surveillance given the malignancy association, especially in the L form Comprises two biochemically distinct enantiomeric disorders identified by chiral separation of urinary 2-hydroxyglutarate into D and L forms L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (L2HGDH defect) causes a fairly characteristic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical white-matter and dentate/basal ganglia involvement, cerebellar signs, and progressive cognitive decline D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria has two genetic subtypes: type I from D2HGDH deficiency and type II from gain-of-function IDH2 mutation, the latter often more severe with cardiomyopathy and epileptic encephalopathy D-2-hydroxyglutarate is an oncometabolite: the IDH-related pathway links it to gliomas and other tumours, and L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria carries an increased lifetime risk of brain tumours The diagnostic signature is elevated urinary 2-hydroxyglutarate, with chiral chromatography needed to determine whether the D or L enantiomer predominates Neuroimaging patterns help differentiate the forms, with L2HGA showing a distinctive symmetric subcortical leukoencephalopathy Both are autosomal recessive except IDH2-related D-2-HGA type II; management is largely supportive with surveillance for tumour and cardiac complications British spelling applies (leukoencephalopathy, tumour, paediatric) New or progressive neurological deficit that may signal an intracranial tumour Cardiomyopathy and epileptic encephalopathy suggesting IDH2-related D-2-HGA type II Rapid neurodevelopmental regression Neonatal severe encephalopathy suggesting the combined D,L form Reporting total 2-hydroxyglutarate without chiral separation, missing the crucial D-versus-L distinction Overlooking the increased brain-tumour risk and omitting surveillance Failing to evaluate the heart in D-2-HGA type II Confusing it with the more severe combined D,L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria 2-hydroxyglutarate exists as D and L enantiomers, normally kept low by the FAD-dependent dehydrogenases D-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase and L-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase, which return them to 2-oxoglutarate. Deficiency of either enzyme allows the corresponding enantiomer to accumulate. Accumulated 2-hydroxyglutarate acts as a competitive inhibitor of 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, disturbing DNA and histone demethylation and cellular metabolism; the D enantiomer in particular is a recognised oncometabolite connected to the IDH mutation pathway seen in gliomas. In D-2-HGA type II, mutant IDH2 gains the capacity to produce D-2-hydroxyglutarate directly. These mechanisms explain the progressive neurological injury, the leukoencephalopathy of the L form, and the increased tumour risk. Outcome varies by form: L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria typically causes slowly progressive neurological decline with a raised tumour risk, whereas D-2-HGA ranges from relatively mild (type I) to severe early encephalopathy with cardiomyopathy (type II). Care is supportive with surveillance for complications.

phenotype It is notably frequent in the Hmong population, in whom it is often clinically silent When symptoms occur they are non-specific and may include hypotonia, lethargy, feeding difficulties or, rarely, metabolic decompensation during illness Newborn screening detects raised C5 (2-methylbutyrylcarnitine), which overlaps with isovaleric acidaemia and requires confirmatory testing Urine organic acids show 2-methylbutyrylglycine, confirming the isoleucine-pathway defect Management, where any is needed, is supportive with avoidance of prolonged fasting and an emergency regimen providing glucose during catabolic illness Metabolic decompensation with hypoglycaemia or acidosis during intercurrent illness Significant lethargy, poor feeding or encephalopathy in a symptomatic infant Failure to thrive or neurodevelopmental concern Marked secondary carnitine depletion Confusing the C5 elevation with isovaleric acidaemia and mismanaging accordingly Over-treating an asymptomatic screen-positive child as though significant disease is present Failing to confirm the diagnosis with urine organic acids and molecular testing Overlooking secondary carnitine deficiency during follow-up Short/branched-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (SBCAD), encoded by ACADSB, catalyses the dehydrogenation of 2-methylbutyryl-CoA in the mitochondrial catabolic pathway of isoleucine. When the enzyme is deficient, 2-methylbutyryl-CoA accumulates and is conjugated to glycine and carnitine, appearing as 2-methylbutyrylglycine in urine and raised 2-methylbutyrylcarnitine (C5) in blood. The metabolic block is usually well tolerated, and most affected individuals remain healthy; only occasionally, and typically under catabolic stress, do non-specific symptoms or mild decompensation arise. Because C5 elevation overlaps with isovaleric acidaemia, biochemical distinction is important. The disorder is generally benign, with most individuals identified by screening remaining asymptomatic and developing normally; rare symptomatic cases have a good outcome with avoidance of fasting and supportive care during illness.

3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency (3-MCC) — 3-MCC deficiency, 3-methylcrotonylglycinuria, MCCC1 deficiency, MCCC2 deficiency, methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency Multiple carboxylase deficiency (holocarboxylase synthetase or biotinidase deficiency) 3-methylglutaconic aciduria Other organic acidaemias raising C5-OH on screening HMG-CoA lyase deficiency Beta-ketothiolase deficiency Maternal 3-MCC detected through the infant's newborn screen Plasma acylcarnitine profile confirming elevated C5-OH (3-hydroxyisovalerylcarnitine) Urine organic acids for 3-methylcrotonylglycine and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid Plasma free and total carnitine to detect secondary deficiency Blood glucose, blood gas and ammonia during any symptomatic episode MCCC1 and MCCC2 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Maternal biochemical testing when an unaffected infant screens positive Autosomal recessive deficiency of 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (MCCC1 or MCCC2 genes), a biotin-dependent enzyme in leucine catabolism, and one of the most common organic acidurias detected by newborn screening Most identified individuals are asymptomatic, so a positive screen frequently represents a benign biochemical phenotype rather than clinical disease When symptomatic, presentation ranges from metabolic decompensation with hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis during catabolic stress to feeding difficulties, hypotonia and developmental delay Newborn screening flags an elevated C5-OH (3-hydroxyisovalerylcarnitine), which overlaps with several other conditions and must be interpreted with confirmatory testing Urine organic acids show 3-methylcrotonylglycine and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid; secondary carnitine depletion is common Maternal 3-MCC can be detected through an abnormal newborn screen in an unaffected infant, so an asymptomatic mother should be considered Management, where indicated, includes avoidance of fasting and prolonged catabolism, carnitine supplementation for secondary deficiency, and an emergency regimen with glucose during illness; a biotin trial may be considered although the enzyme defect is not biotin-responsive Metabolic decompensation with hypoglycaemia and acidosis during intercurrent illness Encephalopathy or reduced consciousness during a catabolic crisis Failure to thrive, marked hypotonia or developmental regression in a symptomatic child Severe secondary carnitine depletion Over-treating or over-investigating an asymptomatic screen-positive child as though clinical disease is certain Failing to consider maternal 3-MCC when an unaffected infant screens positive Assuming the enzyme defect is biotin-responsive like multiple carboxylase deficiency Missing secondary carnitine deficiency during monitoring 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase is a biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme that catalyses a step in the catabolism of the branched-chain amino acid leucine, converting 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA to 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA. Deficiency blocks leucine breakdown, causing accumulation of 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA derivatives that are excreted as 3-methylcrotonylglycine and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid and detected as raised 3-hydroxyisovalerylcarnitine (C5-OH). The accumulating metabolites can sequester coenzyme A and carnitine, producing secondary carnitine deficiency. The biochemical defect is frequently clinically silent, but under catabolic stress a minority develop metabolic decompensation, and unlike multiple carboxylase deficiency the isolated enzyme defect is not corrected by biotin. The large majority of individuals identified by newborn screening remain asymptomatic with a normal outlook, but a minority experience metabolic crises and, rarely, neurological sequelae, so counselling should reflect this generally benign but occasionally clinically significant course.

3-methylglutaconic aciduria — 3-methylglutaconic aciduria, 3-MGA, 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase deficiency (type I, AUH), Barth syndrome (type II, TAZ), Costeff syndrome (type III, OPA3), DNAJC19-related (type V) Other organic acidurias of leucine metabolism (e.g. 3-methylglutaconyl versus 3-methylcrotonyl defects) Primary mitochondrial cytopathies Other causes of infantile or childhood cardiomyopathy Other hereditary optic atrophies Congenital neutropenia syndromes Secondary 3-methylglutaconic aciduria from acquired mitochondrial stress Urine organic acids quantifying 3-methylglutaconic and 3-methylglutaric acids Echocardiography and cardiac assessment (especially for Barth syndrome) Full blood count for neutropenia Ophthalmological assessment for optic atrophy Targeted molecular testing (AUH, TAZ, OPA3, DNAJC19 and mitochondrial genes) Cardiolipin/monolysocardiolipin analysis where Barth syndrome is suspected A biochemically defined group unified by raised urinary 3-methylglutaconic acid (and often 3-methylglutaric acid), but with several genetically and clinically distinct entities Type I reflects a true defect of leucine catabolism (3-methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase, AUH gene); the other types are secondary and largely relate to disturbed mitochondrial membrane/phospholipid biology rather than the leucine pathway Type II is Barth syndrome (X-linked, TAZ gene) with cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, neutropenia, and growth delay Type III is Costeff optic atrophy syndrome (OPA3) with early optic atrophy and later movement disorder, described notably in individuals of Iraqi-Jewish descent So-called type IV is a heterogeneous group of mitochondrial disorders sharing the biochemical marker, and DNAJC19-related dilated cardiomyopathy with ataxia is another form The 3-methylglutaconate elevation in the secondary forms is usually modest and is a clue to a mitochondrial membrane problem rather than the primary defect itself Management is form-specific and supportive, including cardiac care in Barth syndrome and ophthalmological care in Costeff syndrome British spelling applies (cardiomyopathy, paediatric) Cardiomyopathy or heart failure, particularly in a male infant (Barth syndrome) Severe or cyclical neutropenia with infection risk Progressive visual loss from optic atrophy Neurological regression suggesting a mitochondrial disorder Treating the biochemical finding as a single disease rather than pursuing the specific underlying genetic cause Missing Barth syndrome in a boy with cardiomyopathy and neutropenia Assuming a primary leucine-pathway defect when most cases are secondary mitochondrial disorders Overlooking optic atrophy in the Costeff phenotype 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA is an intermediate of leucine degradation, normally hydrated by 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase before onward metabolism. In type I 3-methylglutaconic aciduria this enzyme is deficient, so 3-methylglutaconate and 3-methylglutarate accumulate. In the other, more common types the enzyme is intact and the raised 3-methylglutaconate arises secondarily from disturbed mitochondrial inner-membrane function and phospholipid (cardiolipin) metabolism, as in Barth syndrome where tafazzin deficiency impairs cardiolipin remodelling. Thus the shared biochemical marker points either to a discrete leucine-pathway block or, more often, to a broader mitochondrial membrane disorder with the specific clinical consequences of the underlying gene. Prognosis depends entirely on the specific type: Barth syndrome outcome hinges on cardiac and infective complications, Costeff syndrome causes progressive visual and motor impairment, and type I ranges from mild to more significant neurological involvement. Care is directed at the underlying entity.

COLEC10, often via a gene panel or exome sequencing Craniofacial imaging to assess for craniosynostosis and skull morphology Ophthalmological assessment of ptosis, blepharophimosis, and vision Cleft and palate evaluation with multidisciplinary input Renal and genital assessment for associated structural anomalies Developmental assessment and hearing testing A unifying label for the overlapping Malpuech, Michels, Mingarelli, and Carnevale phenotypes, now recognised as one spectrum Caused by biallelic variants in genes of the lectin complement pathway, including COLEC11, MASP1, and COLEC10 Characteristic facial features include hypertelorism, blepharophimosis, blepharoptosis, and highly arched eyebrows Orofacial clefting, particularly cleft lip and palate, is a frequent finding Craniosynostosis and other cranial anomalies occur in a proportion of individuals Additional features may include growth restriction, developmental delay, genital anomalies, and umbilical abnormalities The complement-pathway proteins involved guide neural crest cell migration during development, explaining the craniofacial emphasis Diagnosis is confirmed by molecular testing of the relevant complement-pathway genes Ptosis or blepharophimosis obstructing vision and risking amblyopia Feeding or airway compromise related to orofacial clefting Raised intracranial pressure from significant craniosynostosis Major associated structural anomaly requiring surgical planning Treating the historical eponymous conditions as distinct rather than as one spectrum, delaying correct testing Overlooking craniosynostosis and its risk of raised intracranial pressure Failing to address vision-threatening ptosis early in childhood Not recognising the autosomal recessive inheritance when counselling consanguineous families 3MC syndrome arises from biallelic loss-of-function variants in genes encoding components of the lectin arm of the complement system, notably the collectins COLEC11 and COLEC10 and the serine protease MASP1/3. Beyond their classical role in innate immunity, these molecules act as extracellular guidance cues that direct the migration of neural crest cells during embryogenesis. When their function is lost, neural crest derivatives fail to migrate correctly, disturbing the development of craniofacial structures and other tissues that depend on neural crest contribution. This accounts for the hypertelorism, clefting, ptosis, craniosynostosis, and the range of additional developmental anomalies that characterise the spectrum, inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. The prognosis varies with the severity of the malformations; many individuals have a normal lifespan, and craniofacial and ocular anomalies are often amenable to surgical correction, while the degree of any intellectual disability and the presence of major internal anomalies principally determine long-term function and support needs.

Karyotype confirming 46,XY Baseline and stimulated testosterone and dihydrotestosterone with calculation of their ratio Anti-Mullerian hormone and gonadotropins to assess testicular function Pelvic and genital imaging to define internal anatomy and gonadal position Molecular genetic testing of SRD5A2 An autosomal recessive 46,XY disorder of sex development caused by mutations in SRD5A2 The enzyme converts testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone, which drives external genital virilisation Affected 46,XY newborns typically have undervirilised or ambiguous external genitalia despite normal testes Wolffian-derived internal structures are usually formed because they depend on testosterone rather than dihydrotestosterone Marked virilisation often occurs at puberty as testosterone levels rise, sometimes prompting a change in perceived sex An elevated ratio of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, especially after stimulation, supports the diagnosis Prostate development and typical male-pattern balding are reduced because these are dihydrotestosterone dependent Ambiguous genitalia in a newborn requiring urgent multidisciplinary assessment Rapid virilisation at puberty causing distress or prompting reconsideration of sex of rearing Undescended or intra-abdominal gonads needing evaluation and monitoring Diagnostic uncertainty that risks incorrect early sex assignment Confusing the condition with partial androgen insensitivity without measuring the testosterone to dihydrotestosterone ratio Making irreversible early decisions about sex of rearing before the diagnosis is clarified Underestimating the degree of virilisation that can occur at puberty Neglecting psychological support during evaluation and management Dihydrotestosterone is the principal androgen responsible for masculinising the external genitalia and prostate during fetal development, and it is produced from testosterone by the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase type 2. In SRD5A2 deficiency, reduced enzyme activity limits dihydrotestosterone formation, so the external genitalia of a 46,XY fetus are incompletely virilised even though testes and testosterone are present. Testosterone-dependent Wolffian structures develop, and anti-Mullerian hormone still causes Mullerian regression. At puberty the surge in testosterone can partially overcome the deficiency and produce substantial virilisation. Prognosis is generally favourable with multidisciplinary care; fertility may be possible in some individuals, and management, including any decisions about hormone therapy or surgery, should be individualised and guided by the person's gender identity.

6-pyruvoyl-tetrahydropterin synthase deficiency — PTPS deficiency, PTS gene deficiency, BH4 deficiency (PTPS type), tetrahydrobiopterin-deficient hyperphenylalaninaemia (PTPS) Classic phenylketonuria (phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency) Dihydropteridine reductase deficiency (BH4 recycling defect) GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency Sepiapterin reductase deficiency Tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency Other neurotransmitter disorders causing infantile dystonia and encephalopathy Urine and blood pterin profile showing raised neopterin with low biopterin Dihydropteridine reductase activity assay (normal, to exclude the recycling defect) Blood phenylalanine and a BH4 loading test demonstrating phenylalanine lowering PTS gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis Cerebrospinal fluid neurotransmitter metabolites (low homovanillic and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid) Developmental and neurological assessment with EEG if seizures occur Autosomal recessive defect of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthesis caused by PTS mutations; it is the most common cause of BH4-deficient hyperphenylalaninaemia It presents as hyperphenylalaninaemia detected on newborn screening but, unlike classic phenylketonuria, dietary phenylalanine restriction alone does not prevent neurological deterioration because central monoamine synthesis is also impaired BH4 is the cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase as well as tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylases, so deficiency causes both elevated phenylalanine and reduced dopamine and serotonin Untreated infants develop progressive encephalopathy with dystonia, hypotonia or hypertonia, oculogyric crises, seizures, and developmental delay despite phenylalanine control Management combines BH4 (cofactor) supplementation to lower phenylalanine with levodopa and a serotonin precursor to replace the deficient neurotransmitters, sometimes with folinic acid Every infant with hyperphenylalaninaemia should be evaluated for a BH4 defect (pterin profile and dihydropteridine reductase activity) so that treatable cofactor and neurotransmitter deficiencies are not missed Neurological deterioration despite adequate phenylalanine control, indicating an untreated cofactor/neurotransmitter defect Progressive dystonia, oculogyric crises, or seizures in an infant with hyperphenylalaninaemia Failure to screen a hyperphenylalaninaemic newborn for a BH4 disorder Feeding and swallowing difficulty from evolving encephalopathy Treating a raised phenylalanine as classic phenylketonuria without excluding a BH4 defect Relying on phenylalanine restriction alone and neglecting the neurotransmitter deficiency Not measuring pterins and dihydropteridine reductase activity to subtype the disorder Under-dosing or delaying neurotransmitter-precursor therapy while focusing on amino-acid control 6-pyruvoyl-tetrahydropterin synthase catalyses the second step of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) biosynthesis. Biallelic PTS mutations reduce BH4, the obligatory cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase, tyrosine hydroxylase, and tryptophan hydroxylase. Consequently phenylalanine accumulates (hyperphenylalaninaemia) while central synthesis of dopamine and serotonin falls. The dual insult explains why treating the amino-acid abnormality alone is insufficient: the neurotransmitter deficiency drives a progressive movement disorder and encephalopathy. The pterin profile shows raised neopterin with low biopterin, reflecting the enzymatic block, and this pattern helps distinguish it from other BH4 defects. With early and combined treatment (cofactor supplementation plus neurotransmitter precursors) neurological outcome can be good, but delayed or incomplete therapy leads to persistent movement disorder, cognitive impairment, and disability. Lifelong specialist metabolic follow-up is required.

Achalasia — achalasia cardia, esophageal achalasia, cardiospasm, failure of LES relaxation, esophageal aperistalsis, megaesophagus Distal esophageal spasm and other esophageal motility disorders Gastroesophageal reflux disease with peptic stricture Esophageal or gastric cardia malignancy causing pseudoachalasia Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi infection) Eosinophilic esophagitis Scleroderma-related esophageal dysmotility Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) causing destruction of myenteric plexus with achalasia-like esophageal dysfunction Barium esophagram — shows esophageal dilation with distal 'bird's beak' tapering and poor emptying High-resolution esophageal manometry — confirms diagnosis via absent peristalsis and impaired LES relaxation, and subtypes achalasia (I–III) Upper endoscopy — mandatory to exclude a mechanical or malignant cause (pseudoachalasia) at or near the gastroesophageal junction Endoscopic ultrasound or CT chest/abdomen — used selectively when pseudoachalasia from tumor infiltration is suspected Serology for Trypanosoma cruzi — considered in patients from endemic regions to exclude Chagas disease Timed barium swallow — assesses esophageal emptying and is useful for monitoring treatment response Chest imaging — may incidentally reveal a dilated, air/fluid-filled esophagus or absent gastric air bubble Peptic or malignant esophageal stricture Esophageal or gastroesophageal junction carcinoma (pseudoachalasia) Diffuse esophageal spasm Scleroderma esophagus Eosinophilic esophagitis Progressive dysphagia to both solids AND liquids from the outset is the classic clue distinguishing achalasia from a mechanical stricture or malignancy, where solid-food dysphagia usually predominates and progresses later to liquids. Regurgitation of undigested food (especially at night, with risk of aspiration) and slow, gradual weight loss are common accompanying features. Retrosternal chest pain/discomfort with meals occurs in a subset of patients, more often early in the disease course. Patients often learn compensatory maneuvers — eating slowly, holding arms overhead, or performing repeated swallows/Valsalva — to help push food through the non-relaxing lower esophageal sphincter. Barium esophagram classically shows a dilated esophagus tapering to a smooth 'bird's beak' narrowing at the gastroesophageal junction. Manometry is the gold standard: it shows absent/incomplete lower esophageal sphincter relaxation together with loss of normal peristalsis in the esophageal body. New-onset 'achalasia-like' symptoms in an older adult, especially with rapid weight loss, should prompt evaluation for pseudoachalasia from a malignancy at the gastroesophageal junction. Chagas disease should be considered in patients from or with travel history to endemic areas of Latin America presenting with an achalasia-like picture. Rapid symptom onset or significant weight loss in an older patient, raising concern for pseudoachalasia due to malignancy Recurrent aspiration pneumonia from nocturnal regurgitation Severe odynophagia or evidence of esophageal perforation Marked, progressive esophageal dilation (megaesophagus) with risk of retained food and aspiration New or worsening symptoms despite treatment, warranting re-evaluation for an underlying malignant cause Attributing dysphagia to reflux disease and delaying manometry, since achalasia can be misdiagnosed as GERD for years Failing to perform endoscopy to exclude a malignant or infiltrative cause before treating for idiopathic achalasia Overlooking Chagas disease in patients with relevant epidemiologic exposure Assuming a normal-caliber esophagus on barium study excludes achalasia; early disease may show minimal dilation despite abnormal manometry Achalasia results from degeneration of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus of the esophagus, leading to loss of coordinated peristalsis in the esophageal body and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax appropriately with swallowing. The cause is usually idiopathic, though an autoimmune or postviral inflammatory process targeting these neurons is suspected in many cases. Similar clinical pictures can arise secondarily from infiltrative or destructive processes affecting the myenteric plexus, such as Chagas disease or tumor invasion at the gastroesophageal junction (pseudoachalasia). With appropriate treatment (pneumatic dilation, surgical myotomy, or peroral endoscopic myotomy), most patients achieve durable symptomatic improvement, though the underlying esophageal aperistalsis is not reversed and long-term surveillance is often needed. Untreated or longstanding disease carries risk of progressive esophageal dilation, aspiration, malnutrition, and a modestly increased long-term risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

Acute Bronchitis — None routinely required — Diagnosis is clinical; investigations are reserved for atypical course, prolonged symptoms, or red-flag features suggesting pneumonia. Chest X-ray (only if pneumonia cannot be excluded clinically) — To rule out consolidation if exam findings are equivocal or symptoms persist beyond expected course. Community-acquired pneumonia (distinguished by a new infiltrate on chest radiography and focal exam findings) (p.1024). Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis / COPD (p.1024). Heart failure (p.1024). Pulmonary embolism (p.1024). Influenza and nonspecific upper respiratory infection, which overlap clinically with lower-tract infection (p.252). Pneumonia (cough plus sputum, dyspnea, chest pain, fever, and a new infiltrate point to pneumonia rather than bronchitis) (p.1537, p.1024). Influenza (overlapping cough and systemic features; can be complicated by secondary bacterial infection) (p.1537). Pertussis / subacute postinfectious tracheobronchitis (a frequent cause of cough persisting 3-8 weeks) (p.272). Chest radiography should be obtained whenever pneumonia is suspected, to confirm the absence of an infiltrate that defines acute bronchitis (p.1537). Specific viral diagnosis is generally unnecessary but, when needed, RT-PCR/multiplex respiratory panels are the most sensitive tests; results must be interpreted cautiously because viral genome can persist for weeks after a resolved infection (p.1537). Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial infarction presenting as cough and dyspnea, illustrated by a fatal case in which exertional dyspnea and chest heaviness were prematurely labeled acute bronchitis (p.21). Cough-variant asthma (p.272). Gastroesophageal reflux (p.272). Rhinosinusitis with postnasal drainage (p.272). ACE-inhibitor-induced cough (p.272). Inhalation of noxious chemicals or smoke, and aspiration, as causes of acute cough (p.272). Defined as a dry or productive cough lasting <3 weeks, occurring without clinical or radiographic signs of pneumonia; it is most common during winter (p.1537). Sputum purulence does not distinguish viral from bacterial cause; in acute bronchitis the cough is predominantly viral, whereas bacteria play a larger role in chronic bronchitis (p.1537). Among acute respiratory infections, only acute otitis media, sinusitis, streptococcal pharyngitis, and pneumonia warrant antibiotics; acute bronchitis is not on that list (p.252). Acute bronchitis and sinusitis are common at all stages of HIV infection, with more severe disease at lower CD4+ counts (p.1595). An individual episode of acute bronchitis does not typically cause lasting reductions in pulmonary function (p.1537 context; long-term lung-function data p. respiratory infections section). Dyspnea, especially exertional dyspnea or chest heaviness/pain, which should trigger consideration of cardiac or thromboembolic disease rather than acute bronchitis (p.21). Cough accompanied by sputum, fever, chest pain, or focal chest signs suggesting pneumonia, prompting chest radiography (p.1537). Hemoptysis or weight loss (raising concern for malignancy or other serious pulmonary disease) (p.272). Cough persisting beyond a few weeks, warranting reassessment and chest radiography for serious causes (sarcoidosis, lymphoma, lung cancer, tuberculosis) (p.272-273). Prescribing antibiotics for acute bronchitis is inappropriate stewardship; roughly half of ambulatory antibiotic prescriptions for acute respiratory infections are unnecessary, and antibiotics cause adverse effects, C. difficile infection, microbiome disruption, and resistance (p.252). Treating purulent sputum as evidence of bacterial infection is a mistake, since purulence does not reliably indicate bacterial etiology in acute bronchitis (p.1537). Premature closure: relying on a rapid 'URI/bronchitis' protocol can cause clinicians to miss life-threatening conditions such as myocardial infarction; a patient who does not look 'sick' may be wrongly assumed to have a benign illness (p.21). Not eliciting a full dyspnea history (exertional onset, chest heaviness, relief with rest) can lead to a dangerous misdiagnosis of acute bronchitis (p.21). Acute bronchitis is predominantly a viral infection of the lower airways below the vocal cords, caused by common respiratory viruses; the inflammatory airway response produces cough that may be dry or productive, without parenchymal consolidation. Bacterial involvement is uncommon, in contrast to chronic bronchitis where bacteria contribute more prominently (p.1537). Acute bronchitis is a self-limited illness; the cough usually resolves within about 3 weeks, and antibiotics neither speed resolution nor prevent complications in most acute respiratory infections. A dry, irritative postbronchitic cough may linger for more than 2 months, particularly in winter, and a residual subacute cough of 3-8 weeks is common after tracheobronchitis (p.252, p.272-273).

(INR generally above 1.5) and any degree of encephalopathy in a patient without pre-existing chronic liver disease, developing within about 26 weeks of illness onset Speed of onset matters clinically: hyperacute presentations (encephalopathy within roughly a week or two of jaundice) are typically from acetaminophen toxicity or viral hepatitis and, despite dramatic cerebral edema risk, often carry better spontaneous recovery odds than slower subacute forms Acetaminophen overdose and drug-induced liver injury are the leading causes in resource-rich settings, while viral hepatitis (especially hepatitis B and E) dominates in many other regions Cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure are the most feared early complications and a major cause of death, particularly in hyperacute presentations Coagulopathy in ALF reflects a rebalanced but fragile hemostatic state rather than pure bleeding tendency; INR is used mainly for prognosis and monitoring, not as a routine transfusion synthetic recovery Delaying transfer to a transplant-capable center while pursuing additional outpatient-type workup — deterioration can be abrupt Overlooking a treatable etiology (Wilson disease, autoimmune hepatitis, pregnancy-related liver disease) because acetaminophen or viral hepatitis seems statistically likely Massive hepatocyte necrosis or dysfunction outstrips the liver's regenerative capacity, causing simultaneous failure of synthetic function (coagulation factors, albumin), detoxification (ammonia, other neurotoxins), and metabolic homeostasis. Accumulating ammonia and inflammatory mediators drive astrocyte swelling and cerebral edema, producing hepatic encephalopathy and raised intracranial pressure. The systemic inflammatory response and impaired hepatic clearance of pathogens also predispose to circulatory dysfunction, renal impairment, and secondary infection, contributing to a multiorgan failure picture. Outcome depends heavily on etiology and speed of onset: hyperacute presentations from acetaminophen or hepatitis A/E often have a better chance of spontaneous recovery than subacute presentations, which have lower native-liver survival. Emergency liver transplantation substantially improves survival in appropriately selected patients who do not recover spontaneously.

from pulmonary involvement Persistent fever despite broad antimicrobial coverage without an identified infectious source Treating as fever of unknown origin with prolonged empiric antibiotics before considering an autoinflammatory cause Missing the diagnosis because the evanescent rash is absent at the time of examination Anchoring on markedly elevated ferritin as diagnostic without excluding lymphoma and macrophage activation syndrome Delaying immunosuppressive therapy while pursuing an exhaustive infectious workup in a clinically deteriorating patient AOSD is an autoinflammatory disorder driven by innate immune activation rather than autoantibody-mediated disease, with overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines including interleukin-1, interleukin-6, interleukin-18, and tumor necrosis factor. This cytokine storm produces the systemic febrile illness, marked acute-phase response, and hyperferritinemia seen clinically. The absence of a clear autoantibody or defined trigger, along with strong similarity to systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, supports its classification as an autoinflammatory rather than autoimmune condition. Course is variable: some patients have a self-limited monophasic illness, others a chronic intermittent pattern, and a subset develop chronic destructive polyarthritis. Most patients respond well to anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive therapy, though macrophage activation syndrome significantly increases morbidity and mortality.

Amoebic Liver Abscess — Abdominal ultrasound or CT — Characterizes the abscess (typically single, right lobe, in amoebic disease) and guides the decision on aspiration. Amoebic serology (IgG) — Highly sensitive for invasive amoebiasis and useful when aspiration is not performed or is inconclusive. Stool microscopy for E. histolytica (trophozoites/cysts) — Supportive if positive, but a substantial proportion of liver abscess patients have negative stool studies at the time of presentation. Diagnostic aspiration (if no improvement in 5-7 days, large/left-lobe abscess, or diagnostic uncertainty) — Classic 'anchovy paste' aspirate supports amoebic etiology; also allows bacterial culture to exclude/identify a pyogenic or mixed process. Pyogenic liver abscess (the most important imaging-based distinction once a hepatic abscess is identified) (p.1801) Malaria (p.1801) Typhoid/enteric fever (p.1801) Pulmonary disease (p.1801) Gallbladder disease (p.1801) Any febrile illness with few localizing signs / fever of unknown origin, since 10-15% present with fever alone (p.1799, p.1801) Pyogenic liver abscess (p.1801) Malaria (p.1801) Typhoid (enteric) fever (p.1801) Serum alkaline phosphatase and aminotransferases (enzymes often normal/minimally elevated; raised aminotransferases suggest acute disease or complication) (p.1800) Full blood count for leukocytosis >10,000/uL, present in about three-quarters of patients, especially with acute or complicated disease (p.1800) Enzyme immunoassay for the Gal/GalNAc lectin antigen, usable on stool and on liver-abscess aspirates (p.1800) Multiplex PCR for E. histolytica DNA (near 100% sensitivity/specificity) (p.1800) Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) on abscess pus as a low-cost molecular option (p.1800) Diagnostic aspirate sent for Gram stain and bacterial culture when distinguishing amebic from pyogenic abscess (p.1801) Gallbladder disease (p.1801) Pulmonary disease presenting with right-sided pleural/pleuritic findings (p.1801) Most patients are febrile with right-upper-quadrant pain that may be dull or pleuritic and may radiate to the shoulder; point tenderness over the liver and a right-sided pleural effusion are common, whereas jaundice is rare (p.1799). Although the colon is the initial site of infection, fewer than one-third of patients with an amebic abscess have active diarrhea at presentation (p.1799). Strongly age- and sex-dependent: men aged 30-60 are infected at a rate roughly 10-12 times that of women in the same age group; testosterone-modulated NK-T-cell interferon-gamma signaling is implicated experimentally (p.1798). Young patients tend to present acutely with prominent symptoms of under 10 days' duration, while older patients from endemic areas more often follow a subacute course over months with weight loss and hepatomegaly; only about one-third of those with chronic presentations are febrile (p.1799). Of travelers who develop an amebic liver abscess after leaving an endemic area, 95% do so within 5 months (p.1799). Amebic liver abscesses are always preceded by intestinal colonization, which may be entirely asymptomatic (p.1799). On imaging, more than 80% of patients symptomatic for over 10 days have a single right-lobe abscess, but about 50% of those symptomatic for under 10 days have multiple abscesses (p.1800). The classic necrotic 'anchovy paste' contents are variable in color and bacteriologically sterile, composed of granular debris with few or no cells; amebae, when present, sit near the abscess capsule rather than in the aspirable necrotic center (p.1799). Liver enzymes are usually normal or only minimally elevated even with large abscesses; alkaline phosphatase is the most commonly elevated value, while aminotransferase elevation suggests acute disease or a complication (p.1800). Invasive amebiasis does not elicit eosinophilia (p.1800). Pleuropulmonary involvement (reported in 20-30%, the most frequent complication): contiguous spread or frank rupture into the pleural space, the latter requiring drainage (p.1799). Large abscess (>10 cm) in the superior right lobe, which may rupture into the pleural space (p.1800). Left-lobe abscess, which may rupture into the pericardium, the complication carrying the gravest prognosis and able to occur even during medical therapy (p.1799-1800). Rupture into the peritoneum, presenting as an indolent leak or as an acute abdomen (p.1799). Hepatobronchial fistula causing cough productive of large amounts of necrotic material (p.1799). Lack of clinical response within 3-5 days or threat of imminent rupture (p.1801). Expecting concurrent dysentery: fewer than one-third of patients have active diarrhea, so a negative stool examination or absent diarrhea does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1799). Trophozoites are rarely recovered from liver aspirates because they reside in the abscess capsule, not in the necrotic center that is actually aspirated (p.1799). Up to 10% of patients with acute amebic liver abscess have negative serology early; titers usually become positive within a week (p.1799). Microscopy cannot distinguish E. histolytica cysts from non-pathogenic E. dispar, E. moshkovskii, or E. bangladeshi; species-specific diagnosis on microscopy requires seeing trophozoites that have ingested erythrocytes (p.1799). In endemic areas serology may stay positive for years (indirect hemagglutination up to ~10 years), complicating interpretation (p.1799). Follow-up imaging may be confusing because abscesses resolve slowly and can transiently enlarge despite a good clinical response (p.1800). Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites invade colonic mucosal venules and travel via the portal venous system to the liver; the organism is resistant to complement-mediated lysis, which is critical to its survival in the bloodstream. An early acute infiltrate (predominantly neutrophils) is followed by lysis of those neutrophils on contact with amebae, and the released neutrophil toxins are thought to contribute to hepatocyte necrosis. The liver parenchyma is progressively replaced by necrotic material surrounded by a thin rim of congested liver tissue, producing the classically described (but variably colored) 'anchovy paste' that is sterile and largely acellular, with amebae found mainly at the capsule. Genetically, a leptin-receptor substitution (Q223R) increases the risk of amebic liver abscess in adults (p.1798-1799). With early diagnosis and treatment, mortality from uncomplicated amebic liver abscess is under 1%, and over 90% of patients respond dramatically with reduced pain and fever within 72 hours; recurrence is rare. Abscesses resolve slowly and may even enlarge despite clinical improvement, so follow-up ultrasonography can be misleading; complete resolution within 6 months is expected in about two-thirds of patients, while roughly 10% have persistent imaging abnormalities for up to a year. A hepatobronchial fistula carries a good prognosis, whereas pericardial rupture (usually from left-lobe abscesses) carries the gravest prognosis (p.1799-1801).

Aspiration Pneumonia — Chest X-ray — Aspiration classically affects dependent lung segments (posterior upper lobes if aspirated supine, basal segments of lower lobes if upright) — helpful in confirming the diagnosis. Swallowing assessment (if recurrent or ongoing risk) — Identifies the underlying mechanism (dysphagia, reduced consciousness) to prevent recurrence. CBC, CRP — Supports severity assessment and baseline for response monitoring. Foreign-body/food aspiration causing major-airway obstruction with atelectasis and nonspecific inflammation, managed by removal rather than antibiotics (p.1418) Chemical (acid) pneumonitis, e.g., Mendelson syndrome from regurgitated gastric contents (p.1418) Pneumococcal pneumonia, distinguished by its more acute presentation (p.1418) Lung abscess (subacute anaerobic infection) as a related/overlapping entity (p.1072, p.1418) Pneumococcal pneumonia presenting more acutely than indolent anaerobic aspiration infection (p.1418) Chest radiography looking for consolidation in dependent lung segments (basilar lower-lobe segments if aspiration occurred upright; posterior segment of the upper lobe or superior segment of the lower lobe if supine) (p.1418) Gram stain of sputum, which characteristically shows a mixed bacterial population with many polymorphonuclear leukocytes (p.1418) Bronchoscopic protected-brush specimens or bronchoalveolar lavage, which may recover anaerobes from the lower tract with less oropharyngeal contamination (role still being defined) (p.1418) Assessment of dentition/oral hygiene, given the association of severe dental disease with aspiration pneumonia (p.1418) Chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome) from aspiration of acidic gastric juices, with rapid alveolar injury and pulmonary edema, often without fever and frequently needing no antibiotics (p.1418) Foreign-body/food aspiration with airway obstruction and atelectasis (p.1418) Aspiration pneumonia is best viewed as a point on a continuum that also includes community-acquired and hospital-acquired pneumonia, defined by a phenotype with macroaspiration risk factors and involvement of characteristic gravity-dependent lung locations (p.1066). Aspiration pneumonia is estimated to account for roughly 5-15% of community-acquired pneumonia cases; reliable figures for the hospital-acquired setting are not available (p.1066). The historical view that aspiration pneumonia is caused mainly by anaerobes has shifted: when acquired in the community or hospital, the likely pathogens mirror those of CAP or HAP, with anaerobes still relevant mainly in poor dentition, lung abscess, necrotizing pneumonia, or empyema (p.1067). Anaerobic aspiration infections tend to follow an indolent course, a clinical clue that helps separate them from more acutely presenting conditions such as chemical pneumonitis or pneumococcal pneumonia (p.1418). Sputum in bacterial aspiration pneumonia is characteristically NOT malodorous unless the process has been ongoing for at least about a week (p.1418). Expectorated sputum is unreliable for anaerobic culture because of inevitable contamination by normal oral microbiota; reliable anaerobic specimens historically required transtracheal or transthoracic aspiration, techniques rarely used now (p.1418). In CAP overall, no specific etiology is identified in more than half of cases despite careful history, examination, and imaging (p.1067). Gross hemoptysis suggesting necrotizing pneumonia (p.1067) Progression to respiratory failure; in chemical pneumonitis a chest x-ray can evolve from normal to a complete bilateral whiteout within 8-24 hours (p.1067, p.1418) Septic shock and organ failure in severe pneumonia (p.1067) Weight loss and anemia indicating a more chronic process (p.1418) Development of lung abscess or complicated/empyematous pleural effusion (pleural fluid pH <7.2, glucose <2.2 mmol/L, or LDH >1000 U/L, or organisms seen/cultured indicates need for drainage) (p.1072) Failing to distinguish chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome) from bacterial aspiration pneumonia: chemical pneumonitis is a non-infectious acid injury that usually resolves with supportive care and does NOT warrant antibiotics unless bacterial superinfection develops (p.1418). Routinely covering anaerobes for all aspiration pneumonia: anaerobic coverage is unnecessary unless dentition is poor or there is lung abscess or necrotizing pneumonia (p.1070). Expecting an acute, foul-smelling presentation: bacterial aspiration pneumonia evolves over days to weeks and sputum is usually not malodorous until the process has lasted about a week (p.1418). Relying on expectorated sputum for anaerobic culture, which is invalid because of oral-flora contamination (p.1418). Macroaspiration of oropharyngeal or gastric contents delivers a high microbial burden directly into the lower airways; lung involvement reflects this rather than invasion of a sterile space, since the lungs normally harbor a microbiota. Mechanical defenses (nasal hairs/turbinates, branching airways, mucociliary clearance, gag and cough reflexes) reduce but do not fully block bacterial access to the lower respiratory tract. Bacterial aspiration pneumonia develops over several days to weeks (not hours) through a combination of increased bacterial burden, increased virulence of aspirated organisms, and potential airway damage from aspirated gastric fluid. This contrasts with chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome), where aspirated acidic gastric juice causes rapid, direct destruction of the alveolar lining with fluid transudation into the alveolar space within hours (p.1066, p.1418).
