requires kidney biopsy with light microscopy showing segmental sclerosis in a subset of glomeruli, since sampling can miss focal lesions Response to immunosuppression is more likely in primary FSGS with diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement than in secondary/adaptive forms, which generally do not respond to immunosuppressive therapy Recurrence in the transplanted kidney is common in primary FSGS, particularly in patients whose native disease progressed rapidly to kidney failure Rapidly rising creatinine or oliguria suggesting an aggressive or collapsing variant Nephrotic syndrome with severe hypoalbuminemia and high thrombotic/infectious risk requiring closer monitoring Resistance to standard immunosuppressive therapy, suggesting secondary/genetic FSGS that will not benefit from continued immunosuppression New heavy proteinuria in a transplant recipient with a history of primary FSGS, raising concern for disease recurrence Uncontrolled hypertension or severe edema/anasarca needing urgent management Treating all FSGS as a single steroid-responsive disease rather than recognizing that secondary/adaptive forms generally do not benefit from immunosuppression Missing the diagnosis on a biopsy specimen that under-samples glomeruli, since the sclerotic lesions are segmental and focal rather than global Failing to search for an underlying secondary cause (obesity, reduced nephron mass, viral infection, drug exposure) before committing a patient to prolonged immunosuppressive therapy Overlooking genetic/familial forms in young patients or those with a family history, which alters both prognosis and treatment approach FSGS results from podocyte injury and loss that a glomerulus cannot adequately repair, leading to segmental capillary collapse and scarring in a portion of glomeruli. In primary disease a circulating permeability factor is suspected to injure podocytes directly, whereas secondary forms arise from maladaptive hyperfiltration in remnant or overworked nephrons, viral cytopathic effects on podocytes, direct podocyte toxicity from certain drugs, or inherited defects in podocyte structural proteins. Ongoing podocyte depletion below a critical threshold triggers a self-perpetuating cycle of glomerulosclerosis and eventual global glomerular loss. Outcomes vary widely by FSGS subtype: primary FSGS achieving remission (spontaneous or treatment-induced) has a favorable long-term renal outlook, whereas resistant primary disease and most secondary/collapsing forms carry a substantial risk of progression to kidney failure over years. The collapsing variant has the most aggressive course among the subtypes.

Acute Gastroenteritis — None routinely required in mild self-limited cases — Most cases resolve without specific identification of organism. Stool routine/microscopy (if symptoms persist beyond 7 days or in immunocompromised) — Identifies parasitic causes (e.g., Giardia) that require specific therapy. Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (O157:H7 / Shiga toxin-producing) - watery progressing to bloody, HUS risk Enteroaggregative E. coli (emerging traveler's-diarrhea pathogen) Cholera (Vibrio cholerae) - profuse rice-water secretory diarrhea Preformed-toxin food poisoning (Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus, Clostridium perfringens) Sapovirus, astrovirus, enteric adenovirus types 40/41 (viral, mainly young children) Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Giardia (esp. travelers, hikers, immunocompromised, persistent cases) Enteric fever / typhoid (penetrating pathogens Salmonella Typhi, Yersinia enterocolitica with fever, relative bradycardia, splenomegaly) Yersinia enterocolitica terminal ileitis mimicking acute appendicitis Clostridioides difficile colitis (recent or current antibiotics; predominant nosocomial cause) Acute viral hepatitis A and other systemic infections (legionellosis, listeriosis, toxic shock, malaria) in which diarrhea is one feature SARS-CoV-2 - diarrhea can be an early symptom Fecal leukocyte smear (methylene blue) or, more sensitively, fecal lactoferrin to distinguish inflammatory from noninflammatory disease Culture-independent multiplex nucleic-acid amplification (PCR) stool panels - now first-line for severe/domestically acquired disease; faster and more sensitive than culture Stool culture for Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter in febrile inflammatory diarrhea acquired outside hospital Sorbitol-MacConkey plating / Shiga-toxin or PCR testing when EHEC (E. coli O157:H7) is suspected (visibly bloody stool) Specific antigen/microscopy for Giardia and Cryptosporidium, and antigen detection for E. histolytica, when suspected or in persistent diarrhea Examination for ova and parasites if diarrhea persists beyond ~10 days Nosocomial diarrhea workup should focus on C. difficile toxin testing; routine stool culture in the hospital is low-yield Endoscopy/imaging reserved for persistent (>30 day) or suspected noninfectious disease; not indicated during the acute episode (risk of false-positive results) Medication side effects (antibiotics, NSAIDs, antidysrhythmics, antihypertensives, some antidepressants, chemotherapy, laxatives) - the most common noninfectious cause Ischemic colitis (age >50, lower abdominal pain preceding watery then bloody diarrhea, spares rectum) Colonic diverticulitis; partial bowel obstruction; graft-versus-host disease Initial presentation or flare of inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's, ulcerative colitis) with abrupt onset mimicking infection Toxic ingestions (organophosphates, amanita/other mushrooms, arsenic) and seafood toxins (ciguatera, scombroid) Food allergy including alpha-gal (delayed mammalian-meat allergy) which can cause systemic collapse and be mistaken for dehydration More than 90% of acute diarrhea episodes are infectious, and most are mild and self-limited; vomiting, fever, and abdominal pain frequently accompany the illness (p.305). The first decision point is to separate noninflammatory (watery, small-bowel, enterotoxin/viral) from inflammatory (dysenteric, colonic, invasion/cytotoxin) disease, since this dichotomy drives the need for stool studies and therapy (p.1078-1079). Clinical timing offers etiologic clues: an abrupt illness with prominent vomiting and little or no fever within hours of eating points to a preformed toxin (e.g., S. aureus, B. cereus), whereas high fever with significant abdominal pain points to invasive or cytotoxin-producing organisms (p.305). Vomiting can be the predominant or sole presenting feature of viral gastroenteritis, especially in children (p.1629). Bloody diarrhea with only low-grade fever or no fever should specifically raise concern for Shiga toxin-producing/enterohemorrhagic E. coli (p.1079, p.1081). Bulky pale/grey stools suggest a malabsorptive small-bowel process, while profuse 'rice-water' stools suggest cholera or a similar toxigenic secretory process (p.1078). Reduced gastric acidity (achlorhydria, gastric surgery, or acid-suppressing drugs such as PPIs/H2 blockers) lowers the infectious barrier and increases susceptibility to Salmonella, Giardia, and other enteric pathogens (p.1077). Immunocompromised hosts (cell-mediated defects/AIDS, hypogammaglobulinemia) get more severe, protracted, and sometimes invasive disease, and may harbor opportunistic pathogens not seen in immunocompetent patients (p.1080, p.305). Tenesmus and frequent small-volume stools indicate a distal colonic/proctitis process (e.g., shigellosis, amebiasis) rather than a small-bowel secretory process (p.1078). Signs of severe dehydration: lethargy/obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, shock Profuse diarrhea with dehydration Overtly bloody stools High fever (>=38.5 C / 101 F) Diarrhea persisting >48 h without improvement (or >2 weeks suggesting a different chronic spectrum) Severe abdominal pain in a patient aged >50 years Elderly (>=70 years) or immunocompromised host Recent antibiotic use (C. difficile concern) Bloody diarrhea with low-grade or absent fever (EHEC / HUS warning) Avoid antimotility agents (e.g., loperamide) and bismuth-based slowing in febrile or bloody/dysenteric diarrhea - they may prolong fever and pathogen shedding in Shigella and other invasive infections; in viral gastroenteritis antibiotics and antimotility agents are not indicated. Do NOT give antibiotics when enterohemorrhagic (Shiga toxin-producing) E. coli is suspected, because antibiotics can increase toxin production and markedly raise the risk of hemolytic-uremic syndrome. Opioid/antimotility therapy can increase the frequency of bacteremia in Salmonella gastroenteritis and prolonged illness in Shigella. Most acute diarrhea needs no microbiologic workup; routine extensive stool testing of mild self-limited disease wastes resources. Do not screen for or endoscope to exclude celiac/Crohn disease or IBD during an acute episode - the risk is low and false-positive results are common. A positive multiplex PCR panel may detect multiple organisms or carriage and can be hard to interpret; lack of an isolate prevents susceptibility testing and outbreak typing, so culture confirmation is still advised after a positive bacterial PCR. Empirical antibacterial coverage is warranted regardless of pathogen recovery in selected high-risk patients (immunocompromised, prosthetic/mechanical heart valves, recent vascular grafts, elderly). Acute infectious diarrhea results when an ingested pathogen overwhelms or bypasses host defenses (gastric acid, intestinal motility/peristalsis, mucus layer, secretory IgA, and the protective resident microbiota). Mechanistically there are two broad patterns. Noninflammatory disease arises in the proximal small bowel and is mediated by enterotoxins (e.g., cholera toxin, E. coli heat-labile [LT] and heat-stable [ST] toxins) or by viral injury; cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates a GTP-binding protein to persistently activate adenylate cyclase, raising cyclic AMP, increasing chloride secretion and decreasing sodium absorption, producing watery secretory diarrhea without mucosal destruction. Inflammatory disease affects the colon or distal small bowel through mucosal invasion (Shigella, enteroinvasive E. coli, Salmonella) or cytotoxins (S. dysenteriae type 1, Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, C. difficile), destroying epithelium and producing dysentery with fecal leukocytes. Viral pathogens (norovirus, rotavirus) injure the small-intestinal villous epithelium: rotavirus destroys mature absorptive enterocytes and the loss of brush-border enzymes leaves unmetabolized disaccharides, generating combined secretory and osmotic diarrhea, with the nonstructural protein NSP4 acting as an enterotoxin. Crucially, glucose-coupled sodium absorption in the small intestine remains intact even during toxin-driven secretion, which is the physiologic basis for oral rehydration therapy (p.1076-1077, p.1081, p.1629). Most acute infectious gastroenteritis is self-limited and resolves within days; viral norovirus/sapovirus illness typically lasts 1-3 days and rotavirus 3-7 days. Death is uncommon in healthy adults but occurs chiefly from dehydration in infants and debilitated elderly; globally acute diarrhea remains a leading cause of childhood death. Oral rehydration has dramatically reduced mortality (e.g., cholera case fatality from >50% untreated to <1%). Recognized post-infectious sequelae include reactive arthritis (after invasive Shigella/Salmonella/Campylobacter/Yersinia), Guillain-Barre syndrome (after Campylobacter), hemolytic-uremic syndrome (after Shiga toxin-producing bacteria), post-infectious IBS (notably after Campylobacter), and transient post-infectious lactase deficiency; recurrent childhood diarrhea in resource-poor settings causes environmental enteropathy with growth and developmental stunting (p.302, p.305, p.1077-1078, p.1081, p.1628-1629). Severity is graded clinically by functional impact and dehydration rather than by a single score. Mild: activity unrestricted. Moderate: activities altered. Severe: incapacitated. Dehydration assessment is the key severity measure on examination - mild = thirst, dry mouth, reduced axillary sweat, decreased urine output, slight weight loss; moderate = orthostatic blood-pressure fall, skin tenting, sunken eyes (or sunken fontanelle in infants); severe = lethargy/obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, and shock. Frequency of stools forewarns impending dehydration. By duration, diarrhea is acute (<2 weeks), persistent (2-4 weeks), or chronic (>4 weeks) (p.302/304, p.307, p.1078).

Antibody deposition activates complement and recruits neutrophils and macrophages, producing crescentic glomerulonephritis and, when pulmonary capillaries are involved, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. Loss of pulmonary capillary integrity (from smoking, infection, or inhalational injury) is thought to expose the alveolar antigen and precipitate lung bleeding in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DR15 association). Outcomes depend heavily on renal function and the extent of crescent formation at diagnosis — patients presenting with dialysis-dependent renal failure or near-total crescents rarely recover independent kidney function, whereas earlier treatment before advanced renal failure preserves function in many cases. Pulmonary hemorrhage, when treated promptly, generally resolves without long-term sequelae, but disease recurrence and progression to end-stage renal disease remain the major long-term concerns.

Hospital Acquired Pneumonia — Sputum/endotracheal aspirate culture — Essential to identify the causative organism and de-escalate from broad empiric therapy. Blood cultures — Identifies bacteremic spread and an organism for targeted therapy. Chest X-ray — Confirms new infiltrate consistent with pneumonia. Procalcitonin (serial) — Supports decisions about duration and early discontinuation if levels fall rapidly with clinical improvement. Purulent tracheobronchitis (notably in chronic ventilator units, where it can impede weaning) (p.1073) Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (as an alternative source of fever/leukocytosis) (p.1074) Central line-associated infection (p.1074) Sinusitis (p.1074) Urinary tract infection (p.1074) Fungal or viral pneumonia (mimics requiring different antimicrobials than VAP) (p.1074) Quantitative culture of deep respiratory tract samples to separate colonisation from true infection; the more distal the sample, the more specific the result and the lower the colony-count threshold (e.g., endotracheal aspirate threshold ~10^6 cfu/mL vs protected specimen brush ~10^3 cfu/mL), at the cost of falling sensitivity for blindly collected distal samples (p.1074) Gram stain of endotracheal aspirate (absence of bacteria argues against pneumonia) (p.1074) Differential cell counts and staining for intracellular organisms on respiratory samples (p.1074) Detection of local protein levels elevated in response to infection (p.1074) Serial / repeat quantitative cultures to track microbiologic response and clarify treatment failure (p.1075) Procalcitonin to help guide duration of therapy in conjunction with the initial clinical response (already curated; Harrison adds the duration-of-therapy context, p.1075) Atypical pulmonary oedema (p.1074) Pulmonary contusion (p.1074) Alveolar haemorrhage (p.1074) Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (p.1074) Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) (p.1074) Pulmonary infarction / pulmonary embolism (p.1074) Pancreatitis (as a non-infective source of fever/leukocytosis) (p.1074) Drug fever (p.1074) VAP is defined as pneumonia with onset 48 hours or more after the start of mechanical ventilation; research on HAP has centred on VAP, but the same principles extend to ventilated HAP and to non-ICU HAP (p.1072). About 70% of HAP cases are acquired outside the ICU and 30% within it; roughly 35% of all HAP patients require mechanical ventilation, which makes ventilated HAP a distinct entity whose bacteriology and outcome resemble those of VAP (p.1072). In nonintubated HAP an expectorated sputum sample is used for microbiologic diagnosis but is confounded by frequent colonisation with oral pathogens; deep lower respiratory tract samples in VAP/ventilated HAP are more reliable yet may still contain colonising organisms (p.1072). The non-MDR 'core pathogens' of VAP closely mirror those of severe CAP and predominate when pneumonia develops in the first 5-7 days of admission; with risk factors (especially prior antibiotics) MDR pathogens become a concern even early (p.1072). Most hospitals contend with P. aeruginosa and MRSA, but the specific MDR organisms are institution-specific and can differ even between critical-care units in the same hospital (p.1072). Prior antibiotic exposure is by far the dominant risk factor for colonisation with pathogenic organisms; P. aeruginosa almost never infects patients with no prior antibiotic exposure (pp.1073, 1076). Only about one-third of colonised intubated patients go on to develop VAP, indicating that the final step is overwhelming of host defences by a large bacterial inoculum rather than colonisation alone (p.1073). Severely ill septic or trauma patients appear to enter a state of immunoparalysis several days after ICU admission, coinciding with the period of greatest VAP risk; hyperglycaemia and frequent transfusions adversely affect immune response (p.1073). Serial changes in oxygenation may detect HAP/VAP earlier than other findings and can also serve to monitor response to therapy (p.1073). Absence of bacteria on a Gram stain of an endotracheal aspirate makes pneumonia an unlikely cause of the fever or infiltrate; presence of an MDR pathogen can be excluded as a target if tracheal aspirate cultures (or sensitive molecular tests) are negative, enabling de-escalation (p.1074). Anaerobes may be somewhat more common in nonintubated HAP than in VAP because of greater macroaspiration risk and lower lower-airway oxygen tension, but they usually contribute only to polymicrobial pneumonia and rarely need specific targeted therapy (p.1076). A bronchopneumonia pattern is most common in nosocomial pneumonias, in contrast to the lobar pattern more typical of bacterial CAP; in VAP, respiratory bronchiolitis may precede a radiologically apparent infiltrate (p.1066). The 'healthcare-associated pneumonia' category has been abandoned because it did not reliably predict resistant-organism infection and drove excessive broad-spectrum antibiotic use; resistance risk should instead be judged individually from comorbidities, recent hospitalisation, and recent antibiotic therapy (p.1066). New or worsening hypoxaemia / serial decline in oxygenation in a ventilated patient (may herald pneumonia before other signs) (p.1073) Septic shock accompanying suspected VAP (influences empirical regimen breadth) (p.1075) Failure to improve clinically by 48-72 h of appropriate therapy (improvement, when it occurs, is usually evident in this window) (p.1076) Necrotising pneumonia (e.g., P. aeruginosa or S. aureus) causing significant pulmonary haemorrhage or empyema (p.1075) Applying CAP-type clinical criteria to ventilated patients consistently overdiagnoses VAP, owing to frequent tracheal colonisation, multiple alternative causes of radiographic infiltrates, and many other sources of fever in the critically ill (pp.1073-1074). No single set of criteria reliably diagnoses pneumonia in a ventilated patient; over-reliance on portable chest radiographs is limited by frequent pre-existing infiltrates and poor portable film quality (p.1073). Effective antibiotic given in the 24-48 h before sampling can drive quantitative cultures below the diagnostic threshold and yield false-negative results; conversely, counts above threshold during therapy suggest the current antibiotics are ineffective (p.1074). Sampling too early in the course, or after an effective host response has already reduced bacterial counts, can also give sub-threshold results; ideally sample as soon as pneumonia is suspected and before starting or changing antibiotics (p.1074). Chest radiographs often worsen initially during treatment, making them less reliable than clinical criteria as indicators of response (p.1076). Recurrent VAP with the same organism can occur because the endotracheal tube biofilm allows persistence and reintroduction; about half of recurrent Pseudomonas cases are actually due to a new strain (p.1075). Three factors are central to VAP pathogenesis: colonisation of the oropharynx with pathogenic organisms, aspiration of those organisms into the lower respiratory tract, and compromise of host defences (p.1073). The endotracheal tube is the single most important risk factor: it bypasses normal anti-aspiration mechanisms, and although it blocks large-volume aspiration, microaspiration is worsened by secretions pooling above the cuff. The tube and suctioning damage tracheal mucosa and facilitate colonisation, and pathogenic bacteria form a protective glycocalyx biofilm on the tube surface that shields them from antibiotics and host defences; biofilm fragments can embolise to distal airways or be dislodged during suctioning to reinoculate the trachea (p.1073). Normal oropharyngeal flora is frequently replaced by pathogenic organisms under antibiotic selection pressure, cross-infection, severe systemic illness, and malnutrition (p.1073). Almost all intubated patients have transient colonisation, but progression to pneumonia reflects a large bacterial inoculum overwhelming host defences amid post-admission immunoparalysis (p.1073). More broadly, pneumonia is now viewed as an emergent disturbance of the lung microbiota driven by self-accelerating inflammatory feedback rather than simple invasion of a sterile space (p.1066). Crude VAP mortality is reported as high as 50-70%, but the key measure is attributable mortality, since many VAP patients have underlying disease that would itself be fatal. Attributable mortality exceeded 25% in one matched-cohort study, whereas more recent estimates are much lower (5-10%); VAP complicating COVID-19 carries higher attributable mortality than other VAP. VAP in trauma patients shows no attributable mortality, likely because many were previously healthy. MDR pathogens carry significantly greater attributable mortality than non-MDR organisms, and some pathogens (e.g., S. maltophilia) chiefly mark a severely immunocompromised, high-risk host. Nonintubated non-ICU HAP has lower mortality and lower risk of antibiotic failure than VAP and ventilated HAP because of better host defences (pp.1076). Harrison frames empirical management around two risk axes rather than a discrete severity score: (1) presence or absence of risk factors for MDR pathogens (prior antibiotic therapy, prior hospitalisation, local antibiogram; for MRSA additionally known MRSA colonisation, chronic haemodialysis, or local MRSA pneumonia rate >10% or unknown), and (2) predicted risk of death, with a mortality risk of 15% or less considered low risk. The frequency of VAP also varies with duration of ventilation, with the highest hazard in the first 5 days, a plateau (~1%/day) after about 2 weeks, and a cumulative rate up to ~70% by 30 days of ventilation (pp.1073, 1075).

entirely without considering overlap syndromes Delaying nephrology and hepatology/transplant referral while pursuing prolonged medical trials in a rapidly deteriorating patient Advanced liver disease with portal hypertension causes marked splanchnic arterial vasodilation, which reduces effective circulating arterial volume despite total-body volume overload. This triggers compensatory activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, sympathetic nervous system, and vasopressin release, producing intense renal vasoconstriction and a progressive fall in glomerular filtration despite normal renal histology. Systemic inflammation and bacterial translocation from the gut further worsen splanchnic vasodilation and renal hypoperfusion, and superimposed infection frequently precipitates the acute form. Historically associated with very high short-term mortality, particularly the rapidly progressive form, unless renal function improves with therapy or the patient undergoes timely liver transplantation. Even with treatment response, underlying hepatic decompensation continues to drive long-term outcomes.

Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) — HLH, Hemophagocytic syndrome, Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, Macrophage activation syndrome, MAS Severe sepsis / septic shock — the principal mimic, with overlapping fever, cytopenias and organ dysfunction Disseminated infection (EBV, CMV and other viruses; tuberculosis; visceral leishmaniasis; severe rickettsial disease) Lymphoma and other haematological malignancies, which can both trigger and mimic HLH Adult-onset Still's disease and systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis complicated by macrophage activation syndrome Thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS) and other causes of fever with cytopenias Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) Severe sepsis / septic shock Disseminated viral infection (EBV, CMV) Visceral leishmaniasis Miliary / disseminated tuberculosis Severe rickettsial or scrub typhus infection Serum ferritin — very high values (often above 10,000 micrograms/L in adults) are highly suggestive Fasting triglycerides and fibrinogen (hypertriglyceridemia and/or hypofibrinogenemia) Full blood count with film (bi- or tri-lineage cytopenias) Soluble CD25 (soluble IL-2 receptor) and NK-cell activity where available Bone marrow aspirate / biopsy for hemophagocytosis (may be absent early — a normal marrow does NOT exclude HLH) Liver function tests and coagulation profile (transaminitis, coagulopathy / DIC) Trigger work-up: EBV / CMV and other viral PCR, blood cultures, and evaluation for lymphoma and autoimmune disease H-score calculation to estimate the probability of secondary HLH in adults Lymphoma / leukaemia Adult-onset Still's disease / systemic JIA with macrophage activation syndrome Thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS) DRESS syndrome HLH is a hyperinflammatory syndrome of uncontrolled immune activation: over-activated CD8 T cells and macrophages drive a cytokine storm and widespread hemophagocytosis (immune cells engulfing blood cells), producing fever, cytopenias and organ injury rather than effective clearance of the trigger. Two broad forms exist — primary/familial HLH from inherited defects of lymphocyte cytotoxicity (e.g. perforin/PRF1, UNC13D), usually presenting in infants and children; and secondary/acquired HLH triggered by infection (classically EBV), malignancy (especially lymphoma), or autoimmune/autoinflammatory disease, where it is termed macrophage activation syndrome (MAS). The clinical hallmark is persistent high fever that does NOT respond to antibiotics, with hepatosplenomegaly and progressive cytopenias affecting two or more lineages — a picture that closely mimics severe sepsis but fails to resolve with antimicrobials alone. A markedly elevated serum ferritin is the most useful bedside clue: values in the tens of thousands are strongly suggestive in adults, and a rising ferritin with falling cell counts and falling fibrinogen should prompt urgent evaluation. Diagnosis commonly uses the HLH-2004 framework (five or more of eight features): fever; splenomegaly; cytopenias in two or more lineages; hypertriglyceridemia and/or hypofibrinogenemia; hemophagocytosis on marrow, spleen or lymph node; low or absent NK-cell activity; ferritin at or above 500 micrograms/L; and elevated soluble CD25 (soluble IL-2 receptor). The H-score is an alternative probability tool for secondary HLH in adults. Persistent high fever unresponsive to broad-spectrum antibiotics with worsening cytopenias Extreme hyperferritinemia (tens of thousands) with falling fibrinogen — impending decompensation Rapidly progressive multi-organ dysfunction, coagulopathy or DIC Neurological involvement (seizures, altered sensorium) indicating CNS-HLH Underlying lymphoma or EBV-driven disease, which carry high mortality and need urgent trigger-directed therapy Anchoring on 'sepsis' and continuing antibiotics while HLH progresses — suspect HLH when a septic picture does not improve and the ferritin is very high. Assuming a normal early bone marrow excludes HLH; hemophagocytosis can appear later, and the diagnosis is clinical plus biochemical, not marrow-dependent. Treating the syndrome without an aggressive search for the trigger (infection, malignancy, autoimmune) — outcome depends on identifying and treating it. Over-relying on a ferritin of 500 micrograms/L alone, which is not specific; it is the very high values and the overall pattern that matter. Defective or overwhelmed cytotoxic lymphocyte function fails to clear antigen-presenting and infected cells, so antigen persists and continuously stimulates CD8+ T cells and macrophages. The result is unrestrained secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (notably interferon-gamma, IL-6, IL-10, TNF and IL-18) — a cytokine storm — that activates macrophages to phagocytose erythrocytes, leukocytes and platelets (hemophagocytosis) in the marrow and reticuloendothelial system. This drives the cardinal features: fever from systemic inflammation, cytopenias from marrow consumption and hemophagocytosis, hepatosplenomegaly and transaminitis from organ infiltration, hyperferritinemia and hypertriglyceridemia from macrophage activation, and hypofibrinogenemia with coagulopathy that can progress to disseminated intravascular coagulation and multi-organ failure. Untreated HLH is frequently fatal. Outcome depends on prompt recognition, the underlying trigger (malignancy- and EBV-associated disease carry the worst prognosis), and timely trigger-directed and immunosuppressive therapy. Macrophage activation syndrome arising in rheumatic disease generally has a better prognosis when recognised and treated early.

Infective Endocarditis — Blood cultures (≥3 sets from separate sites, before antibiotics) — The single most important diagnostic step — identifies the organism and is a major Duke criterion; false-negative cultures from premature antibiotics significantly complicate diagnosis and management. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), followed by transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) if TTE inconclusive or high suspicion persists — Identifies vegetations, abscess, or valve destruction — a major Duke criterion and essential for surgical planning. ECG — Screens for new conduction abnormalities (e.g., new heart block), which can indicate perivalvular abscess extension. CBC, ESR/CRP, renal function — Supports overall assessment of inflammatory burden and any renal involvement (e.g., immune complex glomerulonephritis). Marantic (nonbacterial thrombotic) endocarditis associated with malignancy and chronic wasting disease Atrial myxoma Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome with bland valvular vegetations Systemic lupus erythematosus with sterile (Libman-Sacks-type) vegetations Culture-negative IE due to fastidious organisms (Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella spp., Tropheryma whipplei, Brucella, nutritionally variant Granulicatella/Gemella/Abiotrophia, Corynebacterium/Cutibacterium acnes, Mycobacterium chimaera) Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) detects vegetations in over 90% of definite IE and is preferred over TTE, which misses vegetations under 2 mm and yields inadequate images in about 20% of patients; a negative TEE with high clinical suspicion should be repeated in 7-10 days. Three-dimensional TEE to better define vegetations and perivalvular extension. ECG-gated multislice cardiac CT angiography - superior to TEE for pseudoaneurysm/abscess and can assess coronary patency preoperatively; CTA findings count as a major imaging criterion. 18F-FDG-PET/CT - increases sensitivity in suspected prosthetic-valve IE (including TAVR-PVE), aortic graft, CIED pocket/lead and LVAD infection, and extracardiac foci; false positives within 3 months of valve surgery. Molecular testing of excised/embolized vegetation: organism-specific PCR (C. burnetii, Bartonella, T. whipplei, C. acnes, M. hominis) and broad-range 16S (or 28S for fungi) rRNA PCR with sequencing; only moderately sensitive, so a negative result does not exclude IE. Serologic/PCR testing for culture-negative pathogens: Coxiella burnetii (phase I IgG titer >=1:800) and Bartonella henselae/quintana (IgG titer >=1:800). Brain MRI/MRA in any neurologic signs or symptoms (including unusual headache) to detect emboli, hemorrhage, or mycotic aneurysms. Spine MRI for recalcitrant back pain or focal spinal tenderness to assess for vertebral osteomyelitis/spondylodiscitis and epidural abscess. Routine adjunctive labs: CBC (anemia in 70-90%), ESR (elevated in 60-90%), CRP (elevated in over 90%), microscopic hematuria (30-50%), rheumatoid factor (~50%), creatinine and liver function tests. Marantic endocarditis of malignancy Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome Atrial myxoma SLE-associated sterile endocarditis IE spans a clinical continuum from acute to subacute, and the causative organism largely dictates the tempo: beta-hemolytic streptococci, S. aureus and pneumococci tend to produce an acute, rapidly destructive course, whereas viridans streptococci, enterococci, CoNS and HACEK organisms usually cause subacute disease (Bartonella, T. whipplei, C. burnetii and M. chimaera are exceptionally indolent). Fever is present in 80-90% of cases and a heart murmur in 80-85%, but in subacute IE fever is typically low-grade (rarely above 39.4 C) and may be blunted altogether in elderly, severely debilitated, or renal-failure patients. A new or worsening regurgitant murmur is heard in only 20-50% of cases; in acute IE on a previously normal valve a murmur may be absent at first but is ultimately detected in about 85%. Classic peripheral stigmata (Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, subungual/splinter hemorrhages) appear in only about 2-15% of cases and have become infrequent with earlier diagnosis; their absence does not exclude IE. Janeway lesions are nonsuppurative painless hemorrhagic macules of the palms/soles classically linked to prolonged subacute infection, whereas septic emboli (subungual hemorrhages, Osler nodes) mimicking these lesions are common in acute S. aureus IE. Three independent predictors of embolization are S. aureus etiology, mobile vegetations larger than 10 mm, and involvement of the anterior mitral leaflet. In people who inject drugs, 35-60% of IE is confined to the tricuspid valve and presents with fever but faint or absent murmur and no peripheral stigmata, often with septic pulmonary emboli (cough, pleuritic pain, nodular infiltrates). S. aureus bacteremia carries an 8-14% prevalence of IE and high mortality, so echocardiography (high-quality TTE, preferably TEE) is recommended routinely; intracardiac device, emboli, 2 or more positive cultures, community acquisition, vertebral osteomyelitis or persistent bacteremia each raise IE risk and argue for early TEE. About 12-17% of patients with E. faecalis bacteremia and about 7% with non-beta-hemolytic streptococcal bacteremia have IE, justifying echocardiographic screening when predictive features are present. Up to half of arterial emboli precede the diagnosis of IE; embolic risk falls rapidly once effective antibiotics begin, so emboli occurring late during or after therapy do not by themselves indicate treatment failure. In hemodynamically stable patients with suspected subacute IE, empirical antibiotics can reasonably be withheld initially to allow uncontaminated blood cultures, but patients with sepsis or deteriorating hemodynamics should be treated immediately after the first three culture sets are drawn. Surgery is indicated (as a knowledge concept, distinct from antibiotic regimens) for optimal outcome when there is moderate-severe CHF/shock from valve dysfunction, paravalvular extension with abscess/fistula/heart block, persistent bacteremia without an extracardiac source despite 7-10 days of therapy, lack of effective antimicrobial therapy (fungal, Brucella, multidrug-resistant gram-negative), or an unstable partially dehisced prosthetic valve; it is strongly considered for large (>10 mm) hypermobile vegetations with prior embolus and valve dysfunction, very large (>30 mm) vegetations, S. aureus PVE with intracardiac complications, and relapse after optimal therapy. Removal of all hardware is recommended for established CIED-IE. Congestive heart failure or pulmonary edema/cardiogenic shock from valve dysfunction or intracardiac fistula (develops in 30-40%) - a surgical emergency New electrocardiographic conduction disturbance or new heart block, suggesting paravalvular/septal abscess extension Cerebrovascular embolism (stroke or encephalopathy), which complicates 15-35% of cases Intracranial hemorrhage from hemorrhagic infarct or ruptured mycotic aneurysm Persistent fever or persistently positive blood cultures despite appropriate antibiotics, indicating uncontrolled infection New or worsening regurgitant murmur or prosthetic valve dehiscence Large (over 10 mm) mobile vegetation, particularly on the anterior mitral leaflet, with high embolic risk Acute S. aureus or fungal IE, and any prosthetic-valve involvement Relying on a new/worsening murmur alone - it is a physical-exam minor criterion only; a major imaging criterion requires echocardiographic evidence of new valvular regurgitation, not auscultation. Treating a negative TTE (or even a negative initial TEE) as ruling out IE; TTE misses vegetations under 2 mm and is poor for prosthetic valves, and initial TEE is falsely negative in 6-18% (especially TAVR-PVE) - repeat in 7-10 days when suspicion persists. Forgetting that 5-15% of IE is blood-culture negative, often because of prior antibiotics; withholding empirical therapy when stable preserves diagnostic yield. Interpreting persistent organism DNA detected in excised valves (in ~45% of patients who completed therapy) as antibiotic failure - relapse after surgery for active IE is actually uncommon. Misattributing emboli that occur late during or after effective therapy to treatment failure. Overlooking that prior antibiotics within 2 weeks blunt culture yield and that nontypical organisms require 3 or more positive sets (plus no extracardiac focus) to count as a major criterion. Assuming antithrombotic therapy prevents systemic emboli in NVE - it does not. The prototypic lesion is the vegetation - a mass of platelets, fibrin, microorganisms and scant inflammatory cells - usually on heart valves but also on the low-pressure side of a ventricular septal defect, on mural endocardium injured by aberrant blood jets or foreign bodies, or on intracardiac devices. Intact endothelium resists most bacteria; endothelial injury (e.g., at sites of high-velocity jet impact or on the low-pressure side of a structural lesion) permits direct infection by virulent organisms or formation of a sterile platelet-fibrin thrombus (nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, NBTE) that becomes a nidus for bacterial seeding during transient bacteremia. NBTE is most often associated with mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, ventricular septal defects and complex congenital heart disease, and also arises from hypercoagulable states (marantic endocarditis of malignancy/chronic disease and the bland vegetations of SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome). Circulating organisms adhere via surface adhesins (MSCRAMMs) - fibronectin-binding proteins, S. aureus clumping factor, enterococcal Fss2/Ace/Ebp pili, streptococcal glucans/FimA; S. aureus can even invade intact endothelium via fibronectin-binding proteins and von Willebrand factor, allowing infection of previously normal valves. Adherent organisms proliferate into microcolonies, induce platelet deposition and a local procoagulant (tissue-factor) state, and become buried in fibrin; deep organisms are metabolically inactive and relatively antibiotic-resistant while surface organisms are continuously shed into the blood. Clinical manifestations arise from intracardiac structural damage, embolization of vegetation fragments causing remote infarction/infection, hematogenous seeding during bacteremia, and immune-complex deposition; constitutional symptoms reflect cytokine release. Overall survival in developed countries is about 80-85%, but varies markedly by subgroup. About 85-90% survive NVE caused by viridans streptococci, HACEK organisms, or synergy-susceptible enterococci. Non-injecting patients with S. aureus NVE have 55-70% survival; injecting patients have 85-90%, but 1-year mortality rises to 20-30% if substance-use disorder is not addressed. Prosthetic-valve IE arising within 2 months of surgery carries 40-50% mortality versus only 10-20% for late-onset PVE; elderly TAVR-PVE in-hospital mortality is 35-50%, rising to 60-75% at 1 year. Crude survival after successful treatment is roughly 80-90% at 1 year and 70-80% at 2 years. Death often reflects comorbidities and end-organ complications rather than antibiotic failure. Adverse outcomes are linked to older age, severe comorbidity/diabetes, delayed diagnosis, prosthetic or aortic valve involvement, virulent or resistant pathogens (S. aureus, P. aeruginosa, yeast), intracardiac and major neurologic complications, and health care-associated infection. Diagnosis uses the 2023 Duke-International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases (Duke-ISCVID) update of the modified Duke criteria (sensitivity 80-93%). MAJOR criteria: (1) Microbiologic - a typical IE organism in 2 or more separate blood culture sets (S. aureus, S. lugdunensis, E. faecalis, all streptococci except S. pneumoniae and S. pyogenes, Granulicatella/Abiotrophia/Gemella, HACEK group; and, when intracardiac prosthetic material is present, CoNS, C. striatum, C. jeikeium, S. marcescens, P. aeruginosa, C. acnes, nontuberculous mycobacteria and Candida), OR a nontypical organism in 3 or more sets; positive PCR/single culture/serology for C. burnetii, Bartonella spp. or T. whipplei. (2) Imaging - echocardiography or cardiac CT showing vegetation, perforation/leaflet aneurysm, abscess, pseudoaneurysm or fistula, OR new valvular regurgitation, OR new prosthetic dehiscence; OR abnormal FDG-PET/CT activity on a valve/graft/lead/prosthetic material. (3) Surgical - IE seen at direct surgical inspection. MINOR criteria: predisposing condition (prior IE, injection drug use, prosthetic valve, prior valve repair, congenital heart disease such as bicuspid aortic valve, CIED, more-than-mild regurgitation/stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy); fever over 38.0 C; vascular phenomena (arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial/conjunctival hemorrhage, Janeway lesions); immunologic phenomena (glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, positive rheumatoid factor); microbiologic evidence not meeting a major criterion; and PET/CT activity within 3 months of prosthetic implantation. CLASSIFICATION: DEFINITE IE = pathologic confirmation OR 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. POSSIBLE IE = 1 major + 1 minor, or 3 minor. REJECTED = firm alternative diagnosis, or resolution with under 4 days of antibiotics, or no histologic evidence at surgery/autopsy after under 4 days of therapy. IE is also classified by tempo (acute vs subacute), site (native vs prosthetic valve, right-sided/tricuspid), cause, and predisposition (injection drug use, health care-associated).

IgA nephropathy — iga nephropathy, berger disease, iga glomerulonephritis, synpharyngitic hematuria, ign, berger's disease, mesangial iga disease Thin basement membrane nephropathy (benign familial hematuria) Alport syndrome (hereditary nephritis) Post-infectious (post-streptococcal) glomerulonephritis Lupus nephritis IgA vasculitis with nephritis Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis Infective endocarditis-associated glomerulonephritis Hepatitis-associated glomerulonephritis Urinalysis with microscopy — confirms dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts indicating glomerular bleeding Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour urine protein — quantifies proteinuria for staging and prognosis Serum creatinine and estimated GFR — establishes baseline kidney function and tracks progression Serum complement levels (C3, C4) — typically normal in IgA nephropathy, helping exclude complement-mediated GN Kidney biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy — required for definitive diagnosis and Oxford classification grading Serum IgA level — often elevated but neither sensitive nor specific enough to confirm diagnosis alone ANA, ANCA, and hepatitis serologies — helps exclude secondary causes and mimicking systemic diseases Renal ultrasound — assesses kidney size and excludes obstructive or structural causes of hematuria Thin basement membrane nephropathy Alport syndrome Lupus nephritis ANCA-associated vasculitis with glomerulonephritis Most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide, typically presenting in the second or third decade of life. Classic presentation is episodic gross (macroscopic) hematuria occurring within 1-2 days of an upper respiratory or mucosal infection, distinguishing it from post-streptococcal GN which lags 1-3 weeks. Can also present as asymptomatic microscopic hematuria with mild proteinuria found incidentally on urinalysis. Diagnosis requires kidney biopsy showing dominant or codominant mesangial IgA deposition on immunofluorescence. Course is highly variable: some patients have a benign lifelong course while roughly 20-40% progress to end-stage kidney disease over 20 years. Recurrent gross hematuria episodes typically resolve completely between attacks, but persistent proteinuria or hypertension signals higher risk. IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is considered a systemic variant of the same underlying disease process affecting skin, gut, and joints. Renal biopsy findings are graded using the Oxford (MEST-C) classification to help predict prognosis and guide therapy intensity. Rapidly rising creatinine suggesting crescentic (rapidly progressive) IgA nephropathy requiring urgent nephrology evaluation Nephrotic-range proteinuria or nephrotic syndrome at presentation New or worsening hypertension poorly responsive to therapy Systemic features (purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain) suggesting IgA vasculitis with renal involvement Persistent proteinuria greater than 1 gram per day despite optimized supportive therapy Attributing recurrent gross hematuria solely to urologic causes and delaying nephrology referral or biopsy. Assuming normal complement levels rule out all forms of glomerulonephritis rather than supporting IgA nephropathy specifically. Underestimating long-term risk in patients with isolated microscopic hematuria who lack proteinuria monitoring over time. Confusing timing of hematuria onset relative to infection with post-streptococcal GN, missing the synpharyngitic pattern typical of IgA nephropathy. Disease arises from circulating poorly galactosylated IgA1 molecules that form immune complexes, which deposit in the glomerular mesangium and trigger mesangial cell proliferation and matrix expansion. This deposition activates complement and local inflammatory pathways, leading to variable degrees of mesangial hypercellularity, segmental sclerosis, endocapillary proliferation, and interstitial fibrosis depending on disease severity. Mucosal immune stimulation (e.g., respiratory infection) is thought to transiently boost production of these abnormal IgA1 complexes, explaining the synpharyngitic timing of gross hematuria flares. Course ranges from indolent with preserved kidney function over decades to progressive decline, with an estimated 20-40% of patients reaching end-stage kidney disease within 20 years of diagnosis. Higher risk features include persistent proteinuria, hypertension, reduced GFR at presentation, and unfavorable histology on Oxford classification.

Insulinoma — Insulinoma, Beta-cell tumor, Islet cell tumor, Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor - insulin secreting, Insulin-secreting pNET, Whipple triad tumor, Nesidioblastosis (adult, related entity) Factitious or surreptitious insulin/sulfonylurea administration Non-islet cell tumor hypoglycemia (IGF-2-secreting mesenchymal or epithelial tumors) Post-bariatric surgery hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia / nesidioblastosis Adrenal insufficiency Autoimmune insulin (Hirata) syndrome or insulin receptor autoantibodies Severe hepatic failure or sepsis-related hypoglycemia 72-hour supervised fasting test — reference standard to document Whipple triad with paired glucose, insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin Plasma insulin and C-peptide during hypoglycemia — inappropriately elevated levels confirm endogenous hyperinsulinemia Sulfonylurea/meglitinide screen — excludes factitious hypoglycemia from oral secretagogues Insulin antibody testing — helps exclude autoimmune insulin syndrome or exogenous insulin use Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of pancreas — initial anatomic localization of tumor Endoscopic ultrasound — high sensitivity for small intrapancreatic lesions not seen on cross-sectional imaging Somatostatin-receptor or GLP-1 receptor based functional imaging — localizes lesion when anatomic imaging is negative Genetic/family screening for MEN1 — indicated when tumors are multiple, recurrent, or early-onset Reactive (postprandial) hypoglycemia Alcohol-induced hypoglycemia Adrenal insufficiency Hypopituitarism Factitious hypoglycemia from exogenous insulin or sulfonylureas Presents with Whipple triad: symptoms of neuroglycopenia/adrenergic surge, documented hypoglycemia, and relief with glucose intake. Neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, behavioral change, visual disturbance, seizure, coma) often dominate and can mimic a primary neuropsychiatric or seizure disorder. Fasting-induced hypoglycemia is classic, but symptoms can also occur postprandially or with exertion in some patients. Most insulinomas are small (<2 cm), solitary, benign, and confined to the pancreas; only a minority are malignant or multiple. Multiple or recurrent insulinomas should raise suspicion for MEN1 syndrome, especially in younger patients or with a family history. Weight gain is common because patients learn to eat frequently to avoid symptomatic hypoglycemia. Diagnosis rests on a supervised fasting study demonstrating inappropriately elevated insulin and C-peptide during hypoglycemia, not just cross-sectional imaging. Localization can be difficult since many tumors are very small; a negative scan does not exclude the diagnosis. Severe neuroglycopenia with seizure, coma, or altered mental status requiring urgent glucose correction Recurrent or multifocal tumors suggesting MEN1 and need for broader endocrine screening Imaging or biochemical features suggesting malignant insulinoma with metastatic potential Hypoglycemia unresponsive to standard glucose repletion, suggesting an alternative or coexisting cause Signs of another MEN1-associated tumor (parathyroid, pituitary) in a patient with insulinoma Relying on a single random glucose or insulin level instead of a supervised fasting protocol, leading to missed or false diagnosis. Failing to exclude factitious hypoglycemia (exogenous insulin/sulfonylurea) before pursuing extensive tumor imaging. Assuming a negative CT/MRI excludes insulinoma, when small tumors frequently require endoscopic ultrasound or functional imaging for localization. Overlooking the possibility of MEN1 in patients with multiple or recurrent insulinomas, delaying appropriate family and genetic evaluation. Insulinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor arising from pancreatic beta cells that autonomously secretes insulin independent of glucose feedback regulation. This unregulated insulin release drives glucose into tissues and suppresses hepatic glucose output, producing hypoglycemia. The resulting fall in plasma glucose triggers counter-regulatory adrenergic activation and, when severe or prolonged, neuroglycopenia due to inadequate glucose delivery to the brain. Most tumors are sporadic and benign, but a subset occurs in the context of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1. Most insulinomas are benign and solitary, and surgical resection is curative in the large majority of cases. Malignant or MEN1-associated multifocal disease carries a less favorable outlook and requires longer-term surveillance.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis — idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, IPF, usual interstitial pneumonia, UIP, cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis, idiopathic UIP Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis) Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia Drug-induced pulmonary toxicity Asbestosis or other pneumoconiosis Combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema High-resolution CT chest — identifies UIP pattern and excludes alternative diagnoses Pulmonary function tests with DLCO — documents restrictive pattern and gas-transfer impairment, tracks progression Serologic autoimmune panel (ANA, rheumatoid factor, myositis antibodies) — screens for occult connective tissue disease Six-minute walk test with oximetry — assesses functional capacity and exertional desaturation Surgical or transbronchial cryobiopsy — considered when HRCT is indeterminate and histopathology would change management Echocardiogram — evaluates for pulmonary hypertension as a complication Bronchoalveolar lavage — helps exclude infection or alternative diagnoses in select atypical presentations Detailed exposure and medication history — identifies occupational, environmental, or drug-related causes of fibrosis Congestive heart failure with pulmonary edema Sarcoidosis Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease Pulmonary drug toxicity Consider IPF in an older adult (usually over age 60) with progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough lasting months, especially with a smoking history. Bibasilar, fine 'Velcro-like' end-inspiratory crackles are the classic auscultatory finding. Digital clubbing is present in roughly half of patients and supports the diagnosis. High-resolution CT showing a definite UIP pattern (subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, absence of features suggesting an alternative diagnosis) can obviate the need for lung biopsy. IPF is a diagnosis of exclusion — connective tissue disease, chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, drug toxicity, and occupational/environmental exposures must be ruled out first. Course is highly variable: most patients decline gradually, but acute exacerbations with rapid, often fatal deterioration can occur unpredictably. Antifibrotic therapy slows the rate of decline in lung function but does not reverse existing fibrosis, so early diagnosis and referral matter. Early referral for lung transplant evaluation should be considered at diagnosis given the poor natural history. Acute worsening of dyspnea over days to weeks (acute exacerbation), which carries high short-term mortality Resting hypoxemia or significant desaturation on exertion Rapidly declining forced vital capacity or DLCO on serial testing Signs of cor pulmonale or pulmonary hypertension Superimposed respiratory infection, which can precipitate acute decompensation Attributing crackles and dyspnea to heart failure or COPD without pursuing HRCT, delaying diagnosis Missing an underlying connective tissue disease or exposure history that would reclassify the disease and change management Relying on chest x-ray alone, which is insensitive for early fibrotic change Assuming a stable course; failing to monitor for acute exacerbations or gradual functional decline IPF is thought to result from repeated micro-injury to alveolar epithelium in a genetically susceptible, typically older individual, triggering an aberrant wound-healing response rather than a primarily inflammatory process. This dysregulated repair leads to fibroblast/myofibroblast proliferation and excessive extracellular matrix deposition, producing the patchy, temporally heterogeneous fibrosis and architectural distortion characteristic of the usual interstitial pneumonia pattern. Progressive scarring impairs gas exchange and lung compliance, culminating in restrictive physiology and hypoxemia. IPF carries a poor prognosis with median survival historically around 3-5 years from diagnosis, though the trajectory is heterogeneous and antifibrotic therapy has modestly slowed functional decline. Acute exacerbations and progression to respiratory failure are the major causes of death, and lung transplantation remains the only intervention altering long-term survival.

Kawasaki disease — kawasaki, mucocutaneous lymph node, mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, kawasaki syndrome, infantile polyarteritis, kd Scarlet fever / group A streptococcal infection Measles and other viral exanthems Staphylococcal or streptococcal toxic shock syndrome Stevens-Johnson syndrome / drug hypersensitivity reaction Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) Scarlet fever (group A Streptococcus) Measles Adenovirus infection Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome / toxic shock syndrome Epstein-Barr virus infection Leptospirosis Echocardiogram — baseline and serial imaging to detect coronary artery dilation or aneurysm CBC with differential — leukocytosis early, thrombocytosis typically emerging in the subacute phase ESR and CRP — markedly elevated, supports diagnosis and tracks inflammatory activity Liver function tests — mild transaminitis and hypoalbuminemia are common Urinalysis — sterile pyuria from urethritis supports the diagnosis ECG — screen for arrhythmia or ischemic changes related to coronary involvement Blood culture and throat culture — help exclude streptococcal and other bacterial mimics Lipid panel — baseline assessment given long-term cardiovascular risk in those with aneurysms Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) Stevens-Johnson syndrome / drug reaction Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis Polyarteritis nodosa Acute self-limited vasculitis of childhood, mainly under age 5, that preferentially targets medium-sized arteries, especially the coronary arteries. Classic diagnosis needs fever for five or more days plus four of five criteria: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes (cracked lips, strawberry tongue), polymorphous rash, extremity changes (edema, erythema, later periungual desquamation), and cervical lymphadenopathy usually unilateral and over 1.5 cm. Incomplete (atypical) presentations are common in infants under 6 months and older children, and this group carries a higher, not lower, risk of coronary aneurysm. Irritability out of proportion to exam findings and marked perineal desquamation in the diaper area are supportive clues. Untreated disease leads to coronary artery aneurysms in roughly a quarter of children; timely therapy sharply reduces this risk. Think of Kawasaki disease in any young febrile child with unexplained sterile pyuria, gallbladder hydrops, or aseptic meningitis. Highest risk of coronary aneurysm formation is in the subacute phase, roughly one to four weeks after fever onset, coinciding with marked thrombocytosis. Evidence of coronary artery dilation or aneurysm on echocardiogram warrants urgent cardiology involvement Signs of myocarditis, pericardial effusion, or hemodynamic instability (Kawasaki disease shock syndrome) Persistent or recrudescent fever after initial therapy suggesting treatment resistance Very young infants or children with incomplete presentations, who are at higher risk of coronary complications Marked thrombocytosis in the subacute phase increasing thrombotic risk in dilated vessels Dismissing the diagnosis because not all classic criteria are present, especially in infants who often have incomplete disease with greater cardiac risk Delaying treatment while awaiting full criteria, since early therapy within the first ten days of fever meaningfully lowers aneurysm risk Overlooking overlap with MIS-C in the appropriate epidemiologic context, which requires additional testing and different considerations Failing to arrange long-term cardiology follow-up in children with documented coronary changes Kawasaki disease is thought to arise from an exaggerated innate and adaptive immune response, possibly triggered by an unidentified infectious agent, in a genetically susceptible host. The resulting medium-vessel vasculitis targets the coronary arteries, causing panvasculitis with destruction of the internal elastic lamina and media, which weakens the vessel wall and predisposes to aneurysm formation and later stenosis or thrombosis. Systemic inflammation also produces the mucocutaneous and lymph node findings that define the clinical syndrome. With prompt recognition and treatment most children recover fully with resolution of fever and inflammation within days. Coronary artery aneurysms, when they occur, may regress over time but can also persist, predisposing to late stenosis, thrombosis, or ischemic events, so children with cardiac involvement need long-term surveillance.

Leptospirosis — Leptospira IgM ELISA / MAT (microscopic agglutination test) — Confirms diagnosis serologically; MAT is the reference standard but often only available at referral labs, so treatment should not be delayed pending results. Renal function tests — Assesses for acute kidney injury, a hallmark of severe leptospirosis (Weil's disease) with major prognostic significance. Liver function tests — Jaundice with relatively modest transaminase elevation (compared to viral hepatitis) is a classic pattern in leptospirosis. CBC, coagulation profile — Screens for thrombocytopenia and bleeding risk, relevant to hemorrhagic complications. CPK (creatine phosphokinase) — Often elevated due to myositis, supporting the diagnosis and explaining myalgia. Influenza and SARS-CoV-2 / other respiratory viral infections (when fever, headache, myalgia predominate) Chikungunya Ehrlichiosis / rickettsial diseases Acute HIV infection Hantavirus infection (hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome or hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome) Yellow fever and other viral hemorrhagic fevers (Rift Valley fever, filovirus infections, Lassa fever) when bleeding is present Acute schistosomiasis Dengue (and dengue hemorrhagic fever when bleeding present) Malaria Typhoid fever Scrub typhus (rash may be misattributed) Viral hepatitis Acute HIV infection Hantavirus infection Yellow fever / viral hemorrhagic fevers PCR (notably real-time PCR) of blood/CSF/urine — confirms diagnosis with high accuracy during the first 5 days of illness, before serology becomes positive (p.1443) Microscopic agglutination test (MAT) using live leptospiral strains — paired acute/convalescent sera seeking a fourfold rise; single high titer (1:200-1:800 depending on endemicity) supportive (p.1443) IgM ELISA and commercial rapid lateral-flow / latex agglutination tests (useful where MAT/culture unavailable) (p.1443) Blood/urine/CSF culture (special media; may take weeks to months) (p.1441, 1443) C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, ESR (raised inflammatory markers) (p.1443) Coagulation profile / DIC markers (D-dimer, antithrombin, protein C) in severe disease (p.1443) Serum amylase (often elevated even without overt pancreatitis) (p.1443) Serum electrolytes including magnesium (urinary magnesium loss is characteristic; hypokalemia, hyponatremia) (p.1443) Urinalysis (leukocytes, erythrocytes, hyaline/granular casts, mild proteinuria) (p.1443) Bilirubin, aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase (bilirubin may be high; transaminase rises typically only moderate) (p.1443) Chest radiograph / CT (patchy bilateral lower-lobe alveolar pattern from alveolar hemorrhage; pleura-based densities; ground-glass ARDS pattern) (p.1443) ECG (nonspecific ST/T changes; repolarization abnormalities and arrhythmias are poor prognostic signs) (p.1443) CSF examination when meningitis suspected (pleocytosis from a few to >1000 cells/uL, lymphocytic but may be PMN-predominant early; protein normal or slightly raised, glucose normal) (p.1443) Co-testing for rickettsiae, dengue, and hantavirus given overlap and reported dual infections (p.1443) Classically biphasic: an acute leptospiremic phase (fever lasting ~3-10 days, organism culturable/PCR-detectable in blood) followed by an immune phase in which symptoms may resolve as antibodies appear and leptospires can be recovered from urine; the two phases are not always distinct, mild cases may lack the second phase, and severe disease can be monophasic and fulminant (p.1442). Incubation is usually 1-2 weeks but ranges from 2 to 30 days (p.1442). Conjunctival suffusion (redness without exudate) is a characteristic but non-pathognomonic sign; muscle pain is intense, especially in the calves, back, and abdomen (p.1442). Headache is intense and frontal or retro-orbital, sometimes with photophobia, resembling dengue (p.1442). Weil's syndrome denotes the severe triad of jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage (p.1442-1443). Severe pulmonary hemorrhage (with or without jaundice) is increasingly recognized as an important and widespread presentation; hemoptysis may not become apparent until the patient is intubated (p.1439, 1442). Jaundice occurs in only ~5-10% of patients, can be deep with an orange skin cast, and is usually NOT associated with fulminant hepatic necrosis (p.1442). Aseptic meningitis is more common in children than adults; altered mental status in severe disease may reflect leptospiral meningitis, which can occur in anicteric patients lacking other hallmarks (p.1442-1443). Autoimmune-associated uveitis is a recognized, potentially chronic late sequela (p.1443). Idea that specific serogroups cause distinct clinical syndromes has been refuted, although some serovars tend to cause more severe disease (p.1442). Serology lacks sensitivity in the early acute phase (up to day 5) and cannot guide a timely treatment decision; PCR (notably real-time PCR) can confirm diagnosis during the first 5 days (p.1443). MAT antibodies generally do not reach detectable levels until the second week of illness, and the antibody response may be blunted by early antibiotics (p.1443). Age >40 years Altered mental status Acute kidney injury / oliguria or anuria Respiratory insufficiency, hemoptysis, or pulmonary hemorrhage Hypotension / septic shock Cardiac arrhythmias and repolarization abnormalities on ECG Jaundice with bleeding (Weil's syndrome triad) Thrombocytopenia (platelet count <=100 x10^9/L) — linked to bleeding and renal failure Evidence of coagulation activation / DIC Pregnancy (high fetal mortality) Absence of a travel or freshwater-exposure history does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1443). Absence of renal involvement does not rule out leptospirosis (p.1443). Relying on serology in the first ~5 days risks a false-negative; antibodies are often undetectable until the second week and early antibiotics blunt the response (p.1443). Cross-reactions are frequent in MAT, so the infecting serovar/serogroup cannot be definitively identified without isolating the organism (p.1443). Leptospiral meningitis may present without jaundice or other classic severe-disease hallmarks, making it easy to miss (p.1443). Jaundice can be profound yet usually does not signify fulminant hepatic necrosis, so hepatic transaminase rises are only moderate (p.1442-1443). The transient rash may be misdiagnosed as scrub typhus or a viral exanthem (p.1442). Dual infection (e.g., with dengue, rickettsiae, or hantavirus) can occur, so a positive alternative test does not exclude leptospirosis (p.1443). Leptospires enter through cuts, abraded skin, or mucous membranes (especially conjunctival and oral). The highly motile organisms proliferate, cross tissue barriers, and disseminate hematogenously to all organs (leptospiremic phase), evading innate immune mechanisms such as complement-mediated killing and phagocytosis; an exaggerated proinflammatory response correlates with mortality. With the immune phase, antibodies appear and leptospires clear from blood but persist in liver, lung, kidney, heart, and brain. Renal pathology shows acute tubular damage and interstitial nephritis, progressing to interstitial edema and acute tubular necrosis, with dysregulated nephron transporters causing impaired sodium absorption, potassium wasting, and polyuria. Liver histology shows focal (not widespread) hepatocellular necrosis, inflammation, bile canaliculus plugging, and hepatocyte apoptosis, with disruption of intercellular junctions and bile leakage. Petechiae and hemorrhages occur across many organs. Hemorrhage is associated with thrombocytopenia (likely platelet consumption); a consumptive coagulopathy with elevated coagulation-activation markers, reduced anticoagulant markers, and dysregulated fibrinolysis may progress to overt DIC. Endothelial cell activation (raised soluble E-selectin and von Willebrand factor) correlates with severity, and leptospires/leptospiral proteins disrupt endothelial barrier function, increasing permeability. The LPS has unusually low endotoxic potency, yet serovar-specific anti-LPS antibodies are central to protective humoral immunity (p.1441-1442). Most patients recover, with renal and hepatic function typically returning to normal in survivors (hemodialysis can be lifesaving). Overall mean case-fatality is near 10% for severe cases; severe leptospirosis carries a case-fatality of 1-50%. Mortality is highest in the elderly and those with pulmonary hemorrhage or Weil's syndrome. Untreated leptospiral meningitis has reported mortality of ~13% versus ~2% with antibiotics. Pregnancy is associated with high fetal mortality. Post-leptospirosis sequelae include prolonged fatigue, myalgia, malaise, headache, depression-like symptoms persisting for years, and chronic autoimmune uveitis (p.1443-1444). Harrison distinguishes mild leptospirosis (sudden-onset flu-like febrile illness with headache, myalgia, conjunctival suffusion; usually self-limiting over 7-10 days, low mortality) from severe leptospirosis, which is often rapidly progressive with multiorgan involvement. Severe disease classically presents as Weil's syndrome (triad of jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage) and/or severe pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome, with a case-fatality of 1-50% (p.1442-1443).

Liver Abscess — Abdominal ultrasound or CT — Confirms presence, size, number, and location of abscess(es), and guides drainage planning. Image-guided aspiration with Gram stain, culture, and microscopy — Definitively distinguishes pyogenic from amebic abscess and identifies the specific organism for targeted therapy. Amebic serology (IgG) — Supports diagnosis of amebic liver abscess, especially useful when aspiration is not performed or is inconclusive. Blood cultures — May identify the causative organism in pyogenic abscess, particularly Klebsiella, without requiring aspiration. HbA1c/blood glucose — Diabetes is a major risk factor for Klebsiella liver abscess and affects overall management. Splenic abscess (different clinical setting and organism profile, most often associated with bacterial endocarditis; high index of suspicion needed as it is frequently fatal if untreated) (p.1118) Hepatic actinomycosis (Actinomyces israelii can produce multiple hepatic abscesses, sometimes with a contiguous splenic lesion) (p.1290 region) Candidal (fungal) liver abscess in immunocompromised/post-chemotherapy patients (p.1117) Amebic liver abscess (Entamoeba histolytica) — a treatable alternative with overlapping right-upper-quadrant pain, fever, and point hepatic tenderness; jaundice is rare and fewer than one-third have active diarrhoea at presentation (p.1117, p.1756) Imaging is the most reliable diagnostic modality: ultrasonography, CT, MRI, and indium-labelled-WBC or gallium scintigraphy; more than one study may be needed (p.1117). Chest radiography may give a clue — a newly elevated right hemidiaphragm, right basilar infiltrate, or right pleural effusion (p.1117). Diagnostic aspiration of abscess contents (with Gram stain and culture), together with blood cultures, ideally obtained before starting empirical antibiotics (p.1118). Amebic serology is positive in >95% of amebic liver abscess cases and PCR can also be used; negative results help exclude amebiasis (p.1117). Note enzyme immunoassay for the Gal/GalNAc lectin and LAMP/PCR can also be applied directly to abscess aspirate/pus (p.1756-1757). Supportive labs: leukocytosis (~77%), normochromic normocytic anaemia (~50%), hypoalbuminaemia (~33%); concomitant bacteraemia in one-third to one-half of patients (p.1117). For suspected hypervirulent K. pneumoniae, the string test for hypermucoviscosity is suggestive but not optimally sensitive or specific; the most accurate identification uses the biomarkers iucA, iroB, peg-344, rmpA, and rmpA2 (p.1290). The liver is the visceral organ most prone to abscess formation; in one series of intraabdominal abscesses, hepatic abscesses accounted for roughly half of all visceral abscesses (p.1117). Fever is the most common presenting feature; about half of patients with a liver abscess have no localizing signs (no hepatomegaly, right-upper-quadrant tenderness, or jaundice), so the liver may not be obviously implicated on examination (p.1117). In the elderly, liver abscess may present solely as fever of unknown origin, so abdominal imaging (especially of the right upper quadrant) should form part of any FUO workup (p.1117). An elevated serum alkaline phosphatase is the single most reliable laboratory abnormality, present in about 70% of patients; bilirubin and aminotransferases are often normal or only modestly raised (p.1117). The microbiology of pyogenic liver abscess tracks with the source: biliary-tract origin yields enteric gram-negative aerobic bacilli and enterococci, pelvic/intraperitoneal origin yields a mixed aerobic-anaerobic flora (B. fragilis most common), and haematogenous seeding usually yields a single organism such as S. aureus or a Streptococcus milleri (anginosus)-group streptococcus (p.1117). Anaerobes are not typically involved in liver abscesses arising from biliary infection unless prior surgery has occurred (p.1117). Candida liver abscess characteristically follows fungaemia in patients receiving chemotherapy and often becomes clinically apparent as neutrophil counts recover after a period of neutropenia (p.1117). Features suggesting hypervirulent K. pneumoniae with metastatic spread — concurrent endophthalmitis (threatening vision loss), meningitis/brain abscess, or septic pulmonary nodules — mandate urgent evaluation of distant sites (p.1289-1290). Multiple sizeable abscesses, viscous contents prone to plugging a catheter, presence of yeast, communication with an untreated/obstructed biliary tree, or no clinical response to percutaneous drainage within 4-7 days predict failure of percutaneous drainage and favour surgical intervention (p.1118). Mortality remains appreciable (around 15%) despite treatment (p.1118). Failing to distinguish pyogenic from amebic liver abscess: amebic serology is positive in >95% of amebic cases, amebic abscesses are classically a single right-lobe lesion, and most travellers with amebic abscess present within ~5 months of leaving an endemic area — so travel history, lesion location, and serology should be sought before committing to a purely bacterial diagnosis (p.1117, p.1755-1756). Aspirating an amebic abscess for trophozoites is low-yield: trophozoites reside in the abscess capsule, not in the readily aspirated necrotic ('anchovy-paste') centre, so their absence on aspirate does not exclude amebiasis (p.1756). Up to 10% of patients with acute amebic liver abscess have negative serology early on, usually seroconverting within a week — a single early negative test does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1757). Assuming anaerobic coverage is always required: anaerobes are generally not involved in abscesses of biliary origin (unless prior surgery), whereas pelvic/intraperitoneal-source abscesses are typically polymicrobial with B. fragilis (p.1117). Attributing a cryptogenic pyogenic liver abscess solely to the liver: because biliary, portal (pelvic/appendiceal), and other intra-abdominal infections are leading sources, the underlying source must be sought and addressed (p.1117). Overlooking that ampicillin/amoxicillin exposure within the prior 30 days has been associated with increased risk of the hypervirulent K. pneumoniae liver abscess syndrome, presumably via selection for the causative strain (p.1117). Pyogenic liver abscesses arise either from haematogenous spread of bacteria or from local spread from contiguous intraperitoneal infection. The organism reaches the liver by several routes: ascending biliary infection (currently the most common associated source), portal venous seeding via suppurative thrombosis of the portal vein (pylephlebitis, classically from pelvic or other intra-abdominal infection), direct contiguous spread, or systemic bacteraemic (haematogenous) seeding. Historically, ruptured appendicitis was the leading source. Hypervirulent (hypermucoviscous) K. pneumoniae causes a distinct community-acquired monomicrobial syndrome in which the organism establishes a primary liver abscess and then disseminates metastatically; this contrasts with the polymicrobial, source-driven pattern of biliary or enteric abscesses. (p.1117, p.1289-1290) Mortality from pyogenic liver abscess averaged about 15% despite treatment in the data cited; outcome is poorer with delayed source control or factors predicting failed percutaneous drainage. For hypervirulent K. pneumoniae infection, survivors may suffer catastrophic sequelae from metastatic spread, including vision loss (endophthalmitis) and major neurologic deficits. (p.1118, p.1289)

Lung Abscess — Chest X-ray and CT chest — CT better characterizes cavity size, wall thickness, and surrounding parenchymal involvement, and helps distinguish abscess from other cavitary lesions (e.g., malignancy, TB). Sputum culture (including anaerobic culture if obtainable) — May identify causative organisms, though anaerobic cultures are technically difficult to obtain without invasive sampling. Blood cultures — May identify the organism if bacteremic spread has occurred. Rhodococcus equi, Pneumocystis jirovecii in immunocompromised hosts (p.1034) Empyema / pleural space infection (must be distinguished from a peripheral abscess as it may need urgent drainage) (p.1035)
