therapy fails (p.1035) Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage or protected brush specimen (early if bronchial obstruction is suspected) (p.1035-1036) CT-guided percutaneous needle aspiration (p.1035) Induced sputum for tuberculosis in patients from TB-endemic areas or with TB risk factors such as HIV (p.1036) Bronchoscopy with biopsy in patients with malignancy risk or atypical presentation (p.1036) Cavitary lung cancer (p.1035) Pulmonary infarction (p.1035) Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other vasculitides (p.1035) Sarcoidosis (p.1035) Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (p.1035) Fluid-filled cysts or bullae (p.1035) Pulmonary sequestration (p.1035) Roughly 80% of lung abscesses are primary, arising from aspiration in the absence of an underlying pulmonary or systemic disease; the remaining ~20% are secondary to a predisposing process such as bronchial obstruction or immunocompromise (p.1034). A foul-smelling (putrid) breath, sputum, or empyema is considered essentially diagnostic of an anaerobic lung abscess; abscesses with no isolated pathogen (about 40%) are termed nonspecific and anaerobes are presumed (p.1035). Primary abscesses favor the dependent segments (posterior segments of upper lobes, superior segments of lower lobes), and the right lung is involved more often than the left because the right mainstem bronchus is less angulated (p.1035). Anaerobic abscesses often present indolently with night sweats, fatigue, and anemia, whereas non-anaerobic causes such as S. aureus can produce a fulminant course with high fevers and rapid progression (p.1035-1036). Edentulous patients are thought very unlikely to develop a lung abscess, since teeth (especially with gingivitis/periodontal disease) provide the nidus for the anaerobic/microaerophilic colonization that seeds the lung (p.1034). Lemierre's syndrome (oropharyngeal infection, classically Fusobacterium necrophorum, with septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein) is a recognized embolic source of lung abscess (p.1034-1035). Metronidazole alone is inadequate because it covers anaerobes but not the microaerophilic streptococci that are commonly part of the mixed flora of primary abscesses (p.1036). Life-threatening hemoptysis (p.1036) Massive aspiration of abscess contents into the airway (p.1036) Extension to the pleural space with empyema, which may require urgent drainage (p.1035-1036) Failure to defervesce or radiographic progression despite appropriate therapy (10-20% of patients do not respond) (p.1036) Abscess >6-8 cm in diameter, which is less likely to respond to antibiotics alone (p.1036) Sepsis at presentation (poor prognostic factor) (p.1036) Failure to exclude an obstructing malignancy: in older patients, those with malignancy risk factors, or those lacking clear aspiration risk, early bronchoscopy/biopsy and CT are indicated rather than assuming a primary anaerobic abscess (p.1035-1036). Treating a presumed primary abscess that does not improve without re-evaluating for a secondary cause (obstruction, unusual pathogen) (p.1036). Sputum culture may miss the diagnosis: infection is usually polymicrobial and routine cultures often fail to reflect anaerobes (p.1035). Using metronidazole as monotherapy, which misses microaerophilic streptococci (p.1036). Misclassifying a peripheral abscess as a pleural infection (empyema) or vice versa, since empyema may need urgent drainage (p.1035). Underestimating risk in immunocompromised hosts, who are fragile, infected by a wide pathogen range, and warrant early culture-directed diagnostics (p.1035). A lung abscess is necrosis and cavitation of lung parenchyma after microbial infection, typically a single dominant cavity >2 cm. In primary disease, anaerobes and microaerophilic streptococci colonizing the gingival crevices are aspirated into a susceptible host who carries an overwhelming aspirated burden or cannot clear it. An initial pneumonitis (worsened by gastric-acid tissue damage) progresses over about 7-14 days to parenchymal necrosis and cavitation, with anaerobes driving more extensive synergistic tissue destruction in polymicrobial infection. Secondary abscesses follow the predisposing mechanism: post-obstructive (tumor/foreign body) impairment of secretion clearance, or impaired host defense in immunocompromise allowing a broad pathogen range. Abscesses may also arise hematogenously from septic emboli (e.g., tricuspid endocarditis, Lemierre's syndrome). Mortality for primary lung abscess can be as low as ~2%, but secondary abscesses carry a much higher mortality, reported as high as 75% in some series. Adverse prognostic factors include age >60, malignancy-associated abscess, presence of aerobic bacteria, sepsis at presentation, symptom duration >8 weeks, and abscess size >6 cm. Defervescence on appropriate therapy can take up to 7 days, and 10-20% of patients fail to respond. Larger cavities at presentation predispose to persistent pneumatoceles or bronchiectasis. Prevention centers on airway protection, oral hygiene, minimizing sedation, head-of-bed elevation in aspiration-prone patients, and pathogen prophylaxis in selected immunocompromised hosts (p.1036). Lung abscesses are classified as primary (~80%, aspiration-related, anaerobe-predominant, no underlying lung/systemic disease) versus secondary (underlying obstruction, systemic illness, or immunocompromise); and by chronicity as acute (<4-6 weeks) versus chronic (~40% of cases). Size >6-8 cm marks lesions less responsive to antibiotics alone (p.1034, p.1036).

Malaria — Peripheral blood smear (thick and thin film) — Gold standard for diagnosis, species identification, and parasitemia quantification — directly determines treatment choice and monitoring. Rapid diagnostic test (malaria antigen) — Fast bedside screening tool, useful when smear is not immediately available, though species specificity is more limited than smear. CBC — Thrombocytopenia is a common supportive finding; hemoglobin helps assess severity (severe anemia is a marker of complicated malaria). Renal function tests, blood glucose, LFTs — Screens for organ dysfunction that would classify this as severe/complicated malaria requiring IV therapy and higher level of care. Lactate / blood gas (if unwell) — Acidosis is a severity marker in falciparum malaria with prognostic significance. Acute viral illness / minor febrile viral syndrome (early nonspecific malaria mimics this) (Harrison 22e p.1763) Bacterial meningitis (severe headache in malaria, but neck stiffness and photophobia are absent in malaria) (Harrison 22e p.1763) Sepsis / bacteremia with incidental parasitemia, especially in high-transmission areas (Harrison 22e pp.1765, 1767) Dengue fever (myalgia is prominent but usually more severe in dengue) (Harrison 22e p.1763) Leptospirosis (muscle tenderness, which malaria lacks; petechial hemorrhages a feature) (Harrison 22e p.1763) Typhus/rickettsial illness (tender muscles, unlike malaria) (Harrison 22e p.1763) Viral hemorrhagic fevers (petechial hemorrhages, which are very rare in malaria) (Harrison 22e p.1763) Nontyphoidal Salmonella and other bacteremia complicating or coinciding with malaria (Harrison 22e p.1765) Thick blood film (concentrates parasites ~40-100x over thin film, increasing sensitivity; examine 100-200 fields before calling negative) (Harrison 22e pp.1766-1767) Thin blood film for species identification and parasite quantification (parasitized cells per 1000 RBCs) (Harrison 22e pp.1766-1767) Giemsa (pH 7.2) or other Romanowsky stain; acridine orange for rapid detection of low-level parasitemia (Harrison 22e p.1766) Rapid diagnostic tests detecting PfHRP2, parasite LDH, or aldolase (note PfHRP2/3 gene-deletion false negatives and that RDTs do not quantify parasitemia) (Harrison 22e p.1767) PCR / ultrasensitive PCR for species confirmation and detection of low-density/asymptomatic infection (reference setting; too sensitive for primary diagnosis in endemic areas) (Harrison 22e pp.1767-1768) Plasma lactate and bicarbonate (best biochemical prognosticators in severe malaria) (Harrison 22e p.1764) Coagulation studies (PT, aPTT, fibrinogen) and platelet count in severe disease (Harrison 22e pp.1764-1765, 1768) Assessment of malaria pigment in neutrophils (>5% pigment-containing) and proportion of mature pigmented trophozoites/schizonts as severity/prognostic markers (Harrison 22e pp.1764, 1767) Diabetic ketoacidosis / ketoacidosis (acidotic 'respiratory distress' breathing overlaps with severe malaria acidosis; ketoacidosis can contribute in children) (Harrison 22e pp.1764-1766) Hematologic malignancy / lymphoproliferative disorder (hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly with massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia can be mistaken for it) (Harrison 22e p.1766) Malaria is not a clinical diagnosis: any patient in or from an endemic area with fever needs thick and thin blood smears (or a rapid test if reliable microscopy is unavailable) to confirm infection and identify the species (Harrison 22e p.1766). Early symptoms are nonspecific (malaise, headache, fatigue, abdominal discomfort, myalgia, then fever) and resemble a minor viral illness, so a high index of suspicion is essential (Harrison 22e p.1763). The classic regular febrile paroxysms (chills, rigors, fever spikes at fixed intervals) are now unusual and, when present at presentation, suggest P. vivax or P. ovale (often a relapse); prompt effective treatment prevents the synchronized fever pattern from developing (Harrison 22e p.1763). Mild thrombocytopenia is usual in malaria; a normal platelet count should call the diagnosis into question (Harrison 22e pp.1765, 1768). In falciparum malaria, peripheral parasitemia underestimates true parasite burden because mature parasites sequester in deep vascular beds and only younger ring forms circulate (Harrison 22e p.1762). A PfHRP2-based rapid test can stay positive for weeks after treatment, which helps diagnose severe malaria in a patient who has already taken antimalarials and cleared peripheral parasites but is a drawback in high-transmission settings (Harrison 22e p.1767). Persistent gametocytemia after a full treatment course does not indicate drug resistance or a need to re-treat, because mature P. falciparum gametocytes are unaffected by most antimalarials (Harrison 22e p.1767). Any obtundation, delirium, abnormal behavior, or generalized seizure in falciparum malaria must be taken seriously as a possible herald of cerebral malaria (Harrison 22e pp.1763-1764). Cerebral malaria is a diffuse symmetric encephalopathy without true meningism; focal neurologic signs are unusual and signs of meningeal irritation are absent (Harrison 22e p.1764). Specific retinal changes (patchy retinal opacification/whitening, vessel decolorization, pale-centered hemorrhages) on funduscopy support a diagnosis of cerebral malaria (Harrison 22e pp.1764-1765). In severe malaria the usual adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia (sweating, tachycardia, gooseflesh) are absent and its neurologic effects cannot be distinguished from the disease itself, so glucose must be checked actively (Harrison 22e p.1764). Quinine can provoke hypoglycemia by stimulating pancreatic insulin secretion, compounding the hypoglycemia of severe malaria (Harrison 22e p.1764). Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema may appear even after several days of effective antimalarial therapy and is readily precipitated by over-vigorous IV fluids; mortality exceeds 80% (Harrison 22e p.1764). Acidotic ('respiratory distress') breathing in a child with severe anemia is usually due to metabolic acidosis, not 'anemic heart failure' as previously mislabeled (Harrison 22e pp.1765-1766). Approximately 6% of children and <1% of adults with severe malaria have concomitant bacteremia (higher with >20% parasitemia in adults), and nontyphoidal Salmonella bacteremia is specifically associated with P. falciparum (Harrison 22e p.1765). In high-transmission areas low-density parasitemia is a common incidental finding, so severe malaria is easily overdiagnosed and must be distinguished from sepsis with coincidental parasitemia (Harrison 22e pp.1765, 1767). Sudden delayed hemolysis can follow artesunate treatment of hyperparasitemia in nonimmune patients, from synchronous loss of once-parasitized 'pitted' red cells (Harrison 22e p.1765). Impaired consciousness, delirium, abnormal behavior, or unarousable coma (cerebral malaria) (Harrison 22e pp.1763-1764) Generalized or repeated convulsions (>2 in 24 h), or subtle seizure activity such as tonic-clonic eye movements (Harrison 22e p.1764) Acidotic deep ('respiratory distress') breathing, hyperlactatemia >=5 mmol/L, or acidemia (arterial pH <7.25) (Harrison 22e p.1764) Hypoglycemia (plasma glucose <2.2 mmol/L, <40 mg/dL) (Harrison 22e p.1764) Hypotension/shock with impaired perfusion (Harrison 22e p.1764) Severe anemia (hematocrit <15% or Hb <50 g/L with high parasitemia; Hb <=3 g/dL on presentation carries increased mortality) (Harrison 22e pp.1764-1765) Macroscopic hemoglobinuria / blackwater fever (black, brown, or red urine) (Harrison 22e pp.1764-1765) Acute kidney injury (creatinine >265 umol/L, >3 mg/dL) or anuria (Harrison 22e pp.1764-1765) Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS or O2 saturation <92% with tachypnea (Harrison 22e p.1764) Spontaneous bleeding / DIC (Harrison 22e p.1764) Hyperparasitemia (>5% in nonimmune, >10% in any patient) or >100,000/uL (Harrison 22e pp.1763-1764) Prostration / inability to sit or stand unaided (Harrison 22e p.1764) Low core temperature <36.5C, marked agitation, jaundice (bilirubin >50 umol/L) with vital-organ dysfunction (Harrison 22e p.1764) Treating malaria as a clinical diagnosis; confirmation by smear or rapid test is required (Harrison 22e p.1766). Accepting a normal platelet count without question, as mild thrombocytopenia is the rule in malaria (Harrison 22e pp.1765, 1768). Relying on peripheral parasitemia to gauge true burden in falciparum malaria, since mature parasites are sequestered (Harrison 22e p.1762). Overdiagnosing severe malaria in high-transmission areas where low-density parasitemia is a common incidental finding, missing concurrent sepsis (Harrison 22e pp.1765, 1767). Over-vigorous IV fluid administration, which can precipitate noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (Harrison 22e p.1764). Missing hypoglycemia because its usual autonomic signs are absent in severe disease and its neurologic effects mimic malaria itself (Harrison 22e p.1764). Re-treating on the basis of persistent gametocytemia, which does not signify drug resistance after a full course (Harrison 22e p.1767). False-negative RDTs from PfHRP2/3 gene-deleted parasites (notably in the Horn of Africa); RDTs also cannot quantify parasitemia (Harrison 22e p.1767). Using serology to diagnose acute illness; serology has no role in acute diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1768). Mistaking acidotic breathing in a severely anemic child for 'anemic congestive cardiac failure' (Harrison 22e pp.1765-1766). Infection begins when a female Anopheles inoculates sporozoites, which reach the liver and undergo preerythrocytic schizogony, each sporozoite yielding 10,000 to >30,000 merozoites. Released merozoites invade red cells, becoming trophozoites that multiply roughly 6- to 20-fold each asexual cycle (every 48 h for P. falciparum/P. vivax/P. ovale, 72 h for P. malariae, 24 h for P. knowlesi); symptoms begin around densities of ~50 parasites/uL. In P. vivax and P. ovale a fraction of liver forms persist as dormant hypnozoites for weeks to a year or more, causing the relapses characteristic of these species (P. falciparum, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi do not relapse). Disease results from red-cell invasion and destruction plus the host inflammatory response: schizont rupture releases material that activates monocytes/macrophages and proinflammatory cytokines, producing fever. The central pathology of severe falciparum malaria is cytoadherence: ~12-15 h after invasion 'knobs' on the infected red cell extrude the variant adhesin PfEMP1, which binds endothelial receptors (ICAM-1 and endothelial protein C receptor in brain, VAR2CSA/chondroitin sulfate A in placenta, CD36 elsewhere). Cytoadherence, rosetting (adherence to uninfected red cells), and agglutination sequester mature parasites in vital organs, especially the brain, obstructing microcirculatory flow and metabolism while escaping splenic clearance. Uninfected red cells also become less deformable in severe disease. P. falciparum invades cells of all ages and can reach very high densities (P. knowlesi can also, owing to its 24-h cycle), whereas other species spare most red cells and rarely exceed ~2% parasitemia. The spleen augments clearance and 'pits' damaged ring forms; severe lactic acidosis arises from anaerobic glycolysis in sequestered beds, parasite lactate production, gut-derived acids, and failed hepatic/renal clearance, and hypoglycemia from impaired gluconeogenesis with increased glucose consumption. (Harrison 22e pp.1760-1765) Promptly and appropriately treated uncomplicated falciparum malaria has a mortality of <0.1%, but risk rises steeply once vital-organ dysfunction occurs or parasitemia exceeds 2%. Cerebral malaria carries roughly 20% mortality in adults and 15% in children even with treatment; about 10% of surviving children (especially with hypoglycemia, severe anemia, repeated seizures, or deep coma) have residual neurologic deficits, most of which improve or resolve within 6 months, though persistent language and cognitive deficits, increased epilepsy risk, and reduced life expectancy occur in some. Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema in adults has >80% mortality. Plasma bicarbonate and lactate are the best biochemical prognosticators. Among complications, poor prognosis is indicated by >20% mature pigment-containing parasites or >5% of neutrophils containing pigment, and by hyperparasitemia. In severe acute renal failure that survives, urine flow returns in a median of 4 days and creatinine normalizes in a mean of 17 days; early dialysis improves survival. (Harrison 22e pp.1763-1765, 1767) Severe falciparum malaria (WHO-based criteria, Harrison 22e Table 231-2, p.1764) is defined by one or more of: unarousable coma/cerebral malaria (no localizing response, coma >30 min after a generalized convulsion, Glasgow Coma Score <11 or Blantyre <3 in young children); acidemia/acidosis (arterial pH <7.25, base deficit >8 meq/L, or plasma bicarbonate <15 mmol/L; venous lactate >=5 mmol/L; deep labored 'respiratory distress' breathing); severe normochromic normocytic anemia (hematocrit <15% or Hb <50 g/L with parasite density >10,000/uL); renal failure (creatinine >265 umol/L / >3 mg/dL); noncardiogenic pulmonary edema/ARDS (or O2 sat <92% on room air with respiratory rate >30/min); hypoglycemia (glucose <2.2 mmol/L / <40 mg/dL); hypotension/shock (systolic BP <70 mmHg in children 1-5 y or <80 mmHg in adults with impaired perfusion); significant bleeding/DIC; convulsions (>2 generalized seizures in 24 h); hemoglobinuria (macroscopic black/brown/red urine, not due to oxidant drugs or G6PD deficiency); extreme weakness/prostration; hyperparasitemia (>5% in nonimmune, >10% in any patient); and jaundice (bilirubin >50 umol/L / >3 mg/dL) with parasitemia >100,000/uL or other vital-organ dysfunction. Note: criteria thresholds for renal failure are for adults; lower values define severe disease in children. (Harrison 22e p.1764)

Mixed connective tissue disease — mixed connective tissue, sharp syndrome, MCTD, mixed connective tissue disease, overlap connective tissue disease, anti-U1-RNP disease, undifferentiated connective tissue disease overlap Systemic lupus erythematosus Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) Polymyositis/dermatomyositis Rheumatoid arthritis Undifferentiated connective tissue disease Sjögren syndrome ANA with reflex extractable nuclear antigen panel — screens for anti-U1-RNP, the defining autoantibody Anti-U1-RNP antibody titer — confirms diagnosis when present in high titer, typically without anti-Sm or anti-dsDNA Creatine kinase and aldolase — assess for accompanying myositis Pulmonary function tests with diffusion capacity (DLCO) — detect early interstitial lung disease or pulmonary vascular involvement Transthoracic echocardiogram — screen for pulmonary arterial hypertension, a major prognostic driver High-resolution chest CT — evaluate for interstitial lung disease Esophageal manometry or barium swallow — assess for dysmotility seen in sclerodermoid overlap Urinalysis and renal function panel — screen for renal involvement, which is less common but clinically important Systemic lupus erythematosus Limited or diffuse systemic sclerosis Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy Antisynthetase syndrome Primary Raynaud phenomenon with isolated ANA positivity Consider MCTD in a patient with overlapping features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis who does not neatly fit any single diagnosis. Puffy, swollen ('sausage') fingers and severe Raynaud phenomenon are classic early findings, often preceding other manifestations by years. High-titer anti-U1-ribonucleoprotein (anti-U1-RNP) antibody is the serologic hallmark and is required for diagnosis. Pulmonary arterial hypertension is the leading cause of death and can develop insidiously, so periodic screening is warranted even when patients feel well. Esophageal dysmotility and other sclerodermoid features are common, similar to limited systemic sclerosis. Renal disease and severe CNS involvement are less frequent than in classic SLE, but can occur and should not be dismissed. Clinical phenotype can evolve over time, and some patients eventually reclassify into a more defined connective tissue disease such as scleroderma or SLE. Myositis in MCTD tends to respond well to glucocorticoids compared with some other overlap myopathies. New dyspnea on exertion or signs of right heart strain suggesting evolving pulmonary arterial hypertension Rapidly progressive proteinuria, hematuria, or rising creatinine suggesting renal involvement Severe digital ischemia or ulceration from vasculopathy New neurologic deficits or severe headache raising concern for CNS or cerebrovascular involvement Acute severe muscle weakness or dysphagia suggesting active myositis with aspiration risk Attributing puffy hands and Raynaud phenomenon solely to early scleroderma without checking anti-U1-RNP and considering MCTD. Failing to screen asymptomatic patients periodically for pulmonary arterial hypertension, the dominant cause of mortality. Assuming a single high anti-U1-RNP titer alone confirms diagnosis without correlating with the required overlapping clinical features. Overlooking that clinical features can evolve over years, sometimes prompting reclassification into a more defined connective tissue disease. MCTD is an overlap autoimmune connective tissue disorder characterized by immune-mediated vasculopathy and fibrosis affecting skin, synovium, muscle, esophagus, lungs, and vasculature. It is strongly associated with high titers of antibody against the U1-RNP component of the spliceosome, which is thought to contribute to immune complex formation and endothelial injury. The vascular pathology, particularly intimal proliferation in pulmonary and other vessels, resembles that seen in systemic sclerosis and underlies the propensity for pulmonary arterial hypertension. Overall prognosis is generally better than diffuse systemic sclerosis but variable, with outcomes largely determined by the degree of pulmonary vascular and interstitial lung involvement. Pulmonary arterial hypertension is the most significant predictor of mortality, making regular cardiopulmonary surveillance essential.

travelers Enteric fever or other systemic febrile illness in returning travelers Actinomycosis or nocardiosis Pulmonary tuberculosis Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia with septic emboli Nocardiosis or CT brain in patients with neurologic signs — to detect rare but described CNS melioidosis (brainstem encephalitis) Metastatic malignancy with multiple organ lesions Vasculitis with pulmonary cavitation Lymphoma with splenic/hepatic lesions Caused by the gram-negative soil and water saprophyte Burkholderia pseudomallei, endemic to Southeast Asia and northern Australia, with expanding recognition in South Asia, including India Acquisition is via percutaneous inoculation, inhalation, or ingestion of contaminated soil/water, especially during monsoon/rainy season and after flooding Diabetes mellitus is the dominant risk factor; other predispositions include chronic kidney disease, alcohol excess, chronic lung disease, thalassemia, and immunosuppression Clinical spectrum ranges from localized cutaneous/subcutaneous infection to pneumonia (most common presentation) to overwhelming septicemia with multiple abscesses Classically described as 'the great mimicker' because it can resemble tuberculosis radiographically (cavitary upper-lobe disease) and can produce abscesses in almost any organ, including spleen, liver, and prostate Can present as an acute fulminant illness or as a chronic, indolent infection persisting for months to years, and may reactivate after decades of latency ('Vietnamese time bomb') Requires laboratory alert to the microbiology lab, since B. pseudomallei can be mistaken for a contaminant or misidentified as another Burkholderia/Pseudomonas species on automated systems Treatment is biphasic: an initial intensive intravenous phase followed by a prolonged oral eradication phase, reflecting the organism's propensity to relapse if therapy is inadequate Septic shock or multiorgan dysfunction at presentation, which carries high mortality if treatment is delayed Diabetic patient with fever and pneumonia or unexplained abscesses returning from or residing in an endemic region Evidence of multifocal abscesses (splenic, hepatic, prostatic) suggesting disseminated disease Neurologic signs suggesting brainstem encephalitis, a recognized severe complication Delayed or incorrect microbial identification (mistaken for a contaminant) in a patient with sepsis and tropical exposure history Relapse or recrudescence of symptoms after apparent treatment response, suggesting inadequate eradication-phase therapy Dismissing B. pseudomallei growth in culture as an environmental contaminant, leading to missed or delayed diagnosis Attributing cavitary lung disease to tuberculosis without considering melioidosis in endemic-exposure patients, delaying appropriate therapy Underestimating the need for prolonged eradication-phase oral therapy, which risks relapse if truncated Failing to actively search for occult abscesses (spleen, liver, prostate) once bacteremia or sepsis is confirmed Burkholderia pseudomallei is a motile, aerobic, gram-negative bacillus that survives in soil and surface water in endemic tropical regions and enters the host through skin breaks, inhalation of aerosols, or ingestion. It is a facultative intracellular organism capable of escaping the phagosome, moving between cells via actin-based motility, and inducing multinucleated giant cell formation, which contributes to its capacity for chronic latency and later reactivation. Hematogenous dissemination from a primary site produces multifocal abscesses, and impaired cell-mediated and neutrophil function, as occurs in diabetes, markedly increases susceptibility to severe and disseminated disease. Untreated septicemic melioidosis has historically carried very high mortality, and even with modern intensive-phase antimicrobial therapy, severe disseminated or septic shock presentations remain associated with substantial mortality, particularly in patients with diabetes or other comorbidities. With appropriate biphasic treatment and adequate follow-up, localized and non-septicemic disease generally carries a favorable outcome, though relapse can occur if eradication therapy is incomplete.

Membranous nephropathy — membranous nephropathy, MN, membranous glomerulonephritis, membranous glomerulopathy, epimembranous nephropathy, PLA2R-associated nephropathy, idiopathic membranous nephropathy Minimal change disease Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis Diabetic nephropathy Amyloidosis (AL or AA) Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Lupus nephritis (class V) Hepatitis B virus-associated membranous nephropathy Hepatitis C virus-associated glomerulonephritis Syphilis-associated membranous nephropathy Chronic malaria or schistosomiasis-associated glomerulopathy 24-hour urine protein or spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio — quantify and monitor nephrotic-range proteinuria Serum anti-PLA2R antibody titer — confirms primary autoimmune membranous nephropathy and aids in monitoring immunologic activity Renal biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy — establishes diagnosis and stages disease Age-appropriate malignancy screening — excludes paraneoplastic secondary membranous nephropathy Hepatitis B and C serologies, syphilis serology, ANA/anti-dsDNA, and complement levels — screen for secondary infectious or autoimmune causes Serum albumin and lipid panel — assess severity of nephrotic syndrome and cardiovascular risk Renal function tests (creatinine, eGFR) trended over time — monitor for progression Doppler imaging or cross-sectional imaging of renal veins if clinical suspicion — evaluate for renal vein thrombosis in severe nephrotic syndrome Solid organ malignancy-associated (paraneoplastic) membranous nephropathy Drug-induced membranous nephropathy (e.g., certain NSAIDs or other implicated agents) Systemic lupus erythematosus (class V lupus nephritis) Sarcoidosis-associated glomerulopathy Autoimmune thyroiditis-associated nephropathy Most common cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in non-diabetic White adults, typically presenting with heavy proteinuria and edema but preserved renal function early on. About 70-80% of primary (idiopathic) cases are associated with circulating anti-PLA2R antibodies; a minority have anti-THSD7A antibodies instead. Always screen for an underlying secondary cause (malignancy, autoimmune disease, infection, or drug exposure) before labeling disease as primary/idiopathic, especially in patients over 50-60 years. Follows a 'rule of thirds' natural history in untreated primary disease: roughly one-third spontaneously remit, one-third have persistent proteinuria with stable function, and one-third progress to kidney failure over years. Renal vein thrombosis and other thromboembolic events are disproportionately common because of the profound hypercoagulable state associated with heavy proteinuria and urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins. Microscopic hematuria may be present, but heavy nephritic-range findings (red cell casts, marked hematuria) suggest an alternative or superimposed diagnosis. Immunofluorescence classically shows granular capillary loop deposits of IgG (often IgG4-dominant in primary disease) and C3, with electron microscopy showing subepithelial deposits and spike formation on the basement membrane. Response to therapy is slow (months), so treatment decisions and reassessment of remission should be based on sustained trends in proteinuria rather than short-term fluctuations. Sudden worsening of renal function, flank pain, or asymmetric limb swelling suggesting renal vein thrombosis or other thromboembolic event Rapidly progressive decline in eGFR or emergence of an active urinary sediment suggesting a superimposed crescentic or proliferative process Severe nephrotic syndrome with albumin markedly low, raising risk of thrombosis, infection, and volume complications requiring closer monitoring New signs pointing to occult malignancy or systemic autoimmune disease that would change management from primary to secondary disease pathway Anasarca with respiratory compromise or signs of pulmonary embolism Assuming all membranous nephropathy is primary/idiopathic without adequately excluding secondary causes, particularly malignancy in older patients Making treatment decisions based on a single proteinuria measurement rather than sustained trends, given the naturally fluctuating course and slow treatment response Overlooking the markedly elevated thromboembolic risk and failing to consider prophylactic anticoagulation in severe nephrotic syndrome Misinterpreting a negative anti-PLA2R antibody test as excluding membranous nephropathy, since a meaningful subset of primary cases are antibody-negative or have other target antigens Membranous nephropathy results from in-situ formation of immune complexes along the subepithelial aspect of the glomerular basement membrane, most often triggered by autoantibodies against a native podocyte antigen (chiefly PLA2R, less commonly THSD7A or other targets) or against a planted exogenous/tumor antigen in secondary forms. Complement activation at the site of deposits leads to podocyte injury, cytoskeletal disruption, and a marked increase in glomerular capillary wall permeability to protein without significant inflammatory cell infiltration. Ongoing antigen-antibody deposition drives basement membrane thickening and the characteristic 'spike and dome' appearance seen on silver-stained biopsy over time. This process explains the disease's predominantly nephrotic (rather than nephritic) presentation. Renal outcomes are highly variable, with roughly equal proportions of patients undergoing spontaneous remission, persistent stable proteinuria, or progression to kidney failure over years if untreated; lower proteinuria, preserved renal function at diagnosis, and declining PLA2R antibody titers portend a better outcome, while persistent heavy proteinuria and reduced eGFR predict progression.

Acute Bacterial Meningitis — Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis (cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture) — Confirms the diagnosis, identifies the organism, and guides definitive duration and choice of therapy — but should follow, not precede, empiric antibiotics if there is any delay. Blood cultures (before antibiotics if no delay incurred) — Frequently positive in bacterial meningitis and may identify the organism if LP is delayed or contraindicated. CT head (before LP only if specific indications: papilledema, focal neurological deficit, severely altered consciousness, seizures) — Screens for mass effect/herniation risk before LP in specific high-risk presentations — not required routinely and should not delay antibiotics. Immediate empiric antibiotics required Herpes simplex virus encephalitis (headache, fever, altered consciousness, focal deficits, seizures; distinguished by CSF profile, MRI temporal-lobe changes and HSV CSF PCR) (p.1121) Subacute meningitis presenting acutely: M. tuberculosis, Cryptococcus neoformans, Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Treponema pallidum (p.1122) Mycoplasma pneumoniae CNS infection, which can mimic viral meningitis/encephalitis (p.1124) Viral (aseptic) meningoencephalitis, especially enteroviral and HSV (p.1121) Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Rickettsia rickettsii) with early maculopapular rash that can resemble meningococcemia (p.1121) Ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis (tick-borne) with fever, headache, confusion and sometimes rash (p.1121) Focal suppurative CNS infections: subdural empyema, epidural empyema, brain abscess (consider when focal neurologic findings present) (p.1121) Fungal, tuberculous, Listeria, Brucella, Coxiella, Leptospira meningitis (lymphocytic pleocytosis, hypoglycorrhachia may be absent early) (p.1124) CSF opening pressure measurement: raised (>180 mmH2O) in over 90% of cases, >400 mmH2O in about 20% (p.1120) CSF cell count and differential: PMN pleocytosis, >100 cells/uL in ~90% (p.1120) CSF glucose and CSF/serum glucose ratio: low glucose (<40 mg/dL) and ratio <0.4 are highly suggestive (ratio also low in fungal/TB/carcinomatous meningitis) (p.1120) CSF protein: elevated (>45 mg/dL) in ~90% (p.1120) CSF Gram stain (organisms in >60%) and CSF culture (positive in >70-80%; required for susceptibility testing) (p.1120-1121) CSF multiplex PCR (e.g., FilmArray ME panel) for rapid detection of S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, E. coli, L. monocytogenes, H. influenzae, group B strep; does not include S. aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci or many gram-negatives and cannot replace culture (p.1120-1121) MRI (preferred over CT) for cerebral edema/ischemia; gadolinium meningeal enhancement is non-specific and not diagnostic of meningitis (p.1121) Skin lesion biopsy with Gram stain when petechiae/purpura are present (p.1121) Serum procalcitonin and CSF protein as adjuncts to distinguish bacterial from aseptic meningitis (children) (p.1124) Subarachnoid hemorrhage (the major non-infectious consideration) (p.1121) Medication-induced hypersensitivity (drug-induced) meningitis (p.1121) Chemical meningitis from rupture of tumor contents into CSF (cystic glioma, craniopharyngioma, epidermoid/dermoid cyst) (p.1121) Carcinomatous or lymphomatous (neoplastic) meningitis (p.1121) Inflammatory disorders: sarcoidosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behcet's syndrome (p.1121) Pituitary apoplexy (p.1122) Uveomeningitic syndromes (Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada) (p.1122) The classic triad of fever, headache and nuchal rigidity is useful but each component occurs in over 80% of adult cases while the full triad is frequently incomplete, so its absence does not exclude bacterial meningitis (p.1119). A reduced level of consciousness, ranging from lethargy to coma, is present in more than three-quarters of patients; nausea, vomiting and photophobia are also common (p.1119). Nuchal rigidity is the characteristic sign of meningeal irritation (neck resists passive flexion), but Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs have uncertain sensitivity/specificity and may be absent in the very young, the elderly, the immunocompromised or those with depressed mental status (p.1119-1120). Coexisting cervical spine disease in older patients can produce false-positive neck stiffness (p.1120). Whenever bacterial meningitis is suspected, draw blood cultures immediately and start empirical antibiotics plus adjunctive dexamethasone without delay; if neuroimaging is needed before LP, give antibiotics after blood cultures rather than waiting (p.1120). Antibiotics given a few hours before LP do not meaningfully change CSF WBC count or glucose and are unlikely to prevent Gram-stain visualization or PCR detection of bacterial nucleic acid, so a delayed LP after starting therapy still has diagnostic value (p.1120). Dexamethasone should ideally be given about 20 minutes before, or at the latest with, the first antibiotic dose, because steroids blunt macrophage/microglial TNF-alpha production only if given before those cells are activated by endotoxin; benefit is unlikely if started more than 6 hours after antibiotics (p.1120, p.1123). Petechial or purpuric skin lesions are an important clue to meningococcal infection and, if present, should be biopsied (Gram stain of the lesion may reveal the organism) (p.1119, p.1121). Profound depression of consciousness (stupor/coma), seizures or focal neurologic signs point away from uncomplicated viral meningitis and suggest encephalitis or bacterial/parameningeal disease (p.1123). Petechial or purpuric rash, which may herald fulminant meningococcal disease that can progress to death within hours of symptom onset (p.1119) Signs of raised ICP: deteriorating consciousness, papilledema, dilated poorly reactive pupils, sixth-nerve palsy, decerebrate posturing, Cushing reflex (bradycardia, hypertension, irregular respirations) (p.1120) Seizures at presentation or within the first 24 hours (associated with worse outcome) (p.1120, p.1123) Coma or markedly decreased level of consciousness on admission (p.1123) Indications to obtain CT/MRI before LP: recent head trauma, depressed/abnormal consciousness, papilledema, or focal neurologic deficit (do not delay antibiotics for imaging) (p.1120) Relying on the complete classic triad or on Kernig's/Brudzinski's signs to rule out meningitis; these are insensitive, particularly in elderly, very young or immunocompromised patients (p.1119-1120). Delaying antibiotics and dexamethasone to obtain neuroimaging or LP first; treatment should not wait when bacterial meningitis is suspected (p.1120). Assuming a recent dose of antibiotics renders the LP useless; CSF chemistry, Gram stain and PCR usually remain informative for several hours (p.1120). Interpreting gadolinium meningeal enhancement on MRI as diagnostic of meningitis; it occurs with any condition that increases blood-brain barrier permeability (p.1121). Treating with dexamethasone in settings where it has not shown benefit: trials in low-income countries (late presentation, prior antibiotics, malnutrition, HIV, unproven diagnosis) failed to show efficacy, and patients with a negative CSF Gram stain and culture in those settings should not receive it (p.1123). Forgetting that neurologic injury and complications can progress even after CSF sterilization because much of the damage is immune-mediated (p.1118). Overlooking that a giving of IV glucose (e.g., D50) shortly before LP rarely alters CSF glucose unless several hours have elapsed, so a low CSF glucose remains meaningful (p.1120). Bacterial meningitis is an acute purulent infection of the subarachnoid space accompanied by a CNS inflammatory reaction that can cause decreased consciousness, seizures, raised intracranial pressure and stroke; meninges, subarachnoid space and brain parenchyma are often jointly involved (meningoencephalitis). The leading organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis) first colonize the nasopharynx, cross or breach the epithelium into the bloodstream, evade neutrophil phagocytosis and complement killing via their polysaccharide capsule, and reach the CSF through the choroid plexus or cerebral capillary endothelium. They multiply readily in CSF because normal CSF has few leukocytes and little complement/immunoglobulin, so opsonization and phagocytosis are poor. Much of the neurologic injury comes from the host inflammatory response rather than direct bacterial damage, so injury can progress even after antibiotics sterilize the CSF. Lysis of bacteria releases cell-wall components (gram-negative LPS; pneumococcal teichoic acid and peptidoglycan) that drive production of TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, chemokines and other mediators by microglia, astrocytes, monocytes, endothelium and CSF leukocytes. These cytokines increase blood-brain barrier permeability (vasogenic edema and protein leakage), the proteinaceous/leukocytic exudate obstructs CSF flow and resorption (obstructive and communicating hydrocephalus, interstitial edema), and neutrophil degranulation plus reactive oxygen/nitrogen species and excitatory amino acids produce cytotoxic edema and cell death (notably in the hippocampal dentate gyrus). Cerebral blood flow rises early then falls with loss of autoregulation; vasculitis and thrombosis of arteries, cortical veins and dural sinuses cause ischemia/infarction. The combined interstitial, vasogenic and cytotoxic edema raises ICP and can lead to coma and herniation (p.1118-1120). Case-fatality varies by organism: roughly 3-7% for H. influenzae, N. meningitidis or group B streptococcal meningitis, about 15% for Listeria, and around 20% for pneumococcal meningitis. Risk of death rises with decreased consciousness on admission, seizures within 24 h, signs of raised ICP, age (infancy or >50 years), comorbidities such as shock or need for mechanical ventilation, and delay in starting treatment. A markedly low CSF glucose (<40 mg/dL) and very high CSF protein (>300 mg/dL) predict worse outcomes in some series. About 25% of survivors have moderate-to-severe sequelae, commonly decreased intellectual function, memory impairment, seizures, sensorineural hearing loss with dizziness, and gait disturbance (p.1123). Harrison 22e does not provide a formal graded severity score for acute bacterial meningitis; it frames the disease as a medical emergency (goal: antibiotics within 60 min of arrival) and lists adverse prognostic markers (decreased consciousness on admission, seizures within 24 h, signs of raised ICP, age extremes, comorbidities such as shock/ventilation, treatment delay, very low CSF glucose, very high CSF protein). For distinguishing bacterial from aseptic meningitis in children, the prospectively validated Bacterial Meningitis Score is cited: very low probability (NPV ~99.7%) when all of negative CSF Gram stain, CSF neutrophils <1000/uL, CSF protein <80 mg/dL, peripheral ANC <10,000/uL, and no seizures are met (p.1123-1124).

bacterial overgrowth Chronic Clostridioides difficile infection Giardiasis Chronic bacterial or parasitic enterocolitis Colonoscopy with random biopsies from multiple colonic segments — required for histologic diagnosis since mucosa often appears normal Histopathology — distinguishes collagenous (thickened collagen band) from lymphocytic (intraepithelial lymphocytosis) subtype Celiac serology (tissue transglutaminase IgA) — screens for coexisting celiac disease Thyroid function tests — screens for associated autoimmune thyroid disease Stool studies (culture, C. difficile testing, ova and parasites) — excludes infectious causes of chronic diarrhea Medication review — identifies causative drugs such as NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, and statins Fecal calprotectin — typically normal or only mildly elevated, helps differentiate from classic IBD SeHCAT or serum C4/FGF-19 testing where available — evaluates for concurrent bile acid diarrhea Diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome Bile acid malabsorption Celiac disease Endocrine causes of diarrhea (e.g., hyperthyroidism, neuroendocrine tumors) Classic presentation is chronic, non-bloody, watery diarrhea in an older adult (often 60s-70s) with a grossly and endoscopically normal-appearing colon Female predominance is marked, especially for the collagenous subtype Strongly associated with NSAID use, proton pump inhibitors, SSRIs, and statins — a careful drug history is essential Frequently coexists with autoimmune conditions such as celiac disease, autoimmune thyroiditis, and other connective tissue or rheumatologic disorders Diagnosis requires random biopsies from multiple colonic segments even when mucosa looks endoscopically normal, since gross findings are typically absent Two histologic subtypes — collagenous (thickened subepithelial collagen band) and lymphocytic (increased intraepithelial lymphocytes) — share similar clinical behavior and management Nocturnal diarrhea and fecal urgency/incontinence are common and can significantly impair quality of life despite the benign histology Weight loss and abdominal pain can occur but are typically milder than in classic inflammatory bowel disease Rectal bleeding, anemia, or weight loss suggesting an alternative or coexisting diagnosis rather than uncomplicated microscopic colitis Severe dehydration or electrolyte disturbance from high-volume diarrhea Failure to respond to standard therapy — warrants reassessment for IBD, celiac disease, or bile acid diarrhea New abdominal pain, fever, or peritoneal signs, which are atypical and require evaluation for another process Persistent symptoms despite discontinuation of an implicated drug Assuming a normal-appearing colonoscopy excludes colitis — biopsies are mandatory since gross findings are usually absent Failing to obtain biopsies from multiple segments, as histologic changes can be patchy or segment-specific Overlooking a causative medication and treating chronically without attempting drug discontinuation Missing coexisting celiac disease or bile acid diarrhea, which can perpetuate symptoms despite colitis-directed therapy Microscopic colitis is thought to result from a dysregulated mucosal immune response to luminal antigens (including bile acids, bacterial products, and certain drugs) in a genetically or immunologically susceptible host, producing intraepithelial lymphocytic infiltration with or without subepithelial collagen deposition. This impairs colonic epithelial barrier function and fluid/electrolyte absorption, producing a secretory-type watery diarrhea without gross mucosal ulceration. The strong drug and autoimmune associations support an immune-mediated rather than structural mechanism. Microscopic colitis is a benign, non-progressive condition that does not increase colorectal cancer risk and often responds well to drug withdrawal or medical therapy, though relapses are common after treatment discontinuation and a subset of patients follow a chronic intermittent course.

Minimal change disease — minimal change, MCD, minimal change nephropathy, nil disease, lipoid nephrosis, MCNS Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) Membranous nephropathy Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Diabetic nephropathy IgA nephropathy with heavy proteinuria Amyloidosis or other infiltrative nephropathies Post-infectious glomerulonephritis Hepatitis B/C-associated glomerulonephritis HIV-associated nephropathy Urinalysis with microscopy — assess for selective proteinuria and absence of significant hematuria or cellular casts 24-hour urine protein or spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio — quantify nephrotic-range proteinuria Serum albumin and lipid panel — confirm hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia typical of nephrotic syndrome Renal function panel (creatinine, eGFR) — establish baseline and monitor for atypical renal impairment Renal biopsy with electron microscopy — required in adults or steroid-resistant cases to confirm diagnosis and exclude FSGS/other glomerulopathies Serum complement levels — typically normal in minimal change disease, helps exclude complement-mediated glomerulonephritides Age-appropriate malignancy screening in adults — evaluate for underlying lymphoproliferative disease, especially if steroid-resistant Coagulation studies/consideration of thromboembolic risk — nephrotic syndrome predisposes to venous thromboembolism NSAID-induced acute interstitial nephritis with nephrotic-range proteinuria Paraneoplastic nephrotic syndrome (Hodgkin lymphoma, other lymphoproliferative disorders) Diabetic nephropathy Amyloidosis Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (peak age 2-6 years) but also occurs in adults, sometimes elderly patients. Presents with abrupt-onset heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and edema; renal function and blood pressure are typically preserved at onset. Light microscopy is essentially normal ('minimal change'); diagnosis relies on electron microscopy showing diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement. Excellent response to corticosteroids is characteristic and considered almost diagnostic in children; failure to respond should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis. Frequent relapses and steroid dependence are common, often requiring steroid-sparing agents over time. Can be triggered or associated with recent upper respiratory infection, atopy/allergy, immunizations, NSAID use, or (in adults) underlying lymphoproliferative disease (especially Hodgkin lymphoma). Selective proteinuria (predominantly albumin, low IgG) on urine protein electrophoresis supports the diagnosis. Thromboembolic risk and increased infection susceptibility parallel the severity of nephrotic syndrome regardless of underlying cause. Steroid resistance or failure to achieve remission — reconsider diagnosis (likely FSGS) and pursue biopsy Significant hematuria, hypertension, or renal impairment at presentation — atypical for minimal change disease, suggests alternative diagnosis Signs of thromboembolism (limb swelling, chest pain, dyspnea) given hypercoagulable state of nephrotic syndrome Severe hypovolemia or acute kidney injury from aggressive diuresis in the setting of low oncotic pressure Signs of serious infection (peritonitis, cellulitis, sepsis) due to functional hypogammaglobulinemia and immunosuppressive therapy New systemic symptoms (weight loss, lymphadenopathy, night sweats) in adults raising concern for occult malignancy Assuming a normal light microscopy biopsy excludes glomerular disease without electron microscopy to assess podocyte foot processes Delaying biopsy in adults presenting with nephrotic syndrome, where minimal change disease is less common and other etiologies must be excluded Misclassifying steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome as minimal change disease when it more likely represents FSGS or another glomerulopathy Overlooking secondary causes (drugs, malignancy) in adult-onset minimal change disease Minimal change disease is thought to result from a circulating permeability factor or T-cell/immune dysregulation that injures podocytes, causing effacement of their foot processes and loss of the glomerular filtration barrier's charge/size selectivity without structural glomerular damage visible by light microscopy. This leads to massive selective loss of albumin into the urine, producing hypoalbuminemia, decreased plasma oncotic pressure, and edema, along with compensatory hepatic lipoprotein synthesis causing hyperlipidemia. The glomerular basement membrane and capillary architecture otherwise remain intact, distinguishing it from other primary glomerulopathies. Minimal change disease has an excellent overall prognosis, with the large majority of children and most adults achieving remission with corticosteroid therapy and rarely progressing to chronic kidney disease. However, relapses are common and some patients become steroid-dependent or frequently relapsing, necessitating steroid-sparing immunosuppressive strategies.

Mixed Malaria (P. falciparum + P. vivax) — Peripheral blood smear (thick and thin film) confirming both species — Definitive method to confirm mixed infection and quantify parasitemia of each species, directly determining treatment approach and monitoring intensity. Rapid diagnostic test (combination P.f/P.v if available) — Can support or suggest mixed infection rapidly, though smear remains the definitive confirmatory test. G6PD testing — Mandatory before primaquine administration to avoid precipitating hemolysis in deficient patients. CBC, renal function, blood glucose, LFTs — Screens for organ dysfunction that would classify this as severe/complicated malaria requiring IV therapy and escalated care. Urgent antimalarial therapy required (NOT an antibiotic) Single-species P. falciparum malaria with an undetected coexisting vivax/ovale component (the central diagnostic trap of mixed infection) P. knowlesi infection, which on RDT/microscopy may be misidentified as P. falciparum and can reach dangerously high densities (24-h cycle) Recrudescent falciparum vs. true vivax/ovale relapse vs. reinfection as the cause of recurrent fever after treatment Dengue (myalgia typically more severe than in malaria) Leptospirosis (tender muscles, unlike malaria) Typhus Viral hemorrhagic fevers (petechiae/rash, which are very rare in malaria) Bacterial sepsis with incidental parasitemia (concomitant bacteremia coexists with severe malaria and is hard to distinguish, especially in children) Thick and thin Giemsa-stained blood films examined immediately for parasite demonstration AND species identification; examine 100-200 fields before calling a thick film negative PCR amplification for definitive speciation and genotyping when mixed infection is suspected (more sensitive than microscopy/RDT for detecting and distinguishing species) Combination RDT carrying a P. falciparum-specific antigen plus a pan-malaria or P. vivax band Quantification of parasitemia (RDTs do not quantify) and assessment of parasite maturity/pigment for prognostic stratification G6PD status (knowledge basis for safe hypnozoite-directed therapy of the vivax component) — testing rationale only Mixed infections (most commonly P. falciparum together with P. vivax) are frequently under-detected by light microscopy and rapid antigen tests; PCR is the most sensitive method and is increasingly used specifically for speciation and genotyping in mixed infections (p.1767). Because microscopy and RDTs may detect only the dominant species, a smear or RDT reported as single-species (especially P. falciparum) does not exclude a coexisting vivax/ovale component carrying dormant liver-stage hypnozoites. P. vivax + P. falciparum is recognized as a distinct co-circulating pattern in endemic mapping, with roughly equal prevalence of the two species in Oceania (p.1761-1762). Standard combination RDTs typically carry one P. falciparum-specific band plus a pan-malaria or P. vivax band; this design distinguishes falciparum from the 'less dangerous' malarias but is not optimized to flag concurrent dual infection (p.1766). RDTs may miss low-level P. vivax (and P. ovale/P. malariae) parasitemia and PfHRP2-based tests can be falsely negative where parasites carry HRP2/3 gene deletions — both failure modes can mask one component of a mixed infection (p.1766). The classic regularly-spaced febrile paroxysm at presentation suggests P. vivax or P. ovale (often relapse); its presence in a patient with confirmed falciparum should raise suspicion of a coexisting vivax/ovale component. Apparent vivax/ovale relapses arising after treatment of a mixed infection reflect persistence of liver-stage hypnozoites, which are not cleared by standard blood-stage schizonticides. Coma, obtundation, delirium, or abnormal behavior (cerebral malaria) — attributable to the falciparum component Repeated or generalized convulsions (>2 in 24 h) Respiratory distress / acidotic deep breathing (acidosis, lactate >=5 mmol/L) Hypoglycemia (<2.2 mmol/L) Shock / hypotension with impaired perfusion Severe normocytic anemia (Hct <15%) and/or spontaneous bleeding / DIC Hemoglobinuria (black/brown/red urine) Acute kidney injury (creatinine >265 umol/L) Hyperparasitemia (>2% indicates increased risk; >5-10% defines severe disease) — a falciparum-driven marker Prostration / inability to sit or stand unaided Treating an apparently single-species falciparum infection as if vivax were absent: the coexisting vivax hypnozoite reservoir is not cleared by blood-stage drugs and later causes relapse — manage mixed infection as falciparum AND provide hypnozoite-directed coverage for vivax. Relying on microscopy or RDT alone to exclude a second species — both under-detect the minor component; PCR is needed to confirm/exclude mixed infection. Misreading PfHRP2 RDT positivity that persists for weeks after a prior infection as evidence of the current species mix. Mistaking persistent P. falciparum gametocytemia after treatment for treatment failure or active infection. Attributing all post-treatment fever to falciparum recrudescence when it may be a true vivax/ovale relapse from the mixed-infection liver reservoir. Misidentifying P. knowlesi as P. falciparum on microscopy/RDT, distorting the apparent species picture. Sporozoites inoculated by anopheline mosquitoes reach the liver and undergo pre-erythrocytic schizogony; a single sporozoite yields thousands of merozoites that invade RBCs and multiply (every 48 h for P. falciparum and P. vivax). In P. vivax (and P. ovale) infection, a fraction of intrahepatic forms do not divide but persist as dormant hypnozoites for weeks to a year or more, later reactivating to cause relapses — a feature absent in P. falciparum. In a mixed P. falciparum + P. vivax infection, the falciparum component drives the risk of severe disease through cytoadherence (PfEMP1 binding endothelial receptors), rosetting, and agglutination, causing sequestration of mature parasites in vital organs; only ring forms circulate, so peripheral parasitemia underestimates true burden. P. vivax preferentially invades young reticulocytes and produces lower parasitemia (seldom >2%), while P. falciparum invades RBCs of all ages and can reach very high densities. The simultaneous presence of a vivax hypnozoite reservoir means blood-stage cure of both species does not prevent later vivax relapse (p.1760-1763). Promptly treated uncomplicated falciparum malaria has a mortality of <0.1%, but risk rises steeply once vital-organ dysfunction occurs or parasitemia exceeds ~2%. In a mixed infection the falciparum component dictates the severe-disease prognosis; cerebral malaria carries ~20% mortality in adults and ~15% in children even with treatment, and ~10% of child survivors have residual neurologic deficits (most improving within 6 months). Poor-prognosis features include hyperparasitemia (>100,000/uL), predominance of mature pigment-containing parasites (>20%), pigment in >5% of neutrophils, hypoglycemia, hyperlactatemia, acidemia, and coagulopathy. The vivax component does not usually drive mortality but, if its hypnozoite reservoir is not addressed, predisposes to later relapse and recurrent anemia (p.1763-1767). Severity is governed by the P. falciparum component per Harrison Table 231-2 (Manifestations of Severe Falciparum Malaria): major criteria include unarousable coma/cerebral malaria, acidosis (arterial pH <7.25 / lactate >=5 mmol/L), severe normocytic anemia (Hct <15%), renal failure (creatinine >265 umol/L), noncardiogenic pulmonary edema/ARDS, hypoglycemia (<2.2 mmol/L), hypotension/shock, bleeding/DIC, and repeated convulsions; other criteria include hemoglobinuria, prostration, and hyperparasitemia (>5% nonimmune, >10% any patient). Uncomplicated disease = patient can sit/stand unaided and swallow, with no vital-organ dysfunction and parasitemia <2% (p.1763-1764).

Necrotizing Fasciitis — Urgent surgical exploration (diagnostic AND therapeutic) — The definitive diagnostic test — direct visualization of necrotic fascia confirms the diagnosis and simultaneously allows debridement; imaging should not delay surgery when clinical suspicion is high. Blood cultures and intraoperative tissue/fluid cultures — Identifies the causative organism(s) to guide de-escalation. CT or MRI (only if diagnosis uncertain and patient stable enough to tolerate delay) — May show fascial thickening/gas, but should never delay surgery in a patient with high clinical suspicion. CPK — Markedly elevated levels suggest muscle involvement (myonecrosis), affecting the extent of surgical debridement needed. LRINEC score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis) — Can support clinical suspicion using CRP, WBC, hemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose, though it should not override strong clinical suspicion if score is low. Immediate empiric antibiotics required Clostridial myonecrosis / gas gangrene (distinguished from clostridial NF by muscle biopsy) Streptococcal necrotizing myositis (GAS infection extending into muscle) Pyomyositis (usually S. aureus; localized, shock uncommon unless toxin-producing) Synergistic nonclostridial anaerobic myonecrosis (necrotizing cutaneous myositis / synergistic necrotizing cellulitis) — a mixed aerobic-anaerobic variant Cellulitis / erysipelas (superficial; skin more abnormal but pain mild-moderate) Halophilic Vibrio vulnificus infection (can be as fulminant as NF; Gulf/Atlantic water exposure or raw seafood in cirrhosis) Aeromonas soft-tissue infection (freshwater laceration exposure) Aggressive cellulitis from Vibrio vulnificus or Aeromonas hydrophila Ecthyma gangrenosum (Pseudomonas, neutropenic hosts) Clostridial myonecrosis Soft-tissue plain radiography, CT, and MRI to assess depth of infection and detect tissue gas or a localized abscess — most useful when lesions progress rapidly or SIRS is present; note imaging may show only soft-tissue swelling and is NOT specific for fulminant GAS NF/myonecrosis, where gas is typically absent Gram stain and aerobic/anaerobic culture of surgically excised tissue to identify GAS vs mixed flora vs MRSA vs Clostridium Frozen-section histology of aspirate or punch biopsy (valuable in NF), though aspiration/biopsy is negative in ~80% of cases Serum CPK (markedly elevated when myonecrosis coexists) Lactate, d-dimer, coagulation, liver and renal function as markers of systemic toxicity/organ failure Thrombophlebitis (a common early misdiagnosis) Muscle strain or contusion (the minor trauma at the deep nidus) Pain out of proportion to physical findings is the classic early clue: physical signs may be minimal (only soft-tissue edema and mild erythema) while pain and fever are severe; this disparity helps distinguish NF from superficial cellulitis, where skin appearance is more abnormal but pain is only mild-to-moderate. Early disease is frequently misdiagnosed (e.g., as thrombophlebitis) and patients may be sent home with analgesics, especially in the strep type that begins deep at a site of non-penetrating minor trauma (bruise, muscle strain) with no visible portal of entry. Classic late signs evolve sequentially: swelling and brawny edema/tenderness, then dark-red (violaceous) induration, then bullae filled with blue/purple fluid, then friable bluish-maroon-to-black skin; thrombosis of dermal-papillae vessels is extensive by this stage. Paradoxical decrease in pain or progression to anesthesia over the involved area is an ominous sign reflecting thrombosis of small vessels and infarction of cutaneous nerves. GAS NF can be preceded by varicella, childbirth, or muscle strain, and most patients deny an antecedent streptococcal infection. The inoculation site may be inapparent and remote from clinical involvement (e.g., minor hand trauma manifesting as infection over the shoulder or chest). Myositis/myonecrosis coexists with NF in roughly 20-50% of cases and serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK) may be markedly elevated, signaling deeper muscle involvement. Pain out of proportion to examination findings Rapidly progressing lesion with signs of systemic inflammatory response / toxicity Violaceous (blue/purple) bullae, skin sloughing, dusky/mottled erythema Progression of tenderness to anesthesia over the lesion (cutaneous nerve infarction) Crepitus or gas in deep tissue (suggests mixed/clostridial infection) Renal impairment that may precede shock, plus hypotension/multiorgan failure Urgent surgical exploration supersedes other diagnostic or therapeutic maneuvers — debridement is life-saving and must not be delayed Early physical findings are minimal relative to pain/fever, leading to underestimation of severity and misdiagnosis as thrombophlebitis or simple cellulitis. Absence of gas does NOT exclude NF: gas is usually absent when the cause is GAS or MRSA and is seen mainly with mixed/clostridial infection. Normal or nonspecific imaging does NOT rule out NF — CT/MRI may show only soft-tissue swelling and are not specific for fulminant GAS NF/myonecrosis. A negative aspirate or frozen-section biopsy does NOT exclude NF (negative in ~80% of cases). Decreasing pain should not be reassuring — it can signal nerve infarction and disease progression rather than improvement. Do not wait for imaging or cultures when NF is suspected with systemic toxicity; surgical exploration is both diagnostic and therapeutic. NF is infection of the superficial and/or deep fascia investing the muscles of an extremity or trunk, with extensive necrosis of subcutaneous tissue and fascia. Infection spreads rapidly along fascial planes and via venous channels and lymphatics, typically sparing the muscle itself in pure fasciitis. Two main microbiologic patterns: a mixed aerobic-anaerobic (type I) process beginning with a breach of a mucosal barrier (GI/GU tract), and a monomicrobial group A streptococcal (type II) process. In GAS disease, organisms reach deep fascia either by transient bacteremic seeding at a site of minor non-penetrating trauma (no portal) or by spread from cutaneous infection/penetrating trauma. Thrombosis of dermal vessels produces progressive skin necrosis; infarction of cutaneous nerves causes the characteristic late anesthesia. NF caused by Clostridium perfringens or extending into muscle (clostridial/streptococcal myonecrosis) carries very high systemic toxicity with hemolysis. PVL-producing MRSA strains have been reported as a cause. Mortality for NF is roughly 11-34% overall and rises substantially when associated with toxic shock syndrome. GAS/clostridial fascial-muscle infection historically carried 20-50% mortality with penicillin alone. Survivors of GAS NF often require repeated surgeries including amputation. Clostridial NF/myonecrosis is far more lethal: spontaneous (nontraumatic) myonecrosis mortality exceeds 65% (often C. septicum with underlying malignancy); trunk infection ~63% vs limb ~12% mortality. Any delay in surgery increases the risk of death; early aggressive surgery markedly improves outcomes. Microbiologic/clinical typing: Type I = mixed aerobic-anaerobic, begins at a mucosal-barrier breach (GI/GU), common in diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, malignancy, surgery, or abdominal penetrating injury; Fournier gangrene is the perineal/scrotal form. Type II = monomicrobial group A streptococcal (GAS implicated in ~60% of NF cases), can occur in otherwise healthy hosts, two presentations (with vs without a defined portal of entry). PVL-producing MRSA is a recognized monomicrobial cause. NF qualifies as soft-tissue necrosis under the CDC streptococcal toxic shock syndrome case definition (hypotension plus >=2 of: renal impairment, coagulopathy, hepatic impairment, ARDS, generalized erythematous desquamating rash, soft-tissue necrosis/NF/myositis/gangrene). (LRINEC score not described in this source.)
