airway emergency (Harrison 22e p.302) Peritonsillar abscess — fever, dysphagia, profound throat pain with drooling, trismus, 'hot potato voice', unilateral palate bulge and uvular deviation (Harrison 22e p.302) Retropharyngeal abscess — post-URI in children with sore throat, dysphagia, deep neck pain, neck stiffness, trismus, drooling; severe cases with dyspnea/stridor (Harrison 22e p.302) Submandibular abscess / Ludwig angina — swelling of the floor of the mouth displacing the tongue posteriorly, usually after dental infection or extraction (Harrison 22e p.302) Lemierre syndrome — septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with metastatic infection (Harrison 22e p.302) Candida pharyngitis — cottage-cheese exudate that scrapes off leaving a bleeding surface (Harrison 22e p.300) Rapid GAS antigen test: sensitivity ~80%, specificity ~95%; proper technique (swabbing tonsils/pharynx and any exudate or ulceration) is essential to sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.301) Throat culture: single-swab sensitivity ~85-90%; can be falsely positive in carriers; not recommended for routine adult evaluation given 24-48 h delay (Harrison 22e p.301) Heterophil antibody test for EBV mononucleosis (low early sensitivity, rises by week 3) (Harrison 22e p.302) CBC for atypical lymphocytosis in mononucleosis (absolute lymphocytes >4000/uL or relative >50% with >10% atypical morphology) (Harrison 22e p.302) CT imaging for suspected head and neck abscess (except obvious peritonsillar abscess) (Harrison 22e p.302) Lateral neck radiograph in epiglottitis may show the 'thumb sign' (not required for diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.302) Gastroesophageal reflux / laryngopharyngeal reflux (Harrison 22e p.300) Postnasal drainage (Harrison 22e p.300) Head and neck tumors (Harrison 22e p.300) Thyroiditis (Harrison 22e p.300) Leukoplakia mimicking exudate (cannot be scraped off) (Harrison 22e p.300) Sore throat is not synonymous with pharyngitis: it may also arise from submandibular/retropharyngeal/peritonsillar space infections, thyroiditis, gastroesophageal reflux, tumors, or postnasal drainage (Harrison 22e p.300). Pharyngeal erythema is most commonly seen with viral infection (common cold, influenza), not bacterial disease (Harrison 22e p.300). Pharyngeal exudate can be mimicked by Candida (cottage-cheese appearance, scrapes off leaving a bleeding surface) or leukoplakia (cannot be scraped off) — do not equate exudate with bacterial pharyngitis (Harrison 22e p.300). GAS is the only common cause of sore throat that warrants antibiotics; most non-GAS pharyngitis is viral and self-limited (Harrison 22e p.300). About 10% of adults with sore throat have GAS; in children the prevalence may reach ~35%, peaking at ages 5-15 years, and is higher in winter and early spring (Harrison 22e p.300). Risk of GAS pharyngitis is elevated in health care and child care workers, teachers, parents of young children, and contacts of known strep cases; clinicians should watch for local outbreaks in military and institutional settings (Harrison 22e p.300). GAS carriage is common (up to ~20% of schoolchildren, ~5% of adolescents/young adults); rapid antigen tests and culture cannot distinguish true infection from carriage (Harrison 22e p.301). In adults meeting zero or one Centor criterion, a positive GAS test is very likely a false positive and/or represents carriage; indiscriminate testing of adults with sore throat is discouraged (Harrison 22e p.301). Lower the threshold to test/treat GAS in patients with a history of acute rheumatic fever, documented strep exposure in the past week, those in a community strep epidemic, and diabetic or immunocompromised patients (Harrison 22e p.301). In children the Centor criteria are less specific, so GAS pharyngitis should be confirmed by testing; children with pharyngitis but no viral signs (conjunctivitis, runny nose, cough, hoarseness, nonexudative oral lesions) warrant testing (Harrison 22e p.301). In developed countries the prevalence of rheumatic fever is extremely low, and antibiotic treatment does not prevent poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (Harrison 22e p.300). Full-blown infectious mononucleosis (EBV) appears in only about one-fourth of cases and is a triad of clinical, hematologic, and serologic findings; new EBV causes 1-6% of pharyngitis in young adults and is rare over age 40 (Harrison 22e p.301). Heterophil antibody is detectable in only ~40% of mononucleosis patients in the first week but in 80-90% by the third week, so an early negative test does not exclude EBV (Harrison 22e p.302). Gonococcal pharyngitis is more often asymptomatic than symptomatic; suspect it with persistent sore throat unresponsive to presumptive strep treatment and relevant sexual exposure (Harrison 22e p.302). Diphtheria produces only mild pharyngitis beneath its characteristic grayish pseudomembrane (Harrison 22e p.302). Acute HIV infection causes sore throat in roughly half of cases; consider it when sore throat accompanies headache, fever, myalgias, lymphadenopathy, anorexia, and rash (Harrison 22e p.302). Shaking chills/rigors, neck swelling beyond lymphadenopathy, trouble swallowing, drooling, or symptoms persisting >5 days without improvement should prompt urgent re-evaluation (Harrison 22e p.301) Stridor, dyspnea, hoarseness, or tripod/forward-leaning posture with drooling — suggests epiglottitis and impending airway obstruction (Harrison 22e p.302) Non-GAS pharyngitis that is not resolving in a teenager/young adult with rigors, neck pain or swelling, or extrapharyngeal symptoms — suspect Lemierre syndrome (Harrison 22e p.302) Trismus, 'hot potato voice', and unilateral palate bulge with uvular deviation — peritonsillar abscess (Harrison 22e p.302) Grayish pharyngeal pseudomembrane in a traveler from an endemic area — suspect diphtheria (Harrison 22e p.300, 302) Prescribing antibiotics to the majority of adults with sore throat despite only ~10% having GAS — most cases are viral (Harrison 22e p.300). Testing adults who meet zero or one Centor criterion: 40-60% of adults with pharyngitis fall here, and a positive test is highly likely to be false-positive or carriage (Harrison 22e p.301). Relying on throat culture or rapid test to distinguish active infection from GAS carriage — neither can (Harrison 22e p.301). Applying adult Centor criteria to children, in whom they are less specific (Harrison 22e p.301). Mistaking Candida or leukoplakia for bacterial pharyngeal exudate (Harrison 22e p.300). Attempting to examine or swab the posterior pharynx in suspected epiglottitis — this can provoke laryngospasm and should only be done in a controlled setting (Harrison 22e p.302). Assuming antibiotic treatment of GAS prevents poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis — it does not (Harrison 22e p.300). A negative early heterophil antibody test does not rule out EBV mononucleosis (Harrison 22e p.302). Acute pharyngitis (symptoms generally present for days) is most often caused by respiratory viruses; group A beta-hemolytic streptococci (GAS, Streptococcus pyogenes) are a frequent bacterial cause, with other contributors including Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Epstein-Barr virus, HIV, non-group-A streptococci (groups C and G), Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae. Complications of GAS pharyngitis arise from both suppurative spread (e.g., peritonsillar abscess, sinusitis, other invasive GAS infection) and nonsuppurative immune-mediated sequelae (acute rheumatic fever, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, scarlet fever) (Harrison 22e p.300-301). Both streptococcal and nonstreptococcal pharyngitis should resolve within 3-5 days. Nonsuppurative complications are rare, and even streptococcal pharyngitis is self-limited in the vast majority of cases; outside the U.S., because complications are rare, some guidelines do not recommend routine GAS testing or antibiotic treatment of sore throat (Harrison 22e p.301). Centor criteria (4 findings, 1 point each): history of fever, absence of cough, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and tonsillar exudate or swelling. For an adult pretest probability of ~10%, post-evaluation probability of GAS is ~2% at 0 points, ~3% at 1, ~8% at 2, ~19% at 3, and ~41% at 4 points (area under the curve 0.79). Conceptually: 0-1 criteria -> neither test nor treat; 2-3 -> rapid antigen test to guide management; 4 -> rapid test or empirical treatment. (Harrison 22e p.300-301).

Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria — paroxysmal nocturnal, PNH, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, Marchiafava-Micheli syndrome, PIGA mutation clone, complement-mediated hemolytic anemia Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (warm or cold antibody type) Aplastic anemia Myelodysplastic syndrome Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome Hereditary spherocytosis or other membrane defects G6PD deficiency and other hemolytic enzymopathies Flow cytometry for GPI-anchored proteins (FLAER, CD55, CD59) on granulocytes and erythrocytes — confirms and sizes the PNH clone Complete blood count with reticulocyte count — documents hemolysis and identifies coexisting cytopenias LDH, indirect bilirubin, haptoglobin — supports intravascular hemolysis Urinalysis for hemoglobinuria and urinary hemosiderin — evidence of chronic intravascular hemolysis Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test — should be negative, helping exclude autoimmune hemolysis Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with cytogenetics — assesses for underlying aplastic anemia or MDS Iron studies — chronic hemoglobinuria can cause iron deficiency despite hemolysis Imaging (Doppler ultrasound, CT/MR venography) if thrombosis at an atypical site is suspected Autoimmune hemolytic anemia Microangiopathic hemolytic anemias (TTP/HUS, DIC) Aplastic anemia without a PNH clone Budd-Chiari syndrome from other hypercoagulable states Cold agglutinin disease Acquired clonal stem-cell disorder from a somatic PIGA gene mutation, leading to loss of GPI-anchored surface proteins (including CD55 and CD59) that normally protect red cells from complement attack. Classic triad is intravascular hemolysis, marrow failure/cytopenias, and a marked thrombotic tendency, though most patients present with only one or two of these features. Morning hemoglobinuria is a well-known feature but is actually seen in only a minority of patients; hemolysis is often chronic and low-grade rather than dramatically episodic. Thrombosis is the leading cause of death and characteristically occurs at unusual sites — hepatic (Budd-Chiari), portal, mesenteric, cerebral (dural sinus), and dermal veins. Consider PNH in any patient with unexplained hemolysis plus cytopenia, or with venous thrombosis at an atypical site, especially with a normal or low platelet count. PNH clones frequently coexist with, precede, or follow aplastic anemia and myelodysplastic syndrome, reflecting a shared marrow-failure background. Smooth muscle dystonia (esophageal spasm, erectile dysfunction, abdominal pain) results from free-hemoglobin-mediated nitric oxide scavenging rather than mechanical obstruction. Flow cytometry for GPI-anchored proteins (e.g., FLAER, CD55/CD59) on granulocytes and red cells is the diagnostic test of choice, replacing older Ham's and sucrose lysis tests. Sudden abdominal pain, ascites, or hepatomegaly suggesting Budd-Chiari or mesenteric venous thrombosis New neurologic deficit or severe headache raising concern for cerebral or dural venous sinus thrombosis Rapidly worsening cytopenias suggesting evolution to aplastic anemia or MDS/leukemia Severe abdominal or chest pain with hemolysis flare, which may signal smooth-muscle dystonia or thrombotic event Pregnancy in a known PNH patient, which carries substantially increased maternal thrombotic and fetal risk Acute kidney injury from massive hemoglobinuria or renal vein thrombosis Assuming hemoglobinuria must be present and grossly visible; many patients have only subclinical or intermittent hemolysis Missing the diagnosis in a patient with unexplained thrombosis at an atypical site because cytopenias are mild or absent Relying on outdated Ham's/sucrose lysis tests instead of flow cytometry, which is far more sensitive and specific Overlooking a coexisting or antecedent marrow failure syndrome (aplastic anemia, MDS) when a PNH clone is found PNH arises from an acquired somatic mutation in the X-linked PIGA gene within a hematopoietic stem cell, impairing synthesis of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor required to display several surface proteins. Loss of the complement regulators CD55 (decay-accelerating factor) and CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis) leaves the abnormal red cell clone vulnerable to unchecked complement-mediated intravascular lysis. The clonal population expands, often in the setting of an immune-mediated marrow injury that gives PIGA-mutant cells a relative survival advantage, producing the combination of hemolysis, cytopenias, and a pro-thrombotic state linked to platelet and microparticle complement activation. Historically PNH carried significant mortality, largely from thrombosis and marrow failure, but complement-inhibitor therapy has markedly improved survival and quality of life. Long-term outcome also depends on clone size and any associated bone marrow failure syndrome, with a small risk of progression to MDS or acute leukemia over time.

POEMS syndrome — poems, osteosclerotic myeloma, Crow-Fukase syndrome, Takatsuki syndrome, PEP syndrome, polyneuropathy organomegaly endocrinopathy M-protein skin changes Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) without associated plasma cell disorder Multiple myeloma with peripheral neuropathy Waldenström macroglobulinemia / IgM-related neuropathy Castleman disease (may overlap with or occur alongside POEMS) Amyloidosis (AL) with neuropathy and organomegaly Diabetic or other systemic causes of sensorimotor polyneuropathy Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation — detects and characterizes the monoclonal (typically lambda) protein Serum free light chain ratio — supports clonality assessment Serum VEGF level — supports diagnosis and can track disease activity Skeletal survey and/or whole-body imaging (CT or PET) — identifies characteristic sclerotic or mixed bone lesions Nerve conduction studies/EMG — confirms demyelinating polyneuropathy pattern Bone marrow biopsy — quantifies clonal plasma cells and excludes overt myeloma Endocrine panel (thyroid, gonadal, adrenal, glucose) — screens for associated endocrinopathies Echocardiography and pulmonary function testing — assesses for pulmonary hypertension and extravascular volume overload CIDP (idiopathic) Amyloid neuropathy Diabetic polyneuropathy with unrelated monoclonal gammopathy (MGUS) Castleman disease without POEMS features Hypothyroid-associated neuropathy Rare paraneoplastic disorder driven by an underlying clonal plasma cell process, almost always with lambda light-chain restriction. Peripheral polyneuropathy is typically the presenting and most disabling feature — usually a symmetric, ascending, demyelinating sensorimotor pattern resembling CIDP. Suspect POEMS when 'CIDP' fails to respond to standard immunotherapy, especially if accompanied by systemic features. Sclerotic bone lesions (solitary or multiple) are common and often visible on skeletal survey or CT even without lytic disease typical of myeloma. Papilledema, extravascular volume overload (ascites, edema, effusions), and thrombocytosis/erythrocytosis are distinctive clues that separate POEMS from typical myeloma or CIDP. Markedly elevated serum VEGF is a hallmark biomarker reflecting disease activity. Endocrinopathies (commonly hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, or glucose intolerance) are frequent but nonspecific, and should not be over-interpreted alone. Skin changes (hyperpigmentation, thickening, hypertrichosis, glomeruloid hemangiomas) support the diagnosis when present alongside neuropathy. Rapidly progressive neuropathy with respiratory or bulbar involvement New papilledema suggesting raised intracranial pressure Signs of extravascular volume overload (ascites, pleural effusion, peripheral edema) indicating advancing systemic disease Evidence of pulmonary hypertension or thrombotic events, which portend higher morbidity Rapid rise in serum VEGF or new osteolytic transformation suggesting progression or evolution toward myeloma Misdiagnosing as idiopathic CIDP and treating with standard immunotherapy (e.g., IVIG/plasma exchange) alone, which is typically ineffective since the underlying plasma cell clone is not addressed Overlooking sclerotic bone lesions on imaging because they lack the classic lytic appearance of multiple myeloma Failing to check serum VEGF or overinterpreting an isolated endocrinopathy without considering the full multisystem picture Anchoring on a single feature (e.g., organomegaly) rather than recognizing the required combination of core diagnostic criteria POEMS syndrome arises from an underlying monoclonal, lambda-restricted plasma cell disorder that drives systemic overproduction of proinflammatory and proangiogenic cytokines, most notably vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). This cytokine excess is thought to underlie the vascular, neurologic, and organ-based manifestations rather than direct tumor infiltration, distinguishing the disease from classic multiple myeloma. The resulting syndrome combines a chronic demyelinating polyneuropathy with multisystem involvement including bone, endocrine, dermatologic, and extravascular fluid abnormalities. With clone-directed therapy, many patients achieve meaningful and durable improvement in neuropathy and systemic features, and overall survival is generally more favorable than multiple myeloma. However, residual neurologic deficits are common, and relapse or progression can occur, warranting long-term surveillance of the monoclonal marker and VEGF level.

Very young age of hypertension onset or hypertensive stroke in a young relative, suggesting a familial syndrome Large or irregular adrenal mass on imaging raising concern for adrenocortical carcinoma Failing to correct hypokalemia and withdraw interfering drugs (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, high-dose diuretics) before aldosterone-to-renin ratio testing, leading to false results Relying on adrenal CT alone to decide unilateral versus bilateral disease instead of adrenal vein sampling, risking inappropriate or missed surgery Assuming normokalemia excludes the diagnosis and therefore not screening appropriately hypertensive patients Misattributing resistant hypertension to poor adherence or essential hypertension without screening for secondary causes Autonomous, renin-independent overproduction of aldosterone from one or both adrenal glands leads to sodium retention, potassium and hydrogen ion wasting, and volume-mediated hypertension. The excess mineralocorticoid activity suppresses plasma renin and can produce hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, though many patients remain normokalemic. Beyond hemodynamic effects, chronic aldosterone excess produces direct pro-fibrotic and pro-inflammatory effects on the heart, vasculature, and kidney that account for disproportionate target-organ damage relative to blood pressure alone. With correct subtype classification, unilateral disease treated surgically often achieves cure or major improvement of hypertension and hypokalemia, while bilateral disease managed medically with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists generally achieves good blood pressure control. Untreated or unrecognized disease carries excess risk of cardiovascular events, stroke, and chronic kidney disease compared with blood-pressure-matched essential hypertension.

subset of patients are AMA-negative and require biopsy or specific autoantibodies Missing an overlap syndrome by not screening for autoimmune hepatitis features when transaminases are disproportionately elevated Overlooking screening for associated autoimmune diseases and osteoporosis once diagnosis is established PBC is an autoimmune, T-cell-mediated process that progressively destroys small and medium intrahepatic bile ducts, producing chronic cholestasis. Ongoing bile duct injury leads to periportal inflammation, fibrosis, and eventually biliary-type cirrhosis if untreated. may show onion-skin periductal fibrosis Serum IgG4 — to exclude IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis Colonoscopy with biopsies — to evaluate for concurrent inflammatory bowel disease CA 19-9 and repeat cross-sectional imaging — surveillance for cholangiocarcinoma in patients with dominant strictures or clinical deterioration Autoantibody panel (ANA, ASMA, p-ANCA) — supportive workup, though p-ANCA lacks specificity IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis Ischemic cholangiopathy Post-surgical bile duct strictures Choledocholithiasis with secondary strictures Chronic cholestatic disease marked by progressive fibrosing inflammation and stricturing of intra- and/or extrahepatic bile ducts Strongly linked to inflammatory bowel disease, particularly ulcerative colitis; colitis may be quiescent or diagnosed after PSC Predominantly affects young to middle-aged men; often discovered incidentally via persistently elevated alkaline phosphatase Fluctuating cholestatic pattern (elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT) is typical, with variable bilirubin depending on stricture burden Cholangiography (MRCP preferred over ERCP for initial diagnosis) shows characteristic multifocal strictures alternating with normal or dilated segments (beaded appearance) Any patient with IBD and unexplained cholestatic liver tests should be evaluated for PSC Carries increased lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder cancer, and colorectal cancer (in those with concurrent colitis) No medical therapy has been proven to alter the natural history; liver transplantation is the only definitive treatment for advanced disease Rapid clinical deterioration, weight loss, or new dominant stricture — raise concern for cholangiocarcinoma Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain suggesting superimposed acute bacterial cholangitis Marked rise in CA 19-9 or new mass on imaging New-onset or worsening ascites, variceal bleeding, or encephalopathy indicating progression to cirrhosis and decompensation Colonic dysplasia or malignancy found on surveillance colonoscopy in patients with concurrent IBD Attributing isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation in an IBD patient to the bowel disease alone without pursuing cholangiographic evaluation Missing small-duct PSC, which has a normal cholangiogram and requires biopsy for diagnosis Failing to distinguish IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis, which is often steroid-responsive, from classic PSC Underestimating cholangiocarcinoma risk and not maintaining surveillance in long-standing disease PSC is thought to result from an immune-mediated process in genetically susceptible individuals, possibly triggered by altered gut permeability and microbial translocation related to colonic inflammation, leading to periductal inflammation and concentric fibrosis of bile ducts. Progressive fibro-obliteration produces multifocal strictures with intervening dilations, eventually causing biliary obstruction, secondary bacterial cholangitis, and biliary cirrhosis. The disease can involve both intra- and extrahepatic ducts, and a small-duct variant exists without visible cholangiographic changes. PSC follows a variable but generally progressive course over years to decades, often culminating in biliary cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease; median transplant-free survival historically has been reported around a decade or more from diagnosis, though course varies widely between patients. Cholangiocarcinoma and colorectal cancer (in those with IBD) are major contributors to morbidity and mortality.

Acute Bacterial Prostatitis — Urinalysis and urine culture — Identifies the causative organism; this is preferred over prostatic secretion sampling in the acute setting given bacteremia risk with prostatic massage. Blood cultures (if febrile/systemically unwell) — Bacteremia is not uncommon in acute prostatitis and positive cultures help confirm the organism. Post-void residual / bladder scan (if retention suspected) — Urinary retention is a recognized complication requiring catheterization (suprapubic preferred over urethral if prostatitis is causing obstruction). STI testing (NAAT for gonorrhea/chlamydia) if risk factors present — Identifies sexually transmitted causes requiring different management and partner notification. Chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP) — presents insidiously as recurrent episodes of cystitis, sometimes with pelvic and perineal pain, usually without systemic signs of infection; should be suspected with recurrent UTI not in the context of catheterization (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136). Pyelonephritis — another febrile genitourinary infection that must be excluded as the anatomic source before attributing systemic symptoms to ABP (Harrison 22e p.1136). Acute cystitis in men — uncommon and warrants caution; urine culture should be obtained in all male UTI to help identify a prostatic focus (Harrison 22e p.1089). Pyelonephritis — overlapping febrile UTI presentation; distinguished by flank/costovertebral angle pain and an upper-tract source (Harrison 22e p.1089). Urethritis — urethral pain, pruritus, or discharge should prompt evaluation for sexually transmitted infections (Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium) rather than assuming prostatitis (Harrison 22e p.1087). Urine culture in all male UTI — documenting bacteriuria differentiates bacterial prostatitis from chronic pelvic pain syndrome; dipstick and/or microscopy alone are not sufficient (Harrison 22e p.1089). Cross-sectional imaging (CT or ultrasound) for men with febrile UTI, including the first episode, if not previously done, to evaluate for urinary tract abnormalities or obstruction (Harrison 22e p.1089). Evaluation for urinary retention / prostatic focus in men with recurrent cystitis (Harrison 22e p.1089). Urologic consultation referral if the diagnosis of UTI is unclear or UTI is recurrent (Harrison 22e p.1089). Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (formerly chronic prostatitis) — a noninfectious disorder that is the far more common cause of prostatic-type symptoms, with NO bacteriuria and NO response to antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.1089). Benign prostatic hypertrophy with obstructive uropathy / urinary retention — can produce lower urinary tract symptoms and predispose to UTI (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1131). Acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) typically presents as a severe illness with dysuria, urinary frequency, and pain in the prostatic, pelvic, or perineal region, and may be accompanied by fever, rigors, and/or bladder outlet obstruction (Harrison 22e p.1089). The prostate is involved in the majority of febrile UTI cases in men; ABP should be specifically suspected when a man presents with UTI plus systemic symptoms but no other clear anatomic source such as pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136). Bacteriuria documented on urine culture is what distinguishes the less common bacterial prostatitis syndromes (acute and chronic) from the far more common chronic pelvic pain syndrome, which is NOT associated with bacteriuria and is NOT improved by antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.1089). Men with febrile UTI may show an elevated serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and an enlarged prostate and seminal vesicles on ultrasound, supporting prostatic involvement; PSA is therefore not interpretable as a cancer marker during acute infection (Harrison 22e p.1089). Prostatitis is largely unrepresented in UTI clinical trial data, so complicated-UTI practice guidelines cannot be assumed to apply to prostatitis; older literature suggests prolonged therapy with prostate-penetrating agents may be needed (Harrison 22e p.1087). Bladder outlet obstruction or urinary retention accompanying ABP (Harrison 22e p.1089). Fever and rigors indicating a severe, systemic illness (Harrison 22e p.1089). Identification of a prostatic abscess — should prompt urologic specialist consultation (Harrison 22e p.1136). Symptoms predictive of surgically correctable disease in men with febrile UTI: urinary retention, early UTI recurrence, hematuria at follow-up, and voiding difficulties (Harrison 22e p.1089). Do not attribute prostatic-type symptoms to bacterial prostatitis without bacteriuria; absence of bacteriuria points to chronic pelvic pain syndrome, which will not respond to antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.1089). Do not interpret an elevated PSA during febrile male UTI as a cancer marker — acute prostatic infection itself raises PSA and prostate/seminal vesicle size on imaging (Harrison 22e p.1089). Do not assume complicated-UTI guideline regimens and durations apply to prostatitis, since prostatitis is largely absent from UTI trial data and may require prolonged prostate-penetrating therapy (Harrison 22e p.1087). Do not overlook a prostatic focus or urinary retention in men presenting with recurrent cystitis (Harrison 22e p.1089). Prostatitis can complicate ascending cystitis or arise hematogenously, for example as a metastatic focus of Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia. Infectious prostatitis is almost always bacterial and is far less common than the noninfectious chronic pelvic pain syndrome. In general, most genitourinary infections in men ascend from the urethra to the bladder, with the prostate becoming involved as part of febrile UTI; less than 2% of UTIs are hematogenous, usually from virulent organisms such as S. aureus and Salmonella. Obstruction from prostatic hypertrophy after age 50 promotes urinary stasis and is a major reason UTI incidence in older men approaches that in women (Harrison 22e p.1087, p.1089, p.1131). ABP is typically a severe acute illness but is amenable to therapy with prostate-penetrating antimicrobials. A prostatic abscess is a recognized complication requiring urologic intervention. Chronic bacterial prostatitis recurrences are not uncommon. Men with febrile UTI and none of the warning features (retention, early recurrence, hematuria, voiding difficulty) generally have normal upper and lower urinary tracts on urologic workup, implying a favorable structural prognosis (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136). Prostatitis is categorized as acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) versus chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP). ABP is a typically severe illness with systemic features (fever, rigors, possible bladder outlet obstruction); CBP presents insidiously as recurrent cystitis with pelvic/perineal pain and typically without systemic signs, often managed in the ambulatory setting. Both are distinct from noninfectious chronic pelvic pain syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136).

Pulmonary Tuberculosis — Sputum smear for AFB (at least 2 samples) — Rapid, widely available test; positive smear supports diagnosis and indicates infectiousness for public health purposes. CBNAAT / Xpert MTB-RIF (or equivalent rapid molecular test) — Provides faster diagnosis than culture and simultaneously detects rifampicin resistance, directly informing regimen choice — should be prioritized where available. Sputum culture (liquid or solid media) — Gold standard for diagnosis and allows full drug-susceptibility testing if initial molecular testing suggests resistance or treatment failure occurs. Chest X-ray — Supports diagnosis (upper lobe infiltrates, cavitation) and provides a baseline for treatment response monitoring. HIV testing — TB-HIV co-infection changes management (ART timing, drug interactions) and is a standard part of TB workup per national guidelines. Bronchogenic carcinoma (lung cancer) - upper-lobe mass/cavity, hemoptysis, weight loss; patients with such radiographic findings often undergo bronchoscopy/biopsy to distinguish from TB (p.1393) Nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease (e.g., M. avium complex, M. kansasii) - AFB-positive smear with limited CXR abnormality, favoured by absence of TB risk factors and presence of underlying chronic lung disease (p.1393) Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis / aspergilloma colonising an old TB cavity - hemoptysis, weight loss, fatigue, often misdiagnosed as TB recurrence; Aspergillus IgG precipitins and a fungal ball within a cavity suggest the diagnosis (p.1390-1391) Bacterial lung abscess / necrotising pneumonia (cavitary lesion with air-fluid level) (p.1386) Nontuberculous mycobacteria (M. avium complex, M. kansasii) causing AFB-positive cavitary or nodular lung disease (p.1393) Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis / aspergilloma in residual cavities mimicking TB relapse (p.1390-1391) Bacterial lung abscess or necrotising pneumonia producing upper-lobe cavitation (p.1386) Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra (next-generation NAAT with higher sensitivity in smear-negative and HIV-positive cases) (p.1392) Truenat MTB / MTB Plus and Truenat MTB-Rif Dx - portable, battery-operated molecular tests for peripheral settings (p.1392) Line probe assays (LPAs) for rapid detection of rifampin (rpoB) and isoniazid (katG, inhA) resistance, and second-line LPAs for fluoroquinolone/injectable resistance (p.1393) Liquid culture (MGIT) as WHO reference standard; solid media (Lowenstein-Jensen, Middlebrook 7H10/7H11) require 4-8 weeks (p.1392) Universal drug-susceptibility testing - at minimum rifampin DST on all initial isolates (p.1392-1393) Targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) and whole-genome sequencing for comprehensive resistance profiling (p.1393) Sputum induction with hypertonic saline when spontaneous sputum cannot be produced (p.1393) Fiberoptic bronchoscopy with bronchial brushings, endobronchial/transbronchial biopsy, and bronchoalveolar lavage (submit for Xpert, culture, AFB smear) (p.1393) Early-morning gastric lavage / induced sputum for children unable to expectorate (p.1393) Urine lateral-flow lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) assay in advanced HIV (p.1393) Chest CT to clarify equivocal plain-film findings (p.1393) Tuberculin skin test (TST/PPD) and IFN-gamma release assays (IGRA: QuantiFERON-TB Gold/Plus, T-SPOT.TB) to identify TB infection - note both have low predictive value for who will progress and cannot distinguish infection from active disease (p.1393-1394) M. tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs using ESAT-6/CFP-10) with accuracy similar to IGRA (p.1394) Bronchogenic carcinoma presenting as a cavitary upper-lobe mass with hemoptysis and weight loss (p.1393) Solitary pulmonary nodule - TB can present as one, overlapping with neoplastic causes (p.1393) Sarcoidosis and other granulomatous diseases (caseating vs non-caseating granuloma distinction) (granuloma differential, p.1384) Pulmonary TB is traditionally split into primary (soon after initial infection, often middle/lower lung zones, common in children) and postprimary/adult-type (reactivation or recent reinfection, apical-posterior upper lobes); molecular data show many adult cases in endemic areas reflect recent infection rather than old reactivation (p.1385). Postprimary disease favours the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes and the superior segments of the lower lobes, where higher local oxygen tension favours mycobacterial growth (p.1386). Cough develops in up to ~90% of cases and is often nonproductive initially before becoming purulent; hemoptysis occurs in 20-30%, and constitutional symptoms (diurnal fever, night sweats, weight loss, anorexia, malaise) are typical but nonspecific (p.1386). Absence of fever does not exclude TB; physical examination is frequently normal even with significant parenchymal disease, so reliance on exam findings can mislead (p.1386). Xpert MTB/RIF is the WHO first-line diagnostic, simultaneously detecting M. tuberculosis and rifampin resistance in under 2 hours; overall pulmonary sensitivity ~85% (up to 98% in smear-positive, ~70% in smear-negative), specificity 98% (p.1391-1392). A negative NAAT (Xpert/Ultra) does NOT exclude TB and requires further workup; conversely culture remains the gold standard for definitive diagnosis (p.1390-1393). Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra adds sensitivity (notably in smear-negative/culture-positive cases and PLWH) but its 'trace calls' can detect nonviable bacilli; trace calls in recently treated patients may represent dead-bacillus DNA (p.1392). At least one to two early-morning sputum specimens should be submitted for both AFB smear and mycobacterial culture; tissue for culture must NOT be placed in formaldehyde/preservative (p.1392). In HIV with partially preserved immunity, pulmonary TB looks classic (upper-lobe infiltrates and cavitation); with CD4 <200/uL it shifts to a primary-like pattern with diffuse/subtle interstitial infiltrates, little or no cavitation, pleural effusion and intrathoracic adenopathy (p.1391). Because HIV-associated TB cavitates less, such patients are often less infectious; PLWH with culture- and smear-positive disease may even have a normal chest radiograph (p.1382, p.1391-1393). Urine lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) is a point-of-care adjunct for TB diagnosis specifically in PLWH with advanced disease or low CD4 counts, not a general test (p.1393). MDR-TB is defined as resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampin; rifampin resistance (RR-TB) is used as a practical proxy for MDR; pre-XDR adds fluoroquinolone resistance, and XDR-TB adds resistance to a fluoroquinolone plus at least one additional group A drug (e.g., bedaquiline or linezolid) (p.1380-1382). Massive hemoptysis from erosion of a vessel in a cavity wall or rupture of a Rasmussen's aneurysm - potentially life-threatening (p.1386) Extensive disease causing dyspnea progressing to acute respiratory distress syndrome (p.1386) Features of hematogenous/miliary dissemination (miliary reticulonodular CXR, hepatosplenomegaly, choroidal tubercles) - high mortality if unrecognised (p.1389) Meningismus, headache, altered sensorium or cranial nerve palsy suggesting tuberculous meningitis - uniformly fatal if untreated (p.1388-1389) Advanced HIV with possible TB: NAAT-positive results warrant immediate treatment because diagnostic delay can be fatal (p.1391, p.1393) Treating on clinical/radiographic grounds alone: CXR has high sensitivity but poor specificity and no pattern (including a normal film) is pathognomonic in the HIV era - bacteriologic confirmation must always be pursued (p.1393). Interpreting a negative Xpert/NAAT or negative smear as ruling out TB - smear microscopy sensitivity is only 40-60% and a negative molecular test still requires culture and further workup (p.1392-1393). AFB microscopy cannot distinguish M. tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria, and urine/gastric specimens are prone to false negatives (low organism load) and false positives (commensal mycobacteria) (p.1392). Relying on the chest exam: physical findings are of limited use and may be entirely normal in significant pulmonary TB (p.1386). Missing diagnosis in atypical hosts (elderly nursing-home residents, teenagers, immunosuppressed/PLWH with lower-zone or noncavitary disease) (p.1391). TST/IGRA pitfalls: false-negative TST in immunosuppression and overwhelming TB; false-positive from NTM or BCG; the TST 'boosting phenomenon' can mimic conversion; neither test distinguishes latent infection from active disease (p.1393-1394). Putting tissue intended for culture into formaldehyde, which kills the organism and precludes culture (p.1392). M. tuberculosis is an aerobic acid-fast bacillus whose mycolic-acid-rich cell wall confers acid fastness and low permeability (reducing antibiotic efficacy). Transmission is by airborne droplet nuclei (<5-10 um) from a person with infectious pulmonary or laryngeal TB; cavitary cases are most infectious (10^5-10^7 AFB/mL of sputum). Inhaled bacilli reaching the alveoli are phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages; the bacillus arrests phagosome maturation and phagosome-lysosome fusion, replicates, and (via the ESX-1/RD1 secretion system) ruptures the macrophage to infect newly recruited phagocytes. Around 2-4 weeks, cell-mediated (TH1/IFN-gamma-driven, CD4+ T-cell-dependent) macrophage activation and a delayed-type hypersensitivity tissue-damaging response develop; their balance determines disease form. Granulomas (tubercles) of activated macrophages, epithelioid and giant cells form, with central caseous (cheese-like) necrosis in which low oxygen and pH inhibit but do not kill bacilli. When the macrophage-activating response is weak, delayed hypersensitivity causes progressive caseous liquefaction, bronchial and vascular erosion, and cavity formation; bacilli multiply within cavities and are discharged into airways, driving transmission and bronchogenic spread of satellite lesions. Lymphohematogenous dissemination can seed distant organs (miliary disease, meningitis). The continuum from infection to disease is governed largely by host immune competence; only ~10% of immunocompetent infected persons progress to active disease over a lifetime, about half within ~18 months. (pp.1380-1385) Untreated, TB is often fatal: about one-third of patients die within 1 year of diagnosis, and historically ~70% (weighted mean) of smear-positive cases died within 10 years; paucibacillary smear-negative disease had a lower ~20% case-fatality at 5 years, and ~60% of 5-year survivors underwent spontaneous remission. With timely, proper drug-susceptible treatment the vast majority are cured. Improper therapy lowers mortality but generates chronic infectious, often drug-resistant cases. A substantial proportion of cured survivors suffer post-TB lung disease - chronic airflow impairment, dyspnea, residual cough, bronchiectasis, pulmonary hypertension, and predisposition to aspergilloma/chronic pulmonary aspergillosis in residual cavities. (pp.1383, 1386, 1390-1391) Harrison frames severity primarily by disease form and host rather than a numeric score: primary vs postprimary (cavitary) pulmonary disease; pulmonary vs extrapulmonary vs disseminated (miliary) TB; and by drug-resistance category - drug-susceptible TB, rifampin-resistant (RR-TB), multidrug-resistant (MDR-TB: resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampin), pre-XDR-TB (MDR/RR plus fluoroquinolone resistance), and extensively drug-resistant (XDR-TB: MDR plus fluoroquinolone resistance and resistance to at least one additional group A drug such as bedaquiline or linezolid). Infectiousness grades with cavitation and sputum bacillary load (smear-positive cavitary > smear-negative/culture-positive > culture-negative/extrapulmonary, the last essentially noninfectious). (pp.1380-1386)

Pyrexia of Unknown Origin — Repeat detailed history and serial examinations — New localizing signs often emerge over time and are the single most valuable step in PUO workup. CBC, ESR, CRP, LFTs, RFTs, urinalysis — First-tier screening tests that can reveal a localizing clue (e.g., abnormal LFTs pointing to liver abscess or biliary source). Blood cultures (multiple sets, including for fastidious organisms if endocarditis suspected) — Identifies bacteremic causes including culture-negative endocarditis pathogens with extended incubation. Chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound — First-line imaging to screen for occult infection (TB, abscess) or malignancy. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (second-tier) — More sensitive for occult abscess, lymphadenopathy, or malignancy if first-tier workup is unrevealing. Echocardiography (if any murmur, risk factors, or persistent bacteremia) — Screens for infective endocarditis as a cause of prolonged fever. Infective endocarditis (including culture-negative endocarditis from fastidious organisms - nutritionally variant streptococci, HACEK group, Coxiella burnetii, Tropheryma whipplei, Bartonella) - one of the more common infectious causes (pp.150-151) Extrapulmonary and miliary tuberculosis - up to half of infections in non-Western FUO are M. tuberculosis; miliary TB is especially hard to diagnose (pp.150, 153) Diverticulitis (p.150) Vertebral osteomyelitis / spondylodiscitis (pp.150-151) Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) - consider with rural exposure, animal contact, valve disease, aortic aneurysm, or vascular prosthesis; test by immunofluorescence assay (pp.150-151) Whipple disease (Tropheryma whipplei) - consider with unexplained CNS, GI, or joint symptoms; PCR on stool and blood early (p.150) Intraabdominal / hepatic / renal / pelvic abscesses (p.151) Endemic infections after relevant travel/residence: malaria, visceral leishmaniasis, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis (p.150) Acute HIV infection (p.150) Adult-onset Still's disease (NIID, relatively common in FUO) (p.150) Large-vessel vasculitis and giant cell arteritis / polymyalgia rheumatica (pp.150, 153) Systemic lupus erythematosus (p.150) Sarcoidosis (p.150) Familial Mediterranean fever and other autoinflammatory syndromes (rare except in specific regions) (p.150) Schnitzler's syndrome - urticaria, bone pain, monoclonal gammopathy (p.150) VEXAS syndrome - adult-onset, middle-aged/elderly males, recurrent inflammation, chondritis, skin lesions, lung disease, venous thrombosis, arthritis, MDS; bone-marrow vacuoles in myeloid precursors; somatic UBA1 variants (p.150) Malignant lymphoma - by far the most common neoplastic cause; fever may precede detectable lymphadenopathy (p.150) Common solid tumors causing fever: breast, colon, hepatocellular, lung, pancreatic, renal cell carcinoma (p.151) Culture-negative endocarditis - sterile cultures may simply reflect ongoing antibiotic therapy rather than a noninfectious cause (pp.151-152) Marantic (nonbacterial thrombotic) endocarditis - sterile, paraneoplastic, especially with adenocarcinomas, mimics infective endocarditis (p.151) Sterile endocarditis of SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome (p.151) Obligatory baseline panel: ESR and CRP, platelet count, leukocyte count with differential, hemoglobin, electrolytes, creatinine, total protein, alkaline phosphatase, ALT, AST, LDH, creatine kinase, ferritin, antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, protein electrophoresis, urinalysis, three blood cultures, urine culture, chest x-ray, abdominal ultrasonography, and TST or IGRA (p.149) Cryoglobulins - useful low-cost screening test (p.153) Fundoscopy by an ophthalmologist - early, to exclude retinal vasculitis when PDCs are absent or misleading (p.153) 18F-FDG-PET/CT - established next step when PDC-guided tests are unrevealing; ~50% total diagnostic yield; best performed during active inflammation (elevated CRP/ESR or fever) and before glucocorticoids; outperforms gallium and labeled-leukocyte scintigraphy (pp.152-154) Gallium-67 citrate or 111In/99mTc-labeled leukocyte scintigraphy - alternatives when PET/CT unavailable (lower yield; gallium localizes ~1/3, leukocyte ~1/5 of cases) (p.154) Whole-body MRI - one study reported yield comparable to PET/CT (needs confirmation) (p.154) Echocardiography - low yield without PDCs; reserve for high suspicion of endocarditis (p.153) Liver biopsy (acid-fast smear, culture, PCR) - highest yield if miliary TB suspected; bone marrow / lymph node biopsies are alternatives (p.153) Mycobacterial PCR alongside cultures - may shorten time to TB diagnosis (p.153) Specialized blood cultures held long enough for fastidious organisms (e.g., HACEK); inform the lab and use special media for Histoplasma or Legionella; >3 blood cultures or >1 urine culture is useless without PDCs (p.153) Q fever serology by immunofluorescence assay; T. whipplei PCR on stool/blood (pp.150-151) Temporal artery biopsy in patients >=55 years for suspected giant cell arteritis (p.153) CSF examination (HSV especially type 2, Cryptococcus, M. tuberculosis) when FUO is accompanied by headache (p.153) Later-stage PDC-driven biopsies for pathology and/or microbiology (p.154) Drug-induced fever - virtually any drug, even after long-term use; common culprits include allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, sulfasalazine, furosemide, and antimicrobials (sulfonamides, minocycline, vancomycin, beta-lactams, isoniazid); fever persisting >72h after stopping the drug makes it an unlikely cause (pp.150, 153) DRESS / drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome - often with eosinophilia and extensive lymphadenopathy (p.150) Benign or exercise-induced hyperthermia - elevated temperature WITHOUT raised CRP/ESR or other inflammation; may be postinfectious (triggers similar to chronic fatigue syndrome: EBV, Q fever, COVID-19) (p.150) Factitious fever - artificially induced (e.g., IV injection of contaminated water); suspect with access to medical equipment (p.150) Fraudulent fever - patient is normothermic but manipulates the thermometer; simultaneous multi-site measurement (rectum/ear/mouth) and pulse-temperature dissociation are clues (p.150) Central thermoregulatory disorders - brain tumor, stroke, encephalitis, hypothalamic dysfunction (p.151) Peripheral thermoregulatory causes - hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, heat stroke (p.151) Current (post-Petersdorf) FUO definition requires all of: fever >=38.3C (101F) on at least two occasions, illness lasting at least 3 weeks, no known immunocompromised state, and a diagnosis still uncertain after thorough history, examination, and a defined set of obligatory investigations (p.149). Inflammation of unknown origin (IUO) shares the FUO definition but lacks the temperature criterion (elevated CRP/ESR with normal temperature); its causes and workup are identical to FUO (p.149). FUO usually reflects an ATYPICAL presentation of a COMMON disease rather than a rare disease; pattern recognition explains the higher diagnostic yield at expert centers (pp.150, 153). The cornerstone of the workup is the search for potentially diagnostic clues (PDCs) - all localizing signs, symptoms, and abnormalities pointing toward a diagnosis - via repeated history, examination, and obligatory tests; further testing should be PDC-driven (pp.152-153). Examination should pay special attention to the eyes, lymph nodes, temporal arteries, liver, spleen, prior surgical sites, the entire skin surface, and mucous membranes (p.152). History should capture fever pattern (continuous vs recurrent) and duration, prior medical history, current/recent drugs, family and sexual history, country of origin, recent and remote travel, environmental/hobby exposures, and animal contacts (p.152). Giant cell arteritis is notably prevalent among FUO patients, with rates up to 17% in the elderly; temporal artery biopsy is still recommended for patients >=55 years (p.153). FUO with headache should prompt CSF microbiologic examination for herpes simplex virus (especially type 2), Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii, and M. tuberculosis (p.153). In patients with recurrent/episodic FUO, ask the patient to return DURING a febrile episode; further tests should be done during an inflammatory episode since abnormalities may be absent between episodes (pp.152-153). Geography shapes the differential: infections (especially TB) dominate non-Western cohorts, while noninfectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs) are the most common cause in Western cohorts, accounting for up to one-third of cases (p.150). Investigation of cryoglobulins is a useful low-cost screening test in FUO given the frequent absence of specific symptoms (p.153). Clinical deterioration without new PDCs - the trigger to escalate workup (rather than wait) and the situation where empirical therapy may be justified (pp.152-153) Hemodynamic instability or neutropenia - good indications for empirical antibiotic therapy (p.155) Granulomatous disease on liver or bone marrow biopsy - should prompt (re)consideration of miliary tuberculosis (p.153) Early phase of evaluation carries the highest FUO-related mortality risk (deaths occurred during index admission in cohort data; intravascular lymphoma and pneumonia found at autopsy) (p.154) Starting empirical therapeutic trials before a diagnosis - should be AVOIDED except when the patient is rapidly deteriorating, because most undiagnosed patients resolve spontaneously (p.154). Continuing antibiotics/glucocorticoids during workup - they mask disease: cultures become unreliable and glucocorticoids shrink lymph nodes regardless of cause; stop them before further testing (p.152). Early empirical glucocorticoids - can mask fever while infection or lymphoma spreads and reduce the chance of diagnosing a treatable malignancy; avoid until infection and lymphoma are sufficiently excluded (p.155). Ordering more screening tests without PDCs - low yield; immunologic and microbiologic serologies without PDCs more often give false-positives; better to wait for new PDCs unless the patient deteriorates (pp.153-154). Over-culturing - performing >3 blood cultures or >1 urine culture is useless absent PDCs (p.153). Failing to recognize PDCs already present in available information is a frequent cause of diagnostic delay (p.154). Interpreting a negative TST/IGRA as excluding TB - it does not; results may be indeterminate in miliary TB, malnutrition, immunosuppression, or with anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies (p.153). Misreading PET/CT - physiologic FDG uptake in brain, heart, bowel, kidneys, and bladder can obscure pathology (e.g., cardiac uptake masking endocarditis - mitigate with a pre-scan low-carbohydrate diet) (p.153). Not excluding factitious/fraudulent fever and drug fever early, especially when inflammatory markers are normal (pp.150, 153). FUO is a syndrome, not a single disease - a final prolonged febrile illness in which intensive standard evaluation has failed to localize a cause. Etiologies cluster into four groups: infections, noninfectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs: autoimmune, autoinflammatory, granulomatous, and vasculitides), malignancy, and miscellaneous, with a substantial undiagnosed fraction. The spectrum has shifted over time: intraabdominal abscesses, tumors, and infective endocarditis have declined as CT, ultrasound, blood culture, and echocardiography improved, while entities such as acute HIV and autoinflammatory syndromes are now recognized. NIIDs may precede their typical clinical or laboratory features by months, requiring prolonged observation. The 'FUO paradox' describes how, despite better imaging (CT/MRI/PET-CT), the undiagnosed proportion is now higher (>50% in some Western cohorts) because most febrile illnesses are diagnosed before 3 weeks elapse, leaving only the most difficult cases to meet FUO criteria (pp.149-150). Prognosis depends chiefly on the underlying diagnosis. When FUO remains unexplained after extensive evaluation, outlook is favorable: large cohorts report high rates of spontaneous fever resolution and mortality of 8% or less over several years of follow-up. The greatest mortality risk is during the early diagnostic phase. A normal 18F-FDG-PET/CT is associated with higher rates of spontaneous resolution and may help predict who will resolve. A symptom duration >12 months and a normal PET/CT both lower the chance of ever reaching a final diagnosis (pp.150, 154). FUO categories (by host/setting), each requiring a distinct approach: (1) classic FUO - the immunocompetent adult per the formal definition; (2) nosocomial FUO; (3) neutropenic FUO; and (4) HIV-associated FUO. The contemporary Harrison definition explicitly EXCLUDES immunocompromised states, which need a different, more aggressive approach. Etiologies are grouped into four diagnostic categories - infections, noninfectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs), malignancy, and miscellaneous - with a large 'no diagnosis' fraction (pp.149-150).

Acute Pyelonephritis — Urine culture and sensitivity — Confirms organism and susceptibility, essential for targeted therapy and de-escalation. Blood cultures — Pyelonephritis carries meaningful bacteremia risk; positive cultures confirm systemic involvement and guide duration. Renal ultrasound or CT (if no improvement in 48-72 hours) — Evaluates for obstruction or abscess if the patient fails to improve on appropriate therapy. Acute prostatitis in men presenting with febrile UTI (Harrison 22e p.1137) Complicated UTI (fever in a patient with structural/functional urinary abnormality, immunocompromise, or instrumentation) (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134) Sexually transmitted infection mimicking UTI, particularly Chlamydia trachomatis cervicitis/urethritis (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134) Renal/ureteral calculus with obstruction (renal colic) presenting with flank pain and pyuria (Harrison 22e p.2493) Acute prostatitis (Harrison 22e p.1137) Cervicitis or urethritis due to Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134) Vaginitis (Candida albicans, Trichomonas vaginalis) or herpetic urethritis causing dysuria (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134) Upper-tract imaging (CT or renal ultrasound) to evaluate for obstruction, abscess, or anatomic abnormality, especially in men, in patients not responding within 72 hours, or when complicated infection is suspected (Harrison 22e p.1132, 1137) Urine dipstick (nitrite, leukocyte esterase) and microscopic urinalysis as point-of-care tests; note nitrites detect only Enterobacterales and may be falsely negative with non-Enterobacterales organisms (Harrison 22e p.1134-1135) Imaging for gas in renal/perinephric tissues when emphysematous pyelonephritis is suspected in a diabetic patient (Harrison 22e p.1090) Renal/ureteral stone with proximal obstruction, which may present exactly as acute pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.2493) Interstitial cystitis or noninfectious vulvovaginal irritation causing dysuria (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134) Sloughed renal papilla or blood clot causing ureteral obstruction without infection (Harrison 22e p.2493) Musculoskeletal flank/back pain, herpes zoster, abdominal aortic aneurysm, duodenal ulcer (differential for flank pain) (Harrison 22e p.2493) Fever is the principal feature distinguishing pyelonephritis from simple cystitis; presence of fever, back/flank pain, rigors, nausea or vomiting signals infection that has extended beyond the bladder (Harrison 22e p.1086-1090, 1133). Severity spans a wide spectrum: mild disease may present only with low-grade fever with or without costovertebral angle pain, whereas severe disease manifests with high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain; onset is generally acute and may or may not be preceded by cystitis symptoms (Harrison 22e p.1090). Pyelonephritis represents tissue-invasive disease and patients are often systemically ill, so the threat of progression to bacteremia and urosepsis is real (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137, 1329). In a woman presenting with at least one localizing urinary symptom (dysuria, frequency, hematuria, or back pain) and no complicating factors, the combined probability of acute cystitis or pyelonephritis is about 50% (Harrison 22e p.1133). Men with febrile UTI should undergo upper-tract imaging (CT or ultrasound) if not done previously, to evaluate for urinary tract abnormality or obstruction, and elevated PSA with enlarged prostate/seminal vesicles suggests prostatic involvement (Harrison 22e p.1132). Pregnant patients are at unusually high risk of developing pyelonephritis, which can adversely affect pregnancy outcome (preterm delivery, low birth weight); this underlies routine prenatal screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria (Harrison 22e p.1086, 1329). Acute papillary necrosis with sloughed papillae obstructing the ureter, producing obstructive uropathy that requires intervention to relieve obstruction and preserve renal function (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137) UTI in the setting of ureteral obstruction is a medical emergency requiring immediate restoration of drainage by ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy (Harrison 22e p.2493) Emphysematous pyelonephritis: gas production in renal and perinephric tissues, occurring almost exclusively in patients with poorly controlled diabetes; a particularly severe form (Harrison 22e p.1090) Continued fever and/or bacteremia despite antibacterial therapy should raise suspicion for intraparenchymal, perinephric, or renal cortical abscess (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137) Failure of clinical response within 72 hours warrants evaluation for an uncontrolled source of infection (Harrison 22e p.1137) Persistently elevated/increasing fever, flank pain, and rising neutrophil counts should prompt evaluation for intrarenal/perinephric abscess and/or obstruction (Harrison 22e p.1329) Bilateral papillary necrosis may present first as a rapid rise in serum creatinine (Harrison 22e p.1090) Treating presumed UTI when the true cause is an STI (e.g., C. trachomatis); vaginal discharge should prompt STI consideration since symptoms alone do not reliably distinguish them (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134). Stopping the workup at an abnormal urinalysis in a catheterized or febrile patient: pyuria and bacteriuria are expected with catheterization and do not by themselves establish UTI as the cause of fever (Harrison 22e p.1133-1135). Mistaking an obstructing stone with proximal infection for uncomplicated pyelonephritis and missing the need for emergent drainage (Harrison 22e p.2493). Misattributing xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis to renal malignancy because its mass effect can mimic tumor (Harrison 22e p.1090). Delayed/withheld antimicrobial therapy in true UTI carries a small increased risk of progression to pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.1136). Pyelonephritis usually develops as an ascending infection: uropathogens move from the urethra to the bladder and then continue up the ureter to the renal parenchyma, which is the route for most renal parenchymal infection. Its microbiology therefore mirrors that of acute cystitis. A minority arises hematogenously (<2% of UTIs overall), typically with relatively virulent organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Salmonella; isolation of either from urine should prompt consideration of concomitant bacteremia, and hematogenous seeding can produce focal renal abscesses. Anatomic factors causing urinary obstruction or retention (congenital anomalies, cystocele, pelvic-organ prolapse, neurogenic bladder, benign prostatic hypertrophy) impede the protective flushing action of micturition and predispose to renal involvement. A foreign body such as a stone or catheter provides an inert surface for colonization (Harrison 22e p.1088, 1130-1131). Most pyelonephritis treated effectively resolves, though fever may take 5-7 days to clear completely even with appropriate therapy. Renal parenchymal damage and loss of renal function are uncommon and occur primarily in association with urinary obstruction (preexisting, or, rarely, de novo in diabetic patients with papillary necrosis). Chronic bacterial pyelonephritis is rarely a cause of chronic renal failure because it seldom affects both kidneys. Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis arises from chronic obstruction (often staghorn calculus) plus chronic infection causing suppurative destruction of renal tissue and frequently requires nephrectomy (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137, 1329, 2493). Harrison describes a clinical spectrum rather than a formal score: mild pyelonephritis (low-grade fever, with or without lower back or costovertebral angle pain) versus severe pyelonephritis (high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, flank pain). Distinct severe/complicated entities include emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas-forming, almost exclusively in poorly controlled diabetes), xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (chronic obstruction plus infection causing suppurative renal destruction), and pyelonephritis complicated by papillary necrosis with obstruction or by intrarenal/perinephric abscess. Acute pyelonephritis is one of the systemic UTI presentations that may be grouped as urosepsis or febrile UTI, with or without bacteremia (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1329).

Diagnosis is one of exclusion; there is no single confirmatory laboratory or histologic test Ulcer base often shows purulent, necrotic tissue with a boggy, undermined edge rather than a clean infected wound and pursuing aggressive debridement, which can worsen the ulcer through pathergy Assuming a positive wound culture confirms infection rather than colonization of a chronic ulcer Delaying diagnosis by relying on a single confirmatory test rather than the clinical picture and exclusion of mimics Missing an underlying systemic disease (IBD, arthritis, hematologic disorder) that drives disease activity and recurrence risk Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis thought to arise from dysregulated innate immune activation and neutrophil chemotaxis/function, often in a genetically predisposed host. Cytokine-driven neutrophilic infiltration in the skin, without a demonstrable infectious trigger, produces sterile abscess-like tissue destruction. The tendency for lesions to develop at sites of trauma (pathergy) reflects this exaggerated local inflammatory response. Its frequent association with inflammatory bowel disease, inflammatory arthritides, and myeloid dyscrasias suggests a shared systemic inflammatory or clonal process in many patients. Course is variable and often relapsing, particularly when an underlying systemic disease remains active; lesions can heal with characteristic cribriform (atrophic, often hyperpigmented) scarring. Prompt recognition, avoidance of unnecessary surgical intervention, and treatment of any associated systemic condition improve outcomes.

blennorrhagicum and circinate balanitis — can mimic psoriasis or STI-related dermatoses Synovial fluid is inflammatory and sterile; cultures and PCR are negative for the triggering organism, fluid culture and clinical correlation Missing the diagnosis in incomplete presentations lacking the full urethritis-arthritis-conjunctivitis triad Overlooking a preceding GI or GU infection because the interval before joint symptoms can be several weeks Confusing mucocutaneous lesions (keratoderma blennorrhagicum, circinate balanitis) with psoriasis or sexually transmitted skin disease Reactive arthritis is thought to result from an aberrant immune response to bacterial antigens (or bacterial components/DNA persisting in synovium) following a distant mucosal infection, rather than from direct joint infection. HLA-B27 appears to shape the immune response to these triggering pathogens, promoting a sterile inflammatory synovitis, enthesitis, and mucocutaneous inflammation. It is classified with the spondyloarthritis family, sharing pathogenic overlap with ankylosing spondylitis and psoriatic arthritis. Most episodes resolve within 3-12 months with appropriate anti-inflammatory management, but relapses and progression to chronic spondyloarthritis occur in a meaningful minority, particularly HLA-B27-positive individuals. Chronic disease may involve persistent enthesitis, axial disease, or recurrent ocular inflammation requiring long-term rheumatologic follow-up.

Rickettsial Fever (Spotted Fever Group) — Careful skin examination for eschar and rash characterization — Helps distinguish spotted fever group rickettsiosis (maculopapular/petechial rash, no eschar) from scrub typhus (eschar), though management is similar. Rickettsial serology (IgM/IgG, species-specific where available) or Weil-Felix (less specific) — Supports diagnosis, though treatment should not be delayed pending results when clinical suspicion is high. CBC, LFTs, renal function — Assesses organ involvement; thrombocytopenia and transaminitis are common supportive findings. Human monocytotropic ehrlichiosis (Ehrlichia chaffeensis) and human granulocytotropic anaplasmosis (Anaplasma phagocytophilum) - tick-borne, often rashless, share thrombocytopenia/leukopenia/transaminitis (p.1455-1457) Epidemic (louse-borne) typhus (R. prowazekii) and recrudescent Brill-Zinsser disease (p.1458) Murine (endemic) typhus (R. typhi) (p.1458-1459) Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) (p.1455) Influenza and enteroviral infection (mimic early rashless RMSF) (p.1457) Infectious mononucleosis (p.1457) Viral hepatitis (p.1457) Leptospirosis (p.1457; shares epidemiologic and clinical features, dual infection reported, p.1488) Typhoid fever (epidemic typhus is frequently misdiagnosed as typhoid in tropical countries) (p.1457-1458) Gram-negative or gram-positive bacterial sepsis / septic shock (p.1457) Meningococcemia and disseminated gonococcal infection (p.1457) Secondary syphilis (p.1457) Measles (rubeola) and rubella (p.1457) Dengue and hantavirus infection (share epidemiologic and clinical features) (p.1488) Indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) for SFG IgG - the most common confirmatory test; sensitivity 89-100% and specificity 99-100%, but a reactive titer (>=64) is not detectable until 7-10 days after onset and is usually negative at presentation (p.1458) Immunohistologic examination or PCR of a 3-mm punch biopsy of a rash lesion - the only test useful during acute illness (immunohistology ~70% sensitive, 100% specific; PCR likely higher) (p.1458) PCR of eschar biopsy or eschar swab, or skin biopsy, for SFG rickettsiae (p.1458) Note: PCR of peripheral blood is NOT adequately sensitive because circulating organism quantities are low (p.1458) Platelet count, WBC count, hepatic aminotransferases, serum sodium, and renal function as supportive clues (p.1454-1457) CSF analysis if meningoencephalitis suspected (typically 10-100 cells/uL, mononuclear predominance, normal glucose, mildly elevated protein) (p.1456-1457) Drug hypersensitivity reaction (p.1457) Immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura (p.1457) Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (p.1457) Kawasaki syndrome (p.1457) Immune complex vasculitis (p.1457) Toxic shock syndrome (p.1457) All acute rickettsial illnesses look alike for roughly the first 5 days: fever, headache, and myalgias, often with nausea, vomiting, or cough; the distinguishing features (rash, eschar, pneumonitis, meningoencephalitis) emerge only as the illness progresses (p.1454). An inoculation eschar (tache noire) is a necrotic, often painless black-crusted lesion with a surrounding erythematous halo at the bite site; it can appear during the incubation period and is common in Mediterranean spotted fever (~50%), African tick-bite fever (~90%), and rickettsialpox (~90%), but is essentially absent in classic RMSF (<1%) and in epidemic/murine typhus (p.1455). African tick-bite fever (R. africae) is the rickettsiosis most often imported into Europe and North America via travelers returning from sub-Saharan Africa; because Amblyomma ticks feed in groups, multiple eschars and regional lymphadenopathy are characteristic, and rash may be vesicular, sparse, or absent (p.1457-1458). In RMSF the rash is centrifugal and evolving: erythematous macules begin on wrists and ankles, spread to extremities and trunk, and only later involve palms and soles; macules progress to non-blanching petechiae as vascular damage advances (p.1456). Palm/sole involvement and the classic centripetal/centrifugal spread are late and inconsistent: in RMSF palms/soles are involved after day 5 in only ~43% and never in 18-64% of cases (p.1457). The full classic triad of fever, rash, and recalled tick exposure is present in only ~3% of RMSF patients during the first 3 days, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1457). Characteristic supportive labs across rickettsioses are thrombocytopenia, a normal or low (not elevated) WBC count, mildly elevated hepatic aminotransferases, and hyponatremia (p.1454-1456); hyponatremia in RMSF (~56%) reflects appropriate ADH secretion in a hypovolemic state (p.1457). Spotted fever group serology cross-reacts among species, so a positive titer confirms a SFG rickettsiosis but generally cannot identify the specific organism (p.1458). Hypotension/septic-shock presentation and multiorgan failure (p.1454, p.1457) Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS requiring mechanical ventilation (RMSF: ARDS ~12%) (p.1456-1457) Encephalitis - confusion, lethargy, stupor, delirium, ataxia, seizures, or coma (p.1456-1457) Acute kidney injury from acute tubular necrosis in shock (p.1457) Skin necrosis, peripheral gangrene, or purpura fulminans (severe MSF) (p.1454; p.1488 / Ch.21) Gastrointestinal hemorrhage; severe anemia requiring transfusion (p.1457) Fulminant RMSF (fatal within 5 days), especially in male patients with G6PD deficiency (p.1457) Extremes of age (children <10 years, adults >70 years) and immunosuppression - higher case-fatality (p.1456-1457) Waiting for serology before treating: SFG serology is typically negative at presentation and only turns positive at 7-10 days, so therapy must be started empirically on clinical and epidemiologic suspicion and never delayed for a confirmatory titer (p.1454, p.1458). Excluding the diagnosis because there is no rash or no recalled tick bite: ~10-15% of RMSF patients never develop a rash, rash is present in only ~14% on day 1 and ~49% by day 3, and only ~60% recall a tick bite (p.1455-1457). Treating a positive early SFG titer as proof of current disease: in areas with prevalent low-virulence SFG species (e.g., R. amblyommatis), a positive titer in the first 5-6 days often reflects preexisting cross-reactive antibody, not the acute illness (p.1456, p.1458). Misattributing abdominal pain/vomiting to enterocolitis (has led to unnecessary laparotomy) or CNS findings to primary meningoencephalitis (p.1457). Using ineffective or harmful agents: beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, and erythromycin have no role in RMSF, and sulfa drugs are associated with worse outcomes than no treatment (p.1458). Missing the eschar: it can be small, painless, and located in skinfolds/scalp and frequently goes unnoticed by patient and clinician, yet careful skin examination for an eschar is a key diagnostic clue (p.1454-1459). Rickettsiae and Orientia are obligately intracellular gram-negative coccobacilli that primarily infect vascular endothelial cells. After tick saliva inoculates organisms into the dermis (in RMSF after roughly 6 h of feeding), they spread lymphohematogenously and infect contiguous foci of endothelium throughout the body, producing a widespread infectious vasculitis with increased vascular permeability. The resulting edema, hypovolemia, and tissue ischemia (rather than occlusive thrombosis) drive the organ injury: prerenal azotemia, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and CNS dysfunction. Platelet consumption causes thrombocytopenia in about a third to half of RMSF cases, but frank DIC with hypofibrinogenemia is rare; the coagulation changes appear to be homeostatic responses to endothelial injury forming nonocclusive hemostatic plugs (p.1454, p.1456). Outcome is strongly time-dependent: untreated RMSF carries mortality of roughly 20-25% (historic) with confirmed-case fatality around 9-10% where R. rickettsii is the sole agent, versus ~3-5% when treated early; delayed recognition and treatment markedly increase death. For unclear reasons RMSF case-fatality approaches 50% in Mexico and Brazil. Severe Mediterranean spotted fever has mortality near 50% without treatment but improves dramatically with even a single day of appropriate therapy. Untreated epidemic typhus historically killed up to 60% and still exceeds 10-15% in outbreaks. Many survivors of severe RMSF recover fully, but permanent neurologic deficits and gangrene requiring amputation can follow severe illness (p.1456-1457; p.1488 / Ch.21). Harrison does not give a formal grading scale, but stratifies along a spectrum: (1) self-limited febrile illness that resolves without evolution; (2) classic disease with rash and/or eschar; and (3) severe/complicated disease with organ involvement - pneumonitis/ARDS, meningoencephalitis, acute kidney injury, hemorrhage/skin necrosis/gangrene, sepsis/septic shock, and (rarely) fulminant RMSF fatal within 5 days. Higher-risk groups include children <10 years, adults >70 years, the immunosuppressed, and (for fulminant RMSF) males with G6PD deficiency (p.1454-1457).

adequately excluding infectious mimics (especially TB and fungal disease) can worsen unrecognized infection Relying solely on elevated CSF or serum ACE for diagnosis, as this is neither sensitive nor specific Assuming a favorable steroid response confirms sarcoidosis, since infections and other inflammatory conditions may also improve transiently Overlooking neurosarcoidosis in a patient without known systemic sarcoidosis, since isolated CNS presentation occurs in a meaningful subset of cases Neurosarcoidosis results from non-caseating granulomatous inflammation infiltrating the meninges, cranial nerves, hypothalamic-pituitary axis, brain parenchyma, or spinal cord. The granulomas provoke a perivascular and leptomeningeal inflammatory response that can cause direct compressive or infiltrative neurologic deficits, hydrocephalus from impaired CSF flow, or vasculopathy. Because it is part of a systemic multisystem granulomatous disease, isolated CNS presentations without other organ involvement are diagnostically challenging. Course is variable — many patients respond to immunosuppressive therapy with partial or complete resolution, but a subset experience chronic, relapsing, or progressive disease, particularly with parenchymal brain or spinal cord involvement, which carries a worse functional outcome.

Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis — Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic fluid cell count and culture — Defines the diagnosis (neutrophil count ≥250/mm³) and identifies the organism for targeted therapy — essential before committing to a full antibiotic course where feasible. Blood cultures — Frequently positive and may identify the organism even when ascitic fluid culture is negative (culture-negative neutrocytic ascites). Renal function tests — Guides decision on adjunctive albumin and assesses for hepatorenal syndrome, a major complication of SBP. Liver function tests and coagulation profile — Establishes baseline severity of underlying liver disease, relevant to prognosis and overall management. Secondary bacterial peritonitis from a perforated or inflamed viscus or intraabdominal abscess (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071) Hepatic encephalopathy from other precipitants (GI bleed, volume depletion, hyponatremia, constipation) when SBP presents as altered mentation (Harrison 22e p.2716-2717) Acute kidney injury / hepatorenal syndrome from non-infectious causes when SBP presents as renal deterioration (Harrison 22e p.329, 2716) Secondary bacterial peritonitis (perforated viscus, ruptured appendix/diverticulum/ulcer, intraabdominal abscess) (Harrison 22e p.1071-1072) Spontaneous bacterial empyema complicating hepatic hydrothorax (Harrison 22e p.330) Tuberculous peritonitis (ascitic lymphocytosis; can complicate or mimic infected ascites) (Harrison 22e p.373) Ascitic fluid PMN/neutrophil count (>=250/microL is diagnostic) (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070) Ascitic fluid inoculated into blood-culture bottles at the bedside (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070) Gram stain of ascitic fluid (often negative; does not exclude SBP) (Harrison 22e p.1070) Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) and ascitic total protein to characterize the underlying ascites and assess risk (Harrison 22e p.372) Ascitic glucose and LDH when secondary peritonitis is suspected (Harrison 22e p.373) Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT to seek an intraabdominal source / exclude secondary peritonitis (Harrison 22e p.1070-1071) Chest and abdominal radiography to exclude free air (perforation) when abdominal pain is present (Harrison 22e p.1070) Repeat paracentesis at 48 hours to confirm >=25% fall in ascitic PMN count (Harrison 22e p.329) Peritoneal carcinomatosis / malignant ascites (low-SAAG ascites;
