SBP is rare in malignant ascites) (Harrison 22e p.372-373) Pancreatic ascites (high ascitic amylase, typically >1000) (Harrison 22e p.373) Worsening uncomplicated tense ascites with increased girth but no infection (Harrison 22e p.329) An ascitic-fluid PMN (neutrophil) count of at least 250/microL is diagnostic of SBP, irrespective of whether cultures grow an organism (Harrison 22e p.329, 372, 1070). Fever is the single most common manifestation, present in roughly 80% of cases; abdominal pain, acute onset, and peritoneal signs aid diagnosis but their absence does not rule SBP out (Harrison 22e p.1070). Abdominal tenderness is found in only about 40% of patients and rebound tenderness is uncommon, so a benign abdomen does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.329). SBP can present with no abdominal symptoms at all, instead manifesting as new or worsening hepatic encephalopathy, altered mental status, jaundice, or acute kidney injury without another explanation (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070, 2715). In any cirrhotic patient hospitalized with ascites who deteriorates or shows signs of infection, a diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory; tapping within 12 hours of admission lowers mortality through early SBP detection (Harrison 22e p.329, 2715). Ascitic fluid should be injected directly into blood-culture bottles at the bedside to improve yield, and blood cultures drawn simultaneously, since the organism burden in the fluid is low and bacteremia frequently coexists (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070). Culture samples should be obtained before antibiotics are started to maximize recovery of the organism (Harrison 22e p.1070). SBP is almost always monomicrobial; a single isolate is the rule (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070). Gram stain of ascitic fluid is frequently negative in SBP and a negative result should not deter treatment (Harrison 22e p.1070). SBP virtually always arises on a background of preexisting ascites, which predates the infection (Harrison 22e p.1070). A repeat paracentesis after 48 hours of therapy should confirm at least a 25% fall in the ascitic PMN count from baseline; failure to fall, or persistent ascitic leukocytosis after treatment, should prompt a search for an alternative or secondary diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071). New or worsening hepatic encephalopathy or altered mental status in a cirrhotic with ascites (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070, 2715) Unexplained acute kidney injury, jaundice, or nonlocalizing malaise/fatigue in a susceptible patient (Harrison 22e p.1070) Multiple organisms recovered from ascitic fluid, especially with anaerobes, suggesting secondary peritonitis requiring source control (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071) Free air under the diaphragm on imaging, signaling perforation (Harrison 22e p.1070) Concurrent GI/variceal bleeding, which markedly increases SBP frequency (Harrison 22e p.330, 2716) Failure of the ascitic PMN count to fall, or persistence of WBCs after therapy, indicating treatment failure or an alternative diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071) Diagnosis rests on the ascitic PMN count >=250/microL, not on a positive culture; ascitic cultures are often negative because the organism burden is low (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070). Recovery of more than one organism (a mixed flora, especially with anaerobes) alongside an elevated PMN count points to SECONDARY peritonitis from a ruptured viscus or abscess, not SBP, and demands a search for a surgical source (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071). Multiple organisms WITHOUT an elevated PMN count suggest bowel perforation by the paracentesis needle rather than true infection (Harrison 22e p.329). Failing to perform a diagnostic paracentesis in a decompensated cirrhotic who deteriorates (encephalopathy, AKI, sepsis) misses SBP, since the abdomen may be benign and tenderness is present in only ~40% (Harrison 22e p.329, 2715). A low ascitic total protein (<1.0-1.5 g/dL) reflects low opsonic activity and identifies patients at higher risk for SBP; this group warrants heightened suspicion (Harrison 22e p.330, 1071). The 250/microL PMN threshold is specific to SBP and should not be applied to secondary peritonitis or to peritoneal-dialysis peritonitis, where lower leukocyte cutoffs are used (Harrison 22e p.1070, p.2486 context). Gastric acid suppression (e.g., proton-pump inhibitors) has been associated with increased SBP risk in observational data (Harrison 22e p.1071). SBP is spontaneous infection of ascitic fluid in the absence of an intraabdominal surgical source. The presumed mechanism is bacterial translocation: gut flora cross an edematous, leaky intestinal wall into mesenteric lymph nodes, producing bacteremia that seeds the ascites, which is a good growth medium. Susceptibility in cirrhosis reflects impaired hepatic filtration from a diseased liver and altered portal circulation, low ascitic complement levels (lower than in non-cirrhotic ascites), and diminished opsonic and phagocytic function of PMNs in advanced liver disease. Cirrhosis is also associated with gut dysbiosis (increased Enterobacteriaceae), small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth, reduced Paneth-cell defensins, decreased intestinal motility, reduced pancreatobiliary secretions, and portal-hypertensive enteropathy, all of which promote pathologic translocation. SBP occurs in up to ~30% of hospitalized cirrhotics with ascites but is an uncommon event overall, affecting 10% or fewer of cirrhotic patients. (Harrison 22e p.1070, 2715) SBP is a common and potentially lethal complication of cirrhotic ascites and carries significant morbidity and mortality, largely because it tends to occur in patients with the most advanced liver disease. In-hospital mortality is roughly 17-25%; one tertiary-center series reported ~23% mortality at 30 days and ~37% at 90 days. Recurrence is high, with up to ~70% of patients having another episode within a year. Patients with PBP usually respond to appropriate antibiotics within about 72 hours. The underlying prognosis of cirrhosis with ascites is itself poor, with under 50% surviving 2 years after ascites onset in some series, so SBP should prompt consideration of liver transplantation. (Harrison 22e p.1071, 2715-2716, 373) Harrison does not provide a formal severity grading system specific to SBP. Risk stratification is framed around predictors of poor outcome and renal injury: higher SBP risk in patients with low ascitic-fluid total protein (<1.0-1.5 g/dL), impaired renal function (creatinine >=1.2 mg/dL, BUN >=25 mg/dL, or serum sodium <=130 mEq/L), and advanced liver failure (Child-Turcotte-Pugh score >=9, bilirubin >=3 mg/dL); these are used to identify candidates for prophylaxis. The greatest benefit of adjunctive albumin is seen in those presenting with serum creatinine >=1 mg/dL, BUN >=30 mg/dL, or total bilirubin >=5 mg/dL. (Harrison 22e p.1071)

Scrub Typhus — Careful skin examination for eschar — Eschar (a painless, often overlooked necrotic lesion at the chigger bite site) is highly specific for scrub typhus when found — actively look in skin folds, axillae, groin. Scrub typhus IgM ELISA / Weil-Felix (less specific) — Confirms diagnosis serologically, though treatment should not wait for results when clinical suspicion is high. CBC, LFTs, renal function — Assesses organ involvement; transaminitis and thrombocytopenia are common supportive findings. Chest X-ray (if respiratory symptoms) — Screens for ARDS, a recognized complication of severe/delayed scrub typhus. Other rickettsioses presenting with eschar, rash, fever and headache (e.g., Mediterranean spotted fever, African tick-bite fever, rickettsialpox, murine and epidemic typhus) (Harrison 22e p.1455-1456). Atypical/community-acquired pneumonia, given the cough and dyspnea of pulmonary involvement (Harrison 22e p.1126). Other undifferentiated tropical febrile illnesses with thrombocytopenia and transaminitis. Serology is the mainstay of laboratory diagnosis: indirect fluorescent antibody, indirect immunoperoxidase, enzyme immunoassays, and rapid lateral-flow chromatographic tests (Harrison 22e p.1460). PCR amplification of Orientia genes is effective when performed on eschar material, but is less sensitive on blood (Harrison 22e p.1460). Platelet count: thrombocytopenia is a characteristic laboratory finding in scrub typhus (as in other rickettsioses) (Harrison 22e p.1455). WBC count is typically normal or low (Harrison 22e p.1455). Serum sodium: hyponatremia is a recognized associated finding across the rickettsioses (Harrison 22e p.1455). Hepatic aminotransferases: mild to moderate elevation is commonly seen (Harrison 22e p.1455). The classic triad of an inoculation eschar at the chigger feeding site, regional lymphadenopathy, and a maculopapular rash is the textbook description, but these signs are seldom seen in indigenous (local endemic) patients (Harrison 22e p.1460). Among returning travelers, fewer than 50% develop an eschar and fewer than 40% develop a rash; when a rash does appear it typically emerges on day 4-6 of illness (Harrison 22e p.1460). Eschar formation occurs at the site of mite/chigger feeding and may develop during the incubation period; an eschar is a useful diagnostic clue that should prompt consideration of scrub typhus (Harrison 22e p.1455). Onset after a 6-21 day incubation is characterized by fever, headache, myalgia, cough, and gastrointestinal symptoms; some patients recover spontaneously after a few days while others progress to severe disease (Harrison 22e p.1460). Chigger bites may be asymptomatic, so the absence of a recalled bite does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3773). Immunity to scrub typhus is short-lived: protection against the homologous strain wanes over 1-3 years, and the organism's marked antigenic diversity means cross-protective immunity can be lost in as little as 1 month, so reinfection is possible (Harrison 22e p.1460). Altered mental status / encephalitis (meningoencephalitis is a feature of severe disease) (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1455). Interstitial pneumonia / pneumonitis with dyspnea or progression toward respiratory failure (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1460). Myocarditis (Harrison 22e p.1035). Signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation or hemorrhage (Harrison 22e p.1035). Renal failure (Harrison 22e p.1035). Progressive hypotension and multiorgan failure (a severe-disease pattern shared by the rickettsioses) (Harrison 22e p.1455). Relying on the classic triad: eschar, rash, and lymphadenopathy are frequently absent (eschar <50% and rash <40% of travelers; signs seldom seen in indigenous patients), so a negative skin exam does not exclude scrub typhus (Harrison 22e p.1460). Expecting a recalled bite: chigger bites may be asymptomatic and the mites are tiny and rarely noticed (Harrison 22e p.3773). Assuming geographic exclusion: although classically eastern/southern Asia, northern Australia, and Pacific/Indian Ocean islands, emerging and reemerging foci (e.g., Chile, parts of South/Central America, Africa, Arabian peninsula via related Orientia species) challenge the traditional epidemiology (Harrison 22e p.1460, p.3773). Note that PCR on blood is less sensitive than PCR on eschar material (Harrison 22e p.1460). Some Thai isolates are poorly responsive to doxycycline or chloramphenicol (Harrison 22e p.1460). Scrub typhus is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, an obligate intracellular organism placed in a separate genus within the family Rickettsiaceae. It differs substantially from Rickettsia species both genetically and in cell-wall composition, notably lacking lipopolysaccharide. Disease results from infection of vascular endothelial cells with increased vascular permeability (a mechanism shared across the rickettsioses). The organism is maintained in nature by transovarial transmission within trombiculid mites; infected larval mites (chiggers, the only mite stage that feeds on a vertebrate host) inoculate the organism into the skin during feeding. Severe disease reflects widespread vascular injury, producing the encephalitis and interstitial pneumonia that characterize advanced cases. Closely related Orientia species (O. chuto, Candidatus O. chiloensis) cause scrub typhus-like illness in newly recognized foci (Harrison 22e p.1455-1456, p.1460, p.3773). Illness ranges from mild and self-limiting to fatal. The case-fatality rate for untreated classic cases is about 6% and would likely be lower if all mild cases were captured; overall reported mortality varies widely by location (cited as 1% to 70%). Risk of death rises with increasing age and with the presence of myocarditis, delirium, pneumonitis, or signs of hemorrhage. Recognized in time, the disease responds well to appropriate antibiotic therapy (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1460). Harrison does not give a formal severity score; it contrasts mild/self-limiting illness with severe disease. Severe scrub typhus is marked by encephalitis/meningoencephalitis and interstitial pneumonia due to vascular injury, and may progress to myocarditis, DIC, renal failure, hypotension, and multiorgan failure (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1455, p.1460).

Sepsis — Blood cultures (x2, before antibiotics if feasible) — Identifies the causative organism and susceptibility for de-escalation. Lactate — Core Sepsis-3/Surviving Sepsis Campaign marker of tissue hypoperfusion; guides resuscitation and risk-stratification toward septic shock. Source-specific cultures (urine, sputum, wound, CSF as guided by clinical exam) — Identifies and confirms the infectious source to allow targeted therapy. CBC, renal function, liver function, coagulation profile — Assesses organ dysfunction (SOFA components) and supports staging severity. Imaging directed by suspected source (CXR, abdominal ultrasound/CT) — Localizes the source and identifies any need for source control (drainage, debridement). Immediate empiric antibiotics required Sepsis mimics, retrospectively found in ~25% of ICU 'sepsis' admissions; continuous reevaluation for an alternative diagnosis is imperative when infection is not confirmed (p.2320) Distributive shock from non-septic causes (e.g., neurogenic shock from brain/spinal-cord injury disrupting vascular autonomic tone) (p.2311) Serum procalcitonin / point-of-care pathogen testing where available to support diagnosis (p.2320) Repeat/serial lactate to gauge response to resuscitation, not just a single value (p.2313) Arterial (or venous) blood gas for acid-base assessment; arterial sampling if hypoxemia present (p.2313) Central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2) as a surrogate of oxygen-delivery adequacy in refractory shock (p.2313) Echocardiography / point-of-care ultrasound for sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy, volume responsiveness, and to exclude mimics (tamponade, PE, pulmonary edema, pneumothorax) (p.2293-2294, 2322) EEG, brain imaging, or lumbar puncture if seizure, stroke, or meningoencephalitis is suspected in a septic patient with neurologic findings (p.2321-2322) Coagulation profile / DIC and sepsis-induced-coagulopathy (SIC) markers - platelets, PT/INR, fibrinogen, fibrin split products (p.2323) Abdominal ultrasound in the septic patient with elevated bilirubin to look for biliary obstruction, cholecystitis, or cholangitis (p.2323) Noninfectious inflammatory febrile syndromes - connective tissue diseases and vasculitides (p.2320) Heart failure and other noninfectious causes of pneumonitis or lung injury (the commonest mimic category in one ICU series was cardiovascular, e.g., heart failure, cardiac arrest) (p.2320) Noninfectious abdominal syndromes - mesenteric ischemia and inflammatory bowel disease (p.2320) Acute pancreatitis (a recognized noninfectious cause of distributive/high-output shock) (p.2293, 2311) Adrenal insufficiency / adrenal crisis (distributive shock from cortisol/aldosterone deficiency, unmasked by stress of infection or surgery) (p.2293, 2311) Severe burns (distributive shock with cellular hypoxia from reduced SVR) (p.2311) Acute liver failure (high-output hypotension) (p.2293, 2311) Anaphylaxis (IgE-mediated distributive shock with rapid plasma extravasation) (p.2311) Thyrotoxicosis and large peripheral arteriovenous shunts (other causes of high-output hypotension) (p.2293) Hypovolemia and autonomic dysfunction as noninfectious causes of hypotension (p.2320) Pulmonary embolism / obstructive shock (acute chest pain, dyspnea, hypoxia in the immobile or malignancy patient) (p.2313) Sepsis-3 (2016) reframes sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, not merely a systemic inflammatory state; the older SIRS-based criteria and the term 'severe sepsis' were discarded for poor specificity (p.2316). Operationally, sepsis is identified by an acute rise of >=2 points in the SOFA score over baseline in a patient with suspected or confirmed infection (p.2320). Septic shock is the subset of sepsis with persistent hypotension needing vasopressors to keep MAP >65 mmHg PLUS lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation, reflecting circulatory, cellular, and metabolic derangement that markedly raises mortality (p.2310, 2320). qSOFA (>=2 of: respiratory rate >=22/min, altered mentation/GCS <15, systolic BP <=100 mmHg) flags infected patients at high risk of poor outcome; it is more specific but less sensitive than SIRS and was NOT designed or endorsed as a standalone diagnostic/screening test for sepsis (p.2292, 2320). There is NO gold-standard diagnostic test for sepsis; the diagnosis is a synthesis of epidemiologic, clinical, laboratory, imaging, and microbiologic data (p.2320). Presentation is frequently nonspecific (fever, tachycardia, lethargy, myalgias) and may lack localizing features; the CNS, kidneys, and skin act as accessible 'windows' onto early organ hypoperfusion (altered mentation, oliguria, mottling/delayed capillary refill) (p.2320, 2312). Hypotension or an isolated low BP reading does not by itself define sepsis/shock; interpret BP against the patient's baseline and look for evidence of organ hypoperfusion, since hypertensive patients can decompensate at 'normal' pressures (p.2312). Absence of tachycardia does not exclude sepsis: nodal-blocking drugs or conduction disease can blunt the compensatory heart-rate response (p.2312). Sepsis is the commonest cause of distributive (high-cardiac-output, low-SVR) shock and of high-output hypotension overall; warm extremities with a wide pulse pressure suggest this physiology (p.2310, 2293). Lactate is central to risk-stratifying sepsis: elevation reflects tissue hypoperfusion/anaerobic metabolism, correlates with worse outcome, and serial measurements help track response to resuscitation (p.2313). Most sepsis is community-onset (~88%); the urinary tract is the single most common primary site, followed by respiratory, intra-abdominal, and skin/soft-tissue sources (p.2316). Hospital-onset sepsis tends to involve sicker, more comorbid patients with more intra-abdominal infection and bacteremia from Enterococcus, Candida, and Pseudomonas, and carries higher ICU admission and mortality (p.2317). Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy (reduced LVEF, dilated LV, RV impairment) affects up to half of septic-shock patients and can convert initial distributive shock into a mixed distributive-cardiogenic picture (p.2311, 2322). qSOFA >=2 (RR >=22, altered mentation, SBP <=100) in suspected infection - identifies the most acutely ill subset with higher mortality and ICU need (p.2292, 2320) Persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors plus lactate >2 mmol/L after adequate fluids = septic shock, with mortality up to ~40% (p.2310, 2316) New altered mental status / encephalopathy or new oliguria as early signs that compensatory mechanisms are exhausted (p.2312) Skin mottling, prolonged capillary refill, cool clammy skin - hypoperfusion (p.2312, 2322) Every hour of delay in appropriate antibiotics in bacterial septic shock raises mortality (estimated 7-8% per hour after shock recognition) - empiric antibiotics within 1 h of shock recognition (p.2320-2321) An infection source needing urgent control (intra-abdominal abscess, bowel perforation, cholangitis, obstructed/infected urinary tract, necrotizing soft-tissue infection, infected indwelling catheter/endovascular infection) - source control as fast as possible (p.2321) Failure to confirm infection should prompt active search for a mimic rather than indefinite empiric antibiotics (antibiotic stewardship: stop antibiotics when sepsis is excluded) (p.2315, 2320) Treating sepsis as a single pathogen rather than a syndrome - empiric therapy and workup must be driven by the most likely source (p.2316). Relying on SIRS criteria or a single abnormal vital sign to rule sepsis in or out - poor specificity led to their abandonment in Sepsis-3 (p.2316). Using qSOFA as a diagnostic test - it is a risk-stratification/screening prompt, not a diagnostic criterion (p.2292, 2320). Being falsely reassured by a normal heart rate (beta-blockade/conduction disease) or by a low BP reading in a chronically hypotensive patient (p.2312). Anchoring on 'sepsis' when infection is unconfirmed - up to a quarter of presumed-sepsis ICU cases are mimics; failure to reevaluate delays the correct diagnosis (p.2320). Continuing broad-spectrum antibiotics once infection is excluded, undermining stewardship and risking C. difficile, allergy, and AKI (p.2315, 2321). Over-resuscitation with fluid - excess volume is likely harmful; targeted, dynamically reassessed resuscitation is the goal (p.2294). Attributing all altered mentation to sepsis-associated encephalopathy without excluding seizure, stroke, or CNS infection (p.2321-2322). Missing sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy, which can turn distributive shock into mixed shock and change management (p.2311, 2322). Sepsis arises when an infection provokes a dysregulated, self-amplifying host response rather than a contained local one. Pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs, e.g., LPS, bacterial cell-wall components, microbial nucleic acids) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs, e.g., histones, HMGB1, S100 proteins, mitochondrial/double-stranded DNA, ATP released from injured cells) are sensed by pattern-recognition receptors (TLRs, CLRs, RAGE, RIG-I, NOD-like receptors) on innate immune and parenchymal cells. This triggers exuberant release of cytokines and chemokines and upregulation of vascular adhesion molecules. Myeloid cells (neutrophils, monocytes, M1 macrophages, dendritic cells) drive injury through phagocytosis, degranulation, reactive oxygen/nitrogen species, and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), while emergency granulopoiesis releases immature neutrophils (a poor-prognosis marker). Lymphoid responses are dysregulated, with lymphocyte apoptosis, exhaustion, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells producing a state of immunosuppression that predisposes survivors to secondary infection. The endothelium is activated and injured: glycocalyx breakdown, loss of VE-cadherin/tight junctions, and apoptosis cause capillary leak, interstitial edema, and a widened oxygen-diffusion distance. A prothrombotic shift (increased tissue factor, vWF, PAI-1; depleted antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, and protein C; complement activation with C3a/C5a and the C5b-9 membrane attack complex) generates microvascular thrombi and, once clotting factors and platelets are consumed, bleeding. Excess nitric oxide drives systemic vasodilation. The net result is impaired oxygen delivery, uptake, and utilization; even when oxygen delivery is adequate, mitochondrial and metabolic dysfunction impairs ATP generation and ion homeostasis, producing multiorgan cellular injury and dysfunction (p.2317-2319). Overall in-hospital mortality is roughly 15% among hospitalized adults with sepsis, rising to up to ~40% with septic shock; globally an estimated ~11 million sepsis-related deaths occur yearly (about one in five deaths worldwide). Mortality climbs with age and is higher in men. Elevated SOFA scores and machine-learning-defined phenotypes track population-level outcome (e.g., alpha/beta/gamma/delta phenotypes with ~2%/5%/15%/32% mortality) but cannot reliably predict an individual patient's outcome. Survivorship carries a heavy long-term burden: physical (prolonged fatigue, muscle loss, weakness, reduced functional capacity), cognitive (cognitive decline, dementia), and psychological (depression, reduced quality of life) sequelae, plus increased risk of cardiovascular events, recurrent infection, and readmission. About half of survivors are rehospitalized within a year and roughly one in six die within the first year, with most post-sepsis deaths in the first 6 months and elevated death risk persisting up to ~2 years (p.2316-2317, 2324). No FDA-approved host-targeted/immunomodulatory therapy exists for sepsis (p.2324). Sepsis-3 (Singer et al., JAMA 2016) is the current framework: (1) Infection (suspected or confirmed) without organ dysfunction is not sepsis. (2) Sepsis = suspected/confirmed infection with an acute increase of >=2 points in the SOFA score from baseline (life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response). The SOFA score grades six systems 0-4: respiratory (PaO2/FiO2), coagulation (platelets), liver (bilirubin), cardiovascular (MAP / vasopressor requirement), CNS (Glasgow Coma Scale), and renal (creatinine / urine output). (3) Septic shock = sepsis with vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP >65 mmHg AND serum lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. qSOFA (>=2 of RR >=22/min, altered mentation, SBP <=100 mmHg) is a rapid bedside risk-stratification prompt for poor outcome in suspected infection, not a diagnostic criterion. The prior 1991/1992 SIRS-based definitions and the term 'severe sepsis' are obsolete under Sepsis-3 (p.2292, 2316, 2320).

Septic Shock — Blood cultures (x2) before antibiotics if no meaningful delay — Identifies organism for urgent de-escalation given the broad initial empiric coverage. Lactate (serial) — Tracks resuscitation adequacy and response to therapy. Source-specific cultures and imaging — Identifies source requiring control (e.g., abscess drainage, line removal). Arterial blood gas — Assesses acid-base status and oxygenation in the context of shock. Central venous/arterial line monitoring as per unit protocol — Guides hemodynamic management alongside antibiotic therapy. Immediate empiric antibiotics required Other causes of distributive shock: pancreatitis, severe burns, liver failure, anaphylaxis, neurogenic shock from brain/spinal cord injury, and adrenal insufficiency/adrenal crisis (p.2353-2354) Cardiogenic shock (myocardial infarction, myocarditis, arrhythmia, acute valvular failure) (p.2353-2354) Hypovolemic shock (hemorrhagic from trauma or GI bleeding; nonhemorrhagic from vomiting, diarrhea, osmotic diuresis in DKA or diabetes insipidus, or skin loss) (p.2353-2354) Obstructive shock (tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, air or fat embolism, aortic dissection) (p.2353-2354) Mixed shock, where more than one mechanism coexists (e.g. distributive sepsis plus sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy) (p.2355) Noninfectious pneumonitis or lung injury that mimics pneumonia/respiratory sepsis (p.2320) Noninfectious abdominal syndromes such as mesenteric ischemia and inflammatory bowel disease, which can mimic an intraabdominal source (p.2320) Complete blood count with differential, basic metabolic panel, and liver function tests to assess end-organ dysfunction (p.2320) Coagulation panel (PT/PTT/INR, platelets) to detect sepsis-induced coagulopathy/DIC (p.2320, p.2356) Cultures of blood and other potentially infected sites (urine, sputum, wound) ideally before antimicrobials, plus point-of-care pathogen testing when available (p.2320) Urinalysis and urine sediment to evaluate for pyuria/urinary source (p.2356, p.2320) Cardiac enzymes/troponin to detect a primary or contributory cardiac process (p.2356) Venous or arterial blood gas (arterial if hypoxemia present) to quantify acidosis (p.2356) Focused imaging (chest x-ray, CT, or ultrasound) of suspected sites; point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS, e.g. RUSH/ACES protocols) helps classify undifferentiated and mixed shock (p.2356) SOFA score components for severity (GCS, MAP/vasopressor use, PaO2/FiO2, bilirubin, creatinine, platelets) (p.2317) Noninfectious inflammatory febrile syndromes including connective tissue diseases and vasculitides (p.2320) Heart failure and cardiac arrest (the most common cardiovascular mimics in ICU series, where ~25% of presumed septic patients were later judged to have a mimic) (p.2320) Noninfectious chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation (common respiratory mimic) (p.2320) Hypotension from noninfectious causes: hypovolemia, autonomic dysfunction, and adrenal insufficiency (p.2320) Septic shock under Sepsis-3 is a subset of sepsis with profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic derangements that carry a higher mortality than sepsis alone; sepsis itself is life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection (p.2316). Sepsis-3 abandoned the older SIRS criteria (used by Sepsis-1/2) because of poor specificity for distinguishing infection from other inflammatory states, and eliminated the term 'severe sepsis' (p.2316). Sepsis is operationalized as an acute rise of at least 2 points in the SOFA score from baseline in a patient with suspected or confirmed infection (p.2320). qSOFA (respiratory rate >=22/min, altered mentation with GCS <15, systolic BP <=100 mmHg) is a rapid bedside screen; a score >=2 is more specific but less sensitive than SIRS and flags patients at higher risk of death, ICU admission, and longer stay (p.2313, p.2320). Sepsis presentation can be nonspecific (fever, tachycardia, lethargy, myalgias) with or without localizing findings; there is no single gold-standard diagnostic test, so the diagnosis integrates clinical, laboratory, microbiologic, and imaging data (p.2320). Approximately 88% of sepsis cases are community onset (detected within 48 h of admission); hospital-onset sepsis (after 48 h) tends to involve more comorbidities, intraabdominal infection, and Enterococcus/Candida/Pseudomonas, with higher ICU admission and mortality (p.2316-2317). Among culture-positive community-onset sepsis, the most common primary sites are urinary tract (~49%), respiratory tract (~33%), intraabdominal (~14%), and skin/soft tissue (~10%) (p.2316). About 53% of US sepsis cases are bacterial culture positive with a roughly even gram-positive / gram-negative split; common gram-positives are S. aureus, Streptococcus, and Enterococcus, and common gram-negatives are E. coli, Klebsiella, and P. aeruginosa (p.2316). Persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to keep MAP >65 mmHg plus lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation defines septic shock and marks the highest-mortality end of the spectrum (p.2320, p.2354) Acute rise of >=2 SOFA points from baseline with suspected infection indicates new organ dysfunction (p.2320) qSOFA >=2 (RR>=22, GCS<15, SBP<=100) signals high risk of death and ICU need (p.2313, p.2320) Elevated and rising serial lactate, which correlates with worse outcome and reflects tissue hypoperfusion (p.2356) Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (altered consciousness, cognition, or behavior) signaling CNS organ dysfunction (p.2319) New oliguria / acute kidney injury, occurring in up to two-thirds of septic patients (p.2319) Signs of coagulopathy/DIC with consumption of platelets and clotting factors and bleeding risk (p.2319) Relying on SIRS criteria to define or exclude sepsis: SIRS lacks specificity, which is why Sepsis-3 replaced it (p.2316). Treating shock as a single entity: distributive (septic) shock has low SVR with high cardiac output and low filling pressures, the opposite hemodynamic profile of cardiogenic and hypovolemic shock, so misclassification leads to wrong resuscitation (p.2353-2354). Assuming a single shock type: sepsis frequently coexists with a cardiogenic component (sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy) or hypovolemia, producing mixed shock that POCUS can help dissect (p.2355). A normal hemoglobin/hematocrit early in concurrent hemorrhage, or a normal WBC, does not exclude the relevant process; leukocytosis is suggestive but not diagnostic of infection (p.2356). Anchoring on sepsis when infection is not confirmed: about 25% of presumed septic ICU patients had a mimic, so alternative diagnoses must be continually reconsidered (p.2320). Failure to identify and control the source (e.g. infected catheter, abscess, endocarditis) undermines management even with appropriate antibiotics (p.2321). Septic shock is the most common form of distributive shock, in which the primary hemodynamic derangement is a fall in systemic vascular resistance (vasoplegia) rather than a primary loss of preload or pump function. The vasodilatory profile is distinctive: SVR is reduced, cardiac output is typically increased as a compensatory response, and both central venous pressure (CVP) and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) tend to be low (p.2353-2354). Arterial and venous vasodilation is mediated in part by excess nitric oxide; vasopressin deficiency may also contribute to refractory hypotension. The dysregulated host response begins when pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs, e.g. LPS, microbial nucleic acids) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs, e.g. histones, HMGB1, mitochondrial DNA, ATP) are sensed by pattern-recognition receptors (TLRs, CLRs, RAGE, RIG-I, NOD receptors) on neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, and parenchymal cells, triggering proinflammatory cytokine/chemokine release and upregulation of endothelial adhesion molecules. Activated neutrophils release reactive oxygen species and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs); endothelial activation/injury, glycocalyx degradation, and loss of VE-cadherin tight junctions cause capillary leak, interstitial edema, and increased oxygen-diffusion distance. A prothrombotic state arises from tissue-factor-driven coagulation, platelet/vWF microthrombi, complement activation (C3a, C5a, C5b-9 membrane attack complex), reduced anticoagulants (antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, activated protein C), and impaired fibrinolysis (elevated PAI-1); consumption of clotting factors and platelets can then produce hemorrhage. The net effect is hypotension (from vasodilation, myocardial depression, and hypovolemia), microcirculatory dysfunction, and mitochondrial/metabolic failure, so that oxygen delivery, uptake, and utilization are all impaired and cellular injury occurs even when bulk oxygen delivery appears adequate (p.2317-2320). Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy can add a cardiogenic component, producing mixed shock (p.2355). Septic shock carries up to ~40% mortality, far higher than the ~15% overall mortality among US hospitalized adults with sepsis (p.2316). In emergency-department shock cohorts, septic and cardiogenic shock have the highest 90-day mortality (reported ~56% and ~52% respectively), and septic shock predominates among ICU shock (~62% of ICU shock patients in one multicenter series), whereas hypovolemic shock has lower mortality (p.2355). Mortality rises with age and is higher in men; comorbidities such as diabetes, obesity, neurologic/respiratory/cardiac disease, renal or hepatic insufficiency, cancer, and immunosuppression worsen outcomes (p.2317). SOFA scores predict mortality at the population level but not for individual patients; proposed clinical 'phenotypes' (alpha/beta/gamma/delta) carried roughly 2%, 5%, 15%, and 32% mortality (p.2317). Survivors face substantial long-term sequelae: physical (fatigue, muscle loss, weakness), cognitive and psychological (cognitive decline, dementia, depression), and increased risk of cardiovascular events, recurrent infection, and readmission. Roughly half of survivors are rehospitalized within 1 year and about one in six die within the first year, with most post-sepsis deaths in the first 6 months and elevated risk persisting up to 2 years (p.2321). Sepsis-3 spectrum: (1) Sepsis = life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection, operationalized as an acute increase of >=2 points in the SOFA score in a patient with suspected/confirmed infection. (2) Septic shock = a subset of sepsis with profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities and higher mortality, operationally defined as a septic patient who, despite adequate fluid resuscitation, requires vasopressors to maintain MAP >65 mmHg AND has serum lactate >2 mmol/L. qSOFA (RR>=22, GCS<15, SBP<=100; score >=2) is a rapid risk-stratification screen, not a diagnosis. The historical Sepsis-1/2 terms 'severe sepsis' and SIRS-based septic shock (SBP<90 or drop >=40 mmHg) have been superseded (p.2316, p.2320).

Severe Community Acquired Pneumonia — Blood cultures (x2) — Bacteremia rate is higher in severe CAP; identifies organism and susceptibility for de-escalation. Sputum culture and Gram stain — Helps target and de-escalate empiric therapy. Urinary antigen (pneumococcal and Legionella) — Rapid, useful for severe presentations to guide targeted therapy. ABG — Quantifies hypoxia/hypercapnia and guides ventilatory support decisions. Chest X-ray / CT chest — Defines extent (multilobar disease, effusion, cavitation) which affects prognosis and management. Lactate — Screens for tissue hypoperfusion and helps gauge severity/sepsis overlap. Immediate empiric antibiotics required Acute bronchitis Exacerbation of chronic bronchitis Heart failure / pulmonary edema Pulmonary embolism Lung carcinoma (including postobstructive pneumonia) Tuberculosis (e.g., upper-lobe cavitating lesion) Tuberculosis Endemic/invasive fungal pneumonia Pneumocystis pneumonia (alveolar process despite interstitial radiographic appearance) CT chest (for suspected loculated effusion, cavitary disease, or postobstructive pneumonia from tumor/foreign body) Deep-suction aspirate or bronchoalveolar lavage in intubated ICU patients (high culture yield when sent promptly) Multiplex respiratory PCR / nasopharyngeal swab PCR (influenza, coronaviruses; also Legionella, M. pneumoniae, C. pneumoniae, mycobacteria) MRSA rapid nasal PCR (to guide adding/de-escalating MRSA coverage) Diagnostic pleural fluid sampling (parapneumonic effusion: drainage indicated if pH <7.2, glucose <2.2 mmol/L, LDH >1000 U/L, or organisms seen/cultured) Stains/cultures for M. tuberculosis and fungi in selected cases Bronchoscopy in delayed responders or worsening disease Pulmonary edema Pulmonary embolism / pulmonary infarction Lung carcinoma Radiation pneumonitis Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Connective tissue disease involving the lungs Neither the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) nor CURB-65 accurately determines the need for ICU admission; they predict mortality/site of care but not ICU need (p.1026). Patients with septic shock requiring vasopressors or acute respiratory failure requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation meet a major criterion and should be admitted directly to an ICU (p.1026). Presence of three or more of the nine minor severe-CAP criteria warrants admission to an ICU or high-level monitoring unit (p.1026). Late or delayed ICU admission is associated with increased mortality; less-ill patients placed on a general ward who then deteriorate fare worse than equally ill patients monitored in the ICU from the outset (p.1026). In ICU-admitted CAP specifically, treatment directed at an identified pathogen may be superior to empirical therapy, so etiologic workup carries more weight in severe disease (p.1025). The microbial spectrum of severe (ICU) CAP differs from milder CAP: Legionella tends to cause more serious disease, and S. aureus and gram-negative bacilli become more prominent (p.1024). Prior respiratory-tract isolation of MRSA or P. aeruginosa within the past year is a stronger (more robust) risk factor for these pathogens than recent hospitalization plus parenteral antibiotic exposure (p.1028). Procalcitonin (PCT) is insufficiently accurate to diagnose bacterial CAP and must NOT be used as a basis for withholding initial antibiotics; CRP is even less sensitive than PCT (p.1026). If only a viral pathogen (e.g., influenza or SARS-CoV-2) is found and no bacterial pathogen is evident, antibacterial therapy can be stopped — BUT in severe illness, bacterial-viral co-infection must still be considered (p.1028). Gross hemoptysis suggests necrotizing pneumonia, e.g., due to CA-MRSA (p.1024). In the elderly, severe CAP may present atypically as new-onset or worsening confusion or decompensation of a chronic illness with few classic respiratory findings (p.1025). Recent data show a mortality benefit for corticosteroids in severe CAP, particularly when there is a high level of systemic inflammation (CRP >15 mg/dL) (p.1029). Septic shock requiring vasopressors (major criterion - direct ICU admission) Acute respiratory failure requiring invasive mechanical ventilation (major criterion - direct ICU admission) Three or more minor severe-CAP criteria (warrants ICU/high-level monitoring) O2 saturation <92% on room air (mandates hospitalization) Multiorgan failure Multilobar infiltrates or cavitation on imaging (increased severity) Gross hemoptysis (suggests necrotizing pneumonia, e.g., CA-MRSA) Failure to improve / deterioration by ~day 3 of therapy Using PSI or CURB-65 to decide ICU admission - neither is accurate for that purpose (p.1026). Withholding initial antibiotics based on a low procalcitonin - PCT is too inaccurate to exclude bacterial CAP (p.1026). Assuming hospitalization alone is a significant risk factor for MRSA or P. aeruginosa - it is no longer considered so; severity plus specific risk factors drive coverage decisions (p.1028). Requiring all three drug-resistance risk factors (recent hospitalization, recent oral/IV antibiotics, local validation) before considering resistant pathogens - any can apply (p.1028). Stopping antibacterials when a virus is identified in a severely ill patient without considering bacterial-viral co-infection (p.1028). Attributing failure to improve to the wrong cause: consider resistant or unexpected pathogen (CA-MRSA, M. tuberculosis, fungus), a sequestered focus (lung abscess, empyema), wrong drug/dose, or nosocomial superinfection (p.1029). Routinely covering anaerobes in aspiration-related severe CAP - unnecessary unless poor dentition, lung abscess, or necrotizing pneumonia (p.1027). Pneumonia results from proliferation of microbial pathogens in the alveoli combined with the host inflammatory response. Organisms reach the lower respiratory tract by inhalation, microaspiration of oropharyngeal flora, or direct mucosal spread; mechanical defenses (nasal hairs/turbinates, the branching airway, mucociliary clearance, gag and cough reflexes) are insufficient to fully exclude bacteria, and the lung is now understood to harbor a microbiota rather than being sterile. An inflammatory/epithelial-endothelial injury event releases cytokines, chemokines, and catecholamines that can selectively promote growth of organisms such as S. pneumoniae and P. aeruginosa, generating a positive-feedback loop; in CAP the trigger is often a viral infection compounded by microaspiration. Inflammatory mediators (IL-6, TNF) cause fever, while IL-8 and G-CSF recruit neutrophils; mediators from macrophages and neutrophils produce alveolar-capillary leak with impaired oxygenation, hypoxemia, and radiographic infiltrates. Some pathogens interfere with hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, worsening hypoxemia. Reduced compliance from capillary leak, increased respiratory drive and secretions, and intrapulmonary shunting drive worsening dyspnea, and when severe, reductions in lung volume/compliance and shunting can precipitate respiratory failure. Pathologically, classic (lobar pneumococcal) pneumonia evolves through edema, red hepatization, gray hepatization, and resolution phases. Prognosis depends on age, comorbidities, and site of treatment. For hospitalized CAP, overall mortality ranges from 12% to 40%, the higher end reflecting ICU-level disease and care-process factors such as timely administration of appropriate antibiotics (vs <5% for outpatients). CURB-65 scores >=3 carry an overall ~22% mortality and may indicate ICU admission; PSI class 5 has a ~29.2% mortality. CAP is a leading infectious cause of death in patients >65 years; about 18% of hospitalized CAP patients are readmitted within a month, and recent data show 1-year mortality after CAP (especially in older patients) exceeds 30-day mortality. Severe-CAP complications (respiratory failure, shock, multiorgan failure) and pneumonia-associated cardiovascular events worsen outcomes. IDSA/ATS severe-CAP criteria (Harrison 22e Table 131-3, p.1026). MAJOR criteria (either qualifies for ICU): (1) respiratory failure requiring invasive mechanical ventilation; (2) septic shock requiring vasopressors. MINOR criteria (>=3 warrant ICU/high-level monitoring): respiratory rate >=30 breaths/min; PaO2/FiO2 ratio <=250; multilobar infiltrates; confusion/disorientation; uremia (BUN >=20 mg/dL); leukopenia (WBC <4000/uL); thrombocytopenia (platelets <100,000/uL); hypothermia (core temperature <36 C); and hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation. Prognostic tools PSI (5 mortality classes, class 5 ~29.2%) and CURB-65 (confusion, urea >7 mmol/L, RR >=30, SBP <=90 or DBP <=60 mmHg, age >=65; score >=3 ~22% mortality) assess severity/site of care but are NOT accurate for determining ICU need.

Acute Sinusitis (Rhinosinusitis) — None routinely required — Diagnosis is clinical; imaging is reserved for suspected complications (orbital/intracranial extension) or recurrent/chronic disease. Common cold / nonspecific upper respiratory infection (p. 298) Allergic rhinitis (p. 298) Vasomotor rhinitis (p. 298) Rhinitis medicamentosa from overuse of topical decongestants (p. 298) Drug-induced rhinitis (e.g., aspirin, ibuprofen, beta blockers) (p. 298) Cerebrospinal fluid leak (p. 298) Headache and facial pain syndromes referred to the sinuses (p. 298) Temporomandibular disorder (p. 298) Dental pathology (p. 298) Gastroesophageal reflux causing referred sinus symptoms (p. 298) Nasal foreign body (especially in children) (p. 298) Bacterial superinfection masquerading within an otherwise viral course (p. 299) Invasive fungal rhinosinusitis (Mucorales or Aspergillus) presenting as rapidly progressive sinusitis in immunocompromised hosts (p. 299) Nosocomial sinusitis in intubated critically ill patients presenting as unexplained fever (p. 299) No imaging or laboratory testing is routinely required for uncomplicated acute sinusitis; diagnosis is clinical (pp. 299-300). Sinus transillumination is NOT accurate for diagnosing sinusitis and should not be relied upon (p. 299). Noncontrast CT is the preferred imaging modality when imaging is indicated (e.g., failure to improve, suspected complication, or alternative diagnosis) (p. 300). Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the preferred imaging modality when invasive fungal sinusitis is suspected (p. 299). Nasal endoscopy with biopsy is part of the evaluation for suspected invasive fungal sinusitis (p. 299). Direct rhinoscopy may reveal excess mucus or purulence on examination (p. 299). In recurrent acute sinusitis, consider nasal culture during episodes, imaging between episodes to identify predisposing anatomic abnormalities, and allergic/immunologic evaluation (p. 300). Autoimmune disease such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis (p. 298) Allergic rhinitis and other noninfectious rhinitides (p. 298) Structural causes such as deviated nasal septum or nasal polyps (noted in chronic disease, p. 300) The vast majority of acute sinusitis cases are caused by respiratory viruses; fewer than 2% of episodes are bacterial, yet antibiotics are prescribed at over 70% of office visits, making sinusitis a leading driver of unnecessary antibiotic use in adults (p. 299). By guideline criteria, no more than about 50% of adults (and probably closer to 20%) with sinusitis actually meet thresholds for antibiotic prescribing (p. 299). Symptoms are classified by duration: acute (<4 weeks), subacute (4-12 weeks), and chronic (>=12 weeks) (p. 298). Common features are purulent nasal discharge, facial congestion/fullness, and facial pain or pressure; additional symptoms include fever, hyposmia or anosmia, ear pressure/pain, postnasal drip, halitosis, maxillary toothache, cough, and fatigue (p. 299). Risk factors include age 45-65 years, smoking, asthma, air travel, and allergies (p. 299). For an individual patient with a nonspecific upper respiratory illness, an antibiotic is more likely to cause an adverse reaction than to prevent a complication such as bacterial sinusitis (p. 296). Recurrent acute sinusitis is defined as four or more episodes of acute sinusitis in a year with no signs or symptoms between episodes (p. 299). Nosocomial sinusitis occurs in critically ill patients, often those who are nasotracheally intubated, and should be suspected in hospitalized patients with fever lacking another identifiable source (p. 299). Confusion (possible intracranial complication) (p. 299) Unilateral weakness (p. 299) Proptosis (p. 299) Limited ocular movements / ophthalmoplegia (p. 299) Acute vision changes (p. 299) Orbital swelling, cellulitis, or chemosis (p. 299) Cranial nerve involvement (p. 299) Rapidly progressive facial pain/pressure with headache and fever in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient (suspect invasive fungal disease - an emergency) (p. 299) Recurrent fever >102 degrees F (p. 300) Sinus symptoms that worsen after an initial improvement (double-sickening pattern) (p. 300) Rapid worsening of facial pain that becomes persistent (p. 300) Treating acute sinusitis as bacterial by default - the large majority are viral, and antibiotics are over-prescribed; reserve antibiotics for patients meeting persistent (>=10 days), severe, or worsening criteria (p. 299). Relying on sinus transillumination, which is inaccurate for diagnosis (p. 299). Prescribing a macrolide for sinusitis - specifically not recommended because of high rates of macrolide-resistant S. pneumoniae (p. 300). Missing invasive fungal sinusitis in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient with rapidly progressive disease - delay can be fatal (p. 299). Overlooking nosocomial sinusitis as a hidden source of unexplained fever in nasotracheally intubated ICU patients (p. 299). In children, failing to consider a nasal foreign body as the cause of sinus symptoms (p. 298). Sinusitis is inflammation of the paranasal sinuses; when the nasal passages are also involved the term rhinosinusitis is used. Most acute disease begins as a viral process. Bacterial sinusitis, when it occurs, is usually a secondary superinfection of the obstructed/inflamed sinus and is most often caused by S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, or M. catarrhalis. Invasive fungal disease arises when host defenses are impaired (uncontrolled diabetes, transplant/immunocompromise), allowing Mucorales or Aspergillus to invade tissue and spread beyond the sinus (pp. 298-299). Most acute sinusitis is viral and self-limited. Symptoms of the underlying upper respiratory illness generally peak early but can persist up to about 14 days (p. 296). Complications of sinusitis can be dramatic but are extremely rare (p. 299). Invasive fungal sinusitis is an emergency: in immunocompromised hosts it can progress within days from rhinosinusitis to cranial nerve involvement, orbital and ophthalmic involvement, and critical illness (p. 299). Antibiotic-prescribing indications (Harrison Table 37-2, p. 299): Persistent = symptoms lasting >=10 days; Severe = fever >102 degrees F with either purulent nasal discharge or nasal pain for at least 3-4 consecutive days; Worsening = new fever, headache, or increased nasal discharge following an upper respiratory infection that had lasted 5-6 days and was initially improving (double-sickening). Duration-based: acute <4 weeks, subacute 4-12 weeks, chronic >=12 weeks (p. 298).

Status epilepticus — status epilepticus, SE, convulsive status epilepticus, non-convulsive status epilepticus, NCSE, refractory status epilepticus, seizure emergency, prolonged seizure Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (functional/dissociative attacks) Syncope with convulsive movements Movement disorders (e.g., dystonic storm, severe tremor) Toxic or metabolic encephalopathy without true seizure activity Rigors or shivering from severe sepsis Post-anoxic myoclonus Bacterial meningitis or meningoencephalitis Viral encephalitis (e.g., herpes simplex encephalitis) Cerebral abscess or CNS tuberculosis with seizures Neurocysticercosis Bedside capillary glucose — rapid identification of reversible hypoglycemic cause Serum electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, renal and liver function — screen for metabolic precipitants Anticonvulsant drug levels (if patient on prior therapy) — detect subtherapeutic levels or nonadherence Toxicology screen — identify intoxication or withdrawal etiology Continuous EEG monitoring — detect non-convulsive status epilepticus and confirm electrographic seizure termination Neuroimaging (CT or MRI brain) — identify structural lesion, hemorrhage, or stroke, generally once initially stabilized Lumbar puncture (after imaging if indicated) — evaluate for CNS infection or inflammation when fever or clinical suspicion present Arterial blood gas and core temperature — assess for acidosis and hyperthermia from prolonged seizure activity Acute stroke or intracerebral hemorrhage Severe metabolic derangement (hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, uremia, hepatic encephalopathy) Drug intoxication or withdrawal (alcohol, benzodiazepine, sedative withdrawal; proconvulsant drug toxicity) Autoimmune or paraneoplastic encephalitis Hypoxic-ischemic brain injury Eclampsia in pregnancy Defined operationally as a single seizure lasting beyond the time most seizures of that type would normally stop (roughly 5 minutes for convulsive seizures) or recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness in between. Treat convulsive status epilepticus as a time-critical emergency — earlier treatment initiation strongly predicts easier termination and better outcome. Airway, breathing, circulation, glucose, and thiamine should be addressed simultaneously with, not after, anticonvulsant therapy. Always check a bedside glucose early; hypoglycemia is a rapidly reversible cause that mimics or precipitates status epilepticus. Non-convulsive status epilepticus should be suspected in any patient with unexplained persistent altered consciousness, especially after a convulsive seizure has been treated but the patient fails to wake up. Continuous EEG monitoring is essential once convulsions have stopped to confirm electrographic seizure resolution, particularly in patients who remain unresponsive. Refractory status epilepticus (persisting despite adequate first- and second-line therapy) generally requires escalation to continuous anesthetic infusions with EEG guidance in an ICU setting. Identifying and treating the underlying etiology is as important as stopping the seizure itself, since ongoing precipitants (e.g., infection, toxin, structural lesion) will otherwise perpetuate the episode. Seizure activity continuing beyond the expected duration without response to initial therapy — escalate treatment promptly Persistent unresponsiveness after convulsions have visibly stopped — evaluate for non-convulsive status epilepticus Hemodynamic instability, hyperthermia, or severe acidosis during prolonged seizure activity Focal neurologic signs or papilledema suggesting an acute structural intracranial process Fever with meningismus suggesting an infectious CNS cause requiring urgent antimicrobial coverage Failure to respond to first- and second-line agents, indicating refractory status epilepticus requiring ICU-level anesthetic therapy Assuming convulsions have stopped means the seizure is over — non-convulsive status epilepticus can persist electrographically with only subtle clinical signs. Delaying anticonvulsant administration while awaiting imaging or laboratory results, which worsens the chance of terminating the seizure. Underdosing initial therapy out of caution about respiratory depression, which increases the risk of treatment failure and need for escalation. Failing to search for and treat the underlying precipitant, allowing the episode to recur despite initial seizure control. Status epilepticus arises from a failure of the mechanisms that normally terminate seizure activity, leading to sustained abnormal neuronal hypersynchronization. This results from a relative excess of excitatory (glutamatergic) neurotransmission and depletion or dysfunction of inhibitory (GABAergic) signaling, with progressive receptor trafficking changes that make prolonged seizures increasingly resistant to GABA-acting drugs over time. Prolonged seizure activity can itself cause excitotoxic neuronal injury independent of the underlying cause, and is accompanied by systemic derangements including hyperthermia, acidosis, hypoxia, and autonomic instability that compound neuronal damage. Outcome depends heavily on etiology, age, and duration of status before treatment, with prolonged or refractory episodes carrying substantially higher morbidity and mortality. Even with successful seizure termination, patients face risk of cognitive sequelae and recurrent epilepsy, particularly when status is due to an acute severe brain insult.

Toxic shock syndrome — toxic shock, TSS, staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, STSS, menstrual TSS, tampon-associated shock Kawasaki disease (especially in children with fever, rash, and mucosal changes) Necrotizing fasciitis without full toxic shock physiology Rocky Mountain spotted fever and other rickettsial infections Severe scarlet fever Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) or Stevens-Johnson spectrum Septic shock from another gram-negative or gram-positive source Kawasaki disease Scarlet fever Rocky Mountain spotted fever Leptospirosis (Weil syndrome) Meningococcemia Blood cultures (times two) — often negative in staphylococcal TSS but essential to identify streptococcal bacteremia and guide therapy Wound, vaginal, or device-site cultures — to isolate toxin-producing S. aureus or S. pyogenes and confirm source Complete metabolic panel with renal and hepatic function — documents multi-organ involvement required for diagnosis Complete blood count with differential — assesses for thrombocytopenia and left shift Creatine kinase — elevated with muscular involvement/myositis component Coagulation studies (PT/INR, fibrinogen) — screens for evolving disseminated intravascular coagulation Imaging (CT/MRI or bedside ultrasound) of suspected soft-tissue focus — evaluates for necrotizing infection requiring surgical debridement Serologic/toxin studies where available — can support etiology in atypical or culture-negative presentations Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis Drug hypersensitivity reaction (DRESS) Systemic lupus erythematosus flare with vasculitic rash Adult-onset Still disease Consider TSS in any acute febrile illness with diffuse macular erythroderma, hypotension, and multi-organ involvement, even without an obvious focal infection source. A retained tampon, nasal packing, surgical wound packing, or postpartum/post-surgical site should always be actively sought and removed as part of initial assessment. Streptococcal TSS typically presents with a clear, severe, deep soft-tissue focus (necrotizing fasciitis or bacteremia) and is far more often bacteremic than the staphylococcal form. Desquamation of the palms and soles is a late finding, occurring one to two weeks after illness onset, and should never be relied upon to make the initial diagnosis. Hypotension plus involvement of three or more organ systems (renal, hepatic, hematologic, mucosal, CNS, muscular/GI) in a febrile diffuse-rash illness supports the syndromic diagnosis. Early aggressive fluid resuscitation is often required because of profound capillary leak, and volume needs can be extreme in the first 24-48 hours. Source control (removing foreign material, draining/debriding infected tissue) is as critical as antimicrobial therapy and delays worsen outcomes. Blood cultures are frequently negative in staphylococcal TSS since the syndrome is toxin-mediated rather than driven by bloodstream invasion. Refractory hypotension unresponsive to initial fluid resuscitation, suggesting need for vasopressors and ICU-level care Rapidly spreading pain, swelling, or crepitus over a soft-tissue site raising concern for necrotizing fasciitis requiring emergent surgical exploration Evolving coagulopathy or falling platelet count concerning for disseminated intravascular coagulation Altered mental status or new organ dysfunction indicating rapid progression to multi-organ failure Any retained foreign material (tampon, packing, prosthetic material) not yet identified or removed Dismissing the diagnosis because blood cultures are negative — staphylococcal TSS is toxin-mediated and frequently culture-negative. Waiting for classic desquamation before considering the diagnosis, which delays treatment since desquamation occurs late in the course. Failing to perform a thorough examination for retained foreign bodies (vaginal, nasal, surgical) as the driving source. Underestimating streptococcal TSS severity because the cutaneous findings can be subtler than staphylococcal disease despite higher mortality. TSS results from exotoxins produced by Staphylococcus aureus (notably TSST-1) or by Streptococcus pyogenes acting as superantigens that bind directly to MHC class II molecules and T-cell receptors outside the conventional antigen groove. This bypasses normal antigen processing and triggers massive, non-specific polyclonal T-cell activation with a resulting cytokine storm (IL-1, IL-2, TNF, interferon-gamma). The surge in inflammatory mediators produces capillary leak, vasodilation, hypotension, and secondary multi-organ dysfunction, explaining why the clinical picture can be severe even with a small, localized focus of infection or colonization. Staphylococcal TSS has a lower mortality (roughly a few percent) when recognized early and the source is controlled, whereas streptococcal TSS carries a substantially higher mortality, often cited around 30-70%, particularly when associated with necrotizing soft-tissue infection or bacteremia. Prompt source control, resuscitation, and antimicrobial therapy are the main determinants of outcome.

Tumour lysis syndrome — tumour lysis, tumor lysis, TLS, acute tumor lysis syndrome, spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome, cytolytic syndrome Sepsis-associated multiorgan dysfunction with acute kidney injury Rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalemia and hyperphosphatemia Chemotherapy-induced acute kidney injury from nephrotoxic agents Acute uric acid nephropathy unrelated to malignancy Adrenal insufficiency presenting with hyperkalemia Massive hemolysis syndromes Severe sepsis with acute kidney injury and metabolic derangement mimicking the electrolyte pattern of TLS Serum potassium, phosphate, calcium, uric acid — core panel to confirm the metabolic tetrad and grade severity Creatinine and estimated GFR — assess renal function and monitor for acute kidney injury ECG — screen for hyperkalemia- or hypocalcemia-related conduction changes and arrhythmia risk Urinalysis and urine output monitoring — detect early oliguria or uric acid crystalluria LDH — surrogate marker of tumour burden and cell turnover, useful for risk stratification Baseline and serial renal function before and during cytoreductive therapy Coagulation profile if disseminated intravascular coagulation is suspected concurrently Rhabdomyolysis Acute kidney injury from contrast nephropathy or nephrotoxic drugs Hemolytic states with hyperkalemia Refeeding syndrome (overlapping electrolyte shifts) Emerges when bulky, rapidly proliferating tumours (especially high-grade lymphomas and acute leukemias) undergo massive cell death, either spontaneously or within hours to days of starting cytotoxic therapy Classic biochemical tetrad is hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and secondary hypocalcemia Risk correlates with tumour bulk, proliferation rate, and baseline chemosensitivity — Burkitt lymphoma and acute lymphoblastic leukemia carry the highest risk Pre-existing renal impairment, volume depletion, and acidic urine markedly increase risk of uric acid nephropathy Onset is typically 12–72 hours after initiating effective therapy but can occur before any treatment is given in highly proliferative tumours Acute kidney injury is usually the dominant clinical threat, driven by uric acid and/or calcium phosphate precipitation in renal tubules Cardiac arrhythmia from hyperkalemia and hypocalcemia is the most immediately life-threatening complication Aggressive risk stratification and prophylaxis before chemotherapy is far more effective than treating established syndrome Oliguria or rising creatinine suggesting evolving acute kidney injury ECG changes (peaked T waves, widened QRS, QT prolongation) indicating hyperkalemia or hypocalcemia Symptomatic hypocalcemia (tetany, seizures, arrhythmia) Rapidly rising potassium or phosphate despite supportive measures High tumour bulk with elevated baseline LDH and uric acid before therapy initiation Need for urgent renal replacement therapy in refractory metabolic derangement Assuming TLS only occurs after chemotherapy — spontaneous lysis can precede any treatment in highly proliferative tumours Correcting hypocalcemia aggressively without addressing hyperphosphatemia first, which can worsen calcium-phosphate precipitation Underestimating risk in patients with bulky, chemosensitive tumours and pre-existing renal impairment or dehydration Delaying prophylactic measures until after laboratory abnormalities appear rather than initiating them proactively Rapid destruction of malignant cells releases large quantities of intracellular potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids into the circulation. Nucleic acid catabolism generates a surge of uric acid that can precipitate in the relatively acidic, low-flow environment of the renal tubules, producing obstructive nephropathy. Hyperphosphatemia from cell lysis exceeds the solubility product for calcium phosphate, causing tissue and renal deposition and consequent hypocalcemia. The resulting acute kidney injury further impairs excretion of potassium, phosphate, and uric acid, creating a self-amplifying metabolic crisis. With prompt recognition, risk stratification, and preventive management, most cases resolve without permanent renal impairment; outcomes worsen substantially once oliguric acute kidney injury or refractory hyperkalemia develops, occasionally requiring dialysis.

Upper Respiratory Tract Infection (common cold) — None required — Diagnosis is clinical and investigations rarely change management in uncomplicated URTI. Influenza (more prominent myalgias and systemic symptoms) COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2 can cause virtually any upper respiratory symptom; new loss of taste or smell appears specific for COVID-19) Measles (cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis) Acute HIV infection (sore throat and rash often predominate) Allergic, inflammatory, autoimmune, or neoplastic causes of upper respiratory symptoms Influenza COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2) Acute HIV infection Measles Streptococcal pharyngitis Acute bacterial sinusitis Acute otitis media No specific viral testing is needed for diagnosis; multiplex RT-PCR panels exist but are often unnecessary and may be falsely positive due to recent prior infection (Harrison 22e p.296) Allergic rhinitis / allergic upper respiratory symptoms Other inflammatory upper respiratory conditions Autoimmune causes of upper respiratory symptoms Neoplastic causes of upper respiratory symptoms The nonspecific URI ('common cold') is defined as a respiratory tract infection in which no single symptom predominates, distinguishing it clinically from more localized syndromes such as pharyngitis, sinusitis, or otitis media (Harrison 22e p.296). The overwhelming majority of acute respiratory infections are caused by common respiratory viruses and are self-limited; antibiotics neither speed resolution nor prevent complications, which is why at least half of ambulatory antibiotic prescriptions for these infections are inappropriate (Harrison 22e p.295). Nasal mucus in a viral URI can range anywhere from watery to frankly purulent, so purulent or discolored nasal discharge by itself does not indicate bacterial infection or warrant antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.296). Symptoms typically begin gradually after a 2-8 day incubation, peak early, and usually last 5-10 days but may persist up to 14 days; patients remain infectious as long as symptoms are present (Harrison 22e pp.296-297). Adults average 2-4 URIs per year and children 6-10 per year; reinfection is common because immunity to the many rhinovirus and adenovirus serotypes is serotype-specific and immunity to coronaviruses, parainfluenza, RSV, and metapneumovirus is weak or short-lived (Harrison 22e pp.295-296). Myalgias may occur but are usually less prominent than in influenza, a useful bedside discriminator from influenza (Harrison 22e p.296). Making a specific viral diagnosis is not practical, cost-effective, or necessary; multiplex RT-PCR panels may be overly sensitive and yield false positives from recent prior infection (Harrison 22e p.296). URI can be reduced by hand hygiene, physical distancing, masking, isolation of ill persons, and environmental cleaning (Harrison 22e p.295). Fever above 102 degrees F (38.9 C) Chest pain not attributable to a pulled muscle Shortness of breath Dizziness Confusion New ear or sinus pain (suggesting otitis media or bacterial sinusitis complication) Symptoms lasting longer than 14 days New loss of taste or smell where SARS-CoV-2 is circulating (suggests COVID-19) Prescribing antibiotics for a viral URI: they do not shorten illness or prevent complications and risk adverse drug effects, microbiome disruption, C. difficile infection, increased cost, and antibiotic resistance (Harrison 22e p.295). Interpreting purulent nasal discharge as evidence of bacterial infection; viral URI mucus normally ranges from watery to purulent (Harrison 22e p.296). Drivers of inappropriate prescribing include time pressure, fear of missing a rare bacterial diagnosis, concern about a rare complication, low salience of antibiotic harms, and the mistaken belief that patients demand antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.295). Delayed antibiotic prescriptions are conceptually flawed for self-limited respiratory infections, shift decision-making to patients, and send a mixed message; they should be avoided (Harrison 22e p.296). Procalcitonin testing has been ineffective and CRP testing not durable for reducing inappropriate ambulatory antibiotic use (Harrison 22e p.296). Many popular cold remedies are ineffective, of questionable benefit, or harmful, including echinacea, zinc, inhaled steam, vitamin C, vitamin D, garlic, antihistamines, intranasal corticosteroids, saline nasal irrigation, and antiviral drugs (Harrison 22e p.296). Cough and cold medicines should not be used in children under 6 years because of the risk of adverse effects (Harrison 22e p.296). Nonspecific URI is an acute infection of the respiratory tract above the vocal cords, most commonly caused by respiratory viruses acquired through direct contact with infected people, contaminated surfaces, and large and small respiratory droplets. Susceptibility depends on prior exposure and immunity, general health, genetics, microbiome factors, and psychosocial factors including stress. Because immunity is serotype-specific (rhinovirus, adenovirus) or weak/short-lived (coronaviruses, parainfluenza, RSV, metapneumovirus), reinfection is frequent (Harrison 22e pp.295-296). Nonspecific URI is self-limited. Symptoms peak early and generally resolve within 5-10 days, though some last up to 14 days. Although the cold can occasionally be complicated by otitis media or bacterial sinusitis, for any individual patient an antibiotic is more likely to cause an adverse reaction than to prevent a complication (Harrison 22e pp.296-297).

Ventilator Associated Pneumonia — Quantitative endotracheal aspirate or BAL culture — Gold standard to identify causative organism and guide de-escalation in VAP. Blood cultures — Detects bacteremic spread. Chest X-ray (serial) — Tracks new or progressive infiltrate. Procalcitonin (serial) — Supports shortened duration of therapy when trending down with clinical improvement. Immediate empiric antibiotics required Purulent tracheobronchitis (especially in chronic ventilator units, where it can impede weaning) (p.1030) Fungal pneumonia (requires different antibiotics from those used for bacterial VAP) (p.1031) Viral pneumonia (requires different antibiotics from those used for bacterial VAP) (p.1031) Quantitative deep respiratory tract cultures to separate colonization from true infection: more distal sampling is more specific and uses a lower growth threshold; endotracheal aspirate threshold is 10^6 cfu/mL and protected specimen brush threshold is 10^3 cfu/mL, but sensitivity falls with more distal blind sampling (p.1031). Gram stain of respiratory specimen, differential cell counts, staining for intracellular organisms, and detection of locally elevated infection-related protein levels to increase diagnostic yield (p.1031). Molecular diagnostic methods, which can exclude a suspected MDR pathogen as a therapy target when results are negative (p.1031). Serial procalcitonin and other biomarkers, used together with the initial clinical response to help guide therapy duration (p.1032). Atypical pulmonary edema (p.1031) Pulmonary contusion (p.1031) Alveolar hemorrhage (p.1031) Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (p.1031) Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) (p.1031) Pulmonary infarction / pulmonary embolism (p.1031) Non-pulmonary causes of fever and/or leukocytosis: antibiotic-associated diarrhea, central line-associated infection, sinusitis, urinary tract infection, pancreatitis, and drug fever (p.1031) VAP is defined as pneumonia with onset at or beyond 48 h after the start of mechanical ventilation; the same principles extend to ventilated HAP and to non-ICU HAP (p.1029). About 35% of all HAP patients require mechanical ventilation, which marks ventilated HAP as a distinct entity; roughly 70% of HAP is acquired outside the ICU and 30% within it (p.1029). Three sequential steps drive VAP: oropharyngeal colonization with pathogens, aspiration of these organisms into the lower airway, and compromise of host defenses; almost all intubated patients are at least transiently colonized, yet only about one-third go on to develop VAP (p.1030). Colony counts often rise to high levels days before clinical pneumonia appears, supporting the idea that the final step is overwhelming of host defenses by a large bacterial inoculum (p.1030). Serial changes in oxygenation may detect VAP earlier than other clinical findings and can also be used to track response to therapy (p.1030). Clinical manifestations of HAP and VAP are nonspecific: fever, leukocytosis, increased respiratory secretions, consolidation on examination, and a new or changing radiographic infiltrate (p.1030). Absence of bacteria on a Gram stain of an endotracheal aspirate makes pneumonia an unlikely cause of fever or infiltrates, and absence of an MDR pathogen on culture supports de-escalation of empirical therapy (p.1031). Clinical improvement, when it occurs, is usually evident within 48-72 h of starting therapy, typically as improved oxygenation; chest radiographs often worsen early in treatment and are therefore less useful than clinical criteria for judging response (p.1033). P. aeruginosa essentially never causes infection in patients without prior antibiotic exposure; antibiotic exposure is by far the greatest risk factor for replacement of normal oropharyngeal flora by pathogens (p.1030). On any given day in the ICU, an average of about 10% of patients have pneumonia, the overwhelming majority of which is VAP; reported prevalence ranges from 6 to 52 cases per 100 patients depending on the population (p.1030). Worsening oxygenation, tachypnea, tachycardia, and increased minute ventilation in a ventilated patient (p.1030). Septic shock accompanying suspected VAP (favors broader empirical and combination coverage) (p.1031-1032). Colony counts above the diagnostic threshold while already on antibiotics, suggesting current therapy is ineffective (p.1031). Necrotizing pneumonia (e.g., P. aeruginosa or S. aureus) causing significant pulmonary hemorrhage or empyema (p.1032). VAP complicating COVID-19, which carries higher attributable mortality than other forms of VAP (p.1033). Applying clinical criteria designed for community-acquired pneumonia consistently overdiagnoses VAP, because of frequent tracheal colonization in intubated patients, multiple alternative causes of radiographic infiltrates, and the high frequency of other fever sources in critically ill patients (p.1030-1031). No single set of criteria is reliably diagnostic of pneumonia in a ventilated patient, which undermines both prevention and treatment efforts and even estimates of VAP attributable mortality (p.1030). Recently effective antibiotics given in the 24-48 h before sampling can cause false-negative quantitative cultures; with susceptible organisms a single dose can drop colony counts below threshold, and operating characteristics only normalize after about 3 days (p.1031). Quantitative cultures can also fall below threshold if obtained very early in infection or if delayed until an effective host response has reduced bacterial counts; the specimen should ideally be taken as soon as VAP is suspected and before antibiotics are started or changed (p.1031). Recurrent VAP with the same pathogen can occur because endotracheal-tube biofilm allows persistence and reintroduction; however, about half of recurrent Pseudomonas cases are actually due to a new strain (p.1032). Aggressive early extubation can lead to reintubation and increased aspiration (raising VAP risk), while heavy continuous sedation also increases VAP risk and undersedation risks self-extubation, so tradeoffs must be balanced (p.1033). The endotracheal tube is the single most important risk factor for VAP. While it blocks large-volume aspiration, it worsens microaspiration of secretions that pool above the cuff, and the tube plus suctioning damages tracheal mucosa and promotes tracheal colonization. Pathogenic bacteria form a glycocalyx biofilm on the tube surface that shields them from antibiotics and host defenses; suctioning can dislodge organisms that reinoculate the trachea, and biofilm fragments can embolize to distal airways carrying bacteria. Ventilator circuit tubing can harbor organisms that wash back if manipulated, so circuits are changed only when soiled or with a new patient. In critically ill patients, normal oropharyngeal flora is replaced by pathogens, driven mainly by antibiotic selection pressure, cross-infection, severe systemic illness, and malnutrition. Severely ill patients with sepsis or trauma appear to enter a state of immunoparalysis several days after ICU admission, coinciding with peak VAP risk; the mechanism is unclear but hyperglycemia and frequent transfusions adversely affect immunity (p.1029-1030).
