Crude mortality rates for VAP are reported as high as 50-70%, but the clinically meaningful figure is attributable mortality, since many patients have underlying diseases that would be fatal regardless. Attributable mortality exceeded 25% in one matched-cohort study, while more recent estimates are lower (5-10%); VAP complicating COVID-19 has higher attributable mortality. Mortality varies with patient type and ICU; VAP in trauma patients is generally not associated with attributable mortality (these patients were often previously healthy). The causative pathogen matters: MDR pathogens carry significantly greater attributable mortality than non-MDR pathogens, and infection with organisms such as S. maltophilia mainly marks a severely immunocompromised host at high risk. Beyond death, the major complication is prolonged mechanical ventilation with longer ICU and hospital stays; long-term sequelae of necrotizing infection include bronchiectasis and parenchymal scarring with recurrent pneumonia, prolonged oxygen need, a catabolic state, and (in the elderly) loss of independent function (p.1032-1033). Harrison does not present a formal VAP severity score in this text. Empirical-therapy decisions are instead stratified by (1) the presence of risk factors for MDR pathogens and (2) the predicted risk of death, with a mortality risk of <=15% considered low risk (p.1031).

Acute Viral Hepatitis — Liver function tests — Marked transaminase elevation (often >10x upper limit of normal) with hyperbilirubinemia is characteristic of acute viral hepatitis and helps distinguish it from other causes of jaundice. Hepatitis A IgM, Hepatitis E IgM — Confirms the most likely causes in this setting; both are the standard first-line serologic tests for acute fecal-oral hepatitis. Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), IgM anti-HBc — Identifies acute Hepatitis B, which has different counseling, monitoring, and contact-tracing/vaccination implications than A or E. Coagulation profile (PT/INR) — A rising INR is the key early warning sign of evolving acute liver failure and should be tracked closely. Mental status assessment (serial) — Screens for hepatic encephalopathy, the clinical hallmark of progression to acute liver failure requiring urgent escalation of care. Autoimmune hepatitis (suggested by repeated unexplained episodes of acute hepatitis; can also be triggered after self-limited acute hepatitis A, B, or C) (p.2660) Alcohol-associated hepatitis (aminotransferases usually below ~400 IU/mL with a heavy-drinking history, unlike viral hepatitis) (p.2660) Drug-induced/toxin-induced liver injury, including acetaminophen, and anesthetic-agent hepatotoxicity (p.2660) Acute biliary disease: acute cholecystitis, common-duct stone, or ascending cholangitis (RUQ pain, fever, jaundice overlap) (p.2660) Obstructive jaundice from common-duct stone or pancreatic carcinoma (viral hepatitis in the elderly is often misdiagnosed as this) (p.2660) Wilson disease and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (genetic/metabolic liver disorders) (p.2660) Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD/MASH, formerly NAFLD/NASH) (p.2660) Ischemic (hypoxic) liver injury (a leading cause of aminotransferases >=1000 IU/L, along with drug injury and acute viral hepatitis) (p.2660) Infectious mononucleosis / Epstein-Barr virus (p.2660) Cytomegalovirus hepatitis (p.2643, p.2660) Herpes simplex virus (p.2660) Adenovirus (including the unexplained severe pediatric acute hepatitis linked to adenovirus type 41) (p.2643, p.2660) Coxsackievirus infection (p.2660) Toxoplasmosis (p.2660) SARS-CoV-2 (aminotransferase elevations in ~10% of cases and up to half of severe cases) (p.2660) Leptospirosis (p.2660) Brucellosis (p.2660) Disseminated candidiasis (p.2660) Mycobacterial infection (p.2660) Pneumocystis infection (p.2660) Anti-HCV antibody plus HCV RNA (HCV RNA is the gold standard; needed when anti-HCV is undetectable or in immunosuppressed patients where antibody may be absent) (p.2657-2658) Anti-HDV (IgM/IgG) and/or HDV RNA in HBsAg-positive patients who are at high risk or have severe/fulminant disease (p.2658, p.2659) IgM anti-HEV / HEV RNA when standard A/B/C tests are negative and enteric risk factors are present (specialized labs/CDC) (p.2658) HBeAg and anti-HBe to assess relative infectivity and replication in chronic HBV (p.2656, p.2659) Quantitative HBV DNA (PCR) to gauge replication level and risk of cirrhosis, decompensation, and HCC in chronic HBV (p.2656-2657) Serum albumin (a fall is uncommon in uncomplicated acute hepatitis; signals severe disease) (p.2656) Blood glucose (hypoglycemia can occur in severe hepatitis) (p.2656) Complete blood count / differential (transient neutropenia and lymphopenia, then relative lymphocytosis with 2-20% atypical lymphocytes) (p.2656) Serum bilirubin with conjugated/unconjugated fractions (levels >20 mg/dL persisting late suggest severe disease) (p.2655-2656) Liver biopsy only when the diagnosis is in doubt or chronic/autoimmune hepatitis is suspected; it is rarely needed in acute viral hepatitis (p.2658) Passive hepatic congestion / hypoperfusion from right ventricular failure, shock, severe hypotension, or severe left ventricular failure (p.2660) Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein occlusion) and hepatic veno-occlusive disease (p.2660) Constrictive pericarditis or right atrial myxoma impeding venous return (p.2660) Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (p.2660) Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (p.2660) Eclampsia (p.2660) HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver tests, low platelets) (p.2660) Liver metastases mimicking acute or even fulminant hepatitis (rare) (p.2660) Five hepatotropic viruses cause almost all acute viral hepatitis: HAV, HBV, HCV, HDV (delta), and HEV. All are RNA viruses except HBV, which is a DNA virus that replicates via reverse transcription like a retrovirus (p.2643). All five types produce a clinically similar acute illness, so the type cannot be reliably distinguished by clinical or epidemiologic features alone; specific serologic testing is the accurate way to tell them apart (p.2643, p.2651). Only the bloodborne agents (HBV, HCV, HDV) can become chronic and progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; HAV and HEV do not cause chronic liver disease in immunocompetent hosts (p.2643, p.2659-2660). Hepatitis A is diagnosed during acute illness by detecting IgM anti-HAV; IgM persists ~3 months (rarely 6-12). IgG anti-HAV appears in convalescence, remains detectable indefinitely, and confers lifelong immunity to reinfection (p.2643-2644, p.2656). The serologic/virologic course of acute hepatitis E mirrors hepatitis A: brief fecal shedding and viremia, an early IgM anti-HEV response dominating ~the first 3 months, then long-lasting IgG anti-HEV (p.2658). Acute hepatitis can be evaluated with five serologic tests: HBsAg, IgM anti-HAV, IgM anti-HBc, anti-HCV, and HCV RNA (p.2657-2658). HBsAg positive plus IgM anti-HBc indicates acute (or acute reactivation) hepatitis B; HBsAg positive with IgG anti-HBc (IgM negative) indicates chronic HBV (p.2657-2658). In about 1-5% of acute HBV infections HBsAg is below the detection threshold; in that window the presence of IgM anti-HBc establishes the diagnosis of acute hepatitis B (p.2646, p.2656). The anti-HBc 'window' period (HBsAg already cleared, anti-HBs not yet detectable) is now rarely encountered because of higher-sensitivity HBsAg/anti-HBs assays (p.2646). Isolated anti-HBc usually represents remote past HBV infection (IgG class); rarely it reflects low-level viremia with HBsAg below detection, or a false-positive (p.2646). IgM anti-HBc can reappear with high titer during acute flares of chronic hepatitis B, so IgM vs IgG anti-HBc does not always reliably separate de novo acute hepatitis B from an exacerbation of chronic HBV; history and serial follow-up help (p.2646-2647, p.2657). HBeAg is a qualitative marker of active HBV replication and high infectivity; HBV DNA is the quantitative marker. HBeAg-positive HBsAg-positive mothers transmit to >90% of offspring versus only 10-15% if anti-HBe positive (p.2645-2646). Precore/core-promoter mutant HBV cannot make HBeAg, producing HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis with detectable HBV DNA and anti-HBe; it can run a more aggressive course and is the predominant form in the Mediterranean and Europe (p.2646-2647). Anti-HCV (IgG) is the available antibody marker (no clinically useful IgM anti-HCV exists); with contemporary assays it is detectable early in acute hepatitis C and persists after recovery and during chronic infection (p.2657). HCV RNA is the most sensitive test and the diagnostic gold standard; it appears before aminotransferase rise and before anti-HCV. Detectable anti-HCV with negative HCV RNA signifies cleared/cured infection (p.2657-2658). Recovery from hepatitis C leaves persistent anti-HCV but does NOT protect against reinfection; in people who inject drugs, anti-HCV plus HCV RNA may indicate reinfection rather than chronic infection (p.2657-2658). Serum aminotransferase levels do not correlate well with the degree of liver cell damage; peak ALT/AST does not predict severity (p.2655-2656). A low-grade fever (38-39 C) is more typical of hepatitis A and E than of B or C, except when hepatitis B presents with a serum sickness-like syndrome (p.2655). HDV is a defective virus that requires HBV (HBsAg envelope) for replication; negative HBV serology excludes hepatitis D, and the duration of HDV infection cannot outlast HBV infection (p.2646-2647, p.2658). In acute hepatitis with HBsAg and anti-HDV, the anti-HBc class clarifies the relationship: IgM anti-HBc indicates simultaneous acute HBV-HDV co-infection, whereas IgG anti-HBc indicates HDV superinfection on chronic HBV (p.2658). Among healthy adults, acute hepatitis B is self-limited in ~95-99%, whereas acute hepatitis C is self-limited in only ~15-20% (chronicity is the rule for HCV) (p.2655-2656). Hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, disorientation, somnolence, progression to coma) - hallmark of fulminant hepatitis with very high mortality (>80% in deep coma without transplant) (p.2659) Markedly prolonged prothrombin time / INR (reflects severe synthetic failure and extensive hepatocellular necrosis) (p.2656, p.2658-2659) Rapidly shrinking liver size with rapidly rising bilirubin even as aminotransferases fall - indicates massive hepatic necrosis (p.2659) Ascites and peripheral edema at presentation (poorer prognosis) (p.2658-2659) Hypoglycemia and falling serum albumin in acute hepatitis (severe hepatocellular disease) (p.2656, p.2658-2659) Very high or persistently rising serum bilirubin (>20 mg/dL late in the course) (p.2655-2656, p.2659) Pregnancy with acute hepatitis E - up to 10-20% risk of fulminant hepatitis and death (p.2659, p.2661) HDV superinfection of chronic hepatitis B - clinical deterioration with substantially increased risk of fulminant hepatitis and death (mortality >20% in 'Labrea fever' outbreaks) (p.2659) Advanced age or serious underlying disease, especially pre-existing chronic liver disease (raises risk of severe and fulminant course) (p.2658-2659) Acute hepatitis E or other insult superimposed on chronic liver disease (acute-on-chronic liver failure) (p.2659-2660) Relying on HBsAg alone can miss acute hepatitis B: in ~1-5% of cases HBsAg is below detection and only IgM anti-HBc reveals the diagnosis (p.2656, p.2657-2658). IgM anti-HBc can re-emerge during an acute exacerbation of chronic HBV, so it does not always distinguish true acute hepatitis B from a chronic flare (p.2646-2647, p.2657). False-positive IgM anti-HAV occurs in rheumatologic disease (rheumatoid factor) and rarely in EBV infection; false-positive IgM anti-HBc occurs with high-titer rheumatoid factor (p.2656). Anti-HCV immunoassays can be falsely positive (low pretest probability, rheumatoid factor); confirm with HCV RNA (p.2657). In immunosuppressed patients anti-HCV may be undetectable, so HCV RNA testing is required to diagnose hepatitis C (p.2655, p.2657). HBsAg titer does not reflect disease severity - an inverse correlation exists, with very low HBsAg in fulminant hepatitis (p.2656-2657). Coexisting HBsAg and anti-HBs in chronic HBV does not signal imminent HBsAg clearance; these patients still have chronic HBV infection (p.2646, p.2657). A normal or only mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase and normal albumin are expected in uncomplicated acute hepatitis; abnormal values suggest an alternative or complicated course (p.2656). The serum sickness-like prodrome of acute hepatitis B (arthralgia, rash, angioedema) is often misdiagnosed as a rheumatologic disease before jaundice appears (p.2659). Retrospective diagnosis of self-limited simultaneous acute HBV-HDV co-infection is difficult because anti-HDV is often transient and disappears once HBsAg clears (p.2658). Patients with acute viral hepatitis tolerate surgery poorly; biliary disease should be excluded clinically and with imaging before any operation (p.2660). None of the hepatitis viruses is ordinarily directly cytopathic to hepatocytes; the clinical manifestations and outcome of acute liver injury are largely determined by the host immune (chiefly cell-mediated/cytolytic T-cell) response to infected hepatocytes. In hepatitis B the existence of inactive carriers with normal histology and the more severe disease seen with defective cellular immunity support an immune-mediated mechanism; in immunocompetent adults the degree of liver injury correlates with the level of HBV replication (HBV DNA). HBV enters hepatocytes via the sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP) receptor and replicates through reverse transcription of a pregenomic RNA, forming covalently closed circular DNA in the nucleus. HDV likewise enters via NTCP but depends on HBV helper function for complete virions and liver injury (p.2643-2645, p.2651). Hepatitis A and acute hepatitis B in previously healthy persons usually resolve completely (HBV self-limited in ~95-99% of healthy adults; HAV essentially always), with an overall case-fatality of ~0.1% (1% among hospitalized acute hepatitis B). Hepatitis A and E cause no chronic liver disease in immunocompetent hosts. Acute hepatitis C becomes chronic in ~85-90%; among chronic HCV, cirrhosis develops in up to ~20% over 10-20 years, with an annual decompensation risk ~4% and annual HCC risk ~1-4% (about 3.36%) once cirrhotic - rates declining with effective direct-acting antiviral therapy. Chronic hepatitis B carries an enhanced HCC risk, especially with infection in infancy/childhood and high HBV DNA/HBeAg; risk of cirrhosis and HCC rises with the level of HBV replication. Waterborne hepatitis E (genotypes 1 and 2) in India/Asia has a case-fatality of 1-2%, rising to 10-20% in pregnant women. Acute HBV-HDV co-infection mortality is usually similar to HBV alone (~5% in some injection-drug-user outbreaks), but HDV superinfection of chronic HBV markedly worsens outcome (annual cirrhosis rate ~4% in chronic hepatitis D; annual HCC ~3% once cirrhotic) (p.2658-2660). No formal grading system for acute viral hepatitis is given; severity is judged clinically. Features indicating severe hepatocellular disease warranting prompt hospital admission include prolonged prothrombin time, low serum albumin, hypoglycemia, and very high serum bilirubin; presenting ascites, edema, or encephalopathy indicate a poorer prognosis. Progression to fulminant hepatitis (massive hepatic necrosis) is marked by encephalopathy with rapidly shrinking liver size, rapidly rising bilirubin, and markedly prolonged PT even as aminotransferases fall (p.2658-2659).

Viral (Aseptic) Meningitis — Lumbar puncture with CSF cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture — The decisive test distinguishing viral from bacterial meningitis and guiding the decision to continue or stop empiric antibacterial therapy. CSF viral PCR (enterovirus, HSV) — Identifies the specific viral cause; HSV PCR specifically changes management since HSV meningitis/encephalitis is treated with acyclovir. Blood cultures — Performed alongside LP workup to support the broader diagnostic picture, particularly if bacterial meningitis cannot yet be excluded. Arthropod-borne (arbovirus) meningitis, notably West Nile virus; consider when meningitis/encephalitis clusters occur in a restricted region in summer/early fall (p.1167-1168) Epstein-Barr virus (may produce aseptic meningitis with or without infectious mononucleosis; atypical lymphocytes in CSF/blood are suggestive) (p.1168) Human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) (p.1167) Cytomegalovirus (notably in immunocompromised hosts, where it may cause PMN pleocytosis with low glucose) (p.1167) HSV-1 (less common cause of meningitis than HSV-2) (p.1167) Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) (p.1167, 1169) Mumps (late winter/early spring, male predominance ~3:1) (p.1167, 1168-1169) Zika and other non-WNV arboviruses (p.1167) Human parechovirus (included on the FilmArray ME panel) (p.1167) Untreated or partially treated bacterial meningitis (a key pitfall when CSF shifts toward lymphocytic predominance) (p.1167) Early fungal meningitis (lymphocytic pleocytosis common; RT-PCR ~70% sensitive, useful mainly in immunocompromised patients with poor antibody response) (p.1166, 1168) Arboviral serology demonstrating CSF viral-specific IgM or seroconversion; repeat testing if early study is negative and suspicion is high (p.1168) Throat washing and stool PCR/culture to support enteroviral (and Mycoplasma) diagnosis (stool/throat shedding may persist for weeks) (p.1166-1167) Demonstration of intrathecal HSV-specific or VZV-specific antibody synthesis (less sensitive/specific than PCR; may take >1 week to become positive) (p.1168) Routine bloods: complete blood count with differential, liver and renal function tests, ESR, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, glucose, creatine kinase, aldolase, amylase, and lipase (p.1167) Neuroimaging (MRI preferred over CT) when there is altered consciousness, seizures, focal signs, atypical CSF profile, or immunocompromise (not mandatory in uncomplicated viral meningitis) (p.1167) Serum procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL as a clue favoring bacterial over aseptic meningitis (p.1167) Neoplastic meningitis (p.1167) Medication-induced hypersensitivity (drug-induced) meningitis (p.1167) Systemic lupus erythematosus and other rheumatologic diseases (p.1167) Sarcoidosis (p.1167) Behcet's syndrome (p.1167) Uveomeningitic syndromes (p.1167) Profound alterations in consciousness (stupor, coma, marked confusion), seizures, focal neurologic signs, or neuroimaging evidence of parenchymal involvement do NOT occur in viral meningitis; their presence points instead to encephalitis or another CNS process (p.1166). Headache is almost invariably present, often frontal or retroorbital, with photophobia and pain on eye movement; nuchal rigidity is usually present but may be mild, appearing only near the limit of neck anteflexion (p.1166). A specific viral cause is identified in 60-90% of cases using combined CSF PCR, culture, and serology; roughly two-thirds of culture-negative 'aseptic' meningitis cases have a viral etiology found by CSF PCR (p.1166). Enteroviruses account for >85% of cases with an identified etiology and predominate in summer and fall, especially in children <15 years (p.1167-1168). HSV-2 causes most adult uncomplicated HSV meningitis (HSV-1 causes ~90% of HSV encephalitis); ~20% of HSV meningitis patients develop recurrent attacks, and most recurrent/'aseptic' meningitis, including cases formerly called Mollaret's meningitis, is due to HSV (p.1168). Many HSV meningitis patients give no history and show no active genital herpes lesions at presentation, so absence of genital lesions does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1168). VZV is increasingly recognized as a cause of meningitis even WITHOUT rash, so absence of chickenpox or shingles does not exclude it (p.1168). Cranial nerve palsies (most often V, VII, or VIII) are more common in HIV meningitis than in other viral meningitides; HIV seroconversion may be delayed, so seronegative suspected cases warrant repeat testing (p.1168). Mumps meningitis is suggested by parotitis, orchitis, oophoritis, pancreatitis, or raised serum amylase/lipase, but their absence does not exclude it; a documented prior mumps infection (lifelong immunity) does exclude it (p.1168-1169). Consider LCMV when aseptic meningitis occurs in late fall/winter with exposure to house mice or pet/laboratory rodents or their excreta, particularly when accompanied by leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, or abnormal liver function tests (p.1169). Depressed or markedly altered consciousness (stupor, coma, marked confusion) — suggests encephalitis or alternative diagnosis, not simple viral meningitis (p.1166) Seizures (p.1166) Focal neurologic signs/symptoms or neuroimaging abnormalities indicating parenchymal brain involvement (p.1166) CSF PMN pleocytosis without an established diagnosis — should prompt consideration of bacterial or parameningeal infection (p.1166-1167) Lymphocytic pleocytosis WITH low CSF glucose (hypoglycorrhachia) — should raise suspicion of fungal, tuberculous, or Listeria meningoencephalitis, or noninfectious causes such as sarcoid or neoplastic meningitis (p.1167) Atypical CSF profile or immunocompromising condition/treatment — warrants hospitalization and neuroimaging (p.1167) Failing to recognize partially or incompletely treated bacterial meningitis, which can produce a lymphocytic-predominant CSF that mimics viral meningitis (p.1167) Up to 15% of enteroviral meningitis patients (most often young infants) have a NORMAL CSF leukocyte count, so a normal cell count does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1168) PMNs may predominate during the first 48 h of viral meningitis (e.g., echovirus 9, WNV, EEE, mumps); WNV PMN pleocytosis occurs in ~45% and can persist a week or more before shifting to lymphocytes — do not assume early neutrophilia means bacterial infection (p.1167-1168) Treating a normal CSF glucose as ruling out viral meningitis is wrong, but conversely low CSF glucose can occur in 10-30% of mumps or LCMV and rarely with enteroviruses, HSV-2, or VZV (p.1167) CSF viral culture has generally poor sensitivity for viral meningitis (unlike its utility in bacterial infection), so reliance on culture alone underdiagnoses (p.1167) Enterovirus detected in stool is NOT diagnostic of acute CNS infection — it may reflect residual shedding from a prior infection or asymptomatic carriage during epidemics (p.1167) Enteroviral RT-PCR has low sensitivity for EV71; specific testing may be required (p.1168) EBV CSF PCR false-positives may reflect viral reactivation or latent viral DNA in recruited lymphocytes rather than true EBV meningitis (p.1168) Routine serology is unhelpful for high-seroprevalence viruses (HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV) (p.1167) Viral meningitis is inflammation of the meninges, most often caused by enteroviruses, with a self-limited course in immunocompetent hosts. Inflammation is largely confined to the meninges, producing meningeal irritation without the parenchymal brain involvement that characterizes encephalitis; preservation of higher cerebral function distinguishes meningitis from encephalitis. CSF oligoclonal IgG bands directed against viral proteins can occur, though they are nonspecific (Harrison 22e p.1166-1167). In adults the prognosis for full recovery from viral meningitis is excellent; treatment of almost all cases is primarily symptomatic. Rare adult patients have persisting headache, mild mental impairment, incoordination, or generalized asthenia for weeks to months. Outcome is less certain in infants and neonates (<1 year), in whom intellectual impairment, learning disabilities, hearing loss, and other lasting sequelae have been reported. Enteroviral meningitis outside the neonatal period is usually benign with recovery without sequelae, but chronic/severe infection can occur in neonates and in people with hypo- or agammaglobulinemia (Harrison 22e p.1168-1169). Harrison does not give a formal severity grading for viral meningitis; it instead frames disposition by risk. Immunocompetent patients with a classic CSF profile (lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, negative Gram stain), no focal signs, and no significant alteration in consciousness may not require hospitalization if home monitoring and follow-up are assured. Hospitalization is indicated for immunocompromised patients, those with significant alteration in consciousness, seizures, or focal signs suggesting encephalitis/parenchymal involvement, and those with an atypical CSF profile (Harrison 22e p.1169).

Waldenström macroglobulinaemia — macroglobulinaemia, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia, WM, IgM lymphoma, IgM monoclonal gammopathy-associated lymphoma, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with IgM paraproteinemia Multiple myeloma (IgM myeloma is rare but distinguishable by lytic bone lesions and different marrow morphology) IgM monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma Marginal zone lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation Other B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas with paraproteinemia Amyloidosis (AL) presenting with neuropathy and paraproteinemia Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation — identifies and characterizes the monoclonal IgM spike Serum viscosity — quantifies hyperviscosity risk when symptomatic Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with immunophenotyping — confirms lymphoplasmacytic infiltration MYD88 L265P mutation testing (allele-specific PCR) — supports diagnosis and distinguishes from other lymphomas CXCR4 mutation testing — informs prognosis and response to certain targeted therapies Complete blood count — assesses cytopenias from marrow infiltration Anti-MAG antibody testing — when peripheral neuropathy is present CT imaging of chest/abdomen/pelvis — evaluates lymphadenopathy and organomegaly IgM MGUS Multiple myeloma Chronic lymphocytic leukemia Marginal zone lymphoma Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis from other causes Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) unrelated to paraproteinemia Consider WM in an older adult with fatigue, weight loss, and an incidental monoclonal IgM spike on protein electrophoresis. Hyperviscosity symptoms (visual blurring, headache, mucosal bleeding, dizziness) reflect the very large size of the pentameric IgM molecule rather than tumor burden alone. Bone lesions are characteristically absent, unlike multiple myeloma, which helps distinguish the two at the bedside. Peripheral neuropathy (often demyelinating, anti-MAG antibody mediated) can be a presenting or dominant feature. Cold agglutinin disease and cryoglobulinemia are important IgM-related complications that can cause hemolysis or vasculitis-like skin findings. Bone marrow involvement by small lymphoplasmacytic cells with a mast-cell-rich infiltrate is a classic morphologic clue. MYD88 L265P mutation is present in the great majority of cases and is a useful diagnostic and prognostic marker. Asymptomatic patients with low IgM levels can often be observed without treatment (watch-and-wait). Visual disturbance, headache, confusion, or mucosal bleeding suggesting hyperviscosity syndrome requiring urgent plasmapheresis Rapidly progressive peripheral neuropathy Evidence of cryoglobulinemia with skin ulceration, digital ischemia, or renal involvement Cold agglutinin-mediated hemolysis with severe anemia Marked cytopenias suggesting extensive marrow replacement Transformation to a more aggressive (diffuse large B-cell) lymphoma Attributing an incidental IgM paraprotein to benign MGUS without adequate marrow and clinical evaluation when other features are present Delaying plasmapheresis in symptomatic hyperviscosity while awaiting definitive chemoimmunotherapy Missing WM as a cause of unexplained demyelinating peripheral neuropathy in older adults Confusing WM with IgM myeloma or misinterpreting lytic bone lesions as consistent with WM (they are not typical) Waldenström macroglobulinaemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma in which clonal B-lymphoplasmacytic cells infiltrate the bone marrow (and sometimes lymph nodes and spleen) and secrete large quantities of monoclonal IgM. The pentameric structure of IgM raises serum viscosity disproportionately to its molar concentration, producing the hyperviscosity syndrome, and the paraprotein may also deposit in nerves, precipitate in the cold (cryoglobulinemia), or bind red cells (cold agglutinin disease). Somatic activating mutations in MYD88 (and often CXCR4) drive NF-κB signaling and are central to disease pathogenesis. The disease course is typically indolent with survival often measured in many years, and asymptomatic low-burden disease can be observed safely. Prognosis is influenced by age, cytopenias, beta-2-microglobulin level, and genetic features such as CXCR4 mutation status, with most patients eventually requiring treatment for symptomatic progression.

Chronic secretory diarrhea plus peptic ulcer disease is a classic combination that should prompt gastrin testing. About 20-30% of gastrinomas occur as part of MEN1 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1) — screen for hyperparathyroidism and pituitary tumors. Most gastrinomas arise within the 'gastrinoma triangle' bounded by the cystic duct, junction of the pancreatic head/neck, and duodenal junction. Fasting serum gastrin should be measured off proton pump inhibitors when clinically feasible, since acid suppression can falsely elevate gastrin. A markedly elevated fasting gastrin with an inappropriately low gastric pH strongly supports the diagnosis. Roughly half of gastrinomas are malignant with a tendency for lymph node and hepatic metastases at diagnosis. Somatostatin-receptor imaging (e.g., DOTATATE PET) is the preferred modality for tumor localization given high sensitivity. Multiple or recurrent ulcers despite adequate acid-suppressive therapy Ulcers in atypical locations (distal duodenum, jejunum) Evidence of hepatic or nodal metastases at diagnosis Signs of MEN1 (hypercalcemia, pituitary symptoms) suggesting hereditary syndrome Complications of ulcer disease such as perforation or bleeding Severe secretory diarrhea causing dehydration or electrolyte derangement Failing to hold proton pump inhibitors (when safe to do so) before gastrin testing, leading to false-positive hypergastrinemia Attributing recurrent ulcers solely to H. pylori or NSAIDs without considering gastrinoma in refractory cases Overlooking associated MEN1 features, delaying recognition of a hereditary tumor syndrome Relying on gastrin level alone without confirming inappropriate acid hypersecretion Zollinger-Ellison syndrome results from a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma), most often located in the duodenum or pancreas, that drives unregulated gastric acid hypersecretion. The resulting profound acid load overwhelms mucosal defenses and inactivates pancreatic enzymes, producing severe/recurrent peptic ulceration and secretory diarrhea with malabsorption. A substantial minority of cases occur in association with MEN1, reflecting a hereditary predisposition to multiple endocrine tumors. Prognosis depends primarily on tumor biology and extent of disease at diagnosis; localized, resectable gastrinomas carry a favorable long-term outlook, while metastatic disease (especially hepatic spread) is associated with reduced survival. Effective acid suppression has greatly reduced ulcer-related morbidity, shifting long-term outcome toward tumor-related factors.

AA Amyloidosis (Serum Amyloid A / Reactive Systemic Amyloidosis) — Secondary amyloidosis, Reactive amyloidosis, Inflammatory amyloidosis AL (immunoglobulin light-chain) amyloidosis ATTR and other hereditary amyloidoses Diabetic nephropathy and other causes of nephrotic syndrome Membranous nephropathy and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis Chronic glomerulonephritis Hepatosplenomegaly due to lymphoproliferative disease Abdominal subcutaneous fat aspirate or rectal or renal biopsy with Congo red staining and AA immunohistochemistry Serum amyloid A and C-reactive protein to gauge inflammatory activity Renal function and quantified proteinuria by urine protein to creatinine ratio Serum free light chains and immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis SAP scintigraphy to assess total organ amyloid burden Genetic testing for periodic fever syndromes where clinically suspected Targeted investigations to identify the underlying inflammatory or infective focus AA amyloidosis results from deposition of fragments of serum amyloid A, an acute-phase apolipoprotein whose hepatic synthesis is driven by interleukin-6, interleukin-1 and tumour necrosis factor during sustained inflammation. It complicates chronic inflammatory disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, spondyloarthropathies and inflammatory bowel disease, and chronic infections including bronchiectasis, tuberculosis and osteomyelitis. Hereditary periodic fever syndromes, notably familial Mediterranean fever, TRAPS and the cryopyrin-associated syndromes, are important and treatable causes, particularly in younger patients. The kidney is the dominant target, with proteinuria progressing to nephrotic syndrome and chronic kidney disease as the usual presentation. Hepatosplenomegaly, gastrointestinal involvement with diarrhoea and malabsorption, and less often cardiac disease may occur; macroglossia and periorbital purpura, characteristic of AL, are absent. The circulating serum amyloid A concentration tracks disease activity and is the key monitoring biomarker; sustained suppression can halt or reverse amyloid deposition. The therapeutic cornerstone is aggressive control of the underlying inflammatory drive, using interleukin-6, interleukin-1 or tumour necrosis factor blockade, with colchicine for familial Mediterranean fever. Incidence has fallen substantially with improved control of chronic inflammatory and infective disease. New nephrotic-range proteinuria in a patient with long-standing inflammatory disease Progressive decline in renal function Persistently elevated serum amyloid A and C-reactive protein despite treatment Unexplained hepatosplenomegaly or malabsorption Inferring the amyloid type from the clinical setting rather than confirming it by tissue typing, as AL can coexist with inflammatory disease Failing to search for an occult inflammatory or infective focus Not considering a hereditary periodic fever syndrome in younger patients Relying on C-reactive protein alone when serum amyloid A is the more informative activity marker Persistent activation of the acute-phase response raises hepatic production of serum amyloid A, an HDL-associated apolipoprotein. When the circulating concentration remains chronically elevated, proteolytic processing yields amyloidogenic AA fragments that polymerise into fibrils and deposit in the extracellular space, with particular avidity for the renal glomeruli, interstitium and vasculature, as well as the liver, spleen and gut. Fibril accumulation disrupts tissue architecture and organ function, and the rate of deposition is broadly proportional to the magnitude and duration of the serum amyloid A elevation, so that suppressing inflammation can stabilise or regress disease. Individual susceptibility is modified by serum amyloid A isotype and other genetic factors, which explains why only a minority of patients with chronic inflammation develop amyloidosis. Outcome is largely determined by renal involvement and by the ability to suppress the underlying inflammation. Sustained normalisation of serum amyloid A can arrest progression and permit regression, whereas uncontrolled inflammation leads to end-stage renal disease.

Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm — Bedside aortic ultrasound / CT Crossmatch; vascular surgery NOW Hypotension + back pain + pulsatile mass = surgical emergency Acute mesenteric ischemia (SMA embolism/thrombosis) — also causes severe diffuse abdominal pain, classically pain out of proportion to exam findings (p.154). Thoracic / thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm, which is often contiguous with infradiaphragmatic disease (p.2208). Mycotic (infective) aortic aneurysm from staphylococcal, streptococcal, Salmonella, or fungal seeding — typically saccular and often with positive blood cultures (p.2209). Syphilitic aortitis — uncommon cause, predominantly involves the ascending aorta/arch rather than the abdominal aorta (p.2209). Tuberculous aneurysm — typically affects the thoracic aorta via contiguous spread from hilar nodes or abscess (p.2209). Abdominal ultrasound — delineates transverse and longitudinal dimensions, can detect mural thrombus, and is the tool for serial size surveillance and screening (p.2211). Plain abdominal radiograph — may show a calcified aneurysm outline, but ~25% are non-calcified and not visualized (p.2211). Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI — accurate for location and size and for planning open or endovascular repair (p.2211). Contrast aortography may underestimate true diameter when mural thrombus reduces luminal size, and carries risks of bleeding, allergy, and atheroembolism (p.2211). Renal/ureteric colic — rupturing AAA pain radiating to flank or genitalia can mimic urolithiasis (p.154). Rectus sheath hematoma — abdominal wall mass and pain, especially on anticoagulants (p.154). Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are asymptomatic and are found as an incidental imaging finding or as a palpable, pulsatile, expansile, nontender mass on routine abdominal exam (p.2211). New aneurysmal pain is usually a harbinger of rupture and constitutes a medical emergency; however, acute rupture more often occurs without any prior warning (p.2211). Acute pain plus hypotension is the presentation of frank rupture and mandates emergency open or endovascular repair (p.2211). At least 90% of abdominal aortic aneurysms >4.0 cm are atherosclerotic, and most lie below the level of the renal arteries (infrarenal) (p.2211). Cigarette smoking is the most potent modifiable risk factor; incidence rises with age and the condition is more common in men (p.2211). Mural thrombus within the aneurysm sac can be a source of peripheral (distal) embolization (p.2211). New or worsening aneurysmal pain (abdomen, lower back, chest, or scrotum) signals impending rupture (p.2211). Abdominal pain radiating to sacrum, flank, or genitalia should always raise suspicion of a rupturing AAA (p.154). Acute pain with hypotension indicates rupture — emergency repair required (p.2211). A rupturing AAA can be misattributed to renal/ureteric colic when pain radiates to the flank or genitalia (p.154). Plain x-ray cannot exclude an aneurysm because roughly a quarter are non-calcified (p.2211). Aortography may underestimate aneurysm diameter when mural thrombus narrows the lumen (p.2211). Premonitory pain may persist for several days before rupture and collapse, so an evolving symptomatic aneurysm should not be dismissed (p.154). Aneurysm is a pathologic dilation of the aortic wall; a true aneurysm involves all three wall layers, versus a pseudoaneurysm in which intima and media are disrupted and the dilated segment is contained only by adventitia (and sometimes perivascular clot). Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are degenerative and atherosclerotic. Wall failure results from degradation or abnormal production of the structural matrix proteins elastin and collagen, driven by inflammation, oxidative stress, proteolysis, and biomechanical wall stress. B- and T-lymphocytes, macrophages, inflammatory cytokines, and matrix metalloproteinases degrade elastin and collagen, reducing tensile strength and the aorta's ability to tolerate pulsatile stretch; histology shows elastin/collagen destruction, loss of vascular smooth muscle, neovascularization, and inflammation (p.2208). Prognosis depends on aneurysm size and on the severity of coexisting coronary and cerebrovascular disease. Rupture risk rises sharply with diameter: the 5-year rupture risk is roughly 1-2% for aneurysms <5 cm versus 20-40% for aneurysms >5 cm. At smaller diameters the rupture risk is higher in women than in men (p.2211-2212). Rupture-risk stratification is driven by maximal aortic diameter. Per Harrison: a true abdominal aortic aneurysm is dilation 50% greater than the adjacent normal segment; aneurysms >=4.0 cm affect 1-2% of men >50. 5-year rupture risk is ~1-2% for <5 cm and ~20-40% for >5 cm. Repair thresholds: any size if rapidly expanding or symptomatic; for asymptomatic aneurysms repair is indicated at >=5.5 cm in men and >=5.0 cm in women, with smaller aneurysms followed by ultrasound surveillance (p.2210-2212).

Aagenaes syndrome — lymphoedema-cholestasis syndrome, cholestasis-lymphoedema syndrome, CLS, LCS1, hereditary cholestasis with lymphoedema Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC types 1-5) Alagille syndrome Biliary atresia Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency Primary lymphoedema (Milroy or Meige disease) without hepatic involvement Neonatal hepatitis of other cause Serum bile acids and fractionated (conjugated) bilirubin Liver function tests including gamma-glutamyl transferase and transaminases Fat-soluble vitamin levels (A, D, E) and coagulation studies for vitamin K status Liver biopsy showing cholestasis with variable portal fibrosis and giant-cell change Lymphoscintigraphy or imaging to demonstrate lymphatic hypoplasia Genetic testing and family/pedigree analysis, particularly in individuals of Norwegian ancestry An autosomal recessive disorder combining neonatal cholestasis with chronic lower-limb lymphoedema, described originally in a Norwegian founder population Cholestasis often presents in the neonatal period with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, pruritus, pale stools, and failure to thrive The lymphoedema characteristically affects the lower limbs and may not become clinically obvious until later childhood or adolescence The hepatic component tends to be episodic, with jaundice recurring during infancy and often improving with age, though some progress to fibrosis The disorder maps to a locus on chromosome 15 (LCS1); A defect in lymphatic development is thought to impair drainage from the liver and lower limbs, and reduced hepatic lymph flow may contribute to the cholestasis and periportal fibrosis. The causative gene has not been definitively identified, though linkage studies place the locus (LCS1) on chromosome 15q. Cholestatic episodes tend to be most severe in infancy and to lessen over time, whereas the peripheral lymphoedema is progressive and lifelong. The cholestatic episodes are often most troublesome in infancy and tend to improve with age, and many patients have a near-normal lifespan; however, a minority develop chronic liver disease or cirrhosis, and the lower-limb lymphoedema is lifelong and can be disabling.

anteverted nares, and a widow's peak The genital hallmark is a shawl scrotum, in which scrotal folds surround the base of the penis Hand findings include short broad hands with brachydactyly, clinodactyly and characteristic interdigital webbing Intellectual ability is often normal or only mildly affected, distinguishing it from many other X-linked syndromes Caused by variants in FGD1, encoding a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor that activates the Rho-family GTPase Cdc42 Carrier females may show subtle features such as mild hypertelorism Cervical spine instability (odontoid anomaly) posing a risk during anaesthesia or trauma Cryptorchidism requiring surgical assessment Significant learning or behavioural difficulty Visual impairment from ophthalmic complications Confusing the phenotype with Noonan syndrome and missing FGD1 testing Overlooking possible cervical spine instability before anaesthesia Assuming intellectual disability is invariable and mislabelling the child Missing subtle features in carrier females FGD1 encodes a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor that specifically activates the Rho-family small GTPase Cdc42, a key regulator of the actin cytoskeleton, cell shape and signalling during skeletal and craniofacial development. Loss-of-function variants impair Cdc42 activation, disturbing the cytoskeletal and signalling processes that guide bone growth and morphogenesis, producing the short stature and the facial, limb and genital anomalies. As an X-linked gene, males are predominantly affected while carrier females may show only mild features. Cognition is frequently spared because the developmental effect is weighted toward skeletal and connective-tissue patterning. Most individuals have a good outlook with generally normal or near-normal intellect and manageable skeletal and genital features; short stature persists but adult function is usually good. Care focuses on growth, orthopaedic and genital issues.

Abacavir hypersensitivity (HLA-B*57:01) — abacavir hypersensitivity reaction, AHR, HLA-B*57:01, abacavir HSR, nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor hypersensitivity Intercurrent viral or opportunistic infection in an HIV-positive patient Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome Other drug hypersensitivity reactions (e.g. to co-administered antiretrovirals or antimicrobials) DRESS syndrome from another agent Sepsis Acute gastroenteritis HLA-B*57:01 genotyping (ideally before starting therapy) Full blood count and eosinophil count Liver and renal function tests to assess organ involvement Inflammatory markers Careful medication timeline correlating symptoms with dosing Patch testing in specialist evaluation of uncertain historical reactions A systemic, multiorgan hypersensitivity reaction typically beginning within the first six weeks of starting abacavir, an antiretroviral used in HIV Presents with a combination of fever, rash, gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain), malaise and often respiratory symptoms The reaction is strongly and specifically associated with carriage of the HLA-B*57:01 allele Pre-treatment HLA-B*57:01 screening is standard practice and dramatically reduces the incidence of true immunologically confirmed reactions Symptoms characteristically worsen with each successive dose, in contrast to many self-limiting drug intolerances Management is immediate and permanent discontinuation of abacavir with supportive care Rechallenge after a genuine hypersensitivity reaction is contraindicated because it can precipitate rapid, life-threatening hypotension and collapse Absence of HLA-B*57:01 makes an immunologically confirmed reaction very unlikely but does not entirely exclude other drug intolerance Hypotension or cardiovascular collapse, particularly after re-exposure Rapidly progressive multiorgan symptoms Respiratory distress Any inadvertent rechallenge in a patient with a prior genuine reaction Rechallenging a patient who has had a genuine reaction, risking fatal hypotension Failing to perform HLA-B*57:01 screening before initiating abacavir Attributing early symptoms to a viral illness and continuing the drug Labelling every mild intolerance as hypersensitivity, which unnecessarily removes a useful agent Abacavir hypersensitivity is an HLA-restricted, T-cell-mediated immune reaction. Abacavir binds non-covalently within the antigen-binding groove of the HLA-B*57:01 molecule, altering the repertoire of self-peptides that are presented at the cell surface. This altered peptide display is recognised as foreign by cytotoxic CD8 T cells, driving a clonal T-cell response and release of inflammatory cytokines that produce the systemic multiorgan syndrome. Because the interaction is specific to the HLA-B*57:01 allele, susceptibility is genetically determined and can be predicted by pre-treatment genotyping. Repeat exposure amplifies the primed immune response, explaining the escalating severity and the danger of rechallenge. With prompt and permanent withdrawal, the reaction resolves fully over days and the outlook is excellent. Continued dosing or, especially, rechallenge can cause severe hypotension and death, so lifelong avoidance is mandatory once a genuine reaction has occurred.

Abdominal migraine — abdominal migraine syndrome, childhood periodic syndrome (abdominal type) Functional abdominal pain and irritable bowel syndrome Cyclical vomiting syndrome (a related episodic syndrome) Constipation Intermittent obstruction such as malrotation with volvulus or recurrent intussusception, and recurrent appendicitis Urinary tract infection or pelvi-ureteric junction obstruction Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis Inflammatory bowel disease and coeliac disease Thorough history including an attack diary and family history of migraine Abdominal examination with growth and weight monitoring between attacks Urinalysis to exclude a urinary tract cause Basic bloods including full blood count, inflammatory markers and coeliac serology to exclude organic disease Abdominal ultrasound if structural or renal pathology is suspected Referral for further gastrointestinal evaluation such as endoscopy only if red flags are present An episodic syndrome that may be associated with migraine (ICHD-3), affecting mainly school-age children (peak around 5-10 years) and a recognised cause of recurrent abdominal pain Attacks are recurrent, stereotyped episodes of moderate-to-severe midline or periumbilical dull pain lasting hours (typically up to 72 hours) with completely symptom-free intervals Associated features include anorexia, nausea, vomiting and pallor; the child often looks unwell and withdraws from normal activity The pain is characteristically midline and poorly localised, the abdomen is normal on examination, and the child is entirely well between attacks A personal or family history of migraine is common and many children later develop typical migraine headaches Diagnosis is clinical using ICHD-3 criteria (at least five attacks of midline pain lasting 2-72 hours with at least two of anorexia, nausea, vomiting or pallor and no better explanation) It remains a diagnosis of exclusion, so a careful history and examination are needed to exclude gastrointestinal, renal and surgical causes Management mirrors migraine care with trigger avoidance, reassurance, acute symptomatic measures and migraine prophylaxis in frequent or severe cases Bilious vomiting or pain that is not midline or is localised away from the umbilicus Weight loss, faltering growth or nocturnal waking with pain or diarrhoea Gastrointestinal bleeding, persistent vomiting or signs of obstruction Abnormal examination findings such as a mass, organomegaly or perianal disease Fever, joint symptoms or other systemic features suggesting organic disease Labelling pain as abdominal migraine before excluding organic gastrointestinal, renal or surgical disease Failing to recognise the migraine link and so delaying appropriate migraine-directed management Attributing the pain purely to psychological causes and missing the diagnosis Missing bilious vomiting or faltering growth that signal an alternative diagnosis Over-investigating a child with a typical, stereotyped presentation and a normal examination Abdominal migraine is considered part of the migraine continuum, sharing mechanisms with migraine including trigeminovascular activation, dysregulation of the brain-gut axis and altered central pain processing. The same paroxysmal neuronal excitability and neuropeptide changes thought to drive migraine are expressed with the gut as the principal symptomatic target, producing episodic midline pain with autonomic accompaniments. There is strong familial and genetic overlap with migraine, and attacks are provoked by migraine-type triggers such as stress, fatigue, missed meals and certain foods. Abdominal migraine is benign and self-limiting; attacks typically diminish over time and most children become symptom-free. A substantial proportion, however, develop migraine headaches during adolescence or adulthood.

Sixth nerve palsy — abducens palsy, lateral rectus palsy Thyroid eye disease with restricted medial rectus Medial orbital wall fracture with muscle entrapment Myasthenia gravis Duane retraction syndrome Convergence spasm or divergence insufficiency Internuclear ophthalmoplegia MRI of the brain and orbits, including the cavernous sinus and skull base Assessment for papilloedema and features of raised intracranial pressure Vasculopathic risk-factor evaluation Acetylcholine-receptor antibody testing if myasthenia is suspected Lumbar puncture with opening pressure when intracranial hypertension is suspected Weakness of the lateral rectus causes horizontal binocular diplopia worse at distance and on gaze toward the affected side The affected eye is esotropic and fails to abduct fully beyond the midline in a complete palsy Because the sixth nerve has a long intracranial course it is a poor localiser and can be a false-localising sign of raised intracranial pressure Common causes include microvascular ischaemia, raised intracranial pressure, tumour, trauma and cavernous sinus disease In children, a post-viral benign sixth nerve palsy occurs but a posterior fossa tumour must be excluded Bilateral or progressive palsies and any additional neurological signs mandate neuroimaging Papilloedema or other signs of raised intracranial pressure Additional cranial neuropathies or long-tract signs Progressive, bilateral or paediatric palsy Associated severe headache or systemic features Assuming a microvascular cause and missing raised intracranial pressure Overlooking a posterior fossa tumour in a child Mistaking restrictive or myasthenic limitation for a neurogenic palsy Failing to re-image a palsy that does not recover as expected The abducens nerve supplies the lateral rectus, so its dysfunction impairs abduction and leaves the eye deviated inward by the unopposed medial rectus. Its long course from the pons, up the clivus, over the petrous apex and through the cavernous sinus makes it vulnerable along many segments; stretching from raised intracranial pressure explains its false-localising behaviour. Microvascular ischaemia of the nerve, as in diabetes and hypertension, is a frequent self-limiting cause, whereas compressive, inflammatory or infiltrative lesions produce more persistent or progressive palsies. Isolated microvascular palsies usually recover within weeks to a few months; other causes depend on the underlying pathology, and persistent deviation may need prism or strabismus surgery.

aberrant subclavian artery — arteria lusoria, aberrant right subclavian artery Achalasia and other oesophageal motility disorders Oesophageal stricture or web Oesophageal or mediastinal neoplasm causing extrinsic compression Double aortic arch or other complete vascular ring Right aortic arch with aberrant left subclavian artery Eosinophilic oesophagitis Globus sensation Barium swallow or contrast oesophagogram CT angiography of the aortic arch MR angiography Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to exclude mucosal disease Oesophageal manometry if a motility disorder is suspected Transthoracic echocardiography for associated cardiac anomalies Genetic evaluation given associations with trisomy 21 and 22q11.2 deletion An aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria) is the commonest congenital aortic arch anomaly, arising as the last branch of a left-sided arch and coursing behind the oesophagus. It is usually asymptomatic and found incidentally, but its retro-oesophageal course can produce dysphagia lusoria, typically in adults as the vessel stiffens or becomes aneurysmal. Compression of the trachea may cause stridor or dyspnoea, more often in infants than in adults. The origin is frequently dilated as a Kommerell diverticulum, which carries a risk of aneurysm formation, dissection and rupture. An aberrant right subclavian is associated with an absent (non-recurrent) right laryngeal nerve, a crucial consideration during thyroid and neck surgery to avoid nerve injury. A barium swallow shows a characteristic oblique posterior indentation on the oesophagus, and CT or MR angiography confirms the vessel and any diverticulum. In isolation it does not form a complete ring, whereas an aberrant left subclavian with a right arch and left ligamentum does. Asymptomatic cases are observed, while symptomatic dysphagia or an enlarging diverticulum warrants surgical reimplantation or bypass with division of the aberrant vessel. Rapidly progressive dysphagia or weight loss, prompting exclusion of malignancy An aneurysmal Kommerell diverticulum or signs of dissection Haematemesis suggesting an aorto-oesophageal fistula Stridor or respiratory distress in an infant Attributing dysphagia to the anomaly without excluding a coexisting oesophageal malignancy. Inadvertent injury to a non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve during thyroid surgery when the anomaly is unrecognised. Overlooking an aneurysmal Kommerell diverticulum that requires treatment. Confusing an isolated aberrant subclavian (no ring) with a complete vascular ring. Assuming that symptoms in an infant simply represent benign gastro-oesophageal reflux. The anomaly results from abnormal regression of the embryonic aortic arch system. For an aberrant right subclavian artery, the right fourth arch and proximal right dorsal aorta regress abnormally while a distal segment of the right dorsal aorta persists, so the right subclavian arises as the most distal branch of the left arch and must cross the midline behind the oesophagus to reach the right arm. This retro-oesophageal course places the vessel against the posterior oesophageal wall; in childhood the pliable artery rarely causes symptoms, but with ageing, atherosclerosis and dilatation of the Kommerell diverticulum the vessel becomes rigid and may indent the oesophagus sufficiently to impair swallowing. The great majority of patients remain asymptomatic with a normal life expectancy; symptomatic disease and an aneurysmal diverticulum have good outcomes after appropriate surgical repair.

Without functional MTTP, apoB-containing lipoproteins cannot be assembled or secreted, so dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins are not exported from enterocytes and accumulate as lipid droplets within the cells. The result is severe fat malabsorption and steatorrhoea, extremely low plasma lipids, and progressive deficiency of vitamins A, D, E and K. When diagnosed early and treated with fat restriction and lifelong high-dose vitamin E and other fat-soluble vitamins, the disabling neurological and retinal complications can be largely prevented. Late or untreated disease leads to progressive, often irreversible, neurological and visual deterioration.

acanthocephalan. In the intestine the larva develops into an adult worm that lacks a digestive tract and absorbs nutrients across its surface. Its hallmark is a spiny, retractable proboscis that embeds into the intestinal mucosa, provoking localised inflammation and, with deeper penetration, ulceration or full-thickness injury. Most damage is therefore mechanical and focal at the attachment site; systemic disease is uncommon and severe complications such as perforation are rare. Prognosis is excellent in most cases, as infection is usually mild and self-limited or readily treated; the rare complication of perforation carries the morbidity of any acute abdomen but is uncommon.

Acatalasaemia — Takahara disease, Catalase deficiency, Acatalasia, CAT Necrotising (ulcerative) gingivitis and periodontitis of other cause Immunodeficiency-related oral ulceration and gangrene (for example neutropenia) Other inherited antioxidant enzyme deficiencies Noma (cancrum oris) from severe malnutrition and infection Aggressive periodontal disease Oral manifestations of haematological malignancy Erythrocyte catalase activity assay, which is absent or markedly reduced Simple bedside test observing lack of frothing when blood meets hydrogen peroxide CAT molecular genetic testing Full blood count to exclude neutropenia as a cause of oral gangrene Dental and periodontal assessment of the extent of oral disease Screening for associated oxidative-stress conditions where clinically indicated Acatalasaemia is an autosomal recessive deficiency of the antioxidant enzyme catalase, encoded by CAT, which normally decomposes hydrogen peroxide within peroxisomes It was first described in Japan (Takahara disease) and is often clinically silent, discovered incidentally when blood fails to froth on contact with hydrogen peroxide The best-known manifestation is progressive oral gangrene (Takahara disease), where hydrogen peroxide from oral bacteria is not detoxified, leading to painful ulcerating gum and alveolar lesions Many individuals, especially those with residual enzyme activity (hypocatalasaemia), remain entirely asymptomatic throughout life Reduced antioxidant defence has been linked epidemiologically to increased susceptibility to oxidative-stress-related conditions such as diabetes mellitus in some populations Diagnosis is by demonstrating absent or markedly reduced erythrocyte catalase activity, confirmed by CAT gene analysis Management centres on scrupulous oral hygiene and prompt treatment of oral infection; no specific enzyme replacement exists Progressive oral gangrene with tissue necrosis and secondary infection Spreading orofacial infection threatening deeper structures Severe periodontal destruction with tooth loss Systemic sepsis arising from an oral focus Assuming all affected individuals develop oral disease, when the majority are asymptomatic Overlooking catalase deficiency as a cause of unexplained recurrent oral gangrene Failing to distinguish acatalasaemia from neutropenic or malnutrition-related oral necrosis Not recognising the residual-activity (hypocatalasaemia) state, which is milder and often silent Acatalasaemia results from recessive loss-of-function mutations in CAT, the gene encoding catalase, a haem-containing peroxisomal enzyme that catalyses the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. When catalase activity is largely absent, hydrogen peroxide generated by cellular metabolism or, in the mouth, by peroxide-producing bacteria is inadequately cleared. The accumulating hydrogen peroxide oxidises haemoglobin and damages tissue, and in the oral cavity it causes local ischaemia and ulceration that manifests as the characteristic gangrenous stomatitis. In most tissues, alternative antioxidant systems such as glutathione peroxidase partly compensate, which explains why many individuals are asymptomatic. The prognosis is generally excellent, since most individuals are asymptomatic; where the oral (Takahara) form occurs, outcome is good with meticulous oral hygiene and infection control, and severity tends to lessen after adolescence.

accelerated idioventricular rhythm — AIVR, slow ventricular tachycardia ventricular tachycardia junctional rhythm with aberrant conduction supraventricular rhythm with bundle branch block ventricular escape rhythm in complete heart block paced ventricular rhythm hyperkalaemia producing a wide-complex rhythm twelve-lead ECG to confirm rate and identify fusion and capture beats continuous telemetry to document onset, offset and relationship to sinus rate serial cardiac troponin and ECG in the context of suspected reperfusion serum electrolytes including potassium and magnesium serum digoxin concentration when toxicity is suspected echocardiography to assess ventricular function and structural disease AIVR is a wide-complex ventricular rhythm at a rate of roughly 40 to 120 per minute, faster than the intrinsic ventricular escape rate but slower than ventricular tachycardia. It is the classic and generally benign marker of successful reperfusion following thrombolysis or primary percutaneous intervention in acute myocardial infarction. The rhythm typically emerges when sinus rate slows and the enhanced ventricular focus overtakes it, and it recedes as sinus rate recovers. Onset and offset are gradual, and fusion and capture beats are common at the transitions as the two competing pacemakers interact. It is usually haemodynamically well tolerated and self-limiting, so suppression is rarely required. Loss of atrioventricular synchrony can occasionally reduce cardiac output in patients dependent on the atrial contribution to filling. Other associations include digoxin toxicity, cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, cocaine use and the postoperative cardiac surgical setting. If treatment is needed to restore atrioventricular synchrony, accelerating the sinus rate to overdrive the ectopic focus is preferred over suppressive antiarrhythmics. haemodynamic compromise attributable to loss of atrioventricular synchrony acceleration into sustained rapid ventricular tachycardia occurrence with digoxin toxicity requiring specific management features suggesting active ischaemia rather than reperfusion association with significant electrolyte derangement Misclassifying AIVR as ventricular tachycardia and administering unnecessary or harmful suppressive treatment. Attempting to suppress a benign, self-limiting rhythm rather than supporting sinus rate if symptomatic. Overlooking digoxin toxicity or electrolyte disturbance as a cause outside the reperfusion setting. Assuming reperfusion is complete solely on the basis of AIVR without corroborating clinical and angiographic data. Failing to recognise loss of atrioventricular synchrony as the mechanism of intolerance in filling-dependent patients. AIVR arises from enhanced automaticity of a subsidiary pacemaker within the His-Purkinje system or ventricular myocardium. The abnormal focus discharges faster than its intrinsic escape rate but not fast enough to constitute ventricular tachycardia. Because the focus and the sinus node compete, the ventricular rhythm typically manifests only when it transiently exceeds the sinus rate, such as during sinus slowing or atrioventricular block, and yields to sinus rhythm when the sinus rate rises. In the setting of reperfusion, washout of ischaemic metabolites and calcium loading of injured Purkinje tissue is thought to heighten automaticity. The competing pacemakers frequently generate fusion and capture complexes at onset and termination. AIVR is generally benign, transient and self-limiting, particularly as a reperfusion phenomenon, and rarely requires specific therapy. Prognosis is dominated by the underlying condition rather than the rhythm itself.

Signs of infection or a destructive lesion at the medial midfoot Dismissing medial midfoot pain as simple tendinopathy and missing a symptomatic accessory navicular Failing to recognise associated tibialis posterior dysfunction and flatfoot Overlooking a navicular stress fracture presenting with similar medial pain Excising the ossicle without securing the tibialis posterior insertion, and it is intimately related to the insertion of the tibialis posterior tendon. In the commonly symptomatic type II variant, the ossicle is connected to the navicular by a fibrocartilaginous synchondrosis, and much of the tibialis posterior inserts onto the ossicle rather than directly onto the navicular. Repetitive traction and shear from the tibialis posterior across this synchondrosis, together with direct pressure from footwear on the bony prominence, produce pain, local inflammation, and stress across the junction, which MRI shows as oedema. Because the tibialis posterior is the principal dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch, an insertion compromised by a symptomatic accessory navicular can be associated with tibialis posterior dysfunction and a flexible flatfoot. Acute exacerbations may follow minor trauma or a twisting injury that stresses the synchondrosis. Most symptomatic accessory naviculars settle with conservative measures aimed at offloading the tibialis posterior insertion and supporting the arch, particularly in adolescents whose symptoms often improve with skeletal maturity. When symptoms persist, excision of the ossicle with reattachment or reconstruction of the tibialis posterior gives good pain relief in the majority, although recovery is gradual and associated flatfoot may need to be addressed.

causes of secondary hypothermia Continuous core temperature monitoring with a low-reading thermometer Electrocardiogram and cardiac monitoring for Osborn waves and arrhythmia Blood glucose, trauma, infection, or intoxication Accidental hypothermia is an unintentional fall in core temperature below 35 degrees Celsius and is graded into mild, moderate, and severe categories that guide management Clinical features progress from shivering and tachycardia in mild cases to a fall in consciousness, loss of shivering, bradycardia, and hypotension as cooling deepens The electrocardiogram may show the characteristic Osborn (J) wave, along with bradyarrhythmias and a risk of ventricular fibrillation, especially with rough handling Core temperature should be measured with a low-reading thermometer at a reliable site, as standard thermometers underestimate severe hypothermia Rewarming is tailored to severity: passive external rewarming for mild cases and active external and internal rewarming for moderate to severe cases Afterdrop, a further fall in core temperature after rewarming begins as cold peripheral blood returns centrally, and rewarming-related hypotension should be anticipated In cardiac arrest with severe hypothermia, prolonged resuscitation is warranted because good neurological recovery is possible, and extracorporeal rewarming may be life-saving Absent or severely depressed consciousness with very low core temperature Malignant arrhythmia or cardiac arrest Hypotension and signs of cardiovascular collapse during rewarming Rigidity with no detectable pulse, requiring careful, prolonged assessment before declaring death Declaring death before adequate rewarming, since deep hypothermia can mimic death Rough handling or unnecessary movement precipitating ventricular fibrillation Relying on a standard thermometer that fails to read low temperatures Overlooking afterdrop and rewarming-related hypotension Missing a secondary cause such as hypoglycaemia, hypothyroidism, sepsis, or intoxication Accidental hypothermia results when heat loss exceeds heat production, lowering core temperature and progressively depressing metabolic and organ function. Cold exposure, immersion, impaired thermoregulation, and reduced heat generation all contribute. As temperature falls, initial compensatory shivering and vasoconstriction give way to failure of thermoregulation. Enzyme activity, cardiac conduction, and central nervous system function slow, producing bradycardia, reduced consciousness, cold diuresis, and a shift of fluid that causes intravascular volume depletion. The myocardium becomes increasingly irritable and prone to malignant arrhythmia, particularly ventricular fibrillation, which can be precipitated by jolting movement. During rewarming, return of cold, acidotic peripheral blood to the core can cause afterdrop and cardiovascular instability. Prognosis depends on the depth and duration of cooling, the underlying cause, and the presence of asphyxia or trauma. Isolated hypothermia, even when severe, can have excellent neurological recovery with appropriate rewarming and prolonged resuscitation, which is why the maxim that a patient is not dead until warm and dead is emphasised. Coexisting illness, injury, or hypoxia worsens outcome.

Operating on the fully accommodative component instead of prescribing and continuing glasses Missing a high AC/A ratio by not measuring the near versus distance deviation Discontinuing glasses prematurely and allowing decompensation In a hypermetropic child the unaccommodated retinal image is blurred, so the child accommodates to clear it. Because accommodation is neurologically yoked to convergence (the accommodative convergence per unit of accommodation, or AC/A, relationship), the additional accommodative effort drives excessive convergence. When fusional divergence is insufficient to overcome this, a manifest convergent deviation results. In refractive accommodative esotropia the AC/A ratio is normal and the deviation reflects uncorrected hypermetropia, whereas in the non-refractive (high AC/A) type an abnormally high convergence response per dioptre of accommodation produces a greater deviation at near. A persistent manifest deviation in the visually immature child leads to suppression and amblyopia. With full hypermetropic correction and treatment of any amblyopia, refractive accommodative esotropia has an excellent prognosis with good binocular potential, and some children reduce their hypermetropia and spectacle dependence over time. Partially accommodative cases often need surgery for the non-accommodative component but should continue spectacle correction.
