cognitive decline or new psychiatric symptoms Poorly controlled diabetes with metabolic decompensation Severe or disabling involuntary movements Signs of significant hepatic iron-related dysfunction Confusing the low serum copper and caeruloplasmin with Wilson disease and giving copper-directed therapy while missing the iron-overload picture Overlooking the systemic clues of diabetes and retinopathy that point to the diagnosis Failing to consider a treatable iron-chelation opportunity when NBIA is suspected Not measuring ferritin, which is characteristically high and helps separate this from copper disorders Aceruloplasminaemia results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in CP, which encodes caeruloplasmin, a ferroxidase that oxidises ferrous to ferric iron to enable iron export and loading onto transferrin. Without functional caeruloplasmin, iron cannot be released normally from cells, so it accumulates within the brain and visceral organs including the pancreas, liver, and retina. The resulting iron-mediated oxidative injury produces neurodegeneration concentrated in the basal ganglia and cerebellum together with diabetes and retinopathy, distinguishing this from copper-overload disorders such as Wilson disease. Untreated, the disorder is progressive with worsening neurological disability, diabetes, and retinopathy, but because iron-lowering therapy can retard progression, prognosis is more favourable with early diagnosis than for most other NBIA subtypes.

Achilles tendinopathy — Achilles tendinosis, Achilles tendinitis, mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, insertional Achilles tendinopathy Complete or partial Achilles tendon rupture Retrocalcaneal or superficial calcaneal bursitis Haglund deformity Posterior ankle impingement or os trigonum Calcaneal stress fracture Sural nerve irritation Systemic enthesitis from seronegative spondyloarthropathy Largely a clinical diagnosis Ultrasound to show tendon thickening, hypoechoic areas, neovascularity, and to detect partial tears MRI for detailed assessment in refractory or surgical cases and to characterise insertional pathology Plain radiographs for insertional disease to identify calcification, a Haglund deformity, or spur Consider metabolic and inflammatory screening in atypical, bilateral, or young patients Presents with posterior heel or lower-calf pain and stiffness that is worst on starting activity and after rest, with local tendon thickening and tenderness It is divided into mid-portion disease (a few centimetres above the insertion) and insertional disease at the calcaneal attachment, which are managed differently The mid-portion tendon has a relatively hypovascular zone that predisposes it to degenerative failure under repetitive load It is a degenerative tendinopathy with disorganised collagen and neovascularisation rather than true tendinitis Always distinguish tendinopathy from a complete rupture; a positive Thompson (calf squeeze) test and a palpable gap indicate rupture and need urgent referral Progressive eccentric or heavy slow-resistance calf loading is the cornerstone of treatment for mid-portion disease Insertional disease may respond less well to full-range eccentric loading and often needs modified, reduced-dorsiflexion exercises and heel lifts Corticosteroid injection into or around the tendon is generally avoided because of the risk of rupture Fluoroquinolone antibiotics are associated with tendinopathy and tendon rupture and should be considered in the history Sudden pain with a palpable gap and positive Thompson test indicating tendon rupture Recent fluoroquinolone use raising rupture risk Night pain, systemic symptoms, or a mass suggesting infection or tumour Inflammatory or bilateral enthesitis suggesting spondyloarthropathy Missing a tendon rupture by not performing the Thompson test Injecting corticosteroid into or around the tendon and precipitating rupture Applying mid-portion eccentric protocols to insertional disease and worsening symptoms Advancing loading too quickly and provoking flares, or ignoring contributory training errors Achilles tendinopathy is an overuse condition in which repetitive loading exceeds the tendon's capacity to adapt, causing microtears and a failed healing response. Histology shows collagen disorganisation, increased ground substance, and neovascularisation with accompanying nerve ingrowth rather than inflammatory cells. The mid-portion watershed zone of relative hypovascularity is vulnerable, while insertional disease involves the enthesis and may be associated with a Haglund deformity or retrocalcaneal bursitis. Most patients improve over three to six months with structured loading, though symptoms can be slow to settle and recurrence is common; insertional disease is generally more resistant to conservative treatment than mid-portion disease.

Achondrogenesis — achondrogenesis type 1A (TRIP11), achondrogenesis type 1B (SLC26A2), achondrogenesis type 2 (COL2A1) Thanatophoric dysplasia (FGFR3, lethal short-limbed dysplasia) Osteogenesis imperfecta type II (fractures, poor ossification) Hypophosphatasia, perinatal lethal form Hypochondrogenesis (milder end of the COL2A1 spectrum) Short-rib polydactyly syndromes Fibrochondrogenesis and atelosteogenesis Detailed prenatal ultrasound and, where appropriate, fetal MRI to characterise limb, trunk and thoracic size Postnatal or postmortem skeletal radiographs demonstrating the ossification pattern Molecular testing of TRIP11, SLC26A2 and COL2A1 to define the subtype Histopathology of the cartilage growth plate Placental and fetal examination in perinatal death for diagnostic confirmation Genetic counselling with consideration of parental carrier or gonadal mosaicism testing A group of lethal skeletal dysplasias defined by extreme micromelia (very short limbs), a short trunk and severe deficiency of endochondral ossification Type 1A (Houston-Harris) is caused by TRIP11 mutations and type 1B (Fraccaro) by SLC26A2 mutations, both autosomal recessive; type 2 (Langer-Saldino) is caused by dominant COL2A1 mutations, usually de novo Presents prenatally or at birth with a large head, extremely short limbs, a narrow chest and hydrops or marked soft-tissue oedema The small, poorly compliant thorax causes pulmonary hypoplasia and lethal respiratory failure in the perinatal period Radiographs show virtually absent ossification of the vertebral bodies and sacrum, short ribs (with fractures in type 1A) and severely shortened, poorly modelled long bones Type 2 belongs to the type II collagenopathy spectrum, at the severe end of a continuum that includes hypochondrogenesis and spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia Diagnosis rests on the radiographic pattern, histology of the growth plate and molecular confirmation Because the condition is lethal, care centres on accurate diagnosis, recurrence-risk counselling and compassionate perinatal support Severe pulmonary hypoplasia causing respiratory failure at birth Hydrops fetalis detected antenatally A markedly small thorax on prenatal imaging predicting lethality Recurrence in a subsequent pregnancy indicating recessive inheritance or gonadal mosaicism Confusing it with other lethal short-limbed dysplasias without radiographic and molecular characterisation Assuming a de novo dominant cause and understating recurrence risk in the recessive types Not securing tissue or molecular confirmation before counselling about future pregnancies Overlooking gonadal mosaicism as an explanation for recurrence in type 2 Achondrogenesis is a disorder of cartilage and endochondral bone formation with several molecular causes. Type 1A involves TRIP11, encoding a Golgi protein needed for normal cartilage matrix processing. Type 1B involves SLC26A2, a sulphate transporter required to sulphate cartilage proteoglycans, so undersulphated matrix cannot support normal skeletal growth. Type 2 arises from dominant-negative mutations in COL2A1, the gene for type II collagen, the principal structural collagen of cartilage. In each case, disordered cartilage matrix prevents normal growth-plate function and ossification, producing the profound skeletal deficiency. Achondrogenesis is generally lethal before or shortly after birth because of pulmonary hypoplasia; the value of diagnosis lies in accurate classification, recurrence-risk counselling and support for the family rather than in curative treatment.

Achondroplasia — FGFR3, ACH, rhizomelic short-limbed dwarfism Hypochondroplasia Thanatophoric dysplasia Pseudoachondroplasia Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia Cartilage-hair hypoplasia SHOX-related short stature Skeletal survey demonstrating rhizomelic shortening and characteristic pelvic and spinal changes Targeted FGFR3 molecular testing to confirm the diagnosis Craniocervical MRI and neurological assessment to evaluate foramen magnum stenosis in infancy Polysomnography for suspected central or obstructive sleep apnoea Serial head circumference and disproportionate growth charting on condition-specific curves Spinal imaging for symptomatic canal stenosis or kyphosis The most common non-lethal skeletal dysplasia, characterised by disproportionate short stature with rhizomelic (proximal) limb shortening Nearly all cases arise from a recurrent gain-of-function variant in FGFR3; inheritance is autosomal dominant with high de novo rates, and paternal age is a risk factor Typical features include macrocephaly with frontal bossing and midface hypoplasia, a trident hand configuration, and thoracolumbar kyphosis in infancy Radiographs show short tubular bones, narrowing rather than widening of the interpedicular distance descending the lumbar spine, squared iliac wings, and champagne-glass pelvis Foramen magnum stenosis is a critical early complication that can cause cervicomedullary compression, central apnoea, and sudden death in infancy Later complications include spinal canal stenosis, obstructive sleep apnoea, recurrent otitis media, and genu varum A targeted FGFR3-modulating therapy is now available to promote linear growth, alongside multidisciplinary surveillance Signs of cervicomedullary compression such as central apnoea, hypotonia, or long-tract signs in infancy Rapidly progressive hydrocephalus or raised intracranial pressure Progressive neurogenic claudication or myelopathy from spinal stenosis Severe fixed thoracolumbar kyphosis with neurological involvement Attributing infant apnoea or hypotonia to benign causes and missing foramen magnum compression Plotting growth on standard rather than condition-specific charts Assuming developmental delay when early gross-motor milestones are expectedly slow due to body proportions Overlooking recurrent middle-ear disease and its impact on hearing and speech Achondroplasia is caused by an activating variant in FGFR3, the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 gene. Constitutive receptor signalling suppresses chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation in the growth plate, impairing endochondral ossification. Because long bones grow chiefly through endochondral ossification while membranous ossification is relatively spared, the result is disproportionate shortening of the limbs with a relatively normal trunk length and a large skull. The same mechanism underlies the characteristic craniofacial and spinal features, including a small foramen magnum and narrow spinal canal. Intelligence and lifespan are usually normal with appropriate surveillance, though foramen magnum stenosis raises early infant mortality if unrecognised. Adult stature is markedly reduced, and morbidity later relates chiefly to spinal stenosis, sleep-disordered breathing, and joint problems.

(typical) achromatopsia has total colour blindness, whereas incomplete forms retain some residual cone function and colour discrimination Management is supportive with tinted or red-tinted lenses to reduce photophobia and low-vision aids, and it is a leading candidate condition for gene-replacement therapy trials Nystagmus and photophobia in infancy requiring prompt paediatric ophthalmology and genetics referral Progressive loss of foveal cone structure on imaging Missed diagnosis attributed to a normal-looking fundus delaying appropriate support Attributing infantile nystagmus and poor vision to a normal fundus and missing the electrophysiological diagnosis Confusing achromatopsia with albinism or Leber congenital amaurosis Overlooking the photophobia burden and failing to prescribe appropriate tinted lenses Assuming complete colour blindness in all cases when incomplete forms retain partial function Achromatopsia arises from loss of function of the cone phototransduction cascade. Mutations most commonly affect the cyclic-nucleotide-gated channel subunits CNGB3 and CNGA3, and less often the cone transducin GNAT2 or phosphodiesterase subunits, disrupting the cones' ability to respond to light. Rod-mediated (scotopic) vision remains functional, so vision is relatively better in dim conditions, while bright light saturates the rods and produces disabling photophobia. Because central vision depends on the cone-rich fovea, cone dysfunction causes reduced acuity, nystagmus from lack of a stable foveal fixation signal, and impaired or absent colour perception. Progressive cone photoreceptor structural loss may occur at the fovea over time. Vision is stable in most patients with typically low but non-progressive acuity, though photophobia and colour blindness persist lifelong; the condition is generally non-degenerative, and emerging gene therapies offer future therapeutic promise.

Acinetobacter Infections — Acinetobacter baumannii infection, A. baumannii infection, Acinetobacter calcoaceticus-baumannii complex infection, MDR Acinetobacter, Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter (CRAB) Ventilator-associated/hospital-acquired pneumonia due to other nosocomial gram-negative bacilli (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacterales) Stenotrophomonas maltophilia or Burkholderia infection in the ventilated/immunocompromised host Catheter-related bloodstream infection from other nosocomial pathogens Necrotizing fasciitis or other necrotizing soft tissue infection from streptococcal, clostridial, or polymicrobial causes following trauma Bacterial meningitis due to Neisseria meningitidis (similar gram-negative paired cocci on CSF Gram stain) Neisseria meningitidis on CSF Gram stain (both appear as gram-negative diplococci/paired cocci) Other nonfermenting gram-negative nosocomial pathogens such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for species-level identification Quantitative real-time PCR for identification of A. baumannii Antimicrobial susceptibility testing to guide definitive therapy (given extensive and variable resistance) Respiratory cultures interpreted in clinical context to distinguish colonization from pneumonia Blood cultures (assessing for polymicrobial growth in suspected bacteremia) Rectal surveillance cultures for outbreak detection and infection-control purposes Molecular typing of isolates to differentiate outbreak from nonoutbreak strains Airway colonization without true pneumonia (positive respiratory culture not equating to active infection) Wound colonization rather than soft tissue infection, particularly in burns and trauma Acinetobacter are gram-negative, oxidase-negative, nonmotile, nonfermenting coccobacilli readily grown on standard media; A. baumannii is the most clinically relevant species. Phenotypic differentiation between species is difficult, so molecular methods such as MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry or quantitative real-time PCR are often needed for accurate identification. A. baumannii can survive environmental desiccation for weeks, allowing it to persist on hospital surfaces and equipment - a key reason it drives health care-associated outbreaks. A. baumannii is a notorious cause of nosocomial pneumonia, especially with prolonged mechanical ventilation; onset tends to be later than with other gram-negative bacilli, and the usual clues are fever and increased sputum production. Airway colonization with A. baumannii does not by itself confirm pneumonia, but it is a recognized risk factor for subsequent infection - distinguishing colonization from true infection is a recurring clinical challenge. On a CSF Gram stain, Acinetobacter can mimic Neisseria meningitidis since both appear as gram-negative paired cocci; a petechial rash was described in up to 30% of one meningitis case series. Bloodstream infection most often arises in ICU patients with a central venous catheter or as a secondary complication of ventilator-associated/hospital-acquired pneumonia; fever occurs in over 95% of cases and polymicrobial growth is reported in roughly 20-36% of bacteremia episodes. In combat-trauma soft tissue infection, the described clinical evolution progresses from an edematous peau d'orange appearance to a sandpaper appearance with overlying vesicles, then to a necrotizing process with hemorrhagic bullae; necrotizing fasciitis has been reported. Community-acquired Acinetobacter pneumonia is relatively rare but severe, with fever, prominent respiratory symptoms, multi-organ dysfunction, lobar consolidation on imaging, and mortality exceeding 50%. A. baumannii is an important burn-unit pathogen; large burns provide ideal growth conditions, facilitate patient-to-patient transmission, and wound colonization is a risk factor for bloodstream infection. Risk factors for health care-associated colonization/infection include nursing home residence, prolonged ICU stay, central venous catheterization, tracheostomy, mechanical ventilation, enteral feeding, and prior third-generation cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, or carbapenems; carbapenem-resistant strains are most common after carbapenem exposure. Urinary tract infection is infrequent and usually catheter-associated, reflecting biofilm formation on devices; rare community-acquired cases occur with nephrolithiasis or after renal transplantation. Less common manifestations include contact lens-associated keratitis and native- or prosthetic-valve endocarditis. Septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation, each reported in roughly 25-30% of bloodstream infection cases Infection caused by carbapenem-resistant (extremely drug-resistant) isolates, where delayed adequate therapy drives poor outcomes Evolving necrotizing soft tissue picture (hemorrhagic bullae, necrotizing fasciitis) after combat or disaster-related trauma New A. baumannii in a long-term ventilated ICU patient with fever and rising sputum Multi-organ dysfunction with severe community-acquired pneumonia Treating positive respiratory or wound cultures as proof of infection when they may represent colonization, leading to overtreatment. Underestimating environmental persistence: failure to address desiccation-resistant contamination of surfaces and equipment perpetuates outbreaks. Mistaking Acinetobacter for Neisseria meningitidis on CSF Gram stain. Assuming susceptibility - intrinsic and acquired beta-lactamases (including OXA-type carbapenemases) make empirical choices unreliable without local epidemiology and susceptibility testing. Overlooking Acinetobacter in the differential of soft tissue infection following exposure to tropical/subtropical environments or natural disasters. A. baumannii has greater virulence potential than other Acinetobacter species, partly through its ability to grow at 37 degrees C and resist macrophage uptake. Colonization is facilitated by adherence to surfaces and human cells and by biofilm formation, which is linked to exopolysaccharide production and pilus formation; a quorum-sensing molecule encoded by the abaI autoinducer synthase gene contributes to biofilm on abiotic surfaces. The organism modifies its lipid A structure to survive harsh environments, decreasing susceptibility to antibiotics and antimicrobial peptides and enhancing desiccation survival. An extracellular capsule protects against complement-mediated killing and can be upregulated in the presence of subinhibitory antibiotic levels, producing a hypervirulent phenotype. Phospholipase C and D act as cytotoxic virulence factors aiding epithelial invasion, and siderophore-based iron-acquisition systems permit growth despite host iron limitation. Multiple protein-secretion systems (type II with the LipA lipase substrate, type V trimeric autotransporter mediating biofilm and matrix adherence, and a type VI system secreting antibacterial toxins) plus outer-membrane vesicles carrying OmpA, proteases, and phospholipases contribute to pathogenesis and innate immune activation. Antimicrobial resistance arises from reduced porin expression, overexpressed efflux pumps (removing quinolones, tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, disinfectants, and tigecycline), and beta-lactamases including intrinsic AmpC cephalosporinases (upregulated when the ISAba1 insertion sequence is placed next to the AmpC gene) and acquired serine and metallo-beta-lactamases. Carbapenem resistance is mostly tied to Ambler class D oxacillinases (group 2d), some intrinsic/chromosomal (e.g., OXA-51-like) and others acquired (e.g., OXA-23-, 24-, 58-, 143-, 235-like). The small A. baumannii core genome with a large accessory genome confers high genomic plasticity and ready uptake of resistance genes by horizontal gene transfer. Infections carry high mortality, driven largely by the severity of the patient's underlying illness and by drug resistance of the infecting strain. Crude mortality with nosocomial pneumonia has been reported as high as 65%, though attributable mortality is hard to establish because affected patients are typically debilitated. Community-acquired pneumonia mortality exceeds 50%. Crude bloodstream infection mortality reaches about 40% overall and as high as 70% with carbapenem-resistant isolates. Wound colonization/infection contributes to healing delays and graft loss in burn patients. No formal disease-specific severity score is provided in the source. Severity is gauged clinically by site and host factors: presence of septic shock or DIC in bloodstream infection (~25-30%), need for prolonged mechanical ventilation in pneumonia, and carbapenem/extreme drug resistance, all of which predict markedly higher mortality.

Acinic cell carcinoma — Acinic cell adenocarcinoma Secretory carcinoma (mammary analogue) Normal or hyperplastic acinar tissue Oncocytoma and oncocytic carcinoma Mucoepidermoid carcinoma Cystadenoma or cystadenocarcinoma Metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma Fine-needle aspiration cytology, recognising its known limitations for this tumour Core or excisional biopsy for definitive histology Immunohistochemistry including DOG1 and NR4A3 Molecular testing for NR4A3, and for ETV6 to exclude secretory carcinoma MRI of the primary and ultrasound or CT of the neck for staging Cross-sectional or functional imaging where high-grade transformation is suspected A malignant epithelial tumour showing serous acinar differentiation, with cytoplasmic zymogen granules, most often arising in the parotid. It is generally low-grade and is one of the commoner salivary malignancies of childhood and young adults, with a female predominance. Occasional bilateral parotid involvement is described, an unusual feature among salivary malignancies. Recurrent activation of the transcription factor NR4A3, through enhancer hijacking, is a characteristic molecular event and can be demonstrated by immunohistochemistry. Tumour cells are typically DOG1 positive with an apical or membranous pattern, and the zymogen granules are periodic-acid-Schiff positive and diastase resistant. Architectural patterns include solid, microcystic, follicular and papillary-cystic, the last of which can be misread as a benign cyst. High-grade transformation (dedifferentiation) is the most important adverse event and markedly worsens the outlook. Distinction from secretory carcinoma is essential; secretory carcinoma lacks true zymogen granules, is DOG1 negative and carries an ETV6 fusion. Features of high-grade transformation such as necrosis, marked pleomorphism and high mitotic count Rapid growth or new pain Facial nerve weakness or palsy Cervical nodal disease Evidence of distant metastasis Misclassifying secretory carcinoma as acinic cell carcinoma and missing a targetable fusion Underestimating or failing to sample areas of high-grade transformation Mistaking a low-grade tumour for benign or normal acinar tissue on cytology Achieving inadequate surgical margins because of an infiltrative edge Acinic cell carcinoma arises from cells committed to serous acinar differentiation, recapitulating the zymogen-granule-producing acinar cells of normal salivary tissue. A recurrent structural rearrangement repositions a strong enhancer adjacent to the NR4A3 gene, driving marked overexpression of this nuclear receptor transcription factor and promoting tumour cell proliferation. The neoplastic cells retain the capacity to synthesise serous secretory (zymogen) granules, which underlies both the histological appearance and the periodic-acid-Schiff staining, and they are arranged in solid, microcystic, follicular or papillary-cystic patterns. Although most tumours behave in a low-grade fashion, a subset undergoes high-grade transformation with loss of acinar differentiation, increased mitotic activity, necrosis and a greatly increased propensity for nodal and distant spread. Prognosis is generally favourable for conventional low-grade tumours managed with complete excision. High-grade transformation substantially worsens survival, and late local recurrence or metastasis can occur, so prolonged follow-up is advised.

Anterior cruciate ligament injury — ACL tear, ACL rupture, anterior cruciate ligament rupture, cruciate ligament injury Meniscal tear Collateral (medial or lateral) ligament injury Posterior cruciate ligament injury Patellar dislocation Osteochondral fracture or tibial spine avulsion Knee dislocation with multiligament injury Extensor mechanism rupture MRI of the knee to confirm the tear and detect associated meniscal, chondral, and ligamentous injury Clinical stability testing (Lachman, anterior drawer, pivot-shift) Plain radiographs to exclude fracture, including a Segond fracture as an indirect sign Aspiration of a tense haemarthrosis for symptom relief and diagnostic information where appropriate Assessment for associated multiligament injury if a knee dislocation is suspected Typically follows a non-contact pivoting, twisting, or deceleration injury, often in sport, with the patient reporting a 'pop' and rapid swelling of the knee A tense, blood-filled effusion (haemarthrosis) developing within hours of injury strongly suggests an ACL rupture (or other significant intra-articular injury) The Lachman test is the most sensitive clinical examination; the anterior drawer and pivot-shift tests also demonstrate anterior tibial translation and rotational instability MRI confirms the diagnosis and, importantly, identifies associated meniscal tears, collateral ligament injury, and bone bruising Symptomatic instability with the knee 'giving way' during turning or pivoting is the key indication for reconstruction Management is individualised: reconstruction (usually with a tendon graft) is favoured for young, active, or pivoting-sport patients, while rehabilitation-led treatment suits lower-demand individuals Rehabilitation to restore quadriceps strength and neuromuscular control is essential whether or not surgery is performed Untreated instability predisposes to recurrent meniscal tears and secondary osteoarthritis over time Features of knee dislocation with multiligament injury requiring urgent vascular and neurological assessment (risk to the popliteal artery and peroneal nerve) A locked knee suggesting a displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear needing prompt treatment Signs of neurovascular compromise after significant knee trauma Open injury or associated fracture Missing an ACL rupture by not recognising the significance of an acute haemarthrosis Failing to identify associated meniscal or collateral ligament injury Overlooking a knee dislocation that has spontaneously reduced, with its vascular risk Proceeding to surgery on a stiff, poorly rehabilitated knee, increasing the risk of postoperative stiffness The anterior cruciate ligament runs from the posterior femoral intercondylar notch to the anterior tibial plateau and is the principal restraint to anterior translation of the tibia and a key stabiliser against rotational and pivoting forces. Sudden deceleration, landing, or a valgus-external rotation force with the foot planted overloads the ligament, causing partial or complete rupture, frequently near its femoral origin. Because the ligament is intra-articular and vascular, rupture produces a rapid haemarthrosis. The ACL has poor intrinsic healing capacity, so complete tears generally do not reunite. Persistent instability increases shear on the menisci and articular cartilage, accelerating degenerative change. Outcomes depend on activity demands and associated injuries; reconstruction restores stability and enables return to pivoting sport in most, while appropriately selected patients do well with rehabilitation alone, but chronic instability and untreated meniscal damage increase the long-term risk of osteoarthritis regardless of treatment.

Acne vulgaris — acne, common acne, pimples Rosacea (lacks comedones, features flushing and telangiectasia) Perioral dermatitis Folliculitis (bacterial or fungal) Keratosis pilaris Drug-induced acneiform eruptions (e.g. corticosteroids) Hidradenitis suppurativa when lesions involve flexures Clinical diagnosis; investigations rarely needed for typical presentations Hormonal workup (androgens, and related endocrine tests) when hyperandrogenism or polycystic ovary syndrome is suspected Pregnancy testing and lipid and liver monitoring before and during systemic retinoid therapy Swabs when Gram-negative folliculitis or resistant infection is suspected A disorder of the pilosebaceous unit affecting the face, chest, and back, typically beginning around puberty The hallmark non-inflammatory lesion is the comedo (open blackheads and closed whiteheads); its presence distinguishes acne from other papulopustular eruptions like rosacea Inflammatory lesions range from papules and pustules to deep nodules and cysts, and severe forms lead to scarring and post-inflammatory pigmentation Treatment is chosen by severity: topical retinoids and benzoyl peroxide for comedonal and mild inflammatory disease, adding topical or oral antibacterials for moderate disease Combining benzoyl peroxide with antibacterials reduces bacterial resistance, and antibacterials should not be used as prolonged monotherapy Systemic retinoid therapy is reserved for severe, nodulocystic, or scarring acne resistant to other measures and requires careful monitoring and strict pregnancy precautions given teratogenicity Hormonal therapy can help women with acne linked to androgen excess; consider investigating for hyperandrogenism when there are virilising features or menstrual irregularity Sudden severe nodular acne with fever and joint pain (acne fulminans) is a systemic emergency needing urgent specialist care Acne fulminans: abrupt severe ulcerating nodular acne with fever, malaise, and arthralgia Signs of underlying endocrine disorder such as virilisation or rapid-onset severe acne Extensive scarring or psychological distress requiring escalation of care Suspected retinoid-associated mood disturbance during systemic treatment Prolonged antibacterial monotherapy promoting resistance and relapse Under-treating scarring or nodular acne and delaying referral for systemic retinoid therapy Overlooking the significant psychological burden and risk of low mood Failing to enforce pregnancy prevention during teratogenic systemic retinoid use Acne results from four interacting processes within the pilosebaceous unit: increased sebum production driven by androgens, abnormal keratinisation of the follicular lining producing microcomedones, proliferation of Cutibacterium acnes, and inflammation. Trapped sebum and keratin form comedones; bacterial activity and the host immune response generate inflammatory mediators that produce papules, pustules, and deeper nodules. Rupture of the follicular wall extends inflammation into the dermis, and disordered wound healing can result in atrophic or hypertrophic scarring. Hormonal influences, genetic predisposition, and certain drugs modulate severity. Acne usually improves after adolescence but may persist into adulthood, particularly in women; early effective treatment limits permanent scarring and psychosocial impact.

neurofibromatosis type 2 in young or bilateral cases Acoustic neuroma is a benign neoplasm of Schwann cells, most often originating at the transition zone of the vestibular nerve within or near the internal auditory canal. As it grows it first fills the canal, compressing the cochlear and vestibular fibres and their blood supply to produce sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance. Continued expansion into the cerebellopontine angle displaces and stretches adjacent structures: the trigeminal nerve above, the facial nerve alongside, and eventually the brainstem and cerebellum. Large tumours can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow and raise intracranial pressure. Most cases are sporadic and unilateral, while bilateral tumours are the hallmark of neurofibromatosis type 2. Because the tumour is benign and usually slow growing the prognosis is generally good, and small tumours may simply be observed; treatment outcomes depend on tumour size at diagnosis, with hearing preservation and facial nerve function being more achievable when tumours are small.

Outlook depends on metabolic control and any underlying autoimmune disease; leptin (metreleptin) replacement and vigorous management of triglycerides and glucose improve outcomes, but progressive liver disease and pancreatitis are significant threats if untreated.

acquired haemophilia A — acquired factor VIII inhibitor, autoimmune haemophilia A congenital haemophilia A with an alloantibody inhibitor lupus anticoagulant (prolongs the APTT but predisposes to thrombosis, not bleeding) acquired von Willebrand syndrome other acquired specific clotting factor inhibitors liver disease with impaired synthesis of clotting factors disseminated intravascular coagulation heparin contamination of the sample activated partial thromboplastin time with immediate and incubated mixing studies factor VIII assay Bethesda assay to quantify inhibitor titre von Willebrand factor antigen and activity lupus anticoagulant and antiphospholipid testing prothrombin time and fibrinogen screening for underlying malignancy and autoimmune disease Acquired haemophilia A is caused by spontaneous autoantibodies, usually IgG, directed against coagulation factor VIII, arising in people with no personal or family history of a bleeding disorder. Presentation is typically with sudden extensive bruising and soft-tissue, muscle, mucosal or retroperitoneal bleeding; haemarthrosis, so characteristic of congenital haemophilia, is uncommon. The screening abnormality is an isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal prothrombin time, which does not correct on a mixing study, particularly after incubation at body temperature. Confirmation requires a reduced factor VIII level together with a demonstrable inhibitor quantified by the Bethesda assay. Recognised associations include advanced age, the postpartum period, autoimmune disease, malignancy and certain drugs, although a large proportion of cases remain idiopathic. Factor VIII autoantibodies typically show complex (type II) kinetics, so a measurable residual factor VIII level can coexist with severe bleeding and the inhibitor titre does not reliably predict bleeding severity. Acute bleeding is controlled with bypassing agents such as activated prothrombin complex concentrate or recombinant activated factor VII, or with recombinant porcine factor VIII, rather than with standard human factor VIII. Definitive treatment requires eradication of the inhibitor with immunosuppression, and care should be shared with a specialist haemophilia centre. a large or expanding haematoma, particularly retroperitoneal limb swelling with pain suggesting compartment syndrome or nerve compression airway or neck swelling threatening the airway gross haematuria or gastrointestinal bleeding any feature suggesting intracranial haemorrhage misinterpreting the prolonged APTT as a lupus anticoagulant and failing to test for a factor VIII inhibitor administering standard human factor VIII concentrate and expecting a normal haemostatic response underestimating bleeding risk from the inhibitor titre or from a measurable residual factor VIII level delaying immunosuppression, which prolongs the period of bleeding risk performing intramuscular injections, arterial punctures or invasive procedures without haematological cover The disorder results from a breakdown of self-tolerance leading to polyclonal IgG autoantibodies against factor VIII, most often targeting the A2 or C2 domains that mediate binding to von Willebrand factor, phospholipid and factor IXa. Neutralisation of factor VIII procoagulant activity impairs the intrinsic tenase complex and thus thrombin generation, producing a bleeding tendency. Unlike the alloantibodies seen in congenital haemophilia, these autoantibodies commonly display second-order (type II) kinetics that do not completely inactivate factor VIII, which explains why residual factor activity may be detectable despite clinically significant haemorrhage. The autoimmune process may be triggered by pregnancy, malignancy, drugs or another autoimmune condition, or may be idiopathic. Bleeding-related and treatment-related morbidity and mortality are considerable, especially in the elderly and those with comorbidity, but complete remission of the inhibitor is achieved in the majority with immunosuppression; relapse can occur and warrants ongoing follow-up.

Acute mortality is significant because of severe unheralded bleeding, but with prompt haemostatic control and antibody eradication most patients achieve remission. Relapse can occur, so monitoring after immunosuppression is important, and outcome is also influenced by any underlying disorder.

acquired hypertrichosis lanuginosa — malignant down, hypertrichosis lanuginosa acquisita Drug-induced hypertrichosis (ciclosporin, minoxidil, phenytoin, corticosteroids) Hirsutism from androgen excess (polycystic ovary syndrome, adrenal or ovarian tumour) Congenital hypertrichosis lanuginosa (present from birth) Hypertrichosis of anorexia nervosa or severe malnutrition Hypothyroidism-related hypertrichosis Porphyria cutanea tarda with localised facial hypertrichosis CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis to identify an occult primary Age- and sex-appropriate cancer screening (mammography, colonoscopy, gynaecological assessment) Skin and scalp examination with dermoscopy confirming fine lanugo hair Tumour markers guided by the suspected primary Thyroid function tests Review of the drug history to exclude iatrogenic causes Presents as rapid growth of fine, soft, non-pigmented lanugo hair, often beginning on the face (including the nose and eyelids) and spreading caudally to the trunk and limbs, sparing only the palms and soles. A strong marker of underlying, often advanced malignancy; lung, colorectal and breast carcinoma are the commonest associations. In women breast and gynaecological tumours predominate, while in men lung and colorectal cancers are most frequent. The eruption of malignant down may appear before the tumour is diagnosed and typically indicates advanced or metastatic disease. It is frequently accompanied by glossitis with painful tongue papillae and by other paraneoplastic signs such as acanthosis nigricans and tripe palms. It must be distinguished from drug-induced hypertrichosis and from androgen-dependent hirsutism, which follows a female terminal-hair pattern. Florid facial lanugo growth produces a characteristic elongated, simian facies, often with accompanying weight loss and cachexia. Rapid development of fine lanugo hair on the face of an adult Accompanying weight loss, cachexia or glossitis Coexisting acanthosis nigricans or tripe palms Known or suspected internal malignancy Confusing lanugo hypertrichosis with androgen-driven hirsutism Overlooking a drug cause before attributing the eruption to malignancy Failing to appreciate that it often indicates advanced disease Not examining for accompanying paraneoplastic signs and glossitis The mechanism of acquired hypertrichosis lanuginosa is incompletely understood. Tumour-derived factors are thought to reset hair follicles from the resting or vellus state into active production of lanugo-type hair, possibly through altered growth-factor signalling and disturbance of the normal androgen-independent follicular cycle. The resulting hair is fine and unpigmented, resembling foetal lanugo, which distinguishes it from the pigmented terminal hair of androgen-driven hirsutism. The frequent association with advanced malignancy and cachexia suggests a humoral, tumour-related aetiology. Acquired hypertrichosis lanuginosa usually signifies advanced or metastatic malignancy and therefore carries a poor prognosis; hair growth may regress following successful tumour treatment.

acquired ichthyosis — ichthyosis acquisita, acquired ichthyosis vulgaris Inherited ichthyosis vulgaris (childhood onset, positive family history) Xerosis and asteatotic eczema Hypothyroidism-related dry skin Sarcoidosis with ichthyosiform change Drug-induced ichthyosis Nutritional deficiency (essential fatty acids, vitamin A) HIV-associated acquired ichthyosis Skin biopsy showing compact hyperkeratosis with a reduced or absent granular layer CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis with lymph node assessment for lymphoma Excisional lymph node biopsy where lymphadenopathy is present Full blood count, ESR and LDH Thyroid function tests HIV serology Renal function and nutritional/lipid assessment Presents as generalised, symmetrical fine adherent scaling resembling ichthyosis vulgaris but with onset in adolescence or adulthood and no family history. Extensor surfaces of the limbs and the trunk are typically involved while the flexures are spared; scales are fine and white to brown with a rhomboidal fish-scale pattern. The classic paraneoplastic association is Hodgkin lymphoma; non-Hodgkin lymphoma, mycosis fungoides, multiple myeloma and some solid tumours (breast, lung) are also reported. Numerous non-malignant causes must be excluded, including sarcoidosis, HIV, leprosy, hypothyroidism, chronic renal failure, malnutrition and drugs (nicotinic acid, statins, cimetidine, clofazimine). When paraneoplastic, the ichthyosis tends to parallel tumour activity and may improve with successful treatment of the underlying lymphoma. Palmoplantar keratoderma and keratosis pilaris-like follicular changes may accompany the scaling. New-onset ichthyosis in an adult warrants exclusion of lymphoma, particularly with lymphadenopathy, night sweats or weight loss. New generalised ichthyosis in an adult without a family history Associated lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or B symptoms Rapidly progressive scaling with weight loss Coexisting pruritus and night sweats Dismissing adult-onset scaling as simple xerosis Failing to distinguish acquired from inherited ichthyosis by age of onset and family history Overlooking non-malignant causes such as HIV, sarcoidosis and drugs Not re-evaluating for lymphoma when the scaling recurs Acquired ichthyosis results from disordered keratinocyte differentiation and desquamation producing retention hyperkeratosis. In lymphoproliferative disease, cytokine-driven alterations in epidermal lipid synthesis and stratum corneum cohesion are implicated, and disturbances of vitamin A and essential fatty acid metabolism have been proposed. Reduced or absent keratohyalin (granular layer) with compact orthohyperkeratosis mirrors the histology of inherited ichthyosis vulgaris. In non-malignant cases, systemic disease, drugs or nutritional deficiency similarly impair normal corneocyte shedding, yielding clinically indistinguishable scaling. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; when associated with Hodgkin lymphoma the skin often improves with effective chemotherapy and outcome follows that of the treated malignancy.

Acquired methaemoglobinaemia — toxic methaemoglobinaemia, drug-induced methemoglobinemia Hypoxaemia from cardiac or pulmonary disease Sulfhaemoglobinaemia Congenital methaemoglobinaemia (enzyme or haemoglobin M variants) Carbon monoxide poisoning Cyanide poisoning Co-oximetry to measure the methaemoglobin fraction directly Arterial blood gas demonstrating the saturation gap Careful drug and chemical exposure history Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status before or alongside methylene blue Haemolysis screen where oxidant injury is significant Oxidising drugs and chemicals convert haemoglobin iron to the ferric state, forming methaemoglobin that cannot carry oxygen The hallmark is cyanosis that does not improve with supplemental oxygen, often with chocolate-brown blood There is a characteristic saturation gap, with pulse oximetry reading falsely and the arterial blood gas oxygen tension appearing normal Common precipitants include topical local anaesthetics such as benzocaine, dapsone, nitrites and aniline dyes Methylthioninium chloride (methylene blue) is the specific antidote for significant or symptomatic cases Methylene blue may be ineffective or harmful in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, where alternatives are needed Signs of tissue hypoxia such as chest pain, altered mental state or acidosis High methaemoglobin fraction Ongoing exposure to the causative agent Coexisting anaemia amplifying the effect Being reassured by a normal arterial oxygen tension despite cyanosis Giving methylene blue in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency Failing to identify and remove the causative oxidant Confusing it with primary cardiopulmonary hypoxaemia Methaemoglobin forms when the iron in haemoglobin is oxidised from the ferrous to the ferric state, which cannot bind oxygen and also shifts the oxygen dissociation curve so remaining normal haemoglobin releases oxygen less readily. Oxidant drugs and chemicals overwhelm the physiological reducing systems, chiefly cytochrome-b5 reductase, that normally keep methaemoglobin low. The result is functional anaemia and tissue hypoxia despite adequate arterial oxygen tension, producing cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen. Mild cases resolve once the offending agent is stopped, and symptomatic cases usually respond rapidly to methylene blue; severe or unrecognised cases can cause serious hypoxic injury.

is haemoglobin in which the haem iron is oxidised from the ferrous to the ferric state, which cannot bind oxygen and shifts the oxygen-dissociation curve leftward so remaining ferrous sites release screen for associated renal disease Mistaking the facial fat loss for ageing or an eating disorder Offering leptin replacement despite often near-normal leptin levels Overlooking evolving proteinuria during follow-up Acquired partial lipodystrophy is a progressive loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue that characteristically begins in the face and spreads downward over the trunk and arms while sparing or expanding fat in the lower body. It is closely associated with dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway: many patients have low C3 and circulating C3 nephritic factor, an autoantibody that stabilises the C3 convertase and promotes complement-mediated adipocyte lysis, particularly in fat expressing high levels of complement factor D (adipsin). The same complement dysregulation underlies the linked membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Because lower-body fat depots persist, the severe insulin resistance typical of generalised lipodystrophy is usually absent. The metabolic outlook is generally more favourable than in generalised lipodystrophy because lower-body fat is retained, but long-term prognosis is dominated by the risk of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, which can progress to chronic kidney disease.

acquired perforating dermatosis — acquired perforating disease, perforating dermatosis of chronic renal failure and diabetes prurigo nodularis folliculitis and acneiform eruptions hypertrophic lichen planus multiple keratoacanthomas dermatofibromas perforating granuloma annulare arthropod bite reactions skin biopsy with elastic tissue and connective tissue stains to demonstrate the perforating channel and eliminated material renal function tests (urea, creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate) fasting glucose and glycated haemoglobin liver function tests and thyroid function tests urinalysis for proteinuria full blood count and calcium/phosphate profile age-appropriate malignancy screening where clinically indicated Umbrella term for perforating disorders arising in adults, classically associated with chronic kidney disease and diabetes mellitus, characterised by transepidermal elimination of dermal material. Presents as intensely pruritic, umbilicated papules and nodules with a central keratotic plug, favouring the extensor surfaces of the limbs and the trunk. Koebnerisation is prominent; scratching provokes new lesions arranged in linear streaks, and the itch-scratch cycle perpetuates the eruption. Histology shows a channel of transepidermal elimination extruding degenerate collagen, elastic fibres or keratin through the epidermis or a follicular infundibulum. The four classic perforating dermatoses (Kyrle disease, reactive perforating collagenosis, perforating folliculitis, elastosis perforans serpiginosa) show overlapping features when acquired in adults, hence the unifying term. Strongly linked to end-stage renal disease on haemodialysis and to poorly controlled diabetic nephropathy; screening for occult renal or metabolic disease is warranted at presentation. Management targets the underlying disease and pruritus: emollients, topical retinoids or corticosteroids, phototherapy (narrowband ultraviolet B), and control of uraemia or glycaemia. Reported associations extend beyond renal disease to hypothyroidism, hepatic dysfunction, malignancy and certain drugs (notably targeted anticancer agents). new-onset perforating eruption without known renal or metabolic disease, prompting evaluation for occult systemic illness or malignancy rapidly progressive lesions or systemic symptoms (weight loss, night sweats) suggesting underlying neoplasm signs of secondary bacterial infection of excoriated lesions intractable pruritus indicating poorly controlled uraemia or hyperglycaemia attributing intensely pruritic umbilicated papules to simple prurigo and overlooking the diagnostic transepidermal elimination on biopsy failing to investigate for underlying chronic kidney disease, diabetes or occult malignancy at first presentation biopsying an excoriated or superinfected lesion rather than an intact keratotic papule, obscuring the histology expecting durable clearance from topical therapy alone without addressing the systemic driver and the itch-scratch cycle Acquired perforating dermatosis reflects abnormal transepidermal elimination of altered dermal connective tissue, in which degenerate collagen and/or elastic fibres, and sometimes keratinous debris, are extruded through the epidermis or follicular epithelium. In the setting of chronic kidney disease and diabetes, microangiopathy, deposition of substances that cannot be cleared by failing kidneys, dermal microdeposits (including calcium and urate), and advanced glycation end-products are thought to injure dermal matrix and provoke a foreign-body-like elimination response. Repetitive trauma from scratching (driven by uraemic or metabolic pruritus) initiates and perpetuates lesions through Koebnerisation, and epidermal hyperproliferation forms the characteristic keratotic plug overlying a perforating channel. The eruption tends to be chronic and relapsing, mirroring the course of the underlying renal or metabolic disease; lesions may improve with control of the systemic condition or after renal transplantation but often persist while pruritus and scratching continue.

angiodysplasia New mucocutaneous bleeding in a patient with a known paraprotein or myeloproliferative neoplasm Bleeding with severe aortic stenosis suggesting Heyde syndrome Bleeding refractory to neoplasm, or aortic stenosis Expecting a durable response to replacement when antibody-mediated clearance is rapid Overlooking angiodysplasia as the bleeding source in Heyde syndrome Acquired von Willebrand syndrome develops when a previously normal von Willebrand factor system is disrupted by an underlying disorder. Autoantibodies may accelerate clearance or neutralise function, malignant cells or activated platelets may adsorb the protein, and high shear stress across stenotic valves or in myeloproliferative states can unfold von Willebrand factor and expose it to excessive proteolysis by ADAMTS13. The common consequence is selective loss of the largest, most haemostatically active multimers, impairing platelet adhesion and producing a bleeding phenotype resembling inherited von Willebrand disease. Outcome tracks the underlying disorder, and bleeding often resolves when that condition is treated, for example after valve replacement or control of a clonal disorder. Persistent or untreated causes can lead to recurrent and difficult-to-manage haemorrhage.

acral persistent papular mucinosis — APPM, acral persistent papular mucinosis (localised lichen myxoedematosus) Scleromyxoedema (generalised sclerodermoid lichen myxoedematosus) Granuloma annulare Colloid milium Self-healing juvenile cutaneous mucinosis Digital mucous (myxoid) cyst Syringomas Papular sarcoidosis Skin biopsy with mucin stains such as Alcian blue or colloidal iron Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to exclude a paraprotein Thyroid function tests Fasting glucose to exclude a secondary metabolic association Clinical mapping of lesion distribution to confirm the acral, localised pattern A distinct localised variant of lichen myxoedematosus confined to the dorsa of the hands and the extensor aspects of the distal forearms and wrists. Presents as multiple small, firm, flesh-coloured to ivory-white papules that are persistent and usually asymptomatic. Shows a strong female predominance and typically arises in middle adulthood. Unlike scleromyxoedema, it is not associated with a paraprotein, thyroid dysfunction or systemic organ involvement. Histology shows focal deposition of dermal mucin (mainly hyaluronic acid) in the upper reticular dermis without the fibroblast proliferation and fibrosis of scleromyxoedema. The clinical course is benign and non-progressive, so reassurance rather than aggressive therapy is appropriate. Careful distinction from generalised and sclerodermoid lichen myxoedematosus is essential because the latter carries systemic implications. Induration or sclerosis spreading proximally beyond the hands and forearms, suggesting scleromyxoedema Detection of a monoclonal paraprotein Development of systemic symptoms or organ involvement Mislabelling the condition as scleromyxoedema and subjecting the patient to unnecessary systemic investigation and treatment. Failing to recognise a truly generalised mucinosis with an underlying paraprotein that has been misclassified as the acral variant. Over-treating an asymptomatic, benign eruption. Interpreting focal dermal mucin without clinical correlation, missing the characteristic acral distribution. The condition results from a localised accumulation of dermal mucin, predominantly hyaluronic acid, produced by dermal fibroblasts and deposited in the upper reticular dermis of acral skin. In contrast to scleromyxoedema, there is little or no fibroblast proliferation, no significant fibrosis and no associated circulating paraprotein, and the process remains confined to the distal extremities. The underlying trigger for the localised glycosaminoglycan deposition is unknown. The condition is benign and persistent but non-progressive, with no systemic risk; lesions tend to remain stable over years.

Acrocallosal syndrome (KIF7) — ACLS, Schinzel acrocallosal syndrome, KIF7, GLI3 Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome Hydrolethalus syndrome Joubert syndrome and related disorders Pallister-Hall syndrome Gorlin (naevoid basal cell carcinoma) syndrome Isolated corpus callosum agenesis with polydactyly Brain imaging to assess the corpus callosum and posterior fossa, including for a molar tooth sign Radiographs of the hands and feet to document polydactyly Developmental and neurological assessment Electroencephalography if seizures occur Molecular testing of KIF7 and GLI3 within a ciliopathy gene panel Combines agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum with polydactyly and craniofacial features Macrocephaly with a prominent forehead and hypertelorism is typical Polydactyly is often both preaxial and postaxial, and duplication of the great toe is common Moderate to severe intellectual disability and hypotonia are usual Seizures occur, and some individuals show features overlapping with Joubert syndrome including a molar tooth sign Most cases are caused by biallelic KIF7 variants, with some attributed to GLI3 Overlaps with hydrolethalus and Greig cephalopolysyndactyly, reflecting shared hedgehog and ciliary biology Seizures or progressive neurological decline Feeding difficulty and failure to thrive from hypotonia Hydrocephalus requiring intervention Confusing it with Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome, which usually spares intellect Overlooking a molar tooth sign that would indicate a Joubert-related disorder Attributing the polydactyly to an isolated limb malformation Testing only one of KIF7 or GLI3 and missing the diagnosis Acrocallosal syndrome is caused chiefly by biallelic variants in KIF7, a cilium-associated kinesin that regulates the processing of GLI transcription factors within the hedgehog signalling pathway at the tip of the primary cilium; a minority of cases involve GLI3 itself. Because hedgehog signalling patterns the developing forebrain commissures, cortex and limbs, disturbed ciliary signalling impairs formation of the corpus callosum, contributes to the macrocephaly and dysmorphism, and produces the preaxial and postaxial polydactyly. The dependence of cerebellar and brainstem development on the same pathway explains the overlap with Joubert syndrome and the molar tooth sign seen in some individuals, while shared biology accounts for the resemblance to hydrolethalus and Greig cephalopolysyndactyly. Outcome is variable but significant intellectual disability is common; survival into childhood and adulthood is possible, with the degree of neurological impairment and any associated malformation determining function.

acrocyanosis — acral cyanosis, Crocq disease Raynaud phenomenon Peripheral cyanosis from central hypoxaemia or cardiac disease Cryoglobulinaemia and cold agglutinin disease Antiphospholipid syndrome and other thrombophilias Chilblains (pernio) Peripheral arterial occlusive disease Connective-tissue disease-associated vasculopathy Pulse oximetry and, if indicated, arterial blood gas to exclude central cyanosis Nailfold capillaroscopy to help differentiate from connective-tissue disease Autoimmune serology including antinuclear and antiphospholipid antibodies Cryoglobulins and cold agglutinin titres Full blood count and assessment of blood viscosity/paraproteins Doppler studies and palpation of peripheral pulses to confirm patent large vessels Screening for occult malignancy or eating disorder where clinically suggested Acrocyanosis is a painless, persistent, symmetrical blue-purple discolouration of the hands and feet caused by vasospasm of small cutaneous arteries and arterioles with secondary dilatation of the subpapillary venous plexus. It is distinguished from Raynaud phenomenon by its continuous rather than episodic nature and the absence of the sharply demarcated triphasic white-blue-red colour change. Affected extremities are typically cold and clammy with associated hyperhidrosis, yet peripheral pulses are normal and there is no ulceration, pain or trophic change in the primary form. Primary (idiopathic) acrocyanosis is benign, more common in young women, worsened by cold and emotional stress, and often improves in warm environments and with age. Secondary acrocyanosis may reflect connective-tissue disease, cryoglobulinaemia, antiphospholipid syndrome, malignancy, anorexia nervosa, or drugs, and warrants a search for an underlying disorder. Central cyanosis from hypoxaemia must be excluded, as acrocyanosis is purely peripheral and does not affect the tongue or mucous membranes; oxygen saturation is normal in the primary form. Diascopy and warming help confirm the vasomotor nature, and the discolouration blanches with elevation of the limb, distinguishing it from fixed vascular occlusion. Reassurance, cold avoidance and warmth are the mainstays of management for primary disease; vasodilators are rarely needed and pharmacotherapy is generally unsatisfactory. Digital ulceration, necrosis or pain suggesting a secondary occlusive or ischaemic process Asymmetry or involvement of a single digit indicating structural arterial disease Central cyanosis with low oxygen saturation pointing to cardiopulmonary pathology Systemic features of connective-tissue disease or cryoglobulinaemia Rapid onset in an older patient raising concern for underlying malignancy Confusing continuous acrocyanosis with episodic Raynaud phenomenon and pursuing the wrong work-up Overlooking central cyanosis by assuming all peripheral blueness is acrocyanosis Missing a secondary cause such as cryoglobulinaemia, antiphospholipid syndrome or occult malignancy Attributing unilateral or single-digit discolouration to acrocyanosis when it indicates arterial occlusion Failing to consider anorexia nervosa in a young patient with cold, cyanotic extremities Acrocyanosis results from persistent vasospasm of the small arterioles and cutaneous arteries supplying the acral skin, causing reduced arterial inflow and sluggish capillary perfusion. Compensatory dilatation of the subpapillary venous plexuses leads to pooling of slow-flowing, deoxygenated blood, which produces the sustained bluish discolouration and the associated coolness and sweating. Unlike Raynaud phenomenon, the vasoconstriction is continuous rather than paroxysmal and does not fully occlude flow, so tissue viability is preserved and ischaemic complications do not occur in the primary form. Increased vasomotor tone, heightened sensitivity to cold, and in some cases increased blood viscosity or circulating cryoproteins in secondary disease all contribute. The precise trigger of the primary form is unknown but is thought to reflect a functional abnormality of local vascular reactivity. Primary acrocyanosis is a benign, chronic condition that does not threaten limb viability and frequently improves with warmth and increasing age. The outlook in secondary disease depends on the underlying disorder.

Acrodermatitis enteropathica is caused by variants in SLC39A4, which encodes the intestinal zinc transporter ZIP4 responsible for zinc uptake at the enterocyte apical membrane. Impaired transport leads to systemic zinc deficiency. Zinc is a cofactor for numerous metalloenzymes and is essential for epithelial integrity, immune function and cell proliferation, so its deficiency produces the characteristic dermatitis at sites of friction and around orifices, hair loss, impaired healing and immune dysfunction, together with malabsorptive diarrhoea. Because human milk contains a zinc-binding ligand that aids absorption, symptoms often surface after weaning from breast milk. The inherited form requires lifelong zinc replacement but carries an excellent prognosis once treatment is established, with rapid resolution of skin, gastrointestinal and growth abnormalities. Untreated disease can be life-threatening.

and PTH over time as resistance may evolve Acrodysostosis is a disorder of the cyclic-AMP/protein-kinase-A (PKA) signalling pathway. PRKAR1A encodes the type 1-alpha regulatory subunit of PKA, and PDE4D encodes a phosphodiesterase that degrades cyclic AMP; both regulate intracellular cyclic-AMP-dependent signalling downstream of G-protein-coupled receptors, including receptors for parathyroid hormone and other peptide hormones. Pathogenic variants perturb this signalling in chondrocytes and endocrine target tissues. In cartilage, disturbed PKA signalling accelerates epiphyseal maturation and impairs longitudinal bone growth, producing brachydactyly, cone-shaped epiphyses, and short stature. In hormone-responsive tissues, blunted signalling produces resistance to parathyroid hormone and sometimes other hormones, giving a biochemical picture that can overlap pseudohypoparathyroidism despite a normal GNAS gene. Compatible with survival to adulthood; morbidity relates to short stature, hand deformity, variable hormone resistance, and, in the PDE4D form, cognitive impairment, rather than to a shortened lifespan.

keratolytics, cryotherapy or other destructive methods, and reassurance about the benign nature Rapid change or ulceration in an individual lesion suggesting an alternative diagnosis Widespread florid disease indicating overlap with Darier disease Secondary infection of eroded lesions Diagnostic uncertainty from atypical or verrucous lesions Repeatedly treating the papules as recalcitrant viral warts Overlooking the allelic relationship with Darier disease and its family history Over-treating benign acral papules with aggressive destruction and scarring Failing to reassure the patient about the benign nature of the condition Acrokeratosis verruciformis of Hopf is caused by variants in ATP2A2, encoding the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase isoform 2 (SERCA2), which pumps calcium into the endoplasmic reticulum and maintains the calcium gradients needed for normal keratinocyte adhesion and differentiation. Impaired SERCA2 function disturbs desmosomal assembly and epidermal differentiation, producing focal hyperkeratotic, papillomatous acral papules. Because Darier disease results from variants in the same gene, the two are allelic, and the milder acral phenotype can coexist with or occur in families affected by Darier disease. The condition is benign and chronic with no malignant potential; lesions persist and may slowly increase in number, and the impact is essentially cosmetic.

Acromegaly — growth hormone excess, GH excess, somatotroph adenoma, gigantism (if before epiphyseal fusion) Constitutional large body habitus or familial coarse features Pachydermoperiostosis and other causes of acral enlargement Hypothyroidism causing coarse features and soft-tissue changes Other pituitary masses causing mass effect without GH excess Ectopic GHRH or GH secretion from a neuroendocrine tumour Serum IGF-1 interpreted against age-matched reference ranges as the initial screen Oral glucose tolerance test with GH measurement to confirm non-suppression Pituitary MRI to define adenoma size and relation to the optic chiasm Formal visual field assessment when a macroadenoma abuts the chiasm Evaluation of remaining anterior pituitary axes for co-secretion or hypopituitarism Screening for complications including echocardiography, sleep study, and colonoscopy Insidious onset means diagnosis is often delayed by years; comparing old photographs can reveal the gradual coarsening of features Characteristic findings include enlarging hands and feet, coarse facial features, frontal bossing, prognathism, and interdental spacing Soft-tissue overgrowth commonly causes carpal tunnel syndrome, arthralgia, excessive sweating, and obstructive sleep apnoea Systemic complications include hypertension, glucose intolerance or diabetes, cardiomyopathy, and an increased risk of colonic polyps Because GH secretion is pulsatile, a random GH level is not reliable; IGF-1 is the preferred screening test as it reflects integrated secretion Biochemical confirmation rests on failure of GH to suppress during an oral glucose load Most cases arise from a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma, so pituitary MRI and assessment of other pituitary axes and visual fields are essential Transsphenoidal surgical resection is the usual first-line treatment, with medical therapy or radiotherapy for residual disease Visual field loss or new headache suggesting chiasmal compression by a macroadenoma Features of pituitary apoplexy such as sudden severe headache with ophthalmoplegia Signs of heart failure from acromegalic cardiomyopathy Coexisting hypopituitarism, particularly unrecognised adrenal insufficiency Relying on a single random GH level, which is uninterpretable given pulsatile secretion Attributing carpal tunnel syndrome, sleep apnoea, or new diabetes to common causes without considering acromegaly Missing coexisting hypopituitarism when focusing on GH excess Overlooking the need for long-term surveillance for cardiovascular disease and colonic polyps Acromegaly is caused by chronic excess of growth hormone, almost always from a somatotroph pituitary adenoma, and rarely from ectopic GH or GHRH secretion. Excess GH stimulates hepatic production of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which mediates most of the peripheral growth effects on bone, cartilage, and soft tissue. When GH excess occurs before epiphyseal fusion it produces gigantism; after fusion it produces the acral and soft-tissue overgrowth of acromegaly. The expanding pituitary mass may also compress the optic chiasm and impair other pituitary hormone axes, while GH's counter-regulatory metabolic effects promote insulin resistance and cardiovascular disease. Biochemical control that normalises IGF-1 and GH restores life expectancy toward normal and improves soft-tissue and metabolic features, whereas persistent disease increases cardiovascular, respiratory, and metabolic mortality and the risk of colonic neoplasia.

distribution Assuming dominant inheritance when the Maroteaux type is autosomal recessive Overlooking that heterozygous carriers may have mild isolated short stature Failing to distinguish it from acrodysostosis and pseudohypoparathyroidism, which have distinct biochemistry Acromesomelic dysplasia, Maroteaux type, is caused by loss-of-function variants in NPR2, encoding natriuretic peptide Deficient receptor function reduces growth-plate activity most markedly in the mesomelic and acromelic limb segments, producing their disproportionate shortening. Other genetic forms involve related BMP/GDF signalling components. Intelligence and lifespan are normal; the main issues are disproportionate short stature and limb deformity, which may require orthopaedic correction, with the overall outlook generally favourable.
