Acute coronary syndrome — 12-lead ECG (serial) Troponin Aspirin + cardiology referral STEMI → immediate reperfusion pathway Stable angina (chronic, exertional) Esophageal spasm (can closely mimic angina and may respond to nitroglycerin) Gastroesophageal reflux / peptic ulcer disease Costochondritis / chest wall (musculoskeletal) syndromes Cervical radiculitis / disk disease Panic disorder and related psychiatric conditions (up to ~10% of ED chest pain) High-sensitivity cardiac troponin at presentation, repeated at 1-3 h (1-2 h rapid rule-out possible with hs-assays); conventional troponin repeated at 3-6 h Right-sided ECG leads when ischemia is suspected but standard 12-lead is nondiagnostic Chest radiograph (often normal in ACS; may show pulmonary edema; helps exclude pneumothorax, wide mediastinum) Echocardiography for regional wall-motion abnormality, mechanical complications, or tamponade when diagnosis is uncertain or there is hemodynamic instability Coronary CT angiography for low-intermediate probability (high negative predictive value; also excludes dissection, effusion, PE) Stress nuclear perfusion imaging or stress echocardiography for intermediate-risk patients eligible for further testing Cardiac MRI to characterize troponin elevation without definite CAD and to discriminate ischemic from non-ischemic injury B-type natriuretic peptide and D-dimer as adjuncts (for heart failure and PE exclusion respectively) Acute pericarditis (pleuritic pain, relieved by sitting forward, friction rub, diffuse ST elevation with PR depression) Acute myocarditis (non-ischemic myocardial injury; troponin may rise but should not be labeled MI) Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy (abrupt chest pain/dyspnea after emotional or physical stress; may show ST elevation and elevated biomarkers mimicking MI) Acute aortic syndrome / aortic dissection (sudden tearing or knifelike pain, may radiate to back) Pulmonary embolism (massive PE can cause substernal pain mimicking MI) Pulmonary hypertension (anginal-quality chest pain) Tension pneumothorax Esophageal rupture (Boerhaave) / Mallory-Weiss ACS encompasses unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI, and the term is generally reserved for ischemia precipitated by acute coronary atherothrombosis (Harrison 22e p.145). Unstable ischemic heart disease is sub-classified by whether acute myocardial injury is detectable and whether ST-segment elevation is present: unstable angina = no detectable acute injury; NSTEMI/STEMI = acute injury without/with ST elevation (Harrison 22e p.145). Type 1 MI (acute coronary thrombosis) is distinguished from type 2 MI, which results from another imbalance of myocardial oxygen supply and demand; type 2 may be driven by anemia, hypoxia, hypotension, or intense psychological stress (Harrison 22e p.145, p.150). An ECG is recommended within 10 minutes of presentation, primarily to identify ST-segment elevation candidates for immediate reperfusion (Harrison 22e p.150). Resting ECG sensitivity for ischemia is poor (as low as ~20%), so a normal ECG does not exclude ACS; serial ECGs every 30-60 min are recommended early in suspected ACS (Harrison 22e p.150). Physical examination findings may be entirely normal in unstable ischemic heart disease, so an unremarkable exam is not reassuring (Harrison 22e p.149). Relief of pain by nitroglycerin is neither sensitive nor specific for ischemia (esophageal spasm also responds); relief delayed beyond ~10 min suggests either a non-ischemic cause or severe ischemia such as acute MI (Harrison 22e p.149). Chest wall tenderness on palpation does not exclude myocardial ischemia (Harrison 22e p.150). ST-segment elevation on ECG (candidate for immediate reperfusion) ST-segment depression or symmetric T-wave inversions >=0.2 mV (higher risk of death or recurrent ischemia) Hypotension and significant tachycardia (suggest cardiogenic shock or other severe cause) New murmur of mitral regurgitation or ventricular septal defect (mechanical complication of STEMI) Pulmonary edema / S3 / rales (high-risk LV dysfunction) Pain prolonged >=30 min and not relieved by rest (suggests MI rather than stable angina) Syncope or presyncope with chest pain (consider ischemic arrhythmia, also PE and dissection) Relying on a normal resting ECG or unremarkable physical exam to exclude ACS - both can be normal in unstable ischemic heart disease (Harrison 22e p.149-150). Treating nitroglycerin response as diagnostic - esophageal spasm also responds and ischemic relief is non-specific (Harrison 22e p.149). Attributing pain to the chest wall because palpation reproduces it - tenderness does not exclude ischemia (Harrison 22e p.150). Some patients with ischemia deny 'pain' and report only dyspnea or vague anxiety; women and the elderly may present with anginal equivalents (dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, fatigue, faintness) (Harrison 22e p.149). Inferior MI may present with nausea/vomiting (vagal / Bezold-Jarisch reflex), simulating a GI disorder (Harrison 22e p.149). High-sensitivity troponin detects injury in many non-ACS cardiopulmonary conditions; without a dynamic rise/fall and clinical correlation, a single elevated value can be misinterpreted as MI - chronic elevation occurs with structural heart disease, end-stage renal disease, or interfering antibodies (Harrison 22e p.150). Non-ischemic injury (e.g., myocarditis) can raise troponin but should not be labeled MI (Harrison 22e p.150). Confusing diagnostic decision-aids (HEART, EDACS) with prognostic risk scores (TIMI, GRACE), which are intended for patients with already-established ACS, not for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.151). Myocardial ischemia (angina pectoris) arises from an imbalance between myocardial oxygen demand (raised by heart rate, ventricular wall stress, and contractility) and oxygen supply (set by coronary blood flow and arterial oxygen content). ACS is typically precipitated by acute coronary atherothrombosis. When ischemia is sufficiently severe and prolonged (as little as ~20 min), irreversible cellular injury and MI occur. Symptoms can also be driven predominantly by increased demand (e.g., intense psychological stress) or reduced delivery (anemia, hypoxia, hypotension), underlying the type 2 MI concept (Harrison 22e p.145). Among unselected ED chest-pain populations, only ~10-20% (as low as 5%) are ultimately diagnosed with ACS, while gastrointestinal causes predominate; historically 2-6% of patients discharged with presumed non-ischemic pain were later found to have had a missed MI. In patients stratified as low risk (excluding ST elevation or definite noncardiac pain), the estimated 30-day major cardiovascular event rate was ~2.5%. Validated clinical decision pathways combining ECG and serial high-sensitivity troponin can achieve ACS miss rates <0.5%, and a single very low hs-troponin >2-3 h after symptom onset carries a negative predictive value >99% for MI (Harrison 22e p.145, p.150-151). ACS is categorized along two clinical decision-making lines. (1) Diagnostic/disposition risk in undifferentiated chest pain uses clinical decision pathways such as the HEART score (history, ECG, age, risk factors; low risk 0-3) and EDACS, combined with serial high-sensitivity troponin, to classify patients as low/intermediate/high risk. (2) Prognostic risk in established ACS uses the TIMI and GRACE risk scores to estimate event risk - these are explicitly not intended for diagnostic use. Common high-risk elements across tools: typical ACS symptoms, older age, known/atherosclerotic risk factors, ischemic ECG changes, and elevated troponin (Harrison 22e p.151).

Actinic granuloma (annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma) — annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma, O'Brien actinic granuloma, Miescher granuloma, AEGCG Granuloma annulare Cutaneous sarcoidosis Necrobiosis lipoidica Tinea corporis and other annular infections Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus Mycosis fungoides presenting with annular plaques Skin biopsy demonstrating elastophagocytosis and loss of elastic fibres within a granulomatous infiltrate Elastic tissue stains to highlight the central loss and giant-cell engulfment of elastic fibres Mycological examination to exclude dermatophyte infection in annular lesions Assessment for sarcoidosis when granulomatous histology is found Review of cumulative sun exposure and photodamage Autoimmune serology if lupus is suspected clinically Presents as slowly expanding annular plaques with a raised erythematous border and an atrophic, hypopigmented centre Lesions characteristically arise on chronically sun-damaged skin such as the face, neck, upper chest and dorsa of the forearms The condition is closely related to, and by many considered part of the same spectrum as, annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma Histology shows a granulomatous reaction centred on elastotic (sun-damaged) dermal fibres with multinucleate giant cells engulfing degenerate elastic fibres (elastophagocytosis) A characteristic feature is loss of elastic tissue in the centre of lesions, accounting for the atrophic appearance It is generally asymptomatic and follows an indolent course, though lesions may enlarge over months to years Its relationship to granuloma annulare is debated, but the emphasis on solar elastosis and elastolysis distinguishes it histologically Treatment is often unsatisfactory; strict photoprotection is advised, with topical or intralesional corticosteroids and other agents tried for cosmetically troublesome disease Atypical, rapidly enlarging or ulcerating lesions requiring biopsy to exclude malignancy Granulomatous histology prompting consideration of systemic sarcoidosis Diagnostic uncertainty with annular lymphoma or lupus Extensive photodamage warranting surveillance for skin cancer Mistaking the annular lesions for tinea and prescribing ineffective antifungals Failing to perform elastic tissue stains and missing the characteristic elastolysis Overlooking the relationship to chronic photodamage and neglecting sun protection Confusing it with granuloma annulare and misjudging prognosis and associations Actinic granuloma is thought to arise from a cell-mediated granulomatous response to ultraviolet-damaged (elastotic) dermal elastic fibres. Chronic sun exposure alters elastic tissue so that it becomes antigenic or is otherwise recognised as abnormal, provoking an infiltrate of histiocytes and multinucleate giant cells that phagocytose the degenerate fibres. The result is destruction and clearance of elastic tissue at the advancing granulomatous border, leaving an elastolytic, atrophic centre. This preferential involvement of sun-damaged skin and the prominent elastophagocytosis distinguish the process from other annular granulomatous dermatoses. The condition is benign and typically follows a slow, indolent course; some lesions resolve spontaneously over years while others persist or slowly enlarge, and treatment responses are variable and often disappointing.

horn-like lesion with a firm, tender base warranting histology Dismissing an indurated or growing lesion as a simple actinic keratosis when it is an invasive squamous cell carcinoma Treating allowing recurrent disease Actinic keratosis is an intraepidermal proliferation of atypical, dysplastic keratinocytes driven by cumulative ultraviolet radiation. UV exposure induces characteristic DNA mutations, including in the TP53 tumour-suppressor gene, that impair repair and apoptosis and allow clonal expansion of abnormal keratinocytes confined to the epidermis. The result is disordered maturation and hyperkeratosis producing the palpable scale. Because the whole photo-damaged area shares this mutational burden (field cancerisation), multiple lesions and recurrences are common, and continued genetic damage can lead to full-thickness dysplasia and invasion characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma. Individual actinic keratoses are common and most remain stable or regress, but they mark significant sun damage and carry a small per-lesion risk of transforming into squamous cell carcinoma; with a high lesion burden the cumulative risk becomes clinically important, so treatment and long-term photoprotection and surveillance are worthwhile.

The powerful link with specific HLA-DR4 alleles points to an antigen-presentation abnormality, and the histology and lip involvement suggest an ongoing delayed hypersensitivity response to an ultraviolet-induced cutaneous antigen. The tendency for lesions to persist on covered skin and outside the sunny season distinguishes it immunologically and clinically from ordinary polymorphic light eruption. actinic reticuloid — chronic actinic dermatitis (severe variant), photosensitivity dermatitis and actinic reticuloid syndrome Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma / Sezary syndrome Airborne allergic contact dermatitis Atopic dermatitis with photoaggravation Photoallergic contact dermatitis Drug-induced photosensitivity Systemic photosensitive lupus erythematosus Cutaneous porphyria Monochromator phototesting to define the action spectrum and minimal erythema dose Patch testing and photopatch testing for coexisting contact and photocontact allergy Skin biopsy with assessment of infiltrate and immunophenotype (CD4/CD8 ratio) Peripheral blood flow cytometry and T-cell clonality studies to exclude lymphoma when atypia is marked Autoimmune serology (antinuclear and extractable nuclear antigen antibodies) to exclude lupus Urinary and erythrocyte porphyrin studies to exclude porphyria Represents the most severe end of the chronic actinic dermatitis spectrum, typically in older men with intensely pruritic, thickened, lichenified and infiltrated plaques on sun-exposed skin. The action spectrum is characteristically broad, with abnormal reactivity extending across UVB, UVA and often visible light, so ordinary sunscreens give incomplete protection. Phototesting shows a markedly reduced minimal erythema dose across multiple wavebands, which is central to confirming the diagnosis. Histology may closely mimic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (a pseudolymphomatous pattern with atypical lymphocytes), but the dermal infiltrate is usually CD8 predominant rather than the CD4 predominance of true lymphoma. Coexisting allergic contact or photocontact sensitivity is common, particularly to sesquiterpene lactones (Compositae plants), fragrances and sunscreens, so patch and photopatch testing are essential. Severe disease may generalise to involve covered skin and progress to erythroderma with leonine facial thickening. Strict photoprotection, including from visible light and behind window glass, combined with avoidance of identified contact allergens, is the cornerstone of management. The condition mainly affects skin of the head, neck and dorsal hands, with a sharp cut-off at clothing lines when photo-driven. Progression to erythroderma with systemic upset and temperature dysregulation Persistent lymphadenopathy or circulating atypical lymphocytes raising concern for lymphoma Rapidly enlarging or ulcerating plaques suggesting transformation Failure to improve despite rigorous photoprotection and allergen avoidance Misinterpreting the pseudolymphomatous histology as cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, leading to inappropriate aggressive therapy. Overlooking coexisting contact or photocontact allergy, which perpetuates the eruption. Relying on standard UVB sunscreens that fail to block the visible and UVA wavelengths driving the disease. Attributing generalised involvement to a primary lymphoma rather than to spread of photosensitive dermatitis onto covered skin. Actinic reticuloid is understood as a persistent, delayed-type (cell-mediated) hypersensitivity response in which ultraviolet, and sometimes visible, radiation converts an endogenous cutaneous molecule into a photo-induced antigen. Repeated antigen presentation drives a chronic dermal T-lymphocyte infiltrate that produces the dense, lichenified plaques and the pseudolymphomatous histological appearance. Many patients have concurrent contact or photocontact allergy, which appears to prime or perpetuate the reaction, and abnormal reactivity persists long after the initiating exposure, explaining the chronic, self-sustaining course. The condition tends to be chronic and can persist for many years, but a substantial proportion of patients improve or remit with strict photoprotection and avoidance of identified allergens. Rarely, severe refractory disease requires systemic immunosuppression.

Actinomycosis — Actinomyces infection, lumpy jaw, cervicofacial actinomycosis Malignancy / solid tumor (most common misdiagnosis given mass-like, tissue-plane-crossing behavior) Tuberculosis Nocardiosis Inflammatory bowel disease (when abdominal sinus tracts/fistulas develop) Endometriosis (in pelvic disease) Bacterial pneumonia or lung neoplasm (in thoracic disease) Tuberculosis Nocardiosis Mycetoma due to Nocardia or Actinomadura species Botryomycosis (chronic suppurative bacterial infection forming granule-like clumps) Bacterial pneumonia/empyema from usual organisms Microscopic identification of sulfur granules in pus or tissue (most common diagnostic means; yield improves with additional histopathologic sections and positively charged slides) Anaerobic culture—isolation maximized under anaerobic conditions, typically requiring 5–7 days and potentially up to 2–4 weeks; even a single antibiotic dose can preclude recovery 16S rRNA gene amplification and sequencing to enhance sensitivity and specificity MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry (databases still being optimized) Histologic stains: periodic acid–Schiff (PAS), Grocott methenamine silver (GMS), and Gram stains to identify actinomycotic aggregates CT and MRI for lesion characterization and monitoring; FDG-PET may demonstrate hypermetabolism CT/ultrasound-guided aspiration or biopsy to obtain material in a minimally invasive fashion; endometrial biopsy for pelvic disease Malignant neoplasm / solid tumor Endometriosis Inflammatory bowel disease Lung neoplasm An uncommon, indolent, slowly progressive infection caused by anaerobic or microaerophilic bacteria—primarily Actinomyces species—that normally colonize the mouth, colon, and vagina; it has been called one of the most frequently misdiagnosed diseases (Harrison 22e p.1363). Three classic presentations should trigger suspicion: a chronic mass-like lesion that crosses tissue planes and mimics malignancy, a sinus tract that spontaneously resolves and recurs, and a refractory or relapsing infection after a short course of therapy (Harrison 22e p.1363). Most infections are polymicrobial; companion organisms such as Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Eikenella corrodens, Enterobacteriaceae, Fusobacterium, and Bacteroides are commonly co-isolated, though their pathogenic contribution is uncertain (Harrison 22e p.1363). Disease spreads contiguously, ignoring tissue planes; the characteristic chronic phase produces single or multiple indurated lesions with fibrotic walls classically described as wooden (Harrison 22e p.1364). Central necrosis containing neutrophils and sulfur granules is virtually diagnostic; over time, sinus tracts to skin, adjacent organs, or bone develop (Harrison 22e p.1364). Lymphatic spread with lymphadenopathy and distant hematogenous seeding are uncommon—an important contrast with malignancy and tuberculosis (Harrison 22e p.1364). Oral–cervicofacial disease is the most frequent presentation, typically at the angle of the jaw, often precipitated by dental disease or procedures (Harrison 22e p.1364). Pelvic actinomycosis is strongly associated with intrauterine contraceptive devices (IUDs) and other foreign bodies such as surgical mesh; risk increases the longer the device remains in place and is low when in place under one year (Harrison 22e p.1364-1365). Sulfur granules represent an in vivo matrix of bacteria, calcium phosphate, and host material; on hematoxylin-eosin staining they may be surrounded by a radiating fringe of eosinophilic clubs (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon) (Harrison 22e p.1365). Foreign bodies (especially IUDs) and immunocompromising states—HIV, transplantation, common variable immunodeficiency, chronic granulomatous disease, and certain immunosuppressive therapies—are recognized predisposing factors (Harrison 22e p.1364). FDG-PET may show hypermetabolism in actinomycotic lesions, potentially compounding confusion with malignancy (Harrison 22e p.1365). Chronic mass-like lesion crossing tissue planes and mimicking cancer Sinus tract that spontaneously resolves and recurs Refractory or relapsing infection after a short antibiotic course Lesions crossing fissures/pleura, extending into mediastinum, bone, or chest wall (empyema necessitatis) Wound or fistula that fails to heal, or recurrent abdominal disease CNS involvement (brain abscess, meningitis, cavernous sinus syndrome)—a critical-site presentation Diagnosis is rarely considered prospectively—actinomycosis is often first identified by the pathologist after extensive (and avoidable) surgery (Harrison 22e p.1365). Prior antibiotic exposure or failure to obtain appropriate anaerobic cultures frequently precludes microbiologic identification; even a single antibiotic dose can prevent isolation (Harrison 22e p.1365). Because actinomycetes are normal oral and genital-tract flora, their detection in sputum, bronchial washings, or cervicovaginal secretions without sulfur granules may reflect colonization rather than infection (Harrison 22e p.1365). Detection of Actinomyces-like organisms on Papanicolaou smear in IUD users has low positive predictive value; in an asymptomatic patient this warrants education and follow-up, not routine IUD removal (Harrison 22e p.1365). Isolation of Actinomyces from blood cultures without a defined focus may represent contamination or transient bacteremia from a mucosal site (Harrison 22e p.1366). Elevated CA-125 in pelvic disease and FDG-PET hypermetabolism can reinforce a mistaken cancer diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1365). The etiologic agents are members of the normal oral, gastrointestinal, and female genital flora. The critical initiating step is disruption of the mucosal barrier, allowing local infection. Once established, the infection spreads contiguously in a slow, progressive fashion that disregards normal tissue planes. Although acute inflammation may occur initially, the hallmark is a chronic indolent phase with indurated lesions, central necrosis (neutrophils plus sulfur granules), and dense fibrotic walls. Sinus tracts to skin, adjacent organs, or bone may develop over time. Foreign bodies, particularly IUDs, facilitate infection, and ulcerative mucosal infections (e.g., HSV, CMV) may promote disease (Harrison 22e p.1364). Actinomycosis is usually curable with medical therapy alone, even in extensive disease, and an awareness of its clinical spectrum can expedite diagnosis and minimize unnecessary surgery, morbidity, and mortality. Cure of established disease requires prolonged treatment, and relapse is a clinical hallmark if therapy is stopped too early; refractory disease has been described in HIV-infected individuals (Harrison 22e p.1363, p.1366).

in a young patient with progressive myoclonus Confusing the phenotype with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and delaying genetic testing Overlooking that renal and neurological onset may be separated by years Action myoclonus-renal failure syndrome results from loss-of-function variants in SCARB2, encoding the lysosomal integral membrane protein 2 (LIMP-2). LIMP-2 serves as the sorting receptor that escorts beta-glucocerebrosidase from the endoplasmic reticulum to the lysosome and also maintains lysosomal membrane integrity. Its deficiency impairs lysosomal function in neurons and podocytes. In the nervous system this produces a progressive myoclonic phenotype with cortical hyperexcitability, while in the kidney it disrupts podocyte function, causing proteinuria and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis that can progress to renal failure. The shared reliance of brain and glomerulus on intact lysosomal membrane biology explains the otherwise unusual pairing of neurological and renal disease. A progressive disorder; neurological disability accrues over years and renal disease often advances to end-stage kidney failure, though renal replacement therapy and transplantation can be undertaken.

decline from bronchiectasis Severe or disseminated herpesvirus infection Refractory cytopenias or organomegaly causing functional compromise Labelling the condition common variable immunodeficiency and missing the specific targetable pathway defect Mistaking benign lymphoproliferation for lymphoma or vice versa without histology Overlooking early bronchiectasis because chest examination and spirometry appear normal Failing to monitor and pre-emptively manage EBV Using broad immunosuppression without recognising the option of pathway-specific therapy APDS results from constitutive over-activity of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase delta pathway, either through activating variants in the catalytic subunit p110-delta (PIK3CD) or loss of the inhibitory regulatory subunit p85-alpha (PIK3R1). Outcome varies widely; recurrent infection and bronchiectasis cause chronic morbidity while lymphoma is a major cause of death, but selective PI3K-delta inhibition and, in selected patients, transplantation have improved disease control.

infection, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for severe combined phenotypes Severe bacterial infection with poor wound healing and delayed cord separation Abscesses that fail to form pus despite high neutrophil counts Progressive lymphopenia or an abnormal newborn screen in the activating phenotype Recurrent invasive infection in infancy A family history of early infection consistent with a dominant or other inheritance pattern Confusing the neutrophil-function defect with leucocyte adhesion deficiency without genetic clarification Reassurance based on a normal or high neutrophil count despite defective function Overlooking progressive lymphopenia in activating mutations Giving live vaccines before a combined defect is excluded Delaying definitive treatment while recurrent infections accumulate RAC2 encodes a Rho-family small GTPase expressed almost exclusively in blood cells, where it cycles between active and inactive states to control actin-dependent processes and assembly of the neutrophil oxidase. In neutrophils, RAC2 signalling is needed for directed migration toward chemotactic signals, for the respiratory burst that generates microbicidal superoxide, and for granule release. Dominant-negative mutations block normal RAC2 activity, crippling neutrophil chemotaxis and killing so that bacteria are not cleared despite adequate cell numbers, mimicking a leucocyte adhesion defect. Activating mutations lock the GTPase in a constitutively signalling state that disturbs lymphocyte development and survival, producing progressive lymphopenia and a combined immunodeficiency. The net effect in either case is a serious predisposition to bacterial and, in the activating forms, broader infection. Prognosis depends on the mutation class and severity; the neutrophil-function defect can be life-threatening in infancy and the combined immunodeficiency of activating mutations is severe, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offering the prospect of cure when infections are controlled.

Acute abdomen — surgical abdomen, acute abdominal pain, peritonitis Ruptured or leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm Mesenteric ischaemia or infarction Perforated viscus (peptic ulcer, diverticulum, appendix) Bowel obstruction with or without strangulation Ectopic pregnancy or other gynaecological emergency Inferior myocardial infarction or lower-lobe pneumonia mimicking abdominal pain Erect chest and abdominal radiographs to detect free air or obstruction Bedside ultrasound and CT abdomen for definitive assessment when stable Serum lactate as a marker of ischaemia or hypoperfusion Pregnancy test in women of childbearing age Amylase/lipase, renal and liver function, and inflammatory markers as part of the workup The immediate task is to identify the patient who needs urgent surgery from among the many with self-limiting abdominal pain Assess airway, breathing, and circulation first, since perforation, ischaemia, or bleeding can cause rapid haemodynamic collapse The character, onset, and migration of pain guide the diagnosis; sudden severe pain suggests perforation, rupture, or vascular catastrophe Peritonism (guarding, rigidity, rebound, pain on movement) indicates peritoneal irritation and a likely surgical cause Pain out of proportion to examination findings should raise concern for mesenteric ischaemia Always consider extra-abdominal and vascular causes such as myocardial infarction, ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, and ectopic pregnancy Serial examination and reassessment are valuable when the diagnosis is uncertain, as the picture often evolves Resuscitate, provide analgesia, and involve surgery early rather than delaying for prolonged investigation in the unstable patient Sudden severe pain with peritonism suggesting perforation or vascular rupture needing immediate surgery Haemodynamic instability indicating haemorrhage, ischaemia, or septic shock Pain disproportionate to findings, raising suspicion of mesenteric ischaemia A pulsatile mass or back pain with collapse suggesting ruptured aortic aneurysm Rapidly progressive distension, fever, and toxicity signalling advancing peritonitis Withholding analgesia for fear of masking signs, which is not supported and delays comfort Attributing pain to a benign cause in the elderly, in whom signs are often muted despite serious disease Overlooking vascular and extra-abdominal causes such as aortic aneurysm or myocardial infarction Delaying surgery to complete imaging in an unstable patient Failing to reassess when the initial diagnosis is uncertain Acute abdomen results from inflammation, obstruction, perforation, ischaemia, or haemorrhage of intra-abdominal organs. Visceral pain is initially poorly localised because of autonomic innervation, but once inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum the pain becomes sharp and localised. Perforation releases luminal contents causing chemical then bacterial peritonitis; obstruction causes distension, third-space fluid loss, and potential strangulation; and vascular occlusion causes bowel ischaemia and infarction. These processes can precipitate hypovolaemia, sepsis, and shock, making the acute abdomen a potentially life-threatening presentation. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause and the speed of definitive treatment. Early recognition and surgery for perforation, ischaemia, or haemorrhage improve survival, while delay allows sepsis, bowel infarction, or exsanguination with markedly higher mortality.

hypoxia or hypoglycaemia demanding immediate correction Fluctuating consciousness or new focal neurology suggesting a serious intracranial cause Agitation in a trauma patient indicating possible hypoxia or shock and prompting reassessment Autonomic instability with hyperthermia suggesting a severe toxidrome or serotonin/neuroleptic syndrome Rapid physical exhaustion during prolonged struggle, risking sudden collapse Labelling agitation as psychiatric or drug-related before excluding hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, and head injury Sedating the patient without monitoring, risking airway obstruction and respiratory depression Using prolonged or unmonitored physical restraint Failing to reassess the trauma patient whose agitation reflects worsening shock or hypoxia Overlooking withdrawal states that can escalate dangerously Acute agitation is a final common pathway of many disturbances of brain function. Global cerebral dysfunction (delirium) arises from hypoxia, hypoperfusion, hypoglycaemia, metabolic derangement, sepsis, drug intoxication or withdrawal, and structural brain injury, all of which impair the neural networks governing attention and behaviour. In the trauma setting, agitation may be the earliest external sign of inadequate cerebral oxygen delivery from hypoxia or haemorrhagic shock. Primary psychiatric illness and severe pain also contribute, but organic causes must be excluded because they are frequently reversible and can be fatal if missed. Prognosis depends entirely on the underlying cause. When a reversible medical precipitant is identified and treated, agitation usually resolves, but a missed organic cause such as hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, or intracranial pathology can be rapidly fatal.

creatine phosphokinase and C-reactive protein Respiratory viral panel; selected serologies for HIV, Chagas, CMV, dengue, Lyme, and systemic autoimmune disease (viral titers rarely guide initial therapy) Endomyocardial biopsy (with immunohistochemistry) when ventricular arrhythmias, conduction block, eosinophilia, or autoimmune disease suggest a specific etiology Chest CT (mediastinal lymphadenopathy) and whole-chest FDG-PET for active sarcoid lesions; PCR for T. cruzi in acute Chagas Cardiac sarcoidosis (noncaseating granulomas; may mimic arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy) Giant cell myocarditis Eosinophilic myocarditis / hypereosinophilic syndrome with Loeffler endocarditis Systemic autoimmune disease: polymyositis/dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus (which also causes accelerated CAD, sterile endocarditis, pericarditis, vasculitis) Immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis and vaccine-associated myocarditis Myocarditis is inflammation of heart muscle that can present acutely, subacutely, or insidiously, with outcomes ranging from full resolution to a relapsing course or progression to chronic cardiomyopathy; it is termed acute when symptoms have lasted under a month, often only days (p.2011). Chest pain is the most common symptom of acute myocarditis, occurring in more than 80% of patients, who frequently also have dyspnea or arrhythmias; fever is present in over half of cases and a viral prodrome may precede onset by days to weeks (p.2011). Acute myocarditis in adults typically occurs between roughly 30 and 45 years and is more common in men, whereas women tend to present after age 45 (p.2011). At presentation about one-fourth of acute myocarditis cases have an LVEF below 0.50, ventricular arrhythmias, or shock; fulminant myocarditis (circulatory shock) is reported in about 3-9% of cases (p.2011). Diagnosis can now be made noninvasively when a typical symptomatic presentation is accompanied by elevated troponin plus cardiac MRI showing both myocardial edema and nonischemic injury without another cause; biopsy is no longer strictly required for a 'definite' diagnosis (p.2011-2012). Because chest pain, ECG changes, and elevated troponin overlap between acute myocarditis and myocardial infarction, coronary imaging is often the first differential step; myocarditis is later diagnosed in up to one-third of patients with MINOCA (myocardial infarction with nonobstructed coronary arteries) (p.2011). Eosinophil counts should be checked routinely because hypereosinophilia is present in most cases of eosinophilic myocarditis; right bundle branch block should raise suspicion for sarcoidosis or Chagas rather than typical cardiomyopathies, in which left bundle branch block predominates (p.2011, p.2013, p.2014). Around one in five patients with inflammatory myocarditis carry genetic variants considered pathogenic for cardiomyopathy, and 20-40% of dilated cardiomyopathy patients have variants sufficient to explain their disease; CMR fibrosis patterns once attributed to prior viral myocarditis are now recognized as common in genetic cardiomyopathy too (p.2011, p.2012). Giant cell myocarditis accounts for 10-20% of biopsy-proven myocarditis, occurs equally in men and women (typically older than viral cases), is more often linked to systemic autoimmune disease, and usually presents acutely with rapidly progressive heart failure and tachyarrhythmias (p.2014). Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) is the most common infective cause of cardiomyopathy worldwide; after a usually silent initial infection patients enter an 'indeterminate phase' lasting decades, during which persistent low-level parasitemia is now recognized as the major driver of progression to chronic heart failure (p.2013). Diphtheria toxin (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) interferes with cardiac protein synthesis and especially affects the conduction system; cardiac involvement is the most common cause of death in this infection, and clinical suspicion alone justifies giving antitoxin with higher priority than antibiotics (p.2013). Combined immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis is the most dramatic noninfectious form: troponin is often elevated, biopsy shows extensive lymphocytic infiltration, and it should be suspected immediately with any acute cardiac presentation in a treated patient; CCU admission is recommended for elevated troponin with ECG changes (p.2014). Fulminant presentation with cardiogenic shock or need for high-dose inotropes/mechanical circulatory support (3-9% of cases) Ventricular arrhythmias or syncope, which may precede sudden cardiac death (inflammatory myocarditis found in 3-10% of sudden deaths in previously healthy young adults) New conduction block, especially right bundle branch block (suggests sarcoidosis or Chagas) LVEF <0.50 at presentation (marks higher-risk 'complicated' course and chronic cardiomyopathy risk) Hypereosinophilia (suggests eosinophilic myocarditis, a cause of fulminant disease) Acute cardiac symptoms in a patient on immune checkpoint inhibitors, often with concurrent involvement of other organs Assuming any chest pain/ECG change/troponin elevation is infarction can miss myocarditis, which underlies up to one-third of MINOCA cases (p.2011). Sarcoid granulomas are scattered and commonly missed on endomyocardial biopsy, so a negative biopsy does not exclude cardiac sarcoidosis (p.2014). Eosinophilic myocarditis may be overlooked in milder presentations if hypereosinophilia is not assessed (p.2014). Viral titers and detection of viral genome fragments or anticardiac antibodies in chronic cardiomyopathy are of uncertain significance, as the same viruses (e.g., parvovirus B19, HHV6) are also found in normal control hearts and these assays are not in routine clinical use (p.2011, p.2012). There are no data supporting routine immunosuppression for presumed viral acute myocarditis, and immunosuppression for nonspecific lymphocytic chronic myocarditis has not shown convincing benefit (p.2012). Initial care of suspected checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis should generally not be delayed to obtain endomyocardial biopsy (p.2014). Infectious agents injure the myocardium both by direct cellular invasion (disrupting normal cellular processes) and by activating immune responses, with or without persistent infection. Viral myocarditis has classically been described in three phases from murine enterovirus (coxsackie B) models: (1) direct myocardial invasion, with viral entry sometimes enhanced by coxsackie/adenovirus receptor variants and enteroviral protease degrading dystrophin to trigger apoptosis and impair autophagy; (2) host immune response to conserved antigenic patterns, activating macrophages and expanding T- and B-cell populations, which can produce 'virally triggered' myocarditis even without direct viral injury, possibly via molecular mimicry between viral and cardiac antigens; and (3) progression to chronic cardiomyopathy, demonstrated in animal models. Direct genome entry occurs with enteroviruses, HIV, and dengue, but most common viruses do not appear to damage the heart directly, and early injury is often driven by cytokine storm and nonspecific immune activation. Notably, this initial immune response appears crucial to recovery, since early immunosuppression worsened viral replication and cardiac injury in animals. Viral 'hijacking' of cellular machinery to produce extracellular vesicles carrying viral RNA may allow protected spread to other cells. In Chagas disease, acute infection produces dense parasitic pseudocysts that rupture and cause diffuse myocyte necrosis, while chronic disease reflects persistent parasitemia plus depopulation of cardiac and gastrointestinal parasympathetic neurons. Noninfective inflammatory myocarditis (sarcoid granulomas, giant cell, eosinophilic, autoimmune, checkpoint inhibitor) reflects antigen-driven, dysregulated immune attack on myocardium; the paradigm is cardiac transplant rejection, which showed that antibodies and cytokines, not only lymphocytes, mediate reversible myocardial depression and that antigens are exposed by prior injury or infection (p.2011-2014). Prognosis is good for 'uncomplicated' acute myocarditis (LVEF >=0.50 without ventricular arrhythmias or shock), which represents about three-fourths of patients; spontaneous recovery is common, almost all retain LVEF >=0.50 on follow-up, and they survive without transplantation at 5 years. Among the one-fourth with complicated presentations, roughly 18% die or undergo transplantation over the next 5 years. In fulminant myocarditis, more than half of affected patients recover to near-normal LVEF despite presenting with refractory cardiogenic shock. Reduced LVEF at presentation predicts chronic cardiomyopathy. Chagas cardiomyopathy has lower survival than other cardiomyopathies once overt heart failure develops, and LVEF improvement is uncommon. Most patients with giant cell myocarditis in cardiogenic shock require urgent mechanical support or transplant. Checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis fatality was initially very high but is improving with earlier recognition and treatment (p.2011-2014). Harrison distinguishes uncomplicated acute myocarditis (LVEF >=0.50, no ventricular arrhythmias, no shock; ~75% of cases, good prognosis) from complicated acute myocarditis (LVEF <0.50, ventricular arrhythmias, or shock; ~25%, higher 5-year death/transplant rate). Fulminant myocarditis (~3-9%) denotes circulatory shock requiring high-dose inotropes or mechanical circulatory support. Diagnostically, 'probable myocarditis' requires at least one symptom plus one supporting finding (elevated troponin, consistent ECG, or reduced LVEF/wall-motion abnormality on imaging), while 'definite myocarditis' historically required a positive endomyocardial biopsy with lymphocytic infiltrate (p.2011).

normal pressure once the acute attack settles without confirming the angle is open In predisposed eyes with a shallow anterior chamber and short axial length, the peripheral iris crowds the drainage When the pupil becomes mid-dilated, relative pupillary block impedes aqueous flow from the posterior to the anterior chamber, so pressure builds behind the iris and bows it forward against the trabecular meshwork. This apposition abruptly obstructs aqueous outflow, causing a rapid and severe rise in intraocular pressure that compromises the optic nerve head and corneal endothelium if not relieved promptly. Prompt reduction of pressure and timely iridotomy usually preserve vision, but delayed treatment can cause permanent optic nerve damage and irreversible loss of sight.

Acute Appendicitis and Peritonitis — appendicitis, peritonitis Crohn's disease Cholecystitis or other gallbladder disease Diverticulitis Ectopic pregnancy Endometriosis Gastroenteritis or colitis Gastric or duodenal ulceration Hepatitis Kidney disease including nephrolithiasis Liver abscess Meckel's diverticulitis Mittelschmerz Mesenteric adenitis Omental torsion Pancreatitis Lower lobe pneumonia Pelvic inflammatory disease Ruptured ovarian cyst or other cystic ovarian disease Small-bowel obstruction Urinary tract infection Ovarian torsion (Harrison 22e p.2596) Gastroenteritis or colitis (nausea precedes pain, unlike appendicitis) (Harrison 22e p.2595) Pelvic inflammatory disease (Harrison 22e p.2596) Urinary tract infection / genitourinary infection (Harrison 22e p.2596) Mesenteric adenitis (Harrison 22e p.2595) Hepatitis / liver abscess (Harrison 22e p.2595) Lower lobe pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.2595) COVID-19 infection occasionally coincident (Harrison 22e p.2595) In immunocompromised patients: atypical infections from mycobacteria, Cytomegalovirus, or fungi, and neutropenic enterocolitis (Harrison 22e p.2596) WBC count: only mildly to moderately elevated (~10,000-18,000 cells/uL) in ~70% of simple appendicitis; laboratory testing alone does not identify patients with appendicitis (Harrison 22e p.2596). A left shift toward immature polymorphonuclear leukocytes is present in >95% of cases (Harrison 22e p.2596). Serum amylase and lipase should be measured; sickle cell preparation may be prudent in patients of African, Spanish, Mediterranean, or Indian ancestry (Harrison 22e p.2596). Urinalysis to help exclude genitourinary mimics; a few red or white cells may be a nonspecific finding, and an inflamed appendix abutting the ureter or bladder may cause sterile pyuria or hematuria (Harrison 22e p.2596). Pregnancy test in every woman of childbearing age; cervical cultures if PID is suspected (Harrison 22e p.2596). Anemia and guaiac-positive stools should raise concern for other disease or complications such as cancer (Harrison 22e p.2596). Ultrasonography: highly operator dependent; overall sensitivity ~0.86 and specificity ~0.81; appendix may not be visualized even in skilled hands; especially useful (including intravaginal techniques) for pelvic pathology in women. Suggestive findings: wall thickening, increased appendiceal diameter, free fluid (Harrison 22e p.2596). CT: sensitivity at least 0.94 and specificity at least 0.95; high negative predictive value; suggestive findings include dilatation >6 mm with wall thickening, a lumen that does not fill with enteric contrast, and periappendiceal fatty stranding or air. Presence of luminal air or contrast is NOT consistent with appendicitis; nonvisualization of the appendix is nonspecific and should NOT be used to rule out appendiceal/periappendiceal inflammation (Harrison 22e p.2596). Plain abdominal films are rarely helpful and not routinely obtained; <5% show an opaque fecalith, and a fecalith is not diagnostic of appendicitis (Harrison 22e p.2596). For peritonitis: in stable patients with ascites, diagnostic paracentesis is indicated with testing of fluid for protein and LDH and a cell count; radiographs may show bowel dilatation and wall edema, and free air or other leakage may represent a surgical emergency (Harrison 22e p.2597). Ectopic pregnancy (Harrison 22e p.2596) Ovarian torsion (Harrison 22e p.2596) Ruptured ovarian cyst / cystic ovarian disease (Harrison 22e p.2595) Mittelschmerz (Harrison 22e p.2595) Endometriosis (Harrison 22e p.2595) Nephrolithiasis / ureterolithiasis (Harrison 22e p.2595-2596) Small-bowel obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2595) Omental torsion (Harrison 22e p.2595) Pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2595) Appendiceal tumors / neoplasms (incidence increasing) (Harrison 22e p.2594) Classic history is migration of vague, intermittent, crampy epigastric or periumbilical pain to the right lower quadrant over 12-24 h, where it becomes sharper and localizes as transmural inflammation irritates the parietal peritoneum (p.2595). Maximal tenderness is classically at or near McBurney's point in the right lower quadrant, about one-third of the way along a line from the anterior iliac spine to the umbilicus (p.2596). Nausea, if present, characteristically follows the onset of abdominal pain (helping distinguish appendicitis from gastroenteritis, in which nausea precedes pain); emesis is typically mild and scant and also occurs after pain onset (p.2595). Anorexia is so common that the diagnosis of appendicitis should be questioned in its absence (p.2595). Rovsing's sign: palpation/gentle pressure in the left lower quadrant elicits pain in the right lower quadrant (p.2596). Iliopsoas sign: extending the right hip causes pain along the posterolateral back and hip, suggesting a retrocecal appendix (p.2596). Obturator sign: internal rotation of the hip causes pain, suggesting an inflamed appendix located in the pelvis (p.2596). Patients with appendicitis tend to lie quite still to avoid peritoneal irritation; some report discomfort with a bumpy car ride, coughing, sneezing, or Valsalva-type maneuvers. Parietal peritoneal irritation is often best elicited by gentle percussion, jiggling the bed/gurney, or mildly bumping the feet (p.2596). Simple appendicitis patients usually appear only mildly ill with pulse and temperature only slightly above normal; temperature >38.3 C (~101 F) or rigors should raise concern for another process or for complications such as perforation, phlegmon, or abscess (p.2596). Examine the entire abdomen systematically, starting in a non-tender area; all patients should have a rectal examination, and a pelvic examination in women is mandatory to exclude PID, ectopic pregnancy, and ovarian torsion (p.2596). Appendicitis should be included in the differential diagnosis of abdominal pain for every patient of any age unless it is certain the appendix has been previously removed (p.2595). Free perforation normally causes severe (generalized) peritonitis; perforation risk is ~10-20% and is significantly higher in patients <5 or >65 years of age (Harrison 22e p.2594). Temperature >38.3 C (~101 F) or rigors suggest a complication (perforation, phlegmon, abscess) or another diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2596). Persistent symptoms not improved over 48 h are more likely to perforate or develop other complications (Harrison 22e p.2595). Rare but dreaded complication: infective suppurative thrombosis of the portal vein and its tributaries with intrahepatic abscesses, with very poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2595). Diffuse abdominal tenderness with guarding and rigidity indicates generalized peritonitis; tachycardia, hypotension/volume depletion, significant leukocytosis, and severe acidosis are signs of serious disease (Harrison 22e p.2597). In pregnancy, perforation raises fetal mortality fourfold (from ~5% to ~20%) (Harrison 22e p.2596). Postoperative fever and leukocytosis persisting beyond 5 days should raise concern for an intraabdominal abscess (Harrison 22e p.2597). Atypical presentations and pain patterns are common, especially in the very old and very young; signs and symptoms can be subtle in the elderly, who may not react vigorously, with nausea/anorexia/emesis predominating (Harrison 22e p.2596). Retrocecal or pelvic (below the pelvic brim) appendix may prompt very little anterior abdominal wall tenderness; pelvic appendicitis may present with dysuria, urinary frequency, diarrhea, or tenesmus and only suprapubic or rectal/pelvic-exam tenderness (Harrison 22e p.2596). Appendiceal location varies widely (right lower quadrant, pelvis, right flank, right upper quadrant, or even the left side with malrotation/redundant colon), influencing presentation; delay in diagnosis is more likely when the appendix is unusually positioned (Harrison 22e p.2595). Diagnosing appendicitis in children is challenging (dramatic response to stimulation, difficult history); the smaller pediatric omentum may be less able to wall off a perforation (Harrison 22e p.2596). Pregnancy: appendicitis is the most common extrauterine general surgical emergency in pregnancy; early symptoms (nausea, anorexia) may be overlooked and the enlarging/gravid uterus may displace the appendix higher and obscure typical findings (Harrison 22e p.2596). Immunocompromised patients may present with only mild tenderness; do not be overly cautious and delay operation in those believed to have appendicitis (Harrison 22e p.2596). Laboratory testing alone does not identify appendicitis, and no currently available decision tool obviates the need for expert clinical opinion (Harrison 22e p.2596). A fecalith is not diagnostic of appendicitis, though its presence in an appropriate location with pain is suggestive and associated with greater likelihood of complications (Harrison 22e p.2596). Etiology is not completely understood. Obstruction of the appendiceal lumen (by fecaliths/appendicoliths, incompletely digested food residue, lymphoid hyperplasia, intraluminal scarring, tumors, bacteria, viruses, or inflammatory bowel disease) is believed, though not proven, to be an important early step at least in some cases. Obstruction leads to bacterial overgrowth and luminal distension with increased intraluminal pressure that can inhibit lymph and blood flow; vascular thrombosis and ischemic necrosis with perforation of the distal appendix may then follow. Perforation near the base of the appendix should raise concern for another disease process. Appendicoliths are found in ~50% of patients with gangrenous appendicitis who perforate but are rarely seen in simpler disease, suggesting differing underlying pathophysiology. Uncomplicated appendicitis does not always progress to perforation; some cases of simple acute appendicitis may temporarily resolve or be managed with antibiotics, though at least one-third will subsequently require appendectomy. When perforation occurs, the leak may be contained by omentum or surrounding tissues to form an abscess, whereas free perforation normally causes severe peritonitis (p.2594-2595). Mortality from simple appendicitis is currently <1%, and for uncomplicated nonperforated appendicitis the operative mortality rate is 0.1-0.5% (approximating the risk of general anesthesia). Mortality for perforated or otherwise complicated disease is much higher, ranging from ~3% overall to as high as 15% in the elderly. For acute peritonitis, mortality can be <10% in reasonably healthy patients with relatively uncomplicated, localized disease but >40% in the elderly or immunocompromised (Harrison 22e p.2597). No formal grading scale is presented; disease is broadly distinguished as simple/uncomplicated appendicitis (without gangrenous necrosis, appendicoliths, perforation, or tumors) versus complicated disease (gangrene, perforation, phlegmon, abscess). Peritonitis is classified as secondary (most commonly from perforation of a hollow viscus, e.g., appendix, colonic diverticula, stomach/duodenum) versus primary or spontaneous (no identifiable intraabdominal source; >90% occur in patients with ascites or hypoproteinemia <1 g/L), and either type may be localized or diffuse; aseptic/chemical peritonitis (e.g., from gastric juice, bile, pancreatic enzymes, blood, or urine) is also distinguished (Harrison 22e p.2595-2597).

another cause New relevant inhalational exposure suggesting risk of recurrence if not avoided Excluding the diagnosis because the peripheral blood eosinophil count is normal Treating as refractory bacterial pneumonia or ARDS and delaying bronchoalveolar lavage Overlooking a recent change in smoking behaviour or inhalational exposure as the trigger Failing to exclude infection before starting corticosteroids Acute eosinophilic pneumonia is thought to represent an acute hypersensitivity reaction of the lung, often triggered by a new inhalational insult such as recently started cigarette smoking or dust exposure. There is rapid recruitment and activation of eosinophils within the alveoli and interstitium, with release of granule proteins and cytokines that produce diffuse alveolar damage and a capillary leak. This results in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure with bilateral infiltrates and effusions. Because the process is inflammatory rather than fibrotic and highly steroid responsive, it typically resolves completely without long-term sequelae. With prompt corticosteroid treatment the prognosis is excellent, with rapid and usually complete recovery and, in contrast to chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, little tendency to relapse if the provoking exposure is removed.

Acute Epiglottitis — epiglottitis, supraglottitis, acute supraglottitis Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) Bacterial tracheitis Retropharyngeal or peritonsillar abscess Foreign body aspiration Anaphylaxis with airway angioedema Diphtheria (in unimmunised populations) Direct laryngoscopy under controlled conditions to confirm the diagnosis and secure the airway Blood cultures and epiglottic surface cultures after the airway is protected Lateral neck radiograph only if the child is stable and it will not delay care Full blood count and inflammatory markers once safe to obtain Hib and other relevant serological or PCR testing where indicated A rapidly progressive, life-threatening bacterial infection of the epiglottis and supraglottic structures that can cause sudden complete airway obstruction. Historically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b; its incidence has fallen dramatically since Hib immunisation, so other organisms and unimmunised children now feature prominently. Classic presentation is abrupt onset of high fever, severe sore throat, drooling, muffled 'hot potato' voice, and difficulty swallowing, usually without the barking cough of croup. The child characteristically sits upright in a tripod position, leaning forward with the neck extended to maximise the airway. This is an airway emergency: keep the child calm, avoid distressing procedures such as throat examination or venepuncture, and do not lay the child flat. Definitive airway management is secured in a controlled setting, ideally the operating theatre with experienced anaesthetic and ENT support, before other interventions. Once the airway is secure, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics targeting likely pathogens are given. A lateral neck radiograph may show the classic 'thumbprint' sign, but imaging must never delay airway management and is unnecessary in an unstable child. Direct visualisation of a cherry-red swollen epiglottis confirms the diagnosis but should only be performed where the airway can be immediately secured. Stridor, drooling, and respiratory distress indicating imminent obstruction Tripod positioning and refusal to lie flat Cyanosis, exhaustion, or decreasing level of consciousness Muffled voice with inability to swallow secretions Rapid clinical deterioration Examining the throat or performing painful procedures that can precipitate obstruction Laying the child supine or forcing separation from a caregiver Delaying airway management to obtain imaging or bloods Assuming the diagnosis is excluded in an immunised child, since non-Hib causes still occur Bacterial invasion of the supraglottic tissues produces intense inflammation and oedema of the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, and surrounding structures. Because these tissues sit at the laryngeal inlet, swelling rapidly narrows the airway, and the loose submucosa allows oedema to accumulate quickly. Progressive obstruction, worsened by agitation and secretions, can culminate in acute total airway occlusion. With prompt airway control and antibiotics, recovery is usually rapid and complete; outcomes are poor if the airway obstructs before it is secured, making early recognition critical.

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy — AFLP, acute yellow atrophy of pregnancy HELLP syndrome and severe pre-eclampsia Viral hepatitis, including hepatitis E, and other acute hepatitides Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or haemolytic uraemic syndrome Drug-induced liver injury Fulminant hepatic failure of another cause Sepsis with associated hepatic dysfunction Liver function tests including transaminases and bilirubin, together with serum ammonia Blood glucose, since hypoglycaemia is characteristic and needs frequent monitoring Coagulation screen with fibrinogen and a full blood count Renal function, electrolytes, and urate Viral hepatitis serology and other tests to exclude alternative causes Liver ultrasound, chiefly to exclude other pathology such as a haematoma or Budd-Chiari syndrome Neonatal screening for fatty-acid oxidation disorders after delivery Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare but life-threatening microvesicular fatty infiltration of hepatocytes, typically presenting in the third trimester or early postpartum period It is associated in a proportion of cases with inherited fetal defects of mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation, especially long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, so testing of the newborn is warranted Early symptoms are non-specific, including nausea, vomiting, anorexia, malaise, abdominal pain, and thirst or polyuria, progressing to jaundice and features of acute liver failure Characteristic laboratory findings include hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy with prolonged clotting times and low fibrinogen, raised transaminases and bilirubin, hyperuricaemia, renal impairment, and often a raised white cell count The Swansea criteria provide a helpful clinical framework for diagnosis when a constellation of features is present and other causes are excluded Hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy are hallmarks that help distinguish it from HELLP, although the two can overlap and coexist Management is prompt delivery once the mother is stabilised, with intensive supportive care correcting hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy, and electrolyte disturbance and managing hepatic and renal failure, occasionally requiring referral to a liver unit It demands a high index of suspicion, as delay markedly worsens maternal and fetal outcome Hypoglycaemia with worsening coagulopathy Hepatic encephalopathy or a rising ammonia Acute kidney injury or oliguria Signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation or major haemorrhage Rapid clinical deterioration or fetal compromise Dismissing late-pregnancy nausea and vomiting as benign and missing early disease Failing to check and repeatedly monitor the blood glucose Confusing it with HELLP and overlooking the coagulopathy and hypoglycaemia that guide management Delaying delivery while awaiting confirmatory tests Not arranging neonatal metabolic screening for fatty-acid oxidation disorders Acute fatty liver of pregnancy reflects impaired mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation within hepatocytes, leading to accumulation of microvesicular fat. In many cases the fetus carries a defect of the fatty-acid oxidation pathway, most notably long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency; the metabolic burden of unmetabolised fatty-acid intermediates from the feto-placental unit is thought to overwhelm the maternal liver, whose oxidative capacity is already stressed in late pregnancy. The resulting hepatocellular dysfunction impairs gluconeogenesis, causing hypoglycaemia; synthesis of clotting factors and fibrinogen, causing coagulopathy; and ureagenesis and clearance, causing hyperammonaemia and encephalopathy. Accumulation of toxic metabolites and endothelial dysfunction contribute to renal impairment and, in severe cases, multiorgan failure. Removal of the fetal and placental metabolic load by delivery allows the maternal liver to recover. With early recognition, prompt delivery, and intensive supportive care, maternal survival and hepatic recovery are usual, though maternal and perinatal mortality remain significant when diagnosis is delayed; the liver typically recovers without long-term sequelae, and recurrence is uncommon but recognised, particularly with fatty-acid oxidation defects.

Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis — AGEP, pustular drug eruption Generalised pustular psoriasis Pustular drug eruptions of other type Subcorneal pustular dermatosis DRESS or other severe cutaneous adverse reaction Bacterial folliculitis or impetigo Detailed drug history focusing on recently started agents Full blood count showing neutrophilia Skin biopsy to distinguish from pustular psoriasis Assessment for systemic involvement (usually mild) Documentation of the culprit drug and avoidance An acute severe cutaneous adverse reaction with rapid onset of numerous small sterile non-follicular pustules on an oedematous erythematous base It typically begins in the flexures and face and spreads within hours to days, with fever and neutrophilia Most cases are drug-induced, classically by antibiotics such as beta-lactams and macrolides, with a short latency It resolves rapidly with characteristic superficial desquamation once the culprit drug is stopped The main differential is generalised pustular psoriasis, and histology helps distinguish them Management is withdrawal of the culprit drug and supportive skin care; it has a good prognosis Extensive skin involvement or mucosal involvement Features suggesting overlap with other severe cutaneous adverse reactions Systemic organ involvement Secondary infection of denuded skin Mistaking it for generalised pustular psoriasis and mismanaging Failing to identify and stop the culprit drug Treating the sterile pustules as infection Overlooking a personal history of the same reaction on re-exposure Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis is a T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity reaction, usually to a drug. Drug-specific T cells and neutrophil-recruiting cytokines drive an intense neutrophilic inflammation of the upper dermis and epidermis, producing sterile subcorneal and intraepidermal pustules. The rapid onset after exposure and swift resolution on withdrawal reflect this immune mechanism, and the sterile pustules distinguish it from infective pustular eruptions. The prognosis is generally excellent, with resolution within one to two weeks of stopping the culprit drug, though it is a severe cutaneous adverse reaction requiring recognition and drug avoidance.

Onset is usually rapid, often within a couple of days of starting the responsible drug, most commonly certain antibiotics such as aminopenicillins and macrolides The pustules are sterile, and swab cultures are negative, helping distinguish it from bacterial pustulosis Resolution occurs quickly once the drug is withdrawn, characteristically followed by superficial desquamation of the affected pustular psoriasis, which tends to run a more prolonged and recurrent course and may have a personal or family history of psoriasis Management is prompt withdrawal of the culprit drug with supportive care, topical corticosteroids and monitoring for the uncommon systemic or organ involvement High fever with extensive erythema and rapidly spreading pustulation Evidence of internal organ involvement such as hepatic or renal dysfunction Features overlapping with other severe cutaneous adverse reactions Haemodynamic instability or signs of secondary infection Failure to resolve after drug withdrawal, suggesting pustular psoriasis instead Mistaking the sterile pustules for a bacterial infection and delaying drug withdrawal while giving unnecessary antibiotics Confusing it with generalised pustular psoriasis and misjudging the course and treatment Failing to identify and stop the culprit drug promptly Overlooking uncommon systemic organ involvement Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis is a T-cell-mediated (type IV) drug hypersensitivity reaction with a strong neutrophilic component. Drug-specific T lymphocytes are activated and, through release of neutrophil-recruiting cytokines and chemokines including interleukin-8 (CXCL8), interleukin-17 and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor, drive massive accumulation of neutrophils into the epidermis to form sterile spongiform pustules. Interleukin-36 signalling is also implicated, providing a mechanistic overlap with pustular psoriasis. The rapid onset after drug exposure and swift resolution after withdrawal reflect the reactivation of primed drug-specific T cells and the transient nature of the ensuing sterile inflammatory response. The prognosis is generally favourable, with rapid clearance and desquamation within one to two weeks of stopping the culprit drug, although occasional cases with widespread disease, systemic involvement or in frail patients carry a higher risk of complications.

Acute Glomerulonephritis (Child) — acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, APSGN, acute nephritic syndrome, paediatric acute glomerulonephritis IgA nephropathy Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Lupus nephritis Henoch-Schonlein (IgA) vasculitis nephritis Haemolytic uraemic syndrome Alport syndrome or thin basement membrane disease Urinalysis and microscopy for red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells Serum complement (C3 and C4) Evidence of streptococcal infection (ASO, anti-DNase B, throat or skin swab) Renal function and electrolytes Urine protein quantification Renal biopsy if the course is atypical, complement stays low, or renal function deteriorates The classic nephritic picture is gross haematuria (often described as tea- or cola-coloured urine), oedema, and hypertension. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is the most common cause in children and typically follows a group A streptococcal throat infection by about 1-2 weeks or a skin infection by 3-6 weeks. Although labelled non-infective as a glomerular process, it is an immune-mediated sequela of a preceding streptococcal infection rather than active kidney infection. Look for evidence of recent streptococcal infection with elevated antibody titres (such as ASO) and a low serum C3 that typically normalises within 6-8 weeks. Fluid overload from sodium and water retention can precipitate hypertension, pulmonary oedema, and hypertensive encephalopathy. Urinalysis characteristically shows red blood cells, red cell casts, and mild to moderate proteinuria. Management is largely supportive with salt and fluid restriction and control of hypertension; the condition is generally self-limiting in children. Persistently low complement beyond 8 weeks should prompt consideration of an alternative diagnosis such as membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis or lupus nephritis. Severe hypertension or hypertensive encephalopathy (headache, seizures, altered consciousness) Pulmonary oedema or respiratory distress from volume overload Rapidly rising creatinine suggesting rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis Oligoanuria or features of acute kidney injury requiring dialysis Hyperkalaemia with associated arrhythmia risk Assuming all paediatric nephritis is post-streptococcal and missing lupus or membranoproliferative disease when complement stays persistently low Overlooking hypertension, which may be asymptomatic yet dangerous, by not measuring blood pressure Fluid overloading a child with impaired filtration Attributing dark urine to dehydration rather than examining the urine sediment Immune complexes involving streptococcal antigens deposit in or form within the glomerular basement membrane, activating the complement cascade (predominantly the alternative pathway). This drives glomerular inflammation with endothelial and mesangial proliferation and neutrophil influx, reducing the glomerular filtration surface. The result is a fall in filtration rate, sodium and water retention, haematuria, and proteinuria producing the nephritic syndrome. The great majority of children with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis recover completely, with resolution of gross haematuria within weeks and normalisation of complement within about two months; microscopic haematuria may persist for a year or more. A small minority develop chronic kidney impairment.

Clostridioides difficile Intensifying immunosuppression while missing a concurrent opportunistic infection Under-recognising upper-gut disease presenting only as anorexia and nausea Confusing inflammatory cytokines and exposes host antigens, priming an immune response. Donor T lymphocytes contained within the graft recognise recipient major and minor histocompatibility antigens presented on host cells, become activated, and proliferate. This drives a cytokine-amplified inflammatory cascade in which activated donor effector cells attack epithelial targets in the skin, gut, and liver, producing the characteristic rash, diarrhoea, and cholestasis. The intensity of the response reflects the degree of donor-recipient mismatch and the adequacy of immunosuppressive prophylaxis. Lower-grade disease usually responds to corticosteroids with good outcomes, whereas high-grade or steroid-refractory disease carries substantial mortality driven both by the disease itself and by infection during intensified immunosuppression; acute graft-versus-host disease remains a leading cause of transplant-related morbidity and death.

Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction — AHTR, Immediate haemolytic transfusion reaction Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction Bacterial contamination with septic transfusion reaction Transfusion-related acute lung injury Anaphylactic transfusion reaction Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction presenting early Non-immune haemolysis from mechanical or thermal red-cell damage Immediate clerical recheck of identity and unit against the patient Direct antiglobulin test on a post-transfusion sample Repeat ABO and RhD grouping on pre- and post-transfusion samples and the unit Plasma free haemoglobin, haptoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase and bilirubin Coagulation screen, fibrinogen and D-dimer to detect disseminated intravascular coagulation Renal function, potassium and urine output monitoring with urinalysis for haemoglobin Most severe cases result from ABO incompatibility caused by clerical or sampling error, making patient identification at the bedside the single most important preventive measure. Preformed recipient IgM anti-A or anti-B antibodies bind transfused red cells and drive rapid, complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis. Classical features include fever, chills, loin or back pain, pain at the infusion site, dyspnoea, hypotension and a feeling of impending doom, often after only a small volume. Haemoglobinaemia and haemoglobinuria are hallmark findings; free haemoglobin turns plasma and urine pink to red. The reaction can precipitate disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury and shock, and may be fatal. Immediate management is to stop the transfusion, maintain intravenous access, support blood pressure and preserve renal perfusion with fluids and diuresis. In an anaesthetised or unconscious patient, unexplained hypotension, haemoglobinuria and diffuse bleeding may be the only clues. All reaction samples and the implicated unit must be returned to the laboratory for repeat grouping, direct antiglobulin test and crossmatch. Hypotension and shock developing after only a small transfused volume Loin or back pain with pink or red plasma and urine New diffuse bleeding or oozing indicating disseminated intravascular coagulation Falling urine output and rising creatinine signalling acute kidney injury Unexplained cardiovascular instability during anaesthesia with haemoglobinuria Attributing early fever to a benign febrile reaction and continuing the transfusion. Missing the diagnosis in the anaesthetised patient where pain and anxiety cannot be reported. Failing to check the clerical trail, which is the commonest root cause of ABO mismatch. Under-resuscitating and allowing hypotension to progress to renal injury. Not sending the unit and fresh samples back for laboratory confirmation. Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction is caused by destruction of transfused (or, less often, recipient) red cells by preformed antibodies, most dangerously the naturally occurring IgM anti-A and anti-B of the ABO system. Antibody binding fixes complement to completion, generating the membrane attack complex and causing intravascular lysis with liberation of free haemoglobin. The antigen-antibody complexes and released stroma activate the coagulation cascade and the kinin and complement systems, producing hypotension, bronchospasm and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Free haemoglobin and renal vasoconstriction, together with hypotension and microthrombi, impair renal blood flow and can cause acute tubular necrosis. Cytokine release amplifies the systemic inflammatory response and shock. Severity is dose-related; small volumes may cause mild reactions while larger ABO-incompatible transfusions carry substantial mortality from shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation and renal failure. Prompt recognition, cessation and aggressive supportive care improve outcome, though acute kidney injury may still ensue.

hypotension, back or flank pain, and dark urine during transfusion, indicating an acute haemolytic emergency Unexplained intraoperative hypotension, oozing, and haemoglobinuria under anaesthesia
