central to management The fellow eye is at risk, so timely diagnosis and treatment aim to protect both eyes Rapidly enlarging retinitis threatening the macula or optic nerve New retinal breaks or detachment Involvement or symptoms in the fellow eye Optic neuropathy with acute severe visual loss Mistaking early ARN for idiopathic anterior uveitis and delaying antiviral therapy Attributing the picture to CMV retinitis, which is indolent with little vitritis Underestimating the fellow-eye risk Failing to anticipate and monitor for retinal detachment Reactivation or primary infection with varicella-zoster or herpes simplex virus produces a necrotising retinitis with an occlusive vasculitis of the retinal arterioles. Viral replication in the outer and inner retina causes rapidly enlarging areas of full-thickness necrosis, while the accompanying vasculitis compounds ischaemic damage. As the inflammation resolves the necrotic retina becomes atrophic and develops multiple breaks at the junction of necrotic and healthy retina, predisposing to rhegmatogenous detachment; vitreous inflammation and traction add to the detachment risk. Visual outcome is guarded, dominated by the high rate of retinal detachment and by optic nerve or macular involvement; early antiviral treatment reduces fellow-eye disease and severe complications.

Acute Rheumatic Fever — ARF Always request: electrocardiogram (ECG), echocardiogram, complete blood count (CBC), C-reactive protein (CRP), and streptococcal serology (antistreptolysin O [ASO] and anti-DNase B [ADB]) (Harrison 22e p.2857). Echocardiography should be performed on all possible cases to aid diagnosis (including detection of subclinical carditis/valvulitis) and to establish baseline carditis severity; auscultation is poorly sensitive and specific for RHD in asymptomatic patients (Harrison 22e p.2855, p.2857). Because most cases lack a positive throat swab culture or rapid antigen test, serologic evidence of preceding group A strep infection is usually needed (ASO and anti-DNase B titers), ideally with locally derived age-specific reference ranges (Harrison 22e p.2856). In relevant situations: throat swab, skin sore swab, blood cultures, synovial fluid aspirate (cell count, microscopy, culture, gonococcal PCR), pregnancy test, and creatinine/UEC (since NSAIDs can affect renal function) (Harrison 22e p.2857). Tests to exclude alternative diagnoses (per clinical presentation/local endemic infections): autoantibodies, double-stranded DNA, anti-CCP antibodies; urine molecular testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis; serology for viral hepatitis, Yersinia, CMV, parvovirus B19, respiratory viruses, Ross River virus, Barmah Forest virus (Harrison 22e p.2857). Inflammatory markers should be monitored every 1-2 weeks until normalized (usually within 4-6 weeks), and a repeat echocardiogram performed after 1 month to assess for progression of carditis (Harrison 22e p.2858). ARF is a multisystem autoimmune sequela of group A streptococcal infection; almost all manifestations resolve completely, the major exception being cardiac valvular damage (rheumatic heart disease, RHD), which may persist after other features disappear (Harrison 22e p.2854). Mainly a disease of children aged 5-14 years; initial episodes are rare in persons aged >30 years, whereas recurrent episodes remain relatively common in adolescents and young adults. RHD prevalence peaks between 25 and 40 years (Harrison 22e p.2854). There is no clear gender association for ARF, but RHD more commonly affects females, sometimes up to twice as often as males (Harrison 22e p.2854). Latent period of ~3 weeks (range 1-5 weeks) between the precipitating group A streptococcal infection and onset of ARF; the exceptions are chorea and indolent (low-grade) carditis, which may follow prolonged latent periods of up to 6 months (Harrison 22e p.2855). Most common clinical features are polyarthritis (60-75% of cases) and carditis (50-75%); chorea prevalence varies from <2% to 30% between populations; erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules are now rare, found in <5% of cases (Harrison 22e p.2855). Up to 75% of patients with ARF progress to RHD; the mitral valve is almost always affected, sometimes with the aortic valve. Isolated aortic valve involvement is rare. The characteristic manifestation of carditis in previously unaffected individuals is mitral regurgitation, sometimes with aortic regurgitation (Harrison 22e p.2855). ARF arthritis is typically a migratory polyarthritis of large joints (knees, ankles, hips, elbows), asymmetric, severe and disabling, and highly responsive to salicylates/NSAIDs (Harrison 22e p.2855-2856). Sydenham's chorea often occurs in the absence of other manifestations, follows a prolonged latent period, and is found mainly in females; more than 50% of patients presenting with chorea will have carditis, so echocardiography should be part of the workup (Harrison 22e p.2856). Erythema marginatum is an evanescent serpiginous rash (pink macules clearing centrally) usually on the trunk, sometimes the limbs, but almost never on the face. Subcutaneous nodules are painless, mobile, occur over bony prominences, appear 2-3 weeks after onset, and are commonly associated with carditis (Harrison 22e p.2856). Revised Jones criteria (2015 AHA): for all populations with evidence of preceding group A strep infection, initial ARF requires 2 major OR 1 major plus 2 minor manifestations; recurrent ARF requires 2 major OR 1 major plus 2 minor OR 3 minor manifestations. Separate, more sensitive criteria apply to moderate/high-risk populations versus low-risk populations (Harrison 22e p.2856-2857). Major manifestations: carditis (clinical and/or subclinical), arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules; in moderate/high-risk populations arthritis includes monoarthritis and polyarthralgia (Harrison 22e p.2857). Secondary prevention with long-term penicillin prophylaxis is the mainstay of controlling ARF and RHD, best delivered through a register-based RHD control program; patients should be entered on an ARF registry, educated, and linked to follow-up before discharge (Harrison 22e p.2857-2858). Severe carditis causing congestive heart failure; treatment of heart failure may be lifesaving (Harrison 22e p.2857). Myocardial inflammation affecting conduction, causing P-R interval prolongation (first-degree AV block, rarely higher-level block) (Harrison 22e p.2855). More than 50% of patients presenting with chorea have underlying carditis, mandating echocardiographic workup (Harrison 22e p.2856). Advanced RHD complications: heart failure, arrhythmia, stroke, and infective endocarditis (Harrison 22e p.2856). The preceding group A streptococcal infection is commonly subclinical, so the absence of a reported sore throat or a negative throat swab/rapid antigen test does not exclude ARF; serologic confirmation is usually required (Harrison 22e p.2855-2856). Diagnosis of ARF is often missed, particularly in resource-poor settings, so children, adolescents, and young adults may have undiagnosed RHD; echocardiographic screening can detect these cases (Harrison 22e p.2855). Early commencement of anti-inflammatory medication before the typical migratory pattern is established may produce an atypical presenting picture such as aseptic monoarthritis (Harrison 22e p.2856). Recurrence of fever, joint manifestations, and elevated acute-phase reactants up to 3 weeks after stopping anti-inflammatory medication does NOT indicate a true ARF recurrence and is managed by briefly recommencing anti-inflammatory agents (Harrison 22e p.2857). Glucocorticoid use in ARF carditis remains controversial; two meta-analyses failed to demonstrate benefit over placebo or salicylates, though included studies were >40 years old and used outdated medications (Harrison 22e p.2857-2858). Salicylates/NSAIDs are of no proven value in the treatment of carditis or chorea (they treat arthritis, arthralgia, and fever) (Harrison 22e p.2857). Medications to control choreiform movements do NOT alter the duration or outcome of chorea; IVIg shows no benefit on short- or long-term carditis outcome and is not recommended except in severe chorea refractory to other treatments (Harrison 22e p.2858). ARF results from an autoimmune reaction to group A streptococcal infection, classically of the upper respiratory tract, with increasing evidence for a role of streptococcal skin infection. The most widely accepted theory is molecular mimicry: an immune response to streptococcal antigens (mainly the M protein) cross-reacts with human tissues. Antigen-presenting cells of the innate immune system present streptococcal antigens to T cells, activating humoral and cellular immunity; cross-reactive antibodies bind heart-valve endothelial cells, activating VCAM-1 with recruitment of activated lymphocytes and complement-mediated lysis, releasing peptides (laminin, keratin, tropomyosin) that activate cross-reactive T cells invading the heart, amplifying damage and causing epitope spreading. An alternative hypothesis proposes initial damage from streptococcal invasion of epithelial surfaces with M-protein binding to type IV collagen, rendering it immunogenic but not through molecular mimicry. Susceptibility is inherited (~3-6% of a population susceptible; 44% concordance in monozygotic vs 12% in dizygotic twins; heritability ~60%), with associations to HLA class II alleles, TNF and mannose-binding-lectin polymorphisms, the IGH locus (IGHV4-61*02), and complement factor H (Harrison 22e p.2854-2855). Untreated, ARF lasts on average 12 weeks; with treatment, patients are usually discharged within 1-2 weeks. Almost all non-cardiac manifestations resolve completely. Inflammatory markers usually normalize within 4-6 weeks. Up to 75% of patients with ARF progress to RHD, the long-term consequence being valvular damage; people with RHD are often asymptomatic for many years before progression to cardiac failure. There is no treatment proven to alter the likelihood or severity of RHD; apart from heart-failure management, treatment of ARF is symptomatic. RHD is the most common cause of acquired heart disease in children in low- and middle-income countries and a major cause of adult mortality and morbidity, with >40 million people affected worldwide and >300,000 deaths annually (Harrison 22e p.2854, p.2857-2858). RHD detected by echocardiography is staged (2023 World Heart Federation guidelines) into: Stage A (minimal echocardiographic criteria for RHD, individuals aged <=20 years, mild MR or AR without morphologic features); Stage B (mild RHD, mild valvular regurgitation plus morphologic feature(s)); Stage C (advanced RHD at risk of clinical complications - moderate/severe MR or AR, any MS or AS, pulmonary hypertension, decreased LV systolic function); Stage D (advanced RHD with established clinical complications such as cardiac surgery, heart failure, arrhythmia, stroke, infective endocarditis). The 2015 revised Jones criteria additionally separate low-risk populations (ARF incidence <=2 per 100,000 school-age children, or all-age RHD prevalence <=1 per 1000) from moderate/high-risk populations, applying more sensitive criteria to the latter (Harrison 22e p.2856-2857).

Acute stress disorder — ASD, acute stress reaction Post-traumatic stress disorder once symptoms exceed one month Adjustment disorder in response to a stressor Panic disorder or other anxiety disorders Major depressive episode following trauma Traumatic brain injury or medical sequelae of the event Substance intoxication or withdrawal Brief psychotic disorder with marked stressor Clinical interview characterising the traumatic exposure and symptom onset Structured suicide risk assessment Assessment of dissociative symptoms Medical evaluation for injuries or head trauma related to the event Screening for comorbid depression and substance use The disorder develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation, with symptoms arising and lasting from three days up to one month after the trauma Symptoms span intrusion, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, and arousal, including intrusive memories, distressing dreams, flashbacks, and a sense of unreality or detachment If characteristic symptoms persist beyond one month, the diagnosis is reconsidered as post-traumatic stress disorder rather than acute stress disorder Dissociative features such as depersonalisation, derealisation, or amnesia for part of the event can be prominent in the acute aftermath Many people exposed to trauma recover without progressing to a chronic disorder, so the diagnosis helps identify those at higher risk who may benefit from early support Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy is the recommended intervention, whereas single-session psychological debriefing is not beneficial and may be harmful Medication has a limited role, mainly for specific symptoms such as severe sleep disturbance, and benzodiazepines are generally avoided Assess suicide risk and provide practical support, safety, and psychoeducation as part of early management Suicidal or self-harm ideation following the trauma Ongoing exposure to danger, such as continuing abuse or violence Severe dissociation impairing safety or the ability to seek help Concurrent physical injury or head trauma requiring medical attention Providing single-session psychological debriefing, which is ineffective and potentially harmful Prescribing benzodiazepines, which may impair recovery Assuming all acutely distressed trauma survivors will develop a chronic disorder Overlooking suicide risk or ongoing danger to the patient Missing concurrent physical or head injury from the traumatic event Acute stress disorder reflects the immediate dysregulation of fear and stress-response systems following trauma, with heightened amygdala-driven threat processing, altered prefrontal regulation, and disturbed hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and noradrenergic activity. Impaired encoding and contextualisation of the traumatic memory, together with dissociative responses, are thought to underlie the intrusive and dissociative symptoms, modulated by prior vulnerability and severity of exposure. Many individuals with acute stress disorder recover within weeks, but a significant proportion progress to post-traumatic stress disorder, and the acute diagnosis identifies people who may benefit from early, evidence-based support. Prognosis is better with early trauma-focused intervention, safety, and social support, and worse with severe or ongoing trauma, prominent dissociation, and prior psychiatric illness.

Acute tonsillitis — acute tonsillopharyngitis, acute sore throat, tonsillar infection Viral pharyngitis Infectious mononucleosis Peritonsillar abscess Diphtheria Candidal or other fungal pharyngitis Agranulocytosis or leukaemic infiltration presenting with sore throat Throat examination to assess tonsillar size, exudate and membrane Throat swab or rapid antigen test for group A streptococcus where indicated Full blood count and monospot or heterophile antibody test when mononucleosis is suspected Assessment for splenomegaly and generalised lymphadenopathy Blood glucose and further workup if recurrent or atypical infection suggests immunosuppression Presents with sore throat, painful swallowing, fever, malaise and tender enlarged jugulodigastric lymph nodes The follicular (spotted) form shows yellowish exudate at the tonsillar crypt openings, while the membranous form has a coalescent whitish membrane Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus is the most important bacterial cause because of its non-suppurative sequelae Viral causes are common; features such as prominent cough, coryza and conjunctivitis point away from streptococcal infection Consider infectious mononucleosis when there is marked tonsillar enlargement, membrane formation, generalised lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly Management principles include adequate hydration, analgesia and antibiotics when streptococcal infection is likely, avoiding aminopenicillins if glandular fever is suspected because of the rash Non-suppurative complications of streptococcal infection include rheumatic fever and acute glomerulonephritis, which justify appropriate antibiotic treatment Recurrent tonsillitis meeting frequency criteria, or complications such as abscess, may warrant tonsillectomy Trismus, drooling, muffled voice or unilateral swelling suggesting peritonsillar or deep neck abscess Stridor or respiratory difficulty from airway obstruction A grey adherent membrane bleeding on removal, raising concern for diphtheria Persistent unilateral tonsillar enlargement or ulceration suggesting malignancy Prescribing ampicillin-type antibiotics in undiagnosed glandular fever and precipitating a rash Missing a developing peritonsillar abscess in a patient with worsening unilateral symptoms Treating all sore throats as bacterial when many are viral Overlooking a haematological cause in unusually severe or persistent cases Acute tonsillitis is acute inflammation of the palatine tonsils, usually from viral or bacterial infection of the tonsillar crypts and parenchyma. Pathogens invade the crypt epithelium, provoking an inflammatory response with hyperaemia, oedema and crypt exudate. Streptococcal infection can trigger immune-mediated sequelae elsewhere in the body. Local spread of infection beyond the tonsillar capsule can produce peritonsillar or deep neck space abscesses, and marked tonsillar and adenoid enlargement may compromise the airway. Most episodes are self-limiting or resolve promptly with treatment; complications such as abscess formation and, in streptococcal disease, rheumatic and renal sequelae are largely preventable with appropriate management.

Acute transplant rejection — acute allograft rejection, acute cellular rejection, antibody-mediated rejection, acute rejection Calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity Infection of the allograft such as BK nephropathy or cytomegalovirus disease Recurrence of the primary disease within the graft Surgical or vascular complications such as thrombosis, stenosis, or obstruction Ischaemia-reperfusion injury or delayed graft function early after transplantation Drug-induced organ dysfunction Dehydration or outflow obstruction causing functional decline Allograft biopsy with histological grading, which is the diagnostic standard Donor-specific antibody testing through HLA antibody screening C4d immunostaining on biopsy for antibody-mediated rejection Organ-specific function tests with trend monitoring Immunosuppressant drug levels and assessment of adherence Doppler ultrasound or other imaging to exclude vascular or mechanical causes Screening for graft infection such as BK virus or cytomegalovirus where relevant Immune-mediated injury to a transplanted organ occurring over days to months, classically within the first few months but possible at any time, especially with inadequate immunosuppression or non-adherence Two principal mechanisms operate: T-cell-mediated cellular rejection driven by recipient T lymphocytes, and antibody-mediated rejection driven by donor-specific antibodies against HLA It is often clinically silent early and is detected as a rise in organ-specific markers, such as creatinine in the kidney or transaminases in the liver, or on protocol biopsy Diagnosis rests on allograft biopsy with histological grading, supported by detection of donor-specific antibodies and complement split product C4d staining in antibody-mediated disease Cell-mediated rejection shows mononuclear inflammatory infiltrates, whereas antibody-mediated rejection shows microvascular injury with C4d deposition Risk factors include HLA mismatch, pre-existing sensitisation, previous transplants, and reduced or missed immunosuppression First-line treatment of cellular rejection is high-dose corticosteroids, with lymphocyte-depleting or antibody therapy reserved for severe or steroid-resistant episodes Antibody-mediated rejection is treated by removing or neutralising antibody, for example with plasma exchange and adjunctive agents, alongside optimised immunosuppression Rapid loss of graft function Severe antibody-mediated rejection with widespread microvascular injury Steroid-resistant rejection Rejection from non-adherence or sensitisation with high donor-specific antibody levels Concurrent infection complicating intensified immunosuppression Attributing graft dysfunction to rejection without biopsy and missing infection or drug toxicity Overlooking antibody-mediated rejection by not testing for donor-specific antibodies or C4d Missing non-adherence as a cause, particularly in adolescents Over-immunosuppressing and precipitating infection or malignancy Failing to monitor for chronic rejection after an acute episode Recipient immune cells recognise donor HLA through direct and indirect pathways of allorecognition. In cellular rejection, activated T lymphocytes infiltrate the graft and injure tubular, parenchymal, or endothelial targets. In antibody-mediated rejection, B cells and plasma cells produce donor-specific antibodies that bind graft microvascular endothelium, activate complement with deposition of the split product C4d, and cause microvascular inflammation and injury. Both processes compromise graft perfusion and function and, if unchecked, predispose to chronic rejection. Many cellular rejection episodes reverse with prompt treatment, whereas antibody-mediated and steroid-resistant rejection carry a higher risk of graft loss and predispose to chronic rejection; early detection and treatment improve graft survival.

Acute urinary retention — AUR, acute retention of urine, acute bladder outlet obstruction Benign prostatic hyperplasia with decompensation Prostate cancer causing outlet obstruction Urethral stricture Blood clot retention (clot from haematuria) Neurogenic bladder / cauda equina syndrome Constipation or pelvic mass causing extrinsic compression Drug-induced retention (anticholinergics, opioids, sympathomimetics) Bladder ultrasound to confirm distension and measure retained volume Urinalysis and culture to identify infection Serum creatinine and electrolytes to detect obstructive renal impairment Renal tract ultrasound to assess for hydronephrosis in suspected chronic retention PSA (interpreted with caution, as retention and catheterisation raise levels) Neurological assessment and spinal imaging when cauda equina or cord compression is suspected Presents as the sudden, painful inability to pass urine with a palpable, tender, distended bladder that is dull to percussion In men the commonest precipitant is benign prostatic obstruction, often triggered by infection, constipation, alcohol, immobility, or anticholinergic and sympathomimetic drugs Immediate management is urgent bladder decompression with a urethral catheter; suprapubic catheterisation is used when urethral access fails or is contraindicated Painless retention with a grossly distended bladder suggests chronic-on-acute (high-pressure or high-residual) retention rather than a purely acute event Record the drained volume; a large residual and any renal impairment point toward chronic high-pressure retention with risk of post-obstructive diuresis Post-obstructive diuresis after decompression can cause marked fluid and electrolyte losses, requiring monitoring of urine output, weight, and electrolytes A trial without catheter, often facilitated by an alpha-blocker, is appropriate once the precipitant is treated; failure indicates need for ongoing catheterisation or definitive surgery Always exclude and treat urinary infection, and consider spinal cord compression or cauda equina when neurological features accompany retention Acute urinary retention is itself a urological emergency requiring immediate bladder decompression High-pressure chronic retention with hydronephrosis and renal impairment Post-obstructive diuresis causing dehydration and electrolyte disturbance after decompression Retention with saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg symptoms, or bowel dysfunction suggesting cauda equina syndrome Associated fever or urosepsis in an obstructed system Delaying catheterisation and allowing prolonged painful overdistension Missing high-pressure chronic retention by not measuring residual volume or checking renal function Failing to anticipate and monitor for post-obstructive diuresis Overlooking neurological causes such as cauda equina compression Rapid complete decompression without awareness of possible haematuria ex vacuo Acute urinary retention is the abrupt failure to empty the bladder, arising from mechanical obstruction (most often prostatic enlargement, but also urethral stricture, clot, or stone), increased outlet tone, impaired detrusor contractility, or neurogenic causes. Bladder overdistension raises intravesical pressure and, in high-pressure chronic retention, is transmitted to the upper tracts causing hydronephrosis and renal impairment. Precipitating factors such as anticholinergic drugs, alpha-agonists, infection, pain, and prostatic congestion tip a compensated bladder into decompensation and acute failure to void. Prompt decompression relieves symptoms rapidly; many men can eventually void after a trial without catheter and treatment of precipitants, but recurrent retention often signals the need for definitive prostatic surgery, and delayed relief risks lasting renal damage.

Acute urticaria — acute hives, acute wheals Anaphylaxis (with systemic features) Urticarial vasculitis (weals lasting more than a day, leaving bruising) Angio-oedema without weals (including bradykinin-mediated) Erythema multiforme Mastocytosis Clinical diagnosis from the history and transient weals Assessment for anaphylaxis features requiring immediate treatment Targeted allergy evaluation only where a specific trigger is suspected Consideration of urticarial vasculitis if weals persist or bruise Limited testing, as most acute cases are self-limiting Sudden-onset itchy weals, angio-oedema, or both, lasting less than six weeks Individual weals are transient, each resolving within a day without leaving a mark Common triggers include viral infection, foods, drugs and insect stings, though many cases are idiopathic When accompanied by airway, breathing or circulatory compromise it may be part of anaphylaxis and needs adrenaline It is largely a clinical diagnosis, and extensive investigation is usually unnecessary Non-sedating antihistamines are first-line, with a short corticosteroid course for severe flares Airway compromise, wheeze or hypotension indicating anaphylaxis Angio-oedema of the tongue or throat Weals lasting more than a day or leaving bruising (urticarial vasculitis) Systemic symptoms suggesting another cause Missing evolving anaphylaxis in a patient with urticaria Over-investigating self-limiting acute urticaria Failing to recognise urticarial vasculitis Overlooking bradykinin-mediated angio-oedema, which does not respond to antihistamines Acute urticaria results from activation and degranulation of cutaneous mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine and other mediators that cause vasodilatation, increased vascular permeability (producing weals and angio-oedema) and pruritus. Degranulation may be immunological, classically IgE-mediated in allergy, or non-immunological through direct mast-cell activation by drugs, infections or other stimuli. The transient nature of individual weals reflects the short-lived local mediator response. Acute urticaria is usually self-limiting, resolving within days to a few weeks; a minority evolve into chronic urticaria.

and the trizonal pattern Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography to show ellipsoid zone disruption Automated visual field testing to map and monitor the scotoma and often an enlarged blind spot affects young to middle-aged adults, with a female predominance, and often in patients who are myopic Presents with acute onset of photopsia (shimmering or flickering lights) and one or more zones of visual field loss, frequently in the peripapillary region The fundus characteristically looks normal or near-normal early in the disease, so the retinopathy is described as occult Electroretinography is key to diagnosis, revealing outer retinal dysfunction in affected zones despite an unremarkable fundus appearance Fundus autofluorescence commonly shows a demarcating line or trizonal pattern separating normal from affected retina and is very useful for detecting and monitoring lesions Optical coherence tomography demonstrates disruption or loss of the outer retinal bands (ellipsoid zone) corresponding to the symptomatic field defect Over time affected zones may develop pigmentary changes and retinal pigment epithelial atrophy, and disease can be unilateral or bilateral Management is debated and there is no proven therapy; observation is common and immunosuppression is sometimes used in progressive cases Progressive enlargement of field loss threatening central vision Bilateral or rapidly advancing disease suggesting a more aggressive process Features raising concern for paraneoplastic retinopathy and underlying malignancy Development of secondary choroidal neovascularisation Dismissing a patient with photopsia and field loss as functional because the fundus looks normal Failing to obtain electroretinography and autofluorescence, which reveal the occult pathology Missing an underlying malignancy in what is actually paraneoplastic retinopathy Confusing AZOOR with retinitis pigmentosa given overlapping photoreceptor dysfunction Over-treating stable disease with immunosuppression of unproven benefit Acute zonal occult outer retinopathy is characterised by dysfunction and degeneration of the photoreceptors and outer retina in discrete zones, often beginning adjacent to the optic disc and spreading. The precise mechanism is uncertain, but an autoimmune or inflammatory process targeting photoreceptors, possibly triggered in genetically susceptible individuals, is favoured; a viral prodrome is sometimes reported. Loss of the ellipsoid zone and photoreceptor outer segments produces the field defects and photopsias, while the retinal pigment epithelium and inner retina are relatively preserved early, explaining the near-normal fundus and the value of functional and autofluorescence imaging. Chronic disease leads to zonal outer retinal atrophy. Many patients stabilise with persistent but non-progressive field defects and reasonable central acuity, though photopsias and scotomata may remain; a minority experience progressive or recurrent disease with expanding zones of atrophy and permanent visual field loss.

The condition is progressive and usually fatal in childhood after a period of neurological regression, though the age of decline varies. There is no curative treatment, and management focuses on seizure control, nutrition, and supportive multidisciplinary care.

adamantinoma — adamantinoma of long bones, tibial adamantinoma osteofibrous dysplasia and osteofibrous-dysplasia-like adamantinoma fibrous dysplasia Ewing sarcoma metastatic carcinoma to bone fibrosarcoma of bone non-ossifying fibroma chronic sclerosing osteomyelitis plain radiographs of the tibia demonstrating cortical lytic and sclerotic change MRI to delineate intramedullary and soft-tissue extent CT to assess cortical destruction and lesion architecture representative open biopsy with adequate sampling of epithelial foci cytokeratin and epithelial-marker immunohistochemistry staging CT of the thorax for pulmonary metastases regional imaging for nodal involvement A rare low-grade malignant bone tumour with a striking predilection for the mid-diaphysis of the tibia, typically in adolescents and young adults. It is biphasic, combining epithelial islands with an osteofibrous stroma, and the epithelial cells are reliably cytokeratin positive. It sits on a spectrum with osteofibrous dysplasia and osteofibrous-dysplasia-like adamantinoma, which can complicate diagnosis on small samples. Anterior tibial swelling, often with a long indolent history and sometimes anterior bowing of the leg, is the usual presentation. Radiographs classically show multiple eccentric, lytic, cortically based lesions with sclerotic margins, giving a soap-bubble appearance along the diaphysis. The tumour is essentially resistant to both radiotherapy and chemotherapy, so wide en bloc resection with clear margins is the definitive treatment. Intralesional curettage is inadequate and associated with high local recurrence. Late local recurrence and metastasis, chiefly to the lungs and regional lymph nodes, can occur many years after treatment, mandating prolonged follow-up. rapid increase in size or pain in a long-standing tibial lesion pathological fracture through the diaphysis soft-tissue mass extending beyond the cortex new pulmonary or nodal lesions on staging misclassifying the tumour as benign osteofibrous or fibrous dysplasia on a small biopsy treating with intralesional curettage, which leads to recurrence expecting a response to radiotherapy or chemotherapy curtailing follow-up too early given the risk of late metastasis underestimating intramedullary spread and resecting with inadequate margins Adamantinoma is thought to arise from epithelial elements within bone, and the tumour shows a biphasic pattern in which nests, cords or gland-like islands of epithelial cells are set within a fibrous or osteofibrous stroma. The epithelial component expresses cytokeratins and is regarded as the neoplastic driver, while the osteofibrous background resembles osteofibrous dysplasia. The close morphological and clinical overlap between osteofibrous dysplasia, osteofibrous-dysplasia-like adamantinoma and classic adamantinoma supports a shared histogenetic continuum, with progressive expansion of the epithelial component marking the more overtly malignant end. The tibial diaphyseal cortex is the characteristic site, and slow local growth with the potential for delayed metastatic spread reflects its low-grade biology. With adequate wide resection the outlook is generally good, but the tumour is prone to late local recurrence and delayed metastasis, so long-term surveillance is essential and outcome worsens with inadequate initial surgery.

Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency — APRT deficiency, 2,8-dihydroxyadenine urolithiasis, 2,8-DHA stone disease, DHA crystal nephropathy Uric acid urolithiasis (also radiolucent but pH-responsive) Hereditary xanthinuria and other radiolucent stone disorders Cystinuria and calcium-based stone disease Other crystalline nephropathies (e.g. oxalate, drug crystals) Idiopathic chronic kidney disease of unknown cause Recurrent idiopathic urolithiasis Stone analysis and urine microscopy for characteristic 2,8-DHA crystals Infrared spectroscopy or capillary electrophoresis to confirm 2,8-DHA composition Erythrocyte APRT enzyme activity measurement Molecular genetic testing of the APRT gene Renal function and urinalysis to assess crystal nephropathy Renal tract imaging for radiolucent calculi Autosomal recessive deficiency of adenine phosphoribosyltransferase, an enzyme of the purine salvage pathway Loss of salvage diverts adenine to oxidation by xanthine oxidase, producing the highly insoluble 2,8-dihydroxyadenine (2,8-DHA) 2,8-DHA precipitates as radiolucent urinary stones and as intratubular crystals, causing renal colic, haematuria, recurrent stones and crystal nephropathy It is a major under-recognised cause of chronic kidney disease and can present with graft dysfunction after kidney transplantation if undiagnosed 2,8-DHA stones are radiolucent and can be mistaken for uric acid stones, but unlike uric acid they do not dissolve with urinary alkalinisation Diagnosis rests on identifying 2,8-DHA in stone or crystal analysis (round brown crystals on urine microscopy), enzyme assay or APRT gene testing Management is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor to block 2,8-DHA formation, together with high fluid intake and dietary purine moderation; urinary alkalinisation does not help Progressive or unexplained chronic kidney disease, especially with crystals on biopsy Acute kidney injury from crystal obstruction Early graft dysfunction after renal transplantation from recurrent crystal deposition Recurrent stone disease from infancy or childhood Misclassifying 2,8-DHA stones as uric acid stones and prescribing ineffective alkalinisation Failing to diagnose the condition before kidney transplantation, risking rapid graft injury Overlooking crystalline nephropathy as a cause of unexplained chronic kidney disease Not maintaining lifelong therapy, as crystal formation resumes if treatment stops Missing the diagnosis in adults because it can present at any age Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase normally salvages free adenine by combining it with phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate to form adenosine monophosphate. When the enzyme is deficient, adenine cannot be recycled and is instead oxidised by xanthine oxidase, first to 8-hydroxyadenine and then to 2,8-dihydroxyadenine. This end product is extremely insoluble across the physiological urinary pH range, so it crystallises within the renal tubules and urinary tract, producing stones and progressive crystalline tubulointerstitial damage. Because the enzyme block lies upstream, inhibiting xanthine oxidase effectively prevents 2,8-DHA generation. With early diagnosis and continuous xanthine oxidase inhibitor therapy the prognosis is excellent and renal function can be preserved; delayed diagnosis may lead to irreversible chronic kidney disease or loss of a transplanted kidney.

middle ear effusion and hearing loss Neglecting the possibility of juvenile angiofibroma in an adolescent boy with obstruction and bleeding The adenoid (nasopharyngeal tonsil) is part of Waldeyer's ring and undergoes physiological enlargement with repeated exposure to inhaled and ingested antigens in childhood. Recurrent infection and allergy drive lymphoid hyperplasia so the pad enlarges enough to obstruct the posterior nasal choanae and the nasopharyngeal openings of the Eustachian tubes. Choanal obstruction forces mouth breathing and impairs sinus drainage, while Eustachian tube dysfunction interferes with middle ear ventilation, favouring effusion and recurrent otitis media. Chronic mouth breathing during the years of facial growth alters craniofacial and dental development, and narrowing of the upper airway during sleep produces snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea. The adenoid tissue can also act as a reservoir of infection and biofilm. Adenoid tissue tends to regress naturally with age, so many children improve over time, and adenoidectomy gives prompt and lasting relief of obstruction, sleep-disordered breathing and associated ear disease in those who need surgery.

Adenomyomatosis of the gallbladder — gallbladder adenomyomatosis, adenomyomatous hyperplasia, hyperplastic cholecystosis Gallbladder adenocarcinoma Chronic cholecystitis with wall thickening Gallbladder polyp Porcelain gallbladder Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis Wall thickening from adjacent hepatic or systemic disease High-resolution ultrasound to detect intramural cystic spaces and comet-tail artefacts MRI with heavily T2-weighted sequences to show the pearl-necklace sign of Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses Contrast-enhanced imaging when focal thickening cannot be distinguished from carcinoma Endoscopic ultrasound for detailed assessment of the wall layers in equivocal cases Liver function tests and CA 19-9 if malignancy is a concern Histological examination of the resected specimen for definitive diagnosis A benign, non-inflammatory hyperplastic change of the gallbladder wall characterised by mucosal overgrowth and outpouchings into a thickened muscular layer The pathognomonic feature is Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses, mucosal invaginations that extend into the wall Often asymptomatic and found incidentally, though some patients have biliary-type pain, particularly with the segmental (fundal) form On ultrasound, small cystic intramural spaces and the characteristic comet-tail (ring-down) reverberation artefact from cholesterol crystals within the sinuses are highly suggestive Described as diffuse, segmental, or localised (fundal), with the segmental form sometimes producing an hourglass configuration MRI shows the intramural sinuses as a string-of-beads or pearl-necklace appearance on heavily T2-weighted sequences It is a benign condition, so asymptomatic disease needs no treatment; cholecystectomy is reserved for symptoms or when imaging cannot confidently exclude malignancy Focal or segmental wall thickening that cannot be confidently distinguished from carcinoma An enhancing soft-tissue mass or irregular wall on cross-sectional imaging New or progressive symptoms with concerning imaging features Coexisting features suggesting gallbladder malignancy Mistaking focal or segmental adenomyomatosis for gallbladder carcinoma, or the reverse Overlooking a coexisting malignancy within an area of wall thickening Recommending surgery for confidently benign, asymptomatic disease Failing to recognise the specific comet-tail and pearl-necklace imaging signs Attributing all right upper quadrant symptoms to adenomyomatosis without excluding other causes Adenomyomatosis is a hyperplastic, degenerative change rather than an inflammatory or neoplastic one. Proliferation of the surface epithelium together with hypertrophy of the muscularis leads to thickening of the gallbladder wall, and the mucosa herniates through the muscular layer to form Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses, epithelium-lined intramural diverticula. Bile stagnating within these sinuses tends to deposit cholesterol crystals and small calculi, which generate the characteristic comet-tail reverberation artefact on ultrasound. The process may be diffuse, may affect a segment (often producing focal narrowing), or may be localised to the fundus as a mass-like nodule. Although benign, focal and segmental forms can mimic gallbladder carcinoma and can occasionally coexist with it, which is the principal diagnostic concern. The condition is benign with an excellent prognosis; asymptomatic disease requires no intervention, and cholecystectomy is curative when performed for symptoms or diagnostic uncertainty.

is only mildly enlarged Overlooking the impact on fertility and pregnancy when counselling younger women Adenomyosis develops when endometrial glands and stroma invade the myometrium, thought to occur through invagination of the basal endometrium along the disrupted endometrial-myometrial junction, or from metaplasia of displaced tissue. The ectopic tissue and surrounding smooth muscle undergo hypertrophy and hyperplasia under cyclical hormonal influence, producing a globular, enlarged uterus. Local oestrogen production, altered progesterone signalling, neuroangiogenesis, and inflammation contribute to heavy bleeding and pain, while distortion of the junctional zone and abnormal uterine contractility may impair implantation and contribute to subfertility. Adenomyosis is a benign but often chronic condition; symptoms frequently persist through the reproductive years and typically regress after menopause. Symptom control is achievable in many women with medical therapy, and hysterectomy is definitive when fertility is no longer desired.

the anaemia is usually mild to moderate Severe neonatal jaundice requiring exchange transfusion Aplastic crisis following parvovirus B19 infection Symptomatic anaemia requiring transfusion Transfusional iron overload with long-term support Overlooking the diagnosis by testing only for enzyme deficiencies and not for overactivity Missing the dominant inheritance pattern and its implications for family screening Assuming a membrane disorder when spherocytes are absent Neglecting iron-overload monitoring in transfused patients Adenosine deaminase irreversibly deaminates adenosine to inosine, diverting it away from the salvage pathway that maintains the adenine nucleotide pool. In this disorder the enzyme is markedly overexpressed, so adenosine is degraded excessively and the red cell cannot sustain adequate ATP. The resulting energy deficit compromises the cell's ability to maintain ion gradients and membrane function, shortening survival and producing a chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia; unusually, the mechanism is enzyme excess rather than deficiency and the trait is dominantly inherited. phosphorylating it to AMP. This reaction is important not only for purine handling but also for transmethylation, because clearance of adenosine helps drive the hydrolysis of S-adenosylhomocysteine to homocysteine and adenosine. inflammation followed by fibrosis and contracture of the glenohumeral joint capsule, particularly at the rotator interval and the coracohumeral ligament, with a resulting reduction in joint volume. Fibroblastic proliferation and myofibroblast-driven contracture, mediated by cytokines and growth factors, thicken and tighten the capsule so that movement becomes globally restricted. Diabetes mellitus and thyroid disease predispose to the condition, which is usually self-limiting but resolves only slowly over many months to years. The condition is generally self-limiting but recovery is slow, often taking one to three years; people with diabetes tend to have a more protracted course and some are left with residual stiffness.

Adiaspiromycosis (Emmonsia) — Emmonsia crescens infection, Emmonsia parva infection, adiaspirosis, pulmonary adiaspiromycosis Pulmonary tuberculosis and other mycobacterial disease Histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, and other endemic mycoses Sarcoidosis Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Miliary or metastatic pulmonary nodular disease Emergomycosis (disseminated dimorphic fungal infection in the immunocompromised) Lung biopsy with histopathology demonstrating large thick-walled adiaspores within granulomas Chest imaging (radiograph and CT) to characterise nodular, reticulonodular, or miliary patterns Fungal culture and molecular identification of Emmonsia species Exposure history focusing on soil, rural, and excavation activities Investigations to exclude tuberculosis and endemic mycoses Assessment of immune status to distinguish classical adiaspiromycosis from disseminated dimorphic infection A rare pulmonary infection caused by the dimorphic soil fungi of the Emmonsia genus (notably Emmonsia crescens), which chiefly infect burrowing rodents Humans acquire it by inhaling conidia from soil, an exposure linked to rural, agricultural, and excavation activities The inhaled conidia do not replicate in the lung but enlarge enormously into thick-walled structures called adiaspores, which provoke a granulomatous reaction Because the fungus does not multiply, disease severity depends on the number of spores inhaled: a small inoculum may be asymptomatic while a heavy exposure can cause diffuse illness Clinical presentation ranges from an incidental pulmonary nodule to fever, cough, dyspnoea, and a diffuse reticulonodular or miliary pattern in heavy exposures Diagnosis is histological, showing the characteristic large adiaspores with thick walls surrounded by granulomas, usually on lung biopsy Localised disease is often self-limiting; extensive or symptomatic disease is treated with antifungal agents, sometimes with corticosteroids to dampen the granulomatous response Diffuse bilateral pulmonary involvement with hypoxaemia after heavy spore exposure Progressive dyspnoea or respiratory failure Disseminated disease suggesting an alternative dimorphic fungus in an immunocompromised host Failure to improve, prompting reconsideration of tuberculosis or malignancy Mistaking pulmonary nodules for tuberculosis or malignancy and missing the histological adiaspores Assuming the organism disseminates like other dimorphic fungi, when classical adiaspiromycosis does not replicate in tissue Confusing adiaspiromycosis with disseminated emergomycosis in immunocompromised patients Over-treating incidental, asymptomatic solitary granulomas Emmonsia species are dimorphic fungi that live in soil and infect the lungs of small burrowing mammals. When a person inhales the airborne conidia, body temperature triggers conversion not into replicating yeast but into a unique enlarging spore, the adiaspore, which swells to a large thick-walled sphere without dividing or budding. The lack of replication means the organism cannot disseminate in the usual sense, and the burden of disease is set by the size of the inhaled inoculum. Each adiaspore acts as a persistent antigenic focus that stimulates a granulomatous inflammatory reaction in the surrounding lung. With a light exposure only scattered granulomas form, whereas a massive inhalation produces widespread granulomatous pneumonitis and impaired gas exchange. Note that some organisms formerly grouped with Emmonsia (such as Emergomyces) instead cause true disseminated dimorphic infection in the immunocompromised and are distinct from classical adiaspiromycosis. Localised, low-inoculum disease is frequently self-limiting with an excellent outlook, whereas heavy-exposure diffuse pulmonary disease can cause significant respiratory compromise but usually responds to antifungal therapy and supportive care.

curves A left thoracic curve or other atypical pattern suggesting a non-idiopathic cause Significant or persistent back pain, especially night pain Neurological signs such as weakness, sensory change, gait disturbance, or asymmetric abdominal reflexes Rapid progression, particularly during the growth spurt Onset outside the expected age range or a large curve at first presentation Accepting an idiopathic label for an atypical, painful, or neurologically abnormal curve without imaging Misjudging progression risk by not assessing remaining growth and skeletal maturity Offering a brace after skeletal maturity, when it can no longer alter the curve Underusing bracing in the growing child with a moderate progressive curve Overlooking subtle neurological signs that indicate an intraspinal cause Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is a three-dimensional structural deformity combining lateral curvature, axial vertebral rotation, and alteration of the normal sagittal profile, developing in an otherwise healthy adolescent without congenital or neuromuscular cause. Its aetiology is multifactorial and incompletely understood, with contributions from genetic predisposition and from disturbances of growth, neuromuscular control, connective tissue, and hormonal regulation during the adolescent growth spurt. Asymmetric growth of the vertebrae and the rapid spinal elongation of puberty allow curves to progress, and the vertebral rotation produces the rib prominence seen clinically. Because the label is idiopathic, structural, neurological, and syndromic causes must be excluded before the diagnosis is accepted. Most small curves remain stable and require only monitoring, and appropriately timed bracing can prevent progression in the growing child; large or neglected curves may progress into adulthood with cosmetic, and in severe cases cardiopulmonary, consequences, though surgical correction achieves durable deformity control.

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease — ADPKD, adult polycystic kidney disease, polycystic kidney disease Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease Acquired cystic kidney disease of chronic renal failure Simple renal cysts Tuberous sclerosis or von Hippel-Lindau associated cystic disease Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease Medullary cystic disease Renal ultrasound applying age-adjusted cyst count criteria Cross-sectional imaging and total kidney volume measurement to assess prognosis Blood pressure monitoring and assessment of renal function Urinalysis for haematuria, proteinuria, and infection Liver imaging for hepatic cysts when relevant Targeted cerebral vascular imaging for aneurysm screening in high-risk patients; genetic testing when the diagnosis is uncertain ADPKD is the most common inherited kidney disease and is characterised by progressive bilateral cyst formation that gradually replaces functioning renal tissue Most cases result from mutations in one of two genes, with the more common mutation generally causing earlier and more severe disease than the other Common presentations include hypertension, flank or abdominal pain, haematuria, kidney stones, urinary infections, and a family history of kidney disease Diagnosis is usually established by ultrasound using age-adjusted criteria for the number of cysts, with a positive family history strengthening the diagnosis Extrarenal manifestations are important and include hepatic cysts, intracranial aneurysms, cardiac valve abnormalities, and abdominal wall hernias Screening for intracranial aneurysms is targeted rather than universal, focusing on those with a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid haemorrhage or high-risk occupations Blood pressure control with renin-angiotensin system blockade and generous water intake are core management principles, and a vasopressin antagonist can slow cyst growth in selected rapidly progressing patients Total kidney volume and the specific genotype help predict the rate of progression and identify candidates for disease-modifying therapy Sudden severe headache suggesting rupture of an intracranial aneurysm Cyst infection or haemorrhage causing fever and severe flank pain Rapidly declining renal function or refractory hypertension Obstructing or infected kidney stones Applying uniform ultrasound cyst criteria without adjusting for the patient's age Recommending universal aneurysm screening rather than targeting high-risk patients Missing a cyst infection because it can present without the usual urinary findings Failing to identify rapidly progressing patients who might benefit from disease-modifying therapy ADPKD is caused by mutations in genes encoding polycystin proteins, which are located in the primary cilium and are important for sensing tubular flow and regulating tubular cell proliferation and differentiation. Loss of normal polycystin function disrupts intracellular calcium signalling and increases cyclic AMP, promoting abnormal epithelial proliferation and fluid secretion into forming cysts. Cysts arise from tubular segments, enlarge progressively, and detach from the parent tubule, expanding relentlessly and compressing adjacent normal parenchyma. Vasopressin-driven cyclic AMP signalling is a key driver of cyst fluid secretion and growth, which underlies the therapeutic role of vasopressin blockade. Progressive cyst expansion, interstitial inflammation, and fibrosis gradually reduce functioning nephron mass, while activation of the renin-angiotensin system contributes to the early and often severe hypertension. ADPKD typically progresses over decades, with many patients reaching end-stage kidney disease in mid to later adult life, though the rate varies widely with genotype and total kidney volume. Blood pressure control, treatment of complications, and disease-modifying therapy in appropriate patients can slow progression, and outcomes on dialysis and after transplantation are generally good. Intracranial aneurysm rupture is a serious extrarenal risk in susceptible individuals.

Adrenal crisis — Random cortisol Electrolytes (Na↓ K↑) Empiric hydrocortisone Give IV hydrocortisone if suspected Other causes of distributive/endocrine shock (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic) (p.2353) Hypovolaemic and cardiogenic shock (p.2353) Acute abdomen-like presentation with abdominal tenderness, nausea, vomiting and fever can mimic an intra-abdominal infection (p.3111) Baseline serum cortisol AND plasma ACTH drawn before starting steroids, with formal testing deferred (p.3111) Short cosyntropin (ACTH stimulation) test once stabilised — failure cutoff roughly cortisol <450-500 nmol/L (16-18 ug/dL) at 30-60 min (p.3111) Plasma renin to confirm mineralocorticoid deficiency in primary disease (p.3111) Adrenal steroid autoantibodies to assess for autoimmune adrenalitis (p.3111) Adrenal CT for hemorrhage, infiltration or masses if autoantibodies negative (p.3111) Very-long-chain fatty acids in autoantibody-negative males to exclude X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (p.3111) Hypothalamic-pituitary MRI when ACTH is inappropriately low (secondary cause) (p.3111) Associated labs: hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, raised creatinine, normochromic anaemia, lymphocytosis, eosinophilia (p.3110) Acute abdomen / surgical abdomen (abdominal pain, tenderness, nausea, vomiting) (p.3111) Primary neurologic disease — decreased responsiveness progressing to stupor and coma (p.3111) Adrenal crisis typically emerges after a prolonged prodrome of nonspecific complaints rather than appearing out of the blue (p.3111). Crisis is more frequent in PRIMARY adrenal insufficiency because both glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid secretion are lost (p.3111). Postural hypotension can progress to frank hypovolaemic shock (p.3111). Prospective data: about 8.3 adrenal crises per 100 patient-years and roughly 0.5 crisis-related deaths per 100 patient-years (p.3111). Adrenal crisis is classified as a form of endocrine/distributive shock (p.2353). In suspected crisis, it is reasonable to draw a baseline cortisol (and ACTH), start replacement, and defer formal stimulation testing — diagnostic testing must never delay treatment (p.3111). Starting thyroid hormone replacement in an undiagnosed patient can precipitate adrenal crisis, because thyroid hormone shortens cortisol half-life; screen for adrenal insufficiency before treating hypothyroidism in possible polyendocrine syndrome (p.3133). Refractory or postural hypotension progressing to hypovolaemic shock (p.3111) Decreased responsiveness, stupor or coma (p.3111) Hyperpigmentation suggesting underlying primary adrenal insufficiency (p.3110) Do NOT let diagnostic testing delay treatment in suspected crisis (p.3111). Random/baseline serum cortisol has limited diagnostic value because levels may be coincidentally low from normal diurnal rhythm, and many secondary cases have near-normal baseline cortisol that only fails on stimulation testing (p.3111). Do NOT start thyroid hormone before excluding/treating adrenal insufficiency — it can precipitate crisis (p.3133). Hyperthyroidism increases glucocorticoid inactivation and can trigger crisis (p.3111). Adrenal insufficiency can be masked by concurrent primary hypothyroidism, which prolongs cortisol half-life (p.3133). Acute adrenal insufficiency reflects an absolute or relative deficiency of cortisol, in primary disease compounded by loss of aldosterone (mineralocorticoid). Glucocorticoid deficiency impairs vascular tone, gluconeogenesis and loss of feedback inhibition of AVP release (contributing to hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia), while mineralocorticoid deficiency causes renal salt wasting with volume depletion, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and rising creatinine. The result is hypotension that may decompensate into hypovolaemic shock. Crisis is usually unmasked by a stressor that exceeds the inadequate cortisol reserve — intercurrent illness, surgery or other stress, or increased glucocorticoid inactivation as in hyperthyroidism (p.3111). Acute adrenal insufficiency is potentially lethal (p.636). Even with established care, crises and crisis-related deaths continue to occur (~8.3 crises and ~0.5 deaths per 100 patient-years) (p.3111).

(p.3068) Primary adrenal insufficiency loses both glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid secretion; secondary (central) disease loses glucocorticoid only because the adrenal stays responsive to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Adrenal androgen secretion is lost in both. (p.3067) Hyperpigmentation (palmar creases, friction/shear areas, sun-exposed skin) from excess POMC/ACTH is the hallmark distinguishing primary adrenal insufficiency; secondary insufficiency instead causes an alabaster-pale skin from ACTH lack. (p.3067) Hyponatremia is present in ~80% of primary adrenal insufficiency at presentation and hyperkalemia in ~40%. Hyponatremia can also occur in secondary insufficiency via reduced cortisol inhibition of ADH (mild SIADH-like picture). (p.3067) All patients with an incidentally discovered adrenal mass need a 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test to exclude cortisol excess; add plasma/urine metanephrines if HU >10 (exclude pheochromocytoma), and paired renin/aldosterone plus potassium if hypertensive. Confirm any Cushing's as ACTH-independent by measuring plasma ACTH. (p.3063-3064) On unenhanced CT, adrenal lesion attenuation is the key discriminator: lipid-rich adenomas are typically <10-20 HU, whereas adrenocortical carcinoma and pheochromocytoma have high attenuation (>20 HU). Hounsfield assessment only applies to unenhanced CT, not post-contrast. (p.3064) Mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) = abnormal 1 mg dexamethasone test with no overt clinical Cushing's; it still carries excess risk of hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, osteoporosis, cardiovascular events, and mortality. A subset of primary aldosteronism patients have co-existing MACS ('Connshing' syndrome). (p.3061, p.3064) CYP21A2 (21-hydroxylase) deficiency causes 90-95% of congenital adrenal hyperplasia; it impairs glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid synthesis and drives ACTH-mediated adrenal androgen excess. 17-hydroxyprogesterone is the diagnostic marker steroid. Severity spans classic salt-wasting (neonatal), simple virilizing, to nonclassic (presents in adolescence/adulthood). (p.3071) Adrenal crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency): postural hypotension progressing to hypovolemic shock, often after a prolonged period of nonspecific complaints; may mimic acute abdomen or neurologic decline (stupor/coma); can be triggered by intercurrent illness, surgery/stress, or increased glucocorticoid inactivation (e.g., hyperthyroidism) - treat immediately, do not let testing delay therapy In suspected adrenal crisis, draw a baseline cortisol, start replacement, and defer formal stimulation testing - tests must never delay treatment Cushing's hypercoagulable state with risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism Acute paranoid or depressive psychosis in severe cortisol excess Severe hypokalemia in aldosteronism causing arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, or hypokalemic paralysis; severe alkalosis causing tetany Classic salt-wasting CAH in male neonates presenting as life-threatening adrenal crisis in the first weeks of life Performing imaging or surgery before biochemically confirming Cushing's beyond doubt - pituitary/adrenal nodules are common incidental findings and lead to misdiagnosis Forgetting to exclude exogenous (iatrogenic) glucocorticoid use as the cause before working up endogenous Cushing's Dexamethasone test pitfalls: false non-suppression from oral estrogens/contraceptives (raise CBG/total cortisol; retest after 4-6 weeks off estrogen) and rapid dexamethasone inactivation by CYP3A4 inducers (antiepileptics, rifampicin); antibody-based urinary free cortisol assays have specificity problems improved by tandem mass spectrometry Not normalizing potassium before, or failing to stop MR antagonists (4-6 weeks) before, ARR testing; beta-blockers give false-positive and ACE inhibitors/ARBs false-negative ARR results Relying on the ARR alone when renin is very low increases false positives; only 10-40% of primary aldosteronism patients are hypokalemic, so normokalemia does not exclude it Using random serum cortisol to diagnose adrenal insufficiency - baseline levels may be coincidentally low (diurnal rhythm), and secondary insufficiency often shows near-normal baseline cortisol that fails only on stimulation Stopping exogenous glucocorticoids abruptly can precipitate iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency even though the patient still looks cushingoid Judging adrenal mass attenuation on post-contrast CT - Hounsfield-unit discrimination of benign vs malignant only applies to unenhanced CT; lipid-poor adenomas (high HU) overlap with ACC and pheochromocytoma Mistaking testicular adrenal rest tumors (TART) in CAH for testicular neoplasms The adrenal cortex produces glucocorticoids (cortisol, zona fasciculata under HPA/ACTH control), mineralocorticoids (aldosterone, zona glomerulosa under renin-angiotensin-aldosterone control), and adrenal androgens. Cushing's syndrome reflects chronic glucocorticoid excess: ~90% of endogenous cases are ACTH-dependent (mostly a pituitary corticotrope adenoma = Cushing's disease, or ectopic ACTH from carcinoid/small-cell lung cancer), ~10% are ACTH-independent adrenal causes (adenoma, carcinoma, or bilateral macronodular/pigmented nodular hyperplasia). Cortisol excess upregulates gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and protein catabolism, and when 11beta-HSD2 is overwhelmed cortisol activates the mineralocorticoid receptor, producing hypertension, hypokalemia, and edema. Primary mineralocorticoid excess (primary aldosteronism) is autonomous aldosterone production by the zona glomerulosa (bilateral hyperplasia or unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma/Conn's); MR over-activation causes sodium retention with volume expansion, potassium and hydrogen loss (hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis), and direct cardiac/renal damage. Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's) is destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex (most often autoimmune adrenalitis, also TB, adrenoleukodystrophy, hemorrhage, infiltration, CAH), causing combined glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency; secondary insufficiency is HPA/pituitary-hypothalamic failure (tumor, surgery, irradiation, apoplexy/Sheehan's, or iatrogenic glucocorticoid suppression) with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency. CAH results from inherited steroidogenic enzyme defects (commonly CYP21A2) causing glucocorticoid deficiency, loss of feedback, raised ACTH, and adrenal androgen excess, with mineralocorticoid deficiency or excess depending on the enzymatic block. After successful removal of an ACTH- or cortisol-producing tumor the HPA axis remains suppressed and may take months to years (or never) to recover; recovery rates differ by cause - ectopic ACTH best (~80%, median ~7 months), Cushing's disease intermediate (~60%, ~17 months), adrenal Cushing's lowest (~40%, ~30 months). Even after cure, long-term quality of life can remain impaired with increased cardiovascular and osteoporotic-fracture risk depending on duration and degree of cortisol excess. Primary aldosteronism carries increased osteoporosis, type 2 diabetes, and cognitive dysfunction. Adrenal crisis is potentially lethal, with prospective data of 8.3 crises and 0.5 crisis-related deaths per 100 patient-years. MACS is associated with increased mortality. In CAH, fertility may be compromised (anovulation in women, testicular adrenal rest tumors and fibrosis in men). Adrenal insufficiency is classified as primary (Addison's, combined glucocorticoid + mineralocorticoid deficiency, high ACTH) vs secondary/central (isolated glucocorticoid deficiency, low/inappropriate ACTH), with acute adrenal crisis as the life-threatening acute form. Endogenous Cushing's is classified as ACTH-dependent (~90%; Cushing's disease vs ectopic ACTH) vs ACTH-independent (~10%; adenoma, carcinoma, hyperplasia). Cortisol excess severity ranges from overt Cushing's to mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS). Primary aldosteronism is divided into unilateral (adenoma/Conn's, surgically curable) vs bilateral (hyperplasia, medical therapy). CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency) is graded by severity into classic salt-wasting, simple virilizing, and nonclassic forms. Adrenocortical carcinoma is staged by the ENSAT/TNM system (Stage I T1 <=5 cm to advanced/metastatic).

adrenal haemorrhage — adrenal haematoma, bilateral adrenal haemorrhage haemorrhagic adrenal adenoma or adrenocortical carcinoma phaeochromocytoma with intratumoural haemorrhage adrenal metastasis adrenal abscess retroperitoneal haematoma from other source acute pyelonephritis acute pancreatitis non-contrast and contrast-enhanced CT of the adrenals adrenal MRI with in- and opposed-phase and gradient-echo sequences to characterise and date blood products short Synacthen test with paired ACTH to assess adrenal reserve plasma renin and aldosterone to confirm mineralocorticoid deficiency coagulation screen and platelet count antiphospholipid antibody panel and screening for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia plasma or urinary metanephrines to exclude phaeochromocytoma The adrenal has a rich arterial supply draining through a single central vein, creating a vascular dam that predisposes the medullary-cortical junction to haemorrhage under stress. Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage typically presents non-specifically with abdominal, flank or back pain, fever and progressive hypotension, so acute adrenal crisis is easily overlooked. Suspect it in any critically ill patient with unexplained shock that is refractory to fluids and vasopressors. Antiphospholipid syndrome is the classic cause of spontaneous bilateral haemorrhage, and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia can drive adrenal vein thrombosis with subsequent bleeding. Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome describes haemorrhagic adrenal destruction with disseminated intravascular coagulation, historically in meningococcal sepsis. Neonatal adrenal haemorrhage follows difficult delivery or macrosomia and presents with a flank mass, prolonged jaundice and anaemia. Unilateral haemorrhage usually preserves adrenal function, whereas bilateral involvement threatens Addisonian crisis and warrants empirical glucocorticoid before biochemical confirmation. Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, eosinophilia and hypoglycaemia should prompt urgent cortisol and ACTH testing. haemodynamic instability or shock unresponsive to fluids and vasopressors hyperkalaemia with hyponatraemia suggesting evolving adrenal crisis hypoglycaemia bilateral adrenal enlargement on imaging reduced consciousness or collapse attributing hypotension solely to sepsis and missing coexisting adrenal crisis withholding glucocorticoid while awaiting confirmatory biochemistry mistaking a contrast-enhancing haematoma for a solid tumour failing to investigate an underlying antiphospholipid syndrome or heparin-induced thrombocytopenia continuing anticoagulation without recognising the adrenal as the bleeding source The adrenal cortex receives a rich arterial supply from three separate arteries but drains through a single central vein, so any rise in venous pressure or intra-adrenal arterial flow produces stasis and rupture at the cortico-medullary junction. Physiological stress (sepsis, surgery, burns, trauma) drives an ACTH-mediated surge in adrenal blood flow while catecholamines and cytokines promote vasoconstriction and thrombosis of the small draining veins, culminating in haemorrhagic infarction. Prothrombotic and bleeding states amplify this, including antiphospholipid syndrome, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, anticoagulation and disseminated intravascular coagulation. When both glands are involved, destruction of cortical tissue produces acute primary adrenal insufficiency with combined glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency. Unilateral haemorrhage usually resolves with preservation of adrenal function, whereas bilateral haemorrhage causing acute insufficiency carries substantial mortality if crisis is unrecognised; survivors may recover partially or require lifelong hormone replacement.

Neonatal adrenal haemorrhage — neonatal adrenal haemorrhage, newborn adrenal haemorrhage, perinatal adrenal haemorrhage Neuroblastoma, the key differential of a suprarenal mass Congenital adrenal neoplasm Renal masses such as mesoblastic nephroma or renal vein thrombosis with haemorrhage Adrenal abscess Subdiaphragmatic extralobar pulmonary sequestration Adrenal cyst Serial abdominal ultrasound showing an evolving, involuting suprarenal lesion Haematocrit and haemoglobin monitoring alongside bilirubin Coagulation screen and sepsis evaluation where indicated Urinary catecholamine metabolites to help exclude neuroblastoma MRI if diagnostic uncertainty persists or to characterise a persistent mass Assessment of adrenal function including cortisol and electrolytes if the haemorrhage is bilateral or extensive The adrenal gland is the commonest site of neonatal haemorrhage, favoured by its relatively large size and rich vascularity at birth Recognised risk factors include birth trauma, difficult or breech delivery, macrosomia, perinatal hypoxia or asphyxia, sepsis, and coagulopathy or haemorrhagic disease of the newborn Presentation ranges from an asymptomatic incidental finding to a flank mass, anaemia, prolonged jaundice, or, if bilateral and extensive, adrenal insufficiency It is more common on the right side and may be bilateral Ultrasound is the first-line investigation and typically shows an evolving suprarenal mass that changes and shrinks over serial scans The main differential of a neonatal suprarenal mass is neuroblastoma, which serial imaging and urinary catecholamine metabolites help to distinguish Most cases resolve spontaneously with supportive care, and surgery is reserved for ongoing bleeding or diagnostic uncertainty Signs of adrenal insufficiency such as hypotension, hypoglycaemia and hyponatraemia with bilateral haemorrhage Ongoing haemorrhage with haemodynamic instability or a falling haematocrit A suprarenal mass that fails to involute, raising concern for neuroblastoma Sepsis or coagulopathy requiring urgent treatment Mistaking neuroblastoma for adrenal haemorrhage, or vice versa, without serial imaging and catecholamine testing Missing adrenal insufficiency in bilateral haemorrhage Overlooking an underlying coagulopathy or sepsis Proceeding to surgery for a lesion that would resolve with observation The neonatal adrenal cortex is proportionally large and highly vascular, making it vulnerable to haemorrhage when subjected to the mechanical stress of delivery, hypoxic-ischaemic injury, venous congestion, or the endothelial effects of sepsis. Impaired haemostasis, whether from coagulopathy or vitamin K-dependent haemorrhagic disease, compounds the risk. Extensive bilateral bleeding can destroy enough cortex to cause adrenal insufficiency, whereas unilateral bleeds usually resolve, often leaving residual calcification. Generally excellent for unilateral haemorrhage, which resolves spontaneously and often leaves residual calcification; the outcome is worse with extensive bilateral disease causing adrenal insufficiency or when an underlying illness is severe.

Adrenal incidentaloma — incidental adrenal mass, adrenal nodule, adrenal incidental lesion Non-functioning cortical adenoma Cortisol-secreting adenoma (Cushing syndrome) Aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn syndrome) Phaeochromocytoma Adrenocortical carcinoma Adrenal metastasis or myelolipoma or adrenal cyst Overnight dexamethasone suppression test (and where indicated late-night salivary or 24-hour urinary cortisol) for autonomous cortisol secretion Plasma or urinary metanephrines to exclude phaeochromocytoma Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio in hypertensive or hypokalaemic patients Unenhanced CT for attenuation, with contrast washout study or MRI chemical-shift imaging to characterise indeterminate lesions Serial imaging surveillance for non-operated lesions to assess growth Consideration of adrenal vein sampling when lateralising aldosterone excess before surgery An adrenal incidentaloma is an adrenal mass discovered unexpectedly on imaging performed for an unrelated reason, and its evaluation centres on two questions: is it functional, and is it malignant Every incidentaloma should be screened biochemically for cortisol excess, phaeochromocytoma, and, in hypertensive or hypokalaemic patients, primary aldosteronism Unenhanced CT attenuation is key: a lipid-rich lesion with low Hounsfield values strongly favours a benign adenoma, while high attenuation warrants further characterisation Large size and imaging features such as irregular margins, heterogeneity, and delayed contrast washout raise concern for adrenocortical carcinoma Phaeochromocytoma must be excluded before any biopsy or surgery to avoid a catastrophic hypertensive crisis Surgery (usually laparoscopic adrenalectomy) is indicated for functional tumours, lesions with malignant features, and masses above a threshold size, while smaller non-functioning benign lesions are monitored Biopsy of an adrenal mass is rarely helpful and is reserved for suspected metastasis or infiltrative disease after phaeochromocytoma has been ruled out Undiagnosed phaeochromocytoma before intervention, risking a life-threatening hypertensive crisis on biopsy or induction Large or rapidly enlarging mass with heterogeneous, high-attenuation, poorly washing-out features suggesting adrenocortical carcinoma Severe or resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia indicating a functioning tumour Known extra-adrenal malignancy with a new adrenal lesion suggesting metastasis Proceeding to biopsy or surgery without first excluding a phaeochromocytoma Labelling a mass non-functioning without complete biochemical screening, missing subclinical cortisol excess Underestimating malignant potential by relying on size alone and ignoring washout and morphology Inadequate perioperative alpha- (then beta-) blockade when operating on a catecholamine-secreting tumour Failing to plan perioperative glucocorticoid cover when removing a cortisol-secreting adenoma with a suppressed contralateral gland Adrenal incidentalomas are a heterogeneous group. Most are benign non-functioning cortical adenomas, but the differential spans hormonally active adenomas (secreting cortisol or aldosterone), phaeochromocytomas arising from the adrenal medulla, adrenocortical carcinoma, myelolipomas, cysts, and metastatic deposits. Functional lesions cause disease through autonomous hormone secretion: cortisol excess produces subclinical or overt Cushing syndrome, aldosterone excess produces hypertension and hypokalaemia, and catecholamine excess from a phaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal hypertension and its complications. Malignant potential correlates with size, growth rate, and imaging characteristics reflecting lipid content and vascularity. Most incidentalomas are benign and non-functioning with an excellent outlook and stable behaviour on surveillance. Functional lesions generally do well after adrenalectomy with resolution or improvement of hormone excess, whereas adrenocortical carcinoma carries a poor prognosis, strongly influenced by stage and completeness of resection.
