and any interval growth on follow-up imaging Evaluation for retroperitoneal haemorrhage if the patient presents with acute pain Consideration of further characterisation when imaging features are atypical for benign fat A benign, hormonally inactive adrenal tumour composed of mature adipose tissue admixed with haematopoietic elements, most often found incidentally on imaging The presence of macroscopic (bulk) fat on CT or MRI is the key diagnostic feature and reliably distinguishes it from most other adrenal masses Usually asymptomatic, but large lesions can cause flank or abdominal pain, or present acutely with retroperitoneal haemorrhage Being non-functioning, it does not require the full hormonal excess workup once fat content confirms the diagnosis, though a screening biochemical assessment of an incidentaloma remains prudent Small, uncomplicated lesions can be managed conservatively with surveillance rather than surgery Larger tumours (commonly beyond around 6 to 7 cm) carry a higher risk of spontaneous bleeding and may be considered for resection Can rarely coexist with, or be mimicked by, other fat-containing retroperitoneal lesions such as liposarcoma, which should be considered if imaging is atypical Acute flank or abdominal pain with a fall in haemoglobin suggesting spontaneous haemorrhage Rapid interval growth or heterogeneous soft-tissue components raising concern for liposarcoma Very large lesion causing mass effect on adjacent structures Atypical imaging that fails to confirm benign macroscopic fat Subjecting a clearly fat-containing benign lesion to unnecessary extensive hormonal workup or surgery Mistaking a fat-containing liposarcoma for a benign myelolipoma when imaging is atypical Underestimating the haemorrhage risk of a large lesion Confusing an adrenal myelolipoma with an exophytic renal angiomyolipoma Adrenal myelolipoma is a benign tumour formed by metaplastic transformation of adrenal cortical stromal cells into mature fat and functioning haematopoietic (myeloid and erythroid) tissue. It is not derived from steroidogenic cells and therefore does not secrete hormones. The proportion of fat to marrow elements varies, giving the characteristic mixed density on imaging. Growth is generally slow; the main clinical consequence of larger lesions is mechanical, with the friable, vascular tissue prone to spontaneous or trauma-related haemorrhage. An association with chronic ACTH stimulation and some congenital adrenal disorders has been described. The lesion is benign with an excellent prognosis; most are managed conservatively with imaging surveillance, and surgery, when needed for size or haemorrhage, is generally curative without recurrence.

tumours Acute severe flank or abdominal pain or haemodynamic instability suggesting haemorrhage Large size with mass effect on adjacent structures Atypical imaging with soft-tissue components raising concern for malignancy Rapid growth on surveillance Mistaking a fat-containing myelolipoma for a malignant retroperitoneal fatty tumour Underestimating the haemorrhage risk of a very large lesion mature fat mixed with haematopoietic tissue resembling bone marrow, arising from metaplasia of adrenocortical stromal cells, possibly under hormonal or stress-related stimuli. The lesion is benign and typically non-secreting. As it enlarges, its friable, vascular composition and high fat content predispose to spontaneous haemorrhage, which is the principal complication of large tumours. Excellent; myelolipomas are benign and do not metastasise, and the outlook is determined mainly by size-related complications such as haemorrhage, which resolve well after treatment.

or MRI assessing size, attenuation, washout and local invasion Cross-sectional and functional staging imaging (chest CT, and FDG-PET where available) to detect metastases Histopathology with Weiss cm), irregular margins, heterogeneity, high unenhanced CT attenuation and slow contrast washout are imaging features favouring malignancy Histological malignancy is judged using the Weiss criteria, which combine features such as high mitotic rate, atypical mitoses, venous and capsular invasion and necrosis May occur sporadically or within hereditary syndromes such as Li-Fraumeni (TP53), Beckwith-Wiedemann and Lynch syndrome Complete surgical resection by an experienced adrenal surgeon offers the only realistic chance of cure, with adjunctive adrenolytic and cytotoxic therapy for advanced disease Rapidly progressive combined cortisol and androgen excess (e.g. Cushing with virilisation) Large heterogeneous adrenal mass with local invasion or tumour thrombus New or growing lesions on staging imaging indicating metastatic spread Severe uncontrolled hypercortisolism causing infection, thromboembolism or psychosis Attributing a large adrenal mass to a benign adenoma and delaying definitive surgery Biopsying a suspected adrenocortical carcinoma, which risks tumour seeding and is rarely diagnostic Failing to exclude phaeochromocytoma before operating on an adrenal mass Overlooking subtle androgen or precursor excess that flags malignancy Fragmenting the tumour capsule at surgery, worsening the risk of local recurrence Adrenocortical carcinoma arises from malignant transformation of adrenal cortical cells, frequently involving dysregulation of the IGF-2 growth pathway and inactivation of tumour-suppressor genes such as TP53, together with activation of Wnt/beta-catenin signalling. Many tumours retain steroidogenic capacity but do so inefficiently and in a disordered fashion, producing excess cortisol, adrenal androgens, and sometimes mineralocorticoids or oestrogens, which accounts for the mixed and rapidly evolving endocrine syndromes. The tumours grow to a large size, invade local structures and vessels, and metastasise, particularly to liver, lung and regional nodes. Prognosis is poor overall and strongly stage-dependent; localised tumours amenable to complete resection carry the best outlook, whereas advanced or metastatic disease has low long-term survival despite adrenolytic and cytotoxic therapy. Recurrence is common even after apparently complete excision, mandating close surveillance.

autoimmune or other cause Attention/behavioural disorders in the early cerebral childhood form Plasma very-long-chain fatty acid profile as the principal screening test ABCD1 gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis and enable family testing Brain MRI to detect and stage cerebral demyelination Adrenal function assessment including morning cortisol and ACTH stimulation testing Spinal cord imaging and nerve conduction studies in the adrenomyeloneuropathy phenotype Newborn screening confirmation and genetic counselling for at-risk relatives An X-linked peroxisomal disorder caused by mutations in the ABCD1 gene, leading to accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids in nervous tissue and the adrenal cortex Presents across a wide phenotypic spectrum, from a rapidly progressive childhood cerebral form to the slower adult adrenomyeloneuropathy variant The childhood cerebral form typically begins in a previously healthy boy with behavioural change, declining school performance, visual or auditory deficits, and progressive dementia and spasticity Adrenomyeloneuropathy chiefly affects adult men with a slowly progressive spastic paraparesis, sphincter disturbance, and sensory loss reflecting distal axonopathy of long tracts Adrenal insufficiency (Addison-like) may precede or accompany neurological disease, and some males present first with adrenal failure, so unexplained adrenal insufficiency in a boy or man should prompt VLCFA testing Female carriers can develop a mild myelopathy in later life, so heterozygotes are not always asymptomatic Elevated plasma very-long-chain fatty acids is the key biochemical screening test, confirmed by ABCD1 mutation analysis The disorder is increasingly detected through newborn screening programmes, allowing presymptomatic identification and timely monitoring for cerebral disease and adrenal failure There is no reliable phenotype-genotype correlation, so the same mutation within a family can produce very different clinical courses A previously well boy with rapid cognitive, behavioural, or visual decline suggesting active cerebral demyelination Unexplained primary adrenal insufficiency, especially with hyperpigmentation or adrenal crisis Rapidly enhancing white matter lesions on MRI indicating an inflammatory, aggressive cerebral phase Progressive gait failure with sphincter involvement in an adult male Attributing early cerebral disease in a boy to a behavioural or psychiatric disorder and delaying imaging Overlooking coexisting adrenal insufficiency, which can be life-threatening if untreated Assuming female carriers are always asymptomatic Failing to offer genetic counselling and family screening once a proband is identified Adrenoleukodystrophy results from loss-of-function mutations in ABCD1, which encodes a peroxisomal membrane transporter needed for the import and beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids. Impaired degradation leads to accumulation of these fatty acids in tissues, particularly cerebral white matter, spinal cord long tracts, adrenal cortex, and testis. In the cerebral form, an inflammatory demyelinating process destroys white matter, whereas adrenomyeloneuropathy is characterised by a slowly progressive distal axonopathy of the spinal cord. Adrenocortical cells accumulate abnormal lipid and undergo dysfunction, producing primary adrenal insufficiency. The childhood cerebral form is often relentlessly progressive once inflammatory demyelination is established, whereas adrenomyeloneuropathy advances slowly over years to decades. Early identification through screening allows monitoring and consideration of disease-modifying options in appropriate candidates, and adrenal insufficiency can be effectively treated with hormone replacement, but neurological outcomes remain variable.

adult failure to thrive — geriatric failure to thrive, adult FTT major depressive disorder occult malignancy thyroid dysfunction (hyper- or hypothyroidism) adrenal insufficiency chronic infection such as tuberculosis or infective endocarditis advanced cardiac, renal or hepatic failure dementia or delirium comprehensive geriatric assessment cognitive screening and validated depression screening structured nutritional assessment with albumin and prealbumin full blood count, urea and electrolytes, calcium and glucose thyroid function and a morning cortisol inflammatory markers and targeted malignancy screening or imaging as indicated medication review and swallowing assessment It is a descriptive syndrome, not a diagnosis, so always search for reversible contributors before accepting it as end-stage decline. Four interacting domains dominate: impaired physical function, malnutrition, depression and cognitive impairment. Depression is among the most common and most treatable drivers, so screen every patient formally. Polypharmacy and drug side effects such as anorexia, nausea, sedation and postural hypotension are frequently reversible causes. Exclude occult malignancy, chronic infection such as tuberculosis or endocarditis, thyroid disease and adrenal insufficiency. Low serum albumin, low cholesterol and lymphopenia are recognised markers of poor prognosis. Dysphagia, poor dentition, social isolation and financial hardship limiting food access are commonly missed contributors. Distinguish the syndrome from normal ageing and from an established terminal illness trajectory where the goal shifts to comfort. rapid progressive weight loss new focal neurology or lymphadenopathy suggesting malignancy severe dehydration or electrolyte disturbance suicidal ideation accompanying depression recurrent aspiration or unsafe swallow accepting decline as inevitable ageing and abandoning the diagnostic workup missing treatable depression overlooking polypharmacy as a driver failing to assess swallowing, dentition and social or financial barriers to eating not engaging a multidisciplinary team including dietitian, therapists and social work Adult failure to thrive is a multifactorial state of decline in older people characterised by weight loss, reduced appetite, poor nutrition and physical inactivity, often accompanied by dehydration, depressive symptoms and impaired immunity. It represents a final common pathway of accumulated chronic disease, frailty and sarcopenia, driven in part by a pro-inflammatory cytokine milieu with raised interleukin-6 and tumour necrosis factor that promotes catabolism and anorexia. Age-related dysregulation of appetite signalling through leptin and ghrelin, neuroendocrine changes and reduced physiological reserve interact with depression, cognitive impairment and social adversity to accelerate functional and nutritional loss, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of deconditioning. The syndrome carries high morbidity, risk of institutionalisation and mortality, especially when albumin and functional status are low, yet identification and treatment of a reversible cause, particularly depression or a medication effect, can produce meaningful recovery.

Adult-onset Still disease — AOSD, adult Still's disease, systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis in adults Sepsis and other systemic infections (including viral) Lymphoma and other malignancies Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue diseases Systemic vasculitides Reactive arthritis and other seronegative arthropathies Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) Serum ferritin, characteristically very high, with glycosylated ferritin fraction if available Full blood count showing neutrophilic leucocytosis and inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) Blood cultures and infective screen to exclude sepsis Autoantibody panel (rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody typically negative) Imaging and lymph node biopsy where malignancy or lymphoma needs exclusion Liver function tests, triglycerides, and fibrinogen to detect emerging macrophage activation syndrome Classic triad of high spiking quotidian fevers, an evanescent salmon-pink rash appearing with fever spikes, and arthralgia or arthritis Markedly elevated serum ferritin, often with a low glycosylated ferritin fraction, supports the diagnosis It is a diagnosis of exclusion (e.g. Yamaguchi criteria) requiring the ruling out of infection, malignancy, and other autoimmune disease Sore throat, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and serositis are common accompanying features Rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody are characteristically negative, and there is a neutrophilic leucocytosis Macrophage activation syndrome (secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis) is a life-threatening complication to watch for Treatment ranges from NSAIDs and systemic corticosteroids to IL-1 and IL-6 blockade in refractory or systemic disease Features of macrophage activation syndrome: falling cell counts, very high ferritin, hypertriglyceridaemia, and organ dysfunction Rapidly progressive hepatic dysfunction or coagulopathy Cardiac tamponade or severe serositis Persistent constitutional decline raising concern for occult malignancy Diagnosing it before adequately excluding infection and malignancy Missing evolving macrophage activation syndrome when cytopenias develop Dismissing the diagnosis because the transient rash is absent at the time of review Over-reliance on ferritin alone, which is nonspecific Failing to escalate to cytokine-directed therapy in corticosteroid-refractory disease Adult-onset Still disease is a systemic autoinflammatory disorder driven by dysregulation of the innate immune system rather than autoantibody-mediated autoimmunity. Activation of macrophages and neutrophils with overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines, particularly interleukin-1, interleukin-6, interleukin-18, and tumour necrosis factor, produces the fever, rash, arthritis, and hyperferritinaemia. Interleukin-18 and macrophage activation underlie the extreme ferritin elevation and the propensity to macrophage activation syndrome. A genetic predisposition combined with an infectious or other environmental trigger is thought to initiate the process. The course is variable: some have a self-limiting monocyclic illness, others a polycyclic relapsing course, and a subset develop chronic destructive arthritis; macrophage activation syndrome is the principal cause of mortality.

deficiency of the glycogen branching enzyme encoded by GBE1, which normally introduces branch points into glycogen. Reduced enzyme activity leads to the synthesis of an abnormal, poorly branched, amylopectin-like glycogen that accumulates as intracellular polyglucosan bodies within neurones, glia and peripheral nerves, as well as other tissues. Deposition throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems produces axonal degeneration, demyelination and neuronal dysfunction, manifesting as the characteristic combination of spastic paraparesis, peripheral neuropathy, neurogenic bladder and, in some patients, cognitive impairment. The disorder progresses slowly over years, with accumulating gait impairment, bladder dysfunction and, in some, dementia leading to significant disability; management is supportive, targeting spasticity, bladder symptoms and mobility, and genetic counselling is offered.

chronic destructive arthritis in the articular subtype Adult-onset Still's disease is an autoinflammatory condition driven predominantly by innate immune activation rather than autoantibodies. Excessive activation of macrophages and neutrophils and a cytokine storm involving interleukin-1, interleukin-6, interleukin-18, and interferon-gamma produce the systemic inflammatory picture. Marked hyperferritinaemia reflects macrophage activation. Most systemic cases respond to treatment, but macrophage activation syndrome carries substantial mortality and requires prompt recognition and intensive therapy.

hyperinfection Missing hypercalcaemia as a presenting emergency Misclassifying the clinical variant and therefore mismatching treatment intensity Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma is a mature CD4-positive T-cell neoplasm driven by long-term infection with human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1, usually acquired in infancy through breastfeeding or later through blood or sexual transmission. The viral regulatory proteins, particularly Tax and HBZ, dysregulate host cell proliferation, survival, and genomic stability, and after a long latency a clone of infected T-cells transforms. The neoplastic cells frequently have a regulatory T-cell-like phenotype, contributing to immunosuppression, and secrete factors that stimulate osteoclasts, producing the characteristic hypercalcaemia and lytic bone disease. Only a small proportion of infected individuals develop overt disease. Prognosis depends heavily on subtype: the acute and lymphomatous variants are aggressive with poor survival, whereas chronic and smouldering forms are more indolent though still capable of transformation, and hypercalcaemia and high tumour burden portend worse outcomes.

bacteria that cause disease after ingestion of contaminated water or food, or through direct wound inoculation from freshwater or aquatic animals such as leeches and fish. They elaborate a range of virulence factors, including cytotoxic and haemolytic enterotoxins, proteases and adhesins, which disrupt intestinal epithelium to cause diarrhoea and degrade soft tissue to produce spreading cellulitis and necrosis. In hosts with impaired defences, particularly those with chronic liver disease or malignancy, the organism can invade the bloodstream, and its production of inducible beta-lactamases contributes to treatment difficulty. Self-limited gastroenteritis and localised wound infections generally do well, whereas necrotising soft-tissue disease and bacteraemia in immunocompromised hosts carry significant mortality without prompt antibiotics and surgery.

The behaviour is often habitual and is reinforced by anxiety, eating habits and carbonated drinks, and it may be exacerbated by devices that deliver positive airway pressure. Unlike supragastric belching, the swallowed air genuinely enters the stomach and gut, which accounts for the associated bloating and distension. The condition is benign and often improves with behavioural change and treatment of contributing factors, though it can be persistent, particularly when linked to anxiety or assisted ventilation.

develops when the afferent (biliopancreatic) limb of a gastrojejunostomy becomes obstructed by kinking, adhesions, internal herniation, stenosis, recurrent tumour, or a long redundant loop. Bile and pancreatic secretions accumulate in the closed or partially obstructed limb, raising intraluminal pressure; once the pressure overcomes the obstruction the accumulated fluid is discharged suddenly, producing projectile bilious vomiting and relief of pain. Chronic stasis fosters small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth, deconjugation of bile salts, and consequent fat and vitamin malabsorption, while acute complete obstruction risks duodenal stump rupture and pancreatitis. Acute afferent loop obstruction carries significant risk and requires urgent intervention, whereas chronic partial obstruction can often be corrected surgically with good functional outcomes; untreated stasis leads to progressive malabsorption.

Intracranial haemorrhage or other major spontaneous bleeding Spontaneous splenic rupture or intra-abdominal haemorrhage Thrombotic events, which can occur despite the bleeding phenotype Pregnancy complications including recurrent miscarriage and placental abruption Confusing afibrinogenaemia with dysfibrinogenaemia by relying on a single test rather than both activity and antigen Forgetting that these patients can thrombose as well as bleed Overlooking fibrinogen replacement to sustain pregnancy Attributing grossly abnormal clotting times to DIC or liver disease without measuring fibrinogen Fibrinogen is the soluble plasma protein that thrombin converts to fibrin, the structural scaffold of the clot, and it also supports platelet aggregation by bridging activated platelets. Congenital afibrinogenaemia results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in one of the three fibrinogen genes (FGA, FGB, FGG), abolishing production or secretion of the protein. Without fibrinogen, no fibrin clot can form and platelet aggregation is impaired, so all fibrin-dependent coagulation assays are markedly prolonged and haemostasis fails, producing bleeding that frequently manifests at birth. The same molecule is required for placental integrity, so its absence causes recurrent pregnancy loss and abruption. A coexisting thrombotic tendency reflects loss of fibrinogen's normal role in binding and clearing thrombin, leaving unbound thrombin free to act elsewhere. With fibrinogen concentrate replacement, bleeding episodes can be controlled and pregnancies supported, giving a reasonable outlook, though patients face lifelong risks of both haemorrhage and thrombosis requiring specialist management.

age related functional decline — functional decline in older adults, age-related disability, deconditioning frailty syndrome sarcopenia depression dementia or other cognitive impairment parkinsonism and other gait disorders occult infection or other acute illness anaemia or hypothyroidism comprehensive geriatric assessment functional scales such as the Barthel Index, Lawton instrumental scale, gait speed and Timed Up and Go frailty assessment using the Fried phenotype or Clinical Frailty Scale cognitive and mood screening full blood count, urea and electrolytes and thyroid function vitamin D and vitamin B12 levels medication review with physiotherapy and occupational therapy assessment Decline is defined by loss of basic and instrumental activities of daily living, so quantify it with validated scales rather than relying on diagnoses alone. An abrupt functional decline is frequently the sole presenting sign of acute illness such as infection or myocardial infarction in older adults, and should be treated as a red flag. Hospital-associated deconditioning develops within days of bed rest, so early mobilisation and removal of tethers such as catheters and lines are preventive. Frailty, sarcopenia and disability are overlapping but distinct constructs that guide different interventions. Comprehensive geriatric assessment reduces functional decline and institutionalisation. Correctable contributors such as visual and hearing impairment, foot problems and home hazards are easily overlooked. Progressive resistance exercise combined with adequate protein intake can reverse sarcopenia even in the very old. Always screen for reversible drivers including depression, polypharmacy, pain, malnutrition and undertreated chronic disease. abrupt or stepwise decline suggesting acute illness or stroke recurrent falls with injury new urinary or faecal incontinence rapid unintentional weight loss safeguarding concerns such as neglect or an unsafe home environment attributing acute decline to old age and missing an underlying acute illness prescribing bed rest and promoting deconditioning overlooking sensory impairment and environmental hazards failing to set realistic patient-centred functional goals not reassessing function after a hospital admission Age-related functional decline is the progressive loss of ability to perform activities of daily living arising from the interaction of ageing physiology and superimposed disease. Intrinsic changes include sarcopenia, reduced aerobic capacity and physiological reserve, and sensory decline, which lower the threshold at which stressors overwhelm capacity. Chronic multimorbidity and frailty erode reserve further, while acute precipitants such as illness, hospitalisation, enforced immobility and iatrogenesis trigger rapid deconditioning. Much of the observed decline reflects modifiable disease and inactivity rather than intrinsic ageing, which is why distinguishing usual from successful ageing matters and why targeted intervention can alter the trajectory. Functional decline predicts falls, hospitalisation, institutionalisation and death, but multicomponent interventions combining exercise, nutrition and comprehensive geriatric assessment can slow, halt or partially reverse it, particularly when precipitants are addressed early.

age, family history, and pale iris/light exposure also contribute Intravitreal anti-VEGF injection is the mainstay for neovascular AMD and can stabilise or improve vision Dietary antioxidant and zinc supplementation can reduce progression risk in intermediate dry AMD Sudden central distortion, blurring, or a new scotoma suggesting conversion to neovascular AMD — urgent referral Sudden severe drop in central vision from submacular haemorrhage Rapid progression in the second eye of a patient with unilateral wet AMD Any acute change while on anti-VEGF therapy indicating recurrent activity Dismissing new metamorphopsia as needing new glasses and delaying urgent referral for wet AMD Failing to advise smoking cessation as a key modifiable risk Assuming peripheral vision loss is due to AMD, when it points elsewhere Not checking and monitoring the fellow eye, which is at high risk Age-related macular degeneration results from cumulative damage to the retinal pigment epithelium, Bruch's membrane, and choriocapillaris at the macula. Impaired clearance of metabolic debris leads to drusen deposition, and oxidative stress, complement-mediated inflammation, and lipofuscin accumulation injure the photoreceptor-RPE complex. In the atrophic form this causes progressive loss of central photoreceptors, whereas in the neovascular form ischaemia and VEGF release drive abnormal choroidal new vessels that leak and bleed beneath and within the retina, rapidly destroying central vision. Dry AMD progresses slowly and central vision may remain functional for years, whereas untreated wet AMD can cause rapid severe central loss; prompt anti-VEGF therapy substantially improves outcomes, though peripheral vision is preserved in all forms.

Agenesis of the corpus callosum — ACC, callosal agenesis, corpus callosum dysgenesis, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, partial agenesis of the corpus callosum Holoprosencephaly with absent corpus callosum Interhemispheric cyst with callosal dysgenesis Septo-optic dysplasia Aicardi syndrome Secondary callosal thinning from destructive or hypoxic-ischaemic injury Chromosomal syndromes with callosal involvement Brain MRI to confirm complete or partial agenesis and detect associated malformations Prenatal ultrasound and foetal MRI when suspected antenatally Chromosomal microarray and, where indicated, exome sequencing Metabolic screening for disorders that include callosal agenesis such as certain organic acidaemias Ophthalmological examination, particularly to evaluate for Aicardi syndrome Developmental assessment and electroencephalography if seizures occur Complete or partial absence of the corpus callosum, the major commissure connecting the cerebral hemispheres, and one of the most common brain malformations It may be isolated or, more often clinically significant, part of a wider syndrome, chromosomal disorder, or metabolic condition, so a careful search for associated anomalies is essential Characteristic MRI features include widely spaced parallel lateral ventricles, colpocephaly (dilated occipital horns), a high-riding third ventricle, and radiating medial gyri (the sunburst sign) When complete agenesis is present, longitudinal Probst bundles run anteroposteriorly along the medial ventricular walls instead of crossing the midline Outcome depends heavily on associated malformations and the underlying cause; truly isolated agenesis may be compatible with near-normal development Clinical manifestations when present include developmental delay, epilepsy, and subtle deficits in interhemispheric transfer, and some syndromes such as Aicardi syndrome combine it with distinctive eye and seizure features Diagnosis is by prenatal ultrasound and foetal or postnatal MRI, supplemented by genetic and metabolic testing to identify a cause Seizures, including infantile spasms, especially in the context of Aicardi syndrome Features suggesting an underlying metabolic disorder such as decompensation or regression Multiple associated malformations pointing to a syndromic or chromosomal cause Progressive macrocephaly from an associated interhemispheric cyst or hydrocephalus Labelling the malformation isolated without thorough imaging, genetic, and metabolic evaluation for associated conditions Failing to consider Aicardi syndrome in a girl with callosal agenesis, seizures, and chorioretinal lacunae Giving overly pessimistic prognosis for truly isolated cases Confusing an associated interhemispheric cyst or colpocephaly with hydrocephalus requiring shunting The corpus callosum forms in the first half of gestation as axons from cortical neurons cross the midline, guided by midline glial structures and molecular cues. Agenesis results when these guidance mechanisms fail, so callosal axons cannot cross and instead run longitudinally as Probst bundles along the medial ventricular walls. The malformation can arise from single-gene disorders, chromosomal imbalances, metabolic diseases, or disruptions of midline development, and it frequently coexists with other cerebral and systemic anomalies that determine the clinical picture. Isolated agenesis of the corpus callosum can be compatible with normal or near-normal neurodevelopment, though subtle cognitive and social deficits may emerge. When it is part of a syndromic, chromosomal, or metabolic disorder, the prognosis is dictated by the associated condition.

Aggressive NK-cell leukaemia — ANKL, aggressive natural killer cell leukaemia Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type, in leukaemic phase Chronic lymphoproliferative disorder of NK cells T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukaemia Reactive NK-cell expansion with EBV infection Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis from other causes Acute leukaemia Blood film and flow cytometry demonstrating an aberrant NK-cell population EBV studies including EBV-encoded RNA on tissue and viral load Bone marrow examination with immunophenotyping Assessment for haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and coagulation status Imaging to evaluate hepatosplenomegaly and organ involvement A rare, highly aggressive systemic proliferation of natural killer cells, strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus More prevalent in East Asian and some other populations and tends to affect younger to middle-aged adults Presents with a fulminant course of fever, hepatosplenomegaly and rapidly progressive cytopenias Frequently complicated by disseminated intravascular coagulation and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis Circulating and marrow NK cells show an aberrant immunophenotype and clonal EBV Distinguished from chronic NK-cell lymphoproliferative disorders by its aggressive, often fatal behaviour It overlaps biologically with extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma of nasal type Fulminant illness with high fever and rapidly falling blood counts Evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation Features of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis Rapid multi-organ deterioration Mistaking it for a reactive EBV-driven process or benign NK-cell expansion Attributing cytopenias and fever solely to infection and delaying diagnosis Overlooking associated haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis Using standard regimens without asparaginase, which are typically ineffective Aggressive NK-cell leukaemia is a clonal, EBV-driven malignancy of natural killer cells. Latent EBV infection within the neoplastic cells contributes to their survival and proliferation, and the cells release inflammatory cytokines that drive systemic features and can trigger haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Widespread infiltration of blood, bone marrow, liver and spleen produces profound cytopenias, organ dysfunction and coagulopathy, accounting for the fulminant, rapidly fatal clinical course. Aggressive NK-cell leukaemia has a very poor prognosis with short survival despite intensive therapy; asparaginase-containing regimens and allogeneic stem cell transplantation offer the only realistic prospect of prolonged remission in selected patients.

genetically determined type I interferonopathy in which defects in intracellular nucleic-acid metabolism cause self-derived DNA and RNA to accumulate or to be misrecognised as foreign. The causative genes encode nucleases and nucleic-acid-editing or sensing proteins (for example the exonuclease TREX1, the ribonuclease H2 complex, the deoxynucleotide-regulating enzyme SAMHD1, the RNA-editing enzyme ADAR1, and the cytosolic RNA sensor encoded by IFIH1). When these fail, endogenous nucleic acids trigger innate immune sensors and drive chronic overproduction of type I interferon. Sustained interferon signalling produces the inflammatory encephalopathy, intracranial calcification, white matter injury and systemic features that characterise the disorder. The classic early-onset form often causes severe, permanent neurological disability with significant early mortality, though a wide clinical spectrum exists including milder later-onset presentations; interferon-directed therapies offer the prospect of attenuating disease activity, particularly the systemic and skin manifestations.

infection Overlooking the diagnosis in a girl presenting with infantile spasms Assuming a normal fundus excludes the syndrome without a dilated examination Expecting a defined single-gene test result given the largely clinical diagnosis Aicardi syndrome is a developmental disorder attributed to a presumed X-linked dominant mutation that is lethal in hemizygous males, so surviving affected individuals are almost always female, and cases are typically sporadic and de novo. The disturbance affects early neural and neural crest development, producing agenesis or dysgenesis of the corpus callosum and other cortical malformations, an epileptic encephalopathy manifesting as infantile spasms, and characteristic chorioretinal lacunae from focal maldevelopment of the retinal pigment epithelium and choroid. The optic nerve is often colobomatous or hypoplastic. The combination of severe structural brain abnormality and early seizures underlies the marked neurodevelopmental impairment. The prognosis is generally poor, with significant developmental impairment and often refractory epilepsy; survival and function vary with the severity of the brain malformation and seizure control, though the visual lacunae themselves are non-progressive.

care is supportive and multidisciplinary, with seizure control, spasticity and contracture management, nutrition and family support Refractory seizures or status epilepticus requiring intensive management Progressive microcephaly and neurological regression Severe feeding difficulty with aspiration and faltering growth Respiratory compromise from bulbar and truncal involvement Stopping the genetic workup after a negative PLP1 result and missing AIMP1-related disease Interpreting hypomyelination as delayed myelination without appropriate follow-up imaging Attributing the picture to hypoxic-ischaemic injury or non-specific developmental delay Underestimating the seizure burden and its impact on the child and family Omitting autosomal recessive genetic counselling and recurrence-risk discussion AIMP1-related leukodystrophy is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in AIMP1, which encodes an auxiliary protein (also known as p43) that scaffolds and stabilises the multi-enzyme aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase complex central to protein synthesis. Loss of AIMP1 destabilises this complex and may also disturb additional functions attributed to the protein in cytoskeletal and neuronal regulation. The resulting impairment of protein synthesis and cellular homeostasis affects oligodendrocytes and neurons during a critical developmental window, producing failure of myelination (hypomyelination) alongside progressive neuronal loss and cerebral atrophy, which together account for the severe early-onset encephalopathy. AIMP1-related leukodystrophy is a severe, progressive disorder with early onset; affected children commonly have profound neurodevelopmental impairment, refractory epilepsy and marked motor disability, and life expectancy is significantly reduced in the most severe cases. Care is directed at comfort, seizure control and support for the child and family.

progressive constricting fibrotic process affecting a digit, classically the fifth toe. A hyperkeratotic groove develops and deepens into a circumferential fibrous band that progressively strangulates the soft tissues, impairing local blood flow and lymphatic drainage. The resulting distal congestion causes bulbous swelling, while chronic ischaemia and pressure drive progressive resorption of the underlying phalangeal bone, culminating in spontaneous autoamputation. The idiopathic 'true' form has been linked to chronic trauma from barefoot walking and possibly vascular insufficiency, whereas 'pseudo-ainhum' represents an identical constricting band occurring secondary to systemic or dermatological disease that must be identified. True ainhum is slowly progressive and, if untreated, leads over years to spontaneous autoamputation of the affected digit; early band release can preserve the digit, and outcome in pseudo-ainhum depends on the underlying disease.

excluding pre- and post-renal causes points to an intrinsic parenchymal disease (p.340). Reduced renal perfusion (prerenal) accounts for roughly 40-80% of cases and is typically readily reversible if perfusion is restored promptly (p.340). Urinary tract obstruction (postrenal) accounts for under 5% of cases but is usually reversible and should be excluded early, generally with renal ultrasound looking for ureteric/pelvic dilatation (p.340). Ischaemic and toxic acute tubular necrosis (ATN) together account for about 90% of intrinsic AKI (p.340). Prerenal azotaemia and ATN lie on a spectrum of hypoperfusion: prerenal reverses promptly with restored perfusion, whereas ATN involves structural tubular injury (p.340). Microscopic examination of urine sediment is a key bedside test in AKI; dark (muddy-brown) granular casts and/or tubular epithelial cells strongly suggest ATN (p.340). Because a single kidney can clear adequately, complete obstructive AKI requires bladder-outlet/urethral obstruction, bilateral ureteric obstruction, or unilateral obstruction in a solitary kidney (p.340). RBC casts in the urine indicate glomerular disease (acute nephritic picture) and are an indication for early renal biopsy; they are highly specific but very insensitive for glomerulonephritis (p.341). The kidney is particularly vulnerable to toxic injury because it receives about 25% of cardiac output and concentrates and metabolises toxins (p.340). Distinguishing acute from chronic kidney disease can be difficult because anaemia, hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia occur in both; small echogenic kidneys with cortical thinning on ultrasound and radiographic renal osteodystrophy favour chronicity (p.339-340). Oliguria (24-h output under 400 mL) or anuria (under 100 mL); oliguria is never normal as at least ~400 mL of maximally concentrated urine is needed to excrete the daily osmolar load (p.341) Anuria suggesting complete bilateral obstruction, vascular catastrophe (dissection/arterial occlusion), renal vein thrombosis, myeloma cast nephropathy, cortical necrosis, severe ATN, severe rapidly progressive GN, combined NSAID+ACEi/ARB, or shock (p.341) RBC casts or dysmorphic red cells (acute nephritic/glomerular emergency warranting urgent biopsy) (p.341) Dialysis-indication complications of AKI (refractory hyperkalaemia, severe metabolic acidosis, refractory volume overload/pulmonary oedema, uraemic complications) (existing entry; supported p.2330 RRT criteria for overload/acidosis/hyperkalaemia) Failing to exclude obstruction early; ultrasound can be falsely negative very early in obstruction or when ureters cannot dilate (tumour encasement, retroperitoneal fibrosis) (p.340) Measuring urine eosinophils to diagnose interstitial nephritis: eosinophiluria is raised in many causes of AKI, has no diagnostic utility, and is no longer recommended (p.340) Assuming FENa over 1% always means ATN: it may be under 1% in mild nonoliguric ATN (e.g., rhabdomyolysis) and in prerenal-like states such as CHF, cirrhosis or hepatorenal syndrome (p.340) Over-relying on creatinine-based eGFR: muscle mass, sex, race assumptions can mislead (e.g., a bodybuilder with high creatinine) (p.339) Attributing RBC casts to interstitial nephritis: their presence should instead prompt a search for glomerular disease (p.340-341) In prerenal states, a fall in true or effective arterial volume lowers mean arterial pressure and triggers sympathetic activation, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and vasopressin release; GFR is sustained by prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilatation and angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction. Once mean arterial pressure falls below about 80 mmHg, GFR declines steeply. This autoregulation explains why NSAIDs (which block prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilatation) and ACE inhibitors/ARBs (which reduce efferent constriction) can precipitate hemodynamically mediated AKI when volume or perfusion pressure is already reduced, and why patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis (or stenosis of a solitary kidney) are especially susceptible to a precipitous GFR fall on ACEi/ARBs. Sustained hypoperfusion progresses to ischaemic ATN. Nephrotoxic ATN results from a combination of intrarenal vasoconstriction, direct tubular toxicity, and intratubular obstruction (p.340). Prerenal AKI is usually readily reversible when perfusion is restored, and postrenal AKI is usually reversible once obstruction is relieved if recognised early. In nephrotoxic ATN, stopping the offending agent and stabilising blood pressure often suffice, with regeneration of tubular cells and recovery without dialysis. Nonoliguric ATN tends to have less severe potassium and acid-base disturbance and a more rapid recovery than oliguric AKI (p.340-341). AKI severity is staged by the KDIGO criteria (referenced as Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes; p.341, line ref to KDIGO Controversies Conference). Detailed KDIGO stage cut-offs (serum creatinine rise and urine-output thresholds for stages 1-3) are not specified in this source excerpt and are therefore not reproduced. The source's working framework classifies AKI anatomically into prerenal, intrinsic (renal), and postrenal categories, with supporting urinary indices distinguishing prerenal azotaemia from oliguric ATN (Table 55-2, p.340).

The mesial frontal form involves bilateral injury to the anterior cingulate cortex and supplementary motor area, key hubs linking limbic drive to motor action, commonly from anterior cerebral artery territory infarction or anterior communicating artery aneurysm rupture. Recovery varies widely with cause and lesion extent; some patients improve substantially, particularly when a treatable cause such as hydrocephalus is corrected or with dopaminergic therapy, whereas extensive bilateral injury may leave a persistent deficit.

benign gammopathy while amyloid damages organs Overlooking acquired bleeding risk before invasive procedures AL amyloidosis is driven by a clonal, usually small, population of bone marrow plasma cells that produce an unstable monoclonal immunoglobulin light chain. This light chain misfolds and aggregates into insoluble beta-pleated sheet amyloid fibrils that deposit in the extracellular space of vital organs. The fibrils disrupt tissue architecture, and circulating light chains also exert direct toxicity, particularly on cardiomyocytes. Progressive infiltration of the heart, kidneys, nerves, liver and soft tissues produces the multisystem clinical picture, and the amount and toxicity of the light chain, rather than tumour burden, drive organ damage. Prognosis is dominated by the extent of cardiac involvement; early diagnosis with limited cardiac disease allows good responses to plasma-cell-directed therapy, whereas advanced cardiac amyloidosis carries high early mortality.

Alagille syndrome results from haploinsufficiency of the Notch signalling pathway, most commonly through mutations in the ligand JAG1 and occasionally the receptor NOTCH2. Notch signalling is essential for the differentiation and branching morphogenesis of intrahepatic bile ducts, as well as for cardiac, vascular, renal, skeletal, and ocular development. Impaired signalling leads to progressive loss (paucity) of the interlobular bile ducts, causing chronic intrahepatic cholestasis with retention of bile acids and cholesterol, alongside the syndrome's characteristic extrahepatic malformations. Expressivity is highly variable even within families. Outcome is largely determined by the severity of cardiac and vascular anomalies and the progression of liver disease; many patients do well, but a subset develops end-stage cholestatic liver disease requiring transplantation, and vascular events can cause sudden morbidity or mortality.

to inaccurate recurrence-risk counselling Missing subtle brachydactyly or ectopic ossification that would prompt genetic testing Albright hereditary osteodystrophy stems from inactivating variants in GNAS, the gene for Gs-alpha, the signalling protein that couples numerous hormone receptors to adenylate cyclase and cyclic AMP generation. GNAS is subject to tissue-specific genomic imprinting: in tissues such as the renal proximal tubule, expression is predominantly from the maternal allele. When the inactivating variant is maternally inherited, tissues lose most Gs-alpha activity, so hormones acting through Gs-coupled receptors (notably PTH, and often TSH and gonadotrophins) cannot signal effectively, producing multi-hormone resistance and hypocalcaemia despite elevated PTH. When the same variant is paternally inherited, imprinting preserves signalling in these tissues, so the physical AHO phenotype occurs without hormone resistance. The skeletal and soft-tissue features (brachydactyly, ectopic ossification) reflect impaired Gs-alpha-dependent signalling in developing bone and connective tissue. With appropriate calcium and active vitamin D therapy and surveillance for additional hormone resistances, the metabolic disturbance is manageable and life expectancy is generally normal, though short stature, brachydactyly, and ectopic ossification are permanent.

about 40% of those with AUD meet criteria for a major depressive episode but roughly half are substance-induced and resolve within a month of abstinence (Harrison 22e p.3676-3677) Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and alcohol-related cognitive impairment versus other dementias; there is no single 'alcoholic dementia' entity (Harrison 22e p.3676) Peripheral neuropathy of alcohol versus diabetic neuropathy (both bilateral, distal, with numbness, tingling, paresthesias) (Harrison 22e p.3676) Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT >35 U) - marker of heavy consumption (Harrison 22e p.3678) Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT >20 U/L or >2.6%); combined with GGT for higher accuracy (Harrison 22e p.3679) Mean corpuscular volume (high-normal >=91) and serum uric acid (>7 mg/dL) (Harrison 22e p.3679) Blood ethanol level (e.g., 100 mg/dL = 0.10 g/dL) (Harrison 22e p.3675) Toxicology screen for other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines) and opioids in severe intoxication (Harrison 22e p.3679) AUDIT 10-item screening questionnaire (score >=8 may indicate harmful use) - screening only, not diagnostic (Harrison 22e p.3679-3680) MRI/CT may show ventricular enlargement and widened cortical sulci in ~50% of long-term AUD, usually reversible with abstinence (Harrison 22e p.3676) Diabetes mellitus (alcohol-induced transient hypoglycemia and abnormal glucose tolerance) (Harrison 22e p.3675) Primary depressive, anxiety or psychotic disorder (alcohol-induced psychiatric symptoms during intoxication/withdrawal) (Harrison 22e p.3675, 3676-3677) A standard drink contains roughly 10-12 g of ethanol; one typical drink raises the blood ethanol level by about 0.02 g/dL (Harrison 22e p.3675). Behavioral, psychomotor and cognitive impairment appears at only 0.02-0.04 g/dL (one to two drinks); 'legal intoxication' in most U.S. states is 0.08 g/dL, with 0.04 g/dL applied to pilots and to drivers in some countries (Harrison 22e p.3676). In a person without tolerance, light coma with depressed vital signs occurs around 0.30 g/dL and death between 0.30 and 0.40 g/dL; alcohol probably causes more overdose deaths than any other drug (Harrison 22e p.3676). Heavy drinking while fasting can cause transient hypoglycemia within 6-36 h by suppressing gluconeogenesis, producing temporarily abnormal glucose tolerance that can be misread as diabetes until 2-4 weeks of abstinence (Harrison 22e p.3675). Most ethanol is metabolized in the liver: the cytosolic alcohol dehydrogenase pathway generates acetaldehyde (then cleared by aldehyde dehydrogenase), while the microsomal ethanol-oxidizing system (MEOS) handles >=10% at high blood levels (Harrison 22e p.3675). Blackouts (temporary anterograde amnesia while awake) occur in about 35% of drinkers, with en bloc blackouts at levels >0.20 and fragmentary blackouts at >0.12 (Harrison 22e p.3676). Alcohol disrupts sleep architecture, reducing early-night REM and deep sleep and relaxing pharyngeal muscles to worsen snoring and apnea; sleep apnea symptoms occur in about 75% of men with AUD aged >=60 (Harrison 22e p.3676). DSM-5 diagnoses AUD when >=2 of 11 criteria cluster in the same 12-month period; severity is mild (2-3), moderate (4-5) or severe (>=6 items) (Harrison 22e p.3677-3678). Roughly 60% of the risk for AUD is genetic; a flushing response (ALDH variant seen in Japanese, Chinese and Korean individuals) lowers risk, while a low level of response to alcohol predicts future heavy drinking and problems (Harrison 22e p.3678). Useful blood markers of regular heavy intake are GGT (>35 U) and carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT >20 U/L or >2.6%), with the combination more accurate than either alone; high-normal MCV (>=91) and elevated uric acid also support the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3678-3679). Continued heavy drinking shortens life span by about 10 years, with leading causes of early death being heart disease, cancer, accidents and suicide (Harrison 22e p.3678). 'Holiday heart' refers to atrial or ventricular arrhythmias, especially paroxysmal tachycardia, occurring temporarily after heavy drinking in people with no other evidence of heart disease (Harrison 22e p.3677). Withdrawal seizure (about 2% of patients), with higher risk in older age, concomitant medical problems, polydrug misuse and larger alcohol quantities (Harrison 22e p.3680) Withdrawal delirium / delirium tremens (about 1%): agitated delirium with confusion, fluctuating consciousness, tremor and marked autonomic overactivity (Harrison 22e p.3680) Autonomic overactivity during withdrawal: rising pulse, respiratory rate, sweating and body temperature (Harrison 22e p.3680) Severe intoxication with respiratory depression, cardiac arrhythmias or blood pressure instability; light coma near 0.30 g/dL and death 0.30-0.40 g/dL (Harrison 22e p.3676, 3679) Gastrointestinal bleeding from hemorrhagic gastritis or a Mallory-Weiss tear after violent vomiting (Harrison 22e p.3677) Pregnancy: any drinking risks fetal alcohol spectrum disorder; complete abstinence advised (Harrison 22e p.3677) Misreading alcohol-induced transient hypoglycemia/abnormal glucose tolerance as diabetes before 2-4 weeks of abstinence (Harrison 22e p.3675) Misdiagnosing alcohol ketoacidosis as diabetic ketosis (Harrison 22e p.3675) Treating substance-induced psychiatric symptoms with long-term medication when they typically resolve within days to ~4 weeks of abstinence (only short-term antipsychotics for substance-induced psychosis are usually needed) (Harrison 22e p.3676-3677) Giving routine IV fluids in withdrawal - most patients are normally hydrated or mildly overhydrated, so fluids should be avoided unless there is a specific medical indication, bleeding, vomiting or diarrhea (Harrison 22e p.3680) Relying on questionnaires (e.g., AUDIT) alone - they are screening tools and a face-to-face interview is required for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3679) A false-negative tuberculin skin test from impaired delayed-hypersensitivity in chronic heavy drinkers (Harrison 22e p.3677) Assuming AUD spares affluent or professional patients - lifetime risk among physicians is similar to the general population (Harrison 22e p.3678) Ethanol is a CNS depressant that acutely enhances GABA activity (notably at GABA-A receptors) and inhibits postsynaptic NMDA excitatory glutamate receptors; chronic exposure produces compensatory downregulation of GABA-related activity and upregulation of NMDA receptor subunits. Falling blood levels after chronic use therefore unmask a hyperexcitable state, explaining withdrawal phenomena. Acute alcohol raises dopamine in the ventral tegmentum and nucleus accumbens, releases beta-endorphins, and increases serotonin and stress hormones (cortisol, ACTH), driving reward, craving and relapse. Cellular (pharmacodynamic), metabolic (up to ~30% faster hepatic metabolism after 1-2 weeks) and learned/behavioral mechanisms contribute to acquired tolerance. Cellular adaptations may take weeks to resolve, so rapid drops in blood level produce withdrawal that is most intense in the first 5 days but with protracted symptoms (disturbed sleep, anxiety) lasting up to 4-6 months (Harrison 22e p.3675-3676). With at least a year of follow-up after treatment, more than half of people with AUD achieve a marked reduction in drinking and related problems or full abstinence, and even without formal treatment or self-help groups there is at least a 20% chance of spontaneous long-term remission. Many alcohol-related organ changes are reversible with abstinence: blood pressure normalizes within weeks, GGT/CDT return toward normal within weeks, thrombocytopenia usually resolves within a week (unless cirrhosis or congestive splenomegaly), MRI/CT brain changes generally reverse, and acute myopathy improves though may not fully remit. Continued heavy drinking shortens life span by roughly 10 years, mainly through heart disease, cancer, accidents and suicide (Harrison 22e p.3677-3678). DSM-5 alcohol use disorder severity by number of criteria endorsed in a 12-month period: mild = 2-3 items, moderate = 4-5 items, severe = >=6 of the 11 items (Harrison 22e p.3678). Effects of blood alcohol levels without tolerance: 0.02 decreased inhibitions; 0.08 reduced complex cognition and motor performance; 0.20 slurred speech, incoordination, poor judgment; 0.30 light coma with depressed vital signs; 0.40 death (Harrison 22e p.3676).

Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease — alcoholic hepatitis, alcoholic cirrhosis, ALD Viral hepatitis (e.g., hepatitis B or C) Wilson's disease Severe autoimmune liver disease Drug-induced liver injury (DILI), including amiodarone-related pseudoalcoholic injury Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD) and MetALD Hemochromatosis Ischemic hepatitis Biliary obstruction Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) Viral hepatitis (hepatitis B or C) producing aminotransferase elevation that can be confused with ALD Liver function tests with AST, ALT (AST/ALT ratio), GGT, bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count AUDIT (Alcohol Use Disorders Inventory Test) to identify alcohol use disorder Abdominal ultrasound, MRI, or CT to detect steatosis, nodularity, and signs of portal hypertension Controlled attenuation parameter (CAP) or MR proton density fat fraction (MR-PDFF) for noninvasive hepatic fat quantification Transient elastography / liver stiffness measurement (e.g., FibroScan) for fibrosis staging Fib-4 score (age, AST, ALT, platelets) to exclude advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis (threshold <3.25) Transjugular liver biopsy when confounding factors are present (to confirm alcohol-associated hepatitis) Imaging to exclude biliary obstruction and HCC; AFP and ultrasonography for HCC surveillance in cirrhosis Infection workup: chest x-ray plus blood, urine, and ascites cultures in alcohol-associated hepatitis MASLD/NAFLD (key distinction: ALD typically shows AST/ALT >2:1, whereas NAFLD usually has ALT >= AST) Amiodarone hepatotoxicity producing pseudoalcoholic liver injury (steatosis to alcoholic-hepatitis-like neutrophilic infiltration with Mallory-Denk bodies) Wilson's disease Autoimmune hepatitis Hemochromatosis Ischemic hepatitis ALD is a spectrum: alcohol-associated fatty liver (steatosis) and steatohepatitis progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis; acute alcohol-associated hepatitis is an acute-on-chronic form associated with liver failure and high mortality (p.2697). Characteristic biochemical signature: AST/ALT ratio >1 (commonly cited as >2:1 for alcoholic liver disease), with serum AST rarely exceeding 300 IU/L; in alcohol-associated hepatitis AST and ALT do not exceed 400 IU/L and the AST/ALT ratio is >1.5 with serum bilirubin >3 mg/dL (p.2699). Steatosis and steatohepatitis are clinically silent; symptoms typically appear only when alcohol-associated cirrhosis decompensates or alcohol-associated hepatitis develops (p.2699). Alcohol-associated hepatitis is defined clinically by heavy drinking (>40 g/d women, >50-60 g/d men) for >6 months with <60 days abstinence before symptom onset, presenting with rapid-onset jaundice (bilirubin >3 mg/dL), often with fever, malaise, and tender hepatomegaly (p.2698). Prolonged alcohol abstinence is the most effective therapy to reduce progression and reverse ALD; steatosis and steatohepatitis are reversible with cessation of alcohol consumption (p.2699). There are currently NO approved drugs for treatment of alcohol-associated steatosis or steatohepatitis with or without fibrosis (p.2699). Severity of alcohol-associated hepatitis is stratified by Maddrey discriminant function (MDF) and MELD: severe disease (MDF >=32 or MELD >20) carries high short-term mortality (~30% at 3 months) and may benefit from glucocorticoids; moderate disease (MDF <32 or MELD <=20) still carries ~20% 1-year mortality (p.2700). Lille score >=0.45 after 7 days of glucocorticoid treatment identifies non-responders unlikely to benefit from continued therapy; glucocorticoids should be stopped and early liver transplantation considered (p.2700). Liver transplantation for alcohol-associated decompensated cirrhosis or HCC is the leading indication for liver transplantation in the United States (p.2699-2700). In confirmed cirrhosis, HCC surveillance with liver ultrasonography and serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) every 6 months and upper GI endoscopy to screen for varices are recommended (p.2699). Only 10-20% of individuals with alcohol-induced hepatic steatosis develop progressive liver disease and cirrhosis; women develop ALD at a lower daily alcohol intake (p.2698). Severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (MDF >=32 or MELD >20) - high short-term mortality (~30% at 3 months) Rapid-onset jaundice with serum bilirubin >3 mg/dL, fever, and tender hepatomegaly Clinical signs of hepatic decompensation: ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy Bacterial infection (occurs in 12-26% of severe alcohol-associated hepatitis at admission) Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) Acute kidney injury / hepatorenal syndrome Lille score >=0.45 at day 7 (glucocorticoid non-response) - high 30-day mortality Multiorgan failure and shock Diagnosis of ALD requires exclusion of other liver diseases in heavy drinkers; do not attribute liver disease to alcohol without ruling out viral hepatitis, Wilson's disease, autoimmune liver disease, and DILI. Atypical laboratory values (AST <50 IU/L or >400 IU/L, or AST/ALT ratio <1.5) argue against alcohol-associated hepatitis and warrant transjugular liver biopsy - 10-20% of clinically diagnosed cases have a different disease on biopsy. Do not give glucocorticoids when contraindications are present: uncontrolled infection/sepsis, AKI/hepatorenal syndrome, uncontrolled upper GI bleeding, concomitant viral hepatitis/HCC/pancreatitis/DILI/active TB/HIV, multiorgan failure, or shock; glucocorticoids may be used only once infection, sepsis, and GI bleeding are adequately controlled. Liver biopsy is rarely needed to diagnose simple steatosis or steatohepatitis - reserve invasive biopsy for confounding/atypical cases. Distinguish ALD from NAFLD/MASLD by the AST/ALT pattern (ALD favors AST/ALT >2:1). Ethanol is rapidly absorbed in the upper GI tract and metabolized predominantly in the liver, reaching it via the portal vein. Most ethanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase 1 (ADH1) to acetaldehyde in hepatocytes; chronic consumption also induces CYP2E1, which similarly generates acetaldehyde. Beyond direct acetaldehyde toxicity, ethanol metabolism generates reactive oxygen species causing hepatocyte injury through lipid peroxidation and DNA damage. Acetaldehyde is then oxidized to acetate by acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH); inherited ALDH2 deficiency (common in Asian populations) causes acetaldehyde accumulation with nausea and cutaneous flushing. Steatosis arises because acetate becomes acetyl-CoA feeding fatty acid/triglyceride synthesis, alcohol upregulates lipogenic genes (partly epigenetically) while suppressing fatty acid transport/oxidation, and the increased NADH/NAD+ ratio reduces mitochondrial beta-oxidation; alcohol also mobilizes fatty acids from adipose and intestine into the liver. A subset develop gut dysbiosis and increased intestinal permeability, allowing microbial components (e.g., bacterial LPS) to reach the liver via the portal vein, driving inflammation, hepatocyte death, and fibrotic pathway activation; sustained alcohol use progresses to cirrhosis with portal hypertension. Impaired liver regeneration may contribute to acute alcohol-associated hepatitis arising in underlying cirrhosis (p.2698). Steatosis and steatohepatitis are reversible with abstinence, but only 10-20% of those with steatosis progress to cirrhosis. In alcohol-associated hepatitis, short-term mortality is predicted by MDF, MELD, or ABIC scores: moderate disease (MDF <32 or MELD <=20) carries ~20% 1-year mortality, whereas severe disease (MDF >=32 or MELD >20) carries ~30% 3-month mortality. Glucocorticoids reduce risk of death in severe disease within 28 days but not over the following 6 months. While short-term prognosis depends on disease severity at presentation, long-term prognosis (>1 year) largely depends on alcohol abstinence and underlying cirrhosis. Non-responders to medical therapy have high 30-day mortality (p.2700). Alcohol-associated hepatitis severity: Moderate AH = MDF <32 or MELD <=20 (~20% 1-year mortality); Severe AH = Maddrey discriminant function (MDF) >=32 or MELD >20 (~30% 3-month mortality), candidates for glucocorticoids if no contraindication. MDF = 4.6 x (prothrombin time prolongation above control in seconds) + serum bilirubin (mg/dL). Day-7 Lille score >=0.45 defines glucocorticoid non-response. Cirrhosis prognosis assessed by Child-Pugh-Turcotte (CPT) and MELD (or sodium-MELD). Fibrosis staging by liver stiffness: <6 kPa normal, >8 kPa indicates >=F3 advanced fibrosis, >12.5 kPa indicates F4 cirrhosis.

Alcohol withdrawal syndrome — alcohol withdrawal, delirium tremens, DTs, alcohol withdrawal delirium Delirium from other causes (infection, metabolic derangement) Sedative-hypnotic or benzodiazepine withdrawal Stimulant intoxication Thyroid storm Sepsis or central nervous system infection Wernicke encephalopathy Hepatic encephalopathy Validated withdrawal severity scale to guide symptom-triggered treatment Electrolytes including magnesium and phosphate, glucose, and renal function Liver function tests and full blood count Assessment for infection and other precipitants of delirium Thiamine status and evaluation for Wernicke encephalopathy Occurs on reduction or cessation of heavy, sustained alcohol use, with symptoms typically emerging within hours to a few days Early features include tremor, anxiety, agitation, sweating, nausea, tachycardia, and hypertension; insomnia and irritability are common Withdrawal seizures (typically generalised tonic-clonic) tend to occur early, usually within the first day or two Alcoholic hallucinosis produces hallucinations, often visual, with an otherwise clear sensorium, distinguishing it from delirium tremens Delirium tremens is a later, life-threatening complication with clouded consciousness, disorientation, severe autonomic hyperactivity, and hallucinations, usually appearing after a couple of days Management principles rest on benzodiazepine-based regimens, often symptom-triggered using a standardised withdrawal scale, in a supportive monitored setting Give thiamine before or with glucose to prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy, and correct fluid and electrolyte disturbances Assess withdrawal severity and complication risk with a validated instrument and identify high-risk patients for closer monitoring Delirium tremens with severe autonomic instability, a medical emergency with appreciable mortality if untreated Withdrawal seizures or status epilepticus Signs of Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) Hyperthermia, marked tachycardia, and haemodynamic instability Giving glucose before thiamine and precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy Underestimating severity and under-dosing benzodiazepines in early withdrawal Attributing agitation solely to withdrawal while missing infection, bleeding, or metabolic causes Failing to identify patients at high risk of seizures or delirium tremens Not addressing underlying alcohol use disorder after acute treatment Chronic alcohol exposure enhances inhibitory gamma-aminobutyric acid signalling and suppresses excitatory glutamatergic (NMDA receptor) activity; the brain adapts by downregulating GABA and upregulating glutamate systems. When alcohol is withdrawn, this adaptation leaves a state of central nervous system hyperexcitability and autonomic overactivity, producing the tremor, seizures, and delirium of the withdrawal syndrome. Uncomplicated withdrawal usually resolves within several days with appropriate treatment. Delirium tremens carries significant mortality if unrecognised but is greatly reduced with timely benzodiazepine therapy and supportive care. Long-term prognosis depends on engagement with relapse prevention and treatment of alcohol use disorder.

folate, avoidance of exertional and febrile triggers of muscle breakdown, and splenectomy considered in severe transfusion-dependent haemolysis Acute rhabdomyolysis with risk of acute kidney injury Severe neonatal or childhood jaundice requiring exchange transfusion Aplastic crisis after parvovirus B19 infection Progressive myopathy or failure to thrive Missing the muscle component and attributing symptoms to a purely haematological disorder Failing to check creatine kinase during febrile illness or after exercise Not counselling patients to avoid exertional and febrile triggers of rhabdomyolysis Overlooking transfusional iron overload during long-term follow-up Aldolase A catalyses the cleavage of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into the two triose phosphates that continue through Because the A isoenzyme is also highly expressed in skeletal muscle, deficiency additionally compromises muscle energy metabolism, predisposing to myopathy and exercise- or fever-induced rhabdomyolysis. Outlook depends on the severity of both the haemolytic anaemia and the muscle involvement; well-compensated cases fare well, whereas recurrent rhabdomyolysis and severe transfusion-dependent anaemia carry greater morbidity.

antagonism Severe or resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia raising concern for significant mineralocorticoid excess Profound hypokalaemia causing arrhythmia or muscle weakness A large or radiologically atypical adrenal mass suggesting carcinoma rather than a benign adenoma Hypertensive target-organ damage disproportionate to blood pressure level Screening while on interfering drugs (e.g. mineralocorticoid antagonists) that invalidate the aldosterone-to-renin ratio Relying on CT appearances alone and operating on the wrong side without adrenal vein sampling Missing normokalaemic primary aldosteronism by only testing hypertensive patients with low potassium Failing to replace potassium and control blood pressure before surgery An aldosterone-producing adenoma is a benign cortical tumour, usually arising in the zona glomerulosa, that autonomously secretes aldosterone independent of the renin-angiotensin system. Somatic mutations affecting ion transport (for example in the KCNJ5 potassium channel, or in calcium-handling genes) depolarise glomerulosa cells, increase intracellular calcium and drive constitutive aldosterone synthase activity. Excess aldosterone promotes renal sodium retention and potassium and hydrogen ion excretion, producing volume-dependent hypertension, a tendency to hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis, and suppression of renin. Chronic mineralocorticoid excess also causes target-organ damage disproportionate to the blood pressure. Unilateral adenomas are often cured or substantially improved by adrenalectomy, with normalisation of potassium and improvement in blood pressure, though long-standing hypertension may persist and require ongoing therapy. Untreated primary aldosteronism carries excess cardiovascular and renal risk relative to matched essential hypertension.

Adult-onset Alexander disease (GFAP) — Alexander disease type II, GFAP-related astrocytopathy, adult Alexander disease, hereditary astrocytopathy Multiple system atrophy with brainstem and cerebellar involvement Multiple sclerosis and other inflammatory brainstem disease Brainstem or foramen magnum tumour or structural lesion Progressive bulbar palsy and motor neuron disease Other genetic leukoencephalopathies with brainstem involvement Chronic small-vessel or vascular brainstem disease Brain and cervical spine MRI to identify medullary and upper cord atrophy (the tadpole appearance) and brainstem signal change GFAP sequencing to confirm the diagnosis, including consideration of de novo and mosaic variants Swallow assessment (including videofluoroscopy) given the risk of aspiration Autonomic function testing where dysautonomia is prominent Sleep study if sleep-disordered breathing is suspected CSF and inflammatory workup to help exclude alternative brainstem pathology A primary astrocyte disorder (astrocytopathy) caused by variants in GFAP, the gene for glial fibrillary acidic protein, with Rosenthal fibre accumulation in astrocytes The adult-onset (type II) form differs from the infantile disease and presents predominantly with brainstem and bulbar dysfunction rather than macrocephaly Characteristic features include palatal myoclonus, dysarthria and dysphagia, cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, autonomic disturbance and sleep problems The MRI hallmark is atrophy and signal change of the medulla oblongata and upper cervical spinal cord, producing the recognisable tadpole-like appearance of a thin medulla and cord with relative preservation of the pons Contrast enhancement or signal change of specific brainstem structures may be seen and supports the diagnosis Most cases result from de novo dominant GFAP variants, though inherited and mosaic cases occur, so a negative family history does not exclude the diagnosis There is no disease-modifying therapy; management is supportive and multidisciplinary with attention to swallowing, airway, mobility and autonomic symptoms Severe dysphagia with recurrent aspiration and pneumonia Sleep-disordered breathing or central hypoventilation from brainstem involvement Autonomic instability affecting cardiovascular or bladder function Rapid bulbar deterioration compromising airway protection Not recognising the tadpole medullary and cervical cord atrophy as a specific pointer to the diagnosis Excluding the diagnosis on the basis of a negative family history when many cases are de novo or mosaic Mislabelling the presentation as multiple sclerosis or multiple system atrophy Overlooking palatal myoclonus, a useful clinical clue to brainstem involvement Failing to assess and protect swallowing and the airway as bulbar signs progress Alexander disease is caused by dominant, usually gain-of-function variants in GFAP, which encodes the principal intermediate filament protein of astrocytes. The abnormal protein aggregates within astrocytes as Rosenthal fibres, impairing astrocyte function and disturbing their support of neurons and myelinating cells. In the adult-onset form the pathology preferentially affects the brainstem and upper spinal cord astrocytes, producing the selective medullary and cervical cord atrophy seen on imaging and the associated bulbar, cerebellar and autonomic manifestations, in contrast to the widespread frontal-predominant leukodystrophy of the infantile form. Adult-onset Alexander disease is generally slowly progressive over years, with gradually worsening bulbar, cerebellar and autonomic dysfunction; the course is variable and some patients remain relatively stable for long periods. Prognosis is influenced chiefly by bulbar and respiratory involvement, which can lead to aspiration and other complications.
