or autonomic compromise Acute deterioration superimposed on a chronic course Excluding the diagnosis because there is no family history, despite the predominance of de novo mutations Misreading adult brainstem-predominant disease as a tumour or demyelinating disorder Overlooking the diagnostic value of characteristic MRI patterns Delaying genetic testing while pursuing invasive investigations Alexander disease is caused by gain-of-function mutations in GFAP, the gene for the main intermediate filament protein of astrocytes. Mutant protein accumulates and forms Rosenthal fibres within astrocytes, disturbing astrocyte function and secondarily impairing myelin maintenance, producing a leukodystrophy. The astrocytic dysfunction is considered the primary event, distinguishing this from disorders that primarily affect oligodendrocytes or myelin, and the distribution of pathology accounts for the frontal-predominant cerebral and brainstem clinical features. The infantile form generally carries the poorest prognosis with progressive deterioration over a few years, whereas juvenile and adult forms often follow a slower, more variable course; management remains supportive as no curative therapy exists.

ALG12-CDG (CDG-Ig) — ALG12, congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ig, CDG-Ig, dolichyl-P-mannose:Man7GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol mannosyltransferase deficiency Other type I CDG subtypes (e.g. PMM2-CDG, ALG1-CDG, ALG3-CDG) Primary immunodeficiency with recurrent infection and hypogammaglobulinaemia Syndromic causes of microcephaly with developmental delay Mitochondrial disease in infancy Peroxisomal disorders Chromosomal or copy-number syndromes with dysmorphism Transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry demonstrating a type I pattern ALG12 molecular genetic testing Immunoglobulin levels and immune function assessment Coagulation studies and liver function tests Neuroimaging for microcephaly and structural change Growth, endocrine and dysmorphology evaluation An N-linked type I CDG caused by biallelic ALG12 variants affecting a mannosyltransferase in endoplasmic reticulum assembly of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide Presents in infancy with developmental delay, hypotonia, microcephaly, dysmorphic features and failure to thrive Recurrent infections with hypogammaglobulinaemia are a notable feature, reflecting hypoglycosylation of immunoglobulins Genital and skeletal abnormalities and feeding difficulties are also reported within the phenotype Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing shows a type I pattern from under-occupancy of N-glycan sites Coagulopathy and hepatic involvement can occur as part of the multisystem picture Management is supportive and multidisciplinary; ALG12 sequencing confirms the diagnosis after a suggestive transferrin pattern Recurrent or severe infections indicating clinically significant immunodeficiency Progressive microcephaly or developmental regression Bleeding from coagulation factor deficiency Failure to thrive with multi-organ involvement Investigating recurrent infection as isolated immunodeficiency without recognising an underlying CDG Confusing the type I transferrin pattern with secondary causes Overlooking bleeding risk before procedures Assuming disease-modifying therapy exists when care is supportive ALG12 encodes a dolichol-phosphate-mannose-dependent mannosyltransferase that adds a mannose residue during endoplasmic reticulum assembly of the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide precursor. Deficiency leaves an incomplete precursor that is transferred inefficiently or as a truncated glycan, causing under-occupancy of N-linked sites and a type I transferrin pattern. Hypoglycosylation of immunoglobulins and other proteins contributes to the recurrent infections, developmental and multisystem features. The defect lies in precursor assembly and transfer rather than glycan processing, consistent with its type I classification. ALG12-CDG causes lasting neurodevelopmental disability, and outcome depends heavily on the frequency and severity of infections and other systemic complications. Severity varies with residual enzyme function.

ALG1-CDG (CDG-Ik) — ALG1, congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ik, CDG-Ik, GDP-mannose:GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol mannosyltransferase deficiency Other N-linked type I CDG subtypes (e.g. PMM2-CDG, ALG3-CDG, ALG12-CDG) Early-onset epileptic encephalopathies of other genetic causes Congenital muscular dystrophies with brain involvement Mitochondrial cytopathies presenting in infancy Peroxisomal biogenesis disorders (e.g. Zellweger spectrum) Non-glycosylation causes of neonatal hydrops or nephrotic syndrome Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry to identify a type I glycosylation pattern ALG1 molecular genetic (gene panel or exome) confirmation Coagulation studies including antithrombin, protein C, factor XI and factor IX Liver function tests and abdominal imaging for hepatopathy Endocrine screen including thyroid function Neuroimaging and electroencephalography for encephalopathy and seizures An N-linked type I congenital disorder of glycosylation caused by biallelic ALG1 variants impairing early assembly of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide on dolichol Typically a severe multisystem paediatric disorder with profound developmental delay, hypotonia, drug-resistant epilepsy and frequent early mortality Systemic features overlap the broader CDG phenotype: hepatopathy, coagulopathy with low antithrombin and factor levels, and endocrine abnormalities Nephrotic-range proteinuria, hydrops and oedema are reported and reflect impaired glycosylation of plasma and structural proteins Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing shows a type I pattern (increased asialo- and disialotransferrin) reflecting under-occupancy of N-glycan sites There is no disease-specific pharmacotherapy; management is supportive and multidisciplinary, coordinated through a metabolic service Diagnosis is confirmed by ALG1 molecular genetic testing after a suggestive transferrin pattern Neonatal or infantile hydrops, generalised oedema or nephrotic-range proteinuria Drug-resistant seizures with progressive encephalopathy Bleeding or thrombotic events from combined coagulation factor deficiency Failure to thrive with multi-organ involvement suggesting a severe CDG Attributing the transferrin abnormality to secondary causes such as galactosaemia, alcohol or sepsis without confirmatory genetics Overlooking the coagulopathy, which can cause both bleeding and thrombosis Expecting a disease-modifying pharmacological treatment when only supportive care exists Missing the diagnosis when a normal transferrin pattern occurs, as some CDG subtypes can screen falsely negative ALG1 encodes a mannosyltransferase that adds the first mannose to the growing dolichol-linked oligosaccharide within the endoplasmic reticulum. Loss of function truncates assembly of the lipid-linked precursor, so fewer complete oligosaccharides are transferred en bloc to nascent proteins, producing under-glycosylation at N-linked sites. Because the defect lies in assembly and transfer of the precursor rather than its later trimming, the biochemical signature is a type I transferrin pattern. Widespread hypoglycosylation of enzymes, transport proteins, clotting factors and membrane receptors underlies the multisystem paediatric phenotype. ALG1-CDG is among the more severe glycosylation disorders, and many affected infants die in the first years of life; survivors typically have profound neurodevelopmental disability. Prognosis correlates broadly with residual enzyme activity and the burden of systemic complications.

ALG3-CDG (CDG-Id) — ALG3, congenital disorder of glycosylation type Id, CDG-Id, dolichyl-P-mannose:Man5GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol mannosyltransferase deficiency Other type I CDG subtypes (e.g. ALG1-CDG, ALG12-CDG, PMM2-CDG) Genetic causes of severe microcephaly with epileptic encephalopathy Peroxisomal biogenesis disorders Mitochondrial encephalopathies Congenital causes of optic atrophy with developmental delay Structural brain malformation syndromes Transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry showing a type I pattern ALG3 molecular genetic testing Neuroimaging for microcephaly and structural change Electroencephalography for seizures Ophthalmological assessment including optic nerve evaluation Coagulation and liver function studies An N-linked type I CDG caused by ALG3 deficiency, a mannosyltransferase in endoplasmic reticulum assembly of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide Presents with severe developmental delay, profound microcephaly, hypotonia and drug-resistant seizures Ophthalmological anomalies including optic atrophy and cortical visual impairment are commonly reported Skeletal abnormalities, dysmorphism, feeding difficulties and failure to thrive are part of the phenotype Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing shows a type I pattern from under-occupancy of N-glycan sites Coagulation and hepatic abnormalities may accompany the neurological picture Management is supportive and multidisciplinary; ALG3 sequencing confirms the diagnosis Drug-resistant seizures with progressive encephalopathy Severe or progressive microcephaly Visual deterioration from optic atrophy Failure to thrive with multi-organ involvement Attributing the transferrin abnormality to secondary causes without genetic confirmation Overlooking the coagulopathy before procedures Assuming disease-modifying therapy exists when only supportive care is available Missing associated ophthalmological complications that need surveillance ALG3 encodes a dolichol-phosphate-mannose-dependent mannosyltransferase acting on the endoplasmic reticulum-luminal face during assembly of the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide precursor. Loss of function yields a truncated precursor that is transferred inefficiently to protein, leaving N-linked sites under-occupied and generating a type I transferrin pattern. Because the block is in precursor assembly rather than glycan processing, the disorder is classified as type I. Widespread hypoglycosylation impairs neuronal, ocular and other glycoproteins, producing the severe neurodevelopmental and multisystem phenotype. ALG3-CDG is a severe disorder with profound neurodevelopmental disability and significant early morbidity and mortality; prognosis is generally poor and correlates with residual enzyme activity and complication burden.

ALG6-CDG (CDG type Ic) — ALG6 deficiency, dolichyl-P-Glc:Man9GlcNAc2-PP-dolichyl glucosyltransferase deficiency, CDG-Ic, ALG6 PMM2-CDG and other type 1 CDGs (shared transferrin screening pattern) Genetic/idiopathic epilepsy with developmental delay Mitochondrial disorders Inherited thrombophilias and bleeding disorders Congenital hypotonia of neuromuscular origin Congenital ichthyosis syndromes Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing/mass spectrometry (type 1 pattern) Lipid-linked oligosaccharide (LLO) analysis in fibroblasts ALG6 gene sequencing for confirmation Coagulation panel including antithrombin, protein C and protein S Brain MRI and EEG for epilepsy and structural anomalies Ophthalmological assessment for retinopathy Liver function and glucose monitoring Second most common type 1 CDG after PMM2-CDG, caused by biallelic ALG6 variants Generally milder than PMM2-CDG, with developmental delay, hypotonia and epilepsy predominating Cerebellar hypoplasia is typically less prominent than in PMM2-CDG Features may include failure to thrive, feeding difficulties, and a coagulopathy with low antithrombin and protein C/S Some patients have retinopathy, deep vein thrombosis or ichthyosiform skin changes; virilisation/genital anomalies have been described Serum transferrin analysis shows a type 1 pattern reflecting loss of whole N-glycan chains at the assembly stage Definitive diagnosis rests on lipid-linked oligosaccharide analysis and ALG6 gene sequencing Management is supportive and multidisciplinary; no proven disease-modifying therapy exists Poorly controlled or status epilepticus in infancy Thromboembolic events including deep vein thrombosis Bleeding tendency complicating procedures Acute metabolic or systemic deterioration during intercurrent illness Progressive failure to thrive with feeding failure Stopping the workup at the transferrin screen without identifying the specific CDG subtype Neonatal or infection-related false transferrin patterns misleading interpretation Overlooking coagulation abnormalities before surgery or anticoagulation Assuming a benign course given the milder label and under-monitoring multisystem complications Missing retinopathy or thrombotic risk on long-term follow-up ALG6-CDG is a defect in the endoplasmic reticulum assembly of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor used for N-glycosylation. The ALG6 enzyme is the dolichyl-phosphate glucosyltransferase that adds the first glucose residue to the Man9GlcNAc2 dolichol-linked structure. When this step is impaired, an incompletely glucosylated precursor is transferred less efficiently to nascent proteins, producing hypoglycosylation with loss of complete glycan chains and hence a type 1 serum transferrin pattern. As with other N-glycosylation defects the deficiency affects multiple organ systems, but the neurological phenotype tends to be less severe than PMM2-CDG. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The phenotype is generally milder than PMM2-CDG with better survival, but most patients have persisting intellectual disability, epilepsy and variable multisystem involvement.

Alien hand syndrome — alien limb syndrome, anarchic hand, Dr Strangelove syndrome Corticobasal degeneration (a common progressive cause) Anterior or middle cerebral artery stroke Corpus callosum lesion or surgical callosotomy Frontal or parietal tumour Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease Functional (psychogenic) limb phenomena MRI brain to identify callosal, frontal, or parietal lesions Vascular imaging in suspected stroke Neuropsychological assessment of interhemispheric function and apraxia Investigations for corticobasal degeneration and other neurodegenerative disease Electroencephalography and cerebrospinal fluid studies where prion disease is suspected Bloods and metabolic screen The affected hand performs complex, apparently purposeful movements outside the patient's voluntary control, and is felt as foreign or not their own Patients often personify the limb and may use the other hand to restrain it The callosal (anterior) form typically causes intermanual conflict, where one hand opposes the actions of the other The frontal (medial) form, associated with anterior cerebral artery territory and supplementary motor area lesions, produces compulsive grasping and groping in the dominant hand A posterior (parietal) variant is linked with more withdrawal-type or levitating movements and sensory features Causes include stroke, corticobasal degeneration, tumour, trauma, and callosal surgery Management is supportive, addressing the underlying disorder, with behavioural strategies to occupy or constrain the limb Acute onset indicating a new stroke Rapidly progressive cognitive and motor decline suggesting a neurodegenerative or prion disorder Movements causing self-injury or endangering the patient New focal neurological signs pointing to an expanding lesion Dismissing the complaint as functional or psychiatric without imaging Failing to recognise corticobasal degeneration as an underlying cause Overlooking safety risks from uncontrolled limb movements Confusing the different anatomical subtypes and their localisation Alien hand syndrome reflects a disconnection between the systems that generate movement and those that experience movement as self-willed. In the callosal form, damage to the corpus callosum impairs interhemispheric communication, so the non-dominant hemisphere can drive the hand independently, producing intermanual conflict. In the frontal form, medial frontal lesions involving the supplementary motor area and anterior cingulate release environmentally triggered grasping and reaching behaviours from voluntary inhibitory control. Parietal lesions disrupt the sense of ownership and agency over the limb. In each case, motor acts are produced without the normal accompanying sense of intention, so the hand feels autonomous and alien. Prognosis depends on the cause; the alien hand from stroke may partially improve, whereas that due to corticobasal degeneration or prion disease progresses with the underlying illness, and the phenomenon can be persistently disabling.

Alkaptonuria — AKU, homogentisic aciduria, homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency, ochronosis Other causes of dark urine (haematuria, haemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria, porphyria, drug effects) Tyrosinemia (other tyrosine pathway disorders) Osteoarthritis and ankylosing spondylitis for the arthropathy Exogenous ochronosis (e.g. from hydroquinone or phenol exposure) Degenerative disc and joint disease of other cause Urinary homogentisic acid quantification (diagnostic) Simple test of urine darkening on standing or alkalinisation Molecular testing of the HGD gene Imaging of the spine and large joints for ochronotic arthropathy and disc calcification Echocardiography for valvular involvement in adults Assessment for renal and prostate stones where indicated A rare autosomal recessive defect in tyrosine catabolism caused by deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase, allowing homogentisic acid to accumulate The classic and often earliest sign is urine that turns dark brown or black on standing or on alkalinisation, sometimes noticed as dark-staining nappies in infancy Ochronosis, the bluish-black pigmentation of connective tissue, becomes apparent in adulthood, notably in the ear cartilage and the sclerae A severe, early-onset degenerative arthropathy, particularly of the spine and large joints, is the major cause of morbidity Deposition of ochronotic pigment can also affect heart valves (aortic stenosis and valve calcification), cause pigmented renal and prostate stones, and stiffen tendons Diagnosis is confirmed by markedly elevated urinary homogentisic acid, and the disorder is usually benign in childhood with complications emerging over decades Management is largely symptomatic with analgesia, physiotherapy and joint care; nitisinone, which reduces homogentisic acid production, is being used to slow disease progression It is one of the original inborn errors of metabolism described by Garrod but is not a routine newborn screening target, being clinically mild early in life Symptomatic aortic valve stenosis or significant valve calcification requiring cardiac assessment Severe, disabling spinal or large-joint arthropathy Obstructing pigmented renal or prostatic stones Rapid functional decline from progressive joint destruction in adulthood Dismissing dark urine as a benign curiosity and missing the underlying diagnosis Attributing the arthropathy to ordinary osteoarthritis without recognising ochronosis Overlooking cardiac valve and renal stone complications during long-term follow-up Confusing endogenous ochronosis with exogenous pigmentation from topical or occupational exposure Alkaptonuria results from deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase, an enzyme in the pathway that degrades tyrosine and phenylalanine. The block causes homogentisic acid to accumulate and be excreted in large amounts in urine, where it oxidises and polymerises to a dark pigment, explaining the darkening of urine. Over years, oxidised homogentisic acid deposits as ochronotic pigment in collagen-rich connective tissues, particularly cartilage, tendons, sclerae and heart valves. This pigment makes cartilage brittle and provokes a progressive degenerative arthropathy, and its deposition in other tissues underlies the cardiac, renal and cutaneous manifestations. Alkaptonuria is compatible with a normal lifespan and is largely asymptomatic in childhood, but progressive ochronotic arthropathy and, less often, cardiac and renal complications cause substantial disability in later adult life; disease-modifying therapy aims to slow this progression.

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis — ABPA, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, aspergillus hypersensitivity Poorly controlled asthma without ABPA Cystic fibrosis exacerbation Eosinophilic pneumonia Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss) Bronchiectasis of other cause Invasive or semi-invasive aspergillosis and aspergilloma Total serum IgE, which is characteristically very high and useful for monitoring Aspergillus-specific IgE and IgG (precipitins) and skin testing for sensitisation Peripheral blood eosinophil count High-resolution CT to detect central bronchiectasis and mucoid impaction Sputum examination for Aspergillus and eosinophils ABPA is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus colonising the airways, occurring almost exclusively in patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis Suspect it in poorly controlled asthma with recurrent exacerbations, fleeting pulmonary infiltrates, and expectoration of brownish mucus plugs Markedly elevated total serum IgE and Aspergillus-specific IgE and IgG, with peripheral eosinophilia, support the diagnosis A positive immediate skin test or specific IgE to Aspergillus reflects the underlying sensitisation Imaging classically shows central bronchiectasis and mucoid impaction, sometimes with transient infiltrates Treatment centres on suppressing the immune and inflammatory response with corticosteroids, with antifungal therapy used to reduce fungal burden in selected cases The disease evolves through stages including acute presentation, remission, exacerbation, and, if untreated, fibrotic end-stage lung disease It is a hypersensitivity phenomenon rather than tissue-invasive infection, distinguishing it from invasive aspergillosis and aspergilloma Progressive fixed airflow obstruction or fibrosis indicating advanced disease Frequent severe asthma exacerbations unresponsive to standard therapy Features suggesting invasive aspergillosis in an immunocompromised patient Massive mucoid impaction causing lobar collapse Mistaking ABPA for ordinary difficult asthma and missing the diagnosis Confusing this hypersensitivity condition with invasive aspergillosis and mismanaging treatment Failing to monitor total IgE to gauge disease activity and treatment response Overlooking ABPA as a treatable cause of bronchiectasis In predisposed patients, inhaled Aspergillus fumigatus spores germinate and persist within the viscid airway mucus rather than being cleared. Fungal antigens provoke a vigorous combined type I (IgE-mediated) and type III (immune-complex) hypersensitivity response, with strong Th2 activation, eosinophil recruitment, and high IgE production. The resulting intense airway inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, and mucoid impaction damage the bronchial walls, leading to central bronchiectasis. Recurrent inflammatory episodes can ultimately produce fibrosis and irreversible loss of lung function. With early recognition and appropriate immunosuppressive treatment, exacerbations can be controlled and lung damage limited; however, repeated undertreated flares lead to progressive bronchiectasis and fibrosis with permanent loss of lung function, so long-term monitoring of symptoms and IgE is important.

Food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis — allergic proctocolitis, food protein-induced proctocolitis, cow's milk protein proctocolitis, eosinophilic proctocolitis of infancy Anal fissure Infective colitis from organisms such as Salmonella or Campylobacter Necrotising enterocolitis, especially in the preterm or unwell neonate Swallowed maternal blood in the breast-fed newborn Intussusception or another surgical cause of rectal bleeding Coagulopathy or vitamin K deficiency bleeding Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome or other food allergy Clinical assessment confirming a well, thriving infant, which is the key discriminator Trial of dietary protein elimination with documented resolution of bleeding Full blood count to check for anaemia or eosinophilia when bleeding is notable Stool culture and microscopy to exclude infective causes Examination for an anal fissure Sigmoidoscopy with biopsy only in atypical or non-resolving cases, which shows eosinophilic infiltration Planned reintroduction or rechallenge to confirm the diagnosis where appropriate A non-IgE-mediated food allergy presenting in early infancy with blood-streaked, sometimes mucousy, stools in an otherwise well, thriving baby It is most commonly caused by cow's milk protein, and many affected infants are breast-fed and react to protein passed through maternal milk The infant is characteristically well, feeding normally and gaining weight, and is not systemically unwell despite the visible blood Bleeding is usually low-volume and significant anaemia is uncommon Diagnosis is clinical, supported by resolution of bleeding after removing the culprit protein and recurrence on reintroduction In breast-fed infants, maternal exclusion of cow's milk and sometimes soy is first-line, while formula-fed infants are switched to an extensively hydrolysed formula Allergy tests such as skin-prick and specific IgE are usually negative because the process is non-IgE-mediated The prognosis is excellent, with most infants tolerating the protein and the condition resolving within the first year or two of life A systemically unwell or febrile infant Significant or large-volume rectal bleeding, or anaemia Poor weight gain or faltering growth Abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, or other signs of obstruction Bleeding that does not resolve despite appropriate dietary elimination Over-investigating a well, thriving infant with typical features Attributing all infant rectal bleeding to allergy and missing a fissure, infection, or surgical cause Stopping breast-feeding unnecessarily instead of adjusting the maternal diet Not allowing enough time on elimination before judging the response Failing to plan a supervised reintroduction to confirm resolution and tolerance Food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis is a non-IgE-mediated, eosinophil-predominant immune response to dietary food proteins, most often cow's milk protein reaching the infant directly or through breast milk. The reaction is localised to the distal colon and rectum, where mucosal inflammation causes friability and small-vessel bleeding, producing blood-streaked stools. The condition is benign and self-limiting and is not associated with systemic illness or, in most cases, significant blood loss. The outlook is excellent: this is a benign, self-limiting condition, and most infants outgrow it and tolerate the protein by around one to two years of age with no lasting sequelae.

Allergic rhinitis — hay fever, seasonal allergic rhinitis, perennial allergic rhinitis, allergic rhinosinusitis Non-allergic (vasomotor) rhinitis Infective rhinitis or rhinosinusitis Rhinitis medicamentosa from overuse of decongestant sprays Nasal polyps Structural causes such as deviated nasal septum Hormonal or drug-induced rhinitis Anterior rhinoscopy and nasal endoscopy to assess mucosa and exclude polyps Skin prick testing to identify causative allergens Serum allergen-specific IgE testing where skin testing is unsuitable Nasal smear for eosinophils in selected cases Assessment for coexisting asthma and sinus disease An IgE-mediated hypersensitivity of the nasal mucosa presenting with sneezing, watery rhinorrhoea, nasal itching and congestion Often classified as seasonal (pollen-driven) or perennial (dust mite, animal dander, mould), and by severity and effect on quality of life Commonly associated with allergic conjunctivitis, asthma and eczema as part of the atopic spectrum Examination typically reveals pale, boggy, oedematous nasal mucosa with clear secretions, and children may show an allergic salute crease and allergic shiners Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by skin prick testing or specific IgE assays to identify triggers Management principles begin with allergen avoidance and saline measures, then intranasal corticosteroids and antihistamines according to severity Poorly controlled disease contributes to sinusitis, otitis media with effusion, sleep disturbance and reduced school or work performance Immunotherapy may be considered for confirmed single-allergen sensitivity that is inadequately controlled by standard therapy Unilateral nasal symptoms, bleeding or a mass suggesting a tumour or foreign body Progressive obstruction with facial pain and purulent discharge indicating complicated sinusitis Anosmia or orbital or visual symptoms requiring further evaluation Symptoms of poorly controlled coexisting asthma Missing coexisting asthma that needs concurrent treatment Encouraging prolonged use of topical decongestants leading to rebound rhinitis Attributing unilateral or bloodstained symptoms to allergy rather than investigating for tumour or foreign body Underusing intranasal corticosteroids, the most effective agents, in moderate to severe disease Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated inflammatory response of the nasal mucosa to inhaled allergens. On re-exposure, allergen cross-links IgE bound to mast cells, triggering an early-phase release of histamine and other mediators that produce sneezing, itching, rhinorrhoea and congestion within minutes. A late-phase reaction, driven by recruited eosinophils, basophils and T cells, sustains mucosal inflammation and congestion hours later and heightens nasal reactivity. Chronic inflammation causes mucosal oedema and hyperresponsiveness, and shared airway inflammation links the condition to asthma. Allergic rhinitis is generally a chronic but benign condition; with allergen avoidance and appropriate pharmacotherapy most patients achieve good symptom control, though it may persist for years and contribute to comorbidities.

Allergic transfusion reaction — Urticarial transfusion reaction, Anaphylactic transfusion reaction Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction Transfusion-related acute lung injury Transfusion-associated circulatory overload Septic transfusion reaction from bacterial contamination Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction Unrelated drug reaction or latex allergy Serum tryptase timed from symptom onset to support anaphylaxis Quantitative serum IgA with anti-IgA antibody testing after severe reactions Direct antiglobulin test and haemolysis screen to exclude haemolysis Observation of oxygenation and chest examination to exclude lung injury Review of component type and plasma content Consideration of haptoglobin deficiency testing in relevant populations Allergic reactions span a spectrum from mild urticaria and pruritus to life-threatening anaphylaxis, and are among the commonest reactions to plasma-containing components. Most reactions are due to recipient IgE or IgG antibodies reacting with soluble allergens in donor plasma. Mild urticarial reactions without other features are the only category in which the transfusion may be paused, an antihistamine given, and cautiously restarted if symptoms settle. Anaphylaxis presents with bronchospasm, laryngeal oedema, hypotension and gastrointestinal symptoms, often within minutes and without fever. Severe recurrent anaphylaxis should prompt testing for IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies, and for haptoglobin deficiency in susceptible populations. Adrenaline is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, with airway support, oxygen, fluids and adjunctive antihistamines and corticosteroids. Washed cellular components and plasma-reduced or plasma-free products reduce recurrence in patients with severe or repeated allergic reactions. Platelet additive solutions and washing lower the plasma load and the frequency of allergic reactions to platelet transfusions. Stridor, hoarseness or tongue swelling indicating laryngeal oedema Wheeze and respiratory distress from bronchospasm Hypotension or collapse without fever suggesting anaphylaxis Rapid progression of symptoms after only a small transfused volume History of severe reactions with known or suspected IgA deficiency Restarting transfusion when features beyond simple urticaria are present. Delaying adrenaline in favour of antihistamines when anaphylaxis is evolving. Failing to investigate IgA deficiency after recurrent severe allergic reactions. Overlooking the need for washed or plasma-reduced components in prevention. Confusing an allergic reaction with lung injury or circulatory overload when respiratory symptoms dominate. Allergic transfusion reactions are immediate hypersensitivity responses to soluble constituents of donor plasma. Recipient IgE (and sometimes IgG) antibodies recognise donor plasma proteins or other soluble allergens, cross-link on mast cells and basophils and trigger degranulation with release of histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes and other mediators. Localised mediator release produces urticaria and pruritus, whereas systemic release causes vasodilatation, increased vascular permeability, bronchospasm and mucosal oedema culminating in anaphylaxis. A distinct severe mechanism occurs in individuals with congenital IgA deficiency who form anti-IgA antibodies and react to IgA in transfused plasma; an analogous process is described with anti-haptoglobin antibodies in haptoglobin-deficient individuals. Mild urticarial reactions are benign and often allow completion of the transfusion after treatment, whereas anaphylaxis is potentially fatal but usually responds well to prompt adrenaline and supportive care. Patients with anti-IgA-mediated anaphylaxis require lifelong precautions to prevent recurrence.

Alopecia Areata — AA, patchy hair loss, alopecia totalis, alopecia universalis Tinea capitis (scaly, inflamed, often with broken hairs and positive mycology) Trichotillomania (irregular patches with hairs of varying length) Telogen effluvium (diffuse shedding rather than discrete patches) Traction alopecia at sites of chronic tension Early scarring alopecias such as lichen planopilaris or discoid lupus Secondary syphilis producing a moth-eaten pattern Usually a clinical diagnosis aided by dermoscopy showing exclamation-mark hairs, yellow dots, and black dots Mycology (scrapings or culture) when tinea capitis cannot be excluded Thyroid function and autoantibody testing when clinically indicated Scalp biopsy reserved for atypical or diagnostically uncertain cases Screening for associated autoimmune disease guided by symptoms Presents as sudden, sharply bordered round or oval bald patches on otherwise normal-appearing scalp skin, without scarring or scale Look for exclamation-mark hairs at the margins of active patches, where the shaft narrows towards the scalp A positive hair-pull test at the periphery indicates ongoing disease activity Extensive forms include loss of all scalp hair (totalis) and loss of all body hair (universalis); the ophiasis pattern along the occipital and temporal rim tends to respond poorly Nail involvement such as fine regular pitting or roughening may accompany more severe or persistent disease Associations with thyroid disease, vitiligo, atopy, and other autoimmune conditions warrant a focused history and examination Regrowth often begins as fine depigmented or white hairs that later regain colour Management ranges from watchful waiting in limited disease to intralesional or topical anti-inflammatory therapy, contact immunotherapy, and newer targeted systemic agents for extensive involvement; psychological impact should be addressed directly Rapidly progressive or extensive loss suggesting evolution towards totalis or universalis Scarring, scale, or follicular destruction indicating a different, potentially permanent alopecia Significant psychological distress or impact on functioning requiring support Diffuse hair loss with systemic symptoms prompting evaluation for an underlying disorder Confusing non-scarring alopecia areata with a scarring alopecia and missing the window for treatment Overlooking tinea capitis in children by not performing mycology Attributing patchy loss to alopecia areata when hair-length variation points to trichotillomania Underestimating the psychological burden and failing to offer support or counselling Alopecia areata is an organ-specific autoimmune disorder in which the immune privilege of the hair follicle breaks down, allowing a T-cell-mediated attack focused on the anagen-phase follicular bulb. Interferon-gamma and other cytokines signalling through the JAK-STAT pathway drive a peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate classically likened to a swarm of bees. Affected follicles prematurely enter catagen and telogen and produce dystrophic hairs, but the follicular stem-cell compartment is preserved, which is why regrowth remains possible even after long-standing loss. A polygenic predisposition interacts with environmental triggers, and there is overlap with other autoimmune diseases. Outcome is variable and unpredictable; limited single patches frequently regrow spontaneously within months, whereas early onset, extensive involvement, the ophiasis pattern, nail changes, and atopy predict a more prolonged and relapsing course.

Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome — Alpers syndrome, Alpers disease, Progressive neuronal degeneration of childhood, POLG Other mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes Leigh syndrome Non-metabolic causes of intractable childhood epilepsy with regression Wilson disease and other metabolic liver diseases Acute viral or autoimmune hepatitis with encephalopathy Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis POLG molecular testing as the definitive diagnostic step Liver function tests with coagulation profile to detect synthetic hepatic failure EEG to characterise occipital and multifocal epileptiform activity Brain MRI looking for occipital, thalamic and cerebellar signal change and volume loss Cerebrospinal fluid protein and lactate Blood lactate and, where indicated, quantification of mitochondrial DNA content or muscle respiratory-chain enzymology The classic clinical triad is intractable epilepsy (often with epilepsia partialis continua), psychomotor regression and liver disease progressing to failure It is an autosomal recessive nuclear disorder caused by biallelic mutations in POLG, the gene for the catalytic subunit of mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma, leading to mitochondrial DNA depletion Sodium valproate must be avoided because it can precipitate or accelerate fulminant hepatic failure in POLG disease, and this warning applies whenever POLG is suspected before genetic confirmation Seizures are frequently occipital in onset, drug-resistant, and can evolve into status epilepticus Liver involvement may be present at onset or emerge later, sometimes only after valproate exposure, and includes microvesicular steatosis and eventual cirrhosis Cerebrospinal fluid protein is often raised, and MRI may show occipital and thalamic changes; EEG can show high-amplitude, low-frequency activity with polyspikes Management is supportive, targeting seizure control with mitochondria-sparing agents, nutritional and hepatic support, avoiding hepatotoxic and mitochondrial-toxic drugs Refractory seizures or status epilepticus, including epilepsia partialis continua Rising transaminases, coagulopathy or jaundice indicating hepatic failure Recent valproate exposure with clinical deterioration Rapid neurological regression or coma Giving sodium valproate for the epilepsy before excluding POLG disease, risking fatal hepatotoxicity Attributing the liver failure to the anticonvulsant alone and missing the underlying mitochondrial disorder Waiting for liver disease before considering the diagnosis, since hepatic involvement can be delayed Considering liver transplantation without recognising the systemic, progressive neurological disease Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome is caused by recessive mutations in POLG, which encodes the catalytic subunit of DNA polymerase gamma, the sole polymerase responsible for replicating and repairing mitochondrial DNA. Defective enzyme activity leads to quantitative depletion and qualitative errors of mitochondrial DNA, particularly in post-mitotic tissues with high energy demand such as neurons and hepatocytes. The resulting failure of oxidative phosphorylation causes progressive neuronal loss, spongiform change in grey matter and hepatocellular injury. Valproate further inhibits mitochondrial function and fatty acid oxidation, which explains its propensity to trigger catastrophic liver failure in these patients. Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome is relentlessly progressive with a poor prognosis; most affected children deteriorate over months to a few years, and liver failure, often accelerated by valproate, is a major cause of death.

tomography showing basal panacinar emphysema Liver function tests and hepatic assessment for associated liver disease Family screening and genetic counselling for relatives Suspect in emphysema within hepatocytes Intravenous augmentation therapy with pooled human alpha-1-antitrypsin is the specific disease-directed treatment for emphysema in suitable deficient patients All patients with COPD should be tested at least once, as recommended by guidelines, since the condition is under-recognised Rapidly declining lung function or frequent exacerbations Signs of chronic liver disease such as jaundice, ascites, or deranged synthetic function Continued smoking in a confirmed deficient patient Severe breathlessness or hypoxaemia indicating advanced emphysema Not testing for the deficiency in every patient diagnosed with COPD Attributing early or basal emphysema solely to smoking Overlooking coexisting liver disease Failing to offer family screening once an index case is identified Alpha-1-antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor made in the liver that protects the lung from neutrophil elastase. In the common Z variant of SERPINA1, the abnormal protein misfolds and polymerises within hepatocytes, so little is secreted into the circulation. The resulting deficiency leaves the lung interstitium unprotected against elastase, particularly when neutrophil recruitment is amplified by cigarette smoke, leading to progressive destruction of alveolar walls and panacinar emphysema. Hepatic retention of the polymerised protein separately drives liver injury. Prognosis depends heavily on smoking status and baseline lung function; non-smokers may have near-normal life expectancy, whereas smokers with severe deficiency can develop disabling emphysema early, and augmentation therapy may slow the rate of lung tissue loss in selected patients.

Defective assembly of the collagen IV network weakens the glomerular basement membrane, which progressively thickens, thins, splits, and develops the characteristic basket-weave lamellation seen on electron microscopy. The abnormal membrane cannot maintain a normal filtration barrier, leading to haematuria, progressive proteinuria, glomerulosclerosis, and interstitial fibrosis. Because the same collagen chains are found in the cochlea and the lens and retina, the disorder also produces sensorineural hearing loss and ocular changes. In classic X-linked disease, affected males commonly progress to end-stage kidney disease by early to middle adulthood, whereas female carriers and some autosomal forms have a more variable and often milder course. Early renin-angiotensin blockade can delay progression. Transplantation is generally successful, though a small number of patients develop anti-GBM disease in the graft against the previously absent collagen antigen.

recognised arrhythmia risk in the ATP1A3 spectrum Alternating hemiplegia of childhood is usually caused by de novo missense variants in ATP1A3, which encodes the alpha-3 subunit of the neuronal sodium-potassium ATPase responsible for restoring transmembrane ion gradients after neuronal firing. Impaired pump function disturbs neuronal repolarisation and raises susceptibility to episodic dysfunction, producing paroxysmal hemiplegia, dystonia and oculomotor disturbance that are relieved by the reduced metabolic demand of sleep. Repeated episodes and chronic pump dysfunction are associated with progressive neurological and cognitive decline, and the same gene produces a phenotypic spectrum spanning rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism and CAPOS syndrome. Alternating hemiplegia of childhood is a serious disorder with a generally guarded outlook; although individual hemiplegic attacks resolve, most children accumulate cognitive impairment, dystonia and epilepsy over time. hemosiderin deposits as footprints) Echocardiography (recommended when HAPE occurs below 3000 m or when predisposing cardiopulmonary abnormality is suspected) Lung ultrasound comet-tail/B-line scoring (sensitive but not specific for HAPE) Cardiogenic pulmonary edema / heart failure (HAPE was historically mistaken for heart failure) Acute respiratory distress syndrome (another noncardiogenic edema, but lung architecture is preserved in HAPE) Pulmonary embolism Pneumothorax Anxiety/panic attack Stroke or TIA unrelated to altitude illness Subarachnoid hemorrhage, transient global amnesia, delirium, cranial nerve palsy occurring at altitude outside altitude sickness Altitude illness encompasses a spectrum: acute mountain sickness (AMS, the benign form) and the two life-threatening forms, high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE) and high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) (Harrison 22e p.3754). AMS is a clinical diagnosis presenting 6-12 h after ascent with nonspecific symptoms (headache, nausea, fatigue, dizziness) and few physical findings; the Lake Louise Scoring System is used for research uniformity (Harrison 22e p.3755). AMS and HACE are viewed as opposite ends of one neurologic continuum; HACE (not AMS) is an encephalopathy whose hallmarks are ataxia and altered consciousness with diffuse cerebral involvement, typically without focal deficits, and progression can be rapid (Harrison 22e p.3755). The two most important risk factors for altitude illness are a rapid rate of ascent and a prior history of high-altitude illness; exertion is a risk factor, but lack of physical fitness is not (Harrison 22e p.3755). Illness is likely above 2500 m but has been documented at 1500-2500 m; in the Everest region about 50% of trekkers ascending above 4000 m over 5+ days develop AMS, rising to 84% with direct flight to 3860 m, whereas HACE and HAPE incidence is far lower (roughly 0.1-4%) (Harrison 22e p.3754). HAPE is primarily a pulmonary disorder and need not be preceded by AMS; it develops within 2-4 days of arrival and rarely after 4-5 days at the same altitude owing to vascular remodeling and adaptation (Harrison 22e p.3757). HAPE is a noncardiogenic pulmonary edema with normal pulmonary artery wedge pressure, driven by patchy hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction causing regional overperfusion, capillary pressures above 18 mmHg, and capillary stress failure (Harrison 22e p.3757). Retinal hemorrhages are common at altitudes of 5000 m or more even without AMS/HACE symptoms; most resolve on descent, but macular hemorrhage can cause devastating, occasionally permanent visual loss (Harrison 22e p.3755, 3759). Gradual ascent with time for acclimatization is the best preventive measure; a conservative target above 3000 m is graded gain of no more than ~300 m per sleeping-altitude night with an extra acclimatization day every third day of gain (Harrison 22e p.3756). Sickle cell disease is one of the rare exposures in which altitude can provoke vaso-occlusive crisis, reported even at passes as low as 2500 m; thalassemia has not been linked to high-altitude problems (Harrison 22e p.3759). Hypertensive patients are not more prone to altitude illness, and most with well-controlled hypertension can be reassured that blood pressure stays relatively stable; antihypertensives should be continued at altitude (Harrison 22e p.3759). High-altitude cough can be severe enough to cause rib fracture above 5000 m; it is multifactorial (cold dry air plus hypoxia and respiratory water loss), and infection is generally not a common cause (Harrison 22e p.3758). Ataxia or altered consciousness (hallmarks of HACE) - mandates immediate descent Any hint of HAPE or HACE mandates descent Tachypnea and tachycardia at rest as HAPE progresses Blood-tinged sputum following a dry persistent cough Disproportionate fall in exercise tolerance, or fatigue/dyspnea at rest as the only initial HAPE signs Debilitating fatigue consistent with severe AMS on descent from a summit (important risk factor for death in mountaineers) Papilledema or retinal hemorrhages, especially macular hemorrhage with visual loss Worsening symptoms despite halting ascent Treating AMS as trivial - symptoms overlap with exhaustion, dehydration, hypothermia, hangover, and hyponatremia, and it can progress to life-threatening HACE. Relying on pulse oximetry alone to predict AMS during a trek - readings should not be used predictively unless guided by clinical signs. Assuming HAPE is always preceded by AMS - it is primarily pulmonary and may present without headache or nausea, sometimes only as fatigue and rest dyspnea. Misreading HAPE chest opacities as pneumonia (cold) or as heart failure - Kerley B lines and bat-wing pattern are absent in HAPE. Confusing sudden neurologic events (TIA, stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage, cranial nerve palsy) at altitude with altitude illness - AMS evolves gradually whereas these typically occur suddenly. Mistaking reentry HAPE in returning highlanders for a viral illness. Injudicious prophylactic glucocorticoid use by climbers to boost performance - can be tragic owing to severe side effects, especially with prolonged use. Overhydration - adequate (not excessive) hydration is intended; potent diuretics such as furosemide should be avoided in HAPE. Comet-tail/B-line lung ultrasound is sensitive but not specific, since B-lines also appear in individuals who never develop clinical HAPE - clinical correlation is essential. Ascent lowers barometric pressure and thus the partial pressure of inspired oxygen, reducing the pressure gradient driving oxygen diffusion along the oxygen cascade. Hypobaric hypoxia is the central trigger for all forms of altitude illness. The normal struggle response is increased ventilation (the cornerstone of acclimatization) mediated by the carotid bodies; this can produce marked respiratory alkalosis (arterial pH may exceed 7.7 at extreme altitude) and dehydration, with alkalosis blunting ventilatory drive in sleep and causing periodic breathing and hypoxemia. Early acclimatization includes renal carbonic-anhydrase suppression with dilute alkaline urine to correct pH, plus increased sympathetic tone, rising erythropoietin/hemoglobin and red cell mass, greater tissue capillary density and mitochondrial numbers, and elevated 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate. Hypoxia-inducible factor governs transcriptional hypoxia responses; the EPAS1 gene (HIF-2alpha) and EGLN1/PPARA influence adaptation in Tibetan highlanders (lower hemoglobin than Han Chinese or Andeans). In AMS/HACE, raised intracranial pressure, increased sympathetic activity, relative hypoventilation, fluid retention/redistribution, and impaired gas exchange contribute; MRI evidence points to vasogenic (interstitial) cerebral edema, especially in the splenium of the corpus callosum, that may become cytotoxic in severe HACE, with hemosiderin deposits as long-lasting footprints. Impaired cerebral autoregulation with hypoxic vasodilation, altered blood-brain-barrier permeability via histamine, arachidonic acid, and VEGF, and venous outflow obstruction raising capillary pressure all promote edema. HAPE results from patchy hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction with regional overperfusion and capillary stress failure at normal wedge pressure; endothelial dysfunction with reduced nitric oxide availability and elevated endothelin-1, exaggerated sympathetic drive (pulmonary venoconstriction), and impaired transepithelial alveolar fluid clearance are implicated. Inflammation in HAPE is regarded as an epiphenomenon rather than the primary cause, although inflammatory/viral respiratory processes can predispose to it. AMS is benign and usually self-limited; once symptoms abate (with or without acetazolamide) the patient may reascend gradually. HACE and HAPE are life-threatening but generally reversible with prompt recognition and descent. In HAPE the lung architecture is typically well preserved with rapid reversibility (radiographic opacities can clear in about 2 days), allowing some patients to reascend slowly after a few days of descent and rest; after HACE, reascent within the same trip may be inadvisable. Severe AMS-related debilitating fatigue on descent is an important predictor of death in mountaineers, and macular hemorrhage can rarely cause permanent visual loss. HACE complicated by globus pallidus lesions has been reported to lead to parkinsonism. AMS is graded clinically as mild versus moderate, a subjective judgment based on headache severity and the presence/severity of nausea, fatigue, and dizziness (the Lake Louise Scoring System, without the sleep score, is used for research). The overall spectrum runs from benign AMS to the life-threatening forms HACE (neurologic, the severe end of the AMS-HACE continuum) and HAPE (pulmonary), which can coexist.

Aluminium phosphide poisoning — aluminum phosphide poisoning, celphos poisoning, rice tablet poisoning, phosphine poisoning Other cellular asphyxiants (cyanide, hydrogen sulfide) Cardiogenic shock from other causes Septic shock Other lethal pesticide ingestions Fulminant myocarditis Continuous ECG and cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia and myocarditis Echocardiography to assess ventricular function Arterial blood gas with anion gap and lactate Serum electrolytes including magnesium, renal and liver function Silver nitrate paper test on breath or gastric aspirate to detect phosphine where available A widely used grain fumigant that reacts with moisture and gastric acid to liberate phosphine gas, a potent mitochondrial poison, and is a common agent of fatal deliberate self-harm in some regions There is no specific antidote, so management is entirely supportive and directed at aggressive haemodynamic and metabolic resuscitation Profound, often refractory circulatory shock from direct myocardial toxicity and vasodilatation is the dominant and most lethal feature Severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, myocarditis, arrhythmias, and multi-organ failure develop early A garlicky or decaying-fish odour on the breath or vomitus is a clinical clue to phosphine exposure Rescuers must be protected, as phosphine off-gassed from vomitus and gastric contents can poison staff; ventilate the area and avoid mouth-to-mouth Reported adjuncts include gastric decontamination with agents intended to reduce phosphine liberation, magnesium, high-dose steroids, intravenous lipid emulsion, and vasopressors, though evidence is limited Early intensive-care support with vasopressors, correction of acidosis, and consideration of extracorporeal circulatory support offers the best chance in a highly lethal poisoning Refractory hypotension and shock unresponsive to fluids and vasopressors Severe metabolic acidosis with rising lactate Arrhythmias or echocardiographic evidence of myocardial dysfunction Large ingestion of a fresh (unexposed) tablet, associated with very high mortality Risk of secondary poisoning of healthcare staff from off-gassing Expecting a specific antidote to exist and delaying aggressive supportive resuscitation Underestimating lethality because the patient initially looks stable before rapid deterioration Neglecting staff protection against phosphine off-gassing from the patient Inadequate correction of acidosis and under-resuscitation of shock On contact with water or gastric acid, aluminium phosphide releases phosphine gas, which inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase and generates reactive oxygen species, arresting oxidative phosphorylation across tissues. The heart is especially vulnerable, developing myocardial depression, myocarditis, and arrhythmias, while widespread vasodilatation and cellular energy failure produce profound refractory shock. Lipid peroxidation and oxidative injury drive a severe metabolic (lactic) acidosis and multi-organ dysfunction affecting the liver, kidneys, and adrenal glands. Poisoning carries very high mortality, particularly with fresh tablets and established shock or severe acidosis; death commonly occurs within the first day or two from cardiovascular collapse, and survival is largely determined by ingested dose and speed of intensive supportive care.

Alveolar soft part sarcoma — ASPS, ASPSCR1-TFE3 fusion sarcoma, ASPL-TFE3 sarcoma Metastatic renal cell carcinoma Paraganglioma Granular cell tumour Malignant melanoma Rhabdomyosarcoma Adrenocortical or other metastatic carcinoma MRI of the primary showing a highly vascular soft-tissue mass with prominent flow voids Staging CT of the chest and imaging of bone and brain given the metastatic pattern Biopsy with histological assessment of the alveolar nesting architecture TFE3 nuclear immunohistochemistry and confirmation of the ASPSCR1-TFE3 fusion PAS staining with diastase to demonstrate intracytoplasmic crystals A rare sarcoma of uncertain differentiation that typically arises in the deep soft tissues of the limbs in adolescents and young adults Often painless and slow-growing, so it may reach a considerable size or present first with metastasis before the primary is noticed Highly vascular, and it has a notable propensity for early haematogenous spread to the lungs, bone and brain Defined by a specific ASPSCR1-TFE3 gene fusion resulting from a translocation, producing strong nuclear TFE3 expression on immunohistochemistry Histology shows the characteristic organoid or alveolar nests of large polygonal cells separated by delicate vascular septa Diastase-resistant, PAS-positive intracytoplasmic crystalline material is a helpful diagnostic feature Complete surgical resection is the mainstay for localised disease, while antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitors and immunotherapy are used in advanced disease Pulmonary, bone or brain metastasis at presentation A deep, enlarging, hypervascular soft-tissue mass in a young patient Neurological symptoms suggesting cerebral metastasis Late recurrence or metastasis many years after treatment of the primary Mistaking the organoid pattern for metastatic renal cell carcinoma or paraganglioma Being falsely reassured by slow growth and a painless mass Failing to stage the lungs, bone and brain for occult metastasis Not confirming the diagnosis with TFE3 immunohistochemistry or fusion testing Alveolar soft part sarcoma is a malignant tumour of uncertain lineage defined by an unbalanced translocation that fuses the ASPSCR1 gene to the TFE3 transcription factor gene. The resulting fusion protein acts as an aberrant transcription factor that upregulates targets including MET signalling and angiogenic pathways, driving the tumour's marked vascularity and metastatic propensity. Tumour cells are arranged in distinctive organoid nests separated by thin sinusoidal vascular channels, and the central cells characteristically lose cohesion to create the alveolar pattern. The rich vascular network underlies the tumour's tendency to disseminate haematogenously early in its course. Alveolar soft part sarcoma is an indolent-appearing but ultimately aggressive malignancy with a high rate of late metastasis, and long-term survival is limited by distant disease even when the primary is controlled. Prognosis is more favourable when the tumour is small, localised and completely resected.

Alzheimer's Disease — AD, Alzheimer dementia Vascular dementia (early prominent gait disturbance with only mild memory loss) (Harrison 22e p.3476) Dementia with Lewy bodies (early parkinsonism with fluctuating alertness, visual hallucinations, delusional misidentification) (Harrison 22e p.3476) Parkinson's disease / Parkinson's disease dementia (resting tremor, stooped posture, bradykinesia, masked facies) (Harrison 22e p.3476) Frontotemporal dementia (prominent behavioral changes with intact navigation and focal anterior-predominant atrophy) (Harrison 22e p.3476) Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease / prion disease (rapid progression over weeks-months with rigidity and myoclonus) (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3482) Limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy (LATE) and primary age-related tauopathy (PART) - can mimic AD clinically, especially in biomarker-negative older patients with progressive amnestic dementia (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3477) Huntington's disease and rare hereditary ataxias when family history of dementia is present (Harrison 22e p.3476) Primary or metastatic brain neoplasm (early focal seizure) (Harrison 22e p.3476) Viral or bacterial encephalitides (listed as causes of rapidly progressive dementia in the CJD differential) (Harrison 22e p.3483) MRI/CT structural imaging - mainly to exclude other disorders; AD shows posterior-predominant cortical and medial temporal (hippocampal) atrophy and may be normal early (Harrison 22e p.3476) FDG-PET - shows hypometabolism in posterior temporal-parietal cortex (Harrison 22e p.3476) Amyloid PET ([11C]PIB, [18F]florbetapir, [18F]florbetaben, [18F]flutemetamol) - confirms neuritic/diffuse Abeta plaques (Harrison 22e p.3476) Tau PET ([18F]flortaucipir and research tracers) - estimates density/distribution of neurofibrillary tangles (Harrison 22e p.3476-3477) CSF biomarkers - decreased Abeta42 and Abeta42/Abeta40 ratio, increased p-Tau181/p-Tau217 (Harrison 22e p.3477) Plasma biomarkers - decreased Abeta42/Abeta40 ratio, increased p-Tau181/p-Tau217/p-Tau231 (Harrison 22e p.3477) EEG - usually normal or nonspecific slowing; prolonged EEG to seek intermittent nonconvulsive seizures (Harrison 22e p.3476) ApoE genotyping - recommended before initiating anti-Abeta antibody therapy to inform ARIA risk (Harrison 22e p.3480-3481) Systemic laboratory tests to exclude reversible dementia mimics (Harrison 22e p.3476) Vitamin B12 deficiency (loss of joint position and vibration sensibility with Babinski signs; especially with autoimmune disease, small bowel resection/irradiation, or veganism) (Harrison 22e p.3476) Normal-pressure hydrocephalus (Harrison 22e p.3476) Depression-related cognitive impairment (depressive pseudodementia) (Harrison 22e p.3476) Chronic drug intoxication (history of treatment for insomnia, anxiety, psychiatric disturbance, or epilepsy) (Harrison 22e p.3476) Thyroid and other reversible/metabolic causes of dementia to be excluded per Tables 31-1, 31-3, 31-4 (Harrison 22e p.3476) Hashimoto's encephalopathy, CNS vasculitis, CNS lymphoma, paraneoplastic/autoimmune syndromes (rapidly progressive dementia differential) (Harrison 22e p.3483) Most common cause of dementia, contributing an estimated 60-70% of all cases; in the U.S. ~10% of people over 65 have AD (3% at age 65-74, 17% at 75-84, 32% at 85+) (Harrison 22e p.3475, p.3478). Typical presentation is insidious loss of episodic memory followed by slowly progressive multidomain dementia, with cognitive change progressing from memory to executive, language, and visuospatial deficits (Harrison 22e p.3475-3476). About 20% of patients present with nonmemory complaints; atypical variants include posterior cortical atrophy (visual processing), logopenic progressive aphasia, corticobasal (akinetic-rigid-dystonic) syndrome, and a dysexecutive/behavioral (frontal) variant (Harrison 22e p.3475-3476). Depression, social withdrawal, and anxiety may occur early and represent a prodrome before cognitive symptoms are apparent (Harrison 22e p.3476). ~50% of patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), roughly 12% per year, progress to dementia over 4 years; the MCI construct is increasingly replaced by 'early symptomatic AD' (Harrison 22e p.3476). Preclinical biomarker changes may precede clinical symptoms by 20 years or more, creating a window for early treatment and prevention (Harrison 22e p.3476). Core 1 biomarkers (amyloid PET, CSF/plasma Abeta and p-Tau) are considered necessary and sufficient for biological diagnosis of AD under the revised Alzheimer's Association criteria; tau PET is a core 2 biomarker used for staging (Harrison 22e p.3477). A negative amyloid PET scan in a patient with dementia makes an AD diagnosis unlikely; a positive scan can establish eligibility for amyloid-lowering therapy (Harrison 22e p.3477). Decreases in the CSF Abeta42/Abeta40 ratio and increases in p-Tau181 or p-Tau217 correlate with AD pathology; plasma biomarkers show high concordance with amyloid PET and are entering clinical use (Harrison 22e p.3477). ApoE epsilon4 is the most important genetic risk factor for sporadic AD: one allele raises risk ~2-3 fold (higher in women), two alleles raise it ~10-15 fold; each allele shifts onset ~10 years earlier (Harrison 22e p.3475, p.3479-3480). Lecanemab (anti-Abeta protofibril) and donanemab (anti-pyroglutamate Abeta) are FDA-approved disease-modifying antiamyloid antibodies for early-stage AD, showing ~22-27% slowing of clinical decline; restricted to MCI/mild dementia with biomarker-confirmed Abeta pathology (Harrison 22e p.3480-3481). Antiamyloid antibodies carry risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA-E edema, ARIA-H microhemorrhage/siderosis); risk rises with each ApoE epsilon4 allele and is highest in epsilon4 homozygotes, prompting an FDA box warning (Harrison 22e p.3481). Treatment with lecanemab or donanemab should be considered a contraindication to peripheral thrombolysis, as catastrophic multifocal hemorrhages and death have been reported when antiamyloid-treated patients received thrombolytics for stroke (Harrison 22e p.3482). Medications with strong anticholinergic effects (e.g., diphenhydramine sleep aids, oxybutynin) should be vigilantly avoided in AD (Harrison 22e p.3482). Typical symptomatic duration is 8-10 years (range 1-25 years); death often results from malnutrition, secondary infections, pulmonary emboli, heart disease, or, most commonly, aspiration (Harrison 22e p.3476). Rapid progression over weeks to months with rigidity and myoclonus suggests CJD rather than AD (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3482) Early prominent gait disturbance with mild memory loss suggests vascular dementia or normal-pressure hydrocephalus (Harrison 22e p.3476) Early focal seizure suggests a metastatic or primary brain neoplasm (Harrison 22e p.3476) Loss of joint position/vibration sense with Babinski signs suggests vitamin B12 deficiency (Harrison 22e p.3476) Stroke-like symptoms in a patient on anti-Abeta monoclonal antibody require immediate MRI to differentiate acute stroke from ARIA before any thrombolysis (Harrison 22e p.3482) Seizures (focal or generalized) can herald AD and occur even before dementia onset, especially in younger patients and autosomal dominant mutation carriers (Harrison 22e p.3476) Failing to exclude reversible/treatable mimics early in the course - vitamin B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, and depression-related cognitive impairment should be excluded before attributing dementia to AD (Harrison 22e p.3476). A clinical diagnosis of AD is confirmed at autopsy only ~70-80% of the time; misdiagnoses are usually LATE (with or without hippocampal sclerosis), PART, Lewy body disease, vascular pathology, or FTLD (Harrison 22e p.3476). Amyloid PET positivity is not specific: ~25% of cognitively unimpaired older adults have positive scans, and a positive scan can reflect comorbid (incidental) AD pathology rather than the primary cause of impairment (Harrison 22e p.3476). A completely negative tau PET does not rule out early neurofibrillary pathology (Braak stages I-III) (Harrison 22e p.3477). Increased total tau in CSF is nonspecific - seen in AD but also other neurodegeneration (Harrison 22e p.3477). Plasma Abeta and p-Tau concentrations can be altered by comorbidities (reduced creatinine clearance, elevated BMI), causing false-positive or false-negative results near the threshold (Harrison 22e p.3477). ApoE epsilon4 is neither necessary nor sufficient to cause AD - many AD patients lack epsilon4 and many epsilon4 carriers never develop dementia (Harrison 22e p.3479-3480). Estrogen, statins, vitamin E, ginkgo biloba, and NSAIDs appeared protective in observational studies but did NOT show efficacy in randomized controlled trials; consumer 'memory-enhancing' supplements lack evidence (Harrison 22e p.3478, p.3482). Antipsychotics carry an FDA black box warning in elderly dementia patients (increased risk of death) and should be used with caution for neuropsychiatric symptoms (Harrison 22e p.3482). AD is characterized by extracellular neuritic plaques containing amyloid beta (Abeta) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) of hyperphosphorylated tau, with Abeta also accumulating in cortical and leptomeningeal blood vessel walls (amyloid angiopathy). Abeta is a 39-42 amino acid peptide cleaved from amyloid precursor protein (APP) by beta and gamma secretases; excess production of Abeta42 is a key initiator of cellular damage, and soluble oligomers are thought to be the early toxic species before fibril/plaque formation. Hyperphosphorylated tau can no longer stabilize microtubules and redistributes from axon to cytoplasm and dendrites, with prion-like templating proposed to drive tau spread. Earliest and most severe degeneration is in the medial temporal lobe (entorhinal/perirhinal cortex, hippocampus), inferolateral temporal cortex, and nucleus basalis of Meynert; atrophy spreads to temporoparietal and frontal cortices. Biochemically there is depletion of acetylcholine (degeneration of cholinergic nucleus basalis of Meynert neurons) plus noradrenergic and serotonergic loss from locus coeruleus and dorsal raphe. Genetic contributors include autosomal dominant mutations in APP (chromosome 21), PSEN-1 (chromosome 14, most common cause of early-onset familial AD), and PSEN-2 (chromosome 1), plus the ApoE epsilon4 risk allele (chromosome 19) and >40 minor GWAS risk variants in innate immunity, lipid metabolism, and synaptic pathways (e.g., CLU, PICALM, CR1, TREM2). (Harrison 22e p.3475, p.3478-3480) Typical duration of symptomatic AD is 8-10 years, with a course ranging from 1 to 25 years. Some patients decline steadily while others have prolonged plateaus. Late stages bring rigidity, mutism, incontinence, and a bedridden state with dependence for eating, dressing, and toileting; hyperactive tendon reflexes and myoclonic jerks may occur. Death most commonly results from aspiration, and also from malnutrition, secondary infections, pulmonary emboli, or heart disease. Approved disease-modifying antiamyloid antibodies slow but do not halt clinical decline (~22-27% slowing over the trial periods). (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3480-3481) Clinical staging is performed independent of biomarkers, based on functional impairment along a continuum: preclinical AD (biomarker evidence of amyloid pathology without symptoms) -> subjective cognitive decline -> mild cognitive impairment / early symptomatic AD (functionally compensated) -> dementia stages (early/middle/late/end-stage). Biological staging under the revised Alzheimer's Association criteria uses core 1 biomarkers (amyloid PET, CSF/plasma Abeta and p-Tau) for diagnosis and tau PET (core 2) for biomarker-based disease staging. (Harrison 22e p.3476-3478)

Amatoxin (Amanita) mushroom poisoning — Amanita phalloides poisoning, death cap poisoning, alpha-amanitin poisoning, amanitin toxicity, cyclopeptide mushroom poisoning Gastroenteritis from early-onset (non-amatoxin) mushroom species such as gastrointestinal irritant fungi Viral or bacterial infective gastroenteritis Paracetamol or other drug-induced acute liver failure Acute viral hepatitis Ischaemic hepatitis or hypoxic liver injury Gyromitrin (false morel) or orellanine (nephrotoxic Cortinarius) mushroom poisoning Serial hepatic transaminases, bilirubin and synthetic function including
