radiation, or hidradenitis suppurativa Treatment depends on how much sphincter the track crosses: fistulotomy (lay-open) suits low simple tracks, while sphincter-preserving options (loose or cutting seton, LIFT, advancement flap, fibrin glue or plug) protect continence in high or complex tracks Accurate mapping of the track and internal opening with MRI or endoanal ultrasound is central to avoiding recurrence and incontinence Multiple, complex, or non-healing fistulae suggesting Crohn's disease or immunosuppression Induration, irregularity, or a mass raising suspicion of underlying malignancy Rapidly spreading perianal sepsis or systemic toxicity indicating necrotising infection A new fistula in a patient with previous pelvic radiotherapy Performing fistulotomy on a high transsphincteric track and causing faecal incontinence Missing the internal opening or a secondary track, leading to early recurrence Failing to recognise underlying Crohn's disease before undertaking aggressive surgery Overlooking malignancy in a chronic, indurated, or atypical fistula Most anal fistulae follow the cryptoglandular hypothesis, in which infection of an anal gland at the dentate line lodges in the intersphincteric space and forms an abscess; once this drains, a persistent epithelialised track remains, connecting the internal opening in the anal canal to an external opening on the perianal skin. Chronic inflammation, incomplete drainage, and secondary tracks perpetuate the disease. The relationship of the track to the internal and external sphincters, described by the Parks classification, determines both surgical strategy and the risk to continence. Secondary or atypical fistulae may reflect Crohn's disease, malignancy, or other specific pathology. Simple low fistulae treated by fistulotomy generally heal well with low recurrence, but high, complex, or Crohn's-related fistulae are prone to recurrence and to disturbance of continence, often requiring staged sphincter-preserving procedures.

Anal intraepithelial neoplasia — AIN, anal dysplasia, anal squamous intraepithelial lesion Invasive anal squamous cell carcinoma Condylomata acuminata (anal warts) Perianal Bowen disease and extramammary Paget disease Anal skin tags or benign fibroepithelial lesions Chronic anal dermatoses such as lichen sclerosus or eczema Haemorrhoids or fissure as a cause of bleeding Perianal Crohn disease High-resolution anoscopy with acetic acid and Lugol iodine and targeted biopsy Histopathological grading of biopsies to confirm and stage dysplasia HPV testing and anal cytology where used in screening pathways HIV testing and assessment of immune status Examination under anaesthesia and mapping biopsies for extensive disease Staging imaging (MRI and nodal assessment) if invasion is suspected Anal intraepithelial neoplasia is a human papillomavirus-driven premalignant squamous dysplasia of the anal canal and margin, the precursor of anal squamous cell carcinoma It is graded as low-grade or high-grade dysplasia; contemporary terminology aligns with the two-tier low-grade and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion system High-risk HPV (especially type 16) is the principal driver; major risk groups include people living with HIV, men who have sex with men, immunosuppressed transplant recipients, and those with prior HPV-related anogenital neoplasia It is frequently asymptomatic and detected incidentally, or presents with pruritus, discomfort, bleeding, discharge, or a visible lesion Diagnosis relies on high-resolution anoscopy with targeted biopsy, aided by acetic acid and Lugol iodine staining to identify dysplastic areas High-grade disease carries a risk of progression to invasive carcinoma, which is heightened in immunosuppressed patients, so surveillance is central Management is individualised and ranges from surveillance to topical therapies, ablation, and targeted excision, balancing recurrence and multifocality against the morbidity of wide excision Any suspicion of invasion mandates biopsy and staging, as invasive anal cancer is managed quite differently, typically with chemoradiotherapy An indurated, ulcerated, or bleeding mass suggesting invasive carcinoma Rapid change or progression of a known lesion High-grade dysplasia in an immunosuppressed patient A non-healing anal ulcer or fissure in an at-risk individual Palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy Assuming a visible anal lesion is a simple wart or tag and omitting biopsy Failing to recognise and stage occult invasive carcinoma within apparent dysplasia Overlooking screening in high-risk groups such as people living with HIV Performing wide excision that risks stenosis when multifocal disease will recur regardless Neglecting long-term surveillance after treatment of high-grade disease Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus, principally type 16, is the central driver of anal intraepithelial neoplasia. Viral oncoproteins inactivate host tumour-suppressor pathways (notably p53 and retinoblastoma protein function), driving unregulated proliferation of squamous epithelium of the anal transformation zone and margin. Dysplastic cells accumulate genetic and epigenetic changes, producing progressive loss of maturation and architectural disorder that defines low-grade and then high-grade neoplasia. Immunosuppression, as in HIV infection or transplantation, impairs viral clearance and immune surveillance, favouring persistence, multifocality, and progression. High-grade lesions may, over time, breach the basement membrane to become invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Low-grade lesions frequently regress and rarely progress, whereas high-grade anal intraepithelial neoplasia carries a real, if variable, risk of progression to invasive cancer, greatest in immunosuppressed patients; recurrence after treatment is common, so long-term surveillance is required and early detection of invasion is key to outcome.

Anal skin tag — perianal skin tag, fibroepithelial anal polyp, sentinel tag External haemorrhoid or residual thrombosed haemorrhoid Anal condylomata acuminata (viral warts) Hypertrophied anal papilla protruding at the anal verge Crohn disease-associated perianal tags Anal intraepithelial neoplasia or anal squamous carcinoma Molluscum contagiosum or other perianal skin lesion Prolapsing haemorrhoid or mucosal prolapse Careful inspection and digital rectal examination of the perianal region Proctoscopy to assess for associated haemorrhoids or fissure Examination under anaesthesia where a chronic fissure or Crohn disease is suspected Histopathological examination of any excised or atypical lesion Assessment for Crohn disease (bowel symptoms, endoscopy, imaging) when tags are oedematous or multiple Testing for human papillomavirus-associated disease where warts or neoplasia are suspected An anal skin tag is a benign, soft, fibrovascular projection of perianal skin, usually asymptomatic and found incidentally on examination Tags commonly arise as residua of a previously thrombosed external haemorrhoid, at the site of a healed anal fissure (the sentinel tag/pile), or after anorectal surgery The chief symptoms, when present, are hygiene difficulty, pruritus ani, and irritation rather than pain or bleeding A skin tag associated with a chronic anal fissure typically sits at the posterior midline distal to the fissure and signals the underlying fissure rather than being the primary problem Large, irregular, indurated, or multiple oedematous tags should raise suspicion of Crohn disease, in which characteristic oedematous violaceous tags occur Management is usually reassurance; excision is offered only for troublesome hygiene, persistent irritation, or diagnostic uncertainty Excision should be conservative to avoid wound complications and anal stenosis, and any underlying fissure or Crohn disease must be addressed Histology should be examined after excision to exclude condylomata, intraepithelial neoplasia, or other pathology when appearances are atypical Induration, ulceration, or irregularity suggesting anal neoplasia Multiple oedematous or violaceous tags suggesting Crohn disease Associated bleeding, discharge, or a non-healing perianal wound Rapid growth or change in a previously stable lesion Coexisting perianal fistula or abscess Excising a sentinel tag without recognising and treating the underlying chronic anal fissure Aggressive or circumferential excision leading to painful wounds or anal stenosis Excising oedematous tags in undiagnosed Crohn disease, risking non-healing wounds Mistaking condylomata or a neoplastic lesion for a simple skin tag and omitting histology Offering surgery for asymptomatic tags where reassurance would suffice Anal skin tags are composed of fibrous and vascular connective tissue covered by squamous epithelium of the anal margin. They most often form when the oedema and stretching of an acute external haemorrhoidal thrombosis resolve, leaving redundant, fibrosed perianal skin. Alternatively, the chronic inflammation and induration of a longstanding anal fissure produce a sentinel tag at the distal fissure margin, or postoperative scarring and healing after anorectal procedures leave residual folds. In Crohn disease, transmural inflammation and lymphatic obstruction generate characteristically oedematous, often broad-based perianal tags. The tags themselves have no malignant potential but can impair local hygiene and provoke secondary irritation and pruritus. Anal skin tags are benign with no malignant potential; they cause no harm and often need no treatment, though when excised for symptoms they heal well provided any underlying fissure or Crohn disease is managed, and can recur if the underlying cause persists.

Anal stenosis — anal stricture, anal canal narrowing Functional anal narrowing from chronic fissure with sphincter spasm Anorectal Crohn disease with stricturing Anal or low rectal carcinoma causing luminal narrowing Radiation proctitis or radiation-induced stricture Post-inflammatory stricture from lymphogranuloma venereum or other infection Congenital anal stenosis in younger patients Rectal stricture from ischaemia or anastomotic scarring Careful inspection and gentle digital examination to assess calibre and pliability Examination under anaesthesia when pain precludes adequate assessment Proctosigmoidoscopy to inspect above the stenosis Biopsy of the narrowed segment to exclude Crohn disease, infection, or malignancy Endoanal ultrasound or pelvic MRI where the cause or extent is unclear Assessment of sphincter function and continence before planning surgery Anal stenosis is pathological narrowing of the anal canal with loss of its normal elasticity, most often an anatomical (cicatricial) narrowing due to fibrous scar replacing pliable anoderm The commonest cause is overzealous excisional haemorrhoidectomy with excessive removal of anoderm; other causes include chronic fissure, inflammatory bowel disease, radiation, trauma, and chronic laxative-associated changes Typical symptoms are difficult and painful defecation, thin or pencil-like stools, straining, incomplete evacuation, and bleeding from mucosal splitting A functional narrowing due to sphincter spasm (as in chronic fissure) must be distinguished from true anatomical stenosis with fibrosis, as management differs Severity is graded by the calibre achievable on examination and whether an examining finger or instrument passes; examination may require anaesthesia Mild stenosis often responds to stool bulking, softeners, and dilatation; moderate to severe fibrotic stenosis requires operative correction Surgical options include internal sphincterotomy for a tight functional element and anoplasty with advancement or island flaps to introduce healthy tissue and widen the canal Inflammatory or neoplastic causes must be excluded by biopsy before attributing stenosis to benign scarring, particularly when there is no clear surgical history An indurated or ulcerated stricture suggesting malignancy Stenosis without prior anal surgery, prompting a search for inflammatory or neoplastic causes Progressive obstruction or inability to pass stool Associated fistula, abscess, or perianal Crohn features Bleeding or discharge disproportionate to a benign scar Confusing a functional spasm-related narrowing with true fibrotic stenosis and mismanaging it Attempting forceful dilatation of dense fibrotic stenosis, causing tearing and incontinence Failing to biopsy an atypical stricture and missing Crohn disease or malignancy Performing sphincterotomy alone when tissue deficiency requires flap anoplasty Removing too much anoderm at the index haemorrhoid operation, which is the commonest preventable cause Anal stenosis results from replacement of the elastic, pliable anoderm and mucosa of the anal canal by inelastic fibrous scar, or from fixed narrowing due to inflammatory or neoplastic infiltration. After excisional haemorrhoidectomy or other anal surgery, excessive removal of anoderm leaves broad raw areas that heal by scar contracture, drawing the canal into a rigid, narrowed ring. Chronic anal fissure, Crohn disease, tuberculosis, radiation injury, and chronic dermatoses similarly provoke fibrosis and loss of compliance. The narrowed, non-distensible canal obstructs the passage of stool, causing straining, painful defecation, and mucosal splitting; secondary constipation and stool withholding compound the problem, and any residual sphincter spasm further reduces the effective luminal calibre. Mild anal stenosis often responds well to conservative measures and dilatation, while moderate to severe fibrotic stenosis generally requires anoplasty, which gives good results in experienced hands; outcomes are poorer and recurrence more likely when the underlying cause, such as Crohn disease or radiation, is ongoing.

Analgesic nephropathy — phenacetin nephropathy, analgesic abuse nephropathy, analgesic-induced chronic interstitial nephritis, analgesic kidney Other causes of chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis such as lithium, lead or aristolochic acid (Chinese-herb) nephropathy Reflux nephropathy Chronic pyelonephritis Obstructive uropathy Ischaemic nephropathy Papillary necrosis from other causes A careful analgesic and drug history quantifying cumulative use CT showing small kidneys with an irregular outline and papillary calcification Urinalysis for sterile pyuria and low-grade proteinuria Renal function and assessment of urinary concentrating ability Urine cytology to screen for urothelial malignancy Cross-sectional imaging or cystoscopy if malignancy is suspected A chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis with papillary necrosis caused by prolonged heavy analgesic use, historically phenacetin-containing combinations Cumulative dose over many years is the key exposure, and combination analgesics are more nephrotoxic than single agents Classically described in middle-aged women with chronic pain, headaches or psychiatric comorbidity and a habit of daily analgesic use It presents insidiously with impaired urinary concentration, sterile pyuria, modest proteinuria, hypertension and slowly progressive renal impairment Papillary necrosis may cause haematuria or colic when a papilla sloughs CT typically shows small, scarred kidneys with bumpy contours and papillary calcification There is an increased long-term risk of urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma, so urine cytology surveillance is warranted The essential treatment is to stop all offending analgesics, after which renal decline may stabilise New or persistent haematuria raising concern for urothelial carcinoma Progressive renal impairment despite stopping analgesics Acute obstruction with infection from a sloughed papilla Uncontrolled hypertension Not taking a detailed over-the-counter analgesic history, so the cause is missed Allowing the patient to continue nephrotoxic analgesics for chronic pain Overlooking urothelial malignancy when haematuria develops Attributing the picture to hypertension alone rather than to analgesic injury Long-term ingestion of analgesic mixtures damages the renal medulla by two complementary mechanisms. Phenacetin and its metabolite paracetamol accumulate and generate oxidative injury in the papillary tissue, while aspirin depletes protective prostaglandins, reducing medullary blood flow, and depletes glutathione, potentiating the toxicity. The medulla, already functioning at low oxygen tension, sustains combined ischaemic and oxidative damage leading to papillary necrosis and a surrounding chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis with fibrosis and tubular atrophy. Over years this produces shrunken, scarred kidneys, and chronic urothelial injury predisposes to transitional cell carcinoma. If analgesic use stops early, renal function often stabilises; continued use leads to progressive chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal failure, and a lifelong risk of urothelial cancer persists even after cessation.

Analphalipoproteinaemia — familial HDL deficiency, high-density lipoprotein deficiency, apolipoprotein A-I deficiency, APOA1, ABCA1 Tangier disease (as a specific ABCA1 cause) Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) deficiency Secondary causes of low HDL (severe illness, drugs, metabolic syndrome) Syringomyelia and other cord lesions Vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex Hereditary amyloid neuropathy Fasting lipid panel demonstrating very low HDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein A-I Sequencing of ABCA1 and APOA1 to define the molecular cause Nerve conduction studies to characterise the neuropathy Assessment for hepatosplenomegaly and lipid deposition in tonsils Evaluation for systemic amyloidosis where an APOA1 amyloidogenic variant is suspected Cardiovascular risk assessment in view of altered HDL-mediated protection Term for severe deficiency of high-density lipoprotein, in which plasma HDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein A-I are extremely low or absent Includes ABCA1-related Tangier disease and forms caused by variants in APOA1, the gene encoding the principal HDL apolipoprotein Shares clinical features with Tangier disease, including very low HDL and total cholesterol, hepatosplenomegaly, and in some cases enlarged lipid-laden tonsils Peripheral neuropathy can occur and may be relapsing and multifocal or produce a syringomyelia-like dissociated sensory loss with preferential loss of pain and temperature sensation Certain APOA1 variants also cause hereditary systemic amyloidosis with organ deposition, adding to the phenotypic range A markedly reduced HDL cholesterol on a routine lipid panel is the key laboratory clue and should prompt further evaluation when accompanied by neuropathy or organomegaly Diagnosis combines the characteristic lipid abnormalities with genetic testing of ABCA1 and APOA1 Rapidly progressive multifocal neuropathy causing significant disability Features of systemic amyloidosis such as renal or hepatic involvement with APOA1 variants Progressive dissociated sensory loss raising concern for a spinal cord lesion Painless burns or injuries from unrecognised loss of pain and temperature sensation Dismissing a very low HDL as laboratory error rather than a diagnostic clue Failing to distinguish ABCA1 (Tangier) from APOA1-related disease, which can cause amyloidosis Mistaking pseudosyringomyelic sensory loss for a primary cord lesion Overlooking secondary causes of low HDL before pursuing a genetic diagnosis Analphalipoproteinaemia describes states of profound high-density lipoprotein deficiency arising from defects in HDL metabolism. In ABCA1-related disease (Tangier disease), impaired cholesterol efflux prevents lipidation of apolipoprotein A-I, which is then rapidly degraded; in APOA1-related disease, variants reduce or abolish functional apolipoprotein A-I itself. Either mechanism leaves the body unable to assemble normal HDL particles, so HDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein A-I are very low and cholesterol accumulates within tissue macrophages, producing hepatosplenomegaly and, in some cases, lipid-laden tonsils. Deposition of lipid within Schwann cells and peripheral nerves is thought to drive the neuropathy, which can be multifocal and relapsing or cause a pseudosyringomyelic dissociated sensory loss. Some APOA1 variants additionally form amyloid deposits. Variable and dependent on the underlying gene; neuropathy can be disabling, and APOA1-related amyloidosis may affect vital organs and thereby prognosis, while cardiovascular risk is also altered by the HDL deficiency.

Anaphylaxis — Clinical diagnosis Serum tryptase IM adrenaline immediately Systemic mastocytosis (elevated baseline tryptase; spindle-shaped mast cells on bone marrow) (p. 2813) Pheochromocytoma (elevated urine metanephrines) (p. 2813) Carcinoid syndrome (elevated urine 5-HIAA) (p. 2813) Hereditary angioedema (decreased C4 during attacks) (p. 2813) Acquired angioedema (decreased C1q) (p. 2813) Systemic capillary leak syndrome (severe hypotension with poor response to first-line agents) (p. 2813) Serum tryptase peaks 60-90 min after onset and remains measurable for up to about 5 h; apply the '20% + 2' rule (an acute level >20% above the patient's baseline plus 2 ng/mL is diagnostic of clinically significant mast-cell activation) (p. 2813) Repeat tryptase once the patient is stable to establish the individual baseline, since baseline serum tryptase varies widely and can be raised by hereditary alpha-tryptasemia or high environmental allergen exposure (p. 2813) Serum histamine is of limited use acutely - its measurable window expires within about 1 h of onset (p. 2813) Allergen-specific skin testing or serum-specific IgE to confirm a suspected drug or food trigger (p. 2813) Baseline tryptase in sting-induced anaphylaxis to screen for underlying systemic mastocytosis (p. 2813) Scombroid poisoning (ingested histamine from improperly stored histidine-rich fish such as tuna, mackerel, mahi-mahi); clinically mimics anaphylaxis but tryptase is NOT elevated because histamine is exogenous, and skin test/oral challenge to fish are negative (p. 2813) Direct (pseudoallergic) mast-cell degranulation from opiates, neuromuscular blocking agents, vancomycin, or CT radiocontrast (e.g., via MRGPRX2) - clinically indistinguishable from IgE-mediated reactions but occurs without prior sensitization (p. 2813) Vasovagal (neurally mediated) syncope - provoked by emotion, pain, or orthostatic stress and accompanied by bradycardia, in contrast to the tachycardia and urticaria/angioedema of anaphylaxis (p. 2813; cf. p. 156-157) Onset is typically within seconds to minutes of exposure to the trigger; an exception is the delayed (about 3-6 h) reaction to mammalian meat seen in alpha-gal syndrome (p. 2812-2813). Most episodes (about 80-90%) are uniphasic, but roughly 10-20% are biphasic, with symptoms recurring an hour or more after the initial reaction has resolved (p. 2812). Cutaneous features (urticaria, flushing, generalized warmth) are the most common manifestation, present in over 90% of cases (p. 2812). Cross-linking of allergen with IgE bound to FcepsilonRI receptors on mast cells and basophils is the usual initiating mechanism; sensitization requires prior exposure, so repeated exposure to the antigen is a key risk factor (p. 2812-2813). Some severe reactions are non-IgE-mediated and can occur on first known exposure, because direct mast-cell activation needs no prior sensitization (e.g., via the MRGPRX2 receptor with neuromuscular blockers, quinolones, and icatibant) (p. 2813). Severe Hymenoptera sting anaphylaxis, especially with prominent hypotension, may be the first presentation of underlying systemic mastocytosis; checking a baseline tryptase screens for this (p. 2812-2813). Failure to give epinephrine within the first 20 minutes of symptoms is a risk factor for poor outcomes (p. 2813). About 6% of Western populations carry hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, an extra TPSAB1 allele giving a high baseline tryptase that can confound interpretation and may itself be a risk factor for severe reactions (p. 2813). Hypotension or hypoxia - the most dangerous features, risking cardiovascular collapse or respiratory failure (p. 2812) Laryngeal edema (sensation of a lump in the throat, hoarseness, stridor) or angioedema of the epiglottis/larynx threatening mechanical airway obstruction (p. 2812) Bronchial obstruction (chest tightness, wheezing), especially severe in patients with underlying asthma, who have increased mortality (p. 2812) Underlying asthma or cardiovascular disease - predisposes to more rapid decompensation (p. 2812) Severe GI involvement (vomiting, crampy abdominal pain); bowel-wall angioedema can deplete intravascular volume enough to cause cardiovascular collapse (p. 2812) Treat with epinephrine first - antihistamines, glucocorticoids, and bronchodilators are ancillary agents for residual urticaria/angioedema and bronchospasm once the patient is hemodynamically stable, not initial therapy (p. 2813). Biphasic reactions in 10-20% recur an hour or more after apparent recovery, so a period of observation is needed after initial resolution (p. 2812). A normal tryptase does not exclude anaphylaxis - it is not elevated in scombroid poisoning (exogenous histamine), and an acutely 'normal' value may still be diagnostic relative to a low individual baseline (apply the 20% + 2 rule) (p. 2813). Non-IgE-mediated reactions can occur on first exposure, so the absence of prior exposure does not rule out an anaphylactic reaction (p. 2813). Beta blockers can blunt the response to epinephrine; consider an alternative antihypertensive in patients at high risk of needing emergency epinephrine (p. 2813). Skin/serum specific-IgE testing to foods has relatively poor predictive value, so a positive test alone does not confirm clinical reactivity (p. 2814). Anaphylaxis is driven by mediators released chiefly from mast cells, basophils, and eosinophils. The most common mechanism is allergen cross-linking of IgE bound to FcepsilonRI on mast cells and basophils, triggering degranulation. Preformed granule contents include histamine, proteases (tryptase, chymase), proteoglycans (heparin, chondroitin sulfate), and TNF-alpha; newly generated arachidonic-acid products include cysteinyl leukotrienes, prostaglandin D2, and platelet-activating factor (PAF). Histamine produces flushing, urticaria, pruritus and, at high levels, hypotension and tachycardia; cysteinyl leukotrienes and PGD2 cause bronchoconstriction and increased microvascular permeability, with PGD2 also recruiting eosinophils and basophils. Serum PAF correlates with severity and is inversely related to PAF acetylhydrolase. Tryptase and chymase activate complement (generating the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a) and the kallikrein-kinin system, with mediator effects likely additive or synergistic. Reactions can also be non-IgE-mediated: direct mast-cell activation (e.g., via MRGPRX2 by neuromuscular blockers, quinolones, icatibant; or opiates, vancomycin, radiocontrast, NSAIDs), complement activation (e.g., Cremophor-solubilized paclitaxel), or contact-system/bradykinin generation (e.g., oversulfated chondroitin sulfate heparin contaminant). (p. 2812-2813) Severe and even fatal complications can develop within minutes of symptom onset, making early recognition critical; deaths occur via airway/bronchial obstruction, laryngeal angioedema, or vascular collapse. Delaying epinephrine beyond the first 20 minutes worsens outcomes. Risk is higher with underlying asthma or cardiovascular disease. Natural history varies by trigger: most childhood egg, milk, soy, and wheat allergy resolves, whereas about 80% of peanut allergy persists for life. (p. 2812-2813)

Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma — ATC, undifferentiated thyroid carcinoma, anaplastic carcinoma of thyroid Primary thyroid lymphoma Poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma Medullary thyroid carcinoma Sarcoma of the neck Metastatic carcinoma to the thyroid Riedel (invasive fibrous) thyroiditis Urgent airway assessment including flexible laryngoscopy and cross-sectional imaging of the neck and thorax Core or open biopsy for definitive tissue diagnosis when aspiration is inconclusive Immunohistochemistry to distinguish it from lymphoma, medullary carcinoma, and metastases Expedited molecular testing including BRAF V600E to identify targetable disease Staging cross-sectional or functional imaging to define distant metastasis Serum calcium and thyroid function as part of baseline assessment One of the most aggressive human malignancies, typically presenting in elderly patients as a rapidly enlarging, hard, fixed neck mass over weeks Airway compromise is the dominant early threat, with stridor, dyspnoea, dysphagia, and hoarseness from tracheal and recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement Often arises through dedifferentiation of a pre-existing differentiated thyroid carcinoma or long-standing goitre, frequently accumulating TP53 and TERT promoter mutations Histology shows undifferentiated spindle, giant, or epithelioid cells with brisk mitoses and necrosis, losing thyroid differentiation markers so it does not concentrate iodine Because it is not iodine-avid, radioactive iodine is ineffective and management centres on urgent airway assessment, tissue diagnosis, and multimodal therapy All cases are considered stage IV by convention given the near-universal advanced behaviour at diagnosis BRAF V600E-mutated tumours may respond to targeted BRAF-directed therapy, so molecular testing should be expedited Impending airway obstruction with stridor or dyspnoea requiring emergency airway evaluation Rapidly enlarging fixed neck mass in an elderly patient New hoarseness or dysphagia indicating invasion of the recurrent laryngeal nerve or oesophagus Widespread distant metastases at presentation Delaying airway assessment while awaiting a full diagnostic work-up in a patient with a rapidly growing mass Mistaking anaplastic carcinoma for lymphoma, which has a very different and far more favourable treatment, without immunohistochemistry Expecting benefit from radioactive iodine in a tumour that no longer concentrates iodine Omitting rapid BRAF testing and thereby missing an opportunity for targeted therapy Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is an undifferentiated malignancy of follicular-cell origin that has lost the features of differentiated thyroid cancer, including iodine uptake and thyroglobulin production. It commonly evolves from a pre-existing papillary or follicular carcinoma or a long-standing goitre through progressive genetic hits, characteristically TP53 inactivation and TERT promoter mutations superimposed on earlier BRAF or RAS alterations. The result is a highly proliferative, invasive tumour that rapidly infiltrates the trachea, oesophagus, strap muscles, and great vessels of the neck and disseminates widely, so local airway obstruction and distant metastasis appear early. Prognosis is dismal, with median survival typically only a few months; occasional patients with resectable, intrathyroidal disease or a targetable mutation such as BRAF V600E may survive longer with multimodal treatment.

Andersen disease (GSD IV, branching enzyme) — GSD IV, glycogen storage disease type IV, amylopectinosis, glycogen branching enzyme deficiency, GBE1 deficiency Other causes of infantile cirrhosis and hepatosplenomegaly (e.g. neonatal haemochromatosis, tyrosinaemia, biliary atresia) Other hepatic glycogen storage diseases Congenital muscular dystrophies and congenital myopathies in the neuromuscular form Lafora disease and other polyglucosan-related disorders Adult-onset motor neurone disease or multiple sclerosis mimicking adult polyglucosan body disease Mitochondrial hepatopathy Glycogen branching enzyme activity assay in leucocytes, fibroblasts, or liver Molecular genetic testing of GBE1 Liver biopsy showing PAS-positive, partially diastase-resistant polyglucosan inclusions and fibrosis/cirrhosis Echocardiography and creatine kinase where cardiac or muscle involvement is suspected MRI, nerve conduction studies, and urodynamics in suspected adult polyglucosan body disease Andersen disease (GSD IV) is an autosomal recessive deficiency of glycogen branching enzyme (GBE1), leading to accumulation of abnormal, poorly branched amylopectin-like glycogen (polyglucosan) The classic hepatic form presents in infancy with failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, and progressive liver cirrhosis with portal hypertension, often fatal in early childhood without transplantation Unlike most hepatic glycogenoses, hypoglycaemia is not the dominant feature; progressive liver failure is There is a wide phenotypic spectrum, including a severe neuromuscular perinatal or congenital form with hypotonia, contractures, and cardiomyopathy An adult-onset variant, adult polyglucosan body disease, causes progressive neurogenic bladder, spasticity, peripheral neuropathy, and cognitive change Diagnosis relies on demonstrating deficient branching enzyme activity and characteristic PAS-positive, partially diastase-resistant polyglucosan inclusions, confirmed by GBE1 genetics Liver transplantation can be life-saving in the progressive hepatic form Progressive hepatic decompensation with ascites, coagulopathy, or variceal bleeding Failure to thrive with worsening hepatosplenomegaly in infancy Cardiac failure or arrhythmia from cardiomyopathy Severe neonatal hypotonia with contractures indicating the perinatal neuromuscular form Expecting prominent hypoglycaemia and missing GSD IV, in which liver failure rather than hypoglycaemia dominates Attributing infantile cirrhosis to more common hepatic causes without considering a glycogenosis Not recognising adult polyglucosan body disease as part of the GBE1 spectrum Confusing polyglucosan inclusions with other storage material without enzyme and genetic confirmation Glycogen branching enzyme introduces the alpha-1,6 branch points that give glycogen its soluble, highly branched structure. In GSD IV, deficient GBE1 activity results in synthesis of an abnormal glycogen with few branch points, resembling amylopectin (polyglucosan). This insoluble material precipitates within cells and provokes tissue injury. In the liver it drives inflammation, fibrosis, and cirrhosis; in heart and skeletal muscle it produces cardiomyopathy and myopathy; and in the nervous system polyglucosan bodies accumulate in neurones and axons, underlying the neuromuscular and adult-onset neurological phenotypes. The classic progressive hepatic form is often fatal in early childhood without liver transplantation, whereas non-progressive hepatic and adult-onset forms have more variable, sometimes prolonged courses; the perinatal neuromuscular form carries a poor prognosis.

Andersen-Tawil syndrome — ATS, Andersen syndrome, long QT syndrome type 7, LQT7, KCNJ2, periodic paralysis with cardiac dysrhythmia and dysmorphism Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis Hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis Other congenital long QT syndromes Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis Other syndromic causes of short stature and dysmorphism Twelve-lead electrocardiogram and prolonged rhythm monitoring for U waves, QU prolongation and ventricular ectopy Serum potassium measured during paralytic episodes Echocardiography to assess cardiac structure and function Prolonged exercise electromyography protocol to characterise the periodic paralysis Targeted KCNJ2 genetic testing, with a broader panel if negative Clinical dysmorphology assessment and skeletal imaging as indicated Defined by a clinical triad of periodic paralysis, ventricular arrhythmia with characteristic electrocardiographic changes, and distinctive dysmorphic features Dysmorphism includes low-set ears, hypertelorism, a small mandible, clinodactyly and syndactyly, and short stature The characteristic electrocardiogram shows prominent U waves and a prolonged QU interval with frequent ventricular ectopy, and it is classed as long QT syndrome type 7 Ventricular arrhythmias, including bidirectional and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, are often surprisingly well tolerated but carry a risk of syncope Periodic paralysis in this syndrome can be associated with a low, normal or high serum potassium, so the potassium-shift pattern is variable between families Inherited as an autosomal dominant condition with marked variable expressivity, most often due to mutations in the KCNJ2 gene encoding the inward-rectifier potassium channel Kir2.1 The full triad may be incomplete in any given patient, so a normal cardiac or dysmorphic assessment does not exclude the diagnosis Syncope, palpitations or documented ventricular tachycardia indicating arrhythmic risk Family history of sudden cardiac death Marked QU prolongation with frequent or complex ventricular ectopy Respiratory or severe generalised weakness during a paralytic attack Diagnosing simple periodic paralysis and missing the cardiac and dysmorphic components of the triad Expecting a consistent potassium-shift direction, when the potassium level during attacks is variable Under-appreciating arrhythmic risk because the ventricular tachycardia is often asymptomatic Prescribing QT-prolonging drugs without recognising the underlying repolarisation abnormality Andersen-Tawil syndrome is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in KCNJ2, which encodes the inward-rectifier potassium channel Kir2.1. This channel stabilises the resting membrane potential and shapes the terminal phase of repolarisation in both skeletal and cardiac muscle. Reduced Kir2.1 current, often through a dominant-negative effect on the tetrameric channel, destabilises the resting potential of skeletal muscle to produce periodic paralysis, and prolongs and destabilises cardiac repolarisation to generate the prominent U waves, QU prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias. The same channel and related developmental signalling pathways are implicated in the skeletal and craniofacial dysmorphism that completes the triad. Life expectancy is usually near normal because the ventricular arrhythmias are frequently well tolerated, but syncope and, rarely, sudden cardiac death can occur, so cardiac surveillance is essential and the periodic paralysis and dysmorphic features add variable long-term morbidity.

There is a reduction in Leydig cell number and secretory capacity (a primary testicular component) alongside blunting of luteinising hormone pulse amplitude and altered hypothalamic drive (a secondary central component), so gonadotropins are often only modestly elevated. Comorbidities that accumulate with age, particularly obesity, type 2 diabetes, the metabolic syndrome, and chronic illness, suppress the axis and amplify the fall, meaning much of the observed deficiency is functional rather than fixed organic gonadal failure. With appropriate multidisciplinary care, including psychological support, sex steroid management and individualised decisions about gonadal retention or removal, outcomes are generally good, though fertility is not possible and gender identity should guide management.

principally dihydrotestosterone generated from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase. In susceptible follicles androgens progressively shorten the anagen phase and drive miniaturisation, so successive cycles produce finer, shorter and less pigmented hairs until only vellus hairs remain. Anejaculation — failure of ejaculation, absent ejaculation, aspermia, failure of seminal emission Retrograde ejaculation with backward flow of semen Ejaculatory duct obstruction Severe hypogonadism reducing seminal output Spinal cord injury or neurological disease Medication effect, particularly antidepressants and antipsychotics Psychogenic inhibition of ejaculation Post-orgasmic urine analysis to distinguish failure of emission from retrograde ejaculation Detailed neurological, surgical, and drug history Blood glucose or HbA1c to detect diabetes Serum testosterone and gonadotropins to assess the endocrine axis Scrotal and transrectal ultrasound where obstruction or structural abnormality is suspected Assessment of nocturnal or situational ejaculation to gauge a psychogenic component Anejaculation is the complete absence of antegrade ejaculate, which may occur with or without preserved orgasmic sensation It must be separated from retrograde ejaculation, so a post-orgasmic urine sample is examined; the absence of sperm there indicates true failure of emission rather than backward flow Causes span neurological injury (spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, diabetic autonomic neuropathy), pelvic and retroperitoneal surgery, medications, and psychogenic factors A situational pattern, with normal nocturnal emissions or ejaculation in some circumstances, points towards a psychogenic rather than organic cause In spinal cord injury and other neurogenic cases, penile vibratory stimulation and, if unsuccessful, electroejaculation can induce emission for fertility purposes When induced ejaculation fails or is unsuitable, surgical sperm retrieval from the epididymis or testis provides sperm for intracytoplasmic sperm injection A careful drug history is essential, as antidepressants, antipsychotics, and sympatholytic agents can impair or abolish ejaculation New neurological symptoms suggesting spinal cord disease or demyelination History of recent retroperitoneal or pelvic surgery with autonomic disturbance Sudden loss of ejaculation with other autonomic features Associated erectile failure and sensory loss indicating a broader neurological deficit Failing to examine post-orgasmic urine and thereby confusing anejaculation with retrograde ejaculation Overlooking a causative medication that could be modified Missing an underlying neurological disorder presenting with ejaculatory failure Assuming an organic cause when the pattern is situational and psychogenic Delaying referral for assisted reproductive techniques when natural conception is not feasible Ejaculation is a two-phase spinal reflex: sympathetic-driven emission deposits sperm and seminal fluid into the posterior urethra with simultaneous bladder-neck closure, followed by rhythmic somatic contraction of the pelvic-floor muscles that expels semen. Anejaculation results when the emission phase fails, so no seminal fluid reaches the urethra. This occurs with interruption of the sympathetic outflow through spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, or retroperitoneal surgery that damages the sympathetic chain, and with drugs that block sympathetic transmission. Psychogenic anejaculation reflects central inhibition of the reflex with an intact peripheral apparatus. Unlike retrograde ejaculation, in which emission occurs but is misdirected into the bladder, true anejaculation produces no semen in either the antegrade ejaculate or the post-orgasmic urine. General health is unaffected, and fertility can frequently be achieved using vibratory stimulation, electroejaculation, or surgical sperm retrieval combined with assisted reproduction; psychogenic cases may respond to behavioural or psychological treatment.

Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss — Acute posthemorrhagic anemia, APHA, Posthemorrhagic anemia Hemolytic anemia (the other major cause of anemia with reticulocytosis) (p.807) Iron-deficiency anemia from chronic/protracted blood loss (p.807) Other hypoproliferative or production-failure anemias when reticulocyte count is not elevated (p.807) Serial hemoglobin/hematocrit measurements — recognizing that early values are misleadingly normal and fall over hours as volume is restored (p.807) Reticulocyte count and erythropoietin level — rise during the marrow recovery phase (p.807) Imaging or endoscopy (e.g., sonogram, endoscopy) to localize occult internal bleeding (p.807) Targeted physical examination for signs of concealed hemorrhage (Grey Turner sign, Cullen sign, chest dullness) (p.807) Hemolysis — also presents as anemia with an elevated reticulocyte count and a brisk marrow response, mimicking the recovery phase of acute blood loss (p.807) Hypovolemic shock from non-hemorrhagic causes (dehydration, fluid sequestration) can reproduce the early hypovolemic picture before any fall in hemoglobin (p.807) In the first hours after a sudden large bleed the routine blood count typically does NOT reveal anemia, because hemoglobin concentration is initially unchanged; the dominant problem at this stage is hypovolemia, not a low hemoglobin (p.807). Hemoglobin falls only gradually over several hours to days as the intravascular volume is restored — either by intravenous fluids given acutely, or by the body's own fluid shift from the extravascular into the intravascular compartment (hemodilution) — so the measured hemoglobin lags behind the true blood loss (p.807). The degree of anemia eventually reflects the amount lost: as a rough guide, a hemoglobin around 7 g/dL after about 3 days implies roughly half of the total blood has been lost (p.807). If bleeding stops, the marrow response (rising reticulocyte count and erythropoietin) gradually corrects the anemia; this reticulocyte rise mirrors the marrow response seen in hemolysis (p.807). Acute blood loss and hemolysis are the two principal causes of anemia accompanied by an elevated reticulocyte count (p.807). Signs of vascular instability appear once roughly 25% or more of total blood volume is lost; donating a unit of blood (~20% of volume) is usually only minimally symptomatic (p.807). Bedside signs of concealed bleeding include the Grey Turner sign (flank ecchymosis, suggesting retroperitoneal hemorrhage), the Cullen sign (periumbilical ecchymosis, suggesting intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal bleeding), and dullness to chest percussion (suggesting intrapleural blood) (p.807). The amount of blood lost is frequently overestimated when a scene appears bloody; careful repeated examination and directed investigations (e.g., ultrasound, endoscopy) are needed to localize occult bleeding (p.807). Whenever hemoglobin drops abruptly, acute posthemorrhagic anemia should be suspected regardless of the history initially offered by the patient (p.807). Compensation is partly achieved by a rightward shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve: with mild loss via the Bohr effect (lower pH / higher CO2), and in more chronic anemia via rising intracellular 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, which aids oxygen unloading (p.807). Surgery is an important iatrogenic cause of acute posthemorrhagic anemia; blood loss can be substantial (e.g., up to about 2 L with radical prostatectomy) and should be measured and monitored (p.807-808). Loss of consciousness or acute renal failure early on, reflecting hypovolemic threat to brain and kidneys before any anemia is detectable (p.807) Postural hypotension and tachycardia with a preference to remain supine, indicating sudden loss exceeding ~30% of blood volume that overwhelms sympathetic compensation (p.807) Hypovolemic shock — confusion, dyspnea, diaphoresis, hypotension, tachycardia — indicating loss >40% (>~2 L in an average adult) and significant vital-organ hypoperfusion (p.807) Tachycardia, tachypnea, narrowed pulse pressure, cold, pale, mottled skin and reduced urine output signaling sympathetic compensation for ongoing loss (p.807) Mistakenly excluding significant hemorrhage because an early blood count shows a normal hemoglobin — the fall is delayed until volume is restored (p.807). Overestimating blood loss from the bloody appearance of a scene rather than from careful clinical assessment (p.807). Failing to suspect occult internal bleeding after trauma, where even large losses may not be immediately obvious (p.807). Focusing on the anemia number rather than on hypovolemia and organ perfusion, which are the true early threats in large acute losses (p.807). Blood loss produces anemia by two mechanisms: direct loss of red cells, and — if the bleeding is protracted — gradual depletion of iron stores leading to iron-deficiency anemia (the latter covered separately). Acute posthemorrhagic anemia follows the former. Hemorrhage may be external (trauma, obstetric) or internal (gastrointestinal tract, splenic rupture, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, subarachnoid hemorrhage, leaking aneurysm). After a sudden large loss there are three sequential clinical/pathophysiologic stages: (1) hypovolemia dominates and threatens high-flow organs (brain, kidneys), so impaired consciousness and acute renal failure are early dangers, while the blood count still appears normal because hemoglobin concentration is unchanged; (2) baroreceptor and stretch-receptor activation triggers vasopressin and other peptide release and a shift of fluid from the extravascular into the intravascular space, producing hemodilution that converts hypovolemia into measurable anemia proportional to the volume lost; (3) provided bleeding ceases, increased marrow erythropoiesis (reflected by elevated reticulocytes and erythropoietin) gradually ameliorates the anemia. Tissue oxygen delivery is defended by rightward shifts of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve (acute Bohr effect from lower pH/higher CO2; chronic rise in 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate) and by shunting blood away from organs with relatively rich supply (kidney, gut, skin) (p.807). Outcome depends on the rapidity and volume of loss and on whether the source can be controlled. If bleeding is stopped, the marrow's compensatory rise in red cell production gradually corrects the anemia. The acute danger is not the anemia itself but hypovolemia and impaired organ perfusion: losses above ~30% of blood volume overwhelm normal compensatory mechanisms, and losses >40% (>~2 L in an average adult) produce hypovolemic shock with significant vital-organ perfusion deficits (p.807). Severity tracks the fraction of total blood volume lost: ~20% (one unit) is usually minimally symptomatic; signs of vascular instability emerge at ~25% or more; sudden loss of >30% overwhelms sympathetic compensation and produces postural hypotension and tachycardia; loss of >40% (>~2 L in an average-sized adult) causes hypovolemic shock (confusion, dyspnea, diaphoresis, hypotension, tachycardia). Symptomatic chronic/progressive anemia from slower loss often becomes apparent only when hemoglobin falls below ~70-80 g/L (7-8 g/dL), and intrinsic compensation maintains normal tissue oxygen delivery only across about a 20-30 g/L (2-3 g/dL) hemoglobin deficit (p.807).

at the suspected underlying disorder A common anaemia arising in chronic infection, inflammation and malignancy, driven by immune activation rather than iron deficiency Typically normocytic and normochromic, though it can become mildly microcytic in longstanding cases The hallmark is functional iron restriction, with iron present in stores but unavailable for erythropoiesis Ferritin is normal or raised while transferrin saturation is low, the reverse of the picture in absolute iron deficiency The cytokine-induced hormone hepcidin blocks iron release from macrophages and reduces correcting the inflammation improves the anaemia A disproportionately severe anaemia suggesting an additional cause such as bleeding or marrow disease A low ferritin indicating coexisting iron deficiency that warrants investigation New anaemia as the presenting feature of an occult malignancy or chronic infection Rapidly progressive anaemia not explained by the known chronic illness Diagnosing iron deficiency on microcytosis alone without checking ferritin and saturation Missing coexisting true iron deficiency when ferritin is low-normal in an inflamed patient Giving iron indiscriminately when stores are already adequate but functionally locked away Failing to pursue the underlying inflammatory, infective or neoplastic cause Anaemia of chronic disease is driven by sustained immune activation. Inflammatory cytokines, particularly interleukin-6, stimulate hepatic production of hepcidin, the master regulator of iron. Hepcidin degrades the iron-export protein ferroportin, trapping iron within macrophages and enterocytes so that although stores are adequate the metal cannot reach developing erythroblasts, producing a functional iron restriction. In parallel, cytokines blunt the erythropoietin response and shorten red-cell survival, while direct suppression of erythroid progenitors further limits red-cell production. The net effect is a modest anaemia with high or normal ferritin, low transferrin saturation and raised hepcidin, distinguishing it from absolute iron deficiency in which stores are exhausted. The anaemia is usually mild to moderate and follows the course of the underlying disease; it improves when the inflammatory process is controlled and rarely causes serious symptoms on its own.

hypovolaemia dominates and anemia appears only after fluid shifts/resuscitation (p.850) Spurious/relative changes: serum iron and transferrin saturation vary diurnally, which can mislead iron-status interpretation (p.449) Symptoms and signs of anemia correlate poorly with the actual haemoglobin/haematocrit; clinical severity reflects the rate of onset and the patient's cardiovascular reserve rather than the absolute level (p.444). Slowly developing anemia is remarkably well tolerated because three compensatory mechanisms develop over time: rapid rise in cardiac output (minutes), a rise in 2,3-DPG that lowers haemoglobin oxygen affinity and improves tissue oxygen offloading (hours to days), and an expansion of plasma volume (weeks) (p.444). Plasma-volume expansion can occasionally overwhelm the heart and precipitate features of heart failure/oedema in chronic anemia (p.444). Patients with limited cardiac reserve or atherosclerosis become symptomatic (angina, TIA/stroke) at a higher haematocrit than those with normal cardiovascular function (p.444). The absolute reticulocyte count is the key first branch point for mechanism: an elevated count points to blood loss or haemolysis, while a low or inappropriately low count points to impaired production (p.448-449). Manual percentage reticulocyte counts must be corrected for the haematocrit (a 1% count becomes an apparent 2% at a haematocrit of ~23%); the machine-derived absolute reticulocyte count needs no such correction (p.447). Around 75% of all anemia is hypoproliferative, most often from mild-to-moderate iron deficiency or inflammation (p.449). Anemia is frequently multifactorial (e.g., chronic inflammation plus occult GI blood loss in a patient on anti-inflammatory drugs), so iron status should be evaluated fully before and during treatment of any anemia (p.450). Serum ferritin is an acute-phase reactant: it can be raised several-fold by inflammation and mask coexisting iron deficiency, whereas a ferritin <30 ug/L reliably indicates depleted body iron stores (p.449). A high RDW favours iron deficiency (anisocytosis), whereas a low/normal RDW with microcytosis favours thalassaemia, where cells are more uniform in size (p.449). Iron-deficiency pica and the neuropathy of B12 deficiency are deficiency-specific clues to seek on history and examination (p.444). In acute blood loss the haemoglobin/haematocrit initially does NOT reflect the volume lost; the early picture is hypovolaemia, and the haemoglobin only falls over hours as fluid shifts and resuscitation dilute the blood (p.850). Circulating blasts or other immature white cells, severe pancytopenia, or a very low reticulocyte count (<0.1%) mandating urgent marrow examination (p.448) Myelophthisic blood film (nucleated red cells, teardrop cells, immature white cells) suggesting marrow infiltration/replacement (p.450) Hypotension, angina, or other signs of cardiac compromise as clear indications that the anemia is not being tolerated (p.450) Acute haemorrhage with sudden loss of >25-30% of blood volume: vascular instability and decreased organ perfusion supervene and cannot be compensated by sympathetic mechanisms (p.850-851) Loss of consciousness or acute kidney injury early in major haemorrhage, reflecting hypovolaemic threat to brain and kidneys before any fall in haemoglobin (p.850) Clinical signs of concealed internal bleeding: Grey Turner sign (flank ecchymosis, retroperitoneal), Cullen sign (umbilical ecchymosis), or dullness to chest percussion (intrapleural) (p.850) Anchoring on a normal haemoglobin in early acute haemorrhage and underestimating blood loss; an abrupt fall in haemoglobin should prompt suspicion of acute posthemorrhagic anemia regardless of the given history (p.850). Estimates of blood volume lost at a bloody scene are often overestimated, while concealed internal bleeding may be missed entirely (p.850). Relying on ferritin alone during inflammation, which can falsely normalise or elevate it despite true iron deficiency (p.449). Treating macrocytosis as automatically B12/folate deficiency; if megaloblastic markers (hypersegmentation, macro-ovalocytes) are present but nutritional tests are normal, suspect myelodysplasia and proceed to marrow examination (p.451). Forgetting that the anemia of chronic disease/inflammation frequently has a normal MCV, so a normal MCV does not exclude it (p.449-451). Performing marrow aspiration before biopsy, which distorts the biopsy with aspiration-induced bleeding (p.448). Overlooking drug causes: ACE inhibitors can suppress EPO; chemotherapy and some antiseizure drugs cause macrocytosis (p.449-450). Anemia results from a defect in any of the three requirements for normal red-cell production: renal erythropoietin (EPO) output, a functioning erythroid marrow, and adequate substrate (especially iron). EPO rises logarithmically once haemoglobin falls below ~100-120 g/L, but in chronic kidney disease and chronic inflammation EPO is inappropriately low for the degree of anemia. With adequate EPO and substrate, marrow red-cell output can rise four- to fivefold over 1-2 weeks. Mechanistically anemia is either hyperproductive/regenerative (blood loss or haemolysis, with reticulocytosis) or hypoproliferative (nutritional deficiency, marrow replacement, absent precursors, stem-cell defects, or EPO deficiency). Inflammatory cytokines such as TNF lower EPO and raise hepcidin, which blocks iron absorption and release from stores, producing the anemia of inflammation (p.443-450). Anemia in those over 65 is associated with increased risk of death, hospitalization, and frailty. In acute posthemorrhagic anemia, if bleeding stops the marrow response (reticulocytosis, rising EPO) gradually corrects the anemia. Myelodysplasia has a variable course, from years of stability to rapid evolution into acute leukaemia (p.449-450). Two complementary classifications. (1) By red-cell size (Wintrobe): microcytic (iron deficiency, thalassaemia, sideroblastic, anemia of inflammation), normocytic (renal disease, marrow invasion, myeloma, aplastic anemia, pure red cell aplasia, endocrinopathies), and macrocytic - subdivided into oval macrocytes (B12/folate deficiency, myelodysplasia, drugs) and round macrocytes (alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, hypoxia, reticulocytosis, smoking, dysproteinemia). (2) By mechanism: hyperproductive (blood loss, haemolysis - reticulocytes high) versus underproductive/hypoproliferative (nutritional deficiency, absent precursors, lack of EPO, marrow replacement, stem-cell defects - reticulocytes low/inappropriate). The absolute reticulocyte count plus MCV drive the diagnostic algorithm (p.448-451). For acute blood loss: vascular instability appears with sudden loss of ~25% of total blood volume, and >30% loss exceeds compensatory mechanisms (p.851).

and characteristic fluid-fluid levels on MRI or CT Fluid-fluid levels reflect sedimentation of uncoagulated blood within cystic spaces and are suggestive but not pathognomonic Primary lesions harbour chondroblastoma, osteoblastoma or a telangiectatic osteosarcoma before diagnosing a primary lesion Standard management is intralesional curettage with bone grafting or adjuncts, though sclerotherapy and selective embolisation are increasingly used Local recurrence after curettage is not uncommon, particularly with incomplete removal in young children Rapid growth, a permeative margin or an associated soft-tissue mass suggesting telangiectatic osteosarcoma Spinal lesions causing neurological compromise or vertebral instability Pathological fracture through a weakened expanded cortex Recurrence with more aggressive imaging features after prior treatment Mistaking a telangiectatic osteosarcoma for a benign aneurysmal bone cyst on imaging alone Diagnosing a primary lesion without excluding a secondary aneurysmal change within another tumour Assuming fluid-fluid levels are specific, as they occur in several cystic bone lesions Underestimating recurrence risk after incomplete curettage in skeletally immature patients Aneurysmal bone cyst is a benign but locally destructive neoplasm composed of blood-filled cystic spaces separated by fibrous septa containing osteoclast-type giant cells, reactive woven bone and spindle cells. Primary lesions are driven by rearrangement of the USP6 gene, which places the coding sequence under an active promoter and drives cell proliferation, confirming a true neoplastic rather than purely reactive process. Expansion of the vascular spaces thins and remodels the surrounding cortex, producing the expansile appearance and structural weakening. A morphologically identical secondary process can be superimposed on other primary bone tumours, which lack the USP6 rearrangement. Primary aneurysmal bone cyst is benign and does not metastasise, with generally good outcomes after complete removal, although local recurrence occurs in a minority and repeat treatment may be needed. Outcome depends heavily on excluding a malignant mimic at the outset.

Angelman syndrome — AS, happy puppet syndrome, 15q11-q13 maternal deletion syndrome, UBE3A-related syndrome Rett syndrome Mowat-Wilson syndrome Non-specific cerebral palsy with ataxia Pitt-Hopkins syndrome Other syndromic epileptic encephalopathies DNA methylation analysis of 15q11-q13 as the initial diagnostic test Follow-up studies to define mechanism, including UBE3A sequencing when methylation is normal but suspicion persists Electroencephalography, which often shows a characteristic pattern Neurodevelopmental assessment and communication evaluation Sleep assessment when disturbance is significant Characterised by severe intellectual disability, near-absent speech, and a happy demeanour with frequent laughter and smiling Movement disorder features ataxia, jerky limb movements, and a characteristic wide-based, stiff gait A history of frequent bursts of laughter, hand-flapping, and excitable behaviour is a helpful clinical clue Seizures usually begin in early childhood and are often accompanied by a distinctive EEG pattern even between clinical seizures Microcephaly, a wide mouth with widely spaced teeth, and a prominent chin become more apparent with age Caused by loss of function of the maternally inherited UBE3A gene at 15q11-q13, most commonly a maternal deletion Represents the reciprocal imprinting disorder to Prader-Willi syndrome at the same chromosomal locus Sleep disturbance with reduced sleep need is common and can be very disruptive for families Frequent or prolonged seizures, including status epilepticus, requiring prompt management Feeding and swallowing difficulties with aspiration risk in infancy Scoliosis developing with age needing orthopaedic surveillance Severe communication impairment necessitating augmentative communication support Misdiagnosing as cerebral palsy and missing the genetic cause Assuming a normal methylation test excludes the diagnosis when UBE3A mutation testing is still needed Underrecognising the characteristic EEG changes Overlooking the marked and treatable sleep disturbance Angelman syndrome is caused by loss of function of the maternally expressed UBE3A gene within the imprinted 15q11-q13 region. In neurons, only the maternal UBE3A copy is active because the paternal copy is silenced, so loss of the maternal allele leaves neurons without functional UBE3A, which encodes a ubiquitin ligase important for synaptic regulation. The most common mechanism is a de novo maternal deletion; other causes include paternal uniparental disomy, an imprinting defect, and UBE3A point mutations. The resulting neuronal dysfunction produces the severe developmental impairment, movement disorder, and epilepsy. Life expectancy is near normal, but severe intellectual disability and lack of speech persist lifelong; seizures often improve after childhood, and quality of life depends on multidisciplinary support and communication aids.

Angiodysplasia — gastrointestinal angiodysplasia, vascular ectasia Diverticular bleeding Dieulafoy lesion Gastric antral vascular ectasia Colorectal neoplasm Inflammatory or ischaemic colitis Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia Upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy Capsule endoscopy or device-assisted enteroscopy for small-bowel lesions CT or catheter angiography during active bleeding Full blood count and iron studies Assessment for aortic stenosis and von Willebrand disease in recurrent cases Acquired ectatic submucosal and mucosal blood vessels that are a common cause of obscure gastrointestinal bleeding, especially in older people Most often found in the right colon and caecum, but they occur throughout the gut Bleeding is typically intermittent, painless and can be occult (iron-deficiency anaemia) or overt Associations include chronic kidney disease, aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome) and von Willebrand disease Endoscopy shows characteristic fern-like or spider-like vascular lesions and allows treatment Endoscopic ablation is first-line; refractory or diffuse cases may need medical therapy or, rarely, surgery Haemodynamically significant or transfusion-dependent bleeding Recurrent obscure bleeding despite treatment Coexisting aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome) Features suggesting malignancy as an alternative source Overlooking Heyde syndrome and the role of aortic valve intervention Attributing anaemia to angiodysplasia without excluding malignancy Missing small-bowel lesions requiring capsule or enteroscopy Not addressing contributory bleeding disorders Angiodysplasia consists of dilated, thin-walled, tortuous vessels in the gut wall, thought to arise from chronic, intermittent low-grade obstruction of submucosal veins leading to dilatation of the venules and overlying capillaries and loss of precapillary sphincter competence. The fragile ectatic vessels bleed intermittently. Systemic factors that impair haemostasis, such as acquired von Willebrand syndrome in aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome) and platelet dysfunction in chronic kidney disease, increase bleeding from these lesions. Many lesions are managed successfully with endoscopic therapy, but recurrence is common, particularly with diffuse lesions or predisposing systemic conditions.

ACE-inhibitor / hereditary angioedema — Airway assessment C1-esterase inhibitor / C4 if recurrent Airway swelling — secure airway; not always histamine-mediated Allergic (histaminergic, IgE/mast-cell-mediated) angioedema, typically with concurrent urticaria/pruritus and a more rapid onset and resolution (pp. 2807-2808). Hereditary angioedema (HAE) due to C1-inhibitor deficiency (type 1) or dysfunctional C1INH (type 2), suggested by childhood/adolescent onset, family history, recurrent attacks, and failure to respond to H1 antihistamines (p. 2808). Type 3 (normal-C1INH) HAE, sometimes associated with a mutant factor XII and normal complement protein levels (p. 2808). Acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency from excessive C1INH consumption or an anti-C1INH autoantibody in the setting of lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease, lacking a family history (p. 2808). Idiopathic angioedema without an identifiable trigger (p. 2807). Urticarial vasculitis when lesions are painful rather than pruritic, last >36 h, or scar (p. 2809). Angioedema from other bradykinin-affecting or culprit drugs listed alongside ACE inhibitors: NSAIDs/aspirin, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors, radiocontrast media, opioids, antimicrobials, and angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI/sacubitril-valsartan) (Table 363-1, p. 2807; Ch. 265, p. 1995). Diagnosis of bradykinin-mediated angioedema is largely clinical; the lack of pruritus/urticaria and failure to respond to H1 antihistamines point away from histaminergic causes (p. 2808). For isolated angioedema without urticaria: basic chemistries with liver function tests and complement levels (p. 2809). C1INH antigen level (deficient in type 1 HAE) and a catalytic C1INH functional assay (abnormal in type 2 HAE) to evaluate for C1-inhibitor deficiency (p. 2808). C4 and C2 levels: chronically depleted in C1INH-deficiency states and fall further during attacks; in acquired forms, C1q and C1 function are also reduced (p. 2808). Consider evaluation for paraproteinemia / underlying lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease when acquired C1INH deficiency is suspected (p. 2809). Anaphylaxis / allergic angioedema with airway involvement (histamine-mediated) — important to distinguish because the bradykinin form responds poorly to anaphylaxis therapy (pp. 2807-2808). Hereditary or acquired C1-inhibitor-deficiency angioedema presenting with laryngeal edema or recurrent abdominal colic (p. 2808). An acute surgical abdomen, mimicked by gastrointestinal angioedema causing abdominal colic, nausea, and vomiting (p. 2808). ACE-inhibitor angioedema occurs in roughly 0.2-0.7% of exposed patients and is driven by impaired (delayed) degradation of bradykinin rather than by an IgE/mast-cell allergic mechanism (p. 2807). Recognized risk factors for ACE inhibitor-related angioedema include Black race, prior organ transplant, female sex, smoking, and increasing age (p. 2807). Bradykinin-mediated angioedema (whether from an ACE inhibitor or from C1-inhibitor deficiency) is characterized by the conspicuous ABSENCE of accompanying urticaria or pruritus (p. 2808). Compared with histamine-/mast-cell-driven urticaria-angioedema, bradykinin-mediated swelling tends to be more painful than pruritic, with minimal surrounding erythema, and is slower to resolve, persisting >24 h (pp. 2807-2808). The most common sites of angioedema are periorbital and perioral; lesions are neither symmetric nor dependent in distribution (p. 2808). Gastrointestinal-tract involvement is a frequent feature of bradykinin-mediated angioedema and may present as abdominal colic with or without nausea and vomiting; this can mimic an acute abdomen and lead to unnecessary surgery (p. 2808). ACE inhibitors are a recognized (if uncommon) cause of intestinal angioedema, which can present with diarrhea/abdominal symptoms (Ch. on diarrhea, GI section). No residual scarring follows urticaria or angioedema unless an underlying vasculitic process is present (p. 2808). Upper-respiratory-tract / laryngeal angioedema can cause transient airway obstruction and is potentially life-threatening (p. 2808). Tongue, oropharyngeal, or laryngeal swelling indicating threatened airway (pp. 2807-2808). Progressive or persistent swelling lasting >24 h, characteristic of bradykinin-mediated angioedema and warning against assuming a self-limited allergic course (p. 2808). Because the swelling is bradykinin- and not histamine-mediated, it responds poorly to the standard allergic-angioedema/anaphylaxis measures (adrenaline, antihistamines, glucocorticoids); relying on these can give false reassurance (mechanism is non-histaminergic per p. 2808). Onset is not necessarily immediate after starting the drug — ACE-inhibitor angioedema reflects DELAYED bradykinin degradation and can appear well after therapy has begun, so a long-standing ACE inhibitor should not be dismissed as the cause (delayed-degradation mechanism, p. 2807). Absence of urticaria/pruritus can lead clinicians to overlook angioedema or misattribute it; isolated angioedema without hives is a hallmark of the bradykinin mechanism, not evidence against it (p. 2808). Gastrointestinal angioedema mimicking an acute abdomen may prompt unnecessary surgical intervention (p. 2808). Switching to or overlapping with an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) is hazardous: neprilysin inhibition further blocks bradykinin breakdown, ARNI is contraindicated in anyone with prior angioedema, and a washout gap is required when transitioning from an ACE inhibitor (Ch. 265, p. 1995). ACE inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme, which normally also degrades the vasodilator peptide bradykinin; inhibition leads to delayed bradykinin breakdown and accumulation, increasing vascular permeability in the deep dermis and subcutaneous/submucosal tissues and producing angioedema (pp. 2807, 2024). This is mechanistically the same bradykinin pathway implicated in hereditary angioedema, where deficient or dysfunctional C1 inhibitor (C1INH) fails to restrain activated factor XII (Hageman factor) and kallikrein, generating excess bradykinin (p. 2808). Because the mechanism is bradykinin- rather than histamine-/IgE-mediated, there is no associated urticaria or pruritus, and the process is fundamentally distinct from allergic mast-cell-driven angioedema (p. 2808). The same bradykinin-accumulation mechanism explains the increased angioedema risk seen with combined ACE/neprilysin inhibition, since neprilysin also degrades bradykinin (Ch. 265, p. 1995). Bradykinin-mediated angioedema typically takes hours to days to resolve and persists >24 h, in contrast to the shorter-lived allergic form (pp. 2807-2808). The leading hazard is laryngeal/upper-airway obstruction, which can be life-threatening (p. 2808). No residual scarring occurs unless there is an underlying vasculitis (p. 2808). Harrison classifies urticaria/angioedema by duration as acute (<6 weeks) versus chronic (>6 weeks) rather than by a graded severity scale; this distinction helps identify precipitating factors (pp. 2807, 2809). No formal angioedema severity-grading scheme is given for ACE-inhibitor angioedema in this source.

and detect choroidal neovascularisation Indocyanine green angiography for choroidal detail and neovascular membranes Optical coherence tomography to identify subretinal fluid, haemorrhage and neovascular membranes Fundus autofluorescence to highlight the streaks and pigment epithelial changes Systemic evaluation for pseudoxanthoma elasticum, including skin and cardiovascular assessment Investigations for associated conditions such as Paget disease of bone and haemoglobinopathies where indicated Irregular, reddish-brown to grey linear streaks radiating from the peripapillary area beneath the retinal vessels, representing crack-like breaks in a brittle, calcified Bruch membrane Frequently associated with systemic disease, classically pseudoxanthoma elasticum, and also with Paget disease of bone, sickle cell and other haemoglobinopathies, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, though some cases are idiopathic A characteristic peau d'orange mottling of the posterior pole may accompany the streaks, particularly in pseudoxanthoma elasticum Often asymptomatic until complicated by choroidal neovascularisation, which is the main cause of central visual loss The eyes are vulnerable to choroidal rupture and subretinal haemorrhage after even minor blunt trauma, so protective eyewear and avoidance of contact sports are advised Fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography and optical coherence tomography help delineate the streaks and detect choroidal neovascular membranes Fundus autofluorescence can highlight the streaks and associated retinal pigment epithelial changes Management centres on treating secondary choroidal neovascularisation with anti-VEGF therapy and on investigating and managing the underlying systemic association New distortion, central scotoma or reduced acuity suggesting choroidal neovascularisation Subretinal haemorrhage, particularly following ocular trauma Bilateral macular involvement threatening both eyes Systemic features indicating serious underlying disease such as Paget disease or a haemoglobinopathy Diagnosing angioid streaks without investigating for an underlying systemic association Missing early choroidal neovascularisation because the streaks were assumed to be benign Failing to counsel patients about the risk of choroidal rupture from minor trauma and the need for eye protection Confusing angioid streaks with myopic lacquer cracks or traumatic choroidal rupture Under-monitoring the fellow eye, which is at high risk of neovascular complications Angioid streaks are breaks in Bruch membrane, the elastic layer between the retinal pigment epithelium and choriocapillaris, which becomes abnormally thickened, calcified and brittle. In pseudoxanthoma elasticum and related disorders the underlying defect is degeneration and mineralisation of elastic tissue, which weakens Bruch membrane so that it cracks, producing the visible streaks. These breaks disrupt the barrier between the choroid and retina and predispose to ingrowth of choroidal neovascular membranes, which leak and bleed to cause macular scarring and central visual loss. The same brittleness makes the membrane liable to rupture with subretinal haemorrhage after minor ocular trauma. The streaks themselves are usually asymptomatic, but the long-term visual prognosis is dictated by choroidal neovascularisation, which commonly affects both eyes over time and can cause substantial central visual loss despite treatment; the risk of trauma-related choroidal rupture persists lifelong.

Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma — AITL, angioimmunoblastic lymphadenopathy, TFH-cell lymphoma, nodal T-follicular helper cell lymphoma, angioimmunoblastic type, CD10/CXCL13/PD-1 positive;
