Cross-sectional imaging and bone marrow examination for staging Typically affects older adults with generalised lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, fever, weight loss, and a characteristic skin rash Autoimmune-like features are common, including polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia, haemolytic anaemia with a positive direct antiglobulin test, arthralgia, and circulating immune complexes The neoplastic cell is a T-follicular helper (TFH) lymphocyte expressing CD4 with markers such as CD10, CXCL13, PD-1, ICOS, and BCL6 Nodes show a polymorphous infiltrate, arborising high endothelial venules, and expanded follicular dendritic cell meshworks, which can obscure the malignant clone Epstein-Barr virus-driven B-cell blasts are frequently present and can occasionally transform into a secondary EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Recurrent mutations affect TET2, DNMT3A, IDH2, and RHOA, reflecting an origin often shared with age-related clonal haematopoiesis Immune dysregulation predisposes to opportunistic infection, which contributes significantly to morbidity Rapid clinical deterioration with high fever suggesting aggressive disease or intercurrent opportunistic infection Features of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis such as cytopenias, hyperferritinaemia, and rising triglycerides Emergence of a rapidly enlarging mass indicating transformation to large B-cell lymphoma Severe autoimmune haemolysis causing symptomatic anaemia Misreading the polymorphous, inflammatory-appearing infiltrate as reactive or as Hodgkin lymphoma and missing the malignant TFH clone Attributing systemic symptoms solely to infection or autoimmune disease and delaying biopsy Overlooking a secondary EBV-driven B-cell proliferation or transformation Failing to anticipate and prevent opportunistic infection during immunosuppressive therapy Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma arises from T-follicular helper cells, a subset that normally supports germinal-centre B-cell responses. Early epigenetic mutations in TET2 and DNMT3A may originate in a haematopoietic stem cell, with later acquisition of RHOA and IDH2 changes driving the malignant TFH phenotype. The tumour recreates an aberrant germinal-centre microenvironment, secreting chemokines such as CXCL13 that recruit B cells, plasma cells, eosinophils, and dendritic cells, producing the polymorphous nodal picture. Loss of normal immune regulation explains the prominent autoimmune phenomena, hypergammaglobulinaemia, and reactivation of Epstein-Barr virus in bystander B cells, which can themselves undergo clonal expansion. The disease is generally aggressive with a guarded outlook; many patients relapse after combination chemotherapy, and older age, poor performance status, and infective complications worsen outcome, though epigenetic-targeted approaches are under evaluation.

Angiokeratoma circumscriptum — Angiokeratoma circumscriptum naeviforme Angiokeratoma of Fabry disease (corporis diffusum) Other localised angiokeratomas (Mibelli, Fordyce and solitary types) Verrucous venous malformation (verrucous haemangioma) Malignant melanoma in a pigmented, bleeding lesion Lymphangioma circumscriptum Pyogenic granuloma Dermoscopy showing dark lacunae with a keratotic veil Skin biopsy confirming dilated superficial vessels with overlying hyperkeratosis Ultrasound or MRI if a deeper vascular malformation is suspected Screening for Fabry disease (alpha-galactosidase A activity) if lesions are widespread or symmetrical Assessment of the extent of any associated malformation The rarest form of angiokeratoma, usually congenital or appearing in infancy or childhood and most often on a lower limb. Presents as a unilateral, well-demarcated cluster or plaque of dark-red to blue-black hyperkeratotic vascular papules and nodules, sometimes in a linear or segmental (blaschkoid) pattern. Represents ectatic superficial dermal vessels with overlying epidermal hyperkeratosis and acanthosis. May slowly enlarge and can bleed after minor trauma. Distinct from the systemic angiokeratomas of Fabry disease (angiokeratoma corporis diffusum), which are widespread and symmetrical. Dermoscopy typically shows dark lacunae with an overlying whitish keratotic veil. May coexist with an underlying venous or lymphatic malformation in some cases. Treatment with laser or excision is undertaken for cosmesis or troublesome bleeding, but recurrence is possible. Pigmented or rapidly changing lesion raising suspicion of melanoma Recurrent significant bleeding Widespread symmetrical angiokeratomas suggesting a systemic storage disorder Rapid enlargement suggesting an underlying deeper malformation Confusing localised angiokeratoma circumscriptum with the systemic angiokeratomas of Fabry disease and missing a treatable metabolic condition. Mistaking a bleeding, keratotic and pigmented lesion for melanoma, or the reverse. Treating superficially without recognising a deeper underlying malformation. Incomplete excision leading to recurrence. Angiokeratoma circumscriptum is a localised vascular ectasia in which dilated, thin-walled capillaries and postcapillary venules occupy the superficial papillary dermis, closely apposed to a reactively hyperkeratotic and acanthotic epidermis that may partially enclose the ectatic vessels. Unlike the angiokeratomas of Fabry disease and other lysosomal storage disorders, it is not associated with a systemic enzyme deficiency. It behaves as a localised capillary and venous malformation, sometimes overlying a deeper vascular malformation, with the keratotic surface reflecting secondary epidermal change over long-standing dilated vessels. Angiokeratoma circumscriptum is benign and persists lifelong, tending to enlarge slowly. Treatment is undertaken for bleeding or cosmetic reasons, with a recognised risk of recurrence after ablative therapy.

Angioleiomyoma — Vascular leiomyoma, Angiomyoma Glomus tumour and other painful subcutaneous tumours Angiolipoma Schwannoma or traumatic neuroma Dermatofibroma Haemangioma or vascular malformation Leiomyoma of pilar or genital type at other sites Ultrasound to characterise the subcutaneous nodule and its vascularity MRI when a deeper or larger lesion requires characterisation Excisional biopsy for definitive diagnosis Histology demonstrating smooth muscle bundles around vessels Immunohistochemistry for smooth muscle actin and desmin Clinical correlation with the pattern of pain and provoking factors A benign smooth muscle tumour arising from the muscular wall of veins, hence its vascular architecture It classically presents as a small, solitary, often painful subcutaneous nodule on the lower limb, particularly around the ankle and calf There is a female predominance and a peak in middle adulthood, and pain may be provoked by cold, pressure, or pregnancy Three histological subtypes are recognised: solid, venous, and cavernous, according to the calibre and character of the vessels Microscopically, well-differentiated smooth muscle bundles are arranged around and between vascular channels, staining for smooth muscle actin and desmin It is one of the classic painful subcutaneous tumours to consider alongside glomus tumour, angiolipoma, and neuroma The lesion is well circumscribed and does not infiltrate surrounding tissue Simple excision is curative and recurrence is not expected Rapid growth, large size, or a deep location atypical for a benign lesion Cytological atypia or mitotic activity suggesting a leiomyosarcoma Recurrence after excision Multiplicity prompting consideration of a syndromic smooth muscle disorder Failing to include angioleiomyoma in the differential of a painful subcutaneous nodule Confusing the vascular architecture with a haemangioma or vascular malformation Overlooking atypical features that would suggest a smooth muscle malignancy Attributing chronic limb pain to another cause and delaying diagnosis Angioleiomyoma is a benign neoplasm of smooth muscle that originates from the tunica media of veins within the dermis and subcutis. The tumour is composed of mature, cytologically bland smooth muscle cells that sweep around numerous vascular lumina, with the relative proportion of muscle to vessels and the vessel calibre defining the solid, venous, and cavernous subtypes. The intimate admixture of contractile smooth muscle and vessels is thought to account for the characteristic pain, which may arise from contraction of the muscular component or from local ischaemia and is often precipitated by cold or pressure. The lesion is encapsulated or well demarcated, grows slowly by expansion, and has no capacity for local infiltration or metastasis, in keeping with its benign nature. Angioleiomyoma is benign, and simple complete excision is curative with recurrence being very uncommon. Malignant transformation does not occur, and the main benefit of excision is relief of the often troublesome pain.

Angiolipoma — Angiomyolipoma of soft tissue (historical misnomer to avoid), Vascular lipoma Ordinary lipoma and spindle cell lipoma Other painful subcutaneous tumours such as angioleiomyoma, glomus tumour, and neuroma Haemangioma or vascular malformation Kaposiform or other vascular soft tissue tumour Epidermoid cyst Nodular fasciitis Ultrasound to characterise the subcutaneous nodule and its vascularity MRI showing a fatty lesion with a variable non-fatty vascular component when imaging is required Excisional biopsy for definitive histological diagnosis Histology to demonstrate mature fat with capillary proliferation and fibrin thrombi Assessment for multiplicity and family history given the tendency to multiple lesions Imaging of the muscle compartment if an infiltrating variant is suspected A benign subcutaneous tumour of mature fat and small vessels that characteristically presents as one of the painful soft tissue lumps Typically appears in adolescents and young adults, often multiple, with the forearm and trunk being favoured sites Lesions are small, firm, encapsulated subcutaneous nodules, and tenderness is frequently the presenting complaint The histological hallmark is a mixture of mature adipocytes and a branching capillary network containing characteristic fibrin microthrombi Unlike ordinary lipoma, most angiolipomas have a normal karyotype without the 12q rearrangements typical of lipoma The rare infiltrating angiolipoma is non-encapsulated, extends into skeletal muscle, and has a greater tendency to recur locally There is no malignant potential in the usual encapsulated form Simple excision is curative for symptomatic or troublesome lesions, and asymptomatic nodules may simply be observed A deep or non-encapsulated lesion infiltrating muscle, suggesting the infiltrating variant Recurrence after previous excision Rapid enlargement or increasing pain Extensive multiplicity with functional impairment Attributing tenderness to another cause and overlooking angiolipoma in the differential of a painful subcutaneous lump Failing to recognise the infiltrating variant, leading to incomplete excision and recurrence Confusing the lesion with a vascular malformation on imaging Using the term angiomyolipoma, which properly denotes a distinct renal and perivascular epithelioid tumour Angiolipoma is a benign neoplasm composed of mature adipose tissue admixed with a prominent proliferation of small, thin-walled vessels concentrated at the periphery of the lobules. The defining microscopic feature is the presence of fibrin thrombi within these capillaries, which helps distinguish it from a vascular-rich ordinary lipoma. The vascular component is thought to underlie the pain and tenderness that so often accompany the lesion. In contrast to conventional lipoma, the usual encapsulated angiolipoma typically shows a normal karyotype, indicating a distinct pathogenesis. The uncommon infiltrating variant lacks a capsule and permeates surrounding skeletal muscle and connective tissue, accounting for its higher local recurrence rate although it remains biologically benign. The encapsulated angiolipoma is benign and cured by simple excision, with recurrence being unusual. The infiltrating variant may recur locally because of its permeative growth but does not metastasise or undergo malignant change.

Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma — AFH, angiomatoid malignant fibrous histiocytoma, EWSR1-CREB1 tumour, angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (EWSR1-CREB1) Nodal metastasis or a reactive lymph node, given the lymphoid cuff Aneurysmal (haemorrhagic) benign fibrous histiocytoma Vascular tumours such as haemangioma and angiosarcoma Spindle cell haemangioma Follicular dendritic cell sarcoma Other EWSR1-rearranged tumours including clear cell sarcoma and myoepithelioma Solitary fibrous tumour Immunohistochemistry for desmin, EMA, CD68 and CD99 with exclusion of endothelial and melanocytic markers FISH or molecular testing for EWSR1 (and ATF1/CREB1) or FUS rearrangement Endothelial markers (CD31, ERG) to confirm the pseudovascular spaces lack a true endothelial lining Blood count and inflammatory markers to document reversible systemic effects MRI to characterise the superficial soft-tissue mass Complete excision specimen assessment for margins and depth of invasion A rare tumour of intermediate biological potential that usually arises in the superficial soft tissue of the extremities in children and young adults Classic histology shows nodules of bland ovoid to spindled histiocytoid cells, blood-filled pseudoangiomatous cystic spaces, a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and a peripheral cuff of lymphoid tissue that can mimic a lymph node May cause systemic symptoms such as fever, anaemia, weight loss and raised inflammatory markers, thought to be cytokine-mediated and reversible after resection Most cases harbour an EWSR1-CREB1 fusion; less commonly EWSR1-ATF1 or FUS-ATF1 Immunophenotype is variable but often includes desmin, EMA, CD68 and CD99, with absence of specific melanocytic, vascular and myogenic differentiation The blood-filled spaces are pseudovascular and not lined by endothelium, distinguishing it from a true vascular tumour Despite the historical name, it is not a fibrohistiocytic malignancy and only rarely metastasises Deep, large or infiltrative tumours, which have a higher risk of aggressive behaviour Local recurrence after incomplete excision Rare distant metastasis, most often to lymph nodes and lung Persistent systemic inflammatory symptoms suggesting incomplete resection Misinterpreting the lymphoid cuff as a lymph node and diagnosing metastatic disease Mistaking the pseudovascular spaces for a true vascular tumour Overlooking the diagnosis because the immunophenotype is variable and non-specific Failing to attribute unexplained fever and anaemia to the tumour Assuming the EWSR1 rearrangement indicates Ewing sarcoma or clear cell sarcoma Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma is defined by a recurrent gene fusion, most often EWSR1-CREB1, in which the EWSR1 gene is joined to a CREB-family transcription-factor gene, activating aberrant transcriptional programmes that drive proliferation and may promote cytokine production responsible for systemic symptoms. The lesion forms circumscribed nodules with pseudoangiomatous haemorrhagic spaces, a fibrous pseudocapsule and a lymphoid cuff. The same fusions occur in certain other tumours, so integration of morphology, immunophenotype and molecular findings is needed for a confident diagnosis. Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma is generally cured by complete excision and has an excellent overall prognosis, with local recurrence in a minority and metastasis in only a small percentage of cases; deep or truncal tumours with infiltrative margins carry the greatest risk, and any accompanying systemic symptoms usually resolve once the tumour is removed.

Benign vascular lesions (haemangioma, vascular malformation) Kaposi sarcoma Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma Bruising, haematoma, or cellulitis (for cutaneous lesions) Melanoma (amelanotic) and other cutaneous malignancies Poorly differentiated carcinoma or other high-grade sarcoma MRI or CT of the primary site to assess extent, recognising margins are often underestimated Chest CT for pulmonary metastases Whole-body functional imaging in higher-risk disease Generous, sometimes multiple, biopsies given patchy involvement and diagnostic difficulty Immunohistochemistry for endothelial markers (CD31, ERG, CD34) MYC amplification testing by FISH or immunohistochemistry, especially for radiation- or lymphoedema-associated tumours A malignant tumour of endothelial (vascular or lymphatic) differentiation that can arise in skin, soft tissue, breast, liver, and elsewhere Cutaneous angiosarcoma of the head and neck in elderly patients is the classic form, often presenting as an ill-defined bruise-like or violaceous plaque that is easily mistaken for benign bruising or infection Well-recognised secondary forms include radiation-associated angiosarcoma (for example after breast irradiation) and lymphoedema-associated angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves syndrome) Radiation- and lymphoedema-associated cutaneous angiosarcomas frequently show high-level MYC amplification, a useful diagnostic marker Endothelial markers such as CD31, ERG, and CD34 support the diagnosis, though poorly differentiated tumours can be difficult to recognise Margins are notoriously difficult to define because of infiltrative, multifocal growth, so wide excision may be combined with radiotherapy Multi-agent or targeted systemic therapy is often needed given the high propensity for recurrence and metastasis Overall an aggressive sarcoma with a strong tendency to local recurrence and haematogenous spread, particularly to the lungs An enlarging or non-resolving bruise-like lesion on the scalp or face of an elderly patient New skin changes within a previously irradiated field or a chronically lymphoedematous limb Rapid growth, ulceration, or bleeding of a cutaneous vascular lesion Haemoperitoneum or hepatic mass raising concern for visceral angiosarcoma New respiratory symptoms suggesting pulmonary metastases Dismissing early cutaneous lesions as bruising, infection, or benign vascular change, delaying diagnosis Underestimating tumour extent and achieving inadequate surgical margins Failing to recognise poorly differentiated tumours that mimic carcinoma or other sarcomas without endothelial marker staining Overlooking a history of prior radiotherapy or chronic lymphoedema that should raise suspicion Sampling error from a single biopsy of a multifocal or heterogeneous lesion Angiosarcoma is a malignancy of cells showing endothelial differentiation, forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels or solid sheets in poorly differentiated tumours. It may arise de novo or secondary to chronic lymphoedema, prior radiotherapy, or exposure to certain toxins. Secondary cutaneous forms are characteristically associated with high-level amplification of the MYC oncogene, which drives endothelial proliferation, and additional angiogenic signalling through vascular endothelial growth factor pathways supports tumour growth. Its infiltrative, often multifocal nature reflects diffuse endothelial transformation rather than a single discrete mass, explaining the difficulty in achieving clear margins. Angiosarcoma generally carries a poor prognosis with frequent local recurrence and metastasis; outcome depends on site, size, resectability, and patient factors, with large, deep, or metastatic tumours faring worst and even localised disease showing high relapse rates.

Angiostrongyliasis — Angiostrongylus cantonensis infection, rat lungworm disease, eosinophilic meningitis, neuroangiostrongyliasis Gnathostomiasis and other parasitic causes of eosinophilic meningitis Neurocysticercosis Coccidioidal or other fungal meningitis Tuberculous meningitis Central nervous system malignancy or drug-induced eosinophilic meningitis Viral (aseptic) meningitis Lumbar puncture with measurement of opening pressure and cerebrospinal fluid cell count and differential Cerebrospinal fluid and blood eosinophil quantification Serology or molecular testing for Angiostrongylus where available MRI of the brain for migratory or inflammatory lesions Dietary and exposure history (snails, slugs, prawns, unwashed vegetables) Exclusion of tuberculous, fungal and neoplastic causes of eosinophilic meningitis The leading infective cause of eosinophilic meningitis worldwide, caused by the rat lungworm Angiostrongylus cantonensis Acquired by eating raw or undercooked snails and slugs, or paratenic hosts such as freshwater prawns, crabs and frogs, or contaminated unwashed produce Endemic in Southeast Asia and the Pacific, with expanding distribution including parts of the Americas Presents with severe headache, neck stiffness, nausea and often striking paraesthesiae or hyperaesthesia; cranial nerve palsies can occur Cerebrospinal fluid characteristically shows a raised opening pressure with eosinophilic pleocytosis A related species, Angiostrongylus costaricensis, instead causes abdominal (intestinal) angiostrongyliasis Management is largely supportive, with analgesia, repeated therapeutic lumbar puncture to relieve pressure and headache, and corticosteroids for the inflammatory reaction; the role of anthelmintics is debated Most immunocompetent patients recover, but heavy infections can cause lasting neurological damage or death Depressed consciousness or focal neurological deficit Cranial nerve palsies or visual involvement Rapidly rising intracranial pressure Signs of severe or complicated meningoencephalitis Not requesting a cerebrospinal fluid differential and thereby missing the eosinophilic pleocytosis Overlooking the exposure history to snails, slugs or unwashed produce Giving anthelmintics without corticosteroid cover, which may worsen inflammation as larvae die Failing to relieve raised intracranial pressure with therapeutic lumbar puncture Confusing it with the abdominal disease caused by Angiostrongylus costaricensis Angiostrongylus cantonensis completes its natural cycle in rats and molluscs. Humans become accidental hosts by ingesting third-stage larvae in raw or undercooked snails, slugs or paratenic hosts, or on contaminated produce. The larvae penetrate the intestine, enter the circulation and migrate to the central nervous system, where they cannot complete development. Their migration and death within the brain, meninges and cerebrospinal fluid provoke an intense eosinophil-rich inflammatory response, producing eosinophilic meningitis with raised intracranial pressure. Dying larvae and the surrounding inflammation account for the headache, sensory disturbances and, in severe cases, focal neurological injury. Most immunocompetent patients recover over weeks with supportive care, though headache and paraesthesiae may be prolonged; heavy larval burdens can cause permanent neurological sequelae or death.

Abdominal angiostrongyliasis (A. costaricensis) — Angiostrongylus costaricensis infection, Parastrongylus costaricensis infection, abdominal angiostrongyliasis, intestinal angiostrongyliasis Acute appendicitis Ileocaecal Crohn's disease or other inflammatory bowel disease Intestinal tuberculosis Caecal or colonic carcinoma presenting as a mass Other causes of an eosinophilic mass or eosinophilic enteritis Intestinal lymphoma Full blood count demonstrating marked eosinophilia and leucocytosis Cross-sectional imaging showing ileocaecal wall thickening or an inflammatory mass Serology for Angiostrongylus where available Histopathology of resected bowel demonstrating eggs and worms with eosinophilic vasculitis Inflammatory markers and assessment for obstruction or ischaemia Colonoscopy with biopsy when malignancy or Crohn's disease is considered Caused by the nematode Angiostrongylus costaricensis, endemic in Central and South America, acquired by ingesting infective larvae on vegetation or in slugs and snails contaminating food Larvae migrate to the mesenteric arteries of the ileocaecal region, producing an eosinophilic inflammatory mass Classically presents with right lower quadrant pain, fever, a palpable mass and marked eosinophilia, closely mimicking appendicitis Complications include bowel ischaemia, obstruction and perforation, and the diagnosis is often made only on the surgical specimen Humans are dead-end hosts, so eggs and larvae are not usually found in the stool, unlike many other helminths There is no reliably effective anthelmintic regimen; management is largely supportive and surgical for complications, and anthelmintics may even worsen the inflammatory reaction Prevention relies on washing vegetables thoroughly and avoiding contamination of food by slugs and snails Signs of bowel ischaemia, obstruction or perforation requiring urgent surgery Peritonitis or an acute abdomen A rapidly enlarging abdominal mass Massive lower gastrointestinal haemorrhage Expecting to find eggs or larvae in the stool, which are typically absent in this dead-end infection Assuming anthelmintic therapy is beneficial when it may aggravate the inflammatory response Mistaking the inflammatory mass for malignancy or Crohn's disease Overlooking the diagnosis in a patient from an endemic area with eosinophilia and an appendicitis-like picture Angiostrongylus costaricensis is a nematode whose definitive hosts are rodents and whose intermediate hosts are slugs and snails. Humans acquire infection by ingesting third-stage larvae, either directly in a mollusc or on vegetation and food contaminated by mollusc slime. The larvae penetrate the intestinal wall and migrate to the mesenteric arterial branches supplying the ileocaecal region, where the adult worms lodge and lay eggs. Because humans are unnatural hosts, the eggs and larvae become trapped in the bowel wall rather than reaching the lumen, and they excite an intense eosinophilic and granulomatous vasculitis. This inflammatory reaction thickens the bowel wall, forms a tumour-like mass and can compromise the blood supply, leading to ischaemia, obstruction or perforation of the terminal ileum, caecum and appendix. Many cases resolve spontaneously as the worms die, but those with ischaemia, obstruction or perforation require surgery and can have significant morbidity; overall mortality is low with timely surgical management.

angle recession glaucoma — post-traumatic angle recession glaucoma, contusion angle glaucoma primary open-angle glaucoma traumatic hyphaema with acute pressure rise ghost cell glaucoma following vitreous haemorrhage steroid-induced glaucoma from treatment of the original injury haemolytic or haemosiderotic glaucoma pigmentary glaucoma uveitic glaucoma from post-traumatic inflammation gonioscopy of both eyes to identify and quantify angle recession ultrasound biomicroscopy or anterior segment optical coherence tomography of the angle intraocular pressure measurement and diurnal phasing optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer standard automated perimetry dilated fundus examination for coexisting contusion retinopathy or choroidal rupture optic disc photography for baseline documentation Follows blunt ocular trauma, often years earlier, so a careful history of contusion injury is essential in unilateral glaucoma. Gonioscopy shows an irregularly widened ciliary body band, torn iris processes and a receded iris root, best appreciated by comparison with the fellow eye. The tear is between the longitudinal and circular muscle fibres of the ciliary body; the outflow obstruction, however, is caused by associated trabecular damage and scarring rather than the recession itself. Glaucoma risk rises when recession exceeds around 180 to 270 degrees of the angle circumference. Onset of raised pressure may be immediate, but a substantial proportion present years to decades after the original injury, mandating lifelong follow-up. The fellow, uninjured eye carries an increased lifetime risk of developing primary open-angle glaucoma and should also be monitored. Laser trabeculoplasty tends to respond poorly because the meshwork is scarred; medical therapy and filtration surgery are the mainstays. Associated contusion findings such as sphincter tears, iridodialysis, phacodonesis and commotio retinae support the mechanism. markedly raised pressure with a history of significant blunt trauma progressive optic neuropathy in a previously injured eye recurrent spontaneous hyphaema suggesting neovascularisation or fragile vessels coexisting retinal detachment or dialysis on fundus examination Failing to take a trauma history in unilateral glaucoma and missing the diagnosis. Not examining the fellow eye, which carries an elevated risk of open-angle glaucoma. Relying on laser trabeculoplasty, which is typically ineffective in a scarred angle. Discharging a patient after early normal pressures despite extensive recession, when glaucoma may appear decades later. Overlooking coexisting posterior segment contusion injury that also threatens vision. A blunt, rapid antero-posterior compression of the globe produces an equatorial expansion that transmits shearing forces to the anterior chamber angle. The classic lesion is a cleft within the ciliary body created by separation of the longitudinal from the circular muscle fibres, seen clinically as angle recession. Although the recession itself does not directly obstruct outflow, the same injury damages the adjacent trabecular meshwork, and over subsequent months to years a Descemet-like endothelial membrane proliferates across the damaged angle, the meshwork scleroses and scars, and trabecular outflow facility declines. The resulting chronic rise in intraocular pressure drives a glaucomatous optic neuropathy. Late scarring explains the characteristic delay between trauma and the onset of glaucoma. Glaucoma may develop many years after injury, so lifelong monitoring is required; with timely pressure control the prognosis is reasonable, but the scarred meshwork responds poorly to laser and surgical control can be challenging.

Angular cheilitis — angular stomatitis, perleche, angular cheilosis Herpes simplex or impetigo of the lip Contact or irritant dermatitis of the perioral skin Actinic cheilitis Nutritional deficiency states Orofacial granulomatosis or Crohn disease involvement Clinical diagnosis from the characteristic commissural involvement Assessment of dentition, dentures and vertical facial height Microbiological swab where infection needs targeting Screening for nutritional deficiencies and diabetes where recurrent Consideration of underlying immunosuppression or systemic disease Inflammation, fissuring and crusting at one or both angles of the mouth, often sore or burning It is typically multifactorial, combining mechanical, microbial and nutritional influences Chronic accumulation of saliva at the commissures macerates the skin, promoting overgrowth of Candida and Staphylococcus aureus Reduced facial height from tooth loss or ill-fitting dentures deepens the folds and predisposes to it Nutritional deficiencies (iron, B vitamins, zinc) and immunosuppression are recognised contributors Treatment addresses the underlying cause alongside topical antifungal or antibacterial and barrier preparations Persistent or recurrent disease despite treatment suggesting systemic cause Features of underlying immunosuppression or diabetes Extension beyond the commissures or induration Associated widespread candidosis Treating only the surface infection without correcting mechanical or nutritional causes Overlooking iron or vitamin deficiency in recurrent cases Missing underlying diabetes or immunosuppression Confusing it with herpes labialis or impetigo Angular cheilitis develops where a persistently moist, occluded skin fold at the corner of the mouth becomes macerated and inflamed. Saliva pooling in deepened commissural folds, often due to reduced vertical facial height or drooling, creates conditions favouring colonisation by Candida species and Staphylococcus aureus, which perpetuate the inflammation. Systemic factors such as iron, vitamin B or zinc deficiency and immunosuppression impair mucocutaneous integrity and predispose to the condition, so it is best understood as a multifactorial reactive process rather than a single infection. The condition responds well once contributory factors are corrected, though it recurs if the underlying cause (denture problems, deficiency, dry environment) is not addressed.

Reduced PAX6 dosage disrupts formation of multiple ocular structures, producing iris hypoplasia together with foveal and optic nerve hypoplasia, and predisposing to limbal stem cell deficiency, cataract, and abnormal anterior chamber angle development. The result is a spectrum of structural and functional deficits present from birth. In sporadic cases caused by contiguous gene deletions of 11p13, loss of the neighbouring WT1 tumour-suppressor gene confers a high risk of Wilms tumour, defining the WAGR association. Visual acuity is typically reduced from birth due to foveal hypoplasia and often declines further with progressive glaucoma, cataract, and keratopathy; prognosis in WAGR cases is additionally determined by the outcome of Wilms tumour.

recent raw-seafood meal and misdiagnosing an acute surgical abdomen Attributing allergic reactions to the fish protein rather than to Anisakis sensitisation Relying on anthelmintic drugs rather than endoscopic removal for gastric disease Mistaking the inflammatory mass of intestinal disease for a tumour or Crohn's disease Anisakid nematodes such as Anisakis and Pseudoterranova cycle between marine mammals as definitive hosts and crustaceans and fish or squid as intermediate and paratenic hosts. Humans are accidental hosts who ingest third-stage larvae in raw or undercooked marine seafood. The larva attempts to burrow into the wall of the stomach or intestine but cannot complete its development; its penetration and secreted antigens trigger an intense local inflammatory response with oedema, eosinophil-rich infiltration and eventual granuloma formation around the larva. This underlies the acute pain of gastric disease and the mass-like, sometimes obstructive, lesions of intestinal disease. Sensitised individuals may mount immediate hypersensitivity reactions to larval antigens, producing urticaria, angio-oedema or anaphylaxis independent of, or alongside, the local tissue reaction. Prognosis is excellent once the larva is removed or dies, as symptoms typically settle within days; the main risks are severe allergic reactions and unnecessary surgery when the diagnosis is not considered.

neoplasm Neurological signs suggesting a spinal or cauda equina lesion Diagnosing dyssynergia on a single test rather than corroborating findings Treating with laxatives alone while ignoring the need for biofeedback Missing coexisting slow-transit constipation Attributing pain-related spasm from a fissure to primary dyssynergia Anismus (dyssynergic defecation) is an acquired disorder of defecatory coordination in which the puborectalis and external anal sphincter contract paradoxically or fail to relax during straining, so the anorectal angle does not open and rectal pressure cannot overcome outlet resistance. It is generally a learned or behavioural maladaptation rather than a structural lesion, often reinforced by painful defecation or excessive straining. Rectal propulsive force may also be inadequate. The result is functional outlet obstruction with incomplete evacuation. Biofeedback pelvic floor retraining achieves symptomatic improvement in the majority of adequately selected and motivated patients; response is poorer when slow transit or structural disease coexists.

instability or persistent symptoms if inadequately rehabilitated Inability to bear weight and bony tenderness meeting Ottawa criteria, indicating possible fracture Proximal fibular tenderness suggesting a Maisonneuve fracture Gross instability, deformity, or neurovascular compromise Persistent locking, catching, or effusion suggesting an osteochondral lesion Missing associated fractures such as the fifth metatarsal base or a Maisonneuve injury Failing to identify a syndesmotic sprain and underestimating recovery time Prolonged immobilisation leading to stiffness and deconditioning Omitting proprioceptive rehabilitation, increasing the risk of recurrent sprains An ankle sprain is a ligamentous injury, most often to the lateral complex (anterior talofibular, calcaneofibular, and posterior talofibular ligaments), caused by forced inversion. Excessive load tears collagen fibres, causing bleeding, swelling, and loss of mechanical restraint. Syndesmotic (high ankle) sprains involve the distal tibiofibular ligaments from external rotation. Impaired ligament healing and proprioceptive deficits can lead to mechanical and functional instability. Most low-grade lateral sprains recover within weeks with functional treatment, but up to a third develop residual symptoms or chronic instability; syndesmotic injuries recover more slowly and unstable injuries may require surgery.

untranslated regulatory region Development of additional cytopenias, monocytosis, or circulating blasts Acquisition of a clonal cytogenetic abnormality on marrow monitoring Progressive fall in platelet count or new constitutional symptoms Bleeding disproportionate to the platelet count Misdiagnosis as immune thrombocytopenia leading to needless steroids, immunoglobulin, or splenectomy Failing to arrange surveillance and germline donor screening given the leukaemia predisposition ANKRD26 mutations lie predominantly in the 5' untranslated region and disrupt the normal binding of transcription factors that silence the gene during the terminal stages of megakaryocyte maturation. Persistent ANKRD26 expression sustains aberrant signalling through the thrombopoietin receptor pathway (including MAPK/ERK), impairing proplatelet formation and platelet release. The result is ineffective megakaryopoiesis with a reduced platelet count, and the same disturbance of megakaryocytic and myeloid regulation contributes to the increased risk of clonal myeloid disease over time. Most individuals have a mild bleeding phenotype and a stable platelet count, but the increased lifetime risk of myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukaemia means long-term haematological surveillance is warranted.

AEC syndrome (Hay-Wells) — Hay-Wells syndrome, ankyloblepharon-ectodermal defects-cleft lip/palate syndrome, AEC syndrome, TP63, p63 EEC syndrome (ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-clefting, also TP63) Rapp-Hodgkin syndrome (TP63) Other hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasias Epidermolysis bullosa (for the erosive neonatal skin) Netherton syndrome / congenital erythroderma of other cause Ectodermal dysplasia-skin fragility syndrome Molecular genetic testing of TP63 Ophthalmological examination for ankyloblepharon and lacrimal anomalies ENT/cleft assessment of lip and palate Microbiological swabs of scalp erosions for superinfection Skin biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain Dental, audiological and sweating assessment A p63-related ectodermal dysplasia defined by ankyloblepharon (filiform strands of tissue fusing the eyelid margins), ectodermal defects and cleft lip and/or palate Congenital erythroderma with erosive, weeping scalp dermatitis is a characteristic and troublesome neonatal feature Chronic scalp erosions and scarring alopecia often persist and predispose to infection Sparse wiry hair, nail dystrophy, dental anomalies and reduced sweating are typical ectodermal features Autosomal dominant; caused by mutations in TP63 encoding the transcription factor p63 It overlaps with other p63 disorders such as EEC (ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-clefting), but limb ectrodactyly is not a feature of AEC Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, with intensive scalp wound care, treatment of infection, and ophthalmological, ENT/cleft and dental input Infected, non-healing scalp erosions with risk of sepsis Feeding difficulty and failure to thrive related to clefting Ocular complications from ankyloblepharon or dry eyes Extensive neonatal erythroderma with barrier failure and thermoregulatory instability Mistaking the neonatal erythroderma and erosions for epidermolysis bullosa or infection alone Failing to inspect the eyelids for subtle ankyloblepharon strands Undertreating chronic scalp erosions, allowing recurrent infection and scarring Not distinguishing AEC from EEC (limb ectrodactyly is absent in AEC) when counselling AEC (Hay-Wells) syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in TP63, which encodes p63, a master transcription factor of the p53 family that is essential for the development and maintenance of stratified epithelia and their appendages. In AEC the mutations characteristically affect the sterile alpha motif (SAM) and transactivation-inhibitory domains, disturbing p63's regulation of epithelial adhesion, differentiation and morphogenesis. The result is defective formation of skin, hair, nails, teeth, sweat glands and the palatal and eyelid tissues, producing the ankyloblepharon, clefting and ectodermal defects, together with a fragile, erosive epidermis that manifests as congenital erythroderma and chronic scalp erosions. With intensive neonatal and multidisciplinary care, most children survive and the erythroderma improves, but chronic scalp erosions, scarring alopecia and the sequelae of clefting and ectodermal defects persist. Long-term morbidity relates to skin fragility, infection and the functional impact of cleft and ectodermal features.

after minor trauma Neglecting extra-articular manifestations such as uveitis, bowel disease, and cardiac involvement Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease of the axial skeleton and the prototype of the seronegative spondyloarthritides. Inflammation centres on the entheses (sites where ligaments and tendons attach to bone) and the sacroiliac joints. A strong genetic association with HLA-B27 implicates aberrant antigen presentation and dysregulated IL-23/IL-17 pathway signalling. Chronic enthesitis and osteitis drive a cycle of erosion followed by reactive new bone formation, leading to syndesmophyte development, bony bridging across vertebrae, and ultimately spinal fusion (the 'bamboo spine'). Disease course is variable; many patients maintain good function with exercise and modern therapy, but persistent inflammation can lead to progressive spinal ankylosis, fixed kyphotic deformity, and increased fracture risk. Early diagnosis and biologic therapy have improved symptom control and quality of life.

malignancy Missing the diagnosis when the ring is incomplete and obstruction is subtle Annular pancreas arises from a failure of normal rotation and fusion of the ventral pancreatic bud during The degree of narrowing determines whether obstruction manifests in the newborn period or only later in life, and the abnormal ductal anatomy also predisposes to pancreatitis. Because it is normal pancreatic parenchyma, the ring shares in any inflammatory or neoplastic process affecting the gland. Asymptomatic incidental annular pancreas needs no treatment and has an excellent outlook; symptomatic obstruction generally resolves well after a bypass procedure, though associated congenital anomalies in neonates influence overall outcome.

anomalous left coronary artery — ALCAPA, Bland-White-Garland syndrome dilated cardiomyopathy of other cause viral myocarditis endocardial fibroelastosis critical aortic stenosis or coarctation anomalous left coronary from the right sinus with interarterial course infantile mitral valve disease 12-lead electrocardiogram for anterolateral infarction pattern transthoracic echocardiography with colour Doppler of the coronary origins cardiac catheterisation and selective coronary angiography CT or MR coronary angiography for origin and collateral mapping serum cardiac troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide chest radiograph for cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA) means the left ventricular myocardium is perfused by desaturated pulmonary blood at low pressure once the pulmonary vascular resistance falls after birth. The classic presentation is an infant in the first months of life with irritability, sweating and pallor during feeds, representing angina, often mistaken for colic. As pulmonary pressure declines, flow reverses and the left coronary steals into the pulmonary trunk, producing a coronary steal that worsens ischaemia. Collaterals from the right coronary artery determine survival; an adult type with rich collaterals may present late with a murmur, arrhythmia or sudden death. The electrocardiogram typically shows an anterolateral infarction pattern with deep Q waves and ST-T changes in the lateral leads. Echocardiography shows a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle with mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle ischaemia, and retrograde colour flow into the pulmonary artery. Surgical re-implantation of the anomalous coronary into the aorta to establish a dual coronary system is the definitive treatment. Left ventricular function often recovers remarkably after successful revascularisation even when severely depressed preoperatively. infant with episodic distress and sweating on feeding suggesting angina signs of cardiogenic shock or heart failure in early infancy electrocardiographic infarction pattern in an infant syncope, ventricular arrhythmia or aborted sudden death in an older child Diagnosing idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy or myocarditis without interrogating the coronary origins on echocardiography. Mislabelling feeding-related distress and sweating as colic or reflux. Assuming normal coronaries because the left main appears to arise near the aorta without confirming true aortic origin and flow direction. Underestimating mitral regurgitation as primary valve disease rather than ischaemic papillary muscle dysfunction. Delaying referral in an older asymptomatic child with an incidental murmur and collateral-dependent perfusion. During fetal life the pulmonary arterial pressure and oxygen saturation are high, so a left coronary artery arising from the pulmonary trunk is adequately perfused. After birth the pulmonary vascular resistance and pressure fall, reducing antegrade perfusion pressure and oxygen delivery to the left coronary territory. The myocardium becomes progressively ischaemic, and once right-to-left coronary collaterals develop, blood flows from the higher-pressure right coronary system through collaterals into the left coronary and drains into the low-pressure pulmonary artery, a coronary steal. The result is chronic subendocardial ischaemia and infarction of the anterolateral left ventricle and papillary muscles, causing dilated cardiomyopathy and mitral regurgitation. Untreated infantile ALCAPA carries a high mortality within the first year, but early surgical establishment of a two-coronary system yields excellent long-term survival and frequently full recovery of ventricular function.

testosterone-producing tissue Karyotype to confirm 46,XY and exclude a disorder of sex development Scrotal and abdominal ultrasound or MRI to search for testicular tissue Diagnostic laparoscopy to confirm absence of an intra-abdominal testis or locate a nubbin Anorchia is the absence of testicular tissue in a phenotypically male, 46,XY individual, and may be unilateral or bilateral It is thought to result from a vanishing testis, in which a testis that was present and functional early in fetal life later regresses, often from an intrauterine vascular or torsion event Because early testicular function drove normal male differentiation, the external genitalia and Wolffian structures are typically male, distinguishing it from disorders of sex development In bilateral anorchia the child presents with an empty scrotum and impalpable testes, and the key task is to distinguish absent testes from bilateral intra-abdominal cryptorchidism Hormonal assessment is central: markedly raised gonadotropins with very low or absent inhibin B and anti-Mullerian hormone, and no rise in testosterone after hCG stimulation, support absent functional testicular tissue The hCG stimulation test and measurement of inhibin B and anti-Mullerian hormone help confirm anorchia, but laparoscopy is often required to be certain no intra-abdominal testis or nubbin is present Management includes androgen replacement to induce and maintain puberty in bilateral cases, consideration of a testicular prosthesis, and psychological support and counselling Bilateral impalpable testes requiring urgent distinction from intra-abdominal testes at risk of malignancy Ambiguous genitalia or atypical phenotype suggesting a disorder of sex development Failure to enter or progress through puberty without treatment An intra-abdominal testicular remnant that may need removal because of malignant potential Assuming impalpable testes are absent without excluding intra-abdominal cryptorchidism Relying on imaging alone when laparoscopy is often needed to confirm absent testes Overlooking the malignant potential of an intra-abdominal remnant or undescended testis Delaying androgen replacement and prosthesis discussion, with psychological consequences Mislabelling a disorder of sex development as simple anorchia without a karyotype In congenital anorchia the testis develops and functions early enough in fetal life to drive male differentiation of the genital tract and external genitalia, but subsequently undergoes regression, most likely from an intrauterine vascular accident or perinatal torsion, leaving little or no identifiable testicular tissue, sometimes only a fibrous nubbin with haemosiderin and calcification. The loss of functioning Sertoli and Leydig cells removes the sources of inhibin B, anti-Mullerian hormone, and testosterone, so gonadotropins rise while these markers fall, and there is no testosterone response to hCG stimulation. In bilateral disease this produces hypergonadotropic hypogonadism requiring lifelong androgen replacement. With appropriate androgen replacement, boys with bilateral anorchia can undergo normal virilisation and pubertal development and maintain secondary sexual characteristics and bone health, though natural fertility is not possible; unilateral anorchia with a normal solitary testis usually allows normal development and fertility.

Anorectal abscess — perianal abscess, ischiorectal abscess, perirectal abscess, intersphincteric abscess Thrombosed external haemorrhoid Pilonidal abscess Bartholin abscess (in women) Hidradenitis suppurativa Perianal Crohn's disease Anal or rectal malignancy with sepsis Fournier's gangrene (necrotising perineal infection) Clinical examination and, where pain permits, digital rectal examination to assess deeper spaces Examination under anaesthesia to fully assess and drain the collection and look for a fistula MRI pelvis or endoanal ultrasound for complex, recurrent, or supralevator disease Blood glucose and screening for immunosuppression, and blood cultures if systemically septic Consideration of investigations for Crohn's disease in recurrent or atypical abscesses Presents with acute, constant, throbbing perianal or rectal pain, often with a tender fluctuant swelling, fever, and malaise Classified by anatomical space into perianal, ischiorectal, intersphincteric, and supralevator abscesses, each with characteristic examination findings Most arise from infection of the anal glands opening into the crypts at the dentate line (the cryptoglandular theory) A superficial perianal abscess is visibly red and fluctuant, whereas a deeper ischiorectal or supralevator abscess may cause deep pain and systemic upset with little external sign Treatment is prompt surgical incision and drainage; Pus tracks along planes of least resistance from the intersphincteric space into the perianal, ischiorectal, or supralevator spaces, and can extend circumferentially in a horseshoe pattern. The causative organisms are typically gut flora, including coliforms and anaerobes. Underlying conditions such as Crohn's disease, diabetes, and immunosuppression predispose to formation and to more extensive spread. Persistence of the primary gland infection after drainage creates the epithelialised track of a fistula-in-ano. Simple abscesses drained promptly resolve well, but recurrence and fistula formation are common. Delayed treatment, deep spaces, immunosuppression, or necrotising infection markedly worsen outcomes and can be life-threatening.

and constipation, which correlate with the height of the lesion and the integrity of the sacrum and sphincter complex Progressive abdominal distension and bilious vomiting from unrelieved distal obstruction Absent anus with no fistula, indicating a high lesion that needs urgent surgical decompression Meconium in the urine signalling a rectourinary fistula and risk of urosepsis Associated major cardiac or renal anomalies compromising the neonate Features of a cloacal malformation with a single perineal opening requiring specialist assessment Assuming a visible perineal orifice is a normal anus without confirming its position and calibre Attempting perineal repair or dilatation before determining whether the lesion is high or low Overlooking the VACTERL association and missing a significant cardiac or renal anomaly Failing to recognise a cloacal malformation and its urological implications in a female neonate Neglecting sacral and spinal assessment, which underestimates continence risk Anorectal malformation arises from disordered development of the hindgut and cloaca during early gestation, when the urorectal septum normally partitions the cloaca into an anterior urogenital sinus and a posterior anorectal canal, and the anal membrane subsequently perforates. Failure or incomplete progression of this process leaves the rectum terminating blindly or connecting abnormally to the urinary tract, vagina, or perineum through a fistula. The level at which the bowel ends relative to the levator ani (puborectalis) sling determines whether the lesion is low or high and how well-developed the striated sphincter musculature and sacrum are, which in turn predicts continence. Low lesions with a well-formed sacrum and sphincter complex generally achieve good continence after repair, whereas high or cloacal lesions and sacral hypoplasia carry higher rates of faecal incontinence and constipation. Structured bowel management and long-term multidisciplinary follow-up substantially improve functional outcome.

with anorectal stricturing Radiation proctitis with stricture Ischaemic stricture of the rectum Lymphogranuloma venereum or other infective stricture Diverticular or extrinsic compressive narrowing of the distal bowel Endoscopy (rigid or flexible) to define level, length, and calibre and to obtain biopsies Biopsy of the stricture to exclude malignancy and identify inflammatory causes Examination under anaesthesia for complex, painful, or high strictures Pelvic MRI or CT to assess mural and extramural extent Contrast enema or defecography to characterise length and function Assessment of anastomotic history, prior radiation, and inflammatory bowel disease status An anorectal stricture is a fixed narrowing spanning the distal rectum and/or anal canal, more proximal and often more complex than isolated anal stenosis at the verge Common causes include anastomotic strictures after low anterior resection or stapled anorectal surgery, radiation injury, Crohn disease, ischaemia, chronic inflammation, and neoplasia Presentation includes obstructed defecation, tenesmus, narrow-calibre stool, straining, incomplete evacuation, and, when severe, features of large-bowel obstruction A stricture with no clear benign explanation must be regarded as malignant until proven otherwise, and biopsy is mandatory Anastomotic strictures after colorectal surgery are frequent, particularly after low stapled anastomoses, diverting stomas, or anastomotic leak, and many are short and web-like Endoscopic assessment defines the level, length, and calibre, while cross-sectional imaging and examination under anaesthesia clarify complex or high strictures Short benign strictures often respond to endoscopic or digital dilatation, whereas long, dense, radiation-related, or recurrent strictures may need stricturoplasty, resection, or diversion Treatment must address the underlying disease, as strictures from Crohn disease or radiation behave differently from simple anastomotic scars An irregular, ulcerated, or hard stricture suggesting malignancy A stricture without a clear benign cause Progressive obstruction with abdominal distension and vomiting Rectal bleeding, weight loss, or a rising tumour marker Associated fistula, abscess, or perianal Crohn disease Assuming a stricture is benign and omitting biopsy, thereby missing malignancy Aggressive dilatation of dense or radiation strictures causing perforation Failing to treat the underlying Crohn disease or radiation injury Overlooking a subclinical anastomotic leak as the cause of a postoperative stricture Repeated dilatation of a recurrent stricture without reassessing for underlying disease An anorectal stricture forms when the wall of the distal rectum or anal canal is narrowed by fibrosis, inflammation, ischaemia, or neoplastic infiltration, with loss of the normal distensibility of the lumen. After surgical anastomosis, ischaemia, subclinical leak, or scarring of the staple or suture line contracts the lumen into a fibrous ring. Radiation injury produces progressive obliterative endarteritis and submucosal fibrosis. Crohn disease drives transmural inflammation and fibrosis, and chronic infections or inflammatory dermatoses provoke cicatrisation. Malignant strictures narrow the lumen by mural infiltration. The rigid, non-compliant segment obstructs the passage of stool, causing straining, tenesmus, and proximal loading, and in tight strictures may progress to overt obstruction. Short benign anorectal strictures often do well with dilatation, but long, dense, radiation-related, or recurrent strictures are more difficult and may require major surgery or permanent diversion; the outlook is dominated by the underlying cause, and malignant strictures carry the prognosis of the tumour.

Anorexia nervosa — anorexia, AN Bulimia nervosa Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder Major depressive disorder with appetite loss Hyperthyroidism Malabsorption and gastrointestinal disease Malignancy or chronic infection causing weight loss Body dysmorphic disorder Weight, height, and body mass index with growth trajectory in young people Electrolytes including potassium, phosphate, and magnesium ECG to assess for bradycardia and QT prolongation Full blood count, renal and liver function, and glucose Bone density assessment in prolonged illness Assessment for refeeding risk before and during nutritional rehabilitation Characterised by restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of weight gain, and a disturbance in how body weight or shape is experienced Two patterns are recognised: a restricting type and a binge-eating/purging type Physical consequences include amenorrhoea, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, lanugo hair, and osteopenia Purging behaviours can cause electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, and dental erosion Management principles centre on structured nutritional rehabilitation and weight restoration alongside psychotherapy, with family-based treatment favoured for adolescents Medical stabilisation takes priority in severe cases; feeding must be advanced cautiously to avoid refeeding syndrome Comorbid depression, anxiety, and obsessive-compulsive features are common, and suicide risk is elevated Weigh patients and monitor electrolytes and cardiac status, since bradycardia and QT prolongation can be dangerous Severe bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, or arrhythmia indicating cardiac instability Dangerous electrolyte derangement, particularly hypokalaemia and hypophosphataemia Refeeding syndrome during nutritional restoration Rapid or extreme weight loss and very low body mass index Suicidal ideation Refeeding too rapidly and precipitating life-threatening refeeding syndrome Focusing on weight alone while neglecting electrolyte and cardiac monitoring Underestimating suicide risk Being reassured by a normal weight in the binge-purge type despite dangerous electrolyte disturbance Delaying medical stabilisation while awaiting psychiatric transfer Anorexia nervosa arises from an interaction of genetic and temperamental vulnerability (perfectionism, anxiety, harm avoidance), sociocultural pressures, and neurobiological factors including altered reward and interoceptive processing and serotonergic and dopaminergic dysregulation. Starvation itself perpetuates the disorder through neuroendocrine and cognitive changes, and complications reflect the systemic effects of chronic malnutrition. Anorexia nervosa has one of the highest mortality rates among psychiatric disorders, from both medical complications and suicide. Many patients recover, particularly with early intervention in adolescence, but a substantial proportion follow a chronic or relapsing course.

Anterior cruciate ligament injury — ACL tear, ACL rupture, anterior cruciate ligament sprain Posterior cruciate ligament injury Patellar dislocation with haemarthrosis Meniscal tear Osteochondral fracture Multiligament knee injury Tibial eminence avulsion in skeletally immature patients Lachman, anterior drawer and pivot-shift examination MRI of the knee to confirm the tear and assess meniscal/chondral injury Radiographs to detect a Segond fracture or tibial eminence avulsion Aspiration if characterisation of a tense haemarthrosis is needed Examination under anaesthesia in equivocal or multiligament cases Classically a non-contact pivoting or deceleration injury with an audible pop, rapid effusion and a sense of the knee giving way A rapid (within hours) haemarthrosis after a twisting injury is an ACL rupture until proven otherwise The Lachman test is the most sensitive examination; the pivot-shift correlates with functional instability An associated Segond fracture (lateral capsular avulsion) on radiograph is nearly pathognomonic of ACL rupture Female athletes have a higher incidence, related to neuromuscular and anatomical factors Management is individualised: reconstruction for young pivoting athletes and instability, with rehabilitation appropriate for lower-demand patients Associated meniscal, chondral and collateral injuries (the unhappy triad with MCL and medial meniscus) are common Multiligament injury or knee dislocation with possible popliteal artery injury Inability to bear weight with a locked knee suggesting a displaced meniscal fragment Neurovascular compromise after a high-energy mechanism Dismissing an acute haemarthrosis as a simple sprain and missing the ACL tear Failing to identify a knee dislocation that has spontaneously reduced with vascular risk Overlooking associated meniscal or MCL injury Returning athletes to sport before criteria-based rehabilitation is complete The ACL restrains anterior tibial translation and rotational load. A valgus, rotational or hyperextension force with the foot planted exceeds ligament tensile strength, tearing it (usually mid-substance). Loss of the ACL produces anterior and rotatory instability, abnormal joint kinematics and increased shear on the menisci and cartilage, predisposing to further meniscal tears and later osteoarthritis. Reconstruction restores stability and return to pivoting sport in the majority, though re-rupture and graft failure occur, particularly in young athletes returning early; irrespective of treatment there is an increased long-term risk of osteoarthritis.

especially in inflammatory cases; surgical decompression is reserved for a demonstrable compressive lesion or lack of recovery over an extended period Acute severe shoulder-girdle or forearm pain preceding weakness, indicating neuralgic amyotrophy Inability to flex the distal joints of thumb and index with an intact tenodesis effect, distinguishing palsy from tendon rupture A palpable or amyotrophy as the underlying mechanism in painful acute presentations Rushing to surgical decompression before allowing time for spontaneous recovery in inflammatory cases Confusing it with carpal tunnel or pronator syndrome despite the complete absence of sensory symptoms Failing to isolate pronator quadratus by testing pronation with the elbow flexed The anterior interosseous nerve branches from the median nerve in the proximal forearm, usually just distal to the two heads of pronator teres, and runs on the interosseous membrane to supply flexor pollicis longus, the radial half of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus. Because it is purely motor, lesions produce a distinctive weakness of distal thumb and index-finger flexion and forearm pronation without any sensory deficit. Injury may result from external or internal compression by fibrous arcades, anomalous muscles or vessels and mass lesions, or, frequently, from an immune-mediated inflammatory process (neuralgic amyotrophy) that selectively involves the fascicles destined for the anterior interosseous nerve, producing hourglass-like nerve constrictions demonstrable on imaging. Cases due to neuralgic amyotrophy and to relieved compression frequently recover useful pinch function over several months to about a year, though recovery can be incomplete. Persistent deficits from unresolved fascicular constriction or structural compression may benefit from surgical exploration, nerve reconstruction or tendon transfer.

with acute lens swelling and secondary pressure rise Rapidly progressive myopic shift or fixed astigmatism unresponsive to spectacles in a child at amblyogenic age Haematuria, proteinuria or declining renal function indicating progressive Alport nephropathy Progressive sensorineural hearing loss Attributing the irregular astigmatism to keratoconus and missing the lenticular origin Failing to investigate for Alport syndrome when bilateral anterior lenticonus is found Underestimating anterior capsule fragility, risking uncontrolled tears during capsulorhexis Overlooking co-existing type IV collagen. In Alport syndrome, mutations in the genes encoding the alpha-3, alpha-4 or alpha-5 chains of type IV collagen (most commonly X-linked COL4A5, also autosomal COL4A3 and COL4A4) produce a structurally defective and abnormally thin anterior capsule. Overall prognosis is dominated by the associated Alport nephropathy, which may progress to end-stage renal disease requiring transplantation.

are harmless and missing amblyopia from induced astigmatism Overlooking associated anterior segment dysgenesis and its glaucoma risk Proceeding to unnecessary surgery for a stable, visually insignificant opacity Neglecting refractive correction and occlusion in favour of watching the opacity alone Failing to counsel families about the dominant inheritance and to examine relatives During anterior lens epithelium that proliferates and produces a localised capsular and subcapsular opacity. Most anterior polar cataracts are stationary and visually insignificant, carrying an excellent prognosis with observation alone. When the opacity is large, pyramidal or associated with significant refractive error, the outlook depends on prompt correction of ametropia and treatment of amblyopia, and on the presence of any co-existing anterior segment anomaly.
