The majority are solitary midline scalp lesions; larger or multiple defects and those overlying the spine or trunk warrant a search for associated anomalies. The membranous variant is often surrounded by a collar of long, dark hair (the hair collar sign), which is a marker of possible underlying neural tube or cranial dysraphism. A visible pulsation or bluish translucency at the base suggests an underlying bony defect with exposed dura or a sagittal sinus, raising the risk of haemorrhage and meningitis. Adams-Oliver syndrome links scalp aplasia cutis with terminal transverse limb reduction defects and cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita; screen for these when a scalp defect is found. Truncal or limb defects in a stillborn or macerated co-twin distribution suggest the fetus papyraceus association from intrauterine death of a monozygotic twin. Small defects heal spontaneously by secondary intention with conservative wound care, leaving a hairless atrophic scar; large defects may need surgical closure or grafting. Bart syndrome describes aplasia cutis of the lower limbs in association with epidermolysis bullosa, so blistering elsewhere should prompt investigation for inherited EB. visible dural or sagittal sinus pulsation, or bluish translucency indicating exposed intracranial contents and haemorrhage risk large or deep defect with exposed bone or brain, carrying risk of meningitis and life-threatening bleeding hair collar sign or midline location suggesting underlying neural tube defect signs of local infection with purulence, surrounding cellulitis or systemic sepsis associated limb, cardiac or gastrointestinal anomalies indicating a syndromic diagnosis attributing a scalp defect to birth trauma and missing a true congenital lesion or its syndromic associations overlooking the hair collar sign and failing to image for underlying dysraphism aggressively debriding or grafting a small membranous lesion that would heal conservatively not examining the limbs, heart and skin elsewhere for Adams-Oliver, Bart or Goltz features underestimating haemorrhage risk in lesions overlying the sagittal sinus Aplasia cutis congenita is a heterogeneous developmental defect in which localised interruption of skin formation leaves epidermis, dermis and occasionally deeper structures absent at birth. It is not a single disease but a phenotype with multiple mechanisms, including intrauterine vascular compromise, thrombotic or embolic events (as with a demised co-twin), amniotic membrane adherence, teratogen exposure such as methimazole, and single-gene disorders affecting skin or vascular development. Failure of closure of embryonic fusion lines may explain midline scalp predilection, while defective proliferation or premature degeneration of skin at biomechanical tension points may account for lesions over rapidly growing areas. When the defect extends through the skull, meninges or dura may be exposed, and the underlying dural sinuses are vulnerable to injury. Small solitary scalp defects have an excellent prognosis, healing spontaneously with a residual atrophic hairless scar. Large defects, exposed dura or associated syndromic anomalies carry higher morbidity, with risk of haemorrhage, infection and dependence on surgical reconstruction.

Aplastic anaemia — acquired aplastic anaemia, bone marrow aplasia Hypoplastic myelodysplastic syndrome Inherited bone marrow failure (Fanconi anaemia, dyskeratosis congenita) Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria Marrow infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma, metastasis) Megaloblastic anaemia or drug-induced marrow suppression Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis Full blood count and reticulocytes Bone marrow aspirate and trephine showing hypocellularity Cytogenetics and flow cytometry (including PNH clone testing) Chromosome breakage or telomere studies where inherited syndromes are suspected Screening for viral and drug causes Pancytopenia with a hypocellular bone marrow in the absence of an abnormal infiltrate or fibrosis Presents with anaemia, bleeding from thrombocytopenia and infection from neutropenia Most acquired cases are immune-mediated; others follow drugs, toxins, viral infection or radiation Inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (for example Fanconi anaemia, dyskeratosis congenita) must be excluded, especially in the young Severity is graded by blood counts and marrow cellularity, guiding urgency of treatment Treatment is immunosuppressive therapy or, for suitable patients, allogeneic stem cell transplantation, with supportive transfusion and infection control Severe neutropenia with sepsis Life-threatening bleeding from profound thrombocytopenia Features suggesting an inherited syndrome or evolving clonal disorder Rapidly progressive pancytopenia Missing an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome, which changes management Overlooking a PNH clone or evolving myelodysplasia Attributing pancytopenia to aplasia without excluding marrow infiltration Delaying definitive therapy in severe disease Acquired aplastic anaemia is most often an immune-mediated disorder in which cytotoxic T lymphocytes attack haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, causing their depletion and a markedly hypocellular marrow with resulting pancytopenia. Triggers include certain drugs, toxins (such as benzene), viral infections and, rarely, radiation, though many cases are idiopathic. A minority arise from inherited defects of stem cell maintenance or DNA repair (inherited bone marrow failure syndromes), and there is overlap with clonal disorders such as paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and myelodysplasia. Severe untreated aplastic anaemia is life-threatening, but immunosuppressive therapy and, especially, matched allogeneic transplantation achieve good long-term survival in many patients; clonal evolution remains a long-term risk.

drugs, chemicals (e.g. benzene), viral hepatitis (seronegative), and radiation are recognised triggers Inherited causes such as Fanconi anaemia and dyskeratosis congenita should be considered in younger patients or those with characteristic physical or family features Severity is graded by degree of neutropenia, reticulocytopenia, and thrombocytopenia; very severe disease carries the highest risk of early death from infection or haemorrhage Definitive management is either allogeneic stem cell transplant (favoured in younger patients with a matched sibling donor) or immunosuppressive therapy combining antithymocyte globulin and a calcineurin inhibitor A thrombopoietin receptor agonist can augment haematopoietic recovery when added to immunosuppression Overlap exists with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and hypoplastic myelodysplasia, so flow cytometry for PNH clones and marrow cytogenetics are important at diagnosis Severe neutropenia with fever, indicating potentially fatal sepsis requiring urgent broad-spectrum antibiotics Profound thrombocytopenia with mucosal bleeding or signs of intracranial haemorrhage Rapidly falling counts defining very severe aplastic anaemia and the need for prompt referral to a transplant centre Emergence of dysplastic or cytogenetic abnormalities suggesting clonal evolution to MDS or leukaemia Attributing pancytopenia to a peripheral cause and omitting a marrow biopsy that would reveal hypocellularity Overlooking a coexisting PNH clone or evolving myelodysplasia Delaying HLA typing and transplant referral in young patients with severe disease Failing to recognise an inherited marrow failure syndrome, which changes treatment and family counselling Giving platelet or red cell transfusions without irradiation or leucodepletion in a potential transplant candidate Aplastic anaemia results from destruction or profound suppression of pluripotent haematopoietic stem cells, leaving an empty (hypocellular) marrow and peripheral pancytopenia. In most acquired cases the mechanism is autoimmune: activated cytotoxic T lymphocytes and their cytokines (interferon-gamma, tumour necrosis factor) drive stem cell apoptosis. Environmental exposures, certain drugs, and viral illness can initiate this immune attack, while inherited marrow failure syndromes reflect defects in DNA repair or telomere maintenance that exhaust the stem cell pool. Clonal disorders such as PNH and MDS can emerge from a damaged marrow because surviving abnormal clones gain a survival advantage. Untreated severe aplastic anaemia is frequently fatal from infection or bleeding, but outcomes have transformed with early allogeneic transplantation and effective immunosuppression; younger patients with matched sibling donors have high survival, while older patients rely on immunosuppressive therapy with a meaningful risk of relapse and late clonal disease.

Immature chemoreceptor responses can produce a paradoxical decrease in breathing with hypoxia, and poor pharyngeal tone contributes to obstructive and mixed events. These control problems resolve with maturation of the brainstem respiratory network. New apnoea in a previously stable infant, however, may signal an acquired problem such as infection rather than simple immaturity. Apnoea of prematurity generally resolves with maturation and has a good prognosis; persistent events at term-corrected age or an identified secondary cause require further evaluation.

Apocrine hidrocystoma — apocrine cystadenoma, cyst of Moll, sudoriferous cyst Eccrine hidrocystoma Epidermal inclusion cyst Melanocytic naevus of the eyelid margin Nodular basal cell carcinoma Malignant melanoma of the eyelid Sebaceous (meibomian) cyst / chalazion Cystic sebaceous or sweat-gland adenoma Slit-lamp examination of the lid margin to characterise the cyst Transillumination to confirm the fluid-filled cystic nature Dermoscopy to distinguish from pigmented and vascular lesions External photography for documentation and monitoring Excisional biopsy with histopathology to confirm diagnosis and exclude malignancy in atypical lesions Assessment for associated features of ectodermal dysplasia when lesions are multiple An apocrine hidrocystoma is a benign cystic lesion arising from the apocrine glands of Moll at the eyelid margin, presenting as a smooth, dome-shaped, translucent cyst. It is characteristically solitary and often has a bluish or bluish-black translucent hue owing to the Tyndall effect of clear fluid within the cyst, and it transilluminates. The lesion is filled with clear or slightly milky fluid and, unlike an eccrine hidrocystoma, does not enlarge specifically with heat or sweating. It is typically found at or near the lid margin, most often the inner or outer canthus, and is usually asymptomatic apart from cosmetic concern. Diagnosis is clinical; transillumination helps confirm the cystic, fluid-filled nature and distinguish it from a solid or pigmented lesion. Definitive treatment is complete surgical excision including the cyst wall; simple puncture or incision leads to recurrence because the secretory lining persists. A bluish eyelid-margin lesion must be differentiated from pigmented lesions such as naevus or melanoma, and from a nodular basal cell carcinoma, so atypical lesions warrant histology. Multiple apocrine or eccrine hidrocystomas can occur and, when numerous, may be associated with ectodermal dysplasia syndromes such as Schopf-Schulz-Passarge and Goltz syndromes. Irregular pigmentation, ulceration or induration suggesting melanoma or basal cell carcinoma Rapid growth or recurrence after excision A solid rather than transilluminating lesion, casting doubt on the cystic diagnosis Multiple lesions prompting evaluation for an underlying ectodermal dysplasia syndrome Treating by simple incision or drainage, which leaves the secretory lining and leads to recurrence Mistaking a bluish translucent cyst for a pigmented naevus or melanoma, or vice versa Failing to excise the full cyst wall at the lid margin, risking recurrence or marginal notching Overlooking an associated ectodermal dysplasia syndrome in patients with numerous lesions Not obtaining histology when the lesion has atypical or solid features Apocrine hidrocystomas are adenomatous cystic proliferations (cystadenomas) derived from the apocrine secretory glands of Moll in the eyelid margin, rather than simple retention cysts. The cyst is lined by an inner layer of columnar secretory epithelium showing decapitation (apocrine) secretion and an outer layer of myoepithelial cells, and papillary projections may extend into the lumen. Active apocrine secretion fills the cavity with proteinaceous fluid; the overlying thin wall and clear contents scatter light to give the characteristic translucent bluish appearance. Because the lesion is a true secretory neoplasm with a retained lining, incomplete removal allows continued secretion and recurrence. Benign with an excellent prognosis; complete excision including the cyst wall is curative. Recurrence follows incomplete removal, and multiple lesions may recur individually.

it substantially raises the risk of several kidney diseases Associated phenotypes include focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, HIV-associated nephropathy, hypertension-attributed CKD, and more rapid CKD progression Inheritance behaves recessively for kidney risk, but most people with two risk alleles never develop kidney disease, indicating that a 'second hit' is usually required The variants persist at high frequency because a single copy confers protection against African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) Recognising APOL1 risk has implications for living kidney donation and for donor-derived graft outcomes Genotyping identifies risk but does not by itself diagnose active kidney disease, which still needs clinical and, where appropriate, histological assessment Nephrotic-range proteinuria with rapidly declining renal function Collapsing glomerulopathy on biopsy, often with an interferon-associated trigger Accelerated CKD progression despite blood pressure control Deteriorating graft function in a kidney from a high-risk-genotype donor Treating APOL1 genotype as diagnostic of disease rather than a susceptibility factor Neglecting the impact of the genotype on living-donor evaluation and counselling Assuming a Mendelian dominant pattern rather than the recessive-acting two-hit model Overlooking a treatable second hit such as viral infection driving collapsing disease APOL1 encodes apolipoprotein L1, a circulating and intracellular protein that also confers innate immunity against certain trypanosomes. The G1 and G2 coding variants alter the protein so that, in the presence of a second environmental or genetic stressor (such as interferon-driven inflammation from viral infection), APOL1 becomes toxic to kidney cells, particularly podocytes. This injury drives podocyte dysfunction and loss, producing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, collapsing glomerulopathy and progressive glomerular and interstitial scarring. Because injury generally requires a two-hit process, the high-risk genotype increases susceptibility and accelerates progression rather than being sufficient alone to cause disease. The high-risk genotype is linked to earlier onset and faster progression of kidney disease, but penetrance is incomplete and many carriers retain normal kidney function; outcome depends heavily on the presence of a second injurious trigger and on control of blood pressure and proteinuria.

Apolipoprotein A-I Amyloidosis (AApoAI) — ApoA-I amyloidosis, AApoAI, Hereditary apolipoprotein A-I amyloidosis AL (immunoglobulin light-chain) amyloidosis Other hereditary amyloidoses (fibrinogen, lysozyme, LECT2, transthyretin) AA amyloidosis Primary hepatic disease with cholestasis Other causes of chronic kidney disease Hereditary cardiomyopathy for cardiac-predominant variants Biopsy of the affected organ with Congo red staining Amyloid typing by mass spectrometry and immunohistochemistry APOA1 gene sequencing Renal and liver function with quantified proteinuria Serum free light chains and immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis SAP scintigraphy to assess organ burden Echocardiography and laryngoscopy where the mutation predicts cardiac or laryngeal disease AApoAI is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the APOA1 gene, whose product is the principal apolipoprotein of high-density lipoprotein. It is a multi-organ hereditary amyloidosis in which the pattern of organ involvement is strongly determined by the specific mutation and its position within the protein. Common targets include the kidney, liver, heart, larynx, skin and testes, with hepatic and renal involvement frequently dominant. N-terminal mutations tend to cause hepatic and renal disease, whereas C-terminal mutations more often affect the heart, larynx and skin, providing a useful genotype-phenotype guide. Progression is typically slow, and life expectancy may be near-normal in many kindreds despite organ deposition. Hepatic involvement can cause marked cholestasis and hepatomegaly, while renal involvement is often tubulointerstitial rather than purely glomerular, with modest proteinuria. Organ transplantation of kidney or liver is used for advanced single-organ failure, and outcomes are generally favourable given the indolent course. Unexplained cholestatic liver disease with hepatomegaly Progressive renal impairment with a supportive family history Hoarseness or airway symptoms suggesting laryngeal amyloid Family history of multi-organ disease or premature organ failure Mistyping as AL amyloidosis and giving unnecessary chemotherapy Attributing cholestasis to primary liver disease Underestimating renal involvement because proteinuria is modest Failing to offer genetic counselling and family screening Amyloidogenic variants of apolipoprotein A-I, generated by mutations in APOA1, are cleaved to release an N-terminal fragment that misfolds and aggregates into amyloid fibrils. Because apolipoprotein A-I is central to high-density lipoprotein metabolism and is expressed in the liver and intestine, variant protein circulates widely and deposits in multiple tissues, with the precise tropism dictated by the mutation. Renal deposition is often concentrated in the medulla and interstitium, producing slowly progressive renal impairment with relatively modest proteinuria, while hepatic deposits cause cholestasis. The generally slow kinetics of deposition account for the comparatively indolent clinical course. The course is usually indolent with slow organ deterioration and often near-normal survival. Targeted organ transplantation can provide durable benefit for isolated advanced renal or hepatic failure.

Apolipoprotein A-IV Amyloidosis (AApoAIV) — ApoA-IV amyloidosis, AApoAIV AL (immunoglobulin light-chain) amyloidosis ALECT2 and other renal amyloidoses Wild-type and variant ATTR for cardiac disease AA amyloidosis Age-related and hypertensive nephropathy Other infiltrative cardiomyopathies for cardiac-predominant cases Renal or cardiac biopsy with Congo red staining Amyloid typing by mass spectrometry, which is essential for identification Serum free light chains and immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis Renal function and quantified proteinuria Echocardiography and cardiac biomarkers if cardiac involvement is suspected SAP scintigraphy to assess organ burden Exclusion of ATTR by bone scintigraphy and TTR sequencing where relevant AApoAIV is a rare amyloidosis in which wild-type apolipoprotein A-IV deposits, resembling wild-type ATTR in being an acquired, age-related process rather than a classic hereditary disease. It predominantly affects the kidney, characteristically the renal medulla, and the heart. Renal disease presents as slowly progressive chronic kidney disease, often with only modest proteinuria. It tends to occur in older individuals, consistent with an age-associated deposition of the normal-sequence protein. There is usually no family history and no causative point mutation, which distinguishes it from the hereditary apolipoprotein amyloidoses. Diagnosis requires biopsy with amyloid typing by mass spectrometry, as it is not detected by routine immunohistochemical panels and is easily missed. There is no specific therapy; management is supportive with attention to renal and cardiac function. In AApoAIV the wild-type protein deposits as amyloid, with a distinctive predilection for the renal medullary interstitium and, in some cases, the myocardium. The absence of a destabilising mutation and the older age of affected patients suggest an age-related acquired process analogous to wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis. Medullary deposition can impair urinary concentrating ability and contribute to slowly progressive renal dysfunction, while proteinuria is often modest because glomerular involvement is limited. AApoAIV is typically indolent and age-related, with slowly progressive renal and occasionally cardiac dysfunction. There is no disease-specific treatment, and the prognosis is generally more favourable than that of untreated AL amyloidosis.

tested 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 is a predominantly hepatic and adipose enzyme that regenerates active cortisol from inert cortisone, using NADPH generated within the endoplasmic reticulum by hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase. In cortisone reductase deficiency, loss-of-function mutations in H6PD, and less commonly in the reductase gene itself, deprive the enzyme of cofactor or directly impair it, so cortisol is not efficiently regenerated and its metabolic clearance rises. To maintain circulating cortisol the pituitary increases ACTH secretion, which secondarily stimulates the adrenal cortex to overproduce androgens. The net clinical effect is androgen excess with a broadly compensated cortisol status rather than frank glucocorticoid deficiency. Generally good; androgen-excess features can be managed and, because glucocorticoid status is compensated, patients are usually well, though attention to metabolic health and fertility is worthwhile.

Apparent Life-Threatening Event — ALTE, BRUE, brief resolved unexplained event Gastro-oesophageal reflux with laryngospasm Respiratory infection (including pertussis, RSV) Seizure or other neurological event Cardiac arrhythmia or structural heart disease Inborn error of metabolism Non-accidental injury or inflicted harm Airway anomaly or feeding-related aspiration Thorough history and examination to risk-stratify and seek an underlying cause Observation and pulse oximetry as appropriate ECG when a cardiac cause or arrhythmia is a concern Targeted testing (e.g. for infection, reflux, or seizures) guided by history rather than routinely Evaluation for non-accidental injury when the history is inconsistent or concerning Metabolic screening only if clinical features suggest it The older term ALTE described a frightening episode in an infant involving some combination of apnoea, colour change, altered tone, and choking or gagging as perceived by the observer. Because ALTE was poorly defined, it has largely been replaced by the concept of a brief resolved unexplained event (BRUE) in infants under one year. A BRUE applies only when the infant is asymptomatic on presentation, the episode was brief and has fully resolved, and no explanation is found after appropriate history and examination. A qualifying event involves one or more of: cyanosis or pallor, absent, decreased, or irregular breathing, marked change in tone, or altered responsiveness. The main clinical task is to distinguish low-risk infants, who need little or no intervention, from higher-risk infants requiring evaluation. Low-risk criteria generally include age over about two months, no prematurity, a single brief event, no need for cardiopulmonary resuscitation by a trained provider, and a reassuring history and examination. A careful history and examination frequently reveal an underlying explanation such as reflux, a respiratory infection, a seizure, or feeding difficulty, in which case the event is not a BRUE. Extensive investigation is often unnecessary in low-risk infants, and shared decision-making with caregivers, including reassurance and safety advice, is central to management. Age under two months or history of prematurity Recurrent or multiple events, or a prolonged episode Cardiopulmonary resuscitation required by a trained provider Abnormal examination findings, ongoing symptoms, or failure to return to baseline History inconsistent with the injury or features suggesting non-accidental harm Family history of sudden unexplained death or a sibling with a similar event Applying the BRUE label when the infant is symptomatic or an explanation exists Over-investigating and hospitalising clearly low-risk infants Under-investigating higher-risk infants who need closer evaluation Missing non-accidental injury when the history does not fit the presentation Failing to provide caregiver reassurance, safety advice, and clear follow-up guidance These events are a clinical presentation rather than a single disease, and reflect a transient disturbance of cardiorespiratory or neurological control in the infant. Immature regulation of breathing, airway protective reflexes, and arousal can be perturbed by triggers such as gastro-oesophageal reflux, airway obstruction, infection, seizure activity, or autonomic instability, producing a brief episode that resolves as the infant recovers. When no cause is identified despite adequate assessment, the event is classified as unexplained. Most infants meeting low-risk BRUE criteria have an excellent outcome with a very low risk of recurrence or serious underlying disease, whereas higher-risk infants and those with an identified cause have a prognosis that depends on the specific diagnosis.

Apparent mineralocorticoid excess — AME, HSD11B2 deficiency, 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 deficiency, cortisol-mediated mineralocorticoid excess Liddle syndrome (ENaC gain-of-function) Primary hyperaldosteronism Licorice or carbenoxolone ingestion (acquired AME) Glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism Cushing syndrome Congenital adrenal hyperplasia with mineralocorticoid excess (11-beta or 17-alpha hydroxylase types) Plasma renin activity and aldosterone (both suppressed) Serum potassium and bicarbonate to document hypokalaemic alkalosis Urinary steroid metabolite profile showing an increased cortisol-to-cortisone ratio Screening for licorice, carbenoxolone and other enzyme-inhibiting exposures Renal and cardiac end-organ assessment given severe hypertension Molecular genetic testing of HSD11B2 Apparent mineralocorticoid excess is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in HSD11B2, encoding 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 This enzyme normally converts cortisol to inactive cortisone within mineralocorticoid target cells, protecting the mineralocorticoid receptor from being activated by cortisol When it fails, cortisol floods and activates the mineralocorticoid receptor, producing a mineralocorticoid-excess state despite normal aldosterone The hallmark is severe low-renin hypertension with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, and both renin and aldosterone are suppressed An elevated urinary cortisol-to-cortisone metabolite ratio is characteristic and helps confirm the diagnosis The acquired phenocopy is heavy licorice or carbenoxolone ingestion, which inhibits the same enzyme Management combines mineralocorticoid-receptor blockade and sometimes an ENaC blocker with salt restriction; suppressing endogenous cortisol may be considered in selected cases Severe hypertension presenting in childhood or young adulthood Profound hypokalaemia with weakness or arrhythmia Hypertensive end-organ damage including nephrocalcinosis and left ventricular hypertrophy Failure to thrive or growth restriction in affected children Hypertensive crisis or stroke Attributing the picture to primary hyperaldosteronism despite the suppressed aldosterone Missing a dietary licorice or carbenoxolone cause of an identical biochemical picture Relying on aldosterone antagonism alone when severe disease may also need ENaC blockade and salt restriction Overlooking the recessive inheritance and the need to evaluate siblings Apparent mineralocorticoid excess arises from deficiency of 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, an enzyme expressed in aldosterone-responsive tissues that inactivates cortisol to cortisone. Cortisol binds the mineralocorticoid receptor with affinity similar to aldosterone, but is normally circulating at far higher concentrations; the enzyme provides tissue specificity by locally clearing cortisol so that only aldosterone reaches the receptor. When the enzyme is deficient, intracellular cortisol accumulates and inappropriately activates the mineralocorticoid receptor in the distal nephron, driving sodium retention and potassium and hydrogen loss. The resulting volume expansion causes low-renin hypertension and hypokalaemic alkalosis, while the same volume expansion suppresses aldosterone, so the biochemistry shows mineralocorticoid effects without a raised mineralocorticoid hormone. Outlook depends on how early treatment begins; poorly controlled disease leads to severe hypertensive complications and chronic kidney damage, whereas mineralocorticoid-receptor blockade with salt restriction can achieve reasonable control.

appendiceal mucinous neoplasm — LAMN, appendiceal mucocele acute appendicitis with appendiceal distension appendiceal adenocarcinoma (colonic-type) ovarian mucinous neoplasm with peritoneal spread appendiceal neuroendocrine tumour endometriosis involving the appendix caecal or right-colonic mucinous carcinoma retention mucocele from luminal obstruction contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis MRI to map peritoneal and mucinous disease burden colonoscopy to exclude a synchronous colorectal primary tumour markers including CEA, CA19-9 and CA125 for baseline and monitoring histopathological grading with mucin cellularity assessment molecular testing for KRAS and GNAS where diagnosis is uncertain diagnostic laparoscopy with peritoneal assessment in selected cases A spectrum of mucin-producing appendiceal epithelial tumours ranging from low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm (LAMN) through high-grade (HAMN) to invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma. Often discovered incidentally on imaging as a distended, mucin-filled appendix (mucocele) or at appendicectomy for presumed appendicitis. The defining hazard is peritoneal dissemination producing pseudomyxoma peritonei, a slowly progressive accumulation of gelatinous mucin with epithelial cells throughout the peritoneal cavity. LAMN is characterised by pushing, expansile growth with loss of the muscularis mucosae and absence of infiltrative invasion, distinguishing it from frank adenocarcinoma. CT typically shows a cystic tubular appendiceal mass, sometimes with mural calcification; rupture or extra-appendiceal mucin greatly raises the risk of peritoneal spread. Because puncture or piecemeal removal can seed the peritoneum, an intact en bloc appendicectomy without rupture is essential, and biopsy of a suspected mucocele is avoided. Pathological reporting must document tumour grade, margin status, presence of acellular versus cellular mucin beyond the appendix, and any perforation, as these drive prognosis and follow-up. Established peritoneal disease is managed in specialist centres with cytoreductive surgery combined with heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy where appropriate. appendiceal rupture or free intraperitoneal mucin on imaging new or progressive abdominal distension suggesting pseudomyxoma peritonei cellular mucin beyond the appendiceal wall on histology features of invasive high-grade adenocarcinoma bowel obstruction from peritoneal mucinous disease Rupturing or aspirating a suspected mucocele, seeding the peritoneum with mucin-producing cells. Dismissing acellular peritoneal mucin as harmless without thorough sampling for epithelial cells. Treating pseudomyxoma peritonei as ovarian in origin when the appendix is the true primary. Under-reporting margin, perforation and mucin cellularity, which are essential for risk stratification. Delaying referral to a specialist peritoneal malignancy centre once dissemination is suspected. Appendiceal mucinous neoplasms arise from the appendiceal epithelium, which undergoes mucinous transformation, frequently driven by mutations in KRAS and GNAS that stimulate abundant mucin production. Progressive intraluminal mucin accumulation dilates the appendix to form a mucocele and raises intraluminal pressure, which may cause the wall to thin, ulcerate and eventually rupture. When neoplastic mucin-producing epithelial cells escape into the peritoneal cavity, they redistribute along the flow of peritoneal fluid and implant preferentially at sites of fluid resorption, secreting copious mucin to produce pseudomyxoma peritonei. Even low-grade lesions, despite bland cytology and lack of true stromal invasion, can be lethal through this relentless peritoneal mucinous accumulation causing progressive abdominal distension, adhesions and bowel compromise. Localised, intact low-grade lesions confined to the appendix and completely excised have an excellent outlook, whereas peritoneal dissemination markedly worsens prognosis, with survival strongly dependent on tumour grade and completeness of cytoreduction. High-grade and invasive tumours carry a considerably poorer outcome.

phototherapy and treatment of any underlying disorder A raised haematocrit, splenomegaly or thrombotic history suggesting polycythaemia vera Constitutional symptoms such as weight loss, fever or night skin and overlooking a systemic cause Not reassessing patients over time, since haematological disease may declare itself later Aquagenic pruritus is thought to result from water-triggered activation of cutaneous mast cells and sensory nerves, with release of pruritogenic mediators despite the lack of a visible eruption. In association with myeloproliferative disorders such as polycythaemia vera, abnormal mast cell and basophil activity and increased mediator release are proposed to underlie the itch, and heightened fibrinolytic and neurogenic activity in the skin may contribute. The mechanism in idiopathic cases is less well defined but is presumed to share this neuro-mast-cell pathway. Idiopathic aquagenic pruritus tends to be chronic and can be difficult to control, though symptoms may fluctuate; when it is a manifestation of a myeloproliferative disorder, the prognosis and treatment are governed by the underlying condition, and effective management of that disorder often improves the itch.

daily life given how difficult water avoidance is Not considering omalizumab in disabling, antihistamine-resistant disease Aquagenic urticaria is thought to occur when water contact with the skin generates or mobilises a soluble antigen that diffuses into the epidermis and triggers mast cell degranulation with histamine release, producing weals independent of temperature. aqueous misdirection syndrome — malignant glaucoma, ciliary block glaucoma pupillary block angle-closure glaucoma suprachoroidal haemorrhage annular choroidal effusion or detachment overfiltration with a flat chamber and hypotony after trabeculectomy wound leak with shallow anterior chamber pseudophakic capsular block syndrome posterior segment mass pushing the lens-iris diaphragm forward gonioscopy and assessment of anterior chamber depth centrally and peripherally ultrasound biomicroscopy showing anterior ciliary body rotation and iridolenticular apposition B-scan ultrasonography to exclude suprachoroidal haemorrhage or choroidal effusion anterior segment optical coherence tomography of the angle and chamber assessment of iridotomy patency intraocular pressure measurement over time axial length biometry documenting a short or nanophthalmic eye Characterised by a uniformly shallow or flat anterior chamber, both centrally and peripherally, with raised or normal intraocular pressure. Classically arises after incisional glaucoma or cataract surgery in an eye predisposed by short axial length, a small anterior segment or nanophthalmos. A patent peripheral iridotomy that fails to deepen the chamber effectively excludes pupillary block and points to aqueous misdirection. Central to the mechanism is posterior diversion of aqueous into or behind the vitreous, pushing the whole lens-iris or vitreous face forward. Medical therapy combines cycloplegia to tighten the zonules and posteriorly rotate the ciliary body, aqueous suppressants and hyperosmotic agents to shrink the vitreous. Miotics paradoxically worsen the condition and must be avoided. Nd:YAG laser disruption of the anterior hyaloid, often through an iridotomy or after capsulotomy, can re-establish a normal aqueous pathway in pseudophakic eyes. Refractory cases require pars plana vitrectomy with disruption of the anterior hyaloid, sometimes combined with lens removal, to create a unified fluid compartment. flat anterior chamber with raised pressure unresponsive to iridotomy rapidly rising pressure after intraocular surgery in a small eye features suggesting suprachoroidal haemorrhage requiring urgent differentiation corneal decompensation from lens-corneal touch Administering miotics, which aggravate the anterior displacement of the lens-iris diaphragm. Repeatedly performing or enlarging an iridotomy when pupillary block has already been excluded. Missing an occult suprachoroidal haemorrhage that mimics the flat chamber picture. Failing to warn the patient and plan prophylaxis before surgery on the predisposed fellow eye. Delaying definitive vitrectomy in phakic or refractory cases and allowing prolonged corneal-lens touch. Aqueous humour is abnormally diverted posteriorly, becoming trapped within or behind the vitreous body instead of flowing forward through the pupil to the trabecular meshwork. A postulated ciliolenticular or ciliovitreal block, in which the ciliary processes rotate forward and appose the lens equator, capsule or anterior hyaloid, prevents anterior aqueous movement. Accumulating aqueous in the vitreous cavity raises posterior segment pressure, driving the lens-iris diaphragm or vitreous face anteriorly and flattening the entire anterior chamber. Because the block is at the level of the ciliary body and hyaloid rather than the pupil, peripheral iridotomy does not relieve it. Reduced vitreous fluid conductivity and a crowded, small anterior segment predispose to the self-sustaining cycle. With prompt recognition and a stepwise medical, laser and surgical approach the anterior chamber can usually be re-formed and pressure controlled, but the condition is often recurrent and the fellow eye is at risk after any future intraocular surgery.

infections suggesting immune vulnerability New seizures warranting neurological review Attributing the profound speech delay to isolated language disorder rather than pursuing a genetic diagnosis Failing to screen for congenital heart disease at diagnosis Confusing the condition with allelic KAT6B disorders without careful phenotyping and sequencing Delaying introduction of alternative communication strategies while awaiting speech KAT6A encodes a lysine acetyltransferase of the MYST family that transfers acetyl groups onto histone H3, a modification that loosens chromatin structure and facilitates transcription of target genes. Pathogenic variants reduce or distort this acetyltransferase activity, disturbing the acetylation-dependent control of developmental gene expression, including programmes important for neuronal maturation and for cardiac and craniofacial development. The resulting epigenetic dysregulation manifests as intellectual disability with a distinctive speech deficit, hypotonia, congenital heart disease and dysmorphism, and the position and nature of the variant within the gene help explain the observed variation in severity. Life expectancy is not clearly reduced in most, but intellectual disability is typically moderate to severe and expressive speech may remain very limited, so early augmentative and alternative communication and coordinated developmental support are central; cardiac and feeding issues largely determine morbidity in infancy.

Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) — ARDS Cardiogenic (hydrostatic) pulmonary edema Bilateral pneumonia Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage Acute interstitial lung disease (e.g., acute interstitial pneumonitis) Acute immunologic injury (e.g., hypersensitivity pneumonitis) Toxin injury (e.g., radiation pneumonitis) Neurogenic pulmonary edema Bilateral pneumonia (may also coexist with ARDS) Arterial blood gas to determine PaO2/FiO2 ratio for Berlin severity grading Chest radiograph (bilateral opacities consistent with pulmonary edema, often involving >=three-quarters of lung fields) Echocardiography to exclude hydrostatic/cardiac etiology when no ARDS risk factor is present Chest CT (shows bilateral infiltrates with heterogeneous, often dependent lung involvement) Lung ultrasound permitted as an alternative imaging modality under proposed 2023 Berlin updates, especially in resource-limited settings Cardiogenic pulmonary edema Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage Acute interstitial pneumonitis Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Radiation pneumonitis Neurogenic pulmonary edema ARDS is a clinical syndrome of severe dyspnea of rapid onset, hypoxemia, and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates leading to respiratory failure, caused by diffuse lung injury (Harrison 22e p.2299). By 2012 expert consensus, ARDS is graded as mild, moderate, or severe by the degree of hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 ratio), and these stages correlate with mortality risk and duration of mechanical ventilation in survivors (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2300). Most cases (>80%) arise from a small number of disorders: pneumonia and sepsis (~40-60%), followed by aspiration of gastric contents, trauma, multiple transfusions, and drug overdose; risk rises with more than one predisposing condition (Harrison 22e p.2299). The natural history has three phases - exudative (first ~7 days), proliferative (~day 7-21), and fibrotic - each with characteristic clinical and pathologic features (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2301). Cornerstone of management is recognizing and treating the underlying trigger (pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration, trauma) plus standardized bundled ICU care, rather than ARDS-specific drug therapy (Harrison 22e p.2302). Lung-protective ventilation with low tidal volume (6 mL/kg predicted body weight) and limited plateau pressure (<=30 cmH2O) significantly lowers mortality versus conventional higher tidal volumes; this is the only therapy graded by the strongest evidence (Harrison 22e p.2302, p.2303). Prone positioning early in severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150 mmHg) reduced 28-day mortality in a randomized trial; it requires a team experienced in proning because repositioning critically ill patients can be hazardous (Harrison 22e p.2302). A conservative fluid strategy - reducing left atrial filling pressure with fluid restriction and diuretics - shortens ICU stay and duration of ventilation, limited only by hypotension and organ hypoperfusion (Harrison 22e p.2302). Mortality in ARDS is largely due to nonpulmonary causes, with sepsis and nonpulmonary organ failure accounting for >80% of deaths (Harrison 22e p.2303). Progressive hypoxemia and increasing work of breathing leading to respiratory fatigue and respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation Severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <=100 mmHg) carrying the highest mortality Concurrent sepsis or multiorgan failure, which account for most ARDS deaths Lung biopsy evidence of pulmonary fibrosis in any phase, associated with increased mortality ARDS radiographic findings are characteristic but not specific and can be indistinguishable from cardiogenic pulmonary edema; unlike cardiogenic edema, ARDS often lacks cardiomegaly, pleural effusions, or pulmonary vascular redistribution. Hydrostatic edema must not be the primary cause - if no ARDS risk factor is present, objective evaluation (e.g., echocardiography) is required to exclude a cardiac etiology (Harrison 22e p.2300, p.2301). Mechanical ventilation, though life-saving, can aggravate lung injury via volutrauma (alveolar overdistention from excess tidal volume), barotrauma (high alveolar pressure), and atelectrauma (recurrent alveolar collapse); because ARDS lung is heterogeneous, fully inflating consolidated regions can overdistend and injure more normal lung (Harrison 22e p.2302). Routine glucocorticoids are NOT supported by current evidence for ARDS itself; recruitment maneuvers combined with higher baseline PEEP increased mortality in one study; routine early neuromuscular blockade is not beneficial in all moderate-to-severe ARDS (reserve for ventilatory dyssynchrony despite sedation); surfactant replacement and inhaled vasodilators (e.g., inhaled nitric oxide) do not improve survival (Harrison 22e p.2302, p.2303). Pulse oximetry may overestimate oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin tones, so correlation with PaO2 should be considered when feasible (Harrison 22e p.2300). ARDS results from diffuse lung injury, either direct (e.g., pneumonia, aspiration, toxic inhalation, pulmonary contusion) or indirect (e.g., sepsis, severe trauma, multiple transfusions, pancreatitis). It evolves through three phases. In the EXUDATIVE phase (first ~7 days), alveolar capillary endothelial cells and type I pneumocytes are injured, the tight alveolar barrier is lost, and protein-rich edema fluid accumulates in the interstitial and alveolar spaces. Proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha) and lipid mediators recruit neutrophils, and condensed plasma proteins plus cellular debris and dysfunctional surfactant form hyaline membranes (diffuse alveolar damage). Pulmonary vascular injury occurs early with microthrombi. Dependent alveolar collapse reduces lung compliance, producing intrapulmonary shunting, hypoxemia, and increased work of breathing; microvascular occlusion raises dead space and pulmonary vascular resistance, so hypercapnia and pulmonary hypertension can also occur. The PROLIFERATIVE phase (~day 7-21) brings lung repair, organization of exudates, a shift from neutrophil- to lymphocyte-predominant infiltrates, and proliferation of type II pneumocytes that regenerate surfactant and differentiate into type I cells; most patients recover. Some progress to the FIBROTIC phase, with alveolar-duct and interstitial fibrosis, emphysema-like bullae, vascular occlusion and pulmonary hypertension, increased pneumothorax risk, reduced compliance, and increased dead space (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2300, p.2301, p.2302). Hospital mortality in the LUNG SAFE study was approximately 34.9% for mild, 40.3% for moderate, and 46.1% for severe ARDS, with a trend toward improved outcomes over time. Increasing Berlin-defined severity predicts higher mortality. Most deaths are nonpulmonary, with sepsis and nonpulmonary organ failure causing >80%. Major mortality risk factors are nonpulmonary: advanced age (~60% mortality in patients >75 vs ~20% in those <45), preexisting organ dysfunction (chronic liver disease, chronic alcohol abuse, chronic immunosuppression); direct lung injury carries nearly twice the death risk of indirect injury. Among survivors, the lung has notable resolving power: most regain nearly normal lung function, usually within 6 months, and more than a third have normal spirometry and diffusion capacity one year after extubation. However, exercise limitation and reduced physical quality of life are often documented at 5 years despite near-normal pulmonary function, and survivors and family caregivers carry a substantial burden of depression and posttraumatic stress disorder (Harrison 22e p.2303, p.2304). Berlin definition (2012): severity is graded by oxygenation (PaO2/FiO2 assessed on at least 5 cmH2O PEEP) - Mild: 200 mmHg < PaO2/FiO2 <=300 mmHg; Moderate: 100 mmHg < PaO2/FiO2 <=200 mmHg; Severe: PaO2/FiO2 <=100 mmHg. Onset must be acute (within 1 week of a clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms), chest imaging must show bilateral opacities consistent with pulmonary edema not fully explained by effusions, lobar/lung collapse, or nodules, and respiratory failure must not be primarily due to hydrostatic (cardiogenic) edema (objective evaluation such as echocardiography required if no ARDS risk factor present). Proposed 2023 updates extend criteria to nonintubated patients on high-flow nasal oxygen or noninvasive ventilation, add SpO2/FiO2 (S/F) ratios, permit ultrasound imaging, and allow application in resource-limited settings. A more recent global definition has also been proposed that does not rely on arterial blood gases, chest radiography, or PEEP (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2300).

Untreated disease is progressive with worsening spasticity and cognitive impairment, but early protein restriction, arginine limitation and scavenger therapy can slow or stabilise neurological deterioration and reduce hyperammonaemic episodes.

fumarate. The block prevents completion of ureagenesis, so waste nitrogen cannot be efficiently converted to urea and ammonia accumulates. Early recognition and prompt control of hyperammonaemia improve survival, but neurocognitive impairment, hypertension and hepatic disease may develop even with satisfactory metabolic control, so outcome is more variable than in some other urea cycle disorders.

in dopa-responsive dystonia Missing the diagnosis without CSF neurotransmitter studies Under-recognising the autonomic features and their acute risks Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) catalyses the final step in the synthesis of the monoamine neurotransmitters, converting L-dopa to dopamine and 5-hydroxytryptophan to serotonin. Biallelic DDC variants reduce enzyme activity, so dopamine, noradrenaline, adrenaline and serotonin are all deficient. The resulting monoamine deficiency produces a movement disorder with oculogyric crises, hypotonia, developmental delay and autonomic dysfunction. Because the block is at the decarboxylation step, upstream substrates such as L-dopa and its methylated derivative 3-O-methyldopa accumulate while the downstream metabolites homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid fall, giving the diagnostic CSF pattern. Management aims to boost residual monoamine signalling and, increasingly, to restore enzyme activity through gene therapy. Untreated severe disease causes marked disability, but multi-agent pharmacotherapy and, in particular, gene therapy can produce meaningful gains in motor function and quality of life, so outcome depends on phenotype severity and access to treatment.

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy — ARVC, ARVD, arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, PKP2-related cardiomyopathy Idiopathic right ventricular outflow tract tachycardia Cardiac sarcoidosis Brugada syndrome Dilated cardiomyopathy with predominant right ventricular involvement Athlete's heart with physiological right ventricular remodelling Myocarditis 12-lead ECG for right precordial T-wave inversion, epsilon waves and prolonged terminal activation Signal-averaged ECG to detect late potentials Cardiac MRI to assess right ventricular size, wall motion and fibrofatty infiltration Echocardiography for right ventricular dilatation and regional dysfunction Ambulatory monitoring and exercise testing to quantify ventricular arrhythmia Genetic testing for desmosomal gene variants and cascade family screening A genetic cardiomyopathy in which fibrofatty tissue progressively replaces right ventricular myocardium, predisposing to ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death Typically presents in young adults with palpitations, syncope, or exertional ventricular arrhythmia, and is an important cause of sudden death in athletes Most cases are autosomal dominant and caused by variants in desmosomal proteins, particularly plakophilin-2 (PKP2), desmoplakin, desmoglein-2 and desmocollin-2 The resting ECG may show T-wave inversion in the right precordial leads and an epsilon wave (a low-amplitude terminal QRS deflection) Diagnosis uses the Task Force Criteria, combining imaging, ECG, arrhythmic, tissue and family/genetic categories into major and minor criteria Cardiac MRI demonstrates right ventricular dilatation, regional wall-motion abnormalities and fibrofatty infiltration; left ventricular involvement is increasingly recognised Management centres on arrhythmia risk reduction with exercise restriction, beta-blockers, antiarrhythmic drugs, catheter ablation and an implantable cardioverter defibrillator in high-risk patients Intense endurance exercise accelerates disease progression, so activity counselling is a key part of care Syncope or aborted sudden cardiac death, particularly during exertion Sustained ventricular tachycardia of left bundle branch block morphology Progressive right or biventricular failure Family history of premature sudden death or confirmed ARVC Mislabelling the arrhythmia as benign idiopathic outflow tract tachycardia and missing the underlying cardiomyopathy Confusing physiological athlete's heart remodelling with early ARVC Permitting competitive or endurance exercise, which hastens disease progression Relying on right ventricular imaging alone and overlooking left-dominant or biventricular variants Underestimating arrhythmic risk in gene-positive relatives with subtle findings ARVC is caused predominantly by variants in genes encoding desmosomal proteins that maintain mechanical junctions between cardiomyocytes. Impaired cell-cell adhesion, aggravated by mechanical stress such as vigorous exercise, leads to myocyte detachment and death, with progressive replacement of myocardium by fibrous and fatty tissue. This begins in the right ventricle but can extend to the left. The scarred, electrically heterogeneous myocardium forms re-entry circuits that generate ventricular arrhythmias, while progressive myocardial loss can cause right and eventually biventricular dysfunction. The clinical course is variable; with risk stratification, exercise restriction and appropriate defibrillator therapy many patients do well, but the condition is progressive and carries an ongoing risk of life-threatening arrhythmia and, in advanced cases, heart failure.

Arterial and Venous Thrombosis — Thrombosis, Venous thromboembolism, VTE, Arterial thrombosis, Pathologic thrombosis Atherosclerotic plaque rupture causing acute coronary syndrome Embolism (cardiac source) versus in-situ thrombosis Aortic or arterial dissection Vasculitis causing arterial occlusion Postthrombotic syndrome as sequela of DVT Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension after PE Thrombophilia evaluation (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin, protein C, protein S deficiencies) in selected patients, recognizing many older genetic associations are being questioned in larger contemporary studies Antiphospholipid antibody testing when autoimmune prothrombotic state suspected Plasma homocysteine and MTHFR considerations as historically reported independent risk factors Assessment of acquired risk factors: malignancy screening, recent surgery/trauma, pregnancy status, hormonal therapy use Markers reflecting inflammation-thrombosis crosstalk (e.g., soluble CD40 ligand) noted as research-relevant Acute limb ischemia from arterial embolism rather than local thrombosis Superficial venous thrombophlebitis Lymphedema or cellulitis mimicking DVT-related limb swelling Extrinsic venous compression mimicking thrombotic obstruction Thrombosis is essentially hemostasis occurring in the wrong place at the wrong time; the same processes that protect against hemorrhage can, under certain conditions, produce pathologic arterial or venous occlusion. Hemostasis and thrombosis arise from interplay among three elements: the vessel wall, the coagulation/fibrinolytic proteins, and platelets. Arterial thrombosis is dominated by platelet adhesion to an injured vessel wall and the state of the wall itself, whereas venous thrombosis is driven mainly by activation of the coagulation cascade in the setting of stasis or hypercoagulability. Platelets are small anucleate cells (1-5 microns) circulating at roughly 200,000-400,000/microL with a 7-10 day lifespan, derived from marrow megakaryocytes under the control of thrombopoietin. The platelet GPIb-IX-V complex binds exposed subendothelial von Willebrand factor to initiate adhesion, and signaling converts the GPIIb/IIIa integrin from a low-affinity to a high-affinity fibrinogen receptor that cross-links platelets into an aggregate. Inflammation and infection transiently raise thrombotic risk: acute upper respiratory infection, bacterial and viral infections (including SARS-CoV-2, HIV, hepatitis C, dengue) are linked to increased myocardial infarction, stroke, and VTE. Roughly 5-8% of the U.S. population carries a genetic risk factor predisposing to venous thrombosis, and multiple risk factors frequently coexist in a single patient. Cancer confers an approximately fourfold increased risk of VTE compared with the general population, and VTE in cancer patients is associated with reduced survival. Although factor V Leiden and the prothrombin G20210A mutation are established risk factors for DVT and PE, their contribution to arterial thrombotic events such as acute coronary syndromes is not well established. Loss-of-function CYP2C19 polymorphisms are the strongest single determinant of reduced antiplatelet response to clopidogrel (a prodrug requiring hepatic activation) but account for only about 5-12% of the variability in ADP-induced platelet aggregation. Antithrombin reactions governed by normal endothelium become pivotal in limiting clot extension into adjacent uninjured vessel once a protective clot has formed; antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, heparin cofactor II, and protein C/protein S all restrain thrombin generation. Sudden death from pulmonary embolism (a substantial fraction of new VTE cases die early, with high 30-day mortality) PE in the setting of cancer carries roughly a 25% fatality rate Homozygous protein C or protein S deficiency can produce fatal purpura fulminans Coagulation abnormalities and increased PE/DVT/peripheral thrombosis in hospitalized COVID-19 patients (noted in nearly 20%) Calf-vein thrombus extension into popliteal and proximal veins, where fragments can embolize to the lungs Assuming hypercoagulable (thrombophilic) states that drive venous thrombosis are equally important for arterial events; their role in acute coronary syndromes is poorly defined and often not clinically significant. Genotyping to optimize aspirin therapy is not currently clinically indicated, as ex vivo studies have not firmly established a pharmacogenetic interaction between aspirin and COX1. Over-relying on CYP2C19 genotype for clopidogrel decisions, since loss-of-function alleles explain only a small fraction (about 5-12%) of antiplatelet response variability and genetics do not appreciably affect outcomes with prasugrel or ticagrelor. Forgetting that up to 10% of venous thromboembolic events occur outside the lower extremities and lungs. Treating many older single-gene thrombophilia associations as definitive when larger contemporary studies have called several into question. Thrombus formation reflects dysregulated hemostasis involving the vessel wall, coagulation and fibrinolytic proteins, and platelets. In arterial thrombosis, vessel-wall damage exposes subendothelial collagen and von Willebrand factor; the platelet GPIb-IX-V complex mediates adhesion, platelets are activated through seven-transmembrane receptors (thrombin/PAR1, PAR4, ADP receptors P2Y1 and P2Y12, prostaglandin and lipid receptors), release thromboxane A2, serotonin, and ADP from granules, and undergo a calcium-dependent conformational change in GPIIb/IIIa that allows high-affinity fibrinogen binding and irreversible aggregation. Most arterial thrombi are superimposed on disrupted atherosclerotic plaque whose thrombogenic core triggers platelet-rich thrombus. In venous thrombosis, the coagulation cascade is initiated chiefly by exposure of tissue factor: factor VII/VIIa-tissue factor complex activates factor X (directly or via factor IX/VIIIa), FXa with cofactor FVa converts prothrombin to thrombin, thrombin converts fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin and activates FXIII to cross-link the clot. Amplification lets a small stimulus generate large amounts of fibrin. Venous thrombi typically originate in valve cusps of calf deep veins or muscular sinuses where sluggish flow lowers oxygen delivery, activating endothelial cells that express adhesion molecules; tissue-factor-bearing leukocytes and microvesicles adhere, neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) provide a scaffold that binds and activates platelets and activates factor XII, and impaired clearance of activated clotting factors worsens local thrombosis. Hypercoagulability (heritable or acquired), stasis, and vascular dysfunction (Virchow's elements) underlie venous events. Inflammation links the two: platelet P-selectin binds leukocyte PSGL-1, induces monocyte tissue factor and CD40 ligand expression, and Toll-like receptors (TLR2/3/4, TLR7/8) connect infection to platelet-dependent thrombosis. Thrombosis is a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Coronary disease and stroke account for a large share of deaths; arterial thrombosis underlies most acute MI, ischemic stroke, and limb gangrene. For VTE, up to 30% of patients die within 30 days, about one-fifth experience sudden death from PE, and roughly 30% develop recurrent VTE within 10 years. The ARIC study reported a 9% 28-day fatality from DVT and 15% from PE; cancer-associated PE carries about 25% fatality. Incidence of first DVT rises sharply with age (from about 2-3 per 10,000 person-years at 30-49 years to about 20 per 10,000 at 70-79 years). Increasing age, obesity, malignancy, and acute extremity paresis independently predict recurrence.

Arterial Diseases of the Extremities — Peripheral artery disease, PAD, Peripheral arterial disease, Intermittent claudication, Chronic limb-threatening ischemia, Acute limb ischemia Atherosclerotic peripheral artery disease Fibromuscular dysplasia Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) Takayasu arteritis and giant cell (temporal) arteritis Acute limb ischemia from embolism or in-situ thrombosis Atheroembolism / cholesterol embolization Thoracic outlet compression syndrome (arterial, venous, neurogenic) Popliteal artery entrapment Popliteal artery aneurysm Arteriovenous fistula (congenital or acquired) Raynaud phenomenon (primary and secondary) Acrocyanosis Livedo reticularis / livedo racemosa Pernio (chilblains) Erythromelalgia Frostbite Infective endocarditis as an embolic source producing acute limb ischemia and digital infarcts Ankle-brachial index (ABI) with Doppler at dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries Toe-brachial index (TBI) when arteries are noncompressible Segmental limb pressures and pulse volume recordings to localize stenoses Duplex ultrasonography of native arteries and bypass grafts Treadmill exercise testing with post-exercise ABI Transcutaneous oximetry MRA, CTA, or catheter angiography for revascularization planning Nailfold capillaroscopy in Raynaud evaluation (normal hairpin loops in primary disease) Excisional vessel biopsy with pathology to confirm thromboangiitis obliterans Skin or muscle biopsy showing cholesterol crystals in atheroembolism Chest x-ray for cervical rib in thoracic outlet syndrome; provocative maneuvers (abduction/external rotation, scalene, costoclavicular, hyperabduction) Serologic and hematologic workup for secondary Raynaud (connective tissue disease, cold agglutinins, cryoglobulins, cryofibrinogen) Erythromelalgia (warm, erythematous, painful extremity with preserved pulses, opposite trigger to ischemia) Acrocyanosis (persistent, non-episodic cyanosis with normal pulses, no blanching, distinguishing it from Raynaud) Atheroembolic 'blue toe' confined to one or two digits, not to be confused with Raynaud phenomenon Spinal/neurogenic causes (intervertebral disk disease, syringomyelia, complex regional pain syndrome) mimicking vasospasm Myeloproliferative disorders and hyperviscosity states presenting with digital ischemia or erythromelalgia Peripheral artery disease (PAD) means stenosis or occlusion of the aorta or limb arteries; atherosclerosis is the dominant cause in patients over 40, while thrombosis, embolism, vasculitis, fibromuscular dysplasia, entrapment, cystic adventitial disease, and trauma account for the remainder. Risk factors mirror those for coronary and cerebral atherosclerosis: cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, elevated lipoprotein(a), hypertension, and renal insufficiency; prevalence is similar between sexes but greater in Black than non-Hispanic white persons and in lower socioeconomic groups. More than half of PAD patients are asymptomatic; the classic symptom is intermittent claudication (pain, ache, cramp, numbness, or fatigue in muscle that appears with exertion and resolves with rest), and the symptomatic muscle group lies distal to the obstructing lesion (e.g., buttock/hip/thigh with aortoiliac disease, calf with femoral-popliteal disease). Chronic limb-threatening ischemia produces rest pain or a cold/numb foot that worsens at night when legs are horizontal and improves with dependency; signs include hair loss, thickened nails, shiny atrophic skin, coolness, pallor or cyanosis, and ultimately ulcers or gangrene. Ankle-brachial index (ABI) is the key noninvasive test: normal 1.00-1.40, borderline 0.91-0.99, and abnormal/diagnostic of PAD at 0.90 or below; values above 1.40 indicate noncompressible, calcified vessels (as in diabetes or chronic kidney disease). When the ABI is unreliable because of medial calcification, a toe-brachial index of 0.70 or below is considered abnormal and supports the diagnosis. A drop in ABI immediately after treadmill exercise helps confirm PAD when resting findings are equivocal; MRA, CTA, and catheter angiography are reserved for revascularization planning, not routine diagnosis. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a non-inflammatory hyperplastic arteriopathy of medium and small (sometimes large) arteries, predominant in women, classically renal and carotid/vertebral, with a multifocal 'string of beads' or focal pattern, and can cause stenosis, dissection, aneurysm, or thrombosis. Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is an inflammatory occlusive disorder of distal small and medium arteries and veins, strongly linked to tobacco, typically in men under 40, presenting with a triad of distal claudication, Raynaud phenomenon, and migratory superficial thrombophlebitis; brachial and popliteal pulses are normal while distal pulses are reduced or absent. Acute limb ischemia is sudden cessation of limb blood flow most often from cardiac embolism (atrial fibrillation, MI, ventricular aneurysm, endocarditis, prosthetic valves, atrial myxoma), in-situ thrombosis, dissection, or trauma; emboli lodge at bifurcations, most commonly the femoral artery in the leg. Atheroembolism (cholesterol/fibrin/platelet debris from proximal plaque or aneurysm) classically spares large vessels, so distal pulses remain palpable; it causes the painful 'blue toe' syndrome, livedo reticularis, and may show cholesterol crystals on skin or muscle biopsy. Raynaud phenomenon is episodic digital ischemia with sequential pallor (vasospasm), cyanosis (deoxygenated blood in dilated capillaries), and rubor (reactive hyperemia) after cold or emotional stress; over half of cases are primary/idiopathic, with women affected roughly five times more often and onset typically between ages 20 and 40. Rest pain, ulceration, or gangrene indicating chronic limb-threatening ischemia Sudden severe pain, paresthesia, numbness, coldness, pallor, and pulselessness within an hour signaling acute limb ischemia Paralysis, loss of sensation, and absent Doppler signal in both arteries and veins, marking a nonviable limb requiring amputation Blue toe syndrome with progressive digital necrosis suggesting ongoing atheroembolism Ischemic fingertip ulcers progressing to gangrene and autoamputation in scleroderma-associated Raynaud Subclavian/axillary vein thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter) in venous thoracic outlet syndrome High-output cardiac failure and cardiomegaly from a large arteriovenous fistula Relying on the ABI in calcified, noncompressible vessels (ABI above 1.40) where it falsely appears normal or high; use the toe-brachial index instead. Ordering routine MRA/CTA/angiography for diagnosis when history, examination, and ABI usually suffice and imaging is meant for revascularization planning. Confusing atheroembolic digital ischemia (often one or two digits, palpable distal pulses) with Raynaud phenomenon. Mistaking acrocyanosis for Raynaud phenomenon; acrocyanosis is persistent rather than episodic, extends proximally from the digits, and lacks a blanching phase. Missing the strong tobacco link in Buerger disease and overlooking it in young male smokers presenting with distal ischemia and Raynaud features. Overlooking secondary causes of Raynaud (scleroderma, SLE, blood dyscrasias, drugs, vibration injury) and labeling the disease primary prematurely. Failing to perform provocative maneuvers in suspected thoracic outlet or popliteal entrapment syndromes, where the resting examination is often normal. Applying massage, ice water, or extreme heat to frostbite, which are contraindicated; rewarming should use a 40-44 C water bath. In atherosclerotic PAD, segmental plaques with calcium deposition, medial thinning, patchy loss of muscle and elastic fibers, fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina, and platelet-fibrin thrombi narrow large and medium vessels, preferentially at branch points where turbulence, altered shear stress, and intimal injury occur. Principal sites are the abdominal aorta/iliac arteries (about 30% of symptomatic patients), femoral/popliteal arteries (80-90%), and tibial/peroneal vessels (40-50%); distal disease predominates in the elderly and in diabetics. Hemodynamically significant stenoses lower distal systolic pressure (reflected in a reduced ABI). During exercise, vasodilation distal to a stenosis drops perfusion pressure below interstitial tissue pressure generated by working muscle, producing claudication. Buerger disease shows early neutrophilic infiltration of vessel walls with a preserved internal elastic lamina and a cellular inflammatory luminal thrombus, evolving to mononuclear/giant-cell infiltration, then perivascular fibrosis, organized thrombus, and recanalization. Raynaud phenomenon reflects digital arterial vasospasm; inherited erythromelalgia involves gain-of-function SCN9A (Nav1.7 sodium channel) mutations in sensory/sympathetic nerves. PAD natural history is driven largely by coexisting coronary and cerebrovascular disease: roughly one-third to one-half of symptomatic patients have clinical/ECG evidence of CAD and over half have significant disease on coronary angiography. PAD carries a 15-25% 5-year mortality and a two- to fourfold increased risk of cardiovascular death, with the highest mortality in those with most severe disease. Over 5 years the ABI worsens in nearly 40% and symptoms progress in about 20-25%; roughly 11% of symptomatic patients ultimately develop chronic limb-threatening ischemia, and without revascularization about 25% of those with chronic limb-threatening ischemia undergo amputation within a year. Prognosis is worse in continued smokers and diabetics. In thromboangiitis obliterans the outlook is worse in continued smokers and remains discouraging even after cessation. Primary Raynaud disease is generally mild, with fewer than 1% losing part of a digit, spontaneous improvement in about 15%, and progression in about 30%; primary acrocyanosis and benign livedo reticularis have favorable outcomes without ulceration or gangrene. PAD severity is graded hemodynamically by ABI: normal 1.00-1.40, borderline 0.91-0.99, abnormal/diagnostic at 0.90 or below, and noncompressible above 1.40 (toe-brachial index 0.70 or below abnormal). Clinically the spectrum runs from asymptomatic disease, to intermittent claudication, to chronic limb-threatening ischemia (rest pain, ulceration, gangrene). Acute limb ischemia is assessed for limb viability by presence of sensation, motor function, and Doppler-detectable arterial and venous flow; loss of all three defines a nonviable limb.

Arterial gas embolism — AGE, cerebral arterial gas embolism Decompression sickness Cardiac arrhythmia or myocardial infarction Stroke of another cause Seizure disorder Immersion syncope or near-drowning Immediate clinical recognition based on timing after surfacing or a procedure High-flow oxygen and preparation for recompression without delay Assessment for pulmonary barotrauma including pneumothorax Imaging as feasible, not allowing it to delay recompression Cardiac and neurological monitoring Gas bubbles entering the arterial circulation obstruct end-arteries, most dangerously in the brain and heart In divers it classically follows pulmonary barotrauma during ascent, especially breath-holding on a rapid ascent Symptoms are typically dramatic and immediate on or within minutes of surfacing, including loss of consciousness, seizures, focal deficits or cardiac arrest It can also be iatrogenic, from vascular access, cardiac or pulmonary procedures and mechanical ventilation High-flow oxygen and urgent recompression with hyperbaric oxygen are the definitive treatments Any diver with neurological symptoms immediately after surfacing has gas embolism until proven otherwise Loss of consciousness or cardiac arrest on surfacing Focal neurological deficit or seizure Coexisting tension pneumothorax Rapid deterioration Delaying recompression to complete imaging Confusing it with decompression sickness and mismanaging the urgency Missing a coexisting pneumothorax before recompression Failing to give high-flow oxygen immediately Arterial gas embolism occurs when gas enters the systemic arterial circulation and lodges in small arteries, causing mechanical obstruction, endothelial injury and secondary inflammation and thrombosis. In diving, alveolar rupture from lung overexpansion allows gas to enter the pulmonary veins and reach the systemic arteries, while iatrogenic cases arise from air introduced during procedures. Distribution of bubbles to the cerebral or coronary circulation produces the acute neurological and cardiac manifestations, and reduced perfusion beyond the obstruction drives ischaemic injury. Outcome depends on the bubble burden and speed of recompression; with prompt hyperbaric treatment many recover substantially, but delay or massive embolism can be fatal or leave permanent deficits.

Arterial tortuosity syndrome — ATS, SLC2A10, GLUT10 deficiency Loeys-Dietz syndrome Marfan syndrome Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome Cutis laxa syndromes Menkes disease (given arterial tortuosity) Other heritable thoracic aortic disease and connective-tissue arteriopathies SLC2A10 molecular genetic testing Whole-body magnetic resonance or CT angiography for arterial tortuosity and stenoses Echocardiography for aortic root, pulmonary arteries and cardiac function Blood pressure assessment across limbs Ophthalmological and skeletal evaluation for connective-tissue features Baseline and periodic vascular imaging for surveillance Defined by widespread elongation and tortuosity of large and medium arteries, best appreciated on angiographic imaging Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in SLC2A10, encoding the glucose transporter GLUT10 Arterial stenoses (particularly of the pulmonary arteries and aorta) coexist with the tortuosity and can cause haemodynamic compromise There is a real risk of aneurysm formation, arterial dissection and ischaemic events including stroke Systemic connective-tissue features overlap with other arteriopathies: hyperextensible skin, joint hypermobility, hernias and a marfanoid or dysmorphic facial appearance Whole-body arterial imaging is central to diagnosis and to planning surveillance Management is largely supportive with regular vascular surveillance and consideration of blood-pressure-lowering agents; some clinicians use beta-blockade or angiotensin-pathway blockers as in related aortopathies Prognosis relates chiefly to the severity of vascular stenoses and the risk of dissection or rupture Chest, back or abdominal pain suggesting arterial dissection or rupture New neurological deficit indicating stroke or cerebral ischaemia Haemodynamically significant arterial or pulmonary artery stenosis Rapidly enlarging aneurysm Overlooking the diagnosis when tortuosity is incidental and no dedicated arterial imaging is performed Attributing connective-tissue features to Marfan or Loeys-Dietz without vascular imaging Underestimating the risk of dissection in seemingly stable patients Neglecting lifelong vascular surveillance Arterial tortuosity syndrome is a heritable connective-tissue arteriopathy caused by loss of function of the glucose transporter GLUT10 (SLC2A10). GLUT10 dysfunction is thought to disturb transforming growth factor beta signalling and the metabolism of the arterial wall, impairing elastic fibre organisation in the tunica media. The weakened, disorganised elastic architecture allows the major arteries to elongate and become abnormally tortuous, and predisposes to focal stenoses, aneurysm formation and dissection. The same connective-tissue disturbance produces the skin, joint and facial features. The vascular fragility and stenoses underlie the risks of ischaemia, stroke and arterial rupture. Outcome varies widely and is dominated by the vascular phenotype; severe stenoses, aneurysms and dissection carry significant morbidity and mortality, whereas milder disease with careful surveillance can have a more favourable course.

When resting perfusion falls below the metabolic demand of the tissues, the microcirculation can no longer sustain viability or support wound repair, so minor trauma at acral or pressure-bearing sites fails to heal and instead progresses to ulceration and necrosis. Impaired oxygen and nutrient delivery, endothelial dysfunction and a diminished capacity for angiogenesis mean the ulcer base remains poorly granulating and pale, and unless inflow is restored the deficit extends to frank gangrene. Without revascularisation, arterial ulcers frequently fail to heal and may progress to gangrene and major amputation; timely restoration of perfusion improves limb salvage, but affected patients carry a high burden of coexisting cardiovascular disease and mortality.
