pseudoaneurysm and choosing the wrong treatment Underestimating distal ischaemia caused by arterial steal An arteriovenous fistula creates a low-resistance channel that diverts arterial blood directly into the venous system, bypassing the capillary bed. This produces a steal effect that can reduce distal arterial perfusion, while transmission of arterial pressure into the veins causes venous hypertension, dilatation, and secondary tissue changes. The reduced systemic vascular resistance increases venous return, stroke volume, and cardiac output; a large chronic shunt can lead to cardiac chamber enlargement and high-output heart failure. Congenital lesions reflect abnormal vascular development, whereas acquired fistulae follow penetrating trauma, procedures, or erosion between an adjacent artery and vein. Small fistulae may remain asymptomatic and be safely observed, while large or high-flow lesions can progressively cause limb complications or cardiac strain and generally require intervention. Outcomes after embolisation or surgical repair are favourable when the lesion is anatomically suitable, though congenital malformations can recur.

seizures or deficits to other causes without vascular imaging A cerebral arteriovenous malformation is a congenital vascular anomaly in which feeding arteries drain directly into veins through a nidus of abnormal channels, bypassing the normal capillary network. The absence of intervening capillaries exposes the draining veins to high arterial pressures and flow, causing vessel wall changes and predisposing to rupture. Diversion of blood through the low-resistance shunt can reduce perfusion of surrounding brain (vascular steal), while venous hypertension and gliosis contribute to seizures and focal deficits. Haemorrhage results from rupture of the fragile nidus, draining veins, or associated aneurysms. Prognosis depends on whether the malformation has bled, its size and location, and its venous drainage; haemorrhage carries significant morbidity and a risk of recurrent bleeding, whereas complete obliteration by surgery, radiosurgery, or embolisation can substantially reduce future haemorrhage risk.

arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy — AAION, giant cell arteritis optic neuropathy Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy Central retinal artery occlusion Posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy Optic neuritis Other systemic vasculitides affecting the eye Ocular ischaemic syndrome from carotid disease Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, ideally before starting steroids but never delaying treatment Full blood count for thrombocytosis and anaemia of chronic disease Temporal artery biopsy of an adequate length segment Colour Doppler ultrasonography of the temporal arteries seeking the halo sign Fluorescein angiography showing delayed or patchy choroidal filling Large-vessel imaging such as positron emission tomography or magnetic resonance angiography where extracranial involvement is suspected An ophthalmic emergency caused by giant cell (temporal) arteritis, occurring almost exclusively in patients over 50 and typically over 70. Visual loss is usually severe, frequently counting fingers or worse, and may be preceded by transient obscurations (amaurosis fugax). The swollen disc is characteristically chalky-white and pallid, in contrast to the hyperaemic oedema of the non-arteritic form. Systemic features include jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, new headache, polymyalgia rheumatica, malaise, weight loss and fever. Inflammatory markers are markedly raised, with high erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein and often a reactive thrombocytosis. High-dose systemic corticosteroids must be started immediately on clinical suspicion to protect the fellow eye, without waiting for biopsy. Temporal artery biopsy confirms the diagnosis but skip lesions occur, so a negative biopsy does not exclude the disease and treatment should not be delayed. A concurrent cilioretinal artery occlusion may accompany the optic nerve head infarction and is highly suggestive of an arteritic mechanism. Any systemic symptoms of giant cell arteritis in an older patient with visual loss Transient visual obscurations preceding fixed loss, signalling imminent infarction Symptoms in the fellow eye indicating impending bilateral blindness New diplopia or ocular motor palsy accompanying visual loss Assuming a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate excludes the disease, when C-reactive protein and platelets may still be raised Delaying corticosteroids to await biopsy and risking bilateral blindness Treating with an inadequate corticosteroid dose or tapering too quickly Missing occult giant cell arteritis presenting with visual loss and few or no systemic symptoms Giant cell arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large arteries with a predilection for branches of the external and internal carotid arteries, including the posterior ciliary arteries that supply the anterior optic nerve head. Inflammatory infiltration disrupts the internal elastic lamina, with giant cells and intimal hyperplasia narrowing and occluding the lumen. The resulting thrombotic occlusion produces infarction of the optic nerve head, and the widespread vascular involvement explains the high risk of rapid, bilateral, and often devastating visual loss. Visual loss in the affected eye is usually severe and permanent, with meaningful recovery rare. Prompt high-dose corticosteroid therapy is highly effective at preventing catastrophic fellow-eye involvement, which is the principal goal of treatment.

Mistaking acute hemarthrosis for septic arthritis (or vice versa) in hemophilia; failing to correct clotting factor before aspirating. These arthritides share the theme of an underlying systemic disorder injuring joints rather than a primary autoimmune synovitis. In acromegaly, excess growth hormone and IGF-I stimulate cartilage, periarticular connective tissue, and bone, producing hypertrophic then degenerating cartilage that is prone to fissuring, with ligamentous laxity worsening joint discomfort. In hemochromatosis, parenchymal iron deposition damages cartilage: iron catalyzes superoxide-dependent lipid peroxidation, interferes with collagen formation, increases lysosomal enzyme release from synovium, and inhibits synovial pyrophosphatase, favoring chondrocalcinosis. Hemophilic arthropathy results from repeated intraarticular bleeding; blood persists because intrinsic clotting factors and tissue thromboplastin are absent in the synovium, and recurrent hemarthrosis leads to chronic noninflammatory fibrotic joints. Sickle cell musculoskeletal disease stems from vasoocclusion and marrow/cortical bone infarction, splenic dysfunction predisposing to osteomyelitis and septic arthritis, and avascular necrosis (notably femoral head); marrow hyperplasia widens medullary cavities and thins cortices. In neuropathic joints, loss of deep pain/proprioception plus dysregulated autonomic blood flow leads to bone resorption, repeated microtrauma, ligament tears, and fractures with progressive disorganization. HOA pathogenesis centers on circulating cells/platelet particles and growth factors (PDGF, VEGF) bypassing pulmonary clearance and stimulating peripheral connective tissue and periosteal proliferation, with endothelial activation reflected by elevated von Willebrand factor antigen. Outcomes are determined largely by the underlying disorder. Acromegalic joint pain may persist even after the acromegaly is treated. In hemochromatosis, established arthritis and chondrocalcinosis often progress despite phlebotomy. Hemophilic hemarthrosis usually resolves with joint function returning to baseline over about two weeks, but recurrent bleeding causes chronic fibrotic, flexion-deformed, function-limiting arthropathy. Sickle cell dactylitis resolves without residual damage, but avascular necrosis (about 5% femoral head involvement) and osteomyelitis carry greater morbidity. Neuropathic joints can disorganize rapidly and are largely unaffected by treating the underlying disease; early recognition and offloading of a diabetic Charcot foot can prevent severe disease. In primary HOA, symptoms typically disappear on reaching adulthood. No single formal grading scheme; severity is judged by the staging of the underlying arthropathy. Hemophilic arthropathy progresses radiographically from capsular distention, to juxtaarticular osteopenia with marginal erosions and subchondral cysts, to late joint-space narrowing with osteoarthritis-like bony overgrowth. Neuropathic arthritis evolves from early osteoarthritis-like changes (joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes, effusions) to marked destructive/hypertrophic disorganization. HOA progresses from periostitis with a radiolucent zone between new periosteal bone and cortex to multilayered cortical thickening.

CSF; tissue, thrombus, or autopsy specimens in HPS) Metagenomic / high-throughput sequencing of CSF for arboviral encephalitis CSF analysis (typically modest WBC elevation, early PMN then monocyte predominance, usually normal glucose; lymphocyte counts in the thousands with low glucose in LCM) CBC for thrombocytopenia, leukopenia or leukocytosis with left shift, and circulating atypical lymphocytes/immunoblasts (HPS) Hematocrit/hemoconcentration, serum albumin, lactate, and arterial blood gas in suspected HPS Renal panel (creatinine, potassium), liver transaminases (AST/ALT), and urinalysis for proteinuria in VHF Chest radiography for interstitial then bilateral central alveolar edema with normal cardiac size in HPS Anti-NMDA receptor and other autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitides Metabolic encephalopathy (hyperammonemia, liver failure) Toxic/intoxication states Brain abscess and cerebrovascular events (stroke) Oncologic CNS disease Surgical abdomen / acute pyelonephritis (mimicking the febrile prodrome of HPS) Most arthropod-borne (arbovirus) and rodent-borne zoonotic viral infections in humans are subclinical or unrecognized; humans are usually accidental, dead-end hosts and are not important amplifiers of these viruses (Harrison 22e p.1664-1665). Recognized illness usually falls into one of five overlapping syndromic categories: fever and myalgia (F&M), arthritis and rash (A&R), encephalitis, pulmonary disease, and viral hemorrhagic fever (VHF); a single virus may cause several of these (Harrison 22e p.1664-1665). Fever and myalgia is by far the most common and most benign syndrome, with abrupt fever, chills, intense myalgia, malaise, anorexia, and headache with photophobia/retroorbital pain; true arthritis is absent and physical findings are minimal (Harrison 22e p.1665-1666). A history of tick bite has more diagnostic significance than a history of mosquito exposure; clinical and epidemiologic clues may allow presumptive diagnosis in epidemics, but laboratory confirmation is required in all cases (Harrison 22e p.1664). Arthropod vectors acquire arboviruses from viremic vertebrate blood meals; the virus must disseminate to the salivary glands (extrinsic incubation, typically 1-3 weeks in mosquitoes) before the vector can transmit; transovarial transmission to progeny is an alternative maintenance mechanism (Harrison 22e p.1664). Rodent-borne viruses are maintained by chronically infected rodents; humans are typically infected by inhalation of or contact with aerosolized rodent excreta/secreta, and most show a high degree of rodent-virus specificity (Harrison 22e p.1664). Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is acquired from the house mouse and classically causes a biphasic illness with a febrile phase followed by a CNS (meningeal) phase; patients with neuroinvasive LCM, including frank encephalitis, almost always recover fully, but the virus can cause fetal microcephaly and has been transmitted by organ transplantation (Harrison 22e p.1666-1667). Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) begins after a 2-3 week incubation with a nonspecific 3-4 day prodrome, then rapidly progresses to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and hypoxemic respiratory failure; coincident thrombocytopenia, circulating immunoblasts (atypical lymphocytes), and a left shift are considered almost diagnostic (Harrison 22e p.1673). In suspected HPS, aggressive IV fluid resuscitation is hazardous because of widespread capillary leak and depressed cardiac output; management is hemodynamic/respiratory support, with ECMO for the most critically ill (Harrison 22e p.1673). Lassa fever: most Lassa virus infections are subclinical or mild, onset is gradual (characteristic of mammarenavirus VHFs), and overt hemorrhage occurs in only about 15-30% of patients; about 30% of survivors develop sensorineural deafness (Harrison 22e p.1675-1676). Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is the most significant VHF today, with over 100,000 severe cases annually in Asia; major agents are Hantaan (Eastern Asia), Dobrava (the Balkans), and Puumala (Europe) (Harrison 22e p.1676). Arboviral CNS disease can leave residual deficits; spinal/motor-neuron (poliomyelitis-like) disease has been documented after West Nile virus and Japanese encephalitis virus infection, and difficulty concentrating, fatigability, tremor, and personality change are common during recovery (Harrison 22e p.1671). Altered mental status, seizures, focal neurologic signs, or coma indicating neuroinvasive disease New dry cough, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and early pulmonary edema heralding the HPS cardiopulmonary phase Hypotension, hemoconcentration, and marked thrombocytopenia with left shift Mucosal/overt hemorrhage, marked thrombocytopenia, and CNS dysfunction in suspected VHF CNS features, facial/neck edema, hypotension, hemorrhage, or jaundice in Lassa fever (markers of fatal outcome) Pregnancy, especially the last trimester, in Lassa fever (very high case fatality and ~90% fetal death) Oliguria and rising creatinine signaling acute kidney injury in HPS/VHF Marked confusion, tremor, and cerebellar signs in South American mammarenavirus hemorrhagic fevers Anchoring on the most severe known phenotype of a virus; many agents most commonly cause mild F&M rather than their eponymous severe disease (e.g., West Nile, Venezuelan equine encephalitis, Rift Valley fever). Treating the F&M syndrome as benign and self-limited without watching for evolution into A&R, neuroinvasive, pulmonary, or VHF syndromes for which it can be a prodrome. Using acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) in these febrile illnesses, given the risk of exacerbated bleeding and Reye syndrome. Giving aggressive IV fluids in HPS, which worsens noncardiogenic pulmonary edema because of capillary leak and depressed cardiac output. Relying on a negative CSF RT-PCR to exclude arboviral encephalitis; viruses generally cannot be isolated from blood or CSF and RT-PCR cannot rule out the diagnosis. Misreading the gradual onset of mammarenavirus VHF (Lassa, Argentinian/Bolivian) and expecting prominent early hemorrhage, which is often absent or late. Treating a single positive heterotypic IgG cross-reaction as diagnostic in HPS serology given very low background seroprevalence. Overlooking person-to-person/nosocomial transmission risk (Lassa virus, Andes virus, mammarenaviruses) and sexual transmission during early convalescence. These taxonomically diverse zoonotic RNA viruses (Togaviridae/Alphavirus; Flaviviridae/Orthoflavivirus; the bunyaviricete families Arenaviridae, Hantaviridae, Nairoviridae, Peribunyaviridae, Phenuiviridae; Orthomyxoviridae; Bornaviridae and Rhabdoviridae; and the reovirus families) circulate in nature between arthropod vectors (mosquitoes, ticks, sandflies, midges) or chronically infected rodents and vertebrate reservoirs. Arboviruses establish chronic systemic infection of the vector after a blood meal and reach the salivary glands during extrinsic incubation (1-3 weeks in mosquitoes); vertical transovarial transmission also maintains some viruses. In arboviral encephalitis, an initial lymphoid-origin viremia seeds multifocal CNS entry, presumably via olfactory neuroepithelium/cribriform plate or brain capillary endothelium; CNS injury results partly from direct neuronal infection and partly from edema, inflammation, and host immune response, with focal neuronal necrosis, glial nodules, and perivascular lymphoid cuffing. LCM meningitis is T-cell-mediated immunopathology. VHF agents share a core pathophysiology of disrupted vascular function, stability, and integrity producing multisystem organ dysfunction and capillary leak; in HPS, widespread pulmonary capillary leak with depressed cardiac output produces noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and shock. Outcome depends heavily on syndrome and specific virus. The F&M syndrome generally resolves completely within 2-5 days, though prolonged asthenia may follow LCMV or dengue infection. A&R illness resolves over days, but joint pain/arthritis may persist for months to years without deformity. Encephalitis ranges from full recovery (often slow, over weeks to months) to permanent deficits or death. HPS carries a case-fatality rate of approximately 30-40% even with appropriate care, though most patients surviving the first 48 hours of hospitalization recover without long-term sequelae. Argentinian and Bolivian hemorrhagic fevers can reach case-fatality rates over 50% in individual outbreaks. About 20% of Lassa virus infections become Lassa fever; survivors have roughly a 30% rate of (usually bilateral) sensorineural deafness, and pregnancy markedly worsens prognosis. No single unified severity scale; severity is framed by syndrome. The five-syndrome heuristic (F&M, arthritis and rash, encephalitis, pulmonary disease, viral hemorrhagic fever) stratifies expected severity, with F&M most benign and encephalitis/pulmonary/VHF most severe. Encephalitis severity grades clinically from asymptomatic through febrile headache and aseptic meningitis to full encephalitis with coma. HPS is staged by progression from nonspecific prodrome to the cardiopulmonary phase with respiratory failure and shock. Lassa fever severity/fatality is predicted by high viral load, high serum creatinine and AST, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, CNS features, face/neck swelling, hypotension, hemorrhage, jaundice, and pregnancy.

bronchial carcinoma Rapid clinical or radiological progression Unexplained weight loss in an asbestos-exposed worker Confusing pleural plaques with asbestosis and mislabelling exposure markers as the fibrosing disease Failing to emphasise smoking cessation given the multiplicative lung cancer risk Missing an evolving malignancy by attributing new symptoms to known fibrosis Overlooking the need for a documented occupational history for compensation Assuming a short exposure excludes disease when latency is prolonged Inhaled asbestos fibres that reach the distal airways and alveoli are incompletely cleared and provoke chronic macrophage-driven inflammation with release of reactive oxygen species and fibrogenic mediators. This leads to progressive deposition of collagen and diffuse interstitial fibrosis, initially in the lower zones, impairing gas exchange and lung compliance. The same persistent fibre burden and cellular injury underlie the associated malignant risks of mesothelioma and lung cancer. Asbestosis tends to progress slowly and is irreversible; the overall outlook is dominated by the substantially raised lifetime risk of lung cancer and mesothelioma, which are the leading causes of death in exposed individuals.

Ascariasis — Ascaris lumbricoides infection, roundworm infection, giant intestinal roundworm Other intestinal helminth infections (hookworm, Trichuris, Strongyloides) Non-parasitic causes of eosinophilic pneumonia Mechanical bowel obstruction of other cause Gallstone disease or other biliary obstruction Pancreatitis of other aetiology Asthma or allergic bronchopulmonary disease during the pulmonary phase Drug or allergic eosinophilic pneumonitis Functional abdominal pain in children Stool microscopy for Ascaris eggs Full blood count for eosinophilia, especially during larval migration Abdominal ultrasound or imaging to detect worms in bowel or biliary tree Chest imaging if eosinophilic pneumonitis is suspected Endoscopic evaluation for hepatobiliary or pancreatic complications The most common soil-transmitted helminth worldwide, acquired by ingesting embryonated eggs from faecally contaminated food, water or soil Most infections are light and asymptomatic; heavy worm loads, especially in children, cause malnutrition and growth impairment During larval lung migration patients may develop a transient eosinophilic pneumonitis (Loeffler syndrome) with cough, wheeze and pulmonary infiltrates Heavy intestinal burdens can cause bowel obstruction, particularly in children, and adult worms can migrate into the biliary or pancreatic ducts causing obstruction, cholangitis or pancreatitis It is highly prevalent in parts of India with inadequate sanitation and is targeted by school-based mass deworming programmes Diagnosis is usually by detecting characteristic eggs on stool microscopy; adult worms may be seen passed in stool or vomit or on imaging Antiparasitic (anthelmintic) therapy is highly effective for uncomplicated intestinal infection Biliary or obstructive complications may require endoscopic or surgical intervention in addition to anthelmintics Features of intestinal obstruction (distension, vomiting, absent stool/flatus), particularly in a child Biliary obstruction, cholangitis or pancreatitis from worm migration Respiratory distress during the pulmonary migratory phase Signs of peritonitis suggesting bowel perforation from a heavy worm bolus Overlooking ascariasis as a cause of paediatric bowel obstruction in endemic areas Missing biliary or pancreatic migration as the cause of acute abdominal pain Attributing migratory pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia to asthma alone Neglecting sanitation and re-treatment, allowing reinfection Ingested Ascaris eggs hatch in the small intestine; larvae penetrate the gut wall, travel via the portal circulation to the liver and then the lungs, break into the alveoli, ascend the tracheobronchial tree, are swallowed, and mature into large adult worms in the small intestine. The pulmonary phase provokes an eosinophilic hypersensitivity reaction. In the gut, large numbers of worms can form a bolus that obstructs the lumen, and individual worms may migrate into the biliary tree, pancreatic duct or appendix, producing obstructive and inflammatory complications. Chronic infection contributes to malabsorption and nutritional deficits. Uncomplicated infection has an excellent prognosis and responds promptly to anthelmintic treatment. Morbidity arises from heavy infections causing nutritional compromise in children and from obstructive complications, which can occasionally be life-threatening if not treated in time.

Asherman syndrome — intrauterine adhesions, intrauterine synechiae, uterine synechiae Hypothalamic or other endocrine amenorrhoea Cervical stenosis causing outflow obstruction Premature ovarian insufficiency Pregnancy Endometrial atrophy from other causes Congenital uterine anomaly Diagnostic hysteroscopy to visualise and grade adhesions Saline infusion sonohysterography Hysterosalpingography to assess cavity and tubal patency Transvaginal ultrasound assessing endometrial thickness and pattern Hormonal profile to exclude endocrine causes of amenorrhoea Pregnancy test in any woman with amenorrhoea Asherman syndrome is the formation of intrauterine adhesions that partially or completely obliterate the uterine cavity It classically follows uterine instrumentation, especially curettage after pregnancy loss or postpartum haemorrhage, and sometimes uterine infection or surgery Typical features are reduced or absent menstruation, cyclical pain from trapped blood, recurrent pregnancy loss, and subfertility The diagnosis should be considered in a woman with menstrual change or infertility after intrauterine procedures Hysteroscopy is the reference standard for diagnosis and allows direct visualisation and treatment of adhesions Saline infusion sonography and hysterosalpingography can demonstrate cavity defects and filling irregularities Treatment is hysteroscopic division of adhesions with measures to reduce reformation and encourage endometrial regeneration Outcomes depend on the severity of adhesions and the amount of healthy endometrium remaining Cyclical pelvic pain with amenorrhoea suggesting obstructed, trapped menstruation (haematometra) Recurrent pregnancy loss after uterine instrumentation Signs of abnormal placentation in a subsequent pregnancy New amenorrhoea after a recent postpartum or post-abortal procedure Overlooking the diagnosis in women with menstrual change or infertility after uterine procedures Attributing amenorrhoea solely to endocrine causes without imaging the cavity Aggressive or repeated curettage that worsens endometrial damage Failing to anticipate abnormal placentation in a later pregnancy Asherman syndrome arises when trauma to the basal layer of the endometrium, typically from curettage on a recently pregnant or infected uterus, triggers abnormal healing in which the denuded uterine walls adhere and fibrous adhesions bridge the cavity. Loss of functional endometrium and scarring reduce the responsive tissue available for cyclical growth and shedding, producing hypomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, and can obstruct outflow so that menstrual blood is trapped, causing cyclical pain. Distortion or obliteration of the cavity and impaired endometrial receptivity interfere with implantation and placentation, leading to subfertility, recurrent loss, and later abnormal placentation. Prognosis relates directly to adhesion severity and residual healthy endometrium. Mild adhesions often respond well to hysteroscopic treatment with restoration of menstruation and fertility, while severe, dense scarring with extensive endometrial loss carries a guarded reproductive outlook and a tendency to reform.

Asparagine synthetase deficiency — asparagine synthetase deficiency, ASNS deficiency, ASNSD, congenital microcephaly-severe encephalopathy Other genetic causes of congenital microcephaly with epileptic encephalopathy Serine biosynthesis defects (PHGDH and related) Hyperekplexia from glycine-receptor or transporter mutations Congenital infections causing microcephaly Neonatal-onset mitochondrial encephalopathies Other early epileptic encephalopathies (e.g. channelopathies) Plasma and CSF amino acids looking for low/low-normal asparagine and related changes Brain MRI for microcephaly, simplified gyration, and atrophy EEG to characterise the epileptic encephalopathy Molecular analysis of the ASNS gene (the definitive test) Metabolic screen to exclude other treatable encephalopathies Genetic counselling given autosomal recessive recurrence risk Caused by deficiency of asparagine synthetase (ASNS), which synthesises asparagine from aspartate and glutamine, making asparagine conditionally essential for the developing brain Presents with congenital or progressive microcephaly, severe developmental impairment, intractable seizures, and hyperekplexia-like exaggerated startle or spasticity Because the blood-brain barrier restricts asparagine entry, brain tissue depends on local synthesis, so the defect causes a functional cerebral asparagine deficiency The biochemical picture is subtle: plasma amino acids may be near-normal, and low or low-normal asparagine (sometimes with low glutamine or raised aspartate/glutamate) in plasma or CSF is a clue rather than a definitive marker Diagnosis usually rests on molecular confirmation of ASNS mutations rather than a striking metabolite abnormality There is no established effective therapy; dietary asparagine supplementation has uncertain benefit because brain uptake is limited, and care is largely supportive Inheritance is autosomal recessive with a severe, often early-fatal course British spelling and paediatric context apply Progressive microcephaly with refractory neonatal or infantile seizures Severe startle, spasticity, or encephalopathy from birth Rapid neurological deterioration and early mortality Recurrence risk in future pregnancies requiring counselling Expecting a marked plasma metabolite abnormality when the biochemical changes are subtle Missing the diagnosis without molecular testing Assuming dietary asparagine supplementation will correct the central deficiency Not offering genetic counselling for an autosomal recessive disorder Asparagine synthetase catalyses the ATP-dependent transfer of an amino group from glutamine to aspartate, forming asparagine and glutamate. Neurons depend on endogenous synthesis because asparagine crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly, so loss of enzyme activity produces a functional asparagine deficiency in the central nervous system, and possibly local accumulation of aspartate and glutamate that may be excitotoxic. The resulting disturbance of protein synthesis and amino acid homeostasis in the developing brain causes impaired neuronal proliferation and connectivity, manifesting as congenital microcephaly, severe encephalopathy, and refractory seizures. The peripheral biochemical changes are often mild, reflecting the primarily central nature of the deficiency. The prognosis is generally poor, with severe neurodevelopmental impairment, intractable epilepsy, and frequent death in infancy or early childhood. No disease-modifying therapy is established, and management is supportive.

Aspartylglucosaminuria — AGU, aspartylglucosaminidase deficiency, N-aspartyl-beta-glucosaminidase deficiency, glycosylasparaginase deficiency, AGA deficiency Other oligosaccharidoses such as alpha-mannosidosis and fucosidosis Mucopolysaccharidoses with coarse facies and slow cognitive decline Sanfilippo syndrome given the behavioural and cognitive course Non-syndromic intellectual disability Other lysosomal storage disorders with adult psychiatric presentations Sialidosis and galactosialidosis Leucocyte or fibroblast aspartylglucosaminidase enzyme assay Urinary oligosaccharide analysis detecting aspartylglucosamine AGA gene sequencing, including testing for the Finnish founder variant where relevant Brain MRI for white matter and atrophic changes Developmental and neuropsychological assessment to track decline Skeletal survey for mild dysostosis Caused by deficiency of aspartylglucosaminidase (glycosylasparaginase), which cleaves the linkage between the oligosaccharide and asparagine in glycoprotein degradation Notably enriched in the Finnish population as part of the Finnish disease heritage, though it occurs worldwide Follows a characteristic course: relatively normal early infancy, then slowly progressive intellectual decline through childhood into adulthood Coarse facies, connective tissue laxity, recurrent infections, and mild skeletal changes are typical, with behavioural problems emerging over time Adult patients often show a plateau followed by earlier-than-normal decline, sometimes with psychiatric features Urinary oligosaccharide screening detects aspartylglucosamine, the accumulated glycoasparagine Diagnosis is confirmed by deficient aspartylglucosaminidase activity and AGA gene testing Progressive intellectual decline after relatively normal early development Emerging psychiatric or behavioural disturbance in adolescence or adulthood Recurrent infections Accelerated deterioration in adulthood Attributing the slow cognitive decline to a static intellectual disability and missing the progressive storage disorder Screening only for glycosaminoglycans and missing the oligosaccharide pattern Overlooking the diagnosis outside the Finnish population where it also occurs Failing to consider it in adults presenting with new psychiatric symptoms and intellectual disability Aspartylglucosaminuria is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in AGA, encoding the lysosomal enzyme aspartylglucosaminidase (glycosylasparaginase). This enzyme hydrolyses the bond between N-acetylglucosamine and asparagine, a late step in the degradation of N-linked glycoproteins. Its deficiency causes accumulation of aspartylglucosamine and related glycoasparagines within lysosomes across many tissues, with excretion of aspartylglucosamine in the urine. Progressive storage in the central nervous system underlies the characteristically slow intellectual decline, while systemic accumulation contributes to the coarse features, connective tissue laxity, and skeletal changes. A single founder variant accounts for most Finnish cases. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The disorder is slowly progressive, with many patients reaching adulthood before a phase of more rapid cognitive decline; life expectancy is reduced but survival into middle adulthood is common. Management is supportive, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation has been explored in selected cases.

Aspergillosis — Aspergillus infection, invasive aspergillosis, ABPA Pulmonary tuberculosis (chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and aspergilloma classically mimic and follow TB) Nontuberculous mycobacterial infection Lung carcinoma (Aspergillus nodule may resemble early lung cancer) Bacterial sinusitis (early invasive Aspergillus sinusitis not radiologically distinguishable) Other angioinvasive molds, notably mucormycosis and Fusarium/Scedosporium (histologically can mimic Aspergillus) Mucormycosis (Mucorales) causing invasive pulmonary or sinus disease Fusariosis (Fusarium spp.) Scedosporiosis (Scedosporium/Pseudallescheria boydii) Pulmonary tuberculosis and nontuberculous mycobacterial disease Bacterial sinusitis or pneumonia Galactomannan antigen detection (respiratory sample more sensitive than serum; critical in ICU/ventilated patients) Novel protein antigen assay Serum beta-D-glucan Real-time PCR of respiratory samples and blood (and sputum PCR in chronic disease) Aspergillus IgG antibody (chronic forms) and Aspergillus-specific IgE plus total IgE (allergic forms) High-volume fungal culture on fungal media (also checks for azole resistance) Microscopy/cytology and histopathology of affected tissue (hyaline narrow septate hyphae branching at 45 degrees) Thoracic CT (halo sign, air-crescent, nodules, cavitation); MRI for cerebral and sinus disease Bronchoscopy with tracheobronchial lavage; positron emission tomography for chronic cavitary disease and nodules Lung carcinoma (Aspergillus nodule mimics early carcinoma) COVID-19 itself (nodules with halo signs are a feature of COVID-19; invasive aspergillosis requires supportive evidence) Atelectasis or nonspecific consolidation Granulomatosis with polyangiitis / other cavitary lung disease A. fumigatus causes most invasive aspergillosis, >95% of chronic aspergillosis, and most allergic syndromes; only species that grow at 37C cause invasive infection (Harrison 22e p.1713) The disease spectrum spans three categories: invasive (acute/subacute in the immunocompromised), chronic/saprophytic (chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis, aspergilloma/fungal ball), and allergic (ABPA, severe asthma with fungal sensitization, allergic fungal rhinosinusitis) (Harrison 22e p.1713, 1714) Invasive aspergillosis is one of the most common diagnostic errors revealed at autopsy; keys to early diagnosis are a high index of suspicion, circulating antigen screening (in leukemia), and urgent thoracic CT (Harrison 22e p.1714) On thoracic CT the halo sign (ground-glass hemorrhagic infarction around a nodule/consolidation) appears for ~7 days early in neutropenic patients and is a good prognostic feature reflecting early diagnosis; the air-crescent/cavitation appears later (Harrison 22e p.1716) Galactomannan antigen detection on respiratory samples (e.g., tracheobronchial/BAL fluid) is more sensitive than serum and is critical in ventilated/ICU patients where radiology is nonspecific; positive serum antigen usually precedes clinical or radiologic features by several days (Harrison 22e p.1714, 1716) Antigen, beta-D-glucan, and real-time PCR are faster and far more sensitive than culture, as only 10-30% of invasive aspergillosis cases yield a positive culture; antifungal therapy reduces antigen sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.1716) Aspergillus IgG antibody is detectable in ~90% of chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and ~65% of Aspergillus nodules; ABPA is diagnosed by Aspergillus-specific IgE (or positive skin-prick test) plus elevated total IgE, usually >1000 IU/mL (Harrison 22e p.1714, 1715) Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis follows pulmonary tuberculosis in ~6-13% of treated cases and is often initially mistaken for tuberculosis; >90% of chronic cavitary cases occur in patients with prior lung disease (Harrison 22e p.1713, 1715) On tissue histology Aspergillus hyphae are hyaline, narrow, and septate with branching at 45 degrees; angioinvasion with vascular invasion by hyphae is characteristic in neutropenia (Harrison 22e p.1716) HEPA filtration is often protective and should be installed and monitored in operating rooms, burn units, and areas housing high-risk patients; hospital outbreaks usually relate to a contaminated air source or construction (Harrison 22e p.1713) Life-threatening / massive hemoptysis (the most significant complication of chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and may be the presenting manifestation) Neurologic deterioration: mood change, focal signs, seizures, declining mental status suggesting cerebral aspergillosis (hemorrhagic infarction/abscess) Orbital apex syndrome (blindness and proptosis), facial swelling, cavernous sinus thrombosis or carotid occlusion in invasive/chronic sinusitis Fever progressing despite glucocorticoids in an immunocompromised host Acute keratitis threatening sight Requesting only bacterial culture rather than fungal culture may miss the diagnosis (bacterial agar is less sensitive); only 10-30% of invasive cases have a positive culture Fluconazole is commonly used for prophylaxis but has NO activity against Aspergillus species No prophylactic regimen is completely successful Antifungal therapy reduces the sensitivity of antigen detection Aspergillus IgG may not be positive on initial testing in subacute/nonneutropenic invasive disease A positive respiratory culture may represent only noninvasive disease or airway colonization, not invasion Contrast CT of the brain is often contraindicated by poor renal function and unenhanced CT is usually nonspecific; MRI is the most useful immediate investigation for cerebral disease Surgery is problematic in chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and often causes serious complications; bronchial artery embolization is preferred for problematic hemoptysis Aspergillus is a ubiquitous hyaline septate branching mold whose conidia (spores) are inhaled from indoor/outdoor air; only species growing at 37C cause invasive disease. Disease form depends on host immunity. Invasive disease arises with profound neutropenia, glucocorticoid use, phagocyte dysfunction (CGD, advanced HIV, relapsed leukemia) and underlying respiratory disease, with angioinvasion and hemorrhagic infarction; from the lungs (>80% of cases) it may disseminate hematogenously (most often to brain). Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis occurs in apparently immunocompetent hosts with prior lung disease and a suboptimal TH1-like inflammatory response. Allergic forms (ABPA, SAFS) reflect a TH2-like hypersensitivity response to A. fumigatus, classically complicating asthma and cystic fibrosis. Multiple gene variants underlie susceptibility to each form (Harrison 22e p.1713-1714). Invasive aspergillosis is curable if immune reconstitution occurs, whereas allergic and chronic forms are not curable. Mortality of invasive aspergillosis is 30-70% if treated but ~100% if the diagnosis is missed; cerebral aspergillosis, Aspergillus endocarditis, bilateral extensive invasive pulmonary disease, late-stage AIDS, relapsed uncontrolled leukemia, and liver failure carry very poor outcomes. Untreated chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis causes clinical deterioration in ~70%; with antifungal treatment mortality is 15-20% in the first year, ~40% over 5 years, and 50-60% over 10 years, with treatment failure in ~30% (more with azole resistance). ABPA/SAFS respond to glucocorticoids and antifungals (~60% to itraconazole, ~80% to voriconazole/posaconazole) but relapse after discontinuation is common (Harrison 22e p.1717). By disease category: INVASIVE (acute course <=1 month, subacute 1-3 months) - angioinvasive/nonangioinvasive/granulomatous pulmonary, invasive sinusitis, tracheobronchitis, disseminated, cerebral, endocarditis, cutaneous, keratitis/endophthalmitis. CHRONIC - chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis, chronic fibrosing pulmonary aspergillosis (destroyed lung), Aspergillus bronchitis, Aspergillus nodule, chronic invasive and chronic granulomatous sinusitis. SAPROPHYTIC - aspergilloma (single fungal ball), airway colonization, maxillary sinus fungal ball. ALLERGIC - ABPA, severe asthma with fungal sensitization (SAFS), allergic fungal rhinosinusitis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis (Harrison 22e p.1714-1715).

Aspiration pneumonitis — Mendelson's syndrome, perioperative pulmonary aspiration, acid aspiration syndrome Bronchospasm from asthma or anaphylaxis Pulmonary oedema (cardiogenic or negative-pressure) Pulmonary embolism Acute respiratory distress syndrome from other causes Airway obstruction or laryngospasm Bacterial aspiration pneumonia (later infective complication) Pulse oximetry and arterial blood gas to quantify hypoxaemia Chest radiograph or CT to identify infiltrates, often in dependent lung zones Bronchoscopy to clear particulate material when obstruction is suspected Sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage culture if secondary infection is suspected Serial observation for progression to acute respiratory distress syndrome Results from inhalation of gastric contents, most often during induction, emergence, or in patients with impaired airway protection Chemical injury from acidic gastric fluid produces a rapid inflammatory pneumonitis, which is distinct from later bacterial aspiration pneumonia Risk is highest with a full stomach, delayed gastric emptying, bowel obstruction, pregnancy, obesity, reflux, and emergency or difficult airway situations Signs include hypoxaemia, wheeze or bronchospasm, cough, tachypnoea, and diffuse crackles, sometimes with visible gastric material in the airway Immediate management is to position to limit further soiling, apply suction, secure the airway, and provide oxygen and supportive ventilation with lung-protective strategies Routine antibiotics and corticosteroids are not indicated for pure chemical pneumonitis; antibiotics are reserved for established infection or high-risk contamination Prevention centres on appropriate fasting, rapid-sequence induction with cricoid pressure in at-risk patients, and airway protection with a cuffed tube Aspiration prophylaxis with agents that reduce gastric volume and acidity may be considered in high-risk patients Witnessed massive aspiration with rapid desaturation and airway soiling Progressive hypoxaemia or rising oxygen requirement suggesting evolving acute respiratory distress syndrome Severe bronchospasm with difficult ventilation Haemodynamic instability or the need for escalating respiratory support Giving prophylactic antibiotics and steroids for uncomplicated chemical pneumonitis Underestimating aspiration risk and omitting rapid-sequence induction in at-risk patients Attributing hypoxaemia solely to aspiration and missing another cause Failing to protect the airway promptly and allowing continued soiling Assuming a normal early chest radiograph excludes significant aspiration Aspiration occurs when protective airway reflexes are obtunded, allowing gastric contents to enter the tracheobronchial tree. Acidic fluid causes rapid chemical burn of the alveolar-capillary membrane, triggering an inflammatory cascade with increased permeability, alveolar oedema, surfactant dysfunction, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch that produces hypoxaemia. Particulate matter can cause mechanical obstruction and atelectasis. The initial insult is sterile, but secondary bacterial infection may supervene, and severe injury can progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome. Severity depends on the volume, acidity, and particulate content of the aspirate. Mild chemical pneumonitis often resolves within days with supportive care, but large-volume acidic or particulate aspiration can cause severe respiratory failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and death.

Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease — AERD, Samter triad, NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease Allergic asthma with rhinitis Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps without NSAID sensitivity Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis IgE-mediated NSAID allergy or urticaria Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis Detailed history of respiratory reactions to aspirin or NSAIDs Assessment of asthma control and sinonasal disease including nasal endoscopy and imaging Supervised aspirin (or NSAID) challenge in a controlled setting when diagnosis is uncertain Eosinophil and, where relevant, leukotriene assessment Exclusion of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis A triad of asthma, recurrent nasal polyposis with chronic rhinosinusitis and respiratory reactions to aspirin and other non-selective NSAIDs Ingestion of aspirin or an NSAID provokes upper and lower airway reactions such as rhinorrhoea, nasal congestion, bronchospasm and sometimes flushing The asthma and nasal polyps are typically severe and the polyps recur rapidly after surgery It usually develops in adulthood and is not a classic IgE-mediated allergy Diagnosis may be confirmed by a supervised aspirin challenge where the history is unclear Management includes standard asthma and polyp treatment, avoidance of NSAIDs, and aspirin desensitisation in selected patients Severe bronchospasm after NSAID exposure Features suggesting eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (neuropathy, vasculitic rash) Poorly controlled asthma with frequent exacerbations Rapidly recurrent obstructive nasal polyposis Not warning patients to avoid non-selective NSAIDs Attempting aspirin challenge or desensitisation without appropriate supervision Missing eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis as a mimic Undertreating the underlying asthma and rhinosinusitis Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease is driven by dysregulation of arachidonic acid metabolism. Inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase-1 by aspirin and non-selective NSAIDs reduces protective prostaglandin E2 and shifts metabolism toward overproduction of cysteinyl leukotrienes, which are already elevated at baseline. The resulting eosinophilic inflammation of the upper and lower airways produces severe asthma and nasal polyposis, and NSAID exposure precipitates acute reactions by unmasking this leukotriene excess rather than through an IgE mechanism. The disease is chronic, but with NSAID avoidance, modern asthma and polyp therapies and aspirin desensitisation in appropriate patients, control is often substantially improved.

asplenia syndrome — right atrial isomerism, Ivemark syndrome, bilateral right-sidedness polysplenia syndrome (left isomerism) situs inversus totalis situs solitus with complex cyanotic congenital heart disease surgical or post-traumatic asplenia functional hyposplenism from other causes isolated total anomalous pulmonary venous connection heterotaxy without definite isomerism pattern urgent segmental echocardiography including pulmonary venous drainage assessment abdominal ultrasound confirming absent spleen and midline liver peripheral blood film for Howell-Jolly and Heinz bodies chest imaging for bronchial morphology and pulmonary lobation cardiac CT or MRI angiography for systemic and pulmonary venous mapping twelve-lead ECG documenting atrial rhythm and axis genetic evaluation for laterality and ciliopathy genes in selected cases Asplenia syndrome is the visceral marker of right atrial isomerism (bilateral right-sidedness), characterised by congenital absence of the spleen and duplicated right-sided morphology. Both lungs are trilobed with eparterial bronchi and both atrial appendages are of morphologically right type, features more reliable for classification than the absent spleen itself. Cardiac disease is typically severe and cyanotic, with common atrioventricular canal, single ventricle physiology, pulmonary stenosis or atresia, and total anomalous pulmonary venous connection. Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection, often obstructed, is a defining and life-threatening association demanding urgent recognition in the cyanotic neonate. Absence of the spleen produces lifelong susceptibility to overwhelming encapsulated-organism sepsis, so prophylactic antibiotics and full vaccination are mandatory. Howell-Jolly bodies and Heinz bodies on the blood film confirm the functional consequences of asplenia. A symmetrical midline liver and intestinal malrotation are usual, the latter risking midgut volvulus. Bilateral superior venae cavae and other systemic venous anomalies are common and complicate surgical and catheter approaches. profound neonatal cyanosis, especially with obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous connection fever or rapid clinical deterioration signalling overwhelming post-splenectomy-type sepsis bilious vomiting or abdominal distension from midgut volvulus duct-dependent circulation requiring urgent prostaglandin and intervention shock or acidosis in an infant with known right isomerism Failing to search for obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous connection in the cyanotic neonate. Not recognising the absent spleen and omitting antibiotic prophylaxis and vaccination. Classifying by spleen status alone rather than bronchial and atrial appendage morphology. Overlooking intestinal malrotation until volvulus occurs. Underestimating systemic venous anomalies during surgical or catheter planning. Asplenia syndrome results from a laterality defect in which the embryo fails to establish left-sided identity and instead duplicates right-sided morphology bilaterally. Failure of nodal cilia-generated leftward flow and of the downstream Nodal-Lefty-Pitx2 signalling cascade abolishes the normal asymmetry, so paired organs adopt right-sided features on both sides: the lungs become trilobed with eparterial bronchi and both atria carry morphologically right appendages. The spleen, a structure of left-sided embryonic origin, fails to develop, leaving the child functionally and anatomically asplenic and highly vulnerable to encapsulated bacteria. The same disturbance produces a midline symmetrical liver, anomalous systemic and pulmonary venous connections, and the severe conotruncal and atrioventricular septal malformations that dominate the clinical picture. Intestinal rotation, which depends on normal left-right cues, is likewise disordered. Asplenia syndrome carries the poorest prognosis among the heterotaxy variants because of severe cyanotic cardiac lesions, frequent obstructed anomalous pulmonary venous drainage, and the constant threat of fulminant sepsis. Survival has improved with early surgical palliation and rigorous infection prophylaxis, but morbidity and mortality remain high and many follow a single-ventricle pathway.

Asteroid hyalosis — asteroid bodies, Benson bodies, asteroid hyalitis Synchysis scintillans (cholesterol crystals within a liquefied vitreous that sediment inferiorly) Vitreous haemorrhage or organised old blood Vitritis or inflammatory cells from uveitis or endophthalmitis Vitreous amyloidosis Vitreous infiltration by intraocular lymphoma Physiological floaters from vitreous syneresis and posterior vitreous detachment Dilated slit-lamp biomicroscopy and indirect fundoscopy to characterise the opacities and their movement B-scan ultrasonography showing multiple highly reflective mobile echoes that settle when eye movement stops OCT of the macula to assess for coexisting maculopathy where the direct view is limited Fundus photography to document the appearance and monitor over time Screening for diabetes mellitus where clinically appropriate given the reported association Careful peripheral retinal examination to exclude coexisting pathology obscured by the opacities Composed of calcium-containing phospholipid (calcium soap) spherules that are bound to and suspended within the vitreous collagen framework, so they swing with eye movement and recoil to their original position rather than settling Usually unilateral and asymptomatic, most often discovered incidentally on fundoscopy or when the opacities obscure the examiner's view of the retina Appears as numerous small, yellow-white, highly refractile spheres distributed throughout an otherwise formed vitreous gel Key distinction from synchysis scintillans is that the vitreous is not liquefied and the particles do not sediment inferiorly with gravity when the eye is still Associations with increasing age and diabetes mellitus have been reported but are inconsistent; it is generally regarded as a benign age-related change Vision is characteristically preserved despite a dramatic fundus appearance because light passes between the particles; genuine symptomatic visual disturbance is rare Can significantly hinder retinal examination and imaging and may mask underlying maculopathy or diabetic retinopathy, so B-scan or OCT is sometimes needed Vitrectomy is only rarely indicated, reserved for troublesome symptoms or to allow visualisation and treatment of coexisting sight-threatening retinal disease New floaters or flashes suggesting posterior vitreous detachment or a retinal break rather than stable asteroid bodies Sudden reduction in vision indicating a separate pathology such as haemorrhage or maculopathy Signs of intraocular inflammation pointing to an alternative cause of vitreous opacity Inability to view the retina, potentially masking sight-threatening disease such as proliferative diabetic retinopathy Mistaking the striking appearance for serious vitreous pathology and over-investigating a benign finding Confusing it with synchysis scintillans, which sediments inferiorly and reflects a diseased, liquefied vitreous Attributing visual symptoms to asteroid hyalosis without excluding maculopathy or other retinal disease behind the opacities Assuming the retina is normal when dense opacities have prevented an adequate examination Asteroid bodies are aggregates of calcium and phospholipid, with a hydroxyapatite-like calcium soap composition, that form within and adhere to the collagen fibrils of the vitreous. Because the spherules are bound to an intact gel framework, the vitreous remains formed and the bodies oscillate with ocular movement and return to position, rather than sedimenting. The precise trigger is unknown; proposed contributors include local disturbance of calcium and phospholipid metabolism together with age-related vitreous change. This contrasts with synchysis scintillans, in which crystals move freely within a liquefied, previously diseased vitreous. Visual function is typically spared because incident light is transmitted through the gaps between particles. Asteroid hyalosis is a benign, usually stable condition that rarely affects vision, and the great majority of patients require no intervention. The main clinical significance is its potential to obscure examination of underlying retinal disease.

mechanism noted elsewhere in text) An exacerbation is an episode of acute bronchospasm that may be severe enough to require emergency care or hospitalization and can be fatal (p.2216). During an acute attack patients typically show tachypnea, tachycardia and accessory-muscle use, with wheezing and a prolonged expiratory phase (p.2222). As airway obstruction worsens the chest may become 'silent' with loss of breath sounds, indicating a more dangerous attack rather than improvement (p.2222). Most patients in an attack are hypocapnic from a high respiratory rate; a normal or near-normal PaCO2 in a distressed asthmatic signals impending respiratory failure (p.2227). PEFR, FEV1 and FEV1/FVC are reduced in obstruction, but these may appear normal during an attack or after recent bronchodilator use, so a normal value does not exclude severe disease (p.2222-2223). In urgent care, PEFR/FEV1 should be measured; patients with PEFR >60% predicted often respond to beta2-agonists alone, whereas failure to reach >60% or persistent severe tachypnea over 4-6 h should prompt hospital admission (p.2227). Severe exacerbations requiring systemic corticosteroids may themselves accelerate long-term lung-function decline (p.2221). More than one-third of patients carrying a physician diagnosis of asthma do not actually meet diagnostic criteria, so consider mimics when an 'asthmatic' fails to respond (p.2222). Some patients cannot distinguish an anxiety attack from an asthma attack, which can confound assessment of an apparent exacerbation (p.2222). Being reassured by a normal/normalizing PaCO2 - in a distressed asthmatic this is an ominous sign of impending respiratory failure, not stability (p.2227). Relying on PFT/PEF values that may look normal during an attack or shortly after bronchodilator use (p.2222-2223). Overlooking mimics such as vocal-cord dysfunction, heart failure or COPD in 'difficult' or treatment-refractory presentations - over one-third of diagnosed asthmatics do not meet criteria (p.2222). Missing precipitants such as beta-blockers (including ophthalmic drops), aspirin/NSAIDs in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, or ACE-inhibitor cough (p.2221). Giving antibiotics routinely in an exacerbation - they should be used only if there are signs of infection (p.2227). Asthma is characterized by episodic, usually reversible airway obstruction with airway hyperresponsiveness, generally accompanied by airway inflammation (most often eosinophilic, sometimes neutrophilic, occasionally with no obvious inflammation). Exacerbations are episodes of acute bronchospasm driven by luminal narrowing from airway smooth-muscle constriction, airway edema and mucus secretion, superimposed on chronic airway inflammation. Triggers activate mast cells/basophils and inflammatory cells (releasing bronchoconstrictors and mediators) and stimulate sensory nerves acting on smooth muscle. Allergen exposure can cause an immediate (early) bronchospasm and a late response 2-24 h later with airway narrowing and inflammation. Structural airway-wall thickening (smooth-muscle hypertrophy/hyperplasia, subepithelial collagen deposition, edema, mucosal inflammation) increases the tendency to narrow disproportionately. In severe airflow obstruction there may be air trapping with dynamically elevated FRC and increased residual volume; mild hypoxemia from ventilation-perfusion mismatch (oxygen-responsive) is common (p.2216-2217, p.2221, p.2222-2223). Asthma causes significant morbidity and mortality; roughly 3000-4000 people die from asthma each year in the United States. Death can occur even in mild asthma (at lower rates than severe asthma). Mortality in patients over 65 is about five times that of younger cohorts. High-risk features for asthma death include prior ICU admission or intubation for asthma, illicit drug use, depression, a new diagnosis within the past year, two or more emergency visits in the past 6 months, severe psychosocial problems, lower socioeconomic status, and being on daily prednisone before admission. Severe exacerbations may accelerate long-term lung-function decline (p.2221, p.2227). Harrison stratifies acute deteriorations practically rather than by a fixed table. Mild-to-moderate deteriorations can initially be managed with frequent beta2-agonists; failure to control with hourly beta2-agonists for several hours warrants urgent care. In urgent/ED care, PEFR or FEV1 guides severity: PEFR >60% predicted usually responds to beta2-agonists alone, whereas failure to reach PEFR >60% or persistent severe tachypnea over 4-6 h indicates a severe attack needing admission. Life-threatening / near-fatal features include silent chest, respiratory exhaustion, and a normal or rising PaCO2 signaling impending respiratory failure; status asthmaticus denotes a severe refractory attack with high airway resistance making ventilation difficult (p.2227).

Ataxia-telangiectasia is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the ATM gene, which encodes a kinase that senses DNA double-strand breaks and coordinates the cellular response, including cell-cycle arrest, DNA repair, and apoptosis. Loss of ATM function leaves cells unable to respond properly to DNA damage, causing genomic instability, heightened sensitivity to ionising radiation, and a strong predisposition to malignancy. Progressive death of cerebellar Purkinje and granule cells produces the characteristic neurodegeneration and ataxia, while impaired lymphocyte development and class-switching cause the combined immunodeficiency. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The condition is progressive, with most affected individuals becoming wheelchair-dependent by adolescence and life expectancy reduced, chiefly due to malignancy and chronic respiratory disease.

anti-Ri opsoclonus-myoclonus with breast/lung cancer and neuroblastoma) Anti-GAD65 antibody-associated progressive ataxia without underlying cancer Gluten/antigliadin antibody-associated ataxia (HLA DQB1*0201, may have villus atrophy on small-bowel biopsy) Hyponatremia-associated ataxia Vitamin E deficiency states (abetalipoproteinemia/Bassen-Kornzweig and ataxia with vitamin E deficiency) The core ataxic syndrome is gait impairment, scanning (unclear) speech, blurred vision from nystagmus, limb incoordination, and tremor on movement, reflecting disease of the cerebellum and its afferent/efferent pathways including the spinocerebellar and frontopontocerebellar tracts (p.3533). True cerebellar ataxia is an unsteady, imbalanced gait without vertigo, light-headedness, or sense of movement; vestibular/labyrinthine disorders by contrast produce gait disturbance accompanied by prominent dizziness (p.3533). Sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia can mimic cerebellar imbalance but is distinguished because instability worsens markedly when visual input is removed (positive Romberg sign); rarely proximal leg weakness also mimics cerebellar disease (p.3533). The tempo and pattern of onset guide etiology: gradual, bilateral, symmetric progression points to genetic, metabolic, immune, or toxic causes, whereas focal unilateral signs with headache and depressed consciousness, ipsilateral cranial nerve palsies, and contralateral weakness suggest a space-occupying cerebellar lesion (p.3533). Acute, reversible symmetric ataxias commonly follow intoxication with alcohol, phenytoin, lithium, or barbiturates and exposures such as toluene, gasoline/glue sniffing, methyl mercury, or bismuth (p.3533-3534). Subacute symmetric ataxia raises suspicion of alcoholic-nutritional vermal degeneration (thiamine/B12 deficiency), paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, immune-mediated ataxia, or a prion disorder (p.3533-3534). Friedreich's ataxia is the most common inherited ataxia, accounting for about half of all hereditary ataxias, and is autosomal recessive (p.3536). Friedreich's ataxia features onset before age 25 with progressive staggering gait, areflexia, extensor plantar responses, loss of vibratory/proprioceptive sensation, and frequently pes cavus and scoliosis (p.3536). Among the dominant ataxias, the polyglutamine SCAs (SCA1, SCA2, SCA3/Machado-Joseph, SCA6, SCA7, SCA17) arise from expanded CAG triplet repeats; genotype, not phenotype, is the diagnostic gold standard because clinical pictures overlap (p.3534). Retinal pigmentary degeneration (blue-yellow color blindness progressing to macular degeneration and visual loss) is the distinguishing feature of SCA7 among the spinocerebellar ataxias (p.3535-3536). Episodic ataxia type 1 causes brief (minutes-long) attacks of ataxia with myokymia and nystagmus, while type 2 produces longer attacks lasting hours to days; type 2 stems from CACNA1A mutations (the same calcium-channel gene as SCA6 and familial hemiplegic migraine) (p.3536). A treatable mimic to always exclude in chronic symmetric gait ataxia is hypothyroidism; infectious causes to consider include meningovascular syphilis/tabes dorsalis and Lyme disease (p.3534). Acute focal ataxia with headache, depressed consciousness, and ipsilateral pontine/cranial nerve signs suggesting cerebellar infarction or hemorrhage with brainstem compression Rapidly worsening focal cerebellar signs raising concern for posterior fossa hematoma, abscess, or tumor at risk of rostral (tentorial) or downward (foramen magnum/tonsillar) herniation, which can be devastating and may require emergent surgical decompression Subacute progressive ataxia as the presenting feature of an occult malignancy (paraneoplastic syndrome) Cardiac symptoms in Friedreich's ataxia (cardiomegaly, hypertrophy, conduction defects), since cardiac involvement occurs in about 90% of patients Recurrent pulmonary infections and lymphoreticular malignancy risk in ataxia-telangiectasia Mislabeling vestibular or sensory (proprioceptive) imbalance as cerebellar ataxia; absence of vertigo and a positive Romberg sign help distinguish them. Overlooking readily treatable and reversible causes such as hypothyroidism, vitamin E/B1/B12 deficiency, and intoxications. Relying on clinical phenotype alone to classify inherited ataxias, since SCA phenotypes overlap and genotype is the diagnostic gold standard. In Machado-Joseph disease type I, the stiff broad-based lurching gait results from spasticity rather than true ataxia and lacks truncal titubation, which can be misread. Failing to recognize an acute focal cerebellar lesion as a neurosurgical emergency because of herniation risk. Forgetting that some SCAs have prominent non-cerebellar features (e.g., retinal degeneration in SCA7, parkinsonism/extrapyramidal signs in SCA1/SCA2, peripheral neuropathy in MJD type III). Ataxia results from dysfunction of the cerebellum and the pathways connecting it to the rest of the nervous system, including the spinocerebellar tracts and the frontopontocerebellar pathway arising in the rostral frontal lobe. In the inherited polyglutamine spinocerebellar ataxias, expanded CAG triplet repeats produce mutant ataxin proteins with abnormally long polyglutamine tracts (generally toxic beyond ~40 glutamines); these proteins misfold into beta-pleated aggregates, are abnormally transported into the nucleus, bind and impair other polyglutamine proteins such as TATA-binding protein and CREB-binding protein, disrupt the ubiquitin-proteasome protein-turnover system, and trigger neuronal apoptosis, yielding a relatively disease-specific pattern of neuronal loss and gliosis. Longer repeats correlate with earlier onset and more aggressive disease across generations (anticipation). In Friedreich's ataxia, an expanded GAA repeat in the first intron of the frataxin gene silences frataxin expression; frataxin is a mitochondrial protein involved in iron homeostasis, so its loss causes mitochondrial iron accumulation, deficiency of iron-sulfur cluster enzymes, reduced ATP production, oxidative injury, and irreversible cell death, with predominant degeneration of the spinal cord (spinocerebellar tracts, lateral corticospinal tracts, posterior columns), dorsal root ganglia, and peripheral nerves. Prognosis depends on cause: several acquired ataxias (intoxications, postinfectious ataxia, hypothyroidism, vitamin deficiencies) are reversible, whereas the inherited degenerative ataxias progress relentlessly. In Machado-Joseph disease (SCA3) deficits invariably progress to death from debilitation within about 15 years of onset (especially types I and II), with intellect usually preserved. Friedreich's ataxia has a median age of death around 35 years, and women have a significantly better prognosis than men. Larger triplet-repeat expansions correlate with earlier onset and more aggressive disease, and anticipation produces earlier, more severe disease in successive generations. No single formal severity score is given; etiologic and temporal frameworks are used instead. Cerebellar ataxia is categorized as symmetric/progressive versus focal/ipsilateral, each subdivided by tempo into acute (hours to days), subacute (days to weeks), or chronic (months to years) per Table 450-1. Inherited ataxias are classified genomically by mode of inheritance: autosomal dominant (SCAs, DRPLA, episodic ataxias), autosomal recessive (Friedreich's ataxia, ataxia-telangiectasia, RFC1-related CANVAS), and mitochondrial. Machado-Joseph disease is further graded into clinical types I (ALS-parkinsonism-dystonia), II (ataxic, most common), and III (ataxic-amyotrophic).

produced by a small deep infarct, usually from small-vessel occlusion in the setting of hypertension and diabetes. The lesion, most often in the basis pontis or the posterior limb of the internal capsule and corona radiata, simultaneously interrupts descending corticospinal fibres, causing ipsilateral limb weakness, and corticopontocerebellar or cerebellar outflow fibres, causing ipsilateral incoordination. Because a single strategically placed lacune disrupts both motor and cerebellar-relay pathways, the patient shows weakness combined with ataxia disproportionate to that weakness, without sensory, visual, or cortical involvement. Recovery is often good for a single lacune, with improvement in both weakness and coordination over weeks, though recurrent small-vessel events can cause cumulative gait and cognitive decline.

HOXA1 is a homeobox transcription factor required for correct segmentation and patterning of the embryonic hindbrain into rhombomeres. Deficient HOXA1 activity disrupts the development of brainstem structures that give rise to ocular motor and other cranial nerve pathways, the inner ear, and the neural circuits controlling respiration, alongside the vascular and cardiac derivatives of the region. This shared developmental disturbance produces the combination of horizontal gaze abnormality, deafness, central hypoventilation, and cardiovascular anomalies, distinguishing it from the related Bosley-Salih-Alorainy phenotype partly by population origin and the relative prominence of brainstem dysfunction. The prognosis is chiefly determined by the severity of central hypoventilation and any associated cardiovascular anomaly, which can be life-threatening in infancy; hearing loss and ocular motility limitation are stable and manageable, and with respiratory support and multidisciplinary care survival into later childhood and beyond is possible, though developmental outcome varies.

itch is the cardinal symptom and often precedes visible changes Distribution shifts with age: face and extensor surfaces in infants, flexural creases (antecubital and popliteal fossae) in older children and adults Look for supporting features such as dry skin (xerosis), keratosis pilaris, and a personal or family history of atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis) The disease reflects impaired skin barrier plus immune dysregulation, so consistent emollient use is the foundation of every management plan Flares are treated with topical corticosteroids of potency matched to site and severity, or with topical calcineurin inhibitors on delicate areas Sudden worsening with weeping, crusting, or painful clustered vesicles suggests bacterial superinfection or eczema herpeticum, which needs prompt antiviral treatment Identify and reduce trigger exposure (soaps, heat, sweat, aeroallergens, stress) and consider phototherapy or systemic immunomodulators for severe refractory disease Eczema herpeticum: rapidly spreading painful monomorphic vesicles or punched-out erosions with systemic upset Extensive secondary bacterial infection or signs of sepsis Erythroderma with widespread inflammation and impaired thermoregulation Failure to thrive or recurrent severe infection suggesting underlying immunodeficiency Under-treating flares with insufficiently potent topical steroids while over-worrying about steroid side effects Neglecting regular generous emollient use, the cornerstone of maintenance Missing eczema herpeticum and treating it as a routine bacterial flare Attributing all disease to food allergy and pursuing unnecessary elimination diets Atopic dermatitis arises from the interplay of a defective epidermal barrier and a skewed type-2 immune response. Loss-of-function variants in the filaggrin gene and reduced barrier lipids increase transepidermal water loss and allow penetration of allergens and microbes. This drives activation of type-2 cytokines (including interleukins 4, 13, and 31) that promote inflammation, further barrier breakdown, and the sensation of itch. Scratching perpetuates an itch-scratch cycle, causing lichenification, and the barrier defect predisposes to colonisation and infection with Staphylococcus aureus and herpes simplex virus. Many children improve substantially or clear by adolescence, but a proportion have persistent or adult-onset disease; a relapsing course is typical and long-term control depends on barrier maintenance and trigger avoidance.

atopic eruption of pregnancy — AEP, eczema in pregnancy, atopic dermatitis of pregnancy polymorphic eruption of pregnancy pemphigoid gestationis intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy prurigo of pregnancy (now within this spectrum) allergic or irritant contact dermatitis scabies drug eruption serum bile acids and liver function tests to exclude intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy total and specific serum IgE (often elevated) direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin (negative, to exclude pemphigoid gestationis) skin biopsy in atypical cases (spongiotic dermatitis or non-specific changes) skin swabs if secondary bacterial or eczema herpeticum infection is suspected skin scrapings for scabies when clinically indicated It is the commonest specific dermatosis of pregnancy, accounting for around half of cases. An umbrella term encompassing eczematous (E-type) and papular (P-type) presentations, and it subsumes the older labels prurigo of pregnancy and pruritic folliculitis of pregnancy. Characteristically has an early onset, with the majority of cases starting before the third trimester. Most women have no prior eczema; many experience their first atopic flare during pregnancy, though a personal or family history of atopy is common. E-type disease shows widespread eczematous change favouring flexures, face, neck and hands; P-type shows disseminated small papules or prurigo-like nodules. Diagnosis is clinical with negative direct immunofluorescence; total serum IgE is elevated in a substantial proportion. It carries no maternal or fetal risk but tends to recur in future pregnancies. Managed with emollients, topical corticosteroids, antihistamines and, in resistant cases, narrowband ultraviolet B or short-course systemic corticosteroid. generalised pruritus without primary lesions plus raised bile acids indicating intrahepatic cholestasis with fetal risk tense blisters or periumbilical involvement suggesting pemphigoid gestationis rapidly worsening painful monomorphic vesicles or punched-out erosions suggesting eczema herpeticum spreading erythema, weeping and crusting indicating secondary bacterial infection systemic symptoms or mucosal involvement suggesting an alternative severe drug or infective reaction Failing to check bile acids and missing intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy in a woman presenting with itch. Missing eczema herpeticum in an atopic flare, a dermatological emergency requiring prompt antiviral therapy. Withholding topical corticosteroids through unfounded fear of harm and leaving disease undertreated. Mistaking widespread eczematous AEP for a drug eruption and stopping essential medication unnecessarily. Not recognising that prurigo and pruritic folliculitis of pregnancy fall within this spectrum, causing diagnostic confusion. Atopic eruption of pregnancy reflects a flare of atopic dermatitis-type disease driven by the physiological immunological changes of pregnancy. Gestation promotes a shift from T-helper-1 towards T-helper-2 cytokine predominance with reduced production of interferon-gamma and interleukin-2 and increased interleukin-4 and interleukin-10, an environment that favours the atopic phenotype and skin barrier-related pruritus. In a predisposed woman this unmasks or exacerbates eczematous and papular skin changes. The condition is not autoimmune and has no basement membrane zone antibody, distinguishing it from pemphigoid gestationis, and there is no hepatobiliary disturbance as seen in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Benign for mother and fetus with a good response to topical treatment, though flares may persist through pregnancy and settle after delivery. Recurrence in subsequent pregnancies is common owing to the underlying atopic predisposition.

carrier females are usually unaffected owing to skewed X-inactivation The blood picture may be subtle, so HbH inclusions can be missed unless specifically sought Feeding failure, aspiration or faltering growth in infancy Ambiguous genitalia requiring urgent evaluation Severe constipation or gastrointestinal complications Seizures or significant neurological deterioration Missing the diagnosis because HbH inclusions are absent or not specifically sought Attributing genital anomalies to an isolated disorder of sex development Overlooking the diagnosis in a male with intellectual disability and hypotonic facies Assuming carrier females will be affected ATRX encodes a chromatin-remodelling ATPase of the helicase family that, in partnership with the histone chaperone DAXX, deposits the histone variant H3.3 at heterochromatic regions such as telomeres and, importantly, regulates expression of the alpha-globin gene cluster. Loss-of-function variants impair this chromatin regulation, reducing alpha-globin transcription (producing mild alpha-thalassaemia with HbH inclusions) and disrupting gene expression required for normal brain, genital and skeletal development. Because the gene is on the X chromosome, males are affected while carrier females are protected by skewed X-inactivation. The combined chromatin and globin dysregulation explains the coexistence of intellectual disability and a haematological abnormality. ATR-X syndrome causes lifelong severe intellectual disability with limited speech and independence; the alpha-thalassaemia is usually mild and rarely a major clinical problem. Care is supportive, addressing feeding, gastrointestinal, genital and developmental needs.
