damage is advanced Transferrin is the plasma glycoprotein that binds iron and delivers it to cells, especially erythroid precursors, via the transferrin receptor. In congenital atransferrinaemia the near-absence of transferrin means dietary and recycled iron cannot be transported to the bone marrow, so haemoglobin synthesis is impaired and a microcytic anaemia develops even though total body iron is high. The excess iron, unable to be handled by the normal transferrin pathway, is absorbed avidly from the gut and deposited as haemosiderin in parenchymal organs, producing progressive hepatic, cardiac and endocrine iron toxicity that resembles other iron-overload states. Early recognition with transferrin or plasma replacement to support haematopoiesis and control of iron overload can markedly improve outcome; untreated disease progresses to organ damage from iron deposition, particularly cardiac and hepatic, which determines long-term prognosis.

Atrial fibrillation / arrhythmia — 12-lead ECG Electrolytes, TSH Echocardiogram Rate/rhythm control; anticoagulation per CHA₂DS₂-VASc Multifocal atrial tachycardia (>=3 distinct P-wave morphologies with clear isoelectric intervals and a slower atrial rate than AF; typically in chronic pulmonary disease and acute illness) (p.1989). Other supraventricular tachycardias including atrial flutter, focal atrial tachycardia, AV nodal reentry, and AV reciprocating tachycardia, distinguished by 12-lead ECG appearance and response to AV nodal blockade (p.1976-1977). Preexcited (accessory-pathway) AF, presenting as an irregular wide-complex tachycardia with bizarre, beat-to-beat-variable QRS morphology (p.1985-1986). Transesophageal echocardiography to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus before cardioversion when AF duration is >48 h or unknown (p.1992). Cardiac CT angiography with delayed-acquisition imaging as an alternative to TEE for left atrial appendage thrombus detection, with high sensitivity and specificity (p.1992). Ambulatory ECG monitoring, implantable loop recorders, or wearable/home ECG devices to capture intermittent or subclinical episodes (p.1991, 1993). AF is the most common sustained arrhythmia; prevalence rises steeply with age (~20% of those over 80), and the lifetime risk for a 40-year-old man is roughly one in four (p.1990). On the ECG, AF shows absence of organized atrial activity (no P waves) with an irregularly irregular ventricular response; the chaotic atrial activity is often best seen in lead V1 (p.1990, 1991). The conducted ventricular rate is variable and usually rapid (commonly 110-160/min), but may exceed 200/min, or be inappropriately slow when there is high vagal tone or AV nodal conduction disease (p.1990). Many patients are unaware of the irregular heartbeat, so AF is frequently asymptomatic; absence of AF on intermittent monitoring does not establish low risk (p.1990, 1993). AF is categorized by temporal pattern: paroxysmal (self-terminating, usually within 7 days), persistent (continuous >7 days but <1 year), and long-standing persistent (>1 year); these patterns correlate with progressive left atrial enlargement and scar burden (p.1990, 1991). Stroke and bleeding risks are estimated as concepts using the CHA2DS2-VASc score (stroke risk: congestive heart failure, hypertension, age, diabetes, prior stroke/TIA, vascular disease, sex) and HAS-BLED score (bleeding risk), respectively (p.1993). AF burden does not predict stroke risk; the approach to paroxysmal AF is the same as for persistent AF, and even apparently infrequent episodes carry risk because asymptomatic episodes are common (p.1993). Subclinical AF detectable only on long-term continuous monitoring is associated with roughly 2.5-fold increased stroke risk (p.1993). AF detected after cryptogenic stroke using insertable cardiac monitors in up to ~8.9% of patients within 6 months, supporting prolonged rhythm monitoring in this setting (p.1990). Acute AF with significant haemodynamic compromise, pulmonary oedema, or evidence of coronary ischaemia indicates need for emergent cardioversion (p.1992). Preexcited AF over an accessory pathway with very rapid repetitive conduction (minimum R-R <250 ms occurs in ~25% of preexciting pathways) is potentially life-threatening, predisposing to ventricular fibrillation and sudden death (p.1985-1986). Syncope or presyncope from bradycardia/pauses, including offset pauses on spontaneous conversion to sinus rhythm, suggesting coexisting sinus node dysfunction (tachy-brady syndrome) (p.1992). Sustained uncontrolled rapid ventricular rates risk precipitating heart failure and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (p.1990, 1992). Relying on AF burden or symptom frequency to gauge stroke risk is mistaken; anticoagulation decisions should rest on the risk-factor profile, not how often AF is documented (p.1993). A normal intermittent monitor does not exclude clinically important AF, since asymptomatic episodes are common (p.1993). Cardioverting AF of >48 h (or unknown) duration without anticoagulation or thrombus exclusion risks thromboembolism, which can occur even days later because of post-conversion atrial stunning (delayed recovery of mechanical function) (p.1992). Nonvalvular AF (AF without mitral stenosis) differs in management from valvular AF; rheumatic mitral stenosis and mechanical valves carry especially high thromboembolic risk (p.1993). AF is characterized by disorganized, rapid, irregular atrial electrical activation with loss of organized atrial mechanical contraction; the AV node filters these impulses to produce an irregular ventricular rate. The pathophysiology is multifactorial and incompletely understood, with a proposed 'final common pathway' in which risk factors (age, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, alcohol, sleep-disordered breathing) drive electrophysiologic changes in atrial tissue. Altered membrane channel regulation produces abnormal excitability; pulmonary vein musculature (and other foci such as the posterior left atrial wall, superior vena cava, coronary sinus, vein of Marshall) shows enhanced automaticity generating ectopic beats that initiate AF. Progressive cellular and tissue remodeling shortens atrial refractory periods and creates functional reentry, with eventual fibrosis and left atrial enlargement, explaining the typical progression from paroxysmal to persistent to long-standing persistent disease. Loss of atrial systole reduces cardiac output, and variable ventricular filling produces variable stroke volume (p.1990-1992). AF is not benign: it carries a 1.5- to 1.9-fold increased mortality after adjusting for underlying cardiac disease, and causes approximately 25% of all strokes. It increases the risk of dementia, MRI-detected silent embolic infarcts, congestive heart failure, and cardiomyopathy. Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is generally reversible once ventricular rate is controlled. AF tends to be progressive, with no definitive durable cure, and patients maintaining sinus rhythm generally have better survival than those who remain in AF (p.1990, 1992, 1994). By temporal pattern: paroxysmal AF (self-terminates or is cardioverted within 7 days; normal-to-mildly enlarged left atrium, low scar burden), persistent AF (continuous >7 days but <1 year; mild-to-severe LA enlargement, moderate scar), and long-standing persistent AF (>1 year; severely enlarged LA, high scar burden). A newer staged framework (at risk of AF, pre-AF, AF, permanent AF) reframes AF as a disease continuum. Mitral stenosis defines valvular versus nonvalvular AF for risk purposes (p.1991, 1993, 1996).

atrial flutter — AFL, macroreentrant atrial tachycardia atrial fibrillation focal atrial tachycardia atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia sinus tachycardia with prominent P waves multifocal atrial tachycardia atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia twelve-lead ECG to identify flutter-wave morphology and conduction ratio vagal manoeuvre or adenosine to increase block and reveal flutter waves transthoracic echocardiography to assess chamber size and structural disease transoesophageal echocardiography before cardioversion when indicated to exclude thrombus thyroid function tests and electrolytes to identify precipitants electrophysiological study with entrainment mapping to confirm isthmus dependence Typical atrial flutter is a macroreentrant right atrial circuit dependent on the cavotricuspid isthmus, producing an atrial rate of approximately 250 to 350 beats per minute. Counterclockwise typical flutter shows the classic sawtooth negative flutter waves in the inferior leads and positive deflections in V1. Ventricular response is often regular at a fixed conduction ratio, most commonly 2 to 1, giving a ventricular rate near 150 that should always prompt a search for flutter waves. Vagal manoeuvres or adenosine transiently increase atrioventricular block and unmask the underlying flutter waves without terminating the arrhythmia. Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is highly effective and curative for typical isthmus-dependent flutter. Atypical (non-isthmus-dependent) flutter frequently arises around atrial scar or prior surgical or ablation lesions and requires detailed mapping. Thromboembolic risk parallels that of atrial fibrillation, so anticoagulation decisions follow the same risk-stratification principles. One-to-one atrioventricular conduction can occur when a class Ic antiarrhythmic slows the atrial rate without an AV-nodal blocker, dangerously accelerating the ventricular response. one-to-one atrioventricular conduction producing an extremely rapid ventricular rate haemodynamic instability with hypotension or pulmonary oedema new flutter in the context of acute coronary syndrome or pulmonary embolism rapid uncontrolled rates precipitating tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy flutter with pre-excitation over an accessory pathway Overlooking flutter in a regular narrow tachycardia at about 150 per minute because alternate flutter waves hide within the QRS and T waves. Prescribing a class Ic agent without AV-nodal blockade and provoking 1 to 1 conduction. Neglecting anticoagulation on the mistaken assumption that flutter carries lower thromboembolic risk than fibrillation. Attributing atypical flutter to a typical isthmus-dependent circuit and targeting the wrong ablation site. Failing to look for reversible precipitants such as thyrotoxicosis, sepsis or pulmonary disease. Atrial flutter is a macroreentrant atrial tachycardia in which a single large reentry circuit sustains rapid, organised atrial activation. In typical flutter the wavefront circulates around the tricuspid annulus within the right atrium, constrained anteriorly by the annulus and posteriorly by the crista terminalis and Eustachian ridge, with the cavotricuspid isthmus forming a critical slow-conduction corridor. The atrioventricular node cannot conduct every rapid atrial impulse, so physiological block produces a slower, frequently regular ventricular response. Atypical flutters use alternative circuits, often around regions of atrial scar, surgical incisions or the mitral annulus, and are common in patients with structural or post-operative atrial disease. With rate or rhythm control, anticoagulation and cavotricuspid isthmus ablation for typical flutter, outcomes are generally good and ablation success rates are high. Persistent rapid rates risk tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy, and many patients subsequently develop atrial fibrillation.

Atrial myxoma — cardiac myxoma Mitral stenosis Infective endocarditis Left atrial thrombus Other cardiac tumours (papillary fibroelastoma, sarcoma) Vasculitis or other cause of constitutional illness Echocardiography (transthoracic and transoesophageal) to characterise the mass Cardiac MRI for tissue characterisation and extent Assessment for embolic complications Inflammatory markers Evaluation for Carney complex if multiple, recurrent or young-onset The commonest primary cardiac tumour, benign, and most often arising in the left atrium near the fossa ovalis The classic triad of manifestations is obstructive, embolic and constitutional Obstruction can mimic mitral stenosis, sometimes with a tumour plop and positional symptoms Embolism (systemic from left-sided, pulmonary from right-sided tumours) can cause stroke or limb ischaemia Constitutional features include fever, weight loss and raised inflammatory markers, mimicking endocarditis or vasculitis Most are sporadic, but multiple or recurrent myxomas suggest the Carney complex; treatment is surgical excision Embolic stroke or systemic embolism Syncope or haemodynamic compromise from valve obstruction Features suggesting malignant cardiac tumour Recurrent or multiple tumours suggesting a familial syndrome Mistaking it for infective endocarditis or vasculitis given constitutional features Attributing obstructive symptoms solely to mitral stenosis Overlooking a myxoma as a source of embolic stroke Not considering Carney complex in young or recurrent cases An atrial myxoma is a benign neoplasm of primitive mesenchymal cells, typically pedunculated and attached to the atrial septum. Its gelatinous, friable surface and mobility explain the clinical triad: a pedunculated mass can prolapse into the atrioventricular valve during diastole causing intermittent inflow obstruction, fragments or surface thrombus can embolise, and cytokine production (notably interleukin-6) drives constitutional and inflammatory features. Left atrial tumours embolise systemically, while right atrial tumours embolise to the lungs. Surgical excision is usually curative for sporadic myxomas with an excellent prognosis, though recurrence occurs, particularly in familial (Carney complex) cases requiring surveillance.

Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors — Cardiac myxoma, Left atrial myxoma, Primary cardiac tumor, Cardiac sarcoma, Cardiac neoplasm Mitral stenosis Mitral regurgitation Subaortic or subpulmonic (outflow tract) stenosis from a ventricular tumor Restrictive or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (mimicked by pediatric rhabdomyoma/fibroma) Pericardial constriction Infective endocarditis (myxoma with embolic phenomena, fever, and constitutional symptoms is frequently misdiagnosed as endocarditis) Valvular vegetation Transthoracic echocardiography (initial modality; tumor location, size, attachment site, impact on valves/pericardium) Transesophageal echocardiography (improved characterization and spatial resolution; aids surgical planning) Cardiac MRI with gadolinium (tissue characterization, local invasion, differentiating tumor from thrombus) Gated cardiac CT (anatomic and tissue assessment, calcified lesions, extracardiac involvement; useful when MRI not feasible) Nuclear imaging including FDG-PET (extracardiac disease; some tumor types) and 131I-MIBG scanning for paraganglioma Echocardiographic screening of first-degree relatives when myxoma is familial/syndromic Pericardiocentesis with cytology for malignant pericardial effusion (reported sensitivity ~67-92%) Intracardiac thrombus Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor Myocardial hypertrophy mistaken for a mass Collagen vascular disease (mimicked by myxoma constitutional/laboratory picture) Paraneoplastic syndrome Cardiac tumors are broadly divided into primary tumors (arising in the heart) and metastatic tumors from a distant source; metastatic involvement is far more common and is seen in up to roughly 20% of patients with end-stage metastatic cancer. Primary cardiac tumors are rare (about 1 in 2000 in autopsy series); roughly three-quarters are histologically benign, and most of those benign tumors are myxomas, while malignant primaries (almost all sarcomas) make up about 25%. Myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults, comprising one-third to one-half of cases at postmortem and about three-quarters of surgically treated tumors; it favors the third through sixth decades with a female predilection. Roughly 90% of myxomas are sporadic; the remainder are familial (autosomal dominant), often as part of the Carney complex (cardiac/skin/breast myxomas, lentigines or pigmented nevi, and endocrine overactivity), associated in about 70% of cases with inactivating mutations in the PRKAR1A tumor-suppressor gene. Sporadic myxomas are typically solitary, pedunculated on a fibrovascular stalk, and arise from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis, most often in the left atrium; familial/syndromic myxomas occur in younger patients, are often multiple, may be ventricular, and recur more often. Myxomas most commonly produce obstructive features mimicking mitral valve disease (stenosis from prolapse into the mitral orifice, or regurgitation from valvular trauma); symptoms may be sudden or positional because of gravitational effects on tumor position. A characteristic low-pitched early or mid-diastolic 'tumor plop' may be heard, attributed to the tumor striking the mitral valve or ventricular wall. Myxomas can cause peripheral or pulmonary embolic events (tumor fragments or associated thrombus) and constitutional/cytokine-mediated features (often interleukin-6), so they are frequently misdiagnosed as endocarditis, collagen vascular disease, or a paraneoplastic syndrome. Papillary fibroelastomas are the most common tumors of the cardiac valves (friable, frond-like, usually solitary) and, although often silent, may embolize to cause TIA, stroke, or myocardial infarction. Rhabdomyomas and fibromas are the most common cardiac tumors of infants and children, usually ventricular; rhabdomyomas occur in about 50% of children with tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2 mutations) and tend to regress, whereas fibromas (PTCH1) tend to grow. Malignant primaries are almost all sarcomas (angiosarcoma most common in adults, rhabdomyosarcoma in children), frequently right-sided, rapidly growing, and often invade the pericardium; about one-third are metastatic at diagnosis, usually to the lungs. Tissue histology remains the gold standard for diagnosis; echocardiography is the usual initial test, with cardiac MRI (gadolinium) helping differentiate tumor from thrombus and benign from malignant lesions. Syncope or positional symptoms suggesting intermittent obstruction by a mobile tumor Embolic events (stroke, TIA, peripheral or pulmonary embolism) as the presenting feature Cardiac tamponade or large pericardial effusion (especially with metastatic disease) Rapidly progressive heart failure or chamber/vena caval obstruction suggesting sarcoma New heart block or conduction disturbance (tumors near the AV node, e.g., hemangioma/mesothelioma, can cause sudden death) Misdiagnosing myxoma as infective endocarditis, collagen vascular disease, or a paraneoplastic syndrome because of fever, embolism, and laboratory abnormalities (e.g., elevated ESR/CRP, anemia, hypergammaglobulinemia). Catheterizing the chamber harboring a tumor, which risks tumor embolization; angiography/catheterization is no longer mandatory when noninvasive imaging is adequate and coronary disease is unlikely. Failing to screen first-degree relatives of young patients with multiple myxomas or syndromic features. Attributing cardiac symptoms in cancer patients solely to the tumor when radiotherapy/chemotherapy-induced myocarditis, pericarditis, or cardiomyopathy can produce identical findings. Overlooking that a left-sided sarcoma may be mistaken for a myxoma. Cardiac tumors are classified as primary (benign, chiefly myxoma; or malignant, chiefly sarcoma) or secondary/metastatic. Myxomas are gelatinous masses of myxoma cells in a glycosaminoglycan-rich stroma, usually arising from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis and most often projecting into the left atrium on a fibrovascular stalk. Clinical effects arise from three mechanisms: mechanical obstruction or valvular interference (mimicking mitral stenosis/regurgitation, or outflow obstruction for ventricular tumors), embolization of tumor fragments or associated thrombus, and constitutional effects from tumor-secreted cytokines such as interleukin-6. Familial myxomas relate to PRKAR1A inactivation within the Carney complex. Metastatic tumors reach the heart by hematogenous or lymphangitic spread or direct invasion, most often involving the pericardium, then myocardium of any chamber, and rarely the endocardium or valves. Benign myxoma is generally cured by surgical excision; recurrence is about 1-2% in sporadic cases but 12-22% in familial cases (multifocal disease or incomplete resection). Malignant primary tumors carry a poor prognosis: sarcomas typically progress rapidly to death within weeks to months from hemodynamic compromise, local invasion, or metastasis, and respond poorly to radiotherapy/chemotherapy. The notable exception is primary cardiac lymphoma, the most chemotherapy-sensitive primary cardiac malignancy, with long-term survival in about 40% of treated patients. Metastatic cardiac involvement usually occurs with advanced disease, is clinically apparent only about 10% of the time, is rarely the cause of death, and carries an overall poor prognosis.

Atrial septal aneurysm — ASA, aneurysm of the interatrial septum, interatrial septal aneurysm Patent foramen ovale without aneurysm Secundum atrial septal defect Lipomatous hypertrophy of the atrial septum Atrial septal mass, thrombus, or tumour Sinus venosus atrial septal defect Cor triatriatum or other atrial membrane Transthoracic echocardiography to detect septal bulging and measure its excursion Transoesophageal echocardiography to define the aneurysm and any associated shunt or fenestrations Agitated-saline bubble study with Valsalva to demonstrate right-to-left shunting Cardiac MRI or CT to distinguish an aneurysm from lipomatous hypertrophy or a mass Prolonged rhythm monitoring and embolic-source workup when stroke has occurred A localised redundancy of the interatrial septum, usually at the fossa ovalis, that bulges and oscillates between the atria through the cardiac cycle Defined echocardiographically by the excursion and base width of the mobile septal segment Usually an incidental finding but clinically important because of its strong association with a patent foramen ovale and other interatrial communications The combination of an atrial septal aneurysm and a patent foramen ovale raises the likelihood of paradoxical embolism and cryptogenic stroke compared with either alone May act as a source of thrombus and is associated with atrial arrhythmias in some patients Best characterised by transoesophageal echocardiography with an agitated-saline bubble study to demonstrate any accompanying shunt Management is guided by the associated shunt and any embolic events; device closure may be considered when a high-risk PFO with aneurysm underlies a cryptogenic stroke Cryptogenic stroke or systemic embolism, particularly with a coexisting patent foramen ovale Demonstrable thrombus adherent to the aneurysmal septum Recurrent embolic events despite antithrombotic treatment A large right-to-left shunt provoked by Valsalva in the context of unexplained stroke Reporting the aneurysm without actively searching for an associated shunt with a bubble study Confusing the finding with lipomatous septal hypertrophy or an atrial mass Missing the raised stroke risk conferred by the aneurysm-plus-PFO combination Attributing stroke to the aneurysm before excluding atrial fibrillation and other embolic sources An atrial septal aneurysm is an area of thin, redundant tissue in the interatrial septum, typically involving the region of the fossa ovalis, that billows back and forth with the changing pressure gradient between the two atria. The increased mobility of the septum is frequently accompanied by incomplete sealing of the foramen ovale or by fenestrations, providing a route for right-to-left shunting when right atrial pressure transiently exceeds left. Stasis and the abnormal, mobile surface may promote local thrombus formation, and together with an associated patent foramen ovale this underlies the heightened risk of paradoxical systemic embolism. In isolation an atrial septal aneurysm is generally benign, but when combined with a patent foramen ovale it markedly increases the risk of paradoxical embolism and recurrent cryptogenic stroke, which appropriate treatment can reduce.

Atrial Septal Defect — ASD, atrial septal defects Ventricular septal defect Partial anomalous pulmonary venous return Atrioventricular septal defect (primum type) Innocent pulmonary flow murmur Pulmonary valve stenosis Patent foramen ovale (a normal variant, not a true defect) Echocardiography to define defect type, size, and right heart volume overload Chest radiograph for cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings in significant shunts Electrocardiogram, often showing right axis deviation and right ventricular volume overload (rsR' pattern) Transoesophageal echocardiography or advanced imaging when transthoracic views are inadequate Cardiac catheterisation if pulmonary hypertension needs assessment A communication in the atrial septum permitting left-to-right shunting; the secundum type in the region of the fossa ovalis is the most common form. Most children are asymptomatic and are detected through an incidental murmur or, later, right heart enlargement; heart failure in infancy is uncommon. The characteristic auscultatory finding is a widely and fixedly split second heart sound, accompanied by a soft systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border from increased pulmonary flow. A larger shunt may produce a mid-diastolic rumble at the lower left sternal border from increased flow across the tricuspid valve. The murmur reflects increased flow through the pulmonary valve rather than turbulent flow across the defect itself, which is low-velocity and inaudible. Echocardiography defines the defect type and size, direction of shunt, and degree of right atrial and right ventricular volume overload. Small secundum defects frequently close spontaneously in early childhood; a defect must be distinguished from a normal patent foramen ovale. Significant defects are closed, often by transcatheter device for suitable secundum defects, to prevent later right heart enlargement, arrhythmias, and pulmonary vascular disease. Untreated large defects may lead in adulthood to atrial arrhythmias, pulmonary hypertension, and, rarely, paradoxical embolism. Signs of significant right heart volume overload or pulmonary hypertension Development of atrial arrhythmias Failure to thrive or heart failure in an infant, suggesting an additional or larger lesion New cyanosis suggesting shunt reversal in longstanding, untreated disease Paradoxical embolic events Mistaking a normal patent foramen ovale for a true atrial septal defect Dismissing the subtle findings and missing a significant defect until right heart enlargement is advanced Attributing fixed splitting of the second heart sound to a benign murmur Assuming all defects require closure when many small secundum defects close spontaneously Overlooking associated anomalous pulmonary venous drainage An opening in the atrial septum allows blood to shunt from the higher-compliance left atrium toward the right atrium, the direction favoured because the right ventricle is more compliant than the left. This left-to-right shunt volume-loads the right atrium, right ventricle, and pulmonary circulation while the left-sided output is maintained by the shunt returning through the lungs. Chronic volume overload dilates the right heart; over many years a minority develop elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary hypertension, and the resulting right atrial stretch predisposes to atrial arrhythmias. Isolated secundum defects, whether closed spontaneously, by device, or surgically, have an excellent outlook when addressed before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease. Late, unrepaired large defects carry increasing risk of arrhythmia and pulmonary hypertension in adulthood.

atrioventricular block — AV block, heart block sinus node dysfunction with sinus pauses or arrest blocked atrial premature beats mimicking second-degree block atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response ventriculophasic sinus arrhythmia concealed junctional extrasystoles causing pseudo-AV block atrioventricular dissociation without block due to accelerated junctional rhythm twelve-lead ECG to classify the type and assess escape QRS width ambulatory or inpatient telemetry monitoring to capture intermittent high-grade block serum electrolytes, thyroid function and relevant drug levels serology for Lyme disease and inflammatory or infiltrative causes where indicated echocardiography to evaluate structural and ischaemic heart disease electrophysiological study with His-bundle recording when the level of block is uncertain First-degree block is a fixed PR prolongation with every P wave conducted, whereas third-degree block shows complete atrioventricular dissociation with an independent escape rhythm. Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) second-degree block shows progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat and usually reflects reversible block within the atrioventricular node. Mobitz type II block shows constant PR intervals with sudden non-conducted P waves and localises to the His-Purkinje system, carrying a high risk of progression to complete block. A narrow escape complex suggests a junctional pacemaker with a relatively reliable rate, while a wide, slow escape indicates a ventricular pacemaker that is more likely to fail. The level of block, rather than the numerical degree alone, drives prognosis and the decision to pace. In 2 to 1 block the type cannot be classified by the PR pattern, so accompanying QRS width and response to vagal or exercise manoeuvres help localise the level. Vagal tone slows the sinus rate and improves nodal (Wenckebach) block but worsens infranodal block, whereas exercise or atropine does the reverse, a useful bedside distinction. Reversible causes such as ischaemia, drugs including AV-nodal blockers, hyperkalaemia, hypothyroidism, Lyme disease and raised vagal tone should be excluded before permanent pacing. syncope or presyncope with documented high-grade or complete block Mobitz type II or complete block with a wide, slow or unstable escape rhythm block complicating acute anterior myocardial infarction symptomatic bradycardia with haemodynamic compromise alternating bundle branch block indicating advanced conduction-system disease Classifying 2 to 1 block as type I or type II from the conduction ratio alone rather than from QRS width and provocative manoeuvres. Missing reversible causes such as drug effect, hyperkalaemia, hypothyroidism or Lyme carditis before implanting a permanent device. Mistaking blocked atrial premature beats for genuine second-degree block. Underestimating the danger of Mobitz type II because the resting rate appears adequate. Overlooking that vagal manoeuvres improve nodal but worsen infranodal block when trying to localise the level. Atrioventricular block denotes impaired conduction of the atrial impulse to the ventricles, which may be delayed, intermittently interrupted or completely blocked. The site of disease determines the clinical behaviour. Block within the atrioventricular node is typically decremental, often vagally mediated or drug-related, and tends to produce Wenckebach periodicity with a stable junctional escape. Block within the His-Purkinje system is an all-or-none phenomenon reflecting diffuse conduction-system disease, and it generates Mobitz type II or complete block with an unreliable, slow ventricular escape. Causes span idiopathic age-related fibrosis of the conduction system, ischaemia and infarction, infiltrative and inflammatory disease, congenital block associated with maternal anti-Ro antibodies, drugs, electrolyte disturbance and increased vagal tone. First-degree and Mobitz type I block are usually benign when asymptomatic and reversible causes are addressed, whereas Mobitz type II and complete infranodal block frequently progress and warrant permanent pacing, after which prognosis is largely determined by the underlying cardiac disease. Congenital complete block may be tolerated for years but often eventually requires pacing.

atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia — AVNRT, AV nodal reentry tachycardia atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia using a concealed accessory pathway focal atrial tachycardia atrial flutter with regular conduction sinus tachycardia (including inappropriate sinus tachycardia) permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia junctional ectopic tachycardia twelve-lead ECG during tachycardia and in sinus rhythm to seek pseudo-r' or pseudo-S waves ambulatory or event monitoring to capture onset and offset if episodes are infrequent vagal manoeuvre or adenosine administration with continuous ECG to observe response transthoracic echocardiography to exclude structural heart disease electrophysiological study demonstrating dual AV nodal physiology and a jump in the AH interval thyroid function and full blood count to identify precipitants Commonest regular paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, disproportionately affecting women, typically presenting with abrupt-onset, abrupt-offset palpitations. Substrate is dual atrioventricular nodal physiology: a slow pathway with short refractoriness and a fast pathway with longer refractoriness, permitting a reentry circuit within or adjacent to the compact node. Typical (slow-fast) AVNRT conducts antegradely down the slow pathway and retrogradely up the fast pathway, giving near-simultaneous atrial and ventricular activation. On the surface ECG the retrograde P wave is usually buried in the QRS or produces a pseudo-r' in V1 and a pseudo-S in the inferior leads, a valuable diagnostic clue. Vagal manoeuvres and adenosine terminate the arrhythmia by transiently blocking the AV node, distinguishing it from atrial tachycardias that continue despite block. A neck-pounding sensation (frog sign) reflects simultaneous atrial and ventricular contraction against closed AV valves producing cannon A waves. Atypical (fast-slow or slow-slow) variants show a long RP interval with the retrograde P separated from the QRS, mimicking atrial tachycardia or PJRT. Catheter ablation of the slow pathway near the coronary sinus os is curative in the great majority with a low risk of inadvertent AV block. haemodynamic compromise with hypotension, chest pain or syncope during tachycardia very rapid rates in patients with pre-existing coronary or structural heart disease syncope at onset suggesting an accessory pathway or additional arrhythmia signs of decompensated heart failure during sustained episodes Mistaking the pseudo-r' in V1 for genuine incomplete right bundle branch block and overlooking retrograde atrial activation. Assuming failure of adenosine to terminate excludes a nodal-dependent arrhythmia when subtherapeutic dosing or rapid metabolism is the cause. Labelling atypical long-RP AVNRT as atrial tachycardia and choosing an inappropriate ablation target. Attributing palpitations to anxiety in young women and delaying definitive rhythm documentation. Overlooking coexisting dual pathophysiology when AVNRT and an accessory pathway occur in the same patient. AVNRT arises from functionally and anatomically distinct conduction pathways in the region of the atrioventricular node. A fast pathway conducts rapidly but has a long refractory period, whereas a slow pathway conducts slowly but recovers quickly. A critically timed atrial premature beat blocks in the fast pathway and descends the slow pathway; by the time it reaches the distal node the fast pathway has recovered, allowing retrograde conduction back to the atrium and initiation of a sustained reentrant circuit. In typical slow-fast AVNRT this produces near-simultaneous atrial and ventricular depolarisation, while atypical forms reverse or vary the pathways used. The circuit incorporates perinodal atrial tissue and does not require an accessory pathway or the ventricles for its maintenance. AVNRT is a benign arrhythmia with an excellent long-term prognosis and is not associated with increased mortality in structurally normal hearts. Slow-pathway catheter ablation offers a durable cure in the great majority, and episodes otherwise remain intermittent and self-limiting.

atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia — AVRT, accessory pathway reentrant tachycardia atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia focal atrial tachycardia atrial flutter with rapid conduction ventricular tachycardia (particularly with antidromic AVRT) pre-excited atrial fibrillation permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia twelve-lead ECG in sinus rhythm to seek a delta wave and short PR interval twelve-lead ECG during tachycardia to define RP relationship and QRS alternans transthoracic echocardiography to exclude Ebstein anomaly and other structural disease electrophysiological study to localise the pathway and assess its antegrade refractory period exercise testing to evaluate abrupt loss of pre-excitation suggesting a low-risk pathway ambulatory monitoring to correlate symptoms with rhythm AVRT is a macroreentrant tachycardia that obligatorily uses an accessory atrioventricular pathway as one limb and the AV node as the other. Orthodromic AVRT conducts antegradely through the AV node and retrogradely up the accessory pathway, producing a narrow-complex tachycardia with a retrograde P wave typically after the QRS (RP shorter than PR). Antidromic AVRT conducts antegradely down the accessory pathway and retrogradely through the node, giving a wide, maximally pre-excited QRS that can mimic ventricular tachycardia. A concealed accessory pathway conducts only retrogradely, so the resting ECG is normal and pre-excitation is absent despite recurrent orthodromic tachycardia. QRS alternans and a rate that slows with functional bundle branch block ipsilateral to the pathway (Coumel sign) point to AVRT over AVNRT. Adenosine and vagal manoeuvres terminate orthodromic AVRT by blocking the nodal limb of the circuit. In patients with an antegradely conducting pathway, atrial fibrillation can conduct rapidly to the ventricle and degenerate into ventricular fibrillation, so AV-nodal blocking drugs are hazardous. Catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is highly effective and is first-line for symptomatic or high-risk patients. pre-excited atrial fibrillation with very short RR intervals indicating risk of ventricular fibrillation syncope or presyncope during tachycardia wide-complex tachycardia that is haemodynamically unstable family history of sudden cardiac death with ventricular pre-excitation administration of AV-nodal blockers precipitating haemodynamic collapse in pre-excited AF Giving atrioventricular nodal blocking agents to a patient with pre-excited atrial fibrillation and accelerating ventricular response. Misdiagnosing antidromic AVRT as ventricular tachycardia and withholding appropriate management. Assuming a normal resting ECG excludes an accessory pathway, missing a concealed pathway. Underestimating risk in asymptomatic pre-excitation without electrophysiological risk stratification. Failing to recognise QRS alternans and Coumel sign as clues that favour AVRT over AVNRT. AVRT depends on an accessory pathway, a strand of working myocardium that bridges the atrioventricular groove outside the normal conduction axis and electrically connects atrium to ventricle. This creates the potential for a large reentrant loop in which the impulse travels down one connection and up the other. In orthodromic tachycardia the AV node and His-Purkinje system form the antegrade limb and the accessory pathway the retrograde limb, yielding a narrow QRS. In antidromic tachycardia the direction reverses and the ventricle is activated entirely through the pathway, producing a fully pre-excited wide complex. Pathways may conduct in both directions, only antegradely, or only retrogradely (concealed). The circuit is initiated by a premature beat that blocks in one limb and returns through the other once refractoriness has resolved. Prognosis is excellent when the pathway lacks rapid antegrade conduction, and catheter ablation provides a durable cure in most patients. The principal risk is sudden death from pre-excited atrial fibrillation degenerating to ventricular fibrillation in those with a rapidly conducting antegrade pathway.

The resulting defect allows shunting at atrial and/or ventricular level and produces a common or abnormal atrioventricular valve that is often regurgitant. A large left-to-right shunt increases pulmonary blood flow, causing heart failure in infancy and, if uncorrected, progressive pulmonary vascular remodelling toward irreversible pulmonary hypertension (Eisenmenger physiology). ATTR Amyloidosis (Transthyretin Amyloidosis) — Transthyretin amyloidosis, ATTRv and ATTRwt, Familial amyloid polyneuropathy AL (immunoglobulin light-chain) amyloidosis Hypertensive heart disease and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Other infiltrative cardiomyopathies (Fabry disease, cardiac sarcoidosis, haemochromatosis) Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy and diabetic polyneuropathy AA and other hereditary amyloidoses Hereditary sensorimotor neuropathies such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease Echocardiography with longitudinal strain showing apical sparing Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement and T1 or extracellular volume mapping Bone scintigraphy with DPD, PYP or HMDP graded by the Perugini scale Serum free light chains with serum and urine immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis TTR gene sequencing to distinguish variant from wild-type disease Tissue biopsy with Congo red staining and amyloid typing by mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry when required Cardiac biomarkers (NT-proBNP and troponin) and nerve conduction studies according to phenotype ATTR arises from transthyretin, a hepatically synthesised transport protein for thyroxine and retinol-binding protein; disease reflects dissociation of its stabilising tetramer into amyloidogenic monomers. Two forms exist: hereditary variant disease (ATTRv) from autosomal dominant TTR mutations, and acquired wild-type disease (ATTRwt), which predominantly affects older men with a cardiac phenotype. Genotype shapes phenotype: Val30Met tends toward polyneuropathy with endemic clusters in Portugal, Sweden and Japan, whereas Val122Ile and Thr60Ala favour cardiomyopathy. Cardiac ATTR presents as heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, increased ventricular wall thickness on echocardiography, and a discordantly low-voltage or pseudo-infarct ECG. Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis and spontaneous biceps tendon rupture are red-flag musculoskeletal harbingers that often precede cardiac disease by years. Bone-avid scintigraphy with technetium-labelled DPD, PYP or HMDP showing grade 2 to 3 myocardial uptake, once a monoclonal protein is excluded, permits a non-biopsy diagnosis of cardiac ATTR. Disease-modifying options include transthyretin tetramer stabilisers and gene-silencing agents (small interfering RNA and antisense oligonucleotides); liver transplantation historically removed the variant protein source. Autonomic neuropathy with orthostatic hypotension, gastrointestinal dysmotility and erectile dysfunction is prominent in the neuropathic form and limits tolerance of heart failure therapy. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, increased wall thickness and low ECG voltages Hypotension or intolerance when standard heart failure or antihypertensive drugs are introduced New high-grade atrioventricular block or need for pacing Rapidly progressive sensorimotor neuropathy with autonomic failure Attributing increased ventricular wall thickness to hypertension and missing the diagnosis Assuming all cardiac amyloid is AL type and delaying bone scintigraphy Interpreting a positive bone scan as diagnostic without excluding a monoclonal protein, as co-existent MGUS is common in the elderly Overlooking the early musculoskeletal clues of carpal tunnel syndrome and spinal stenosis Transthyretin circulates as a homotetramer; destabilisation, driven either by an inherited point mutation in ATTRv or by ageing-related factors acting on the normal sequence in ATTRwt, promotes dissociation into monomers that misfold and aggregate into insoluble amyloid fibrils. These fibrils deposit in the extracellular matrix of the myocardium, peripheral and autonomic nerves, and the tenosynovium and ligaments, producing a stiff non-compliant myocardium and length-dependent axonal degeneration. The relative tropism for heart versus nerve is strongly influenced by the specific mutation, whereas wild-type disease is almost exclusively cardiac and musculoskeletal. Deposition is progressive and, untreated, culminates in restrictive cardiomyopathy with conduction disease or disabling sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathy. Untreated cardiac ATTR carries a poor prognosis with median survival of only a few years, although wild-type disease generally progresses more slowly than many variant forms. Stabiliser and gene-silencing therapies now improve survival and functional outcomes, particularly when started early.

The dysgranulopoiesis produces functionally abnormal neutrophils and their precursors in the blood, while ineffective haematopoiesis can cause cytopenias, and the disease has a substantial risk of progression to acute myeloid leukaemia. Prognosis is generally poor with short median survival in many series and a significant risk of transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia; allogeneic transplantation is the main potentially curative option.

that cannot assess depth of invasion Atypical fibroxanthoma is a superficial pleomorphic mesenchymal tumour arising in the dermis of severely sun-damaged skin, with ultraviolet radiation implicated as the principal driver through characteristic UV-signature mutations, notably in TP53. The lesion is composed of atypical spindled, epithelioid, and multinucleated cells with numerous, often atypical, mitotic figures. It is confined to the dermis and lacks the deep infiltration, tumour necrosis, and lymphovascular or perineural invasion that define its more aggressive counterpart, pleomorphic dermal sarcoma. True atypical fibroxanthoma has an excellent prognosis after complete excision, with low recurrence and rare metastasis; prognosis worsens substantially if the lesion is in fact a pleomorphic dermal sarcoma, which carries a meaningful risk of recurrence and metastasis.

awaiting genetic results Confusing it with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and mismanaging accordingly Attributing the picture to typical HUS and withholding complement-directed therapy Forgetting uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway on endothelial surfaces. Under normal conditions, regulatory proteins such as complement factor H, factor I and membrane cofactor protein restrain complement amplification; loss-of-function variants in these regulators, or gain-of-function variants in the C3 convertase components C3 and factor B, allow persistent complement activation and generation of the terminal membrane attack complex. The resulting endothelial injury, particularly in the renal microvasculature, promotes platelet activation and microthrombus formation, which mechanically shears red cells to produce microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, consumes platelets to cause thrombocytopenia, and obstructs glomerular capillaries to cause acute kidney injury. A genetic predisposition typically requires an environmental trigger such as infection or pregnancy to precipitate an episode. Before complement-targeted therapy many patients progressed to end-stage kidney disease or died; terminal complement inhibition has greatly improved renal and overall outcomes, though prognosis still depends on the underlying genetic variant and the promptness of treatment.

investigations, leading to inadequate treatment planning Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour is driven by inactivation of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling complex, most commonly through loss of the SMARCB1 (INI1) tumour-suppressor gene and, in a minority, SMARCA4. Loss of this complex disrupts control of gene transcription and cellular differentiation, producing a poorly differentiated, rapidly proliferating tumour with characteristic rhabdoid cytology. atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumour — AT/RT, ATRT, atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour Medulloblastoma Other central nervous system embryonal tumours (e.g., embryonal tumour with multilayered rosettes) Ependymoma Choroid plexus carcinoma High-grade glioma Central nervous system metastasis of an extracranial rhabdoid tumour Pineoblastoma for pineal-region lesions MRI of the brain and whole spine with contrast for tumour extent and drop metastases Cerebrospinal fluid cytology once safe with respect to intracranial pressure SMARCB1/INI1 and SMARCA4 immunohistochemistry on tumour tissue DNA-methylation profiling for molecular subgroup assignment Germline SMARCB1/SMARCA4 testing and genetic counselling Abdominal and renal imaging to exclude synchronous extracranial rhabdoid tumour Ophthalmological and baseline endocrine assessment where relevant to tumour site A highly malignant embryonal central nervous system tumour of infancy and early childhood, classified as WHO CNS grade 4. Defined molecularly by loss of SMARCB1 (INI1), or rarely SMARCA4 (BRG1), with absent nuclear INI1 staining on immunohistochemistry being diagnostic. Histology is heterogeneous, containing rhabdoid cells alongside primitive neuroectodermal, mesenchymal, and epithelial elements, historically causing confusion with medulloblastoma and other embryonal tumours. Three epigenetic molecular subgroups are recognised (ATRT-TYR, ATRT-SHH, and ATRT-MYC), differing in age, location, and outcome. It occurs in both the posterior fossa and supratentorial compartments, with infratentorial tumours predominating in the youngest infants. Leptomeningeal dissemination is common, mandating imaging of the whole neuraxis and cerebrospinal fluid cytology at staging. A significant proportion carry a germline SMARCB1/SMARCA4 mutation (rhabdoid tumour predisposition syndrome), warranting germline testing and screening for synchronous extracranial rhabdoid tumours. Presentation reflects raised intracranial pressure and posterior fossa dysfunction: vomiting, lethargy, a bulging fontanelle, head tilt, ataxia, and cranial neuropathies. Rapidly progressive raised intracranial pressure with impaired consciousness Acute hydrocephalus requiring urgent cerebrospinal fluid diversion Evidence of leptomeningeal dissemination on neuraxis imaging A concurrent renal or soft-tissue mass suggesting germline predisposition Misdiagnosing the tumour as medulloblastoma or another embryonal tumour without INI1 immunohistochemistry. Omitting germline SMARCB1/SMARCA4 testing and failing to screen for synchronous extracranial rhabdoid tumours. Understaging by not imaging the whole neuraxis or sampling cerebrospinal fluid. Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour is driven by biallelic inactivation of SMARCB1 (INI1/hSNF5), or less often SMARCA4 (BRG1), core subunits of the SWI/SNF (BAF) chromatin-remodelling complex. Loss of these subunits deregulates chromatin accessibility and enhancer activity, blocking differentiation and driving an aggressive embryonal phenotype, yet the genome is otherwise strikingly stable with SMARCB1 loss frequently the sole recurrent event. Distinct DNA-methylation and expression programmes define the ATRT-TYR (tyrosinase, melanosomal), ATRT-SHH (sonic hedgehog and NOTCH), and ATRT-MYC subgroups. The tumour recapitulates rhabdoid morphology with variable teratoid components and disseminates readily through the cerebrospinal fluid; a germline SMARCB1/SMARCA4 alteration predisposes to multifocal central nervous system and synchronous extracranial rhabdoid tumours. Historically dismal, though intensified multimodal regimens (surgery, high-dose or conventional chemotherapy, and radiotherapy where age permits) have improved survival for some. Very young age, metastatic disease, incomplete resection, and germline predisposition remain adverse factors.

pursuing HNRNPK testing Overlooking craniosynostosis and its risk of raised intracranial pressure Failing to screen for cardiac and renal anomalies at diagnosis Assuming inheritance from a parent when most cases are de novo Au-Kline syndrome is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in HNRNPK, which encodes a heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein that binds nucleic acids and participates in the regulation of transcription, RNA splicing, messenger RNA stability, and translation. Through these activities HNRNPK influences the expression of many genes during development, and reducing its dosage disrupts the coordinated developmental programmes of the brain, heart, kidneys, and skeleton. The resulting haploinsufficiency produces the intellectual disability, hypotonia, characteristic facial features, and the cardiac, renal, and skeletal anomalies of the syndrome. The condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and typically arises de novo. Lifespan is generally not markedly shortened, and the outlook is dominated by intellectual disability of variable degree together with the management of any cardiac, renal, and skeletal anomalies; developmental progress is expected with support, and the presence and severity of major structural anomalies principally shape the long-term outcome.

hearing aids will suffice without evaluating implant candidacy in poor discriminators In auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder the cochlear outer hair cells continue to function, so otoacoustic emissions and the cochlear microphonic persist, but transmission of a synchronised signal along the auditory pathway is disrupted. The lesion may be presynaptic, at the inner hair cell to auditory nerve synapse (synaptopathy, as with otoferlin dysfunction), or neural, affecting spiral ganglion neurones or the auditory nerve itself. Loss of neural synchrony degrades the timing cues that underpin speech understanding, especially in noise, which explains why discrimination is far worse than the pure-tone thresholds would predict. The distinction between synaptopathic and neural forms is central because a functioning nerve can be stimulated directly by a cochlear implant. Outcomes vary widely; some children with milder or maturational forms improve, whereas persistent cases, especially synaptopathic ones, often do well with cochlear implantation, while true neural lesions carry a more guarded prognosis.

Autism Spectrum Disorder — ASD, autism, autistic spectrum disorder, pervasive developmental disorder Global developmental delay or intellectual disability Isolated language disorder or hearing impairment Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder Social (pragmatic) communication disorder Anxiety disorders and selective mutism Rett syndrome and other genetic or metabolic syndromes Severe early deprivation or attachment disorder Formal audiology assessment to exclude hearing loss Structured diagnostic observation and developmental history Genetic evaluation (chromosomal microarray, fragile X testing, targeted panels) Assessment of cognitive and adaptive functioning Screening for co-occurring conditions such as epilepsy or sleep disorders Metabolic testing when clinical features suggest an inborn error A neurodevelopmental disorder defined by persistent deficits in social communication and interaction together with restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests, or activities. Symptoms are present from early development, though they may become fully apparent only when social demands exceed the child's capacities. It is more frequently diagnosed in boys and shows a strong genetic contribution, with increased recurrence risk in siblings. Early signs include reduced eye contact, limited joint attention and pointing, absent or delayed social smiling, and lack of response to name. Repetitive behaviours may include hand-flapping, lining up objects, insistence on routines, and unusual sensory responses. Diagnosis is clinical and based on developmental history and structured observation rather than a laboratory test. Routine developmental surveillance and autism-specific screening in toddlerhood aid early identification. Early intensive behavioural and educational intervention improves functional outcomes. Common co-occurring conditions include intellectual disability, ADHD, anxiety, epilepsy, sleep problems, and gastrointestinal symptoms, and no evidence links vaccines to autism. Regression or loss of previously acquired language or social skills Absence of babbling, pointing, or other gestures by around 12 months No single words by 16 months or no two-word phrases by 24 months Seizures or focal neurological signs suggesting an underlying disorder Concern for self-injurious behaviour or safety Attributing early social and language concerns to shyness and delaying referral Failing to test hearing before attributing delay to autism Overlooking treatable co-occurring conditions such as epilepsy, anxiety, or sleep disturbance Assuming intellectual ability from verbal fluency alone Autism arises from atypical early brain development influenced by a strong and heterogeneous genetic basis, including many single-gene syndromes, copy number variants, and polygenic risk, interacting with prenatal and perinatal factors. These influences alter neuronal connectivity, synaptic function, and the balance of excitation and inhibition during critical periods, affecting circuits underlying social cognition, language, and behavioural flexibility. No single mechanism or biomarker accounts for all cases, reflecting the disorder's biological heterogeneity. Outcomes vary widely; language ability and cognitive level are important predictors, and early intervention improves adaptive functioning, though most individuals have lifelong needs requiring ongoing support.

Autoimmune inner ear disease — AIED, immune-mediated sensorineural hearing loss Sudden sensorineural hearing loss Meniere disease Otosyphilis or other infective labyrinthitis Vestibular schwannoma or other retrocochlear lesion Cogan syndrome and systemic vasculitides Ototoxicity Serial audiometry to document progression and treatment response Assessment for systemic autoimmune disease and vasculitis MRI to exclude a retrocochlear lesion Investigations to exclude otosyphilis and other infective causes Monitored trial of corticosteroids as a diagnostic and therapeutic step A rare cause of bilateral, rapidly progressive sensorineural hearing loss evolving over weeks to months The tempo is faster than age-related loss but slower than sudden sensorineural hearing loss Vestibular symptoms such as imbalance and dizziness may accompany the hearing loss It may be primary (isolated to the ear) or secondary to a systemic autoimmune disease such as vasculitis or Cogan syndrome A response to a trial of corticosteroids supports the diagnosis, which lacks a specific confirmatory test Prompt immunosuppressive treatment offers the best chance of preserving hearing Rapidly progressive bilateral hearing loss Features of systemic vasculitis or Cogan syndrome Interstitial keratitis with audiovestibular symptoms Asymmetric loss suggesting a retrocochlear tumour Attributing progressive bilateral loss to presbyacusis and missing a treatable cause Failing to exclude otosyphilis and retrocochlear lesions Delaying corticosteroids while awaiting non-specific tests Overlooking an underlying systemic autoimmune disease Autoimmune inner ear disease is thought to result from immune-mediated injury to cochlear and vestibular structures, whether through antibodies, immune complexes or cell-mediated mechanisms directed at inner ear antigens. The resulting inflammation damages the cochlea and sometimes the vestibular apparatus, producing progressive sensorineural hearing loss and imbalance. In secondary forms the inner ear is one target of a broader systemic autoimmune or vasculitic process, and the potential reversibility with early immunosuppression reflects the immune rather than purely degenerative basis. Hearing can be preserved or partially recovered if immunosuppression is started early, but delayed treatment often results in permanent loss; cochlear implantation may help advanced cases.

Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome — ALPS, Canale-Smith syndrome Lymphoma and other lymphoproliferative malignancies Common variable immunodeficiency with autoimmune features Evans syndrome from other causes Chronic viral infection causing lymphadenopathy (for example EBV) Other immune dysregulation syndromes such as activated PI3K-delta syndrome Flow cytometry to quantify alpha-beta double-negative T cells Full blood count and direct antiglobulin test for autoimmune cytopenias Serum vitamin B12, IL-10, and soluble FAS ligand as supportive biomarkers In vitro lymphocyte apoptosis assays Genetic testing (FAS, FASLG, CASP10 and related genes) Imaging and, where indicated, lymph node biopsy to exclude lymphoma Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome is a disorder of defective lymphocyte apoptosis, most often caused by mutations in the FAS (TNFRSF6) pathway Impaired programmed cell death allows autoreactive lymphocytes to accumulate, producing chronic non-malignant lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly A hallmark laboratory finding is an expanded population of 'double-negative' T cells (CD3-positive, TCR alpha-beta-positive, but CD4- and CD8-negative) Autoimmune cytopenias are characteristic, particularly autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, immune thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia Unlike most primary immunodeficiencies, the dominant clinical problem is immune dysregulation and autoimmunity rather than recurrent infection, though hyposplenism after splenectomy raises infection risk Supportive biomarkers include raised serum vitamin B12, elevated IL-10 and soluble FAS ligand, and increased IgG There is a substantially increased lifetime risk of lymphoma, warranting long-term surveillance Treatment targets the autoimmune manifestations with immunosuppression and, in refractory cases, agents such as sirolimus or mycophenolate; splenectomy is generally avoided because of infection risk and often incomplete benefit Rapidly enlarging, asymmetric, or hard lymph nodes or systemic B symptoms suggesting lymphoma and needing urgent evaluation Severe autoimmune cytopenia (profound anaemia or thrombocytopenia) causing symptomatic disease Overwhelming infection risk if the patient is asplenic, requiring vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis Massive splenomegaly at risk of rupture Mistaking the chronic lymphadenopathy for lymphoma and vice versa, delaying correct management Performing splenectomy for cytopenias without recognising the resulting infection risk and often limited durable benefit Overlooking the diagnostic value of double-negative T cells and supportive biomarkers Attributing recurrent cytopenias to isolated Evans syndrome without investigating for ALPS Neglecting long-term lymphoma surveillance Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome results from defects in the FAS-mediated (extrinsic) apoptotic pathway that normally deletes activated and autoreactive lymphocytes at the end of an immune response. Germline or somatic mutations in FAS, or in FAS ligand or caspase-10, impair this death signal, so lymphocytes fail to undergo apoptosis and accumulate. This produces the chronic lymphoproliferation (lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly) and the expansion of the unusual alpha-beta double-negative T-cell population. The persistence of autoreactive clones and disturbed immune homeostasis drives autoimmune cytopenias and other autoimmune features, and the impaired deletion of proliferating lymphocytes underlies the elevated risk of lymphoma. Many patients do well with control of autoimmune complications, and lymphoproliferation may lessen with age, but the markedly increased risk of Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma means lifelong surveillance is essential and largely determines long-term outcome.

FAS ligand and caspase-10 defects also occur, and somatic FAS mutations are recognised Supportive biomarkers include raised vitamin B12, soluble FAS ligand, interleukin-10 and interleukin-18 There is a substantially increased lifetime risk of Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma Immunosuppression targeting the autoimmune cytopenias is used rather than routine splenectomy, which carries added sepsis risk in these patients Rapidly enlarging, asymmetric or B-symptom-associated lymphadenopathy suggesting lymphoma transformation Severe autoimmune haemolysis or thrombocytopenia with bleeding Overwhelming sepsis, particularly if the spleen has been removed New cytopenias or organomegaly warranting re-evaluation for malignancy Misdiagnosing the lymphoproliferation as lymphoma and administering unnecessary chemotherapy Performing splenectomy for cytopenias without recognising the heightened post-splenectomy sepsis risk Overlooking the diagnosis in a child labelled as having idiopathic Evans syndrome Failing to arrange long-term lymphoma surveillance Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome results from impaired programmed cell death (apoptosis) of lymphocytes through the FAS receptor pathway. Under normal circumstances, activated lymphocytes that are no longer needed, including autoreactive clones, are removed when FAS engages its ligand and triggers a caspase-dependent death signal. Mutations affecting FAS, its ligand, or downstream caspase-10 disrupt this deletion, so lymphocytes accumulate, producing chronic lymphoproliferation and a characteristic expansion of immature double-negative T cells. The persistence of autoreactive cells drives autoimmunity, predominantly directed at blood cells, and the failure of a key tumour-suppressive apoptotic checkpoint underlies the elevated lymphoma risk. Many patients have a chronic but manageable course with autoimmune cytopenias controlled by immunosuppression and lymphoproliferation that may lessen with age, but the persistently raised risk of lymphoma requires lifelong surveillance and tempers the overall outlook.
