renal, or salivary involvement that supports systemic IgG4-related disease Failing to monitor type 1 patients for relapse after tapering therapy Autoimmune pancreatitis is a corticosteroid-responsive fibroinflammatory disorder of the pancreas. In type 1 disease the pancreas is one target organ of systemic IgG4-related disease, in which an aberrant immune response drives infiltration by IgG4-positive plasma cells and lymphocytes, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis, producing diffuse glandular swelling and a peripheral rim of oedema and fibrosis. Type 2 disease is confined to the pancreas and is characterised histologically by neutrophilic infiltration of the duct epithelium (granulocytic epithelial lesions) without the raised IgG4 or multi-organ features of type 1. Both forms compress the pancreatic and intrapancreatic bile ducts, causing strictures, obstructive jaundice, and secondary exocrine impairment, and both typically regress with immunosuppression. Both subtypes usually respond promptly and completely to corticosteroids, with resolution of jaundice and normalisation of gland size; type 1 disease relapses in a substantial proportion of patients and may need maintenance immunosuppression, whereas type 2 rarely relapses. Long-standing or recurrent disease can lead to pancreatic atrophy with exocrine and endocrine insufficiency.

Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndromes — APS, APS-1, APS-2, APECED, autoimmune polyglandular syndrome, polyglandular deficiency syndrome Isolated autoimmune Addison's disease without polyglandular involvement Isolated autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis or Graves' disease Isolated type 1 diabetes mellitus Idiopathic/isolated hypoparathyroidism IPEX syndrome (immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, X-linked) Insulin autoimmune syndrome (Hirata's syndrome) Adult combined pituitary hormone deficiency with anti-Pit1 autoantibodies (anti-Pit1 syndrome) POEMS syndrome Kearns-Sayre and DIDMOAD (Wolfram) syndromes as causes of multiple endocrine deficiencies Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis from primary immunodeficiencies other than APS-1 (e.g., STAT1 gain-of-function) Congenital rubella associated with thyroiditis and/or diabetes AIRE gene sequencing in suspected APS-1 Anti-interferon alpha and anti-interferon omega antibodies (identify nearly 100% of APS-1) Anticytokine antibodies to IL-17 and IL-22 (support candidiasis of APS-1) Anti-21-hydroxylase (and anti-17-hydroxylase) autoantibodies for Addison's disease risk Morning ACTH and cortisol; cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test if abnormal Serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH for hypoparathyroidism TSH with anti-TPO/anti-thyroglobulin and anti-TSH receptor antibodies Islet autoantibodies (insulin, GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8) and hemoglobin A1c for type 1 diabetes Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies for celiac disease Vitamin B12, CBC, and anti-parietal cell/intrinsic factor antibodies for pernicious anemia Peripheral blood smear for Howell-Jolly bodies to detect asplenism (with splenic ultrasound if positive) Immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced endocrinopathies producing multiple gland failure Sequential isolated autoimmune endocrinopathies occurring by chance Trisomy 21 and Turner's syndrome associated autoimmune endocrine disease Autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes (APS) are divided into two principal categories: APS type 1 (APS-1) and APS type 2 (APS-2); some authors further split APS-2 into APS-3 and APS-4, but this added subdivision adds little to understanding pathogenesis or guiding management (Harrison 22e p.3089). Although the underlying autoimmunity predominantly targets endocrine glands, many nonendocrine tissues can be affected, so a range of nonendocrine disorders is recognized as part of these syndromes (Harrison 22e p.3089). APS-1 (APECED) is defined by a triad of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison's disease; the diagnosis is usually made clinically when two of these three major components are present (Harrison 22e p.3089). APS-1 is rare (<500 reported cases) and classically is autosomal recessive, caused by mutations in the AIRE gene on chromosome 21; AIRE is most highly expressed in thymic medullary epithelial cells where it drives expression of tissue-specific self-antigens such as insulin (Harrison 22e p.3089). Anticytokine autoantibodies are characteristic of APS-1: anti-IL-17A, anti-IL-17F, and anti-IL-22 underlie the mucocutaneous candidiasis, while detection of anti-interferon alpha and anti-interferon omega antibodies identifies nearly 100% of APS-1 cases and is not seen in other autoimmune disorders (Harrison 22e p.3089-3090). APS-1 typically begins in infancy with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (mouth and nails more than skin/esophagus), followed by hypoparathyroidism (>85% of cases) and then Addison's disease (nearly 80%); the interval between components can be many years and the order is variable (Harrison 22e p.3089-3090). APS-2 is more common (prevalence 1-2 per 100,000), shows a female predominance (at least 3:1), has multigenerational inheritance, and usually presents in adulthood with peak incidence between 20 and 60 years (Harrison 22e p.3090). APS-2 is defined by two or more of: primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease, 50-70%), Graves' disease or autoimmune thyroiditis (15-69%), type 1 diabetes (40-50%), and primary hypogonadism; associated conditions include celiac disease, myasthenia gravis, vitiligo, alopecia, serositis, and pernicious anemia (Harrison 22e p.3090). Adrenal insufficiency can be masked by coexisting primary hypothyroidism because low thyroid hormone prolongs the half-life of cortisol; patients with hypothyroidism and possible APS should be screened for adrenal insufficiency, since starting thyroid hormone first can precipitate an adrenal crisis (Harrison 22e p.3090). Antibody screening can detect risk years before clinical disease: anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies are highly predictive of future adrenal insufficiency, and presence of two or more islet autoantibodies with normal glucose tolerance is defined as stage 1 type 1 diabetes with a near-100% lifetime risk of clinical disease (Harrison 22e p.3091). About 50% of patients with Addison's disease develop another autoimmune disorder during their lifetime, so a new diagnosis of Addison's should prompt broader screening for linked conditions (Harrison 22e p.3091). New thyroid hormone replacement in an undiagnosed patient with adrenal insufficiency can precipitate an adrenal crisis Treatment of mucocutaneous candidiasis with ketoconazole in a patient with subclinical adrenal insufficiency may also precipitate adrenal crisis Hyperpigmentation, unexplained hyponatremia/hyperkalemia, or hypotension signaling evolving Addison's disease Tetany or seizures from hypocalcemia indicating hypoparathyroidism Howell-Jolly bodies on smear indicating functional asplenism and increased infection risk in APS-1 Refractory diarrhea or obstipation suggesting autoimmune destruction of enterochromaffin(-like) cells Chronic oral candidiasis with leukoplakia-like atrophic change carrying a risk of future carcinoma Initiating thyroid hormone before excluding/treating adrenal insufficiency, precipitating adrenal crisis Failing to recognize that one component disorder warrants screening for others, and that siblings of an APS-1 patient should be considered affected even with a single component Attributing chronic candidiasis purely to local infection rather than recognizing it as a marker of APS-1 Missing functional asplenism (Howell-Jolly bodies) in APS-1, which raises infection risk Overlooking subclinical/preclinical disease detectable only by autoantibodies and physiologic testing APS-1 is a monogenic, classically autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the AIRE (autoimmune regulator) gene on chromosome 21. AIRE is most highly expressed in thymic medullary epithelial cells, where it promotes expression of tissue-specific self-antigens; its loss reduces this expression and is thought to allow autoreactive T cells to escape central (thymic) deletion. Over 100 mutations are described, with higher frequency in certain ethnic groups (Iranian Jews, Sardinians, Finns, Norwegians, Irish). Newly recognized autosomal dominant mutations cluster in the PHD1 domain and tend to cause later-onset, less aggressive disease. Patients develop anticytokine autoantibodies (anti-IL-17A, IL-17F, IL-22, and type 1 interferons). In contrast, APS-2 is polygenic, with the dominant risk in the HLA complex on chromosome 6: Addison's disease in APS-2 is strongly linked to HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4, with additional contributions from HLA-B8, DQ2, DQ8, and DRB1 subtypes. Non-HLA immune genes including MIC-A (the 5.1 allele strongly associated with Addison's), PTPN22, CTLA4, and IL-2R-alpha variants further modulate susceptibility. Organ damage in both syndromes is mediated by organ-specific autoantibodies and autoreactive T cells against targets such as 21-hydroxylase, GAD65, thyroid peroxidase, transglutaminase, and intrinsic factor (Harrison 22e p.3089-3091). These are chronic, progressive disorders in which individual component diseases continue to emerge over years to decades, so cumulative prevalence rises with age and lifelong surveillance is required. APS-1 typically presents earliest (often infancy) and its chronic candidiasis is nearly always present and poorly responsive to treatment. In APS-2, autoantibodies can precede clinical disease by many years, allowing early detection; about half of patients with Addison's disease develop an additional autoimmune disorder over their lifetime, and individuals with two or more islet autoantibodies have a near-100% lifetime risk of clinical type 1 diabetes. With timely hormone replacement and monitoring, prognosis for individual endocrinopathies is generally favorable, but unrecognized adrenal insufficiency or precipitated adrenal crisis is potentially fatal (Harrison 22e p.3089-3091). No formal severity grading is defined; classification is by type (APS-1 vs APS-2, with proposed APS-3/APS-4 subtypes) based on the constellation of component autoimmune disorders. For type 1 diabetes risk within APS-2, presence of two or more islet autoantibodies with normal glucose tolerance is staged as stage 1 disease (Harrison 22e p.3089-3091).

Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 — APS-1, APECED, autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 Isolated autoimmune Addison disease or hypoparathyroidism Other primary immunodeficiencies with candidiasis IPEX syndrome DiGeorge syndrome (for hypoparathyroidism) Assessment of the endocrine components (calcium, adrenal, gonadal, thyroid, glucose) AIRE genetic testing Autoantibody profiling, including anti-interferon-omega Evaluation for chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis Ongoing periodic surveillance for evolving components A rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene The classic triad is chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and primary adrenal insufficiency Diagnosis is usually made when two of the three classic components are present It typically presents in childhood, often with candidiasis first, then hypoparathyroidism, then adrenal failure Many other autoimmune features occur, including hypogonadism, type 1 diabetes, hepatitis, enamel and nail dystrophy and keratopathy Lifelong surveillance is needed because components accrue over time; interferon-omega and anti-cytokine antibodies are characteristic markers Adrenal crisis from unrecognised adrenal insufficiency Severe hypocalcaemia from hypoparathyroidism Autoimmune hepatitis or malabsorption New endocrine failure during follow-up Failing to anticipate additional components developing over time Missing evolving adrenal insufficiency (life-threatening) Attributing candidiasis to simple immunodeficiency without recognising the syndrome Overlooking the autosomal recessive inheritance and need for family evaluation Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 results from loss-of-function mutations in the AIRE gene, which normally drives expression of tissue-specific self-antigens in the thymus to delete autoreactive T cells. Defective AIRE function impairs central immune tolerance, allowing autoreactive lymphocytes to escape and attack multiple endocrine and non-endocrine tissues. The chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis reflects autoantibodies against T-helper-17 cytokines (such as IL-17 and IL-22), while organ-specific autoimmunity produces the endocrine failures and other manifestations. The condition is lifelong with morbidity from cumulative organ involvement; with hormone replacement, antifungal treatment and vigilant monitoring, prognosis is much improved, though adrenal crisis and other complications remain risks.

Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 — APS-2, Schmidt syndrome Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 Isolated autoimmune Addison disease Isolated autoimmune thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes IPEX syndrome Secondary (pituitary) endocrine failure Assessment of adrenal, thyroid and glucose status Relevant autoantibodies (adrenal/21-hydroxylase, thyroid, islet, transglutaminase) Screening for coeliac disease and pernicious anaemia HLA and family assessment where appropriate Periodic surveillance for new components The commonest autoimmune polyglandular syndrome, defined by primary adrenal insufficiency with autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes It is more common in adults and in women, with a polygenic and HLA-associated inheritance rather than a single gene The combination of Addison disease and autoimmune thyroid disease is known as Schmidt syndrome Other associated autoimmune conditions include coeliac disease, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo and premature ovarian insufficiency Starting thyroid hormone before treating coexisting adrenal insufficiency can precipitate an adrenal crisis Screening at-risk individuals and relatives for evolving endocrine autoimmunity is important Adrenal crisis, especially if thyroid hormone is started first Unexplained hypoglycaemia or reduced insulin requirement signalling adrenal insufficiency Severe hyponatraemia New autoimmune component during follow-up Giving thyroid hormone before excluding or treating adrenal insufficiency Attributing improving diabetes control to good management when it reflects Addison disease Missing associated coeliac disease or pernicious anaemia Failing to monitor for evolving components Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 is a polygenic disorder of immune tolerance, strongly associated with particular HLA haplotypes and other susceptibility genes, in which organ-specific autoantibodies and autoreactive T cells target several endocrine glands. Unlike type 1, there is no single causative gene. Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex, thyroid and pancreatic beta cells produces the characteristic cluster, and the tempo of gland involvement varies, with components often appearing years apart. With appropriate hormone replacement and monitoring the prognosis is good, but unrecognised adrenal insufficiency, particularly during intercurrent illness or after starting thyroxine, can be life-threatening.

Autoimmunity and Autoimmune Diseases — Autoimmune disease, AD, Loss of immune tolerance, Autoimmunity Organ-specific AD (e.g., Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves disease, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia/autoimmune gastritis, myasthenia gravis, multiple sclerosis, vitiligo, autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis) (p.2822) Systemic AD (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, primary antiphospholipid syndrome, Sjogren syndrome, systemic sclerosis, idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, mixed connective tissue disease) (p.2822) Systemic vasculitides (giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, polyarteritis nodosa, ANCA-associated vasculitis, anti-GBM/Goodpasture disease, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, IgA/Henoch-Schonlein vasculitis, Behcet disease) (p.2822) Paraneoplastic autoimmune syndromes (Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, paraneoplastic pemphigus, dermatomyositis, anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis with ovarian cancer) (p.2826) Drug-induced lupus (antihistone-antibody positive) and immune checkpoint inhibitor-related immune adverse events (p.2826) Infections that trigger or mimic autoimmune flares: group A streptococcal infection underlying rheumatic fever via M-protein/myosin cross-reactivity (p.2825) Coxsackievirus (myocarditis, Hashimoto thyroiditis, T1DM) and influenza A (T1DM, IgA vasculitis) as proposed autoimmune triggers (p.2825) Epstein-Barr virus linked to SLE, MS, RA, celiac disease, and Sjogren syndrome (p.2825) SARS-CoV-2-associated myocarditis, antiphospholipid syndrome, MIS-C, Kawasaki disease, and Guillain-Barre syndrome (p.2826) Disease-specific autoantibody panels: anti-dsDNA and anti-RNP (SLE); anti-Ro/anti-La and rheumatoid factor (Sjogren); ACPA, anti-carbamylated antibodies, rheumatoid factor (RA); anti-MPO and anti-PR3 (ANCA-associated vasculitis); anti-type IV collagen (Goodpasture) (p.2825) Anti-TSH-receptor antibodies (Graves); anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin (Hashimoto) (p.2825) Islet-related antibodies in T1DM: anti-insulin, anti-GAD (glutamic acid decarboxylase), anti-protein-tyrosine-phosphatase/IA-2; antibodies to multiple targets confer higher risk of progression (p.2825) Anti-parietal cell antibodies in pernicious anemia (present in 70-90% of patients) and antimitochondrial antibodies (anti-pyruvate dehydrogenase) in primary biliary cholangitis (p.2825) Myositis-specific antibodies (anti-aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, anti-Mi2, anti-MDA5, anti-TIF1-gamma, anti-HMGCR, anti-cN1A) for risk stratification in inflammatory myopathies (p.2825) Antihistone antibodies for suspected drug-induced lupus (p.2826) Serum tryptase, 24-h urinary 5-HIAA, and metanephrines to exclude mast-cell, carcinoid, and pheochromocytoma mimics when relevant (contextual) (p.2821) Paraneoplastic syndromes presenting before a cancer diagnosis (e.g., dermatomyositis, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, immune thrombocytopenia, vitiligo, thyroiditis) (p.2826) Drug-induced autoimmunity from antibiotics, antihypertensives, antiarrhythmics, TNF inhibitors, antiseizure agents (p.2826) Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia and mast-cell activation disorders presenting with multisystem symptoms (contextual, adjacent chapter) (p.2821) Autoimmunity (development of autoantibodies or autoreactive T-cell responses against self-antigens) is present in essentially all individuals and tends to increase with age; it does not by itself imply disease. Autoimmune disease (AD) arises only when a loss of tolerance produces clinically relevant, pathogenic responses (p.2821-2822). Roughly 150 organ-specific and systemic ADs have been described; in 2009 the U.S. prevalence was estimated at 7.6-9.4% of the population (about 25-31 million people), likely an underestimate, with an apparent ongoing rise in incidence and prevalence (p.2822). ADs predominantly affect women and, as a group, rank among the top 10 leading causes of death in women; an affected person carries a higher risk of developing a second autoimmune condition, of autoimmunity in relatives, and of certain cancers and premature cardiovascular disease (p.2822). AD is a multistep process: genetic and environmental factors drive immune dysregulation and loss of tolerance, and autoantibodies can be detectable years before clinical symptoms appear (p.2822-2825). HLA haplotype is considered the best single predictor of AD risk; specific HLA-DR types, complement-component deficiencies, and genes in the type I interferon and B-/T-cell pathways raise risk, and many susceptibility genes (e.g., STAT4, PTPN22) are shared across several ADs (p.2822-2823). Autoantibodies serve as diagnostic tools and, in some diseases, as markers of activity or worse outcome; however, for several autoantibodies a specific pathogenic role has not been established, and the relevant autoantigens of many ADs remain unknown (p.2825). Natural autoantibodies are mainly IgM, encoded by unmutated V(D)J genes with moderate self-affinity, and are not pathogenic; the harmful autoantibodies of AD are high-affinity, somatically mutated IgG generated by somatic hypermutation, class switching, and antigen-driven clonal selection (p.2824-2825). Dysregulated type I interferon signaling is implicated across SLE, primary Sjogren syndrome, and idiopathic inflammatory myopathies; neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation externalizes modified autoantigens and is implicated in SLE, ANCA-associated vasculitis, myopathies, antiphospholipid syndrome, and RA (p.2823-2824). Many ADs are female-predominant; two X chromosomes (women, and men with Klinefelter XXY) increase expression of X-linked immunity genes such as TLR-7/8 and IRAK-1, and breakdown of X-inactivation has been linked to autoimmunity (p.2823). Infections can both trigger AD and provoke flares via molecular mimicry, epitope spreading, bystander/adjuvant effects, release of hidden self-antigens, and epigenetic changes; EBV is linked to SLE, MS, RA, celiac disease, and Sjogren, and SARS-CoV-2 has been associated with myocarditis, new APS, MIS-C, Kawasaki disease, and Guillain-Barre (p.2825-2826). Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) cause immune-related adverse events in up to 85% of treated patients (dermatitis, arthritis, thyroiditis, colitis among the most common); most are mild and overall survival/time to progression is generally not influenced by their occurrence (p.2826). Drug-induced lupus is a well-recognized iatrogenic AD characterized by antihistone antibodies; in many cases discontinuing the offending drug is sufficient to abate symptoms (p.2826). New autoimmune-pattern symptoms in a patient on an immune checkpoint inhibitor (irAE such as colitis, thyroiditis, arthritis, dermatitis) — can be severe and may persist after stopping therapy (p.2826) Sudden new autoimmunity or autoantibody synthesis following SARS-CoV-2 or other viral infection (APS, myocarditis, MIS-C, Guillain-Barre) (p.2826) Autoimmune presentation that may herald an occult malignancy (paraneoplastic syndromes often precede cancer diagnosis) (p.2826) Anti-Ro-positive pregnancy: IgG anti-Ro crosses the placenta and can cause neonatal lupus and congenital heart block in the fetus (p.2825) Multiple positive autoantibody specificities (e.g., several islet antibodies in at-risk individuals) signaling high likelihood of progression to overt disease (p.2825) Equating autoimmunity with autoimmune disease: autoantibodies/autoreactivity occur in healthy individuals (and relatives) and increase with age without necessarily causing disease (p.2821-2822, p.2825). Assuming any detected autoantibody is pathogenic — several are used only as diagnostic or activity/outcome markers without a proven causal role (p.2825). Overlooking that classification criteria (e.g., for SLE) were designed for clinical-trial enrollment, not for individual diagnosis (contextual, p.2827). Attributing AD to infection on circumstantial grounds — causality is often unproven and supported mainly by animal models (p.2825-2826). Missing iatrogenic causes: failing to recognize drug-induced lupus (antihistone antibodies) or checkpoint-inhibitor irAEs, where stopping the agent may resolve symptoms (p.2826). Autoimmune disease reflects a failure of self-tolerance in a genetically predisposed host exposed to environmental and stochastic 'hits'. Central tolerance (deletion of autoreactive T cells in the thymus and high-affinity autoreactive B cells in the marrow) and peripheral tolerance (anergy from lack of costimulation, regulatory lymphocyte suppression, inhibitory costimulation, removal of autoreactive cells) normally restrain autoreactivity; impairment of these mechanisms allows pathogenic autoimmune responses. Susceptibility is largely polygenic (HLA-DR types, complement deficiencies, type I IFN-pathway and B-/T-cell genes such as STAT4 and PTPN22), with rare monogenic forms, and epigenetic programming (histone modifications, altered DNA methylation, trained immunity) further shapes risk. On the innate side, dysregulated or proinflammatory cell death (apoptosis, pyroptosis, necroptosis, NETosis) plus impaired clearance of dead-cell debris and defective nucleases prolong exposure of modified nucleic-acid autoantigens; endosomal TLR-7/8/9 and cytosolic sensors then drive type I interferon production and inflammasome activation. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (major IFN-alpha producers), conventional dendritic cells, neutrophils/low-density granulocytes with aberrant NET formation, monocytes/macrophages with defective phagocytosis, and NK cells are all implicated. On the adaptive side, autoreactive CD4/CD8 T cells, Treg deficiency, and imbalance between costimulatory and inhibitory pathways (PD-1, CTLA-4) and cytokines (IL-2, IL-6, IL-17, IL-33) promote disease; pathogenic high-affinity IgG autoantibodies form immune complexes that deposit in tissue, fix complement, opsonize, engage activating Fc receptors, and drive type I IFN production. Inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-17, type I IFNs) sustain and amplify tissue injury. Female sex (sex hormones, X-chromosome dosage) and immune aging (inflammaging with senescent, proinflammatory cells) further potentiate autoimmunity. ADs are described as chronic, incurable conditions that significantly impair quality of life and, in many cases, carry accelerated mortality; as a group they are among the top 10 leading causes of death in women. An individual with one AD has elevated risk of additional autoimmune conditions, certain cancers, and premature cardiovascular disease. Autoantibodies (e.g., ACPA in RA, islet antibodies in T1DM, antimitochondrial antibodies in PBC) may precede clinical disease by years to a decade and can mark worse prognosis. Better understanding of pathophysiology is hoped to enable primary or secondary prevention (e.g., trials of oral insulin in T1DM-autoantibody-positive infants and at-risk RA studies), though more data are needed (p.2822, p.2825-2826). No single unifying severity grading exists for autoimmunity as a whole; severity and classification are disease-specific and covered in the individual disease chapters. Autoantibody breadth/titer (e.g., number of islet antibodies in T1DM risk) and specific specificities (e.g., anti-TIF1-gamma marking cancer-associated myositis, anti-HMGCR statin-induced myositis, anti-cN1A inclusion body myositis) help stratify risk and outcome (p.2825).

infection as a trigger Skin survey for pressure injury, ingrown toenail, or other cutaneous triggers ECG and, when neurological features are present, brain imaging to exclude intracranial haemorrhage A life-threatening emergency occurring in patients with spinal-cord injury at or above the sixth thoracic (T6) level Triggered by a noxious stimulus below the level of the lesion, most often bladder distension from a blocked catheter or bowel impaction Presents with severe paroxysmal hypertension, a pounding headache, and flushing and sweating above the lesion, with pallor, piloerection, and cool skin below it Reflex bradycardia and nasal congestion are common, and blurred vision and anxiety may occur Uncontrolled hypertension can cause seizures, intracranial haemorrhage, retinal detachment, or death Immediate management: sit the patient upright, loosen tight clothing, and urgently identify and remove the triggering stimulus (relieve the bladder or bowel) If severe hypertension persists after the trigger is removed, rapid-onset, short-acting antihypertensive agents are used Patient and carer education on prevention and early recognition is essential, as episodes commonly recur Blood pressure rising markedly above the patient's baseline Severe headache with neurological signs suggesting intracranial haemorrhage Seizures or acute visual loss Hypertension persisting despite removal of the presumed trigger Laying the patient flat, which raises blood pressure further, instead of sitting them upright Failing to look for and relieve a blocked catheter or bowel impaction as the first step Missing the diagnosis in a patient whose baseline blood pressure is low, so a 'normal' reading is actually a dangerous surge Treating the hypertension pharmacologically without removing the underlying noxious stimulus Autonomic dysreflexia arises when a spinal-cord lesion at or above the sixth thoracic segment disconnects the splanchnic sympathetic outflow from supraspinal inhibitory control. A noxious stimulus below the injury, such as a full bladder, generates afferent impulses that trigger an unmodulated reflex sympathetic discharge below the lesion, producing widespread vasoconstriction and a steep rise in blood pressure. Baroreceptors detect the hypertension and drive compensatory parasympathetic (vagal) outflow, causing bradycardia together with vasodilatation, flushing, and sweating above the level of the lesion. However, descending inhibitory signals cannot cross the injury to switch off the sympathetic storm below it, so the hypertension persists until the offending stimulus is removed. With prompt recognition and removal of the trigger an episode usually resolves quickly, but delayed treatment of the hypertensive surge can cause stroke, seizures, or death; recurrent episodes are common in susceptible patients and warrant preventive strategies.

Autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia — ADH, ADH type 1 (activating CASR), autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia with hypercalciuria, activating calcium-sensing receptor mutation Idiopathic or autoimmune hypoparathyroidism Post-surgical hypoparathyroidism DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) and other syndromic hypoparathyroidism Vitamin D deficiency or resistance Hypomagnesaemia causing functional hypoparathyroidism Pseudohypoparathyroidism (with raised rather than suppressed PTH) Serum calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormone (hypocalcaemia with low or inappropriately normal PTH) Serum magnesium (activating receptor may also lower magnesium) Urinary calcium excretion demonstrating relative hypercalciuria CASR (and GNA11) gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis and subtype Renal ultrasound to detect nephrocalcinosis or renal stones Vitamin D status and, where relevant, family biochemical screening Autosomal dominant hypocalcaemia type 1 is caused by activating (gain-of-function) mutations in the calcium-sensing receptor gene (CASR); a type 2 form results from GNA11 mutations The activated receptor perceives normal calcium as high, so parathyroid hormone is suppressed and hypocalcaemia occurs with inappropriately low or normal PTH rather than the raised PTH expected as a compensatory response In the kidney the overactive receptor also reduces tubular calcium reabsorption, producing relative hypercalciuria for the level of serum calcium Many patients are mildly symptomatic or asymptomatic, but some present with paraesthesia, tetany, or seizures, and it is a cause of hypoparathyroidism-like biochemistry The key management caution is that standard treatment with calcium and active vitamin D readily worsens hypercalciuria, risking nephrocalcinosis, renal stones, and impaired renal function, so treatment is reserved for symptomatic hypocalcaemia and kept modest It should be considered in familial or apparently idiopathic hypoparathyroidism, and distinguished from it because the treatment threshold and targets differ Symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany, laryngospasm, or seizures Nephrocalcinosis or declining renal function, often precipitated or worsened by treatment Marked hypercalciuria during calcium and active vitamin D therapy Prolonged QT interval or cardiac manifestations of severe hypocalcaemia Treating to a normal serum calcium as in ordinary hypoparathyroidism, provoking hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis Misdiagnosing as isolated idiopathic hypoparathyroidism and missing the familial, receptor-based cause Overlooking coexisting hypomagnesaemia that can aggravate the biochemical picture Failing to monitor urinary calcium and renal imaging during calcium and active vitamin D therapy The calcium-sensing receptor is a G-protein-coupled receptor on parathyroid and renal tubular cells that monitors extracellular calcium and sets the threshold for parathyroid hormone secretion and renal calcium handling. Activating CASR mutations (or GNA11 mutations affecting downstream signalling) lower this set point, so the receptor signals as if calcium were elevated even at normal or low concentrations. Parathyroid hormone secretion is therefore inappropriately suppressed, causing hypocalcaemia, while enhanced receptor signalling in the renal tubule decreases calcium reabsorption and increases urinary calcium excretion. The combination gives hypocalcaemia with low or inappropriately normal PTH and a tendency to hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis. Prognosis is generally good when the diagnosis is recognised and treatment is restrained; many patients tolerate mild hypocalcaemia without therapy, but aggressive correction can cause hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, and chronic kidney disease. The aim is to relieve symptoms while keeping serum calcium in the low-normal range and limiting urinary calcium.

proteolytic inactivation. Stabilised FGF23 accumulates and suppresses renal sodium-phosphate cotransport, producing phosphaturia and hypophosphataemia, while also inhibiting 1-alpha-hydroxylase so that 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is inappropriately low or normal. Because iron deficiency stimulates FGF23 transcription while normally increasing cleavage, in ADHR the uncleavable mutant accumulates during iron-deficient states, explaining the disease's characteristic fluctuation and its links to menstruation, pregnancy, and growth. The net result is defective mineralisation manifesting as rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults. Course is variable, ranging from spontaneous resolution to persistent phosphate wasting; with phosphate and active vitamin D therapy and attention to iron status, most affected children achieve improved growth and bone health, though monitoring for treatment complications is required.

secreted protein that bridges presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes through interactions with ADAM proteins and helps regulate synaptic excitability and network maturation in the lateral temporal Inherited LGI1-related lateral temporal epilepsy is generally benign, with infrequent focal seizures that usually respond well to antiseizure medication and normal cognition between events. This contrasts with the acquired anti-LGI1 encephalitis, which is a more serious condition requiring immunotherapy.

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (PKD1/PKD2) — ADPKD, PKD1, PKD2, polycystin, adult polycystic kidney disease Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease Simple renal cysts or acquired cystic disease of chronic kidney disease Tuberous sclerosis complex with renal cysts and angiomyolipomas Von Hippel-Lindau disease with renal cysts and tumours Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease Nephronophthisis and other ciliopathies Renal ultrasound applying age-specific cyst-number diagnostic criteria MRI or CT for total kidney volume measurement and prognostication Blood pressure assessment and renal function monitoring Urinalysis for haematuria, proteinuria and infection MR angiography screening for intracranial aneurysm in selected patients (family history or high-risk occupation) Genetic testing of PKD1 and PKD2 when imaging is inconclusive or for family or reproductive planning The commonest inherited kidney disease, characterised by progressive bilateral renal cyst formation and enlarging kidneys Most disease results from mutations in PKD1 (encoding polycystin-1); PKD2 (polycystin-2) disease is generally milder with later kidney failure Typical presentations include hypertension, flank or abdominal pain, haematuria, urinary tract infection, stones, or an incidental family finding Extrarenal features include hepatic cysts, intracranial aneurysms, cardiac valve abnormalities and abdominal wall or inguinal hernias Diagnosis is usually by ultrasound using age-adjusted cyst-count criteria in an at-risk individual, with genetic testing where imaging is equivocal Total kidney volume is a validated marker of disease progression and helps identify rapid progressors Blood pressure control with renin-angiotensin blockade and, in selected rapidly progressing patients, a vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist can slow decline Sudden severe headache suggesting rupture of an intracranial aneurysm Cyst infection or haemorrhage with fever, severe pain or sepsis Rapidly rising blood pressure or accelerating decline in renal function Gross haematuria with clot colic or haemodynamic compromise Applying adult ultrasound cyst criteria to young at-risk relatives, in whom absence of cysts does not exclude disease Undertreating hypertension, a major modifiable driver of cardiovascular risk and progression Offering aneurysm screening indiscriminately rather than to those with family history or specific risk Missing cyst infection because standard imaging and cultures can be unremarkable ADPKD is caused by heterozygous mutations in PKD1 or PKD2, encoding polycystin-1 and polycystin-2, proteins that localise to the primary cilium and regulate tubular cell proliferation, differentiation and fluid secretion. A somatic second hit in individual tubular cells is thought to trigger focal cyst initiation, and cysts then expand through cell proliferation and fluid secretion driven in part by cyclic AMP and vasopressin signalling. Progressive cyst growth distorts and compresses the surrounding parenchyma, causing interstitial fibrosis, activation of the renin-angiotensin system, hypertension and gradual loss of glomerular filtration over decades. Progression is variable, with many PKD1 patients reaching end-stage kidney disease in mid-to-late adulthood while PKD2 disease progresses more slowly; blood pressure control and, in rapid progressors, vasopressin antagonism can delay kidney failure.

Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease — ADTKD, UMOD-related kidney disease, MUC1-related kidney disease, uromodulin kidney disease, familial juvenile hyperuricaemic nephropathy, medullary cystic kidney disease type 2 Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease HNF1B-associated kidney disease (RCAD) Chronic hypertensive or ischaemic nephropathy Reflux nephropathy and chronic obstructive uropathy Analgesic or other chronic interstitial nephritis Nephronophthisis and other ciliopathies Serum urate, especially seeking early-onset or disproportionate hyperuricaemia Urinalysis and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio demonstrating bland sediment and low-grade proteinuria Renal ultrasound to assess kidney size and any medullary cysts Detailed multigenerational family history and eGFR trajectory Targeted genetic testing (UMOD, MUC1, HNF1B, REN) with specialised MUC1 assays where standard sequencing is negative Kidney biopsy in selected cases showing nonspecific tubulointerstitial fibrosis A group of autosomal dominant disorders causing slowly progressive chronic kidney disease with a bland urinary sediment and little or no proteinuria The commonest subtypes are caused by variants in UMOD (uromodulin) and MUC1 (mucin-1); other genes include HNF1B, REN and SEC61A1 The UMOD form is classically associated with early-onset hyperuricaemia and gout, sometimes preceding renal impairment Imaging and urinalysis are typically unremarkable, so a strong family history of unexplained CKD across generations is often the key clue Kidneys may be normal or small with occasional medullary cysts; overt cysts are inconstant, so absence does not exclude the diagnosis Progression to kidney failure usually occurs over decades, with wide variability even within the same family Definitive diagnosis relies on genetic testing, as histology shows nonspecific tubulointerstitial fibrosis; MUC1 variants may need specialised assays Rapidly declining renal function inconsistent with the usual indolent course Anaemia disproportionate to CKD stage, suggesting the REN subtype Recurrent or tophaceous gout at a young age Progression to advanced CKD requiring planning for renal replacement or transplantation Dismissing the diagnosis because imaging and urinalysis look normal Missing the diagnosis when standard gene panels fail to detect the MUC1 variant Attributing early gout solely to lifestyle rather than considering UMOD disease Overlooking the autosomal dominant inheritance and failing to screen at-risk relatives ADTKD is a family of monogenic tubulointerstitial diseases in which a defective protein disrupts tubular epithelial cell function and triggers progressive interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy. In the UMOD form, mutant uromodulin misfolds and is retained within the endoplasmic reticulum of thick ascending limb cells, causing cellular stress, impaired sodium handling that promotes urate retention (hyperuricaemia and gout), and eventual nephron loss. In the MUC1 form, a frameshift variant generates an abnormal mucin-1 protein that accumulates and injures tubular cells. Regardless of gene, the shared final pathway is chronic tubulointerstitial injury with fibrosis, producing slowly declining glomerular filtration with characteristically bland urine and minimal proteinuria. The disease progresses slowly, typically over several decades, culminating in kidney failure at a variable age even within families; the extrarenal burden is limited, and kidney transplantation is not complicated by disease recurrence in the graft.

and falls support Rapid deterioration or new focal signs suggesting an alternative or superimposed process Severe spasticity causing painful contractures and immobility Recurrent falls with injury Overlooking retinal nerve fibre hypermyelination, a valuable and relatively specific clue Missing the characteristic pontine MRI changes that support the diagnosis Failing to test for treatable recessive ataxias before settling on ARSACS ARSACS is caused by biallelic mutations in SACS, encoding sacsin, a very large multidomain protein with chaperone-like activity that is important for protein quality control and mitochondrial dynamics, and is highly expressed in cerebellar Purkinje cells. Loss of functional sacsin impairs handling of misfolded proteins and disturbs the mitochondrial network and neurofilament organisation, leading to degeneration of Purkinje cells, corticospinal tracts and peripheral nerves. This combined central and peripheral pathology produces the hallmark triad of cerebellar ataxia, pyramidal spasticity and peripheral neuropathy, with the retinal nerve fibre hypermyelination reflecting the disorder's effect on the retinal nerve fibre layer. ARSACS is slowly progressive; ambulation is typically preserved into adulthood before wheelchair dependence develops in later life, and disability accrues from worsening spastic ataxia and neuropathy, though life expectancy is often only modestly reduced.

(ARHR2) Both genes normally restrain osteocyte FGF23 production, so their loss leads to excess circulating FGF23 and the familiar phosphaturic biochemical picture Presents with rickets, short stature, bowing, and bone pain in children and osteomalacia in adults, similar to X-linked and autosomal dominant forms Biochemistry shows hypophosphataemia, renal phosphate wasting, and inappropriately low or normal 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D with normal calcium and parathyroid hormone ENPP1 loss also reduces pyrophosphate and is associated with generalised arterial calcification of infancy, so cardiovascular assessment matters in ARHR2 Because it is recessive, a family history may be absent, and consanguinity increases risk Treatment follows the FGF23-driven paradigm with oral phosphate salts and active vitamin D, or FGF23-directed antibody therapy where available Signs of arterial calcification or cardiovascular compromise in an infant with ENPP1 disease Severe progressive skeletal deformity or growth failure Enthesopathy and joint stiffness limiting mobility Nephrocalcinosis or hyperparathyroidism emerging on therapy Overlooking the recessive inheritance when there is no affected parent Missing arterial calcification in ENPP1 deficiency by focusing only on the bone disease Failing to distinguish ARHR from X-linked disease, altering genetic counselling Inducing nephrocalcinosis and secondary hyperparathyroidism with unmonitored conventional therapy Dentin matrix protein 1 (DMP1) and ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterase 1 (ENPP1) are expressed by osteocytes and normally suppress FGF23 synthesis. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations release this brake, so osteocytes overproduce FGF23. Elevated FGF23 drives renal phosphate wasting through downregulation of proximal sodium-phosphate cotransporters and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase, leaving 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D inappropriately low. Chronic hypophosphataemia impairs skeletal mineralisation, producing rickets and osteomalacia. In ARHR2, ENPP1 deficiency additionally lowers extracellular pyrophosphate, an inhibitor of ectopic mineralisation, which paradoxically predisposes to arterial and periarticular calcification alongside the phosphate-wasting bone disease. Skeletal outcome with phosphate and active vitamin D therapy resembles other FGF23-driven rickets, but ARHR2 carries an added burden from ENPP1-related vascular calcification that can dominate the prognosis and requires dedicated cardiovascular follow-up.

from pulmonary hypoplasia Severe or poorly controlled hypertension in an infant or child Variceal bleeding or features of decompensated portal hypertension Ascending cholangitis with fever and sepsis children Failing to arrange surveillance for portal hypertension and cholangitis ARPKD results from biallelic mutations in PKHD1, encoding fibrocystin (polyductin), a protein of the primary cilium and basal body of renal and biliary epithelium. Defective fibrocystin disrupts normal tubular and ductal development, producing non-obstructive fusiform dilatation of the renal collecting ducts and abnormal remodelling of the biliary tree (ductal plate malformation) with congenital hepatic fibrosis. Massive kidney enlargement in utero can restrict lung growth and amniotic fluid, while progressive tubular and interstitial injury impairs renal concentrating ability and glomerular filtration, and hepatic fibrosis leads to portal hypertension. Outcome depends heavily on surviving the neonatal period, since perinatal respiratory failure is a major early risk; children who survive infancy can live into adulthood but face progressive kidney failure and complications of congenital hepatic fibrosis requiring lifelong specialist care.

Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia (ARSACS / SACS) — ARSACS, autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay, SACS-related spastic ataxia, sacsin deficiency Friedreich ataxia Hereditary spastic paraplegia with cerebellar features, such as SPG7 Other recessive ataxias including ataxia with oculomotor apraxia and ataxia-telangiectasia Cerebral palsy in young children presenting with spasticity and incoordination Leukodystrophies affecting cerebellar and corticospinal pathways Treatable metabolic ataxias such as vitamin E deficiency and cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis Brain MRI to identify vermian atrophy, linear pontine hypointensities and a bulky pons Nerve conduction studies to document the peripheral neuropathy Optical coherence tomography or fundoscopy for retinal nerve fibre thickening SACS sequencing by gene panel or exome, with copy-number analysis Screening for treatable recessive ataxias (vitamin E level, plasma cholestanol) Family history and consanguinity assessment to support recessive inheritance Autosomal recessive spastic ataxias are a group in which cerebellar ataxia combines with pyramidal spasticity; the prototype is ARSACS, caused by biallelic variants in SACS, which encodes the chaperone-like protein sacsin ARSACS classically presents in early childhood with a triad of progressive cerebellar ataxia, lower-limb spasticity and a peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy A characteristic feature is thickening of the retinal nerve fibres, demonstrable on fundoscopy or optical coherence tomography Brain MRI often shows superior cerebellar vermian atrophy together with linear pontine hypointensities and a bulky pons, forming a recognisable pattern Although first described in the Charlevoix-Saguenay region of Quebec, ARSACS is now identified worldwide with a wide range of SACS variants Other recessive spastic ataxias, including SPG7-related and metabolic causes, should be considered where the picture is atypical Diagnosis combines the clinical triad, the characteristic MRI and retinal findings, and molecular confirmation, usually by sequencing or a gene panel There is no cure; management is supportive, addressing spasticity, ataxia, neuropathy and mobility Rapid deterioration or regression suggesting an alternative or acquired disorder Severe bulbar or respiratory involvement requiring supportive intervention Cognitive decline or white-matter change raising the possibility of a leukodystrophy A treatable metabolic mimic on screening (vitamin E deficiency or cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis) that must not be missed Missing a treatable recessive mimic such as vitamin E deficiency or cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis before settling on ARSACS Mislabelling a young child with spasticity and incoordination as having cerebral palsy Overlooking the retinal and MRI clues that strongly suggest ARSACS Not testing SACS or not recognising the broader recessive spastic ataxia group Failing to address consanguinity and recessive inheritance in genetic counselling ARSACS results from loss-of-function variants in SACS, which encodes sacsin, a very large multidomain protein with chaperone-like activity that supports protein folding and mitochondrial dynamics and distribution, and is important in Purkinje cells and in long motor and sensory axons. Deficiency of sacsin disturbs protein quality control and mitochondrial function, causing Purkinje cell abnormalities, corticospinal tract dysfunction and a length-dependent peripheral neuropathy. These combined effects produce the characteristic spastic, ataxic and neuropathic phenotype, and the broader group of recessive spastic ataxias reflects related disturbances of neuronal maintenance from other genes. ARSACS is progressive over years, and many affected individuals lose independent ambulation and become wheelchair-dependent in mid-adult life, with the tempo and severity varying by variant; other recessive spastic ataxias differ in course, so prognosis is best individualised once the specific gene is known.

depth, and certain high-risk settings such as obstetric, cardiac, and trauma anaesthesia Total intravenous techniques carry particular risk if drug delivery fails or is interrupted, so vigilance over the infusion is essential Prevention includes confirming delivery and adequate dosing of anaesthetic, monitoring end-tidal volatile concentration, checking equipment, and considering processed EEG depth-of-anaesthesia monitoring in high-risk cases When paralysed, patients cannot signal distress, so clinical signs of light anaesthesia (movement, autonomic changes) may be blunted and must be interpreted with care If awareness is suspected or reported, a compassionate response, honest explanation, and structured psychological support and follow-up are important Documentation and use of a structured interview help confirm the event and guide support and any formal reporting Reports of explicit recall with pain or the sensation of paralysis Evidence of severe psychological distress or post-traumatic stress after surgery Recognised anaesthetic delivery failure during a paralysed case Signs of inadequate anaesthesia in a paralysed patient at high risk Relying on movement to gauge depth in a neuromuscularly blocked patient Failing to notice interrupted or failed intravenous anaesthetic delivery Dismissing or disbelieving a patient's report of awareness Not offering timely psychological support and follow-up Omitting depth monitoring in recognised high-risk situations General anaesthesia suppresses consciousness by acting on the brain, and adequate depth depends on delivering sufficient anaesthetic to the effect site relative to individual requirement and surgical stimulation. Awareness occurs when brain anaesthetic concentration is inadequate to prevent consciousness while the patient is unable to communicate, often because neuromuscular blockade prevents movement. Contributing mechanisms include underdosing to protect a compromised circulation, equipment or infusion failure, increased anaesthetic requirement, and pharmacokinetic variability. Explicit memory formation during light anaesthesia can lead to conscious recall and psychological sequelae. Many episodes are brief with limited recall, but distressing awareness can cause persistent anxiety, sleep disturbance, and post-traumatic stress disorder; early acknowledgement and psychological support improve outcomes.

infant suggesting early glaucoma Family history of anterior segment anomalies and glaucoma indicating dominant inheritance Regarding posterior embryotoxon or iris changes as benign and not screening for glaucoma Assuming the glaucoma is a one-off, when lifelong surveillance is required Overlooking the systemic dental and umbilical features that support the diagnosis Failing to examine and counsel relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome results from abnormal development of neural-crest-derived tissues forming the anterior segment of the eye, driven by mutations in developmental transcription-factor genes such as PITX2 and FOXC1. Faulty migration and differentiation of these cells produces incomplete regression and anomalous development of structures at the iridocorneal angle and iris, giving the characteristic angle strands, prominent Schwalbe line and iris defects. Maldevelopment of the trabecular meshwork and drainage angle impairs aqueous outflow, leading to raised intraocular pressure and glaucoma. The same transcription factors act in the development of teeth, the umbilicus and midface, explaining the associated systemic features. The ocular anomalies themselves are static, but glaucoma is common, may be difficult to control, and is the principal threat to vision; with early detection and effective pressure control the visual prognosis is good, whereas late or refractory glaucoma can cause irreversible optic nerve damage.

neurological deficit suggesting an alternative spinal pathology Biochemical abnormalities pointing to a treatable systemic osteomalacia instead Features suggesting malignancy or Paget disease rather than axial osteomalacia Treating with vitamin D and phosphate as though it were deficiency osteomalacia, which is ineffective here Misreading the coarse axial trabeculae as Paget disease or metastatic infiltration Overlooking the normal mineral biochemistry that separates it from systemic osteomalacia Escalating investigation or therapy for what is usually a stable, benign disorder Axial osteomalacia is a mineralisation defect confined mainly to the axial skeleton, in which osteoblasts produce osteoid that mineralises slowly, leaving excess unmineralised matrix demonstrable on undecalcified bone biopsy with tetracycline labelling. Unlike the common forms of osteomalacia, it is not caused by vitamin D deficiency, phosphate wasting, or hypophosphatasia, and the mineral-regulating biochemistry is characteristically normal. The underlying cause is unknown, and it appears to reflect an intrinsic, possibly localised osteoblast dysfunction rather than a systemic hormonal abnormality. Because mineral homeostasis is intact, the disease tends to remain limited and stable, producing the coarse axial trabecular pattern and modest symptoms without the progressive deformity and fractures of systemic osteomalacia. The condition is generally benign and non-progressive, with stable symptoms over long follow-up; because it does not stem from a correctable deficiency, expectations should focus on symptom control rather than radiographic reversal.

Axial spondyloarthritis — axSpA, radiographic and non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis Mechanical (non-inflammatory) back pain Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis Psoriatic or enteropathic spondyloarthritis Osteitis condensans ilii Infective sacroiliitis Assessment of inflammatory back pain features HLA-B27 testing MRI of the sacroiliac joints for active inflammation Radiographs of the sacroiliac joints and spine Inflammatory markers and screening for extra-articular disease A chronic inflammatory disease of the axial skeleton, encompassing ankylosing spondylitis (radiographic) and non-radiographic forms The hallmark is inflammatory back pain: insidious onset before middle age, morning stiffness, improvement with exercise and not with rest, and night pain It is strongly associated with HLA-B27 and with sacroiliitis on imaging Extra-articular features include acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease MRI detects active sacroiliitis before radiographic changes appear, enabling earlier diagnosis Management combines exercise and NSAIDs with biologic therapy (TNF or IL-17 inhibitors) for active disease Features suggesting infective sacroiliitis or malignancy Acute anterior uveitis Rapid loss of spinal mobility or spinal fracture in ankylosed spine Cauda equina syndrome (rare, in long-standing disease) Dismissing chronic back pain in a young adult as mechanical Relying on radiographs alone and missing early disease detectable on MRI Overlooking extra-articular clues such as uveitis Forgetting the high fracture risk of an ankylosed spine after trauma Axial spondyloarthritis is an immune-mediated inflammatory disorder centred on the entheses and sacroiliac joints, in which inflammation at sites of ligament and tendon insertion is followed by reactive new bone formation. Genetic susceptibility, especially HLA-B27, and dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity involving the interleukin-23/17 axis drive the process. Over time, inflammation of the spine and sacroiliac joints can lead to syndesmophyte formation, ankylosis and loss of spinal mobility, while shared immunopathology explains the associated uveitis, psoriasis and bowel inflammation. Course is variable; early diagnosis and modern therapy can control symptoms and improve function, though some progress to spinal ankylosis with disability.

chromosomal disorders Y-chromosome microdeletion History of cryptorchidism or testicular torsion Gonadotoxic chemotherapy or radiotherapy Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism producing a secretory picture with low gonadotropins Repeat centrifuged semen analysis to confirm the absence of sperm Serum follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone, and testosterone, with a raised follicle-stimulating hormone supporting spermatogenic failure Karyotype to detect Klinefelter syndrome and other chromosomal abnormalities Y-chromosome microdeletion analysis to establish cause and guide retrieval prospects Scrotal ultrasound to assess testicular volume and exclude associated pathology Prolactin and, where a central cause is suspected, pituitary assessment Diagnostic and therapeutic testicular sperm extraction, ideally by microdissection technique Non-obstructive azoospermia is the absence of ejaculated sperm due to failed or severely impaired sperm production rather than a blockage The typical picture is of small, soft testes with a raised follicle-stimulating hormone, reflecting loss of the negative feedback normally provided by an intact germinal epithelium This contrasts with obstructive azoospermia, where testicular volume and follicle-stimulating hormone are normal, and the distinction guides the entire management pathway Recognised causes include Klinefelter syndrome, establish a cause and because certain deletions predict whether surgical sperm retrieval is likely to succeed Despite globally impaired production, focal areas of spermatogenesis may persist, so microdissection testicular sperm extraction can recover sperm in a meaningful proportion of men Any retrieved sperm are used with intracytoplasmic sperm injection, and genetic counselling is important given the heritable causes A trial of hormonal optimisation may be considered in selected men with a secondary (hypogonadotropic) component before retrieval A testicular mass detected on examination or ultrasound Features of Klinefelter syndrome prompting broader endocrine and metabolic surveillance A complete azoospermia-factor deletion predicting little chance of retrievable sperm Signs of a pituitary lesion where gonadotropins are inappropriately low Failing to differentiate non-obstructive from obstructive azoospermia by integrating testicular size with follicle-stimulating hormone Omitting karyotype and Y-microdeletion testing before attempting retrieval Proceeding to sperm extraction without genetic counselling about heritable causes Assuming no sperm can be found and denying a man a properly performed microdissection retrieval Overlooking a treatable secondary hypogonadotropic component Non-obstructive azoospermia results from a primary failure of the seminiferous epithelium to produce sperm in sufficient numbers to appear in the ejaculate, with a patent excurrent duct system. The spectrum of histology ranges from maturation arrest to hypospermatogenesis and complete germ-cell aplasia (Sertoli-cell-only pattern). Because functioning germ cells are reduced or absent, inhibin feedback falls and pituitary follicle-stimulating hormone rises, while the testes lose volume and become soft. Underlying mechanisms include chromosomal disorders such as Klinefelter syndrome, deletions of the azoospermia factor regions of the Y chromosome, the aftermath of undescended testes, and damage from cytotoxic treatment, though many cases remain idiopathic. Even in severely affected testes, spermatogenesis can be patchy, which underpins the rationale for meticulous surgical exploration. The reproductive outlook is more guarded than in obstructive disease, but microdissection testicular sperm extraction retrieves usable sperm in a substantial minority to allow fatherhood through intracytoplasmic sperm injection; the likelihood is influenced by the underlying cause and specific genetic findings.

Associated renal anomaly on imaging, which may accompany unilateral vasal agenesis Features suggesting the azoospermia is in fact non-obstructive, altering the retrieval strategy Labelling a man azoospermic without examining a centrifuged specimen on more than one occasion Failing to check ejaculate volume, pH, and fructose, which localise distal obstruction Omitting cystic-fibrosis gene testing when the vasa are impalpable Confusing obstructive with non-obstructive azoospermia by not integrating testicular volume with follicle-stimulating hormone Overlooking retrograde ejaculation as a cause of an apparently empty ejaculate In obstructive azoospermia sperm production within the seminiferous tubules is preserved, but a mechanical blockage anywhere along the excurrent pathway, from the epididymis through the vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and ejaculatory ducts, prevents sperm from entering the ejaculate. Because the pituitary-testicular axis and germ-cell production are intact, follicle-stimulating hormone and testicular volume remain normal. Obstruction may be congenital, as in bilateral absence of the vas deferens linked to cystic-fibrosis gene mutations, or acquired through infection, iatrogenic injury, prior vasectomy, or ejaculatory duct obstruction from cysts or calculi. When the distal ducts or seminal vesicles are involved, ejaculate volume falls and fructose, a seminal-vesicle product, is reduced or absent. The reproductive outlook is generally favourable because spermatogenesis is intact, so surgical sperm retrieval combined with intracytoplasmic sperm injection has high success, and selected acquired obstructions can be reconstructed with restoration of sperm in the ejaculate.

Progressive neurological deterioration Treating the hydrocephalus or malformation without recognising an underlying glycosylation disorder Not distinguishing type I from type II defects on transferrin analysis Overlooking the coagulopathy before neurosurgical procedures Assuming a specific therapy exists when management is supportive B4GALT1 encodes a Golgi beta-1,4-galactosyltransferase that transfers galactose onto the N-acetylglucosamine of maturing complex N-glycans. Deficiency leaves glycan antennae lacking terminal galactose, a processing defect that produces a type II transferrin pattern on isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry. Because the enzyme acts after the oligosaccharide has been transferred to protein, the glycans are structurally incomplete rather than absent. As a very rare disorder, prognosis is defined by a small number of reports; outcome depends on the severity of the brain malformation, hydrocephalus and systemic complications, with variable neurodevelopmental disability. No treatment corrects the enzymatic defect.

warranting re-evaluation Attributing pain to incidental kissing spines without confirming the source Overlooking coexisting facet or discogenic pain Proceeding to surgery without a positive diagnostic injection Baastrup disease arises when adjacent spinous processes come into abnormal contact (kiss) because of loss of intervertebral disc height and increased lumbar lordosis. Repetitive contact in extension produces bony changes, including flattening, sclerosis, and enlargement of the opposing spinous processes, and inflammation of the interspinous ligament, often with formation of an adventitial interspinous bursa. Stimulation of nociceptors in the inflamed interspinous tissues and periosteum generates midline mechanical pain that worsens with extension. The condition is benign and usually responds to conservative treatment and postural measures; local injections are often helpful, and the rare patient who needs surgery generally does well.

Babesiosis — Babesia Lyme disease (concurrent or co-transmitted by the same tick) Anaplasmosis (Anaplasma phagocytophilum) Borrelia miyamotoi infection HELLP syndrome in pregnant women at risk of tick exposure (babesiosis is an imitator) Other causes of febrile hemolytic anemia Malaria (Plasmodium falciparum and others) — intraerythrocytic febrile illness most readily confused with babesiosis Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi) Anaplasmosis (Anaplasma phagocytophilum) Borrelia miyamotoi infection Giemsa-stained thin blood smear (microscopy) — definitive diagnosis; trophozoites appear as ring/ameboid forms, and merozoites arranged in tetrads form the pathognomonic 'Maltese cross' Real-time PCR amplifying the parasite 18S rRNA gene (detects 1–10 parasites/uL; allows speciation; used to monitor low-grade infection and relapse risk) Complete blood count (anemia, often severe thrombocytopenia preceding severe anemia; WBC may be low, normal, or high) and reticulocyte count Hemolysis markers: low haptoglobin, elevated LDH, elevated total bilirubin Liver enzymes (alkaline phosphatase, AST, ALT) and renal function (BUN, creatinine) Urinalysis (urobilinogen, hemoglobinuria, proteinuria) Indirect fluorescent antibody serology (IgM and IgG titers) — a single positive result is NOT sufficient for diagnosis because antibodies can persist for over a year CT for suspected splenic infarction or rupture HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) in pregnancy Other hemolytic anemias / thrombotic microangiopathies presenting with hemolysis and thrombocytopenia Emerging tick-borne infection caused by intraerythrocytic protozoa of the genus Babesia that invade and lyse red blood cells; most U.S. cases are due to Babesia microti, transmitted by the deer tick Ixodes scapularis, with ~90% presenting June through August (p.1775, 1777). Presents as a flu-like illness: gradual-onset fatigue/malaise followed within days by fever (can reach 40.9 C) with chills, night sweats, headache, myalgia, and anorexia; dark urine and jaundice raise suspicion of severe hemolytic anemia (p.1777). Because the same I. scapularis tick co-transmits Borrelia burgdorferi and Anaplasma phagocytophilum, co-infection is common: about one-half of patients diagnosed with babesiosis are also infected with B. burgdorferi, so a babesiosis diagnosis should prompt evaluation for Lyme disease, and vice versa (p.1778). Most symptomatic patients (~80%) are 50 years or older; hospitalized patients are roughly a decade older (median 68 years) (p.1777). Splenic complications (infarction, subcapsular hematoma, rupture) can occur even with low-grade parasitemia (median ~1%) and typically affect young, healthy patients (p.1777, 1780). Severe disease especially in asplenic (congenital, functional, or post-splenectomy), elderly, and immunocompromised (HIV/AIDS, transplant, malignancy, B-cell-depleting/rituximab therapy) patients Dark urine and jaundice indicating severe hemolytic anemia, with scleral icterus on examination Left-sided abdominal pain, unexplained hypotension with tachycardia, or hemodynamic instability suggesting splenic infarction or rupture Acute renal failure (leading complication, ~20%) and acute respiratory failure (~7%); also DIC, shock, arrhythmia, heart failure Parasitemia >4% (risk factor for severe, complicated disease; can reach 30–40% in immunocompromised patients) Diagnosis delayed >7 days after symptom onset predisposes to severe complicated disease Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis from massive phagocytosis of blood cells (fatal) Misidentifying Babesia as malaria on the blood smear: distinguish by absence of central brownish hemozoin pigment, presence of extracellular merozoites, absence of gametocytes and schizonts, and the pathognomonic tetrad ('Maltese cross'); a negative BinaxNOW malaria test helps rule out falciparum malaria when microscopy is ambiguous (p.1779). Relying on a single positive serology for diagnosis — antibodies persist for over a year after the parasite is cleared (p.1779). Missing co-infection: failing to evaluate for Lyme disease (and other tick-borne pathogens) when babesiosis is diagnosed, or for babesiosis when Lyme symptoms worsen or fail to abate on appropriate antibiotics (p.1778). Overlooking splenic complications, which can occur with low-grade parasitemia and in young, otherwise healthy patients (p.1777, 1780). Routine follow-up PCR is not recommended in immunocompetent patients (parasite DNA detectable up to 3 months) since relapse is unlikely, and persistent fatigue alone does not warrant extending or resuming therapy (p.1779). Babesia parasites invade and lyse red blood cells. RBC debris from hemolysis can accumulate in the renal vasculature and cause renal failure. Free hemoglobin is complexed by haptoglobin, then the oxidized heme group by hemopexin; excess free hemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, promoting thrombus formation and vascular inflammation. RBC lysis in splenic capillaries can trigger localized necrosis and splenic infarction; oxidatively stressed, poorly deformable RBCs are filtered and phagocytosed by splenic macrophages, and erythrophagocytosis with the immune response contributes to splenomegaly and rupture. Fever, chills, and sweats reflect a systemic inflammatory response to RBC lysis, and excessive inflammation drives end-organ (renal and pulmonary) damage. The spleen is the immunodominant organ, explaining why asplenia is a major risk factor for severe disease; protective immunity involves CD4+ Th1 cells (severe disease in AIDS and transplant recipients), and B cells/antibodies appear critical for clearance in some patients (relapsing disease after rituximab). Persistent anemia after infection clears has been attributed to autoantibodies tagging RBCs for clearance (p.1778). With first-line atovaquone plus azithromycin, a fatal outcome is rare; of 7612 CDC-reported cases in 2011–2015, 46 (0.6%) ended in death. Older regimens (clindamycin plus quinine) had fatality rates of 5–9%. Death is more frequent in those 65 years or older. Among Medicare recipients diagnosed 2006–2013, ~1% died within 30 days; fatality was ~3% among hospitalized patients. Fatality is high in immunocompromised patients (~20%) and in those with splenic rupture or infarction (~6%). Fatigue may persist for weeks to months after treatment. Highly immunocompromised patients are at risk of persistent, relapsing infection (p.1778). Severe babesiosis requires hospital admission (median stay 4 days). Severe, complicated babesiosis is defined as illness requiring ICU admission; complicated by ARDS, heart failure, or shock; or requiring dialysis, intubation, or RBC exchange. Diarrhea and nausea/vomiting are strong predictors of severe disease, and asplenia and autoimmune disorders predispose to it. Parasitemia is typically 0.1–10% in immunocompetent patients (up to 30–40% in immunocompromised); parasitemia >4% is a risk factor for severe complicated disease (p.1777-1778).

or metastatic vascular tumour Verruga peruana (Bartonella bacilliformis) in endemic regions Disseminated fungal infection with cutaneous lesions Angiosarcoma Skin or tissue biopsy with Warthin-Starry Bartonella quintana, and characterised by a vasoproliferative response to infection Occurs predominantly in immunocompromised hosts, especially those with advanced HIV and low CD4 counts, and rarely in immunocompetent individuals Bartonella henselae is associated with cat and cat-flea exposure, whereas Bartonella quintana is linked to body lice, homelessness and poor hygiene The hallmark is one or more friable, red to purple vascular papules or nodules that can bleed readily and may resemble pyogenic granuloma or Kaposi sarcoma Visceral disease includes hepatic and splenic bacillary peliosis, and lesions may also involve bone, causing painful osteolytic lesions, and other organs Histology of a lesion shows lobular vascular proliferation with clumps of bacilli demonstrable on Warthin-Starry silver staining Prolonged antimicrobial therapy is required, and the condition responds well, distinguishing it from the Kaposi sarcoma it can mimic clinically Haemorrhage from friable lesions Hepatosplenic peliosis with abdominal pain, fever or cytopenias Undiagnosed underlying HIV or other profound immunosuppression Systemic bacteraemic illness with fever and weight loss Misidentification as Kaposi sarcoma delaying curative antibiotic therapy Mistaking lesions for Kaposi sarcoma and missing a treatable infection Using too short an antibiotic course, leading to relapse Failing to test for and address underlying immunosuppression Overlooking visceral or osseous involvement in a patient with cutaneous disease Not eliciting cat, flea or body-louse exposure that points to the causative species Bartonella species are fastidious Gram-negative bacteria that, in the susceptible host, invade endothelial cells and stimulate a marked angioproliferative response. Bacterial factors promote endothelial cell proliferation and inhibit apoptosis, generating the characteristic lobular capillary proliferations seen in skin, liver, spleen, bone and other tissues. The impaired cellular immunity of the host permits this proliferative, rather than granulomatous or self-limiting, response, and the resulting friable neovascular lesions account for the bleeding tendency and the peliotic blood-filled spaces in affected viscera. Bacillary angiomatosis is a treatable and generally curable infection that responds well to prolonged antibiotics, but untreated visceral or disseminated disease can be life-threatening, and relapse may occur if therapy is too short.
