airway support Deep coma with loss of brainstem reflexes Seizures Haemodynamic instability or significant bradycardia Suspected intrathecal pump failure or withdrawal with hyperthermia and autonomic instability Mistaking reversible deep coma with absent brainstem reflexes for irreversible brain injury Extubating or discharging prematurely before prolonged effects resolve Overlooking impaired renal clearance that prolongs toxicity Failing to recognise and urgently treat baclofen withdrawal Attributing withdrawal to sepsis or another hyperthermic syndrome and delaying baclofen restoration Baclofen is a structural analogue of the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid and acts as an agonist at gamma-aminobutyric-acid type B receptors, predominantly in the spinal cord, reducing excitatory neurotransmission and muscle tone. In overdose, excessive receptor stimulation causes marked central nervous system depression, hypotonia, respiratory depression and coma, with cardiovascular effects and a lowered seizure threshold in some patients. Baclofen is largely renally eliminated, so impaired renal function prolongs and intensifies toxicity. Sudden withdrawal removes chronic inhibitory tone, producing a hyperexcitable rebound state with severe spasticity and autonomic dysregulation. Overdose generally has a good prognosis with supportive care and mechanical ventilation, with full neurological recovery even after profound coma, though recovery may be slow in renal impairment; unrecognised withdrawal, especially from intrathecal therapy, can be fatal.

Bacterial keratitis — microbial keratitis, bacterial corneal ulcer, infective keratitis, corneal ulcer Herpes simplex (dendritic) keratitis Fungal keratitis Acanthamoeba keratitis Marginal (hypersensitivity) keratitis Sterile contact-lens-related infiltrates Anterior uveitis or acute angle-closure glaucoma (for the red painful eye) Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining to define the infiltrate and epithelial defect Corneal scraping for Gram stain, culture, and sensitivities Contact lens and lens case cultures where relevant Measurement of infiltrate size and assessment of corneal thinning Confocal microscopy or specialised staining if Acanthamoeba or fungal infection is suspected Presents with a painful red eye, photophobia, watering, discharge, and reduced vision, usually developing over hours to days Examination shows a focal white or grey corneal infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect that stains with fluorescein; a hypopyon may be present in severe cases Contact lens wear (especially overnight or poor hygiene) is the leading risk factor, alongside corneal trauma, ocular surface disease, and previous surgery Pseudomonas is an important and rapidly destructive pathogen in contact lens wearers; Staphylococci and Streptococci are also common Corneal scraping for Gram stain and culture should ideally be taken before starting intensive treatment in significant ulcers Management is with intensive topical broad-spectrum antibiotics, initially given very frequently, and stopping contact lens use Central ulcers, large infiltrates, or delayed treatment risk scarring, perforation, and permanent visual loss Sight-threatening — central or large ulcers can scar the visual axis or perforate the cornea Rapid progression, especially in a contact lens wearer, suggesting Pseudomonas Hypopyon, corneal thinning, or descemetocele indicating impending perforation Worsening despite treatment raising suspicion of fungal or Acanthamoeba infection Prescribing topical steroids or a patch that can worsen infection, particularly with undiagnosed herpetic or fungal disease Failing to scrape a significant ulcer for culture before starting treatment Underestimating the aggressiveness of contact-lens-associated Pseudomonas keratitis Missing Acanthamoeba in a contact lens wearer with pain out of proportion to signs Bacterial keratitis develops when the corneal epithelial barrier is breached (by trauma, contact lens wear, dry eye, or surgery), allowing bacteria to invade the corneal stroma. Bacterial proliferation and the release of enzymes and toxins, together with the host inflammatory response and recruited neutrophils, cause stromal necrosis and an infiltrate. Collagen-degrading enzymes can rapidly thin the cornea, leading to ulceration, descemetocele formation, and perforation. Healing occurs with scarring that reduces corneal clarity, particularly when the visual axis is involved. Prompt intensive antibiotic treatment usually controls infection, but a central scar, large ulcer, or delayed care can leave permanent visual impairment; perforation may require corneal grafting.

Bacterial Vaginosis — BV, vaginal dysbiosis, Gardnerella vaginitis, anaerobic vaginosis Vulvovaginal candidiasis Trichomonas vaginalis infection Physiological or cyclical vaginal discharge Retained foreign body such as a tampon Desquamative inflammatory vaginitis Cervicitis from gonorrhoea or chlamydia Measurement of vaginal pH, which is typically elevated above 4.5 Whiff (amine) test with potassium hydroxide to detect a fishy odour Saline wet-mount microscopy for clue cells and reduced lactobacilli Gram stain scoring of vaginal flora where laboratory diagnosis is used Testing for co-existing sexually transmitted infections when risk factors are present Bacterial vaginosis reflects a shift in the vaginal microbiome away from protective lactobacilli toward an overgrowth of anaerobes rather than a single infecting pathogen The characteristic feature is a thin, homogeneous, greyish-white discharge with a fishy odour that is often most noticeable after intercourse It is typically not associated with significant inflammation, so vulval itching and soreness are usually mild or absent, distinguishing it from candidiasis and trichomoniasis Clinical diagnosis using the Amsel criteria combines discharge characteristics, raised vaginal pH, a positive whiff test with potassium hydroxide, and clue cells on microscopy Clue cells are vaginal epithelial cells studded with adherent bacteria and are a hallmark microscopic finding Treatment targets anaerobes with agents such as metronidazole or clindamycin, but recurrence is common and reflects failure to re-establish a lactobacillus-dominant flora In pregnancy it is associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, late miscarriage, and postpartum endometritis, so symptomatic pregnant women are treated It also increases susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections including HIV and to post-procedural pelvic infection Symptomatic bacterial vaginosis in pregnancy given the association with preterm birth and miscarriage Signs of ascending infection such as pelvic pain, fever, or cervical motion tenderness suggesting pelvic inflammatory disease Bacterial vaginosis before termination or intrauterine procedures, increasing post-procedure infection risk Persistent atypical discharge not responding to treatment, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Coexisting features of a sexually transmitted infection Mistaking it for candidiasis and treating with antifungals Overtreating asymptomatic women outside pregnancy or pre-procedure settings Failing to consider it in recurrent or malodorous discharge with minimal inflammation Not screening for concurrent sexually transmitted infections when risk exists Overlooking its role in preterm birth in symptomatic pregnant women The healthy vagina is dominated by lactobacilli that produce lactic acid and hydrogen peroxide, maintaining an acidic environment that suppresses other organisms. In bacterial vaginosis this population is depleted and replaced by a polymicrobial overgrowth of anaerobes such as Gardnerella vaginalis, Prevotella, Mobiluncus, and Atopobium, often organised into a biofilm on the epithelium. The resulting rise in vaginal pH and production of amines generates the typical odour and discharge, while the biofilm contributes to treatment resistance and recurrence. Symptoms usually respond well to appropriate antibiotic therapy, but recurrence within months is frequent because the protective lactobacillus flora and the biofilm are difficult to eradicate permanently. It is not itself a serious infection but its associations with adverse pregnancy outcomes, post-procedural infection, and enhanced susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections give it clinical importance.

episignature aiding interpretation Severe feeding difficulty with faltering growth in infancy Recurrent aspiration linked to hypotonia and swallowing problems Developmental regression, which would prompt reassessment New seizures warranting neurological review Confusing Bainbridge-Ropers syndrome with Bohring-Opitz syndrome and wrongly instituting Wilms tumour surveillance or expecting the BOS posture Misdiagnosing the child as Angelman or Pitt-Hopkins syndrome without appropriate molecular testing Delaying augmentative communication while awaiting speech that may not develop Underestimating early feeding difficulties driven by hypotonia ASXL3 encodes a member of the additional sex combs-like family of polycomb group proteins, which regulate chromatin by influencing histone ubiquitination and the balance of polycomb-mediated gene repression. Constitutional truncating variants disturb this epigenetic regulation, deranging the developmental programmes of gene expression that guide neuronal maturation and craniofacial patterning. The resulting dysregulation produces severe intellectual disability, speech impairment, hypotonia and a distinctive facial gestalt; although ASXL3 is closely related to ASXL1, differences in their developmental roles explain why Bainbridge-Ropers syndrome lacks the fixed posture and tumour predisposition seen in Bohring-Opitz syndrome. The disorder causes lifelong severe intellectual disability with major speech limitation and dependence on augmentative communication; survival is generally not curtailed in the absence of severe feeding or respiratory complications, and management focuses on developmental, feeding and behavioural support.

phimosis Non-specific or infective balanitis, including candidal balanitis Zoon (plasma cell) balanitis Psoriasis or lichen planus of the genitalia Penile intraepithelial neoplasia or invasive xerotica obliterans is the genital form of lichen sclerosus in men, producing white, atrophic, scarring change of the glans and prepuce It characteristically affects the foreskin and glans and may extend to the meatus, causing a firm white sclerotic ring, phimosis, and meatal narrowing Presenting features include a non-retractile foreskin, painful erections, splitting or bleeding of the prepuce, and a poor or deflected urinary stream from meatal stenosis Meatal and urethral involvement can lead to stricture disease and obstructed voiding, so the urethra should always be assessed It is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis rather than an infection, and topical high-potency corticosteroid is the mainstay of medical treatment Circumcision is frequently both diagnostic and therapeutic and often resolves preputial disease, while meatal or urethral involvement may require reconstructive surgery There is a recognised, if uncommon, association with penile squamous cell carcinoma, so persistent, atypical, or non-healing lesions should be biopsied and lesions kept under review Histological confirmation is advisable in doubtful cases and mandatory where malignancy is suspected A persistent ulcer, indurated plaque, or exophytic lesion suggesting penile squamous cell carcinoma Progressive meatal stenosis or urethral stricture causing obstructed voiding or retention Rapidly worsening or treatment-resistant disease New nodularity or bleeding within an established plaque Treating recurrent balanitis symptomatically without recognising underlying lichen sclerosus Overlooking meatal and urethral involvement and the resulting stricture disease Failing to biopsy a suspicious or non-healing lesion and missing an early carcinoma Assuming circumcision alone always cures disease that has extended to the meatus or urethra Neglecting long-term follow-up given the malignant association Balanitis xerotica obliterans is a chronic lymphocyte-mediated inflammatory dermatosis of the genital skin, regarded as the male genital manifestation of lichen sclerosus. Immune-mediated inflammation in the dermis drives hyalinisation and homogenisation of the upper dermal collagen with epidermal atrophy, producing the characteristic pale, sclerotic, and fragile tissue. Chronic scarring contracts the prepuce to cause acquired phimosis and narrows the external meatus, and progressive fibrosis may extend proximally into the anterior urethra to produce strictures. The persistent inflammation and epithelial change are believed to underlie the small but definite increase in risk of penile squamous cell carcinoma associated with long-standing disease. The cause is incompletely understood, with genetic, autoimmune, and local factors, including chronic exposure to urine under an unretractable foreskin, all implicated. Most preputial disease is controlled by topical corticosteroid or cured by circumcision, but meatal and urethral involvement can be recurrent and may need reconstructive surgery, and lifelong awareness of the small malignant potential warrants ongoing surveillance of persistent lesions.

Balantidiasis (Balantidium coli) — Balantidium coli infection, Balantidiosis, Neobalantidium coli infection, ciliate dysentery Amoebic colitis Bacillary dysentery (shigellosis) Inflammatory bowel disease Campylobacter or non-typhoidal Salmonella colitis Ischaemic colitis Other invasive enteric protozoa Fresh stool wet-mount microscopy for large motile ciliated trophozoites Stool concentration methods to detect cysts Repeated stool examination because shedding is intermittent Sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy with biopsy of ulcer edges in invasive disease Full blood count and markers of inflammation and dehydration Assessment of nutritional and immune status Balantidium coli is the largest protozoan parasite of humans and the only ciliate that causes human disease Pigs are the principal reservoir, and infection follows ingestion of cysts in food or water contaminated by porcine faeces, so it clusters where people live in close contact with pigs Most infections are asymptomatic, but invasive disease produces a colitis resembling amoebic dysentery with abdominal pain, tenesmus and bloody, mucoid diarrhoea The trophozoite is large, ciliated and rapidly motile on a fresh wet stool preparation, with a characteristic macronucleus, making it recognisable microscopically Colonic ulceration mirrors that of amoebiasis and can lead to perforation; extraintestinal spread is rare but described Malnutrition, alcoholism and immunosuppression predispose to symptomatic and severe disease Tetracycline is the usual first-line treatment, with metronidazole as an effective alternative Severe bloody dysentery with dehydration and haemodynamic compromise Signs of colonic perforation or peritonitis Fulminant colitis in a malnourished or immunosuppressed patient Failure to respond to appropriate therapy Mistaking invasive balantidial colitis for amoebiasis and not identifying the ciliate Relying on a single stool sample despite intermittent trophozoite and cyst shedding Overlooking the epidemiological clue of pig contact Underestimating severity in malnourished or immunosuppressed patients Balantidium coli exists as a large motile trophozoite and a resistant cyst that transmits infection. After cysts are ingested, excystation in the small intestine releases trophozoites that colonise the large bowel. Secreting proteolytic enzymes such as hyaluronidase, the trophozoites can invade the colonic mucosa, producing flask-shaped ulcers closely resembling those of amoebic colitis with surrounding inflammation and haemorrhage. Tissue invasion drives the dysenteric illness, and in severe cases confluent ulceration may cause perforation and peritonitis. Host factors such as malnutrition, achlorhydria and immunosuppression favour invasion and more severe disease. Asymptomatic carriage and mild disease resolve well with treatment; invasive colitis carries a more serious outlook, and fulminant or perforating disease, particularly in debilitated hosts, can be fatal.

posterior cortical atrophy, and other bilateral posterior lesions Acute onset following hypotension or hypoxia suggesting watershed infarction Progressive course suggesting posterior cortical atrophy or another degenerative process Associated focal neurological signs indicating extensive posterior damage Rapid deterioration requiring urgent imaging Mistaking the profound functional impairment for blindness despite intact visual fields Attributing the picture to psychiatric or non-organic causes Overlooking a treatable systemic precipitant of watershed ischaemia Failing to recognise posterior cortical atrophy as an underlying degenerative cause Balint syndrome follows bilateral damage to the parieto-occipital junction, disrupting the dorsal visual stream that mediates spatial attention and visuomotor integration. Loss of this network produces simultanagnosia (a constricted attentional window), oculomotor apraxia (inability to voluntarily shift gaze), and optic ataxia (inaccurate visually guided reaching). Because primary visual cortex is relatively spared, elementary vision and fields can be preserved even though the patient behaves as if severely visually impaired. Typical causes are bilateral watershed infarction from hypotension, posterior cortical atrophy, and other diffuse or multifocal posterior pathology. Prognosis depends on the cause; some recovery may occur after an isolated ischaemic or hypoxic insult with rehabilitation, whereas neurodegenerative causes progress, and the functional disability is often severe.

urinalysis and quantification of tubular (low-molecular-weight) proteinuria Renal ultrasound documenting small, symmetrically shrunken kidneys Regular urine cytology and upper-tract imaging for urothelial carcinoma surveillance Renal biopsy showing outer-cortical interstitial fibrosis in selected cases Aristolochic-acid-DNA adduct or mutational signature analysis where available A chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy occurring in defined rural communities along tributaries of the Danube in the Balkan region Now widely attributed to chronic dietary exposure to aristolochic acid from Aristolochia seeds contaminating locally grown grain Characterised by slowly progressive renal impairment with small, shrunken kidneys, tubular proteinuria and relatively bland urinary sediment Carries a markedly increased risk of upper urothelial (renal pelvis and ureter) carcinoma, often multifocal Biopsy shows hypocellular interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy, most pronounced in the outer cortex Familial clustering reflects shared environmental exposure rather than a simple inherited disorder, though genetic susceptibility contributes There is no specific antidote, so management is avoidance of the causative exposure and supportive care, with lifelong surveillance for urothelial malignancy Haematuria or an upper-tract mass indicating possible urothelial carcinoma Rapid decline in renal function suggesting an additional insult New flank pain or hydronephrosis Bilateral or multifocal urothelial disease Failing to appreciate the aristolochic acid link and shared environmental cause Missing upper-tract urothelial carcinoma by omitting cytology and imaging surveillance Attributing the disease purely to genetics because of familial clustering Overlooking tubular proteinuria because dipstick albumin is low Assuming stopping exposure halts progression, when established fibrosis may still advance Balkan endemic nephropathy is now regarded as a form of chronic aristolochic acid nephropathy resulting from prolonged, low-level dietary exposure to aristolochic acid, a nephrotoxic and carcinogenic compound derived from Aristolochia plants that contaminate wheat in affected regions. Aristolochic acid is metabolised to reactive intermediates that form characteristic DNA adducts, injuring proximal tubular cells and driving progressive interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy, predominantly in the superficial cortex. The same adducts induce mutations, including a signature TP53 mutation, in urothelial cells, explaining the strong association with upper-tract urothelial carcinoma. The insidious, cumulative nature of exposure accounts for the slow, relentless decline in renal function and the late age of clinical presentation. The nephropathy is slowly but relentlessly progressive, and many patients eventually reach end-stage kidney disease over years to decades. The dominant long-term threat is upper-tract urothelial carcinoma, which is frequently multifocal and requires lifelong surveillance; overall prognosis is heavily influenced by early detection of malignancy.

disease Balo concentric sclerosis is an inflammatory demyelinating process in which bands of myelin loss alternate with bands of preserved or partially preserved myelin, producing the concentric lamellated pattern. The rings are thought to arise from a tissue preconditioning mechanism in which hypoxia-like metabolic stress and protective upregulation at the advancing lesion edge spare a rim of myelin, so that successive waves of demyelination leave alternating layers. Oligodendrocyte injury with relative axonal preservation in the earlier layers underlies the potential for recovery, and the disorder is considered part of the multiple sclerosis spectrum. Outcome is variable; some patients recover well and follow a relapsing-remitting course while others sustain significant deficits, and the historically fulminant fatal form is now less commonly seen with modern treatment.

Band keratopathy — calcific band keratopathy, calcium band degeneration, band-shaped keratopathy Spheroidal (climatic droplet) degeneration Calcific plaques from chronic exposure or scarring Anterior corneal dystrophies affecting the Bowman layer Salzmann nodular degeneration Gelatinous drop-like corneal dystrophy Corneal scarring from prior keratitis Slit-lamp examination documenting the interpalpebral calcific band with lucid interval and clear holes Serum calcium, phosphate, and albumin to detect hypercalcaemia or altered calcium-phosphate product Parathyroid hormone and vitamin D assessment when a metabolic cause is suspected Renal function tests to identify chronic renal failure Evaluation for underlying uveitis or chronic ocular inflammation Investigation for sarcoidosis or other systemic causes of hypercalcaemia when indicated A degeneration in which calcium (hydroxyapatite) is deposited at the level of the Bowman layer in the interpalpebral band across the cornea The band begins peripherally with a clear lucid interval separating it from the limbus and spreads centrally over time Characteristic small clear holes (Swiss-cheese appearance) within the plaque correspond to nerves penetrating the Bowman layer Common ocular causes include chronic anterior uveitis (especially juvenile idiopathic arthritis-associated), long-standing keratitis, and phthisical or chronically inflamed eyes Systemic causes relate to raised calcium or phosphate, including hypercalcaemia (hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, vitamin D excess) and chronic renal failure Symptoms include foreign body sensation, irritation, and reduced vision when the band crosses the visual axis; the surface may break down Management is chelation with topical EDTA to remove superficial calcium, with phototherapeutic keratectomy for deeper or recurrent deposits, alongside treatment of the underlying cause Recurrence is common if the underlying ocular inflammation or systemic calcium disturbance is not controlled Band encroaching on the visual axis with progressive visual loss Surface breakdown with pain and risk of secondary infection Underlying hypercalcaemia signalling a serious systemic disorder requiring investigation Rapid recurrence indicating uncontrolled ocular inflammation or metabolic disturbance Treating the cornea without investigating and addressing an underlying cause such as hypercalcaemia or chronic uveitis Overlooking juvenile idiopathic arthritis-associated uveitis in a child with band keratopathy Attempting deep removal that risks scarring when superficial chelation would suffice Failing to anticipate recurrence when the driving condition persists Band keratopathy results from the deposition of calcium salts, chiefly hydroxyapatite, in and beneath the Bowman layer within the interpalpebral zone of the cornea. Evaporation of tears in the exposed interpalpebral strip raises local pH and concentrates calcium and phosphate, favouring precipitation, while chronic ocular inflammation and elevated serum calcium or phosphate promote deposition. Calcification typically begins at the periphery with a clear zone next to the limbus and advances centrally as a horizontal band, sparing regions where nerves pierce the Bowman layer, which appear as clear holes. As the band thickens it disrupts the epithelium and reduces vision when it reaches the visual axis. Removal of superficial calcium by chelation or phototherapeutic keratectomy usually improves comfort and vision, but band keratopathy tends to recur unless the underlying ocular inflammation or systemic calcium disturbance is controlled.

macrocephaly for insignificant findings and missing the unifying diagnosis Confusing pigmented penile macules or hamartomas with unrelated dermatological conditions Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome is caused by germline inactivation of PTEN, a tumour suppressor that dephosphorylates the products of PI3K signalling and thereby restrains the PI3K/AKT/mTOR growth pathway. Loss of PTEN function releases this brake, driving cell growth, proliferation, and survival, which manifests as macrocephaly, hamartomatous overgrowth of multiple tissues, and lifelong susceptibility to benign and malignant tumours. The same signalling dysregulation underlies the neurodevelopmental features seen in some children. Childhood features are usually benign and overgrowth tends to stabilise, but because the disorder is part of the PTEN spectrum the principal long-term concern is an elevated lifetime cancer risk, making adherence to structured surveillance essential. With surveillance and early treatment of tumours the outlook is favourable.

and hypertension Hepatic or cardiac involvement in atypical presentations Excluding the diagnosis when a cardinal feature is absent in an atypical case Relying on a single gene result and missing an dysfunction of the BBSome, a protein complex, and its associated chaperonins that together traffic membrane proteins into and along the primary cilium. Because the primary cilium is a near-ubiquitous sensory and signalling organelle, its impairment affects many tissues, producing the retinal photoreceptor degeneration, hypothalamic dysregulation of appetite, limb patterning defect, gonadal and renal maldevelopment and cognitive effects that define the syndrome. Most cases follow autosomal recessive inheritance, but in some families the phenotype is modulated by additional variants at a second BBS locus (oligogenic or triallelic inheritance), which helps explain the variable expression and the atypical presentations in which one or more cardinal features are absent or a single organ dominates. Long-term outlook is dominated by renal disease and progressive visual loss, compounded by the metabolic consequences of obesity; the atypical and oligogenic forms show wide variability, so prognosis must be individualised.

baritosis — barium pneumoconiosis, baryta pneumoconiosis silicosis stannosis and other benign inert-dust pneumoconioses siderosis (iron oxide pneumoconiosis) mixed-dust fibrosis coal workers' pneumoconiosis pulmonary sarcoidosis miliary tuberculosis or metastatic nodular disease detailed occupational history of barite mining, milling or barium use chest radiography showing dense discrete nodular opacities high-resolution CT to characterise nodules and exclude fibrosis pulmonary function tests to confirm preserved lung function assessment for concomitant silica or other fibrogenic dust exposure serial imaging to document regression after exposure ceases workplace air sampling and mineralogical dust analysis Baritosis is a benign inert-dust pneumoconiosis caused by inhalation of insoluble barium compounds, chiefly barium sulfate (baryte) and barium oxide/carbonate dusts. Like stannosis, it produces striking radiographic shadowing with little or no symptoms or functional impairment, because barium is highly radiodense. Chest radiographs show very dense, discrete, rounded nodular opacities distributed through both lungs, reflecting the high radio-opacity of barium rather than fibrosis. Exposure occurs in barite mining and milling, and in industries using barium in glass, paint, rubber, ceramics and drilling muds. A characteristic feature is partial regression of the radiographic opacities after exposure ceases, as inert dust is gradually cleared. Lung function is typically preserved and there is no progression to fibrosis, tuberculosis or malignancy from the barium dust itself. Soluble barium salts are systemically toxic (notably causing hypokalaemia and muscle effects), but baritosis specifically results from insoluble, non-toxic barium dust in the lung. The clinical priority is to separate benign baritosis from silicosis or mixed-dust fibrosis, considering silica co-exposure in mined ore. true fibrosis or functional impairment suggesting concomitant silica exposure progressive breathlessness or cough not explained by inert dust retention atypical radiographic features such as masses, cavitation or effusion constitutional symptoms prompting exclusion of infection or malignancy features of systemic toxicity implying exposure to soluble barium salts Mistaking the dense nodular radiograph for silicosis or metastatic disease. Attributing coexisting fibrosis to barium rather than to concurrent silica exposure. Confusing benign insoluble-barium lung disease with systemic soluble-barium toxicity. Performing unnecessary invasive tests in an asymptomatic worker with a clear history. Failing to obtain follow-up imaging that would demonstrate characteristic regression. Inhaled insoluble barium sulfate and related barium dusts deposit in the alveoli and are engulfed by alveolar macrophages. These compounds are biologically inert and non-fibrogenic, so they accumulate as dust-laden macrophage collections around bronchioles and vessels without provoking collagen deposition, granulomas or destruction of lung architecture. Gas exchange and lung mechanics are therefore preserved. The dense nodular shadowing on imaging results from the high atomic number and radio-opacity of barium, greatly overstating the trivial tissue reaction. Because the dust is inert and clearable, macrophage-mediated clearance over time can produce partial regression of the radiographic changes once exposure stops. Any fibrosis or functional decline should raise suspicion of concomitant silica or other fibrogenic dust exposure, and soluble barium compounds, in contrast to the insoluble dust, carry separate systemic toxicity that is not part of baritosis. Baritosis is benign, with preserved lung function and no progression to fibrosis or malignancy from the barium dust itself; radiographic opacities may partially regress after exposure ends. The outlook is excellent provided coexisting fibrogenic exposures are excluded.

Barodontalgia — tooth squeeze, aerodontalgia, dental barotrauma Maxillary sinus barotrauma referring pain to upper teeth Pulpitis or periapical disease unrelated to pressure Temporomandibular joint disorder Trigeminal neuralgia Referred pain from other orofacial pathology Dental examination and imaging to identify the underlying pathology History correlating pain with ascent or descent Assessment of recent dental treatment Exclusion of sinus barotrauma as a source of referred pain Vitality testing of the implicated tooth Tooth pain provoked by changes in ambient pressure during flying or diving It is almost always a symptom of pre-existing dental pathology rather than a disease in itself Underlying causes include caries, defective restorations, pulpitis, periapical disease and recent dental work Pain classically occurs on ascent in flight or on descent when diving, as trapped gas expands or contracts Severe dental barotrauma can rarely cause tooth or restoration fracture Prevention rests on maintaining dental health and deferring diving or flying after certain dental procedures Severe pain with in-flight or in-water incapacitation risk Evidence of tooth or restoration fracture Features suggesting acute infection Recurrent episodes indicating untreated dental disease Treating the pain without identifying and managing the underlying dental disease Confusing referred sinus barotrauma pain with true barodontalgia Clearing personnel to dive or fly with untreated dental pathology Overlooking recent dental work as a precipitant Barodontalgia arises when ambient pressure changes act on gas trapped within a tooth or its surrounding tissues, or when pressure change stimulates a diseased or inflamed pulp. According to Boyle's law, gas trapped beneath a restoration or within carious or periapical spaces expands as pressure falls and contracts as it rises, producing pain, while an already inflamed pulp becomes sensitive to these changes. The pain is therefore a manifestation of underlying dental disease unmasked by the pressure environment. The symptom resolves once the underlying dental problem is treated, and prevention is effective with good dental care and appropriate timing of diving or flying after dental work.

disorder Renovascular hypertension Drug or sympathomimetic effect Continuous or ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring to document lability Baroreflex sensitivity testing during formal autonomic assessment Plasma and urinary metanephrines to exclude phaeochromocytoma Imaging of the neck to identify prior surgery, radiotherapy, or tumour-related damage Cardiovascular autonomic reflex tests including the Valsalva manoeuvre and deep breathing Heart-rate variability analysis Presents with labile, volatile blood pressure, with episodic severe hypertension alternating with hypotension, reflecting loss of buffering of blood-pressure fluctuations Hypertensive surges are often accompanied by tachycardia, headache, flushing, sweating, and emotional distress Commonly follows neck surgery or radiotherapy for head and neck cancer, bilateral carotid body tumour resection, or damage to the glossopharyngeal and vagal afferents May mimic phaeochromocytoma because of paroxysmal hypertension with catecholamine surges A later chronic phase can show orthostatic tachycardia and pressure lability rather than sustained hypertension A reduced parasympathetic component can produce marked tachycardia, and the volatile swings make treatment difficult Diagnosis is supported by demonstrating impaired baroreflex sensitivity on autonomic testing Management focuses on damping the swings and avoiding emotional and physical triggers, with specialist input Severe hypertensive surges risking stroke or cardiac events Symptoms strongly suggesting phaeochromocytoma requiring exclusion Profound hypotensive episodes causing syncope and injury A new neurological deficit occurring during a surge Misdiagnosing the paroxysmal hypertension as phaeochromocytoma and missing the true cause Treating the hypertension aggressively and precipitating dangerous hypotension Overlooking a history of neck surgery or radiotherapy Underestimating the role of emotional and physical arousal as triggers The arterial baroreflex normally buffers moment-to-moment changes in blood pressure: baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch sense arterial stretch and, via glossopharyngeal and vagal afferents to the brainstem, adjust sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow to keep pressure stable. Baroreflex failure occurs when these afferent limbs or their central connections are damaged, for example by surgery, radiotherapy, tumour, or neck trauma, so that blood pressure is no longer buffered. Sympathetic outflow becomes unrestrained and highly sensitive to arousal and stress, producing large surges of hypertension and tachycardia interspersed with hypotension when sympathetic drive falls. Loss of vagal baroreflex control adds heart-rate instability. Blood-pressure lability may lessen over time as partial compensation develops, but many patients have persistent, difficult-to-control fluctuations; prognosis depends on the extent of afferent damage and on avoiding hypertensive complications.

Middle ear barotrauma — aural barotrauma, ear squeeze, barotitis media Inner ear barotrauma or perilymph fistula External ear barotrauma Acute otitis media Eustachian tube dysfunction without barotrauma Decompression sickness affecting the vestibular system Otoscopy to grade the tympanic membrane injury Audiometry and tympanometry if hearing loss or effusion is present Assessment for inner ear involvement if vertigo or sensorineural loss occurs Evaluation of Eustachian tube function and nasal pathology Consideration of a diving-medicine review before return to diving The commonest injury in divers and a frequent problem in air travellers, caused by failure to equalise middle ear pressure during descent Inability to open the Eustachian tube, often from upper respiratory congestion, prevents pressure equalisation Features range from ear fullness and pain to tympanic membrane haemorrhage, effusion and, in severe cases, rupture Conductive hearing loss and vertigo may occur, and forceful equalisation can cause inner ear barotrauma Otoscopy grades the injury from mild retraction and erythema to frank haemorrhage or perforation Prevention centres on gentle equalisation techniques and avoiding diving or flying with nasal congestion Sensorineural hearing loss or persistent vertigo suggesting inner ear barotrauma Tympanic membrane rupture Signs of secondary infection Symptoms suggesting vestibular decompression sickness Missing coexisting inner ear barotrauma when there is vertigo or sensorineural loss Advising continued diving or flying with nasal congestion Confusing it with acute otitis media Overlooking a perforation requiring follow-up During descent the ambient pressure rises and, unless the middle ear is equalised through the Eustachian tube, the relative negative pressure in the middle ear draws the tympanic membrane inward and engorges and ruptures mucosal vessels, producing effusion and haemorrhage. If the tube cannot be actively opened, the pressure differential increases until tissue injury or membrane rupture occurs. Forceful attempts at equalisation against a blocked tube can transmit pressure to the inner ear and cause more serious inner ear barotrauma. Most cases resolve over days to weeks with conservative care; perforations often heal spontaneously, but inner ear barotrauma can cause permanent hearing loss.

Barth syndrome — TAZ deficiency, tafazzin deficiency, 3-methylglutaconic aciduria type II, X-linked cardioskeletal myopathy with neutropenia, BTHS Other genetic dilated cardiomyopathies and left ventricular non-compaction Primary mitochondrial cardiomyopathies and other causes of 3-methylglutaconic aciduria Congenital or cyclical neutropenia of other causes Congenital myopathies and muscular dystrophies Viral or other acquired myocarditis Glycogen storage disease with cardiac involvement (for example Pompe disease) Cardiolipin analysis with the monolysocardiolipin-to-cardiolipin ratio in blood spots or tissue Molecular genetic testing of TAZ Urine organic acids showing raised 3-methylglutaconic acid Serial full blood counts to characterise cyclical or persistent neutropenia Echocardiography and cardiac assessment for cardiomyopathy and non-compaction Creatine kinase and assessment of skeletal muscle function X-linked recessive disorder caused by variants in TAZ (also called TAFAZZIN), encoding the enzyme tafazzin, so it almost exclusively affects males Tafazzin remodels cardiolipin, the signature phospholipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane, so its deficiency impairs mitochondrial structure and oxidative phosphorylation The core clinical triad is cardiomyopathy (often dilated, sometimes with left ventricular non-compaction), skeletal myopathy with proximal weakness, and cyclical or persistent neutropenia Growth delay is common in childhood, sometimes with a characteristic catch-up growth in later adolescence Recurrent bacterial infections result from the neutropenia and can be life-threatening A useful biochemical clue is raised urinary 3-methylglutaconic acid (a form of 3-methylglutaconic aciduria) and an abnormal monolysocardiolipin-to-cardiolipin ratio Cardiomyopathy may present in utero, in infancy or later, and can fluctuate in severity Diagnosis is confirmed by cardiolipin analysis and TAZ genetic testing; management is supportive with attention to cardiac failure and infection risk Heart failure from dilated cardiomyopathy in an infant or child Serious or recurrent bacterial infection during neutropenic episodes Ventricular arrhythmia or sudden deterioration in cardiac function Severe hypotonia and weakness impairing feeding or breathing Overlooking the diagnosis in a boy with dilated cardiomyopathy by not checking for neutropenia or 3-methylglutaconic aciduria Attributing recurrent infections to an unrelated immune problem Assuming the cardiomyopathy is static, when it can fluctuate and worsen Missing the raised urinary 3-methylglutaconic acid as a diagnostic clue Barth syndrome is caused by deficiency of tafazzin, a transacylase that remodels immature cardiolipin into its mature form containing predominantly unsaturated fatty acyl chains. Mature cardiolipin is concentrated in the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it stabilises the respiratory chain complexes and supports oxidative phosphorylation, membrane curvature and cristae structure. Loss of tafazzin leaves an abnormal cardiolipin profile with accumulation of the intermediate monolysocardiolipin, destabilising the respiratory chain and impairing energy production. Tissues with high energy demand, particularly cardiac and skeletal muscle, are most affected, and mitochondrial dysfunction in the bone marrow contributes to the neutropenia. The disturbed leucine and mitochondrial metabolism underlies the 3-methylglutaconic aciduria. Historically Barth syndrome carried high early mortality from heart failure and infection, but with modern cardiac care, monitoring and management of neutropenia many patients now survive into adulthood. Prognosis depends largely on the severity and course of the cardiomyopathy and on preventing serious infections.

abscesses Spreading vulval cellulitis, systemic sepsis, or features suggesting necrotising infection Rapidly enlarging or irregular mass, or one in a postmenopausal woman, raising suspicion of carcinoma Recurrent abscesses that may indicate underlying diabetes or immunosuppression Severe pain with induration extending beyond the gland Failure to resolve after adequate drainage Treating with antibiotics alone without adequate drainage Relying on simple incision and drainage, which frequently recurs, instead of a definitive drainage procedure Failing to test for sexually transmitted infections when relevant Overlooking Bartholin carcinoma in an older woman with a persistent solid mass Not investigating recurrent abscesses for underlying diabetes Obstruction of the Bartholin duct, often following inflammation or inspissated secretions, causes retention of mucus and cystic dilatation of the gland. Stasis within the obstructed duct favours bacterial proliferation, and secondary infection with mixed vaginal, enteric, and occasionally sexually transmitted organisms produces a walled-off collection of pus. The resulting abscess generates local inflammation, oedema, and pain, and if untreated may point and rupture spontaneously or recur once the duct re-obstructs. Most Bartholin abscesses resolve well after adequate drainage, and techniques that create a lasting drainage tract, such as catheter placement or marsupialisation, substantially lower recurrence. Recurrent disease may require repeat procedures or gland excision, and the outlook is excellent overall provided malignancy is excluded in older or atypical cases.

a woman over forty, raising concern for carcinoma Rapidly spreading cellulitis, systemic sepsis, or features suggesting necrotising infection Recurrent abscesses that may indicate underlying diabetes or immunosuppression Non-healing lesion after appropriate drainage Performing simple incision and drainage without a marsupialisation or catheter technique, leading to recurrence Missing a Bartholin gland carcinoma by assuming any posterior vulval mass in an older woman is a benign cyst Prescribing antibiotics for a fluctuant abscess instead of draining it Failing to consider diabetes or immunosuppression in recurrent disease Mistaking other vulval or vaginal cysts for a Bartholin cyst because of location The greater vestibular (Bartholin) glands lie deep to the posterior vulva and secrete mucus through ducts opening into the vestibule to lubricate the introitus. When a duct becomes obstructed, often after inflammation or minor trauma, secretions are retained and the duct distends into a cyst. If the retained fluid becomes secondarily infected, typically by mixed vaginal and enteric organisms, an abscess develops with the classic features of acute inflammation. Because the underlying problem is a blocked duct, treatments that merely evacuate the contents without maintaining an open drainage tract allow re-obstruction and recurrence. Most Bartholin cysts and abscesses resolve well after drainage with a fistulising technique, though recurrence can occur; the rare Bartholin gland carcinoma carries a far more serious prognosis and must not be missed in older women.

Bartonellosis — cat scratch disease, Bartonella infection, bacillary angiomatosis, Carrion's disease Mycobacterial lymphadenitis (tuberculous or atypical) Lymphoma and other causes of regional lymphadenopathy Toxoplasmosis Pyogenic bacterial lymphadenitis Other causes of culture-negative endocarditis (e.g. Coxiella) Kaposi sarcoma (for the vascular lesions of bacillary angiomatosis) Tuberculous lymphadenitis Toxoplasmosis Coxiella (Q fever) endocarditis Pyogenic lymphadenitis Bartonella serology (indirect immunofluorescence or EIA) as a first-line test PCR of blood, lymph node aspirate, or tissue for Bartonella DNA Histopathology of affected nodes or skin lesions, with special stains such as Warthin-Starry silver stain Echocardiography and repeated cultures when endocarditis is suspected HIV testing and immune status assessment when bacillary angiomatosis is considered Bartonella species cause a spectrum of illness; Bartonella henselae is the usual agent of cat scratch disease, typically following a scratch or bite from a young cat or flea exposure Cat scratch disease classically presents with a papule or pustule at the inoculation site followed by regional lymphadenopathy that is often tender and can suppurate Most immunocompetent patients have a self-limiting illness, and management is often supportive with antibiotics reserved for more severe or systemic disease In immunocompromised patients, particularly those with advanced HIV, Bartonella can cause bacillary angiomatosis with vascular proliferative skin and visceral lesions Bartonella is an important cause of culture-negative endocarditis, so it should be considered when blood cultures remain sterile Atypical presentations include prolonged fever of unknown origin, hepatosplenic granulomatous disease, neuroretinitis with a macular star, and encephalopathy Diagnosis relies on serology, PCR, or special stains and histology, as the organism is fastidious and difficult to culture by routine methods Culture-negative endocarditis with embolic phenomena or heart failure Neuroretinitis with visual loss, or encephalopathy and seizures Disseminated vascular lesions (bacillary angiomatosis) in an immunocompromised patient Persistent high fever, hepatosplenic lesions, or systemic deterioration Overlooking Bartonella as a cause of culture-negative endocarditis Failing to elicit a history of cat or flea exposure in regional lymphadenopathy Not assessing immune status when vascular proliferative lesions are found Draining or excising nodes unnecessarily in what is often a self-limiting illness Bartonella are fastidious, facultatively intracellular Gram-negative bacteria that infect erythrocytes and endothelial cells. Transmission occurs through animal scratches or bites and arthropod vectors such as fleas and lice depending on species. In immunocompetent hosts the infection typically provokes a granulomatous immune response producing localised lymphadenitis. The bacterium's ability to invade endothelium and stimulate vascular proliferation underlies bacillary angiomatosis and peliosis seen in immunocompromised patients, and its persistence within red cells and on cardiac valves accounts for bacteraemia and endocarditis. Cat scratch disease in immunocompetent people usually resolves spontaneously over weeks to months, while endocarditis, disseminated disease, and complications in immunocompromised hosts require prolonged antibiotic therapy and carry greater morbidity.

Bartonellosis (Carrion disease) — Bartonella bacilliformis infection, Carrion's disease, Oroya fever, verruga peruana, verruca peruana Malaria and other causes of febrile haemolytic anaemia Enteric fever and other bacteraemias Bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella henselae/quintana, especially in HIV) Pyogenic granuloma Kaposi sarcoma (for the eruptive nodules) Haemangioma or other vascular tumours Cutaneous leishmaniasis Peripheral blood smear for intra-erythrocytic bacilli in the acute phase Blood cultures (including for secondary pathogens such as Salmonella) Full blood count and haemolysis markers documenting anaemia Skin biopsy and histology of eruptive lesions showing endothelial proliferation Serology and PCR for Bartonella bacilliformis where available Screening for co-infection given immunosuppression in the acute phase Carrion disease is caused by Bartonella bacilliformis and is transmitted by sandflies (Lutzomyia species) in the Andean valleys of Peru, Ecuador and Colombia The illness is classically biphasic: an acute haematic phase (Oroya fever) followed weeks to months later by a chronic eruptive phase (verruga peruana) Oroya fever is an acute febrile illness with severe haemolytic anaemia caused by intra-erythrocytic bacteria, and carries high mortality if untreated, often compounded by secondary infections such as Salmonella Verruga peruana is characterised by crops of red-purple vascular skin nodules (angiomatous papules) that can resemble pyogenic granulomas or bacillary angiomatosis Diagnosis in the acute phase uses peripheral blood smear showing bacilli within red cells and blood culture; the eruptive phase is supported by histology of skin lesions and serology or PCR Asymptomatic carriage occurs and sustains transmission, and immunity after infection modifies the presentation in endemic residents versus travellers Treatment differs by phase, using antibiotics effective against Bartonella; severe Oroya fever requires cover for concurrent bacteraemias and supportive transfusion Severe haemolytic anaemia with haemodynamic compromise in Oroya fever Signs of secondary bacteraemia or sepsis (e.g. Salmonella) Neurological involvement or altered consciousness Profound immunosuppression during the acute phase Failure to improve on antibiotics suggesting concurrent infection Attributing febrile haemolysis to malaria alone and missing the blood-smear bacilli Overlooking secondary Salmonella or other bacteraemia in acute-phase patients Mistaking verruga peruana nodules for pyogenic granuloma, Kaposi sarcoma or bacillary angiomatosis Using the same treatment approach for both phases without accounting for their differences Underestimating transfusion and supportive needs in severe anaemia Bartonella bacilliformis is inoculated during the bite of an infected sandfly. The bacterium invades and multiplies within erythrocytes, causing massive intravascular and extravascular haemolysis that produces the profound anaemia of the acute Oroya fever phase; immunosuppression during this phase predisposes to superimposed infections. After the acute illness resolves the organism persists and, in the eruptive phase, stimulates vascular endothelial proliferation, producing the angiomatous cutaneous nodules of verruga peruana. Cell-mediated immunity governs progression between phases, and partial immunity in endemic populations attenuates disease. Untreated Oroya fever has a high mortality from haemolysis and secondary infection, whereas prompt antibiotic and supportive treatment greatly improves survival; the eruptive verruga phase is generally benign and self-limiting though lesions can bleed and persist.

hypertension is expected Management principles include generous potassium and salt repletion, potassium-sparing strategies, and blockade of prostaglandin synthesis to reduce salt wasting Severe hypokalaemia causing arrhythmia or profound weakness Marked volume depletion and dehydration, especially in neonates Failure to thrive or growth retardation in children Progressive nephrocalcinosis with declining renal function Mistaking surreptitious diuretic or laxative abuse for a genetic tubulopathy without appropriate screening Confusing Bartter with Gitelman syndrome by not checking urinary calcium and serum magnesium Overlooking the diagnosis in a normotensive patient with unexplained hypokalaemic alkalosis Inadequate potassium and magnesium repletion leaving the patient symptomatic Bartter syndrome comprises a group of autosomal recessive defects in the ion transporters of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, the site of action of loop diuretics. Loss of function in the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter or its associated potassium and chloride channels impairs sodium chloride reabsorption, causing renal salt and water wasting. The resulting volume contraction activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, and the combination of increased distal sodium delivery and high aldosterone drives potassium and hydrogen secretion, producing hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. Because the transporter normally contributes to the electrochemical gradient favouring calcium reabsorption, its loss leaves calcium excretion normal or elevated. Overproduction of prostaglandins amplifies the salt wasting and the activation of renin. With consistent electrolyte and fluid replacement and prostaglandin inhibition, most patients maintain reasonable growth and function, though lifelong therapy is required. Severe antenatal forms carry higher perinatal risk, and chronic hypokalaemia and nephrocalcinosis can gradually impair renal function.

dehydration and electrolyte disturbance Profound hypokalaemia risking cardiac arrhythmia Failure to thrive with growth restriction Progressive nephrocalcinosis with declining renal function Mistaking the presentation for surreptitious diuretic use, or vice versa Confusing it with Gitelman syndrome, which characteristically causes hypocalciuria and hypomagnesaemia rather than hypercalciuria Interpreting the very high aldosterone as primary hyperaldosteronism despite normal or low blood pressure Overlooking transient neonatal hyperkalaemia in ROMK-related disease Neglecting nephrocalcinosis surveillance and cumulative renal injury Antenatal Bartter syndrome results from inherited loss of salt reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, where the NKCC2 cotransporter (SLC12A1) and the apical ROMK channel (KCNJ1) normally drive sodium, potassium and chloride uptake and recycle potassium back into the tubular lumen. When these fail, sodium chloride is lost in the urine, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and increasing distal sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ion, which produces hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Impaired salt handling also dissipates the transepithelial voltage that normally drives paracellular calcium reabsorption, causing hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis. Compensatory renal prostaglandin synthesis amplifies polyuria and systemic vasodilatation, explaining the severe fetal and neonatal phenotype and the benefit of prostaglandin inhibition. With early salt and potassium replacement and prostaglandin inhibition, many children stabilise and grow, though nephrocalcinosis and a degree of chronic kidney impairment may persist. Long-term outcome depends on the genetic subtype and on avoiding recurrent severe electrolyte crises.

Basal cell adenoma — Monomorphic adenoma, Dermal analogue tumour (membranous type) Pleomorphic adenoma (cellular type) Adenoid cystic carcinoma Basal cell adenocarcinoma Canalicular adenoma Basaloid squamous cell carcinoma Myoepithelioma Fine-needle aspiration cytology, with core biopsy if a basaloid lesion is uncertain Ultrasound of the gland MRI for well-defined lesions and to assess extent Immunohistochemistry including beta-catenin and myoepithelial markers Examination and history for cutaneous cylindromas or trichoepitheliomas (Brooke-Spiegler syndrome) Histological examination of the excised specimen A benign monomorphic adenoma composed of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and a distinct basement-membrane-like rim, most commonly in the parotid. The defining negative feature is the absence of the chondromyxoid stroma of pleomorphic adenoma, which aids histological distinction. Recognised architectural subtypes are solid, trabecular, tubular and membranous. The membranous (dermal analogue) subtype is associated with Brooke-Spiegler syndrome, with synchronous cutaneous cylindromas and trichoepitheliomas and germline CYLD alteration. Non-membranous subtypes frequently harbour CTNNB1 (beta-catenin) mutations, with nuclear beta-catenin accumulation on immunohistochemistry. It typically presents in older adults as a slow-growing, mobile, painless mass with a slight female predominance. The membranous subtype is more often multifocal and recurs more readily than other subtypes. A basaloid aspirate on cytology overlaps substantially with adenoid cystic carcinoma, so caution is needed before a benign report. Infiltrative or ill-defined margins suggesting basal cell adenocarcinoma Rapid growth or new pain Perineural symptoms such as numbness or facial weakness pointing towards adenoid cystic carcinoma Multifocal tumours with syndromic cutaneous features Fixation to surrounding tissues Misclassifying a basaloid aspirate as adenoid cystic carcinoma or vice versa Failing to identify the underlying Brooke-Spiegler syndrome in membranous tumours Mistaking an infiltrative basal cell adenocarcinoma for a benign adenoma Assuming complete excision without recognising the multifocality of the membranous subtype Basal cell adenoma is a benign epithelial neoplasm arising from the basal reserve cells of the salivary duct system, showing both luminal ductal and abluminal (basal/myoepithelial) differentiation but lacking the mesenchymal-type chondromyxoid matrix of pleomorphic adenoma. In most non-membranous tumours, activating mutations in CTNNB1 lead to nuclear translocation of beta-catenin and constitutive WNT pathway signalling, promoting basaloid proliferation. The membranous subtype is genetically distinct, associated with inactivation of the CYLD tumour suppressor in the context of Brooke-Spiegler syndrome, which predisposes to multiple adnexal and salivary basaloid tumours. Growth is expansile and encapsulated in most subtypes, although the membranous type is characteristically multinodular and less well demarcated. Prognosis is excellent after complete excision for non-membranous subtypes, with malignant transformation rare. The membranous subtype has a higher rate of local recurrence and multicentricity and warrants closer follow-up.

syndrome or prior radiation exposure Advise lifelong photoprotection and skin surveillance, as a diagnosis of BCC predicts further skin cancers A non-healing, ulcerating, or bleeding lesion on sun-exposed skin, which is a hallmark of malignancy An ill-defined, indurated, scar-like plaque suggesting an infiltrative or morphoeic tumour with deep spread Lesions at high-risk facial sites (eyes, nose, ears) where local destruction threatens vital structures Numerous or early-onset tumours suggesting an inherited cancer syndrome or prior radiotherapy Mistaking a morphoeic BCC for a scar and underestimating its true extent Treating a superficial BCC as eczema or psoriasis and delaying diagnosis Choosing a non-surgical or narrow-margin approach for high-risk or recurrent facial tumours Failing to arrange ongoing skin surveillance after a first diagnosis Basal cell carcinoma is a malignancy of the basal keratinocytes of the epidermis and follicular structures, driven predominantly by ultraviolet-induced DNA damage. Aberrant activation of the Hedgehog signalling pathway, commonly through inactivating mutations in the PTCH1 tumour-suppressor gene or activating changes in SMO, is central to tumour development, alongside UV signature mutations in TP53. The tumour grows as nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and a surrounding fibromyxoid stroma. Its behaviour is locally invasive rather than metastatic, and infiltrative or morphoeic patterns spread with subclinical extension that explains higher recurrence when margins are inadequate. The prognosis is excellent because metastasis is exceedingly rare, and appropriately treated tumours are usually cured; however, incompletely excised or high-risk subtypes recur and can cause significant local morbidity, and patients remain at higher lifetime risk of further skin cancers requiring ongoing surveillance.

Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System — Cardiovascular system biology, Cardiac and vascular cell biology, Cardiovascular developmental biology Flow-mediated dilatation of the brachial artery by ultrasound (cuff occlusion/release) to assess endothelial vasodilator function in vivo The heart arises from crescent-shaped fields of lateral splanchnic mesoderm; a primary (first) heart field forms the linear heart tube while a second heart field, marked by Islet-1 expression, later adds myocardium to the inflow/outflow poles and contributes much of the right ventricle and outflow tract. Neural crest cells are required for aortic arch remodeling and truncus arteriosus septation; because these cells are sensitive to vitamin A and folic acid, maternal deficiency of these vitamins is associated with congenital defects of aortic arch remodeling. Coronary arteries depend on epicardial cells derived from the proepicardial organ (a septum transversum derivative that also forms the fibrous diaphragm and contributes to the liver), which supply coronary smooth muscle and help pattern the vessels. The cardiac conduction system differentiates from cardiomyocyte precursors into slow-conducting proximal components (SA and AV nodes) and fast-conducting distal components (His bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers); developmental defects can produce congenital heart block or pre-excitation (Wolff-Parkinson-White). Decremental conduction across the AV node delays atrial-to-ventricular impulse transmission to allow sequential contraction and protects the ventricle by limiting transmission of rapid atrial rates. The endothelium is a selectively permeable barrier and a major homeostatic organ: under physiologic conditions it favors vasodilation, an antithrombotic/profibrinolytic state, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties; endothelial dysfunction reverses each of these (vasoconstriction, prothrombotic, proinflammatory, prooxidant, impaired barrier). Endothelium-derived vasodilators include nitric oxide (NO), prostacyclin, endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factor, and hydrogen peroxide; flow-mediated dilatation (brachial artery cuff occlusion/release with ultrasound) is used to assess endothelial vasodilator function in humans. Excess reactive oxygen species (e.g., superoxide generated under high angiotensin II exposure) inactivate NO, and inflammatory stimuli/endotoxin/angiotensin II drive endothelial production of PAI-1 and tissue factor, shifting balance toward thrombosis (contributing to DIC in sepsis and to hyperglycemia-related prothrombotic states). Vascular smooth-muscle contraction is governed by cytosolic calcium and the balance of myosin light chain kinase (calcium/calmodulin-activated) versus myosin light chain phosphatase; voltage-dependent L-type calcium channels and IP3-triggered sarcoplasmic reticulum release raise intracellular calcium. Cardiac contraction follows the sliding-filament model: an L-type calcium current during the action potential plateau triggers calcium-induced calcium release from the SR via the ryanodine receptor RyR2; calcium binds troponin C, relieving troponin-tropomyosin inhibition so actin and myosin cross-bridge cycling (ATP-dependent) can occur. Relaxation depends on lowering cytosolic calcium by SR reuptake via SERCA2A (regulated by phospholamban) and sarcolemmal Na+/Ca2+ exchange; PKA phosphorylation of phospholamban speeds reuptake and produces the lusitropic (enhanced relaxation) effect. Cytoplasmic calcium is the principal determinant of inotropic state: positive inotropes such as digitalis glycosides and beta-adrenergic agonists act by raising cytosolic calcium (beta agonists via Gs-adenylyl cyclase-cyclic AMP-PKA phosphorylation of sarcolemmal calcium channels). Ventricular stroke volume is set by three factors: preload (muscle length at contraction onset), afterload (tension developed during contraction), and contractility; contractile force is optimal near a sarcomere length of about 2.2 micrometers, the structural basis of the Frank-Starling relationship. Inherited or acquired disturbances of SR calcium handling (RyR2/regulatory protein abnormalities) can impair contraction and predispose to heart failure or ventricular arrhythmias. Mutations in sarcomeric and cytoskeletal proteins (including titin, dystrophin/dystroglycan complex) cause Mendelian cardiomyopathies and sensitize the heart to toxic insults such as alcohol or chemotherapy and to inflammatory or peripartum cardiomyopathy. Developmental conduction-system defects may present as congenital heart block or pre-excitation (Wolff-Parkinson-White). Treating these molecular and developmental concepts as purely theoretical: shared embryonic origins of cardiovascular cell types explain syndromic associations between congenital heart disease and extracardiac anomalies. Overlooking that true regeneration of a complete three-layered blood vessel does not normally occur in adult mammals, so adult arteriogenesis/angiogenesis reflects growth and collateral expansion rather than new full-thickness vessel formation. Assuming adult vascular smooth-muscle cells are quiescent; they proliferate and migrate after injury or inflammatory activation, contributing to atherosclerotic stenosis, hypertensive arteriolar remodeling, and restenosis. The cardiovascular system develops from cardiac progenitors in lateral splanchnic mesoderm that fuse into a linear heart tube of endocardium and spontaneously beating cardiomyocytes, then undergo asymmetric looping and chamber specification with continued addition of second-heart-field cells (Islet-1 positive). Septation separates the cardiac chambers and divides the truncus arteriosus into aorta and pulmonary artery; endocardial cushions, rich in hyaluronic-acid 'cardiac jelly', undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transformation to form valves. Neural crest cells direct aortic arch remodeling and supply smooth muscle to the great vessels, while proepicardial cells form coronary vasculature. Blood vessels share a trilaminar architecture (intimal endothelium, smooth-muscle media, fibroblast-rich adventitia), with capillaries reduced to an endothelial tube and pericytes and large vessels nourished by vasa vasorum. The endothelium maintains vascular homeostasis through balanced production of vasodilators (NO, prostacyclin) and vasoconstrictors (endothelin), regulation of leukocyte adhesion, and modulation of coagulation; loss of these functions underlies atherosclerosis, hypertension, capillary-leak states, and immune-mediated vascular injury. Vascular smooth-muscle tone is set by intracellular calcium and myosin light chain phosphorylation, integrated through sympathetic, parasympathetic, and nonadrenergic/noncholinergic (nitrergic, peptidergic) autonomic signaling. In the myocardium, the sarcomere is the contractile unit; excitation-contraction coupling links the action potential and T-tubular calcium entry to RyR2-mediated SR calcium release, troponin C activation, and actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling, with relaxation driven by SERCA2A reuptake and Na+/Ca2+ exchange. Cardiac output reflects the interplay of preload, afterload, and contractility (Frank-Starling mechanism). As a foundational chapter, prognosis is framed at the level of mechanism: increased arterial stiffness with aging or disease raises left ventricular afterload and portends a poor outcome, and sustained high-flow states (e.g., left-to-right shunts) drive pulmonary smooth-muscle proliferation and pulmonary hypertension. Outcomes in specific cardiovascular diseases are detailed in their respective chapters.

Basic calcium phosphate crystal arthropathy — BCP crystal arthropathy, basic calcium phosphate deposition, apatite-associated arthropathy, calcific periarthritis Gout Calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis (pseudogout) Septic arthritis or bursitis Rotator cuff tear or subacromial impingement Osteoarthritis Cellulitis Radiographs for amorphous periarticular calcification and to track its resorption Ultrasound for calcific tendinitis or deposits and to guide aspiration Joint or bursal aspiration with cell count and culture to exclude infection Polarised microscopy (which will not show the crystals) with alizarin red staining to suggest BCP MRI where soft-tissue or rotator cuff pathology needs clarification Electron microscopy in cases of diagnostic uncertainty or for research confirmation Basic calcium phosphate (BCP) crystals, predominantly carbonate-substituted hydroxyapatite, deposit in periarticular soft tissues such as tendons and bursae and also within joints The commonest clinical expression is calcific periarthritis or tendinitis, classically calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff at the shoulder BCP crystals are minute and non-birefringent, so they are not seen on standard polarised microscopy; clumps may stain with alizarin red, but definitive confirmation needs special techniques such as electron microscopy Acute calcific periarthritis presents with sudden severe periarticular pain, swelling, and tenderness, most often at the shoulder, and can mimic gout, infection, or acute CPP arthritis Radiographs may show amorphous, cloud-like periarticular calcific deposits that can change or resorb over time, unlike the linear chondrocalcinosis of CPPD BCP deposition is implicated in severe destructive arthropathies, most notably Milwaukee shoulder syndrome Treatment is largely symptomatic, using anti-inflammatory therapy, aspiration or needling (barbotage) of deposits, and physiotherapy, as there is no specific crystal-dissolving agent Rapidly destructive shoulder or joint pathology suggesting Milwaukee shoulder Features indicating possible septic arthritis or bursitis Large deposits causing mechanical symptoms or nerve compression Missing BCP disease because the crystals are invisible on routine polarised microscopy Confusing amorphous BCP calcification with the linear chondrocalcinosis of CPPD Treating self-limiting acute calcific periarthritis as infection unnecessarily Overlooking an underlying destructive arthropathy driven by the crystals Basic calcium phosphate crystals, chiefly hydroxyapatite, form and deposit in periarticular structures and cartilage, often at sites of tissue turnover or degeneration. When crystals are shed into a bursa, tendon sheath, or joint they provoke an acute inflammatory reaction, producing calcific periarthritis. Within joints, BCP crystals can stimulate synovial cells to release proteolytic enzymes that degrade cartilage and periarticular tissue, contributing to rapidly destructive arthropathies. Because the crystals are non-birefringent and extremely small, their detection is far harder than for urate or calcium pyrophosphate crystals. Acute calcific periarthritis is usually self-limiting and the deposits may resorb, with good recovery; however, BCP-associated destructive arthropathies such as Milwaukee shoulder can cause substantial and progressive joint damage.

Basic calcium phosphate deposition disease — BCP deposition disease, hydroxyapatite deposition disease Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease Gout Rotator cuff tear or tendinopathy Septic arthritis or bursitis Osteoarthritis Radiographs showing periarticular calcification Ultrasound to identify calcific tendinitis Synovial fluid analysis (crystals not seen on standard microscopy; alizarin red where available) Exclusion of infection when acutely inflamed Assessment of joint destruction in suspected Milwaukee shoulder Deposition of basic calcium phosphate (mainly hydroxyapatite) crystals in periarticular and articular tissues Calcific tendinitis, especially of the rotator cuff, is a common manifestation causing acute severe shoulder pain In the shoulder it can cause the destructive Milwaukee shoulder syndrome with a large effusion and cuff arthropathy The crystals are too small to see with ordinary light microscopy and are not birefringent, unlike urate and CPP crystals Alizarin red staining or advanced techniques are needed to identify the crystals Radiographs show amorphous periarticular calcification; treatment is largely symptomatic with some cases needing aspiration or barbotage Rapidly destructive arthropathy (Milwaukee shoulder) Features suggesting septic arthritis or bursitis Severe acute calcific tendinitis Progressive functional loss Failing to detect the crystals because they are invisible on standard microscopy Confusing it with CPPD or gout Missing septic arthritis in an acutely inflamed joint Underestimating the destructive potential in the shoulder Basic calcium phosphate deposition disease involves the accumulation of hydroxyapatite and related crystals in tendons, bursae and joints. In tendons this causes calcific tendinitis, and crystal shedding provokes acute inflammation. Within joints, particularly the shoulder, the crystals stimulate release of enzymes that degrade cartilage and cause a rapidly destructive arthropathy (Milwaukee shoulder). gastrointestinal mass Rapid enlargement or systemic spread of disease Extensive organ involvement (liver, colon) on imaging Diagnostic confusion leading to inappropriate cancer or Crohn's therapy Human subcutaneous disease is thought to follow inoculation through minor skin trauma or insect bites, while gastrointestinal disease probably results from ingestion of contaminated soil, food, or water. In the tissues the fungus provokes a chronic granulomatous and intensely eosinophilic inflammatory response rather than the vascular invasion typical of true zygomycetes, so infarction is uncommon. The hyphae are surrounded by eosinophilic Splendore-Hoeppli material, and the reaction slowly forms fibrotic masses. In the bowel this transmural inflammation and mass effect closely imitates Crohn's disease or carcinoma, and can lead to obstruction or perforation. Subcutaneous disease usually responds well to prolonged antifungal therapy with a good outlook; gastrointestinal disease carries higher morbidity because of late diagnosis and complications, though combined surgery and antifungals achieve cure in many patients.
