rapidly deteriorating child Overlooking raccoon exposure and pica in the history Attributing eosinophilic meningitis solely to more familiar causes Failing to give corticosteroids alongside anthelmintic therapy to temper the inflammatory response Baylisascaris procyonis is an ascarid roundworm whose adults live in the intestine of raccoons, which shed vast numbers of environmentally hardy eggs. Humans are accidental hosts who ingest embryonated eggs from contaminated soil, hands or objects. Larvae hatch in the intestine and, rather than maturing, migrate aggressively through the tissues (visceral, ocular and neural larva migrans). The larvae continue to grow as they migrate and show a marked neurotropism, penetrating the central nervous system where they cause mechanical destruction of neural tissue and provoke an intense eosinophilic inflammatory reaction, producing a fulminant eosinophilic meningoencephalitis. In the eye they damage the retina and incite inflammation. The severity reflects both the larvae's large size and continued growth and the vigorous host immune response along their migratory tracks. Prognosis is grave once neural larva migrans is established, with a high risk of death or severe permanent neurological disability; early treatment before extensive central nervous system invasion offers the best, though still limited, chance of a good outcome.

bazex syndrome — acrokeratosis paraneoplastica, acrokeratosis paraneoplastica of Bazex Psoriasis, especially acral or palmoplantar disease Chronic acral eczema or hyperkeratotic hand and foot dermatitis Pityriasis rubra pilaris Systemic or chilblain lupus erythematosus with acral involvement Reactive arthritis-associated keratoderma blennorrhagicum Dermatophyte (tinea) infection of the hands and feet Bazex-Dupre-Christol syndrome (genodermatosis) ENT examination with nasendoscopy and laryngoscopy for upper aerodigestive squamous carcinoma CT or MRI of the head and neck, chest and mediastinum Panendoscopy including oesophagoscopy and bronchoscopy as indicated Biopsy of cervical lymphadenopathy for metastatic squamous carcinoma Skin biopsy showing non-specific hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis and dyskeratosis PET-CT to locate an occult primary when initial imaging is negative A psoriasiform, violaceous, acral dermatosis symmetrically affecting the ears, nose, fingers, toes and nails, often with adherent scale. Almost invariably paraneoplastic and strongly associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the upper aerodigestive tract (oropharynx, larynx, oesophagus, lung) and with metastatic cervical or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. It predominantly affects men over 40, frequently with a history of smoking and/or alcohol use. The eruption evolves in stages: initially acral (ears, nose, digits, nails) while the tumour is occult, then extending to the hands, feet and cheeks, and eventually more widely as disease advances. Nail dystrophy, paronychia-like change and a painful palmoplantar keratoderma are common features. Skin disease is typically resistant to topical therapy but improves with treatment of the underlying carcinoma, and recurrence signals tumour relapse. It must be distinguished from the unrelated Bazex-Dupre-Christol syndrome, an inherited disorder featuring follicular atrophoderma and early basal cell carcinomas. Acral psoriasiform eruption in a middle-aged male smoker or drinker Nail dystrophy with violaceous acral scaling unresponsive to topical therapy Cervical lymphadenopathy, dysphagia, hoarseness or haemoptysis Recurrence of the eruption after tumour treatment Misdiagnosing the eruption as treatment-resistant psoriasis or eczema and delaying the tumour search Confusing it with the unrelated Bazex-Dupre-Christol genodermatosis Not performing ENT and aerodigestive evaluation when the primary is occult Overlooking recurrence as a marker of tumour relapse The pathogenesis of acrokeratosis paraneoplastica is uncertain. Proposed mechanisms include tumour-derived growth factors such as transforming growth factor alpha, insulin-like growth factor 1 and epidermal growth factor driving epidermal hyperproliferation. An immunological hypothesis invokes molecular mimicry, whereby antibodies or cytotoxic T cells directed against tumour antigens cross-react with structurally similar antigens in the epidermis and basement membrane zone. Disturbances of zinc and vitamin A metabolism have also been implicated. The acral distribution and the close temporal relationship with tumour activity favour a humoral, tumour-related process. Prognosis reflects the associated squamous cell carcinoma, which is often advanced with regional nodal spread at diagnosis; the skin lesions typically resolve with successful tumour therapy and their recurrence heralds relapse.

follow-up Missing the diagnostic significance of crumpled ears Assuming no cardiac assessment is needed despite occasional aortic involvement Failing to distinguish it from arthrogryposis syndromes with different prognoses Beals syndrome is caused by variants in FBN2, a gene closely related to FBN1 that encodes fibrillin-2, a component of the microfibrils that form during early elastic-fibre assembly. Fibrillin-2 is expressed prominently in developing tissues, so its deficiency chiefly disturbs early skeletal and joint development, producing congenital contractures, long slender digits, and a tall marfanoid build. Because fibrillin-2 has a more limited role in the mature aortic wall and lens zonules than fibrillin-1, the severe progressive aortopathy and ectopia lentis of Marfan syndrome are generally absent, which is the key clinical distinction. The outlook is generally good, with contractures often improving over childhood and a life expectancy usually within the normal range. Kyphoscoliosis is the main source of long-term morbidity, and the aorta, when involved, is usually only mildly affected.

During the period of impaired activity a thinner segment of plate is laid down, which appears as a transverse depression once that portion emerges from beneath the proximal nail fold and grows distally. limb-girdle muscular dystrophy without genetic confirmation Underusing cardiac imaging in patients with mild or subclinical muscle disease Becker muscular dystrophy is caused by DMD gene variants that Because the variants are usually in-frame, some partially functional dystrophin is still produced, so membrane stabilisation is impaired rather than absent. Repeated contraction-induced sarcolemmal damage leads to calcium influx, fibre necrosis, and progressive replacement of muscle by fat and fibrous tissue, but at a slower rate than in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. The same protein deficiency in cardiac muscle causes dilated cardiomyopathy, which can be severe even when skeletal weakness is mild. Progression is slower than in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and many patients remain ambulant well into adulthood with a substantially longer life expectancy. Cardiomyopathy is often the main determinant of prognosis, so cardiac surveillance and timely heart-failure treatment are essential.

laser can address pigmentation and hair, though results are variable and recurrence is common Associated breast/nipple hypoplasia or skeletal anomaly indicating Becker naevus syndrome Atypical change, nodularity or rapid growth prompting exclusion of another lesion Marked induration suggesting a prominent smooth-muscle hamartoma component Confusing it with a congenital melanocytic naevus or a large café-au-lait macule Overlooking Becker naevus syndrome when there are associated anomalies Over-treating a benign lesion, with variable and often incomplete laser results Attributing the hypertrichosis to an endocrine disorder rather than the naevus itself Becker naevus is regarded as a mosaic organoid hamartoma showing increased epidermal melanisation and melanocyte activity, epidermal acanthosis and hyperplasia of arrector pili smooth muscle, rather than a proliferation of naevus cells. Local upregulation of androgen receptors is thought to underlie its typical onset at puberty, its predilection for males and the development of terminal hair. The associated smooth-muscle hamartoma explains the occasional induration and follicular prominence. The naevus is benign and stable, persisting lifelong with permanent pigmentation and hypertrichosis; it carries no meaningful malignant potential, and treatment is undertaken only for cosmetic reasons.

The prognosis is generally good; the cutaneous lesion is benign with negligible malignant potential, and the main issues relate to cosmetic appearance and to any associated skeletal or breast asymmetry, which may need orthopaedic or reconstructive management.

to the specific molecular subtype Assuming all cases are sporadic and not identifying inherited CDKN1C variants with recurrence risk Attributing isolated hemihypertrophy to normal variation without considering tumour surveillance Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is an imprinting disorder of the 11p15.5 region, which contains two differentially methylated control domains regulating growth-promoting IGF2 and growth-restraining genes such as CDKN1C. Molecular lesions that increase IGF2 expression or reduce CDKN1C activity, including loss of methylation at IC2, gain of methylation at IC1, paternal uniparental disomy, or CDKN1C mutation, tip the balance toward excess tissue growth. This produces generalised or asymmetric overgrowth, organomegaly, hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia, and a predisposition to embryonal tumours in affected tissues. With early management of hypoglycaemia and structured tumour surveillance the long-term outlook is generally good, and overgrowth and organomegaly tend to normalise with age. Tumour risk declines after early childhood, and most individuals have normal cognition and life expectancy.

Behçet Syndrome — Behçet's disease, Behcet syndrome, Behcet disease Crohn's disease (gastrointestinal Behçet can be clinically and endoscopically indistinguishable; distinction often relies on extraintestinal features) Recurrent aphthous stomatitis / ordinary canker sores Acne vulgaris (papulopustular lesions are indistinguishable in appearance and pathology) Other systemic vasculitides Inflammatory bowel disease more broadly Herpetic and other infectious genital/oral ulceration causing recurrent ulcers Diagnosis is clinical; no specific laboratory, imaging, or histologic test confirms it, so investigations mainly serve to exclude mimics. International Study Group (ISG) criteria: recurrent oral ulceration (at least 3 times in 12 months) plus two of recurrent genital ulcers, skin lesions, eye lesions, or a positive pathergy test (sensitivity ~95%, specificity ~96%). Pathergy test: dermal insertion of a 20-gauge (20-21 gauge) needle, read at 24-48 h. HLA-B*51 testing may support but cannot establish the diagnosis. Endoscopy for suspected gastrointestinal involvement (ulcers typically single or fewer than five, deep, round, confined to the ileocecal area, prone to perforation). Vascular and neuroimaging when vascular or CNS involvement is suspected (e.g., pulmonary artery aneurysm, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, parenchymal CNS lesions). Crohn's disease (especially with ileocecal ulcers) Acne vulgaris Recurrent aphthous stomatitis A systemic vasculitis presenting with various combinations of oral and genital ulcers, skin lesions, uveitis, arthritis, large vessel (arterial and venous) disease, and gastrointestinal and neurologic involvement, with manifestations appearing in differing sequences over time. Oral ulcers occur in essentially all patients (~98%) and are usually the first manifestation; they are typically multiple, resemble ordinary canker sores, last about 10 days, and recur unless treated, with only the uncommon major ulcers tending to scar. Genital ulcers are the most specific lesion, most often on the scrotum or labia; they are larger, deeper, slower to heal than oral ulcers, and tend to scar. The pathergy reaction (a papule or pustule forming 24-48 h after a needle prick) is a fairly unique nonspecific skin hyperreactivity and is part of the diagnostic criteria. Hypopyon (intense anterior chamber inflammation), seen in about 10% of patients with eye disease, is quite specific for Behçet syndrome. Superficial thrombophlebitis often occurs in men and is associated with deep-vein thrombosis; its presence should prompt a workup for other vascular involvement including pulmonary artery aneurysm. HLA-B*51 is positive in up to 50-60% of patients depending on geographic origin, but it is not diagnostic because roughly 20% of the normal population also carries it. Most prevalent in Turkey (about 1 in 250 adults); patients are most commonly from the Middle East, Mediterranean, and Far East. Onset before the late teens or after age 50 is uncommon. Sexes are affected roughly equally, but males tend to have more severe disease and worse outcomes; eye involvement may reach ~70% in males. Ocular disease (most often bilateral panuveitis) usually appears within the first 2 years after diagnostic criteria are met, is most severe early, then tends to abate. Most new manifestations appear within the first 5 years, and the natural history for most patients is one of diminishing symptoms that may culminate in remission. Superficial thrombophlebitis in a male should trigger evaluation for deeper vascular involvement including pulmonary artery aneurysm. Pulmonary artery aneurysms carry a 5-year mortality of about 20-25%. Subacute severe headache with cranial nerve palsy, dysarthria, ataxia, or hemiparesis suggests parenchymal CNS involvement (telencephalic-diencephalic junction, brainstem, spinal cord). Deep, round ileocecal ulcers are prone to perforation. Clustering thrombotic events (deep-vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, IVC syndrome, intracardiac thrombosis, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis). Diagnosis may take months to years as the full constellation of features evolves; a tentative diagnosis often precedes a definitive one. HLA-B*51 is not a diagnostic test because it is common in the general population. Gastrointestinal Behçet is easily mistaken for Crohn's disease unless extraintestinal manifestations are evident. Pathergy and eye lesions each occur in only about half of patients, so their absence does not exclude the diagnosis. Regional variation matters: gastrointestinal involvement is common in Japan and seen in ~30% of US patients but rare in Turkey. The cause and pathogenesis are unknown. Family studies suggest a possible genetic predisposition, and heightened inflammation with involvement of both innate and adaptive immunity is implicated. Neutrophil hyperreactivity is present, though it is unclear whether this is primary or secondary to cytokine-driven activation. The disorder sits between classic autoimmune and autoinflammatory conditions: unlike typical autoimmune disease it is not generally associated with autoantibodies, Raynaud's phenomenon, Sjögren's syndrome, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, photosensitivity, serosal involvement, or increased risk of other autoimmune diseases; unlike classic autoinflammatory disease it tends to abate over time, lacks the mutations seen in autoinflammatory syndromes, and is more prevalent than disorders such as familial Mediterranean fever. Retrospective cohort data suggest distinct disease clusters (e.g., acne lesions clustering with arthritis and enthesitis) that may have differing pathogeneses. Most patients follow a course of diminishing symptoms over time with potential remission, often eventually requiring no ongoing medication, and most new manifestations emerge within the first 5 years. Young male patients tend to have worse outcomes. Poor ocular prognostic factors include male sex, posterior involvement, frequent attacks (>3 per year), strong vitreous opacity, and macular edema. Pulmonary artery aneurysms are associated with a 5-year mortality of about 20-25%. No formal severity grade; management and outlook are stratified by the type and severity of organ involvement (mucocutaneous, ocular, vascular, gastrointestinal, neurologic), with young male sex and posterior/severe eye disease marking higher-risk disease.

testing Failing to appreciate loss of insight, so that patient self-report understates the problem Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia results from progressive degeneration of the frontal and anterior temporal lobes, with the underlying frontotemporal lobar degeneration most often characterised by abnormal accumulation of either tau or TDP-43 protein, and less commonly FUS. Preferential involvement of frontal-subcortical and salience networks, together with early loss of specialised neurones such as von Economo cells, underlies the disinhibition, apathy and executive impairment. Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia is progressive and currently incurable, with gradual decline in behaviour, cognition and eventually motor function. Survival is generally shorter than in Alzheimer's disease and is particularly reduced when there is coexisting motor neurone disease. Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, focusing on behavioural strategies, carer support, safety and advance care planning.

and risking irreversible vision loss Managing vascular thrombosis with anticoagulation alone without addressing the underlying inflammation, and overlooking coexisting aneurysms Attributing neurological symptoms to other causes rather than neuro-Behçet Assuming absence of pathergy or HLA-B51 excludes the diagnosis Behçet disease is a chronic relapsing inflammatory disorder classified as a variable-vessel vasculitis because it can affect vessels of any size and type, both arterial and venous. Its cause is uncertain but involves genetic susceptibility (notably HLA-B51) and dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity with prominent neutrophil hyperactivity, elevated Th1/Th17 responses, and inflammation triggered in predisposed individuals. Vascular inflammation produces thrombosis, aneurysm formation, and tissue damage, while immune-mediated inflammation drives the recurrent mucocutaneous, ocular, neurological, and gastrointestinal lesions. Course is relapsing and remitting and tends to be more severe in young men. Mucocutaneous disease is troublesome but not dangerous, whereas ocular, neurological, and major vascular involvement drive the risk of blindness, disability, and death. Early aggressive treatment of organ-threatening disease improves outcome.

disease typically presents in the secondary stage with mucous patches of the mouth and oropharynx and moist condyloma-like lesions in skin folds Secondary features include angular stomatitis (split papules at the mouth angles), laryngitis and generalised skin lesions, with osteoperiostitis of long bones Late (tertiary) bejel produces gummatous destruction of skin, nasopharynx and bone, including gangosa, similar to late yaws Serology and dark-field microscopy are indistinguishable from those of venereal syphilis and the other endemic treponematoses Treatment of the endemic treponematoses uses benzathine penicillin, with a macrolide alternative for penicillin-allergic patients and mass-treatment campaigns Destructive nasopharyngeal (gangosa) lesions causing disfigurement Airway or swallowing compromise from laryngeal or oropharyngeal involvement Extensive gummatous bone destruction with deformity Difficulty distinguishing from venereal syphilis in adolescents or adults Reappearance of lesions after treatment Misinterpreting positive treponemal serology as venereal syphilis, with inappropriate social and clinical implications Overlooking the largely unnoticed primary stage and only recognising disease when secondary lesions appear Failing to treat contacts and address shared-utensil transmission Confusing bejel with yaws or pinta without geographic and clinical context Neglecting nutritional and hygiene factors in affected communities Treponema pallidum subspecies endemicum is transmitted through direct mucosal contact or shared utensils in communities with limited hygiene. After entering through the oral mucosa or skin the treponeme multiplies locally and disseminates, producing mucosal and cutaneous secondary lesions and bone involvement over weeks to months. A latent phase may be followed years later by destructive tertiary gummatous lesions of skin, bone and the nasopharynx. As with yaws, the cardiovascular and neurological complications and congenital transmission characteristic of venereal syphilis are not features of bejel. Early bejel responds well to penicillin with full recovery, but untreated late disease may cause permanent, disfiguring destruction of the oronasopharynx and bone; the endemic treponematoses are targets for elimination programmes.

or slow to recover for an underlying structural lesion Bell's palsy is an acute mononeuropathy of the facial (seventh cranial) nerve, widely attributed to inflammation and oedema of the nerve, often linked to reactivation of herpes simplex virus. Swelling of the nerve within the narrow bony facial canal causes compression, ischaemia, and demyelination, producing unilateral weakness of all facial muscles on the affected side. Depending on the segment involved, taste, lacrimation, and stapedius function may also be impaired. Most patients with Bell's palsy recover well, and the majority regain normal or near-normal function, particularly with early corticosteroid treatment and when weakness is incomplete. A minority, especially those with complete paralysis, are left with residual weakness, synkinesis, or contracture. Recovery beginning within the first few weeks predicts a favourable outcome.

Benign cephalic histiocytosis — BCH, histiocytosis with intracytoplasmic worm-like bodies Juvenile xanthogranuloma Generalised eruptive histiocytosis Langerhans cell histiocytosis Urticaria pigmentosa / cutaneous mastocytosis Flat warts (verruca plana) Xanthoma disseminatum Molluscum contagiosum Skin biopsy with histology and immunohistochemistry (CD68, factor XIIIa, CD1a, langerin) Electron microscopy demonstrating comma-shaped bodies and absent Birbeck granules where diagnosis is uncertain Clinical review to confirm absence of systemic involvement Blood glucose and assessment for diabetes insipidus if suggestive symptoms arise Dermoscopy to distinguish from mastocytosis and other papular disorders Serial photography to document the characteristic evolution and regression A self-limiting non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis of early childhood presenting with multiple small red-brown to yellowish macules and flat-topped papules. Onset is usually in the first three years of life, with lesions beginning on the head and face, particularly the cheeks, forehead and around the eyes and ears. Lesions subsequently spread in a cephalocaudal direction to the neck, upper trunk and proximal limbs while sparing mucosae, palms and soles. The condition is asymptomatic and, by definition, has no visceral, ocular or bony involvement. Spontaneous resolution over months to a few years is the rule, often leaving transient hyperpigmentation or slight atrophy. Histology shows a well-demarcated dermal infiltrate of histiocytes that are CD68 positive and CD1a and langerin negative, with characteristic comma-shaped or worm-like bodies on electron microscopy and absence of Birbeck granules. It is considered by many authorities to lie on a spectrum with juvenile xanthogranuloma and generalised eruptive histiocytosis within the cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses. Rare reports describe coexistent diabetes insipidus or diabetes mellitus, so evolving systemic symptoms merit review. Development of polyuria and polydipsia suggesting diabetes insipidus Hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy suggesting an alternative systemic histiocytosis Mucosal, palmar or plantar involvement, which is atypical and should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis Progressive rather than eventually regressing disease Systemic symptoms such as fever or failure to thrive Misinterpreting the papules as cutaneous mastocytosis or flat warts and instituting unnecessary treatment. Confusing it with Langerhans cell histiocytosis; immunohistochemistry for CD1a and langerin distinguishes the two. Subjecting a child to extensive systemic investigation for what is a benign self-limiting condition. Failing to counsel families that lesions may continue to appear for a time before regression begins. Overlooking the rare emergence of diabetes insipidus during follow-up. Benign cephalic histiocytosis is a reactive proliferation of dermal macrophage-lineage histiocytes belonging to the cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses. The infiltrating cells are dendrocyte-derived histiocytes that express macrophage markers such as CD68 but lack the Langerhans cell markers CD1a and langerin and contain no Birbeck granules; ultrastructurally they show distinctive comma-shaped or worm-like bodies and coated vesicles. Unlike the xanthomatous histiocytoses, the histiocytes contain little or no lipid early in the course, though lipidisation may develop over time, supporting the view that benign cephalic histiocytosis, juvenile xanthogranuloma and generalised eruptive histiocytosis represent overlapping expressions of a single reactive histiocytic process. The self-limiting behaviour reflects eventual clearance of the reactive infiltrate rather than a clonal neoplastic proliferation. The prognosis is excellent; the eruption is entirely benign and resolves spontaneously over months to several years, usually without residual scarring, and no treatment is required.

Benign familial neonatal epilepsy is caused by autosomal dominant loss-of-function variants in KCNQ2 or KCNQ3, which together form the Kv7 potassium channel generating the neuronal M-current. Modest reduction of this stabilising current transiently increases neuronal excitability in the maturing neonatal brain, producing seizures that resolve as channel expression and network development mature. The milder functional impact compared with the dominant-negative variants of KCNQ2 encephalopathy explains the self-limited course and favourable developmental outcome. The prognosis is generally excellent, with seizures remitting within weeks to months and normal neurodevelopment in most children. A minority develop later seizures, so long-term outcome is favourable but not uniformly seizure-free.

Overall prognosis is mainly determined by the associated thyroid and pulmonary features, which respond to appropriate treatment.

The outlook is excellent; it is a benign self-limiting condition that resolves spontaneously by around 2 years of age with a normal neurodevelopmental outcome.

further investigation is usually unnecessary Recognition avoids unnecessary antiepileptic treatment, invasive investigation and parental anxiety Jerks that persist or occur during wakefulness Abnormal neurological examination, encephalopathy or poor feeding Failure to abolish the movements by waking the infant Associated apnoea, colour change or autonomic features Developmental delay or regression, or persistence beyond several months Misdiagnosis as neonatal seizures leading to unnecessary antiepileptic drugs and investigation Attempting to suppress the jerks by restraint, which can worsen them Prescribing benzodiazepines, which may paradoxically increase the myoclonus Not obtaining a home video to demonstrate the sleep-only, arousal-abolished pattern Overlooking hyperekplexia or a metabolic cause when features are atypical The precise mechanism is unknown but is presumed to reflect transient immaturity of brainstem and spinal motor control and of serotonergic pathways that regulate sleep-related motor activity in the developing nervous system. benign paroxysmal positional vertigo — BPPV, positional vertigo, canalithiasis central positional vertigo or nystagmus from posterior fossa or craniocervical junction lesions vestibular migraine with positional features Menière's disease orthostatic hypotension persistent postural-perceptual dizziness vestibular neuritis in the acute phase alcohol-induced positional nystagmus Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre for posterior and anterior canal disease supine roll (Pagnini-McClure) test for horizontal canal disease video-nystagmography or Frenzel goggles to remove visual fixation and characterise nystagmus pure-tone audiometry when there are cochlear symptoms MRI of the brain when central features are present or the presentation is atypical serum vitamin D and orthostatic blood pressure in recurrent or secondary cases The commonest cause of recurrent positional vertigo, produced by displaced utricular otoconia entering a semicircular canal; brief spinning is triggered by changes in head position relative to gravity such as lying down, rolling over in bed, or looking up. The posterior semicircular canal is affected in the large majority of cases; individual attacks are brief, typically settling within a minute even if the provoking position is maintained. The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre is diagnostic for posterior canal disease, provoking an upbeating torsional nystagmus with a short latency, a crescendo-decrescendo time course, and fatigability on repetition. Horizontal (lateral) canal involvement is identified with the supine roll (Pagnini-McClure) test, producing a horizontal nystagmus that is geotropic in canalithiasis and apogeotropic in cupulolithiasis. Canalithiasis (free-floating debris within the canal) and cupulolithiasis (debris adherent to the cupula) generate different nystagmus latencies and durations and guide the choice of repositioning manoeuvre. Treatment is with canalith repositioning: the Epley or Semont manoeuvre for the posterior canal, and the Lempert (barbecue) roll or Gufoni manoeuvre for the horizontal canal; medication has little role. Secondary BPPV follows head trauma, vestibular neuritis, prolonged recumbency, inner-ear surgery, and ageing, and is associated with reduced vitamin D and osteopenia; these cases recur more often. The direction and plane of the nystagmus localise the affected canal — posterior (upbeat-torsional), horizontal (geotropic or apogeotropic), and the rare anterior canal (predominantly downbeat). positional nystagmus that is purely downbeat, direction-changing, or does not fit a single canal plane, suggesting a central lesion positional nystagmus lacking latency, adaptation, or fatigability associated neurological signs, intractable vomiting, or imbalance out of proportion to the vertigo new-onset severe headache or occipital pain with positional symptoms sensorineural hearing loss developing alongside the positional vertigo mistaking central positional vertigo for BPPV and thereby overlooking posterior fossa pathology omitting positional testing in a patient reporting positional dizziness performing a repositioning manoeuvre for the wrong canal or the wrong side concluding treatment has failed after a single manoeuvre without re-testing and repeating it attributing chronic, non-positional dizziness to BPPV when persistent postural-perceptual dizziness or another disorder is responsible Otoconia — calcium carbonate crystals normally embedded in the utricular macula — become dislodged and migrate into one of the semicircular canals, most often the gravity-dependent posterior canal. In canalithiasis the free-floating particles move under gravity when the head is repositioned, dragging endolymph and deflecting the cupula abnormally, which generates a transient sensation of rotation and a characteristic nystagmus with latency and fatigability. In cupulolithiasis the particles adhere to the cupula itself, rendering it gravity-sensitive and producing a more immediate and persistent deflection. The resulting inappropriate canal signal conflicts with the otolith and visual inputs, giving rise to vertigo. Degeneration and demineralisation of otoconia with age, trauma, ischaemia, and other inner-ear disease predispose to their detachment. The prognosis is excellent, with most patients responding to a single or small number of repositioning manoeuvres and many resolving spontaneously; recurrence is common, affecting a substantial minority within a few years, particularly in secondary and idiopathic elderly cases.

The condition is benign and self-limiting, resolving spontaneously in early childhood; some children later develop migraine or other episodic syndromes.

most affected children have a strong family history of migraine or later develop migraine themselves Presents in toddlers and preschool children (typically 2-4 years) with recurrent, sudden, brief attacks of vertigo and unsteadiness lasting minutes and resolving spontaneously During an attack the child suddenly appears frightened, off-balance or refuses to walk, may clutch a parent and become pale, sweaty or nauseated; observable nystagmus supports the diagnosis Consciousness is fully preserved with no ictal confusion or postictal drowsiness, which helps distinguish attacks from epileptic seizures Attacks are stereotyped and self-limiting and the child is entirely well between episodes, with a normal neurological and audiological examination Diagnosis is clinical using ICHD-3 criteria (at least five stereotyped attacks with spontaneous resolution and normal examination and investigations between attacks); routine investigation is not needed in typical cases The condition remits spontaneously over months to a few years and is often followed by more typical migraine headaches later in childhood or adolescence Reassurance is the mainstay of management; migraine-preventive strategies are reserved for frequent or disabling attacks Persistent or interictal nystagmus, ataxia or other neurological signs suggesting a posterior fossa lesion Hearing loss or tinnitus pointing to a peripheral or structural cause Headache with early-morning vomiting, papilloedema or increasing head circumference Progressive or worsening attacks, or a new focal neurological deficit Altered consciousness during episodes, which points towards seizures Misdiagnosing attacks as epileptic seizures and starting antiepileptic drugs Failing to recognise the strong link with migraine and the family history Overlooking a posterior fossa tumour when interictal neurological signs are present Ordering unnecessary investigations in a child with a typical, self-limiting picture Confusing it with benign paroxysmal torticollis or other paroxysmal infantile syndromes Benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood is regarded as part of the migraine spectrum and a migraine precursor. Attacks are thought to arise from transient dysfunction of central vestibular pathways, plausibly driven by the same paroxysmal neuronal excitability, channel dysfunction and brainstem/trigeminovascular mechanisms that underlie migraine. The strong association with a personal or family history of migraine, and the tendency to evolve into typical migraine, support a shared pathophysiology; a subset overlaps with the calcium-channel dysfunction seen in familial hemiplegic migraine. The outlook is excellent; it is a benign, self-limiting condition that resolves spontaneously over months to a few years. Many children subsequently develop migraine in later childhood or adolescence.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia — BPH, benign prostatic enlargement, BPE, prostatic hyperplasia Prostate cancer Urethral stricture Bladder neck stenosis or contracture Neurogenic bladder / detrusor dysfunction Overactive bladder Urinary tract infection or prostatitis Bladder stone or bladder tumour Urinalysis to exclude infection and haematuria Serum creatinine and renal function assessment PSA measurement with counselling about interpretation Post-void residual volume by bladder ultrasound Uroflowmetry to assess flow rate and obstructive pattern Renal and bladder ultrasound to assess upper tracts, bladder wall, and residual urine Pressure-flow urodynamics in equivocal or complex cases Typically affects men over 50 and presents with lower urinary tract symptoms that are grouped into voiding (hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency, straining, incomplete emptying) and storage (frequency, urgency, nocturia) categories Symptom severity correlates poorly with prostate size, so a large gland may be asymptomatic while a small gland can cause significant obstruction Digital rectal examination usually reveals a smooth, firm, symmetrically enlarged gland; nodularity, asymmetry, or a hard area should raise suspicion of malignancy The International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) is useful for quantifying symptom burden and monitoring response to treatment Medical management principles include alpha-blockers to relax prostatic smooth muscle for rapid symptom relief and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors to shrink the gland over months in larger prostates Absolute surgical indications include refractory retention, recurrent urinary infection, bladder stones, recurrent haematuria, and upper tract dilatation or renal impairment from obstruction Transurethral resection of the prostate remains the reference surgical standard, with newer minimally invasive and laser techniques offering alternatives PSA may be mildly elevated due to gland volume, but a significantly raised or rising level warrants evaluation for prostate cancer Acute urinary retention, a urological emergency requiring prompt catheterisation Obstructive uropathy with hydronephrosis and renal impairment Recurrent urinary infection or urosepsis associated with an obstructed, incompletely emptying bladder Gross or persistent haematuria requiring exclusion of malignancy Hard, nodular, or asymmetric prostate on examination suggesting cancer Attributing all lower urinary tract symptoms to the prostate and missing bladder dysfunction, cancer, or stricture Overlooking chronic high-residual retention presenting with overflow incontinence and silent renal impairment Relying on prostate size alone to judge the need for treatment Failing to counsel that 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors lower PSA and take months to act Missing prostate cancer masked by a benign clinical picture Benign prostatic hyperplasia is a proliferation of glandular epithelial and stromal cells in the transition zone of the prostate, driven by ageing and androgen (dihydrotestosterone) activity. The enlarging gland produces a static component of obstruction by mechanical narrowing of the prostatic urethra and a dynamic component from increased smooth muscle tone mediated by alpha-1 adrenergic receptors. Chronic outflow obstruction leads to detrusor muscle hypertrophy, trabeculation, and eventually detrusor decompensation, incomplete emptying, and rising post-void residual volumes, with risk of upper tract dilatation and renal impairment in advanced cases. BPH is a slowly progressive condition; many men remain stable or improve with medical therapy, but a subset progress to retention or complications requiring surgery, which generally produces durable symptom relief.

without considering an inherited cause Failing to recognise the shared genetic basis and low-GGT pattern linking it to progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis Assuming progression to cirrhosis and pursuing transplantation inappropriately in classic disease Overlooking identifiable triggers such as drugs or hormonal changes Undertreating disabling pruritus during acute episodes Benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis arises from partial-function mutations in the same canalicular transport proteins implicated in progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis: the aminophospholipid flippase FIC1 (ATP8B1) in type 1 and the bile salt export pump BSEP (ABCB11) in type 2. Because residual transporter function is retained, hepatocyte bile acid secretion is only intermittently impaired, typically when an additional stress such as infection, hormonal change, or a drug tips the balance. During an episode, bile acids and conjugated bilirubin accumulate and cholestasis with pruritus develops, but between episodes bile flow normalises and the liver recovers without lasting structural injury. The normal or low gamma-glutamyl transferase reflects that, as in the corresponding PFIC subtypes, the underlying lesion does not damage the bile duct epithelium. The condition is benign with a normal life expectancy; episodes are self-limiting and, by definition, do not progress to chronic liver disease or cirrhosis, although attacks can be prolonged and debilitating during the cholestatic phase.

Bennett fracture (thumb base intra-articular) — Bennett fracture-dislocation, first metacarpal base fracture-dislocation, two-part thumb base fracture Rolando fracture (comminuted intra-articular thumb base) Extra-articular first metacarpal base fracture First carpometacarpal dislocation without fracture Trapezium fracture Ulnar collateral ligament injury of the thumb (gamekeeper/skier thumb) of the first metacarpal, characteristically a two-part injury A volar-ulnar fragment held by the anterior oblique (beak) ligament remains reduced against the trapezium while the metacarpal shaft mechanism is an axial load along a partially flexed thumb metacarpal Anatomical restoration of the joint surface is the goal, achieved by closed reduction with percutaneous Kirschner-wire fixation or open reduction and internal fixation Distinguishing the two-part Bennett from the comminuted Rolando pattern guides fixation strategy Residual articular incongruity or subluxation predisposes to painful trapeziometacarpal arthritis Articular step-off or incongruity predisposing to early arthritis Persistent subluxation of the trapeziometacarpal joint after reduction Comminution reclassifying the injury as a Rolando pattern Loss of reduction due to unopposed abductor pollicis longus pull Accepting a non-anatomical reduction of the articular surface Failing to counter the deforming pull of abductor pollicis longus, allowing loss of reduction Confusing the injury with a comminuted Rolando pattern Under-imaging and missing the extent of articular involvement An axial force transmitted along a flexed first metacarpal fractures the volar-ulnar corner of its base. This small volar fragment is anchored to the trapezium by the strong anterior oblique (beak) ligament and therefore stays in place, while the remainder of the metacarpal displaces. The abductor pollicis longus and adductor pollicis then pull the shaft proximally, dorsally, radially and into supination, producing the characteristic subluxation at the trapeziometacarpal joint. Because the injury involves the articular surface of a highly mobile joint, incongruent healing accelerates degenerative change. Anatomical reduction with stable fixation generally yields good thumb function, whereas residual articular incongruity or subluxation predisposes to early trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis and pain.

Benzodiazepine overdose — benzodiazepine poisoning, benzodiazepine toxicity, sedative overdose Opioid overdose Alcohol or other sedative-hypnotic intoxication Hypoglycaemia Structural or metabolic causes of coma Carbon monoxide or other toxic causes of reduced consciousness Capillary blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia Pulse oximetry and, if indicated, arterial blood gas for hypoventilation Paracetamol and salicylate levels and an ECG to screen for co-ingestants Urine or serum toxicology where it will change management CT head if reduced consciousness is unexplained or focal signs are present Produces a sedative-hypnotic toxidrome of drowsiness, slurred speech, ataxia, and depressed consciousness, typically with preserved or only mildly depressed vital signs Taken alone, benzodiazepines rarely cause death; serious respiratory depression usually reflects co-ingestion of alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives, or the parenteral route The mainstay of care is supportive - airway protection, breathing support, and observation - rather than any specific antidote in most cases Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist that reverses sedation, but its use is limited because it can precipitate seizures and a withdrawal state, particularly in chronic users or mixed overdoses Flumazenil is especially hazardous when a proconvulsant (such as a tricyclic antidepressant) has been co-ingested, as it removes the seizure threshold-raising effect of the benzodiazepine Marked or fluctuating conscious level, disproportionate hypotension, or significant respiratory depression should prompt a search for a co-ingested agent Activated charcoal offers little benefit and risks aspiration in a drowsy patient, so it is generally not recommended Consider alternative causes of coma (hypoglycaemia, head injury, other intoxicants) if the clinical picture does not fit a pure benzodiazepine effect Significant respiratory depression or hypoxaemia Deep or fluctuating coma suggesting a co-ingested agent Hypotension out of proportion to isolated benzodiazepine effect Loss of airway protective reflexes with aspiration risk Seizures, which should raise concern for a proconvulsant co-ingestant rather than benzodiazepine alone Reflexively giving flumazenil and precipitating seizures or acute withdrawal, especially in chronic users or mixed overdose Attributing deep coma or hypotension to benzodiazepines alone and missing a co-ingestant Overlooking hypoglycaemia or another treatable cause of reduced consciousness Administering charcoal to a drowsy patient and causing aspiration Benzodiazepines enhance the inhibitory action of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) at the GABA-A receptor by increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening, producing central nervous system depression. Because they modulate rather than directly open the channel, there is a ceiling to their respiratory depressant effect when taken alone, which explains their relatively wide margin of safety in isolated overdose. When combined with other central depressants such as opioids or alcohol, this ceiling is lost and dangerous synergistic respiratory depression can occur. Isolated benzodiazepine overdose usually has an excellent prognosis with supportive care, but outcome worsens considerably with co-ingestion of other central depressants or when aspiration or prolonged hypoxia occurs.

neuropathy Guillain-Barre syndrome Other causes of delirium and ataxia Fluid overload from renal, hepatic, or cardiac disease Clinical assessment with dietary and alcohol history Erythrocyte transketolase activity or blood thiamine level where available Assessment of cardiac function in suspected wet beriberi Neurological and cognitive assessment for Wernicke-Korsakoff features Evaluation for coexisting deficiencies in the malnourished or alcohol-dependent Wet beriberi presents with high-output cardiac failure, oedema, and warm extremities, whereas dry beriberi is a symmetrical peripheral polyneuropathy Thiamine deficiency also causes Wernicke encephalopathy, with the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia, which can progress to irreversible Korsakoff amnesia It is associated with diets based on polished (milled) white rice, chronic alcohol use, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery, and prolonged unsupplemented parenteral feeding Infantile beriberi can occur in breastfed infants of thiamine-deficient mothers and may be acute and life-threatening Thiamine should be given before or with any glucose load in at-risk patients, as glucose can precipitate acute Wernicke encephalopathy A rapid improvement in cardiac output after thiamine strongly supports wet beriberi Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by the response to treatment, since laboratory confirmation may be slow Acute high-output cardiac failure or cardiovascular collapse (fulminant wet beriberi) Wernicke encephalopathy, a medical emergency requiring immediate thiamine Rapid deterioration in an infant with suspected infantile beriberi Glucose administration in an at-risk patient without prior thiamine Giving intravenous glucose before thiamine in an at-risk patient and precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy Failing to recognise high-output failure as a treatable nutritional cardiomyopathy Waiting for laboratory confirmation before treating in suspected Wernicke encephalopathy Overlooking deficiency after bariatric surgery, in hyperemesis, or on prolonged parenteral nutrition Thiamine, as thiamine pyrophosphate, is a cofactor for key enzymes of carbohydrate metabolism including pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase. Deficiency impairs oxidative energy production and causes accumulation of pyruvate and lactate, hitting tissues with high energy demand such as heart, peripheral nerves, and brain. Cardiovascular (wet) disease reflects impaired myocardial energetics and peripheral vasodilatation producing high-output failure, while neural (dry) disease and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome reflect neuronal energy failure. Carbohydrate loading raises thiamine demand and can unmask or worsen deficiency. Cardiac and early neurological features often improve rapidly with thiamine, but delayed treatment of Wernicke encephalopathy risks permanent Korsakoff amnesia, and severe peripheral neuropathy may recover only partially.

Bernard-Soulier syndrome (GP Ib-IX-V) — BSS, GP1BA, GP1BB, GP9, giant platelet syndrome Glanzmann thrombasthenia Von Willebrand disease (including type 2B) Immune thrombocytopenia Other inherited Willebrand studies to exclude von Willebrand disease Review of the film to exclude pseudothrombocytopenia and other macrothrombocytopenias Genetic testing of GP1BA, GP1BB and GP9 An autosomal recessive platelet disorder caused by deficiency or dysfunction of the glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex, the platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor It produces a mucocutaneous bleeding tendency together with mild thrombocytopenia and characteristically large (giant) platelets on the film The triad of thrombocytopenia, giant platelets and a mucocutaneous bleeding history should prompt consideration of the diagnosis The distinctive aggregometry pattern is absent agglutination to ristocetin that is not corrected by adding normal plasma, with preserved aggregation to other physiological agonists This ristocetin pattern is the mirror image of Glanzmann thrombasthenia, where ristocetin response is preserved but other agonist responses are absent Diagnosis is confirmed by reduced glycoprotein Ib-IX-V expression on flow cytometry and by GP1BA, GP1BB or GP9 genetic testing Management uses local measures, antifibrinolytics, desmopressin in some settings and platelet transfusion for significant bleeding, mindful of alloimmunisation risk Major haemorrhage such as gastrointestinal or intracranial bleeding Severe menorrhagia or postpartum bleeding with haemodynamic compromise Uncontrolled peri-operative or post-traumatic bleeding Platelet refractoriness from alloimmunisation Misdiagnosing the low platelet count as immune thrombocytopenia and treating with immunosuppression Automated analysers undercounting the giant platelets, exaggerating the apparent thrombocytopenia Confusing the ristocetin defect with von Willebrand disease without a mixing (normal plasma) study Overusing platelet transfusion and provoking alloimmunisation Bernard-Soulier syndrome is caused by biallelic mutations in GP1BA, GP1BB or GP9, which encode subunits of the platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex. This complex is the receptor through which platelets bind von Willebrand factor on exposed subendothelium, the first step of platelet adhesion under high shear. When the complex is deficient or defective, platelets cannot tether to the vessel wall, so primary haemostasis is impaired. The same molecular defect disturbs normal megakaryocyte and platelet development, producing mild thrombocytopenia and abnormally large platelets, and the combined adhesion failure and low platelet number underlie the bleeding phenotype. With appropriate supportive care and bleeding prophylaxis around procedures, most patients do well, although serious spontaneous or provoked bleeds can occur and repeated transfusion carries a risk of alloimmunisation.

fibrosis Connective tissue disease-associated lung disease Beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test on blood and/or bronchoalveolar lavage High-resolution CT of the chest Bronchoscopy with lavage and to diagnosis Presentation is with progressive exertional breathlessness, cough and fatigue, sometimes with systemic features, developing after a variable latent period Acute beryllium disease, a chemical pneumonitis from intense exposure, is now rare because of exposure controls Treatment relies on removing further exposure and, for progressive disease, immunosuppression with corticosteroids, since there is no cure Workplace surveillance with beryllium sensitisation testing allows early identification of affected workers Acute high-level exposure causing chemical pneumonitis and respiratory failure Rapidly progressive breathlessness or hypoxaemia Cor pulmonale from advanced fibrotic disease Systemic involvement of other organs Labelling the disease as sarcoidosis without seeking a beryllium exposure history Not performing beryllium-specific testing when granulomatous lung disease is found in an exposed worker Assuming low exposure excludes disease when susceptibility governs risk Failing to institute workplace surveillance for coworkers Beryllium acts as a hapten that, in genetically susceptible individuals (linked to particular HLA-DP variants), drives an Accumulation of these sensitised T cells in the lung leads to formation of non-caseating granulomas and chronic inflammation, progressing to interstitial fibrosis and impaired gas exchange, in a picture that is histologically indistinguishable from sarcoidosis. The course is variable; some remain stable for years while others progress to disabling fibrosis and respiratory failure. Removal from exposure and immunosuppression can slow progression, but the disease is not curable.

testing for BEST1 mutations and family screening Autosomal dominant macular dystrophy caused by mutations in the BEST1 gene encoding bestrophin-1, a chloride channel in the retinal pigment epithelium The hallmark early lesion is a round, yellow, yolk-like (vitelliform) deposit at the fovea, best appreciated on fundus examination Progresses through recognised stages: previtelliform, vitelliform (egg-yolk), pseudohypopyon (layering of material), vitelliruptive (scrambled egg), and atrophic or fibrotic scarring The electro-oculogram (EOG) is diagnostic and characteristically abnormal, with a markedly reduced Arden light-rise ratio even when the full-field electroretinogram (ERG) is normal Optical coherence tomography shows subretinal accumulation of hyperreflective vitelliform material subretinal haemorrhage or fluid at the macula Rapid progression to atrophy or fibrotic scarring with central scotoma Misdiagnosing the vitelliform lesion as age-related macular degeneration and missing the genetic diagnosis Relying on a normal electroretinogram to exclude the condition when the diagnostic test is the electro-oculogram Overlooking choroidal neovascularisation as a treatable cause of acute visual loss Failing to screen at-risk family members given autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity Best vitelliform macular dystrophy results from mutations in BEST1, which encodes bestrophin-1, a calcium-activated chloride channel located on the basolateral membrane of retinal pigment epithelial cells. Dysfunction of this channel disturbs ion and fluid transport across the retinal pigment epithelium and impairs the standing potential of the eye, which underlies the abnormal electro-oculogram. Lipofuscin-like material accumulates within and beneath the retinal pigment epithelium in the subretinal space at the macula, forming the characteristic vitelliform lesion. Over time this deposited material breaks down and disperses, leading to photoreceptor loss, geographic atrophy, and sometimes fibrous scarring, with the risk of secondary choroidal neovascularisation. Prognosis is generally favourable, with many patients retaining good central vision into later life; however, the fellow eye is usually affected and vision can decline significantly if atrophy, scarring, or choroidal neovascularisation develops.

Beta-2 Microglobulin Amyloidosis (Dialysis-Related Amyloidosis) — Dialysis-related amyloidosis, Abeta2M amyloidosis, Haemodialysis-associated amyloidosis Other causes of carpal tunnel syndrome Inflammatory and crystal arthropathies Renal osteodystrophy Septic or destructive arthritis Multiple myeloma bone disease Other systemic amyloidoses such as AL and ATTR Plain radiographs or ultrasound showing subchondral cysts and synovial thickening MRI of affected joints Nerve conduction studies for carpal tunnel syndrome Synovial or bone biopsy with Congo red staining and amyloid typing where needed Serum beta-2 microglobulin with review of dialysis modality and vintage Serum free light chains and immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis Genetic testing where a hereditary variant is suspected The acquired form arises in patients on long-term dialysis, in whom beta-2 microglobulin, normally cleared by the kidney, accumulates and is poorly removed by conventional membranes. The phenotype is predominantly osteoarticular, comprising carpal tunnel syndrome, chronic large-joint arthropathy (especially the shoulders) and destructive spondyloarthropathy. Subchondral bone cysts (amyloidomas) and an increased risk of pathological fracture are characteristic radiological findings. Risk rises with duration of dialysis and older age at commencement, and disease was more common before high-flux and more biocompatible membranes. Carpal tunnel syndrome is frequently the earliest manifestation and is often bilateral. A distinct rare hereditary form results from a variant beta-2 microglobulin (Asp76Asn) that causes visceral, gastrointestinal and autonomic disease unrelated to dialysis. Successful renal transplantation lowers beta-2 microglobulin levels and generally halts progression, and improved dialysis techniques reduce incidence. Destructive arthropathy or pathological fracture in a long-term dialysis patient Rapidly progressive joint destruction Spinal involvement with neurological compromise Visceral or autonomic symptoms suggesting the hereditary variant Attributing shoulder or wrist symptoms in dialysis patients to age or overuse rather than amyloid Overlooking subchondral bone cysts as a fracture risk Assuming all amyloid in a dialysis patient is beta-2 microglobulin without excluding AL Failing to recognise the distinct hereditary variant Beta-2 microglobulin is the invariant light chain of MHC class I molecules and is normally filtered and catabolised by the kidney. In renal failure, and especially during prolonged dialysis with membranes that clear it inefficiently, serum concentrations rise many-fold. Over years the protein, sometimes modified by advanced glycation, aggregates into amyloid fibrils that deposit with particular affinity for synovium, tendon sheaths, articular cartilage and bone. The resulting infiltration produces carpal tunnel compression, erosive arthropathy and cystic bone lesions. In the rare hereditary variant, an unstable mutant protein deposits in the viscera independent of renal function. In dialysis-related disease morbidity is largely musculoskeletal and progresses with dialysis vintage; renal transplantation arrests progression. The rare hereditary visceral form is slowly progressive and systemic.

Beta-blocker overdose — beta-adrenergic antagonist poisoning, beta blocker toxicity Calcium-channel-blocker poisoning Digoxin toxicity Clonidine or other central sympatholytic overdose Cholinergic (organophosphate) poisoning Primary cardiac conduction disease or myocardial infarction Continuous cardiac monitoring and serial electrocardiograms Blood glucose (may be low) and electrolytes Assessment of the specific agent, formulation and co-ingestants Blood gas and lactate to gauge perfusion Echocardiography in refractory shock to guide support The core features are bradycardia and hypotension from reduced cardiac chronotropy and inotropy Hypoglycaemia can occur, especially in children, in contrast to the hyperglycaemia typical of calcium-channel-blocker poisoning Lipophilic agents such as propranolol can cause seizures, coma and sodium-channel blockade with QRS widening Agents with membrane-stabilising activity or mixed effects produce more severe cardiotoxicity Treatment escalates from fluids and atropine to glucagon, high-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy and vasopressors Refractory shock may prompt consideration of lipid emulsion or mechanical circulatory support Profound bradycardia or high-grade heart block Hypotension refractory to initial measures Wide QRS or seizures suggesting membrane-stabilising toxicity Ingestion of a modified-release preparation with delayed deterioration Confusing it with calcium-channel-blocker poisoning (glucose typically low versus high) Underdosing high-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy in refractory shock Missing delayed toxicity from modified-release formulations Overlooking co-ingestants that compound cardiotoxicity Beta-blocker overdose produces excessive antagonism of beta-adrenergic receptors, reducing heart rate and myocardial contractility and blunting the compensatory sympathetic response to hypotension. Impaired cyclic AMP generation reduces intracellular calcium available for contraction. Lipophilic and membrane-stabilising agents add central nervous system toxicity and sodium-channel blockade, worsening conduction and precipitating seizures. The net effect is cardiogenic shock with, in some cases, metabolic and neurological complications. Many patients recover with aggressive supportive care, but massive ingestions, membrane-stabilising agents and delayed presentation can cause fatal refractory shock.

Beta-ketothiolase deficiency (T2/ACAT1) — mitochondrial acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase deficiency, T2 deficiency, ACAT1 deficiency, 3-oxothiolase deficiency, 2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA thiolase deficiency Succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase (SCOT) deficiency Diabetic ketoacidosis Other organic acidaemias (methylmalonic, propionic, isovaleric) Maple syrup urine disease during decompensation Salicylate or other toxic ingestion causing anion-gap acidosis Glycogen storage disease with ketotic hypoglycaemia Urine organic acid analysis for 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyrate, 2-methylacetoacetate and tiglylglycine Plasma acylcarnitine profile by tandem mass spectrometry looking for raised C5:1 and C5-OH Blood gas, glucose, electrolytes and calculated anion gap during acute presentations Blood and urine ketone quantification to document ketoacidosis Molecular genetic testing of ACAT1 to confirm the diagnosis Enzyme assay or in-vitro loading studies in fibroblasts where genetics are inconclusive Autosomal recessive defect of the mitochondrial enzyme (ACAT1 gene) that acts in both ketone-body utilisation and isoleucine catabolism, so the disorder combines a ketolysis defect with an organic aciduria Typically presents in infancy or early childhood with intermittent ketoacidotic crises precipitated by intercurrent infection, fasting, or a high-protein load, often with normal health between episodes Urine organic acids classically show 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyrate, 2-methylacetoacetate and tiglylglycine, reflecting the block in isoleucine breakdown Blood acylcarnitine profile characteristically shows raised C5:1 (tiglylcarnitine) and C5-OH (2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyrylcarnitine) Severe ketoacidosis during crises can be striking, but unlike SCOT deficiency the ketosis is episodic rather than permanent Acute management centres on reversing catabolism with intravenous glucose and correcting acidosis; long-term care uses avoidance of prolonged fasting and modest protein moderation with an emergency regimen for illness Neurological outcome is variable and basal ganglia injury has been reported after severe crises, so prompt treatment of acidotic episodes is important Severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with heavy ketosis in an unwell child Reduced consciousness or seizures suggesting cerebral involvement during a crisis Recurrent unexplained ketoacidotic episodes triggered by illness or fasting Haemodynamic instability from profound dehydration and acidosis Attributing severe ketoacidosis to presumed diabetes or gastroenteritis and missing the underlying metabolic disorder Assuming a normal interictal examination excludes a serious inherited condition Failing to send urine organic acids and acylcarnitines during the acute episode when abnormalities are most informative Under-treating catabolism by not providing adequate intravenous glucose during illness Beta-ketothiolase deficiency results from loss of mitochondrial acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase (T2), encoded by ACAT1. The enzyme participates both in the terminal step of ketone-body metabolism and in the catabolism of isoleucine at the level of 2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA. Its deficiency impairs ketone-body handling and blocks isoleucine degradation, so intermediates such as 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyrate, 2-methylacetoacetate and tiglylglycine accumulate. During catabolic stress, when fatty-acid oxidation and ketogenesis are upregulated, the inability to process ketoacids leads to profound ketoacidosis. Episodes are typically intermittent, with metabolic decompensation triggered by fasting, infection, or protein loading. Prognosis is generally favourable when crises are recognised and treated promptly, and many individuals develop normally with few episodes after childhood. However, severe or poorly managed ketoacidotic crises can cause basal ganglia injury and lasting neurological sequelae.

Beta Thalassaemia — beta-thalassaemia major, Cooley anaemia, beta-thalassaemia intermedia, beta thalassemia Iron deficiency anaemia Alpha thalassaemia Sickle cell disease and other haemoglobinopathies Anaemia of chronic disease Sideroblastic anaemia Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia Full blood count with red cell indices (low MCV and MCH) Peripheral blood film Haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC quantifying HbA, HbA2, and HbF Reticulocyte count Iron studies and serum ferritin to distinguish iron deficiency and monitor overload Genetic mutation analysis of the beta-globin gene Serial ferritin and cardiac/hepatic MRI (T2*) to monitor iron burden An inherited disorder of reduced or absent beta-globin chain production, most common in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, South Asian, and Southeast Asian populations. Beta-thalassaemia major typically presents in the second half of the first year of life as protective fetal haemoglobin declines, with progressive pallor, poor growth, and hepatosplenomegaly. The blood film shows a severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia with marked anisopoikilocytosis, target cells, and nucleated red cells. Haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC demonstrates elevated HbF and often raised HbA2, with little or no HbA in the major form. Chronic transfusion is required in transfusion-dependent disease to sustain growth and suppress ineffective erythropoiesis. Repeated transfusion inevitably causes iron overload, so iron chelation is essential to prevent cardiac, hepatic, and endocrine damage. Untreated or under-transfused children develop characteristic skeletal changes from marrow expansion, including frontal bossing and maxillary overgrowth. Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offers a potential cure, and newer gene-based therapies are emerging. Splenomegaly may lead to hypersplenism and rising transfusion requirements; genetic counselling and antenatal screening are important for at-risk families. Symptomatic severe anaemia with cardiac decompensation Signs of iron overload cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia Rapidly enlarging spleen with falling counts (hypersplenism) Growth failure and delayed puberty from chronic anaemia or endocrine iron toxicity Features of extramedullary masses causing compressive symptoms Misdiagnosing microcytic anaemia as simple iron deficiency and giving unnecessary iron Under-transfusing and allowing marrow expansion and skeletal deformity to progress Neglecting or delaying iron chelation, leading to preventable organ damage Overlooking endocrine complications such as hypothyroidism, diabetes, and delayed puberty Mutations in the beta-globin gene reduce (beta+) or abolish (beta0) beta-chain synthesis, creating an imbalance with relatively excess alpha-globin chains. Unpaired alpha chains precipitate within red cell precursors, causing their destruction in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) and shortened survival of circulating red cells (haemolysis). The resulting chronic anaemia drives erythropoietin-mediated marrow expansion and extramedullary haematopoiesis, while increased gastrointestinal iron absorption and transfusional iron together produce progressive tissue iron overload. With regular transfusion and effective iron chelation, survival into adulthood with good quality of life is achievable; outcomes are limited chiefly by iron-related cardiac and endocrine complications, and stem cell transplant can be curative in selected patients.

Outcome depends on how quickly adrenal insufficiency is recognised and treated and on the severity of the underlying illness; delayed steroid replacement can be fatal, whereas prompt treatment allows recovery, though some patients are left with permanent adrenal insufficiency requiring lifelong replacement.

bilateral adrenal hyperplasia — idiopathic hyperaldosteronism, bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia, primary bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia aldosterone-producing adenoma unilateral adrenal hyperplasia familial hyperaldosteronism including glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism ACTH-dependent Cushing's disease ectopic ACTH syndrome congenital adrenal hyperplasia phaeochromocytoma aldosterone-to-renin ratio after appropriate adjustment of interfering antihypertensives confirmatory saline suppression or fludrocortisone suppression testing adrenal vein sampling for lateralisation low-dose dexamethasone suppression test and late-night salivary cortisol for autonomous cortisol dedicated adrenal-protocol CT germline ARMC5 and PRKAR1A genetic testing where indicated serum electrolytes and acid-base assessment Bilateral idiopathic hyperplasia of the zona glomerulosa is the commonest cause of primary aldosteronism, exceeding aldosterone-producing adenoma in frequency. Adrenal vein sampling is the pivotal test to distinguish surgically curable unilateral disease from bilateral disease before any adrenalectomy. Bilateral aldosterone excess is managed medically with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists rather than surgery. Screen with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio in resistant hypertension, hypertension with hypokalaemia, or hypertension with an adrenal incidentaloma; potassium may be normal. Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia can cause overt or subclinical Cushing's, sometimes via aberrant membrane receptors producing food- or posture-dependent cortisol secretion. Germline ARMC5 mutations underlie many familial macronodular cases, so relatives should be offered assessment. Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease in a young patient suggests Carney complex, prompting a search for cardiac myxoma and skin lentigines. Cross-sectional imaging cannot reliably lateralise aldosterone excess, and apparently normal adrenals do not exclude hyperplasia. severe or resistant hypertension with cardiovascular or cerebrovascular complications profound hypokalaemia with arrhythmia or weakness florid hypercortisolism with proximal myopathy, fragility fracture or opportunistic infection an adrenal nodule with radiological features suspicious for malignancy proceeding to adrenalectomy on CT appearance alone without adrenal vein sampling excluding primary aldosteronism because serum potassium is normal inadequate preparation and drug washout before measuring the aldosterone-to-renin ratio labelling bilateral nodules as non-functioning and missing subclinical Cushing's misclassifying ACTH-dependent hyperplasia as a primary adrenal disorder Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia denotes diffuse or nodular expansion of both adrenal cortices with autonomous hormone secretion. In the aldosterone-producing form (idiopathic hyperaldosteronism) the zona glomerulosa is hyperplastic with dysregulated aldosterone output, producing sodium retention, potassium wasting, suppressed renin and hypertension. In cortisol-producing macronodular disease, aberrant expression of membrane receptors for gastric inhibitory polypeptide, catecholamines, vasopressin or luteinising hormone couples cortisol release to non-ACTH stimuli, and germline ARMC5 mutations promote nodular growth. Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease arises from PRKAR1A defects within Carney complex. These primary adrenal processes must be distinguished from ACTH-driven bilateral hyperplasia of pituitary or ectopic Cushing's and from congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to steroidogenic enzyme deficiency. Bilateral idiopathic hyperaldosteronism is controlled but not cured by mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and cardiovascular risk persists if untreated; macronodular disease causing hypercortisolism improves after unilateral or bilateral adrenalectomy, though replacement therapy may then be required.

vestibulo-ocular and vestibulospinal reflexes that stabilise gaze and posture. Because the loss is symmetrical there is no static imbalance signal to generate spinning vertigo; instead the failure of the vestibulo-ocular reflex causes retinal image slip during head movement, perceived as oscillopsia, and loss of vestibulospinal support causes gait unsteadiness that worsens when vision and proprioception cannot compensate, such as in darkness. Peripheral vestibular function rarely recovers, but sustained vestibular rehabilitation improves gaze stability and gait, though oscillopsia and darkness-related unsteadiness often persist to some degree.

Normally most conjugated bile acids are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and recycled; when this reabsorption fails (from ileal disease or resection) or when hepatic bile acid synthesis is inappropriately high (from impaired negative feedback by the ileal hormone FGF19), the bile acid load overwhelms colonic capacity. Cholecystectomy and other conditions can also alter bile acid delivery and enterohepatic cycling. Most patients respond well to bile-acid sequestrants, though tolerability can limit adherence; symptoms tend to persist without treatment, and outcome also depends on any underlying disease.

In these inborn errors, deficiency of a specific enzyme in the pathway prevents formation of normal cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid and causes accumulation of upstream sterol and bile acid intermediates. The lack of normal bile acids reduces the osmotic driving force for bile flow, producing cholestasis and malabsorption of fat and fat-soluble vitamins, while the abnormal intermediates that build up are themselves hepatotoxic and drive progressive liver injury. Because the accumulating intermediates fail to suppress the pathway through feedback, provision of primary bile acids both downregulates their production and restores bile flow. Several of these disorders are highly treatable, and timely primary bile acid replacement can normalise liver biochemistry and prevent progression to cirrhosis or transplantation; delayed diagnosis may allow irreversible liver failure to develop.

Biliary Atresia — extrahepatic biliary atresia, EHBA Neonatal (idiopathic) hepatitis Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency Choledochal cyst Alagille syndrome and other intrahepatic cholestatic syndromes Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis Inspissated bile / bile plug syndrome Congenital infection (TORCH) Fractionated (total and conjugated) serum bilirubin Liver function tests including GGT and aminotransferases Abdominal ultrasound (gallbladder, triangular cord sign, exclusion of choledochal cyst) Hepatobiliary scintigraphy assessing excretion into the intestine Percutaneous liver biopsy Intraoperative cholangiogram to confirm the diagnosis Studies to exclude alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency and metabolic causes The most common cause of neonatal cholestasis leading to liver transplantation, resulting from progressive inflammatory obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts. Classic presentation is a term infant with prolonged jaundice, pale (acholic) stools, and dark urine, usually with otherwise good early growth. Any infant jaundiced beyond about two weeks of age should have a fractionated bilirubin measured; a raised conjugated (direct) fraction signals cholestasis and needs urgent evaluation. Early diagnosis is critical because the success of surgery falls sharply with age, ideally before about 8 weeks (60 days) of life. The Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy aims to restore bile drainage; the earlier it is performed, the better the chance of clearing jaundice. Even after a successful Kasai procedure, many children progress to cirrhosis and ultimately require liver transplantation. A subset have the biliary atresia splenic malformation syndrome with situs and other congenital anomalies. Ultrasound may show an absent or small gallbladder and the 'triangular cord' sign; a hepatobiliary scan shows hepatic uptake without excretion into the bowel. Acholic (pale, clay-coloured) stools Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia at any age in an infant Jaundice persisting beyond two weeks of life Signs of coagulopathy or vitamin K deficiency bleeding Hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, or other features of advanced liver disease Dismissing prolonged neonatal jaundice as physiological or breast-milk jaundice without checking a split bilirubin Failing to inspect stool colour Delaying referral and surgery beyond the window where the Kasai procedure is most effective Relying on a normal ultrasound to exclude the diagnosis Overlooking associated congenital anomalies in the splenic malformation syndrome A fibro-obliterative process destroys the extrahepatic and often intrahepatic bile ducts, obstructing bile flow. Retained bile causes progressive hepatocellular injury, portal tract inflammation, and bile ductular proliferation, leading to fibrosis and, if untreated, biliary cirrhosis with portal hypertension and liver failure. The initiating cause is uncertain and probably heterogeneous, involving developmental, immune, and possibly viral mechanisms. Outcome depends heavily on the age at surgery; early Kasai portoenterostomy can restore bile flow and delay or avoid transplantation, but many children eventually progress to end-stage liver disease. Overall long-term survival is good when transplantation is available.
