ERCP is the gold standard and also therapeutic, MRCP often the initial test (p.325) Plain abdominal film detects only the radiopaque minority of stones (~10-15% of cholesterol, ~50% of pigment) and has low yield (p.2730) Functional dyspepsia / non-ulcer dyspepsia presenting with post-prandial epigastric discomfort (p.2461) Gastroesophageal reflux / pill esophagitis (biliary colic itself can be mistaken for unexplained upper-GI symptoms) (p.2728) Irritable bowel syndrome (most common cause of abdominal pain alongside functional dyspepsia) (p.2461) Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction and acalculous cholecystopathy (biliary-type pain without calculi) (p.2732, p.2734) Cardiac/precordial referral — gallbladder pain may occasionally be referred to the precordium (p.2728) Biliary colic is the most specific symptom of gallstone disease, yet 'colic' is a misnomer: the pain is steady rather than waxing-and-waning, reflecting non-relievable distention of the gallbladder/duct against a stone obstructing the cystic duct or CBD (p.2731). A typical episode begins abruptly and lasts roughly 30 minutes to 5 hours before easing; pain that persists beyond ~5 hours should prompt suspicion of acute cholecystitis rather than uncomplicated colic (p.2731). Pain is characteristically a severe steady ache or fullness in the epigastrium or right upper quadrant, often radiating to the interscapular region, right scapula, or shoulder (p.2731). Attacks may be triggered by a fatty meal, a large meal after prolonged fasting, or even a normal meal, and are frequently nocturnal, occurring within a few hours of going to bed (p.2731). Nausea and vomiting commonly accompany the pain, but fever/chills are NOT features of uncomplicated colic and signal a complication (p.2731). Vague short-lived epigastric fullness, dyspepsia, belching, or flatulence after fatty food are nonspecific and occur with or without gallstones; they should not be equated with true biliary pain (p.2731). Most asymptomatic gallstones stay silent: 60-80% remain symptom-free over follow-up up to 25 years, so incidentally found stones without referable symptoms generally do not warrant intervention (p.2731). Once colic occurs, the disease has 'declared' itself; complications requiring surgery are far more common in patients who have developed biliary pain than in the asymptomatic group, and most patients who develop complications had prior warning symptoms (p.2731). Sudden awakening from sleep by pain favors an organic cause such as biliary colic over a functional gut-brain disorder (p.2461). Pain persisting beyond ~5 hours — suspect acute cholecystitis (p.2731) Fever, chills, or rigors with biliary pain — implies a complication (cholecystitis, cholangitis, or pancreatitis), not uncomplicated colic (p.2731) Jaundice and/or rising bilirubin or alkaline phosphatase — suggests common-bile-duct stone or obstruction (p.2731) Charcot's triad (biliary pain + jaundice + spiking fever/chills) — acute cholangitis (p.2735) Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation) with RUQ tenderness, fever, and leukocytosis — acute cholecystitis (p.323, p.2732) Severe pain persisting for days, with confusion/sepsis features — suggests pancreatitis or suppurative cholangitis (p.2461, p.2735) Treating the term 'colic' literally and expecting intermittent crampy pain — biliary colic is steady, and waiting for it to fluctuate can delay recognition (p.2731). Attributing nonspecific fatty-food dyspepsia, belching, or bloating to gallstones; these symptoms are equally common in people without stones and do not establish a biliary cause (p.2731). Assuming an incidental gallstone explains a patient's symptoms — most stones are silent, and a coexisting non-biliary disorder (e.g., reflux, peptic ulcer, IBS) may be the true cause (p.2731, p.2735). Missing that fever or jaundice has converted 'colic' into a complication requiring different (often urgent) management (p.2731). Relying on a plain abdominal film, which misses most cholesterol stones, instead of ultrasound (p.2730). Overlooking acalculous causes of biliary-type pain (sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, acalculous cholecystopathy) when ultrasound shows no stones (p.2732, p.2734). Biliary colic results from transient obstruction of the cystic duct (or common bile duct) by a gallstone migrating out of the gallbladder. The obstruction raises intraluminal pressure and distends the viscus; because repetitive biliary contractions cannot overcome or relieve the blockage, a steady visceral pain is generated. When the stone disimpacts or falls back, pressure normalizes and the pain resolves spontaneously, so an uncomplicated episode is self-limited and is NOT accompanied by inflammation, fever, or sustained cholestasis. Underlying stones are usually cholesterol stones (>90% in Western populations), which form when bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol, cholesterol monohydrate crystals nucleate, and gallbladder hypomotility allows stasis and stone growth; gallbladder emptying is frequently impaired in stone formers. Distinct mechanisms (mechanical, chemical from lysolecithin, and bacterial) convert simple obstruction into acute cholecystitis when the cystic duct stays blocked (p.2727-2732). Uncomplicated biliary colic is self-limited; the individual attack resolves once the transient obstruction clears. The natural history of the underlying gallstones is generally favorable: 60-80% of asymptomatic stone carriers stay symptom-free for up to 25 years, the chance of developing symptoms is only ~2-4% per year in the first 5 years after diagnosis (falling to 1-2% thereafter), and the yearly incidence of complications is only ~0.1-0.3%. The cumulative risk of death from gallstone disease under expectant management is small. However, once biliary pain has occurred, the likelihood of recurrent attacks and of complications requiring intervention rises substantially; younger patients at diagnosis are more likely to become symptomatic than those over 60 (p.2731). Harrison frames the spectrum by clinical course rather than a formal grading scale: uncomplicated biliary colic = transient cystic-duct obstruction giving self-limited pain (30 min-5 h) WITHOUT fever, inflammation, or jaundice; progression/complication is signalled by pain >5 h, fever/chills, or jaundice, and corresponds to acute cholecystitis (sustained cystic-duct obstruction with inflammation), choledocholithiasis with cholangitis (CBD obstruction + infection, Charcot's triad), or gallstone pancreatitis. Acute cholecystitis is itself triaged by complications (e.g., empyema, gangrene, perforation, Mirizzi's syndrome) (p.2731-2735).

Functional gallbladder disorder is thought to arise from abnormal gallbladder motility and impaired emptying, sometimes accompanied by visceral hypersensitivity and altered neurohormonal signalling of the biliary tract. Ineffective contraction in response to cholecystokinin, whether from a primary motility defect or from a functional narrowing at the cystic duct or sphincter, is proposed to generate biliary-type pain despite the absence of stones. A reduced gallbladder ejection fraction on cholescintigraphy is the objective correlate of this impaired emptying, although the correlation between measured ejection fraction and symptom relief after surgery is imperfect. The condition is benign but can be chronic and relapsing; selected patients with a low ejection fraction and classic pain often improve after cholecystectomy, though a proportion have persistent symptoms, underscoring the need for careful selection.

biliary hamartoma — von Meyenburg complex, bile duct hamartoma hepatic microabscesses hepatic metastases simple hepatic cysts Caroli disease polycystic liver disease primary sclerosing cholangitis peribiliary cysts MRI with MRCP as the key confirmatory study abdominal ultrasound including assessment for comet-tail artefact contrast-enhanced CT to assess enhancement pattern liver biochemistry renal imaging to assess for associated polycystic kidney disease liver biopsy reserved for genuinely indeterminate lesions Biliary hamartomas (von Meyenburg complexes) are benign, usually incidental lesions representing a ductal plate malformation of the small interlobular bile ducts. They are typically multiple, small, and scattered throughout both lobes, and are almost always asymptomatic with normal liver biochemistry. On MRI they appear as numerous tiny cystic foci of uniform small size that do not communicate with the biliary tree, best shown on heavily T2-weighted and MRCP sequences. Their multiplicity and small size can closely mimic hepatic metastases or microabscesses, a critical consideration in patients with known malignancy. Ultrasound may show tiny hyperechoic or hypoechoic foci sometimes with comet-tail artefact from the dilated ductules. They lie within the fibropolycystic liver disease spectrum and may coexist with polycystic liver or kidney disease and Caroli disease. MRCP is the key investigation to confirm the diagnosis non-invasively and avoid unnecessary intervention. Malignant transformation to cholangiocarcinoma is exceedingly rare but has been reported, so significant interval change warrants review. an enlarging lesion or one developing a mural nodule or solid component obstructive jaundice, which points to an alternative diagnosis new dominant mass distinct from the uniform hamartomatous pattern constitutional symptoms suggesting malignancy rising tumour markers in the appropriate clinical context misdiagnosing the lesions as diffuse hepatic metastases and instituting unnecessary oncological treatment failing to obtain MRCP, which best distinguishes them from communicating biliary disease attributing abnormal liver tests to the hamartomas rather than seeking another cause confusing them with microabscesses in a septic or immunocompromised patient over-investigating an otherwise classic incidental finding Von Meyenburg complexes arise from an arrest in the remodelling of the ductal plate, the embryonic template from which the intrahepatic bile ducts form. The result is small clusters of disorganised, variably dilated and often tortuous bile ductules embedded in an abundant fibrous or fibrocollagenous stroma, situated in or adjacent to the portal tracts. The ductules may contain inspissated bile but characteristically do not communicate with the functioning biliary tree, which accounts for their cystic appearance on imaging without biliary dilatation. Because the underlying defect is one of ductal plate malformation, biliary hamartomas share pathogenesis with the wider fibropolycystic spectrum, including congenital hepatic fibrosis, Caroli disease, and autosomal dominant polycystic disease, with which they frequently coexist. The lesions are benign with an excellent prognosis and generally require no treatment. Malignant transformation to cholangiocarcinoma is exceptionally rare.

Deficiency impairs these carboxylases, disturbing energy and lipid metabolism in the skin, hair follicles and nervous system and producing the dermatitis, alopecia and neurological features. escalate treatment urgently during febrile crises Overlooking atypical infantile or adult-onset presentations The disease arises from deficient function of thiamine transporter-2 encoded by SLC19A3, which mediates thiamine uptake into cells. Because thiamine (as thiamine pyrophosphate) is an essential cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase, transporter failure produces intracellular thiamine deficiency and impaired oxidative energy metabolism. The basal ganglia, with high metabolic demand, are especially vulnerable, so metabolic stress such as fever or fasting precipitates acute energy crises with cytotoxic oedema and neuronal injury. Supraphysiological biotin and thiamine are thought to drive residual transporter activity and alternative uptake pathways, restoring intracellular thiamine. Prognosis depends critically on how early treatment begins; when high-dose biotin and thiamine are started promptly, recovery from acute crises can be near-complete. Delayed or missed episodes cause cumulative basal ganglia damage with residual dystonia, dysarthria and cognitive impairment.

Biotinidase deficiency — BTD deficiency, late-onset multiple carboxylase deficiency, juvenile multiple carboxylase deficiency, biotin recycling defect Holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency (neonatal multiple carboxylase deficiency) Other organic acidaemias Mitochondrial and other causes of lactic acidosis Acrodermatitis enteropathica (zinc deficiency) for the skin and hair findings Epileptic during symptomatic episodes Urine organic acids for the characteristic carboxylase-deficiency pattern Audiological and ophthalmological assessment Molecular testing of the BTD gene to define profound versus partial deficiency Caused by deficiency of biotinidase, the enzyme that recycles biotin from biocytin and liberates dietary protein-bound biotin, leading to functional biotin deficiency Typical untreated features include seizures, hypotonia, developmental delay, ataxia, alopecia and a scaly periorificial skin rash Sensorineural hearing loss and optic atrophy are important complications that screening (enzyme activity assay), allowing pre-symptomatic treatment and excellent outcomes Metabolic decompensation with lactic acidosis, ketosis and encephalopathy in an untreated infant compromise during acute decompensation Failing to consider a treatable cause in an infant with seizures, hypotonia and skin or hair changes Stopping biotin therapy, since it must be continued lifelong the cofactor for several carboxylase enzymes involved in gluconeogenesis, fatty acid synthesis and amino acid catabolism. Biotinidase cleaves biocytin to release free biotin, recycling it, and also frees biotin bound to dietary protein. When biotinidase is deficient, biotin is progressively lost and cannot be adequately reused, producing a functional deficiency that impairs the biotin-dependent carboxylases (pyruvate carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase, 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase). The resulting metabolic block causes lactic acidosis and abnormal organic acid accumulation, while the neurological, cutaneous, ophthalmological and auditory features reflect tissue biotin deficiency. Supplemental free biotin bypasses the recycling defect. Prognosis is excellent when biotin supplementation is started early, and screen-detected infants treated before symptoms usually develop normally; however, hearing loss, optic atrophy and neurological damage that occur before diagnosis may not fully reverse, underscoring the value of early detection.

Bipolar disorder — bipolar affective disorder, manic depression, manic-depressive illness, BPAD Major depressive disorder (unipolar) Schizoaffective disorder Schizophrenia Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder Borderline personality disorder Substance-induced mood or psychotic disorder Hyperthyroidism or steroid-induced mood elevation Collateral history to identify prior manic or hypomanic episodes Thyroid, renal function, and pregnancy testing prior to mood stabiliser use Serum drug-level monitoring for agents with narrow therapeutic indices such as lithium Substance use screening Structured mood charting to track episode pattern Defined by episodes of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy and activity, alternating over time with depressive episodes A manic episode involves a distinct sustained period (about a week or requiring hospitalisation) with features such as inflated self-esteem or grandiosity, reduced need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, and risky goal-directed behaviour Bipolar I requires at least one full manic episode; bipolar II is defined by hypomania plus major depressive episodes without a full mania Bipolar depression is easily misdiagnosed as unipolar depression; a careful history for past highs is essential, since antidepressant monotherapy can precipitate mania or rapid cycling Mood stabilisers (such as lithium or certain anticonvulsants) and atypical antipsychotics are the mainstays of acute and maintenance treatment, described here as principles without specific dosing Lithium reduces suicide risk but has a narrow therapeutic index and requires monitoring of serum levels, renal function, and thyroid function Psychoeducation, regularising sleep and daily routines, and treatment adherence are central to preventing relapse Screen for psychotic features, which may accompany severe mania or depression and can be mood-congruent or incongruent Suicidal ideation, which carries high risk across both manic and depressive phases Psychotic symptoms or severe agitation requiring urgent stabilisation Reckless behaviour endangering the patient or others during mania Signs of lithium toxicity such as tremor, confusion, vomiting, and ataxia Treating bipolar depression with an antidepressant alone and triggering a manic switch or rapid cycling Missing a history of hypomania and misdiagnosing unipolar depression Failing to monitor lithium levels and organ function Overlooking suicide risk during depressive and mixed states Attributing early mania to intoxication and delaying appropriate treatment Bipolar disorder is a highly heritable condition involving dysregulation of monoaminergic and intracellular signalling systems, disturbances of circadian rhythm and sleep, and abnormalities in the connectivity and function of prefrontal-limbic circuits governing mood and reward. Episodes are often precipitated by sleep disruption, stress, or substances acting on an underlying biological vulnerability. Bipolar disorder is a lifelong, recurrent illness with substantial risk of functional impairment and elevated suicide rate. Prognosis improves with early diagnosis, mood-stabiliser adherence, and relapse-prevention strategies, whereas repeated episodes, substance misuse, and poor adherence worsen outcomes.

electroretinogram indicating widespread retinal dysfunction Features atypical for the diagnosis raising concern for intraocular lymphoma Development of choroidal neovascularisation or optic atrophy vitreoretinal lymphoma masquerading as birdshot uveitis Assuming a negative HLA-A29 result excludes the diagnosis in an otherwise classic case Neglecting objective monitoring with electroretinography and angiography when relying on symptoms alone Birdshot chorioretinopathy is an organ-specific autoimmune inflammation of the choroid and retina, occurring almost exclusively in genetically predisposed HLA-A29-positive individuals. An autoreactive T-cell response, possibly directed against retinal antigens, drives multifocal granulomatous infiltration of the choroid, producing the characteristic depigmented birdshot lesions. Associated retinal vasculitis and breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier lead to cystoid macular oedema, while progressive photoreceptor and retinal pigment epithelial dysfunction cause the electroretinographic abnormalities and night-vision loss. Chronic inflammation results in choroidal and retinal atrophy over time. Birdshot chorioretinopathy is a chronic, relapsing disease; with sustained immunosuppression many patients maintain good central vision, but untreated or poorly controlled disease leads to progressive macular oedema, retinal atrophy and irreversible loss of night vision, colour vision and peripheral field.

recognising the underlying syndrome and its renal risk Assuming a single renal oncocytoma is sporadic and not screening for further multifocal or contralateral tumours Mistaking fibrofolliculomas for encoding folliculin, a tumour-suppressor protein that participates in the AMP-activated protein kinase and mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signalling pathways and in regulation of cellular Loss of folliculin function, typically with a somatic second hit in renal tissue, dysregulates growth and energy-sensing pathways and underlies the development of benign skin tumours, lung cysts and renal neoplasms. BK polyomavirus nephropathy — BK virus nephropathy, BKVN, polyomavirus-associated nephropathy, BK polyomavirus (BKPyV) infection Acute cellular allograft rejection Calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity Cytomegalovirus nephritis or disease Adenovirus nephritis or haemorrhagic cystitis Obstructive uropathy or ureteric stenosis from other causes Recurrent or de novo glomerular disease in the graft Quantitative plasma BK virus DNA by PCR for screening and monitoring of viraemia Urine BK virus DNA quantification and urine cytology for decoy cells Renal allograft biopsy with SV40 large T antigen immunohistochemistry Serial serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate Assessment of net immunosuppression, including drug levels of calcineurin inhibitors and antiproliferative agents Imaging of the urinary tract to exclude ureteric stenosis or obstruction Caused by reactivation of BK polyomavirus, a ubiquitous virus latent in the urinary tract epithelium that reactivates under the intense immunosuppression of kidney transplantation It is a leading infectious cause of allograft dysfunction and loss, typically emerging within the first year after transplantation Usually silent until an asymptomatic rise in serum creatinine appears; frank cystitis or ureteric stenosis is less common than in haemorrhagic cystitis after stem-cell transplant Urine cytology may reveal decoy cells, tubular epithelial cells bearing enlarged nuclei with ground-glass viral inclusions that mimic malignant cells Surveillance uses quantitative plasma BK virus DNA (viraemia), which correlates with nephropathy better than urinary viral load alone Definitive diagnosis requires allograft biopsy showing viral cytopathic changes in tubular cells with confirmatory SV40 large T antigen immunostaining The cornerstone of management is judicious reduction of immunosuppression to allow virus-specific cellular immunity to recover, balanced against the risk of rejection Rising allograft creatinine with high-level BK viraemia Biopsy features overlapping with acute rejection creating diagnostic and therapeutic conflict Ureteric stenosis with obstructive graft dysfunction Persistent high viral load despite reduction of immunosuppression Mistaking BK nephropathy for acute rejection and intensifying immunosuppression, which worsens viral replication Relying on urinary viral load or decoy cells alone, which are sensitive but not specific for invasive nephropathy Delaying protocol screening so that infection is only detected once irreversible scarring has occurred Reducing immunosuppression too aggressively and precipitating rejection BK polyomavirus infects most people in childhood and thereafter persists latently within the epithelium of the renal tubules and urinary tract. In the transplanted kidney, heavy pharmacological immunosuppression allows the virus to reactivate and replicate, first producing viruria, then viraemia, and finally invasive infection of tubular epithelial cells. Lytic viral replication causes cell injury and denudation of the tubular basement membrane, with an accompanying interstitial inflammatory infiltrate and progressive tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis. The inflammatory response is difficult to distinguish histologically from acute rejection, and untreated infection leads to scarring and irreversible loss of graft function. Ureteric involvement can cause stenosis and obstruction. Outcome depends on how early infection is detected and immunosuppression reduced; caught during viraemia the graft is often preserved, but established nephropathy with extensive fibrosis frequently progresses to allograft failure despite intervention.

Black hairy tongue — lingua villosa nigra, hairy tongue Pseudo-black hairy tongue from bismuth or food staining Oral hairy leukoplakia Acanthosis nigricans of the tongue Pigmented fungiform papillae Melanotic or other pigmented mucosal lesions Clinical diagnosis from the characteristic appearance Medication and habit history (tobacco, mouthwashes, antibiotics) Assessment of oral hygiene and salivary flow Biopsy only if an alternative pigmented or keratotic lesion is suspected A benign condition in which elongated, poorly desquamated filiform papillae give the dorsum of the tongue a matted, hair-like appearance The colour ranges from brown to black depending on pigment-producing organisms, foods, tobacco and staining substances The colour comes from trapped debris and chromogenic micro-organisms rather than from true pigmentation It is usually asymptomatic but can cause a gagging sensation, halitosis or altered taste Risk factors include poor oral hygiene, smoking, a soft diet, xerostomia and certain medications and mouthwashes Management centres on tongue debridement, improved oral hygiene and removing precipitating factors Persistent lesion despite hygiene measures suggesting an alternative diagnosis Associated immunosuppression raising concern for oral hairy leukoplakia Ulceration or induration Rapidly changing pigmented lesion Mistaking it for oral hairy leukoplakia or a pigmented neoplasm Overlooking contributory medications or mouthwashes Failing to address smoking and dry mouth Investigating a clearly benign appearance excessively Black hairy tongue arises from defective desquamation and consequent hypertrophy and elongation of the filiform papillae on the tongue dorsum. The elongated papillae trap keratin, food debris and micro-organisms, and chromogenic bacteria and yeasts together with exogenous stains produce the characteristic discoloration. Predisposing factors that reduce mechanical cleansing of the tongue, such as a soft diet, dry mouth, smoking and poor hygiene, promote the papillary overgrowth; microbial colonisation contributes to colour but is not a primary infection. The condition is entirely benign and reversible, resolving with debridement, better oral hygiene and correction of precipitating factors.

Bladder & Urinary Tract Cancer — urothelial carcinoma, transitional cell carcinoma Hematuria from malignancy in females is frequently mistaken for a urinary tract infection (Harrison 22e p.691). Urine cytology (detects cancer in only about 50% of high-grade bladder cancers) (Harrison 22e p.691). Cystoscopy for direct bladder visualization; blue light or narrow-band imaging cystoscopy improves detection of small or flat noninvasive tumors and is used routinely in monitoring (Harrison 22e p.691). CT urogram (or MR urogram if renal function is impaired) for the kidneys and upper tract (Harrison 22e p.691). Adjunct urine molecular tests (FISH for chromosomal changes, nuclear mitotic proteins, bladder tumor-associated antigens) used mainly for detecting recurrence, as they can be falsely positive (Harrison 22e p.691). Ureteroscopy or retrograde pyelography when upper-tract tumors are suspected with a normal bladder (Harrison 22e p.691). Transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) or endoscopic resection of upper tract tumors for histologic diagnosis and staging (Harrison 22e p.691). Genomic sequencing of tumor tissue and/or circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) recommended in all metastatic patients (Harrison 22e p.690). In females, malignant hematuria may be misattributed to menstrual bleeding (Harrison 22e p.691). Intravesical BCG side effects (dysuria, urinary frequency, bladder spasms, hematuria) overlap with infection/cystitis, and in <5% a systemic inflammatory response can mimic disseminated BCG infection (Harrison 22e p.692). Painless hematuria, either gross or microscopic, is the initial manifestation of urinary tract cancer in most patients; in males painless hematuria is almost always abnormal and must be worked up (Harrison 22e p.691). In females, hematuria due to malignancy is often mistaken for a urinary tract infection or menstrual bleeding; antibiotics are warranted if a concurrent UTI is found, but persistent hematuria still requires further workup (Harrison 22e p.691). Initial investigation in either sex includes urine cytology plus visual examination of the bladder by cystoscopy, together with radiographic evaluation of the kidneys and upper tract by CT urogram (MR urogram if renal function is poor) (Harrison 22e p.691). Smoking of tobacco products is the overwhelming leading risk factor; 90% of new bladder cancer diagnoses occur in current or former smokers, and roughly one-third of cases could be prevented by smoking cessation (Harrison 22e p.692). Urothelial carcinoma (formerly transitional cell carcinoma) is the most common histology, seen in about 90% of cases; nonurothelial variants (squamous cell, adenocarcinoma, small-cell, carcinosarcoma) collectively account for 10% or less (Harrison 22e p.690-691). Disease is divided into non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC: carcinoma in situ, Ta, or T1 not reaching the muscularis propria; ~75% at presentation) and muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC: T2 invasion of muscularis propria and beyond) (Harrison 22e p.691-692). Urothelial carcinoma shows a biphasic phenotype: low-grade papillary tumors that frequently recur but rarely invade or metastasize, and high-grade often flat tumors that invade early and lead to lethal metastatic disease (Harrison 22e p.691). Painless gross or microscopic hematuria warrants investigation for urothelial cancer; in males it is almost always abnormal (Harrison 22e p.691). Persistent hematuria despite treatment of a concurrent UTI requires further workup (Harrison 22e p.691). Flank pain with an upper tract renal pelvis/ureter cancer, or hydronephrosis from a bladder tumor obstructing the ureteral orifice (Harrison 22e p.691). Cachexia and widespread metastatic disease at presentation (rare) (Harrison 22e p.691). Urine cytology is insensitive, identifying cancer in only about 50% of high-grade bladder cancers, so a negative cytology does not exclude malignancy (Harrison 22e p.691). Treating presumed UTI without follow-up risks missing malignancy; persistent hematuria after antibiotics still requires workup (Harrison 22e p.691). Adjunct urine molecular tests may be abnormal in patients without cancer (false positives) and are best reserved for surveillance of known cancer (Harrison 22e p.691). Systemic inflammatory reaction after intravesical BCG can mimic disseminated BCG infection (Harrison 22e p.692). Urothelial carcinoma arises from the lining of the bladder, renal pelvis, ureter, and urethra and displays a biphasic clinical behavior. Loss of portions of chromosomes 9q and 9p (loss of heterozygosity) is an early molecular event in both phenotypes; candidate genes in these regions include CDKN2A and TSC1. Low-grade papillary tumors are characterized by RAS/RAF pathway alterations with activating FGFR3 mutations or fusions in 60-80% of patients, whereas the high-grade invasive phenotype features early deleterious TP53 and RB1 mutations, CDH1 (E-cadherin) alterations, and increased VEGFR2 expression. Chronic inflammatory states drive squamous-type bladder cancer, classically chronic schistosomiasis infection and chronic indwelling catheters in paraplegic patients. Carcinogenic exposures include aromatic amines (benzidine, beta-naphthylamine) in industrial dyes and arsenic-contaminated drinking water. The Cancer Genome Atlas defined five intrinsic molecular subtypes (luminal papillary, luminal infiltrated, luminal, basal squamous, neuronal) resembling breast cancer subclasses (Harrison 22e p.691-692). Outcomes correlate closely with stage at diagnosis. About 75% present with non-muscle-invasive disease, 18% with muscle-invasive disease, and only 3% with metastatic spread. 5-year overall survival is 70-90% for disease confined to the bladder (stage I-II), 39-50% for disease penetrating through the bladder or involving regional lymph nodes (stage III), and only 8% for metastatic disease (stage IV) (Harrison 22e p.692). Staging is driven primarily by depth of invasion (T stage). NMIBC: Tis (CIS) and Ta (epithelial layer only) or T1 (into connective tissue/lamina propria below urothelium but not muscularis propria). MIBC: T2 (into muscularis propria), T3 (through muscularis propria to serosa), T4 (adjacent pelvic organs - rectum, prostate, vagina, cervix). Nodal: N1 (single true pelvic node), N2 (two true pelvic nodes), N3 (common iliac nodes); disease beyond common iliac nodes or distant spread is M1. Stages 0a-II are defined by T stage alone without nodal/metastatic disease; regional pelvic or common iliac nodal involvement is stage III; any distant metastasis is stage IV (Harrison 22e p.691-692).

Bladder diverticulum — Vesical diverticulum, Bladder pouch Bladder outlet obstruction with detrusor trabeculation and sacculation Ureterocele or ectopic ureteric insertion Vesicoureteric reflux with a dilated distal ureter Urachal remnant or urachal cyst Bladder ear (transient extraperitoneal herniation in infants) Patent processus or inguinoscrotal bladder herniation Neurogenic bladder with sacculation Voiding cystourethrography to demonstrate the diverticular neck and any vesicoureteric reflux CT urography or MRI to define size, wall, ureteric relationship and detect intradiverticular tumour Cystoscopy to inspect the diverticular neck and interior for tumour and calculi Uroflowmetry with post-void residual measurement Urodynamic study to confirm and characterise outlet obstruction or detrusor dysfunction Urine culture and urine cytology Renal function assessment and upper tract ultrasound Congenital diverticula are typically solitary, occur near the ureteric orifice (Hutch diverticulum) and have otherwise normal detrusor; acquired diverticula are usually multiple and arise secondary to bladder outlet obstruction with a trabeculated bladder. The diverticular wall is deficient in organised detrusor muscle, so it empties poorly and predisposes to stasis, recurrent infection and stone formation. A large Hutch diverticulum adjacent to the ureterovesical junction can distort the antireflux mechanism and cause vesicoureteric reflux or functional ureteric obstruction. Post-void residual urine within the diverticulum produces a characteristic pattern of double micturition or a sensation of incomplete emptying. Urinary stasis carries a recognised risk of malignancy within the diverticulum, most often urothelial carcinoma but with a relatively higher proportion of squamous cell and adenocarcinoma than in the main bladder. Because the diverticular wall lacks a muscle layer, any tumour arising within it can invade beyond the bladder early, worsening the stage at presentation. Voiding cystourethrography and cross-sectional imaging define the neck, size and relationship to the ureters and guide whether diverticulectomy is needed. Management of acquired diverticula must address the underlying outlet obstruction, otherwise diverticula recur or symptoms persist after excision. Visible haematuria or positive cytology suggesting malignancy within the diverticulum A solid filling defect or enhancing mass inside the diverticulum on imaging New hydronephrosis or deteriorating renal function from ureteric compression or reflux Recurrent urosepsis or a large retained infected residual Rapidly enlarging diverticulum causing bladder outlet or ureteric obstruction Excising the diverticulum without relieving the causative outlet obstruction, leading to recurrence or persistent symptoms Overlooking an intradiverticular tumour because the diverticular interior is difficult to inspect fully at cystoscopy Failing to recognise the close relationship to the ureter, risking ureteric injury during diverticulectomy Attributing incomplete emptying solely to the diverticulum when concurrent detrusor underactivity is present Assuming all diverticula are acquired and missing a congenital Hutch diverticulum in a child with reflux A bladder diverticulum is a herniation of bladder urothelium and lamina propria through a defect or weakness in the detrusor muscle, producing an outpouching whose wall contains little or no organised muscle. Congenital diverticula reflect a primary focal weakness of the detrusor, classically at the ureterovesical junction (Hutch diverticulum), and occur in an otherwise normal, non-obstructed bladder. Acquired diverticula develop when chronically raised intravesical voiding pressure, most often from bladder outlet obstruction (benign prostatic obstruction, urethral stricture or neurogenic dysfunction), forces mucosa between hypertrophied detrusor bundles of a trabeculated bladder. Because the diverticulum contracts poorly, urine pools within it during and after voiding; the resulting stasis underlies recurrent infection, calculus formation and an elevated long-term risk of malignant transformation of the diverticular urothelium. Small asymptomatic diverticula with the underlying obstruction relieved carry an excellent outlook and can be observed. Prognosis worsens substantially when malignancy arises within a diverticulum, because the muscle-deficient wall permits early extravesical spread and a more advanced stage at diagnosis.

in males than females Management is staged or single-stage surgical reconstruction aimed at secure abdominal/bladder closure, epispadias repair, and eventual continence, often with bladder neck reconstruction Long-term surveillance is needed for reflux, upper-tract deterioration, continence, sexual function, and an increased lifetime risk of bladder malignancy Upper-tract dilatation or deteriorating renal function on follow-up Recurrent urinary tract infection with high-grade reflux after closure Wound dehiscence or bladder prolapse after primary closure New bladder mass or haematuria in adulthood raising concern for malignancy Delaying or mishandling initial closure, jeopardising later continence and upper-tract preservation Failing to recognise associated pubic diastasis and its implications for pelvic reconstruction Neglecting long-term cancer surveillance of reconstructed or augmented bladders Underestimating the psychosocial, sexual, and fertility impact into adulthood Bladder exstrophy arises from a developmental failure during formation of the lower abdominal wall and anterior bladder wall. An abnormally developed or prematurely ruptured cloacal membrane is thought to prevent medial migration of mesenchyme, so the structures that should form the anterior abdominal wall, anterior bladder, and anterior urethra fail to close in the midline. The bladder is left open and everted, the pubic bones are separated, and the genitalia are epispadic. The severity depends on the timing and extent of the developmental disturbance, giving the spectrum of the exstrophy-epispadias complex. With modern staged or single-stage reconstruction most children can achieve satisfactory continence and preservation of renal function, though multiple operations are common and long-term risks include reflux, sexual and fertility issues, and an elevated risk of bladder cancer requiring lifelong follow-up.

Bladder pain syndrome — Interstitial cystitis, Painful bladder syndrome, IC/BPS Recurrent or chronic urinary tract infection Carcinoma in situ of the bladder Overactive bladder without pain Endometriosis and other gynaecological pelvic pain Bladder calculus or foreign body Radiation or ketamine-associated cystitis Pelvic floor myofascial pain and chronic pelvic pain syndrome Urinalysis and culture, including tests for fastidious organisms where indicated Urine cytology to help exclude carcinoma in situ Frequency-volume bladder diary documenting small voided volumes Cystoscopy with hydrodistension to identify Hunner lesions and capacity Bladder biopsy where malignancy or Hunner lesion needs confirmation Validated symptom and pain questionnaires Pelvic imaging or gynaecological assessment to exclude other pelvic pathology Bladder pain syndrome is chronic pelvic pain, pressure or discomfort perceived to relate to the bladder, accompanied by urinary frequency and urgency, in the absence of infection or other identifiable cause. The defining feature that distinguishes it from overactive bladder is pain or discomfort that worsens with bladder filling and is relieved, at least transiently, by voiding. It is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring confident elimination of infection, malignancy, carcinoma in situ, stones and other treatable pelvic pathology. Cystoscopy with hydrodistension identifies a phenotype with Hunner lesions, which behaves differently and responds to lesion-directed treatment, distinct from the non-Hunner phenotype. Glomerulations after hydrodistension are non-specific and are not sufficient alone to confirm the diagnosis. It frequently overlaps with other chronic pain and functional conditions such as fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome and chronic pelvic pain, favouring a multidisciplinary approach. Management is stepwise: education, dietary and stress modification, pelvic floor physical therapy and oral agents, escalating to intravesical therapy, and reserving major surgery for refractory disease. Long courses of empirical antibiotics are inappropriate once infection has been excluded and should be avoided. Visible haematuria requiring exclusion of malignancy Positive or suspicious urine cytology suggesting carcinoma in situ A history of pelvic irradiation or ketamine use pointing to a specific cystitis Sterile pyuria that may indicate genitourinary tuberculosis Rapidly worsening symptoms or systemic features atypical for the syndrome Diagnosing the syndrome without adequately excluding infection, malignancy and carcinoma in situ Missing a treatable Hunner lesion by omitting cystoscopy in a patient with persistent pain Over-relying on non-specific glomerulations to confirm the diagnosis Prescribing repeated empirical antibiotic courses after infection has been excluded Neglecting pelvic floor dysfunction and coexisting chronic pain conditions that need concurrent treatment Bladder pain syndrome is understood as a multifactorial disorder rather than a single disease, with several interacting mechanisms proposed. A defective urothelial glycosaminoglycan layer is thought to increase urothelial permeability, allowing urinary potassium and other solutes to penetrate the bladder wall and irritate sensory nerves and detrusor muscle. Mast cell activation and neurogenic inflammation amplify the response, while peripheral and central sensitisation of afferent pathways lowers the pain threshold and helps explain the frequent overlap with other chronic pain syndromes. In the Hunner lesion phenotype there is a distinct picture of localised chronic inflammation with epithelial denudation and a dense inflammatory infiltrate. Reduced functional bladder capacity, autoimmune and microvascular contributions, and psychosocial factors that modulate pain perception are also implicated. No single mechanism accounts for all cases, and the clinical presentation reflects a combination of bladder-centred and systemic processes. Bladder pain syndrome is typically chronic and relapsing, and most patients require ongoing, individualised management rather than achieving cure; symptom control and preserved quality of life are realistic goals. The Hunner lesion phenotype often responds well to lesion-directed treatment, whereas widespread central sensitisation predicts a more refractory course.

significant blast exposure Aggressive positive-pressure ventilation aggravating blast lung and air embolism Failing to anticipate delayed bowel perforation Underestimating severity of injuries sustained in enclosed spaces An explosion generates a high-pressure blast wave that transmits energy across tissue interfaces of differing density. Where gas meets fluid or solid, as in the alveoli, middle ear, and gut, shearing and implosion-reexpansion forces rupture delicate structures, producing pulmonary haemorrhage and oedema (blast lung), tympanic perforation, and bowel contusion or perforation. Secondary injury results from fragments propelled by the blast causing penetrating wounds, tertiary injury from the body being thrown, and quaternary effects from burns, crush, inhalation, and toxic exposure. Blast lung can allow air to enter pulmonary veins, producing systemic air embolism to the brain or coronary circulation. Prognosis depends on the dominant mechanism and injury burden. Blast lung and multi-mechanism injuries carry significant early mortality, while many fragment and displacement injuries are survivable with prompt trauma care; delayed presentations such as bowel perforation add later risk.

arising from precursors of plasmacytoid dendritic cells, the interferon-producing cells of the innate immune system. Malignant blasts overexpress the interleukin-3 receptor alpha chain (CD123) and retain markers of plasmacytoid dendritic cell lineage while co-expressing CD4 and CD56. Recurrent genetic lesions affect tumour suppressor and epigenetic regulatory genes, and there is molecular overlap with myeloid neoplasia that underlies the frequent association with myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukaemia. The disease is aggressive with historically poor outcomes; targeted CD123-directed therapy and consolidation with allogeneic transplantation in eligible patients have improved responses, but relapse remains common.

when indicated Full blood count and inflammatory markers Blastocystis is an anaerobic stramenopile protist and one of the most commonly detected organisms in human stool worldwide, particularly in tropical and resource-limited settings Its clinical significance is debated, as it is frequently found in asymptomatic people and its detection does not reliably prove it is the cause of symptoms When symptoms are attributed to it they are non-specific, including abdominal discomfort, bloating, flatulence, intermittent watery diarrhoea and nausea It is transmitted by the faecal-oral route through contaminated food or water, with the cyst as the resistant transmissible form The vacuolar form is the most recognisable on microscopy, appearing as a rounded body with a large central vacuole Diagnosis rests on stool microscopy, though sensitivity is improved by culture or molecular methods, and there are numerous genetically distinct subtypes Treatment is reserved for symptomatic patients in whom other pathogens have been excluded, with metronidazole or cotrimoxazole commonly used Weight loss, rectal bleeding or nocturnal diarrhoea suggesting an alternative serious diagnosis Persistent symptoms despite treatment, prompting a search for another cause Symptomatic infection in an immunocompromised host Systemic features that would be atypical for uncomplicated colonisation Assuming Blastocystis is the cause of symptoms without excluding other pathogens and functional disorders Treating asymptomatic carriage unnecessarily Anchoring on a positive stool result and missing a coexisting diagnosis such as coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease Repeated courses of antimicrobials when symptoms are in fact functional Blastocystis is a polymorphic anaerobic protist that colonises the large intestine, existing in vacuolar, granular, amoeboid and cyst forms, the cyst being responsible for faecal-oral transmission. Whether and how it causes disease remains uncertain: proposed mechanisms include degradation of the intestinal mucus barrier, protease activity, alteration of gut permeability and immune activation, and pathogenicity may vary between the many genetic subtypes. Because heavy colonisation is common in healthy people and symptoms overlap with functional bowel disorders, attribution of illness requires exclusion of other causes rather than mere detection of the organism. Generally benign; most carriage is asymptomatic and self-limiting, and where symptoms are genuinely attributable they usually respond to antimicrobial therapy, though persistence of symptoms often points to another underlying disorder.

Blastomycosis — Blastomyces dermatitidis Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (p.1701) Viral pneumonia (p.1701) Tuberculosis (p.1701-1702) Lung cancer / malignancy (p.1701-1702) Skin cancer (for cutaneous lesions) (p.1701) Sarcoidosis (p.1701) Pyoderma gangrenosum (p.1701) Laryngeal cancer (rare mimic) (p.1701) Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (p.1701) Viral pneumonia (p.1701) Tuberculosis (p.1701-1702) Histoplasmosis (B. helicus small yeast can be confused with Histoplasma; antigen cross-reactivity with H. capsulatum, Paracoccidioides, T. marneffei) (p.1702-1703) Microscopy of stained clinical specimens for broad-based budding yeast with doubly refractile cell wall (sputum, tracheal aspirate, BAL fluid, or purulent drainage stained with calcofluor, 10% KOH, or Papanicolaou; sensitivity 50-90%) (p.1702) Histopathology of tissue stained with Gomori methenamine silver or periodic acid-Schiff, assessed for pyogranulomatous inflammation and broad-based budding yeast (Gram and H&E do not visualize the yeast well) (p.1702) Fungal culture on special media (Sabouraud dextrose, potato dextrose, brain-heart infusion); 5-28 days incubation; definitive diagnosis (p.1702) Chemiluminescent DNA probe or PCR to confirm identification (does not distinguish among species) (p.1702) Urine, serum, BAL, and CSF galactomannan antigen testing (urine sensitivity 85-93%, serum 57-82%); useful to monitor response (p.1702-1703) Anti-BAD1 antibody serologic test (sensitivity 87%, specificity 94-99%) (p.1702) Lung cancer / malignancy (p.1701-1702) Skin cancer (cutaneous lesions) (p.1701) Sarcoidosis (cutaneous lesions) (p.1701) Pyoderma gangrenosum (cutaneous lesions) (p.1701) Laryngeal cancer (rare) (p.1701) A pyogranulomatous disease acquired by inhaling Blastomyces conidia or hyphal fragments from disturbed soil; typically a pulmonary infection, with a subset progressing to disseminated disease involving skin, bone, brain, or genitourinary system (p.1699). A primary fungal pathogen: it infects persons with intact as well as impaired immune systems (p.1699). Endemic mainly in North America (Mississippi/Ohio and St. Lawrence River basins, Great Lakes states, southeastern states) but of global importance with cases in Africa and Asia; outbreaks linked to construction, soil excavation, water sports, compost piles, and beaver dams (p.1699-1700). Yeast form (37 degrees C) is a broad-based budding yeast, 4-29 micrometers, with a doubly refractile cell wall, allowing distinction from other fungi (p.1700, 1702). After a 3-week to 3-month incubation, about 50% of those exposed develop symptomatic infection; the long incubation means cases present year-round (p.1701). Pulmonary disease occurs in 69-93% of symptomatic patients (most common feature) and may present as asymptomatic infection, influenza-like illness, acute pneumonia, chronic pneumonia, or ARDS (p.1701). Disseminated disease occurs in 15-48%; skin is the most common site (papules, ulcers, verrucous lesions, abscesses), followed by bone (osteomyelitis of spine, long bones, ribs) (p.1701). CNS (meningitis/abscess/mass), laryngeal, and genitourinary (prostate, epididymis) dissemination each occur in fewer than 10%, usually with concurrent lung or skin involvement (p.1701). Diagnosis combines microscopy of stained specimens, fungal culture, and antigen testing; serology (complement fixation 9%, immunodiffusion 28%) is diagnostically dispensable, though a newer anti-BAD1 antibody test has higher sensitivity/specificity (p.1702). Urine galactomannan antigen testing (sensitivity 85-93% urine, 57-82% serum) has supplanted older serology and can monitor treatment response as levels decline (p.1702-1703). Treatment is recommended for ALL patients because there are no criteria to identify which untreated cases will self-resolve; antifungals are amphotericin B formulations and triazoles (p.1699, 1703). Unexplained respiratory failure or ARDS in a person from or visiting an endemic area; 4-15% of pulmonary cases develop ARDS with a fulminant course and 40-89% mortality (p.1701) Pneumonia that fails to improve despite antibiotics, or pneumonia with extrapulmonary features (skin lesions, osteomyelitis, CNS involvement) (p.1701) Skin ulcers unresponsive to standard therapy (p.1701) AIDS with CD4+ count <100/microliter: increased risk of CNS dissemination (p.1702) B. helicus infection (commonly causes fungemia, usually in immunosuppressed hosts, high mortality ~71%) (p.1702) Called 'the great pretender' because it mimics infectious and noninfectious diseases; pulmonary blastomycosis is commonly misdiagnosed, and patients often receive two or three antibiotic courses before diagnosis (p.1701). No distinctive radiographic features differentiate blastomycosis from other pulmonary diseases (consolidation, mass, nodules, miliary, cavitary patterns all possible); a mass lesion can mimic malignancy (p.1701). Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion and a detailed exposure history (about 50-60% of patients have environmental risk factors); failure to consider Blastomyces in the differential delays treatment (p.1701). Serology by complement fixation/immunodiffusion has poor sensitivity and is diagnostically dispensable (p.1702). Echinocandins are ineffective (minimal beta-(1,3)-glucan in the yeast cell wall) and should not be used (p.1703). Antigen testing cross-reacts with other dimorphic fungi, notably H. capsulatum which shares the same endemic region (p.1703). Blastomyces is a thermally dimorphic species complex (including B. dermatitidis, B. gilchristii, B. helicus, B. percursus, B. emzantsi). In soil at 22-25 degrees C it grows as septate hyphae producing infectious conidia; inhalation into the lungs and conversion at the mammalian core temperature of 37 degrees C yields a pathogenic broad-based budding yeast that upregulates yeast-phase virulence factors and downregulates host immune defenses, eliciting pyogranulomatous inflammation. Shared virulence traits with other dimorphic fungi (Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Sporothrix, Paracoccidioides) include thermotolerance at 37 degrees C, intracellular survival, and the ability to infect immunocompetent hosts. Blastomyces can also replicate outside macrophages. Notably, immunosuppression has only minimal influence on dissemination, suggesting fungal virulence factors outweigh host defenses; the infecting species and duration of pulmonary symptoms (and concomitant AIDS) influence dissemination, with B. dermatitidis more likely to disseminate than B. gilchristii. (p.1700-1702) Overall mortality ranges from 5 to 13% (7.9% in 11,776 U.S. hospital admissions, 2010-2020), with most deaths from respiratory failure due to ARDS. Mortality is higher in older patients and those with COPD or concomitant solid/hematologic malignancy, and is increased when diagnosis is delayed. The vast majority who recover from pulmonary blastomycosis do not have long-term loss of pulmonary function; cutaneous blastomycosis typically heals with scarring. (p.1703) Harrison does not give a formal numeric severity scale. Severe blastomycosis is operationally defined as disease requiring hospitalization (medical ward, intermediate care, or ICU). Risk factors for severe pulmonary disease include diabetes, solid organ transplantation, immunosuppression, and multilobar pneumonia; ARDS (in 4-15%) represents the most severe pulmonary form with high mortality. Special high-risk/severity categories warranting intensified management include CNS, severe pulmonary, and severe disseminated disease. (p.1701-1703)

oedema Diagnosing early-onset sarcoidosis without recognising the genetic Blau syndrome in a young child with the triad Underestimating and under-monitoring the uveitis, allowing preventable visual loss Confusing the gain-of-function Blau NOD2 mutations with the loss-of-function Crohn-associated variants Mistaking the boggy tenosynovitis for ordinary juvenile idiopathic arthritis Blau syndrome is an autosomal dominant granulomatous disorder caused by gain-of-function mutations in NOD2 (also called CARD15), an intracellular pattern-recognition receptor that senses bacterial peptidoglycan fragments. The disease-causing mutations lie in the nucleotide-binding domain and render the receptor constitutively active, driving ligand-independent activation of the pro-inflammatory transcription factor NF-kB and dysregulated innate immune signalling. This sustained activation promotes formation of non-caseating epithelioid granulomas in the joints, skin and eyes. The mutations are mechanistically and topographically distinct from the Crohn-disease-associated NOD2 variants, which impair rather than enhance receptor function. The joint and skin disease are often manageable, but the chronic uveitis is the principal threat to long-term outcome and can lead to visual loss if not aggressively monitored and treated; systemic involvement in atypical cases can broaden morbidity.

Blepharitis — anterior blepharitis, posterior blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction, lid margin inflammation Dry eye disease Allergic or bacterial conjunctivitis Sebaceous gland carcinoma of the eyelid (in atypical, unilateral disease) Rosacea-associated ocular surface disease Demodex lash infestation Contact dermatitis of the eyelids Slit-lamp examination of the lid margins, lashes, and meibomian gland orifices Assessment of tear film stability and ocular surface staining for associated dry eye Lid margin or lash swab in severe or atypical cases Lid margin biopsy when malignancy is suspected (unilateral disease with lash loss and induration) A common, chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins presenting with burning, grittiness, crusting, and redness that is typically bilateral and worse in the mornings Divided into anterior blepharitis (affecting the lash bases, often staphylococcal or seborrhoeic) and posterior blepharitis (meibomian gland dysfunction) Anterior staphylococcal disease shows hard crusts and collarettes around the lashes, with lash loss and misdirection in chronic cases Posterior disease shows capped, plugged, or inspissated meibomian orifices and a poor-quality, foamy tear film with associated evaporative dry eye Strongly associated with rosacea and seborrhoeic dermatitis; recurrent chalazia and styes are common complications The mainstay of management is lid hygiene with warm compresses and lid margin cleaning; topical antibiotic ointment helps anterior disease and oral tetracyclines help refractory meibomian dysfunction Recurrent, unilateral, or asymmetrical lid margin disease with lash loss should raise suspicion of eyelid malignancy such as sebaceous gland carcinoma Patients should be counselled that it is a chronic, relapsing condition controlled rather than cured Unilateral or markedly asymmetrical disease with localised lash loss and lid thickening suggesting sebaceous gland carcinoma Associated corneal involvement (marginal keratitis or ulceration) threatening vision Failure to respond to appropriate treatment prompting re-evaluation of the diagnosis Recurrent chalazia at the same site raising concern for malignancy Expecting a cure rather than long-term control and stopping lid hygiene prematurely Missing sebaceous gland carcinoma masquerading as recurrent unilateral blepharitis or chalazion Overlooking associated dry eye and rosacea that require concurrent management Prolonged unmonitored topical steroid use with risk of raised intraocular pressure Blepharitis is chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins with overlapping mechanisms. Anterior blepharitis involves bacterial (chiefly staphylococcal) colonisation of the lash bases and an inflammatory reaction to bacterial products, or seborrhoeic changes with excessive scaling. Posterior blepharitis reflects meibomian gland dysfunction, in which altered and inspissated meibomian secretions block the glands, destabilise the lipid layer of the tear film, and promote evaporative dry eye. Bacterial lipases and inflammatory mediators contribute to ocular surface irritation, and the condition is frequently linked to rosacea. Blepharitis is a chronic relapsing condition that is generally controlled well with sustained lid hygiene, though symptoms recur if treatment lapses; complications such as recurrent chalazia and evaporative dry eye can be troublesome but vision is usually preserved.

Blepharochalasis — blepharochalasis syndrome Dermatochalasis Allergic or angioneurotic eyelid oedema Floppy eyelid syndrome Thyroid eye disease Cutis laxa or other elastic-tissue disorder Clinical diagnosis from the history of recurrent painless lid swelling Documentation of episodes and resulting lid changes Exclusion of allergic, thyroid and systemic causes of lid oedema Assessment of levator function and lacrimal gland position Photography to monitor progression and quiescence A rare condition of recurrent episodes of painless upper eyelid oedema, typically beginning in youth Repeated attacks stretch and thin the eyelid skin, leaving redundant, atrophic, crinkled tissue It is distinct from dermatochalasis, which is age-related redundant lid skin without inflammatory episodes Chronic changes can include ptosis, lacrimal gland prolapse and fat atrophy or herniation It usually affects the upper lids and may be unilateral or bilateral Surgery is deferred until the disease has quiesced, as operating during active swelling gives poor results Features suggesting an alternative systemic cause of recurrent oedema Rapidly progressive changes Functional visual impairment from ptosis or dermatochalasis Signs of thyroid eye disease Confusing it with simple age-related dermatochalasis Operating during active inflammatory episodes Overlooking associated ptosis or lacrimal gland prolapse Failing to exclude allergic or systemic causes of lid oedema Blepharochalasis is characterised by recurrent bouts of eyelid angio-oedema-like swelling of uncertain cause, thought to involve localised inflammation with elastolysis. Repeated inflammatory episodes degrade elastic fibres in the eyelid skin, producing progressive atrophy, laxity and thinning, and can weaken the levator aponeurosis and orbital septum, leading to ptosis, fat herniation and prolapse of the lacrimal gland. The condition tends to enter a quiescent phase in later life once the acute episodes subside. The condition is benign but episodes can recur for years before quiescence; surgical correction of the residual deformity gives good results once the disease is inactive.

in affected females with type I disease Overlooking amblyopia while focusing on the cosmetic deformity Attempting standard levator surgery when poor function mandates frontalis suspension Neglecting genetic counselling for the wider family The syndrome arises from mutations in FOXL2, a transcription factor essential for eyelid and ovarian development. Disrupted FOXL2 signalling impairs formation of the periocular structures, producing shortened palpebral fissures, dystrophic eyelid tissue with poor levator development, and abnormal medial canthal anatomy seen as telecanthus and epicanthus inversus. Because FOXL2 also governs maintenance of ovarian follicles, mutation types that abolish its ovarian function additionally cause premature ovarian insufficiency, defining type I disease, whereas mutations that spare ovarian function give the eyelid-only type II phenotype. Eyelid appearance and function can be substantially improved with staged surgery, though results depend on the degree of levator dysfunction; visual prognosis is good if amblyopia is managed early, but affected females with type I face reduced fertility from ovarian insufficiency.

Blepharospasm is usually chronic and can fluctuate but is not life-threatening; most patients gain substantial and repeatable relief from botulinum toxin, though the condition generally requires ongoing treatment.

weight loss and malnutrition Severe or neurological features of vitamin B12 deficiency Symptoms suggesting an underlying stricture, fistula or malignancy Failure to respond to antibiotics, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis and anatomy Diagnosing irritable bowel syndrome without considering bacterial overgrowth in at-risk patients Overlooking the underlying anatomical or motility cause that perpetuates overgrowth Failing to replace vitamin B12 and fat-soluble vitamins Relying on a single breath test result given its limited sensitivity and specificity Blind loop syndrome, or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, occurs when excessive numbers of colonic-type bacteria colonise the normally sparsely populated small intestine. Normal protective mechanisms include gastric acid, intact intestinal motility that sweeps the lumen, the ileocaecal valve and immune defences; anatomical stasis from a surgically created blind loop, strictures, fistulae or diverticula, or impaired motility, allows bacteria to proliferate. These bacteria deconjugate bile acids, impairing fat absorption and causing steatorrhoea, consume dietary vitamin B12 leading to deficiency, and synthesise folate. They also injure the mucosa and produce gas and toxic metabolites, giving rise to the diarrhoea, bloating and malabsorption that characterise the syndrome. Symptoms usually improve with antibiotic treatment and correction of deficiencies, but relapse is common when a fixed anatomical or motility abnormality cannot be corrected, and some patients need recurrent or cyclical therapy.

progressive growth failure in infancy Using standard-dose radiotherapy or DNA-damaging chemotherapy without accounting for the extreme treatment sensitivity Attributing early growth restriction to nutritional causes and missing the underlying diagnosis Failing to maintain a low threshold for investigating possible malignancy Overlooking associated immunodeficiency and diabetes in ongoing care Bloom syndrome is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in BLM, which encodes a RecQ-family DNA helicase essential for maintaining genomic stability during DNA replication and repair, particularly in resolving recombination intermediates and stalled replication forks. Loss of BLM function leads to excessive homologous recombination and a striking increase in sister chromatid exchanges, the cytogenetic signature of the disorder. This genomic instability drives the profound cancer predisposition and contributes to the growth failure and other systemic features. The condition is more frequent in the Ashkenazi Jewish population owing to a founder variant. Life expectancy is significantly reduced, largely because of the exceptionally high and early risk of multiple cancers, which are the leading cause of death. Infections, diabetes and chronic pulmonary disease add to morbidity, and management is supportive with intensive cancer awareness and cautious use of DNA-damaging treatments.

aspect of the proximal tibial growth plate. Excessive mechanical compressive load across the medial physis, favoured by obesity and early weight-bearing, is thought to inhibit growth there while the lateral physis continues, producing progressive varus angulation. Early infantile disease may respond to bracing, but established or later-onset deformity usually requires orthopaedic correction; outcomes are good with timely treatment, though delayed intervention risks residual deformity and early degenerative knee change.

the priority is early recognition and supportive ventilation until the toxin is cleared First aid with pressure immobilisation is appropriate to delay systemic spread of this neurotoxic venom Complete recovery is expected if effective ventilation is maintained through the period of paralysis Perioral or facial paraesthesiae progressing to weakness Bulbar dysfunction or difficulty speaking and swallowing Falling respiratory effort or oxygen saturation Rapidly ascending paralysis Preserved awareness with inability to move, indicating impending respiratory arrest Dismissing a painless bite and failing to anticipate rapid paralysis Assuming loss of movement means loss of awareness, leading to inadequate reassurance and analgesia/sedation Delaying airway support until respiratory arrest occurs Searching for an antivenom that does not exist instead of prioritising supportive ventilation Blue-ringed octopuses (Hapalochlaena) secrete saliva containing tetrodotoxin, produced by symbiotic bacteria, which is introduced through a small bite. Tetrodotoxin binds voltage-gated sodium channels on nerve and muscle membranes, blocking sodium influx and preventing action potential propagation. This produces a rapidly progressive flaccid paralysis affecting sensory, motor and respiratory function, with respiratory muscle failure being the lethal effect. Because the toxin does not cross the blood-brain barrier appreciably or affect the cortex, consciousness is preserved despite profound paralysis. The outcome depends entirely on airway and ventilatory support; with timely and sustained ventilation through the paralytic phase, patients recover fully, whereas untreated respiratory failure is rapidly fatal.

Blue rubber bleb naevus syndrome — Bean syndrome, BRBNS Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia Isolated or multifocal venous malformations Maffucci syndrome Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome Glomuvenous malformations Gastrointestinal angiodysplasia Full blood count and iron studies showing iron-deficiency anaemia Upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy Video capsule endoscopy and device-assisted enteroscopy for the small bowel MRI to map visceral and soft-tissue lesions Faecal occult blood testing TEK (TIE2) mutation analysis Rare disorder characterised by multifocal venous malformations of the skin and gastrointestinal tract. Cutaneous lesions are soft, compressible, blue-black rubbery nodules that refill after compression and are often present from infancy. Gastrointestinal venous malformations cause chronic occult bleeding with iron-deficiency anaemia and can bleed acutely anywhere from mouth to anus. Usually sporadic and associated with somatic (rarely germline) TEK (TIE2) mutations. The small bowel is frequently involved, making capsule endoscopy and deep enteroscopy valuable. Lesions may also involve the liver, spleen, central nervous system and other organs. Sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor) can reduce lesion size, bleeding and transfusion requirements. Management is multidisciplinary, with endoscopic and surgical treatment targeting dominant bleeding lesions. Acute gastrointestinal haemorrhage with haemodynamic instability Severe or transfusion-dependent iron-deficiency anaemia Intussusception or volvulus arising from bowel lesions Central nervous system lesions with neurological symptoms Overlooking the gut as the source of unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in a patient with blue skin nodules. Attempting to resect every gastrointestinal lesion rather than targeting dominant bleeders. Missing small-bowel lesions with standard endoscopy alone. Confusing the condition with hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. Blue rubber bleb naevus syndrome is a venous malformation disorder in which multiple thin-walled, dysplastic venous channels develop in the skin, gastrointestinal tract and viscera. Most cases are sporadic and driven by somatic activating mutations in the endothelial receptor TIE2 (TEK), which promote PI3K/AKT signalling and abnormal venous channel formation. The gastrointestinal lesions bleed readily because of their thin walls and mucosal location, producing chronic blood loss and iron-deficiency anaemia. The condition is distinguished from hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and from isolated venous malformations by its characteristic multifocal cutaneous and gut distribution. Life expectancy is usually normal with appropriate management, but chronic gastrointestinal bleeding causes significant morbidity and transfusion dependence. Sirolimus has substantially improved control of bleeding in many patients.
