evaluation of occult bleeding Blue rubber bleb naevus syndrome is a disorder of multifocal slow-flow venous malformations affecting the skin and, characteristically, the gastrointestinal tract. The malformations consist of ectatic, thin-walled venous channels lined by quiescent endothelium, and somatic activating changes in the TEK (TIE2) receptor tyrosine kinase pathway drive their formation. Because venous channels can trap and consume clotting factors, extensive lesions may produce a localised intravascular coagulopathy. Bowel lesions bleed chronically, leading to iron-deficiency anaemia, and can rarely precipitate acute haemorrhage or mechanical complications. Cutaneous lesions are largely a cosmetic and comfort issue, but gastrointestinal disease often requires lifelong management of anaemia and recurrent bleeding; with iron replacement, medical therapy and targeted endoscopic or surgical treatment most patients do well, though extensive bowel involvement can be difficult to control.

Body Dysmorphic Disorder — Dysmorphophobia, BDD Obsessive-compulsive disorder Social anxiety disorder Major depressive disorder Eating disorders where the concern is weight or shape Delusional disorder, somatic type Gender dysphoria where distress concerns sex characteristics Normal appearance concern or actual disfigurement Structured assessment such as the BDD-YBOCS and validated screening questions Suicide risk assessment, which is essential Screening for depression, social anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and eating disorder Assessment of insight and delusionality History of cosmetic or dermatological procedures sought or undergone Substance use assessment Collateral history regarding functioning and behaviours Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects in appearance that are unobservable or appear only slight to others, causing marked distress or impairment. Classified within the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders spectrum. Repetitive behaviours such as mirror-checking or avoidance, grooming, skin-picking, reassurance-seeking, and comparing, or mental acts, occur in response to appearance concerns. Common foci are the skin, hair, nose, and other facial features; muscle dysmorphia, a preoccupation with insufficient muscularity, is a recognised specifier. High rates of depression and social anxiety accompany notably high suicidality, which is a leading clinical concern. Frequently presents to dermatology, cosmetic, and maxillofacial or plastic surgery services rather than psychiatry, and cosmetic procedures rarely satisfy and may worsen the condition. Insight is often poor and may reach delusional intensity as a specifier, yet the condition still responds to serotonergic and cognitive-behavioural treatment. First-line management combines serotonin reuptake inhibitors, often requiring higher-range dosing and prolonged trials, with cognitive-behavioural therapy incorporating exposure and response prevention. Active suicidal ideation or previous attempts, indicating high risk Escalating pursuit of cosmetic surgery or self-performed procedures Severe social isolation and functional collapse Skin-picking causing tissue damage or infection Missing the diagnosis behind depression, social anxiety, or repeated cosmetic requests Underestimating suicide risk Endorsing or facilitating cosmetic procedures that typically fail to help Under-dosing or curtailing serotonergic trials and omitting exposure-based cognitive-behavioural therapy Body dysmorphic disorder shares mechanisms with obsessive-compulsive disorder, involving fronto-striatal and limbic circuitry and serotonergic dysfunction. Patients show abnormal visual processing biased toward detailed, piecemeal analysis of appearance rather than global or holistic processing, with heightened activity in visual and orbitofrontal-striatal systems. Cognitive-behavioural models emphasise selective attention to perceived flaws, distorted self-image, maladaptive appearance-related beliefs, and safety and checking behaviours that maintain distress. Emotional processing biases, such as interpreting neutral facial expressions as contemptuous, reinforce social anxiety and avoidance. Without treatment the disorder tends to be chronic; with adequate-dose serotonergic medication and cognitive-behavioural therapy many patients improve substantially, though relapse can occur if treatment is stopped prematurely.

Body Integrity Dysphoria — Body integrity identity disorder, Apotemnophilia Body dysmorphic disorder Gender dysphoria, an analogous identity-body mismatch in a different domain Somatic delusional disorder or psychosis Factitious disorder Obsessive-compulsive disorder Paraphilic disorder where a sexual motive predominates Self-harm in the context of personality disorder Detailed developmental and psychosexual history Mental state examination to confirm that the belief is non-delusional Assessment of self-harm and self-amputation risk and any prior attempts Screening for depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and body dysmorphic disorder Capacity, ethical, and multidisciplinary review where surgical requests arise Neuropsychological assessment of body representation where available Risk assessment for dangerous pretending or self-injury An intense and persistent desire to be disabled, most often through amputation of a specific limb but sometimes paralysis, blindness, or deafness, arising from a mismatch between the experienced and the actual body. Affected individuals feel their able body is over-complete, and the desired site of impairment is highly specific and stable over time, frequently dating from childhood. Now recognised in ICD-11 as body integrity dysphoria, having previously been termed body integrity identity disorder or apotemnophilia. Some engage in pretending, using wheelchairs or crutches, and a minority attempt dangerous self-amputation or self-injury to force surgical amputation. Distinguished from a psychotic or somatic delusion (the belief is not delusional), from body dysmorphic disorder (the concern is not about ugliness), and from factitious disorder (there is no deception to obtain the sick role). A subset report sexual arousal linked to the desired disability, but the core is an identity-based desire rather than a primarily paraphilic one. A proposed neurological basis lies in right parietal, particularly superior parietal lobule, dysfunction affecting the body schema. Management is ethically fraught, since elective amputation of healthy limbs is not sanctioned, and focuses on distress reduction and safety. Plans or attempts at self-amputation or dangerous self-injury to induce disability Use of ischaemia, cold, or trauma to damage the target limb Severe depression with suicidal ideation Pursuit of unregulated or unsafe surgical amputation Misclassifying the condition as psychosis, body dysmorphic disorder, or a purely paraphilic disorder Underestimating the risk of self-inflicted limb damage Ethical missteps around requests for elective amputation Missing treatable comorbid depression, anxiety, or obsessive-compulsive disorder Body integrity dysphoria is hypothesised to result from a disturbance of the cortical body schema, particularly involving the right superior parietal lobule and related networks that construct the sense of body ownership. The affected limb, though normally innervated, is not fully incorporated into the internal body representation, producing a persistent sense of mismatch and a desire to bring the physical body into line with the internal image. Supportive evidence includes altered parietal responses and reduced skin-conductance responses below the desired amputation line. The condition is developmental in many cases, with onset in early childhood, and is categorised as a disorder of bodily distress and experience rather than a psychosis or paraphilia, although paraphilic features coexist in a subset. The desire is typically persistent and stable over years; distress and safety can be improved with psychological support and treatment of comorbidity, but no established treatment reliably removes the desire, and a minority who obtain amputation report relief while incurring significant risks.

and underestimating severity Using barium rather than water-soluble contrast when perforation is suspected Underestimating fluid and antibiotic needs in a septic patient Boerhaave syndrome is a spontaneous full-thickness rupture of the oesophagus caused by a sudden rise in intraluminal pressure against a closed upper oesophageal sphincter, typically during forceful vomiting or retching. The pressure surge tears the wall, usually at the weaker distal left posterolateral segment. Gastric and oral contents then contaminate the mediastinum and, because the rupture communicates with the left pleural cavity, frequently the left pleural space, provoking a fulminant chemical and bacterial mediastinitis and pleuritis with sepsis. The condition is distinct from iatrogenic perforation and from the partial-thickness mucosal tears of Mallory-Weiss syndrome. Outcome depends critically on time to diagnosis and treatment; early intervention gives reasonable survival, whereas delay beyond about a day markedly increases mortality from mediastinitis and sepsis.

modifications governing gene repression, in part through the PR-DUB complex which removes ubiquitin from histone H2A and thereby balances polycomb silencing. continuously remodeled by a basic multicellular unit: osteoblasts (mesenchymal origin) lay down and mineralize osteoid, osteoclasts (hematopoietic/macrophage lineage) resorb matrix, and long-lived embedded osteocytes coordinate both and act as mechanosensors (Harrison 22e p.3259). Roughly half of total serum calcium is ionized; the rest is bound to albumin/immunoglobulins or complexed to anions, so total calcium must be interpreted with the serum protein level. A useful correction adds about 0.8 mg/dL to total calcium for each 1 g/dL the albumin is below normal, but in acute illness measure ionized calcium directly with a calcium-selective electrode (Harrison 22e p.3261-3262). Acidosis raises ionized calcium by reducing calcium binding to protein; alkalosis does the opposite, which helps explain tetany seen with respiratory alkalosis (Harrison 22e p.3262). Serum phosphate varies by up to 50% over a day with a morning nadir, and IV dextrose, insulin, or alkalosis can drop it acutely, so phosphate should be measured fasting and in the basal state (Harrison 22e p.3262-3263). Because only about 1% of body magnesium is in the extracellular fluid, a normal serum magnesium does not exclude significant total-body magnesium depletion (Harrison 22e p.3266-3267). Hypomagnesemia frequently causes refractory hypocalcemia and hypokalemia; at very low serum magnesium (below roughly 0.4 mmol/L) PTH secretion is impaired and there is cellular PTH resistance, so calcium and potassium will not correct until magnesium is repleted (Harrison 22e p.3267). FGF23, secreted by osteocytes, is a phosphaturic hormone that both lowers proximal-tubule phosphate reabsorption and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase (lowering 1,25(OH)2D); excess FGF23 underlies XLH, ADHR, and tumor-induced osteomalacia, whereas deficient/inactive FGF23 causes tumoral calcinosis (Harrison 22e p.3263-3265). Vitamin D is effectively a hormone, not a true vitamin: skin synthesizes it from 7-dehydrocholesterol under UV light, the liver performs unregulated 25-hydroxylation (25(OH)D is the storage/measured form), and the kidney performs the tightly regulated 1-alpha-hydroxylation to active 1,25(OH)2D (Harrison 22e p.3268). Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase is stimulated by PTH and hypophosphatemia and suppressed by calcium, FGF23, and 1,25(OH)2D itself; granuloma/lymphoma macrophages express an unregulated 1-alpha-hydroxylase, explaining hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis and lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.3268). Optimal intestinal calcium absorption requires gastric acid; achlorhydria, proton pump inhibitors, or post-bariatric surgery impair absorption of poorly dissociable salts like calcium carbonate, so calcium citrate or dosing with meals is preferred (Harrison 22e p.3262). Active vitamin D-dependent transcellular calcium and phosphate absorption uses specific apical channels/transporters (TRPV6 and Npt2b in the gut, TRPV5 in the distal tubule); thiazides lower urinary calcium (useful in hypercalciuria) while loop diuretics and saline promote calciuresis (Harrison 22e p.3262). rapid phosphate correction risks heterotopic calcification if the calcium-phosphorus product is allowed to rise Mineral homeostasis is maintained by integrated handling of calcium, phosphate, and magnesium across gut, kidney, and bone under hormonal control by PTH, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, and FGF23. Bone provides both mechanical support and the major reservoir of these ions; it is constantly remodeled, with osteoblasts (mesenchymal lineage, driven by Runx2, osterix, Ihh, Wnt and BMP signaling) forming and mineralizing type I collagen matrix and osteoclasts (hematopoietic lineage, driven by M-CSF and RANK ligand, opposed by osteoprotegerin) resorbing it via acidification and proteases such as cathepsin K. Osteocytes sense mechanical load, secrete the Wnt inhibitor sclerostin and the phosphaturic hormone FGF23, and orchestrate remodeling. Ionized calcium in the extracellular fluid is sensed by the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells and renal tubule; low calcium raises PTH, which mobilizes bone calcium, enhances distal renal calcium reabsorption, lowers renal phosphate reabsorption, and stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase to make 1,25(OH)2D, which in turn increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption. Phosphate balance is governed largely by proximal tubular NaPi-2a/2c transporters, which are downregulated by PTH and FGF23; FGF23 from osteocytes additionally suppresses 1,25(OH)2D synthesis. Vitamin D is produced in skin or absorbed from diet, 25-hydroxylated in liver, and 1-alpha-hydroxylated in kidney, with 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1) providing inactivation. Disturbances at any node (dietary extremes, renal failure, hormone deficiency/excess, intestinal disease, or genetic transporter/enzyme defects) disrupt the narrow regulation of ionized calcium and lead to skeletal and systemic disease. Prognosis depends entirely on the underlying disorder rather than on bone and mineral metabolism per se. Acute redistributive electrolyte derangements (hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia) are typically reversible with appropriate repletion, and respiratory/cardiac dysfunction from severe hypophosphatemia improves with phosphate replacement. Tumor-induced osteomalacia resolves within hours to days after successful tumor resection. Chronic renal phosphate-wasting disorders (XLH, ADHR) generally cannot be fully normalized but can be controlled. Persistent dysregulation, as in chronic kidney disease with secondary hyperparathyroidism and hyperphosphatemia, leads to progressive skeletal and vascular consequences. Hypophosphatemia is graded by serum phosphate (mild-moderate ~0.5-0.8 mmol/L [1.5-2.5 mg/dL] with mainly musculoskeletal/reversible cardiorespiratory effects; severe <0.5 mmol/L [<1.5 mg/dL]; life-threatening <0.25 mmol/L [<0.8 mg/dL] with paralysis, seizures, rhabdomyolysis). Hyperphosphatemia in adults is defined as fasting phosphate >1.8 mmol/L (5.5 mg/dL). Hypomagnesemia is usually asymptomatic above ~0.5 mmol/L; defects in PTH secretion appear below ~0.4 mmol/L. Hypermagnesemia produces vasodilation/neuromuscular blockade above ~2 mmol/L, coma and hyporeflexia above ~4 mmol/L, and asystole near 10 mmol/L.

Bone island — Enostosis, Solitary enostosis Osteoblastic metastasis (notably prostate and breast carcinoma) Osteoid osteoma (with a lucent nidus) Osteoblastoma Low-grade or sclerosing osteosarcoma Osteopoikilosis when lesions are multiple Healed or sclerotic phase of a prior benign lesion Plain radiographs demonstrating a dense focus with radiating spiculated margins CT to document very high attenuation approaching that of cortical bone Bone scintigraphy to assess for the intense uptake that would favour metastasis Comparison with prior imaging to confirm stability or characterise growth MRI in selected uncertain cases, where the lesion is low signal on all sequences Correlation with tumour markers and primary tumour history when metastasis is a concern A focus of compact cortical bone within the cancellous medullary bone, most often an incidental finding in the pelvis, proximal femur and other long bones. The hallmark radiographic feature is a homogeneously dense sclerotic focus with radiating spiculated thorny or brush-border margins that blend into the surrounding trabeculae. The lesion is typically asymptomatic and stable, although slow growth can occur over years. Bone scintigraphy usually shows little or no increased uptake, which helps distinguish it from osteoblastic metastasis that is typically intensely avid, though large or growing islands may show mild uptake. CT attenuation is very high, often in the range of dense cortical bone, which helps separate it from lower-attenuation sclerotic metastases. Multiple bone islands define osteopoikilosis, an autosomal dominant condition caused by LEMD3 mutations that may occur with the skin lesions of Buschke-Ollendorff syndrome (dermatofibrosis lenticularis disseminata). A lesion larger than about 2 cm is termed a giant bone island; slow growth is acceptable but marked or rapid enlargement warrants scrutiny. No treatment is required; the key clinical value is confident recognition to avoid unnecessary biopsy or oncological work-up. Significant interval growth, particularly more than about 1 cm per year Associated lucency, cortical destruction or a soft-tissue mass Intense uptake on bone scintigraphy with a known primary malignancy or rising tumour markers New localised pain attributable to the lesion Misinterpreting a bone island as an osteoblastic metastasis, or dismissing a true metastasis as a bone island Proceeding to unnecessary biopsy of a radiographically classic lesion Failing to act on documented marked interval growth Overlooking the pattern of osteopoikilosis and its familial and cutaneous associations A bone island, or enostosis, is a benign developmental hamartomatous focus of mature compact (lamellar) bone situated within the spongiosa. It is thought to result from a localised failure of osteoclastic resorption during endochondral ossification and remodelling, leaving an island of dense cortical-type bone that maintains continuity with the surrounding trabeculae through its characteristic radiating bony spicules. Histologically it consists of normal lamellar bone with Haversian systems, and it possesses no malignant potential. When multiple and symmetrically distributed, particularly in a periarticular distribution, the lesions represent osteopoikilosis, linked to loss-of-function mutations in the LEMD3 gene. The prognosis is excellent; the bone island is entirely benign with no malignant potential and requires only recognition rather than treatment.

the syndromes are categorized by the dominant marrow morphology, with aplastic anemia (fatty/empty marrow), MDS (dysplastic marrow), and single-lineage aplasias forming a related spectrum. Immune (acquired) aplastic anemia is classically a young person's disease with abrupt pancytopenia in a previously well adolescent or young adult; the age distribution is biphasic with peaks in the teens-twenties and again in older adults. In aplastic anemia bleeding (bruising, gum oozing, epistaxis, menorrhagia, petechiae) is typically the earliest symptom, whereas infection as a first symptom is unusual; lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly are highly atypical and should prompt search for another cause of pancytopenia. Clues to an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome: short stature and cafe au lait spots with thumb/radial anomalies (Fanconi anemia); dystrophic nails, mucosal leukoplakia and reticular hyperpigmentation (dyskeratosis congenita); premature hair graying plus a family history of pulmonary or hepatic fibrosis (telomere biology disorders); recurrent warts and unusual infections (GATA2 deficiency). A detectable PNH clone by flow cytometry is found in up to half of patients at presentation of aplastic anemia and strongly suggests immune-mediated pathophysiology and likely responsiveness to immunosuppression; patients can later cross over between aplastic and hemolytic PNH phenotypes. MDS is predominantly a disease of older adults (mean onset over 70) with a slight male predominance; anemia (often macrocytic) dominates the early course and at least half of patients are asymptomatic, discovered incidentally on routine blood counts. Persistent parvovirus B19 infection is a treatable cause of pure red cell aplasia; the marrow shows giant pronormoblasts (the cytopathic signature), and diagnosis requires detection of viral DNA because IgG/IgM antibodies are commonly absent in immunodeficient hosts. B19 parvovirus uses the erythrocyte P antigen as its receptor; in patients with underlying hemolysis it can precipitate a transient aplastic crisis with abrupt worsening of anemia from arrested erythropoiesis. Macrocytosis (elevated MCV) is a frequent finding across marrow failure states; in aplastic anemia the smear shows large red cells with a paucity of platelets and granulocytes, near-absent reticulocytes, and the elevated MCV often persists even after recovery. Marrow blast percentage is the strongest morphologic prognostic determinant in MDS; the WHO threshold of 20% marrow blasts separates AML from MDS, and blasts should be enumerated manually on smear and by flow cytometry. 5q deletion MDS arises from heterozygous loss of a ribosomal protein gene, effectively mimicking constitutional red cell aplasia; SF3B1 mutation is strongly associated with ring sideroblasts and a relatively favorable outcome. Severity grading in aplastic anemia and recovery thresholds are defined by blood counts (see severity criteria); absolute reticulocyte and lymphocyte numbers are better predictors of treatment response than the classic severity definition in the immunosuppression era. Profound neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count <500/uL) with fever mandates urgent empirical broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics without awaiting cultures Persistent or recrudescent fever despite antibacterials implies invasive fungal disease (Candida, Aspergillus) Severe thrombocytopenia with central nervous system or retinal bleeding can be catastrophic (intracranial or retinal hemorrhage) Platelet count below 5000/uL sharply increases risk of gut bleeding Systemic symptoms, weight loss, lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly point away from simple aplastic anemia toward malignancy or systemic disease Emergence of new cytogenetic abnormalities, rising blasts, marrow fibrosis or abrupt worsening of pancytopenia signals clonal evolution to MDS/leukemia Family history of AML/MDS or unexplained cytopenias should trigger evaluation for an inherited predisposition syndrome Clinical drug/chemical and viral associations with aplastic anemia are not proof of causation; the implicated agent may merely have been used to treat the earliest symptoms (antibiotics for fever, NSAIDs causing petechiae in an already thrombocytopenic patient). Marrow cellularity correlates imperfectly with disease severity: 'empty' biopsies can occur in moderate disease and focal 'hot spots' of hematopoiesis can be seen in severe aplasia, so a single small or dilute sample can mislead (a dry tap suggests fibrosis or myelophthisis rather than aplasia). Distinguishing acquired from constitutional aplastic anemia is essential; constitutional marrow is usually morphologically indistinguishable and physical anomalies may be subtle or absent (adults with telomere disorders can present without anomalies, only premature graying). Hypocellular MDS can be mistaken for aplastic anemia; the boundary with low-risk MDS is blurred (del 13q/20q may respond to immunosuppression, and DNMT3A/ASXL1 mutations occur in both). Dysplastic marrow changes are not specific to MDS, occurring with vitamin deficiencies, copper deficiency, drug effects, alcohol and acute viral infection; interobserver agreement on dysplasia morphology is imperfect. Germline genomic panel results may take weeks to return, a problem in the severely pancytopenic patient who needs prompt management. In transplant-eligible aplastic anemia patients, transfusing blood from family members risks alloimmunization and should be avoided; HLA typing should be ordered as soon as the diagnosis is made. Glucocorticoids are not effective primary therapy for aplastic anemia and increase fungal infection risk. Bone marrow failure results from severe damage to the hematopoietic cell compartment. In aplastic anemia the marrow is replaced by fat, CD34+ early hematopoietic cells are greatly diminished, and the stem cell pool in severe disease may be reduced to about 1% or less of normal. Three principal mechanisms underlie an empty marrow: physical/chemical damage (high-dose radiation, benzene and its reactive hydroquinone/quinolone metabolites, cytotoxic chemotherapy), immune-mediated stem cell destruction, and constitutional genetic defects. Acquired aplastic anemia is most often immune: activated cytotoxic T cells suppress hematopoietic progenitors, type 1 cytokines including interferon-gamma upregulate Fas on CD34+ cells driving apoptosis, and immune selection can produce HLA-loss and PNH clones. Genetically determined immune-response features (HLA, cytokine and T-cell polarization gene polymorphisms) likely convert a normal response into sustained autoimmunity, explaining why aplasia is rare despite common exposures. Idiosyncratic drug-induced aplasia is attributed to abnormal generation of or failure to detoxify reactive electrophilic drug intermediates that bind cellular macromolecules. Constitutional syndromes are intrinsic stem cell defects: Fanconi anemia involves a DNA interstrand cross-link repair pathway (most often FANCA; the gene products monoubiquitinate FANCD2), telomere biology disorders involve telomerase complex (DKC1, TERC, TERT) or shelterin (TINF2) defects that limit replicative capacity, and GATA2/RUNX1 mutations disrupt hematopoietic transcriptional regulation; Diamond-Blackfan and Shwachman-Diamond syndromes are ribosomopathies. MDS is a clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder of aging marrow characterized by disordered proliferation, impaired differentiation and ineffective hematopoiesis producing cytopenias plus risk of leukemic progression; both chromosomal instability (non-random losses of 5, 7, 20, trisomy 8) and accumulating somatic mutations in ~100 recurrently mutated myeloid genes drive disease, with clonal succession of founder clones acquiring further mutations during evolution to AML. Untreated severe aplastic anemia deteriorates rapidly and is fatal; spontaneous recovery is rare. The dominant prognostic factor is the blood count: severe disease has historically required two of three of an absolute neutrophil count <500/uL, platelets <20,000/uL and corrected reticulocyte count <1% (or absolute reticulocytes <60,000/uL), while in the immunosuppression era higher absolute reticulocytes (>25,000/uL) and lymphocytes (>1000/uL) better predict response and survival. A PNH clone, very short telomeres and somatic myeloid mutations (e.g., ASXL1) further influence outcome and risk of clonal evolution. Clonal evolution to MDS or leukemia occurs in roughly 10-15% of immunosuppression-treated patients over a decade. In MDS, median survival ranges from years (5q- or sideroblastic anemia) to only months (high blast count disease); the IPSS-R and emerging molecularly informed IPSS-M stratify risk. Even lower-risk MDS carries meaningful morbidity and mortality; most patients die of complications of pancytopenia rather than leukemic transformation, and about a third die of unrelated comorbidities. Therapy-related MDS has an extremely poor prognosis with rapid progression to refractory AML. Pure red cell aplasia is generally compatible with long-term survival with supportive care, and persistent parvovirus B19 PRCA almost always responds to immunoglobulin. Severe aplastic anemia has historically been defined by the presence of at least two of three criteria: absolute neutrophil count <500/uL, platelet count <20,000/uL, and corrected reticulocyte count <1% (or absolute reticulocyte count <60,000/uL). In the immunosuppressive-therapy era, absolute reticulocyte count >25,000/uL and absolute lymphocyte count >1000/uL are better predictors of response and long-term outcome. For MDS, prognostic severity is assessed by the Revised International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS-R), which integrates marrow blast percentage (categories at <=2%, >2-<5%, 5-10%, >10-30%), refined cytogenetic risk groups, depth of cytopenias (hemoglobin, platelets, neutrophils), and additional features (age, performance status, ferritin, LDH, beta-2-microglobulin) into five risk categories; the molecularly enhanced IPSS-M is emerging as the current standard.

The mechanism is uncertain and probably multifactorial, involving transient alterations in local perfusion, increased intraosseous pressure and a reparative or neurovascular response. Its migratory and self-limiting nature and the absence of necrosis distinguish it from avascular necrosis, though the two may overlap on a spectrum. The syndrome is benign and self-limiting, generally resolving over several months, though symptoms may migrate to other joints before settling.

psychotic-level symptoms beyond transient stress-related phenomena Severe comorbid substance misuse increasing danger during crises Reacting to crises with escalating polypharmacy rather than psychotherapy and structure Dismissing chronic suicidality and thereby missing genuine acute risk Allowing splitting to divide the treating team through inconsistent boundaries Misdiagnosing affective instability as bipolar disorder Overlooking comorbid trauma and substance use disorders Borderline personality disorder is understood through a biosocial model in which a heritable predisposition to emotional vulnerability and impulsivity interacts with an invalidating or traumatic developmental environment. Neurobiological findings include altered function of limbic structures such as the amygdala and of prefrontal regulatory regions, contributing to heightened emotional reactivity and impaired regulation, with disturbances in serotonergic and stress-response systems. Contrary to older pessimistic views, many patients with borderline personality disorder show substantial improvement over time, with reduced impulsivity and self-harm and often remission of full criteria, though interpersonal and functional difficulties can persist. Prognosis is better with engagement in structured psychotherapy and stable support, and worse with severe early trauma, persistent substance misuse, and repeated high-lethality self-harm.

delayed puberty Attributing obesity to lifestyle alone and missing the syndromic diagnosis PHF6 encodes a plant homeodomain (PHD) finger protein that localises to the nucleus and nucleolus and participates in chromatin-associated transcriptional regulation, including interactions with chromatin-remodelling and ribosome-biogenesis machinery. Loss-of-function variants impair this transcriptional control during development of the brain and endocrine tissues, producing intellectual disability together with the hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction that underlies the obesity and hypogonadism. As an X-linked gene, PHF6 variants affect males more consistently, while carrier females show variable expression. The combined effect on neuronal and endocrine gene expression accounts for the characteristic syndromic picture. Affected males have lifelong intellectual disability with obesity and hypogonadism that require ongoing endocrine and metabolic management; carrier females are usually more mildly affected. Care is supportive and multidisciplinary.

HOXA1 is essential for patterning the rhombomeres of the embryonic brainstem, from which cranial nerve nuclei, inner ear structures, and adjacent vascular and cardiac derivatives arise. to assess deep tissue, bone or visceral involvement Antimicrobial susceptibility testing to direct prolonged therapy Assessment of immune status and search for a retained foreign body Botryomycosis is a retained foreign body Visceral botryomycosis, particularly of the lungs, is less common and tends to occur in immunocompromised or debilitated hosts Discharging sinuses may extrude visible granules Extension of infection into bone or deep structures Non-healing sinuses despite standard antibiotic courses Diagnostic uncertainty requiring exclusion of mycetoma or malignancy Mistaking bacterial grains for fungal mycetoma and giving inappropriate antifungal therapy Relying on antibiotics alone without surgical removal of affected tissue or foreign body Truncating therapy before the chronic infection is fully cleared Overlooking underlying immunosuppression in visceral disease Botryomycosis develops when common pyogenic bacteria establish a chronic, walled-off infection rather than being cleared, often in the setting of local trauma, a foreign body or impaired host defences. The bacteria aggregate into grains encased in an eosinophilic, immunoglobulin-rich matrix (the Splendore-Hoeppli reaction), which shields them from immune attack and antibiotics. Surrounding chronic suppurative and granulomatous inflammation produces nodules, abscesses and sinus tracts, closely mimicking the clinical and histological picture of fungal or actinomycotic mycetoma despite being purely bacterial in origin. Localised cutaneous disease usually responds well to prolonged antibiotics combined with surgical excision, whereas visceral disease in compromised hosts is more difficult to eradicate and carries a poorer outcome.

Botulism — Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) Myasthenia gravis Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome Tick paralysis Basilar stroke producing nonlateralizing/symmetric bulbar palsies Tetrodotoxin or shellfish poisoning Antimicrobial-associated paralysis Guillain-Barre syndrome following Campylobacter jejuni or viral infection Detailed neurologic examination (the key to clinical diagnosis, uncovering invariable cranial nerve deficits) Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis (protein usually normal in botulism, in contrast to GBS; may help distinguish) Electromyography by an experienced operator (neuromuscular junction blockage with normal axonal conduction and potentiation on rapid repetitive stimulation) Brain imaging (normal in botulism; helps exclude basilar stroke) Serologic antibody tests and rapid nerve stimulation tests (to evaluate myasthenia gravis) Mouse bioassay (gold standard for BoNT identification and serotyping in clinical or food specimens) Detection of BoNT in serum or stool, or isolation of BoNT-producing Clostridium from stool or wound cultures; toxin in suspected food In vitro assays: real-time PCR for bont genes, Endopep mass spectrometry, immune-based and cell-based assays Myasthenia gravis Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (proximal limb weakness, often with advanced cancer) Tick paralysis Basilar stroke Intoxication from alcohol or other substances (ptosis, dysarthria, and gait instability can be misattributed) Classic syndrome: bilateral cranial nerve palsies followed by symmetric, descending flaccid paralysis, in a patient who is afebrile and fully conscious with normal sensorium (Harrison 22e p.1235). First neurologic manifestation is usually ptosis, which can be striking; ocular findings include blurred/fuzzy vision or diplopia from extraocular palsies of cranial nerves III, IV, and VI (Harrison 22e p.1235). Bulbar onset: dysarthria, difficulty swallowing, and nasal/oral regurgitation reflect cranial nerve involvement; descending weakness then spreads to neck, shoulders, and limbs, with proximal groups affected before distal (Harrison 22e p.1235). Paralysis descends symmetrically and distal tendon reflexes diminish symmetrically; constipation from intestinal paralysis develops in almost all patients (Harrison 22e p.1235-1236). In a U.S. series of 332 cases, the most common reported symptoms were difficulty swallowing (86%), fatigue (85%), blurred vision (80%), and slurred speech (78%); signs included afebrile temperature (99%), descending paralysis (93%), alert/oriented status (93%), and ptosis (81%) (Harrison 22e p.1236). BoNTs irreversibly block acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, so paralysis persists for weeks to months until nerve endings regenerate; the clinical approach is the same for all toxin types causing human illness (Harrison 22e p.1234, p.1236). Four naturally occurring forms (foodborne, infant, wound, adult intestinal colonization) plus iatrogenic and inhalational forms; the neurologic syndrome is essentially identical across all forms and all ages (Harrison 22e p.1233-1235). Every case of foodborne botulism is a public health emergency, as it may be the first in an outbreak; clinicians should contact the state health department emergency line to reach a CDC botulism consultant (Harrison 22e p.1235, p.1237). More than 95% of noninfant botulism patients in the U.S. recover, and the infant botulism survival rate is near 100% (Harrison 22e p.1236). Pharyngeal muscle flaccidity causing airway collapse and respiratory arrest early in the course Falling vital capacity / diaphragmatic and accessory muscle weakness signaling impending respiratory failure Rapidly progressive descending paralysis (especially BoNT type A or F) A placid, expressionless appearance masking the agitation expected with respiratory distress Autonomic dysfunction producing hemodynamic instability Two or more patients with the same syndrome (near-pathognomonic and signals an outbreak / public health emergency) Misclassifying the paralysis as ascending: botulism is a DESCENDING (cranial-first, then downward) symmetric flaccid paralysis, whereas GBS presents as an ASCENDING paralysis in about 95% of cases - this descending-versus-ascending distinction is central, though the Miller Fisher GBS variant (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia) may resemble early descending paralysis (Harrison 22e p.1236). Mistaking intact sensorium for altered consciousness: cranial nerve palsies, ptosis, dysarthria, and gait instability can give a false impression of obtundation or be wrongly attributed to alcohol/substance intoxication, even though patients remain fully conscious (Harrison 22e p.1235-1236). Sporadic (lone) cases are commonly misdiagnosed because of the rarity of botulism and clinician unfamiliarity; an incomplete neurologic examination is a frequent cause of delayed or missed diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1236). Waiting for laboratory confirmation: confirmation may take >=24 h, so treatment must rely on rapid clinical diagnosis rather than awaiting lab results (Harrison 22e p.1236-1237). Assuming normal CSF excludes GBS too early: in GBS, CSF protein elevation may lag symptom onset by days, so a normal early CSF must be interpreted with symptom duration and the lumbar puncture may need repeating (Harrison 22e p.1236). Reported paresthesias are not explained by the known activity of botulinum toxin, and GI symptoms (nausea/vomiting) are seen in foodborne but have NOT been reported in wound botulism (Harrison 22e p.1235-1236). Disease is caused by botulinum neurotoxins (BoNTs) produced by Clostridium botulinum (rarely C. butyricum or C. baratii), gram-positive, spore-forming, anaerobic bacteria whose heat-resistant spores are ubiquitous in soil. Serotypes A, B, E, and F cause human disease. BoNT is a metalloprotease whose heavy chain mediates neurospecific binding and internalization and whose light chain enters the cytosol and cleaves SNARE-family proteins (e.g., SNAP-25, VAMP), disrupting synaptic vesicle fusion and blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, producing flaccid paralysis of voluntary muscles. Toxin binding is effectively irreversible, so recovery requires regeneration of nerve endings over weeks to months. Routes differ by form: foodborne (ingestion of preformed toxin in improperly preserved foods, often home-canned low-acid vegetables), wound (spore germination in wounds/necrotic tissue, notably from black tar heroin injection), infant and adult intestinal colonization (in situ toxin production by colonizing Clostridium), iatrogenic (high-dose therapeutic BoNT injection), and inhalational (aerosolized toxin as a bioweapon). (Harrison 22e p.1233-1234) More than 95% of noninfant botulism patients in the United States recover, often after protracted intensive care and rehabilitation, even without antitoxin; the survival rate for infant botulism is near 100%. Paralysis lasts weeks to months while affected nerve endings regenerate. Serotype A is associated with more rapid progression, more frequent respiratory compromise and mechanical ventilation, and longer-duration paralysis; type B is milder and shorter; type F progresses rapidly but recovers faster. Untreated, early death results from airway obstruction and inadequate tidal volume from respiratory muscle paralysis. (Harrison 22e p.1236) Harrison does not provide a formal numeric severity score; severity is described as varying greatly between patients and is probably governed by toxin dose. At the mild end, some untreated patients progress no further than ptosis and mild palsy of one or two cranial nerves; at the severe end, others develop fulminant cranial nerve palsies and rapidly progressive descending flaccid paralysis affecting most or all voluntary muscles with respiratory failure requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation within hours. (Harrison 22e p.1236)

interphalangeal joint The Elson test to identify an acute central slip injury before the deformity is fully established Plain radiographs to detect a dorsal avulsion fragment and assess the joint Serial clinical assessment to detect an evolving deformity Ultrasound or MRI to evaluate the central slip when the diagnosis is unclear Screening for an inflammatory arthropathy when the deformity is atraumatic Characterised by proximal interphalangeal joint flexion combined with distal interphalangeal joint hyperextension The primary lesion is disruption of the central slip at its insertion on the dorsal base of the middle phalanx As the central slip fails, the lateral bands migrate volar to the axis of the proximal interphalangeal joint so that they flex it and hyperextend the distal joint The Elson test detects an acute central slip injury, showing weak proximal interphalangeal extension and a rigid distal joint when the joint is flexed over an edge Common causes include forced flexion of an extended finger, volar dislocation, dorsal laceration, and attritional rupture in rheumatoid arthritis The deformity characteristically develops over the days following injury rather than appearing immediately It must be distinguished from a pseudo-boutonniere, in which a volar plate injury causes a proximal interphalangeal flexion contracture without distal joint hyperextension Generic management is proximal interphalangeal extension splinting with the distal joint left free for closed acute injuries, and surgery for displaced avulsions, open injuries or established deformity An open laceration over the proximal interphalangeal joint involving the extensor mechanism and joint A displaced intra-articular avulsion fracture Septic arthritis of the joint A fixed established contracture that limits treatment options Missing the acute central slip injury because the deformity is delayed, which the Elson test helps avoid Confusing the deformity with a pseudo-boutonniere and mismanaging it Unnecessarily splinting the distal interphalangeal joint Under-recognising rheumatoid arthritis as the underlying cause A boutonniere deformity develops when the central slip insertion at the dorsal base of the middle phalanx is disrupted, removing the principal extensor of the proximal interphalangeal joint. The triangular ligament that normally tethers the lateral bands dorsally becomes attenuated, allowing the lateral bands to subluxate volar to the joint axis. In this displaced position the lateral bands act as flexors of the proximal interphalangeal joint and hyperextensors of the distal interphalangeal joint, and progressive contracture fixes the posture. In rheumatoid arthritis the same imbalance is produced by synovitis-driven attenuation of the extensor mechanism. Early recognition and splinting give good results, whereas an established fixed deformity is difficult to correct and the outcomes of reconstructive surgery are less predictable.

patient Overlooking pneumobilia or an ectopic stone on imaging Undertaking extensive combined stone and fistula surgery in a frail patient when simple stone extraction would suffice Attributing the presentation to malignancy or peptic disease and delaying appropriate treatment Recurrent gallbladder inflammation causes the gallbladder to adhere to and then erode into the adjacent duodenum or stomach, creating a cholecystoduodenal or cholecystogastric fistula. A large gallstone passes through this fistula directly into the proximal gastrointestinal tract and becomes impacted at the pylorus or duodenum, where the lumen is relatively narrow, producing gastric outlet obstruction. Because the stone lodges proximally rather than at the ileocaecal valve, the clinical picture is one of upper rather than lower gastrointestinal obstruction. The fistula also allows air to reflux into the biliary tree, giving the pneumobilia seen on imaging. Prognosis is reasonable once the obstruction is relieved, but mortality is not negligible given the typically elderly, comorbid population, so a minimally invasive, staged approach that prioritises relieving the obstruction is often favoured.

Assessment for bacterial overgrowth Presents with recurrent crops of small erythematous macules that evolve into papules, vesiculopustules and purpuric lesions, typically on the upper trunk and proximal limbs The eruption is accompanied by a non-deforming, often migratory polyarthralgia or arthritis and frequently by fever and malaise It was first described after jejunoileal bypass surgery for obesity but also occurs with inflammatory bowel disease and other conditions causing a blind loop or bacterial overgrowth The syndrome can arise without any bowel surgery ('bowel bypass syndrome without bowel bypass') Episodes are recurrent and self-limited, lasting days at a time, and belong to the neutrophilic dermatoses Biopsy shows a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate resembling early Sweet syndrome, sometimes with leucocytoclasis Management addresses the underlying bowel abnormality, for example antibiotics for bacterial overgrowth or surgical revision of a bypassed segment Features suggesting septic arthritis or disseminated gonococcal infection requiring urgent exclusion Systemic sepsis in a patient with a blind bowel loop Progressive or destructive joint disease Underlying inflammatory bowel disease with complications Mistaking the eruption and arthritis for a septic process and missing the bowel-related cause Failing to look for bacterial overgrowth or a bypassed loop in a patient without prior surgery Treating flares symptomatically while ignoring the underlying gut abnormality Confusing it with Sweet syndrome without considering the bowel association Bowel-associated dermatosis-arthritis syndrome is thought to arise from bacterial overgrowth within a bypassed, diverticular or diseased segment of bowel. Bacterial antigens, particularly peptidoglycan components, stimulate formation of circulating immune complexes that deposit in the skin and synovium, triggering a neutrophil-rich inflammatory response. This immune-complex-mediated, cross-reactive process produces the recurrent neutrophilic dermatosis and the accompanying arthralgia. The link to intestinal bacterial overgrowth explains why the syndrome responds to measures that reduce the bacterial burden. Individual episodes are self-limited, but without correction of the underlying bowel problem the syndrome tends to recur; treating the intestinal cause, whether by antibiotics or surgical revision, generally controls the disease and carries a good outlook.

Bowel obstruction — Erect/supine abdominal X-ray or CT NG decompression Surgical review Strangulation / perforation → emergency surgery Adynamic / paralytic ileus (loss of peristalsis with absent bowel sounds) rather than mechanical obstruction Colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome) — colonic dilatation without a mechanical lesion Severe constipation / fecal impaction causing abdominal distension and discomfort Sigmoid or cecal volvulus as a cause of colonic obstruction Gastric outlet obstruction (malignancy or chronic peptic stenosis of the pylorus) presenting with vomiting of partially digested food hours after eating Esophageal obstruction by impacted food bolus / foreign body (proximal obstruction mimic) Low-dose CT is preferred over plain abdominal radiography when the indication for surgical/medical intervention is unclear in nontraumatic acute abdominal pain Plain upright/lateral-decubitus abdominal radiographs can show dilated bowel loops suggesting obstruction or ileus, but have limited utility and may be unnecessary when the cause (e.g., strangulated external hernia) is already evident Water-soluble contrast enema can be diagnostic in suspected colonic obstruction without perforation; oral barium sulfate should be avoided if colonic obstruction is suspected Serum amylase may be raised by strangulating intestinal obstruction (also by perforated ulcer, cholecystitis), so an elevation neither confirms nor excludes the need for operation Leukocytosis is non-specific (a WBC >20,000/uL may follow perforation but also pancreatitis, cholecystitis, infarction) and should never be the sole determinant of operative need; a normal count does not exclude perforation Endoscopy can diagnose and often manage gastroduodenal and colonic obstruction/pseudo-obstruction, but small-bowel obstruction from surgical adhesions is generally neither diagnosed nor treated endoscopically Acute mesenteric arterial occlusion — early diffuse cramping pain from hyperperistalsis with 'pain out of proportion to physical findings' can mimic early obstruction; tenderness and rigidity may be absent until vascular collapse Porphyria and lead colic — severe hyperperistalsis makes the pain difficult to distinguish from intestinal obstruction Diabetic ketoacidosis — can both precipitate and mimic an acute abdomen; if pain does not resolve with metabolic correction, suspect an organic cause such as obstruction Irritable bowel syndrome — functional pain with altered bowel habit, but nausea/vomiting are rare and localized tenderness/spasm inconsistent (a non-obstructive mimic of altered bowel habit) Small-bowel obstruction characteristically produces poorly localized, intermittent peri-/supra-umbilical colicky pain; as the bowel progressively dilates and loses muscular tone the colicky quality of the pain may actually diminish, which can be falsely reassuring (p.110). Colonic obstruction tends to cause lower-intensity colicky pain located in the infraumbilical area, often radiating to the lumbar region, in contrast to the more periumbilical pain of small-bowel obstruction (p.110). High-pitched, hyperactive bowel sounds are characteristic of mechanical obstruction, whereas loss of bowel sounds points toward ileus; however, once proximal bowel becomes markedly distended and edematous, peristaltic sounds may become weak or absent even without peritonitis. Auscultation is one of the least revealing parts of the abdominal exam: a strangulating small-intestinal obstruction can occur with normal-sounding peristalsis, so normal bowel sounds do not exclude a catastrophe (p.113). Patients with obstructive colic tend to be restless and may thrash about, in contrast to the peritonitic patient who lies still to avoid movement — a useful bedside discriminator when ischaemia/perforation supervenes (p.110). Inability to pass stool or flatus combined with nausea/vomiting and increasing abdominal girth suggests bowel obstruction (or severe constipation/ileus); retained feces in the colon itself adds to the distension (p.327). Continuous diffuse pain with absent tenderness/rigidity ('pain out of proportion to findings') in a patient at vascular risk — suspect superior mesenteric artery occlusion / intestinal ischaemia Spread of pain to the lower lumbar region — may indicate strangulating obstruction with traction on the mesenteric root Truly silent abdomen with sudden severe pain — suggests chemical peritonitis from a perforated viscus Catastrophic intra-abdominal events may present with minimal or no pain/muscle spasm in obtunded, debilitated, immunosuppressed, or elderly patients — a slowly developing process also attenuates guarding Relying on auscultation or bowel-sound quality: strangulating obstruction can occur with normal peristaltic sounds, and distended/edematous proximal bowel may be quiet even without peritonitis (p.113). Interpreting waning colicky pain as improvement — pain may diminish simply because the dilated bowel has lost muscular tone (p.110). Using leukocytosis or serum amylase as a deciding factor for surgery — both are non-specific in obstruction and infarction (p.113). Giving oral barium when colonic obstruction is possible (risk of inspissation above the obstruction); use water-soluble contrast instead. Missing intestinal ischaemia, which classically elicits severe pain but little tenderness (GI evaluation chapter). Mechanical obstruction of a hollow viscus classically elicits intermittent (colicky) pain that is less well localized than the parietal pain of peritoneal irritation; distension of the viscus may also produce steady pain with only occasional paroxysms. With superimposed strangulating obstruction, traction on the root of the mesentery can refer pain to the lower lumbar region. As the obstructed proximal bowel progressively dilates it loses muscular tone, so colicky pain may wane and peristaltic sounds may weaken. Obstruction must be distinguished from adynamic ileus (loss of peristalsis) and from colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome), in which the bowel is dilated without a mechanical lesion (Harrison 22e pp.110-113, p.327).

Box jellyfish (Chironex) envenomation — Chironex fleckeri sting, sea wasp sting, box jellyfish sting, cubozoan envenomation, marine stinger sting Irukandji syndrome from other cubozoans Other jellyfish or marine stings Primary cardiac arrest or arrhythmia from another cause Anaphylaxis to a marine allergen Drowning or immersion-related collapse Sea snake or stonefish envenomation Continuous cardiac monitoring and electrocardiography for arrhythmia and ischaemia Cardiac troponin and echocardiography if myocardial injury is suspected Full blood count and haemolysis markers Electrolytes, particularly potassium, and renal function Assessment of the extent of tentacle contact/skin involvement to gauge severity Chironex fleckeri causes immediate excruciating pain with characteristic whip-like, ladder-pattern skin markings from tentacle contact Life-threatening envenomation can cause rapid cardiovascular collapse and cardiac arrest within minutes of a large sting, sometimes before other features develop Extensive tentacle contact (roughly the surface area covering a large proportion of a child's body) is associated with the highest risk of fatal outcome First aid principles are to remove the patient from the water, douse adherent tentacles with vinegar (acetic acid) to inhibit undischarged nematocysts, and begin resuscitation as needed Box jellyfish antivenom exists and may be given for severe envenomation, though its efficacy in arrest is debated and resuscitation takes priority Do not rinse with fresh water or rub the area, as this can trigger further nematocyst discharge Prolonged resuscitation may be warranted given the potential for reversible venom-mediated cardiac toxicity Cardiac arrest or peri-arrest state after a large sting Extensive tentacle contact, especially in a child Arrhythmia, hypotension or evidence of myocardial injury Respiratory distress or altered consciousness Rapid clinical deterioration within minutes of the sting Rinsing with fresh water or rubbing the sting, provoking further nematocyst discharge Delaying or abandoning resuscitation prematurely despite the potential reversibility of venom cardiotoxicity Focusing on antivenom before ensuring effective basic and advanced life support Underestimating a large sting in a child given the surface-area risk relationship Box jellyfish deliver venom through nematocysts on their tentacles that inject rapidly on contact. The venom contains porins that form pores in cell membranes, causing potassium leakage and rise in intracellular calcium in cardiomyocytes and red cells. This produces near-instant cardiotoxicity with catastrophic cardiovascular collapse, arrhythmia and cardiac arrest, alongside intense dermal pain and potential skin necrosis. Systemic effects can include hypertension followed by cardiovascular failure; the speed of cardiac toxicity distinguishes Chironex from most other marine stings. Minor stings cause severe pain and skin marks that heal, sometimes with scarring. Major envenomation can be rapidly fatal from cardiac arrest, but prompt resuscitation, vinegar decontamination and antivenom offer the best chance of survival, and full recovery is possible if circulation is restored.

Boxer fracture (fifth metacarpal neck) — fifth metacarpal neck fracture, brawler fracture, puncher fracture Fifth metacarpal shaft fracture Metacarpal head fracture Carpometacarpal fracture-dislocation of the little finger Base of metacarpal fracture Fight-bite injury with metacarpophalangeal joint involvement Hamate fracture Anteroposterior, lateral and oblique hand radiographs Measurement of the degree of neck angulation on the lateral view Clinical assessment of rotational alignment via the finger cascade during flexion Careful wound inspection for a fight-bite breach of the metacarpophalangeal joint CT reserved for suspected intra-articular extension A fracture of the neck of the fifth metacarpal, usually caused by striking a hard object with a clenched fist There is characteristic apex-dorsal angulation with volar tilt of the metacarpal head; considerable angulation is tolerated here because of the mobility of the fifth carpometacarpal joint Rotational malalignment, detected as scissoring or overlap of the fingers on flexion, is not tolerated and must be assessed and corrected Always inspect for an overlying wound suggesting a fight bite (tooth injury), which carries a serious risk of joint infection Most fractures are managed conservatively with buddy strapping or an ulnar gutter splint and early mobilisation Markedly angulated, rotated or multiple fractures may require closed reduction and immobilisation or fixation Pseudoclawing on attempted extension indicates significant angulation requiring correction Rotational deformity with scissoring of the fingers An open wound over the metacarpophalangeal joint (fight bite) with infection risk Excessive angulation causing pseudoclawing or functional deficit Signs of established joint or hand infection Missing malrotation because the sagittal angulation appears acceptable Overlooking a fight-bite wound and subsequent joint sepsis Over-treating minor angulation that would remodel or be well tolerated Failing to check active flexion for finger scissoring An axial force transmitted along the fifth metacarpal during a punch concentrates stress at the metaphyseal neck. The thin dorsal cortex fails in tension while the volar cortex is compressed, producing apex-dorsal angulation, and the pull of the intrinsic muscles further flexes the distal fragment volarly. The generous mobility of the fifth carpometacarpal joint compensates for residual angulation in the sagittal plane, so functional loss is usually minor unless there is malrotation, which foreshortens and crosses the affected finger over its neighbours during flexion. Most fractures heal well with good function even with moderate residual angulation because of the mobility of the fifth carpometacarpal joint; rotational malunion and an untreated fight-bite infection are the principal causes of a poor outcome.

Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo — BPPV, positional vertigo, benign positional vertigo Vestibular neuritis Meniere's disease Central positional vertigo from posterior fossa pathology Vestibular migraine Orthostatic hypotension Perilymph fistula Dix-Hallpike test for posterior canal involvement Supine roll (head-turn) test for suspected horizontal canal disease Otoscopy and hearing assessment to exclude other otological causes Neurological examination to exclude central causes Imaging of the brain and posterior fossa only if central pathology is suspected The most common cause of peripheral vertigo, characterised by brief spinning episodes triggered by changes in head position Typical triggers include rolling over in bed, lying down, looking up or bending forward Each episode is short-lived, usually lasting seconds to under a minute, and there is no associated hearing loss or tinnitus The posterior semicircular canal is most often involved because of its dependent position The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces symptoms and elicits characteristic positional nystagmus with a brief latency and fatigability Management principles rely on canalith repositioning manoeuvres such as the Epley manoeuvre rather than long-term drug therapy Vestibular sedatives are generally unhelpful and may hinder central compensation if used long term Recurrences are common but usually respond again to repositioning; atypical or persistent features should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis Atypical nystagmus that is purely vertical, direction-changing or non-fatiguing suggesting a central cause Associated neurological signs, severe headache or gait ataxia Accompanying hearing loss or tinnitus pointing to alternative inner ear disease Persistent continuous vertigo rather than brief positional episodes Mistaking central positional vertigo for BPPV and missing serious pathology Relying on vestibular suppressant drugs instead of repositioning manoeuvres Failing to identify the affected canal, leading to ineffective treatment Overlooking coexisting hearing loss that indicates a different diagnosis Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is caused by displacement of otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) from the utricular macula into a semicircular canal, most often the posterior canal. In the common canalithiasis form, these free-floating particles move under gravity when the head changes position, creating abnormal endolymph flow that deflects the cupula and generates a transient, mismatched sensation of rotation. The brief latency, short duration and fatigability of symptoms reflect the settling of the particles. A less common cupulolithiasis form, with particles adherent to the cupula, produces more persistent positional nystagmus. The condition is benign and often self-limiting, with excellent response to repositioning manoeuvres, although recurrences over time are common and occasionally require repeat treatment.

Brachial neuritis — neuralgic amyotrophy, Parsonage-Turner syndrome, idiopathic brachial plexopathy, acute brachial plexus neuropathy Cervical radiculopathy from disc or spondylosis Rotator cuff disease or other primary shoulder pathology Compressive or traumatic brachial plexopathy Neoplastic or radiation-induced plexopathy Thoracic outlet syndrome Mononeuritis multiplex from vasculitis Electromyography and nerve conduction studies to confirm multifocal, mainly axonal involvement MRI of the brachial plexus or high-resolution nerve ultrasound to identify constrictions and exclude structural lesions Cervical spine MRI when radiculopathy is a competing diagnosis Basic inflammatory and infective screen when a systemic cause is suspected Consideration of genetic testing (SEPT9) in recurrent or familial cases Characterised by abrupt, severe pain around the shoulder and upper arm, followed within days to weeks by patchy weakness and wasting as the pain subsides The distribution is often patchy and does not conform to a single nerve or root, reflecting involvement of individual nerves or plexus branches The long thoracic nerve is frequently affected, producing scapular winging, and the anterior interosseous and suprascapular nerves are also commonly involved Often follows an antecedent trigger such as infection, immunisation, surgery, or physical stress Sensory symptoms are usually less prominent than the motor deficit and the early pain A hereditary recurrent form exists (linked to SEPT9), so a family history and recurrent episodes should be explored Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by electromyography showing multifocal denervation, with imaging used to exclude structural or compressive lesions Management is mainly supportive with analgesia and physiotherapy, as most patients recover over months Progressive or non-resolving deficit suggesting a compressive, neoplastic, or infiltrative plexopathy A history of cancer or radiotherapy raising concern for malignant or radiation plexopathy Bilateral or systemic features suggesting an alternative diagnosis such as vasculitis Rapidly worsening weakness that warrants urgent structural imaging Mistaking the initial severe pain for a primary shoulder or rotator cuff problem and delaying diagnosis Confusing it with cervical radiculopathy because both cause arm pain and weakness Overlooking scapular winging from long thoracic nerve involvement Failing to consider a hereditary recurrent form in patients with repeated attacks Assuming a compressive lesion and pursuing unnecessary surgery in a self-limiting inflammatory condition Brachial neuritis (neuralgic amyotrophy) is thought to be an immune-mediated inflammatory disorder of the brachial plexus and its branches, often triggered by antecedent infection, vaccination, surgery, or other immunological stressors. Inflammation causes multifocal axonal damage to individual nerves or fascicles, sometimes with focal nerve constrictions or torsions demonstrable on high-resolution imaging. The predominantly axonal injury explains the muscle wasting and the protracted recovery as reinnervation occurs. A hereditary form associated with SEPT9 mutations produces recurrent attacks. Most patients recover useful function over many months to a few years, though recovery can be incomplete with residual weakness or scapular winging, and the hereditary form tends to recur.

Brachioradial pruritus — BRP, brachioradial summer pruritus, solar pruritus of the elbows Notalgia paraesthetica and other neuropathic localised pruritus Cervical radiculopathy or spinal cord pathology presenting with itch Polymorphic light eruption Atopic or contact dermatitis of the forearms Prurigo nodularis Photoallergic or drug-induced photosensitivity History elicting the ice-pack sign, summer predominance and forearm localisation Neurological examination and assessment for cervical spine disease Imaging of the cervical spine (radiography or magnetic resonance imaging) where radiculopathy is suspected Phototesting only if a primary photodermatosis is being considered Skin biopsy in atypical cases, which is usually non-specific Review of the pattern to exclude a systemic cause of generalised pruritus A localised neuropathic itch, often with burning or stinging, affecting the dorsolateral forearms over the brachioradialis region, which may extend to the upper arms and shoulders It is typically bilateral, though often asymmetrical, and characteristically worse in summer and in fair-skinned people with substantial sun exposure The 'ice-pack sign' is highly characteristic: patients gain relief from applying something cold rather than from scratching, which distinguishes it from most other pruritic conditions There is a recognised association with cervical spine disease such as degenerative change or nerve-root compression, and the affected dermatomes often correspond to lower cervical levels The interplay of chronic ultraviolet exposure and underlying cervical nerve pathology is thought to sensitise cutaneous nerves and produce the itch The skin may look normal or show only secondary excoriation and lichenification from rubbing Management combines photoprotection with neuropathic-itch measures and, where relevant, assessment and treatment of cervical spine pathology Neurological deficit, limb weakness or sensory loss suggesting significant cervical cord or nerve-root compression Rapidly progressive or unilateral symptoms warranting spinal imaging Features of an inflammatory dermatosis or systemic pruritus that do not fit a neuropathic pattern Intractable itch with severe secondary skin damage Treating it as an inflammatory dermatitis with topical steroids alone, which are generally ineffective for neuropathic itch Overlooking the ice-pack sign, which is a valuable diagnostic clue Failing to consider and investigate underlying cervical spine disease Not advising photoprotection despite the clear relationship with sun exposure Brachioradial pruritus is understood as a neuropathic itch arising from dysfunction of cutaneous sensory nerves, in which chronic ultraviolet-induced damage to nerve endings acts together with proximal cervical nerve-root irritation from degenerative spine disease to lower the threshold for itch signalling. The characteristic relief from cold and the frequent correspondence of symptoms to cervical dermatomes support a neurogenic rather than a primary inflammatory mechanism. The summer predominance reflects the contribution of accumulated sun exposure to peripheral nerve sensitisation. Brachioradial pruritus tends to be chronic and relapsing with a seasonal, sun-related pattern, but symptoms are often controllable with photoprotection, cold application and neuropathic-itch therapy; addressing any underlying cervical spine pathology can improve outcomes, though complete resolution is variable.

HV interval for His-Purkinje ≤55 ms) reserved for selected/uncertain cases; SNRT/SACT rarely used and NOT an absolute pacing indication Drug/medication effect (beta blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, digoxin, amiodarone and other antiarrhythmics, clonidine, lithium, etc.) Hypothyroidism and other endocrine disease Hyperkalemia/electrolyte disturbance Increased vagal tone (sleep, well-conditioned athlete, cough/micturition/vasovagal, carotid sinus hypersensitivity) Sleep apnea (high vagal tone during apneic events) Hypothermia, hypoxia, raised intracranial pressure Infiltrative cardiomyopathy (sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, hemochromatosis) Neuromuscular disease (myotonic dystrophy, Kearns-Sayre, Lamin A/C cardiomyopathy) Iatrogenic: cardiac/valve surgery, TAVR, alcohol septal ablation, catheter ablation injury, spinal cord injury, post heart transplant Sinus node dysfunction (SND), also termed sick sinus syndrome, typically presents with fatigue, exercise intolerance, dyspnea, or syncope from a slow rate or pauses; the key diagnostic step is correlating symptoms with bradycardia/pauses on ECG or ambulatory monitoring (p.1917-1918). Tachycardia-bradycardia (tachy-brady) syndrome is a subset of SND: high rates (most commonly atrial fibrillation) alternating with symptomatic bradycardia or offset pauses after the tachycardia terminates; the drugs needed for rate control often worsen the bradycardia, frequently prompting pacemaker implantation (p.1919). AV block is classified on ECG: first-degree = fixed PR prolongation >200 ms with all impulses conducted; second-degree = intermittent failure of conduction (Mobitz I/Wenckebach with progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat vs Mobitz II with fixed PR before a dropped beat); third-degree = complete AV dissociation with ventricular rate slower than atrial rate (p.1925-1926). Mobitz I (Wenckebach) AV block typically involves the AV node, is hemodynamically stable, and in the absence of symptoms does NOT usually warrant pacing; Mobitz II is usually infranodal, associated with QRS widening and a less reliable escape rhythm, carries a risk of sudden death, and requires permanent pacing even when asymptomatic (p.1925). Escape morphology localizes block: a narrow QRS escape implies AV-nodal/proximal-His block with a faster, more stable junctional rhythm, whereas a wide QRS escape implies distal His or bundle-branch block with a slower, less reliable rhythm (p.1926). AV block from acute MI is more common with inferior MI but is usually proximal (AV node), with a stable narrow escape >40/min and often reversible; AV block in anterior MI is usually distal/infranodal, gives wide unstable escape rhythms, and carries a worse prognosis with high mortality (p.1926-1927). Lyme carditis is a classic reversible infectious cause of AV block (usually nodal, narrow junctional escape >40/min) that typically resolves within about a week of antibiotic therapy; AV block with infective endocarditis should raise concern for a perivalvular abscess requiring urgent surgical consultation (p.1927). AV block that develops at a younger age (≤60 years) warrants advanced imaging (cardiac MRI, CT, or FDG-PET) to evaluate for infiltrative disease such as sarcoidosis, since age-related progressive conduction-system fibrosis is otherwise the most common cause (p.1928). Permanent pacing is the only reliable long-term therapy for symptomatic irreversible bradycardia; there is NO established heart-rate threshold below which pacing is automatically indicated, and the decision is driven by symptom-bradycardia correlation (p.1917, p.1922). Initial management of any bradyarrhythmia is to identify and eliminate reversible causes and assess the safety/reliability of the escape rhythm before deciding on temporary or permanent pacing (p.1922, p.1929). Missing reversible causes (drugs, hypothyroidism, hyperkalemia/electrolytes, ischemia, sleep apnea, increased vagal tone, hypothermia, raised ICP) before committing to permanent pacing. Overlooking Lyme carditis as a reversible cause of AV block (typically resolves within ~1 week of antibiotics) - a treatable cause that should not lead to an unnecessary permanent pacemaker. Failing to suspect a perivalvular abscess when AV block develops during infective endocarditis. In 2:1 AV block, ECG cannot reliably distinguish Mobitz I from Mobitz II; clues (PR <160 ms with wide QRS suggesting infranodal) or EP study may be needed. Missing chronotropic incompetence because a patient achieves a normal maximum heart rate on standard exercise testing despite inadequate rate during daily activity. Misjudging a normal heart-transplant resting rate (~90-110/min due to denervation) as normal when it may represent chronotropic incompetence. Bradyarrhythmias arise from abnormalities of the specialized conduction tissues. The sinoatrial (SA) node is the natural pacemaker (resting rate 60-100/min); its pacemaker cells have no true resting potential and depolarize spontaneously in phase 4 driven by the funny current (If) plus T- and L-type calcium currents, with calcium (not sodium) carrying the slow phase-0 upstroke. SA node function is dominated by parasympathetic tone at baseline (intrinsic heart rate ~100-110/min after autonomic blockade); intrinsic rate declines ~5-6 beats/min per decade of age. SA node dysfunction reflects problems of impulse formation (sinus arrest) or impulse conduction (sinoatrial exit block), and is most often due to age-related fibrosis and loss of pacemaker myocytes. In the AV node, conduction is decremental and depends on L-type calcium current; the node and proximal His are richly innervated by autonomic input, whereas the His bundle and distal conduction system are NOT influenced by autonomic tone. Acquired AV conduction disease is most commonly due to fibrosis/sclerosis/calcification of the conduction system (~50% of cases: senile degeneration/Lev's disease, Lenegre's disease, aortic-annular calcification). Block is anatomically nodal (vagally modulated, stable narrow escape) or infranodal (His-Purkinje, unstable wide escape, higher risk). Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia has NOT been associated with adverse outcomes and generally does not warrant pacing; symptomatic SND is benign in terms of mortality and is treated to relieve symptoms. AV block prognosis depends critically on the level of block: AV-nodal (Mobitz I) block tends to be stable with a reliable junctional escape and good prognosis, whereas infranodal block (Mobitz II, distal third-degree) has unreliable escape rhythms and risk of sudden death. AV block complicating anterior MI carries high mortality, while inferior-MI nodal block is often transient and reversible. With appropriate permanent pacing, symptomatic bradyarrhythmias have an excellent prognosis. An HV interval >100 ms predicts ~10% annual progression to complete block. ECG-based AV block grading: First-degree (PR >200 ms, all impulses conducted, usually AV-nodal delay) -> Second-degree (intermittent failure; Mobitz I/Wenckebach = progressive PR prolongation before dropped beat, usually nodal/stable; Mobitz II = fixed PR before dropped beat, usually infranodal/wide QRS/unstable) -> Third-degree/complete (complete AV dissociation, ventricular rate slower than atrial). SND subtypes: sinus arrest, sinoatrial exit block (type I, type II Mobitz I/II), tachy-brady syndrome, chronotropic incompetence. Pacing-indication classes (ACC/AHA/HRS): Class I (complete/high-grade or acquired Mobitz II block when irreversible - pace regardless of symptoms; symptomatic irreversible 2nd/3rd-degree block), Class IIa/IIb (symptom- or disease-dependent for milder block), Class III: Harm (asymptomatic physiologic bradycardia/pauses).

many patients have both (p.716). The classic morning-predominant headache that eases through the day occurs in only a minority of patients; brain-tumour headache is more often a nondescript dull ache, and migraine produces this pattern far more often than tumour (p.716, p.157). Vomiting preceding headache by weeks is highly characteristic of posterior fossa tumours, and headache disturbs sleep in about 10% (p.157). Seizures from a brain tumour always have a focal onset whether or not this is clinically apparent (p.716). On MRI, malignant tumours (primary or metastatic) typically enhance with gadolinium, have central necrosis and surrounding white-matter edema, whereas low-grade gliomas usually do NOT enhance and are best seen as increased signal on FLAIR (p.716).
