Leptomeningeal disease produces multilevel neuraxis signs (radiculopathies, cranial neuropathies, seizures, confusion, raised-ICP encephalopathy); isolated focal deficits like hemiparesis are rarely from it unless brain is directly infiltrated (p.724). Parinaud's syndrome (impaired upgaze and accommodation) points to a pineal-region mass (p.720). Progressive, subacute focal/lateralizing deficit (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual field loss) (p.716) New-onset focal-onset seizures (p.716) Morning-predominant headache or headache with raised-ICP features (nausea/vomiting, worse with exertion or position change) (p.716, p.157) Vomiting preceding headache by weeks - suggests a posterior fossa mass (p.157) New de novo headache in a patient with known systemic cancer (p.157) Personality change/apathy that may be mistaken for depression (p.716) A ring-enhancing lesion is non-specific - the differential includes brain abscess, toxoplasmosis, PCNSL, demyelination, sarcoidosis, radiation necrosis and primary brain tumour, so do not assume tumour without context (p.721, p.723). Withholding the diagnosis of glioma can be hard for diffusely infiltrative non-enhancing tumours (formerly gliomatosis cerebri), which often present only with cognitive decline and confluent FLAIR signal without mass effect (p.718). Do not give glucocorticoids before biopsy in suspected PCNSL - their cytolytic effect can yield non-diagnostic tissue (p.720). Prophylactic antiepileptic drugs have no role in tumour patients who have not had a seizure (only perioperative use is sometimes appropriate) (p.716). Brain metastases spread hematogenously, lodging in terminal arterioles at the grey-white junction in watershed territory, so distribution follows blood flow (~85% supratentorial, ~15% posterior fossa) (p.723). Outcome is tumour-specific. Low-grade (grade 2) IDH-mutant astrocytoma usually transforms to higher grade with median survival around 10 years; high-grade IDH-mutant astrocytoma roughly 3-9 years (p.718). Oligodendrogliomas (IDH-mutant, 1p/19q co-deleted) are more therapy-responsive with median survival in excess of 10 years (p.718). Glioblastoma (IDH wild-type) is the most common malignant primary tumour and invariably recurs; with standard combined therapy median survival is ~15-18 months and 5-year survival ~10%; adverse factors include older age, unmethylated MGMT promoter, poor performance status and unresectable tumour (p.718-719). Pilocytic astrocytoma (grade 1) and completely resected meningiomas/ependymomas can be cured (p.719-721). WHO CNS grading (2021 integrated histologic + molecular classification): diffuse gliomas graded 2-4 by histologic malignancy and molecular markers, with CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion conferring grade 4 to otherwise lower-grade IDH-mutant astrocytomas; pilocytic astrocytoma is grade 1. that is apparent only on optical coherence tomography Failing to arrange ongoing review for late neovascular complications At an arteriovenous crossing the retinal artery and vein are enclosed within a shared adventitial sheath, so age-related arteriolar wall thickening compresses the underlying vein. The resulting turbulence and endothelial injury promote local thrombosis and venous outflow obstruction. Pressure rises in the venules and capillaries upstream of the block, producing haemorrhage, plasma leakage with macular oedema, and variable capillary non-perfusion within the drained sector. Injuring adjacent structures such as the great vessels or cranial nerves during dissection Branchial cleft anomalies result from failure of the branchial (pharyngeal) apparatus to fully regress during embryonic development. Persistent epithelial remnants of a cleft or pouch give rise to cysts, sinuses or fistulae in characteristic locations determined by the arch of origin. The second branchial cleft accounts for the majority; its tract, when complete, passes from the tonsillar fossa between the internal and external carotid arteries to the lower lateral neck. The main clinical hazard is misclassifying a malignant cystic metastasis as a benign branchial cyst, which delays cancer treatment.

antibiotics alone rarely cure a collection Breastfeeding or expression from the affected side should generally continue to relieve stasis in lactational cases A non-lactational or non-resolving abscess, particularly in an older woman, requires exclusion of inflammatory breast cancer and other malignancy Recurrent periareolar abscess with a mammary duct fistula may need duct excision once inflammation settles Non-resolving or recurrent inflammatory changes suggesting inflammatory breast cancer Overlying skin necrosis or spreading cellulitis with systemic sepsis Immunosuppression or diabetes with rapidly progressive infection A persistent mass after treatment requiring triple assessment Treating with antibiotics alone and failing to drain an established collection Missing inflammatory breast cancer masquerading as a non-resolving abscess Advising cessation of breastfeeding unnecessarily, worsening milk stasis Not addressing smoking in recurrent non-lactational disease A breast abscess is a localised collection of pus within breast tissue. In lactating women, milk stasis and nipple trauma allow skin organisms, chiefly Staphylococcus aureus, to enter and proliferate, progressing from mastitis to a walled-off abscess. In non-lactating women, periductal mastitis, strongly linked to smoking, causes duct damage, squamous metaplasia, and duct obstruction, with secondary infection by mixed aerobic and anaerobic organisms producing periareolar collections and sometimes a mammary duct fistula. Untreated collections enlarge, may point to the skin, and can cause tissue necrosis. Most breast abscesses resolve fully with timely drainage and appropriate antibiotics. Non-lactational and smoking-related disease is prone to recurrence and mammary duct fistula, and outcome improves with smoking cessation and, when indicated, duct excision.

Breast Cancer — breast carcinoma Inflammatory breast cancer is sometimes confused with mastitis or other breast infection (Harrison 22e p.638). Benign breast pathology such as atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia (raises risk about four- to fivefold) and lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS, raises risk 7- to 12-fold) (Harrison 22e p.633). Mastitis or other breast infection can be mimicked by inflammatory breast cancer, which presents with rapid onset of erythema, swelling, and tenderness of the breast; breast or skin biopsy is critical when breast inflammation fails to resolve after antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.638). Image-guided core biopsy for pathologic confirmation, tumor grade/morphology, and biomarker testing (ER, PR, HER2 protein, and potentially HER2 gene amplification) (Harrison 22e p.634). Diagnostic breast imaging: mammography, ultrasonography, and MRI if indicated; bilateral breast imaging because up to 3% have unsuspected contralateral disease (Harrison 22e p.634). Germline panel testing for breast cancer susceptibility mutations on DNA from peripheral blood or saliva after appropriate counseling (not recommended for the general population) (Harrison 22e p.633). For symptoms or findings of advanced disease (large tumor, skin changes, extensive adenopathy): CT and radionuclide bone scanning to look for overt metastatic disease, with biopsy of suspicious lesions to confirm metastatic disease (Harrison 22e p.635). Genomic transcriptional profiling assays for early-stage ER-positive disease (Oncotype Dx 21-gene, MammaPrint 70-gene, ProSigna 50-gene, EndoPredict 12-gene, Breast Cancer Index) to inform adjuvant chemotherapy decisions; ordering more than one per case is discouraged (Harrison 22e p.636). Skin biopsy showing dermal lymphatic invasion with tumor cells supports diagnosis of inflammatory breast cancer (Harrison 22e p.638). Evolving changes in the pregnant breast can make diagnosis of breast cancer during pregnancy difficult, so suspicious lumps or skin or nipple changes still require formal evaluation (Harrison 22e p.638). Most common nonskin cancer in women worldwide; predominantly a disease of prolonged estrogen exposure, with female gender and increasing age the most common risk factors (about 70% diagnosed at 55 years or older, median age 63) (Harrison 22e p.632). Clinical signs and symptoms suggestive of breast cancer may include a breast lump, skin or nipple changes, or palpable regional nodes; with mammographic screening many patients are asymptomatic and present only with an imaging abnormality (mass, distortion, or suspicious microcalcifications) (Harrison 22e p.634). Diagnosis rests on pathologic confirmation, generally by image-guided core biopsy, which also assesses tumor grade and morphology and performs biomarker evaluation for estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and HER2 protein expression and potentially HER2 gene amplification (the triple assessment of clinical/imaging/pathology with biomarkers) (Harrison 22e p.634). Suspicious axillary nodes should be biopsied via image-guided techniques, and both breasts should be imaged because up to 3% of women with newly diagnosed breast cancer have unsuspected contralateral disease (Harrison 22e p.634). Invasive breast cancer is divided into at least four molecular subtypes: luminal A and luminal B (both ER positive; luminal B has reduced PR or higher Ki67 proliferation and worse outcome), HER2 subtype (high HER2 expression, benefits from HER2-targeted therapy), and basal/triple-negative (TNBC, lacking ER, PR, and HER2) (Harrison 22e p.636). Most invasive breast cancers are ductal; about 10-15% are lobular, which are usually ER positive and HER2 negative, distinguished by absence of E-cadherin, and have a propensity to spread to serosal surfaces (omentum, pleura, meninges) and parenchyma (ovaries, GI tract) (Harrison 22e p.636). Family history is a critical risk factor, yet only 20% of women diagnosed with breast cancer have a family history; a first-degree relative with breast cancer doubles the risk (Harrison 22e p.633). Inflammatory breast cancer: rapid onset of erythema, swelling, and tenderness of the breast (a subset of locally advanced disease); breast inflammation failing to resolve after antibiotics warrants breast or skin biopsy, and up to one-third have detectable metastasis at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.638). Any unexplained mass or lesion palpable on physical examination needs further assessment including biopsy where warranted; a normal mammogram does NOT rule out cancer in a woman with a palpable breast lump (Harrison 22e p.45). Locally advanced features: large primary tumor, involvement of skin or chest wall, or fixed tumor or axillary nodes (Harrison 22e p.638). A common disease-specific diagnostic pitfall is ordering a mammogram for a woman with a palpable breast lump and, when it returns normal, reassuring her that cancer has been ruled out; any unexplained palpable mass needs further testing and biopsy where warranted (Harrison 22e p.45). Lobular cancers can recur at unusual sites (serosal surfaces, ovaries, GI tract), producing atypical presentations that may delay diagnosis if metastatic disease is not considered (Harrison 22e p.636). Up to 3% of newly diagnosed patients have unsuspected contralateral disease, so both breasts must be imaged (Harrison 22e p.634). Inflammatory breast cancer may be mistaken for mastitis or infection; biopsy is critical when inflammation fails to resolve after antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.638). Germline panel testing can yield variants of unknown significance (VUS) and includes genes with poorly defined clinical risk, causing patient confusion and discomfort (Harrison 22e p.633). Breast cancer is predominantly a disease resulting from prolonged exposure of the breast to estrogen. Most breast cancers begin in epithelial cells within the lobules or ducts and proceed through a conceptual continuum of atypia and hyperplasia to in situ malignancy, then invasion into surrounding tissue, intravasation into lymph and blood channels, spread to regional lymph nodes, and distant metastases (though not all cancers progress through every stage). Hereditary breast cancer susceptibility genes account for 5-10% of cases; these genes participate in DNA damage repair, and inherited autosomal dominant mutations generally cause protein truncation and loss of function of DNA repair proteins. The most common are BRCA1 (chromosome 17q21) and BRCA2 (chromosome 13q12), conferring a 50-80% lifetime risk of invasive breast cancer by age 80 and a 30% risk of ovarian cancer; other germline mutations include TP53 (Li-Fraumeni), PALB2, ATM, STK11 (Peutz-Jeghers), and PTEN (Cowden). Ashkenazi Jews have a higher BRCA mutation incidence (Harrison 22e p.632-633). 5-year relative survival in the United States is currently about 91%. Outcomes are directly related to stage at presentation (and vary by race/ethnicity): 5-year relative survival is over 99% for stage I, about 93% for stage II, about 75% for stage III, and about 29% for stage IV. Less than 10% present with de novo metastatic (M1) disease. Luminal B tumors carry a poorer outcome than luminal A; TNBC carries a poorer prognosis; mucinous and pure medullary cancers have very favorable prognoses with local therapy only; higher Nottingham grade is associated with poorer prognosis. About 20-25% of patients treated for early breast cancer subsequently develop metastatic disease (Harrison 22e p.635-638). Staging follows the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) eighth edition TNM (tumor-node-metastasis) system, which has evolved to incorporate molecular biomarkers (ER, PR, HER2) and certain genomic tests (e.g., Oncotype 21-gene assay). Conceptually, stages I and II are early-stage disease confined to breast and ipsilateral nodes; stage III is locally advanced disease; and stage IV (M1) is metastatic disease. Staging may be clinical (c), pathologic after surgery (p), or post-neoadjuvant (y prefix). Common metastatic sites are soft tissues, lung, bone, liver, and brain (Harrison 22e p.634-635).

Breast cyst — Simple breast cyst, Gross cyst Fibroadenoma Galactocoele in a lactating woman Intracystic papilloma Intracystic (encysted) papillary carcinoma Fibrocystic change with prominent cysts Abscess or inflammatory collection Well-circumscribed invasive carcinoma Breast ultrasound with cyst characterisation Mammography in the appropriate age group as part of triple assessment Diagnostic or therapeutic needle aspiration of tense or symptomatic cysts Cytology of aspirate only when blood-stained Image-guided core biopsy of any solid or complex component Post-aspiration ultrasound to confirm resolution Pneumocystography in selected recurrent cysts (historical) Fluid-filled, epithelial-lined cavities that are among the commonest causes of a discrete breast lump in perimenopausal women aged roughly 35 to 50. Often present suddenly as a smooth, mobile, sometimes tender lump; multiple and bilateral cysts are frequent. Regarded as an aberration of normal breast involution within the ANDI framework rather than a disease. Ultrasound classification into simple, complicated and complex cysts guides management and determines the need for intervention. A simple anechoic cyst with imperceptible walls and posterior enhancement is benign and needs no aspiration unless symptomatic. Aspiration is indicated for painful or tense cysts; clear or green-brown fluid can be discarded without cytology. Blood-stained aspirate, a residual mass after aspiration, or rapid refilling should prompt imaging and biopsy to exclude an intracystic carcinoma or papilloma. Complex cysts with thick septa, mural nodules or solid components require image-guided core biopsy. Blood-stained cyst aspirate Persistent palpable or sonographic mass after complete aspiration Rapid symptomatic refilling of an aspirated cyst Mural nodule or thick irregular septa on ultrasound Associated skin tethering, nipple change or suspicious microcalcification Sending clear cyst fluid for cytology, which is low-yield and unnecessary Failing to re-examine and image after aspiration to exclude a residual mass Dismissing a complex cyst as simple and missing an intracystic carcinoma Attributing a blood-stained aspirate to a traumatic tap and delaying biopsy Overlooking that hormone replacement therapy can drive cyst formation after the menopause Breast cysts arise from the terminal duct lobular unit during the involutional phase of breast development, when lobular stroma regresses faster than its epithelium, leaving distended acini that coalesce into macroscopic fluid-filled spaces. The lining may be flattened atrophic epithelium or show apocrine metaplasia, the latter associated with cysts that secrete potassium-rich fluid and tend to recur. Hormonal fluctuation influences cyst formation, explaining their peak incidence in the perimenopausal years and regression after the menopause unless hormone replacement therapy is used. Simple cysts are benign with an excellent prognosis and only a marginal, if any, increase in future breast cancer risk. Recurrence after aspiration is common, but reassurance and symptom-directed management are usually sufficient.

Breast fibroadenoma — fibroadenoma, breast mouse, FAD, benign breast fibroadenoma Phyllodes tumour Breast cyst Fibrocystic change Breast carcinoma (particularly in older patients) Hamartoma of the breast Lipoma or other benign stromal lesion Breast ultrasound as first-line imaging in younger women Mammography in older patients or where imaging is indeterminate Core needle biopsy for histological confirmation and to exclude phyllodes tumour or malignancy Fine-needle aspiration cytology in selected settings as part of triple assessment Clinical follow-up imaging for lesions managed conservatively Fibroadenoma is the commonest benign solid breast lump in young women, typically presenting as a smooth, firm, well-defined, highly mobile mass, hence the nickname breast mouse It is usually painless and often discovered incidentally; multiple and bilateral lesions occur in a minority Assessment follows triple assessment: clinical examination, imaging (ultrasound in younger women, with mammography added in older patients), and needle biopsy where indicated Ultrasound characteristically shows a well-circumscribed, hypoechoic, oval lesion with a benign appearance Core biopsy is used to confirm the diagnosis and, importantly, to distinguish a fibroadenoma from a phyllodes tumour, which can behave more aggressively Many small, biopsy-proven fibroadenomas can be safely observed, as a proportion regress, while excision is offered for large, enlarging, symptomatic, or diagnostically uncertain lesions or patient preference A giant fibroadenoma or a rapidly enlarging lesion should prompt careful exclusion of a phyllodes tumour Rapid growth or a large (giant) lesion suggesting a phyllodes tumour Irregular, hard, or fixed features or suspicious imaging raising concern for malignancy New solid breast mass in an older woman requiring careful exclusion of cancer Discordance between clinical, imaging, and pathology findings on triple assessment Assuming a solid mass in an older woman is a fibroadenoma without excluding carcinoma Failing to distinguish a phyllodes tumour from a fibroadenoma, leading to inadequate excision margins Ignoring discordance within triple assessment and falsely reassuring the patient Over-treating small, biopsy-proven, asymptomatic fibroadenomas that could be safely observed Neglecting follow-up of a lesion managed conservatively that later enlarges A fibroadenoma is a benign biphasic tumour arising from the breast lobule, composed of both epithelial and stromal (fibrous) elements that proliferate together. It is regarded as an aberration of normal breast development and involution rather than a true neoplasm, and its growth is hormonally responsive, which explains its predominance in the reproductive years, occasional enlargement during pregnancy, and tendency to regress after the menopause. The lesion is well encapsulated and mobile within the breast tissue. The main clinical distinction is from phyllodes tumours, which share stromal and epithelial components but have greater stromal cellularity and a spectrum of behaviour from benign to malignant. The prognosis is excellent; fibroadenomas are benign, a significant proportion regress or remain stable, and they carry little or no increase in subsequent breast cancer risk in the usual simple form. Recurrence after complete excision is uncommon, though new fibroadenomas may develop elsewhere.

Breast hamartoma — Fibroadenolipoma, Lipofibroadenoma, Adenolipoma Fibroadenoma Lipoma Phyllodes tumour Galactocoele Pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia Well-circumscribed carcinoma Fibrocystic change forming a mass Mammography to demonstrate the mixed-density encapsulated lesion Breast ultrasound to assess the heterogeneous circumscribed mass Core needle biopsy with radiological-pathological correlation Breast MRI for large or atypical lesions Excisional biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain Assessment for features of Cowden syndrome if multiple lesions Interval imaging to confirm stability A benign, well-circumscribed overgrowth of disorganised but otherwise normal breast tissue, comprising glandular, fibrous and adipose elements. Often presents as a soft, mobile, painless mass or as an incidental screening finding, most commonly in women in their fourth to fifth decade. The mammographic appearance is characteristic: an encapsulated lesion containing both fat and soft-tissue density, described as a 'breast within a breast'. A thin radiolucent capsule separating the lesion from surrounding tissue supports the diagnosis. Because it contains all normal breast constituents, core biopsy can appear deceptively 'normal', making radiological correlation essential. Proportions of fat, fibrous stroma and glandular tissue vary, giving rise to the synonyms fibroadenolipoma and adenolipoma. Treatment is reassurance for typical asymptomatic lesions, with excision reserved for large, symptomatic or diagnostically uncertain masses. Multiple hamartomas, particularly with mucocutaneous features, should prompt consideration of Cowden syndrome. Rapid or asymmetric enlargement of a previously stable mass Suspicious microcalcification or an intralesional solid nodule Skin tethering, nipple retraction or fixity Discordance between benign biopsy and suspicious imaging Multiple hamartomas with mucocutaneous stigmata of Cowden syndrome Interpreting deceptively 'normal' core biopsy tissue as a benign result without imaging correlation Mistaking a hamartoma for a simple fibroadenoma or lipoma Overlooking an incidental carcinoma developing within the lesion Failing to recognise the 'breast within a breast' mammographic sign Missing the link between multiple hamartomas and Cowden syndrome A breast hamartoma is a developmental, tumour-like malformation rather than a true neoplasm, arising from the localised disorganised proliferation of the mature tissue elements normally present in the breast. Ducts, lobules, fibrous stroma and mature adipose tissue are haphazardly arranged within a thin pseudocapsule that demarcates the lesion from adjacent parenchyma. Because the constituent tissues are cytologically normal, the hamartoma behaves as a slowly enlarging, well-defined mass. Its recognition rests largely on the interplay of fatty and glandular densities on imaging, since histology of a small sample may be indistinguishable from ordinary breast tissue. Breast hamartoma is benign with an excellent prognosis, and simple excision is curative when required. Malignancy arising within a hamartoma is rare and generally reflects an incidental coexisting lesion rather than transformation of the hamartoma itself.

Breath-holding spells — breath-holding attacks, cyanotic and pallid infantile syncope Epileptic seizures, particularly tonic or atonic seizures Cardiac arrhythmia including long QT syndrome and other causes of reflex anoxic syncope Vasovagal or neurally mediated syncope Brainstem or posterior fossa lesion causing central apnoea Gastro-oesophageal reflux with apnoea, or a brief resolved unexplained event Central hypoventilation or other disorder of respiratory control Detailed eyewitness account confirming the typical trigger-and-sequence pattern Full blood count with ferritin and iron studies to detect iron deficiency ECG to exclude long QT syndrome or arrhythmia in atypical, pallid or severe cases EEG only if the diagnosis is uncertain or seizures are strongly suspected Echocardiography or cardiology referral if a cardiac cause is suspected Developmental and growth assessment to confirm an otherwise normal child Common, benign, non-epileptic paroxysmal events of infants and toddlers, with peak occurrence between 6 and 18 months and usual resolution by 5-6 years of age Two main types are recognised: cyanotic (blue) spells triggered by anger, frustration or vigorous crying, and pallid (white) spells triggered by pain, sudden fright or minor injury The typical sequence is a provoking stimulus, then crying, then breath held in expiration, then colour change and limpness with possible brief loss of consciousness; prolonged spells may end in a few tonic-clonic movements (a reflex anoxic seizure) Pallid spells are mediated by a vagally driven cardiac asystole or profound bradycardia, whereas cyanotic spells involve prolonged expiratory apnoea with altered respiratory control Recovery is rapid and spontaneous with prompt return to normal activity, and there is no prolonged postictal confusion as seen with epilepsy Iron deficiency, with or without anaemia, is a recognised association and iron supplementation reduces spell frequency in many children Diagnosis is clinical from a clear temporal and eyewitness account; investigations are usually unnecessary, though an ECG helps exclude a long QT or arrhythmia mimic in atypical cases Management centres on parental reassurance and education, avoiding reinforcement of the behaviour, with the clear message that spells do not cause brain damage and are not epilepsy Events without a clear provoking trigger, or occurring during sleep Prolonged loss of consciousness, focal neurological features or a true postictal state Family history of sudden cardiac death, or syncope on exertion or startle suggesting long QT syndrome Developmental regression or an abnormal interictal neurological examination Onset in the newborn period or persistence well beyond the expected age Misdiagnosing spells as epilepsy and initiating antiepileptic drugs Failing to check for and treat iron deficiency Missing an underlying long QT syndrome or arrhythmia in atypical or unprovoked events Alarming parents unnecessarily, or conversely dismissing genuinely atypical events without an ECG Reinforcing the behaviour by altering normal discipline for fear of provoking spells Breath-holding spells reflect dysregulated autonomic control in an immature nervous system. In cyanotic spells, provoked crying leads to prolonged expiratory apnoea with hypoxaemia and cerebral hypoxia, causing loss of consciousness and occasionally a reflex anoxic seizure. In pallid spells, a noxious stimulus triggers an exaggerated vagal reflex producing transient cardiac asystole or profound bradycardia with cerebral hypoperfusion. Iron deficiency may contribute through its effects on neurotransmitter function and autonomic regulation, and a familial predisposition is common. The outlook is excellent; spells resolve spontaneously in almost all children by school age with no long-term neurological sequelae. A minority of children with pallid spells develop vasovagal syncope in later life.

Brenner tumour — transitional cell tumour of ovary, ovarian Brenner tumour Ovarian fibroma or fibrothecoma Granulosa cell tumour Mucinous cystadenoma Krukenberg or other metastatic tumour Struma ovarii Transitional-cell (urothelial-type) carcinoma metastatic from the urinary tract Transvaginal ultrasound showing a solid, often calcified ovarian mass Pelvic MRI or CT to characterise a solid lesion and detect coexisting cysts Tumour markers (CA125 and others) mainly to exclude malignant or metastatic disease Endometrial assessment if oestrogenic effects such as postmenopausal bleeding are present Histology with immunohistochemistry to confirm transitional-type epithelium and grade the lesion Urinary tract imaging or cystoscopy if a metastatic urothelial carcinoma is considered An uncommon surface-epithelial ovarian tumour composed of nests of transitional-type (urothelium-like) epithelium set in a dense fibrous stroma The overwhelming majority are benign, small, solid, and discovered incidentally in middle-aged or older women Frequently unilateral and often coexists with a mucinous cystadenoma in the same ovary The epithelial nests may show longitudinal nuclear grooves, giving a coffee-bean appearance, and are thought to derive from Walthard cell rests of transitional metaplasia Coarse calcification within a solid ovarian mass on imaging is a helpful pointer Borderline and malignant variants exist but are rare; malignant Brenner tumours behave as transitional-type carcinomas Occasionally the stroma is hormonally active and produces oestrogen, causing postmenopausal bleeding or endometrial hyperplasia A solid ovarian mass with rapid growth or solid enhancing components suggesting a malignant variant Postmenopausal bleeding indicating oestrogenic stromal activity requiring endometrial evaluation Ascites or peritoneal disease pointing to a malignant or metastatic process Confusing a solid, calcified Brenner tumour with a fibroma or malignant ovarian mass on imaging Overlooking a coexisting mucinous cystadenoma in the same ovary Failing to investigate oestrogenic symptoms such as postmenopausal bleeding Assuming all transitional-type epithelium is benign and missing a malignant variant Brenner tumours are surface-epithelial-stromal neoplasms in which islands of transitional-type epithelium, resembling urothelium, are embedded in an abundant fibromatous stroma. The epithelium is believed to originate from metaplastic transitional cells, analogous to the Walthard cell nests found near the tubo-ovarian junction. In benign lesions the nests are well circumscribed with bland, grooved nuclei and frequent central cystic change or mucinous metaplasia, which explains the common association with mucinous cystadenomas. Malignant transformation, when it occurs, produces frankly invasive transitional-cell carcinoma. Some tumours have a hormonally active stroma capable of oestrogen secretion, accounting for occasional endometrial effects. Benign Brenner tumours are cured by simple excision with an excellent outlook. Borderline lesions rarely recur, whereas malignant Brenner tumours carry a prognosis comparable to other invasive ovarian carcinomas and depend on stage at diagnosis.

brenner tumour — Brenner tumor, transitional cell tumour of ovary ovarian fibroma or fibrothecoma granulosa cell tumour mucinous cystadenoma or borderline mucinous tumour metastatic urothelial carcinoma to the ovary high-grade serous or endometrioid carcinoma (for malignant Brenner) struma ovarii Walthard cell nests and other benign inclusions transvaginal and abdominal pelvic ultrasound MRI of the pelvis to characterise a solid, often calcified mass CT of abdomen and pelvis when malignancy is suspected for staging serum CA125 and other epithelial tumour markers endometrial assessment if there is abnormal or post-menopausal bleeding immunohistochemistry including GATA3, p63 and cytokeratins histological search for a coexisting mucinous or other epithelial component A surface epithelial-stromal ovarian tumour composed of nests of transitional-type (urothelial-like) epithelium set in a dense fibrous stroma; the great majority are benign. Most benign Brenner tumours are small and discovered incidentally in peri- and post-menopausal women, often within an oophorectomy specimen removed for another reason. They frequently coexist with other epithelial neoplasms, particularly mucinous cystadenomas, in the same or contralateral ovary. Characteristic histology shows well-demarcated epithelial nests with longitudinal nuclear grooves (coffee-bean nuclei) and often central microcystic change, with frequent stromal calcification. Borderline (atypical proliferative) and malignant Brenner tumours are rare; malignancy is suggested by a solid mass with an infiltrative stromal invasion and frank cytological atypia. The stroma may be hormonally active and occasionally produces oestrogen, so a minority present with post-menopausal bleeding or endometrial hyperplasia. Immunohistochemistry typically shows the epithelial nests expressing urothelial-type markers such as GATA3, along with p63 and cytokeratins, aiding distinction from other ovarian tumours. Benign tumours are cured by simple excision or oophorectomy, whereas malignant Brenner tumours are staged and managed like other malignant ovarian epithelial cancers. a large predominantly solid ovarian mass raising concern for a borderline or malignant Brenner tumour rapid growth, ascites or extra-ovarian spread suggesting malignancy post-menopausal bleeding from oestrogenic stromal activity requiring endometrial evaluation imaging features of stromal invasion or an admixed malignant epithelial component bilateral or metastatic transitional-type tumour prompting exclusion of a urinary tract primary Assuming any solid, calcified ovarian mass is benign without excluding a malignant Brenner tumour on adequate sampling. Overlooking a coexisting mucinous or other epithelial neoplasm in the same specimen. Misinterpreting transitional-type epithelium as metastatic urothelial carcinoma without appropriate immunohistochemistry and clinical correlation. Failing to evaluate the endometrium when an oestrogenic Brenner tumour causes post-menopausal bleeding. Confusing a cellular fibrous stroma with a sex-cord stromal tumour when the diagnostic epithelial nests are sparsely sampled. Brenner tumours belong to the surface epithelial-stromal group of ovarian neoplasms and are thought to arise from metaplasia of the ovarian surface epithelium or of Walthard cell nests near the tubo-ovarian junction into transitional (urothelial-like) epithelium. The benign tumour consists of sharply circumscribed nests of bland transitional cells embedded in an abundant, often calcified fibrous stroma. A metaplastic-to-neoplastic sequence is proposed, whereby benign tumours may progress through a borderline (atypical proliferative) phase to malignant Brenner tumour, the last showing stromal invasion, high-grade atypia and, molecularly, alterations distinct from urothelial carcinoma of the bladder. The associated dense stroma can undergo luteinisation and secrete steroid hormones, accounting for the occasional oestrogenic manifestations, and the common coexistence with mucinous tumours reflects the shared metaplastic potential of the ovarian epithelium. Benign Brenner tumours have an excellent prognosis and are cured by excision, while borderline tumours behave indolently after complete removal; malignant Brenner tumours are uncommon and their outlook depends on stage, being poorer when disease extends beyond the ovary.

Brittle nail syndrome — Onychorrhexis, Fragilitas unguium Onychomycosis Nail lichen planus Nail psoriasis Iron deficiency and koilonychia Thyroid dysfunction affecting the nails Twenty-nail dystrophy (trachyonychia) Chemical or occupational nail damage Full blood count and ferritin for iron deficiency Thyroid function tests Nail clipping for mycology to exclude onychomycosis Dermoscopy of the nail plate and folds Assessment for signs of lichen planus or psoriasis elsewhere Occupational and cosmetic exposure history Brittle nail syndrome describes nails that split, flake, crumble or break easily, and is common, affecting a large proportion of adults and women more than men. Two morphological patterns are recognised: onychoschizia, a lamellar splitting of the free edge into horizontal layers, and onychorrhexis, longitudinal ridging and splitting. The dominant mechanism is repeated cycles of hydration and dehydration, worsened by frequent hand washing, wet work and exposure to detergents, solvents and nail cosmetics. It may be idiopathic and age-related or secondary to dermatoses such as lichen planus and psoriasis, or to systemic factors including iron deficiency and thyroid disease. A careful history should explore occupational and domestic wet work, cosmetic and solvent exposure, and any relevant systemic symptoms. Management emphasises protecting the nails, minimising water and irritant exposure, regular emollient and the consistent use of emollients or nail hydrating agents; supplementation is reserved for demonstrated deficiency. Biotin supplementation has traditional support for nail fragility, but it can interfere with several laboratory immunoassays and should be noted before testing. The condition is chiefly one of quality of life and cosmesis rather than a threat to health, though it can be a clue to underlying disease. Brittleness confined to a single nail or with a subungual mass, raising concern for a tumour Associated nail dystrophy with scarring suggesting lichen planus Systemic features such as fatigue and pallor pointing to iron deficiency or thyroid disease Rapidly progressive dystrophy of all nails Prescribing biotin without noting its interference with laboratory immunoassays such as thyroid and troponin testing Overlooking onychomycosis or nail dermatoses as the true cause of fragility Failing to check for iron deficiency or thyroid disease in appropriate patients Expecting rapid improvement rather than the several months dictated by nail growth The nail plate depends for its strength on the orderly adhesion of corneocytes and on an appropriate water and lipid content. In brittle nail syndrome this integrity is disturbed, most often by repeated wetting and drying that fatigues the intercellular bonds between the layered keratinocytes of the plate, so that the distal nail delaminates (onychoschizia) or splits along its long axis (onychorrhexis). Reduced cohesion may also follow matrix disease that produces a structurally poor plate, as in lichen planus, or from generalised nail thinning with age. Nutritional deficiency, particularly of iron, and endocrine disturbance such as thyroid dysfunction can further impair keratinisation. The common final pathway is a plate with diminished flexibility and cohesion that fractures under normal mechanical stress. Brittle nail syndrome is benign but often chronic and relapsing, improving with consistent protective measures and correction of any underlying cause. Because nails grow slowly, visible improvement typically takes several months.

the diagnosis Progressive fixed weakness, which is atypical and suggests an alternative disorder Labelling the delayed relaxation as true myotonia without noting that electromyography is silent Being reassured by a normal creatine kinase and dismissing a genuine muscle disorder Overlooking the anaesthetic implications of abnormal calcium handling Confusing it with metabolic myopathies that also cause exercise-induced contractures Brody myopathy is caused by mutations in ATP2A1, which encodes SERCA1, the calcium ATPase of the sarcoplasmic reticulum in fast-twitch (type II) muscle fibres. SERCA1 pumps calcium from the cytoplasm back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum to terminate contraction and allow relaxation. When SERCA1 activity is deficient, cytoplasmic calcium is cleared too slowly after a contraction, so relaxation is delayed and repeated contractions cause cumulative stiffness, particularly during sustained or rapid exercise and in the cold. Because the impaired relaxation results from defective calcium reuptake rather than abnormal membrane excitability, the phenomenon is electrically silent, distinguishing it from the true myotonias. Brody myopathy is generally non-progressive and compatible with a normal lifespan, and although exercise-induced stiffness can be functionally limiting, most patients manage well with pacing of activity, warming-up and avoidance of cold.

bronchial atresia — congenital bronchial atresia, bronchocoele Endobronchial tumour such as carcinoid causing mucoid impaction Inhaled foreign body with distal air trapping Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis with mucoid impaction Congenital lobar emphysema Congenital pulmonary airway malformation Intralobar pulmonary sequestration Swyer-James (MacLeod) syndrome High-resolution and contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax Bronchoscopy to exclude an obstructing endobronchial lesion Contrast-enhanced MRI to characterise mucocoele signal Ventilation-perfusion assessment showing a matched regional reduction Pulmonary function testing if disease is extensive Histopathological examination of any resected specimen Characterised by focal obliteration or interruption of the lumen of a segmental or subsegmental bronchus, with normal development of the airways and alveoli distal to the atretic segment. The apicoposterior segment of the left upper lobe is the classic site, although any lobe may be affected. Mucus secreted distal to the blind-ending bronchus cannot drain and accumulates as a mucocoele (bronchocoele), producing the characteristic branching tubular gloved-finger opacity. The lung distal to the lesion is ventilated only through collateral channels (pores of Kohn, canals of Lambert), causing regional air trapping and hyperinflation. Most cases are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on imaging in adolescents or young adults. CT is diagnostic, showing the combination of a mucocoele with surrounding oligaemic, hyperlucent, hyperinflated lung. It must be distinguished from an obstructing endobronchial tumour or foreign body, which are acquired causes of a similar appearance. Management is usually conservative, with segmentectomy or lobectomy reserved for recurrent infection or diagnostic uncertainty. A new or enlarging soft-tissue component suggesting tumour rather than a benign mucocoele Recurrent infection localised to the affected segment Haemoptysis, which should prompt exclusion of malignancy Progressive hyperinflation causing mediastinal shift or respiratory compromise in a neonate Misinterpreting the mucocoele as a neoplasm and proceeding to unnecessary aggressive intervention. Conversely, assuming a mucoid-impaction pattern is congenital and missing an obstructing endobronchial cancer in an older patient. Overlooking the surrounding hyperlucency, which is the key clue distinguishing it from other tubular opacities. Confusing the entity with pulmonary sequestration when imaging is incomplete. Bronchial atresia is thought to result from a focal interruption of the developing bronchus, attributed either to an in-utero vascular insult to the bronchial supply or to a defect in bronchial budding occurring after the distal airway has already formed. The consequence is a segmental bronchus that ends blindly, with normal lung parenchyma beyond it. Secretions produced by the mucosa distal to the atresia have no route of egress and collect to form a mucus-filled bronchocoele, while the distal parenchyma, receiving air only via collateral ventilation and unable to expel it efficiently, becomes hyperinflated and oligaemic through reflex hypoxic vasoconstriction. Prognosis is excellent; most patients remain asymptomatic for life, and those requiring resection for complications generally do very well.

Persistent bacterial presence provokes chronic neutrophilic inflammation with release of proteases and reactive oxygen species that progressively damage the bronchial wall, weakening and dilating the airways. The damaged, dilated airways clear secretions still less effectively, perpetuating infection and inflammation and leading to further structural destruction. Prognosis varies widely with the underlying cause and disease extent; many patients remain stable for years with good airway clearance and infection control, but frequent exacerbations, chronic Pseudomonas colonisation, and extensive disease predict faster decline in lung function and higher mortality.

Bronchiolitis — acute bronchiolitis, RSV bronchiolitis, viral bronchiolitis Viral-induced wheeze / early asthma Pneumonia Congenital heart disease with heart failure Foreign body aspiration Gastro-oesophageal reflux with aspiration Pertussis Pulse oximetry to assess oxygenation Nasopharyngeal viral testing (mainly for cohorting or in severe/atypical cases) Chest radiograph only if diagnosis is unclear or deterioration is unexplained Blood gas in severe respiratory distress or impending failure Capillary or venous blood tests only when a bacterial complication is suspected A common lower respiratory tract infection of infants, typically under 2 years and peaking around 2-6 months, most often caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Begins with upper respiratory symptoms (coryza, cough, low-grade fever) that progress over a few days to tachypnoea, wheeze, crackles, and increased work of breathing. Diagnosis is clinical; routine viral testing, chest radiographs, and blood tests are usually unnecessary and can be misleading. Management is supportive: ensure adequate hydration and feeding, maintain oxygenation, and provide gentle nasal suction as needed. Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics are generally not beneficial in typical bronchiolitis and are not routinely recommended. Apnoea can be an early and sometimes presenting sign, particularly in young or premature infants. Risk factors for severe disease include prematurity, age under 2-3 months, congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease, and immunodeficiency. Most cases are self-limiting over 1-2 weeks, though cough can persist longer. Apnoea or episodes of colour change Persistent hypoxaemia or rising oxygen requirement Severe respiratory distress: marked recession, grunting, nasal flaring, head bobbing Inability to feed or signs of dehydration Exhaustion, lethargy, or signs of impending respiratory failure Overusing bronchodilators, steroids, or antibiotics that provide no benefit in typical disease Relying on transient oxygen desaturation readings and over-treating stable, feeding infants Missing apnoea as a presenting feature in very young infants Ordering routine chest radiographs, which may prompt unnecessary antibiotics for atelectasis mistaken for infiltrate Viral infection of the small airway epithelium causes inflammation, oedema, and necrosis of epithelial cells with increased mucus production. Sloughed cellular debris and mucus, together with airway wall swelling, partially or completely obstruct the small bronchioles. Because infant airways are narrow, this obstruction produces air trapping, hyperinflation, atelectasis, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch, leading to wheeze, hypoxaemia, and increased work of breathing. Most previously healthy infants recover fully within one to two weeks; a minority, especially high-risk infants, require hospitalisation, and some children have recurrent wheeze afterwards.

Bronchiolitis obliterans — constrictive bronchiolitis, obliterative bronchiolitis, popcorn lung Asthma Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease Cryptogenic organising pneumonia Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Bronchiectasis Other small airways disease Spirometry demonstrating fixed airflow obstruction Expiratory high-resolution CT showing mosaic attenuation and air trapping Assessment for transplant rejection or connective tissue disease Occupational and inhalational exposure history Lung biopsy in selected diagnostically uncertain cases An irreversible obstructive lung disease from fibrosis and narrowing of the small airways (bronchioles) Presents with progressive breathlessness and dry cough, often with relatively preserved chest radiograph findings It is distinct from cryptogenic organising pneumonia (the older term bronchiolitis obliterans organising pneumonia causes confusion) Recognised causes include lung and haematopoietic stem cell transplant rejection, connective tissue disease, inhalational injury and certain infections Spirometry shows fixed airflow obstruction, and expiratory CT demonstrates mosaic attenuation and air trapping Treatment aims to halt progression and address the underlying cause, as established fibrosis does not reverse Rapidly declining lung function, especially after transplantation Progressive hypoxaemic respiratory failure Features of an underlying connective tissue disease Significant occupational inhalational exposure Confusing it with organising pneumonia, which is steroid-responsive Misdiagnosing it as asthma or COPD Missing an occupational inhalational cause Overlooking chronic rejection in a transplant recipient Bronchiolitis obliterans is characterised by concentric fibrosis of the submucosa of terminal and respiratory bronchioles, progressively narrowing and obliterating their lumen (constrictive bronchiolitis). An initiating injury, whether immune (as in chronic transplant rejection or connective tissue disease), toxic (inhaled fumes such as diacetyl), or post-infective, triggers airway epithelial damage and a fibroproliferative repair response. The resulting fixed small-airway obstruction increases air trapping and reduces expiratory flow, and because the process is fibrotic it is largely irreversible. Established disease is generally irreversible and can progress to respiratory failure, though early recognition and treatment of the cause may stabilise lung function; prognosis is worse in post-transplant disease.

diagnosis, relieve symptoms, and prevent complications Acute airway compromise or stridor from tracheobronchial compression Signs of infection or abscess formation within the cyst Rapid enlargement or haemorrhage into the cyst Dysphagia from oesophageal compression Mistaking a high-density mucoid cyst on CT for a solid tumour and missing the diagnosis Attributing symptoms to another cause when a cyst is compressing the airway or oesophagus Assuming an incidental cyst is always safe to leave when complications or diagnostic uncertainty exist Incomplete excision leaving epithelial remnants that predispose to recurrence Bronchogenic cysts result from abnormal budding of the ventral foregut, the primitive tracheobronchial tree, during early embryonic development. A group of cells becomes separated from the developing airway and forms a closed cyst lined by ciliated respiratory epithelium, often with cartilage, smooth muscle, and mucous glands in its wall. The cyst fills with clear or mucoid secretion and enlarges slowly. Because it does not communicate with the airway it usually remains sterile, but a connection or bacterial seeding can lead to infection, and expansion may compress the trachea, bronchi, or oesophagus. Bronchogenic cysts are benign, and complete excision is curative with an excellent long-term outlook; untreated cysts may enlarge or become infected, and malignant change is very rare.

broncholithiasis — broncholith, endobronchial calculus endobronchial tumour (carcinoid or bronchogenic carcinoma) aspirated calcified or radiopaque foreign body calcified endobronchial tuberculosis or fungal granuloma mucoid impaction from other causes of bronchial obstruction bronchiectasis from unrelated cause carcinoid or hamartoma with calcification broncholith mimicking a bronchial stone within a congenital sequestration high-resolution and contrast CT of the chest to localise the calcified focus and assess vascular relations flexible and, where indicated, rigid bronchoscopy to confirm and characterise the broncholith sputum examination and culture for mycobacteria and fungi assessment for prior granulomatous exposure (tuberculin or interferon-gamma release testing, fungal serology) CT angiography where erosion into a vessel or significant haemoptysis is suspected contrast swallow or CT if broncho-oesophageal fistula is considered histological examination of expectorated or extracted material Broncholithiasis denotes calcified or ossified material within the airway lumen, most often a calcified peribronchial lymph node that erodes into an adjacent bronchus. It classically follows healed granulomatous infection — historically tuberculosis and, in endemic regions, histoplasmosis — where calcified nodes gradually breach the bronchial wall. Lithoptysis, the expectoration of gritty stone or sand-like material, is pathognomonic but occurs in only a minority of patients. Common presentations are chronic cough, recurrent focal infection, localised wheeze and haemoptysis, the last resulting from erosion into bronchial vessels. A broncholith adjacent to a vessel can cause massive haemoptysis or, rarely, erode into the oesophagus producing a broncho-oesophageal fistula. CT typically shows a calcified endobronchial or peribronchial focus with distal atelectasis, obstructive pneumonitis, mucoid impaction or bronchiectasis. Bronchoscopy may reveal a whitish, hard, mobile intraluminal stone; forceful blind extraction of a partially eroded broncholith risks torrential bleeding and should be avoided. Management ranges from bronchoscopic removal of loose stones to surgical resection when the broncholith is embedded, associated with fistula, or causing recurrent haemoptysis or infection. massive or recurrent haemoptysis suggesting erosion into a bronchial or pulmonary vessel recurrent obstructive pneumonia in the same segment features of broncho-oesophageal fistula such as coughing on swallowing or recurrent aspiration signs of a large-airway obstruction with atelectasis or lobar collapse Attempting forceful bronchoscopic extraction of a partially embedded broncholith and precipitating catastrophic haemorrhage. Missing a small calcified endobronchial focus on non-contrast or low-resolution imaging. Attributing recurrent focal pneumonia to simple infection without seeking an obstructing broncholith. Overlooking an evolving broncho-oesophageal fistula in a patient with cough on swallowing. Assuming a systemic disorder of calcium metabolism rather than recognising the granulomatous nodal origin. Broncholithiasis usually begins with granulomatous inflammation of hilar or mediastinal lymph nodes, most often from healed tuberculosis or fungal infection such as histoplasmosis, silicosis being a less common contributor. Over years the affected nodes calcify and harden. Continuous transmission of respiratory and cardiac motion between the rigid calcified node and the pliable adjacent bronchial wall produces chronic mechanical erosion, allowing the calcified material to migrate into or through the wall and project into the lumen. Once endobronchial, the broncholith obstructs airflow and mucus clearance, causing distal atelectasis, post-obstructive infection, mucoid impaction and bronchiectasis. Erosion into accompanying bronchial or pulmonary vessels produces haemoptysis that may be severe, and erosion between airway and oesophagus or mediastinum can create fistulae. The process is mechanical and inflammatory rather than a disorder of systemic calcium metabolism. Outcome is generally favourable once the broncholith is removed and complications addressed, though embedded stones, fistulae or recurrent haemoptysis may require surgery and calcified nodal disease can occasionally produce further broncholiths over time.

Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia — BPD, chronic lung disease of prematurity, chronic lung disease of infancy Recurrent aspiration Congenital heart disease with left-to-right shunt or pulmonary oedema Pulmonary hypertension from other causes Recurrent or persistent lower respiratory infection Interstitial lung disease of infancy Tracheobronchomalacia Chest radiograph showing hyperinflation, cystic or coarse interstitial changes Pulse oximetry and, where indicated, blood gas analysis Echocardiography to screen for pulmonary hypertension Assessment of growth and nutritional status Selected infants may need chest CT or bronchoscopy for airway evaluation A chronic lung disease of prematurity, usually defined by a persisting need for supplemental oxygen or respiratory support at around 36 weeks postmenstrual age. Occurs mainly in very preterm, very-low-birth-weight infants, often those who required prolonged mechanical ventilation and oxygen for respiratory distress syndrome. The modern ('new') form reflects arrested alveolar and pulmonary vascular development rather than the severe fibrotic airway injury seen historically. Contributing factors include oxygen toxicity, ventilator-induced volutrauma and barotrauma, inflammation, infection, and a patent ductus arteriosus. Lung-protective strategies, such as early CPAP, gentle ventilation targeting acceptable gas exchange, and judicious oxygen targeting, help prevent it. Management emphasises adequate nutrition and calories for lung growth, careful fluid balance, and weaning of respiratory support as tolerated. Systemic corticosteroids can facilitate extubation but carry neurodevelopmental risks, so their use is weighed carefully and generally limited. Affected infants are prone to recurrent wheeze, respiratory infections, and pulmonary hypertension, and benefit from RSV prophylaxis and immunisation. Caffeine therapy for apnoea of prematurity is associated with a lower rate of bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Escalating oxygen or ventilatory requirement Signs of pulmonary hypertension or cor pulmonale Failure to gain weight despite adequate calories Frequent acute deteriorations or hypoxaemic spells Recurrent lower respiratory tract infections requiring hospitalisation Using liberal oxygen targets that worsen lung and retinal injury Overlooking pulmonary hypertension as a cause of persistent oxygen need Excess fluid administration precipitating pulmonary oedema Prolonged or high-dose systemic steroid courses despite neurodevelopmental risk Underestimating nutritional needs required for lung repair and growth In the immature lung, the combination of oxidative stress from supplemental oxygen, mechanical injury from positive-pressure ventilation, inflammation, and antenatal or postnatal infection disrupts normal alveolar septation and pulmonary microvascular growth. The result is fewer, larger, simplified alveoli with an abnormal vascular bed, variable airway smooth-muscle and interstitial changes, and impaired gas exchange. Pulmonary vascular remodelling can lead to pulmonary hypertension. Most infants gradually improve as the lung grows during early childhood, but many have increased respiratory morbidity, exercise limitation, and abnormal lung function later; severe disease with pulmonary hypertension carries higher mortality and long-term risk.

retaining a primitive systemic arterial supply from the aorta rather than acquiring a normal pulmonary connection. The sequestered tissue therefore does not participate in gas exchange and lacks normal bronchial communication. In extralobar sequestration the accessory tissue has its own pleural investment and systemic venous drainage, while in intralobar sequestration the abnormal tissue is incorporated within a normal lobe and tends to drain via pulmonary veins. Absent normal airway clearance predisposes intralobar lesions to recurrent infection, and hybrid lesions sharing features with congenital pulmonary airway malformation are recognised. Prognosis is generally excellent after complete resection, which is curative and prevents recurrent infection and shunt-related complications. Large fetal lesions causing hydrops carry a poorer outlook, and outcome may be influenced by coexisting anomalies, particularly with extralobar disease.

Brooke-Spiegler syndrome — BSS, CYLD cutaneous syndrome, familial cylindromatosis (overlapping spectrum), turban tumour syndrome Sporadic solitary cylindroma, spiradenoma, or trichoepithelioma Multiple familial trichoepithelioma (allelic condition) Familial cylindromatosis (allelic condition) Cowden syndrome and other hamartoma syndromes Multiple basal cell carcinomas / basal cell naevus syndrome Nevoid follicular tumours and adnexal hamartomas Detailed skin examination mapping cylindromas, spiradenomas, and trichoepitheliomas Skin biopsy of representative lesions for histological confirmation CYLD germline genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and enable family counselling Family history and examination of at-risk relatives Imaging and surgical planning for extensive confluent scalp disease Biopsy of any rapidly changing lesion to exclude malignant transformation An autosomal dominant genodermatosis caused by germline CYLD mutations predisposing to multiple adnexal tumours Characteristic tumours are cylindromas, spiradenomas, and trichoepitheliomas, which may coexist and even collide within a single lesion (spiradenocylindroma) Cylindromas favour the scalp and may coalesce into disfiguring turban tumours, while trichoepitheliomas cluster on the central face and nasolabial folds It forms a clinical spectrum with familial cylindromatosis and multiple familial trichoepithelioma, all linked to CYLD Lesions typically appear from adolescence and increase in number and size through adult life, with female predominance in some kindreds The CYLD gene encodes a deubiquitinase that negatively regulates NF-kB signalling; its loss promotes adnexal tumorigenesis Malignant transformation of cylindromas or spiradenomas is uncommon but recognised, so changing lesions warrant biopsy A rapidly growing, ulcerating, or bleeding lesion suggesting malignant transformation of a cylindroma or spiradenoma Extensive disfiguring turban-tumour disease with functional impact New neurological or local symptoms from large or deep tumours Emergence of aggressive histology on biopsy of a long-standing tumour Treating a patient's tumours as isolated sporadic lesions and missing the hereditary diagnosis Failing to offer genetic counselling and family screening Overlooking malignant transformation in a long-standing changing lesion Inadequate excision of confluent scalp tumours leading to recurrence Brooke-Spiegler syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition arising from germline loss-of-function mutations in the CYLD tumour-suppressor gene, with a somatic second hit inactivating the remaining allele in tumour tissue. CYLD encodes a deubiquitinating enzyme that removes regulatory ubiquitin chains from signalling intermediates, thereby restraining nuclear factor-kappa B and related pro-survival pathways. Loss of this brake enhances cell survival and proliferation in follicular and apocrine/eccrine adnexal structures, generating the syndrome's hallmark cylindromas, spiradenomas, and trichoepitheliomas. Because the underlying defect is shared, individual lesions can display overlapping or combined histological features, and the same genotype produces the overlapping phenotypes of familial cylindromatosis and multiple trichoepithelioma. The syndrome is chronic and progressive with recurring benign tumours that cause cosmetic and functional morbidity and often require repeated surgery; life expectancy is generally normal, but the small risk of malignant transformation necessitates lifelong surveillance.

cause Progressive deficit suggesting an expanding compressive lesion or haematoma Traumatic injury with spinal instability requiring immobilisation New sphincter dysfunction indicating more extensive cord involvement An ascending sensory or motor level over hours Expecting sensory loss on the same side as the weakness and forgetting that spinothalamic loss is contralateral Missing a subtle contralateral pinprick deficit and thereby overlooking the diagnosis Assuming the syndrome only follows penetrating trauma and neglecting compressive or inflammatory causes Mislocating the lesion by relying on the lower contralateral pain and temperature level rather than the higher ipsilateral signs Failing to image urgently when a compressive cause is potentially reversible Brown-Sequard syndrome results from injury to one lateral half of the spinal cord, which interrupts three long tracts with differing decussation patterns. The corticospinal tract has already crossed in the medulla, so its interruption causes weakness on the same side as the cord lesion; the dorsal columns ascend uncrossed to the lower medulla, so their damage causes ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration; the spinothalamic tract, by contrast, decussates within one or two segments of entering the cord, so its interruption causes contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning just below the lesion. This anatomy explains the distinctive dissociated and laterally divided pattern of deficit and the slight vertical offset between the sensory modalities. Brown-Sequard syndrome carries the most favourable prognosis of the incomplete cord syndromes, and the majority of patients regain the ability to walk and achieve useful bladder control. Outcome is best when a treatable cause is addressed promptly before secondary cord injury accrues.

from bulbar and diaphragmatic weakness Rapidly advancing dysphagia with aspiration risk Acute deterioration during intercurrent catabolic illness Progressive visual loss from optic atrophy Mislabelling the presentation as motor neurone disease or a non-treatable neurodegeneration and missing a treatable cause Delaying empirical riboflavin while awaiting genetic results Assuming a normal plasma flavin or acylcarnitine profile excludes the diagnosis Overlooking deafness as an early and pivotal diagnostic clue The syndrome arises from defective cellular uptake of riboflavin (vitamin B2) due to loss-of-function variants in the riboflavin transporter genes SLC52A2 and SLC52A3. Impaired riboflavin transport lowers tissue levels of the flavin cofactors FMN and FAD, which are essential for numerous flavoenzymes, particularly those of mitochondrial fatty-acid beta-oxidation and the respiratory chain. Because the defect is one of cofactor delivery rather than an irreparable structural lesion, supplying supraphysiological riboflavin can restore flavoenzyme activity and halt neurodegeneration. Untreated disease is progressive and can be fatal from respiratory or bulbar failure, but early high-dose riboflavin supplementation frequently stabilises and partially reverses neurological deficits, so prognosis depends heavily on prompt recognition and treatment.

Brucellosis — undulant fever, Malta fever Tuberculosis is the most important differential for vertebral osteomyelitis or septic arthritis; vertebral destruction or spinal cord impingement is rare in brucellosis and usually suggests tuberculosis (p.1333). Typhoid fever and malaria as causes of fever in endemic areas (p.1333). Glandular fever-like illness (EBV, Toxoplasma, cytomegalovirus, HIV, or Mycobacterium tuberculosis) when hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy is present (p.1333). Mumps and surgical conditions such as testicular torsion when epididymo-orchitis occurs (p.1333). Neurotuberculosis, atypical leptospirosis, and noninfectious conditions when lymphocytic meningoencephalitis develops (p.1333). Tuberculosis Typhoid fever Malaria Leptospirosis Epstein-Barr virus infection Cytomegalovirus infection Toxoplasmosis HIV infection Mumps Blood, CSF, bone marrow, joint fluid, or tissue aspirate/biopsy culture under containment conditions for dangerous pathogens; alert the laboratory when brucellosis is suspected (p.1333). Standard tube/plate/microagglutination serology as the mainstay, with complement fixation, Coombs antiglobulin, and ELISA tests; repeat after 2-4 weeks to detect a rising titer (p.1334). Peripheral blood PCR / nucleic acid amplification (e.g., targeting rrs-rrl spacer, outer-membrane protein genes, IS711, BCSP31) which is more sensitive and quicker than culture and avoids biohazard risk (p.1334). MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for identification in well-resourced laboratories, with the caveat that earlier implementations often failed to identify Brucella correctly (p.1333). Isotope bone scanning, more sensitive than plain x-ray for bony disease (p.1333). CSF/joint fluid analysis showing lymphocytosis and low glucose; tissue biopsy may show noncaseating granulomas without acid-fast bacilli (p.1333). Noninfectious causes of lymphocytic meningoencephalitis Chronic fatigue syndromes (in the context of a suspected chronic brucellosis state) Other causes of excessive sweating such as alcohol abuse and obesity A bacterial zoonosis caused by Brucella species, transmitted directly or indirectly from infected animals, predominantly domesticated ruminants and swine; B. melitensis (sheep, goats, camels) is the most common cause of symptomatic human disease, with B. abortus (cattle/buffalo), B. suis (swine), and B. canis (dogs) also implicated (p.1331). Human infection is usually associated with occupational or domestic animal exposure (farmers, shepherds, goatherds, veterinarians, slaughterhouse and meat-processing workers, laboratory staff); travelers and urban residents typically acquire it through contaminated food (p.1332). Dairy products, especially soft cheeses, unpasteurized milk, and ice cream, are the most frequently implicated sources; acquisition may occur by ingestion, inhalation, or mucosal/percutaneous exposure (p.1332). Almost invariably causes fever, which may be accompanied by profuse sweats, especially at night; untreated, the fever classically shows an undulating pattern persisting for weeks before an afebrile period that may be followed by relapse (p.1332-1333). Fever is associated with musculoskeletal symptoms and signs in about half of patients; nonspecific features include apathy, fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, myalgia, headache, and chills (p.1333). Presentation often fits one of three patterns: a typhoid-like febrile illness but less severe; fever with acute monoarthritis (typically hip or knee) in a young child; and long-lasting fever with misery and low-back or hip pain in an older person, especially men (p.1333). Focal musculoskeletal involvement is the most common complication (~40%): osteomyelitis favors lumbar and low thoracic vertebrae, and septic arthritis most often affects knee, hip, sacroiliac, shoulder, and sternoclavicular joints, as monoarthritis or polyarthritis (p.1333). Roughly one-quarter of patients have hepatosplenomegaly and 10-20% have significant lymphadenopathy; up to 10% of men develop acute epididymo-orchitis (p.1333). Endocarditis occurs in about 1% of cases, most often affecting the aortic valve (native or prosthetic), and is the usual cause of death when the outcome is fatal (p.1333, p.1335). Diagnosis rests on a history of potential exposure, a compatible presentation, and supporting laboratory findings, because the clinical picture is not distinctive (p.1333). Isolation of brucellae from blood, CSF, bone marrow, joint fluid, or a tissue aspirate/biopsy is definitive and succeeds in about 50-70% of cases; modern automated blood culture systems (e.g., Bactec) usually turn positive within 7 days (p.1333). Serology often provides the only positive laboratory finding; in endemic or occupationally exposed settings agglutinin titers of 1:320-1:640 or higher are considered diagnostic, while in nonendemic areas a titer of at least 1:160 is significant, with no single universal cutoff (p.1334). Endocarditis, most often of the aortic valve (native or prosthetic), the leading cause of death in fatal cases (p.1333, p.1335). Neurobrucellosis: lymphocytic meningoencephalitis mimicking neurotuberculosis, and rarely intracerebral abscess, cranial nerve deficits, or ruptured mycotic aneurysms (p.1333). Vertebral osteomyelitis (spondylitis) and sacroiliitis (p.1333). Disseminated intravascular coagulation with raised fibrinogen degradation products and thrombocytopenia (p.1333). Increased fetal loss in infected pregnant women (though teratogenicity has not been described and abortion is much less pronounced in humans than in animals) (p.1333). The clinical picture is not distinctive and definitive diagnostic signs may be lacking, so exposure history and laboratory support are essential (p.1331, p.1333). Routine biochemistry is usually normal; peripheral leukocyte counts are typically normal or low with relative lymphocytosis, so normal blood counts do not exclude the disease (p.1333). Brucella may be misidentified by gallery strips as Agrobacterium, Ochrobactrum, or Psychrobacter (Moraxella) phenylpyruvicus; after taxonomic changes Ochrobactrum isolates may now be reported as a Brucella subspecies despite completely different management, so culture reports should be confirmed with the laboratory before therapeutic decisions (p.1333-1334). Rough strains such as B. canis and B. ovis do not react in conventional serologic tests and will give false-negative results; consult the laboratory if B. canis is suspected (p.1334). Serologic cross-reactions occur with other gram-negative bacteria including Yersinia enterocolitica O:9, E. coli O157, Francisella tularensis, Salmonella enterica group N, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, and Vibrio cholerae (p.1334). Live B. abortus vaccine strain RB51 does not elicit antibody in tests using smooth antigens, which must be considered when following accidental vaccine exposures (p.1334). Elevated CSF adenosine deaminase cannot be used to distinguish tubercular meningitis, as it may also be raised in brucellosis (p.1333). Existence of a prolonged chronic brucellosis state after successful treatment remains controversial; evaluation requires careful exclusion of malingering, chronic fatigue syndromes, and other causes of sweating such as alcohol abuse and obesity (p.1335). Brucellae are small, gram-negative, unencapsulated, nonsporulating coccobacilli that behave as facultative intracellular parasites. Following entry by ingestion, inhalation, or mucosal/percutaneous exposure, initial replication is presumed to occur within cells of the lymph nodes draining the entry point, with subsequent hematogenous spread that can establish chronic localizing infection at almost any site, most often the reticuloendothelial system, musculoskeletal tissues, and genitourinary system. The macrophage is the key target cell; Brucella is a "stealth" pathogen that evades innate immunity and survives within monocytic cells by restricting fusion of type IV secretion system-dependent Brucella-containing vacuoles with lysosomes, inhibiting apoptosis of infected cells, and preventing dendritic cell maturation and T-cell activation. Smooth LPS has low endotoxin activity and contributes to pyrogenicity and resistance to phagocytosis and serum killing. Antibodies aid clearance of extracellular organisms but alone cannot eradicate infection; control depends on macrophage activation and IFN-gamma/TH1 responses. Tissue responses range from acute and chronic inflammation to granuloma formation, with or without necrosis and caseation, and abscesses may develop in chronic localized infection (p.1332). Fewer than 1% of patients die of brucellosis; when fatal, death is usually due to cardiac involvement and, more rarely, severe neurologic disease. Despite low mortality, recovery is slow and the illness can cause prolonged inactivity. Relapse occurs in up to 30% of poorly compliant patients, so clinical follow-up for up to 2 years is recommended; relapse responds to a prolonged repeat course of the original therapy. General well-being and body weight are better guides to absence of relapse than serology, since IgG agglutination titers can stay in the diagnostic range for more than 2 years after cure. Immunity is not solid and reinfection can occur after repeated exposures (p.1335). Harrison distinguishes acute nonfocal brucellosis (duration under about 1-2 months) from complex or focal disease (e.g., spondylitis, neurobrucellosis, endocarditis), the latter requiring more prolonged and tailored therapy. Patterns by species are also noted: B. melitensis tends toward a more acute, aggressive presentation, B. suis toward focal abscess formation, and B. abortus toward a more insidious onset that is more likely to become chronic (p.1333-1334).
