The course is variable; recurrent fractures, progressive deformity, scoliosis and short stature cause significant disability, though bone-protective care, rehabilitation and orthopaedic surgery can improve function, and cognition and lifespan are usually preserved.

Brugada syndrome — Brugada, Brugada pattern, SCN5A channelopathy, sudden unexpected nocturnal death syndrome Right bundle branch block Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy Acute right precordial ST elevation from ischaemia or pericarditis Electrolyte disturbance mimicking a Brugada pattern Early repolarisation variants Drug-induced or fever-induced phenocopies of the pattern 12-lead ECG including high right precordial lead placement to detect the coved pattern Sodium-channel-blocker provocation testing under monitoring when the resting ECG is non-diagnostic Assessment during febrile illness given fever-induced unmasking Genetic testing and cascade family screening Echocardiography or cardiac imaging to exclude structural disease such as ARVC Electrophysiology study in selected cases for risk stratification Brugada syndrome is an inherited arrhythmia disorder characterised by a distinctive coved ST-segment elevation in the right precordial leads and a risk of polymorphic ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death in a structurally normal heart Only the type 1 coved pattern is diagnostic; the saddleback type 2 pattern is suggestive and may need provocation or repositioned high leads to confirm Arrhythmic events characteristically occur at rest or during sleep and may be triggered by fever, which can unmask the pattern Certain drugs (including some sodium-channel blockers, and various psychotropic and anaesthetic agents) can precipitate or accentuate the pattern and should be avoided It disproportionately affects young to middle-aged men and can present as syncope, nocturnal agonal breathing, or aborted sudden death Diagnosis integrates the ECG pattern with clinical and family history, and a drug provocation test may be used when the resting ECG is non-diagnostic An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is the mainstay of protection in high-risk patients, and prompt treatment of fever is advised Family screening and genetic counselling are important given autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expression MEDICAL EMERGENCY: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation causing syncope, cardiac arrest, or sudden death Syncope or nocturnal agonal respiration in a patient with a type 1 pattern indicating high arrhythmic risk Spontaneous (not drug-induced) type 1 pattern, which carries greater risk Fever in a known patient, which can precipitate malignant arrhythmia Treating a non-diagnostic saddleback pattern as definitive Brugada syndrome Failing to place high right precordial leads or to consider provocation when suspicion is high Prescribing drugs that can precipitate the pattern or omitting prompt fever control Neglecting family screening after a diagnosis Brugada syndrome is most often linked to loss-of-function mutations in the cardiac sodium channel gene SCN5A, reducing inward sodium current. The leading explanation involves heterogeneity of repolarisation and depolarisation predominantly in the right ventricular outflow tract, producing a transmural voltage gradient that generates the characteristic ST-segment changes and a substrate for phase 2 reentry. This can trigger polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. Factors that reduce sodium current or increase transient outward current, such as fever and specific drugs, accentuate the abnormality and increase arrhythmic risk, which is why events cluster at rest, during sleep, and with febrile illness. Asymptomatic individuals with only a drug-induced pattern generally have a low event rate, whereas those with a spontaneous type 1 pattern and prior syncope or aborted arrest are at substantially higher risk; defibrillator therapy and avoidance of triggers markedly improve outcomes in high-risk patients.

in most patients, most notably myeloproliferative neoplasms (including JAK2-associated disease), so a thrombophilia workup is essential Doppler ultrasound is the usual first-line test, with CT or MR venography to define the level and extent of the obstruction The caudate lobe often drains directly into the inferior vena cava and is characteristically spared and hypertrophied while the rest of the liver is congested Management is stepwise: anticoagulation for essentially all patients, then angioplasty or stenting of short-segment stenoses, transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting, and finally liver transplantation for refractory or fulminant cases Acute presentation with rapid-onset jaundice, coagulopathy, and encephalopathy represents acute liver failure and is a medical emergency specialist and transplant assessment Rapidly worsening liver function or tense refractory ascites Concurrent inferior vena cava obstruction with lower-limb oedema and renal impairment Evidence of an aggressive underlying myeloproliferative disorder Attributing ascites and hepatomegaly to more common cirrhosis and missing outflow obstruction Failing to search for and treat an underlying prothrombotic disorder, allowing rethrombosis Delaying escalation from anticoagulation to interventional or transplant options in deteriorating patients Misinterpreting caudate lobe hypertrophy as a mass lesion Obstruction of hepatic venous outflow raises sinusoidal pressure and causes hepatic congestion, hypoxic injury to hepatocytes, and centrilobular necrosis. The resulting portal hypertension produces ascites and, over time, congestive fibrosis progressing to cirrhosis. Most cases stem from thrombosis on a background prothrombotic disorder, commonly a myeloproliferative neoplasm, inherited thrombophilia, antiphospholipid syndrome, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, pregnancy, or oral contraceptive use; in some regions membranous webs of the inferior vena cava predominate. The caudate lobe, with its independent venous drainage into the vena cava, escapes congestion and hypertrophies. Speed and completeness of obstruction determine whether the course is fulminant, acute, or chronic. Outcome depends on the rapidity and extent of obstruction and the response to a staged treatment strategy. Many patients do well with anticoagulation and interventional or shunt procedures, but fulminant presentations carry high mortality without transplantation, and untreated chronic disease progresses to cirrhosis.

progressive digital necrosis, particularly with continued smoking Ascending infection of an ischaemic digit Involvement of multiple limbs signalling extensive disease Diagnosing atherosclerotic disease in a young smoker and missing thromboangiitis obliterans Underemphasising that continued smoking, including any tobacco or nicotine exposure, drives progression Pursuing revascularisation where the distal small-vessel pattern makes it unsuitable Failing to exclude an embolic source or systemic vasculitis before settling on the diagnosis Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) is a segmental non-atherosclerotic vasculitis affecting small and medium arteries and veins of the extremities. There is an inflammatory, highly cellular thrombus with relative sparing of the vessel wall and internal elastic lamina, distinguishing it histologically from atherosclerosis and other vasculitides. Tobacco exposure is central to pathogenesis, likely through an immune-mediated and endothelial mechanism, and continued use drives progression. Occlusion of distal vessels produces critical ischaemia of the digits with limited collateral compensation. Prognosis is closely tied to smoking behaviour: complete cessation usually arrests the disease and greatly reduces amputation risk, whereas continued tobacco use commonly leads to recurrent ischaemia and progressive tissue loss. Life expectancy is generally near normal, but limb and digit loss is the major morbidity.

SSRIs (notably fluoxetine) are the pharmacological principle of choice Comorbid depression, anxiety, substance use, and impulsivity are common, and suicide risk should be assessed Behaviours are often concealed, so specific, non-judgemental enquiry is needed to detect them Severe hypokalaemia or other electrolyte disturbance with arrhythmia risk Haematemesis or oesophageal tear (Mallory-Weiss or Boerhaave) from forceful vomiting Suicidal ideation or self-harm Marked dehydration and haemodynamic instability from purging Assuming a normal body weight excludes serious medical risk from purging Missing dangerous hypokalaemia and its arrhythmic potential Not asking directly about purging behaviours that patients tend to conceal Overlooking comorbid depression and suicide risk Failing to offer evidence-based cognitive behavioural therapy Bulimia nervosa involves interacting genetic, temperamental, and sociocultural factors, with dysregulation of serotonergic systems affecting satiety, mood, and impulse control. Dietary restraint promotes binge episodes, and the binge-purge cycle is maintained by both physiological drives and psychological reinforcement, while overvaluation of shape and weight sustains the disorder. Bulimia nervosa often has a fluctuating course, but many patients improve substantially with cognitive behavioural therapy. Comorbid substance use, personality disorder, and persistent purging are associated with a more chronic course and greater medical risk.

risk Over-reliance on high-dose systemic steroids in frail patients when potent topical steroids may suffice Failing to identify a drug trigger that could be withdrawn Bullous pemphigoid is caused by This produces a subepidermal split, giving tense blisters with an intact epidermal roof. The urticarial prodrome reflects the inflammatory phase before frank blistering. Disease predominates in the elderly and may be associated with neurological disease and, in some cases, drug exposure. Bullous pemphigoid is often a self-limiting disease over months to a few years and generally responds to treatment, but morbidity and mortality are notable in elderly patients, largely driven by comorbidity and treatment-related complications.

bunionette is a lateral forefoot deformity analogous to hallux valgus but affecting the fifth ray, in which the fifth metatarsal head becomes prominent laterally and the little toe deviates medially. The prominence may result from an intrinsically wide or laterally bowed fifth metatarsal, from an increased angle between the fourth and fifth metatarsals that splays the forefoot, or simply from an enlarged lateral condyle of the metatarsal head. Constricting footwear that compresses the forefoot contributes by pressing on and irritating the lateral eminence. Chronic pressure between the bony prominence and the shoe produces a reactive callosity and an inflamed adventitial bursa, which are the usual sources of pain. When the prominence is plantar as well as lateral, a plantar keratosis can develop. The deformity frequently accompanies hallux valgus and a generally splayed, broad forefoot. Most bunionettes are controlled with footwear modification and padding, and symptoms often settle once pressure on the lateral eminence is relieved. When surgery is needed, lateral eminence resection or a metatarsal osteotomy chosen according to the deformity type gives good pain relief in the majority, although recurrence, transfer symptoms, or under-correction can occur, particularly if constricting footwear is resumed or the underlying angular deformity is not corrected.

arises from a germinal-centre B cell and is driven by translocation of the MYC oncogene, usually to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus, causing constitutive MYC overexpression that powerfully drives proliferation and metabolic reprogramming. In endemic disease Epstein-Barr virus infection and chronic immune stimulation, including from malaria, contribute to lymphomagenesis, whereas immunodeficiency-associated cases relate to impaired immune surveillance in HIV infection. Cooperating mutations, for example in TCF3 and ID3, sustain tonic B-cell receptor and PI3K signalling. The resulting extremely high proliferative rate produces the characteristic starry-sky histology and the marked propensity for rapid tumour growth and tumour lysis. Despite its aggressiveness Burkitt lymphoma is highly curable with intensive short-course chemoimmunotherapy and central nervous system prophylaxis, particularly in children and in limited-stage disease; prognosis is worse with advanced age, bulky or central nervous system disease, and delays in initiating treatment.

inhalation injury until airway swelling makes intubation difficult Failing to reassess deep dermal burns, which may convert to full thickness and need grafting Neglecting hypothermia, analgesia, and nutrition during the acute phase Missing the need for escharotomy in circumferential deep burns A burn causes coagulative tissue necrosis whose severity depends on temperature and contact time. Jackson described three zones: a central zone of coagulation (irreversible necrosis), a surrounding zone of stasis with compromised perfusion that can be salvaged or progress to necrosis, and an outer zone of hyperaemia. Large burns trigger a systemic inflammatory response with release of mediators that increase capillary permeability, causing fluid shift from the intravascular space into the interstitium and burn oedema. This produces hypovolaemia (burn shock) and, if inadequately treated, organ hypoperfusion. Loss of the skin barrier impairs thermoregulation and fluid balance and predisposes to infection and hypermetabolism. Outcome depends on burn size and depth, age, inhalation injury, and comorbidity. Superficial and superficial partial thickness burns generally heal without surgery and with minimal scarring, whereas deep dermal and full thickness burns require grafting and are prone to hypertrophic scarring and contracture. Timely resuscitation, early excision, infection control, and rehabilitation markedly improve survival and functional recovery.

Defined by a persistent burning or scalding sensation of the oral mucosa, most often the anterior tongue, in the absence of any visible mucosal abnormality It is a diagnosis of exclusion: the diagnosis of primary (idiopathic) burning mouth syndrome requires that local and systemic causes have been ruled out Symptoms are frequently accompanied by altered taste (dysgeusia) and a sensation of diabetes, xerostomia, contact allergy, and denture problems Management combines reassurance, treatment of any contributing factor, and neuropathic agents such as clonazepam (often topical), alpha-lipoic acid, or low-dose tricyclics A visible mucosal ulcer, white patch, or mass, which excludes primary burning mouth syndrome and requires biopsy Unilateral fixed symptoms with a discrete lesion suggesting malignancy Rapidly progressive symptoms with systemic illness Neurological deficits suggesting a central lesion Labelling a patient with primary burning mouth syndrome before excluding candidiasis, deficiency states, and xerostomia Overlooking a subtle mucosal lesion that requires biopsy Neglecting associated anxiety, depression, or cancerophobia Assuming reported dry mouth reflects true hyposalivation without measuring salivary flow Repeatedly investigating without offering symptomatic neuropathic treatment Primary burning mouth syndrome is regarded as a chronic oral neuropathic pain disorder. Evidence points to dysfunction of small-fibre sensory and taste pathways, with degeneration of intra-epithelial nerve fibres, altered central pain processing, and interactions between taste and trigeminal systems; declining gonadal and neuroactive steroid levels around the menopause may contribute. The result is spontaneous burning dysaesthesia without a structural mucosal lesion. Secondary burning mouth symptoms, by contrast, arise from identifiable local or systemic conditions (such as candidiasis, nutritional deficiency, or xerostomia) that irritate or sensitise the oral mucosa. Primary burning mouth syndrome tends to be chronic and fluctuating; a proportion of patients improve spontaneously over time, and many gain partial relief with neuropathic agents and management of psychological factors, though complete resolution is not the norm. Secondary cases resolve when the underlying cause is treated.

Buruli ulcer — Mycobacterium ulcerans infection, Bairnsdale ulcer, Daintree ulcer, Searls ulcer Tropical phagedenic ulcer Cutaneous leishmaniasis Venous or arterial leg ulcer Pyoderma gangrenosum Squamous cell carcinoma (including within chronic ulcers) Other mycobacterial or deep fungal infection Necrotising bacterial infection PCR for the IS2404 sequence on swab or tissue (most sensitive confirmatory test) Ziehl-Neelsen microscopy of swab or tissue for acid-fast bacilli Culture of M. ulcerans (slow-growing, requires lower incubation temperature) Histopathology showing necrosis with clumps of extracellular acid-fast bacilli Imaging to assess deep or bone involvement in extensive disease Assessment of functional impairment where lesions cross joints Caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans, an environmental mycobacterium associated with slow-moving or stagnant water; most cases occur in West and Central Africa, with foci in Australia and elsewhere The organism produces the toxin mycolactone, which causes tissue necrosis and local immunosuppression, explaining the characteristically painless lesion Early disease presents as a painless nodule, plaque or oedematous area; without treatment it progresses to a painless ulcer with widely undermined edges The undermined, deeply excavated ulcer with necrotic base extending beyond the visible skin margin is the hallmark of established disease Diagnosis is confirmed by PCR for the IS2404 insertion sequence, supported by microscopy for acid-fast bacilli, culture and histopathology Because lesions are painless, patients often present late with extensive tissue loss, and disease over joints can cause disabling contractures Treatment combines prolonged rifampicin-based anti-mycobacterial therapy with wound care, and surgery or skin grafting for larger lesions; physiotherapy prevents contractures Rapidly enlarging or oedematous lesions suggesting aggressive disease Lesions crossing joints with impending contracture and disability Bone involvement (osteomyelitis) Malignant transformation in a long-standing chronic ulcer Extensive tissue loss requiring reconstructive surgery Attributing a painless chronic ulcer to trivial trauma and delaying diagnosis Underestimating the true extent of necrosis, which extends beyond the visible ulcer margin Relying on surgery alone without anti-mycobacterial therapy, risking recurrence Neglecting physiotherapy, allowing preventable contractures Missing malignant change in long-standing ulcers Mycobacterium ulcerans is acquired from aquatic environments, though the precise mode of transmission remains uncertain. Once in subcutaneous tissue it secretes mycolactone, a diffusible lipid toxin that induces coagulative necrosis of fat and dermis while suppressing local immune and pain responses, accounting for the painless, minimally inflamed lesion. Necrosis spreads laterally in the subcutaneous plane, producing ulcers whose undermined edges extend well beyond the surface defect. As anti-mycobacterial therapy reduces bacillary load, the local immunosuppressive effect lifts and healing can proceed, sometimes with a paradoxical inflammatory reaction. Early nodular disease can heal with antibiotics alone and minimal scarring, but late, extensive ulceration frequently leaves disfiguring scars, contractures and functional disability; relapse is uncommon with adequate combination therapy.

Buschke-Ollendorff syndrome (LEMD3) — dermatofibrosis lenticularis disseminata with osteopoikilosis, connective tissue naevi with osteopoikilosis, LEMD3, BOS Isolated osteopoikilosis without cutaneous naevi Tuberous sclerosis (shagreen patch and sclerotic bone islands) Pseudoxanthoma elasticum Isolated connective-tissue naevus or nevus lipomatosus Osteoblastic skeletal metastases (radiographic mimic of the bone foci) Focal dermal hypoplasia and other elastic-tissue disorders Skin examination and biopsy of a representative papule for elastin and collagen assessment Plain radiographs or skeletal survey demonstrating the osteopoikilosis-type foci Bone scintigraphy where malignancy needs to be excluded LEMD3 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Family assessment including skin examination and targeted imaging of relatives Dermatological photography to document and monitor cutaneous lesions Defined by the combination of cutaneous connective-tissue naevi (elastomas rich in elastin, or collagenomas) with the spotty sclerotic bone lesions of osteopoikilosis Skin lesions are typically firm, skin-coloured or yellowish papules and plaques, often on the trunk and limbs, and may be present from childhood Shares the same causal gene as isolated osteopoikilosis, LEMD3, so the two conditions represent a spectrum with variable cutaneous expression Autosomal dominant inheritance with marked intrafamilial variability means some relatives show only skin lesions and others only bone findings The bone foci are asymptomatic incidental findings and, like osteopoikilosis, show no increased scintigraphic uptake Skin biopsy of a naevus confirms disorganised or increased dermal elastin/collagen and supports the diagnosis Management is reassurance; skin lesions may be removed for cosmetic reasons but this is not medically necessary New focal bone pain or a lesion with cortical destruction or increased uptake, prompting exclusion of metastatic disease Rapidly changing or ulcerating skin lesion atypical for a benign connective-tissue naevus Family history of a severe or unexplained bone disorder warranting broader evaluation Interpreting the sclerotic bone foci as osteoblastic metastases and triggering an unwarranted oncological workup Failing to link coexisting skin naevi and bone lesions, thereby missing the unifying diagnosis Overlooking the autosomal dominant inheritance and the need to counsel and examine relatives Assuming the skin lesions require aggressive treatment when observation is appropriate Buschke-Ollendorff syndrome is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in LEMD3, the same inner nuclear membrane protein implicated in osteopoikilosis, which normally restrains bone morphogenetic protein and transforming growth factor-beta signalling. In this disorder the dysregulated signalling manifests in both mesenchymal tissues: the dermis develops connective-tissue naevi with excess or disordered elastic and collagen fibres, while the skeleton develops the scattered sclerotic enostosis-like foci of osteopoikilosis. The variable balance of skin and bone involvement within a single family reflects the pleiotropic effect of the shared genetic defect rather than distinct disorders. The syndrome is benign with a normal life expectancy; both the skin naevi and bone foci are harmless, and the principal risk is unnecessary intervention prompted by misdiagnosis of the sclerotic lesions as malignancy.

C1 inhibitor deficiency (hereditary angioedema types I and II) — hereditary angioedema, HAE, C1-INH deficiency, SERPING1, C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency, HAE type I, HAE type II Histaminergic (mast-cell/allergic) angio-oedema with or without urticaria ACE-inhibitor-induced angio-oedema Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency associated with lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease Hereditary angioedema with normal C1 inhibitor (e.g. factor XII or plasminogen mutations) Idiopathic recurrent angio-oedema Gastrointestinal or surgical causes of recurrent abdominal pain Complement C4 level as an initial screen C1-inhibitor antigenic (quantitative) level C1-inhibitor functional assay to distinguish type II C1q level to help separate hereditary from acquired deficiency SERPING1 genetic testing when biochemistry is equivocal or for family studies Investigation for underlying lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease if acquired deficiency is suspected Causes recurrent non-pruritic, non-urticarial angio-oedema of the skin, gastrointestinal tract and upper airway, with attacks that are bradykinin-mediated Type I (about 85 percent) has low antigenic and functional C1 inhibitor; type II has normal or high antigenic level but reduced C1-inhibitor function A persistently low complement C4 is a useful screening clue between and during attacks Attacks lack the wheals of histaminergic angio-oedema and characteristically do not respond to antihistamines, corticosteroids or adrenaline Laryngeal oedema can be fatal, and unexplained abdominal attacks may mimic a surgical abdomen Attacks are triggered by trauma, dental or surgical procedures, infection, oestrogens and ACE inhibitors Management separates on-demand attack treatment, short-term procedural prophylaxis, and long-term prophylaxis using C1-inhibitor concentrate or bradykinin-pathway-directed agents rather than antihistamines/steroids Laryngeal or tongue swelling with any voice change, stridor or difficulty swallowing Rapidly progressive facial or neck oedema threatening the airway Severe unexplained abdominal attacks that could be mistaken for an acute surgical abdomen Attacks provoked or worsened by an ACE inhibitor or oestrogen therapy Treating bradykinin-mediated attacks as allergic and relying on antihistamines, corticosteroids or adrenaline, which do not work for hereditary angioedema attacks Being falsely reassured by a normal C1-inhibitor antigenic level in type II, where function is the abnormal parameter Continuing ACE inhibitors or oestrogen-containing therapy that provoke attacks Overlooking short-term prophylaxis before dental or surgical procedures Hereditary angioedema from C1 inhibitor deficiency is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by SERPING1 mutations that reduce the quantity (type I) or function (type II) of C1 inhibitor. C1 inhibitor is the principal brake on the contact (kallikrein-kinin) system as well as on the classical complement and fibrinolytic pathways. When it is deficient, unrestrained activation of plasma kallikrein cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen to release bradykinin, a potent vasodilator that increases vascular permeability. The resulting fluid extravasation produces the localised, self-limiting but potentially life-threatening swelling, and the mechanism explains why the swelling is bradykinin-driven rather than histamine-driven and does not respond to antiallergic therapy. With accurate diagnosis and access to modern on-demand and prophylactic therapy the outlook is good and quality of life can be near normal, but untreated laryngeal attacks carry a real risk of asphyxiation, making airway attacks the principal cause of mortality.

C1q deficiency — C1q deficiency, Complement C1q deficiency, Hereditary C1q deficiency Idiopathic systemic lupus erythematosus without complement deficiency Other early-component complement deficiencies (C1r/C1s, C4, C2) Hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis Other primary immunodeficiencies with autoimmunity Familial chilblain lupus and type I interferonopathies Acquired hypocomplementaemia from active immune-complex disease CH50 classical-pathway haemolytic assay (markedly low or absent) AH50 alternative-pathway assay (typically preserved) C1q antigenic level and functional activity Genetic testing of the C1q genes Autoimmune serology including ANA and anti-dsDNA Renal function and urinalysis for lupus nephritis Documentation of vaccination status and infection history C1q deficiency is the complement defect most strongly associated with early-onset systemic lupus erythematosus, often with prominent cutaneous and central nervous system disease. It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and usually presents in childhood. Impaired clearance of apoptotic cells and immune complexes is the key mechanism linking the deficiency to lupus-like autoimmunity. There is also increased susceptibility to encapsulated and pyogenic infections owing to defective classical-pathway activation. The CH50 (total classical-pathway haemolytic complement) is markedly reduced or absent, while the alternative-pathway assay (AH50) is preserved. Specific C1q antigenic and functional assays confirm the diagnosis after an absent CH50 is found. Some patients have functionally defective C1q with normal antigen levels, so functional testing matters. Management centres on treating the autoimmune disease, vaccination against encapsulated organisms and prompt treatment of infection. Invasive infection with encapsulated organisms or signs of meningitis or sepsis Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis Neuropsychiatric features suggesting CNS lupus Severe cytopenias Early-onset severe photosensitive or ulcerating skin disease Overlooking an inherited complement defect in a child presenting with early, severe lupus. Stopping at an absent CH50 without measuring individual components to localise the defect. Missing functionally defective C1q when only the antigen level is checked. Neglecting vaccination and infection prophylaxis against encapsulated organisms. Attributing persistently low complement solely to disease activity rather than a primary deficiency. C1q is the recognition subunit of the first component of the classical complement pathway, binding immune complexes and the surfaces of apoptotic cells. In C1q deficiency the classical pathway cannot be activated, so opsonisation and lysis of certain pathogens are impaired, predisposing to pyogenic infection. Critically, C1q also tethers apoptotic cell debris for clearance by phagocytes; without it, dying cells and nuclear antigens accumulate, are inadequately removed and provoke a break in self-tolerance. This drives the strong association with systemic lupus erythematosus, in which autoantibodies form against these persisting nuclear self-antigens. Defective clearance of circulating immune complexes further contributes to tissue deposition and inflammation. Outcome is largely determined by the severity of associated lupus and the frequency of serious infections; the majority of individuals with complete deficiency develop lupus-like disease. Vigilant management of autoimmunity and infection prophylaxis improve outcomes.

C1q nephropathy without excluding systemic lupus erythematosus Ignoring the underlying light-microscopic lesion that guides treatment and prognosis Over-treating a minimal-change-like course with prolonged aggressive immunosuppression Failing to monitor for later evolution into lupus Regarding mesangial C1q staining as diagnostic in isolation C1q nephropathy is characterised by mesangial deposition of C1q, the recognition component of the classical complement pathway, together with immunoglobulins, forming immune-type deposits without the serological hallmarks of lupus. The mechanism is uncertain: C1q may be deposited as part of immune complexes or bind altered mesangial antigens, activating the classical pathway and provoking a variable injury response that ranges from a pure podocytopathy to mesangial or endocapillary proliferation. The resulting disturbance of the glomerular filtration barrier produces proteinuria, and more proliferative lesions add haematuria and functional decline. Because C1q deposition also features prominently in lupus nephritis, exclusion of systemic lupus is central to the definition. Outcome largely follows the underlying histological pattern and the response of proteinuria to treatment: minimal-change-like disease may respond well, whereas focal segmental glomerulosclerosis or proliferative lesions with steroid resistance carry a higher risk of progressive renal impairment. Long-term follow-up is needed because a minority later manifest systemic lupus.

C2 deficiency — C2 deficiency, Complement C2 deficiency, Hereditary C2 deficiency Idiopathic systemic lupus erythematosus Other early-component deficiencies (C1q, C4) Specific antibody or other primary immunodeficiency with recurrent pneumococcal infection Asplenia or hyposplenism Hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis Acquired hypocomplementaemia from active immune-complex disease CH50 classical-pathway haemolytic assay (low or absent) AH50 alternative-pathway assay (normal) Specific C2 antigenic level Genetic testing for the common C2 deletion Autoimmune serology including ANA where a lupus-like syndrome is suspected Vaccination status and functional antibody responses Documentation of invasive infection history and organisms C2 deficiency is the commonest inherited complement deficiency in people of European ancestry and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Many individuals are asymptomatic, but there is an increased risk of invasive infection with encapsulated organisms, especially Streptococcus pneumoniae. It is associated with autoimmune disease, particularly a lupus-like syndrome that is often photosensitive but tends to be milder and less renal-predominant than C1q-related lupus. The classical-pathway assay (CH50) is markedly reduced or absent while the alternative-pathway assay (AH50) is normal. A specific low C2 level confirms the diagnosis once an isolated classical-pathway defect is identified. A common two base-pair deletion (type I deficiency) accounts for most cases in populations of European descent. Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccination is central to management, alongside prompt treatment of febrile illness. Because the alternative and lectin pathways remain intact, infections are generally less severe than in terminal-pathway defects. Invasive pneumococcal or meningococcal infection Recurrent severe or unusual bacterial infections Signs of meningitis or fulminant sepsis Progressive glomerulonephritis in associated lupus Failure to mount protective responses to vaccination Assuming that being asymptomatic excludes the deficiency, as penetrance is variable. Failing to prioritise pneumococcal and other encapsulated-organism vaccination. Interpreting a low CH50 without confirming which component is deficient. Overlooking C2 deficiency as an underlying cause of a lupus-like syndrome. Delaying antibiotics in a febrile deficient patient while awaiting confirmation. C2 is a component shared by the classical and lectin complement pathways; it is cleaved to form the C3 convertase that amplifies complement activation. In C2 deficiency these pathways cannot efficiently generate C3 convertase, impairing opsonisation and clearance of encapsulated bacteria and predisposing to invasive pneumococcal disease. Reduced classical-pathway function also compromises the clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic material, promoting autoantibody formation and a lupus-like syndrome. Because the alternative pathway is preserved and can still be triggered directly on microbial surfaces, residual complement activity persists, which is why many individuals remain asymptomatic and infections are usually less severe than in complete terminal-pathway deficiency. Many individuals lead normal lives, but there is a lifelong increased risk of invasive encapsulated-organism infection and of developing a usually milder lupus-like autoimmune disease. Vaccination and prompt antibiotic treatment markedly reduce infective mortality.

C3 deficiency — C3 deficiency, Complement C3 deficiency, Hereditary C3 deficiency Secondary C3 consumption (C3 nephritic factor, factor H or factor I deficiency) Other early-component complement deficiencies Severe antibody deficiency or combined immunodeficiency Asplenia or hyposplenism Idiopathic systemic lupus erythematosus C3 glomerulopathy from complement dysregulation C3 antigenic level (markedly low or absent) CH50 and AH50, both reduced in primary deficiency Assays for C3 nephritic factor and regulatory proteins (factor H, factor I) to exclude secondary consumption Genetic testing of the C3 gene Renal function, urinalysis and, where indicated, renal biopsy Autoimmune serology including ANA Vaccination status and infection history documentation C3 is the central convergence point of all complement pathways, so its deficiency produces the most severe complement-related infective phenotype. Patients suffer recurrent, often severe, pyogenic infections with encapsulated organisms from early childhood. Immune-complex disease, including a lupus-like syndrome and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, is an important complication. Both CH50 and AH50 are markedly reduced because C3 is shared by classical, lectin and alternative pathways. A very low or absent C3 antigenic level confirms primary deficiency once secondary consumption is excluded. Secondary C3 lowering from consumption (for example by C3 nephritic factor or factor H/I deficiency) must be distinguished from primary genetic deficiency. Vaccination against encapsulated organisms and prompt, often prophylactic, antibiotic strategies are central to care. Impaired opsonisation is the dominant defect, reflecting the loss of C3b-mediated coating of pathogens. Fulminant sepsis or meningitis Recurrent invasive encapsulated-organism infection Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis Heavy proteinuria or declining renal function Failure to thrive with recurrent infection in a child Failing to distinguish primary genetic deficiency from secondary consumptive hypocomplementaemia. Underestimating the severity of infective risk given C3's central role. Omitting assessment for C3 nephritic factor and regulatory-protein defects. Neglecting vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis in affected children. Missing associated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis until renal function declines. C3 lies at the hub of the complement system, where the classical, lectin and alternative pathways converge; its cleavage products C3b and C3a drive opsonisation, immune-complex solubilisation and downstream membrane attack complex formation. In complete C3 deficiency none of these functions proceeds effectively, so bacteria are poorly opsonised and cleared, leading to recurrent severe pyogenic infection with encapsulated organisms. The failure to solubilise and clear immune complexes and apoptotic debris promotes their tissue deposition, giving rise to lupus-like autoimmunity and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Because C3 is upstream of the terminal components, its absence also impairs the bactericidal membrane attack complex, though opsonic failure predominates clinically. The infective risk is substantial and can be life-threatening, particularly in early childhood, but improves with vaccination and prompt antibiotic treatment; renal involvement is a key long-term determinant of outcome. Overall prognosis is generally more serious than for early-component deficiencies.

C3 glomerulopathy — C3G, dense deposit disease, C3 glomerulonephritis, C3 GN, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis type II, C3 nephritic factor Immune-complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (infection- or immune-complex-mediated) Post-infectious glomerulonephritis Lupus nephritis Cryoglobulinaemic glomerulonephritis Monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance IgA nephropathy Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (also complement-mediated but a thrombotic microangiopathy) Kidney biopsy with immunofluorescence (C3-dominant staining) and electron microscopy to subclassify Serum complement (low C3 with normal C4 typical of alternative-pathway activation) Complement functional assays and detection of C3 nephritic factor and other autoantibodies Assessment of complement regulator levels (e.g. factor H) and terminal complement activity Screening for monoclonal gammopathy, especially in older adults Genetic testing of alternative-pathway complement genes C3 glomerulopathy is defined by glomerular deposition of complement C3 with little or no immunoglobulin on immunofluorescence, reflecting dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway It encompasses two entities distinguished on electron microscopy: dense deposit disease, with dense intramembranous deposits, and C3 glomerulonephritis, with subendothelial and mesangial deposits Presentation ranges from asymptomatic haematuria or proteinuria to nephrotic syndrome or a nephritic picture, often with low serum C3 and a normal C4 An acquired autoantibody, the C3 nephritic factor, stabilises the alternative-pathway C3 convertase and perpetuates complement consumption in many patients Inherited or acquired abnormalities of complement regulators (such as factor H) or activators can underlie the disease Diagnosis rests on kidney biopsy with immunofluorescence and electron microscopy, supported by a complement functional and genetic workup Management combines general glomerular disease measures with immunosuppression in some cases; complement-targeted therapy is used in selected or refractory disease Dense deposit disease may be associated with retinal drusen and acquired partial lipodystrophy Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with crescents Nephrotic-range proteinuria with declining renal function Severe hypertension Progression toward end-stage kidney disease Recurrence in a kidney transplant Misclassifying it as immune-complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis without careful immunofluorescence Overlooking an underlying monoclonal gammopathy driving complement dysregulation in older patients Failing to perform a complement functional and genetic workup once the biopsy pattern is recognised Not anticipating disease recurrence in the allograft Confusing it with atypical HUS, which shares complement dysregulation but presents as thrombotic microangiopathy C3 glomerulopathy results from persistent activation and dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway in the fluid phase, leading to deposition of C3 breakdown products within the glomerulus. Normally the alternative-pathway C3 convertase is tightly regulated by proteins such as factor H and factor I; in this disease acquired autoantibodies (notably C3 nephritic factor, which stabilises the convertase) or genetic abnormalities in complement regulators or activators allow uncontrolled convertase activity and continuous C3 turnover. The resulting C3 fragments accumulate along the glomerular basement membrane and mesangium, producing the characteristic complement-dominant, immunoglobulin-poor staining. This drives glomerular inflammation and a membranoproliferative pattern of injury, manifesting clinically as haematuria, proteinuria and progressive loss of kidney function, with correspondingly low circulating C3. C3 glomerulopathy is frequently progressive, with a substantial proportion of patients reaching end-stage kidney disease over years, and it commonly recurs after transplantation; outcome varies with histological severity and the underlying complement abnormality.

C5 deficiency — C5 deficiency, Complement C5 deficiency, Terminal complement deficiency (C5) Other terminal-component deficiencies (C6, C7, C8, C9) Properdin deficiency Factor D or alternative-pathway defects Asplenia or hyposplenism Antibody deficiency predisposing to infection Acquired complement consumption CH50 and AH50, both markedly reduced in terminal-pathway defects Specific C5 antigenic and functional level Serum bactericidal activity against Neisseria where available Genetic testing of the C5 gene Cultures and PCR during acute infection to identify serogroup Documentation of meningococcal and other vaccination status Screening of at-risk relatives once an index case is identified C5 deficiency is a terminal-pathway defect that markedly predisposes to invasive and recurrent Neisseria infection, particularly meningococcal disease. Meningococcal infections in terminal-complement deficiency often involve unusual or non-groupable serogroups and may recur. It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and, unlike C3 deficiency, is not associated with severe pyogenic infection or major autoimmune disease. CH50 and AH50 are both markedly reduced or absent because the terminal lytic pathway is shared, while individual upstream components are normal. A low or absent C5 antigenic level confirms the diagnosis after terminal-pathway failure is demonstrated. C5 also generates the potent anaphylatoxin C5a, but the clinical phenotype is dominated by defective membrane attack complex formation. Meningococcal vaccination, including serogroup B and the quadrivalent conjugate vaccine, is a cornerstone of management. Any febrile illness warrants urgent assessment and empirical antibiotics because meningococcaemia can progress rapidly. Fever with headache, neck stiffness or a non-blanching rash Rapidly evolving meningococcaemia or septic shock Recurrent episodes of neisserial infection Disseminated gonococcal infection Any febrile illness in a known terminal-complement-deficient patient Not testing for terminal-complement deficiency after a first or recurrent meningococcal infection. Assuming standard childhood immunisation is sufficient without serogroup B and conjugate meningococcal vaccines. Delaying empirical antibiotics in a febrile deficient patient. Confusing terminal-pathway deficiency with early-component defects, which have a different phenotype. Failing to screen and counsel affected family members. C5 is the first component of the terminal complement pathway; once cleaved, C5b nucleates assembly of the C5b-9 membrane attack complex that lyses susceptible organisms, most importantly Neisseria species. In C5 deficiency the membrane attack complex cannot form, so serum bactericidal activity against Neisseria is lost, explaining the striking susceptibility to meningococcal and gonococcal infection. Upstream complement functions such as opsonisation and immune-complex clearance remain intact, which is why pyogenic infection with other encapsulated organisms and lupus-like autoimmunity are not prominent. Loss of C5a generation also blunts a component of chemotaxis, but the dominant clinical consequence is failure of complement-mediated killing of Neisseria. With meningococcal vaccination, patient education and prompt treatment of febrile illness, most individuals do well; the principal risk is recurrent neisserial infection, which although often less fatal than in the general population can still be life-threatening if not treated promptly.

The altered collagen is thought to provoke an inflammatory, periosteal reaction with exuberant subperiosteal new bone formation over affected cortices, accompanied by overlying soft-tissue swelling. or over-replacing glucocorticoid, risking either androgen excess or iatrogenic Cushingoid effects Failing to arrange sensitive multidisciplinary care for ambiguous genitalia 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder of adrenal steroidogenesis caused by variants in CYP11B1, which encodes the enzyme catalysing the final step of cortisol synthesis in the zona fasciculata. Because cortisol cannot be produced efficiently, the loss of negative feedback increases pituitary ACTH secretion, driving adrenal hyperplasia and diverting accumulated precursors down the androgen pathway; the resulting androgen excess produces virilisation, presenting as ambiguous genitalia in genetic females and early virilisation in males. At the same time, the enzyme block causes accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone, a steroid with intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity, which drives sodium retention and volume-dependent, low-renin hypertension often accompanied by hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. This mineralocorticoid excess distinguishes the condition from the salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase form. With glucocorticoid replacement to control ACTH-driven androgen and precursor overproduction, virilisation and hypertension can be managed and growth optimised, though long-standing or poorly controlled disease may leave residual hypertension and its cardiovascular consequences.

Loss of both activities lowers cortisol and sex steroids, and the reduced cortisol removes negative feedback so ACTH rises and drives steroidogenesis into the intact mineralocorticoid pathway. Accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone and corticosterone, both with mineralocorticoid activity, causes sodium retention, volume expansion and low-renin hypertension with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, while the raised corticosterone provides enough glucocorticoid effect to usually prevent adrenal crisis. Sex-steroid deficiency impairs sexual development, producing hypogonadism with absent puberty and, in 46,XY individuals, undervirilised or female-appearing genitalia because androgen synthesis fails. With glucocorticoid therapy to reverse the mineralocorticoid excess and control blood pressure and potassium, plus sex-hormone replacement to induce and maintain secondary sexual characteristics, patients can do well; fertility is impaired and long-term outcome depends on blood-pressure control and adherence.

tendinitis results from deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite crystals within tendon substance, classically the rotator cuff. The process is described as passing through phases: a precalcific phase, a formative phase in which chalk-like calcium accumulates within fibrocartilaginous metaplastic tissue, a resorptive phase in which the deposit softens to a toothpaste-like consistency and is reabsorbed by a vascular and cellular response, and a post-calcific healing phase. The resorptive phase is associated with the most intense pain, owing to raised intratendinous pressure and surrounding inflammation. Because it is a crystal-deposition process, it is distinct from an overload-related degenerative tendinosis. The natural history is often favourable, with many deposits resorbing spontaneously and symptoms settling; barbotage and shockwave help resistant cases, and only a minority require surgery.

Typically affects adults in middle age and shows a female predominance; an association with diabetes and thyroid disorders is recognised. The natural history is self-limiting and cyclical, passing through precalcific, formative (resting), resorptive and postcalcific healing phases. The resorptive phase produces the most severe, acute and often incapacitating pain, correlating with a soft, fluffy, ill-defined deposit on imaging. Dense, well-defined homogeneous deposits usually indicate the quiescent formative phase and tend to be less painful but more persistent. Ultrasound-guided barbotage (needling and lavage), with or without corticosteroid, is an effective option for symptomatic deposits resistant to conservative care. Extracorporeal shockwave therapy can promote fragmentation and resorption of larger, chronic formative-phase deposits. Migration of calcium into the subacromial bursa or intraosseously can mimic infection or malignancy, so correlate radiological appearances with the clinical phase. Fever, systemic upset or markedly raised inflammatory markers suggesting infection rather than the resorptive phase Rapidly enlarging bony or soft-tissue mass raising concern for malignancy Persistent weakness suggesting an associated significant cuff tear Atypical, aggressive or destructive bone changes on imaging Mistaking the acutely painful resorptive phase for septic arthritis and undertaking unnecessary aggressive intervention. Interpreting intraosseous migration of calcium as a destructive tumour or osteomyelitis. Attempting to surgically excise a deposit during the soft resorptive phase when it may resolve spontaneously. Overlooking underlying metabolic or endocrine disease in recurrent or bilateral disease. Calcific tendinitis is a cell-mediated, reactive process rather than a simple dystrophic calcification. In the formative phase, tenocytes undergo fibrocartilaginous metaplasia and mediate deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite crystals within the tendon substance, typically in a hypovascular zone. The deposit may remain quiescent for a prolonged period before entering the resorptive phase, in which vascular ingrowth and macrophage-driven phagocytosis remove the calcium; the accompanying rise in intratendinous pressure and inflammatory response generates acute severe pain. Once resorption is complete, granulation tissue remodels and the tendon architecture is largely restored during the postcalcific phase. The trigger for the cycle is not fully understood, though local hypoxia and metabolic factors are implicated. The majority of cases resolve spontaneously as the deposit is resorbed, with restoration of tendon function and good long-term outcomes. A minority with large persistent formative-phase deposits have prolonged symptoms and may require barbotage, shockwave therapy or, rarely, surgical removal.

Management is multidisciplinary and includes correction of calcium-phosphate imbalance and hyperparathyroidism, sodium thiosulfate, meticulous wound care, analgesia, and avoidance of precipitants such as warfarin Rapidly enlarging necrotic ulcers with surrounding cellulitis and systemic sepsis Severe pain disproportionate to visible skin changes signalling early disease Truncal or proximal (central) lesions carrying a worse prognosis Signs of overwhelming infection in an immunocompromised or dialysis-dependent patient Dismissing severe pain before ulceration appears and delaying diagnosis Continuing warfarin, which aggravates the disease, when an alternative anticoagulant may be appropriate Aggressive debridement or biopsy that can extend non-healing wounds if not carefully weighed Failing to address the underlying calcium-phosphate and parathyroid derangement Calciphylaxis is driven by progressive calcification of the media of small dermal and subcutaneous arterioles, accompanied by intimal fibrosis and microthrombosis, which occludes the vessels and causes ischaemic necrosis of skin and fat. In the uraemic form, chronic kidney disease with a deranged calcium-phosphate product, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and reduced levels of circulating calcification inhibitors allow vascular smooth-muscle cells to transform into an osteoblast-like, calcifying phenotype. A hypercoagulable tendency, exacerbated by warfarin's inhibition of vitamin-K-dependent calcification inhibitors, promotes the thrombotic occlusion that completes tissue infarction. The condition carries high morbidity and mortality, with sepsis from infected necrotic wounds the usual cause of death; central and ulcerated lesions fare worse than distal non-ulcerated disease, though early multidisciplinary intervention can improve outcomes.

Calcium-channel-blocker overdose — calcium antagonist poisoning, CCB toxicity Beta-blocker poisoning Digoxin toxicity Clonidine or central sympatholytic overdose Septic or other distributive shock Primary cardiac conduction disease Continuous cardiac monitoring and serial electrocardiograms Blood glucose (often high) and electrolytes including calcium Identification of the agent and whether it is a modified-release formulation Blood gas and lactate for perfusion Echocardiography in refractory shock Non-dihydropyridine agents (verapamil, diltiazem) typically cause bradycardia, heart block and hypotension Dihydropyridine agents mainly cause vasodilatory hypotension, sometimes with a reflex tachycardia, at least early on Hyperglycaemia is characteristic and reflects blockade of insulin release, helping distinguish it from beta-blocker poisoning A relatively preserved conscious level despite marked hypotension is a recognised feature Management includes calcium, high-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy, vasopressors and supportive care Modified-release preparations can cause delayed and prolonged toxicity requiring extended monitoring Refractory hypotension or high-grade heart block Rising lactate indicating poor perfusion Ingestion of a modified-release preparation with potential delayed collapse Deteriorating conscious level indicating severe shock Confusing it with beta-blocker poisoning (glucose typically high versus low) Failing to anticipate delayed toxicity from modified-release formulations Underusing high-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy Discharging too early after a modified-release ingestion Calcium-channel-blocker overdose blocks L-type calcium channels in cardiac and vascular smooth muscle and in pancreatic islet cells. Reduced calcium entry impairs myocardial contractility and conduction and causes vasodilatation, producing hypotension and, with non-dihydropyridines, bradycardia and block. Blockade of calcium-dependent insulin secretion causes hyperglycaemia and shifts myocardial metabolism away from carbohydrate use, which underlies the benefit of high-dose insulin therapy. Outcomes vary with the agent and dose; with prompt high-dose insulin therapy and vasoactive support many recover, but massive or modified-release ingestions can cause prolonged refractory shock and death.

Calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis — calcium oxalate stones, calcium oxalate kidney stones, CaOx stones, calcium oxalate urolithiasis Uric acid stones, which are radiolucent Calcium phosphate stones Struvite (infection) stones Cystine stones Renal or ureteric urothelial tumour causing haematuria Musculoskeletal or biliary pain mimicking renal colic Acute pyelonephritis Non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder to confirm and localise the stone Analysis of any retrieved stone by infrared spectroscopy or X-ray diffraction Two 24-hour urine collections measuring volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium and pH Serum calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone to exclude primary hyperparathyroidism Urine microscopy for crystalluria and dipstick for haematuria Serum urea, electrolytes and creatinine to assess renal function The commonest type of urinary stone; typically presents with acute loin-to-groin colic accompanied by haematuria, nausea and a restless patient unable to find a comfortable position The principal metabolic drivers are hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, hypocitraturia and a persistently low urine volume Stones are radio-opaque and usually visible on plain imaging, but non-contrast CT is the diagnostic standard for confirming and localising them Urine microscopy classically shows bipyramidal (envelope-shaped) calcium oxalate dihydrate crystals A full metabolic evaluation with repeated 24-hour urine collections is indicated in recurrent stone-formers to target preventive therapy General prevention rests on a generous fluid intake to keep the urine dilute, moderating dietary sodium and animal protein, and maintaining a normal dietary calcium intake Thiazide diuretics lower urinary calcium and potassium citrate corrects hypocitraturia, both reducing recurrence in selected patients Restricting dietary calcium is counterproductive because it frees intestinal oxalate for absorption and raises urinary oxalate Fever or systemic sepsis with an obstructing stone, indicating an infected obstructed kidney that is a urological emergency Acute kidney injury, or obstruction of a solitary or transplanted kidney Intractable pain or persistent vomiting requiring admission Bilateral or complete obstruction Advising a low-calcium diet, which increases oxalate absorption and worsens stone formation Omitting a metabolic evaluation in patients with recurrent stones Overlooking primary hyperparathyroidism as a treatable cause of hypercalciuria Attributing all loin pain to a stone and missing an infected obstructed system Calcium oxalate stones form when the urine becomes supersaturated with calcium and oxalate, permitting crystal nucleation, growth and aggregation. Many stones begin on Randall's plaques, deposits of calcium phosphate in the papillary interstitium that erode through the urothelium and provide a scaffold for calcium oxalate to accrete. Crystallisation is promoted by high urinary calcium and oxalate and by concentrated urine, while citrate and magnesium act as natural inhibitors that complex calcium and oxalate; deficiency of these inhibitors, particularly hypocitraturia, tips the balance toward stone formation. High animal-protein and sodium intake, metabolic acidosis and low fluid intake together create a lithogenic urinary environment. With adequate fluid intake and targeted metabolic treatment the recurrence rate falls substantially, but untreated stone-formers have a high likelihood of a further stone within a few years, and repeated obstruction or intervention can contribute to chronic kidney disease.

Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease — CPPD, calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, pyrophosphate arthropathy, chondrocalcinosis Osteoarthritis Rheumatoid arthritis Gout Haemochromatosis arthropathy Hyperparathyroid bone and joint disease Septic arthritis during acute flares Basic calcium phosphate crystal arthropathy Synovial fluid polarised microscopy for positively birefringent rhomboid CPP crystals Radiographs of the knees, wrists, and pelvis (including the symphysis pubis) for chondrocalcinosis Ultrasound for crystal deposits within cartilage Metabolic screen: ferritin and transferrin saturation, calcium and parathyroid hormone, magnesium, and alkaline phosphatase Synovial fluid cell count and culture to exclude infection during flares Cross-sectional imaging or CT where deep joints or the spine are involved Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease is the umbrella term for the pathology caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition, encompassing several distinct clinical phenotypes Recognised phenotypes include asymptomatic chondrocalcinosis (an imaging finding), acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout), chronic CPP crystal inflammatory arthritis, and CPPD occurring alongside osteoarthritis Chondrocalcinosis on radiographs, the linear calcification of fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage, is the imaging hallmark but is often asymptomatic Chronic CPPD can mimic osteoarthritis, especially in atypical joints such as the wrist, metacarpophalangeal joints, and shoulder, or resemble rheumatoid arthritis with a symmetrical inflammatory pattern, so it is easily misdiagnosed Prevalence rises steeply with age; onset in a younger patient should prompt a search for metabolic causes including haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia, and hypophosphatasia Diagnosis rests on identifying positively birefringent rhomboid CPP crystals in synovial fluid together with supportive imaging There is no crystal-dissolving therapy, so management targets inflammation in the acute and chronic inflammatory forms, treats any underlying metabolic disorder, and applies standard measures for associated osteoarthritis A younger patient with chondrocalcinosis, pointing to an underlying metabolic disorder An acute hot joint requiring exclusion of sepsis Axial (spinal) involvement causing neurological symptoms, as in crowned dens syndrome with acute neck pain and stiffness Labelling chronic CPPD as osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis and missing the crystal diagnosis Overlooking metabolic causes in younger patients Assuming asymptomatic chondrocalcinosis accounts for all of a patient's joint symptoms Forgetting that acute flares can coexist with, or closely mimic, infection CPPD disease results from excessive generation of inorganic pyrophosphate within cartilage and its combination with calcium to form calcium pyrophosphate crystals, which are deposited in fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage. Ageing cartilage and certain metabolic disturbances, such as iron overload, the hypercalcaemia of hyperparathyroidism, and low magnesium, favour crystal formation. Shedding of crystals into the joint provokes acute inflammatory attacks, while chronic deposition contributes to progressive cartilage damage and a degenerative or inflammatory arthropathy, giving rise to the range of clinical phenotypes. Outcomes vary by phenotype: asymptomatic chondrocalcinosis needs no treatment, acute attacks settle with anti-inflammatory therapy, and chronic forms may cause progressive joint damage; identifying and treating an underlying metabolic disease is important, particularly in younger patients.

Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease — CPPD, pseudogout, chondrocalcinosis Gout Septic arthritis Osteoarthritis Rheumatoid arthritis Basic calcium phosphate deposition disease Synovial fluid analysis for crystals and to exclude infection Radiographs showing chondrocalcinosis Screening for metabolic associations (ferritin/transferrin saturation, calcium and parathyroid hormone, magnesium) Inflammatory markers during acute attacks Joint aspiration to exclude septic arthritis when acute Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in cartilage and joints, causing several clinical patterns Acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) presents as an acute monoarthritis, classically of the knee or wrist Chondrocalcinosis is the radiographic finding of cartilage calcification, often of the knee menisci and wrist triangular fibrocartilage Synovial fluid shows positively birefringent, rhomboid crystals, distinguishing it from gout It may mimic osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis or septic arthritis Younger patients or florid disease should prompt a search for metabolic associations such as haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism and hypomagnesaemia Features indistinguishable from septic arthritis requiring aspiration Young-onset or florid disease suggesting a metabolic cause Rapidly destructive arthropathy Systemic upset with an acutely hot joint Assuming an acute hot joint is CPPD without excluding infection Confusing the crystals and management with gout Missing haemochromatosis or hyperparathyroidism in young patients Attributing joint damage solely to osteoarthritis Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease results from the formation and deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals within articular cartilage and fibrocartilage, promoted by abnormal pyrophosphate metabolism and ageing cartilage. Shedding of crystals into the joint space triggers an acute inflammatory response (pseudogout), while chronic deposition contributes to a degenerative arthropathy. Metabolic disorders that alter pyrophosphate or mineral handling, such as haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism and hypomagnesaemia, predispose to earlier or more extensive disease. Acute attacks are self-limiting and treatable, but chronic CPPD can cause a progressive degenerative arthropathy; treating any underlying metabolic disorder is important.

Calve disease (vertebra plana) — Calve vertebral osteochondrosis, vertebra plana of childhood Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma) Vertebral osteomyelitis (including tuberculosis) Leukaemia or lymphoma involving the spine Ewing sarcoma or metastasis Traumatic compression fracture Spinal radiographs showing vertebra plana with preserved discs MRI to characterise the lesion and adjacent structures Biopsy where histiocytosis, infection or tumour must be confirmed Assessment for multifocal histiocytosis Inflammatory and infective screen as indicated Historically described as an osteochondrosis of a vertebral body producing marked flattening (vertebra plana) Most cases originally labelled Calve disease are now recognised to be Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the vertebra Presents in children with back pain and, sometimes, a mild kyphosis, usually without neurological deficit Radiographs show a uniformly flattened vertebral body with preserved adjacent discs The key task is to exclude serious causes of vertebra plana such as histiocytosis, infection and tumour When due to histiocytosis it often reconstitutes with growth, and management is usually conservative Neurological deficit or spinal instability Features suggesting infection or malignancy Multifocal disease suggesting systemic histiocytosis Progressive collapse or deformity Assuming a benign osteochondrosis without excluding histiocytosis, infection or tumour Missing multifocal or systemic histiocytosis Overlooking spinal instability or cord compromise Attributing vertebra plana to trauma without a clear injury Calve disease refers to collapse of a vertebral body to a flattened (vertebra plana) configuration in a child. Although classically attributed to an avascular osteochondrosis, most cases represent an eosinophilic granuloma (Langerhans cell histiocytosis) that weakens and collapses the vertebral body while sparing the intervertebral discs. Other causes of vertebra plana, including infection and neoplasm, share the appearance, so the term describes a radiographic pattern with several possible underlying processes. When due to histiocytosis, remodelling and partial height restoration often occur with growth. When due to Langerhans cell histiocytosis, single-level vertebra plana in a child often reconstitutes with growth and has a good prognosis, though outcome depends on the underlying cause.

Coeliac disease or other small-bowel causes of iron-deficiency anaemia Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with careful inspection of the hernia sac, including retroflexion, to identify the linear erosions Full blood count and iron studies to characterise the anaemia Faecal occult blood testing where occult loss is suspected Repeat or second-look endoscopy if initial examination is negative but suspicion remains Evaluation of the remainder of the gastrointestinal tract to exclude a second source of bleeding Cross-sectional imaging or contrast study to define the size of the hiatus hernia movement together with acid injury and local mucosal ischaemia Often asymptomatic, being discovered during endoscopy for anaemia, though they can occasionally cause acute overt bleeding Easily missed at endoscopy unless the hernia sac is carefully inspected on both forward and retroflexed views Managed with acid suppression and iron replacement, with surgical hernia repair reserved for refractory or recurrent bleeding Acute overt gastrointestinal bleeding with haemodynamic compromise Transfusion-dependent or recurrent anaemia despite medical therapy A large or complex hiatus hernia with strangulation risk Failure of anaemia to correct on iron and acid suppression Missing the lesions by not carefully examining and retroflexing within the hernia sac Attributing iron-deficiency anaemia to another cause and overlooking the hernia Assuming absence of symptoms excludes clinically important blood loss Not considering surgical repair when bleeding recurs despite medical treatment Cameron lesions are linear erosions or ulcers that develop on the crests of gastric folds where they are compressed by the diaphragmatic hiatus within a hiatus hernia. Their formation is attributed to a combination of mechanical trauma from repetitive movement of the herniated stomach against the diaphragm, chronic acid exposure, and localised mucosal ischaemia at the point of constriction. The resulting slow, repetitive blood loss commonly manifests as iron-deficiency anaemia, and the risk increases with the size of the hernia. Most cases respond well to acid suppression and iron replacement with resolution of anaemia, and surgical repair of the hiatus hernia is effective for the minority with refractory or recurrent bleeding.
