hypophosphatasia Skeletal survey demonstrating long-bone bowing, hypoplastic scapulae, and thoracic changes Karyotype and molecular testing of SOX9 to confirm the diagnosis Assessment of genital anatomy and gonadal status with imaging and endocrine input Respiratory and airway evaluation including for laryngotracheomalacia Cervical spine imaging for instability Audiological assessment given frequent hearing loss Characterised by bowing (campomelia) of the long bones, particularly the tibiae and femora, often with a cutaneous dimple over the apex of the bend Caused by dominant variants in or around SOX9, a master transcription factor for chondrocyte differentiation and testis development Sex reversal is a key association, with many chromosomally male (46,XY) infants having female or ambiguous external genitalia Respiratory distress is common and frequently fatal in the neonatal period, related to a small thorax, tracheobronchomalacia, and hypotonia Additional features include a large head with a flat face and small chest, cleft palate, talipes, and hypoplastic scapulae Radiographs show bowed long bones, hypoplastic scapulae, non-mineralised thoracic pedicles, small iliac wings, and only eleven pairs of ribs in many cases Diagnosis relies on the radiographic pattern, karyotype with genital assessment, and SOX9 molecular testing Severe neonatal respiratory failure from a small thorax and airway malacia Airway collapse requiring urgent support Discordance between chromosomal and phenotypic sex requiring sensitive multidisciplinary management Cervical instability with neurological signs Assuming phenotypic sex reflects the karyotype and mismanaging gonadal and genital issues Attributing long-bone bowing solely to osteogenesis imperfecta without genetic testing Underestimating airway malacia as a cause of respiratory failure Overlooking hearing loss and cervical instability in survivors Campomelic dysplasia arises from haploinsufficiency of SOX9, a transcription factor essential both for chondrocyte differentiation and cartilage matrix gene expression and for testis determination. Disrupted SOX9 function impairs endochondral ossification, producing bowed and hypoplastic bones and a small thorax, while defective testicular development in genetically male fetuses causes the frequent gonadal sex reversal. Airway cartilage deficiency and a narrow chest contribute to the respiratory insufficiency that dominates the neonatal course. The classic form is frequently lethal in the neonatal period owing to respiratory failure, though a milder acampomelic variant and rare longer-term survivors exist. Survivors face significant respiratory, orthopaedic, and developmental morbidity and require multidisciplinary care.

Camurati-Engelmann disease (progressive diaphyseal dysplasia, TGFB1) — progressive diaphyseal dysplasia, Engelmann disease, TGFB1-related diaphyseal dysplasia, CED Other craniotubular hyperostoses such as sclerosteosis and Van Buchem disease Osteopetrosis Ribbing disease (a related but more localised diaphyseal sclerosis) Hyperostosis from chronic osteomyelitis Paget disease of bone Primary inflammatory myopathy given the muscle weakness Plain radiographs demonstrating symmetrical fusiform diaphyseal cortical thickening Skeletal survey or bone scintigraphy to assess extent and activity Genetic testing for TGFB1 mutations Bone turnover markers and inflammatory markers Cranial imaging when skull-base involvement or cranial neuropathy is suspected Assessment of muscle strength and, where needed, tests to exclude primary myopathy An autosomal dominant sclerosing bone dysplasia caused by activating mutations in TGFB1 Presents in childhood or adolescence with limb pain, a waddling gait, muscle weakness and wasting, and easy fatigability Radiographs show symmetrical fusiform cortical thickening of the diaphyses of the long bones, sparing the epiphyses and metaphyses The skull base may thicken and narrow foramina, occasionally producing cranial neuropathies, headache, and hearing or visual disturbance The proximal myopathy and slender body habitus with reduced muscle bulk can dominate the clinical picture and mimic a primary muscle disorder Bone turnover markers may be raised, and disease activity can wax and wane over time Management is symptomatic; glucocorticoids can relieve bone pain and improve strength in many patients, and physical rehabilitation is important Progressive cranial neuropathy with visual loss, deafness, or facial weakness from skull-base narrowing Features of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus Severe intractable bone pain limiting mobility Rapidly worsening weakness suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis Misdiagnosing the proximal myopathy as a primary muscle disease and overlooking the bone dysplasia Attributing headaches and hearing loss to unrelated causes rather than skull-base hyperostosis Failing to recognise the symmetrical diaphyseal pattern that distinguishes it from focal lesions Not offering a trial of glucocorticoids for disabling bone pain when appropriate Camurati-Engelmann disease results from gain-of-function mutations in the gene encoding transforming growth factor beta 1 (TGFB1). The mutations increase TGF-beta signalling, which enhances osteoblast activity and bone formation at the periosteal and endosteal surfaces of the diaphyses. The excessive but disorganised cortical apposition produces symmetrical diaphyseal hyperostosis with narrowing of the medullary canal. Involvement of the skull base can encroach on cranial nerve foramina, and altered marrow space and cytokine signalling may contribute to the anaemia and systemic features seen in some patients. The course is variable and often chronic; many patients have significant bone pain and weakness but a normal lifespan, and symptoms may improve in adulthood or with glucocorticoid therapy, though skull-base disease can cause lasting neurological deficits.

Canalicular adenoma — Canalicular type monomorphic adenoma Basal cell adenoma Pleomorphic adenoma Adenoid cystic carcinoma Polymorphous adenocarcinoma Mucocele (clinical mimic on the lip) Other minor salivary gland adenomas Incisional or excisional biopsy for definitive histology Fine-needle aspiration cytology (of limited value in the lip) Ultrasound of the lip or cheek where useful Immunohistochemistry including S100 and bcl-2 MRI for larger or deeper lesions to assess extent Clinical examination of other minor gland sites for multifocal nodules A benign minor salivary gland adenoma with a striking predilection for the upper lip, and less commonly the buccal mucosa. It typically affects older adults with a slight female predominance and presents as a slow-growing, submucosal, painless nodule. The histological hallmark is columnar to cuboidal cells arranged in single or double branching, anastomosing cords that periodically separate to form bead-like canaliculi. The stroma is characteristically loose, hypocellular and richly vascular, unlike the stroma of basal cell adenoma. Multifocality is well recognised and can present as several discrete nodules within the upper lip. In contrast to most salivary tumours, it lacks a true myoepithelial component; tumour cells are S100 positive and often bcl-2 positive. It is readily mistaken clinically for a mucocele of the upper lip, but its solid nature at excision distinguishes it. The principal serious differential is adenoid cystic carcinoma, which the cords and canaliculi can superficially resemble on small biopsies. Infiltrative growth or ill-defined margins on histology Rapid growth or new pain Mucosal ulceration Perineural symptoms such as numbness suggesting a malignant mimic Fixation to underlying tissues Misdiagnosing it as adenoid cystic carcinoma on a small or fragmented biopsy Overlooking multifocal nodules within the upper lip Mistaking it clinically for a simple mucocele and delaying excision Proceeding to overly aggressive surgery for a benign lesion Canalicular adenoma is a benign neoplasm arising from the ductal (luminal) epithelial cells of minor salivary glands, most typically those of the upper lip. The neoplastic columnar cells retain ductal differentiation and are notable for the absence of a neoplastic myoepithelial population, which sets it apart from pleomorphic and basal cell adenomas. The tumour cells form long, branching, anastomosing cords that intermittently draw apart to create elongated canalicular lumina, set within a conspicuously loose and highly vascularised stroma that is prone to haemorrhage and cystic change. Its frequent multifocality within the upper lip suggests a field origin from multiple minor gland ducts rather than a single clonal focus. Prognosis is excellent, as the tumour is benign and local excision is curative. Apparent recurrence usually reflects a separate multifocal nodule rather than incomplete removal.

Canaliculitis — lacrimal canaliculitis Chronic or recurrent conjunctivitis Dacryocystitis Punctal or canalicular tumour Nasolacrimal duct obstruction Herpetic or other viral lid disease Clinical diagnosis from the pouting punctum and expressible concretions Microbiological examination and culture of expressed material Assessment of the lacrimal drainage system Imaging only if a tumour or extensive disease is suspected Examination for concretions at the time of any procedure A chronic infection of the lacrimal canaliculus that is frequently misdiagnosed as recurrent conjunctivitis Presents with a red, tender, pouting punctum, unilateral discharge and epiphora Expression of the canaliculus may release characteristic concretions (sulphur-like granules) The classic organism is Actinomyces israelii, though other bacteria and fungi occur It is often unilateral and resistant to topical antibiotics alone Definitive treatment usually requires removal of the concretions, commonly by canaliculotomy and curettage A mass or atypical lesion suggesting canalicular tumour Spread to dacryocystitis or surrounding tissues Failure to resolve after concretion removal Marked recurrent disease Treating it repeatedly as conjunctivitis and missing the diagnosis Relying on topical antibiotics without removing concretions Overlooking a canalicular tumour Not sending expressed material for microbiology Canaliculitis is infection within the lacrimal canaliculus, most classically by the filamentous bacterium Actinomyces israelii, which forms concretions (dacryoliths) within the lumen. These concretions harbour organisms and perpetuate the infection, causing chronic inflammation, a pouting inflamed punctum and discharge. Because topical antibiotics cannot eradicate organisms sequestered within the concretions, mechanical removal is generally required for cure. The prognosis is excellent once the concretions are removed, though cases treated with antibiotics alone tend to recur until the sequestered material is cleared.

Canavan disease — aspartoacylase deficiency, ASPA deficiency, spongy degeneration of the brain Other infantile leukodystrophies including Alexander disease Metachromatic leukodystrophy and Krabbe disease Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts Mitochondrial encephalopathies Other causes of macrocephaly with developmental regression Urinary N-acetylaspartate measurement ASPA gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis Brain MRI showing diffuse symmetric white matter change MR spectroscopy demonstrating an elevated N-acetylaspartate peak Carrier screening and genetic counselling for at-risk families Developmental and feeding assessments for supportive care An autosomal recessive leukodystrophy caused by mutations in the ASPA gene resulting in deficiency of aspartoacylase Enzyme deficiency leads to accumulation of N-acetylaspartate, which is measurably elevated in urine and can be detected as a raised NAA peak on MR spectroscopy Classic infantile disease presents in the first months with hypotonia, poor head control, macrocephaly, and progressive developmental failure As disease progresses, hypotonia often gives way to spasticity, with seizures, feeding difficulties, and optic atrophy It is one of the leukodystrophies with increased carrier frequency in the Ashkenazi Jewish population, making carrier screening relevant in that group MRI shows diffuse, symmetric white matter disease, and elevated N-acetylaspartate on spectroscopy strongly supports the diagnosis Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating elevated urinary N-acetylaspartate and by ASPA gene testing Macrocephaly in an infant with developmental regression should raise suspicion and prompt appropriate metabolic and imaging workup Progressive loss of milestones with seizures in an infant Feeding and swallowing failure risking aspiration and malnutrition Rapidly enlarging head circumference Respiratory compromise in advanced disease Attributing macrocephaly to benign causes without considering a leukodystrophy Overlooking the diagnostic value of urinary N-acetylaspartate and MR spectroscopy Failing to offer carrier screening and counselling in high-risk populations Delaying supportive measures for feeding and seizures Canavan disease arises from biallelic ASPA mutations causing deficiency of aspartoacylase, the enzyme that hydrolyses N-acetylaspartate in the brain. The resulting accumulation of N-acetylaspartate is thought to disturb myelin maintenance and fluid balance, producing spongy vacuolar degeneration of white matter. The intramyelinic oedema and dysmyelination give the characteristic diffuse leukodystrophy and clinical picture of progressive neurological failure with macrocephaly. Classic infantile Canavan disease is progressive with limited life expectancy and no curative therapy, so care is supportive; milder variants with later onset follow a more variable and slower course.

Cancer cachexia — cachexia, cancer anorexia-cachexia syndrome, tumour cachexia, wasting syndrome Simple starvation or undernutrition from inadequate intake Sarcopenia of ageing without underlying malignancy Malabsorption or gastrointestinal obstruction Depression causing anorexia and weight loss Hyperthyroidism or other hypermetabolic states Adrenal insufficiency Documentation of weight trajectory and body-mass index over time Assessment of muscle mass and function where available Inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein and albumin as prognostic indicators Nutritional assessment including intake and symptoms limiting eating Screening for reversible contributors such as nausea, constipation, oral problems, and depression Cancer cachexia is a multifactorial syndrome of ongoing loss of skeletal muscle, with or without fat loss, that cannot be fully reversed by conventional nutritional support It is driven by both reduced intake (anorexia) and metabolic derangement, so simply increasing calories does not restore muscle mass A consensus framework stages it as pre-cachexia, cachexia, and refractory cachexia, which guides how aggressively to intervene Diagnostic pointers include weight loss over roughly five percent in six months, or lesser weight loss in the setting of low body-mass index or sarcopenia Systemic inflammation, reflected in raised C-reactive protein and other markers, is central and correlates with worse outcomes Management is multimodal: nutritional support, resistance exercise where feasible, symptom control of nausea and early satiety, and treatment of the underlying cancer when possible In refractory cachexia near the end of life the emphasis shifts from reversing weight loss to comfort, and aggressive artificial feeding usually offers little benefit Family distress about reduced eating is common and benefits from explanation that appetite loss is part of the illness, not a failure of care Rapid, accelerating weight and muscle loss suggesting progressive or refractory disease Profound weakness with inability to maintain basic function Evidence of impending gastrointestinal obstruction limiting intake Severe deconditioning increasing risk of falls, pressure injury, and infection Assuming increased calorie provision alone will reverse muscle loss Pursuing burdensome artificial nutrition in refractory, end-stage disease with no meaningful benefit Overlooking treatable symptoms that limit intake, such as nausea, constipation, and oral candidiasis Failing to address family anxiety about the patient not eating Missing depression as a contributor to anorexia and weight loss Cancer cachexia results from tumour- and host-derived pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IL-1) and tumour-specific catabolic factors that drive a hypermetabolic, catabolic state. These mediators increase resting energy expenditure, promote skeletal muscle proteolysis and lipolysis, induce insulin resistance, and act centrally to suppress appetite. The net effect is a negative energy and protein balance dominated by muscle wasting that persists despite feeding, distinguishing cachexia from simple starvation in which muscle is relatively spared. Cachexia is a marker of advanced disease and independently predicts reduced tolerance of anticancer treatment, poorer quality of life, and shorter survival. Refractory cachexia, typically in the setting of advanced, treatment-unresponsive cancer with a short prognosis, is not reversible, and care goals appropriately shift toward comfort.

therapy Total pain acknowledges that physical, psychological, social, and spiritual distress interact, so addressing suffering broadly improves pain control Signs of opioid toxicity such as excessive sedation, confusion, myoclonus, pinpoint pupils, or slowed respiration requiring urgent dose review New back pain with neurological signs suggesting malignant spinal cord compression Sudden severe pain suggesting pathological fracture or visceral perforation Rapidly escalating opioid requirement indicating disease progression or an emergent complication Failing to prescribe prophylactic laxatives when starting an opioid Under-dosing because of undue fear of addiction or respiratory depression in appropriate palliative use Relying on opioids alone for neuropathic pain that needs adjuvants Ignoring reduced renal clearance in older adults, risking accumulation and toxicity Treating physical pain while neglecting the psychological and spiritual dimensions of suffering Cancer pain may be nociceptive (somatic pain from bone or soft-tissue involvement, or visceral pain from organ infiltration and stretch) or neuropathic (from tumour compression or infiltration of nerves, or from treatment such as chemotherapy or radiation). Persistent nociceptive input sensitises peripheral nociceptors and central pathways, producing hyperalgesia and allodynia. Opioids act at central and peripheral opioid receptors to modulate pain transmission, while adjuvants target neuropathic mechanisms, inflammation, or specific complications, and the multiplicity of mechanisms underpins the use of combination therapy. Most cancer pain can be well controlled with systematic assessment and stepwise pharmacological management, allowing meaningful quality of life. Poorly controlled or neuropathic pain, or pain complicating advanced disease, may be more difficult and often requires specialist palliative input and multimodal or interventional approaches.

Ocular involvement threatening vision Isolation of Candida auris or other resistant species with implications for treatment and infection control Dismissing a positive Candida blood culture as a contaminant Delaying effective antifungal therapy while awaiting species identification Leaving an infected central catheter in place Omitting fundoscopy and follow-up cultures, missing ocular disease or persistent infection Candida species are common commensals of the gastrointestinal tract, skin, and mucosa. Disruption of these barriers, by mucosal breakdown, surgery, or indwelling devices, together with impaired host defences from neutropenia, immunosuppression, or broad-spectrum antibiotics that eliminate competing bacterial flora, allows Candida to translocate into the bloodstream or seed from a catheter biofilm. Once in the circulation, the organism can disseminate haematogenously to the eyes, heart valves, bones, and deep organs, producing metastatic foci that are difficult to eradicate without prolonged therapy and source control. Candidemia carries high attributable mortality, especially with delayed effective antifungal therapy, failure to remove infected catheters, persistent fungaemia, or severe underlying illness; earlier appropriate treatment and source control improve survival.

Candidiasis — Candida infection, invasive candidiasis, candidemia Dermatophytosis (tinea) on glabrous skin (Chap. 60, p.432) Tinea (pityriasis) versicolor due to Malassezia furfur (Chap. 60, p.432) Lichen planus / oral leukoplakia for oral white lesions Other invasive fungal infections in neutropenia: invasive aspergillosis and other molds (Chap. 79, p.578) Invasive aspergillosis and other molds (necrotic nodules) in immunocompromised hosts (Chap. 79, p.578; rash chapter) Disseminated cryptococcosis (molluscum-like nodular lesions) (rash chapter) Mucormycosis (rash chapter) Bacterial/septic endophthalmitis, including from endocarditis (Roth's spots also in leukemia, diabetes) (Chap. 34, p.269) KOH preparation of skin/mucosal scrapings demonstrating yeast and pseudohyphae for mucocutaneous candidiasis (Chap. 60, p.433) Culture of lesional material (Chap. 60, p.433) Blood cultures for candidemia (note insensitivity; see pitfalls) (Chap. 34, p.269; Chap. 79) Dilated funduscopic examination to detect candidal endophthalmitis in candidemia (Chap. 34, p.269) Erythema nodosum (tender lower-extremity nodules) for nodular eruptions (rash chapter) Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) (rash chapter) Psoriasis / eczema in intertriginous areas Candidiasis spans a spectrum: mucocutaneous disease (oral thrush, esophageal, vulvovaginal, intertriginous, paronychia/onycholysis) that is usually localized, versus rare systemic, life-threatening invasive disease such as candidemia and disseminated candidiasis (Chap. 60, p.432-433). The usual causative organism is Candida albicans; these yeasts are normal saprophytic inhabitants of the gastrointestinal tract that overgrow and cause disease when host defenses are altered (Chap. 60, p.432-433). Oral candidiasis (thrush) appears as white plaques on the tongue or buccal mucosa; angular fissured macerated lesions at the mouth corners (perleche) are seen with poorly fitting dentures and may be candidal (Chap. 60, p.432-433). Intertriginous candidal lesions are characteristically edematous, erythematous, and scaly with scattered 'satellite pustules'; in males the penis, scrotum, and inner thighs are often involved (Chap. 60, p.432-433). In contrast to dermatophyte infections, candidal infections are frequently painful and accompanied by a marked inflammatory response (Chap. 60, p.432-433). Disseminated candidiasis (often due to Candida tropicalis) may present with a triad of fever, myalgias, and eruptive nodules; hematogenous cutaneous disease shows multiple raised papules with systemic signs (rash chapter, p.190; Chap. 79, p.621). Candidemia and chronic disseminated candidiasis are recognized complications in neutropenic patients because Candida species are endogenous gastrointestinal flora (Chap. 79, p.578). Candidemia is a recognized cause of endogenous endophthalmitis from hematogenous seeding; Roth's spots and retinal hemorrhages were illustrated in a liver transplant patient with candidemia from immunosuppression (Chap. 34, p.269). Candidemia or suspected disseminated candidiasis in a neutropenic or immunosuppressed host (Chap. 79, p.578) Visual loss, ocular pain, or floaters in a patient with candidemia or indwelling IV catheters (endophthalmitis) (Chap. 34, p.269) Fever, myalgias, and eruptive cutaneous nodules suggesting disseminated candidiasis (rash chapter, p.190) Presence of an indwelling intravascular catheter or central line in a patient with candidemia (Chap. 34, p.269; Chap. 79) Systemic therapy is usually reserved for immunosuppressed patients or those with chronic/recurrent disease who fail topical therapy, NOT routine mucocutaneous cases (Chap. 60, p.433). Oral nystatin is effective ONLY for candidiasis of the gastrointestinal tract, not for systemic disease (Chap. 60, p.433). Failure to remove predisposing factors (broad-spectrum antibiotics, chronic moisture/maceration) leads to treatment failure (Chap. 60, p.433). In endogenous endophthalmitis, visual loss may sometimes be the ONLY symptom even without prominent ocular pain or injection (Chap. 34, p.269). Candida species (most often C. albicans) are normal saprophytic commensals of the gastrointestinal tract and skin. They overgrow and become pathogenic when local or systemic host defenses are disrupted, e.g., by broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, diabetes mellitus, or immunosuppression. Mucocutaneous disease results from overgrowth at moist, macerated surfaces; invasive disease arises when the organism gains bloodstream access, frequently via intravascular catheters or the gut in neutropenic hosts (endogenous flora), producing candidemia and hematogenous (disseminated) seeding to organs, skin, and the eye (Chap. 60, p.432-433; Chap. 79, p.578). Mucocutaneous candidiasis is generally benign and responds to removal of predisposing factors plus topical or, when needed, systemic antifungal therapy. Systemic involvement is rare but life-threatening; candidemia and chronic disseminated candidiasis are serious complications in neutropenic and immunosuppressed patients (Chap. 60, p.432-433; Chap. 79, p.578). Harrison frames candidiasis along a clinical spectrum rather than a formal grading scale: localized mucocutaneous disease (oral, esophageal, vulvovaginal, intertriginous, cutaneous) versus rare systemic/invasive disease (candidemia, chronic disseminated/hepatosplenic candidiasis). Invasive disease risk rises with prolonged profound neutropenia (ANC <500/uL) (Chap. 60, p.432-433; Chap. 79, p.578).

developmental delay A type I interferonopathy caused by mutations affecting the proteasome, classically PSMB8, impairing protein degradation Presents in infancy or early childhood with recurrent fevers, violaceous annular skin plaques, and progressive lipodystrophy Facial and limb fat loss produces a characteristic pinched appearance, while periorbital oedema and swelling are common Additional features include arthralgia, hepatosplenomegaly, growth impairment, and delayed physical development A raised interferon signature in blood is a key laboratory clue supporting an interferonopathy Skin biopsy shows an atypical mononuclear and neutrophilic dermal infiltrate rather than a simple neutrophilic dermatosis Janus kinase (JAK) inhibition targets the interferon pathway and can improve systemic and cutaneous features, though damage may be only partly reversible Progressive organ dysfunction from sustained interferon-driven inflammation Severe growth failure and developmental delay Intracranial calcification or neurological involvement Refractory systemic inflammation despite conventional immunosuppression Attributing early features to juvenile dermatomyositis or systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and missing the interferonopathy Failing to request an interferon signature when standard autoimmune workup is inconclusive Expecting full reversal of lipodystrophy with treatment Relying on conventional immunosuppression that inadequately targets interferon signalling CANDLE syndrome is a proteasome-associated autoinflammatory disease, most often from mutations in PSMB8 and related proteasome or immunoproteasome subunit genes. Defective proteasome function impairs clearance of ubiquitinated and oxidised proteins, causing cellular stress that triggers excessive type I interferon production. This interferon-dominated inflammation drives recurrent fevers, an atypical neutrophilic dermatosis, panniculitis with resulting lipodystrophy, and multi-organ involvement. The prominent interferon signature explains both the clinical phenotype and the rationale for JAK inhibition, which dampens interferon signalling. CANDLE is a chronic progressive disease; JAK inhibition can substantially reduce inflammation and improve quality of life, but established lipodystrophy and organ damage may persist.

Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome — CHS Cyclic vomiting syndrome Gastroparesis Bowel obstruction Raised intracranial pressure or other central cause of vomiting Metabolic or endocrine causes of recurrent vomiting History of chronic cannabis use and the hot-water bathing behaviour Targeted tests to exclude obstruction and metabolic causes rather than repeated broad workup Assessment of hydration and electrolytes during acute episodes Consideration of cyclic vomiting syndrome in the differential Confirmation by resolution with cannabis cessation Recurrent episodes of severe nausea and vomiting in the context of long-term, regular cannabis use A highly characteristic feature is temporary symptom relief from hot showers or baths The clinical pattern resembles cyclic vomiting syndrome, with well periods between attacks It is frequently misdiagnosed, and patients often undergo repeated investigations before it is recognised Definitive resolution follows sustained cessation of cannabis, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic Acute episodes are managed supportively, and topical capsaicin and certain antiemetic or sedative agents are used adjunctively Severe dehydration or electrolyte disturbance Features suggesting bowel obstruction Neurological signs suggesting a central cause Haematemesis or severe abdominal pain Not asking about cannabis use and the hot-water pattern Repeated extensive investigation before recognising the syndrome Attributing episodes to cyclic vomiting syndrome without exploring cannabis use Overlooking dehydration and electrolyte disturbance in acute attacks Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome is a paradoxical effect of chronic cannabis use, in which prolonged stimulation of the endocannabinoid system disrupts its normal regulation of gastrointestinal motility, the emetic reflex and thermoregulation. Proposed mechanisms include downregulation or dysregulation of cannabinoid receptors and effects on hypothalamic thermoregulatory centres, which may explain the relief obtained from hot water. The syndrome resolves when the causative cannabinoid exposure is removed, confirming its central role. The syndrome resolves fully with sustained cannabis cessation, but recurs if use resumes; complications relate mainly to dehydration and electrolyte disturbance during severe attacks.

Cannabis and Cannabis Use Disorder — Marijuana use disorder, CUD, Cannabis dependence, Marijuana abuse Primary psychotic disorder (schizophrenia) versus cannabis-induced psychosis Other substance use disorders (alcohol, nicotine, opioids, stimulants) often co-occurring Primary anxiety, depressive, or panic disorder versus cannabis-induced symptoms Cyclic vomiting syndrome versus cannabis hyperemesis syndrome Other causes of impaired cognition, low IQ, or poor school performance in adolescents Urine immunoassay/confirmatory testing for 11-nor-carboxy-THC (11-COOH-THC), the inactive long-lived metabolite DSM-5 criteria-based clinical assessment for cannabis use disorder severity Screening for comorbid substance use (alcohol, nicotine, opioids, stimulants) and for psychiatric comorbidity (psychosis, depression, suicidality) In pregnancy: assessment of fetal growth given association with lower birth weight and preterm delivery Cyclic vomiting syndrome (mimics cannabis hyperemesis syndrome) Primary schizophrenia or other psychotic disorder (mimics cannabis-induced psychosis) Primary anxiety/panic disorder (mimics acute high-dose cannabis intoxication) EVALI (e-cigarette/vaping product use-associated lung injury) linked to vitamin E acetate diluent in black-market THC e-liquids Cannabis is among the most widely used psychoactive substances; surveys cited estimate tens of millions of monthly users in the U.S., including a substantial number of adolescents and young adults aged 12-25. Marijuana is legally distinguished from hemp by Delta-9-THC content: material exceeding 0.3% Delta-9-THC by dry weight is marijuana, while 0.3% or less is hemp; the principal euphoric and medicinal effects are mediated by Delta-9-THC acting on type 1 cannabinoid receptors (CB1R). Product potency has risen sharply: flower can contain 20-30% Delta-9-THC, vape concentrates are advertised up to ~75%, and solid extracts ('shatter') up to ~95%, though many high claims appear exaggerated; higher potency is linked to greater addiction and psychosis risk. Inhalation (smoking, vaping, 'dabbing') gives rapid, highly bioavailable absorption with quick onset, conditions associated with increased addiction risk; edibles have slower, less predictable onset and carry a higher risk of accidental overdose, particularly in children and inexperienced users. Following smoking, plasma Delta-9-THC peaks within 5-10 minutes, but a hysteresis exists because brain levels keep rising during the early distribution (alpha) phase (t1/2 ~6 min) even as plasma falls; subjective peak effects occur at 20-30 minutes and total effect lasts roughly 4-8 hours. Urine drug testing detects the inactive metabolite 11-nor-carboxy-THC (11-COOH-THC), whose terminal half-life is ~20 to 35+ hours, so cannabis remains detectable for days in occasional users and weeks in frequent users with saturated fat stores. Regular use produces tolerance, so a given plasma Delta-9-THC level does not reliably predict impairment, which has hampered regulation of cannabis-impaired driving; Delta-9-THC nonetheless impairs judgment, motor coordination, and reaction time, increasing crash risk. Cannabis use disorder (CUD) is a DSM-5 diagnosis defined by a problematic pattern of use causing clinically significant impairment or distress; criteria include craving, tolerance, a withdrawal syndrome, and failure to meet role obligations from recurrent use and drug seeking. The withdrawal syndrome peaks within 1-3 days of stopping and manifests as anxiety, restlessness, insomnia, depression, and reduced appetite; most symptoms resolve within about 2 weeks, but insomnia often persists longer and may drive relapse. Chronic high-dose use can cause cannabis hyperemesis syndrome, presenting as recurrent cycles of severe nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, and is a growing reason for ED visits and hospitalization. High-potency cannabis (>10% THC) can trigger acute psychotic episodes even on first exposure; these are usually transient but may become chronic with continued use and can trigger or worsen schizophrenia in vulnerable individuals. Synthetic Delta-9-THC (dronabinol) is approved for chemotherapy-induced nausea and appetite stimulation, and a Delta-9-THC:CBD formulation is approved in some countries for chronic pain and MS-related spasticity (efficacy in MS largely based on patient report); there are currently no FDA-approved medications specifically for CUD. Acute psychosis, severe anxiety, paranoia, or panic after high-potency or high-dose exposure Tachycardia with acute cannabis toxicity, especially in children or naive users who accidentally ingest edibles Cannabis hyperemesis syndrome with intractable vomiting, dehydration, and abdominal pain Depression and suicidality, particularly with adolescent onset of use Respiratory symptoms suggesting EVALI in vaping users Use in pregnancy given fetal growth and neurodevelopmental concerns Assuming a plasma Delta-9-THC level reliably reflects impairment; tolerance breaks this correlation and complicates impaired-driving assessment. Underestimating edible dosing: delayed and variable onset (amplified by fatty meals increasing bioavailability 200-400%) leads naive users to redose and overdose. Overstating the clinical role of minor cannabinoids (e.g., CBD) or terpenes at the concentrations found in marijuana, where evidence of relevance is limited and largely unproven. Trusting product potency labels, which testing has shown to be frequently inflated. Perceiving intoxicating hemp-derived products (e.g., Delta-8-THC and others) as safe or 'legal'; some such products can be considerably more potent than Delta-9-THC. Overlooking EVALI risk historically tied to vitamin E acetate diluent rather than cannabis itself. Delta-9-THC is mainly a partial agonist at G protein-coupled cannabinoid receptors CB1R and CB2R, with euphorigenic effects mediated through CB1Rs on excitatory glutamatergic and inhibitory GABAergic interneurons and glial cells in brain regions processing stress, mood, and reward. These receptors are effectors of the endocannabinoid system (ECS), physiologically driven by endogenous ligands 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG, a full agonist) and anandamide (a partial agonist) that are synthesized and degraded on demand to give temporally and regionally precise modulation. Exogenous cannabinoids, defined by dose and duration rather than this 'just-in-time' synaptic signaling, disrupt ECS neuroregulation. Reward is thought to be mediated by modulation of glutamatergic and GABAergic activity in the ventral tegmental area, from which dopaminergic neurons project to the nucleus accumbens where rewarding experiences are reinforced; anxiolytic effects are mediated via the amygdala. Regular use is associated with broad but reversible reduction in cannabinoid receptor density (recovering by ~28 days of abstinence). Perturbation of ECS signaling during early fetal development can affect neuronal development, migration, and connectivity. Most acute psychotic episodes are transient, but regular use can render them chronic, and cannabis may trigger or worsen schizophrenia in vulnerable individuals; adolescent and higher-frequency, higher-potency use carries the strongest associations with later psychotic disorder. Receptor downregulation is largely reversible, recovering toward control levels within about 28 days of abstinence. Withdrawal generally resolves within roughly 2 weeks, although insomnia may persist and promote relapse. Earlier age of initiation, higher use frequency, and higher-THC products increase the risk of developing CUD and of progression to other substance use disorders. Adolescent use has been associated with lower grades, lower IQ, and higher school dropout, though causation is not established. Cannabis use disorder is diagnosed and graded by DSM-5 criteria (problematic use pattern causing clinically significant impairment or distress), with features including craving, tolerance, a withdrawal syndrome, and failure to fulfill role obligations from recurrent use and drug seeking.

complication of chronic heavy use Assess and address comorbid mental illness, since cannabis is frequently used to self-medicate anxiety, insomnia, or low mood Emergence of psychotic symptoms, particularly in adolescents or those with a family history Suicidal ideation, especially with comorbid depression Severe dehydration or electrolyte disturbance from cannabinoid hyperemesis Escalating use with functional decline in education, work, or relationships Dismissing cannabis use as harmless and missing a genuine use disorder Overlooking cannabis as a contributor to anxiety, low mood, or psychosis Missing cannabinoid hyperemesis and attributing vomiting to other causes Neglecting the recognised withdrawal syndrome that maintains use Failing to address comorbid psychiatric illness driving self-medication Cannabis use disorder involves the endocannabinoid system, with delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol acting as a partial agonist at CB1 receptors and modulating dopaminergic reward signalling in the mesolimbic pathway. Chronic exposure produces receptor downregulation and neuroadaptation underlying tolerance and withdrawal, and heavy adolescent use during neurodevelopment may have lasting effects on cognition and psychosis risk, modulated by genetic and environmental vulnerability. Cannabis use disorder often follows a chronic course, particularly with early-onset heavy use, but many people reduce or stop use with psychosocial treatment and maturation. Prognosis is better with later onset, lower potency use, strong social support, and treatment of comorbid disorders, and worse with adolescent onset, high-potency use, and untreated psychiatric comorbidity.

Cap myopathy — Cap disease, Congenital cap myopathy Nemaline myopathy Congenital fibre type disproportion Centronuclear and myotubular myopathy Core myopathies (central core, multiminicore) Congenital muscular dystrophy Congenital myasthenic syndromes Muscle biopsy with oxidative, trichrome and immunohistochemical stains plus electron microscopy Gene testing for TPM2, TPM3 and ACTA1 Serum creatine kinase Pulmonary function and overnight respiratory studies Electromyography and nerve conduction studies Spinal imaging for scoliosis Cardiac assessment where indicated A rare congenital myopathy defined by peripheral, crescent-shaped caps of disorganised sarcomeres beneath the sarcolemma, rich in thin-filament proteins and lacking ATPase activity. Associated most often with mutations in TPM2 and TPM3 (beta- and alpha-tropomyosin) and occasionally ACTA1. Presents with congenital or childhood-onset hypotonia, proximal and facial weakness, an elongated myopathic face and a high-arched palate. Respiratory involvement is common and is often the leading source of morbidity. Regarded as part of the tropomyosin-related thin-filament myopathy spectrum, overlapping with nemaline myopathy and congenital fibre type disproportion. Caps stain for actin, tropomyosin and alpha-actinin and are best demonstrated on oxidative and trichrome preparations. Skeletal deformity, including scoliosis and chest-wall changes, may develop. Nocturnal hypoventilation or overt respiratory failure Feeding and swallowing difficulty with aspiration risk Rapidly progressive scoliosis Failure to thrive in infancy Missing small caps when oxidative and immunostains are not performed. Labelling the disease nemaline myopathy without recognising the cap pathology on the same thin-filament spectrum. Underestimating respiratory compromise. Not pursuing genetic confirmation for counselling. Cap myopathy arises from mutations, predominantly in tropomyosin genes, that alter regulation of the actin-myosin interaction and the calcium sensitivity of the thin filament. Mutant tropomyosin disturbs sarcomere assembly, producing peripheral subsarcolemmal zones of poorly organised, incompletely developed myofilaments (the caps) that are rich in thin-filament proteins. Impaired regulation of contraction underlies the muscle weakness. The disorder is usually static or slowly progressive, and long-term outlook depends chiefly on respiratory muscle involvement and orthopaedic complications, with many patients retaining ambulation.

Capgras syndrome — Capgras delusion, delusion of doubles, illusion des sosies, imposter syndrome (delusional) Fregoli syndrome (belief that strangers are a familiar persecutor in disguise) Prosopagnosia (impaired face recognition without delusion) Lewy body and other dementias with misidentification Schizophrenia and delusional disorder Delirium with misidentification phenomena Reduplicative paramnesia for place Cognitive assessment to detect underlying dementia or focal deficits Neuroimaging (MRI brain) to identify right hemisphere, frontal, or degenerative changes Bloods and metabolic screen to exclude reversible organic causes Electroencephalography where delirium or seizures are considered Psychiatric evaluation for a primary psychotic or mood disorder Medication and toxicology review The archetypal delusional misidentification syndrome, in which the patient believes a familiar person (often spouse or parent) has been replaced by an identical-looking imposter or double The face is recognised as looking correct, but the sense of familiarity or emotional connection is absent, producing the conviction of substitution May also extend to pets, objects, or places believed to have been duplicated or replaced Classically described in schizophrenia and mood disorders but increasingly recognised in organic disease, including dementia (especially Lewy body), stroke, and traumatic brain injury Right hemisphere and frontal dysfunction are frequently implicated, and organic causes should always be excluded Can carry a risk of aggression directed at the supposed imposter Management targets the underlying psychiatric or neurological disorder, with antipsychotics used for the delusional content Threats or violence directed at the misidentified person Abrupt onset with fluctuating consciousness suggesting delirium or acute brain lesion Rapid cognitive decline pointing to a neurodegenerative process Focal neurological signs indicating structural pathology Assuming a purely psychiatric cause and missing an organic or neurodegenerative disorder Overlooking the risk of violence toward the supposed imposter Confusing Capgras with prosopagnosia or with Fregoli syndrome Failing to reassess cognition over time as dementia may declare itself later Capgras syndrome is a delusional misidentification thought to arise from a disconnection between intact facial recognition and the affective response that normally accompanies recognition of a familiar person. Damage to or dysfunction of pathways linking face-processing regions (fusiform cortex) with limbic structures (amygdala) that assign emotional significance leaves the face recognised but stripped of its felt familiarity. The mismatch is then rationalised as the person being an imposter. Right frontal and temporoparietal dysfunction, impairing belief evaluation and self-monitoring, is proposed to allow the aberrant belief to be maintained. It occurs in both primary psychiatric illness and a range of neurodegenerative and structural brain disorders. Outcome depends on the underlying cause; delusions accompanying treatable psychiatric illness may resolve with therapy, whereas those due to progressive dementia tend to persist or recur. The associated risk of harm to the misidentified individual requires active safety planning.

Intestinal capillariasis — Capillaria philippinensis infection, intestinal capillariosis, Paracapillaria philippinensis infection Other soil-transmitted or fish-borne helminthiases Giardiasis and other malabsorptive protozoal infections Coeliac disease and tropical sprue Inflammatory bowel disease Other causes of protein-losing enteropathy Chronic infective diarrhoea from other pathogens Stool microscopy for characteristic eggs, larvae and adult worms Repeated stool examination given intermittent and sometimes scanty shedding Serum albumin and total protein to assess protein loss Electrolyte measurement to detect depletion Full blood count and assessment of nutritional status Small-bowel biopsy when stool examination is repeatedly negative Intestinal capillariasis is caused by the nematode Capillaria philippinensis, acquired by eating raw or undercooked small freshwater or brackish-water fish, and is endemic to parts of Southeast Asia It is a potentially fatal helminthiasis, distinguished from most intestinal worms by its ability to build up enormous worm numbers through internal autoinfection The illness presents with chronic watery diarrhoea, borborygmi, abdominal pain and progressive weight loss Severe infection causes a protein-losing enteropathy with malabsorption, leading to hypoproteinaemia, electrolyte depletion, muscle wasting and oedema, and death if untreated Diagnosis rests on identifying the characteristic peanut-shaped eggs, larvae or adult worms in the stool, sometimes requiring repeated examination Because autoinfection sustains and amplifies the burden, prolonged anthelmintic courses are needed rather than a single dose Albendazole or mebendazole given as an extended course is the mainstay, together with correction of fluid, electrolyte and protein deficits Severe hypoproteinaemia with generalised oedema Profound electrolyte disturbance and dehydration Marked cachexia from prolonged malabsorption Relapse after apparently successful treatment due to ongoing autoinfection Giving a single short anthelmintic course, which fails to control autoinfection and permits relapse Missing the diagnosis when stool shedding is scanty and only one sample is examined Attributing chronic diarrhoea and wasting to other malabsorptive disease without stool parasitology in endemic areas Underestimating the severity of fluid, electrolyte and protein losses Capillaria philippinensis normally cycles between fish-eating birds and freshwater fish, with humans infected by consuming raw fish containing infective larvae. The larvae mature into adults that burrow into the mucosa of the small intestine. Crucially, the females can produce larvae that develop in situ and reinvade the same host's intestine, a process of internal autoinfection that allows the worm population to multiply to very large numbers over time. This heavy mucosal infestation damages the small-bowel epithelium, causing villous atrophy and a severe protein-losing enteropathy with malabsorption of nutrients, protein and electrolytes; the resulting hypoproteinaemia, wasting, oedema and electrolyte disturbance account for the potentially fatal course of untreated disease. Untreated heavy infection is frequently fatal, but with an adequate prolonged anthelmintic course and correction of protein, fluid and electrolyte deficits the outlook is good, though relapse can occur if treatment is too short.

Capillary malformation — Port-wine stain, Naevus flammeus Naevus simplex (salmon patch) Macular precursor of an early infantile haemangioma Arteriovenous malformation Capillary malformation of an overgrowth syndrome (Klippel-Trenaunay, CLOVES, Sturge-Weber) Angioma serpiginosum Cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita Clinical diagnosis, with dermoscopy as an adjunct Contrast-enhanced brain MRI when Sturge-Weber syndrome is suspected (V1 distribution) Ophthalmology review with intraocular pressure measurement for at-risk facial lesions Limb imaging and length assessment where overgrowth is suspected Genetic testing (GNAQ, RASA1, PIK3CA) in syndromic presentations Slow-flow malformation present at birth as a flat, sharply demarcated pink to red patch that grows proportionately with the child and does not involute. Caused by somatic activating mutations in GNAQ (and related genes such as GNA11), the same pathway implicated in Sturge-Weber syndrome. Facial lesions in the frontal or ophthalmic (V1) distribution carry a risk of Sturge-Weber syndrome with leptomeningeal and ocular involvement. Tends to darken, thicken and develop nodular cobblestoning with age. Overgrowth of underlying soft tissue and bone can occur, especially with segmental facial or limb lesions. Pulsed dye laser is the treatment of choice for cosmetically significant lesions and is most effective when started early. Distinguish from the common, transient naevus simplex (salmon patch or stork bite), which usually fades in infancy. A geographic, well-demarcated capillary stain on a limb may signal an overgrowth syndrome such as capillary malformation-arteriovenous malformation (RASA1) or a PIK3CA-related overgrowth disorder. V1 or forehead facial distribution with seizures or developmental concern (Sturge-Weber syndrome) Glaucoma risk with periocular lesions Progressive limb overgrowth or asymmetry Warmth, thrill or bruit suggesting a high-flow arteriovenous malformation Confusing a persistent port-wine stain with a self-resolving salmon patch. Failing to screen V1-distribution facial lesions for Sturge-Weber syndrome and glaucoma. Overlooking a limb overgrowth syndrome behind an apparently simple capillary stain. Missing an evolving arteriovenous malformation masquerading as a capillary stain. Capillary malformation is a congenital slow-flow malformation of dermal capillaries and postcapillary venules arising from somatic mosaic activating mutations, most commonly in GNAQ, which constitutively activate Galpha-q signalling through the MAPK/ERK pathway in endothelial cells. This causes progressive ectasia of superficial dermal vessels and deficient perivascular neural regulation. Unlike vascular tumours there is no endothelial proliferation; the vessels are structurally abnormal and dilate over time, accounting for progressive darkening and thickening of the lesion. A capillary malformation is a lifelong lesion that tends to darken and thicken with age. Laser therapy lightens most lesions, and the wider prognosis depends on any associated syndromic features.

syndrome results from germline loss-of-function variants in RASA1 or EPHB4, genes that regulate RAS-MAPK signalling in vascular endothelium and thereby control the balance between arterial, venous and Most affected individuals have only benign multifocal capillary stains and a good prognosis, but the presence of a fast-flow arteriovenous malformation, particularly in the brain or spine, can lead to serious or life-threatening complications; lifelong awareness and targeted surveillance are advised for gene carriers.

It is relatively resistant to killing by complement and phagocytes and evades early innate immune clearance, which allows it to establish bacteraemia. In hosts with impaired splenic function or other immune compromise the organism proliferates unchecked, triggering an intense systemic inflammatory response, endotoxin-driven activation of coagulation and disseminated intravascular coagulation. The resulting microvascular thrombosis produces purpura fulminans, peripheral gangrene, septic shock and multi-organ failure. Localised bite-wound infection generally does well with prompt antibiotics, but fulminant Capnocytophaga sepsis, particularly in asplenic or immunocompromised patients, carries a high mortality and survivors may suffer limb loss from gangrene, underscoring the need for early recognition and treatment.

This pressure impedes venous and lymphatic return, causing serosanguinous fluid to accumulate diffusely in the scalp. Because the fluid is superficial and not confined by periosteal attachments, it crosses suture lines and resolves quickly as the fluid is reabsorbed. Caput succedaneum is benign and resolves spontaneously within days without sequelae.

recessive genetic risk CARASIL is caused by biallelic mutations in HTRA1, a serine protease that normally represses transforming growth factor-beta signalling. Loss of HTRA1 function dysregulates this pathway and impairs extracellular matrix homeostasis in the walls of small cerebral arteries, leading to intimal thickening, loss of smooth muscle cells, and hyaline arteriosclerosis. The resulting non-atherosclerotic arteriopathy causes chronic ischaemia and a diffuse leukoencephalopathy, while the same signalling disturbance contributes to the associated alopecia and degenerative spondylosis. CARASIL is relentlessly progressive, with accumulating motor and cognitive disability from early adulthood and shortened life expectancy; there is no treatment that alters the underlying arteriopathy.

Carbamate poisoning — carbamate insecticide poisoning, carbamate cholinergic toxicity Organophosphate poisoning Nerve agent exposure Cholinergic mushroom (muscarinic) poisoning Asthma or acute pulmonary oedema (for respiratory features) Other causes of coma with excess secretions Clinical recognition of the cholinergic toxidrome and exposure history Red-cell (and plasma) cholinesterase activity where available Oxygenation and airway assessment given bronchorrhoea risk Cardiac monitoring Assessment for co-ingestants, especially the solvent carrier Carbamates inhibit acetylcholinesterase and cause a cholinergic toxidrome similar to organophosphate poisoning Features combine muscarinic effects (salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, bronchorrhoea and bronchospasm), nicotinic effects (fasciculations and weakness) and central effects Bronchorrhoea and respiratory failure are the main causes of death Unlike organophosphates, the enzyme inhibition is reversible and self-limiting, so recovery is usually faster Atropine is the mainstay to counter muscarinic effects; routine use of an oxime is generally considered unnecessary The classic intermediate syndrome and delayed neuropathy of organophosphates are not typical of carbamates Copious respiratory secretions or respiratory failure Bradyarrhythmia or haemodynamic instability Depressed consciousness with an unprotected airway Seizures Assuming the prolonged course and oxime need of organophosphate poisoning Under-atropinising and failing to dry pulmonary secretions Overlooking the toxic hydrocarbon solvent carrier Delaying airway support in a patient with bronchorrhoea Carbamates bind and inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic and nicotinic synapses and producing the cholinergic syndrome. In contrast to organophosphates, the carbamate-enzyme bond does not undergo irreversible ageing and dissociates spontaneously within hours, so cholinesterase activity recovers relatively quickly. This reversibility explains the generally shorter course and the reduced role for oxime therapy compared with organophosphate poisoning. Because enzyme inhibition is reversible, prognosis is generally better than for organophosphates, and most patients recover within a day or two with prompt atropinisation and respiratory support.

enzyme assay requires liver tissue and is now rarely needed Acute management is emergency ammonia removal (haemodialysis/haemofiltration if severe), nitrogen scavengers, arginine and protein restriction; liver transplantation is definitive for severe disease Neonatal hyperammonaemic coma requiring emergency dialysis Cerebral oedema and raised intracranial pressure from severe hyperammonaemia Rapidly rising ammonia with deteriorating consciousness at any age Decompensation during catabolic illness, high protein intake or surgery Failure of ammonia to fall despite scavenger and dietary measures Delaying ammonia measurement and dialysis in an encephalopathic neonate Confusing CPS1 with OTC deficiency by not checking orotic acid Not separating CPS1 from NAGS deficiency, missing the carglumic-acid-responsive disorder Under-dialysing when ammonia is dangerously high and scavengers alone are inadequate Failing to establish an emergency regimen and long-term dietary/scavenger plan Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 is the mitochondrial enzyme that initiates the urea cycle by condensing ammonia and bicarbonate into carbamoyl phosphate, a reaction that absolutely requires N-acetylglutamate as an allosteric activator. When CPS1 activity is deficient, waste nitrogen cannot enter the urea cycle, so ammonia accumulates to toxic levels while downstream urea cycle intermediates (citrulline, arginine) are low. Because carbamoyl phosphate is not overproduced, it is not shunted into the pyrimidine pathway, so orotic acid excretion remains low, a key feature shared with NAGS deficiency and distinguishing both from the more distal OTC deficiency. Hyperammonaemia is directly neurotoxic, causing cerebral oedema and encephalopathy, particularly in the neonate. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The severe neonatal form carries a high risk of death or permanent neurological disability related to the depth and duration of hyperammonaemia, whereas milder late-onset disease can be managed medically; liver transplantation corrects the hepatic enzyme defect and can prevent further crises.

Carbon monoxide poisoning — CO poisoning, carbon monoxide toxicity, carboxyhaemoglobinaemia Viral illness or gastroenteritis Migraine or tension headache Cyanide poisoning (smoke inhalation) Diabetic or other metabolic coma Acute coronary syndrome Blood carboxyhaemoglobin level by co-oximetry (venous or arterial) Arterial blood gas with metabolic acidosis and lactate ECG and cardiac biomarkers to detect myocardial ischaemia Neuroimaging in severe cases (basal ganglia changes) Pregnancy test in women of childbearing age given fetal risk Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with far greater affinity than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and causing profound tissue hypoxia despite a normal arterial oxygen tension Symptoms are non-specific (headache, nausea, dizziness, confusion) and are frequently misdiagnosed as viral illness or food poisoning, especially when several household members are affected Standard pulse oximetry is misleading because it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin; a co-oximeter or blood carboxyhaemoglobin level is required The classic cherry-red skin appearance is uncommon and unreliable, and its absence does not exclude poisoning The cornerstone of treatment is high-flow 100 percent oxygen, which greatly shortens the elimination half-life of carboxyhaemoglobin Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is considered for severe poisoning (loss of consciousness, neurological signs, cardiac involvement, pregnancy, or very high levels) to reduce delayed neurological sequelae Delayed neuropsychiatric syndrome (cognitive impairment, movement disorders, personality change) can develop days to weeks after apparent recovery Suspect concurrent cyanide poisoning in victims of smoke inhalation from enclosed-space fires Any loss of consciousness, seizure, or focal neurological deficit Chest pain, arrhythmia, or ECG evidence of ischaemia Metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate indicating severe tissue hypoxia Pregnancy, as the fetus is disproportionately affected Multiple people from the same environment falling ill simultaneously Trusting a normal pulse oximeter reading and normal arterial oxygen tension to exclude poisoning Attributing symptoms to a viral illness and discharging the patient back to the source Relying on the cherry-red sign, which is usually absent Overlooking coexisting cyanide toxicity in fire victims Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas produced by incomplete combustion. It binds haemoglobin with roughly 200-250 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin, which both reduces oxygen-carrying capacity and shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve leftward, impairing oxygen release to tissues. CO also binds myoglobin and inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, causing cellular hypoxia and oxidative stress. The brain and heart, with high oxygen demand, are most vulnerable, and a lipid peroxidation and inflammatory cascade underlies the delayed neurological injury. Mild poisoning usually resolves fully with oxygen, but severe exposure can cause death or lasting neurological and cardiac damage; delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae may appear after seemingly complete recovery, and early high-flow or hyperbaric oxygen reduces this risk.

to localise and stage the tumour Carcinoid heart disease is a complication of the carcinoid syndrome caused by vasoactive substances, particularly serotonin, released by metastatic neuroendocrine tumours It characteristically affects the right-sided heart valves, producing tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis or regurgitation with fibrous plaque-like thickening of the endocardium Left-sided valve involvement is uncommon because the lungs inactivate circulating serotonin, but it can occur with a patent foramen ovale or bronchial carcinoid It usually develops in patients with liver metastases, since hepatic clearance of tumour products is then bypassed Right heart failure with peripheral oedema, ascites, and elevated venous pressure is the typical late presentation Urinary while significant valve disease may require surgical valve replacement Progressive right heart failure with ascites and oedema Carcinoid crisis with flushing, haemodynamic instability, and bronchospasm, especially around procedures Severe symptomatic valve dysfunction requiring surgical evaluation Rapidly rising cardiac biomarkers indicating advancing cardiac disease Attributing right heart failure to more common causes and missing an underlying neuroendocrine tumour Not screening for cardiac involvement in patients with established carcinoid syndrome Failing to prevent and treat carcinoid crisis around surgery and interventions Delaying valve surgery until right ventricular function is irreversibly impaired Metastatic neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumours, typically of midgut origin with hepatic metastases, secrete serotonin and other vasoactive mediators into the systemic circulation. These substances stimulate fibroblast proliferation and deposition of fibrous tissue on the endocardium and valve leaflets, predominantly on the right side of the heart. The resulting plaque-like fibrosis retracts and immobilises the tricuspid and pulmonary valves, causing regurgitation and stenosis that lead to volume overload and right ventricular failure. Pulmonary inactivation of serotonin largely protects the left heart. Cardiac involvement is a major determinant of survival in carcinoid syndrome and historically indicated advanced disease with a poor outlook, but somatostatin analogue therapy, tumour-directed treatment, and timely valve surgery have improved outcomes.
