cardiac MRI can further characterise disease and right ventricular function Controlling the tumour and serotonin secretion with somatostatin analogues and other antitumour therapies is central but does not reverse established valvular fibrosis Valve replacement surgery in appropriately selected patients is the only effective treatment for severe valvular disease and can improve symptoms and prognosis Progressive right heart failure with ascites, oedema and hepatic congestion Severe tricuspid regurgitation or pulmonary stenosis on echocardiography Syncope or low cardiac output Rapidly rising NT-proBNP or urinary 5-HIAA Need for non-cardiac surgery where carcinoid crisis risk compounds cardiac risk Not screening for cardiac involvement with echocardiography and NT-proBNP in patients with carcinoid syndrome Attributing oedema and ascites to the tumour or liver metastases rather than to right heart failure Delaying valve surgery until right ventricular function is irreversibly impaired Assuming medical control of the tumour will reverse established valvular disease Failing to plan perioperative carcinoid crisis prophylaxis for cardiac or non-cardiac surgery Carcinoid heart disease is driven by chronic exposure of the endocardium to circulating serotonin and other vasoactive mediators released by a metastatic neuroendocrine tumour. Serotonin stimulates fibroblast proliferation and deposition of fibrous tissue (carcinoid plaque) on the valve leaflets, subvalvular apparatus and endocardium, causing leaflet thickening, retraction and immobility. Because the pulmonary vascular bed inactivates these mediators, disease is characteristically right-sided; left-sided disease implies mediators reaching the left heart via a bronchial primary or an intracardiac shunt. The result is tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary valve stenosis or regurgitation, leading to volume and pressure overload of the right heart and progressive right ventricular failure. Carcinoid heart disease is a leading cause of death in carcinoid syndrome and markedly worsens prognosis once right heart failure develops; timely valve replacement in selected patients can relieve symptoms and improve survival, although established fibrosis is irreversible.

Carcinoid tumour — well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour, neuroendocrine tumour (carcinoid), gastrointestinal or bronchial carcinoid Poorly differentiated (high-grade) neuroendocrine carcinoma Adenocarcinoma of the same primary site such as bowel or lung Other functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours Lymphoma or gastrointestinal stromal tumour of the small bowel Appendicitis or appendiceal mucocoele for appendiceal lesions Inflammatory bowel disease or mesenteric ischaemia mimicking mesenteric involvement Metastatic neuroendocrine tumour of unknown primary Chromogranin A, with 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA if functional disease is suspected Somatostatin receptor PET/CT (DOTATATE) for staging and receptor status Multiphase contrast CT or MRI to define primary, mesenteric and hepatic disease Endoscopy, colonoscopy or bronchoscopy for accessible primaries, with biopsy Histology with Ki-67 index and mitotic count for WHO grading Echocardiography if carcinoid syndrome or a raised 5-HIAA suggests cardiac involvement FDG-PET in higher-grade tumours to assess more aggressive biology Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour arising most often in the gastrointestinal tract (notably small bowel, appendix and rectum) and the bronchopulmonary system; current WHO classifications increasingly use the term neuroendocrine tumour in place of carcinoid Classified by embryological origin into foregut (bronchus, stomach, duodenum, pancreas), midgut (jejunoileum, appendix, proximal colon) and hindgut (distal colon, rectum), which influences secretory profile and behaviour Most are non-functioning and present late with local or mass effects or with metastases; small bowel tumours characteristically incite a mesenteric desmoplastic reaction causing obstruction or ischaemia Carcinoid syndrome develops in only a minority and usually implies hepatic metastases, or a bronchial or ovarian primary that bypasses portal clearance Appendiceal and small rectal tumours are frequently incidental and, when small and localised, have an excellent prognosis after local resection Grading by Ki-67 index and mitotic count (WHO G1 to G3) is central to prognosis and distinguishes well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour from poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma Chromogranin A is the main circulating tumour marker and somatostatin receptor PET/CT (DOTATATE) is the imaging modality of choice for staging Somatostatin analogues control symptoms and slow progression, with peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, targeted agents and liver-directed therapies available for advanced disease Small bowel obstruction or mesenteric ischaemia from the desmoplastic reaction New carcinoid syndrome indicating likely hepatic metastases Rapidly progressive disease or a high Ki-67 suggesting a high-grade tumour Carcinoid heart disease with right heart failure or a new murmur Risk of carcinoid crisis around surgery, anaesthesia or tumour manipulation Assuming all carcinoids are benign, when higher-grade and metastatic tumours behave aggressively Omitting Ki-67 grading, which changes prognosis and treatment Overlooking a small bowel primary as the cause of an unexplained mesenteric mass or obstruction Failing to give perioperative somatostatin analogue prophylaxis against carcinoid crisis Confusing well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour with poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma, which require very different management Carcinoid (well-differentiated neuroendocrine) tumours arise from enterochromaffin and other neuroendocrine cells dispersed through the gut and bronchial epithelium. They can synthesise bioactive amines and peptides, most notably serotonin, stored in neurosecretory granules. When these mediators drain into the portal circulation they are largely inactivated by the liver, so systemic effects (carcinoid syndrome) usually appear only with hepatic metastases or extra-portal primaries. Locally, midgut tumours provoke a fibrotic desmoplastic reaction in the mesentery that can cause bowel obstruction or ischaemia. Tumour behaviour ranges from indolent low-grade lesions to more aggressive higher-grade tumours, stratified by proliferative activity. Well-differentiated, localised carcinoid tumours, especially small appendiceal and rectal lesions, have an excellent prognosis; in metastatic disease prognosis depends on grade and tumour burden but is frequently indolent, with prolonged survival achievable using modern therapies.

Carcinoma of Unknown Primary — CUP, Cancer of Unknown Primary, Occult primary malignancy, Metastatic carcinoma of unknown origin Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (commonly misdiagnosed as liver-presenting CUP) (Harrison 22e p.731) Extragonadal germ cell tumor in men with poorly/undifferentiated midline adenopathy (Harrison 22e pp.732, 735) Occult breast carcinoma in women with isolated axillary adenopathy (Harrison 22e pp.732, 735) Primary peritoneal papillary serous carcinoma versus colon or pancreaticobiliary cancer in women with peritoneal carcinomatosis (Harrison 22e p.735) Prostate carcinoma in men with blastic bone-only metastases and elevated PSA (Harrison 22e p.735) Lung or head-and-neck primary in older smokers presenting with mediastinal adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.735) Contrast CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis is the standard baseline workup in all CUP patients absent contraindication (Harrison 22e p.732) Thorough history (risk factors, prior surgeries, family history) and physical exam including digital rectal exam in men and breast/pelvic exam in women (Harrison 22e p.731) Mammography (and breast MRI if mammogram/ultrasound negative) in women with metastatic adenocarcinoma, especially isolated axillary adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.732) For cervical squamous CUP: CT/MRI plus laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy, upper endoscopy, and consideration of staging tonsillectomy (Harrison 22e p.732) 18-FDG-PET, most useful in squamous cervical CUP (identifies a head/neck primary in about 21-30%) and in solitary metastasis or bone-metastasis candidates for aggressive multimodality therapy (Harrison 22e p.732) Serum PSA in men with adenocarcinoma and osteoblastic metastasis; beta-hCG and AFP for suspected extragonadal germ cell tumor (Harrison 22e pp.731-732) Detailed pathology with hematoxylin-eosin and a tiered IHC panel (e.g., CK7/CK20, TTF-1, CDX-2, GCDFP-15/GATA3, PSA, thyroglobulin) plus molecular/tissue-of-origin profiling and next-generation sequencing (Harrison 22e pp.732-734) Endoscopy/colonoscopy/bronchoscopy reserved for symptomatic patients or those with findings suggesting high diagnostic yield (Harrison 22e p.732) Lymphoma, metastatic melanoma, and metastatic sarcoma (excluded from CUP because they have specific histology/staging) (Harrison 22e p.731) Peritoneal mesothelioma mislabeled as peritoneal carcinomatosis (calretinin/D2-40 positive; BerEp4/MOC-31 negative) (Harrison 22e p.735) CUP is a biopsy-proven malignancy whose anatomic site of origin stays unidentified despite a standardized, detailed diagnostic workup; it ranks among the 10 most frequently diagnosed cancers worldwide and accounts for roughly 3-5% of all malignancies (Harrison 22e p.731). Most authorities restrict the CUP label to epithelial or undifferentiated cancers and exclude lymphoma, metastatic melanoma, and metastatic sarcoma, since those have distinct histology and stage-based management even without an identified primary (Harrison 22e p.731). On light microscopy about 60-65% of CUP is adenocarcinoma and roughly 5% is squamous cell carcinoma, with the remaining 30-35% being poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma/carcinoma or poorly differentiated neoplasm; neuroendocrine tumors make up about 2% (Harrison 22e p.732). Most serum tumor markers (CEA, CA-125, CA 19-9, CA 15-3) are nonspecific and do not localize the primary; in contrast, PSA tissue/serum staining and thyroglobulin are among the most specific markers but have low yield because prostate and thyroid cancers rarely present as CUP (Harrison 22e pp.731-732). CK7 and CK20 cytokeratin patterns help narrow the putative primary: CK7 marks lung, ovary, endometrium, breast, and upper GI/pancreaticobiliary tumors, while CK20 is expressed in GI epithelium, urothelium, and Merkel cells (Harrison 22e p.733). TTF-1 nuclear staining is positive in about 68% of lung adenocarcinomas and roughly 25% of squamous lung cancers and helps distinguish a lung primary from metastatic adenocarcinoma in pleural, mediastinal, or parenchymal sites (Harrison 22e p.733). Comprehensive genomic profiling shows about 85% of CUP samples carry at least one clinically relevant genomic alteration, averaging about 4.2 alterations per tumor; the most common are TP53 (about 55%), KRAS (about 20%), CDKN2A (about 19%), and ARID1A (about 11%) (Harrison 22e pp.733-734). Tissue-agnostic biomarkers matter in a minority of CUP cases: MSI-high / mismatch-repair-deficient tumors and high tumor mutational burden tumors, as well as NTRK fusion-positive tumors, identify candidates for established histology-agnostic therapy (Harrison 22e p.734). Adequate tissue acquisition (preferably excisional or core needle biopsy rather than fine-needle aspiration alone) is critical, both for histology/IHC and for molecular profiling that can suggest a primary and actionable biomarkers (Harrison 22e p.732). Liver is a common site of CUP presentation, so intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is frequently misdiagnosed as CUP; cholangiocarcinoma incidence is rising while CUP incidence is declining, partly due to improved molecular diagnostics and clinician awareness (Harrison 22e p.731). DNA methylation profiling predicted a primary in about 87% of 216 CUP patients in one study, and tissue-of-origin classifier assays suggest a plausible primary in roughly 70-80% of patients, though accuracy cannot be fully verified because the true primary is by definition unconfirmed (Harrison 22e pp.733-734). Latent primary cancers (a new primary emerging after months to years) are uncommon with modern imaging, occurring in 5% or fewer of CUP patients, typically in indolent presentations or highly treatment-responsive disease (Harrison 22e p.732). Liver, brain, or adrenal metastatic involvement, which carries a poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.735) Disseminated disease with two or more involved sites (Harrison 22e pp.734-735) Poor performance status and elevated serum LDH, which are adverse prognostic factors (Harrison 22e p.734) Peritoneal carcinomatosis from metastatic adenocarcinoma, raising concern for gastric, appendiceal, colon, or pancreaticobiliary primaries (Harrison 22e p.735) No IHC stain is 100% sensitive or specific; under- or overinterpretation should be avoided, and poor differentiation reduces sensitivity even of hallmark markers (Harrison 22e p.732). CDX-2 positivity, while used for GI adenocarcinomas, can also occur in tumors with enteric/mucinous differentiation from other sites such as mucinous ovarian cancer (Harrison 22e p.733). Tissue antigenicity and IHC interpretation are affected by antigen retrieval, fixation/processing, observer variability, antibody performance, and tissue heterogeneity or inadequacy from small biopsies (Harrison 22e p.733). Pathologic features should not always override clinical or radiologic findings when deciding to test for therapeutic biomarkers such as EGFR, ALK, or HER2 (Harrison 22e p.733). More IHC stains are not necessarily better; staining must be interpreted alongside clinical presentation and imaging, with close clinician-pathologist communication (Harrison 22e p.732). Not all peritoneal carcinomatosis in women is primary peritoneal serous carcinoma; careful pathology can reveal a colon or pancreaticobiliary profile or mislabeled mesothelioma (Harrison 22e p.735). Two randomized trials of gene-expression-directed site-specific therapy versus empiric chemotherapy failed to show a significant survival benefit, so molecular classifier results must be interpreted cautiously (Harrison 22e pp.733-734). The reasons cancers present without an identifiable primary remain unclear. One hypothesis is that the primary tumor regresses after seeding metastases or stays too small to detect, possibly contained or eliminated by host defenses including the immune system. Alternatively, CUP may reflect a distinct malignant event producing increased metastatic spread or survival relative to the primary; whether CUP metastases represent a genetically and phenotypically unique clone is unresolved. Searches for a unique CUP signature have been unrevealing: aneuploidy occurs in about 70% of metastatic adenocarcinoma/undifferentiated CUP, and overexpression of RAS, BCL2 (about 40%), HER2 (about 11%), and P53 (about 26-53%) is seen but is shared with many other malignancies. Adenocarcinoma CUP is more often driven by RTK/Ras/MAPK pathway alterations than non-adenocarcinoma CUP. No distinct molecular signature has been established (Harrison 22e pp.731-734). Median survival for most patients with disseminated CUP is about 6-10 months, and the prognosis for advanced disease remains poor with early resistance to available cytotoxic therapy. Prognosis is heterogeneous: favorable subsets (e.g., women with isolated axillary adenopathy treated as breast cancer, women with primary peritoneal serous carcinoma treated as ovarian cancer, men with midline poorly differentiated carcinoma resembling germ cell tumor, squamous cervical adenopathy, solitary metastatic sites, low-grade neuroendocrine tumors, and men with blastic bone metastases and elevated PSA) can achieve prolonged survival and occasionally cure. Recognized prognostic factors include performance status, site and number of metastases, response to therapy, and serum LDH; prognostic models (Culine using performance status and LDH; Raghav nomogram using gender, ECOG performance status, histology, number of metastatic sites, and neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio) stratify outcomes (Harrison 22e pp.734-735). No single formal staging system; risk stratification distinguishes favorable prognostic subsets (treatable as a specific putative primary, with potential for prolonged survival/cure) from unfavorable disseminated disease. Prognostic models include the Culine model (performance status plus serum LDH, dividing patients into two outcome subgroups) and the Raghav nomogram (gender, ECOG performance status, histology, number of metastatic sites, and neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio) (Harrison 22e pp.734-735).

When a phagocyte detects a fungus, these receptors normally activate CARD9, which assembles a signalling complex that switches on nuclear factor kappa B and drives production of cytokines needed for neutrophil recruitment and for the development of interleukin-17-producing T cells that protect skin and mucosa. With prolonged antifungal treatment many patients are controlled, but central-nervous-system fungal disease carries appreciable morbidity and mortality, relapse is frequent, and lifelong surveillance or suppressive therapy is often required.

defibrillation of a shockable rhythm Focusing on drugs and airway while neglecting the search for reversible causes Applying standard medical algorithms to traumatic arrest without treating haemorrhage, tension pneumothorax, and tamponade Neglecting structured post-resuscitation care after return of spontaneous circulation Cardiac arrest is the sudden cessation of effective cardiac output. Shockable rhythms arise from disorganised (ventricular fibrillation) or excessively rapid (pulseless ventricular tachycardia) electrical activity that prevents coordinated contraction, most often on a background of ischaemic heart disease. Non-shockable arrest reflects either absent electrical activity (asystole) or organised electrical activity without a pulse (pulseless electrical activity), commonly due to a profound reversible insult. Regardless of mechanism, cessation of circulation causes global ischaemia; the brain tolerates only minutes before injury begins, so restoration of perfusion by chest compressions and treatment of the cause is time-critical. Outcome depends on the initial rhythm, the promptness of high-quality resuscitation and defibrillation, and whether a reversible cause is corrected. Witnessed shockable arrests with early bystander CPR and defibrillation have the best prognosis, whereas unwitnessed asystolic arrest and prolonged downtime carry poor survival and higher risk of neurological injury.

cardiac haemochromatosis — iron-overload cardiomyopathy, haemochromatotic heart disease cardiac amyloidosis cardiac sarcoidosis Fabry cardiomyopathy idiopathic restrictive cardiomyopathy hypertrophic cardiomyopathy dilated cardiomyopathy of other aetiology glycogen storage cardiomyopathy cardiac magnetic resonance with myocardial T2* mapping serum ferritin and transferrin saturation HFE genotyping (C282Y, H63D) in suspected hereditary disease echocardiography with diastolic and tissue Doppler assessment ambulatory ECG monitoring for arrhythmia and conduction disease liver iron quantification (MRI R2/R2*) and liver function tests endocrine screen including fasting glucose, thyroid and gonadal axes Myocardial iron deposition may arise from hereditary haemochromatosis (typically HFE C282Y homozygosity) or from secondary/transfusional iron overload (thalassaemia major, sideroblastic anaemia, myelodysplasia); the secondary forms often cause the most severe cardiac disease because transfused iron bypasses regulatory absorption controls. The cardiomyopathy characteristically evolves through an early restrictive/diastolic phase into a later dilated phase with systolic impairment, so a normal ejection fraction does not exclude significant iron loading. Iron preferentially accumulates in ventricular myocardium and the conduction system, producing a mixed picture of heart failure plus atrial and ventricular arrhythmias and heart block. Cardiac T2* magnetic resonance is the pivotal non-invasive tool: a myocardial T2* below the accepted threshold identifies clinically important iron loading before ejection fraction falls, and it guides intensification of chelation. Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation reflect total body iron but correlate poorly with myocardial iron, so cardiac assessment must not rely on ferritin alone. Iron-related cardiac dysfunction is substantially reversible if chelation (or venesection in primary disease) is instituted before end-stage fibrosis develops, distinguishing it from most other restrictive cardiomyopathies. In transfusion-dependent patients, combining or intensifying iron chelators for cardiac indications can recover ventricular function and reduce arrhythmic death. Coexisting endocrinopathy (diabetes, hypogonadism, hypothyroidism) and hepatic disease frequently accompany the cardiomyopathy and worsen overall prognosis. new or progressive heart failure in a transfusion-dependent patient high-grade atrioventricular block or symptomatic bradyarrhythmia sustained ventricular arrhythmia or syncope falling ejection fraction with markedly reduced myocardial T2* rapid decompensation suggesting advanced iron-related systolic failure relying on serum ferritin, which does not reliably reflect myocardial iron burden assuming a normal ejection fraction excludes dangerous iron loading attributing arrhythmia or heart block to other causes and missing reversible iron toxicity under-dosing or delaying chelation once cardiac involvement is evident overlooking secondary transfusional overload because HFE testing is negative Excess iron, whether from dysregulated intestinal absorption in hereditary haemochromatosis or from repeated transfusion, saturates transferrin and circulates as non-transferrin-bound iron that is taken up by cardiomyocytes largely through L-type and T-type calcium channels. Intracellular labile iron catalyses Fenton-type generation of reactive oxygen species, causing lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial injury and impaired excitation-contraction coupling. Iron is deposited within lysosomes and myofibrils, initially stiffening the ventricle and impairing relaxation (a restrictive physiology), and later provoking myocyte loss and replacement fibrosis that culminate in ventricular dilatation and systolic failure. Iron loading of the sinoatrial node, atrioventricular node and conducting tissue underlies the associated bradyarrhythmias, heart block and atrial and ventricular tachyarrhythmias. Prognosis is favourable when iron overload is detected and treated before irreversible fibrosis, with substantial recovery of ventricular function and rhythm; established dilated systolic failure or advanced conduction disease carries high morbidity and mortality, and cardiac iron loading remains a leading cause of death in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia.

resection in familial disease Cardiac myxoma is a benign neoplasm arising from primitive multipotent mesenchymal cells, most often on a stalk attached to the interatrial septum in the left atrium. The gelatinous, friable tumour projects into the cardiac chamber, where it can intermittently obstruct the mitral valve orifice, producing haemodynamic effects resembling mitral stenosis. Fragments of the friable surface, or overlying thrombus, may detach and embolise into the systemic or pulmonary circulation. The tumour secretes cytokines, notably interleukin-6, which account for the fever, weight loss, raised inflammatory markers, and other constitutional and immunological manifestations. The familial form is associated with Carney complex. Surgical excision is curative for most sporadic myxomas with an excellent outlook, but recurrence is more likely in familial (Carney complex) disease, warranting long-term echocardiographic surveillance.

rhabdomyomas Overlooking arrhythmia or pre-excitation as a mechanism of symptoms Confusing a rhabdomyoma with a cardiac fibroma, which does not regress and behaves differently Cardiac rhabdomyoma is a benign hamartomatous tumour of cardiac muscle, considered a myocyte hamartoma rather than a true neoplasm. It is closely linked to tuberous sclerosis complex, in which loss of function of the TSC1 or TSC2 genes leads to unchecked mTOR pathway activation and abnormal cell growth. The tumours are composed of enlarged, vacuolated myocytes, classically including spider cells, and appear as multiple firm nodules within the ventricular myocardium and septum. They can obstruct blood flow, distort valves, or provide a substrate for arrhythmia and accessory-pathway conduction. Because the abnormal cells lose their proliferative drive after birth, the tumours frequently involute spontaneously during infancy. The outlook is generally good because most rhabdomyomas regress spontaneously and cause no lasting harm; prognosis in symptomatic cases depends on the haemodynamic burden and on any associated tuberous sclerosis manifestations.

cardiac tamponade — pericardial tamponade, acute cardiac compression constrictive pericarditis right ventricular myocardial infarction massive pulmonary embolism with obstructive shock tension pneumothorax restrictive cardiomyopathy severe acute right heart failure from any cause superior vena cava obstruction transthoracic echocardiography (chamber collapse, IVC plethora, Doppler respiratory variation) 12-lead ECG (low voltage, electrical alternans, sinus tachycardia) chest radiograph (enlarged globular 'water-bottle' cardiac silhouette if effusion is large) pericardial fluid analysis after drainage (cytology, culture, protein, LDH, adenosine deaminase) CT or CMR when loculated or regional effusion, haemopericardium or aortic dissection is suspected coagulation screen and full blood count right heart catheterisation showing equalisation of diastolic pressures in equivocal cases Tamponade is a clinical and haemodynamic diagnosis, not merely an echocardiographic one; a pericardial effusion of any size compressing the heart may cause tamponade if it accumulates faster than the parietal pericardium can stretch. The rate of accumulation matters more than absolute volume: rapid bleeding of a small volume (e.g. after cardiac perforation or aortic dissection) can be fatal, whereas a slowly accumulating chronic effusion may exceed a litre before compromise. Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, raised jugular venous pressure) is classically described but present in a minority; a high index of suspicion in the appropriate context is essential. Pulsus paradoxus (an exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic pressure greater than 10 mmHg) reflects enhanced ventricular interdependence and is a key bedside sign, though it may be absent in aortic regurgitation, atrial septal defect, severe hypotension or regional tamponade. The jugular venous pressure shows a preserved or prominent systolic x descent with an attenuated or absent diastolic y descent, distinguishing tamponade from constrictive pericarditis. Echocardiography demonstrates early diastolic right ventricular collapse (specific) and late diastolic/systolic right atrial collapse (sensitive), a dilated non-collapsing inferior vena cava and exaggerated respiratory variation in transvalvular Doppler inflow. Low-voltage QRS complexes and electrical alternans on the ECG suggest a large effusion with the heart swinging within it. Definitive treatment is drainage (echo-guided pericardiocentesis or surgical drainage); intravenous fluids may temporise but vasodilators and diuretics are harmful, and positive-pressure ventilation can precipitate cardiovascular collapse. hypotension with raised jugular venous pressure and tachycardia after cardiac procedure, trauma or in suspected aortic dissection pulseless electrical activity or peri-arrest in a patient with known or suspected effusion pulsus paradoxus greater than 10 mmHg with progressive breathlessness echocardiographic right ventricular diastolic collapse with a dilated non-collapsing inferior vena cava rapidly enlarging effusion following myocardial infarction (suggesting free wall rupture) Assuming a small effusion excludes tamponade; rapidly accumulating fluid causes compromise at low volumes. Administering diuretics, vasodilators or nitrates, which reduce preload and can precipitate cardiovascular collapse. Missing regional (loculated) tamponade after cardiac surgery, where localised clot compresses one chamber without the classic circumferential effusion. Delaying drainage to await confirmatory imaging in a peri-arrest patient. Attributing absent pulsus paradoxus to exclusion of tamponade, overlooking confounders such as aortic regurgitation or an atrial septal defect. Accumulation of fluid, blood, pus or gas within the relatively non-distensible pericardial sac raises intrapericardial pressure. Once this pressure approaches and then exceeds the diastolic filling pressures of the cardiac chambers, transmural distending pressure falls and diastolic filling is progressively impeded, beginning with the lower-pressure right-sided chambers. As total cardiac volume becomes fixed, the ventricles compete for a shared volume across the interventricular septum (enhanced ventricular interdependence): inspiratory augmentation of right ventricular filling shifts the septum leftward and reduces left ventricular stroke volume, producing pulsus paradoxus. Compensatory tachycardia, increased adrenergic tone and elevated systemic venous pressure maintain output until, at a critical intrapericardial pressure, stroke volume and cardiac output fall precipitously, culminating in obstructive shock and pulseless electrical activity. Prognosis depends chiefly on the underlying cause and the speed of recognition and drainage; promptly relieved tamponade has excellent haemodynamic recovery, whereas unrecognised tamponade from myocardial rupture or aortic dissection carries very high mortality. Malignant effusions frequently recur and portend a poor overall outlook.

Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation — Heart transplantation, Orthotopic heart transplant, Left ventricular assist device therapy, LVAS, LVAD, Mechanical circulatory support, Total artificial heart Other causes of advanced/refractory heart failure warranting evaluation: restrictive and infiltrative cardiomyopathy (e.g., amyloidosis), congenital heart disease, and chronic-infection-associated cardiomyopathy (Chagas disease, viral hepatitis-related, tuberculosis) Allograft dysfunction differential after transplant: acute cellular rejection vs antibody-mediated rejection vs cardiac allograft vasculopathy vs primary graft dysfunction Surveillance endomyocardial biopsy to grade and monitor rejection Immunofluorescence for immunoglobulin deposition and complement fixation, plus circulating donor-specific antibody testing, when AMR is suspected Cardiopulmonary exercise testing for peak VO2 to assess transplant/LVAS candidacy Invasive hemodynamic assessment of pulmonary vascular resistance and transpulmonary gradient (PVR >3 Wood units or transpulmonary gradient >15 are relative transplant contraindications unless reactive) Intravascular ultrasound or optical coherence tomography (more sensitive than angiography) and noninvasive coronary flow reserve for CAV detection and prognosis Prospective or virtual cross-match in allosensitized recipients with preformed antibodies Doppler-derived mean arterial pressure measurement in continuous-flow LVAS patients Lactate dehydrogenase as a hemolysis biomarker to screen for pump thrombosis Advanced heart failure is a distinct syndrome marked by refractoriness to conventional therapy, intolerance of guideline-dose neurohormonal antagonists, worsening renal function, poor cardiopulmonary reserve, and a low-output state with elevated pulmonary pressures; therapeutic goals shift toward surgical support of the failing heart (Harrison 22e p.2028). Transplant candidacy generally requires refractory heart failure with a peak VO2 below ~14 mL/kg per min (below 12 if on beta blockers) or percent-predicted VO2 under 50%, combined with intolerance of disease-modifying therapy, cardiorenal syndrome, inotrope dependence, or need for an LVAS (Harrison 22e p.2028). Age is not an absolute contraindication, but frailty is a relative one; BMI above 35 should prompt weight loss, eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 is a relative contraindication possibly requiring combined kidney transplant, and tobacco use in any form must cease for at least 6 months (Harrison 22e p.2028). The transplanted heart is surgically denervated and unresponsive to sympathetic or parasympathetic stimuli; early postoperatively high-dose catecholamines are needed, and allograft bradycardia does NOT respond to atropine, so isoproterenol or temporary pacing is used (Harrison 22e p.2029). Donor ischemia (out-of-body) time is typically limited to about 4 hours unless novel ex situ normothermic perfusion transport techniques are used; allocation considers urgency, waiting-list time, distance, and ABO blood group, while HLA matching is usually impractical given time constraints (Harrison 22e p.2029). Acute cellular rejection (ACR) is a T cell-mediated process with myocardial lymphocytic infiltrates that occurs early and declines after about 6 months, whereas antibody-mediated rejection (AMR) is a noncellular, donor-specific antibody-driven process with complement fixation, endothelial swelling, and arteriolar vasculitis that carries worse allograft survival and predisposes to vasculopathy (Harrison 22e p.2029-2030). Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) is an accelerated, diffuse coronary intimal proliferation that is commonly clinically silent; intravascular ultrasound or optical coherence tomography is more sensitive than routine angiography for detection (Harrison 22e p.2030). Angiographic CAV is present in roughly 30% of patients by 5 years and about 50% by 10 years after transplant; retransplantation is the only definitive therapy for advanced CAV (Harrison 22e p.2030). Continuous-flow LVAS generate forward flow dependent on the pressure gradient between the LV cavity and aorta, so flow is critically sensitive to systemic blood pressure; because pulse is often undetectable, blood pressure is measured by Doppler (mean/opening pressure) and the target mean arterial pressure is at or below 90 mmHg (Harrison 22e p.2032). LVAS-related shear stress can cause low-grade hemolysis and acquired von Willebrand disease (loss of high-molecular-weight vWF multimers), predisposing to gastrointestinal bleeding from intestinal arteriovenous malformations and to iron-deficiency anemia (Harrison 22e p.2032). Lactate dehydrogenase is an excellent though nonspecific biomarker of hemolysis and can herald pump thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.2032). Posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders are usually Epstein-Barr virus driven and are the most frequent malignancy; solid cancers most often manifest as basal- and squamous-cell skin malignancies, so routine sunscreen is advised (Harrison 22e p.2030). Cardiac transplantation replaces the failing heart with an allograft that is surgically denervated, so it depends initially on circulating catecholamines and cannot mount reflex heart-rate responses. Allograft rejection follows two mechanisms: ACR, a T cell-mediated lymphocytic assault on donor myocardium (perivenular in mild disease, diffuse interstitial with myocyte necrosis and hemorrhage in severe disease), and AMR, an antibody/complement-mediated injury with immunoglobulin deposition, endothelial swelling, interstitial edema, and arteriolar vasculitis. Over the long term, immunologic insults (brain death, ischemia-reperfusion, alloimmunity) combined with nonimmunologic metabolic factors (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, dysglycemia from chronic immunosuppression) drive cardiac allograft vasculopathy, a diffuse fibrotic intimal proliferation narrowing the coronary tree. For mechanical support, continuous-flow LVAS divert blood from the LV apex to the aorta via a pump whose output depends on the LV-to-aorta pressure gradient; the non-physiologic flow path imposes shear stress that degrades von Willebrand factor multimers and causes hemolysis. LV unloading lowers right-sided afterload, but increased device flow raises RV preload and the displaced septum reduces RV contractile efficiency, promoting RV dilatation and maladaptation. More than 150,000 patients have undergone cardiac transplantation worldwide, with 1-year survival above 80%, median survival of ~12.5 years, and conditional survival of ~14.8 years for those surviving the first year. With the fully magnetically levitated HeartMate 3 LVAS, median survival exceeds 5 years (about 60% survival at 5 years), and in younger patients (under 50) without comorbidity and an uncomplicated course the 5-year survival can rival transplantation (~75%). Without such support, patients with severe refractory systolic heart failure (peak VO2 <12 mL/kg per min or inotrope dependence) often have a median survival under 1 year. CAV grade correlates with prognosis and remains a leading limit on late allograft survival. Cardiac allograft vasculopathy is graded by the ISHLT 2010 scheme as CAV0 (absent), CAV1 (mild), CAV2 (moderate), and CAV3 (severe), based on extent of angiographic disease and presence of allograft dysfunction by echocardiography or restrictive physiology. Transplant allocation urgency is tiered, with the highest status for critically ill patients on ECMO or temporary biventricular mechanical support, then those needing daily invasive hemodynamic monitoring plus IV inotropes or with durable LVAD complications, and lower status for ambulatory patients stable at home.

Cardiac Trauma — Blunt cardiac injury, BCI, Myocardial contusion, Penetrating cardiac injury, Commotio cordis Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial infarction (traumatic coronary dissection or thrombosis can produce STEMI) Aortic dissection (traumatic aortic rupture can mimic its presentation) Acute pericarditis Cardiac tamponade from other causes Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy following emotional or physical trauma Musculoskeletal chest wall pain from rib or sternal injury 12-lead ECG in all patients with chest trauma (repeat as needed for evolving conduction disturbance/arrhythmia) Serial cardiac troponin (I or T); normal serial levels make cardiac injury very unlikely Transthoracic echocardiography in all suspected BCI and all penetrating chest injuries to assess wall motion, effusion, valves, and shunts Transesophageal echocardiography when adequate TTE images cannot be obtained Chest x-ray (mediastinal widening suggests aortic injury) Cardiac catheterization to confirm a suspected mechanical complication (shunt/valvular lesion) Non-traumatic acute myocardial infarction Non-traumatic aortic dissection Idiopathic or other-cause acute pericarditis Takotsubo cardiomyopathy Cardiac injury is broadly divided into penetrating trauma (most often gunshot or knife wounds, where the entry site is usually obvious) and nonpenetrating, or blunt cardiac injury (BCI). BCI most commonly follows motor vehicle collisions (rapid deceleration or chest impact) but can also result from falls, crush and blast injuries, assault, or vigorous contact in sports; significant cardiac injury may occur even when there are no external signs of thoracic trauma. There is no single sign, symptom, or test that confirms BCI, and clinical, laboratory, and radiographic findings are frequently nonspecific in the setting of major trauma, so a high index of suspicion is essential. An ECG should be obtained in every patient presenting with chest trauma; abnormalities can resemble those of infarction or pericarditis and include sinus tachycardia, RBBB, heart block, ST-T changes, and atrial or ventricular arrhythmias. Cardiac troponin is more specific than CK-MB for myocardial damage; a normal troponin combined with a normal ECG at 6-8 hours after chest trauma essentially excludes BCI. Echocardiography is the most useful modality for detecting the structural and functional sequelae of BCI, including regional wall motion abnormalities, pericardial effusion, valvular dysfunction, and ventricular or septal rupture; the RV, interventricular septum, and LV apex are most commonly involved. Commotio cordis is ventricular fibrillation triggered by a blunt, often innocent-appearing chest impact in the absence of structural injury, occurring most often in adolescents during sports when the blow lands during the vulnerable phase of repolarization (just before the T-wave peak); survival depends on prompt defibrillation. Sudden emotional or physical stress, even without direct cardiac trauma, may precipitate a transient catecholamine-mediated cardiomyopathy (takotsubo / apical ballooning syndrome). Because of its anterior position in the chest, the right ventricle is the most frequently injured chamber in penetrating trauma, followed by the left ventricle; isolated atrial injury is uncommon. Iatrogenic cardiac perforation can complicate central/intracardiac catheter placement, pacemaker or defibrillator lead insertion, RV endomyocardial biopsy, and intracoronary stent deployment. Post-cardiac injury syndrome (an inflammatory process resembling the postpericardiotomy syndrome) can develop weeks to months after blunt chest trauma, presenting with pericarditis and/or pericardial effusion. Survivors of penetrating cardiac injury may present days to weeks later with a new murmur or heart failure from an occult or evolving valvular regurgitation or intracardiac shunt, so trauma patients should be re-examined several weeks after injury. Hemodynamic instability or collapse at presentation (penetrating injury mortality approaches 90% in those in hemodynamic collapse) New loud murmur with rapidly progressive heart failure (traumatic valvular rupture) Signs of pericardial tamponade (pericardial rub, distant heart sounds, hypotension) ST-segment elevation suggesting coronary dissection/occlusion Mediastinal widening on chest x-ray with upper-extremity hypertension and diminished lower-extremity pulses (aortic rupture) Sudden collapse during chest impact in an athlete (commotio cordis requiring immediate defibrillation) Even a small pericardial effusion on echo in a penetrating chest injury (suggests occult cardiac perforation) Overlooking cardiac injury because attention is focused on more obvious external injuries. Relying on sternal or rib fractures to gauge cardiac risk; there is no proven association, and significant cardiac injury can occur with a normal-appearing chest wall. Using CK-MB to confirm BCI; it is elevated in only ~20% of blunt chest trauma and is falsely raised by massive skeletal muscle injury. Attributing post-traumatic chest pain solely to musculoskeletal causes when it may reflect myocardial ischemia or pericardial injury. Assuming a hemodynamically stable penetrating chest injury excludes cardiac involvement; up to ~20% harbor occult cardiac trauma. Missing delayed complications (post-cardiac injury syndrome, late valvular regurgitation, intracardiac shunt) by not re-examining the patient weeks after injury. Blunt forces (rapid deceleration, direct chest impact, crush, or blast) and penetrating objects damage the myocardium, valves, coronary arteries, pericardium, and great vessels. Myocardial contusion produces injury pathologically similar to infarction, with necrosis arising either directly or from traumatic coronary laceration, dissection, or thrombosis, predisposing to arrhythmias and conduction block. More severe injury causes free wall rupture (hemopericardium and tamponade) or ventricular septal rupture (intracardiac shunting). Valvular apparatus rupture (most often tricuspid or aortic) causes acute incompetence. Aortic rupture or transection, typically just above the aortic valve or at the ligamentum arteriosum tethering point, is the most common vascular deceleration injury. Commotio cordis represents a purely electrical mechanism: a chest blow during the susceptible repolarization window induces ventricular fibrillation without structural damage. Outcome depends on injury mechanism, chambers involved, and clinical condition at presentation. Although myocardial rupture is generally fatal, up to ~40% of patients reach a specialized trauma center alive. In penetrating injury, gunshot wounds carry higher mortality than stab wounds (about 20% of shooting victims survive versus up to ~65% of stabbing victims), partly because ballistic injuries more often involve multiple chambers; multichamber involvement carries a worse prognosis than single-chamber injury, and RV injury may carry a better prognosis than LV injury. Patients in hemodynamic collapse on arrival have a mortality near 90%, whereas roughly 75% of those stable enough to reach the operating room survive. Iatrogenic penetrating injuries generally have a better prognosis owing to more limited injury and prompt corrective therapy. Blunt cardiac abnormalities span a spectrum: ECG changes (sinus tachycardia, RBBB, heart block, ST-T changes, arrhythmias), elevated biomarkers (troponin most specific), focal wall motion abnormality or hematoma (RV free wall, LV apex, septum), valvular insufficiency (most often mitral/tricuspid, occasionally aortic), myocardial rupture (VSD or free wall), coronary artery injury (often LAD, presenting as STEMI), and pericardial effusion/tamponade. Risk stratification: stable patients with a normal ECG and normal serial troponins are low risk; an abnormal ECG and/or elevated troponin with a normal echo warrants telemetry monitoring; mechanical complications and hemodynamic instability constitute the highest-acuity group.

ectodermal disorder Cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome is a RASopathy caused by germline activating variants in components of the RAS-MAPK (mitogen-activated protein kinase) signalling cascade, principally BRAF and the downstream kinases MEK1 and MEK2, with a minority in KRAS. This pathway transduces growth-factor signals to control cell proliferation, differentiation and survival. Constitutive over-activation dysregulates these processes during development, producing the characteristic craniofacial, cardiac, ectodermal and neurodevelopmental abnormalities shared, with variation, across the RASopathy spectrum. Prognosis depends heavily on the cardiac phenotype, particularly hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and on the severity of feeding and neurological problems; many individuals have moderate to severe intellectual disability. With multidisciplinary care most survive into adulthood, though medical needs remain substantial.

Objective parameters (cardiac index, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure) help confirm a cardiac cause but are not mandatory for the diagnosis (p.2324). Compensatory rise in systemic vascular resistance is typical; left-ventricular processes elevate PCWP whereas right-ventricular processes elevate CVP (p.2311). Occasionally BP is maintained by very high SVR despite established shock, so normotension does not exclude cardiogenic shock (p.2326). Only about 10% of patients present with shock on admission; roughly 90% develop it during hospitalisation, so serial reassessment is essential (p.2123, p.2325). A new systolic murmur after MI should trigger urgent echocardiography to look for VSR, papillary muscle rupture or free-wall rupture; a murmur may be absent in up to 50% of acute MR cases (p.334, p.1894). Pericardial thrombus on imaging after MI strongly suggests myocardial rupture and is a surgical emergency (p.1894). Patients who develop shock typically have severe multivessel disease with 'piecemeal' necrosis extending beyond the original infarct zone (p.2123). Missing a mechanical complication: a murmur is absent in up to 50% of acute papillary-muscle-rupture MR (p.334). Overlooking RV infarction in inferior MI, where fluid management differs (volume to maintain RV preload) (p.2123). Treating presumed cardiogenic shock as hypovolaemia — filling pressures (PCWP/CVP) are elevated, not low (p.2311). Failing to recognise mixed shock (e.g. sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy superimposed on distributive shock) (p.2311). A profound fall in myocardial contractility initiates a self-perpetuating spiral: reduced cardiac output and stroke volume lower blood pressure and coronary perfusion, worsening ischaemia and further depressing contractility, which left untreated leads to death. Ineffective stroke volume is the inciting event, but inadequate circulatory compensation also contributes. Early peripheral vasoconstriction may transiently improve coronary and peripheral perfusion but raises afterload and can worsen ischaemia. Over time, systemic inflammation from acute cardiac injury induces pathologic vasodilatation; inflammatory cytokines and inducible/endothelial nitric oxide synthase increase NO and its by-product peroxynitrite, which are negatively inotropic and cardiotoxic. Lactic acidosis and hypoxaemia compound the cycle because severe acidosis blunts the efficacy of endogenous and exogenous catecholamines. Bleeding and transfusion during ICU care can further trigger inflammation. Left-ventricular failure accounts for roughly 80% of cardiogenic shock complicating acute MI, with acute severe mitral regurgitation, ventricular septal rupture, predominant RV failure, and free-wall rupture/tamponade making up the remainder (p.2325). In-hospital mortality ranges from roughly 40-60% depending on shock severity and underlying cause; cardiogenic and septic shock carry the highest mortality among shock types (90-day mortality around 52% for cardiogenic shock in one ED cohort). Higher lactate, elevated admission glucose, hepatic hypoperfusion and progressive renal impairment are adverse markers. Untreated shock progresses through compensated (preshock), decompensated, and finally irreversible stages with permanent organ dysfunction and multi-organ failure. Reperfusion and modern care have reduced the incidence of shock complicating acute MI to about 5-10% (p.2311, p.2325). SCAI shock classification (2019, updated): Stage A 'at risk' — no current signs/symptoms; Stage B 'beginning'/preshock — relative hypotension or tachycardia without hypoperfusion; Stage C 'classic' — manifest hypoperfusion requiring intervention (inotropes, vasopressors or MCS, excluding ECMO) beyond volume; Stage D 'deteriorating' — like C but worsening and failing initial therapy; Stage E 'extremis' — cardiac arrest with ongoing CPR and/or ECMO. The updated definition adds a three-axis model: (1) shock severity, (2) phenotype/aetiology, (3) risk modifiers such as cardiac arrest. Lactate >8 mmol/L marks stage E (p.2325-2326).

collapse is sudden loss of effective circulation that may revert spontaneously (e.g., neurocardiogenic syncope) or require intervention; cardiac arrest is abrupt cessation of cardiac function with loss of circulation potentially reversible by prompt intervention; and sudden cardiac death is unexpected death from cardiac arrest occurring within roughly 1 hour of symptom onset (p.2332-2333). Sudden cardiac death accounts for about 15% of all deaths and roughly half of all cardiac deaths; in the United States the text cites an estimated 350,000 EMS-attended out-of-hospital arrests and 210,000 sudden cardiac deaths in adults yearly (p.2332). Up to two-thirds of sudden cardiac deaths occur as the first clinical manifestation of previously undiagnosed heart disease, limiting the ability to predict and prevent events at the population level (p.2332). Coronary heart disease underlies the majority of sudden cardiac deaths, but the proportion attributable to coronary disease varies markedly by demographics: roughly 70% in white men versus 40-50% in women and black individuals, and under 40% in Asian populations (p.2333-2334). The text emphasizes the chain of survival for out-of-hospital arrest, and that survival is strongly time-dependent: neurologic recovery falls rapidly and is under 30% by 5 minutes from collapse to return of spontaneous circulation when no bystander CPR is given (p.2335-2338). Gasping (agonal) respirations and brief seizure-like activity are common during arrest and may be misinterpreted as breathing or responsiveness, leading to delayed resuscitation; a pulse check by a trained provider should take no longer than 10 seconds (p.2335-2336). The initial recorded rhythm carries prognostic and etiologic weight: ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation (shockable rhythms) have the best outcomes, while pulseless electrical activity and asystole carry a poor prognosis (p.2335-2336). The proportion of arrests found in ventricular fibrillation has fallen from over half in the 1970s to only 20-25% in recent series, with pulseless electrical activity and asystole now most common; because arrhythmias are unstable after collapse, the rhythm at EMS arrival may not reflect the initiating rhythm (p.2334). Inherited arrhythmia syndromes without structural heart disease (long QT, Brugada, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, early repolarization, idiopathic VF) are a more important cause of sudden death in the young and in Asian populations, accounting for around 10% of cases in Asia versus 1-2% in Western countries (p.2334). Depressed left ventricular function is the best-validated risk marker in structural heart disease; after myocardial infarction, SCD risk rises gradually as LVEF falls toward 40% and then increases exponentially below that (p.2338-2339). Following an MI, the risk of sudden death rises up to roughly 10-fold, with the highest absolute rates in the first 30 days; early deaths are more often non-arrhythmic (myocardial rupture, reinfarction) while later deaths are predominantly scar-related ventricular arrhythmias (p.2334-2335). Commotio cordis - ventricular fibrillation triggered by blunt, non-penetrating precordial impact - is a rare cause of sudden death in otherwise healthy individuals, especially after a chest blow during the vulnerable repolarization window (p.2335). while still under sedation/hypothermia or before the recommended 72 hours of normothermia Implanting an ICD for arrhythmia driven by a transient reversible cause (e.g., hyperkalemia, drug-induced torsades, or VF within 48 h of acute MI), where it is generally not indicated Withholding consideration that arrhythmia may signal end-stage heart disease, in which an ICD will not change the course absent transplant or assist-device candidacy Overlooking treatable PEA/asystole causes such as pulmonary embolism, hypovolemia, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, hypoxia, acidosis, hyperkalemia, hypothermia, toxins, and massive MI Attributing sudden death in the young to coronary disease, when HCM, coronary anomalies, myocarditis, ARVC, and channelopathies are more often responsible Most sudden cardiac death stems from a lethal ventricular tachyarrhythmia (polymorphic VT degenerating to ventricular fibrillation) arising on a vulnerable myocardial substrate, though bradyarrhythmia, asystole, and pulseless electrical activity are increasingly common terminal rhythms. Coronary artery disease is the predominant substrate, acting through acute ischemia/infarction or through reentry around scar from a healed infarct. Nonischemic processes - dilated, hypertrophic, infiltrative, and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathies, valvular disease, congenital surgical scars, and myocarditis - produce replacement fibrosis, hypertrophy, ventricular stretch, electrical heterogeneity, altered ion-channel function, and abnormal calcium handling that lower the threshold for sustained arrhythmia. In structurally normal hearts, inherited channelopathies (long QT, Brugada, CPVT), pre-excited atrial fibrillation in Wolff-Parkinson-White, and QT-prolonging drug toxicity cause primary electrical arrest. Pulseless electrical activity reflects mechanical or metabolic catastrophe - massive MI, pulmonary embolism, exsanguination, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, profound hypoxia or acidosis. Heightened autonomic (sympathetic) tone is the common thread linking precipitants such as vigorous exertion, emotional and environmental stress to arrhythmogenesis. After return of circulation, global ischemia-reperfusion brain injury becomes the dominant determinant of outcome. Outcomes are dominated by time to resuscitation and the presenting rhythm. Survival to hospital discharge for out-of-hospital arrest has improved but remains low - the chapter states about 90% of patients do not survive to discharge, and roughly 20% of survivors are left with severe neurologic or physical disability. Shockable rhythms (VT/VF) carry the best prognosis, with survival approaching 30% in some regions, whereas PEA and asystole carry poor outcomes. Success of resuscitation declines sharply after 5 minutes from collapse. Ischemia-reperfusion brain injury accounts for over two-thirds of post-arrest deaths; reliable neurologic prognostication is generally deferred at least 72 hours after return to normothermia (typically 4-5 days post-arrest). Features predicting poor neurologic outcome include absent pupillary light reflex, status myoclonus, absent EEG reactivity, and persistent burst suppression. Harrison frames the spectrum by terminology and reversibility: cardiovascular collapse (may revert spontaneously, includes syncope) -> cardiac arrest (rarely reverts spontaneously; reversibility depends on mechanism, setting, and speed of intervention) -> sudden cardiac death (death within ~1 hour of symptom onset). Acute risk and outcome stratify by presenting rhythm - shockable (VT/VF, better) versus non-shockable (PEA/asystole, worse). Chronic SCD risk in structural heart disease is graded chiefly by LVEF and presence of heart failure, with risk rising gradually as LVEF falls to 40% and exponentially below it.

counselling Assuming progressive muscle disease when the weakness is typically static Carey-Fineman-Ziter syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in MYMK, which encodes myomaker, a membrane protein required for the fusion of myoblasts into multinucleated muscle fibres during development. Impaired myoblast fusion produces a congenital myopathy with reduced muscle bulk and strength. The consequent foetal weakness and reduced movement contribute to micrognathia and the Pierre Robin sequence, to facial diplegia resembling Moebius sequence, and in some patients to joint contractures. Because the primary defect is in muscle formation rather than ongoing degeneration, the weakness tends to be static, and feeding and respiratory difficulties dominate the early clinical picture. The outlook depends on the severity of weakness and airway/feeding involvement; the myopathy is generally non-progressive and many children stabilise with supportive care, though feeding, respiratory and craniofacial problems cause significant early morbidity.

PRKAR1A, which encodes the type 1-alpha regulatory subunit of protein kinase A. This subunit normally restrains the catalytic activity of protein kinase A; its loss leads to unregulated cyclic-AMP-dependent protein kinase A signalling. Overactive protein kinase A signalling promotes proliferation in hormonally responsive and other susceptible tissues, explaining the endocrine tumours, myxomas, pigmented skin lesions and schwannomas. Tumour development follows a tumour-suppressor mechanism with a somatic second hit. A minority of cases involve other loci, and some show genetic heterogeneity. Cardiac myxomas are the leading cause of mortality through embolic events, obstruction and surgical risk, and can recur, so lifelong cardiac surveillance is essential. With regular monitoring and timely surgery for tumours, overall outlook is improved, though endocrine and other tumours require ongoing management.

palpitations and headache indicating a catecholamine-secreting tumour Gastrointestinal bleeding or a gastric mass from a stromal tumour A rapidly enlarging or metastatic tumour A hypertensive crisis during a procedure in an unblocked patient Confusing the syndrome with the non-hereditary Carney triad and missing the germline SDHx cause Expecting a succinate dehydrogenase-deficient GIST to respond like a KIT-mutated tumour to standard inhibitors Operating on a secretory paraganglioma without adequate preoperative adrenergic blockade Failing to screen for paraganglioma when a young patient presents with a wild-type gastric GIST The syndrome results from germline loss-of-function variants in genes encoding subunits of the succinate dehydrogenase complex, a mitochondrial enzyme shared by the tricarboxylic acid cycle and the electron transport chain. Inactivation of the complex causes succinate to accumulate, which inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases and stabilises hypoxia-inducible factors, producing a pseudohypoxic, pro-angiogenic state and widespread epigenetic changes. These effects promote the development of succinate dehydrogenase-deficient gastrointestinal stromal tumours and paragangliomas that characterise the condition. Succinate dehydrogenase-deficient GISTs tend to be indolent but can metastasise, notably to lymph nodes and liver, and respond poorly to standard targeted therapy, so surgery is central to management. Paragangliomas vary in behaviour, and with lifelong surveillance and appropriate perioperative preparation overall outcomes are often reasonable.

Carney triad — Carney triad, gastric GIST paraganglioma pulmonary chondroma, GIST-paraganglioma-chondroma triad Carney-Stratakis syndrome (dyad of GIST and paraganglioma) Sporadic KIT/PDGFRA-mutant gastrointestinal stromal tumour Hereditary paraganglioma-phaeochromocytoma syndromes (SDHx germline) Neurofibromatosis type 1 with GIST Carney complex von Hippel-Lindau disease Cross-sectional imaging of the abdomen for gastric stromal tumours Chest imaging for pulmonary chondromas Biochemical screening for catecholamine excess (plasma or urinary metanephrines) Functional and anatomical imaging to localise paragangliomas Immunohistochemistry for SDHB loss on tumour tissue Molecular testing to distinguish SDH-deficient from KIT/PDGFRA-mutant tumours A rare non-hereditary syndrome defined by the association of gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumours, paragangliomas, and pulmonary chondromas It overwhelmingly affects young women and is distinct from the autosomal dominant Carney-Stratakis dyad of GIST and paraganglioma The gastric stromal tumours are typically multifocal, wild-type for KIT and PDGFRA, and characterised by loss of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) activity Patients rarely have all three components at once; two of the three, or one plus another related tumour, may fulfil the diagnosis over time Additional associated lesions include phaeochromocytoma, oesophageal leiomyoma, and adrenocortical adenoma Management is tumour-directed surgery with lifelong surveillance, as the SDH-deficient GISTs behave differently from conventional GISTs and often respond poorly to standard tyrosine kinase inhibitors Consider Carney triad in a young woman with a wild-type, SDH-deficient gastric GIST, and screen for paraganglioma and pulmonary chondroma Gastrointestinal bleeding or anaemia from a gastric stromal tumour Paroxysmal hypertension, palpitations, or sweating from a catecholamine-secreting tumour Metastatic spread of an SDH-deficient GIST New or enlarging masses on surveillance imaging Treating an SDH-deficient GIST like a conventional GIST and expecting a good response to standard tyrosine kinase inhibitors Missing an occult catecholamine-secreting tumour before surgery Failing to recognise that the full triad rarely presents simultaneously Confusing the non-hereditary triad with the inherited Carney-Stratakis dyad Carney triad is associated with deficient function of the succinate dehydrogenase enzyme complex, most often through epigenetic silencing (such as hypermethylation of the SDHC promoter) rather than germline mutation, which is why the condition is generally not inherited. Loss of succinate dehydrogenase impairs mitochondrial energy metabolism and stabilises hypoxia-inducible factors, promoting a pseudohypoxic, pro-angiogenic state that drives tumour formation. This mechanism underlies the SDH-deficient gastric stromal tumours, the paragangliomas and phaeochromocytomas, and the other component lesions. Because the SDH-deficient GISTs differ molecularly from KIT- or PDGFRA-driven tumours, they follow an indolent but persistent course and respond less predictably to conventional targeted therapy. The SDH-deficient gastric tumours are frequently multifocal and can metastasise, yet often follow a protracted indolent course, so long-term survival can be favourable with surgery and surveillance despite recurrent disease; paraganglioma-related morbidity depends on catecholamine excess and tumour location.

intravenous glucose to suppress lipolysis, avoids fasting, and supports cardiac and hepatic function Chronic care uses long-chain fat restriction with medium-chain triglyceride substitution, frequent feeds and a strict emergency regimen Neonatal cardiac arrhythmia or conduction block with haemodynamic instability Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy and hyperammonaemia Cardiomyopathy with rapid deterioration Recurrent life-threatening decompensation during intercurrent illness Mistaking the biochemistry for CPT2 deficiency without confirmatory genetics Under-treating catabolism, allowing lipolysis to drive cardiac toxicity Overlooking arrhythmia as the presenting feature of metabolic collapse Permitting any fasting in a diagnosed infant The carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase is the inner mitochondrial membrane antiporter that imports long-chain acylcarnitine into the matrix in exchange for free carnitine, an essential step of the carnitine cycle linking CPT1 and CPT2. When the carrier is deficient, long-chain fatty acids cannot reach the matrix for beta-oxidation, so heart, muscle and liver are deprived of fatty-acid-derived energy during fasting or stress and ketogenesis fails. Accumulation of long-chain acylcarnitines is arrhythmogenic and cardiotoxic, accounting for the prominent cardiac features, and impaired acetyl-CoA generation contributes to hyperammonaemia. The neonatal-onset severe form carries high mortality despite intensive treatment, whereas individuals with residual carrier activity and milder disease can survive with careful metabolic management; early diagnosis and aggressive prevention of catabolism are critical.

uptake and renal reabsorption Presentations range from infantile hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and hepatic encephalopathy to a childhood dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and skeletal myopathy Some carnitine is markedly low, and renal carnitine wasting is characteristic of the primary transporter defect Secondary carnitine deficiency is far more common and results from other organic acidaemias and fatty acid oxidation defects, renal loss, malnutrition, or certain drugs Cardiomyopathy and muscle weakness in primary disease often respond well to carnitine replacement, making early recognition important Management principle is supplementation with L-carnitine and, for secondary forms, treatment of the underlying disorder and avoidance of fasting Detectable on newborn screening through a low free-carnitine level, which also flags affected mothers Acute hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy during fasting or illness Decompensated cardiomyopathy with heart failure or arrhythmia Sudden cardiac events in an at-risk individual Newborn screen showing very low carnitine, which may indicate an affected and vulnerable mother Failing to distinguish primary transporter deficiency from the much commoner secondary forms Overlooking the diagnosis in unexplained childhood cardiomyopathy that could respond to carnitine Missing an affected mother identified through her infant's abnormal newborn screen Not investigating for an underlying fatty acid oxidation defect or organic acidaemia when carnitine is low Carnitine is essential for transporting long-chain fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane for beta-oxidation. In primary carnitine deficiency, loss-of-function of the OCTN2 plasma-membrane transporter prevents carnitine entry into cardiac and skeletal muscle and impairs its reabsorption in the renal tubule, causing systemic depletion and urinary carnitine wasting. Without adequate carnitine, long-chain fatty acids cannot be oxidised, so energy production fails during fasting and fatty acid-dependent tissues such as heart and muscle are especially vulnerable, producing cardiomyopathy, myopathy and hypoketotic hypoglycaemia. Secondary deficiency occurs when carnitine is consumed conjugating accumulated acyl groups or is lost through the kidney. Primary carnitine deficiency generally has an excellent prognosis with carnitine supplementation, as cardiomyopathy and myopathy often reverse and metabolic crises are preventable; untreated disease, however, can cause sudden death or progressive cardiac failure. Prognosis of secondary deficiency depends on the underlying disorder.

disease, including autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease and PKHD1 mutations Bile stasis within the dilated ducts predisposes to intraductal stone formation, recurrent bacterial cholangitis, and abscess The central dot sign on cross-sectional imaging, representing a portal vein branch surrounded by dilated duct, is a characteristic feature There is an increased long-term risk of cholangiocarcinoma requiring vigilance Management addresses cholangitis and stones, with segmental resection for localised disease and liver transplantation for diffuse or complicated disease Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain indicating acute cholangitis or sepsis Progressive weight loss or a dominant stricture raising concern for cholangiocarcinoma Features of portal hypertension when congenital hepatic fibrosis coexists Recurrent severe infective episodes suggesting the need for definitive surgical management Confusing Caroli disease with primary sclerosing cholangitis or simple obstructive dilatation Failing to distinguish isolated Caroli disease from Caroli syndrome with hepatic fibrosis and portal hypertension Overlooking associated renal cystic disease Underestimating the long-term risk of cholangiocarcinoma and omitting surveillance Delaying definitive surgical assessment in localised, recurrently infected disease Caroli disease results from arrested remodelling of the embryonic ductal plate affecting the larger intrahepatic bile ducts, leaving them congenitally and permanently dilated in a saccular or fusiform pattern that communicates with the biliary tree. The abnormal ducts promote stasis of bile, which encourages the formation of pigment stones and repeated ascending bacterial infection, producing recurrent cholangitis and sometimes hepatic abscesses. When the same ductal plate malformation also involves the smallest ducts it produces the periportal fibrosis of congenital hepatic fibrosis, giving rise to Caroli syndrome with additional portal hypertension. The shared ciliopathy mechanism, often linked to PKHD1, accounts for the frequent association with renal cystic disease, and chronic biliary inflammation underlies the raised risk of cholangiocarcinoma. Prognosis depends on the extent of ductal involvement and the frequency of infective complications; localised disease may be cured by resection, whereas diffuse disease carries recurrent cholangitis, stone disease, and an elevated cholangiocarcinoma risk, with transplantation considered for advanced or complicated cases.
