Carotid duplex ultrasound to estimate stenosis severity and plaque characteristics CT angiography or MR angiography to confirm stenosis and evaluate arch and intracranial vessels Brain imaging (CT or MRI) to identify infarction in symptomatic patients Cardiac evaluation including ECG and echocardiography to exclude a cardioembolic source Vascular risk-factor profiling including lipids and glucose Most lesions occur at the carotid bifurcation and proximal internal carotid artery, where atherosclerotic plaque and turbulence predispose to thromboembolism Symptomatic disease typically presents as ipsilateral transient ischaemic attack, amaurosis fugax, or hemispheric stroke rather than global symptoms A cervical bruit is neither sensitive nor specific and its absence does not exclude significant stenosis Duplex ultrasound is the usual first-line imaging, with CT or MR angiography used to confirm the degree of narrowing and assess the aortic arch and intracranial circulation Risk stratification hinges on whether the lesion is symptomatic and on the percentage stenosis, as benefit from intervention is greatest in recently symptomatic high-grade lesions Best medical therapy with antiplatelet agents, lipid lowering, blood pressure control, and smoking cessation is fundamental for all patients regardless of intervention Carotid endarterectomy and carotid artery stenting are the two revascularisation options, with choice guided by anatomy, age, comorbidity, and operative risk Intervention for symptomatic disease is most effective when performed early after the index neurological event Recent transient ischaemic attack, amaurosis fugax, or stroke with high-grade ipsilateral stenosis, indicating high early stroke risk and need for urgent assessment Crescendo TIAs or stroke-in-evolution suggesting an unstable plaque Acute focal neurological deficit requiring emergency stroke pathway activation Contralateral occlusion or near-occlusion increasing haemodynamic vulnerability Relying on a bruit or its absence to gauge stenosis severity Delaying revascularisation in recently symptomatic patients, forfeiting the greatest window of benefit Overestimating benefit of intervention in asymptomatic patients with limited life expectancy Neglecting global vascular risk-factor modification while focusing only on the carotid lesion Carotid artery stenosis is usually caused by atherosclerotic plaque forming at the carotid bifurcation, a site of low and oscillating wall shear stress. Progressive plaque growth narrows the lumen, but the dominant mechanism of stroke is artery-to-artery thromboembolism from an unstable, ulcerated, or haemorrhagic plaque rather than simple flow limitation. Plaque rupture exposes thrombogenic material, generating platelet-fibrin and cholesterol emboli that lodge in the ophthalmic or middle cerebral territory. In severe stenosis or occlusion, cerebral perfusion may also become haemodynamically compromised, particularly when collateral supply through the circle of Willis is inadequate. Recently symptomatic high-grade stenosis carries a substantial short-term risk of recurrent stroke that is markedly reduced by timely revascularisation combined with medical therapy. Asymptomatic disease has a lower annual stroke risk, and modern medical therapy has narrowed the margin of benefit from intervention.

Carotid body tumour — carotid body paraganglioma, chemodectoma, carotid body tumor, cervical paraganglioma Cervical lymphadenopathy (reactive or malignant) Branchial cleft cyst Vagal or other head and neck paraganglioma Carotid artery aneurysm Salivary gland tumour Metastatic neck node or nerve sheath tumour Duplex ultrasound and CT or MR angiography demonstrating a vascular mass splaying the carotid bifurcation Catheter angiography where detailed vascular mapping or embolisation is planned Functional and biochemical testing for catecholamine secretion when a secretory tumour is suspected Genetic testing (including succinate dehydrogenase genes) and screening for multifocal or bilateral disease Cross-sectional imaging to assess local extent and identify additional paragangliomas A paraganglioma arising from the chemoreceptor tissue of the carotid body at the carotid bifurcation Typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, pulsatile neck mass at the angle of the jaw The mass is classically mobile from side to side but not vertically because it is tethered to the bifurcation (Fontaine sign) Most are benign and non-functional, but a minority secrete catecholamines or behave malignantly with nodal or distant spread A significant proportion are familial and linked to succinate dehydrogenase gene mutations, warranting genetic assessment and screening for multiple or bilateral tumours Imaging shows a highly vascular mass splaying the internal and external carotid arteries, producing the characteristic lyre sign on angiography Biopsy is generally avoided because of the vascularity and bleeding risk; diagnosis relies on characteristic imaging Surgical resection is the mainstay for suitable lesions, with radiotherapy considered for high-risk or unresectable disease, and preoperative embolisation used in selected large tumours Features suggesting malignant paraganglioma with regional or distant spread Catecholamine excess with paroxysmal hypertension or arrhythmia requiring assessment before intervention Rapid growth or new cranial nerve deficits indicating local invasion Bilateral or familial disease prompting genetic evaluation and family screening Performing biopsy of a highly vascular mass and precipitating significant haemorrhage Failing to test for catecholamine secretion before surgery in a functional tumour Overlooking hereditary disease and the need for genetic testing and screening for additional paragangliomas Underestimating the risk of cranial nerve injury with resection of large tumours The carotid body is a small chemoreceptor organ at the carotid bifurcation that senses arterial oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH. A carotid body tumour is a paraganglioma arising from its neural crest-derived chief cells. Chronic hypoxic stimulation, such as living at high altitude, can promote hyperplasia and tumour development, and hereditary forms result from germline mutations in succinate dehydrogenase subunit genes. The tumour is intensely vascular and grows within the crotch of the bifurcation, progressively splaying and encasing the internal and external carotid arteries and potentially involving adjacent cranial nerves. Most are non-functional, but some secrete catecholamines. Most carotid body tumours are benign and slow-growing, and complete resection offers an excellent outcome, though larger lesions carry greater risk of cranial nerve injury and vascular complications. A minority are malignant, and prognosis then depends on the extent of spread and completeness of treatment.

Carotid body tumour — Carotid paraganglioma, Chemodectoma Branchial cleft cyst Reactive or malignant lymphadenopathy Other paraganglioma such as glomus vagale or glomus jugulare Carotid artery aneurysm or marked tortuosity Schwannoma of the vagus or sympathetic chain Salivary gland tumour Metastatic cervical node Duplex ultrasound showing a vascular mass at the bifurcation Contrast-enhanced CT angiography MRI or MR angiography demonstrating 'salt-and-pepper' flow voids Plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary catecholamines when a functional tumour is suspected Genetic testing for succinate dehydrogenase mutations and screening for familial or multifocal disease Functional imaging such as somatostatin-receptor or MIBG studies for multifocality and metastasis Catheter angiography, often combined with preoperative embolisation A paraganglioma arising from the chemoreceptor tissue of the carotid body at the carotid bifurcation, and the commonest head and neck paraganglioma. Classically a slow-growing, painless, pulsatile lateral neck mass that is mobile from side to side but not vertically (Fontaine's sign). Splays the internal and external carotid arteries apart, producing the 'lyre sign' on angiography. Usually non-functional, but a minority secrete catecholamines and cause flushing, palpitations and hypertension, so biochemical screening is warranted when symptomatic. Associated with succinate dehydrogenase gene mutations (especially SDHD) and hereditary paraganglioma syndromes, and with chronic hypoxia such as high altitude or cyanotic heart disease. The Shamblin classification (I to III) grades the degree of carotid encasement and predicts operative difficulty and vascular risk. Cross-sectional and duplex imaging show a highly vascular mass at the bifurcation; percutaneous biopsy is contraindicated because of bleeding risk. Treatment is usually surgical excision, with preoperative embolisation to reduce vascularity in large tumours and radiotherapy reserved for unresectable or elderly patients. Rapid growth, pain or a new cranial nerve palsy (hoarseness, tongue deviation, dysphagia) suggesting aggressive or malignant behaviour. Symptoms of catecholamine excess such as paroxysmal hypertension, palpitations, headache and sweating. Bilateral or multifocal masses indicating a hereditary syndrome. Evidence of regional or distant metastasis. Airway compromise from a large mass. Performing incisional or fine-needle biopsy of a pulsatile neck mass and precipitating haemorrhage. Failing to screen for catecholamine secretion before intervention, risking an intraoperative haemodynamic crisis. Missing hereditary or multifocal disease by not offering genetic testing and paraganglioma surveillance. Underestimating cranial nerve injury risk in high Shamblin-grade tumours. Delayed referral allowing progressive carotid encasement that complicates resection. The carotid body is a chemoreceptor organ at the carotid bifurcation that senses arterial oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH. Sustained hypoxaemia from high altitude, chronic lung disease or cyanotic heart disease causes hyperplasia and predisposes to tumour formation. Tumours comprise chief (type I) cells arranged in nests (the Zellballen pattern) surrounded by sustentacular cells and a rich capillary network, accounting for their marked vascularity. Hereditary forms arise from germline mutations in succinate dehydrogenase subunit genes, producing pseudohypoxic signalling that drives paraganglioma development. Progressive growth splays and encases the carotid vessels and may involve adjacent cranial nerves. Most are benign and cured by complete excision with excellent long-term outcomes, while a small proportion (around 5 to 10%) are malignant with nodal or distant spread. Operative risk, chiefly cranial nerve injury and stroke, rises with tumour size and Shamblin grade.

Carotid-cavernous fistula — CCF, carotid-cavernous sinus fistula, cavernous sinus fistula Thyroid eye disease (Graves' orbitopathy) Orbital cellulitis Cavernous sinus thrombosis Orbital tumour or arteriovenous malformation Conjunctivitis or scleritis (for the red eye of an indirect fistula) Orbital pseudotumour or inflammatory orbital disease CT and MRI of the orbits and brain (dilated superior ophthalmic vein, bulging cavernous sinus, proptosis) CT or MR angiography to demonstrate the fistula Catheter (digital subtraction) cerebral angiography as the definitive diagnostic and treatment-planning study Measurement of intraocular pressure and ophthalmic assessment of vision and ocular motility Orbital colour Doppler ultrasound showing arterialised flow in the superior ophthalmic vein Assessment for cortical venous drainage or reflux, which indicates higher risk An abnormal communication between the carotid arterial system and the cavernous sinus, which arterialises the venous sinus and its tributaries Classified as direct (high-flow, often traumatic or from a ruptured intracavernous carotid aneurysm) or indirect (dural, low-flow, arising spontaneously, often in older women or with hypertension) The classic triad is pulsatile proptosis, chemosis, and an ocular or orbital bruit; a whooshing noise in the head is often reported Arterialisation of orbital veins produces dilated conjunctival (corkscrew) vessels, raised intraocular pressure, and ophthalmoplegia from involvement of the cranial nerves in the sinus, and can threaten vision Direct high-flow fistulae usually present dramatically after head trauma, whereas indirect dural fistulae are more insidious with a red eye that can mimic conjunctivitis or thyroid eye disease Diagnosis uses orbital imaging (CT or MRI showing a dilated superior ophthalmic vein and an enlarged cavernous sinus) with catheter angiography as the definitive study Management is usually endovascular closure (transarterial or transvenous embolisation); some low-flow dural fistulae close spontaneously or after manual carotid compression Deteriorating visual acuity or signs of ocular ischaemia (sight-threatening) Uncontrolled raised intraocular pressure Cortical venous drainage or reflux indicating a risk of intracranial haemorrhage Rapidly worsening proptosis or new cranial nerve palsies Misdiagnosing the red eye of an indirect fistula as conjunctivitis or thyroid eye disease Missing the diagnosis when no bruit is audible in a low-flow fistula Overlooking cortical venous reflux that raises the risk of haemorrhage Delaying imaging or angiography in a patient with progressive visual loss A carotid-cavernous fistula is an abnormal shunt between the carotid artery and the cavernous sinus. In direct fistulae a tear in the intracavernous internal carotid artery, from trauma or a ruptured aneurysm, allows high-pressure arterial blood directly into the sinus; in indirect (dural) fistulae, meningeal branches of the internal or external carotid feed the sinus at low flow. Arterial pressure within the cavernous sinus reverses venous drainage and engorges and arterialises the orbital veins. This raises orbital, episcleral, and intraocular pressure, produces proptosis, chemosis, and a bruit, and compromises the cranial nerves traversing the sinus to cause ophthalmoplegia; venous congestion and ocular ischaemia can threaten sight. Indirect low-flow dural fistulae may resolve spontaneously or after conservative measures, whereas direct high-flow fistulae usually require endovascular treatment; with timely closure the ocular signs generally regress, but delayed treatment risks permanent visual loss.

Carotid sinus hypersensitivity — carotid sinus syndrome, CSH, carotid sinus syncope Reflex (vasovagal) syncope Orthostatic hypotension Cardiac arrhythmia such as sick sinus syndrome or heart block Structural cardiac disease such as aortic stenosis Epileptic seizure Transient ischaemic attack Carotid sinus massage, supine and upright, with continuous ECG and beat-to-beat blood pressure 12-lead ECG and ambulatory ECG monitoring Head-up tilt-table testing to assess coexisting reflex syncope or orthostatic hypotension Echocardiography to exclude structural heart disease Carotid duplex before massage where vascular disease is suspected Medication review for bradycardic or hypotensive agents An exaggerated response to carotid sinus stimulation causing syncope or unexplained falls, chiefly in older people Two components are recognised: a cardioinhibitory response with asystole or marked bradycardia (conventionally a pause of at least three seconds) and a vasodepressor response with a fall in systolic pressure (conventionally at least 50 mmHg); a mixed pattern is common Symptoms may be provoked by head turning, tight collars, shaving, or neck extension, though a clear trigger is often absent Carotid sinus massage under continuous ECG and blood-pressure monitoring, performed supine and upright on a tilt table, is the diagnostic test An important reversible cause of unexplained falls and syncope in the elderly, sometimes without a warning Asymptomatic hypersensitive responses are common in older people, so results must be correlated with symptoms Carotid massage is avoided when there are carotid bruits or recent stroke or TIA because of embolic risk Management is reassurance and trigger avoidance; cardiac pacing is considered for a dominant cardioinhibitory type, while the vasodepressor component is harder to treat Syncope during exertion or with chest pain suggesting a cardiac cause A carotid bruit or recent stroke or TIA contraindicating carotid massage Recurrent injurious falls or 'drop attacks' Documented prolonged asystole Diagnosing carotid sinus hypersensitivity from a positive massage without correlating it to the patient's symptoms Performing carotid massage despite bruits or a recent cerebrovascular event Implanting a pacemaker when the dominant problem is vasodepressor rather than cardioinhibitory Overlooking it as a cause of unexplained falls in the elderly The carotid sinus baroreceptors normally sense arterial stretch and, via glossopharyngeal afferents, modulate autonomic outflow to regulate blood pressure and heart rate. In carotid sinus hypersensitivity this reflex is exaggerated, so that ordinary mechanical stimulation of the neck provokes an excessive efferent response. A cardioinhibitory response reflects a surge of vagal (parasympathetic) outflow producing profound bradycardia or asystole, whereas a vasodepressor response reflects sympathetic withdrawal causing vasodilatation and a fall in blood pressure. The result is transient cerebral hypoperfusion, syncope, or an unexplained fall. The condition is associated with ageing and with neurodegenerative disease, and its mechanism is incompletely understood. With trigger avoidance and, where appropriate, cardiac pacing for the cardioinhibitory form, many patients have fewer syncopal events; however, the vasodepressor component responds less well, and recurrent falls remain a concern in frail older people.

carpal boss — carpometacarpal boss, carpal bossing, os styloideum Dorsal wrist ganglion Extensor tendon tenosynovitis Second or third carpometacarpal osteoarthritis Gouty tophus or crystal deposition Dorsal osteophyte from scaphotrapeziotrapezoid arthritis Anomalous extensor digitorum brevis manus muscle Osteochondroma or other bony tumour Focused dorsal hand radiographs including a partially supinated oblique carpal boss view Lateral radiograph with the wrist slightly flexed to profile the prominence CT to define an os styloideum and associated carpometacarpal arthritis MRI if a soft-tissue mass or occult ganglion is suspected Ultrasound to distinguish a solid boss from a cystic ganglion Diagnostic local anaesthetic injection to confirm the pain source A carpal boss is a firm bony prominence on the dorsum of the hand at the base of the second and third carpometacarpal joints, over the capitate-trapezoid-metacarpal junction. It may represent a degenerative osteophyte or an accessory ossicle (os styloideum) and is frequently associated with dorsal carpometacarpal osteoarthritis. The prominence becomes more visible with the wrist flexed and is hard and fixed, distinguishing it from the softer, mobile dorsal wrist ganglion. A dorsal wrist ganglion may coexist and arise adjacent to the boss, complicating the clinical picture. Many bosses are asymptomatic and found incidentally; symptomatic cases usually present with activity-related dorsal pain. Extensor tendons may snap over the prominence, and a small overlying bursa or extensor tendon irritation can develop. A dedicated carpal boss view, taken partially supinated, ulnar-deviated and slightly flexed, best profiles the ossicle. Rapidly enlarging or aggressive-looking bony lesion suggesting neoplasm Features of inflammatory or crystal arthropathy Extensor tendon attrition or rupture over the prominence Confusing a hard, fixed carpal boss with a mobile dorsal ganglion. Missing coexisting carpometacarpal osteoarthritis as the true pain source. Using inadequate radiographic views that fail to demonstrate the ossicle. Performing incomplete excision, which leads to symptomatic recurrence. The carpal boss is a bony excrescence at the second and third carpometacarpal joints, arising either as a degenerative osteophyte from the carpometacarpal articulation or from an unfused ossification centre (os styloideum) that persists as an accessory bone. Repetitive dorsal stress and osteoarthritic change at these tightly constrained carpometacarpal joints generate the prominence, which can mechanically irritate the overlying extensor tendons and a superficial bursa, producing localised dorsal pain. Most carpal bosses are benign and either asymptomatic or settle with activity modification; surgical excision relieves symptoms in refractory cases, though recurrence and residual dorsal ache can occur.

Carpal tunnel syndrome — median nerve compression at the wrist, CTS, median neuropathy at the carpal tunnel Cervical radiculopathy (particularly C6/C7) Proximal median nerve entrapment (e.g. pronator syndrome) Peripheral polyneuropathy (e.g. diabetic) Thoracic outlet syndrome Other nerve entrapments (ulnar neuropathy) Thenar osteoarthritis (first carpometacarpal joint) Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to confirm and grade median nerve compression Clinical provocative tests (Tinel's and Phalen's) and thenar strength assessment Blood tests for associated conditions (glucose/HbA1c, thyroid function) where indicated Wrist radiographs if there is a history of fracture, deformity, or arthritis Ultrasound of the nerve in selected or atypical cases The commonest peripheral nerve entrapment, caused by compression of the median nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum at the wrist Typically presents with numbness, tingling, and pain in the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger, characteristically worse at night and relieved by shaking the hand Symptoms may radiate up the forearm; in advanced cases there is weakness and wasting of the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis) Often idiopathic but associated with pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, obesity, and repetitive wrist use Provocative signs include Tinel's (tapping over the nerve) and Phalen's (sustained wrist flexion) tests, though their sensitivity is limited Nerve conduction studies confirm the diagnosis and grade severity, and are useful before surgery or in atypical cases Mild or intermittent disease often responds to nocturnal wrist splinting, activity modification, and treatment of any underlying condition; corticosteroid injection can give temporary relief Surgical division of the flexor retinaculum (carpal tunnel release) is indicated for persistent symptoms, failure of conservative treatment, or established motor deficit and sensory loss Progressive thenar muscle wasting and weakness indicating advanced nerve damage warranting timely decompression Persistent dense sensory loss that may not fully recover Acute severe symptoms after a wrist fracture suggesting acute median nerve compression Bilateral or rapidly progressive neuropathy suggesting a systemic cause needing investigation Attributing hand symptoms to carpal tunnel syndrome when the cause is cervical radiculopathy or a more proximal lesion Delaying surgery until irreversible thenar wasting and sensory loss develop Overlooking a treatable underlying condition such as hypothyroidism or diabetes Relying solely on provocative clinical tests, which can be falsely negative The carpal tunnel is a rigid osseofibrous canal bounded by the carpal bones and roofed by the flexor retinaculum, through which the median nerve passes alongside the flexor tendons. Any increase in the contents or reduction in the capacity of this fixed space raises pressure on the median nerve. Compression impairs the nerve's microcirculation and, if sustained, causes segmental demyelination and eventually axonal loss. Conditions that increase tissue volume (fluid retention in pregnancy, synovial thickening in rheumatoid arthritis, tenosynovitis from overuse) or reduce tunnel size (wrist fractures, deformity) precipitate symptoms. Sensory fibres are usually affected first, with motor weakness and thenar wasting appearing later. Most patients with mild to moderate disease improve with conservative measures or gain lasting relief from surgical release; however, longstanding severe compression with thenar wasting and marked axonal loss may leave incomplete recovery of strength and sensation despite decompression.

anomalies Assuming a uniformly poor developmental outcome Carpenter syndrome is caused predominantly by biallelic loss-of-function variants in RAB23, a small GTPase that governs vesicular trafficking to the primary cilium and acts as a negative regulator of hedgehog signalling; a subset of cases result from variants in MEGF8. Because hedgehog signalling at the cilium coordinates cranial suture patterning, limb development and cardiac morphogenesis, its dysregulation produces the multi-suture craniosynostosis with acrocephaly, the preaxial polydactyly and syndactyly, and the congenital heart disease characteristic of the condition. The variable involvement of growth, cognition and the genitalia reflects the broad developmental role of ciliary hedgehog signalling, and the pattern places Carpenter syndrome within the acrocephalopolysyndactyly ciliopathies. With staged cranial surgery and management of cardiac and airway problems many individuals do well; intellectual outcome is variable, and the presence of associated malformations influences the overall prognosis.

Prognosis depends heavily on the severity of the craniosynostosis and any associated cardiac disease; with surgical correction and multidisciplinary support many children do well, though intellectual outcome is variable and some have significant learning difficulty.

Prognosis depends largely on the severity of the immunodeficiency and the lifelong increased risk of malignancy; those with severe combined immune impairment have a poorer outlook and may require haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, whereas milder cases can have near-normal survival with surveillance and infection prevention.

left-dominant/dilated Delaying cardiological referral until cardiac symptoms appear Not screening at-risk family members for arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy Carvajal syndrome is usually an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in DSP, which encodes desmoplakin, an obligate component of the desmosomal plaque that anchors intermediate filaments to the cell membrane. Desmosomes provide mechanical coupling between cells, and desmoplakin dysfunction weakens cell-cell adhesion in tissues subject to mechanical stress. In the epidermis this produces the keratoderma and, with hair-shaft involvement, woolly hair; in the myocardium impaired desmosomal integrity leads to myocyte detachment, fibrofatty replacement and an arrhythmogenic, dilated (frequently left-ventricular predominant) cardiomyopathy that predisposes to arrhythmia and sudden death. The cutaneous and hair features are benign, but prognosis is dictated by the cardiomyopathy, which can cause heart failure, life-threatening arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death, sometimes in childhood or adolescence. Early cardiac surveillance and intervention substantially influence outcome.

Loss of CASPR2 function reduces potassium-channel clustering and raises axonal and neuronal excitability, generating peripheral neuromyotonia and, centrally, limbic hyperexcitability and encephalopathy. Many patients respond well to immunotherapy and tumour treatment, though recovery of neuropathic pain and dysautonomia can lag. Cast nephropathy — myeloma kidney, myeloma cast nephropathy Other myeloma-related renal disease (light chain deposition disease, AL amyloidosis) Hypercalcaemic acute kidney injury Contrast or drug-induced acute kidney injury Acute tubular necrosis of other cause Tumour lysis syndrome Serum free light chain assay and serum/urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation Renal function, calcium and urinalysis (often dipstick-negative for protein) Full blood count and bone marrow assessment for myeloma Renal biopsy in selected cases Identification and correction of precipitating factors The commonest cause of acute kidney injury in multiple myeloma, from precipitation of monoclonal free light chains in the tubules It presents as acute or subacute kidney injury, often precipitated by dehydration, hypercalcaemia, infection or nephrotoxins The urine dipstick is typically negative for protein because it detects albumin, not the light chains Serum free light chain assay and serum/urine electrophoresis are key to diagnosis Precipitating factors such as hypercalcaemia and nephrotoxic drugs should be corrected urgently Rapid reduction of the offending light chains with anti-myeloma therapy offers the best chance of renal recovery Severe or dialysis-requiring acute kidney injury Hypercalcaemia with dehydration Very high free light chain levels Concurrent nephrotoxin exposure Being falsely reassured by a negative urine dipstick for protein Failing to check free light chains in unexplained acute kidney injury in older patients Not correcting hypercalcaemia and volume depletion urgently Continuing nephrotoxins that promote cast formation In cast nephropathy, an excess of monoclonal free light chains produced by a plasma cell neoplasm is filtered and reaches the distal tubule, where they bind Tamm-Horsfall protein and precipitate to form obstructing tubular casts. The casts cause intratubular obstruction and a local inflammatory and toxic injury to tubular cells. Volume depletion, hypercalcaemia, loop diuretics and nephrotoxins promote cast formation, so these factors both precipitate and worsen the injury. Reducing the circulating light chain burden is central to reversing it. Renal recovery is possible if light chains are reduced rapidly and precipitants corrected early, but delayed treatment or prolonged injury can lead to dialysis dependence.

Bartonellosis (incl. Cat-Scratch Disease) — Bartonella infection, cat-scratch disease Pyogenic (bacterial) lymphadenitis Mycobacterial infection (incl. tuberculous lymphadenitis) Brucellosis Syphilis Tularemia Plague Toxoplasmosis Sporotrichosis Histoplasmosis Serology (immunofluorescence or enzyme immunoassay) is the most commonly used diagnostic, but has variable sensitivity/specificity; CSD serodiagnosis is often based on IgG alone (in the absence of IgM) and seroconversion may take a few weeks, complicating interpretation (p.1352). PCR of pus aspirated from a lymph node or the primary inoculation lesion is highly sensitive and specific and is particularly useful for definitive, rapid diagnosis in seronegative patients; PCR of a lymph node biopsy specimen may be less sensitive (possibly due to sampling error) (p.1352). Histopathology shows early lymphoid hyperplasia, later stellate granulomata with necrosis, coalescing microabscesses and occasional multinucleated giant cells (nonspecific but may narrow the differential) (p.1352). For endocarditis: blood cultures (even with lysis-centrifugation or EDTA tubes) are positive in only ~25% of cases (mostly B. quintana, rarely B. henselae) and require prolonged incubation up to 6 weeks; high-titer (>=1:800) IgG serology supports the diagnosis but cross-reacts between B. quintana and B. henselae and with C. burnetii and Chlamydia; species-level identification usually requires PCR and DNA sequencing of valve tissue (p.1353). For bacillary angiomatosis/peliosis: diagnosis is by histologic examination; Warthin-Starry silver staining of lesions reveals clusters of bacilli; cultures are usually negative though blood cultures may be positive (p.1355). Lymphoma / malignancy (weight loss and night sweats of CSD, and CSD-associated FUO, can mimic malignancy) Kaposi's sarcoma (differential for cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis) Pyogenic granuloma (differential for cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis) Subcutaneous tumors (differential for cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis) Bartonella are fastidious, facultative intracellular, slow-growing gram-negative bacteria; clinical presentation depends on both the infecting species and the host's immune status. Of the >40 species/subspecies, B. bacilliformis, B. quintana and B. henselae are most commonly identified human pathogens (p.1350). B. henselae is the principal etiologic agent of cat-scratch disease (CSD); rare cases are associated with Afipia felis and other Bartonella species. Apparently healthy bacteremic cats (especially kittens) are the major reservoir; person-to-person transmission does not occur and intrafamilial clustering is rare (p.1351). Typical CSD (85-90% of cases) is a usually self-limited subacute regional lymphadenopathy; a small (0.3-1 cm) painless erythematous papule/pustule appears at the inoculation site within days to 2 weeks in about one-third to two-thirds of patients, with nodes enlarging 1-3 weeks (or longer) after cat contact (p.1351-1352). Affected nodes are usually painful and suppurate in ~10% of cases; axillary/epitrochlear nodes are most commonly involved, then head/neck, then inguinal/femoral. About 50% have fever, malaise and anorexia; weight loss and night sweats can mimic lymphoma (p.1351-1352). Atypical (extranodal) CSD occurs in 10-15% and includes Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome, neuroretinitis (often unilateral visual deterioration), hepatosplenic disease, encephalitis/seizures/myelitis/cranial-nerve palsies, FUO, pneumonitis, debilitating myalgia, arthritis/arthralgia (mostly women >20 yr), osteomyelitis (incl. multifocal) and erythema nodosum (p.1353). CSD-associated FUO is a unique, sometimes severe and debilitating syndrome that often mimics malignancy and may involve multiple organs (hepatosplenic space-occupying lesions, abdominal/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, ocular disease, multifocal osteomyelitis); fever may be continuous or relapsing (p.1353). In elderly patients (>60 yr), lymphadenopathy is more often absent, whereas encephalitis and FUO are more common than in younger patients (p.1353). Coxiella burnetii and Bartonella species are the most common causes of culture-negative endocarditis; in one French series Bartonella accounted for 28% of 348 culture-negative endocarditis cases. B. quintana and B. henselae are the species most often implicated (p.1353). Bartonella endocarditis often presents as a prolonged, minimally febrile or even afebrile indolent illness lasting weeks to months; initial echocardiography may not show vegetations and acute aggressive disease is rare. Most cases are native-valve, ~60% aortic; B. henselae usually infects preexisting valvulopathy while B. quintana often infects normal valves (p.1353). Bacillary angiomatosis (caused by B. henselae or B. quintana) is a neovascular proliferative disease of severely immunocompromised patients, presenting as non-painful tan/red/purple cutaneous lesions, tender subcutaneous nodules, ulcerated plaques or verrucous growths; nodular forms resemble fungal or mycobacterial infection (p.1354-1355). Bacillary peliosis is a related angioproliferative disorder caused by B. henselae involving primarily the liver (peliosis hepatis) and also spleen and lymph nodes, with blood-filled cystic structures (microscopic to several mm). In advanced immunodeficiency, B. henselae and B. quintana are important causes of FUO (p.1355). Trench fever (5-day/quintan fever) is caused by B. quintana, transmitted by the human body louse; it has reemerged as chronic bacteremia in homeless people (urban/contemporary trench fever), with alcoholism and louse infestation as risk factors (p.1354). Persistent constitutional symptoms with failure of spontaneous regression of node size, and negative acute- and convalescent-phase sera (10-20% of CSD patients) — malignancy must be ruled out (p.1352). Seronegative CSD with lymphadenopathy and severe complications (encephalitis or neuroretinitis) — early biopsy is important to establish a specific diagnosis (p.1352). Unilateral visual deterioration (neuroretinitis) in suspected CSD — ophthalmologic manifestations may occasionally cause moderate to severe vision loss (p.1353). Culture-negative endocarditis, especially in a homeless/alcoholic patient with body louse infestation (B. quintana) or significant cat exposure (B. henselae) (p.1353). Bartonella is a key but easily missed cause of culture-negative endocarditis; routine blood cultures are positive in only ~25% of cases and serology cross-reacts with C. burnetii and Chlamydia, so a high titer to one organism may reflect cross-reactivity rather than the true pathogen (p.1353). CSD is a frequently overlooked cause of FUO; CSD-associated FUO can mimic malignancy with multiorgan space-occupying lesions, leading to unnecessary investigation for cancer (p.1353). Negative serology does not exclude CSD: 10-20% of patients have negative acute- and convalescent-phase sera, and seroconversion may take weeks; PCR of aspirated pus is preferred in seronegative patients (p.1352). Suppurative nodes should be drained by large-bore needle aspiration, NOT by incision and drainage, to avoid chronic draining tracts (p.1353). In elderly patients, lymphadenopathy is more often absent, so CSD may be missed when it presents instead as encephalitis or FUO (p.1353). Bartonella adapt to specific domestic/wild mammalian hosts where prolonged intraerythrocytic and endothelial-cell infection creates an immune-protected reservoir, producing chronic bacteremia that may persist even after prolonged antimicrobial therapy. Adhesion and entry to endothelial cells and erythrocytes is facilitated by Bartonella adhesin A or variably expressed outer-membrane proteins; the organism evades host immunity by modifying virulence factors (lipopolysaccharide, flagella) and attenuating the immune response. Humans are incidental hosts for most species except B. quintana and B. bacilliformis (which are not zoonotic). In CSD, the cat-to-human transmission mode is undetermined: B. henselae-infected cat saliva spreads to claws by self-licking and contaminated flea feces can be inoculated by a scratch or bite (mucous-membrane/conjunctival inoculation also possible). Lymphatic drainage to regional nodes in immunocompetent hosts triggers a TH1 response producing necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis, with dendritic cells and chemokines driving granuloma formation. In bacillary angiomatosis, Bartonella angiogenic factor A (a proangiogenic autotransporter in B. henselae) activates the host vascular endothelial growth factor pathway to drive angiogenesis (p.1350-1355). In immunocompetent individuals, CSD (whether typical or atypical) usually resolves without treatment and without sequelae; resolution is slow, requiring weeks for fever/pain and months for node shrinkage, and lifelong immunity is the rule. Some ophthalmologic manifestations may occasionally result in moderate to severe vision loss. Bartonella endocarditis is often diagnosed late, and the proportion of patients requiring valvular surgery (~60%) is high, probably as a consequence of delayed diagnosis (p.1352-1353). Cat-scratch disease is described along clinical lines rather than a formal grading scale: (1) Typical CSD (85-90%) — subacute regional lymphadenopathy, usually self-limited; (2) Atypical/extranodal CSD (10-15%) — extranodal manifestations (Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome, neuroretinitis, hepatosplenic disease, neurologic disease, FUO, osteomyelitis, etc.). Severe/disseminated Bartonella disease (bacillary angiomatosis and peliosis) occurs primarily in HIV-infected persons with CD4+ T-cell counts <100/uL and in other immunosuppressed patients; Bartonella endocarditis is a separate severe culture-negative-endocarditis presentation (p.1351-1355).

Cataract — lens opacity, senile cataract, age-related cataract, nuclear sclerosis, cortical cataract, posterior subcapsular cataract Refractive error Age-related macular degeneration Diabetic retinopathy or macular oedema Open-angle glaucoma Corneal opacity or dystrophy Vitreous opacities Visual acuity and refraction Slit-lamp examination to grade and localise the opacity Assessment of the red reflex Dilated fundus examination to exclude co-existing macular or retinal disease Biometry (keratometry and axial length) for intraocular lens power calculation before surgery Presents with gradual painless blurring of vision, glare and haloes around lights, and reduced contrast, often worse in bright sunlight or oncoming headlights Nuclear sclerotic cataract can cause a temporary myopic shift ('second sight') allowing reading without glasses before vision deteriorates Posterior subcapsular cataract disproportionately impairs near vision and glare and is associated with steroid use and diabetes The red reflex is reduced or shows dark opacities against the glow on ophthalmoscopy Age is the commonest cause; With age, lens proteins (crystallins) undergo aggregation, oxidation, and cross-linking, while accumulation of pigment and changes in hydration reduce lens transparency and scatter incoming light. Depending on where these changes concentrate, opacity develops in the nucleus, cortex, or beneath the posterior capsule, each producing a distinct visual disturbance. Metabolic, traumatic, inflammatory, and toxic insults accelerate similar biochemical changes. Cataract surgery is one of the most effective and successful operations, restoring good vision in the great majority provided the retina and optic nerve are healthy.

breathing pattern during sleep in which expiration becomes greatly prolonged and airflow is vocalised against a partially adducted larynx, producing the groaning sound. Catathrenia is benign with no known harmful consequences for the sleeper, but it tends to be persistent and its main impact is disturbance to a bed partner; response to treatment, including continuous positive airway pressure, is inconsistent.

of food and fluids leading to dehydration, aspiration, or venous thromboembolism New neurological signs, seizures, or fever suggesting encephalitis Attributing immobility and mutism solely to depression or psychosis and overlooking treatable catatonia Giving antipsychotics, which may precipitate malignant catatonia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome Failing to escalate to electroconvulsive therapy in malignant or benzodiazepine-refractory cases Missing an underlying autoimmune, metabolic, or structural cause Neglecting supportive care for dehydration, thromboprophylaxis, and pressure areas Catatonia is best understood as a final common motor pathway of diverse insults rather than a unitary disease. Prevailing models implicate dysregulation of frontal-subcortical and basal ganglia circuits, with reduced GABA-A signalling in orbitofrontal and prefrontal cortex, altered glutamatergic (NMDA) transmission, and relative dopamine hypoactivity. This produces impaired top-down control of movement, volition, and speech. The rapid response to GABA-enhancing benzodiazepines supports the role of cortical GABAergic underactivity, while the risk of deterioration with dopamine-blocking antipsychotics links catatonia mechanistically to neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Underlying triggers span primary psychiatric illness, autoimmune (e.g. anti-NMDA-receptor) encephalitis, metabolic and toxic states, and structural lesions. Simple catatonia usually responds well and often rapidly to benzodiazepines or electroconvulsive therapy, with outcome largely determined by the underlying cause. Malignant catatonia carries a high risk of death without prompt recognition and aggressive treatment, and prolonged immobility increases the risk of thromboembolic, infective, and pressure complications.

Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia — CPVT Long QT syndrome Andersen-Tawil syndrome Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation Vasovagal syncope Digoxin toxicity (bidirectional VT) Exercise stress testing to provoke the arrhythmia Ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring Resting electrocardiogram and echocardiography (typically normal) Genetic testing for RYR2 and CASQ2 Family screening and cascade genetic testing An inherited arrhythmia syndrome causing exercise- or emotion-induced polymorphic or bidirectional ventricular tachycardia Presents with syncope or cardiac arrest triggered by adrenergic stress, typically in children and young adults The resting electrocardiogram and cardiac structure are characteristically normal Most cases involve mutations in the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RYR2) or, less often, calsequestrin (CASQ2) Exercise testing or ambulatory monitoring reproducing the arrhythmia is central to diagnosis Beta-blockade is first-line, with flecainide, sympathetic denervation and an implantable defibrillator in selected cases Exertional or emotional syncope or cardiac arrest Documented bidirectional or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia Family history of sudden cardiac death in the young Breakthrough events despite treatment Misdiagnosing exertional syncope as vasovagal Relying on a normal resting electrocardiogram to exclude it Overlooking family history of sudden death Prescribing drugs that increase adrenergic tone Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is caused by abnormal handling of calcium within cardiomyocytes. Mutations affecting the ryanodine receptor or calsequestrin lead to inappropriate release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum during adrenergic stimulation. The resulting calcium overload triggers delayed afterdepolarisations and triggered activity, which under conditions of high sympathetic tone generate bidirectional and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation. Because the substrate is functional rather than structural, the heart appears normal at rest. With beta-blockade and activity modification many patients do well, but the condition carries a real risk of sudden cardiac death, particularly if untreated or non-adherent, and some require additional therapies.

Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia — CPVT, RYR2-related CPVT, CASQ2-related CPVT, familial polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, bidirectional ventricular tachycardia Long QT syndrome (especially exercise-triggered LQT1) Andersen-Tawil syndrome with bidirectional ectopy Digoxin toxicity causing bidirectional ventricular tachycardia Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy Vasovagal or neurocardiogenic syncope Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation Exercise treadmill or bicycle stress testing to provoke reproducible ectopy and bidirectional VT Ambulatory (Holter) monitoring to capture exertional arrhythmia burden 12-lead resting ECG (usually normal, helps exclude QT prolongation and other channelopathies) Echocardiography and cardiac MRI to confirm structurally normal heart and exclude cardiomyopathy Targeted genetic testing for RYR2 and CASQ2 variants Cascade genetic and clinical screening of first-degree relatives Presents in childhood or adolescence with syncope, seizures, or cardiac arrest triggered by exercise or intense emotion, in a structurally normal heart The resting ECG is typically normal, so a high index of suspicion and provocative testing are essential Exercise or catecholamine stress testing reproducibly elicits ventricular ectopy that progresses to bidirectional and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia as heart rate rises Most cases follow autosomal dominant inheritance through cardiac ryanodine receptor (RYR2) variants; a rarer autosomal recessive form is caused by calsequestrin (CASQ2) variants Beta-blockers, particularly non-selective agents such as nadolol, are the cornerstone of therapy and reduce arrhythmic events Flecainide is a useful adjunct that suppresses calcium-driven ectopy, and left cardiac sympathetic denervation is an option for refractory disease An implantable cardioverter defibrillator is reserved for survivors of cardiac arrest or those with breakthrough events despite optimal medical therapy Family cascade genetic screening and counselling are important because relatives may carry the variant while appearing clinically normal Exertional or emotion-triggered syncope or seizure in a young person Aborted cardiac arrest or documented polymorphic ventricular tachycardia Family history of sudden death, drowning, or unexplained syncope in youth Recurrent arrhythmic events despite beta-blocker therapy Dismissing exertional syncope as vasovagal because the resting ECG and echocardiogram are normal Relying on a single resting ECG rather than provocative exercise testing to make the diagnosis Under-dosing beta-blockade or accepting poor adherence, leaving breakthrough arrhythmia Placing an ICD as sole therapy, since painful shocks can trigger an adrenergic surge and further arrhythmia Overlooking the need to screen and counsel apparently healthy relatives CPVT arises from dysregulated calcium handling in cardiac myocytes. Variants in the ryanodine receptor (RYR2) or calsequestrin (CASQ2) genes destabilise the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release channel complex, so that during adrenergic stimulation calcium leaks into the cytosol during diastole. This calcium overload drives delayed afterdepolarisations and triggered activity, which under the influence of circulating catecholamines generate the characteristic exercise- or emotion-induced bidirectional and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia despite an anatomically normal heart. Sustained runs may degenerate into ventricular fibrillation and sudden death. With early diagnosis, adherence to beta-blockade with or without flecainide, and activity modification, arrhythmic events can be substantially reduced; however, untreated or poorly controlled CPVT carries a high risk of sudden cardiac death from adolescence onward.

perineal symptoms and missing the diagnosis until retention is established Delaying MRI or specialist referral, forfeiting the window for effective decompression Failing to examine perineal sensation and anal tone Assuming normal voiding excludes the syndrome without checking post-void residual volume Cauda equina syndrome results from compression of the bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots within the spinal canal below the termination of the spinal cord. Because these are peripheral nerve roots, compression produces lower motor neuron deficits, radicular pain, and disruption of the sacral parasympathetic and somatic supply to the bladder, bowel, and perineum. Sustained compression causes ischaemia and mechanical injury to the roots, and delayed relief risks irreversible loss of sphincter and sexual function. Outcome depends heavily on the speed of diagnosis and decompression. Surgery performed before the onset of established urinary retention gives the best functional results, whereas delayed treatment is associated with persistent bladder, bowel, sexual, and motor deficits. Some residual dysfunction is common even after timely surgery in severe cases.

Haemodynamic instability or systemic acidosis High-grade circumferential or deep injury on endoscopy Assuming a normal oral examination excludes serious distal injury Attempting to neutralise the agent or induce vomiting, worsening tissue damage Giving activated charcoal, which is ineffective and obscures endoscopic assessment Delaying airway management until obstruction is established Failing to arrange follow-up for stricture and malignancy surveillance Caustic agents injure tissue on contact according to their pH, concentration, volume and contact time. Strong alkalis produce liquefactive necrosis, saponifying fats and dissolving proteins so injury extends deeply into and potentially through the oesophageal wall. Strong acids cause coagulative necrosis, forming a superficial eschar that can limit but not prevent deep penetration, and often preferentially injure the stomach. Tissue damage evolves over days through inflammation, then granulation and fibrosis, which underlies later stricture formation, while full-thickness injury risks perforation, mediastinitis and peritonitis. Minor mucosal injury usually heals without sequelae, but deep circumferential burns frequently lead to oesophageal strictures requiring dilatation, and severe transmural injury carries substantial morbidity and mortality; there is a lasting increased risk of oesophageal malignancy.

and its surrounding sympathetic plexus, the abducens nerve within its lumen, and the oculomotor, trochlear, and ophthalmic (and often maxillary) trigeminal nerves in its lateral wall. Lesions here produce painful or painless ophthalmoplegia with trigeminal sensory loss, and the proximity of sympathetic fibres to the abducens nerve can yield a combined sixth nerve palsy and Horner syndrome. Outcome is determined by the cause; thrombosis and fistulae can be managed with good results if treated promptly, while malignant infiltration carries a poorer prognosis, and residual ophthalmoplegia may persist after resolution.

degradation, thereby restraining RAS-MAPK signalling. Germline heterozygous variants impair this negative feedback, so the pathway remains inappropriately active, producing the developmental and growth features shared with Noonan syndrome. In haematopoietic progenitors, a second somatic hit that removes the remaining functional allele can drive uncontrolled proliferation and juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia, although the same event may later self-correct, explaining the occasional spontaneous regression. Outlook varies widely; many individuals have a mild syndromic phenotype with normal life expectancy, but the risk of juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia is significant, and although some cases regress spontaneously others require intensive haematological treatment.

for this autosomal recessive condition CEDNIK syndrome results from loss of function of SNAP29, a soluble NSF attachment protein receptor (SNARE) that mediates fusion of intracellular vesicles and In the epidermis, SNAP29 is required for the secretion of lamellar bodies that deliver barrier lipids to the stratum corneum, so its deficiency disrupts keratinocyte maturation and produces ichthyosis and palmoplantar keratoderma. The same defect in vesicular trafficking during nervous system development underlies the cerebral dysgenesis and peripheral neuropathy that characterise the syndrome. Prognosis is guarded and dominated by the severity of the cerebral malformation and neurological impairment; many affected children have significant developmental disability, while the cutaneous features are chronic but manageable.

cement dermatitis — bricklayer's dermatitis, cement eczema irritant contact dermatitis from other construction materials allergic contact dermatitis to rubber gloves or boots alkaline chemical burn from wet cement atopic or endogenous hand eczema pompholyx (dyshidrotic eczema) palmar psoriasis epoxy or resin contact dermatitis in construction workers detailed occupational history linking symptoms to cement and concrete work patch testing to potassium dichromate and cobalt chloride patch testing to rubber accelerators and other construction allergens assessment of protective clothing, gloves and cement type used skin swab if secondary bacterial infection is suspected clinical assessment for alkaline burns in kneeling or boot-contact areas workplace review of chromate-reduced cement availability and hygiene practices Cement causes two overlapping problems: an irritant contact dermatitis from its strong alkalinity, abrasive particles and hygroscopic drying effect, and an allergic contact dermatitis, chiefly to hexavalent chromium and cobalt. Wet cement is highly alkaline and can produce not only eczema but full-thickness alkaline (caustic) burns, classically on the knees, feet and lower legs of kneeling concrete workers. Chromate is the dominant allergen in cement dermatitis; adding ferrous sulfate to reduce hexavalent to trivalent chromium has markedly lowered the incidence where mandated. The eruption typically affects the hands, wrists and forearms, and any skin in prolonged contact with wet concrete through clothing or boots. Allergic cement dermatitis tends to be chronic and persistent, often continuing despite avoidance because of the ubiquity of chromate and the entrenched sensitisation. A history of an itchy hand eczema that flares at work and settles on holiday, in a construction or masonry worker, is highly suggestive. Patch testing to potassium dichromate and cobalt chloride confirms the allergic component and guides prognosis and workplace advice. Prevention relies on low-chromate (ferrous-sulfate-treated) cement, waterproof protective clothing and gloves, prompt washing of skin contamination and avoiding kneeling in wet concrete. deep or extensive alkaline burns from prolonged wet-cement contact circumferential or full-thickness skin loss requiring surgical assessment severe secondarily infected eczema with systemic features persistent disabling dermatitis threatening the worker's livelihood signs of concurrent chromate exposure such as nasal septal ulceration Assuming all cement dermatitis is irritant and omitting patch testing for chromate and cobalt. Underestimating wet cement as a cause of serious alkaline burns, especially on the knees. Expecting resolution on avoidance and failing to warn of the chronicity of chromate allergy. Relying on ordinary gloves that are permeable to wet cement or fail with prolonged contact. Overlooking coexisting rubber-glove allergy contributing to hand eczema. Cement injures skin by several mechanisms. Its high alkalinity (calcium hydroxide and related species when hydrated) saponifies lipids and denatures keratin, producing irritant dermatitis and, with prolonged contact, alkaline caustic burns; the abrasive mineral particles and desiccating properties add mechanical and drying injury that further disrupts the barrier. Superimposed on this is allergic contact dermatitis: hexavalent chromium and cobalt present as soluble contaminants penetrate the compromised epidermis, bind proteins to form haptens and elicit a delayed (type IV) T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity, giving a chronic spongiotic eczema. Barrier damage from the irritant effects enhances allergen penetration and perpetuates sensitisation, so the two processes reinforce each other. Reducing hexavalent to trivalent chromium (for example with added ferrous sulfate) lowers the allergenic load and the risk of new sensitisation. Irritant cement dermatitis often improves with barrier protection and good skin care, but allergic (chromate) cement dermatitis is frequently chronic and may persist even after leaving the trade because of established sensitisation and ubiquitous exposure. Alkaline burns can cause significant scarring.

inner root sheath lead to follicular destruction and perifollicular fibrosis, beginning at the vertex and expanding outward. A genetic predisposition, including variants in the PADI3 gene that affect hair-shaft formation, appears to interact with hairdressing practices that impose traction, heat and chemical trauma. The final common pathway is irreversible loss of follicular stem cells with replacement by fibrous tracts. Progression can be halted or slowed with early anti-inflammatory treatment and modification of hair care, but established scarred areas will not regrow, so late presentation carries a poorer cosmetic outcome.

Abnormal channel function disturbs excitation-contraction coupling and calcium handling, and over time regions of affected fibres lose mitochondria and oxidative enzyme activity, producing the characteristic amorphous central cores. Predominant involvement of type 1 fibres accounts for the proximal, often relatively non-progressive weakness. Weakness is often static or only slowly progressive and many affected individuals achieve independent ambulation, though orthopaedic and, less commonly, respiratory complications may require ongoing management. The dominant lifelong risk is malignant hyperthermia during anaesthesia, which is preventable with appropriate precautions.

The mononuclear stromal cells are regarded as the proliferating component, recruiting and fusing to form the giant cells, which resorb bone and generate the expansile lytic lesion. Although its precise trigger is uncertain and it was once attributed to trauma or reactive repair, it is now considered a benign proliferative process; crucially, systemic hyperparathyroidism produces a histologically identical brown tumour that must be excluded biochemically. Most lesions are cured by thorough curettage or enucleation, although aggressive lesions and a proportion of others recur and may need repeated or more extensive treatment; the outlook is excellent once hyperparathyroidism has been excluded or treated.

Central neurocytoma — central neurocytoma, intraventricular neurocytoma, WHO grade 2 neurocytoma, synaptophysin-positive neurocytoma Oligodendroglioma Ependymoma Subependymoma Intraventricular meningioma Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma Metastasis to the ventricular region Contrast-enhanced brain MRI to characterise the intraventricular mass and hydrocephalus Assessment of relationship to the septum pellucidum and foramen of Monro Histopathology showing uniform round cells in a neuropil background Synaptophysin immunohistochemistry to confirm neuronal differentiation IDH, 1p/19q and ATRX testing to exclude oligodendroglioma Ki-67/MIB-1 proliferation index to identify atypical, higher-risk tumours A typically benign neuronal tumour (CNS WHO grade 2) of young and middle-aged adults, arising within the lateral ventricles Characteristically attached near the septum pellucidum or foramen of Monro, where it obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow Usually presents with headache and other features of raised intracranial pressure from obstructive hydrocephalus Histology resembles oligodendroglioma with uniform round cells, but neuronal differentiation is confirmed by strong synaptophysin positivity Retained ATRX and absence of IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion help distinguish it from oligodendroglioma Extraventricular neurocytomas with similar morphology can occur in the brain parenchyma Gross total resection is often curative; atypical variants with higher proliferation may recur Acute obstructive hydrocephalus with rapidly rising intracranial pressure Intraventricular haemorrhage from the tumour High proliferation index or atypical features indicating recurrence risk Sudden deterioration in consciousness from cerebrospinal fluid obstruction Misdiagnosing it as oligodendroglioma and applying inappropriate glioma management Not performing synaptophysin staining to establish neuronal differentiation Overlooking an elevated proliferation index that flags an atypical, recurrence-prone tumour Delaying relief of obstructive hydrocephalus in a symptomatic patient Central neurocytoma is a neuronal tumour believed to arise from bipotential progenitor cells or neuronal precursors near the septum pellucidum and the walls of the lateral ventricles. It grows as a well-circumscribed intraventricular mass composed of uniform round cells with clear cytoplasm and finely speckled chromatin, set in a fibrillary neuropil-like background, frequently with calcification and microcystic change. Despite a superficial resemblance to oligodendroglioma on light microscopy, it shows neuronal differentiation demonstrated by synaptophysin expression and lacks the molecular signatures of diffuse glioma. Symptoms result largely from mechanical obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid at the foramen of Monro. Prognosis is generally favourable, with gross total resection frequently curative and long-term survival common. Atypical central neurocytomas with an elevated proliferation index carry a higher risk of recurrence, and adjuvant radiotherapy may be considered for incompletely resected or recurrent disease.

carries a higher risk of underlying pathology Very rapid pubertal progression with markedly advancing bone age threatening final height Signs of raised intracranial pressure or new focal neurological deficit Relying on a single basal LH value, which may be prepubertal, rather than performing a stimulation test when suspicion is high Omitting brain imaging in young children and in boys, in whom peripheral cause that has secondarily triggered central puberty Central precocious puberty results from premature reactivation of pulsatile hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone secretion, which stimulates pituitary release of LH and FSH and consequent gonadal sex-steroid production. The activated axis reproduces normal puberty but at an inappropriately early age, so the sequence and progression of pubertal events are physiological. Triggers include disinhibition of the GnRH pulse generator by hypothalamic lesions (hamartoma, tumours, hydrocephalus, cranial irradiation, or previous chronic sex-steroid exposure), genetic changes affecting the pubertal timing network (such as MKRN3 loss of function), and, most commonly in girls, no identifiable cause. The premature sex-steroid exposure accelerates skeletal maturation, advancing bone age ahead of height gain. Idiopathic central precocious puberty generally responds well to GnRH analogue therapy, with arrest of pubertal progression and preservation of adult height potential when treatment is started early; prognosis in secondary forms depends on the underlying central nervous system cause.

OCT and fluorescein angiography as adjuncts Presents as sudden, painless, profound loss of vision in one eye, often to counting fingers or worse A relative afferent pupillary defect is present in the affected eye Fundoscopy shows a pale, oedematous retina with a classic cherry-red spot at the fovea and attenuated, segmented ('cattle-trucking') arterioles It is effectively a stroke of the eye — treat as a time-critical emergency and investigate the same as an acute cerebral ischaemic event Always exclude giant cell arteritis in older patients by asking about jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and headache and checking inflammatory markers Immediate measures aim to dislodge or reperfuse (ocular massage, lowering intraocular pressure), though evidence for benefit is limited once the window has passed Urgent referral for stroke workup (carotid imaging, cardiac source, vascular risk factors) is essential to prevent a subsequent cerebral stroke Time-critical emergency — inner retinal infarction becomes irreversible within a short window, so treat and refer immediately Suspected giant cell arteritis threatens the fellow eye and requires urgent systemic treatment without waiting for biopsy It is a warning of systemic embolic disease with high risk of subsequent cerebral stroke Bilateral or ophthalmic artery involvement suggesting a major vascular or arteritic process Failing to consider and treat giant cell arteritis in an older patient, risking loss of the second eye Treating it as an isolated eye problem rather than initiating urgent stroke and vascular workup Dilating or delaying assessment and missing the narrow reperfusion window Confusing it with vein occlusion, which shows haemorrhages rather than retinal pallor Central retinal artery occlusion results from acute interruption of blood flow in the central retinal artery, most often from an embolus (carotid or cardiac) or from thrombosis, arteritis, or vasospasm. The inner retina, supplied by this artery, is exquisitely sensitive to ischaemia; sudden occlusion causes rapid infarction and oedema of the inner retinal layers. The fovea, supplied by the underlying choroid, retains its colour and stands out as a cherry-red spot against the surrounding pale, opaque ischaemic retina. Irreversible neuronal damage occurs within a short ischaemic window. Visual prognosis is generally poor, with permanent severe visual loss common; the main priority becomes preventing a devastating cerebral stroke and protecting the fellow eye.

arteriosclerotic thickening of the artery compresses the vein and promotes turbulent flow and thrombus formation. The resulting rise in venous and capillary pressure causes widespread retinal haemorrhage, oedema, and, when perfusion fails, capillary non-perfusion and retinal ischaemia. Ischaemic retina releases vascular endothelial growth factor, driving macular oedema and neovascularisation of the retina, optic disc, and iris, which can lead to neovascular glaucoma. Non-ischaemic CRVO often has a reasonable visual outcome, though some cases convert to the ischaemic form over time. Ischaemic CRVO carries a poor visual prognosis and a high risk of neovascular glaucoma; timely anti-VEGF therapy for macular oedema and laser for ischaemia improve outcomes but vision is frequently limited.
