suggesting secondary choroidal neovascularisation such as haemorrhage, lipid exudate or a sudden change in vision Bilateral or atypical multifocal detachment prompting exclusion of inflammatory, hypertensive or neoplastic causes Ongoing high-dose corticosteroid exposure that cannot be withdrawn Misdiagnosing chronic disease as wet macular degeneration and giving unnecessary treatment, or vice versa Overlooking occult corticosteroid exposure such as inhalers, skin creams or joint injections Prescribing corticosteroids for a presumed inflammatory cause and thereby worsening the fluid Intervening too early in acute cases that would resolve spontaneously, exposing the patient to treatment risk Failing to recognise secondary choroidal neovascularisation developing on a background of chronic disease Central serous chorioretinopathy is thought to arise from choroidal vascular hyperpermeability and congestion (part of the pachychoroid spectrum), which raises hydrostatic pressure beneath the retinal pigment epithelium. This overwhelms and damages the pumping and barrier function of the epithelium, allowing fluid to pass into the subretinal space and produce a localised serous detachment of the neurosensory retina at the macula. Corticosteroids and elevated endogenous cortisol are believed to potentiate this choroidal dysfunction, which explains the strong association with steroid use, stress and Cushingoid states. Persistent or repeated fluid accumulation leads to chronic retinal pigment epithelial atrophy and photoreceptor damage. Acute central serous chorioretinopathy usually resolves spontaneously within a few months with good visual recovery, but recurrences are common. Chronic or repeated disease may cause irreversible retinal pigment epithelial atrophy, photoreceptor loss and secondary neovascularisation, with lasting reduction in acuity and quality of vision.

Central sleep apnoea — CSA, central sleep apnea, central apnoea, Cheyne-Stokes breathing Obstructive sleep apnoea Mixed (complex) sleep apnoea Obesity hypoventilation syndrome Nocturnal breathlessness from decompensated heart failure Periodic breathing at high altitude Neuromuscular or chest-wall hypoventilation disorders Attended polysomnography to characterise and quantify central versus obstructive events Echocardiography and cardiac assessment when heart failure is suspected Daytime arterial or capillary blood gas to identify chronic hypercapnia Brain and brainstem imaging if a central neurological cause is suspected Review of opioid and sedative medication as a reversible contributor Central sleep apnoea reflects a transient loss of respiratory drive, so airflow and respiratory effort stop together, distinguishing it from obstructive events where effort continues against a closed airway Unlike the loud habitual snoring of obstructive disease, patients may present chiefly with fragmented sleep, frequent awakenings, nocturnal breathlessness, or witnessed pauses without much snoring A Cheyne-Stokes crescendo-decrescendo breathing pattern is characteristic and points strongly towards underlying heart failure The disorder clusters into hypercapnic forms (blunted drive, as in brainstem disease or opioid use) and non-hypercapnic forms driven by an unstable, oversensitive ventilatory control loop Polysomnography is required to confirm the diagnosis and to separate central from obstructive and mixed events Treatment is directed at the underlying cause; optimising heart failure therapy often reduces central events, and supplemental oxygen or adaptive ventilatory support may be considered in selected patients Long-term opioid therapy is an increasingly common and reversible contributor that should be actively sought in the history Adaptive servo-ventilation should be used cautiously and is contraindicated in patients with symptomatic heart failure and reduced ejection fraction Cheyne-Stokes breathing indicating underlying heart failure requiring cardiac evaluation and optimisation New central apnoea with focal neurology suggesting a brainstem lesion or stroke Central events emerging or worsening on chronic opioid therapy Daytime hypercapnia, cor pulmonale, or morning headache signalling chronic ventilatory failure Assuming all sleep apnoea is obstructive and missing the absent respiratory effort that defines central events Prescribing adaptive servo-ventilation to patients with symptomatic reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure, in whom it may be harmful Overlooking chronic opioid use as a treatable cause Failing to investigate and treat underlying heart failure or brainstem pathology Central sleep apnoea arises from intermittent failure of the brainstem respiratory rhythm generator to signal the respiratory muscles, so both airflow and inspiratory effort cease simultaneously. In non-hypercapnic (high loop gain) forms, ventilatory control is unstable: an oversensitive chemoreceptor response drives arterial CO2 below the apnoeic threshold, breathing stops until CO2 rises again, and overshoot perpetuates a cyclical pattern. Prolonged circulation time in heart failure delays chemoreceptor feedback and produces the crescendo-decrescendo Cheyne-Stokes cycling. In hypercapnic forms, reduced central drive or neuromuscular capacity (brainstem lesions, opioids, chronic hypoventilation) causes sustained underventilation with superimposed central pauses. Recurrent apnoeas generate cyclical hypoxaemia, arousals, and sympathetic surges. Prognosis is largely determined by the underlying disorder; central sleep apnoea complicating advanced heart failure is a marker of poorer outcome, whereas apnoea from reversible causes such as opioids or high altitude often improves once the trigger is addressed.

Centrally mediated abdominal pain syndrome — CAPS, functional abdominal pain syndrome Irritable bowel syndrome Narcotic bowel syndrome Chronic pancreatitis or other structural abdominal disease Abdominal wall pain (for example nerve entrapment) Somatic symptom disorder Focused history and examination, including the Carnett test for abdominal wall pain Limited, targeted testing to exclude structural disease rather than repeated investigation Assessment of psychological comorbidity and functional impact Review of analgesic, especially opioid, use Consideration of prior imaging to avoid duplication Near-constant or frequent abdominal pain that is poorly related to eating, defecation or menstruation The pain reflects central amplification of visceral signals rather than a gut-based trigger It is often associated with loss of daily function and with psychological comorbidity There may be behavioural clues such as the closed-eyes sign and a discrepancy between reported severity and examination It is distinct from irritable bowel syndrome, in which pain is linked to bowel function Management centres on a therapeutic relationship, central neuromodulators and psychological therapies rather than repeated investigation New alarm features such as weight loss, bleeding or a mass Escalating opioid use with worsening pain Features suggesting a specific structural disease Significant psychiatric risk Repeated investigation and surgery in search of a structural cause Escalating opioids and precipitating narcotic bowel syndrome Missing abdominal wall pain, which the Carnett test can identify Failing to address psychological and gut-brain contributors Centrally mediated abdominal pain syndrome arises from dysregulation of central pain processing, in which descending pain-modulatory pathways fail to dampen, and instead amplify, visceral afferent input. This central sensitisation means pain is experienced largely independently of gut events. Psychological factors and prior experiences influence the pain through the gut-brain axis, and repeated negative investigations and escalating analgesia, particularly opioids, can perpetuate the syndrome. The condition is chronic, but a supportive clinician relationship with neuromodulator and psychological treatment can substantially reduce pain and improve function; repeated testing and opioids worsen outcomes.

Centronuclear/myotubular myopathy — CNM, X-linked myotubular myopathy, XLMTM, MTM1, DNM2, BIN1 Nemaline myopathy Central core disease Congenital myotonic dystrophy Congenital myasthenic syndrome Congenital muscular dystrophy Spinal muscular atrophy Muscle biopsy demonstrating central nuclei and perinuclear oxidative staining patterns Genetic testing of MTM1, DNM2 and BIN1 with appropriate X-linked inheritance analysis Serum creatine kinase Respiratory function assessment, critical in neonates with the X-linked form Ophthalmological assessment for ptosis and ophthalmoplegia Electromyography and, where relevant, hepatic and coagulation monitoring in severe MTM1 disease The severe X-linked form (myotubular myopathy, MTM1) presents in affected males at birth with profound hypotonia, weakness, respiratory failure and often a history of polyhydramnios and reduced fetal movements Autosomal dominant (DNM2) and recessive (BIN1) centronuclear forms are generally milder with later onset and slower progression Ophthalmoplegia and ptosis are common and are a useful clinical clue, alongside a long face and proximal weakness Muscle biopsy hallmark is centrally placed nuclei in a high proportion of fibres, often with a central zone of oxidative enzyme activity surrounded by a pale halo, resembling fetal myotubes Male infants with the X-linked form frequently have macrosomia, long digits and elongated face Creatine kinase is usually normal or mildly elevated Carrier females for MTM1 variants may occasionally show mild or asymmetric weakness Neonatal respiratory failure requiring immediate ventilatory support Recurrent aspiration from bulbar weakness Signs of hepatic peliosis or bleeding described in severe X-linked disease Progressive hypoventilation in older children with dominant or recessive forms Failing to arrange urgent respiratory support in a hypotonic newborn with the X-linked form Overlooking ptosis and ophthalmoplegia that point toward centronuclear myopathy Assuming a female carrier is unaffected when mild manifestations can occur Interpreting central nuclei as regenerating fibres rather than the primary pathology Centronuclear myopathies are congenital myopathies characterised by centrally located nuclei in muscle fibres. The severe X-linked form is caused by loss-of-function variants in MTM1, which encodes myotubularin, a phosphoinositide phosphatase important for membrane trafficking and the organisation of the triad and T-tubule system. Autosomal dominant disease is usually caused by DNM2 (dynamin 2) variants and recessive disease by BIN1 (amphiphysin 2) variants; all converge on disturbed membrane remodelling and excitation-contraction coupling. The resulting maldevelopment of the sarcotubular system impairs contractile function and, in severe cases, arrests fibres at a myotube-like stage. The severe X-linked form carries high early mortality from respiratory failure, though intensive respiratory support has improved survival in some cases. Autosomal dominant and recessive centronuclear forms are typically slowly progressive and compatible with prolonged survival, with disability determined mainly by limb and respiratory muscle involvement.

Cephalohaematoma — cephalhaematoma, subperiosteal haemorrhage of the newborn Caput succedaneum Subgaleal haemorrhage Skull fracture with associated swelling Cranial meningocele or encephalocele Clinical diagnosis from a fluctuant swelling limited by sutures Bilirubin monitoring for associated jaundice Skull imaging only if an underlying fracture or intracranial injury is suspected Assessment for anaemia if the collection is large Distinguishing it from subgaleal haemorrhage clinically A subperiosteal collection of blood over a skull bone, confined by the periosteal attachments at the sutures It does not cross suture lines, in contrast to caput succedaneum and subgaleal haemorrhage It often becomes apparent hours after birth and enlarges over the first day or two, then resolves over weeks It is associated with instrumental delivery and may overlie a linear skull fracture in a minority Resorption of the blood can contribute to jaundice, and a firm rim may calcify as it heals Management is expectant; the collection should not be aspirated because of infection risk A swelling that crosses sutures and is diffuse, suggesting subgaleal haemorrhage Signs of significant blood loss or anaemia Features suggesting depressed or complex skull fracture or intracranial injury Signs of secondary infection of the collection Confusing it with subgaleal haemorrhage, which is far more dangerous Aspirating the collection and introducing infection Overlooking associated hyperbilirubinaemia Missing an underlying skull fracture when clinically indicated A cephalohaematoma forms when shearing forces during birth, often with instrumental delivery, rupture blood vessels beneath the periosteum of a skull bone. Because the periosteum is firmly attached at the suture margins, the accumulating blood is confined to the surface of a single bone and cannot cross the sutures. The collection resorbs gradually; breakdown of the trapped blood adds to the bilirubin load, and organisation at the margins can produce a calcified rim during healing. Cephalohaematoma is usually benign and resolves over weeks to a few months; the main issues are exaggerated jaundice, occasional anaemia and, rarely, calcification or infection.

Cerebellar ataxia — cerebellar syndrome, ataxia, cerebellar dysfunction Sensory ataxia from dorsal column or large-fibre neuropathy disease Vestibular disorders causing imbalance Frontal gait disorder and normal pressure hydrocephalus Intoxication (alcohol, anticonvulsants, other drugs) Functional gait disorder Weakness or extrapyramidal disorders mimicking incoordination MRI of the brain focusing on the posterior fossa to identify structural, vascular, or demyelinating lesions Blood tests for metabolic, endocrine, nutritional (including vitamin B12 and E), and toxic causes Paraneoplastic antibody panel and search for underlying malignancy when subacute cerebellar degeneration is suspected Genetic testing for hereditary ataxias in chronic progressive cases Cerebrospinal fluid analysis when an inflammatory, infective, or paraneoplastic cause is considered A clinical syndrome of incoordination arising from cerebellar dysfunction, causing a wide-based unsteady gait, limb dysmetria, and impaired balance Characteristic signs include intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, dysmetria on finger-nose and heel-shin testing, and scanning dysarthria Midline (vermis) lesions predominantly affect gait and truncal stability, whereas hemispheric lesions cause ipsilateral limb ataxia Nystagmus and impaired smooth pursuit and saccades commonly accompany cerebellar disease Cerebellar ataxia is distinguished from sensory ataxia, in which imbalance worsens markedly with eyes closed (positive Romberg) due to proprioceptive loss Causes are broad, spanning stroke, tumour, demyelination, alcohol and toxins, hereditary and paraneoplastic syndromes, and metabolic disturbance Acute cerebellar signs, particularly with headache or reduced consciousness, may indicate a cerebellar stroke or haemorrhage that can cause life-threatening brainstem compression and hydrocephalus Investigation is guided by tempo of onset, with acute presentations requiring urgent imaging and chronic ones prompting evaluation for hereditary, degenerative, and metabolic causes Acute cerebellar signs with headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness suggesting cerebellar stroke or haemorrhage that can cause brainstem compression and obstructive hydrocephalus requiring emergency neurosurgical assessment Rapidly progressive ataxia suggesting a paraneoplastic, inflammatory, or toxic cause Associated cranial nerve or long-tract signs indicating brainstem involvement New ataxia in a patient on potentially toxic drug levels such as anticonvulsants Failing to distinguish cerebellar from sensory or vestibular ataxia, leading to the wrong workup Missing a cerebellar stroke or haemorrhage that can rapidly deteriorate into brainstem compression Overlooking reversible causes such as drug toxicity, vitamin deficiency, or hypothyroidism Not pursuing a paraneoplastic cause in subacute progressive cerebellar degeneration Cerebellar ataxia reflects impaired function of the cerebellum or its afferent and efferent connections, which normally coordinate the timing, force, and accuracy of movement and maintain balance and posture. Damage to the cerebellar hemispheres, vermis, or connecting peduncles disrupts these predictive and error-correcting mechanisms, producing dysmetria, tremor, and incoordination. The underlying pathology may be vascular, inflammatory, neoplastic, toxic, metabolic, degenerative, or genetic. Prognosis depends entirely on the underlying cause. Some causes, such as drug toxicity, vitamin deficiency, or an inflammatory process, are reversible with treatment, whereas hereditary and neurodegenerative ataxias are typically progressive. Acute cerebellar strokes can be life-threatening but may recover substantially with timely intervention.

Cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy, vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS, RFC1) — CANVAS, RFC1 disease, RFC1 AAGGG biallelic repeat expansion, RFC1-related ataxia with chronic cough Other late-onset sporadic or genetic cerebellar ataxias Sensory neuronopathies from other causes (paraneoplastic, Sjogren syndrome, toxic, idiopathic) Bilateral vestibulopathy from ototoxicity or other causes Multiple system atrophy, cerebellar type Friedreich ataxia and other recessive ataxias with neuropathy Vitamin E deficiency or other treatable sensory ataxias Targeted RFC1 biallelic AAGGG repeat-expansion analysis Nerve conduction studies demonstrating a non-length-dependent sensory neuronopathy Vestibular function testing including the head-impulse test and caloric or video head-impulse assessment MRI brain to document cerebellar atrophy Screening for acquired sensory neuronopathy causes (autoimmune, paraneoplastic, Sjogren) Assessment of chronic cough and autonomic function Late-onset, slowly progressive syndrome defined by a triad of cerebellar ataxia, sensory (ganglionopathy-type) neuropathy and bilateral vestibular failure Caused by a biallelic AAGGG pentanucleotide repeat expansion in an intron of RFC1, inherited autosomal recessively A longstanding dry chronic cough often precedes the neurological features by years and is a valuable diagnostic clue Bilateral vestibular areflexia is demonstrated by an abnormal (impaired) bidirectional head-impulse test and impaired visually enhanced vestibulo-ocular reflex The sensory neuropathy is a non-length-dependent sensory neuronopathy causing sensory ataxia and areflexia Autonomic symptoms and oscillopsia on head movement are common associated features MRI frequently shows cerebellar (especially vermian) atrophy; nerve conduction studies show a sensory neuronopathy Management is supportive, centred on balance and vestibular rehabilitation, falls prevention and cough evaluation Rapidly progressive sensory neuronopathy raising concern for a paraneoplastic cause Recurrent falls with injury from combined sensory, cerebellar and vestibular loss Severe dysautonomia causing syncope or cardiovascular instability Marked dysphagia in advanced disease with aspiration risk Investigating the ataxia, neuropathy and vestibular loss as unrelated problems and missing the unifying diagnosis Overlooking a longstanding chronic cough that offers a strong diagnostic pointer Failing to test the vestibulo-ocular reflex and thus missing bilateral vestibular failure Not confirming the biallelic (recessive) nature of the RFC1 expansion, which is required for diagnosis CANVAS is caused by a biallelic AAGGG pentanucleotide repeat expansion within an intron of RFC1, which encodes the large subunit of replication factor C. The recessive expansion is thought to impair normal gene expression and RNA handling, producing a slowly progressive degeneration that converges on three vulnerable systems: the cerebellum, the dorsal root ganglia (giving a sensory neuronopathy) and the vestibular apparatus (giving bilateral vestibular failure). Involvement of sensory and autonomic ganglia and brainstem pathways also explains the frequent chronic cough and dysautonomia. The combined sensory, vestibular and cerebellar deficits summate to produce a severe multimodal balance disorder. CANVAS is slowly progressive over years to decades, with balance impairment and falls being the main sources of disability; life expectancy is usually preserved but mobility and independence decline gradually. Recognition allows targeted rehabilitation and avoidance of unnecessary investigation.

Cerebral amyloid angiopathy — CAA, congophilic angiopathy, cerebral amyloid angiopathy (sporadic, amyloid-beta type) Hypertensive deep intracerebral haemorrhage Haemorrhage from an underlying tumour or vascular malformation Coagulopathy or anticoagulant-related haemorrhage Hypertensive or other microangiopathy causing microbleeds Ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack when presenting with transient episodes Primary or secondary CNS vasculitis in the inflammatory subtype Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome with cortical bleeding MRI of the brain including susceptibility-weighted imaging to detect lobar microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis CT of the head in the acute setting to identify and localise haemorrhage Blood pressure assessment and coagulation studies to evaluate contributing factors Vascular imaging to exclude an underlying structural lesion in appropriate cases Amyloid PET and cerebrospinal fluid amyloid and tau markers where cognitive assessment or Alzheimer overlap is relevant Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and, rarely, biopsy when the inflammatory subtype is suspected A major cause of spontaneous lobar intracerebral haemorrhage in older adults, typically sparing the deep grey structures affected by hypertensive haemorrhage Susceptibility-weighted MRI reveals lobar cerebral microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis, which are key imaging biomarkers Transient focal neurological episodes, sometimes called amyloid spells, can mimic transient ischaemic attacks or seizures and are associated with superficial siderosis Progressive cognitive impairment is common, and the condition frequently coexists with Alzheimer disease pathology The Boston criteria integrate clinical and imaging features to estimate the probability of cerebral amyloid angiopathy Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy substantially raise the risk of further haemorrhage and require careful individual risk assessment A rare inflammatory form, cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related inflammation, presents with subacute encephalopathy and oedematous white matter change that may respond to immunosuppression Acute lobar intracerebral haemorrhage with rising intracranial pressure or deteriorating consciousness Recurrent haemorrhage, particularly in patients on antithrombotic therapy Subacute encephalopathy with oedematous white matter change suggesting the inflammatory subtype Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities developing during anti-amyloid antibody treatment Prescribing anticoagulants or antiplatelets without weighing the elevated haemorrhage risk in known or suspected cerebral amyloid angiopathy Misinterpreting transient focal episodes as transient ischaemic attacks and starting antithrombotic therapy Overlooking the treatable inflammatory subtype in a patient with subacute encephalopathy and white matter oedema Failing to recognise amyloid-related imaging abnormalities as a caveat of anti-amyloid antibody therapy Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is caused by progressive deposition of amyloid-beta protein within the walls of small and medium-sized arteries and arterioles of the cerebral cortex and leptomeninges. The amyloid-laden vessels become fragile and prone to rupture, producing lobar haemorrhages, microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis from repeated small bleeds, and impaired vascular function contributes to cognitive decline. The same amyloid-beta peptide is central to Alzheimer disease, explaining the frequent overlap, and an immune reaction against vascular amyloid can produce the inflammatory subtype. Deposition of vascular amyloid also underlies the amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) seen with anti-amyloid antibody therapies. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy carries a high risk of recurrent lobar haemorrhage and progressive cognitive decline, with prognosis depending on haemorrhage burden and comorbidity; the inflammatory subtype may improve with immunosuppression, but there is no disease-modifying treatment for the underlying angiopathy.

Cerebral aneurysm — intracranial aneurysm, berry aneurysm, saccular aneurysm Other causes of thunderclap headache (reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome) Perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal haemorrhage Arteriovenous malformation Intracerebral haemorrhage from hypertension Bacterial meningitis Migraine or primary headache Non-contrast CT head to detect subarachnoid blood Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia when CT is negative but suspicion persists CT angiography or digital subtraction angiography to define aneurysm location and morphology MRI/MR angiography for detection and follow-up of unruptured aneurysms Monitoring of sodium, and transcranial Doppler or imaging for vasospasm after haemorrhage Most intracranial aneurysms are saccular (berry) lesions arising at branch points of the circle of Willis, and many are asymptomatic until they rupture Rupture causes aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, classically a sudden thunderclap headache described as the worst ever, often with vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, and reduced consciousness A non-contrast CT performed early is highly sensitive for subarachnoid blood; if negative but suspicion remains, lumbar puncture looking for xanthochromia is used An enlarging unruptured aneurysm can cause warning signs such as a painful third nerve palsy from a posterior communicating artery lesion Risk factors include hypertension, smoking, family history, polycystic kidney disease, and connective tissue disorders After rupture, priorities are securing the aneurysm by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping to prevent rebleeding, alongside management of complications Delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm, hydrocephalus, hyponatraemia, and seizures are important complications after subarachnoid haemorrhage Management of unruptured aneurysms weighs rupture risk (influenced by size, site, and morphology) against the risks of treatment, and small stable lesions may be monitored Sudden thunderclap headache suggesting aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage requiring emergency imaging Reduced or fluctuating consciousness and focal deficit indicating a large bleed or rebleeding New painful third nerve palsy as a warning sign of an enlarging or symptomatic aneurysm Acute hydrocephalus or deterioration from delayed cerebral ischaemia after haemorrhage Dismissing a sudden severe headache as migraine and missing subarachnoid haemorrhage Relying on a late CT alone, when sensitivity falls and lumbar puncture may be needed Failing to secure a ruptured aneurysm promptly, risking early rebleeding Overlooking delayed complications such as vasospasm, hyponatraemia, and hydrocephalus A cerebral aneurysm is a focal outpouching of an intracranial artery wall, typically forming at bifurcations where haemodynamic stress is greatest and the muscular and elastic layers are relatively deficient. Over time, wall degeneration and turbulent flow allow the sac to enlarge. Rupture releases arterial blood into the subarachnoid space, abruptly raising intracranial pressure and irritating the meninges. Subsequent breakdown products can trigger arterial vasospasm days later, causing delayed cerebral ischaemia, while blood interfering with cerebrospinal fluid circulation can produce acute or communicating hydrocephalus. Unruptured aneurysms may remain quiescent, but rupture carries substantial mortality and morbidity, with many deaths occurring before or soon after hospital arrival; early securing of the aneurysm and management of vasospasm and hydrocephalus improve outcomes for survivors.

Cerebral folate deficiency — CFD, FOLR1 deficiency, folate receptor alpha deficiency, neurodegeneration due to cerebral folate transport deficiency Mitochondrial cytopathies including Kearns-Sayre syndrome Rett syndrome and other regression syndromes Primary neurotransmitter biosynthesis disorders Inborn errors of folate metabolism (e.g. DHFR or MTHFR deficiency) Autoimmune (folate receptor antibody) cerebral folate deficiency Leukodystrophies with infantile regression CSF 5-methyltetrahydrofolate measurement (the diagnostic cornerstone) FOLR1 molecular genetic testing Serum and red-cell folate to confirm normal peripheral status Serum folate receptor autoantibody assay Brain MRI for hypomyelination or leukoencephalopathy EEG for seizure characterisation Defined biochemically by a low cerebrospinal fluid 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-MTHF) concentration despite normal peripheral folate status The hereditary form is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in FOLR1, encoding folate receptor alpha, which mediates folate transport across the choroid plexus into the central nervous system Typically presents in late infancy with developmental regression, irritability, movement disorder, acquired microcephaly, ataxia and drug-resistant seizures Folinic acid (a reduced folate that can bypass the transport defect) is the specific treatment and can improve or stabilise neurological function, especially when started early Some children have a leukoencephalopathy or hypomyelination on MRI that may partly reverse with treatment Folate receptor autoantibodies and secondary causes (mitochondrial disease, Kearns-Sayre syndrome) can produce an acquired cerebral folate deficiency phenotype Standard oral folic acid is not the correct therapy; reduced folate is needed to restore central nervous system folate Lumbar puncture for CSF 5-MTHF is central to diagnosis and should be considered in unexplained infantile regression with movement disorder Developmental regression with drug-resistant seizures Acquired microcephaly signalling ongoing neurodegeneration Progressive movement disorder or ataxia Visual deterioration Measuring only peripheral folate, which is typically normal, and thereby missing the diagnosis Treating with plain folic acid instead of a reduced folate such as folinic acid Attributing the picture to non-specific epileptic encephalopathy without CSF studies Failing to distinguish hereditary FOLR1 disease from autoantibody-mediated or mitochondrial secondary forms Cerebral folate deficiency is a state of low central nervous system folate in the presence of normal systemic folate. In the hereditary FOLR1 form, loss of functional folate receptor alpha at the choroid plexus prevents transport of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate from blood into cerebrospinal fluid. The resulting central folate deficit impairs one-carbon metabolism, methylation reactions and neurotransmitter synthesis in the developing brain, leading to hypomyelination, neuronal dysfunction and a progressive encephalopathy. Because folinic acid is a reduced folate that can reach the brain through alternative routes, supplementation can raise CSF folate and mitigate the neurological damage. Early folinic acid treatment can arrest regression and improve development, but delayed diagnosis is associated with irreversible neurological impairment, so outcome is strongly time-dependent.

Cerebral Palsy — CP, spastic diplegia, static encephalopathy Progressive neurodegenerative or metabolic disorders Spinal muscular atrophy and other neuromuscular disorders Dopa-responsive dystonia Hereditary spastic paraplegia Structural spinal cord lesions Global developmental delay without a motor disorder MRI of the brain to identify structural or ischaemic lesions EEG when seizures are suspected Metabolic or genetic testing if the presentation is atypical or progressive Assessment of vision and hearing Hip surveillance imaging to detect subluxation Evaluation of feeding, swallowing, and nutrition A group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive injury or malformation of the developing brain, though the clinical picture can change as the child grows. It is the most common cause of chronic motor disability beginning in childhood. Classified by motor type (spastic, dyskinetic, ataxic, or mixed) and by topography (hemiplegia, diplegia, quadriplegia). Spastic forms are most common; early signs include abnormal tone, persistent primitive reflexes, delayed motor milestones, and early hand preference before one year. Preterm birth, low birth weight, intrauterine growth restriction, perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic injury, infection, kernicterus, and brain malformations are recognised risk factors. Frequent comorbidities include intellectual disability, epilepsy, visual and hearing impairment, feeding and swallowing difficulties, communication problems, and orthopaedic complications such as hip subluxation and contractures. Diagnosis is largely clinical; MRI often identifies the underlying lesion and helps establish aetiology. Management is multidisciplinary and supportive, aiming to maximise function and participation with therapy, orthotics, spasticity treatment, and orthopaedic care rather than cure. Because the disorder is static, clear progression or regression of neurological signs should prompt a search for an alternative, evolving diagnosis. Loss of previously acquired skills or clear neurological progression (suggests an alternative diagnosis) New or worsening seizures Signs of aspiration or faltering growth from feeding difficulty Progressive scoliosis or hip dislocation Rapidly increasing spasticity or dystonia causing pain or care difficulty Labelling a child with cerebral palsy when the course is actually progressive (missing a treatable metabolic or genetic disorder) Focusing only on motor impairment and overlooking epilepsy, sensory, or feeding comorbidities Neglecting hip surveillance, allowing silent dislocation Underestimating cognition in non-verbal children with good comprehension Delaying nutritional and communication support Cerebral palsy results from injury or maldevelopment of the immature brain from any of a range of prenatal, perinatal, or early postnatal insults. In preterm infants, periventricular white-matter injury (periventricular leukomalacia) commonly affects descending motor tracts, producing spastic diplegia; in term infants, hypoxic-ischaemic injury, malformations, stroke, or kernicterus may be responsible. The primary lesion is non-progressive, but secondary musculoskeletal changes such as contractures and bony deformity evolve over time. The motor impairment itself is non-progressive, and life expectancy is often near normal in milder forms; outcome depends on severity, mobility level, and comorbidities, with severe quadriplegia, epilepsy, intellectual disability, and feeding problems associated with greater disability and shorter survival.

Cerebro-oculo-facio-skeletal syndrome — COFS syndrome, Pena-Shokeir syndrome type 2, cerebrooculofacioskeletal syndrome, ERCC6, ERCC5, ERCC2, ERCC1 Cockayne syndrome Pena-Shokeir syndrome type 1 (foetal akinesia deformation sequence) Congenital cytomegalovirus and other congenital infections Neuronal migration disorders with contractures Congenital muscular dystrophies with brain and eye involvement Peroxisomal disorders such as Zellweger syndrome Neuroimaging showing microcephaly, calcification and structural brain malformation Ophthalmological examination for cataract, microphthalmia and retinal changes Molecular genetic testing for nucleotide-excision-repair genes (ERCC1/2/5/6 and related) DNA-repair functional studies in cultured fibroblasts where genetics is inconclusive Assessment of feeding, swallowing and respiratory function Skeletal survey to characterise contractures and exclude other diagnoses A severe autosomal recessive DNA-repair disorder within the nucleotide-excision-repair spectrum, overlapping clinically with Cockayne syndrome Characterised by microcephaly with brain malformation, congenital cataracts and/or microphthalmia, a characteristic facial appearance and multiple joint contractures (arthrogryposis) Prenatal or early-onset growth failure and profound developmental impairment are typical Progressive neurological deterioration, feeding difficulty and recurrent respiratory infection are common Caused by variants in nucleotide-excision-repair genes such as ERCC1, ERCC2, ERCC5 and ERCC6, linking it to Cockayne syndrome and xeroderma pigmentosum Historically labelled Pena-Shokeir syndrome type 2, but distinct from the akinesia-based Pena-Shokeir type 1 Management is supportive and palliative, with genetic counselling for the recessive inheritance Progressive neurological deterioration and intractable feeding difficulty Recurrent aspiration and respiratory infection Failure to thrive with severe growth failure Recurrence risk in future pregnancies given autosomal recessive inheritance Confusing the DNA-repair-based COFS syndrome with the akinesia-based Pena-Shokeir type 1 despite the shared eponym Overlooking the link to Cockayne syndrome and the wider nucleotide-excision-repair spectrum Missing congenital cataract or microphthalmia on examination Failing to provide recurrence counselling for the recessive inheritance Cerebro-oculo-facio-skeletal syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in genes of the nucleotide-excision-repair pathway (including ERCC1, ERCC2, ERCC5 and ERCC6), the same pathway disrupted in Cockayne syndrome and xeroderma pigmentosum. Defective repair of transcription-coupled DNA damage impairs the survival and function of neurons and other cells during development, producing microcephaly, brain malformation and progressive neurodegeneration. Associated foetal neurological impairment reduces movement in utero, leading to arthrogryposis, while abnormal development gives the ocular anomalies (cataract, microphthalmia) and the distinctive facial features. The disorder lies on a continuum with Cockayne syndrome, representing a severe, early-onset end of that spectrum. The prognosis is very poor, with most affected children dying in early childhood from neurological deterioration and respiratory complications; care is supportive and palliative, focused on comfort, feeding support and family counselling.

Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis — CTX, sterol 27-hydroxylase deficiency, CYP27A1 deficiency, cholestanolosis Familial hypercholesterolaemia with tendon xanthomata Sitosterolaemia (xanthomata with a plant-sterol defect) Other hereditary spastic paraplegias and cerebellar ataxias Multiple sclerosis or other progressive neuroinflammatory disease Early-onset dementia or leukodystrophy of other cause Neonatal cholestasis from other bile acid synthesis defects Plasma cholestanol concentration (characteristically raised) Urinary bile alcohol analysis Molecular genetic testing of the CYP27A1 gene Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, which may show cerebellar and dentate nucleus changes Slit-lamp examination for juvenile cataract and clinical assessment of tendon xanthomata Lipid profile, noting cholesterol may be normal or low despite xanthomata Autosomal recessive defect of bile acid synthesis caused by deficiency of the mitochondrial enzyme sterol 27-hydroxylase (CYP27A1) The block impairs bile acid production and diverts cholesterol to cholestanol, which accumulates in the brain, tendons and other tissues A highly treatable but frequently missed cause of progressive neurological decline; early diagnosis is critical to prevent irreversible damage The classic triad comprises tendon xanthomata (especially the Achilles tendon), early-onset (juvenile) bilateral cataracts and progressive neuropsychiatric and cerebellar dysfunction Early clues in childhood include neonatal cholestasis, intractable or chronic diarrhoea and learning difficulty, preceding the neurological syndrome The biochemical hallmark is raised plasma cholestanol with normal or low cholesterol and increased urinary bile alcohols Treatment is replacement with chenodeoxycholic acid, which suppresses abnormal synthesis and can halt or improve disease if started early; a statin may be added Progressive cognitive, psychiatric or cerebellar decline in a young person with tendon xanthomata Early-onset bilateral cataracts in a child or young adult Neonatal cholestasis or intractable childhood diarrhoea of unknown cause Delay in starting bile acid replacement, risking irreversible neurological damage Assuming tendon xanthomata always indicate familial hypercholesterolaemia, since cholesterol is often normal here Missing the diagnosis during the early non-neurological phase (cholestasis, diarrhoea, cataract) Overlooking juvenile cataract as an early diagnostic clue Delaying treatment while awaiting genetic confirmation, forfeiting a treatable window Failing to screen and counsel at-risk relatives given the recessive inheritance Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis is caused by deficiency of sterol 27-hydroxylase, an enzyme in the mitochondrial pathway of bile acid synthesis from cholesterol. Loss of this step reduces production of the primary bile acid chenodeoxycholic acid, removing the normal negative feedback on the rate-limiting enzyme of bile acid synthesis and driving overproduction of bile acid intermediates. These intermediates are shunted into cholestanol and bile alcohols, which accumulate in tissues. Deposition of cholestanol and cholesterol in the central nervous system, tendons and lens produces the characteristic xanthomata, cataracts and progressive neurodegeneration. Replacing the deficient bile acid restores feedback inhibition and reduces the toxic accumulation. If chenodeoxycholic acid replacement is started before significant neurological damage, progression can be halted and some deficits improve, giving a good outlook; late diagnosis after established neurodegeneration carries a poorer prognosis with irreversible disability.

Cervical Cancer — carcinoma of the cervix, cervical carcinoma, cervical malignancy, invasive cervical cancer Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (pre-invasive disease) Cervical polyp or ectropion Most infections clear spontaneously, but persistent infection produces cervical intraepithelial neoplasia that may progress over years to invasive carcinoma. Invasion typically begins at the transformation zone and extends locally into the cervical stroma, vagina, and parametrium, then to pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes and distant sites. Prognosis depends strongly on stage at diagnosis: disease confined to the cervix carries high cure rates, whereas parametrial extension, nodal involvement, and distant spread substantially reduce survival. Tumour size, histological subtype, and depth of invasion further influence outcome, and screening plus vaccination continue to shift diagnosis toward earlier, more curable stages.

idiopathic (primary), but secondary causes should be considered Fixed posture present from birth or in early childhood suggesting a structural or congenital cause Rapid progression or generalisation suggesting a secondary process Associated focal neurological signs, myelopathy or systemic illness Features of Wilson's disease in a younger patient Overlooking the sensory trick, which is a valuable diagnostic clue Attributing the abnormal posture and pain to a primary orthopaedic or musculoskeletal cause Missing a drug-induced or structural secondary cause Under-treating the associated neck pain, which is often the most disabling symptom Cervical dystonia arises from dysfunction of the basal ganglia and the wider sensorimotor network, with impaired inhibition and abnormal sensorimotor integration leading to excessive, inappropriate co-contraction of the cervical muscles. The effectiveness of a sensory trick illustrates the strong influence of afferent input on the abnormal motor output. Most cases are idiopathic and may have a genetic predisposition, although structural, drug-induced and other secondary causes are recognised. Cervical dystonia is generally chronic; while it can be painful and disabling, it does not shorten life, and severity often stabilises after the early years. Botulinum toxin injection into the overactive muscles is the treatment of choice and produces meaningful, repeatable benefit in most patients; oral medication, physiotherapy and, in refractory cases, deep brain stimulation are additional options.

Cervical ectropion — Cervical ectopy, Cervical erosion Cervical polyp Cervicitis of infective origin Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia or early cervical carcinoma Nabothian cysts Cervical condyloma Contact bleeding from another cervical or vaginal cause Speculum examination as the basis of clinical diagnosis Cervical cytology and HPV testing in line with the screening programme Colposcopy when cytology is abnormal or the lesion looks suspicious Endocervical swabs for sexually transmitted infections where there is discharge or bleeding Pregnancy test and hormonal history Directed biopsy if there is any suspicion of neoplasia Cervical ectropion is the presence of endocervical columnar epithelium everted onto the ectocervix around the external os, and it is a normal physiological finding rather than a true erosion. It is common in high-oestrogen states such as adolescence, pregnancy and combined hormonal contraceptive use. It appears as a red, velvety zone around the os because the thin single-layered columnar epithelium reveals the underlying vasculature. Most are asymptomatic, but the fragile epithelium may produce postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding and a copious, non-offensive mucoid discharge. It is benign and usually requires only reassurance, with no treatment needed. Symptoms often settle once the hormonal stimulus is withdrawn, for example on stopping the combined pill, as squamous metaplasia re-covers the area. Persistently troublesome symptoms can be treated by ablation such as cryotherapy or diathermy once other causes are excluded. The transformation zone lies at the squamocolumnar junction within the ectropion and is the key site sampled during cervical screening. Abnormal cervical cytology or high-risk HPV positivity An irregular, friable or contact-bleeding lesion suspicious for malignancy Presentation in a postmenopausal woman, in whom an oestrogen-driven ectropion is unexpected Persistent symptoms despite appropriate treatment Associated infective symptoms that fail to resolve Using the misleading term erosion, which can needlessly alarm the patient. Attributing abnormal bleeding to ectropion without excluding cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, carcinoma and infection. Ablating the cervix before excluding neoplasia and infection. Overlooking chlamydial cervicitis, which can resemble an ectropion. Performing unnecessary ablation during early pregnancy. Under oestrogenic influence the squamocolumnar junction migrates outward onto the ectocervix, exposing delicate endocervical columnar epithelium to the vaginal environment. Because this epithelium is a single vascular layer, it bleeds easily on contact and secretes abundant mucus, accounting for the typical symptoms. Over time the acidic vaginal pH induces squamous metaplasia that forms the transformation zone, and the junction eventually recedes; the process is neither inflammatory nor truly erosive despite the historical term erosion. The prognosis is excellent as the condition is benign and frequently self-limiting, with symptoms resolving spontaneously or after simple ablative treatment, and it carries no malignant potential in itself.

Cervical Incompetence — cervical incompetence, cervical insufficiency, incompetent cervix, cervical insufficiency of pregnancy Preterm labour with contractions Chorioamnionitis or intra-amniotic infection Placental abruption Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes Uterine anomaly causing recurrent loss Antiphospholipid syndrome and other causes of recurrent mid-trimester loss Serial transvaginal ultrasound cervical length measurement with assessment for funnelling Speculum examination to assess dilatation and detect bulging or ruptured membranes Screening for infection including genital and urinary cultures where relevant Review of obstetric and surgical history for prior losses and cervical procedures Assessment for alternative causes of recurrent loss such as thrombophilia or uterine anomaly where indicated Cervical incompetence is painless progressive cervical dilatation in the second trimester leading to mid-trimester pregnancy loss or spontaneous preterm birth in the absence of contractions or labour The hallmark history is recurrent second-trimester losses that are painless, often with rupture of membranes or bulging membranes and rapid, non-laborious delivery Risk factors include previous cervical surgery (cone biopsy, large loop excision), cervical trauma from dilatation, congenital collagen or Mullerian abnormalities, and prior mechanical dilatation Transvaginal ultrasound measurement of cervical length is the key surveillance tool, with progressive shortening and funnelling of the internal os indicating risk Cervical cerclage, a stitch placed to reinforce the cervix, is offered based on history, ultrasound findings, or examination findings depending on the clinical scenario Vaginal progesterone is used to reduce preterm birth risk in women with a short cervix, and can complement or substitute for cerclage in selected cases History-indicated cerclage is typically placed electively in early second trimester, whereas ultrasound- or examination-indicated (rescue) cerclage is placed when shortening or dilatation is detected Emergency rescue cerclage on a dilated cervix with exposed membranes carries higher risks of membrane rupture and infection and requires careful case selection The diagnosis is clinical and somewhat retrospective, as no single definitive test confirms it, so it must be distinguished from preterm labour and infection Painless cervical dilatation with bulging or exposed fetal membranes in the second trimester Rupture of membranes at previable or early gestation Signs of intra-amniotic infection (fever, uterine tenderness, offensive discharge, maternal or fetal tachycardia) Rapidly progressive cervical shortening on surveillance scanning Onset of contractions or bleeding suggesting labour or abruption rather than pure insufficiency Attributing painless mid-trimester loss to bad luck and not investigating for insufficiency Placing a rescue cerclage without recognising established infection or advanced labour Overlooking infection as either a cause or a contraindication to intervention Relying on a single cervical length measurement rather than trends Failing to plan surveillance or cerclage early in a subsequent at-risk pregnancy The cervix normally remains firm and closed under load until term, maintained by its collagen-rich connective tissue. In cervical insufficiency, structural or functional weakness of this tissue, whether congenital, from collagen disorders, or acquired through surgical or traumatic disruption, means the cervix cannot withstand the increasing mechanical stress of the growing pregnancy. It shortens, effaces, and dilates painlessly. As the cervix opens, the fetal membranes prolapse into the vagina, becoming exposed to ascending flora; membrane rupture and mid-trimester loss or preterm delivery follow, often without the coordinated contractions of true labour. With recognition and appropriate intervention, whether cerclage, progesterone, or close surveillance, many women achieve substantially prolonged gestation and improved neonatal outcomes in subsequent pregnancies. Prognosis is poorer when membranes are already prolapsed or ruptured, or when infection supervenes. Recurrence risk in future pregnancies is significant, warranting proactive planning.

history, ultrasound-detected shortening, or as a rescue procedure for premature dilatation It must be distinguished from preterm labour and from infection or abruption, which change management Excluding infection and ruptured membranes is essential before intervention such as rescue cerclage Painless cervical dilatation with bulging or exposed membranes Signs of intra-amniotic infection such as fever, tenderness, or offensive discharge Ruptured membranes with cervical change Rapidly progressing dilatation in the mid-trimester Placing a cerclage without excluding infection or ruptured membranes Labelling a first mid-trimester loss as insufficiency without considering other causes Missing coexisting preterm labour or abruption and delaying appropriate care Failing to monitor cervical length in women with relevant risk factors Cervical insufficiency reflects structural or functional weakness of the cervix so that it cannot retain the pregnancy against the increasing mechanical load of the growing uterus. Deficient cervical stroma, whether from congenital collagen abnormality or acquired damage after surgery or trauma, leads to progressive painless shortening, funnelling, and dilatation, often in the second trimester. As the cervix opens, membranes may prolapse and become exposed to the vaginal flora, predisposing to rupture, ascending infection, and subsequent loss or preterm delivery. In practice a spectrum exists, with inflammation and subclinical infection frequently interacting with mechanical weakness. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause, gestation, and timeliness of intervention. History-indicated and ultrasound-indicated cerclage can improve outcomes in appropriately selected women, whereas advanced dilatation with prolapsing membranes or infection carries a high risk of loss or extreme preterm birth.

Cervical polyp — Endocervical polyp, Cervical mucous polyp Endometrial polyp prolapsing through the os Prolapsed submucosal fibroid Cervical ectropion Cervical carcinoma Retained products of conception or decidual reaction in pregnancy Nabothian cyst Cervical condyloma or papilloma Speculum examination to establish the diagnosis Histopathological examination of the excised polyp Cervical cytology in accordance with the screening programme Transvaginal ultrasound or saline sonohysterography to assess the endometrium Hysteroscopy when endometrial pathology is suspected or the polyp is broad-based Endometrial biopsy when abnormal uterine bleeding is accompanied by risk factors High vaginal and endocervical swabs where there is associated discharge Cervical polyps are common benign outgrowths of endocervical, and occasionally ectocervical, tissue, most frequent in multiparous women in the fourth to sixth decades. They are often asymptomatic and found incidentally at speculum examination, but when symptomatic they cause intermenstrual, postcoital or postmenopausal bleeding, or a mucoid discharge. The typical appearance is a smooth, reddish, pedunculated lesion protruding through the external os. Malignant change is very rare, affecting well under one per cent, yet every removed polyp should be sent for histological examination. Small symptomatic polyps can frequently be removed in clinic by grasping and twisting the base, whereas a broad-based lesion may require hysteroscopic resection. Coexisting endometrial polyps are common, particularly when there is abnormal bleeding, so the endometrial cavity should be assessed. Visible bleeding still warrants exclusion of cervical and endometrial malignancy, even when a polyp is present. An endometrial polyp can prolapse through the cervix and mimic a cervical polyp, and recurrence after removal is possible. Postmenopausal bleeding, which mandates endometrial investigation regardless of a visible polyp A friable, irregular or necrotic-looking lesion suspicious for malignancy Persistent abnormal bleeding after polyp removal Rapid growth of the lesion Abnormal cervical cytology Assuming all bleeding arises from the polyp and failing to investigate the cervix and endometrium for malignancy. Not submitting the removed specimen for histology. Mistaking a prolapsed endometrial polyp or submucosal fibroid for a cervical polyp. Removing a polyp during pregnancy without accounting for the increased risk of bleeding. Overlooking an associated endometrial polyp in women with abnormal uterine bleeding. A cervical polyp is a focal benign proliferation of endocervical columnar epithelium and its supporting stroma, generally attributed to chronic inflammation, local vascular congestion or oestrogenic stimulation. It consists of a vascular connective-tissue core covered by epithelium, and the fragile surface vessels bleed readily on contact, producing the characteristic postcoital or intermenstrual spotting. The covering epithelium may undergo squamous metaplasia, and less commonly microglandular hyperplasia develops in association with progestogen exposure or pregnancy. The prognosis is excellent, as cervical polyps are benign with very low malignant potential and simple removal is usually curative, although recurrence can occur.

Cervical radiculopathy — cervical nerve root compression, brachialgia, pinched nerve in the neck, cervical nerve root impingement Cervical spondylotic myelopathy when long-tract signs are present
