peripheral entrapment Plain and oblique radiographs to assess foraminal narrowing and alignment CT to characterise osteophytes when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated Diagnostic selective nerve-root block to confirm the symptomatic level Compression or irritation of a cervical nerve root causes dermatomal arm pain, paraesthesiae, and sometimes myotomal weakness The C6 and C7 roots are most commonly affected: C6 radiates to the thumb and C7 to the middle finger The Spurling test (extension, ipsilateral rotation, and axial compression of the neck) reproduces radicular arm symptoms The shoulder abduction relief sign, in which resting the arm on the head eases symptoms, supports a radicular cause Reflex changes help localise the level: a reduced biceps or brachioradialis jerk suggests C6 and a reduced triceps jerk suggests C7 Most cases arise from either a soft disc herniation in younger patients or foraminal narrowing from spondylosis in older patients The natural history is usually favourable, with most patients improving on conservative treatment (analgesia, physiotherapy, activity modification, nerve-root injection) Progressive weakness, myelopathic signs, or failure of conservative care prompt MRI and consideration of foraminotomy, discectomy, or fusion Signs of myelopathy such as gait disturbance, hand clumsiness, or hyperreflexia indicating cord compression Progressive or profound motor weakness Constitutional features or a history of malignancy suggesting a neoplastic cause Confusing radiculopathy with primary shoulder pathology or peripheral nerve entrapment Missing coexisting myelopathy by not examining for long-tract signs Operating for pain alone without a corroborating match between imaging and the clinical level Cervical radiculopathy is dysfunction of a cervical nerve root caused by mechanical compression and chemical irritation. In younger patients a soft posterolateral disc herniation is the usual cause, whereas in older patients narrowing of the intervertebral foramen by uncovertebral and facet osteophytes (spondylosis) predominates. Compression together with accompanying inflammation of the root produces pain, sensory disturbance, and, in a myotomal distribution, motor weakness and reflex loss corresponding to the affected level. Most patients with cervical radiculopathy improve within weeks to a few months with conservative measures, and surgery reliably relieves arm pain in those who fail conservative treatment or develop significant weakness.

Cervical spondylosis — cervical degenerative disc disease, cervical osteoarthritis, cervical spondylotic myelopathy, cervical radiculopathy Cervical disc prolapse Peripheral nerve entrapment (e.g. carpal or cubital tunnel syndrome) Brachial plexopathy or thoracic outlet syndrome Motor neuron disease and other neurodegenerative conditions Multiple sclerosis or intramedullary cord lesion Shoulder pathology (rotator cuff disease) referring pain to the arm Spinal tumour or infection MRI of the cervical spine to assess cord and root compression Plain cervical radiographs (including flexion/extension views) for alignment and degenerative change Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to distinguish radiculopathy from peripheral entrapment CT for detailed bony anatomy when MRI is contraindicated or surgery is planned Neurological examination for upper and lower limb signs of myelopathy Age-related degeneration of the cervical discs and facet joints causing neck pain, stiffness, and sometimes referred occipital headache; it is extremely common and often asymptomatic on imaging Nerve-root compression by osteophytes or disc material produces radiculopathy with dermatomal arm pain, sensory change, weakness, and reflex loss, most often at C5/6 and C6/7 Cord compression from a narrowed canal produces cervical spondylotic myelopathy, the most important complication, which can develop insidiously Myelopathy is suggested by gait disturbance, clumsy hands, loss of dexterity, and upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Hoffmann's sign, extensor plantars, sometimes bladder involvement) Most patients with axial neck pain or radiculopathy improve with conservative measures such as analgesia, activity modification, and physiotherapy MRI is the investigation of choice to demonstrate cord and root compression when myelopathy or persistent radiculopathy is suspected Progressive myelopathy is an indication for surgical decompression to halt deterioration, since established cord damage recovers poorly Radiographic degenerative change correlates poorly with symptoms, so imaging findings must be interpreted alongside the clinical picture Signs of cervical myelopathy (gait disturbance, hand clumsiness, hyperreflexia, sphincter dysfunction) requiring urgent specialist assessment Rapidly progressive neurological deficit Features suggesting infection or malignancy (fever, weight loss, night pain, cancer history) Acute deterioration after neck trauma in a spondylotic, stenotic spine Missing early myelopathy by attributing gait or hand-function changes to age or arthritis Over-relying on degenerative radiographic findings that are common and often asymptomatic Delaying decompression in progressive myelopathy until irreversible cord damage occurs Aggressive manipulation of a stenotic, myelopathic cervical spine With ageing the cervical intervertebral discs lose height and hydration, transferring load to the facet and uncovertebral joints, which develop osteophytes. These bony spurs, together with disc bulging, ligamentum flavum thickening, and reduced canal diameter, encroach on the neural foramina and spinal canal. Foraminal narrowing compresses nerve roots to cause radiculopathy, while central canal stenosis compresses the spinal cord, producing myelopathy through direct pressure and impaired vascular supply. Dynamic factors during neck movement can aggravate cord compression. The degenerative process is gradual, and neurological compromise may accumulate slowly before becoming clinically apparent. Axial neck pain and radiculopathy usually follow a fluctuating but generally benign course with conservative care; cervical spondylotic myelopathy tends to progress in a stepwise manner, and while surgery can arrest decline, neurological recovery of established deficits is often incomplete, making timely intervention important.

Cervical spondylotic myelopathy — CSM, cervical myelopathy, degenerative cervical myelopathy, spondylotic cervical myelopathy Motor neurone disease (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) Multiple sclerosis or other demyelinating disease Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency Intramedullary or extramedullary spinal tumour Normal-pressure hydrocephalus or other central gait disorder Peripheral neuropathy MRI of the cervical spine to show compression and any cord signal change Flexion-extension radiographs to assess alignment and instability CT to characterise osteophytes and ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament Nerve conduction studies and EMG to help distinguish motor neurone disease or peripheral neuropathy Vitamin B12 and metabolic screen when subacute combined degeneration is possible The commonest cause of spinal cord dysfunction in adults over 50, resulting from degenerative narrowing of the cervical canal Presents insidiously with clumsy hands (difficulty with buttons, handwriting, and dropping objects) and an unsteady, broad-based gait Upper motor neurone signs appear below the level of compression: hyperreflexia, clonus, extensor plantar responses, and spasticity A positive Hoffmann sign (flicking the middle fingernail provokes thumb and index flexion) and an inverted supinator reflex point to cervical cord involvement The Lhermitte phenomenon, an electric-shock sensation down the spine or limbs on neck flexion, may be reported The myelopathic hand shows the finger escape sign and difficulty with rapid grip-and-release movements Neck pain may be mild or absent, and sensory symptoms and sphincter disturbance tend to appear later MRI demonstrates cord compression and may show intramedullary signal change; surgical decompression is the mainstay for progressive myelopathy because conservative treatment rarely reverses established deficits Rapidly progressive weakness, gait deterioration, or new sphincter disturbance Acute deterioration after minor neck trauma suggesting a central cord syndrome in a stenotic neck Significant cord compression with myelomalacia on imaging Misattributing early myelopathy to ageing, arthritis, or peripheral neuropathy and delaying imaging Ascribing bilateral hand clumsiness and hyperreflexia to carpal tunnel syndrome Failing to recognise the risk of catastrophic central cord injury from minor falls in a stenotic neck Cervical spondylotic myelopathy results from age-related degenerative change: disc-height loss, osteophyte (spondylotic bar) formation, facet and uncovertebral hypertrophy, and infolding of a thickened ligamentum flavum progressively narrow the cervical spinal canal, and a congenitally narrow canal predisposes. Static compression is compounded by dynamic factors, as the cord is pinched during extension and stretched over ventral osteophytes during flexion. Repetitive mechanical injury together with impaired microvascular perfusion produces demyelination and grey-matter loss, particularly in the lateral and posterior columns, giving rise to the characteristic long-tract signs. The natural history is typically one of stepwise deterioration; established neurological deficits often do not fully recover even after surgery, so timely decompression before severe or long-standing signs develop offers the best functional outcome.

Cervicogenic headache — CGH, cervical headache Migraine, especially when accompanied by neck pain Tension-type headache Occipital neuralgia Hemicrania continua Temporomandibular joint disorder Cervical radiculopathy or myelopathy Examination of cervical range of motion and provocation of pain by neck manoeuvres Assessment of upper cervical joint and muscle tenderness Cervical spine imaging with X-ray or MRI when structural or red-flag features are present Diagnostic anaesthetic blocks of cervical facet joints or nerves for confirmation Review for migrainous features to distinguish overlapping headache types Pain is referred to the head from a disorder of the cervical spine, typically the upper C1 to C3 segments It is usually side-locked and unilateral without side-shift, beginning in the neck or occiput and radiating to the fronto-temporal region Attacks are provoked by neck movement, sustained awkward postures, or pressure over the upper cervical joints or muscles Restricted cervical range of motion and ipsilateral neck, shoulder or arm discomfort are common Relief of pain after a diagnostic anaesthetic block of a cervical structure or nerve strongly supports the diagnosis Autonomic and migrainous features are usually mild, helping distinguish it from migraine and the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias Imaging changes of cervical spondylosis are common with age and do not by themselves confirm causation Neurological signs of cervical myelopathy or radiculopathy A history of significant neck trauma, malignancy or infection Systemic symptoms, fever or unexplained weight loss Sudden severe neck pain with headache suggesting arterial dissection Attributing headache to incidental cervical spondylosis seen on imaging Missing vertebral or carotid artery dissection presenting with neck pain and headache Confusing it with migraine, which also frequently involves neck pain Relying on imaging rather than on clinical provocation and diagnostic blocks Cervicogenic headache arises because sensory afferents from the upper three cervical segments converge with trigeminal afferents in the trigeminocervical complex of the upper spinal cord and lower brainstem. Nociceptive input from the upper cervical joints, discs, ligaments or muscles is therefore perceived as pain in trigeminal territory, that is, in the head, and the pattern of referral depends on the specific cervical structure generating the pain. Prognosis depends on the underlying cervical disorder; many patients improve with physiotherapy, manual therapy and targeted injections, though pain can be chronic and recurrent when degenerative changes persist.

Cestode (Tapeworm) Infections — neurocysticercosis, Taenia, echinococcosis, hydatid disease Intestinal taeniasis presenting only with passage of proglottids or vague abdominal symptoms (T. saginata, T. asiatica, T. solium, D. latus, D. caninum) Megaloblastic / pernicious-type anemia from vitamin B12 deficiency in D. latus fish tapeworm infection Seizure disorder / epilepsy of other cause in regions where neurocysticercosis is endemic Obstructive or communicating hydrocephalus from ventricular or subarachnoid cysticerci Sparganosis presenting as a migrating subcutaneous, periorbital or CNS mass (Spirometra plerocercoid) Coenurosis presenting as a CNS or subcutaneous space-occupying cystic lesion (T. multiceps, T. serialis) Tuberculoma / CNS tuberculosis (major cause of focal CNS mass lesions in India and East Asia) Toxoplasma encephalitis (ring-enhancing CNS lesions, especially in immunocompromised/HIV) Pyogenic brain abscess Other tissue helminths producing CNS or hepatic cysts (e.g., schistosomiasis, sparganosis) Stool microscopy for eggs/proglottids; perianal cellophane-tape swab when taeniasis suspected (eggs of the three Taenia species are morphologically indistinguishable) Examination of mature proglottids or scolex, or molecular testing, to distinguish T. solium from T. saginata/T. asiatica Neuroimaging (MRI and CT) for neurocysticercosis, including FIESTA/3D-CISS for ventricular/subarachnoid cysts and susceptibility-weighted imaging for calcifications Enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot (EITB) on serum for cysticercosis antibody CSF analysis (lymphocytic, neutrophilic or eosinophilic pleocytosis; protein may be raised; glucose usually normal but occasionally markedly reduced) Funduscopic / dilated ophthalmologic exam in all patients with suspected neurocysticercosis Ultrasound, CT or MRI with WHO ultrasound staging (CL, CE1-CE5) for hepatic cystic echinococcosis; chest x-ray/CT for pulmonary cysts ELISA/immunoblot serology for echinococcosis (cannot exclude disease if negative) PET to follow disease activity in alveolar echinococcosis Primary or metastatic brain tumor (parenchymal neurocysticercosis or spinal cysticercus can mimic intraspinal tumor) CNS lymphoma Hepatic neoplasm or simple/biliary hepatic cyst (alveolar echinococcosis mimics a slow-growing liver tumor; cystic hydatid mimics benign liver cyst) Cholelithiasis (biliary leakage/compression by a hepatic hydatid cyst) Cestodes (tapeworms) cause two clinically distinct patterns: intestinal infection by adult worms (taeniasis) and somatic/larval-tissue infection (e.g., cysticercosis, hydatid disease) (Harrison 22e p.1832). Neurocysticercosis is the most common parasitic disease of the CNS worldwide; humans acquire it by ingesting food contaminated with Taenia solium eggs, not by eating cysticerci-containing pork (which instead causes intestinal taeniasis) (Harrison 22e p.1833, p.1138). Seizures are the most frequent manifestation of neurocysticercosis and are associated with inflammation of brain parenchyma around the cysticercus; new-onset partial seizures with or without secondary generalization are the classic presentation (Harrison 22e p.1833, p.1138). On neuroimaging a cystic lesion with a mural nodule representing the scolex ('dot-in-hole') is diagnostic of neurocysticercosis; lesions evolve through vesicular, colloidal, granulonodular and nodular-calcified stages (Harrison 22e p.1833-1834, p.1138). CT is more sensitive for calcified lesions, whereas MRI is more sensitive for small cystic lesions, scolices and enhancement; FIESTA/3D-CISS sequences best detect ventricular and subarachnoid cysts (Harrison 22e p.1834). The enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot (EITB) using lentil-lectin-purified glycoproteins is >99% specific/sensitive in patients with multiple cysts, but patients with a single intracranial lesion or only calcifications may be seronegative; serum is more sensitive than CSF (Harrison 22e p.1834). Crude-antigen ELISA antibody tests have high false-positive and false-negative rates and should be avoided for neurocysticercosis (Harrison 22e p.1834). In endemic-area patients with a single enhancing 5-20 mm round CT lesion, seizures, a normal exam and no systemic disease (no fever, adenopathy or chest abnormality), the lesion is almost always neurocysticercosis (validated in India) (Harrison 22e p.1834). Antiparasitic treatment of neurocysticercosis is never an emergency; initial management focuses on controlling seizures and hydrocephalus and on excluding intraocular disease before any cysticidal therapy (Harrison 22e p.1834). High-dose glucocorticoids should always accompany antiparasitic therapy of neurocysticercosis, since dying parasites provoke an inflammatory response that can worsen seizures or hydrocephalus (Harrison 22e p.1834). Bruns' syndrome is intermittent acute hydrocephalus triggered by positional change, caused by a ventricular cysticercus acting as a ball valve (Harrison 22e p.1833). In Latin America and immigrants from Latin America, T. solium (neurocysticercosis) is the most common cause of brain abscess / focal CNS mass lesion (Harrison 22e p.1136). Echinococcosis (hydatid disease) is larval Echinococcus infection: E. granulosus sensu lato causes unilocular cystic hydatid disease; E. multilocularis causes locally invasive, tumor-like alveolar disease (Harrison 22e p.1835-1836). In cystic echinococcosis the liver is involved in about two-thirds and the lungs in about 20% of cases; alveolar echinococcosis involves the liver in nearly all cases (Harrison 22e p.1836). Echinococcal cysts often remain asymptomatic for years and are frequently found incidentally on x-ray or ultrasound (Harrison 22e p.1836). Identification of daughter cysts within a larger cyst, or eggshell/mural calcification on CT, is diagnostic of cystic echinococcosis; 'hydatid sand' is visible protoscolices/brood capsules within cyst fluid (Harrison 22e p.1837). ELISA/immunoblot serology is positive in about 90% of hepatic hydatid disease but only about 50% of pulmonary cysts, and a negative test cannot exclude echinococcosis (Harrison 22e p.1837). The fish tapeworm Dibothriocephalus latus (formerly Diphyllobothrium latum) is the longest human tapeworm (up to 25 m) and its avid vitamin B12 receptors can cause B12 deficiency with megaloblastic/pernicious-type anemia and neurologic sequelae (Harrison 22e p.1838-1839). Rodentolepis nana (dwarf tapeworm, formerly Hymenolepis nana) is the most common human cestode infection and the only one not requiring an intermediate host, perpetuated by intestinal autoinfection (Harrison 22e p.1838). New-onset seizures or focal neurologic deficit in a patient from a cysticercosis-endemic area (e.g., Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa, China, India, Southeast Asia) Signs of raised intracranial pressure or obstructive hydrocephalus (headache, vomiting, papilledema, altered mental status) from intraventricular/subarachnoid cysticerci Bruns' syndrome: intermittent acute hydrocephalus precipitated by head position change Subarachnoid/basal cysticerci causing chronic meningitis, arachnoiditis, vasculitis, infarction or hemorrhage Sudden pruritus, urticaria, eosinophilia or anaphylaxis from rupture/leakage of a hydatid cyst Pulmonary hydatid rupture into the bronchial tree (sudden expectoration of cyst fluid/membranes) or pleura (hydatid empyema) Do not aspirate or rupture a hydatid cyst carelessly: spillage of protoscolices can disseminate infection and provoke anaphylaxis; aspiration/PAIR should only be done by experienced operators with albendazole cover and through solid tissue. Never start antiparasitic drugs in neurocysticercosis with elevated intracranial pressure, and avoid them in diffuse cerebral edema from multiple inflamed lesions (glucocorticoids are the mainstay there). Always give high-dose glucocorticoid cover when treating neurocysticercosis, because dying cysticerci can worsen seizures and hydrocephalus. Treating T. solium intestinal taeniasis with praziquantel may occasionally trigger a CNS inflammatory response if occult (cryptic) cysticercosis is present. Avoid antiparasitic drugs before neurosurgical removal of ventricular cysticerci: they make the cyst friable and harder to extract. Crude-antigen ELISA antibody tests for cysticercosis are unreliable (high false-positive/false-negative rates) and should not be used. A negative echinococcosis serology cannot exclude the diagnosis, and sensitivity is especially low (~50%) for pulmonary cysts. Eggs/proglottids are shed intermittently, so single stool examination may miss intestinal taeniasis; Taenia species eggs are morphologically indistinguishable. For ocular and spinal cysticercosis, drug-induced inflammation may cause irreversible damage; intraocular disease should be managed surgically. Infusion of scolicidal agents during surgery is no longer recommended because of hypernatremia, intoxication and sclerosing cholangitis. Cestodes are segmented flatworms (Platyhelminthes, subphylum Cestoda) whose adult worms live in the gut of the definitive host while larval cystic forms inhabit tissues of the intermediate host. The adult tapeworm attaches to intestinal mucosa by suckers or hooks on a scolex; proglottids bud from the neck to form the ribbon-like strobila and shed eggs. In intestinal taeniasis humans are definitive hosts (T. saginata, T. asiatica, T. solium, D. latus, D. caninum). In somatic disease, ingested eggs release oncospheres that penetrate the gut wall, disseminate via blood, and encyst as a cysticercus (single scolex), coenurus (multiple scolices) or hydatid (cyst with daughter cysts and protoscolices). Cysticercosis follows ingestion of T. solium eggs (fecal-oral, including autoinfection in tapeworm carriers); lodged cysticerci initially provoke little inflammation, but as the cyst degenerates an inflammatory response develops, producing seizures, and accompanying arachnoiditis or ventricular obstruction can cause hydrocephalus. In echinococcosis ingested eggs of canine tapeworms release oncospheres that seed liver, lung and other organs; E. granulosus forms slowly enlarging unilocular hydatid cysts containing brood capsules and protoscolices, while E. multilocularis grows by invasive peripheral budding of the germinal layer like a malignancy. (Harrison 22e p.1832-1837) Intestinal tapeworm infections (taeniasis, R. nana, diphyllobothriasis, dipylidiasis) are usually mild or asymptomatic and respond to a single course of treatment. In neurocysticercosis, single enhancing lesions often resolve and seizure medication can frequently be tapered after about 6 months; calcified lesions carry a higher risk of recurrent seizures, particularly with perilesional edema, and subarachnoid/ventricular (extraparenchymal) disease is more difficult to treat and requires prolonged therapy. Cystic echinococcosis is often curable with stage-appropriate medical therapy, PAIR or surgery, with relapse rates after skilled PAIR comparable to surgery; inactive CE4/CE5 cysts need only periodic surveillance. Alveolar echinococcosis behaves like a malignancy: most cases are diagnosed too late for complete resection and require indefinite antiparasitic therapy, since even after liver transplantation immunosuppression promotes parasite recurrence. (Harrison 22e p.1834-1838) Cystic echinococcosis of the liver is staged by the WHO Informal Working Group ultrasound classification, reflecting cyst viability: active cysts (CL = cystic lesion with no visible wall, CE1 = visible wall with internal echoes/snowflake sign, CE2 = visible wall with internal septation), transitional cysts (CE3a = detached laminar membranes, CE3b = partially collapsed), and inactive cysts (CE4 = nonhomogeneous mass, CE5 = thick calcified wall). Neurocysticercosis is categorized by parasite location and viability and by lesion stage on imaging (vesicular, colloidal, granulonodular, nodular-calcified); diagnosis uses the Del Brutto revised criteria (absolute, neuroimaging [major/confirmative/minor], and clinical/exposure criteria). (Harrison 22e p.1834-1837)

Trypanosomiasis (Chagas & Sleeping Sickness) — Chagas disease, American trypanosomiasis, African sleeping sickness Chagas chronic cardiomyopathy: other dilated cardiomyopathies including ischemic heart disease (advanced Chagas carries a worse prognosis) (p.1790) Chagas megaesophagus: achalasia and other causes of dysphagia (p.1789) Chagas megacolon: Hirschsprung's disease and other causes of severe chronic constipation (p.1789) T. b. gambiense HAT systemic features: hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency (but thyroid/adrenal function tests are normal) (p.1794) HAT neuropsychiatric presentation: primary psychiatric illness (mental disorder is a key HAT feature easily misdiagnosed) (p.1794) T. b. rhodesiense acute febrile illness: malaria (suspect HAT especially if malaria tests are negative) (p.1794) Malaria (acute febrile illness overlapping T. b. rhodesiense HAT; HAT suspected when malaria tests are negative) (p.1794) Other febrile/systemic infections in returned travelers from endemic areas (p.1794) Chagas acute/reactivation: blood microscopy after concentration (Strout method, microhematocrit) or PCR of peripheral blood, CSF, or other body fluids (p.1790) Chagas chronic: serology for anti-T. cruzi IgG - conventional/recombinant ELISA and immunofluorescence; two positive tests with different techniques/antigens to confirm (third test if discordant); immunochromatographic rapid tests for first-line screening where labs are limited (p.1790) Chagas congenital: cord/peripheral blood microscopy or PCR in first days/weeks (testing after 4 weeks most accurate; earlier PCR may be falsely positive); serology at 9 months once maternal antibodies cleared (p.1790) Chagas cardiac staging: 12-lead ECG with 30-s strip; echocardiography and 24-h Holter for chamber dilation, apical aneurysm, ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmias; MRI or electrophysiologic studies as indicated (p.1791) Chagas digestive staging: barium esophagography and barium enema (first-line); esophageal manometry (p.1791) Chagas comorbidity workup: screen for other cardiovascular risk factors, immunosuppressive conditions, and other chronic infections (e.g., Strongyloides stercoralis, HIV) (p.1791) HAT T. b. gambiense screening: card agglutination test for trypanosomiasis (CATT) or lateral flow tests; ELISA/immunofluorescence/indirect hemagglutination in reference labs (p.1795) HAT confirmation: microscopy of trypanosomes in lymph (cervical lymph node puncture), blood (microhematocrit centrifugation; most sensitive is miniature anion-exchange centrifugation, ~90%), skin biopsy, or CSF; thin/thick Giemsa smears and concentration for T. b. rhodesiense (p.1795) HAT staging: lumbar puncture with CSF examination (leukocyte count, trypanosomes after centrifugation) (p.1795) Supportive HAT labs (nonspecific): anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated C-reactive protein and IgM (p.1794) Achalasia (Chagas megaesophagus) (p.1789) Hirschsprung's disease (Chagas megacolon) (p.1789) Dilated/ischemic cardiomyopathy (Chagas cardiomyopathy) (p.1790) Hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency (HAT systemic features, but endocrine tests normal) (p.1794) Primary psychiatric illness (HAT neuropsychiatric features) (p.1794) Three trypanosome species cause human disease: T. cruzi causes Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis); T. brucei gambiense and T. b. rhodesiense cause human African trypanosomiasis (HAT, 'sleeping sickness'). Both are vector-borne neglected tropical diseases (p.1788). Chagas is transmitted mainly by intradomiciliary triatomine ('reduviid') bugs whose feces, deposited during a nighttime blood meal, carry the infective metacyclic form that enters through skin breaks, mucosae, or conjunctivae; nonvectorial routes include congenital, blood transfusion, organ/tissue transplant, and oral (contaminated food/drink) transmission (p.1788). Acute Chagas is asymptomatic or a mild febrile illness in >90% of cases; characteristic local swelling at the inoculation site is the Romaña sign (eyelid) or chagoma (skin) (p.1789-1790). After acute infection T. cruzi persists for life in most patients; 60-70% remain in the indeterminate form (no apparent tissue damage), while 30-40% progress over decades to determinate disease - cardiac (20-30%), digestive (5-20%), or mixed (5-10%) (p.1789). Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy produces a dilated cardiomyopathy with fibrosis, segmental contractility loss, left ventricular apical aneurysm, ventricular arrhythmias, and conduction system disease; advanced cardiac damage carries a worse prognosis than other cardiomyopathies including ischemic disease (p.1789-1790). Digestive Chagas (megaviscera) results from destruction of intramural autonomic ganglion cells: esophageal involvement mimics achalasia and colonic involvement mimics Hirschsprung's disease, with severe constipation, fecaloma, and risk of volvulus and toxic dilation; megacolon is diagnosed when sigmoid/descending colon diameter is >=6.5 cm (p.1789, 1791). Chagas diagnosis is stage-dependent: detect circulating parasites by blood microscopy after concentration (Strout, microhematocrit) or PCR during acute phase/reactivation; rely on serology (anti-T. cruzi IgG) once parasitemia is subpatent in the chronic phase - two positive tests using different techniques and antigens confirm chronic infection (p.1790). 12-lead ECG (with 30-s strip) is a good screening test for Chagas cardiomyopathy; common abnormalities are right bundle branch block, left anterior fascicular block, ventricular premature beats, repolarization disorders, Q waves, and low QRS voltage (p.1791). HAT is restricted to sub-Saharan Africa, matching the range of its tsetse fly (Glossina) vector; T. b. gambiense (western/central Africa, humans are main reservoir, slow chronic course) differs from T. b. rhodesiense (eastern/southeastern Africa, zoonotic animal reservoirs, acute course) (p.1792-1793). T. b. gambiense HAT is a slowly evolving illness with a long incubation (months to years); T. b. rhodesiense HAT is an acute febrile illness with a short (<3-week) incubation and a shorter (weeks to months) course (p.1794). A trypanosomal chancre may develop at the tsetse bite site (more common in travelers and in T. b. rhodesiense); it is nonpurulent, painful, itchy, and resolves spontaneously in 1-3 weeks (p.1794-1795). Enlarged cervical lymph nodes are a classic HAT sign (38-85% of patients); posterior cervical involvement is the Winterbottom sign - cervical palpation is essential in suspected HAT (p.1794). HAT is called 'sleeping sickness' because of CNS (second-stage) sleep disturbances - daytime somnolence, nocturnal insomnia, dysregulated sleep/wake cycle and fragmented sleep - plus neuropsychiatric features (mood/behavioral change, psychosis, motor/extrapyramidal/cerebellar syndromes) that may mimic primary psychiatric illness (p.1794). HAT staging is by CSF examination: second-stage (CNS) disease is defined by CSF leukocytes >5/uL and/or trypanosomes; T. b. gambiense screening uses serology (card agglutination test, CATT, or lateral flow tests) and confirmation by microscopy of trypanosomes in lymph, blood, skin, or CSF (p.1795). T. b. rhodesiense diagnosis is usually simpler because parasites are more numerous in blood; wet mounts, thin/thick Giemsa smears, and concentration techniques serve for both screening and confirmation, and parasites may be seen in chancre aspirate (p.1795). T. cruzi evades immunity to persist as low-grade amastigote replication; immunosuppression (HIV, post-transplant, hematologic malignancy) can cause reactivation with increased parasitemia and CNS/cardiac/skin lesions - clinically manifest reactivation is an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection (~20% risk in untreated HIV when CD4 <100/uL) (p.1789). Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy with high risk of sudden death - bundle branch block is often the first sign and may be asymptomatic for years before serious conduction disease, arrhythmias, and LV dysfunction; 5-year mortality 2-63% depending on cardiac damage, leading causes cardiac failure and sudden death, then stroke (p.1790) Chagas digestive determinate disease: dysphagia, regurgitation, severe constipation, fecaloma, volvulus, and toxic colonic dilation (p.1790) Intramural thrombus or LV apical aneurysm in Chagas cardiomyopathy - risk of cardioembolic stroke (p.1790-1791) Chagas reactivation in immunosuppression (HIV with CD4 <100/uL, post-transplant, hematologic malignancy): myocarditis, Toxoplasma-like focal brain lesion, meningoencephalitis - AIDS-defining when clinically manifest (p.1789-1790) Untreated HAT is usually lethal - early diagnosis is crucial; second-stage (CNS) disease with decreased consciousness, dementia, epilepsy progressing to coma and death (p.1794) T. b. rhodesiense terminal sepsis-like illness with disseminated intravascular coagulation and multi-organ failure, plus more rapid evolution to coma and death than gambiense (p.1794) Severe second-stage HAT signs warranting non-fexinidazole staging/treatment: mental confusion, abnormal behavior, logorrhea, anxiety, ataxia, tremor, motor weakness, speech impairment, abnormal gait/movements, or seizures (p.1795) More than 90% of Chagas infections go undiagnosed and are often identified late once chronic complications develop; the majority of infected individuals are asymptomatic (indeterminate form) (p.1790) International tourists visiting endemic areas are at very low risk of Chagas and travel-related cases are rare - the at-risk group is migrants from endemic regions, not casual travelers (p.1789) There is no evidence that bedbugs transmit T. cruzi to humans despite laboratory potential (p.1788) There is no predictor of which chronic-phase Chagas patients will progress to clinical disease (p.1790) Chronic-phase Chagas PCR has limited sensitivity (50-80%): a negative result cannot be interpreted, so patients with negative PCR but persistent positive serology should still be considered potentially infective (p.1790, 1792) Early congenital Chagas PCR may be falsely positive (maternal T. cruzi DNA fragments); testing after 4 weeks of age is most accurate (p.1790) In adults with chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy, benznidazole has no impact on disease progression or mortality, and neither benznidazole nor nifurtimox is effective against digestive complications (KNOWLEDGE only - no dosing) (p.1791-1792) HAT clinical/biologic features (anemia, thrombocytopenia, raised CRP and IgM) are not specific enough to treat on suspicion - diagnostic confirmation is required in all patients (p.1794) Absence of fever does not rule out T. b. gambiense HAT (fever is more frequent in travelers than natives) (p.1794) HAT systemic features may mimic hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency but thyroid/adrenal tests are normal; mental disorder may be misdiagnosed as primary psychiatric illness (p.1794) Trypanids (HAT rashes) are almost impossible to detect on dark skin and have been reported only in Caucasians (p.1794) HIV co-infection does not appear to increase HAT risk, and the virus's effect on HAT presentation is unknown (p.1794) Eflornithine is ineffective against T. b. rhodesiense, so melarsoprol remains in use for second-stage rhodesiense disease (KNOWLEDGE only) (p.1796) Chagas (T. cruzi): trypomastigotes inoculated via triatomine feces enter the bloodstream, infect nucleated cells (notably cardiac, skeletal, and smooth muscle) and differentiate into amastigotes. An innate response to parasite mucins/DNA drives a predominantly Th1 response with proinflammatory cytokines and CD8+ T-cell activation that reduces parasitemia to subpatent levels in 4-8 weeks (end of acute phase). Immune evasion permits lifelong low-intensity amastigote proliferation. Chronic damage is thought to arise from parasite persistence plus a dysregulated host immune response (Th1/Th2 imbalance, excess proinflammatory cytokines), with secondary microcirculatory abnormalities and dysautonomia; the role of autoimmune mechanisms remains unresolved. In myocardium, chronic inflammation causes cellular destruction and fibrosis, segmental loss of contractility, chamber dilation, apical aneurysm, ventricular arrhythmias, and conduction-system scarring, plus autonomic (vagal/sympathetic) denervation. In the gut, a direct toxic effect on intramural autonomic ganglion cells causes loss of neural cells, motility disorders, and organ dilation (megaviscera). African trypanosomiasis (T. b. gambiense/rhodesiense): these subspecies infect humans because they resist human serum lytic factor apolipoprotein L-1 (T. b. rhodesiense via serum resistance-associated protein; T. b. gambiense via TgsGP glycoprotein and other mechanisms). After tsetse bite and local inflammation (chancre), parasites disseminate through the hematolymphatic system, multiply in blood (with cyclic density fluctuation due to variant surface glycoprotein antigenic switching - a repertoire of ~1000 VSGs) and extravascular tissues (skin, muscle, serous membranes, heart). CNS invasion (second stage) follows weeks-to-months (rhodesiense) or months-to-years (gambiense), with predominantly white-matter perivascular astrocyte/microglial proliferation and Mott (morular) cells containing IgM; the cortex and neurons are spared until terminal stages, and inflammatory lesions are largely reversible so neuropsychiatric features may resolve with treatment (p.1789-1790, 1793-1794). Chagas: 5-10% of acute (early) infections resolve spontaneously without treatment; most become chronic, of whom 60-70% never develop tissue damage (indeterminate form) and 30-40% progress over decades to cardiac, digestive, or mixed disease. Acute-phase mortality is low (0.1-5% with oral transmission or myocarditis/encephalitis). Determinate chronic disease 5-year mortality is 2-63% depending on extent of cardiac damage, with cardiac failure, sudden death, and stroke the leading causes; advanced cardiac damage carries a worse prognosis than other cardiomyopathies. African trypanosomiasis: untreated HAT is usually fatal. With properly followed guidelines, >95% of first- and second-stage T. b. gambiense HAT patients are definitively cured (fexinidazole, pentamidine, nifurtimox-eflornithine), overall case-fatality <1% except in very advanced cases; relapses can occur long after treatment, so follow-up every 6 months for at least 2 years is advised. Second-stage T. b. rhodesiense HAT carries a 5-10% risk of death during/after melarsoprol treatment, though relapses are very rare (p.1790, 1796). Chagas (T. cruzi infection stages, Table 234-1): Acute phase (including congenital, vector-borne, oral, transfusion, transplant) lasting 2-8 weeks, mostly asymptomatic; Chronic indeterminate form (normal exam and ECG, no attributable mortality, lifelong or until determinate phase); Chronic determinate form (cardiac, digestive, or mixed organ damage years to decades after infection); Acute reactivation in severe immunosuppression. Diagnostic procedure of choice by stage: microscopy after concentration / PCR for acute, early congenital, and reactivation; serology (two positive tests) for chronic indeterminate and determinate. HAT staging: First stage (hemolymphatic, no CNS involvement) vs Second stage (CNS/meningoencephalitic), defined by CSF leukocytes >5/uL and/or trypanosomes; nonsevere second stage = 6-99 leukocytes/uL CSF, severe second stage = >=100 leukocytes/uL CSF (p.1790, 1795).

Chalazion — meibomian cyst, tarsal cyst, meibomian granuloma Internal or external hordeolum (stye) Sebaceous gland carcinoma of the eyelid Basal cell or squamous cell carcinoma of the lid Preseptal cellulitis (if acutely inflamed) Pyogenic granuloma Epidermal inclusion cyst Clinical slit-lamp examination and eversion of the eyelid to assess the tarsal conjunctival surface Refraction and assessment for induced astigmatism in large lesions Histopathological examination of excised or curetted tissue in recurrent or atypical cases to exclude malignancy A chalazion is a chronic, sterile lipogranulomatous swelling of a blocked meibomian gland, presenting as a firm, painless nodule within the tarsal plate Unlike a stye (hordeolum), it is typically non-tender once the acute phase has passed and points towards the conjunctival rather than skin surface It is strongly associated with blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction, and rosacea, and recurrences are common in these patients A large chalazion can press on the cornea and induce astigmatism with blurred vision Many small lesions resolve spontaneously or with conservative treatment using warm compresses and lid massage over several weeks Persistent lesions are treated with incision and curettage through a conjunctival approach, or with intralesional steroid injection A recurrent chalazion at the same site, or one with atypical features, should be biopsied to exclude sebaceous gland carcinoma It should be distinguished from an internal hordeolum, which is an acute infective abscess of a meibomian gland Recurrence at the same site or failure to resolve, raising suspicion of sebaceous gland carcinoma Associated madarosis (lash loss), lid margin distortion, or induration suggesting malignancy Rapid growth or ulceration of the overlying skin Signs of secondary infection with spreading cellulitis Assuming any recurrent lid nodule is benign and not sending atypical or recurrent lesions for histology Confusing a sterile chalazion with an infective hordeolum and prescribing unnecessary antibiotics Overlooking underlying blepharitis and meibomian gland dysfunction that drive recurrence Missing chalazion-induced astigmatism as a cause of blurred vision A chalazion forms when a meibomian gland orifice becomes obstructed and retained sebaceous secretions leak into the surrounding tarsal tissue. This lipid material provokes a chronic granulomatous (lipogranulomatous) inflammatory reaction rather than an infection, producing a firm nodule within the tarsal plate. Predisposing factors include meibomian gland dysfunction, blepharitis, and rosacea, all of which alter meibomian secretions and promote gland blockage. The prognosis is excellent; most chalazia resolve with conservative measures or minor surgery, though recurrences are common in patients with underlying meibomian gland disease. Rarely, a persistent or atypical lesion proves to be a malignancy, which is why histology is important in suspicious cases.

complications Progressive hepatic dysfunction or cirrhosis developing from chronic steatosis Marked collodion presentation in the neonate with fluid, electrolyte and temperature instability Rising creatine kinase or clinical myopathy suggesting significant muscle involvement Progressive sensorineural hearing loss or visual impairment Labelling the child as simple congenital ichthyosis and never examining a blood film for Jordans anomaly Overlooking hepatic steatosis, which can progress silently to fibrosis Attributing raised creatine kinase to another cause and missing the lipid myopathy Assuming skin-directed therapy alone is sufficient without multisystem surveillance Chanarin-Dorfman syndrome arises from loss-of-function variants in ABHD5, which encodes the co-activator protein CGI-58 that normally stimulates adipose triglyceride lipase. When this co-activator is deficient, triglycerides cannot be efficiently hydrolysed and neutral lipid droplets accumulate within the cytoplasm of many cell types, including keratinocytes, hepatocytes, myocytes and circulating leucocytes. In the epidermis, disordered lipid metabolism disrupts the lamellar barrier of the stratum corneum and produces an ichthyosiform erythroderma, while lipid storage elsewhere accounts for hepatic steatosis, myopathy and the characteristic vacuolated leucocytes. The ichthyosis is lifelong but generally manageable; prognosis is chiefly determined by systemic organ involvement, particularly the risk of progressive liver disease, and by myopathic, auditory and neurological complications.

Missing the associated intra-abdominal injury Failing to recognise a ligamentous variant by relying on CT without MRI Underestimating the instability of the injury Overlooking the fracture on inadequate imaging A flexion-distraction force with its fulcrum anterior to the spine, as when a lap belt restrains the pelvis during sudden deceleration, places the posterior and middle spinal columns under tension. Failure propagates horizontally, either through bone in the classic Chance fracture, through the disc and ligaments in a purely soft-tissue variant, or through a combination of both. The same abrupt flexion compresses the abdominal viscera against the spine, explaining the frequent association with hollow viscus and mesenteric injuries. Whether the injury is stable depends on the integrity of the posterior ligamentous complex. Purely osseous injuries through cancellous bone generally heal well with bracing, whereas ligamentous variants are unstable and require fixation; associated abdominal injuries may dominate the early clinical course.

Chancroid — soft chancre, Haemophilus ducreyi infection, ulcus molle Primary syphilis (painless indurated chancre) Genital herpes simplex ulceration Lymphogranuloma venereum Granuloma inguinale (donovanosis) Traumatic or fixed drug eruption ulcer Syphilitic chancre Herpes simplex virus genital ulcers Lymphogranuloma venereum with inguinal buboes Donovanosis with beefy granulomatous ulcers Dark-field microscopy and syphilis serology to exclude primary syphilis HSV PCR or culture from the ulcer to exclude herpes Nucleic acid amplification or PCR for Haemophilus ducreyi where available Gram stain and special culture media (low sensitivity) if molecular testing unavailable HIV testing at presentation and on follow-up A sexually transmitted cause of genital ulceration produced by the Gram-negative coccobacillus Haemophilus ducreyi, now uncommon but still important in the differential of genital ulcer disease The ulcer is typically painful, non-indurated (soft) with a ragged undermined edge and a purulent base, contrasting with the painless firm ulcer of primary syphilis Tender, often unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy that may become fluctuant and suppurate into a bubo is characteristic The combination of one or more painful genital ulcers with suppurative inguinal nodes strongly suggests chancroid Culture requires special enriched media and is insensitive, so diagnosis is often clinical after excluding syphilis and herpes; molecular testing is most reliable where available Because genital ulcer disease facilitates HIV transmission, testing for HIV and syphilis is essential, with follow-up serology as needed Treatment uses recommended antibiotics such as a macrolide, ceftriaxone or a fluoroquinolone, and fluctuant buboes may require needle aspiration or incision Rapidly enlarging or fluctuant bubo threatening rupture and needing drainage Coexisting HIV infection, which impairs healing and alters treatment response Failure of ulcers to heal after appropriate therapy, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Extensive tissue destruction or secondary bacterial superinfection Assuming a painful ulcer excludes syphilis or coinfection, when mixed infections occur Incising a bubo when aspiration through healthy skin is preferred to avoid sinus formation Relying on insensitive culture and missing the diagnosis Neglecting partner notification and HIV screening Haemophilus ducreyi enters through breaks in genital epithelium during sexual contact. It secretes a cytolethal distending toxin and other virulence factors that cause keratinocyte and epithelial cell damage, producing a necrotic, ulcerative lesion with a neutrophil-rich inflammatory infiltrate. The organism resists phagocytic killing and provokes a suppurative regional lymphadenitis. The disrupted mucocutaneous barrier and inflammatory milieu markedly enhance the risk of HIV acquisition and shedding, linking chancroid epidemiologically to HIV spread. With appropriate antibiotic therapy ulcers heal over one to two weeks and buboes resolve, though large nodes may need aspiration and healing is slower in people with HIV; untreated disease causes progressive ulceration and scarring.

Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A is a hereditary demyelinating (type 1) motor and sensory neuropathy caused in most cases by a 1.5 Mb duplication on chromosome 17 that includes PMP22, resulting in overexpression of peripheral myelin protein 22. The gene-dosage excess disrupts the normal formation and maintenance of compact myelin by Schwann cells, leading to repeated cycles of demyelination and remyelination and the formation of concentric onion-bulb structures. Slowed and inefficient saltatory conduction, together with secondary axonal loss over time, produces the length-dependent distal weakness, wasting and sensory loss. The reciprocal deletion of the same region causes hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies. The disorder progresses slowly over decades and life expectancy is normal; most affected individuals remain ambulant, though many require orthoses, foot surgery or walking aids and experience meaningful disability from deformity and balance impairment.

cheiralgia paraesthetica — Wartenberg syndrome, superficial radial nerve entrapment, handcuff neuropathy de Quervain tenosynovitis C6 cervical radiculopathy lateral antebrachial cutaneous neuropathy posterior interosseous or radial tunnel syndrome first carpometacarpal joint osteoarthritis complex regional pain syndrome intersection syndrome of the forearm superficial radial sensory nerve conduction studies with contralateral comparison high-resolution ultrasound of the superficial radial nerve in the distal forearm magnetic resonance imaging if a mass or structural lesion is suspected wrist and thumb radiographs to assess the carpometacarpal joint diagnostic local anaesthetic block of the superficial radial nerve cervical spine imaging when radiculopathy is a consideration examination for coexisting de Quervain tenosynovitis with the Finkelstein manoeuvre Entrapment or compression of the superficial (sensory) branch of the radial nerve over the distal radial forearm and wrist, producing purely sensory symptoms over the dorsoradial hand. Patients describe pain, numbness and tingling over the dorsum of the thumb and dorsoradial hand, often provoked by tight wristbands, watch straps or handcuffs. Because the branch is purely sensory, there is no motor weakness and no wrist drop, distinguishing it from a radial nerve or posterior interosseous lesion. The nerve becomes subcutaneous as it emerges between brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus, where forearm pronation can pinch it (a scissoring mechanism). A Tinel sign over the distal radial forearm and a positive response to forced pronation and ulnar wrist flexion support the diagnosis. Overlap with de Quervain tenosynovitis is common, and the two may coexist, so the first dorsal compartment should be examined carefully. Symptoms frequently follow external compression, direct trauma, or surgery and cannula placement in the region. Sensory nerve conduction studies of the superficial radial nerve, compared with the asymptomatic side, help confirm the lesion. any true motor weakness, which indicates a more proximal radial nerve lesion rather than this sensory syndrome a progressive or palpable mass along the nerve course suggesting a peripheral nerve tumour features of complex regional pain syndrome such as trophic and vasomotor change multifocal sensory symptoms suggesting a generalised or inflammatory neuropathy mistaking the sensory symptoms for de Quervain tenosynovitis and overlooking coexistence of the two attributing motor findings to this syndrome, which is by definition purely sensory failing to identify a modifiable external compressive source such as a tight strap or handcuffs generating a painful neuroma through surgical intervention in a poorly selected case The superficial radial nerve travels beneath brachioradialis in the forearm and emerges to become subcutaneous roughly at the junction of the middle and distal thirds, passing over the tendons of the first dorsal compartment to supply sensation to the dorsoradial hand and dorsum of the thumb and adjacent fingers. Forearm pronation causes the tendons of brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus to scissor across the nerve, and external circumferential pressure, direct trauma or local scarring produce focal demyelination and axonal irritation. As the branch carries no motor fibres, the clinical picture is confined to sensory disturbance and pain. Removal of external compression and conservative treatment resolve symptoms in most cases, and the outlook is generally good. Refractory or post-traumatic cases may need neurolysis, though painful neuroma and persistent dysaesthesia can complicate recovery.

hydrofluoric acid is a special case Hydrofluoric acid causes deep tissue penetration and dangerous systemic effects including hypocalcaemia and cardiac dysrhythmia, and is treated specifically with calcium The apparent surface appearance can underestimate the true depth, which may only declare itself over hours to days Eye exposure is a sight-threatening emergency requiring immediate, prolonged irrigation and urgent ophthalmology assessment, with pH checking to guide adequacy of rinsing Some agents (for example phenol, hydrofluoric acid and cyanide-releasing compounds) are absorbed and cause systemic toxicity, so treat the whole patient, not just the wound Rescuer safety, removal of contaminated clothing and correct decontamination are essential to prevent further and secondary injury MEDICAL EMERGENCY: extensive or deep burns, airway or inhalational involvement, or eye exposure threatening sight Hydrofluoric acid exposure with hypocalcaemia and cardiac dysrhythmia Signs of systemic toxicity from absorbed agents such as phenol Circumferential burns risking compartment syndrome or airway compromise Delaying irrigation while trying to identify the chemical or find a specific antidote Underestimating burn depth from the initial surface appearance, especially with alkalis Failing to recognise and specifically treat hydrofluoric acid injury and its hypocalcaemia Neglecting systemic absorption and toxicity while focusing only on the wound Inadequate rescuer protection and decontamination leading to secondary injury Corrosive chemicals damage tissue by disrupting cell membranes and denaturing or dissolving proteins and lipids. Acids cause coagulative necrosis that tends to limit their own penetration, whereas alkalis cause liquefactive necrosis that allows continued deep spread. Some agents also produce heat or are absorbed to cause systemic metabolic disturbance, such as the calcium and magnesium binding and consequent hypocalcaemia seen with hydrofluoric acid. Prompt, thorough irrigation and appropriate specific treatment greatly improve outcome; however, deep or extensive burns, delayed decontamination, ocular involvement and systemic toxicity from certain agents can cause scarring, visual loss or death.

flash) Severe infective keratitis or corneal ulcer Toxic keratoconjunctivitis from other agents Corneal foreign body or abrasion Measurement of ocular surface pH before and after irrigation to guide continued irrigation Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein to assess epithelial defect size and corneal clarity Assessment and grading of limbal and conjunctival ischaemia Intraocular pressure measurement, as burns can cause acute and chronic pressure rise Eyelid eversion and fornix inspection for retained particulate chemical A true ocular emergency in which immediate, copious irrigation cause coagulative necrosis that tends to limit deeper penetration Irrigation should continue until the tear film pH returns to neutral, and the fornices must be swept and everted to remove any retained particulate matter (e.g. lime or cement) The degree of limbal ischaemia (blanching) and corneal clarity are the key prognostic signs, forming the basis of grading systems such as Roper-Hall and Dua A deceptively white, non-injected eye after an alkali burn can indicate severe limbal ischaemia rather than a mild injury Later management principles aim to promote epithelial healing, control inflammation with topical steroids, prevent infection, support the ocular surface, and control intraocular pressure Severe burns can be complicated by limbal stem cell deficiency, symblepharon, corneal melting and perforation, glaucoma, and eventual scarring Bilateral injury and workplace or assault-related exposures require attention to both eyes and appropriate safeguarding and indicating a severe, sight-threatening burn A deceptively white, quiet eye masking severe ischaemic damage after alkali injury Rising intraocular pressure, corneal melting, or threatened perforation requiring urgent specialist care Delaying irrigation to complete history or examination first Stopping irrigation before the pH has normalised or failing to check pH Not everting the lids and sweeping the fornices, leaving retained caustic particles Underestimating a white, non-inflamed eye that actually reflects severe limbal ischaemia Chemical injury damages the ocular surface through direct chemical action on cells and the extracellular matrix. Alkalis dissolve cell membrane lipids and penetrate deeply by liquefactive necrosis, reaching the anterior chamber and damaging the limbal stem cells, corneal stroma, trabecular meshwork, and intraocular structures. Acids denature and precipitate proteins, producing coagulative necrosis that can form a barrier limiting deeper spread, though strong acids still cause severe injury. Destruction of limbal stem cells impairs corneal epithelial regeneration, leading to persistent epithelial defects, conjunctivalisation, and scarring, while ischaemia and inflammation predispose to stromal melting and perforation. Prognosis correlates closely with the initial extent of limbal ischaemia and corneal opacification; mild burns with minimal limbal involvement usually heal well, whereas severe burns with extensive limbal stem cell loss risk chronic surface failure, scarring, and permanent visual loss despite intensive treatment. Prompt and thorough irrigation is the single most important factor improving outcome.

cherry angioma — Campbell de Morgan spot, senile angioma, cherry haemangioma angiokeratoma pyogenic granuloma amelanotic or nodular melanoma spider naevus petechia or purpura Kaposi sarcoma glomus tumour dermoscopy demonstrating red lacunae diascopy to assess blanching clinical photography for monitoring multiple lesions excisional biopsy of an atypical or rapidly changing lesion review of medication and chemical exposure history in eruptive cases Presents as a small, bright cherry-red to violaceous dome-shaped papule, most numerous on the trunk of middle-aged and older adults. Lesions are usually multiple and increase in number and size with advancing age; they are among the commonest acquired vascular proliferations. Diascopy shows only partial blanching because the vascular spaces are relatively fixed, distinguishing them from simple telangiectasia. Dermoscopy reveals well-demarcated red or red-blue lacunae separated by pale septa, confirming the vascular nature. Traumatised lesions may bleed briskly or thrombose, turning dark and mimicking a melanocytic or vascular malignancy. An abrupt eruption of numerous lesions has been associated with pregnancy, certain chemical exposures and some drugs, though most cases are idiopathic. No treatment is required; electrocautery, laser or shave removal is used for cosmetic reasons or recurrent bleeding. A rapidly enlarging or atypical solitary vascular papule should be biopsied to exclude amelanotic melanoma or other malignancy. a rapidly enlarging or ulcerated solitary vascular lesion raising concern for amelanotic melanoma or angiosarcoma an eruptive shower of angiomas prompting review of drug and chemical exposures persistent bleeding uncontrolled by simple pressure atypical dermoscopic features lacking the characteristic lacunar pattern Mistaking a thrombosed cherry angioma for a melanocytic lesion because of its dark colour. Attributing an eruptive crop solely to ageing and overlooking a drug or chemical trigger. Assuming any red papule is benign and missing an amelanotic melanoma or pyogenic granuloma. Inadequate haemostasis during removal leading to troublesome bleeding. Cherry angiomas are benign proliferations of dilated post-capillary venules and capillaries within the papillary dermis, lined by flattened endothelium and often accompanied by dermal oedema and collagen homogenisation. Increased local expression of angiogenic factors and somatic mutations affecting the GNAQ and GNA11 signalling pathway have been implicated in their development. Their strong association with ageing, and reported clustering during pregnancy or after certain chemical and drug exposures, points to hormonal and environmental modulation of cutaneous angiogenesis. The lesions are stable, non-involuting vascular hamartomatous proliferations without malignant potential. Cherry angiomas are entirely benign and persist indefinitely without malignant transformation. Cosmetic removal is generally curative, though new lesions continue to appear with age.

hyperparathyroidism without checking calcium and parathyroid hormone Overlooking orbital involvement and vision risk in extensive maxillary disease Failing to recognise the autosomal dominant inheritance and counsel the family Cherubism arises from autosomal dominant gain-of-function variants in SH3BP2, an adaptor protein that modulates signalling in cells of the myeloid and osteoclast lineage. The variants increase SH3BP2 stability and amplify downstream signalling, promoting excessive osteoclast formation and a local inflammatory, fibro-osseous process that replaces normal jaw bone with giant-cell-rich fibrous tissue. This produces the expansile, cyst-like lesions of the mandible and maxilla and the resulting facial swelling. The disease characteristically follows an age-dependent course, expanding through childhood, stabilising around puberty and frequently involuting thereafter as the abnormal osteoclastic drive subsides and the lesions ossify. The prognosis is generally favourable because the lesions tend to stabilise after puberty and often regress, leaving variable residual jaw deformity; extensive disease with orbital or airway involvement carries greater morbidity.

Chiari malformation — Arnold-Chiari malformation, Chiari I malformation, Chiari II malformation, cerebellar tonsillar ectopia Primary headache disorders (migraine, tension-type) Idiopathic intracranial hypertension Posterior fossa tumour Multiple sclerosis or other myelopathy Craniocervical junction anomalies (e.g. basilar invagination) MRI brain and whole spine to measure tonsillar descent and identify a syrinx Cine or CSF flow MRI at the craniocervical junction in selected cases Assessment for hydrocephalus and, in type II, for an associated neural tube defect Dynamic craniocervical imaging when bony instability or basilar invagination is suspected Chiari malformation describes downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils (and, in some types, the brainstem and fourth ventricle) through the foramen magnum The type I form often presents in adolescence or adulthood with a suboccipital headache classically worsened by coughing, straining, or Valsalva Associated features can include neck pain, dizziness, imbalance, and lower cranial nerve or brainstem symptoms such as swallowing difficulty A frequent and important association is syringomyelia, a fluid-filled junction and can stabilise or improve symptoms and an associated syrinx Progressive brainstem or lower cranial nerve dysfunction, including swallowing or breathing problems Rapidly enlarging syrinx with advancing weakness or sensory loss Signs of raised intracranial pressure or associated obstructive hydrocephalus Acute deterioration in an infant with type II malformation and myelomeningocele Attributing coughing-related occipital headache to migraine without considering the malformation Failing to image the whole spine and missing an associated syringomyelia Over-treating small, asymptomatic incidental tonsillar ectopia Overlooking coexisting hydrocephalus or craniocervical instability Chiari malformations involve herniation of hindbrain structures below the foramen magnum. In the type I form the cerebellar tonsils descend into the upper cervical canal, often with a small or crowded posterior fossa, obstructing normal cerebrospinal fluid movement across the craniocervical junction. This altered CSF dynamics is thought to drive syrinx formation within the spinal cord. The type II form is a more complex hindbrain anomaly with caudal displacement of the brainstem and fourth ventricle, strongly associated with open neural tube defects and hydrocephalus. Symptoms arise from direct compression of neural structures and from disturbed CSF flow. Many patients with mild or incidental type I malformation remain stable; symptomatic patients often improve or stabilise after decompression, though an established syrinx and any fixed neurological deficits may only partially recover. Type II outcomes depend heavily on the severity of associated anomalies.

Chilaiditi syndrome — Chilaiditi's syndrome, hepatodiaphragmatic interposition of the colon, Chilaiditi sign Pneumoperitoneum (free subdiaphragmatic air) from a perforated viscus Subphrenic or hepatic abscess with gas Colonic volvulus Bowel obstruction Diaphragmatic hernia Right basal lung pathology causing referred discomfort Erect chest and abdominal radiography noting haustral folds within the subdiaphragmatic gas to distinguish it from free air Computed tomography of the abdomen to confirm bowel interposition and exclude perforation or other pathology Clinical assessment for signs of obstruction, volvulus, or peritonitis Full blood count and inflammatory markers where complications are suspected Assessment for predisposing conditions such as cirrhosis or chronic lung disease Contrast studies in selected cases to define colonic anatomy Refers to interposition of the colon (or small bowel) between the liver and the right hemidiaphragm The radiological Chilaiditi sign is an incidental finding of interposed bowel; Chilaiditi syndrome is the term reserved for when this interposition causes symptoms Symptoms, when present, are usually non-specific and include abdominal pain, distension, constipation, nausea, and occasionally respiratory discomfort The key pitfall is mistaking the interposed gas-filled colon for free subdiaphragmatic air (pneumoperitoneum), which can lead to unnecessary surgery Predisposing factors include a redundant mobile colon, laxity or absence of suspensory ligaments, chronic constipation, cirrhosis, and chronic lung disease Recognising haustral markings within the subdiaphragmatic gas helps distinguish it from true free air Most cases are managed conservatively with bowel rest, hydration, laxatives, and decompression, with surgery reserved for complications such as obstruction, volvulus, or ischaemia Features of bowel obstruction, volvulus, or ischaemia of the interposed segment Peritonitis or clinical deterioration suggesting true perforation rather than the benign sign Intractable pain, vomiting, or distension unresponsive to conservative measures Respiratory compromise attributable to the interposition Misinterpreting the interposed colonic gas as free air and performing an unnecessary laparotomy Labelling an incidental sign as a syndrome in the absence of attributable symptoms Overlooking a genuine complication such as volvulus in a patient with the anatomy Attributing all right upper quadrant or respiratory symptoms to the interposition without excluding other causes Chilaiditi anatomy arises when a loop of colon, and sometimes small bowel, becomes interposed in the space between the liver and the right hemidiaphragm. This is favoured by anatomical factors such as an elongated, redundant, and mobile colon, laxity or congenital absence of the suspensory ligaments of the liver or colon, a small or atrophic liver, and conditions that enlarge the subphrenic space or increase colonic mobility. When the interposition is merely a radiological observation it is termed the Chilaiditi sign, whereas the syndrome denotes symptomatic interposition, in which distension, altered motility, or occasional volvulus of the interposed segment produces the clinical picture. The incidental Chilaiditi sign is benign and requires no treatment, and most symptomatic cases settle with conservative management; the outlook is only guarded when complications such as volvulus, obstruction, or ischaemia supervene and require surgery.

immersion foot (non-freezing cold injury of prolonged wet exposure) Acrocyanosis Vasculitis or embolic acral lesions Clinical diagnosis based on history of cold, damp exposure and characteristic acral lesions Autoimmune screen (including antinuclear antibodies) in recurrent, severe, or atypical cases Cold agglutinins and cryoglobulins where an alternative vasculopathy is suspected Skin biopsy in diagnostic uncertainty or when connective tissue disease is considered Assessment for peripheral vascular disease in older patients An inflammatory cold injury, not a freezing injury, caused by repeated exposure to cold but non-freezing, often damp conditions Presents with itchy or painful erythematous to violaceous papules, plaques, or nodules on acral sites such as toes, fingers, ears, and fixed inflammatory lesions rather than transient colour change Rewarming should be gradual, with keeping the affected part dry and warm and avoiding further cold exposure Persistent, recurrent, or of management Ulceration, necrosis, or secondary infection of lesions Features suggesting underlying connective tissue disease or systemic vasculitis Persistent lesions unresponsive to cold avoidance Signs of concurrent freezing injury (frostbite) after severe exposure Mistaking pernio for frostbite and applying inappropriately aggressive rewarming Failing to investigate recurrent or atypical cases for connective tissue disease Rubbing or applying direct heat, which can aggravate the inflammatory injury Overlooking secondary infection of blistered or ulcerated lesions Chilblains represent an abnormal inflammatory response to cold, non-freezing exposure. Cold-induced vasoconstriction of dermal vessels, followed by a poorly regulated inflammatory and vascular reaction on rewarming, produces localised tissue oedema, a perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, and the characteristic tender discoloured acral lesions. Unlike frostbite there is no ice crystal formation, so the injury is inflammatory rather than a direct freezing necrosis. A subset of cases reflects an underlying autoimmune or connective tissue disorder that predisposes to the exaggerated vascular response. Acute chilblains usually resolve over one to three weeks with cold avoidance and supportive care; chronic or recurrent perniosis can persist through cold seasons and, when linked to autoimmune disease, follows the course of the underlying condition.

CHILD syndrome — congenital hemidysplasia with ichthyosiform naevus and limb defects, NSDHL, CHILD naevus Conradi-Hunermann-Happle syndrome (X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia punctata, EBP) Inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal naevus (ILVEN) Epidermal naevus / naevus sebaceus Ichthyosis with confetti and other mosaic ichthyoses Incontinentia pigmenti (verrucous stage) Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma Skin biopsy showing psoriasiform hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis and a characteristic verruciform xanthoma-like dermal infiltrate Molecular genetic testing for NSDHL mutations Radiographs for chondrodysplasia punctata (epiphyseal stippling) and limb defects Echocardiography and renal imaging for ipsilateral visceral anomalies Neuroimaging where central nervous system involvement is suspected Sterol profiling to demonstrate distal cholesterol-pathway abnormality Acronym for Congenital Hemidysplasia with Ichthyosiform naevus and Limb Defects, characteristically strikingly lateralised (one side of the body) The ichthyosiform erythroderma stops abruptly at the midline and typically follows the lines of Blaschko, with a waxy yellowish scale Ipsilateral limb hypoplasia or defects and skeletal stippling (chondrodysplasia punctata) are hallmark associations Caused by mutations in NSDHL, an X-linked dominant gene in the distal cholesterol biosynthesis pathway, and is lethal in most affected males Ptychotropism (a predilection for skin folds) is a distinctive feature of the naevus Ipsilateral visceral, cardiac, renal and central nervous system anomalies may accompany the cutaneous and limb findings Management is supportive with emollients/keratolytics; topical cholesterol-pathway (statin/cholesterol) preparations have been used to target the metabolic defect Cardiac or renal malformation causing functional compromise in the neonate Extensive erythroderma with barrier failure and risk of infection or dehydration Progressive scoliosis or limb dysfunction requiring orthopaedic intervention Central nervous system anomaly with neurological deterioration Mistaking the lateralised naevus for a simple epidermal naevus or psoriasis and missing the syndromic limb and visceral defects Failing to screen for internal anomalies once the cutaneous diagnosis is made Overlooking the diagnosis in a male, in whom it is rare and often lethal or associated with mosaicism Assuming skin-directed therapy alone is sufficient without multidisciplinary evaluation CHILD syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in NSDHL (NAD(P)H steroid dehydrogenase-like protein), an enzyme acting in the distal (post-squalene) cholesterol biosynthetic pathway. The gene is X-linked, and the disorder behaves as an X-linked dominant trait that is generally lethal in hemizygous males, so affected individuals are almost always female. Random X-inactivation (lyonisation) produces functional mosaicism, which explains the sharply lateralised, Blaschko-linear distribution of skin and limb involvement. Deficient cholesterol synthesis and accumulation of toxic sterol precursors impair epidermal barrier formation and normal morphogenesis of limbs and viscera on the affected side. Prognosis depends chiefly on the extent of internal organ and skeletal involvement rather than the skin disease. The cutaneous naevus persists lifelong but is compatible with a normal lifespan when major visceral malformations are absent; associated cardiac or renal anomalies are the main determinants of outcome.

Childhood Obesity — paediatric obesity, childhood overweight, obesity in children and adolescents Exogenous (lifestyle-related) obesity Hypothyroidism Cushing syndrome Growth hormone deficiency Monogenic obesity (e.g. leptin or MC4R pathway defects) Syndromic obesity (e.g. Prader-Willi, Bardet-Biedl syndromes) Hypothalamic obesity (e.g. after CNS tumour or its treatment) BMI plotted on age- and sex-specific percentile charts, with blood pressure measurement Fasting glucose and/or HbA1c and fasting lipid profile Liver function tests and assessment for fatty liver disease Thyroid function testing where clinically indicated Evaluation for obstructive sleep apnoea when symptoms suggest it Genetic or endocrine work-up for early-onset severe or syndromic obesity In children and adolescents obesity is defined using body mass index relative to age- and sex-specific percentiles rather than fixed adult cut-offs, with obesity typically at or above the 95th percentile. The vast majority of cases are related to lifestyle and energy balance; a monogenic or endocrine cause is uncommon but should be considered in specific circumstances. A tall child growing well who is obese is usually exogenously obese, whereas an obese child who is short or growing poorly raises suspicion of an endocrine or syndromic cause. Ask about diet, physical activity, screen time, sleep, family history, and psychosocial factors, as these shape both cause and management. Screen for comorbidities including type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and obstructive sleep apnoea. Acanthosis nigricans is a clinical clue to insulin resistance and increased type 2 diabetes risk. Management centres on sustainable family-based lifestyle change addressing nutrition, activity, sleep, and behaviour rather than short-term restrictive dieting. Early-onset severe obesity, particularly with hyperphagia, may suggest a monogenic cause and warrants specialist evaluation. Obesity combined with poor linear growth or short stature suggesting an endocrine cause Symptoms of type 2 diabetes such as polyuria, polydipsia, or an incidental very high glucose Signs of obstructive sleep apnoea including loud snoring, apnoeic pauses, or daytime somnolence Features of Cushing syndrome (central obesity, striae, hypertension, growth deceleration) Early-onset severe obesity with extreme hyperphagia suggesting a monogenic disorder Hip or knee pain suggesting a slipped capital femoral epiphysis Assuming all obesity is lifestyle-related and missing an endocrine, syndromic, or monogenic cause when growth is impaired Failing to screen for comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes, fatty liver, and sleep apnoea Focusing on the child alone rather than engaging the whole family in change Overlooking psychosocial factors, stigma, and mental health in management Childhood obesity results from a chronic positive energy balance in which caloric intake exceeds expenditure, leading to excess adipose tissue. This arises from a complex interplay of genetic susceptibility, dietary patterns, physical inactivity, sleep, and environmental and socioeconomic influences. Expanded and dysfunctional adipose tissue drives insulin resistance, low-grade inflammation, and altered adipokine signalling, which underlie the associated metabolic, hepatic, cardiovascular, and endocrine complications. Rare monogenic and syndromic disorders disrupt central appetite regulation (notably the leptin-melanocortin pathway). Childhood obesity frequently persists into adulthood and raises the long-term risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and other complications; early sustained family-based lifestyle intervention can improve trajectory and reduce comorbidity.
