torsion must be excluded promptly) Intrauterine contraceptive device-induced cervical inflammation Functional urinary symptoms / non-infectious dysuria (acute urethral syndrome in women) Reactive arthritis / spondyloarthropathy in the differential of HLA-B27-associated joint disease C. trachomatis genital infection is the most prevalent bacterial STI worldwide and is reported more than any other infectious disease in the United States; case counts are heavily dependent on screening coverage (Harrison 22e p.1469). Most genital infections are silent: up to 80-90% of women and >50% of men with C. trachomatis genital infection lack symptoms, and pharyngeal/rectal infection is typically asymptomatic and may persist for years, sustaining a large transmission reservoir (Harrison 22e p.1469). C. trachomatis is the most common cause of nongonococcal urethritis (NGU) and postgonococcal urethritis (PGU), implicated in 30-50% of NGU cases (Harrison 22e p.1469-1470). NAATs are the CDC-recommended diagnostic assay of choice; less-invasive specimens (urine for both sexes, vaginal swabs for women) are acceptable, and self-collected or clinician-collected vaginal swabs are slightly more sensitive than urine in women (Harrison 22e p.1472-1473). Because of frequent co-infection, testing for or treating chlamydia should be considered in patients diagnosed with N. gonorrhoeae (Harrison 22e p.1474). Trachoma (serovars A, B, Ba, C) remains a leading cause of preventable infectious blindness worldwide; the WHO SAFE-era programs target elimination as a public health problem by 2030 (Harrison 22e p.1474-1475). LGV (serovars L1, L2, L3) is an invasive STI presenting classically as a transient painless genital ulcer followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy with bubo formation, or as hemorrhagic proctocolitis in MSM (Harrison 22e p.1469, 1472). C. pneumoniae causes atypical (community-acquired) pneumonia, bronchitis, pharyngitis and sinusitis, accounting for as many as 10% of CAP cases though more typically 1-2%; PCR of respiratory secretions is the preferred diagnostic method (Harrison 22e p.1476). Psittacosis (C. psittaci) is a zoonosis acquired from birds (psittacines, poultry) presenting as atypical pneumonia or systemic febrile illness; person-to-person transmission has never been demonstrated (Harrison 22e p.1475). Neonatal exposure during vaginal delivery causes inclusion conjunctivitis (in ~20-30% of exposed infants) and, in 10-15%, pneumonia at 2 weeks to 4 months of age; standard gonococcal ocular prophylaxis does NOT prevent chlamydial conjunctivitis (Harrison 22e p.1471-1472). Acute unilateral testicular pain - exclude testicular torsion promptly by imaging or surgical exploration before attributing to epididymitis Failure of unilateral intrascrotal pain/swelling to respond to antimicrobials - exclude testicular tumor or chronic infection such as tuberculosis Hemorrhagic proctocolitis with severe anorectal pain in MSM - consider invasive LGV serovars (often with HIV co-infection) Right-upper-quadrant pain/fever/nausea in a sexually active woman - suspect perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis), associated with extensive tubal scarring Trichiasis and entropion in trachoma - lashes abrade the cornea leading to ulceration and blindness if untreated Severe psittacosis pneumonia - can be fatal in up to 10% of untreated cases and may require ICU care, with hepatitis, endocarditis or myocarditis Untreated maternal infection - risk of neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis and infant pneumonia NAATs detect nucleic acid, not viable organisms - residual DNA may yield a positive result for up to 3 weeks after effective therapy, so NAATs should not be used as a test of cure before 3 weeks; routine test of cure is not recommended except in pregnancy. Single-dose penicillins or cephalosporins used for gonorrhea lack activity against chlamydiae - hence postgonococcal urethritis and the need to co-treat or exclude chlamydia. Standard gonococcal ocular prophylaxis does NOT prevent neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis; the most effective prevention is antenatal screening and treatment. Chlamydial and gonococcal conjunctivitis cannot be distinguished from other neonatal conjunctivitis on clinical grounds - laboratory diagnosis is required. CF and LPS-based serologic tests identify chlamydiae only to the genus level (cross-reactive across all chlamydiae) and must be interpreted cautiously. Serology (including a single high IgG titer) over-attributes C. pneumoniae to atypical pneumonia; cross-reactivity limits specificity, and PCR is preferred. Serology is never recommended for diagnosis of uncomplicated genital cervical/urethral/lower-tract infection or for asymptomatic screening. Fluoroquinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy; beta-lactams and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are not active against C. pneumoniae. Most genital infections are asymptomatic, so clinical recognition of cervicitis requires a high index of suspicion - no genital symptom is specific for chlamydial cervical infection. C. psittaci is a biohazard category B biothreat agent associated with laboratory-acquired infections. Chlamydiae are nonmotile, gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacteria that lack peptidoglycan (structural integrity depends on disulfide cross-linking of outer-membrane proteins) and are energy parasites using host-cell ATP. They have a unique biphasic growth cycle alternating between the infectious, extracellular-adapted elementary body (0.25-0.35 um) and the metabolically active, non-infectious intracellular reticulate body (0.5-1 um), which divides by binary fission within a membrane-bound cytoplasmic inclusion while preventing phagosome-lysosome fusion; the cycle lasts ~48-72 h, giving a long clinical incubation (generally 1-3 weeks). C. trachomatis has two biovars (trachoma and LGV) and 18 serovars (trachoma A/B/Ba/C; oculogenital D-K; LGV L1-L3); the trachoma biovar parasitizes squamocolumnar epithelium whereas the more invasive LGV biovar involves lymphoid cells. Disease is driven largely by immunopathology rather than direct cytotoxicity: the chlamydial heat-shock protein shares epitopes with human and other bacterial proteins and, with repeated/persistent infection, drives fibrosis and mucosal scarring leading to tubal-factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain (genital) or cicatricial trichiasis and blindness (ocular). Antigenic variation in the major outer-membrane protein (omp1) permits reinfection because immunity to one serovar is not protective against others (Harrison 22e p.1467-1469). Uncomplicated genital chlamydial infection responds well to recommended antibiotics, and clinically significant drug resistance has not been observed in C. trachomatis; apparent treatment failure usually reflects non-adherence or reinfection. However, untreated or recurrent genital infection causes substantial long-term morbidity through mucosal scarring - PID with tubal-factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain - and women bear the greatest burden of sequelae. Reactive arthritis episodes typically last 2-6 months. Untreated ocular disease progresses to blinding trachoma; the WHO estimates ~6 million people have been blinded and ~1.3 million remain blind from trachoma. Untreated psittacosis pneumonia can be fatal in up to 10% of cases. Previous chlamydial infection raises the risk of reinfection, prompting rescreening at 3 months (Harrison 22e p.1469-1475). No formal grading scale. Genital C. trachomatis infections are categorized as uncomplicated (lower genital tract) versus complicated (e.g., PID, epididymitis) requiring longer therapy; LGV is treated as invasive disease with extended therapy. Trachoma is described by phase - active trachoma (follicular conjunctivitis) versus cicatricial disease (conjunctival scarring, trichiasis, entropion) - underpinning the WHO clinical signs used for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1474-1475).

chloracne — chloracne (MADISH), metabolising acquired dioxin-induced skin hamartomas acne vulgaris acne cosmetica or pomade acne oil folliculitis and coal-tar or mineral-oil acne steroid or drug-induced acneiform eruption favre-racouchot solar comedones nevoid comedones or dilated pore lesions milia or eruptive vellus hair cysts detailed occupational, environmental and exposure history including timeline serum or adipose tissue dioxin/PCB concentrations where available liver function tests and fasting lipid profile urinary and plasma porphyrins to assess for porphyria cutanea tarda skin biopsy showing comedones, keratin cysts and sebaceous gland atrophy neurological assessment for peripheral neuropathy public-health and workplace exposure investigation to identify co-exposed individuals Chloracne is the most specific and sensitive cutaneous marker of systemic exposure to dioxins and dioxin-like halogenated aromatic hydrocarbons; its presence should trigger a search for a significant exposure. The hallmark lesions are numerous comedones (open and closed) and small pale-yellow keratin cysts, distributed characteristically over the malar cheeks, retroauricular skin, axillae and groin rather than the usual sebaceous acne zones. Involvement behind the ears and in the axillae/groin, sparing of the nose, and a paucity of inflammatory pustules help distinguish chloracne from acne vulgaris. Causative agents include polychlorinated dibenzodioxins and dibenzofurans, polychlorinated biphenyls, chlorinated naphthalenes and certain chlorophenol/herbicide contaminants. Exposure may be occupational (chemical manufacture, waste incineration, transformer work), environmental (contamination incidents) or from deliberate poisoning, and can be inhaled, ingested or absorbed through skin. Because dioxins are highly lipophilic and slowly eliminated, chloracne can appear weeks after exposure and persist for years, sometimes fluctuating long after contact has ended. Associated systemic effects may include hepatic dysfunction, deranged lipids, porphyria cutanea tarda, peripheral neuropathy and, with heavy exposure, an increased long-term malignancy risk, so evaluation must extend beyond the skin. Management centres on identifying and removing the source, supportive skin care and comedo extraction; the eruption is often relatively resistant to conventional acne therapies. history suggesting deliberate poisoning or a mass contamination incident hepatic dysfunction, photosensitive blistering or other features of porphyria cutanea tarda neurological symptoms indicating systemic dioxin toxicity widespread or rapidly progressive eruption implying heavy ongoing exposure co-exposure of colleagues, family members or a community requiring public-health action Dismissing the eruption as ordinary acne and failing to investigate a significant toxic exposure. Overlooking the diagnostic retroauricular, axillary and groin distribution and sparing of the nose. Focusing only on the skin and missing hepatic, porphyric or neurological involvement. Expecting a rapid response to standard acne therapy and underestimating persistence. Not pursuing source identification, biological monitoring and screening of co-exposed contacts. Dioxins and dioxin-like compounds are potent ligands of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR). On binding, the AhR translocates to the nucleus and alters transcription of genes controlling xenobiotic metabolism, cell proliferation and epidermal differentiation. In the pilosebaceous unit this drives metaplasia of sebaceous glands and follicular epithelium, with loss of sebocytes and squamous metaplasia of the sebaceous ducts, so that follicles become filled with keratin to form comedones and keratin cysts — reflected in the concept of metabolising acquired dioxin-induced skin hamartomas. The extreme lipophilicity and metabolic stability of these compounds explain their bioaccumulation in adipose tissue, prolonged half-life, delayed onset and persistence of lesions, and the potential for concurrent hepatic, porphyric, neurological and carcinogenic effects mediated through the same receptor pathway. Chloracne is often persistent, lasting months to many years and sometimes leaving scarring, because the causative compounds are eliminated very slowly; severe cases may be resistant to treatment. The systemic outlook depends on the magnitude of exposure and any associated hepatic, neurological or malignancy risk.

Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine are aminoquinolines with membrane-stabilising, quinidine-like activity. They block cardiac sodium channels, slowing depolarisation and widening the QRS complex, and block potassium channels, prolonging repolarisation and the QT interval, together predisposing to ventricular tachyarrhythmias. Negative inotropy and vasodilatation produce hypotension and cardiovascular collapse. The drugs also drive potassium into cells, causing hypokalaemia whose severity broadly parallels the ingested dose. Central nervous system depression and seizures may occur, and the very large volume of distribution limits the usefulness of extracorporeal removal. Severe acute overdose carries a high risk of sudden cardiovascular collapse and death, but early aggressive supportive care including ventilation, sedation and vasopressors has improved survival; milder ingestions and most chronic therapeutic toxicity have a good outcome.

for atresia Overlooking CHARGE and other syndromic associations in bilateral cases Underestimating the risk of postoperative restenosis and not planning appropriate follow-up Choanal atresia results from persistence of tissue that should break down during development of the posterior nasal apertures, leaving the choana occluded by bone, membrane, or a combination of the two. Several embryological explanations have been proposed, including failure of rupture of the bucconasal membrane and abnormal mesodermal persistence. Because newborns preferentially breathe through the nose, complete bilateral obstruction prevents effective nasal airflow, so the infant becomes cyanotic at rest and improves paradoxically when crying opens the mouth, giving the classic cyclical pattern. In unilateral disease the patent side maintains the airway, and the condition presents insidiously with chronic one-sided obstruction and discharge. With prompt airway management and surgical repair the outlook is good, though restenosis can occur and may require revision, and prognosis in bilateral cases is influenced by any associated syndromic anomalies.

gemcitabine plus platinum chemotherapy is the systemic backbone, and molecular profiling for targetable alterations such as FGFR2 fusions and IDH1 mutations can guide targeted therapy Relieving biliary obstruction with stenting is central to palliation and to controlling cholangitis and pruritus Progressive painless obstructive jaundice with weight loss Cholangitis with fever and rigors on a background of biliary stricture New dominant biliary stricture in a patient with primary sclerosing cholangitis Rapidly enlarging intrahepatic mass with vascular involvement on imaging Assuming obstructive jaundice is benign and delaying malignancy workup Relying on a normal or mildly raised CA 19-9 to exclude cancer Aggressive biliary instrumentation causing cholangitis before definitive staging Missing a dominant malignant stricture within primary sclerosing cholangitis Cholangiocarcinoma is a malignancy of the epithelial cells lining the intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile ducts, most often adenocarcinoma. Chronic inflammation and cholestasis, as seen in primary sclerosing cholangitis, chronic infection, or biliary stones, produce repeated epithelial injury and repair that promotes dysplasia and malignant transformation. The tumours are frequently desmoplastic and grow along the bile ducts, causing obstruction; perihilar lesions readily invade the portal structures and liver, while intrahepatic tumours behave as mass-forming liver cancers with early lymphatic and vascular spread. Prognosis is generally poor because most patients present with unresectable disease; complete resection with negative margins offers the best survival, while advanced disease treated with systemic therapy has limited long-term survival though molecularly targeted agents can extend it in selected patients.

Choledochal cyst — bile duct cyst, congenital biliary dilatation, choledochal malformation Biliary atresia (in the neonate) Obstruction from a biliary or gallstone Pancreatic pseudocyst Hepatic or mesenteric cyst Caroli disease (intrahepatic ductal dilatation) Abdominal ultrasound as the initial imaging test Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography to delineate biliary and pancreaticobiliary anatomy Liver function tests and inflammatory markers to assess cholestasis and cholangitis Serum amylase/lipase if pancreatitis is suspected Intraoperative cholangiography when needed to clarify ductal anatomy A congenital cystic dilatation of the biliary tree, most often affecting the extrahepatic common bile duct, and more common in females and in East Asian populations The classic triad of abdominal pain, jaundice, and a palpable right upper quadrant mass is present in only a minority; most children show one or two of these features Infants often present with obstructive jaundice and an abdominal mass, whereas older children more often have intermittent pain and cholangitis The Todani classification describes the anatomical types, with type I (fusiform extrahepatic dilatation) being the most frequent An anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction allowing reflux of pancreatic enzymes into the bile duct is thought to contribute to many cases Ultrasound is the usual first-line study, with MRCP providing detailed mapping of the biliary anatomy before surgery Treatment is complete excision of the cyst with reconstruction by hepaticojejunostomy, because the abnormal epithelium carries a lifelong risk of malignancy Even after excision, long-term surveillance is needed for anastomotic stricture, recurrent cholangitis, and biliary malignancy Ascending cholangitis with fever, pain, and jaundice requiring prompt treatment Cyst rupture causing biliary peritonitis, a surgical emergency Features suggesting malignant transformation, especially in longstanding or previously untreated cysts Progressive obstructive jaundice with signs of biliary sepsis Performing simple internal drainage rather than complete cyst excision, leaving malignancy risk Confusing neonatal presentation with biliary atresia and delaying appropriate imaging Failing to identify and address an anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction Neglecting long-term surveillance for late strictures, cholangitis, and biliary cancer Choledochal cysts are congenital dilatations of part of the biliary tree. A widely accepted mechanism is an anomalous union of the pancreatic and bile ducts outside the duodenal wall, creating a long common channel that allows pancreatic secretions to reflux into the biliary system. Enzymatic damage weakens and dilates the duct wall, and chronic inflammation predisposes the abnormal biliary epithelium to stricturing, stone formation, cholangitis, and, over time, malignant change (cholangiocarcinoma). Complete surgical excision with biliary reconstruction gives good long-term results in most children and reduces but does not abolish the malignancy risk. Internal drainage procedures that leave the cyst in place are inadequate because they carry ongoing risks of cholangitis, stones, and cancer, so lifelong follow-up remains important.

stones and missing an underlying malignant stricture Common bile duct stones are usually cholesterol or mixed stones that form in the gallbladder and pass through the cystic duct into the common bile duct; primary duct stones (typically pigment stones) form within the duct, favoured by biliary stasis, stricture, or infection. A stone obstructing the duct raises biliary pressure and causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and cholestasis. Obstruction at the ampulla can block pancreatic outflow and trigger acute pancreatitis. Stagnant, obstructed bile readily becomes infected, and rising ductal pressure allows bacteria and endotoxin to translocate into the circulation, producing ascending cholangitis and potentially biliary sepsis. With timely stone clearance and, where appropriate, cholecystectomy the outlook is excellent and complications are prevented. Prognosis is worse when choledocholithiasis is complicated by severe cholangitis or pancreatitis, especially with delayed biliary decompression, but urgent drainage markedly improves survival in cholangitis.

Cholera — Vibrio cholerae infection Other secretory/toxigenic watery diarrhoeas: enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (produces a heat-labile toxin like cholera toxin), and other dehydrating secretory diarrhoeal illnesses to which the term cholera has historically and loosely been applied (p.1325) Diarrhoea due to non-O1/O139 (noncholera) V. cholerae, which generally do not produce cholera toxin and do not cause large epidemics (p.1330) Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (heat-labile enterotoxin resembling cholera toxin causing secretory diarrhoea) (p.1325-1326) Other Vibrio gastroenteritis, e.g. Vibrio parahaemolyticus and non-O1/O139 V. cholerae (p.1330) Stool culture on a selective medium such as taurocholate-tellurite-gelatin (TTG) agar or thiosulfate-citrate-bile salts-sucrose (TCBS) agar; the organism must be specifically sought (p.1328) Direct dark-field microscopy of a wet mount of fresh stool, with serotype discernible by immobilisation with specific antisera (p.1328) Point-of-care antigen-detection cholera dipstick (rapid diagnostic test) for field use or where laboratory facilities are lacking (p.1328) Cary-Blair transport medium and/or alkaline-peptone water-enrichment medium if sample processing will be delayed (p.1328) Vibrios are oxidase-positive; standard Enterobacteriaceae biochemical testing suffices for identification (p.1328) Supportive labs in dehydrated patients: elevated haematocrit (haemoconcentration) in non-anaemic patients, mild neutrophilic leukocytosis, raised blood urea nitrogen and creatinine (prerenal azotaemia), normal sodium/potassium/chloride, markedly reduced bicarbonate (<15 mmol/L), elevated anion gap and low arterial pH (~7.2) (p.1328) Severely dehydrating secretory diarrhoea of non-infectious aetiology, to which the term cholera has at times been loosely applied (p.1325) Cholera is an acute toxin-mediated diarrhoeal disease caused by Vibrio cholerae serogroup O1 or O139 (the serogroups with epidemic potential) that can progress to profound, rapidly progressive dehydration and death within hours (p.1325-1326). After a 24-48 h incubation in a non-immune individual, illness begins with the sudden onset of painless watery diarrhoea that can rapidly become voluminous; vomiting is common and fever is usually absent (p.1327). The characteristic stool is non-bilious, gray, slightly cloudy fluid flecked with mucus, containing no blood, with a fishy, inoffensive odour, described as rice-water stool because it resembles water in which rice has been washed (p.1327). In severe cases (cholera gravis) volume loss can exceed 250 mL/kg in the first 24 h, and muscle cramps from electrolyte disturbance are common (p.1327). Symptoms parallel the degree of volume contraction: thirst at <5% body-weight loss; postural hypotension, weakness, tachycardia and decreased skin turgor at 5-10%; and oliguria, weak or absent pulses, sunken eyes (sunken fontanelles in infants), wrinkled washerwoman skin, somnolence and coma at >10% (p.1327-1328). If fluids and electrolytes are replaced adequately, complications are averted and the illness is self-limited, resolving in a few days (p.1328). Profound, rapidly progressive dehydration developing within hours (p.1325) Signs of severe dehydration: unconsciousness, lethargy or floppiness, weak or absent pulse, inability to drink, sunken eyes (sunken fontanelles in infants), >10% loss of body weight (p.1328) Voluminous ongoing stool losses (volume loss exceeding 250 mL/kg in the first 24 h in severe cases) (p.1327) Features of hypovolaemic shock, oliguria, somnolence and coma (p.1327-1328) Acute watery diarrhoea or death from acute watery diarrhoea in a patient >=5 years, even where cholera is not known to be present (p.1328) The organism is not recovered on routine media; V. cholerae must be specifically sought using selective medium, or the diagnosis will be missed (p.1328). Diagnosis is often syndromic and many endemic countries under-report to the WHO, so the true burden and distribution are unknown and cases may be unrecognised (p.1326). Cholera should still be suspected in severe acute watery diarrhoea or death even in areas not known to have cholera (p.1328). Fever is usually absent, so its absence should not dissuade from the diagnosis (p.1327). Immunity to V. cholerae O1 is not protective against O139 (and vice versa), so prior infection does not guarantee protection against the other serogroup (p.1327). Cholera is fundamentally a toxin-mediated disease. After ingestion (most often via faecally contaminated water, though contaminated food and human-to-human transmission also contribute), V. cholerae colonises the small intestine, a process dependent on the toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP), with cholera toxin, TCP and other virulence factors coordinately regulated by ToxR and by quorum sensing. The organism elaborates cholera toxin, a protein enterotoxin made of a monomeric enzymatic A subunit and a pentameric B-subunit binding moiety. The B pentamer binds GM1 ganglioside on the epithelial cell surface, delivering the A subunit, whose activated form (A1) irreversibly ADP-ribosylates the GTP-binding regulatory component of adenylate cyclase. This upregulates adenylate cyclase, raising intracellular cyclic AMP, which inhibits absorptive sodium transport in villus cells and activates secretory chloride transport in crypt cells, driving accumulation of sodium chloride in the lumen; water follows passively to maintain osmolality, producing isotonic fluid that exceeds the gut's reabsorptive capacity and results in watery diarrhoea. Cholera toxin also enhances secretion via prostaglandins and/or neural histamine receptors. Unless lost fluid and electrolytes are replaced, profound dehydration leads to hypovolaemic shock and bicarbonate loss leads to acidosis. The cholera toxin genes (ctxAB) are carried on the bacteriophage CTX-phi, which uses TCP as its receptor, allowing horizontal transfer to generate new toxigenic strains (p.1326-1327). Death from cholera is due to hypovolaemic shock. Historically the disease carried high mortality, but prompt aggressive fluid repletion and supportive care can obviate this. With adequate fluid and electrolyte replacement, complications are averted and the illness is self-limited, resolving over a few days. Complications derive exclusively from volume and electrolyte depletion and include renal failure due to acute tubular necrosis. Untreated cholera carries very high case-fatality (historically >50% in untreated severe cases), which falls dramatically with rehydration (p.1326, p.1328). Harrison stratifies dehydration in cholera into: (1) None or mild (diarrhoea present) - thirst in some cases, <5% loss of total body weight; (2) Moderate - thirst, postural hypotension, weakness, tachycardia, decreased skin turgor, dry mouth/tongue, no tears, 5-10% loss of total body weight; and (3) Severe - unconsciousness, lethargy or floppiness, weak or absent pulse, inability to drink, sunken eyes (sunken fontanelles in infants), >10% loss of total body weight. This dehydration assessment guides the intensity of rehydration (p.1328).

Cholesteatoma — keratoma, epidermosis of middle ear, unsafe chronic otitis media Tubotympanic (safe) chronic suppurative otitis media Keratosis obturans of the external canal Aural polyp or granulation from other causes Middle ear or external canal malignancy Glomus tumour of the middle ear Foreign body with surrounding inflammation Otoscopy and microscopy to identify retraction pockets, keratin debris and granulations High-resolution CT of the temporal bone to define extent and bony erosion Diffusion-weighted MRI to detect residual or recurrent cholesteatoma Pure tone audiometry to document conductive or mixed hearing loss Culture of discharge to guide treatment of secondary infection Fistula test if erosion into the labyrinth is suspected Cholesteatoma is a collection of keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear cleft; despite the name it contains neither cholesterol nor a tumour It is characteristically associated with attic or posterosuperior marginal perforations, which is why this is called the unsafe or atticoantral type of chronic otitis media Typical symptoms are scanty, foul-smelling ear discharge with progressive conductive hearing loss Otoscopy may reveal a retraction pocket, whitish debris or granulations and a crust in the attic; a polyp or aural granulation should raise suspicion It is locally destructive because the matrix and surrounding inflammation erode bone, threatening the ossicles, facial nerve, labyrinth and dura Congenital cholesteatoma can occur behind an intact drum with no history of infection Imaging with high-resolution CT maps disease extent and bony erosion, and MRI (including diffusion-weighted sequences) helps detect or confirm residual or recurrent disease The mainstay of treatment is surgical eradication by mastoidectomy and tympanoplasty, since medical therapy alone cannot cure it Vertigo or a positive fistula sign suggesting labyrinthine erosion Facial nerve weakness indicating involvement of the facial canal Severe headache, fever, neck stiffness or altered consciousness suggesting intracranial complication (an emergency) Sudden worsening of hearing or new sensorineural loss Postauricular swelling or abscess signalling spread beyond the mastoid Dismissing scanty foul discharge as trivial and missing an unsafe ear Failing to inspect the attic and posterosuperior quadrant where retraction pockets hide Relying on medical treatment alone when surgery is needed for cure Not recognising an aural polyp as a possible marker of underlying cholesteatoma Neglecting long-term surveillance for residual or recurrent disease Cholesteatoma consists of a sac of keratinising stratified squamous epithelium (matrix) that sheds keratin into the middle ear and mastoid, where it accumulates and cannot escape. Acquired disease most often follows persistent Eustachian tube dysfunction that produces a retraction pocket in the pars flaccida or posterosuperior pars tensa; trapped desquamated epithelium enlarges the pocket, or squamous epithelium migrates through a marginal perforation. The expanding mass and its associated chronic inflammation release enzymes and mediators that resorb surrounding bone, progressively destroying the ossicular chain and eroding toward the facial nerve, semicircular canals and intracranial cavity. Superimposed infection produces the characteristic foul discharge and accelerates the destructive process. With complete surgical removal the disease can be controlled and complications prevented, but cholesteatoma has a tendency to recur or leave residual matrix, so long-term follow-up is essential; neglected disease leads to serious intratemporal and intracranial complications.

cholesterol embolisation syndrome — atheroembolism, cholesterol crystal embolism Contrast-induced acute kidney injury Systemic vasculitis (e.g. polyarteritis nodosa, ANCA-associated) Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and other thrombotic microangiopathies Infective endocarditis with septic emboli Antiphospholipid syndrome Drug-induced interstitial nephritis Thromboembolic limb ischaemia Full blood count looking for peripheral eosinophilia Renal function, urinalysis and inflammatory markers (often raised ESR/CRP, hypocomplementaemia) Fundoscopy for Hollenhorst plaques Skin, muscle or renal biopsy demonstrating cholesterol clefts in occluded vessels Vascular imaging of the aorta and large arteries to identify the embolic source Autoimmune and vasculitis serology to exclude mimics Blood cultures and echocardiography where endocarditis is a consideration Cholesterol embolisation syndrome occurs when cholesterol crystals are showered from ulcerated atherosclerotic plaques into small distal arteries, most often after angiography, vascular surgery or anticoagulation in a patient with widespread atherosclerosis. The classic triad is livedo reticularis, blue or discoloured toes with preserved peripheral pulses, and acute or subacute kidney injury developing days to weeks after an inciting vascular event. Peripheral eosinophilia is a valuable, though transient, clue and helps distinguish atheroembolism from contrast-induced nephropathy, which typically follows a different time course. Preserved distal pulses despite ischaemic digits are characteristic because the occlusion is at the microvascular level rather than in the large conduit arteries. Hollenhorst plaques, bright refractile cholesterol crystals seen at retinal arteriolar bifurcations on fundoscopy, provide supportive evidence of systemic atheroembolism. Renal impairment often progresses in a stepwise fashion over weeks reflecting recurrent showers, in contrast to the rapid rise and recovery of contrast nephropathy. Definitive diagnosis requires demonstration of biconvex, needle-shaped cholesterol clefts within occluded small arteries on biopsy of skin, muscle or kidney, though the diagnosis is often clinical. Management is largely supportive with aggressive control of atherosclerotic risk factors and statin therapy; anticoagulation may worsen the syndrome by destabilising plaques and is generally avoided if possible. Progressive acute kidney injury following angiography or vascular surgery Digital ischaemia or necrosis with intact peripheral pulses Mesenteric ischaemia presenting with abdominal pain or gastrointestinal bleeding Neurological deficits suggesting cerebral or spinal atheroembolism Rapid multi-organ deterioration after an intravascular procedure Mistaking the renal injury for contrast-induced nephropathy and missing the atheroembolic time course Attributing blue toes to large-vessel occlusion despite the preserved pulses Continuing or starting anticoagulation, which may perpetuate embolisation Overlooking eosinophilia and Hollenhorst plaques as diagnostic clues Misdiagnosing the multisystem picture as a primary systemic vasculitis Cholesterol embolisation syndrome arises when the fibrous cap of an ulcerated atheromatous plaque, typically in the aorta or large arteries, is disrupted, releasing cholesterol crystals and atheromatous debris into the circulation. These crystals lodge in small arteries and arterioles of 100-200 micrometres, causing mechanical occlusion followed by a foreign-body inflammatory reaction with endothelial injury, giant-cell infiltration and intimal proliferation that further narrows the lumen. The resulting distal ischaemia produces the cutaneous, renal, gastrointestinal, muscular and neurological manifestations. Because the process is showered and inflammatory rather than a single large occlusion, organ dysfunction typically evolves subacutely and in a stepwise manner. Plaque disruption is frequently precipitated by intravascular instrumentation, vascular surgery, thrombolysis or anticoagulation, the last of which is thought to prevent protective thrombus formation over ulcerated plaque and allow continued embolisation. Cholesterol embolisation syndrome carries significant morbidity and mortality, particularly when renal and mesenteric involvement occur; renal recovery is often incomplete and many patients progress to chronic kidney disease, with outcome reflecting the extent of atherosclerotic burden and organ ischaemia.

hyperplastic cholecystoses along with adenomyomatosis, though the two are histologically and mechanistically distinct The condition is unrelated to systemic hypercholesterolaemia and reflects local disturbance of gallbladder cholesterol handling rather than serum lipid levels A gallbladder polyp that is large, sessile, or shows interval growth on surveillance A solitary polyp associated with wall thickening or loss of normal wall layering Coexisting gallstones with a polyp in an older patient or one with primary sclerosing cholangitis, raising malignancy risk New or progressive jaundice or biliary obstruction Detected vascularity within a polyp suggesting a neoplastic lesion Assuming any gallbladder polyp is a benign cholesterol polyp and thereby missing a neoplastic lesion that distinct hyperplastic cholecystosis Wrongly linking the condition to serum hypercholesterolaemia and instituting unnecessary lipid investigation Failing to arrange appropriate surveillance for polyps that fall below the threshold for immediate surgery Cholesterolosis arises from a local abnormality of cholesterol metabolism within the gallbladder wall in which excess cholesterol, derived from cholesterol-supersaturated bile, is absorbed across the mucosa and esterified. The esterified cholesterol and triglyceride accumulate within macrophages (foam cells) that aggregate in the lamina propria at the tips of the mucosal villi, producing the yellow speckling of the diffuse form. Where these lipid-laden aggregates enlarge and become covered by hyperplastic epithelium on a slender stalk, they form pedunculated cholesterol polyps that project into the lumen. The deposits are confined to the mucosa without inflammation or muscular hypertrophy, distinguishing cholesterolosis from adenomyomatosis. Although the process shares the biliary cholesterol supersaturation that also underlies cholesterol gallstones, it correlates poorly with serum cholesterol concentrations, indicating that altered mucosal handling and biliary lipid composition, rather than systemic hyperlipidaemia, are the key drivers. Cholesterolosis is entirely benign with an excellent prognosis, carries no malignant potential, and typically requires no treatment when asymptomatic; symptomatic patients or those with polyps meeting resection criteria are cured by cholecystectomy.

Partial deficiency in cholesteryl ester storage disease leads to lysosomal accumulation of cholesteryl esters and triglycerides, predominantly in hepatocytes, Kupffer cells, intestinal mucosa and the arterial wall. The net effect is that any stimulus raising body temperature can provoke widespread mediator release in predisposed individuals. Cholinergic urticaria often persists for several years but tends to improve over time, and most patients are well controlled with trigger moderation and antihistamines; the main concern is the small subset with associated systemic reactions, in whom careful assessment and an emergency plan may be needed.

Chondroblastoma is a benign neoplasm of immature cartilage-producing cells (chondroblasts) that arises in the secondary ossification centre, explaining its typical epiphyseal or apophyseal location in growing bone. The tumour is composed of sheets of chondroblasts with characteristic nuclear grooves, admixed osteoclast-like giant cells and a distinctive fine pericellular (chicken-wire) calcification of the chondroid matrix. Recurrent driver mutations in the histone gene H3F3B underpin its development and provide a diagnostic immunohistochemical and molecular signature. Although benign, the lesion can breach the growth plate or extend to the articular surface, and rare pulmonary implants have been reported. With adequate curettage and grafting the prognosis is very good, though local recurrence can occur, particularly with incomplete removal or aggressive lesions. Malignant behaviour is exceptional, and rare pulmonary implants are usually indolent.

chondromalacia patellae — patellar chondromalacia, patellofemoral chondrosis, retropatellar cartilage softening Patellofemoral pain syndrome without structural cartilage change Patellofemoral osteoarthritis Patellar instability or maltracking Patellar tendinopathy Hoffa's fat pad impingement Medial synovial plica syndrome Osteochondritis dissecans in adolescents or referred hip and lumbar pain Skyline/Merchant and lateral radiographs to assess patellar tilt, subluxation, joint space and alignment MRI with cartilage-sensitive sequences such as fat-suppressed proton density to grade chondral change Clinical assessment of the Q-angle and lower limb rotational alignment Evaluation of patellar tracking and vastus medialis obliquus function Assessment of hip abductor and core strength Arthroscopy for direct Outerbridge grading in refractory or surgical cases Denotes true softening, fibrillation and degeneration of the patellar articular cartilage, distinct from though overlapping with patellofemoral pain syndrome. Retropatellar pain is worse on stairs, squatting, kneeling and prolonged sitting, the classic theatre or cinema sign. The Outerbridge classification grades severity arthroscopically from softening through fissuring to full-thickness cartilage loss with exposed bone. Crepitus and a positive patellar grind test are common but non-specific findings. Typically affects younger, often female patients with maltracking, quadriceps imbalance or an increased Q-angle. Articular cartilage is aneural, so pain arises from the innervated subchondral bone, synovium and peripatellar soft tissues rather than the cartilage lesion itself. Management is predominantly conservative, centred on activity modification, quadriceps and hip strengthening and patellar taping. Arthroscopic chondroplasty is reserved for selected refractory cases and does not reverse the underlying process. Effusion with warmth suggesting inflammatory or septic arthritis Locking or true giving way suggesting a chondral flap or loose body Progressive rest or night pain or systemic symptoms suggesting neoplasm or infection Rapidly progressive joint space loss indicating established osteoarthritis Using the term interchangeably with patellofemoral pain syndrome and overcalling structural disease. Over-relying on imaging when chondral findings correlate poorly with symptoms. Neglecting proximal hip and core contributions to patellar maltracking. Proceeding to early surgery such as lateral release or chondroplasty before exhausting rehabilitation. Missing an underlying instability or malalignment that is driving the cartilage wear. Chondromalacia patellae describes structural degeneration of the patellar articular cartilage that progresses from softening and swelling, through fissuring and fibrillation, to fragmentation and eventual full-thickness loss exposing subchondral bone. It is driven by abnormal patellofemoral contact stress arising from maltracking, lateral patellar tilt or subluxation, muscle imbalance with a weak vastus medialis obliquus and a tight lateral retinaculum, malalignment such as an increased Q-angle or trochlear dysplasia, or direct trauma, all of which concentrate load on focal cartilage areas. Because articular cartilage is avascular and aneural, the lesion is not itself the direct pain generator; symptoms arise from altered load transmission to richly innervated subchondral bone, synovial irritation and peripatellar soft tissues. In some patients it represents an early stage on the continuum towards patellofemoral osteoarthritis. Symptoms frequently improve with sustained conservative rehabilitation, but established high-grade cartilage lesions may persist and can progress to patellofemoral osteoarthritis; surgical outcomes are variable.

The prognosis is favourable, with cure expected after complete curettage or excision, although local recurrence is recognised, particularly after incomplete removal in younger patients. Malignant transformation is very rare.

The relatively avascular, matrix-rich nature of cartilaginous tumours limits the delivery and efficacy of chemotherapy and radiotherapy, explaining their characteristic treatment resistance. Higher-grade and dedifferentiated tumours acquire further genetic alterations that confer aggressive behaviour. Prognosis is governed principally by histological grade and completeness of resection; low-grade tumours have an excellent outcome after adequate surgery, whereas high-grade, dedifferentiated, and axial or pelvic tumours that are difficult to resect completely carry a markedly worse prognosis.

Chordoma is a slow-growing but relentlessly recurring tumour; long-term outcome depends chiefly on achieving complete en bloc resection and on tumour location, with incompletely resected skull base and sacral tumours prone to repeated recurrence and eventual metastasis in a proportion of patients.

Chorea-acanthocytosis is a progressive, life-limiting neurodegenerative disorder that typically advances over one to two decades, with increasing disability from movement, cognitive and psychiatric features. Management is supportive and symptomatic, and premature death often relates to seizures, aspiration or intercurrent complications.

chorea gravidarum — gestational chorea, pregnancy-associated chorea Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome Systemic lupus erythematosus Recurrent or persistent Sydenham chorea Wilson disease unmasked in pregnancy Thyrotoxicosis-associated chorea Polycythaemia and other metabolic choreas Functional (psychogenic) movement disorder Antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I) Antinuclear and extractable nuclear antigen antibodies for lupus Anti-streptolysin O / anti-DNase B titres and echocardiography if rheumatic history Thyroid function tests Serum caeruloplasmin, copper and slit-lamp examination for Wilson disease Full blood count for polycythaemia MRI brain (used selectively, with appropriate gestational precautions) Chorea gravidarum is a descriptive term for any chorea arising during pregnancy, not a single disease entity; it reflects an underlying predisposition unmasked by the hormonal state. Historically most cases followed prior Sydenham chorea or rheumatic fever, but with declining rheumatic disease, antiphospholipid syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus are now leading causes. Onset is typically in the first half of pregnancy and often remits spontaneously after delivery or termination. A comparable oestrogen-related mechanism produces chorea with combined oral contraceptive use, supporting a hormonal trigger. Chorea may be unilateral or generalised and can be severe enough to interfere with feeding, sleep and safety. A prior episode strongly predicts recurrence in subsequent pregnancies or with oestrogen exposure. Thorough evaluation for an underlying secondary cause is mandatory, as management and prognosis depend on the aetiology rather than the pregnancy itself. Treatment is reserved for disabling symptoms, favouring the lowest effective dose of agents with the most reassuring gestational safety profile after specialist counselling. Features of antiphospholipid syndrome such as thrombosis or recurrent pregnancy loss requiring anticoagulation assessment Systemic features of active lupus (rash, arthritis, nephritis, cytopenias) Severe chorea threatening maternal exhaustion, rhabdomyolysis or fetal wellbeing New neurological or cardiac signs suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis Hyperthyroid crisis features accompanying the chorea Regarding chorea gravidarum as a benign self-contained diagnosis and failing to investigate for antiphospholipid syndrome or lupus. Overlooking a missed antiphospholipid syndrome that also endangers the pregnancy through thrombosis. Prescribing dopamine-blocking drugs without specialist counselling on gestational safety. Missing thyrotoxicosis or Wilson disease as reversible contributors. Not advising on recurrence risk with future pregnancies and oestrogen-containing contraception. Chorea gravidarum arises when the physiological rise in oestrogen and progesterone during pregnancy sensitises or unmasks striatal dopaminergic pathways in a predisposed individual. Oestrogens are thought to modulate dopamine receptor sensitivity within the basal ganglia, and in those with prior basal ganglia injury (notably previous Sydenham chorea) or circulating antibodies (antiphospholipid or anti-basal ganglia antibodies in lupus), this heightened dopaminergic responsiveness precipitates dysfunction of the striatal indirect pathway. The resultant reduction in inhibitory output produces disinhibited involuntary movements. The frequent postpartum remission mirrors the fall in sex hormone levels, and the same mechanism explains contraceptive-induced chorea. Chorea gravidarum usually remits after delivery or termination and carries a good prognosis when no serious underlying disorder is present, although it commonly recurs in later pregnancies or with oestrogen exposure. Overall outlook is determined by the underlying cause, particularly antiphospholipid syndrome or lupus.

Inflammation of the membranes, cord, and placenta may compromise the fetus directly through infection and indirectly through the fetal inflammatory response syndrome, which is implicated in preterm birth and neurological injury. With prompt antibiotics and timely delivery most mothers recover fully, though the condition carries risks of postpartum infection, haemorrhage from uterine atony, and rarely septic shock. Neonatal outcome depends on gestation and the severity of the fetal inflammatory response; term infants generally do well with treatment, whereas preterm infants exposed to intrauterine infection face higher risks of sepsis and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment.

choroid plexus papilloma — CPP, choroid plexus tumour choroid plexus carcinoma atypical choroid plexus papilloma ependymoma papillary meningioma metastatic papillary carcinoma villous hypertrophy of the choroid plexus central neurocytoma contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain showing an enhancing intraventricular mass MRI of the whole neuraxis to assess cerebrospinal fluid dissemination surgical resection with histological grading immunohistochemistry including transthyretin and cytokeratins assessment of cerebrospinal fluid dynamics and ventricular size germline TP53 testing where carcinoma or a suggestive family history is present developmental and ophthalmological assessment when Aicardi syndrome is suspected A CNS WHO grade 1 intraventricular tumour that in children favours the lateral ventricles and in adults the fourth ventricle. Hydrocephalus is the dominant clinical problem, arising from cerebrospinal fluid overproduction, obstruction of flow, or impaired reabsorption after microhaemorrhage. Imaging shows a well-defined, lobulated, avidly and homogeneously enhancing intraventricular mass with a cauliflower-like surface. Histology recapitulates normal choroid plexus, with delicate fibrovascular fronds lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar epithelium. Tumour cells commonly express transthyretin and cytokeratins, helping distinguish them from metastatic papillary carcinoma. It forms a spectrum with atypical papilloma (grade 2) and choroid plexus carcinoma (grade 3), graded largely on mitotic activity and anaplasia. Choroid plexus tumours, especially carcinoma, are associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome and germline TP53 mutation, and papilloma may occur in Aicardi syndrome. Complete surgical resection is usually curative for papilloma and often resolves the hydrocephalus. rapidly progressive hydrocephalus with raised intracranial pressure macrocephaly and bulging fontanelle in an infant intratumoural or intraventricular haemorrhage features suggesting carcinoma such as brain invasion or dissemination assuming hydrocephalus will always resolve after resection when a shunt may still be needed misgrading a carcinoma as a benign papilloma on limited sampling confusing the tumour with reactive villous hypertrophy or normal plexus overlooking an underlying Li-Fraumeni syndrome and the need for family counselling underestimating intraoperative bleeding from these vascular tumours Choroid plexus papilloma is a benign neoplasm derived from the modified ependymal epithelium of the choroid plexus, and it faithfully reproduces the papillary architecture of normal plexus with fibrovascular cores covered by a single orderly layer of epithelium. Hydrocephalus results from a combination of active cerebrospinal fluid oversecretion by the expanded epithelial surface, mechanical obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid pathways, and reduced arachnoid reabsorption following recurrent microhaemorrhage that raises fluid protein content. A subset arises in the setting of germline TP53 mutation, linking the choroid plexus tumour spectrum to Li-Fraumeni syndrome, and progression to atypical papilloma and carcinoma is accompanied by increasing mitotic activity, cellular anaplasia and loss of the orderly papillary pattern. Papilloma carries an excellent prognosis with prolonged survival and frequent cure after complete resection, in marked contrast to choroid plexus carcinoma, which behaves aggressively.

distinguishing them helps localise the underlying cause Management is directed at the underlying cause; longstanding idiopathic folds are usually stable and asymptomatic, although a hyperopic shift or mild distortion may occur New unilateral folds with proptosis or a hyperopic shift suggesting an orbital or retrobulbar mass Pain, especially on eye movement, accompanying folds and suggesting posterior scleritis Associated disc swelling raising the possibility of raised intracranial pressure Hypotony with a shallow anterior chamber or a bleb leak after surgery Dismissing new choroidal folds as idiopathic without imaging to exclude an orbital mass or posterior scleritis Confusing choroidal folds with angioid streaks Missing hypotony as a cause after glaucoma surgery or trauma Overlooking associated papilloedema and raised intracranial pressure Choroidal folds arise when the outer coats of the eye, namely the sclera, choroid, Bruch's membrane and retinal pigment epithelium, are compressed, thickened or rendered redundant, throwing the choroid and overlying RPE into a series of parallel undulations. Any process that shortens or indents the posterior globe or expands the choroid may be responsible. Orbital masses and thyroid orbitopathy compress the globe, posterior scleritis inflames and thickens the sclera and choroid, hypotony allows the eye wall to collapse and fold, and raised intracranial pressure transmitted along the optic nerve sheath produces peripapillary folds with disc oedema. In idiopathic cases a short, thick sclera in a hyperopic eye is implicated. The crest of each fold has stretched, thinned RPE while the trough has heaped RPE, which produces the characteristic angiographic pattern. Idiopathic and longstanding choroidal folds are usually stable and visually insignificant. When secondary, the outcome depends on the underlying cause, and the folds may resolve if that cause, such as hypotony, an orbital mass or scleritis, is treated, although longstanding RPE changes can persist.

Choroidal melanoma arises from malignant transformation of melanocytes within the choroidal stroma. Growth breaches Bruch membrane in many tumours, producing the characteristic mushroom shape and disrupting the overlying retinal pigment epithelium and retina, which leads to serous detachment and lipofuscin deposition. Chromosomal changes, notably loss of one copy of chromosome 3 and gains of chromosome 8q, correlate with an aggressive metastatic phenotype. Spread is almost exclusively haematogenous with a strong hepatic tropism, sometimes appearing years after successful local treatment. Prognosis is determined mainly by tumour size, cell type, extraocular extension, and cytogenetics; small tumours with disomy 3 have a favourable survival outlook, whereas large tumours with monosomy 3 or chromosome 8q gain carry a high risk of fatal hepatic metastasis, and local eye-preserving radiotherapy controls the tumour without necessarily altering metastatic risk.

Prognosis is guarded, and management is supportive and multidisciplinary.

chrome ulcers — chrome holes, chromate ulcers chromate allergic contact dermatitis pyoderma gangrenosum cutaneous anthrax or ecthyma (infective ulcer) traumatic or factitious ulcer squamous cell carcinoma or other ulcerated neoplasm vasculitic or ischaemic ulcer atypical mycobacterial or deep fungal ulcer detailed occupational and exposure history with workplace hygiene assessment clinical examination of hands, forearms and nasal septum for coexisting lesions patch testing to potassium dichromate to detect concurrent chromium sensitisation swab of the ulcer base for microbiology to exclude secondary or primary infection skin biopsy if the ulcer is atypical, non-healing or malignancy is suspected environmental and biological monitoring of chromium (air sampling, urinary chromium) assessment of surface and airborne hexavalent chromium contamination in the workplace Punched-out, painless ulcers with rolled or undermined edges and a hard-crusted base, arising at sites of skin trauma exposed to hexavalent chromium, classically over the dorsa of hands, fingers, forearms and around the nail folds. The nasal septum is the other characteristic site: chromate exposure produces septal ulceration that may progress to painless perforation, so always examine the nose in any worker with chrome ulcers. Hexavalent chromium (chromate, dichromate) is the corrosive, ulcerogenic and sensitising species; trivalent chromium is far less toxic to skin, which is central to understanding both prevention and substitution. Classic exposures include electroplating, chrome tanning of leather, chromate pigment and dye manufacture, welding of stainless steel, and cement/anti-corrosion work. A pre-existing break in the skin (cut, abrasion, cuticle tear) is usually the portal; intact skin is relatively resistant, so minor wounds must be covered before chromate work. Ulcers are indolent and slow to heal while exposure continues but typically heal with atrophic or depressed scars once contact ceases and the wound is protected. Chrome ulceration reflects direct corrosive injury and is distinct from chromate allergic contact dermatitis, although a worker may have both; patch testing to potassium dichromate helps identify concurrent sensitisation. Prevention hinges on barrier protection, prompt wound care, substitution to trivalent formulations where feasible, and reducing airborne and surface chromate contamination. nasal septal ulceration or perforation indicating significant mucosal chromate exposure non-healing or expanding ulcer with atypical margins raising concern for malignancy clinical signs of secondary infection such as spreading cellulitis or systemic upset multiple or recurrent ulcers signalling ongoing uncontrolled workplace exposure features suggesting systemic chromate toxicity or coexisting respiratory disease Mistaking a painless chrome ulcer for a trivial wound and allowing exposure to continue. Failing to examine the nasal septum and missing early ulceration or perforation. Confusing the corrosive ulcer with chromate allergic dermatitis and omitting patch testing when both may coexist. Attributing a non-healing ulcer solely to chromium and overlooking malignant transformation or infection. Neglecting workplace hygiene and colleagues, so that source control and case-finding are incomplete. Hexavalent chromium compounds are strong oxidising agents that penetrate skin readily, particularly through breaches in the epidermal barrier. On contact with tissue they are reduced to trivalent chromium, generating reactive intermediates and free radicals that produce direct cytotoxic and corrosive coagulative necrosis of keratinocytes and dermal tissue. This yields a localised, sharply demarcated area of tissue destruction — the chrome ulcer — with a necrotic base and surrounding reactive changes. Because chromate is not appreciably painful and impairs the local inflammatory and healing response, ulcers enlarge and persist while exposure continues. The same oxidative injury on the nasal mucosa causes septal ulceration and perforation. Separately, chromium can act as a hapten binding tissue proteins to drive a delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity, but the ulcer itself is a toxic-corrosive rather than immunological lesion. Individual ulcers usually heal with atrophic or depressed scarring once chromate contact ceases and the wound is protected, though healing is slow. Continued exposure leads to recurrent, persistent lesions and risks nasal septal perforation, so the outlook depends on effective exposure control.

apparently trivial skin lesion in a systemically unwell patient Chromobacterium violaceum is an environmental facultative anaerobe that gains entry through skin wounds contaminated by soil or freshwater. Localised skin infection may resolve with drainage and antibiotics, but disseminated disease carries substantial mortality; outcome improves with early recognition, appropriate agents chosen for the organism's resistance pattern, and prolonged therapy with abscess drainage.

The host mounts a chronic mixed suppurative and granulomatous response with pseudoepitheliomatous epidermal hyperplasia, producing the characteristic verrucous surface. Small early lesions may be cured with prolonged antifungal therapy or excision, but extensive long-standing disease is often refractory, prone to relapse, and can lead to disabling fibrosis, lymphoedema and, rarely, malignant transformation.

In the actinic reticuloid variant the dense dermal lymphocytic infiltrate can resemble cutaneous T-cell lymphoma histologically, although the process is benign and reactive. Chronic actinic dermatitis tends to be persistent and can be markedly disabling, but with strict photoprotection, allergen avoidance and immunosuppressive therapy many patients improve, and slow resolution over years is possible; the actinic reticuloid variant is benign despite its lymphoma-like appearance, though it warrants careful follow-up.

Chronic and Recurrent Meningitis — Chronic meningitis, Recurrent meningitis, Chronic lymphocytic meningitis, Mollaret's meningitis, Basal meningitis Infectious: M. tuberculosis, Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii, syphilis, Lyme disease (Bannwarth's syndrome), Brucella, Nocardia, Actinomyces, Whipple's disease, partially treated bacterial meningitis, parameningeal infection Fungal: Coccidioides, Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Candida, Aspergillus, Sporothrix Parasitic/helminthic: cysticercosis (Taenia solium), Gnathostoma, Angiostrongylus, Baylisascaris, Toxoplasma, trypanosomiasis, Acanthamoeba/Balamuthia Viral: HSV-2 (Mollaret's, recurrent), mumps, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, enteroviruses (in agammaglobulinemia/B-cell depletion), HIV acute retroviral syndrome Malignancy: carcinomatous/lymphomatous meningitis (breast, lung, stomach, pancreas, melanoma, leukemia, gliomatosis) Inflammatory/autoimmune: neurosarcoidosis, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome, Behcet's, SLE, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, IgG4-related hypertrophic pachymeningitis, primary CNS vasculitis, Sjogren's Monogenic autoinflammatory: TRAPS, CAPS, NOMID, complement factor I deficiency Chemical: leakage from epidermoid/dermoid tumor, craniopharyngioma, cholesteatoma; drug hypersensitivity (NSAIDs, sulfonamides, IVIG, others) Carcinomatous or lymphomatous meningitis (CSF seeding by malignant cells) Neurosarcoidosis (low CSF glucose can mimic tuberculous/fungal meningitis) Chemical meningitis from leaking epidermoid/dermoid cyst or craniopharyngioma Drug-induced aseptic meningitis Primary CNS or systemic vasculitis with meningitis and stroke Measure opening CSF pressure; brain imaging before LP if raised ICP is suspected, as a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus risks herniation CSF cell count and differential, glucose, protein, Gram's stain; bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures (large volumes) CSF VDRL (highly specific, low sensitivity); serum treponemal antibodies; consider empiric neurosyphilis treatment if CSF VDRL negative but serum positive with unexplained pleocytosis Cryptococcal antigen, India ink/fungal wet mount, oligoclonal bands, and cytology/flow cytometry for malignant cells Pathogen-specific PCR; broad-range 16s rRNA PCR (bacteria, useful in partially treated meningitis), 18s/28s rRNA PCR (fungi), CSF beta-glucan assay, and unbiased metagenomic next-generation sequencing for enigmatic cases Contrast-enhanced MRI/CT of brain and spinal cord to detect meningeal enhancement, parameningeal infection, cord encasement, or nodular deposits; angiography if arteritis/stroke suspected Systemic workup: tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay, chest radiograph or chest CT/MRI and sputum exam, urinalysis, CBC, renal/liver function, alkaline phosphatase, ESR, ANA, anti-Ro/anti-La, rheumatoid factor, serum IgG4 FDG-PET to locate a systemic biopsy site in suspected carcinomatous meningitis or sarcoidosis; genetic testing for monogenic autoinflammatory disorders Meningeal biopsy targeting contrast-enhancing regions when CSF is non-diagnostic and the patient is severely disabled, needs ventricular decompression, or is deteriorating rapidly Subarachnoid hemorrhage in the preceding week presenting with xanthochromia and pleocytosis IgG4-related hypertrophic pachymeningitis Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome and Behcet's syndrome (recurrent forms) Multiple sclerosis and Sjogren's syndrome Chronic meningitis is defined by a characteristic neurologic syndrome persisting beyond 4 weeks together with a sustained CSF inflammatory response (white cell count >5/uL); appropriate treatment hinges entirely on identifying the underlying cause. Five disease categories account for most cases: meningeal infections, malignancy, autoimmune inflammatory disorders, chemical meningitis, and parameningeal infections; some recurrent cases reflect monogenic autoinflammatory disorders. Cardinal manifestations are persistent nonfocal headache, signs of hydrocephalus, cranial neuropathies, radiculopathies, and cognitive or personality change; classic meningeal signs (Kernig/Brudzinski) are actually uncommon in the chronic form. Basal meningitis, where exudate collects at the skull base, presents as multiple cranial neuropathies; lower cranial nerves are involved more often because the inflammatory exudate gravitates to the base of the brain. Spinal involvement produces multiple radiculopathies (radicular pain, sensory loss, weakness, sphincter dysfunction) and may progress to arachnoiditis with clumping of lower nerve roots, again because cells settle at the bottom of the intrathecal space. Two clinical forms exist: a chronic persistent form and a recurrent form in which all clinical and CSF abnormalities resolve completely between discrete episodes (e.g., Mollaret's meningitis from HSV-2, chemical leak from epidermoid tumor, autoimmune conditions, drug hypersensitivity). Worldwide, M. tuberculosis is the most common infectious cause, followed by Cryptococcus neoformans; in immunosuppressed patients these may present with little or no headache, fever, or meningeal signs and even a pauci-cellular CSF. In most chronic (non-recurrent) meningitides mononuclear cells predominate; a neutrophilic CSF after 3 weeks points to Nocardia, Actinomyces, Brucella, certain fungi (Blastomyces, Candida, Histoplasma, Aspergillus, Pseudallescheria, Cladophialophora), or noninfectious causes (SLE, chemical meningitis). An eosinophilic CSF response suggests parasitic disease (Angiostrongylus, Gnathostoma, Baylisascaris, Toxocara, cysticercosis, schistosomiasis, echinococcosis, toxoplasmosis), coccidioidal fungal meningitis (6-20% eosinophils with lymphocytic pleocytosis), neoplasia, or sarcoidosis. Meningeal enhancement patterns localize the process: leptomeningeal enhancement follows gyri and basal cisterns (typical of infection), whereas pachymeningeal enhancement is thick, linear or nodular along dura/falx/tentorium (e.g., lymphoma, IgG4-related disease). In about one-third of cases the cause remains undiagnosed despite thorough evaluation; many causative organisms require weeks of culture, so diagnostic patience is balanced against the risk of progressive neurologic deterioration. Repeated large-volume lumbar CSF samples (three or more), and if needed cervical cisternal sampling near the basal meninges, raise the yield for fungal and malignant causes; ventricular fluid may appear sterile despite active lower lumbar infection. Signs of raised intracranial pressure (vomiting, drowsiness, papilledema, visual loss, impaired upgaze, sixth-nerve palsy) warranting imaging before lumbar puncture Rapidly progressive neurologic deterioration requiring urgent treatment rather than awaiting culture results Multiple progressive cranial neuropathies or evolving radiculopathy/myelopathy indicating widespread CSF dissemination Focal cerebral signs suggesting brain abscess, parameningeal infection, or infarction Immunosuppression or untreated HIV, where meningeal signs are attenuated and any persistent headache or mental status change mandates CSF examination Low CSF glucose with lymphocytic pleocytosis, prompting empiric coverage for tuberculosis given the potential for devastation within weeks Performing lumbar puncture before imaging when raised ICP from a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus exists risks brain herniation Assuming a normal or pauci-cellular CSF excludes meningitis in immunosuppressed or HIV patients, in whom signs are attenuated Relying on a single small-volume CSF sample; fungal and malignant causes often require repeated large-volume sampling, and some organisms take weeks to grow in culture Interpreting a transient response to empiric glucocorticoids as confirmation of a noninfectious cause, since tuberculosis, cysticercosis, and lymphoma may also respond temporarily Overlooking false-negative cryptococcal antigen or CSF VDRL results due to the prozone effect at high antibody/antigen titers Attributing dural enhancement to disease when it can be a benign post-LP, post-neurosurgical, post-concussion, or post-CSF-leak finding Failing to recognize that ventricular CSF can appear sterile while active infection persists in the lower lumbar space Chronic inflammation of the meninges (pia, arachnoid, dura) generates neurologic deficits whose pattern is determined by the anatomic site of inflammation and its consequences. CSF, produced by the choroid plexus and circulating from the ventricles through the basal cisterns over the convexities to arachnoid villi, provides a conduit for rapid spread of infectious or infiltrative processes over the brain, cord, and nerve roots; organisms may also track along perivascular (Virchow-Robin) spaces into brain parenchyma. Intracranial inflammation stimulates meningeal nociceptive fibers (headache, neck/back pain) and may obstruct CSF flow at the cerebral aqueduct or arachnoid villi, causing hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure. Inflammatory exudate seeded around the brainstem and cranial nerves at the skull base produces basal meningitis with multiple cranial neuropathies, while spinal exudate injures nerve roots and may encircle the cord to cause myelopathy. Vasculitis of subarachnoid vessels can lead to infarction and cognitive/behavioral decline. A recently identified dural lymphatic system drains the dura, but its role in chronic meningitis is not yet established. Outcome depends on the underlying etiology and the speed of diagnosis and treatment; many causes are effectively treatable, but untreated disease produces progressive, potentially fatal damage to the CNS, cranial nerves, and roots. Even with treatment, tuberculous meningitis carries high rates of morbidity. Fatal levels of raised intracranial pressure can occur (notably in cryptococcal meningitis) even without ventricular enlargement, and repetitive or continuous CSF drainage may be needed to prevent abrupt deterioration and death. Some recurrent forms (e.g., chronic benign lymphocytic meningitis) resolve over 2-6 months. No formal grading scale is given; severity is gauged clinically by the rate of neurologic progression, the presence of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus, and the degree of disability, which together determine whether to await culture results or proceed to meningeal biopsy and empiric therapy.

patient Family history of colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease Features of obstruction such as severe pain, distension, and vomiting Escalating laxatives without recognising an underlying defecatory disorder that needs biofeedback Failing to exclude secondary and structural causes before treating symptomatically Overlooking constipating medications, particularly opioids Omitting the rectal examination, which often reveals the mechanism of constipation Chronic constipation reflects disordered colonic transit, defecatory mechanics, or both. In slow-transit constipation, reduced colonic propulsive activity, often linked to abnormalities of enteric neurons and interstitial cells of Cajal, delays stool passage. In defecatory disorders, impaired coordination of the pelvic floor and anal sphincter (dyssynergia) or structural pelvic floor abnormalities prevent effective evacuation. Normal-transit constipation, the most common type, involves normal stool movement with perceived difficulty, often overlapping with irritable bowel syndrome. Secondary causes act through metabolic, endocrine, neurological, or pharmacological effects on gut motility. Chronic constipation is generally benign but frequently persistent and can significantly reduce quality of life; most patients improve with lifestyle measures and laxatives, and biofeedback is effective for defecatory disorders, though a minority remain refractory.

Chronic eosinophilic leukaemia — CEL Reactive eosinophilia (parasitic infection, allergy, drugs) Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome Myeloid neoplasm with PDGFRA/PDGFRB/FGFR1 rearrangement Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Lymphocyte-variant hypereosinophilia Full blood count and film quantifying eosinophilia Bone marrow examination with cytogenetics Molecular testing for PDGFRA, PDGFRB and FGFR1 rearrangements Exclusion of reactive causes including parasites and allergy Cardiac assessment (troponin, echocardiography) for eosinophilic heart disease A myeloproliferative neoplasm with clonal proliferation of eosinophils causing persistent marked eosinophilia Organ damage from eosinophil infiltration and granule release can affect the heart, skin, lungs, gut and nervous system It must be distinguished from reactive eosinophilia and from idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome Clonality is shown by cytogenetic or molecular abnormalities or an increase in blasts Cases with rearrangements of PDGFRA, PDGFRB or FGFR1 are classified separately and are important because PDGFR-driven disease responds dramatically to tyrosine kinase inhibitors Endomyocardial fibrosis is a serious complication of sustained eosinophilia Cardiac involvement (eosinophilic myocarditis, endomyocardial fibrosis) Thromboembolic or neurological complications Rising blasts suggesting progression Very high eosinophil counts with organ dysfunction Failing to test for PDGFR rearrangements, missing a highly treatable subtype Attributing clonal eosinophilia to a reactive cause Overlooking cardiac involvement Confusing it with idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome Chronic eosinophilic leukaemia is a clonal stem cell neoplasm in which acquired genetic lesions drive autonomous eosinophil production. In an important subset, fusion genes involving PDGFRA (such as FIP1L1-PDGFRA), PDGFRB or FGFR1 constitutively activate tyrosine kinase signalling; these are now categorised as a distinct group of myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia. The expanded eosinophils release granule proteins that damage tissues, with the heart particularly vulnerable to eosinophilic myocarditis and progressive endomyocardial fibrosis. Prognosis varies with the genetic subtype; PDGFR-rearranged disease usually responds very well to tyrosine kinase inhibitors, whereas other forms depend on organ damage and risk of leukaemic progression.

develop Attributing persistent eosinophilia solely to allergy or parasites This group of disorders results from clonal proliferation of eosinophil precursors, most often driven by constitutively active tyrosine kinases created by gene rearrangements involving PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1 or JAK2. These fusion kinases signal continuously to expand the eosinophil lineage independent of normal cytokine control. Where no specific rearrangement is found but clonality or increased blasts are demonstrable, the disorder is classified as chronic eosinophilic leukaemia not otherwise specified. Sustained eosinophilia releases granule proteins that injure tissues, with the heart being especially vulnerable to progressive endomyocardial fibrosis and thrombosis. Prognosis depends on the molecular subtype; PDGFRA- and PDGFRB-rearranged disease responds dramatically to tyrosine kinase inhibition with excellent outcomes, whereas FGFR1-rearranged and blast-phase disease is aggressive with poorer survival.
