there is asthma with extrapulmonary features such as neuropathy or vasculitis Exclude drug reactions and parasitic infection as secondary causes of pulmonary eosinophilia Extrapulmonary features such as mononeuritis multiplex, cardiac or renal involvement suggesting systemic vasculitis Frequent relapse or steroid dependence requiring steroid-sparing therapy Progressive breathlessness or hypoxaemia despite treatment Very high eosinophil counts raising concern for hypereosinophilic syndrome Failing to recognise the peripheral photographic-negative-of-oedema pattern on imaging Stopping corticosteroids too early and provoking relapse Missing an evolving eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis when systemic features appear Not excluding drug and parasitic causes of pulmonary eosinophilia Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia is characterised by sustained accumulation of eosinophils within the alveoli and interstitium, driven by eosinophil-active cytokines and chemokines in a background that is often atopic or asthmatic. Persistent eosinophil infiltration and release of cytotoxic granule proteins produce dense alveolar filling, predominantly in the peripheral and upper lung zones, giving the characteristic reverse-oedema distribution. The inflammation is corticosteroid sensitive but tends to recur, and prolonged uncontrolled disease can occasionally lead to fibrotic change. The response to corticosteroids is usually excellent and rapid, but relapse is frequent when treatment is reduced or stopped, so many patients need prolonged therapy; long-term outcome is generally good provided disease is controlled.

Chronic exertional compartment syndrome — CECS, exertional compartment syndrome Medial tibial stress syndrome Tibial stress fracture Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome Nerve entrapment (for example peroneal) Vascular claudication Dynamic intracompartmental pressure measurement before and after exercise Clinical reproduction of symptoms with exertion MRI or bone imaging to exclude stress fracture Vascular studies where arterial entrapment is considered Assessment of nerve involvement if there are neurological symptoms Exercise-induced pain, tightness and sometimes numbness in a muscle compartment, most often the leg, that predictably comes on at a given level of exertion Symptoms are relieved by rest within minutes and recur on resuming activity, unlike acute compartment syndrome It commonly affects runners and other endurance athletes and is frequently bilateral The anterior compartment of the leg is most often involved, sometimes with foot drop or paraesthesiae during exertion Diagnosis is confirmed by measuring raised intracompartmental pressures with exercise Activity modification may suffice, but fasciotomy is the definitive treatment for refractory cases Symptoms that do not resolve with rest, raising concern for acute compartment syndrome Progressive or persistent neurological deficit Vascular signs suggesting arterial entrapment Features suggesting stress fracture Confusing it with medial tibial stress syndrome or stress fracture Assuming the risk profile of acute compartment syndrome Missing popliteal artery entrapment as a vascular mimic Diagnosing without objective pressure measurement Chronic exertional compartment syndrome arises when exercise-induced expansion of muscle within a relatively non-compliant fascial compartment raises intracompartmental pressure, impairing perfusion and causing reversible ischaemic pain and sometimes nerve dysfunction. Unlike acute compartment syndrome, the pressure rise is transient and resolves with rest, so tissue is not permanently damaged. The mismatch between muscle volume during exercise and the fixed compartment size, sometimes with a thickened or tight fascia, underlies the recurrent symptoms. The condition is not limb-threatening; many manage with activity modification, and fasciotomy provides good relief for those who wish to continue high-level activity, though results vary by compartment.

lung disease is often asymptomatic Neglecting infection prophylaxis during prolonged immunosuppression Under-treating ocular and oral sicca and allowing avoidable complications Overlooking the increased risk of secondary malignancy on long-term follow-up Alloreactive donor T cells, together with dysregulated B-cell responses and autoantibody formation, sustain chronic immune-mediated inflammation. Damage to the thymus impairs the development of tolerance, allowing autoreactive and alloreactive clones to persist. Ongoing inflammation drives progressive tissue fibrosis across multiple organs, producing a phenotype that resembles scleroderma and other autoimmune connective-tissue diseases rather than the acute epithelial injury of acute graft-versus-host disease. The course is variable: limited disease may resolve, whereas extensive sclerodermatous or pulmonary disease causes long-term disability and contributes to non-relapse mortality; an associated graft-versus-tumour effect can reduce the risk of underlying disease relapse.

syndrome) Congenital or acquired neutropenia Inflammatory bowel disease (granulomatous colitis can mimic Crohn disease) Mycobacterial infection and Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease Cystic fibrosis or bronchiectasis with recurrent pulmonary infection Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency causing a CGD-like oxidative defect Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow-cytometric assay of the neutrophil oxidative burst Nitroblue tetrazolium test where DHR is unavailable Genetic testing to identify the affected oxidase subunit and inheritance pattern Microbiologic sampling and culture of infected sites, including for fungi and Nocardia Cross-sectional imaging to localise deep abscesses and granulomatous complications Carrier testing and genetic counselling for family members CGD is a primary phagocyte disorder in which defective NADPH oxidase prevents the respiratory burst, so neutrophils and macrophages ingest but cannot kill certain microbes Infections are characteristically caused by catalase-positive organisms, notably Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia, Nocardia, and the mould Aspergillus Recurrent deep-seated infections-pneumonia, lymphadenitis, liver and other abscesses, and osteomyelitis-are typical and often present in early childhood Exuberant granuloma formation reflects dysregulated inflammation and can obstruct hollow viscera, causing gastrointestinal or genitourinary problems that mimic inflammatory bowel disease Most cases are X-linked (gp91phox/CYBB) and therefore affect boys, with autosomal recessive forms tending to run a milder course Diagnosis relies on tests of the oxidative burst, historically the nitroblue tetrazolium test and now the more quantitative dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow-cytometric assay, with genetic confirmation Long-term prophylaxis against bacteria and fungi plus interferon-gamma reduces serious infections, and prompt aggressive treatment of intercurrent infection is essential Invasive aspergillosis and other fungal infections are leading causes of death, so a high index of suspicion and early antifungal therapy are important Allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation is the established curative option, and gene therapy is an evolving approach Invasive fungal infection, particularly aspergillosis, with respiratory or systemic decline Deep abscess, sepsis, or rapidly progressive pneumonia requiring urgent intervention Bowel or urinary obstruction from granulomatous inflammation Infection with Burkholderia or Nocardia signalling severe, potentially fatal disease Underestimating fungal risk and delaying antifungal therapy in a febrile CGD patient Mistaking granulomatous colitis for ordinary inflammatory bowel disease and missing the underlying immunodeficiency Stopping antimicrobial and antifungal prophylaxis during periods of apparent wellness Failing to pursue genetic diagnosis, carrier testing, and consideration of curative transplantation CGD is caused by mutations in any of the subunits of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex (gp91phox, p22phox, p47phox, p67phox, p40phox). This enzyme normally generates superoxide and downstream reactive oxygen species that drive the microbicidal respiratory burst within the phagosome. Without a functional oxidase, phagocytes engulf organisms but fail to kill catalase-positive microbes that can neutralise their own hydrogen peroxide. Persistence of viable organisms and impaired resolution of inflammation lead to chronic granuloma formation and tissue damage. The most common form is X-linked (CYBB), with autosomal recessive forms accounting for the remainder. Prophylactic antibacterial and antifungal therapy with interferon-gamma has substantially improved survival, though serious infections and inflammatory complications still occur. Invasive fungal disease remains a leading cause of death. Haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation can be curative, especially with well-matched donors performed before major organ damage.

Chronic Hepatitis — chronic hepatitis B, chronic hepatitis C, autoimmune hepatitis Wilson disease (especially in adolescents, before neurologic signs/Kayser-Fleischer rings) Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Primary biliary cholangitis Cryptogenic cirrhosis Celiac disease Ischemic liver disease Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic venous outflow obstruction) Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) hepatitis Chronic hepatitis B Chronic hepatitis C Chronic hepatitis D (delta) superimposed on hepatitis B Hepatitis E (chronic in immunosuppressed/post-transplant hosts) Liver biochemical tests (AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time) HBV markers: HBsAg, IgG anti-HBc, HBeAg/anti-HBe, HBV DNA HCV markers: anti-HCV, HCV RNA HDV markers: anti-HDV, HDV RNA Autoantibodies: ANA (homogeneous), anti-smooth-muscle antibody (anti-actin), anti-LKM1, anti-SLA, anti-LC1, F-actin, atypical pANCA Serum immunoglobulins/globulins (hypergammaglobulinemia >2.5 g/dL in AIH; IgG level) Liver biopsy for grading (HAI/METAVIR) and staging of fibrosis Noninvasive fibrosis assessment: FIB-4, Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) score, liver elastography/stiffness imaging Ceruloplasmin, serum/urinary copper and liver copper (to exclude Wilson disease) Autoimmune hepatitis Drug- or toxin-induced liver injury (including minocycline) Alcohol-associated hepatitis Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH/NASH) Wilson disease Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Primary biliary cholangitis Rheumatologic disorders (rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus) given extrahepatic features and autoantibodies Chronic hepatitis is defined as hepatic inflammation and necrosis continuing for at least 6 months; milder forms are nonprogressive or slowly progressive, whereas more severe forms cause scarring and architectural reorganization that, when advanced, lead ultimately to cirrhosis (p.2673). Classification rests on three axes: (1) cause, (2) histologic activity or grade (necroinflammatory activity), and (3) degree of progression based on fibrosis or stage; neither clinical features alone nor histology alone are sufficient to characterize disease (p.2673). Grade reflects necroinflammatory activity (periportal/piecemeal necrosis or interface hepatitis, bridging necrosis, focal lobular necrosis, portal inflammation) and is scored by the histologic activity index (HAI, used in the U.S.) or METAVIR (used in Europe); chronic hepatitis is graded mild, moderate, or severe (p.2673-2674). Stage reflects fibrosis on a numerical scale (0-6 HAI or 0-4 METAVIR); when fibrous septa surround parenchymal nodules and alter normal lobular architecture, the lesion is defined as cirrhosis (p.2674). Hyperglobulinemia and circulating autoantibodies are distinctly ABSENT in chronic hepatitis B, in contrast to autoimmune hepatitis; this helps distinguish viral from autoimmune disease (p.2674). Autoimmune hepatitis has a strong female predominance (~75% of cases) with a bimodal age distribution (one peak age <30, a second often >60); fatigue is the most common symptom (~85%) and ~25% are diagnosed when asymptomatic on abnormal liver tests (p.2694-2695). Type I AIH (classic, North America/northern Europe, young women) is associated with ANA in a homogeneous pattern and anti-smooth-muscle antibody (ASMA); type II AIH (often children, Mediterranean) is associated with anti-LKM1 (directed against cytochrome P450 2D6) rather than ANA (p.2695). Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (>2.5 g/dL) is common in AIH; smooth-muscle antibodies are detected in 63% of cases and, combined with a positive ANA, have high specificity (p.2695). Anti-LKM1 (against cytochrome P450 2D6) seen in type II AIH is the same antibody found in some patients with chronic hepatitis C; rarely AIH patients with hyperglobulinemia give false-positive anti-HCV immunoassays (p.2685-2695). Cirrhosis from any cause of chronic hepatitis carries a risk of hepatocellular carcinoma; in cirrhotic hepatitis C the annual HCC rate is 1-4%, occurring primarily after 30 or more years of infection, warranting HCC surveillance (p.2685). Liver biopsy is imperative to diagnose AIH; classic features include interface hepatitis extending beyond portal tracts, plasma cells in the infiltrate, central vein perivenulitis, hepatocellular rosette formation, and frequent septal/bridging fibrosis and cirrhosis (p.2695). Complications of cirrhosis: ascites, edema, bleeding gastroesophageal varices, hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy, hypersplenism Intermittent deepening of jaundice with worsening malaise/anorexia/fatigue, often coinciding with virologic reactivation, which may cause hepatic decompensation when superimposed on cirrhosis Severe AIH: aminotransferases >10x normal, marked hyperglobulinemia, multilobular collapse or bridging necrosis on histology (6-month untreated mortality up to ~40%) Failure of serum bilirubin to improve after 2 weeks of therapy in AIH (poor prognostic sign) Multilobular collapse at initial presentation in AIH (poor prognostic sign) Development of hepatocellular carcinoma in established cirrhosis Histopathologic-only classification (chronic persistent/lobular vs chronic active hepatitis) has been replaced because its presumed prognostic implications were not corroborated; classification now combines cause, grade, and stage (p.2673). Laboratory features of chronic hepatitis B do not reliably distinguish histologically mild from severe disease (p.2674). Low-titer ANA or ASMA occurs in other liver diseases including MASLD (~20% ANA-positive, ~14% ASMA-positive in one series) and viral hepatitis, so positive autoantibodies are not specific for AIH (p.2695). Rarely AIH patients with hyperglobulinemia have false-positive anti-HCV; conversely some confirmed chronic hepatitis C patients have circulating anti-LKM1, blurring the distinction between viral and autoimmune disease (p.2685-2695). ICI hepatitis resembles AIH but lacks female preponderance and is less likely to have ANA (low-titer if present) or plasma cell infiltrates (p.2695). Overlapping types of hepatitis (e.g., viral plus steatotic, alcohol plus nonalcohol steatotic) are encountered not infrequently given the high prevalence of steatotic liver disease (p.2673). Chronic hepatitis comprises liver disorders of varying cause in which hepatic inflammation and necrosis persist for at least 6 months. Broad categories include chronic viral hepatitis (B, B plus D, C), drug- or toxin-induced chronic hepatitis, alcohol-associated liver disease, metabolic dysfunction-related (steatotic) liver disease, and autoimmune chronic hepatitis; idiopathic/cryptogenic cases are also believed largely autoimmune. In chronic hepatitis B, all forms can be progressive but progression occurs primarily in patients with active HBV replication, and HCC risk is highest with continued high-level replication. In autoimmune hepatitis, progressive injury results from a cell-mediated immunologic attack on hepatocytes in the setting of lost/failed tolerance for self-liver antigens; predisposition is inherited (HLA-B8, DR3, DR4, DRB1*0301/*0401) while liver specificity is triggered by environmental factors (chemicals, drugs such as minocycline, viruses, and reported triggers including COVID-19 and COVID-19 vaccination); molecular mimicry activates infiltrating CD4+ T cells and impaired regulatory CD4+CD25+ T-cell control contributes (p.2673, 2693-2694). Outcome depends on grade and stage. In untreated chronic hepatitis B, 5-year survival was 97% for mild, 86% for moderate-to-severe, and 55% for those with cirrhosis (15-year survival 77%, 66%, 40% respectively); all forms can progress, primarily with active HBV replication. In chronic hepatitis C, liver histology is the best prognostic indicator; mild disease has an excellent prognosis, while moderate-to-severe necroinflammation or bridging fibrosis makes cirrhosis highly likely over 10-20 years. In compensated HCV cirrhosis, 10-year survival is ~80%, with mortality 2-6%/year, decompensation 4-5%/year, and HCC 1-4%/year. In autoimmune hepatitis, 10-year survival is 80-98% for treated versus 67% for untreated patients; severe symptomatic disease carries up to ~40% 6-month mortality without therapy; in a Dutch cohort, mortality exceeded the general population only in patients with cirrhosis (p.2674, 2685-2686, 2694-2695). Graded by necroinflammatory activity as mild, moderate, or severe using the histologic activity index (HAI, 0-18) or METAVIR (A0-A3). Staged by fibrosis: HAI 0-6 or METAVIR F0-F4, with cirrhosis defined when fibrous septa surround parenchymal nodules and alter lobular architecture (Table 352-2, p.2674).

pseudo-obstruction is a severe motility disorder in which the bowel behaves as though obstructed despite the absence of any mechanical blockage. It arises from dysfunction of the neuromuscular apparatus that generates coordinated propulsion, and is classified as neuropathic when the enteric nervous system is affected, myopathic when the intestinal smooth muscle is abnormal, or mesenchymopathic when the interstitial cells of Cajal are deficient. It may be idiopathic or secondary to systemic diseases including connective-tissue disorders, endocrine and metabolic disease, amyloidosis, paraneoplastic processes and mitochondrial cytopathies. Ineffective peristalsis causes luminal stasis, bowel dilatation, bacterial overgrowth and malabsorption. The disorder is typically chronic and often progressive, with significant morbidity from malnutrition, recurrent hospital admissions and complications of nutritional support; prognosis depends on the extent of gut involvement and any underlying systemic disease.

vessels are calcified and incompressible Attributing all leg pain to arterial disease and missing neurogenic or musculoskeletal causes Focusing on the limb while neglecting the high systemic cardiovascular risk Delaying referral in limb-threatening ischaemia, allowing avoidable tissue loss Chronic limb ischaemia results from progressive atherosclerotic narrowing of the aortoiliac, femoropopliteal, or tibial arteries, reducing perfusion to the lower limb. In claudication, resting flow is adequate but cannot meet the increased metabolic demand of exercising muscle, producing reversible ischaemic pain. As stenoses progress and collateral capacity is exceeded, resting perfusion falls below tissue requirements, causing rest pain, ulceration, and tissue loss. Diabetes and renal disease accelerate distal and calcified disease, and the combination of impaired inflow and microvascular dysfunction underlies poor wound healing. Most patients with claudication remain stable and only a minority progress to limb-threatening ischaemia, but overall mortality is high because of concurrent coronary and cerebrovascular disease. Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia carries a substantial risk of amputation and death without timely revascularisation and wound care.

Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) — CLL, small lymphocytic lymphoma, SLL Mantle cell lymphoma (CD5+, but CD23-negative, cyclin D1+, moderate/bright CD20 and surface Ig) — distinguished by immunophenotype (p.852) Marginal zone lymphoma (CD5 -/+, CD23 -/+, bright surface Ig) (p.852) Follicular lymphoma (CD5-negative, CD10-positive, CD23-positive) (p.852) Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (clonal B cells below the CLL threshold without organ involvement or cytopenias) (p.852) Small lymphocytic lymphoma (tissue-based counterpart with identical molecular features) (p.852) B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia arising from CLL (clinically and therapeutically distinct, though classified under Richter's transformation) (p.853-854) Reactive lymphocytosis from viral infection — viral infections produce larger reactive lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm, in contrast to the increased small lymphocytes and smudge cells of CLL (p.443) Flow cytometry of peripheral blood for the characteristic immunophenotype (CD19, CD20, CD22, CD23, CD200, CD5, dim surface Ig) — diagnostic test of choice (p.852) FISH for recurrent abnormalities del(13)(q14.3), trisomy 12, del(11)(q22.3), del(17)(p13.1); repeated before each line of therapy to detect acquired del(17p) (p.851) Stimulated metaphase karyotype, including assessment for complex karyotype (≥3 abnormalities) (p.851) Sequencing for TP53 and IGHV mutational status for prognostication (p.854) β2-microglobulin and LDH (prognostic; component of CLL International Prognostic Index) (p.853-854) Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test for warm IgG antibody when autoimmune hemolytic anemia is suspected (Coombs-negative cases can occur) (p.853) Reticulocyte count, bilirubin, LDH, haptoglobin to evaluate suspected hemolysis (p.853) 18FDG-PET/CT to localize a biopsy site when Richter's transformation is suspected (SUV <5 consistent with CLL; SUV >5 suspicious; ≥10 very concerning); excisional biopsy preferred over fine-needle aspiration (p.853-854) CLL International Prognostic Index integrating TP53 status, IGHV status, β2-microglobulin, clinical stage, and age (p.854) Other CD5+ or low-grade B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders (mantle cell, marginal zone, follicular lymphoma) distinguishable by flow cytometry immunophenotype, morphology, or cytogenetics (p.852) CLL is a monoclonal proliferation of mature B lymphocytes defined by an absolute clonal B-cell count of ≥5 × 10⁹/L in the blood; it is a disease of older adults (median age at diagnosis 71) (p.849). Most commonly diagnosed incidentally on routine blood work showing an elevated lymphocyte count in an asymptomatic individual; the natural history is heterogeneous, with some patients never requiring therapy (p.849, p.853). On the peripheral blood smear, the small lymphocytes are increased and many rupture during smear preparation, leaving nuclear material without surrounding cytoplasm — smudge cells, which are rare in the absence of chronic lymphoid leukemia (p.443). Diagnosis is confirmed by flow cytometry on peripheral blood; the typical immunophenotype is CD19+, CD20+, CD22+, CD23+, CD200+, the T-cell marker CD5+, and dim surface immunoglobulin (kappa or lambda). A clonal B-cell count ≥5 × 10⁹/L needs no further workup to confirm CLL (p.852). Small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) is the tissue-based counterpart of CLL (lymphadenopathy/splenomegaly with a small clonal blood population); genetic and molecular features are identical and SLL is managed identically to CLL (p.852). Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (MBL) is a precursor: clonal B cells below the CLL threshold without nodal/organ involvement or cytopenias; high-count MBL progresses to overt CLL at ~1–2% per year, whereas low-count MBL has a negligible progression rate (p.849, p.852). IGHV mutational status is a key prognostic factor: ~60% have IGHV ≥2% mutated from germline (more indolent course), while ~40% are IGHV-unmutated (more rapid progression, shorter survival before BCR-targeted therapy) (p.850). B-cell receptor (BCR) signaling is central to CLL pathogenesis, characterized by low-level IgM expression and tonic activation of antiapoptotic pathways promoting tumor survival (p.850). FISH (with or without karyotype) should be checked before every line of therapy because cytogenetics can evolve even without treatment, mainly to detect acquisition of del(17)(p13.1) (p.851). Bone marrow biopsy is not undertaken until therapy is initiated, except in cases of unexplained cytopenias; CT imaging is usually unnecessary at diagnosis (p.854). A watchful-waiting strategy is used for most patients, with therapy reserved for symptomatic disease, as multiple trials show no survival advantage to earlier therapy (p.854). Hypogammaglobulinemia affects all immunoglobulin subclasses and occurs in ~85% of patients at some point; low IgG and IgA correlate with infection risk, but isolated IgM reduction does not seem to confer excess infection risk (p.852). Richter's transformation — transformation to an aggressive lymphoma (most commonly DLBCL; Hodgkin lymphoma is a recognized variant). Suspect with rapid progression of adenopathy (often localized), constitutional symptoms (fatigue, night sweats, fever, weight loss), and usually high LDH (p.853-854) del(17)(p13.1)/TP53 loss or mutation — poorest prognosis, rapid progression, poor response to DNA-damaging therapy (p.850-851) Complex karyotype (≥3 abnormalities) — adverse impact on time to treatment and overall survival, worsening with increasing complexity (p.851) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia — death from uncontrolled AIHA can occur without appropriate supportive care; immediate therapy is almost always necessary (p.853) Symptoms indicating need for therapy: progressive marrow failure, massive/progressive/symptomatic splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy, lymphocyte doubling time <6 months, autoimmune cytopenia unresponsive to standard therapy, or constitutional symptoms (p.854) When anemia or thrombocytopenia appear, distinguish autoimmune cytopenia from marrow replacement — the therapeutic approaches differ, and autoimmune cytopenias often respond without treating the underlying CLL (p.853) AIHA can be Coombs-negative, so a negative direct antiglobulin test does not exclude it (p.853) ITP can be hard to distinguish from disease progression because no lab test directly identifies the platelet-destruction mechanism; isolated thrombocytopenia and rapid platelet decline without alternative cause point to ITP (p.853) del(13)(q14.3) seen on banded karyotype (rather than only on FISH) indicates a larger deletion involving the retinoblastoma gene, which negates the favorable prognosis usually associated with this marker (p.850) Live vaccines should be avoided in CLL because of the small risk of viral reactivation in an immunocompromised host (p.853) Fine-needle aspiration should be discouraged for diagnosing suspected Richter's transformation; excisional biopsy is preferred (p.854) Cytogenetics can change without therapy, so prior FISH results may be outdated — recheck before each line of treatment (p.851) CLL is a monoclonal expansion of mature B lymphocytes; the definitive cell of origin is not established (mature/memory B cell, stepwise transformation, or hematopoietic stem cell are all proposed). Distinct BCR signaling — low-level IgM, tonic antiapoptotic pathway activation — drives tumor survival, with upregulation of BCR-pathway genes in lymph nodes and marrow versus blood. The CLL genome is relatively simple (~20 nonsynonymous and ~5 structural changes) with no unifying driver; recurrent mutations include SF3B1, NOTCH1, MYD88, ATM, and TP53 (mostly enriched in IGHV-unmutated disease, except MYD88 which favors IGHV-mutated/indolent disease). Key cytogenetic lesions: del(13)(q14.3) (sole, indolent; causes loss of the miR15/16 cluster that normally suppresses BCL2 and other antiapoptotic genes), trisomy 12 (intermediate), del(11)(q22.3)/ATM (bulky disease, aggressive), and del(17)(p13.1)/TP53 (poorest prognosis). Immune dysregulation pervades the disease: innate defects (reduced complement, neutrophil and NK cell defects), adaptive defects (CD4+ T-cell exhaustion, Th1-to-Th2 shift, expanded T regulatory cells), nurse-like tumor-associated macrophages, and humoral hypogammaglobulinemia (p.849-852). Heterogeneous: many patients are asymptomatic and never require therapy while others need multiple lines and die of disease. Overall survival has improved markedly (5-year OS 70% in 1980, 92% in 2015, likely higher today), and only a small minority now die of CLL itself. Infections cause ~30–50% of CLL-related deaths. Favorable markers: IGHV-mutated disease, sole del(13)(q14.3), MYD88 mutation. Adverse markers: IGHV-unmutated disease, del(17p)/TP53, del(11q)/ATM, NOTCH1, complex karyotype, and high β2-microglobulin/LDH. The CLL International Prognostic Index stratifies 5-year survival from ~93% (low risk) to ~23% (very high risk) in training-set data, though it has not been validated in the era of novel targeted therapies. Richter's transformation carries a poor prognosis, with median survival of 6–16 months for clonally related DLBCL versus ~5 years for clonally unrelated lymphomas (p.849, p.851, p.853-854). Two staging systems, both based on physical exam and labs (no imaging or marrow required). Rai system (more common in the US): low risk (stage 0) = lymphocytosis only; intermediate risk (stage I/II) = lymphocytosis with lymphadenopathy, with or without splenomegaly/hepatomegaly; high risk (stage III/IV) = lymphocytosis with anemia or thrombocytopenia from marrow involvement. Binet system (more common in Europe): A = <3 areas of lymphadenopathy; B = ≥3 areas of lymphadenopathy; C = hemoglobin ≤10 g/dL and/or platelets <100,000/μL. The CLL International Prognostic Index refines outcome prediction using TP53 status, IGHV status, β2-microglobulin, clinical stage, and age (p.854).

Chronic mesenteric ischaemia — Intestinal angina, Chronic mesenteric arterial insufficiency Peptic ulcer disease or gastritis Chronic pancreatitis Biliary colic or cholecystitis Intra-abdominal malignancy such as gastric or pancreatic cancer causing weight loss Median arcuate ligament syndrome Functional or irritable bowel disorders Mesenteric vasculitis Mesenteric duplex ultrasound with fasting and postprandial velocities CT angiography of the mesenteric vessels MR angiography as an alternative Catheter angiography with a lateral aortogram, often with intervention Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and cross-sectional imaging to exclude malignancy or ulceration Nutritional assessment and baseline blood tests Screening for vasculitis where the presentation is atypical The classic triad is postprandial abdominal pain (intestinal angina), fear of eating (sitophobia) and weight loss. Almost always caused by atherosclerotic stenosis or occlusion of two or more of the three mesenteric vessels (coeliac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric arteries) because of rich collateralisation. Predominantly affects older women who smoke and have widespread atherosclerosis. Pain characteristically begins within about 15 to 30 minutes of eating and is disproportionate to examination findings. Weight loss stems from reduced intake because of food fear rather than malabsorption, and can closely mimic malignancy. Duplex ultrasound is a useful screening test; CT angiography confirms the diagnosis and plans revascularisation. Endovascular angioplasty and stenting is now first-line revascularisation for most patients, with open bypass or endarterectomy reserved for complex disease or endovascular failure. Untreated disease can progress to acute-on-chronic mesenteric ischaemia and bowel infarction. Sudden severe constant abdominal pain, or pain out of proportion, signalling acute-on-chronic ischaemia or infarction. Peritonism, lactic acidosis or a rising white cell count. Gastrointestinal bleeding or bloody diarrhoea. Rapid, profound weight loss and malnutrition. Haemodynamic instability. Attributing weight loss and pain to occult malignancy and pursuing an exhaustive negative work-up while missing the vascular cause. Assuming single-vessel stenosis explains symptoms when disease of at least two vessels or specific superior mesenteric artery involvement is usually required. Delaying revascularisation until acute infarction supervenes. Overlooking median arcuate ligament compression in younger patients. Providing inadequate surveillance after stenting and missing restenosis. Progressive atherosclerotic narrowing of the ostia of the coeliac axis and superior mesenteric artery reduces splanchnic blood flow. Because of the extensive collateral network, including the pancreaticoduodenal arcades and the marginal artery of Drummond with the arc of Riolan, symptoms usually develop only when at least two of the three main vessels are critically diseased. After eating, splanchnic oxygen demand rises but the stenotic vessels cannot augment flow, producing a supply-demand mismatch and ischaemic visceral pain, with blood effectively diverted from the intestinal to the gastric circulation. Chronic ischaemia impairs mucosal integrity, and acute thrombosis of a critical vessel precipitates transmural infarction. Non-atherosclerotic causes include median arcuate ligament compression, vasculitis and fibromuscular dysplasia. Successful revascularisation relieves symptoms, restores weight and prevents progression to infarction in the great majority, whereas untreated disease risks acute mesenteric infarction with very high mortality. Endovascular treatment carries lower perioperative morbidity but higher restenosis than open repair, mandating surveillance.

ischaemia and bowel infarction Rising lactate, acidosis, peritonism, or shock requiring emergency surgical evaluation Rapid, marked weight loss with intractable food aversion Progression of symptoms despite conservative measures indicating imminent vascular compromise Attributing chronic postprandial pain and weight loss to malignancy or functional disease and missing a vascular cause Failing to recognise that significant multi-vessel disease is usually needed to cause symptoms, leading to under-treatment of critical single-vessel lesions Delaying revascularisation until acute infarction supervenes Neglecting cardiovascular risk-factor management after treating the mesenteric lesions Chronic mesenteric ischaemia develops when atherosclerotic stenosis of the splanchnic arteries limits the increase in blood flow required to meet the metabolic demand of the gut after meals. The resulting mismatch produces postprandial ischaemic pain. Because of extensive collateral pathways among the three main mesenteric arteries, symptomatic disease typically requires high-grade stenosis or occlusion of at least two vessels, or a critical single-vessel lesion where collaterals are inadequate. Chronic hypoperfusion impairs absorption and causes food avoidance and weight loss. Acute thrombosis superimposed on a stenosed vessel can precipitate acute mesenteric ischaemia with bowel infarction. With timely revascularisation, symptoms usually resolve, weight is regained, and the risk of catastrophic bowel infarction falls. Untreated disease carries a substantial risk of progression to acute mesenteric ischaemia, which has high mortality. Overall outlook is also influenced by the patient's generalised atherosclerotic burden.

Chronic mountain sickness — Monge disease, chronic high-altitude polycythaemia Secondary polycythaemia from chronic lung or cardiac disease Polycythaemia vera Obstructive sleep apnoea with hypoxaemia High-altitude pulmonary hypertension Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease Full blood count documenting excessive erythrocytosis Oxygen saturation and arterial blood gas showing hypoxaemia Echocardiography for pulmonary hypertension and right heart function Assessment for coexisting sleep-disordered breathing or lung disease Exclusion of primary polycythaemia where appropriate A syndrome of excessive erythrocytosis and severe hypoxaemia in long-term residents of high altitude Symptoms include headache, dizziness, breathlessness, sleep disturbance, cyanosis and mental slowing Marked polycythaemia raises blood viscosity and predisposes to thrombosis and pulmonary hypertension Over time it can progress to pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure (cor pulmonale) It is distinguished from acute altitude illness by its chronic course in acclimatised long-term dwellers Descent to lower altitude is the most effective treatment, with phlebotomy and respiratory stimulants as adjuncts Signs of right heart failure or severe pulmonary hypertension Thrombotic complications Very high haematocrit with hyperviscosity symptoms Progressive cognitive or functional decline Attributing the polycythaemia to a primary haematological disorder Overlooking coexisting sleep apnoea worsening hypoxaemia Relying on phlebotomy without addressing altitude exposure Missing early pulmonary hypertension Chronic mountain sickness develops in some long-term high-altitude residents who lose adequate ventilatory and other adaptations, leading to accentuated hypoxaemia. The chronic hypoxia drives excessive erythropoietin-mediated red-cell production, producing severe polycythaemia that increases blood viscosity and impairs oxygen delivery. Sustained hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and vascular remodelling cause pulmonary hypertension, which ultimately strains the right heart. The combination of hypoxaemia, hyperviscosity and pulmonary hypertension underlies the symptoms and complications. Symptoms and erythrocytosis typically improve substantially with descent; if residence at altitude continues, progression to pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure worsens the outlook.

Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis — CMC, chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, CMCD, candidiasis of skin nails and mucosae STAT1 gain-of-function disease APECED (AIRE deficiency) IL-17 pathway defects (IL17RA, IL17F, ACT1) CARD9 deficiency with invasive fungal disease Acquired immunosuppression, diabetes or endocrinopathy predisposing to candidiasis DOCK8 or STAT3 hyper-IgE syndromes Enumeration of circulating T-helper-17 (IL-17-producing) cells STAT1 phosphorylation assay and STAT1 gene sequencing Screening for autoantibodies against interleukin-17 cytokines and for AIRE variants when APECED is suspected Serum immunoglobulins and endocrine autoantibody and hormone screen Targeted or panel gene sequencing covering IL17RA, IL17F, ACT1, CARD9 and RORgammaT Mycological confirmation and assessment for invasive or deep fungal disease where indicated Describes persistent or recurrent infection of the skin, nails and mucous membranes with Candida, typically without invasive dissemination in isolated forms It is a phenotype rather than a single disease and reflects a defect in the interleukin-17-dependent T-helper-17 pathway that governs mucosal antifungal defence Recognised monogenic causes include gain-of-function variants in STAT1, defects in the IL-17 axis (IL17RA, IL17F, IL17RC, ACT1), CARD9 deficiency and RORgammaT deficiency It is a cardinal feature of APECED (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy) due to AIRE deficiency, where it accompanies autoimmune endocrinopathy CARD9 deficiency is distinctive because it can allow deep-seated and central nervous system fungal invasion rather than purely superficial disease Associated features vary by genotype and may include autoimmunity, endocrinopathy, aneurysms and, with chronic mucosal inflammation, a raised risk of squamous cell carcinoma Diagnostic workup should look beyond confirming Candida to define the underlying immunological and genetic mechanism Management combines antifungal therapy with treatment directed at the underlying defect, such as a JAK inhibitor in STAT1 gain-of-function disease Neurological signs suggesting central nervous system fungal invasion, particularly in CARD9 deficiency New oral or oesophageal lesion raising concern for squamous cell carcinoma Features of autoimmune endocrine crisis such as adrenal insufficiency in APECED Evidence of invasive or disseminated fungal infection Vascular symptoms in genotypes associated with aneurysm Treating the candidiasis symptomatically without investigating the underlying inborn error Failing to screen for the autoimmune endocrinopathy of APECED Underestimating the risk of invasive and CNS fungal disease in CARD9 deficiency Overlooking the long-term squamous malignancy risk in chronically inflamed mucosa Assuming a single mechanism when the phenotype has several distinct genetic causes Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis arises from impaired T-helper-17 immunity, the arm of adaptive defence that produces interleukin-17 and interleukin-22 to recruit neutrophils and maintain antifungal barrier function at skin and mucosal surfaces. Different genetic lesions converge on this pathway: STAT1 gain-of-function suppresses T-helper-17 differentiation, defects in interleukin-17 or its receptor block downstream signalling, AIRE deficiency generates neutralising autoantibodies against interleukin-17 cytokines, and CARD9 deficiency impairs the innate sensing of fungi. The shared consequence is inadequate mucosal control of Candida, producing persistent superficial infection, while the specific genotype determines the accompanying autoimmune, endocrine, vascular or invasive features. Isolated chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis is often chronic but manageable with antifungal therapy, whereas outcome in syndromic forms depends on the associated autoimmune, endocrine, vascular or invasive complications and the response to genotype-directed treatment.

Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) — CML Leukemoid reaction (reactive leukocytosis) - distinguished from CML by a high/normal leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score (CML has a LOW LAP) and absence of BCR::ABL1 (Harrison 22e p.837) Atypical CML (BCR::ABL1-negative) - lacks the Ph chromosome/BCR::ABL1, does not respond to TKI therapy, associated with SETBP1 (about 25%) and some CSF3R mutations, poor prognosis with median survival ~2-3 years (Harrison 22e p.835) Chronic neutrophilic leukemia - frequently CSF3R-mutated (about 80%); may respond to ruxolitinib (Harrison 22e p.835) Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (Harrison 22e p.835) Myelodysplastic syndrome/myeloproliferative neoplasms, including MDS/MPN-RS-T (SF3B1-mutated) (Harrison 22e p.835) Essential thrombocythemia and other Ph-negative MPNs presenting with thrombocytosis - when JAK2 V617F is absent, cytogenetics/FISH for BCR::ABL1 are required to exclude CML (Harrison 22e p.832-833) Bone marrow aspiration with routine G-banding cytogenetics - required to confirm the Ph chromosome, detect additional chromosomal abnormalities (which FISH will not detect), and quantify marrow blasts and basophils; a diagnosis of CML must always rely on marrow analysis with cytogenetics (Harrison 22e p.837) FISH analysis for BCR::ABL1 on peripheral blood - quantifies percentage of Ph-positive cells; preferred when a Ph cytogenetic study is negative or for monitoring (Harrison 22e p.837) Quantitative RT-PCR for BCR::ABL1 transcripts on the International Scale - baseline transcript typing at diagnosis (to avoid spurious 'undetectable' results on follow-up with atypical transcripts) and serial molecular monitoring of response (Harrison 22e p.837-838) ABL1 kinase domain mutation analysis - assessed when resistance/loss of response is suspected (e.g., to detect T315I) (Harrison 22e p.836-837) Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score - characteristically LOW in CML, helping distinguish it from a leukemoid reaction (Harrison 22e p.837) Supportive biochemistry - high vitamin B12, uric acid, lactate dehydrogenase, and lysozyme are commonly seen (Harrison 22e p.837) Leukemoid reaction (reactive leukocytosis from infection, inflammation, or other stress) - mimics the leukocytosis with left shift of CML but lacks BCR::ABL1 and shows a high/normal (not low) leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score (Harrison 22e p.837) Other myeloproliferative neoplasms and MDS/MPN overlap syndromes that can produce leukocytosis, basophilia, or splenomegaly without the Philadelphia chromosome (Harrison 22e p.835) CML is a clonal hematopoietic myeloproliferative stem cell neoplasm driven by the BCR::ABL1 chimeric gene, which encodes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase (Harrison 22e p.834). BCR::ABL1 results from a balanced reciprocal translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 9 and 22, t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2), known as the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph); the t(9;22) is present in >90% of classical CML cases (Harrison 22e p.834-835). The most common transcript in CML encodes the p210BCR::ABL1 oncoprotein; p190BCR::ABL1 is present in two-thirds of Ph-positive ALL but rare in CML, and p230BCR::ABL1 is rare and associated with a more indolent course (Harrison 22e p.835). Untreated, CML is typically biphasic or triphasic: an early indolent chronic phase, often followed by an accelerated phase, and a terminal blastic phase (Harrison 22e p.834). Most patients (about 90%) present in chronic phase; in developed countries 50-60% are diagnosed on routine blood tests with minimal symptoms such as fatigue (Harrison 22e p.836). Common symptoms, when present, are manifestations of anemia and splenomegaly: fatigue, malaise, weight loss, early satiety, and left upper quadrant pain or mass (Harrison 22e p.836). Splenomegaly is the most common physical finding (20-70% depending on screening frequency); hepatomegaly (5-10%) and lymphadenopathy (5%) are less common (Harrison 22e p.836-837). Untreated CML shows leukocytosis (10-500 x 10^9/L) with left-shifted myeloid hematopoiesis: neutrophils plus bands, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, promyelocytes, and blasts (usually <=5%); basophils and/or eosinophils are frequently increased (Harrison 22e p.837). Thrombocytosis is common; thrombocytopenia is rare and, when present, suggests worse prognosis, disease acceleration, or an unrelated etiology. Anemia is present in one-third of patients (Harrison 22e p.837). Diagnosis depends on documenting t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2), identified by G-banding in 90% of cases; FISH and PCR aid diagnosis and estimate disease burden, and can be done on peripheral blood (Harrison 22e p.837). TKIs have revolutionized CML: the estimated 10-year survival with imatinib now exceeds 85% and approaches that of a normal age-matched population; allogeneic HSCT (curative but riskier) is offered as later-line therapy after TKI failure (Harrison 22e p.834). Molecular monitoring on the International Scale (IS) guides therapy: complete cytogenetic response (0% Ph) is roughly equivalent to BCR::ABL1 <=1% (MR2); major molecular response (MMR/MR3) is BCR::ABL1 <=0.1%; deep molecular response MR4 is <=0.01% and MR4.5 is <=0.0032% (Harrison 22e p.837-838). The T315I 'gatekeeper' kinase-domain mutation prevents binding of, and causes resistance to, imatinib and the second-generation TKIs (dasatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib); third-generation agents (e.g., ponatinib, asciminib) retain activity against it (Harrison 22e p.836). Unexplained, sustained leukocytosis (with or without splenomegaly) should prompt marrow examination and cytogenetic analysis (Harrison 22e p.837) Increasing/therapy-resistant leukocytosis, worsening anemia, fever and constitutional symptoms, and rising blasts and basophils signal disease progression (Harrison 22e p.838) New thrombocytopenia (<100 x 10^9/L unrelated to therapy) suggests worse prognosis or disease acceleration (Harrison 22e p.837-838) Extramedullary disease (skin/subcutaneous lesions, soft tissue, or lytic bone lesions) with biopsy showing blast predominance indicates transformation (Harrison 22e p.837-838) Hyperleukocytosis/hyperviscosity or marked thrombocytosis with thrombotic events (priapism, MI, venous thrombosis, visual disturbance, CVA) or bleeding diathesis (Harrison 22e p.836) PITFALL: Mistaking a reactive leukemoid reaction for CML - the leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score is LOW in CML but high/normal in a leukemoid reaction, and CML requires demonstration of BCR::ABL1 (Harrison 22e p.837). Atypical transcripts (e13a3, e14a3, e19a2, etc.) not detected at diagnosis can produce falsely 'negative/undetectable' BCR::ABL1 on follow-up PCR, giving a false impression of complete molecular response; transcript type must be documented at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.835, 837). FISH does NOT detect additional chromosomal abnormalities, so a marrow cytogenetic analysis is still required at diagnosis; relying on FISH/PCR alone can miss clonal evolution (Harrison 22e p.837). Both FISH and PCR can be falsely positive at low levels or falsely negative for technical reasons, so diagnosis must always rely on marrow analysis with routine cytogenetics (Harrison 22e p.837). In about 10% of patients marrow blasts and basophils are significantly higher than in peripheral blood, conferring poorer prognosis or representing transformation that peripheral counts alone would miss (Harrison 22e p.837). Failure to achieve MMR or DMR should NOT automatically be considered 'failure' of a given TKI or an indication to switch TKI or proceed to allogeneic HSCT (Harrison 22e p.838). CML is a clonal myeloproliferative stem cell neoplasm caused by the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene arising from the reciprocal balanced translocation t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2) (the Philadelphia chromosome). DNA from the ABL1 proto-oncogene on chromosome 9 is juxtaposed to the breakpoint cluster region (BCR) gene on chromosome 22, generating a hybrid oncogene whose product (most commonly the p210BCR::ABL1 oncoprotein from e13a2 or e14a2 transcripts) has constitutive tyrosine kinase activity. This drives increased proliferation and reduced apoptosis, giving CML cells a growth advantage and progressively suppressing normal hematopoiesis. Constitutive BCR::ABL1 activation triggers autophosphorylation and downstream signaling via RAS, MAP kinases, STAT, PI3K, MYC and others, mediated by adapter proteins (GRB-2, CRK, CRK-L, SHC). Most TKIs bind the ATP-binding domain to inhibit kinase activity; asciminib (a STAMP inhibitor) instead binds the ABL1 myristoyl pocket. BCR::ABL1 induces genetic instability favoring acquisition of additional defects (e.g., double Ph, trisomy 8, isochromosome 17/17p loss of TP53, 3q26 abnormalities, mutations in TP53, RB1, RUNX1, p16) that drive transformation from chronic to accelerated to blastic phase. Notably, the BCR::ABL1 rearrangement is detectable in the blood of up to 25% of normal adults and 5% of infants but is not sufficient to cause overt CML in the overwhelming majority. (Harrison 22e p.834-836) TKIs have transformed CML prognosis. Before the TKI era median survival was 3-7 years with annual mortality of 10% in the first 2 years and 15-20% thereafter. With imatinib, annual mortality has fallen to about 1-2%, the 10-year survival rate is about 85% (CML-specific survival ~90%), and the 10-year incidence of blastic transformation is only 5-6%; more than half of deaths are now from non-CML causes. Treatment-related response milestones are the dominant modern prognostic factors: achievement of complete cytogenetic response (MR2) is the major endpoint associated with improved survival, while durable deep molecular response (MR4/MR4.5) may permit treatment-free remission (TFR rate about 50% after 2+ years of durable DMR and 80%+ after 5+ years). Historical pretreatment models (Sokal, Hasford, EUTOS) and adverse features (age, splenomegaly, anemia, high blasts/basophils, marrow fibrosis, additional chromosomal abnormalities) have lost much of their prognostic weight in the TKI era. Accelerated phase (historical median survival <2 years) and blastic phase carry the worst outcomes; de novo accelerated phase on TKI now has an estimated 8-year survival of 60-70%, and lymphoid blastic phase responds to ALL-type chemotherapy plus TKIs (complete response ~70%, median survival ~3 years). (Harrison 22e p.834, 838-839) CML is staged by clinical phase. Chronic phase: indolent, marrow blasts typically <=5%, where ~90% of patients present. Accelerated phase (historically median survival <2 years): >=15% peripheral blasts, >=30% peripheral blasts plus promyelocytes, >=20% peripheral basophils, cytogenetic clonal evolution (additional chromosomal abnormalities beyond Ph), or thrombocytopenia <100 x 10^9/L unrelated to therapy. Blastic phase: >=30% peripheral or marrow blasts, or sheets of blasts in extramedullary disease (commonly myeloid in ~60%, lymphoid in ~25%). The newest WHO classification suggests eliminating accelerated phase and reclassifying such patients as high-risk CML, but the text argues the accelerated-phase definition should be maintained because their survival is significantly worse than high-risk CML. Risk models (Sokal, Hasford, EUTOS) were used historically. (Harrison 22e p.838)

Chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia — CMML Reactive monocytosis (infection, inflammation, malignancy) Chronic myeloid leukaemia (BCR-ABL1 positive) Myelodysplastic syndrome Atypical chronic myeloid leukaemia Juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia (in children) Full blood count and film confirming sustained monocytosis Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics BCR-ABL1 testing to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia Molecular panel (for example TET2, SRSF2, ASXL1) Assessment for reactive causes of monocytosis A clonal disorder with overlapping myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative features, defined by persistent peripheral blood monocytosis It occurs mainly in older adults and presents with cytopenias, monocytosis, splenomegaly or constitutional symptoms Diagnosis requires sustained monocytosis with monocytes forming a significant fraction of the white cells, and exclusion of other causes The BCR-ABL1 fusion must be absent, distinguishing it from chronic myeloid leukaemia Common mutations include TET2, SRSF2 and ASXL1, and prognostic scores guide management It carries a risk of progression to acute myeloid leukaemia Rising blast count indicating progression to acute leukaemia Worsening cytopenias with bleeding or infection Rapidly enlarging spleen or proliferative features Severe constitutional symptoms Attributing persistent monocytosis to a reactive cause without excluding CMML Not testing for BCR-ABL1 to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia Underusing prognostic scoring to guide therapy Missing progression to acute leukaemia Chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia is a clonal haematopoietic stem cell neoplasm with both dysplastic (ineffective haematopoiesis causing cytopenias) and proliferative (monocytosis, sometimes leucocytosis and organomegaly) features. Recurrent mutations in epigenetic regulators and splicing genes such as TET2, SRSF2 and ASXL1 drive the clonal expansion and the characteristic monocyte proliferation. Ineffective and dysplastic maturation produces the peripheral cytopenias, and accumulation of blasts over time can culminate in transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia. The course is heterogeneous; prognosis depends on blast percentage, cytogenetics, mutations and blood counts, ranging from indolent disease to rapid progression to acute myeloid leukaemia.

Chronic neutrophilic leukaemia — CNL Reactive neutrophilia (leukaemoid reaction, infection, inflammation) Neutrophilia driven by an underlying plasma cell neoplasm Chronic myeloid leukaemia (BCR-ABL1 positive) Atypical chronic myeloid leukaemia Other myeloproliferative neoplasms Full blood count and film showing mature neutrophilia CSF3R mutation analysis BCR-ABL1 testing to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia Bone marrow examination with cytogenetics Exclusion of a plasma cell neoplasm and reactive causes A rare myeloproliferative neoplasm with sustained mature neutrophilia without significant dysplasia Splenomegaly and, sometimes, hepatomegaly are common The majority of cases carry an activating CSF3R mutation, which is a key diagnostic and therapeutic marker It requires exclusion of reactive neutrophilia and of other myeloid neoplasms, and BCR-ABL1 must be absent A plasma cell neoplasm can drive a reactive neutrophilia that mimics it, so this must be excluded CSF3R mutation status can guide targeted therapy with JAK or other kinase inhibitors Rising blasts indicating accelerated or blast phase Worsening cytopenias or organomegaly Very high white cell count with hyperviscosity Features suggesting an underlying plasma cell disorder Mistaking a leukaemoid reaction or plasma-cell-driven neutrophilia for CNL Not testing CSF3R, which informs diagnosis and therapy Omitting BCR-ABL1 testing Missing progression to a blast phase Chronic neutrophilic leukaemia is a clonal stem cell disorder characterised by proliferation of the neutrophil lineage producing sustained mature neutrophilia. Activating mutations of the colony-stimulating factor 3 receptor gene (CSF3R), most commonly a membrane-proximal mutation, drive downstream JAK-STAT and SRC-family signalling to promote neutrophil production. Unlike a leukaemoid reaction, the neutrophilia is autonomous and clonal, and the marrow shows granulocytic hyperplasia; disease can progress with accelerated or blast phases over time. The course is variable and often progressive; prognosis depends on disease phase and response to therapy, with a risk of transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia.

composed of mature segmented neutrophils and band forms Splenomegaly and sometimes hepatomegaly are common, and the neutrophils lack significant dysplasia or a left shift to immature precursors leukaemoid reaction and of other myeloproliferative neoplasms, particularly BCR-ABL1 positive chronic myeloid leukaemia Unlike a reactive process, the leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score tends to be normal or raised and there is no infective or inflammatory driver Coexisting plasma cell disorders can drive a reactive neutrophilia that mimics the condition, so a monoclonal protein should be sought CSF3R mutation status guides prognosis and targeted approaches such as JAK pathway inhibition Rising blast count indicating transformation to acute leukaemia Progressive anaemia or thrombocytopenia signalling marrow failure Massive or painful splenomegaly Hyperleukocytosis with hyperviscosity symptoms Accepting a reactive leukaemoid reaction as the diagnosis without molecular confirmation Failing to exclude BCR-ABL1 positive chronic myeloid leukaemia Missing an occult plasma cell neoplasm driving the neutrophilia Overlooking CSF3R testing that establishes the diagnosis and informs therapy Chronic neutrophilic leukaemia is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm in which activating mutations of the granulocyte colony-stimulating factor receptor gene (CSF3R) drive unchecked signalling through the JAK/STAT and SRC-family kinase pathways. This produces sustained expansion of the mature neutrophil compartment without the dysplasia or maturation arrest seen in other myeloid disorders. The proliferating granulocytes accumulate in blood, marrow and spleen. Over time additional mutations may accrue and the disease can transform to acute leukaemia. A morphologically similar picture can be produced reactively by cytokines from an occult plasma cell neoplasm, which must be distinguished. The clinical course is variable; some patients remain stable for years while others progress to marrow failure or transform to acute myeloid leukaemia, and outcome is influenced by mutation burden and additional cytogenetic changes.

Chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis (CNO) — CNO, chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, CRMO, chronic non-bacterial osteitis Bacterial (including subacute) osteomyelitis Malignancy such as leukaemia, Ewing sarcoma, osteosarcoma or metastatic neuroblastoma Langerhans cell histiocytosis Benign bone tumours (e.g. osteoid osteoma) Bone infarction Metabolic or fibrous bone lesions Whole-body MRI to identify multifocal and clinically silent lesions Inflammatory markers, which may be normal or only mildly raised Blood cultures and, where needed, bone biopsy with culture to exclude infection and malignancy Plain radiographs showing mixed lytic and sclerotic change Bone biopsy histology when malignancy cannot otherwise be excluded Screening for associated psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease Spinal imaging to detect vertebral involvement An autoinflammatory bone disease producing sterile, often multifocal osteomyelitis, with the recurrent multifocal form termed CRMO Presents with insidious bone pain, local swelling and sometimes low-grade fever, frequently affecting the metaphyses of long bones, clavicle, spine and pelvis Clavicular involvement is a characteristic clue, and the sternoclavicular region may be affected It is a diagnosis of exclusion; cultures are negative and there is no response to antibiotics, which helps distinguish it from bacterial osteomyelitis Whole-body MRI is valuable for detecting clinically silent lesions and defining the full extent of disease Associations include psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and palmoplantar pustulosis (within the SAPHO spectrum in older patients) Treatment uses NSAIDs first line, with bisphosphonates (particularly for vertebral disease), TNF inhibition or other agents for refractory or spinal involvement Vertebral involvement with risk of collapse and spinal deformity Neurological signs from spinal disease Features suggesting malignancy such as an aggressive lesion, night pain or systemic upset High fever and systemic toxicity suggesting genuine infection Treating repeatedly for presumed bacterial osteomyelitis despite negative cultures and no antibiotic response Failing to perform whole-body MRI and thereby underestimating disease extent Missing vertebral disease and the risk of collapse Not excluding malignancy before settling on the diagnosis Overlooking associated skin and bowel disease Chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis is an autoinflammatory disorder in which dysregulated innate immunity produces sterile inflammation of bone. An imbalance between proinflammatory cytokines and inadequate anti-inflammatory signalling, with activation of the inflammasome and osteoclast-driven bone remodelling, leads to osteitis, bone oedema, lytic and sclerotic change and, in the spine, vertebral collapse. The absence of an infective organism and the frequent overlap with other autoinflammatory and immune-mediated conditions such as psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease underline its immune-mediated basis. The course is variable, ranging from a single self-limiting episode to a chronic relapsing disease over years. Most children do well with treatment, but vertebral involvement can cause permanent deformity, and some have persistent or recurrent symptoms into adulthood.

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease — COPD, Emphysema, Chronic bronchitis, Chronic obstructive lung disease Asthma (substantial overlap in older patients; both feature airway hyperresponsiveness and may share genetic/environmental factors) Bronchiectasis Interstitial lung disease Congestive heart failure Chronic thromboembolic disease / pulmonary hypertension Lung cancer (especially when new clubbing appears) Tuberculosis-associated chronic airflow limitation (important in absence of tobacco history) Pneumonia (frequently found on imaging during presumed exacerbation) Acute bronchitis Tuberculosis (can produce chronic airflow limitation with emphysematous and fibrotic change and airway remodeling) HIV-associated emphysema/COPD (increased risk with lower CD4 counts; often underdiagnosed) Post-bronchodilator spirometry (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC) for diagnosis and severity grading (GOLD vs ATS/ERS Z-scores) Lung volumes (TLC, FRC, RV, RV/TLC) and diffusing capacity (DLCO) - DLCO reduced in emphysema Arterial blood gas and oximetry for resting/exertional hypoxemia, alveolar ventilation and acid-base status (key in exacerbation assessment) Complete blood count with differential (blood eosinophil count; hematocrit for chronic hypoxemia) Chest CT (definitive for emphysema pattern/distribution, airway disease, coexisting ILD/bronchiectasis; annual low-dose CT for lung cancer screening in eligible smokers) Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level with PI-type determination (isoelectric focusing, mass spectrometry/genotyping, or DNA sequencing) when low 6-minute walk distance for exercise capacity and BODE index C-reactive protein (incorporated into proposed objective criteria for staging exacerbation severity) Congestive heart failure Pulmonary embolism (incidence increased during exacerbations; should be considered) Pneumothorax (asymmetric chest findings can mimic an exacerbation) Large airway obstruction COPD is defined by persistent respiratory symptoms with airflow obstruction, and the umbrella term spans emphysema (alveolar destruction with air-space enlargement), chronic bronchitis (chronic cough and phlegm), and small airway disease (narrowing and loss of small bronchioles); these coexist in varying proportions between patients. Fixed airflow obstruction is the spirometric hallmark: a chronically reduced FEV1/FVC ratio that does not normalize after bronchodilator. The classic threshold is FEV1/FVC <0.7 (GOLD), with the ATS/ERS alternative using Z-scores of FEV1 below the lower limit of normal. The three cardinal symptoms are cough, sputum production, and exertional dyspnea; many patients have symptoms for months to years before presenting, and a careful history often reveals respiratory symptoms preceding an apparent acute onset. Activities involving arm work at or above shoulder level are particularly poorly tolerated, whereas activities that let the patient brace the arms and recruit accessory muscles (pushing a shopping cart, treadmill) are better tolerated. Early disease typically has a normal physical exam; advanced disease shows prolonged expiration, wheeze, barrel chest, poor diaphragmatic excursion, accessory muscle use, the tripod posture, and cyanosis of lips/nail beds. Digital clubbing is NOT a feature of COPD; its appearance should trigger a search for another cause, most commonly lung cancer in this population. The blood eosinophil count (on CBC with differential) is used to guide therapy aimed at reducing exacerbation risk; an elevated hematocrit suggests chronic hypoxemia. Chest CT is the definitive test for establishing presence, pattern, and distribution of emphysema and for medium/large airway disease; chest x-ray may be consistent with COPD (hyperinflation, flat diaphragm, bullae, hyperlucency) but cannot reliably make the diagnosis. Guidelines recommend testing for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in ALL patients with COPD or with asthma plus chronic airflow obstruction; serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level is the initial test, with PI-type determination for confirmation when levels are low. Approximately only 1% of COPD patients have severe alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, yet it is the proven monogenic risk factor and demonstrates the powerful role of genetics in susceptibility; PiZ individuals often develop early-onset COPD, accelerated by smoking. The strongest single predictor of future exacerbations is a prior exacerbation, and the single greatest risk factor for hospitalization with an exacerbation is a history of previous hospitalization. The BODE index (Body mass index, airflow Obstruction, Dyspnea, Exercise capacity by 6-minute walk) predicts mortality better than FEV1 alone. New digital clubbing - investigate for lung cancer, not attributable to COPD Respiratory acidosis with hypercarbia (PaCO2 >45 mmHg) signaling acute ventilatory failure New or worsening hypoxemia Mental status changes (confusion, sleepiness), inability to speak in full sentences, paradoxical abdominal wall motion Tachycardia, tachypnea, accessory muscle use, perioral/peripheral cyanosis Cachexia with significant weight loss (independent poor prognostic factor) Signs of cor pulmonale / right heart failure (lower extremity edema, persistent activity limitation) Chest x-ray cannot reliably diagnose COPD or establish chronicity; do not rely on it to confirm emphysema. Pulmonary function testing during an exacerbation has not been shown helpful in diagnosis or management (unlike in asthma exacerbations). Smokers with normal spirometry are not necessarily spared - many have reduced quality of life, reduced exercise capacity, emphysema/airway disease on CT, and may have exacerbations (pre-COPD). Attributing new clubbing to COPD itself - it is not a feature and warrants a cancer workup. Failing to test for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in COPD patients, missing a treatable genetic cause; only a small minority of the ~1 in 3000 with severe deficiency in the US have been identified. Overlooking pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, heart failure, or pneumothorax during a presumed exacerbation (about 25% of x-rays in moderate/severe distress are abnormal). Underestimating viral causes of exacerbations - PCR studies show viruses may cause >50% of exacerbations. Race-specific reference equations for pulmonary function may be inappropriate; race-neutral interpretation may be preferable. Chronic inhaled exposures (most commonly cigarette smoke, also biomass fuels, and increasingly vaping/inhaled cannabis) in genetically susceptible individuals trigger inflammatory and immune cell recruitment in large and small airways and terminal air spaces. Large-airway changes (mucus gland enlargement, goblet cell hyperplasia, squamous metaplasia) produce cough and sputum and define chronic bronchitis. Small airways (<=2 mm) are the major site of increased airflow resistance, narrowed by goblet cell metaplasia replacing surfactant-secreting club cells, smooth-muscle hypertrophy, fibrosis, mucus, edema, and cellular infiltration; small-airway narrowing and drop-out precede emphysematous destruction. Emphysema results from a four-step paradigm: inflammatory/immune recruitment; proteinase release damaging extracellular matrix; oxidant-induced structural cell death, cellular senescence and proteolytic loss of cell-matrix attachments; and disordered repair of elastin. The elastase:antielastase imbalance (epitomized by alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency permitting unopposed neutrophil elastase) plus matrix metalloproteinases (notably MMP12) degrade elastin and collagen, generating chemotactic fragments that fuel a positive-feedback inflammatory loop. Oxidative stress (with NRF2 and SOD3 implicated, and oxidant inactivation of HDAC2 unleashing NF-kB-driven transcription of MMPs, IL-8, TNF-alpha) and impaired macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells and bacteria contribute. Physiologically, airflow obstruction with air trapping causes hyperinflation (raised residual volume, RV/TLC, and total lung capacity); a flattened diaphragm becomes mechanically inefficient. Ventilation-perfusion mismatch accounts for essentially all of the reduction in PaO2 (shunt is minimal), explaining why modest supplemental oxygen corrects hypoxemia. Inflammation can persist even after smoking cessation in susceptible individuals. Risk of death from COPD is closely tied to reduced FEV1 and the presence of emphysema. Mortality is predicted better by the multidimensional BODE index than by FEV1 alone. The absolute annual loss of FEV1 is highest in mild COPD and lowest in very severe disease. Cachexia/wasting is an independent poor prognostic factor. Smoking cessation slows the rate of FEV1 decline (greatest benefit when earlier) and improves survival. Among survival-improving interventions are smoking cessation, long-term oxygen in chronically hypoxemic patients, and lung volume reduction surgery in selected emphysema patients. Patients with PRISm (preserved ratio-impaired spirometry) physiology carry increased risk of mortality and respiratory and cardiovascular events. Exacerbations are episodic acute worsenings (usually <14 days) that increase in frequency as obstruction worsens (severe obstruction with FEV1 <50% predicted averages 1-3 episodes per year) and account for most COPD-related health-care costs; there is currently no cure except lung transplantation. Spirometric severity of airflow obstruction (GOLD, post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7): Mild FEV1 >=80% predicted; Moderate FEV1 50 to <80%; Severe FEV1 30 to <50%; Very severe FEV1 <30% predicted. ATS/ERS alternative uses FEV1/FVC < lower limit of normal with FEV1 Z-scores (borderline zFEV1 > -1.645; mild -1.65 to -2.5; moderate -2.51 to -4; severe < -4.1). The GOLD ABE assessment additionally incorporates respiratory symptom burden (mMRC dyspnea scale or COPD Assessment Test) and annual exacerbation frequency to guide therapy. Multidimensional BODE index (BMI, obstruction, dyspnea, exercise capacity) is used for prognosis. Ventilatory failure is defined as PaCO2 >45 mmHg, classified as acute (with acidemia) or chronic by arterial pH.

Chronic orchialgia — chronic testicular pain, chronic scrotal pain, orchialgia, chronic orchidalgia Chronic epididymitis and post-vasectomy pain syndrome Varicocele Spermatocele or epididymal cyst Testicular tumour Referred pain from ureteric calculus or inguinal hernia Nerve entrapment following inguinal or scrotal surgery Musculoskeletal or hip pathology referring to the scrotum Detailed
