examination is needed to localise the pain and to exclude a testicular mass, varicocele, epididymal pathology, and hernia Referred pain must be considered, as ureteric calculi, inguinal hernia, hip pathology, and nerve entrapment can all present as scrotal pain Scrotal ultrasound is commonly performed largely to reassure and to exclude significant pathology rather than because it usually reveals the cause Initial management is conservative, with reassurance, supportive underwear, analgesia, anti-inflammatory measures, and treatment of any identifiable contributor Neuropathic pain agents and pain-clinic input help selected men, and spermatic cord blocks can be both diagnostic and therapeutic Surgery, including microsurgical denervation of the spermatic cord or orchidectomy, is reserved for carefully selected refractory cases after detailed counselling A discrete or hard testicular mass on examination or imaging Sudden severe pain with swelling raising the possibility of torsion Systemic features suggesting infection or malignancy Associated haematuria or flank pain suggesting a urological cause requiring investigation Attributing all scrotal pain to infection and giving repeated unnecessary antibiotics Missing a testicular tumour presenting as chronic pain Failing to consider and treat a referred cause such as a ureteric stone or hernia Proceeding to orchidectomy without exhausting conservative options and counselling about persistent pain Neglecting the neuropathic and psychological components amenable to pain-clinic input Chronic orchialgia represents a persistent scrotal pain state that in many men cannot be attributed to a single structural lesion. Recognised contributors include previous inflammation or infection, varicocele, spermatocele, prior scrotal or inguinal surgery, and vasectomy, but a substantial proportion is idiopathic. The prevailing understanding is of a neuropathic and centrally sensitised pain process, in which the afferent nerves travelling in the spermatic cord become hypersensitive and pain is amplified within the nervous system, sometimes long after any initial insult has resolved. Referred pain, in which pathology in the ureter, hernia, hip, or lumbar nerves is perceived in the testis owing to shared innervation, is an important and treatable mechanism. Psychological factors and coexisting chronic pelvic pain frequently modulate the experience of pain. The condition is benign but often chronic and difficult to eradicate; many men gain adequate relief with conservative and pain-directed measures, while a smaller group with intractable pain may consider surgery, which offers benefit in selected cases but carries no guarantee of cure.

Chronic pain management — chronic pain, persistent pain, chronic pain syndrome Progressive or undiagnosed structural disease (e.g. malignancy) Inflammatory or autoimmune conditions Neuropathic pain from a specific nerve lesion Fibromyalgia and other nociplastic pain conditions Depression and anxiety contributing to pain and disability Medication-related problems including opioid-induced hyperalgesia Comprehensive biopsychosocial assessment including function, mood, and sleep Validated pain and disability questionnaires to track outcomes Targeted imaging or nerve conduction studies only when a specific treatable cause is suspected Screening for depression, anxiety, and substance use Medication review including opioid risk assessment Chronic pain persists beyond normal tissue healing, commonly defined as lasting more than about three months, and often becomes a condition in its own right rather than a symptom It is best understood through a biopsychosocial model, since biological, psychological, and social factors all influence the pain experience and disability Assessment should characterise the pain (nociceptive, neuropathic, or mixed and nociplastic), functional impact, mood, sleep, and the patient's goals Management is multidisciplinary and multimodal, combining physical rehabilitation, psychological therapies such as cognitive behavioural approaches, and carefully selected medications Neuropathic pain often responds better to agents such as certain antidepressants and anticonvulsants than to conventional analgesics Interventional options, including nerve blocks, radiofrequency procedures, and neuromodulation, may help selected patients within a broader plan Long-term opioid therapy has limited benefit for most chronic non-cancer pain and carries risks of tolerance, dependence, hyperalgesia, and harm, so it requires careful selection, review, and often deprescribing Realistic goals emphasising improved function and quality of life, rather than complete pain elimination, guide effective long-term care New or changing pain with features suggesting malignancy, infection, or fracture Progressive neurological deficit or signs of cord or cauda equina compression Systemic features such as weight loss, fever, or night pain Signs of opioid misuse, escalating use, or overdose risk Managing chronic pain with escalating opioids despite limited benefit and rising harm Neglecting psychological and social contributors within a biomedical-only approach Failing to identify neuropathic pain that needs different medication Missing red-flag features that indicate serious underlying pathology Setting unrealistic goals of complete pain elimination rather than improved function Chronic pain involves persistent changes in the peripheral and central nervous systems. Ongoing nociceptor activity and inflammation can sensitise peripheral nerves, while repeated input drives central sensitisation with amplified spinal and cortical responses, reduced descending inhibition, and reorganisation of pain-processing networks. Neuropathic pain follows damage or disease of the somatosensory system, producing ectopic firing and maladaptive plasticity. In nociplastic pain, altered central processing generates pain without clear tissue damage. Psychological and social factors modulate these pathways, and this neuroplasticity explains why chronic pain often persists independently of the original injury. Chronic pain is frequently a long-term condition; while cure is often not achievable, multidisciplinary management can substantially improve function, mood, and quality of life, whereas reliance on escalating opioids tends to worsen outcomes.

Chronic Pancreatitis — Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (must be excluded on imaging) Autoimmune pancreatitis (type 1 AIP / IgG4-related disease; type 2 / idiopathic duct-centric) Pancreatic pseudocyst Fecal elastase-1 (random level on a formed stool specimen) to confirm exocrine pancreatic insufficiency Abdominal CT (initial imaging modality of choice) to show calcifications, dilated pancreatic/biliary ducts, atrophy, and to exclude pseudocyst and cancer MRI/MRCP, secretin-enhanced MRCP Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS); five or more of nine endosonographic features considered diagnostic, though not specific for early disease EUS with endoscopic pancreatic function testing (EUS-ePFT) Direct pancreatic function test using secretin (best sensitivity; becomes abnormal when >=60% of exocrine function is lost) Plain abdominal film for diffuse calcifications Serum amylase/lipase (usually not strikingly elevated), serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase (may indicate cholestasis from biliary stricture) Serum IgG4 (supportive of type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis) Pancreatic cancer (a poor response to glucocorticoids in suspected autoimmune pancreatitis should raise suspicion of pancreatic cancer) Autoimmune pancreatitis (type 1 can mimic primary sclerosing cholangitis via IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis) Patients typically present with abdominal pain or symptoms of maldigestion; pain is variable in location, severity, and frequency, may be constant or intermittent, and can be exacerbated by eating, leading to fear of eating and weight loss (p.2752). There is often a disparity between the reported severity of abdominal pain and the physical findings, which mainly consist of nonfocal abdominal tenderness (p.2752). In contrast to acute pancreatitis, serum amylase and lipase are usually NOT strikingly elevated in chronic pancreatitis; low serum pancreatic enzyme levels are moderately specific but have poor sensitivity (p.2752). Cumulative prevalence of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency exceeds 80%; overt steatorrhea in a patient with chronic pancreatitis is highly suggestive of this complication (p.2752). A random fecal elastase-1 level on a formed stool specimen can help confirm exocrine pancreatic insufficiency in patients with milder symptoms (p.2752). Diffuse calcifications on a plain abdominal film usually indicate significant pancreatic damage and are pathognomonic for chronic pancreatitis; tropical pancreatitis (often SPINK1-associated) characteristically shows bulky calcifications (p.2752). Lifetime prevalence of chronic pancreatitis-related diabetes exceeds 80%; most develop hyperglycemia from insulin deficiency due to islet cell loss, but diabetic ketoacidosis, diabetic coma, and end-organ damage (retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy) are uncommon (p.2752). Cigarette smoking is an independent, dose-dependent risk factor for chronic pancreatitis and recurrent acute pancreatitis; continued alcohol and smoking exposure are associated with disease progression including fibrosis and calcifications (p.2750). Metabolic bone disease is highly prevalent, with about 65% of patients having osteopenia or osteoporosis (p.2752). Increased risk of pancreatic cancer: cumulative risk is 4% at 20 years after diagnosis of chronic calcific pancreatitis; hereditary PRSS1 and tropical pancreatitis carry an even higher risk than other forms. Jaundice, cholestasis, and biliary cirrhosis from chronic inflammation around the intrapancreatic common bile duct. Gastrointestinal bleeding from peptic ulceration, gastritis, a pseudocyst eroding into the duodenum, arterial bleeding into the pancreatic duct (hemosuccus pancreaticus), or ruptured varices from splenic vein thrombosis. Diagnosis of early or mild chronic pancreatitis is challenging because there is no accurate biomarker, and serum amylase/lipase are usually not strikingly elevated (unlike acute pancreatitis) (p.2752). EUS is not specific enough to diagnose early chronic pancreatitis alone and may show positive features in patients with diabetes, a smoking history, or even normal aging individuals (p.2752). Elevated serum IgG4 has a low positive predictive value for autoimmune pancreatitis when used in isolation from other clinical findings (p.2751). Complete correction of steatorrhea with pancreatic enzyme replacement is uncommon, even though enzyme therapy usually controls diarrhea and improves fat absorption (p.2753). Meta-analyses show no consistent benefit of enzyme therapy at reducing pain; any pain relief may reflect improvement of dyspepsia from maldigestion (p.2753). Chronic pancreatitis is characterized by irreversible damage to the pancreas (in contrast to the reversible changes of acute pancreatitis), defined by histologic abnormalities including chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and progressive destruction (atrophy) of both exocrine and endocrine tissue. Irrespective of the mechanism of injury, pancreatic stellate cell activation leads to cytokine expression and production of extracellular matrix proteins contributing to inflammation and collagen deposition. Proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6) and oxidants induce stellate cell activity with new collagen synthesis; TGF-beta-mediated autocrine self-activation pathways may explain disease progression even after removal of noxious stimuli. Etiologies are framed by the TIGAR-O classification (Toxic-metabolic, Idiopathic, Genetic, Autoimmune, Recurrent and severe acute pancreatitis, Obstructive). Heavy alcohol use is the most common clinically apparent cause in U.S. adults, though additional factors are required for disease development (not all heavy drinkers develop disease). Genetic predisposition (e.g., PRSS1 cationic trypsinogen mutations preventing destruction of prematurely activated trypsin; CFTR and SPINK1 disease modifiers) accounts for up to 15% of previously idiopathic cases. Cardinal manifestations are abdominal pain, steatorrhea, weight loss, diabetes mellitus, and, less commonly, pancreatic cancer (p.2750-2752). Chronic pancreatitis is an irreversible disease; there are currently no therapies to reverse or delay disease progression, so management is focused on screening for and treating complications. Patients have impaired quality of life and significant morbidity with frequent health encounters. Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (cumulative prevalence >80%) and chronic pancreatitis-related diabetes (lifetime prevalence >80%) commonly develop. The 20-year cumulative risk of pancreatic cancer in chronic calcific pancreatitis is 4%, higher in hereditary PRSS1 and tropical forms (p.2752-2754). Etiologic classification follows the TIGAR-O system: Toxic-metabolic (alcohol, tobacco smoking, hypercalcemia, hyperlipidemia/hypertriglyceridemia, chronic renal failure), Idiopathic (early onset, late onset, tropical), Genetic (PRSS1 cationic trypsinogen, CFTR, CASR, CTRC, SPINK1), Autoimmune (type 1 IgG4-related; type 2 idiopathic duct-centric), Recurrent and severe acute pancreatitis (postnecrotic, recurrent acute), and Obstructive (pancreas divisum, duct obstruction by tumor, preampullary duodenal wall cysts, posttraumatic duct strictures). Some genetic conditions are disease modifiers requiring additional factors to cause disease (p.2750).

Chronic pelvic pain — CPP, chronic pelvic pain syndrome, CPPS Endometriosis or adenomyosis Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome Irritable bowel syndrome or inflammatory bowel disease Pudendal neuralgia or other nerve entrapment Pelvic floor myofascial dysfunction Chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men Pelvic congestion syndrome or adhesions Thorough pelvic and musculoskeletal examination including assessment of pelvic floor tone and trigger points Urinalysis and targeted urological evaluation for bladder pain syndrome Pelvic ultrasound and, where indicated, frequently reflects overlapping contributions from gynaecological, urological, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, neurological, and psychological systems, so evaluation must be broad Pelvic floor muscle dysfunction with hypertonicity and myofascial trigger points is a common and treatable contributor that is easily overlooked Central sensitisation is often present and helps explain pain that is disproportionate to examination findings and associated with other chronic pain conditions A careful history should screen for endometriosis, interstitial cystitis or bladder pain syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, pudendal neuralgia, and a history of physical or sexual trauma Pelvic floor physical therapy is a cornerstone of management, alongside neuropathic pain agents, treatment of identified contributors, and psychological therapies A multidisciplinary, biopsychosocial approach with realistic functional goals is more effective than repeated searches for a single surgical cause Trigger-point injection and, in selected cases, nerve blocks such as pudendal blocks may be used within a broader programme Abnormal vaginal or rectal bleeding, postmenopausal bleeding, or a pelvic mass suggesting malignancy Unexplained weight loss, fever, or night sweats Acute severe pain with peritonism suggesting a surgical emergency Haematuria or new bowel symptoms warranting urgent investigation New neurological deficit in the pelvic or lower limb distribution Repeated surgery or invasive procedures in pursuit of a single structural cause when pain is centrally mediated Overlooking pelvic floor muscle dysfunction as a treatable contributor Ignoring psychological factors and a history of trauma that maintain the pain Long-term opioid use, which is generally unhelpful and harmful in this setting Failing to screen for red-flag features of malignancy or a surgical emergency Chronic pelvic pain typically arises from the interaction of peripheral visceral and somatic nociceptive input with central pain processing changes. Viscero-somatic and viscero-visceral convergence in the spinal cord means input from one pelvic organ can amplify and refer pain to others. Persistent nociception promotes peripheral and central sensitisation, with reduced descending inhibition, so pain becomes self-sustaining and disproportionate to any ongoing tissue damage. Pelvic floor muscle overactivity, myofascial trigger points, and psychological factors including anxiety, depression, and prior trauma further modulate and maintain the pain. Chronic pelvic pain often follows a fluctuating long-term course, but many patients achieve meaningful improvement in pain and function with a coordinated multidisciplinary programme that addresses physical, neurological, and psychological contributors. Outcomes are poorer when treatment focuses narrowly on a single organ and ignores central and musculoskeletal factors.

Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (chronic prostatitis, NIH category III) — chronic prostatitis, CP/CPPS, NIH category III prostatitis, chronic nonbacterial prostatitis, prostatodynia Chronic bacterial prostatitis (category II) Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome Benign prostatic enlargement with lower urinary tract symptoms Urethral stricture Pudendal neuralgia Pelvic-floor dysfunction Prostate or bladder malignancy Urinalysis with mid-stream urine culture Lower urinary tract localisation using pre- and post-prostatic-massage specimens (Meares-Stamey or two-glass test) NIH Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index questionnaire Uroflowmetry and post-void residual measurement Sexually transmitted infection screening, including urethral swab or nucleic acid amplification testing PSA where appropriate, and cystoscopy or imaging to exclude other pathology NIH category III prostatitis: chronic pelvic pain present for at least three of the previous six months in the absence of a demonstrable urinary tract infection Pain is typically felt in the perineum, suprapubic area, penis, testes, or lower back, and is often accompanied by ejaculatory or post-ejaculatory discomfort Lower urinary tract symptoms such as frequency, urgency, hesitancy, and a sense of incomplete emptying, along with sexual dysfunction, commonly coexist and reduce quality of life Subdivided into IIIA (inflammatory, with leucocytes in expressed prostatic secretions, semen, or post-massage urine) and IIIB (non-inflammatory, with no leucocytes) By definition standard bacterial cultures are negative, distinguishing it from acute (category I) and chronic bacterial (category II) prostatitis Best assessed with a validated symptom score such as the NIH Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index, and understood as a multifactorial disorder with pelvic-floor, neuropathic, and psychosocial contributions Management is multimodal and phenotype-directed (for example the UPOINT approach) - pelvic-floor physiotherapy, neuromodulatory and analgesic strategies, alpha-blockers, and attention to anxiety or depression - rather than repeated antibiotic courses Visible haematuria PSA elevation or an abnormal prostate on examination Systemic features suggesting acute bacterial prostatitis or a prostatic abscess Unexplained weight loss Neurological deficit or saddle anaesthesia Prescribing repeated prolonged antibiotic courses when cultures are negative and there is no bacterial infection Overlooking pelvic-floor muscle dysfunction and the value of physiotherapy Ignoring the psychosocial dimension of anxiety, depression, and catastrophising that strongly influences outcome Missing an alternative diagnosis such as bladder pain syndrome or, rarely, malignancy Chronic pelvic pain syndrome is a heterogeneous condition with no single identifiable cause. Proposed and frequently overlapping mechanisms include an initial infective or inflammatory insult that triggers ongoing neurogenic inflammation, pelvic-floor muscle dysfunction and spasm, central sensitisation of pain pathways, autoimmune or chemical inflammation from reflux of urine into the prostatic ducts, and psychological stress that amplifies symptom perception. Because cultures are negative and the disorder spans several systems, it is best conceptualised as a chronic pain syndrome centred on the pelvis rather than a simple prostatic infection, which underpins the move away from antibiotics towards multimodal, phenotype-directed therapy. A chronic, often relapsing-remitting condition; symptoms fluctuate and can be frustrating, but many men improve substantially with a tailored multimodal programme, although a subset have persistent symptoms.

Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO/CNO) — CRMO, chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis, CNO, chronic non-bacterial osteitis Bacterial (pyogenic) osteomyelitis Ewing sarcoma and osteosarcoma Leukaemia and lymphoma with bone involvement Langerhans cell histiocytosis Bone metastasis (e.g. neuroblastoma) SAPHO syndrome (adult overlap) Whole-body MRI to identify multifocal, often children and adolescents, with recurrent bone pain and swelling but negative cultures Lesions are frequently multifocal and symmetrical, favouring the metaphyses of long bones, the clavicle, pelvis and vertebrae Regarded as the paediatric counterpart of SAPHO syndrome, sharing autoinflammatory pathophysiology Commonly associated with psoriasis, palmoplantar pustulosis and inflammatory bowel disease Whole-body MRI is the key modality to detect clinically silent lesions and define the multifocal distribution A diagnosis of exclusion made after infection and malignancy are ruled out, often confirmed by biopsy showing sterile inflammation Treated with NSAIDs first-line, escalating to bisphosphonates, TNF inhibitors or other DMARDs for persistent or spinal disease Systemic features (persistent fever, weight loss, night pain) raising concern for malignancy Solitary aggressive lytic lesion where sarcoma or infection cannot be excluded without biopsy Vertebral involvement with collapse or neurological signs Failure to respond to treatment, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Treating as bacterial osteomyelitis with repeated antibiotics or surgery despite sterile cultures Missing additional silent lesions by relying on targeted rather than whole-body imaging Overlooking vertebral disease that risks compression fracture Not screening for associated skin and bowel inflammatory conditions Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, also termed chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis, is an autoinflammatory disease driven by dysregulated innate immunity rather than infection. An imbalance between pro-inflammatory cytokines (including interleukin-1, tumour necrosis factor and interleukin-17) and anti-inflammatory signalling leads to sterile osteoclast-mediated bone inflammation with reactive sclerosis and hyperostosis. Genetic contributions are recognised, with monogenic forms such as those involving IL-1 pathway dysregulation informing understanding of the sporadic disease. The process produces recurrent, often multifocal and symmetrical osteitis, and overlaps mechanistically with SAPHO syndrome as part of the same sterile osteomyelitis spectrum. Many children have a self-limiting or relapsing-remitting course with eventual remission, but a substantial minority develop chronic disease; vertebral involvement can lead to fracture and deformity, so early detection and treatment are important.

Chronic rhinosinusitis — CRS, chronic sinusitis, chronic rhinosinusitis with or without nasal polyps Allergic and non-allergic rhinitis Recurrent acute rhinosinusitis Nasal polyps from other causes with unilateral disease Nasal endoscopy to document mucopus, oedema and polyps CT of the paranasal sinuses to assess extent and osteomeatal complex anatomy Allergy testing where an allergic component is suspected Nasal or sinus swab for culture in resistant or complicated cases Biopsy of atypical or unilateral lesions to exclude neoplasia or granulomatous disease Investigations for immune deficiency or ciliary dysfunction in recalcitrant disease Chronic rhinosinusitis is symptomatic inflammation of the nose and paranasal sinuses persisting for at least twelve weeks Diagnosis requires two or more cardinal symptoms, at least one being nasal blockage or nasal discharge, alongside facial pressure/pain or reduction in sense of smell It is broadly classified into disease with nasal polyps and disease without polyps, which differ in inflammatory pattern and treatment response Objective evidence of inflammation on nasal endoscopy or CT is needed to confirm the diagnosis, as symptoms alone are non-specific Obstruction of the osteomeatal complex impairing sinus ventilation and mucociliary clearance is central to the disease Contributing factors include allergy, asthma, aspirin sensitivity, structural abnormalities, biofilms and, in some cases, fungal disease and immune deficiency First-line treatment is medical, centred on saline irrigation and topical intranasal corticosteroids, with other measures directed at the underlying driver Functional endoscopic sinus surgery is reserved for disease that fails maximal medical therapy or where complications or specific anatomy demand it Strictly unilateral symptoms or bloody discharge suggesting neoplasm Periorbital swelling, proptosis, visual disturbance or ophthalmoplegia indicating orbital complication (an emergency) Severe headache, high fever, neck stiffness or neurological signs suggesting intracranial spread Clear watery rhinorrhoea after trauma or surgery suggesting a cerebrospinal fluid leak Rapidly progressive symptoms with facial numbness or palatal changes in an immunocompromised patient (invasive fungal disease) Diagnosing chronic rhinosinusitis on symptoms alone without objective endoscopic or CT confirmation Overlooking a unilateral lesion that could be a tumour Treating repeatedly with antibiotics rather than addressing the underlying inflammatory driver Missing orbital or intracranial complications during an acute exacerbation Failing to consider allergy, asthma or immune deficiency in recurrent disease Chronic rhinosinusitis reflects a persistent inflammatory process of the sinonasal mucosa rather than simple ongoing infection. Anatomical narrowing or mucosal swelling at the osteomeatal complex obstructs sinus outflow, disrupting ventilation and mucociliary clearance so that secretions stagnate and mucosal inflammation is perpetuated. Host factors (allergy, asthma, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, immune dysfunction, ciliary disorders) and environmental factors (microbial biofilms, fungi, irritants) drive different inflammatory endotypes; polypoid disease is often eosinophilic and type 2 driven, whereas non-polypoid disease tends to be more neutrophilic. Chronic inflammation causes mucosal oedema, polyp formation and epithelial remodelling that further obstruct drainage, creating a self-sustaining cycle. Most patients achieve good symptom control with appropriate medical therapy and, where needed, surgery, but the condition is often chronic and relapsing, particularly the polypoid, eosinophilic and aspirin-sensitive forms, which frequently recur and may require long-term treatment including biologics.

Chronic subdural haematoma — cSDH, chronic SDH, subdural haematoma (chronic) Acute or subacute subdural haematoma Ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack Intracranial neoplasm or metastasis Normal pressure hydrocephalus Neurodegenerative dementia Subdural empyema or hygroma Non-contrast CT head to identify the crescentic collection, its density, and midline shift MRI brain when the diagnosis or age of blood is uncertain or isodense collections are suspected Full blood count, coagulation profile, and platelet function assessment Review of antiplatelet and anticoagulant medication and relevant drug levels or reversal targets Typically affects older adults, often with only trivial or forgotten head trauma weeks earlier, and is more common in those on antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy Presentation is usually insidious over days to weeks, with headache, confusion, gait disturbance, focal weakness, or a fluctuating conscious level that can mimic dementia or stroke Brain atrophy in the elderly and in chronic alcohol use increases the subdural space and stretches bridging veins, predisposing to slow venous bleeding On CT the collection is classically crescent-shaped over the convexity and hypodense or mixed density relative to acute blood; layering or membranes suggest recurrent bleeding of differing ages Symptomatic collections causing mass effect are commonly managed with surgical drainage (burr-hole or craniotomy), while small asymptomatic collections may be observed Correction of coagulopathy and careful review of anticoagulation are central to management and to reducing recurrence Recurrence after drainage is relatively frequent, and subdural drains plus adequate brain re-expansion help lower this risk Bilateral collections can mask midline shift, so symmetry on imaging should not be taken as reassurance Rapid deterioration in conscious level or new pupillary asymmetry suggesting acute rebleeding or herniation Large collection with significant midline shift and effacement of basal cisterns New or worsening focal deficit or seizures Bilateral collections with clinical deterioration despite symmetric imaging Attributing gradual cognitive or gait decline to dementia and overlooking a treatable collection Missing an isodense collection on CT, especially when bilateral and symmetric Resuming anticoagulation without weighing rebleeding risk against thrombotic risk Assuming complete resolution immediately after drainage when residual or recurrent collections are common A chronic subdural haematoma is a slowly accumulating collection of blood and its breakdown products in the subdural space, between the dura and arachnoid. It often begins with minor tearing of bridging cortical veins, particularly where cerebral atrophy has enlarged the subdural space. An encapsulating membrane forms with fragile, leaky neovessels, and repeated micro-haemorrhages together with osmotic and inflammatory factors allow the collection to expand over weeks. Gradual enlargement produces mass effect on the underlying cortex, causing progressive or fluctuating neurological signs. Many patients recover well after drainage of a symptomatic collection, but outcome is worse in the frail elderly and those with marked preoperative neurological impairment; recurrence and the need for repeat surgery are recognised problems.

Chronic suppurative otitis media — CSOM, chronic otitis media, chronic middle ear infection Otitis externa with discharge Otitis media with effusion Tuberculous otitis media Middle ear or external canal malignancy Granulomatous disease of the ear Retained foreign body with secondary infection Otoscopy and otomicroscopy to define perforation type and detect cholesteatoma Pure tone audiometry to characterise conductive or mixed hearing loss Culture and sensitivity of ear discharge High-resolution CT of the temporal bone to map cholesteatoma extent and bony erosion MRI where intracranial complications or residual cholesteatoma are suspected Defined by a persistent or recurrent ear discharge through a chronic tympanic membrane perforation with associated hearing loss Traditionally divided into a tubotympanic (mucosal, safe) type and an atticoantral (squamous, unsafe) type associated with cholesteatoma The tubotympanic type typically causes intermittent painless mucoid discharge and a central perforation, with a comparatively low complication risk The atticoantral type is dangerous because cholesteatoma erodes bone and predisposes to serious intratemporal and intracranial complications Foul-smelling scanty discharge, an attic or marginal perforation, or visible keratin debris should raise suspicion of cholesteatoma Management principles include aural toileting, topical and systemic antibiotics for active disease, and surgery to eradicate disease and reconstruct hearing Cholesteatoma is essentially a surgical disease requiring mastoid exploration to remove the sac and prevent complications Audiometry usually shows conductive loss, but a sensorineural component suggests inner ear involvement Foul discharge with an attic or marginal perforation suggesting cholesteatoma Vertigo or a positive fistula sign indicating labyrinthine erosion Facial nerve palsy from facial canal involvement Severe headache, fever, neck stiffness or altered consciousness suggesting intracranial extension Treating a discharging ear as simple otitis externa and missing an underlying cholesteatoma Failing to recognise attic or marginal perforations as high-risk Overlooking early complications such as vertigo or facial weakness Relying on medical therapy alone when surgical clearance of cholesteatoma is required Chronic suppurative otitis media is long-standing inflammation of the middle ear cleft with a non-intact tympanic membrane. In the tubotympanic type, persistent Eustachian tube dysfunction and recurrent infection maintain mucosal inflammation and a central perforation, with reversible mucosal changes. In the atticoantral type, retraction pockets or migration of squamous epithelium form a cholesteatoma, an expanding keratinising sac whose enzymatic and pressure effects erode ossicles and surrounding bone. This bony destruction can breach the facial canal, labyrinth, or dural plates, opening routes for intracranial spread. The mucosal (tubotympanic) type generally does well with medical treatment and reconstructive surgery, while the atticoantral type with cholesteatoma carries a higher risk of serious complications and requires surgical eradication with ongoing follow-up for recurrence.

Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension — CTEPH, group 4 pulmonary hypertension, chronic thromboembolic disease Idiopathic or heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension Acute pulmonary embolism Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease (group 2) Pulmonary hypertension due to lung disease or hypoxia (group 3) In situ pulmonary artery sarcoma or tumour embolism Large-vessel pulmonary arteritis (e.g. Takayasu) Fibrosing mediastinitis compressing pulmonary vessels Ventilation-perfusion scintigraphy as the primary screen for mismatched perfusion defects Right heart catheterisation to confirm pre-capillary haemodynamics and quantify severity Pulmonary angiography (conventional or CT/MR) to define the anatomy and surgical accessibility of obstruction Transthoracic echocardiography to assess right ventricular function and estimate pressures Thrombophilia and antiphospholipid antibody screening given the thromboembolic basis Cardiopulmonary exercise testing and six-minute walk distance for functional and prognostic assessment Constitutes group 4 pulmonary hypertension and is the pre-capillary form that is potentially curable by surgery, making its identification essential in every patient Results from incomplete resolution of pulmonary emboli that organise into fibrotic material obstructing the pulmonary arteries, though many patients have no documented prior acute event Presents with progressive exertional breathlessness and fatigue, sometimes with signs of right heart failure, developing months to years after a thromboembolic insult The ventilation-perfusion scan is the key screening test, showing multiple segmental mismatched perfusion defects, and is more sensitive than CT pulmonary angiography for excluding the disease Diagnosis requires persistent pulmonary hypertension despite at least several months of therapeutic anticoagulation, confirmed at right heart catheterisation Lifelong anticoagulation is standard, and patients should be assessed at an experienced centre to determine operability Pulmonary endarterectomy is the treatment of choice for surgically accessible disease and can be curative; balloon pulmonary angioplasty and targeted medical therapy help inoperable or residual disease Syncope or presyncope on exertion suggesting critically limited pulmonary flow Signs of decompensated right heart failure with hypotension or hepatic congestion Haemoptysis, which may reflect enlarged bronchial collaterals Persisting or worsening pulmonary hypertension despite adequate anticoagulation, mandating operability assessment Relying on CT pulmonary angiography alone, which can miss disease that a ventilation-perfusion scan would detect Attributing symptoms to residual acute embolism and not screening breathless patients months after an event Labelling disease inoperable without assessment at an experienced surgical centre Starting targeted pulmonary vasodilator therapy in an operable patient and thereby delaying curative surgery Failing to establish lifelong anticoagulation and investigate an underlying thrombophilia Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension develops when acute pulmonary thromboembolism fails to resolve and instead organises into fibrous, endothelialised material that becomes incorporated into the pulmonary arterial wall, producing webs, bands, and stenoses that mechanically obstruct flow. Over time a secondary small-vessel arteriopathy develops in non-obstructed territories, resembling the remodelling of arterial pulmonary hypertension and contributing to the rise in pulmonary vascular resistance. The chronically obstructed and remodelled circulation imposes a progressive afterload on the right ventricle, leading to hypertrophy, dilatation, and eventual failure. Because the proximal obstructing material is fibrotic rather than fresh clot, it is amenable to surgical removal, which distinguishes the disorder from other forms of pulmonary hypertension. Untreated, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension carries a poor prognosis that worsens with rising pulmonary vascular resistance, but pulmonary endarterectomy can normalise haemodynamics and offer a functional cure in operable disease. Inoperable or residual disease is managed with balloon pulmonary angioplasty and targeted therapy at expert centres, with outcomes that continue to improve.

Chronic Venous Disease & Lymphedema — venous insufficiency, varicose veins, lymphedema Congestive heart failure (bilateral leg swelling) Hypoalbuminemia from nephrotic syndrome or severe hepatic disease Myxedema from hypothyroidism, or pretibial myxedema with Graves' disease Drug-induced edema (dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, thiazolidinediones) Lipedema (adipose accumulation thigh-to-ankle sparing the feet, usually in women) Ruptured leg muscle, hematoma from trauma, popliteal (Baker's) cyst (unilateral swelling) Acute deep-vein thrombosis Cellulitis (erythema and swelling of the affected limb) Bacterial lymphangitis Venous duplex ultrasonography - principal test; detects obstruction (no flow, echogenic thrombus, non-compressible vein) and reflux (prolonged flow reversal on Valsalva or cuff release) Air/strain-gauge plethysmography to quantify venous reflux and calf-muscle-pump efficiency MR, CT, or conventional venography for suspected IVC/iliofemoral obstruction, IVC filter occlusion, extrinsic compression, or May-Thurner syndrome Bedside Brodie-Trendelenburg test (deep vs superficial reflux) and Perthes test (deep-venous obstruction) - now used infrequently For lymphedema: abdominal/pelvic ultrasound and CT for obstructing neoplasm; MRI of the limb (honeycomb epifascial pattern; distinguishes lipedema) Lymphoscintigraphy and lymphangiography (rarely needed) to confirm and distinguish primary from secondary lymphedema Near-infrared fluorescence optical imaging for quantitative superficial lymph-flow assessment, useful operatively Lymphedema vs chronic venous insufficiency (venous edema is softer with stasis dermatitis, hyperpigmentation, and superficial varicosities) Lipedema (spares the feet; differentiated by MRI) Myxedema Leg ulcers from severe peripheral artery disease / chronic limb-threatening ischemia, diabetic neuropathy, skin cancer, vasculitis, or rarely hydroxyurea (distinct from venous ulcers by location and characteristics) Chronic venous disease spans a spectrum: telangiectasias and reticular veins, to varicose veins, to chronic venous insufficiency with edema, skin changes, and ulceration (p.2179). Chronic venous insufficiency arises from incompetent veins with venous hypertension and extravasation of fluid and blood elements into the limb; it may occur with superficial venous disease, but more advanced manifestations are usually caused by deep-vein disease (p.2180). Secondary deep-venous insufficiency most often follows deep-vein thrombosis (post-thrombotic syndrome): valve leaflets become thickened and contracted, losing the ability to prevent retrograde flow, and the vein wall becomes rigid and thick-walled (p.2180). Lipodermatosclerosis is the combination of induration, hemosiderin deposition, and inflammation, typically in the lower leg just above the ankle (the gaiter area) (p.2180). Atrophie blanche is a white patch of scar tissue, often with focal telangiectasias and a hyperpigmented border, usually developing near the medial malleolus (p.2180). A venous ulcer is typically shallow with an irregular border, a base of granulation tissue, and exudate, and occurs near the medial and lateral malleoli (p.2180). Venous edema is usually pitting early on, but over time may become less pitting and more indurated, particularly with secondary development of lymphatic dysfunction (phlebolymphedema) (p.2180). Lymphedema is generally a painless condition; it initially involves the foot and progresses up the leg, with early soft pitting edema that later becomes nonpitting with a woody, indurated, fibrotic texture (p.2183-2184). Stemmer's sign (inability to tent the skin at the base of the toes) and peau d'orange (orange-peel dimpling), along with squaring of the toes, are characteristic skin findings of lymphedema (p.2184). Worldwide, the most common cause of secondary lymphedema is lymphatic filariasis; in developed countries it is surgical excision or irradiation of axillary/inguinal lymph nodes for cancer (p.2183). Recurrent bacterial lymphangitis, usually streptococcal, is a very common cause of lymphedema, and lymphedema in turn predisposes to recurrent cellulitis/lymphangitis - a vicious cycle (p.2183-2184). Acute unilateral leg swelling raising concern for deep-vein thrombosis (duration of edema helps distinguish DVT from chronic venous insufficiency) Suspected proximal venous obstruction (IVC/iliofemoral) warranting intervention Infected or rapidly worsening venous ulcer Lymphangiosarcoma - a rare but highly lethal complication of long-standing uncontrolled lymphedema Recurrent cellulitis/lymphangitis in a lymphedematous limb Lymphedema is often confused with chronic venous insufficiency, and the two can coexist as phlebolymphedema when venous insufficiency impairs lymphatic function - do not assume a single cause (p.2180). Distinguish bilateral venous edema and lymphedema from systemic causes (heart failure, hypoalbuminemia, myxedema, drug-induced edema) before attributing swelling to venous disease (p.2180). Distinguish unilateral leg swelling of chronic venous insufficiency/lymphedema from acute deep-vein thrombosis - the duration of edema helps differentiate them (p.2180, 2183). Compression garments improve symptoms and aid ulcer healing but are NOT curative and do NOT prevent progression of varicose veins (p.2181). Antibiotics are NOT indicated for a venous ulcer unless it is infected (p.2181). Diuretics are contraindicated in lymphedema - they may cause intravascular volume depletion and metabolic abnormalities (p.2184). No drugs are FDA-approved for chronic venous insufficiency, and there is insufficient evidence to recommend general use of venoactive herbal supplements (p.2182). In chronic venous disease, incompetent (refluxing) or obstructed veins produce sustained venous hypertension with extravasation of fluid and blood elements into limb tissues. Primary varicose veins arise from defective saphenous valves, intrinsic vein-wall weakness, and high intraluminal pressure; secondary varicosities and chronic venous insufficiency result from deep-venous obstruction or valvular incompetence, classically post-thrombotic (valve leaflets thicken and contract after DVT, the vein becomes rigid, and distal valves become incompetent as high pressure distends the vein). Other secondary causes include May-Thurner syndrome, extrinsic compression by tumor/retroperitoneal fibrosis, arteriovenous fistulas, deep-vein agenesis, and venous malformations. Lymphedema results from impaired lymph transport: deficiency, reflux, or obstruction of lymph vessels causes an imbalance between lymph production and absorption (governed by Starling forces), so protein-rich fluid accumulates in the interstitium and raises tissue osmotic load. Persistent lymphedema triggers inflammatory/immune responses with infiltration of mononuclear cells, fibroblasts, and adipocytes, leading to adipose and collagen deposition in skin and subcutaneous tissues (p.2180, 2182-2183). Approximately 20% of patients with chronic venous insufficiency develop venous ulcers. Recurrent varicose veins occur in up to 50% of patients by 5 years after ligation and stripping. Endovenous thermal ablation achieves 1- and 5-year occlusion rates exceeding ~90%; sclerotherapy averages ~81% and ~74% at 1 and 5 years. Iliac venous stenting has technical success >85% with long-term patency ~75%; venous bypass long-term patency generally exceeds 60%. Lymphedema is a chronic, generally progressive condition; failure to control limb edema may lead to recurrent infections, progressive trophic skin changes, and rarely the highly lethal complication of lymphangiosarcoma (p.2179, 2182-2184). CEAP (Clinical, Etiologic, Anatomic, Pathophysiologic) classification of chronic venous disease. Clinical: C0 no signs; C1 telangiectasias/reticular veins; C2 varicose veins (C2r recurrent); C3 edema; C4 skin/subcutaneous changes (C4a pigmentation or eczema, C4b lipodermatosclerosis or atrophie blanche, C4c corona phlebectatica); C5 healed venous ulcer; C6 active venous ulcer (C6r recurrent). Etiologic: Ep primary, Es secondary (Esi intravenous, Ese extravenous), Ec congenital, En none identified. Anatomic: As superficial, Ap perforator, Ad deep, An none. Pathophysiologic: Pr reflux, Po obstruction, Pr,o both, Pn none. Lymphedema is staged by the International Society of Lymphology: Stage 0/Ia latent/subclinical; Stage I early protein-rich edema reduced by elevation, may pit; Stage II elevation rarely reduces swelling, pitting manifest then later non-pitting as fat/fibrosis supervene; Stage III lymphostatic elephantiasis with trophic skin changes, acanthosis, fat/fibrosis, warty overgrowths (p.2181, 2184).

Chronic venous insufficiency — CVI, chronic venous disease, venous stasis, venous insufficiency Peripheral arterial disease or arterial ulcer Lymphoedema Cardiac, renal, or hepatic oedema Cellulitis Diabetic neuropathic ulcer Vasculitic ulcer or pyoderma gangrenosum Acute deep vein thrombosis Venous duplex ultrasound to map reflux and obstruction Ankle-brachial pressure index to exclude significant arterial disease before compression Photoplethysmography or venous filling assessment where indicated Cross-sectional venography (CT or MR) for suspected proximal or iliac obstruction Ulcer swab and, if atypical or non-healing, biopsy to exclude malignancy Assessment for coexisting cardiac, renal, or hepatic causes of oedema Results from sustained venous hypertension due to valvular incompetence (reflux), venous obstruction, or calf-muscle pump failure, or a combination of these The clinical spectrum runs from telangiectasia and varicose veins to oedema, skin changes (haemosiderin pigmentation, venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche), and venous ulceration The CEAP classification (Clinical, aEtiological, Anatomical, Pathophysiological) grades severity, with clinical classes C0 to C6, C6 being an active venous ulcer Venous ulcers characteristically occur in the gaiter area around the medial malleolus, are shallow with irregular margins, and are often preceded by lipodermatosclerosis Venous duplex ultrasound is the key investigation, mapping reflux and obstruction to guide treatment Compression therapy is the cornerstone of management once significant arterial disease is excluded by the ankle-brachial pressure index; it promotes ulcer healing and prevents recurrence Correcting superficial reflux by endovenous ablation (thermal or non-thermal) or surgery improves symptoms and ulcer healing in suitable patients A non-healing or atypical ulcer requiring biopsy to exclude malignancy (Marjolin's ulcer) Coexisting significant arterial disease making compression hazardous Signs of deep vein thrombosis or spreading cellulitis A rapidly deteriorating limb or systemic sepsis Applying compression without checking the ankle-brachial pressure index for arterial disease Attributing all leg ulcers to venous disease and missing arterial, malignant, or vasculitic causes Under-treating with inadequate compression, leading to non-healing Neglecting to treat correctable superficial reflux Chronic venous insufficiency stems from persistent ambulatory venous hypertension in the lower limb. Valvular incompetence in the superficial, deep, or perforating veins allows reflux, while venous outflow obstruction (for example after deep vein thrombosis) and calf-muscle pump failure also contribute. The elevated venous pressure is transmitted to the microcirculation, causing capillary leakage, fibrin deposition, leucocyte activation, and chronic inflammation. This produces oedema, characteristic skin changes such as haemosiderin staining and lipodermatosclerosis, and ultimately tissue breakdown and venous ulceration, typically in the gaiter region. A chronic, relapsing condition; compression and correction of reflux heal most venous ulcers, but recurrence is common without ongoing compression and risk-factor control, and advanced skin changes are only partly reversible.

structures, recognises modified histones and helps regulate access to chromatin and the expression of downstream genes. Loss-of-function variants and deletions reduce the available protein (haploinsufficiency), disturbing this chromatin-reading function and the gene-expression programmes it supports, including those influencing neurodevelopment and the central regulation of appetite and energy balance. The resulting dysregulation manifests as developmental delay and intellectual disability with a characteristic behavioural profile, alongside a predisposition to obesity, positioning the condition within the broader group of Mendelian disorders of the epigenetic machinery. Life expectancy is not clearly reduced, but intellectual disability is usually mild to moderate and behavioural difficulties and obesity often persist, so long-term outcome is improved by early developmental support, behavioural intervention and proactive management of weight and its metabolic consequences.

pancreatic disease without lipid and biopsy evaluation Neglecting long-term surveillance for hepatic steatosis Chylomicron retention disease is caused by variants in SAR1B, which encodes a small GTPase essential for COPII vesicle formation and the intracellular transport of prechylomicron particles from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi. When SAR1B is defective, newly formed chylomicrons cannot be trafficked and secreted from enterocytes, so dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins are trapped within the cells. This produces fat malabsorption, steatorrhoea and deficiency of vitamins A, D, E and K, with characteristic lipid-laden enterocytes. Because the defect is selective for the intestinal chylomicron pathway, hepatic VLDL secretion is comparatively spared and plasma apolipoprotein B is reduced rather than absent. With early dietary fat restriction and lifelong fat-soluble vitamin, especially vitamin E, supplementation, growth improves and the usually milder neurological and retinal complications can be limited. Long-term monitoring for vitamin deficiency and hepatic changes is needed.

tamponade from a large or rapidly accumulating chylous effusion Recurrent reaccumulation after drainage indicating an unresolved lymphatic leak Features suggesting an underlying mediastinal malignancy or lymphangiomatosis Nutritional and immune depletion from chronic high-volume chyle loss Mistaking chylous fluid for pus and missing the diagnosis without triglyceride analysis Confusing chylopericardium with a pseudochylous cholesterol effusion Draining the effusion without addressing the ongoing lymphatic leak, leading to recurrence Overlooking an underlying malignancy or lymphatic disorder in secondary cases Chylopericardium arises when lymph rich in triglyceride-laden chylomicrons drains abnormally from the thoracic duct or its tributaries into the pericardial sac. In primary disease this reflects congenital or acquired abnormal lymphatic channels communicating with the pericardium, sometimes with reflux from the thoracic duct; in secondary disease the duct or its branches are disrupted by surgery, trauma, tumour, or radiation. The accumulating chyle raises intrapericardial pressure and, if large or rapid, impairs cardiac filling to cause tamponade, while chronic loss of chyle can deplete fat-soluble nutrients, protein, and lymphocytes. Primary chylopericardium often responds to dietary measures and drainage but can recur and require surgical or interventional treatment, whereas the outlook in secondary disease is largely determined by the underlying cause.

depletion Signs of malnutrition, hypovolaemia, or lymphopenia-related infection Underlying malignancy such as lymphoma requiring urgent evaluation Respiratory compromise from a large or rapidly reaccumulating effusion Assuming turbid pleural fluid is empyema without measuring triglycerides Overlooking a false-negative milky appearance in a fasting patient Allowing prolonged high-volume drainage without addressing nutritional and immune depletion Failing to investigate for an underlying malignancy in non-traumatic cases The thoracic duct conveys chyle, rich in triglycerides absorbed from the gut, from the abdomen to the systemic venous circulation. When the duct is disrupted by surgery or trauma, or obstructed by tumour or fibrosis, chyle leaks into or backs up into the pleural space. Because chyle contains chylomicrons and high triglyceride content, the effusion has a characteristic milky appearance and high triglyceride level. Ongoing leakage depletes the body of nutrients, immunoglobulins, and lymphocytes, and the volume loss can cause hypovolaemia and metabolic disturbance. Outcome depends on the underlying cause and leak volume; traumatic and postsurgical chylothoraces often settle with conservative measures, whereas malignant or high-output leaks are more difficult to control and prolonged chyle loss risks serious malnutrition and immunosuppression if not addressed.

Ciguatera fish poisoning — ciguatera, ciguatoxin poisoning, reef fish poisoning, CFP Scombroid (histamine) fish poisoning Paralytic or neurotoxic shellfish poisoning Tetrodotoxin poisoning Viral or bacterial gastroenteritis Peripheral neuropathy of other cause Anxiety or hyperventilation with paraesthesiae Clinical diagnosis based on reef-fish ingestion and characteristic features Electrocardiography for bradycardia and conduction changes Electrolytes and hydration status given gastrointestinal losses Blood pressure and heart rate monitoring in the acute phase Detection of ciguatoxin in remaining fish where specialised assays are available Neurological assessment to document sensory disturbance Follows ingestion of large, predatory tropical reef fish (such as barracuda, grouper, snapper) that have accumulated ciguatoxins up the food chain Combines gastrointestinal symptoms (vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain) early with a distinctive neurological and cardiovascular picture Cold allodynia, often described as a reversal of hot and cold sensation, is a characteristic feature, along with perioral and limb paraesthesiae and pruritus Bradycardia and hypotension can occur in the acute phase and may need cardiovascular support Neurological symptoms can persist or relapse for weeks to months and may be provoked by alcohol, exercise or eating fish again Management is supportive; symptoms are often self-limiting acutely, and patients should avoid fish, alcohol and nuts during recovery to reduce relapse The toxin is heat-stable and odourless, so the fish looks, smells and tastes normal and cooking does not prevent poisoning Symptomatic bradycardia or hypotension Significant dehydration or electrolyte disturbance from vomiting and diarrhoea Neurological features in pregnancy or with significant comorbidity Respiratory or bulbar involvement (uncommon but serious) Severe or rapidly worsening symptoms Attributing the illness to simple gastroenteritis and missing the neurological signature Assuming cooking or freezing makes the fish safe, as the toxin is heat-stable Failing to advise avoidance of fish, alcohol and nuts during recovery, risking relapse Overlooking bradycardia and hypotension needing monitoring Ciguatoxins are produced by the dinoflagellate Gambierdiscus and bioaccumulate and biomagnify in reef fish. The toxins bind voltage-gated sodium channels and hold them open, increasing sodium influx and neuronal excitability, and also affect calcium handling. This heightened excitability produces the sensory disturbances, paraesthesiae and characteristic cold allodynia, together with autonomic effects such as bradycardia and hypotension. The toxins are lipid-soluble, heat-stable and undetectable by taste or smell, and their persistence in tissues underlies the prolonged and relapsing neurological course. Acute symptoms usually settle over days, but neurological symptoms such as paraesthesiae and cold allodynia can persist or relapse for weeks to months; recurrence can be triggered by alcohol, exertion and further fish consumption, though the illness is rarely fatal.

ciliated hepatic foregut cyst — CHFC, ciliated foregut cyst of the liver simple hepatic cyst hydatid cyst mucinous cystic neoplasm (biliary cystadenoma) hepatic abscess cystic metastasis intrahepatic bronchogenic cyst Caroli disease abdominal ultrasound to characterise the subcapsular cyst contrast-enhanced CT of the liver MRI for soft-tissue characterisation and surgical planning histopathology with immunohistochemistry to confirm the ciliated foregut lining serology to exclude hydatid disease where relevant assessment for solid components suggesting malignant transformation Ciliated hepatic foregut cysts are rare, usually solitary lesions that characteristically lie in segment IV of the left lobe in a subcapsular position. The wall shows four distinctive layers: an inner ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium, subepithelial connective tissue, one or more smooth muscle layers, and an outer fibrous capsule. They share an embryological origin with bronchogenic and oesophageal cysts, arising from a detached remnant of the embryonic foregut. Most are small and asymptomatic, discovered incidentally on imaging or at operation for another reason. The presence of a smooth muscle layer and ciliated lining distinguishes them histologically from simple hepatic cysts. Unlike most benign hepatic cysts, they carry a recognised potential for malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma. Enlargement, solid or mural components, or wall thickening should raise concern for malignant change. Excision is advocated for larger or symptomatic lesions and where the diagnosis is uncertain or malignancy cannot be excluded. rapid interval growth of a previously stable cyst solid, papillary, or mural nodular components on imaging irregular wall thickening features suggesting squamous cell carcinoma transformation new symptoms such as pain or a palpable mass in a previously silent lesion dismissing the lesion as a simple hepatic cyst and overlooking its malignant potential confusing it with a mucinous cystic neoplasm and mismanaging accordingly relying on aspiration cytology, which is often non-diagnostic and risks spillage failing to recognise the characteristic segment IV subcapsular location inadequate histological sampling that misses focal malignant change The ciliated hepatic foregut cyst is believed to originate from an aberrant detached bud of the embryonic foregut, the same anlage that gives rise to the tracheobronchial tree and oesophagus, which becomes incorporated into the developing liver. This shared derivation explains the histological resemblance to bronchogenic cysts, notably the ciliated respiratory-type epithelium and the muscular wall. The characteristic four-layered wall comprises ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium overlying loose subepithelial connective tissue, a smooth muscle coat, and an outer fibrous capsule. The lesion is typically unilocular and contains mucoid or serous fluid. Chronic epithelial irritation is thought to underlie the well-documented, though uncommon, progression through squamous metaplasia to squamous cell carcinoma, which accounts for the interest in definitive excision. Prognosis is excellent for benign lesions treated by complete excision. Malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma, though uncommon, markedly worsens the outlook.

Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder — CRSWD, circadian rhythm sleep disorder, delayed sleep phase syndrome, shift work disorder, jet lag disorder Psychophysiological (behavioural) insomnia Primary hypersomnia disorders Depression or other mood disorder affecting sleep timing Poor sleep hygiene Substance or medication effects on sleep-wake timing Neurodegenerative disease with irregular sleep-wake rhythm Detailed sleep-wake history with a prospective sleep diary over one to two weeks Actigraphy to objectively document sleep-wake timing patterns Assessment of light exposure, work schedule, and travel history Where available, markers of circadian phase such as dim-light melatonin onset Screening for coexisting mood disorder or other sleep pathology Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders arise from a mismatch between the internal biological clock and the desired or socially required sleep-wake schedule, so total sleep is often normal if the patient sleeps at their preferred times Common subtypes include delayed and advanced sleep phase disorders, non-24-hour rhythm, irregular sleep-wake rhythm, and the externally imposed shift work and jet lag disorders Delayed sleep phase disorder is typical of adolescents and young adults, who cannot fall asleep or wake at conventional times and are mislabelled as insomniacs Advanced sleep phase disorder, with early evening sleepiness and early morning waking, is more common in older adults Non-24-hour rhythm disorder is characteristic of totally blind people who lack light entrainment of the clock A sleep diary, often circadian principles, are the mainstays of realigning the clock Shift work and jet lag disorders are managed with strategic light, scheduled sleep, and planned adaptation, since the environmental demand usually cannot be removed Sleepiness during shift work causing accidents or dangerous errors Irregular sleep-wake rhythm emerging with cognitive decline, suggesting neurodegenerative disease Severe social, educational, or occupational impairment from persistent misalignment Coexisting depression with the circadian disturbance Misdiagnosing delayed sleep phase disorder as primary insomnia and prescribing hypnotics Giving light or melatonin at the wrong circadian time and worsening the misalignment Overlooking blindness as the cause of a free-running non-24-hour rhythm Ignoring the occupational safety consequences of shift work sleepiness The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus generates an intrinsic rhythm slightly longer than twenty-four hours that is entrained to the environment chiefly by light detected through retinal photoreceptors, with melatonin secretion providing an internal darkness signal. Circadian rhythm disorders occur when this clock is misaligned with the external day. Intrinsic disorders reflect altered clock timing or entrainment: a long intrinsic period or reduced morning light sensitivity delays the phase, an advanced phase shortens it, absent light input (blindness) causes free-running non-24-hour rhythms, and weakened clock output produces an irregular rhythm as seen in neurodegenerative disease. Extrinsic disorders (shift work, jet lag) arise when behaviour and light exposure are acutely forced out of step with the still-entrained internal clock, producing sleepiness, insomnia, and impaired performance until re-entrainment occurs. Intrinsic disorders such as delayed sleep phase can usually be improved with disciplined light and melatonin timing, though relapse is common if the regimen lapses; shift work and jet lag disorders resolve with adaptation or cessation of the schedule, and outcomes are poorer when the environmental demand cannot be altered.

the main etiologic groups are alcohol-associated, chronic viral hepatitis B/C, biliary, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH, formerly NASH), and miscellaneous (cardiac, cryptogenic) (p.2708). Alcohol-associated cirrhosis is classically micronodular (nodules <3 mm); with abstinence larger nodules may form, giving a mixed micronodular/macronodular pattern (p.2708). In alcohol-related liver disease the AST is typically higher than the ALT, usually in roughly a 2:1 ratio, and aminotransferases are generally <400 IU/mL (p.2708-2709). Stigmata of chronic liver disease include scleral icterus, palmar erythema, spider angiomas, parotid enlargement, digital clubbing, muscle wasting, and in men decreased body hair, gynecomastia and testicular atrophy; these are often reversible with abstinence (p.2710). Portal hypertension is defined as a hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) >5 mmHg; clinically significant portal hypertension is an HVPG >=10 mmHg, carrying substantial risk of decompensation (variceal bleeding, ascites, encephalopathy) (p.2713). A serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) >=1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension as the cause of ascites; cardiac ascites also shows SAAG >=1.1 g/dL but with ascitic protein >2.5 g/dL, whereas SAAG <1.1 g/dL points to infectious or malignant causes (p.2715). Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed when the ascitic absolute neutrophil count is >250/uL; ascitic protein <1.5 g/dL marks patients at higher risk for SBP (p.2715-2716). Most common SBP organisms are Escherichia coli and other gut flora; growth of more than two organisms should raise suspicion for secondary peritonitis from a perforated viscus (p.2716). Hepatorenal syndrome is functional renal failure without renal histopathology; HRS-AKI (old type 1) is rapidly progressive while HRS-CKD (old type 2) is more stable with a better prognosis (p.2716). In hepatic encephalopathy ammonia is usually elevated, but its level correlates poorly with disease severity, so most hepatologists do not rely on ammonia to diagnose or follow the condition; asterixis (liver flap) is a key bedside sign (p.2716-2717). Standard PT/INR do not reliably measure clotting capacity in cirrhosis because both pro- and anticoagulant factor synthesis fall (rebalanced hemostasis); adequate thrombin generation occurs at platelet counts above ~50,000-60,000/L (p.2717). Acute-on-chronic liver failure is acute decompensation of cirrhosis with failure of one or more organ systems, behaves like a sepsis-type systemic inflammatory syndrome, and carries 28-day mortality of roughly 20-70% rising with the number of organ failures (p.2717). Variceal hemorrhage - immediately life-threatening, with about 20-30% mortality per bleeding episode New or worsening hepatic encephalopathy, especially with violent agitation or progressive obtundation Rapidly rising creatinine in a patient with tense ascites suggesting HRS-AKI Fever, abdominal pain, altered mental status or new AKI in a patient with ascites suggesting SBP Acute-on-chronic liver failure with multiorgan failure Refractory ascites failing maximal diuretics Relying on PT/INR (or routinely correcting it before procedures) to gauge bleeding risk in cirrhosis - hemostasis is rebalanced and these tests are unreliable Trusting ammonia levels to diagnose or grade hepatic encephalopathy despite poor correlation with severity Restricting dietary protein for encephalopathy, which worsens malnutrition and is strongly discouraged Missing SBP because classic signs may be absent - a high index of suspicion and paracentesis are needed in hospitalized ascitic patients Using nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides) or unmonitored ACE inhibitors/ARBs in patients with ascites, precipitating renal failure Forgetting albumin replacement after large-volume paracentesis (>=5 L) to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction Overlooking sarcopenia masked by obesity or edema in decompensated cirrhosis Chronic, repeated hepatocellular injury (toxic, viral, immune, metabolic, cholestatic, or congestive) drives Kupffer cell activation and release of profibrogenic cytokines that activate hepatic stellate cells, producing excess collagen and extracellular matrix. Connective tissue links portal triads to central veins, hepatocytes are lost, and regenerative nodules form, so the liver contracts and loses normal architecture - a process taking years to decades. The resulting distorted vasculature raises intrahepatic resistance, which together with splanchnic arterial vasodilation (driven by mediators such as nitric oxide) produces portal hypertension. Splanchnic vasodilation causes effective arterial underfilling, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and sympathetic systems, leading to renal sodium and water retention, plasma volume expansion, and a hyperdynamic circulation; combined with low oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia, this generates ascites and edema. Portosystemic shunting plus reduced hepatic mass allows gut-derived neurotoxins (ammonia, false neurotransmitters, mercaptans) to reach the brain and cause encephalopathy (p.2708, p.2713-2717). Severity and bleeding risk are stratified by Child-Pugh class and MELD score. Once clinically significant portal hypertension leads to decompensation, median survival is under 2 years. Less than half of patients survive 2 years after the onset of ascites. Patients with complicated cirrhosis who keep drinking have under 50% 5-year survival, whereas abstinence markedly improves outlook. Development of encephalopathy is a poor prognostic sign, and HRS (AKI or CKD type) carries a poor prognosis without transplantation. ACLF 28-day mortality ranges from roughly 20-70%, rising with the number of failing organs. Liver transplantation is the definitive option for end-stage disease and can reverse HRS (p.2709, p.2713, p.2715-2717). Compensated cirrhosis (HVPG 5-10 mmHg) may be asymptomatic for >=10 years; clinically significant portal hypertension is HVPG >=10 mmHg. Decompensation is marked by variceal bleeding, ascites, or encephalopathy. Overall severity is graded by Child-Pugh class and MELD score, which also predict variceal bleeding risk and guide transplant prioritization. Acute kidney injury is defined as a creatinine rise of 0.3 mg/dL over 48 h or a 50% rise from baseline; SBP is defined by ascitic neutrophils >250/uL (p.2713, p.2715-2716).

Citrate toxicity — Citrate-induced hypocalcaemia, Transfusion citrate toxicity Hypocalcaemia from other causes such as hypoparathyroidism Hypomagnesaemia of independent cause Transfusion-associated hyperkalaemia causing arrhythmia Hypothermia-related cardiac dysfunction during massive transfusion Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction Local anaesthetic or other drug-induced arrhythmia Ionised calcium measurement during rapid or massive transfusion Serum magnesium level Electrocardiogram assessing the corrected QT interval and rhythm Arterial blood gas to detect accompanying alkalosis Total calcium and albumin for context Continuous cardiac monitoring during high-volume transfusion or apheresis Citrate is the anticoagulant in blood components and chelates ionised calcium; toxicity is effectively acute hypocalcaemia and sometimes hypomagnesaemia. Occurs when citrate is infused faster than the liver can metabolise it, as in massive or rapid transfusion, exchange transfusion, and apheresis procedures. Neonates, patients with hepatic impairment, hypothermia or poor perfusion are at particular risk because citrate clearance is reduced. Early symptoms include perioral and peripheral tingling, and this is a common experience for apheresis donors. Progressive hypocalcaemia causes tremor, tetany, a prolonged QT interval, arrhythmias and reduced myocardial contractility with hypotension. Ionised calcium, not total calcium, should guide assessment because citrate binds the ionised fraction. Management is to slow or pause the infusion and replace calcium, with magnesium replacement if deficient. Citrate is metabolised to bicarbonate, so a metabolic alkalosis may follow large citrate loads once the acute phase passes. Tetany or carpopedal spasm during transfusion Prolonged QT interval or new arrhythmia Hypotension with reduced myocardial contractility during massive transfusion Seizures attributable to severe hypocalcaemia Rapid citrate load in a neonate or patient with hepatic failure Relying on total rather than ionised calcium to gauge severity. Overlooking concurrent hypomagnesaemia that perpetuates hypocalcaemia. Failing to anticipate toxicity in neonates, hepatic failure and hypothermia. Attributing arrhythmia to hyperkalaemia alone and missing hypocalcaemia. Neglecting the later metabolic alkalosis from citrate conversion to bicarbonate. Citrate toxicity is a metabolic complication of transfusion rather than an immune reaction. Citrate anticoagulants prevent clotting by chelating calcium ions, and when large volumes of citrated blood are infused rapidly, or when calcium is returned slowly as in apheresis, the plasma concentration of ionised calcium falls. Under normal conditions citrate is rapidly metabolised by the liver, kidney and skeletal muscle via the citric acid cycle to bicarbonate, so toxicity only occurs when the infusion rate exceeds metabolic capacity, which is more likely in hepatic dysfunction, hypothermia, shock and in neonates. The resulting acute hypocalcaemia, sometimes accompanied by hypomagnesaemia, impairs neuromuscular and cardiac function, producing paraesthesiae, tetany, QT prolongation, arrhythmia and depressed myocardial contractility. Subsequent conversion of the citrate load to bicarbonate can produce a metabolic alkalosis. Citrate toxicity is readily reversible when recognised, by slowing the infusion and replacing calcium, and rarely causes lasting harm. Severe unrecognised hypocalcaemia during massive transfusion can, however, precipitate life-threatening arrhythmia and cardiac depression.

abnormal threonine/serine) Liver function tests and coagulation in cholestatic infants Plasma and urine galactose/galactitol in NICCD Serum pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor where available SLC25A13 gene sequencing for confirmation Fasting lipid profile and glucose tolerance assessment Brain imaging in adults with encephalopathy to exclude other causes Caused by biallelic SLC25A13 variants affecting citrin, the mitochondrial aspartate-glutamate carrier, not a urea cycle enzyme itself Age-dependent phenotypes: neonatal cholestasis (NICCD), a childhood failure-to-thrive/dyslipidaemic stage, and adult-onset citrullinaemia (CTLN2) NICCD presents with intrahepatic cholestasis, galactosuria, hypoproteinaemia and often self-limited jaundice in infancy Adult CTLN2 causes recurrent hyperammonaemic encephalopathy with neuropsychiatric symptoms, often precipitated by alcohol, medication or carbohydrate load A striking clue is a self-selected diet rich in protein and fat with an aversion to carbohydrates and sweets Biochemistry shows raised citrulline and ammonia with an elevated arginine and abnormal threonine-to-serine ratio; pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor (PSTI) may be raised Confirmed by SLC25A13 sequencing; the disorder is especially prevalent in East Asian populations High-carbohydrate treatment is harmful; management favours a low-carbohydrate, higher-protein/fat diet, avoidance of glycerol/high-glucose infusions, arginine and nitrogen scavengers, with liver transplantation for severe CTLN2 Adult hyperammonaemic encephalopathy with rapid neurological decline Cerebral oedema during a CTLN2 crisis Precipitation of coma by high-carbohydrate/glucose infusion or glycerol Progressive cholestatic liver failure in an affected infant Recurrent unexplained neuropsychiatric episodes with hyperammonaemia Giving high-glucose or glycerol-containing infusions, which can precipitate or worsen a crisis Applying a standard high-carbohydrate, protein-restricted urea-cycle diet, which is counterproductive here Misattributing adult encephalopathy to alcohol or psychiatric disease and missing citrin deficiency Overlooking NICCD as a cause of neonatal cholestasis Ignoring the diagnostic clue of carbohydrate aversion and protein/fat preference Citrullinaemia type 2 is caused by deficiency of citrin, the liver-type mitochondrial aspartate-glutamate carrier encoded by SLC25A13, a component of the malate-aspartate shuttle. Citrin exports aspartate from mitochondria to the cytosol, where aspartate is required by argininosuccinate synthetase to combine with citrulline in the urea cycle and for the shuttle that transfers reducing equivalents (NADH) into mitochondria. Loss of citrin therefore both limits cytosolic aspartate for ureagenesis, causing citrulline accumulation and hyperammonaemia, and impairs the malate-aspartate shuttle, raising the cytosolic NADH:NAD ratio and disturbing carbohydrate/lipid metabolism. This explains the characteristic carbohydrate intolerance, the harm from glucose loading, and the preference for protein- and fat-rich foods. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. NICCD usually resolves with supportive care and appropriate feeding, but adult CTLN2 can be life-threatening with recurrent hyperammonaemic crises and may require liver transplantation; dietary management markedly influences outcome.
