>1 cm length discrepancy suggests unilateral/renovascular disease (p.2394-2395) Kidney biopsy reserved for early CKD with diagnostic uncertainty or suspected superimposed active process - NOT advised once kidneys are small/scarred (technically hazardous, scarring obscures diagnosis, no therapeutic window) (p.2395) Genetic testing (large CKD gene panels, microarray, exome/genome sequencing) for familial disease, consanguinity, extrarenal/syndromic features, steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, cystic disease, or young-onset unexplained CKD (p.2395) Acute or subacute kidney injury that is potentially reversible - the single most important distinction from true CKD; prior creatinine values establish chronicity (p.2395) Acute-on-chronic kidney failure from a superimposed reversible insult: ECFV depletion (GI losses, over-diuresis), urinary tract infection, new obstructive uropathy, nephrotoxin/contrast/NSAID exposure, or flare of the primary disease (e.g., lupus, vasculitis) (p.2389, 2395-2396) Progression risk in CKD tracks three things together: the current GFR, the trajectory of GFR over time, and the degree of albuminuria - not GFR alone (p.2385). Once nephron mass is reduced, surviving nephrons undergo compensatory hyperfiltration and hypertrophy; these short-term adaptations become maladaptive, driving glomerulosclerosis and ongoing GFR loss even after the original insult has resolved (p.2385-2386, 2396). A normal serum creatinine can mask substantial GFR loss in older patients and women (lower muscle mass); an elderly woman with a 'normal' creatinine may have a GFR under 50 mL/min/1.73 m2 (p.2387). Loss of urinary concentrating ability gives an obligate output of ~2 L/day and nocturia; paradoxically, resolution of nocturia may feel like improvement but can actually signal worsening oliguria (p.2362). Cardiac troponin is frequently chronically elevated in CKD without acute ischemia - serial trending over hours is more informative than a single value, and persistently elevated levels independently predict adverse cardiovascular events (p.2392). Most CKD patients die of cardiovascular disease before ever reaching stage 5; cardiovascular risk is increased roughly 10- to 200-fold versus age/sex-matched controls depending on stage (p.2391). In advanced CKD a malnutrition-inflammation state can paradoxically reverse classic risk factors (lowering blood pressure and lipids) and is itself a marker of poor prognosis - so 'improving' numbers can be ominous (p.2392). A drop in GFR of up to ~30% after starting an ACEi/ARB is often a benign reflection of relieved intraglomerular hyperfiltration; if stable it can be tolerated, but a progressive rise in creatinine suggests underlying renovascular disease (p.2392, 2396). A normal-sized kidney does not exclude CKD: diabetic nephropathy (early), amyloidosis, and HIV nephropathy can show normal or enlarged kidneys despite advanced disease; polycystic kidneys are typically enlarged (p.2394-2395). Hyperkalemia disproportionate to the GFR decline points to hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism (e.g., diabetes) or distal-nephron disease such as obstructive uropathy or sickle cell nephropathy (p.2389). PTH is itself a uremic toxin - high levels are associated with muscle weakness, cardiac fibrosis, ESA-resistant anemia (via marrow fibrosis), and constitutional symptoms (p.2390). Erythrocytosis rather than anemia can occur in some CKD-associated conditions: urinary tract obstruction, polycystic kidney disease, renovascular disease, and renal cell carcinoma (p.2362). Uremic pericarditis (pleuritic chest pain with friction rub; ECG with PR depression and diffuse ST elevation) - absolute indication for urgent dialysis; risk of hemorrhagic effusion and tamponade, so dialyze without heparin (p.2392) Asterixis, myoclonus, seizures, or coma in advanced untreated kidney failure - uremic encephalopathy (p.2393) Peripheral neuropathy without another cause is an indication to start renal replacement therapy (p.2393) Calciphylaxis - painful livedo reticularis and subcutaneous nodules progressing to ischemic skin necrosis/ulceration (legs, thighs, abdomen, breasts); warfarin is a risk factor and should be stopped (p.2390-2391) Diuretic-resistant intractable edema and hypertension, refractory hyperkalemia, or refractory pulmonary edema in advanced CKD - indications to initiate dialysis (p.2389, 2392) Accelerating rate of GFR decline - prompts search for a reversible superimposed acute/subacute process (p.2396) Acute systemic features (fever, polyarthritis, rash) with renal impairment suggest an acute systemic illness rather than chronic CKD (p.2395) Treating an elevated creatinine as chronic without checking prior values - missing a reversible acute or acute-on-chronic process (p.2395). Assuming normal kidney size excludes CKD (diabetic nephropathy early, amyloid, HIV nephropathy retain normal/large kidneys) (p.2394-2395). Stopping ACEi/ARB for a modest (<30%) non-progressive GFR fall - discontinuation in CKD is associated with increased death/cardiovascular events; the small drop usually reflects relieved hyperfiltration (p.2392). Combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB - greater incidence of AKI and adverse cardiac events; avoid dual blockade (p.2396). Overlooking occult potassium sources (dietary salt substitutes) and potassium-retaining drugs (RAS inhibitors, MRAs, potassium-sparing diuretics) as causes of hyperkalemia (p.2389). Gadolinium MRI contrast in advanced CKD - risk of nephrogenic systemic/fibrosing dermopathy; minimize in stage 3 and avoid in stages 4-5 unless essential (older agents) (p.2394). Iodinated radiographic contrast - contrast-induced nephropathy, especially in diabetic nephropathy; avoid where possible (p.2395). Pruritus and skin pigmentation often persist despite dialysis; first rule out unrelated causes (e.g., scabies) and treat hyperphosphatemia (p.2394). Metformin and sulfonylureas are contraindicated below ~half-normal GFR; insulin requirements fall as renal degradation of insulin declines (p.2394). CKD results from two overlapping processes: (1) initiating mechanisms specific to the underlying cause (developmental/genetic, immune-complex, inflammatory, metabolic, microvascular, or toxic injury to vascular, glomerular, or tubulointerstitial compartments), and (2) a nonspecific final common pathway in which loss of nephron mass triggers compensatory hyperfiltration and hypertrophy of remaining nephrons. Intrarenal renin-angiotensin activation with blunted tubuloglomerular feedback raises intraglomerular pressure; this adaptation becomes maladaptive, distorting glomerular architecture, impairing podocyte function and the filtration barrier, and producing progressive sclerosis and nephron dropout. The uremic syndrome arises from three spheres of dysfunction: accumulation of retained solutes (urea and creatinine are only readily-measured but incomplete surrogates for many retained toxins), loss of non-excretory kidney functions (fluid/electrolyte homeostasis, hormone production/regulation - EPO, calcitriol, with altered PTH, FGF-23, insulin), and progressive systemic inflammation (elevated CRP, falling albumin/fetuin) feeding a malnutrition-inflammation-atherosclerosis/calcification syndrome (p.2385-2389). Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality at every stage, and most patients die of it before reaching stage 5; only 30-45% of those who reach stage 5 have advanced cardiovascular complications at that point. Left ventricular hypertrophy and dilated cardiomyopathy are among the strongest predictors of cardiovascular death. Hyperphosphatemia, high FGF-23, and persistently elevated troponin independently predict worse cardiovascular outcomes. A superimposed malnutrition-inflammation-calcification state in advanced disease carries a poor prognosis. Nephrotic-range proteinuria and heavy persistent proteinuria predict faster progression and worse outcomes. Survivors of dialysis-requiring AKI are at high risk of progressive CKD, with up to ~10% developing ESKD (p.2384, 2391-2392, 2362). KDIGO classification stratifies CKD by GFR category and albuminuria, both predicting all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, and progression. GFR categories: G1 >=90, G2 60-89, G3a 45-59, G3b 30-44, G4 15-29, G5 <15 mL/min/1.73 m2. Albuminuria (UACR) categories: A1 <30, A2 30-299, A3 >=300 mg/g. Harrison Table 319-3 stages (abnormality >3 months): Stage 1 (>60 with abnormal urinalysis/imaging), Stage 2 (>60, mild progression risk), Stage 3a (45-60), Stage 3b (30-45), Stage 4 (15-30, prepare for RRT), Stage 5 (<15, highest RRT need). Stages 1-2 are usually asymptomatic; complications emerge in stages 3-4; the full uremic syndrome appears at stage 5 (GFR <15) (p.2385-2388, 2362, Table 319-3).

detailed family history of cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, conduction disease, tachyarrhythmia, and sudden death Chemistries including sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, glucose/glycohemoglobin, creatinine/BUN, albumin and liver tests, lipid profile, TSH, serum iron and transferrin saturation, creatine kinase isoforms, and cardiac troponin Hematology including CBC with differential, total eosinophil count if abnormal, and ESR Targeted infection workup when suspected: HIV, Chagas', Lyme and other tick-borne disease, toxoplasmosis, trichinosis; respiratory pathogen panel in acute respiratory syndromes Endomyocardial biopsy (with electron microscopy sample) when a specific diagnosis with therapeutic implications is suspected Coronary angiography/catheterization in patients with evidence of ischemia or infarction who are candidates for intervention Athlete's heart (mimics HCM and can show LV noncompaction) Severe chronic hypertension (mimics HCM) Aortic stenosis (mimics HCM and should be excluded) Cardiac amyloidosis (causes RCM and can produce asymmetric septal thickening mimicking HCM, especially in older patients) Storage diseases mimicking HCM morphology: GLA/Anderson-Fabry, PRKAG2, and LAMP2/Danon disease Cardiac sarcoidosis (often DCM-pattern or regional wall-motion abnormalities, or RV involvement with arrhythmias, rather than classic restrictive morphology) Coronary artery disease/prior infarction and primary valve disease as structural causes mimicking DCM Radiation, scleroderma-type connective tissue disease, and drugs such as doxorubicin causing an RCM phenotype PVC-related cardiomyopathy versus genetic ACM in patients with frequent PVCs or nonsustained VT Cardiomyopathy denotes primary disease of the heart muscle itself; strictly it excludes myocardial dysfunction secondary to other cardiovascular disease, though common usage also folds in ischemic, valvular, and hypertensive cardiomyopathy. The traditional morphologic scheme recognizes three major phenotypes: hypertrophic (HCM), dilated (DCM), and restrictive (RCM) cardiomyopathy. HCM is characterized by increased left ventricular wall thickness (roughly 13-15 mm depending on context) with a normal or high ejection fraction; LV chamber volume is normal or smaller, and EF is usually above 0.60. DCM is defined when LVEF is at or below 0.50, although most patients present clinically with LVEF at or below 0.40; an LVEF persistently at or below 0.30-0.35 is the threshold considered for primary-prevention ICD. RCM is the least common phenotype and is defined more by physiology (moderate-to-severe diastolic dysfunction and/or elevated cardiac filling pressures) than by morphology; wall thickness is often increased but may appear normal, EF is usually only mildly reduced, and marked atrial enlargement with predominant right heart failure is typical. Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC, originally arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia) is a fourth, predominantly genetic phenotype marked by life-threatening arrhythmias and abnormal RV structure/function with variable LV involvement. Evolving genotype-driven terminology reframes arrhythmogenic disease as ACM-RV (RV-predominant, formerly ARVC), ACM-LV (LV-predominant), and biventricular arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy; in ACM-LV ventricular arrhythmias can dominate before LVEF is severely reduced, so primary-prevention ICD may be considered even with LVEF above 0.35. Phenotypes overlap and shift over time: DCM can undergo reverse remodeling toward higher EF and smaller ventricles with recommended therapy, and about 5% of HCM evolves to a reduced-EF, more restrictive state (HCM-rEF). Mid-range LVEF (0.40-0.50) commonly represents a transition state, either deterioration from early DCM or improvement into DCM remission. Clinical expression frequently follows a two-hit model in which an inherited predisposition is triggered by an acquired insult such as infection, toxic exposure, pregnancy, or tachycardia. Echocardiography is the initial imaging modality; cardiac MRI adds tissue characterization, with late gadolinium enhancement mapping fibrosis and T1/T2 mapping identifying focal and diffuse inflammation. Left ventricular noncompaction is a trait (often assessed by a noncompacted-to-compacted myocardium ratio above 2.3) that can accompany HCM, DCM, dystrophies, and syndromes, but can also appear in normal hearts, in pregnancy, and more often in athletes. Ventricular tachyarrhythmias or nonsustained VT, which may dominate before EF is severely reduced in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy Family history of sudden death, cardiomyopathy, conduction disorders, or skeletal myopathy Embolic events from atrial fibrillation or apical ventricular thrombus as a presentation of unrecognized cardiomyopathy Progressive exertional breathlessness, fatigue, orthopnea, edema, and abdominal symptoms indicating the congestion syndrome Marked wall thickening suggesting amyloidosis, inherited storage disease, or inborn metabolic disease Treating 'congestive heart failure' as a diagnosis or etiology; it is a nonspecific congestion syndrome common to many cardiac conditions (including congenital heart disease, primary pulmonary hypertension, and valve disease) and requires full etiologic evaluation. Over-relying on morphologic phenotype, since phenotypes overlap and shift over time and many entities (sarcomeric variants, storage diseases) can present as either HCM or RCM. Missing amyloidosis in older patients, where it can both cause RCM and mimic the asymmetric septal thickening of HCM. Misclassifying sarcoidosis as restrictive when it more often produces DCM-pattern, regional wall-motion abnormalities, or RV involvement with arrhythmias. Failing to distinguish PVC-related cardiomyopathy from a genetic arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy that itself causes both the arrhythmias and the muscle disease. Interpreting LV noncompaction as inherently pathologic, since it can occur in normal hearts, in pregnancy, and in athletes. Cardiomyopathy reflects intrinsic disease of the myocardium producing characteristic structural and functional abnormalities. In HCM, abnormal myocyte/sarcomere biology drives increased wall thickness with preserved or supranormal systolic function but impaired filling. In DCM, the ventricle dilates with depressed systolic function (low LVEF). In RCM, the dominant abnormality is impaired ventricular filling from a stiff myocardium causing markedly elevated filling pressures and atrial enlargement, often with relatively preserved EF. Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy involves fibrofatty or fibrotic remodeling that creates a substrate for ventricular arrhythmias with variable RV and/or LV structural change. An expanding catalog of pathogenic genetic variants underlies heritable cardiomyopathy, and inherited differences in immune-response pathways contribute to infectious and noninfectious inflammation that can manifest as myocarditis and cardiomyopathy. Clinical disease often requires a second acquired insult superimposed on a genetic predisposition. Prognosis depends on the specific phenotype and underlying cause rather than on classification alone. DCM may improve substantially with reverse remodeling on guideline-directed therapy, whereas about 5% of HCM deteriorates to a reduced-EF, restrictive state. Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy carries a risk of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias that can precede heart failure. Persistent severe LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF at or below 0.30-0.35) identifies patients considered for primary-prevention ICD. Morphologic/functional classification: Hypertrophic (HCM) - septal thickness >=15 mm in men, >=13 mm in women (13-14 mm may suffice in relatives of a proband or with a positive genetic test), LVEF normal or high (usually >0.60), normal/small LV volume. Dilated (DCM) - early: LVEF <=0.50 and/or LV end-diastolic volume >112% of normal for age/sex or LVEDD >95th percentile; LVEF <=0.40 is the threshold for traditionally recommended heart-failure therapy; persistent LVEF <=0.30-0.35 is the threshold for primary-prevention ICD. Restrictive (RCM) - functional diagnosis based on moderate-to-severe diastolic dysfunction and/or elevated filling pressures, usually mildly reduced LVEF, with marked atrial enlargement. Mid-range LVEF (0.40-0.50) represents a transition zone. Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy - ACM-LV (usually DCM morphology), ACM-RV/ARVC (2010 modified task force criteria combining major and minor criteria), and biventricular forms. LV noncompaction trait assessed by noncompacted/compacted ratio >2.3.

cerebellar stroke Overlooking the third nerve palsy when the ataxia dominates the presentation Claude syndrome results from a paramedian dorsal midbrain tegmental lesion, typically ischaemic, in the The infarct damages the oculomotor fascicles, giving an ipsilateral third nerve palsy, together with the inferior red nucleus and the crossing superior cerebellar peduncle (dentatorubrothalamic) fibres, giving contralateral cerebellar ataxia and dysmetria. Because the lesion spares the ventral corticospinal fibres, limb strength is generally preserved, and the movement disorder is one of incoordination rather than the coarse rubral tremor that characterises the more ventrally extending Benedikt syndrome. The oculomotor palsy often improves partially over weeks to months, and the cerebellar ataxia frequently lessens with rehabilitation, giving a generally more favourable functional outcome than syndromes with added hemiparesis.

compromises surgical healing Claw toe results from a muscle imbalance in which the intrinsic muscles of the foot are weak or fail to counterbalance the long extrinsic tendons. The long extensor hyperextends the metatarsophalangeal joint while the long flexor flexes both interphalangeal joints, producing the characteristic clawed posture across several toes. Because the deforming mechanism frequently reflects generalised intrinsic weakness, clawing is strongly linked to neuromuscular disorders such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and other peripheral neuropathies, and to cavus foot deformity, diabetes, and inflammatory arthritis. The hyperextended metatarsophalangeal joint drives the metatarsal head into a plantarflexed and prominent position, increasing plantar pressure and causing metatarsalgia and callosities, while the dorsally elevated interphalangeal joints rub against footwear. Initially flexible, the deformity becomes fixed as capsular and tendon contractures develop. When an underlying neuromuscular cause is stable, flexible claw toes respond well to tendon balancing and offloading, and fixed deformities improve with arthrodesis and metatarsophalangeal realignment. However, recurrence is more likely than with isolated hammer toe because the deforming intrinsic imbalance often persists, and outcomes depend heavily on recognising and managing the underlying disorder and protecting the insensate or ischaemic foot.

Clear cell sarcoma (EWSR1-ATF1, melanoma of soft parts) — clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue, malignant melanoma of soft parts, EWSR1-ATF1 fusion sarcoma, EWSR1-CREB1 fusion sarcoma Metastatic malignant melanoma Synovial sarcoma Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour with melanocytic features Epithelioid sarcoma Perivascular epithelioid cell tumour (PEComa) Other spindle or epithelioid soft-tissue sarcomas MRI of the primary site to define deep extent and relation to tendons and fascia Regional lymph node assessment given the propensity for nodal spread Chest CT for pulmonary metastases Whole-body functional imaging for staging Biopsy with careful tract planning and immunohistochemistry for melanocytic markers Molecular testing for EWSR1 rearrangement and, where needed, assessment for BRAF mutation to help exclude melanoma A rare soft-tissue sarcoma with melanocytic differentiation, historically called malignant melanoma of soft parts Typically affects young to middle-aged adults and characteristically involves the deep soft tissue of the distal extremities, especially around the foot, ankle, and tendons or aponeuroses Often presents as a slowly growing, sometimes painful deep mass attached to tendons or fascia Expresses melanocytic markers such as S100, SOX10, HMB-45, and Melan-A, closely resembling metastatic melanoma histologically Distinguished from cutaneous melanoma by a defining EWSR1-ATF1 (or less commonly EWSR1-CREB1) fusion and by the absence of BRAF mutations typical of melanoma Molecular demonstration of the EWSR1 rearrangement is essential to separate it from metastatic melanoma when morphology and immunohistochemistry overlap Wide surgical excision is the primary treatment, with radiotherapy for local control; it responds poorly to conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy Has a marked tendency for regional lymph node involvement as well as distant metastasis, so nodal assessment is important A deep, enlarging soft-tissue mass near tendons of the distal extremity in a young adult Regional lymphadenopathy accompanying an extremity soft-tissue mass A mass with melanocytic marker positivity but no cutaneous primary melanoma identified New respiratory symptoms suggesting pulmonary metastases Local recurrence after prior excision Misdiagnosing the tumour as metastatic melanoma on the basis of melanocytic markers alone Omitting molecular testing for the EWSR1 fusion that distinguishes it from melanoma Neglecting regional lymph node evaluation despite its notable nodal spread Relying on conventional chemotherapy, to which the tumour is largely resistant Poor biopsy planning that complicates limb-sparing surgery Clear cell sarcoma is a translocation-associated malignancy showing melanocytic differentiation, defined by a EWSR1-ATF1 fusion gene (or the less common EWSR1-CREB1 variant). The chimeric fusion protein aberrantly activates the microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF) pathway, driving melanocytic gene expression and accounting for the tumour's pigment-related markers and melanoma-like appearance. Despite this resemblance, it is genetically distinct from cutaneous melanoma, lacking the characteristic melanoma driver mutations, and its defining fusion provides the basis for accurate diagnosis. The tumour's origin from a primitive neural crest-derived cell explains its melanocytic phenotype in a deep soft-tissue location. Clear cell sarcoma carries a guarded prognosis with frequent late recurrence and metastasis to lymph nodes and lung; outcome relates to tumour size, resectability, and nodal status, and its poor response to conventional chemotherapy contributes to the difficulty of controlling advanced disease.

Overlooking associated anomalies or an underlying syndrome Underestimating feeding and airway difficulties in the neonatal period Neglecting audiological follow-up, allowing undetected hearing loss to impair speech development Timing palate repair without balancing speech benefit against effects on midface growth Orofacial clefting results from failure of fusion of the embryonic facial processes. Cleft lip arises from incomplete fusion of the medial nasal and maxillary processes, which normally unite to form the primary palate, during early facial development. Cleft palate results from failure of the palatal shelves to elevate, meet, and fuse in the midline to form the secondary palate. The aetiology is multifactorial, involving genetic susceptibility and environmental influences such as maternal smoking, alcohol, folate deficiency, and certain medications, and clefts can also occur as part of recognised syndromes. With coordinated multidisciplinary care most children achieve good functional and aesthetic outcomes, normal feeding, and intelligible speech, though some require secondary speech surgery, alveolar bone grafting, orthodontics, and orthognathic surgery into adolescence. Outcomes are influenced by cleft severity, associated syndromes, and access to specialist team care.

cleft mitral valve — isolated cleft anterior mitral leaflet, mitral valve cleft Partial or complete atrioventricular septal defect Mitral valve prolapse Rheumatic mitral regurgitation Double-orifice mitral valve Leaflet perforation from endocarditis Congenital mitral valve dysplasia Transthoracic echocardiography with parasternal short-axis imaging Three-dimensional transthoracic or transoesophageal echocardiography Cardiac MRI for regurgitant fraction Electrocardiography, where a left superior axis suggests the atrioventricular septal defect spectrum Screening for ostium primum atrial septal defect and inlet ventricular septal defect Cardiac catheterisation if pulmonary hypertension is suspected Isolated cleft mitral valve is a slit in the anterior leaflet pointing towards the left ventricular outflow tract, distinct from the atrioventricular septal defect cleft, which points towards the ventricular septum. It presents with mitral regurgitation ranging from an incidental finding to heart failure. It is best seen on parasternal short-axis and 3D echocardiography as a V-shaped indentation in the leaflet during diastole. Atrioventricular septal defect and other endocardial cushion anomalies must always be excluded, as the septal-type cleft accompanies a common atrioventricular junction with an inlet ventricular septal defect or ostium primum atrial septal defect. The regurgitant jet often arises through the cleft and may be eccentric, so severity should be quantified carefully. It is associated with conotruncal anomalies and heterotaxy in some patients. Surgical closure with cleft suture, with or without annuloplasty, is the usual repair and is generally durable. Severe mitral regurgitation with left ventricular dilatation or dysfunction Pulmonary hypertension Heart failure symptoms or failure to thrive Features of an associated atrioventricular septal defect with a significant shunt Mislabelling an atrioventricular septal defect cleft as an isolated cleft despite its different orientation and associations Missing the cleft on standard long-axis views when short-axis or 3D imaging is needed Underestimating eccentric regurgitant jets Overlooking an associated ostium primum atrial septal defect A cleft is a congenital slit-like division of a mitral leaflet, most often the anterior leaflet. An isolated cleft points towards the left ventricular outflow tract and is regarded as a distinct developmental anomaly of the mitral valve, whereas the cleft seen in atrioventricular septal defect represents the commissure between the left superior and inferior bridging leaflets of a common atrioventricular valve and points towards the ventricular septum. In both, the resulting failure of leaflet coaptation produces mitral regurgitation of variable severity, and chronic volume loading leads to left atrial and left ventricular dilatation. An isolated cleft with mild regurgitation may remain stable, whereas significant regurgitation responds well to surgical cleft closure with good long-term durability, although some residual or recurrent regurgitation can occur.

intramembranous and endochondral bone formation. Reduced RUNX2 activity impairs ossification of bones that depend heavily on membranous ossification, especially the clavicles and cranial vault, and disrupts the tooth-forming programme. The result is clavicular hypoplasia, delayed cranial and dental maturation, and a range of skeletal ossification defects, with relative preservation of overall growth. Prognosis is excellent with a normal lifespan and intelligence. Morbidity is mainly dental and orthodontic, together with a modest increase in fracture risk and reduced bone density; multidisciplinary dental care is central to management.

arrange long-term radiological surveillance CLIPPERS is characterised by a chronic, predominantly T-lymphocytic perivascular inflammatory infiltrate concentrated in the pons, brainstem, and The inflammation surrounds small vessels and correlates with the punctate perivascular contrast enhancement seen on MRI. No specific antigen or antibody has been identified, and the disorder is defined clinically, radiologically, and pathologically together with its striking corticosteroid responsiveness. Because similar perivascular inflammation can herald lymphoma or other conditions, CLIPPERS is regarded as a syndrome requiring exclusion of mimics and ongoing surveillance. Cloacal exstrophy — OEIS complex, vesicointestinal fissure, exstrophy of the cloaca Classic bladder exstrophy Omphalocele or gastroschisis in isolation Cloacal malformation (persistent cloaca) in females Anorectal malformation with associated anomalies Caudal regression syndrome Limb-body wall complex Renal and abdominal ultrasound to assess the upper tracts and associated anomalies Spinal ultrasound and MRI to detect dysraphism and tethered cord Echocardiography and skeletal imaging for associated anomalies Karyotype and multidisciplinary DSD evaluation to guide gender and genital management Contrast studies of the bowel to define hindgut anatomy Serial renal function assessment The most severe form of the exstrophy-epispadias complex, in which an exstrophied segment of hindgut/caecum lies between two exstrophied bladder halves on the lower abdominal wall Frequently occurs as the OEIS complex: Omphalocele, Exstrophy of the cloaca, Imperforate anus, and Spinal defects Associated anomalies are the rule and include omphalocele, imperforate anus with a foreshortened or blind-ending hindgut, spinal dysraphism and tethered cord, and skeletal, renal, and genital anomalies Genital anomalies are marked; in males the phallus is often bifid or diminutive, historically raising complex questions of gender assignment now guided by multidisciplinary DSD care Because of the visceral and neural involvement, management is far more complex than for classic bladder exstrophy Neonatal care requires a coordinated team addressing the omphalocele, bowel diversion, staged closure of the exstrophy, and neurosurgical assessment of any spinal cord lesion Long-term goals include urinary and faecal continence (often via reconstruction and stomas), preservation of renal function, and attention to sexual and psychosocial outcomes Neonatal instability from the omphalocele, exposed viscera, or associated cardiac disease Progressive neurological deficit from a tethered or dysraphic spinal cord Upper-tract obstruction or deteriorating renal function Sepsis from exposed bowel and bladder plates or after reconstruction Treating it as a more severe bladder exstrophy while overlooking the bowel, spinal, and genital components Missing occult spinal dysraphism or tethered cord that needs neurosurgical input Making premature or unilateral decisions on gender assignment outside a multidisciplinary DSD framework Failing to coordinate the many specialties required for staged reconstruction Cloacal exstrophy results from a very early and extensive developmental failure of the lower abdominal wall, in which an abnormal, prematurely disrupted cloacal membrane and defective mesenchymal migration occur before the urorectal septum has divided the cloaca. As a result the bladder is split into two halves that flank an exstrophied central plate of hindgut, and the anus is imperforate. Because the insult occurs so early and involves the cloaca, associated omphalocele, spinal dysraphism, and genital and skeletal anomalies are common, reflecting a global disturbance of caudal embryonic development rather than an isolated urinary tract defect. Survival has improved markedly with modern neonatal and staged surgical care, but children face multiple reconstructive operations and lifelong management of urinary and faecal continence, renal function, spinal and orthopaedic issues, and sexual and psychosocial development, so outcomes remain guarded and highly individual.

atresia Abdominal distension or failure to pass meconium indicating bowel obstruction before diversion Mislabelling a cloaca as a simple imperforate anus and failing to recognise the single perineal prognosis Attempting definitive reconstruction outside an experienced specialist centre without fully delineating the anatomy Failing to plan for menstrual outflow and Mullerian anomalies, which may present with obstruction at puberty A cloacal malformation arises from failure of normal partitioning of the embryonic cloaca, the common terminal chamber into which the hindgut and urogenital sinus drain. In normal development the urorectal septum descends to divide this chamber into an anterior urogenital sinus and a posterior anorectal canal, while the cloacal membrane breaks down to create separate perineal openings. When this septation and descent are disturbed, the urinary tract, genital tract and rectum remain confluent and drain through a single common channel that opens onto the perineum. The length of this common channel reflects how early and how severely development was disrupted, and associated maldevelopment commonly affects the sacrum, spinal cord, kidneys and Mullerian structures, producing the frequently duplicated or obstructed vagina and uterus and the renal and neurological anomalies that accompany the malformation. Outcome depends heavily on the length of the common channel, the quality of the sacrum and spinal cord, and associated renal anomalies; children with short channels and good sacral anatomy often achieve satisfactory urinary and faecal continence, whereas long common channels are associated with greater need for intermittent catheterisation, bowel management and reconstructive interventions. Preservation of renal function and attention to future menstrual, sexual and reproductive function are central long-term goals.

Clonorchiasis — Clonorchis sinensis, Chinese liver fluke infection, Oriental liver fluke Opisthorchiasis (Opisthorchis viverrini/felineus), clinically and morphologically very similar Fascioliasis and other liver flukes Ascending bacterial cholangitis from other causes Choledocholithiasis and biliary strictures Cholangiocarcinoma arising de novo Recurrent pyogenic cholangitis of other aetiology Stool microscopy (with concentration) for the characteristic small operculated eggs Duodenal or bile aspirate examination when stool is negative but suspicion is high Full blood count for eosinophilia Liver function tests to assess cholestasis Abdominal ultrasound, CT or MRCP to show ductal dilatation, flukes, stones or a mass Serological or antigen testing where available as an adjunct Caused by the trematode Clonorchis sinensis and endemic in East Asia, including China, Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and eastern Russia, where freshwater fish is a dietary staple Acquired by eating raw, undercooked, pickled or smoked freshwater fish containing infective metacercariae The adult flukes reside in the intrahepatic bile ducts; The larvae excyst in the duodenum, migrate up the ampulla into the biliary tree, and mature into adult flukes that live in the intrahepatic bile ducts for years. Mechanical irritation, secretions and immune-mediated inflammation produce biliary epithelial hyperplasia, periductal fibrosis and ductal dilatation. Chronic stasis predisposes to intrahepatic stone formation and recurrent pyogenic (bacterial) cholangitis, and long-standing epithelial injury with hyperplasia underlies the increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma. Light infections carry an excellent prognosis and respond well to anthelmintic therapy, but heavy chronic infection can lead to irreversible biliary fibrosis, recurrent cholangitis and a significantly increased lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma.

Clouston syndrome — hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia type 2, GJB6, connexin 30 Anhidrotic (hypohidrotic) ectodermal dysplasia (EDA/EDAR pathway) Pachyonychia congenita Other hereditary palmoplantar keratodermas Keratitis-ichthyosis-deafness (KID) syndrome (also connexin-related) Nail-patella syndrome Dyskeratosis congenita Molecular genetic testing of GJB6 Nail assessment and mycological sampling for secondary onychomycosis Trichoscopy and hair examination Assessment of palmoplantar keratoderma and function Family history and pedigree analysis Dental and audiological review to help distinguish from other ectodermal dysplasias An autosomal dominant hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia defined by the triad of nail dystrophy, palmoplantar keratoderma and hair defects Caused by variants in GJB6, which encodes the gap-junction protein connexin 30 Crucially, sweating is normal (hidrotic), distinguishing it from the anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasias where heat intolerance is a major concern Nail changes are prominent, with thickened, slow-growing, discoloured and dystrophic nails that are prone to infection Hair is sparse, fine and brittle, with partial or total alopecia of the scalp, eyebrows and body hair A diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma and hyperpigmentation over the knuckles and other bony prominences are common Diagnosis is clinical, supported by family history and GJB6 molecular testing; management is supportive with nail, hair and keratoderma care Recurrent or severe nail-bed infection Painful fissuring of palmoplantar keratoderma impairing function Features atypical for a hidrotic dysplasia suggesting an alternative syndrome Significant psychosocial impact from alopecia and nail changes Confusing it with anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia and warning unnecessarily about heat intolerance Overlooking secondary onychomycosis superimposed on dystrophic nails Attributing hair loss to a primary alopecia rather than the ectodermal dysplasia Neglecting genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant condition Clouston syndrome is caused by dominant variants in GJB6, encoding connexin 30, a gap-junction protein that forms intercellular channels in the epidermis and its appendages. Defective connexin 30 impairs communication between keratinocytes and disturbs the development and maintenance of ectodermal structures derived from surface ectoderm, namely nails, hair and the palmoplantar epidermis. Because eccrine sweat glands are relatively spared, sweating remains normal, which clinically separates this hidrotic dysplasia from the anhidrotic forms caused by defects in the ectodysplasin pathway. The condition is compatible with a normal lifespan and, because sweating is preserved, lacks the heat-intolerance risks of anhidrotic dysplasias; the main burden is cosmetic and from nail and keratoderma complications.

affected tissue and wrongly excluding a mosaic PIK3CA variant Confusing CLOVES with Klippel-Trenaunay or Proteus syndrome despite differing genetics and complications Underestimating thrombotic risk in extensive vascular malformations Neglecting spinal surveillance for scoliosis or cord compromise CLOVES syndrome results from somatic mosaic gain-of-function variants in PIK3CA, which encodes the catalytic subunit of phosphoinositide 3-kinase. Constitutive activation of PIK3CA drives the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, promoting unregulated cell growth, proliferation, and survival in the tissues carrying the variant. Because the mutation arises after fertilisation, only a subset of cells is affected, producing the segmental, asymmetric overgrowth of fat, vessels, skin, and bone that defines the phenotype; the distribution and burden of mutant cells determine clinical severity. The course is highly variable and depends on the extent and location of overgrowth and vascular involvement; some individuals have limited disease while others face progressive functional and orthopaedic complications. Emerging targeted pathway inhibitors and multidisciplinary care have improved management of severe disease.

Clubfoot — congenital talipes equinovarus, CTEV, talipes, congenital clubfoot Postural (positional) talipes that corrects fully with manipulation Metatarsus adductus Congenital vertical talus Neuromuscular clubfoot (e.g. secondary to spina bifida or arthrogryposis) Syndromic foot deformity Tibial or fibular deficiency Clinical examination to assess rigidity and classify severity Full musculoskeletal and neurological examination to detect associated conditions Examination and, if indicated, imaging of the hips for developmental dysplasia Antenatal ultrasound detection and postnatal confirmation Spinal imaging or specialist assessment where a neuromuscular cause is suspected A congenital deformity present at birth in which the foot is held in equinus, hindfoot varus, midfoot cavus, and forefoot adductus (remembered as the components of talipes equinovarus) The key clinical distinction is between a rigid, structural clubfoot and a flexible 'postural' foot that corrects with gentle manipulation It is often idiopathic but may be associated with neuromuscular conditions (e.g. spina bifida), syndromes, or oligohydramnios, so a general and neurological examination is important Diagnosis is clinical; the deformity is frequently detected on antenatal ultrasound, and examination should exclude associated abnormalities such as developmental dysplasia of the hip The Ponseti method of serial casting is the mainstay of treatment, gradually correcting the deformity, usually followed by a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy to address residual equinus Maintenance with a foot-abduction (boots-and-bar) orthosis is essential to prevent relapse, and poor brace compliance is the commonest cause of recurrence Treatment should begin early in the neonatal period when the tissues are most amenable to correction Surgery is reserved for resistant, relapsed, or neglected deformities not corrected by casting Associated neuromuscular disorder or spinal dysraphism requiring broader assessment Failure to progress with casting, or early relapse, indicating a resistant or syndromic foot Neglected or late-presenting rigid deformity limiting non-surgical correction Signs of an alternative diagnosis such as congenital vertical talus Mistaking a rigid structural clubfoot for a flexible postural foot and delaying treatment Under-emphasising brace compliance, the leading cause of relapse Overlooking an associated neuromuscular or syndromic condition, or concurrent hip dysplasia Attempting forceful correction or premature surgery instead of graduated casting Congenital talipes equinovarus arises from abnormal development and positioning of the bones, joints, muscles, and soft tissues of the foot and ankle, with contracture of the medial and posterior soft tissues (including the tendo Achillis, tibialis posterior, and plantar structures) and abnormal alignment of the talus, calcaneus, and navicular. The exact cause is multifactorial, with genetic predisposition and intrauterine factors implicated; in syndromic or neuromuscular cases an underlying disorder disturbs the muscle balance across the developing foot. The result is a fixed deformity combining hindfoot equinus and varus with midfoot cavus and forefoot adduction, which becomes increasingly rigid and structurally established if untreated. With early Ponseti treatment and disciplined brace use, most idiopathic clubfeet achieve a functional, plantigrade, pain-free foot, though a minority relapse and need repeat casting or surgery; syndromic and neuromuscular clubfeet are stiffer, more prone to recurrence, and have a less predictable outcome.

Cluster headache — trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia, histamine headache, suicide headache Migraine, particularly unilateral migraine Paroxysmal hemicrania (indomethacin-responsive) SUNCT/SUNA syndromes Trigeminal neuralgia Acute angle-closure glaucoma Secondary headache from a pituitary or posterior fossa lesion or carotid dissection MRI of the brain with attention to the pituitary and cavernous sinus to exclude secondary causes MR or CT angiography when a vascular cause such as dissection or aneurysm is suspected Pituitary hormone screen if imaging suggests a sellar lesion ECG before starting verapamil and monitoring during dose changes Characterised by attacks of severe, strictly unilateral pain centred on the orbit or temple, usually lasting between 15 minutes and 3 hours Attacks are accompanied by ipsilateral cranial autonomic features such as lacrimation, conjunctival redness, nasal congestion or rhinorrhoea, and sometimes a partial Horner syndrome Unlike migraine sufferers who prefer to lie still, patients are typically restless and agitated during an attack, often pacing or rocking Attacks cluster into bouts lasting weeks to months separated by remission periods, and there is a striking circadian and seasonal rhythm with nocturnal attacks common Alcohol and other vasodilators can reliably provoke attacks during an active cluster period but not during remission High-flow oxygen and fast-acting triptan therapy are the mainstays of acute abortive treatment, while verapamil is a common preventive principle The condition shows a male predominance and is strongly linked with tobacco use Neuroimaging is warranted at presentation to exclude a structural or pituitary lesion mimicking the syndrome First or worst attack, or a change in established attack pattern, suggesting a secondary cause Persistent Horner syndrome or other fixed neurological deficit between attacks Features suggesting carotid dissection such as neck pain with Horner syndrome Papilloedema or other signs of raised intracranial pressure Misdiagnosing the attacks as migraine or sinusitis and delaying effective treatment Overlooking paroxysmal hemicrania, which is exquisitely responsive to indomethacin, in short frequent attacks Failing to obtain neuroimaging to exclude a secondary or pituitary cause Starting verapamil without baseline and follow-up ECG monitoring for conduction effects Cluster headache is the most common trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia. The pain reflects activation of the trigeminovascular system, while the accompanying autonomic signs arise from cranial parasympathetic outflow and sympathetic dysfunction. The pronounced circadian and seasonal periodicity implicates the posterior hypothalamus, which shows activation on functional imaging during attacks and is thought to act as the disorder's generator or pacemaker. Episodic cluster headache typically follows a relapsing course with prolonged remissions, whereas a minority develop chronic cluster headache with little or no remission. Preventive therapy substantially reduces attack frequency in most patients, but the disorder can be highly disabling during active bouts.

Coagulation Disorders — hemophilia, von Willebrand disease, bleeding disorders Hemophilia A versus hemophilia B (clinically indistinguishable; require factor assays to differentiate) (Harrison 22e p.930) Von Willebrand disease with low FVIII versus hemophilia A (VWD must be excluded in a patient with prolonged aPTT and low FVIII and no known hemophilia history) (Harrison 22e p.930) Factor XI deficiency (hemophilia C) and other rare inherited factor deficiencies (FII, FV, FVII, FX, FXIII, fibrinogen) (Harrison 22e p.928, 931-932) Qualitative platelet function disorders (e.g., Glanzmann thrombasthenia, Bernard-Soulier syndrome, storage pool disorder) as a cause of mucocutaneous bleeding with normal coagulation factor levels (Harrison 22e p.926) PT and aPTT as first-line screens for clotting factor deficiency (Harrison 22e p.928) Mixing study (correction with normal plasma indicates factor deficiency; failure to correct indicates an inhibitor or anticoagulant) (Harrison 22e p.928) Individual factor activity assays to identify the specific deficient factor (Harrison 22e p.928) Bethesda assay to define inhibitor specificity and titer (expressed in Bethesda units; classifies low- vs high-responder patients) with annual aPTT/mixing-study screening at hemophilia centers (Harrison 22e p.930-931) VWD laboratory panel: aPTT, VWF antigen, VWF activity, FVIII activity, and multimer analysis to classify type 1, 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N, and 3 (Harrison 22e p.926-927) Chromogenic FVIII activity assay using bovine substrates when emicizumab is present (routine aPTT and FVIII activity are inaccurate) (Harrison 22e p.931) Molecular/genetic testing for F8 or F9 mutations to enable precise carrier diagnosis in affected families (Harrison 22e p.930) Acquired von Willebrand syndrome from lymphoproliferative disorders / MGUS / multiple myeloma / Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (suspect with new-onset severe mucosal bleeding, especially in the elderly) (Harrison 22e p.927) Acquired VWD due to high shear: cardiac valvular disease and Heyde syndrome (aortic stenosis with GI bleeding from angiodysplasia; shear unfolds VWF causing loss of large multimers, reversed by valve replacement) (Harrison 22e p.927) Acquired VWD in myeloproliferative disorders with markedly elevated platelet counts (>1.5 million) due to platelet-VWF binding and clearance (Harrison 22e p.926) Acquired inhibitors (autoantibodies) to clotting factors in patients without genetic deficiency: postpartum, autoimmune or neoplastic disease, idiopathic, or rarely after topical bovine thrombin exposure in complex surgery (Harrison 22e p.928) Liver disease, DIC, and vitamin K deficiency as acquired multifactor coagulopathies (Harrison 22e p.928) The most common inherited factor deficiencies are the hemophilias, X-linked recessive diseases due to deficiency of factor VIII (hemophilia A, ~80% of cases) or factor IX (hemophilia B); hemophilia A and B are clinically indistinguishable (Harrison 22e p.928, 930). Disease phenotype correlates with factor activity level: severe (<1%), moderate (1-5%), mild (6-30%). Severe and moderate disease cause bleeding into joints (hemarthrosis), soft tissues, and muscles after minor trauma or spontaneously; mild disease bleeds infrequently and usually only after trauma (Harrison 22e p.930). Recurrent hemarthroses (knees, elbows, ankles, shoulders, hips) damage a joint to create a chronically affected 'target joint' with synovitis and progressive deformity; deep-muscle hematomas can cause compartment syndrome by compressing arteries, veins, or nerves (Harrison 22e p.930). Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder (symptomatic prevalence ~1 in 1000 to 1 in 10,000); VWF tethers platelets to subendothelium and is the carrier protein that prolongs the FVIII half-life (Harrison 22e p.927). Most VWD symptoms are 'platelet-like' (mucocutaneous: bruising, epistaxis, heavy menstrual bleeding); type 1 (parallel reduction in VWF protein, function, and FVIII) is most common (>=80% of cases) (Harrison 22e p.926-927). Type 2N VWD ('autosomal hemophilia') is caused by VWF variants that impair FVIII binding, markedly shortening the FVIII half-life and lowering FVIII levels (Harrison 22e p.927). Screening hemostasis tests: an isolated prolonged PT suggests FVII deficiency; a prolonged aPTT indicates an intrinsic-pathway deficiency, most commonly FVIII, FIX, or FXI; prolongation of both PT and aPTT suggests deficiency of FV, FX, FII, or a fibrinogen abnormality (Harrison 22e p.928). Mixing study principle: adding normal pooled plasma corrects a prolonged PT/aPTT due to a factor deficiency but fails to correct when an inhibitor (antibody) is present; if it corrects, individual factor activity assays identify the deficient factor (Harrison 22e p.928). Inhibitor (alloantibody) formation is the major complication of hemophilia treatment, with prevalence ~30% in severe hemophilia A, ~10% in nonsevere hemophilia A, and only 3-5% in hemophilia B; inhibitors increase morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.930-931). Acquired coagulation factor deficiencies are more frequent than congenital disorders; the most common are the hemorrhagic diathesis of liver disease, DIC, and vitamin K deficiency, each typically involving more than one clotting factor (Harrison 22e p.928). Bleeding into the oropharyngeal spaces, central nervous system, or retroperitoneum is life-threatening and requires immediate therapy (Harrison 22e p.930) Retroperitoneal hemorrhage may form a calcified inflammatory mass (pseudotumor syndrome) and damage the femoral nerve; pseudotumors can also form in long bones (Harrison 22e p.930) Deep-muscle hematomas of the distal limbs can cause compartment syndrome from external compression of arteries, veins, or nerves (Harrison 22e p.930) Failure to respond to factor replacement at therapeutic doses suggests an inhibitor; early detection is critical (Harrison 22e p.930) In carriers/women, postpartum hemorrhage risk rises after delivery as the pregnancy-induced rise in clotting factor levels falls rapidly (Harrison 22e p.931) FXII (Hageman factor), high-molecular-weight kininogen, and prekallikrein deficiencies markedly prolong the aPTT but do NOT cause bleeding (no bleeding phenotype; treatment is not indicated) — do not treat the lab abnormality (Harrison 22e p.928). Not all patients with low VWF levels bleed; mildly decreased VWF should be diagnosed as VWD only with bleeding symptoms and/or a family history, and type O blood physiologically lowers VWF (overlapping the diagnostic range) (Harrison 22e p.926-927). Bleeding phenotype does not always correlate with factor activity in FXI deficiency, and a negative bleeding history with prior procedures does NOT exclude increased hemorrhage risk (Harrison 22e p.931-932). Family history of hemophilia is absent in ~30% of cases (de novo mutations), so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.930). Antifibrinolytic drugs are NOT indicated for hematuria because of the risk of an occlusive clot obstructing the genitourinary tract (Harrison 22e p.931). Plasma coagulation factor deficiencies impair secondary hemostasis (the coagulation cascade). Inherited hemophilia A and B are X-linked recessive disorders from mutations in F8 and F9 respectively; affected males bleed while carrier women are generally asymptomatic, although a wide range of factor activity from random X-inactivation (lyonization) can produce bleeding in some carriers. FVIII has a very short intrinsic circulating half-life (~25-30 min) that is extended to roughly 12 h when complexed with von Willebrand factor (VWF). VWD reflects quantitative or qualitative defects of VWF, which serves both as the adhesion molecule tethering platelets to exposed subendothelium (function dependent on large VWF multimers) and as the FVIII carrier; loss of high-molecular-weight multimers (e.g., via excessive ADAMTS13 cleavage in type 2A/2B, or shear-induced unfolding) impairs platelet adhesion. Acquired deficiencies (liver disease, DIC, vitamin K deficiency) usually involve multiple factors and perturb both primary (platelet/vessel wall) and secondary (coagulation) hemostasis. (Harrison 22e p.926-930) Without treatment severe hemophilia may limit life expectancy; with modern recombinant factor concentrates, prophylaxis, and viral-inactivated products, life expectancy of severe hemophilia is now only ~10 years shorter than the general male population and near normal in mild/moderate disease. Since 1998 no new viral hepatitis or HIV infections have been reported in hemophilia patients, though aging patients carry burdens of arthropathy, chronic pain, and prior HCV/HIV infection (hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common cause of death in HIV-negative patients). TTP-related microangiopathy and inhibitors worsen prognosis when present. (Harrison 22e p.930-932) Hemophilia A/B by factor VIII or IX activity: severe (<1%), moderate (1-5%), mild (6-30%); patients with baseline activity >25% may be detected only after major trauma or as an isolated prolonged aPTT. VWD classified into types 1, 2 (subtypes 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N), and 3 (severe, with virtually absent VWF and FVIII usually <10%) using VWF antigen, VWF activity, FVIII activity, and multimer pattern. Inhibitor patients classified as low responders (<5 Bethesda units) or high responders (>5 BU or anamnestic rise). (Harrison 22e p.926-931)

Coal workers' pneumoconiosis — CWP, black lung disease, coal miner's lung, anthracosis (severe) Silicosis and mixed-dust pneumoconiosis Pulmonary tuberculosis (may coexist and complicate) Sarcoidosis Pulmonary metastases or primary lung carcinoma (masses) Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis Rheumatoid lung nodules Chest radiograph with ILO classification of small opacities and large opacity categories High-resolution CT to characterise nodularity, conglomerate masses, and emphysema Detailed occupational and exposure history Spirometry and lung volumes to define obstructive, restrictive, or mixed impairment Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide Consideration of tuberculosis testing where masses cavitate or grow rapidly Arises from chronic inhalation of coal mine dust, with risk tied to cumulative exposure and to the rank (carbon content) of the coal Simple pneumoconiosis is often asymptomatic and detected on imaging as small upper-zone nodular opacities Progressive massive fibrosis (complicated CWP) is defined by coalescent conglomerate masses, typically in the upper zones, causing breathlessness and airflow limitation Caplan syndrome describes rounded fibrotic nodules occurring in coal (and other dust) exposure alongside rheumatoid arthritis The coal macule, a dust-laden macrophage collection around respiratory bronchioles, is the fundamental histological lesion and drives focal (centrilobular) emphysema A careful occupational history including years underground and job type is central to diagnosis, as there is no curative treatment Disease may progress even after exposure has ceased, so surveillance and cessation of further dust exposure are key Rapidly enlarging or cavitating mass suggesting superimposed tuberculosis or malignancy Accelerated progressive massive fibrosis with rapid decline in lung function Haemoptysis prompting exclusion of carcinoma or mycobacterial disease New systemic symptoms or weight loss requiring evaluation for alternative pathology Attributing all coal-worker breathlessness to pneumoconiosis while missing coexistent COPD or heart disease Overlooking superimposed tuberculosis or malignancy within a conglomerate mass Assuming disease stabilises once mining stops, when progression can still occur Failing to take an adequate occupational history in a patient presenting with upper-zone nodules Inhaled coal dust particles that reach the small airways and alveoli are engulfed by macrophages, which accumulate around respiratory bronchioles to form pigmented coal macules, the earliest lesion. Persistent dust burden and the resulting release of inflammatory mediators and reactive oxygen species provoke fibroblast activation and collagen deposition, producing fibrotic nodules. In simple disease these remain small and discrete, but with heavy exposure nodules enlarge and coalesce into large conglomerate masses (progressive massive fibrosis), which distort lung architecture, destroy vasculature, and cause focal emphysema. Coexisting silica in mixed dusts accelerates and worsens fibrosis. Simple coal workers' pneumoconiosis often remains stable and asymptomatic, whereas progressive massive fibrosis causes progressive breathlessness, respiratory failure, and increased mortality; there is no reversal, so prevention through dust control and exposure cessation is paramount.

Coarctation of the Aorta — CoA, aortic coarctation, coarctation Interrupted aortic arch Hypoplastic left heart syndrome Critical aortic stenosis Other duct-dependent systemic circulation lesions Essential hypertension in an older child Peripheral vascular disease Four-limb blood pressure measurement and simultaneous upper- and lower-limb pulse assessment Echocardiography to define coarctation site, severity, and associated lesions such as bicuspid valve Chest radiograph for rib notching and aortic contour in older children CT or MR angiography for detailed arch anatomy Assessment for acidosis and end-organ perfusion in the collapsing neonate A narrowing of the aorta, most often just distal to the left subclavian artery near the ductal region, obstructing flow to the lower body. The hallmark examination finding is diminished, delayed, or absent femoral pulses compared with the upper limbs, with a blood pressure gradient higher in the arms than the legs. Severe coarctation may be duct-dependent in the neonate: as the ductus arteriosus closes, lower-body perfusion falls, producing shock, acidosis, and heart failure. A prostaglandin infusion is used to reopen or maintain ductal patency and restore lower-body perfusion while stabilising a critically ill neonate before repair. Older children may be asymptomatic and present with an incidentally found murmur, upper-limb hypertension, headaches, or leg claudication. Coarctation is commonly associated with a bicuspid aortic valve and may occur with other left-sided obstructive lesions and Turner syndrome. Chest radiograph in older children can show rib notching from collateral vessels and a figure-3 aortic contour. Echocardiography defines the site and severity of narrowing and associated lesions; CT or MR angiography is useful for detailed anatomy. Repair by surgery or catheter intervention relieves the obstruction, but lifelong follow-up is needed for recoarctation and persistent hypertension. Neonatal circulatory collapse with shock and acidosis as the ductus arteriosus closes in duct-dependent coarctation Absent or markedly weak femoral pulses with an upper-to-lower limb blood pressure gradient Signs of heart failure and poor lower-body perfusion in an infant Severe upper-limb hypertension with headaches or hypertensive complications Evidence of end-organ hypoperfusion such as oliguria or feeding intolerance Failing to palpate femoral pulses and compare limb blood pressures in an unwell neonate or hypertensive child Missing a duct-dependent coarctation until the neonate collapses as the ductus closes Attributing upper-limb hypertension in a child to essential hypertension without checking for a gradient Overlooking associated bicuspid aortic valve and other left-sided lesions Assuming successful repair eliminates the need for ongoing hypertension and recoarctation surveillance A discrete or long-segment narrowing of the aortic lumen creates a mechanical obstruction to systemic outflow. Proximal to the obstruction, pressure rises, producing upper-body hypertension and left ventricular pressure overload; distal to it, perfusion pressure falls, causing weak lower-body pulses. In severe neonatal coarctation, lower-body perfusion depends on right-to-left flow through the ductus arteriosus, so ductal closure precipitates hypoperfusion, metabolic acidosis, and circulatory collapse. In slowly progressive disease, collateral arterial channels develop to bypass the obstruction. Early repair of significant coarctation gives a good outlook, but patients need lifelong surveillance for recoarctation, residual or late hypertension, aneurysm formation, and associated valve disease. Unrecognised severe neonatal coarctation can be rapidly fatal.

Coarctation of the aorta — aortic coarctation Interrupted aortic arch Other causes of neonatal collapse (sepsis, metabolic, other duct-dependent lesions) Secondary hypertension of other cause Aortic arch hypoplasia Middle aortic syndrome Four-limb blood pressure and pulse assessment Echocardiography to define the coarctation and associated lesions CT or MR angiography for anatomy and collaterals Chest radiograph (rib notching, aortic contour) Assessment for bicuspid aortic valve and Turner syndrome A narrowing of the aorta, typically just distal to the left subclavian artery near the ductal insertion Presents in neonates with collapse as the duct closes, or later with hypertension and reduced leg pulses The classic sign is radio-femoral delay with upper-limb hypertension and weak, delayed femoral pulses Rib notching from collateral vessels and a figure-of-three aortic contour may be seen on imaging in older children and adults It is strongly associated with bicuspid aortic valve and with Turner syndrome Duct-dependent neonatal presentations require prostaglandin to maintain the duct before repair Neonatal collapse as the duct closes Severe upper-limb hypertension or heart failure Features suggesting aortic aneurysm or dissection in adults Recoarctation after repair Missing the diagnosis by not checking femoral pulses and leg blood pressure Failing to start prostaglandin in a collapsing duct-dependent neonate Overlooking associated bicuspid aortic valve Assuming cure after repair and not monitoring for recoarctation and hypertension Coarctation is a discrete narrowing of the aortic lumen, usually in the juxtaductal region, that obstructs systemic outflow. In duct-dependent neonates, closure of the arterial duct unmasks severe obstruction, causing left ventricular failure and shock. In those presenting later, chronic obstruction drives upper-body hypertension and the development of collateral arteries bypassing the narrowing, while the left ventricle hypertrophies against the increased afterload. Associated bicuspid aortic valve and aortopathy contribute to long-term risk. With timely repair prognosis is good, but lifelong follow-up is needed for recoarctation, persistent or recurrent hypertension, and aortopathy-related complications.

Coats disease (retinal telangiectasia) — Coats' disease, retinal telangiectasia, exudative retinopathy, Leber miliary aneurysms Retinoblastoma Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy Retinopathy of prematurity Persistent fetal vasculature Ocular toxocariasis Von Hippel-Lindau retinal capillary haemangioblastoma Incontinentia pigmenti-associated retinopathy Dilated fundus examination, often under anaesthesia in children, to map telangiectasia, exudate and detachment Fluorescein angiography to demonstrate aneurysmal vessels, non-perfusion and leakage B-scan ultrasonography to assess detachment and exclude the calcification typical of retinoblastoma Optical coherence tomography to evaluate macular exudate and subretinal fluid where media permit Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) when retinoblastoma cannot be excluded clinically Wide-field retinal imaging to document extent and monitor treatment response Predominantly affects young boys and is usually unilateral, often presenting with leukocoria, strabismus or reduced vision detected incidentally or by a parent Hallmark findings are retinal telangiectasia and aneurysmal (light-bulb) vessel dilatation with massive intraretinal and subretinal lipid (yellow exudate) Exudation can progress to an exudative (non-rhegmatogenous) retinal detachment, which in advanced cases fills much of the vitreous cavity A key differential is retinoblastoma, and distinguishing the two is critical because management and prognosis differ radically Fluorescein angiography highlights the telangiectatic and aneurysmal vessels, areas of capillary non-perfusion and leakage Management principles centre on ablating abnormal vessels with laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy, with anti-VEGF or steroid adjuncts and surgery for advanced detachment The condition is typically sporadic and non-hereditary, though somatic mutations affecting retinal vascular development are implicated Early detection and treatment give the best chance of preserving vision and avoiding enucleation for a blind painful eye Leukocoria in a child, which mandates urgent exclusion of retinoblastoma Total exudative retinal detachment threatening irreversible visual loss Neovascular glaucoma producing a painful blind eye Rapid progression of exudation despite treatment Mistaking Coats disease for retinoblastoma or vice versa, with catastrophic consequences for management Underestimating the extent of peripheral telangiectasia and undertreating abnormal vessels Delaying examination under anaesthesia in an uncooperative child, allowing progression Failing to monitor for recurrence of exudation after apparently successful ablation Coats disease is an idiopathic disorder of retinal vascular development in which the retinal capillaries, arterioles and venules become telangiectatic and form saccular aneurysms. Breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier in these abnormal vessels allows lipid-rich plasma to leak into and beneath the retina, producing the characteristic yellowish exudate. Progressive exudation and fluid accumulation lead to an exudative retinal detachment, and long-standing disease can cause neovascular glaucoma, cataract and a blind, painful eye. The process is usually unilateral and sporadic, reflecting a localised abnormality of retinal endothelial integrity rather than a systemic vascular disease. Outcome depends on the stage at diagnosis: eyes treated before macular involvement or extensive detachment can retain useful vision, whereas advanced disease with total detachment or neovascular glaucoma often results in poor vision and may require removal of a painful blind eye.

Cobalamin A/B defect (vitamin B12-responsive methylmalonic acidaemia) — cblA defect, cblB defect, MMAA deficiency, MMAB deficiency, vitamin B12-responsive methylmalonic aciduria, adenosylcobalamin deficiency Methylmalonic acidaemia from methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (mut) deficiency Combined methylmalonic acidaemia and homocystinuria (cblC/cblD defects) Propionic acidaemia Dietary or maternal vitamin B12 deficiency Other organic acidaemias with hyperammonaemia Transcobalamin and intrinsic-factor cobalamin transport defects Urine organic acids demonstrating markedly elevated methylmalonic acid Plasma acylcarnitine profile showing raised propionylcarnitine (C3) Plasma total homocysteine (normal here, distinguishing from cblC/cblD) Blood gas, ammonia, glucose and lactate during acute presentations A supervised hydroxocobalamin responsiveness trial Complementation studies and MMAA/MMAB molecular genetic testing to define the subtype Autosomal recessive disorders of intramitochondrial adenosylcobalamin synthesis (cblA due to MMAA, cblB due to MMAB) that impair methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, causing isolated methylmalonic acidaemia They are the classic vitamin B12-responsive forms of methylmalonic acidaemia, and the cblA subtype in particular often responds well to hydroxocobalamin Present with metabolic acidosis, hyperammonaemia, vomiting, lethargy and failure to thrive, typically precipitated by protein load or catabolic illness Because adenosylcobalamin (not methylcobalamin) synthesis is affected, homocysteine is normal, distinguishing these from the combined cblC/cblD defects Urine organic acids show markedly elevated methylmalonic acid; blood acylcarnitines show raised propionylcarnitine (C3) A cobalamin-responsiveness trial with hydroxocobalamin is a key part of assessment, alongside protein restriction and carnitine supplementation Management combines vitamin B12 (hydroxocobalamin) for responsive patients, avoidance of fasting and protein moderation, an emergency regimen with glucose during illness, and treatment of hyperammonaemia during crises Severe metabolic acidosis with hyperammonaemia and encephalopathy during a crisis Recurrent vomiting, lethargy and poor feeding with failure to thrive Rapid deterioration triggered by protein load or intercurrent illness Evolving renal impairment, a recognised long-term complication of methylmalonic acidaemia Not performing a formal cobalamin-responsiveness trial and missing a treatable form Failing to measure homocysteine and thereby confusing these defects with combined cblC/cblD disease Overlooking hyperammonaemia and secondary carnitine deficiency during crises Neglecting long-term monitoring of renal function Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase requires adenosylcobalamin as its cofactor to convert methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the pathway that handles propiogenic substrates (certain amino acids, odd-chain fatty acids and cholesterol side-chains). The cblA (MMAA) and cblB (MMAB) defects impair the mitochondrial synthesis and delivery of adenosylcobalamin, so mutase activity is reduced despite a structurally normal enzyme. Methylmalonyl-CoA and its derivative methylmalonic acid accumulate, and propionyl-CoA is diverted to propionylcarnitine and related metabolites; secondary inhibition of the urea cycle contributes to hyperammonaemia during decompensation. Because only adenosylcobalamin is affected, methionine synthase activity and homocysteine remain normal. Provision of pharmacological hydroxocobalamin can restore cofactor supply in responsive patients, particularly the cblA type. The cobalamin-responsive forms, especially cblA, generally have a better prognosis than mutase-deficient methylmalonic acidaemia, and many respond well to hydroxocobalamin with dietary management; nonetheless, poorly controlled disease carries risks of neurological injury and progressive renal impairment.

Cobalamin C deficiency (cblC) — cblC disease, MMACHC deficiency, combined methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria type cblC, methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria cblC type Isolated methylmalonic acidaemia (mutase or other cobalamin defects) Classic homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency) Other remethylation defects (MTHFR deficiency, cblE/cblG) Nutritional vitamin B12 deficiency Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome / thrombotic microangiopathy Other causes of infantile encephalopathy with retinopathy Transcobalamin deficiency Plasma and urine methylmalonic acid Plasma total homocysteine and methionine Plasma acylcarnitine profile (raised C3 propionylcarnitine) Full blood count and film for megaloblastic/haemolytic changes MMACHC gene sequencing and complementation studies where needed Ophthalmological assessment for maculopathy/pigmentary retinopathy Renal function and markers of thrombotic microangiopathy Most common inborn error of intracellular cobalamin (vitamin B12) metabolism, caused by biallelic MMACHC variants Impaired processing of cobalamin blocks synthesis of both adenosylcobalamin and methylcobalamin, so both dependent pathways fail Biochemical signature is combined methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria with low-to-normal methionine Early-onset (infantile) disease brings failure to thrive, feeding problems, hypotonia, encephalopathy, seizures and a pigmentary retinopathy Haematological clue is megaloblastic anaemia, sometimes with a thrombotic microangiopathy (haemolytic-uraemic-like picture) Late-onset disease can present with cognitive decline, psychiatric symptoms, myelopathy or thromboembolism Confirmed by plasma/urine metabolites (raised methylmalonic acid and total homocysteine) plus MMACHC sequencing Treatment centres on parenteral hydroxocobalamin, with betaine, folinic acid and sometimes carnitine; oral B12 is inadequate Encephalopathy with seizures and rapid neurological deterioration in infancy Thrombotic microangiopathy with renal impairment (HUS-like presentation) Severe metabolic acidosis with feeding failure Thromboembolic events in older patients Progressive visual loss from maculopathy Treating with oral cyanocobalamin instead of parenteral hydroxocobalamin, which is far less effective Diagnosing isolated methylmalonic acidaemia without measuring homocysteine and missing the combined defect Overlooking the retinopathy, which can progress despite metabolic control Mistaking the thrombotic microangiopathy for primary atypical HUS Failing to recognise late-onset presentations with psychiatric or myelopathic features Cobalamin C disease results from deficiency of the MMACHC protein, which performs an early cytosolic step in intracellular processing of dietary cobalamin, dealkylating/decyanating incoming cobalamin so it can be converted into its two active cofactor forms. Loss of function prevents generation of both adenosylcobalamin, the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, and methylcobalamin, the cofactor for methionine synthase. Consequently methylmalonyl-CoA cannot be isomerised, causing methylmalonic acid accumulation, and homocysteine cannot be remethylated to methionine, causing hyperhomocysteinaemia with low methionine. The combined metabolic block produces neurological injury, endothelial damage with thrombotic microangiopathy, megaloblastic haematopoiesis and retinopathy. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Early-onset disease often has a guarded prognosis with persistent neurological and visual impairment even when treated, whereas late-onset disease responds better to early hydroxocobalamin-based therapy; outcome depends strongly on age at diagnosis and treatment.
