of haemorrhage and cord ischaemia from an untreated arteriovenous malformation Cobb syndrome is a metameric neurocutaneous vascular disorder in which a vascular malformation of the spinal cord and its coverings coexists with a cutaneous vascular lesion in the matching body segment. The shared segmental distribution is thought to arise from a developmental event affecting cells destined for a single metamere, so that skin, vertebral, meningeal, and cord tissues derived from that segment carry the vascular anomaly. The neurological consequences stem from the spinal arteriovenous malformation, which can injure the cord by direct compression, by diverting blood and raising venous pressure with resulting cord ischaemia, or by haemorrhage. The condition is characteristically sporadic. Outcome depends on the size, location, and haemodynamics of the spinal malformation and on the degree of cord injury at presentation. Timely diagnosis and treatment can stabilise or improve neurological function, whereas late presentation with established cord damage or haemorrhage carries a risk of permanent disability.

Cocaine, Other Psychostimulants, and Hallucinogens — Cocaine intoxication, Methamphetamine use disorder, Stimulant use disorder, MDMA (ecstasy/Molly), Cathinone / bath salts, Hallucinogen use disorder, LSD / PCP / psilocybin / ketamine Sympathomimetic toxidrome from other agents (e.g., synthetic cathinones/bath salts, prescription stimulant misuse) Anticholinergic toxidrome Serotonin syndrome Neuroleptic malignant syndrome / malignant hyperthermia (hyperthermia, rigidity) Thyroid storm Pheochromocytoma / catecholamine excess Primary psychiatric psychosis or mania Alcohol or sedative withdrawal Sepsis with hyperthermia and tachycardia CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis) presenting with agitation, fever, altered mental status Electrocardiogram for chest pain or arrhythmia evaluation Chest radiograph in cocaine-associated chest pain Cardiac biomarkers to exclude myocardial infarction Core body temperature monitoring (hyperthermia) Note that emerging substances/NPS are often NOT detected on standard ED drug screens or postmortem toxicology Hyperthyroidism / thyroid storm Pheochromocytoma Serotonin syndrome Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Primary psychotic or manic episode Hypoglycemia or hypoxemia (must be excluded before treating agitation) Cocaine blocks reuptake at the dopamine transporter, raising synaptic dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin in both CNS and PNS; this monoaminergic excess underlies its euphoric and sympathomimetic effects. Smoked or vaporized cocaine (freebase/crack) reaches the brain almost as fast as the IV route because of the large pulmonary vasculature, producing a rapid, intense, transient high that increases addictive potential. Acute psychostimulant intoxication produces a uniform syndrome regardless of agent: euphoria, increased energy, reduced need for sleep, decreased appetite, heightened alertness, increased libido, plus peripheral tremor, diaphoresis, hypertonia, tachypnea, hyperreflexia, and hyperthermia. Many psychostimulant effects are biphasic: low doses improve psychomotor performance and increase vagal tone (lowering heart rate), whereas high doses cause tremor/convulsions and raise heart rate and blood pressure. Combining cocaine with alcohol generates the metabolite cocaethylene, whose cardiovascular toxicity is additive to cocaine's, intensifying pathophysiologic harm. Methamphetamine is more potent than amphetamine, producing higher synaptic dopamine and greater nerve-terminal toxicity; the dextrorotatory (d-) enantiomer has 3-5 times the CNS activity of the l-form, and smoked bioavailability (~90%) far exceeds oral (~67%). MDMA acts mainly on serotonin transporters, increasing release of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine; animal data show moderate-to-high doses can cause loss of serotonergic nerve endings and permanent damage. Classic (serotonergic) hallucinogens such as LSD, psilocybin, mescaline/peyote, DMT, and ayahuasca disrupt serotonin and glutamate signaling; oral onset is ~20-90 min with duration up to 6-12 h (salvia ~30 min). Dissociative agents (PCP, ketamine, high-dose dextromethorphan, salvia) distort perception of time, motion, color, sound, and self and can cause respiratory depression, heart-rate abnormalities, and a withdrawal syndrome with craving, confusion, headache, and sweating. Psychostimulant withdrawal features hypersomnia, increased appetite, and depressed mood; acute withdrawal lasts ~7-10 days but residual symptoms may persist for months. Conditioned (cue-triggered) craving, not physical withdrawal, is considered the primary driver of ongoing use. Stimulant use disorder is diagnosed by DSM-5 when at least 2 of 11 criteria occur within 12 months; for hallucinogen use disorder only the first 10 criteria apply because the withdrawal criterion does not apply (use is typically not chronic). Adulterants are a major and underappreciated hazard: cocaine/methamphetamine are increasingly cut with fentanyl-related opioids (overdose deaths), levamisole (agranulocytosis, leukoencephalopathy, cutaneous vasculitis with skin necrosis), clenbuterol (tachycardia, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia), and xylazine (sedation, necrotic soft-tissue lesions). Severe psychomotor agitation, hypertension, tachycardia, headache, and mydriasis indicating sympathetic overactivity / overdose Hyperthermia (goal to cool to core temperature <39 C within 30 min) Seizures, coma, or focal neurologic signs Intracranial hemorrhage or cerebral infarction Chest pain, cardiac ischemia/arrhythmia, left ventricular dysfunction, aortic dissection/rupture Respiratory failure, airway burns or bronchospasm from inhaled crack ('crack lung') Rhabdomyolysis with metabolic acidosis / renal infarction Concurrent opioid co-ingestion (e.g., fentanyl-adulterated cocaine) precipitating fatal overdose 'Bad trip' with panic, paranoia, or psychosis (hallucinogens), which may persist up to 24 h Beta blockers should generally be avoided in cocaine users because unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation from beta blockade may cause coronary vasoconstriction, ischemia, and infarction; if essential, mixed alpha/beta agents (e.g., labetalol, carvedilol) are preferred over nonselective beta blockers. Succinylcholine is relatively contraindicated for rapid-sequence intubation in cocaine use; a nondepolarizing agent (e.g., rocuronium) is the alternative. Before treating psychomotor agitation, hypoglycemia and hypoxemia must be ruled out first. Drugs sold as 'Molly'/MDMA frequently contain methylone, ethylone, or other synthetic cathinones rather than MDMA, so the reported drug may not match the actual exposure. Emerging/new psychoactive substances are often missed on standard drug tests, so a negative screen does not exclude intoxication. Fentanyl, xylazine, levamisole, and other adulterants can produce effects (and overdose) not anticipated from the intended drug. MDMA, LSD, and psilocybin remain Schedule I in the United States despite FDA breakthrough-therapy designations; investigational use does not equal approved therapy. Psychostimulants increase synaptic monoamines. Cocaine binds the dopamine transporter and blocks reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, raising their levels centrally and peripherally; repeated exposure induces long-term neuronal changes including adaptations in glutamate-releasing neurons. Methamphetamine, a cationic lipophilic molecule structurally similar to monoamine transporters, reverses transporter function to dump newly synthesized catecholamines from storage vesicles into the synapse and also inhibits monoamine oxidase, attenuating monoamine metabolism; it is more potent than amphetamine with greater nerve-terminal toxicity. MDMA acts predominantly on serotonin transporters to release serotonin (and norepinephrine/dopamine) and can damage serotonergic nerve endings. Cathinone (from khat) increases dopamine release and reduces its reuptake. Classic hallucinogens disrupt serotonin (affecting mood, perception, sleep, appetite, temperature, sexual behavior, muscle control) and glutamate (affecting pain perception, environmental responses, emotion, learning/memory). The sympathomimetic surge drives the cardiovascular, neurologic, pulmonary, renal, and hyperthermic complications. Acute overdose is a medical emergency that can be fatal through cerebral hemorrhage/infarction, cardiac arrhythmia or ischemia, respiratory failure, hyperthermia, or rhabdomyolysis, and management is largely supportive in an ICU/telemetry setting. Co-ingestion of other drugs (especially opioids) markedly increases morbidity and mortality, and overdose deaths involving cocaine and psychostimulants have risen sharply (cocaine-related overdose deaths more than quintupled from 2011 to 2022; psychostimulant-involved deaths reached ~36,000 in 2023). Early abstinence is frequently complicated by depression, guilt, insomnia, and anorexia that can be as severe as a major affective disorder and may persist for months to years. Contingency management has robust evidence of efficacy for stimulant use disorder with benefit lasting up to 2 years after treatment ends; no FDA-approved pharmacotherapy exists for stimulant or hallucinogen addiction. Chronic hallucinogen/dissociative use can leave persistent psychosis, memory loss, anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation, and flashbacks lasting a year or more. No single graded severity scale; DSM-5 stimulant use disorder severity is rated mild (2-3 criteria), moderate (4-5), or severe (>=6) of 11 criteria over 12 months. Acute clinical severity ranges from intoxication to life-threatening overdose marked by sympathetic overactivity (agitation, hypertension, tachycardia), hyperthermia, seizures, intracranial or cardiac events, respiratory failure, and rhabdomyolysis. Complications of psychostimulant use are catalogued in Table 468-1 across cardiovascular, CNS/PNS, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, renal, endocrine, and other organ systems.

Coccidioidomycosis — Valley fever, Coccidioides Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis is often misdiagnosed as this) (Harrison 22e p.1697) Pulmonary malignancy (coccidioidal nodules are difficult to distinguish radiographically and, like malignancies, may enhance on PET) (Harrison 22e p.1697) Histoplasmosis (can cause false-positive coccidioidal antigen results) (Harrison 22e p.1698) Blastomycosis (can cause false-positive coccidioidal antigen results) (Harrison 22e p.1698) Tuberculosis / other chronic granulomatous pulmonary infections (upper lobe infiltrate, cavities, hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy mimic) (Harrison 22e p.1697) EIA for IgM and IgG antibodies (recommended for initial diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.1698) Confirmatory immunodiffusion (IDTP/IDCF) or traditional tube-precipitin and complement-fixation assays with CF titer (CF titer is an important prognostic tool) (Harrison 22e p.1698) Culture of sputum/respiratory fluids and tissue (grows within 3-7 days at 37 degrees C on artificial media including blood agar) (Harrison 22e p.1698) Direct microscopy of respiratory specimens (Papanicolaou, Gomori methenamine silver, or calcofluor white) or fixed tissue (H&E or GMS) for spherules (Harrison 22e p.1698) Coccidioidal antigen test (antigenuria/antigenemia), including CSF assay in suspected meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1698) CSF examination in suspected meningitis (lymphocytic pleocytosis, profound hypoglycorrhachia, elevated protein, occasional CSF eosinophilia; CF antibody in CSF) (Harrison 22e p.1697) MRI with gadolinium in meningitis (frequently shows basilar meningeal enhancement; dilated ventricles indicate hydrocephalus) (Harrison 22e p.1697) Chest imaging/CT for nodules and cavities (multiple nodules and microsatellite lesions favor coccidioidomycosis over malignancy) (Harrison 22e p.1697) Pulmonary malignancy (solitary or multiple nodules, PET-avid, may require biopsy to distinguish) (Harrison 22e p.1697) Caused by dimorphic soil-dwelling fungi of the genus Coccidioides (C. immitis and C. posadasii), which are clinically indistinguishable; infection follows inhalation of airborne arthroconidia (Harrison 22e p.1696). Endemic to the Western Hemisphere between 40 degrees N and 40 degrees S; areas of high endemicity in the US include the southern San Joaquin Valley of California (hence 'Valley fever') and south-central Arizona, with other foci across the southwestern US, northern Mexico, Central America, and parts of South America (Harrison 22e p.1696). In endemic areas most human cases occur without obvious soil or dust exposure; periods of aridity following rainy seasons are associated with increases in symptomatic infections (Harrison 22e p.1696). After infection, 60% of individuals are completely asymptomatic; the other 40% have symptoms related primarily to pulmonary infection (fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain) appearing several days to up to 3 weeks after inhalation, with risk of symptomatic illness increasing with age (Harrison 22e p.1697). Immunologic manifestations of primary pulmonary disease include cutaneous reactions: a diffuse erythematous maculopapular rash ('toxic erythema'), erythema nodosum (typically over the lower extremities), erythema multiforme (often in a necklace distribution), and Sweet syndrome lesions; cutaneous manifestations are especially common in women (Harrison 22e p.1697). Symmetrical arthralgias ('desert rheumatism'), often involving the ankles, knees, and hips, may occur with or without cutaneous manifestations (Harrison 22e p.1697). Serology is the most common diagnostic method; EIA for IgM and IgG is recommended for initial diagnosis, with positive results confirmed by immunodiffusion (IDTP/IDCF) or traditional tube-precipitin and complement-fixation assays (Harrison 22e p.1697). Rising complement-fixation (CF) titers reflect fungal growth and correlate with clinical progression; high CF titers (e.g., 1:32 or greater) suggest unrestrained fungal growth and the possibility of extrathoracic dissemination, while CF antibody in CSF is indicative of coccidioidal meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1698). Spherules (up to 200 microns) are unique to Coccidioides and can be demonstrated in respiratory specimens after Papanicolaou, Gomori methenamine silver, or calcofluor white staining, or in fixed tissue with hematoxylin-eosin or Gomori methenamine silver (Harrison 22e p.1698). A commercial coccidioidal antigen test (antigenuria/antigenemia) is useful in immunosuppressed patients with severe or disseminated disease and when assaying CSF in suspected meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1698). Coccidioidal meningitis is the most dire disseminated syndrome and is uniformly fatal if untreated; patients present with a persistent dull headache often with lethargy and confusion, and nuchal rigidity, if present, is not severe (Harrison 22e p.1697). Disseminated disease (occurs in approximately 1% of infections; defined as fungus found outside the thoracic cavity), more likely in male patients, those of African and perhaps Filipino ancestry, and persons with depressed cellular immunity (Harrison 22e p.1697) Coccidioidal meningitis: persistent dull headache, lethargy, confusion; uniformly fatal if untreated, may progress to communicating hydrocephalus with declining mental status and gait disturbance (Harrison 22e p.1697) Immunocompromised hosts at risk for dissemination: HIV-1 infection with CD4 count <250/microL, chronic glucocorticoid therapy, allogeneic solid-organ transplant recipients, and patients on TNF-alpha antagonists or other biological response modifiers (Harrison 22e p.1697) New coccidioidal infection acquired during the second or third trimester of pregnancy or postpartum (significant risk for disseminated disease) (Harrison 22e p.1697) Diffuse reticulonodular pneumonia with dyspnea and fever in intense exposure or profoundly suppressed cellular immunity (e.g., untreated HIV with markedly low CD4), associated with unrestrained fungal growth and frequent fungemia (Harrison 22e p.1697) High serum CF titer (e.g., 1:32 or greater) predicting disease activity and possible extrathoracic dissemination (Harrison 22e p.1698) Pulmonary cavity rupture into the pleural space causing pyopneumothorax (acute dyspnea, collapsed lung with pleural air-fluid level) (Harrison 22e p.1697) Primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis is often misdiagnosed as community-acquired bacterial pneumonia; rash, symmetrical arthralgias, night sweats, marked fatigue, peripheral-blood eosinophilia, failure to improve with antibacterial therapy, or upper lobe infiltrate / hilar or mediastinal adenopathy should suggest the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1697). Coccidioides poses a significant laboratory hazard if inadvertently inhaled; the clinical laboratory should always be alerted to the possibility of this diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1698). Coccidioidal pulmonary nodules can be difficult to distinguish radiographically from malignancy and, like malignancies, often enhance on PET; biopsy may be required (Harrison 22e p.1697). The IgM EIA in particular is occasionally falsely positive; results should be interpreted cautiously when screening asymptomatic individuals (Harrison 22e p.1698). The EIA IgG optical density does not correlate with the IDCF/traditional CF titer and should not be used as a surrogate for a titer (Harrison 22e p.1698). Coccidioidal antigen testing may yield false-positive results in histoplasmosis or blastomycosis (Harrison 22e p.1698). The fungus is isolated from CSF in fewer than one-third of meningitis cases, so a negative CSF culture does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1697). Potassium hydroxide preparation of sputum is rarely fruitful for identifying Coccidioides (Harrison 22e p.1698). PCR genomic detection does not appear to be more sensitive than culture, though it can be more rapid (Harrison 22e p.1698). Coccidioides exists as filamentous mold (mycelia) in the environment, producing barrel-shaped airborne spores (arthroconidia, ~2 x 5 microns) that, when inhaled, are small enough to evade mucosal defenses and reach deep into the bronchial tree to initiate infection. Within the host, arthroconidia enlarge into spherules (up to 200 microns, unique to Coccidioides) containing endospores; spherules rupture and release endospores that form new spherules, propagating infection locally. A robust cellular immune response is critical to host control: resolved pulmonary infection shows necrotizing granulomas containing spherules, whereas uncontrolled disseminated disease shows poorly formed or absent granulomas and a polymorphonuclear leukocyte response. In persons with protective cellular immunity, spherules may persist in the lungs for prolonged periods (possibly lifelong) in a latent state, conferring protective immunity but creating a risk of recurrent active disease if that immunity wanes (Harrison 22e p.1696-1697). In most patients, primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis resolves without sequelae over several weeks. Clinical dissemination occurs in approximately 1% of infected individuals and, when it occurs, is usually evident within the first 6 months after primary infection. Coccidioidal meningitis is uniformly fatal if untreated; even with treatment, relapse is common after stopping therapy. Antibodies disappear over time in persons whose illness resolves, but the presence of coccidioidal antibodies in serum does not indicate immunity or control of infection (Harrison 22e p.1696-1698). Clinical presentations and their approximate frequencies (Table 219-1, Harrison 22e p.1698): asymptomatic infection (60%); primary focal pneumonia (40%); diffuse pneumonia (<1%); pulmonary sequelae (~5%: nodule, cavity, chronic pneumonia); and disseminated disease (1% or less, including skin/bone/joint/soft tissue disease and meningitis). High CF titers (e.g., 1:32 or greater) and features such as night sweats >3 weeks, weight loss >10%, CF titer >1:16, and extensive pulmonary involvement indicate greater severity.

with feeding difficulty and aspiration risk Marked visual or hearing deterioration affecting development Signs of renal or hepatic impairment as part of multisystem decline Mistaking the intracranial calcification for congenital infection Confusing photosensitivity with xeroderma pigmentosum and expecting a high skin-cancer risk Overlooking progressive hearing and visual loss that are amenable to supportive intervention Failing to recognise milder later-onset forms because growth failure is less striking Cockayne syndrome results from biallelic variants in ERCC6 or ERCC8, whose protein products are essential for transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair. Failure to remove transcription-blocking DNA lesions leads to stalled RNA polymerase, impaired gene expression and increased cellular vulnerability to oxidative and ultraviolet-induced damage. The condition is progressive and life-limiting; the severe early-onset form is often fatal in early childhood, while the classic form typically leads to death in the first or second decade. Care is supportive and multidisciplinary, with sun protection to limit photosensitivity.

Coenurosis (Taenia multiceps) — Taenia multiceps infection, Multiceps multiceps infection, coenurus cyst disease, Taenia serialis coenurosis Neurocysticercosis (Taenia solium larval disease) Hydatid disease (Echinococcus) of brain or soft tissue Cerebral abscess or primary brain tumour Arachnoid or other benign intracranial cyst Sparganosis and other larval cestode infection Soft-tissue lipoma, cyst or abscess MRI or CT to characterise the cystic lesion and detect internal scolices Full blood count for eosinophilia Serology for cestode infection to help distinguish from cysticercosis and hydatid disease Histological examination of the excised cyst confirming the multi-scolex coenurus Ophthalmological assessment in suspected ocular disease Cerebrospinal fluid examination where clinically appropriate Caused by the larval coenurus stage of Taenia (Multiceps) species, with humans as accidental intermediate hosts after ingesting eggs shed by dogs and other canids The coenurus is a fluid-filled bladder containing many invaginated protoscolices, distinguishing it from the single-scolex cysticercus and from hydatid cysts Cerebral and spinal coenurosis presents with raised intracranial pressure, seizures, focal deficits or cord compression depending on cyst location Subcutaneous and intramuscular coenuri present as slowly enlarging soft-tissue swellings, and ocular disease can threaten vision Imaging shows a cystic lesion that may contain multiple scolices, and eosinophilia may be present Definitive management is complete surgical excision of the cyst; anthelmintic drugs such as albendazole and corticosteroids may be adjuncts, particularly when surgery is difficult Prevention relies on deworming dogs, safe disposal of infected sheep offal and good personal hygiene to avoid ingesting eggs Signs of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus Seizures or progressive focal neurological deficit Spinal cord compression from a spinal cyst Visual loss from an ocular or orbital coenurus Mistaking a coenurus for neurocysticercosis or a hydatid cyst on imaging Incomplete excision or intraoperative rupture provoking an inflammatory reaction and relapse Relying on medical therapy alone for large space-occupying cysts Overlooking the canine egg exposure history in the epidemiological assessment Taenia multiceps and related species are tapeworms whose adults inhabit the intestine of dogs and wild canids, with sheep and other herbivores as usual intermediate hosts. Humans become accidental intermediate hosts by ingesting eggs from canine faeces. Oncospheres hatch in the intestine, penetrate the mucosa and are carried in the blood to tissues, most importantly the brain, spinal cord, eye and subcutaneous tissue, where they develop into a coenurus, a large fluid-filled larval bladder studded with numerous protoscolices. The expanding cyst acts as a space-occupying lesion, causing mass effect, raised intracranial pressure, seizures or cord compression in the nervous system and progressive swelling elsewhere. Surrounding inflammation and, if the cyst ruptures, release of larval contents can intensify the local reaction. Prognosis after complete excision of an accessible cyst is favourable, but cerebral and spinal disease can cause serious morbidity and carries a guarded outlook when the cyst is inoperable or diagnosed late.

supplementation rather than escalating immunosuppression alone Muscle biopsy may show reduced activities of coenzyme Q10-dependent respiratory chain segments (complex I+III and II+III) with preserved complex-specific activities, and direct measurement of muscle coenzyme Q10 is diagnostically useful Because the response to treatment can be striking, prompt recognition and a supplementation trial are central to management while awaiting genetic confirmation Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome progressing towards renal failure that has not been trialled on coenzyme Q10 Rapidly progressive encephalopathy or multiorgan involvement in infancy Emerging seizures or profound hypotonia indicating severe mitochondrial compromise Progressive cerebellar ataxia with functional decline Escalating immunosuppression in steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome without considering a treatable coenzyme Q10 deficiency Delaying a supplementation trial while awaiting genetic results when clinical suspicion is high Attributing the picture solely to a generic mitochondrial disorder and missing the specific, treatable defect Failing to distinguish primary biosynthetic deficiency from secondary coenzyme Q10 reduction, which alters counselling and expectations Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) is a lipid-soluble electron carrier that shuttles electrons from respiratory-chain complexes I and II to complex III and also serves as a lipophilic antioxidant. Biallelic mutations in genes of the coenzyme Q10 biosynthetic pathway reduce ubiquinone synthesis, impairing oxidative phosphorylation and increasing oxidative stress. Tissue involvement reflects the affected gene and residual synthesis, producing phenotypes ranging from isolated steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (podocyte-predominant) to cerebellar ataxia, encephalomyopathy, and severe multisystem infantile disease. Because the deficient metabolite can be partially replaced, exogenous supplementation may restore electron transport and reverse or arrest organ dysfunction. Outcome depends on the genotype, affected organs, and how early treatment begins; some patients, particularly those with the nephrotic or ataxic forms, improve substantially with coenzyme Q10 supplementation, whereas severe infantile multisystem disease carries a poor prognosis despite treatment. Early supplementation before irreversible damage offers the best chance of benefit.

Because the defect lies in Golgi processing rather than precursor assembly, transferrin shows a type II pattern. The breadth of affected glycoproteins accounts for the multisystem phenotype, and the specific subunit affected influences severity. Prognosis varies widely by subunit and severity, from lethal neonatal forms to milder presentations with survival and moderate disability; outcome is dominated by hepatic, infective and neurological complications. supranuclear control of horizontal saccades, the fast eye movements that redirect gaze, while the pathways for reflexive and vertical movements are relatively spared. To compensate, the child throws the head towards a new target, using the intact vestibulo-ocular reflex to drag the eyes across, then re-centres the head once fixation is achieved. In many children the sign is isolated and improves with maturation, but it is frequently a marker of underlying cerebellar and brainstem malformation, especially the molar tooth malformation of Joubert syndrome and related ciliopathies, in which disordered ciliary signalling disturbs mid-hindbrain development. It also occurs in neurodegenerative and metabolic disorders such as ataxia-telangiectasia and the ataxias with oculomotor apraxia, so its recognition should prompt a search for such causes. When isolated, the compensatory head thrusts tend to lessen with age and the outlook is good; when it is part of a syndrome the prognosis is determined by the underlying disorder and its systemic complications.

Cogan syndrome — Cogan's syndrome, interstitial keratitis with audiovestibular dysfunction, oculo-audiovestibular syndrome Syphilitic interstitial keratitis Meniere disease Susac syndrome Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other systemic vasculitides Sarcoidosis Autoimmune inner ear disease Slit-lamp examination to identify interstitial keratitis, scleritis, or uveitis Audiometry and vestibular testing to characterise and monitor audiovestibular involvement Serological testing to exclude syphilis and other infective causes Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) and autoimmune screen Echocardiography and vascular imaging when aortitis or aortic valve disease is suspected MRI of the brain and inner ear to exclude alternative pathology A rare autoimmune vasculitic disorder combining inflammatory eye disease with audiovestibular dysfunction, usually in young adults The classic ocular feature is interstitial keratitis causing photophobia, eye pain, redness, and blurred vision, though scleritis and uveitis also occur Inner ear involvement resembles Meniere disease with sudden sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo, and tinnitus, and can progress to deafness Ocular and audiovestibular features may not appear simultaneously, so a high index of suspicion is needed when one precedes the other A systemic large-vessel vasculitis, including aortitis and aortic valve involvement, complicates a proportion of cases There is no specific diagnostic test; diagnosis is clinical after excluding infective causes such as syphilis Prompt systemic corticosteroids are the mainstay for hearing preservation, with immunosuppressive or biologic agents in refractory or systemic disease Rapidly progressive sensorineural hearing loss threatening permanent deafness Signs of aortitis or new aortic regurgitation indicating systemic vasculitis Neurological features suggesting central nervous system involvement or an alternative diagnosis Systemic vasculitic manifestations requiring urgent immunosuppression Delaying corticosteroids and losing the window to preserve hearing Attributing audiovestibular symptoms to Meniere disease and missing the ocular link Failing to exclude syphilis before diagnosing autoimmune interstitial keratitis Not screening for systemic and aortic vasculitic complications Managing eye and ear disease in isolation without recognising the unifying diagnosis Cogan syndrome is regarded as an autoimmune vasculitis, possibly triggered by preceding infection, in which the immune response cross-reacts with shared antigens in the cornea and inner ear. Autoantibodies directed against inner ear and endothelial antigens have been described. Immune-mediated inflammation of the corneal stroma produces interstitial keratitis, while inflammation and damage to the cochlea and vestibular apparatus cause hearing loss and vertigo. In some patients the process extends to a systemic vasculitis affecting large vessels, leading to aortitis and aortic regurgitation. With prompt corticosteroid therapy ocular inflammation usually settles, but hearing loss is frequently permanent and may progress to bilateral deafness; associated large-vessel vasculitis and aortic valve disease carry additional morbidity and mortality.

presentation EED encodes an essential scaffolding component of Polycomb Repressive Complex 2, a multiprotein assembly that, through its catalytic partner EZH2, deposits the repressive histone mark H3K27me3 to silence target genes during development. Pathogenic EED variants impair the complex's ability to establish or read this mark, reducing repression of genes that promote cellular proliferation and growth. The resulting loss of appropriate transcriptional silencing manifests as generalised overgrowth, accelerated skeletal maturation and disordered neurodevelopment, and because the same complex is affected in Weaver and Imagawa-Matsumoto syndromes these conditions share a common mechanistic basis and overlapping features. Long-term data are limited because of rarity, but children typically show persistent overgrowth with intellectual disability of variable severity; life expectancy is not clearly reduced in the absence of malignancy, and management centres on developmental support, orthopaedic monitoring and vigilance for tumours as advised for the wider PRC2 overgrowth group.

poisoning Iron or other multi-organ toxin ingestion Ricin or other plant-toxin poisoning Primary haematological failure or aplastic crisis Distributive or cardiogenic shock from another cause Serial for rhabdomyolysis Coagulation profile and troponin with electrocardiogram for cardiac involvement Careful history of tablet ingestion or plant exposure Colchicine has a narrow therapeutic index and serious overdose can occur at doses only modestly above therapeutic, so risk assessment should be cautious Toxicity classically evolves in three phases: an early gastrointestinal phase, a phase of multi-organ failure, and, in survivors, a recovery phase The initial phase brings nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal pain with fluid losses within hours of ingestion The second phase, over subsequent days, features bone-marrow suppression, cardiovascular collapse, acute kidney injury, hepatic dysfunction and metabolic derangement A relatively well-appearing patient after the gastrointestinal phase can be deceptive, as multi-organ failure may follow Plant sources such as autumn crocus and glory lily can cause identical toxicity and may be mistaken for edible plants There is no widely available antidote in routine practice, so meticulous supportive and intensive care is the mainstay, with early poisons-centre involvement Late alopecia and a rebound leucocytosis are recognised features during recovery Large reported ingestion or ingestion of concentrated plant material Progressive cytopenias, particularly worsening neutropenia Hypotension, arrhythmia or evidence of cardiogenic shock Acute kidney injury, hepatic dysfunction or lactic acidosis Deterioration after an apparently settling gastrointestinal phase Being reassured by a well patient after the gastrointestinal phase and discharging prematurely Underestimating toxicity because the ingested dose seems only slightly supratherapeutic Failing to monitor serial blood counts for delayed marrow suppression Not recognising plant sources such as autumn crocus and glory lily Overlooking drug interactions that raise colchicine concentrations in therapeutic users Colchicine binds tubulin and prevents microtubule polymerisation, arresting mitosis and disrupting intracellular transport, cell division and structural integrity. Tissues with high turnover, including gastrointestinal epithelium and bone marrow, are affected early, producing profuse gastrointestinal losses and later pancytopenia. Impaired cellular function and mitochondrial dysfunction contribute to multi-organ failure with cardiovascular collapse, acute kidney injury, hepatic dysfunction, lactic acidosis and rhabdomyolysis. The delayed, evolving course reflects the time required for microtubule-dependent processes and rapidly dividing cell populations to fail. Mild ingestions may cause only self-limiting gastrointestinal upset, but significant overdose carries a high mortality driven by cardiovascular collapse and multi-organ failure; those who survive the second phase generally recover marrow and organ function.

autoantibodies that bind red cells optimally at cold temperatures Symptoms worsen on cold exposure and include acrocyanosis and mottling of the extremities, ears and nose, with haemolytic anaemia The direct antiglobulin test is positive for complement (C3d) and negative or weak for IgG, reflecting complement-mediated haemolysis Cold agglutinins cause red cell clumping that can spuriously raise the patient warm, with rituximab-based therapy for significant disease Severe or rapidly falling haemoglobin requiring transfusion Haemoglobinuria indicating brisk intravascular haemolysis Acute exacerbation on cold exposure with cardiovascular compromise Features suggesting underlying lymphoma requiring investigation Being misled by spurious red cell indices from cold-induced agglutination in unwarmed samples Using warm-antibody treatments such as corticosteroids and splenectomy, which are relatively ineffective here Transfusing without warming blood and the patient, worsening haemolysis Failing to investigate for an underlying B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder Cold agglutinin disease is caused by monoclonal (in primary disease) or polyclonal (in secondary disease) IgM autoantibodies, usually directed against the I antigen on red cells, that bind most avidly in the cooler peripheral circulation. Antibody binding fixes complement on the red cell surface; as cells return to the warmer core the IgM detaches but deposited complement drives predominantly extravascular clearance by the liver, with some intravascular haemolysis. Agglutination of red cells in cold peripheral vessels also produces the circulatory symptoms. In primary disease a clonal marrow B-cell lymphoproliferative process produces the pathogenic monoclonal IgM. Primary cold agglutinin disease is usually chronic; many patients have mild, manageable haemolysis while others need directed therapy, and prognosis is also shaped by any underlying lymphoproliferative disorder. Secondary post-infectious cases are often self-limiting.

Cold panniculitis — popsicle panniculitis, cold-induced panniculitis, equestrian panniculitis (cold-related) Erythema nodosum Chilblains (perniosis) Cellulitis Trauma-induced (factitial) panniculitis a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermal-subcutaneous junction The history of preceding cold exposure is the key to diagnosis and avoids unnecessary investigation Management is reassurance and avoidance of further cold exposure, as lesions resolve spontaneously Features suggesting cellulitis or abscess requiring antimicrobial treatment Recurrent or widespread lesions disproportionate to cold exposure Systemic symptoms or evidence of an underlying cold-sensitivity disorder Ulceration or necrosis, which is atypical and warrants review Misdiagnosing it as cellulitis and prescribing unnecessary antibiotics Failing to elicit the history of cold exposure Overinvestigating a self-limiting condition Not recognising the higher susceptibility of infants' fat to cold injury Cold panniculitis is a localised injury to subcutaneous fat provoked by exposure to cold. Adipose tissue with a higher proportion of saturated fatty acids, as in infants, solidifies and is damaged at higher temperatures than adult fat, explaining the predisposition in young children. The cold induces crystallisation and injury of adipocytes with a resulting inflammatory response in the fat lobules. The reaction is self-limited once the cold stimulus is removed, and lesions typically resolve without scarring. The condition is benign and self-limiting; lesions usually resolve over one to a few weeks without scarring once cold exposure ceases. Recurrence can occur with repeated cold contact.

Cold-stimulus headache — ice-cream headache, brain freeze, cold-induced headache Migraine attack triggered by cold Primary stabbing headache Trigeminal neuralgia Sinus or dental pain provoked by cold Secondary headache if the temporal link to cold is unclear Clinical diagnosis from the clear temporal relationship to a cold stimulus Neurological examination to confirm no focal signs Investigation only if features are atypical or examination is abnormal A brief headache triggered by a cold stimulus applied to the head or passing over the palate and posterior pharynx The pain is short-lived, usually frontal or temporal, and resolves within seconds to a couple of minutes of removing the stimulus The palatal (ingested-cold) form is the familiar response to rapidly eating or drinking something very cold It is very common in the general population and especially frequent in people with migraine No investigation is needed when the trigger is clear and the examination is normal Simple avoidance or slowing intake of cold food and drink is sufficient management Headache that outlasts the cold stimulus substantially Focal neurological signs Progressive or new pattern unrelated to cold exposure Associated systemic or alarm features Confusing a cold-triggered migraine with a simple cold-stimulus headache Investigating an obviously benign, stimulus-locked headache Overlooking that it flags an underlying tendency to migraine Attributing an unrelated persistent headache to cold exposure Cold-stimulus headache is a referred pain response in which sudden cooling of the palate, pharynx or head activates trigeminal sensory afferents and provokes transient changes in local blood vessels, generating brief referred pain to the frontotemporal region. It is a benign physiological phenomenon rather than a disease, though its heightened frequency in migraine suggests a lower threshold of trigeminovascular activation in those individuals. The condition is entirely benign and self-limiting, with pain resolving promptly once the cold stimulus is withdrawn.

diagnosis and gauge threshold History clarifying the rewarming pattern and any systemic symptoms with extensive exposure Cryoglobulins and cold agglutinins in atypical or secondary cases Full blood count and inflammatory markers where an underlying disorder is suspected Screening for associated infection where clinically indicated Assessment of systemic reaction risk to guide adrenaline provision An inducible urticaria in which itchy weals develop on skin exposed to cold, most typically as it rewarms after contact with cold air, water or objects The ice-cube test is the key bedside investigation: an ice cube (usually in a thin bag to avoid wetting) is applied to the forearm and a weal appears on rewarming in a positive result Most cases are acquired and idiopathic, arising in adolescents and young adults, and are usually self-limiting over a few years The greatest danger is a systemic reaction from extensive cold exposure, particularly swimming in cold water, which can cause hypotension, collapse and even drowning Angioedema of the lips can follow cold food or drink, and oropharyngeal swelling is a recognised hazard Rare familial and secondary forms exist, the latter occasionally linked to cryoglobulins or infection, so atypical cases merit further evaluation Management combines strict avoidance of sudden cold exposure with non-sedating antihistamines, with omalizumab reserved for resistant disease and adrenaline provision for those at risk of systemic reactions History of faintness, wheeze or collapse with widespread cold exposure such as swimming Oropharyngeal angioedema after cold food or drink Atypical features suggesting cryoglobulinaemia or another systemic disorder Onset in infancy or a family history suggesting a hereditary autoinflammatory syndrome Failing to warn patients against swimming in cold water because of the risk of systemic collapse and drowning Omitting the simple ice-cube test that readily confirms the diagnosis Not screening for cryoglobulins or infection in atypical or secondary presentations Overlooking the need for an adrenaline auto-injector in those at risk of anaphylaxis Cold urticaria results from cold-triggered activation and degranulation of cutaneous mast cells, releasing histamine and other mediators that produce weals and, when exposure is extensive, systemic effects. In many patients the reaction is thought to involve cold-dependent autoantigens or IgE-mediated mechanisms, while secondary forms may relate to cryoglobulins or other cold-precipitable proteins associated with infection or systemic disease. Because the response scales with the area and duration of cold exposure, large surface-area cooling such as swimming can precipitate life-threatening mediator release. Acquired idiopathic cold urticaria commonly remits spontaneously within a few years and is well controlled with avoidance and antihistamines, but it carries a real risk of serious systemic reactions during large-area cold exposure, which patients must be counselled about; secondary forms follow the course of the underlying disorder.

subepithelial collagen band thickness Coeliac serology and thyroid function tests Stool studies to exclude infection Medication review for non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and proton-pump unintentional weight loss requiring exclusion of malignancy or coeliac disease Severe dehydration or electrolyte disturbance from high-volume diarrhoea New iron-deficiency anaemia suggesting an alternative diagnosis Labelling the patient as irritable bowel syndrome and not taking biopsies of normal-looking mucosa Taking biopsies from only one colonic segment and missing patchy disease Failing to review and stop drugs that can trigger or perpetuate the condition Confusing it with lymphocytic colitis rather than distinguishing by the collagen band Collagenous colitis is a form of microscopic colitis in which the colonic mucosa appears macroscopically normal but shows a characteristic thickened subepithelial band of collagen together with increased chronic inflammatory cells in the lamina propria and surface epithelial injury. The mechanism is thought to involve an abnormal mucosal immune response to luminal antigens, including drugs and possibly bile acids, in genetically predisposed individuals, leading to altered fluid and electrolyte handling and a secretory, watery diarrhoea. The thickened collagen band, rather than being purely structural, reflects abnormal subepithelial fibroblast activity. The condition is benign and does not carry an increased colorectal cancer risk; symptoms often respond well to treatment, although relapse after stopping therapy is common and some patients require maintenance treatment.

management is empirical and supportive, including iron repletion and trials of acid suppression or corticosteroids Significant or refractory iron-deficiency anaemia requiring transfusion or intravenous iron Marked weight loss or failure to thrive in children Severe or dehydrating diarrhoea in the adult diarrhoeal pattern Overlooking the diagnosis when the mucosa looks endoscopically normal and biopsies are not taken or not specially stained Failing to search for coexisting coeliac disease or collagenous colitis Attributing the iron-deficiency anaemia solely to another cause and missing the gastric source Confusing the entrapped surface changes with a neoplastic process Collagenous gastritis is a rare disorder in which an abnormally thick, patchy band of subepithelial collagen is deposited immediately beneath the gastric surface epithelium, associated with a chronic inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria and often entrapped dilated capillaries and detached surface cells. The mechanism is uncertain but is presumed to reflect an aberrant reparative or immune-mediated response of the subepithelial fibroblast sheath, mirroring the process seen in collagenous colitis, with which it may coexist. The abnormal mucosa can bleed and impair nutrient handling, contributing to the iron-deficiency anaemia commonly seen in affected children and young adults. The condition tends to be chronic and relapsing; the subepithelial collagen band often persists on repeat biopsy, but symptoms can be controlled and serious complications are uncommon, with prognosis largely determined by associated coeliac or colonic disease.

therapy in HIV-associated disease Collapsing glomerulopathy is a podocytopathy in which a severe injury drives podocytes to lose their differentiated markers and proliferate, forming a hyperplastic cap over a collapsed, wrinkled glomerular basement membrane. APOL1 high-risk variants render podocytes susceptible, and a 'second hit' such as viral infection, interferon exposure or another stressor precipitates the collapsing response. The intense podocyte injury produces massive proteinuria, while associated severe tubular injury with microcyst formation contributes to the rapid loss of function. The combination of tuft collapse and epithelial proliferation distinguishes it histologically from other FSGS variants and accounts for its worse prognosis. Collapsing glomerulopathy carries the worst prognosis among FSGS patterns, with rapid progression to end-stage kidney disease in many patients despite treatment. Outcomes are better when a reversible trigger such as HIV or an offending drug is identified and addressed early, but APOL1-associated idiopathic disease often responds poorly to immunosuppression.

Collecting duct carcinoma — Bellini duct carcinoma, carcinoma of the collecting ducts of Bellini Renal medullary carcinoma Upper tract urothelial carcinoma High-grade papillary renal cell carcinoma Clear cell renal cell carcinoma with infiltrative growth Metastatic carcinoma involving the kidney Renal pelvis inflammatory or infective mass Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis to define the infiltrative mass and nodal spread Chest imaging for pulmonary metastases Tissue diagnosis with immunohistochemistry to distinguish from urothelial and medullary carcinoma Urine cytology and evaluation of the upper urinary tract Baseline renal function and staging investigations A rare, aggressive renal carcinoma arising from the collecting ducts of Bellini in the renal medulla Tends to present at a younger age than clear cell carcinoma, often with advanced disease Common presenting features include haematuria, flank pain, an abdominal mass and constitutional symptoms Imaging typically shows a centrally located, infiltrative medullary mass rather than a well-defined cortical tumour Histology shows irregular tubular and papillary structures with a marked desmoplastic stromal reaction It behaves more like an aggressive urothelial cancer than a typical renal cell carcinoma Early lymph node and distant metastases are frequent at diagnosis Infiltrative central renal mass with haematuria and systemic symptoms Bulky regional lymphadenopathy at presentation Evidence of distant metastatic disease Rapid clinical deterioration Mistaking an infiltrative medullary tumour for upper tract urothelial carcinoma or vice versa Attributing a central renal mass to infection and delaying oncological work-up Assuming standard clear cell targeted therapy will be effective Underestimating the likelihood of occult metastatic disease Collecting duct carcinoma originates from the principal cells of the distal collecting ducts within the medulla. It is a high-grade tumour with infiltrative growth, extensive desmoplasia and early vascular and lymphatic invasion. Its central medullary origin explains the infiltrative imaging pattern and the tendency to involve the renal pelvis and regional nodes. Its biology overlaps with high-grade urothelial carcinoma, and it is distinguished from renal medullary carcinoma by retained SMARCB1 expression and the absence of an obligatory link to sickling haemoglobinopathies. The prognosis is generally poor, with many patients presenting at an advanced stage and limited response to systemic therapy; complete surgical resection of localised disease offers the best chance of prolonged survival.

Colles' fracture — distal radius fracture, dorsally displaced distal radial fracture, dinner-fork deformity fracture Smith's fracture (volar displacement) and Barton's fracture (intra-articular shear) Scaphoid fracture Distal radial physeal injury in adolescents Wrist sprain or ligamentous injury Carpal dislocation (perilunate/lunate) Distal radioulnar joint injury Posteroanterior and lateral wrist radiographs to assess dorsal tilt, radial length and inclination, and articular involvement CT for complex intra-articular or comminuted patterns to plan fixation Post-reduction radiographs to confirm and monitor alignment Assessment for osteoporosis and secondary fracture prevention in older patients Clinical assessment of median nerve function before and after reduction Classically a fracture of the distal radius within a few centimetres of the wrist with dorsal displacement and angulation, producing the 'dinner-fork' deformity Typically caused by a fall onto the outstretched hand in an older, osteoporotic patient; displaced fractures usually require closed reduction and immobilisation, checking that radial length and volar tilt are restored Unstable, markedly comminuted, or intra-articular fractures often need surgical fixation such as a volar locking plate or K-wires to maintain alignment Median nerve symptoms (acute carpal tunnel) can arise from swelling or displacement and must be sought before and after reduction Watch for later complications including malunion, extensor pollicis longus tendon rupture, stiffness, and complex regional pain syndrome Early finger, elbow, and shoulder mobilisation during cast treatment helps prevent stiffness and disuse Progressive median nerve symptoms indicating acute carpal tunnel syndrome requiring urgent decompression or reduction Open fracture or skin compromise Marked deformity with vascular compromise of the hand Fracture from trivial trauma signalling significant underlying osteoporosis Accepting a poor reduction with persistent dorsal tilt or radial shortening, leading to symptomatic malunion Failing to recognise or monitor acute median nerve compression Immobilising the wrist in excessive flexion (Cotton-Loder position), which risks stiffness and nerve compression Neglecting finger and shoulder movement during cast treatment, causing stiffness and complex regional pain syndrome A Colles' fracture occurs when a fall onto the dorsiflexed, outstretched hand transmits force through the distal radius, which fails in its metaphyseal cancellous bone. Osteoporosis lowers the threshold for injury, explaining its predominance in postmenopausal women and older adults. The distal fragment tilts and displaces dorsally and radially and impacts proximally, shortening the radius and disrupting the normal volar tilt and radial inclination of the articular surface. Associated soft-tissue swelling or bony displacement may compress the median nerve in the carpal tunnel, and disruption of the distal radioulnar joint or triangular fibrocartilage can affect forearm rotation. Most stable distal radial fractures unite and recover good function with appropriate reduction and rehabilitation, but malunion with residual dorsal tilt and radial shortening can leave weakness, reduced grip, and cosmetic deformity, and intra-articular incongruity predisposes to post-traumatic arthritis.

suggesting an alternative neoplastic diagnosis Widespread or atypical distribution prompting reconsideration of amyloidosis New pigmented deposits raising concern for ongoing hydroquinone-related and require careful correlation Overlooking hydroquinone use as a cause of the pigmented variant Treating aggressively without recognising the benign, purely cosmetic nature of the condition Failing to reinforce sun protection, allowing the adult form to progress Assuming solitary amber papules on sun-damaged skin are benign without biopsy when features are atypical Colloid milium is defined by accumulation of amorphous colloid material in the upper dermis, but the origin differs by subtype. In the common adult form, chronic ultraviolet exposure drives severe solar elastosis, and the colloid is thought to derive from actinically degenerated elastic fibres, accumulating as fissured eosinophilic masses in the papillary dermis. The juvenile form, by contrast, appears to arise from filamentous degeneration of epidermal keratinocytes, producing colloid that is immunohistochemically distinct and often keratin-related, closer in nature to the amyloid seen in keratinocyte-derived cutaneous amyloidosis. The pigmented variant reflects colloid deposition associated with topical hydroquinone and shares features with exogenous ochronosis. Colloid milium is a benign, largely cosmetic condition; the adult form tends to persist and may slowly progress with continued sun exposure, whereas the juvenile form may stabilise or regress after puberty. There is no risk of systemic involvement, and outcomes are good with photoprotection and, where desired, physical removal.

Uveal/ocular coloboma and CHARGE-associated coloboma — uveal coloboma, chorioretinal coloboma, iris coloboma, CHARGE syndrome, CHD7 Microphthalmia and anophthalmia within the same developmental coherence tomography and ultrasound to assess involved structures Systemic evaluation for CHARGE features including cardiac and choanal assessment Audiological assessment given the frequent ear and hearing involvement Molecular genetic testing including CHD7 and a broader panel where syndromic Coloboma is a gap in one or more ocular structures resulting from failure of the embryonic optic (choroidal) fissure to close, classically located inferonasally It can affect the iris (producing a keyhole pupil), ciliary body, choroid, retina and optic disc, alone or in combination Visual impact ranges from minimal, when only the iris is involved, to severe, when the macula or optic nerve is affected Colobomatous eyes are prone to retinal detachment, so patients should know the warning be part of wider syndromes Symptoms of retinal detachment such as flashes, floaters or a visual field shadow Choanal atresia or cardiac anomaly in a neonate with coloboma requiring urgent care Optic disc or macular involvement threatening central vision Feeding, breathing or growth difficulties suggesting CHARGE syndrome Treating coloboma as purely a cosmetic iris finding and not examining the posterior segment Failing to evaluate for CHARGE syndrome and associated hearing loss Overlooking the raised retinal detachment risk and not counselling on warning symptoms Attributing all visual loss to the coloboma without excluding amblyopia or detachment Ocular coloboma results from incomplete closure of the optic (choroidal) fissure during early eye development, normally completed in the sixth week of gestation. Persistence of this fissure leaves a defect in the affected layers of the eye, characteristically in the inferonasal quadrant, and the retina and choroid overlying the gap are absent or malformed. In CHARGE syndrome, mutations in the chromatin-remodelling gene CHD7 disrupt development of multiple neural-crest and placode-derived structures during the same embryonic window, so coloboma coexists with cardiac, choanal, growth, genital and ear or hearing anomalies. The malformed retina at the coloboma margin is structurally weak, accounting for the raised risk of retinal detachment. Visual prognosis depends on which structures are involved, being good for isolated iris coloboma but guarded when the optic nerve, macula or a large chorioretinal area is affected, and further limited by the lifelong risk of retinal detachment; in CHARGE syndrome overall outcome is shaped by the systemic anomalies.

Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction — Ogilvie, Ogilvie syndrome, ACPO, acute colonic pseudo-obstruction Mechanical large-bowel obstruction (tumour, stricture, volvulus) Toxic megacolon from severe colitis Sigmoid or caecal volvulus Generalised paralytic ileus Faecal impaction with distension Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction Abdominal radiograph to document colonic and caecal diameter CT of the abdomen or water-soluble contrast enema to exclude a mechanical cause and assess for ischaemia or perforation Electrolyte panel including potassium, magnesium, calcium, and phosphate Review of the medication chart for motility-impairing drugs Serial clinical and radiological monitoring of caecal size and abdominal signs Massive dilatation of the colon, especially the caecum and right colon, in the absence of any mechanical obstructing lesion Typically occurs in hospitalised or debilitated patients after surgery, severe illness, trauma, infection, or in the setting of electrolyte disturbance and certain medications Presents with progressive abdominal distension, often with relatively little pain, and variable nausea, vomiting, and altered bowel output A mechanical obstruction and toxic megacolon must be excluded, usually with abdominal imaging and often a water-soluble contrast study or CT The main danger is progressive caecal dilatation leading to ischaemia and perforation, with risk rising sharply as caecal diameter increases and as distension persists Initial management is conservative: correct electrolyte abnormalities, stop contributing drugs (especially opioids and anticholinergics), decompress with a nasogastric tube, and mobilise the patient If conservative measures fail and there is no perforation, pharmacological decompression with a parasympathomimetic agent is effective, given under cardiac monitoring Colonoscopic decompression or, as a last resort, surgery is reserved for refractory cases or when ischaemia or perforation is suspected Progressive caecal dilatation, especially beyond a critical diameter, indicating high risk of ischaemia and perforation Abdominal tenderness, peritonism, fever, or rising lactate suggesting colonic ischaemia or perforation Failure to improve with conservative management over 24-48 hours Sudden clinical deterioration or signs of sepsis pointing to perforation requiring emergency surgery Assuming distension is a simple ileus and failing to exclude mechanical obstruction or monitor caecal diameter Continuing opioids or anticholinergic drugs that perpetuate the problem Delaying decompression until the caecum reaches a dangerous size and perforation risk is high Giving pharmacological decompression without cardiac monitoring or ignoring its contraindications Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction reflects a disturbance of the autonomic regulation of colonic motility, with a relative imbalance favouring reduced parasympathetic (excitatory) drive or excess sympathetic (inhibitory) tone in the distal colon. This produces a functional adynamic segment and proximal dilatation without any mechanical block. Precipitants include major surgery, severe systemic illness, sepsis, metabolic and electrolyte derangements, and drugs that impair gut motility. As the caecum distends, its wall tension rises (in keeping with the law of Laplace, tension increases with radius), compromising perfusion and risking ischaemic necrosis and perforation. Most patients recover with correction of precipitating factors and conservative or pharmacological decompression. Prognosis worsens substantially if ischaemia or perforation develops, which carries high mortality, so early recognition and monitoring of caecal size are critical.

Influenza and other nonspecific viral febrile illnesses Relapsing fever from Borrelia species Early Lyme disease RT-PCR on blood for viral RNA during acute illness Immunofluorescent detection of viral antigen in erythrocytes Paired acute and convalescent serology Full blood count showing leucopenia and thrombocytopenia Investigations to exclude Rocky Mountain spotted fever given overlapping presentation Cerebrospinal fluid analysis if meningoencephalitis is suspected Caused by a coltivirus transmitted by the Rocky Mountain wood tick (Dermacentor andersoni) at higher altitudes in the western United States and western Canada The illness is classically biphasic (saddleback fever), with fever, headache, myalgia, and photophobia that remit briefly and then recur after a few days The virus infects erythroid precursors and persists inside red blood cells, so leucopenia and thrombocytopenia are common and viraemia may be prolonged Because virus persists in erythrocytes for weeks, affected patients should be deferred from blood donation to avoid transfusion transmission Rash is less prominent than in the rickettsial tick-borne diseases, and the absence of an eschar or petechial manifestations with marked thrombocytopenia Persistent high fever failing to follow the expected self-limiting course Signs suggesting an alternative treatable tick-borne infection such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever Prolonged or severe cytopenias Withholding empirical treatment for Rocky Mountain spotted fever while awaiting confirmation, since that infection can be rapidly fatal Not deferring blood donation despite prolonged erythrocyte-associated viraemia Overlooking the mountain travel and tick-exposure history Attributing prolonged cytopenias to another cause Assuming a rash must be present to consider a tick-borne infection Colorado tick fever virus is introduced during the bite of an infected Dermacentor tick and infects haematopoietic progenitor cells in the bone marrow, including erythroid precursors. As infected cells mature, the virus remains sequestered within circulating erythrocytes, protecting it from immune clearance and producing prolonged viraemia. Marrow suppression accounts for the characteristic leucopenia and thrombocytopenia, and the biphasic fever pattern reflects waves of viral replication and host response. Rare severe manifestations include meningoencephalitis and haemorrhagic disease, particularly in children. The illness is usually self-limiting with full recovery, although convalescent fatigue and weakness may persist for weeks; severe complications such as encephalitis or haemorrhage are rare and occur mainly in children.

Colorectal Cancer — colon cancer, rectal cancer, bowel cancer Hemorrhoids or benign anorectal disease as a cause of rectal bleeding (rectal bleeding and altered bowel habits still demand DRE and sigmoidoscopy) (Harrison 22e p.656) Other causes of iron-deficiency anemia from chronic occult GI blood loss (Harrison 22e p.656) Inflammatory bowel disease (both a risk factor and a differential for altered bowel habit and bleeding) (Harrison 22e p.655) Colonoscopy of the entire large bowel (gold standard for detecting cancer and synchronous neoplasms/polyps) (Harrison 22e p.656) Flexible sigmoidoscopy as a screening modality (Harrison 22e p.655-656) Stool-based tests: fecal occult blood test, fecal immunochemical test (FIT), and fecal DNA testing (Harrison 22e p.655-656) Serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) (Harrison 22e p.656) Complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel (Harrison 22e p.656) Chest, abdomen, and pelvic CT scan; MRI and PET as dictated by CT findings (Harrison 22e p.656) Pelvic MRI for rectal cancer to assess mesorectal margin and nodal status (Harrison 22e p.658) Tumor MMR/microsatellite instability testing (IHC or MSI) and germline genetic testing where indicated (Harrison 22e p.654, 656) Investigational: plasma circulating tumor DNA as a biomarker for residual/recurrent disease (Harrison 22e p.658) Symptoms vary by tumor location. Right-sided cancers (cecum, ascending colon) can grow large without obstruction because stool is still liquid, and they tend to ulcerate, causing chronic insidious blood loss and presenting as iron-deficiency anemia (Harrison 22e p.656). Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia in any adult mandates a thorough endoscopic and/or radiographic visualization of the entire large bowel; the possible exception is a premenopausal, multiparous woman (Harrison 22e p.656). Left-sided (transverse/descending colon) tumors impede passage of more formed stool, producing abdominal cramping, occasional obstruction, and even perforation, classically the annular constricting 'apple-core' lesion on imaging (Harrison 22e p.656). Rectosigmoid cancers cause hematochezia, tenesmus, and narrowing of stool caliber; these may be mistaken for hemorrhoids, but rectal bleeding and/or altered bowel habits demand prompt digital rectal exam and sigmoidoscopy (Harrison 22e p.656). Most colorectal cancers arise from adenomatous polyps (not hyperplastic, hamartomatous, or serrated polyps); only a minority of adenomas progress, with risk tied to polyp size and histology, and villous adenomas becoming cancer about threefold more often than tubular adenomas (Harrison 22e p.653). Universal testing of colorectal tumors for MMR defects is recommended, by immunohistochemistry for MMR proteins or microsatellite instability testing; MSI-high tumors are dramatically sensitive to immune checkpoint inhibition and less sensitive to chemotherapy (Harrison 22e p.653-654, 656). Serum CEA is used for staging workup and follow-up; some authorities measure plasma CEA at 3-month intervals after curative resection because of its sensitivity as a marker for otherwise undetectable recurrence (Harrison 22e p.656-658). Liver is the most frequent visceral metastatic site, being the initial site of distant spread in about one-third of recurring cancers and involved in over two-thirds of patients at death; complete resection of metastases isolated to one site (liver, lung, peritoneum) is considered curative (Harrison 22e p.657-658). Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia in any adult (mandates evaluation of the entire large bowel) Change in bowel habit / altered bowel habits Rectal bleeding (hematochezia) or guaiac-positive stool Tenesmus and narrowing of the caliber of the stool (rectosigmoid lesions) Abdominal cramping or obstruction (left-sided lesions) Strong family history or known hereditary syndrome (FAP, MUTYH-associated polyposis, Lynch syndrome) Attributing rectal bleeding to hemorrhoids and not pursuing DRE and sigmoidoscopy (Harrison 22e p.656) Relying on fecal occult blood testing alone: about 50% of patients with documented colorectal cancer have a negative FOBT due to intermittent bleeding, and a colorectal neoplasm is NOT found in most asymptomatic individuals with a positive test (Harrison 22e p.655-656) Sigmoidoscopy alone misses proximal lesions: about 1.5% of individuals with a normal sigmoidoscopy harbor a high-risk polyp or adenocarcinoma in the proximal colon (Harrison 22e p.656) Lynch syndrome may not be associated with multiple polyps and is therefore often unrecognized (Harrison 22e p.654) Disease stage cannot be determined accurately before surgical resection and pathologic analysis unless gross metastatic disease is present (Harrison 22e p.656) Initial treatment should be delayed until MMR/microsatellite status is known when possible, since MSI-high rectal cancers may be cured with checkpoint inhibitors (PD-1 antibodies) without surgery, radiation, or chemotherapy (Harrison 22e p.656) The majority of colorectal cancers develop through the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence, in which adenomatous polyps accumulate sequential genetic and epigenetic events involving tumor suppressor genes and oncogenes. Three major sporadic molecular pathways exist: the chromosomal instability (CIN) pathway (the most common), characterized by early loss of the APC tumor suppressor gene followed by sequential MAP-kinase oncogene mutations such as KRAS and BRAF, with loss of p53 as a common final step; the mismatch repair (MMR) pathway, often caused by hypermethylation of MMR gene promoters, producing a microsatellite-instability-high (MSI-high) phenotype; and the CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP), with tumors that are often right-sided and associated with MLH1 methylation. These pathways are not mutually exclusive and can overlap in individual cancers (Harrison 22e p.653-654). Prognosis is stage-related and depends on depth of tumor penetration into the bowel wall, regional lymph node involvement, and distant metastases (TNM). Stage I (T1-2N0M0) confers a high cure rate (>90-95% 5-year survival); 5-year survival declines through stage II (T3-4N0M0), stage III (node-positive), and stage IV (distant metastasis, <5% in colon). Stage I patients are considered cured after complete resection. A minimum of 12 sampled lymph nodes is considered necessary to accurately define stage. Poor-prognosis features include penetration through the bowel wall into pericolic fat, poorly differentiated histology, perforation and/or adherence to adjacent organs, venous invasion, preoperative CEA >5 ng/mL, BRAF mutation, and right-sided primary location. Tumors with MSI/MMR defects have an improved prognosis (enhanced immune response), and left-colon tumors fare better than right-colon tumors. Notably, primary tumor size does not influence prognosis once adjusted for nodal involvement and differentiation. Most recurrences occur within the first 5 years (Harrison 22e p.656-658). TNM classification (American Joint Committee on Cancer / Union for International Cancer Control): T = depth of tumor penetration (T1 submucosa, T2 muscularis, T3 through muscularis, T4 adjacent structures), N = regional lymph node involvement (N1 = 1-3 nodes, N2 = >=4 nodes), M = distant metastasis. Stage I = T1-2N0M0; Stage II = T3-4N0M0; Stage III = any T, N1-2, M0; Stage IV = any T, any N, M1. The older Dukes classification was historically used for colorectal cancer (Harrison 22e p.656).
