major trauma requiring dual-factor replacement Menorrhagia causing anaemia Unrecognised diagnosis before major surgery Treating only one factor and leaving the other uncorrected during bleeding Assuming a low factor VIII reflects von Willebrand disease without checking factor V Confusing the inherited transport defect with an acquired combined deficiency Overlooking the diagnosis when both prolonged clotting times are attributed to liver disease Combined factor V and factor VIII deficiency results from loss-of-function variants in LMAN1 (encoding ERGIC-53) or its cofactor MCFD2. Together these proteins form a cargo receptor that transports factor V and factor VIII from the endoplasmic reticulum through the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment for secretion. When this transport machinery fails, both factors are inefficiently secreted, so their plasma levels fall in parallel despite normal factor V and factor VIII genes. The shared secretory pathway explains why two functionally distinct factors are deficient at once. The disorder generally causes only mild to moderate bleeding, and with appropriate replacement around surgery and childbirth the long-term outlook is good. Spontaneous severe bleeding is uncommon.

Combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema — CPFE, Emphysema with pulmonary fibrosis Isolated idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis Isolated chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with emphysema Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease with emphysema Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis with emphysema Pulmonary hypertension of other causes Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis HRCT thorax demonstrating upper-zone emphysema with lower-zone fibrosis Full pulmonary function tests with transfer factor, showing preserved volumes but a disproportionately low gas transfer Echocardiography and, where indicated, right heart catheterisation for pulmonary hypertension Six-minute walk test with oximetry documenting exertional desaturation Autoimmune serology to exclude connective tissue disease Surveillance imaging and vigilance for lung cancer Arterial blood gas analysis A distinct syndrome combining upper-lobe emphysema with lower-lobe pulmonary fibrosis, occurring predominantly in male heavy smokers. Characterised by relatively preserved lung volumes and spirometry, because the opposing mechanical effects of emphysema and fibrosis offset one another, but with a markedly and disproportionately reduced transfer factor. Severe exertional breathlessness and hypoxaemia on exercise are typical despite near-normal spirometry. HRCT shows upper-zone emphysema coexisting with lower-zone fibrosis, often with a UIP pattern. There is a high prevalence of pulmonary hypertension, which is the main determinant of poor prognosis. The risk of lung cancer is markedly increased and warrants ongoing vigilance. It is not a standalone consensus disease entity but an important recognisable phenotype that alters management and prognosis. Smoking cessation is essential, and management targets the fibrotic and pulmonary vascular components and associated comorbidities. Signs of pulmonary hypertension or right heart failure A new nodule or mass given the high risk of lung cancer Severe resting or exertional hypoxaemia Rapidly progressive breathlessness or an acute exacerbation of fibrosis Being falsely reassured by near-normal spirometry and missing severe disease Attributing symptoms to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease alone and overlooking the fibrosis, or vice versa Failing to investigate for pulmonary hypertension Not maintaining lung cancer vigilance and overlooking the diagnosis because it is not a formal single disease entity Tobacco smoke, and sometimes other inhaled exposures, produces concurrent emphysematous destruction of the upper-zone parenchyma and fibrotic remodelling of the lower zones. The coexistence yields pseudonormalised lung volumes and airflow, because hyperinflation from emphysema offsets the restriction of fibrosis, while gas transfer is severely impaired and pulmonary vascular remodelling frequently produces pulmonary hypertension. The outlook is worse than for emphysema alone; survival is strongly influenced by the presence and severity of pulmonary hypertension and by lung cancer, with high overall mortality.

Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias — Typical atrial flutter, Cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent atrial flutter, Atypical atrial flutter, Macroreentrant atrial tachycardia, Multifocal atrial tachycardia, MAT Atrial fibrillation Focal atrial tachycardia Atypical (non-CTI-dependent) atrial flutter vs typical flutter Left atrial / perimitral flutter Sinus tachycardia 12-lead ECG to identify sawtooth flutter waves and conduction ratio Vagal/AV-nodal-blocking maneuvers to unmask flutter waves at higher conduction ratios Electrophysiology study with electroanatomic mapping to define circuit and confirm mechanism in atypical flutter or to distinguish from focal AT CHA2DS2-VASc scoring for thromboembolic risk and bleeding-risk assessment Atrial fibrillation (irregular, no isoelectric baseline between atrial activations) versus MAT (isoelectric intervals present, slower atrial rate) Focal atrial tachycardia versus left atrial/atypical flutter (distinguished by P-wave morphology and often only by electrophysiology study) Common (typical) right atrial flutter is a macroreentrant circuit that revolves around the tricuspid valve annulus, passing through the cavotricuspid (sub-Eustachian) isthmus, which is why it is termed cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent flutter and is amenable to interruption at that isthmus (Harrison 22e p.1943). Counterclockwise rotation of the typical flutter circuit produces the characteristic negative sawtooth flutter waves in the inferior leads II, III, and aVF and positive flutter (P) waves in V1; clockwise (reverse typical) rotation produces the opposite vectors (Harrison 22e p.1943). The atrial rate in typical flutter is usually 240-300 beats/min but may be slower with atrial disease or antiarrhythmic drugs (Harrison 22e p.1943). Typical flutter often conducts to the ventricle with 2:1 AV block, yielding a regular tachycardia near 140-150 beats/min, where flutter waves can be obscured within the T wave (Harrison 22e p.1943). Maneuvers or AV nodal disease/agents that increase AV block raise the conduction ratio and unmask flutter waves, aiding diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1943). Typical flutter frequently coexists with atrial fibrillation and is associated with atrial scarring from aging or prior cardiac surgery; AF may precede the onset of flutter (Harrison 22e p.1943). Atrial conduction-slowing antiarrhythmics (flecainide, propafenone, amiodarone) can convert a patient's AF presentation into atrial flutter by promoting reentry while suppressing ectopic triggers (Harrison 22e p.1943). Atypical (non-cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent) flutters arise in either atrium, are almost universally tied to atrial scar, and are commonly seen after right atriotomy, extensive left atrial ablation for AF, or mitral valve surgery (Harrison 22e p.1943-1944). Left atrial flutter and perimitral left atrial flutter resemble common flutter clinically but show different P-wave morphologies and can mimic focal atrial tachycardia (Harrison 22e p.1944). Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT) is defined by at least three distinct P-wave morphologies with rates typically 100-150 beats/min and is mechanistically attributed to triggered automaticity from multiple atrial foci (Harrison 22e p.1946). Unlike atrial fibrillation, MAT shows clear isoelectric intervals between P waves and a slower atrial rate, helping distinguish the two (Harrison 22e p.1946). MAT is characteristically seen in patients with chronic pulmonary disease during acute illness (Harrison 22e p.1946). Hemodynamic instability with rapid ventricular response (may warrant urgent electrical cardioversion) Severe symptoms attributable to the arrhythmia Difficult-to-control ventricular rate, as rate control in flutter is frequently more challenging than in AF Elevated thromboembolic risk by CHA2DS2-VASc requiring attention before rhythm conversion In 2:1 conducted flutter, flutter waves hidden in the T wave can be mistaken for another regular narrow-complex tachycardia; failing to use AV-nodal-slowing maneuvers may miss the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1943). Assuming AF and flutter are independent: antiarrhythmics given for AF (e.g., flecainide, propafenone, amiodarone) may unmask or organize the rhythm into flutter (Harrison 22e p.1943). Attempting electrical cardioversion for MAT, which is ineffective for this automatic arrhythmia (Harrison 22e p.1946). Mislabeling atypical/left atrial flutter as focal atrial tachycardia without electrophysiologic confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1944). Assuming MAT carries the same thromboembolic risk as AF or flutter; in MAT this risk remains unclear and is not considered equivalent (Harrison 22e p.1946). Macroreentrant atrial tachycardia depends on a large anatomic reentry circuit, frequently involving areas of atrial scar with slow conduction. In common (typical) flutter, the wavefront encircles the tricuspid valve annulus, bounded anteriorly by the annulus and posteriorly by the inferior vena cava and Eustachian ridge, passing through the cavotricuspid isthmus between the IVC and tricuspid annulus. The circuit usually rotates counterclockwise as viewed from the ventricular apex; reversed (clockwise) rotation gives reverse typical flutter. AF and typical flutter are mechanistically interrelated: a line of functional block or coalescence of fibrillatory wavelets around barriers such as the crista terminalis and Eustachian valve may convert AF into organized flutter, and conduction-slowing antiarrhythmics promote this reentry. Atypical flutters are macroreentrant circuits not using the cavotricuspid isthmus, almost always associated with atrial scar. MAT arises from triggered automaticity in multiple atrial foci, producing multiple P-wave morphologies (Harrison 22e p.1943-1946). Typical flutter is highly treatable, with cavotricuspid isthmus catheter ablation achieving success rates greater than 95% with low complication and recurrence rates; however, up to half of patients undergoing such ablation later develop atrial arrhythmias, most often atrial fibrillation. With antiarrhythmic drug therapy alone, over 70% of patients experience recurrence. MAT prognosis is largely tied to the underlying pulmonary or systemic illness; electrical cardioversion is ineffective for MAT (Harrison 22e p.1944-1946). No formal severity grading scale; thromboembolic risk in flutter is stratified by the CHA2DS2-VASc score, and hemodynamic stability/symptom severity guides urgency of intervention (Harrison 22e p.1944).

tense compartment or severe disproportionate pain suggesting compartment syndrome Confusing a peroneal palsy with L5 radiculopathy by failing to test ankle inversion and plantarflexion Missing an intraneural ganglion or nerve sheath tumour in painful or recurrent presentations Attributing foot drop solely to positioning while overlooking a persisting structural cause Not fitting an ankle-foot orthosis early, allowing an equinus contracture to develop Overlooking a proximal sciatic lesion in which the peroneal division is selectively vulnerable The common peroneal (fibular) nerve is the lateral division of the sciatic nerve, carrying predominantly L4-S1 fibres. After separating in the popliteal fossa it curves around the lateral aspect of the fibular neck, where it lies superficially against bone with little protective soft tissue before dividing into the deep peroneal nerve (ankle and toe dorsiflexors, first dorsal web-space sensation) and the superficial peroneal nerve (evertors, dorsal foot sensation). This superficial, tethered course over rigid bone makes it highly vulnerable to external compression, stretch during knee flexion and inversion injury, and to focal masses such as ganglia. Injury produces focal demyelination with conduction block in mild cases and axonal loss in severe or prolonged compression, manifesting as weakness of dorsiflexion, toe extension and eversion with corresponding sensory loss. Neuropraxic palsies from transient compression usually recover over weeks to a few months once the precipitant is removed, and an ankle-foot orthosis maintains function in the interim. Lesions with substantial axonal loss or an unresected structural cause recover more slowly and less completely, and may leave a persistent foot drop.

common variable enteropathy — CVID enteropathy, CVID-associated enteropathy coeliac disease giardiasis and other chronic gastrointestinal infections inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn's disease autoimmune enteropathy small intestinal bacterial overgrowth intestinal lymphoma tropical sprue quantitative immunoglobulins and vaccine responses to establish CVID duodenal and colonic biopsies for villous atrophy and reduced plasma cells stool microscopy and antigen testing for Giardia and Cryptosporidium with stool culture cytomegalovirus PCR and immunohistochemistry on biopsy faecal calprotectin nutritional panel including iron, B12, folate and fat-soluble vitamins cross-sectional imaging or enteroscopy and a hydrogen breath test for bacterial overgrowth Common variable enteropathy is a chronic non-infective enteropathy of common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), presenting with chronic diarrhoea, malabsorption and weight loss despite immunoglobulin replacement. Histology often resembles coeliac disease with villous atrophy, but characteristically shows a paucity or absence of lamina propria plasma cells and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, and does not respond to a gluten-free diet. Other patterns include lymphoid nodular hyperplasia, a graft-versus-host-like appearance and changes resembling inflammatory bowel disease; gastric involvement may cause atrophic gastritis. Treatable infective mimics such as Giardia, cytomegalovirus, Cryptosporidium, small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth and Campylobacter must be excluded first. IgA-based coeliac serology is unreliable in antibody deficiency, so diagnosis rests on histology and exclusion of infection rather than serology. The enteropathy is associated with other non-infective CVID complications, including nodular regenerative hyperplasia of the liver, granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease, autoimmune cytopenias and an increased lymphoma risk. Immunoglobulin replacement corrects infection risk but does not treat the enteropathy; corticosteroids (including budesonide) and steroid-sparing immunomodulators are used for refractory disease. Nutritional support and surveillance for gastric carcinoma and lymphoma are important components of long-term care. rapid weight loss or severe malabsorption refractory diarrhoea despite treatment of identified infection features suggesting lymphoma such as a mass, night sweats or rising LDH gastrointestinal bleeding hepatosplenomegaly or signs of portal hypertension from nodular regenerative hyperplasia relying on coeliac serology in an antibody-deficient patient assuming villous atrophy equals coeliac disease and prescribing a gluten-free diet missing treatable infection such as Giardia or cytomegalovirus attributing symptoms solely to CVID without obtaining biopsies neglecting malignancy surveillance The enteropathy reflects the dysregulated mucosal immunity of CVID rather than a single mechanism. Deficient B-cell differentiation and a striking reduction in mucosal plasma cells impair local secretory antibody, while T-cell dysregulation, aberrant innate immune signalling and an altered gut microbiome contribute to immune-mediated small-bowel injury. The result is villous atrophy and chronic inflammation histologically overlapping with coeliac disease and inflammatory bowel disease, but distinguished by the paucity of plasma cells. Chronic infection and immune dysregulation coexist, and the same immune defects underlie the systemic non-infective complications seen in CVID. The course is variable but often chronic and difficult to treat, and the enteropathy is associated with poorer outcomes in CVID and with increased risks of lymphoma and malnutrition.

and/or IgM plus a poor antibody response to vaccines, in the absence of another defined cause of hypogammaglobulinaemia It is far more than an infection disorder: autoimmune cytopenias, granulomatous disease, enteropathy, lymphoid hyperplasia, and an increased risk of lymphoma are common and drive much of the morbidity Diagnosis is often delayed for years, so recurrent bacterial infections or should generally be avoided and are unreliable, and antibody responses to immunisation are used diagnostically rather than for protection Autoimmune and inflammatory complications may need immunosuppression, which must be balanced carefully against the underlying immune deficiency Because it is a heterogeneous diagnosis of exclusion, secondary causes such as protein loss, drugs, and haematologic malignancy must be ruled out Severe or overwhelming bacterial infection or sepsis in an untreated antibody-deficient patient Rapidly enlarging lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, or systemic symptoms suggesting lymphoma Progressive respiratory decline from bronchiectasis or interstitial lung disease Severe autoimmune cytopenia or refractory enteropathy causing haemodynamic or nutritional compromise Delaying diagnosis by not measuring immunoglobulins in adults with recurrent sinopulmonary infection or unexplained bronchiectasis Attributing autoimmune or granulomatous complications to a separate disease rather than to CVID itself Giving live vaccines or relying on vaccination for protection in an antibody-deficient patient Failing to exclude secondary and malignant causes of hypogammaglobulinaemia before labelling CVID CVID is a heterogeneous group of primary immunodeficiencies characterised by defective differentiation of B cells into immunoglobulin-secreting plasma cells and impaired class switching and memory B-cell formation, resulting in low serum immunoglobulins and failure of specific antibody responses. Although predominantly a humoral defect, many patients also have T-cell and innate immune abnormalities and dysregulated immune tolerance, which explain the frequent autoimmune and granulomatous-lymphoproliferative complications. Most cases are sporadic; a minority carry identifiable monogenic defects (e.g. in TACI/TNFRSF13B, ICOS, CD19 complex, NFKB pathways). The combined immune dysfunction predisposes to both infection and immune dysregulation, including malignancy. With regular immunoglobulin replacement and prompt treatment of infection, life expectancy has improved substantially. Prognosis is worst in patients who develop non-infectious complications-bronchiectasis, chronic lung disease, autoimmune disease, granulomatous-lymphoproliferative disease, and lymphoma-which are now the main determinants of mortality.

Common Viral Respiratory Infections, Other Than COVID-19 — Common cold, Viral upper respiratory tract infection, Non-COVID respiratory virus infection, Acute viral rhinosinusitis Bacterial pneumonia or secondary bacterial superinfection (notably staphylococcal/streptococcal after influenza) Streptococcal pharyngitis versus viral pharyngitis Bacterial sinusitis complicating viral rhinosinusitis Asthma or COPD exacerbation triggered by viral infection Allergic rhinitis mimicking the common cold Influenza COVID-19 / SARS-CoV-2 Bacterial pharyngitis, sinusitis, otitis media Bacterial or atypical pneumonia Pertussis presenting as prolonged cough EBV mononucleosis with exudative pharyngitis Primary HIV infection with pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy RT-PCR molecular testing and multiplex respiratory panels (most sensitive/specific) Rapid antigen detection for influenza and RSV in nasopharyngeal secretions Viral culture in a reference laboratory (gold standard for isolation) Direct/indirect fluorescent antibody detection in nasal secretions Chest radiograph in all patients with suspected pneumonia Pulse oximetry / oxygenation assessment in lower-tract disease Allergic rhinitis / vasomotor rhinitis Asthma or reactive airway disease COPD exacerbation from non-infectious triggers Aspiration or chemical/pollutant airway irritation Cardiac dyspnea masquerading as lower respiratory illness Respiratory virus infections are the most frequent infections in humans; many agents (rhinovirus, RSV, hMPV, parainfluenza, adenovirus, influenza, non-COVID coronaviruses) produce overlapping syndromes, so epidemiology, season, age, and exposure history narrow the differential more reliably than symptoms alone (Harrison 22e p.1531-1532). The vocal cords mark the boundary between upper and lower respiratory tract; syndrome correlates with the cell types a virus prefers, e.g. rhinitis/common cold, sinusitis, otitis media, pharyngitis and laryngitis above versus tracheitis, bronchitis, bronchiolitis and pneumonia below (Harrison 22e p.1532). Rhinoviruses are the single most common cause of the common cold, account for at least half of cases, and exist as more than 100 serotypes; because most adults develop radiographic sinus changes during a cold that resolve spontaneously, the entity is better termed rhinosinusitis (Harrison 22e p.1534-1535). RSV is among the most transmissible human viruses and a leading cause of severe lower respiratory tract illness and hospitalization in both infants and the frail elderly; it has a single serotype with two antigenic subgroups (A and B) that are only about 25 percent cross-related, partly explaining lifelong reinfection (Harrison 22e p.1533). Human metapneumovirus resembles RSV but is roughly half as likely to cause severe lower-tract disease, attributed to its lack of the nonstructural interferon-antagonist genes RSV uses to blunt innate immunity (Harrison 22e p.1533-1534). Measles is probably the most contagious respiratory virus, spreading by small-particle aerosol; the classic triad is the '3 Cs' (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis) with high fever, a maculopapular rash within days, and pathognomonic Koplik's spots in the setting of typical rash and fever (Harrison 22e p.1534). Coxsackievirus pharyngitis presents as herpangina (palatal vesicles/ulcers with fever, odynophagia and throat pain), and enterovirus A71 outbreaks of hand-foot-and-mouth disease can be complicated by neurologic disease; enterovirus D68 is linked to wheezing and acute flaccid myelitis (Harrison 22e p.1535). Adenovirus species B and C dominate respiratory disease, can establish persistent shedding from tonsils/adenoids for months to years, and classically cause pharyngoconjunctival fever; acute respiratory disease (ARD, types 4 and 7) historically devastated crowded military-recruit settings (Harrison 22e p.1535-1536). Acute bronchitis is a cough of under 3 weeks without pneumonia signs or radiographic infiltrate and is predominantly viral, whereas bacteria figure more prominently in chronic bronchitis; antibiotics do not improve uncomplicated viral respiratory infection in healthy patients (Harrison 22e p.1537). RT-PCR (including multiplex panels) is the most sensitive and specific diagnostic, but extreme sensitivity is a pitfall: prolonged genome persistence in secretions for weeks after recovery means a positive result may reflect a recently resolved rather than a currently active infection (Harrison 22e p.1537). Primary infection is generally far more severe than reinfection for the acute respiratory viruses; most primary (and thus many severe) infections occur in the first years of life, yet severe disease rises again in the elderly due to immune senescence (Harrison 22e p.1536). Contact and droplet precautions with rigorous hand hygiene suffice for most respiratory viruses; measles virus and varicella-zoster virus are notable exceptions that require airborne precautions because they spread by small-particle aerosol (Harrison 22e p.1537). Hypoxia or respiratory failure requiring oxygen or mechanical ventilation Tachypnea, dyspnea, chest pain or hypoxemia indicating pneumonia EBV tonsillar swelling severe enough to threaten airway occlusion Severe disease in immunocompromised hosts (HSCT/solid-organ transplant, chemotherapy-induced leukopenia, advanced HIV) Neurologic complications with enterovirus A71 or acute flaccid myelitis with enterovirus D68 Exposure history suggesting high-mortality zoonotic agents (avian influenza H5N1/H7N9, MERS-CoV) Dehydration from fever, tachypnea or poor oral intake (esp. young children with primary HSV stomatitis) Treating uncomplicated viral respiratory infection with antibiotics, which does not improve outcome in otherwise healthy patients Over-interpreting RT-PCR positives, since viral genome can persist for weeks post-recovery and asymptomatic individuals (e.g. rhinovirus, bocavirus) frequently test positive Applying rapid tests indiscriminately, lowering positive predictive value; testing is best targeted to high-risk exposures in the appropriate season Laboratory PCR contamination from prior reactions producing false positives Assuming rhinovirus is confined to the upper tract; it is now linked to wheezing, asthma exacerbations and (rhinovirus C) pneumonia/COPD exacerbation Missing secondary bacterial pneumonia complicating influenza Respiratory viruses enter via the respiratory tract and replicate in epithelium whose cell type dictates the resulting syndrome. Purely respiratory viruses (e.g. rhinoviruses) replicate only in respiratory epithelium, whereas systemic viruses (e.g. measles, SARS-CoV) disseminate via the bloodstream and may also injure the airway. Wheezing arises from smooth-muscle contraction plus luminal obstruction by mucus and sloughed epithelium, predominantly at the narrow-caliber bronchioles (bronchiolitis); croup reflects inflammation of larynx, trachea and bronchi causing inspiratory difficulty. Because non-viremic respiratory viruses elicit incomplete or waning immunity, reinfection with the same virus and even the same strain is common across life. Each virus type harbors vast antigenic diversity (e.g. influenza drift/shift, >100 rhinovirus serotypes), limiting durable cross-protection. Influenza pneumonia is notable for a high rate of secondary staphylococcal and streptococcal bacterial superinfection (Harrison 22e p.1531-1534). Most acute viral respiratory infections in immunocompetent hosts are self-limited, with reinfection generally milder than primary infection. Severe and sometimes fatal disease concentrates in infants, the frail/institutionalized elderly, those with underlying lung disease (especially COPD and oxygen-dependent disease) or cardiovascular disease, and immunocompromised patients, in whom conventional viruses may cause chronic and even fatal infection. Selected agents carry high lethality: the 2002-2003 SARS-CoV epidemic (>8000 cases) had mortality approaching 10 percent, and MERS-CoV mortality is approximately 35 percent. Measles, though often milder in immunocompetent children, causes high mortality in low-resource settings, especially with malnutrition (Harrison 22e p.1533-1536). No formal grading scheme; severity is stratified clinically by anatomic level (upper vs lower respiratory tract), presence of pneumonia or respiratory failure/hypoxia, and host risk (extremes of age, underlying lung/cardiac disease, COPD, obesity, immunocompromise). Accumulation of multiple risk factors markedly increases risk of severe lower respiratory tract disease (Harrison 22e p.1536).

commotio cordis — cardiac concussion, impact-induced sudden cardiac death myocardial contusion from blunt chest trauma traumatic coronary artery dissection underlying hypertrophic cardiomyopathy inherited arrhythmia syndrome such as long QT or Brugada aortic or great-vessel injury vasovagal or neurocardiogenic syncope exercise-associated collapse from heat illness immediate rhythm assessment with a defibrillator or monitor post-resuscitation twelve-lead electrocardiogram serial cardiac troponin to exclude significant contusion transthoracic echocardiography to confirm structural normality cardiac magnetic resonance to exclude occult cardiomyopathy genetic and family evaluation for inherited arrhythmia in survivors toxicology screen where recreational drug use is possible Sudden cardiac arrest triggered by a blunt, non-penetrating blow to the precordium in a structurally normal heart, without myocardial contusion or rib fracture. Classically occurs in young athletes struck by a projectile such as a baseball, hockey puck, lacrosse ball or a bodily collision during sport. The mechanism is induction of ventricular fibrillation when impact falls within a narrow vulnerable window on the upsloping phase of the T wave. The impact is often modest and would be considered innocuous, making the collapse appear disproportionate to the trauma sustained. Immediate collapse follows the blow, although a brief interval of consciousness before arrest has occasionally been described. Survival depends critically on prompt recognition, early cardiopulmonary resuscitation and rapid defibrillation, so access to an automated external defibrillator at sporting venues is vital. Autopsy in fatal cases reveals no causative structural cardiac abnormality, distinguishing it from cardiac contusion and from underlying inherited heart disease. Chest protectors have not reliably prevented events, and prevention centres on rule modification, softer training balls, and defibrillator availability. instantaneous collapse and unresponsiveness after a precordial blow absent pulse with ventricular fibrillation on initial rhythm check delay in initiating bystander resuscitation or defibrillation recurrent syncope or a family history of premature sudden death Underestimating the event because the causative blow seemed trivial and the heart is structurally normal. Delaying defibrillation while awaiting emergency services rather than using an on-site automated external defibrillator. Assuming a chest protector worn during sport excludes the diagnosis. Failing to evaluate survivors for an underlying inherited arrhythmia syndrome before return to play. Commotio cordis arises when a sudden blunt impact over the cardiac silhouette is transmitted to the myocardium at a precise, narrow phase of the cardiac cycle coinciding with the vulnerable period of repolarisation just before the T-wave peak. The mechanical energy activates ion channels, plausibly including mechanosensitive potassium channels, generating a premature depolarisation that captures the myocardium during heterogeneous repolarisation and precipitates ventricular fibrillation. The probability of a fatal event depends on the timing relative to this window, the location of impact directly over the heart, and the velocity and hardness of the striking object, whereas the heart itself is structurally normal. Historically survival was poor, but outcomes have improved substantially with widespread automated external defibrillator access and prompt bystander resuscitation; neurological recovery is favourable when defibrillation is delivered within the first minutes.

Acute compartment syndrome — compartment syndrome, acute limb compartment syndrome, ACS Arterial injury or acute limb ischaemia Deep vein thrombosis Cellulitis or necrotising soft-tissue infection Fracture or crush injury pain without compartment syndrome Peripheral nerve injury Chronic exertional compartment syndrome (in the appropriate setting) Serial clinical assessment of pain, pain on passive stretch, and neurology (the mainstay) Intracompartmental pressure measurement, especially in obtunded or equivocal cases Serum creatine kinase and renal function to detect rhabdomyolysis Urinalysis for myoglobinuria Radiographs to characterise any underlying fracture A surgical emergency in which raised pressure within a closed fascial compartment compromises tissue perfusion, leading to muscle and nerve ischaemia if not decompressed The cardinal early sign is pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch of the muscles in the affected compartment It commonly follows tibial or forearm fractures, crush injuries, reperfusion after vascular occlusion, or tight casts and dressings Pulselessness, pallor, paraesthesia, and paralysis are late signs; waiting for them risks irreversible damage, so a normal distal pulse does not exclude the diagnosis Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by compartment pressure measurement, particularly in the unconscious or unreliable patient Definitive treatment is urgent open fasciotomy to decompress all involved compartments; casts and constrictive dressings must be split or removed immediately while preparing for surgery The limb should be kept at heart level rather than elevated, and hypotension avoided, to maintain perfusion pressure Missed or delayed treatment leads to Volkmann's ischaemic contracture, permanent deficit, rhabdomyolysis with renal failure, and potential limb loss SURGICAL EMERGENCY: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch mandate urgent fasciotomy without delay Do not wait for pulselessness or paralysis, which are late and indicate established ischaemic damage Rapidly rising creatine kinase with dark urine indicating rhabdomyolysis and impending renal failure A tense, swollen limb after fracture, crush, or reperfusion, or beneath a tight cast Relying on the presence of distal pulses to exclude compartment syndrome Attributing escalating analgesic requirements solely to the fracture rather than recognising ischaemic pain Elevating the limb above heart level, which reduces perfusion pressure Delaying decompression pending imaging or specialist availability, allowing irreversible injury Acute compartment syndrome develops when pressure within a non-compliant osseofascial compartment rises to a level that impedes capillary perfusion. Bleeding, oedema, or external constriction increases compartment volume or reduces its capacity, raising interstitial pressure until it exceeds the perfusion gradient. Ischaemia increases capillary permeability, causing further oedema in a vicious cycle. Muscle and nerve are highly sensitive to ischaemia; sustained pressure elevation for a few hours produces irreversible necrosis. Because arterial inflow pressure is much higher than compartment pressure, distal pulses are often preserved until very late, making them an unreliable marker. With prompt fasciotomy, usually within a few hours of onset, muscle and nerve can recover fully; delay leads to ischaemic necrosis, fixed contracture (Volkmann's), sensory and motor deficits, chronic pain, and in severe cases systemic complications or amputation.

Complement C1 inhibitor deficiency — Hereditary angioedema, C1-INH deficiency, HAE types I and II Histaminergic (allergic) angioedema and urticaria ACE-inhibitor-induced angioedema Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency with lymphoproliferative disease Hereditary angioedema with normal C1-INH (factor XII or plasminogen mutations) Idiopathic non-histaminergic angioedema Gleich syndrome (episodic angioedema with eosinophilia) Systemic capillary leak syndrome Serum C4 level (low during and between attacks) C1 inhibitor antigenic (protein) concentration C1 inhibitor functional activity assay C1q level to distinguish acquired from hereditary forms SERPING1 gene sequencing when diagnosis is uncertain Screening for underlying lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disorder in suspected acquired disease Family screening of first-degree relatives Deficiency or dysfunction of C1 esterase inhibitor causes recurrent, non-pruritic, non-urticarial angioedema of skin, gut and airway mediated chiefly by bradykinin. Type I (about 85 percent) shows low antigenic and functional C1-INH, whereas type II shows normal or high antigenic levels with reduced function. A persistently low C4 between and during attacks is a useful screening clue; confirmation requires C1-INH antigenic and functional assays. Attacks are self-limiting over 2 to 5 days but laryngeal involvement can be fatal from asphyxiation. Abdominal attacks mimic a surgical abdomen with colic, vomiting and ascites, frequently leading to unnecessary laparotomy. Triggers include trauma, dental work, oestrogens, ACE inhibitors and emotional stress; lesions do not respond to antihistamines, corticosteroids or adrenaline. Acute treatment uses C1-INH concentrate, a bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist or a kallikrein inhibitor; prophylaxis employs C1-INH, attenuated androgens or a plasma kallikrein inhibitor. Acquired C1-INH deficiency, associated with lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease, features low C1q and later onset without family history. Laryngeal oedema with voice change, dysphagia or stridor threatening the airway Rapidly progressive facial or neck swelling Severe abdominal attack with hypovolaemia from third-space fluid loss First presentation of angioedema in an older adult suggesting acquired deficiency and occult malignancy Failure of swelling to respond to adrenaline, antihistamine and corticosteroid Treating bradykinin-mediated angioedema as an allergic reaction with adrenaline, steroids and antihistamines, which are ineffective. Proceeding to laparotomy for recurrent abdominal attacks misdiagnosed as a surgical emergency. Prescribing ACE inhibitors or oestrogen-containing contraceptives, which precipitate attacks. Relying on a single normal C4 to exclude the diagnosis, since it is most reliably low during an attack. Overlooking acquired C1-INH deficiency by not checking C1q in late-onset disease. C1 inhibitor is a serine protease inhibitor that regulates the classical complement pathway, the contact (kallikrein-kinin) system, the coagulation cascade and fibrinolysis. In hereditary angioedema, autosomal dominant mutations in SERPING1 reduce the quantity (type I) or function (type II) of C1-INH. Loss of inhibition permits unchecked activation of plasma kallikrein, generating excess bradykinin from high-molecular-weight kininogen. Bradykinin acts on endothelial B2 receptors to increase vascular permeability, producing localised subcutaneous and submucosal oedema. Consumption of C4 and C2 through unregulated classical pathway activity explains the characteristically low C4. With modern on-demand and prophylactic therapy most patients achieve good control and a normal life expectancy, but untreated laryngeal attacks carry a significant mortality. Disease severity and attack frequency vary widely even within a single family.

Complement C3 deficiency — C3 deficiency, hereditary C3 deficiency Other complement component deficiencies (for example early classical pathway or terminal pathway defects) Antibody deficiencies causing recurrent encapsulated bacterial infection Asplenia or hyposplenism Systemic lupus erythematosus from other causes Secondary complement consumption (for example membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis with C3 nephritic factor) Total haemolytic complement (CH50) and alternative pathway (AH50) screening Quantitative C3 (and C4) levels Assays of individual complement components and function Investigation for C3 nephritic factor and autoantibodies where consumption is suspected Renal assessment (urinalysis, renal function, and biopsy if glomerulonephritis is suspected) Autoimmune serology for lupus-like disease C3 is the central component of the complement system, shared by the classical, alternative, and lectin pathways, so its deficiency produces broad impairment of complement function Complete C3 deficiency causes severe susceptibility to recurrent pyogenic infections with encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Neisseria species Because C3 is essential for opsonisation, patients cannot efficiently coat bacteria for phagocytosis, leading to invasive infections including sepsis, meningitis, and pneumonia In addition to infection, C3 deficiency predisposes to immune complex disease, notably a lupus-like syndrome and various forms of glomerulonephritis The defect can be inherited (autosomal recessive) or arise secondary to consumption, for example in the presence of C3 nephritic factor Laboratory screening typically shows a very low or undetectable total haemolytic complement (CH50) together with a low AH50, reflecting the shared central role of C3 Preventive care emphasises vaccination against encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus, and Haemophilus influenzae type b) and prompt treatment of infections Some patients benefit from antibiotic prophylaxis, and screening for associated renal and autoimmune disease is important Invasive infection such as meningitis, sepsis, or pneumonia with encapsulated organisms requiring urgent treatment Recurrent severe pyogenic infection warranting complement evaluation Signs of glomerulonephritis (haematuria, proteinuria, declining renal function) Features of a systemic lupus-like illness Failing to measure complement in a patient with recurrent invasive encapsulated bacterial infection Attributing a lupus-like presentation solely to primary autoimmune disease without considering complement deficiency Not ensuring vaccination against pneumococcus, meningococcus, and Haemophilus influenzae type b Overlooking associated glomerulonephritis Confusing primary genetic deficiency with secondary consumptive low C3 C3 sits at the convergence of all three complement activation pathways, and its cleavage generates C3b, the principal opsonin, and C3a, an anaphylatoxin, while enabling assembly of the C5 convertase and downstream membrane attack complex. In C3 deficiency, opsonisation of encapsulated bacteria fails and phagocytic clearance is severely impaired, producing recurrent invasive pyogenic infection. C3 and its fragments also contribute to the clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic debris and to the regulation of B-cell responses; their absence permits immune complex deposition in tissues such as the kidney and skin, explaining the lupus-like autoimmune manifestations and glomerulonephritis. The deficiency may be primary (genetic) or secondary to unregulated consumption of C3. With vaccination against encapsulated organisms, prompt treatment of infections, and where appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis, many patients do well, but the risk of severe invasive infection persists and the outlook is also influenced by any associated renal or autoimmune disease.

Complement deficiency — complement component deficiency, inherited complement deficiency, terminal complement deficiency Asplenia or hyposplenism with encapsulated-organism infection Antibody deficiencies (e.g. CVID, specific antibody deficiency) Acquired complement consumption from active autoimmune or immune-complex disease Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective-tissue diseases Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome from complement-regulatory defects Hereditary angioedema from C1-inhibitor deficiency CH50 (classical pathway) and AH50 (alternative pathway) functional screens Individual complement component assays to identify the specific deficiency C3, C4, and C1q levels, distinguishing inherited deficiency from consumption Autoimmune serology (e.g. ANA, dsDNA) when immune-complex disease is suspected Genetic testing in selected or familial cases Microbiologic confirmation and serogrouping of neisserial and other invasive infections The infection and disease pattern in complement deficiency tracks the part of the cascade affected, so localising the defect predicts clinical risk Deficiencies of the terminal components (C5-C9) and of properdin impair formation of the membrane attack complex and cause a striking susceptibility to recurrent Neisseria infection, especially meningococcal disease Early classical-pathway deficiencies (C1q, C1r/s, C4, C2) predispose strongly to systemic lupus erythematosus and other immune-complex diseases because complement is needed to clear apoptotic cells and immune complexes C3 deficiency, at the hub of all pathways, produces both severe pyogenic infection with encapsulated bacteria and immune-complex disease Recurrent or unusual neisserial infection, or a single episode with an uncommon meningococcal serogroup, should prompt complement evaluation The CH50 screens the classical pathway and the AH50 the alternative pathway; a near-absent total haemolytic complement points to a specific component deficiency to be confirmed by individual assays Prevention centres on vaccination against encapsulated organisms-meningococcus (including serogroup B), pneumococcus, and Haemophilus influenzae type b-with prompt treatment of febrile illness C1-inhibitor deficiency is a distinct entity causing bradykinin-mediated hereditary angioedema rather than the infection-prone phenotypes of other complement defects Acquired complement consumption from active immune-complex disease must be distinguished from inherited deficiency, since low levels may simply reflect ongoing disease activity Meningococcal or other invasive neisserial infection, or meningitis with rapid deterioration, requiring emergency antibiotics Recurrent invasive infection with encapsulated bacteria signalling significant deficiency Sepsis in a known complement-deficient or asplenic patient Features of severe systemic lupus with major organ involvement in early-component deficiency Failing to evaluate complement after recurrent or unusual neisserial infection Interpreting a low complement level as inherited deficiency when it reflects consumption by active disease Neglecting to give and update the full schedule of vaccines against encapsulated organisms Confusing C1-inhibitor deficiency (angioedema) with the infection-prone complement defects The complement system comprises the classical, lectin, and alternative pathways that converge on C3 and the terminal pathway that assembles the C5b-9 membrane attack complex. Its functions include opsonisation, chemotaxis and inflammation, direct lysis of certain pathogens, and clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic debris. Inherited deficiency of a component removes the corresponding function: loss of early classical components impairs immune-complex handling and predisposes to lupus-like autoimmunity; deficiency of C3 or opsonic components causes pyogenic infection with encapsulated bacteria; and deficiency of terminal components or properdin cripples membrane-attack-complex killing of Neisseria. Regulatory-protein defects produce different phenotypes, such as C1-inhibitor deficiency causing angioedema and factor H/I defects causing atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome. With appropriate vaccination, prompt treatment of infection, and in some cases antibiotic prophylaxis, most patients with complement deficiency do well. Prognosis is worse when invasive infection is not recognised early, and outcomes in early-component deficiency are additionally shaped by the severity of associated autoimmune disease.

46,XX gonadal dysgenesis — 46,XX complete gonadal dysgenesis, XX gonadal dysgenesis, XX pure gonadal dysgenesis, hypergonadotropic ovarian dysgenesis Turner syndrome and its mosaic forms Swyer syndrome (46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis) Premature ovarian insufficiency of other cause Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (uterus absent) Galactosaemia-associated ovarian failure Karyotype confirming 46,XX and excluding a Y-bearing line Serum follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone and oestradiol demonstrating hypergonadotropic hypogonadism Pelvic ultrasound or MRI confirming a uterus and streak gonads Genetic testing including FSHR and syndromic genes where indicated Audiometry to detect associated sensorineural hearing loss (Perrault syndrome) Bone mineral density assessment given oestrogen deficiency A 46,XX individual with a female phenotype, normal internal mullerian structures, but bilateral streak gonads that fail to produce oestrogen Typically presents with primary amenorrhoea and absent or arrested puberty in a girl of normal stature, without the somatic stigmata of Turner syndrome Biochemistry shows hypergonadotropic hypogonadism with high gonadotropins and low oestradiol Often inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, with variants in genes such as FSHR and other ovarian-determining and DNA-repair genes; some cases form part of syndromes (for example Perrault syndrome with sensorineural deafness) The uterus is present and normal, so pregnancy is achievable through oocyte donation after adequate hormonal preparation Unlike dysgenesis involving a Y chromosome, there is no gonadoblastoma risk, so prophylactic gonadectomy is not indicated on tumour grounds Management centres on oestrogen and progestogen replacement to induce puberty, maintain secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone Associated sensorineural deafness or neurological features suggesting a syndromic diagnosis Severe osteoporosis or fragility fracture from untreated oestrogen deficiency Delayed diagnosis with prolonged absence of pubertal development Any evidence of a Y-chromosome line on karyotype, which would change tumour-risk management Attributing primary amenorrhoea to constitutional delay and missing hypergonadotropic hypogonadism Recommending gonadectomy despite the absence of a Y chromosome and tumour risk Confusing it with androgen insensitivity, in which the uterus is absent Overlooking associated syndromic features such as deafness In 46,XX gonadal dysgenesis the karyotype is normal female, but the ovaries fail to develop and are replaced by fibrous streak gonads, so oestrogen production is absent. This may follow biallelic defects in genes required for ovarian development or gonadotropin signalling (such as the follicle-stimulating hormone receptor) or occur within multisystem syndromes. The mullerian ducts, whose development does not depend on gonadal hormones, form a normal uterus and upper vagina, while the absence of oestrogen prevents pubertal maturation and drives compensatory elevation of gonadotropins. Because no Y-chromosome material is present, the streak gonads do not carry the germ cell tumour risk seen in Y-bearing dysgenesis. With oestrogen and progestogen replacement, pubertal development and bone health can be established and maintained, and pregnancy is feasible through oocyte donation because the uterus is intact. The absence of a Y line means germ cell tumour risk is not a concern in this karyotype.

Complete heart block — third-degree AV block, complete AV block, CHB, third-degree atrioventricular block Second-degree AV block (Mobitz I and II) High-grade AV block with occasional conduction AV dissociation without true complete block Sinus bradycardia or sinus arrest with a junctional escape Drug or electrolyte induced bradyarrhythmia Junctional rhythm from other causes 12-lead ECG and continuous rhythm monitoring to confirm AV dissociation and characterise the escape Electrolytes including potassium and review of AV-nodal-blocking medications Assessment for acute ischaemia or infarction including cardiac biomarkers Echocardiography to assess ventricular function and structural or infiltrative disease Evaluation for infiltrative, inflammatory, or infective conduction system disease when suspected In complete heart block there is no conduction from atria to ventricles, so atrial and ventricular activity are entirely independent, giving AV dissociation with a slower, regular ventricular rate driven by an escape rhythm The ECG shows P waves and QRS complexes marching independently, with the atrial rate faster than the ventricular rate The reliability and rate of the escape rhythm depend on its origin: a narrow junctional escape is usually faster and more stable, whereas a wide ventricular escape is slower and less dependable Presentations include fatigue, breathlessness, presyncope, syncope, and haemodynamic collapse, and it can precipitate cardiac arrest if the escape fails Common causes are age-related conduction system fibrosis, ischaemia or infarction (particularly inferior), drugs affecting the AV node, and infiltrative or post-procedural disease Reversible causes such as offending drugs, hyperkalaemia, and ischaemia should be sought and corrected Symptomatic or high-risk complete heart block is an indication for cardiac pacing, temporary in the acute setting and permanent for irreversible block In acute inferior infarction the block is often transient and nodal, whereas anterior infarction with block implies extensive damage and a worse prognosis MEDICAL EMERGENCY: haemodynamic instability, syncope, or an unreliable slow wide-complex escape rhythm at risk of asystole, requiring urgent temporary pacing Complete heart block complicating acute anterior myocardial infarction, indicating extensive damage Recurrent syncope (Stokes-Adams attacks) from transient ventricular standstill Escape rhythm failure progressing to asystole and cardiac arrest Mistaking marked AV dissociation from other mechanisms for true complete block, or vice versa Failing to identify and reverse causes such as AV-nodal drugs, hyperkalaemia, or ischaemia before committing to permanent pacing Underestimating the instability of a wide-complex ventricular escape rhythm Delaying temporary pacing in a symptomatic or unstable patient Complete heart block arises when conduction through the AV node or the His-Purkinje system is entirely interrupted, so no atrial impulse reaches the ventricles. Ventricular activity then depends on a subsidiary escape pacemaker distal to the block. Block within the AV node typically produces a junctional escape with a narrow QRS and a relatively faster, more stable rate, whereas block in the His-Purkinje system produces a ventricular escape with a wide QRS, slower rate, and greater risk of asystole. Causes include degenerative fibrosis of the conduction system, ischaemic damage, increased vagal or drug-induced nodal suppression, electrolyte disturbance, and infiltrative processes. Untreated symptomatic complete heart block carries a high risk of syncope and sudden death, but permanent pacing restores a normal prognosis in most; outcome is worse when block complicates extensive anterior infarction or advanced structural heart disease, and better when a reversible cause is corrected.

Complex regional pain syndrome — CRPS, reflex sympathetic dystrophy, RSD, causalgia, CRPS type I, CRPS type II Peripheral neuropathy or specific peripheral nerve injury Deep vein thrombosis Cellulitis or other soft-tissue infection Inflammatory or crystal arthropathy Compartment syndrome Vascular insufficiency or thoracic outlet syndrome Factitious or self-induced limb dysfunction Clinical assessment against the Budapest diagnostic criteria as the primary basis for diagnosis Plain radiographs, which may show patchy periarticular osteopenia in established disease Three-phase bone scintigraphy showing periarticular uptake in supportive cases Quantitative sensory testing and infrared thermography to document sensory and temperature asymmetry Investigations to exclude mimics, including venous Doppler, inflammatory markers, and nerve conduction studies where a nerve lesion is suspected Presents as regional pain that is disproportionate in severity and duration to the inciting event, often following a fracture, sprain, surgery, or immobilisation of a limb The diagnosis is clinical and rests on the Budapest criteria, requiring symptoms and signs across sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor/oedema, and motor/trophic domains with no better alternative explanation Type I follows tissue injury without a defined nerve lesion, whereas type II (causalgia) follows an identifiable peripheral nerve injury Characteristic features include allodynia, hyperalgesia, temperature and colour asymmetry between limbs, sweating changes, swelling, and later trophic changes to skin, hair, and nails Early mobilisation and functional restoration through physical and occupational therapy are the cornerstone of treatment, with pain control used to enable participation in rehabilitation rather than as an end in itself Graded motor imagery and mirror therapy can help address the cortical remapping and body-perception disturbances seen in the condition Pharmacological principles favour agents targeting neuropathic pain such as gabapentinoids and certain antidepressants, alongside bisphosphonates and short courses of corticosteroids in selected early cases Sympathetic nerve blocks and, in refractory cases, spinal cord stimulation may be considered as part of a multidisciplinary programme Untreated or under-treated disease can progress to fixed contractures, disuse atrophy, and permanent functional loss, so timely recognition matters Rapidly spreading swelling, erythema, or systemic features suggesting infection or deep vein thrombosis rather than CRPS Progressive fixed contracture or dystonia threatening irreversible loss of limb function Signs of compartment syndrome in an acutely painful, tense limb Severe refractory pain with escalating opioid use and psychological deterioration New or evolving focal neurological deficit implying an untreated nerve or spinal lesion Prolonged immobilisation or splinting of the affected limb, which worsens stiffness and reinforces disuse Delaying the diagnosis by attributing persistent disproportionate pain to the original injury alone Focusing on pain elimination with escalating medication instead of restoring function through active therapy Overlooking coexisting anxiety, depression, or catastrophising that undermine rehabilitation Relying on imaging to confirm the diagnosis when the criteria are fundamentally clinical Complex regional pain syndrome is a maladaptive response to injury involving several overlapping mechanisms. Peripheral and central sensitisation amplify nociceptive signalling, while neurogenic inflammation driven by neuropeptide release produces oedema, vasodilation, and warmth. Autonomic dysregulation causes vasomotor and sudomotor changes, and cortical reorganisation of the somatosensory and motor maps contributes to distorted body perception, motor dysfunction, and persistent pain. An exaggerated inflammatory and immune response, together with possible autoimmune contributions, is thought to perpetuate the disorder beyond the expected healing time of the original injury. Outcomes vary widely; many patients improve substantially with early diagnosis and active functional rehabilitation, but a minority develop chronic, treatment-resistant disease with lasting pain, stiffness, and disability. Delay in diagnosis, prolonged immobilisation, and untreated psychological distress are associated with poorer recovery.

Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries — Traumatic brain injury, TBI, Concussion, Mild TBI, mTBI, Head injury, Closed head injury Postconcussion symptom overlap with preinjury mood or anxiety disorders (e.g., depression, PTSD) Transient ischemic attack (chronic subdural hematoma may mimic with brief hemiparesis or aphasia) Intracranial neoplasm or abscess (evolving contusion with surrounding enhancement and edema can be mistaken for these) Carotid or vertebral artery dissection presenting as focal deficit after trauma Vasovagal syncope after injury Drug or alcohol intoxication confounding the neurologic exam Cervical spine injury (may be clinically inapparent) Noncontrast CT - first-line for skull fracture, extra-axial hematoma, contusion, traumatic SAH, and large TAI lesions with blood MRI (including gradient-echo/susceptibility-weighted and diffusion sequences) - more sensitive than CT for microhemorrhage and axonal injury; detects intracranial abnormalities in ~27% of CT-negative mild TBI patients and has prognostic value Advanced/multimodal MRI (functional MRI, cerebral blood flow, diffusion) - increasing sensitivity for subtle injury Blood-based biomarkers GFAP and UCHL1 - point-of-care detection and prognostication across the TBI spectrum GCS scoring before sedation/paralysis or intubation Validated symptom inventories (e.g., Rivermead Post-Concussion Symptom Questionnaire) to quantify and track recovery Intracranial pressure monitoring (ventricular catheter or fiberoptic device) in severe TBI to guide therapy (note: has not been shown to improve outcome) Cervical spine imaging given risk of concurrent occult injury Chronic subdural hematoma mimicking TIA, dementia, or personality change in the elderly Contusion with delayed contrast enhancement mimicking tumor or abscess Trochlear (fourth nerve) palsy after minor head injury mimicking primary ocular motility disorder Persistent postconcussion symptoms attributable instead to preinjury psychiatric illness, migraine, or adjustment reaction CTE clinical criteria overlapping with other neurodegenerative conditions (low specificity) TBI is defined as an externally caused alteration in brain function or other evidence of brain pathology, marked by any of the following: loss/decrease in consciousness, retrograde or posttraumatic amnesia, neurologic deficits, or altered mental state at the moment of injury (p.3571). Incidence shows a bimodal age distribution: motor vehicle crashes predominate in younger persons (more often men), while falls are the leading cause in older adults (more often women); roughly 70-90% (most estimates ~85%) of treated TBIs are mild (p.3570, p.3572). Severity is graded with the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS): mild 13-15, moderate 9-12, severe 3-8; the individual eye/verbal/motor components (e.g., E3V4M6) are more informative than the summed total, which should only describe groups (p.3571). In moderate-to-severe TBI, GCS plus the duration of loss of consciousness (LOC) and posttraumatic amnesia (PTA) predict outcome well; in mild TBI, LOC and PTA are far less predictive of recovery time and outcome, and postinjury symptom burden is the most robust predictor (p.3571, p.3574). Epidural hematoma classically follows tearing of the middle meningeal artery beneath a temporal-bone fracture, evolves rapidly, and may be preceded by a lucid interval; rapid surgical evacuation usually yields a favorable outcome (p.3572). Acute subdural hematoma is usually venous in origin, can occur without major trauma (especially in the elderly or anticoagulated, or from acceleration/whiplash forces), and carries significant morbidity and mortality when surgery is required - in contrast to the generally better-treated epidural hematoma (p.3572). Contusions follow coup (under the impact) and contrecoup (antipolar) mechanisms; blunt deceleration typically bruises the orbitofrontal and anterior/basal temporal lobes, and old contusion sites become gliotic scars that are highly epileptogenic (p.3573). Traumatic axonal injury (TAI) from shearing forces is among the most common TBI lesions; four or more foci constitute diffuse axonal injury (DAI), which when widespread is proposed to underlie prolonged coma and the vegetative state (p.3573). Anosmia and apparent loss of taste occur in ~10% of serious head injuries (especially falls onto the back of the head) from shearing of olfactory filaments at the cribriform plate; persistent bilateral anosmia for several months carries a poor prognosis (p.3573-3574). Second-impact syndrome is a rare, often fatal diffuse cerebral swelling that follows a second minor head injury before the first has resolved - a key reason no athlete should return to play until fully asymptomatic and cleared (p.3575). Blood biomarkers GFAP (astroglial injury) and UCHL1 (neuronal injury) are now usable at point of care; GFAP in particular discriminates intracranial abnormalities and helps stratify CT+, CT-/MRI+, and CT-/MRI- patients, with both diagnostic and prognostic value (p.3574). Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) - tau deposition in superficial cortical layers, perivascular regions, and the depths of sulci - is linked to repetitive head impacts but remains a postmortem diagnosis; proposed clinical criteria lack specificity and in vivo imaging/biomarker findings have been inconsistent (p.3576-3577). Lucid interval followed by neurologic deterioration (suggests epidural or, less often, subdural hematoma) Stupor or coma, hemiparesis, and unilateral pupillary enlargement (larger hematoma with mass effect) Coma from the moment of injury - requires immediate resuscitation and neurologic attention Persistent confusion, repeated vomiting (two or more episodes), palpable skull fracture, seizure, or >30 min of retrograde/persistent anterograde amnesia - sensitive indicators of intracranial hemorrhage warranting CT Age >65 years, underlying coagulopathy or anticoagulant use, or concurrent serious bodily injury - lower the threshold for imaging CSF leak (orthostatic headache, rhinorrhea/otorrhea), hemotympanum, Battle sign, or raccoon eyes - signs of basilar skull fracture Large contusion or hemorrhage after only minor trauma - raises concern for coagulopathy or anticoagulation Bilateral anosmia persisting for months - poor prognostic sign Grading severity solely on acute injury characteristics can mislead - some severe TBI patients recover fully while some mild TBI patients have lifelong disability. Relying on the summed GCS total rather than its components loses information; the score is confounded if recorded after sedation, paralysis, or intubation. Assuming a normal CT excludes injury in mild TBI - MRI reveals intracranial abnormalities in about 27% of CT-negative patients and 3T MRI can show contusion/microhemorrhage. Prescribing prolonged rest after concussion - inactivity beyond ~5 days can be detrimental and prolong recovery; supervised subthreshold exercise shortens symptom duration. Overusing dependence-producing drugs for postconcussion symptoms. Missing chronic subdural hematoma in the elderly, where trauma may be trivial or forgotten and the clot can become isodense and inapparent on CT between 2-6 weeks. Overlooking concurrent occult cervical spine injury or drug/alcohol intoxication in injuries of intermediate severity. Diagnosing CTE in vivo - it remains a postmortem diagnosis and proposed clinical criteria lack specificity. Therapeutic nihilism in severe TBI, reinforced by the common but premature 6-month outcome endpoint - recovery may continue for years. TBI results from external mechanical force - the head being struck or striking an object, acceleration/deceleration of the brain, penetration, or blast/explosion - producing primary structural lesions and secondary injury. A skull fracture marks the site and severity of impact and, when the arachnoid is torn, opens a pathway for CSF leak and bacterial entry (meningitis risk); basilar fractures may cause CSF leak, pneumocephalus, and delayed cavernous-carotid fistula. Extra-axial hematomas arise from torn meningeal arteries (epidural) or bridging veins (subdural) and exert mass effect that raises intracranial pressure. Cortical surface bruising (contusion) occurs at coup and contrecoup sites with petechial hemorrhage, edema, and tissue destruction. Shearing of axons (traumatic/diffuse axonal injury) at impact, with associated microhemorrhages, disrupts white-matter connectivity. Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage from rupture of small cortical vessels is common and, when diffuse after severe TBI, increases mortality. In concussion/mild TBI, conventional CT is often normal while higher-resolution 3T MRI may reveal contusion or microhemorrhage; advanced imaging shows reduced cerebral blood flow, altered functional connectivity, and white-matter microstructural change that broadly track injury severity and recovery, though subtle changes may persist after clinical recovery (a neurobiologic recovery 'tail'). The typical concussion syndrome has a good prognosis with little risk of subsequent deterioration. After sport-related concussion, recovery is generally favorable: in a large collegiate cohort, median symptom resolution was about 6.4 days and median return to sport 12.8 days, with ~92% symptom resolution and ~85% clearance to return by one month; most athletes across ages fully recover over 1-4 weeks. A subset develop persistent postconcussion symptoms (PPCS) beyond ~3 months; preinjury mental health disorder, migraine, and prior concussion predispose to prolonged recovery. Recovery from severe TBI can take years, and long-term outcome prediction is limited and often incorrect; best practice recommends aggressive therapy for at least 72 h (absent brain death). TBI is now recognized as a chronic, dynamic condition, with meaningful improvement or decline observed 2-7 years post-injury regardless of initial severity. TBI (mild to severe) is associated with a 63-96% increased risk of all-cause dementia, with risk greatest after severe injury; TBI with LOC >1 h has been linked to subsequent Parkinson's disease and Lewy body accumulation. Glasgow Coma Scale-based grading: mild/concussion GCS 13-15, moderate GCS 9-12, severe GCS 3-8 (scores range 3-15). Mild TBI with CT and/or MRI abnormality is termed 'complicated mTBI' and carries a higher risk of unfavorable outcome. Loss of consciousness and posttraumatic amnesia duration further characterize severity. CTE neuropathology has been proposed to be staged as 'low' or 'high' severity (criteria not yet established).

condensing osteitis clavicle — condensing osteitis of the clavicle, sternoclavicular osteosclerosis sternoclavicular septic arthritis or osteomyelitis SAPHO syndrome and sternocostoclavicular hyperostosis Friedrich disease (osteonecrosis of the medial clavicle) osteoblastic metastasis or primary bone tumour Paget disease of the clavicle osteoarthritis of the sternoclavicular joint plain radiography of the clavicle and sternoclavicular joint CT to confirm sclerosis with intact cortex and joint space MRI to assess marrow oedema and exclude a soft-tissue mass bone scintigraphy to gauge activity and screen for multifocal disease inflammatory markers to help exclude infection and SAPHO biopsy reserved for atypical or diagnostically uncertain lesions Condensing osteitis of the clavicle is a benign, non-infective sclerosis of the medial clavicle, typically in women of childbearing age. It presents with localised pain and sometimes swelling over the medial clavicle near the sternoclavicular joint, aggravated by shoulder movement. Radiographs show sclerosis and mild expansion of the inferomedial clavicle with preservation of the sternoclavicular joint space and no bony destruction. The absence of joint erosion, periostitis and soft-tissue mass distinguishes it from infection and malignancy. It is thought to reflect a chronic stress or mechanical reaction of the medial clavicle rather than an inflammatory or infective arthropathy. CT best demonstrates the sclerosis and confirms an intact cortex and joint, while MRI may show marrow oedema during painful phases. It must be differentiated from SAPHO syndrome and sternocostoclavicular hyperostosis, which cause more florid hyperostosis and often skin lesions. Management is conservative with analgesia and reassurance, and symptoms commonly settle over time. fever, warmth and rising inflammatory markers suggesting sternoclavicular infection destructive or expansile change with a soft-tissue mass indicating tumour palmoplantar pustulosis or acne pointing to SAPHO syndrome progressive symptoms or atypical imaging warranting biopsy Mistaking the sclerosis for osteoblastic metastasis and pursuing an oncological work-up. Overlooking sternoclavicular infection, which can present similarly but requires urgent treatment. Failing to screen for the skin lesions and multifocal bone involvement of SAPHO syndrome. Performing unnecessary biopsy of a radiologically characteristic benign lesion. Confusing it with Friedrich disease, which is osteonecrosis rather than reactive sclerosis. Condensing osteitis of the clavicle is regarded as a reactive sclerosing process of the medial clavicle, probably driven by chronic mechanical stress across the sternoclavicular region, which is subject to considerable load during upper limb and shoulder use. Repetitive stress is thought to provoke increased osteoblastic activity and trabecular thickening of the inferomedial clavicular bone, producing dense sclerosis without the cortical destruction, sequestration or periosteal reaction seen in infection, and without the neoplastic matrix of a bone tumour. The condition is not associated with an identifiable organism or systemic inflammatory disorder, and its self-limiting course supports a mechanical rather than infective or autoimmune aetiology. The condition is benign and self-limiting, with symptoms typically resolving or becoming quiescent over months to years and no risk of malignant change.

may reduce progression toward antisocial personality disorder in adulthood Serious violence or use of weapons posing danger to others Cruelty to people or animals and fire-setting Suicidal ideation or self-harm, which can coexist with the disorder Signs of abuse, neglect, or exploitation requiring safeguarding action Confusing oppositional defiant disorder with the more severe conduct disorder Missing treatable comorbid ADHD or mood disorder that worsens behaviour Relying on medication as a primary treatment rather than psychosocial intervention Overlooking safeguarding concerns and adverse home circumstances Failing to assess for coexisting suicidality and self-harm Conduct disorder arises from an interaction of genetic and temperamental factors, such as difficult temperament and low behavioural inhibition, with adverse environmental influences including harsh or inconsistent parenting, maltreatment, and socioeconomic adversity. Neurobiological correlates include altered function in circuits underlying emotional processing, reward, and threat appraisal, and blunted autonomic responsiveness, particularly in the callous-unemotional subgroup. The course is variable; adolescent-onset conduct disorder often remits by adulthood, whereas childhood-onset and callous-unemotional presentations carry a higher risk of persistence, antisocial personality disorder, substance misuse, and poor social outcomes. Prognosis improves with early, sustained psychosocial intervention, treatment of comorbidities, and a supportive family and school environment.

is an inherited degeneration confined largely to the cone photoreceptor system. Defects in genes controlling cone phototransduction and guanylate cyclase signalling (for example GUCA1A, GUCY2D, PDE6C) disturb the recovery phase of the cone light response and lead to progressive cone dysfunction and cell death. Because rod photoreceptors are relatively preserved, patients retain night vision while losing central acuity, colour discrimination and photopic sensitivity. Over years some cases develop rod involvement and reclassify as cone-rod dystrophy. Central vision declines slowly but progressively over years, and most patients reach the low-vision range; the tempo and endpoint depend on the underlying genotype.

Cone-rod dystrophy — CORD, cone-rod retinal dystrophy, ABCA4, CRX, GUCY2D, peripherin/RDS Rod-cone dystrophy (retinitis pigmentosa) with a rod-first pattern Stargardt disease and ABCA4-related maculopathy Isolated cone dystrophy without rod involvement Hydroxychloroquine or other toxic bull's-eye maculopathy Bardet-Biedl and other syndromic retinal dystrophies Central areolar choroidal dystrophy Full-field electroretinography to confirm cone responses reduced disproportionately to rod responses Multifocal electroretinography to map central cone dysfunction Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography of the macula for outer retinal and ellipsoid zone loss Fundus autofluorescence to detect bull's-eye or ring abnormalities Colour vision and formal perimetry to characterise functional deficit Molecular genetic testing with a retinal dystrophy gene panel Cone dysfunction dominates early, so patients describe reduced central acuity, colour-vision disturbance and photophobia before nyctalopia appears, in contrast to the reverse order seen in classic rod-cone retinitis pigmentosa Genetically heterogeneous with autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive and X-linked inheritance; ABCA4 is a common recessive cause and CRX, GUCY2D and peripherin/RDS underlie dominant forms Fundoscopy typically shows a bull's-eye or atrophic maculopathy with later peripheral pigmentary change and attenuated vessels as rod involvement supervenes Full-field electroretinography demonstrates photopic (cone) responses depressed out of proportion to scotopic (rod) responses, the electrophysiological signature that separates it from rod-cone dystrophy Optical coherence tomography shows loss of the outer retinal layers and ellipsoid zone at the fovea, and fundus autofluorescence often reveals a ring or bull's-eye of abnormal signal Progressive by definition, distinguishing it from the stationary cone dysfunction syndromes, and central vision is affected relatively early Management is supportive with refraction, tinted glasses or filters for glare, low-vision aids, genetic counselling and enrolment in registries or gene-therapy trials where relevant Rapid central acuity loss in a young patient prompting urgent genetic and electrophysiological assessment Features suggesting a syndromic association requiring systemic evaluation Development of night blindness and peripheral field constriction signalling rod recruitment and disease progression Family members with undiagnosed visual loss who may benefit from screening and counselling Labelling the condition as retinitis pigmentosa and missing the cone-first electrophysiological pattern Attributing an early bull's-eye maculopathy to drug toxicity without a genetic and drug history Reassuring a patient that the disorder is stationary when it is inherently progressive Overlooking a syndromic diagnosis by failing to take a systemic history Cone-rod dystrophy is a group of inherited retinal degenerations in which photoreceptor loss begins predominantly in the cones and later extends to the rods. Mutations in genes governing the phototransduction cascade, the visual cycle (for example ABCA4) or photoreceptor development and structure (for example CRX, GUCY2D, peripherin/RDS) impair cone metabolism and survival, causing early central and colour-vision failure. As the disease advances, rod photoreceptors also degenerate, producing peripheral field loss and night blindness, so the final picture can resemble widespread retinal dystrophy but with a cone-first temporal sequence. Prognosis is generally worse than for many rod-cone dystrophies because central vision is lost early and progressively; most patients become significantly visually impaired, though the rate varies with the underlying gene.
