minocycline Attributing a negative potassium hydroxide result to sampling error rather than reconsidering the diagnosis Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis is best understood as a disturbance of epidermal keratinisation. The leading hypotheses invoke an aberrant cutaneous reaction to microbial colonisation, with the actinomycete Dietzia papillomatosis and the commensal yeast Malassezia both proposed as triggers, while a subset of cases is linked to endocrine and metabolic factors such as insulin resistance and obesity. Whatever the initiating factor, the epidermis responds with papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, and increased basal pigmentation, producing the confluent central plaques and reticulate peripheral pattern. The frequently rapid response to minocycline supports a microbial or anti-inflammatory contribution to the mechanism. Benign and largely cosmetic in impact; it usually responds well to minocycline with clearance over weeks, although relapses can occur and maintenance or repeat courses may be required.

Confusional arousals — sleep drunkenness, Elpenor syndrome Sleep terrors Sleepwalking Sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy REM sleep behaviour disorder Nocturnal hypoglycaemia or other metabolic causes of confusion Clinical diagnosis from a characteristic history and event description Screening for precipitants such as sleep deprivation and obstructive sleep apnoea Video polysomnography if events are atypical, injurious or possibly epileptic Medication and substance review Assessment for coexisting parasomnias A non-REM parasomnia in which the person is partially awakened from deep sleep and appears confused and disoriented in time and place Behaviour is typically slow and clumsy rather than the fearful, agitated flight of a sleep terror Episodes arise from slow-wave sleep, usually in the first third of the night, and there is amnesia for the event It is most common in young children and tends to diminish with age Priming factors include sleep deprivation, other sleep disorders such as apnoea, shift work and certain sedatives Management centres on reassurance, adequate sleep and treating any underlying sleep disorder Injurious or aggressive behaviour during episodes Stereotyped features suggesting nocturnal seizures New onset in an adult without clear precipitant Associated excessive daytime sleepiness suggesting untreated apnoea Confusing confusional arousals with sleep terrors or nocturnal seizures Overlooking obstructive sleep apnoea as a driver in adults Attributing an adult's new confusional episodes to parasomnia without excluding metabolic or epileptic causes Failing to address sleep deprivation as a key precipitant Confusional arousals reflect incomplete transition out of slow-wave sleep, so that arousal systems partially activate while the brain remains largely in deep sleep, producing a mixed state of wakefulness and sleep. This dissociation, favoured by factors that deepen sleep or fragment it, leaves cognition and orientation impaired during the episode. As with other non-REM parasomnias there is a genetic predisposition and a tendency to run in families, and precipitants that increase slow-wave sleep pressure or cause arousals trigger events. The disorder is benign and usually self-limiting, particularly in children, with events reduced by adequate sleep and by addressing precipitating factors.

congenital absence of pericardium — congenital pericardial defect, pericardial agenesis atrial septal defect or other left-to-right shunt (from radiographic pulmonary artery prominence) right ventricular volume overload of other cause mediastinal or cardiac mass displacing the heart pneumopericardium or pneumomediastinum acquired pericardial defect after surgery or trauma arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (given apparent RV enlargement) dextroposition of the heart from pulmonary or pleural pathology cardiac MRI (definitive demonstration of pericardial absence and lung interposition) ECG-gated cardiac CT (defect delineation, chamber herniation) chest radiography (leftward cardiac shift, lung interposition signs) transthoracic echocardiography (abnormal windows, exaggerated cardiac swing) 12-lead ECG (rightward axis, poor R-wave progression, incomplete RBBB) screening for associated anomalies (bronchogenic cysts, congenital heart disease, pulmonary sequestration) exercise or ambulatory monitoring if positional symptoms or arrhythmia are reported Congenital absence of the pericardium ranges from a small localised foramen to complete bilateral absence; partial left-sided defects are the most common form encountered clinically. It results from premature atrophy of the left common cardinal vein (duct of Cuvier), which compromises the blood supply to the developing pleuropericardial membrane, hence the predominance of left-sided defects. Most patients are asymptomatic and the diagnosis is made incidentally; when symptoms occur they are typically positional atypical chest pain, palpitations or dyspnoea. Complete absence is usually benign, but partial defects carry the risk of herniation and strangulation of a cardiac chamber (especially the left atrial appendage) through the rim of the defect, which can be life-threatening. Chest radiography classically shows leftward shift of the cardiac silhouette with a prominent pulmonary artery/left atrial appendage and interposition of lung between the aorta and pulmonary artery or beneath the heart. The ECG often reveals rightward axis, poor R-wave progression and incomplete right bundle branch block due to cardiac displacement and rotation. Echocardiography can be technically difficult and may show unusual windows, exaggerated cardiac motion and apparent right ventricular enlargement; CT or MRI is the definitive means of demonstrating the defect and any lung interposition. Asymptomatic complete defects require no treatment, whereas symptomatic or partial defects at risk of herniation may warrant surgical pericardioplasty, defect enlargement or, occasionally, left atrial appendage excision. positional or exertional chest pain with syncope suggesting chamber herniation or strangulation new arrhythmia in a patient with a known partial defect evidence of left atrial appendage incarceration on imaging haemodynamic instability with abrupt severe chest pain sudden cardiac death in a young person with an undiagnosed partial defect Misinterpreting the displaced cardiac silhouette and RV prominence as an atrial septal defect or right ventricular pathology. Assuming all pericardial defects are benign and overlooking the herniation risk specific to partial defects. Attributing technically difficult or unusual echocardiographic windows to poor acoustic access rather than the underlying defect. Failing to search for associated congenital anomalies once the defect is identified. Delaying surgical referral in a symptomatic partial defect until an acute strangulation event occurs. During embryogenesis the pleuropericardial membranes, which are nourished by the left duct of Cuvier (common cardinal vein), grow to separate the pericardial from the pleural cavity. Premature involution of this venous channel deprives the left pleuropericardial membrane of its blood supply, so that it fails to develop fully; the consequence is a partial or complete, usually left-sided, pericardial defect. In complete absence the heart is abnormally mobile within the thorax and shifts leftward, but haemodynamics are generally preserved. In a partial defect the free edge of the residual pericardium can act as a constricting ring: a portion of the heart, most often the left atrial appendage, may herniate through and become incarcerated, leading to strangulation, myocardial ischaemia, arrhythmia or sudden death. The abnormal position and rotation of the heart account for the characteristic radiographic and electrocardiographic findings. Complete absence of the pericardium generally carries a benign prognosis and normal life expectancy, whereas partial defects have a less predictable course because of the risk of chamber herniation and strangulation, which can be fatal but is preventable with timely surgical correction.

Spermatogenesis is usually normal, so testicular volume and follicle-stimulating hormone are typically preserved, confirming an obstructive rather than a productive problem The bilateral form is undergo cystic-fibrosis gene testing, with genetic counselling before conception because of the risk of an affected child The unilateral form and some bilateral cases are associated with ipsilateral renal anomalies, so upper-tract imaging is recommended, particularly when cystic-fibrosis mutations are not found Fertility is achievable through surgical sperm retrieval from the epididymis or testis combined with intracytoplasmic sperm injection The diagnosis is largely clinical, resting on the absence of palpable vasa, and is supported by seminal analysis and imaging Detection of cystic-fibrosis gene mutations in the partner, substantially raising the risk of an affected child An associated solitary or ectopic kidney requiring surveillance Features suggesting overt cystic fibrosis such as recurrent respiratory disease Findings inconsistent with obstruction that suggest an alternative diagnosis Failing to palpate for the vasa and thus missing the diagnosis in an azoospermic man Omitting cystic-fibrosis gene testing of the man and, crucially, his partner before assisted conception Neglecting renal imaging, particularly in cases without cystic-fibrosis mutations Misclassifying the low-volume ejaculate as ejaculatory duct obstruction without checking for palpable vasa Proceeding to assisted reproduction without genetic counselling about the risk to children Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens arises from failure of development of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct derivatives, so the vasa deferentia, and often the distal epididymis and seminal vesicles, are absent or rudimentary. Because sperm cannot pass from the testis into the ejaculate, the result is obstructive azoospermia with intact testicular sperm production. Most bilateral cases are caused by mutations in the cystic-fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator gene, placing the condition within the spectrum of cystic-fibrosis-related disease; the same gene defects that impair chloride transport disrupt Wolffian duct development. A subset, more often unilateral, is instead associated with abnormal embryological development of the mesonephric duct and coexisting renal agenesis or ectopia, reflecting the shared origin of the reproductive and upper urinary tracts. General health is usually unaffected in the absence of overt cystic fibrosis, and because spermatogenesis is intact, fatherhood is readily achievable with surgical sperm retrieval and intracytoplasmic sperm injection; the principal consideration is the genetic risk to offspring, which is addressed through partner testing and counselling.

Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia — CAH, 21-hydroxylase deficiency, adrenogenital syndrome Other causes of ambiguous genitalia and disorders of sex development Pyloric stenosis or sepsis in a vomiting, dehydrated neonate Other forms of primary adrenal insufficiency Rarer enzyme defects (11-beta-hydroxylase, 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency) Precocious puberty from other causes Polycystic ovary syndrome (for non-classic presentations) Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone (baseline and, if needed, after ACTH stimulation) Serum electrolytes, glucose, and acid-base status Plasma renin activity and aldosterone Adrenal androgens (androstenedione, testosterone) Karyotype and pelvic ultrasound in ambiguous genitalia Genetic analysis of the CYP21A2 gene A group of autosomal recessive disorders of adrenal steroid synthesis, the great majority caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency. The classic salt-wasting form presents in the first weeks of life with vomiting, poor feeding, weight loss, dehydration, and shock from combined cortisol and aldosterone deficiency. Female infants with the classic form often show virilisation of the external genitalia (ambiguous genitalia), whereas affected males may appear normal at birth and are at particular risk of unrecognised salt-wasting crisis. Characteristic biochemistry includes hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and metabolic acidosis in the salt-wasting crisis, with markedly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone. A non-classic (late-onset) form presents later with signs of androgen excess such as premature pubarche, hirsutism, or menstrual irregularity. Newborn screening measuring 17-hydroxyprogesterone allows early detection before a life-threatening crisis. Treatment principle is glucocorticoid replacement to correct cortisol deficiency and suppress excess adrenal androgen, with mineralocorticoid replacement (and salt supplementation in infancy) for salt-wasting forms. Additional stress steroid cover is essential during illness, surgery, or major stress to prevent adrenal crisis. Management of affected girls includes multidisciplinary care regarding virilised genitalia, and genetic counselling is important for families. Salt-wasting adrenal crisis with dehydration, hypotension, or shock Severe hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia Hypoglycaemia Vomiting and poor feeding in a neonate, particularly a male infant Intercurrent illness or surgery without adequate stress steroid cover Missing salt-wasting crisis in a male infant with normal genitalia Failing to provide stress steroid cover during illness or surgery Over-treating with glucocorticoids, impairing growth, or under-treating, allowing androgen excess Misattributing a neonatal collapse to sepsis or pyloric stenosis without checking electrolytes and adrenal steroids A deficiency of an enzyme in the adrenal cortisol synthesis pathway, most often 21-hydroxylase, reduces cortisol production. The resulting loss of negative feedback drives increased ACTH secretion, which stimulates adrenal hyperplasia and diverts steroid precursors into the androgen pathway, causing androgen excess and virilisation. In the severe salt-wasting form, aldosterone synthesis is also impaired, leading to sodium loss, hyperkalaemia, and volume depletion, while accumulation of the precursor 17-hydroxyprogesterone serves as a diagnostic marker. With early diagnosis, hormone replacement, and stress dosing, children generally grow and develop well; risks include life-threatening adrenal crises, effects of over- or under-treatment on growth and puberty, and fertility and psychosocial issues in classic disease.

Congenital adrenal hypoplasia (NR0B1/DAX1) — congenital adrenal hypoplasia, X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita, AHC, NR0B1 deficiency, DAX1 deficiency Congenital adrenal hyperplasia Other causes of primary adrenal insufficiency such as adrenoleukodystrophy or autoimmune adrenalitis ACTH resistance syndromes and familial glucocorticoid deficiency Adrenal hypoplasia from steroidogenic factor-1 (NR5A1/SF1) defects Secondary adrenal insufficiency Isolated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism such as Kallmann syndrome Serum electrolytes and glucose with paired cortisol and ACTH, expected to show low cortisol and high ACTH in primary failure Plasma renin and aldosterone to confirm mineralocorticoid deficiency ACTH (Synacthen) stimulation test showing an impaired cortisol response Gonadotropins (LH and FSH) and sex steroids, expected to be low in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism 17-hydroxyprogesterone and a steroid profile to exclude congenital adrenal hyperplasia NR0B1 (DAX1) genetic testing and evaluation for contiguous Xp21 gene deletions Adrenal imaging where structural assessment is needed A rare cause of primary adrenal insufficiency; the classic X-linked form results from mutations in the NR0B1 gene encoding the nuclear receptor DAX1 It typically presents in male infants with a salt-wasting adrenal crisis (hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and hypotension) or with more insidious glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency in childhood It is characteristically combined with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, which becomes apparent as absent or arrested puberty Because it is X-linked, affected individuals are usually boys with carrier mothers, and a family history of infant deaths or adrenal insufficiency may be present It is distinguished from congenital adrenal hyperplasia by the absence of a steroidogenic enzyme block and virilisation and by low gonadotropins Management is lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement, with induction of puberty and fertility issues addressed later Contiguous gene deletions at Xp21 can associate it with Duchenne muscular dystrophy and glycerol kinase deficiency A salt-wasting adrenal crisis in a male infant requiring emergency treatment A family history of infant deaths or X-linked adrenal disease Failure to enter or progress through puberty Features suggesting a contiguous gene syndrome such as muscular dystrophy or developmental delay Misdiagnosing it as congenital adrenal hyperplasia and missing the correct genetic cause Failing to anticipate pubertal failure and delaying induction of puberty Under-recognising precipitants of adrenal crisis and giving inadequate sick-day dosing Overlooking an associated Xp21 contiguous gene deletion syndrome DAX1, encoded by NR0B1, is a nuclear receptor essential for development of the adrenal cortex and of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Loss-of-function mutations impair formation of the definitive adrenal cortex, producing primary adrenal insufficiency with deficient cortisol and aldosterone, and disrupt gonadotropin secretion and gonadal function, causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Impaired spermatogenesis tends to persist even with gonadotropin therapy, reflecting a combined central and gonadal defect. With early diagnosis and lifelong hormone replacement the outlook is good, but survival depends on prompt recognition and treatment of adrenal crises; fertility is usually impaired despite treatment, and associated gene deletions worsen the prognosis.

anaemia Serial counts and marrow surveillance for evolving pancytopenia and clonal change An autosomal recessive disorder caused by MPL mutations that disable the thrombopoietin receptor on megakaryocytes and stem cells Presents in the neonatal period with severe isolated thrombocytopenia and bleeding, typically without the skeletal anomalies seen in TAR syndrome The marrow shows platelet transfusion provides interim support Neonatal or early infant bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage, from severe thrombocytopenia Falling haemoglobin or neutrophils signalling progression to aplastic anaemia Emerging cytogenetic abnormality or dysplasia indicating clonal evolution or leukaemia Failure to identify a curative donor while marrow function declines Mistaking it for immune neonatal thrombocytopenia and delaying marrow evaluation Overlooking the progression from isolated thrombocytopenia to pancytopenia Confusing it with TAR syndrome despite the absence of radial anomalies Failing to pursue transplantation planning early in the disease course Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in MPL, the gene encoding the thrombopoietin receptor (c-MPL). Thrombopoietin acting through this receptor is the principal driver of megakaryocyte proliferation and platelet production, so its absence causes a profound reduction in megakaryocytes and severe thrombocytopenia from birth. Because thrombopoietin signalling additionally supports the survival and self-renewal of haematopoietic stem cells, the same defect progressively exhausts the stem cell pool, and the initially isolated thrombocytopenia commonly evolves into aplastic anaemia with pancytopenia. Circulating thrombopoietin rises to high levels because the non-functional receptor neither transduces its signal nor mediates its clearance. There is also an increased predisposition to clonal evolution and myeloid malignancy. Without transplantation the outlook is poor because most patients progress to marrow failure, but haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can be curative, making early diagnosis and donor identification critical.

Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract — CAKUT, renal dysplasia, renal hypoplasia, renal agenesis, posterior urethral valves, vesicoureteric reflux, PAX2, HNF1B Autosomal recessive or dominant polycystic kidney disease Nephronophthisis and other ciliopathies Acquired obstructive uropathy Reflux nephropathy from acquired causes Syndromic disorders with renal involvement (e.g. branchio-oto-renal syndrome) Neurogenic bladder Renal tract ultrasound to define structural anatomy and hydronephrosis Micturating cystourethrogram to assess reflux and posterior urethral valves Functional renography (e.g. isotope scanning) to quantify differential function and drainage Serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate, with urinalysis for proteinuria Blood pressure monitoring Genetic and chromosomal testing (including HNF1B and PAX2) when syndromic or familial disease is suspected CAKUT is an umbrella term for a spectrum of developmental malformations of the kidneys, collecting systems, bladder and urethra, and is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease in children It includes renal agenesis, hypoplasia and dysplasia, multicystic dysplastic kidney, duplex systems, pelvi-ureteric and vesico-ureteric junction obstruction, vesicoureteric reflux and posterior urethral valves Many cases are detected on antenatal ultrasound as hydronephrosis or abnormal renal appearance, prompting postnatal evaluation It can be isolated or part of a syndrome; monogenic causes and copy-number variants (for example involving HNF1B or PAX2) are increasingly recognised, and HNF1B disease may be associated with abnormal glucose metabolism and electrolyte disturbance Posterior urethral valves in males cause bladder outlet obstruction and are an important, potentially treatable cause of obstructive uropathy Reduced functioning nephron mass predisposes to hypertension, proteinuria and progressive kidney disease over time Management is largely supportive and urological, with relief of obstruction, prevention and treatment of urinary infection, and long-term surveillance of blood pressure and kidney function Bladder outlet obstruction from posterior urethral valves in a newborn male Oligohydramnios with pulmonary hypoplasia in severe bilateral disease Rapidly declining renal function Recurrent or febrile urinary tract infections with scarring Severe or resistant hypertension Failing to arrange timely postnatal follow-up of an antenatally detected renal abnormality Missing posterior urethral valves in a male infant with poor urinary stream or bladder distension Underestimating the long-term risk of hypertension and chronic kidney disease from reduced nephron mass Overlooking associated extrarenal or syndromic features and the yield of genetic testing (e.g. HNF1B) Neglecting prevention and prompt treatment of urinary tract infection in refluxing or obstructed systems CAKUT arises from disruption of the tightly orchestrated developmental interactions between the ureteric bud and the metanephric mesenchyme that form the kidney and drainage system during embryogenesis. Abnormal budding, branching, nephron induction or lower-tract development produces the wide morphological spectrum, from complete absence or dysplasia of a kidney to obstruction and reflux within the collecting system and bladder outlet. Genetic factors (single-gene variants such as HNF1B and PAX2, and chromosomal copy-number changes) together with environmental influences during nephrogenesis contribute to the phenotype. A reduced or maldeveloped nephron endowment lowers renal functional reserve, so affected individuals are prone to hypertension, proteinuria and gradual decline in glomerular filtration, while obstruction and reflux add risk of infection and further parenchymal injury. Outcome varies enormously with the type and severity of the anomaly and the amount of functioning renal tissue; many children do well with monitoring, but bilateral dysplasia, severe obstruction or extensive scarring can progress to chronic and end-stage kidney disease, so lifelong follow-up of blood pressure, proteinuria and renal function is important.

Congenital aphakia — primary congenital aphakia, secondary congenital aphakia Anterior lenticonus or severe lens coloboma Ectopia lentis with a dislocated lens out of the visual axis Microphthalmia with lenticular anomalies Persistent fetal vasculature Surgical (acquired) aphakia Examination and imaging (for example ultrasound biomicroscopy) to confirm lens absence Assessment for associated anterior segment dysgenesis and microphthalmia Refraction and visual development assessment Genetic evaluation where syndromic features are present Amblyopia assessment and monitoring A rare congenital absence of the crystalline lens, present from birth Primary aphakia reflects failure of lens induction with severe anterior segment dysgenesis Secondary aphakia occurs when a lens that did form is resorbed or extruded during development It causes high hyperopia and is a cause of visual deprivation and amblyopia in the affected eye It is frequently accompanied by other ocular malformations such as microphthalmia and anterior segment dysgenesis Management focuses on optical correction and aggressive amblyopia therapy during the critical period Dense amblyopia risk requiring urgent optical correction Associated glaucoma or other sight-threatening malformation Bilateral involvement affecting overall visual development Syndromic features suggesting a broader disorder Delaying optical correction and losing the amblyopia treatment window Missing associated glaucoma or anterior segment dysgenesis Confusing it with ectopia lentis Overlooking a syndromic association Congenital aphakia results from disturbance of lens development. In primary aphakia the surface ectoderm fails to differentiate into lens placode and vesicle, so no lens forms and the anterior segment develops abnormally. In secondary aphakia a lens is initially formed but is subsequently resorbed or expelled in utero, for example after intrauterine inflammation or with other developmental anomalies. Absence of the lens removes a major refractive element, producing marked hyperopia and, without correction, dense form-deprivation amblyopia. Visual prognosis depends on the severity of associated malformations and on the timeliness of optical correction and amblyopia therapy, and is often guarded, particularly in primary aphakia.

of visual development is crucial A careful family history and examination of parents can reveal an inherited pattern, often autosomal dominant Dense bilateral cataract in an infant requiring urgent referral to prevent amblyopia Associated systemic illness or failure to thrive suggesting a metabolic disorder Signs of raised intraocular pressure or coexisting glaucoma Leukocoria where retinoblastoma has not yet been excluded Missing a treatable metabolic cause such as galactosaemia by omitting a metabolic screen Delaying surgery beyond the critical period and allowing irreversible opacification of the lens present at or soon after birth, arising when the normal transparency and orderly arrangement of lens fibres is disturbed during development. In syndromic forms this may result from mutations in genes encoding lens crystallins, membrane and cytoskeletal proteins, or developmental transcription factors, or from systemic metabolic derangements (such as abnormal galactose metabolism) that alter the osmotic and biochemical environment of the lens. Chromosomal abnormalities and multisystem genetic syndromes disrupt lens development as one of several affected tissues. A dense opacity blocks formation of a clear retinal image during the sensitive period, causing amblyopia unless treated promptly. Visual outcome depends on the density and laterality of the cataract and the timeliness of surgery and amblyopia therapy; early treatment of bilateral cataracts and of reversible metabolic causes can give good vision, whereas late-treated dense unilateral cataracts often have a guarded prognosis.

neural-crest tumour Signs of bowel obstruction suggesting Hirschsprung disease Attributing neonatal hypoventilation to lung immaturity or sepsis and missing the central cause Underestimating complications Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome results from mutations in PHOX2B, a transcription factor essential for development of the autonomic nervous system and of central chemosensory pathways derived from the neural crest. The defect blunts the brainstem ventilatory response to rising carbon dioxide and falling oxygen, so automatic breathing fails, most profoundly during sleep when voluntary drive is absent. Because PHOX2B guides broad neural-crest development, the same mutation predisposes to Hirschsprung disease, wider autonomic dysregulation, and neural-crest tumours. With reliable ventilatory support and coordinated multidisciplinary care survival into adulthood is expected, but outcome depends on adherence to assisted ventilation, prevention of hypoxic injury, and management of autonomic, cardiac, and tumour-related complications.

substitution allows near-normal growth and development Severe dehydration and circulatory compromise in the neonate from ongoing salt and water loss Profound hypokalaemia and alkalosis with risk of arrhythmia Antenatal features misinterpreted as bowel obstruction leading to unnecessary surgery Renal impairment or nephrocalcinosis from chronic volume depletion and electrolyte loss Overlooking watery stool mistaken for urine in a wet nappy, delaying recognition Interpreting metabolic alkalosis as inconsistent with diarrhoea and missing the diagnosis Failing to measure faecal chloride, which is the key discriminating test Under-replacing potassium and chloride, allowing chronic volume depletion and renal injury Congenital chloride diarrhoea results from loss of function of the apical SLC26A3 (DRA) chloride/bicarbonate exchanger in the ileum and colon. Failure of this exchanger prevents chloride absorption and bicarbonate secretion, so chloride is retained in the lumen and osmotically drives water loss, producing a secretory watery diarrhoea rich in chloride. Impaired bicarbonate loss into the gut and secondary activation of sodium- and potassium-conserving pathways lead to systemic hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Chronic volume depletion can cause secondary hyperaldosteronism and renal complications if replacement is inadequate. With early diagnosis and consistent chloride, sodium and potassium replacement, growth, development and renal function are usually preserved. Inadequate substitution predisposes to growth failure, renal damage and electrolyte crises.

Congenital Cytomegalovirus Infection — cCMV, congenital CMV, congenital cytomegalovirus Other congenital infections in the TORCH group (toxoplasmosis, rubella, syphilis, herpes simplex, Zika) Neonatal sepsis or bacterial infection Congenital toxoplasmosis (also causes intracranial calcification) Haemolytic disease of the newborn Inherited metabolic or genetic disorders causing microcephaly Neonatal haematological disorders causing thrombocytopenia CMV detection by PCR from urine or saliva within the first three weeks of life Newborn and serial audiological (hearing) assessment Cranial imaging (ultrasound and/or MRI) for calcification and brain abnormalities Ophthalmological examination for chorioretinitis Full blood count, platelets, and liver function tests Dried blood spot testing when late confirmation is needed The most common congenital viral infection and a leading non-genetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss and neurodevelopmental disability in children. Most infected newborns are asymptomatic at birth, yet a proportion of these still go on to develop late-onset hearing loss. Symptomatic disease may include small size for gestational age, microcephaly, petechiae, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and low platelets. Neurological features can include intracranial calcifications (often periventricular), chorioretinitis, and seizures. Both primary maternal infection and non-primary (reactivation or reinfection) during pregnancy can transmit to the fetus, with primary infection carrying higher risk. Diagnosis must be confirmed within the first three weeks of life to distinguish congenital from perinatally acquired infection, using viral detection from urine or saliva. Because of the risk of progressive hearing loss, confirmed cases need structured audiological surveillance over time, not just a single newborn screen. Antiviral therapy is considered for symptomatic infants, particularly those with central nervous system involvement, to improve hearing and neurodevelopmental outcomes. Microcephaly or abnormal neuroimaging indicating central nervous system involvement Confirmed or progressive sensorineural hearing loss Symptomatic disease with thrombocytopenia, hepatitis, or petechiae Chorioretinitis threatening vision Seizures in the neonatal period Failure to confirm the diagnosis within three weeks, losing the ability to prove congenital infection Missing the diagnostic window by testing after three weeks of age and being unable to distinguish congenital from acquired infection Assuming a normal newborn hearing screen excludes future hearing loss Overlooking asymptomatic infection, which still carries a risk of late sequelae Attributing intracranial calcification solely to toxoplasmosis without confirming CMV Failing to arrange long-term audiological and developmental surveillance Cytomegalovirus, a herpesvirus, crosses the placenta following maternal infection and disseminates in the fetus, where it replicates in multiple organs. The developing central nervous system is particularly vulnerable: infection disrupts neuronal migration and brain development and causes an inflammatory response that produces calcifications, microcephaly, and migrational abnormalities. Involvement of the inner ear leads to progressive sensorineural hearing loss, while infection of the liver, bone marrow, and reticuloendothelial system accounts for hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, and jaundice. Asymptomatic infants generally do well but remain at risk of late-onset hearing loss, warranting ongoing audiological follow-up; symptomatic infants, especially those with neurological involvement, have a higher risk of hearing loss, developmental delay, and other long-term deficits, though early antiviral therapy can improve outcomes in selected cases.

(alignment, ptosis and head-posture correction) with genetic counselling, as the underlying dysinnervation cannot be reversed A progressive course or new neurological deficit, suggesting an acquired or alternative diagnosis Progressive scoliosis with a horizontal gaze palsy (HGPPS), requiring spinal monitoring Bulbar dysfunction with aspiration risk, as in the Mobius spectrum Corneal exposure from lagophthalmos or a poor Bell's phenomenon Systemic features indicating a syndromic genetic cause that requires multisystem work-up Treating a dysinnervation disorder as a primary muscle problem and missing the neurogenic basis Overlooking synkinesis, for example not testing adduction for globe retraction in Duane or jaw movement in Marcus Gunn Failing to screen for syndromic or systemic features such as scoliosis, hearing loss, limb and cardiac anomalies Not counselling families about the genetic basis and recurrence risk Expecting surgery to restore normal motility rather than to improve head posture and alignment The congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders arise from maldevelopment of cranial motor neurons and/or their axonal pathways during embryogenesis, producing absent, deficient or misdirected (aberrant) innervation of the ocular, facial and other cranial-nerve-supplied muscles. Causative genes encode proteins for axon guidance, motor-neuron specification and cytoskeletal function, for example ROBO3 (midline axon crossing) in horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis, CHN1 (alpha-2-chimaerin, axon guidance) in Duane, PHOX2A and MAFB (motor-neuron and nucleus development), and KIF21A and TUBB3 (axonal transport and microtubule structure) in CFEOM. Aberrant reinnervation produces the characteristic synkinetic movements, while abnormal muscle development leads to secondary fibrosis and restriction. The disorders are congenital and non-progressive, with rare exceptions such as the progressive scoliosis component of HGPPS. These disorders are congenital and non-progressive, so vision and function are generally stable, and multidisciplinary and surgical management improves alignment, head posture, lid position and cosmesis. The aberrant innervation and associated motility limitation usually persist, and prognosis in syndromic forms depends on the associated systemic features.

Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia — CDH, Bochdalek hernia, diaphragmatic hernia Congenital pulmonary airway malformation Congenital lobar emphysema Pulmonary sequestration Pneumothorax or large pleural effusion Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn of other cause Eventration of the diaphragm Antenatal ultrasound and, where available, fetal MRI with lung volume estimation Chest and abdominal radiograph showing thoracic bowel loops and mediastinal shift Echocardiography to assess pulmonary hypertension and exclude associated cardiac lesions Blood gas and pre- and post-ductal oxygen saturations to gauge shunting Evaluation for associated anomalies and genetic conditions A defect in the diaphragm allows abdominal viscera to herniate into the thorax during fetal development, impairing lung growth; the posterolateral (Bochdalek) defect, more often left-sided, is most common. The principal problems are pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension rather than the anatomical defect itself. Many cases are detected on antenatal ultrasound, allowing delivery at a centre with neonatal surgical and intensive care support. A typical presentation is respiratory distress soon after birth with a scaphoid (sunken) abdomen and a shifted apex or heart sounds, and reduced breath sounds on the affected side. Bowel sounds may be audible in the chest, and the chest radiograph shows bowel loops in the thorax with mediastinal shift. Bag-mask ventilation should be avoided because it distends the herniated bowel and worsens lung compression; early endotracheal intubation and gastric decompression are preferred. Initial management focuses on gentle, lung-protective ventilation, cardiorespiratory stabilisation, and treatment of pulmonary hypertension before surgery. Surgical reduction and repair of the defect is undertaken after the infant is physiologically stabilised, not as an emergency. Severe cases may need advanced support such as inhaled pulmonary vasodilators or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Severe respiratory distress and hypoxaemia at or shortly after birth Persistent pulmonary hypertension with right-to-left shunting refractory to therapy Deterioration after bag-mask ventilation distends intrathoracic bowel Signs of inadequate oxygenation and rising acidosis Associated major cardiac or other anomalies worsening the outlook Using bag-mask ventilation and inflating herniated bowel, worsening lung compression Rushing to surgery before stabilising pulmonary hypertension and gas exchange Attributing neonatal distress to primary lung disease and missing the diagnosis on examination and radiograph Using aggressive high-pressure ventilation that risks barotrauma to hypoplastic lungs Overlooking associated cardiac and genetic anomalies that affect management and prognosis Failure of the diaphragm to close completely during embryogenesis permits abdominal organs to occupy the thoracic cavity while the lungs are developing. The space-occupying viscera restrict growth of the ipsilateral (and to a lesser extent contralateral) lung, producing pulmonary hypoplasia with fewer alveoli and abnormal, muscularised pulmonary arterioles. After birth these abnormal vessels fail to relax normally, causing persistent pulmonary hypertension with right-to-left shunting, hypoxaemia, and acidosis. The combination of reduced functional lung tissue and elevated pulmonary vascular resistance drives the respiratory failure that dominates the clinical course. Outcome depends chiefly on the degree of pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension and on associated anomalies. With optimal perinatal care many infants survive, though survivors may have chronic lung disease, feeding and growth problems, and neurodevelopmental sequelae. Severe hypoplasia and refractory pulmonary hypertension carry a poor prognosis.

Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia — CDA, HEMPAS (CDA type II), hereditary dyserythropoietic anaemia Myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts or multilineage dysplasia Thalassaemia syndromes and other causes of ineffective erythropoiesis Megaloblastic anaemia from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency Hereditary haemolytic anaemias (membrane, enzyme or unstable haemoglobin defects) Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, given the historical acidified-serum overlap Hereditary haemochromatosis, when the iron-loading phenotype dominates Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Full blood count with red cell indices and reticulocyte count (characteristically low for the anaemia) Blood film for anisopoikilocytosis and basophilic stippling Bone marrow aspirate and trephine for characteristic erythroblast morphology and to exclude myelodysplasia Bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin as markers of haemolysis and ineffective erythropoiesis Iron studies with ferritin and transferrin saturation, plus hepatic and cardiac MRI (T2*) for iron quantification Targeted gene sequencing or a CDA panel (SEC23B, CDAN1, CDIN1, KIF23, GATA1, KLF1) Exclusion tests including haemoglobin analysis and flow cytometry for a paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria clone A heterogeneous group of inherited disorders defined by ineffective erythropoiesis and pathognomonic multinuclearity and dysplastic changes of bone marrow erythroblasts, with an anaemia that is characteristically reticulocytopenic for its severity Type II (SEC23B) is the commonest form; type I (CDAN1, more rarely CDIN1) and type III (KIF23) are rarer, and transcription-factor variants (e.g. GATA1, KLF1) are increasingly recognised Presentation ranges from antenatal or neonatal anaemia and hydrops through to incidental diagnosis in adulthood; jaundice, splenomegaly and pigment gallstones are common The anaemia is typically normocytic or macrocytic with an inappropriately low reticulocyte count, reflecting intramedullary destruction of abnormal erythroblasts rather than peripheral haemolysis alone Parenchymal iron overload develops even without transfusion because ineffective erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin, and it may be the dominant clinical problem Type II red cells show increased lysis by acidified ABO-compatible sera (the historical acidified-serum, or Ham, reaction) reflecting abnormal membrane band 3 glycosylation, hence the older name HEMPAS Marrow morphology guides typing (binucleate erythroblasts in type II, internuclear chromatin bridges and megaloblastoid change in type I, giant multinucleate erythroblasts in type III), now confirmed by molecular genetics Careful distinction from myelodysplasia, thalassaemia and other causes of ineffective erythropoiesis is essential to avoid inappropriate therapy Antenatal presentation with hydrops fetalis or severe neonatal anaemia Iron overload with cardiac, hepatic or endocrine dysfunction Transfusion-dependence with rising ferritin Symptomatic pigment gallstones or biliary obstruction Aplastic crisis, for example with parvovirus B19, causing abrupt worsening Misdiagnosing CDA as myelodysplasia and exposing young patients to inappropriate therapy Overlooking iron overload because the patient has never been transfused Attributing an inappropriately low reticulocyte count to marrow failure rather than ineffective erythropoiesis Missing the diagnosis in a mildly anaemic adult labelled as chronic haemolysis of unknown cause Assuming splenectomy is curative, when it may reduce transfusion needs but does not correct ineffective erythropoiesis and carries thrombotic and infective risk The congenital dyserythropoietic anaemias arise from mutations in genes governing erythroblast nuclear division, cytokinesis and membrane maturation. Type I reflects defects in codanin-1 (CDAN1) or CDIN1 that disturb chromatin and nuclear architecture, type II results from SEC23B mutations impairing COPII-mediated vesicular transport and glycosylation of membrane proteins such as band 3, and type III arises from KIF23 mutations disrupting cytokinesis. The common consequence is apoptosis and destruction of morphologically abnormal erythroid precursors within the marrow, so effective red cell output fails to match demand. The resulting ineffective erythropoiesis, together with hepcidin suppression driven by erythroferrone and related mediators, produces anaemia and progressive parenchymal iron loading that is independent of transfusion. Many patients follow a mild to moderate course compatible with a normal lifespan, but morbidity is driven chiefly by iron overload and its complications. Transfusion-dependent forms and those with unrecognised iron loading fare less well, although much of this is preventable with monitoring and chelation.

Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia — CDA, CDA type I, CDA type II, HEMPAS, CDAN1-related anaemia, SEC23B-related anaemia, KLF1/KIF23-related dyserythropoiesis Thalassaemia syndromes Myelodysplastic syndrome with dyserythropoiesis Megaloblastic anaemia from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency Congenital haemolytic anaemias such as hereditary spherocytosis Sideroblastic anaemias Erythropoietic porphyrias with dyserythropoiesis Bone marrow aspirate examining erythroblast multinuclearity and chromatin bridges Full blood count, reticulocyte count, and blood film to characterise the anaemia Haemolysis markers including bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, and haptoglobin Iron studies (ferritin, transferrin saturation) and hepatic iron quantification by MRI Targeted genetic testing (CDAN1, C15orf41, SEC23B, KLF1, KIF23) Electron microscopy of erythroblasts in selected cases to define subtype A group of inherited anaemias characterised by ineffective erythropoiesis and morphologically abnormal, often multinucleated, erythroblasts in the marrow Type I (CDAN1 or C15orf41) shows megaloblastoid erythroblasts with internuclear chromatin bridges; type II (SEC23B), the commonest, shows binucleate late erythroblasts Type II is also known as HEMPAS, in which red cells lyse in a proportion of acidified normal sera and show characteristic membrane glycoprotein abnormalities The anaemia is typically macrocytic or normocytic with inappropriately low reticulocytes for the degree of anaemia Iron overload is common and progresses even without transfusion because ineffective erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin Splenomegaly and jaundice from haemolysis of the abnormal cells are frequent, and gallstones may develop Diagnosis rests on marrow morphology plus genetic testing, distinguishing CDA from thalassaemia and myelodysplasia Signs of iron overload affecting heart, liver, or endocrine organs even without transfusion Severe anaemia in infancy requiring frequent transfusion Hydrops or profound anaemia detected antenatally in severe variants Progressive cytopenias or dysplasia raising concern for an alternative marrow disorder Mislabelling the marrow appearances as myelodysplasia and pursuing inappropriate therapy Failing to monitor and treat iron overload in non-transfused patients Confusing the macrocytosis with B12 or folate deficiency and missing the congenital cause Overlooking the diagnosis in a family member with milder compensated disease Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemias are disorders of terminal erythroid maturation in which erythroblasts undergo abnormal nuclear division and cytokinesis, generating characteristic multinucleate and internuclear-bridged forms. The underlying genes govern nuclear envelope integrity and chromatin organisation (CDAN1 in type I), endoplasmic reticulum vesicle transport and glycoprotein processing (SEC23B in type II), and erythroid transcription or cytokinesis machinery in rarer subtypes. Defective maturation leads to apoptosis of erythroid precursors within the marrow, producing ineffective erythropoiesis with a low reticulocyte response relative to the anaemia. As with other ineffective erythropoieses, expanded but futile erythroid activity suppresses hepcidin and drives excess intestinal iron absorption, so tissue iron overload accumulates independently of transfusion. Many patients have a moderate, compatible-with-life anaemia, but long-term morbidity is dominated by iron overload and its organ complications, making iron monitoring and chelation central to care regardless of transfusion status.

requiring transfusion Worsening cytopenias or marrow dysplasia raising concern for an alternative diagnosis Features of decompensated haemolysis such as aplastic crisis after parvovirus infection Attributing iron overload solely to transfusion and missing the intrinsic ineffective-erythropoiesis mechanism Confusing dyserythropoietic marrow with myelodysplasia and pursuing inappropriate treatment Relying on iron studies alone and delaying genetic confirmation Failing to screen for and treat iron loading in patients who are not transfused Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia type I results from biallelic loss of function of codanin-1 (or its partner C15orf41), proteins involved in nuclear-envelope and chromatin regulation during erythroid maturation. Defective chromatin condensation and abnormal nuclear division produce dysplastic erythroblasts with internuclear bridges and spongy heterochromatin, and many maturing red-cell precursors are destroyed within the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis). The resulting anaemia and low hepcidin state drive inappropriate iron absorption and progressive tissue iron overload, which becomes a major long-term complication. Many patients maintain a moderate, non-transfusion-dependent anaemia, and interferon alpha can raise haemoglobin, but iron overload accumulates over decades and, if unmonitored, drives the main morbidity and mortality.

monitor it Misinterpreting the dyserythropoietic marrow as myelodysplasia Delaying genetic confirmation when morphology and membrane studies are already suggestive SEC23B encodes a component of the COPII vesicle coat that transports cargo from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi. Biallelic loss of function impairs glycoprotein trafficking and glycosylation during erythroid maturation, producing abnormal, hypoglycosylated band 3 and other membrane proteins and the aberrant surface antigen responsible for the positive acidified-serum test. Disordered maturation yields bi- and multinucleated erythroblasts and marked intramedullary destruction (ineffective erythropoiesis); the chronic anaemia suppresses hepcidin and drives progressive iron overload. Congenital ectropion uveae — congenital ectropion uvea Acquired ectropion uveae (from rubeosis or chronic inflammation) Axenfeld-Rieger spectrum Iridocorneal endothelial syndrome Iris melanoma or other iris lesion (for pigment change) Neurofibromatosis-associated iris changes Slit-lamp examination of the pupillary margin and iris Gonioscopy of the drainage angle Intraocular pressure measurement and glaucoma assessment Evaluation for neurofibromatosis type 1 and other associations Serial monitoring for glaucoma over time A non-progressive anomaly in which iris pigment epithelium extends from the pupillary margin onto the anterior iris surface It appears as a dark cuff of pigment around the pupil where the posterior pigment layer is visible anteriorly It is usually unilateral and is a marker of anterior segment maldevelopment It is strongly associated with glaucoma, which may be present at birth or develop later Associations include neurofibromatosis type 1, Prader-Willi syndrome and other anterior segment dysgenesis Lifelong glaucoma surveillance is the key management priority Raised intraocular pressure or glaucomatous optic neuropathy Progressive visual field loss Features of neurofibromatosis or another syndrome New iris changes suggesting an acquired cause Failing to screen for and monitor glaucoma Confusing it with acquired ectropion uveae from neovascularisation Overlooking neurofibromatosis type 1 and other associations Assuming a benign course without angle assessment Congenital ectropion uveae results from abnormal development of the anterior segment in which the iris posterior pigment epithelium migrates anteriorly over the pupillary margin onto the iris face. It is thought to reflect a neural crest-related developmental abnormality, and the same maldevelopment involves the drainage angle, producing a high-insertion or dysgenic angle that impairs aqueous outflow and causes glaucoma. The pigment ectropion itself is stable, but the associated angle anomaly drives the visually important complication. The anomaly is stable, and visual prognosis depends on detecting and controlling the associated glaucoma; with effective glaucoma management outcomes can be good.

there are no neurovisceral attacks Management is largely supportive with rigorous lifelong sunlight avoidance and photoprotection; severe cases may be considered for haematopoietic stem cell transplantation Severe transfusion-dependent haemolytic anaemia Progressive mutilating scarring with functional loss of digits or facial structures Secondary infection of ulcerated photodamaged skin Presentation in a neonate with red-staining urine and blistering requiring urgent photoprotection Missing the diagnosis in an infant with staining of the nappy dismissed as dietary or infective Inadequate lifelong photoprotection allowing progressive irreversible damage Confusing it with erythropoietic protoporphyria, which causes pain without blistering Underestimating the burden of chronic haemolysis and splenomegaly Failing to offer genetic counselling given the recessive inheritance Congenital erythropoietic porphyria results from markedly deficient uroporphyrinogen III synthase, the fourth enzyme of the haem pathway, which converts hydroxymethylbilane to uroporphyrinogen III. When this step fails, hydroxymethylbilane cyclises non-enzymatically to the type I isomer, which cannot be used for haem and accumulates as uroporphyrin I and coproporphyrin I. These photoreactive type I porphyrins accumulate massively in erythrocytes, plasma, urine, bone and teeth. Deposition in the skin causes light-induced generation of reactive oxygen species and severe phototoxic damage, while porphyrin-laden erythrocytes undergo haemolysis, producing the anaemia and splenomegaly. Prognosis depends on disease severity; many patients have progressive disfigurement and chronic haemolysis with a substantially affected quality of life, though rigorous photoprotection and, in selected severe cases, stem cell transplantation can improve outcomes.

Congenital fibre type disproportion — Congenital fibre-type disproportion, CFTD, Fibre-type disproportion myopathy Nemaline myopathy Central core and multiminicore disease Centronuclear and myotubular myopathy Congenital muscular dystrophy Spinal muscular atrophy Congenital myasthenic syndromes Secondary type 1 fibre smallness (for example myotonic dystrophy) Muscle biopsy with fibre-type morphometry using ATPase or immunohistochemistry Targeted or panel gene testing (TPM3, ACTA1, SELENON, RYR1, MYH7) Serum creatine kinase Pulmonary function testing and overnight respiratory monitoring Electromyography and nerve conduction studies Echocardiography where MYH7 is implicated Spinal and skeletal imaging for scoliosis and contractures A congenital myopathy defined histologically by type 1 (slow) fibres being consistently smaller than type 2 fibres, without other structural lesions. Genetically heterogeneous, with recognised causes in TPM3, ACTA1, SELENON (SEPN1), RYR1 and MYH7. Presents with neonatal or infantile hypotonia and proximal weakness, often with facial weakness, an elongated myopathic face and a high-arched palate. Contractures, spinal rigidity and scoliosis may develop; associated external ophthalmoplegia points to particular genotypes. Respiratory muscle weakness can be disproportionate to limb weakness, particularly with SELENON-related disease. Diagnosis relies on quantitative morphometry showing type 1 fibres roughly 35 to 40 per cent smaller than type 2 fibres. Type 1 fibre predominance commonly accompanies the disproportion. The course is usually static or slowly progressive and strength may improve through childhood. Nocturnal hypoventilation and daytime hypercapnia Respiratory decline out of proportion to limb weakness Feeding difficulty with aspiration Progressive scoliosis compromising respiration Diagnosing the disorder without excluding secondary causes of type 1 fibre smallness. Underestimating respiratory involvement because limb strength appears preserved. Not pursuing a genetic diagnosis despite its prognostic and cardiac implications with MYH7. Congenital fibre type disproportion is a pathological pattern rather than a single disease, in which slow type 1 myofibres fail to reach normal size relative to fast type 2 fibres. The underlying mutations affect thin-filament and sarcomeric proteins such as tropomyosin, actin and slow myosin, the ryanodine receptor calcium-release channel, or selenoprotein N involved in redox regulation of calcium handling. These disturb fibre-type maturation and trophic regulation, impairing contractile function and producing the characteristic size discrepancy. Most cases are non-progressive or slowly progressive, with stable or slowly improving strength. Respiratory insufficiency is the principal determinant of morbidity and mortality, especially in SELENON-related disease.

Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles — CFEOM, congenital fibrosis syndrome, congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder, KIF21A, PHOX2A Congenital third nerve palsy Duane retraction syndrome Congenital myasthenic syndromes Congenital myopathies and mitochondrial ophthalmoplegia Thyroid eye disease (in older patients) Orbital fibrosis from other causes Möbius syndrome Orthoptic assessment of ductions, versions and head posture Forced duction testing under anaesthesia MRI of the orbits and brainstem to assess nerves and muscles Genetic testing including KIF21A, PHOX2A and TUBB3 Cycloplegic refraction and amblyopia assessment Assessment for associated cranial nerve or systemic anomalies A congenital, non-progressive restrictive ophthalmoplegia now classified among the congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders rather than a primary muscle disease Children typically present with bilateral ptosis and eyes fixed in a downgaze position, adopting a compensatory chin-up head posture Attempted upgaze is severely limited and there may be anomalous convergence or aberrant movements on attempted gaze Forced duction testing is positive, reflecting secondary fibrosis of the involved muscles Several genetic subtypes exist; CFEOM1 is linked to KIF21A, CFEOM2 to PHOX2A and CFEOM3 to TUBB3, affecting oculomotor nucleus and nerve development The primary defect lies in maldevelopment of the oculomotor and trochlear nuclei and nerves, with muscle fibrosis a secondary consequence of chronic denervation Management focuses on ptosis correction to clear the visual axis and strabismus surgery to improve head posture and alignment Acquired or progressive ophthalmoplegia suggesting an alternative neurological or myopathic cause Amblyopia developing behind a ptotic lid requiring prompt intervention Associated systemic or brain malformations in syndromic TUBB3 disease Fatigable ptosis pointing to a myasthenic disorder rather than CFEOM Mistaking the restrictive picture for an isolated cranial nerve palsy Neglecting amblyopia treatment while awaiting surgery Assuming a primary muscle disease and missing the dysinnervation mechanism Overlooking the familial pattern and not offering genetic counselling Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles is a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder in which the oculomotor (and sometimes trochlear) nuclei and their nerves develop abnormally. Mutations in genes such as KIF21A and TUBB3 disrupt axon guidance and microtubule-based transport in developing motor neurons, while PHOX2A affects nucleus formation. The resulting aberrant or deficient innervation of the extraocular muscles leads to chronic dysfunction and secondary fibrotic, restrictive change in the muscles themselves. Clinically this produces fixed, restricted eye positions, ptosis and anomalous gaze-evoked movements, with positive forced ductions confirming the mechanical restriction. The ophthalmoplegia is stable and non-progressive; surgery can improve head posture, lid position and alignment, but full ocular motility is not restored and binocular function often remains limited.

with arrhythmia in susceptible subtypes Uncontrolled insulin-resistant diabetes with severe hyperglycaemia Attributing the muscular, veiny habitus to athleticism and missing the diagnosis Overlooking severe resistance Failing to arrange genetic confirmation and family counselling Congenital generalised lipodystrophy is an inherited near-total failure to develop or maintain functional adipose tissue, caused by biallelic mutations in genes governing triglyceride synthesis (AGPAT2), lipid-droplet/adipocyte formation (BSCL2/seipin), or caveolar structure (CAV1, PTRF/CAVIN1). Without a normal fat depot, dietary and endogenous lipid cannot be stored subcutaneously and is deposited ectopically in liver, skeletal muscle, and other organs, driving profound insulin resistance. The tiny fat mass secretes very little leptin, removing satiety signalling and provoking hyperphagia that worsens the lipid overload. The resulting phenotype combines hypertriglyceridaemia, hepatic steatosis, acanthosis nigricans, and early insulin-resistant diabetes. Prognosis depends on metabolic control; leptin (metreleptin) replacement and aggressive management of triglycerides and glucose substantially improve outcomes, but untreated disease carries risks of pancreatitis, progressive liver disease, and cardiac complications.

amblyopia Attributing infant watering solely to nasolacrimal duct obstruction and missing glaucoma Overlooking early buphthalmos because both eyes are symmetrically enlarged Relying on medical therapy alone when the definitive treatment is surgical Failing to manage amblyopia and refractive error alongside pressure control Mistaking Haab striae or corneal oedema for a primary corneal disorder Primary congenital glaucoma arises from maldevelopment of the anterior chamber angle, in which abnormal differentiation of the trabecular meshwork and related tissues impairs aqueous outflow and raises intraocular pressure. Many cases are autosomal recessive and associated with mutations in the CYP1B1 gene. Because the collagen of an infant's cornea and sclera is still elastic, sustained pressure elevation stretches the whole globe, enlarging the corneal diameter and axial length to produce buphthalmos. Rapid corneal stretching ruptures Descemet membrane, giving the horizontal or curvilinear breaks known as Haab striae, and causes corneal oedema. The developing optic nerve is vulnerable, and cupping can progress quickly but may partly reverse after successful pressure control. With early angle surgery many eyes achieve good long-term pressure control and useful vision, but outcomes worsen with late presentation, marked corneal clouding, and high pressures; amblyopia, refractive error, and corneal scarring commonly limit final vision even after successful pressure control.

Congenital haemangioma — Rapidly involuting congenital haemangioma (RICH), Non-involuting congenital haemangioma (NICH), Partially involuting congenital haemangioma (PICH) Infantile haemangioma Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma Infantile fibrosarcoma Venous or arteriovenous malformation Soft-tissue sarcoma or myofibroma Cutaneous metastatic neuroblastoma Antenatal and postnatal Doppler ultrasound demonstrating a fast-flow mass MRI to define deep extent and flow characteristics GLUT1 immunohistochemistry (negative) if biopsied Full blood count and coagulation screen in the neonatal period GNAQ/GNA11 mutation analysis where available Serial photography to document involution Fully formed at birth and does not undergo postnatal proliferation, unlike infantile haemangioma. GLUT1-negative, which reliably separates it from infantile haemangioma. Three subtypes are recognised: rapidly involuting (RICH), non-involuting (NICH) and partially involuting (PICH). Somatic activating mutations in GNAQ and GNA11 are characteristic. RICH often regresses within the first year, sometimes leaving atrophic skin or anetoderma; NICH persists and grows proportionately with the child. Typical appearance is a violaceous plaque or exophytic mass with a peripheral pallor halo, coarse telangiectasia and a central depression or ulcer. Large RICH may cause a transient, self-limited thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy, milder than the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. Frequently detected on antenatal ultrasound as a fast-flow mass. High-output cardiac failure from large shunting lesions Transient consumptive coagulopathy with thrombocytopenia Ulceration, bleeding or haemorrhage Diagnostic uncertainty with more aggressive tumours such as fibrosarcoma or kaposiform haemangioendothelioma Mislabelling the lesion as infantile haemangioma and expecting the same natural history or beta-blocker response. Overlooking transient neonatal coagulopathy in a large RICH. Assuming that all congenital lesions will involute, when NICH will not. Failing to consider malignancy in an atypical, rapidly growing neonatal mass. Congenital haemangiomas are benign vascular tumours that proliferate in utero and are fully grown at delivery. They are GLUT1-negative and harbour somatic mosaic activating mutations in GNAQ or GNA11, affecting Galpha subunits that drive downstream MAPK and related proliferative signalling within endothelial cells. Histologically they show lobules of capillaries surrounded by fibrous tissue with abnormal draining channels and, in involuting forms, progressive lobular loss and fibrosis. Subtype behaviour (RICH, NICH, PICH) reflects the degree of postnatal regression. RICH commonly involutes within months, though residual atrophy or redundant skin may require correction. NICH persists indefinitely and may need excision or embolisation, but malignant transformation does not occur.

Adult Congenital Heart Disease — ASD, VSD, tetralogy of Fallot, Eisenmenger Atrial septal defect (secundum, primum, sinus venosus, coronary sinus types) — most common cause of right heart dilation from a shunt Patent foramen ovale (distinct from ASD; not associated with right heart dilation) Ventricular septal defect (membranous/perimembranous, muscular, AV-canal/inlet, subpulmonary/conal types) Patent ductus arteriosus Partial anomalous pulmonary venous return Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve Tetralogy of Fallot (most common cyanotic CHD) Transposition of the great arteries (D-loop and congenitally corrected L-loop) Coarctation of the aorta (with associated bicuspid aortic valve) Single ventricle physiology (tricuspid atresia, double inlet LV, hypoplastic left heart) post-Fontan Eisenmenger syndrome (any unrepaired left-to-right shunt that has reversed) Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography with agitated saline (bubble) contrast — needed to diagnose PFO and non-secundum ASDs; color flow Doppler for VSDs and shunt-ratio estimation Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging — routine surveillance of RV size, function, and mass in repaired tetralogy of Fallot and other complex CHD; cross-sectional imaging detects PAPVR Surface ECG — incomplete right bundle branch block in ASD; QRS duration >=180 ms in repaired TOF flags risk of ventricular tachycardia/sudden death; ventricular pre-excitation (WPW) in up to 20% of Ebstein anomaly Cardiac catheterization — shunt quantification and hemodynamic assessment, particularly when pulmonary hypertension is suspected Genetic evaluation — testing for 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge) in conotruncal defects (clues: right aortic arch, aberrant subclavian artery); recognition of trisomy 21, Noonan (PTPN11), Williams (7q11.23), and Turner syndromes Fetal echocardiogram between 18 and 22 weeks of gestation for pregnant patients with CHD Atrial septal defect may be mistaken for mitral stenosis; features favoring ASD over MS include a pulmonary mid-to-upper left sternal border flow murmur, and large left-to-right shunts can produce findings overlapping with MS (Harrison 22e p.2065 / Chap. on MS). Arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy and Uhl's anomaly are non-shunt myocardial causes of right heart dilation that can mimic the dilated right heart of an ASD. At least 1.4 million U.S. adults are living with congenital heart disease (CHD); the majority were diagnosed in childhood, but a substantial percentage have CHD first recognized in adulthood, so lifelong follow-up with ACHD expertise is recommended (Harrison 22e p.2067). ASD physiology is predominantly a left-to-right shunt; the degree of shunting (and thus right heart volume loading) depends on defect size and the diastolic properties of the heart. As patients age, diabetes, hypertension, and atherosclerosis reduce left-heart compliance and may increase left-to-right shunting and symptoms (Harrison 22e p.2070). The classic ASD physical finding is a wide, FIXED splitting of the second heart sound, due to prolonged RV ejection and increased pulmonary artery capacitance delaying pulmonary valve closure; the ECG commonly shows incomplete right bundle branch block (Harrison 22e p.2070). Secundum ASD (defect in the region of the fossa ovalis) is the most common type and can often be closed percutaneously with an occluder device; a patent foramen ovale (PFO) is distinct, is NOT associated with right-sided dilation, and persists in up to 25% of adults (Harrison 22e p.2070). Surgical closure (not percutaneous) is required for primum ASDs, sinus venosus defects, and coronary sinus septal defects; a sinus venosus defect is not actually a defect of the atrial septum but a communication near the SVC- or IVC-atrial junction with right pulmonary veins (Harrison 22e p.2070-2071). VSDs are the most common congenital anomaly recognized at birth but account for only ~10% of adult CHD, owing to the high rate of spontaneous closure of small VSDs in early life; the most common location is the membranous (perimembranous/outlet) septum (Harrison 22e p.2071-2072). Outcome for adults with small VSDs WITHOUT ventricular dilation or pulmonary hypertension is generally excellent; small muscular defects persisting into adulthood are often pressure- and flow-restricted with no significant hemodynamic consequence (Harrison 22e p.2072). Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common form of cyanotic CHD (~0.5 per 1000 live births) and comprises anterior conal-septal deviation causing RV outflow tract obstruction, a VSD, RV hypertrophy, and an overriding aorta (Harrison 22e p.2073). In repaired tetralogy of Fallot, pulmonary regurgitation is common and is usually associated with RV dilation; accurate quantification of RV size, function, and mass is particularly important because RV dilation, dysfunction, and hypertrophy are associated with adverse outcomes, and cardiac MRI is routinely used for surveillance (Harrison 22e p.2073-2074). Eisenmenger syndrome is the consequence of a long-standing high-volume or pressurized left-to-right shunt: excessive pulmonary blood flow leads to severely increased pulmonary vascular resistance that eventually REVERSES the shunt, creating bidirectional or right-to-left flow and cyanosis; it can complicate any CHD with an initial left-to-right shunt (Harrison 22e p.2078). Selective pulmonary vasodilators such as bosentan or sildenafil are efficacious in Eisenmenger syndrome; select patients may be candidates for combined heart-lung transplantation, or preferably lung transplantation with concomitant repair of the intracardiac defect when feasible (Harrison 22e p.2078). Endocarditis prophylaxis before dental procedures is advised in high-risk CHD lesions: unrepaired cyanotic CHD (including palliative shunts/conduits), completely repaired defects during the first 6 months after repair, and repaired CHD with residual defects adjacent to prosthetic material (Harrison 22e p.745, Table 133-9). Reversal of a left-to-right shunt to right-to-left flow with cyanosis = Eisenmenger syndrome; develops from severely elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and is a multi-organ condition Right heart dilation in an unrepaired ASD without other cause signals risk of progression to symptomatic right heart failure, atrial arrhythmias, and pulmonary arterial hypertension QRS duration >=180 ms on resting ECG in repaired tetralogy of Fallot — associated with increased risk of ventricular tachycardia and sudden cardiac death Systemic RV dysfunction after atrial switch (Mustard/Senning) for D-loop TGA — the most worrisome long-term complication, with no proven effective medical therapy Pregnancy in a woman with Eisenmenger syndrome is contraindicated due to high risk of maternal mortality; pulmonary arterial hypertension and severe systemic ventricular dysfunction are WHO class IV (extremely high maternal risk) New exercise-capacity decline in ACHD may be unrecognized by the patient; by the time symptoms appear, irreversible physiologic changes may already have occurred Confusing a PFO (flap-valve patency, present in up to 25% of adults, no right heart dilation) with a true secundum ASD. Assuming all ASDs are amenable to percutaneous closure — large defects, inadequate tissue rims, and anomalous draining pulmonary veins make device closure unfavorable, and primum/sinus venosus/coronary sinus defects require surgery. Overlooking that a sinus venosus defect is not in the atrial septum itself, so it may be missed without dedicated imaging. Routine phlebotomy in an asymptomatic adult with Eisenmenger syndrome is contraindicated; elevated hematocrit appropriate to the degree of cyanosis should not be lowered reflexively, and iron deficiency should be corrected because it impairs quality of life and function. Using teratogenic medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, direct oral anticoagulants, endothelin receptor blockers) in CHD patients of childbearing potential; estrogen-containing contraception should be avoided in Eisenmenger syndrome due to thrombogenicity. Failing to test adults with conotruncal defects for 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge) — many were never tested, and unrecognized cognitive/psychiatric disability may go untreated. Treating an ACHD patient's seemingly minor lesion without recognizing limited hemodynamic reserve and subclinical multi-organ dysfunction before noncardiac surgery. The normal heart is analyzed segmentally (atria, ventricles, great arteries joined by the atrioventricular canal and conus), with attention to alignment (what drains into what) and connection (how segments are physically linked). The heart forms from the third week of gestation and is nearly complete by 8 weeks; cardiac neural crest cells migrating in weeks 5-6 are essential for outflow septation, semilunar valve formation, and aortic arch patterning, so disturbance of these processes underlies conotruncal defects. Shunt lesions are defined by the relative compliance, pressure, and outflow resistance of the connected chambers/vessels and the defect size. Left-to-right shunts (ASD, VSD, PDA) move oxygenated blood toward the deoxygenated (right) side, volume-loading the pulmonary circulation: ASD/PAPVR (proximal to the tricuspid valve) cause right heart dilation, whereas VSD/PDA (below the tricuspid valve) cause left heart dilation. Sustained high-volume or pressurized left-to-right shunting can raise pulmonary vascular resistance to the point that the shunt reverses (Eisenmenger physiology, right-to-left, cyanosis). Tetralogy of Fallot produces a right-to-left shunt across the VSD because RV outflow obstruction raises right-sided systolic pressure, mixing deoxygenated blood into the LV and causing systemic arterial cyanosis. In transposition of the great arteries the aorta arises from the RV and the pulmonary artery from the LV, creating parallel rather than series circulations that are incompatible with life unless mixing exists (ASD, VSD, or PDA). Outcomes vary widely by lesion. Adults with small VSDs without ventricular dilation or pulmonary hypertension generally have an excellent prognosis. Repaired coarctation patients generally do well but remain at risk for systemic hypertension, premature atherosclerosis, LV failure, and aortic aneurysm/dissection and recoarctation. In repaired tetralogy of Fallot, one prospective cohort of 144 adults showed 72% survival at 40 years but only 25% cumulative event-free survival (events: reintervention, most commonly pulmonary valve replacement; symptomatic arrhythmia; heart failure); LV dysfunction is present in at least 20%. The arterial switch operation for D-loop TGA has produced substantial long-term survival, whereas atrial switch leaves a systemic RV prone to dysfunction. Adults with Eisenmenger syndrome have significant morbidity but generally survive longer than patients with other forms of pulmonary arterial hypertension. In aggregate, adults with CHD have quality-of-life-limiting comorbidities and premature mortality far exceeding age-matched controls, and nearly all can be classified as stage A heart failure or greater; care within a center that has an ACHD specialty program is associated with improved overall survival. The chapter applies the modified World Health Organization (mWHO) classification of maternal risk in heart disease during pregnancy, graded mWHO I (no detectable increased mortality risk, e.g., small/mild lesions) through mWHO IV (extremely high maternal mortality risk; pregnancy generally contraindicated). Examples by class: mWHO II includes unoperated ASD/VSD and repaired tetralogy of Fallot; mWHO III includes mechanical valve, systemic RV, and Fontan circulation; mWHO IV includes pulmonary arterial hypertension, severe systemic ventricular dysfunction (EF <30% or NYHA III-IV), severe aortic dilatation, and Fontan with any complication. The CARPREG II weighted-risk score is also described (highest 3-point factors: prior cardiac event/arrhythmia, NYHA >=III, mechanical valve), stratifying predicted cardiac-event risk from 5% (<=1 point) to 41% (>4 points). For repaired tetralogy of Fallot, potential sequelae are catalogued in Table 280-3 and long-term sequelae of D-loop TGA surgery in Table 280-4.
