Generally poor, with severe disability and, in the most affected infants, early respiratory compromise; outcome depends on the specific variant, and some children survive with major motor impairment.

Congenital hypothyroidism — CH, neonatal hypothyroidism, cretinism, congenital thyroid deficiency Transient neonatal hypothyroidism (e.g. maternal antithyroid drugs, iodine exposure, maternal antibodies) Central (secondary/tertiary) hypothyroidism Other causes of prolonged neonatal jaundice Down syndrome and other conditions with hypotonia and feeding difficulty Constitutional causes of poor feeding and lethargy Newborn screening TSH and/or T4 on heel-prick blood Confirmatory serum free T4 and TSH Thyroid imaging (ultrasound and/or radionuclide scan) to define aetiology Maternal thyroid history and antibody status where relevant Knee radiograph for bone age in some cases to assess in utero severity One of the most common preventable causes of intellectual disability, resulting from inadequate thyroid hormone at birth or in early infancy. Most affected newborns appear normal at birth because of transplacental maternal thyroid hormone, so clinical detection is unreliable and newborn screening is essential. The commonest cause worldwide is thyroid dysgenesis (aplasia, hypoplasia, or an ectopic gland); dyshormonogenesis and, in some regions, iodine deficiency also contribute. Later clinical features include prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, lethargy, constipation, a large fontanelle, macroglossia, umbilical hernia, hypotonia, and hoarse cry. Screening measures TSH and/or T4 on a heel-prick sample; a raised TSH with low T4 confirms primary hypothyroidism. Treatment is early thyroid hormone replacement with levothyroxine, and the key to normal neurodevelopment is starting therapy as early as possible. Regular monitoring of growth, development, and thyroid function is needed to keep levels in the target range during infancy. Delay in starting treatment is associated with irreversible loss of cognitive potential, making prompt recognition critical. Positive newborn screen requiring urgent confirmation and treatment Signs of significant hypothyroidism (marked lethargy, poor feeding, hypothermia) Prolonged unexplained neonatal jaundice Delayed diagnosis beyond the early weeks of life, risking neurodevelopmental harm Relying on clinical signs, which are usually absent or subtle in the newborn period Delaying treatment while awaiting further tests once screening is clearly abnormal Under- or over-treating due to infrequent monitoring during infancy Missing central hypothyroidism when screening is TSH-based only Thyroid hormone is essential for normal brain growth and myelination, particularly in the first years of life. In congenital hypothyroidism, deficient hormone production results from failure of thyroid gland development, an enzymatic defect in hormone synthesis (dyshormonogenesis), inadequate iodine substrate, or, less commonly, hypothalamic-pituitary (central) dysfunction. In primary disease, low circulating thyroid hormone removes negative feedback on the pituitary, raising TSH. Because maternal thyroid hormone crosses the placenta, the fetus is partly protected in utero, but after birth the untreated infant becomes progressively hypothyroid, and prolonged deficiency during the critical window of brain development produces permanent neurological injury. With early diagnosis through screening and prompt, adequately dosed replacement, neurodevelopmental outcome is typically normal; delayed or inadequate treatment risks permanent intellectual impairment.

It may occur in isolation as a packaging phenomenon from abnormal intrauterine position, particularly with breech presentation and oligohydramnios, or as part of a generalised condition such as arthrogryposis or Larsen syndrome in which multiple joints are affected by connective-tissue laxity or contracture. Isolated, reducible dislocations treated early with serial casting generally achieve a stable, functional, well-flexing knee, whereas irreducible or syndromic cases have a more guarded outlook and often require surgery and prolonged rehabilitation.

Without functional lactase, dietary lactose cannot be hydrolysed to glucose and galactose in the small intestine. The unabsorbed disaccharide is osmotically active, drawing water into the lumen and passing to the colon where bacterial fermentation generates gas and short-chain acids. Prognosis is excellent with a strict lactose-free diet, and growth and development proceed normally. The enzyme deficiency is permanent, so dietary avoidance is lifelong.

steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (StAR) transports cholesterol into mitochondria, the essential first committed step for synthesising all steroid hormones. When StAR function is lost, cholesterol cannot be delivered for conversion, so production of glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids and sex steroids fails across the adrenal cortex and gonads. Survival depends on prompt recognition and lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement with stress dosing during illness; gonadal steroid replacement is needed at puberty, and fertility is generally severely impaired.

Lobectomy in symptomatic infants is generally curative with a good long-term outcome, as the remaining lung compensates well. Mildly symptomatic or incidentally found cases may remain stable without surgery under observation.

membrane, extracellular matrix, or the glycosylation machinery that modifies alpha-dystroglycan. Respiratory involvement is often the principal determinant of outcome, so early respiratory surveillance and support are critical.

stretching physiotherapy Associated developmental dysplasia of the hip Progressive facial asymmetry or severe fixed contracture Assuming every infantile head tilt is muscular and missing a bony, ocular, or neurological cause Failing to examine the hips and overlooking coexisting dysplasia Delaying stretching physiotherapy, which is most effective in the early months Neglecting positioning advice, allowing plagiocephaly and facial asymmetry to worsen Persisting with conservative treatment indefinitely when surgical release is indicated Congenital muscular torticollis results from localised fibrosis and shortening of the sternocleidomastoid, thought to follow a compartment-like injury or ischaemia of the muscle related to intrauterine position or a difficult, often breech, delivery. Fibrous tissue replaces part of the muscle, sometimes forming a palpable tumour early on, and the resulting contracture tethers the head into tilt toward the affected side and rotation away from it. Because the deforming posture is constant, the growing skull and face remodel asymmetrically, producing plagiocephaly and hemifacial flattening. The same intrauterine crowding that injures the muscle is thought to underlie the association with developmental hip dysplasia and other moulding deformities. The outlook is excellent when treatment begins early, as most infants achieve full correction with stretching and positioning; later presentation or a persistent tight band carries a greater chance of residual deformity and a need for surgical release.

family history Episodic apnoea or respiratory crises, particularly during febrile illness in infants Rapidly worsening bulbar weakness with aspiration Deterioration after starting an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, suggesting a subtype that it worsens Feeding difficulty with failure to thrive Misdiagnosing a congenital myasthenic syndrome as seronegative autoimmune myasthenia and giving immunotherapy Prescribing acetylcholinesterase inhibitors empirically in subtypes where they are harmful Overlooking episodic apnoea syndromes that require an emergency respiratory plan Assuming absent antibodies means no neuromuscular junction disorder Congenital myasthenic syndromes arise from inherited defects in proteins essential for neuromuscular transmission, classified by the location of the defect as presynaptic, synaptic (basal lamina) or postsynaptic. Postsynaptic forms are the most common, including acetylcholine receptor deficiency (often CHRNE), kinetic abnormalities of the receptor channel (slow- and fast-channel syndromes), and defects in receptor clustering proteins such as rapsyn and the agrin-MuSK-DOK7 pathway. Each defect reduces the safety factor for transmission, so that acetylcholine release, receptor function or endplate architecture is insufficient to reliably generate a muscle action potential, producing fatigable weakness. Because the process is structural or kinetic rather than immune-mediated, there is no autoantibody and responses to specific therapies depend on the underlying mechanism. Prognosis varies widely by subtype: many forms are compatible with long, functional lives especially once correctly treated, while some cause significant disability or life-threatening apnoeic episodes. Accurate genetic diagnosis substantially improves outcomes by guiding targeted therapy.

Congenital mydriasis — congenital mydriasis syndrome, iridoplegia with congenital mydriasis, ACTA2-related mydriasis Aniridia Iris coloboma and other structural iris defects Pharmacological (mydriatic) pupil dilatation Traumatic mydriasis or sphincter rupture Adie tonic pupil Third nerve palsy with pupil involvement Congenital ectropion or iris hypoplasia Slit-lamp examination of iris structure and pupillary margin Pharmacological pupil testing to assess sphincter and dilator responsiveness Cycloplegic refraction and assessment of near function Genetic testing for ACTA2 and related smooth-muscle genes Echocardiography and vascular imaging where a smooth-muscle syndrome is suspected Cerebrovascular imaging in ACTA2-related disease Persistently dilated, poorly reactive pupils present from birth with an essentially normal-appearing but functionally unresponsive iris Both light and near responses are typically impaired, and pupils show little reaction to pharmacological miotics or mydriatics The condition reflects maldevelopment or dysfunction of the iris sphincter and dilator smooth muscle rather than a neurological lesion Photophobia and difficulty with near focusing are common because of the fixed large aperture Reported in association with ACTA2 mutations as part of a smooth-muscle dysfunction syndrome that includes patent ductus arteriosus and cerebral and aortic vascular disease Structural iris disorders such as aniridia and iris coloboma, and pharmacological or traumatic mydriasis, must be excluded Management is supportive with tinted or photochromic lenses and refractive correction; the systemic associations may require cardiovascular and cerebrovascular surveillance Features suggesting an ACTA2 smooth-muscle syndrome with aortic aneurysm or dissection risk Cerebrovascular symptoms indicating associated arteriopathy Signs of a patent ductus arteriosus or other cardiac anomaly New anisocoria or ptosis suggesting an acquired neurological cause rather than a congenital condition Assuming a neurological cause and pursuing unnecessary third nerve investigation Overlooking the systemic ACTA2 associations and their vascular risks Confusing it with pharmacological or traumatic mydriasis Neglecting refractive and photophobia management Congenital mydriasis is characterised by fixed pupillary dilatation from birth due to a primary abnormality of the iris musculature. Rather than a defect of the parasympathetic pathway, the sphincter pupillae and dilator smooth muscle are maldeveloped or dysfunctional, so the pupil neither constricts to light and near effort nor responds normally to pharmacological agents. In a recognised subset, mutations in ACTA2, which encodes smooth-muscle alpha-actin, disturb smooth muscle throughout the body, producing not only iris dysfunction but also patent ductus arteriosus, aortic aneurysm and dissection, and cerebrovascular disease. The fixed large pupil impairs the eye's ability to regulate retinal illumination and contributes to photophobia and near difficulty. The ocular condition is stable and chiefly causes photophobia and near difficulty managed with optical measures, but prognosis in ACTA2-related cases is dominated by the potentially serious cardiovascular and cerebrovascular complications.

from the hypercoagulable state Severe refractory oedema with respiratory or feeding compromise Progressive decline toward end-stage kidney disease requiring renal replacement Trialling corticosteroids or immunosuppression, which are ineffective in this genetic barrier defect Overlooking secondary hypothyroidism from urinary loss of thyroxine-binding globulin Underestimating infection and thrombosis risk from urinary loss of immunoglobulins and anticoagulant proteins Delaying genetic diagnosis, which is essential for prognosis and family counselling Congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in NPHS1, encoding nephrin, a transmembrane protein that forms the structural backbone of the glomerular slit diaphragm between podocyte foot processes. Loss of functional nephrin disrupts this size- and charge-selective filtration barrier, so plasma proteins, chiefly albumin, leak massively into the urine from before birth. The resulting hypoalbuminaemia produces severe oedema, while urinary loss of immunoglobulins, anticoagulant and hormone-binding proteins predisposes to infection, thrombosis and endocrine disturbance, and ongoing podocyte injury leads to progressive glomerulosclerosis and kidney failure. Without intensive supportive care the outlook in infancy is poor, but with modern management of protein losses, nutrition and infection, and progression to dialysis and transplantation, long-term survival is achievable in specialist centres.

surgery (Kestenbaum-Anderson) for a significant head posture Oscillopsia, vertical or dissociated nystagmus, or other neurological signs suggesting acquired disease Asymmetric or unilateral nystagmus with head nodding requiring exclusion of intracranial pathology Poor vision suggesting a significant underlying retinal or optic nerve disorder Rapid change in the nystagmus pattern or new onset in an older child Assuming all infantile nystagmus is benign and missing an underlying sensory or neurological cause Failing to correct refractive error and treat amblyopia Overlooking a subtle anomalous head posture that indicates a shiftable null zone Misinterpreting a compensatory head turn as a primary musculoskeletal (torticollis) problem Infantile nystagmus reflects instability of the ocular motor fixation-maintenance system, producing involuntary rhythmic to-and-fro eye movements from early life. In sensory forms an afferent visual deficit such as albinism, a retinal dystrophy, or optic nerve hypoplasia degrades the fixation signal that normally stabilises gaze; in idiopathic (motor) forms the afferent pathway is intact and the defect lies in ocular motor control itself. A null zone develops where slow-phase drift is minimised, and the brain adopts a head turn to keep the eyes in that position, optimising visual acuity. Idiopathic infantile nystagmus is compatible with useful, often good, vision that tends to stabilise with age; visual outcome in sensory forms is determined by the underlying afferent disorder, and head-posture surgery can meaningfully improve an abnormal head position.

Congenital Pneumonia — neonatal pneumonia, intrauterine pneumonia, early-onset neonatal pneumonia Respiratory distress syndrome (surfactant deficiency) Transient tachypnoea of the newborn Meconium aspiration syndrome Early-onset sepsis without pneumonia Congenital heart disease Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn Chest radiograph Blood culture and full blood count with differential Inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein Pulse oximetry and blood gas Lumbar puncture when sepsis or meningitis is suspected Maternal history and cultures (group B streptococcus status, chorioamnionitis) Pneumonia acquired before or during birth typically presents as respiratory distress in the first hours to days of life and often forms part of early-onset neonatal sepsis. Infection may be acquired transplacentally, by ascending spread from the genital tract (especially with prolonged rupture of membranes or chorioamnionitis), or during passage through the birth canal. Group B streptococcus and Escherichia coli are leading bacterial causes; other organisms include Listeria, and congenital infections such as certain viruses can also involve the lungs. Clinical features overlap with other causes of neonatal respiratory distress, so it is often difficult to distinguish pneumonia from surfactant deficiency or transient tachypnoea on presentation. Maternal and perinatal risk factors, particularly chorioamnionitis, prolonged membrane rupture, and maternal group B streptococcus colonisation, raise the likelihood and guide management. Chest radiographs may show diffuse or patchy opacities, but findings can mimic respiratory distress syndrome, so imaging is supportive rather than definitive. Because differentiating infection from non-infectious causes is difficult, empirical antibiotics covering likely organisms are usually started while cultures and the clinical course are followed. Supportive care to maintain oxygenation, ventilation, temperature, and perfusion is essential alongside antimicrobial therapy. Severe or worsening respiratory distress and rising oxygen requirement Signs of septic shock or poor perfusion Apnoea Persistent pulmonary hypertension with labile oxygenation Deterioration despite initial supportive measures Attributing respiratory distress solely to surfactant deficiency and delaying antibiotics in an at-risk infant Underweighting maternal risk factors such as chorioamnionitis or prolonged membrane rupture Relying on chest radiograph appearance to exclude infection given its overlap with other conditions Failing to evaluate for accompanying bacteraemia or meningitis Organisms reach the fetal or newborn lung by several routes: transplacental spread during maternal bloodstream infection, ascending colonisation of amniotic fluid after membrane rupture or with chorioamnionitis, and aspiration of infected amniotic fluid or genital secretions around delivery. Once in the alveoli, pathogens trigger an inflammatory response with exudate, impaired gas exchange, and interference with surfactant function. In early-onset disease this frequently coexists with bacteraemia and systemic sepsis, so lung involvement is often one component of a generalised infection in the vulnerable newborn. With prompt recognition and appropriate antibiotics and supportive care many infants recover well, but outcome depends on the organism, gestational age, and severity; fulminant early-onset sepsis with pneumonia, particularly from group B streptococcus, can be life-threatening.

Congenital portosystemic shunt (Abernethy malformation) — Abernethy malformation, congenital portosystemic shunt, CPSS, congenital extrahepatic portosystemic shunt Acquired portosystemic collaterals from portal hypertension Urea-cycle or other inherited metabolic causes of hyperammonaemia Neonatal cholestatic syndromes Hepatopulmonary syndrome from chronic liver disease Focal nodular hyperplasia or hepatocellular tumours of other aetiology Hepatic arteriovenous malformation Doppler ultrasound to identify the shunt and assess intrahepatic portal flow Contrast-enhanced CT or MR angiography to define shunt anatomy and classify the malformation Serum ammonia and bile-acid measurement Echocardiography and evaluation for associated cardiac and other anomalies Cross-sectional imaging surveillance for liver nodules Assessment for hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension An abnormal communication that diverts portal blood into the systemic circulation, bypassing the liver, classified as extrahepatic (Abernethy) or intrahepatic Abernethy type 1 has complete diversion with absent intrahepatic portal supply, whereas type 2 preserves some portal perfusion via a side-to-side shunt May be detected antenatally, in the neonate with cholestasis or galactosaemia-like screening abnormalities, or later with hepatic encephalopathy Loss of hepatic first-pass nodules, including focal nodular hyperplasia-like lesions and hepatocellular tumours, arise because of the altered hepatic perfusion Frequently associated with congenital heart disease and other anomalies, prompting a search for coexisting malformations Management ranges from shunt closure by embolisation or surgical ligation when intrahepatic portal vasculature can recruit, to transplantation for type-1 lesions Progressive hepatic encephalopathy or marked hyperammonaemia Hypoxaemia from hepatopulmonary syndrome or signs of portopulmonary hypertension Development or growth of hepatic nodules suggesting malignant change Severe associated congenital cardiac disease Attributing hyperammonaemia solely to a metabolic disorder and missing the vascular anomaly Closing a shunt without confirming that the intrahepatic portal vasculature can accommodate restored flow Assuming a liver nodule is benign without surveillance for malignant transformation Overlooking associated cardiac and pulmonary complications A congenital portosystemic shunt is a developmental anomaly of the portal venous system in which portal blood is shunted directly into a systemic vein, partially or completely bypassing hepatic sinusoidal metabolism. Diversion of nutrient- and hormone-rich portal blood deprives the liver of trophic and metabolic exposure, producing hyperammonaemia, deranged bile-acid and galactose handling, and abnormal vasoactive-substance clearance that predisposes to hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension. Altered intrahepatic haemodynamics also promote the formation of regenerative and neoplastic liver nodules. Outcome depends on shunt type and complications; many type-2 and intrahepatic shunts do well after closure with recruitment of the portal system, whereas type-1 lesions with absent portal supply may ultimately require liver transplantation.

chin-up head posture and brow action indicate the child is using accessory means to clear the visual axis Marcus Gunn jaw-winking should be excluded by observing lid movement during sucking or jaw movement Timing of surgery balances the amblyogenic risk against the need to assess levator function accurately, using a levator resection or a frontalis suspension when function is poor Anisocoria suggesting Horner syndrome, which may signal an underlying neuroblastoma Associated ophthalmoplegia or pupil involvement indicating a third nerve palsy Fatigable or variable ptosis pointing to a myasthenic disorder Occlusion of the visual axis with developing amblyopia requiring prompt intervention Overlooking amblyopia while focusing on the lid position Missing jaw-winking synkinesis before planning surgery Failing to detect Horner syndrome and its possible sinister cause Misjudging levator function and choosing an inappropriate procedure Congenital ptosis most commonly reflects a developmental dystrophy of the levator palpebrae superioris, in which muscle fibres are replaced by fibrous and fatty tissue, reducing both the muscle's contractile power (poor lifting) and its ability to relax (lid lag on downgaze). The absent or high skin crease reflects deficient levator aponeurotic attachment to the skin. Less commonly the ptosis is neurogenic, aponeurotic or part of a syndrome. The functional consequences depend on whether the lid obscures the visual axis or induces corneal astigmatism, either of which can cause amblyopia in the developing visual system. With appropriate timing of surgery and amblyopia management the outlook is good, and most children achieve a functional and cosmetically acceptable lid position, though undercorrection or recurrence can require revision.

Fetal hydrops or significant mediastinal shift on prenatal imaging Recurrent or severe infection within the malformation Features suggesting pleuropulmonary blastoma rather than a benign lesion Rapid enlargement or tension physiology causing cardiorespiratory compromise Assuming a normal postnatal chest radiograph excludes a lesion seen antenatally Failing to look for a systemic feeding vessel and misclassifying a hybrid lesion Confusing a large cyst with congenital diaphragmatic hernia or lobar emphysema Attributing recurrent pneumonia to ordinary infection and missing an underlying malformation Overlooking the possibility of pleuropulmonary blastoma in an atypical cystic lesion Congenital pulmonary airway malformation arises from abnormal branching morphogenesis of the developing airways, producing a mass of disorganised, adenomatoid or cystic terminal respiratory structures that maintain communication with the bronchial tree but lack normal alveolar architecture. Depending on the level and timing of the developmental error, lesions vary from large single cysts to microcystic and solid tissue. Unlike bronchopulmonary sequestration, the blood supply is usually from the pulmonary circulation. Large lesions exert mass effect in utero, compressing normal lung and mediastinal structures, whereas after birth the abnormal, poorly draining airspaces predispose to air trapping and recurrent infection, and hybrid lesions with features of sequestration occur. Many small lesions are asymptomatic with an excellent outlook, and resection is generally curative with good long-term lung function. Large lesions causing fetal hydrops or severe pulmonary hypoplasia carry a worse prognosis, and the small associated malignancy risk supports specialist follow-up or elective resection.

Congenital radioulnar synostosis — radioulnar synostosis, proximal radioulnar synostosis, congenital forearm synostosis, congenital fusion of the forearm bones Post-traumatic (acquired) radioulnar synostosis Congenital dislocation of the radial head without synostosis Pulled elbow (nursemaid's elbow), which is transient Arthrogryposis affecting the elbow and forearm Multiple hereditary exostoses tethering the forearm Malunion after a forearm fracture limiting rotation Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the forearm and elbow to confirm proximal fusion and assess the radial head CT with three-dimensional reconstruction to define the bony bridge before surgical planning Clinical measurement of the forearm rotation arc and the fixed pronation angle Karyotype or targeted genetic evaluation when syndromic features or bilateral involvement are present Examination for associated musculoskeletal anomalies in other limbs, the hips, and the knees A bony or fibrous bridge unites the proximal radius and ulna, so forearm rotation (pronation and supination) is absent or severely restricted while the elbow and wrist may move normally The forearm is characteristically fixed in pronation, and the degree of fixed pronation determines the functional disability Presentation is often delayed because children compensate with shoulder and wrist motion; difficulty with supination-dependent tasks (accepting coins, catching, self-feeding) prompts recognition It is frequently bilateral and may be associated with chromosomal abnormalities (including sex-chromosome aneuploidies) and other syndromes Radiographs confirm the proximal fusion; the radial head may be absent, hypoplastic, or dislocated posteriorly Mild deformity with acceptable pronation frequently needs no treatment, and surgery is considered only for severe fixed pronation limiting function Surgery is usually a derotational osteotomy to reposition the forearm nearer neutral rather than an attempt to restore rotation, because recreating a mobile joint is unreliable and prone to re-fusion Severe fixed hyperpronation of both forearms causing major functional limitation An associated syndromic or chromosomal disorder requiring broader assessment Neurovascular compromise or compartment syndrome following a large corrective osteotomy Attempting to excise the synostosis to restore rotation, which commonly re-fuses and disappoints Over-correcting the derotational osteotomy and precipitating compartment syndrome or neurovascular injury Missing bilaterality and an associated syndrome Delaying diagnosis because unilateral cases compensate so well Early in limb development the proximal radius and ulna share a common cartilaginous anlage and normally undergo longitudinal segmentation to separate; congenital radioulnar synostosis reflects a failure of this differentiation, leaving the bones fused proximally. Because the forearm forms in a pronated position, the fused segment locks the limb in fixed pronation. The abnormality is therefore one of failure of differentiation and segmentation rather than of formation, and it may be linked to genetic or chromosomal disturbances, which explains its frequent bilaterality and syndromic associations. Many children function surprisingly well through compensatory shoulder and wrist motion and need no intervention; when correction is required, derotational osteotomy reliably improves the resting position of the hand, although forearm rotation itself is not restored and large corrections carry a risk of neurovascular complications.

monitoring Whole-spine magnetic resonance imaging to define intraspinal anomalies such as tethered cord or diastematomyelia Renal ultrasound to screen for the frequently associated urinary-tract anomalies Echocardiography to detect associated congenital cardiac lesions Computed tomography with three-dimensional reconstruction to characterise the vertebral anomaly before surgery Neurological examination and assessment for other VACTERL-associated malformations Scoliosis arising from congenital vertebral anomalies present from birth, caused by errors in the embryonic formation and segmentation of the vertebrae The anomalies are classified as failure of formation (for example a hemivertebra), failure of segmentation (for example a unilateral unsegmented bar), or a mixed pattern, and the combination determines the growth imbalance A unilateral unsegmented bar with a contralateral hemivertebra is the most progressive combination because growth is tethered on one side and unopposed on the other Because the vertebrae, heart, and kidneys form at the same embryonic stage, congenital scoliosis carries frequent VACTERL-type associations, so cardiac and renal evaluation is essential Intraspinal anomalies such as tethered cord, diastematomyelia, and syrinx are common, making whole-spine magnetic resonance imaging a routine part of assessment Serial standing radiographs with Cobb-angle measurement track progression, which depends on the type of anomaly and the growth remaining rather than on bracing responsiveness Bracing is generally ineffective for the primary structural curve, and progressive deformity is treated surgically, sometimes with early growth-preserving techniques A unilateral unsegmented bar with a contralateral hemivertebra, the most progressive pattern Neurological signs indicating cord tethering, diastematomyelia, or other intraspinal anomaly Associated cardiac or renal anomalies within a VACTERL pattern Rapid curve progression, especially during periods of accelerated growth Cutaneous markers of spinal dysraphism such as a hairy patch, dimple, or naevus over the spine Failing to screen for cardiac and renal anomalies given the VACTERL association Omitting magnetic resonance imaging and missing a tethered cord or diastematomyelia before surgery Relying on bracing for a structural congenital curve that will not respond Underestimating the progressive potential of a unilateral unsegmented bar Delaying surgical intervention until the deformity and any compensatory curve are advanced Congenital scoliosis results from anomalous development of the vertebral column during the first weeks of embryogenesis, producing asymmetric vertebral growth that drives a lateral curve. Failure of formation leaves a wedge or hemivertebra with deficient bone on one side, while failure of segmentation leaves vertebrae fused by a bar that prevents growth on that side; either imbalance, and especially their combination, causes the spine to curve as it grows. Because vertebral segmentation coincides with development of the cardiac and renal systems and the neural tube, the same insult frequently produces associated cardiac, renal, and intraspinal anomalies, the basis of the VACTERL association and of the high rate of cord tethering and dysraphism. The outlook depends on the specific anomaly, as balanced defects may progress little while a unilateral bar with a contralateral hemivertebra progresses relentlessly; early recognition and timely surgery can control progression, but associated cardiac, renal, and neural anomalies also influence overall prognosis.

Blood lead, copper and zinc, with assessment for alcohol and drug causes Investigation of syndromic features including lactate, pancreatic exocrine function, audiometry, glucose tolerance and neurological assessment Hepatic and cardiac iron quantification by MRI (T2*) A genetically heterogeneous group of inherited anaemias united by ring sideroblasts in the marrow due to defective mitochondrial haem synthesis, iron-sulphur cluster biogenesis or wider mitochondrial metabolism Divided into non-syndromic forms confined to erythropoiesis and syndromic forms with additional extra-haematological features The commonest non-syndromic causes are ALAS2 (X-linked, often pyridoxine-responsive) and SLC25A38 (autosomal recessive, typically more severe and transfusion-dependent) Syndromic forms include Pearson marrow-pancreas syndrome (mitochondrial DNA deletion with exocrine pancreatic failure), thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anaemia (SLC19A2, with diabetes and sensorineural deafness, Rogers syndrome), mitochondrial myopathy with lactic acidosis and sideroblastic anaemia (MLASA; PUS1, YARS2), sideroblastic anaemia with ataxia (ABCB7), and SIFD (TRNT1, with immunodeficiency, periodic fevers and developmental delay) The anaemia is usually microcytic and hypochromic in haem-synthesis defects but may be normocytic or macrocytic in some mitochondrial or syndromic forms Iron overload is common and treatment-limiting, occurring even without transfusion because of ineffective erythropoiesis, so iron therapy must be avoided A pyridoxine trial is worthwhile, notably in ALAS2 disease, and thiamine benefits the SLC19A2 form; otherwise care centres on transfusion and iron chelation Diagnosis integrates marrow morphology with Perls staining, the systemic phenotype and targeted gene or panel testing including mitochondrial DNA analysis Iron overload with cardiac, hepatic or endocrine failure Pancytopenia, lactic acidosis or multiorgan involvement suggesting Pearson or another mitochondrial syndrome Transfusion-dependence with faltering growth in infancy Recurrent fevers with immunodeficiency, suggesting TRNT1-related SIFD Inadvertent iron therapy aggravating overload Treating the anaemia as iron deficiency and giving iron, which worsens overload Failing to look for a syndromic or mitochondrial diagnosis, for example missing Pearson syndrome Not trialling pyridoxine or thiamine where the genotype makes it relevant Assuming ring sideroblasts always indicate myelodysplasia in a young patient Underestimating non-transfusional iron loading and its complications Congenital sideroblastic anaemias arise from inherited defects that impair the terminal mitochondrial steps of haem synthesis (for example ALAS2, and SLC25A38 which supplies mitochondrial glycine), iron-sulphur cluster assembly and export (GLRX5, ABCB7), or broader mitochondrial function including mitochondrial DNA integrity, RNA processing and translation (Pearson syndrome, PUS1, YARS2, TRNT1) and thiamine-dependent metabolism (SLC19A2). The common end point is failure to incorporate iron delivered to the erythroblast mitochondrion into protoporphyrin and haem, so iron accumulates in perinuclear mitochondria to form ring sideroblasts. Impaired haemoglobinisation and ineffective erythropoiesis produce anaemia, while hepcidin suppression drives systemic iron overload, and syndromic forms add multisystem features reflecting the affected mitochondrial or metabolic pathway. Outlook varies widely by genotype: vitamin-responsive forms (ALAS2, SLC19A2) may do well, whereas SLC25A38 and many syndromic or mitochondrial forms are severe, and Pearson syndrome in particular carries a poor prognosis. Iron overload is a major and largely preventable cause of morbidity across the group.

Congenital sideroblastic anaemia — hereditary sideroblastic anaemia, X-linked sideroblastic anaemia, ALAS2-related sideroblastic anaemia, SLC25A38 sideroblastic anaemia, XLSA, congenital sideroblastic anemia Acquired clonal sideroblastic anaemia (myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts) Iron deficiency and other microcytic anaemias Thalassaemia syndromes Lead poisoning impairing haem synthesis Copper deficiency or zinc excess causing sideroblastic change Alcohol- or drug-induced (for example isoniazid) reversible sideroblastic anaemia Bone marrow aspirate with Perls (Prussian blue) iron stain to demonstrate ring sideroblasts Full blood count and blood film assessing red cell indices and dimorphism Iron studies including ferritin and transferrin saturation to gauge overload Targeted next-generation sequencing panel (ALAS2, SLC25A38, and syndromic genes) A supervised pyridoxine trial where ALAS2 disease is likely Screening for syndromic features such as diabetes, deafness, or exocrine pancreatic dysfunction A group of inherited anaemias defined by ring sideroblasts in the marrow, reflecting iron-laden mitochondria encircling the erythroblast nucleus The commonest form is X-linked, caused by ALAS2 mutations affecting the first enzyme of haem synthesis, and characteristically responds to pyridoxine Autosomal recessive SLC25A38 disease is the next most frequent and tends to be more severe and pyridoxine-unresponsive Syndromic variants exist, including mitochondrial DNA deletion in Pearson syndrome and SLC19A2-related thiamine-responsive anaemia with diabetes and deafness The blood film typically shows a dimorphic or hypochromic microcytic anaemia, though the mean cell volume can be normal or raised in some forms Systemic iron overload develops even without transfusion because ineffective erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin and enhances iron absorption Diagnosis combines iron-stained marrow showing ring sideroblasts with targeted gene panels; a pyridoxine trial is warranted where ALAS2 disease is suspected Evidence of iron overload with cardiac, hepatic, or endocrine dysfunction despite few or no transfusions Severe transfusion-dependent anaemia presenting in infancy Syndromic features suggesting mitochondrial disease such as lactic acidosis or multiorgan failure Progressive cytopenias raising concern for clonal or marrow-failure evolution Assuming a microcytic anaemia is iron deficiency and giving iron, which worsens overload Missing the pyridoxine-responsive ALAS2 phenotype and failing to trial the vitamin Confusing congenital disease with acquired myelodysplasia, which requires different management Neglecting iron chelation because the patient is not transfusion dependent Congenital sideroblastic anaemias result from defects that impair mitochondrial haem biosynthesis, iron-sulphur cluster assembly, or mitochondrial protein handling within developing erythroblasts. When haem synthesis stalls, iron that has been imported into the mitochondrion cannot be incorporated into protoporphyrin and instead accumulates as insoluble deposits in perinuclear mitochondria, producing the pathognomonic ring sideroblast. ALAS2 mutations cripple delta-aminolaevulinate synthase, the pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent first committed step of the pathway; SLC25A38 disrupts the mitochondrial glycine transporter that supplies substrate. The failure of effective haemoglobinisation causes ineffective erythropoiesis, and the accompanying suppression of hepcidin drives excess dietary iron absorption and progressive parenchymal iron loading. Outcome depends on subtype: pyridoxine-responsive ALAS2 disease can be well controlled, whereas SLC25A38 and syndromic forms are more severe, and long-term morbidity is dominated by iron overload requiring vigilant monitoring and chelation.

linked to SLC9A3 and activating GUCY2C variants Presents in the neonatal period with profuse watery diarrhoea and heavy faecal sodium loss The biochemical picture is high faecal sodium with hyponatraemia and metabolic acidosis, distinguishing it from the alkalosis of congenital chloride diarrhoea May be preceded antenatally by polyhydramnios and distended bowel loops A syndromic form associated with SPINT2 features additional congenital anomalies such as choanal or anal atresia Management relies on aggressive sodium, fluid and bicarbonate replacement to restore balance and support growth Some patients tolerate gradual weaning of supplementation as intestinal adaptation occurs Severe hyponatraemia and dehydration threatening circulation in the neonate Significant metabolic acidosis requiring correction Associated congenital anomalies indicating the syndromic form Growth failure from inadequate sodium replacement Confusing the acidotic, high-sodium picture with congenital chloride diarrhoea Underestimating ongoing sodium losses and under-replacing, causing chronic depletion and poor growth Overlooking the diagnosis in a neonate with diarrhoea attributed to feed intolerance Failing to look for associated anomalies that suggest the SPINT2-related syndrome Congenital sodium diarrhoea reflects failure of electroneutral sodium absorption across the intestinal epithelium. Loss-of-function variants in SLC9A3, which encodes the apical sodium/hydrogen exchanger NHE3, impair sodium and fluid reabsorption. Activating variants in GUCY2C (guanylate cyclase 2C) raise intracellular cyclic GMP, inhibiting NHE3 and promoting chloride and fluid secretion, mimicking an enterotoxin-driven state. In both routes luminal sodium and water are retained, producing a secretory diarrhoea with high faecal sodium, systemic sodium depletion, and metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss. The SPINT2-associated syndromic form combines the enteropathy with developmental anomalies. Adequate and sustained sodium, fluid and bicarbonate replacement generally permits satisfactory growth, and some children reduce supplementation over time with intestinal adaptation. Syndromic disease carries added morbidity from associated anomalies.

Congenital stationary night blindness — CSNB, Schubert-Bornschein type, Riggs type, NYX, CACNA1F, GRM6, TRPM1 Retinitis pigmentosa and other progressive rod-cone dystrophies Oguchi disease and fundus albipunctatus (other stationary night-blindness disorders) Vitamin A deficiency retinopathy X-linked retinoschisis (also electronegative) Enhanced S-cone syndrome Melanoma-associated or other TRPM1 and others) Fundus examination and imaging to confirm an otherwise normal retina Non-progressive rod-system disorder presenting from birth with night blindness, and often nystagmus, myopia and reduced acuity, especially in X-linked forms A normal-appearing fundus in a patient with lifelong nyctalopia is a strong clue to the diagnosis The Schubert-Bornschein type shows a characteristic electronegative electroretinogram, where the b-wave is reduced below the a-wave under scotopic bright-flash conditions, reflecting impaired signalling from photoreceptors to bipolar cells It subdivides into complete (ON-bipolar dysfunction, for example NYX, GRM6, TRPM1) and incomplete (ON and OFF pathway, for example CACNA1F) forms distinguished by detailed electrophysiology The Riggs type shows reduced rod a-wave amplitude without the electronegative configuration, reflecting a phototransduction defect Inheritance is commonly X-linked (NYX, CACNA1F) but autosomal recessive and dominant forms exist The condition is stationary, so management is refractive correction, low-vision advice where needed, and genetic counselling rather than treatment of progression Documented progression of field loss or fundus change, which should prompt reconsideration of a degenerative diagnosis Systemic features or malabsorption suggesting acquired vitamin A deficiency Sudden onset of night blindness later in life indicating an acquired cause such as autoimmune retinopathy New maculopathy raising suspicion of an alternative diagnosis Mislabelling a stable patient as having progressive retinitis pigmentosa Overlooking the electronegative electroretinogram or failing to perform electrophysiology in a patient with lifelong nyctalopia and a normal fundus Confusing acquired night blindness (vitamin A deficiency, autoimmune retinopathy) with the congenital disorder Not distinguishing complete from incomplete forms, which carry different associated features Congenital stationary night blindness is caused by mutations that disrupt rod-mediated signal transmission. In the common Schubert-Bornschein group, defects in genes controlling the photoreceptor-to-bipolar synapse (NYX, GRM6, TRPM1 for the complete form; CACNA1F for the incomplete form) impair transmission to depolarising bipolar cells, producing the electronegative electroretinogram despite preserved photoreceptor phototransduction. In the rarer Riggs type, the primary defect is in rod phototransduction itself, reducing the rod a-wave. Because the abnormality is developmental and non-degenerative, visual function remains stable over life. By definition the disorder is stationary; night vision and acuity remain stable throughout life, though associated myopia and nystagmus may limit best-corrected acuity.

Congenital syphilis — congenital syphilis, prenatal syphilis, Treponema pallidum, vertically transmitted syphilis Other congenital (TORCH) infections such as cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, rubella, and herpes simplex Neonatal sepsis or other bacterial infection Neonatal hepatitis or haemolytic disease causing jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly Non-accidental injury or metabolic bone disease as a cause of bony changes and irritability Blistering or desquamating dermatoses of the newborn Immune or non-immune hydrops fetalis from other causes Maternal treponemal and non-treponemal serological testing with review of treatment history Quantitative non-treponemal titre in the infant compared with the maternal titre Dark-field microscopy or molecular detection of Treponema pallidum from nasal discharge, mucocutaneous lesions, or placenta Cerebrospinal fluid examination for cell count, protein, and treponemal testing to assess neurosyphilis Long-bone radiographs to detect periostitis, osteochondritis, and metaphyseal changes Full blood count, liver function tests, and additional imaging or ophthalmological and audiological assessment as indicated Placental and, where relevant, autopsy histopathology in stillbirth Congenital syphilis follows transplacental (and occasionally perinatal) transmission of Treponema pallidum from an infected mother, and the risk is highest with untreated early maternal syphilis It is almost entirely preventable through antenatal syphilis screening and timely maternal treatment with benzathine penicillin, so every case reflects a missed prevention opportunity Outcomes range from miscarriage, stillbirth, and hydrops to a live-born infant who may be asymptomatic at birth yet still infected Early congenital syphilis (within the first two years) features include snuffles (infectious nasal discharge), a maculopapular or desquamating rash often involving palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, lymphadenopathy, and periostitis or osteochondritis causing painful pseudoparalysis Late stigmata (after two years) include Hutchinson teeth, mulberry molars, interstitial keratitis, sensorineural deafness, a saddle-nose deformity, frontal bossing, and sabre shins Diagnosis integrates maternal treponemal and non-treponemal serology, comparison of infant and maternal non-treponemal titres, direct detection from lesions or body fluids, and assessment for neurosyphilis Treatment of the infant is with penicillin, and management must be coordinated with maternal treatment history and adequacy A confirmed or suspected case mandates public health notification, maternal partner tracing, and evaluation of the mother's own syphilis stage Hydrops fetalis, stillbirth, or a severely unwell neonate Signs of neurosyphilis or abnormal cerebrospinal fluid findings Pseudoparalysis of a limb indicating painful bony involvement Interstitial keratitis or new sensorineural deafness suggesting active or late disease Maternal syphilis untreated or inadequately treated before delivery Assuming an asymptomatic newborn of an infected mother is uninfected without appropriate evaluation Judging maternal treatment adequate without confirming the agent, timing, and titre response (only benzathine penicillin given in good time is reliable) Misinterpreting infant serology, since transplacental maternal antibody can produce a positive result without infection Overlooking neurosyphilis by not examining the cerebrospinal fluid when indicated Failing to notify public health services and trace and treat the mother's partners Congenital syphilis results when the spirochaete Treponema pallidum crosses the placenta from an infected pregnant woman to the fetus, an event that can occur at any gestation but is most efficient during maternal spirochaetaemia in early (primary and secondary) syphilis. Disseminated fetal infection provokes widespread inflammation and endarteritis affecting the liver, bones, skin, mucous membranes, and central nervous system, and the resulting tissue injury underlies presentations from fetal hydrops and stillbirth to the multisystem features of early congenital disease. If the child survives untreated, chronic inflammation and scarring of developing structures such as the teeth, eyes, ears, nose, and long bones produce the classic late stigmata. Maternal treatment before or early in pregnancy prevents fetal infection, which is why antenatal screening is central to control. When the mother is screened and adequately treated in good time, fetal infection is usually prevented and the outlook is excellent; established infection treated promptly in the neonate generally does well, but untreated disease carries substantial mortality and, in survivors, irreversible late stigmata such as deafness and dental and skeletal deformity.

Congenital TTP (Upshaw-Schulman, ADAMTS13) — Upshaw-Schulman syndrome, congenital thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, hereditary TTP, ADAMTS13 deficiency Immune (acquired, autoantibody-mediated) thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura Complement-mediated (atypical) haemolytic uraemic syndrome Shiga toxin-associated haemolytic uraemic syndrome Disseminated intravascular coagulation HELLP syndrome and other pregnancy-related microangiopathies Severe vitamin B12 deficiency causing pseudo-microangiopathy Full blood count and blood film to identify thrombocytopenia and schistocytes Haemolysis markers including lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, bilirubin, and a direct antiglobulin test ADAMTS13 activity assay demonstrating severe deficiency ADAMTS13 inhibitor and antibody testing to exclude the immune form ADAMTS13 gene sequencing to confirm biallelic pathogenic variants Assessment of renal, neurological, and cardiac involvement during acute episodes A hereditary thrombotic microangiopathy from severe congenital deficiency of the von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease ADAMTS13 The classic picture combines microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia, often with neurological, renal, or cardiac involvement Blood film shows fragmented red cells (schistocytes) with a raised lactate dehydrogenase and low haptoglobin, and the direct antiglobulin test is negative May present in the neonatal period with jaundice and thrombocytopenia, or later, with pregnancy and infection acting as common triggers for acute episodes Distinguished from immune TTP by demonstrating severe ADAMTS13 deficiency without a detectable inhibitor, confirmed by biallelic ADAMTS13 variants Unlike immune TTP, plasma exchange to remove an autoantibody is not required; the deficiency is corrected by supplying the missing enzyme Regular plasma infusion provides ADAMTS13 replacement for prophylaxis and treatment of acute episodes Neurological features such as confusion, seizures, or focal deficits Cardiac involvement with chest pain, arrhythmia, or troponin rise Acute kidney injury with worsening microangiopathic haemolysis Neonatal presentation with severe jaundice and profound thrombocytopenia Assuming all TTP is immune and instituting plasma exchange and immunosuppression when replacement suffices Missing the diagnosis in neonatal jaundice attributed solely to haemolytic disease of the newborn Not measuring ADAMTS13 activity before plasma therapy, which can obscure the baseline result Overlooking cardiac involvement, which can be clinically silent yet dangerous ADAMTS13 is the metalloprotease that cleaves ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers released from endothelium into smaller, less adhesive forms. In Upshaw-Schulman syndrome, biallelic loss-of-function ADAMTS13 variants cause severe enzyme deficiency, so ultra-large multimers persist and spontaneously bind platelets under high shear. This drives platelet-rich microthrombi in the small vessels, consuming platelets and mechanically shearing red cells to produce schistocytes. The resulting microvascular occlusion causes ischaemic organ dysfunction, particularly in the brain, kidneys, and heart, and episodes are often precipitated by inflammatory or physiological stress. With regular ADAMTS13 replacement and prompt treatment of acute episodes, long-term outcomes are good and organ damage is largely preventable. Untreated or unrecognised disease carries a substantial risk of recurrent microangiopathic crises and cumulative organ injury.

Congenital vertical talus — vertical talus, congenital convex pes valgus, rocker-bottom foot, CVT Flexible calcaneovalgus foot, which is supple and positional Oblique talus, a milder reducible variant intermediate between normal and vertical talus Flexible flatfoot with a supple, correctable arch Tarsal coalition presenting as a rigid flatfoot in older children Congenital talipes equinovarus at the opposite end of the deformity spectrum Paralytic or neuromuscular flatfoot from cerebral palsy or myelomeningocele Weight-bearing or simulated weight-bearing anteroposterior and lateral foot radiographs Forced plantarflexion lateral radiograph to confirm the irreducible talonavicular dislocation Forced dorsiflexion lateral view to demonstrate fixed hindfoot equinus Assessment for associated neuromuscular disease including a full neurological examination Genetic evaluation and karyotype where a syndrome or chromosomal disorder is suspected Spinal imaging when a neural-tube or cord anomaly is considered A rare rigid flatfoot deformity in which the talus is fixed in a near-vertical position and the navicular is irreversibly dislocated dorsally onto the talar neck The classic appearance is a rocker-bottom foot with a convex plantar surface, a prominent talar head medially in the sole, and the forefoot dorsiflexed and everted The deformity is rigid and cannot be passively corrected, which is the crucial distinction from a flexible calcaneovalgus or positional flatfoot About half of cases are associated with neuromuscular disease, chromosomal abnormalities, or syndromes such as arthrogryposis, so a broader examination is essential Lateral radiographs taken in maximal plantarflexion show the talus remaining vertical and failing to align with the first metatarsal, confirming the fixed dislocation Modern management favours a reverse-Ponseti (Dobbs) serial-casting technique to stretch the dorsolateral soft tissues, usually followed by minimally invasive surgery to reduce the talonavicular joint Untreated, the foot becomes painful and functionally disabling with callosity over the prominent talar head and difficulty with shoe wear A truly rigid rocker-bottom foot that resists all passive correction Features of arthrogryposis, a chromosomal disorder, or another syndrome Signs of an underlying neuromuscular condition or spinal dysraphism Bilateral deformity with a positive family history suggesting a genetic cause Progressive callosity, pain, or skin breakdown over the plantar talar prominence Mislabelling the rigid deformity as a benign flexible flatfoot and delaying treatment Omitting the forced plantarflexion radiograph, which is needed to distinguish vertical from oblique talus Failing to screen for associated neuromuscular disease or genetic syndromes Attempting correction with casting alone and expecting full reduction without surgery Underestimating the likelihood of recurrence and the need for prolonged follow-up Congenital vertical talus is a fixed dorsal dislocation of the navicular on the talus, locking the talus into a vertical, plantarflexed orientation while the calcaneus is held in equinus and valgus. Contracture of the dorsolateral soft tissues, including the tibialis anterior, extensor tendons, and the peroneals, together with a tight Achilles tendon, maintains the deformity, and the head of the talus is forced plantar-medially to create the convex sole. The condition may be an isolated idiopathic malformation but is frequently a manifestation of an underlying neuromuscular imbalance or genetic syndrome, and abnormalities of the HOXD10 gene have been described in some familial idiopathic cases. With early serial casting and appropriately timed surgery a plantigrade, functional foot can usually be achieved, though results are less predictable in syndromic or neuromuscular cases; late or untreated deformity leads to a painful, stiff, poorly shod foot.

Conjunctival melanoma — malignant melanoma of the conjunctiva, conjunctival malignant melanoma Conjunctival naevus Primary acquired melanosis without atypia Complexion-associated (racial) melanosis Ocular surface squamous neoplasia (especially pigmented or amelanotic overlap) Conjunctival pigmented pyogenic granuloma or foreign-body pigmentation Extension of uveal melanoma or ciliary body tumour Conjunctival lymphoma (for salmon-patch amelanotic lesions) Detailed slit-lamp examination mapping pigmentation, nodularity, and feeder vessels Excisional biopsy with a no-touch technique and adjunctive cryotherapy Map (multiple conjunctival) biopsies to delineate primary acquired melanosis extent Histopathology with assessment of thickness, invasion, and margins Regional lymph node examination and imaging, with sentinel node biopsy in selected cases Systemic staging imaging for higher-risk or recurrent tumours A malignant melanocytic tumour of the conjunctiva presenting as a variably pigmented, often nodular and vascularised lesion, though amelanotic forms occur Most cases arise from primary acquired melanosis with atypia; a minority arise from a pre-existing naevus or de novo Primary acquired melanosis appears as flat, patchy, acquired conjunctival pigmentation in middle-aged and older patients and must be assessed for atypia Location beyond the bulbar conjunctiva (palpebral, forniceal, caruncular, or tarsal) and thicker tumours carry a worse prognosis Diagnosis relies on excisional biopsy with a no-touch technique; incomplete or incisional biopsy of the primary tumour is discouraged where excision is feasible Management combines wide local excision with adjunctive cryotherapy to the margins, with topical chemotherapy for diffuse primary acquired melanosis and map biopsies to define extent Regional (preauricular and cervical) nodes are the first site of metastatic spread, so nodal assessment and sometimes sentinel node biopsy are relevant New nodularity, rapid growth, or increasing vascularity within an area of conjunctival pigmentation Extrabulbar involvement of the fornix, palpebral conjunctiva, caruncle, or tarsus Palpable preauricular or cervical lymphadenopathy Recurrence after treatment or extensive diffuse primary acquired melanosis with atypia Dismissing acquired flat conjunctival pigmentation without assessing primary acquired melanosis for atypia Performing incisional biopsy or non-excisional manipulation of a resectable primary tumour Omitting adjunctive cryotherapy and map biopsies, increasing recurrence and missing diffuse disease Overlooking amelanotic melanoma and mistaking it for squamous neoplasia or a benign lesion Conjunctival melanoma is a malignant proliferation of conjunctival melanocytes. The commonest precursor is primary acquired melanosis with atypia, an acquired intraepithelial melanocytic proliferation in which increasing atypia predicts transformation to invasive melanoma; less often the tumour develops from a pre-existing conjunctival naevus or arises de novo. Ultraviolet exposure and characteristic driver mutations contribute to melanocytic transformation. Malignant melanocytes proliferate within and beneath the conjunctival epithelium, and invasive disease can spread through conjunctival lymphatics to regional preauricular and cervical nodes and thereafter haematogenously; extrabulbar sites and greater tumour thickness are associated with higher risks of recurrence and metastasis. Prognosis depends on tumour thickness, location, and completeness of excision; bulbar limbal tumours that are thin and completely excised fare better, whereas extrabulbar, thick, or recurrent tumours carry a substantial risk of local recurrence and regional or distant metastasis with corresponding mortality.

Conjunctivitis — pink eye, red eye, bacterial conjunctivitis, viral conjunctivitis, allergic conjunctivitis Acute anterior uveitis Acute angle-closure glaucoma Bacterial keratitis or corneal ulcer Scleritis and episcleritis Subconjunctival haemorrhage Dry eye and blepharitis Clinical examination assessing discharge type, follicles/papillae, and preauricular nodes Visual acuity and fluorescein staining to exclude corneal involvement Conjunctival swabs for culture in severe, hyperacute, neonatal, or non-resolving cases Testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea in suspected sexually transmitted or neonatal conjunctivitis Slit-lamp examination to exclude keratitis, uveitis, and angle closure Presents with a red, gritty, or irritable eye with discharge, but crucially with normal vision, a clear cornea, normal pupil, and no significant pain — features that distinguish it from serious causes of the red eye Bacterial conjunctivitis produces purulent, sticky discharge with lids stuck together in the morning; it is usually self-limiting Viral (often adenoviral) conjunctivitis gives watery discharge, follicles, a preauricular node, and is highly contagious, frequently following an upper respiratory infection Allergic conjunctivitis is bilateral and itchy with watery discharge, chemosis, and papillae, often with a personal history of atopy Redness is diffuse and superficial, sparing the circumcorneal zone seen in keratitis and uveitis Most cases are managed supportively with hygiene measures; topical antibiotics are used for bacterial cases and antihistamine/mast-cell stabiliser drops for allergic disease Hyperacute, profuse purulent discharge suggests gonococcal infection and is an emergency because it can rapidly perforate the cornea Reduced vision, significant pain, or photophobia — points away from simple conjunctivitis to a sight-threatening cause Circumcorneal injection, a hazy cornea, or an abnormal pupil suggesting keratitis, uveitis, or angle closure Hyperacute profuse purulent discharge (possible gonococcal infection) risking rapid corneal perforation Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum), which requires urgent evaluation for chlamydia and gonococcus Labelling any red eye as conjunctivitis and missing keratitis, uveitis, or angle-closure glaucoma Prescribing topical steroids inappropriately and worsening an undiagnosed herpetic keratitis Overlooking contact lens wear, which raises the risk of sight-threatening keratitis Failing to recognise hyperacute gonococcal or neonatal conjunctivitis as emergencies Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the mucous membrane lining the eyelids and covering the sclera. It arises from infection (bacterial or viral), allergy, or irritation. Inflammatory mediators dilate conjunctival vessels (causing redness) and increase vascular permeability (causing chemosis and discharge), while the cellular response produces follicles in viral and chlamydial disease or papillae in bacterial and allergic disease. Because the process is confined to the conjunctiva and spares the cornea, anterior chamber, and intraocular structures, vision and pupil responses remain normal in uncomplicated cases. Most bacterial, viral, and allergic conjunctivitis is self-limiting or responds readily to treatment with an excellent visual prognosis; serious outcomes occur mainly with gonococcal, chlamydial, or misdiagnosed sight-threatening mimics.

Conjunctivochalasis — redundant bulbar conjunctiva, CCh Aqueous-deficient or evaporative dry eye disease Punctal or nasolacrimal duct obstruction causing epiphora Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis Conjunctival lymphangiectasia or chemosis Pinguecula or pterygium Involutional lower-lid malposition (ectropion, entropion) Allergic conjunctivitis with chemosis Slit-lamp assessment of conjunctival folds in primary gaze, downgaze and on blinking Tear film evaluation with break-up time and ocular surface staining Fluorescein clearance / tear meniscus assessment to demonstrate impaired tear drainage Lissamine green staining of redundant folds Assessment of lid position and punctal patency to distinguish other causes of epiphora Anterior-segment photography to document extent and monitor progression Conjunctivochalasis is redundant, loose bulbar conjunctiva that folds over the lower lid margin, most prominent in the inferior interpalpebral zone, and is a very common age-related change often mistaken for simple dry eye. Symptoms are variable and position-dependent: irritation, foreign-body sensation, unstable tear film and either epiphora (when folds obstruct the inferior punctum and tear meniscus) or paradoxical dryness. The redundant folds disrupt the tear meniscus and are aggravated by blinking and downgaze, so symptoms characteristically worsen on reading and looking down. Diagnosis is clinical at the slit lamp; asking the patient to blink and look down, and gently pressing the lid against the globe, demonstrates the mobile conjunctival folds interposed between globe and lid. First-line management is conservative with ocular lubricants and topical anti-inflammatory measures, and treatment of any coexisting dry eye and lid disease. Surgery (conjunctival resection with primary closure, cautery or amniotic-membrane grafting) is reserved for symptoms refractory to medical therapy. It frequently coexists with, and is confused for, aqueous-deficient or evaporative dry eye; recognising the redundant folds explains symptoms that persist despite adequate lubrication. Mechanical chafing from the folds can cause localised conjunctival injection, subconjunctival haemorrhage and, occasionally, epithelial breakdown. Persistent unilateral redundancy or a mass-like fold that could represent conjunctival neoplasia Progressive epiphora with signs of nasolacrimal obstruction requiring lacrimal evaluation Corneal epithelial breakdown or dellen from chronic mechanical exposure Symptoms disproportionate to findings prompting reassessment of the diagnosis Labelling the patient as pure dry eye and escalating lubricants while missing the mechanical role of the redundant folds Attributing epiphora solely to lacrimal obstruction and performing unnecessary lacrimal surgery Failing to examine in downgaze and on blinking, so the folds are not appreciated Overlooking coexisting lid malposition or dry eye that must be treated concurrently Proceeding to surgery before an adequate trial of medical therapy Age-related degeneration weakens the attachment of the bulbar conjunctiva to the underlying Tenon capsule and sclera, so redundant conjunctiva accumulates and prolapses over the lower lid margin. Elastotic degeneration, increased matrix metalloproteinase activity, chronic mechanical friction between the lid and globe during blinking, and local inflammation with lymphatic dilatation all contribute to loss of elastic tissue and conjunctival laxity. The redundant folds disrupt the tear meniscus and tear distribution, may occlude the inferior punctum causing epiphora, and by delaying tear clearance perpetuate ocular surface inflammation. A benign, chronic degenerative condition; most patients are controlled with lubricants and conservative measures. Surgical correction of symptomatic cases generally gives good and durable symptomatic relief.

isomerase in cholesterol biosynthesis) Because it is X-linked dominant, it is usually seen in females and is typically lethal in most affected males, with survivors often mosaic Features follow a mosaic distribution along the lines of Blaschko, producing patchy skin changes (early ichthyosiform erythroderma, later follicular atrophoderma and patchy alopecia) Skeletal features include often asymmetric or sectorial, are a common and important association The stippled epiphyses tend to disappear after infancy, so early imaging is more informative A key differential is a phenocopy from maternal warfarin exposure in pregnancy, so a medication history is essential Diagnosis is supported by a characteristic sterol profile (raised 8-dehydrocholesterol and 8(9)-cholestenol) and confirmed by EBP testing Dense or progressive cataracts threatening vision in infancy Rapidly progressive scoliosis requiring orthopaedic intervention Severe neonatal skin involvement with barrier compromise An affected male, prompting evaluation for mosaicism and a guarded prognosis Missing a warfarin-exposure phenocopy through inadequate medication history Delaying radiographs so that transient stippled epiphyses are no longer visible Overlooking asymmetric cataracts that need timely ophthalmic treatment Assuming autosomal recessive rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata and mismanaging counselling Conradi-Hunermann syndrome is caused by mutations in EBP, encoding emopamil-binding protein, an enzyme (sterol delta-8, delta-7 isomerase) acting late in cholesterol biosynthesis. Loss of enzyme activity leads to accumulation of abnormal sterol precursors and a relative deficiency of cholesterol in developing tissues, disturbing sterol-dependent developmental signalling and cartilage and skin development. Because the gene is X-linked and the trait behaves as dominant, random X-inactivation in females produces the mosaic, Blaschko-line pattern of skin and skeletal involvement, while non-mosaic affected males usually do not survive. Affected females usually survive with variable orthopaedic, ophthalmological and dermatological problems and generally normal cognition, whereas the non-mosaic male phenotype is typically severe or lethal; long-term care focuses on scoliosis, cataracts and skin.

always be distinguished before puberty starts Missing an underlying chronic illness or nutritional disorder presenting as pubertal delay Interpreting short stature as pathological without accounting for the delayed bone age Overlooking the psychological impact and withholding a reasonable short course of priming therapy Failing to arrange follow-up to confirm that puberty eventually progresses Constitutional delay of growth and puberty represents a benign, self-limited lag in maturation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, so the reawakening of pulsatile GnRH secretion and the pubertal growth spurt occur later than average but ultimately proceed normally. Skeletal maturation is correspondingly delayed, meaning bone age lags behind chronological age but remains concordant with the child's height, which preserves growth potential and normal adult stature. The tendency is strongly familial. The principal clinical challenge is that the biochemical picture of low gonadotropins and sex steroids is shared with permanent hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, from which it can be difficult to distinguish before puberty finally begins. Excellent, with spontaneous onset of puberty and a normal growth spurt leading to an adult height within the genetic target range; the main morbidity is psychosocial, arising from the discrepancy with peers during the waiting period.

Constrictive pericarditis — pericardial constriction, chronic constrictive pericarditis, constrictive pericardial disease Restrictive cardiomyopathy including amyloidosis Right heart failure from restrictive cardiomyopathy Targeted workup for underlying cause including tuberculosis and connective tissue disease A rigid, often calcified pericardium prevents normal diastolic filling, producing predominantly right-sided heart failure with preserved or near-preserved systolic function Presents with progressive breathlessness, fatigue, marked peripheral oedema, ascites, and hepatic congestion, sometimes mislabelled as liver disease Examination classically reveals a raised jugular venous pressure with a prominent y descent, Kussmaul's sign, and a pericardial knock Causes include prior cardiac surgery, radiotherapy, tuberculosis and other infections, connective tissue disease, and idiopathic or post-viral pericarditis The hallmark physiology is dissociation of intrathoracic and intracardiac pressures with enhanced ventricular interdependence, giving a septal bounce and respiratory variation in ventricular filling Pericardial calcification on chest radiograph or CT and pericardial thickening on imaging support the diagnosis, though thickness can be normal The key differential is restrictive cardiomyopathy, distinguished by echocardiographic, haemodynamic, and imaging features of interdependence and respiratory variation Definitive treatment for chronic constriction is surgical pericardiectomy, while transient constriction after acute pericarditis may resolve with anti-inflammatory therapy Progressive congestion with refractory ascites, oedema, and cachexia Hepatic dysfunction and renal impairment from chronic venous congestion Haemodynamic decompensation with low cardiac output Failure to distinguish from restrictive cardiomyopathy, risking inappropriate management Misdiagnosing the syndrome as cirrhosis because of ascites and hepatic congestion Failing to distinguish constriction from restrictive cardiomyopathy before considering surgery Assuming normal pericardial thickness excludes constriction Overlooking a transient, reversible constriction that may respond to anti-inflammatory treatment In constrictive pericarditis the pericardium becomes thickened, fibrotic, and often calcified following inflammation, so it forms a rigid shell around the heart. Early diastolic filling is initially unimpeded but halts abruptly when the ventricles reach the limit set by the stiff pericardium, producing rapid early filling followed by a plateau. Because the total cardiac volume is fixed by the rigid sac, the ventricles compete for space, so filling of one comes at the expense of the other, creating exaggerated ventricular interdependence and a septal bounce. The pericardium also isolates the cardiac chambers from the respiratory swings in intrathoracic pressure, driving the characteristic respiratory variation in transvalvular flow and systemic venous congestion. Chronic constriction is progressive without treatment, but pericardiectomy can substantially relieve symptoms in suitable patients; outcomes are worse with radiation-induced or advanced disease and significant myocardial or hepatic involvement.

Contact dermatitis — contact eczema, allergic contact dermatitis, irritant contact dermatitis Atopic dermatitis Seborrhoeic dermatitis Nummular (discoid) eczema Tinea (dermatophyte infection) Psoriasis on the hands or feet Cellulitis when acute unilateral limb involvement mimics infection Patch testing to identify causative allergens in suspected allergic contact dermatitis Detailed occupational, cosmetic, and hobby exposure history Skin swabs if secondary bacterial infection is suspected Skin scrapings or mycology to exclude dermatophyte infection Skin biopsy in atypical or diagnostically uncertain cases Distinguish irritant contact dermatitis (direct chemical or physical damage, no prior sensitisation, often stinging or burning) from allergic contact dermatitis (a delayed hypersensitivity reaction that is typically itchy) The distribution of the rash is the key clue to the culprit; sharply demarcated eruptions localised to sites of contact point to an external cause Common irritants include water, soaps, detergents, and solvents, while frequent allergens include nickel, fragrances, preservatives, rubber accelerators, and topical medicaments Acute lesions are erythematous, oedematous, and vesicular; chronic exposure produces dryness, scaling, fissuring, and lichenification Patch testing is the definitive method to identify a contact allergen, whereas irritant dermatitis is largely a clinical diagnosis Cornerstone management is identification and avoidance of the offending agent alongside barrier restoration with emollients and, for flares, topical corticosteroids Occupational exposure is a common driver (e.g. hairdressers, healthcare and construction workers), so take a detailed work and hobby history Widespread or erythrodermic involvement with systemic upset Rapidly spreading eruption with fever suggesting secondary infection or an alternative diagnosis Airborne or facial involvement with eyelid swelling affecting vision Occupational disease threatening ability to work and requiring formal assessment Failing to perform patch testing and thus missing a treatable allergen Overlooking a relevant occupational or cosmetic exposure in the history Assuming persistent hand eczema is purely irritant when a superimposed allergy exists Applying a topical product that itself contains a sensitising allergen and perpetuates the dermatitis Contact dermatitis has two principal mechanisms. Irritant contact dermatitis results from direct, non-immunological damage to the epidermal barrier by chemical or physical agents, triggering innate inflammation; severity relates to the concentration and duration of exposure. Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV, T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity reaction: after an initial sensitisation phase in which small-molecule haptens bind skin proteins and prime allergen-specific T cells, re-exposure elicits an inflammatory eczematous response over one to several days. Repeated insult impairs the barrier further, perpetuating inflammation and, over time, chronic lichenified changes. Prognosis is excellent when the causative agent is identified and avoided; persistent exposure, especially occupational, leads to chronic relapsing dermatitis and may necessitate a change of work.
