angioedema, wheeze or anaphylaxis requiring emergency treatment Widespread reaction beyond the site of contact History of previous severe systemic reaction on re-exposure Respiratory symptoms accompanying skin reactions Confusing immediate contact urticaria with delayed allergic contact dermatitis and choosing the wrong test Performing provocation testing without resuscitation facilities in a potentially anaphylactic patient Failing to recognise latex as a cause and continuing latex glove use Overlooking associated respiratory allergy Not providing an emergency plan for those at risk of systemic reactions In the immunological form, prior sensitisation leads to allergen-specific IgE on mast cells; re-exposure cross-links IgE and triggers rapid mast cell degranulation with histamine release, producing the immediate wheal and flare and, if extensive, systemic effects. In the non-immunological form, substances act directly to release vasoactive mediators without prior sensitisation, generally causing localised reactions. Symptoms usually resolve once the causative contact is avoided, and the outlook is good with effective avoidance; however, sensitised individuals remain at risk of severe reactions on re-exposure, and latex allergy in particular can have systemic consequences.

Contrast-induced nephropathy — CIN, contrast-associated acute kidney injury, CA-AKI, contrast nephropathy Ischaemic acute tubular necrosis from hypotension or the underlying illness Atheroembolic (cholesterol embolisation) renal disease after arterial procedures Prerenal azotaemia from volume depletion Other nephrotoxic drug injury Obstructive uropathy Progression of underlying chronic kidney disease Baseline and serial serum creatinine with estimated GFR before and after contrast exposure Urinalysis and urine microscopy to help distinguish tubular injury from other causes Assessment of volume status and review of the medication list for other nephrotoxins Consideration of atheroembolic disease (eosinophilia, skin changes) after arterial catheterisation Renal ultrasound if obstruction or another structural cause is suspected Contrast-induced nephropathy is an acute, usually reversible decline in renal function occurring within a few days of intravascular iodinated contrast, once other causes have been excluded The rise in creatinine typically begins within one to three days and peaks around three to five days, with recovery over one to two weeks in most cases Pre-existing chronic kidney disease is the strongest risk factor, and the risk rises steeply when diabetic nephropathy is also present Volume depletion, heart failure, higher contrast volumes, and concurrent nephrotoxins compound the risk The most effective preventive measure is adequate intravenous volume expansion with isotonic fluid before and after contrast exposure Non-essential nephrotoxic drugs should be withheld around the time of the study and the smallest necessary volume of contrast used The true incidence of contrast-related injury after intravenous contrast in modern practice is lower than once believed, and the need for imaging should be weighed against a frequently modest risk Progressive or non-recovering renal function suggesting an alternative or additional cause Oliguria or features of established acute kidney injury requiring supportive care Signs of atheroembolism such as livedo, digital ischaemia, and eosinophilia after arterial procedures Hyperkalaemia, acidosis, or fluid overload indicating a need for closer monitoring or dialysis Withholding a clinically necessary contrast study out of exaggerated fear of nephropathy in a low-risk patient Failing to provide adequate periprocedural volume expansion in high-risk patients Attributing all post-contrast creatinine rises to contrast without considering atheroembolism or ischaemic injury Overlooking continued exposure to other nephrotoxic drugs during the vulnerable period Contrast-induced nephropathy is thought to arise from a combination of renal medullary ischaemia and direct tubular toxicity. Iodinated contrast alters intrarenal haemodynamics, causing vasoconstriction and reduced medullary blood flow, which is particularly damaging to the metabolically active outer medulla. Contrast media also generate reactive oxygen species and exert direct toxic effects on tubular epithelial cells, and their osmotic and viscosity properties can impair tubular flow. The result is a predominantly acute tubular injury pattern. Patients with reduced baseline renal reserve, impaired autoregulation, or reduced effective circulating volume are least able to compensate for these insults, which explains the clustering of risk in chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and volume depletion. Most episodes are mild and self-limiting, with renal function returning toward baseline within one to two weeks. However, an episode is associated with longer hospital stay, higher risk of needing dialysis in susceptible patients, and worse long-term cardiovascular and renal outcomes, so prevention in high-risk individuals remains important.

Conus medullaris syndrome — conus syndrome, conus medullaris injury, terminal cord syndrome Cauda equina syndrome Conus tumour such as ependymoma or metastasis Transverse myelitis affecting the lower cord Spinal arteriovenous malformation or fistula Tethered cord syndrome Lumbosacral plexopathy Urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine with contrast to identify a compressive or intrinsic lesion Bladder contraction Cerebrospinal fluid analysis where an inflammatory or neoplastic process is suspected Oncological work-up and tumour markers when a mass lesion is identified The conus medullaris is the tapered caudal end of the cord, lying at about the first lumbar vertebral level in adults, and contains the sacral segments that govern bladder, bowel and sexual reflex arcs A lesion here causes early and severe sphincter disturbance, with urinary retention and overflow incontinence, faecal incontinence and erectile dysfunction, often out of proportion to limb weakness Sensory loss is typically symmetrical and confined to the saddle region, and pain tends to be less prominent than in cauda equina syndrome Because it is the junction of cord and roots, the syndrome can combine upper and lower motor neurone signs, so ankle reflexes may be lost while other reflexes are variably preserved The distinction from cauda equina syndrome matters, as the latter is more asymmetrical, more painful and radicular, with purely lower motor neurone features and later bladder involvement Epiconus lesions just above the conus cause more pronounced lower limb weakness with relatively preserved sphincter function Common causes include central disc prolapse, intramedullary and extramedullary tumours, trauma and cord ischaemia Acute retention with saddle anaesthesia is a neurosurgical emergency requiring urgent imaging and decompression Acute urinary retention with saddle anaesthesia, which constitutes a surgical emergency Rapidly progressive lower limb or sphincter deficit Loss of anal tone or absent bulbocavernosus reflex Bilateral leg symptoms with a sensory level suggesting cord involvement Confusing the syndrome with cauda equina compression and delaying urgent imaging Performing an incomplete examination that omits saddle sensation and anal tone Attributing urinary retention to a primary urological cause and missing the neurological lesion Interpreting overflow incontinence as preserved or normal voiding Failing to appreciate the mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs and thus mislocating the lesion The conus medullaris houses the second to fifth sacral cord segments, which contain the parasympathetic and somatic centres controlling micturition, defaecation and sexual reflexes, together with the sacral dermatomal representation of the saddle area. A lesion of the conus damages these segmental reflex centres directly, producing early autonomic failure and symmetrical saddle sensory loss. Because the conus is also the site where the lower lumbar and sacral nerve roots begin to exit, a lesion here can additionally injure these roots, generating a mixture of upper motor neurone signs from cord damage and lower motor neurone signs from root involvement; the anatomical compactness of the sacral segments explains why relatively small lesions cause disproportionately severe sphincter and saddle deficits. Bladder, bowel and sexual function often recover incompletely once deficits are established, and sphincter recovery tends to lag behind motor recovery. Early recognition and prompt decompression of a compressive cause offer the best chance of preserving function.

relieve symptoms when exercises alone are insufficient New or atypical convergence insufficiency in an adult should prompt exclusion of a neurological cause Sudden-onset convergence problems with other neurological signs suggesting dorsal midbrain syndrome Associated pupillary or eyelid abnormalities, or a gaze palsy Convergence failure following significant head trauma with persistent symptoms Progressive or fatigable diplopia suggesting a neuromuscular disorder Attributing reading difficulty to a learning or attentional problem without checking the near point of convergence Overlooking uncorrected refractive error or accommodative dysfunction Missing a neurological cause of acquired convergence failure in adults Prescribing reading glasses that relieve accommodation but worsen the exophoria Convergence insufficiency is a disorder of the near-response fusional vergence system in which the eyes cannot sustain the inward turning needed for comfortable single binocular vision at near. Fusional convergence reserves are inadequate to control an exophoric tendency that is greatest at near fixation, so maintaining alignment during reading demands excessive effort, producing asthenopic symptoms and intermittent diplopia. It is usually idiopathic, but reduced convergence can also follow head injury or accompany neurological disorders that affect the midbrain vergence centres. Convergence insufficiency generally responds well to vision therapy, with many patients achieving durable relief of symptoms; recurrence can occur and may require refresher exercises, while cases secondary to neurological disease follow the course of the underlying condition.

COPD exacerbation (non-infective) — ABG CXR to exclude pneumonia/pneumothorax Distinguish infective trigger — may need antibiotics Pneumonia (a common abnormal finding on chest imaging during a presumed exacerbation) (p.2258) Congestive heart failure / decompensated heart failure (a frequent imaging finding and recognized comorbidity that can mimic or coexist with exacerbation) (p.2258) Pneumothorax (asymmetric chest findings or large-airway obstruction can mimic an exacerbation) (p.2258) Pulmonary embolism, whose incidence is increased in the setting of COPD exacerbation and should be actively considered (p.2258, p.2259) Pneumonia identified on chest x-ray or CT in a patient presenting as an exacerbation (~25% of x-rays in moderate/severe distress are abnormal, most often pneumonia) (p.2258) Arterial blood gas in patients with advanced COPD, a history of hypercarbia, mental status change (confusion, sleepiness), or significant distress; hypercarbia is defined as Pco2 >45 mmHg and carries treatment implications (p.2258) Use of arterial pH alongside Pco2 to classify ventilatory failure (Pco2 >45 mmHg) as acute (acidemic) versus chronic, since pH changes ~0.08/10 mmHg acutely versus ~0.03/10 mmHg chronically (p.2255) Chest x-ray or chest CT in patients with severe underlying COPD, moderate-to-severe distress, or focal findings, to detect pneumonia, heart failure, or pneumothorax (p.2258) Consideration of investigation for pulmonary embolism given its increased incidence in exacerbations (p.2259) Complete blood count with differential for blood eosinophil count to guide exacerbation-risk management (p.2255) An expert-consensus objective scheme using dyspnea, vital signs, C-reactive protein, and arterial blood gases to diagnose and stage exacerbation severity (more applicable in the emergency department than outpatient setting) (p.2259) Congestive heart failure (frequent abnormal imaging finding mimicking exacerbation) (p.2258) Pneumothorax (may produce chest asymmetry mimicking an exacerbation) (p.2258) Pulmonary embolism (increased incidence during COPD exacerbations) (p.2259) An exacerbation is an episodic acute worsening of respiratory symptoms (increased dyspnea, cough, and/or change in sputum amount or character), typically evolving over less than 14 days; it may or may not be accompanied by fever, myalgias, or sore throat (p.2258). COPD exacerbation is fundamentally a clinical diagnosis; spirometry/pulmonary function testing has not been shown to help diagnose or manage an exacerbation, in contrast to its role in asthma (p.2259). The single strongest predictor of future exacerbations is a prior exacerbation, and the greatest single risk factor for hospitalization is a previous hospitalization for exacerbation (p.2258). Exacerbation frequency rises as airflow obstruction worsens; patients with severe obstruction (FEV1 <50% predicted) average about 1-3 episodes per year, though some severely obstructed patients exacerbate infrequently (p.2258). Assess both the severity of the current exacerbation and the severity of the underlying COPD, because the more severe either component, the greater the likelihood of needing hospital admission (p.2258). Examination should focus on degree of distress, tachycardia, tachypnea, accessory muscle use, cyanosis, ability to speak in full sentences, mental status, and paradoxical abdominal wall motion (p.2258). Blood eosinophil count (from CBC differential) is used to stratify exacerbation risk and to guide whether inhaled corticosteroids are added; counts below 100 cells/microliter derive no benefit while benefit rises above 100 and is favored above 300 (p.2255, p.2256). Non-infective precipitants are well recognized: air pollution (including extreme-heat days), allergens, pulmonary embolism, and medication nonadherence; in a notable minority no precipitant is identified (p.2253, p.2258). Environmental exposure and Aspergillus sensitization can drive some COPD exacerbations, relevant to the eosinophilic/allergic exacerbation phenotype (p.1756). Cor pulmonale (overt right heart failure) is now relatively uncommon since supplemental oxygen became standard, but pulmonary hypertension should be considered in patients with persistent activity limitation or lower-extremity edema; it typically arises with FEV1 <25% predicted and chronic hypoxemia (Pao2 <55 mmHg), though some develop it from vascular destruction independent of obstruction severity (p.2252, p.2254). Respiratory acidosis with hypercarbia (Paco2 >45 mmHg and pH <=7.35) indicating acute respiratory failure and a need for ventilatory support (p.2255, p.2259) New or worsening hypoxemia (p.2259) Mental status change (confusion, sleepiness), inability to speak in complete sentences, or impaired cooperation (p.2258, p.2259) Paradoxical abdominal wall motion, marked accessory muscle use, and central cyanosis signaling impending respiratory failure (p.2258) Significant comorbidity such as heart failure, or an unsafe living situation, favoring inpatient management (p.2259) New digital clubbing is NOT a feature of COPD itself and should prompt a search for another cause such as lung cancer (p.2254) Withholding needed supplemental oxygen for fear of CO2 retention: oxygen targeted to SpO2 88-92% is appropriate, and although it may modestly raise arterial Pco2 in some hypercarbic patients by altering ventilation-perfusion relationships, this should not deter correction of hypoxemia (p.2259). Relying on spirometry to diagnose or manage an acute exacerbation, which is not supported by evidence (unlike in asthma) (p.2259). Overlooking pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pneumonia, or heart failure, since each can mimic or accompany an exacerbation (p.2258, p.2259). Attributing all exacerbations to bacterial infection: PCR-based studies show viral respiratory infections may cause more than 50% of exacerbations, and in a notable minority no specific precipitant is identifiable (p.2258). A range of stimuli converge on a final common pathway of airway inflammation and worsening respiratory symptoms. The underlying COPD substrate is fixed airflow obstruction (chronically reduced, non-normalizing FEV1/FVC) compounded by hyperinflation and air trapping; a flattened diaphragm becomes mechanically disadvantaged, raising the work of breathing during any acute decompensation. Gas exchange is impaired chiefly by ventilation-perfusion mismatching (shunt is minimal), which explains why modest supplemental oxygen usually corrects COPD hypoxemia. Hypoxemia tends not to appear until FEV1 falls below ~50% predicted, and CO2 retention is not expected until FEV1 is below ~25% predicted. Acutely, worsening obstruction and dynamic hyperinflation can precipitate alveolar hypoventilation with rising arterial CO2 and respiratory acidosis (p.2251-2252, p.2255, p.2258). Mechanical ventilatory support for a COPD exacerbation carries a hospital mortality of roughly 17-49%. After a hospitalization for COPD, about 20% of patients are rehospitalized within 30 days and 45% within a year, with mortality around 20% in the year following discharge. Exacerbations are also associated with greater longitudinal loss of lung function (notably in those with better baseline function) and account for the majority of COPD-related health-care expenditure (p.2253, p.2259). Underlying COPD severity is graded by post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7 plus FEV1 % predicted: GOLD 1 (mild) >=80%, GOLD 2 (moderate) 50-79%, GOLD 3 (severe) 30-49%, GOLD 4 (very severe) <30%. The GOLD ABE assessment further classifies patients using symptom burden (mMRC dyspnea scale or CAT score) and annual exacerbation history: groups A and B for those with 0-1 moderate exacerbations not leading to hospitalization (A = mMRC 0-1/CAT <10, B = mMRC >=2/CAT >=10), and group E for those with >=2 moderate exacerbations or >=1 leading to hospitalization. The ATS/ERS alternative grades obstruction by FEV1 z-scores rather than percent predicted. For an acute exacerbation, severity itself is a clinical determination; an expert-consensus scheme stages it using dyspnea, vital signs, CRP, and arterial blood gases (p.2255, p.2256, p.2259).

Copper deficiency — hypocupraemia, acquired copper deficiency myeloneuropathy Vitamin B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration) Myelodysplastic syndrome (for the marrow findings) Vitamin E deficiency Other causes of sensory ataxic myelopathy HIV or other myelopathy Serum copper and caeruloplasmin Serum zinc (to detect zinc excess as the cause) Full blood count and, where relevant, bone marrow examination Vitamin B12 to exclude the main mimic History of gastrointestinal surgery, supplements and denture-cream use Causes a myeloneuropathy that closely mimics vitamin B12 subacute combined degeneration Haematological features include anaemia and neutropenia, sometimes with ring sideroblasts mimicking myelodysplasia Common causes are prior upper gastrointestinal surgery, malabsorption and, importantly, excess zinc intake Zinc excess (from supplements or denture creams) induces intestinal metallothionein that blocks copper absorption A sensory ataxia with dorsal column signs and spastic gait is typical Copper repletion and removing the cause (for example stopping excess zinc) halt progression Progressive myelopathy with gait disturbance Marrow findings mistaken for myelodysplasia Ongoing high zinc exposure Severe cytopenias Overlooking zinc excess as the cause Misdiagnosing the marrow appearance as myelodysplastic syndrome Attributing the myeloneuropathy solely to vitamin B12 deficiency Not checking copper in unexplained myelopathy after gastric surgery Copper is a cofactor for enzymes essential to haematopoiesis and to the integrity of the nervous system. Deficiency, from malabsorption, prior gastric or bariatric surgery, or zinc-induced blockade of copper absorption, impairs these enzymes, producing a myeloneuropathy affecting the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts and a marrow disturbance causing anaemia and neutropenia. Excess zinc upregulates enterocyte metallothionein, which binds copper and prevents its absorption, a frequently overlooked mechanism. The neurological picture closely resembles vitamin B12 deficiency. Haematological abnormalities usually recover well with copper repletion, but neurological deficits may only stabilise rather than fully reverse if treatment is delayed.

distension Signs of right heart failure include raised jugular venous pressure, a left parasternal heave, a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, hepatomegaly, and peripheral oedema Echocardiography helps assess right ventricular size and function and estimate pulmonary artery pressure, while right heart catheterisation confirms pulmonary hypertension Treatment is directed primarily at the underlying lung disease and at correcting hypoxaemia, since chronic hypoxia drives pulmonary vasoconstriction Long-term oxygen therapy in chronically hypoxaemic patients can reduce pulmonary vascular resistance and improve survival Diuretics can relieve congestion but require caution to avoid reducing preload excessively or worsening metabolic alkalosis Rapidly worsening right heart failure with hypotension or syncope Severe hypoxaemia or hypercapnic respiratory failure Signs suggesting acute or chronic pulmonary embolism as a cause Refractory fluid overload despite therapy Attributing right heart failure to lung disease without excluding left heart disease or thromboembolism Failing to correct hypoxaemia, a key reversible driver of pulmonary hypertension Over-diuresis reducing right ventricular preload and cardiac output Overlooking treatable causes such as chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension Chronic lung disease or pulmonary vascular disease raises pulmonary vascular resistance through several mechanisms: alveolar hypoxia causes pulmonary arteriolar vasoconstriction, destruction or remodelling of the pulmonary vascular bed reduces its cross-sectional area, and acidosis and polycythaemia further increase resistance. The right ventricle, facing sustained pressure overload, initially hypertrophies to maintain output but ultimately dilates and fails. Rising right-sided filling pressures produce systemic venous congestion, hepatic congestion, and peripheral oedema. Prognosis is largely determined by the severity and reversibility of the underlying pulmonary disorder; the onset of overt right heart failure generally marks advanced disease and portends a poorer outlook, though correcting hypoxaemia and optimising the underlying condition can improve symptoms and survival.

raised pulmonary pressures Features pointing to chronic thromboembolic disease that may be surgically treatable Attributing right heart failure to lung disease without excluding left heart disease or chronic thromboembolism Over-diuresis that lowers right ventricular preload and reduces cardiac output Using pulmonary vasodilators intended for pulmonary arterial hypertension in cor pulmonale from lung disease, worsening gas exchange Failing to identify and treat correctable hypoxaemia and sleep-disordered breathing Chronic cor pulmonale develops when a respiratory disorder raises pulmonary vascular resistance and pressure. Alveolar hypoxia causes pulmonary arteriolar vasoconstriction and, over time, vascular remodelling; loss or destruction of the pulmonary vascular bed in emphysema or fibrosis and obliteration by chronic thromboembolism add a fixed component. The right ventricle responds to this sustained afterload with hypertrophy and then dilatation, and as it fails, right atrial pressure rises and systemic venous congestion produces the characteristic oedema, hepatic congestion, and ascites. Correcting hypoxaemia can relieve the reversible vasoconstrictive element of the pulmonary hypertension. The outlook is largely governed by the underlying lung disease; the onset of overt right heart failure signals advanced disease and a poorer prognosis, though long-term oxygen therapy improves survival in chronically hypoxaemic patients.

Cor triatriatum — cor triatriatum sinister, divided left atrium, triatrial heart, subdivided left atrium Congenital mitral stenosis Supravalvar mitral ring Total or partial anomalous pulmonary venous return Pulmonary vein stenosis Left atrial myxoma or other mass Restrictive cardiomyopathy Transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiography to visualise the dividing membrane and measure the orifice gradient Doppler assessment of flow across the membrane and estimation of pulmonary artery pressure Cardiac CT or MR angiography to define pulmonary venous connections and chamber anatomy Chest radiograph to assess pulmonary venous congestion and cardiac silhouette Cardiac catheterisation when pulmonary vascular resistance or coexisting lesions need clarification Electrocardiogram to detect right ventricular hypertrophy or atrial arrhythmia A fibromuscular membrane divides the left atrium into a proximal chamber receiving the pulmonary veins and a distal chamber containing the appendage and mitral valve Haemodynamics mimic mitral stenosis, with pulmonary venous congestion, pulmonary hypertension and, in severe cases, low cardiac output Severity depends on the size of the communicating orifice in the membrane; a small orifice presents in infancy while a large one may be silent until adulthood Presentation ranges from breathlessness, recurrent chest infections and failure to thrive in infants to exertional dyspnoea or atrial arrhythmia in older patients The dividing membrane sits above the level of the atrial appendage and fossa ovalis, distinguishing it from a supravalvar mitral ring Associated lesions include atrial septal defect and anomalous pulmonary venous connection, which may modify the clinical picture Definitive treatment is surgical resection of the obstructing membrane, which usually gives excellent relief when performed before fixed pulmonary vascular changes develop Severe pulmonary venous congestion or pulmonary oedema in a distressed infant Signs of low cardiac output or shock from critical membrane obstruction Rapidly progressive pulmonary hypertension New atrial arrhythmia with haemodynamic compromise Mistaking the obstructing membrane for congenital mitral stenosis or a supravalvar ring, which changes surgical planning Overlooking a small membrane orifice because a coexisting atrial septal defect masks the pressure gradient Attributing an infant's respiratory distress to recurrent infection rather than pulmonary venous obstruction Failing to search for associated anomalous pulmonary venous connections Cor triatriatum sinister arises when a fibromuscular membrane partitions the left atrium into a posterosuperior chamber that receives the pulmonary veins and an anteroinferior chamber bearing the left atrial appendage and mitral valve. The embryological basis is incomplete incorporation of the common pulmonary vein into the left atrium. Blood must cross a restrictive orifice within the membrane, producing an obstruction functionally equivalent to mitral stenosis. The upstream chamber and pulmonary veins become congested, pulmonary venous and then pulmonary arterial pressures rise, and right heart pressure loading follows. The degree of obstruction, and hence age at presentation, is governed by the diameter of the communicating orifice and any associated atrial septal communication that may decompress the proximal chamber. Surgical resection of the membrane is generally curative with low operative mortality and an excellent long-term outlook when performed before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease. Untreated severe obstruction in infancy carries high mortality.

Spinal cord compression — Urgent whole-spine MRI Neurosurgical / oncology review Time-critical for neurological recovery; high-dose steroids if malignant Intradural extramedullary tumours (meningioma, neurofibroma/schwannoma) - usually slow-growing and benign; long symptom duration favours an intradural origin (p.3606) Intramedullary lesions (ependymoma, haemangioblastoma, low-grade astrocytoma, rarely metastasis) - present with poorly localised burning pain and SACRAL SPARING rather than radicular pain (p.3604, 3606) Cervical spondylotic / degenerative cervical myelopathy - osteophytes, ossified posterior longitudinal ligament/ligamentum flavum, disk degeneration; insidious, stepwise; early signs are subtle (paraesthesia, loss of hand dexterity, 'clumsiness') (p.173) Acute spondylytic myelopathy from hyperextension injury on a pre-existing stenotic canal, sometimes producing a central cord syndrome (p.3606) Conus medullaris syndrome - saddle anaesthesia (S3-S5), early prominent bladder/bowel dysfunction with lax anal tone, preserved leg strength (p.3604) Spinal epidural abscess - midline spinal/neck pain, fever and progressive limb weakness; mostly Staphylococcus aureus (consider MRSA), with gram-negative bacilli, streptococci, anaerobes and fungi less commonly; risk factors include diabetes, IV drug use, alcoholism, renal failure, malignancy, HIV and recent spinal surgery/anaesthesia/trauma (pp.3606-3607) Vertebral osteomyelitis / diskitis - neurological deficit in about a third of cases, mostly mediated by epidural abscess; fever may be absent, especially in cervical disease (pp.131, 1105) Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott's disease) with epidural extension - an important cause in the developing world (p.3607) Infectious noncompressive myelitis to consider once compression excluded (VZV, HSV, CMV, HIV, HTLV-1, Borrelia, Listeria, syphilis, Mycoplasma) (p.3603) MRI with gadolinium centred on the suspected level is the initial procedure; imaging the entire spine is important because up to ~40% with compression at one level have asymptomatic epidural metastases elsewhere (and multiple epidural deposits are present in ~25%) (pp.632, 3605) CT myelography reserved for patients who cannot undergo MRI promptly or have non-diagnostic MRI (pp.632, 768) ESR and CRP are valuable for excluding spinal infection (raised in ~98-100% of vertebral osteomyelitis) (p.1105) Blood cultures (positive in over half of epidural abscess cases); image-guided or open biopsy/aspiration when cultures are negative (pp.1105, 3607) If cord compression suspected but only radicular symptoms without myelopathy, imaging may safely be deferred 24-48 h - but suspected myelopathic compression is imaged immediately (p.3605) In compression from an unknown primary, a simple workup (chest imaging, mammography, PSA, abdominal CT) often reveals the malignancy (p.632) Osteoporotic vertebral collapse (p.631) Spinal epidural haematoma - acute focal/radicular pain then cord or conus signs; predisposed by anticoagulation, trauma, tumour or blood dyscrasias, occasionally post-LP or epidural anaesthesia (p.3607) Hematomyelia - acute painful transverse myelopathy from intramedullary haemorrhage (trauma, vascular malformation, vasculitis, coagulopathy) (p.3607) Spinal cord infarction / anterior spinal artery syndrome - sudden myelopathy without antecedent pain, with preserved vibration/position sense (pp.3604-3605) Radiation myelopathy, neoplastic leptomeningitis and spinal lipomatosis (p.631) Subacute combined degeneration (vitamin B12 deficiency), copper deficiency (p.3602) Inflammatory/demyelinating myelopathy - multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica, sarcoidosis (p.3602) A horizontally demarcated sensory level (identified by moving a pinprick or cold stimulus up the trunk) below which sensory, motor and autonomic function is impaired is the hallmark of a cord lesion; for the spinothalamic tract the true level may sit one to two segments above the clinically detected level (p.3603). The upper border of sensory loss often lies one or two vertebrae BELOW the actual site of compression, so the radiographic target may be higher than the clinical level suggests (p.631). Pain is usually the first symptom of metastatic compression and can precede neurological signs by days to months; it characteristically worsens when supine/recumbent and at night, helping distinguish it from degenerative disk pain which is often relieved by lying down (pp.631, 768, 3605). Lhermitte's sign (an electric tingling shooting down the back and limbs on neck flexion/extension) can be an EARLY clue to cervical cord compression (p.631). Loss of bowel/bladder control is usually a LATE feature; motor and sensory loss typically precede sphincter disturbance (p.631). Useful trunk sensory landmarks for localising a thoracic level are the nipples (T4) and umbilicus (T10) (p.3604). Spinal column infection (osteomyelitis/abscess) characteristically crosses the disk space to involve the adjacent vertebral body, whereas tumour tends to respect the disk space - a distinguishing imaging feature (p.3605). Vertebral collapse is not a reliable marker of malignancy - about 20% of collapses, especially in older and postmenopausal patients, are due to osteoporosis rather than tumour (p.632). Pedicle erosion (the 'winking owl' sign) is the earliest plain-film sign of vertebral tumour, but plain films are insensitive and a normal film does not exclude malignancy (p.632). Established motor deficit (paraplegia/quadriplegia) present >12 h rarely improves, and beyond 48 h the prognosis for meaningful motor recovery is poor - urgency is measured in hours (p.3606) Autonomic dysfunction (decreased anal tone, reduced perineal sensation, distended bladder, absent anal wink or bulbocavernosus reflex) signals cord involvement and is an unfavourable prognostic sign (p.631) Once weakness appears in spinal epidural abscess, progression can be rapid and irreversible (p.3606) Recent-onset persistent thoracic back pain in a cancer patient is suspicious for vertebral metastasis (the thoracic spine is rarely involved by spondylosis) (p.3605) Pain crescendo pattern, pain aggravated by cough/Valsalva/recumbency, and Lhermitte's sign warrant urgent imaging (p.632) Mistaking a myelopathy for polyneuropathy or Guillain-Barre syndrome: ascending paraesthesias suggest neuropathy, but a sharply demarcated sensory level plus bladder disturbance points to a cord origin (pp.213, 3605). Acute severe transverse lesions cause initial FLACCID weakness and areflexia ('spinal shock') that can be misread as anterior horn cell disease or acute polyneuropathy before hyperreflexia supervenes over days to weeks (p.3604). Cauda equina syndrome (low back/radicular pain, saddle/perineal sensory loss, asymmetric leg weakness, sphincter and sexual dysfunction, lost ankle/bulbocavernosus/anal reflexes) reflects nerve-root rather than cord compression and must be distinguished from conus and cord syndromes - mass lesions low in the canal often produce a mixed picture (pp.132, 632, 3604). Gadolinium enhancement can deceptively 'normalise' vertebral metastases by raising their signal to that of normal marrow on MRI (p.3605). Cervical osteomyelitis/epidural abscess may present without fever, delaying recognition - keep it in mind for neck pain with IV drug use, immunosuppression or diabetes (p.131). Because the cord packs nearly the entire motor output and sensory input of the trunk and limbs into a small cross-section, even a small compressive mass causes disproportionately severe, often reversible-if-treated-early, deficits (p.3559). In neoplastic compression, metastases lodge in the vertebral body or pedicle (the axial skeleton is rich in marrow); the enlarging deposit compresses the underlying dura, or a paravertebral mass (lymphoma, myeloma, paediatric tumours) extends through the intervertebral foramen into the canal. Expanding extradural tumour injures axons and myelin mechanically and compromises blood flow, producing ischaemia and infarction (pp.589, 3563). In spinal epidural abscess, as the collection expands it causes additional cord damage through venous congestion and thrombosis, so that once weakness appears deterioration can be rapid and irreversible (p.3606). The thoracic spine is the commonest site of metastatic compression (~70%), followed by lumbosacral (~20%) and cervical (~10%) (p.631). Outcome is strongly time- and function-dependent: treatment is most successful in patients who are still ambulatory and have intact sphincter control when therapy begins, and a good response is expected in those ambulatory at presentation - treatment usually prevents new weakness and up to a third regain some motor function (pp.632, 3606). Motor deficits fixed for more than 12 h seldom improve, and beyond 48 h substantial recovery is unlikely (p.3606). For spinal epidural abscess, prompt diagnosis and treatment allow significant recovery in up to two-thirds, but surgery is unlikely to reverse deficits fixed for more than a few days (p.3607). Recovery from paraparesis is better after surgery than radiotherapy alone, though survival may be short with widespread metastatic disease (p.768). Harrison frames management decisions for malignant compression using the NOMS framework (Memorial Sloan Kettering): Neurologic status (degree of epidural compression, myelopathy, functional radiculopathy), Oncologic status (tumour radiosensitivity), Mechanical stability of the spine, and Systemic factors; high-grade epidural compression from a radioresistant tumour favours separation surgery followed by stereotactic body radiotherapy (pp.589-590). Clinically, prognosis is best stratified by ambulatory and sphincter status at presentation and by duration of any motor deficit (p.3606).

Umbilical Cord Prolapse — cord prolapse, umbilical cord prolapse, prolapsed cord, overt cord prolapse, occult cord prolapse Vasa praevia with fetal vessel rupture Placental abruption causing acute fetal compromise Uterine rupture Cord compression from oligohydramnios (nuchal or true knot) without frank prolapse Maternal supine hypotension causing transient fetal heart rate changes Continuous electronic fetal heart rate monitoring to detect bradycardia or variable decelerations Vaginal examination to confirm a palpable pulsating cord and assess cervical dilatation and presenting part Rapid bedside assessment of fetal viability Ultrasound where time allows to confirm presentation and fetal heart activity Preparation for theatre including maternal bloods and cross-match as part of emergency delivery Cord prolapse is descent of the umbilical cord below the presenting part after membrane rupture (overt) or alongside it with intact membranes (occult), threatening the fetal blood supply It is an acute obstetric emergency because compression of the cord and reflex vasospasm rapidly cause fetal hypoxia and can lead to stillbirth if delivery is delayed Predisposing factors include a high or poorly applied presenting part, malpresentation (breech, transverse, oblique), polyhydramnios, prematurity, multiple pregnancy, and long cord Iatrogenic rupture of membranes when the presenting part is not engaged is a recognised trigger, so artificial rupture should be avoided with an unengaged head The classic sign is an abrupt, severe fetal heart rate deceleration or bradycardia immediately after membrane rupture; a loop of cord may be palpable or visible at the introitus Immediate management aims to relieve cord compression: elevate the presenting part manually or by filling the bladder, position the mother knee-chest or in steep head-down tilt, and minimise handling of an exposed cord to prevent vasospasm Definitive treatment is the fastest safe delivery, usually emergency caesarean section, unless vaginal delivery is imminent and quicker Tocolysis may buy time by reducing contractions while preparations for delivery are made Outcome depends chiefly on the interval from diagnosis to delivery and on the setting, with the best results when it occurs in hospital with rapid theatre access OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY: sudden fetal bradycardia or profound decelerations after membrane rupture demanding immediate delivery Visible or palpable pulsating cord at or beyond the introitus Loss of cord pulsation suggesting critical fetal compromise Malpresentation or unengaged presenting part with ruptured membranes Any delay in achieving delivery once prolapse is confirmed Performing artificial rupture of membranes with a high or unengaged presenting part Excessive handling or attempts to replace an exposed cord, provoking vasospasm Delaying transfer to theatre while arranging investigations Failing to relieve cord compression by positioning or bladder filling while awaiting delivery Not maintaining manual elevation of the presenting part during preparation for caesarean When the umbilical cord slips past the presenting part, it becomes trapped between the fetus and the maternal pelvis or lower uterine segment. Mechanical compression occludes the umbilical vessels, and exposure of the cord to cold air or handling induces vasospasm of the umbilical arteries. Both mechanisms interrupt oxygenated blood flow from the placenta to the fetus, producing acute fetal hypoxaemia, acidosis, and, if unrelieved, hypoxic-ischaemic injury or death. A poorly fitting presenting part leaves space for the cord to descend, which explains the association with malpresentation, prematurity, and polyhydramnios. When cord prolapse is recognised promptly and delivery is expedited, particularly in a hospital setting, perinatal survival is good and long-term neurological outcomes are usually favourable. Prognosis worsens markedly with longer diagnosis-to-delivery intervals, out-of-hospital events, and prematurity, where hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy and perinatal death become more likely.

Cori disease (glycogen storage disease type III) — glycogen storage disease type III, GSD III, Forbes disease, debrancher enzyme deficiency, amylo-1,6-glucosidase deficiency, AGL deficiency, limit in childhood Hepatic causes of hepatomegaly with transaminitis Muscular dystrophies or metabolic myopathies when muscle involvement predominates Blood glucose, ketones, lactate, and uric acid during controlled fasting Liver function tests demonstrating elevated transaminases Creatine kinase and cardiac assessment (echocardiography, ECG) in suspected type IIIa Fasting studies distinguishing ketotic from lactic-acidotic hypoglycaemia Molecular genetic testing of the AGL gene Muscle or liver enzyme assay where diagnostic confirmation is needed Autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme (AGL gene), leading to accumulation of abnormal, short-branched glycogen (limit dextrin) Presents in childhood with fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia and prominent hepatomegaly, often resembling a milder von Gierke disease Type IIIa affects both liver and muscle, whereas type IIIb affects the liver only Because gluconeogenesis is intact, hypoglycaemia is typically ketotic and lactate and uric acid are usually normal, unlike type I Serum transaminases are often markedly elevated, and hepatomegaly frequently improves after puberty In type IIIa a progressive myopathy and cardiomyopathy can emerge in later childhood or adult life Management centres on avoiding fasting with frequent feeds, uncooked cornstarch therapy, and a diet relatively high in protein Symptomatic hypoglycaemia with reduced consciousness or seizures Progressive muscle weakness or exercise intolerance suggesting myopathy Features of cardiomyopathy such as heart failure or arrhythmia in type IIIa Progression to hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis Mistaking Cori disease for von Gierke disease and expecting lactic acidosis and hyperuricaemia Overlooking muscle and cardiac involvement in type IIIa during follow-up Assuming hepatomegaly and transaminitis reflect primary liver disease Neglecting cardiac surveillance in patients with muscle-affecting disease Cori disease results from deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme, which normally works with phosphorylase to fully degrade glycogen at its branch points. Loss of debranching activity halts glycogenolysis once the outer glucose chains are removed, leaving an abnormal glycogen molecule with short outer branches (limit dextrin) that accumulates in liver and, in type IIIa, in skeletal and cardiac muscle. Because gluconeogenesis remains functional, patients can still generate glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors, so fasting hypoglycaemia is generally milder than in type I and is accompanied by ketosis rather than lactic acidosis. Chronic glycogen and metabolic stress produce hepatomegaly and transaminitis, and in muscle-involving disease lead to progressive myopathy and cardiomyopathy. Hepatic and hypoglycaemic manifestations often improve after puberty and overall prognosis is better than type I; however, in type IIIa progressive myopathy and cardiomyopathy can dominate the long-term course and determine outcome.

Corneal abrasion — corneal epithelial defect, scratched cornea Microbial (bacterial) keratitis Herpes simplex dendritic keratitis Recurrent corneal erosion syndrome Retained corneal or subtarsal foreign body Ultraviolet (arc eye) photokeratitis Corneal ulcer Fluorescein staining to delineate the epithelial defect Upper lid eversion to exclude a retained subtarsal foreign body Slit-lamp examination to assess depth and look for infiltrate suggesting infection Contact lens history and, if infiltrate present, corneal scrape for microbiology Presents with sudden severe pain, foreign body sensation, tearing, photophobia, and blepharospasm, usually after minor trauma such as a fingernail, branch, or contact lens Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals the epithelial defect as a bright green area Always evert the upper lid and inspect for a retained subtarsal foreign body, especially with vertical linear (ice-rink) abrasions Topical anaesthetic aids examination but must never be prescribed for ongoing use as it delays healing and masks damage Small uncomplicated abrasions heal within one to two days; treatment is supportive with lubrication and topical antibiotic prophylaxis Contact lens-related abrasions and those from vegetable or organic matter carry higher infection risk and warrant closer follow-up Patching is generally avoided, particularly in contact lens wearers, as it may promote infection A white corneal infiltrate, mucopurulent discharge, or anterior chamber reaction suggesting microbial keratitis Contact lens wearers with pain out of proportion, indicating possible Pseudomonas or Acanthamoeba infection Failure to heal within expected time or worsening pain and redness Suspicion of penetrating injury or high-velocity foreign body Sending patients home with topical anaesthetic, which delays healing and can cause severe corneal damage Failing to evert the lid and missing a retained foreign body Patching a contact lens wearer and precipitating infection Assuming all painful epithelial defects are simple abrasions and missing herpetic or microbial keratitis A corneal abrasion is a defect in the corneal epithelium, most often from mechanical trauma. Loss of the epithelial barrier exposes richly innervated subepithelial nerve endings, producing intense pain and reflex tearing and blepharospasm. The epithelium normally regenerates rapidly by sliding and mitosis of surrounding cells. Contamination, retained foreign material, or contact lens wear can convert a simple abrasion into a microbial keratitis, and repeated or poorly healing defects may reflect an underlying epithelial basement membrane dystrophy causing recurrent erosions. Simple abrasions heal quickly with no lasting visual effect, but infection, deep central lesions, or recurrent erosions can cause scarring and reduced vision.

Corneal dystrophy — corneal dystrophies, hereditary corneal dystrophy, Fuchs endothelial dystrophy Corneal degenerations such as band keratopathy or Salzmann nodular degeneration Keratoconus and other ectatic disorders Pseudophakic or aphakic bullous keratopathy Interstitial keratitis from prior infection Corneal deposits from systemic or drug causes Recurrent erosion from prior corneal trauma Slit-lamp biomicroscopy to define the affected layer and deposit pattern Corneal pachymetry to quantify thickness and oedema in endothelial disease Specular or confocal microscopy to assess endothelial cell density and guttata Corneal topography or tomography to exclude ectasia and plan surgery Family history and, where available, genetic testing to confirm the subtype Corneal dystrophies are inherited, usually bilateral and symmetrical, non-inflammatory disorders that progress slowly and are typically classified by the corneal layer chiefly affected Anterior (epithelial and Bowman) dystrophies such as epithelial basement membrane dystrophy often cause recurrent corneal erosions with episodic pain, tearing, and morning symptoms Stromal dystrophies (lattice, granular, macular) deposit characteristic material and progressively reduce clarity and vision Fuchs endothelial dystrophy causes progressive endothelial cell loss, corneal guttata, and stromal oedema that leads to worse vision on waking that improves through the day Slit-lamp examination and family history are central to diagnosis, and the pattern of deposits helps identify the subtype Specular or confocal microscopy and corneal pachymetry help assess endothelial function and corneal thickness in endothelial disease Management ranges from lubricants and hypertonic agents for symptomatic relief to phototherapeutic keratectomy for anterior disease and lamellar or penetrating keratoplasty for advanced visual loss Some stromal dystrophies can recur in a corneal graft, which is relevant when planning surgery Sudden pain and redness suggesting a ruptured epithelial bulla or secondary microbial keratitis rather than the dystrophy itself Rapid loss of vision that is out of keeping with a slowly progressive dystrophy Corneal decompensation after intraocular surgery in an eye with borderline endothelial function Graft failure or dystrophy recurrence after keratoplasty Mistaking a bilateral inherited dystrophy for a unilateral infective or degenerative process Treating recurrent erosions symptomatically without recognising an underlying epithelial basement membrane dystrophy Proceeding to cataract surgery without assessing endothelial reserve in suspected Fuchs dystrophy Overlooking the risk of dystrophy recurrence when counselling about corneal grafting Corneal dystrophies are genetically determined disorders in which abnormal material accumulates within, or normal cells are progressively lost from, a specific corneal layer. Many stromal dystrophies (lattice, granular, and the related TGFBI group) result from mutations causing deposition of amyloid or hyaline material that scatters light. Macular dystrophy reflects a defect in keratan sulphate metabolism with mucopolysaccharide deposition. In Fuchs endothelial dystrophy the endothelial pump fails as cells are lost and guttata form, so the stroma imbibes fluid and swells, producing oedema and, in advanced cases, epithelial bullae. Anterior dystrophies disrupt epithelial adhesion, predisposing to recurrent erosions. Most dystrophies progress slowly over years; anterior disease is often controlled with conservative measures, while advanced stromal opacity or endothelial decompensation may require keratoplasty, which restores useful vision in many cases although some stromal dystrophies can recur in the graft.

Cornelia de Lange syndrome — CdLS, Brachmann-de Lange syndrome, NIPBL, SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21, HDAC8, cohesinopathy Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder Coffin-Siris syndrome Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome Fryns syndrome Duplication 3q syndrome KBG syndrome Targeted gene-panel or exome sequencing covering NIPBL, SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21 and HDAC8 Testing of tissues such as buccal cells or fibroblasts when mosaicism is suspected despite negative blood results Chromosomal microarray to exclude copy-number mimics Echocardiography to detect congenital heart disease Upper gastrointestinal evaluation and monitoring for reflux and malrotation Hearing and ophthalmology assessment including for ptosis and refractive error A distinctive facial gestalt with synophrys (confluent eyebrows), long philtrum, thin down-turned upper lip, and long curly eyelashes is the diagnostic hallmark Prenatal and postnatal growth restriction with microcephaly is characteristic and often severe Upper-limb reduction defects range from small hands with proximally placed thumbs to severe oligodactyly or phocomelia Generalised hirsutism, a low anterior and posterior hairline, and cutis marmorata are frequently seen Most cases follow autosomal dominant inheritance from de novo NIPBL variants, with X-linked (SMC1A, HDAC8) and other cohesin-related genes accounting for milder phenotypes Gastro-oesophageal reflux is common and easily overlooked, and can drive irritability, feeding refusal and self-injurious behaviour Intellectual disability, autistic features, and expressive language deficits are typical, with severity broadly tracking the causative gene and mutation type Unexplained irritability or feeding refusal suggesting severe gastro-oesophageal reflux or oesophagitis Cyanosis or poor feeding indicating an undiagnosed congenital heart defect Bilious vomiting raising concern for intestinal malrotation with volvulus Recurrent aspiration and respiratory compromise Excluding the diagnosis on a negative blood test when tissue mosaicism can still be present Attributing behavioural disturbance to the syndrome itself and missing treatable reflux or pain Overlooking hearing loss that compounds language delay Failing to screen for occult congenital heart disease and genitourinary anomalies Cornelia de Lange syndrome is a cohesinopathy caused by dysfunction of the cohesin complex or its regulators, which normally hold sister chromatids together and also regulate transcription and chromatin architecture. Loss-of-function or missense variants in NIPBL (the commonest) or in the structural and regulatory subunits SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21 and HDAC8 disturb the expression of developmental gene networks. This dysregulation during embryogenesis produces the multisystem pattern of growth failure, limb reduction, craniofacial malformation and neurodevelopmental impairment. Somatic mosaicism is well recognised and can lead to false-negative blood testing. Prognosis varies widely with genotype and severity; individuals with classic NIPBL-related disease often have significant intellectual disability and medical comorbidity, whereas milder variants permit better cognitive and functional outcomes. Life expectancy is largely determined by cardiac, gastrointestinal and respiratory complications.

Coronary arteriovenous fistula — coronary cameral fistula, coronary artery fistula Patent ductus arteriosus (continuous murmur) Ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm Aortopulmonary window Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation Anomalous origin of a coronary artery Echocardiography with colour Doppler Coronary CT angiography or invasive coronary angiography to define the fistula Assessment for ischaemia where coronary steal is suspected Quantification of shunt where large Cardiac MRI in selected cases An abnormal communication between a coronary artery and a cardiac chamber or great vessel, bypassing the myocardial capillary bed Most are congenital, though some follow cardiac procedures or trauma Many are small and asymptomatic, found incidentally on echocardiography or angiography as a continuous murmur Large fistulae can cause a left-to-right shunt, coronary steal with ischaemia, heart failure or aneurysm formation A continuous murmur, often atypical in location, is a clue Small asymptomatic fistulae are observed; large or symptomatic ones are closed by catheter or surgery Angina or ischaemia from coronary steal Heart failure from a large shunt Coronary aneurysm or thrombosis Endocarditis risk at the fistula site Attributing a continuous murmur solely to a patent ductus Overlooking coronary steal as a cause of ischaemia Closing small asymptomatic fistulae unnecessarily Missing associated coronary aneurysm A coronary arteriovenous fistula is a direct connection that shunts blood from a coronary artery into a low-pressure cardiac chamber or vein, diverting it from the myocardial capillary network. The shunt volume and drainage site determine the effects: diversion of coronary flow can cause a steal phenomenon with distal myocardial ischaemia, while a large left-to-right shunt increases volume load and can cause chamber dilatation and heart failure. Chronic high flow may lead to aneurysmal dilatation of the feeding coronary artery and predisposes to thrombosis. Small fistulae often remain asymptomatic with a benign course, whereas large or symptomatic ones can cause ischaemia or heart failure and generally do well after catheter or surgical closure.

embryological development in which a coronary ostium arises from an inappropriate aortic sinus or from the opposite coronary. The clinical danger of certain variants arises from the anomalous vessel taking an interarterial course between the aorta and the pulmonary trunk. During exertion the aortic root expands and the increased flow demands widen these great vessels, which can compress the interarterial segment; an associated acute-angle take-off, slit-like ostium, or intramural course within the aortic wall further compromises the lumen. The resulting dynamic reduction in coronary flow can precipitate myocardial ischaemia, malignant arrhythmia, and sudden death, characteristically during or just after strenuous activity, which is why exertional symptoms in a young person warrant careful evaluation. Prognosis varies widely with the specific anatomy; many variants are benign and require no intervention, whereas a high-risk interarterial course carries a real risk of sudden cardiac death, particularly during vigorous exertion. Appropriately selected surgical repair can relieve symptoms and reduce risk, and activity guidance is an important part of management.

aneurysmal dilatation of the feeding artery and its thrombotic risk A coronary artery fistula is a direct channel connecting a coronary artery to a cardiac chamber or great vessel, so blood bypasses the intramyocardial capillary network. Because the drainage site is usually a lower-pressure right-sided structure, flow runs continuously throughout the cardiac cycle, producing a continuous murmur and a left-to-right shunt when drainage is into the venous circulation. The chronically high flow dilates and can aneurysmally enlarge the feeding artery. Flow preferentially runs down the low-resistance fistulous track rather than into the higher-resistance distal myocardial bed, a coronary steal that may cause regional ischaemia. Large shunts impose volume loading on the receiving chambers and can lead to heart failure and pulmonary overcirculation over time. Small fistulae often remain benign and may close spontaneously, while large or symptomatic fistulae carry risks of ischaemia, heart failure and aneurysm; outcomes after device or surgical closure are generally favourable.

coronary slow flow phenomenon — coronary slow flow, cardiac syndrome Y, primary slow coronary flow microvascular angina vasospastic angina obstructive coronary artery disease no-reflow following percutaneous coronary intervention takotsubo cardiomyopathy myocarditis non-cardiac chest pain quantitative coronary angiography with corrected TIMI frame count twelve-lead electrocardiogram during symptomatic episodes cardiac troponin measurement during chest pain coronary flow reserve or index of microcirculatory resistance assessment transthoracic echocardiography to exclude structural disease metabolic and lipid profiling for associated risk factors cardiac magnetic resonance to exclude alternative myocardial pathology Defined angiographically as delayed opacification of the distal coronary vasculature in the absence of obstructive epicardial disease, quantified by an elevated corrected TIMI frame count. Presents most often as recurrent rest or exertional chest pain, frequently prompting repeated emergency attendances and angiography with unremarkable epicardial findings. Predominantly affects younger to middle-aged men, and cigarette smoking and metabolic syndrome features are commonly associated. Should be distinguished from the no-reflow phenomenon that follows percutaneous intervention or infarction, which has a different mechanism and context. Resting electrocardiogram and biomarkers are usually normal between episodes, though transient ischaemic changes and occasionally raised troponin can occur during pain. The disorder is generally considered a marker of small-vessel and microvascular dysfunction rather than a benign angiographic curiosity. Calcium-channel blockers, particularly dihydropyridines, and addressing risk factors form the mainstay of symptom management, with nitrates often disappointing. Recurrent chest pain, arrhythmia and, rarely, sudden cardiac death have been reported, so the phenomenon is not uniformly innocuous. chest pain accompanied by a rise in cardiac troponin documented ventricular arrhythmia or syncope haemodynamic compromise during an episode progressive escalation in frequency or severity of symptoms Labelling the angiogram simply normal and reassuring the patient without recognising the slow-flow pattern and its microvascular basis. Confusing primary slow coronary flow with post-procedural no-reflow, which has distinct causes and treatment. Assuming a completely benign course and thereby dismissing recurrent disabling symptoms. Relying on nitrates, which frequently provide little benefit in this microvascular disorder. Coronary slow flow phenomenon reflects delayed passage of contrast through angiographically smooth epicardial arteries, attributed principally to structural and functional abnormality of the coronary microcirculation. Contributing mechanisms include microvascular endothelial dysfunction with impaired vasodilator response, small-vessel medial hypertrophy and myointimal proliferation, heightened microvascular resistance and tone, subclinical diffuse atheroma, and low-grade inflammation and oxidative stress. The net effect is a raised distal resistance and impaired coronary flow reserve producing intermittent myocardial ischaemia despite the absence of a flow-limiting epicardial stenosis. Most patients have a relatively favourable survival outlook but suffer recurrent chest pain with impaired quality of life and repeated healthcare use; occasional reports of arrhythmia and sudden death indicate the condition is not entirely benign.

coronary steal syndrome — coronary steal, coronary-subclavian steal syndrome progressive obstructive coronary artery disease graft stenosis or occlusion vasospastic angina microvascular angina subclavian steal syndrome affecting the vertebrobasilar circulation aortic dissection involving arch vessels peripheral arterial disease of the upper limb bilateral upper-limb blood pressure comparison invasive coronary and subclavian angiography duplex ultrasonography of the subclavian and internal mammary arteries myocardial perfusion imaging with vasodilator stress computed tomographic or magnetic resonance angiography of the arch and grafts coronary physiology assessment with fractional flow reserve twelve-lead electrocardiogram during induced or exertional symptoms Occurs when blood is diverted away from an ischaemic myocardial territory towards an adjacent bed with lower vascular resistance, worsening rather than relieving regional ischaemia. Vasodilator stress agents such as adenosine, regadenoson and dipyridamole can provoke steal by maximally dilating normal vessels while a stenosis limits flow reserve in the dependent territory. Coronary-subclavian steal arises after use of an internal mammary artery graft when a proximal subclavian stenosis reverses flow, drawing blood from the myocardium to the arm. Suspect coronary-subclavian steal in a bypass patient with recurrent angina, an inter-arm blood pressure difference and arm claudication or a diminished ipsilateral pulse. Collateral-dependent myocardium supplied through vessels from a bed with a proximal stenosis is particularly vulnerable to the steal effect. Symptoms typically emerge during exertion or pharmacological vasodilatation, when the resistance gradient between beds is greatest. Management targets the culprit lesion, most often percutaneous revascularisation of a subclavian stenosis in the coronary-subclavian variant. Duplex ultrasound and angiography demonstrating reversed internal mammary or subclavian flow confirm the diagnosis. recurrent angina after internal mammary artery bypass grafting significant inter-arm systolic blood pressure difference ischaemia or haemodynamic deterioration provoked by vasodilator stress testing arm claudication or absent pulse with concurrent chest pain Measuring blood pressure in only one arm and missing the inter-arm gradient that signals subclavian stenosis. Interpreting stress-induced ischaemia as fixed disease progression without considering a steal mechanism. Overlooking a proximal subclavian lesion in a symptomatic internal mammary graft recipient. Assuming symptoms reflect graft failure when flow reversal is the true cause. Coronary steal reflects the redistribution of limited coronary blood flow governed by differences in vascular resistance between adjacent perfusion beds. When a territory is supplied through a fixed proximal stenosis or through collaterals, its distal arterioles are already near-maximally dilated to preserve resting flow, leaving little reserve. Administration of a potent arteriolar vasodilator, or physiological demand, further lowers resistance in the normally perfused neighbouring bed, so flow preferentially follows the path of least resistance and is diverted away from the dependent, resistance-exhausted territory, deepening its ischaemia. In the coronary-subclavian variant a proximal subclavian obstruction reverses flow in an internal mammary artery graft, siphoning coronary blood into the upper limb. Outcome is favourable once the responsible lesion is corrected, with revascularisation of a subclavian stenosis typically abolishing angina in the coronary-subclavian variant; untreated, the diverted myocardial supply predisposes to recurrent ischaemia.

coronary vasospasm — vasospastic angina, Prinzmetal angina, variant angina obstructive atherosclerotic angina acute coronary syndrome due to plaque rupture microvascular angina myocardial bridging takotsubo cardiomyopathy oesophageal spasm or reflux cocaine-induced myocardial ischaemia twelve-lead electrocardiogram captured during an episode ambulatory ST-segment monitoring to detect transient elevation invasive coronary angiography with intracoronary provocation testing cardiac troponin to detect associated myonecrosis coronary CT angiography to characterise coexisting plaque urine toxicology screen for sympathomimetic drugs serum magnesium and thyroid function assessment Characterised by transient, reversible focal or diffuse epicardial coronary spasm causing myocardial ischaemia, classically at rest and often between midnight and early morning rather than on exertion. Transient ST-segment elevation during a spontaneous attack is the electrocardiographic hallmark; ST depression or T-wave changes may occur, and the tracing normalises as symptoms resolve. Preserved or even enhanced exercise tolerance despite rest angina should raise suspicion, as attacks are frequently unrelated to increased myocardial oxygen demand. Provocative spasm testing in the catheter laboratory with acetylcholine or ergonovine is the reference standard when the diagnosis is uncertain and obstructive disease has been excluded. Calcium-channel blockers, often combined with long-acting nitrates, are the cornerstone of prophylaxis; non-selective beta-blockers may worsen spasm by leaving alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed. Smoking is the single most important modifiable trigger; magnesium deficiency, hyperventilation, cold exposure, emotional stress and certain vasoconstrictors including cocaine and sumatriptan can precipitate attacks. Spasm may coexist with non-obstructive or obstructive plaque and can precipitate acute coronary syndrome, malignant arrhythmia or sudden death during a prolonged episode. The condition is more common in East Asian populations and, unlike atherosclerotic angina, may affect relatively younger patients with fewer conventional risk factors apart from smoking. prolonged rest chest pain with persistent ST elevation suggesting evolving infarction syncope or documented ventricular arrhythmia during an attack recurrent nocturnal episodes escalating in frequency or duration haemodynamic instability or cardiac arrest associated with an episode Attributing rest angina with a normal resting electrocardiogram to non-cardiac causes because a coronary angiogram between attacks appears unobstructed. Prescribing a non-selective beta-blocker, which can aggravate spasm through unopposed alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction. Failing to capture the diagnostic transient ST-segment shift because it resolves before a tracing is obtained. Overlooking modifiable precipitants such as smoking, cocaine use or vasoconstrictor medications. Coronary vasospasm results from transient intense contraction of vascular smooth muscle in an epicardial coronary segment, producing dynamic subtotal or total occlusion and abrupt reduction in myocardial blood flow. Endothelial dysfunction with impaired nitric oxide bioavailability, coupled with smooth-muscle hyperreactivity mediated by enhanced Rho-kinase activity and disturbed autonomic and calcium handling, renders the vessel hypersensitive to vasoconstrictor stimuli such as acetylcholine, catecholamines, cold and hyperventilation-induced alkalosis. The resulting supply-side ischaemia is typically distinct from the demand-driven ischaemia of fixed atherosclerotic stenosis, although spasm frequently localises to or near sites of subclinical plaque where endothelial function is most impaired. With smoking cessation and calcium-channel blocker therapy the long-term outlook is generally favourable and most patients become symptom-controlled, though multivessel or refractory spasm carries a higher risk of arrhythmia, infarction and sudden death.

When coronin-1A is deficient, T cells are inefficiently released from the thymus and fail to persist and move normally in the periphery, so naive T-cell numbers fall and T-cell responses are weakened. Because effective control of Epstein-Barr virus depends on cytotoxic T-cell surveillance, this T-cell defect allows the virus to drive B-cell proliferation and predisposes to lymphoproliferative disease and lymphoma. The resulting combined immunodeficiency underlies the susceptibility to recurrent and opportunistic infection. Prognosis depends on severity and on timely recognition; severe infantile disease is life-threatening without haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and the risk of Epstein-Barr-virus-driven lymphoproliferation adds to morbidity, so early transplantation offers the best outcome.

Underestimating the volume of haemoperitoneum, particularly in anticoagulated patients Overlooking coexisting ovarian torsion in a woman with a luteal cyst Proceeding to surgery for a cyst that would have resolved with observation After ovulation the ruptured follicle normally organises into a corpus luteum that regresses if pregnancy does not occur. When involution fails, the corpus luteum persists and accumulates fluid or blood, forming a cyst. Bleeding from the vascular granulosa lining into the cyst cavity distends it and may cause pain; if the wall gives way, blood escapes into the peritoneal cavity. The extent of any resulting haemoperitoneum is greater in women taking anticoagulants or with a bleeding tendency. Corpus luteum cysts are benign and typically resolve spontaneously within one or two menstrual cycles; even after rupture, most women recover well with conservative management, and surgery is only occasionally required.

emphysema or free air on imaging Assuming a normal mouth excludes serious oesophageal or gastric damage Attempting to neutralise the corrosive or induce vomiting, which aggravates injury Giving activated charcoal, which is ineffective and hinders endoscopy Delaying airway management in a patient with evolving laryngeal oedema Corrosive agents produce tissue destruction on contact. Strong alkalis (e.g. lye, drain cleaner) cause liquefactive necrosis, saponifying fats and dissolving proteins, allowing deep penetration and full-thickness oesophageal injury with risk of perforation and mediastinitis. Strong acids cause coagulative necrosis with eschar formation that can limit depth of penetration but tends to pool in and damage the stomach, risking gastric perforation and peritonitis. Injury severity depends on the agent, concentration, volume, and contact time. Healing of deep circumferential burns leads to fibrosis and stricture, and chronic injury raises long-term malignancy risk. Minor mucosal injury usually heals well, but deep circumferential burns commonly progress to strictures needing repeated dilatation or surgery, and full-thickness injury with perforation carries high mortality; survivors have a lifelong increased risk of oesophageal cancer.

four-repeat tauopathy with neuronal and glial tau deposition, including astrocytic plaques, and ballooned achromatic neurons, affecting the cerebral cortex (especially frontoparietal) and the basal cortisol producing adenoma — cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma, adrenal Cushing syndrome (adenoma), autonomous cortisol-secreting adenoma Pituitary ACTH-dependent Cushing disease (corticotroph adenoma) Ectopic ACTH syndrome from a neuroendocrine tumour Adrenocortical carcinoma with cortisol secretion ACTH-independent macronodular adrenal hyperplasia or primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease Non-functioning adrenal incidentaloma Exogenous (iatrogenic) glucocorticoid excess Pseudo-Cushing states such as severe obesity, uncontrolled diabetes, depression or alcohol hypercortisolism Plasma ACTH and DHEA-sulphate to establish ACTH-independence and support a benign adenoma Dedicated adrenal CT with unenhanced attenuation and contrast washout, or chemical-shift MRI, to characterise the mass Biochemical exclusion of co-secreting phaeochromocytoma (plasma or urinary metanephrines) before any surgery Assessment of complications: blood pressure, glucose and HbA1c, lipids and bone mineral density In equivocal or bilateral disease, adrenal venous sampling or additional functional imaging to lateralise the source A benign, ACTH-independent cortical adenoma that (central obesity, moon facies, dorsocervical fat pad, wide violaceous striae, proximal myopathy, thin skin and easy bruising) to mild autonomous cortisol secretion detected incidentally on imaging replacement is mandatory The overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test is the pivotal screen: failure of morning cortisol to suppress, together with low or undetectable ACTH, points to an autonomously functioning adrenal source Loss of circadian rhythm with a raised late-night salivary or midnight serum cortisol, and increased urinary free cortisol, corroborate hypercortisolism; a suppressed DHEA-sulphate is a useful pointer to a benign cortisol-producing adenoma Cross-sectional imaging typically shows a well-defined, lipid-rich unilateral mass with low unenhanced attenuation and rapid contrast washout on CT, features that favour a benign adenoma over carcinoma or phaeochromocytoma Even mild autonomous cortisol secretion is not harmless, being associated with hypertension, dysglycaemia, dyslipidaemia, osteoporosis and increased cardiovascular and mortality risk, so it warrants active assessment rather than simple reassurance Laparoscopic unilateral adrenalectomy is the definitive treatment for a unilateral adenoma, with perioperative and postoperative steroid cover until the suppressed axis recovers Rapid onset or rapidly progressive Cushingoid features, marked virilisation or a large or heterogeneous mass suggesting adrenocortical carcinoma Severe hypokalaemic alkalosis with very high cortisol, raising concern for ectopic ACTH secretion Hypertensive crisis, palpitations or headache suggesting an unrecognised co-existing phaeochromocytoma Postoperative adrenal insufficiency (hypotension, hyponatraemia, collapse) if glucocorticoid cover is inadequate New psychosis, severe infection or venous thromboembolism complicating florid hypercortisolism Attributing an incidentally found adrenal mass to a non-functioning lesion without screening for autonomous cortisol secretion Omitting or under-dosing postoperative glucocorticoid replacement, precipitating an adrenal crisis from the atrophic contralateral gland Failing to exclude phaeochromocytoma with metanephrines before adrenalectomy Misreading a pseudo-Cushing state as true endogenous hypercortisolism, or vice versa, without confirmatory dynamic testing Overlooking features that suggest adrenocortical carcinoma rather than a benign adenoma and delaying appropriate oncological management A cortisol-producing adenoma is a monoclonal benign neoplasm of the adrenal zona fasciculata that synthesises glucocorticoid independently of pituitary ACTH. Constitutive activation of the cyclic AMP / protein kinase A signalling pathway, frequently through somatic activating variants in PRKACA (and in some tumours changes in GNAS, CTNNB1 or components of the PKA pathway), drives steroidogenesis regardless of physiological feedback. The resulting chronic cortisol excess suppresses hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing hormone and pituitary ACTH, so circulating ACTH falls and the non-tumorous adrenal tissue, including the contralateral gland, atrophies. Sustained glucocorticoid excess then produces the multisystem features of Cushing syndrome through catabolic effects on skin, muscle and bone, insulin resistance and gluconeogenesis, mineralocorticoid-like and vascular effects raising blood pressure, and immunosuppressive and neuropsychiatric consequences. Unilateral adrenalectomy is usually curative for a benign cortisol-producing adenoma, with resolution of hypercortisolism and gradual improvement in metabolic, skeletal and cardiovascular consequences, although recovery of the suppressed hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis may take many months and requires interim steroid replacement. Untreated or long-standing cortisol excess, including mild autonomous secretion, carries excess cardiovascular, metabolic, skeletal and mortality risk.

institute tumour surveillance given the high embryonal cancer risk Misclassifying it as Noonan or cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome, altering cancer risk counselling Overlooking atrial tachyarrhythmia
