Capgras or other misidentification phenomena Cotard syndrome is a nihilistic delusional state proposed to arise from a global loss of the emotional resonance normally attached to perceptions of oneself and the world. Where Capgras involves loss of felt familiarity for a specific person, Cotard is conceptualised as an extension of this affective disconnection to the self, so that internal and external experiences feel unreal, leading to the conviction of being dead or non-existent. Dysfunction of frontal, temporoparietal, and limbic networks that integrate self-perception with emotional salience, combined with the depressive substrate that often accompanies it, is implicated. It occurs in severe affective and psychotic illness and in organic brain disease. With treatment of the underlying disorder, including electroconvulsive therapy in severe cases, the delusion often remits, though relapse can occur and outcome depends on the primary illness. Untreated, the syndrome carries a serious risk of death from suicide or self-neglect.

COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2) — SARS-CoV-2, coronavirus disease 2019 Influenza and other viral lower respiratory tract infections (RSV, human metapneumovirus, parainfluenza, rhinovirus) Other coronaviruses: SARS-CoV-1, MERS-CoV, and common-cold coronaviruses HCoV-OC43 and HCoV-HKU1 Community-acquired or health care-associated bacterial pneumonia Any respiratory symptom occurring where SARS-CoV-2 is circulating should be considered a potential manifestation of COVID-19 Influenza Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection Human metapneumovirus and parainfluenza virus infections Rhinovirus / common cold (including HCoV-OC43, HCoV-HKU1 coronaviruses) SARS-CoV-1 and MERS-CoV infections Bacterial community-acquired pneumonia Molecular nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), usually RT-PCR on nasopharyngeal swab or saliva - most sensitive; cannot be done at home and is processed in a reference laboratory Antigen tests (rapid / at-home) detecting SARS-CoV-2 proteins - reliable but less accurate than molecular tests, especially in exposed asymptomatic persons CBC: lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia Inflammatory markers: elevated IL-6, TNF-alpha, ferritin, C-reactive protein Elevated liver enzymes and lactate dehydrogenase Elevated markers of acute kidney injury Elevated D-dimer and prothrombin time (coagulopathy) Elevated troponin and creatine phosphokinase (cardiac/muscle injury) Chest radiograph: bilateral consolidation and ground-glass opacities, especially in lower lung regions (may be normal despite respiratory compromise) Chest CT: ground-glass opacification +/- consolidation, pleural thickening, interlobular septal thickening, air bronchograms - interpretable as typical, indeterminate, or atypical; more sensitive than radiograph but should be used for management, not as a primary diagnostic tool Lung ultrasound to detect lung abnormalities SARS-CoV-2 is an enveloped, positive-sense RNA betacoronavirus; its trimeric spike (S) protein is primed by the host protease TMPRSS2 and attaches via a receptor-binding domain to the human ACE2 receptor (p.1539). Disease course varies widely: asymptomatic infection, mild disease, moderate disease, or severe disease needing hospitalization, oxygen, intensive care, and mechanical ventilation. Possibly about a third of those infected are asymptomatic yet can still transmit the virus (p.1540). Onset of disease typically manifests within 4-5 days after exposure and nearly always within 14 days; common symptoms are cough, fever, myalgia, headache, dyspnea, sore throat, and GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) (p.1541). Sudden-onset dysgeusia and anosmia (loss of taste and smell) occur in a substantial number of cases and often resolve over weeks to months (p.1541). Spread is primarily via respiratory droplets between persons in close proximity; airborne transmission by small particles may occur but airborne transmission over long distances is unlikely. Fomite (contaminated-surface) transmission occurs, so hand washing is advised (p.1540). The basic reproduction number (R0) of SARS-CoV-2 has been estimated to peak around 6, substantially higher than seasonal influenza (typically 1-2); densely populated settings (prisons, cruise ships, nursing homes, airplanes, large indoor gatherings) facilitate high transmission, while outdoor transmission is less common (p.1540). RNA-dependent RNA polymerases are error-prone, so variants arise frequently; the WHO classifies variants under monitoring (VUMs), of interest (VOIs), and of concern (VOCs). Rapid variant evolution affecting transmission, severity, antigenicity, therapy effectiveness, and diagnostic accuracy is a distinguishing feature of the pandemic (p.1540). An excessive proinflammatory host response to infection likely contributes directly to pulmonary pathology and disease severity; later in the clinical course pathogenesis is driven more by tissue and systemic inflammation than by direct viral cytopathic effect (p.1541-1542). Children have lower rates of severe disease than adults, and schools have not been considered a primary driver of population transmission (p.1540). Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C / PMIS) is associated with COVID-19: persistent fever, multi-organ involvement (GI, dermatologic, cardiac, renal, hematologic, neurologic), and elevated inflammatory markers; highest US risk is in Black and Latino children aged 3-12 years. A similar adult syndrome (MIS-A) may rarely occur (p.1540). Long COVID is a chronic condition occurring after infection, present for at least 3 months, with a wide range of symptoms (respiratory, metabolic, neuropsychiatric, pain) that may improve, worsen, or be ongoing; affected people may have increased suicidal ideation and suicide risk (p.1541). Vaccination's principal goal is preventing severe COVID-19 (critical illness, death, hospitalization, emergency/urgent-care visits); preliminary data also suggest vaccinated persons with COVID are less likely than unvaccinated persons to develop long COVID (p.1543). Oxygen saturation <=94% on room air Respiratory rate >30 breaths/min PaO2/FiO2 <300 mmHg Lung infiltrates occupying >50% of lung fields on chest radiograph Moderate to severe dyspnea or cyanosis Change in mental status (confusion, delirium) or new-onset mental status changes Chest pain Reduced urine output or anuria Acute respiratory distress syndrome / respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation Multiorgan failure or shock Persistent fever with multiorgan disease and elevated inflammatory markers (excessive inflammatory response - high risk of fatal outcome) Thromboembolic events (VTE/PE/DVT, arterial thrombosis, acute stroke, limb ischemia) Antibiotics are NOT generally indicated, as bacterial infection is an uncommon complication of COVID-19; reserve empiric antibiotics for diagnostic uncertainty or proven secondary infection, and deescalate or stop if no evidence of bacterial infection. Chest CT should NOT be used as a primary diagnostic tool for COVID-19; it is principally for medical management of respiratory disease. COVID-19-specific therapy is NOT recommended for individuals with asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection. Antigen (rapid/at-home) tests are less accurate than molecular tests, especially when testing exposed persons without symptoms. Chest radiographs may be normal despite respiratory compromise, so a normal film does not exclude significant disease. Possible association between NSAID use and worse outcomes has been raised; acetaminophen is the preferred antipyretic where possible (knowledge point - doses omitted). Antibody-based therapies and EUAs are repeatedly revoked as new variants escape their activity, so confirm current authorization status before relying on a monoclonal antibody or long-acting antibody product. Effectiveness of masking in community or health settings has been difficult to assess (most studies observational and confounded), so evidence is uncertain rather than absent. SARS-CoV-2 (genus Betacoronavirus) is an enveloped positive-sense RNA virus with a ~30,000-nucleotide genome encoding four structural proteins (S spike, E envelope, M membrane, N nucleocapsid) plus a large polyprotein cleaved into 16 nonstructural proteins. The trimeric S protein is a type-1 fusion machine primed by the host transmembrane protease TMPRSS2 and mediates attachment via a receptor-binding domain (RBD) to the human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (hACE2) receptor, allowing viral entry into respiratory epithelium. Infection spreads chiefly by respiratory droplets, with possible short-range airborne and fomite spread. Disease results from direct viral pathogenesis in tissues and the associated immune response. An excessive proinflammatory host response contributes directly to pulmonary pathology; early in infection viral load (peak titer) correlates with severity, whereas later disease is increasingly driven by tissue and systemic inflammatory responses (cytokine storm) rather than direct viral cytopathic effect. The hyperinflammatory and hypercoagulable state drives severe multi-organ complications. Symptomatic infection is usually an acute syndrome that resolves within about 2 weeks in roughly 80% of persons, especially after mild or moderate disease. Severe disease often needs several months for recovery. Advanced age is the principal risk factor for severe illness: >95% of deaths occur in persons older than 45 years and >80% in those older than 65; male sex carries higher risk (odds ratio ~1.8), and most who die have preexisting comorbidities. Risk rises markedly with elevated BMI (overweight, obesity, severe obesity). As of September 2024 the virus had caused >700 million cases and >7 million deaths worldwide. A subset progress to recurring or persisting symptoms (long COVID); those with severe acute pulmonary or cardiac injury may have persisting respiratory or cardiac impairment, and adverse long-term mental-health consequences are common. Spectrum: asymptomatic infection; mild disease (symptomatic, no pneumonia - most symptomatic cases); moderate disease; severe disease (pneumonia with dyspnea, radiographic involvement of more than half the lung, and/or hypoxia with oxygen saturation <=94%, typically requiring hospitalization and oxygen); critical disease (respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, multiorgan failure, or shock - requires intensive care).

cutaneous anthrax or a necrotising bacterial infection Failing to distinguish cowpox from mpox during outbreaks, delaying appropriate public health action Overlooking cat contact as the usual modern source of infection Underestimating the risk of dissemination in atopic or immunocompromised patients Cowpox virus is an orthopoxvirus maintained in wild rodent populations, from which it spills over into cats and occasionally cattle and humans. Infection follows inoculation of the virus through broken skin during contact with an infected animal, most often a scratch or bite from a pet cat carrying the virus. The virus replicates locally in the epidermis and dermis, producing an evolving pox lesion that becomes vesicular, then pustular and haemorrhagic, before forming a firm black eschar as the tissue necroses. A vigorous local and systemic immune response accounts for the accompanying lymphadenopathy and constitutional symptoms. Because orthopoxviruses share antigens, previous smallpox vaccination offers some cross-protection, and disseminated disease is more likely where immunity or the skin barrier is impaired, as in atopic dermatitis. In healthy people cowpox is self-limiting and heals over several weeks, often leaving a scar; disseminated infection in immunocompromised or severely atopic patients can be serious and occasionally life-threatening.

Cow's Milk Protein Allergy — CMPA, cow's milk protein intolerance, milk allergy in infants Lactose intolerance Infantile colic Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease Infectious gastroenteritis Other food protein-induced enteropathies or proctocolitis Eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorders Trial of dietary elimination and planned reintroduction Specific IgE or skin prick testing (for IgE-mediated disease) Supervised oral food challenge Stool examination for blood if allergic proctocolitis suspected Growth monitoring and, if needed, nutritional assessment This is an immune-mediated reaction to cow's milk proteins, distinct from lactose intolerance, which is a non-immune enzyme deficiency. Reactions are broadly divided into IgE-mediated (rapid onset urticaria, angioedema, vomiting, wheeze, and rarely anaphylaxis) and non-IgE-mediated (delayed gastrointestinal symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhoea, blood or mucus in stool, and colic-like distress). It is one of the most common food allergies in infancy and can occur in both formula-fed and exclusively breastfed infants exposed to milk protein through maternal diet. Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by a compatible history, a trial of milk protein elimination, and improvement followed by recurrence on reintroduction. For IgE-mediated disease, specific IgE testing or skin prick testing can support the diagnosis, whereas these tests are unhelpful in non-IgE-mediated presentations. Management centres on strict avoidance of cow's milk protein, using an appropriate hypoallergenic formula in formula-fed infants and maternal dietary exclusion in breastfed infants. A supervised oral food challenge is the most reliable way to confirm or refute the diagnosis and to assess whether tolerance has developed. Most children outgrow cow's milk protein allergy during early childhood, so periodic reassessment for acquired tolerance is important to avoid unnecessary long-term restriction. Anaphylaxis or significant respiratory compromise after milk exposure Significant gastrointestinal bleeding or severe enteropathy Faltering growth or failure to thrive Severe dehydration or shock (as in food protein-induced enterocolitis reactions) Signs suggesting an alternative serious diagnosis Confusing cow's milk protein allergy with lactose intolerance and giving inappropriate dietary advice Relying on IgE tests to diagnose non-IgE-mediated disease Maintaining prolonged, unnecessary dietary restriction without reassessing for tolerance Using inadequately hypoallergenic substitutes or overlooking nutritional adequacy of exclusion diets The disorder results from an abnormal immune response to proteins in cow's milk, principally caseins and whey proteins. In IgE-mediated allergy, sensitisation leads to specific IgE that, on re-exposure, triggers mast cell and basophil degranulation with rapid release of histamine and other mediators, producing immediate symptoms. In non-IgE-mediated allergy, cell-mediated and mixed immune mechanisms cause a more delayed inflammatory response in the gastrointestinal tract, resulting in mucosal inflammation, altered motility, and enteropathy. Because the offending proteins can pass into breast milk, exclusively breastfed infants can react to maternal dietary intake. The prognosis is generally favourable, with the majority of children achieving tolerance during the preschool years; IgE-mediated allergy, particularly with high specific IgE levels, may persist longer than non-IgE-mediated disease.

coxa saltans — snapping hip syndrome, dancer's hip Greater trochanteric pain syndrome / trochanteric bursitis Iliopsoas bursitis or tendinopathy Acetabular labral tear Intra-articular loose body or synovial chondromatosis Femoroacetabular impingement Hip instability or subluxation Dynamic ultrasound of the iliopsoas tendon and the lateral peritrochanteric structures MRI or MR arthrography to identify intra-articular causes and associated bursitis Radiographs to exclude bony abnormality, loose bodies and proximal femoral morphology Image-guided diagnostic injection of the iliopsoas sheath or trochanteric bursa Dynamic iliopsoas assessment or bursography where ultrasound is inconclusive Classified as external, internal or intra-articular, and defining the type clinically directs both investigation and treatment. External coxa saltans is a palpable or visible lateral snap as the posterior iliotibial band or anterior border of gluteus maximus flips over the greater trochanter during flexion and extension. Internal coxa saltans is an audible or palpable groin clunk from the iliopsoas tendon catching over the iliopectineal eminence or femoral head as the hip moves from flexion-abduction-external rotation into extension. Intra-articular snapping from a labral tear, loose body or chondral flap produces true mechanical clicking and warrants intra-articular imaging. The snapping itself is frequently painless; it becomes symptomatic once secondary bursitis or tendinopathy develops. It is common in dancers, gymnasts, runners and young women, and is often bilateral. Dynamic ultrasound is the investigation of choice for internal and external types because it demonstrates the abnormal tendon movement in real time. Management is predominantly conservative with stretching and physiotherapy; iliopsoas or iliotibial band lengthening is reserved for painful cases refractory to non-operative treatment. Snapping accompanied by locking or giving way, suggesting intra-articular derangement or a loose body Progressive, rest or night pain rather than mechanical, activity-related symptoms New snapping after hip surgery or trauma, suggesting tendon subluxation or hardware impingement Fixed deformity or restricted rotation indicating an alternative structural diagnosis Assuming that all snapping is pathological, when a painless snap in a young athlete frequently requires only reassurance. Missing an intra-articular cause by omitting arthrography or arthroscopic assessment in true mechanical clicking. Over-releasing the iliopsoas and producing symptomatic hip flexor weakness. Proceeding to surgery without first clearly distinguishing internal from external snapping by dynamic examination and ultrasound. Coxa saltans occurs when a musculotendinous structure abruptly catches and releases over a bony prominence. In the external type the posterior iliotibial band or the anterior edge of gluteus maximus snaps across the greater trochanter during hip flexion and extension, often provoking overlying trochanteric bursitis. In the internal type the iliopsoas tendon snaps over the iliopectineal eminence, femoral head or lesser trochanter as the hip transitions from a flexed, abducted, externally rotated position into extension and internal rotation. Intra-articular snapping reflects mechanical derangement within the joint such as a labral tear, loose body or synovial chondromatosis. Repetitive snapping incites peritendinous inflammation, bursal thickening and tendinopathy that convert a painless mechanical phenomenon into a painful syndrome. The outlook is excellent, as most cases are painless or settle with stretching and activity modification. Surgical lengthening for refractory painful snapping is usually successful but carries a risk of transient hip flexor or abductor weakness and occasional recurrence.

Confusing the condition with milder sclerosing dysplasias and underestimating its progressive course Overlooking foramen magnum stenosis and the risk of brainstem compression Failing to anticipate re-growth of bone after surgical decompression Craniodiaphyseal dysplasia is driven by defective sclerostin activity; sclerostin, the product of SOST, normally inhibits the WNT/beta-catenin pathway and thereby limits osteoblastic bone formation. When this brake is lost, unchecked WNT signalling produces extreme, continuous bone deposition. In the craniofacial skeleton this yields gross hyperostosis and sclerosis with grotesque facial thickening, while in the appendicular skeleton the diaphyses widen and lose their normal shape. The expanding cranial bone progressively narrows neural foramina and the foramen magnum, compressing cranial nerves and the brainstem and raising intracranial pressure, which accounts for the serious neurological complications that dominate the clinical course. The prognosis is poor in severe cases because of progressive cranial-nerve compression, raised intracranial pressure and the tendency of decompressed bone to reform; early and repeated surgical intervention may preserve function but does not halt the underlying overgrowth.

transport machinery (the IFT-A complex), including IFT122, WDR35, WDR19 and IFT43. These proteins move cargo back towards the cell body along the primary cilium, and their loss impairs the assembly and maintenance of cilia and the hedgehog and other signalling pathways that depend on them. Because the primary cilium is required for normal growth-plate chondrocyte signalling, epithelial patterning and renal tubular function, the resulting ciliary dysfunction produces the combination of short ribs and limbs, ectodermal abnormalities of hair, teeth and nails, a chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy, hepatic fibrosis, and retinal degeneration that characterises the condition. Outcome is variable; thoracic constriction is usually less severe than in Jeune syndrome, but progressive renal failure is a leading cause of morbidity and may require dialysis or transplantation, and hepatic and retinal disease add to the long-term burden.

Craniometaphyseal dysplasia — CMD, ANKH-related craniometaphyseal dysplasia, GJA1-related craniometaphyseal dysplasia Craniodiaphyseal dysplasia (more severe, diaphyseal) Osteopetrosis (generalised increased bone density) Pyle disease (metaphyseal dysplasia with mild skull change) Frontometaphyseal dysplasia (otopalatodigital spectrum) Van Buchem disease and sclerosteosis (SOST-related sclerosis) Fibrous dysplasia of the craniofacial bones Molecular testing of ANKH (and GJA1 for suspected recessive disease) Skull and facial radiographs or CT to document hyperostosis and foraminal narrowing Long-bone radiographs to demonstrate metaphyseal flaring Audiological assessment for conductive and sensorineural hearing loss Cranial nerve examination and imaging of the skull base foramina Ophthalmological and nasal airway assessment where symptoms suggest compression A sclerosing bone dysplasia combining progressive craniofacial hyperostosis with abnormal metaphyseal modelling of the long bones The autosomal dominant form is caused by mutations in ANKH; a rarer autosomal recessive form is linked to GJA1 Facial features include a broad nasal bridge, paranasal bossing and hypertelorism that progress with age Cranial nerve compression from thickened skull base bone can cause facial palsy, hearing loss and, less often, visual impairment Nasal airway obstruction and choanal narrowing may occur from hyperostosis of the facial bones Radiographs show a widened, club-shaped or 'Erlenmeyer flask' metaphyseal deformity of the long bones alongside diffuse cranial sclerosis It must be distinguished from craniodiaphyseal dysplasia, which is far more severe with predominantly diaphyseal involvement Management is largely supportive with surgical decompression of foramina considered for symptomatic cranial nerve compression Progressive facial nerve palsy or hearing loss from foraminal narrowing Visual deterioration suggesting optic nerve compression Significant nasal airway obstruction from facial hyperostosis Rapid clinical progression raising concern for craniodiaphyseal dysplasia Confusing it with the much more severe craniodiaphyseal dysplasia, altering prognosis Attributing hearing loss solely to middle-ear disease and missing bony foraminal compression Delaying decompression until cranial nerve deficits become irreversible Overlooking the metaphyseal long-bone changes that support the diagnosis Craniometaphyseal dysplasia is a disorder of bone modelling. The dominant form results from mutations in ANKH, a transmembrane protein that transports inorganic pyrophosphate, a key inhibitor of mineralisation, out of cells; disturbed pyrophosphate handling alters the balance of bone deposition and resorption. The consequence is excessive, poorly remodelled bone in the skull and face (hyperostosis and sclerosis) together with defective tubulation of the long-bone metaphyses. The recessive form involves the gap-junction protein connexin 43 encoded by GJA1. Progressive skull-base thickening narrows the neural foramina and causes the cranial neuropathies. Life expectancy is usually normal, but the craniofacial changes are progressive and cranial nerve compression can cause lasting facial weakness, hearing loss or visual problems, so long-term surveillance and timely surgical decompression are important.

Craniopharyngioma — adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma, papillary craniopharyngioma, Rathke pouch tumour, suprasellar craniopharyngioma Pituitary adenoma Rathke cleft cyst Meningioma of the sellar region Germ cell tumour of the suprasellar region Hypothalamic or optic pathway glioma Lymphocytic hypophysitis Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary and hypothalamic region Computed tomography to demonstrate calcification Formal visual acuity and visual field assessment Full anterior pituitary hormone profile Assessment of posterior pituitary function including for diabetes insipidus Histological and molecular characterisation of resected tissue A benign but locally aggressive sellar/suprasellar tumour arising from remnants of Rathke's pouch along the craniopharyngeal duct Shows a bimodal age distribution, with the adamantinomatous type predominating in children and a papillary type more typical in adults Compression of the optic chiasm classically causes bitemporal visual field loss, while hypothalamic-pituitary involvement produces endocrine deficits Growth hormone and gonadotrophin deficiencies are common; diabetes insipidus and other posterior pituitary problems may occur, particularly after surgery The adamantinomatous variant characteristically shows cystic components, calcification and a mixed solid-cystic appearance on imaging Cyst fluid is often described as machinery-oil-like, cholesterol-rich material at operation Hypothalamic damage, whether from tumour or treatment, can lead to obesity, disordered temperature and thirst regulation, and behavioural change Management balances surgical resection, often transsphenoidal or transcranial, with radiotherapy and long-term hormone replacement to preserve function Rapidly progressive visual loss from chiasmal compression Raised intracranial pressure or obstructive hydrocephalus Acute hypopituitarism or adrenal insufficiency Hypothalamic dysfunction with disturbed thirst, temperature or consciousness New-onset diabetes insipidus Mistaking a cystic calcified suprasellar mass for a simple pituitary adenoma Failing to assess and monitor visual fields before and after treatment Overlooking cortisol deficiency before surgery or before starting thyroid replacement Underestimating the risk of postoperative diabetes insipidus and hypothalamic obesity Assuming complete cure after resection despite a high recurrence rate Craniopharyngiomas develop from epithelial remnants of the craniopharyngeal duct and Rathke's pouch in the sellar and suprasellar region. Although histologically benign, they enlarge and encroach on adjacent structures, compressing the optic chiasm, pituitary gland and stalk, hypothalamus and third ventricle. The adamantinomatous subtype, linked to Wnt/beta-catenin pathway activation, tends to be cystic and calcified, whereas the papillary subtype, associated with BRAF mutation, is usually solid. Mass effect and infiltration produce the visual, endocrine and hydrocephalic manifestations, and hypothalamic disruption underlies the metabolic and regulatory sequelae. Overall survival is generally good given the benign histology, but recurrence is frequent and long-term morbidity from hypopituitarism, visual impairment and hypothalamic obesity substantially affects quality of life, so lifelong endocrine and ophthalmic follow-up is required.

Craniosynostosis — premature suture fusion, scaphocephaly, plagiocephaly (synostotic), syndromic craniosynostosis Positional (deformational) plagiocephaly Microcephaly with a small but normally shaped clinical clues Most single-suture cases are non-syndromic and isolated, but multi-suture or syndromic forms (such as Apert, Crouzon, or Pfeiffer) carry higher risks and associated anomalies Multi-suture involvement can raise intracranial pressure and threaten vision and neurodevelopment, so fundoscopy and developmental monitoring are important Cranial CT with three-dimensional reconstruction confirms the diagnosis and defines the sutures involved when clinical assessment is uncertain Treatment is usually surgical remodelling to correct the deformity and allow normal brain growth, with timing and approach tailored to the sutures affected and the child's age Multi-suture fusion with signs of raised intracranial pressure such as papilloedema Progressive skull deformity with developmental delay or visual compromise Features of a craniofacial syndrome with airway or midface concerns Rapidly abnormal head growth or a bulging appearance suggesting elevated pressure Confusing positional plagiocephaly, which improves with repositioning, with true synostosis Missing raised intracranial pressure in multi-suture disease by omitting fundoscopy Underestimating associated anomalies and genetic implications in syndromic cases Delaying referral so that the optimal surgical window is missed Craniosynostosis arises when one or more cranial sutures fuse prematurely, before the underlying brain has finished its rapid early growth. Because bone cannot expand across the fused suture, compensatory growth occurs at the remaining open sutures, distorting the skull into a predictable shape determined by which suture is involved. When several sutures fuse, the overall cranial volume may become inadequate for the growing brain, leading to raised intracranial pressure. Syndromic forms are often driven by identifiable genetic mutations affecting fibroblast growth factor signalling and are associated with midface and limb anomalies. Isolated single-suture craniosynostosis generally has an excellent outcome after timely surgical correction; multi-suture and syndromic forms are more complex, carry a greater risk of raised intracranial pressure and neurodevelopmental problems, and often require staged, multidisciplinary management.

and pharmacological measures in GAMT to lower guanidinoacetate The creatine transporter defect responds poorly to supplementation because the transporter needed for brain uptake is defective Urine and plasma creatine, guanidinoacetate and the creatinine metabolite ratio help distinguish the three subtypes Global developmental delay with epilepsy and prominent speech impairment Refractory seizures and a movement disorder suggesting GAMT deficiency Regression or deterioration during intercurrent illness Family history consistent with X-linked inheritance in males Overlooking a treatable cause of intellectual disability by not requesting spectroscopy or guanidinoacetate testing Assuming all creatine deficiency syndromes respond to supplementation, when the transporter defect does not Missing raised guanidinoacetate as a marker of the treatable GAMT form Delaying treatment in synthesis defects, when early therapy is most effective Creatine and its phosphorylated form provide a rapid energy buffer for tissues with high and fluctuating energy demands, notably brain and muscle. Creatine is synthesised in two steps: AGAT (encoded by GATM) forms guanidinoacetate, which GAMT then methylates to creatine; creatine is delivered to the brain and taken up by cells via the SLC6A8 transporter. Loss of any step causes cerebral creatine depletion and impaired energy homeostasis, producing neurodevelopmental impairment. In GAMT deficiency, guanidinoacetate additionally accumulates and is neurotoxic, contributing to seizures and movement disturbance. In the transporter defect, creatine is made normally but cannot enter the brain. Outcomes in the treatable synthesis defects (AGAT and GAMT) are substantially improved by early creatine supplementation, and pre-symptomatic treatment can prevent much of the neurological damage. The X-linked creatine transporter defect has a less favourable prognosis because supplementation does not restore brain creatine.

Cri-du-chat syndrome — cat cry syndrome, 5p deletion syndrome, 5p minus syndrome, Lejeune syndrome, monosomy 5p Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome Other subtelomeric deletion syndromes Trisomy 21 Cornelia de Lange syndrome Prader-Willi syndrome in the hypotonic neonate Non-specific syndromic intellectual disability Chromosomal microarray to define the deletion and its size Karyotype to detect an underlying translocation, with parental karyotypes for recurrence risk FISH targeting the 5p critical region where confirmation is needed Echocardiography for congenital heart disease Feeding and swallowing assessment in infancy Hearing and vision testing to support developmental progress The high-pitched, monotone, cat-like cry in infancy gives the syndrome its name and reflects abnormal laryngeal and neurological development; it often diminishes with age Caused by a partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, with phenotype severity broadly correlating with deletion size and specific critical regions Facial features include microcephaly, a rounded face, hypertelorism, epicanthic folds, down-slanting palpebral fissures and low-set ears, with the face lengthening over time Prenatal-onset growth restriction, marked feeding difficulty and hypotonia are common in infancy Most deletions are de novo, but a minority arise from an unbalanced parental translocation, so parental karyotyping is essential for recurrence-risk counselling Severe intellectual disability with markedly limited expressive language is typical, though receptive skills are relatively better Behavioural features can include hyperactivity, self-injury and stereotypies Failure to thrive from severe feeding difficulty and recurrent aspiration Unrecognised congenital heart disease causing cardiorespiratory compromise Stridor or airway obstruction related to laryngeal abnormality Self-injurious behaviour requiring safeguarding and specialist input Assuming a normal standard karyotype excludes the diagnosis when small deletions require microarray or FISH Omitting parental karyotyping and mis-stating recurrence risk when a translocation is present Attributing feeding failure to behaviour rather than oromotor dysfunction Underestimating relatively preserved receptive language and social ability Cri-du-chat syndrome arises from a terminal or interstitial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p), producing haploinsufficiency for genes in this region. Loss of specific critical intervals correlates with the characteristic cry and with the degree of intellectual disability, and candidate genes such as those influencing telomerase regulation and neuronal cytoskeletal proteins have been implicated. The reduced dosage of these developmentally important genes disrupts laryngeal, craniofacial and central nervous system formation. Deletions are commonly de novo and paternal in origin, but can result from malsegregation of a balanced parental rearrangement. Most individuals have severe intellectual disability but can achieve some self-care and communication skills with early intervention; survival into adulthood is usual. Outcome depends largely on associated malformations, especially cardiac and respiratory, and on deletion size.

type 1, in which such a response is absent Type 1 management relies on intensive phototherapy to keep bilirubin in a safe range, with liver transplantation being the definitive cure It is distinguished from the milder, common Gilbert syndrome, which also involves reduced UGT1A1 activity but does not cause dangerous bilirubin levels Rising unconjugated bilirubin with lethargy, hypotonia, or abnormal tone signalling impending kernicterus Failure of bilirubin to respond to intensive phototherapy Intercurrent illness, fasting, or drugs precipitating a sharp rise in bilirubin Progressive loss of phototherapy efficacy as skin surface area increases with growth Confusing severe Crigler-Najjar with benign Gilbert syndrome and underestimating kernicterus risk Failing to appreciate that phototherapy becomes progressively less effective with age and growth Prescribing drugs that displace bilirubin from albumin or that are conjugated by the same pathway Delaying liver transplantation assessment in type 1 disease Overlooking precipitants such as fasting, infection, or stress that acutely worsen jaundice Bilirubin produced from haem breakdown must be conjugated with glucuronic acid by the hepatic enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 before it can be excreted in bile. In Crigler-Najjar syndrome, biallelic mutations in UGT1A1 abolish (type 1) or severely reduce (type 2) this enzyme activity, so unconjugated bilirubin cannot be efficiently processed and accumulates in the blood. Because unconjugated bilirubin is lipid soluble it can cross the blood-brain barrier, and at high concentrations it deposits in the basal ganglia and brainstem, causing bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus). The liver is otherwise structurally normal with no cholestasis or hepatocellular injury. Type 2 disease is generally compatible with a normal life expectancy and low neurological risk when managed appropriately, whereas untreated type 1 carries a high risk of kernicterus and death; sustained phototherapy delays complications, and liver transplantation offers definitive correction of the enzyme defect.

Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever — CCHF, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, viral haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), VHF Other viral haemorrhagic fevers (Ebola, Lassa, hantavirus, Kyasanur Forest disease) Severe dengue with haemorrhage Severe leptospirosis (Weil's disease) Meningococcaemia and other bacterial sepsis with DIC Severe malaria Rickettsial disease with haemorrhage Dengue haemorrhagic fever Leptospirosis Meningococcal sepsis Severe malaria Other viral haemorrhagic fevers RT-PCR for CCHF viral RNA in early illness, performed in an appropriately biosafe laboratory CCHF-specific IgM and IgG serology later in the course Full blood count, coagulation profile, liver and renal function to gauge severity Careful exclusion of dengue, malaria, and leptospirosis given overlapping presentations All sampling and testing conducted under enhanced biosafety with prior laboratory notification A tick-borne viral haemorrhagic fever caused by an orthonairovirus, transmitted mainly by Hyalomma ticks and by contact with blood or tissues of infected livestock In India it is a recognised emerging threat, with documented outbreaks in Gujarat and neighbouring regions and cases among livestock handlers and healthcare workers Onset is abrupt with fever, severe headache, myalgia, and prostration, progressing over days to a haemorrhagic phase with petechiae, ecchymoses, mucosal bleeding, and multi-organ involvement Nosocomial and slaughterhouse transmission is well described, so a history of tick exposure, animal contact, or care of a bleeding patient is a critical clue Laboratory features include thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and rising transaminases, with deranged coagulation heralding severe disease This is a medical emergency requiring strict infection-control and barrier precautions, patient isolation, and safe handling of body fluids and laboratory specimens Management is chiefly supportive with careful correction of coagulopathy and organ support; suspected and confirmed cases must be promptly notified to public health authorities Spontaneous mucosal or gastrointestinal bleeding, extensive ecchymoses, or evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation Rapidly falling platelet count with rising transaminases and deteriorating coagulation Hypotension, shock, or signs of multi-organ failure Any suspected case demands immediate isolation, barrier nursing, and public health notification because of nosocomial transmission risk Failing to institute isolation and barrier precautions early, exposing staff and other patients to a highly transmissible pathogen Anchoring on dengue or malaria and overlooking CCHF in someone with relevant tick or livestock exposure Performing invasive procedures or unprotected phlebotomy that increase bleeding and transmission risk Not notifying public health authorities and the receiving laboratory before sending specimens CCHF virus is an enveloped RNA virus that, following tick bite or exposure to infected blood or tissues, replicates and disseminates widely. It infects endothelial cells and cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system, and a dysregulated inflammatory and cytokine response together with direct endothelial injury leads to increased vascular permeability, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and haemorrhage. Hepatic involvement and marrow suppression contribute to the coagulopathy and cytopenias, and severe cases progress to shock and multi-organ failure. Case fatality is high, especially with delayed recognition and severe coagulopathy or multi-organ failure; early supportive care and meticulous infection control improve outcomes, and survivors who pass the acute haemorrhagic phase generally recover.

disturbance and deficiencies of vitamins and trace elements It is thought to be immune-mediated and treatment centres on nutritional support with corticosteroids and other immunosuppression There is an associated increased risk of gastrointestinal malignancy warranting surveillance Severe hypoalbuminaemia with oedema and effusions Profound weight loss and malnutrition Gastrointestinal bleeding or an obstructing or suspicious polyp raising concern for malignancy Severe electrolyte disturbance from high-volume diarrhoea Mistaking it for an inherited polyposis syndrome and missing the ectodermal clues Overlooking and undertreating the protein-losing enteropathy and micronutrient deficiencies Failing to institute cancer surveillance Attributing the diarrhoea to a functional disorder despite systemic features Cronkhite-Canada syndrome is a rare acquired condition characterised by diffuse gastrointestinal polyposis together with ectodermal abnormalities. The polyps are inflammatory and hamartomatous in type, with oedematous, inflamed lamina propria and cystic gland dilatation, and they diffusely involve the stomach, small intestine and colon. The cause is uncertain but growing evidence points to an autoimmune or chronic inflammatory mechanism, supported by the presence of IgG4-positive plasma cells in some cases and response to immunosuppression. Widespread mucosal disease leads to malabsorption and a protein-losing enteropathy, producing the hypoalbuminaemia, electrolyte loss and nutritional deficiencies that dominate the clinical picture. The syndrome can be serious with significant mortality from malnutrition and complications, but many patients improve with nutritional support and immunosuppression; the associated cancer risk means long-term surveillance is required.

Rising proliferation indices suggesting aggressive behaviour or progression toward carcinoma Visual deterioration from mass effect Grading it as an ordinary adenoma and under-estimating the recurrence risk Missing the diagnosis without cytokeratin immunostaining Assuming a silent tumour is a benign non-functioning adenoma rather than an aggressive corticotroph variant Providing inadequate long-term follow-up after apparently complete resection The Crooke cell adenoma is a corticotroph-lineage pituitary tumour in which the tumour cells display Crooke hyaline change, a dense perinuclear accumulation of cytokeratin intermediate filaments. In non-neoplastic corticotrophs this change is induced by glucocorticoid excess and reflects feedback; when it dominates a tumour it defines an aggressive adenoma subtype. Crooke cell adenomas are aggressive, with high rates of recurrence and resistance to conventional therapy; multimodal treatment with surgery, radiotherapy and medical therapy is often required and long-term surveillance is essential, with a subset progressing despite treatment.

Crossed fused renal ectopia — crossed renal ectopia with fusion, crossed fused ectopia, crossed renal ectopia Horseshoe kidney Simple renal ectopia (pelvic kidney) without crossing Unilateral renal agenesis with compensatory hypertrophy Retroperitoneal or pelvic mass or tumour Multicystic dysplastic kidney Other renal fusion variants such as a lump or pancake kidney Nephroptosis Renal tract ultrasound showing an empty renal fossa with both moieties on one side Contrast-enhanced CT or CT/MR urography to define the fusion type, rotation and vascular supply before any surgery MAG3 or DMSA scintigraphy for differential function and drainage Micturating cystourethrogram where vesicoureteric reflux is suspected Assessment for associated skeletal, cardiac and genital anomalies Metabolic stone work-up when calculi are present In crossed renal ectopia one kidney lies on the side opposite its ureteric insertion; the crossed kidney sits contralaterally while its ureter still enters the bladder on the original side, crossing the midline Fusion of the crossed kidney to the orthotopic kidney occurs in the great majority of cases, and several morphological types are described including unilateral fused ectopia, sigmoid or S-shaped, L-shaped or tandem, and lump or disc kidneys Left-to-right crossing is the more frequent pattern, and the crossed kidney is usually inferior, malrotated and supplied by anomalous vessels arising from the nearby aorta or iliac arteries Most cases are asymptomatic incidental findings; when symptomatic, the features stem from urinary stasis, namely infection, calculi and obstruction, particularly at the pelviureteric junction Malrotation and a variable, aberrant blood supply make surgery technically demanding and increase the risk of pelviureteric junction obstruction, and the ectopic mass can be mistaken for an abdominal or pelvic tumour It is associated with vesicoureteric reflux and with skeletal, cardiac, anorectal and genital anomalies, and sits within the wider spectrum of renal fusion and ectopia that includes the horseshoe kidney A solitary crossed fused ectopic kidney represents the patient's entire functioning renal mass and therefore warrants protection and appropriate counselling Febrile urinary tract infection, pyelonephritis or urosepsis Pelviureteric junction obstruction with pain or deteriorating function Impaired function in a solitary crossed fused ectopic kidney A large obstructing calculus Mistaking the ectopic fused renal mass for a tumour or lymphadenopathy on imaging Misinterpreting the empty renal fossa as unilateral renal agenesis Overlooking the anomalous and variable blood supply during surgery and risking haemorrhage Attributing loin pain solely to stones without assessing for pelviureteric junction obstruction Failing to recognise and protect solitary functioning renal tissue Crossed fused renal ectopia arises from an error during the ascent and rotation of the metanephric kidneys. Abnormal migration of one nephrogenic blastema, or malpositioning of its ureteric bud, causes one developing kidney to cross the midline; contact between the two renal masses before rotation and encapsulation are complete then leads to their fusion. Because the ureter of the crossed kidney was already committed to its side of origin, it continues to enter the bladder orthotopically even though the parenchyma now lies contralaterally. The malrotation, abnormal hilar orientation and aberrant blood supply from local vessels reflect the abnormal position of the kidney when it acquired its vasculature, and the resulting distorted drainage predisposes to stasis, reflux, infection and stone formation. The prognosis is excellent in the asymptomatic majority, with normal renal function and life expectancy. It worsens only if complications such as obstruction, recurrent infection or stones damage the parenchyma, which is more consequential when the fused unit constitutes solitary functioning renal tissue.

Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) — laryngotracheobronchitis, laryngotracheitis, viral croup, acute laryngotracheobronchitis Epiglottitis Bacterial tracheitis Foreign body aspiration Retropharyngeal or peritonsillar abscess Anaphylaxis / angioedema Spasmodic (recurrent) croup Clinical severity assessment (e.g. presence of stridor at rest and recession) Pulse oximetry Anteroposterior neck radiograph only if diagnosis is uncertain (steeple sign) Avoid interventions that distress the child until the airway is secured in severe cases A common viral illness of young children, typically 6 months to 3 years, most often caused by parainfluenza viruses, producing upper airway obstruction at the subglottis. Characterised by a barking (seal-like) cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness, usually preceded by coryza and worse at night. Diagnosis is clinical; a frontal neck radiograph may show subglottic narrowing (the steeple sign) but is not required. Corticosteroids are the mainstay and benefit essentially all severities, reducing symptoms and the need for further intervention. Nebulised adrenaline (epinephrine) provides rapid, temporary relief in moderate to severe cases and mandates a period of observation for rebound. Keeping the child calm and comfortable is important, as agitation and crying worsen airway obstruction. Stridor at rest, marked recession, or hypoxaemia indicates significant obstruction requiring active treatment. Consider alternative diagnoses when the presentation is atypical: sudden toxic appearance suggests epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis, and drooling with dysphagia is a warning sign. Stridor at rest with marked chest wall recession Cyanosis, hypoxaemia, or altered mental status / lethargy Drooling, dysphagia, or a toxic-appearing child suggesting epiglottitis Rapidly worsening obstruction or exhaustion despite treatment Biphasic stridor indicating severe fixed obstruction Distressing the child with unnecessary examination or procedures, worsening obstruction Withholding corticosteroids in mild cases where they still provide benefit Discharging a child after nebulised adrenaline without an adequate observation period for rebound Failing to recognise epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis presenting with a croup-like picture Viral infection produces inflammation and oedema of the larynx, trachea, and subglottic tissues. Because the subglottis is the narrowest part of a child's airway and is encircled by rigid cricoid cartilage, even modest mucosal swelling markedly narrows the lumen, dramatically increasing airway resistance and producing turbulent airflow heard as inspiratory stridor and the characteristic barking cough. Increased work of breathing follows, and severe obstruction can cause hypoxaemia and fatigue. Most children have mild, self-limiting illness that resolves within a few days; severe airway compromise is uncommon and the need for intubation is rare with appropriate treatment.

of raised intracranial pressure Progressive hydrocephalus or symptomatic Chiari malformation Severe obstructive sleep apnoea causing hypoxia Overlooking the diagnosis because intelligence and limbs are normal Failing to protect the exposed globe in a child with marked proptosis Missing evolving hydrocephalus or hindbrain herniation on follow-up Not screening for hearing loss and treating it, which can compound developmental delay Crouzon syndrome arises from activating mutations in fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2) that heighten receptor signalling in cranial suture mesenchyme. Overactive signalling accelerates osteoblast differentiation and premature ossification, so the calvarial sutures and cranial base synchondroses fuse early. This restricts the growth of the skull and, importantly, the midface, producing shallow orbits, proptosis and maxillary retrusion, while limb development is spared. An allelic form linked to an FGFR3 mutation additionally shows acanthosis nigricans. Cognition is usually normal, and with timely craniofacial and neurosurgical management most children do well, but ongoing surveillance for raised intracranial pressure, visual and airway complications is essential throughout growth.

crushed part Delaying fluid resuscitation until after the limb is freed, when the potassium surge is already underway Overlooking hyperkalaemia and failing to monitor the electrocardiogram during extrication Missing evolving compartment syndrome in the injured limb Under-resuscitating and allowing pigment nephropathy to progress Attributing dark urine to visible blood rather than myoglobin Prolonged compression of muscle causes ischaemic and pressure necrosis (rhabdomyolysis). While compressed, the injury is largely contained, but on release reperfusion washes the accumulated intracellular contents into the systemic circulation. Potassium, myoglobin, phosphate, and organic acids surge, producing hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, and hypocalcaemia. Myoglobin precipitates in the renal tubules, and combined with hypovolaemia from fluid sequestration into damaged muscle, causes acute kidney injury. Massive fluid shifts and the release of vasoactive and inflammatory mediators can cause shock, while swelling within fascial compartments produces compartment syndrome. Early and aggressive fluid resuscitation with prevention and treatment of hyperkalaemia and pigment nephropathy improves outcome. Untreated crush syndrome carries high mortality from arrhythmia and renal failure, though renal function often recovers with timely supportive care and dialysis where needed.

Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis — Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis, Mixed cryoglobulinaemia syndrome, Cryoglobulinaemic small-vessel vasculitis IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schoenlein purpura) ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis Hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis Polyarteritis nodosa Septic vasculitis or infective endocarditis with embolic purpura Thrombotic microangiopathy Drug-induced (hypersensitivity) vasculitis Serum cryoglobulin assay with cryocrit, using strict 37 degrees Celsius collection and transport Hepatitis C serology and HCV RNA, plus hepatitis B and HIV testing Complement levels (characteristically low C4, relatively preserved C3) and rheumatoid factor Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation to detect a monoclonal component Renal function, urinalysis and urine protein quantification for glomerulonephritis Skin or renal biopsy demonstrating immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Nerve conduction studies where peripheral neuropathy is suspected Cryoglobulins are immunoglobulins that precipitate reversibly below core body temperature; the resulting immune-complex deposition drives a small-vessel vasculitis. The classic clinical triad is palpable purpura of the lower limbs, arthralgia and fatigue (Meltzer triad), often with peripheral neuropathy. Type II (mixed monoclonal IgM with rheumatoid factor activity plus polyclonal IgG) is the commonest vasculitic type and is strongly linked to chronic hepatitis C. Type I cryoglobulinaemia (single monoclonal immunoglobulin) reflects an underlying lymphoproliferative or plasma-cell disorder and tends to cause hyperviscosity and occlusive acral ischaemia rather than classic vasculitis. Low C4 with relatively preserved C3 is a characteristic complement pattern; rheumatoid factor is typically positive. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is the dominant renal lesion and a major determinant of long-term outcome. Correct sampling is essential: blood must be collected and transported at 37 degrees Celsius or the cryoglobulin may be missed (false negative). Treatment addresses the underlying cause (antiviral therapy for hepatitis C, B-cell depletion for severe or refractory disease) rather than immunosuppression alone. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with rising creatinine or heavy proteinuria Digital or acral necrosis and impending gangrene Mononeuritis multiplex or rapidly progressive sensorimotor neuropathy Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage or gastrointestinal ischaemia Hyperviscosity features (visual disturbance, confusion, mucosal bleeding) suggesting type I disease Missing the diagnosis because blood was not kept at 37 degrees Celsius, giving a false-negative cryoglobulin result. Attributing purpura to simple hypersensitivity and failing to screen for hepatitis C and an underlying B-cell clone. Immunosuppressing hepatitis C-driven disease without concurrent antiviral therapy, risking viral flare. Overlooking type I cryoglobulinaemia as a marker of occult myeloma, Waldenstroem macroglobulinaemia or lymphoma. Interpreting a normal C3 as excluding active disease when the key finding is a disproportionately low C4. Cryoglobulins are circulating immunoglobulins that undergo reversible precipitation at temperatures below 37 degrees Celsius. In mixed (type II and type III) disease a chronic antigenic stimulus, most often hepatitis C virus, drives expansion of rheumatoid-factor-producing B cells; the resulting IgM-IgG immune complexes deposit in small vessel walls, activate the classical complement pathway and recruit neutrophils, producing a leukocytoclastic small-vessel vasculitis. In type I disease a monoclonal immunoglobulin from an underlying B-cell or plasma-cell clone precipitates and occludes vessels, causing hyperviscosity and thrombotic acral ischaemia. Cold exposure promotes precipitation, explaining the distal, cool, dependent distribution of skin lesions. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause and on renal and neurological involvement; hepatitis C-associated disease often improves markedly with sustained virological clearance. Severe renal disease, extensive vasculitic ulceration or an underlying malignant lymphoproliferative disorder carry a worse outlook.

immunosuppression alone when an underlying infection or clonal disorder needs directed therapy Cryoglobulins are immunoglobulins that reversibly precipitate at temperatures below core body temperature and redissolve on warming. In mixed cryoglobulinaemia a polyclonal or monoclonal immunoglobulin with rheumatoid-factor activity binds polyclonal IgG, forming immune complexes that deposit in small and medium vessels, activate complement, and trigger a leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Chronic hepatitis C virus infection is the dominant driver, providing sustained antigenic stimulation that expands rheumatoid-factor-producing B-cell clones. Vascular deposition produces cutaneous purpura, immune-complex glomerulonephritis (often membranoproliferative), and vasa nervorum involvement causing neuropathy. Outcome depends on the underlying cause and organ involvement; hepatitis-C-related disease often improves markedly with viral eradication, whereas severe renal disease, extensive neuropathy, and underlying lymphoproliferative disorders worsen prognosis.

NLRP3, including analysis for somatic mosaicism when routine testing is negative Audiometry to detect sensorineural hearing loss Ophthalmology assessment for conjunctivitis, uveitis and papilloedema signalling AA amyloidosis Visual compromise from papilloedema or uveitis Mislabelling the recurrent rash as ordinary allergic urticaria and giving antihistamines Missing the diagnosis when standard NLRP3 sequencing is negative because of somatic mosaicism Delaying interleukin-1 blockade until irreversible hearing or neurological damage has occurred Neglecting audiological and renal surveillance Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes are driven by gain-of-function mutations in NLRP3, which encodes cryopyrin, a sensor protein of the innate immune system. Cryopyrin nucleates the NLRP3 inflammasome, a multiprotein complex that activates caspase-1. The mutations lower the threshold for or constitutively enhance inflammasome assembly, leading to excessive caspase-1-mediated cleavage of pro-interleukin-1 beta into its active form. The resulting overproduction of interleukin-1 beta produces systemic and organ-specific inflammation, and the severity of the phenotype broadly tracks the degree of inflammasome dysregulation. Chronic interleukin-1-driven inflammation underlies the sensorineural deafness, central nervous system disease, and predisposition to AA amyloidosis. Milder cold-induced disease has a favourable outlook, but untreated Muckle-Wells syndrome and NOMID cause progressive deafness, neurological damage and amyloidosis; early and sustained interleukin-1 inhibition can halt organ damage and greatly improve prognosis.

Cryptococcosis — Cryptococcus neoformans infection, cryptococcal meningitis Tuberculous (chronic) meningitis Other fungal meningitides (e.g., Coccidioides, Histoplasma) Subacute dementia or depression (indolent CNS cryptococcosis mimic) Carcinomatous meningitis Pulmonary malignancy or other causes of lung nodules/masses (pulmonary cryptococcosis found incidentally on chest radiograph) Tuberculosis (chronic meningitis and pulmonary disease) Molluscum contagiosum (cutaneous cryptococcosis in highly immunosuppressed patients resembles its lesions) Other disseminated/endemic fungal infections (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis) CSF examination: opening pressure, protein, glucose, cell count, Gram stain, cultures India ink stain of CSF for encapsulated yeast Cryptococcal antigen (CRAg) assay in CSF and blood; point-of-care lateral flow assay Fungal cultures of CSF and blood (blood cultures often positive) Serum CRAg screening in HIV with low CD4+ counts PCR (confirm positive or negative results with independent methods such as CRAg and culture) Chest imaging for pulmonary disease (nodules, infiltrates, masses) Biopsy for CNS cryptococcoma or to distinguish inadequately treated infection from immune reconstitution syndrome Carcinomatous (neoplastic) meningitis Subacute dementia Depression Pulmonary malignancy (cryptococcoma/nodule mimicking neoplasm) Caused by Cryptococcus, a genus of yeast-like fungi; WHO declared C. neoformans a critical priority pathogen in 2022 (p.1703). C. neoformans and C. gattii are now regarded as species complexes; for clinical purposes both cause indistinguishable disease termed cryptococcosis (p.1703-1704). High-risk hosts for C. neoformans: hematologic malignancy, solid-organ transplant, advanced liver disease, diabetes, glucocorticoid therapy, and advanced HIV with CD4+ counts <200/uL (p.1704). C. gattii disease is NOT generally associated with specific immune deficits and often occurs in immunocompetent individuals; associated with autoantibodies to GM-CSF (p.1704). Disease usually presents as pulmonary disease and/or chronic meningoencephalitis, but cryptococcosis can affect any tissue or organ (p.1704-1705). Cryptococcal meningitis differs from bacterial meningitis: many patients present with symptoms of several weeks' duration and classic meningismus may be absent; indolent cases can present as subacute dementia or depression (p.1705). In AIDS patients, cryptococcal meningitis is the initial AIDS-defining illness in ~2% and generally occurs with CD4+ counts <100/uL; about one-third also have pulmonary disease (p.1606). Diagnosis requires demonstration of cryptococcal cells or antigen in normally sterile tissue; India ink of CSF shows encapsulated yeast and CRAg (serum/CSF) is both sensitive and specific with rapid point-of-care lateral flow assays (p.1705). Increased intracranial pressure in cryptococcal meningoencephalitis is managed by repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures and shunt placement; mannitol and acetazolamide are NOT effective (p.1706). Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) can occur after starting ART in HIV; recommended to start ART 4-6 weeks after initiating antifungal therapy (p.1706). Serum CRAg screening is recommended for asymptomatic people with HIV and CD4+ counts <100-200/uL to identify those at high risk of cryptococcal disease (p.1705-1706). Raised intracranial pressure in cryptococcal meningoencephalitis requiring serial therapeutic lumbar puncture drainage (and possible shunt placement) Sudden catastrophic vision loss from meningeal cryptococcosis Cranial nerve paresis, vision and hearing loss Altered mental status, headache, and blurred vision as clues to elevated ICP Refractory cryptococcosis despite antifungal therapy (prompt susceptibility testing) India ink and Gram stain may be falsely negative with low fungal burden or misread as positive by inexperienced operators (p.1705). CRAg is often negative in pulmonary cryptococcosis, so it is less useful for diagnosing pulmonary disease and of only limited use in monitoring response to therapy (p.1705). Cryptococcal cells with negative cultures on CSF staining and persistently elevated CSF/blood cryptococcal antigen long after culture clearance do NOT indicate treatment failure (p.1705). Categorizing cryptococcosis as 'extrapulmonary without CNS involvement' should be made only after CSF evaluation reveals no evidence of cryptococcal infection (p.1705). Prophylactic dexamethasone in HIV-associated cryptococcosis is NOT recommended (associated with reduced fungal clearance and increased mortality); glucocorticoids are not helpful for raised ICP unless from a mass lesion with edema (p.1706). Echinocandins are NOT effective against Cryptococcus species (p.1706). IRIS can be difficult to distinguish from relapsing/refractory infection (p.1706). Cryptococcal infection is almost always acquired by inhalation of aerosolized particles (small desiccated yeast cells or basidiospores); occasionally by direct skin inoculation. C. neoformans is found in soils contaminated with avian (pigeon) excreta, whereas C. gattii inhabits arboreal species such as eucalyptus and is not found in bird feces. Infection is acquired in childhood and is common, but disease is rare in the absence of impaired immunity, indicating that intact pulmonary defenses effectively contain the fungus. Some infections lead to latency with viable organisms harbored in granulomas. Extrapulmonary dissemination to the CNS may occur via direct fungal migration across endothelium and via macrophage 'Trojan horse' carriage. Virulence factors include the antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule, melanin production, and enzymes (phospholipase, urease). Copious release of capsular polysaccharide into tissues interferes with local immune responses, and infection may elicit little or no inflammatory response; capsular polysaccharide is the antigen measured diagnostically (p.1704). Even with antifungal therapy, cryptococcosis carries high morbidity and mortality. The most important prognostic factors are the extent and duration of the underlying immunologic deficit. Disease is often curable in those with no apparent immune dysfunction, but in irreversible immunosuppression the goal is remission maintained by lifelong suppressive therapy. Before ART, median survival for AIDS patients with cryptococcosis was <1 year. Cryptococcosis with underlying neoplastic disease has a particularly poor prognosis. Poor prognostic markers for CNS disease: positive India ink on initial CSF exam (heavy fungal burden), high CSF pressure, low CSF glucose, low CSF pleocytosis (<2/uL), recovery of yeast from extraneural sites, absence of antibody to capsular polysaccharide, CSF or serum cryptococcal antigen level >=1:32, and concomitant glucocorticoid therapy or hematologic malignancy. Relapse is common even with relatively intact immunity (p.1706). Nonsevere disease limited to the lungs or other non-CNS sites is distinguished from severe disease or CNS involvement; severe/CNS cryptococcosis is treated with induction, consolidation, and maintenance phases (p.1705).

resonance imaging of the brain to identify cryptococcomas and hydrocephalus Computed tomography of the chest to characterise pulmonary nodules or masses Species identification to distinguish C. gattii from C. neoformans and HIV testing to assess immune status An encapsulated environmental yeast associated with certain trees (classically eucalyptus) and soil, historically tropical/subtropical but with a recognised temperate focus in the Pacific Northwest of North America Unlike Cryptococcus neoformans, which predominantly affects those with advanced HIV or other immunosuppression, C. gattii frequently causes disease in apparently immunocompetent hosts It has a propensity to form space-occupying mass lesions, with pulmonary cryptococcomas and cerebral cryptococcomas that can mimic tumours Presentations include chronic cough with lung masses and subacute meningoencephalitis with headache, cranial nerve palsies, and features of raised intracranial pressure Neurological disease may
