and maintenance strategy using amphotericin-based and azole antifungal agents, with repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures to manage raised pressure Diagnosis uses cryptococcal antigen testing (serum and cerebrospinal fluid), India ink microscopy, culture, and neuroimaging to define cryptococcomas Features of markedly raised intracranial pressure such as reduced consciousness, papilloedema, or cranial nerve palsies Large cerebral cryptococcomas causing mass effect Progressive neurological deficit despite antifungal therapy Respiratory compromise from extensive pulmonary disease Hydrocephalus requiring cerebrospinal fluid diversion Assuming cryptococcosis only occurs in immunocompromised patients and dismissing it in an immunocompetent host Mistaking pulmonary or cerebral cryptococcomas for malignancy Neglecting management of raised intracranial pressure, a major driver of morbidity Failing to distinguish C. gattii from C. neoformans, which affects expected course and management Underestimating the prolonged treatment and possible surgery needed for large mass lesions Cryptococcus gattii is acquired by inhaling infectious propagules from environmental sources associated with trees and soil. The yeast's polysaccharide capsule is a key virulence factor that impairs phagocytosis and modulates the immune response. After a pulmonary portal of entry the organism can disseminate haematogenously with a strong neurotropism, seeding the central nervous system. In contrast to C. neoformans, C. gattii tends to elicit a granulomatous response and to form discrete mass lesions (cryptococcomas) in the lung and brain, and it is capable of causing significant disease in hosts with no identifiable immune defect. With prompt antifungal therapy and diligent control of intracranial pressure many patients recover, but large cryptococcomas respond slowly, neurological sequelae can occur, and disease in immunocompetent hosts may still be protracted and require prolonged treatment.

Cryptogenic organising pneumonia — COP, Idiopathic bronchiolitis obliterans organising pneumonia, BOOP Non-resolving infective pneumonia Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia Pulmonary vasculitis or diffuse alveolar haemorrhage Lymphoma or invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma Connective tissue disease-associated organising pneumonia Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Sarcoidosis HRCT thorax to characterise distribution and migratory nature of consolidation Bronchoalveolar lavage to exclude infection and characterise cellularity Transbronchial or surgical lung biopsy for histological confirmation Autoimmune serology to exclude connective tissue disease Review of drug and radiation exposure Pulmonary function tests with transfer factor Inflammatory markers and cultures to exclude active infection Formerly termed idiopathic bronchiolitis obliterans organising pneumonia (BOOP). Presents subacutely over weeks with dry cough, breathlessness, low-grade fever, malaise and weight loss, frequently mistaken for a community-acquired pneumonia that fails to resolve on antibiotics. HRCT shows patchy, often peripheral or peribronchial consolidation that may be migratory; the reversed halo (atoll) sign is suggestive but not specific. Histology reveals intraluminal plugs of granulation tissue (Masson bodies) filling distal airspaces and alveolar ducts with preserved lung architecture. Diagnosis of cryptogenic disease requires exclusion of secondary organising pneumonia due to infection, drugs, radiation, connective tissue disease, aspiration or malignancy. Bronchoalveolar lavage typically shows a mixed cellularity with lymphocytosis and often foamy macrophages. There is an excellent response to corticosteroids, but relapse during dose reduction is common and usually responds to re-treatment. Pulmonary function is normal or shows a restrictive defect, and transfer factor is commonly reduced. Rapidly progressive or fulminant organising pneumonia with respiratory failure Haemoptysis suggesting an alternative diagnosis such as vasculitis Failure to respond to corticosteroids, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Features suggesting underlying malignancy or systemic vasculitis Repeated courses of antibiotics for 'non-resolving pneumonia' that delay the diagnosis Failing to search for a secondary cause before labelling the disease cryptogenic Withdrawing corticosteroids too rapidly and precipitating relapse Overlooking a rapidly progressive fibrotic variant that requires escalated treatment Alveolar epithelial injury triggers an exuberant organising repair response in which fibroblasts and myofibroblasts migrate into alveolar spaces, ducts and terminal bronchioles to form plugs of loose connective tissue. Because the underlying lung architecture is preserved, the process is typically reversible, distinguishing it from the fibrosing interstitial pneumonias. When no precipitating cause is identified the disorder is termed cryptogenic. Most patients recover fully with corticosteroid therapy; relapses during dose reduction are frequent but usually respond to re-treatment, and only a minority follow a rapidly progressive fibrosing course.

Cryptogenic organising pneumonia — COP, idiopathic bronchiolitis obliterans organising pneumonia, idiopathic BOOP, organising pneumonia Community-acquired or atypical infective pneumonia Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia Lymphoma or bronchoalveolar-pattern adenocarcinoma Vasculitis (e.g. granulomatosis with polyangiitis) Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease High-resolution CT to identify migratory peripheral/peribronchial consolidation, the reversed halo sign, and perilobular opacities Bronchoalveolar lavage showing mixed cellularity, useful mainly to exclude infection, eosinophilia, and malignancy Surgical or transbronchial (including cryobiopsy) lung biopsy demonstrating intraluminal granulation-tissue plugs Connective tissue disease and vasculitis serology to detect a secondary cause Review of drug history and prior radiotherapy as potential triggers Pulmonary function tests, typically showing a restrictive defect with reduced gas transfer A subacute illness with cough, breathlessness, malaise, low-grade fever, and weight loss over weeks, often mistaken initially for a community-acquired pneumonia that fails to respond to antibiotics The term cryptogenic denotes the idiopathic form; identical organising pneumonia can be secondary to infection, drugs, connective tissue disease, radiation, or aspiration High-resolution CT typically shows patchy peripheral or peribronchial consolidation and ground-glass opacity that is frequently migratory over time Suggestive CT signs include the reversed halo (atoll) sign and a perilobular pattern of consolidation Histology shows intraluminal plugs of granulation tissue (Masson bodies) within distal airspaces and alveolar ducts, with preserved lung architecture Response to corticosteroids is characteristically prompt and often dramatic, which supports the diagnosis Relapse is common when steroids are tapered too quickly, so treatment is usually prolonged and reduced gradually Always search for a secondary cause before labelling organising pneumonia as cryptogenic Rapidly progressive or fulminant respiratory failure suggesting an aggressive fibrosing variant Failure to improve with corticosteroids, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Features pointing to an underlying vasculitis, connective tissue disease, or malignancy Frequent relapse on tapering requiring re-evaluation and treatment intensification Persisting with repeated antibiotic courses for a 'pneumonia' that is actually organising pneumonia Labelling the disease cryptogenic without excluding drug, infection, radiation, and connective tissue disease causes Tapering corticosteroids too rapidly and precipitating relapse Relying on non-specific bronchoalveolar lavage findings rather than correlating imaging and, when needed, histology Organising pneumonia is a stereotyped repair response of the distal lung to epithelial injury. Damage to the alveolar and bronchiolar epithelium allows leakage of plasma proteins and recruitment of fibroblasts that organise into buds of granulation tissue filling the alveolar ducts and alveoli (Masson bodies), sometimes extending into respiratory bronchioles. Because the underlying lung architecture and interstitial framework are preserved, the process is largely reversible and responds well to corticosteroids. When no trigger such as infection, drug, radiation, or connective tissue disease is identified, the disorder is termed cryptogenic organising pneumonia. Most patients with cryptogenic organising pneumonia respond well and often completely to corticosteroids, although relapses during dose reduction are common; a minority have a progressive fibrosing course with a poorer outcome.

Cryptorchidism — undescended testis, undescended testicle, maldescended testis, empty scrotum Retractile testis (a normal variant due to an active cremasteric reflex) Ascending or acquired undescended testis Anorchia or vanishing testis (testicular regression) Ectopic testis lying outside the normal line of descent Disorder of sex development presenting with bilateral impalpable gonads Congenital adrenal hyperplasia in an undervirilised or apparently 'cryptorchid' infant Careful, warm-handed physical examination to determine whether the testis is palpable and retractile Karyotype and disorder-of-sex-development assessment when gonads are bilaterally impalpable or ambiguity is present Serum LH, FSH, testosterone, and anti-Müllerian hormone/inhibin B to assess for testicular tissue hCG stimulation test to detect functioning testicular tissue in bilateral non-palpable cases Diagnostic laparoscopy to localise or confirm absence of an intra-abdominal testis Adrenal hormone profile (including 17-hydroxyprogesterone) where congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a concern The most common genital anomaly in male infants, defined by failure of one or both testes to reach a normal scrotal position, and more frequent in preterm boys It must be distinguished from a retractile testis, which can be manipulated into the scrotum and remains there, and which does not require surgery Spontaneous descent may occur in the first months of life, but is unlikely after around 6 months of corrected age, after which surgical correction is planned The undescended testis carries an increased lifetime risk of malignancy (typically a germ cell tumour) and of impaired fertility, particularly with bilateral or intra-abdominal testes Bilateral non-palpable testes, especially with any genital ambiguity or hypospadias, may indicate a disorder of sex development or congenital adrenal hyperplasia and require urgent karyotype and hormonal evaluation Orchidopexy, ideally performed in infancy, relocates and fixes the testis in the scrotum to optimise fertility potential and to allow easier examination for later malignancy An acquired or ascending testis can present in an older boy whose testis was previously scrotal, and also warrants surgical correction Bilateral non-palpable testes with any genital ambiguity, which may represent a virilised female with congenital adrenal hyperplasia and a salt-wasting risk A previously descended testis that has ascended, requiring surgical referral Acute pain and swelling in the region of an undescended testis suggesting torsion A new inguinal or abdominal mass raising concern about malignant change Mistaking a retractile testis for a truly undescended one and performing unnecessary surgery Failing to recognise bilateral impalpable testes as a potential endocrine and disorder-of-sex-development emergency Deferring orchidopexy well beyond infancy and losing the fertility and surveillance benefits of early correction Relying on imaging to 'find' an impalpable testis rather than proceeding to laparoscopy Overlooking an acquired ascending testis in an older boy assumed to have been treated Testicular descent proceeds in two hormonally regulated phases: a transabdominal phase governed largely by insulin-like factor 3 acting on the gubernaculum, and an inguinoscrotal phase dependent on androgen action. Disruption of these processes, through hormonal, mechanical, or genetic factors, leaves the testis arrested along its normal path of descent, most often in the inguinal region. The abnormally high position exposes the testis to a warmer environment than the scrotum, which impairs germ cell maturation over time and contributes to reduced fertility, while the underlying developmental abnormality also predisposes to malignant change. Bilateral non-palpable testes may reflect anorchia, intra-abdominal testes, or an underlying disorder of sex development. Early orchidopexy improves the outlook for fertility and facilitates surveillance, but an increased relative risk of testicular malignancy persists and fertility is lower with bilateral or intra-abdominal disease; unilateral corrected cryptorchidism is generally compatible with normal paternity.

Cryptosporidiosis — Cryptosporidium infection, crypto, cryptosporidial diarrhoea Other protozoal enteritides (giardiasis, cyclosporiasis, microsporidiosis) Bacterial and viral gastroenteritis Other opportunistic enteric infections in HIV Inflammatory bowel disease Non-infective malabsorption syndromes Other opportunistic causes of chronic diarrhoea in advanced HIV Small bowel malabsorption of non-infective cause Secretory diarrhoea from other pathogens Modified acid-fast (Kinyoun) staining of stool for oocysts Stool antigen detection or PCR for sensitive diagnosis HIV testing and CD4 count assessment when severe or chronic Evaluation of hydration and electrolyte status Imaging or biliary studies if cholangiopathy is suspected in the immunocompromised A protozoal infection caused by Cryptosporidium species, transmitted faecal-orally through contaminated water, food or contact, with a very low infectious dose In immunocompetent hosts it causes a self-limiting watery diarrhoea, but in the immunocompromised, especially advanced HIV, it can cause severe, chronic and life-threatening diarrhoea A recognised cause of waterborne outbreaks because the oocysts are highly resistant to routine chlorination An important contributor to childhood diarrhoea and to malnutrition and growth faltering in Indian children In profound immunosuppression infection may extend beyond the gut to the biliary tract, causing sclerosing cholangitis, and to the respiratory tract Restoration of immune function, particularly antiretroviral therapy in HIV, is central to control in immunocompromised patients Diagnosis requires specific tests: modified acid-fast staining of stool, antigen detection or PCR, as the oocysts are missed on routine microscopy Management emphasises rehydration; antiprotozoal drug options are limited and work best when immunity is restored Severe or high-volume dehydrating diarrhoea, especially in infants or the immunocompromised Chronic diarrhoea with weight loss in a patient with advanced HIV/AIDS Right upper quadrant pain and cholestasis suggesting biliary involvement Failure of diarrhoea to settle, signalling underlying immunodeficiency Failing to request specific staining, antigen or PCR tests, so oocysts are missed on routine stool microscopy Not testing for HIV in a patient with severe or persistent cryptosporidial diarrhoea Relying on antiprotozoal drugs alone in the immunocompromised without addressing the underlying immune deficit Underestimating waterborne outbreak potential given oocyst resistance to chlorination Ingested Cryptosporidium oocysts release sporozoites that invade the apical surface of intestinal epithelial cells, residing in an intracellular but extracytoplasmic compartment. Infection blunts villi, impairs absorption and increases secretion, producing a watery, non-bloody diarrhoea. In immunocompetent people a robust cellular immune response clears the parasite, but when T-cell immunity is deficient the organism proliferates unchecked, causing high-volume chronic diarrhoea, malabsorption and spread to biliary and respiratory epithelium. In immunocompetent individuals the illness resolves spontaneously over one to two weeks. In severely immunocompromised patients it can be chronic, debilitating and fatal unless immune function is restored, and outcome is closely tied to recovery of cellular immunity.

Crystal arthritis (gout / pseudogout) — Joint aspiration + polarised microscopy Serum urate (off-attack) Septic arthritis must be excluded by aspiration Palindromic rheumatism (Harrison 22e p.2958) Psoriatic arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2958) Osteoarthritis - CPPD pseudo-osteoarthritis variant mimics progressive OA, often in atypical joints (MCP, wrist, elbow, shoulder, ankle) (Harrison 22e p.2960-2961) Rheumatoid arthritis - chronic symmetric CPP synovitis can clinically resemble RA (Harrison 22e p.2961) Neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy - severe destructive CPPD may radiographically mimic it (Harrison 22e p.2961) Cellulitis - acute gout flare with warm, red, swollen periarticular tissue may mimic cellulitis (pseudocellulitis) (Harrison 22e p.2958) Septic arthritis - crystal arthritis closely mimics it; aspiration with Gram stain and culture is essential, especially as bacterial infection can coexist with crystals in synovial fluid (Harrison 22e p.2958, p.2961) Polarized light microscopy of synovial fluid - MSU: needle/rod-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent; CPP: rhomboid/rod-shaped, weakly positively or non-birefringent; apatite: non-birefringent (requires alizarin red S staining or electron microscopy); calcium oxalate: bipyramidal, variable/strong birefringence, alizarin red S positive (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961-2962) Synovial fluid Gram stain and culture to exclude coexisting septic arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2958, p.2961) Synovial fluid leukocyte count - gout flare typically 5000-75,000/uL; acute CPPD ~24,000/uL (range several thousand to 100,000); apatite and calcium oxalate usually <2000/uL (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961-2962) Arthrocentesis of an unaffected first MTP joint or knee between flares can still demonstrate MSU crystals (Harrison 22e p.2959) Plain radiographs - advanced gout: well-defined erosions with sclerotic/overhanging margins, soft tissue tophi; CPPD: punctate/linear chondrocalcinosis in fibrocartilage or hyaline cartilage (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961) Musculoskeletal ultrasound - double-contour sign over articular cartilage indicating MSU deposition; can also reveal chondrocalcinosis in CPPD (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961) Dual-energy CT - identifies MSU crystals by chemical composition (Harrison 22e p.2959) Baseline labs to assess comorbidities and treatment safety: serum creatinine, liver function tests, hemoglobin, WBC count, HbA1c, lipids (Harrison 22e p.2959) In CPPD patients under 50, evaluate for metabolic/familial causes: serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, magnesium, iron, transferrin (Harrison 22e p.2960) HLA-B*5801 screening before allopurinol in high-prevalence populations (Southeast Asian, Pacific Islander/Native Hawaiian, Black patients) to reduce risk of severe cutaneous adverse reactions (knowledge point) (Harrison 22e p.2960) Acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) mimics acute gout flares (Harrison 22e p.2960) Apatite (basic calcium phosphate) deposition disease (Harrison 22e p.2961) Calcium oxalate arthropathy - acute presentation may be indistinguishable from MSU, CPP, or apatite crystal disease (Harrison 22e p.2962) Osteoarthritis (pseudo-osteoarthritis pattern of CPPD) (Harrison 22e p.2961) Initial gout flares are usually monoarticular; the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) is involved in 70-90% of cases, followed by tarsal joints, ankles, and knees. Oligo- and polyarticular flares emerge over time (Harrison 22e p.2958). Gout flares often begin at night to early morning, are among the most painful conditions humans experience, and the affected joint becomes warm, red, tender, and very swollen, frequently mimicking cellulitis (pseudocellulitis) (Harrison 22e p.2958). Untreated flares usually subside spontaneously within 1-2 weeks, with symptom-free intervals (intercritical gout) until the next episode (Harrison 22e p.2958). Serum urate can be normal or low during an acute flare because inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 are uricosuric and can lower urate by about 2 mg/dL; seek historical or post-flare urate values instead (Harrison 22e p.2959). In CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) the knee is most commonly affected, followed by the wrist; the first MTP joint (podagra) is rarely involved, a useful distinguishing clue from gout (Harrison 22e p.2960). Initial acute CPPD attacks tend to last longer than typical gout flares, sometimes weeks to months (Harrison 22e p.2960). Acute CPPD can be precipitated by trauma, severe medical illness, or surgery (especially parathyroidectomy, which rapidly lowers serum calcium and magnesium and sheds crystals) (Harrison 22e p.2960). Women account for only about 5-20% of gout patients; most are postmenopausal, elderly, and often on diuretics with coexisting osteoarthritis, hypertension, or mild renal insufficiency. Premenopausal gout is rare (Harrison 22e p.2958). Hyperuricemia in a prepubertal boy should prompt consideration of inherited enzyme defects such as HPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan spectrum) or PRPP synthetase superactivity (Harrison 22e p.2958). Apatite (basic calcium phosphate) arthropathy can cause an extremely destructive arthropathy of the elderly, classically the shoulder (Milwaukee shoulder), with low synovial fluid leukocyte counts despite dramatic symptoms (Harrison 22e p.2961). Hyperuricemia and gout are part of the insulin-resistance syndrome and associate with cardiometabolic-kidney comorbidities: obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction, stroke, CKD, and urate nephrolithiasis (Harrison 22e p.2956). Crystal-proven arthritis does not exclude concurrent septic arthritis - bacterial infection can coexist with MSU or CPP crystals in synovial fluid; always Gram stain and culture (Harrison 22e p.2958, p.2961) Acute CPPD can produce systemic features (fever, chills, raised acute-phase reactants), with low-grade fever in up to 50% and temperatures occasionally as high as 40C - mandates microbial culture to exclude infection (Harrison 22e p.2960, p.2961) CPPD onset before age 50 warrants workup for underlying metabolic disease (hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypophosphatasia, hypomagnesemia) or hereditary CPPD (Harrison 22e p.2960) Relying on a normal serum urate during an acute flare to exclude gout - urate is often normal or low at flare onset (Harrison 22e p.2959). Attributing a destructive 'osteoarthritis' in atypical joints (MCP, wrist, elbow, shoulder, ankle) to primary OA rather than recognizing pseudo-osteoarthritis from CPPD (Harrison 22e p.2961). Assuming chondrocalcinosis on imaging is always CPPD - calcium oxalate deposition in chronic renal failure is an exception (Harrison 22e p.2961). Missing apatite arthropathy because individual apatite crystals are not visible on routine polarized light microscopy and need alizarin red S staining or electron microscopy (Harrison 22e p.2961). Overlooking inherited enzyme defects when hyperuricemia/gout presents in a young patient, particularly a prepubertal boy (Harrison 22e p.2958). Gout arises from an increased body urate pool due to chronic hyperuricemia, leading to supersaturation and crystallization of monosodium urate (MSU) within joints and connective tissue. Hyperuricemia is predominantly due to impaired renal urate excretion (~90%) and less often urate overproduction (~10%); a minority (~10%) of cases reflect inherited metabolic disorders (PRPP synthetase superactivity, HPRT deficiency). Crystal shedding from inert synovial deposits, triggered by metabolic factors, diuresis, rapid urate changes (including urate-lowering therapy initiation), local trauma, or medical illness, activates resident synovial phagocytes (monocytes/macrophages, mast cells) and the NLRP3 inflammasome, generating IL-1beta and other proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha). Phagocytosis of MSU crystals by neutrophils with a respiratory burst amplifies the acute inflammatory response. Persistent MSU deposition produces tophi (granulomatous inflammation around crystals) and chronic erosive gouty arthritis. In CPPD, increased cartilage inorganic pyrophosphate (largely from extracellular ATP breakdown, regulated by the ANKH transporter) combines with calcium to form CPP crystals; their release similarly drives inflammasome-mediated inflammation, analogous to hyperuricemia in gout. Apatite and calcium oxalate crystals can likewise stimulate synovial cell proliferation and release of proteases, collagenases, and prostaglandin E2, contributing to joint destruction (Harrison 22e p.2956-2962). Untreated gout flares typically resolve spontaneously within 1-2 weeks, but recurrent flares over years can progress to chronic gouty arthritis with persistent low-grade synovitis, subcutaneous tophi, joint deformity, and erosive bony destruction. Controlling the underlying chronic hyperuricemia (urate-lowering therapy to a subsaturation target) can prevent recurrent flares and dissolve tophi, generally requiring lifelong therapy. For chronic CPPD there is no means to remove established CPP crystal deposits from cartilage and synovium (unlike urate lowering in gout), and progressive destructive large-joint disease may require joint replacement. Apatite-associated destructive arthropathy (e.g., Milwaukee shoulder) progresses indolently and may also lead to joint replacement (Harrison 22e p.2958-2962).

CTLA4 haploinsufficiency — CTLA4, CHAI, CTLA-4 haploinsufficiency with autoimmune infiltration, CTLA4 insufficiency Common variable immunodeficiency LRBA deficiency Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS) IPEX and IPEX-like syndromes Activated PI3K-delta syndrome Sarcoidosis or other granulomatous disease Lymphocyte subsets and quantification of regulatory T cells Flow cytometry for CTLA-4 protein expression and transendocytosis function where available Serum immunoglobulins and specific antibody responses documenting evolving hypogammaglobulinaemia Autoantibody screen and direct antiglobulin test for autoimmune cytopenias CTLA4 gene sequencing for heterozygous loss-of-function variants Organ-directed imaging and biopsy for interstitial lung disease or enteropathy Presents as a disorder of immune dysregulation combining autoimmunity, lymphoproliferation and a variable degree of immunodeficiency rather than pure infection susceptibility Common features include autoimmune cytopenias, enteropathy with chronic diarrhoea, and lymphocytic infiltration of the lungs, gut, liver, marrow and central nervous system Progressive hypogammaglobulinaemia frequently develops, so the phenotype can overlap with and be misdiagnosed as common variable immunodeficiency Respiratory disease may take the form of granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease Penetrance is incomplete and expressivity highly variable, so asymptomatic carriers occur within affected families Inheritance is autosomal dominant, resulting from heterozygous loss-of-function variants that reduce the dose of functional CTLA-4 protein There is an increased risk of lymphoma and of end-organ autoimmune damage over time CTLA4-Ig fusion therapy (abatacept) can replace the missing inhibitory signal and control severe dysregulation, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is used in refractory disease New or progressive neurological deficit from CNS lymphocytic infiltration Rapidly enlarging lymphadenopathy or organomegaly suggesting lymphoma Severe autoimmune cytopenia with bleeding or profound anaemia Progressive breathlessness from interstitial lung disease Refractory enteropathy with malnutrition Diagnosing common variable immunodeficiency and stopping short of genetic testing that reveals a treatable pathway defect Overlooking asymptomatic carriers because of incomplete penetrance Attributing multi-organ infiltration to sarcoidosis or malignancy without immunological evaluation Failing to distinguish it from the phenotypically similar LRBA deficiency Delaying targeted therapy until irreversible organ damage has occurred CTLA-4 is an inhibitory receptor expressed by regulatory and activated T cells that outcompetes the co-stimulatory receptor CD28 for the ligands CD80 and CD86 and removes them from antigen-presenting cells by transendocytosis, thereby restraining T-cell activation. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants leave insufficient CTLA-4 protein (haploinsufficiency), impairing regulatory T-cell function and allowing unchecked effector T-cell activation and lymphocytic infiltration of multiple organs. The resulting loss of tolerance manifests as widespread autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation, while progressive B-cell dysfunction produces hypogammaglobulinaemia and susceptibility to infection. The disorder is chronic and often progressive with cumulative autoimmune organ damage and a raised lymphoma risk; targeted CTLA4-Ig replacement and, in severe cases, transplantation can achieve substantial disease control and improve outlook.

over the medial epicondyle Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to localise the lesion and demonstrate conduction slowing across the elbow Provocative testing with the elbow flexion test and Tinel percussion over the cubital tunnel Plain radiographs of the elbow for osteoarthritis, deformity or old fracture Ultrasound to assess nerve enlargement and demonstrate dynamic subluxation MRI when a compressive mass lesion or ganglion is suspected Cervical spine imaging when radiculopathy needs exclusion The second most common compression neuropathy of the upper limb after carpal tunnel syndrome Patients report paraesthesiae of the little finger and the ulnar half of the ring finger, characteristically provoked or worsened by sustained elbow flexion Weakness of grip and pinch develops with wasting of the ulnar-innervated intrinsic muscles, notably the first dorsal interosseous and hypothenar eminence A positive Froment sign (thumb interphalangeal flexion substituting for a weak adductor pollicis during key pinch) indicates significant motor involvement Wartenberg sign describes persistent abduction of the little finger from unopposed extensor digiti minimi and weak intrinsics Potential compression sites include the arcade of Struthers, the medial intermuscular septum, the retrocondylar groove and Osborne band, and the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris The ulnar paradox means a more proximal lesion produces less clawing than a distal one because the flexor digitorum profundus to the ulnar digits is also weakened Generic management includes activity modification, night-time elbow extension splinting, and surgical in-situ decompression or anterior transposition for progressive or severe disease Rapidly progressive intrinsic muscle wasting or dense motor loss requiring prompt surgical decompression An apical lung or supraclavicular mass suggesting a Pancoast tumour Features of myelopathy or motor neurone disease rather than a focal entrapment Bilateral, rapidly worsening symptoms suggesting a systemic or central cause Attributing ulnar symptoms to the wrist when the lesion is at the elbow, or vice versa Overlooking a double-crush lesion combining cervical and peripheral compression Failing to detect a subluxating nerve that dictates the choice of surgical procedure Inadequate protection or handling of the nerve leading to persistent or worsened symptoms after surgery The ulnar nerve is vulnerable as it passes behind the medial epicondyle through the cubital tunnel, where elbow flexion narrows the canal and increases both intraneural pressure and longitudinal traction on the nerve. Repetitive or sustained flexion, a shallow or unstable retrocondylar groove allowing subluxation, cubitus valgus, osteophytes, ganglia or previous trauma contribute to injury. Sustained compression first produces focal demyelination with conduction slowing across the elbow and, if unrelieved, progresses to axonal loss with intrinsic muscle wasting and fixed sensory deficit. Early and mild cases often improve with conservative measures, whereas established intrinsic wasting and long-standing sensory loss may not recover fully even after successful decompression, so timely diagnosis is important.

Currarino syndrome (sacral agenesis + anorectal + presacral mass) — Currarino triad, Currarino-Silverman syndrome, sacral agenesis with presacral mass, ASP triad Isolated anorectal malformation without sacral or presacral anomaly Sacrococcygeal teratoma Isolated anterior sacral meningocele Caudal regression syndrome Hirschsprung disease as a cause of chronic constipation Tethered cord syndrome Sacral and pelvic radiographs to demonstrate the scimitar hemisacrum Pelvic and spinal MRI to characterise the presacral mass and detect tethered cord or meningocele Ultrasound of the spine and pelvis in the neonate MNX1 (HLXB9) genetic testing and screening of first-degree relatives Contrast studies or examination to define the anorectal anatomy Assessment for associated urogenital and spinal anomalies Defined by a triad of a sacral bony defect, an anorectal malformation, and a presacral mass The characteristic sacral anomaly is a hemisacrum with a crescentic (scimitar) sacral defect that spares the first sacral segment The anorectal component ranges from anal stenosis and chronic constipation to a frank anorectal malformation The presacral mass is most often an anterior meningocele, a teratoma, an enteric duplication cyst, or a combination of these Frequently familial with autosomal dominant inheritance linked to MNX1 (HLXB9) mutations, so family screening is worthwhile Chronic refractory constipation from birth, especially with a sacral abnormality on radiograph, should prompt evaluation for the triad Management is individualised, addressing the anorectal defect surgically and resecting or repairing the presacral mass with neurosurgical input for a meningocele Meningitis or signs of central nervous system infection from a communicating anterior meningocele Neurological deterioration suggesting tethered cord or cord compression Features raising concern for malignant change within a presacral teratoma Severe obstructive symptoms from a large presacral mass Recurrent urinary or faecal complications from the associated malformations Treating chronic constipation without imaging the sacrum and missing the underlying triad Overlooking an anterior meningocele and risking meningitis during transrectal or perineal procedures Assuming a presacral mass is benign without appropriate imaging and follow-up Failing to screen family members despite autosomal dominant inheritance Neglecting spinal cord tethering when planning management Currarino syndrome is a developmental disorder of the caudal cell mass and notochord, in which abnormal separation of the neuroectoderm and endoderm and defective sacral formation produce the characteristic combination of anomalies. Many cases carry mutations in the MNX1 (HLXB9) homeobox gene, which is important in caudal and hindgut development. The resulting hemisacrum leaves a persistent anterior sacral defect through which a presacral mass such as an anterior meningocele, teratoma, or enteric duplication protrudes, while concurrent maldevelopment of the hindgut yields the anorectal malformation or anal stenosis. Tethered cord and other spinal dysraphic features may coexist. With recognition of all three components and appropriate surgical and neurosurgical management, prognosis is generally good, though continence outcomes depend on the anorectal lesion and sacral integrity. Undiagnosed meningocele risks life-threatening meningitis, and a small proportion of presacral teratomas may undergo malignant transformation.

commonest cause of a Cushingoid appearance Simple exogenous obesity, where growth velocity is usually normal or increased Ectopic ACTH secretion, which is rare in children Adrenal adenoma or carcinoma causing ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease and Carney complex McCune-Albright syndrome Pseudo-Cushing states Documentation of the growth curve and height velocity alongside weight Late-night salivary or midnight serum cortisol to demonstrate loss of the diurnal rhythm 24-hour urinary free cortisol Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test Plasma ACTH to establish ACTH dependence Pituitary MRI, recognising that a microadenoma may be small or unseen Inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH stimulation to confirm the pituitary source and lateralisation In children an ACTH-secreting pituitary corticotroph adenoma is the commonest cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome beyond infancy The hallmark is weight gain together with growth arrest, so a decelerating height velocity in a child who is gaining weight should prompt evaluation Other features include facial rounding and plethora, striae, hypertension and fatigue, often more subtle than in adults Delayed or arrested puberty and declining school performance may occur The adenomas are usually small microadenomas that can be difficult to see on MRI Diagnosis follows the standard hypercortisolism workup with late-night salivary or serum cortisol, 24-hour urinary free cortisol and low-dose dexamethasone suppression, then confirmation of ACTH dependence Inferior petrosal sinus sampling is valuable to confirm a pituitary source and to lateralise when MRI is equivocal First-line treatment is transsphenoidal selective adenomectomy, after which catch-up growth and recovery of the axis need monitoring Progressive growth arrest with weight gain in a child Severe hypertension or hypokalaemia Very high cortisol or ACTH suggesting aggressive disease or an ectopic or adrenal malignancy Vertebral fracture from osteoporosis, or significant psychiatric disturbance Reassuring an obese child without checking the growth curve, since normal growth argues against Cushing disease and arrested growth is a red flag Over-relying on a normal or equivocal MRI to exclude a microadenoma Omitting inferior petrosal sinus sampling when imaging is negative but disease is ACTH-dependent Failing to anticipate and treat postoperative adrenal insufficiency and to monitor for recurrence Paediatric Cushing disease is caused by a corticotroph adenoma of the anterior pituitary that autonomously secretes ACTH, driving bilateral adrenal cortisol overproduction. Chronic glucocorticoid excess suppresses the growth hormone and IGF-1 axis and directly inhibits growth-plate chondrocytes and bone formation, so linear growth slows or halts even as adiposity increases, giving the characteristic divergence of the height and weight curves in children. Cortisol excess also suppresses gonadotropin secretion and so delays puberty, raises blood pressure, impairs glucose tolerance and alters mood and immune function. The tumours are usually microadenomas, and the excess ACTH retains partial responsiveness to high-dose glucocorticoid feedback, which underlies the diagnostic testing. Transsphenoidal surgery by an experienced neurosurgeon achieves remission in most children; catch-up growth is often incomplete so final height may be reduced, and there is a risk of persistent or recurrent disease requiring further surgery, radiotherapy or medical therapy, along with temporary secondary adrenal insufficiency during axis recovery.

Cushing syndrome — hypercortisolism, Cushing's syndrome, cortisol excess, Cushing disease (pituitary-dependent) Exogenous (iatrogenic) glucocorticoid effect Pseudo-Cushing states from severe obesity, depression, or heavy alcohol use Metabolic syndrome with central obesity Polycystic ovary syndrome Poorly controlled diabetes with weight gain Ectopic ACTH from neuroendocrine malignancy Late-night salivary cortisol to detect loss of the normal evening nadir 24-hour urinary free cortisol, ideally on more than one collection Low-dose (overnight or 48-hour) dexamethasone suppression testing Plasma ACTH to separate ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent disease Pituitary MRI, adrenal CT, or cross-sectional imaging for ectopic sources as directed by biochemistry Inferior petrosal sinus sampling to localise ACTH-dependent disease when imaging is equivocal Typical features include central weight gain, a rounded plethoric face, a dorsocervical fat pad, thin skin, and easy bruising Wide purple abdominal striae, proximal muscle weakness, and unexplained osteoporosis are among the more discriminating clinical signs Exogenous glucocorticoid use is by far the most common cause and should be excluded by careful drug history before pursuing endogenous disease Diagnosis proceeds in two stages: first confirm cortisol excess, then determine whether it is ACTH-dependent or ACTH-independent Screening rests on demonstrating loss of normal cortisol regulation using late-night salivary cortisol, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, or a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test A suppressed ACTH points to an adrenal source, whereas a normal or elevated ACTH indicates a pituitary tumour or an ectopic source Pituitary-dependent disease (Cushing disease) accounts for most endogenous ACTH-dependent cases, while ectopic ACTH is often from neuroendocrine tumours Associated metabolic consequences include hypertension, glucose intolerance or diabetes, dyslipidaemia, and increased thrombotic and infection risk Definitive management is directed at the underlying cause, most often surgical removal of the responsible tumour Rapid onset with marked hypokalaemia and pigmentation suggesting aggressive ectopic ACTH secretion New severe hypertension, hyperglycaemia, or thromboembolism from florid hypercortisolism Features of adrenal carcinoma such as very high androgen or cortisol levels with a large adrenal mass Severe proximal weakness, fractures, or psychosis reflecting advanced disease Overlooking exogenous steroid exposure, including inhaled, topical, or injected preparations Interpreting a single borderline test as diagnostic rather than repeating and combining screening tests Confusing pseudo-Cushing states with true disease during acute illness, depression, or alcohol excess Assuming a pituitary microadenoma on imaging proves the source without confirmatory biochemistry Cushing syndrome results from chronic exposure to excess glucocorticoid. This may be exogenous, from prescribed or surreptitious steroid use, or endogenous. Endogenous disease is divided into ACTH-dependent forms, in which a pituitary corticotroph adenoma or an ectopic ACTH-secreting tumour drives adrenal cortisol output, and ACTH-independent forms, in which an adrenal adenoma, carcinoma, or bilateral hyperplasia autonomously produces cortisol. Sustained cortisol excess disrupts the normal negative-feedback of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, abolishes the circadian rhythm of cortisol, and produces widespread catabolic, metabolic, immunosuppressive, and mineralocorticoid effects on multiple tissues. With successful treatment of the underlying cause many features regress over months, though hypertension, bone loss, and psychological effects may persist; untreated hypercortisolism carries substantial cardiovascular, metabolic, infective, and thrombotic mortality, and ectopic ACTH from malignancy has a poor outlook.

Cutaneous angiosarcoma — angiosarcoma of skin, cutaneous malignant haemangioendothelioma, Stewart-Treves syndrome (lymphoedema-associated) Bruise or haematoma (for the early patch stage) Amelanotic or nodular melanoma Kaposi sarcoma Squamous or basal cell carcinoma of the scalp Benign vascular lesions such as haemangioma or pyogenic granuloma Cellulitis or rosacea (for facial erythematous change) Atypical fibroxanthoma / pleomorphic dermal sarcoma Incisional biopsy, often multiple, given ill-defined and multifocal spread Histopathology demonstrating anastomosing atypical vascular channels Immunohistochemistry for endothelial markers (CD31, ERG) and D2-40, plus MYC assessment Cross-sectional and chest imaging to assess local extent and pulmonary metastasis Mapping biopsies to define subclinical margins before surgery Multidisciplinary sarcoma-team assessment for combined surgery and radiotherapy A malignant tumour of vascular (endothelial) origin that classically affects the scalp and face of elderly patients Presents deceptively as a bruise-like violaceous patch or plaque that fails to resolve, often with ill-defined margins and later nodularity or bleeding Three main clinical settings are idiopathic head-and-neck disease in the elderly, post-irradiation angiosarcoma, and lymphoedema-associated Stewart-Treves syndrome Stewart-Treves syndrome arises in chronically lymphoedematous limbs, historically after mastectomy with axillary clearance Histology shows irregular anastomosing vascular channels dissecting collagen, lined by atypical endothelial cells, with variable solid and epithelioid areas Endothelial markers such as CD31, ERG, and often the lymphatic marker D2-40 confirm the diagnosis; MYC amplification supports radiation- and lymphoedema-associated forms Wide surgical excision with radiotherapy is the mainstay, but multifocal subclinical spread makes clear margins difficult and recurrence common A persistent bruise-like scalp or facial lesion in an elderly patient that does not resolve New vascular tumour arising in a chronically lymphoedematous limb (Stewart-Treves) Cutaneous vascular malignancy within a previously irradiated field Rapid growth, ulceration, or bleeding of an ill-defined violaceous plaque Respiratory symptoms suggesting pulmonary metastasis Dismissing an early bruise-like lesion as a simple contusion or rosacea and delaying biopsy Underestimating margins because of diffuse multifocal subclinical spread Failing to consider angiosarcoma in a chronically lymphoedematous limb or previously irradiated site Not obtaining endothelial immunohistochemistry when the tumour is poorly differentiated or epithelioid Cutaneous angiosarcoma is an aggressive malignancy of endothelial-cell origin in which atypical cells form irregular, anastomosing vascular channels that dissect through dermal collagen and infiltrate widely. Several predisposing contexts are recognised: chronic ultraviolet and actinic damage of the head and neck in the elderly; prior therapeutic irradiation; and long-standing lymphoedema, as in Stewart-Treves syndrome following axillary node clearance, where amplification of the MYC oncogene is characteristic in radiation- and lymphoedema-associated tumours. The neoplastic endothelium retains vascular differentiation, expressing markers such as CD31 and ERG, but grows in a diffuse, often multifocal fashion with extensive subclinical spread that underlies the high rates of local recurrence and early haematogenous metastasis, particularly to lung. Cutaneous angiosarcoma has a poor prognosis with high rates of local recurrence and early metastasis, particularly to the lungs; extensive subclinical spread frequently precludes clear surgical margins, and larger tumour size and head-and-neck or metastatic disease predict worse survival.

women as rapidly growing red-blue tumours on one or both lower legs and carries a markedly worse outlook, though morphologically identical tumours can arise elsewhere Immunophenotype separates the subtypes: follicle centre lymphoma is BCL6 positive with variable CD10 and usually lacks strong BCL2, marginal zone lymphoma shows monotypic light-chain restriction with plasmacytic differentiation, and leg type expresses strong BCL2, MUM1/IRF4 and FOXP1 Primary cutaneous marginal zone lymphoma has been linked to Borrelia burgdorferi infection in some endemic regions, and antibiotic therapy has occasionally induced regression Indolent forms are treated with skin-directed measures such as excision, radiotherapy or intralesional therapy, whereas leg type requires systemic anthracycline-based chemoimmunotherapy Rapidly enlarging red-blue tumour on the lower leg of an elderly patient, suggesting aggressive leg-type disease Ulceration, systemic B symptoms or a rising lactate dehydrogenase Lymphadenopathy or organomegaly indicating possible systemic dissemination Extracutaneous involvement detected on staging investigations Misclassifying a systemic lymphoma with skin involvement as primary cutaneous by omitting adequate staging Confusing reactive cutaneous lymphoid hyperplasia with a low-grade B-cell lymphoma Over-treating indolent disease with aggressive systemic chemotherapy Assuming BCL2 positivity necessarily indicates nodal follicular lymphoma Missing leg-type diffuse large B-cell lymphoma when the tumours arise outside the lower legs Cutaneous B-cell lymphomas result from clonal proliferation of B lymphocytes at differing stages of maturation that home to and expand within the skin. Marginal zone lymphoma derives from post-germinal-centre marginal zone / memory B cells and may be driven by chronic antigenic stimulation, including Borrelia in endemic areas. Follicle centre lymphoma arises from germinal-centre B cells but, unlike its nodal follicular counterpart, usually lacks the t(14;18) BCL2 rearrangement. Leg-type diffuse large B-cell lymphoma originates from activated non-germinal-centre B cells, characteristically over-expressing BCL2 and MUM1/IRF4 and frequently harbouring MYD88 mutation and other lesions that drive constitutive NF-kB signalling, underlying its aggressive behaviour. Primary cutaneous marginal zone and follicle centre lymphomas are indolent with excellent long-term survival despite frequent cutaneous relapses, whereas primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, leg type, has a substantially poorer prognosis, worsened by multiple lesions and leg location.

cutaneous calcinosis — calcinosis cutis, cutaneous calcification Calciphylaxis (calcific uraemic arteriolopathy) when painful ischaemic ulceration predominates Cutaneous ossification (osteoma cutis) and osteoma cutis of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy Gouty tophi and other crystal deposition Subcutaneous nodules of rheumatoid disease or rheumatic fever Epidermoid or pilar cysts and other adnexal tumours Gouty or xanthomatous nodules Foreign-body granuloma Serum calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and alkaline phosphatase to define the metabolic type Renal function tests to identify chronic kidney disease Plain radiography (and where needed CT) to map the distribution and burden of calcification Skin biopsy with von Kossa or alizarin red staining to confirm calcium deposition Autoimmune serology including antinuclear and myositis-specific antibodies when connective tissue disease is suspected Screening for sarcoidosis or occult malignancy where metastatic calcification is unexplained Deposition of insoluble calcium salts in the skin and subcutis, presenting as firm white or yellow papules, nodules or plaques that may ulcerate and extrude chalky, toothpaste-like material Classified into four main types: dystrophic (much the commonest), metastatic, idiopathic and iatrogenic, with calciphylaxis considered a distinct and dangerous vascular variant Dystrophic calcinosis occurs in damaged tissue with normal serum calcium and phosphate, classically complicating connective tissue disease such as juvenile dermatomyositis and systemic sclerosis (the C of CREST) Metastatic calcinosis reflects a deranged calcium-phosphate product, seen in chronic kidney disease, hyperparathyroidism, hypervitaminosis D, sarcoidosis and milk-alkali syndrome Idiopathic forms include idiopathic scrotal calcinosis, subepidermal calcified nodules and tumoral calcinosis, while iatrogenic disease follows extravasation of calcium- or phosphate-containing infusions Investigation is directed at the calcium-phosphate axis and any underlying connective tissue disease, with radiographs delineating the extent and distribution of deposits Treatment is difficult and evidence is limited; options include correcting metabolic drivers, medical therapies such as sodium thiosulfate, warfarin, bisphosphonates, minocycline and diltiazem, and surgical excision of symptomatic deposits Rapidly enlarging, exquisitely painful retiform ulceration suggesting calciphylaxis Secondary infection or systemic sepsis arising from ulcerated deposits Widespread metastatic calcification indicating severe metabolic derangement Functional loss from periarticular deposits causing contracture or nerve compression Assuming normal serum calcium excludes significant disease, when most cutaneous calcinosis is dystrophic with a normal calcium-phosphate axis Overlooking an underlying connective tissue disease, particularly juvenile dermatomyositis or systemic sclerosis Missing calciphylaxis, which requires urgent recognition and differs fundamentally in management and prognosis Aggressive surgery precipitating poor wound healing, recurrence at operative sites and new dystrophic deposits Failing to review medications and infusions as an iatrogenic source of calcium loading Cutaneous calcinosis results from precipitation of calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) or amorphous calcium salts within the dermis or subcutaneous tissue. In dystrophic disease, local tissue injury, inflammation and mitochondrial calcium overload in damaged cells provide a nidus for mineralisation despite normal circulating calcium and phosphate; release of phosphate-binding proteins and denatured collagen and elastin favour crystal nucleation. In metastatic disease, a raised calcium-phosphate product drives deposition in otherwise normal tissue, particularly where local pH or tissue conditions promote precipitation. Idiopathic and iatrogenic forms reflect, respectively, unexplained local deposition and direct introduction of calcium salts, while calciphylaxis involves medial calcification and thrombosis of small dermal and subcutaneous vessels causing ischaemic necrosis. Prognosis depends on the type and underlying cause: idiopathic and iatrogenic deposits may resolve or remain stable, whereas dystrophic calcinosis of connective tissue disease is often chronic, recurrent and resistant to therapy. Metastatic calcinosis improves when the calcium-phosphate disturbance is corrected, while calciphylaxis carries high morbidity and mortality.

Cutaneous Larva Migrans — CLM, creeping eruption, sandworm disease, hookworm-related cutaneous larva migrans Larva currens due to Strongyloides (faster-moving track, often perianal) Scabies Contact dermatitis Tinea (especially of the feet) Erythema migrans of Lyme disease Loiasis or other migratory parasitic eruptions in the appropriate exposure setting Diagnosis is clinical, based on the characteristic migrating track and exposure history Dermoscopy may help visualise the larval track Blood eosinophilia is variable and non-specific Biopsy is usually unhelpful because the larva lies ahead of the visible track and is rarely captured Assessment for secondary bacterial infection when the site is inflamed or purulent The hallmark is an intensely itchy, serpiginous (snake-like), slightly raised erythematous track that advances a short distance each day It commonly affects the feet, buttocks, and other skin that contacts contaminated sand or soil, reflecting exposure during beach holidays or barefoot activity in warm climates Take a travel and exposure history, as most cases in temperate regions are imported from tropical and subtropical areas The larva itself lies just ahead of the visible track, so the leading edge marks its current position It is a self-limiting zoonotic infestation because the human is a dead-end host in which the animal hookworm larva cannot complete its life cycle Antihelminthic therapy shortens symptoms and is warranted for troublesome disease; the itch responds as the larva dies and the track resolves Secondary bacterial infection from scratching and, less often, a localised allergic reaction can complicate the picture Preventive advice includes wearing footwear and using barriers on contaminated sand or soil Extensive involvement or numerous tracks suggesting heavy exposure or an immunocompromised host Rapidly moving perianal tracks or features suggesting Strongyloides, which can disseminate and requires different management Signs of secondary bacterial infection such as spreading erythema, pain, or pus Systemic symptoms or respiratory features prompting reconsideration of a diagnosis with visceral involvement Failing to elicit a travel or sand-exposure history and missing the diagnosis Confusing it with the faster-moving larva currens of Strongyloides, which carries a risk of dissemination Performing an unhelpful biopsy at the visible track rather than treating clinically Overlooking secondary bacterial infection driven by scratching Cutaneous larva migrans is caused by the larvae of animal hookworms, most often Ancylostoma species from dogs and cats, whose eggs are shed in animal faeces and hatch into infective larvae in warm, moist sand or soil. On contact these larvae penetrate intact human skin but lack the enzymes to cross the basement membrane, so they remain trapped in the epidermis. As the larva migrates it provokes a local eosinophilic inflammatory and hypersensitivity response that produces the itchy, advancing serpiginous track. Because humans are accidental dead-end hosts, the parasite cannot mature or disseminate and eventually dies, giving the self-limiting course. The condition is benign and self-limiting, as the larva dies within weeks to a few months even without treatment; antihelminthic therapy shortens the intensely itchy course and speeds resolution, and lasting sequelae are uncommon apart from transient post-inflammatory change.

Cutaneous mastocytosis — mastocytosis of the skin Systemic mastocytosis with skin involvement Urticaria Juvenile xanthogranuloma or other histiocytoses Post-inflammatory pigmentation Bullous disorders (in diffuse cutaneous disease of infancy) Clinical diagnosis with elicitation of Darier sign Skin biopsy demonstrating increased dermal mast cells where confirmation is needed Serum baseline tryptase to screen for systemic involvement Assessment for systemic symptoms, especially in adults Referral for systemic workup if features suggest systemic mastocytosis Accumulation of mast cells confined to the skin, most commonly presenting in childhood Major forms are maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (urticaria pigmentosa), diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis and solitary mastocytoma Stroking a lesion causes urtication and erythema (a positive Darier sign), a useful bedside clue Childhood-onset disease often regresses around puberty, whereas adult-onset skin disease more often reflects underlying systemic mastocytosis Mediator symptoms such as flushing and pruritus can occur, and extensive disease risks more serious reactions Management is largely supportive with trigger avoidance and mediator-targeted therapy, reserving systemic workup for suggestive features Adult onset raising concern for systemic mastocytosis Systemic symptoms such as recurrent anaphylaxis or organ involvement Extensive blistering disease in infancy A markedly raised tryptase Assuming adult cutaneous disease is skin-limited without checking for systemic mastocytosis Provoking severe mediator release by triggering extensive lesions Missing the Darier sign as a diagnostic clue Overlooking anaphylaxis risk in extensive disease Cutaneous mastocytosis results from clonal accumulation of mast cells within the dermis, frequently associated with activating KIT mutations. The excess dermal mast cells release mediators such as histamine when mechanically or chemically triggered, producing the characteristic weal-and-flare on stroking (Darier sign) and symptoms of flushing and itch. In children the process is usually limited to the skin and tends to involute, whereas in adults cutaneous involvement is commonly a marker of systemic disease. Childhood cutaneous mastocytosis often improves or resolves by adolescence with an excellent prognosis, whereas adult disease frequently persists and may indicate systemic mastocytosis.

cutaneous mucinosis — cutaneous mucinoses, dermal mucinosis Scleromyxoedema and localised lichen myxoedematosus Scleroedema Pretibial myxoedema and generalised myxoedema of hypothyroidism Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis Reticular erythematous mucinosis and lupus erythematosus tumidus Follicular mucinosis with or without mycosis fungoides Systemic sclerosis and morphoea Skin biopsy with Alcian blue or colloidal iron staining to confirm and localise mucin Thyroid function tests and thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibodies where pretibial myxoedema is suspected Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to detect a paraprotein Autoimmune serology when a connective tissue disease is considered Assessment for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, including clonality studies, in persistent follicular mucinosis Investigations tailored to the suspected specific subtype and its systemic associations An umbrella group of disorders defined by abnormal accumulation of mucin (glycosaminoglycans, chiefly hyaluronic acid) in the dermis or hair follicles, produced by fibroblasts Broadly divided into primary mucinoses, where mucin deposition is the defining pathology, and secondary mucinoses, where mucin is an incidental finding in another disease such as lupus erythematosus Primary degenerative-inflammatory forms include lichen myxoedematosus and scleromyxoedema, scleroedema, reticular erythematous mucinosis, self-healing juvenile cutaneous mucinosis and papular mucinosis Pretibial myxoedema (thyroid dermopathy) is a distinctive form seen in Graves disease, driven by thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibodies, presenting as firm plaques and nodules over the shins Follicular mucinosis (alopecia mucinosa) shows mucin within hair follicles and may be idiopathic or a marker of mycosis fungoides, so persistent or atypical lesions warrant exclusion of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma Investigation combines biopsy with mucin stains (Alcian blue, colloidal iron) and a search for associations such as thyroid disease, paraproteinaemia and connective tissue disease Management is directed at the specific subtype and any underlying disorder, since prognosis and treatment differ widely across the group Follicular mucinosis with atypical or persistent lesions suggesting underlying mycosis fungoides Widespread papular mucinosis with a paraprotein indicating scleromyxoedema and possible systemic involvement Neurological, cardiac or gastrointestinal features accompanying a sclerodermoid mucinosis Rapid progression or systemic symptoms prompting evaluation for an associated systemic disorder Treating all mucinoses as a single entity rather than identifying the specific subtype, which determines prognosis and therapy Missing an associated systemic disorder such as thyroid disease, paraproteinaemia or connective tissue disease Failing to exclude mycosis fungoides in persistent follicular mucinosis Overlooking mucin as a secondary clue to lupus erythematosus or other connective tissue disease Relying on routine histology without specific mucin stains, so that subtle dermal mucin is missed The cutaneous mucinoses share deposition of mucin, a jelly-like mixture of acid glycosaminoglycans (predominantly hyaluronic acid) secreted by dermal fibroblasts, within the connective tissue or, in follicular mucinosis, within the follicular epithelium. In many primary forms, fibroblasts are stimulated to overproduce glycosaminoglycans by circulating factors: paraproteins in scleromyxoedema, thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibodies and other cytokines in pretibial myxoedema, and immune or inflammatory mediators in reticular erythematous mucinosis and lupus-associated disease. Accumulated hyaluronic acid is hygroscopic and separates collagen bundles, producing the induration, papules, plaques or oedematous changes characteristic of each subtype. In follicular mucinosis, mucin accumulates between keratinocytes of the follicle, sometimes in association with a lymphomatous infiltrate. Prognosis varies greatly by subtype: self-healing juvenile cutaneous mucinosis and post-infectious scleroedema may resolve, pretibial myxoedema and macular forms are usually chronic but benign, whereas scleromyxoedema and lymphoma-associated follicular mucinosis carry the potential for serious systemic disease. Outcome depends on accurate subtyping and management of the underlying condition.

including electrocardiography Ophthalmological review for uveitis and other ocular involvement Serum and urinary calcium to detect dysregulated vitamin D metabolism Sarcoidosis is a multisystem
