plaques to nodules, and diascopy classically reveals an apple-jelly colour Lupus pernio describes indurated violaceous plaques on the nose, cheeks and ears and is strongly associated with chronic disease and upper respiratory tract or pulmonary involvement Scar sarcoidosis is the appearance of granulomatous infiltration within old scars or tattoos and should always raise suspicion of systemic disease Erythema nodosum is a reactive, non-specific eruption that, with hilar lymphadenopathy and arthralgia (Lofgren syndrome), carries a favourable prognosis Histology shows non-caseating epithelioid granulomata with sparse surrounding lymphocytes (naked granulomas), but infection must always be excluded Because cutaneous signs may herald internal organ disease, every patient needs assessment for pulmonary, ophthalmic, cardiac and other systemic involvement Treatment is directed at the underlying disease and ranges from potent topical or intralesional corticosteroids for limited skin disease to systemic corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents for extensive or organ-threatening disease Lupus pernio or extensive skin disease signalling chronic systemic sarcoidosis Symptoms of cardiac involvement such as palpitations, syncope or conduction disturbance Progressive breathlessness suggesting significant pulmonary disease Visual disturbance from ocular sarcoidosis Hypercalcaemia with renal impairment Assuming skin disease is isolated and failing to screen for potentially serious internal organ involvement Diagnosing sarcoidosis without excluding tuberculosis and other granulomatous infections Overlooking granulomatous change within scars or tattoos as a clue to the diagnosis Missing asymptomatic cardiac or ocular disease that requires urgent treatment Sarcoidosis is characterised by the formation of non-caseating epithelioid granulomata in affected tissues, thought to represent an exaggerated cell-mediated immune response to an as-yet-unidentified antigen in a genetically susceptible host. Activated CD4 T-helper lymphocytes and macrophages accumulate and organise into compact granulomata, driven by a T-helper-1 cytokine profile. In the skin this produces the varied papules, plaques and nodules seen clinically, while similar granulomata elsewhere account for the multisystem nature of the disease. The granulomata may resolve spontaneously or progress to fibrosis, and their tendency to arise within scars and foreign material reflects a localised granulomatous response to tissue disruption. Outcome varies widely: acute presentations such as Lofgren syndrome and erythema nodosum often resolve spontaneously within months, whereas lupus pernio and infiltrative plaques tend to be chronic and may cause disfigurement, and prognosis ultimately depends on the extent and severity of internal organ involvement.

Cutis laxa — dermatochalasis (generalised), elastolysis, ELN-related cutis laxa, ATP6V0A2-related cutis laxa Ehlers-Danlos syndrome Pseudoxanthoma elasticum De Barsy syndrome Geroderma osteodysplasticum Wrinkly skin syndrome Age-related or actinic skin laxity Skin biopsy with elastic-tissue staining to assess elastic-fibre number and structure Molecular genetic testing with a cutis laxa gene panel to define the subtype Echocardiography and vascular imaging for aneurysm and arterial tortuosity Pulmonary function testing and chest imaging for emphysema Developmental and growth assessment in children Investigation for an underlying cause when an acquired form is suspected A heterogeneous group of disorders characterised by loose, inelastic, sagging skin that hangs in redundant folds and does not recoil when stretched It may be inherited or acquired; inherited forms include autosomal dominant (often ELN), autosomal recessive, and X-linked (occipital horn) types with differing systemic risks Unlike Ehlers-Danlos syndrome the skin is lax rather than hyperextensible, and joint hypermobility is not the dominant feature Systemic elastic-tissue involvement can cause emphysema, aortic and arterial aneurysm or tortuosity, and hollow-viscus diverticula depending on subtype Autosomal recessive and some syndromic forms may include developmental delay, growth restriction, and skeletal anomalies Acquired cutis laxa can follow inflammatory skin disease, drug reactions, or systemic conditions and may be a marker of underlying disease Diagnosis combines the clinical appearance, skin biopsy showing sparse or fragmented elastic fibres, and molecular genetic testing to define the subtype Management is supportive, with cardiorespiratory and vascular surveillance in at-risk subtypes and plastic-surgical options for the skin Acute chest, back, or abdominal pain suggesting arterial aneurysm rupture or dissection Progressive breathlessness from emphysema or spontaneous pneumothorax Signs of bowel or bladder diverticular complications New neurological signs suggesting cerebrovascular involvement Rapidly progressive acquired skin laxity indicating serious underlying disease Confusing lax, non-recoiling skin with the hyperextensible skin of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome Treating it purely as a cosmetic problem and missing systemic elastic-tissue disease Failing to arrange cardiovascular and pulmonary surveillance in high-risk subtypes Overlooking an underlying systemic trigger in acquired cutis laxa Not defining the subtype, which is essential for prognosis and counselling Cutis laxa reflects a defect in the formation, cross-linking, or maintenance of elastic fibres in connective tissue. Inherited forms disrupt elastin itself (for example ELN variants) or proteins and enzymes required for elastic-fibre assembly, copper-dependent cross-linking, or intracellular trafficking, leaving elastic fibres sparse, fragmented, or disorganised. Loss of functional elastic tissue removes the normal recoil of the skin and can weaken the walls of the lungs, arteries, and hollow organs, explaining the sagging skin together with emphysema, arterial aneurysm and tortuosity, and diverticula in the more severe systemic subtypes. Acquired forms arise from elastic-fibre destruction driven by inflammation or other secondary insults. Prognosis varies widely by subtype: isolated cutaneous disease is mainly a cosmetic and functional concern with a normal lifespan, whereas forms with pulmonary, cardiovascular, or multisystem involvement can significantly reduce life expectancy. Surveillance of at-risk systems guides outcome.

cutis marmorata — physiological livedo reticularis, marbled skin Livedo reticularis (persistent/pathological forms) Livedo racemosa associated with antiphospholipid syndrome or vasculitis Cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita Neonatal lupus and other connective-tissue disease-related livedo Sneddon syndrome Cholesterol embolisation-associated livedo Physiological acrocyanosis of the newborn Careful clinical observation of reversibility on rewarming (usually diagnostic; no tests needed for physiological form) Thyroid function tests where persistent neonatal mottling raises concern for hypothyroidism Chromosomal/genetic evaluation if dysmorphic features suggest a syndromic association Antinuclear antibody and antiphospholipid antibody screen if a fixed livedo pattern emerges Skin biopsy reserved for atypical or persistent lesions to exclude vasculopathy Assessment of perfusion, blood pressure and lactate in an acutely unwell patient with new mottling Doppler or vascular imaging if a congenital vascular malformation is suspected Cutis marmorata is a transient, symmetrical reticulated blue-red mottling of the skin provoked by cold exposure and resolving fully on rewarming, reflecting a physiological vasomotor response rather than fixed structural vessel disease. It is extremely common in neonates and infants because of immature autonomic control of the cutaneous vasculature, and typically diminishes with age. The pattern arises from cold-induced constriction of the ascending arterioles supplying dermal vascular cones, so surrounding venous plexuses dilate and deoxygenated blood pools in a net-like configuration. Distinguish physiological cutis marmorata from persistent, non-reversible livedo reticularis or livedo racemosa, which suggest underlying vasculopathy, thrombophilia or connective-tissue disease and warrant investigation. Persistent or pronounced cutis marmorata in a neonate should prompt consideration of hypothyroidism, Down syndrome, trisomy 18, Cornelia de Lange syndrome and other neurodevelopmental disorders. It must be differentiated from cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita, a fixed congenital vascular malformation that does not fully disappear on warming and may be associated with limb atrophy or asymmetry. No treatment is required for the physiological form; reassurance and avoidance of cold exposure suffice, with the reticulate colour normalising once ambient or core temperature rises. Reappearance or accentuation of a marbled pattern in a critically ill adult may signal peripheral hypoperfusion, shock or impending cardiovascular collapse and should not be dismissed as benign. Mottling that persists on rewarming or has a broken, irregular (racemosa) pattern New or worsening skin marbling in an acutely unwell or hypotensive patient Associated dysmorphic features, developmental delay or failure to thrive in an infant Ulceration, atrophy or limb asymmetry accompanying the reticulate pattern Systemic symptoms such as arthralgia, neurological deficit or thrombotic events Mislabelling a fixed, pathological livedo racemosa as benign cutis marmorata and missing an underlying thrombophilia or vasculitis Overlooking new skin mottling as an early sign of shock or poor perfusion in a deteriorating patient Confusing cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita with the transient physiological form Failing to screen for hypothyroidism or a genetic syndrome when neonatal mottling is persistent and marked Over-investigating a clearly reversible, cold-induced pattern in an otherwise well child Cutis marmorata represents an exaggerated but physiological vasomotor reaction of the cutaneous microcirculation to cold. The dermal blood supply is organised into cone-shaped units in which a central ascending arteriole feeds a superficial capillary bed drained by a peripheral venous plexus. On cooling, sympathetically mediated vasoconstriction narrows the central arterioles while the peripheral venules dilate and fill with slow-flowing, deoxygenated blood. This produces the characteristic reticulated, bluish-red network delineating areas of relative venous stasis around islands of better-perfused skin. Because the change is purely functional and driven by neurovascular tone, it reverses completely with rewarming. Immaturity of autonomic vascular regulation explains its prevalence in neonates, whereas in adults a similar reversible pattern may reflect labile vasomotor tone or, in the unwell patient, systemic hypoperfusion. Physiological cutis marmorata is entirely benign and self-limiting, typically becoming less prominent as autonomic vascular control matures. Persistent or syndrome-associated patterns carry the prognosis of the underlying condition rather than the skin change itself.

Cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita — CMTC, van Lohuizen syndrome, congenital generalised phlebectasia Physiological cutis marmorata (resolves on warming) Reticulate capillary (port-wine) malformation Neonatal lupus and other neonatal livedo Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome Adams-Oliver syndrome (with aplasia cutis and limb defects) Diffuse capillary malformation with overgrowth Clinical examination documenting the fixed reticulated pattern and its distribution Ophthalmological assessment for glaucoma when periocular skin is involved Limb-length and girth measurement to assess asymmetry Imaging (ultrasound or MRI) if significant limb asymmetry or other anomaly is suspected Skin assessment for atrophy or ulceration Developmental review where broader syndromic features are present A congenital vascular malformation producing a fixed, reticulated, marbled (livedoid) violaceous pattern of the skin present from birth The mottling is persistent and does not fully resolve on warming, distinguishing it from benign physiological cutis marmorata It often has a segmental or localised distribution, and the affected area may show mild atrophy, ulceration or dilated superficial veins A degree of limb or body asymmetry (hypoplasia or, less often, hypertrophy) can accompany the skin changes It is usually sporadic and tends to improve gradually over the first years of life Associated anomalies are described, including glaucoma when facial skin around the eye is involved, so ophthalmology assessment is warranted in periocular disease Diagnosis is clinical; imaging is reserved for evaluating associated limb asymmetry or other suspected anomalies Management is largely supportive, with monitoring of associated features and protection of atrophic or ulcerated skin Periocular involvement with signs of raised intraocular pressure or glaucoma Significant or progressive limb-length discrepancy Persistent ulceration or non-healing skin breakdown Features suggesting an associated syndrome requiring further workup Neurological or developmental concerns Confusing it with benign physiological cutis marmorata that resolves on warming Omitting ophthalmology review when the skin around the eye is affected Overlooking limb asymmetry that may need orthopaedic follow-up Assuming all cases are isolated without checking for associated anomalies Cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita is a sporadic congenital malformation of the cutaneous microvasculature in which persistently dilated capillaries and venules produce a fixed reticulated, marbled discolouration of the skin. The affected vessels and surrounding dermis may be structurally abnormal, accounting for associated skin atrophy, ulceration and prominent superficial veins. The underlying cause is not fully defined and most cases occur without a clear inheritance pattern; the reticulated pattern tends to soften with time as the microvasculature matures. The cutaneous mottling commonly fades and improves over the first few years of life, and isolated disease has a good prognosis; outlook is determined by any associated anomalies such as glaucoma or substantial limb asymmetry, which require targeted follow-up.

Cutis tricolor — cutis tricolor parvimaculata, paired hyper- and hypopigmented macules with normal skin Isolated café-au-lait macules and naevus depigmentosus Segmental pigmentary mosaicism (hypomelanosis of Ito, segmental hyperpigmentation) Phakomatosis pigmentovascularis Speckled lentiginous naevus Incontinentia pigmenti (later stages) Neurofibromatosis type 1 Detailed skin mapping of paired hyper- and hypopigmented lesions Wood's lamp examination to accentuate hypopigmented macules Skin biopsy where diagnosis is uncertain Neurological and developmental assessment where systemic features are suspected Skeletal imaging where deformity or asymmetry is present MRI of the brain in patients with neurological symptoms Describes the coexistence of hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules in close proximity against a background of normally pigmented skin It is understood as an example of twin spotting (didymosis), in which two mosaic clones of opposite pigmentary tendency arise from a single post-zygotic event The pigmentary lesions typically follow the lines of Blaschko or a segmental pattern reflecting their mosaic origin It may occur in isolation or as part of a wider malformation syndrome with neurological and skeletal features Reported associations include developmental delay, skeletal anomalies and, in some cases, features overlapping recognised overgrowth or dysmorphic syndromes Diagnosis is clinical, supported by careful mapping of the paired pigmentary lesions Management is generic: reassurance and cosmetic camouflage for isolated skin disease, with developmental and skeletal assessment where systemic features are present Developmental regression or new neurological signs Progressive skeletal deformity Features suggesting a defined overgrowth or dysmorphic syndrome Seizures warranting neuroimaging Overlooking the diagnostic pairing of hyper- and hypopigmented lesions and treating each in isolation Failing to assess for systemic involvement when pigmentary mosaicism is extensive Confusing the hypopigmented component with vitiligo Not using Wood's lamp, which can miss subtle hypopigmented macules Cutis tricolor is regarded as a pigmentary manifestation of twin spotting, in which a single post-zygotic somatic recombination event produces two genetically distinct daughter clones with opposing pigmentary behaviour, one hyperpigmented and one hypopigmented, adjacent to each other on a background of unaffected skin. Because the event occurs during embryonic development, the paired macules follow the lines of Blaschko or a segmental distribution. When the underlying mosaic clones also affect neuroectodermal or mesodermal tissue, the associated neurological and skeletal anomalies of the syndromic form arise, whereas involvement limited to melanocyte precursors produces isolated cutaneous disease. Isolated cutis tricolor is benign with an excellent prognosis and is mainly of cosmetic significance, whereas the syndromic form carries a prognosis determined by the associated neurological and skeletal abnormalities.

Cyanide poisoning — hydrogen cyanide poisoning, cyanide toxicity, prussic acid poisoning, smoke inhalation cyanide toxicity, nitrile poisoning Carbon monoxide poisoning Hydrogen sulphide poisoning Other causes of high anion-gap lactic acidosis such as toxic alcohols or metformin Septic shock with profound lactic acidosis Simple asphyxiant or smoke inhalation without systemic toxin Sudden cardiac or neurological catastrophe Arterial and central/mixed venous blood gases with lactate to assess acidosis and oxygen extraction Carboxyhaemoglobin and co-oximetry, particularly in fire victims with concurrent carbon monoxide exposure Whole-blood lactate, which correlates with severity in the appropriate context Electrocardiogram and cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia and ischaemia Whole-blood cyanide concentration for later confirmation rather than acute decision-making Basic metabolic panel and anion-gap calculation Cyanide poisoning is a diagnosis made on clinical suspicion and context, since confirmatory blood levels are not available in real time Consider it in enclosed-space fire victims with soot, altered consciousness and unexplained profound metabolic acidosis, often coexisting with carbon monoxide poisoning A high anion-gap metabolic acidosis with a raised lactate and a narrowed arterio-venous oxygen difference is a classic clue to impaired cellular oxygen use Venous blood may appear bright red and retinal veins arterialised because tissues cannot extract oxygen from arterial blood Sources include combustion of synthetic materials, industrial nitriles, laetrile/amygdalin and prolonged sodium nitroprusside infusion Empirical antidotal therapy should not wait for laboratory confirmation when suspicion is high in a deteriorating patient Hydroxocobalamin, or the combination of a nitrite with sodium thiosulfate, are the principal antidotes, alongside high-flow oxygen and supportive care Hydroxocobalamin is generally preferred in fire victims because nitrite-induced methaemoglobinaemia can worsen oxygen delivery when carboxyhaemoglobin is also elevated Rapidly declining consciousness or seizures after smoke or chemical exposure Severe unexplained high anion-gap lactic acidosis with a markedly elevated lactate Cardiovascular collapse or refractory hypotension in a fire victim Apnoea or cardiac arrest requiring immediate empirical antidote Coexisting evidence of carbon monoxide poisoning compounding tissue hypoxia Waiting for confirmatory cyanide levels before giving antidote in a deteriorating patient Overlooking concurrent cyanide toxicity in fire victims treated only for carbon monoxide Using nitrites in smoke inhalation where induced methaemoglobinaemia may further impair oxygen carriage Attributing collapse solely to hypoxia or shock and missing histotoxic hypoxia Forgetting prolonged sodium nitroprusside infusion as an iatrogenic source Cyanide binds avidly to the ferric iron of cytochrome c oxidase in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, arresting aerobic adenosine triphosphate production. Cells are forced into anaerobic metabolism, generating lactic acid and a high anion-gap acidosis despite adequate oxygen delivery, a state of histotoxic hypoxia. Because oxygen cannot be utilised, venous oxygen saturation rises and the arterio-venous oxygen difference narrows. The brain and heart, being most dependent on oxidative metabolism, fail first, producing rapid loss of consciousness, seizures, cardiovascular collapse and death. Untreated severe cyanide poisoning can be fatal within minutes, but prompt antidotal therapy and supportive care can produce full recovery; survivors of significant hypoxic insult may develop delayed neurological sequelae including parkinsonism.

Cyclic neutropenia — cyclical neutropenia, ELANE-related cyclic neutropenia, periodic neutropenia Severe congenital neutropenia (persistent, not cyclical) Autoimmune neutropenia Chronic idiopathic neutropenia PFAPA and other periodic fever syndromes Infection- or drug-induced transient neutropenia Large granular lymphocyte-associated neutropenia Serial full blood counts two to three times weekly over six to eight weeks to document the cycle ELANE genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Bone marrow examination in atypical cases to assess maturation and exclude other pathology Antineutrophil antibody testing to exclude autoimmune neutropenia Inflammatory markers and cultures during febrile episodes to guide infection management Dental and oral assessment for recurrent gingivitis and ulceration An autosomal dominant disorder caused by ELANE mutations in which neutrophil counts oscillate, typically with a regular cycle of about three weeks During the nadir, patients develop recurrent fever, mouth ulcers, gingivitis, cervical adenopathy, and skin or respiratory infections The characteristic periodicity distinguishes it from severe congenital neutropenia, which is persistent rather than oscillating Diagnosis requires serial blood counts two or three times weekly for six to eight weeks to capture the cyclical pattern Unlike severe congenital neutropenia, cyclic neutropenia carries little or no increased risk of leukaemic transformation G-CSF shortens and shallows the neutrophil nadir and reduces infection during vulnerable periods Monocytes and other cell lines often oscillate reciprocally, and symptoms tend to lessen with age Serious deep-seated infection or sepsis during a neutrophil nadir Clostridial or necrotising soft-tissue infection, a recognised hazard during severe nadirs Failure of counts to recover between cycles, prompting reconsideration of severe congenital neutropenia Persistent oral or perianal infection despite treatment Making the diagnosis from a single blood count rather than serial sampling across a cycle Confusing it with severe congenital neutropenia and overstating the leukaemia risk Underestimating the danger of clostridial or necrotising infection during a deep nadir Attributing recurrent mouth ulcers to an unrelated cause and missing the periodicity Cyclic neutropenia is caused by heterozygous mutations in ELANE, the gene for neutrophil elastase, which produce a misfolded protein that stresses developing myeloid precursors and periodically curtails granulopoiesis. The oscillation reflects a disturbance in the feedback regulation of the haematopoietic stem and progenitor compartment, so neutrophil production rises and falls in a regular rhythm of roughly three weeks. During each production trough the circulating neutrophil count falls to very low levels, leaving the patient transiently susceptible to bacterial infection and mucosal ulceration, before recovering as the next wave of granulopoiesis emerges. Although the same gene is implicated in severe congenital neutropenia, the mutational spectrum and cellular consequences differ, which is thought to explain why cyclic disease does not share the marked predisposition to myeloid malignancy. Cyclic neutropenia generally has a good long-term outlook, symptoms often attenuate with age, and it lacks the marked leukaemic risk of severe congenital neutropenia, though infections during nadirs can occasionally be life-threatening.

of intense vomiting that are self-limiting and separated by well intervals of completely normal health Attacks are strikingly similar for a given patient in onset time, duration, and symptom pattern, often starting in the early morning Strong personal or family history of migraine is common, and the disorder is regarded as part of the migraine spectrum Episodes may be triggered by psychological or Diagnosis is largely clinical and requires exclusion of metabolic, neurological, and obstructive mimics Coalescence of attacks or loss of symptom-free intervals suggests an alternative diagnosis or transformation Bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, or signs of mechanical obstruction Focal neurological deficit, severe headache, or vomiting worse on waking with papilloedema Onset associated with fasting, intercurrent illness, or lethargy suggesting a metabolic crisis Progressive weight loss or loss of the characteristic symptom-free intervals Attributing repeated presentations to a psychiatric or behavioural cause and missing the stereotyped pattern Overlooking cannabinoid hyperemesis in patients who compulsively hot-bathe for relief Failing to exclude malrotation or a metabolic disorder before labelling the illness functional Under-treating dehydration and electrolyte loss during severe attacks Cyclic vomiting syndrome is a functional gut-brain disorder in which recurrent, discrete episodes of severe nausea and vomiting arise on a background of normal health between attacks. The mechanism is thought to overlap with migraine, involving dysregulation of the brain-gut axis, autonomic instability, and heightened activation of central emetic pathways, with possible roles for mitochondrial energy dysfunction, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal stress responses, and altered neuroendocrine signalling. Triggers such as stress, infection, and fasting appear to lower the threshold for a stereotyped emetic cascade that then runs a self-limiting course. Many children improve or remit with maturity, although a proportion evolve into migraine headaches, and adult-onset disease tends to be more chronic. With effective prophylaxis and trigger avoidance, attack frequency and severity can often be substantially reduced.

detection when microscopy is negative Dehydration and electrolyte disturbance from prolonged diarrhoea Marked weight loss and malabsorption from protracted infection Severe or unremitting disease suggesting underlying immunosuppression Cluster of cases pointing to a contaminated food source requiring public health action Failing to request specific stool staining, so oocysts are overlooked on routine microscopy Attributing persistent traveller's diarrhoea to a purely functional cause without parasitological testing Assuming person-to-person transmission and missing the food or water source Under-treating immunocompromised patients who require longer courses Cyclospora cayetanensis is a coccidian parasite that infects the epithelium of the small intestine. Ingested sporulated oocysts release sporozoites that invade enterocytes, where asexual and sexual cycles generate oocysts excreted unsporulated in the faeces; environmental maturation over days renders them infectious, explaining the food- and water-borne pattern. Mucosal invasion causes villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and inflammation with malabsorption and a secretory diarrhoea. Illness is typically self-limiting in immunocompetent people but can be prolonged and relapsing, and is more severe and persistent when cell-mediated immunity is impaired. Self-limiting over weeks in most immunocompetent people but often protracted and relapsing without treatment; antimicrobial therapy produces rapid improvement, while immunocompromised hosts may need extended or suppressive courses.

Cylindroma — dermal cylindroma, turban tumour, Spiegler tumour Spiradenoma Trichoepithelioma Basal cell carcinoma Adenoid cystic carcinoma (histological mimic) Epidermoid cyst of the scalp Cutaneous adnexal carcinoma Excisional or incisional biopsy with histopathology demonstrating the jigsaw pattern and hyaline sheaths Clinical mapping of the scalp and head-neck region for multiple lesions Family history and examination for spiradenomas and trichoepitheliomas CYLD genetic testing when Brooke-Spiegler syndrome is suspected Imaging of extensive confluent scalp disease to plan surgery A benign adnexal tumour with apocrine/eccrine differentiation, presenting as a firm smooth pink to red nodule usually on the scalp, head, or neck Solitary lesions are usually sporadic; multiple confluent scalp nodules may coalesce into the classic turban tumour appearance Multiplicity, especially with trichoepitheliomas and spiradenomas, points to CYLD-related Brooke-Spiegler syndrome Histology shows islands of basaloid cells arranged in a jigsaw-puzzle pattern separated and surrounded by a thickened hyaline basement-membrane material Droplets of hyaline basement-membrane material are also seen within the tumour nests, a helpful diagnostic clue Germline or somatic loss of the CYLD tumour-suppressor deregulates NF-kB signalling and predisposes to these adnexal tumours Most are benign, but long-standing or rapidly changing lesions can rarely undergo malignant transformation to cylindrocarcinoma Rapid growth, ulceration, or bleeding of a previously stable nodule suggesting malignant transformation Extensive confluent turban-tumour disease causing functional or cosmetic morbidity Family clustering of adnexal tumours indicating a hereditary syndrome Misinterpreting the histology as adenoid cystic carcinoma or basal cell carcinoma Overlooking the syndromic context when multiple adnexal tumours are present Failing to recognise features of malignant change in long-standing lesions Incomplete excision of confluent lesions leading to recurrence Cylindroma is a benign cutaneous adnexal neoplasm showing apocrine and eccrine differentiation. It is composed of nests and cords of basaloid epithelial cells arranged in an interlocking jigsaw-puzzle pattern, each nest sheathed by and interspersed with abundant hyaline basement-membrane material. Loss-of-function alterations in the CYLD gene, a tumour suppressor that normally restrains nuclear factor-kappa B signalling by removing regulatory ubiquitin chains, deregulate this pathway and promote survival and proliferation of the adnexal cells. When CYLD is affected in the germline, patients develop multiple cylindromas, spiradenomas, and trichoepitheliomas as part of Brooke-Spiegler syndrome, whereas sporadic solitary lesions may harbour somatic CYLD changes. Cylindromas are benign and slow-growing with an excellent prognosis after excision; syndromic patients develop numerous recurrent lesions requiring repeated intervention, and malignant transformation, though rare, carries a more serious outlook.

Cystathioninuria — cystathioninuria, cystathionase deficiency, cystathionine gamma-lyase deficiency, gamma-cystathionase deficiency, CTH Classical homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase primary trait is desired Autosomal recessive deficiency of cystathionine gamma-lyase (cystathionase), the enzyme that cleaves cystathionine to cysteine in the transsulfuration pathway Characterised biochemically by raised cystathionine in plasma and urine It is regarded as a benign trait with no consistent disease association, often discovered incidentally Many cases are pyridoxine (vitamin B6) cystathioninuria is commoner than the primary trait and occurs in vitamin B6 deficiency, liver disease, thyrotoxicosis and neuroblastoma The main practical task is to recognise it as benign and avoid unnecessary investigation or treatment It must be distinguished from classical homocystinuria, in which cystathionine is low rather than high Raised homocysteine accompanying the cystathionine, which points away from a benign trait Clinical or biochemical evidence of an underlying tumour such as neuroblastoma Signs of liver disease or thyrotoxicosis suggesting a secondary cause Symptoms attributed to cystathioninuria itself, prompting reassessment Treating a benign trait as a significant disease and overinvestigating the patient Failing to distinguish primary cystathioninuria from important secondary causes such as neuroblastoma Confusing it with classical homocystinuria without measuring homocysteine Overlooking simple pyridoxine responsiveness when documenting the biochemistry In the transsulfuration pathway, homocysteine is condensed with serine to form cystathionine, which cystathionine gamma-lyase then cleaves to cysteine and alpha-ketobutyrate. When this enzyme is deficient, cystathionine accumulates and spills into the urine, producing cystathioninuria, while the downstream synthesis of cysteine is reduced but usually compensated by dietary intake. Because the enzyme is pyridoxal phosphate dependent, activity is often improved by pyridoxine. The accumulated cystathionine appears to be metabolically inert and non-toxic, which is why the primary deficiency is a benign biochemical trait rather than a disease. The primary trait is benign with a normal outlook and no need for long-term treatment; when cystathioninuria is secondary, prognosis is that of the underlying condition.

Cystic adventitial disease — Adventitial cystic disease, Cystic adventitial degeneration Atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome Thrombosed popliteal artery aneurysm Baker's cyst Fibromuscular dysplasia Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease) Extrinsic compression by a soft-tissue mass Ankle-brachial pressure index, which may fall with knee flexion or exercise Duplex ultrasound showing an eccentric cystic wall lesion with a preserved distal artery MRI or MR angiography, which best demonstrates the adventitial cyst and its content CT angiography Catheter angiography showing a smooth 'scimitar' or hourglass narrowing Provocative positional testing of pulses and pressures Histology of the resected cyst to confirm the diagnosis A rare non-atherosclerotic cause of claudication in which a mucin-containing cyst within the arterial adventitia compresses the lumen; the popliteal artery is by far the commonest site. Characteristically affects relatively young or middle-aged men without conventional cardiovascular risk factors. Produces intermittent, sometimes rapidly progressive, calf claudication, with symptoms that may vary with knee position. Ishikawa's sign describes loss of a palpable distal pulse on knee flexion as the cyst compression increases. Imaging shows smooth extrinsic narrowing, the 'scimitar' sign on angiography, or an eccentric well-defined cyst on ultrasound and MRI without atherosclerosis elsewhere. MRI is particularly useful, demonstrating the cystic fluid collection within the vessel wall. Treatment is surgical, by cyst evacuation or resection with bypass or interposition graft; simple aspiration has a high recurrence rate. It should be considered in any young patient with claudication and otherwise normal, non-atherosclerotic arteries. Acute limb ischaemia from complete arterial occlusion or thrombosis. Rapidly worsening short-distance claudication or rest pain. Loss of distal pulses, especially provoked by knee flexion. New sensory or motor changes in the foot. Recurrence of symptoms after previous treatment. Misdiagnosing it as ordinary atherosclerotic claudication and missing the extrinsic cause in a young patient. Relying on simple cyst aspiration, which is prone to recurrence. Failing to recognise an associated communication with the knee joint. Attempting angioplasty or stenting of an extrinsic compressive lesion, which tends to fail. Confusing it with popliteal entrapment or a thrombosed aneurysm without dedicated cross-sectional imaging. A mucinous, gelatinous cyst resembling a ganglion develops within the adventitia of the artery and progressively encroaches on the lumen. Several origins are proposed: a developmental theory invoking embryonic mesenchymal rests, a degenerative ganglion-like process, and an articular theory in which a communication with the adjacent knee joint capsule allows synovial-type mucin to track along vascular branches into the adventitia. The cyst content is a mucopolysaccharide-rich fluid. Because the underlying problem is extrinsic compression of an otherwise healthy artery, symptoms depend on cyst volume and the position-dependent geometry of the vessel, and complete luminal thrombosis can occur. Outcomes after surgical treatment are generally good, with resolution of symptoms, although recurrence is well recognised, particularly after aspiration alone or when a joint communication is not addressed. Long-term patency is favourable when the diseased segment is resected and reconstructed.

Cystic Fibrosis — CF, CFTR disease Non-CF bronchiectasis (CF carrier status predisposes; heterozygous CFTR mutations implicated) (p.2247) Chronic rhinosinusitis (associated with relative CFTR deficiency) (p.2247) Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens as an isolated forme fruste of CFTR mutation (p.2247) Idiopathic/recurrent pancreatitis associated with CFTR mutation in at least one allele (p.2247) Sweat chloride after pilocarpine iontophoresis (chloride >=60 mEq/L supports diagnosis; highly specific) (p.2246-2247) CFTR mutation analysis / panels of several hundred variants, or complete CFTR sequencing with splice-junction analysis (p.2246-2247) Immunoreactive trypsinogen (newborn screening) (p.2246) Fecal elastase-1 (low in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency) (p.2246) Sputum culture surveillance for resistant pathogens (Burkholderia cepacia complex, Stenotrophomonas, Achromobacter, mucoid P. aeruginosa, atypical mycobacteria, MRSA) (p.2248) FEV1 (% predicted) for monitoring and transplant referral thresholds (p.2248) Annual diabetes mellitus testing in adults; monitor liver function and CYP3A drug interactions on modulator therapy (p.2248) Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive exocrinopathy affecting multiple epithelial tissues; the gene product CFTR is an apical anion (chloride and bicarbonate) channel that regulates the volume and composition of exocrine secretion (p.2245). Major morbidity and mortality arise from pulmonary disease: copious hyperviscous adherent secretions obstruct small and medium airways, and a complex flora including Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa is routinely cultured from CF sputum (p.2245). P. aeruginosa shows stereotypic pathogenesis: an early sentinel colonization often becomes lifelong infection by the same strain, and over years evolves a mucoid (alginate-producing) phenotype that confers selective advantage and poor host prognosis (p.2245). Radiographic sinusitis occurs in most patients with CF; the sinuses may act as a reservoir for bacterial seeding of the lower airways (p.2245). Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency causes chronic malabsorption, poor growth, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency; high blood immunoreactive trypsinogen (used in newborn screening) and low fecal elastase-1 are characteristic (p.2245-2246). CF-related diabetes mellitus occurs in >30% of adults and is multifactorial (endocrine pancreatic destruction plus, in some, insulin resistance); annual diabetes testing is recommended for adults with CF (p.2246, p.2248). Men typically show complete involution of the vas deferens despite functioning spermatogenesis, and ~99% of males with CF are infertile (unable to conceive without in vitro fertilization) (p.2246). Diagnosis is confirmed by disease-causing variants on both CFTR alleles and/or sweat chloride >=60 mEq/L together with characteristic exocrine manifestations; sweat electrolyte testing follows pilocarpine iontophoresis (p.2246-2247). Several severe defects (F508del, G551D, nonsense alleles) predict pancreatic insufficiency, present in ~80% of patients; F508del alone accounts for ~85% of defective CFTR alleles in the United States (p.2247). CFTR modulators (ivacaftor potentiator; lumacaftor/tezacaftor/elexacaftor correctors) are highly effective modulator therapy (HEMT); triple combination therapy is projected to benefit >90% of patients and improves FEV1, reduces exacerbations, and lowers sweat chloride (p.2247-2248). Pulmonary exacerbation poor-prognosis pathogens that are rigorously monitored include Burkholderia cepacia complex, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Achromobacter, mucoid P. aeruginosa, and atypical mycobacteria; MRSA may also signal worse outcomes (p.2248). Infection commonly persists despite modulator therapy, so chronic respiratory infection and inflammation continue even after substantial clinical improvement on HEMT (p.2248). Hemoptysis requiring hospitalization (p.2248) Pneumothorax requiring hospitalization (p.2248) Sputum culture growing Burkholderia cepacia complex, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Achromobacter, mucoid P. aeruginosa, or atypical mycobacteria (poor prognostic indicators) (p.2248) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (~5% of patients) suggested by failure to respond to aggressive inpatient antibiotics (p.2248) FEV1 <30% predicted (threshold for lung transplant referral) (p.2248) Hyperviscosity of eccrine sweat is NOT a feature of CF; the sweat test reflects defective ductal chloride reabsorption, not thick sweat (p.2247). Anion flux through CFTR does NOT involve active transport against a concentration gradient (p.2245-2246). Genotype does NOT reliably predict respiratory prognosis or longevity, even though some severe alleles predict pancreatic insufficiency (p.2247). A subset of patients with F508del respond poorly to triple combination therapy, so modulator benefit is not universal (p.2248). HEMT may reduce sputum bacterial density but does NOT eradicate infection; chronic respiratory infection and inflammation persist (p.2248). CF has been underdiagnosed outside historically white populations (Eastern Europe, Latin America, Asia, India, and US minorities), often due to rare/poorly characterized variants and limited access to DNA/sweat testing (p.2249). Mutation of CFTR, an apical epithelial anion channel that conducts chloride and bicarbonate (~1480 amino acids, gated by ATP hydrolysis without active transport against gradient), impairs hydration and clearance of exocrine secretions. In the airway, loss of CFTR-dependent anion secretion depletes the periciliary fluid layer, causing ciliary collapse and failure to clear overlying mucus; mucoobstruction with chronic infection drives an aggressive, unrelenting neutrophilic inflammatory response with proteases and oxidants, leading to airway remodeling and bronchiectasis. Low airway-surface-fluid pH may impair bacterial killing. Similar mechanisms affect pancreatic acini/ducts (fibrotic destruction, cyst formation, exocrine and eventually endocrine insufficiency), hepatobiliary tissue (biliary obstruction, focal/multilobular cirrhosis, portal hypertension), and intestine (meconium ileus, distal intestinal obstructive syndrome). Over 2000 CFTR allelic variants are described and grouped into classes I-VI by molecular mechanism (e.g., F508del is a class II protein-maturation/folding defect degraded in the endoplasmic reticulum; G551D is a class III gating defect). Modulator and other therapies have transformed CF from a disease that historically led to death in early childhood to one with frequent survival well into the fifth decade and beyond; US median survival now exceeds 60 years. Genotype is of limited value for predicting respiratory rate of decline or longevity. End-stage pulmonary failure may be treated with lung transplantation (median survival >9 years among adults). Marked geographic disparity exists: median survival is <30 years in much of Latin America versus >60 years in the United States (p.2248-2249). CFTR mutations are categorized by molecular mechanism into classes I-VI: class I, absent synthesis (e.g., nonsense mutations G542X, R553X, W1282X); class II, defective protein maturation and premature degradation (e.g., F508del, ~85% of US alleles, the most common); class III, disordered gating/regulation (e.g., G551D, ~4% of patients); class IV, defective conductance through the channel pore; class V, reduced transcript number from promoter/splicing abnormality; class VI, accelerated turnover from the cell surface. Severity is not formally graded by stage; FEV1 <30% predicted is used as a lung-transplant referral threshold (p.2246, p.2248).

Cystic Fibrosis (Paediatric) — CF, cystic fibrosis, mucoviscidosis, paediatric cystic fibrosis Primary ciliary dyskinesia Immunodeficiency with recurrent infections Asthma with recurrent chest infections Protracted bacterial bronchitis Coeliac disease or other causes of malabsorption and failure to thrive Shwachman-Diamond syndrome Newborn screening (immunoreactive trypsinogen) with confirmatory testing Sweat chloride testing CFTR genetic analysis Assessment of pancreatic function (e.g. faecal elastase) Respiratory cultures to identify airway pathogens Chest imaging and, in older children, lung function testing Nutritional assessment and fat-soluble vitamin levels An autosomal recessive multisystem disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, the most common of which is F508del. It is a genetic disease, not an infection, though recurrent respiratory infections dominate its course and morbidity. Suspect it in a child with chronic productive cough, recurrent chest infections, failure to thrive, and greasy, bulky, foul-smelling stools from fat malabsorption. Meconium ileus in a newborn is highly suggestive and is often the earliest presentation. Many countries diagnose it through newborn screening, but a positive screen must be confirmed, classically with an elevated sweat chloride test. Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency is common and requires enzyme replacement and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation, with attention to overall nutrition. Chronic airway infection, notably with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, drives progressive bronchiectasis and lung function decline. Care is delivered by a specialist multidisciplinary team, and CFTR modulator therapies have transformed outcomes for eligible genotypes. Failure to thrive or faltering growth reflecting malabsorption and increased energy demands New or persistent Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection requiring eradication Acute pulmonary exacerbation with increased cough, sputum, breathlessness, or falling lung function Haemoptysis or pneumothorax Distal intestinal obstruction syndrome or meconium ileus in the newborn Signs of CF-related diabetes or liver disease emerging over time Attributing recurrent chest infections and loose stools to common childhood illness and missing the diagnosis Assuming a negative newborn screen fully excludes CF, since screening can miss some cases Underestimating nutritional needs and failing to optimise pancreatic enzyme and vitamin replacement Delaying treatment of new Pseudomonas infection when early eradication is most effective Overlooking emerging complications such as CF-related diabetes and liver disease Mutations in the CFTR gene impair the CFTR chloride and bicarbonate channel at epithelial surfaces. Defective ion transport produces thick, dehydrated secretions across multiple organs. In the airways, viscous mucus impairs mucociliary clearance, promoting chronic infection, neutrophilic inflammation, and progressive bronchiectasis. In the pancreas, ductal obstruction leads to exocrine insufficiency and malabsorption; similar mechanisms affect the intestine, biliary tree, sweat glands (hence high sweat chloride), and reproductive tract. Survival has improved dramatically with multidisciplinary care, aggressive infection and nutrition management, and CFTR modulator therapy, with many people now living well into adulthood; prognosis is largely determined by the rate of progressive lung disease and nutritional status.

Cystic hygroma — lymphatic malformation, lymphangioma, macrocystic lymphatic malformation Branchial cleft cyst Haemangioma or other vascular malformation Thyroglossal cyst (if midline) Lipoma or other soft-tissue mass Cervical abscess or lymphadenitis Neck and soft-tissue ultrasound to confirm the cystic nature and transillumination correlate MRI to map the full extent and involvement of adjacent structures Antenatal ultrasound and karyotyping when detected in the fetus Airway assessment (including nasendoscopy or cross-sectional imaging) for large cervical lesions Assessment for associated syndromes when clinically indicated A congenital lymphatic malformation that most often presents as a soft, compressible, painless swelling in the posterior triangle of the neck or the axilla The lesion characteristically transilluminates brightly because it is filled with clear lymphatic fluid Many are detected antenatally or in early infancy; fetal nuchal cystic hygroma is associated with chromosomal abnormalities such as Turner and Down syndromes The swelling may enlarge suddenly following intracystic bleeding or with an upper respiratory infection Large cervical lesions can extend toward the floor of the mouth or mediastinum and threaten the airway or swallowing Ultrasound and MRI define the extent and whether the lesion is macrocystic or microcystic, guiding treatment choice Management options include sclerotherapy (often effective for macrocystic lesions) and surgical excision, though complete removal can be difficult when the malformation infiltrates vital structures Because the malformation crosses tissue planes and encases nerves and vessels, incomplete excision and recurrence are common Airway compromise from a large or rapidly enlarging cervical or oral lesion, which may be life-threatening Sudden painful swelling due to intracystic haemorrhage Signs of infection within the malformation causing rapid expansion Feeding or swallowing difficulty from mass effect on the pharynx Attempting aggressive complete excision at the cost of damaging encased nerves and vessels Underestimating airway risk in large cervical lesions before intervention Assuming the lesion will spontaneously resolve, unlike infantile haemangiomas Overlooking associated chromosomal or cardiac anomalies in antenatally detected cases Cystic hygroma is a malformation of the lymphatic system in which sequestered lymphatic channels fail to connect normally with the venous drainage, producing dilated, fluid-filled cystic spaces. These may be macrocystic (large cysts) or microcystic and tend to infiltrate along tissue planes rather than respect anatomical boundaries. Accumulated lymph distends the cysts, and intralesional haemorrhage or infection can cause rapid, sometimes dangerous, enlargement. The malformation grows with the child and does not spontaneously regress in most cases. Small, well-localised macrocystic lesions often respond well to sclerotherapy or excision. Extensive, infiltrative, or microcystic malformations are harder to eradicate, recur frequently, and may require repeated interventions. Fetal cystic hygromas associated with chromosomal or cardiac anomalies carry a guarded prognosis.

Cystic leukoencephalopathy (RNASET2) — RNASET2-related leukoencephalopathy, cystic leukoencephalopathy without megalencephaly, RNASET2 deficiency, CMV-like leukoencephalopathy Congenital cytomegalovirus infection and other congenital (TORCH) infections Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome and other interferonopathies Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts (MLC1/GLIALCAM) Vanishing white matter disease and other cystic leukoencephalopathies Mitochondrial leukoencephalopathy with cystic change Congenital muscular dystrophies with brain malformation and white matter change Brain MRI to demonstrate multifocal white matter lesions with bilateral anterior temporal cysts Congenital cytomegalovirus testing, including PCR of stored neonatal blood spots where possible RNASET2 sequencing, with leukodystrophy panel or exome if targeted testing is negative Audiometry for associated sensorineural hearing loss Electroencephalography where seizures are present Developmental assessment to guide supportive intervention An autosomal recessive leukoencephalopathy caused by variants in RNASET2, which encodes a ribonuclease The MRI pattern closely mimics congenital cytomegalovirus infection, with multifocal patchy white matter lesions and bilateral anterior temporal subcortical cysts Because of this imaging overlap, a key diagnostic step is to exclude congenital cytomegalovirus, including testing of stored neonatal blood spots where available Children usually present in infancy with psychomotor delay, hypotonia and often seizures, and sensorineural hearing loss may be present The clinical course is frequently non-progressive or only slowly progressive, distinguishing it from many other leukodystrophies Diagnosis rests on the characteristic imaging combined with exclusion of congenital infection and confirmation of biallelic RNASET2 variants Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, with seizure control, developmental support, hearing rehabilitation and physiotherapy Poorly controlled seizures or status epilepticus Unexpected neurological regression prompting reassessment of the diagnosis Progressive hearing loss impairing communication and development Feeding difficulty with aspiration risk Diagnosing congenital cytomegalovirus purely on imaging without genetic testing, or vice versa, given their close resemblance Overlooking the anterior temporal cysts as a specific pattern clue Assuming a progressive leukodystrophy and giving an unduly pessimistic prognosis for what is often a static condition Failing to test stored neonatal blood spots when congenital infection needs to be excluded Not arranging hearing assessment and developmental support This leukoencephalopathy is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in RNASET2, which encodes a ribonuclease of the transferase T2 family that participates in RNA turnover and lysosomal RNA degradation. Loss of enzyme activity is thought to disturb RNA processing and clearance, with downstream effects on neuroinflammation and glial function during early brain development. The resulting injury produces the distinctive combination of multifocal white matter abnormality and anterior temporal cysts, a pattern that strikingly resembles the sequelae of intrauterine cytomegalovirus infection despite the genetic cause. The disorder is often static or only slowly progressive, with fixed motor and cognitive impairment of variable severity and, in many children, associated epilepsy and hearing loss; because it is largely non-progressive, prognosis relates mainly to the initial extent of brain injury and the burden of seizures rather than to ongoing degeneration.

neurological involvement is the most important form Subcutaneous and muscular cysts may be palpable as painless nodules and can calcify, sometimes visible on imaging Ocular cysticercosis can threaten vision and requires careful assessment before any antiparasitic therapy It is a major public-health problem in India and other regions where pigs are raised with poor sanitation Serology (antibody detection) supports the diagnosis, but imaging is central to defining cyst location and burden Antiparasitic therapy is used with adjunctive corticosteroids to control the inflammation provoked by dying cysts, and treatment decisions depend heavily on the site and stage of cysts New-onset seizures or focal neurological deficits indicating central nervous system involvement Features of raised intracranial pressure requiring urgent evaluation Visual disturbance suggesting an ocular cyst that could be harmed by antiparasitic-induced inflammation Rapid neurological deterioration during or after starting antiparasitic therapy Starting antiparasitic drugs without first excluding ocular cysts, risking sight-threatening inflammation Overlooking a coexisting intestinal tapeworm that perpetuates transmission Attributing all soft-tissue nodules to benign causes without imaging in endemic areas Failing to give adjunctive anti-inflammatory cover when treating heavy or CNS cyst burdens When humans ingest Taenia solium eggs, oncospheres hatch in the intestine, penetrate the mucosa and disseminate through the bloodstream to tissues, where they mature into fluid-filled cysticerci. Living cysts often provoke little inflammation, but as they degenerate they release antigens that trigger a host inflammatory and immune response. This inflammation, together with mass effect and eventual calcification, produces most of the clinical manifestations, especially when cysts lie within the brain or eye. Isolated subcutaneous or muscular cysticercosis is generally benign and often asymptomatic. Prognosis is largely determined by neurological and ocular involvement, where outcome depends on cyst location, number, and the inflammatory response to treatment; many patients do well but some suffer chronic epilepsy or visual loss.

SLC7A9 (encoding b0,+AT). Defective reabsorption leaves large amounts of cystine in the tubular fluid; because cystine is relatively insoluble, especially in acidic and concentrated urine, it becomes supersaturated and crystallises. Solubility improves markedly as the urine is diluted and alkalinised, which underpins the therapeutic approach. The disorder generates recurrent stones from early life and, without control, a substantial cumulative stone burden. A lifelong condition with a strong tendency to recur; with rigorous hydration, alkalinisation and thiol therapy the stone rate can be greatly reduced, but adherence is demanding and chronic kidney disease may develop after repeated interventions.

Overlooking cystinosis as a cause of Fanconi syndrome and rickets in a young child Failing to examine for corneal crystals that support the diagnosis Underestimating the importance of adherence to cystine-depleting therapy and electrolyte replacement Assuming renal transplantation cures the disorder, when extrarenal cystine accumulation continues Cystinosis is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in CTNS, which encodes cystinosin, the transporter that moves cystine out of the lysosome. Impaired transport leads to intralysosomal cystine accumulation and crystal formation in cells across many tissues, including the kidney, cornea, thyroid, muscle, pancreas, and brain. In the kidney, damage to the proximal tubule produces a generalised reabsorptive defect (Fanconi syndrome) and, over time, progressive glomerular and interstitial injury leading to renal failure. Continued crystal accumulation elsewhere accounts for the later multisystem complications. Untreated nephropathic cystinosis progresses to end-stage renal failure in childhood with multisystem complications. Early and sustained cystine-depleting therapy with supportive care substantially delays renal deterioration and reduces extrarenal complications, improving long-term survival, though adherence is critical and complications may still accrue over time.

With lifelong high fluid intake, urinary alkalinisation and monitoring, stone recurrence can be markedly reduced, but adherence is demanding and recurrent stones or interventions may lead to chronic kidney disease over decades.

analogue glaucoma drop as a contributing factor Failing to treat the underlying vascular or inflammatory cause and treating only the fluid Cystoid macular oedema results from breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier, allowing fluid to accumulate in cystic spaces of the macula. Inflammatory mediators, particularly prostaglandins and vascular endothelial growth factor, increase perifoveal capillary permeability. After cataract surgery the trigger is a self-limiting inflammatory response, whereas in diabetes and vein occlusion it reflects chronic vascular incompetence and ischaemia. Vitreomacular traction and epiretinal membranes can contribute mechanically. Sustained fluid accumulation distorts and eventually damages photoreceptors. Post-surgical cystoid macular oedema often resolves with anti-inflammatory treatment and a good visual outcome, but oedema secondary to diabetes, vein occlusion, or chronic uveitis tends to recur and can cause lasting central visual impairment if fluid persists.

is unusual among enteric protozoa Stopping treatment too early in immunosuppressed patients, allowing relapse Cystoisospora belli is an obligate intracellular coccidian parasite of the small-intestinal epithelium. Sporulated oocysts ingested from contaminated food or water release sporozoites that invade enterocytes, where the parasite undergoes both asexual and sexual replication before immature oocysts are passed in the stool and mature in the environment. Epithelial invasion produces villous blunting, crypt hyperplasia and a mucosal inflammatory infiltrate rich in eosinophils, impairing absorption and driving a secretory, watery diarrhoea. In immunocompetent people the illness is usually self-limiting, but defective cell-mediated immunity permits heavy, persistent infection, extraintestinal spread and chronic malabsorption. Immunocompetent patients usually recover fully, though relapses can occur; in immunocompromised hosts the illness may be chronic and debilitating, but responds well to antimicrobial therapy combined with immune reconstitution.

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Infection — CMV Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infectious mononucleosis (heterophile-positive, with prominent exudative pharyngitis and cervical adenopathy) versus CMV mononucleosis (heterophile-negative) Congenital cytomegalic inclusion disease must be distinguished from congenital syphilis, toxoplasmosis, rubella, Zika, herpes simplex virus, and bacterial sepsis (p.1513) CMV pneumonitis differential includes Pneumocystis, other viral/bacterial/fungal pneumonias, pulmonary hemorrhage, and irradiation or cytotoxic drug injury (p.1514) CMV retinopathy must be distinguished from toxoplasmosis, candidiasis, and herpes simplex virus retinitis (p.1514) Epstein-Barr virus mononucleosis Toxoplasmosis Congenital rubella, Zika, herpes simplex virus, and syphilis (in neonates) Pneumocystis pneumonia Herpes simplex virus and Candida retinitis/esophagitis Quantitative nucleic acid testing (QNAT) for CMV DNA by PCR in blood or other specimens (preferred; same assay should be used for serial comparison) CMV pp65 antigenemia immunofluorescence assay on peripheral-blood leukocytes CMV DNA PCR in cerebrospinal fluid for suspected encephalitis or polyradiculopathy Viral culture on human fibroblast monolayers, including the rapid overnight shell vial assay with monoclonal antibody to immediate-early antigen Serology: CMV IgG (may take up to 4 weeks to rise after primary infection) and CMV IgM (false positives possible with rheumatoid factor); serology mainly stratifies transplant risk and is NOT recommended to diagnose acute disease in immunocompromised patients Histopathology/biopsy demonstrating 'owl's eye' cytomegalic inclusions for tissue-invasive disease Pulmonary hemorrhage and radiation- or cytotoxic-drug-induced lung injury (mimicking CMV pneumonitis) Allograft rejection (overlapping with CMV syndrome in transplant recipients) CMV is a beta-herpesvirus carried for life after infection; the infection is usually silent, and reactivation syndromes emerge predominantly when T-lymphocyte-mediated immunity is compromised (organ transplantation, lymphoid neoplasms, HIV, or critical illness in the ICU) (p.1512). In immunocompetent hosts beyond the neonatal period, the most common manifestation is a heterophile-antibody-negative mononucleosis syndrome; unlike EBV mononucleosis, exudative pharyngitis and cervical lymphadenopathy are rare, though splenomegaly, prolonged high fever, fatigue and malaise are common (p.1513-1514). The characteristic laboratory finding in CMV mononucleosis is relative lymphocytosis with >10% atypical lymphocytes (predominantly activated CD8+ T cells); heterophile antibodies are absent (p.1514). Congenital CMV is the commonest congenital infection; most congenital infections are clinically inapparent at birth, yet 7-11% of asymptomatically infected infants develop sensorineural hearing loss over 5 years (p.1512-1513). Clinical disease in the fetus/newborn is related largely to PRIMARY maternal infection rather than reactivation; primary first-trimester infection carries up to 40-50% risk of sensorineural complications (p.1513). Preferred diagnosis is detection of virus/antigen/DNA, most commonly quantitative nucleic acid testing (QNAT) by PCR; the pp65 antigenemia immunofluorescence assay is an alternative, and CMV DNA in CSF aids diagnosis of CMV encephalitis or polyradiculopathy (p.1515). In persons with HIV, end-organ CMV disease (especially retinitis) occurs particularly when CD4+ counts fall below 50/uL; flares of CMV retinitis can occur shortly after starting antiretroviral therapy as an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) (p.1514). An immune-complex glomerulopathy has been observed in some CMV-infected patients after renal transplantation, and CMV mononucleosis can produce transient autoantibodies (cryoglobulins, rheumatoid factors, cold agglutinins, antinuclear antibodies) via polyclonal B-cell activation (p.1512-1514). Pathology shows enlarged 'cytomegalic' cells (2-4x normal) with an eccentric intranuclear inclusion surrounded by a clear halo producing the classic 'owl's eye' appearance (p.1513). Retinitis in an immunocompromised host (especially HIV with CD4+ <50/uL) - threat to vision Colitis or gastrointestinal ulceration with risk of bleeding or perforation Pneumonitis (tachypnea, hypoxemia, nonproductive cough with bilateral interstitial/reticulonodular infiltrates) Encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis or subacute progressive polyradiculopathy Persistent viremia with multi-organ involvement, pancytopenia and hypotension (associated with fatal disease) Symptomatic congenital infection (petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, microcephaly with cerebral calcifications, intrauterine growth retardation) Tissue-invasive CMV disease (e.g., gastrointestinal) may be present despite NEGATIVE blood CMV antigenemia and viral-load testing - diagnosis may require endoscopic biopsy with histopathology, not blood viremia alone (p.1514). Isolation of CMV from urine, stool, or saliva does NOT by itself prove acute infection, since excretion may persist for months to years; detection of viremia by QNAT or antigenemia is a better predictor (p.1515). Serology is NOT recommended to diagnose acute disease in immunocompromised patients; IgG may not rise for up to 4 weeks and rheumatoid factor can cause false-positive IgM (p.1515). CMV detection in blood does not equate to end-organ disease; clinical and tissue correlation is required. Universal ganciclovir/valganciclovir prophylaxis is bone-marrow suppressive, favoring preemptive strategies in HSCT recipients (p.1515). CMV is a beta-herpesvirus with double-stranded DNA, icosahedral symmetry and a lipoprotein envelope; it replicates in the cell nucleus and can establish either lytic/productive or latent infection. After primary infection the virus persists indefinitely in multiple cell types and organs (silent latency). Primary infection in late childhood/adulthood elicits a vigorous CD8+ T-lymphocyte response producing atypical lymphocytes and a mononucleosis-like illness, with polyclonal B-cell activation generating autoantibodies. When host T-cell responses are compromised by disease or iatrogenic immunosuppression, latent virus reactivates; chronic antigenic stimulation under immunosuppression (e.g., post-transplant) is an ideal setting for CMV disease, and potent T-cell suppressants (antithymocyte globulin, alemtuzumab) markedly raise CMV syndrome rates. CMV itself further depresses T-lymphocyte responsiveness, predisposing to superinfection by other opportunists. Congenital disease arises chiefly from primary maternal infection; transmission to transplant/transfusion recipients reflects silent infection in donor tissues (p.1512-1513). Immunocompetent CMV mononucleosis is almost always self-limited (illness lasting 2-6 weeks); most patients recover without sequelae, though postviral asthenia may persist for months and fatal infection is rare. Severely affected congenitally infected infants have a poor prognosis with a mortality of about 5% and few survivors escaping intellectual or hearing impairment; 7-11% of asymptomatically infected neonates still develop sensorineural hearing loss over 5 years. In immunocompromised hosts, untreated CMV may progress to severe end-organ disease; CMV disease is an independent risk factor for both graft loss and death after organ transplantation, and high blood viral loads in HIV predict severe disease and death (p.1513-1514). Harrison frames CMV by host and syndrome rather than a formal grading scale: (1) congenital CMV - subclinical to severe disseminated cytomegalic inclusion disease; (2) perinatal CMV - usually asymptomatic; (3) immunocompetent CMV mononucleosis - heterophile-negative, self-limited; (4) CMV in the immunocompromised host - asymptomatic infection/viremia, 'CMV syndrome' (febrile leukopenia), and tissue-invasive end-organ disease (pneumonitis, colitis/GI disease, hepatitis, esophagitis, retinitis, encephalitis/polyradiculopathy), stratified by population in Table 200-1 (fetus/neonate, organ transplant recipient, HSCT recipient, person with HIV) (p.1513).

nutritional support Structural brain malformation on imaging indicating disturbed neuronal migration Rapid early neurological deterioration Diagnosing Zellweger syndrome without pursuing single-enzyme peroxisomal defects when biogenesis markers are normal Relying on VLCFA alone and missing the branched-chain and bile-acid abnormalities that point to the bifunctional protein Underestimating milder phenotypes that survive longer and present beyond the neonatal period Not offering genetic counselling and carrier testing given the autosomal recessive inheritance D-bifunctional protein deficiency arises from HSD17B4 mutations that impair the D-bifunctional protein, a peroxisomal enzyme providing the 2-enoyl-CoA hydratase and 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase steps of peroxisomal beta-oxidation for both very-long-chain and branched-chain (pristanic) fatty acids and bile-acid precursors. The classic presentation is severe, with most affected infants having little developmental progress, refractory seizures, and death typically within the first years of life, although milder variants with longer survival are recognised. Treatment is supportive without a disease-modifying option.

D-glyceric aciduria — D-glycerate kinase deficiency, GLYCTK deficiency, D-glyceric acidaemia Other organic acidaemias presenting with encephalopathy L-glyceric aciduria (primary hyperoxaluria type 2), a biochemically distinct disorder Serine biosynthesis defects Mitochondrial disease with lactic acidosis Other causes of infantile epileptic encephalopathy Non-metabolic causes of developmental delay and hypotonia Urine organic acids demonstrating increased D-glyceric acid GLYCTK molecular genetic testing Blood gas and lactate to assess metabolic acidosis Neuroimaging and electroencephalography where symptomatic Developmental and growth assessment Exclusion of other organic acidaemias on the same organic acid profile A rare inborn error of serine and fructose metabolism caused by deficiency of D-glycerate kinase (GLYCTK) The clinical spectrum is broad and variable, ranging from severe encephalopathy with seizures and developmental delay to essentially asymptomatic individuals Reported features in symptomatic cases include hypotonia, microcephaly, seizures, metabolic acidosis and failure to thrive The biochemical marker is markedly increased urinary D-glyceric acid on organic acid analysis The variable phenotype means the metabolite finding does not reliably predict clinical severity Management is supportive; no specific corrective therapy is established, and dietary measures are individualised through a metabolic service Diagnosis rests on urine organic acids with confirmatory GLYCTK molecular testing Metabolic acidosis with acute encephalopathy Drug-resistant seizures Developmental regression Failure to thrive with progressive neurological signs Confusing D-glyceric aciduria with L-glyceric aciduria (primary hyperoxaluria type 2) Assuming the metabolite level predicts clinical severity Over-treating an incidentally detected, asymptomatic biochemical abnormality Attributing all neurological findings to the disorder without excluding co-existing causes D-glycerate kinase phosphorylates D-glycerate to 2-phosphoglycerate, linking the metabolism of serine and fructose to glycolytic intermediates. Enzyme deficiency causes accumulation and urinary excretion of D-glyceric acid. The mechanism by which the metabolite relates to the neurological features is not fully defined, and because some individuals with the biochemical defect remain well, the accumulated acid may not be directly and uniformly neurotoxic. The disorder is therefore biochemically defined but clinically heterogeneous. Prognosis is highly variable: some patients have severe neurological impairment while others are asymptomatic, so counselling must reflect this heterogeneity rather than the biochemical finding alone.

Dacryoadenitis — lacrimal gland inflammation Idiopathic orbital inflammation (lacrimal subtype) Lacrimal gland tumour (pleomorphic adenoma, lymphoma, carcinoma) IgG4-related dacryoadenitis Sarcoidosis Preseptal or orbital cellulitis Ruptured dermoid cyst Assessment for systemic infective features and preauricular nodes CT or MRI of the orbit where the diagnosis is unclear or orbital extension is suspected Viral and bacterial studies as clinically indicated Serum IgG4, angiotensin-converting enzyme and autoimmune screen for chronic disease Lacrimal gland biopsy for chronic, bilateral or mass-like presentations Inflammation of the lacrimal gland presenting with pain, swelling and redness over the outer third of the upper eyelid The upper lid may take on a characteristic S-shaped contour from lateral gland enlargement Acute dacryoadenitis is most often infective, classically viral (such as mumps or Epstein-Barr virus) or bacterial Chronic or bilateral disease is more often non-infective, from sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, Sjogren syndrome or granulomatosis with polyangiitis Fever, preauricular lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms point to an infective cause Imaging and, in atypical or chronic cases, biopsy help distinguish infection from inflammatory or neoplastic disease Proptosis, ophthalmoplegia or visual loss suggesting orbital extension A firm mass or chronic painless enlargement suggesting tumour Systemic features suggesting sarcoidosis or vasculitis Failure to respond to appropriate treatment Assuming all lacrimal swelling is infective and missing a tumour or IgG4-related disease Overlooking orbital extension of a bacterial infection Failing to investigate chronic or bilateral disease for a systemic cause Delaying biopsy of a suspicious mass Dacryoadenitis is inflammation of the lacrimal gland that may be infective or non-infective. Acute infective dacryoadenitis follows viral or bacterial infection reaching the gland, producing acute painful enlargement with an inflammatory response. Non-infective forms arise from systemic granulomatous or autoimmune disease infiltrating the gland. The enlarged, inflamed gland displaces the globe and deforms the upper lid, and untreated bacterial infection can progress to abscess or orbital involvement. Acute infective dacryoadenitis usually resolves with treatment of the underlying infection; prognosis of non-infective disease depends on the systemic condition, and a neoplastic cause must not be missed.
