management is with systemic antibiotics and warm compresses in the acute phase Incision and drainage may be needed for a pointing abscess, but definitive treatment of the underlying obstruction is dacryocystorhinostomy once inflammation settles Congenital dacryocystitis in infants relates to a persistent membrane at the valve of Hasner and may need probing if it does not resolve Acute dacryocystitis can be complicated by preseptal or orbital cellulitis and rarely by fistula formation Spread to preseptal or orbital cellulitis with proptosis, restricted eye movements, or reduced vision A firm, irregular, or bloody lacrimal sac mass suggesting a lacrimal sac tumour rather than simple infection Systemic features of sepsis in an unwell patient Neonatal dacryocystitis, which can progress rapidly and needs prompt treatment Attempting probing or surgery during acute inflammation rather than treating the infection first Mislabelling the medial canthal swelling as preseptal cellulitis and missing the underlying sac infection Failing to recognise a lacrimal sac tumour presenting as atypical dacryocystitis Not addressing the underlying duct obstruction, leading to repeated infections Dacryocystitis is inflammation of the lacrimal sac, almost always resulting from obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct. Obstruction leads to retention and stagnation of tears and mucus within the sac, providing a medium for bacterial overgrowth. Acute infection produces a tense, inflamed sac that may progress to abscess formation, while chronic obstruction causes a mucocele with recurrent low-grade infection and persistent watering. In infants, incomplete canalisation of the duct at the valve of Hasner is the usual cause. Acute dacryocystitis usually responds well to antibiotics, but recurrence is common until the underlying nasolacrimal duct obstruction is corrected surgically; dacryocystorhinostomy is highly effective at relieving obstruction and preventing further episodes.

Dacryops — lacrimal ductal cyst Lacrimal gland tumour (pleomorphic adenoma, others) Dermoid or epidermoid cyst Dacryoadenitis with swelling Prolapsed lacrimal gland Orbital lymphangioma or other cystic orbital lesion Clinical examination with transillumination Imaging (ultrasound, CT or MRI) showing a cystic lacrimal lesion Assessment of size fluctuation and effect on the globe Exclusion of a solid lacrimal gland tumour Histology of the cyst wall if excised A cystic lesion arising from the ductal system of the lacrimal gland (or accessory glands) It presents as a smooth, fluctuant, sometimes bluish swelling in the region of the lacrimal gland or superolateral fornix It may fluctuate in size and can cause a foreign-body sensation or, if large, mechanical effects Transillumination and imaging demonstrate its cystic, fluid-filled nature It is benign and distinct from solid lacrimal gland tumours Management ranges from observation to marsupialisation or excision for symptomatic lesions A solid or rapidly enlarging mass suggesting neoplasm Proptosis or globe displacement Pain or inflammation suggesting infection Recurrence after drainage Mistaking a solid lacrimal gland tumour for a benign cyst Simple aspiration leading to recurrence rather than definitive marsupialisation Overlooking associated lacrimal gland pathology Attributing a fluctuant swelling to infection Dacryops results from cystic dilatation of a lacrimal gland duct, thought to follow ductal obstruction or a valve-like mechanism that traps secretions, leading to a fluid-filled cyst lined by ductal epithelium. Because it communicates with, or arises from, the secretory ductal system, it may enlarge with lacrimal stimulation. It is a benign cystic lesion rather than a neoplasm, which imaging and its fluctuant, transilluminating character help confirm. Dacryops is benign with an excellent prognosis; symptomatic lesions do well after marsupialisation or excision, though recurrence can occur.

Dandy-Walker malformation — DWM, Dandy-Walker complex, Dandy-Walker syndrome, cystic posterior fossa malformation Mega cisterna magna Blake pouch cyst Posterior fossa arachnoid cyst Cerebellar vermis hypoplasia of other cause including Joubert syndrome Rhombencephalosynapsis Pontocerebellar hypoplasia Brain MRI to characterise the vermis, fourth ventricle, and posterior fossa and to distinguish it from milder variants Prenatal ultrasound and foetal MRI when suspected antenatally Chromosomal microarray and, where indicated, exome sequencing Evaluation for associated supratentorial and systemic anomalies Serial head circumference measurement and imaging to monitor for hydrocephalus Developmental assessment and neurosurgical review if hydrocephalus develops A posterior fossa malformation defined by hypoplasia or agenesis of the cerebellar vermis, cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle communicating with the cyst, and an enlarged posterior fossa with upward displacement of the tentorium and torcula Hydrocephalus is common but often develops after the neonatal period rather than at birth It should be distinguished from milder posterior fossa variants such as an isolated mega cisterna magna or a Blake pouch cyst, which have a different prognosis It may be isolated or associated with other central nervous system anomalies such as agenesis of the corpus callosum, and with chromosomal and single-gene syndromes Presentation ranges from an incidental finding to macrocephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia, ataxia, and signs of raised intracranial pressure Neurodevelopmental outcome depends strongly on the presence of associated brain malformations and any underlying genetic syndrome rather than the posterior fossa cyst alone Diagnosis is by prenatal ultrasound and foetal or postnatal MRI, with genetic evaluation when other anomalies coexist Progressive hydrocephalus with raised intracranial pressure requiring neurosurgical intervention Rapidly increasing head circumference in an infant Apnoea or brainstem signs from posterior fossa mass effect Multiple associated anomalies suggesting a serious underlying syndrome Overdiagnosing Dandy-Walker malformation when the finding is actually a benign mega cisterna magna or Blake pouch cyst Giving a uniformly poor prognosis without assessing for associated anomalies and genetic cause Assuming hydrocephalus is always present at birth and not monitoring for its later development Neglecting a full genetic and structural evaluation in apparently isolated cases Dandy-Walker malformation arises from abnormal development of the cerebellar vermis and the roof of the fourth ventricle in early gestation. Failure of normal vermian formation and of the developing fourth ventricular roof leads to cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle that balloons into an enlarged posterior fossa, elevating the tentorium and torcula. Disturbed cerebrospinal fluid dynamics predispose to hydrocephalus. The malformation may occur in isolation or as part of chromosomal, single-gene, or teratogenic disorders, and coexisting supratentorial anomalies largely determine the neurological outcome. Prognosis varies widely. Isolated Dandy-Walker malformation with a normally formed vermis apart from the cyst can have a favourable neurodevelopmental outcome, whereas cases with vermian agenesis, associated brain malformations, or a genetic syndrome often have significant developmental disability.

abnormalities support the diagnosis The disease is rapidly progressive in males, and cardiac transplantation is often required at a young age Defibrillator therapy is considered because of the high arrhythmic and sudden death risk Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis and enables screening of at-risk relatives Rapidly progressive heart failure in a young male Syncope or documented ventricular arrhythmia Marked left ventricular hypertrophy with pre-excitation on ECG Family history consistent with X-linked inheritance and early cardiac death Labelling the cardiomyopathy as ordinary sarcomeric hypertrophic disease and missing the storage aetiology Overlooking the diagnostic clues of pre-excitation, raised creatine kinase and mild myopathy Underestimating disease severity and the need for early transplant assessment in males Assuming female relatives are unaffected rather than at risk of later disease Delaying genetic confirmation and family screening Danon disease is caused by variants in LAMP2, which encodes lysosome-associated membrane protein 2, a protein essential for autophagy and lysosomal function. Its deficiency impairs the fusion of autophagosomes with lysosomes, so autophagic vacuoles and glycogen accumulate within cardiac and skeletal muscle and other tissues. This storage and disrupted autophagy lead to progressive cardiomyocyte dysfunction and hypertrophy, conduction tissue involvement causing pre-excitation and arrhythmia, and skeletal muscle weakness. Because the gene is X-linked, hemizygous males are affected early and severely, while heterozygous females show a milder and later phenotype through variable X-inactivation. The prognosis is poor in affected males, with rapidly progressive cardiomyopathy and high arrhythmic risk often necessitating transplantation in adolescence or early adulthood; female carriers generally have a later and more variable course.

involvement or skin detachment Renal impairment or other organ dysfunction Persistent high fever with haemodynamic instability Severe methaemoglobinaemia or haemolysis compounding the picture Mistaking the delayed multiorgan reaction for infection and continuing dapsone Confusing the immune syndrome with the separate dose-related methaemoglobinaemia and haemolysis Stopping corticosteroids too rapidly and precipitating relapse Reintroducing dapsone after recovery Not considering HLA-B*13:01 screening in high-prevalence populations Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome is a delayed, T-cell-mediated immune reaction. Dapsone is metabolised, partly via cytochrome P450, to reactive hydroxylamine and other intermediates; these reactive metabolites can act as haptens that modify host proteins and trigger an adaptive immune response, with the risk shaped by genetic factors including the HLA-B*13:01 allele. The activated immune response, similar to other DRESS reactions, produces fever, a widespread cutaneous eruption, eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy and inflammation of internal organs, especially the liver. This immune-mediated syndrome is mechanistically separate from dapsone's predictable, dose-dependent oxidant effects on red cells, which cause methaemoglobinaemia and haemolysis (the latter particularly in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency). With early withdrawal and corticosteroid treatment most patients recover, but the syndrome can be fatal, chiefly from hepatic failure. The course may be prolonged with relapses, and lifelong avoidance of dapsone is required.

examination of nails and mucosa for corroborating signs Autosomal dominant disorder caused by variants in ATP2A2, which encodes the SERCA2 endoplasmic reticulum calcium pump Presents in adolescence with greasy, warty, malodorous keratotic papules coalescing in seborrhoeic distribution (chest, back, scalp margins, flexures) Nail changes are highly characteristic: alternating red and white the eruption, so flares are common in summer Neuropsychiatric associations, including mood disorders, are recognised in affected families Superimposed herpes simplex (Kaposi varicelliform eruption) can cause abrupt, painful deterioration Sudden painful monomorphic vesicles or erosions suggesting Kaposi varicelliform eruption from herpes superinfection Widespread erosions with systemic upset and secondary bacterial infection Rapidly enlarging or ulcerated lesion raising concern for squamous change Missing herpes superinfection and attributing a painful flare simply to disease activity Mistaking flexural involvement for intertrigo or fungal infection Overlooking the characteristic nail and palmar signs that clinch the diagnosis Failing to advise on heat, sweat, and sun avoidance that reduces flares Darier disease results from loss-of-function variants in ATP2A2, encoding the SERCA2 pump that transports calcium into the endoplasmic reticulum of keratinocytes. Impaired intracellular calcium regulation disrupts the calcium-dependent assembly and function of desmosomal adhesion complexes. The consequence is loss of cohesion between keratinocytes (acantholysis) together with abnormal keratinisation of individual cells (dyskeratosis), giving the histological hallmarks of suprabasal acantholysis with corps ronds and grains. Environmental triggers such as heat, ultraviolet light, and mechanical friction further destabilise the fragile epidermis and precipitate clinical flares. It is a chronic, relapsing condition that persists lifelong with seasonal flares, but most patients maintain reasonable control with skin care, avoidance of triggers, and oral retinoids in severe cases; it does not shorten life expectancy.

subcutaneous fat contributing to the aged look Joint laxity and dislocations may occur alongside the skin findings Management is supportive, addressing feeding, growth, developmental needs and the ophthalmic abnormalities Failure to thrive with significant feeding difficulty Progressive neurological deterioration or intractable movement disorder Visual impairment from cataract or corneal clouding Complications of severe hypotonia such as recurrent aspiration Confusing it with other progeroid or cutis laxa syndromes without molecular confirmation Overlooking the movement disorder and attributing hypotonia to a non-specific cause Missing the ophthalmic abnormalities that need early assessment Assuming a uniformly poor prognosis when expressivity varies considerably De Barsy syndrome is a progeroid cutis laxa caused by biallelic variants in ALDH18A1 or PYCR1, enzymes of the mitochondrial pathway that synthesises proline and ornithine from glutamate. Disruption of this pathway impairs collagen and elastin synthesis and mitochondrial function, weakening dermal connective tissue to produce lax, aged-looking skin and contributing to the neurological, ocular and growth abnormalities. The combined connective tissue and metabolic effects explain the striking progeroid appearance alongside the movement disorder and developmental delay. The outlook is variable and often guarded, with significant developmental impairment and growth failure; some children have a shortened lifespan while milder cases survive longer with supportive care.

and wrist movement and by gripping and lifting It affects the first dorsal extensor compartment, involving abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis as they pass under the extensor rather than a purely inflammatory tenosynovitis First-line management is activity modification, a thumb spica splint, and analgesia by principle Corticosteroid injection into the first dorsal review Confusing it with thumb basal joint arthritis, which needs different treatment Injuring or overlooking the superficial radial nerve during injection or surgery Failing to recognise a compartment septum causing injection failure Neglecting activity modification so symptoms persist or recur De Quervain tenosynovitis is a stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal extensor compartment of the wrist. Repetitive or sustained thumb and wrist loading causes thickening and myxoid degeneration of the tendon sheath and retinaculum, narrowing the fibro-osseous tunnel through which abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis run. The resulting friction and impaired tendon gliding produce pain over the radial styloid. Most cases respond well to splinting and corticosteroid injection, and postpartum cases often settle as hormonal and mechanical factors resolve; a minority need surgical release, which is generally successful.

De Quervain thyroiditis — subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, subacute painful thyroiditis Suppurative (infective) thyroiditis Graves disease Silent and postpartum thyroiditis (painless) Haemorrhage into a thyroid nodule Riedel thyroiditis Thyroid function tests through the phases Inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP), typically very high Radioactive iodine uptake (low in the thyrotoxic phase) Thyroid ultrasound Follow-up thyroid function to detect persistent hypothyroidism A painful subacute thyroiditis, typically following a viral upper respiratory infection Presents with a tender, firm goitre, neck pain often radiating to the jaw or ears, and systemic upset It follows a triphasic course of thyrotoxicosis, then hypothyroidism, then recovery Inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) are characteristically markedly raised, unlike in other thyroiditides Radioactive iodine uptake is low during the thyrotoxic phase because the process is destructive It is managed with analgesia or anti-inflammatory drugs, or corticosteroids for severe pain; beta-blockade eases thyrotoxic symptoms Features suggesting suppurative thyroiditis (high fever, fluctuant tender mass) Severe compressive symptoms Persistent hypothyroidism Diagnostic uncertainty with Graves disease Treating the thyrotoxic phase with antithyroid drugs, which are ineffective in destructive thyroiditis Confusing it with suppurative thyroiditis or Graves disease Overlooking the markedly raised inflammatory markers as a diagnostic clue Not following up for permanent hypothyroidism De Quervain thyroiditis is a self-limiting inflammatory thyroiditis widely attributed to a viral or post-viral immune response, with a granulomatous infiltrate damaging thyroid follicles. Follicular destruction releases stored hormone, producing a transient thyrotoxic phase, after which hormone depletion causes a hypothyroid phase before the gland recovers. The intense inflammation accounts for the pain, tenderness and markedly elevated inflammatory markers, and the destructive (rather than hyperfunctioning) mechanism explains the low radioiodine uptake. Although virally triggered, it is not a suppurative infection of the gland. Most patients recover normal thyroid function within months, though a minority develop permanent hypothyroidism, and recurrence is uncommon.

by the first major event — ascites/edema, variceal hemorrhage, hepatic encephalopathy, or jaundice. (p.2756, p.2754) Once clinically significant portal hypertension (HVPG ≥5 mmHg, with substantial decompensation risk at ≥10 mmHg) progresses to overt decompensation, median survival is under 2 years. (p.2756) Encephalopathy in chronic liver disease is almost always triggered by an identifiable precipitant (GI bleeding, infection, volume depletion/overdiuresis, hyponatremia, constipation, uremia, sedatives/narcotics) rather than spontaneous progression. (p.2673, p.2759) Ammonia levels correlate poorly with the severity of encephalopathy or liver disease; the diagnosis of hepatic encephalopathy is clinical, and most hepatologists do not rely on ammonia to make the diagnosis or follow progress. (p.2759) A new or worsening encephalopathy episode mandates a search for occult infection — if ascites is present it should be tapped to exclude SBP. (p.2759) A hyperdynamic circulation (widened pulse pressure, increased cardiac output, reduced peripheral resistance from splanchnic vasodilation) is a hallmark of advanced cirrhosis. (p.2673) Acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) is acutely decompensating cirrhosis with one or more extrahepatic organ failures, behaves like a sepsis syndrome, and carries 28-day mortality of 20-70% rising with the number of failing organs; it is most often precipitated by bacterial/fungal infection or alcoholic hepatitis. (p.2760) Variceal hemorrhage carries a 20-30% mortality per bleeding episode and is an immediate life-threatening event (p.2756) A stepwise progressive rise in creatinine with large-volume ascites suggests hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI), a poor-prognosis functional renal failure (p.2759) ACLF with four or more organ failures persisting after 3-7 days of ICU support, when transplant is not an option, signals a transition toward palliative care (p.2760) Avoid NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, and use ACE inhibitors/ARBs cautiously — they precipitate renal failure in cirrhotic ascites (p.371, p.2758) New-onset or worsening encephalopathy, jaundice, or tense ascites in known cirrhosis should prompt an urgent search for a precipitant (p.2759) Relying on ammonia levels to diagnose or track hepatic encephalopathy — they correlate poorly with disease severity (p.2759) Attributing altered mental status to encephalopathy without excluding electrolyte disturbance, sedatives, and renal/respiratory failure (p.2673) Failing to tap the ascites in a decompensated cirrhotic with new symptoms — abdominal tenderness is present in only ~40% of SBP and rebound is uncommon, so SBP can be clinically silent (p.372) Multiple organisms on ascitic culture with a raised PMN count indicate secondary (not spontaneous) peritonitis and a surgical source; multiple organisms without raised PMN suggest bowel perforation by the paracentesis needle (p.372) Withholding paracentesis for fear of coagulopathy — paracentesis is safe even in coagulopathic patients (p.371) Restricting dietary protein for encephalopathy — its harm to nutrition outweighs benefit and it is strongly discouraged (p.2760) Decompensation is driven by portal hypertension plus renal sodium and water retention. Portal hypertension (elevation of the hepatic venous pressure gradient >5 mmHg) arises from two simultaneous processes: increased intrahepatic resistance from fibrosis disrupting sinusoidal architecture, stellate-cell-mediated smooth-muscle contraction, regenerative nodules, microthrombi, and reduced intrahepatic endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) causing intrahepatic vasoconstriction; and increased splanchnic blood flow from systemic vasodilation. Systemically, raised nitric oxide, VEGF and TNF cause splanchnic arterial vasodilation, pooling blood and reducing effective circulating volume; the kidneys sense this as hypovolemia and activate ADH, the sympathetic nervous system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, producing free-water and sodium retention (ascites/edema). Encephalopathy results from gut-derived neurotoxins bypassing the liver via portosystemic shunting and reduced hepatic mass. (p.370, p.2756, p.2759) Decompensation defines a poor-prognosis state: with clinically significant portal hypertension that decompensates, median survival is under 2 years, and fewer than 50% of patients survive 2 years after the onset of ascites. Encephalopathy in chronic liver disease is a poor prognostic sign. HRS (both AKI and CKD types) carries a poor prognosis unless liver transplantation is achieved. ACLF 28-day mortality ranges from 20-70%, rising with the number of organ failures. Severity and transplant priority are graded by Child-Pugh class and the MELD/MELD-Na (MELD 3.0) systems. (p.371, p.2675-2676, p.2756, p.2759-2760) Child-Pugh score (5 factors: bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time/INR, ascites, encephalopathy; range 5-15) classifies cirrhosis as class A (5-6, compensated), B (7-9), or C (10-15); a score ≥7 (class B) defines decompensation. MELD score uses INR, bilirubin, and creatinine to predict short-term mortality and allocate organs; it was extended with serum sodium and reweighted as MELD-Na / MELD 3.0 for transplant listing. PELD is the pediatric equivalent. Clinically significant portal hypertension is defined by HVPG ≥10 mmHg. (p.2675-2676, p.2756, p.2754)

Decompression illness — DCI, decompression sickness, the bends, arterial gas embolism Inner ear or other barotrauma Immersion pulmonary oedema Musculoskeletal strain unrelated to diving Stroke or transient ischaemic attack from another cause Seizure disorder or cardiac syncope Marine envenomation or other diving-related injury Migraine with aura Detailed dive profile review including depth, bottom time, ascent rate, and decompression stops Full neurological examination to detect spinal cord and cerebral involvement Skin examination for cutis marmorata and joint assessment for the bends Assessment of oxygenation and cardiorespiratory status Investigation for a patent foramen ovale (e.g. bubble contrast echocardiography) in appropriate cases Consultation with a diving medicine or hyperbaric service to guide recompression An umbrella term encompassing decompression sickness, from bubbles forming out of dissolved inert gas, and arterial gas embolism, from pulmonary barotrauma driving gas into the arterial circulation Decompression sickness ranges from musculoskeletal joint pain (the bends) and a mottled skin rash (cutis marmorata), to serious neurological forms with spinal cord or cerebral involvement Arterial gas embolism typically presents dramatically within minutes of surfacing, with stroke-like deficits, loss of consciousness, or seizure Symptoms usually begin during or within hours of surfacing; any neurological complaint after diving should be treated as decompression illness until proven otherwise Definitive treatment is recompression in a hyperbaric chamber with hyperbaric oxygen, alongside high-flow surface oxygen, lying flat, and fluids during transfer Flying after diving too soon reduces ambient pressure further and can precipitate or worsen decompression illness, so recommended pre-flight surface intervals must be observed The dive profile, including depth, bottom time, ascent rate, and any missed decompression stops, is central to assessing risk A patent foramen ovale increases the risk of paradoxical bubble embolisation in some divers Neurological deficit, altered consciousness, or seizure after diving Rapid stroke-like onset within minutes of surfacing, suggesting arterial gas embolism Respiratory distress or chest pain suggesting pulmonary barotrauma Rapidly progressing symptoms or a history of missed decompression stops or rapid ascent Cutis marmorata, which may herald more serious decompression sickness Dismissing joint pain or vague post-dive symptoms and delaying recompression Failing to give high-flow surface oxygen while arranging transfer Allowing the patient to fly too soon after diving, worsening the illness Overlooking arterial gas embolism when stroke-like symptoms follow surfacing Not considering a patent foramen ovale in unexplained or recurrent cases Decompression illness has two overlapping mechanisms. In decompression sickness, inert gas (usually nitrogen) that dissolved into tissues under pressure comes out of solution as bubbles when ambient pressure falls too quickly on ascent; these bubbles obstruct vessels, distort tissue, and trigger inflammatory and clotting cascades, causing joint pain, skin mottling (cutis marmorata), and neurological injury, particularly of the spinal cord. In arterial gas embolism, over-expansion of the lungs on ascent (pulmonary barotrauma) forces gas into the pulmonary veins and systemic arteries, embolising to the brain and producing acute stroke-like features. Reducing ambient pressure further, as with flying soon after diving, exacerbates bubble formation. Prompt recompression and hyperbaric oxygen give many patients a good or full recovery, but delay in treatment, severe neurological (especially spinal) involvement, or arterial gas embolism can leave lasting deficits; early recognition and surface oxygen substantially improve outcomes.

interval excludes serious disease During exposure to raised pressure, inert gas (usually nitrogen) dissolves into body tissues in proportion to the pressure and time. If pressure is reduced faster than the gas can be safely eliminated through the lungs, it comes out of solution and forms bubbles within tissues and blood. These bubbles cause mechanical obstruction of vessels, mechanical tissue distortion, and secondary inflammatory and coagulation responses, producing the musculoskeletal, neurological, pulmonary and other manifestations. Prompt recompression and oxygen therapy give a good chance of full recovery, especially in milder disease; delay in treatment, severe neurological involvement or arterial gas embolism carry a higher risk of permanent deficit.

deep gluteal syndrome — deep gluteal space sciatic nerve entrapment, non-discogenic sciatic nerve entrapment Lumbar radiculopathy from disc herniation or stenosis Proximal hamstring tendinopathy or avulsion Ischiofemoral impingement Sacroiliac joint dysfunction Intra-articular hip pathology such as a labral tear Pudendal neuralgia Ischiogluteal or trochanteric bursitis MRI of the pelvis and hip with MR neurography of the sciatic nerve MRI of the lumbar spine to exclude a discogenic cause Electrodiagnostic studies including nerve conduction studies and EMG, with positional testing where available Dynamic ultrasound of the sciatic nerve in the deep gluteal space Image-guided perineural diagnostic local anaesthetic injection Describes non-discogenic entrapment of the sciatic nerve within the deep gluteal (subgluteal) space, presenting as posterior hip and buttock pain with sciatica not attributable to the lumbar spine. Symptoms are characteristically aggravated by prolonged sitting, and patients often shift weight or cannot tolerate sitting for extended periods. Piriformis syndrome is one subset; entrapment may equally arise from fibrovascular bands, the obturator internus and gemelli, proximal hamstring pathology, ischiofemoral narrowing or vascular structures. Provocation tests include the seated piriformis stretch test, the active piriformis test, and the flexion-adduction-internal-rotation manoeuvre; the Pace and Freiberg signs may also be positive. A normal lumbar spine examination and imaging in a patient with sciatica should prompt consideration of an extraspinal source in the deep gluteal space. MR neurography helps localise the entrapment site and characterise the nerve, while lumbar imaging is needed to exclude a discogenic cause. Management begins with physiotherapy emphasising neural mobilisation and stretching, alongside image-guided perineural injection that is both therapeutic and diagnostic. Endoscopic sciatic nerve decompression offers good outcomes in correctly selected patients who fail conservative treatment. Progressive motor weakness or foot drop indicating significant nerve compromise Bowel or bladder dysfunction or saddle anaesthesia, suggesting cauda equina syndrome from a central cause Constant severe night pain with systemic features, raising concern for a pelvic or presacral mass Bilateral symptoms with rapidly evolving neurological signs Anchoring on a diagnosis of piriformis syndrome and overlooking the other entrapment sites within the deep gluteal space. Failing to exclude the lumbar spine as the true pain generator before attributing symptoms to the deep gluteal space. Relying on normal static imaging, since entrapment is frequently dynamic and posture-dependent. Injecting near the sciatic nerve without image guidance, risking intraneural injection and nerve injury. The deep gluteal or subgluteal space is bounded anteriorly by the posterior hip capsule and proximal femur, posteriorly by gluteus maximus, medially by the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments and the ischium, and superiorly by the sciatic notch. The sciatic nerve courses through this space and may be compressed or tethered by several structures: the piriformis, including anatomical variants in which the nerve or its divisions pierce or straddle the muscle; fibrovascular bands; hypertrophied or inflamed short external rotators such as the obturator internus and gemelli; proximal hamstring scarring; a narrowed ischiofemoral interval; or aberrant vessels. Loss of the normal gliding and excursion of the nerve, often dynamic and posture-dependent, produces neuropathic buttock and posterior thigh pain. Many patients improve with conservative treatment and image-guided perineural injection. Endoscopic decompression provides good pain relief and functional recovery in appropriately selected patients with a clearly identified entrapment, although recovery of longstanding neurological deficit can be incomplete.

also assesses RV size and alternative diagnoses) Ventilation/perfusion lung scan (second-line, for patients unable to tolerate contrast) Chest radiograph (Westermark's sign, Hampton's hump, Palla's sign) MR venography with gadolinium (for equivocal leg/pelvic ultrasound) and MR pulmonary angiography (detects large proximal PE only) Echocardiography (to detect PE mimics and indirect signs such as McConnell's sign) Invasive pulmonary angiography and contrast phlebography (reserved for nondiagnostic CT or when intervention is planned) Ruptured Baker's cyst Muscle strain/injury Postthrombotic syndrome / venous insufficiency Congestive heart failure Acute coronary syndrome and myocardial infarction Pericarditis and pericardial tamponade Aortic dissection Pneumothorax / rib fracture Anxiety and vasovagal syncope PE is described as the great masquerader; symptoms and signs are nonspecific, and unexplained breathlessness is its most common symptom. Failure to improve despite standard therapy for concurrent heart failure or pneumonia is a clue to coexisting PE. The most common DVT symptom is a persistent, intensifying calf cramp or 'charley horse'; physical findings may be limited to mild lower-calf tenderness, although massive DVT can produce marked thigh swelling, tenderness, and erythema. A diffusely edematous leg makes ordinary DVT unlikely, with the important exception of phlegmasia cerulea dolens, the most severe form of DVT. Recurrent left thigh edema, especially in young women, should raise suspicion for May-Thurner syndrome (right common iliac artery compressing the left iliac vein), which may be associated with DVT. Wells point scores estimate clinical likelihood of DVT/PE and are validated in ambulatory but not hospitalized patients; low-likelihood DVT or low-to-moderate-likelihood PE can be evaluated with d-dimer alone, while high-likelihood patients should skip d-dimer and go straight to imaging. Age-adjusted d-dimer (age x 10 ng/mL as the upper limit for patients over 50 with low/intermediate PE probability) reduces unnecessary CT pulmonary angiograms, but it does NOT apply to suspected acute DVT. Venous ultrasound diagnoses DVT chiefly through loss of vein compressibility; a normal vein collapses with gentle transducer pressure (the 'wink'), whereas an acutely thrombosed vein stays distended and non-compressible. CT pulmonary angiography is the principal imaging test for PE; an RV-to-LV diameter ratio greater than 1 (RV enlargement) on CT predicts increased 30-day mortality. ECG S1Q3T3 is relatively specific but insensitive for PE; the most common ECG abnormalities are sinus tachycardia and T-wave inversion in leads V1-V4 from RV strain/ischemia. McConnell's sign on echocardiography (RV free-wall hypokinesis with preserved or hyperkinetic RV apex) is a recognized indirect sign of PE, but most PE patients have a normal echocardiogram, so echo is not a reliable rule-out test. Many patients with PE have no demonstrable DVT because the leg thrombus has already embolized; paradoxical embolism to the arterial circulation can occur through a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect. Antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired (not inherited) thrombophilia predisposing to both venous and arterial thrombosis, and patients often warrant lifetime anticoagulation even when the index VTE was provoked. Systemic arterial hypotension with extensive thrombosis - massive (high-risk) PE, accounting for 5-10% of cases, presenting with dyspnea, syncope, hypotension, cyanosis, and possible cardiogenic shock and multisystem organ failure RV dysfunction on echocardiography or RV enlargement on CT despite normal systemic pressure - submassive (intermediate-risk) PE Combination of right heart failure with elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin), indicating high risk of clinical deterioration Phlegmasia cerulea dolens - the most serious form of DVT with diffuse leg edema Hemodynamic instability portending high risk of adverse outcomes despite anticoagulation Relying on d-dimer in hospitalized patients - levels are frequently elevated by systemic illness, so d-dimer rarely has a useful role in inpatients. Applying the age-adjusted d-dimer cutoff to suspected acute DVT - it is validated only for ruling out PE in patients over 50 with low/intermediate probability. Using echocardiography as a rule-out test for PE - most PE patients have normal echocardiograms; echo is better for detecting mimics like MI, tamponade, and aortic dissection. Assuming absence of DVT excludes PE - the leg thrombus may have already fully embolized. Treating antiphospholipid syndrome with DOACs - warfarin, not DOACs, is the standard for APS. Mistaking a diffusely edematous leg for routine DVT and overlooking phlegmasia cerulea dolens; conversely attributing all calf pain to DVT (consider ruptured Baker's cyst) and all dyspnea to PE. Confusing cellulitis (fever, chills) with DVT. Overlooking nonthrombotic embolism (fat, tumor, bone marrow, air, amniotic fluid, cement, talc/hair in IV drug users) as a cause of PE. VTE arises from Virchow's triad of venous stasis, hypercoagulability, and endothelial injury, typically coupled with an inflammatory trigger. Activated platelets release microparticles bearing proinflammatory mediators that recruit neutrophils to form neutrophil extracellular traps; the contained histones drive platelet aggregation and platelet-dependent thrombin generation, and thrombi flourish in conditions of stasis, low oxygen tension, and upregulated proinflammatory genes. Inherited prothrombotic states include factor V Leiden (resistance to protein C) and the prothrombin gene mutation; deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C, and protein S are associated with VTE but rare. Lower-extremity DVT usually begins in the calf and may propagate to the popliteal, femoral, and iliac veins; when thrombi detach they embolize through the vena cava and right heart to lodge in the pulmonary arteries. PE impairs gas exchange, causing arterial hypoxemia and a widened alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient, increased anatomic and physiologic dead space, increased pulmonary vascular resistance (from mechanical obstruction and vasoconstrictors such as serotonin), reflex hyperventilation, increased airway resistance, and reduced pulmonary compliance. Rising pulmonary artery pressure increases RV wall tension, causing RV dilation and dysfunction with BNP release; the interventricular septum bows into and compresses the left ventricle, impairing LV filling; elevated RV wall tension also compresses the right coronary artery, producing RV ischemia/microinfarction with troponin release, and LV underfilling can culminate in falling cardiac output, hypotension, circulatory collapse, and death. Prognosis depends on PE severity and RV function. Low-risk PE (about 65-75% of cases) carries an excellent prognosis. Submassive (intermediate-risk) PE (20-25%) with RV dysfunction and biomarker elevation has a high risk of clinical deterioration, and massive (high-risk) PE (5-10%) can cause cardiogenic shock, multisystem organ failure, and death. US PE-related mortality fell from 6 to about 4.5 per 100,000 between 2000 and 2017 but is rising among young and middle-aged adults, with the median age at PE death dropping from 73 (2000) to 68 (2018) and roughly 50% higher mortality in African Americans than Caucasians; mortality is consistently higher in socioeconomically disadvantaged communities. The 30-day all-cause readmission rate after PE hospitalization is about 11% and the 90-day rate about 15%, with recurrent PE the most common readmission cause. Long-term, roughly half of PE patients report persistent dyspnea, fatigue, and reduced exercise capacity and about a quarter have persistent RV dysfunction - the post-PE syndrome; chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) develops in about 2% of acute PE patients. DVT can lead to postthrombotic syndrome (chronic venous insufficiency) with calf/ankle swelling, leg aching, and, in severe cases, deep skin ulceration. Pulmonary embolism is stratified into three categories: Massive (high-risk) PE - 5-10% of cases, systemic arterial hypotension with thrombosis involving at least half the pulmonary vasculature, presenting with dyspnea, syncope, hypotension, and cyanosis and capable of causing cardiogenic shock and death. Submassive (intermediate-risk) PE - 20-25% of cases, RV dysfunction despite normal systemic arterial pressure; right heart failure with biomarker (troponin) release marks high risk of deterioration. Low-risk PE - about 65-75% of cases, excellent prognosis. (Wells clinical decision rules in Table 290-2 stratify pretest probability of DVT and PE rather than anatomic severity.)

adenosine deaminase 2 results from biallelic mutations in the ADA2 gene, reducing the activity of a secreted enzyme important for endothelial integrity and the differentiation of monocytes and Prognosis is worse when severe haematological or immune involvement dominates, in which case stem cell transplantation may be curative.

nodosa in a young patient without testing ADA2 Overlooking the immunodeficiency and cytopenia phenotype that can present without prominent vasculitis Delaying tumour necrosis factor inhibition, which is the key stroke-preventing therapy DADA2 is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the ADA2 gene, which encodes the secreted enzyme adenosine deaminase 2. Unlike the intracellular ADA1 enzyme whose deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency, ADA2 is released chiefly by cells of the myeloid lineage and acts as a growth factor influencing endothelial integrity and the differentiation of monocytes and macrophages. Loss of ADA2 skews macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype, impairs endothelial stability, and produces a vasculopathy affecting small and medium vessels, together with excess tumour necrosis factor-driven inflammation. The endothelial and vascular damage underlies the strokes and vasculitis, while effects on haematopoiesis and lymphocytes account for the immunodeficiency and cytopenias. Untreated DADA2 carries a high burden of recurrent stroke and cumulative neurological disability, but tumour-necrosis-factor inhibition markedly reduces stroke recurrence and controls vasculitis; severe haematological or immune disease may require transplantation, and early diagnosis substantially improves outcome.

deficiency of il1 receptor antagonist — DIRA, IL1RN deficiency, deficiency of the interleukin-1 receptor antagonist Deficiency of the interleukin-36 receptor antagonist (DITRA) with generalised pustular psoriasis Infectious multifocal osteomyelitis Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis and chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis Neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease Majeed syndrome Langerhans cell histiocytosis Neonatal sepsis IL1RN gene sequencing for biallelic loss-of-function variants, including targeted testing for known founder alleles Skeletal survey for multifocal osteolytic lesions, periostitis and rib-end widening Skin biopsy demonstrating intraepidermal and subcorneal neutrophilic pustules Bone biopsy and cultures to confirm sterility and exclude infective osteomyelitis Acute-phase reactants and full blood count showing a neutrophilic leucocytosis Blood and tissue cultures to exclude infection before and during immunomodulatory therapy Autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function IL1RN variants that abolish functional interleukin-1 receptor antagonist, leaving interleukin-1 alpha and interleukin-1 beta signalling unopposed. Presents in the neonatal period with a triad of pustular skin disease, sterile multifocal osteomyelitis and periostitis, and marked systemic inflammation. Skin involvement ranges from scattered pustules to generalised pustulosis with an ichthyosiform appearance, and nail changes such as pustular onychomadesis are characteristic. Bone disease produces painful swelling with radiographic multifocal osteolytic lesions, periosteal new bone, widening of the anterior rib ends and balloon-like expansion of ribs and clavicles. Fever is often absent or only low grade despite a striking acute-phase response, which can be a diagnostic clue distinguishing it from infection and from many other autoinflammatory syndromes. Recombinant interleukin-1 receptor antagonist replacement is dramatically effective and life-saving, essentially replacing the missing protein. Agents that block only interleukin-1 beta give a less complete response because interleukin-1 alpha signalling also contributes to disease. Founder loss-of-function variants have been described in several geographically distinct populations, aiding targeted genetic testing. Respiratory distress from thoracic involvement or interstitial lung disease in a neonate Widespread pustulosis with systemic inflammation mimicking overwhelming sepsis Multifocal bone lesions in an infant that are repeatedly culture negative Clinical deterioration or incomplete response when only interleukin-1 beta is blocked Mistaking sterile multifocal osteomyelitis for bacterial infection and pursuing prolonged antibiotics Being reassured by the frequent absence of high fever and underestimating the severity of inflammation Expecting a full response from interleukin-1 beta-selective blockade rather than receptor-level antagonism Confusing the phenotype with the clinically overlapping deficiency of the interleukin-36 receptor antagonist The interleukin-1 receptor antagonist is a naturally occurring inhibitor that competes with interleukin-1 alpha and interleukin-1 beta for binding to the type 1 interleukin-1 receptor without triggering signalling. Loss-of-function IL1RN variants remove this brake, so even physiological amounts of interleukin-1 drive unopposed and amplified receptor signalling. The result is intense innate immune activation with neutrophil recruitment to skin and bone, producing sterile pustulosis, multifocal osteomyelitis and periostitis, and a vigorous systemic acute-phase response. Because both interleukin-1 alpha and interleukin-1 beta act on the receptor, complete control requires blockade at the receptor level rather than neutralisation of a single ligand. Untreated disease carries a high risk of severe morbidity and death from uncontrolled systemic inflammation and its complications. Prompt recombinant interleukin-1 receptor antagonist replacement usually induces rapid and sustained remission with a good long-term outlook.

neurological deficit Constitutional symptoms, night pain, or a history of malignancy suggesting tumour Fever or features suggesting discitis or osteomyelitis Over-interpreting ubiquitous age-related disc changes on MRI as the definite pain source Recommending fusion for poorly localised, multilevel degeneration Neglecting psychosocial contributors to chronic back pain Degenerative disc disease describes the symptomatic consequences of intervertebral disc ageing. Progressive loss of proteoglycan and water content reduces the disc's ability to distribute load, leading to disc-height loss, annular fissuring, and altered biomechanics. Pain is thought to arise from stimulation of nociceptors in the outer annulus and vertebral endplates, sometimes accompanied by ingrowth of nerves and blood vessels into the degenerate disc and by inflammatory endplate (Modic) changes. Because degeneration is almost universal with age, structural changes correlate poorly with symptoms. The condition tends to fluctuate but is usually self-limiting or manageable over the long term with conservative measures; most people do not require surgery, and surgical outcomes for axial discogenic pain are less predictable than for radicular symptoms.

degos disease — malignant atrophic papulosis, Kohlmeier-Degos disease Antiphospholipid syndrome Systemic lupus erythematosus and lupus vasculopathy Systemic sclerosis and other connective-tissue diseases Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis Cholesterol embolisation and other embolic vasculopathies Lymphomatoid papulosis (early papular lesions) Sneddon syndrome Skin biopsy showing wedge-shaped ischaemic dermal necrosis over a thrombosed vessel Antiphospholipid antibody and lupus anticoagulant testing Antinuclear antibody and connective-tissue disease serology Thrombophilia screen Gastrointestinal endoscopy or imaging if abdominal symptoms occur Brain MRI and neurological assessment for suspected CNS involvement Ophthalmological review for retinal and conjunctival lesions Degos disease is a rare occlusive vasculopathy producing pathognomonic skin lesions: small papules that evolve into atrophic, porcelain-white centres surrounded by an erythematous, telangiectatic rim. It exists as a benign cutaneous-only variant and a malignant systemic form in which the same vasculopathy affects the gastrointestinal tract and central nervous system with high mortality. Gastrointestinal involvement causes bowel infarction and perforation, while central nervous system disease produces strokes, seizures and neurological deficits, together accounting for most deaths. The characteristic histology is a wedge-shaped area of dermal ischaemic necrosis and connective-tissue atrophy overlying a thrombosed vessel, with interface changes and mucin deposition. There is no established diagnostic serological marker; diagnosis rests on recognising the clinical morphology supported by biopsy, and on excluding lupus and antiphospholipid syndrome. The condition can mimic or overlap with connective-tissue disease and antiphospholipid syndrome, so a thorough autoimmune and thrombophilia work-up is essential. Anecdotal benefit has been reported with antiplatelet agents, and in systemic disease with treatments targeting complement (eculizumab) and endothelial pathways (treprostinil), reflecting a presumed thrombotic-endothelial mechanism. The purely cutaneous form may remain stable for years, but new systemic symptoms mandate urgent evaluation because visceral involvement can be rapidly fatal. New abdominal pain suggesting bowel ischaemia or perforation Neurological symptoms such as stroke, seizures or headache indicating CNS disease Rapid appearance of numerous new lesions Systemic symptoms in a patient previously thought to have cutaneous-only disease Signs of peritonism requiring urgent surgical assessment Dismissing early non-specific papules and missing the diagnostic porcelain-white atrophic lesions Assuming cutaneous-only disease is permanently benign and failing to monitor for systemic conversion Confusing Degos disease with antiphospholipid syndrome or lupus vasculopathy Delaying surgical review when acute abdominal signs develop Interpreting the vasculopathy as a true inflammatory vasculitis and mistreating accordingly Degos disease is a thrombo-occlusive vasculopathy of small and medium arteries in which progressive endothelial injury and intimal proliferation lead to luminal narrowing and thrombosis. The resulting occlusion produces wedge-shaped ischaemic infarcts in the skin and viscera, manifesting in the dermis as connective-tissue necrosis capped by an atrophic, porcelain-white epidermis. The precise trigger is unknown, but proposed mechanisms include a primary endothelial cell disorder, complement-mediated (particularly C5b-9 membrane attack complex) endothelial damage, and dysregulated interferon signalling, with secondary platelet activation and thrombosis. Because the same process affects the gut and brain vasculature, systemic disease causes bowel infarction, perforation and cerebral ischaemia. The absence of a prominent inflammatory infiltrate distinguishes it from a true vasculitis and supports a primarily occlusive, endotheliopathic pathogenesis. The benign cutaneous-only variant may persist for years without systemic progression, whereas the malignant systemic form carries a poor prognosis with substantial mortality from bowel perforation and cerebral infarction, though complement- and prostacyclin-directed therapies have improved some outcomes.

Dehydrated hereditary stomatocytosis — hereditary xerocytosis, xerocytosis, DHSt Overhydrated hereditary stomatocytosis and other stomatocytosis variants Hereditary spherocytosis and hereditary elliptocytosis Hereditary haemochromatosis, when the iron-overload phenotype dominates Other causes of a raised MCHC, such as cold agglutinins or sample artefact Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia Thalassaemia and other haemoglobinopathies Full blood count with MCHC (raised) and reticulocyte count Blood film for stomatocytes, target cells and desiccated forms Osmotic gradient ektacytometry, showing a characteristic left-shifted curve where available Osmotic fragility, typically decreased Iron studies with hepatic iron quantification by MRI (T2* or R2*) Molecular testing of PIEZO1 and KCNN4 with family segregation studies Exclusion of HFE and other haemochromatosis genes when iron loading dominates An autosomal dominant red cell membrane cation-leak disorder in which red cells are dehydrated (xerocytes), most often from gain-of-function variants in PIEZO1 (a mechanosensitive cation channel) and less commonly KCNN4 (the Gardos channel) Causes a compensated or mild to moderate haemolytic anaemia with a characteristically raised MCHC and increased reticulocytes; the film may show few overt stomatocytes but target and desiccated cells Iron overload is common and can occur out of proportion to transfusion, sometimes as the presenting problem, mimicking hereditary haemochromatosis Perinatal oedema, transient hydrops fetalis or ascites is a recognised feature of PIEZO1-related disease and may resolve spontaneously Splenectomy is contraindicated: it does not reliably correct the anaemia and carries a high risk of subsequent venous thromboembolism, including portal and pulmonary thrombosis Osmotic fragility is typically decreased because the dehydrated cells resist osmotic lysis, and osmotic gradient ektacytometry shows a characteristic left-shifted curve The overlapping and heterogeneous stomatocytosis syndromes require careful characterisation, since management, particularly avoidance of splenectomy, hinges on correct classification Perinatal hydrops fetalis, ascites or unexplained oedema Progressive iron overload with hepatic or cardiac dysfunction Venous or arterial thrombosis, especially after prior splenectomy Symptomatic pigment gallstones Performing splenectomy, which is contraindicated and carries a high thrombotic risk Misattributing iron overload solely to transfusion or to primary haemochromatosis Missing the diagnosis because stomatocytes are sparse on the film Confusing it with overhydrated stomatocytosis, which behaves differently Overlooking the dominant family history and perinatal oedema as diagnostic clues Dehydrated hereditary stomatocytosis is caused by dominant gain-of-function variants in red cell membrane cation channels, chiefly PIEZO1 (a mechanosensitive non-selective cation channel) and occasionally KCNN4 (the calcium-activated Gardos potassium channel). Abnormal channel gating produces a net cation leak in which potassium loss exceeds sodium gain, so intracellular monovalent cation and water content fall and the cell becomes dehydrated with an increased haemoglobin concentration. The resulting rigid, poorly deformable red cells have a shortened lifespan and undergo haemolysis, while disordered iron regulation with relative hepcidin suppression promotes parenchymal iron loading independent of transfusion. The haemolytic anaemia is usually mild and compatible with a normal lifespan, but iron overload and thrombotic complications, particularly after splenectomy, drive long-term morbidity. Outcomes are good when splenectomy is avoided and iron status is monitored and treated.

The disorder is generally more severe and disabling than typical Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, often with early and significant motor impairment, though the course varies with the underlying mutation; management remains supportive.

Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction — DHTR, Delayed serologic and haemolytic transfusion reaction Ongoing bleeding causing a falling haemoglobin Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction Hyperhaemolysis syndrome in sickle cell disease Infection-related anaemia or marrow suppression Drug-induced immune haemolysis Direct antiglobulin test on a current sample Repeat antibody screen and identification panel comparing pre- and post-transfusion sera Elution studies to identify antibody bound to transfused cells Lactate dehydrogenase, bilirubin, haptoglobin and reticulocyte count Full blood count and film for spherocytes and evidence of haemolysis Comparison of haemoglobin increment with the expected post-transfusion value Occurs typically several days to two weeks after transfusion due to an anamnestic antibody response against a red-cell antigen to which the recipient was previously sensitised. Most commonly implicates antibodies of the Kidd, Rh, Duffy, Kell and MNS systems, with Kidd (anti-Jk) antibodies notorious for evanescence and for causing severe delayed reactions. Antibody levels fall below detection between exposures, so the pre-transfusion antibody screen may be negative; the antibody reappears rapidly on re-exposure. Presents insidiously with an unexplained fall in haemoglobin, low-grade fever, mild jaundice and a failure of transfused red cells to sustain the expected increment. Haemolysis is predominantly extravascular, mediated by IgG-coated cells removed by the reticuloendothelial system, so overt haemoglobinuria and shock are uncommon. A positive direct antiglobulin test with newly detectable alloantibody and spherocytes on the film supports the diagnosis. Management is usually supportive; future transfusions must use antigen-negative units, and the antibody should be recorded permanently to prevent recurrence. In sickle cell disease a delayed reaction can trigger hyperhaemolysis, an important and dangerous overlap to recognise. Unexpected drop in haemoglobin days after transfusion with jaundice New positive direct antiglobulin test with a previously negative screen Haemoglobinuria suggesting a more brisk haemolytic process Rapidly worsening anaemia in a patient with sickle cell disease raising concern for hyperhaemolysis Renal impairment accompanying significant haemolysis Overlooking the diagnosis and attributing the falling haemoglobin to bleeding. Relying on a negative pre-transfusion screen despite historical alloimmunisation. Failing to permanently record identified antibodies, risking recurrence at other sites. Not recognising the overlap with hyperhaemolysis in sickle cell disease. Transfusing further antigen-positive units and compounding the haemolysis. A delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction reflects a secondary (anamnestic) immune response. Prior transfusion or pregnancy sensitises the recipient to a foreign red-cell antigen, but the resulting alloantibody wanes over time and may be undetectable at the next crossmatch. When antigen-positive cells are transfused, memory B cells rapidly produce IgG antibody over several days. These antibodies coat the transfused cells, which are then cleared extravascularly by splenic and hepatic macrophages via Fc-receptor-mediated phagocytosis. Because destruction is gradual and largely extravascular, the clinical picture is of a progressive unexplained anaemia with rising unconjugated bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase rather than acute intravascular haemolysis, although brisk complement-fixing antibodies such as those of the Kidd system can occasionally produce more acute haemolysis. Most delayed reactions are mild and self-limiting, resolving as the incompatible cells are cleared, provided antigen-negative blood is given thereafter. Occasionally, brisk haemolysis causes clinically significant anaemia or renal impairment, and in sickle cell disease evolution to hyperhaemolysis can be life-threatening.

Re-exposure rapidly boosts antibody production over the following days, and the antibodies coat the transfused cells, which are then cleared largely by the mononuclear phagocyte system in the spleen and liver. features raising suspicion of Turner syndrome Evidence of a chronic systemic illness or eating disorder underlying the delay Labelling all delay as constitutional and missing a treatable or serious underlying cause Overlooking anosmia, which would point to Kallmann syndrome Failing to consider chronic illness, undernutrition, or an eating disorder as functional causes Not arranging a karyotype in suspected Turner or Klinefelter syndrome Puberty begins with reactivation of pulsatile hypothalamic gonadotrophin-releasing hormone secretion, which stimulates pituitary LH and FSH and thereby gonadal steroid production and gametogenesis. Delayed puberty results from any interruption of this axis. In constitutional delay the axis is intrinsically normal but activates late, with a correspondingly delayed bone age. Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism arises from functional suppression (chronic disease, malnutrition, intense athletic training, eating disorders, hyperprolactinaemia) or permanent central defects (Kallmann syndrome with anosmia, other congenital GnRH deficiencies, pituitary tumours or infiltration). Hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism reflects primary gonadal failure, as in chromosomal disorders (Turner, Klinefelter), gonadal dysgenesis, or damage from chemotherapy or radiation, where absent negative feedback drives gonadotrophins high. Constitutional delay carries an excellent prognosis with spontaneous progression through normal puberty and attainment of adult height and fertility; outcomes in pathological causes depend on the specific disorder and on timely diagnosis and hormone replacement.

tumour or systemic disease Failing to measure testicular volume, the key sign that puberty has begun Overlooking anosmia, the clue to Kallmann syndrome, in a boy with low gonadotropins Not arranging a Delayed puberty results from disturbance at any point along this axis. In constitutional delay the axis is simply reactivated later than average, following a familial timetable, and maturation is ultimately complete. In hypogonadotropic hypogonadism there is deficient central drive, whether congenital, as in Kallmann syndrome with associated anosmia, or acquired through pituitary or hypothalamic lesions, systemic illness, or undernutrition. Delirium — acute confusional state, acute brain syndrome, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy (psychiatric framing) Dementia and other major neurocognitive disorders Depression, especially where hypoactive delirium mimics low mood Acute psychosis or mania Non-convulsive status epilepticus Wernicke encephalopathy Alcohol or sedative withdrawal states Focal neurological events such as stroke Bedside attention testing and validated delirium screening instruments Search for precipitants: infection screen, oxygenation, glucose, electrolytes, renal and liver function Medication review for deliriogenic drugs Neuroimaging when a structural cause is suspected EEG if non-convulsive seizures are considered An acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness accompanied by additional cognitive changes such as disorientation, memory deficit, or perceptual disturbance Onset is acute (hours to days) and the course typically fluctuates over the day, often with worsening in the evening and at night (sundowning) It is a direct physiological consequence of a medical condition, substance intoxication or withdrawal, medication, or multiple causes, and is best regarded as acute brain failure Recognised as hyperactive, hypoactive, or mixed; the hypoactive form is easily missed and carries a worse prognosis The essential intervention is identifying and treating the underlying cause and reviewing offending medications, together with supportive care Non-pharmacological measures are first-line: reorientation, sensory aids, sleep-wake regulation, mobilisation, hydration, and a calm familiar environment Antipsychotics are reserved for severe agitation or distress that threatens safety, at the lowest effective level, while benzodiazepines are generally avoided except in alcohol or sedative withdrawal Distinguish from dementia (chronic, stable, with preserved alertness early) and from primary psychiatric illness; delirium can be superimposed on dementia Underlying life-threatening cause such as sepsis, hypoxia, or hypoglycaemia Sudden focal neurological signs suggesting stroke or intracranial pathology Delirium tremens or severe withdrawal states Profound hypoactive delirium with reduced consciousness and aspiration risk Missing hypoactive delirium and mislabelling it as depression or fatigue Attributing acute confusion to dementia and failing to seek a reversible cause Using benzodiazepines routinely and worsening confusion (outside alcohol or sedative withdrawal) Sedating agitation without identifying and treating the underlying medical trigger Overlooking medication and polypharmacy as precipitants Delirium reflects diffuse, usually reversible cerebral dysfunction arising from systemic insults. Proposed mechanisms include neurotransmitter imbalance (notably cholinergic deficiency and dopaminergic excess), neuroinflammation, impaired oxidative metabolism, and disruption of neuronal networks supporting attention and arousal. Common precipitants include infection, hypoxia, metabolic and electrolyte derangements, drug effects and withdrawal, and the disorder is often multifactorial in vulnerable individuals such as the elderly. Delirium often resolves once the precipitant is treated, but it is associated with prolonged hospital stay, functional decline, increased risk of subsequent dementia, and higher mortality, particularly in older and hypoactive cases. Recovery can be incomplete and protracted in vulnerable patients.

antipsychotics are reserved for severe agitation posing a safety risk Benzodiazepines and anticholinergic drugs generally worsen delirium and should be minimised except for specific indications such as alcohol withdrawal Sudden confusion with focal neurological signs suggesting a stroke Delirium accompanied by hypoxia, sepsis, or severe metabolic derangement Features suggesting alcohol or sedative withdrawal with autonomic instability Severe agitation posing a risk of harm to the patient or others Missing hypoactive delirium because the patient is quiet rather than agitated Mislabelling delirium as dementia and failing to seek reversible causes Using benzodiazepines or anticholinergics that worsen confusion Reaching for antipsychotics before addressing underlying precipitants Neglecting non-pharmacological preventive measures in high-risk patients Postoperative delirium reflects acute global brain dysfunction arising from the interaction of a vulnerable brain and perioperative stressors. Proposed mechanisms include neuroinflammation from the surgical stress response, neurotransmitter imbalance (notably cholinergic deficiency and dopamine excess), impaired cerebral oxygen delivery, disrupted sleep-wake regulation, and the effects of sedative and analgesic drugs. Patients with reduced cognitive reserve are more susceptible, so relatively minor insults can precipitate delirium. The condition is typically multifactorial, and cumulative contributions from pain, infection, metabolic derangement, and medications drive the acute confusional state. Delirium is often reversible when precipitants are treated, but it is associated with longer hospital stay, functional decline, increased risk of long-term cognitive impairment, and higher mortality, particularly in the hypoactive form.
