Delta storage pool deficiency — Dense granule deficiency, Delta-SPD, Delta storage pool disease Alpha granule deficiency (grey platelet syndrome) Combined alpha-delta storage pool deficiency von Willebrand disease Glanzmann thrombasthenia Platelet release/signalling (secretion) defects Antiplatelet drug or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory effect Acquired platelet dysfunction (uraemia, myeloproliferative neoplasm) Light transmission platelet aggregometry with ADP, collagen, adrenaline and arachidonic acid Whole-mount transmission electron microscopy for dense granule enumeration Flow-cytometric mepacrine uptake and release assay Platelet nucleotide content and ADP:ATP ratio with secretion studies Full blood count and blood film to confirm normal platelet number von Willebrand factor antigen and activity to exclude von Willebrand disease Examination and testing for syndromic features (albinism, immune defects) with targeted genetics An inherited platelet function disorder characterised by a reduced number or content of platelet dense (delta) granules. Dense granules store the small molecules ADP, ATP, calcium, serotonin and polyphosphate that amplify platelet activation and recruitment. Clinically presents with lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding: easy bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia and excessive surgical or dental bleeding. The platelet count is normal, so the disorder is a qualitative rather than quantitative defect. Aggregometry classically shows an absent or blunted second wave with impaired response to ADP and collagen and a diminished response to arachidonic acid. Confirmation uses whole-mount electron microscopy for dense granule count, mepacrine uptake and release by flow cytometry, or measurement of the platelet ADP:ATP ratio and secretion. May be isolated or syndromic, occurring in Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (with albinism and pulmonary fibrosis) and Chediak-Higashi syndrome (with immunodeficiency). Treatment employs antifibrinolytics and desmopressin for minor bleeding and procedures, reserving platelet transfusion for major haemorrhage. Major haemorrhage after surgery, trauma or childbirth Severe menorrhagia producing symptomatic iron-deficiency anaemia Features of Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome such as progressive pulmonary fibrosis or granulomatous colitis Recurrent severe infections or accelerated-phase lymphohistiocytosis suggesting Chediak-Higashi syndrome Uncontrolled bleeding despite antifibrinolytic and desmopressin therapy Overlooking a qualitative platelet defect because the platelet count is normal. Missing an underlying syndrome by not examining for oculocutaneous albinism or a history of recurrent infection. Misinterpreting aggregometry performed after recent aspirin or non-steroidal drug use. Relying on a single aggregometry result, as dense granule defects can give subtle or variable patterns. Repeated platelet transfusion causing alloimmunisation and later refractoriness. Delta storage pool deficiency arises from defective biogenesis or cargo loading of platelet dense granules, the lysosome-related organelles that store the non-protein mediators ADP, ATP, calcium, serotonin and inorganic polyphosphate. Upon activation, normal platelets secrete dense granule contents, and released ADP engages P2Y receptors to amplify aggregation and recruit further platelets, producing the second wave of aggregation. When dense granules are reduced in number or content, this positive-feedback amplification fails, so platelet activation and thrombus consolidation are impaired even though adhesion and initial shape change are intact. In syndromic forms, mutations in genes governing the biogenesis of lysosome-related organelles (as in Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome) or vesicle trafficking (as in Chediak-Higashi syndrome) simultaneously affect melanosomes and other organelles, accounting for the associated albinism and immune defects. Isolated delta storage pool deficiency usually causes mild to moderate lifelong bleeding with a normal life expectancy when peri-procedural precautions are observed. In syndromic disease the outlook is dominated by associated features such as pulmonary fibrosis in Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome or immunodeficiency in Chediak-Higashi syndrome.

Dementia with Lewy Bodies — DLB, Lewy body disease, Lewy body dementia Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) Alzheimer's disease (and DLB with co-existing AD pathology) Multiple system atrophy (MSA) Vascular parkinsonism / vascular cognitive impairment Delirium from drugs, infection, or metabolic disturbance Brain MRI to exclude vascular parkinsonism or subdural hematoma and to look for the MSA 'hot-cross buns' pontine sign Polysomnography demonstrating REM sleep behavior disorder without atonia Seed amplification assays (e.g., RT-QuIC) detecting alpha-synuclein in CSF Skin biopsy showing cutaneous alpha-synuclein deposition I-123 MIBG cardiac scintigraphy showing postganglionic sympathetic denervation Dopamine transporter imaging by SPECT or PET showing reduced striatal (particularly putaminal) dopamine transporter FDG-PET showing occipital hypometabolism with relative posterior cingulate sparing (cingulate island sign) CSF or blood phospho-tau217/phospho-tau181 when concurrent Alzheimer pathology is suspected Multiple system atrophy, in which autonomic disturbance occurs earlier and is more severe and cognition is relatively preserved (anosmia favors LBD over MSA) Alzheimer's disease, suggested by prominent early episodic memory and semantic naming impairment Vascular parkinsonism or subdural hematoma identifiable on MRI Drug-induced, infectious, or metabolic encephalopathy producing reversible cognitive change DLB and Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) are viewed as points along a single spectrum of Lewy body disease (LBD); LBD is the second most common neurodegenerative dementia after Alzheimer's disease (Harrison 22e p.3491). The timing between parkinsonism and dementia distinguishes the two: when dementia and neuropsychiatric symptoms precede or emerge alongside parkinsonism, the diagnosis is DLB; when dementia appears in a patient with long-standing PD, it is PDD (Harrison 22e p.3492). Core diagnostic features of DLB are early psychosis with well-formed visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and parkinsonism (Harrison 22e p.3491). The cognitive profile shows severe executive, attentional, and visuospatial deficits with relatively preserved episodic memory; prominent early episodic memory impairment instead suggests comorbid Alzheimer pathology (Harrison 22e p.3491-3492). Fluctuations in attention and concentration can be marked, with short episodes of confusion or severe lethargy that may resolve rapidly (Harrison 22e p.3492). Patients are highly sensitive to infectious and metabolic disturbances, and delirium precipitated by infection, a new medication, or systemic illness can be the first manifestation (Harrison 22e p.3492). RBD, in which dream enactment occurs because normal dreaming muscle atonia is lost (sometimes causing injury to patient or bed partner), is a characteristic and often prodromal feature that may precede the syndrome by years (Harrison 22e p.3492). A sense of a presence behind the person may precede well-formed hallucinations; delusions are less frequent and usually involve misidentification, infidelity, theft, or persecution (Harrison 22e p.3491-3492). Autonomic and nonmotor features such as anosmia, constipation, depression, anxiety, orthostatic hypotension, and erectile dysfunction may appear early (Harrison 22e p.3492). Incidence of DLB is roughly 7 per 100,000 person-years; prevalence of both DLB and PDD rises with age and both are more common in men (Harrison 22e p.3491). About 10% of PD patients develop PDD per year, with most eventually progressing to dementia over time (Harrison 22e p.3491). A profound cholinergic deficit from basal forebrain and pedunculopontine nucleus involvement underlies the fluctuations, inattention, and visual hallucinations (Harrison 22e p.3492). New-onset delirium precipitated by infection, a new medicine, or systemic illness as the presenting feature Severe sensitivity to dopaminergic medications and to typical neuroleptics, the latter risking neuroleptic malignant syndrome and death Recurrent falls from early postural instability and orthostatic hypotension causing syncope Violent dream enactment in RBD causing injury to patient or bed partner Misclassifying DLB as Alzheimer's disease because frequent AD co-pathology makes prediction of underlying disease challenging; prominent early episodic memory loss points to comorbid AD Confusing DLB with MSA when autonomic features appear early; MSA autonomic dysfunction is earlier and more severe with relatively preserved cognition Exposing patients to typical neuroleptics, anticholinergics, or dopamine agonists, which can trigger neuroleptic malignant syndrome or worsen symptoms Overlooking that scattered Lewy body pathology in substantia nigra, amygdala, or olfactory bulb can be an incidental finding in healthy older individuals Attributing fluctuating confusion solely to delirium and missing the underlying DLB diagnosis DLB is a synucleinopathy: the defining neuropathologic lesions are Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites distributed through specific brainstem nuclei, the substantia nigra, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, and ultimately the neocortex. Lewy bodies are intraneuronal cytoplasmic inclusions composed of straight 7-20 nm neurofilaments with surrounding amorphous material; they stain with PAS and ubiquitin and are now identified by antibodies to the presynaptic protein alpha-synuclein. Accumulation of alpha-synuclein aggregates in neurons and glia classifies DLB and PDD molecularly as synucleinopathies, though neuronal and synaptic loss (rather than Lewy pathology itself) best predicts clinical deficits. Pathology progresses through three stages: brainstem-predominant, transitional limbic, and diffuse neocortical. Disease is thought to propagate via a prion-like mechanism in which misfolded alpha-synuclein spreads transneuronally along connection pathways; PD often begins in the enteric nervous system and ascends via the vagus nerve, and/or in the olfactory bulb. A profound cholinergic deficit from basal forebrain and pedunculopontine nucleus loss drives fluctuations, inattention, and hallucinations, while locus coeruleus adrenergic deficits impair arousal and alerting. Both genetic and environmental factors contribute; alpha-synuclein gene duplications/triplications and GBA (glucocerebrosidase) mutations are linked to PDD/DLB presentations, supporting a double-hit hypothesis of toxins acting on a susceptible genetic background (Harrison 22e p.3492). DLB is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with no currently available disease-modifying therapy; only symptomatic management exists. Severity of behavioral, sleep, and autonomic symptoms correlates with substantial caregiver burden, depression, and reduced caregiver quality of life (Harrison 22e p.3492-3493). Neuropathologic staging recognizes three stages of LBD progression: (1) brainstem-predominant, (2) transitional limbic, and (3) diffuse neocortical. Both DLB and PDD have a prodromal mild cognitive impairment (MCI) phase; prodromal MCI-Lewy body (MCI-LB) is distinguished from prodromal MCI-AD by clinical and biomarker features (Harrison 22e p.3492).

Dengue haemorrhagic fever — DHF, severe dengue, dengue shock syndrome, DSS Other viral haemorrhagic fevers Chikungunya and Zika co-circulating arboviral illness Severe malaria Leptospirosis Enteric fever Rickettsial infection (e.g. scrub typhus) Sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation Acute leukaemia or other causes of thrombocytopenia with bleeding Immune thrombocytopenia Hantavirus or other capillary-leak syndromes NS1 antigen in early illness and dengue IgM/IgG serology or RT-PCR Serial full blood counts monitoring haematocrit and platelet trends Coagulation profile and liver enzymes to assess severity Ultrasound to detect plasma leakage (ascites, pleural effusion, gallbladder wall oedema) Blood grouping and cross-match if significant bleeding occurs A severe form of dengue, a mosquito-borne flaviviral infection spread by Aedes aegypti, with recurrent large outbreaks across India The defining features are plasma leakage (haemoconcentration, effusions, ascites), bleeding tendency and thrombocytopenia, which can progress to dengue shock syndrome The critical, most dangerous period begins around the time of defervescence, when capillary leak peaks, so patients can deteriorate just as fever settles WHO warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, hepatomegaly, fluid accumulation and a rising haematocrit with falling platelets) flag patients at risk of severe disease Secondary infection with a different dengue serotype increases the risk of severe disease through antibody-dependent enhancement Management is meticulous fluid balance guided by haematocrit and clinical status; there is no specific antiviral, and both under- and over-resuscitation are harmful Platelet transfusion is not indicated purely for a low count and should be reserved for significant bleeding Diagnosis uses NS1 antigen early and IgM/IgG serology or PCR, with serial full blood counts to track haematocrit and platelets WHO warning signs: severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, restlessness or lethargy, and clinical fluid accumulation Rising haematocrit with a rapidly falling platelet count indicating intensifying plasma leak Signs of shock (narrow pulse pressure, cold clammy peripheries, tachycardia, hypotension) marking dengue shock syndrome Deterioration around defervescence, the classic timing of the critical phase Assuming a patient is improving when fever settles, missing the onset of the critical plasma-leak phase Over-transfusing platelets based on the count alone rather than for clinical bleeding Excessive intravenous fluids causing fluid overload and respiratory compromise, or inadequate fluids allowing shock Giving NSAIDs or other agents that worsen bleeding and gastric irritation Following an infective Aedes bite, dengue virus replicates and causes a systemic febrile illness. In severe dengue an intense host immune and cytokine response transiently increases vascular permeability, allowing plasma to leak from the intravascular compartment; this manifests as haemoconcentration, serous effusions and, if severe, hypovolaemic shock. Concurrent thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, coagulopathy and vascular fragility produce the bleeding diathesis. Pre-existing heterotypic antibodies from a prior infection can enhance viral uptake into cells (antibody-dependent enhancement), heightening the risk of severe disease on secondary infection. With early recognition and careful fluid management the great majority recover fully. Untreated or poorly managed severe dengue with prolonged shock or major haemorrhage carries significant mortality, but timely, judicious supportive care dramatically reduces death rates.

obstructing renal stones or symptomatic nephrocalcinosis Growth failure in a child suggesting significant tubular or renal impairment Features suggesting evolving extrarenal disease in OCRL-related cases Overlooking the diagnosis because dipstick testing detects albumin poorly and misses low-molecular-weight proteinuria Attributing recurrent stones to idiopathic hypercalciuria without checking for tubular proteinuria Failing to distinguish Dent disease 2 from Lowe syndrome when OCRL is involved Assuming female relatives are entirely unaffected Dent disease is an inherited disorder of the renal proximal tubule caused by loss of function of the endosomal chloride/proton exchanger encoded by CLCN5, or of the phosphatase encoded by OCRL. Both proteins are required for normal acidification and trafficking within the endocytic machinery that reabsorbs filtered low-molecular-weight proteins via the megalin-cubilin receptor system. Defective endosomal function impairs receptor-mediated endocytosis, so filtered proteins escape into the urine, producing the hallmark low-molecular-weight proteinuria. Associated disturbances of calcium and phosphate handling generate hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis and stones, and cumulative tubular and interstitial damage leads to progressive decline in kidney function. Dent disease is slowly progressive; many affected males develop chronic kidney disease and a proportion reach kidney failure between the third and fifth decades, while proteinuria and hypercalciuria are usually present from childhood. Progression rate varies and extrarenal disease is generally mild.

Dental caries — tooth decay, cavities, carious lesion Dental erosion from intrinsic or extrinsic acids Enamel hypoplasia or developmental defects Dentine hypersensitivity from gingival recession Fluorosis or intrinsic staining mimicking lesions Cracked tooth or fracture line Visual-tactile examination with good lighting and drying of surfaces Bitewing and periapical radiographs for interproximal and root lesions Caries risk assessment including diet and salivary evaluation Pulp sensibility testing when pulpal involvement is suspected Adjunctive detection methods (transillumination, laser fluorescence) where available Caries is a chronic, biofilm-mediated disease driven by repeated acid production from fermentable carbohydrates, not a simple one-off infection Early lesions appear as chalky white spots that represent subsurface demineralisation and can still remineralise before cavitation occurs Pit-and-fissure surfaces, interproximal contacts, and exposed root surfaces in older patients are the sites most prone to decay Symptoms often lag behind disease; sensitivity to sweet, cold, or hot stimuli suggests progression toward the pulp Bitewing radiographs are key for detecting interproximal lesions that are hidden on visual examination Management balances remineralisation strategies (fluoride, diet control, oral hygiene) for early lesions against operative restoration once cavitation is established High caries risk should prompt assessment of salivary flow, diet, fluoride exposure, and plaque control rather than only drilling and filling Untreated caries is the usual precursor to pulpitis, periapical infection, and eventual tooth loss Spreading facial swelling, fever, or trismus indicating odontogenic infection extending beyond the tooth Rampant or early childhood caries suggesting major dietary or salivary dysfunction Signs of pulpal necrosis or periapical involvement requiring urgent endodontic assessment Restoring cavities without addressing underlying diet and hygiene, leading to recurrent decay Overlooking interproximal or hidden root-surface lesions on clinical inspection alone Mistaking arrested or remineralised lesions for active disease and over-treating Ignoring salivary hypofunction as a driver of rapid caries progression Dental caries results from an ecological shift in the dental plaque biofilm favouring acidogenic and aciduric bacteria such as mutans streptococci and lactobacilli. Frequent intake of fermentable sugars fuels bacterial acid production, lowering plaque pH below the critical threshold and driving demineralisation of enamel hydroxyapatite. When acid attacks outpace the buffering and remineralising capacity of saliva and fluoride, subsurface mineral loss progresses to surface cavitation. The lesion then advances through dentine, where tubular structure allows faster spread, ultimately reaching and infecting the pulp if untreated. Early non-cavitated lesions can be arrested or reversed with preventive measures, while cavitated lesions require restoration but carry a good prognosis when risk factors are controlled; neglected disease progresses to pulpitis, abscess, and tooth loss.

non-accidental injury Aspirated or unaccounted-for tooth fragments needing chest imaging Storing an avulsed tooth in water or letting it dry, damaging periodontal ligament cells Reimplanting avulsed primary teeth and harming the permanent successor Assuming an initially vital tooth will remain so and skipping follow-up sensibility testing Focusing on the obvious dental injury and missing alveolar or jaw fractures or non-accidental injury Dental trauma results from a direct or indirect force exceeding the resistance of the tooth and its supporting structures. Depending on the vector and magnitude, energy is dissipated as enamel or dentine fracture, pulp exposure, displacement of the tooth within or out of its socket (luxation or avulsion), or fracture of the alveolar bone. Injury to the neurovascular supply at the apex can lead to reversible or irreversible pulpal damage and later necrosis, while disruption of the periodontal ligament and its cells governs the likelihood of successful healing after repositioning or reimplantation. Extra-oral drying and delay compromise ligament cell viability and predispose to replacement resorption. Outcome depends on injury type, maturity of the tooth, and speed of appropriate care; minor fractures and promptly managed luxations often do well, whereas avulsions with prolonged dry time and mature apices frequently develop pulp necrosis or root resorption.

urgent management Misdiagnosing it as Huntington disease or another spinocerebellar ataxia without genetic confirmation Overlooking DRPLA in the differential of progressive myoclonus epilepsy in children Failing to counsel families about anticipation and paternal transmission risk Attributing white matter changes to an unrelated process Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy is a polyglutamine disorder caused by an expanded CAG repeat in ATN1, which encodes atrophin-1. Longer repeat expansions produce earlier onset and more severe disease, and paternal transmission tends to increase repeat size, explaining the pronounced anticipation and the shift toward the juvenile epileptic phenotype in successive generations. results from expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat in ATN1, yielding an atrophin-1 protein with an elongated polyglutamine tract. DRPLA is progressive and ultimately fatal; juvenile-onset disease advances rapidly with early severe disability, whereas adult-onset disease progresses more slowly over years to a couple of decades. Prognosis worsens with larger repeat expansions and earlier onset.

immunosuppression Denys-Drash syndrome arises from constitutional pathogenic variants in WT1, a transcription factor essential for normal development of the kidney and gonads. Missense variants, characteristically in the zinc-finger domains that bind DNA, act in a dominant-negative manner and disrupt the transcriptional programmes that govern podocyte and glomerular development, producing diffuse mesangial sclerosis and progressive proteinuric renal failure. Because WT1 also directs gonadal differentiation, the same variants cause disorders of sex development and gonadal dysgenesis, and the dysgenetic gonadal tissue is prone to malignant change. Loss of WT1 tumour-suppressor function in nephrogenic rests underlies the strong predisposition to Wilms tumour of the developing kidney. The renal prognosis is poor, with early progression to end-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis and transplantation, though the nephropathy does not recur in the allograft; overall outcome depends heavily on timely detection and management of Wilms tumour and gonadal malignancy risk.

disease DEPDC5 is part of the GATOR1 complex, which inhibits mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) signalling, a pathway controlling cell growth, protein synthesis, and neuronal Loss-of-function variants relieve this inhibition, causing constitutive mTOR pathway overactivity. In the brain this promotes epileptogenesis and, when a somatic second hit occurs in a clone of cells, can produce focal cortical dysplasia. Depersonalisation-Derealisation Disorder — Depersonalisation disorder, Derealisation disorder Panic disorder and other anxiety disorders Post-traumatic stress disorder and other dissociative disorders Depressive disorder Substance-induced states (cannabis, hallucinogens, ketamine) Temporal lobe epilepsy or aura Psychotic disorder where reality-testing is lost Migraine with aura or vestibular disorders Structured clinical interview and validated scales such as the Cambridge Depersonalisation Scale Screening for anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and trauma history Substance use history and toxicology EEG where temporal lobe epilepsy is suspected Neuroimaging where focal features or atypical onset are present Thyroid and metabolic screen Assessment for vestibular or migraine contributors Persistent or recurrent depersonalisation (detachment from one's own thoughts, feelings, body, or actions) and/or derealisation (a sense of unreality of the surroundings). Reality-testing remains intact and the experience is recognised as subjective, which distinguishes it from psychosis. Onset is typically in adolescence or early adulthood, often precipitated by severe stress, trauma, cannabis or hallucinogen use, or panic. Transient depersonalisation is very common and non-pathological; the disorder requires persistence, distress, and impairment. Frequently comorbid with anxiety disorders, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder, and is often under-recognised or misdiagnosed. Patients describe feeling like an automaton, being in a dream, watching from behind glass, or being emotionally numb, and find this distressing. Cannabis and dissociative agents such as ketamine are recognised precipitants. The course is often chronic and under-treated, and psychoeducation reduces the fear of losing one's mind. Emergent loss of reality-testing suggesting psychosis Focal neurological signs or seizure features Suicidal ideation with severe depression Abrupt onset in later life suggesting an organic cause Misdiagnosing the condition as psychosis and prescribing antipsychotics inappropriately Overlooking the diagnosis behind prominent anxiety or depression Missing cannabis or hallucinogen use as a trigger Failing to reassure that the experience, though distressing, is not a sign of madness Depersonalisation-derealisation disorder is thought to involve dysregulation of the neural systems that integrate emotion with bodily and self-awareness. Neuroimaging implicates altered activity in prefrontal regions, notably the right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, with reciprocal suppression of limbic responses in the amygdala and insula, producing a dampening of the emotional colouring of experience. This has been interpreted as a hard-wired response to overwhelming stress that becomes persistent, with associated autonomic blunting to emotional stimuli. Trauma, anxiety, and drug exposure, especially cannabis, can trigger the state, which then self-perpetuates through catastrophic appraisal and heightened self-monitoring. The disorder frequently runs a chronic, fluctuating course, but symptoms and distress can improve substantially with psychoeducation, treatment of comorbid anxiety or depression, and psychological therapy.

Dermatitis herpetiformis is an autoimmune blistering disease driven by gluten sensitivity in genetically predisposed individuals carrying HLA-DQ2 or DQ8. Dietary gluten triggers production of IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase and, in the skin, cross-reactivity with epidermal transglutaminase. IgA immune complexes deposit in the dermal papillae, recruiting neutrophils that form the characteristic papillary microabscesses and cause subepidermal separation with vesicle formation. The same gluten-driven autoimmunity produces the small-bowel villous atrophy of coeliac disease, so skin and gut manifestations share a common mechanism and both respond to gluten withdrawal. Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic condition, but a strict gluten-free diet usually controls the skin disease, allows medication to be reduced or stopped over time, heals the associated enteropathy, and lowers the long-term lymphoma risk; lapses in the diet typically provoke relapse.

Gravity and chronic sun exposure contribute to the redundant, lax skin. The excess upper eyelid tissue can hang over the lid margin and lashes, mechanically limiting the superior visual field, while lower-lid changes are largely cosmetic. The condition is benign and slowly progressive; blepharoplasty reliably improves the visual field and appearance, though ageing changes may continue.

and histiocytic cells confined largely to the dermis, with some lesions extending into the superficial subcutis. The cells are arranged in a characteristic storiform, or cartwheel, pattern and characteristically entrap thickened collagen bundles at the periphery of the lesion. The overlying epidermis typically shows acanthosis with hyperpigmentation of the basal layer and sometimes induction of hair follicle-like or basaloid structures, producing the clinically apparent surface pigmentation. There is longstanding debate as to whether the lesion is a true clonal neoplasm or a reactive fibrosing response, often to minor trauma or an arthropod bite, and evidence exists on both sides. The immunophenotype, with expression of factor XIIIa and absence of CD34, is diagnostically important because it is the mirror image of dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans and helps separate these two entities. Dermatofibroma is benign with an excellent prognosis and most lesions remain stable indefinitely, requiring no treatment. Cellular, aneurysmal, and atypical variants have a small risk of local recurrence but essentially no metastatic potential.

taking inadequate margins, leading to recurrence Mistaking it for a benign dermatofibroma, keloid or scar and delaying treatment Overlooking fibrosarcomatous transformation on histology Failing to COL1A1-PDGFB gene fusion, typically carried on a supernumerary ring chromosome derived from chromosomes 17 and 22. The fusion places platelet-derived growth factor B under the control of the collagen COL1A1 promoter, resulting in continuous autocrine PDGF receptor beta activation and tumour cell proliferation. The tumour grows as a storiform proliferation of CD34-positive spindle cells that infiltrates the dermis and subcutis in an insidious, finger-like fashion far beyond the visible lesion. A high-grade fibrosarcomatous transformation can occur, conferring greater metastatic risk. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans has an excellent prognosis when excised with adequate margins, but it recurs locally at high rates if margins are inadequate because of its infiltrative growth. Metastasis is rare and occurs mainly with fibrosarcomatous transformation.

biopsy shows perifascicular atrophy and perivascular inflammation There is a well-recognised association with occult malignancy, so age-appropriate cancer screening is essential, particularly around diagnosis Interstitial lung disease is common and may be rapidly progressive, especially with anti-MDA5 antibodies, which also carry a characteristic cutaneous ulcerating phenotype Myositis-specific antibodies (e.g. anti-Mi-2, anti-TIF1-gamma, anti-MDA5, antisynthetase) predict distinct patterns of skin, lung, and malignancy risk Treatment uses corticosteroids with steroid-sparing immunosuppressants, photoprotection and topical therapy for skin, and prompt management of lung involvement Rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease, particularly with anti-MDA5 antibodies, which can be life-threatening Clinical features pointing to an underlying malignancy (weight loss, new mass, cytopenias) Dysphagia and respiratory muscle weakness with aspiration or ventilatory risk Cutaneous ulceration and severe vasculopathy associated with anti-MDA5 disease Cardiac involvement with arrhythmia or heart failure Failing to perform malignancy screening in newly diagnosed adults Overlooking amyopathic disease when weakness is absent despite classic skin findings Missing or underestimating rapidly progressive lung disease, especially with anti-MDA5 antibodies Undertreating skin disease and neglecting photoprotection Assuming normal creatine kinase excludes active or amyopathic disease Dermatomyositis is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterised by humorally mediated, complement-dependent microangiopathy. Immune complex deposition and complement activation (membrane attack complex) on endomysial capillaries cause capillary loss, ischaemia, and the perifascicular atrophy typical of muscle biopsy. A strong type I interferon signature is present in muscle and skin. The same immune-mediated vasculopathy affects skin and other organs, and paraneoplastic mechanisms link it to underlying malignancy in a substantial proportion of adults. Prognosis depends heavily on associated interstitial lung disease, malignancy, and cardiac involvement rather than the myositis itself. Skin and muscle disease often respond to immunosuppression, but rapidly progressive lung disease and paraneoplastic cases carry significant mortality.

tinea incognito that obscures the diagnosis Failing to confirm the diagnosis mycologically before long courses of systemic antifungals Using topical-only therapy for scalp or nail infection, which will not eradicate it Neglecting reservoirs such as untreated tinea pedis or animal contacts, leading to recurrence Dermatophytosis is caused by dermatophyte fungi of the genera Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton, which possess keratinases enabling them to invade and digest keratin in the stratum corneum, hair, and nails. Infection is acquired from other people (anthropophilic), animals (zoophilic), or soil (geophilic), with zoophilic species often producing more inflammatory reactions. The fungus spreads centrifugally through the stratum corneum, producing the characteristic annular lesion with an active advancing scaly margin. The host inflammatory response accounts for erythema and, in strongly inflammatory infections such as kerion, pustulation and potential scarring. Warmth, moisture, occlusion, and impaired immunity favour infection. Prognosis is excellent with correct diagnosis and appropriate topical or systemic antifungal therapy; nail infections require prolonged treatment and relapse is common, while delayed treatment of inflammatory scalp disease can leave permanent scarring alopecia.

dermatosis papulosa nigra — DPN seborrhoeic keratosis melanocytic naevi verruca plana (flat warts) syringoma acrochordon (skin tag) adnexal tumours such as trichoepithelioma angiofibroma clinical diagnosis based on morphology and distribution dermoscopy showing seborrhoeic-keratosis-like features biopsy reserved for atypical or diagnostically uncertain lesions clinical photography to monitor cosmetic treatment outcomes test-spot treatment to assess pigmentary response before wider therapy Presents as multiple small, smooth, dark brown to black dome-shaped papules on the face, especially the malar region and periorbital skin. It is regarded as a variant of seborrhoeic keratosis occurring predominantly in people of African and, less commonly, Asian descent. Onset is typically in adolescence or early adulthood, with lesions increasing in number and size over time. There is a strong familial tendency and a female predominance, and lesions are entirely benign. The papules are asymptomatic and of cosmetic concern only, though occasional lesions may become pruritic or catch on clothing. Diagnosis is clinical; dermoscopy shows features shared with seborrhoeic keratosis such as comedo-like openings and a cerebriform pattern. Treatment is for cosmetic reasons and includes light electrodesiccation, curettage, snip excision or laser, undertaken cautiously given the risk of dyspigmentation. Careful test treatment of a few lesions is advised in richly pigmented skin because of the risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and keloid scarring. an individual lesion showing asymmetry, irregular pigmentation or ulceration suggesting melanoma rapid change in a solitary lesion within the field keloid formation or marked dyspigmentation following treatment atypical distribution or morphology prompting biopsy Aggressive or extensive destructive treatment causing post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation or keloid scarring in darker skin. Failing to perform a test treatment before treating numerous lesions. Overlooking an atypical lesion within the field that warrants biopsy. Confusing the condition with flat warts and applying inappropriate therapy. Dermatosis papulosa nigra is considered a clinical variant of seborrhoeic keratosis, with histology showing hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and elongation of rete ridges in an epidermal proliferation of basaloid and squamoid keratinocytes. A pronounced familial and genetic predisposition in people with darker skin phototypes underlies the characteristic distribution and early onset, and a naevoid or developmental defect of the pilosebaceous follicle has been proposed. Increased epidermal melanisation accounts for the dark colour. As with seborrhoeic keratosis, the lesions are benign proliferations without malignant potential. Dermatosis papulosa nigra is entirely benign with no malignant potential; lesions persist and slowly accumulate over life. Cosmetic treatment can improve appearance but carries a risk of dyspigmentation and scarring in richly pigmented skin.

arises from an exaggerated response of cutaneous mast cells to mechanical shearing forces, such that minor stroking or rubbing triggers histamine and mediator release with a localised weal and flare along the line of trauma. The stimulus is thought to release or unmask an antigen that provokes IgE-dependent mast cell degranulation in susceptible skin. The result is a reproducible, mechanically induced urticaria that follows the exact pattern of the applied friction. Symptomatic dermographism is benign and often persists for several years before gradually resolving; most patients achieve good control with avoidance of friction and regular antihistamines, and the condition does not carry the systemic risks of some other physical urticarias.

Descending perineum syndrome — perineal descent syndrome, abnormal perineal descent Rectocele causing obstructed defecation Rectal intussusception or full-thickness rectal prolapse Anismus (paradoxical puborectalis contraction) Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome Pudendal neuropathy from other causes Enterocele or multi-compartment pelvic organ prolapse Slow-transit constipation Defecating proctography to quantify perineal descent and associated abnormalities Dynamic pelvic-floor MRI for multi-compartment assessment Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion for evacuatory and sphincter function Pudendal nerve terminal motor latency or neurophysiological testing where available Endoanal ultrasound to assess sphincter integrity in incontinent patients Perineometry to measure descent clinically Descending perineum syndrome is excessive downward descent of the perineum and pelvic floor during straining, reflecting weakness of the pelvic-floor musculature and its supports It presents with obstructed defecation, a sensation of incomplete evacuation, perineal aching or pain, and, over time, faecal incontinence as pudendal neuropathy develops Chronic excessive straining is both a cause and a consequence, creating a self-perpetuating cycle of descent, incomplete evacuation, and further straining The condition is closely linked to repeated stretch injury of the pudendal nerves, which progressively weakens the sphincter and pelvic floor and contributes to incontinence Clinically the perineum balloons below the plane of the ischial tuberosities on straining, and this can be quantified with a perineometer or on defecating proctography It frequently coexists with rectocele, rectal intussusception, and solitary rectal ulcer syndrome as part of a spectrum of pelvic-floor dysfunction Management is predominantly conservative: avoidance of straining, stool bulking and softening, and biofeedback pelvic-floor retraining Surgery has a limited and carefully selected role, as operations may not reverse established neuropathy and outcomes for isolated perineal descent are unpredictable Rectal bleeding, weight loss, or a mass suggesting neoplasia A persistent solitary rectal ulcer requiring biopsy to exclude malignancy Rapidly progressive incontinence or neurological deficit New external prolapse requiring assessment Symptoms disproportionate to findings, prompting a wider search Encouraging or overlooking continued straining, which perpetuates descent and nerve injury Attributing symptoms to a single finding and missing the wider pelvic-floor disorder Expecting surgery to reverse established pudendal neuropathy and incontinence Failing to biopsy a coexisting solitary rectal ulcer Neglecting biofeedback and bowel regulation as first-line therapy The pelvic floor normally provides dynamic support that limits downward movement of the perineum during defecation. In descending perineum syndrome, weakness of the levator ani and supporting connective tissue, often following childbirth, ageing, and years of excessive straining, allows abnormal downward ballooning of the perineum when intra-abdominal pressure rises. This descent stretches and repeatedly injures the pudendal nerves as they pass around the ischial spines, producing a progressive neuropathy that weakens the external anal sphincter and pelvic floor and predisposes to faecal incontinence. The descent also impairs the normal anorectal angulation and evacuatory mechanics, causing incomplete emptying that provokes further straining, perpetuating both the descent and the nerve injury. Associated mucosal prolapse and intussusception may produce solitary rectal ulcer changes. Descending perineum syndrome tends to be chronic and progressive; conservative measures and biofeedback can relieve symptoms and slow progression, but established pudendal neuropathy and incontinence are difficult to reverse, and surgical results for isolated perineal descent are unpredictable.

surgery has a limited and unreliable role It forms part of the spectrum of pelvic floor weakness and often coexists with pelvic organ prolapse Progressive faecal incontinence indicating an advancing pudendal neuropathy New bleeding, weight loss, or a mass suggesting malignancy Rapidly progressive symptoms or neurological signs suggesting a spinal cause Ulceration with atypical features requiring biopsy Attempting surgery with the expectation of a reliable cure Overlooking the underlying straining or evacuatory disorder Missing early pudendal neuropathy before incontinence is established Failing to address coexisting pelvic organ prolapse Descending perineum syndrome results from chronic excessive straining that progressively weakens and stretches the pelvic floor, so that on defecatory effort the perineum balloons abnormally downward. The prolapsing anterior rectal mucosa produces a sensation of obstruction, provoking further straining in a vicious cycle. Sustained descent stretches the pudendal nerves as they course around the ischial spines, causing a progressive pudendal neuropathy with denervation of the sphincter and pelvic floor and eventual faecal incontinence. It overlaps with mucosal prolapse and solitary rectal ulcer syndrome. Generally a chronic, slowly progressive condition; established pudendal neuropathy and incontinence are difficult to reverse, so prevention through avoiding straining and early conservative management is important, and surgical results are inconsistent.

Desensitization — Drug desensitization, Rapid drug desensitization, Temporary drug tolerance induction Type I IgE-mediated drug allergy IgE-independent mast cell activation (complement-mediated, COX-1 inhibition, MRGPRX2-mediated) Cytokine release reaction (IL-6 driven) Mixed reaction (combined type I and CRR features) Delayed type IV maculopapular eruption Hereditary alpha tryptasemia Infusion reaction (non-allergic) Serum tryptase within 30 min to 4 h of reaction (and baseline tryptase) Baseline tryptase with TPSAB1 genotyping if elevated (hereditary alpha tryptasemia) Serum IL-6 (elevated in CRR and mixed reactions) Skin testing (epicutaneous/intradermal) for IgE-mediated reactions Basophil activation test (in vitro evidence of IgE sensitization) Drug-specific serum IgE (e.g., penicillin, platins; low sensitivity) Skin patch testing for delayed type IV reactions (high specificity, low sensitivity) Lymphocyte transformation test for SCARS-causing drugs HLA genotyping for SCARS risk (abacavir, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, vancomycin) Non-allergic infusion reaction Anxiety/vasovagal episode during infusion Kounis syndrome (allergic coronary vasospasm) Takotsubo cardiomyopathy from drug-induced anaphylaxis Drug desensitization (DD) is a temporary immunotherapy that delivers sequential, incremental small doses of a culprit drug over hours to safely reach the full therapeutic dose, taking advantage of mast cell/basophil inhibitory pathways rather than producing lasting tolerance. Tolerance achieved by DD is transient: it does not produce sustained tolerance and must be repeated for each new course, or when the interval between doses equals two or more drug half-lives; continued exposure (e.g., ongoing antibiotics or aspirin/COX-1 inhibitors) can maintain the desensitized state. Roughly 10-20% of the health-care-engaged population claims a penicillin allergy, but most labels are unconfirmed; low-risk patients can be delabeled, and single-dose oral challenges have been shown safe in low-risk children and adults. Serum tryptase is the specific biomarker of anaphylaxis: a level above the normal range (11.4 ng/mL) or above a patient's baseline (a 1.6-fold rise), measured within 30 min to 4 h of symptom onset, supports type I or mixed reactions. A baseline tryptase of 7.5 ng/mL or higher may signal hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HαT) from TPSAB1 gene duplication on chromosome 16, an autosomal dominant trait in 4-6% of Caucasians that can worsen anaphylaxis severity. Cytokine release reactions (CRRs) present with fever, chills, and back/chest/pelvic pain and headache with a transient IL-6 rise; mixed reactions combine type I and CRR features with both tryptase and IL-6 elevations. The most widely used standardized protocol uses three bags (1/100, 1/10, and undiluted target concentration) with 12 doubling steps every 15 min, reaching target dose in about 5.7 h, adaptable to IV, oral, SC, IM, intraperitoneal, intraocular, and intrathecal routes. Breakthrough reactions occur in roughly 10-30% of protocols, are usually mild and resemble the initial reaction, and do not prevent completion of DD in about 99% of cases; no deaths from DD have been reported. Corticosteroids do NOT protect against anaphylaxis during desensitization; omalizumab (anti-IgE) has been used as an adjuvant in highly sensitized patients with severe IgE-mediated reactions. Skin testing reliability falls with greater time since the index reaction and after severe anaphylaxis (mediator depletion can cause false negatives); anaphylaxis to penicillin or carboplatin has not been reported in skin-test-negative patients. Platinum-drug IgE sensitization usually requires six or more exposures (fewer in BRCA-mutation carriers); skin testing is positive in over 85% of patients with recent reactions, and reexposure of skin-test-positive patients carries high anaphylaxis risk. Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS, AGEP) - contraindication to desensitization, avoid the drug Type II cytotoxic, type III immune-complex, vasculitis, and single-organ toxic reactions - contraindications to DD Hypotension with cardiovascular collapse, throat tightening, oxygen desaturation (grade 3 anaphylaxis) Kounis syndrome or takotsubo cardiomyopathy from drug-induced anaphylaxis - contraindications to DD Oxaliplatin-induced immune-mediated thrombocytopenia with bleeding - precludes further DD Markedly elevated tryptase well above baseline indicating severe mast cell activation Assuming corticosteroid premedication prevents anaphylaxis during DD - it does not. Treating SCARS or other contraindicated phenotypes with DD, where even minute drug amounts can trigger severe reactions. Expecting durable tolerance - DD is temporary and must be repeated each course or after a gap of two or more half-lives. Relying on a negative skin test performed long after the index reaction or after severe anaphylaxis (false negatives from mediator depletion or time elapsed). Maintaining unconfirmed penicillin allergy labels, leading to use of less effective, costlier second-line antibiotics. Overusing one-bag protocols in highly sensitized type I patients, associated with more epinephrine use and failure to complete treatment. Missing phenotype switching in oxaliplatin DD (type I converting to CRR/mixed reactions). Drug hypersensitivity reactions are classified by timing, mechanism (endotype), and biomarkers. Type I reactions arise from mast cell and basophil activation, either IgE-dependent (requiring prior repeated sensitizing exposures, as with antibiotics, chemotherapy, and some biologics) or IgE-independent (first-exposure reactions via complement activation, COX-1 inhibition, or MRGPRX2 receptor activation by quinolones, vancomycin, icatibant, basic compounds, and certain THIQ-motif general anesthetics). Cytokine release reactions reflect T-cell and other immune-cell activation with transient IL-6 elevation. Delayed type IV reactions are T-cell mediated. Desensitization works because rapid, stepwise delivery of incremental antigen doses recruits inhibitory phosphatases to the IgE receptor, blocking signal transduction and mediator release so that the target dose can be reached without anaphylaxis; desensitized patients show transient conversion of skin tests from positive to negative. Mechanisms for non-IgE phenotypes are less well understood. Rapid multistep desensitization is highly effective and safe across thousands of patients with infections, chronic inflammatory diseases, and malignancies. Protocols are completed in roughly 95-100% of cases (taxane series completed 95-100%), breakthrough reactions occur in about 10-30% and are usually mild, and no deaths attributable to DD have been reported. Drug delivery via DD achieves efficacy equal to standard administration (expected clearance of infection, reduced inflammation, comparable cancer responses); survival of platinum-desensitized cancer patients is noninferior to that of nonallergic patients, and ovarian cancer patients undergoing carboplatin DD have shown a 5-year life-expectancy advantage in one large series. Hypersensitivity reactions are graded by organ involvement and vital signs: grade 1 (mild, one organ), grade 2 (moderate, two or more organs), grade 3 (severe, with changes in vital signs/cardiovascular collapse). Reactions are also categorized by timing as acute/immediate (during or within 1-6 h of exposure) versus delayed (6 h to days or weeks), and by endotype (type I IgE/non-IgE, cytokine release, mixed, and type II-IV delayed reactions).

The course is highly variable, and a meaningful proportion stabilise or regress, which underpins the shift towards active surveillance rather than immediate intervention.

In sporadic disease this results from somatic activating mutations in CTNNB1, the gene encoding beta-catenin, which stabilise the protein so that it accumulates and translocates to the nucleus to drive transcription of proliferative target genes. The resulting proliferation of uniform spindle cells within a dense collagenous matrix infiltrates adjacent muscle and fascia along tissue planes, encasing rather than destroying structures. Local factors such as prior surgery, trauma, and the hormonal milieu of pregnancy appear to promote tumour development, consistent with the observed clinical associations, while the absence of metastatic potential reflects the tumour's fibroblastic, non-epithelial biology. Desmoid tumours do not metastasise, and many stabilise or regress under active surveillance, but they cause significant morbidity through local infiltration and have a high propensity for recurrence after surgery. Long-term outcome depends on site, since mesenteric and head and neck lesions can be life-threatening, whereas abdominal wall tumours generally behave more indolently.

Desmoplastic small round cell tumour is driven by a balanced chromosomal translocation that fuses the EWSR1 gene with the Wilms tumour gene WT1, generating a chimeric protein in which the transcriptional activation domain of EWSR1 is joined to the DNA-binding zinc-finger domain of WT1. This aberrant transcription factor dysregulates target genes, including those encoding growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor, which is thought to drive the intense desmoplastic stromal reaction that characterises the tumour. The tumour has a marked tropism for mesothelial-lined surfaces, spreading diffusely across the peritoneum as multiple implants rather than a single dominant mass, which underlies its typical widespread intra-abdominal presentation and difficulty in achieving durable control. Desmoplastic small round cell tumour carries a poor prognosis, with frequent relapse and low long-term survival even after intensive multimodal therapy. The best outcomes are seen when complete or near-complete cytoreduction can be achieved in the context of systemic treatment.

Detrusor sphincter dyssynergia — DSD, Detrusor-external sphincter dyssynergia, Vesicosphincteric dyssynergia Anatomical bladder outlet obstruction (benign prostatic obstruction, urethral stricture) Primary bladder neck obstruction / dysfunction Fowler's syndrome (impaired sphincter relaxation in young women) Dysfunctional voiding in neurologically intact patients Detrusor underactivity or acontractile bladder Non-relaxing pelvic floor dysfunction Learned or behavioural voiding dysfunction Video-urodynamics with external sphincter electromyography Renal function tests and serial upper tract ultrasound MRI of the spinal cord or brain to define the neurological lesion Post-void residual measurement Cystoscopy to exclude structural outlet obstruction Isotope renography to assess differential function and drainage Urine culture given the high infection risk Detrusor sphincter dyssynergia is the involuntary contraction of the external urethral sphincter during a detrusor contraction, producing functional outlet obstruction, and is a hallmark of suprasacral spinal cord pathology. It arises from a lesion between the pontine micturition centre and the sacral cord, most commonly spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, transverse myelitis or myelomeningocele; a lesion above the pons does not cause it. The dangerous consequence is sustained high detrusor storage and voiding pressure, which threatens the upper tracts with vesicoureteric reflux, hydronephrosis and renal failure. Diagnosis is made by video-urodynamics showing simultaneous detrusor contraction and increased external sphincter electromyographic activity with a characteristic obstructed flow pattern. Symptoms overlap with mechanical obstruction: hesitancy, interrupted or staccato flow, incomplete emptying and recurrent infection, so urodynamic confirmation is essential before treatment. Management prioritises conversion of a high-pressure system to a safe low-pressure reservoir, commonly with clean intermittent catheterisation combined with detrusor pressure-lowering therapy. Chemical relaxation of the sphincter with botulinum toxin, or pharmacological or surgical outlet reduction, may be used, and afferent-modulating neuromodulation is emerging in selected patients. Lifelong upper tract surveillance is mandatory because renal deterioration can progress silently despite apparently adequate bladder emptying. When a neurological lesion interrupts the pathways between the pons and the sacral spinal cord, this coordination is lost: the sacral reflex arcs mediating detrusor contraction and sphincter activity become dissociated, so the external sphincter contracts involuntarily during detrusor contraction rather than relaxing. The bladder therefore contracts against a closed or intermittently closing outlet, generating high intravesical pressure with poor and inefficient urine flow. Sustained elevation of storage and voiding pressures produces detrusor wall thickening and reduced compliance, promotes vesicoureteric reflux and impedes ureteric drainage, ultimately endangering renal function. The severity and pattern correlate with the level and completeness of the underlying cord lesion. With early urodynamic diagnosis and a management strategy that maintains low storage and voiding pressures, most patients preserve renal function and avoid serious upper tract damage. Untreated or poorly controlled detrusor sphincter dyssynergia carries a substantial long-term risk of progressive renal impairment and recurrent sepsis.

Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip — DDH, congenital dislocation of the hip, hip dysplasia Benign hip clicks Septic arthritis of the hip Transient synovitis Neuromuscular hip dysplasia (e.g. in cerebral palsy or spina bifida) Proximal focal femoral deficiency or other congenital femoral anomalies Leg-length discrepancy from other causes Hip ultrasound in the first months of life Anteroposterior pelvic radiograph after the femoral head ossifies Careful serial clinical examination including Barlow, Ortolani, and Galeazzi tests Targeted imaging for high-risk infants (breech, family history) A spectrum of abnormal development of the hip ranging from mild acetabular dysplasia to frank dislocation, present at or developing after birth. Major risk factors include female sex, breech presentation, oligohydramnios, first-born status, and a positive family history. Newborn screening uses the Barlow manoeuvre (to dislocate a reducible hip) and the Ortolani manoeuvre (to relocate a dislocated hip). In older infants, signs include limited hip abduction, asymmetric thigh or gluteal skin creases, and apparent limb-length discrepancy (Galeazzi sign). Ultrasound is the imaging test of choice in early infancy before the femoral head ossifies; plain radiographs become useful after a few months of age. Early treatment of a reducible hip with an abduction device such as the Pavlik harness is usually successful and avoids surgery. The later the diagnosis, the more likely that closed or open reduction and casting, or surgical procedures, will be needed. Untreated or late-treated dysplasia leads to a limp, gait abnormality, and premature degenerative hip arthritis in adulthood. Persistent clicks alone are usually benign, whereas a palpable 'clunk' of dislocation or relocation is significant. Without a well-seated femoral head, the acetabulum fails to develop its normal depth and shape, perpetuating instability and, over time, leading to secondary degenerative change. When detected and treated in early infancy, most hips develop normally with excellent long-term function; delayed diagnosis increases the need for surgery and the risk of residual dysplasia, avascular necrosis, and early osteoarthritis.

obstruction The nasal septum is formed by the septal cartilage, the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid and the vomer, meeting the maxillary and palatine crests. Deviation arises when these components grow at differing rates or are displaced by trauma, so the septum buckles or angulates away from the midline. The deviation narrows the airway on the concave side and may obstruct the osteomeatal complex, impairing sinus ventilation and mucociliary drainage. Compensatory hypertrophy of the turbinate on the wider side can paradoxically cause obstruction there as well. dextrocardia — dextrocardia situs solitus, isolated dextrocardia, dextroversion dextroposition from pulmonary hypoplasia or agenesis dextroposition from congenital diaphragmatic hernia mediastinal shift from large left pleural effusion or pneumothorax situs inversus totalis with mirror-image heart isolated levocardia with abdominal situs anomaly congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries heterotaxy syndrome transthoracic echocardiography with full segmental analysis chest radiograph localising apex, gastric bubble and aortic arch ECG with right-sided or mirror-image lead placement abdominal ultrasound to define visceral situs and spleen number cross-sectional cardiac imaging (CT or MRI) for complex anatomy assessment for primary ciliary dyskinesia when situs inversus coexists with respiratory disease genetic and laterality evaluation in selected cases Dextrocardia denotes a heart whose apex points to the right hemithorax and must be distinguished from dextroposition, where an extracardiac process merely displaces a normally formed heart rightward. The clinical significance depends entirely on the accompanying visceral situs: dextrocardia with situs inversus usually accompanies a structurally normal heart, whereas dextrocardia with situs solitus carries a high burden of complex congenital heart disease. Dextrocardia with situs solitus (isolated dextrocardia) is frequently associated with congenitally corrected transposition, ventricular septal defect and pulmonary stenosis. A segmental sequential analysis of atrial situs, ventricular loop and great-artery connection is essential to characterise the malformation before any intervention. On examination the apex beat and heart sounds are maximal on the right, and the ECG shows reversed praecordial R-wave progression with abnormal frontal axis unless leads are repositioned. Right-sided praecordial leads or mirror-image electrode placement are required to obtain an interpretable ECG. Dextroposition from right pulmonary hypoplasia, diaphragmatic hernia or large left effusion should be excluded before labelling true dextrocardia. Association with primary ciliary dyskinesia should be considered when dextrocardia accompanies situs inversus and chronic respiratory disease. neonatal cyanosis or heart failure indicating complex associated congenital heart disease rapid respiratory distress suggesting dextroposition from an acute intrathoracic process murmur, abnormal pulses or failure to thrive in an infant with rightward apex chronic sinopulmonary disease pointing to primary ciliary dyskinesia planned surgery or line placement where malposition risks a wrong-side procedure Confusing true dextrocardia with dextroposition and missing the underlying pulmonary or diaphragmatic cause. Interpreting the standard-placement ECG as ischaemic or lead-reversed artefact. Assuming a normal heart without performing full segmental echocardiography, especially in situs solitus. Overlooking congenitally corrected transposition and its late complications. Failing to alert procedural teams to the reversed cardiac position. Dextrocardia arises from abnormal direction of embryonic cardiac looping and its interaction with overall body situs. In normal development the straight heart tube undergoes rightward (D-loop) looping so the morphological right ventricle lies rightward and the apex swings left. When looping and situs are coordinately reversed, as in situs inversus totalis, the apex points right but atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial concordance is preserved in mirror image, usually yielding a normal heart. When cardiac position is reversed independently of visceral situs (dextrocardia with situs solitus), there is a mismatch between the direction of looping and atrial arrangement, which strongly predisposes to segmental discordances such as congenitally corrected transposition and to septal and outflow malformations. True dextrocardia is thus an intrinsic developmental malposition, in contrast to dextroposition, where a normally formed and normally looped heart is secondarily shifted rightward by loss of lung volume or a space-occupying process in the left hemithorax. Dextrocardia associated with situs inversus and an otherwise normal heart has an excellent outlook, whereas dextrocardia with situs solitus often accompanies complex congenital heart disease and carries a prognosis governed by those lesions and their reparability. Outcome therefore ranges from normal life expectancy to that of severe cyanotic congenital heart disease.

progression prompting review for autoimmune or other treatable causes Marked asymmetry suggesting a superimposed structural lesion Emergence of systemic features that would reclassify the disorder as syndromic Progression to severe loss limiting communication despite aiding Dismissing a dominant familial pattern as ordinary age-related hearing loss Not using the audiometric configuration to prioritise likely genes Overlooking reversible causes of accelerated decline Assuming uniform severity across a family despite variable penetrance The DFNA group comprises many distinct loci, each caused by a variant in a gene important to cochlear function, and most act through a dominant-negative or gain-of-function mechanism that disrupts a shared multimeric protein or ion channel. For example, KCNQ4 encodes a potassium channel in outer hair cells whose dysfunction causes progressive high-frequency loss, while WFS1 (wolframin) variants produce a characteristic low-frequency loss. Because a single altered allele can poison the assembled channel or structural complex, heterozygotes are affected, and the progressive nature reflects cumulative hair cell or supporting cell dysfunction over time rather than a fixed congenital lesion. Most forms progress gradually over decades, and while amplification maintains communication for many years, cochlear implantation offers reliable rehabilitation once hearing aids no longer provide adequate benefit.

and consanguinity increases risk DFNB1 (GJB2/GJB6) is by far the commonest locus, but many other genes such as SLC26A4, MYO15A, and OTOF contribute Most forms are stable, though SLC26A4-related DFNB4 (with enlarged vestibular aqueduct) fluctuates and progresses The phenotype is usually bilateral and symmetrical without systemic features, distinguishing it from syndromic deafness Vestibular
