fluctuation suggesting SLC26A4-related disease with an enlarged vestibular aqueduct Emerging visual, thyroid, renal, or cardiac features indicating a syndrome Delayed speech and language from under-recognised loss Cardiac syncope or prolonged QT raising concern for Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome Stopping at a single GJB2 variant without excluding a GJB6 deletion or another locus Missing an evolving syndrome by not screening for extra-auditory features Overlooking congenital cytomegalovirus as a treatable or coexisting cause Delaying intervention while awaiting complete genetic results The DFNB group encompasses numerous loci in which biallelic loss-of-function variants disrupt proteins essential to cochlear development or function, including gap-junction proteins, hair cell stereocilia and motor proteins, and ion transporters. Because both alleles must be affected, heterozygous carriers are typically asymptomatic and disease appears in the offspring of two carriers. The resulting lesion is usually cochlear and often severe and congenital, reflecting failure of hair cell mechanotransduction, endolymph homeostasis, or synaptic transmission depending on the gene involved. The central auditory pathway is generally intact, which is why direct cochlear stimulation is effective. Most DFNB forms are stable, and with early amplification or cochlear implantation and structured habilitation children typically develop good spoken language; fluctuating SLC26A4-related disease carries a more variable course.

Dhat Syndrome — Dhat, Semen-loss anxiety Depressive disorder Generalised anxiety or somatic symptom disorder Sexual dysfunction (premature ejaculation, erectile dysfunction) Genito-urinary infection or urethral discharge Prostatitis Illness anxiety disorder Diabetes mellitus presenting with fatigue and sexual dysfunction Detailed history including sexual and cultural beliefs Mental state examination for depression and anxiety Urinalysis and microscopy to exclude infection and to demonstrate absence of semen Screening for genito-urinary infection where indicated Fasting glucose or HbA1c where fatigue and sexual dysfunction are prominent Assessment of sexual function Assessment of psychoeducational needs and collateral history Culture-bound syndrome of the Indian subcontinent involving distressing conviction that vital semen is being lost in urine, through nocturnal emission, or through masturbation, causing weakness. Presents with fatigue, weakness, poor concentration, anxiety, low mood, and multiple somatic complaints attributed to dhat, a whitish urinary discharge. Rooted in traditional Ayurvedic concepts that semen (dhatu) is a precious vital essence whose loss depletes the body. Predominantly affects young men, often recently married or experiencing sexual guilt and anxiety. Frequently overlaps with depression, anxiety disorders, and sexual dysfunction such as premature ejaculation or erectile difficulty. Management centres on culturally sensitive psychoeducation, correcting misconceptions, and treating comorbid depression or anxiety. Often presents first to general practitioners, traditional healers, or genito-urinary and andrology clinics rather than to psychiatry. Significant comorbid depression with suicidal ideation Severe functional impairment or social withdrawal Self-treatment with harmful traditional remedies Genuine genito-urinary pathology being overlooked Ordering repeated unnecessary investigations that reinforce illness beliefs Missing treatable comorbid depression or anxiety Dismissive or culturally insensitive reassurance that alienates the patient Failing to address the underlying sexual dysfunction Dhat syndrome arises from culturally embedded beliefs, drawn from traditional Ayurvedic medicine, that semen is a finite vital essence whose loss depletes bodily and mental vigour. Sexual guilt, misinformation, and anxiety focus attention on normal physiological phenomena such as nocturnal emission and phosphaturia causing cloudy urine, which are reinterpreted as pathological semen loss. This cognitive misattribution generates a self-perpetuating cycle of somatic symptom amplification and health anxiety. It commonly coexists with, and may serve as a cultural idiom of distress for, underlying depressive and anxiety disorders. With culturally sensitive reassurance, education, and treatment of comorbid depression or anxiety the outlook is generally good, though symptoms may become chronic if misconceptions and comorbidity are not addressed.

Diabetes insipidus — DI, arginine vasopressin deficiency, AVP deficiency (central DI), AVP resistance (nephrogenic DI) Primary (psychogenic or dipsogenic) polydipsia Osmotic diuresis from uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (hyperglycaemia) Diuretic use Hypercalcaemia or hypokalaemia causing acquired nephrogenic DI Chronic kidney disease with impaired concentrating ability Post-obstructive or recovery-phase polyuria Paired serum and urine osmolality with serum sodium 24-hour urine volume to confirm true polyuria Water deprivation test followed by desmopressin challenge Plasma copeptin, ideally with hypertonic saline or arginine stimulation Serum glucose, calcium, and potassium to exclude secondary causes Pituitary and hypothalamic MRI when central DI is confirmed to seek a structural or infiltrative lesion Presents with persistent polyuria and polydipsia, typically with large volumes of dilute (hypotonic) urine and a strong thirst that drives high fluid intake The key distinction is between central DI, from deficient vasopressin secretion, and nephrogenic DI, from renal resistance to vasopressin Primary polydipsia, in which excessive drinking suppresses vasopressin, must be separated from true DI as management differs completely Serum sodium is often high-normal or elevated in true DI, whereas primary polydipsia tends toward low-normal sodium A water deprivation test with subsequent desmopressin assesses urinary concentrating ability and response to exogenous hormone Copeptin measurement, particularly after hypertonic saline stimulation, is increasingly used as a more reliable discriminator Central DI usually responds to desmopressin, whereas nephrogenic DI is managed by treating the underlying cause and supportive measures Where thirst perception is intact and access to water is preserved, patients can defend their sodium; the danger is when thirst or water access is impaired Rapidly rising sodium with altered consciousness from unreplaced free water losses DI arising after pituitary surgery or head injury, which may fluctuate through a triphasic pattern Absent or impaired thirst (adipsic DI) predisposing to dangerous hypernatraemia Loss of a previously present suprasellar lesion signal or new mass suggesting infiltrative or neoplastic disease Confusing osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia with true DI Giving desmopressin to a patient with primary polydipsia and precipitating water intoxication Restricting fluids in a patient who cannot concentrate urine, causing hypernatraemic dehydration Overlooking lithium or hypercalcaemia as reversible causes of nephrogenic DI Diabetes insipidus reflects an inability to concentrate urine appropriately. In central (cranial) DI there is deficient secretion of arginine vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) due to disease of the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary, such as tumours, infiltrative disease, trauma, or surgery. In nephrogenic DI the kidney fails to respond to circulating vasopressin, from inherited receptor or aquaporin defects, drugs such as lithium, hypercalcaemia, or hypokalaemia. In both, the collecting duct cannot reabsorb enough free water, producing large volumes of dilute urine; if water intake cannot keep pace, plasma osmolality and sodium rise. Primary polydipsia is a separate entity in which excessive fluid intake physiologically suppresses vasopressin. Central DI is generally well controlled with vasopressin replacement and normal life expectancy when thirst and water access are intact; nephrogenic DI depends on reversibility of the underlying cause, and adipsic forms carry ongoing risk of severe sodium disturbances.

Diabetes Mellitus — type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, DM Monogenic diabetes / MODY (autosomal dominant, onset usually <25 y, impaired secretion; HNF-4alpha, glucokinase, HNF-1alpha/1beta mutations; glucokinase MODY = mild stable hyperglycemia; HNF-1alpha MODY often responds to sulfonylureas) (p.3195-3196, 3203) Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) - glucose intolerance arising in 2nd/3rd trimester; diabetes in 1st trimester is classified as pre-existing pregestational diabetes (p.3196) Atypical diabetes (features of both type 1 and type 2, not single-gene; includes ketosis-prone diabetes) and latent autoimmune diabetes of adults (5-10% of phenotypic type 2 have GAD/ICA) (p.3196, 3204) Pancreatogenic (type 3c) DM from pancreatitis, pancreatectomy, cystic fibrosis (CF-related diabetes prevalence ~50%), hemochromatosis (p.3203) Endocrinopathy-related hyperglycemia: acromegaly, Cushing's syndrome, glucagonoma, pheochromocytoma, somatostatinoma, hyperthyroidism (p.3196) Drug/chemical-induced diabetes: glucocorticoids, calcineurin/mTOR inhibitors, pentamidine, nicotinic acid, statins, HIV/protease-inhibitor therapy, thiazides, second-generation antipsychotics, immune checkpoint inhibitors (p.3196, 3203) Neonatal diabetes (onset <6 months; ATP-sensitive K+ channel subunit mutations may respond to sulfonylureas) (p.3196, 3203) HbA1c (lab method NGSP-aligned to DCCT reference) for diagnosis and monitoring; affected by hemoglobinopathies and ancestry (p.3196-3197) Fasting plasma glucose and 75-g OGTT (OGTT mainly for pregnancy/GDM and CF-related diabetes screening) (p.3197) Islet cell autoantibodies (GAD, IA-2, ZnT8, insulin) to classify type 1 vs type 2 and identify presymptomatic type 1 DM (p.3200-3201, 3204) C-peptide as a marker of endogenous insulin secretion (distinguishes endogenous vs exogenous insulin) (p.3198) Spot urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) plus estimated GFR annually for nephropathy (screen 5 y after type 1 onset and at type 2 diagnosis); albuminuria = UACR >30 mg/g, severe >300 mg/g (p.3224) Annual dilated retinal exam (or retinal photography) - nondilated primary-care exams are inadequate (p.3224) Annual foot exam with 10-g monofilament, 128-Hz vibration, ankle reflexes, pedal pulses; annual DSPN screening for LOPS (p.3204, 3226) In DKA/HHS: serum/plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate (preferred over nitroprusside which detects acetoacetate), glucose, electrolytes with corrected sodium, anion gap, bicarbonate, BUN/creatinine (p.3216) Stress/illness-related transient hyperglycemia from counterregulatory hormone excess (surgery, infection, critical illness) - hyperglycemia in a hospitalized patient need not indicate established DM (p.3217) Other causes of increased anion-gap acidosis when DKA is suspected: starvation ketosis and alcoholic ketoacidosis (bicarbonate usually >15 meq/L) (p.3216) DM is a group of metabolic disorders sharing the phenotype of hyperglycemia; it is defined as the level of glycemia at which a diabetes-specific complication (e.g., retinopathy) occurs, not as a deviation from a population mean (p.3195, 3197). Diagnostic criteria (any one, confirmed by repeat testing on a different day unless unequivocal hyperglycemia/acute metabolic decompensation): HbA1c >=6.5% (>=48 mmol/mol); fasting plasma glucose (FPG) >=7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL, fasting = no calories >=8 h); 2-h plasma glucose >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) on a 75-g OGTT; or a random plasma glucose >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) PLUS classic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) (p.3197). Prediabetes (each identifies different individuals via different biologic mechanisms): HbA1c 5.7-6.4%; impaired fasting glucose (IFG) FPG 5.6-6.9 mmol/L (100-125 mg/dL) per ADA; impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) 2-h glucose 7.8-11.0 mmol/L (140-199 mg/dL). WHO defines IFG as FPG >6.1 mmol/L (110 mg/dL). All three confer increased risk of type 2 DM and cardiovascular disease (p.3197). Type 1 DM = autoimmune beta cell destruction with insulin deficiency; 25-50% present with DKA; ~40% of new type 1 DM now has onset after age 30 and is often initially misdiagnosed as type 2. Islet cell autoantibodies (ICAs: insulin, GAD, IA-2, ZnT8) are present in >85% at new onset and define a 3-stage model: stage 1 = >=2 autoantibodies + normoglycemia, stage 2 = autoimmunity + dysglycemia, stage 3 = overt hyperglycemia (p.3199-3201). Type 2 DM = heterogeneous: insulin resistance + impaired insulin secretion + increased hepatic glucose production; >=80% of patients are obese (central/visceral). Insulin resistance usually precedes the secretory defect, but diabetes appears only once secretion becomes inadequate for the degree of resistance (p.3195, 3201-3202). Type 2 DM may be asymptomatic for up to a decade before diagnosis, so some patients already have diabetes-specific complications at the time of diagnosis (p.3198, 3221). HbA1c can be misleading with hemoglobinopathies and varies by ancestry; OGTT is reserved mainly for pregnancy/GDM and cystic fibrosis-related diabetes screening, not routine care (p.3197). Symptoms of hyperglycemia: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, fatigue, weakness, blurred vision (lens water-content change, resolves with control), recurrent superficial infections (vaginitis, fungal skin infections), slow wound healing (p.3203). Microvascular complications usually do not appear until the second decade of hyperglycemia; macrovascular (ASCVD) risk, driven by insulin resistance and dyslipidemia, may develop before hyperglycemia is established (p.3221). Distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSPN) is the most common diabetic neuropathy and occurs in ~50% of long-standing DM; up to 50% are asymptomatic, so annual screening for loss of protective sensation (LOPS) is required - LOPS is a major risk factor for foot ulceration and amputation (p.3226). Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): hyperglycemia (glucose >13.9 mmol/L [250 mg/dL]; may be near-normal = euglycemic DKA, especially on SGLT-2 inhibitors), ketosis, anion-gap metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate <15-18 mmol/L); nausea/vomiting, severe abdominal pain (may mimic acute pancreatitis), Kussmaul respirations, fruity breath, volume depletion, lethargy progressing to coma; cerebral edema is a serious complication mainly in children (p.3216) Hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (HHS): older patient, more pronounced dehydration, marked hyperglycemia (often 33.3-66.6 mmol/L [600-1200 mg/dL]) with mental status changes; mortality up to 15% (higher than DKA) (p.3217) Hypoglycemia (<3.0 mmol/L, <54 mg/dL); hypoglycemia unawareness from autonomic neuropathy raises risk of severe events and can prolong QTc - sudden death has been attributed to cardiac autonomic neuropathy (p.3203, 3226) New blindness risk: proliferative retinopathy with neovascularization and vitreous hemorrhage; clinically significant macular edema (p.3222-3223) Loss of protective sensation / foot ulceration predisposing to lower-extremity amputation (p.3226) Silent (painless) myocardial ischemia is common - absence of chest pain does not exclude coronary disease; consider cardiac evaluation before major surgery (p.3228) Do not over-rely on classic features (age of onset, obesity, insulin need) to classify DM - many adult-onset type 1 cases are misdiagnosed as type 2, and many new type 1 patients are now overweight/obese; measure ICAs when type 1 features are present (p.3199, 3204). Euglycemic DKA can occur (notably with SGLT-2 inhibitors) - a near-normal glucose does not exclude DKA; check ketones and acid-base (p.3216). In DKA, hyperamylasemia is usually salivary in origin and does NOT diagnose pancreatitis; obtain serum lipase if pancreatitis is suspected (p.3216). Measured serum sodium is falsely lowered by hyperglycemia (correct ~1.6 mmol/L per 5.6 mmol/L [100 mg/dL] glucose rise); a normal sodium in DKA signals a profound water deficit (p.3216). Serum potassium may be normal or high at DKA presentation despite a large total-body potassium deficit (acidosis/volume depletion shift) (p.3216). Nitroprusside ketone tests detect acetoacetate, not the predominant beta-hydroxybutyrate, and give false positives with captopril, penicillamine, or valproic acid - prefer serum beta-hydroxybutyrate (p.3216). Glycemic control may transiently worsen established retinopathy in the first 6-12 months of improvement, and GLP-1 receptor agonists with marked glycemic improvement have been associated with worsening retinopathy (p.3224). CKD without retinopathy in type 1 DM should prompt a search for an alternative (non-diabetic) cause of kidney disease (p.3224). Very strict glycemic control in acutely/critically ill patients (NICE-SUGAR) increased mortality and severe hypoglycemia - avoid overly tight targets in hospital (p.3217). Hyperglycemia results from reduced insulin secretion, decreased peripheral glucose utilization, and/or increased hepatic glucose production, with the relative contribution depending on the DM type. Insulin is produced by pancreatic beta cells (from preproinsulin -> proinsulin -> insulin + C-peptide); glucose is the key secretagogue: it enters the beta cell via GLUT transporters, glucokinase phosphorylation is rate-limiting, glycolysis generates ATP that closes the ATP-sensitive K+ channel (target of sulfonylureas/meglitinides), causing depolarization, calcium influx, and insulin release; incretins (GLP-1, GIP) amplify glucose-stimulated secretion only when glucose is above fasting. Type 1 DM arises from interacting genetic (HLA region accounts for ~50% of risk; DR3-DQ2 and DR4-DQ8 predisposing), environmental, and immunologic factors leading to CD8+ T cell-mediated beta cell destruction and absolute insulin deficiency; alpha-cell dysfunction adds fasting/postprandial hyperglucagonemia with impaired glucagon response to hypoglycemia. Type 2 DM combines impaired insulin secretion, insulin resistance (post-receptor defects in skeletal muscle, liver, fat; lipid intermediate accumulation; low-grade metabolic inflammation), excessive hepatic glucose production (failure to suppress gluconeogenesis), abnormal fat metabolism (increased free fatty acids, altered adipokines, reduced adiponectin), giving the characteristic dyslipidemia (high triglycerides, low HDL, small dense LDL); beta cell function is reduced ~50% at onset and declines progressively. Complications stem from chronic hyperglycemia driving advanced glycosylation end products (AGEs), increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, epigenetic changes ("metabolic memory"), and growth factors such as VEGF-A in proliferative retinopathy. DM is a major cause of mortality (8th leading cause of death in the US, 2021; likely underreported) and was responsible for ~6.7 million deaths worldwide in 2021 (12.2% of global all-cause mortality in adults 20-79); about one-third of diabetes-related deaths occur before age 60. Cardiovascular disease is the main cause of morbidity and mortality, with ASCVD events and mortality 2-4 times greater in type 2 DM. In the US, DM is the leading cause of end-stage renal disease, nontraumatic lower-extremity amputation, and adult blindness; ~20-40% of patients develop diabetic nephropathy. Intensive glycemic control has durable benefit ("metabolic memory"/legacy effect lasting >=10 years): DCCT/EDIC showed reductions in retinopathy (47%), albuminuria (39%), clinical nephropathy (54%), neuropathy (60%), later a 57% reduction in cardiovascular events and 33% reduction in mortality; UKPDS showed each 1% HbA1c reduction lowered microvascular complications by 35%, and blood pressure control reduced complications even more than glycemic control. Diagnosis at younger age worsens prognosis (~3-4 years of reduced life expectancy per decade of earlier diagnosis). Glucose homeostasis is a spectrum: normal -> impaired (IFG/IGT/HbA1c 5.7-6.4%, i.e., prediabetes) -> diabetes mellitus. DKA severity by ADA: mild (pH 7.25-7.30, bicarbonate 15-18 meq/L, normal mental status), moderate (pH 7.0-7.25, bicarbonate 10-15 meq/L, mildly reduced mental status), severe (pH <7.0). Diabetic retinopathy: nonproliferative (microaneurysms, blot hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots) vs proliferative (neovascularization) +/- clinically significant macular edema. Albuminuria: moderately increased UACR 30-299 mg/g vs severely increased >300 mg/g creatinine. Neuropathy categories: distal symmetric polyneuropathy, autonomic neuropathy, mononeuropathy, and radiculopathy/polyradiculopathy.

Diabetes Mellitus: Complications — Diabetic complications, Microvascular and macrovascular complications of diabetes, Diabetic retinopathy, Diabetic nephropathy, Diabetic neuropathy, Diabetic foot Diabetic neuropathy is a diagnosis of exclusion - confirm only after excluding other neuropathy causes (e.g., B12/folate deficiency, alcohol, other metabolic/toxic neuropathies) Chronic kidney disease without retinopathy in type 1 diabetes should prompt investigation for an alternative (non-diabetic) cause of renal disease Type IV renal tubular acidosis (hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism) as a cause of hyperkalemia/acidemia in diabetic patients Renovascular hypertension when blood pressure is not readily controlled in type 2 diabetes Celiac disease in type 1 diabetes presenting with diarrhea/constipation (associated anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies) Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease, possibly autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome) in type 1 diabetes with orthostatic hypotension Gas gangrene appearance in a diabetic foot may develop in the absence of clostridial infection Superficial culture of any foot ulcer yields multiple bacterial species of uncertain significance - infected ulcer is a clinical diagnosis, not a culture diagnosis Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common with diabetic cystopathy and generally does not require treatment Dilated retinal examination by optometrist/ophthalmologist or retinal photography with remote reading (nondilated primary-care exams are inadequate); fluorescein angiography and optical coherence tomography to detect macular edema Spot urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) plus estimated GFR, screening annually (start 5 years after type 1 diagnosis, at diagnosis for type 2) Annual neuropathy screening with 10-g monofilament and vibration testing to detect loss of protective sensation; begin 5 years after type 1 diagnosis and at diagnosis of type 2 Gastric scintigraphy after a radiolabeled meal to document delayed gastric emptying (may not correlate with symptoms) in suspected gastroparesis Ankle-brachial index for screening asymptomatic PAD in diabetic patients over 50 with risk factors Foot ulcer workup: probe-to-bone testing with a blunt sterile instrument, plain radiographs for osteomyelitis in chronic non-healing ulcers, MRI (most specific) with nuclear/labeled-WBC studies as alternatives; cultures from debrided ulcer base or purulent aspirate Cardiac stress testing in diabetic patients with symptoms (even atypical) suggestive of ischemia (routine screening of asymptomatic patients is not recommended) Transient worsening of established retinopathy during the first 6-12 months of improved glycemic control (and with GLP-1 receptor agonist-associated rapid glycemic improvement) can mimic disease progression but is temporary UACR can be falsely elevated by strenuous exercise, fever, infection, congestive heart failure, marked hyperglycemia, marked hypertension, or prostate disease - confirm on 2-3 occasions over 3-6 months Acute painful diabetic neuropathy may be treatment-related, triggered by improved glycemic control Diabetes-related complications are split into vascular (microvascular: retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy; macrovascular: coronary heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, cerebrovascular disease, heart failure) and nonvascular (infections, dermatologic changes, cheiroarthropathy, hearing loss, cataracts, glaucoma, fractures, cognitive impairment); patterns are similar in type 1 and type 2 disease. Microvascular complications generally do not become evident until the second decade of hyperglycemia, whereas atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk (driven by insulin resistance and dyslipidemia) may precede frank hyperglycemia, so type 2 patients often have complications already present at diagnosis. Landmark trials established that chronic hyperglycemia is causative for microvascular disease: in the DCCT, intensive control (HbA1c 7.3% vs 9.1%) reduced retinopathy ~47%, albuminuria ~39%, clinical nephropathy ~54%, and neuropathy ~60%; the UKPDS showed each 1-percentage-point HbA1c reduction lowered microvascular complications by about 35%. A 'metabolic memory' / legacy effect exists: a period of improved glycemic control yields reduced cardiovascular events and mortality more than a decade later even after glycemic separation between groups disappears (DCCT/EDIC showed ~57% fewer cardiovascular events and ~33% lower mortality long term). Diabetic retinopathy is staged as nonproliferative (microaneurysms, blot hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, venous caliber change, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities) and proliferative (neovascularization from retinal hypoxemia, risking vitreous hemorrhage and traction retinal detachment); neovascularization is the hallmark of the proliferative stage. Macular edema can occur at either retinopathy stage and is a key cause of moderate vision loss; duration of diabetes and degree of glycemic control are the strongest predictors of retinopathy, with hypertension, nephropathy, and dyslipidemia as additional risk factors. Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease and stage 5 CKD; screening combines a spot urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) and estimated GFR because some patients lose GFR without albuminuria. Albuminuria is a persistently increased UACR >30 mg/g (moderate 30-299 mg/g, severe >300 mg/g). Diabetic neuropathy affects roughly half of long-standing patients and includes distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSPN), autonomic neuropathy, and mononeuropathy/radiculopathy; up to 50% of those with DSPN are asymptomatic, so screening for loss of protective sensation (10-g monofilament, vibration) is essential. Cardiovascular disease (CHD, PAD, cerebrovascular disease, heart failure) is the major cause of death in diabetes; heart failure is about twice as common (HFpEF, HFmrEF, or HFrEF) and 'silent ischemia' with absent chest pain is frequent, warranting a cardiac evaluation before major surgery. Diabetes is the leading cause of nontraumatic lower-extremity amputation; foot ulcers arise from the interaction of neuropathy, abnormal biomechanics, peripheral arterial disease, and poor wound healing, and a wound that probes to bone is highly likely to harbor osteomyelitis. Patients have greater frequency and severity of infections; certain severe infections occur almost exclusively in diabetes: rhinocerebral mucormycosis, emphysematous cholecystitis/pyelonephritis/cystitis, and malignant (invasive) otitis externa (usually Pseudomonas aeruginosa). Characteristic dermatologic findings include xerosis/pruritus, diabetic dermopathy (pigmented pretibial papules), bullosis diabeticorum, necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum (predominantly young women), acanthosis nigricans (severe insulin resistance), and vitiligo/alopecia areata in type 1 disease. Neovascularization, vitreous hemorrhage, or traction involving the macula - urgent panretinal laser photocoagulation and/or anti-VEGF; surgical vitrectomy for severe proliferative disease with vitreous hemorrhage Foot wound that probes to bone (high likelihood of osteomyelitis) or rapidly spreading cellulitis/severe infection requiring IV broad-spectrum coverage and possible surgical debridement Severe infections seen largely in diabetes: rhinocerebral mucormycosis, malignant (invasive) otitis externa progressing to osteomyelitis/meningitis, emphysematous pyelonephritis/cystitis/cholecystitis - consider especially with severe hyperglycemia Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy with resting tachycardia, reduced heart-rate variability, orthostatic hypotension, and QTc prolongation - associated with silent ischemia and reports of sudden death Hypoglycemia unawareness from autonomic neuropathy/reduced counterregulation, increasing the risk of severe hypoglycemia Hyperkalemia/acidemia from type IV RTA, potentially exacerbated by ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists Risk of radiocontrast-induced nephrotoxicity (preexisting nephropathy, volume depletion) Routine urinalysis does not detect low-level albuminuria - use UACR; and some patients lose GFR without albuminuria, so always assess both eGFR and UACR Nondilated eye exams by primary providers miss diabetic eye disease - a dilated/photographic retinal exam is required Once advanced retinopathy or moderate albuminuria is established, improving glycemic control provides less benefit - early detection is critical Diagnosing diabetic neuropathy without excluding other etiologies; metformin can lower vitamin B12 and pernicious anemia is more common in type 1 disease Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria unnecessarily; basing diabetic foot infection diagnosis on superficial swab cultures rather than clinical judgment and deep cultures Failure to hold metformin around iodinated contrast and to monitor creatinine 24-48 h afterward; failing to reassess glucose-lowering drug choice/dose as GFR falls (sulfonylureas and metformin contraindicated in advanced renal insufficiency; SGLT-2 inhibitors ineffective below eGFR 20) Overlooking silent ischemia given frequent absence of chest pain, and failing to evaluate before major surgery Chronic hyperglycemia is the principal etiologic driver of microvascular complications, though the precise mechanisms remain incompletely defined and are likely multifactorial. Proposed pathways include hyperglycemia-induced epigenetic changes altering gene expression, formation of advanced glycosylation end products (e.g., pentosidine, glucosepane, carboxymethyllysine) that cross-link proteins and bind cell-surface receptors causing endothelial and glomerular dysfunction and accelerated atherosclerosis, local growth-factor effects (VEGF-A drives proliferative retinopathy), and a unifying hypothesis that hyperglycemia raises mitochondrial reactive oxygen species/superoxide that activate downstream injury pathways. In nephropathy, soluble mediators (angiotensin II, endothelin, AGEs), hemodynamic alterations (glomerular hyperfiltration, increased capillary pressure), and structural changes (basement-membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, fibrosis) lead from early hyperfiltration/renal hypertrophy to irreversible albuminuria and GFR decline. Macrovascular disease additionally reflects insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and inflammation, with insulin failing to suppress adipose lipolysis and causing ectopic lipid accumulation (triglycerides, diacylglycerol, ceramides). In neuropathy both myelinated and unmyelinated fibers are lost; foot ulceration arises from sensory loss removing protective mechanisms, autonomic anhidrosis causing dry/fissured skin, motor changes producing deformity, and PAD impairing healing. Complications account for most diabetes-related morbidity and mortality. Diagnosis at a younger age increases lifetime complication burden (one estimate: 3-4 fewer years of life expectancy per decade of earlier diagnosis). Intensive glycemic control substantially improves outcomes: DCCT projections estimated several additional years free of vision loss, end-stage renal disease, and amputation, with overall added life expectancy, and 30-year follow-up showed durable reductions in retinopathy, nephropathy, and cardiovascular events (legacy/metabolic-memory effect). About 20-40% of patients develop diabetic nephropathy, and CKD on dialysis carries a poor prognosis. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death and outcomes after CHD are worse than in nondiabetic patients; CHD tends to involve multiple vessels and revascularization (PCI/CABG) is less durable, though CABG plus optimal medical therapy generally outperforms PCI. Diabetic polyradiculopathies (including amyotrophy) are usually self-limited, resolving over 6-12 months. Foot ulcers carry a substantial amputation risk (about 14-24% with that or subsequent ulceration). Some patients never develop retinopathy or nephropathy despite long-standing disease, suggesting genetic protection. Retinopathy: nonproliferative (mild to severe, with microaneurysms, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, venous beading, IRMA) versus proliferative (neovascularization), with clinically significant macular edema as a separate sight-threatening category. Albuminuria/CKD: UACR normal (<30 mg/g), moderately increased (30-299 mg/g), severely increased (>300 mg/g), staged alongside eGFR; nephrology referral when eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2, UACR >300 mg/g, or atypical features (hematuria, rapid decline). Diabetic neuropathy categorized as diffuse (distal symmetric polyneuropathy and/or autonomic), focal mononeuropathy, or radiculopathy/polyradiculopathy. Foot infection severity stratified clinically from mild/non-limb-threatening (oral antibiotics) to severe (IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, offloading, debridement).

Diabetes Mellitus: Management and Therapies — DM management, comprehensive diabetes care, diabetic ketoacidosis, DKA, hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state, HHS, euglycemic DKA Starvation ketosis (bicarbonate typically preserved) Alcoholic ketoacidosis (bicarbonate usually >15 meq/L) Other causes of high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis Acute pancreatitis or surgical abdomen (DKA abdominal pain can mimic these; hyperamylasemia in DKA is usually salivary, so serum lipase is needed) Lactic acidosis (a small anion-gap acidosis from lactate can accompany HHS) HbA1c at initial evaluation and at least twice yearly when at goal, every 3 months when control is inadequate or therapy changed (interpret with caution in hemoglobinopathies, anemias, reticulocytosis, transfusion, uremia, G6PD variants, hemodialysis, erythropoietin or HIV therapy) Continuous glucose monitoring or capillary blood glucose monitoring for short-term control and time-in-range Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate (preferred over urine nitroprusside ketone assays) Serum electrolytes with anion gap, potassium, phosphate and magnesium (every 4 h in early DKA), bicarbonate, arterial pH Serum/plasma glucose every 1-2 h during acute crises BUN and creatinine (intravascular volume depletion / prerenal azotemia), serum osmolality Serum lipase if pancreatitis suspected (amylase in DKA is often salivary and nondiagnostic) Workup for precipitant: cultures, chest x-ray, ECG; corrected sodium calculation Fructosamine or glycated albumin as alternative measures reflecting glycemia over the prior 2-4 weeks Acute pancreatitis / acute surgical abdomen presenting with abdominal pain mimicking DKA Other high-anion-gap metabolic acidoses (starvation, alcohol, toxins) Alternative causes of altered mental status or coma (stroke, hypoxemia, intoxication) overlapping with severe DKA/HHS presentation The three overarching goals of diabetes care are to relieve hyperglycemic symptoms, reduce or prevent long-term microvascular and macrovascular complications, and allow as normal a lifestyle as possible; symptoms usually resolve once plasma glucose is below ~200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L), so therapy mainly targets complication prevention. (Harrison 22e p.3205) HbA1c reflects average glycemia over the prior 2-3 months because erythrocytes live ~120 days, with the most recent month contributing roughly half the value; it does not capture short-term variability or recent intercurrent illness the way continuous (CGM) or fingerstick (BGM) monitoring does. (Harrison 22e p.3207-3208) Continuous glucose monitoring measures interstitial glucose, which is in equilibrium with blood glucose but can lag when glucose changes rapidly or during exercise; an ambulatory glucose profile summarizes time-in-range, time above/below target, the glucose management indicator (correlating with HbA1c), and glucose variability. (Harrison 22e p.3207) The general HbA1c goal is below 7% (or <=6.5% for selected patients), but a more lenient target of <7.5-8% is appropriate for those with cognitive impairment, hypoglycemia unawareness, or limited life expectancy; about one in four people over 65 has diabetes, so elderly targets must be individualized. (Harrison 22e p.3208) A consensus CGM time-in-range goal for most patients with type 1 or type 2 DM is >70% of time within 70-180 mg/dL (3.9-10.0 mmol/L), with <4% below 70 mg/dL and <1% below 54 mg/dL. (Harrison 22e p.3208) Ketones (preferably blood beta-hydroxybutyrate rather than urine nitroprusside assays, which detect only acetoacetate and acetone) should be checked in type 1 DM whenever plasma glucose persistently exceeds 250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L) or during intercurrent illness with nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. (Harrison 22e p.3216) DKA arises mostly in type 1 DM and HHS mostly in type 2 DM, but the two exist along a continuum of hyperglycemia and up to one-third of patients show features of both. (Harrison 22e p.3216) Ketosis-prone diabetes can present with DKA at diagnosis in obese young adults of Hispanic or African descent who later recover insulin secretory capacity and can discontinue insulin after weeks to months. (Harrison 22e p.3216) SGLT-2 inhibitor therapy can precipitate euglycemic DKA in type 2 DM, where glucose is normal or only mildly elevated because of glucosuria, so a normal glucose does not exclude ketoacidosis; resolution should be tracked by bicarbonate correction rather than by glucose. (Harrison 22e p.3216-3217) In DKA the measured serum sodium is artifactually low; the correction adds ~1.6 mmol/L of sodium for each 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) rise in glucose, and a normal measured sodium in DKA signals a profound free-water deficit. (Harrison 22e p.3217) Inpatient hyperglycemia predicts worse outcomes, yet very strict glycemic control in the critically ill worsens outcomes; the NICE-SUGAR trial showed higher mortality and more severe hypoglycemia with a target of 81-108 mg/dL versus a moderate goal of <180 mg/dL, supporting a hospital target of roughly 140-180 mg/dL. (Harrison 22e p.3219) Sliding-scale insulin alone (reactive treatment only when glucose is already high) is inadequate for inpatient management; scheduled basal plus prandial and corrective dosing is preferred, and CGM/automated insulin delivery are not FDA approved for ICU use. (Harrison 22e p.3219-3220) Nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain in a person with type 1 DM (warrants immediate evaluation for DKA) Kussmaul respirations and a fruity (acetone) breath odor Lethargy progressing to obtundation or coma; cerebral edema (especially in children during DKA resolution) Hypotension and tachycardia from volume depletion Plasma glucose persistently >250 mg/dL or, in HHS, markedly elevated (>1000 mg/dL) with hyperosmolality (>300 mOsm) Normal measured serum sodium during DKA (indicates profound water deficit) Hypoglycemia, particularly recurrent, nocturnal, or with hypoglycemia unawareness Signs of a precipitating event (infection, myocardial infarction, stroke, pancreatitis) even without fever Assuming a normal or only mildly elevated glucose excludes ketoacidosis; euglycemic DKA occurs with SGLT-2 inhibitors and resolution must be judged by bicarbonate, not glucose Relying on urine nitroprusside ketone tests, which miss beta-hydroxybutyrate (the dominant ketone) and give false positives with captopril, penicillamine, or valproic acid Interpreting hyperamylasemia in DKA as pancreatitis when it is usually salivary in origin; obtain lipase Failing to correct serum sodium for hyperglycemia, masking a true free-water deficit Misreading the early/at-presentation serum potassium as adequate; total-body potassium is depleted despite a normal or high initial level, and hypokalemia develops during insulin/fluid therapy Trusting HbA1c in conditions that alter red-cell turnover (hemoglobinopathy, anemia, reticulocytosis, transfusion, uremia, dialysis, erythropoietin or HIV therapy) Using sliding-scale insulin alone for inpatients, which is inadequate Applying overly strict inpatient glucose targets, which increases severe hypoglycemia and can worsen outcomes (NICE-SUGAR) Substances interfering with glucose sensors/meters (e.g., acetaminophen, ascorbic acid, hydroxyurea, mannitol/sorbitol for CGM; uric acid, galactose, xylose, L-DOPA for BGM) Hyperglycemia in diabetes reflects relative or absolute insulin deficiency with impaired glucose utilization and unrestrained hepatic glucose production. In acute decompensation, severe hyperglycemia drives osmotic diuresis with volume depletion. DKA results from relative or absolute insulin deficiency combined with excess counterregulatory hormones (glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, growth hormone); the low insulin-to-glucagon ratio promotes hepatic gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, and ketone body formation, while increased lipolysis releases free fatty acids that are shifted toward ketogenesis, producing ketonemia and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Inflammatory markers (cytokines, C-reactive protein) are elevated in both DKA and HHS. HHS is caused by relative (less severe) insulin deficiency plus inadequate fluid intake; insulin deficiency raises hepatic glucose output and impairs muscle uptake, and osmotic diuresis with poor fluid replacement produces extreme hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and dehydration. The absence of significant ketosis in HHS is incompletely understood but is attributed to only partial insulin deficiency, lower counterregulatory hormone and free-fatty-acid levels, and an insulin/glucagon balance that does not favor ketogenesis. During exercise or acute illness, surges in counterregulatory hormones and cytokines cause transient insulin resistance and can tip toward hyperglycemia or, with relative hyperinsulinemia, hypoglycemia. With appropriate therapy, DKA mortality is low (<1%) and relates more to the underlying or precipitating event (infection/pneumonia, COVID-19, pregnancy, end-stage renal disease, myocardial infarction) than to the metabolic derangement itself; venous thrombosis, upper GI bleeding, ARDS, and cerebral edema (chiefly in children, during resolution) can complicate the course. Even a single DKA episode carries a substantially increased 1-year mortality, and recurrent DKA may signal underlying mental health issues or barriers to care such as insulin cost. HHS carries a substantially higher mortality (up to ~15% in some series) because patients are typically older with serious precipitating illness and comorbidities. Improved glycemic control reduces microvascular complications regardless of baseline level, and early intensive control in type 1 DM (DCCT/EDIC) lowered later cardiovascular events nearly two decades on. DKA severity is graded by pH, serum bicarbonate, and mental status: mild (pH 7.25-7.30, bicarbonate 15-18 meq/L, normal mentation); moderate (pH 7.0-7.25, bicarbonate 10-15 meq/L, mildly reduced mentation); severe (pH <7.0, bicarbonate <10-15 meq/L, reduced mental status or coma). Representative presenting laboratory ranges: DKA glucose ~250-600 mg/dL with bicarbonate <18 meq/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate >3.0 mmol/L, and elevated anion gap; HHS glucose ~600-1200 mg/dL (may exceed 1000) with osmolality >300, bicarbonate >18, pH >7.3, and absent/minimal ketones; euglycemic DKA glucose ~100-250 mg/dL with bicarbonate <18 and beta-hydroxybutyrate >3.0.

glycaemic control, vascular assessment, and antibiotics targeted to severity and likely organisms Deep abscess, extensive necrosis, or gas-forming infection requires urgent surgical drainage or debridement Deep abscess, extensive necrosis, or gas in tissues requiring urgent surgical drainage or debridement Rapidly spreading infection with systemic toxicity indicating limb- or life-threatening sepsis Critical limb ischaemia threatening tissue viability and demanding urgent vascular input Probing to bone or radiographic bone destruction suggesting osteomyelitis Treating on the basis of a superficial swab that reflects colonisation rather than a deep specimen Overlooking peripheral arterial disease that undermines healing and antibiotic delivery Missing underlying osteomyelitis and treating for too short a duration Neglecting offloading and debridement while relying on antibiotics alone Diabetic foot infection develops when skin integrity is breached, usually over a pressure point, in a foot compromised by sensory neuropathy (loss of protective sensation), motor and autonomic dysfunction (deformity and dry, fissured skin), and often peripheral arterial disease. Impaired neutrophil function and microvascular disease blunt the immune response and reduce tissue perfusion, allowing colonising skin flora to invade soft tissue, tendon sheaths, and bone. Infection can spread rapidly along fascial and tendon planes, producing deep abscesses and osteomyelitis. Outcomes depend on infection severity, adequacy of perfusion, and glycaemic control; mild soft-tissue infection often resolves, whereas deep infection with ischaemia or osteomyelitis carries a substantial risk of amputation and is associated with reduced long-term survival.

Diabetic foot ulcer — diabetic foot wound, diabetic foot lesion, diabetic plantar ulcer Neuropathic ulcer from a non-diabetic cause Arterial (ischaemic) ulcer Venous leg ulcer Charcot neuroarthropathy with ulceration Osteomyelitis Acute gout or another inflammatory foot lesion Malignant ulcer such as a Marjolin ulcer Structured foot assessment with a monofilament and palpation of pulses Ankle-brachial and toe pressures with arterial duplex Plain radiograph and MRI for osteomyelitis or Charcot changes Deep tissue or bone culture rather than a superficial swab to guide antibiotics Inflammatory markers and glycaemic assessment including glucose and glycated haemoglobin Blood cultures if the patient is systemically unwell Diabetic foot ulcers arise from the interplay of peripheral neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease and susceptibility to infection, and are a leading cause of non-traumatic lower-limb amputation Ulcers are broadly neuropathic, ischaemic or mixed neuroischaemic; neuropathic ulcers form at plantar pressure points with surrounding callus, whereas ischaemic ulcers affect the margins, toes and heel Loss of protective sensation, foot deformity, high plantar pressures, callus and previous ulceration or amputation are major risk factors, and structured screening stratifies future risk Infection is a clinical diagnosis and may be limb- and life-threatening; deep infection, abscess and osteomyelitis are common and their usual signs can be muted by neuropathy and ischaemia The ability to probe to bone, or a large or long-standing ulcer, raises the likelihood of osteomyelitis, and imaging with plain film then MRI, and where needed bone biopsy, helps confirm it Assessment must include perfusion through pulses, ankle-brachial and toe pressures and duplex, as ischaemia impairs healing and mandates vascular assessment for revascularisation Management is delivered by a multidisciplinary diabetic foot team and combines offloading, debridement, infection control with appropriate antibiotics, revascularisation where indicated, glycaemic optimisation and wound care Prevention through education, regular podiatry, appropriate footwear and prompt presentation is central to reducing recurrence and amputation Spreading cellulitis, abscess, wet gangrene or systemic sepsis Suspected osteomyelitis with the ability to probe to bone or a chronic non-healing ulcer Critical limb ischaemia with rest pain, dependent rubor or gangrene A rapidly deteriorating foot An unexplained warm, swollen foot suggesting Charcot neuroarthropathy Relying on superficial swabs rather than deep tissue or bone samples Missing underlying osteomyelitis or significant ischaemia Underestimating infection because neuropathy and ischaemia mask the usual signs Providing inadequate offloading, or delaying vascular or surgical referral Over-relying on an ankle-brachial index that may be falsely elevated in calcified vessels Chronic hyperglycaemia drives peripheral neuropathy affecting sensory, motor and autonomic fibres and accelerates atherosclerosis of the leg and foot arteries. Sensory loss removes protective pain, motor neuropathy deforms the foot and concentrates pressure on prominences, and autonomic dysfunction produces dry, fissured skin and arteriovenous shunting. Superimposed arterial disease reduces perfusion and healing capacity. In this setting minor trauma at high-pressure sites goes unnoticed and fails to heal, while impaired neutrophil function and the metabolic effects of hyperglycaemia predispose to rapidly spreading soft-tissue and bone infection, so a superficial ulcer can progress swiftly to a limb-threatening problem. Outcomes vary with ulcer depth, infection and ischaemia; many ulcers heal with prompt multidisciplinary care, but recurrence is frequent and an infected, ischaemic ulcer carries a high risk of amputation and mortality.

Diabetic kidney disease — DKD, diabetic nephropathy, diabetic glomerulosclerosis Hypertensive nephrosclerosis Primary or secondary glomerulonephritis Ischaemic nephropathy from renovascular disease Membranous nephropathy Obstructive uropathy Other causes of chronic kidney disease coexisting with diabetes Quantification of albuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio) and serial estimated GFR Urinalysis with microscopy to detect an active sediment suggesting an alternative diagnosis Fundoscopy to assess for diabetic retinopathy Blood pressure assessment and cardiovascular risk evaluation Renal ultrasound to assess kidney size and exclude obstruction Consideration of biopsy when the clinical picture is atypical for diabetic disease Diabetic kidney disease is the leading cause of end-stage kidney disease worldwide and develops in a substantial proportion of people with long-standing type 1 or type 2 diabetes The classic course progresses from glomerular hyperfiltration through rising albuminuria to declining glomerular filtration, though not every patient follows this sequence Persistent albuminuria is both an early marker of kidney involvement and an independent predictor of cardiovascular risk Coexisting diabetic retinopathy supports the diagnosis, and its absence in type 1 diabetes should prompt consideration of a non-diabetic cause Features that argue against pure diabetic disease include an active urinary sediment, rapid loss of function, heavy proteinuria without retinopathy, or a short duration of diabetes Control of blood pressure, glycaemia, and albuminuria, together with blockade of the renin-angiotensin system, are the mainstays of slowing progression Newer agents that reduce intraglomerular pressure and albuminuria have been shown to slow decline and reduce cardiovascular events, changing modern management principles Regular screening with albuminuria measurement and estimated GFR allows early intervention before irreversible damage accumulates Rapid decline in renal function suggesting a superimposed or alternative process Nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema Active urinary sediment or haematuria pointing to glomerulonephritis Refractory hypertension or hyperkalaemia complicating renin-angiotensin blockade Assuming all kidney disease in a diabetic patient is diabetic nephropathy and missing a treatable alternative Neglecting albuminuria screening so that intervention starts only after significant function is lost Failing to intensify renin-angiotensin blockade and other kidney-protective therapy in albuminuric patients Overlooking the high cardiovascular risk that accompanies diabetic kidney disease Diabetic kidney disease develops from chronic hyperglycaemia acting through several interlinked pathways. Excess glucose drives formation of advanced glycation end products, activation of protein kinase C, and oxidative stress, which damage the glomerular filtration barrier. Early on, altered afferent and efferent arteriolar tone produces glomerular hypertension and hyperfiltration, increasing shear stress on the capillary wall. Over time the glomerular basement membrane thickens, the mesangium expands with accumulation of matrix, and podocytes are lost, culminating in the nodular and diffuse glomerulosclerosis characteristic of the disease. These changes progressively increase albumin leakage and reduce filtration surface area. Systemic and intraglomerular hypertension, along with tubulointerstitial fibrosis, accelerates the decline toward end-stage kidney disease. Without intervention, diabetic kidney disease tends to progress steadily to end-stage kidney disease, and it markedly increases cardiovascular mortality. Intensive control of glycaemia and blood pressure, renin-angiotensin blockade, reduction of albuminuria, and modern kidney-protective therapies can substantially slow decline and reduce cardiovascular events, so early detection and comprehensive risk-factor management materially improve outcomes.

uraemia or fluid overload requiring renal replacement planning Assuming all renal impairment in a diabetic patient is diabetic nephropathy and missing a treatable alternative Failing to screen for dominant cause of death in these patients Sustained hyperglycaemia and glomerular hypertension drive haemodynamic and metabolic injury to the kidney. Early glomerular hyperfiltration, mesangial expansion, glomerular basement membrane thickening, and podocyte injury progress to nodular and diffuse glomerulosclerosis, the nodular lesions being the classic Kimmelstiel-Wilson change. Advanced glycation end-products, oxidative stress, and activation of the renin-angiotensin system promote albuminuria, tubulointerstitial fibrosis, and progressive loss of filtration. Without intervention diabetic nephropathy progresses to end-stage renal disease and carries a high cardiovascular mortality, but early detection and aggressive control of glucose and blood pressure, renin-angiotensin blockade, and SGLT2 inhibition can substantially slow progression.

sensorimotor polyneuropathy that begins in the feet and progresses proximally in a stocking-and-glove distribution Sensory loss predisposes to unnoticed foot injury, ulceration, and Charcot arthropathy, making regular foot examination essential Painful neuropathy can coexist with sensory loss, causing burning, tingling, and allodynia that are often worse at night Autonomic involvement can produce postural hypotension, resting tachycardia, gastroparesis, bladder dysfunction, and erectile dysfunction It is a diagnosis of exclusion, so other causes of neuropathy such as vitamin B12 deficiency, alcohol, uraemia, and hypothyroidism should be considered Optimised glycaemic control is central to prevention and slowing progression, particularly in type 1 diabetes Management of painful neuropathy relies on agents active in neuropathic pain rather than simple analgesics, alongside foot protection strategies Foot ulceration, deformity, or signs of Charcot arthropathy Rapidly progressive, asymmetric, or predominantly motor deficits suggesting an alternative diagnosis Severe autonomic features such as symptomatic postural hypotension or gastroparesis Signs of limb ischaemia or infection complicating a neuropathic foot Attributing all neuropathy to diabetes without excluding treatable alternative causes Neglecting routine foot inspection and patient education, allowing preventable ulcers Undertreating painful neuropathy or relying on ineffective simple analgesics Missing autonomic neuropathy as the cause of unexplained postural symptoms or gastrointestinal complaints Chronic hyperglycaemia damages peripheral nerves through several linked mechanisms, including accumulation of advanced glycation end-products, activation of the polyol and protein kinase C pathways, oxidative stress, and microvascular ischaemia of the vasa nervorum. These processes injure axons and Schwann cells, producing a length-dependent loss of both small and large fibres. Involvement of autonomic fibres disrupts cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary regulation, while focal ischaemia or entrapment can cause mononeuropathies and radiculopathies. Neuropathy tends to progress with duration and poor control of diabetes, and established nerve damage is largely irreversible, so the emphasis is on prevention of ulceration and amputation and on symptom control; autonomic neuropathy carries an adverse cardiovascular prognosis.

tomography to detect and quantify macular oedema Fluorescein angiography to map ischaemia and neovascularisation Visual acuity assessment Systemic review of HbA1c, blood pressure, lipids, and renal function A leading cause of blindness in working-age adults and directly related to duration of diabetes and quality of glycaemic control Early (non-proliferative) disease is usually asymptomatic, underscoring the value of regular screening fundus photography Non-proliferative signs include microaneurysms, dot-and-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots, and venous beading Proliferative disease is defined by neovascularisation of the disc or retina, which risks vitreous haemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment Diabetic maculopathy (macular oedema) is the commonest cause of visual loss and can occur at any stage Anti-VEGF intravitreal therapy is first-line for centre-involving macular oedema, while panretinal laser photocoagulation is used for proliferative disease Blood pressure, lipid, and glycaemic control materially slow progression alongside ophthalmic treatment Sudden visual loss or floaters suggesting vitreous haemorrhage New vessels on the disc or elsewhere indicating sight-threatening proliferative disease Centre-involving macular oedema threatening central vision Rubeosis iridis (iris new vessels) heralding neovascular glaucoma Assuming good vision means no retinopathy and skipping screening Missing macular oedema that requires OCT rather than fundoscopy alone to detect Rapid tightening of glycaemic control causing transient worsening of retinopathy Overlooking pregnancy as an accelerator of progression Chronic hyperglycaemia damages retinal capillaries through pathways including accumulation of advanced glycation end-products, oxidative stress, and pericyte loss. This weakens vessel walls (forming microaneurysms), increases permeability (causing exudation and macular oedema), and causes capillary occlusion leading to retinal ischaemia. Ischaemic retina releases vascular endothelial growth factor and other mediators that drive pathological new-vessel formation; these fragile vessels bleed and contract, producing vitreous haemorrhage and tractional detachment in advanced proliferative disease. With timely screening, good systemic control, and prompt laser or anti-VEGF treatment, most severe visual loss is preventable; neglected proliferative disease and macular oedema carry a high risk of blindness.

Diamond-Blackfan anaemia — DBA, congenital hypoplastic anaemia, RPS19, pure red cell aplasia of infancy Transient erythroblastopenia of childhood Parvovirus B19-associated red cell aplasia Pearson marrow-pancreas syndrome Fanconi anaemia and other inherited marrow-failure syndromes Acquired pure red cell aplasia Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemias Full blood count and reticulocyte count showing macrocytic anaemia with reticulocytopenia Bone marrow examination demonstrating erythroid hypoplasia Erythrocyte adenosine deaminase activity Fetal haemoglobin measurement Molecular genetic testing of ribosomal protein genes Assessment for congenital anomalies with echocardiography, renal imaging and limb radiographs Inherited ribosomopathy causing a congenital pure red cell aplasia, frequently caused by variants in ribosomal protein genes such as RPS19 Typically presents in the first year of life with severe macrocytic anaemia, reticulocytopenia and a normal white cell and platelet count Bone marrow shows a selective paucity of erythroid precursors with otherwise normal cellularity Around half of patients have congenital anomalies, including craniofacial (Cathie facies), thumb (triphalangeal or duplicated), cardiac and genitourinary defects, and short stature Raised erythrocyte adenosine deaminase activity and elevated fetal haemoglobin support the diagnosis Corticosteroids induce a response in many patients; others become dependent on long-term red cell transfusion with attendant iron overload There is an increased risk of myelodysplastic syndrome, acute leukaemia and solid tumours over a lifetime Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can cure the haematological disease and is used for transfusion dependence or clonal progression Evolving neutropenia or thrombocytopenia suggesting progression to marrow failure or myelodysplasia Clonal cytogenetic change or blasts indicating malignant transformation Symptomatic iron overload from chronic transfusion Severe anaemia with cardiovascular compromise at presentation Confusing it with transient erythroblastopenia of childhood, which recovers spontaneously Overlooking parvovirus B19 as a cause of acute red cell aplasia Failing to monitor and treat transfusional iron overload Neglecting long-term malignancy surveillance Diamond-Blackfan anaemia is caused by haploinsufficiency of genes encoding ribosomal proteins, impairing ribosome biogenesis. Disrupted assembly of the ribosomal subunits activates stabilisation of p53 and stress pathways to which erythroid progenitors are especially sensitive, producing selective failure of red cell production. The same ribosomal stress and secondary genomic instability contribute to the congenital malformations and the heightened risk of malignancy. Many patients achieve stable disease with corticosteroids or transfusion support, and some undergo spontaneous remission; long-term outcome is influenced by transfusional iron overload and the lifelong increased risk of myelodysplasia, leukaemia and solid tumours. Transplantation is curative for the haematological disease.

Diastrophic dysplasia — SLC26A2, DTD, diastrophic dwarfism, DTDST Atelosteogenesis type II (also SLC26A2-related) Achondrogenesis type IB (also SLC26A2-related) Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita Pseudoachondroplasia Larsen syndrome Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia Skeletal survey documenting short tubular bones, epiphyseal changes, and spinal deformity SLC26A2 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Cervical spine imaging to assess kyphosis and instability, particularly before anaesthesia Serial spinal imaging to monitor progressive scoliosis Hip imaging to detect dysplasia and dislocation Airway and respiratory assessment given craniofacial and thoracic involvement An autosomal recessive dysplasia characterised by short-limbed short stature with multiple joint contractures and severe progressive scoliosis Caused by biallelic variants in SLC26A2, a sulphate transporter needed for proper sulphation of cartilage proteoglycans The hitch-hiker thumb, produced by a proximally placed, abducted first metacarpal, is a highly characteristic hand sign Cystic swelling of the external ear in infancy that later calcifies (cauliflower ear) and cleft palate are recognised features Radiographs show short broad tubular bones, flattened irregular epiphyses, cervical kyphosis, and progressive scoliosis and hip dysplasia Cervical spine kyphosis and instability, together with a small airway, create important anaesthetic and respiratory risks Diagnosis combines the clinical and radiographic pattern with SLC26A2 molecular confirmation Cervical kyphosis or instability threatening the spinal cord, especially around anaesthesia Rapidly progressive scoliosis with restrictive lung disease Airway compromise related to cleft palate, micrognathia, or laryngotracheal involvement Neurological deterioration from spinal deformity Missing cervical kyphosis and precipitating cord injury during airway management Overlooking the hitch-hiker thumb and ear findings that point to the diagnosis Underestimating the rate of scoliosis progression Confusing it with arthrogryposis without appropriate radiographic and genetic assessment Diastrophic dysplasia results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in SLC26A2, a transporter that supplies sulphate for the sulphation of proteoglycans in cartilage matrix. Undersulphated proteoglycans produce structurally abnormal cartilage, impairing endochondral ossification and the integrity of articular and physeal cartilage. This underlies the short limbs, epiphyseal abnormalities, joint contractures and dislocations, spinal deformity, and the distinctive ear and hand features. The same transporter defect underlies a spectrum of recessive chondrodysplasias of varying severity. Intelligence and lifespan are usually normal, but disability is often considerable owing to severe scoliosis, contractures, hip and knee deformity, and premature joint degeneration. Early cervical spine complications and respiratory compromise from spinal deformity are the main threats.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation — PT/APTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer Blood film Treat the underlying trigger Often secondary to sepsis/malignancy — treat the cause Severe liver disease (thrombocytopenia from sequestration/portal hypertension/hypersplenism, decreased factor and natural-anticoagulant synthesis, elevated d-dimer) — distinguished because liver-disease parameters do not change rapidly, unlike DIC (p.977). Immune thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) — acute thrombocytopenia, red cell fragmentation, multiorgan failure, but identified by ADAMTS13 inhibitor (p.977). Vitamin K deficiency (isolated PT prolongation as earliest finding) (p.977-978). Gram-negative bacterial systemic infection (DIC is most commonly seen here) (p.974). COVID-19-associated coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia (p.974). ISTH overt-DIC score using platelet count, d-dimer, PT prolongation, and fibrinogen (p.977). Peripheral blood smear for schistocytes (red cell fragmentation) (p.977). Serial/repeated PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, d-dimer measurements (every 6-8 h in critically ill; daily if overt DIC) to assess trajectory and distinguish from liver disease (p.977). Fibrin degradation products (FDP) (p.976-977). ADAMTS13 activity/inhibitor when TTP is in the differential (p.977). Severe/fulminant liver disease and cirrhosis (coexisting chronic or acute DIC can also occur) (p.977-978). Thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP, HUS) (p.977). Dysfibrinogenemia of liver disease (p.978). DIC is an acquired syndrome of intravascular activation of coagulation with loss of localization, which can damage the microvasculature and, if severe enough, cause organ dysfunction (ISTH 2001 definition) (p.976). The central event is uncontrolled thrombin generation, compounded by disruption of physiologic anticoagulant mechanisms and abnormal fibrinolysis, producing systemic fibrin deposition in small and mid-size vessels (p.976). Fibrin deposition can compromise blood supply to lung, kidney, liver and brain, causing organ failure; pulmonary microvascular thrombosis is a component of ARDS (p.976). Most common causes: bacterial sepsis (also viral and fungal), trauma, obstetric events (abruptio placentae, amniotic fluid embolism), and malignancy (especially mucin-producing adenocarcinomas and acute promyelocytic leukemia) (p.976). Sepsis-driven DIC reflects thrombo-inflammation: increased tissue factor expression, neutrophil/monocyte activation with cytokine release, neutrophil extracellular traps, and polyphosphate release driving thrombin generation (p.976). Bleeding manifestations dominate clinically: petechiae, ecchymoses, oozing from venipuncture sites, and severe hemorrhage from GI tract, lung, or CNS; thrombosis of large vessels and cerebral embolism can also occur (p.977). Chronic (low-grade, compensated) DIC is seen with giant hemangioma, metastatic carcinoma, and late-gestation fetal demise; bleeding is discrete and limited to skin/mucosa, with elevated FDP/d-dimer but PT/aPTT/fibrinogen often normal or high and only mild thrombocytopenia (p.977). In critically ill patients, coagulation parameters should be repeated over 6-8 h because patients can deteriorate rapidly; an overt-DIC score should be rechecked daily (p.977). Hemodynamic instability and shock are common in acute DIC; mortality ranges from 30% to over 80% (p.977). Purpura fulminans — extensive skin thrombosis, especially in children post-infection or with protein C pathway deficiency (p.976). Bleeding into the CNS, lung, or GI tract (p.977). Rapidly deteriorating coagulation parameters in a critically ill patient (p.977). Distinguishing DIC from severe liver disease is challenging and requires serial laboratory measurements — both share thrombocytopenia, reduced factor synthesis, and elevated d-dimer, but liver-disease values do not change rapidly (p.977). The ISTH overt-DIC scoring tool is not validated for pregnant patients; a separate tool exists for pregnancy (p.977). d-Dimer assays are not standardized and have differing normal ranges; degree of increase must be interpreted against the local laboratory range (p.977). A single low score does not exclude evolving DIC — a non-overt score (<5) should be repeated every 1-2 days (p.977). DIC arises from uncontrolled thrombin generation triggered by multiple mechanisms, with simultaneous disruption of physiologic anticoagulant pathways and abnormal fibrinolysis. In sepsis and trauma, activation of inflammatory pathways increases tissue factor expression, activates neutrophils and monocytes with cytokine release and neutrophil extracellular trap formation, and releases polyphosphates that cross-talk with the coagulation system (thrombo-inflammation); endothelial damage causes loss of native antithrombotic properties. The result is systemic fibrin deposition in small and mid-size vessels causing microvascular occlusion, ischemic organ damage, and red cell fragmentation/hemolysis. Sustained activation consumes platelets and clotting factors, producing systemic bleeding that is aggravated by secondary hyperfibrinolysis in late stages. Purpura fulminans is a severe form of DIC with extensive cutaneous thrombosis, predominantly in young children after viral or bacterial infection, especially with inherited or acquired protein C pathway deficiency (p.976). Morbidity and mortality in DIC are primarily driven by the underlying disease; acute DIC carries mortality ranging from 30% to greater than 80%. Many patients with overt DIC are critically ill and require intensive care (p.977). ISTH overt-DIC score: Platelets >100x10^9/L = 0, 50-100 = 1, <50 = 2; d-dimer normal = 0, moderate increase = 2, severe increase = 3; PT prolongation <3 s = 0, 3-6 s = 1, >6 s = 2; fibrinogen >1 g/L = 0, <1 g/L = 1. Total <5 = non-overt/low-grade DIC (repeat in 1-2 days); >5 = overt DIC (repeat labs daily). Not for use in pregnant patients (p.977).

loss-of-function allele Surveillance focuses on chest imaging in early childhood, pelvic and abdominal assessment, and thyroid monitoring Respiratory distress or a cystic or solid lung lesion in a young child A pelvic or abdominal mass suggesting ovarian or renal tumour A rapidly enlarging or suspicious thyroid nodule Neurological signs raising concern for pineoblastoma or other intracranial tumour Dismissing childhood lung cysts as benign congenital lesions and missing early pleuropulmonary blastoma Overlooking the diagnosis because of incomplete penetrance and an unremarkable family history Failing to monitor the thyroid, especially after chemotherapy or radiotherapy Not offering cascade testing and paediatric surveillance to at-risk relatives DICER1 encodes an endoribonuclease that cleaves precursor microRNAs into mature microRNAs, which fine-tune the expression of many genes controlling growth and differentiation. In this syndrome a germline loss-of-function variant is combined with a characteristic somatic missense mutation in the RNase IIIb catalytic domain of the other allele, a distinctive two-hit mechanism that selectively impairs processing of one class of microRNAs. The resulting imbalance in microRNA regulation disrupts developmental control of susceptible tissues, giving rise to the diverse embryonal and mesenchymal tumours that define the condition. Penetrance is variable and many carriers stay healthy, but pleuropulmonary blastoma can be aggressive, so early detection through surveillance improves outcomes. Most other tumours are treatable when identified early, and long-term thyroid monitoring is warranted given the increased malignancy risk, particularly after cancer therapy.

Dicrocoeliasis (lancet liver fluke) — Dicrocoelium dendriticum infection, lancet fluke infection, lancet liver fluke disease Fascioliasis and opisthorchiid liver fluke infection Spurious egg passage after eating infected liver Cholelithiasis with biliary colic Functional dyspepsia or non-ulcer dyspepsia Ascending bacterial cholangitis Other causes of eosinophilia with hepatobiliary symptoms Stool microscopy for the characteristic dark operculated eggs Repeat stool examination after several days on a liver-free diet to exclude spurious infection Full blood count for eosinophilia Liver function tests Abdominal ultrasound for biliary changes in symptomatic disease Duodenal aspirate examination where diagnosis remains uncertain Caused by the lancet liver fluke Dicrocoelium dendriticum, primarily a parasite of grazing herbivores; human infection is uncommon The life cycle is unusual, using land snails and then ants as intermediate hosts, with humans infected by accidentally swallowing infected ants on vegetation Genuine infection may cause right upper quadrant discomfort, dyspepsia, flatulence and, in heavier disease, biliary symptoms Spurious infection is a well-known trap: eggs appear in stool after eating infected animal liver, without the person actually being parasitised Diagnosis requires finding characteristic dark operculated eggs in stool, ideally after excluding a liver-containing meal and re-testing on a liver-free diet Praziquantel is used for treatment, with triclabendazole considered in some settings Peripheral eosinophilia and mild derangement of liver function tests may be present Progressive jaundice or biliary obstruction Fever with right upper quadrant pain suggesting cholangitis Persistent symptoms after treatment prompting reassessment Marked hepatic dysfunction Diagnosing genuine infection without excluding spurious egg passage from a recent liver-containing meal Treating an asymptomatic person on the basis of a single positive stool Confusing the eggs with those of other liver flukes Overlooking the ant intermediate host when tracing the source of exposure Dicrocoelium dendriticum is a small liver fluke that inhabits the bile ducts of sheep, cattle and other herbivores. Its life cycle is distinctive: eggs passed in faeces are eaten by land snails, larvae are shed in slime balls, and these are consumed by ants, which serve as the second intermediate host. An infected ant is behaviourally altered so that it clings to vegetation and is grazed, allowing the definitive host to ingest the metacercariae. In the rare true human infection, larvae ascend the biliary tree and mature into adults in the intrahepatic bile ducts, where chronic irritation produces ductal inflammation, epithelial hyperplasia and periductal fibrosis analogous to other biliary flukes. More commonly, apparent infection is spurious, reflecting passage of eggs from ingested infected animal liver rather than established parasitism. True infection is generally mild and responds to anthelmintic treatment; the main clinical importance is avoiding misdiagnosis, since most positive stools represent harmless spurious egg passage.

Dientamoeba fragilis infection — dientamoebiasis, Dientamoeba fragilis, Dientamoeba infection Giardiasis Blastocystis infection Enterobiasis Irritable bowel syndrome Other enteric protozoal infections Inflammatory bowel disease Stool microscopy using permanent stained smears rather than wet mount alone Prompt fixation of stool given rapid trophozoite degeneration Molecular PCR, which is highly sensitive Perianal tape test for coexisting pinworm Full blood count for peripheral eosinophilia Testing to exclude other enteric pathogens in persistent symptoms Dientamoeba fragilis is a trichomonad-related flagellate that, despite its name, has no external flagella and historically no recognised cyst stage, existing chiefly as a fragile trophozoite It is a common colonic protozoan whose pathogenic role is debated, but it is increasingly linked to chronic non-bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain, bloating and anorexia, especially in children Peripheral eosinophilia can accompany infection, an unusual feature among enteric protozoa It is thought to be co-transmitted with the pinworm Enterobius vermicularis, whose eggs may serve as a protective vehicle for the delicate trophozoite The trophozoite typically has two nuclei, and the organism degenerates rapidly in stool, so prompt fixation and permanent staining greatly improve detection Routine wet-mount microscopy frequently misses it; permanent stained smears or molecular PCR are far more sensitive Metronidazole is commonly used for symptomatic infection, and concurrent treatment of coexisting pinworm should be considered Persistent symptoms despite treatment, prompting reassessment for another diagnosis Weight loss or growth faltering in an affected child Bloody diarrhoea or systemic features atypical for this organism Failure to eradicate infection suggesting reinfection from untreated pinworm Relying on wet-mount microscopy alone, which frequently fails to detect the fragile trophozoite Delaying stool fixation so the organism degenerates before examination Overlooking and failing to treat concurrent pinworm infection Attributing all symptoms to Dientamoeba without considering functional bowel disorders Dientamoeba fragilis is a flagellate protozoan that colonises the lumen and mucosal surface of the large intestine without demonstrable tissue invasion. The trophozoite is osmotically fragile and does not survive well outside the host, and a robust cyst stage has not been reliably demonstrated, which has long puzzled parasitologists regarding its transmission. The leading hypothesis is that it is carried within the eggs of the pinworm Enterobius vermicularis, explaining frequent co-infection. Mucosal irritation and mild inflammation, rather than invasion, are thought to underlie the abdominal pain and diarrhoea attributed to symptomatic infection, and an eosinophilic response may occur. Benign overall; symptomatic infection generally responds well to antiprotozoal treatment, though relapse or persistence can occur if coexisting pinworm infection is not also addressed.
