with a tattoo or clip aids relocation if bleeding recurs or surgery is required Angiographic embolisation or surgical wedge resection is reserved for endoscopic failure Massive haematemesis with haemodynamic instability requiring resuscitation Recurrent obscure bleeding with negative initial endoscopy Rebleeding after apparently successful endoscopic therapy Ongoing transfusion requirement despite treatment Dismissing normal-looking mucosa and overlooking the tiny bleeding point Failing to mark the site, making relocation difficult if bleeding recurs Relying on a single endoscopy when bleeding is intermittent Delaying angiography or surgery after repeated endoscopic failure A Dieulafoy lesion is an abnormally large, tortuous submucosal artery that retains a wide calibre as it approaches the mucosal surface instead of tapering into a capillary bed. Pulsatile pressure and possibly local mucosal thinning lead to erosion of a pinpoint mucosal defect overlying the vessel, exposing the artery and allowing sudden, often torrential arterial haemorrhage. Because the surrounding mucosa is otherwise normal and there is no ulcer or mass, the lesion can be extremely difficult to identify, particularly between bleeding episodes when it may not be actively spurting. With prompt endoscopic haemostasis the outlook is generally good and definitive control is achieved in most patients, though the lesion has a notable tendency to rebleed, and mortality rises when diagnosis is delayed or bleeding is massive.

Difficult airway — difficult intubation, difficult mask ventilation, CICO, can't intubate can't oxygenate Laryngospasm Bronchospasm or anaphylaxis limiting ventilation Airway foreign body or obstructing tumour Airway oedema from angioedema or infection Oesophageal intubation mistaken for a difficult airway Equipment failure or circuit disconnection Bedside airway assessment scores and examination of relevant pathology Nasendoscopy or flexible airway endoscopy to evaluate obstructing lesions Imaging (radiograph, CT) to characterise airway anatomy and masses when indicated Capnography to confirm tracheal placement and ventilation Review of previous anaesthetic records and airway alerts A difficult airway describes difficulty with mask ventilation, supraglottic device placement, laryngoscopy, intubation, or surgical airway access, and may be anticipated or unexpected Preoperative assessment combines several predictors (mouth opening, Mallampati class, thyromental distance, neck mobility, prognathism, prior difficulty, and pathology) since no single test is reliable A structured plan with pre-formulated backup steps and clear failure criteria is essential, and progression through a difficult-airway algorithm should be deliberate and time-limited Preoxygenation and apnoeic oxygenation extend safe apnoea time and are central to preventing hypoxic injury When intubation fails, the priority shifts from securing the tube to maintaining oxygenation using face mask or supraglottic devices A can't-intubate-can't-oxygenate situation is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate front-of-neck access (cricothyroidotomy) without delay For a known or predicted difficult airway, an awake technique with a flexible bronchoscope preserves spontaneous ventilation and airway reflexes Limiting repeated laryngoscopy attempts reduces trauma, bleeding, and oedema that can convert a difficult airway into an impossible one; documentation and patient alerting are vital afterwards Can't-intubate-can't-oxygenate scenario requiring immediate front-of-neck access Progressive desaturation despite optimal mask and supraglottic ventilation Rapidly worsening airway obstruction from oedema, bleeding, or an expanding mass Repeated failed attempts causing trauma, bleeding, and deteriorating airway conditions Persisting with repeated intubation attempts instead of prioritising oxygenation Failing to declare and act on a can't-intubate-can't-oxygenate emergency in time Inadequate preoxygenation before induction Not preparing backup equipment and a clear stepwise plan in advance Failing to document the difficulty and alert the patient for future anaesthetics Airway difficulty arises from anatomical or pathological factors that impair alignment of the oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes or obstruct airflow. Congenital syndromes, obesity, limited neck extension, restricted mouth opening, tumours, infection, trauma, previous surgery, radiation, and airway oedema all contribute. Under anaesthesia, loss of muscle tone can collapse the pharynx and worsen obstruction. When ventilation and oxygenation fail, progressive hypoxaemia leads within minutes to bradycardia, hypoxic brain injury, cardiac arrest, and death, so oxygenation rather than intubation is the overriding physiological goal. Most anticipated difficult airways are managed safely with planning and appropriate techniques; unanticipated failure with delayed rescue oxygenation can cause hypoxic brain injury or death within minutes.

Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage — DAH Pulmonary oedema Pneumonia or other infection Acute respiratory distress syndrome Pulmonary embolism with infarction Malignancy Aspiration Sequential bronchoalveolar lavage demonstrating persistent or increasing blood Chest imaging and full blood count for anaemia Autoimmune serology (ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA and others) Renal assessment for a pulmonary-renal syndrome Coagulation studies and echocardiography as indicated A syndrome of bleeding into the alveoli from the pulmonary microcirculation, not a single disease Classic features are haemoptysis, diffuse alveolar infiltrates, anaemia and hypoxaemia, though haemoptysis can be absent A falling haemoglobin with new alveolar shadowing should raise the possibility even without haemoptysis Sequential bronchoalveolar lavage returning progressively bloodier aliquots confirms alveolar haemorrhage Causes include small-vessel vasculitis, anti-GBM disease, connective tissue disease, drugs and coagulopathy, grouped by the presence or absence of capillaritis Management combines supportive care with urgent immunosuppression when an immune cause is identified Rapidly progressive hypoxaemic respiratory failure Associated acute kidney injury (pulmonary-renal syndrome) Massive or recurrent bleeding Haemodynamic instability Excluding the diagnosis because haemoptysis is absent Mistaking it for infection or pulmonary oedema and delaying immunosuppression Missing an associated renal component Failing to identify a treatable immune cause Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage arises from disruption of the alveolar-capillary basement membrane, allowing red cells to enter the alveolar spaces. The commonest mechanism is pulmonary capillaritis, a neutrophilic inflammation of the microvasculature seen in small-vessel vasculitides and connective tissue disease. Other cases result from bland haemorrhage without inflammation (as in coagulopathy or raised pulmonary venous pressure) or from diffuse alveolar damage. Accumulated blood impairs gas exchange, and recurrent bleeding can lead to haemosiderosis and fibrosis. Prognosis depends on the cause and speed of treatment; immune capillaritis can respond well to prompt immunosuppression, but delayed treatment or severe disease carries significant mortality.

treatment of any underlying cause Rapidly progressive hypoxaemic respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support Concurrent acute kidney injury suggesting a pulmonary-renal vasculitic syndrome Massive haemorrhage with haemodynamic compromise Falling haematocrit with expanding infiltrates indicating ongoing bleeding Excluding the diagnosis because haemoptysis is absent Mistaking the infiltrates for pneumonia or pulmonary oedema and missing an underlying vasculitis Failing to check renal function and urinalysis for an associated glomerulonephritis Overlooking the diagnostic value of sequential bronchoalveolar lavage aliquots and a raised carbon monoxide transfer factor Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage results from disruption of the alveolar-capillary basement membrane, allowing red cells to flood the alveolar spaces. Three broad mechanisms are recognised. In pulmonary capillaritis there is neutrophilic inflammation and fibrinoid necrosis of the alveolar capillaries, most often from ANCA-associated vasculitis or anti-glomerular basement membrane disease. In bland haemorrhage the capillaries bleed without inflammation, as in coagulopathy, mitral stenosis, or idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis. In the third group, haemorrhage accompanies diffuse alveolar damage from infection, drugs, or toxins. Extravasated blood is phagocytosed by macrophages, which accumulate haemosiderin over the ensuing days. Outcome depends heavily on the underlying cause and speed of treatment; immune capillaritis can respond well to prompt immunosuppression, but severe or recurrent haemorrhage, especially with renal involvement, carries significant morbidity and mortality.

Diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis — DCM Other cutaneous mastocytosis (urticaria pigmentosa, mastocytoma) Epidermolysis bullosa or other blistering disorders of infancy Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome Erythroderma of other cause Systemic mastocytosis Skin biopsy showing dense diffuse dermal mast cell infiltration Serum baseline tryptase (often very high) Assessment for systemic involvement Identification of triggers and a documented anaphylaxis plan Monitoring for complications during illness or procedures A rare, severe form of cutaneous mastocytosis of infancy with diffuse mast cell infiltration of the whole skin The skin is thickened with a doughy or leathery texture rather than discrete lesions Extensive blistering and erythroderma can occur, and the large mast cell burden risks severe mediator release Massive histamine release can cause flushing, hypotension and life-threatening reactions, sometimes triggered by handling or medications Baseline tryptase is often markedly elevated reflecting the high mast cell load Careful trigger avoidance, anaphylaxis preparedness and mediator-targeted therapy are essential Hypotension, extensive blistering or shock from mediator release Severe reactions triggered by handling, drugs or infection Very high tryptase with systemic symptoms Failure to thrive or systemic involvement Underestimating the risk of catastrophic mediator release Using known mast cell-degranulating drugs without caution Confusing extensive blistering with a primary bullous disease Failing to equip carers with an anaphylaxis plan In diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis, clonal mast cells infiltrate the entire dermis rather than forming discrete lesions, giving generalised skin thickening. The very large cutaneous mast cell burden means that degranulation, provoked by mechanical trauma, temperature change, drugs or infection, can release enough mediator to cause extensive blistering and dangerous systemic effects including hypotension and shock. The high mast cell mass is reflected in a markedly raised tryptase, and affected infants are vulnerable to severe, potentially fatal mediator crises. The condition can improve over childhood, but the infantile course may be complicated by dangerous mediator crises; with careful management and avoidance of triggers, many children improve with age.

cardiac ischaemia Progressive dysphagia, weight loss, or regurgitation suggesting achalasia or malignancy Food impaction requiring urgent endoscopy Odynophagia or alarm features warranting mucosal assessment Attributing chest pain to the oesophagus before excluding cardiac disease Diagnosing spasm on a single abnormal swallow rather than a consistent manometric pattern Missing spastic achalasia, which is managed differently Overlooking reflux as a treatable trigger of spastic contractions Distal oesophageal spasm is a motility disorder characterised by uncoordinated, simultaneous or premature contractions of the distal oesophageal smooth muscle. Impaired inhibitory neuronal signalling, particularly a deficiency of nitric-oxide-mediated inhibition, shortens the normal latency between swallowing and contraction, so that contractions occur prematurely and out of sequence. This disordered propagation disrupts orderly bolus transit, producing intermittent dysphagia, while the vigorous, poorly coordinated contractions generate episodic chest pain. The course is variable and often benign, with many patients managed symptomatically; a minority have refractory pain or dysphagia, and some overlap with or progress towards spastic achalasia.

physiotherapy, and surgery is reserved for complications such as severe dysphagia or myelopathy Progressive dysphagia or airway compromise from large cervical osteophytes Neurological deficit suggesting myelopathy or associated spinal canal stenosis Unstable spinal fracture through an ankylosed, brittle segment after minor trauma New severe pain that could indicate fracture, infection or malignancy in a stiff spine Confusing DISH with ankylosing spondylitis and missing the preserved discs and sacroiliac joints Underestimating fracture risk in the rigid, brittle ankylosed spine after minor trauma Overlooking cervical osteophytes as a cause of unexplained dysphagia Failing to assess and manage the associated metabolic syndrome Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis is a non-inflammatory ossifying diathesis in which new bone is laid down at entheses and along the spine, particularly the anterolateral vertebral margins, through progressive endochondral and membranous ossification. The disc spaces, sacroiliac joints and facet joints remain intact, distinguishing it from inflammatory spondyloarthropathy. Metabolic factors are strongly implicated: hyperinsulinaemia, insulin-like growth factor and other growth-promoting mediators associated with metabolic syndrome, diabetes and obesity are thought to stimulate osteoblast activity and enthesial new bone formation. The accumulating anterior bridging osteophytes stiffen the spine and, in the cervical region, can mechanically impinge on the oesophagus and airway. DISH is generally benign and slowly progressive; many patients remain asymptomatic, but spinal ankylosis increases fracture risk after minor trauma and large osteophytes can occasionally cause dysphagia or neurological compromise.

diffuse oesophageal spasm — distal oesophageal spasm, corkscrew oesophagus, DES type III (spastic) achalasia jackhammer (hypercontractile) oesophagus gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with reflux-induced chest pain cardiac ischaemia and microvascular angina functional chest pain of presumed oesophageal origin eosinophilic oesophagitis oesophageal hypersensitivity high-resolution oesophageal manometry with distal latency measurement timed barium oesophagram (may show corkscrew or segmental spasm) upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsies to exclude mucosal and structural disease ambulatory oesophageal pH-impedance monitoring to assess reflux contribution cardiac assessment (ECG and stress or perfusion testing) to exclude ischaemia provocative or pharmacological testing during manometry where available functional lumen imaging probe (FLIP) to assess oesophagogastric junction distensibility Defined on high-resolution manometry (Chicago Classification) by premature (spastic) contractions with a shortened distal latency in at least 20% of swallows, with normal or near-normal lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation. Presents with intermittent dysphagia to both solids and liquids and retrosternal chest pain that may closely mimic cardiac angina; symptoms are often unpredictable and precipitated by hot or cold liquids or emotional stress. The classic 'corkscrew' or 'rosary bead' barium appearance reflects simultaneous non-peristaltic contractions but is seen in a minority and correlates poorly with symptoms. Cardiac causes of chest pain must be excluded before attributing symptoms to oesophageal spasm, as the two are clinically indistinguishable at the bedside. There is meaningful overlap with type III (spastic) achalasia; impaired LOS relaxation on manometry shifts the diagnosis toward achalasia rather than diffuse spasm. Gastro-oesophageal reflux frequently coexists and may drive spastic motor activity, so an empirical trial of acid suppression is a reasonable early step. Smooth-muscle relaxants (nitrates, calcium-channel blockers), and neuromodulators for visceral hypersensitivity are mainstays; peppermint oil can abolish simultaneous contractions. Refractory cases may respond to endoscopic botulinum toxin injection or, rarely, to a long myotomy including peroral endoscopic myotomy tailored to the spastic segment. progressive dysphagia, especially to solids, or significant weight loss suggesting stricture or malignancy chest pain with cardiac risk factors or exertional pattern requiring urgent cardiac exclusion food bolus impaction or inability to swallow saliva new anaemia or gastrointestinal bleeding onset in older patients over a short period, raising concern for pseudoachalasia from an infiltrating tumour Attributing non-cardiac chest pain to spasm without first excluding coronary disease. Over-reliance on the barium 'corkscrew' sign, which is neither sensitive nor specific and correlates poorly with symptoms. Missing impaired lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation on manometry and thereby mislabelling type III achalasia as diffuse spasm. Failing to recognise coexistent gastro-oesophageal reflux as a treatable driver of spastic activity. Proceeding to a short myotomy without mapping the length of the spastic segment, risking incomplete symptom relief. Diffuse (distal) oesophageal spasm is a primary motor disorder of the oesophageal body characterised by loss of the normal orderly, sequential peristaltic wave in the smooth-muscle segment. The core defect is impaired deglutitive inhibition, attributed to dysfunction of inhibitory myenteric neurons that release nitric oxide; reduced nitrergic tone allows contractions to begin prematurely and propagate simultaneously rather than in an aboral sequence. This is reflected manometrically by a shortened distal latency. The resulting rapidly propagated or simultaneous contractions produce dysphagia and chest pain, and superimposed oesophageal hypersensitivity amplifies symptom perception. Unlike achalasia, lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation is typically preserved, though some patients show a spectrum bridging toward spastic achalasia. The condition is typically chronic and relapsing but benign, with symptoms fluctuating over years rather than progressing relentlessly; a substantial minority improve with reassurance, reflux control and neuromodulation. A subset evolve toward spastic achalasia over time, and response to invasive therapy is less predictable than in classic achalasia.

syndrome is most often caused by a recurrent hemizygous microdeletion at chromosome 22q11.2, encompassing the TBX1 gene among others. TBX1 is critical for development of the pharyngeal arches and pouches, and its haploinsufficiency disrupts formation of the thymus, parathyroid glands, and cardiac outflow tract, producing immunodeficiency, hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcaemia, and conotruncal heart defects. The deletion typically arises de novo from misalignment of flanking low-copy repeats, though it can be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Similar phenotypes rarely result from other causes such as maternal diabetes or teratogen exposure. Outcome depends chiefly on the severity of cardiac disease and immunodeficiency; most children with milder immune involvement do well, while those with complete thymic aplasia face life-threatening infection unless treated with thymic or immune reconstitution.

myxoid cyst is a benign, dome-shaped, translucent swelling overlying the distal interphalangeal joint or the proximal nail fold of a finger It is strongly associated with osteoarthritis of the observation and simple drainage to more definitive treatments addressing the joint connection, such as excision, with recurrence being a recognised problem Rapid growth, ulceration, or atypical joint connection Persistent nail dystrophy that could reflect an alternative underlying lesion Mistaking the cyst for a nail tumour and pursuing unnecessary aggressive investigation Treating the nail groove without recognising and addressing the overlying cyst Simple drainage alone, which frequently leads to recurrence via the joint pedicle Overlooking the risk of introducing infection into the joint during intervention A digital myxoid cyst is a mucin-filled swelling that develops near the distal interphalangeal joint, typically in the setting of underlying osteoarthritis. It is thought to arise either from local overproduction of mucin by fibroblasts in the dermis or from herniation of degenerate joint fluid through a capsular defect, often with a persistent connecting pedicle to the joint. When the cyst lies over the proximal nail fold it presses on the matrix beneath, disturbing plate production and creating a longitudinal groove in the nail; the frequent communication with the joint explains why lesions recur if the connection is not dealt with and why they may intermittently discharge gelatinous fluid. Digital myxoid cysts are benign, and the associated nail groove usually resolves once the cyst is successfully treated and matrix pressure is relieved, but recurrence is common, especially when the connection to the osteoarthritic joint is not addressed.

automaticity with conduction block Overlooking chronic toxicity because the digoxin level is only modestly raised Failing to correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia that perpetuate arrhythmia in severe hyperkalaemia Digoxin inhibits the myocardial sodium-potassium ATPase, raising intracellular sodium and, through sodium-calcium exchange, intracellular calcium, which increases contractility but also enhances automaticity and the tendency to arrhythmia. It also augments vagal tone, slowing sinoatrial and atrioventricular conduction. In acute overdose, widespread inhibition of the pump drives potassium out of cells, producing hyperkalaemia that reflects the degree of poisoning. Electrolyte disturbances (low potassium or magnesium, high calcium) and renal impairment increase myocardial sensitivity and reduce clearance, precipitating chronic toxicity at therapeutic or near-therapeutic levels. With timely recognition, correction of electrolytes, and use of digoxin-specific antibody fragments for severe cases, most patients recover; untreated life-threatening arrhythmias and marked hyperkalaemia in acute overdose carry high mortality.

When the enzyme is deficient, the supply of tetrahydrofolate and its derivatives, including the 5-methyltetrahydrofolate needed in the central nervous system and the folate cofactors required for nucleotide synthesis, falls. Impaired DNA synthesis in the marrow produces megaloblastic anaemia, while depletion of reduced folate in the brain causes cerebral folate deficiency with seizures and developmental problems. Because folic acid needs this same enzyme to become active, treatment relies on already-reduced folates such as folinic acid. With early recognition and treatment using reduced folates the haematological abnormality corrects and neurological outcome can be favourable, but delayed treatment of the cerebral folate deficit may leave lasting neurological impairment.

Dihydropteridine reductase deficiency — DHPR deficiency, QDPR gene deficiency, BH4 recycling defect (DHPR), tetrahydrobiopterin-deficient hyperphenylalaninaemia (DHPR) Classic phenylketonuria (phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency) 6-pyruvoyl-tetrahydropterin synthase deficiency (BH4 synthesis defect) GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency Sepiapterin reductase deficiency Cerebral folate deficiency from other causes Other neurotransmitter disorders causing infantile dystonia and encephalopathy Dihydropteridine reductase enzyme activity assay (deficient) in blood spots Blood and urine pterin profile (biopterin normal or elevated) with blood phenylalanine QDPR gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis Cerebrospinal fluid neurotransmitter metabolites and 5-methyltetrahydrofolate to detect cerebral folate deficiency Brain MRI/CT for demyelination and basal ganglia calcification BH4 loading test to characterise phenylalanine responsiveness Autosomal recessive defect of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) recycling caused by QDPR mutations, in which dihydropteridine reductase cannot regenerate BH4 from its oxidised form Like other BH4 disorders it presents as hyperphenylalaninaemia on newborn screening but is not corrected by dietary phenylalanine restriction alone, because dopamine and serotonin synthesis is also impaired A distinguishing feature is secondary cerebral folate deficiency, so treatment includes folinic acid alongside neurotransmitter precursors, and untreated disease can cause intracranial calcification and a demyelinating course Untreated children develop a progressive encephalopathy with dystonia, hypotonia, seizures, oculogyric crises, and developmental regression Because BH4 recycling rather than synthesis is impaired, giving BH4 alone is often insufficient; management centres on controlling phenylalanine plus levodopa, a serotonin precursor, and folinic acid The biochemical clue is normal or raised biopterin with markedly deficient dihydropteridine reductase enzyme activity, differentiating it from PTPS and GTPCH defects Neurological regression despite good phenylalanine control, indicating untreated cofactor and folate deficiency Seizures, dystonia, or oculogyric crises evolving in an infant with hyperphenylalaninaemia Intracranial calcification or demyelination on neuroimaging Failure to add folinic acid, allowing progressive cerebral folate deficiency Managing as classic phenylketonuria and omitting the essential folinic acid and neurotransmitter therapy Assuming BH4 supplementation alone suffices when the problem is cofactor recycling Not measuring dihydropteridine reductase activity, so the specific recycling defect is missed Overlooking cerebral folate deficiency and associated calcification/demyelination Dihydropteridine reductase regenerates tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) from quinonoid dihydrobiopterin, sustaining the active cofactor pool. Biallelic QDPR mutations impair this recycling, so BH4 becomes functionally deficient despite adequate synthesis, disabling phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan hydroxylases. This produces hyperphenylalaninaemia together with central dopamine and serotonin deficiency. The defect additionally reduces regeneration of folate cofactors, causing cerebral folate deficiency that contributes to demyelination and basal ganglia calcification. The combined amino-acid, neurotransmitter, and folate disturbances underlie the progressive neurological deterioration seen when treatment is inadequate. Early combined treatment with phenylalanine control, neurotransmitter precursors, and folinic acid can substantially improve outcome, but delayed or incomplete therapy, especially neglect of cerebral folate deficiency, leads to progressive neurological damage and disability. Lifelong metabolic follow-up is essential.

without checking DPD status Assuming a normal genotype excludes deficiency, as phenotype testing may add information Attributing severe early chemotherapy toxicity to chance rather than to enzyme deficiency Failing to use the specific antidote promptly when severe toxicity occurs Overlooking that heterozygous partial deficiency can still cause serious toxicity Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase catalyses the rate-limiting first step in the degradation of the pyrimidine bases uracil and thymine. Deficiency causes accumulation of these bases and their precursors in body fluids. Clinically, the disorder has two faces. As an inborn error it can cause a variable neurological phenotype, thought to relate to accumulated metabolites and, in some, associated abnormalities of the neurotransmitter pool. More importantly for adult medicine, fluoropyrimidine drugs are analogues of uracil that are normally inactivated by this enzyme; when it is deficient, the active drug and its cytotoxic metabolites persist, producing severe dose-related toxicity even at standard doses. Constitutional cases range from entirely asymptomatic to significant neurodevelopmental impairment; the critical determinant of outcome is recognition before fluoropyrimidine exposure, since unrecognised deficiency can cause life-threatening or fatal drug toxicity.

Dilated Cardiomyopathy — DCM, cardiomyopathy Ischaemic cardiomyopathy / coronary artery disease or prior infarction (structural heart disease that can mimic or cause DCM, p.2002) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), including the ~5% that evolve to reduced EF with restrictive physiology (HCM-rEF) (p.2001-2002) Restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) - functional diagnosis based on diastolic dysfunction/elevated filling pressures; some sarcomeric variants and storage diseases overlap (p.2002) Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM-LV / ACM-RV/ARVC) where ventricular arrhythmias dominate before severely reduced LVEF (p.2002) Primary valvular disease Takotsubo (stress-induced) cardiomyopathy - distinct acute presentation with apical ballooning, often resolving (p.2019) Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) - overlaps with proposed obesity and diabetic cardiomyopathy (p.2018) Viral myocarditis (coxsackie, adenovirus, COVID-19, influenza, HIV) progressing to dilated cardiomyopathy (p.2015-2016) Chagas' disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) and other parasitic infection (toxoplasmosis, trypanosomiasis) (p.2016) Bacterial (diphtheria), spirochetal (Lyme disease - Borrelia burgdorferi), rickettsial (Q fever), and fungal myocarditis (p.2016) Echocardiography (initial imaging modality to define morphology and function) (p.2002) Cardiac MRI for myocardial tissue characterization, late gadolinium enhancement patterns of fibrosis, and T1/T2 mapping for focal/diffuse inflammation (note: avoid gadolinium in pregnancy) (p.2002, 2018) Electrocardiogram and chest radiograph (p.2003) Chemistry including sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, glucose/glycohemoglobin, renal and liver function, lipids, thyroid-stimulating hormone, serum iron and transferrin saturation, urinalysis, creatine kinase isoforms, cardiac troponin (p.2003) Hematology including CBC with differential, eosinophil count, ESR (p.2003) Genetic counseling and multigene cardiomyopathy panel (p.2003) Targeted infectious work-up when suspected (HIV, Chagas', Lyme, toxoplasmosis, trichinosis); rheumatologic serologies (p.2003) Endomyocardial biopsy (including electron microscopy) when a specific diagnosis with therapeutic implications is suspected (p.2003) Coronary angiography in patients with evidence of ischemia/infarction who are candidates for intervention (p.2003) Granulomatous inflammatory disease - sarcoidosis (often regional wall-motion abnormality, DCM phenotype, or RV involvement) and giant cell myocarditis (p.2002, 2016) Eosinophilic myocarditis / Loeffler endocarditis (can progress to restrictive physiology) (p.2015-2016) Collagen vascular / connective tissue disease, polymyositis, dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus (p.2015-2016) Immune checkpoint-inhibitor myocarditis (most dramatic noninfectious inflammatory myocarditis) (p.2016) Hemochromatosis / iron overload (variably classified as metabolic or restrictive but often presents as DCM) (p.2018-2019) Endocrinopathy - thyroid disease, pheochromocytoma; very-high-renin states (renal artery stenosis) (p.2017-2018) Nutritional deficiency - thiamine (beriberi), selenium (Keshan's disease), carnitine, calcium, phosphate (p.2018) DCM is defined by decreased left ventricular systolic function, typically with increased LV dimensions, although dilation may be minimal in some cases (p.2015). Quantitatively, DCM is defined when LVEF is <=0.50, but most clinical presentations occur with LVEF <=0.40; persistent LVEF <=0.30-0.35 is the threshold for primary-prevention ICD (p.2001-2002). Despite multiple etiologies and variable initial presentations, DCM often progresses into a convergent clinical phenotype similar to that following acute myocardial infarction, with myocyte death, apoptosis, compensatory hypertrophy, and neurohormonal activation (p.2015). Mitral regurgitation commonly develops as the ventricle dilates and the valvular apparatus is distorted, and is commonly moderate to severe by the time heart failure is advanced (p.2015). Right ventricular dilation and dysfunction may result directly from the initial injury but more often develop later from elevated afterload due to secondary pulmonary hypertension and mechanical interaction with the failing LV (p.2015). Alcohol is the most common toxin implicated in chronic DCM, but alcoholic cardiomyopathy is relatively rare and remains a diagnosis of exclusion; atrial fibrillation occurs commonly both early ('holiday heart') and in advanced stages (p.2016). Truncating variants in TTN and other DCM disease genes can be found in about 10% of patients with presumed alcohol cardiomyopathy and about 15% of peripartum cardiomyopathy, indicating that environmental triggers can unmask genetic predisposition (p.2016-2017). Chemotherapy agents are the most common drugs implicated in toxic cardiomyopathy; doxorubicin cardiotoxicity generally does NOT cause marked LV dilation, so stroke volume and perfusion can be low with only a modest fall in ejection fraction (p.2016). Tests of thyroid function are part of the routine evaluation of cardiomyopathy because clinical signs of thyroid disease may be masked; hyperthyroidism should always be considered with new-onset atrial fibrillation or ventricular tachycardia (p.2017). Heritability is present in at least 30% of DCM without other clear etiology, and expanded genetic testing reveals pathogenic variants sufficient to cause cardiomyopathy in 20-40% of DCM patients (p.2003, 2013). Sudden cardiac death risk: ventricular arrhythmias may be presenting events; persistent LVEF <=0.30-0.35 is the threshold for primary-prevention ICD (p.2001-2002, 2002) Embolic events from atrial fibrillation or apical LV thrombi can be the first presentation (p.2002) Peripartum cardiomyopathy with LVEF <0.35 carries higher risk of life-threatening arrhythmias at presentation and early after discharge, and marked dilation/LVEF <0.35 raises LV thrombus and embolic risk (p.2017-2018) Acute cardiac presentation (elevated troponin, conduction blocks, bizarre arrhythmias) in a patient on immune checkpoint inhibitors warrants immediate coronary-care-unit admission and high-dose glucocorticoids without delay for biopsy (p.2016) Hyperthyroidism combined with heart failure is a dangerous combination that may decompensate precipitously and fatally during titration of antithyroid therapy (p.2017) 'Congestive heart failure' should NOT be considered a diagnosis or an etiology of cardiomyopathy - it is a nonspecific syndrome of congestion common to many cardiac diagnoses and requires thorough etiologic evaluation (p.2002). Phenotypes overlap and evolve over time (DCM can reverse-remodel to higher EF; HCM can evolve to reduced EF), so reliance on a single morphologic phenotype is diminishing (p.2001-2002). Alcoholic cardiomyopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion, and many patients are fully functional without apparent stigmata of alcoholism (p.2016). Anthracycline cardiotoxicity can produce low stroke volume/perfusion with only modestly reduced EF because marked LV dilation is usually absent (p.2016). In peripartum cardiomyopathy, edema and dyspnea may be mistakenly attributed to pregnancy itself; renin-angiotensin system inhibitors should NOT be given before delivery due to adverse fetal effects, and gadolinium should NOT be used on MRI during pregnancy (p.2017-2018). Detection of anticardiac antibodies and viral genome fragments in chronic cardiomyopathy is of uncertain significance (possible cause vs neutral bystander) and is not in routine clinical use (p.2013). Immunosuppression for nonspecific chronic lymphocytic myocarditis has not demonstrated convincing benefit (p.2013). DCM is characterized by decreased LV systolic function, typically with LV chamber dilation (LVEF <=0.50, usually <=0.40 at presentation). Multiple causes (idiopathic, familial/genetic, prior myocarditis, ischaemic, toxic/alcohol, chemotherapy, peripartum, tachycardia-mediated, metabolic/endocrine) converge on a common phenotype resembling post-infarct injury: early myocyte death, later apoptosis, and compensatory hypertrophy of remaining myocytes in response to increased wall stress. Local and circulating neurohormonal factors drive deleterious secondary remodeling; dynamic remodeling of the interstitial scaffold affects diastolic function and the degree of dilation. As the ventricle dilates, the mitral valve apparatus is distorted, producing functional mitral regurgitation. RV dilation/dysfunction develops directly from injury or, more often, secondarily from pulmonary hypertension and ventricular interaction. Chronic inflammation contributes to progression even when not initially implicated, and many 'acute' presentations have progressed silently over months to years (Harrison 22e p.2015). DCM secondary responses are often modifiable or reversible. Almost a third of patients with recent-onset cardiomyopathy without coronary artery disease show substantial spontaneous recovery to normal ejection fraction, and partial recovery to LVEF >0.40 ('heart failure with improved ejection fraction') is common with guideline-directed neurohormonal therapy, CRT for LBBB, and diuretics. Alcoholic cardiomyopathy can improve markedly within 3-6 months of abstinence but has a grim prognosis if heavy drinking continues. In peripartum cardiomyopathy, LVEF improves to >=0.50 in 50-80% of cases (often within 6 months); recovery is less likely with LVEF <0.30, LV end-diastolic dimension >=0.60, black race, and presentation >6 weeks postpartum; U.S. 1-year mortality ranged 4-11% and up to twofold higher in Africa. Takotsubo syndrome has a generally good long-term prognosis (lowest mortality with emotional rather than physical triggers) but in-hospital complications/mortality resemble acute MI, with ~10% recurrence (Harrison 22e p.2002, 2016-2019). Classification of cardiomyopathies: DCM phenotype - Early: LVEF <=0.50 and/or LVEDV >112% normal for age/sex or LVEDD >95% predicted for sex/height; LVEF <=0.40 is the threshold for traditional heart-failure therapies for low LVEF; persistent LVEF <=0.30-0.35 is the threshold for primary-prevention ICD. Mid-range LVEF 0.40-0.50 is often a transitional state (deterioration from early DCM or improvement into DCM remission). DCM is distinguished from HCM (increased wall thickness, septal >=15 mm men / >=13 mm women, LVEF >=normal usually >0.60), RCM (functional diagnosis from diastolic dysfunction/elevated filling pressures, often marked atrial enlargement), and arrhythmogenic CM (ACM-LV/ACM-RV/ARVC, ventricular arrhythmias dominating). (Harrison 22e p.2001-2002).

Diogenes Syndrome — Senile squalor syndrome, Severe domestic self-neglect Dementia, including frontotemporal dementia Hoarding disorder Obsessive-compulsive disorder Depression with self-neglect Chronic psychotic illness such as schizophrenia Alcohol-related brain damage Learning disability or longstanding personality difficulties Cognitive assessment and neuropsychological or executive-function testing Neuroimaging (MRI or CT) for frontal and cerebrovascular pathology Capacity assessment regarding care and residence Nutritional and physical health screen (full blood count, metabolic panel, vitamins, thyroid function) Home and environmental assessment via occupational therapy and environmental health Alcohol use assessment Screening for infection and infestation Syndrome of extreme self-neglect, domestic squalor, social withdrawal, and often hoarding (syllogomania), with a characteristic lack of shame or insight. Typically affects older adults living alone and may occur with or without a diagnosable mental illness. The eponym, drawn from the Greek philosopher Diogenes, is widely regarded as a misnomer. Around half of cases have no primary psychiatric diagnosis; the remainder are associated with frontal-lobe dysfunction, dementia, alcohol misuse, or psychosis. Frontal and executive dysfunction is a recurrent theme, with behaviour reflecting impaired judgement and self-regulation. Frequently comes to attention through neighbours, environmental health, or crisis rather than self-referral. Carries high morbidity and mortality, with presentations including malnutrition, hypothermia, infestation, or untreated medical illness. Capacity assessment and multi-agency working with social care and environmental health are central to management. Malnutrition, dehydration, or hypothermia Untreated serious physical illness or pressure injuries Fire or public-health hazard arising from hoarding Loss of capacity with inability to keep oneself safe Rapid cognitive decline Assuming that self-neglect equates to lack of capacity, or the reverse, without formal assessment Attributing the picture solely to eccentricity and missing dementia or depression Neglecting assessment of frontal-lobe function One-off clearance of the home without addressing the underlying cause, leading to relapse Diogenes syndrome is a behavioural syndrome rather than a single disease, characterised by breakdown of self-care and of socially normative standards of cleanliness. A substantial proportion of cases are linked to frontal-lobe and executive dysfunction, whether from neurodegeneration, cerebrovascular disease, or alcohol-related damage, impairing planning, judgement, and insight. Premorbid personality traits such as aloofness, stubbornness, and suspiciousness, together with adverse life events, may precipitate decompensation in vulnerable older people. In others the picture is secondary to dementia, psychosis, depression, or obsessive hoarding, and the final common presentation is profound self-neglect with abnormal decision-making about the home environment. Mortality is high, particularly where physical complications are advanced, and recurrence of squalor after intervention is common; outcome improves with treatment of any underlying disorder and sustained multi-agency support.

Bisphosphoglycerate mutase deficiency — 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate mutase deficiency, diphosphoglycerate mutase deficiency, DPGM deficiency, BPGM gene High-oxygen-affinity haemoglobin variants Primary polycythaemia (polycythaemia vera) Secondary erythrocytosis from hypoxia or erythropoietin excess Congenital erythrocytosis from erythropoietin receptor or oxygen-sensing pathway mutations Relative (apparent) polycythaemia Methaemoglobinaemia with altered oxygen delivery Red-cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate measurement Bisphosphoglycerate mutase enzyme activity assay Oxygen dissociation curve (p50) analysis Full blood count showing erythrocytosis with serum erythropoietin Haemoglobin variant analysis to exclude a high-affinity variant Molecular testing of the BPGM gene A rare defect of the Rapoport-Luebering shunt that characteristically causes erythrocytosis rather than haemolytic anaemia Deficiency lowers red-cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, increasing haemoglobin's oxygen affinity and reducing oxygen release to tissues The resulting tissue hypoxia drives a compensatory increase in erythropoietin and a secondary polycythaemia It is an important consideration in the workup of unexplained erythrocytosis with a low 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate and left-shifted oxygen dissociation curve Inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, so consanguinity or affected relatives may be present Diagnosis rests on demonstrating a low red-cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, reduced enzyme activity and a BPGM mutation Management is generally conservative; the erythrocytosis is compensatory and venesection is usually unnecessary and may be counterproductive Symptoms of hyperviscosity from marked erythrocytosis Thrombotic events attributable to a high haematocrit Misclassification as polycythaemia vera leading to inappropriate cytoreductive treatment Inappropriate aggressive venesection worsening tissue oxygen delivery Mistaking the compensatory erythrocytosis for polycythaemia vera and treating with cytoreduction Performing unnecessary or over-aggressive venesection that impairs oxygen delivery Failing to measure 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate and the oxygen dissociation curve in unexplained erythrocytosis Overlooking a high-affinity haemoglobin variant as an alternative explanation Bisphosphoglycerate mutase drives the Rapoport-Luebering shunt, converting 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, the principal regulator of haemoglobin oxygen affinity in the red cell. When the enzyme is deficient, 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate concentrations fall, shifting the oxygen dissociation curve to the left so that haemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly and releases less to the tissues. The consequent tissue hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin and produces a secondary erythrocytosis; because ATP-generating glycolysis is largely preserved, haemolysis is not a prominent feature. The prognosis is generally good; the erythrocytosis is a compensatory response to increased oxygen affinity and most patients remain well without specific intervention.

Diphtheria — Corynebacterium diphtheriae infection Group A streptococcal pharyngitis (exudative, but its exudate is not tightly adherent unlike the diphtheritic pseudomembrane) (p.1223) Group C streptococcal pharyngitis (p.1223) Respiratory virus pharyngitis (rhinovirus, influenza, parainfluenza, coronavirus, adenovirus) (p.1223) Herpes simplex virus and Epstein-Barr virus (infectious mononucleosis) pharyngitis (p.1223) Atypical bacterial pharyngitis (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae) (p.1223) Acute HIV infection, gonococcal pharyngitis, and fusobacterial infection / Lemierre's syndrome (p.1223) Candida (thrush) pharyngitis (p.1223) Corynebacterium ulcerans / C. pseudotuberculosis, which express the same toxin and cause diphtheria-like disease (p.1222) Culture of pseudomembrane fragments or submembranous swabs on selective medium (Loffler's or Tinsdale's, tellurite/colistin/nalidixic-acid based) plus nonselective medium such as blood agar (p.1223-1224) Histopathologic demonstration of compatible gram-positive organisms / characteristic local lesions (p.1223-1224) Notify the laboratory that diphtheria is being considered so special selective medium and biochemical differentiation from commensal corynebacteria are performed (p.1224) Toxigenicity testing; report all toxigenic C. diphtheriae isolates to the state health department (reportable disease) (p.1224) Nasopharyngeal culture in patients with cutaneous diphtheria (p.1224) Repeat throat culture ~2 weeks after completing antimicrobial therapy to document eradication (p.1224) Cardiac workup to assess for myocarditis (p.1225) Antitoxin (antibody) titer measurement after recovery, performed 6 months after antitoxin administration (p.1224) Respiratory diphtheria is clinically diagnosed by the constellation of sore throat, adherent tonsillar/pharyngeal/nasal pseudomembranous lesions, and low-grade fever (p.1223). The diphtheritic pseudomembrane is gray or whitish and sharply demarcated; unlike the exudate of streptococcal pharyngitis it is tightly adherent to underlying tissue, and attempts to dislodge it may cause bleeding (p.1223). A few patients develop 'bull-neck' diphtheria from edema of the submandibular and paratracheal region, with massive tonsillar swelling, foul breath, thick speech, and stridorous breathing (p.1223). Diphtheria should be considered in any patient with severe pharyngitis, especially with difficulty swallowing, respiratory compromise, or signs of systemic disease (myocarditis, generalized weakness); a pharyngeal pseudomembrane or extensive exudate should prompt consideration (p.1222-1223). Toxigenic strains most often cause pharyngeal disease, while nontoxigenic strains commonly cause cutaneous disease; in tropical latitudes cutaneous diphtheria is more common than respiratory diphtheria (p.1221-1222). Once a clinical diagnosis is made, diphtheria antitoxin should be obtained and administered as rapidly as possible because antitoxin cannot neutralize cell-bound toxin (p.1224). Hoarseness suggests laryngeal diphtheria, in which laryngoscopy may be diagnostically helpful (p.1223). Antibiotics in diphtheria are used primarily to prevent transmission to contacts and to halt further toxin production; they are not a substitute for antitoxin (p.1224). Patients who recover should be vaccinated, since natural infection does not reliably confer protective immunity; antitoxin levels should be measured (6 months after antitoxin administration) (p.1224). Neck (submandibular/paratracheal) edema and difficulty breathing in advanced cases carry a poor prognosis (p.1223) Airway obstruction is a major early risk and accounts for 60-65% of deaths, usually in the first 1-2 weeks; sloughing pseudomembranes may obstruct the airway or extend to larynx/tracheobronchial tree (children especially prone) (p.1224) Toxic cardiomyopathy/myocarditis (cardiac arrhythmias or congestive heart failure), a late manifestation arising >=1 week after respiratory symptoms, accounting for 20-25% of deaths (p.1223-1224) Bull-neck diphtheria, ventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, or complete heart block (p.1224) Polyneuropathy 3-5 weeks after onset: cranial nerve involvement (lingual/facial numbness, dysphonia, dysphagia), then weakness of respiratory and abdominal muscles, limb paresis, sensory ataxia, and autonomic dysfunction with hypotension (~15% of deaths) (p.1224) Large or extensive pseudomembranes and laryngeal/tracheal/bronchial involvement indicate severe disease and poor prognosis (p.1223-1224) Antitoxin cannot neutralize cell-bound toxin, so delay in administration worsens outcome; do not wait for laboratory confirmation once diphtheria is clinically suspected (p.1224). Antibiotics are not a substitute for antitoxin; they mainly prevent transmission and further toxin production (p.1224). Glucocorticoids have NOT been shown to reduce the risk of myocarditis or polyneuropathy (p.1225). Cutaneous diphtheria lesions are not characteristic and are indistinguishable from other dermatoses, so diagnosis requires laboratory confirmation; the punched-out appearance is only occasional, not consistent (p.1224). Corynebacterium pseudodiphtheriticum is a nontoxigenic normal throat commensal and does not pose significant risk; it must be differentiated from C. diphtheriae (p.1224). Drug-resistant and multidrug-resistant C. diphtheriae strains exist and are increasing; consider resistance when eradication efforts fail (p.1224). Natural infection does not reliably confer immunity, so survivors must be vaccinated (p.1224). Disease is driven by diphtheria toxin produced by toxigenic (tox+) strains of C. diphtheriae. The tox structural gene is carried by lysogenic corynebacteriophage beta, and nontoxigenic strains can be converted to the toxigenic phenotype; iron-limiting conditions optimize toxin expression. The toxin is a single-chain 535-amino-acid protein produced in the pharyngeal pseudomembranous lesion, taken up into the bloodstream and distributed to all organs. After binding its receptor (a heparin-binding EGF-like precursor) it is internalized by receptor-mediated endocytosis; the A fragment enters the cytosol and irreversibly inhibits protein synthesis via NAD+-dependent ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2, causing cell death. Pseudomembranes consist of an inner fibrin band and a luminal neutrophil band overlying toxin-induced mucosal ulcers with edema, hyperemia, and vascular congestion; initially white and firmly adherent, they turn gray/green/black as necrosis advances and may extend into bronchial airways (p.1221-1223). A systematic review of >20 outbreaks found a case-fatality ratio of 29% among unvaccinated, untreated individuals, with children under 5 at 1.5-fold higher mortality risk. Fatal pseudomembranous diphtheria typically occurs in unimmunized patients or those with nonprotective antibody titers. Risk factors for death include bull-neck diphtheria; myocarditis with ventricular tachycardia; atrial fibrillation; complete heart block; age >60 or <6 months; alcoholism; extensive pseudomembrane elongation; and laryngeal/tracheal/bronchial involvement. A key predictor of fatal outcome is the interval between onset of local disease and administration of antitoxin. Cutaneous diphtheria has a low mortality rate and is rarely associated with myocarditis or peripheral neuropathy. Polyneuropathy is typically reversible in patients who survive the acute phase (p.1224-1225). CDC case definitions: confirmed respiratory diphtheria (laboratory proven or epidemiologically linked to a culture-confirmed case) vs probable respiratory diphtheria (clinically compatible but not laboratory proven or epidemiologically linked). Carriers are individuals with positive C. diphtheriae cultures who are asymptomatic or symptomatic but lack pseudomembranes (p.1223).

the worm Assuming all megaloblastic anaemia is due to pernicious anaemia The adult Diphyllobothrium attaches by its bothria to the small-intestinal mucosa and can reach great length. Humans are infected by eating raw or undercooked fish harbouring the plerocercoid larva, which develops into the adult tapeworm over weeks. Positioned in the proximal small intestine, the worm competes with the host for luminal vitamin B12, binding and absorbing it far more efficiently than the host and thereby depleting available B12; with a favourably situated heavy worm, this can produce B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anaemia and, occasionally, subacute combined degeneration and other neurological manifestations. Local symptoms are otherwise mild and reflect the mechanical presence of the worm rather than tissue invasion. Excellent; the tapeworm is readily eradicated, and B12 deficiency with its haematological and neurological consequences resolves with treatment and vitamin replacement, though established neurological damage may only partly recover.

Dipylidiasis (Dipylidium caninum) — Dipylidium caninum infection, cucumber seed tapeworm infection, double-pored dog tapeworm disease, flea tapeworm infection Enterobiasis (pinworm) causing perianal irritation Taenia species tapeworm infection with proglottids in stool Hymenolepis nana or diminuta infection Threadworm or other cause of childhood pruritus ani Non-specific functional abdominal pain in children Anxiety over passage of undigested food mistaken for proglottids Macroscopic and microscopic identification of proglottids passed in stool Stool microscopy for the characteristic egg packets Perianal examination for migrating segments Full blood count, which may show mild eosinophilia History of pet ownership and flea infestation Repeat stool or proglottid examination if the first is inconclusive Caused by the dog and cat tapeworm Dipylidium caninum and seen mainly in infants and young children in close contact with flea-infested pets Infection follows accidental ingestion of an infected flea, which is the intermediate host carrying the larval cysticercoid Most children are asymptomatic; the usual presentation is the alarming discovery of motile, cucumber-seed-shaped proglottids in the stool, nappy or perianal area Symptomatic children may have mild abdominal discomfort, perianal irritation, restlessness or diarrhoea Diagnosis rests on identifying the characteristic proglottids or the distinctive egg packets rather than single eggs Praziquantel is highly effective, and a single course usually clears the infection Preventing reinfection requires treating pets for both tapeworms and fleas and improving hand hygiene Recurrent infection indicating ongoing exposure to infected fleas or untreated pets Significant weight loss or failure to thrive prompting search for another cause Persistent gastrointestinal symptoms after treatment Diagnostic uncertainty about the identity of passed segments Failing to treat the pet and its fleas, allowing repeated reinfection of the child Misidentifying proglottids as those of Taenia and misdirecting the diagnostic workup Searching for single eggs rather than the distinctive egg packets Overlooking the flea intermediate host when advising families on prevention Dipylidium caninum is a common tapeworm of dogs and cats whose life cycle depends on fleas (and occasionally chewing lice) as intermediate hosts. Flea larvae ingest tapeworm eggs from the environment, and the cysticercoid develops within the flea. Humans, typically young children, become accidental definitive hosts by swallowing an infected flea, often during close play with pets. The larva is released in the intestine and matures into an adult tapeworm attached to the small bowel mucosa, where it usually causes little more than mild local irritation. Gravid proglottids detach and migrate actively, and their emergence at the anus produces perianal itching and the visible cucumber-seed segments that prompt medical attention. The proglottids disintegrate to release characteristic egg packets, completing the cycle when ingested by flea larvae. Prognosis is excellent, with prompt cure after anthelmintic treatment and no long-term sequelae; the main issue is reinfection unless the pet and flea source is addressed.

sterility and exclude infection Skin biopsy showing neutrophilic pustular infiltrate Bone biopsy where infection cannot otherwise be excluded A recessively inherited monogenic autoinflammatory disease caused by loss-of-function mutations in IL1RN, which encodes the interleukin-1 receptor antagonist Presents in the neonatal period with pustular skin eruption, painful bone swelling, and systemic inflammation, typically without high spiking fever The hallmark is sterile multifocal osteomyelitis with periosteal reaction, often affecting the ribs and long bones, alongside widespread pustulosis Radiographs may show balloon-like widening of anterior ribs, multifocal osteolytic lesions, and periosteal new bone formation Inflammatory markers are markedly elevated but blood and bone cultures are sterile, reflecting an autoinflammatory rather than infective process Responds strikingly to interleukin-1 blockade, which replaces the missing antagonist and rapidly controls skin and bone disease Untreated disease can be fatal in infancy from systemic inflammatory complications, so early recognition is critical Overwhelming systemic inflammation in a neonate with respiratory compromise Extensive multifocal bone involvement causing pathological fracture or deformity Failure to thrive with unremitting inflammation despite antibiotics Life-threatening vasculitis or thrombosis complicating severe inflammation Misdiagnosing the sterile bone and skin lesions as infective osteomyelitis and pursuing prolonged antibiotics Delaying genetic testing and targeted IL-1 blockade while awaiting cultures Underestimating disease severity because high spiking fever may be absent Attributing the pustular rash to neonatal infection or common dermatoses DIRA arises from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in IL1RN, the gene encoding the naturally occurring interleukin-1 receptor antagonist. Without this antagonist, interleukin-1 alpha and beta signal unopposed through the IL-1 receptor, driving unchecked activation of neutrophils and pro-inflammatory pathways. The resulting excess of IL-1 signalling produces sterile neutrophilic inflammation in skin and bone, manifesting as pustulosis and multifocal osteomyelitis with periosteal reaction. Because the defect lies in a soluble regulatory protein, pharmacological IL-1 blockade effectively substitutes for the missing brake and reverses the disease. Untreated DIRA carries a high risk of death in infancy from systemic inflammation, but sustained interleukin-1 blockade generally induces durable remission of skin and bone disease with a good long-term outlook.

the skin Lichen planus, including follicular (lichen planopilaris) on the scalp Psoriasis or actinic keratoses on sun-exposed sites Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma arising within a chronic plaque features) indicating progression to systemic lupus Rapidly progressive scalp involvement threatening permanent scarring alopecia Features suggesting overlap with other connective tissue disease alopecia to other causes and delaying treatment until hair loss is irreversible Not screening for systemic lupus or overlooking its later emergence Missing malignant transformation within a chronic plaque Underestimating the cosmetic and psychological burden of facial scarring Discoid lupus erythematosus is a chronic autoimmune interface dermatitis in which ultraviolet light and other triggers provoke keratinocyte injury and expose nuclear antigens. A cytotoxic lymphocytic response targets the basal epidermis, producing vacuolar degeneration at the dermo-epidermal junction, follicular plugging, basement-membrane thickening, and a perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate. Immune complex and complement deposition at the junction can be demonstrated on direct immunofluorescence. Sustained inflammation destroys adnexal structures, leading to the scarring, atrophy, and permanent alopecia characteristic of established lesions. Genetic predisposition, ultraviolet exposure, and smoking all contribute. Skin-limited discoid lupus often follows a chronic relapsing course; with photoprotection and treatment many lesions become inactive, but scarring, dyspigmentation, and alopecia may be permanent, and a minority of patients evolve towards systemic lupus, warranting periodic review.

with serotyping and Shiga toxin testing to identify O157 STEC Scombroid (fish) poisoning, in which Proteus-mediated histamine generation in spoiled fish produces a histamine-toxicity syndrome rather than infection Adherent-invasive E. coli associated with Crohn disease (causal role unproven; does not produce acute diarrheal illness) The enteric gram-negative bacilli (GNB) that most often cause extraintestinal infection belong to the order Enterobacterales and include Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterobacter, Serratia, Citrobacter, Morganella, Providencia, Cronobacter, and Edwardsiella; Salmonella, Shigella, and Yersinia are covered separately as mainly enteric pathogens. Isolation of a GNB from a normally sterile site almost always signifies true infection, whereas recovery from nonsterile sites (open wounds, respiratory tract, catheterized urine) needs clinical correlation because it may represent only colonization. E. coli and, to a lesser extent, Klebsiella are the most virulent of this group and can cause severe disease even in previously healthy ambulatory people; the other genera behave mainly as opportunists in long-term-care and hospitalized patients. The urinary tract is the single most common extraintestinal site infected by extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli (ExPEC), and E. coli is the leading uropathogen across essentially all UTI syndromes and host groups. The urinary tract is also the most common source of E. coli bacteremia (roughly one-half to two-thirds of episodes); the abdomen is the second most common source (about one-quarter), and some abdominal sources such as abscesses can be clinically silent and require imaging. E. coli and group B Streptococcus are leading causes of neonatal meningitis; most neonatal E. coli meningitis strains carry the K1 capsular antigen, and ventriculomegaly is a common complication. Hypervirulent K. pneumoniae (hvKp), first recognized in Taiwan in 1986, classically presents as community-acquired monomicrobial pyogenic liver abscess in patients without prior hepatobiliary disease, often diabetic, with a striking tendency to spread metastatically (e.g., endophthalmitis, brain/splenic/prostatic abscess, meningitis, necrotizing fasciitis). Proteus produces urease, which hydrolyzes urea to ammonia and alkalinizes the urine; this promotes struvite and carbonate-apatite crystals, catheter biofilms, and staghorn calculi, and the organism typically cannot be cleared without removing the stone or catheter. Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) are classified by CDC and WHO as an urgent, critical-priority threat and were estimated to cause more than 100,000 deaths globally in 2019, with the heaviest burden in low- and middle-income regions such as the Indian subcontinent. Pneumonia, sepsis, and septic shock arising from any GNB focus are especially dangerous, carrying reported mortality rates of about 20 to 60 percent. Serratia marcescens is notable for environmental and outbreak associations (contaminated infusates, prefilled syringes, soaps, even chlorhexidine); some strains produce red pigment that can cause distinctive findings such as pink breast milk, pink hypopyon, or pseudohemoptysis. In children with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC/EHEC) infection, antibiotics should be avoided because they may increase the risk of hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS), and adequate volume expansion may help protect the kidneys. rather than true infection (e.g., asymptomatic bacteriuria or a positive sputum culture without pneumonia), which drives resistance and harm without benefit Attributing E. coli bacteremia to a urinary source in the absence of characteristic UTI signs, especially given high rates of asymptomatic bacteriuria in elderly and functionally compromised patients, thereby missing an occult abdominal focus resistance can emerge during therapy and cause clinical failure, particularly in bacteremia Giving antibiotics for STEC/EHEC infection, which may increase the incidence of HUS through increased Shiga toxin release Assuming carbapenems cover all Enterobacterales: Proteus, Morganella, and Providencia are intrinsically resistant to imipenem, and tetracycline derivatives and polymyxins are poorly active against the tribe Proteeae and Serratia and may achieve inadequate urine/blood levels Failing to achieve source control (abscess drainage, debridement of necrotic tissue, removal of infected foreign bodies), without which antimicrobial therapy often fails Empirical reliance on fluoroquinolones in critically ill patients, which is now unreliable given widespread GNB resistance often linked to ESBL production Enteric GNB are predominantly extracellular pathogens that normally reside in the colonic microbiota and environmental niches. Their outer membrane (lipopolysaccharide and capsule) is central both to virulence and to antimicrobial resistance via permeability barriers and efflux pumps. Disease requires accessory virulence genes: multiple adhesins (e.g., type 1, S, and F1C fimbriae and P pili in E. coli) for attachment; iron-acquisition systems (siderophores) and other nutrient-scavenging tools; capsule and O-antigen to resist complement and phagocytosis in the absence of antibody; and toxins (e.g., E. coli hemolysin) that cause tissue damage facilitating spread. The lipid A moiety of lipopolysaccharide acts as a PAMP that, through pattern-recognition receptors, can trigger an exuberant proinflammatory cascade leading to septic shock, with DAMPs such as HMGB1 propagating injury. Extensive antigenic variation (E. coli alone has more than 150 O, ~80 K, and ~53 H antigens) permits immune evasion and repeated infection and has hampered vaccine development. Host defenses are innate (intact skin/mucosa, complement, antimicrobial peptides, phagocytes, nutrient withholding) and humoral; impairment of these increases both susceptibility and severity. Intestinal pathogenic E. coli use distinct, pathotype-specific mechanisms (Shiga toxin, heat-stable/labile enterotoxins, attaching-and-effacing lesions, epithelial invasion, aggregative adherence). Outcomes correlate with severity of illness, underlying host status, and the resistance profile of the infecting organism, which can lead to suboptimal therapy. Pneumonia, sepsis, and septic shock from any GNB focus carry mortality rates of roughly 20 to 60 percent; ExPEC pneumonia specifically has high crude (20-60%) and attributable (10-20%) mortality. Uncomplicated cystitis is largely self-limited and rarely progresses, whereas pyelonephritis can take 5-7 days for fever to resolve even with effective therapy and only uncommonly causes renal parenchymal loss (mainly with obstruction). hvKp infections can be life- and organ-threatening even in young healthy hosts, with survivors often left with catastrophic sequelae such as vision loss or major neurologic deficits. Pandrug-resistant strains exist, and extensive resistance can leave few or no ideal therapeutic options. Disease is stratified clinically rather than by a single formal score: localized/uncomplicated infection (e.g., uncomplicated cystitis with dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain) versus systemic/severe infection (febrile or systemic UTI/urosepsis, pyelonephritis, prostatitis, pneumonia, bacteremia, sepsis syndrome defined as dysfunction of at least one organ/system, and septic shock). Resistance is graded as multidrug-resistant (MDR), extensively drug-resistant (XDR), and pandrug-resistant; resistance mechanisms range from broad-spectrum beta-lactamases through ESBLs and AmpC enzymes to carbapenemases (Ambler class A serine [KPC], class B metallo-beta-lactamases [NDM, VIM, IMP], and class D [OXA-48]).

the clinical history is central to evaluation (Harrison 22e p.2503). Dysphagia for both liquids and solids suggests a motility disorder such as achalasia, whereas dysphagia for solids alone suggests a structural lesion (stricture, web, ring, or tumor) (Harrison 22e p.2504). Patient localization of where food 'hangs up' is notoriously imprecise; about 30% of distal esophageal obstructions are perceived as cervical (neck) dysphagia (Harrison 22e p.2504). Intermittent solid-food dysphagia that is unchanged or slowly progressive over years points to a benign process (Schatzki ring or eosinophilic esophagitis), whereas dysphagia progressing over weeks to months raises concern for neoplasia (Harrison 22e p.295). Odynophagia is uncommon with reflux esophagitis; its presence should raise suspicion of an alternative etiology, particularly pill-induced or infectious esophagitis (Harrison 22e p.2505, p.2513). Achalasia is diagnosed by barium swallow and/or esophageal manometry; the barium study shows a dilated esophagus with poor emptying, an air-fluid level, and a tapered 'beak-like' narrowing at the LES (Harrison 22e p.2507). Manometric hallmarks of achalasia are impaired (incomplete) deglutitive LES relaxation plus absent peristalsis; manometry is the most sensitive test as it detects disease before esophageal dilatation (Harrison 22e p.2507-2508). Endoscopy is a necessary part of the achalasia evaluation to exclude pseudoachalasia from tumor infiltration at the cardia/distal esophagus, which accounts for up to 5% of suspected cases (Harrison 22e p.2507). The GERD injury spectrum progresses from esophagitis to stricture to Barrett metaplasia to adenocarcinoma; esophageal adenocarcinoma incidence is rising in parallel with GERD (Harrison 22e p.2509). Erosive esophagitis at the esophagogastric junction is the endoscopic hallmark of GERD but is found in only about one-third of GERD patients (Harrison 22e p.2510). Eosinophilic esophagitis should be strongly considered in children and adults presenting with dysphagia and food impaction, especially with an atopic history (Harrison 22e p.2511). EoE is confirmed histologically by esophageal mucosal eosinophilia with a peak density of 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, in the setting of esophageal symptoms (Harrison 22e p.2512). Progressive solid-food dysphagia with weight loss - classic presentation of esophageal cancer; warrants prompt endoscopy (Harrison 22e p.2507). Odynophagia (painful swallowing) - usually indicates ulceration; raises suspicion of pill-induced or infectious esophagitis (Harrison 22e p.295, p.2513). Iron-deficiency anemia / chronic occult GI bleeding accompanying esophageal symptoms. Hoarseness developing after dysphagia - may indicate recurrent laryngeal nerve compromise by malignancy (Harrison 22e p.295). Abrupt onset of symptoms (<1 year), advanced age, and weight loss in apparent achalasia - suggests pseudoachalasia from malignancy (Harrison 22e p.2507). Food impaction with inability to pass a bolus even with liquids - typical of structural dysphagia (Harrison 22e p.295). Severe cough with swallowing - may signal tracheoesophageal fistula. Finding of high-grade dysplasia in Barrett esophagus - high rate of progression to and coexisting prevalence of adenocarcinoma; mandates intervention (Harrison 22e p.2511). Treating presumed GERD empirically without recognizing that persistent dysphagia or chest pain may instead reflect eosinophilic esophagitis, peptic stricture, motility disorder, esophageal cancer, or coronary artery disease (Harrison 22e p.2510). Attributing 'heartburn' to GERD when the term is misused for indigestion or other sensations - clarify the patient's meaning (Harrison 22e p.2503). Assuming neck-localized dysphagia is oropharyngeal - about 30% of distal esophageal lesions refer pain proximally (Harrison 22e p.2504). Mistaking pseudoachalasia (tumor infiltration, up to 5% of cases) for primary achalasia - omit endoscopy at peril (Harrison 22e p.2507). Diagnosing distal esophageal spasm before excluding the more common peptic and infectious esophagitis and, above all, cardiac disease (Harrison 22e p.2509). Aggressive esophageal dilation in EoE - the stiff-walled esophagus risks deep mural laceration or perforation (Harrison 22e p.2512). Relying on peripheral blood eosinophilia (present in only 25-50%) or allergy testing (poor sensitivity/specificity) to diagnose EoE or identify trigger foods (Harrison 22e p.2512). Over-interpreting nonspecific minor manometric findings (hypertensive/hypotensive peristalsis) as a defined motility disorder; reflux and anxiety/depression are common in these patients (Harrison 22e p.2509). The esophagus is a muscular tube with a sphincter at each end (UES, LES) that transports food and otherwise remains empty. Disease manifests as impaired function (swallowing disorders, excessive gastroesophageal reflux) or pain. Dysphagia is subclassified by mechanism: structural/mechanical narrowing (lumen <13 mm reliably causes solid-food dysphagia) versus propulsive/motor disorders of peristalsis and deglutitive inhibition. In achalasia, autoimmune-mediated loss of myenteric plexus ganglion cells (involving both excitatory cholinergic and inhibitory nitric-oxide neurons), linked to latent HSV-1 infection plus genetic susceptibility, produces impaired deglutitive LES relaxation and absent peristalsis. GERD results from excessive reflux of gastric acid and pepsin causing a cytokine-mediated (rather than directly caustic) inflammatory mucosal injury; pathologic reflux follows progressive distortion of esophagogastric junction architecture (hiatus widening, loss of intraabdominal esophageal segment/flap valve, axial hiatal hernia, increased junction compliance) compounded by impaired acid clearance from disrupted peristalsis or reduced salivation. Eosinophilic esophagitis is an immunologic disorder driven by antigen (chiefly food allergen) sensitization in susceptible individuals, with eosinophil-predominant inflammation. (Harrison 22e p.2503, p.2506-2510, p.2511) Esophageal cancer carries poor survival even when small because abundant esophageal lymphatics permit early regional nodal metastasis. Barrett metaplasia progresses to adenocarcinoma at an estimated 0.1-0.3% per year through low- and high-grade dysplasia, with greatest risk in obese white males in the sixth decade. Untreated achalasia predisposes to stasis esophagitis and increases squamous cell cancer risk roughly 17-fold; durable therapies (pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy, POEM) achieve symptom relief in about 80-90% of patients, though peristalsis does not recover and chest pain responds less well than dysphagia. EoE is chronic with nearly universal recurrence on stopping therapy, requiring maintenance treatment. Erosive esophagitis and peptic strictures have become increasingly rare in the era of potent acid suppression. (Harrison 22e p.2507-2508, p.2510-2512) GERD esophageal injury spectrum: esophagitis -> stricture -> Barrett metaplasia -> adenocarcinoma; reflux testing defines GERD as esophageal pH <4 for >6% of the day. Barrett progression staged histologically as no dysplasia -> low-grade dysplasia -> high-grade dysplasia -> adenocarcinoma. High-resolution manometry differentiates three achalasia subtypes: type I classic (minimal esophageal-body pressurization), type II with esophageal compression/pressurization, and type III spastic achalasia. EoE histologic threshold: peak >=15 eosinophils per high-power field. (Harrison 22e p.2508-2511)
