pleural fluid tests: amylase (pancreatic disease/esophageal rupture), eosinophils (drug-induced), NT-proBNP (heart failure, >1500 pg/mL suggests cardiac origin), cholesterol/triglycerides (chylothorax, triglyceride >110 mg/dL), hematocrit (hemothorax), glucose and pH (rheumatoid disease), Congo red staining (amyloidosis), flow cytometry (lymphoma) TB markers: pleural fluid adenosine deaminase >40 IU/L or interferon-gamma >140 pg/mL; AFB culture, pleural biopsy CT/ultrasound-guided pleural biopsy or thoracoscopy when cytology is non-diagnostic CT angiography for suspected pulmonary embolism; lymphangiogram and chest CT for chylothorax without obvious trauma Pleural manometry to help confirm trapped lung Pulmonary embolism mimicking infectious pleuritis with an exudative effusion and pleuritic pain Malignant effusion (including mesothelioma) mimicking empyema or chronic infection Rheumatoid or lupus pleuritis mimicking infectious exudate (low glucose in rheumatoid disease) Pleural effusion ex vacuo / trapped lung mimicking persistent active disease The pleural space normally holds only a thin film of fluid acting as a coupling system, kept at roughly -3 to -5 cmH2O by the balance between lung elastic recoil (visceral pleura) and chest-wall outward expansion (parietal pleura). The first diagnostic step in any pleural effusion is distinguishing transudate from exudate via thoracentesis; this dictates whether further work-up is needed, since exudates require investigation to define their cause. Light's criteria define an exudate when at least one is met: pleural fluid/serum protein >0.5, pleural fluid/serum LDH >0.6, or pleural fluid LDH greater than two-thirds the upper normal serum limit; transudates meet none. Light's criteria misclassify about 25% of transudates as exudates ('pseudoexudates'), often in a diuresed transudate; a serum-to-pleural-fluid protein gradient >3.1 g/dL or albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL helps reclassify these (high sensitivity in heart failure and hepatothorax). Left ventricular failure is the single most common cause of pleural effusion (a transudate from raised hydrostatic pressure); cirrhosis is the next leading transudative cause in the United States. Parapneumonic effusions occur in up to 50% of community-acquired pneumonias and are generally the most common exudative effusion in the U.S.; about 10% become complicated or progress to empyema (fibrinopurulent or grossly purulent fluid). Malignant pleural effusions are the second most common exudate; lung carcinoma, breast carcinoma, and lymphoma together cause roughly 75% of cases, and dyspnea is often out of proportion to effusion size. Pulmonary embolism is the diagnosis most commonly overlooked in an undiagnosed exudative effusion; the fluid is almost always exudative and dyspnea is the predominant symptom. Tuberculous pleuritis arises largely as a hypersensitivity reaction to tuberculous protein in the pleural space and yields a lymphocyte-predominant exudate; pleural biopsy culture yield exceeds that of pleural fluid. Chylothorax produces milky fluid with a triglyceride level exceeding 110 mg/dL (1.2 mmol/L); prolonged chest-tube drainage should be avoided because chyle loss causes malnutrition and immunologic incompetence. Hemothorax is defined when pleural fluid hematocrit exceeds half the peripheral blood hematocrit; most are traumatic. About half of patients with an initial primary spontaneous pneumothorax (from rupture of apical subpleural blebs) will have a recurrence. Tension pneumothorax is a medical emergency: positive intrapleural pressure throughout the respiratory cycle impairs ventilation and reduces venous return, lowering cardiac output. Tension pneumothorax: enlarged hemithorax with absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, contralateral mediastinal shift, and hypotension; treat as an emergency with immediate needle decompression (large-bore needle in the second anterior intercostal space). Difficulty ventilating or high peak inspiratory pressures during mechanical ventilation/resuscitation strongly suggest tension pneumothorax. Complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema markers indicating need for drainage: loculated fluid, pleural fluid pH <7.20, glucose <60 mg/dL (<3.3 mmol/L), positive Gram stain or culture, gross pus, and elevated pleural fluid LDH (>900 IU/L). Hemothorax with ongoing pleural hemorrhage exceeding 200 mL/h warrants angiographic embolization, thoracoscopy, or thoracotomy. Secondary pneumothorax in a patient with underlying lung disease can be more life-threatening because of reduced pulmonary reserve. Relying on Light's criteria alone can misclassify roughly 25% of transudates as exudates; failing to apply protein/albumin gradients in a clinically transudative setting leads to unnecessary work-up. Overlooking pulmonary embolism as the cause of an otherwise undiagnosed exudative effusion. Being overly aggressive in pursuing a diagnosis in a clinically improving patient whose effusion is likely viral and self-limited. Failing to recognize trapped lung: a thick pleural rind, air on imaging after thoracentesis (pneumothorax ex vacuo), and rapid re-accumulation indicate a lung that will not re-expand without decortication. Prolonged tube thoracostomy drainage of a chylothorax, which can cause malnutrition and immunologic incompetence. Not performing diagnostic thoracentesis in a presumed heart-failure effusion that is unilateral, asymmetric, febrile, or pleuritic, or that persists despite therapy. Pleural fluid normally enters from parietal pleural capillaries and is cleared by parietal pleural lymphatics, which can absorb up to 20 times the normal rate of fluid formation; fluid can also enter from lung interstitium via the visceral pleura or from the peritoneal cavity through diaphragmatic openings. An effusion forms when the hydrostatic-oncotic balance is disturbed and fluid production overwhelms lymphatic removal. Transudates result from altered systemic factors (e.g., elevated left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure in heart failure raising hydrostatic pressure, or low oncotic pressure), whereas exudates result from altered local factors such as inflammation, infection, or malignancy increasing capillary permeability or impairing lymphatic drainage. Parapneumonic effusions begin as a sterile reactive exudate and can progress through exudative, fibrinopurulent, and organizing (pleural peel) phases. Hepatic hydrothorax reflects direct movement of ascitic fluid through small diaphragmatic defects into the pleural space. Pneumothorax results from gas entering the pleural space, abolishing the negative pressure that couples lung to chest wall; in tension pneumothorax a one-way mechanism produces sustained positive pleural pressure. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause. Transudative effusions from heart failure or cirrhosis improve when the primary condition is treated, and undiagnosed viral effusions usually resolve spontaneously without long-term residua. A malignant pleural effusion usually portends a poor prognosis (often less than 6-month survival) and reflects disseminated disease that is generally not curable with chemotherapy. Untreated complicated parapneumonic effusions can organize into a restrictive pleural peel (trapped lung). Tension pneumothorax is rapidly fatal from inadequate cardiac output or marked hypoxemia if not relieved. Surgical pleurodesis prevents pneumothorax recurrence in nearly 100% of cases. Parapneumonic effusions are staged along a continuum from simple (free-flowing, reactive) to complicated (loculated, pH <7.20, glucose <60 mg/dL, positive Gram stain/culture) to empyema (frank pus), with progression through exudative, fibrinopurulent, and organizing (pleural peel) phases guiding the need for escalating intervention. Pneumothorax is categorized as primary spontaneous, secondary, traumatic (including iatrogenic), and tension.

Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System — Male hypogonadism, Testicular failure, Testosterone deficiency syndrome, Androgen deficiency in men Erectile dysfunction without testosterone deficiency (the two are distinct disorders that may coexist) Self-limited (constitutional) delayed puberty versus congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in adolescents Hyperprolactinemia / prolactinoma causing secondary hypogonadism Hemochromatosis (pituitary and/or testicular iron deposition) Sellar mass lesions / pituitary adenoma impairing gonadotropin secretion Functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from systemic illness, malnutrition, eating disorders, or opioid use Androgen insensitivity / 5-alpha-reductase deficiency / aromatase (CYP19) deficiency Mumps orchitis (and orchitis from echovirus, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, group B arboviruses) causing acquired primary testicular failure HIV infection associated with low testosterone (primary or central) Lepromatous leprosy causing testicular atrophy through direct mycobacterial invasion Fasting early-morning total testosterone (LC-MS/MS preferred, CDC HoST-certified); repeat if borderline (200-400 ng/dL) and add free testosterone Free testosterone by equilibrium dialysis when SHBG is altered (aging, obesity, chronic illness) LH and FSH to separate primary (high LH/FSH) from secondary (low/inappropriately normal LH) hypogonadism Karyotype in men with low testosterone, elevated LH, and small testes to diagnose Klinefelter syndrome Serum prolactin and ferritin/transferrin saturation; pituitary MRI when secondary hypogonadism is found Inhibin B (Sertoli cell product) to assess seminiferous tubule integrity Semen analysis and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing (AZFa/AZFb/AZFc) in oligo-/azoospermia For gynecomastia: testosterone, estradiol, estrone, androstenedione, LH, hCG (beta), TSH; testicular ultrasound and adrenal/chest imaging if an estrogen- or hCG-secreting tumor is suspected Lipomastia (excess adipose) mimicking glandular gynecomastia Retractile testis mimicking cryptorchidism Age-related decline in testosterone overlapping with symptomatic hypogonadism Obesity-related lowering of total testosterone (with often normal free testosterone) due to reduced SHBG A low serum testosterone with an elevated LH localizes the defect to the testis (primary/hypergonadotropic hypogonadism), whereas a low or inappropriately normal LH points to a hypothalamic-pituitary defect (secondary/hypogonadotropic hypogonadism) (p.3107, p.3118). Acquired androgen-deficient men commonly report decreased libido, fewer sexual thoughts and acts, low energy, low mood, and (less often) hot flushes; eunuchoid body proportions (arm span >2 cm greater than height) indicate that deficiency predated epiphyseal fusion (p.3110). Klinefelter syndrome (classically 47,XXY) is the most common chromosomal cause of testicular dysfunction and male infertility, occurring in about 1 in 600 live-born males, with markedly small testes (often 1-2 mL), azoospermia, low testosterone, raised estradiol, undervirilization, and gynecomastia (p.3110, p.3114). True glandular gynecomastia (palpable firm, cord-like tissue >4 cm, often tender) reflects an increased estrogen-to-androgen ratio and must be distinguished from excess adipose (lipomastia); recent rapid onset, tenderness, or occurrence in a lean man warrants workup (p.3115). Testicular volume is a useful clinical index: normal adult testes are 3.5-5.5 cm long (about 12-25 mL by Prader orchidometer), and very small testes in a hypogonadal man should prompt a karyotype to exclude Klinefelter syndrome (p.3110, p.3119). Mumps is the classic cause of viral orchitis; orchitis develops in up to one-fourth of affected adult men, is unilateral in about two-thirds, and semen analysis normalizes in three-fourths after unilateral but only one-third after bilateral involvement (p.3114). Total testosterone can mislead when SHBG is altered (low in obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome; high in aging, hyperthyroidism, estrogen, HIV/hepatitis B and C, some anticonvulsants); measure free testosterone (ideally by equilibrium dialysis) in these settings (p.3106, p.3108). Cryptorchidism, even when corrected before puberty, carries increased risk of malignancy, infertility, inguinal hernia, and torsion, and is considered part of the testicular dysgenesis syndrome along with hypospadias, impaired spermatogenesis, and testicular cancer (p.3114). Selective elevation of FSH (with relatively normal LH) suggests seminiferous tubule/Sertoli cell damage, because reduced inhibin B removes the negative feedback restraining FSH (p.3104, p.3107). Up to two-thirds of pubertal boys and about half of hospitalized men have benign palpable breast tissue, so not all gynecomastia requires extensive investigation (p.3116). Kallmann syndrome is the anosmic form of congenital GnRH-deficient hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, arising from defective olfactory bulb morphogenesis and failed migration of GnRH neurons; micropenis and a history of cryptorchidism favor a congenital central defect over self-limited delayed puberty (p.3112, p.3110). Recent-onset, rapidly growing, or tender gynecomastia in a lean man, or breast tissue fixed to underlying tissue (evaluate for tumor/malignancy) Markedly elevated estradiol with suppressed LH, suggesting a testicular or adrenal estrogen-secreting tumor Elevated hCG (beta) prompting search for an hCG-producing germ cell or other tumor Very small testes with low testosterone and high LH (consider Klinefelter syndrome and its associated breast cancer risk) Diabetes insipidus accompanying hypogonadism, suggesting craniopharyngioma or infiltrative hypothalamic lesion Hyperprolactinemia with visual field defects suggesting a pituitary mass Relying on a single random or afternoon testosterone level — values are pulsatile, diurnal, lower in the late afternoon and after meals, and depressed by acute illness, so confirm with a fasting early-morning sample (p.3108, p.3118). Interpreting total testosterone without accounting for SHBG changes, leading to over- or under-diagnosis in obesity, aging, thyroid disease, or chronic illness (p.3106, p.3108). Mislabeling the normal aging decline as 'andropause' — there is no discrete andropause and population screening of all older men is not recommended (p.3117). Subjecting every man with gynecomastia to extensive workup, when most pubertal and many hospitalized men have benign glandular tissue (p.3116). Confusing retractile testis (no treatment needed) with true cryptorchidism (p.3114). Assuming corrected unilateral cryptorchidism guarantees normal fertility — sperm counts can remain reduced (p.3114). Overlooking drug, alcohol, opioid, marijuana, or anabolic-androgenic steroid use as reversible causes of suppressed testosterone (p.3114, p.3119). The hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis governs androgen production and spermatogenesis. Pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH (regulated by kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin in KNDy neurons) drives pituitary LH and FSH roughly every 1-3 h. LH stimulates Leydig cell testosterone synthesis (rate-limited by StAR-mediated cholesterol transport into mitochondria and CYP11A1 side-chain cleavage); FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis and inhibin B production, the latter selectively suppressing FSH. Testosterone is converted by 5-alpha-reductase (SRD5A2) to the more potent DHT (required for external genital virilization and prostate growth) and aromatized by CYP19 to estradiol (mediating effects on bone, epiphyseal closure, libido). Disorders arise from gonadotropin deficiency (secondary/hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, congenital such as GnRH-deficient/Kallmann syndrome or acquired from sellar masses, hyperprolactinemia, hemochromatosis, illness, drugs, obesity) or primary testicular failure (hypergonadotropic), e.g., Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, orchitis, chemo/radiation, torsion. Resistance syndromes (androgen receptor mutations, 5-alpha-reductase or aromatase deficiency) impair androgen action or conversion. Gynecomastia results from a relative excess of estrogen action on breast tissue (p.3102-3116). Outcomes depend on the underlying disorder. Secondary (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism is highly amenable to fertility restoration with pulsatile GnRH or gonadotropins, and 10-20% of congenital GnRH-deficient men may have spontaneous reversal in adulthood. In Klinefelter syndrome azoospermia is the rule, though sperm can sometimes be retrieved surgically (including in some non-mosaic men) for ICSI. After mumps orchitis the testis may recover or atrophy. Radiation effects on spermatogenesis are dose-dependent (transient decline below 1 Gy, temporary azoospermia at 1-2 Gy, usually permanent azoospermia above 2 Gy), while Leydig cells are relatively radioresistant (dysfunction generally only above 20 Gy). The age-related testosterone decline is gradual and progressive without a discrete abrupt fall (p.3107, p.3114-3115, p.3117). Diagnostic stratification of male testosterone deficiency (Harrison Fig. 403-8): early-morning total testosterone >350-400 ng/dL makes androgen deficiency unlikely; borderline values 200-350 ng/dL should be repeated with free testosterone; consistently low levels (notably <200 ng/dL) in association with symptoms confirm deficiency. Localization: high LH/FSH = primary (hypergonadotropic) testicular failure; low/inappropriately normal LH = secondary (hypogonadotropic). Harmonized normal total testosterone reference range in healthy young men is 264-916 ng/dL (p.3108, p.3117-3118).

Disorders of Ventilation — Alveolar hypoventilation, Hypoventilation syndromes, Chronic hyperventilation, Obesity hypoventilation syndrome, Central hypoventilation syndrome, Ondine's curse Parenchymal lung disease (obstructive such as COPD; restrictive such as interstitial lung disease; atelectasis; pulmonary embolus) Chest wall disorders (kyphoscoliosis, obesity, abdominal distention/ascites) Neuromuscular disease (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, phrenic nerve injury, spinal cord lesion, myopathy, muscular dystrophy) Depressed respiratory drive (narcotic/sedative use, brainstem stroke, hypothyroidism, primary alveolar hypoventilation) Brainstem structural lesions of the pons or medulla (stroke, tumor) Recurrent pneumonia from ineffective cough in neuromuscular disease can mimic or precipitate acute respiratory deterioration Arterial blood gas (the diagnostic hallmark): Paco2 >=45 mmHg defines hypoventilation; venous blood gas is an alternative, recognizing venous Pco2 runs a few points higher than arterial Serum bicarbonate (total CO2) as a sensitive but nonspecific screen: a level <27 mmol/L with normal renal function makes hypoventilation very unlikely, while >=27 mmol/L should prompt Paco2 measurement Chest x-ray and/or CT to identify lung/chest wall disease Pulmonary function testing including seated-versus-supine FVC (a 15-25% supine drop suggests diaphragmatic weakness) plus maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures Polysomnography to demonstrate nocturnal hypercapnia, central versus obstructive apneas/hypopneas, and to screen for OSA Brain CT or MRI to detect pontine/medullary structural lesions OSA screening tools (Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Berlin Questionnaire, STOP-Bang) recognizing their limited sensitivity/specificity Genetic testing for PHOX2b abnormalities in suspected congenital central hypoventilation syndrome Anxiety disorders and panic attacks (overlap with but are not equivalent to chronic hyperventilation) Mild asthma producing respiratory alkalosis (must be excluded before diagnosing chronic hyperventilation) Diabetic ketoacidosis presenting as acute hyperventilation Normal arterial CO2 (Paco2) sits between roughly 37 and 43 mmHg at sea level; all ventilatory disorders manifest as an abnormal Paco2 (Harrison 22e p.2273). Because Paco2 is governed by Paco2 = k(VCO2)/VA, every disturbance reflects altered CO2 production, minute ventilation, or dead-space fraction; a patient can breathe rapidly with a high minute ventilation yet still hypoventilate at the alveolar level if dead space is increased (Harrison 22e p.2273). Respiratory rhythm is generated in the brainstem (dorsal respiratory group and ventral respiratory column); the pre-Botzinger complex within the VRC is critical for inspiration, and its lesioning abolishes breathing entirely (Harrison 22e p.2273). Normal sleep brings an attenuated response to hypercapnia and hypoxemia, producing mild nocturnal hypoventilation that corrects on awakening (Harrison 22e p.2273). New-onset orthopnea is one of the earliest signs of reduced diaphragmatic force generation; 'paradoxical breathing' (abdomen moving inward on deep inspiration while supine) signals significant diaphragmatic weakness or paralysis (Harrison 22e p.2274). Chronic hypoventilation follows a characteristic sequence: an asymptomatic stage with normal daytime gases, then nocturnal hypoventilation appearing first in REM then non-REM sleep, then falling vital capacity, and finally daytime hypercapnia (Harrison 22e p.2274). The shared hallmark of all alveolar hypoventilation syndromes is a rise in alveolar and arterial Pco2 with a compensatory increase in plasma bicarbonate; the rising Paco2 displaces alveolar oxygen and commonly causes hypoxemia (Harrison 22e p.2274). Chronic hypoxemia from hypoventilation can drive secondary erythrocytosis, and the combination of chronic hypoxemia and hypercapnia can cause pulmonary vasoconstriction leading to pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular hypertrophy, and right heart failure (Harrison 22e p.2274). Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) requires BMI >=30 kg/m2 plus chronic daytime hypoventilation (Paco2 >=45 mmHg) with no other explanation; obstructive sleep apnea coexists in nearly 90% of cases, with about 70% having severe OSA (Harrison 22e p.2275). In OHS, the depressed ventilatory responsiveness appears to be a consequence rather than a primary cause, since central drive often improves once sleep-disordered breathing is treated without weight change (Harrison 22e p.2276). Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (Ondine's curse, CCHS) is linked to PHOX2b gene abnormalities; affected patients lack ventilatory responses to hypoxia/hypercapnia, have mild waking hypercapnia, markedly elevated Paco2 in non-REM sleep, yet can paradoxically normalize Paco2 during exercise and REM sleep (Harrison 22e p.2276). In chronic hyperventilation, anxiety/panic are not synonymous with the condition; sustaining hypocapnia needs only about a 10% increase in alveolar ventilation, achievable through subtle pattern changes such as occasional sigh breaths or frequent yawning (Harrison 22e p.2277). Paradoxical (abdominal) breathing while supine indicating significant diaphragmatic weakness or paralysis New-onset orthopnea heralding reduced respiratory muscle force in neuromuscular disease Progressive 15-25% supine fall in FVC signaling impending chronic respiratory failure Daytime hypercapnia developing on top of established nocturnal hypoventilation Signs of secondary erythrocytosis, pulmonary hypertension, or right heart failure from chronic hypoxemia/hypercapnia Equating high minute ventilation with adequate alveolar ventilation: increased dead space can produce alveolar hypoventilation despite rapid breathing (Harrison 22e p.2273). Diagnosing primary respiratory drive disorder without excluding far more common secondary causes such as sedatives, chronic narcotics, and significant hypothyroidism (Harrison 22e p.2275). Misattributing chronic hyperventilation symptoms to cardiopulmonary disease and failing to exclude acute causes (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis, mild asthma) before labeling it chronic (Harrison 22e p.2276-2277). Overlooking that supplemental oxygen, even at low concentrations, can worsen hypercapnia in some hypoventilating patients (Harrison 22e p.2276). Failing to recognize that a serum bicarbonate elevated out of proportion to chronic respiratory acidosis (excess metabolic alkalosis) can itself aggravate hypoventilation (Harrison 22e p.2276). Adequate ventilation depends on a balance between respiratory drive and neuromuscular strength on one side and the elastic plus resistive loads of the respiratory system on the other. Reduced drive, impaired neuromuscular competence, or a markedly increased load lowers effective minute ventilation and produces hypercapnia; conversely, normal muscle strength combined with excessive drive yields hyperventilation and hypocapnia. Diseases reducing minute ventilation or increasing dead space fall into four broad categories: parenchymal lung/chest wall disease, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular disease, and respiratory drive disorders. 'Pump failure' encompasses disorders of drive, neural pathways, the neuromuscular junction, and muscle. In OHS the mechanism is multifactorial, combining OSA, increased work of breathing, respiratory muscle impairment against an excess-adiposity load, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and blunted central responsiveness to hypoxemia and hypercapnia. Chronic hyperventilation is conceptualized as having initiating and sustaining factors, with an initial event dropping Paco2 toward ~20 mmHg and resultant symptoms perpetuating overbreathing (Harrison 22e p.2273-2277). Chronic hypercapnia in COPD marks more advanced disease and carries worse survival than in equally severe normocapnic patients. Documented daytime hypercapnia treated with nocturnal noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation is associated with improved daytime gas exchange, prolonged survival, and better health-related quality of life. In OHS with severe OSA, both CPAP and NIPPV improve long-term Paco2/bicarbonate and reduce cardiovascular and overall mortality. Progressive neuromuscular disease tends to advance from sleep-only to round-the-clock ventilatory support need, though modern home ventilation can delay tracheostomy and institutionalization (Harrison 22e p.2275-2276). Diagnostic thresholds rather than a formal grading scale: hypoventilation is defined by Paco2 >=45 mmHg; OHS requires BMI >=30 kg/m2 plus Paco2 >=45 mmHg without another cause; severe OSA is an apnea-hypopnea index >30 events/h; stable chronic hypercapnic COPD considered for home high-intensity ventilation typically has Paco2 >52 mmHg with normal pH (Harrison 22e p.2275-2276).

therapy, drainage of abscesses, and oral retinoid or biologic therapy in refractory disease, with surgery for scarred sinuses Extensive interconnecting sinuses with progressive scarring and keloid formation Signs of deep or systemic infection Long-standing disease with new indurated or non-healing areas, given the rare risk of squamous carcinoma Severe refractory disease affecting quality of life, prompting escalation to systemic therapy Treating recurrent nodules as isolated abscesses rather than recognising the interconnected disease Missing the association with hidradenitis suppurativa and other occlusion-tetrad conditions Under-treating with short antibiotic courses, allowing progression to scarring Overlooking the small long-term risk of malignant change in chronic sinuses Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp begins with follicular hyperkeratosis and occlusion, leading to follicular rupture, deep dermal and subcutaneous neutrophilic inflammation, abscess formation and interconnecting sinus tracts. Secondary bacterial colonisation amplifies the suppuration. As a component of the follicular occlusion tetrad it shares this pathogenic mechanism with hidradenitis suppurativa and acne conglobata. Chronic inflammation and sinus formation destroy follicles and produce extensive fibrosis with permanent, scarring alopecia. The course is chronic and relapsing with a tendency to permanent scarring alopecia and keloids; response to treatment is variable and often incomplete, and refractory disease may require systemic retinoids, biologics or surgery.

from bloodstream spread of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, often from an asymptomatic mucosal focus in the genital tract, rectum, or pharynx It classically presents in one of two overlapping forms: an arthritis-dermatitis (bacteraemic) syndrome and a localised purulent (septic) arthritis The arthritis-dermatitis form features migratory or additive polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis (often of the wrists, hands, and ankles), and scattered painful pustular or haemorrhagic skin lesions, usually with negative synovial cultures The purulent-arthritis form produces a frankly septic mono- or oligoarthritis with an inflammatory effusion from which the organism is more often recovered Because the responsible mucosal infection is frequently silent, a high index of suspicion and a full sexual history are needed, and it is comparatively more common in women Blood, synovial fluid, skin lesions, and all relevant mucosal sites should be sampled, using culture and nucleic acid amplification testing, with antimicrobial susceptibility testing given rising resistance Treatment is with a parenteral third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone, with joint drainage for purulent arthritis and coverage for co-existing chlamydia as guided by local policy Deficiency of terminal complement components (and functional or anatomical asplenia) predisposes to recurrent or disseminated neisserial infection and should prompt complement screening in recurrent cases Features suggesting gonococcal endocarditis or meningitis A hot, swollen, immobile joint indicating septic arthritis requiring urgent drainage Sepsis with haemodynamic compromise Recurrent disseminated neisserial infection pointing to terminal complement deficiency Rapidly evolving haemorrhagic or necrotic skin lesions Not considering disseminated gonococcal infection in a sexually active patient with polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, and pustular skin lesions Excluding the diagnosis because genital symptoms or mucosal cultures are absent, when the source is often silent Omitting sampling of all relevant mucosal sites and skin lesions, reducing diagnostic yield Failing to screen for terminal complement deficiency in recurrent cases Overlooking concurrent chlamydia or other sexually transmitted infection Disseminated gonococcal infection occurs when Neisseria gonorrhoeae invades from a mucosal surface into the bloodstream, a step favoured by particular gonococcal strains that resist normal serum bactericidal activity and by host factors. Circulating organisms and the immune response to them seed the skin, tenosynovium, and joints, producing an immune-complex-influenced arthritis-dermatitis picture in the early bacteraemic phase and, later or in other patients, direct bacterial seeding of a joint with suppurative arthritis. The organism's marked antigenic variation helps it evade immunity, while an intact terminal complement (membrane attack complex) pathway is critical for killing Neisseria, so individuals deficient in these complement components are strikingly susceptible to disseminated and recurrent neisserial disease. With prompt parenteral antibiotics and, where needed, joint drainage the outlook is generally very good and most patients recover fully, though delayed treatment of purulent arthritis can cause lasting joint damage, and rare complications such as endocarditis or meningitis carry higher risk.

disseminated intravascular coagulation — DIC, consumptive coagulopathy, defibrination syndrome thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura haemolytic uraemic syndrome severe hepatic failure with coagulopathy HELLP syndrome and other pregnancy-associated coagulopathies primary hyperfibrinolysis vitamin K deficiency or warfarin effect heparin-induced thrombocytopenia prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time fibrinogen level (interpreted as a trend, since it is an acute phase reactant) D-dimer or fibrin degradation products serial platelet count blood film for schistocytes and thrombocytopenia ISTH DIC score in a compatible clinical context investigations directed at the trigger (blood cultures and septic screen, imaging, obstetric assessment) DIC is never a primary disease; it is always secondary to an underlying disorder such as sepsis, major trauma, malignancy, obstetric catastrophe (abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, retained products), severe pancreatitis or extensive burns, and treating the trigger is the single most important intervention. There is simultaneous systemic activation of coagulation and fibrinolysis, so patients may present with bleeding, with microvascular and macrovascular thrombosis, or with both at once. The characteristic laboratory picture is a falling platelet count, prolonged prothrombin and activated partial thromboplastin times, a low or falling fibrinogen and markedly raised D-dimer or fibrin degradation products. The trend of serial results is far more informative than any single value; repeat testing over hours guides both diagnosis and component replacement. The ISTH scoring system, applied only when a compatible clinical setting is present, helps to separate overt (decompensated) from non-overt DIC. The blood film usually shows some fragmented red cells (schistocytes), but fragmentation is typically less florid than in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or haemolytic uraemic syndrome. Management is largely supportive and directed at the cause; blood component replacement is reserved for active bleeding or a high bleeding risk rather than for correcting numbers alone. A chronic, compensated form (classically with adenocarcinoma, giant haemangioma or a retained dead fetus) may present with thrombosis or migratory thrombophlebitis rather than bleeding. spontaneous bleeding from multiple unrelated sites including venepuncture and cannula sites purpura fulminans or rapidly spreading skin necrosis acral cyanosis or digital ischaemia progressing to gangrene new organ dysfunction (oliguria, hypoxaemia, altered consciousness) rapidly falling fibrinogen and platelet count on serial testing relying on a single set of results rather than the trend, so that early evolving DIC is missed interpreting a normal fibrinogen as reassuring when it is in fact falling from a high baseline as an acute phase reactant giving prophylactic component therapy to correct numbers in a non-bleeding patient rather than treating the cause overlooking the chronic compensated form that presents with thrombosis, so anticoagulation is withheld inappropriately failing to search actively for and treat the precipitating disorder DIC arises when a systemic stimulus, most often the release of tissue factor from injured or activated cells or from tumour, drives unregulated generation of thrombin throughout the microcirculation. Widespread thrombin activity converts fibrinogen to fibrin, deposits fibrin in small vessels and consumes platelets and clotting factors faster than they can be replaced. Natural anticoagulant pathways (antithrombin, protein C and tissue factor pathway inhibitor) are overwhelmed and depleted, and endothelial injury with impaired fibrinolytic regulation compounds the process. The resulting intravascular fibrin causes microvascular occlusion and organ dysfunction, mechanical fragmentation of red cells produces a microangiopathic haemolytic picture, and secondary reactive fibrinolysis generates large amounts of fibrin degradation products that themselves impair haemostasis. The net clinical effect is a paradoxical combination of thrombosis and consumptive bleeding. Outcome is dominated by the underlying cause and the degree of organ failure, and mortality is high when DIC complicates sepsis or multi-organ dysfunction. Prompt reversal of the trigger and supportive haematological care allow recovery when the precipitant is treatable.

infection caused by Mycobacterium avium complex, ubiquitous environmental organisms found in soil and water, acquired through inhalation or ingestion Disseminated disease occurs almost exclusively in profoundly immunocompromised hosts, classically people with advanced HIV and very low CD4 counts The typical presentation is insidious fever, night sweats, weight loss and wasting, fatigue, and abdominal symptoms with hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy Cytopenias (especially anaemia) and a raised alkaline phosphatase are common laboratory clues in advanced HIV Diagnosis is best confirmed by mycobacterial blood cultures, with bone marrow, lymph node, or liver biopsy showing acid-fast bacilli and granulomas as alternatives Treatment is prolonged combination antimycobacterial therapy (a macrolide-based regimen) together with antiretroviral therapy for immune restoration, and macrolide monotherapy must be avoided to prevent resistance Starting antiretroviral therapy can precipitate an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome with paradoxical worsening, particularly focal lymphadenitis Progressive wasting with high fevers in a patient with very low CD4 count Severe cytopenias from marrow infiltration Marked hepatosplenomegaly or bulky abdominal lymphadenopathy Paradoxical worsening after starting antiretroviral therapy suggesting immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome Features overlapping with disseminated tuberculosis requiring urgent differentiation Using macrolide monotherapy, which rapidly selects for resistance Failing to distinguish disseminated MAC from tuberculosis before committing to therapy Overlooking the diagnosis in a wasting, febrile patient with advanced HIV Not anticipating immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome when antiretroviral therapy is started Discontinuing therapy prematurely before adequate immune recovery is achieved Mycobacterium avium complex organisms are environmental mycobacteria encountered through water and soil, entering the body via the gastrointestinal or respiratory tract. In people with intact cell-mediated immunity infection is contained, but in those with profound immunosuppression, particularly advanced HIV with very low CD4 counts, the organisms proliferate within macrophages and disseminate widely through the reticuloendothelial system. Heavy infiltration of bone marrow, liver, spleen, gut, and lymph nodes with mycobacteria-laden macrophages produces the constitutional wasting, cytopenias, organomegaly, and cholestatic liver findings that characterise disseminated disease. With combination antimycobacterial therapy and immune restoration through antiretroviral treatment, disseminated MAC is generally controllable and prognosis has improved markedly, though outcomes remain worse with very advanced immunosuppression or delayed diagnosis.

Alternate cover testing, observing the covered eye elevate and the uncovered eye re-fixate downward Assessment in all positions of gaze to separate DVD from inferior oblique overaction Documentation of any associated latent nystagmus and abnormal head posture Attempted prism measurement, recognising the inherent variability, and testing under different fixation conditions Assessment of the associated horizontal deviation, usually an infantile esotropia Fundus torsion assessment and full orthoptic evaluation An anomalous eye movement in which the non-fixating or occluded eye drifts slowly upward, and often extorts, then returns downward when fixation is resumed; because it violates Hering's law it is not a true hypertropia Strongly associated with early-onset (infantile) esotropia and frequently accompanied by latent nystagmus, inferior oblique overaction and an abnormal head posture It is typically bilateral though often asymmetric: either eye elevates under cover, unlike a genuine unilateral hypertropia where covering either eye gives reciprocal movements consistent with Hering's law The hallmark on cover testing is that the covered eye elevates and, on uncovering, re-fixates and moves down without any corresponding downward movement of the fellow eye It frequently has no fixed measurement, being variable and dissociated, and may be brought out by fatigue or dissociation, with a Bielschowsky darkening phenomenon sometimes demonstrable It is usually asymptomatic and well controlled, so treatment (superior rectus recession or inferior oblique anterior transposition) is reserved for manifest, cosmetically or functionally significant deviations Distinguishing it from inferior oblique overaction is important: DVD elevates regardless of horizontal gaze and without a true contralateral hypotropia, whereas inferior oblique overaction elevates in adduction and obeys Hering's law It commonly coexists with other features of the infantile strabismus complex, so latent nystagmus and horizontal motility anomalies should be sought An acquired vertical deviation with neurological symptoms, prompting reconsideration of a paretic or central cause A constant large manifest deviation causing symptoms or poor cosmesis Diplopia, which is unusual in DVD and warrants reassessment Misdiagnosing DVD as a simple hypertropia and planning inappropriate surgery Confusing DVD with inferior oblique overaction by not testing adherence to Hering's law Expecting a fixed, reproducible measurement when the deviation is inherently variable Overlooking the associated latent nystagmus and infantile esotropia Operating on asymptomatic, well-controlled deviations Dissociated vertical deviation is an innervational anomaly that usually arises in the context of disrupted binocular development from early-onset strabismus. The upward drift of the covered or non-fixating eye does not obey Hering's law of equal innervation, indicating that it is not a simple vertical muscle imbalance but a dissociated, supranuclear innervational phenomenon. It has been linked to primitive dorsal light and righting reflexes and to the abnormal binocular development seen with infantile esotropia and latent nystagmus. The magnitude of the deviation is modulated by the degree of dissociation between the two eyes, for example under occlusion or with reduced visual input to one eye. DVD is usually benign and often subclinical, controlled by the child without symptoms; when manifest and significant, surgery reduces the deviation although it may not abolish it and can recur or require further procedures. It does not itself threaten vision beyond the amblyopia associated with the underlying infantile strabismus.

can correlate with neurological findings Hypotonia, foot deformities and variable facial dysmorphism are common Immune abnormalities, particularly IgA deficiency, occur and may predispose to infection Phenotype and severity vary with the size and breakpoint of the deletion Chromosomal microarray defines the deletion and its extent Significant hearing loss impairing communication and development Faltering growth suggesting growth hormone deficiency Recurrent or severe infection raising concern about immune deficiency Seizures or neurological deterioration requiring evaluation Missing conductive hearing loss and aural atresia that compound developmental difficulty Overlooking growth hormone deficiency as a treatable cause of short stature Failing to recognise IgA deficiency and other immune problems predisposing to infection Confusing the distal deletion with the proximal 18q deletion, which differs clinically Distal 18q deletion syndrome results from loss of the terminal long arm of chromosome 18, usually as a de novo terminal deletion of variable size, though unbalanced translocations also occur. It behaves as a contiguous-gene syndrome in which haploinsufficiency of multiple dosage-sensitive genes produces the neurodevelopmental, growth, auditory and immune features. Loss of genes influencing myelination is thought to contribute to the white-matter changes seen on imaging. The variability in deletion size and breakpoint largely accounts for the range of clinical severity. Most individuals have mild to moderate intellectual disability and can achieve meaningful function with early support, particularly when hearing loss is identified and managed and growth is optimised. Long-term outlook depends on the severity of the developmental, auditory and immune involvement, which correlates broadly with deletion size.

typically normal, and there is no progressive muscle weakness once contractures are established The hand posture is characteristic: a tightly clenched fist with the thumb held across the palm (cortical thumb) at birth Early passive stretching, serial casting and splinting improve range of motion, with surgical release reserved for fixed deformities Family examination and a three-generation pedigree are essential because the phenotype is often milder in relatives Feeding or respiratory difficulty in the neonate suggesting more widespread neuromuscular involvement Progressive weakness, which would point away from a static distal arthrogryposis toward a myopathy Facial involvement or micrognathia raising concern for a syndromic distal arthrogryposis Scoliosis developing during growth and requiring orthopaedic surveillance Assuming sporadic occurrence and missing a mildly affected parent, leading to inaccurate recurrence counselling Labelling the clubfoot as idiopathic and overlooking the associated hand contractures Delaying passive stretching and splinting, allowing contractures to become fixed Attributing the condition to a progressive muscle disease and initiating unnecessary investigation or treatment Distal arthrogryposis type 1 arises from pathogenic variants in genes coding for components of the fast-twitch skeletal muscle sarcomere, including beta-tropomyosin, troponin I and myosin-binding protein C. These variants disturb the regulation of the actin-myosin interaction and calcium sensitivity of contraction, altering muscle tone and force generation in the developing foetus. Reduced or unbalanced foetal movement (akinesia) during a critical window of limb development permits periarticular connective tissue to become fibrotic and joints to fixate in flexion, producing the congenital contractures of the hands and feet without a primary bone or nerve lesion. The prognosis is generally favourable, with normal intellect and lifespan; contractures are static and functional outcomes are good after physiotherapy and, where needed, orthopaedic surgery, though some residual deformity and reduced grip may persist.

troponin-tropomyosin-myosin complex (TNNI2, TNNT3, TPM2, MYH3). These variants perturb the calcium-regulated actin-myosin interaction, altering muscle tone during foetal development. Diminished and unbalanced foetal movement permits periarticular fibrosis and fixed distal joint contractures. Because it shares causative genes with Freeman-Sheldon syndrome and with distal arthrogryposis type 1, DA2B represents an intermediate point on a continuous phenotypic and genetic spectrum, corresponding clinically to Sheldon-Hall syndrome. The outlook is favourable, with normal intellect and lifespan; the contractures are static and respond well to physiotherapy and orthopaedic surgery, although some residual limb deformity may persist.

or spinal CMT Weakness usually begins in the feet and lower legs with foot drop and pes cavus, later involving the hands in many subtypes Numerous causative genes are recognised (for example HSPB1, HSPB8, GARS1, BSCL2, DYNC1H1), inherited in dominant, recessive or X-linked patterns Some subtypes have distinctive features such as predominant hand and upper-limb onset, vocal cord or diaphragmatic involvement, or pyramidal signs overlapping with hereditary spastic paraplegia and motor neuron disease Nerve conduction studies show reduced motor amplitudes with preserved sensory responses, and EMG confirms chronic denervation Sensory nerve action potentials being normal is the key electrophysiological discriminator from CMT Management is supportive, with physiotherapy, orthoses (e.g. ankle-foot orthoses), footwear and occupational therapy Prominent or progressing upper motor neuron signs and bulbar involvement suggesting motor neuron disease Diaphragmatic weakness causing respiratory compromise in specific subtypes Vocal cord paralysis with stridor or airway risk Rapid progression or conduction block pointing to a treatable acquired neuropathy Labelling the condition Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease without noting the preserved sensory responses that define dHMN Missing a treatable acquired motor neuropathy such as multifocal motor neuropathy Overlooking respiratory or vocal cord involvement in subtypes where it occurs Failing to recognise overlap with motor neuron disease when pyramidal signs are present The distal hereditary motor neuropathies are inherited disorders in which the pathology is largely restricted to the motor system, involving distal motor axons and/or anterior horn cells with relative sparing of sensory neurons. The many causative genes converge on core neuronal processes essential for long motor axons, including axonal transport (for example dynein and kinesin components), protein folding and chaperone function (small heat-shock proteins such as HSPB1 and HSPB8), aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase activity (GARS1) and lipid metabolism (BSCL2). Disruption of these pathways causes a length-dependent, dying-back degeneration of the longest motor fibres, producing progressive distal weakness and wasting. Most distal hereditary motor neuropathies progress slowly, remain confined to the distal limbs and do not shorten life; disability arises mainly from foot drop, hand weakness and deformity, though rare subtypes with respiratory or bulbar involvement carry a more serious outlook.

involvement Conduction block indicating potentially treatable multifocal motor neuropathy Sensory loss, which should prompt reconsideration of the pure motor diagnosis Missing treatable multifocal motor neuropathy, which can mimic distal motor neuropathy Confusing early hand wasting with motor neurone disease Overlooking the shared GARS spectrum with CMT2D Attributing pure motor weakness to a myopathy without electrophysiology Distal hereditary motor neuropathy type V is a dominantly inherited motor axonopathy caused by variants in genes such as GARS, which encodes glycyl-tRNA synthetase, and BSCL2, which encodes seipin. Glycyl-tRNA synthetase is required for protein translation and appears to have additional roles in the axon; pathogenic variants are thought to exert a toxic effect that preferentially damages the longest and most metabolically demanding motor axons, especially those supplying intrinsic hand muscles. Typically slowly progressive with disability largely confined to distal limb function; ambulation is usually preserved and life expectancy is normal.

Distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis, hereditary — type 1 RTA, classic distal RTA, SLC4A1, ATP6V0A4, ATP6V1B1 Proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis and Fanconi syndrome Type 4 (hyperkalaemic) renal tubular acidosis from hypoaldosteronism Gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss from chronic diarrhoea Acquired distal RTA from Sjogren syndrome or other autoimmune disease Medullary sponge kidney with nephrocalcinosis Toxin- or drug-induced distal tubular dysfunction Serum electrolytes, bicarbonate and calculation of a normal serum anion gap Simultaneous urine pH and assessment of urinary anion gap or ammonium excretion Ammonium chloride or furosemide-fludrocortisone acidification testing where diagnosis is unclear Renal ultrasound or CT for nephrocalcinosis and stones Audiometry to detect associated sensorineural hearing loss Targeted genetic testing of SLC4A1, ATP6V1B1 and ATP6V0A4 Hereditary distal RTA reflects a failure of the distal nephron to secrete hydrogen ions, producing a normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis The hallmark biochemical clue is an inappropriately alkaline urine (pH persistently high) despite systemic acidosis Hypokalaemia is characteristic and can cause muscle weakness, and profound hypokalaemia may precipitate paralysis or arrhythmia Chronic acidosis mobilises bone buffer, causing hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia and consequent nephrocalcinosis and stone formation Autosomal recessive forms (ATP6V1B1, ATP6V0A4) are often associated with sensorineural hearing loss and present early; autosomal dominant SLC4A1 disease is generally milder Children may present with failure to thrive, rickets and polyuria, whereas adults may present with stones, osteomalacia or unexplained hypokalaemia Alkali replacement (for example potassium citrate or bicarbonate) corrects the acidosis, replaces potassium and raises citrate to limit nephrocalcinosis Severe hypokalaemia causing muscle paralysis or cardiac arrhythmia Failure to thrive or rickets in an infant or young child Progressive nephrocalcinosis with declining renal function Obstructing stone with infection requiring urgent intervention Missing the diagnosis by not measuring urine pH during systemic acidosis, when it should be inappropriately high Overlooking associated hearing loss in recessive forms Attributing the hypokalaemia to diuretics or diarrhoea rather than tubular loss Correcting acidosis with sodium bicarbonate alone and worsening hypokalaemia by not replacing potassium Type 1 (distal) renal tubular acidosis arises from impaired hydrogen ion secretion by the alpha-intercalated cells of the collecting duct. Inherited forms result from mutations affecting the apical H+-ATPase (ATP6V1B1, ATP6V0A4) or the basolateral chloride-bicarbonate exchanger AE1 (SLC4A1). Because the distal nephron cannot generate a steep enough pH gradient, net acid excretion falls and a hyperchloraemic normal anion gap acidosis develops with inappropriately alkaline urine. Persistent acidosis drives calcium out of bone, raises urinary calcium and lowers citrate, promoting nephrocalcinosis and stones, while potassium wasting produces hypokalaemia. With sustained alkali and potassium replacement, growth, bone health and biochemistry usually improve and stone or nephrocalcinosis progression slows, though established nephrocalcinosis and chronic kidney impairment may persist.

Distichiasis — accessory eyelash row Trichiasis Entropion Epiblepharon Cicatricial conjunctival disease Chronic blepharitis Slit-lamp examination identifying lashes from meibomian orifices Assessment of corneal involvement with fluorescein Family history and examination for limb lymphoedema (lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome) Genetic evaluation where a hereditary syndrome is suspected Assessment for underlying cicatrising disease in acquired cases An abnormal additional row of eyelashes emerging from the meibomian gland orifices along the posterior lid margin These aberrant lashes are often finer and less pigmented and may rub on the cornea causing irritation It may be congenital, sometimes inherited, or acquired following chronic lid inflammation or cicatrisation The congenital form is associated with lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome linked to FOXC2 mutations It should be distinguished from trichiasis, in which normally sited lashes are misdirected Treatment targets the aberrant follicles with cryotherapy, electrolysis or lid-splitting procedures Corneal abrasion or scarring threatening vision Associated lymphoedema suggesting a genetic syndrome Progressive cicatrising conjunctival disease Extensive or recurrent aberrant lashes Confusing distichiasis with trichiasis, which differ in origin and treatment Missing lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome and its cardiovascular associations Overlooking corneal damage Simple epilation alone, which is followed by regrowth Distichiasis arises when meibomian glands, which are modified sebaceous glands, differentiate abnormally into complete pilosebaceous units that produce lashes from the posterior lid margin. In the congenital form this reflects a developmental abnormality, classically with FOXC2 mutations in lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome, whereas acquired distichiasis follows metaplasia of the glands after chronic inflammation or cicatrising conjunctival disease. The posteriorly placed lashes can abrade the ocular surface, causing irritation and, if chronic, corneal damage. Vision is preserved with appropriate follicle-directed treatment, though recurrence can occur; the associated lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome carries its own systemic implications.

Disturbances of Respiratory Function — Respiratory dysfunction, Disorders of lung ventilation and gas exchange, Pulmonary physiology disturbances Restrictive pattern from increased lung elastic recoil (e.g., idiopathic/interstitial pulmonary fibrosis) Restrictive pattern from chest-wall abnormality (e.g., obesity, kyphoscoliosis) Restrictive pattern from respiratory muscle weakness (e.g., myasthenia gravis, diaphragmatic paralysis, neuromuscular disease) Obstructive pattern from airway narrowing (e.g., asthma, chronic bronchitis) Obstructive pattern from loss of elastic recoil (e.g., emphysema) Pulmonary vascular disease (suggested by isolated low DLCO with otherwise preserved volumes) Upper/central airway obstruction (e.g., tracheal adenoma, post-tracheostomy stricture, tracheomalacia) Pneumonia or other alveolar-filling processes reduce respiratory system compliance and increase work of breathing, mimicking other causes of restrictive dyspnea Spirometry (FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC, flow-volume loop) to characterize obstructive vs restrictive physiology and localize airway obstruction Absolute lung volumes by inert-gas (helium/neon) dilution or body plethysmography (plethysmography preferred in airflow obstruction, as dilution underestimates trapped gas) Single-breath diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) Arterial blood gas with calculation of the alveolar-arterial oxygen tension difference (A-a)DO2 and the alveolar gas equation Pulse oximetry for noninvasive hemoglobin saturation; capnography (end-tidal CO2) for noninvasive ventilation assessment Maximal inspiratory/expiratory mouth pressures and supine-vs-upright FVC to detect respiratory muscle / diaphragmatic weakness Chest imaging: ultrasound, plain radiograph (PA and lateral), CT (with contrast and/or PET when indicated) Further studies as guided by suspicion: bronchoscopy with lavage/biopsy, hypercoagulable and serologic testing, sputum analysis, echocardiography, surgical lung biopsy Pulmonary edema (alveolar filling reducing compliance) Anemia (lowers DLCO and oxygen content, mimicking a gas-transfer defect) Polycythemia or pulmonary hemorrhage (can elevate DLCO) Obstructive sleep apnea with associated pulmonary arterial hypertension lowering DLCO in an obese patient Cardiac causes of dyspnea (enlarged heart functioning as part of the chest-wall load) The respiratory system can be conceptualized as three functionally independent components: the lung (with its airways), the neuromuscular system (the force generated by respiratory muscles), and the chest wall (everything else, including the muscle mass itself, an obese abdomen, and an enlarged heart). Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the passive resting volume where outward recoil of the chest wall is exactly balanced by inward recoil of the lung; at FRC, negative intrapleural pressure offsets positive intrapulmonary pressure giving an airway pressure of 0. The combined respiratory system pressure-volume relationship is sigmoid: stiffness at high lung volumes is imparted by the lung, stiffness at low volumes by the chest wall (or airway closure), with compliance greatest in the mid-range where normal tidal breathing occurs. Expiratory airflow limitation is a normal lung property arising from collapsible (not rigid) bronchial airways: as gas accelerates toward the mouth the Bernoulli effect lowers intraluminal and transmural pressure, narrowing the airway, so harder effort yields no net increase in flow. Inspiratory airflow limitation is rarely caused by diffuse intrathoracic airway disease because more negative pleural pressure during inspiration increases airway transmural pressure and expands airways; instead, inspiratory flow limitation points toward extrathoracic/upper-airway narrowing (e.g., tracheal lesion, post-tracheostomy stricture). Adequacy of alveolar ventilation is reflected in PaCO2: alveolar and arterial CO2 tensions are equal, the controller normally targets ~40 mmHg, so PaCO2 below 40 indicates hyperventilation and above 40 indicates hypoventilation, with ventilatory failure being extreme hypoventilation. Only the tidal volume that exceeds the anatomic dead space delivers fresh gas to alveoli; dead space is increased functionally when ventilated lung receives no perfusion (e.g., distal to a large pulmonary embolus), 'wasting' that ventilation. Oxygen uptake in normal lung is perfusion-limited rather than diffusion-limited: hemoglobin is typically fully saturated by the time blood traverses only about one-third of the alveolar capillary. Hypoxemia from true shunt (perfusion of nonventilated lung) is refractory to supplemental oxygen, whereas hypoxemia from ventilation/perfusion heterogeneity (low V/Q regions) typically improves with oxygen therapy — a key bedside discriminator. DLCO interpretation: it falls in diseases that thicken or destroy alveolar membrane (pulmonary fibrosis, emphysema), curtail the pulmonary vasculature (pulmonary hypertension), or reduce capillary hemoglobin (anemia); it can be elevated in asthma, polycythemia, and pulmonary hemorrhage. In severe airflow obstruction, slowed expiratory flow prevents complete exhalation, raising operating FRC (dynamic hyperinflation / auto-PEEP); at these high volumes the system is less compliant, so the patient senses difficulty INHALING even though the root problem is EXPIRATORY obstruction. A normal FEV1/FVC ratio does not exclude airflow obstruction: obstruction can raise residual volume and lower FVC, rendering the ratio 'artifactually normal' — lung volumes should scale together (~85-115% predicted) in health, so disproportion is a clue. Hypoxemia refractory to supplemental oxygen, suggesting true shunt physiology rather than simple V/Q mismatch Rising PaCO2 above 40 mmHg indicating alveolar hypoventilation, with extreme elevation signaling impending ventilatory failure Inspiratory flow plateau on the flow-volume loop, indicating extrathoracic/upper-airway obstruction Precipitous fall in PaO2 on exertion in emphysema, reflecting inability to raise cardiac output across a destroyed pulmonary vascular bed Supine FVC decrement greater than about 10-25% (versus the normal 3-8%) indicating significant diaphragmatic/neuromuscular weakness Isolated reduction in DLCO with preserved spirometry and volumes, prompting evaluation for pulmonary vascular disease Interpreting a normal FEV1/FVC ratio as excluding obstruction when raised RV has lowered FVC and made the ratio artifactually normal Relying on single-breath inert-gas dilution in airflow obstruction, which underestimates true lung volumes because poorly ventilated regions do not receive the inert gas Assuming alveolar hypoventilation alone explains severe hypoxemia at sea level breathing air — the alveolar gas equation shows this is uncommon unless barometric pressure is reduced (altitude) Forgetting that a normal chest radiograph does not exclude respiratory disease, especially airway and pulmonary vascular disorders Attributing a low DLCO to parenchymal disease without considering anemia, while overlooking that DLCO may be elevated in polycythemia or pulmonary hemorrhage Misreading dyspnea on inhalation in severe obstruction as a primary inspiratory problem when it stems from dynamic hyperinflation due to expiratory flow limitation Effective respiration requires tidal ventilation to freshen alveolar gas, perfusion of each alveolus proportional to its ventilation, and adequate diffusion of O2 and CO2 across the thin alveolar membrane (roughly 70 m2 of surface in about 7 L of thorax via multigenerational airway and vascular branching). Ventilation depends on the volume-related (elastic/static) and flow-related (dynamic) mechanical properties of lung, neuromuscular system, and chest wall; lung recoil rises with inflation while the passive chest wall stiffens at low volume. Disease deranges these properties in a limited number of ways: increased lung elastic recoil restricts volumes (e.g., idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis lowers TLC/FRC/RV/FVC and DLCO but raises flow relative to volume); chest-wall abnormality (e.g., moderate obesity) blunts outward chest recoil and lowers FRC; reduced muscle strength (e.g., myasthenia gravis) lowers TLC and raises RV, reducing FVC/FEV1 as bystanders; decreased airway diameter (e.g., acute asthma) raises resistance and scoops the flow-volume loop; and decreased elastic recoil (e.g., severe emphysema) causes hyperinflation with very elevated TLC/FRC/RV and reduced DLCO. Gas-exchange failure (hypoxemia) results from low inspired oxygen tension, severe alveolar hypoventilation, perfusion of low-V/Q or unventilated (shunt) units, and, rarely, diffusion limitation; shunt blood disproportionately lowers arterial PaO2 because of the nonlinear oxyhemoglobin relationship. Hypercarbia accompanies disorders of ventilation, including severe obstruction and progressive restriction. Prognosis is determined by the underlying disorder rather than the physiologic pattern itself; the same abnormalities may arise from very different diseases, so pulmonary function testing alone often cannot discriminate among conditions. Many functional disturbances are reversible (e.g., bronchodilator-responsive airflow obstruction in acute asthma), whereas others reflect fixed structural loss (e.g., capillary and alveolar destruction in emphysema or fibrosis) that progressively impairs gas exchange and exercise capacity. No single formal severity grade applies; physiologic severity is judged by the degree of deviation from predicted values. Most lung-function measures are normal at 85-115% of predicted, and in health volumes scale together. Examples of marked derangement cited include severe emphysema (TLC ~130%, RV ~310%, FEV1 ~35% predicted, low DLCO ~40%) versus pulmonary fibrosis (TLC/FVC/FRC/RV ~60%, low DLCO). Airway resistance (Raw) is normally <2 cmH2O/L/s, and maximal mouth pressures >±60 cmH2O at FRC make significant muscle weakness unlikely.

Disulfiram-ethanol reaction — disulfiram reaction, Antabuse reaction, acetaldehyde syndrome, disulfiram-alcohol reaction, disulfiram-like reaction Anaphylaxis or anaphylactoid reaction Acute coronary syndrome (chest pain and diaphoresis) Carcinoid syndrome or other flushing disorders Vasovagal or panic reaction Sepsis with vasodilatation Other drug-induced flushing reactions Clinical diagnosis based on the temporal relationship to alcohol intake Blood pressure and cardiac monitoring during the reaction Electrocardiogram to assess for arrhythmia or ischaemia in severe cases Electrolytes and hydration status Careful history of hidden alcohol sources and disulfiram-like agents Blood alcohol concentration where diagnosis is unclear Occurs when alcohol is consumed by a patient taking disulfiram, used as a deterrent in alcohol dependence Symptoms begin within minutes of alcohol ingestion and include flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting, sweating, palpitations and chest tightness More severe reactions cause marked hypotension, tachycardia, dyspnoea and, rarely, arrhythmias or cardiovascular collapse The reaction is caused by accumulation of acetaldehyde due to inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase Similar 'disulfiram-like' reactions can be provoked by metronidazole, certain cephalosporins and other agents Patients must be counselled to avoid all sources of alcohol including some mouthwashes, tonics and topical or oral preparations Management is supportive, with fluids and antiemetics; there is no specific antidote and the reaction is self-limiting as acetaldehyde is cleared The enzyme inhibition is long-lasting, so reactions can occur for up to two weeks after stopping disulfiram Profound or refractory hypotension Chest pain or signs of myocardial ischaemia Significant arrhythmia Depressed consciousness or respiratory compromise Failing to warn patients about hidden sources of alcohol in mouthwashes, tonics and topical preparations Not recognising that metronidazole and some cephalosporins cause a similar reaction Assuming safety immediately after stopping disulfiram despite persisting enzyme inhibition Mistaking a severe reaction for acute coronary syndrome and overlooking the drug-alcohol interaction Ethanol is normally metabolised to acetaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase, and acetaldehyde is then oxidised to acetate by aldehyde dehydrogenase. Disulfiram irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so when alcohol is consumed, acetaldehyde accumulates to concentrations many times higher than normal. Acetaldehyde is a potent vasoactive and toxic intermediate that causes cutaneous vasodilatation, catecholamine and histamine effects, and stimulation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone, producing the flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia and hypotension of the reaction. Because the enzyme inhibition is irreversible, recovery of aldehyde dehydrogenase activity depends on synthesis of new enzyme, explaining the prolonged period of susceptibility after the drug is stopped. Most reactions are unpleasant but self-limiting, resolving over hours as acetaldehyde is metabolised. Severe reactions with marked hypotension or cardiac effects can occasionally be life-threatening, particularly in patients with cardiovascular disease.

threatening maternal and fetal wellbeing Treating a pustular flare as bacterial infection and missing the autoinflammatory diagnosis Abruptly withdrawing systemic corticosteroids, which can precipitate a severe flare Failing to recognise generalised pustular psoriasis as distinct from plaque psoriasis Overlooking metabolic and fluid derangements during extensive skin involvement DITRA results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in IL36RN, encoding the interleukin-36 receptor antagonist. Loss of this antagonist removes the normal brake on interleukin-36 signalling, so IL-36 cytokines drive amplified activation of keratinocytes and recruitment of neutrophils. The resulting cytokine cascade, involving downstream interleukin-8, interleukin-17 and interleukin-23 pathways, produces the sterile neutrophilic pustulosis and systemic inflammation characteristic of generalised pustular psoriasis. Because IL-36 signalling is central, biologics targeting this and related axes can control disease. The disease follows a relapsing-remitting course; individual flares can be severe or life-threatening, but targeted anti-cytokine therapy has improved control and long-term outcomes for many patients.
