In the common age-related form, degenerative changes in the orbital connective-tissue pulleys and extraocular muscle mechanics are thought to contribute. Because reduced divergence can also result from pontine or cerebellar disease and from raised intracranial pressure, a secondary neurological cause must be considered when onset is acute or accompanied by other signs. The benign age-related form is generally stable and responds well to prisms; prognosis in secondary cases depends on the underlying neurological cause.

Diverticular Disease — diverticulitis, diverticulosis Colorectal cancer (parallel epidemiology and overlapping presentation; must exclude with colonoscopy after an episode) Irritable bowel syndrome (SCAD can mimic it) Crohn's disease (diverticulitis can be confused with CD clinically and radiographically) Appendicitis Ischemic colitis Twisted ovarian cyst / gynecologic pathology Acute appendicitis Infectious colitis Pelvic inflammatory disease / tubo-ovarian abscess Contrast-enhanced abdominal/pelvic CT (diagnostic modality of choice for diverticulitis) Multiplanar CT angiography for active diverticular bleeding localization Nuclear medicine tagged red-cell scan for bleeding localization Mesenteric angiography (allows superselective coil embolization if active bleeding is localized) Colonoscopy ~6 weeks after resolution to exclude malignancy (avoid during the acute attack) CRP and WBC count to gauge inflammation/disease progression risk Colorectal cancer Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis) Irritable bowel syndrome Ischemic colitis Giant sigmoid diverticulum (air-fluid level in LLQ on plain film) Diverticulosis is the most common cause of hematochezia (brisk lower-GI bleed) in patients >60 years; bleeding is abrupt in onset, usually painless, sometimes massive, and often from the right colon. Chronic or occult bleeding is NOT characteristic (Harrison 22e p.2496, 2579). Only ~20% of patients with diverticulosis will ever have GI bleeding; most bleeds are self-limited and stop spontaneously with bowel rest (colonic diverticula stop bleeding spontaneously in >=90% of patients). Lifetime risk of rebleeding is ~25% (Harrison 22e p.2496, 2579). Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis characteristically presents with fever, anorexia, left lower quadrant abdominal pain, and obstipation (Harrison 22e p.2579). Diagnosis of diverticulitis is best made on a contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT showing sigmoid diverticula, thickened colonic wall >4 mm, and pericolic fat inflammation WITHOUT extravasation of contrast or fluid (Harrison 22e p.2579). Diverticula commonly affect the left and sigmoid colon and the rectum is always spared; however in Asian populations 70% of diverticula are in the right colon and cecum (Harrison 22e p.2579). The pseudodiverticulum (protrusion of mucosa and submucosa only, through the muscularis propria) is the most common type seen in the colon; a true diverticulum is herniation of the entire bowel wall (Harrison 22e p.2578). Perforated diverticular disease is staged using the Hinchey classification (I: confined paracolic abscess; II: distant/pelvic abscess after spontaneous closure; III: noncommunicating perforation with purulent peritonitis; IV: free perforation with fecal peritonitis); modified to add stage Ia for phlegmon/early abscess (Harrison 22e p.2580). Pneumaturia or passage of stool/air through the vagina or skin signals a fistula (colovesical, colovaginal, or colocutaneous); colovaginal fistulas are more common in women who have undergone hysterectomy (Harrison 22e p.2579). Colonoscopy should be considered ~6 weeks AFTER resolution of a first episode, because colon cancer prevalence is low overall (<2%) but higher after complicated diverticulitis (6-8%) (Harrison 22e p.2580). Routine antibiotics do NOT shorten time to symptom resolution or reduce complications/recurrence in immunocompetent patients with uncomplicated diverticular disease (AVOD and DIABOLO trials, plus meta-analysis) (Harrison 22e p.2580). Diverticulosis affects about half the population aged >60 years and the majority remain asymptomatic; only ~5% develop acute diverticular disease (Harrison 22e p.2578). Signs of peritonitis indicating diverticular perforation Abscess formation (~16% of complicated disease) with abdominal distention and localized peritonitis Free perforation with fecal peritonitis (Hinchey IV) Fistula (colovesical with pneumaturia, colovaginal, colocutaneous) Obstruction/stricture Air-fluid level in LLQ on plain film suggesting giant sigmoid diverticulum (impending perforation) Massive or refractory lower-GI hemorrhage, hemodynamic instability, or large-volume transfusion requirement Immunocompromise, chronic renal failure, or collagen-vascular disease (fivefold greater perforation risk on recurrent attacks) Do NOT perform colonoscopy during acute diverticulitis (risk of perforation); defer it ~6 weeks until the attack resolves. Do not reflexively give antibiotics for uncomplicated diverticulitis in immunocompetent patients - trials show no benefit. The historical advice to avoid nuts, corn, and popcorn rests on anecdotal data only and is not evidence-based; higher intake was actually associated with lower recurrence risk. Mesalazine appears to help symptoms in SUDD but shows no benefit once objective inflammation (CRP, imaging) is considered. A systematic review found no benefit to probiotics used alone. Right-sided diverticula predominate in Asian populations, so a right-colon source should not be dismissed. Diverticula form where the nutrient artery (vasa recta) penetrates the muscularis propria, creating a point of weakness in the colonic wall; most arise in the sigmoid colon, likely reflecting its high-pressure zone where higher-amplitude contractions and firm/constipated stool act on a weak segment. Pathogenesis is now viewed as multifactorial rather than simply low-fiber diet: gut dysbiosis, chronic low-grade inflammation driving neuronal degeneration with resulting dysmotility and high intraluminal pressure, and abnormal collagen cross-linking causing loss of compliance all contribute. Genome-wide association studies (Iceland, Denmark, UK biobanks) link LAMB4 (extracellular-matrix laminin family) and TNFSF15 (TNF family, inflammation) variants to early-onset severe disease. Complications occur when the vasa recta is compressed or eroded (bleeding) or a diverticulum perforates (Harrison 22e p.2578-2579). Most patients with diverticulosis stay asymptomatic; only ~5% develop acute diverticular disease, and 10-25% of those with diverticular disease have recurrent symptoms with up to 10% requiring surgery. Diverticular bleeds are largely self-limited (spontaneous cessation in >=90%), with lifetime rebleeding risk ~25%. After complicated diverticulitis the risk of underlying colon cancer rises to 6-8% (vs <2% overall). Elective surgical resection for recurrent SUDD improved quality of life and was more cost-effective at 5 years (DIRECT trial) (Harrison 22e p.2578-2581). Hinchey classification of perforated diverticulitis: Stage I - perforation with confined paracolic abscess (modified stage Ia = phlegmon/early abscess); Stage II - perforation that closed spontaneously with distant (pelvic) abscess; Stage III - noncommunicating perforation with purulent peritonitis (diverticular neck closed off); Stage IV - free perforation communicating with the peritoneum producing fecal peritonitis. Clinically, disease is divided into uncomplicated (~75%) and complicated (~25%: abscess 16%, perforation 10%, stricture 5%, fistula 2%) (Harrison 22e p.2579-2580).

Diabetic ketoacidosis — Venous gas Blood & urine ketones Glucose, electrolytes Search for precipitant (infection) DKA protocol; look for precipitating infection Alcoholic ketoacidosis — high-anion-gap acidosis (predominantly beta-hydroxybutyrate) without hyperglycaemia, usually with preserved renal function, in chronic alcohol use with vomiting and poor intake (p.413). Starvation ketoacidosis — ketoacidosis with normal or low glucose (p.413). Other high-anion-gap acidoses: lactic acidosis, toxic ingestions (e.g. salicylates), and renal failure/uraemia (p.413). Plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate measured directly (more reliable than urine nitroprusside ketones) (p.413). Anion gap calculation, including assessment for a mixed non-anion-gap / high-anion-gap acidosis when the change in bicarbonate exceeds the change in anion gap (p.413). Acute pancreatitis can mimic DKA (and vice versa), with overlapping abdominal pain; DKA may itself be accompanied by amylase elevation, complicating the distinction (p.2788). An acetone-like fruity odour on the breath is a classic bedside clue to ketoacidosis (p.93). Urine dipstick (nitroprusside reaction) detects acetoacetate but not beta-hydroxybutyrate, so it can underestimate the true degree of ketosis; measure plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate directly (p.413). As the circulation is restored with fluids, beta-hydroxybutyrate is converted to acetoacetate, so the nitroprusside ketone reading may paradoxically become more positive during treatment rather than reflecting worsening disease (p.413). Glucose may be normal or only mildly raised in euglycaemic DKA (SGLT2-inhibitor associated) and in starvation ketoacidosis, so a normal glucose does not exclude ketoacidosis (p.413). Excretion of ketoacids obligates loss of cations (sodium, potassium), worsening volume depletion and promoting chloride retention (p.413). Mucormycosis risk: DKA patients are at high risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis; acidosis frees iron from carrier proteins and beta-hydroxybutyrate upregulates fungal adherence/penetration receptors — consider in a DKA patient with sinus/orbital/facial signs (p.1761). Severe acidaemia (pH <7.00) or shock identifies the small subset where bicarbonate may be considered; cerebral oedema risk limits its use (p.413). Hyperchloraemic (non-anion-gap) acidosis and volume overload can be precipitated by aggressive isotonic saline during treatment (p.413). Relying on urine ketone dipstick, which misses beta-hydroxybutyrate and underestimates ketosis (p.413). Interpreting a rising nitroprusside ketone result during fluid resuscitation as deterioration, when it reflects the beta-hydroxybutyrate-to-acetoacetate shift (p.413). Assuming a normal/near-normal glucose excludes DKA, missing euglycaemic DKA on SGLT2 inhibitors (p.413). Over-resuscitation with isotonic saline causing volume overload and/or hyperchloraemic acidosis (p.413). DKA results from increased fatty acid metabolism with accumulation of the ketoacids acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, producing hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia and a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. It typically occurs in insulin-dependent diabetes when insulin is stopped or when an intercurrent illness (e.g. infection, gastroenteritis, pancreatitis, myocardial infarction) acutely raises insulin requirements. In euglycaemic DKA caused by SGLT2 inhibitors, glycosuria drives an osmotic diuresis and volume depletion while plasma glucose stays in the normal range despite the ketoacidosis (p.413).

early-onset severe infection Lymphopenia or abnormal lymphocyte function on screening A family history of early childhood death from infection or consanguinity Mistaking the picture for a purely antibody deficiency and delaying definitive treatment Underestimating the antiviral defect and giving live vaccines Attributing recurrent infection to environmental exposure rather than an inborn error Delaying referral for transplantation while infections accumulate Relying on lymphocyte counts alone, which may be misleadingly preserved DOCK2 is a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor expressed mainly in haematopoietic cells that activates the small GTPase Rac, thereby controlling reorganisation of the actin cytoskeleton. This actin remodelling underlies many leucocyte functions: the migration of lymphocytes and neutrophils toward chemokines, the formation of the immunological synapse during T-cell activation, B-cell responses, and natural killer cell and interferon-driven antiviral defence. When DOCK2 is absent, lymphocytes and phagocytes cannot properly polarise, move, or signal, so adaptive and innate responses are broadly impaired. The result is a combined immunodeficiency in which affected children fail to contain bacterial, viral, and fungal pathogens, with the antiviral deficit being especially prominent. Untreated, the disorder carries a poor prognosis with early life-threatening infection; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offers the prospect of cure and is the treatment of choice, with outcomes best when undertaken early before infective damage accumulates.

reticulum enzyme that phosphorylates dolichol to dolichol phosphate. Deficiency limits precursor assembly and transfer, giving under-occupied N-glycosylation sites and a type I transferrin pattern. Impaired glycosylation and O-mannosylation of cardiac and other structural proteins is thought to underlie the characteristic dilated cardiomyopathy and, in severe forms, the cutaneous and neurological features. Prognosis is largely determined by the cardiomyopathy, which can progress to end-stage heart failure and early death; the severe multisystem form carries high infant mortality, whereas more isolated cardiac disease may be amenable to heart failure treatment or transplantation.

when pathogenic variants affect proteins important to both Schwann cells and axons, so that myelination and axonal integrity are simultaneously compromised. Dynamin 2 (DNM2) participates in membrane trafficking and cytoskeletal regulation; tyrosyl-tRNA synthetase (YARS) is required for protein synthesis and appears to have additional axonal functions; INF2 regulates actin dynamics in both nerve and kidney. Because both the myelin sheath and the axon are affected, conduction slowing is only moderate and response amplitudes are reduced, producing velocities intermediate between the markedly slow demyelinating range and the near-normal axonal range. The mixed pathology also explains the wide intrafamilial variability. Generally slowly progressive with preserved ambulation in most patients, though severity varies by gene and variant. Associated organ involvement, particularly renal disease with INF2, can influence overall outcome.

systemic features of DOA-plus Dominant optic atrophy usually results from heterozygous mutations in OPA1, a nuclear-encoded protein embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane that governs mitochondrial fusion, cristae architecture and control of programmed cell death. Impaired mitochondrial dynamics render the metabolically demanding retinal ganglion cells vulnerable, with preferential degeneration of the small fibres of the papillomacular bundle. The result is progressive loss of ganglion cells and their axons, clinically expressed as central visual and colour deficits with temporal disc pallor. Because the mechanism is one of haploinsufficiency or a dominant-negative effect with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity, phenotype ranges from asymptomatic carriers to severe syndromic disease. Vision usually declines slowly and often stabilises at a moderate level, with most patients retaining useful sight, though a minority progress to legal blindness and DOA-plus cases carry additional systemic morbidity.

with a congenital infection Donohue syndrome results from severe loss-of-function mutations in both copies of the insulin receptor gene (INSR), so insulin can bind but cannot transmit its signal. Insulin normally suppresses hepatic glucose output and promotes tissue glucose uptake and growth; when receptor signalling is almost absent, tissues cannot use glucose or grow normally despite grossly elevated insulin concentrations. This produces intrauterine growth restriction, near-total loss of adipose tissue and muscle, and a paradoxical glucose profile of fasting hypoglycaemia (from insulin's residual and IGF-mediated effects and poor counter-regulation) with severe postprandial hyperglycaemia. Impaired insulin/IGF signalling also underlies the dysmorphism, hypertrichosis, and organ abnormalities. Prognosis is poor, with most affected infants dying within the first one to two years of life from metabolic instability and infection, although recombinant IGF-1-based therapy may modestly improve metabolic control and survival in some children.

Donovanosis — Granuloma inguinale, Granuloma venereum Primary syphilitic chancre (Harrison 22e p.1357) Secondary syphilis with condylomata lata (Harrison 22e p.1357) Chancroid (Harrison 22e p.1357) Lymphogranuloma venereum (Harrison 22e p.1357) Genital herpes (Harrison 22e p.1357) Genital neoplasm / carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.1357) Amebiasis (Harrison 22e p.1357) Rhinoscleroma on histology (Harrison 22e p.1357) Leishmaniasis on histology (Harrison 22e p.1357) Histoplasmosis on histology (Harrison 22e p.1357) Tissue smear for Donovan bodies stained with rapid Giemsa or Wright stain (Harrison 22e p.1357) Crush preparation of granulation tissue spread between two slides (Harrison 22e p.1357) Histologic biopsy showing chronic inflammation, microabscesses, and rete ridge elongation (Harrison 22e p.1357) phoE gene PCR with colorimetric detection to differentiate K. granulomatis from related Klebsiella species (Harrison 22e p.1357) Multiplex genital-ulcer PCR including K. granulomatis (Harrison 22e p.1357) Cervical carcinoma (cervical lesions may mimic it) (Harrison 22e p.1357) Genital neoplasm (Harrison 22e p.1357) Chronic, progressive bacterial infection that predominantly involves the genital region and is regarded as a sexually transmitted infection of low infectivity (Harrison 22e p.1356). Caused by Klebsiella granulomatis comb nov; the older name Calymmatobacterium granulomatis is still favored by some authorities based on 16S rRNA gene sequence analysis (Harrison 22e p.1356). Diagnosis is confirmed by microscopic identification of intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies (about 1.5 x 0.7 micrometers) within large mononuclear Pund cells, where they appear as gram-negative cysts with a characteristic safety-pin appearance (Harrison 22e p.1356-1357). When donovanosis is suspected clinically, the smear for Donovan bodies should be obtained before swabs for other genital ulcer pathogens so adequate material is collected; smears can be read at the bedside with rapid Giemsa or Wright stain (Harrison 22e p.1357). An experienced clinician's diagnosis based on lesion appearance has a high positive predictive value, and donovanosis is probably the most readily recognizable cause of genital ulceration (Harrison 22e p.1357-1358). Four lesion types are described: classic beefy-red ulcerogranulomatous ulcer that bleeds easily on touch, hypertrophic/verrucous ulcer with a raised irregular edge, necrotic foul-smelling destructive ulcer, and sclerotic/cicatricial fibrous lesion (Harrison 22e p.1357). Genitalia are affected in about 90% of patients and the inguinal region in about 10%; lymphadenitis is uncommon, in contrast to other ulcerative STIs (Harrison 22e p.1357). Cervical lesions can mimic cervical carcinoma, and in men lesions are associated with lack of circumcision (Harrison 22e p.1357). Extragenital lesions occur in about 6% of cases and may involve the lip, gums, cheek, palate, pharynx, larynx, and chest; hematogenous spread to liver and bone has been reported (Harrison 22e p.1357). Donovanosis is a recognized risk factor for HIV infection, and its global decline likely reflects more effective management of genital ulcers given their role in HIV transmission (Harrison 22e p.1357). The estimated incubation period is approximately 50 days based on experimental human infection, though it remains uncertain (Harrison 22e p.1357). A diagnostic PCR exploits two unique base changes in the phoE gene that eliminate Hae111 restriction sites, distinguishing K. granulomatis from related Klebsiella species; a multiplex genital-ulcer PCR including K. granulomatis exists (Harrison 22e p.1357). Late presentation with extensive ulceration (Harrison 22e p.1357-1358) Cervical lesion mimicking carcinoma requiring exclusion of malignancy (Harrison 22e p.1357) Neoplastic change developing within chronic lesions (Harrison 22e p.1357) Stenosis of the urethra, vagina, or anus (Harrison 22e p.1357) Pseudoelephantiasis from lymphatic involvement (Harrison 22e p.1357) Lesions in newborns (may present as ear infection) or children, prompting evaluation for source of infection (Harrison 22e p.1357) Collecting other genital-ulcer swabs before the Donovan body smear can leave insufficient material for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1357). Serologic tests are only poorly specific and are not currently used, so they should not be relied upon (Harrison 22e p.1357). Mixed infections with other genital ulcer pathogens are common and may obscure the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1357). Lymphadenitis is uncommon, so its absence should not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1357). Cervical lesions can be mistaken for cervical carcinoma and vice versa (Harrison 22e p.1357). During pregnancy lesions develop more quickly and respond more slowly, so closer monitoring is needed (Harrison 22e p.1357). Donovanosis is a chronic granulomatous infection caused by the intracellular gram-negative organism Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium granulomatis). The lesion begins as a papule or subcutaneous nodule that ulcerates, often after trauma. The organism resides within macrophages and the stratum malpighii as intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies inside large mononuclear (Pund) cells; these cysts rupture and release infective organisms. Histology shows chronic inflammation with infiltration by plasma cells and neutrophils, and epithelial changes including ulceration, microabscesses, and elongation of the rete ridges. The organism resisted reproducible culture until the mid-1990s, when isolation in peripheral-blood monocytes and human epithelial cell lines was achieved (Harrison 22e p.1356-1357). Donovanosis is a treatable condition, and reassurance is an important part of care given the embarrassment and low self-esteem many patients experience. It is now confined to a few specific geographic locations, has been almost entirely eliminated in Australia and is close to elimination in South Africa, and its global eradication is considered a distinct possibility. Surgery may be required for very advanced lesions, and patients treated for shorter courses require monitoring until lesions heal completely (Harrison 22e p.1357-1358). No formal severity grading is given. Lesions are categorized morphologically into four types: classic ulcerogranulomatous, hypertrophic/verrucous, necrotic/destructive, and sclerotic/cicatricial (Harrison 22e p.1357).

Doose syndrome — Myoclonic-atonic epilepsy, Myoclonic-astatic epilepsy, Epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures Lennox-Gastaut syndrome Childhood absence epilepsy Dravet syndrome Epilepsy with myoclonic absences GLUT1 deficiency syndrome Progressive myoclonic epilepsies Eyelid myoclonia with absences (Jeavons) Video-EEG capturing ictal drop attacks and interictal discharges MRI brain, usually normal, to exclude a structural cause Genetic testing including SLC2A1 and epilepsy gene panels CSF-to-blood glucose ratio or SLC2A1 analysis for GLUT1 deficiency Metabolic screening where the presentation is atypical Neuropsychological assessment Genetic generalised epilepsy of early childhood characterised by myoclonic, atonic and combined myoclonic-atonic (drop) seizures. Onset is usually between 1 and 5 years in a previously normal child, with a male predominance. Drop attacks from myoclonic-atonic seizures cause frequent falls and injury. EEG shows generalised spike-wave and polyspike-wave, often with a biparietal or central theta rhythm; the background may initially be normal. Generalised tonic-clonic and absence seizures frequently coexist, and non-convulsive status epilepticus can occur. Ketogenic dietary therapy is notably effective and is often introduced early. Sodium-channel-blocking drugs and vigabatrin may aggravate seizures and are generally avoided. Outcome ranges from seizure freedom with normal cognition to refractory epilepsy with intellectual impairment. Frequent injurious drop attacks Cognitive or behavioural regression Non-convulsive status epilepticus with fluctuating responsiveness Seizure aggravation after starting an antiseizure medication Confusing it with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, which features tonic seizures, slow spike-wave and a worse prognosis. Using sodium-channel blockers that may worsen seizures. Missing GLUT1 deficiency, which is amenable to ketogenic therapy. Overlooking non-convulsive status as a cause of apparent regression. Doose syndrome is a genetically influenced generalised epilepsy in which thalamocortical network hyperexcitability produces bilaterally synchronous epileptic discharges. The basis is usually polygenic, with monogenic contributions in a minority, including SLC2A1 (GLUT1 deficiency), SCN1A and others; GLUT1 deficiency is important to identify because it responds to ketogenic therapy. The combination of positive (myoclonic) and negative (atonic) motor phenomena reflects rapidly generalising cortical discharges. Highly variable; a substantial proportion achieve seizure freedom with preserved cognition, while others develop drug-resistant epilepsy and intellectual disability. Early effective treatment, including the ketogenic diet, may improve outcome.

neurotransmitter and pterin analysis and by phenylalanine loading, and confirmed by molecular genetic testing Unlike most dystonias the disorder is eminently treatable, so recognition carries a high clinical payoff Diurnally fluctuating dystonia in a child that has been labelled cerebral palsy without a levodopa trial Progressive dystonia with developmental regression suggesting a broader neurotransmitter disorder Severe generalised dystonia impairing gait, feeding, or respiration Failure to respond to an adequate levodopa trial, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Failing to undertake a levodopa trial in young-onset dystonia and thereby missing an eminently treatable disorder Accepting a longstanding label of cerebral palsy or spastic paraplegia without questioning atypical features such as diurnal fluctuation Attributing a partial or absent response to inadequate trial duration rather than reassessing the diagnosis Overlooking the recessive tyrosine hydroxylase and sepiapterin reductase forms, which may have a more complex phenotype Dopa-responsive dystonia is a disorder of dopamine biosynthesis. In the common autosomal dominant form, variants in GCH1 reduce GTP cyclohydrolase 1 activity, the first and rate-limiting step in producing tetrahydrobiopterin, the essential cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase. Reduced cofactor availability lowers dopamine synthesis in nigrostriatal neurons without causing their degeneration, so the deficit is biochemical rather than structural. Because the neurons remain intact, replacing the downstream product with levodopa restores near-normal dopaminergic signalling, explaining the sustained and complete response and the absence of levodopa-related motor complications. With levodopa treatment the prognosis is excellent: most patients achieve near-complete, durable symptom control and normal or near-normal function, and the benefit is sustained for decades without the motor complications typical of Parkinson disease. Untreated, symptoms progress and cause significant disability.

hypoglycaemia, and collapse Recurrent syncope with injury Severe exercise intolerance limiting daily function Coexisting supine hypertension complicating treatment Missing this treatable diagnosis in a young person with severe orthostatic hypotension Not measuring plasma catecholamines to reveal the characteristic dopamine-to-noradrenaline profile Confusing it with pure autonomic failure or multiple system atrophy Overlooking supine hypertension that can arise during treatment Dopamine beta-hydroxylase is the enzyme that converts dopamine to noradrenaline within sympathetic nerve terminals and the adrenal medulla. In dopamine beta-hydroxylase deficiency, biallelic loss-of-function variants abolish enzyme activity, so noradrenaline and adrenaline cannot be produced and dopamine is released instead from sympathetic nerves. The absence of noradrenergic vasoconstriction causes severe orthostatic hypotension, while excess circulating dopamine may contribute to renal and other effects. Parasympathetic and cholinergic sympathetic (sudomotor) functions, which do not depend on this enzyme, are preserved. Because the defect is a single missing biosynthetic step, supplying a precursor that is decarboxylated directly to noradrenaline can restore noradrenergic signalling. With precursor replacement therapy many patients gain substantial and durable relief of orthostatic hypotension and can lead near-normal lives, which makes recognition important; untreated, disabling orthostatic symptoms persist, and perinatal presentations carry early morbidity.

double aortic arch — complete vascular ring, double arch Right aortic arch with aberrant left subclavian artery and a left ligamentum (another complete ring) Pulmonary artery sling Innominate artery compression syndrome Laryngomalacia or primary tracheomalacia Viral croup or recurrent bronchiolitis Gastro-oesophageal reflux with aspiration Mediastinal mass or lymphadenopathy CT angiography of the thorax MR angiography as a radiation-free alternative Transthoracic echocardiography for screening and associated cardiac lesions Contrast oesophagogram (barium swallow) Flexible or rigid bronchoscopy to assess airway compression and malacia Chest radiograph noting the side of the aortic arch and tracheal deviation Genetic testing including 22q11.2 microdeletion where indicated The most common complete vascular ring, in which both the right and left aortic arches persist and encircle the trachea and oesophagus. The right (posterior) arch is dominant in the majority of cases, with the left arch smaller and occasionally atretic. Symptoms arise from tracheo-oesophageal compression, including biphasic or expiratory stridor, a barking cough, recurrent respiratory infection and feeding difficulty with dysphagia. Reflex apnoea or so-called dying spells, sometimes precipitated by feeding, can occur in infants. CT or MR angiography defines the arch anatomy, the dominant arch and the airway compression, and is the mainstay of diagnosis. A barium swallow classically shows bilateral indentations of the oesophagus with a prominent posterior compression. Bronchoscopy demonstrates pulsatile external tracheal compression and helps assess associated tracheomalacia. Treatment is surgical division of the ring, usually through division of the smaller (commonly left) arch, relieving the constriction around the airway and oesophagus. Acute life-threatening events or reflex apnoea during feeds Severe stridor with respiratory distress or cyanosis Failure to thrive from feeding-related airway compromise Recurrent pneumonia suggesting significant airway obstruction Prolonged misdiagnosis as asthma, croup or reflux, delaying definitive imaging. Relying on echocardiography alone, which may not fully delineate the ring or the airway. Underestimating persistent tracheomalacia after division and expecting immediate symptom resolution. Dividing the dominant rather than the smaller arch, compromising systemic perfusion. Failing to identify an atretic segment that alters the surgical approach. A double aortic arch reflects failure of normal regression within the embryonic aortic arch system. Normally the right fourth arch and dorsal aorta regress distal to the right subclavian origin to leave a single left arch, but when both arches persist the ascending aorta divides into two limbs that pass on either side of the trachea and oesophagus and rejoin posteriorly to form the descending aorta. The two arches, together with the ligamentum arteriosum, create a complete ring that mechanically constricts the enclosed airway and oesophagus, and chronic pulsatile compression frequently produces secondary tracheomalacia. Surgical division is curative with low operative mortality and excellent long-term outcomes, although residual tracheomalacia may cause symptoms that resolve gradually over months to years.

double orifice mitral valve — double-orifice mitral valve, DOMV Atrioventricular septal defect Congenital mitral stenosis from parachute valve or supravalvar ring Cleft mitral valve Cor triatriatum Rheumatic mitral valve disease Mitral leaflet fenestration Transthoracic echocardiography with parasternal short-axis imaging Three-dimensional transoesophageal echocardiography Doppler inflow gradient measurement Cardiac MRI Screening for atrioventricular septal defect and left-heart obstruction Electrocardiography Double-orifice mitral valve divides the inflow into two orifices through a fibrous bridge, each often with its own subvalvar apparatus. Three morphological types are described: complete bridge, incomplete bridge and duplicate or hole type, best defined on short-axis and 3D echocardiography. It is frequently an incidental finding with normal function but may cause stenosis or regurgitation. There is a strong association with atrioventricular septal defect and other left-heart lesions such as coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve. Parasternal short-axis imaging shows two distinct orifices with a double-barrel appearance in diastole. Surgeons should avoid dividing the bridge to create a single orifice, as this can worsen regurgitation, so repair is tailored to the dominant lesion. Balloon or surgical intervention is reserved for significant stenosis or regurgitation rather than for the morphology itself. Severe mitral stenosis with pulmonary hypertension Severe regurgitation with left ventricular volume overload Heart failure or failure to thrive Coexisting significant atrioventricular septal defect or outflow tract obstruction Mistaking the two orifices for vegetations or an intracardiac mass Surgically dividing the bridge and precipitating severe regurgitation Missing an associated atrioventricular septal defect Underestimating stenosis when each individual orifice is small A fibrous bridge of tissue divides the mitral orifice into two openings, each usually supported by its own set of chordae and papillary muscle. In the complete bridge type the division extends from annulus to leaflet edge producing two separate orifices; in the incomplete or eccentric type the division is confined to the leaflet margin; and in the duplicate or hole type a small accessory orifice sits within one leaflet. Valve function is often normal, but stenosis can arise when the orifices are small or the subvalvar apparatus is abnormal, and regurgitation can occur through deficient coaptation. The anomaly is strongly associated with atrioventricular septal defect and other left-heart obstructive lesions. When valve function is normal the anomaly needs no treatment and prognosis is excellent; outcome in symptomatic cases depends on the severity of stenosis or regurgitation and associated defects, with repair being more complex than for a single-orifice valve.

heart failure from pulmonary overcirculation A subaortic defect with pulmonary stenosis mimics tetralogy of Fallot with cyanosis A subpulmonary defect (Taussig-Bing anomaly) directs left ventricular blood to the pulmonary artery and behaves like transposition with cyanosis A wide anatomical spectrum means individualised surgical planning is essential, guided by defect location and great-artery transposition-like streaming Heart failure from unobstructed pulmonary overcirculation Progressive pulmonary vascular disease from a long-standing large shunt Duct-dependent circulation with critical outflow obstruction Assuming a fixed physiology when the picture depends heavily on defect location and pulmonary stenosis Failing to recognise the Taussig-Bing subtype and its transposition-like cyanosis Underestimating pulmonary vascular disease in an unobstructed large-shunt lesion Neglecting to screen for associated chromosomal and conotruncal anomalies Double outlet right ventricle is a conotruncal anomaly in which both great arteries connect entirely or mostly to the morphological right ventricle, so the left ventricle can eject only through a ventricular septal defect. The haemodynamics depend on how the defect relates to the great vessels and whether pulmonary outflow is obstructed. When the defect lies beneath the aorta, oxygenated blood streams preferentially to the aorta and the physiology resembles a simple ventricular septal defect, or tetralogy if pulmonary stenosis coexists. When the defect lies beneath the pulmonary artery, oxygenated left ventricular blood is directed into the pulmonary circulation while systemic output is relatively desaturated, producing a transposition-like picture with cyanosis. The balance of pulmonary and systemic flow and the presence of outflow obstruction thus govern cyanosis and heart failure. Outcome varies widely with anatomy; favourable subtypes have good results after biventricular repair, while complex forms with remote defects or straddling valves may require single-ventricle palliation and carry a more guarded prognosis.

pigmentation as acanthosis nigricans Overlooking the autosomal dominant family history Missing an association with hidradenitis suppurativa in relevant cases Expecting significant benefit from currently available treatments Dowling-Degos disease is a genetically determined disorder of keratinocyte and follicular biology. Mutations, classically in keratin 5 and also in genes of the Notch signalling and protein-glycosylation pathways, disturb keratinocyte adhesion, melanosome transfer, and follicular development. The result is abnormal downgrowth of pigmented rete ridges and irregular deposition of melanin, producing the reticulate hyperpigmentation and the follicular, comedo-like lesions. Because the abnormality is intrinsic to the epidermis and follicle rather than driven by an external stimulus, the pigmentation is progressive and does not resolve spontaneously. Benign but chronic and slowly progressive; it does not resolve spontaneously, and currently available treatments offer only limited cosmetic improvement.

Down Syndrome — trisomy 21, Down's syndrome, trisomy 21 syndrome Other trisomies (trisomy 18, trisomy 13) Congenital hypothyroidism (overlapping hypotonia and coarse features) Zellweger and other syndromes with hypotonia Other syndromic causes of intellectual disability Non-syndromic congenital heart disease Karyotype to confirm trisomy 21 and identify translocation or mosaicism Echocardiography to detect congenital heart disease Thyroid function testing at birth and on a scheduled basis Hearing and vision assessments Full blood count to screen for transient myeloproliferative disorder and later leukaemia Cervical spine assessment when symptoms suggest atlantoaxial instability The most common autosomal chromosomal disorder and a leading genetic cause of intellectual disability, resulting from an extra copy of chromosome 21. Most cases are due to meiotic nondisjunction, with incidence rising markedly with advancing maternal age; a minority result from translocation or mosaicism. Recognisable features include hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, a flat nasal bridge, small ears, a single transverse palmar crease, and a sandal gap between the toes. Congenital heart disease is common, particularly atrioventricular septal defects, so early echocardiography is recommended. Gastrointestinal anomalies such as duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease occur more frequently. There is increased risk of hypothyroidism, hearing and visual impairment, obstructive sleep apnoea, and atlantoaxial instability, warranting scheduled surveillance. Children have a higher risk of transient myeloproliferative disorder in the newborn period and of leukaemia in childhood. Diagnosis is confirmed by karyotype, which also identifies translocations relevant to recurrence risk and family counselling. Early developmental support and coordinated multidisciplinary care improve developmental and health outcomes. Signs of significant congenital heart disease or heart failure Bilious vomiting or abdominal signs suggesting intestinal obstruction Neurological signs of cervical cord compression from atlantoaxial instability Persistent pallor, bruising, or abnormal blood counts suggesting leukaemia Severe obstructive sleep apnoea Assuming a normal heart without echocardiographic screening Overlooking hypothyroidism, which can mimic or worsen developmental delay Missing atlantoaxial instability before activities or anaesthesia in symptomatic children Failing to follow structured health surveillance recommendations The presence of a third copy of chromosome 21 leads to over-expression of the genes it carries, disrupting normal development across multiple organ systems in a dosage-dependent manner. This gene-dosage imbalance affects neurodevelopment, cardiac and gastrointestinal morphogenesis, immune function, and haematopoiesis. Most trisomy 21 arises from failure of chromosomal separation during meiosis (nondisjunction), while translocation and mosaic forms produce the extra genetic material through other mechanisms. Life expectancy has improved substantially with modern medical and surgical care and now commonly extends into adulthood; outcomes depend largely on cardiac disease and other complications, and most individuals have mild to moderate intellectual disability with early-onset Alzheimer-type changes in later life.

Dracunculiasis (Guinea worm disease) — Guinea worm disease, Dracunculus medinensis infection, dracontiasis, Medina worm, guinea worm infection Cutaneous larva migrans and other migratory helminth infections Bacterial skin abscess or cellulitis Tropical (phagedenic) ulcer Myiasis Foreign body granuloma or retained foreign material Cutaneous larva currens (strongyloidiasis) Clinical identification of the emerging adult worm at the skin ulcer Microscopy of fluid expressed from the lesion for larvae after water contact Wound assessment for secondary bacterial infection Plain radiography, which may reveal a calcified dead worm in chronic cases Review of tetanus immunisation status Assessment of drinking-water source and exposure history for public health action Caused by the nematode Dracunculus medinensis, acquired by drinking stagnant water containing infected copepods (water fleas, Cyclops) The target of an international eradication programme, so cases are now rare and geographically restricted, but recognition remains important After a prolonged incubation of about a year, the gravid female worm migrates to the skin, most often of the lower leg or foot, forming a painful blister that ulcerates Contact of the lesion with water triggers the worm to discharge larvae, producing intense local burning that patients relieve by immersing the limb in water, perpetuating transmission Diagnosis is clinical, based on the visible emerging worm; larvae may be seen when the ulcer contacts water There is no reliable curative drug; management is by slow, careful extraction of the worm over days by winding it onto a stick, with wound care and prevention of secondary bacterial infection Prevention centres on safe drinking water (filtering or treating), health education, and containment of cases to interrupt the life cycle Secondary bacterial infection with spreading cellulitis, abscess, or sepsis Features suggesting tetanus from a contaminated wound Septic arthritis or contracture if a worm ruptures near a joint Severe systemic hypersensitivity if the worm breaks during extraction Pulling the worm out too quickly and rupturing it, provoking severe inflammation Neglecting tetanus prophylaxis and secondary bacterial infection of the ulcer Missing the diagnosis outside classically endemic areas as eradication progresses Failing to counsel patients to avoid water contact, which perpetuates transmission Dracunculiasis results from ingesting water containing copepods infected with Dracunculus medinensis larvae. Gastric acid frees the larvae, which penetrate the intestinal wall and migrate into the abdominal and retroperitoneal tissues where they mature and mate. Over roughly a year the fertilised female worm grows to great length and migrates through subcutaneous tissue, usually to a distal limb. There it induces a painful blister; on contact with water the worm ruptures the skin and expels motile larvae, which are ingested by copepods to complete the cycle. Most symptoms arise from the migrating and emerging worm and the intense local inflammatory and allergic response, with pain, blistering, and ulceration. Secondary bacterial infection, cellulitis, abscess, tetanus, or joint involvement can complicate the emergence, and a retained or broken worm can provoke severe inflammation. The infection is rarely fatal and the worm is ultimately expelled or extracted, but the process is protracted and disabling; prognosis is good with careful wound care, though secondary infection or joint involvement can cause lasting morbidity.

Dravet syndrome — SCN1A, severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy, SMEI, polymorphic epilepsy of infancy Simple or complex febrile seizures Genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+) PCDH19-related epilepsy Other early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (e.g. KCNQ2, SCN2A) Mitochondrial or metabolic epilepsies Structural focal epilepsy on neuroimaging Targeted or panel gene testing for SCN1A and related epilepsy genes Prolonged or video EEG, which may be normal early and later shows generalised or multifocal epileptiform discharges Brain MRI, typically normal Presents in a previously healthy infant, typically in the first year of life, with prolonged febrile and afebrile hemiclonic or generalised seizures often triggered by fever, illness or vaccination The great majority of cases are caused by loss-of-function variants in the SCN1A gene encoding a voltage-gated sodium channel alpha subunit Seizures are characteristically sensitive to temperature elevation and can be precipitated by hot baths, exertion or environmental heat Multiple seizure types emerge over the second year, including myoclonic, atypical absence, focal and atonic seizures, with a tendency to status epilepticus Development is usually normal at onset but slows or regresses from the second year, with later intellectual disability, ataxia and behavioural difficulties epilepsy (SUDEP), so seizure control and safety counselling are priorities Prolonged or repeated febrile seizures progressing to convulsive status epilepticus Developmental slowing or regression in the second year of life Seizure aggravation after introduction of a sodium-channel-blocking agent Features suggesting elevated SUDEP risk such as frequent nocturnal convulsions Dismissing early prolonged febrile seizures as simple febrile convulsions and delaying genetic testing Prescribing sodium-channel blockers, which commonly worsen seizures in this condition Assuming a normal early EEG or MRI excludes the diagnosis Overlooking fever, illness and heat as consistent seizure triggers requiring aggressive fever management Dravet syndrome is a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy caused in most patients by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SCN1A, which encodes the Nav1.1 voltage-gated sodium channel. Nav1.1 is expressed preferentially in inhibitory GABAergic interneurons, so reduced channel function impairs interneuron firing and disinhibits cortical and hippocampal networks, producing hyperexcitability and a low threshold for seizures, particularly with rises in body temperature. The same interneuron dysfunction is thought to underlie the associated cognitive, motor and behavioural impairments that define the encephalopathy. Seizures typically persist into adulthood and are often drug-resistant, with associated intellectual disability, gait disturbance and behavioural problems. Mortality is elevated, largely from SUDEP and status epilepticus, so long-term multidisciplinary care and safety planning are essential.

dressler syndrome — post-myocardial infarction syndrome, post-cardiac injury syndrome early peri-infarction (epistenocardiac) pericarditis recurrent or reinfarction / acute coronary syndrome pulmonary embolism with pleuritic pain post-pericardiotomy syndrome (when after surgery) viral or idiopathic acute pericarditis pneumonia or pleurisy of other cause heart failure with effusions 12-lead ECG (diffuse concave ST elevation, PR-segment depression) transthoracic echocardiography (pericardial effusion, tamponade assessment) inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) and full blood count chest radiography (cardiomegaly, pleural effusion, pulmonary infiltrate) cardiac troponin to help exclude reinfarction cardiac MRI in equivocal cases (pericardial inflammation/enhancement) cross-sectional imaging or catheterisation if constriction is suspected Dressler syndrome is a delayed, immune-mediated pericarditis (a form of post-cardiac injury syndrome) that classically develops weeks to a few months after myocardial infarction, cardiac surgery or other myocardial or pericardial injury. It should be distinguished from early peri-infarction (epistenocardiac) pericarditis, which occurs within the first few days of infarction and reflects direct transmural inflammation rather than an immune mechanism. Its incidence has fallen markedly in the reperfusion era, as prompt revascularisation limits the extent of myocardial injury and antigen exposure. The typical picture combines pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward, low-grade fever, a pericardial friction rub, a pericardial and/or pleural effusion and raised inflammatory markers. Diagnosis rests on the clinical syndrome supported by ECG (diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression), echocardiographic effusion and elevated CRP/ESR, in the appropriate temporal context after cardiac injury. First-line treatment is high-dose non-steroidal anti-inflammatory therapy (aspirin is often preferred after recent myocardial infarction) combined with colchicine, which reduces recurrence. Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory or contraindicated cases because they are associated with a higher recurrence rate and, early after infarction, theoretical concern regarding myocardial healing. Recognised complications include recurrent pericarditis, large effusion with tamponade and, rarely, constrictive pericarditis. hypotension with raised jugular venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus indicating tamponade large or rapidly accumulating pericardial effusion features suggesting reinfarction or a new acute coronary syndrome rather than pericarditis haemodynamic compromise in a patient on anticoagulation with a growing effusion signs of evolving constrictive physiology (progressive right heart failure, raised venous pressure) Confusing delayed Dressler syndrome with early peri-infarction pericarditis, which differ in timing, mechanism and implications. Overlooking tamponade in a patient on anticoagulation after myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery. Reaching for corticosteroids first line, given their association with higher recurrence rates. Attributing recurrent post-infarction chest pain solely to ischaemia and missing the pericardial nature of the pain. Omitting colchicine, which reduces the risk of recurrence when added to anti-inflammatory therapy. Dressler syndrome is understood as an autoimmune or immune-mediated inflammatory response triggered by injury to the myocardium and pericardium. Necrosis exposes previously sequestered cardiac (particularly pericardial and myocardial) antigens to the immune system, and in susceptible individuals this provokes the formation of anti-heart antibodies and a delayed hypersensitivity reaction. The resulting immune complex-mediated and cell-mediated inflammation involves the pericardium and frequently the adjacent pleura and lung, producing a pericarditis often accompanied by pericardial and pleural effusions and occasionally pulmonary infiltrates. The characteristic latent interval of weeks to months reflects the time required to mount this adaptive immune response, distinguishing it mechanistically from the immediate, direct inflammation of early peri-infarction pericarditis. With appropriate anti-inflammatory therapy the syndrome is usually self-limiting and carries a good prognosis, though recurrences are not uncommon; serious sequelae such as tamponade or constrictive pericarditis are infrequent but clinically important.

Drowning — submersion injury, near-drowning, immersion injury Primary cardiac arrest with secondary immersion Seizure or syncope precipitating submersion Cervical spinal cord injury from diving Intoxication (alcohol or drugs) as a contributing factor Acute coronary syndrome or arrhythmia Arterial blood gas to quantify hypoxaemia and acidosis Chest imaging to assess for aspiration and pulmonary oedema Core temperature measurement for hypothermia ECG and cardiac monitoring Capillary glucose, electrolytes, and cervical spine imaging where trauma is suspected Drowning is the process of respiratory impairment from submersion or immersion in liquid; outdated terms such as near-drowning, wet, dry, and secondary drowning are no longer recommended The central injury is hypoxaemia; the historical distinction between fresh and salt water has little practical bearing on resuscitation Correcting hypoxia takes priority - rescue breathing and early effective ventilation are the most important interventions, and resuscitation should begin with airway and breathing rather than the usual circulation-first approach Aspirated water washes out surfactant and injures the alveolar-capillary membrane, and pulmonary oedema or acute respiratory distress syndrome may evolve over the following hours Symptomatic survivors need a period of observation, as respiratory deterioration can be delayed; a completely asymptomatic patient with normal oxygenation after several hours is at low risk Suspect and manage hypothermia, which frequently accompanies submersion and can be protective of the brain, so resuscitation should continue until the patient is rewarmed Consider precipitating and associated conditions, including cervical spine injury (in diving), seizures, arrhythmia, intoxication, and hypoglycaemia Prophylactic antibiotics and routine corticosteroids are not recommended; antibiotics are reserved for established infection or grossly contaminated water Hypoxaemia, respiratory distress, or need for ventilatory support Reduced conscious level or coma indicating hypoxic brain injury Cardiac arrest or significant arrhythmia Severe hypothermia requiring continued resuscitation during rewarming Delayed worsening of oxygenation over the observation period Prioritising chest compressions over ventilation in a hypoxia-driven arrest Discharging a symptomatic patient too early and missing delayed respiratory deterioration Terminating resuscitation before adequately rewarming a hypothermic patient Overlooking a precipitating cause such as seizure, arrhythmia, cervical injury, or intoxication Submersion triggers breath-holding, then involuntary aspiration of water or laryngospasm, leading to progressive hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis. Aspirated fluid disrupts and washes out pulmonary surfactant and damages the alveolar-capillary membrane, causing atelectasis, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, and potentially acute respiratory distress syndrome. Sustained hypoxia causes global tissue injury, with the brain most vulnerable to hypoxic-ischaemic damage. Cardiac arrhythmias and arrest follow severe hypoxia and acidosis, and coexisting hypothermia alters both the injury and the resuscitation. Outcome is largely determined by the duration of submersion and hypoxia and the neurological status at the scene and on arrival; prolonged submersion and persistent coma predict poor neurological recovery, whereas patients who are alert with normal oxygenation generally do well, and hypothermia can occasionally allow good recovery after prolonged arrest.

requiring immediate intramuscular adrenaline Mucosal erosions, skin blistering or pain, or positive Nikolsky sign suggesting SJS/TEN Fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and organ involvement suggesting DRESS Any severe cutaneous adverse reaction, in which re-exposure or desensitisation is contraindicated Accepting an unverified allergy label and defaulting to broader, more toxic alternatives Attempting desensitisation or re-challenge after a severe cutaneous reaction Mistaking a viral rash or predictable side effect for true allergy, or vice versa Failing to document the reaction clearly and counsel the patient about cross-reacting agents Immune-mediated drug reactions occur when a drug or its reactive metabolite, often after binding host protein as a hapten, is recognised by the adaptive immune system. Type I reactions involve drug-specific IgE on mast cells and basophils, producing immediate mediator release. Type II reactions are antibody-mediated cytotoxicity against drug-coated cells (e.g. immune haemolysis, thrombocytopenia), and type III reactions involve immune-complex deposition (serum sickness, vasculitis). Type IV delayed reactions are T-cell-driven and range from benign exanthems to severe cutaneous reactions; the p-i concept describes direct, non-covalent drug interaction with immune receptors, and specific HLA alleles predispose to particular severe reactions. Most benign exanthems and immediate reactions resolve fully once the drug is withdrawn and future exposure avoided. Severe cutaneous adverse reactions carry significant morbidity and mortality, particularly toxic epidermal necrolysis, and require urgent specialist and supportive care.

drug induced chorea — iatrogenic chorea, medication-induced chorea Sydenham chorea and other autoimmune chorea Huntington disease and phenocopies Metabolic chorea (non-ketotic hyperglycaemia, thyrotoxicosis) Vascular (post-stroke) chorea Wilson disease Chorea gravidarum and oestrogen-related chorea Functional (psychogenic) movement disorder Detailed medication, over-the-counter and illicit substance history with timeline Serum drug levels where relevant (e.g. phenytoin, lithium) Urine toxicology screen for stimulants and cocaine Metabolic screen including glucose and thyroid function Full blood count and peripheral film if neuroacanthocytosis considered MRI brain to exclude structural or vascular lesions Genetic testing for Huntington disease if features persist after drug withdrawal Drug-induced chorea should be considered in any acquired chorea, as a careful medication and substance history is often more revealing than extensive investigation. Levodopa and dopamine agonists are the commonest culprits, producing peak-dose or diphasic dyskinesia in treated Parkinson disease. Chronic dopamine-receptor-blocking drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) cause tardive dyskinesia, characteristically orobuccolingual and sometimes irreversible. Other implicated agents include anticonvulsants (notably phenytoin toxicity), stimulants and cocaine ('crack dancing'), oral contraceptives, lithium and certain antihistamines. Onset ranges from acute (stimulants, phenytoin toxicity, levodopa) to delayed after months or years of exposure (tardive dyskinesia). A predisposing basal ganglia state (previous Sydenham chorea, pregnancy, hyperthyroidism, structural lesion) lowers the threshold for drug-induced chorea. Management centres on identifying and withdrawing or reducing the offending agent, though tardive dyskinesia may persist or transiently worsen on withdrawal. VMAT2 inhibitors are the evidence-based pharmacological treatment for persistent tardive dyskinesia when the causative drug cannot be stopped. Hyperpyrexia, rigidity and autonomic instability suggesting neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin toxicity Signs of severe anticonvulsant or lithium toxicity requiring urgent level measurement and management Cardiovascular compromise with stimulant or cocaine intoxication Severe generalised chorea causing rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia or exhaustion Persistent chorea after drug withdrawal, prompting a search for an alternative diagnosis Failing to take a thorough medication and substance history, including recently stopped drugs. Abruptly withdrawing a neuroleptic and precipitating worsening (withdrawal-emergent) dyskinesia. Mistaking tardive dyskinesia for a primary neurodegenerative chorea. Attributing dyskinesia in Parkinson disease to disease progression rather than levodopa dosing. Overlooking predisposing factors such as pregnancy or hyperthyroidism that unmask drug-induced chorea. Drug-induced chorea reflects pharmacological disturbance of dopaminergic and other neurotransmitter balance within the basal ganglia. Dopaminergic excess, as with levodopa and dopamine agonists, overstimulates striatal receptors and drives the indirect pathway toward disinhibited, choreic output, often superimposed on the maladaptive plasticity of chronic denervation. Conversely, chronic dopamine-receptor blockade induces post-synaptic receptor supersensitivity and compensatory changes that manifest as tardive dyskinesia. Stimulants and cocaine acutely increase synaptic dopamine, while anticonvulsant toxicity and other agents perturb striatal function through less well-defined mechanisms. In each case the final common pathway is dysregulation of striatal control over thalamocortical motor circuits. Chorea from acute intoxication or dopaminergic overtreatment usually resolves promptly once the drug is withdrawn or the dose adjusted. Tardive dyskinesia has a more guarded prognosis, being persistent or irreversible in a substantial proportion, although VMAT2 inhibitors and early causative-drug withdrawal improve outcomes.

Drug-induced immune haemolytic anaemia — DIIHA Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Cold agglutinin disease Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (oxidative drug haemolysis) Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction Direct antiglobulin test and drug-dependent antibody studies Detailed drug history including recent additions Full blood count, reticulocytes and haemolysis markers Blood film Rechallenge avoidance and documentation of the culprit drug Immune-mediated red cell destruction triggered by a drug or its metabolites It can mimic warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia clinically and serologically Implicated drugs classically include some cephalosporins, penicillins and, historically, methyldopa, among others Mechanisms include drug-dependent antibodies (drug adsorption or immune-complex types) and true drug-independent autoantibodies The direct antiglobulin test is usually positive, and identifying the culprit drug is central The mainstay of treatment is stopping the offending drug, with supportive care and transfusion if required Severe or intravascular haemolysis after a new drug Haemodynamic compromise from rapid anaemia Renal impairment from intravascular haemolysis Ongoing exposure to the culprit drug Failing to take a thorough drug history and identify the culprit Mistaking it for idiopathic warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Overlooking oxidative (G6PD-related) drug haemolysis, which is a different mechanism Re-exposing the patient to the offending drug Drug-induced immune haemolytic anaemia arises when a drug provokes an antibody response that leads to red cell destruction. In the drug-adsorption mechanism the drug binds firmly to the red cell membrane and antibodies target the drug-coated cell; in the immune-complex mechanism drug-antibody complexes attach to red cells and activate complement; and some drugs induce true autoantibodies indistinguishable from those of warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. The result is accelerated clearance of antibody- or complement-coated red cells, causing extravascular or, with strong complement activation, intravascular haemolysis. Haemolysis usually resolves after withdrawal of the offending drug, though it can be severe acutely; recovery is generally complete once the drug is stopped and avoided.

Overlooking that some agents (e.g. nitrofurantoin) cause both acute and chronic forms Drugs injure the lung through several mechanisms: direct cytotoxicity to alveolar epithelial and endothelial cells (as with cytotoxic chemotherapy), oxidant-mediated damage, phospholipid accumulation (as with amiodarone), and immune or hypersensitivity reactions in which the drug or its metabolites trigger an inflammatory response. The resulting injury manifests as varied histological patterns depending on the agent, dose, and host susceptibility, ranging from reversible inflammatory pneumonitis and organising pneumonia to diffuse alveolar damage and established fibrosis. Immune checkpoint inhibitors act differently, unleashing T-cell-mediated inflammation of the lung as an autoimmune-like adverse event. Recognition of the offending drug and its withdrawal are central, as continued exposure risks progression to irreversible fibrosis. Many inflammatory patterns improve after drug withdrawal, with or without corticosteroids for drug-induced ILD, but agents causing diffuse alveolar damage or established fibrosis, and severe checkpoint-inhibitor pneumonitis, carry a substantial risk of persistent impairment or death.

renal impairment accompanying liver failure Overlooking herbal, dietary supplement or over-the-counter agents in the drug history Attributing injury to a chronic medication while missing a recently introduced drug or a completed antibiotic course Failing to recognise that cholestatic injury can begin after the culprit drug has been stopped Delaying N-acetylcysteine in staggered or unclear-timing paracetamol exposure while awaiting levels Rechallenging the patient with the suspected drug and precipitating severe recurrence Drug-induced liver injury arises either from intrinsic, dose-related toxicity or from idiosyncratic reactions that depend on host factors. In intrinsic injury, exemplified by paracetamol, saturation of normal conjugation pathways diverts metabolism to cytochrome P450, generating the reactive intermediate NAPQI which depletes glutathione and binds hepatocyte proteins, causing centrilobular necrosis. Idiosyncratic injury reflects unpredictable interactions between reactive metabolites, mitochondrial stress and adaptive immune responses, often with a genetic (including HLA) predisposition, and may be immunoallergic with fever, rash and eosinophilia. The biochemical picture reflects the target: hepatocellular necrosis raises transaminases, while injury to bile ducts or canalicular transport produces a cholestatic pattern with raised alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin. Most idiosyncratic injury resolves after the offending drug is stopped, though cholestatic injury may take months to normalise. Development of jaundice in a hepatocellular pattern (Hy's law) predicts a substantial risk of death or need for transplantation, and fulminant failure carries a poor outcome without transplantation.

involvement with proteinuria or an active urinary sediment (uncommon, prompts reassessment) Marked cytopenias Persistent or worsening symptoms despite withdrawal of the suspected agent Mistaking drug-induced lupus for idiopathic systemic lupus and committing the patient to long-term immunosuppression Failing to review the full medication list, including recently started antihypertensives, antiarrhythmics and biologics Assuming a positive antinuclear antibody alone confirms the diagnosis without the compatible clinical picture Not appreciating that biologic-induced lupus can behave atypically with anti-dsDNA positivity Drug-induced lupus is a systemic autoimmune reaction triggered by chronic drug exposure. Several mechanisms are proposed, including drug-induced disruption of central immune tolerance, inhibition of DNA methylation altering T-cell gene expression, and formation of reactive metabolites (often by activated neutrophils or hepatic oxidation) that modify nuclear proteins and break self-tolerance. This drives production of antinuclear antibodies, particularly against the histone-DNA complex, giving the characteristic anti-histone antibody positivity. Slow acetylators accumulate parent drug and are at higher risk with hydralazine and procainamide. Unlike idiopathic disease, immune complex deposition rarely causes significant nephritis, and manifestations typically remit once the drug and its metabolites are cleared. The prognosis is generally excellent; clinical features usually resolve within weeks to months of stopping the culprit drug, though serological abnormalities may persist longer. Serious organ-threatening disease is rare, and permanent sequelae are unusual.

drug induced parkinsonism — iatrogenic parkinsonism, neuroleptic-induced parkinsonism idiopathic Parkinson disease atypical parkinsonian syndromes such as multiple system atrophy and progressive supranuclear palsy vascular parkinsonism essential tremor tardive syndromes coexisting with parkinsonism normal-pressure hydrocephalus hypothyroidism or depression with psychomotor slowing comprehensive medication review including antiemetics, calcium-channel blockers and antidepressants dopamine transporter (DaT) SPECT imaging to distinguish reversible drug effect from underlying nigrostriatal degeneration MRI brain to assess for vascular disease, hydrocephalus or atypical parkinsonian features thyroid function tests and metabolic screen for treatable mimics structured assessment for coexisting tardive dyskinesia and dystonia monitored reassessment of parkinsonian signs over months after withdrawal of the offending drug The commonest cause of secondary parkinsonism, produced by dopamine-receptor-blocking or dopamine-depleting drugs, and a leading mimic of idiopathic Parkinson disease. Classically more symmetrical than Parkinson disease, with bradykinesia and rigidity predominating; a symmetrical postural and action tremor may occur, though asymmetry does not exclude the diagnosis. Onset typically within weeks to a few months of starting or increasing the offending drug, and it is potentially reversible after withdrawal, though recovery may take many months. Common culprits include typical and atypical antipsychotics, the antiemetics metoclopramide and prochlorperazine, and dopamine-depleting agents; less-appreciated contributors include some calcium-channel blockers, valproate and certain antidepressants. Persistent or progressive symptoms after drug withdrawal should raise suspicion of unmasked underlying Parkinson disease. Coexisting tardive dyskinesia or orolingual dyskinesia alongside parkinsonism strongly favours a drug-induced aetiology. Dopamine transporter (DaT) imaging is normal in pure drug-induced parkinsonism but abnormal where an underlying degenerative process has been unmasked, aiding difficult cases. First-line management is identifying and stopping or substituting the causative agent; where an antipsychotic is essential, switching to a lower-liability agent (such as quetiapine or clozapine) is preferred, and antiparkinsonian drugs are generally reserved for refractory disability. markedly asymmetrical or rapidly progressive signs suggesting an underlying degenerative disorder rigidity with fever, autonomic instability and altered consciousness indicating possible neuroleptic malignant syndrome early falls, prominent autonomic failure or gaze palsy pointing to an atypical parkinsonian syndrome failure to improve, or continued progression, after adequate withdrawal of the causative agent assuming symmetry is required for the diagnosis and missing drug-induced parkinsonism when signs are asymmetrical overlooking hidden culprits such as metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, flunarizine or cinnarizine starting levodopa or dopamine agonists rather than removing the causative drug expecting immediate resolution and prematurely concluding the drug was not responsible failing to arrange DaT imaging or follow-up when symptoms persist, thereby missing unmasked Parkinson disease Drug-induced parkinsonism results from functional dopaminergic hypofunction in the nigrostriatal pathway. Dopamine-receptor antagonists (antipsychotics and antiemetics) block striatal postsynaptic D2 receptors, while dopamine-depleting agents reduce presynaptic dopamine availability; both shift the basal ganglia towards the parkinsonian state via overactivity of the indirect pathway and increased inhibitory output from the globus pallidus internus and substantia nigra pars reticulata. Non-dopaminergic mechanisms are implicated for some drugs such as calcium-channel blockers and valproate. Susceptibility increases with older age, higher potency and dose, and in some patients subclinical nigral degeneration lowers the threshold, such that the drug unmasks incipient Parkinson disease. Most patients improve after the offending drug is withdrawn, though resolution can take several months and a proportion have persistent deficits reflecting unmasked underlying Parkinson disease. Early recognition and drug cessation offer the best chance of full recovery.

involves loss of adhesion between keratinocytes (acantholysis) mediated by autoantibodies against the desmosomal proteins desmoglein 1 and desmoglein 3. Thiol-containing drugs such as penicillamine are thought to interact directly with sulphydryl groups in the desmoglein molecules or in the enzymes maintaining desmosomal integrity, disrupting cell-cell adhesion and, in some patients, provoking a true autoantibody response. Non-thiol drugs may act as haptens or otherwise trigger an autoimmune reaction that more closely mirrors idiopathic pemphigus. The result is intraepidermal blistering with flaccid bullae and erosions. Because part of the mechanism can be biochemical rather than purely immune, thiol-induced disease frequently resolves once the drug is cleared, whereas antibody-driven non-thiol cases can persist. Thiol-induced pemphigus often remits within weeks to months of stopping the drug, whereas non-thiol-induced disease may persist and require ongoing immunosuppression. Overall prognosis is generally better than idiopathic pemphigus when the trigger is identified and removed early.
