Relying on the uncorrected QT rather than a rate-corrected QTc Missing drug interactions that raise plasma concentrations of a QT-prolonging agent Failing to monitor the electrocardiogram after initiating a high-risk medication Ventricular repolarisation depends heavily on the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current (IKr) conducted by the hERG channel. Many structurally diverse drugs block this channel, prolonging the action potential duration and the QT interval on the surface electrocardiogram. Delayed repolarisation predisposes to early afterdepolarisations, which can trigger torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a twisting axis. Susceptibility is increased when repolarisation reserve is already reduced by electrolyte disturbance (particularly low potassium, magnesium or calcium), bradycardia, structural heart disease, or subclinical congenital long QT mutations. Drug interactions that raise plasma levels of a QT-prolonging agent, or combine several such agents, further impair repolarisation and heighten arrhythmic risk. With prompt recognition, drug withdrawal and correction of precipitants, the QT usually normalises and the arrhythmic risk resolves. Untreated torsades can be rapidly fatal, but appropriately managed episodes generally have a good outcome.

Drug-induced vasculitis — Drug-induced vasculitis, Drug-associated vasculitis, Drug-induced ANCA-associated vasculitis Idiopathic ANCA-associated vasculitis IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schoenlein purpura) Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis Infection-associated vasculitis Connective tissue disease-associated vasculitis Septic emboli or infective endocarditis Thrombotic or occlusive vasculopathy Detailed drug, over-the-counter and illicit substance history including timeline ANCA testing with antigen specificity (MPO and PR3), noting high titres or dual positivity Skin biopsy confirming leukocytoclastic vasculitis Renal function and urinalysis to detect glomerulonephritis Full blood count looking for neutropenia (as with levamisole) Complement, cryoglobulins and infection screen to exclude alternatives Urine toxicology where illicit drug exposure is suspected Drug-induced vasculitis most often manifests as a small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis with palpable purpura on dependent areas, typically days to weeks after starting the culprit drug. A distinct drug-induced ANCA-associated vasculitis is well recognised, classically with antimyeloperoxidase antibodies, and can affect the kidneys and lungs. Antithyroid drugs, hydralazine, minocycline, certain anti-tumour necrosis factor agents and cocaine adulterated with levamisole are among the well-described triggers. Very high-titre antimyeloperoxidase antibodies, antibodies to multiple antigens, or combined MPO and PR3 positivity should raise suspicion of a drug cause. Withdrawal of the offending agent is the cornerstone of management and often leads to resolution of milder cutaneous disease. Severe organ-threatening disease (glomerulonephritis, alveolar haemorrhage) may still require immunosuppression despite drug cessation. Levamisole-adulterated cocaine characteristically causes retiform purpura with ear involvement, neutropenia and positive ANCA. A detailed drug and substance history, including over-the-counter agents and illicit drugs, is essential to identify the trigger. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with rising creatinine Pulmonary haemorrhage or hypoxia Extensive retiform purpura with skin necrosis Severe neutropenia or agranulocytosis Systemic features persisting despite drug withdrawal Failing to take a complete drug and substance history, including illicit drugs and supplements. Not recognising drug-induced ANCA vasculitis and treating it as idiopathic while continuing the trigger. Missing levamisole-adulterated cocaine as a cause of retiform purpura with neutropenia. Assuming all drug-induced vasculitis is benign and self-limiting when severe organ involvement can occur. Rechallenging the patient with the causative drug, precipitating relapse. Drug-induced vasculitis arises when a drug or its metabolites trigger an immune-mediated attack on blood vessel walls. In hypersensitivity small-vessel vasculitis the drug acts as a hapten, driving immune-complex formation and deposition in postcapillary venules with complement activation and neutrophil-mediated leukocytoclastic injury. In drug-induced ANCA-associated vasculitis certain agents promote the generation of antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, often against myeloperoxidase; some drugs are thought to alter neutrophil extracellular trap formation or unmask sequestered antigens, breaking tolerance. The result ranges from purely cutaneous disease to a necrotising small-vessel vasculitis with renal and pulmonary involvement indistinguishable from idiopathic disease. Cutaneous-limited disease usually resolves after the culprit drug is stopped, but organ-threatening ANCA-associated forms can cause lasting renal impairment if not treated promptly. Rechallenge with the offending agent risks recurrence and should be avoided.

Drug intoxication / poisoning — Toxidrome assessment Paracetamol/salicylate levels ABG, osmolar gap Specific antidotes where available Characterise overall physiologic state and toxidrome from vital signs and neuromuscular exam (p.3704) Anion gap (raised AGMA in methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate, or any poisoning causing organ failure, seizures or shock; low anion gap with bromide, calcium, iodine, lithium, magnesium) (p.3705) Osmolal gap (>10 mmol/L suggests a low-molecular-weight solute such as an alcohol or glycol) (p.3705) Serum lactate (low relative to anion gap in alcohol/glycol intoxication, high and near the anion gap in hypoperfusion) (p.3705) Glucose, electrolytes, ketones (hypo-/hyperglycaemia and hypo-/hyperkalaemia patterns can implicate specific agents) (p.3705) ECG (bradycardia/AV block, QRS and QT prolongation, ventricular tachyarrhythmias suggest specific agent classes) (p.3706) Abdominal/chest radiograph (radiopaque densities suggest heavy metals, drug packets, iron, enteric-coated or salicylate tablets; CXR for pulmonary edema/aspiration) (p.3706) Quantitative serum levels (acetaminophen, alcohols incl. ethylene glycol/methanol, anticonvulsants, barbiturates, digoxin, iron, lithium, salicylate, theophylline, carboxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin) guide management (p.3706) Coagulation (PT/INR) for warfarin/rodenticide risk stratification, though unreliable for direct oral anticoagulant overdose (p.3705) Psychogenic illness / anxiety reaction (mass hysteria, fear of poisoning) producing symptoms inconsistent with the exposure history (p.3705) Structural CNS lesion - focal neurologic findings are uncommon in poisoning and should prompt evaluation for a structural cause (p.3703) Diagnosis of an unknown poisoning rests on pattern recognition: first classify the overall physiologic state as stimulated, depressed, discordant, or normal, then look for a recognizable toxidrome (p.3704). Core temperature is the single most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant (e.g. cocaine) poisoning or in drug/alcohol/GHB withdrawal, so it must be measured even in difficult or combative patients (p.3704). Mydriasis is common to all stimulant states but is most marked with anticholinergics (muscarinic loss of pupil reactivity); cocaine and other sympathomimetics enlarge pupils yet retain some light reactivity (p.3704). The anticholinergic toxidrome is distinguished from other stimulant states by hot, dry, flushed skin, decreased bowel sounds and urinary retention, whereas sympathomimetic states cause diaphoresis and increased bowel activity (p.3704). Miosis points to a depressed state from opioids or cholinergic agents; muscarinic/nicotinic features separate cholinergic poisoning from opioid poisoning (p.3704-3705). In opioid and sedative-hypnotic poisoning, vital-sign derangements are secondary to CNS depression and do not appear until consciousness is markedly reduced (grade 3-4 depression); marked cardiovascular depression with preserved consciousness instead suggests a peripherally acting sympatholytic (p.3705). Rotatory nystagmus among stimulated patients is essentially specific to phencyclidine and ketamine (p.3704). A near-normal exam may reflect a nontoxic exposure, psychogenic illness, or a 'toxic time-bomb' (slowly absorbed, slowly distributed, requiring metabolic activation, or disrupting metabolism); once-daily reformulations have made these increasingly common (p.3705). Rapid response of altered mental status to IV dextrose, naloxone or flumazenil is virtually diagnostic of hypoglycemia, opioid poisoning and benzodiazepine intoxication respectively (p.3706). Most patients who are or become asymptomatic by 6 h after ingestion are unlikely to develop later toxicity and may be discharged, but longer observation is required after 'toxic time-bomb' ingestions (p.3707). Temperature elevation (grade 4 stimulation) - most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant poisoning and withdrawal (p.3704) Coma, seizures or cardiovascular collapse (grade 4 physiologic stimulation or depression) (p.3705) Focal neurologic findings - uncommon in poisoning and suggest a structural CNS lesion (p.3703) Suspicion of 'body packing'/'body stuffing' in patients ill after foreign travel or arrest (p.3703) High blood levels of agents with more toxic metabolites (acetaminophen, ethylene glycol, methanol) signalling need for antidote or dialysis (p.3707) Rapid hospital urine drug-of-abuse screens are screening tests only, cannot confirm the exact substance, and are not diagnostic or forensic; false positives (e.g. fluoroquinolones triggering false-positive opiate screens) and false negatives are common (p.3706). A negative drug screen does not exclude poisoning - the agent may be undetectable by the assay (e.g. synthetic cannabinoids/spice, cathinones/bath salts, kratom) or present below the limit of detection at the time of sampling; repeat testing later may turn positive (p.3706). Qualitative drug screens are not clinically useful or cost-effective when the patient is asymptomatic or the picture fits the reported history; reserve them for severe or unexplained toxicity (coma, seizures, cardiovascular instability, acidosis, nonsinus rhythms) (p.3706). Blood levels obtained during absorption/distribution may exceed tissue levels and may not correlate with toxicity (p.3707). In polydrug overdose a clear toxidrome may be obscured when different drug classes counteract each other's physiologic effects (p.3704). Physostigmine fully reverses anticholinergic poisoning but can also produce some arousal in CNS depression of any cause, so arousal alone is not specific (p.3706). Overdose effects begin sooner, peak later and last longer than therapeutic-dose effects, and an agent's published (therapeutic) pharmacokinetics differ from its toxicokinetics in overdose (p.3707). Poisoning is a dose-related adverse effect from exposure to a chemical, drug or other xenobiotic. Responses to a given dose vary with genetic polymorphism, enzyme induction or inhibition by co-ingestants, and acquired tolerance. Toxicity may be local or systemic depending on route, the agent's physicochemical properties and mechanism, and its severity/reversibility depends on the functional reserve of the patient or target organ (influenced by age and pre-existing disease) (p.3703). Overall mortality is low (<1% of all poison exposures) but rises to 1-2% among hospitalised patients with intentional (suicidal) overdose or complications of drugs of abuse, who account for most serious poisonings. About 20-25% of exposures need bedside professional evaluation and ~5% need hospitalisation. Acetaminophen is the pharmaceutical most often implicated in fatal poisoning, while carbon monoxide is the leading overall cause of poisoning death (often fatal before discovery). Most patients asymptomatic at 6 h are unlikely to deteriorate (p.3703, p.3707). Harrison grades physiologic stimulation and depression in poisoning/withdrawal: Stimulation - grade 1 anxious/tremulous with normal vital signs; grade 2 agitated, mildly-moderately raised vitals but can follow commands; grade 3 delirious with motor hyperactivity and markedly raised vitals, possible tachyarrhythmias; grade 4 coma, seizures, cardiovascular collapse. Depression - grade 1 lethargic but arousable to voice/touch; grade 2 responds to pain not voice, brainstem reflexes intact; grade 3 unresponsive to pain, depressed brainstem reflexes, reduced tone/respiration/temperature; grade 4 flaccid, absent brainstem reflexes and respirations, depressed cardiovascular signs (p.3705).

patients Attributing all irritation to dryness and missing allergy, infection, or medication toxicity Long-term use of preserved drops aggravating ocular surface toxicity Dry eye disease is a multifactorial disorder of the ocular surface characterised by loss of tear film homeostasis. Reduced aqueous production (as in Sjogren and non-Sjogren lacrimal dysfunction) or excessive evaporation (chiefly from meibomian gland dysfunction with an unstable lipid layer) leads to tear hyperosmolarity. Hyperosmolarity triggers a self-perpetuating cycle of ocular surface inflammation, epithelial damage, and neurosensory dysfunction, which further destabilises the tear film. Goblet cell loss and reduced mucin worsen wetting, sustaining the inflammatory cascade. Dry eye disease is usually chronic and requires ongoing management; most patients achieve good symptom control, but severe or autoimmune-associated disease can cause persistent surface damage and visual impairment.

osteonecrosis risk in patients on antiresorptive therapy Dry socket is a painful complication of tooth extraction caused by disintegration or loss of the protective blood clot, exposing alveolar bone Severe throbbing pain characteristically begins two to four days after extraction, later than the pain of the surgery itself The socket appears empty with exposed bone and often malodour, but there is indicated Management is supportive: irrigation, gentle debridement, and placement of a sedative dressing to relieve pain and protect the bone Preventive measures include atraumatic technique, avoiding smoking, and good postoperative care Spreading swelling, fever, trismus, or purulent discharge suggesting true infection rather than simple dry socket Failure to heal or exposed necrotic bone in a patient on antiresorptive or antiangiogenic drugs raising concern for osteonecrosis Persistent numbness or worsening pain suggesting nerve injury or osteomyelitis Prescribing antibiotics for uncomplicated dry socket, which is not an infection Mistaking spreading infection or osteomyelitis for simple alveolar osteitis Overlooking a retained root fragment as the cause of persistent socket pain Failing to consider medication-related osteonecrosis in at-risk patients with non-healing sockets Dry socket, or alveolar osteitis, develops when the blood clot that normally fills and protects an extraction socket is lost prematurely, often through excessive local fibrinolysis. Breakdown of the clot exposes the alveolar bone and nerve endings to the oral environment, producing intense pain. Contributing factors such as smoking, bacterial contamination, trauma during extraction, and elevated fibrinolytic activity impair clot stability and delay the normal organisation and healing of the socket. The condition is characterised by inflammation of the exposed bone rather than an established suppurative infection. Dry socket is self-limiting and typically resolves over one to two weeks with supportive care and adequate analgesia, without long-term sequelae in most patients.

malformation with impaired function Cardiac anomaly identified during evaluation of overlapping syndromes Cytopenias raising concern for an alternative diagnosis such as Fanconi anaemia Progressive hearing loss impairing communication Confusing the condition with Holt-Oram or Townes-Brocks syndrome and testing the wrong gene Missing mildly affected relatives because of the highly variable expression Overlooking renal or hearing involvement by focusing on the limb and eye features Failing to consider Fanconi anaemia when cytopenias accompany radial ray defects Duane-radial ray syndrome results from heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SALL4, a zinc-finger transcription factor of the spalt-like family that regulates gene expression during limb, eye, ear, kidney, and heart development. Haploinsufficiency of SALL4 disturbs these developmental programmes, and its role in the developing abducens motor system underlies the Duane retraction anomaly, while its function in limb patterning produces the radial ray defects. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with marked variability in expression. Lifespan is usually normal, and the outlook is determined by the severity of limb, renal, and hearing involvement; the ocular motility limitation is stable and the limb anomalies are often amenable to surgical and rehabilitative management, so most individuals function well with appropriate multidisciplinary care.

Duane retraction syndrome — Duane syndrome, Duane's retraction syndrome, DRS, congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder, CHN1 Congenital or acquired sixth nerve palsy Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles Möbius syndrome Infantile esotropia with cross-fixation Brown syndrome (for restricted elevation patterns) Congenital third nerve palsy with aberrant regeneration Orthoptic assessment of ductions, palpebral fissure changes and head posture Cover testing for deviation in primary position Cycloplegic refraction and amblyopia assessment Audiometry and systemic examination for associated anomalies (e.g. Wildervanck, Goldenhar) Neuroimaging if the presentation is atypical or acquired features arise Genetic evaluation in familial or syndromic cases A congenital eye movement disorder marked by limited abduction, globe retraction and narrowing of the palpebral fissure on attempted adduction Caused by aberrant innervation in which the lateral rectus is supplied partly by a branch of the oculomotor nerve owing to absence or hypoplasia of the abducens nucleus and nerve Co-contraction of the medial and lateral recti on adduction pulls the globe back into the orbit, narrowing the lid fissure, with widening on abduction Traditionally classified into three types by the pattern of abduction and adduction limitation (Huber types) More common in the left eye and in females, and usually unilateral Many children maintain binocular vision by adopting a compensatory face turn; amblyopia is relatively uncommon Surgery is reserved for a significant anomalous head posture, manifest deviation in primary position, or marked up- or down-shoots Acquired abduction deficit that could represent a true sixth nerve palsy needing urgent workup Associated hearing loss or vertebral anomalies suggesting a wider syndrome Amblyopia developing in the affected eye A large primary-position deviation or head posture affecting development Confusing it with a sixth nerve palsy and pursuing unnecessary neurological investigation Attempting to restore full abduction surgically, which is not achievable Overlooking associated systemic anomalies Neglecting amblyopia screening in unilateral cases Duane retraction syndrome is a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder arising from maldevelopment of the abducens nucleus and nerve. In the absence of normal sixth nerve supply, the lateral rectus receives anomalous branches from the oculomotor nerve. On attempted adduction, both horizontal recti contract simultaneously, retracting the globe and narrowing the palpebral fissure, while abduction is deficient because the lateral rectus is not properly innervated for that action. The condition is usually sporadic, though familial cases and the associated gene CHN1 implicate disordered axon guidance during brainstem development, and it can occur within broader syndromes such as Wildervanck. Generally a stable, non-progressive condition with good functional outcome; many patients retain binocular vision via head posture, and surgery can improve alignment and posture though it cannot restore normal abduction.

fails to visualise the gallbladder, and biliary scintigraphy shows delayed hepatic clearance Jaundice may be precipitated or worsened by pregnancy, oral contraceptives, or intercurrent illness No warranting exclusion of other cholestatic disease Mistaking benign conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia for obstructive or hepatocellular disease and pursuing invasive workup Overlooking the distinguishing coproporphyrin isomer pattern that separates it from Rotor syndrome Attributing the abnormal liver pigment to malignancy on biopsy Failing to reassure patients, leading to unnecessary anxiety and investigation Assuming imaging non-visualisation of the gallbladder implies pathological obstruction MRP2, encoded by ABCC2, is the canalicular transporter responsible for secreting conjugated bilirubin and other organic anions from the hepatocyte into bile. In Dubin-Johnson syndrome, biallelic loss-of-function mutations impair this export step, so conjugated bilirubin that has been normally taken up and glucuronidated cannot be efficiently excreted and refluxes back into the blood, producing conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. A parallel disturbance of organic anion handling shifts urinary coproporphyrin excretion toward the isomer I fraction. The retained dark pigment, thought to derive from adrenaline metabolites, accumulates in lysosomes and gives the liver its distinctive black appearance, but hepatocyte function and architecture remain otherwise normal. Dubin-Johnson syndrome is benign with a normal life expectancy and does not progress to cirrhosis; jaundice may fluctuate with hormonal or physiological stress but requires no specific therapy.

Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy — DMD, Duchenne dystrophy, pseudohypertrophic muscular dystrophy Becker muscular dystrophy (milder allelic disorder) Limb-girdle muscular dystrophies Spinal muscular atrophy Congenital myopathies Inflammatory myopathy Metabolic myopathy Serum creatine kinase (markedly elevated) Genetic testing for DMD gene deletions, duplications, and point mutations Muscle biopsy with dystrophin immunostaining when genetics are inconclusive Electrocardiogram and echocardiography for cardiomyopathy surveillance Pulmonary function testing to monitor respiratory muscle strength The most common and most severe childhood muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive disorder that therefore affects boys, caused by absence of functional dystrophin. Symptoms usually appear in early childhood with delayed walking, frequent falls, difficulty running and climbing stairs, and a waddling gait. Gower sign - using the hands to 'climb up' the legs when rising from the floor - reflects proximal, especially pelvic girdle, weakness. Calf pseudohypertrophy from fatty and fibrous replacement of muscle is a characteristic finding. Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated, often into the thousands, even before overt weakness. Weakness is progressive; most boys lose independent ambulation by around the early teens without disease-modifying therapy. Cardiomyopathy and respiratory muscle weakness are the main causes of morbidity and death, so cardiac and pulmonary surveillance is essential. Glucocorticoids slow progression and prolong ambulation and are a mainstay of care; multidisciplinary management improves outcomes. Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing for dystrophin gene mutations, with muscle biopsy reserved for uncertain cases; learning and behavioural difficulties are more common than in the general population. Declining respiratory function or nocturnal hypoventilation Symptoms or signs of cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia Rapid loss of motor milestones or ambulation Recurrent chest infections with weak cough Perioperative risk, including reactions to certain anaesthetic agents Attributing early motor delay and clumsiness to normal variation and delaying creatine kinase testing Overlooking the diagnosis in a boy presenting with isolated raised transaminases (from muscle, not liver) Neglecting cardiac and respiratory surveillance in an ambulant child Using certain anaesthetic agents that can trigger dangerous reactions Failing to offer genetic counselling and carrier testing to the family Mutations in the DMD gene abolish functional dystrophin, a cytoskeletal protein that links the muscle fibre cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix through the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex. Without it the sarcolemma is unstable and is damaged by contraction, leading to repeated cycles of muscle fibre degeneration and regeneration, calcium influx, inflammation, and eventual replacement of muscle by fat and fibrous tissue. Dystrophin deficiency in cardiac muscle produces cardiomyopathy. Without disease-modifying treatment, progressive weakness leads to loss of ambulation in the early teens, with respiratory and cardiac complications limiting survival; corticosteroids, cardiac and respiratory support, and multidisciplinary care have substantially improved life expectancy.

with other features raising concern for carcinoma Associated axillary lymphadenopathy Discordant triple assessment findings Attributing nipple retraction or a subareolar mass to duct ectasia without before completing triple assessment Confusing physiological discharge with pathological discharge Duct ectasia involves progressive dilatation of the large ducts beneath the nipple, with accumulation The stagnant luminal contents and leakage of material into surrounding tissue provoke a chronic inflammatory and fibrotic response, which over time shortens and scars the ducts. This fibrosis can tether and retract the nipple and produce a firm subareolar mass, features that clinically overlap with carcinoma. The condition is degenerative and age-related and is closely related to periductal mastitis, in which the inflammatory component predominates and is strongly linked to smoking. Duct ectasia is a benign condition with a good prognosis; symptoms frequently settle with conservative management, and surgery is curative for persistent discharge, although periductal inflammation can recur, particularly in smokers.

clinical pattern, supported where needed by a provocation test or documentation of postprandial hypoglycaemia First-line management is dietary modification with smaller, more frequent low-carbohydrate meals and separating solids from liquids Refractory cases may need pharmacological therapy to slow transit or, rarely, surgical revision Severe or recurrent hypoglycaemia with neuroglycopenic symptoms Significant weight loss or malnutrition Symptoms suggesting a mechanical complication such as afferent loop obstruction Features suggesting an endocrine tumour rather than dumping Overlooking late dumping as a cause of postprandial hypoglycaemic spells after gastric surgery Failing to give thorough dietary advice before escalating to drugs or surgery Confusing dumping with afferent loop syndrome or gastroparesis Attributing vasomotor symptoms to anxiety rather than to rapid emptying Dumping syndrome follows loss of normal gastric reservoir and pyloric control after surgery, allowing hyperosmolar gastric contents to pass rapidly into the small bowel. In early dumping, the osmotic load draws fluid into the lumen, causing distension and diarrhoea, and triggers release of vasoactive gut hormones that produce the vasomotor symptoms. In late dumping, rapid delivery and absorption of carbohydrate provokes an exaggerated insulin (and incretin) surge that outlasts the glucose load, resulting in reactive hypoglycaemia one to three hours after the meal. Most patients improve substantially with dietary modification, and symptoms often lessen over time; a minority have persistent, disabling symptoms requiring pharmacological or surgical measures.

with bilious vomiting and upper abdominal fullness with a scaphoid lower abdomen Vomiting is usually bilious because most obstructions lie distal to the ampulla of Vater, though a proximal lesion can cause non-bilious vomiting The classic radiographic finding is the double-bubble sign, two gas-filled bubbles from the distended stomach and proximal duodenum with little or no distal bowel gas in fluid and electrolyte disturbance, and evaluation for associated anomalies before definitive surgical repair A partial obstruction from a duodenal web or stenosis may present later and more subtly with intermittent vomiting and feeding difficulty Bilious vomiting in a neonate, which mandates urgent exclusion of malrotation with volvulus Signs of bowel ischaemia such as abdominal tenderness, distension, or bloody stool Severe dehydration and electrolyte or acid-base disturbance from persistent vomiting Coexisting critical congenital heart disease or other major anomaly affecting stability associated cardiac, renal, or chromosomal conditions before surgery Delaying gastric decompression and fluid resuscitation while awaiting definitive imaging Attributing the double-bubble sign solely to duodenal atresia without considering annular pancreas or malrotation Duodenal atresia is thought to arise from failure of recanalisation of the duodenal lumen during early embryonic development, when the normally solid cord of proliferating epithelium fails to reopen. This produces a spectrum from complete atresia to a stenosis or a fenestrated web (windsock deformity). The obstruction is most often located near the ampulla of Vater, and because it is usually distal to the bile duct opening the vomiting is characteristically bilious. Proximal bowel becomes distended while distal bowel is decompressed, giving the double-bubble appearance. The developmental timing overlaps with that of other structures, which accounts for the frequent association with Down syndrome and with cardiac, renal, and other gastrointestinal anomalies. With timely diagnosis and surgical correction the outlook for isolated duodenal atresia is very good and most infants achieve normal feeding and growth. Prognosis is influenced mainly by prematurity and by associated anomalies, particularly complex congenital heart disease and the syndromic burden in Down syndrome.

Duplex collecting system — duplex kidney, duplicated collecting system, ureteral duplication Ureteropelvic junction obstruction of a single system Ureterocele or ectopic ureter in a single system Vesicoureteric reflux without duplication Primary obstructive megaureter Multicystic dysplastic upper-pole moiety Continuous incontinence from other cause in girls Renal and bladder ultrasound to demonstrate duplication and moiety dilatation Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) to detect reflux, usually into the lower moiety MAG3 or DMSA renography to assess function of each moiety and drainage MR urography to define complex ductal anatomy and ectopic insertions Cystoscopy to locate ureteric orifices and any ureterocele Urinalysis and culture during infection One of the commonest congenital urinary tract anomalies, ranging from a partial (incomplete) duplication where the two ureters join before the bladder, to complete duplication with two separate ureteric orifices The Weigert-Meyer rule governs complete duplication: the upper-pole ureter inserts more caudally and medially (ectopic, prone to obstruction and ureterocele), while the lower-pole ureter inserts more superolaterally and is prone to vesicoureteric reflux Many duplex systems are incidental and asymptomatic and require no treatment Symptomatic presentations include urinary tract infection, antenatal hydronephrosis, obstruction of the upper moiety, reflux into the lower moiety, and continuous incontinence in girls from an ectopic ureter inserting below the sphincter In partial duplication, ureteroureteral (yo-yo) reflux between the two limbs can cause stasis and infection Imaging aims to define which moiety is affected, its function, and the presence of reflux, obstruction, or an ectopic insertion/ureterocele Management is dictated by function and pathology, from surveillance to upper-pole heminephrectomy, ureteric reimplantation, or ureteroureterostomy Obstruction of the upper moiety with declining function or infection High-grade reflux into the lower moiety with recurrent pyelonephritis or scarring Continuous urinary leakage from an ectopic ureter indicating an insertion below the sphincter Urosepsis in an obstructed or refluxing duplex system Misapplying the Weigert-Meyer rule and treating the wrong moiety Missing an ectopic ureter as the cause of continuous incontinence in a girl Overlooking a poorly functioning obstructed upper pole on standard imaging Assuming all duplex systems require surgery when many are incidental A duplex collecting system arises when the ureteric bud undergoes abnormal branching during development. Early splitting of a single bud produces incomplete duplication with a bifid system joining before the bladder, whereas two separate ureteric buds produce complete duplication with two ureters and orifices. The differing sites at which the buds contact the developing bladder explain the Weigert-Meyer relationship: the more caudally arising upper-pole ureter inserts ectopically and inferomedially, predisposing to obstruction and ureterocele, while the lower-pole ureter inserts superolaterally with a short intramural tunnel, predisposing to reflux. The associated renal moieties may show variable dysplasia depending on the position of bud contact with the metanephric blastema. Asymptomatic duplex systems have an excellent prognosis and need no intervention; symptomatic systems generally do well when the specific pathology (obstruction, reflux, or ectopia) is appropriately treated, with overall renal function usually preserved.

Duplex kidney — duplex collecting system, duplicated collecting system, ureteral duplication Pelviureteric junction obstruction or simple hydronephrosis Single-system ectopic ureter or ureterocele Vesicoureteric reflux in a single system Multicystic dysplastic upper pole moiety Neurogenic bladder or other functional cause of incontinence Bladder diverticulum Ureteric stricture Renal tract ultrasound to show two pelvicalyceal systems, upper pole hydronephrosis, a dilated ureter or a ureterocele Micturating cystourethrogram to assess reflux and demonstrate a ureterocele MAG3 or DMSA renal scintigraphy for the differential function and drainage of each moiety MR urography for anatomical delineation and localisation of an ectopic ureter Urinalysis and culture to confirm and characterise urinary tract infection Baseline serum renal function One of the commonest congenital urinary tract anomalies; a duplex kidney drains through two pelvicalyceal systems, either partial (the ureters unite before reaching the bladder, giving a bifid or Y-shaped ureter) or complete (two separate ureters with two bladder orifices) The Weigert-Meyer rule states that in complete duplication the upper pole ureter inserts ectopically, inferomedial to the lower pole ureter, and tends to obstruct, often with a ureterocele, while the lower pole ureter inserts more laterally and superiorly and tends to reflux As a result the upper moiety tends towards obstruction and dysplasia, and the lower moiety towards vesicoureteric reflux and reflux nephropathy An ectopic upper pole ureter that inserts below the sphincter in a girl (into the vagina, urethra or vestibule) causes continuous dribbling incontinence despite otherwise normal voiding, a classic diagnostic clue In boys the upper pole ureter cannot insert below the continence mechanism, so incontinence does not occur; instead it may drain into wolffian derivatives and present with epididymitis or a seminal vesicle cyst Presentations include antenatal hydronephrosis, recurrent urinary tract infection, incontinence or an incidental finding, and a ureterocele may prolapse into the urethra to cause bladder outlet obstruction Management is guided by function and symptoms and ranges from conservative observation to endoscopic ureterocele puncture, ureteric reimplantation, ureteroureterostomy or heminephrectomy of a non-functioning moiety Febrile urinary tract infection, pyelonephritis or urosepsis A prolapsing ureterocele causing bladder outlet obstruction with bilateral upper tract dilatation and renal impairment An obstructed non-functioning upper pole moiety Severe bilateral antenatal hydronephrosis Missing a duplex system on ultrasound when only the lower pole is well visualised Overlooking an ectopic ureter in a girl with continuous wetness despite normal voiding and mislabelling it functional incontinence Failing to apply the Weigert-Meyer rule and attributing obstruction or reflux to the wrong moiety Removing a moiety that retains recoverable function Not recognising a prolapsing ureterocele as a cause of bladder outlet obstruction Duplication of the collecting system results from anomalous development of the ureteric bud from the mesonephric (wolffian) duct. Two separate ureteric buds induce complete duplication with two ureters and two orifices, whereas a single bud that bifurcates early produces incomplete (partial) duplication. In keeping with the Weigert-Meyer relationship, the bud destined for the upper pole is carried more caudally and medially and joins the bladder ectopically with a tendency to obstruct and to form a ureterocele, while the lower pole bud reaches the bladder earlier and more laterally with a short intramural tunnel that predisposes to reflux. Whether the ectopic upper pole ureter terminates above or below the continence mechanism determines whether continuous incontinence occurs. The prognosis is generally good; many duplex systems are asymptomatic and require no intervention. Outcomes depend on preserving renal function and controlling infection and reflux, and even moieties needing surgery usually do well overall.

cannot lay the palm flat against a table, indicating a functionally significant contracture Metacarpophalangeal joint contractures generally correct more reliably than proximal interphalangeal joint contractures, which tend to be more resistant Associated with northern European ancestry, family history, male sex, increasing age, diabetes, alcohol excess, smoking and antiepileptic use Ectopic family history and ectopic involvement) predicts aggressive behaviour and recurrence Generic management ranges from observation of mild non-contracting disease to needle aponeurotomy, collagenase interphalangeal contracture with skin maceration or secondary infection Signs of digital neurovascular compromise Aggressive early-onset diathesis with rapid recurrence in a young patient Mistaking a benign nodule for a tumour, or conversely dismissing a genuine soft-tissue neoplasm as Dupuytren tissue Iatrogenic injury to a neurovascular bundle displaced by a spiral cord during aponeurotomy or fasciectomy Intervening too aggressively in mild, non-contracting disease that only warrants observation Underestimating the likelihood of recurrence and failing to counsel patients accordingly Dupuytren disease is a benign proliferative fibromatosis of the palmar and digital fascia in which myofibroblasts proliferate and lay down disorganised, contractile type III collagen, converting the normal fascial bands into pathological cords. The process is classically described in proliferative, involutional and residual phases, driven by growth factors such as transforming growth factor beta acting on genetically predisposed tissue. Contraction of the cords progressively flexes the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, while a spiral cord can displace the neurovascular bundle superficially and towards the midline, placing it at risk during surgery. The condition is benign but typically progressive and prone to recurrence, particularly in those with a diathesis; metacarpophalangeal contractures respond well to treatment whereas established proximal interphalangeal contractures are less predictable and may leave residual deformity.

Dupuytren disease — Dupuytren contracture, palmar fibromatosis Stenosing tenosynovitis (trigger finger) with a palpable nodule Camptodactyly Post-traumatic or burn scar contracture Ulnar nerve palsy causing clawing Soft-tissue sarcoma or other palmar mass Diabetic cheiroarthropathy (limited joint mobility syndrome) Epithelioid sarcoma of the hand Diagnosis is clinical; imaging is rarely required Serial goniometric measurement of MCP and PIP contracture angles Hueston tabletop test documentation Ultrasound to characterise an atypical palmar mass when the diagnosis is uncertain MRI reserved for suspected sarcoma or atypical rapidly enlarging lesions Screening for associated diabetes mellitus where clinically indicated Photographic record for monitoring progression Benign fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar and digital fascia producing nodules, cords and progressive flexion contracture, most often of the ring and little fingers. Strong association with northern European ancestry, positive family history, male sex and increasing age; alcohol misuse, diabetes mellitus, smoking and antiepileptic therapy are recognised associations. The pathological cord contracts the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints; MCP contracture is more readily corrected than PIP contracture, which tends to be more resistant and prone to recurrence. A positive Hueston tabletop test (inability to lay the palm flat on a flat surface) is a useful clinical indicator that intervention should be considered. Dupuytren diathesis (early onset, bilateral disease, strong family history, ectopic lesions) predicts aggressive behaviour and higher recurrence. Ectopic disease includes knuckle pads (Garrod nodes), plantar fibromatosis (Ledderhose disease) and penile fibromatosis (Peyronie disease). Treatment options include limited fasciectomy, percutaneous needle fasciotomy and collagenase clostridial injection; choice balances contracture severity, joint involved, patient fitness and recurrence risk. Recurrence is common regardless of technique, and the condition is controlled rather than cured; realistic counselling about recurrence and the aim of function is essential. Rapidly enlarging, painful or firm fixed mass suggesting sarcoma rather than benign fibromatosis Progressive fixed PIP flexion contracture threatening hand function Skin ulceration, maceration or fixed web-space contracture impairing hygiene Sensory or vascular compromise of a digit from severe contracture Mistaking a Dupuytren nodule for a trigger finger nodule or a ganglion and mismanaging it Operating too early on a soft palmar nodule without contracture, exposing the patient to surgical risk for little functional gain Underestimating the difficulty and recurrence rate of correcting fixed PIP contractures Failing to recognise digital neurovascular bundle displacement by spiral cords, risking iatrogenic injury during fasciectomy Overlooking diathesis features that should temper prognostic expectations Dupuytren disease is a fibroproliferative condition in which myofibroblasts within the longitudinal palmar and digital fascia proliferate and deposit disorganised type III collagen. Progression classically passes through a proliferative nodular phase rich in contractile myofibroblasts, an involutional phase in which cords align along lines of tension, and a residual phase of relatively acellular collagenous cord. Dysregulated cytokine signalling, particularly transforming growth factor beta and platelet-derived growth factor, together with local oxidative stress and a genetic predisposition involving Wnt signalling pathway variants, drives contraction of the diseased fascia and secondary joint contracture. A benign but chronic and progressive condition that is controlled rather than cured, with recurrence common after any intervention, particularly in patients with a strong diathesis. Function is generally well preserved with appropriate timing of treatment, though established PIP contractures respond less predictably.

Deep vein thrombosis — Compression ultrasound (Doppler) D-dimer Wells score Anticoagulate; assess for PE Ruptured Baker's cyst (sudden severe calf discomfort) (Harrison 22e p.2159) Muscle strain or injury (Harrison 22e p.2159) Acute postthrombotic syndrome / chronic venous insufficiency (Harrison 22e p.2159) May-Thurner syndrome (iliac vein compression) presenting as recurrent leg edema (Harrison 22e p.2159) Cellulitis - fever and chills more often herald cellulitis than DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159) Loss of vein compressibility is the primary ultrasound criterion for DVT; a normal vein collapses (a 'wink') under gentle transducer pressure, whereas an acutely thrombosed vein stays distended and may show central, homogeneous, low-echogenicity thrombus (Harrison 22e p.2160). Doppler interrogation adds flow data: calf compression normally augments flow, and loss of respiratory variation suggests an obstructing DVT or a pelvic obstructive process (Harrison 22e p.2160). Contrast (gadolinium) MR venography is an excellent option when pelvic or leg ultrasound is equivocal or technically nondiagnostic (Harrison 22e p.2160-2161). Contrast phlebography is now reserved mainly for when an interventional procedure is planned (Harrison 22e p.2161). An age-adjusted d-dimer cutoff (age x 10 ng/mL in patients >50 years) is endorsed for ruling out PE but does NOT apply to suspected acute DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159-2160). d-Dimer rarely helps in hospitalized patients because levels are frequently elevated by systemic illness (MI, pneumonia, sepsis, cancer, postoperative state, pregnancy) (Harrison 22e p.2159). Ruptured Baker's cyst (Harrison 22e p.2159) Muscle strain or injury (Harrison 22e p.2159) Chronic venous insufficiency / postthrombotic syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2156, 2159) The classic DVT symptom is a calf cramp or 'charley horse' that persists and worsens over several days, rather than a sudden event (Harrison 22e p.2159). A diffusely edematous (whole-leg) limb actually makes ordinary DVT less likely, with the important exception of phlegmasia cerulea dolens, the most severe form of DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159). Recurrent left thigh edema, especially in a young woman, should raise suspicion of May-Thurner syndrome, in which the right common iliac artery compresses the left common iliac vein and may precipitate DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159). Upper extremity DVT may show only subtle asymmetry of the supraclavicular fossa or upper-arm circumference; it is increasingly linked to PICC lines and rises with larger catheter diameter and more lumens (Harrison 22e p.2158-2159, 2161). Superficial vein thrombosis presents with erythema, tenderness and a palpable cord and carries a risk of extension into the deep venous system (Harrison 22e p.2158). An idiopathic (no clear precipitant) VTE is the strongest predictor of recurrence in patients without malignancy (Harrison 22e p.473). Testing for inherited thrombophilia in adults should be reserved for the rare situation where the result would actually change management (Harrison 22e p.473-474). Phlegmasia cerulea dolens - massive proximal DVT with a diffusely swollen, painful, cyanotic limb, the most serious form of DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159). Signs of pulmonary embolism (unexplained breathlessness, syncope, hypotension, cyanosis) since DVT can embolize; many PE patients have no detectable residual DVT because the leg clot has already embolized (Harrison 22e p.2158-2159). Active malignancy as the underlying driver - up to ~15% of patients who develop DVT have cancer, and unprovoked VTE may be its first manifestation (Harrison 22e p.~705). Not all leg pain is DVT - sudden severe calf pain may be a ruptured Baker's cyst, and fever/chills point more to cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.2159). Wells point-score rules are validated in ambulatory but NOT in hospitalized patients (Harrison 22e p.2159). Using d-dimer to rule out DVT in hospitalized or systemically ill patients is futile because it is frequently elevated by non-thrombotic illness (Harrison 22e p.2159). The age-adjusted d-dimer threshold validated for PE does not extend to suspected acute DVT (Harrison 22e p.2160). In cancer patients, elevated d-dimer is far less predictive of DVT than in patients without cancer (Harrison 22e p.~705). IVC filters can paradoxically increase the DVT rate by acting as a nidus for clot, and may still let small-to-medium clots pass via collateral veins (Harrison 22e p.2163). Warfarin (not a DOAC) is the standard anticoagulant for antiphospholipid syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2163). DVT arises from Virchow's triad of venous stasis, hypercoagulability and endothelial injury, now understood to be typically coupled with an inflammatory trigger. Activated platelets release proinflammatory microparticles that recruit neutrophils to form neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs); these histone-rich, web-like networks promote platelet aggregation and platelet-dependent thrombin generation. Thrombi form and propagate in an environment of stasis, low oxygen tension and upregulated proinflammatory genes. Lower-extremity thrombi usually begin in the calf veins and can propagate proximally to the popliteal, femoral and iliac veins; detached thrombi embolize through the vena cava and right heart into the pulmonary circulation, and rarely cross a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect to cause paradoxical (arterial) embolism. VTE shares inflammation, hypercoagulability and endothelial injury with arterial atherothrombosis, so VTE patients have more than double the risk of future MI or stroke and vice versa. Common genetic prothrombotic states are factor V Leiden (resistance to protein C) and the prothrombin gene mutation (raised prothrombin level); deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C and protein S also predispose but are rare; antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired thrombophilia causing both venous and arterial thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.2156-2158). Postthrombotic syndrome (chronic venous insufficiency) is the main long-term morbidity: damaged venous valves cause ankle/calf swelling and leg aching after prolonged standing, and in its most severe form deep skin ulceration near the medial malleolus. Notably, graduated compression stockings prescribed for asymptomatic newly diagnosed acute DVT do NOT prevent postthrombotic syndrome (they are used only for symptomatic swelling relief). Recurrence risk after stopping anticoagulation is stratified (ESC 2019) as low (<3%/yr, e.g., major surgery/trauma), intermediate (3-8%/yr, e.g., minor surgery, hospitalization for acute illness, pregnancy/estrogen, long-haul flight, IBD, autoimmune disease, or no identifiable risk factor) and high (>8%/yr, active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome). Harrison de-emphasizes the 'provoked vs unprovoked' dichotomy because many provoked VTEs recur at rates similar to unprovoked ones, and enduring risk factors (heart failure, chronic lung disease, IBD) raise recurrence risk. The Post-VTE Functional Status scale (grades 0-4) can track functional recovery (Harrison 22e p.2156-2157, 2163). Wells clinical prediction rule for DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159): low likelihood if score <=0, moderate if 1-2, high if >=3. Points: active cancer +1; paralysis/paresis or recent cast +1; bedridden >3 days or major surgery <12 weeks +1; tenderness along distribution of deep veins +1; entire-leg swelling +1; unilateral calf swelling >3 cm +1; pitting edema +1; collateral superficial nonvaricose veins +1; alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT -2. Pretest-probability strategy: patients with low DVT likelihood undergo d-dimer first and need no imaging if it is normal, whereas high-likelihood patients should skip d-dimer and proceed straight to compression ultrasound imaging.

diagnostic clue Dyggve-Melchior-Clausen syndrome is caused by loss-of-function variants in DYM, which encodes dymeclin, a protein required for normal Golgi apparatus organisation and intracellular trafficking. Impaired Golgi function disturbs the processing and secretion of extracellular matrix components in chondrocytes and, in neurones, contributes to the associated intellectual disability. The result is abnormal endochondral ossification affecting vertebrae, epiphyses and metaphyses, producing platyspondyly, the distinctive lacy iliac crest, and generalised skeletal dysplasia. The allelic disorder Smith-McCort dysplasia shares the skeletal phenotype without cognitive impairment. Life expectancy is often near normal, but morbidity from short stature, progressive spinal deformity, joint contractures and (in classic DMC) intellectual disability is significant; cervical instability requires vigilance to prevent cord injury.

Dismissing isolated dysarthria and hand clumsiness as non-neurological or functional Assuming a lacunar cause without excluding large-vessel or cardioembolic sources Overlooking subtle cortical signs that would reclassify the syndrome Relying on early CT, which often fails to reveal a small acute lacune Dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome is a lacunar syndrome caused by a small deep infarct, typically from small-vessel occlusion related to hypertension and diabetes. The lesion, most often in the basis pontis or the genu and posterior limb of the internal capsule, interrupts corticobulbar fibres supplying the bulbar musculature, producing dysarthria and often mild facial and tongue weakness, together with corticospinal fibres to the hand, producing clumsiness and impaired fine motor control. Because the lesion is small and spares sensory, visual, and cortical pathways, the deficit is limited to speech and hand dexterity with only mild associated pyramidal signs. The syndrome usually carries a favourable prognosis with good recovery of speech and hand function after a single lacune, although recurrent small-vessel disease may lead to cumulative disability.

Dysbaric osteonecrosis — caisson disease of bone, diver's bone necrosis Avascular necrosis from other causes (corticosteroids, alcohol, sickle cell disease) Osteoarthritis Bone infarct of another aetiology Bone tumour or metastasis Osteomyelitis Plain radiography and MRI to detect and characterise lesions Occupational history of diving or compressed-air work and decompression incidents Assessment for other causes of osteonecrosis Joint imaging where articular collapse is suspected Surveillance imaging in exposed workers Avascular necrosis of bone occurring in divers and compressed-air (caisson) workers exposed to repeated or inadequate decompression It characteristically affects the humeral and femoral heads and the shafts of long bones Shaft (medullary) lesions are typically asymptomatic, whereas juxta-articular lesions can progress to joint surface collapse and arthritis There is often a latent period of months to years between exposure and radiological changes It is associated with cumulative dysbaric exposure and with episodes of decompression sickness Screening imaging is used in occupationally exposed groups, and established joint disease may require orthopaedic treatment Joint pain suggesting articular surface collapse Rapidly progressive joint destruction Features suggesting an alternative cause such as malignancy or infection Multiple or bilateral juxta-articular lesions Attributing osteonecrosis to diving without excluding steroids, alcohol and other causes Overlooking asymptomatic lesions that need monitoring Missing early juxta-articular disease before collapse Failing to review decompression practice in affected workers Dysbaric osteonecrosis is thought to result from impaired blood supply to bone related to decompression, with proposed mechanisms including intraosseous or intravascular gas bubbles, fat embolism and altered coagulation compromising the end-arterial supply of bone. The resulting ischaemia causes death of bone and marrow, and subsequent attempted repair produces the characteristic lesions. Juxta-articular necrosis weakens the subchondral bone, leading to collapse of the articular surface and secondary degenerative joint disease. Shaft lesions are usually asymptomatic and stable, but juxta-articular disease can progress to disabling joint collapse requiring arthroplasty; prevention through safe decompression is key.

dyschromatosis — dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria, dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria Dowling-Degos disease Reticulate acropigmentation of Kitamura Xeroderma pigmentosum Vitiligo with perilesional hyperpigmentation Poikiloderma of various causes Naevoid pigmentary mosaicism Acropigmentation of Dohi variants Detailed three-generation family pedigree to establish inheritance pattern Molecular genetic testing for ADAR1 (DSH) and ABCB6 and related genes (DUH) Skin biopsy of paired hyper- and hypopigmented macules showing corresponding melanin changes Wood's lamp examination to characterise the pattern of pigment change Neurological assessment where dystonia or developmental features are present in DSH Dermoscopy to define the reticulate pigmentary pattern A group of inherited pigmentary genodermatoses characterised by the coexistence of hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules producing a mottled or reticulate pattern. Dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (DSH) is caused by mutations in ADAR1 (DSRAD) and typically presents with symmetrical reticulate macules on the dorsa of the hands and feet. Dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria (DUH) shows generalised, more widespread mixed macules and is associated with ABCB6 and other loci. Onset is usually in infancy or early childhood, with lesions becoming established before puberty and remaining largely stable thereafter. Inheritance is most often autosomal dominant, though recessive kindreds are described, so a detailed pedigree is valuable. DSH may rarely be associated with neurological features such as dystonia and developmental delay, reflecting the wider role of ADAR1 in RNA editing. The face, trunk, and limbs can be involved in DUH, and mucosae and nails are usually spared. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by family history and, where available, molecular confirmation; histology shows corresponding increases and decreases in epidermal melanin. Neurological deterioration, dystonia, or developmental regression suggesting ADAR1-related systemic involvement Marked photosensitivity or early cutaneous malignancy raising suspicion of xeroderma pigmentosum Progressive poikiloderma with atrophy and telangiectasia indicating an alternative genodermatosis Rapidly changing or ulcerating pigmented lesions warranting exclusion of malignancy Confusing the reticulate pattern with Dowling-Degos disease or Kitamura acropigmentation, which have distinct distributions and genetics Overlooking xeroderma pigmentosum when photosensitivity or early skin cancers accompany the dyschromia Failing to enquire about neurological symptoms in suspected DSH Assuming a purely cosmetic disorder and omitting genetic counselling for affected families Attempting aggressive depigmenting or laser therapy for a stable, benign, and genetically determined pattern The dyschromatoses arise from disturbed regulation of melanin production and distribution rather than melanocyte loss. In dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria, loss-of-function mutations in ADAR1, which encodes an adenosine deaminase acting on double-stranded RNA (RNA editing enzyme), disrupt post-transcriptional RNA editing; the resulting dysregulation of melanocyte gene expression produces adjacent zones of increased and decreased epidermal melanin, giving the reticulate acral pattern. In dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria, mutations in ABCB6, a mitochondrial and lysosomal porphyrin transporter contributing to melanosome function, and in other identified loci, similarly perturb the balance of melanogenesis to yield widespread mixed macules. Histologically the hyperpigmented macules show increased basal melanin and the hypopigmented macules show reduced melanin, with melanocytes generally preserved in number, confirming that the disorder reflects abnormal pigment regulation within a normal melanocyte population. The dyschromatoses are benign, stable, and lifelong pigmentary disorders that do not undergo malignant change, and the cutaneous findings are of cosmetic rather than medical concern. Prognosis is chiefly determined by any associated systemic features, notably the rare neurological involvement described in some ADAR1-related cases.

benign imaging change to progression and over-investigating Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumour is a benign, developmental glioneuronal tumour arising in the cerebral cortex, thought to originate from progenitor cells during cortical development, in keeping with its frequent association with focal cortical dysplasia. Its defining feature is the specific glioneuronal element: columns of axons oriented perpendicular to the cortical surface, lined by small oligodendrocyte-like cells, with neurons appearing to float within pools of pale mucoid matrix. Proliferative activity is minimal and the lesion is essentially non-progressive. Molecular studies commonly identify alterations of the FGFR1 gene. Its intracortical location and disruption of local circuitry underlie the epileptogenic behaviour that dominates the clinical picture. Prognosis is excellent, as the tumour is benign and non-progressive; complete surgical resection commonly achieves long-term seizure freedom, particularly when associated cortical dysplasia is also removed. Malignant transformation is very rare, and incidental or well-controlled lesions may be monitored.

Dysfibrinogenaemia — congenital dysfibrinogenaemia, acquired dysfibrinogenaemia, FGA/FGB/FGG variants, qualitative fibrinogen disorder Afibrinogenaemia and hypofibrinogenaemia (quantitative fibrinogen defects) Liver disease causing acquired fibrinogen dysfunction Disseminated intravascular coagulation Direct thrombin inhibitor or heparin effect prolonging the thrombin time Other inherited thrombophilias when thrombosis predominates Factor XIII deficiency when clot instability is prominent Clauss functional fibrinogen assay compared with fibrinogen antigen to demonstrate a functional-to-antigen discrepancy Thrombin time and reptilase time to detect impaired fibrin polymerisation Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time as screening tests Fibrinogen gene sequencing (FGA, FGB, FGG) to confirm a congenital variant Liver function tests to identify an acquired hepatic cause Thrombophilia workup and imaging when a thrombotic event has occurred A qualitative fibrinogen defect in which a structurally abnormal molecule is produced, so functional fibrinogen is low while immunological (antigen) levels are near normal The clinical picture is heterogeneous: many carriers are asymptomatic, some bleed, and a notable minority have a paradoxical tendency to thrombosis The hallmark laboratory pattern is a discrepancy between a reduced Clauss (functional) fibrinogen and a normal or near-normal antigen level Prolonged thrombin time and reptilase time are characteristic, reflecting defective fibrin polymerisation Congenital forms arise from variants in the fibrinogen genes (FGA, FGB, FGG); acquired forms occur with liver disease and some malignancies Certain variants are strongly linked to venous thrombosis, so a bleeding-only mindset can be misleading Management is guided by the individual and family phenotype, using fibrinogen replacement for bleeding and anticoagulation for thrombotic presentations rather than a fixed protocol Unexplained venous or arterial thrombosis in a patient labelled as having a bleeding disorder Severe or postoperative bleeding out of proportion to the platelet count Pregnancy loss or thrombotic complications during pregnancy Rapidly falling fibrinogen suggesting acquired consumption or hepatic decompensation Assuming a low fibrinogen means bleeding risk when the variant is actually prothrombotic Measuring only antigen and missing the functional deficit Overlooking acquired dysfibrinogenaemia in a patient with liver disease Failing to relate the laboratory abnormality to the individual and family bleeding or thrombotic history Dysfibrinogenaemia results from an amino-acid substitution or other structural abnormality in one of the fibrinogen chains, yielding a molecule that is synthesised and secreted but functions abnormally. Depending on the site of the defect, fibrin monomer polymerisation, fibrinopeptide release, cross-linking, or interaction with thrombin and plasmin is impaired. Some variants produce a fibrin clot that resists fibrinolysis or fails to bind thrombin normally, explaining the paradoxical thrombotic phenotype, while others yield a friable clot that bleeds. Acquired dysfibrinogenaemia typically reflects abnormal glycosylation of fibrinogen in hepatic disease. Outlook is variable and phenotype-dependent; many individuals live normally, whereas those with bleeding-prone or thrombosis-prone variants face event-related morbidity. Recognising the specific familial phenotype allows tailored prophylaxis and generally favourable long-term outcomes.

risk of malignant change Rising tumour markers indicating progression or a mixed germ-cell component Assuming a solid ovarian mass in a young woman is benign and delaying diagnosis Failing to karyotype patients with features of gonadal dysgenesis, missing a Y-chromosome cancer risk Interpreting a raised AFP as consistent with pure dysgerminoma rather than a mixed germ-cell tumour Performing unnecessarily radical surgery when fertility-sparing treatment would suffice Dysgerminoma is a malignant germ-cell tumour composed of primitive germ cells that have not differentiated towards embryonic or extra-embryonic tissues, so its cells resemble the primordial oocytes and mirror testicular seminoma. Sheets and nests of uniform cells with clear cytoplasm are separated by fibrous septa infiltrated by lymphocytes, and scattered syncytiotrophoblast-like cells may secrete small amounts of beta-hCG. The tumour commonly shows gain of the short arm of chromosome 12 as an isochromosome 12p. In individuals with dysgenetic gonads carrying Y-chromosome material, a precursor gonadoblastoma can give rise to dysgerminoma, which is why karyotyping and consideration of gonadectomy are important in such patients. The tumour is intrinsically radiosensitive and chemosensitive, a key determinant of its favourable outlook. Excellent, particularly for early-stage disease, and even advanced or recurrent tumours frequently achieve cure because of high sensitivity to platinum-based chemotherapy; fertility can often be preserved.

reticulate skin hyperpigmentation, nail dystrophy, and oral leukoplakia Bone marrow failure is the leading cause of early mortality and may present as cytopenias or aplastic anaemia Markedly increased Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome adds cerebellar hypoplasia and immunodeficiency Very short telomeres for age (measured by flow-FISH) strongly support the diagnosis alongside gene testing Progressive pancytopenia or evolving bone marrow failure Features of myelodysplasia or acute leukaemia Non-healing or indurated oral leukoplakia suggesting squamous carcinoma Progressive dyspnoea from pulmonary fibrosis Treating apparent acquired aplastic anaemia without recognising an underlying telomere disorder, which alters transplant conditioning Using standard-intensity chemotherapy or radiotherapy that is poorly tolerated in these patients Overlooking pulmonary and hepatic complications by focusing only on skin and marrow Failing to screen at-risk relatives given variable inheritance and anticipation Dyskeratosis congenita is caused by defects in the telomere maintenance machinery, including the telomerase enzyme complex and shelterin proteins that protect chromosome ends. Inadequate telomere maintenance leads to accelerated telomere shortening, so highly proliferative tissues such as bone marrow, skin, mucosa, and lung exhaust their replicative capacity prematurely. Cells undergo senescence or apoptosis, producing the progressive stem-cell failure that underlies bone marrow failure, mucocutaneous changes, and organ fibrosis. Genomic instability from dysfunctional telomeres also explains the heightened predisposition to haematological and epithelial malignancies. Prognosis is guarded and shortened, dominated by bone marrow failure, malignancy, and pulmonary or hepatic fibrosis; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can address marrow failure but does not remove the ongoing cancer and organ-fibrosis risks, so lifelong surveillance is essential.

Dyslipidemia — hyperlipidemia, hypercholesterolemia, hypertriglyceridemia Fasting lipid profile: total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides (Harrison 22e p.2046). Lipoprotein(a) measurement, given its role as an independent cardiovascular risk predictor (Harrison 22e p.2017, p.2046). Apolipoprotein B as a marker of atherogenic particle burden (Harrison 22e p.3237). Screening for secondary contributors: glucose/HbA1c and urinalysis for diabetes and renal disease, and thyroid function testing when indicated (Harrison 22e p.2046). High-sensitivity C-reactive protein may be considered as an independent cardiovascular risk marker informing therapeutic decisions (Harrison 22e p.2046). Elevated plasma LDL cholesterol is a major modifiable driver of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; globally high LDL is estimated to contribute to ~41% of ischemic heart disease deaths and ~9% of stroke deaths (Harrison 22e p.2017). Lipoprotein(a) appears to be an independent predictor of cardiovascular risk beyond total or LDL cholesterol, and is elevated in roughly 20% of the global population; levels are reported higher in those of African descent and intermediate in East and South Asians (Harrison 22e p.2017). Tendon xanthomas (e.g., Achilles and extensor finger tendons), xanthelasma, and plane/tuberous xanthomas reflect hypercholesterolemia (hyperlipoproteinemia types II and III); eruptive xanthomas are most commonly associated with hypertriglyceridemia (types I, IV, V) (Harrison 22e p.234, p.1860). Palmar (palmar crease) xanthomas are specific for type III hyperlipoproteinemia, and severe hypertriglyceridemia can produce eruptive xanthomatosis and lipemia retinalis (Harrison 22e p.1860). Loss-of-function PCSK9 variants are associated with lower LDL cholesterol and reduced coronary artery disease, which led to development of PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies; rare gain-of-function PCSK9 variants are a cause of familial hypercholesterolemia (Harrison 22e p.260). Tendon xanthomas with premature coronary artery disease, suggesting familial hypercholesterolemia (Harrison 22e p.234, p.260). Severe hypertriglyceridemia, which can precipitate acute pancreatitis and may manifest with eruptive xanthomatosis and lipemia retinalis (Harrison 22e p.1860). Attributing dyslipidemia solely to primary lipid disorders while overlooking secondary causes such as diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, and excess alcohol intake (Harrison 22e p.2046). Underrecognizing familial hypercholesterolemia in patients with tendon xanthomas and premature coronary disease (Harrison 22e p.234, p.260). Atherogenic lipoproteins, principally LDL, deposit cholesterol within the arterial wall and disturb normal endothelial functions (control of vascular tone, maintenance of an antithrombotic surface, and regulation of inflammatory cell adhesion and diapedesis), promoting atherosclerosis; LDL, cigarette smoking, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus vary in their relative impact on these endothelial functions. Lipoprotein(a) is thought to add risk through increased cellular lipid accumulation, endothelial dysfunction, and effects on coagulation. Severe hypertriglyceridemia (chylomicron/VLDL accumulation) can precipitate acute pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2017, p.2046). LDL-driven dyslipidemia is a leading contributor to atherosclerotic cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, including ischemic heart disease and stroke; lowering LDL (e.g., a 50% or greater reduction with high-intensity statin therapy in patients with established atherosclerotic disease) reduces the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, and death (Harrison 22e p.2017, p.2056).

obstruction Focused history and pelvic examination to distinguish primary from secondary causes Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound to assess for fibroids, adenomyosis, and adnexal pathology Screening for sexually transmitted infection where pelvic inflammatory disease is suspected Diagnostic laparoscopy when endometriosis is suspected and symptoms persist Pregnancy test to exclude pregnancy-related pain Primary dysmenorrhoea is painful menstruation without underlying pelvic pathology and typically begins within a year or two of menarche once ovulatory cycles are established Secondary dysmenorrhoea arises from identifiable pelvic disease, most often endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, or pelvic inflammatory disease, and tends to begin later or change in character The pain of primary dysmenorrhoea is cramping and suprapubic, often radiating to the back and thighs, and coincides with the onset of menstrual flow Prostaglandin-driven myometrial contractions and uterine ischaemia underlie primary dysmenorrhoea, which explains the effectiveness of prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors First-line management combines non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with hormonal suppression of ovulation such as combined hormonal contraception Features suggesting secondary causes include pain that starts before bleeding or persists after it, deep dyspareunia, abnormal bleeding, or poor response to standard treatment A careful history and examination, with pelvic ultrasound and consideration of laparoscopy, help identify secondary pathology when suspected Symptoms of primary dysmenorrhoea often improve with age and after childbirth Pain beginning well after menarche or changing markedly in character, suggesting secondary pathology Associated abnormal or heavy uterine bleeding Deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, or cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms suggesting endometriosis Fever, abnormal discharge, or pelvic tenderness suggesting infection Failure to respond to first-line therapy, warranting further evaluation Assuming all menstrual pain is primary and missing endometriosis or adenomyosis Failing to reassess when standard treatment does not work Overlooking pelvic inflammatory disease as a treatable secondary cause Not offering hormonal suppression alongside anti-inflammatory therapy Attributing new-onset severe pain in an older woman to simple period pain In primary dysmenorrhoea, the fall in progesterone at the end of the luteal phase triggers release of arachidonic acid and increased endometrial production of prostaglandins, particularly PGF2-alpha. These stimulate intense, poorly coordinated myometrial contractions that raise intrauterine pressure and reduce uterine blood flow, producing ischaemic pain analogous to angina; leukotrienes and vasopressin contribute. In secondary dysmenorrhoea the pain results instead from a structural or inflammatory disorder such as ectopic endometrial tissue, myometrial invasion by endometrium, leiomyomas, or infection. Primary dysmenorrhoea is benign and commonly improves over time and after childbirth, with most women achieving good symptom control from anti-inflammatory and hormonal treatment. The prognosis of secondary dysmenorrhoea depends on the underlying condition, and outcomes improve when that cause is correctly identified and managed.

markers of bone turnover to characterise the disorder Molecular genetic testing including SLC29A3 and TNFRSF11A Dental review for associated dental anomalies A rare sclerosing bone dysplasia combining generalised osteosclerosis with flattened vertebral bodies (platyspondyly) and, characteristically, sclerosis that spares or under-modifies the metaphyses Presents in childhood with short stature, fractures despite dense bone, and sometimes developmental delay Recognised causes include recessive variants in SLC29A3 and in TNFRSF11A, reflecting genetic heterogeneity within the phenotype The paradox of dense yet fragile bone reflects disordered bone modelling and impaired resorption rather than simply increased mass Radiographs typically show a dense skull base, platyspondyly and abnormal is supportive and orthopaedic, with fracture care, monitoring for cranial-nerve compression and decompression of affected foramina where indicated Progressive visual or hearing loss suggesting cranial-nerve foraminal compression Recurrent fractures despite dense bone indicating significant bone fragility Neurological signs of brainstem or spinal cord compromise Features of marrow failure suggesting an osteopetrosis-like process Assuming dense bone is strong bone and underestimating the fracture risk Confusing the disorder with osteopetrosis and missing the characteristic platyspondyly Neglecting surveillance for cranial-nerve compression from skull-base sclerosis Not pursuing molecular testing given the genetic heterogeneity and implications for counselling Dysosteosclerosis is a heterogeneous recessive disorder of bone modelling in which osteoclast-mediated resorption and the normal shaping of bone are disturbed, producing generalised osteosclerosis together with distinctive platyspondyly. Variants in SLC29A3, a nucleoside transporter, and in TNFRSF11A (RANK), central to osteoclast differentiation, have both been implicated, indicating that different molecular lesions converge on impaired bone remodelling. The accumulated bone is abnormally dense yet mechanically defective, explaining the coexistence of sclerosis and fracture susceptibility. Sclerosis of the skull base can narrow neural foramina and compromise cranial nerves, while the vertebral flattening and abnormal metaphyseal modelling reflect the same failure of orderly bone turnover. The prognosis varies with severity and genetic subtype, ranging from relatively mild disease with orthopaedic morbidity to more severe presentations complicated by cranial-nerve deficits and recurrent fractures.
