evaluate deep pelvic causes such as endometriosis Assessment of pelvic floor muscle tone and psychosexual contributors Dyspareunia is persistent or recurrent genital pain associated with sexual intercourse and is a common but frequently underreported complaint A key clinical step is to localise the pain as superficial (at the entrance) or deep (with deep penetration), since this narrows the likely causes Superficial pain often reflects vulvovaginal conditions such as atrophy, vestibulodynia, dermatoses, infection, or inadequate lubrication Deep pain suggests pelvic pathology including endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, adhesions, fibroids, or ovarian pathology Postmenopausal dyspareunia is commonly due to genitourinary syndrome of menopause from oestrogen deficiency and responds well to local oestrogen and lubrication Dyspareunia and vaginismus frequently coexist and reinforce each other, and both fall within genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder A careful history and a gentle, systematic examination to reproduce and localise the pain are central to diagnosis Management is directed at the identified cause and often combines physical treatment with attention to the anxiety and relationship consequences of chronic sexual pain Postcoital bleeding or an abnormal pelvic mass suggesting significant gynaecological pathology Features of endometriosis or pelvic inflammatory disease requiring directed investigation History of sexual trauma needing sensitive, specialised support Chronic pain driving significant psychological distress or relationship breakdown Failing to distinguish superficial from deep pain, leading to misdirected investigation Overlooking easily treatable atrophic changes in postmenopausal women Missing endometriosis or other pelvic pathology as a cause of deep dyspareunia Neglecting the secondary pelvic floor tension and anxiety that perpetuate the pain Dyspareunia is a symptom with diverse underlying mechanisms rather than a single disease. Superficial (entry) pain arises from disorders of the vulva and introitus: oestrogen-deficient atrophy thinning and drying the tissue, provoked vestibulodynia with localised hypersensitivity, inflammatory or infective vulvovaginitis, dermatoses, or insufficient arousal and lubrication. Deep (pelvic) pain results from structures reached during deep penetration, so endometriosis, chronic pelvic inflammatory disease, adhesions, fibroids, and ovarian or uterine pathology can generate pain when moved or compressed. Persistent pain from any of these causes commonly triggers protective pelvic floor muscle tension and anticipatory anxiety, so a peripheral organic problem can evolve into a mixed pain syndrome with secondary vaginismus, blurring the line between physical and psychological contributors. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; menopausal atrophic dyspareunia responds very well to local oestrogen, infective and inflammatory causes resolve with treatment, and even complex or chronic pain often improves with a combined physical and psychosexual approach, though deep pain from conditions such as endometriosis may require longer-term management.

neurological signs Assuming an intact cough reflex excludes aspiration and thereby missing silent aspiration Neglecting oral hygiene, which strongly influences aspiration pneumonia risk Delaying endoscopy in progressive solid-food dysphagia with weight loss Defaulting to tube feeding in advanced dementia without a goals-of-care discussion Overlooking medications and dry mouth as contributors to swallowing difficulty Normal swallowing requires precise coordination of oral, pharyngeal, and oesophageal phases under neural control, with timely airway protection by laryngeal elevation and epiglottic closure. Oropharyngeal dysphagia arises from neuromuscular disorders (stroke, Parkinson disease, motor neuron disease, dementia) or local structural lesions that disrupt this coordination, impairing bolus transfer and airway protection so that material may enter the larynx and lungs. Oesophageal dysphagia results from mechanical obstruction (stricture, tumour, ring) or motility disorders that impede transit through the oesophagus. Age-related changes in muscle strength and sensation lower reserve and predispose to aspiration. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause. Post-stroke dysphagia often improves over weeks with rehabilitation, whereas dysphagia from progressive neurodegenerative disease tends to worsen and, in advanced dementia, signals a poor overall prognosis. Untreated dysphagia leads to aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, dehydration, and reduced quality of life; timely assessment and tailored management reduce these complications.

Dyssynergic defecation — pelvic floor dyssynergia, anismus, defecatory disorder Slow-transit constipation Functional constipation of normal transit Structural outlet obstruction (rectocele, intussusception) Hirschsprung disease (in appropriate patients) Neurological disease affecting defecation Anorectal manometry to demonstrate the dyssynergic pattern Balloon expulsion test Defecography where structural outlet problems are suspected Colonic transit study to assess for coexisting slow transit Digital rectal examination as an initial screen for impaired relaxation A functional defecation disorder in which impaired coordination of the abdominal, rectal and pelvic floor muscles prevents effective evacuation Patients strain excessively, feel incomplete evacuation and may use digital manoeuvres to pass stool There is paradoxical contraction or inadequate relaxation of the anal sphincter and pelvic floor during attempted defecation, or inadequate propulsive force It is a common and often overlooked cause of refractory constipation Diagnosis requires anorectal physiology testing, including manometry and a balloon expulsion test Biofeedback-based pelvic floor retraining is the treatment of choice and is more effective than laxatives alone Alarm features suggesting organic disease Suspected structural outlet obstruction requiring surgery Features suggesting Hirschsprung disease Neurological signs Treating refractory constipation with escalating laxatives without testing for dyssynergia Overlooking the diagnosis on a normal-appearing colon Missing a coexisting structural outlet problem Not referring for biofeedback, the definitive treatment Dyssynergic defecation is a disorder of the coordinated neuromuscular sequence required for normal evacuation. Rather than the normal rise in rectal pressure with relaxation of the anal sphincter and pelvic floor, affected patients show paradoxical pelvic floor and sphincter contraction, incomplete relaxation, or insufficient rectal propulsive force. This learned incoordination obstructs stool passage despite otherwise normal colonic function, and because it is a behavioural motor-control problem it responds to retraining rather than to laxatives targeting transit. The prognosis is good, with the majority improving through biofeedback-directed pelvic floor retraining; outcomes are poorer if the diagnosis is missed and only laxatives are used.

treatable dopa-responsive dystonia Overlooking Wilson disease, a treatable cause, in a young patient Not recognising drug-induced dystonia and continuing the offending dopamine-blocking agent Mislabelling dystonia as functional, or vice versa, without adequate assessment Dystonia arises from dysfunction of motor networks centred on the basal ganglia and their connections with the cerebellum, thalamus, and cortex, leading to loss of inhibition, abnormal sensorimotor integration, and maladaptive plasticity. Co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles with overflow to adjacent muscles produces the abnormal postures. Causes range from inherited (isolated or combined genetic forms) and idiopathic disease to acquired lesions, drugs, and neurodegenerative or metabolic disorders. Prognosis varies with cause and distribution. Focal dystonias are usually chronic but not life-threatening and often respond well to botulinum toxin. Dopa-responsive dystonia can improve dramatically with treatment. Young-onset genetic generalised dystonia tends to spread and be more disabling, though deep brain stimulation can help selected patients.

essential-tremor treatments Dystonic tremor is considered a manifestation of the same disordered basal ganglia and cerebello-thalamo-cortical network dysfunction that underlies dystonia, with deficient inhibition and abnormal sensorimotor integration producing both the sustained abnormal postures and the superimposed oscillation. Its position dependence and its responsiveness to sensory tricks reflect the strong influence of afferent input on this dysfunctional motor control, and help to distinguish it physiologically from essential tremor. Dystonic tremor tends to be chronic and can be difficult to treat, but it is not life-threatening. Focal presentations, particularly head and hand tremor, may respond to botulinum toxin injection into the overactive muscles, and some patients benefit from oral medication; refractory, disabling cases may be considered for deep brain stimulation. Overall function is usually preserved with appropriate symptom management.

of death in adulthood Management is multidisciplinary and supportive, with meticulous wound care, nutritional support, contracture prevention, and vigilant skin cancer surveillance A new, enlarging, or non-healing indurated lesion suspicious for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma Progressive dysphagia and weight loss from oesophageal strictures Severe anaemia and failure to thrive from chronic wounds and poor intake Progressive pseudosyndactyly and contractures impairing function Failing to institute skin cancer surveillance in severe recessive disease Overlooking oesophageal strictures as a cause of malnutrition Not preventing hand and foot contractures and pseudosyndactyly with early therapy and dressings Confusing dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa with the autoimmune condition epidermolysis bullosa acquisita Underestimating the multidisciplinary nutritional, dental, and psychological support required Type VII collagen, encoded by COL7A1, forms the anchoring fibrils that tether the lamina densa of the basement membrane to the underlying papillary dermis. In dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, mutations reduce or abolish functional type VII collagen so anchoring fibrils are deficient or absent, and the skin separates beneath the lamina densa in the superficial dermis in response to minor trauma. Because the split lies within the dermis, repair occurs with fibrosis, producing scarring, milia, and progressive contractures rather than clean healing. Dominant mutations typically retain more residual collagen function and cause milder disease, whereas recessive loss-of-function mutations produce severe generalised disease with extensive scarring, mucosal strictures, and the chronic wounds that predispose to squamous cell carcinoma. The dominant forms are generally compatible with a near-normal life expectancy, whereas severe generalised recessive disease is disabling, with progressive contractures, strictures, and a markedly increased risk of aggressive squamous cell carcinoma that is the leading cause of premature death.

respiration Status dystonicus with severe, unremitting muscle contractions Features atypical for isolated dystonia (cognitive decline, ataxia, weakness) suggesting an alternative diagnosis Bulbar involvement compromising swallowing or airway Omitting a levodopa trial and missing coexisting or mimicking dopa-responsive dystonia Interpreting reduced penetrance incorrectly, for example reassuring a carrier that they cannot be affected or over-predicting risk Attributing childhood limb dystonia to a functional cause without genetic evaluation Delaying referral for deep brain stimulation in medically refractory generalised disease DYT1 dystonia is caused by a recurrent in-frame trinucleotide (GAG) deletion in TOR1A, which removes a glutamic acid residue from torsinA, an ATPase of the endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear envelope. The abnormal protein disturbs nuclear envelope and endoplasmic reticulum function and impairs neuronal development and connectivity within motor circuits, particularly the basal ganglia-thalamocortical and cerebellar pathways. The result is abnormal sensorimotor integration and defective inhibition producing sustained co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles, without neurodegeneration, which is why brain structure appears normal. The dystonia is usually static or slowly progressive after an initial spreading phase and does not shorten life or cause cognitive decline; disability depends on the extent of generalisation. Many refractory cases achieve substantial, durable benefit from pallidal deep brain stimulation.

Eagle syndrome (elongated styloid) — stylohyoid syndrome, elongated styloid process syndrome, styloid-carotid artery syndrome Glossopharyngeal neuralgia Trigeminal neuralgia Temporomandibular joint dysfunction Chronic tonsillitis or peritonsillar pathology Cervical spine or carotid artery disease Pharyngeal or tongue-base malignancy Migraine or cluster-type facial pain CT of the neck with three-dimensional reconstruction to measure and characterise the styloid process Panoramic dental radiography (orthopantomogram) as an initial screen for styloid elongation Palpation of the tonsillar fossa to reproduce symptoms Diagnostic local anaesthetic infiltration of the tonsillar fossa to confirm the pain source CT or MR angiography of the carotid vessels when a vascular variant is suspected Flexible laryngoscopy to exclude mucosal or neoplastic causes of throat pain Presents with recurrent throat and neck pain, a foreign-body or globus sensation, pain on swallowing, and referred otalgia The classic (pharyngeal) form often follows tonsillectomy and produces pain aggravated by swallowing or turning the head The vascular (styloid-carotid) form arises when the elongated process impinges on the carotid vessels, causing pain radiating along the artery and, rarely, transient neurological symptoms A firm styloid tip may sometimes be palpated in the tonsillar fossa, reproducing the patient's pain Diagnosis rests on demonstrating an elongated (over about 2.5-3 cm) or ossified styloid process/stylohyoid ligament, best shown on CT with three-dimensional reconstruction Conservative options include analgesia, neuropathic agents, and local anaesthetic/steroid infiltration; surgical styloidectomy (transoral or transcervical) is definitive for refractory cases Symptoms result from mechanical irritation of adjacent neurovascular structures rather than the mere presence of an elongated styloid, which is often incidental Transient ischaemic or stroke-like symptoms suggesting carotid impingement (vascular Eagle syndrome) Unilateral throat pain with a mucosal lesion or mass raising suspicion of malignancy Progressive dysphagia or weight loss Syncope associated with head turning Treating an incidentally elongated styloid seen on imaging in an asymptomatic patient Overlooking the vascular variant and its cerebrovascular risk Attributing symptoms to Eagle syndrome without excluding pharyngeal malignancy Confusing the pain with glossopharyngeal or trigeminal neuralgia and missing the mechanical cause Relying on plain radiographs alone, which under-characterise the styloid Eagle syndrome results from an abnormally elongated styloid process or ossification/calcification of the stylohyoid ligament. The elongated bony spur, or the rigid ossified ligament, mechanically irritates adjacent structures during movement and swallowing. In the classic form it impinges on the pharyngeal mucosa and nearby cranial nerves (glossopharyngeal, trigeminal, facial), producing throat pain, dysphagia, and referred otalgia. In the vascular variant the process compresses or irritates the internal or external carotid artery and its periarterial sympathetic plexus, producing pain along the vessel and occasionally transient cerebral ischaemic symptoms. Elongation is common in the general population, so it is symptomatic only when it contacts and irritates these structures. The condition is benign but can be chronically disabling. Conservative measures relieve milder cases, while surgical shortening of the styloid process gives good long-term relief in appropriately selected patients; the rare vascular variant carries the additional risk of cerebrovascular events.

eales disease — idiopathic retinal periphlebitis, primary perivasculitis of the retina Tuberculous retinal vasculitis with active systemic infection Sarcoid retinal periphlebitis (candle-wax drippings) Behcet disease with occlusive retinal vasculitis Branch retinal vein occlusion Diabetic retinopathy with peripheral neovascularisation Sickle cell (and other haemoglobinopathy) proliferative retinopathy Ocular ischaemic syndrome from carotid disease Fundus fluorescein angiography to map capillary non-perfusion and neovascular leakage B-scan ultrasonography when vitreous haemorrhage obscures the fundus, to exclude retinal detachment Tuberculin skin testing or interferon-gamma release assay Chest imaging to screen for pulmonary tuberculosis or sarcoidosis Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and inflammatory markers Optical coherence tomography for associated macular oedema Wide-field retinal imaging to document peripheral involvement over time Classically affects young adult men, typically presenting with sudden painless loss of vision or floaters from vitreous haemorrhage rather than from the underlying vasculitis itself. The disease is an idiopathic obliterative peripheral retinal periphlebitis; venous involvement predominates over arterial, distinguishing it from many other retinal vasculitides. Diagnosis is one of exclusion, made only after systemic and infective causes of retinal vasculitis have been actively ruled out. A strong association with hypersensitivity to tuberculoprotein is recognised, particularly in the Indian subcontinent, though active systemic tuberculosis is usually absent. The natural history progresses through three overlapping phases: active periphlebitis, peripheral retinal capillary non-perfusion (ischaemia), and neovascularisation with its haemorrhagic complications. Fundus fluorescein angiography is central to management, delineating the extent of peripheral capillary non-perfusion and areas of leakage that guide laser photocoagulation. Bilateral involvement is common though often asymmetrical, so the fellow eye must always be examined and monitored even when asymptomatic. Corticosteroids control the inflammatory (vasculitic) phase while sectoral or scatter laser photocoagulation addresses the ischaemic and neovascular phases. Sudden marked loss of vision indicating fresh dense vitreous haemorrhage New floaters or a shadow in the peripheral field suggesting tractional retinal detachment Neovascularisation of the optic disc, carrying high risk of recurrent bleeding Non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage requiring surgical intervention Rubeosis iridis or raised intraocular pressure signalling anterior segment neovascularisation Labelling any peripheral retinal vasculitis as Eales disease without first excluding tuberculosis, sarcoidosis and Behcet disease. Overlooking the asymptomatic fellow eye, which may harbour early treatable periphlebitis or ischaemia. Attributing painless visual loss solely to the vasculitis and missing an underlying tractional retinal detachment behind vitreous haemorrhage. Treating the inflammatory phase with corticosteroids while neglecting laser ablation of established peripheral non-perfusion. Failing to arrange long-term follow-up, so recurrent neovascular bleeding goes undetected until vision is lost. Eales disease is an idiopathic inflammatory occlusive vasculopathy centred on the peripheral retinal veins. An initial perivascular inflammatory infiltrate (periphlebitis) causes vessel wall thickening, sheathing and progressive luminal occlusion. The resulting peripheral capillary non-perfusion generates retinal ischaemia, which upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor and drives the formation of fragile retinal and optic disc neovascular tufts. These new vessels bleed readily into the vitreous, producing the characteristic recurrent vitreous haemorrhage, and later fibrovascular proliferation may exert tractional forces leading to retinal detachment. A delayed hypersensitivity response to mycobacterial (tuberculoprotein) antigen is strongly implicated as a trigger of the immune-mediated vascular injury in predisposed individuals, alongside proposed roles for oxidative stress and altered retinal autoimmunity, but no single causative organism is consistently demonstrated within the affected tissue. With timely laser photocoagulation of ischaemic retina and control of the inflammatory phase, visual prognosis is generally favourable and many eyes retain good vision. Outcomes worsen with recurrent vitreous haemorrhage, macular involvement or tractional retinal detachment, though modern vitreoretinal surgery salvages useful vision in a substantial proportion of advanced cases.

Ear barotrauma — middle ear barotrauma, barotitis media, aerotitis, ear squeeze Sinus barotrauma Inner ear barotrauma or perilymph fistula Inner ear decompression sickness Alternobaric vertigo Acute otitis media or externa Temporomandibular joint dysfunction Otoscopy to assess the tympanic membrane and grade middle-ear barotrauma Assessment of hearing, distinguishing conductive from sensorineural loss Tuning fork tests and formal audiometry where hearing loss is present Review of the dive profile and equalisation history Urgent specialist (ENT) referral and vestibular assessment if inner ear injury is suspected The most common injury in diving, occurring when the pressure in the middle ear cannot be equalised with the surrounding environment, classically during descent On descent, failure to equalise creates a relative negative middle-ear pressure (an ear squeeze) that draws the tympanic membrane inward, causing pain, fullness, and sometimes bleeding or rupture Presents with ear pain, a blocked sensation, conductive hearing loss, and occasionally vertigo or tinnitus Otoscopy is central to diagnosis and may show retraction, congestion, haemorrhage behind the drum, or perforation, graded by severity Inner ear barotrauma is a more serious variant causing sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo, and warrants urgent specialist assessment Prevention relies on gentle, early, and frequent equalisation manoeuvres and not diving with upper respiratory congestion Divers should never force descent against an ear that will not equalise Sensorineural hearing loss, persistent vertigo, or tinnitus suggesting inner ear barotrauma Tympanic membrane rupture, especially with cold water causing caloric vertigo Symptoms suggesting inner ear decompression sickness rather than barotrauma Signs of secondary infection of the middle ear Forcing descent or aggressive equalisation, worsening the injury Missing inner ear barotrauma by attributing vertigo and hearing loss to the middle ear Confusing inner ear barotrauma with inner ear decompression sickness, which differ in management Allowing diving to continue with upper respiratory congestion The middle ear is a rigid, air-filled space that depends on the Eustachian tube to equalise its pressure with the environment. During descent the ambient pressure rises rapidly and, if the Eustachian tube does not open to admit air, the middle-ear pressure becomes relatively negative. This pressure gradient retracts and congests the tympanic membrane and middle-ear mucosa, causing oedema, haemorrhage, and, if severe, rupture of the drum. Round or oval window disruption can extend the injury to the inner ear, producing sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo. Most middle-ear barotrauma resolves over days to a couple of weeks with conservative care, and small perforations often heal spontaneously; inner ear barotrauma has a more guarded outlook, with hearing recovery dependent on prompt recognition and management.

metabolic encephalopathy Elevated CSF glycine indicating non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia Failure of vitamin-responsive trials Rapid clinical deterioration pointing to a progressive metabolic disorder Failing to send CSF and plasma glycine to detect non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia Not trialling vitamin-responsive therapies before concluding refractoriness Confusing erratic myoclonus with benign neonatal sleep myoclonus Attributing seizures to structural causes without a full metabolic workup Early myoclonic encephalopathy is a neonatal-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy strongly linked to inborn errors of metabolism, particularly non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia. Accumulation of neurotoxic metabolites and disturbance of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission in the immature brain produce marked cortical and subcortical hyperexcitability. This generates erratic fragmentary myoclonus and the burst-suppression pattern, while the underlying metabolic derangement causes the severe and early developmental impairment. The prognosis is generally very poor with high early mortality and profound neurodevelopmental disability in survivors, largely determined by the underlying metabolic disorder. Seizures are usually refractory to antiseizure medication.

Early repolarisation syndrome — J-wave syndrome, early repolarization syndrome Benign early repolarisation pattern Brugada syndrome Acute myocardial ischaemia or pericarditis Hypothermia (Osborn waves) Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation Twelve-lead electrocardiogram characterising the J-point changes Assessment of the clinical context and any arrhythmic events Ambulatory monitoring Exclusion of ischaemia and other causes of J-point elevation Family assessment where a syndrome is confirmed Defined by an early repolarisation pattern on the electrocardiogram together with otherwise unexplained ventricular arrhythmia or sudden cardiac arrest The electrocardiographic pattern is J-point elevation with notching or slurring in the inferior or lateral leads The early repolarisation pattern alone is extremely common and usually benign; it becomes a syndrome only with arrhythmic events It belongs to the J-wave syndromes, sharing mechanistic overlap with Brugada syndrome It should be distinguished from the benign pattern and from ischaemia and other causes of J-point elevation Management of the syndrome may include an implantable defibrillator and isoproterenol or quinidine for electrical storm Unexplained cardiac arrest or ventricular fibrillation with the pattern High-risk electrocardiographic features (high-amplitude J waves, horizontal ST segments) Family history of sudden cardiac death Recurrent syncope Labelling the common benign pattern as a dangerous syndrome Missing ischaemia or pericarditis as a cause of J-point changes Underestimating risk when high-risk features and events coexist Failing to assess the family after a confirmed syndrome Early repolarisation syndrome is thought to arise from heterogeneity of repolarisation between the epicardium and endocardium, related to a prominent transient outward potassium current that exaggerates the early repolarisation notch. This transmural dispersion of repolarisation creates a substrate for phase-2 re-entry and closely coupled ventricular ectopy that can precipitate ventricular fibrillation. The same electrocardiographic pattern occurs benignly in many healthy people, so the arrhythmic risk depends on additional factors and clinical context. The isolated pattern is benign in the vast majority; the syndrome, defined by arrhythmic events, carries a risk of recurrent life-threatening arrhythmia requiring definitive management.

Early repolarisation syndrome — ERS, early repolarisation syndrome, J-wave syndrome, early repolarization pattern with arrhythmia Benign early repolarisation pattern without arrhythmia Brugada syndrome Acute pericarditis (diffuse ST elevation) Acute myocardial ischaemia or infarction Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation Hypothermia (Osborn J waves) 12-lead ECG characterising J-point elevation morphology and distribution Ambulatory and event monitoring to capture arrhythmia Echocardiography and cardiac MRI to exclude structural disease Coronary assessment to exclude ischaemia in appropriate patients Genetic testing and family screening in selected high-risk or familial cases Exclusion of other channelopathies including drug-provocation testing where indicated Defined by an early repolarisation ECG pattern (J-point elevation or notching/slurring at the QRS-ST junction) in the inferior and/or lateral leads together with documented ventricular arrhythmia or resuscitated cardiac arrest The early repolarisation ECG pattern alone is common and usually benign; the syndrome label requires an associated malignant arrhythmic event Considered one of the J-wave syndromes, sharing mechanistic overlap with Brugada syndrome Higher-risk features include marked J-point elevation, a horizontal or descending ST segment, and inferior or global lead distribution Typically presents in young to middle-aged adults, often men, with syncope or aborted sudden death, sometimes during sleep or at rest Most cases are sporadic, but familial clustering occurs and variants in cardiac ion-channel genes have been described in a minority Diagnosis is one of exclusion after structural heart disease and other channelopathies have been ruled out Resuscitated cardiac arrest or documented polymorphic ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation Unexplained syncope with a high-risk early repolarisation pattern Family history of sudden unexplained death at a young age Marked J-point elevation with a horizontal or descending ST segment Labelling every early repolarisation ECG pattern as dangerous and causing undue alarm Missing higher-risk morphological features when assessing an early repolarisation ECG Confusing the pattern with pericarditis or ischaemia Failing to exclude structural disease and other channelopathies before diagnosing the syndrome Early repolarisation syndrome is thought to arise from heterogeneity in the early phases of the ventricular action potential, particularly an accentuated transient outward potassium current relative to inward currents in the epicardium. This creates a voltage gradient across the ventricular wall that produces the characteristic J-point elevation on the ECG and, when pronounced, favours phase-2 re-entry and closely coupled ventricular ectopy that can trigger polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. The tendency is modulated by autonomic tone, explaining events at rest or during sleep. A subset of patients carry variants in genes controlling these ionic currents, placing the disorder among the inherited J-wave syndromes, though for most individuals no single causal gene is identified. The isolated ECG pattern carries a very low absolute risk, whereas the full syndrome with a prior malignant arrhythmic event confers a meaningful risk of recurrence; risk stratification and secondary prevention, including defibrillator therapy in survivors of cardiac arrest, guide outcome.

(Seizures, Sensorineural deafness, Ataxia, Mental retardation, Electrolyte imbalance) Seizures usually begin in infancy, followed by a non-progressive cerebellar ataxia and developmental delay The diagnosis in any child with early seizures plus an unexplained salt-losing tubulopathy, and confirm with KCNJ10 sequencing Poorly controlled or status epilepticus in infancy Severe symptomatic hypokalaemia risking cardiac arrhythmia Profound hypomagnesaemia precipitating tetany or seizures Failure to thrive and developmental regression Labelling the tubulopathy as isolated Gitelman syndrome and overlooking the neurological features Attributing the seizures to a primary epilepsy without checking electrolytes Under-recognising hypomagnesaemia as a contributor to seizure threshold Missing early hearing loss that would benefit from amplification Kir4.1 is an inwardly rectifying potassium channel expressed in glial cells of the brain, the stria vascularis of the cochlea, and the basolateral membrane of the distal convoluted tubule. In the kidney it recycles potassium to maintain the activity of the basolateral sodium-potassium ATPase, so that loss of Kir4.1 function impairs sodium chloride reabsorption in the distal tubule, producing a Gitelman-like picture of renal salt wasting, hypokalaemic alkalosis, hypomagnesaemia, and reduced urinary calcium. Loss of the channel in astrocytes disturbs potassium buffering and glutamate handling, giving rise to epilepsy and cerebellar dysfunction, while its absence in the inner ear disrupts the endocochlear potential and causes sensorineural deafness. Seizures and electrolyte disturbances are usually manageable with treatment and the ataxia is typically non-progressive, but neurodevelopmental delay and permanent sensorineural deafness contribute to long-term disability; renal salt wasting generally does not progress to renal failure.

Eastern equine encephalitis — EEE, eastern equine encephalitis virus infection, EEEV infection, sleeping sickness (equine) Herpes simplex virus encephalitis West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease Other arboviral encephalitides such as St Louis or La Crosse encephalitis Bacterial meningoencephalitis Autoimmune or paraneoplastic encephalitis Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis Serum and cerebrospinal fluid IgM serology for eastern equine encephalitis virus Cerebrospinal fluid analysis typically showing pleocytosis and raised protein Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain looking for basal ganglia and thalamic involvement Molecular testing (RT-PCR) on cerebrospinal fluid where available, recognising limited sensitivity late in disease Electroencephalography to characterise seizure activity and encephalopathy Testing to exclude treatable causes, particularly herpes simplex virus A mosquito-borne alphavirus of eastern North America maintained in a bird reservoir with Culiseta mosquitoes, spilling over to humans and horses via bridge-vector mosquitoes near freshwater swamps Most infections are asymptomatic or febrile, but eastern equine encephalitis produces the most severe of the arboviral encephalitides in North America with very high mortality among those with neuroinvasive disease Neuroinvasive illness presents with high fever, headache, vomiting, seizures, and rapidly progressive obtundation, often after a brief prodrome Young children and older adults are at greatest risk of severe disease and neurological sequelae Magnetic resonance imaging characteristically shows lesions in the basal ganglia and thalami, which can help differentiate it from other encephalitides There is no specific antiviral or licensed human vaccine; management is intensive supportive and neuroprotective care with seizure and intracranial pressure control Diagnosis rests on cerebrospinal fluid and serum serology (IgM) and, where available, molecular testing, alongside a summer mosquito-exposure history Rapidly declining consciousness or coma Status epilepticus or recurrent seizures Signs of raised intracranial pressure Focal neurological deficits with basal ganglia or thalamic lesions on imaging Extremes of age with neuroinvasive disease Delaying empirical aciclovir for possible herpes simplex encephalitis while awaiting arboviral results Relying on molecular testing alone, since RT-PCR sensitivity in cerebrospinal fluid is limited and serology is often required Underestimating rapid deterioration and delaying intensive care admission Overlooking the summer mosquito-exposure history in swampy endemic regions Failing to recognise characteristic deep grey-matter imaging findings Eastern equine encephalitis virus cycles between passerine birds and ornithophilic mosquitoes in freshwater swamp habitats, with bridge-vector mosquitoes transmitting to incidental hosts such as humans and horses that do not sustain transmission. After a bite, viral replication and viraemia can be followed by neuroinvasion across the blood-brain barrier. In the central nervous system the virus causes widespread neuronal infection, intense inflammation, and vasculitis, with a predilection for deep grey-matter structures, producing severe oedema and neuronal destruction that underlie the high fatality and neurological sequelae. Neuroinvasive eastern equine encephalitis carries one of the highest case-fatality rates of the arboviral encephalitides, and many survivors are left with significant long-term neurological disability.

infection-prevention measures in healthcare settings Profuse vomiting and diarrhoea with signs of severe volume depletion and shock Bleeding, bruising, or laboratory evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation Confusion, agitation, or other neurological deterioration Any suspected case is a public health emergency requiring immediate isolation, full PPE, and notification, given the extreme transmission risk Failing to isolate and don appropriate PPE promptly, risking healthcare-associated outbreaks Under-resuscitating patients by focusing on bleeding while overlooking massive gastrointestinal fluid losses Attributing illness solely to malaria or typhoid in an outbreak or travel context and delaying containment Neglecting safe burial practices and contact tracing, which are central to outbreak control Ebolaviruses are enveloped RNA filoviruses that infect a broad range of cells, including macrophages, dendritic cells, and endothelium, while actively suppressing interferon-based innate immunity. Widespread viral replication drives a massive dysregulated inflammatory and cytokine response, impaired coagulation with disseminated intravascular coagulation, and increased vascular permeability. The combination of capillary leak, huge gastrointestinal fluid losses, and coagulopathy produces intravascular volume depletion, shock, and multi-organ failure, which underlie the high mortality. Untreated Ebola virus disease has historically carried very high case-fatality, but early presentation, intensive supportive care, and specific antibody therapies markedly improve survival; convalescence can be prolonged and survivors may experience persistent symptoms and viral persistence in immune-privileged sites.

Ebstein anomaly — Ebstein's anomaly, Ebstein malformation of the tricuspid valve, tricuspid valve displacement, atrialised right ventricle Tricuspid valve dysplasia without displacement Tricuspid atresia Right atrial enlargement from other causes Uhl anomaly and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum Pericardial effusion causing an enlarged cardiac silhouette Echocardiography to measure leaflet displacement, quantify regurgitation and assess right ventricular function Electrocardiogram for pre-excitation, right atrial enlargement and conduction abnormalities Cardiac MRI to assess right ventricular volumes and the atrialised segment Electrophysiological study when accessory pathways or tachyarrhythmias are suspected Chest radiograph, which may show marked cardiomegaly with a globular heart Assessment of an atrial-level shunt and its direction The septal and posterior tricuspid leaflets are displaced apically into the right ventricle, so part of the ventricle becomes incorporated into the right atrium as an atrialised chamber The malformed valve is usually regurgitant, and the functional right ventricle is small and often poorly contractile Severity is highly variable, from a critically cyanotic neonate to an incidental finding in an adult An atrial-level communication is common and allows right-to-left shunting with cyanosis, especially when right heart pressures are high There is a well-recognised association with accessory pathways and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, predisposing to tachyarrhythmias Neonatal presentation can be severe because high pulmonary resistance worsens tricuspid regurgitation and cyanosis, improving as resistance falls Management ranges from observation to arrhythmia ablation and surgical tricuspid repair or reconstruction (cone repair) depending on severity Severe neonatal cyanosis with a massively enlarged heart and low output Symptomatic tachyarrhythmia, particularly with an accessory pathway Progressive right heart failure from severe tricuspid regurgitation Syncope or haemodynamic collapse during arrhythmia Underestimating the arrhythmia risk from an associated accessory pathway Misinterpreting neonatal cyanosis that may improve as pulmonary resistance falls and prompting premature intervention Confusing the atrialised right ventricle with global right ventricular dilatation of other cause Overlooking a right-to-left atrial shunt as the source of cyanosis and paradoxical embolism In Ebstein anomaly the tricuspid valve leaflets fail to delaminate normally from the right ventricular wall, so the septal and posterior leaflets are displaced towards the apex. This incorporates the inflow portion of the right ventricle into the right atrium as a thin, poorly contractile atrialised segment, leaving a reduced functional right ventricle. The abnormal valve is typically regurgitant, and the combination of tricuspid regurgitation, a large functionally impaired right atrium and a small right ventricle limits forward pulmonary flow. When right atrial pressure exceeds left, blood shunts right to left across an associated atrial communication, producing cyanosis. Disordered conduction tissue and accessory atrioventricular pathways underlie the frequent association with pre-excitation and reentrant tachyarrhythmias. Outcome spans a wide range: mild disease is compatible with a normal life, while severe neonatal presentations carry high mortality; arrhythmias add risk, and modern tricuspid repair offers durable improvement in selected patients.

eccrine poroma — poroma, acrospiroma, poroma of the sweat duct pyogenic granuloma amelanotic melanoma basal cell carcinoma squamous cell carcinoma porocarcinoma viral wart or verruca irritated seborrhoeic keratosis dermoscopy to characterise the vascular pattern excisional biopsy with histopathology immunohistochemistry demonstrating ductal (EMA/CEA) differentiation where required sentinel lymph node assessment if porocarcinoma is confirmed staging imaging when malignancy with metastatic potential is diagnosed Presents as a solitary, slowly growing, often reddish or skin-coloured papule or nodule, classically on the sole or side of the foot. The palms, and increasingly other sites such as the trunk and head, may also be affected, reflecting derivation from any acrosyringeal duct. Lesions are frequently vascular in appearance and may sit in a shallow cup-shaped depression with a surrounding keratotic collarette. They can bleed readily on minor trauma and are commonly mistaken for a pyogenic granuloma or amelanotic melanoma. Dermoscopy may show polymorphous vessels, a pink-white structureless background and a vascular pattern that overlaps with malignant lesions. Histology shows a well-demarcated proliferation of small, monomorphous cuboidal poroid cells connected to the epidermis, with ductal differentiation. Porocarcinoma, the malignant counterpart, may arise de novo or within a long-standing poroma and shows atypia, infiltration and mitoses. Complete excision with histopathological confirmation is the treatment of choice, given the difficulty of clinical differentiation from malignancy. rapid growth, ulceration or bleeding suggesting porocarcinoma an infiltrative, indurated or fixed lesion recurrence after excision regional lymphadenopathy indicating possible metastatic porocarcinoma Mistaking a bleeding vascular poroma for a pyogenic granuloma and destroying it without histology. Overlooking porocarcinoma arising within a long-standing poroma that suddenly changes. Failing to excise completely, allowing recurrence. Confusing the lesion with a plantar wart and applying inappropriate keratolytic or destructive therapy. Poroma is a benign adnexal neoplasm arising from the terminal portion of the sweat duct, the acrosyringium, and although traditionally termed eccrine it may show apocrine or folliculosebaceous differentiation. Tumour cells are small, uniform poroid keratinocytes forming broad anastomosing cords connected to the overlying epidermis, punctuated by ductal lumina reflecting the sweat-duct lineage. Recurrent gene fusions involving YAP1 with MAML2 or NUTM1 have been identified, indicating a shared oncogenic driver across the poroma-porocarcinoma spectrum. Malignant transformation to porocarcinoma involves acquisition of cytological atypia, infiltrative growth and a capacity for lymphatic and distant spread. Benign poroma is cured by complete excision with a low recurrence rate. Porocarcinoma carries a less favourable outlook, with potential for local recurrence and lymphatic or distant metastasis, so early recognition is important.

Eclampsia — eclamptic seizure, eclamptic convulsion, convulsive pre-eclampsia Epilepsy and other primary seizure disorders Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis Intracranial haemorrhage or ischaemic stroke Hypoglycaemia or other metabolic derangement CNS infection (meningitis, encephalitis) Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura Bloods as for severe pre-eclampsia: full blood count, liver enzymes, renal function, coagulation, and lactate dehydrogenase Blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia Neuroimaging (CT or MRI) if seizures are atypical, focal, recurrent despite magnesium, or if focal neurological deficit persists Continuous fetal monitoring after maternal stabilisation Magnesium level monitoring where clinically indicated during infusion Defined as new-onset generalised tonic-clonic seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia that cannot be attributed to another cause Seizures may occur antepartum, intrapartum, or postpartum, and a substantial proportion arise after delivery Premonitory features include severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain, and hyperreflexia, though seizures can occur without warning Magnesium sulfate is the treatment of choice for controlling and preventing recurrent seizures and is superior to conventional anticonvulsants in this setting Immediate priorities are maternal airway protection, oxygenation, and prevention of injury and aspiration during the seizure Blood pressure must be controlled with antihypertensives to reduce the risk of intracranial haemorrhage Delivery is undertaken once the mother is stabilised; eclampsia itself is not an indication for immediate caesarean if vaginal delivery is achievable and conditions are favourable Magnesium toxicity is monitored clinically (loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression) and calcium gluconate is the antidote Recurrent or prolonged seizures despite magnesium sulfate (status eclampticus) Focal neurological deficit or reduced conscious level suggesting intracranial haemorrhage Severe uncontrolled hypertension threatening stroke Signs of magnesium toxicity such as respiratory depression or absent reflexes Maternal hypoxia, aspiration, or airway compromise during a seizure Attributing a peripartum seizure to epilepsy and delaying magnesium therapy Discontinuing magnesium too early after delivery when postpartum eclampsia remains a risk Rushing to caesarean during an active seizure rather than stabilising the mother first Overlooking magnesium toxicity by not monitoring reflexes and respiratory rate Neglecting ongoing postpartum blood pressure surveillance Eclampsia represents the cerebral manifestation of the endothelial dysfunction and vasospasm of pre-eclampsia. Loss of cerebral autoregulation and endothelial injury lead to hyperperfusion, vasogenic and cytotoxic oedema (often in the posterior circulation, akin to posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome), and focal ischaemia, which lower the seizure threshold and provoke generalised convulsions. Cerebral haemorrhage is the most feared and lethal complication. With prompt seizure control, blood pressure management, and delivery, most women recover without lasting neurological deficit. However, eclampsia is associated with significant maternal mortality and morbidity worldwide, particularly from intracranial haemorrhage, aspiration, and organ failure, and with increased perinatal loss.

Ectoparasite Infestations and Arthropod Injuries — Scabies, Pediculosis, Pthiriasis, Lice infestation, Myiasis, Tungiasis, Chigger bites, Tick bites and tick paralysis, Spider bites, Scorpion stings, Hymenoptera stings, Pentastomiasis, Delusional infestation Psoriasis (mimicked by crusted scabies) Eczematous dermatitis / contact dermatitis Papular urticaria from other arthropod bites Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis (purpuric papules resembling chigger bites) Cutaneous larva migrans (resembling serpiginous migratory fly-larva eruptions) Bacterial cellulitis (mimicked by large local hymenopteran sting reactions) Peritonitis / acute surgical abdomen (mimicked by widow spider envenomation abdominal rigidity) Seizure (mimicked by scorpion-induced muscle twitching/jerking) Guillain-Barre syndrome (mimicked by tick paralysis) MRSA and other bacterial skin infections misattributed to spider bites Impetigo / cellulitis as secondary infection of scabies or louse excoriations Bacterial cellulitis confused with large local Hymenoptera sting reactions Microscopic examination of skin scrapings from unroofed burrows for mites, eggs, and fecal pellets (scabies) Skin biopsy, cellophane-tape or cyanoacrylate adhesive lift, and dermatoscopy of papulovesicular lesions Direct identification of the offending arthropod from a collected specimen (taken from patient, traps, or environment) with proper fixation/preservation for taxonomic review Examination of clothing seams for body lice and nits; inspection of hair for live lice Skin tests and venom-specific RAST for Hymenoptera hypersensitivity to guide immunotherapy PCR of captured lice has detected pathogenic bacteria in research settings Delusional infestation (Ekbom syndrome / delusory parasitosis), with self-induced excoriations and ulcers and no true parasite Pseudo-nits (debris, dry skin flakes, hair fungi) mistaken for louse eggs Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis Psoriasis versus crusted scabies Of all organisms in this chapter, only the human itch mite (Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis) and human-infesting lice are obligate human parasites; humans are accidental or dead-end hosts for most others. Scabies affects roughly 250 million people worldwide and is spread mainly by direct skin-to-skin contact; transmission via shared bedding or clothing is less common than widely assumed, and mites usually die within about a day off a suitable host. Scabies pruritus reflects a sensitization reaction; an initial infestation can stay asymptomatic for up to about 6 weeks, but reinfestation provokes prompt hypersensitivity. Itch typically worsens at night and after hot showers. Crusted (formerly Norwegian) scabies arises in glucocorticoid use, immunodeficiency (including HIV/AIDS), and neuropsychiatric conditions that blunt itching/scratching; it harbors thousands of mites, is highly contagious, often non-pruritic, lacks classic burrows, and can mimic psoriasis. Confirmation of louse infestation should rest on finding a live louse, not on nits alone, since hatched/dead eggs (and pseudo-nits of debris/dander/fungi) remain cemented to hair for months and are frequently misread as active disease. Body lice (not head lice) are the recognized vectors of epidemic (louse-borne) typhus, louse-borne relapsing fever, and trench fever; outbreaks track societal upheaval, crowding, and inability to launder clothing. Furuncular myiasis (e.g., Dermatobia hominis, Cordylobia anthropophaga) presents as a boil-like nodule with a central breathing pore that emits bubbles when submerged in water, and the patient may sense movement within the skin. Brown recluse (Loxosceles) envenomation classically produces a painful lesion with central induration, a pale ischemic zone, and surrounding erythema, sometimes evolving to a necrotic black eschar; widow spider (Latrodectus) bites cause minimal local injury but severe neurotoxic muscle cramps via alpha-latrotoxin. Removing hard ticks within the first 24 hours of attachment generally prevents transmission of Lyme disease, babesiosis, anaplasmosis, and ehrlichiosis, though tick-borne viruses may transmit faster. Tick paralysis is an acute ascending flaccid Guillain-Barre-like paralysis from a salivary toxin; sensory exam and lumbar puncture are typically normal, and finding/removing the hidden tick (often under scalp hair) reverses it within hours. Alpha-gal syndrome (red-meat allergy) follows tick bites that induce IgE against galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose, a carbohydrate present in non-primate mammalian muscle; in the US it is linked to the lone star tick. Most reported 'spider bites' are not spider-related; acute tender noduloulcerative lesions are frequently due to minor trauma or bacterial infection, particularly MRSA. Ascending flaccid paralysis with cranial-nerve involvement after tick attachment (tick paralysis) progressing to respiratory failure if the tick is not found and removed Rapid anaphylaxis after Hymenoptera or reduviid bite (upper-airway edema, bronchospasm, hypotension, shock) usually beginning within 10 minutes Stings to the tongue or mouth causing life-threatening upper-airway edema Scorpion envenomation with cranial-nerve dysfunction, neuromuscular hyperexcitability, hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia, pulmonary edema, or rhabdomyolysis Widow spider envenomation with severe muscle cramping, respiratory distress, hypertension, or premature labor Recluse spider envenomation with systemic hemolysis, renal failure, or expanding necrosis Lonomia obliqua caterpillar contact causing disseminated coagulopathy and hemorrhagic shock Halzoun/marrara (Linguatula serrata pentastomiasis) with severe pharyngeal edema requiring tracheostomy Aeromonas hydrophila sepsis, myonecrosis, or intractable bleeding complicating medicinal leech therapy Diagnosing scabies or an 'outbreak' without confirmation; unrelated skin diseases are frequently misdiagnosed as scabies. Treating residual nits as active louse infestation; onerous 'no-nit' school exclusion policies are increasingly viewed as unjustified and counterproductive. Over-treating with topical scabicides/pediculicides, which can cause irritant contact dermatitis (especially repeated permethrin). Treating environmental (non-burrowing) mites such as chiggers with acaricides on the patient, which is discouraged because these mites do not reside on humans. Attributing necrotic skin lesions to spider bites without observation of a spider; many are bacterial (often MRSA) or traumatic. Delaying tick removal by applying heat or occlusive substances, which merely prolongs attachment; ticks should be removed by traction with fine-tipped forceps at the mouthparts. Mistaking widow spider abdominal rigidity for a surgical abdomen and performing unnecessary surgery (the abdomen is not tender on palpation). Interpreting childhood eyelash (pubic louse) infestation as incontrovertible proof of sexual abuse. Failing to recognize delusional infestation, leading to repeated futile antiparasitic treatment. Ectoparasites are arthropods and organisms of other phyla that infest skin or hair; they may remain superficial (anchored by mouthparts or claws) or penetrate into epidermis, dermis, or subcutaneous tissue. Injury arises through several mechanisms: direct mechanical damage, consumption of blood or nutrients, hypersensitivity reactions to saliva/secretions/excretions, inoculation of toxins or venoms, transmission of pathogens, and creation of skin portals for secondary bacterial infection. In scabies, gravid female mites burrow within the stratum corneum and lay eggs; rash and pruritus result from delayed-type sensitization, with burrows surrounded by infiltrates of eosinophils, lymphocytes, and histiocytes. Lice are obligate blood feeders whose saliva produces a pruritic morbilliform/urticarial reaction in sensitized hosts. Venom-mediated injury is prominent in arachnid and hymenopteran envenomation: widow spider alpha-latrotoxin binds irreversibly to presynaptic terminals causing release then depletion of acetylcholine and norepinephrine; bark scorpion neurotoxins hold sodium channels open producing cranial-nerve and neuromuscular hyperexcitability; some scorpion venoms trigger massive catecholamine release with cardiopulmonary toxicity. Hymenopteran venoms contain amines, kinins, and enzymes (e.g., melittin, phospholipases, hyaluronidase) producing local and systemic effects, with most fatalities due to IgE-mediated type 1 anaphylaxis. Tick salivary secretions are biologically active anticoagulants that can transmit pathogens and provoke sterile inflammatory responses, fever, and toxin-mediated paralysis. Most infestations and bites are self-limited or readily treated. Scabies becomes noncommunicable within about a day of proper treatment, though hypersensitivity pruritus may persist for weeks as dead mites and debris are cleared; secondary streptococcal infection can lead to poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis and possibly acute rheumatic fever. Brown recluse lesions usually heal within about 3 months, and verified deaths from North American brown recluse bites have not been confirmed. Widow spider pain typically begins subsiding within the first 12 hours but may recur over days to weeks; fatal outcomes are rare and concentrated in the very young, elderly, or debilitated. Bark scorpion envenomation peaks around 5 hours and subsides over a day or two, with fatal respiratory arrest mainly in young children and the elderly. Tick paralysis generally resolves within hours to days after tick removal but can be fatal from respiratory paralysis or aspiration if untreated. Hymenoptera-related deaths (>=100/year in the US) result almost entirely from anaphylaxis. No formal numeric staging is given; severity is graded clinically by host reaction and systemic involvement. Scabies ranges from ordinary (typically <=10-15 burrows) to crusted/hyperinfested (thousands of mites, highly contagious). Arthropod envenomations are stratified from local-only reactions (most scorpion and spider bites: pain, edema) to systemic/life-threatening envenomation (cranial-nerve and neuromuscular dysfunction, cardiopulmonary toxicity, hemolysis, renal failure). Hymenoptera reactions span uncomplicated local stings, large local hypersensitivity reactions spreading >=10 cm over 1-2 days, and systemic type 1 anaphylaxis.

excess, and bilateral adrenalectomy is a last resort for refractory hypercortisolism Severe hypokalaemia with metabolic alkalosis and arrhythmia risk Rapidly progressive hypercortisolism with profound myopathy Opportunistic infection or sepsis from immunosuppression Venous thromboembolism from a hypercoagulable state Psychosis or severe metabolic decompensation Assuming a pituitary source and missing an occult ectopic tumour Relying on dexamethasone suppression alone given the overlap with pituitary disease Overlooking severe hypokalaemia and its cardiac risk Delaying control of hypercortisolism while searching for the primary tumour Underestimating infection and thrombosis risk in profound hypercortisolism Ectopic adrenocorticotrophic hormone syndrome results from autonomous secretion of the hormone, or occasionally corticotrophin-releasing hormone, by a tumour outside the pituitary. The excess hormone drives bilateral adrenal hyperplasia and sustained cortisol overproduction that is not subject to normal negative feedback. Because many causative tumours are aggressive and secrete large amounts rapidly, patients often present with severe metabolic derangement, including hypokalaemic alkalosis (aggravated by cortisol's mineralocorticoid effect at high concentrations) and hyperpigmentation from the melanocyte-stimulating activity of the precursor peptide, sometimes before the classic physical stigmata of Cushing syndrome develop. Outlook is dominated by the nature of the underlying tumour; occult indolent neuroendocrine tumours that can be localised and resected may be curable, whereas ectopic secretion from aggressive malignancy such as small-cell lung cancer carries a poor prognosis despite cortisol-lowering measures.

together with the thymus, from the third pouch. Variations in this migration leave glands in unexpected positions, including retro-oesophageal and paraoesophageal tissue, the carotid sheath, within the thyroid, or descended into the anterior mediastinum with thymic tissue. When such a gland becomes an autonomously hyperfunctioning adenoma or hyperplastic gland, it produces primary hyperparathyroidism, but its aberrant location makes it difficult to find, and it is a frequent reason for failed neck exploration and persistent disease. Once the ectopic hyperfunctioning gland is accurately localised and completely removed, hyperparathyroidism is usually cured; the main difficulty is localisation, and undetected glands lead to persistent disease and repeat surgery.

The invading trophoblast erodes the tubal wall, which lacks the capacity to accommodate a growing gestation. This leads to distension and bleeding into the tube, and eventually to tubal rupture with potentially massive intraperitoneal haemorrhage, or to tubal abortion where the products are expelled through the fimbrial end. With early diagnosis and treatment the maternal outlook is excellent and fertility is often preserved. Rupture remains an important cause of maternal death, especially where access to care is delayed. Women who have had one ectopic pregnancy carry an increased risk of recurrence and of subtly reduced fertility.

effusive-constrictive pericarditis two processes coexist: fluid accumulates within the pericardial space while the visceral pericardium becomes inflamed, thickened, and rigid. ehlers danlos hypermobile — hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, hEDS, EDS type III classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome Marfan syndrome Loeys-Dietz syndrome generalised (benign) joint hypermobility without syndromic features osteogenesis imperfecta hypermobility spectrum disorder Beighton score assessment with age-appropriate thresholds and application of the 2017 hEDS diagnostic criteria genetic testing (including panels for other EDS subtypes and heritable connective-tissue disorders) primarily to exclude alternative diagnoses transthoracic echocardiography to assess aortic root dimensions and valves orthostatic vital signs or tilt-table testing where dysautonomia is suspected bone density assessment where fragility or osteogenesis imperfecta is considered targeted imaging of symptomatic joints for instability or early osteoarthritis assessment for pelvic-floor dysfunction and hernias when indicated The commonest subtype of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and the only one still without a confirmed molecular marker, so diagnosis remains clinical using the 2017 international criteria. Diagnosis requires generalised joint hypermobility (assessed by the Beighton score with age-adjusted cut-offs) plus a combination of systemic connective-tissue features, positive family history and musculoskeletal complications, after exclusion of other heritable connective-tissue disorders. Skin is soft and mildly hyperextensible with a velvety texture but, unlike classical EDS, lacks marked fragility, wide atrophic scarring or severe bruising. Chronic widespread pain, fatigue, recurrent joint subluxations/dislocations and premature osteoarthritis are the dominant sources of morbidity. Frequently overlaps with dysautonomia (including postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome), functional gastrointestinal disorders, and mast cell activation symptoms. Cornerstones of management are physiotherapy for joint stabilisation and proprioception, graded exercise, pacing, and multidisciplinary chronic-pain and fatigue management rather than surgery. In contrast to vascular EDS, life-threatening arterial or hollow-organ rupture is not a feature; however, cardiovascular assessment (including echocardiography for aortic root) is reasonable at diagnosis. Pelvic-floor dysfunction, hernias, pelvic organ prolapse, and pregnancy-related complications are more frequent and merit anticipatory care. features suggesting vascular EDS (translucent skin, easy arterial/organ rupture, acrogeria) requiring urgent COL3A1 evaluation aortic root dilatation or lens dislocation pointing towards Marfan or Loeys-Dietz syndrome significant skin fragility with abnormal scarring suggesting classical EDS acute severe abdominal or chest pain that could indicate a vascular or visceral catastrophe and must not be dismissed as chronic pain diagnosing hEDS on hypermobility alone without applying the full 2017 criteria or excluding other heritable connective-tissue disorders attributing every symptom to hEDS and overlooking a treatable comorbidity or an alternative EDS subtype with vascular risk recommending joint surgery prematurely when conservative rehabilitation is first-line and surgical outcomes are often poor in lax tissue missing associated dysautonomia, gastrointestinal or mast cell symptoms that are amenable to specific treatment Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a heritable disorder of connective tissue in which the extracellular matrix supporting joints, skin and vessels is qualitatively abnormal, producing tissue laxity and reduced tensile strength. Although inheritance appears autosomal dominant with variable expressivity and a female preponderance in clinical series, no single causative gene has been reliably identified, and the condition is presumed genetically heterogeneous, possibly involving collagen processing, minor collagens or matrix regulatory proteins. The resulting ligamentous laxity leads to recurrent joint instability, microtrauma and secondary chronic pain and osteoarthritis, while altered matrix in autonomic and visceral tissues is thought to contribute to the commonly co-occurring dysautonomia, gastrointestinal dysmotility and pelvic-floor dysfunction. Life expectancy is normal, but many patients experience chronic pain, fatigue and recurrent joint instability that can substantially impair function and quality of life; outcomes are improved by early multidisciplinary rehabilitation and self-management.

wall stress and avoidance of arterial catheterisation and elective vascular procedures are important Sudden severe abdominal, chest, or flank pain suggesting arterial or visceral rupture in vascular EDS Unexplained bruising with a family history of premature sudden death from vascular causes Pregnancy in vascular EDS, given the risk of uterine and arterial rupture Rapidly expanding haematoma or signs of internal haemorrhage Recurrent large-joint dislocations causing severe disability Treating all EDS as benign and missing the life-threatening vascular subtype Performing arterial catheterisation or elective vascular surgery in vascular EDS without weighing the high rupture risk Assuming a normal molecular test excludes hypermobile EDS, which has no confirmed gene Underestimating chronic pain, fatigue, and autonomic symptoms in affected patients Neglecting genetic counselling and family screening, particularly for vascular EDS The Ehlers-Danlos syndromes result from defects in the synthesis, structure, or processing of collagen and related extracellular matrix components. Depending on the subtype, variants affect fibrillar collagens (such as type V in classical EDS and type III in vascular EDS) or enzymes and cofactors involved in collagen modification and cross-linking. Abnormal collagen fibrils reduce the tensile strength and integrity of skin, ligaments, blood vessels, and hollow organs, producing hypermobility, skin fragility with poor wound healing, and, in the most severe forms, catastrophic vascular and visceral rupture. The wide phenotypic range reflects which matrix component and tissue are predominantly affected. Prognosis depends heavily on subtype: most patients with classical or hypermobile EDS have a normal lifespan with chronic musculoskeletal symptoms, whereas vascular EDS carries a substantially reduced life expectancy from arterial and organ rupture. Early recognition of the vascular subtype and appropriate precautions are the most important determinants of outcome.

Pregnancy, which carries very high maternal mortality Paradoxical embolism causing stroke or systemic embolism, and features of hyperviscosity Prescribing systemic vasodilators that reduce systemic resistance and deepen right-to-left shunting Routine venesection for erythrocytosis without hyperviscosity symptoms, which causes iron deficiency and paradoxically increases risk Failing to counsel firmly against pregnancy and to advise safe, non-oestrogen contraception Overlooking the risk of paradoxical embolism during intravenous access, requiring meticulous air-bubble precautions A large communication between the systemic and pulmonary circulations initially drives a high-volume left-to-right shunt. Sustained exposure of the pulmonary vasculature to high flow and pressure causes progressive remodelling with medial hypertrophy, intimal proliferation, and plexiform lesions, raising pulmonary vascular resistance irreversibly. When pulmonary resistance approaches or exceeds systemic resistance the shunt reverses, so deoxygenated blood enters the systemic circulation and causes cyanosis. Chronic hypoxaemia stimulates erythropoietin and secondary erythrocytosis, increasing viscosity, while the loss of the pulmonary filter allows paradoxical embolism; these mechanisms underlie the multisystem complications and explain why lowering systemic vascular resistance is dangerous. Eisenmenger syndrome shortens life expectancy but many patients survive into adulthood with specialist care; prognosis worsens with syncope, haemoptysis, right heart failure, and pregnancy, and transplantation is considered in advanced disease.

Chronic mechanical friction between the inferior scapula and the underlying rib cage is thought to induce abnormal production and degeneration of elastic fibres within a dense collagenous stroma. The result is a poorly circumscribed mass characterised by numerous swollen, fragmented and beaded elastic fibres admixed with collagen and entrapped fat. Its stereotyped deep periscapular location reflects this mechanical aetiology. Elastofibroma dorsi is entirely benign with no malignant potential, and observation is appropriate for asymptomatic lesions. Marginal excision is curative for symptomatic disease, and recurrence is rare.

elastosis perforans serpiginosa — EPS, perforating elastosis reactive perforating collagenosis perforating folliculitis Kyrle disease granuloma annulare (annular and perforating variants) tinea corporis porokeratosis annular sarcoidosis skin biopsy with elastic tissue stain (Verhoeff-van Gieson) to demonstrate abnormal elastic fibres and their transepidermal elimination medication history focused on penicillamine and duration of use clinical and, where indicated, genetic assessment for associated connective-tissue disorders karyotype or clinical evaluation for Down syndrome when phenotypic features present ophthalmic and cardiovascular review if pseudoxanthoma elasticum or Marfan syndrome is suspected dermoscopy to highlight keratotic plugs in an annular arrangement A perforating dermatosis defined by transepidermal elimination of abnormal elastic fibres, presenting as keratotic papules arranged in serpiginous or arcuate (annular) configurations. Typically affects adolescents and young adults, with a male predominance, and favours the sides of the neck, the face, upper limbs and flexures. Idiopathic in many cases, but classically associated with inherited connective-tissue and metabolic disorders: Down syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, pseudoxanthoma elasticum, Marfan syndrome and osteogenesis imperfecta. A distinctive drug-induced form is caused by penicillamine, which produces bizarre 'lumpy-bumpy' or 'bramble-bush' abnormal elastic fibres on staining. Histology shows increased and abnormal elastic fibres in the papillary dermis being extruded through a channel in the hyperplastic epidermis; elastic tissue stains (Verhoeff-van Gieson) are diagnostic. Lesions are often asymptomatic or mildly pruritic and may resolve spontaneously over months to years, sometimes leaving atrophic or reticulate scarring. Treatment is challenging and often unsatisfactory; options include topical retinoids or corticosteroids, cryotherapy, and laser or cautery for limited disease, with withdrawal of penicillamine in drug-induced cases. The serpiginous configuration reflects centrifugal spread with central clearing rather than a single perforating focus. current or prior penicillamine therapy indicating a drug-induced form requiring drug review features of an underlying heritable connective-tissue disorder with systemic (ocular, cardiovascular, skeletal) implications extensive or rapidly spreading serpiginous plaques causing significant scarring secondary infection of excoriated or treated lesions omitting an elastic tissue stain, so the diagnostic abnormal elastic fibres are missed on routine sections failing to elicit a penicillamine history in a young patient with connective-tissue disease mistaking annular lesions for tinea corporis or granuloma annulare and treating empirically aggressive destructive therapy leading to disfiguring scarring given the tendency to spontaneous resolution Elastosis perforans serpiginosa results from focal accumulation of qualitatively and quantitatively abnormal elastic fibres in the papillary dermis, which the skin eliminates transepidermally as a foreign-body-type response. The epidermis surrounding a follicular or interfollicular channel becomes hyperplastic and forms a narrow perforating canal through which the altered elastic material, admixed with keratinous and inflammatory debris, is expelled. In heritable connective-tissue disorders the elastic fibres are intrinsically abnormal, while penicillamine directly interferes with elastin cross-linking (by inhibiting lysyl oxidase-dependent desmosine formation), producing the characteristic serrated 'thorny' elastic fibres seen on histology. Often a self-limiting condition that resolves over months to a few years, though it may leave atrophic or reticulate scarring; drug-induced and syndrome-associated forms can be more persistent and recurrence after destructive treatment is common.
