genetically predisposed individuals, including carriers of HLA-B27 for the axial phenotype, inflammation of the gut mucosa in inflammatory bowel disease is thought to allow translocation of luminal antigens and trafficking of activated immune cells that promote inflammation at the joints, entheses, and axial skeleton. This shared gut-joint immune axis links intestinal and musculoskeletal inflammation and places the disorder within the spondyloarthritis spectrum, helping explain why type 1 peripheral disease often parallels bowel activity while axial disease pursues an independent course. Type 1 peripheral arthritis is usually self-limiting and improves as the bowel disease is controlled, whereas type 2 peripheral and axial disease tend to be more persistent and can, like ankylosing spondylitis, lead to structural spinal damage if untreated; the overall outlook is improved by coordinated control of both gut and joint inflammation.

Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma — EATL, type I enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, coeliac-associated T-cell lymphoma, intestinal T-cell lymphoma, CD3+/CD103+/CD30-variable intraepithelial-derived lymphoma Refractory coeliac disease type II without overt lymphoma Monomorphic epitheliotropic intestinal T-cell lymphoma Crohn's disease or other inflammatory bowel disease with ulceration Intestinal diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Adenocarcinoma of the small bowel Infective or ischaemic ulceration of the small intestine Endoscopic or surgical biopsy with immunohistochemistry (CD3, CD103, CD30, CD8, CD56) and cytotoxic markers T-cell receptor clonality analysis on tumour and background mucosa Coeliac serology and HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing to confirm the enteropathy background Video capsule endoscopy or enteroscopy to map multifocal small-bowel disease Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI enterography) and PET for staging Bone marrow examination and assessment of nutritional and metabolic status Arises on a background of coeliac disease, often in patients with refractory coeliac disease type II, and usually presents in adults of northern European origin Common presentations include abdominal pain, weight loss, and recurrence of malabsorptive symptoms despite a gluten-free diet, or an acute surgical picture of bowel perforation or obstruction The jejunum is the most frequent site; tumours are often multifocal with ulceration and may present as multiple ulcers rather than a single mass Neoplastic cells derive from intraepithelial T-lymphocytes and typically express CD3 and CD103, with variable CD30 and cytotoxic markers, and characteristically lack CD8 and CD56 in the classic form Adjacent mucosa usually shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and an abnormal intraepithelial lymphocyte population confirming the enteropathy link Distinguish from monomorphic epitheliotropic intestinal T-cell lymphoma, which is not coeliac-associated and expresses CD8 and CD56 Association with the coeliac-related HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotype underpins the disease Signs of bowel perforation or peritonitis requiring urgent surgical assessment Gastrointestinal haemorrhage or obstruction Rapidly worsening malabsorption with profound weight loss and hypoalbuminaemia Refractory coeliac disease failing to respond to a strict gluten-free diet, signalling possible progression Attributing recurrent symptoms to dietary non-adherence and delaying investigation for lymphoma Failing to distinguish classic EATL from monomorphic epitheliotropic intestinal T-cell lymphoma, which differ in coeliac association and immunophenotype Underestimating perforation risk when starting cytotoxic therapy Overlooking profound malnutrition that limits treatment delivery Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma develops from intraepithelial T-lymphocytes of the small intestine in the setting of long-standing coeliac disease. Chronic gluten-driven mucosal immune activation, particularly in refractory coeliac disease type II, gives rise to an aberrant, clonal intraepithelial lymphocyte population that has lost normal surface T-cell antigens. Accumulation of genetic changes, including alterations in the JAK-STAT signalling pathway, drives progression from this precursor state to overt lymphoma. The tumour cells retain gut-homing characteristics such as CD103 expression, and their transmural, ulcerating growth accounts for the high rate of perforation. The outlook is poor, with frequent presentation as a surgical emergency, high relapse rates, and limited tolerance of intensive therapy owing to malnutrition; consolidation with autologous stem-cell transplant is used in fit patients.

Enterovirus, Parechovirus, and Reovirus Infections — Nonpolio enterovirus infection, Coxsackievirus infection, Echovirus infection, Poliovirus infection / poliomyelitis, Human parechovirus (HPeV) infection, Reovirus infection, Summer grippe, Hand-foot-and-mouth disease, Herpangina, Bornholm disease (pleurodynia) Bacterial sepsis (especially in neonatal generalized enteroviral disease) Partially treated bacterial meningitis (can be hard to exclude from enteroviral meningitis) Mumps meningitis (distinguished by low CSF glucose, vs normal in enterovirus) Rubella (enteroviral rubelliform rash lacks lymphadenopathy and occurs in summer) Measles (enteroviral enanthems may mimic Koplik's spots) Herpetic stomatitis (vs herpangina, which lacks gingivitis) Adenoviral or Chlamydia trachomatis conjunctivitis (vs acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis) Bacterial sepsis of the newborn Bacterial (including partially treated) meningitis Mumps virus meningitis Herpes simplex stomatitis / encephalitis Adenovirus and Chlamydia trachomatis ocular infection Other respiratory viruses causing cold/pneumonia PCR is now the primary diagnostic method; pan-enterovirus reverse-transcription PCR detects all human enteroviruses (CSF PCR ~70-100% sensitive, over 80% specific, faster than culture) but does NOT detect parechoviruses. CSF PCR is less likely positive if presentation is 3 or more days after meningitis onset or with EV71; in those cases throat or rectal swab PCR (less specific) should be considered. Serum PCR is highly sensitive/specific for disseminated disease and useful for diagnosis/monitoring in immunodeficient patients on immunoglobulin whose cultures may be negative; antigen detection is less sensitive than PCR. Viral culture of CSF, serum, body-cavity fluid, or tissue is positive less often but a positive result is diagnostic; throat isolation is more meaningful than stool because shedding is shorter; coxsackievirus A may need special cell lines or suckling-mouse inoculation. For suspected poliomyelitis: obtain two or more fecal and throat swabs at least 1 day apart for culture; a positive stool culture within the first 2 weeks confirms diagnosis when CSF culture is negative, and any poliovirus isolate must be sent to CDC to distinguish wild-type from vaccine virus. Serotype identification is mainly for epidemiology; serologic diagnosis (paired acute and ~4-week convalescent neutralizing titers, the most accurate method) is limited by the many serotypes and absence of a common antigen. Dedicated parechovirus PCR (performed by CDC and research labs; often unavailable commercially) when HPeV is suspected. In acute flaccid myelitis: spinal-cord MRI may show gray-matter changes; CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and mildly elevated protein; EV-D68 antibodies are most often found in CSF though the virus itself is rarely detected there. Guillain-Barre syndrome (also associated with enterovirus but a key paralytic mimic) Idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy (as a sequela/overlap of enteroviral myocarditis) Erythema multiforme and other drug or immune exanthems Type 1 diabetes mellitus (epidemiologically associated with prolonged enteroviral shedding) Idiopathic dermatomyositis (chronic enteroviral infection in agammaglobulinemia mimics it) Enteroviruses are Picornaviridae with single-stranded RNA and a non-enveloped icosahedral capsid; being non-enveloped they are acid-stable (survive the stomach), resist alcohol and detergent disinfectants, persist for days at room temperature, but are susceptible to chlorine-containing cleansers. More than 50% of nonpolio enterovirus infections and over 90% of poliovirus infections are subclinical; when symptomatic, the most common picture is a nonspecific febrile illness ('summer grippe'), and in temperate climates disease clusters in summer and fall. In children and young adults enteroviruses account for up to 90% of aseptic meningitis cases with an identifiable agent; CSF shows pleocytosis that shifts from neutrophil to lymphocyte predominance within a day, total cell count usually under 1000/uL, normal glucose, and normal-to-slightly-elevated protein. A normal CSF glucose in enteroviral meningitis helps distinguish it from mumps meningitis, in which CSF glucose is low; enteroviral meningitis tends to be more severe in adults than children but neurologic sequelae are rare. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (most often coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71) is highly infectious with attack rates near 100% in young children; coxsackievirus A6 causes a more extensive atypical form, and a B16/EV71 epidemic in Taiwan (1998) and yearly EV71 epidemics in China since 2008 produced brainstem encephalitis, pulmonary edema/hemorrhage, and deaths, mostly in children 5 years or younger. Herpangina (usually coxsackievirus A) produces grayish-white papulovesicular ulcerating lesions concentrated in the posterior mouth (soft palate, anterior tonsillar pillars, uvula) and, unlike herpetic stomatitis, is NOT associated with gingivitis. Pleurodynia (Bornholm disease), usually coxsackievirus B, causes paroxysms of knifelike pleuritic chest or upper-abdominal pain lasting 15-30 minutes with tender muscles and possible pleural rub; WBC and chest x-ray are typically normal. Enteroviruses cause up to one-third of acute myocarditis cases; patients (over two-thirds male, often neonates/adolescents/young adults) present after a respiratory prodrome with chest pain, arrhythmia, ST/T-wave changes and elevated cardiac enzymes; up to 10% progress to dilated cardiomyopathy. Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis (enterovirus 70, coxsackievirus A24) presents with sudden severe eye pain, subconjunctival hemorrhage, chemosis, and preauricular adenopathy; its abrupt onset and short course (recovery in ~10 days) distinguish it from adenoviral or chlamydial eye disease, and EV70 cases have been linked to paralysis during epidemics. Humoral immunity is critical: patients with agamma-/hypogammaglobulinemia can develop chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis (often echovirus 11) with a dermatomyositis-like syndrome and chronic hepatitis, and may relapse even while on immunoglobulin; hypogammaglobulinemic patients can shed poliovirus for more than 20 years. Human parechoviruses (HPeV, also Picornaviridae) mimic enteroviral disease (neonatal generalized disease, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, seizures, hepatitis, rash) but pan-enterovirus PCR does NOT detect HPeV, so a dedicated PCR is required; infant deaths have been associated with HPeV-1, HPeV-3, and HPeV-6. Reoviruses are double-stranded RNA viruses; most childhood infection is asymptomatic or causes mild upper respiratory symptoms, and reovirus is only a rare cause of mild gastroenteritis or meningitis, with speculative (unproven) links of reovirus type 3 to neonatal hepatitis and biliary atresia. Neonatal enteroviral illness resembling sepsis with myocarditis/hypotension, fulminant hepatitis with DIC, meningoencephalitis, or pneumonia (serious disease most often in the first week of life, up to 3 months). Rapid onset of flaccid limb paralysis after fever/respiratory symptoms (acute flaccid myelitis or paralytic enteroviral disease). Brainstem encephalitis with myoclonus, tremor/ataxia, plus pulmonary edema or hemorrhage in young children (severe enterovirus 71 disease). Bulbar involvement causing dysphagia, dysphonia, or respiratory insufficiency/circulatory collapse in poliomyelitis. Chest pain, arrhythmia, ST-segment changes, and elevated cardiac enzymes after a respiratory prodrome (enteroviral myocarditis, risk of dilated cardiomyopathy). Chronic meningoencephalitis or dermatomyositis-like syndrome in an agamma-/hypogammaglobulinemic patient. Glucocorticoids are contraindicated in enterovirus infections. A positive enterovirus culture from stool, nasopharynx, or throat does NOT prove disease causation, since these sites are colonized for weeks during subclinical infection; throat isolation is more meaningful than stool. Pan-enterovirus PCR does not detect human parechoviruses, so HPeV can be missed unless a dedicated assay is used. CSF PCR may be falsely negative if obtained 3 or more days into meningitis or in EV71 infection. Neonatal enteroviral disease can be indistinguishable from bacterial sepsis; a recent viral illness in the mother is a useful clue. Cultures may be falsely negative due to neutralizing antibody, unsuitable cell lines, or improper specimen handling. Oral poliovirus vaccine can revert to neurovirulence (vaccine-associated/vaccine-derived poliomyelitis), with risk roughly 2000-fold higher in immunodeficient persons; tonsillectomy predisposes to bulbar polio and IM injections increase paralysis risk in the involved limb. Enteroviruses multiply in the gastrointestinal tract. Based largely on poliovirus studies, after ingestion the virus infects mucosal epithelium and replicates in submucosal lymphoid tissue (tonsils, Peyer's patches), spreads to regional lymph nodes and into a viremic phase with replication in reticuloendothelial organs; a secondary viremia may seed other tissues and cause symptomatic disease. CNS entry is thought to occur via the bloodstream (viremia precedes neurologic disease), but evidence also supports direct neural spread: the poliovirus receptor is an immunoglobulin-superfamily member expressed at the neuromuscular end-plate, and animal/transgenic-mouse studies show that cutting the sciatic nerve prevents spinal-cord involvement after IM virus injection, implying axonal transport from muscle to anterior horn cells. Poliovirus is culturable from blood 3-5 days after infection (before neutralizing antibody); it is shed from the oropharynx up to ~3 weeks and from the GI tract up to ~12 weeks (over 20 years in hypogammaglobulinemia), and attenuated oral vaccine virus can revert toward neurovirulence during GI replication. Capsid protein VP1 is the main neutralizing-antibody target, conferring lifelong serotype-specific protection that does not prevent reinfection or shedding; IgM persists under ~6 months and IgG for life. Mucosal/secretory IgA limits GI replication and shedding, and breast-milk IgA is protective. Acute flaccid myelitis and poliomyelitis both target anterior horn cells of the spinal cord. Most enterovirus infections are mild and self-limited, resolving within about a week. Enteroviral aseptic meningitis carries an excellent prognosis with rare neurologic sequelae (though CSF abnormalities can persist weeks); immunocompetent encephalitis patients generally do well. Pleurodynia resolves in days with rare recurrence; acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis usually recovers completely in ~10 days. Myocarditis in older children and adults usually resolves fully, but neonates often have severe disease and up to 10% progress to chronic dilated cardiomyopathy, with chronic constrictive pericarditis a possible sequela. In paralytic poliomyelitis most patients regain some function over weeks to months but about two-thirds have residual neurologic sequelae; postpolio syndrome has a generally good prognosis with slow progression and plateaus of 1-10 years. Acute flaccid myelitis usually leaves persistent neurologic deficits. EV71 CNS disease can leave lasting dysphagia, cranial-nerve palsies, hypoventilation, limb weakness/atrophy, and impaired cognition. HPeV infection is usually mild (HPeV-1) but has caused infant deaths. Poliovirus infection severity spectrum: asymptomatic (most) -> minor/abortive poliomyelitis (~5%: fever, malaise, sore throat, myalgia, headache, resolving in ~3 days) -> nonparalytic poliomyelitis/aseptic meningitis (~1%) -> paralytic poliomyelitis (least common; asymmetric, proximal-predominant weakness, may be bulbar/respiratory). Paralytic disease is more frequent in older individuals, pregnant women, and those exercising or experiencing trauma at symptom onset. Postpolio syndrome occurs 20-40 years after initial paralytic disease. Vaccine-associated paralytic risk is about 1 per 2.5 million OPV doses.

Enthesitis-related arthritis — ERA, enthesitis-related JIA, juvenile spondyloarthritis, HLA-B27-associated JIA Mechanical or overuse enthesopathy and apophysitis (e.g. Osgood-Schlatter, Sever disease) Reactive arthritis following gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection Inflammatory bowel disease-associated arthritis Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis Other JIA subtypes Psoriatic arthritis HLA-B27 typing to support the diagnosis Inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein) MRI of the sacroiliac joints to detect early sacroiliitis before radiographic change Ultrasound of entheses to confirm active enthesitis Ophthalmology assessment for symptomatic anterior uveitis Screening for inflammatory bowel disease when gastrointestinal symptoms are present Radiographs of affected joints and sacroiliac joints in established disease Falls within the juvenile spondyloarthritis spectrum and typically affects older boys, often with a family history of HLA-B27-associated disease Enthesitis, inflammation at the insertion of tendons and ligaments into bone, is characteristic and commonly affects the Achilles tendon, plantar fascia and around the knee Peripheral arthritis is usually asymmetrical and predominantly affects the lower limbs, including hips Axial and sacroiliac involvement may develop over time, producing inflammatory back pain with morning stiffness that improves with activity Acute symptomatic anterior uveitis (a painful, red, photophobic eye) is typical, in contrast to the chronic silent uveitis of oligoarticular disease Strong association with HLA-B27, and overlap with reactive arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease-related arthropathy Management uses NSAIDs, intra-articular corticosteroids and, for persistent or axial disease, TNF inhibition Progressive inflammatory back pain with restricted spinal mobility indicating axial disease Acute painful red eye requiring urgent ophthalmology review Fever and systemic upset suggesting infection Weight loss, bloody diarrhoea or anaemia suggesting inflammatory bowel disease Dismissing entheseal heel and knee pain as mechanical growing pains Overlooking early sacroiliitis because plain radiographs are insensitive early on Assuming HLA-B27 negativity excludes the diagnosis Missing associated inflammatory bowel disease Failing to warn families about symptomatic acute uveitis Enthesitis-related arthritis is a juvenile spondyloarthropathy in which inflammation centres on the enthesis, the site where tendons, ligaments and joint capsules insert into bone. In genetically predisposed children, particularly those carrying HLA-B27, aberrant innate and adaptive immune responses, with a prominent role for the interleukin-23/interleukin-17 axis, drive entheseal and synovial inflammation and, in some, sacroiliitis and spinal involvement. Chronic inflammation can lead to new bone formation, ankylosis and progressive axial disease resembling ankylosing spondylitis in adulthood. The course is variable; some children have limited peripheral disease, while others progress to axial spondyloarthritis with sacroiliitis and reduced spinal mobility in adulthood. Early recognition and TNF inhibition can improve symptom control and may modify axial progression.

Entomophthoromycosis — Conidiobolus coronatus, Basidiobolus ranarum, conidiobolomycosis (rhinofacial), basidiobolomycosis, subcutaneous zygomycosis Angioinvasive mucormycosis (in immunocompromised hosts) Soft-tissue tumours (benign or malignant) Lymphoedema or filariasis (for limb swelling) Cellulitis or other subcutaneous infection Inflammatory bowel disease or abdominal malignancy (for the gastrointestinal form) Rhinoscleroma or other causes of destructive facial swelling Biopsy with histology showing broad sparsely septate hyphae and the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon Fungal culture to identify Conidiobolus or Basidiobolus Full blood count (peripheral eosinophilia is common) Imaging (CT/MRI) to define the extent of facial or abdominal disease Endoscopy and biopsy for suspected gastrointestinal involvement Assessment of immune status to distinguish from mucormycosis Entomophthoromycosis is a chronic subcutaneous fungal infection caused by the Entomophthorales, principally Conidiobolus coronatus and Basidiobolus ranarum, seen in tropical Africa, Asia and Latin America Unlike the angioinvasive mucormycoses of immunocompromised patients, these infections typically occur in immunocompetent hosts and are slow, localised and non-angioinvasive Conidiobolus infection (rhinofacial/rhinoentomophthoromycosis) affects adults, producing painless, firm swelling of the central face, nose and paranasal tissues that can cause gross disfigurement Basidiobolus infection presents mainly in children as a firm, mobile, painless subcutaneous swelling of the limbs, shoulder or trunk with a well-defined edge, and can less commonly involve the gastrointestinal tract Gastrointestinal basidiobolomycosis mimics abdominal malignancy or inflammatory bowel disease and is often diagnosed only after surgery Diagnosis is histological, showing broad, thin-walled, sparsely septate hyphae surrounded by eosinophilic material (the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon), with culture for confirmation Prolonged medical therapy with agents such as oral potassium iodide or azole antifungals is used, sometimes combined with surgery, but rhinofacial disease can leave permanent disfigurement Progressive facial swelling threatening the airway, orbit or vision Gastrointestinal disease with obstruction, perforation or a mass mimicking cancer Rapid progression or angioinvasive features suggesting mucormycosis instead Extensive disfiguring disease unresponsive to therapy Relapse after treatment Confusing indolent entomophthoromycosis with aggressive angioinvasive mucormycosis and mismanaging accordingly Stopping prolonged therapy prematurely, leading to relapse Missing gastrointestinal basidiobolomycosis, which mimics malignancy or inflammatory bowel disease Failing to obtain adequate tissue for histology and culture Underestimating the disfigurement and functional impact of rhinofacial disease The Entomophthorales are environmental saprophytes of soil and decaying vegetation and are also found in the gut of amphibians and reptiles. Infection follows implantation into subcutaneous tissue through minor trauma or insect contact, or, for Conidiobolus, inhalation of spores into the nasal mucosa. The fungi grow slowly within subcutaneous or submucosal tissue, eliciting a chronic granulomatous and eosinophilic inflammatory response rather than invading blood vessels, which distinguishes them clinically from the acute mucormycoses. Progressive local extension produces firm, indurated swelling; gastrointestinal disease arises from mucosal implantation and causes inflammatory masses. Subcutaneous basidiobolomycosis of the limbs often responds well to prolonged medical therapy, whereas rhinofacial conidiobolomycosis frequently leaves permanent facial disfigurement despite treatment; gastrointestinal disease carries higher morbidity and can be serious if diagnosed late.

Entropion — inturned eyelid, inverted eyelid Trichiasis (misdirected lashes with normal lid position) Epiblepharon (extra lower lid skin fold, often in children) Distichiasis (aberrant accessory lash row) Spastic entropion from ocular irritation Blepharospasm Slit-lamp examination to assess lash-cornea contact and corneal integrity Fluorescein staining to detect epithelial damage Assessment of horizontal lid laxity (snap-back and distraction tests) Evaluation of the conjunctival fornices for scarring in suspected cicatricial disease The eyelid margin turns inward so that lashes rub against the cornea and conjunctiva, causing irritation, foreign body sensation, tearing, and redness The involutional (age-related) type is the commonest and usually affects the lower lid, driven by tissue laxity Cicatricial entropion follows conjunctival scarring from conditions such as trachoma, chemical burns, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and ocular cicatricial pemphigoid Chronic lash-cornea contact risks epithelial breakdown, secondary microbial keratitis, and corneal scarring Temporary measures include lubrication, taping the lid outward, and botulinum toxin, while lid-everting sutures give short-term relief Definitive management is surgical correction tailored to the underlying mechanism Distinguish from trichiasis, where lashes are misdirected but the lid margin itself is correctly positioned Corneal epithelial defect or infiltrate indicating secondary keratitis and threatened vision Progressive conjunctival scarring suggesting cicatrising disease such as pemphigoid requiring systemic workup Persistent lash-cornea contact despite temporising measures Treating symptoms with lubricants alone while ongoing lash contact damages the cornea Failing to identify a cicatricial cause requiring different surgical planning and systemic evaluation Confusing entropion with trichiasis and choosing the wrong intervention Overlooking recurrence after involutional repair due to unaddressed lid laxity Entropion is inward rotation of the eyelid margin. Involutional entropion arises from age-related horizontal lid laxity, attenuation or disinsertion of the lower lid retractors, and overriding of the preseptal orbicularis, which together destabilise the lid and allow it to rotate inward. Cicatricial entropion results from contracture of scarred tarsoconjunctiva pulling the margin toward the globe. Spastic entropion is triggered by orbicularis spasm from ocular irritation, and congenital entropion reflects a structural lid defect. In all forms the inturned lashes abrade the ocular surface, causing chronic irritation and potential corneal damage. Surgical correction is generally effective with good long-term results, though cicatricial cases may recur and require repeated intervention; untreated chronic disease can cause corneal scarring and visual loss.

Eosinophilia — peripheral blood eosinophilia, hypereosinophilia, eosinophilic disorders Helminth and other parasitic infections Atopic disease: asthma, atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis Drug hypersensitivity, including DRESS Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and eosinophilic lung diseases Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other vasculitides Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and reactive eosinophilia in solid tumours or lymphoma Adrenal insufficiency and, rarely, HIV infection Repeat full blood count to confirm and quantify the absolute eosinophil count Stool microscopy and relevant parasite serology, with Strongyloides testing before immunosuppression Serum tryptase, vitamin B12, and IgE with review of medications Molecular testing for FIP1L1-PDGFRA and other tyrosine-kinase fusions, plus marrow examination and cytogenetics when clonal disease is suspected Troponin and echocardiography (and cardiac MRI if indicated) to assess cardiac involvement Targeted imaging and biopsy of affected organs Eosinophilia is defined by an absolute eosinophil count above the normal range, with hypereosinophilia denoting persistently very high counts; the degree and persistence guide the urgency of evaluation A practical framework separates causes into reactive/secondary (allergy, parasites, drugs, malignancy) and primary/clonal (myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms) plus idiopathic disease Worldwide, helminth infection is the leading cause, so travel and exposure history and stool and serologic studies are essential, especially before immunosuppression that could disseminate strongyloidiasis In high-income settings, atopic disease and drug reactions are common causes, and a careful medication review can reveal the culprit Hypereosinophilic syndrome is diagnosed when marked eosinophilia persists with evidence of eosinophil-mediated organ damage and no identifiable secondary cause Cardiac involvement (endomyocardial fibrosis and thrombosis) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, so troponin and echocardiography are important in significant hypereosinophilia The FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion defines an imatinib-responsive myeloid variant, making molecular testing pivotal because it changes treatment entirely Corticosteroids are the mainstay for symptomatic reactive and idiopathic hypereosinophilia, but empiric anti-parasitic cover for Strongyloides is prudent before starting them where exposure is possible Peripheral counts do not always reflect tissue eosinophilia, so organ-specific disease can occur with only modestly raised or normal blood counts Cardiac involvement with troponin rise, heart failure, or intracardiac thrombus Neurologic deficits, thromboembolism, or rapidly progressive organ dysfunction Very high, persistent counts (hypereosinophilia) with systemic symptoms suggesting evolving organ damage Features of an underlying haematologic malignancy such as splenomegaly, cytopenias, or blasts Starting corticosteroids without excluding Strongyloides, risking fatal hyperinfection Attributing eosinophilia to allergy without considering clonal or parasitic causes Relying on blood counts alone and missing tissue eosinophilic organ damage Overlooking treatable molecular subtypes by not sending fusion-gene testing Eosinophil production and survival are driven principally by interleukin-5, along with IL-3 and GM-CSF. In reactive eosinophilia these cytokines are overproduced by activated T cells or tumour cells in response to allergens, parasites, drugs, or malignancy. In clonal (primary) eosinophilia, a genetic lesion in the myeloid lineage-most classically the FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion, or rearrangements of PDGFRB, FGFR1, and JAK2-produces autonomous eosinophil proliferation. A lymphocytic variant arises from an aberrant T-cell population secreting eosinophilopoietic cytokines. Tissue injury results from release of eosinophil granule proteins (major basic protein, eosinophil cationic protein), reactive oxygen species, and prothrombotic and profibrotic mediators, damaging heart, lungs, skin, gut, and nervous system. Reactive eosinophilia usually resolves once the trigger is removed or treated. Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome outcome depends on organ involvement and treatment response; the FIP1L1-PDGFRA variant generally responds very well to targeted tyrosine-kinase inhibition, whereas untreated cardiac disease carries a poor prognosis.

Eosinophilic cellulitis (Wells syndrome) — Wells syndrome, eosinophilic cellulitis, recurrent granulomatous dermatitis with eosinophilia Bacterial cellulitis / erysipelas Acute contact dermatitis Urticaria and angio-oedema Arthropod bite reactions Hypereosinophilic syndrome with skin involvement Sweet syndrome Skin biopsy demonstrating tissue eosinophilia and flame figures Full blood count for peripheral eosinophilia Investigation for triggers (recent bites, drugs, infections) Stool examination for parasites where relevant Evaluation for underlying haematological or myeloproliferative disease in persistent cases Inflammatory markers to help distinguish from infective cellulitis Presents with acute, often itchy or burning, oedematous erythematous plaques that closely resemble bacterial cellulitis but fail to respond to antibiotics and lack fever Lesions may evolve over days into slate-grey or greenish infiltrated plaques as they resolve, and the eruption tends to recur It is a reactive hypersensitivity process rather than an infection, often triggered by insect bites, drugs, infections or, occasionally, underlying haematological disease Peripheral blood eosinophilia is common but not invariable The histological hallmark is dermal eosinophilic infiltration with 'flame figures', formed by eosinophil granule proteins coating collagen bundles Diagnosis rests on recognising the mismatch between a cellulitis-like appearance and the biopsy findings Treatment is with systemic corticosteroids for troublesome disease and identification of any trigger; many cases eventually remit Marked or persistent eosinophilia suggesting hypereosinophilic syndrome with organ involvement Failure to respond, prompting reassessment for underlying malignancy or myeloproliferative disease Genuine secondary bacterial infection of oedematous skin Extensive or blistering lesions with systemic upset Repeatedly treating it as bacterial cellulitis with escalating antibiotics Not biopsying antibiotic-unresponsive 'cellulitis' to reveal the eosinophilic pattern Assuming flame figures are specific, when they occur in other eosinophil-rich dermatoses Overlooking an underlying haematological disorder in persistent or severe cases Wells syndrome is thought to represent a hypersensitivity reaction with abnormal eosinophil recruitment and activation in the skin, often in response to an identifiable stimulus such as an arthropod bite, drug, infection or underlying disorder. Activated eosinophils infiltrate the dermis and degranulate, depositing major basic protein and other granule proteins onto collagen fibres to create the characteristic flame figures, surrounded by histiocytes and giant cells in later stages. This eosinophil-driven tissue reaction produces the oedematous, cellulitis-like plaques and their tendency to recur. The condition is benign but characteristically relapsing, with individual episodes resolving over weeks, sometimes leaving transient discoloration; most patients eventually enter remission, though recurrent flares can be troublesome and steroid-dependent.

Eosinophilic colitis — EC, Eosinophilic proctocolitis Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease) Parasitic colitis (Strongyloides, Trichuris, schistosomiasis) Drug-induced colonic eosinophilia Hypereosinophilic syndrome with colonic involvement Connective tissue disease or vasculitis Cow's milk protein allergy in infants Colorectal malignancy or lymphoma Ileocolonoscopy with segmental biopsies and eosinophil counts against regional norms Full blood count with eosinophil count Stool microscopy and serology for parasites Faecal calprotectin Allergy assessment where food allergy is suspected Cross-sectional imaging if wall thickening or a mass is present Screen for hypereosinophilic syndrome and vasculitis where indicated The rarest of the eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorders in adults, with a bimodal age distribution affecting infants and adults. The infantile form (allergic proctocolitis) is typically benign, cow's milk protein-related and resolves with dietary change. The adult form presents with diarrhoea, abdominal pain and sometimes rectal bleeding, and is often idiopathic. Physiological colonic eosinophil counts vary by site, being higher in the caecum and right colon, so biopsies must be interpreted against regional norms. It is a diagnosis of exclusion: rule out parasites, drugs, inflammatory bowel disease, connective tissue disease, hypereosinophilic syndrome and malignancy. Peripheral eosinophilia is less consistent than in upper gastrointestinal eosinophilic disorders. Treatment is dietary elimination in infants and corticosteroids or other agents in persistent adult disease. Multiple biopsies across colonic segments are required to make the diagnosis. Significant rectal bleeding or anaemia Weight loss or failure to thrive in infants Features suggesting inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy or systemic vasculitis Severe or refractory diarrhoea with dehydration Overdiagnosis by ignoring the normal regional variation in colonic eosinophils Missing an underlying parasitic infection or drug cause Labelling inflammatory bowel disease-related eosinophilia as primary eosinophilic colitis Starting immunosuppression before excluding Strongyloides Eosinophilic colitis is an eosinophilic infiltration of the colonic mucosa, and sometimes deeper layers, driven by Th2 allergic mechanisms that are most clearly food-antigen (cow's milk protein) related in infants. Eosinophil recruitment and degranulation cause mucosal inflammation, altered motility and secretory diarrhoea. Because baseline colonic eosinophil density is normally high and regionally variable, distinguishing pathological infiltration from physiological presence is central and challenging. Infantile allergic proctocolitis has an excellent prognosis and usually resolves with dietary modification, whereas adult eosinophilic colitis is more variable and often relapsing but is generally not life-threatening.

Eosinophilic enteritis — Eosinophilic enteropathy, Eosinophilic gastroenteritis (small-bowel) Parasitic infestation (Strongyloides, Anisakis, hookworm) Coeliac disease Crohn's disease Hypereosinophilic syndrome with bowel involvement Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Small-bowel lymphoma or other malignancy Drug-induced enteropathy Device-assisted enteroscopy or capsule endoscopy with small-bowel biopsies Full blood count with eosinophil count Stool microscopy and Strongyloides serology Coeliac serology (tissue transglutaminase IgA) with total IgA Serum albumin and markers of protein-losing enteropathy CT or MR enterography for wall thickening, obstruction or ascites ANCA and connective tissue screen where vasculitis is suspected Eosinophilic infiltration of the small bowel, part of the eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorders and frequently overlapping with gastric involvement as eosinophilic gastroenteritis. The Klein depth classification applies: mucosal disease causes malabsorption, diarrhoea, protein-losing enteropathy and iron deficiency; muscular disease causes obstruction; serosal disease causes eosinophilic ascites. Malabsorption and weight loss are prominent with mucosal involvement. Peripheral eosinophilia is common and atopy is frequent. Diagnosis rests on small-bowel biopsies (which may need enteroscopy or capsule endoscopy) showing excess eosinophils after excluding secondary causes. Parasitic infection such as Strongyloides, Anisakis or hookworm is a key mimic and must be excluded. Corticosteroids are the mainstay, with dietary elimination in selected cases. Patchy, deep or transmural disease may be missed on standard mucosal biopsy. Small-bowel obstruction from muscular disease Severe malabsorption with weight loss and hypoalbuminaemia Gastrointestinal haemorrhage Features suggesting lymphoma or systemic vasculitis Missing patchy or deep (muscular or serosal) disease with superficial biopsies alone Failing to exclude Strongyloides before immunosuppression Confusing the picture with coeliac disease or Crohn's disease Attributing the eosinophilia to the bowel while overlooking systemic hypereosinophilic syndrome Eosinophilic enteritis reflects antigen-driven Th2 inflammation of the small intestine, with interleukin-5 and interleukin-13-mediated recruitment of eosinophils whose degranulation injures the mucosa and deeper layers. Mucosal infiltration disrupts the absorptive surface and enteric barrier, causing malabsorption and protein loss; muscular involvement thickens and stiffens the bowel wall producing subacute obstruction; and serosal involvement generates eosinophil-rich ascites. Food allergens and an atopic diathesis are frequently implicated. Eosinophilic enteritis often responds well to corticosteroids with symptomatic and histological improvement, but relapse is common and some patients require long-term immunomodulation or dietary therapy.

response to corticosteroids raising concern for an alternative fibrosing disorder Aplastic anaemia or myeloproliferative features in association with the fasciitis Mistaking it for systemic sclerosis and missing the sparing of digits and absence of Raynaud phenomenon Taking too superficial a biopsy that fails to sample the fascia and yields a non-diagnostic result Assuming a normal eosinophil count excludes the diagnosis when eosinophilia is transient Delaying treatment and allowing fixed contractures to develop Failing to screen for an underlying haematological disorder in refractory cases Eosinophilic fasciitis is an uncommon fibrosing disorder characterised by inflammation and thickening of the deep fascia. The trigger is unknown but strenuous physical exertion frequently precedes onset. An immune-mediated process recruits eosinophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells into the fascia, with release of profibrotic mediators driving collagen deposition and fascial fibrosis. The resulting induration tethers overlying skin and can cause joint contractures. Peripheral eosinophilia and hypergammaglobulinaemia reflect the underlying inflammatory activation, and an association with clonal haematological disease is recognised. Many patients achieve substantial improvement or remission with prompt corticosteroid therapy, though residual induration or contractures may persist, and relapse can occur on tapering. An associated haematological disorder worsens the outlook.

Eosinophilic gastritis — EG, Eosinophilic gastroenteropathy Secondary gastric eosinophilia from parasitic infection (Strongyloides, Anisakis) Drug-induced eosinophilia Hypereosinophilic syndrome with gastric involvement Helicobacter pylori gastritis Gastric carcinoma or lymphoma Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Crohn's disease with gastric involvement Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with multiple gastric biopsies and eosinophil quantification Full blood count with eosinophil count Stool microscopy and Strongyloides serology Serum IgE and allergy testing Cross-sectional imaging for wall thickening or ascites Ascitic fluid analysis for eosinophils in serosal disease Screen for hypereosinophilic syndrome and ANCA-associated vasculitis where indicated One of the eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorders, defined by gastric-predominant eosinophilic infiltration without a secondary cause. The Klein classification describes disease by depth: mucosal (commonest, causing pain, nausea, bleeding and protein loss), muscular (obstruction and gastric outlet narrowing) and serosal (eosinophilic ascites). Peripheral eosinophilia is common but not universal, and most patients have an atopic background. Diagnosis requires gastric biopsies showing excess eosinophils together with exclusion of parasites, drugs, malignancy, hypereosinophilic syndrome and connective tissue disease. Normal-appearing mucosa does not exclude the diagnosis, so take multiple biopsies. Serosal disease may present with eosinophil-rich ascites. Corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment, with dietary elimination in selected and paediatric cases. Exclude Strongyloides infection before starting immunosuppression to avoid hyperinfection. Gastric outlet obstruction or intractable vomiting Significant gastrointestinal haemorrhage Marked hypoalbuminaemia from protein-losing enteropathy Features suggesting malignancy or systemic vasculitis Starting corticosteroids before excluding Strongyloides, risking hyperinfection Relying on peripheral eosinophilia, which may be absent Taking too few biopsies from normal-looking mucosa Overlooking serosal disease presenting as unexplained eosinophilic ascites Eosinophilic gastritis is a Th2-mediated eosinophilic infiltration of the gastric wall driven by interleukin-5, interleukin-13 and eotaxin, frequently in atopic individuals reacting to food antigens. Eosinophil degranulation releases major basic protein and other cytotoxic granule proteins that damage tissue, and the depth of infiltration determines the phenotype: mucosal disease causes malabsorption and protein loss, muscular disease causes obstruction, and serosal disease produces eosinophilic ascites. Prognosis is generally good given corticosteroid responsiveness, but many patients relapse and require maintenance therapy, and a subset follows a chronic remitting-relapsing course.

Eosinophilic gastroenteritis — eosinophilic gastroenteropathy, EGE, eosinophilic gastritis and enteritis Parasitic infection (e.g. strongyloidiasis, anisakiasis) causing tissue eosinophilia Hypereosinophilic syndrome with gastrointestinal involvement Inflammatory bowel disease Coeliac disease and other malabsorptive enteropathies Drug-induced eosinophilic mucosal injury Systemic vasculitis such as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Full blood count and blood film to detect and quantify peripheral eosinophilia Upper and lower endoscopy with multiple biopsies from grossly normal and abnormal mucosa Stool microscopy and serology to exclude parasitic infection Coeliac serology and total IgE with allergy assessment Cross-sectional imaging to assess bowel-wall thickening and ascites Diagnostic paracentesis of ascitic fluid for eosinophil count in suspected serosal disease Symptoms depend on which bowel layer is infiltrated: mucosal disease causes abdominal pain, diarrhoea, vomiting and malabsorption; muscular disease causes obstructive symptoms; and serosal disease produces eosinophilic ascites Peripheral blood eosinophilia is common but not universal, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis Many patients have a personal or family history of atopy, asthma, eczema or food allergy Diagnosis rests on demonstrating dense eosinophilic infiltration on biopsy after excluding secondary causes such as parasitic infection, drug reaction and connective-tissue disease Endoscopic appearances range from normal mucosa to erythema, nodularity or ulceration, so multiple biopsies from several sites are needed even when the mucosa looks normal Serosal disease characteristically presents with eosinophil-rich ascites that improves rapidly with corticosteroids Management centres on dietary elimination and corticosteroids for eosinophilic gastroenteritis, with corticosteroid-sparing agents reserved for relapsing disease Features of bowel obstruction suggesting transmural muscular disease Rapidly accumulating eosinophilic ascites Weight loss, gastrointestinal bleeding or a mass raising concern for malignancy Very high peripheral eosinophil counts suggesting hypereosinophilic syndrome with end-organ damage Excluding the diagnosis because peripheral eosinophilia is absent Taking too few biopsies or sampling only visibly abnormal mucosa and missing patchy infiltration Attributing tissue eosinophilia to eosinophilic gastroenteritis without excluding parasites, drugs and vasculitis Overlooking muscular disease as a cause of unexplained obstruction Eosinophilic gastroenteritis is characterised by abnormal eosinophil accumulation within the wall of the stomach and small bowel in the absence of an identifiable secondary cause such as parasitic infection or drug reaction. Allergen exposure and a T-helper-2 driven immune response promote release of cytokines such as interleukin-5 and eotaxin, which recruit and activate eosinophils; their degranulation releases toxic granule proteins that damage tissue and cause dysmotility, oedema and increased permeability. The clinical picture is determined by the depth of infiltration, with mucosal, muscular and serosal patterns producing distinct presentations. The condition typically follows a relapsing-remitting course; most patients respond well to dietary and corticosteroid therapy, though some require long-term maintenance treatment, and serosal disease usually responds most briskly.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis — EGPA, Churg-Strauss syndrome, Churg-Strauss, allergic granulomatosis and angiitis Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis Hypereosinophilic syndrome (including clonal/myeloproliferative variants) Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis Parasitic infection with eosinophilia Drug reaction with eosinophilia (DRESS) Polyarteritis nodosa and other systemic vasculitides Full blood count documenting peripheral eosinophilia and inflammatory markers ANCA testing with anti-MPO and anti-PR3 specificities Chest imaging for pulmonary infiltrates and sinus assessment Cardiac evaluation with ECG, troponin, echocardiography, and cardiac MRI as indicated Nerve conduction studies for suspected mononeuritis multiplex Urinalysis and renal function for glomerulonephritis, with tissue biopsy of an affected organ where feasible EGPA is an eosinophil-rich, often ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis that almost always arises on a background of adult-onset, frequently difficult-to-control asthma The illness classically evolves through phases: an allergic phase with asthma and rhinosinusitis, an eosinophilic phase with blood and tissue eosinophilia, and a vasculitic phase with systemic involvement Peripheral blood eosinophilia is a hallmark, and its degree helps distinguish EGPA from other ANCA-associated vasculitides Neurologic involvement, especially mononeuritis multiplex causing asymmetric sensorimotor deficits, is a characteristic and clinically important feature Cardiac involvement-myocarditis, heart failure, and coronary or pericardial disease-is a leading cause of death and mandates cardiac assessment even when asymptomatic ANCA (usually anti-MPO/p-ANCA) is positive in a minority; ANCA-positive disease tends toward vasculitic manifestations such as neuropathy and glomerulonephritis, while ANCA-negative disease more often shows cardiac and lung involvement Diagnosis integrates the clinical picture with eosinophilia and, where feasible, biopsy showing eosinophilic tissue infiltration, extravascular granulomas, and necrotising vasculitis Corticosteroids are the foundation of treatment, with additional immunosuppression for organ-threatening disease and anti-IL-5 (eosinophil-directed) biologic therapy used to control eosinophilic disease and spare steroids A recognised though debated association exists between leukotriene-receptor antagonists and unmasking of EGPA, often linked to reduction of background corticosteroids Cardiac involvement with myocarditis, heart failure, or arrhythmia, the principal cause of mortality Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with rising creatinine Mononeuritis multiplex or other acute neurologic deficit indicating active vasculitis Gastrointestinal ischaemia, alveolar haemorrhage, or other organ-threatening manifestations requiring urgent immunosuppression Attributing worsening asthma and eosinophilia to poorly controlled asthma alone and missing evolving vasculitis Failing to assess the heart in apparently stable patients, given the high mortality of cardiac disease Overlooking mononeuritis multiplex as a marker of active organ-threatening vasculitis Confusing EGPA with hypereosinophilic syndrome or other eosinophilic lung disease without appropriate ANCA testing and biopsy EGPA is a systemic disorder combining marked eosinophilia with small- and medium-vessel necrotising vasculitis and extravascular eosinophilic granulomas. Th2-driven immune responses with elevated interleukin-5 promote eosinophil production, survival, and tissue infiltration; eosinophil granule proteins cause direct tissue and endothelial damage, particularly in the heart, lungs, nerves, skin, and gut. In a subset, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (typically anti-myeloperoxidase) contribute to a neutrophil-mediated necrotising vasculitis, giving rise to glomerulonephritis, purpura, and peripheral neuropathy. The two mechanisms-eosinophilic tissue infiltration and ANCA-associated vasculitis-broadly correspond to the different clinical phenotypes. With corticosteroids and, when needed, additional immunosuppression and eosinophil-directed biologics, remission is achievable in most patients, though relapse is common and asthma often persists. Prognosis is worst when there is cardiac, severe gastrointestinal, or renal involvement, which are the main determinants of mortality.

wrist drop Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage causing hypoxaemia and haemoptysis Gut ischaemia from mesenteric vasculitis presenting as severe abdominal pain Assuming a negative ANCA excludes EGPA when eosinophilia and asthma are present Overlooking silent cardiac involvement, which carries the worst prognosis Attributing worsening respiratory symptoms solely to asthma and missing evolving vasculitis Failing to consider that leukotriene-receptor antagonists or steroid tapering can unmask disease rather than cause it EGPA is a small-to-medium vessel necrotising vasculitis characterised by eosinophil-rich granulomatous inflammation of the respiratory tract alongside tissue and blood eosinophilia. It is considered one of the ANCA-associated vasculitides, though ANCA is detectable in only a subset. Dysregulated T-helper-2 immunity drives eosinophil recruitment and activation through interleukin-5 and related cytokines; eosinophil degranulation releases cytotoxic granule proteins that injure tissue, particularly heart, nerve, and lung. In ANCA-positive disease, autoantibody-mediated neutrophil activation contributes a more classic pauci-immune vasculitic and glomerular phenotype, whereas ANCA-negative disease is dominated by eosinophilic tissue infiltration. With glucocorticoids and modern immunosuppression most patients achieve remission, but relapses are common and steroid dependence for residual asthma is frequent. Cardiac involvement remains the principal determinant of mortality.

Eosinophilic oesophagitis — EoE, Allergic oesophagitis Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease Infective oesophagitis (candida, herpes simplex, cytomegalovirus) Eosinophilic gastritis or enteritis with oesophageal involvement Achalasia or other primary oesophageal motility disorder Pill-induced or caustic oesophagitis Hypereosinophilic syndrome with oesophageal involvement Crohn's disease of the oesophagus Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with graded (EREFS) assessment Multiple oesophageal biopsies from proximal and distal levels with eosinophil counts Treatment trial and histological reassessment on a proton pump inhibitor Full blood count for peripheral eosinophilia Allergy assessment (skin prick or specific IgE) when dietary therapy is considered Barium or timed oesophagram to define strictures and calibre Oesophageal manometry if a motility disorder or achalasia is suspected A chronic, antigen-driven Th2 immune disease of the oesophagus, most common in young atopic men. Adults present with dysphagia and food bolus impaction; children present with feeding difficulty, vomiting and failure to thrive. Diagnosis requires symptoms of oesophageal dysfunction plus at least 15 eosinophils per high-power field on biopsy, with other causes excluded. Take multiple biopsies from proximal and distal oesophagus because involvement is patchy. Endoscopic features include fixed rings (trachealisation), linear furrows, white exudates, oedema, strictures and crepe-paper mucosa graded by the EREFS score. Proton pump inhibitor-responsive oesophageal eosinophilia is now regarded as part of the disease spectrum, so proton pump inhibitors are a first-line treatment rather than only a diagnostic filter. Therapeutic options include proton pump inhibitors, swallowed topical corticosteroids, dietary elimination and endoscopic dilation of strictures. Untreated inflammation drives fibrostenotic remodelling with progressive strictures and recurrent impaction. Acute food bolus impaction requiring emergency endoscopy Complete dysphagia or inability to manage secretions Oesophageal perforation after impaction or dilation Significant weight loss or failure to thrive in children Diagnosing on a single biopsy or from one level and missing patchy disease Failing to treat and reassess, allowing silent progression to strictures Attributing symptoms solely to reflux and missing the diagnosis Aggressive dilation without anti-inflammatory therapy, risking mucosal tears Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic Th2-mediated immune response to food and possibly aeroallergens in genetically predisposed individuals. Antigen exposure triggers release of interleukin-5 and interleukin-13, eosinophil recruitment via eotaxin-3, and mast cell activation, producing an eosinophil-predominant inflammation confined to the oesophagus. Sustained inflammation causes epithelial barrier dysfunction, subepithelial fibrosis and smooth muscle dysfunction, generating the rings, strictures and dysmotility that underlie dysphagia and bolus impaction. Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic relapsing condition that is not life-limiting but tends to recur off treatment; maintenance therapy and surveillance prevent progression to fibrostenotic strictures and recurrent impaction.

Eosinophilic proctocolitis of infancy — Food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis (FPIAP), Allergic proctocolitis, Dietary protein proctocolitis Anal fissure Swallowed maternal blood in the breastfed neonate (Apt-Downey test) Infective colitis (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, shiga-toxin Escherichia coli) Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES) Necrotising enterocolitis in the preterm or ill neonate Very-early-onset inflammatory bowel disease Vitamin K deficiency bleeding or coagulopathy Trial of dietary protein elimination (both diagnostic and therapeutic) Stool microscopy and culture to exclude infective colitis Full blood count with differential for peripheral eosinophilia and anaemia Apt-Downey test to distinguish swallowed maternal blood in the neonate Faecal calprotectin (raised but non-specific in early infancy) Flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy with mucosal biopsy in atypical or refractory disease Coagulation studies if bleeding is unexpectedly brisk Typically presents within the first weeks to months of life in a well-appearing, thriving infant with mucousy, blood-streaked stools and no systemic upset. Most commonly triggered by cow's milk protein, with soy a frequent co-trigger; it occurs in both breastfed and formula-fed infants. In breastfed infants the offending proteins reach the gut via the maternal diet, so maternal elimination of cow's milk (and sometimes soy) is first-line rather than stopping breastfeeding. It is a non-IgE-mediated hypersensitivity, so skin-prick tests and specific IgE are usually negative and are not required for diagnosis. The infant remains systemically well without prominent vomiting, dehydration or shock, which distinguishes it from food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES). Rectal bleeding usually settles within days to a couple of weeks after the trigger protein is removed, supporting the diagnosis. Diagnosis is clinical; endoscopy with biopsy is reserved for atypical or refractory cases and shows eosinophilic mucosal infiltration and lymphonodular hyperplasia. Formula-fed infants generally respond to an extensively hydrolysed formula, reserving amino-acid formula for those who fail hydrolysate. Faltering growth, poor weight gain or weight loss Vomiting, lethargy, pallor, dehydration or shock suggesting FPIES or an alternative diagnosis Brisk or large-volume rectal bleeding, or clinically significant anaemia Abdominal distension, bilious vomiting or systemic toxicity suggesting surgical or obstructive pathology Onset outside the typical infant age range or persistence despite thorough protein elimination Attributing all infant rectal bleeding to allergy and missing an anal fissure or an infective or surgical cause. Ordering IgE-based allergy tests, which are typically negative in this non-IgE-mediated condition and can mislead. Stopping breastfeeding prematurely rather than trialling maternal dietary elimination. Incomplete maternal elimination with hidden milk or soy, producing apparent treatment failure. Failing to attempt planned reintroduction, leading to unnecessary prolonged dietary restriction. The condition is a non-IgE-mediated, predominantly cell-mediated hypersensitivity to ingested food proteins, most often cow's milk protein and less commonly soy, egg or other proteins. Antigen exposure, either directly through formula or indirectly through maternal dietary protein secreted into breast milk, drives an eosinophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate within the lamina propria of the distal colon and rectum. The resulting mucosal eosinophilia and lymphonodular hyperplasia render the mucosa friable, producing the characteristic low-grade bleeding and mucus. Inflammation remains localised to the gut without systemic features, and immunological tolerance to the offending protein typically develops during the first years of life. The condition is benign and self-limiting, with most infants developing tolerance to the offending protein and successful dietary reintroduction between one and three years of age. Growth and long-term gut health are unaffected.

Epidemic (louse-borne) typhus — louse-borne typhus, Rickettsia prowazekii infection, classic typhus, jail fever, Brill-Zinsser disease (recrudescent form) Murine (endemic) typhus Spotted fever group rickettsioses Meningococcaemia Typhoid fever Relapsing fever Leptospirosis Viral haemorrhagic fever in endemic areas Indirect immunofluorescence antibody serology on paired sera PCR of blood or tissue where available Full blood count and film Renal function and liver enzymes Serum sodium to detect hyponatraemia Examination of clothing and body for lice to support the epidemiological diagnosis Caused by Rickettsia prowazekii and transmitted by the human body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis); infection occurs when louse faeces are scratched into the bite site or contact mucosae, not directly from the bite Classically epidemic in conditions of overcrowding, cold, war, famine and poor hygiene where body lice thrive, hence historical names such as jail and camp fever After an incubation of about 1-2 weeks there is abrupt high fever, severe headache, myalgia and prostration, often with marked neurological features A rash typically begins on the trunk in the axillae and spreads centrifugally to the limbs, usually sparing the palms, soles and face, and may become petechial Doxycycline is highly effective, often with a single-dose response, and should be given empirically on clinical and epidemiological suspicion Brill-Zinsser disease is a milder recrudescence occurring years later from latent organisms and can seed new louse-borne outbreaks Humans are the main reservoir, and flying squirrels are recognised as a sylvatic reservoir in North America Altered consciousness, delirium, seizures or coma indicating encephalitic involvement Petechial or purpuric rash with hypotension and shock Gangrene of digits or extremities from severe vasculitis Occurrence in a refugee, prison or disaster setting signalling outbreak potential Acute kidney injury or myocardial involvement Not considering the diagnosis outside historical contexts despite ongoing risk in crowded, impoverished and displaced populations Waiting for serology before treating in a clinically suspicious case Confusing the centrifugal, palm-and-sole-sparing rash with a spotted fever Overlooking Brill-Zinsser disease as a source of new outbreaks Neglecting delousing and public-health measures alongside treatment Rickettsia prowazekii is an obligate intracellular bacterium that, once inoculated through louse-faeces contamination of broken skin, invades vascular endothelial cells and multiplies until the cell ruptures. Progressive endothelial infection produces a widespread small-vessel vasculitis with increased permeability, perivascular inflammation and microthrombus formation. This vasculitis affects the skin, brain, myocardium, kidneys and other organs, accounting for the rash, encephalitic features, hypovolaemia and multi-organ dysfunction of severe disease. Latent survival of organisms explains later recrudescence as Brill-Zinsser disease. Untreated epidemic typhus carries a high mortality that rises with age, but prompt doxycycline is dramatically effective; recrudescent Brill-Zinsser disease is generally milder.

Epidermal naevus syndrome — Schimmelpenning syndrome, Solomon syndrome, Epidermal nevus syndrome Other neurocutaneous syndromes (tuberous sclerosis, neurofibromatosis, incontinentia pigmenti) Proteus syndrome and PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum Encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis Isolated naevus sebaceus without systemic involvement McCune-Albright syndrome Focal dermal hypoplasia (Goltz syndrome) Skin examination and biopsy of naevi with histopathology MRI brain for hemimegalencephaly and other malformations EEG where seizures occur Ophthalmological assessment Skeletal survey or targeted imaging for deformity Molecular testing of affected lesional tissue for mosaic mutations Renal and other organ imaging guided by phenotype An umbrella term for mosaic neurocutaneous disorders in which epidermal naevi are associated with extracutaneous abnormalities of the central nervous system, eyes and skeleton. Arises from post-zygotic somatic mutations producing genetic mosaicism, so the naevi follow the lines of Blaschko. Several distinct entities are recognised, including Schimmelpenning syndrome with naevus sebaceus, naevus comedonicus syndrome, CHILD syndrome, Becker naevus syndrome and phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica. Common driver mutations involve the RAS-MAPK pathway (HRAS, KRAS, NRAS) and FGFR3, with PIK3CA in some overgrowth phenotypes. Neurological features include seizures, developmental delay, intellectual disability and hemimegalencephaly. Ocular findings include colobomas, lipodermoids and choristomas, while skeletal features include scoliosis and limb hypoplasia. Naevus sebaceus carries a small risk of secondary benign and, less often, malignant tumours in adulthood. Management is multidisciplinary and directed at the specific systems involved. New-onset or refractory seizures Rapid growth, ulceration or change within a naevus suggesting tumour transformation Progressive neurological deficit Skeletal deformity compromising function Regarding epidermal naevi as purely cosmetic and missing systemic associations. Testing blood rather than lesional tissue for the mosaic mutation. Overlooking the small malignant potential of naevus sebaceus. Failing to arrange multidisciplinary surveillance. Epidermal naevus syndromes result from post-zygotic somatic activating mutations, most often in RAS-MAPK pathway genes or FGFR3, present in a mosaic distribution. Cells carrying the mutation populate ectodermally derived tissues along embryonic migration lines, producing epidermal naevi and, where the mutation affects neural, ocular or skeletal precursors, corresponding extracutaneous malformations. The pattern and severity depend on the timing and lineage of the mutational event. Highly variable and dependent on the extent of extracutaneous involvement; isolated cutaneous disease has an excellent outlook, whereas extensive central nervous system involvement carries a risk of intractable epilepsy and intellectual disability.

symptomatic naevi New-onset or refractory seizures Progressive neurological deficit or developmental regression Rapid growth, ulceration or nodularity within a naevus Unexplained bone pain or fractures suggesting hypophosphataemic rickets Treating an extensive epidermal naevus as cosmetic without screening for systemic involvement Missing hypophosphataemic rickets as a correctable cause of skeletal symptoms Failing to recognise that the syndrome comprises several genetically distinct subtypes Delaying neuroimaging in a child with an extensive naevus and seizures Epidermal naevus syndrome results from post-zygotic mosaic variants affecting epidermal progenitor cells during embryogenesis. Depending on the affected gene and cell lineage, the variant produces a keratinocytic, sebaceous or other organoid naevus distributed along the lines of Blaschko. Several causative variants involve growth-signalling pathways, including FGFR3 and PIK3CA in keratinocytic naevi and RAS-pathway genes in sebaceous forms. When the mosaic clone also contributes to neuroectodermal, ocular or mesenchymal tissues, the corresponding brain, eye and skeletal malformations arise, giving the syndrome its characteristic multisystem pattern. Outcome is governed by the extent of extracutaneous disease; limited cutaneous involvement carries an excellent prognosis, while extensive neurological disease with intractable seizures and cognitive impairment is associated with greater morbidity.

epidermoid cyst — epidermal inclusion cyst, infundibular cyst, sebaceous cyst (misnomer) pilar (trichilemmal) cyst lipoma dermoid cyst abscess steatocystoma multiplex cutaneous metastasis or adnexal tumour calcinosis cutis clinical examination for a central punctum ultrasonography demonstrating a well-defined cystic dermal or subcutaneous lesion histopathology of the excised cyst wall bacterial swab and culture if genuine secondary infection is suspected evaluation for Gardner syndrome when multiple or atypical cysts are present Presents as a firm, mobile, dome-shaped dermal or subcutaneous nodule, commonly on the face, neck, trunk and scrotum. A central punctum representing the connection to the follicular infundibulum is the key clinical sign. Expressed contents consist of macerated keratin with a characteristic malodour, not true sebum, making 'sebaceous cyst' a misnomer. The wall is a true epidermis-like lining with a granular layer, and the cyst fills with laminated keratin produced by that lining. Rupture releases keratin into the dermis, provoking a brisk foreign-body inflammatory response that mimics bacterial infection. Multiple epidermoid cysts, especially at atypical sites or from childhood, should prompt consideration of Gardner syndrome. Definitive treatment is complete surgical excision of the cyst wall; incomplete removal leads to recurrence. An inflamed cyst is usually sterile inflammation from rupture rather than true infection, so incision and drainage with delayed excision is often preferred. multiple cysts with osteomas or intestinal polyps suggesting Gardner syndrome rapid enlargement, fixation or induration raising concern for malignant transformation spreading cellulitis, systemic upset or fluctuance indicating genuine secondary infection atypical firm nodule that could represent a cutaneous metastasis or adnexal carcinoma Attempting definitive excision during acute inflammation, when tissue planes are obscured and recurrence is likely. Labelling every inflamed cyst as infected and prescribing antibiotics when the process is sterile keratin-induced inflammation. Leaving cyst wall remnants in situ, resulting in recurrence. Overlooking Gardner syndrome in a patient with multiple cysts and a relevant family history. Epidermoid cysts arise from the follicular infundibulum, most often through proliferation of surface or follicular epidermal cells that become implanted or occluded within the dermis. The cyst is lined by stratified squamous epithelium possessing a granular layer, which desquamates keratin into the cavity, producing the laminated keratinous contents. Traumatic implantation of epidermis, as on the palms and soles, and human papillomavirus infection at some sites, are alternative mechanisms. Rupture of the wall discharges keratin into the surrounding dermis, triggering a granulomatous foreign-body reaction. Numerous cysts may reflect an underlying genetic disorder such as Gardner syndrome or naevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome. Epidermoid cysts are benign and often stable for years; complete excision is curative, whereas incomplete removal of the wall predisposes to recurrence. Malignant transformation is exceedingly rare.

carcinoma Epidermolysis bullosa is a group of inherited disorders in which minor friction or trauma causes blistering and skin fragility, usually presenting at or soon after birth It is classified by the level of skin cleavage: simplex (within the epidermis), junctional (at the basement membrane zone), dystrophic (below the basement membrane), and Kindler EB (mixed levels) The plane of splitting predicts scarring: intra-epidermal simplex forms tend to heal without scarring, whereas dystrophic forms scar and can cause fusion of digits (mitten deformity) Extracutaneous involvement is common in severe subtypes, including oral, oesophageal, ocular, and genitourinary mucosae, leading to feeding difficulty, strictures, and malnutrition Care is multidisciplinary and centres on meticulous wound care, non-adherent dressings, infection control, pain management, nutrition, and prevention of trauma Handle affected neonates and children gently, avoiding shearing forces, adhesive tapes, and friction that can strip the skin Junctional EB includes a severe generalised form with high infant mortality, while severe recessive dystrophic EB carries a substantial lifetime risk of aggressive squamous cell carcinoma Accurate subtyping through skin biopsy with mapping and genetic testing guides prognosis, genetic counselling, and emerging targeted therapies Extensive blistering and skin loss in a neonate with fluid, electrolyte, and thermoregulatory compromise and high infection risk Sepsis arising from chronically open wounds New, non-healing, or indurated ulcer in severe dystrophic EB suggesting aggressive squamous cell carcinoma Oesophageal stricturing causing dysphagia, malnutrition, and failure to thrive Airway or ocular involvement compromising breathing or vision Assuming all EB is mild and underestimating the severity of junctional or dystrophic subtypes Using adhesive dressings or tapes that strip fragile skin Neglecting nutrition, pain, and psychological support in chronic disease Failing to arrange skin cancer surveillance in severe dystrophic EB Delaying accurate subtyping and genetic counselling that guide management and family planning Epidermolysis bullosa results from mutations in genes encoding structural proteins that anchor the layers of skin together. Defects in keratins (such as KRT5 and KRT14) weaken the basal keratinocyte cytoskeleton in simplex forms; defects in laminin-332 and other hemidesmosomal components disrupt adhesion at the basement membrane in junctional forms; and defects in type VII collagen, the main component of anchoring fibrils, undermine attachment of the epidermis to the dermis in dystrophic forms. The specific protein deficiency determines the level at which the skin separates under mechanical stress, the tendency to scar, and the pattern of extracutaneous complications. Repeated blistering, wound healing, and chronic inflammation drive fibrosis and, in severe dystrophic disease, malignant transformation. Outcome varies enormously by subtype: localised simplex forms are compatible with a near-normal lifespan, whereas severe junctional disease can be fatal in infancy and severe recessive dystrophic disease causes progressive disability, contractures, malnutrition, and a high risk of fatal squamous cell carcinoma in adulthood.

salt-split skin study to identify dermal-side binding Underestimating scarring and mucosal complications, including ocular disease Confusing acral blistering with porphyria cutanea tarda Expecting a prompt response to therapy when the disease is characteristically resistant Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita is mediated by IgG (and sometimes IgA) autoantibodies against type-VII collagen, the structural protein of the anchoring fibrils that tether the epidermal basement membrane to the papillary dermis. Antibody binding beneath the lamina densa impairs dermo-epidermal adhesion; in the mechanobullous form this produces fragile skin that blisters with minor trauma, whereas complement activation and inflammatory cell recruitment drive the inflammatory variants. Because the cleavage plane lies below the lamina densa and anchoring fibrils are damaged, healing is often accompanied by scarring and milia, mirroring hereditary dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa. Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita tends to run a chronic, relapsing course and is often refractory to treatment; scarring, milia, and functional impairment from mucosal disease can accumulate over time.
