involvement occurs in severe variants Rapidly spreading skin loss suggesting an alternative severe blistering diagnosis Assuming all epidermolysis bullosa scars, when the simplex form typically heals without scarring Failing to distinguish it from junctional and dystrophic forms, which have a worse prognosis and deeper cleavage plane Mistaking neonatal blistering for infection such as staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome Neglecting measures to reduce friction and overheating that precipitate blistering Overlooking secondary bacterial infection of eroded skin Epidermolysis bullosa simplex is a disorder of the mechanical integrity of the basal layer of the epidermis. Keratins 5 and 14 assemble into the intermediate filament network that gives basal keratinocytes their structural resilience; pathogenic mutations, usually dominant-negative, produce a defective keratin cytoskeleton that cannot withstand mechanical stress. As a result, minor friction or trauma causes the basal cells to rupture and split, so blister formation occurs within the epidermis above the dermo-epidermal junction. Because the basement membrane and dermis remain intact, healing generally proceeds without the scarring characteristic of deeper cleavage-plane disease. Most forms, particularly the localised variant, are compatible with a normal life expectancy and improve after childhood, though severe generalised subtypes cause more troublesome blistering; because the cleavage plane is superficial, healing is usually without scarring.

Epidermolytic ichthyosis — bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, BCIE, KRT1, KRT10 Other congenital ichthyoses (lamellar ichthyosis, congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma) Epidermolysis bullosa (for neonatal blistering) Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome Ichthyosis with confetti Superficial epidermolytic ichthyosis (ichthyosis bullosa of Siemens, KRT2) Epidermolytic epidermal naevus Skin biopsy showing epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (vacuolar/reticular degeneration with clumped tonofilaments) Molecular genetic testing of KRT1 and KRT10 (and KRT2 for the superficial variant) Microbiological swabs of eroded or malodorous skin Assessment of palmoplantar involvement to help localise the mutation (KRT1 vs KRT10) Neonatal monitoring of fluid balance, temperature and infection Family history and pedigree analysis, with counselling regarding mosaic naevi Presents at birth with widespread erythroderma, superficial blistering and skin fragility, evolving into a chronic hyperkeratotic phenotype Older children and adults show thick, ridged, often verrucous ('corrugated') hyperkeratosis, most marked in the flexures A characteristic malodour and a tendency to recurrent bacterial skin infection accompany the hyperkeratosis Caused by dominant mutations in the suprabasal keratins KRT1 or KRT10; KRT1 mutations tend to involve the palms and soles The histological hallmark is epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (vacuolar degeneration of the upper epidermis with clumped keratin) An epidermal naevus with the same histology can occur; if it involves the gonads, offspring may inherit generalised disease (mosaicism) Management is supportive with emollients/keratolytics, oral retinoids in severe cases, and antiseptic/antimicrobial measures for infection and odour Neonatal barrier failure with dehydration, temperature instability or sepsis Rapidly spreading skin infection Extensive erosions with fluid and electrolyte loss Severe hyperkeratosis causing fissuring, pain or functional impairment Mistaking neonatal blistering for epidermolysis bullosa or staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome Overusing keratolytics or high-dose retinoids that aggravate erosions and fragility Neglecting antimicrobial care, so recurrent infection and malodour persist Failing to counsel that a localised epidermolytic naevus may transmit generalised disease through gonadal mosaicism Epidermolytic ichthyosis is usually an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in KRT1 or KRT10, which encode the suprabasal keratins K1 and K10 that pair to form the intermediate-filament cytoskeleton of differentiating keratinocytes in the spinous and granular layers. The mutations, typically in conserved helix-boundary regions, exert a dominant-negative effect that destabilises the keratin network, so suprabasal keratinocytes cannot withstand mechanical stress and undergo cytolysis, producing blistering and the histological picture of epidermolytic hyperkeratosis. Compensatory hyperproliferation and abnormal cornification yield the thick hyperkeratosis of later life, while barrier disruption predisposes to bacterial colonisation, infection and odour. Postzygotic mutation can produce a mosaic epidermal naevus with the same histology and a risk of transmitting generalised disease if gonadal tissue is involved. The neonatal blistering phase carries risks of infection and fluid loss but usually gives way to a chronic, stable hyperkeratotic phenotype compatible with a normal lifespan. The condition is lifelong and not curable; hyperkeratosis, odour and recurrent infection require ongoing management, and oral retinoids can help but may increase skin fragility.

Epididymal cyst — epididymal cystic swelling, simple epididymal cyst, epididymal cyste Spermatocele Hydrocele Varicocele Epididymitis Testicular or epididymal tumour Inguinoscrotal hernia Cyst of the appendix testis or appendix epididymis Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler Transillumination test at the bedside Clinical examination confirming the lump is separate from the testis Testicular tumour markers if any solid component is seen Interval review where there is diagnostic uncertainty A benign, fluid-filled cyst of the epididymis, usually arising from the head and containing clear serous fluid, in contrast to the sperm-laden fluid of a spermatocele Presents as a painless, smooth, mobile swelling felt separate from and usually above and behind the testis Transilluminates brightly, reflecting its clear fluid content Often multiple and bilateral, and very common as an incidental finding Scrotal ultrasound confirms a thin-walled anechoic cyst separate from the testis and is the key investigation The distinction from a spermatocele is largely academic, resting on content rather than behaviour, as both are benign and managed the same way Most need only reassurance; excision is reserved for large, painful, or bothersome cysts, with counselling about the small risk to fertility from epididymal surgery A solid or vascular component on ultrasound An associated painful, hard testicular mass Rapid enlargement of the swelling Systemic or infective features An irregular or fixed swelling Excising asymptomatic cysts and risking epididymal obstruction and fertility impairment Failing to obtain ultrasound to exclude a solid testicular lesion behind a scrotal lump Confusing an epididymal cyst with a hydrocele or with a spermatocele Under-counselling younger men about the fertility implications of surgery An epididymal cyst arises from cystic dilatation of the epididymal tubules or efferent ductules, probably from obstruction or from embryological ductal remnants, producing a thin-walled sac of clear serous fluid. Unlike a spermatocele, this fluid does not contain spermatozoa. The cysts are lined by flattened epithelium, grow slowly, and are entirely benign with no malignant potential; they become clinically important only when large enough to cause discomfort or anxiety. Excellent, as epididymal cysts are benign and often remain stable or fluctuate in size; even when excised the outlook is good, with only a small risk to ipsilateral epididymal function.

multidisciplinary pain management, and surgery such as epididymectomy is a last resort with counselling about uncertain benefit A discrete or hard testicular mass on examination or ultrasound requiring tumour exclusion Acute severe pain with swelling suggesting torsion or superimposed acute infection Systemic features of infection such as fever and rigors Progressive or unexplained scrotal swelling Repeatedly prescribing antibiotics in the absence of proven infection Overlooking a testicular tumour presenting as chronic scrotal discomfort Failing to consider referred pain from the ureter, hernia, or entrapped nerves Proceeding to surgery without realistic counselling about uncertain outcomes Neglecting the psychological impact and the value of a chronic-pain approach Chronic epididymitis denotes long-standing epididymal pain that in most cases is not due to ongoing infection. It may follow an episode of acute epididymitis, with residual inflammation, fibrosis, and scarring of the epididymal tubules, or arise from congestion and obstruction, as can occur after vasectomy. In many men no infective or structural cause is identified and the condition is best understood as a chronic inflammatory or neuropathic pain state involving sensitisation of scrotal afferent nerves. Coexisting or overlapping chronic pelvic pain and referred pain from the lower urinary or musculoskeletal structures frequently contribute. The distinction from acute infective epididymitis is important because it changes management away from antimicrobial therapy towards a chronic-pain approach. The condition is benign but can be persistent and frustrating, with symptoms often waxing and waning; many men improve with conservative measures and time, though a subset have long-lasting pain that is difficult to abolish and requires ongoing pain-focused management.

resistant organism, abscess, or alternative diagnosis Misdiagnosing torsion as epididymo-orchitis and delaying surgical exploration Choosing antibiotics that do not cover the likely organism for the urinary tract pathology in older or recurrent cases Epididymo-orchitis is inflammation of the epididymis, frequently extending to the adjacent testis, usually caused by retrograde ascent of organisms from the urethra or bladder along the vas deferens. In younger men sexually transmitted pathogens predominate, whereas in older men Gram-negative urinary organisms associated with obstruction, catheterisation, or instrumentation are more common. The resulting inflammatory oedema, hyperaemia, and swelling can progress to suppuration, abscess, or testicular infarction from compromised blood supply. Viral causes such as mumps produce orchitis through haematogenous spread. Most cases resolve with appropriate antibiotics and supportive care, though swelling and discomfort can take weeks to settle; complications include abscess, chronic epididymitis, testicular atrophy, and, particularly with mumps or bilateral disease, impaired fertility.

Spinal epidural abscess — SEA, spinal epidural abscess, epidural empyema, extradural abscess Vertebral osteomyelitis or discitis without abscess Transverse myelitis Spinal cord tumour or metastasis Acute disc herniation with cord compression Guillain-Barre syndrome in the setting of ascending weakness Metastatic epidural cord compression from malignancy Epidural haematoma Demyelinating myelopathy Mechanical radiculopathy from disc prolapse Urgent MRI of the whole spine with contrast to localise the abscess and assess cord compression Blood cultures and inflammatory markers Culture of aspirated or surgically drained pus to guide antibiotics Screening for a primary source such as endocarditis or vertebral osteomyelitis Assessment for skip lesions, since abscesses may involve multiple non-contiguous levels A collection of pus in the spinal epidural space that is a neurosurgical emergency because of the risk of irreversible cord compression The classic triad of back pain, fever, and neurological deficit is present in only a minority, so a high index of suspicion is essential Symptoms often progress through localised back pain, then radicular pain, then motor or sensory deficit and sphincter dysfunction, and finally paralysis Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism, and infection may spread haematogenously or contiguously from vertebral osteomyelitis or paraspinal infection Risk factors include injecting drug use, diabetes, immunosuppression, indwelling catheters, spinal instrumentation, and recent epidural procedures Urgent MRI with contrast is the investigation of choice and should not be delayed once the diagnosis is considered Management principles combine emergency surgical decompression and drainage for neurological compromise with prolonged targeted antibiotics; selected stable patients without deficit may be managed medically with close monitoring Once a significant neurological deficit is established, the window for functional recovery is short, making speed of intervention critical Any new or progressing motor weakness, sensory level, or bladder or bowel dysfunction indicating cord or cauda equina compression requiring emergency decompression Rapid neurological deterioration signalling a closing window for recovery Back pain with fever in an injecting drug user or immunocompromised patient Sepsis complicating the abscess Waiting for the full triad of back pain, fever, and deficit before considering the diagnosis Delaying MRI or surgical referral once suspicion is raised Failing to image the entire spine and missing non-contiguous abscesses Underestimating how quickly a mild deficit can progress to permanent paralysis A spinal epidural abscess forms when bacteria reach the epidural space by haematogenous seeding, contiguous spread from vertebral osteomyelitis or a paraspinal focus, or direct inoculation during a spinal procedure. Accumulating pus causes neurological injury through two mechanisms: direct mechanical compression of the spinal cord or cauda equina and vascular compromise, with septic thrombophlebitis and arterial disruption producing cord ischaemia and infarction. This combination explains why deficits can progress rapidly and become irreversible if decompression is delayed. Outcome hinges on neurological status at the time of intervention; patients treated before a major deficit develops usually do well, whereas established paralysis, especially if present for more than a day or two before decompression, often does not recover fully.

Epilepsy with myoclonic absences — Myoclonic absence epilepsy, Tassinari syndrome Childhood and juvenile absence epilepsy Doose syndrome (myoclonic-atonic epilepsy) Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy Lennox-Gastaut syndrome Eyelid myoclonia with absences (Jeavons) Progressive myoclonic epilepsy Video-EEG with polygraphic EMG to demonstrate the time-locked myoclonias MRI brain to exclude a structural cause Chromosomal microarray and genetic testing Metabolic screen if progressive features emerge Neuropsychological assessment Hyperventilation-activated EEG A generalised epilepsy defined by absence seizures accompanied by rhythmic bilateral myoclonic jerks, predominantly of the shoulders and arms, with a tonic component. Onset is around 7 years, spanning early childhood to pre-adolescence, with a male predominance. Seizures are frequent, occurring many times a day, and can be triggered by hyperventilation. EEG shows bilateral synchronous rhythmic 3 Hz spike-wave discharges time-locked to the myoclonias, confirmed by polygraphic EMG. Consciousness is variably impaired during events. Associated intellectual disability is common and other seizure types, including generalised tonic-clonic seizures, may occur. A proportion have an identifiable cause such as a chromosomal abnormality or structural lesion. Treatment response is often incomplete, and valproate combined with ethosuximide is a common regimen. Cognitive decline or regression Emergence of tonic or atonic seizures suggesting evolution to Lennox-Gastaut syndrome Drug-resistant, very frequent seizures Abnormal neurological examination or imaging Mistaking the myoclonic absences for simple typical absences and under-treating. Not performing polygraphic EEG-EMG to confirm the time-locked myoclonias. Overlooking an underlying chromosomal or structural cause. Using drugs that aggravate generalised seizures. Epilepsy with myoclonic absences is a generalised epilepsy in which thalamocortical oscillatory circuits generate rhythmic 3 Hz spike-wave discharges. The distinctive rhythmic myoclonias arise as the motor cortex is entrained by these generalised discharges, producing a positive motor phenomenon with a superimposed tonic contraction, demonstrable on combined EEG-EMG polygraphy. Underlying genetic or, in some, structural and chromosomal abnormalities contribute to the network dysfunction and the associated cognitive impairment. Variable and often guarded; seizures may be difficult to control and cognitive impairment is common, although isolated cases without other seizure types can remit. Evolution to other epileptic encephalopathies occurs in some.

epiphrenic diverticulum — epiphrenic oesophageal diverticulum, distal oesophageal pulsion diverticulum achalasia without diverticulum distal oesophageal spasm or hypercontractile oesophagus hiatus hernia (para-oesophageal) oesophageal duplication cyst peptic or malignant distal oesophageal stricture intramural pseudodiverticulosis traction diverticulum from mediastinal inflammation barium swallow to delineate the sac, its neck and associated dysmotility high-resolution oesophageal manometry to identify the underlying motility disorder upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to exclude malignancy and mucosal disease within the sac computed tomography of the chest to define mediastinal anatomy before surgery ambulatory pH or reflux monitoring where gastro-oesophageal reflux is suspected timed barium oesophagogram to assess emptying if achalasia is present An epiphrenic diverticulum is a pulsion (false) diverticulum of the distal oesophagus, typically within the terminal few centimetres above the diaphragm, and is almost always associated with an underlying oesophageal motility disorder. Achalasia, distal oesophageal spasm, hypercontractile (jackhammer) oesophagus and other outflow-obstruction disorders raise intraluminal pressure and drive mucosal herniation, so manometry is essential in the work-up. Typical symptoms are dysphagia, regurgitation of retained and sometimes fermented food, nocturnal aspiration, chest pain and halitosis, though many diverticula are asymptomatic and found incidentally. Barium swallow best demonstrates the sac and any associated motility abnormality; endoscopy is needed to exclude malignancy within the diverticulum. Because the diverticulum is a consequence of the motility disorder, effective surgery must address the distal obstruction, usually by adding a myotomy to any diverticulectomy. Surgical repair combines diverticulectomy (or diverticulopexy), an extended myotomy across the lower oesophageal sphincter and often a partial fundoplication to prevent reflux. The staple line after diverticulectomy is prone to leak if a distal myotomy is not performed, because unrelieved outflow resistance keeps intraluminal pressure high. Rare but important complications include carcinoma arising within a long-standing diverticulum, so persistent or atypical symptoms warrant careful endoscopic assessment. progressive dysphagia with significant weight loss suggesting malignancy recurrent aspiration pneumonia or nocturnal choking haematemesis or evidence of ulceration within the sac chest pain with fever or sepsis suggesting perforation a mass or filling defect within the diverticulum on imaging Performing diverticulectomy without an accompanying myotomy, leading to staple-line leak or recurrence. Failing to perform manometry and missing the causative motility disorder. Overlooking a carcinoma developing within a long-standing diverticulum. Attributing symptoms solely to the sac size when the motility disorder is the true driver. Omitting an antireflux procedure after myotomy and producing troublesome reflux. An epiphrenic diverticulum is a herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the muscular layers of the distal oesophagus, classifying it as a pulsion (false) diverticulum. It develops because a functional or mechanical outflow obstruction at the oesophagogastric junction, most often an underlying motility disorder such as achalasia, distal oesophageal spasm or a hypercontractile oesophagus, generates sustained high intraluminal pressure during swallowing against a poorly relaxing or spastic segment. This pressure forces the mucosa outward at a point of relative muscular weakness just above the diaphragm. Retention of food and secretions within the sac produces stasis symptoms, regurgitation and aspiration risk, and chronic inflammation of the retained material can rarely predispose to malignant change. Because the pressure gradient is the driving force, the diverticulum will tend to recur or the repair to leak unless the distal obstruction is relieved. Asymptomatic small diverticula can be observed with a good prognosis, whereas symptomatic lesions treated with combined diverticulectomy and myotomy generally do well, provided the underlying motility disorder is addressed. Staple-line leak and recurrence are the main risks when the distal obstruction is not relieved.

Epiretinal membrane (macular pucker) — ERM, macular pucker, cellophane maculopathy, premacular fibrosis, surface wrinkling retinopathy Vitreomacular traction syndrome Full-thickness or lamellar macular hole Cystoid macular oedema Choroidal neovascular membrane in age-related macular degeneration Diabetic macular oedema Central serous chorioretinopathy Myopic traction maculopathy Optical coherence tomography to characterise the membrane, foveal contour and retinal thickness Amsler grid testing to quantify and monitor metamorphopsia Best-corrected visual acuity measurement to track functional change Fundus examination and imaging to detect vessel distortion and any macular hole Fluorescein angiography where secondary vascular pathology or leakage is suspected Assessment for underlying causes such as prior retinal tears, vascular occlusion or uveitis in secondary cases A fibrocellular membrane proliferating on the inner surface of the retina at the macula, common in older adults and often bilateral though usually asymmetric Most cases are idiopathic and related to posterior vitreous detachment; secondary membranes follow retinal tears or detachment, vascular occlusion, uveitis, trauma or intraocular surgery Symptoms depend on severity and range from none, through a subtle cellophane sheen, to metamorphopsia, reduced acuity and micropsia as contraction increases Fundus examination shows glistening or wrinkled inner retina with distorted, straightened or dragged retinal vessels Optical coherence tomography is the key investigation, demonstrating the membrane, retinal thickening, loss of the foveal pit and, in advanced cases, a lamellar or pseudohole The Amsler grid is a simple bedside and home tool for detecting and monitoring distortion Many mild membranes remain stable and warrant observation, with intervention reserved for troublesome distortion or declining vision Management of visually significant disease is surgical, with pars plana vitrectomy and membrane peel, often including internal limiting membrane peel Rapidly worsening distortion or acuity suggesting progressive traction Development of a lamellar or full-thickness macular hole Features of an underlying secondary cause such as retinal vascular occlusion or a retinal tear New symptoms suggesting associated retinal detachment Attributing reduced vision to a mild membrane while missing a coexisting cause such as macular oedema or neovascular disease Overlooking a secondary membrane and failing to identify and treat the underlying pathology Recommending surgery for a stable, minimally symptomatic membrane Missing an evolving macular hole beneath the membrane on OCT Setting unrealistic expectations about the speed and completeness of visual recovery after peeling An epiretinal membrane forms when glial cells, retinal pigment epithelial cells and other cell types migrate onto and proliferate along the inner retinal surface, laying down a contractile fibrocellular sheet. In idiopathic cases this is typically triggered by a posterior vitreous detachment that leaves residual cortical vitreous and breaks in the internal limiting membrane, allowing cells to gain access to the retinal surface. Contraction of the membrane wrinkles the underlying retina, distorts the foveal architecture and displaces retinal vessels, producing metamorphopsia and reduced acuity. Persistent traction can cause macular oedema and, uncommonly, a lamellar or full-thickness macular hole. Many idiopathic membranes remain stable with good vision; when surgery is performed for visually significant disease, distortion and acuity usually improve, though recovery is gradual and often incomplete, and some residual metamorphopsia may persist.

Episcleritis — simple episcleritis, nodular episcleritis Scleritis Conjunctivitis Anterior uveitis Inflamed pterygium or pinguecula Subconjunctival haemorrhage Foreign body or localised irritation Slit-lamp examination and topical phenylephrine test to confirm superficial vessel involvement Assessment of visual acuity to confirm it is preserved Limited systemic workup only in recurrent, nodular, or atypical cases (e.g. inflammatory markers, autoimmune screen, urate) A common, benign, usually self-limiting inflammation of the episclera presenting with acute redness and mild discomfort or grittiness rather than severe pain Redness may be sectoral or diffuse with a bright red appearance, and visual acuity is preserved The superficial episcleral vessels blanch with topical phenylephrine, unlike the deeper vessels of scleritis Classified as simple (diffuse) or nodular; in nodular disease a mobile, tender nodule is seen over the sclera Most cases are idiopathic, though a minority are linked to systemic inflammatory conditions such as gout, rosacea, or connective-tissue disease It is distinguished from scleritis by the absence of deep boring pain, vessel blanching with phenylephrine, and a benign course Management is largely reassurance with lubricants; topical or short courses of oral NSAIDs and, occasionally, mild topical steroids help troublesome or nodular cases Severe boring pain, deep violaceous vessels, or failure to blanch with phenylephrine suggesting scleritis instead Reduced visual acuity, which should not occur in simple episcleritis Frequently recurrent disease suggesting an underlying systemic inflammatory condition Confusing episcleritis with scleritis and over-investigating or over-treating a benign condition Conversely, dismissing genuine scleritis as episcleritis and missing sight-threatening disease Prolonged unnecessary topical steroid use with its attendant risks of raised intraocular pressure Overlooking an associated systemic disease in recurrent cases Episcleritis is inflammation confined to the episclera, the thin vascular layer of connective tissue between the conjunctiva and the sclera. The process is typically a localised, non-granulomatous inflammatory response affecting the superficial episcleral vascular plexus, producing vasodilatation and mild oedema without the deep scleral destruction of true scleritis. It is usually idiopathic and self-limiting, though recurrent or nodular episodes can occasionally be associated with systemic inflammatory disease. Episcleritis is benign and self-limiting, typically resolving within one to two weeks without lasting visual consequences, although recurrences are common.

Episodic ataxia (types 1 and 2) — EA1, EA2, KCNA1-related episodic ataxia, CACNA1A-related episodic ataxia, paroxysmal cerebellar ataxia Vestibular migraine and basilar-type migraine Transient ischaemic attacks affecting the posterior circulation Peripheral vestibular disorders (e.g. Meniere disease, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo) Paroxysmal movement disorders and other paroxysmal neurological syndromes Metabolic episodic ataxias (e.g. related to pyruvate dehydrogenase or urea-cycle disorders) Functional or anxiety-related episodic symptoms Early progressive spinocerebellar ataxia (notably SCA6) Targeted KCNA1 and CACNA1A genetic testing guided by attack duration and associated features MRI brain to assess for cerebellar atrophy and exclude structural lesions Electromyography to detect myokymia supporting EA1 Vestibular and oculomotor testing to characterise interictal nystagmus Metabolic screening when a metabolic episodic ataxia is suspected A trial of acetazolamide as a supportive diagnostic and therapeutic measure in EA2 Autosomal dominant channelopathies causing recurrent, discrete episodes of ataxia rather than steady progression EA1 is caused by KCNA1 potassium-channel mutations and features brief attacks (seconds to minutes) often with interictal myokymia, frequently triggered by startle or exertion EA2 is caused by CACNA1A calcium-channel mutations and features longer attacks (minutes to hours) often with vertigo, nausea and nystagmus, frequently triggered by stress, exercise or caffeine Interictal downbeat or gaze-evoked nystagmus is common in EA2 and may persist between attacks EA2 is allelic with SCA6 and familial hemiplegic migraine, and progressive cerebellar atrophy with fixed ataxia can develop over time Acetazolamide is a recognised prophylactic option, particularly effective in EA2; carbamazepine can help the myokymia and attacks of EA1 MRI may be normal early but can show cerebellar (vermian) atrophy in longstanding EA2 Diagnosis rests on the episodic history, family history and targeted KCNA1 or CACNA1A testing Focal neurological deficit or first presentation in later life suggesting cerebrovascular disease Progressive fixed ataxia developing between attacks indicating cerebellar degeneration Attacks with reduced consciousness or hemiplegic features prompting reassessment for hemiplegic migraine or seizures Metabolic decompensation with encephalopathy pointing to an inborn error of metabolism Misdiagnosing recurrent attacks as vestibular migraine or anxiety and missing a treatable channelopathy Not offering a trial of acetazolamide in EA2, where it can markedly reduce attacks Overlooking interictal myokymia or nystagmus that point to the specific subtype Assuming a normal early MRI excludes the diagnosis or future cerebellar atrophy The episodic ataxias are inherited ion-channel disorders of the cerebellum. EA1 results from mutations in KCNA1, encoding the Kv1.1 voltage-gated potassium channel; impaired potassium conductance causes neuronal hyperexcitability that manifests as peripheral myokymia and brief cerebellar attacks. EA2 results from mutations in CACNA1A, encoding the alpha-1A subunit of the P/Q-type calcium channel densely expressed in Purkinje cells; disturbed calcium signalling produces longer attacks of ataxia and vertigo and, over years, can lead to Purkinje cell loss and progressive cerebellar atrophy. CACNA1A's allelic relationship with SCA6 and familial hemiplegic migraine reflects a shared channel dysfunction. Attack frequency often lessens with prophylaxis, and many patients function well between episodes; EA1 generally does not cause fixed deficits, whereas EA2 may lead to slowly progressive cerebellar signs and atrophy over time. Overall life expectancy is typically normal.

Episodic ataxia type 1 (KCNA1) — EA1, KCNA1-related episodic ataxia, episodic ataxia with myokymia, Kv1.1 potassium channel disorder Episodic ataxia type 2 (CACNA1A) Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia Other paroxysmal dyskinesias Vestibular migraine and migraine with brainstem aura Functional or psychogenic paroxysmal attacks Metabolic episodic ataxias KCNA1 sequencing within an ataxia or channelopathy gene panel Electromyography to demonstrate myokymia or neuromyotonic discharges A structured attack diary and trigger history to characterise the episodes Brain MRI to exclude a structural cerebellar lesion CACNA1A testing where features overlap with episodic ataxia type 2 Electroencephalography if associated seizures are suspected An autosomal dominant channelopathy caused by missense variants in KCNA1, which encodes the Kv1.1 voltage-gated potassium channel, resulting in neuronal and peripheral-nerve hyperexcitability Attacks are brief, usually lasting seconds to a few minutes, and consist of ataxia and dysarthria, sometimes occurring several times a day Attacks are commonly provoked by sudden movement or startle (kinesigenic triggers), exercise, emotional stress or vestibular stimulation The hallmark interictal sign is myokymia, a continuous fine rippling of muscles often seen around the eyes or in the hands, and demonstrable on electromyography Some individuals additionally have epilepsy, and skeletal features such as muscle stiffness or contractures may occur Acetazolamide can reduce attack frequency in many patients, and anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine may help the myokymia, alongside advice on avoiding triggers Diagnosis is clinical, supported by electromyography demonstrating myokymia and by KCNA1 sequencing It should be distinguished from episodic ataxia type 2, caused by CACNA1A, which produces longer attacks with prominent nystagmus and interictal gaze abnormalities A progressive fixed cerebellar deficit rather than purely episodic symptoms, suggesting an alternative diagnosis Frequent disabling attacks with falls and injury New focal neurological signs indicating a structural lesion Seizures requiring specific assessment and management Mistaking brief kinesigenic attacks for functional or psychogenic episodes Overlooking myokymia, which is the key interictal clue to the diagnosis Confusing the condition with episodic ataxia type 2 and giving inappropriate prognostic expectations Not offering a therapeutic trial of acetazolamide when attacks are frequent Failing to provide genetic counselling given autosomal dominant inheritance Episodic ataxia type 1 arises from dominant missense variants in KCNA1, encoding the Kv1.1 delayed-rectifier potassium channel expressed in cerebellar basket cells, peripheral nerve and elsewhere. The mutations reduce potassium current through loss-of-function or dominant-negative effects, impairing repolarisation and increasing excitability of neurons and peripheral nerves. Enhanced firing of cerebellar interneurons transiently disrupts Purkinje cell output, producing the brief episodes of ataxia and dysarthria, while sustained peripheral-nerve hyperexcitability generates the continuous myokymia that characterises the condition. The outlook is generally good; attacks often lessen with treatment and may improve in adulthood, and the disorder is usually non-progressive with normal life expectancy, although quality of life can be affected by recurrent attacks and persistent myokymia.

Epispadias — dorsal urethral defect, isolated epispadias, epispadias-exstrophy complex Hypospadias (ventral meatus) Classic bladder exstrophy (more severe complex) Buried or webbed penis with abnormal meatal appearance Female urethral or clitoral duplication anomalies Ambiguous genitalia from a disorder of sex development Isolated dorsal chordee without meatal abnormality Clinical examination to define meatal position, chordee, and continence Renal and bladder ultrasound to assess the upper tracts Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) to evaluate reflux and bladder neck Pelvic imaging to assess pubic diastasis for surgical planning Urodynamic assessment where continence is in question Assessment for other associated anomalies of the complex A congenital anomaly in which the urethral meatus opens on the dorsal (upper) surface of the penis in boys or between a bifid clitoris in girls, representing the mildest end of the exstrophy-epispadias complex In males it is classified by meatal position as glanular, penile, or penopubic; the more proximal (penopubic) the defect, the greater the likelihood of associated sphincteric incompetence and incontinence The penis is typically short and broad with dorsal chordee (upward curvature) Continence depends on the integrity of the bladder neck and sphincter, which are more commonly deficient in proximal epispadias Pubic diastasis of a lesser degree than in exstrophy may be present, reflecting the shared developmental spectrum It must be distinguished from hypospadias, in which the meatus lies on the ventral surface Management is surgical reconstruction to reposition the meatus, correct chordee, and, when needed, bladder neck reconstruction to achieve continence Urinary incontinence indicating a deficient bladder neck or sphincter Associated upper-tract dilatation or reflux with infection Features suggesting a more severe exstrophy variant Ambiguity of the genitalia requiring evaluation for a disorder of sex development Confusing epispadias with hypospadias and mis-planning the repair Underestimating sphincteric incompetence in proximal defects, leading to persistent incontinence Failing to recognise membership of the wider exstrophy-epispadias complex Neglecting upper-tract evaluation before reconstruction Epispadias arises from an abnormality of early cloacal and genital tubercle development within the exstrophy-epispadias spectrum, in which the developing genital structures form more caudally than normal, so the urethral plate ends up on the dorsal aspect of the phallus. Depending on the extent of the developmental disturbance, the defect ranges from a distal glanular opening to a proximal penopubic opening with an incompetent bladder neck and sphincter mechanism, and there may be associated separation of the pubic symphysis. The dorsal position of the urethral plate and abnormal corporal development produce the characteristic dorsal chordee and foreshortened penis. Distal epispadias generally has an excellent functional and cosmetic outcome after reconstruction, whereas proximal (penopubic) forms more often require additional bladder neck surgery for continence and may need staged procedures, with fertility and sexual function requiring long-term attention.

Epistaxis — nosebleed, nasal haemorrhage Bleeding from a nasal or sinonasal tumour Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia Coagulopathy or anticoagulant-related bleeding Haemoptysis or upper gastrointestinal bleeding mimicking nasal bleeding Trauma including base of skull fracture with CSF or blood Anterior rhinoscopy and nasal endoscopy to localise the bleeding point Blood pressure measurement and assessment of haemodynamic status Full blood count, coagulation profile and group and save or crossmatch in significant bleeds Review of anticoagulant and antiplatelet medication Imaging (CT or MRI) and referral where a sinonasal tumour or vascular lesion is suspected Bleeding is broadly classified as anterior or posterior, which differ in likely source, severity and management Most bleeds are anterior and arise from Little's area on the nasal septum, where several vessels anastomose (Kiesselbach's plexus) Posterior bleeds tend to occur in older patients, are more profuse, and are harder to control, with a higher risk of airway soiling and significant blood loss Causes are grouped into local (trauma, digital picking, foreign body, infection, tumour) and general (hypertension, coagulopathy, anticoagulants, hereditary telangiectasia) First aid principles are sitting upright, leaning forward and pinching the soft part of the nose, with attention to airway and circulation Stepwise management progresses from cautery of an identified bleeding point to anterior packing and then posterior packing or balloon devices Refractory bleeding may require endoscopic or surgical arterial ligation or embolisation of the offending vessel Unilateral persistent or recurrent bleeding, especially with nasal obstruction, warrants evaluation for a tumour such as juvenile angiofibroma in adolescent males Profuse or posterior bleeding with hypovolaemia or haemodynamic instability requiring resuscitation Airway compromise from blood aspiration in heavy or bilateral bleeding Bleeding uncontrolled by packing needing arterial ligation or embolisation Recurrent unilateral bleeding with a mass suggesting malignancy or angiofibroma Failing to assess and resuscitate the patient while focusing only on the nose Overlooking a posterior source when anterior examination appears clear Missing an underlying tumour in recurrent unilateral bleeding Neglecting to review anticoagulation and correct coagulopathy Epistaxis is bleeding from the nasal mucosa, whose rich, superficial vascular supply from branches of both the internal and external carotid systems makes it prone to haemorrhage. Anterior bleeding usually comes from the low-pressure anastomotic vessels of Little's area, provoked by drying, trauma or minor mucosal injury. Posterior bleeding tends to arise from larger branches such as the sphenopalatine artery and is aggravated by hypertension and vascular fragility in older patients. Systemic factors such as bleeding disorders, anticoagulation and platelet dysfunction impair haemostasis and prolong or worsen bleeding. Most anterior nosebleeds settle with simple first aid or cautery, whereas posterior and recurrent bleeds, particularly in patients with hypertension or coagulopathy, can be severe or life-threatening and may need aggressive intervention.

Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma — EHE, WWTR1-CAMTA1 fusion tumour, epithelioid haemangioendothelioma of soft tissue Metastatic adenocarcinoma Epithelioid angiosarcoma Epithelioid sarcoma Epithelioid haemangioma Metastatic melanoma Sclerosing or metastatic carcinoma of the liver or lung Cross-sectional imaging of the affected organ and staging to map multifocal disease Biopsy with histological assessment of epithelioid cords in myxohyaline stroma Endothelial immunohistochemistry with CD31, ERG and CD34 CAMTA1 nuclear staining as a surrogate for the WWTR1-CAMTA1 fusion Molecular confirmation of WWTR1-CAMTA1 or YAP1-TFE3 fusion in ambiguous cases A malignant vascular tumour of intermediate to low-grade behaviour that can arise in soft tissue, bone, liver, lung and other organs Frequently multifocal within an organ or presents synchronously in several sites, which can be mistaken for metastatic carcinoma Defined in most cases by a WWTR1-CAMTA1 gene fusion, with a smaller subset carrying a YAP1-TFE3 fusion CAMTA1 nuclear immunohistochemistry serves as a useful surrogate marker for the characteristic fusion Histology shows cords and nests of epithelioid endothelial cells in a distinctive myxohyaline or chondroid stroma, with intracytoplasmic vacuoles representing primitive lumina The cells express endothelial markers such as CD31, ERG and CD34, confirming vascular differentiation Behaviour ranges from indolent to aggressive, and management spans surveillance, resection and systemic therapy depending on burden and risk features Large tumour size or high mitotic activity indicating more aggressive behaviour Widespread multiorgan involvement or rapid progression Pleural effusion, haemoptysis or significant pain suggesting aggressive disease Features overlapping with epithelioid angiosarcoma, which is more aggressive Misdiagnosing multifocal disease as metastatic carcinoma Confusing it with the more aggressive epithelioid angiosarcoma Overlooking vascular differentiation without endothelial immunostains Assuming a uniformly indolent course without assessing risk features Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma is a malignant tumour of endothelial (vascular) origin defined in the great majority of cases by a WWTR1-CAMTA1 gene fusion, with a minority driven by a YAP1-TFE3 fusion. The fusion dysregulates the Hippo signalling pathway, leading to constitutive activation of transcriptional coactivators that promote endothelial cell proliferation. Tumour cells are epithelioid and grow as cords and small nests set in a characteristic myxohyaline stroma, and individual cells often contain intracytoplasmic vacuoles that represent attempts at forming primitive vascular lumina. Its multifocal presentation reflects the disease biology rather than metastatic spread from a single primary. Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma has variable behaviour, and many cases follow an indolent course while others progress and metastasise, particularly those with larger size and higher mitotic activity. Risk stratification using size and mitotic count helps predict outcome and guide the intensity of treatment.

immunohistochemistry in the large majority of cases Histology shows nodules of epithelioid and spindled cells with central necrosis, sometimes creating a granuloma-like appearance Tumour cells co-express epithelial markers (cytokeratin, EMA) and CD34, an unusual combination that aids diagnosis It spreads along fascial planes and via lymphatics, with a high rate of local recurrence and regional nodal and distant metastasis A non-healing ulcer or persistent nodule on the hand or forearm not responding to expected treatment Regional lymphadenopathy suggesting nodal metastasis Proximal-type tumour of the pelvis or perineum, which is more aggressive Local recurrence or distant metastasis during follow-up Mistaking a necrotising nodule for benign granulomatous disease and delaying diagnosis Interpreting keratin positivity as evidence of carcinoma rather than epithelioid sarcoma Failing to perform INI1 staining, which typically shows diagnostic loss Neglecting nodal staging given the unusual lymphatic spread of this sarcoma Epithelioid sarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumour defined in most cases by inactivation of the SMARCB1 (INI1) tumour suppressor gene, a core subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling complex. Loss of SMARCB1 function disrupts normal chromatin regulation and gene expression, promoting oncogenesis, and is detected as loss of nuclear INI1 staining. The tumour grows as nodules of epithelioid cells that frequently undergo central necrosis, producing a deceptively granuloma-like or necrobiotic pattern. It characteristically infiltrates along tendons, fascia and nerves and has a marked propensity for lymph node involvement, which is unusual among sarcomas. Epithelioid sarcoma is an aggressive malignancy prone to local recurrence and to regional nodal and distant metastasis, and it often follows a protracted but ultimately unfavourable course. The proximal-type variant, large size and metastatic disease at presentation carry a worse prognosis.

Erb's palsy — Erb-Duchenne palsy, upper brachial plexus birth palsy Klumpke (lower plexus) palsy Clavicular or humeral fracture causing pseudoparalysis Total brachial plexus palsy Cervical spinal cord injury Osteomyelitis or septic arthritis of the shoulder (as a cause of a still arm) Clinical examination of the posture, active movement and reflexes Assessment for Horner syndrome suggesting root avulsion Radiographs to exclude clavicular or humeral fracture Neurophysiology and MRI in persistent or severe cases Serial examination to track recovery A birth-related brachial plexus injury affecting the upper roots (C5-C6, sometimes C7) The affected arm lies adducted and internally rotated with the forearm pronated and wrist flexed, the classic waiter's tip posture The Moro reflex is asymmetric, but grasp is preserved because the lower roots are spared Risk factors include shoulder dystocia, macrosomia, instrumental delivery and breech birth An intact grasp helps distinguish it from lower plexus (Klumpke) palsy, and Horner syndrome suggests a more severe root avulsion Most cases recover with early physiotherapy; persistent deficit at a few months warrants specialist referral for possible surgery Horner syndrome or a flail arm suggesting severe avulsion or total plexus injury Respiratory distress suggesting phrenic nerve involvement No recovery of biceps function by a few months of age Bilateral involvement Missing an associated fracture causing pseudoparalysis Overlooking Horner syndrome as a marker of severe injury Failing to refer non-recovering cases in time for surgical options Neglecting early physiotherapy and joint contracture prevention Erb's palsy results from traction on the upper brachial plexus during delivery, typically when the shoulder is depressed as the head is delivered, as in shoulder dystocia. Stretching injures the C5-C6 (and sometimes C7) nerve roots, ranging from neurapraxia to rupture or root avulsion. The upper-root distribution explains the weakness of shoulder abduction and external rotation, elbow flexion and forearm supination, producing the characteristic posture, while preserved lower roots maintain hand function. The severity of the nerve injury determines the potential for recovery. The majority of infants recover spontaneously or with physiotherapy over weeks to months; a minority with severe injury have persistent weakness and may benefit from nerve or later orthopaedic surgery.

Erdheim-Chester disease — ECD, non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis, polyostotic sclerosing histiocytosis Langerhans cell histiocytosis Rosai-Dorfman disease IgG4-related disease and retroperitoneal fibrosis Metastatic malignancy with osteosclerosis Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis Sarcoidosis Biopsy of an affected site showing foamy CD68-positive, CD1a-negative histiocytes with Touton giant cells Molecular testing for BRAF-V600E and other MAPK pathway mutations Plain radiographs and technetium bone scan showing symmetrical long-bone osteosclerosis CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis for perirenal 'hairy kidney' and periaortic 'coated aorta' MRI of brain and cardiac imaging to assess neurological and cardiac infiltration PET imaging to map disease extent and monitor treatment response A rare non-Langerhans histiocytosis, now recognised as a clonal myeloid neoplasm, usually presenting in middle-aged and older adults Bilateral symmetrical osteosclerosis of the long bones (particularly around the knees) with bone pain is the most consistent finding Perirenal infiltration produces the characteristic 'hairy kidney' appearance and periaortic encasement the 'coated aorta' on cross-sectional imaging Central nervous system, retro-orbital, cardiac (periaortic and right atrial pseudotumour), and pituitary involvement (diabetes insipidus) are common and drive morbidity A large majority carry activating BRAF-V600E or other MAPK pathway mutations, which are both diagnostic and therapeutic targets Histology shows foamy (lipid-laden) CD68-positive, CD1a-negative histiocytes with Touton giant cells and surrounding fibrosis Targeted BRAF and MEK inhibition has transformed treatment of mutation-positive disease; interferon has historically been used Cardiac infiltration or pericardial involvement threatening haemodynamic compromise Central nervous system involvement with neurological deterioration Diabetes insipidus and other hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction Renal impairment from perirenal and periureteric encasement Mistaking foamy histiocytes for Langerhans cell histiocytosis without immunostaining (CD1a) and molecular testing Attributing bone pain to degenerative disease and missing the symmetrical osteosclerosis Overlooking cardiac and central nervous system involvement that determine prognosis Failing to test for BRAF-V600E, which guides targeted therapy Confusing periaortic and perirenal disease with retroperitoneal fibrosis alone Erdheim-Chester disease is a clonal histiocytic neoplasm arising from myeloid precursors, driven in most cases by activating mutations of the MAPK/ERK signalling pathway, most commonly BRAF-V600E. Constitutive pathway activation leads to accumulation and tissue infiltration by foamy, lipid-laden non-Langerhans histiocytes accompanied by fibrosis and an inflammatory milieu. This produces the characteristic bilateral long-bone osteosclerosis, perirenal and periaortic sheathing, and infiltration of the central nervous system, orbit, heart, and hypothalamic-pituitary axis, the last causing diabetes insipidus. Prognosis depends on the extent and site of involvement; central nervous system and cardiac disease historically carried high mortality, but targeted BRAF/MEK inhibition has markedly improved outcomes in mutation-positive patients.

Erectile dysfunction — ED, impotence, erectile failure Psychogenic erectile dysfunction Vascular (arteriogenic or veno-occlusive) dysfunction Neurogenic causes (diabetic neuropathy, pelvic surgery, spinal cord disease) Endocrine causes (hypogonadism, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease) Drug-induced erectile dysfunction Peyronie's disease Reduced libido or relationship factors Fasting glucose or HbA1c and lipid profile to assess cardiovascular and metabolic risk Morning serum testosterone, with prolactin and other hormones if deficiency is suspected Blood pressure and cardiovascular risk assessment Validated questionnaires such as the International Index of Erectile Function Penile Doppler ultrasound and specialist vascular studies in selected complex or younger patients Erectile dysfunction is the persistent inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual activity, and it is common with increasing age Causes are broadly organic (vascular, neurogenic, hormonal, anatomical, drug-induced) or psychogenic, and the two frequently coexist Vascular disease is the leading organic cause, so ED often shares risk factors with, and can be an early warning sign of, cardiovascular disease and diabetes A history distinguishing gradual organic onset from sudden situational psychogenic ED is key; preserved spontaneous nocturnal or early-morning erections point toward a psychogenic cause Assessment should review medications (antihypertensives, antidepressants, antiandrogens), lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol, obesity), and endocrine and psychological status First-line pharmacological management is with phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, alongside optimisation of cardiovascular risk factors and lifestyle modification PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated with nitrate therapy because of the risk of profound hypotension Second-line options include intracavernosal or intraurethral vasoactive agents and vacuum devices, with penile prosthesis implantation reserved for refractory cases ED as a sentinel marker of undiagnosed cardiovascular disease or diabetes Erectile dysfunction with neurological signs suggesting spinal cord or cauda equina pathology Concurrent nitrate use, which contraindicates PDE5 inhibitors Features suggesting a pituitary lesion (hyperprolactinaemia, visual field changes) requiring endocrine evaluation Prescribing PDE5 inhibitors to a patient taking nitrates Treating ED symptomatically without addressing underlying cardiovascular or metabolic disease Overlooking hypogonadism or hyperprolactinaemia as reversible causes Failing to consider medication side effects as a contributor Neglecting the psychological and relationship dimensions of the problem Penile erection depends on neurally mediated relaxation of cavernosal smooth muscle, increased arterial inflow, and veno-occlusion that traps blood within the corpora cavernosa; nitric oxide and the cyclic GMP pathway are central to this process. Erectile dysfunction arises when any of these mechanisms fails: arterial insufficiency from atherosclerosis reduces inflow, veno-occlusive dysfunction allows leak, neuropathy (for example from diabetes or pelvic surgery) impairs signalling, and hormonal deficiency (notably hypogonadism) reduces desire and erectile capacity. Psychogenic factors act through central inhibition of the erectile response. Many patients have a mixed, multifactorial aetiology. Erectile dysfunction is highly treatable in most men, with many responding to PDE5 inhibitors and risk-factor modification; prognosis depends on the underlying cause, and it should prompt evaluation and management of associated cardiovascular risk.

penile structural disorders Medication-induced dysfunction, including antihypertensives and antidepressants Chronic systemic disease such as renal or hepatic failure Neurological disease or the questionnaire Early-morning serum testosterone, repeated if low, with luteinising hormone and prolactin where indicated Fasting glucose or HbA1c and a lipid profile to assess cardiometabolic risk
