erectile side effects Thyroid and renal function where systemic disease is suspected Organic erectile dysfunction typically develops gradually, is present in most sexual situations, and is accompanied by loss of spontaneous nocturnal and early-morning erections By contrast, a psychogenic pattern is often abrupt, situational, and retains nocturnal erections, though many men have a mixed picture The commonest organic mechanism is vascular, and dysfunction frequently precedes overt coronary or peripheral arterial disease, serving as an early marker of endothelial disease Every man presenting with erectile dysfunction should undergo cardiovascular risk assessment, as the small penile arteries may signal disease in larger vessels before symptoms elsewhere Diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, smoking, obesity, and hypogonadism are important and often modifiable contributors A directed history, examination, and measurement of morning testosterone and metabolic parameters identify most causes without invasive testing First-line treatment is with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors alongside risk-factor modification, with intracavernosal or intraurethral agents, vacuum devices, and penile prosthesis reserved for non-responders Coexisting hypogonadism should be corrected as it can both cause dysfunction and reduce the response to oral therapy Erectile dysfunction as a sentinel symptom of undiagnosed cardiovascular disease requiring cardiac assessment Associated symptoms of hypogonadism or a pituitary lesion such as visual disturbance New neurological signs pointing to spinal or central disease Penile deformity, pain, or plaque suggesting Peyronie disease Priapism or a history of prolonged erections as a treatment complication Treating erectile dysfunction symptomatically without assessing cardiovascular risk Overlooking coexisting hypogonadism that reduces the response to oral therapy Missing a culprit medication that could be changed Attributing an organic problem to psychological causes and delaying appropriate investigation Failing to counsel on priapism and nitrate interactions before prescribing phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors Penile erection is a neurovascular event in which parasympathetic and nitric-oxide-mediated signalling relaxes cavernosal smooth muscle, allowing arterial inflow to engorge the sinusoids and compress the subtunical venules to trap blood. Organic erectile dysfunction arises when any component of this pathway is impaired. Vasculogenic disease, driven by atherosclerosis and endothelial dysfunction, reduces arterial inflow and impairs the veno-occlusive mechanism. Neurogenic causes interrupt the autonomic and somatic innervation, as after pelvic surgery, in diabetes, or with neurological disease. Endocrine causes, chiefly testosterone deficiency and hyperprolactinaemia, blunt libido and the erectile response. Because the cavernosal arteries are of small calibre, endothelial compromise manifests here early, which is why organic erectile dysfunction commonly heralds systemic cardiovascular disease. Most men respond well to phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and risk-factor modification, and identifying and treating the underlying cardiometabolic disease benefits overall health; where oral therapy fails, injectable agents, devices, and prosthetic surgery offer highly effective alternatives.

Erotomania — de Clérambault syndrome, Delusional erotomania Schizophrenia Bipolar affective disorder with mania Other delusional disorder subtypes (grandiose, persecutory) Organic or neurological disease (frontal syndromes, dementia) Substance-induced psychosis Obsessional non-delusional infatuation Intense but non-delusional unrequited love Detailed psychiatric and forensic risk assessment Collateral history from family and, where appropriate, the named object's account of contact Mood assessment to identify mania or depression Neuroimaging where onset is late or organic features are present Organic screen bloods including thyroid function Substance and toxicology screen Structured stalking and violence risk instruments Delusional conviction that another person, typically of higher social status or otherwise unattainable, is secretly in love with the patient. In the classical form the object is believed to have made the first advances and to communicate covertly through gestures, media, or coincidences. More common in women in the primary or pure form, but forensically important in men, who more often stalk. May be primary (de Clérambault's pure erotomania within delusional disorder) or secondary to schizophrenia, manic states, or organic disease. Rejection is reinterpreted as concealed affirmation (the paradoxical conviction), so denials by the object reinforce rather than dispel the belief. Carries forensic significance through harassment, stalking, and occasional violence toward the object or perceived rivals. The pure form is frequently long-standing and encapsulated, with otherwise preserved functioning. Escalating stalking or approach behaviour toward the love object Threats toward the object or perceived rivals Weapon access or a forensic history Comorbid mania or psychosis increasing impulsivity and risk Underestimating forensic and stalking risk, especially in men Misclassifying manic or schizophrenic erotomania as primary delusional disorder Dismissing the delusion as harmless infatuation Reassuring the object without a safety plan Erotomania is a monothematic delusional disorder in which affect and belief converge on the fixed conviction of being loved. In the primary form it arises within delusional disorder, without prominent thought disorder or hallucinations. Secondary forms occur within schizophrenia, mania, or organic brain disease, where mood elevation or psychotic mechanisms drive the belief. Cognitive models emphasise abnormal salience attribution and self-referential bias, whereby neutral cues are interpreted as coded declarations of love; dopaminergic dysregulation is implicated where erotomania complicates psychotic or manic illness. The pure primary form is frequently chronic and treatment-resistant, whereas secondary erotomania often resolves as the underlying mood or psychotic disorder is treated.

Erysipeloid — Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae infection, erysipeloid of Rosenbach, fish-handler's disease, seal finger (related occupational presentation) Erysipelas or cellulitis due to streptococci or staphylococci Contact or irritant dermatitis Herpetic whitlow Orf or other parapoxvirus infection Tularaemia or other inoculation zoonoses Gout or acute inflammatory arthritis of a digit Culture of a full-thickness skin biopsy from the advancing edge of the lesion (surface swabs are often unrewarding) Blood cultures where systemic infection or endocarditis is suspected Echocardiography, including transoesophageal study, in bacteraemic patients Gram stain of biopsy material showing Gram-positive bacilli Inflammatory markers to gauge severity of invasive disease Caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, a Gram-positive bacillus widely distributed in animals, fish and shellfish, and acquired through occupational skin inoculation Typically affects butchers, abattoir workers, fishermen, fish handlers and veterinarians, so an occupational history is central to recognition The usual localised cutaneous form appears after a short incubation of about 1-4 days as a well-demarcated, violaceous, painful and often intensely itchy plaque, characteristically on a finger or hand The lesion tends to spread slowly at its advancing edge while clearing centrally and is not usually associated with suppuration or systemic upset A rarer diffuse cutaneous form with more widespread skin involvement and a serious systemic form with bacteraemia and endocarditis also occur The organism has a notable propensity to cause endocarditis, which may affect previously normal valves, so unexplained bacteraemia warrants echocardiography Penicillin-class agents are highly active and are first-line; importantly the organism is intrinsically resistant to vancomycin, a key point when treating suspected bacteraemia empirically New or changing murmur, embolic phenomena or heart failure suggesting endocarditis Fever and systemic toxicity indicating invasive rather than localised disease Rapidly spreading or diffuse skin involvement Sepsis in an occupationally exposed patient Empirical use of vancomycin, which is ineffective, in suspected Erysipelothrix bacteraemia Missing the occupational exposure and misdiagnosing the plaque as ordinary cellulitis Relying on surface swabs rather than a deep biopsy for culture Choosing empirical vancomycin, to which the organism is intrinsically resistant Failing to investigate for endocarditis when bacteraemia is documented Assuming all cases are trivial and overlooking the diffuse and systemic forms Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae is introduced through minor cuts or abrasions during handling of contaminated animal or fish products. In the localised form it multiplies in the dermis, producing a slowly advancing inflammatory plaque with the characteristic violaceous colour and central clearing, generally without pus formation. In susceptible hosts the organism can invade the bloodstream, and its ability to adhere to and colonise cardiac valve endothelium underlies its striking tendency to cause endocarditis, sometimes on structurally normal valves, with the potential for systemic embolic and destructive valvular complications. The localised cutaneous form is self-limiting and resolves within a few weeks, and responds promptly to penicillin; invasive disease and endocarditis carry a much more serious prognosis and require prolonged intravenous therapy and sometimes valve surgery.

Erythema annulare centrifugum — EAC, figurate erythema, gyrate erythema Tinea corporis Erythema gyratum repens Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (annular type) Annular urticaria and urticarial vasculitis Granuloma annulare Erythema migrans of Lyme disease Skin scrapings and mycology to exclude dermatophyte infection Skin biopsy to confirm the reaction pattern and exclude mimics Screening for infective and drug triggers guided by history Full blood count and inflammatory markers Age-appropriate malignancy screen if lesions are persistent or atypical Autoantibody testing where lupus is a consideration Presents as slowly enlarging annular or polycyclic erythematous lesions that spread centrifugally with central clearing, favouring the trunk and proximal limbs A trailing scale on the inner edge of the advancing border is characteristic of the superficial type It is a reactive figurate erythema and often a marker of an underlying trigger rather than a primary disease Recognised triggers include infections (dermatophytes, viruses, bacteria), drugs, foods and, less commonly, underlying malignancy The superficial form is often mildly itchy with the classic trailing scale, whereas the deep form is indurated, non-scaling and more sharply defined Biopsy of the superficial type shows a tight ('coat-sleeve') perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate in the dermis Management focuses on identifying and treating the underlying cause; the eruption often settles once the trigger is removed Rapidly progressive or atypical lesions raising concern for erythema gyratum repens and internal malignancy Persistent eruption unresponsive to treatment of obvious triggers Systemic symptoms suggesting an underlying serious illness Features overlapping with subacute cutaneous lupus Mistaking it for tinea and not confirming with mycology, or vice versa Failing to distinguish it from erythema gyratum repens, which prompts a malignancy search Overlooking a drug or infective trigger Assuming an underlying malignancy in every case, when most are idiopathic or reactive to benign triggers Erythema annulare centrifugum is regarded as a hypersensitivity reaction pattern in which the skin responds to a variety of antigenic stimuli, such as microbial antigens, drugs or, occasionally, tumour-associated antigens. The reactive process produces a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate in the dermis; the superficial variant additionally shows spongiosis and parakeratosis accounting for the trailing scale, while the deep variant has a denser, deeper infiltrate without epidermal change. Centrifugal spread with central clearing gives the characteristic annular and polycyclic configurations. The course is variable, from lesions clearing within weeks to a chronic relapsing pattern lasting months or years; prognosis largely reflects the identifiable underlying trigger, and the eruption often resolves once that is addressed.

Erythema elevatum diutinum — EED, chronic fibrosing leukocytoclastic vasculitis, extracellular cholesterosis (historical) Granuloma annulare Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis of other cause Rheumatoid nodules Bacillary angiomatosis or Kaposi sarcoma (especially in HIV) Xanthomas Skin biopsy showing leukocytoclastic vasculitis in early lesions and fibrosis in older ones Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation for IgA monoclonal gammopathy HIV testing Autoimmune and inflammatory disease screening (including for rheumatoid and connective-tissue disorders) Full blood count and evaluation for haematological disease Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase level before dapsone therapy A rare chronic cutaneous vasculitis presenting as persistent red-brown to violaceous papules, plaques, and nodules Lesions are characteristically symmetrical over extensor surfaces and joints, notably the dorsal hands, elbows, knees, and ankles Early lesions are soft and inflammatory but become firm and fibrotic over time as the disease persists It is considered a chronic form of leukocytoclastic vasculitis with secondary dermal fibrosis Strong associations include IgA monoclonal gammopathy, HIV infection, autoimmune and inflammatory disorders, and haematological disease Histology evolves from a neutrophilic leukocytoclastic vasculitis to a fibrotic picture in older lesions Dapsone is often strikingly effective, reflecting the neutrophilic nature of the infiltrate Detection of a monoclonal gammopathy or haematological disorder requiring haematology review Newly identified HIV infection needing specialist management An underlying systemic autoimmune or inflammatory disease Progressive nodular disease impairing joint function Mistaking it for granuloma annulare or rheumatoid nodules and missing the vasculitic basis Failing to screen for IgA gammopathy and HIV Assuming a single acute vasculitis rather than recognising the chronic fibrosing course Starting dapsone without checking glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status Erythema elevatum diutinum is regarded as a chronic, localised leukocytoclastic vasculitis, probably driven by immune-complex deposition in dermal vessels. Repeated bouts of neutrophilic small-vessel inflammation, with leukocytoclasis and fibrin deposition, lead over time to reactive dermal fibrosis, giving the persistent firm papules and plaques over joints. Circulating immune complexes, frequently in the setting of IgA gammopathy, HIV, or other chronic immune stimulation, are thought to underlie the recurrent vascular injury, which explains both the extensor-surface distribution and the responsiveness to dapsone. Erythema elevatum diutinum is typically chronic and persistent over years, often waxing and waning; it frequently responds well to dapsone, but relapse on withdrawal is common and outcome is influenced by any associated systemic condition.

Erythema gyratum repens — EGR, Gammel's disease, gyrate erythema (wood-grain) Erythema annulare centrifugum Widespread tinea corporis Bullous pemphigoid (figurate/urticarial phase) Pityriasis rubra pilaris Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus Erythrokeratoderma variabilis Urgent search for internal malignancy including chest imaging Age- and risk-appropriate cancer screening (breast, gastrointestinal, gynaecological) Skin biopsy to exclude specific mimics Direct immunofluorescence to exclude bullous pemphigoid Full blood count, inflammatory markers and general health screen Mycology to exclude extensive dermatophytosis Presents as striking concentric, whorled erythematous bands with a fine trailing scale, producing a 'wood-grain' or 'zebra-stripe' pattern The eruption migrates rapidly, sometimes several centimetres per day, and is usually widespread and pruritic It is one of the most specific paraneoplastic dermatoses and should prompt an urgent search for internal malignancy Lung carcinoma is the most frequently associated tumour, followed by oesophageal, breast and other cancers The rash often precedes the diagnosis of the underlying cancer, so recognition offers a chance for earlier detection Biopsy shows non-specific changes such as a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with spongiosis and parakeratosis, so diagnosis is largely clinical Treatment of the underlying tumour typically clears the eruption, whereas symptomatic measures alone are of limited benefit The eruption itself, given its very high association with underlying cancer Weight loss, cough, haemoptysis or other symptoms of internal malignancy Failure of the rash to respond, implying an undetected or untreated tumour Rapidly progressive, widespread involvement Treating the rash symptomatically without pursuing the mandatory malignancy workup Confusing it with the slower, less florid erythema annulare centrifugum Stopping the cancer search after an initial negative screen when the rash persists Overlooking a paraneoplastic cause because biopsy findings are non-specific Erythema gyratum repens is considered a paraneoplastic phenomenon in which tumour-associated antigens are thought to trigger an immune response that cross-reacts with skin antigens, producing a migrating figurate erythema. Immune complex deposition and altered cutaneous antigen expression have been proposed as mechanisms. The rapidly shifting concentric wave-like erythema reflects a dynamic hypersensitivity reaction in the skin, and the close temporal link with an underlying, often occult, malignancy is central to its behaviour. The skin prognosis is favourable once the underlying malignancy is treated, with the eruption usually resolving; however, overall prognosis is dominated by the frequently advanced associated cancer, so the outlook depends chiefly on tumour stage and treatability.

Erythema induratum (nodular vasculitis) — nodular vasculitis, Bazin disease, erythema induratum of Bazin, tuberculid panniculitis Erythema nodosum Polyarteritis nodosa (cutaneous) Superficial thrombophlebitis Pancreatic panniculitis Cutaneous polyarteritis and other vasculitides Lupus panniculitis Deep incisional or excisional skin biopsy capturing subcutaneous fat to show lobular panniculitis with vasculitis Tuberculin skin test and interferon-gamma release assay Chest radiograph and evaluation for active or latent tuberculosis Tissue mycobacterial staining, culture, and polymerase chain reaction for mycobacterial DNA Assessment of venous insufficiency in the lower limbs Screening for alternative infective, drug, or systemic triggers in non-tuberculous cases A lobular panniculitis with vasculitis presenting as tender, indurated, often ulcerating nodules on the posterior lower legs (calves) Predominantly affects women, and lesions tend to be more posterior than the anterior shins typical of erythema nodosum Lesions frequently ulcerate and heal with atrophic scarring and pigmentation, distinguishing it from non-ulcerating erythema nodosum When associated with tuberculosis it is regarded as a tuberculid, an immune (hypersensitivity) reaction to Mycobacterium tuberculosis rather than direct skin infection The term nodular vasculitis is used for clinically and histologically identical disease without demonstrable tuberculous association A strongly positive tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay supports the tuberculid form Cases linked to tuberculosis respond to antituberculous therapy, so evaluating for latent or active infection is essential Evidence of active tuberculosis requiring prompt antituberculous treatment and public-health measures Chronic non-healing ulceration with secondary infection Systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss) suggesting disseminated infection or systemic vasculitis Recurrent disease despite treatment, prompting re-evaluation of the underlying cause Confusing it with erythema nodosum and missing the posterior-leg distribution, ulceration, and vasculitis Taking a biopsy too superficial to sample the subcutaneous fat Failing to investigate for tuberculosis before attributing the disease to another cause Overlooking treatable contributors such as chronic venous insufficiency or a drug trigger Erythema induratum is a lobular panniculitis accompanied by vasculitis of the small and medium vessels within the subcutaneous fat, leading to ischaemic fat necrosis, nodule formation, and ulceration. In the classic Bazin form it represents a tuberculid: a delayed-type hypersensitivity response to mycobacterial antigens disseminated from a distant focus, rather than viable organisms in the skin, so mycobacterial cultures of lesions are typically negative while molecular tests may detect mycobacterial DNA. Identical disease without tuberculous association is termed nodular vasculitis and may follow other infections, drugs, or chronic venous insufficiency. The condition tends to be chronic and relapsing with recurrent crops of nodules and scarring; tuberculid cases usually improve substantially with antituberculous therapy, whereas idiopathic nodular vasculitis may persist and require anti-inflammatory treatment.

Erythema infectiosum — fifth disease, slapped cheek syndrome, parvovirus B19 infection Rubella Measles Scarlet fever Enteroviral exanthem Drug eruption Systemic lupus erythematosus (when arthropathy predominates in adults) Rubella Enteroviral rash illness Other viral arthropathies such as chikungunya or rubella-associated arthritis Clinical diagnosis usually adequate in a well child with the classic rash Parvovirus B19 IgM and IgG serology to confirm recent infection, particularly in pregnancy or arthropathy B19 DNA PCR in immunocompromised patients or when serology is unreliable Full blood count and reticulocyte count where aplastic crisis is suspected Fetal ultrasound surveillance for hydrops after maternal infection in pregnancy Caused by parvovirus B19 and most common in school-aged children, often occurring in community outbreaks The typical rash begins with bright red cheeks giving a slapped-cheek appearance, followed by a lacy, reticular erythematous eruption on the limbs and trunk The rash can wax and wane over weeks and may flare with warmth, sunlight, or exercise By the time the rash appears the child is usually no longer infectious, since viral shedding peaks earlier during the mild prodrome Adults, especially women, more often develop a symmetrical polyarthropathy affecting hands, wrists, and knees rather than a prominent rash Because the virus targets erythroid precursors, it can precipitate transient aplastic crisis in patients with chronic haemolytic disorders and chronic anaemia in the immunocompromised Infection in pregnancy carries a risk of fetal anaemia and hydrops fetalis, warranting fetal surveillance after maternal exposure Sudden severe anaemia with a low reticulocyte count in a patient with an underlying haemolytic disorder (aplastic crisis) Persistent anaemia or marrow suppression in an immunocompromised patient Maternal infection in pregnancy with signs of fetal hydrops or anaemia Profound pancytopenia suggesting a broader marrow process Isolating the child once the rash appears, when infectivity has usually already passed Missing an evolving aplastic crisis in a patient with sickle cell disease or other haemolytic anaemia Overlooking recent parvovirus exposure as a cause of new symmetrical polyarthropathy in an adult Failing to arrange fetal monitoring after documented maternal infection in pregnancy Parvovirus B19 is transmitted mainly by respiratory droplets and binds the P antigen (globoside) on erythroid progenitor cells, halting red cell production. In healthy hosts this transient arrest is clinically silent, and the exanthem and arthropathy that follow are largely immune-complex mediated, appearing as antibody develops. In people who depend on high red cell turnover the production arrest causes an acute aplastic crisis, while persistent infection in immunocompromised patients produces chronic anaemia. Transplacental infection can cause severe fetal anaemia and hydrops. In immunocompetent children and adults the illness is self-limiting with an excellent outcome, though adult arthropathy may linger for weeks to months; the serious outcomes are aplastic crisis in haemolytic disease, chronic anaemia in the immunocompromised, and fetal loss or hydrops in pregnancy.

Erythema multiforme — EM, erythema multiforme minor, erythema multiforme major Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis Urticaria and urticarial vasculitis Fixed drug eruption Bullous or autoimmune blistering disease Viral exanthem Acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus Clinical diagnosis based on the characteristic target lesions and distribution Testing for herpes simplex virus and Mycoplasma pneumoniae when a trigger is sought Skin biopsy in atypical cases to distinguish from other reactions Review of recent medications to help differentiate from drug-induced severe reactions Assessment of mucosal and ocular involvement, with ophthalmology input where indicated An acute, usually self-limiting hypersensitivity reaction characterised by target (iris) lesions with three concentric zones Lesions are typically symmetrical and acral, favouring the extensor surfaces of the hands, forearms, feet, and often the palms and soles Herpes simplex virus is the commonest trigger, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae is an important cause, particularly in children Erythema multiforme major involves significant mucosal disease (oral, ocular, or genital) in addition to skin lesions, whereas the minor form has little or no mucosal involvement It is now regarded as distinct from Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, which have different triggers (mainly drugs), morphology, and far greater skin detachment and mortality Management is largely supportive with removal or treatment of the trigger; recurrent herpes-associated disease may warrant suppressive antiviral therapy Recurrent or persistent disease should prompt a search for an underlying herpes infection or other trigger Extensive skin detachment or a positive Nikolsky sign suggesting Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis Severe mucosal involvement impairing oral intake, vision, or urination Systemic upset with fever and mucosal disease requiring urgent assessment Ocular involvement threatening long-term visual complications Confusing erythema multiforme with Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis and mismanaging severity Overlooking an underlying herpes simplex or Mycoplasma trigger, especially in recurrent disease Failing to assess and manage mucosal and ocular involvement Attributing a target-like drug eruption to infection and missing a culprit medication Erythema multiforme is a cell-mediated immune reaction, most often provoked by infection, in which cytotoxic T lymphocytes target keratinocytes expressing antigens derived from the trigger. In herpes-associated disease, viral DNA fragments are transported to the skin and drive a T-cell response with interferon-gamma-mediated inflammation at the dermo-epidermal junction, producing the characteristic target lesions with central epidermal damage. This immunopathology and its infective triggers distinguish it from the drug-driven, tumour-necrosis-factor and granulysin-mediated widespread keratinocyte apoptosis of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. Erythema multiforme minor is generally self-limiting and resolves over a few weeks without scarring; the herpes-associated form is prone to recurrence, and prognosis is far better than for the more severe drug-induced blistering syndromes it must be distinguished from.

erythema toxicum neonatorum — toxic erythema of the newborn, erythema neonatorum transient neonatal pustular melanosis neonatal herpes simplex infection bullous impetigo or staphylococcal pustulosis congenital or neonatal candidiasis neonatal cephalic pustulosis (neonatal acne) infantile acropustulosis miliaria (rubra or crystallina) Wright or Giemsa stain of pustule contents showing predominant eosinophils Gram stain and bacterial culture to exclude staphylococcal infection when unwell viral swabs and PCR for herpes simplex if vesicular and clinical suspicion exists potassium hydroxide preparation to exclude candidal pustulosis full blood count where peripheral eosinophilia is being assessed septic screen including blood culture if the neonate is systemically unwell skin biopsy only in atypical or diagnostically uncertain presentations A very common, benign, self-limiting eruption of the term newborn, typically appearing in the first few days of life and rarely present at birth. Lesions are blotchy erythematous macules with central urticarial papules, vesicles or pustules, giving the classic flea-bitten appearance. The palms and soles are characteristically spared, reflecting the eruption's association with hair follicles which are absent at those sites. The eruption waxes and wanes and migrates over different body regions over hours to days, then resolves without sequelae. Wright or Giemsa stain of a pustule shows abundant eosinophils, and a peripheral blood eosinophilia may accompany florid cases. It is more frequent in term and post-term, larger infants and is uncommon in the preterm, which helps in bedside reasoning. Diagnosis is clinical; the well appearance of the infant and characteristic morphology distinguish it from serious infective causes of neonatal pustules. No treatment is required and parents should be reassured, but atypical, persistent or pustular eruptions in an unwell neonate warrant a septic and viral screen. an unwell, febrile or poorly feeding neonate, which is inconsistent with benign erythema toxicum grouped vesicles, especially on the scalp or presenting part, raising concern for neonatal herpes simplex pustules with a positive Gram stain or culture indicating bacterial infection lesions present at birth or persisting beyond the expected transient course involvement of palms and soles, which is atypical and should prompt reconsideration mistaking the benign eruption for neonatal sepsis or, conversely, dismissing true infection as erythema toxicum in an unwell baby failing to consider neonatal herpes simplex when vesicles are present over-investigating a well term infant with classic morphology confusing it with transient neonatal pustular melanosis, which is present at birth and leaves pigmented macules not recognising that palm and sole involvement argues against the diagnosis Erythema toxicum neonatorum is a benign inflammatory dermatosis of the newborn whose precise trigger is unknown. Histology shows an eosinophil-rich infiltrate centred on the pilosebaceous unit, with eosinophils and some neutrophils accumulating in the upper follicle and adjacent dermis, and pustules forming in a subcorneal or intrafollicular location. The follicular localisation explains sparing of the palms and soles. Current thinking favours an innate immune or transient inflammatory response, possibly reflecting activation of the neonatal immune system on early microbial colonisation of the skin and hair follicles after birth, rather than any toxic, infective or allergic process. The condition is entirely reactive and leaves no residual pigmentary or scarring change. The prognosis is excellent; the eruption is entirely benign and resolves spontaneously within days to a couple of weeks, leaving no scarring or pigmentary change, and recurrence is unusual.

Erythroderma — exfoliative dermatitis, generalised exfoliative dermatitis, red man syndrome (dermatological) Erythrodermic psoriasis Atopic or other eczema progressing to erythroderma Drug reaction, including DRESS Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma / Sezary syndrome Pityriasis rubra pilaris Inherited ichthyoses and pemphigus foliaceus in specific settings Skin biopsy, often repeated, to help identify the underlying dermatosis Peripheral blood film and flow cytometry to look for circulating atypical (Sezary) cells Bloods assessing fluid, electrolyte, albumin, and infection status Drug history review and consideration of eosinophilia and organ involvement suggesting DRESS Cultures if secondary infection or sepsis is suspected Erythroderma is defined as erythema and scaling affecting more than about 90 per cent of the body surface, and is a clinical syndrome rather than a single disease The most frequent underlying causes are pre-existing dermatoses (psoriasis, atopic and other eczemas), drug reactions, and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with a proportion remaining idiopathic Always take a careful history of prior skin disease and recent drug exposures, as these often reveal the trigger Look for diagnostic clues within the redness: nail and scalp changes suggesting psoriasis, lymphadenopathy raising concern for lymphoma, or an eruption temporally linked to a new medication Widespread skin failure impairs thermoregulation, fluid balance, and the barrier against infection, so treat these patients as systemically unwell Management centres on supportive care (warmth, fluids, emollients, nutrition) alongside identification and treatment of the underlying cause and withdrawal of any culprit drug Repeated skin biopsies over time may be needed because early histology is frequently non-specific and the cause can declare itself later Beware secondary infection and consider it in any patient who deteriorates or develops systemic upset Dermatological emergency: extensive skin failure causes impaired thermoregulation and a high-output cardiac state requiring urgent supportive management Fluid, electrolyte, and protein loss leading to dehydration, hypotension, and metabolic derangement Secondary bacterial infection or sepsis complicating the compromised barrier Features suggesting DRESS or an evolving lymphoma requiring specialist input Frail, elderly, or comorbid patients in whom cardiovascular decompensation is more likely Focusing on the skin alone and neglecting fluid balance, temperature, and nutritional support Assuming a single early biopsy excludes lymphoma or a specific dermatosis Failing to identify and stop a causative drug Underestimating the cardiovascular strain of high cutaneous blood flow in older patients Missing secondary infection as a cause of clinical deterioration Erythroderma reflects a massive inflammatory response in the skin, whatever the trigger, with markedly increased epidermal turnover and a dense dermal inflammatory infiltrate producing generalised erythema and scaling. Loss of the intact cutaneous barrier over almost the entire surface leads to substantial transepidermal water loss, protein and heat loss, and high cutaneous blood flow. The resulting physiological derangements include impaired temperature regulation, fluid and electrolyte disturbance, hypoalbuminaemia, and high-output cardiac demand. The specific microscopic pattern depends on the underlying disease, which is why histology and clinical correlation are both required. Outcome depends heavily on the underlying cause and the patient's comorbidities; many drug-related and dermatosis-related cases resolve with treatment, but lymphoma-associated and idiopathic erythroderma may run a protracted or relapsing course, and severe cases carry meaningful morbidity and mortality.

Progressive symmetric erythrokeratodermia — PSEK, Gottron syndrome, erythrokeratodermia progressiva symmetrica, KRT83/LOR/GJB variants Erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva Pityriasis rubra pilaris Psoriasis Ichthyosis (lamellar or ichthyosiform erythroderma) Netherton syndrome KID (keratitis-ichthyosis-deafness) syndrome Skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis Molecular genetic testing of connexin, LOR and keratin genes as indicated Family history and pedigree analysis Assessment for palmoplantar keratoderma Clinical photography to document progression and symmetry Exclusion of psoriasis and pityriasis rubra pilaris where clinically uncertain Characterised by fixed, symmetrical, well-demarcated erythematous hyperkeratotic plaques, typically over the extensor limbs, buttocks and face Lesions are relatively stable in position (unlike the migratory figures of erythrokeratodermia variabilis) but slowly progress, often during childhood A palmoplantar keratoderma is present in many affected individuals Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant, and it shows genetic overlap with erythrokeratodermia variabilis, with variants reported in connexin and other keratinisation genes such as KRT83 and LOR There is considerable clinical and genetic overlap with erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva, and the two are often considered a spectrum Diagnosis is clinical, supported by biopsy showing hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis; molecular testing may identify a causative variant Management is supportive with emollients and keratolytics, and oral retinoids can substantially improve the hyperkeratosis in severe disease Rapid extension or erythroderma with barrier compromise Deep painful fissuring of associated palmoplantar keratoderma Secondary infection of hyperkeratotic plaques Atypical features prompting reconsideration of an inflammatory or syndromic diagnosis Misdiagnosing the fixed plaques as psoriasis or pityriasis rubra pilaris Failing to recognise the overlap with erythrokeratodermia variabilis Overlooking an associated palmoplantar keratoderma Stopping effective retinoid therapy abruptly with subsequent relapse Progressive symmetric erythrokeratodermia is a genetically heterogeneous disorder of keratinisation. Reported causes include variants affecting gap-junction connexins, loricrin and hair-keratin genes such as KRT83, which disturb keratinocyte communication, cornified-envelope formation and terminal differentiation. The result is a chronic disturbance of epidermal proliferation and differentiation, generating persistent symmetric erythematous hyperkeratotic plaques with a background of increased epidermal turnover, and a frequently associated palmoplantar keratoderma. Its overlap with erythrokeratodermia variabilis reflects shared molecular pathways. The condition is chronic and tends to progress through childhood before stabilising; it is not life-threatening, and many patients respond well to oral retinoids, though relapse on withdrawal is common.

Erythrokeratodermia variabilis — GJB3, GJB4, connexin 31, connexin 30.3, erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva, Mendes da Costa syndrome Progressive symmetric erythrokeratoderma KID syndrome Netherton syndrome Pityriasis rubra pilaris Psoriasis Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma Skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis Molecular genetic testing of GJB3 and GJB4 Clinical documentation/photography of the migratory erythema over time Examination for palmoplantar keratoderma Family history and pedigree analysis Exclusion of inflammatory mimics where the presentation is atypical Characterised by two coexisting features: transient, migratory erythematous patches that change shape over hours to days, and fixed, well-demarcated hyperkeratotic plaques The migratory erythema can be provoked by temperature change, emotion and mechanical trauma Onset is usually in infancy or early childhood, and the fixed plaques often favour the extensor limbs, buttocks and face Most commonly autosomal dominant, caused by mutations in GJB3 (connexin 31) or GJB4 (connexin 30.3) Palmoplantar keratoderma may be present in a proportion of cases Sensation and general health are typically normal, distinguishing it from more severe ichthyoses Management is supportive with emollients/keratolytics and oral retinoids for the fixed keratotic component, and avoidance of provoking factors Rapidly progressive or generalised keratoderma causing functional impairment Secondary infection of fissured hyperkeratotic plaques Atypical features suggesting an alternative ichthyosis or syndrome Significant psychosocial impact from visible, fluctuating erythema Mistaking the migratory erythema for urticaria or an inflammatory dermatosis Overlooking the coexistence of transient erythema and fixed plaques, which is the diagnostic hallmark Assuming systemic or dangerous internal disease when general health is in fact preserved Not counselling on trigger avoidance for the labile erythematous component Erythrokeratodermia variabilis is most often an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in GJB3 or GJB4, which encode the gap-junction proteins connexin 31 and connexin 30.3. Connexins oligomerise into channels that permit direct exchange of ions and small signalling molecules between adjacent keratinocytes, coordinating epidermal differentiation and homeostasis. The mutations disturb assembly and function of these channels and may exert dominant-negative effects, disrupting intercellular communication in the epidermis. This produces two clinical components: labile vasomotor/erythematous change that migrates in response to stimuli, and abnormal terminal differentiation manifesting as fixed hyperkeratotic plaques. Erythrokeratodermia variabilis is a chronic condition that tends to be stable or slowly progressive; the migratory erythema often lessens after childhood while the fixed plaques persist. General health and lifespan are normal, and oral retinoids can markedly improve the keratotic component.

Erythromelalgia — erythermalgia, Mitchell disease, erythromelalgia, red extremity pain syndrome Peripheral neuropathy, including small-fibre and diabetic neuropathy Complex regional pain syndrome Raynaud phenomenon and other vasospastic disorders Cellulitis or other infective causes of a hot red limb Gout and inflammatory arthritis Peripheral arterial disease or vasculitis Full blood count to detect polycythaemia vera or essential thrombocythaemia JAK2 mutation analysis and haematology referral when a myeloproliferative cause is suspected Genetic testing for SCN9A mutations in early-onset or familial disease Screening for secondary causes including autoimmune, neuropathic and drug-related triggers Assessment of skin for cold-immersion damage, maceration and secondary infection Vascular and neurological assessment to exclude mimics such as ischaemia or neuropathy Characterised by episodes of burning pain, marked redness and heat, most often affecting the feet and sometimes the hands Symptoms are triggered or worsened by warmth, exercise and dependency, and are characteristically relieved by cooling and elevation of the affected part Patients often seek relief by immersing the limbs in cold water, which can itself lead to maceration, ulceration and non-healing skin damage The disorder is divided into primary (idiopathic or inherited) and secondary forms, the latter most importantly associated with myeloproliferative disease Myeloproliferative-associated erythromelalgia, particularly with polycythaemia vera or essential thrombocythaemia (often JAK2-related), characteristically responds to low-dose aspirin An inherited primary form is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the SCN9A gene encoding the Nav1.7 sodium channel, presenting early in life A full blood count is essential in every patient to detect an underlying myeloproliferative disorder, which may precede an overt haematological diagnosis Management combines cooling, elevation and avoidance of triggers with aspirin for myeloproliferative-associated disease and treatment of any underlying cause; primary neuropathic forms are often difficult to control An underlying myeloproliferative disorder revealed by an abnormal blood count Tissue damage, ulceration or infection from repeated cold-water immersion Rapid onset or severe unremitting pain suggesting a secondary or ischaemic cause Thrombotic or bleeding complications in myeloproliferative-associated disease Omitting a full blood count and missing an underlying myeloproliferative disorder that may respond to aspirin Encouraging or overlooking harmful prolonged cold-water immersion that damages the skin Attributing the hot red limb to cellulitis and giving unnecessary antibiotics Failing to consider an inherited sodium-channel cause in early-onset or familial cases Erythromelalgia reflects a mismatch between skin perfusion and metabolic demand, with maldistribution of blood flow causing both increased superficial perfusion (redness and warmth) and paradoxical tissue hypoxia that generates burning pain. In myeloproliferative-associated disease, platelet-mediated microvascular occlusion and inflammation within the small vessels are thought to drive the symptoms, which is why antiplatelet therapy with aspirin is so effective. In the inherited primary form, gain-of-function mutations in the SCN9A gene increase the excitability of the Nav1.7 sodium channel in peripheral sensory and sympathetic neurons, lowering the threshold for pain and vasomotor dysregulation. Secondary erythromelalgia may also accompany drugs, connective tissue disease and neuropathies, reflecting varied vascular and neural mechanisms. Prognosis varies with the cause: myeloproliferative-associated erythromelalgia often improves markedly with aspirin and treatment of the blood disorder, whereas primary and neuropathic forms tend to be chronic and refractory, and complications may arise from aggressive cooling behaviours.

erythromelalgia primary — primary erythromelalgia, erythermalgia, Mitchell disease Complex regional pain syndrome Peripheral small-fibre neuropathy Raynaud phenomenon (opposite triggers and colour change) Fabry disease Peripheral arterial disease Cellulitis Acute gout or inflammatory arthritis Full blood count with JAK2 mutation analysis to exclude a myeloproliferative neoplasm SCN9A genetic testing when there is early onset or a family history Small-fibre neuropathy assessment including skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density and quantitative sensory testing Thermography or skin temperature monitoring during an episode Autoimmune and connective tissue disease screen Review of medications known to provoke the condition Characterised by episodes of burning pain, erythema and increased warmth of the extremities, affecting the feet more often than the hands and usually bilateral and symmetrical. Symptoms are provoked by heat, exercise and limb dependency and are relieved by cooling and elevation. Patients often immerse the limbs in cold water for relief, which can cause maceration, non-healing wounds and immersion injury. The primary (inherited) form is linked to gain-of-function mutations in SCN9A encoding the Nav1.7 sodium channel, with autosomal dominant inheritance and early onset. Secondary erythromelalgia is most importantly associated with myeloproliferative neoplasms, particularly polycythaemia vera and essential thrombocythaemia. Erythromelalgia due to thrombocythaemia responds dramatically to aspirin, whereas primary channelopathy-related disease typically does not. There is considerable overlap with small-fibre neuropathy, and many patients have abnormal intraepidermal nerve fibre findings. Skin breakdown, ulceration or immersion injury from repeated cooling Features of a myeloproliferative neoplasm such as thrombosis, splenomegaly or abnormal blood counts Rapidly progressive or treatment-refractory symptoms Signs of secondary infection in macerated skin Permitting prolonged cold-water immersion, which causes tissue damage and non-healing wounds. Missing an underlying myeloproliferative neoplasm as a treatable cause. Misdiagnosing an acute episode as cellulitis and giving unnecessary antibiotics. Failing to recognise a heritable sodium-channelopathy in a child or young adult with a positive family history. Erythromelalgia reflects a mismatch between skin metabolic demand and perfusion, with maldistribution of cutaneous blood flow and arteriovenous shunting that leaves the skin relatively hypoxic despite increased total flow, producing the red, hot, painful extremity. In the primary inherited form, gain-of-function mutations in the SCN9A gene alter the Nav1.7 voltage-gated sodium channel expressed in nociceptive and sympathetic neurons, lowering their firing threshold and causing hyperexcitability and neuropathic burning pain. Secondary forms arise from platelet-mediated microvascular occlusion in myeloproliferative disease or from other neuropathic and vasomotor disturbances. The primary form is often lifelong and may be refractory to treatment, whereas secondary erythromelalgia usually improves when the underlying cause is addressed, and thrombocythaemic disease characteristically responds to aspirin.

erythromelalgia secondary — secondary erythermalgia, acquired erythromelalgia Primary (hereditary SCN9A) erythromelalgia Complex regional pain syndrome Peripheral (small-fibre) neuropathy of other cause Cellulitis or other localised infection Raynaud phenomenon with reperfusion hyperaemia Fabry disease acroparaesthesiae Peripheral arterial disease with rest pain Full blood count and peripheral blood film to detect myeloproliferative neoplasm JAK2 V617F and related myeloproliferative mutation testing Fasting glucose and HbA1c to assess for diabetes mellitus Autoimmune serology including antinuclear antibodies for connective-tissue disease Nerve conduction studies and small-fibre assessment (e.g. skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density) Medication review to identify vasodilator or other drug triggers Screening for occult malignancy where a paraneoplastic cause is suspected Secondary erythromelalgia is characterised by episodic burning pain, marked erythema and warmth of the extremities, most often the feet, triggered by heat, exercise or dependency and relieved by cooling and elevation. Unlike the inherited primary form caused by SCN9A sodium-channel mutations, the secondary type arises from an identifiable underlying disorder, most classically a myeloproliferative neoplasm such as polycythaemia vera or essential thrombocythaemia. Myeloproliferative-associated erythromelalgia frequently responds dramatically to low-dose aspirin, reflecting a platelet-mediated arteriolar inflammatory-thrombotic mechanism, a response that is a useful diagnostic clue. Other secondary causes include connective-tissue disease, diabetes mellitus, peripheral neuropathy, drugs such as calcium-channel blockers and certain vasodilators, and paraneoplastic states. Patients characteristically immerse affected limbs in cold water or seek cold surfaces for relief, which can lead to maceration, immersion injury or secondary infection. A full blood count with examination of the film is mandatory in any adult presenting with erythromelalgia to exclude an occult myeloproliferative neoplasm, which may precede overt blood-count abnormalities. Management targets the underlying cause together with symptom control using cooling, limb elevation, and agents such as aspirin for platelet-driven disease or neuropathic-pain modulators for neuropathic forms. Aggressive cooling should be discouraged as prolonged immersion can precipitate ulceration, necrosis and infection, worsening long-term outcome. Abnormal full blood count or splenomegaly suggesting an underlying myeloproliferative neoplasm Digital ulceration, necrosis or gangrene from disease or excessive cooling Signs of secondary infection following repeated cold immersion Rapidly progressive neurological deficit accompanying the limb symptoms Systemic features suggesting occult malignancy or active connective-tissue disease Failing to check a full blood count and thereby missing an occult myeloproliferative neoplasm Mistaking the warm, red painful limb for cellulitis and prescribing unnecessary antibiotics Permitting prolonged cold immersion, which causes maceration, ulceration and infection Assuming all erythromelalgia is primary and overlooking a treatable secondary trigger such as a drug Attributing symptoms to peripheral arterial disease and missing the diagnosis Secondary erythromelalgia results from a maldistribution of skin blood flow in which there is inappropriate arteriovenous shunting and microvascular hypoperfusion despite overall increased flow and erythema, so tissue oxygenation is paradoxically reduced during attacks. In myeloproliferative disease, abnormal, hyperreactive platelets adhere to and inflame arteriolar walls, producing platelet-fibrin thrombi and a local inflammatory response that generates burning pain and compensatory vasodilatation; this platelet-driven mechanism underlies the striking sensitivity to aspirin. In neuropathic and connective-tissue-associated forms, dysregulation of small-fibre sensory and autonomic nerves alters vasomotor control and nociceptive signalling. Heat and dependency lower the threshold for symptomatic vasodilatation, while cooling and elevation reduce metabolic demand and shunting, temporarily relieving symptoms. Prognosis largely follows the underlying cause; platelet-driven myeloproliferative erythromelalgia often improves markedly with treatment of the neoplasm and aspirin, whereas neuropathic and idiopathic secondary forms tend to be chronic and harder to control.

Erythronychia — Red nail streaks, Longitudinal erythronychia Onychopapilloma Glomus tumour Bowen disease or squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the nail unit Amelanotic subungual melanoma Lichen planus of the nail Darier disease Graft-versus-host disease affecting the nails Dermoscopy of the nail plate and free edge Nail matrix and bed biopsy of a solitary or symptomatic band Examination of all twenty nails to distinguish mono- from polydactylous disease Skin and mucosal examination for lichen planus or Darier disease Imaging such as MRI for suspected glomus tumour Histopathology of the free-edge subungual keratosis Erythronychia denotes red discolouration of the nail, seen most usefully as one or more longitudinal red bands running from the lunula to the free edge. Longitudinal erythronychia reflects a thinned ventral nail plate overlying a vascular focus, often accompanied by distal splinter haemorrhage, a V-shaped nick or subungual keratosis at the free margin. Single-band (monodactylous) longitudinal erythronychia in one nail should prompt concern for a localised tumour, classically onychopapilloma, but also glomus tumour, Bowen disease or amelanotic melanoma. Polydactylous longitudinal erythronychia affecting multiple nails is more often associated with systemic or inflammatory dermatoses such as lichen planus, Darier disease or graft-versus-host disease. Darier disease characteristically produces alternating longitudinal red and white bands with distal wedge-shaped nicking. Dermoscopy and, where a single symptomatic or evolving band exists, matrix and bed biopsy are central to excluding neoplasia. A painful single red band, particularly with cold sensitivity and pinpoint tenderness, suggests a glomus tumour. Because a solitary band can harbour malignancy, persistent monodactylous erythronychia should not be dismissed as cosmetic. A single persistent or evolving red band, especially if painful or bleeding Associated nail plate destruction, ulceration or a distal nodule Rapid change in width, colour or symptoms of a longitudinal band Erythronychia with a subungual mass or bony change on imaging Dismissing a solitary longitudinal red band as trivial and missing an underlying tumour Attributing all erythronychia to systemic disease without examining the individual band morphology Overlooking a glomus tumour as a cause of an exquisitely tender red streak Failing to sample the free-edge keratosis, which often holds the diagnostic clue The red colour is produced when the nail bed vasculature becomes more visible through a nail plate that has been focally thinned or has lost its normal attachment. In localised longitudinal erythronychia a discrete lesion in the distal matrix or bed, such as an onychopapilloma or glomus tumour, alters keratinisation so that the overlying plate is thinned along a narrow channel, allowing the dilated capillaries of the bed to show through as a red line; fragility of this channel accounts for the associated splinter haemorrhages and distal notch. In polydactylous disease a generalised inflammatory or dyskeratotic matrix process, as in lichen planus or Darier disease, produces the same thinning across several nails. The band is therefore a window onto matrix and bed pathology rather than a primary vascular abnormality. Prognosis depends entirely on the cause: benign onychopapilloma and inflammatory dermatoses do well, whereas an unrecognised subungual carcinoma or melanoma carries the prognosis of the underlying malignancy. Solitary bands therefore merit histological clarification.

Erythropoietic protoporphyria — EPP, ferrochelatase deficiency, FECH deficiency, protoporphyria, X-linked protoporphyria (ALAS2 variant) Polymorphic light eruption and solar urticaria Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (blistering photosensitivity) Porphyria cutanea tarda and other bullous porphyrias Contact or phototoxic dermatitis Hydroa vacciniforme Secondary protoporphyrinaemia from lead poisoning or iron deficiency Erythrocyte protoporphyrin measurement, distinguishing free (metal-free) from zinc-bound protoporphyrin Plasma fluorescence scanning with a characteristic emission peak Molecular genetic testing of the FECH gene (and ALAS2 for the X-linked form) Liver function tests and monitoring for protoporphyric hepatopathy Iron studies, as iron status can influence the phenotype Abdominal imaging where gallstones or hepatic involvement are suspected Caused by deficient ferrochelatase, the final enzyme of haem biosynthesis; a phenotypically similar X-linked form results from gain-of-function ALAS2 mutations Typically presents in early childhood with immediate painful, burning photosensitivity on sun exposure, often without prominent visible skin lesions Acute reactions cause intense stinging or burning pain, erythema and oedema; chronic changes include waxy thickening and shallow scars over the knuckles and nose The characteristic pain without blistering distinguishes it from the bullous cutaneous porphyrias and often leads to years of diagnostic delay The biochemical hallmark is markedly raised free (metal-free) erythrocyte protoporphyrin, with normal urinary porphyrins because protoporphyrin is not water-soluble A minority develop protoporphyric hepatopathy, as excess protoporphyrin is excreted in bile and can precipitate as gallstones or cause cholestatic liver failure Management centres on strict sunlight and visible-light avoidance and photoprotection; afamelanotide is an approved treatment to increase light tolerance Signs of protoporphyric liver disease such as jaundice, rising bilirubin or hepatic failure Rapidly worsening photosensitivity suggesting deteriorating liver function Severe, disabling phototoxic pain limiting daily activity Gallstone-related biliary obstruction Long diagnostic delay because painful photosensitivity without blistering is not recognised as porphyria Relying on urinary porphyrins, which are normal, and missing the diagnosis Overlooking progressive liver disease until it is advanced Failing to protect the skin and eyes from visible as well as ultraviolet light Not screening relatives, as inheritance and the low-expression FECH allele complicate risk assessment Erythropoietic protoporphyria results from reduced activity of ferrochelatase, the last enzyme of haem biosynthesis, which inserts iron into protoporphyrin IX to form haem; in the X-linked variant, increased ALAS2 activity overproduces protoporphyrin. Either mechanism causes accumulation of lipophilic, photoreactive protoporphyrin, chiefly in erythrocytes. On exposure to visible light of the appropriate wavelength, protoporphyrin in dermal blood vessels generates reactive oxygen species that cause an acute, painful phototoxic reaction. Because protoporphyrin is water-insoluble it is cleared in bile rather than urine, and biliary overload can lead to gallstones and, in a minority, progressive cholestatic liver disease. Most patients have a normal lifespan with a chronic burden of painful photosensitivity; the main serious risk is the small proportion who develop rapidly progressive protoporphyric liver failure requiring specialist and sometimes transplant management.

Escobar syndrome — non-lethal multiple pterygium syndrome, multiple pterygium syndrome, Escobar variant, Escobar variant multiple pterygium syndrome, CHRNG Lethal multiple pterygium syndrome Distal surveillance Caused by autosomal recessive variants in CHRNG, encoding the gamma subunit of the foetal acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction Because the foetal (gamma) receptor is downslanting palpebral fissures, a small mouth and micrognathia Management is supportive with physiotherapy, splinting and surgical release, noting that pterygia often contain neurovascular structures that complicate surgery Rapidly progressive scoliosis compromising respiratory function Neurovascular injury risk during pterygium release surgery Restrictive lung disease from thoracic and spinal deformity Feeding or airway difficulty in infants with facial involvement Confusing the non-lethal Escobar variant with the lethal multiple pterygium syndrome Operating on pterygia without recognising that they may contain nerves and vessels Under-monitoring for progressive scoliosis Missing the autosomal recessive inheritance and its recurrence implications Escobar syndrome is caused by loss-of-function variants in CHRNG, the gene for the gamma subunit of the acetylcholine receptor. This subunit is part of the foetal-type receptor that mediates neuromuscular transmission before birth, when it is normally replaced by the adult epsilon subunit. Deficient foetal neuromuscular transmission reduces foetal movement during development, producing joint contractures and the skin webs (pterygia) that bridge the flexed joints. Because the adult receptor takes over after birth, there is no ongoing myasthenic weakness, and the phenotype is essentially static, distinguishing the Escobar variant from the lethal form. Lifespan is usually normal and intellect is typically preserved; however affected individuals face significant orthopaedic morbidity from contractures and progressive scoliosis, and surgical correction of pterygia is challenging because of contained neurovascular bundles.

(as a coexisting anomaly rather than mimic) Attempted passage of a radio-opaque orogastric tube with chest radiograph showing coiling in the upper pouch Chest and abdominal radiograph to assess distal atresia with distal fistula (most common) to isolated atresia, isolated (H-type) fistula, and proximal fistula variants Strongly linked to the VACTERL association, so vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, renal, and limb anomalies should be screened for Management is surgical repair with ligation of any fistula and oesophageal anastomosis, primarily or in stages when the gap is long Recurrent cyanotic and choking episodes with aspiration before repair Marked gaseous abdominal distension from a large distal fistula worsening ventilation Coexisting major congenital heart disease affecting operative risk Respiratory failure requiring ventilation, which can force fistula gas into the stomach Anastomotic leak, stricture, or recurrent fistula after repair Feeding a drooling neonate before excluding oesophageal atresia Missing an isolated H-type fistula, which can present later with recurrent chest infections Overlooking the VACTERL association and undetected cardiac or renal anomalies Failing to identify a right-sided aortic arch, which alters the surgical approach Attributing all postoperative feeding problems to stricture without considering dysmotility or recurrent fistula Oesophageal atresia with or without tracheo-oesophageal fistula results from abnormal separation of the primitive foregut into the trachea and oesophagus during early gestation, when the tracheoesophageal septum normally divides the two structures. Faulty septation leaves the oesophagus discontinuous and frequently maintains an abnormal communication between the airway and oesophagus. A distal fistula allows air to enter the stomach and permits reflux of gastric contents into the lungs, while secretions pooling in the blind upper pouch spill into the trachea, both contributing to aspiration and respiratory compromise. Associated tracheomalacia and dysmotility of the repaired oesophagus are common longer-term issues. Survival is excellent for infants without severe cardiac or chromosomal anomalies, and most achieve satisfactory swallowing. Long-gap atresia, major associated anomalies, and prematurity worsen outcomes, and many children have ongoing reflux, oesophageal strictures, dysmotility, or tracheomalacia requiring follow-up.

May be congenital or acquired and can be associated with mucocutaneous or autoimmune conditions Progressive rather than intermittent dysphagia suggesting stricture or malignancy Weight loss, odynophagia, or bleeding Post-cricoid web with iron deficiency, given the increased risk of hypopharyngeal cancer Food impaction requiring urgent endoscopy Missing a thin web on endoscopy because it ruptures on scope passage Failing to recognise and treat the associated iron deficiency Attributing dysphagia to a web without excluding malignancy Confusing a proximal web with a distal Schatzki ring An oesophageal web is a thin, shelf-like protrusion of mucosa and submucosa that partially occludes the lumen. Webs may be congenital or acquired, the latter linked to chronic iron deficiency, mucosal inflammation, and certain immune-mediated dermatoses. The membrane narrows the effective luminal diameter, so that bolus transit of solids is intermittently obstructed, producing dysphagia; because the wall muscle is not involved, peristalsis is preserved and symptoms depend chiefly on the degree of luminal compromise. Symptomatic webs generally respond well to endoscopic disruption or dilatation, though they can recur; the main concern with post-cricoid webs is the associated long-term risk of hypopharyngeal squamous carcinoma.

Essential palatal tremor — essential palatal myoclonus, primary palatal tremor Symptomatic (oculopalatal) tremor Middle-ear myoclonus (stapedius or tensor tympani) Other causes of objective tinnitus (vascular, patulous Eustachian tube) Functional movement disorder Temporomandibular joint clicking Direct examination of the soft palate for rhythmic movement Otological assessment of the clicking tinnitus MRI of the brainstem to exclude a lesion causing symptomatic tremor Assessment for functional signs such as distractibility and variability Audiological evaluation where indicated Rhythmic involuntary movement of the soft palate with no identifiable structural brain lesion The characteristic complaint is an objective clicking tinnitus that the examiner may also hear, produced by rhythmic opening of the Eustachian tube Contraction of the tensor veli palatini muscle is responsible for the ear click It typically stops during sleep, unlike the symptomatic form which often persists MRI is normal, in contrast to symptomatic palatal tremor with hypertrophic olivary degeneration A proportion of cases are functional, so positive functional signs should be sought Persistence during sleep or associated pendular nystagmus suggesting the symptomatic form Brainstem or cerebellar signs A lesion on imaging Progressive additional neurological features Failing to distinguish it from symptomatic palatal tremor by imaging and sleep behaviour Overlooking middle-ear myoclonus as an alternative cause of objective clicking Not considering a functional cause Dismissing the objective tinnitus as subjective Essential palatal tremor is characterised by rhythmic contraction of the tensor veli palatini, which rhythmically opens the Eustachian tube and generates an audible click perceived as objective tinnitus. Unlike symptomatic palatal tremor, there is no lesion in the Guillain-Mollaret triangle and no hypertrophic olivary degeneration, and the underlying mechanism is uncertain, with some cases having a functional basis. The absence of a structural substrate and the frequent disappearance during sleep distinguish it from the symptomatic form. The condition is benign though the click can be distressing; it may remit spontaneously or fluctuate, and various treatments including botulinum toxin to the palatal muscle are used with variable success.

Essential thrombocythaemia — essential thrombocythemia, primary thrombocythaemia, ET Reactive (secondary) thrombocytosis Polycythaemia vera or primary myelofibrosis (prefibrotic) Chronic myeloid leukaemia Myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative overlap with thrombocytosis Iron deficiency with reactive thrombocytosis Full blood count and blood film JAK2, CALR and MPL mutation analysis Bone marrow examination assessing megakaryocyte morphology Exclusion of reactive causes (inflammation, iron deficiency, bleeding) von Willebrand assessment at very high platelet counts A myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by a persistently raised platelet count from clonal megakaryocyte proliferation Driver mutations are found in JAK2, CALR or MPL, with a minority triple-negative Many patients are asymptomatic; others have vasomotor symptoms such as headache, erythromelalgia and visual disturbance Both thrombosis and, at very high platelet counts, bleeding (from acquired von Willebrand syndrome) can occur It is a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring reactive thrombocytosis and other myeloproliferative neoplasms to be ruled out Risk-adapted management uses aspirin and, in higher-risk patients, platelet-lowering cytoreduction Arterial or venous thrombosis Bleeding with extreme thrombocytosis (acquired von Willebrand syndrome) Progressive splenomegaly or cytopenias suggesting fibrotic transformation Blasts suggesting leukaemic transformation Treating reactive thrombocytosis as essential thrombocythaemia Giving aspirin at extreme counts without checking for acquired von Willebrand syndrome Missing prefibrotic myelofibrosis on marrow morphology Overlooking CALR/MPL in JAK2-negative cases Essential thrombocythaemia is a clonal stem cell disorder in which mutations in JAK2, CALR or MPL activate thrombopoietin-receptor signalling, driving excess megakaryopoiesis and a sustained rise in platelets. The qualitatively abnormal platelets, together with the raised count and interactions with the vessel wall, increase thrombotic risk. Paradoxically, extreme thrombocytosis can cause bleeding through an acquired von Willebrand syndrome, as large von Willebrand multimers are adsorbed and degraded. Long-term clonal evolution can lead to myelofibrosis or, less often, acute leukaemia. Life expectancy is near-normal for many patients with appropriate risk management, though thrombosis and haemorrhage cause morbidity and a minority transform to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia.

Essential thrombocythaemia — ET, essential thrombocythemia, essential thrombocytosis, primary thrombocythaemia Reactive (secondary) thrombocytosis from iron deficiency, infection, or inflammation Chronic myeloid leukaemia Polycythaemia vera Primary myelofibrosis (prefibrotic stage) Myelodysplastic syndrome with thrombocytosis Post-splenectomy thrombocytosis Full blood count and blood film to confirm sustained thrombocytosis and assess morphology Molecular testing for JAK2 V617F, and if negative, CALR and MPL mutations BCR-ABL1 testing to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia Bone marrow aspirate and trephine showing enlarged, clustered megakaryocytes Iron studies, inflammatory markers, and screening for occult malignancy to exclude reactive causes Assessment for acquired von Willebrand syndrome when counts are very high or bleeding occurs A myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by a sustained rise in platelet count from clonal overproduction of megakaryocytes Many patients are asymptomatic and detected on a routine blood count, while others present with vasomotor symptoms such as headache, erythromelalgia (burning red extremities), and visual disturbance Both arterial and venous thrombosis and, paradoxically, bleeding can occur; bleeding risk rises with very high platelet counts due to acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency Most cases carry a driver mutation in JAK2, CALR, or MPL, which supports clonality and helps distinguish ET from reactive thrombocytosis Reactive causes of a high platelet count (iron deficiency, infection, inflammation, malignancy, post-splenectomy) must be excluded before diagnosing ET Treatment intensity is guided by thrombotic risk, factoring in age, prior thrombosis, and JAK2 status; low-dose aspirin is used for microvascular symptoms and thrombosis prevention Cytoreduction (for example with hydroxyurea) is reserved for higher-risk patients to lower the platelet count and reduce thrombotic events Long-term risks include transformation to myelofibrosis or, less commonly, acute leukaemia Acute arterial or venous thrombosis, including stroke, myocardial infarction, or splanchnic vein thrombosis Significant haemorrhage, particularly with extreme thrombocytosis and acquired von Willebrand deficiency Transient neurological or visual symptoms indicating microvascular ischaemia Features of transformation to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia such as worsening cytopenias or new blasts Diagnosing ET without excluding reactive thrombocytosis and chronic myeloid leukaemia Prescribing aspirin at very high platelet counts without recognising acquired von Willebrand syndrome and bleeding risk Underestimating thrombotic risk in JAK2-positive or older patients Attributing microvascular symptoms to unrelated causes and missing the underlying disorder Failing to reassess for transformation when the blood picture changes ET is a clonal disorder of the haematopoietic stem cell in which constitutive activation of the JAK-STAT signalling pathway, most often through JAK2 V617F, CALR, or MPL mutations, drives excessive megakaryocyte proliferation and platelet production independent of normal regulatory signals. The expanded platelet mass and qualitatively abnormal platelets promote thrombosis in the microcirculation and larger vessels. At very high counts, platelets adsorb and clear large von Willebrand factor multimers, producing an acquired von Willebrand syndrome and a paradoxical bleeding tendency. Over years the clone may evolve towards marrow fibrosis or acute leukaemia. Life expectancy in ET is close to that of the general population for many patients, with the principal threats being thrombosis and haemorrhage; a minority progress over years to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia, which markedly worsens outlook.

that may produce or amplify tremor DaTscan or specialist assessment when distinguishing from Parkinson disease is difficult The hallmark is a bilateral, largely symmetric postural and kinetic (action)
