anticonvulsant primidone Deep brain stimulation of the ventral intermediate thalamic nucleus can help severe, medication-refractory cases Onset spans a wide age range, and prevalence and severity tend to increase with age Strictly unilateral tremor, a resting component, or associated bradykinesia and rigidity suggesting Parkinson disease Abrupt onset or rapid progression suggesting a structural, toxic, or metabolic cause Young age of onset with Kayser-Fleischer rings or hepatic dysfunction suggesting Wilson disease Accompanying cerebellar signs, ataxia, or other focal neurological deficits Confusing essential tremor with early Parkinson disease, which delays appropriate management Overlooking a reversible cause such as thyrotoxicosis, medication, or excess caffeine Missing Wilson disease in a young patient with tremor Assuming the disorder is trivial and underestimating its impact on daily function and quality of life Essential tremor is a common movement disorder thought to arise from abnormal oscillatory activity within cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuits, with the inferior olive and cerebellum implicated as key nodes of a central oscillator. It is often familial with autosomal dominant inheritance and variable penetrance, though the precise genetic and neurodegenerative substrate remains incompletely defined, and some evidence points to cerebellar pathology. Essential tremor is typically slowly progressive over years. Although often labelled benign, it can become functionally and socially disabling, impairing writing, eating, and drinking; many patients gain useful relief from medication or, in refractory cases, from surgical neuromodulation.

esthesioneuroblastoma — olfactory neuroblastoma, esthesioneurocytoma Sinonasal undifferentiated carcinoma Sinonasal neuroendocrine or small cell carcinoma Rhabdomyosarcoma (particularly in the paediatric population) Ewing sarcoma / primitive neuroectodermal tumour Sinonasal mucosal melanoma Sinonasal lymphoma (extranodal NK/T-cell type) Olfactory groove meningioma or pituitary adenoma Nasal endoscopy with representative biopsy of the vault mass Contrast-enhanced MRI of the paranasal sinuses and brain to define dural, intracranial and orbital extension and interface cysts High-resolution CT of the sinuses to assess cribriform plate and lamina papyracea erosion Immunohistochemistry panel (synaptophysin, chromogranin, S100 sustentacular pattern, cytokeratin) to confirm diagnosis Whole-body PET-CT for staging and detection of distant disease Neck imaging and ultrasound for regional nodal assessment Ophthalmology review with visual fields where orbital involvement is suspected Rare malignant neuroectodermal tumour arising from the olfactory neuroepithelium high in the nasal vault (cribriform plate, superior turbinate, upper septum). Classic bimodal age distribution with peaks in the second and sixth decades, and no strong sex predilection. Typical presentation is unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis; hyposmia or anosmia is frequent but often unnoticed by the patient. A dumbbell-shaped mass straddling the cribriform plate with intracranial and intranasal components is a characteristic imaging appearance. Kadish staging (A confined to nasal cavity, B nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses, C extension beyond, D nodal or distant disease) and Hyams histological grade together drive prognosis and management. Histology shows small round blue cells in lobules with neurofibrillary stroma, Homer Wright and occasionally Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. Immunohistochemistry shows synaptophysin and chromogranin positivity with S100-positive sustentacular cells at lobule peripheries and usually negative or only focal cytokeratin. Craniofacial or expanded endoscopic resection with negative skull-base margins plus adjuvant radiotherapy is the mainstay; late neck-node and delayed local recurrence mandate prolonged surveillance. Intracranial or dural extension with headache, altered mental state or CSF rhinorrhoea Orbital invasion causing proptosis, diplopia or visual loss New or enlarging neck lump suggesting nodal metastasis Cranial neuropathy indicating skull-base spread Progressive unilateral nasal obstruction with epistaxis and anosmia in an adult Mistaking the mass for a benign inflammatory nasal polyp, delaying diagnosis and biopsy Interpreting the biopsy as another small round blue cell tumour without a neuroendocrine immunohistochemistry panel Relying on CT alone and underestimating intracranial or orbital extension that MRI would reveal Failing to survey for late nodal and distant recurrence during follow-up Leaving positive skull-base margins after resection The tumour arises from the basal neuronal precursor cells of the olfactory neuroepithelium lining the roof of the nasal cavity, showing malignant neuroectodermal and neuroendocrine differentiation. It grows in an organoid lobular pattern within a neurofibrillary matrix and characteristically erodes the cribriform plate to invade the anterior cranial fossa, dura and orbit; cysts at the tumour-brain interface are a helpful marker of intracranial spread. Hyams grading (I to IV) reflects preservation of lobular architecture, degree of rosette formation, mitotic activity, nuclear pleomorphism and the presence of necrosis, with higher grades behaving more aggressively. Low Kadish stage and low Hyams grade with complete craniofacial resection and adjuvant radiotherapy carry a favourable long-term outlook. Higher stage, high grade, dural or intracranial extension and nodal spread worsen survival, and late recurrences occur many years later, so lifelong follow-up is essential.

Ethylene glycol poisoning — antifreeze poisoning, ethylene glycol toxicity, glycol poisoning Methanol poisoning Diabetic ketoacidosis Lactic acidosis from other causes Salicylate poisoning Uraemia and other high anion-gap acidoses Serum ethylene glycol level where available Arterial blood gas with calculated anion gap Serum osmolality with calculated osmolal gap Serum calcium, electrolytes, urea, and creatinine Urine microscopy for calcium oxalate crystals and ECG for QT interval Ethylene glycol, found in antifreeze and coolants, is itself relatively harmless but is metabolised to glycolic and oxalic acids that cause severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis and organ injury The course classically evolves in stages: an early neurological phase resembling alcohol intoxication, then a cardiopulmonary phase, and finally a renal phase with acute kidney injury Precipitation of calcium oxalate crystals causes renal tubular damage and produces hypocalcaemia, which may manifest as tetany or QT prolongation Suspect it in unexplained high anion-gap metabolic acidosis with a raised osmolal gap; calcium oxalate crystals may be seen on urine microscopy Fomepizole is the antidote of choice, inhibiting alcohol dehydrogenase to prevent formation of toxic acids; ethanol is an alternative where fomepizole is not available Cofactor therapy with thiamine and pyridoxine is given to divert metabolism toward non-toxic products Haemodialysis removes the parent compound and its metabolites and corrects acidosis, and is indicated for severe acidosis, renal failure, or high levels Urinary fluorescence under Wood's lamp (from fluorescein added to some antifreeze) is unreliable and should not be used to confirm or exclude the diagnosis Severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis Acute kidney injury with oliguria Hypocalcaemia with tetany, seizures, or QT prolongation Reduced consciousness or coma Rising anion gap with a falling osmolal gap indicating ongoing metabolism to toxic acids False reassurance during the early intoxication-like phase before acidosis and renal injury develop Delaying antidote to await a confirmatory ethylene glycol level in a suggestive presentation Relying on urine fluorescence to make or exclude the diagnosis Missing life-threatening hypocalcaemia and its cardiac effects Ethylene glycol is oxidised by alcohol dehydrogenase to glycoaldehyde, then to glycolic acid and finally oxalic acid. Glycolic acid is the main contributor to the profound high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, while oxalic acid combines with calcium to form insoluble calcium oxalate crystals that deposit in renal tubules, causing acute kidney injury, and lower serum calcium. Accumulating toxic metabolites also impair oxidative metabolism, producing lactic acidosis. The parent alcohol raises serum osmolality, giving an early osmolal gap that later falls as the anion gap widens. Prompt antidote and, when needed, dialysis before significant metabolite accumulation usually allow full recovery; delayed treatment can lead to permanent renal failure, neurological injury, and death.

the metabolic and vascular picture together is highly suggestive Management is supportive; combined metronidazole (to reduce sulphide-producing gut flora) and N-acetylcysteine has shown some benefit Rapidly progressive encephalopathy with developmental regression Recurrent haemorrhagic/petechial skin lesions and acrocyanosis Severe lactic acidosis during intercurrent illness Refractory chronic diarrhoea with failure to thrive Neurological deterioration with new basal ganglia lesions Attributing ethylmalonic aciduria solely to short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency and missing ETHE1 disease Interpreting the petechiae as a primary bleeding or vasculitic disorder Overlooking the diagnostic value of combining the metabolic and vascular/gastrointestinal features Delaying targeted therapy while pursuing an extensive alternative workup Assuming a purely mitochondrial cocktail will help without addressing sulphide toxicity Ethylmalonic encephalopathy is caused by loss of function of ETHE1, a mitochondrial matrix sulphur dioxygenase (persulphide dioxygenase) that is essential for the detoxification of hydrogen sulphide generated by gut bacteria and endogenous metabolism. When ETHE1 activity is lost, hydrogen sulphide accumulates in tissues where it inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) of the respiratory chain and short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase. This produces a mitochondrial energy-failure state with lactic acidosis, accumulation of ethylmalonic acid and short-chain acylcarnitines, and toxic injury to the highly perfused brain, gastrointestinal mucosa and vascular endothelium, accounting for the encephalopathy, chronic diarrhoea and relapsing petechial/vascular skin lesions. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The disorder is typically severe and progressive with early death in classic cases, although combined metronidazole and N-acetylcysteine therapy may slow progression in some patients; overall prognosis remains guarded.

ventilation tubes or balloon dilation are options in selected refractory cases Persistent unilateral effusion in an adult mandates examination of the nasopharynx to exclude a tumour Persistent unilateral middle-ear effusion in an adult, which requires exclusion of nasopharyngeal carcinoma Cranial nerve deficits, neck mass or epistaxis suggesting a nasopharyngeal tumour Progressive retraction pocket or features suggesting developing cholesteatoma Sudden hearing loss or vertigo indicating alternative inner-ear pathology Failing to examine the nasopharynx in an adult with persistent unilateral effusion and missing a carcinoma Confusing the patulous form with obstructive dysfunction and prescribing inappropriate decongestion Overlooking progressive tympanic membrane retraction that heralds cholesteatoma Attributing autophony to obstructive dysfunction without considering a third-window disorder The eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx and normally opens intermittently, chiefly through tensor veli palatini action during swallowing, to ventilate the middle ear and equalise pressure. In obstructive dysfunction, inflammation, mucosal oedema, allergy, reflux, adenoidal hypertrophy or a nasopharyngeal mass impairs tubal opening, so the middle ear cannot be ventilated. Trapped air is absorbed by the mucosa, generating negative pressure that draws the tympanic membrane inward and can promote transudation of an effusion. Chronic negative pressure and retraction may lead to retraction pockets and cholesteatoma. In the less common patulous form the tube remains abnormally patent, transmitting nasopharyngeal sounds and causing autophony. Many cases are self-limiting or improve once contributing nasal and nasopharyngeal factors are treated. A subset develops chronic effusion or tympanic membrane retraction that may require ventilation tubes or balloon dilation, and untreated chronic retraction can progress to cholesteatoma.

The thyroid test abnormalities themselves are benign and resolve with recovery; a markedly low thyroxine reflects severe underlying illness and is associated with worse outcomes.

Evaluation and Management of Obesity — Obesity evaluation, Overweight and obesity assessment, Adiposity-based chronic disease Polycystic ovarian syndrome Hypothyroidism Cushing's syndrome Hypothalamic disease Monogenic/syndromic obesity (e.g., Bardet-Biedl syndrome, POMC, PCSK1, or leptin receptor deficiency) Fasting lipid profile (total, LDL, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides) Glycated hemoglobin and chemistry panel for diabetes and metabolic screening Blood pressure measurement Waist circumference / waist-to-hip ratio for visceral adiposity Targeted endocrine workup (thyroid, cortisol/Cushing evaluation) when secondary obesity is suspected Sleep evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea when symptoms or risk factors present Drug-induced weight gain (diabetes agents such as insulin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones; steroid hormones; antipsychotics such as clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone; lithium; tricyclic antidepressants, MAO inhibitors, paroxetine, mirtazapine; antiepileptics such as valproate, gabapentin, carbamazepine) Peripheral edema mimicking fat gain (NSAIDs, calcium channel blockers do not increase body fat) More than 70% of U.S. adults are overweight or have obesity, and prevalence is rising in most industrialized nations, with accelerating rates in children and adolescents. BMI (weight in kg divided by height in m squared, or weight in lb divided by height in in squared times 703) is used to classify weight status: healthy weight 18.5-24.9, overweight 25.0-29.9, obesity class I 30.0-34.9, class II 35.0-39.9, and extreme/class III obesity 40 or greater. BMI only reflects body size; it does not capture body composition, fat distribution, or individual health, so it functions as a screening and population tool rather than a direct measure of adiposity. Waist circumference is a surrogate for visceral adipose tissue and independently predicts metabolic syndrome, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease; it should be measured in the horizontal plane above the iliac crest, particularly when BMI is 35 or below. Ethnic-specific waist cutpoints differ: for Europeans, greater than 94 cm in men and greater than 80 cm in women; for South Asians and Chinese, greater than 90 cm in men and greater than 80 cm in women. Lower BMI thresholds for overweight and obesity have been proposed for the Asia-Pacific population because metabolic risk appears at lower body weights. The obesity-focused history is best approached using neutral language (weight, excess weight, BMI, unhealthy weight) because terms like obesity, morbid obesity, or fatness are perceived as stigmatizing. Recommended baseline workup for all patients includes a fasting lipid profile (total, LDL, and HDL cholesterol plus triglycerides), a chemistry panel, glycated hemoglobin, and blood pressure measurement. Physical fitness and sedentary behavior are independent predictors of all-cause mortality regardless of BMI or body composition, underscoring the importance of an activity history. Staging tools such as the AACE/ACE complication-based system (stage 0 with no complications, stages 1-2 with mild-moderate or severe complications) and the Edmonton Obesity Staging System (graded 0-4 across medical, functional, and psychological domains, independent of BMI) help identify high-risk patients beyond BMI alone. As BMI rises by 5 kg/m2, cancer mortality is estimated to increase by about 10%, and obesity has reportedly overtaken smoking as the leading risk factor for cancer in some countries. Not every patient meeting a BMI obesity threshold requires treatment, but those with obesity-related complications and comorbidities should be managed proactively. Features suggesting a secondary cause (e.g., signs of Cushing's syndrome, hypothyroidism, hypothalamic disease) warranting further evaluation Severe hypertriglyceridemia sufficient to risk pancreatitis Symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea or hypoventilation (heavy snoring, daytime somnolence, dyspnea) Idiopathic intracranial hypertension presentation in a patient with obesity Rapidly progressive metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease/NASH with signs of fibrosis or cirrhosis Relying on BMI alone, which does not measure body composition or fat distribution and can misclassify individual risk. Using stigmatizing language (obesity, morbid obesity, fatness) that leaves patients feeling judged and can undermine engagement. Overlooking secondary or drug-induced causes of weight gain before attributing obesity solely to lifestyle. Initiating lifestyle change when the patient is not ready, which can cause frustration and hamper future efforts. Assuming all patients with a BMI in the obesity range require treatment, when BMI is an imperfect measure of disease. Neglecting waist circumference, which adds independent risk information about visceral adiposity. Obesity arises from a chronic imbalance in which energy intake exceeds energy expenditure, leading to expansion of adipose depots. It is a highly heterogeneous condition strongly influenced by underlying genetic variation, with environmental factors ubiquitous in developed and developing countries; in some individuals it is attributable entirely to genetic causes. Insulin resistance is one of the earliest complications: muscle (glucose disposal) and liver (glucose production) become less responsive to insulin, prompting compensatory hyperinsulinemia. Two main hypotheses link adiposity to insulin resistance—macrophage- and inflammatory-cell products in obese adipose tissue disturbing insulin action, and the limited storage capacity of adipose tissue causing ectopic lipid deposition in muscle and liver (human data are stronger for the ectopic-fat mechanism). The metabolic, endocrine, and cardiovascular consequences may stem from chronic overnutrition and ectopic fat rather than fat mass per se, whereas certain complications (osteoarthritis, reflux esophagitis, obstructive sleep apnea) relate more directly to mass and volume effects. Obesity is a serious chronic disease associated with increased morbidity and mortality through multiple complications—type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, atherothrombotic cardiovascular disease, stroke, heart failure (often diastolic dysfunction) and atrial fibrillation, obstructive sleep apnea, fatty liver disease that can progress to NASH and cirrhosis, several cancers, osteoarthritis, and gout. Risk generally rises with increasing levels of obesity and with central (visceral) fat distribution. Obesity also worsens outcomes from some infections (notably COVID-19) and raises susceptibility to wound infection and postoperative sepsis. Realistic initial treatment goals (around 8-10% weight loss over 6 months) can meaningfully improve obesity-related complications and quality of life. WHO/BMI classification: underweight under 18.5; healthy weight 18.5-24.9; overweight 25.0-29.9 (increased disease risk); obesity class I 30.0-34.9 (high risk); class II 35.0-39.9 (very high risk); class III/extreme obesity 40 or greater (extremely high risk). Complication-based staging (AACE/ACE): stage 0 no complications, stage 1 one or more mild-moderate complications, stage 2 at least one severe complication. The Edmonton Obesity Staging System grades 0-4 across medical, functional, and psychological domains independent of BMI.

Evaluation of Liver Function — Liver function tests, LFTs, Liver biochemical tests, Hepatic panel Hepatocellular pattern (predominant aminotransferase elevation): viral hepatitis, ischemic/hypoxic hepatitis, drug- or toxin-induced injury, autoimmune hepatitis, nonalcoholic/metabolic-associated fatty liver disease, alcohol-related liver disease Cholestatic pattern (predominant alkaline phosphatase/bilirubin elevation): bile duct obstruction by stone, stricture, or tumor; primary biliary cholangitis; sclerosing cholangitis; drug-induced cholestasis Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia: hemolysis, Gilbert's syndrome, Crigler-Najjar syndrome Isolated conjugated hyperbilirubinemia without other test abnormalities: Dubin-Johnson and Rotor syndromes Isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation: infiltrative liver disease, Paget's bone disease, Hodgkin's disease, hyperthyroidism, diabetes, congestive heart failure, amyloidosis AIDS cholangiopathy due to cytomegalovirus or cryptosporidial infection causing marked alkaline phosphatase elevation Hepatic tuberculosis with biliary involvement Sepsis producing an intrahepatic cholestatic pattern Battery of bilirubin (with fractionation), AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, and prothrombin time/INR; repeat over days to weeks for a diagnostic pattern Fractionation of alkaline phosphatase, or 5'-nucleotidase or GGT, to confirm hepatic versus bone origin of an isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation Serum globulin isotypes: IgG in autoimmune hepatitis, IgM in primary biliary cholangitis, IgA in alcoholic liver disease Etiologic workup for chronically abnormal tests: hepatitis C antibody, hepatitis B surface antigen, iron studies/ferritin, ANA and serum protein electrophoresis, ceruloplasmin if under 40, antimitochondrial antibody, and ultrasound for fatty liver Blood ammonia (limited value; poor correlation with encephalopathy severity, though arterial levels correlate with outcome in fulminant failure) Liver biopsy (percutaneous with ultrasound guidance, or transjugular when ascites or prolonged INR present) for unexplained hepatocellular disease, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, indeterminate lesions, fever of unknown origin, or lymphoma staging Noninvasive fibrosis assessment: FibroTest/FibroSure, Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) test, FIB-4 index, transient elastography (FibroScan), and magnetic resonance elastography Ultrasonography (first-line for suspected cholestasis or Budd-Chiari), with CT, MRCP, or ERCP as directed Hypoalbuminemia from protein malnutrition, protein-losing enteropathy, or nephrotic syndrome mimicking the low albumin of chronic liver disease Vitamin K deficiency or warfarin therapy prolonging the prothrombin time independent of hepatic synthetic failure Bone-origin alkaline phosphatase elevation (Paget's disease, growing children, late pregnancy from placental isoenzyme) mimicking hepatic cholestasis Postprandial intestinal alkaline phosphatase rise in blood group O and B individuals Serum biochemical tests labeled 'liver function tests' are useful to detect liver disease, distinguish disorder types, gauge severity, and follow treatment response, but most do not actually measure synthetic liver function; aminotransferases and alkaline phosphatase instead detect hepatocyte damage or impaired bile flow (Harrison 22e p.2633). Tests should be used as a battery rather than singly; when more than one is abnormal, or abnormalities persist on serial testing, the probability of liver disease is high, whereas normal results make occult disease unlikely (Harrison 22e p.2633). Total bilirubin normally runs about 1-1.5 mg/dL (95% of normals 0.2-0.9 mg/dL); if the direct fraction is under 15% of total, the bilirubin is considered essentially all indirect (unconjugated) (Harrison 22e p.2634). Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia points to hemolysis or genetic conditions such as Gilbert's or Crigler-Najjar syndromes; in an otherwise healthy person without hemolysis it can be attributed to Gilbert's syndrome with no further workup needed (Harrison 22e p.2634). Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia almost always implies hepatobiliary disease; because the rate-limiting step is canalicular transport rather than conjugation, the conjugated fraction can rise in any liver disease, including fulminant failure (Harrison 22e p.2634). Aminotransferase elevations above 1000 IU/L occur almost exclusively with extensive hepatocellular injury: viral hepatitis, ischemic/hypoxic injury, or drug/toxin injury; levels up to ~300 IU/L are nonspecific (Harrison 22e p.2635). The absolute aminotransferase level does not correlate with degree of liver cell damage and has no prognostic significance in acute hepatocellular disease; necrosis is not required for enzyme release, only increased membrane permeability (Harrison 22e p.2635). An AST:ALT ratio over 2:1 suggests, and over 3:1 strongly suggests, alcohol-related liver disease; AST is rarely above 300 IU/L in alcoholic liver disease and ALT is often normal/low because of pyridoxal phosphate deficiency (Harrison 22e p.2635). Alkaline phosphatase elevation greater than ~4x normal points to cholestatic disorders, infiltrative diseases (tumor, amyloidosis), or high-turnover bone disease such as Paget's; less than 3x elevation is nonspecific (Harrison 22e p.2635). Because clotting factors (except factor VIII, made by endothelium) are made only in hepatocytes and turn over rapidly (factor VII half-life ~6 h), the prothrombin time/INR is the single best acute marker of hepatic synthetic function (Harrison 22e p.2636). Any bilirubin in the urine is conjugated, since unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and not filtered; bilirubinuria implies liver disease or obstructive jaundice and clears before serum bilirubin during recovery (Harrison 22e p.2634). Ultrasonography is the first test when cholestasis is suspected (to assess for dilated ducts or gallstones) and is also the first study ordered when Budd-Chiari syndrome is suspected, using Doppler to assess vessel patency and flow direction (Harrison 22e p.2636). Aminotransferases above 1000 IU/L indicating extensive hepatocellular injury (viral, ischemic, or toxin/drug) Prothrombin time prolonged more than 5 seconds above control and uncorrected by parenteral vitamin K, a poor prognostic sign in acute viral and other liver disease Albumin below 3 g/dL in apparent hepatitis raising concern for underlying chronic liver disease Elevated total bilirubin in drug-induced liver injury signaling more severe injury Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, which nearly always implies hepatobiliary disease and can occur even in fulminant liver failure Liver tests lack sensitivity and specificity; results can be normal in serious liver disease and abnormal in non-hepatic disease, and rarely indicate a specific diagnosis on their own (Harrison 22e p.2633). Relying on the absolute aminotransferase value for prognosis is an error, since it does not correlate with the degree of damage in acute hepatocellular disease (Harrison 22e p.2635). Except with isolated hyperbilirubinemia, fractionating bilirubin rarely identifies the cause of jaundice (Harrison 22e p.2634). Alkaline phosphatase level does not distinguish intrahepatic from extrahepatic cholestasis (Harrison 22e p.2635). Albumin is insensitive to acute or mild hepatic dysfunction owing to its long half-life and is not specific for liver disease; it should not be ordered to screen patients without suspected liver disease (Harrison 22e p.2636). Liver biopsy should not be the first procedure for cholestasis; the biliary tree must first be evaluated for obstruction, and biopsy is subject to sampling error in focal disease (Harrison 22e p.2636). Blood ammonia correlates poorly with both presence and severity of encephalopathy and with hepatic function, and can be elevated from portal shunting despite near-normal liver function (Harrison 22e p.2636). Serum liver tests reflect distinct mechanisms rather than overall hepatic function. Aminotransferases (AST, ALT) leak from hepatocytes when cell-membrane permeability increases; ALT is comparatively liver-specific while AST is also present in cardiac and skeletal muscle, kidney, brain, pancreas, lung, leukocytes, and red cells. Cholestasis-associated enzymes (alkaline phosphatase, 5'-nucleotidase, GGT) rise with impaired bile flow; alkaline phosphatase and 5'-nucleotidase localize near the canalicular membrane, whereas GGT, found in endoplasmic reticulum and bile-duct epithelium, is more diffuse and less specific. Bilirubin, the end product of heme catabolism, circulates unconjugated and albumin-bound until hepatocellular uptake, intracellular binding, glucuronide conjugation, and canalicular secretion render it water-soluble and excretable; the rate-limiting step is canalicular transport of conjugated bilirubin. Biosynthetic capacity is reflected by albumin (hepatocyte-synthesized, half-life 18-20 days, so insensitive to acute injury) and the clotting factors (rapid turnover, making PT/INR a sensitive acute marker). Gamma globulins rise in chronic liver disease because the cirrhotic liver fails to clear gut-derived bacterial antigens, increasing antibody synthesis (Harrison 22e p.2634-2636). Individual tests carry prognostic weight: in viral hepatitis a higher serum bilirubin reflects greater hepatocellular damage, total bilirubin correlates with poor outcome in alcoholic hepatitis and with prognosis in primary biliary cholangitis, and an elevated bilirubin signals more severe drug-induced injury. A prothrombin time prolonged more than 5 seconds above control and not corrected by parenteral vitamin K is a poor prognostic indicator in acute viral and other liver diseases, and elevated arterial ammonia correlates with outcome in fulminant hepatic failure. Bilirubin, INR, creatinine, albumin, and sodium are integrated into the MELD 3.0 score used to gauge hepatic decompensation and prioritize transplant allocation (Harrison 22e p.2634-2636). Liver test patterns are categorized by pattern recognition (Harrison Table 348-1): hemolysis/Gilbert's (isolated indirect bilirubin, no bilirubinuria, otherwise normal); acute hepatocellular necrosis (aminotransferases often above 500 IU/L with ALT exceeding AST, bilirubinuria, PT prognostic); chronic hepatocellular disorders (aminotransferases usually below 300 IU/L, often low albumin and prolonged PT not corrected by vitamin K); alcoholic hepatitis/cirrhosis (AST:ALT above 2); and intra/extrahepatic cholestasis or infiltrative disease (alkaline phosphatase often above 4x normal). Disease severity in chronic liver disease/cirrhosis is graded by the Child-Pugh classification and, for transplant prioritization, the MELD 3.0 score (bilirubin, INR, creatinine, albumin, sodium) (Harrison 22e p.2636-2637).

Children presenting with Evans syndrome warrant evaluation for an underlying immune dysregulation disorder Severe thrombocytopenia with significant or intracranial bleeding Rapidly falling haemoglobin with haemodynamic compromise Features suggesting thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura that require urgent exclusion Evidence of an aggressive underlying lymphoproliferative disorder Treating the anaemia or thrombocytopenia in isolation without recognising the combined syndrome Missing an underlying autoimmune, lymphoproliferative or immunodeficiency disorder Failing to consider thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura before attributing cytopenias to autoimmunity Underestimating the relapsing course and stopping immunosuppression prematurely Evans syndrome represents a breakdown of immune tolerance that generates autoantibodies against more than one blood-cell lineage. Warm IgG autoantibodies coat red cells, which are cleared extravascularly by splenic macrophages to cause haemolytic anaemia, while separate antiplatelet autoantibodies drive splenic destruction of platelets producing immune thrombocytopenia; some patients also form antineutrophil antibodies. The underlying immune dysregulation may be idiopathic or secondary to systemic autoimmune disease, lymphoproliferative disorders or inherited defects of immune regulation such as autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome and common variable immunodeficiency. The multilineage nature of the autoimmunity accounts for the relapsing course and the frequent need for prolonged immunosuppression. The syndrome typically runs a chronic, relapsing course that is often harder to control than isolated autoimmune cytopenias, with outcome shaped by the response to immunosuppression and by any underlying disease.

Ewing sarcoma (EWSR1-FLI1) — Ewing's sarcoma, Ewing sarcoma family of tumours, EWSR1-FLI1 fusion sarcoma, primitive neuroectodermal tumour, PNET, CD99-positive small round cell tumour Acute or chronic the permeative lytic pattern and periosteal reaction Chest CT to detect pulmonary metastases Whole-body staging with functional imaging and skeletal survey to identify distant bony disease Bone-marrow aspirate and trephine to exclude marrow involvement Image-guided or open biopsy with molecular testing (FISH or RT-PCR) for EWSR1 rearrangement and immunohistochemistry including CD99 and NKX2.2 Typically affects children, adolescents, and young adults, with a peak in the second decade and a modest male predominance Classically arises in the diaphysis or metadiaphysis of long bones and in the flat bones of the pelvis, although extraskeletal soft-tissue forms occur Presents with localised pain and swelling that may mimic osteomyelitis, sometimes with fever, raised inflammatory markers, and a lamellated (onion-skin) periosteal reaction on plain films Histologically a small round blue cell tumour with strong, diffuse membranous CD99 (MIC2) expression, though CD99 is not specific and must be interpreted with molecular confirmation Defined by recurrent FET-ETS gene fusions, most commonly EWSR1-FLI1 from a t(11;22) translocation, with EWSR1-ERG the next most frequent Multimodality care combines multi-agent chemotherapy with local control by surgery, radiotherapy, or both, reflecting inherent chemo- and radiosensitivity Around a fifth to a quarter of patients have overt metastatic disease at diagnosis, most often to lung, bone, and marrow, which strongly influences outcome Staging must include cross-sectional imaging of the primary, chest CT, whole-body assessment, and bone-marrow evaluation before treatment begins A destructive bone lesion with a soft-tissue mass in a child or young adult, mistaken for infection and treated with antibiotics alone Systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, and raised inflammatory markers accompanying a bone lesion Rapidly enlarging mass, pathological fracture, or neurological compromise from spinal or paraspinal disease Symptoms of widespread disease (bone pain, cytopenias) suggesting marrow or multifocal involvement Attributing the presentation to osteomyelitis and delaying biopsy and imaging Placing the biopsy tract without discussion with the treating surgeon, potentially compromising later limb-sparing resection Relying on CD99 positivity alone, since it is shared by lymphoblastic and other tumours, without molecular confirmation Omitting bone-marrow evaluation and thereby understaging the disease Underestimating late effects of therapy, including second malignancies and treatment-related toxicity in long-term survivors Ewing sarcoma is an aggressive small round cell malignancy driven by a chimeric transcription factor produced when a FET-family gene (usually EWSR1) fuses with an ETS-family partner (most often FLI1, less commonly ERG). The resulting fusion protein acts as an aberrant transcription factor that reprogrammes gene expression, binds GGAA microsatellite repeats to switch on oncogenic targets, and blocks the differentiation of a permissive mesenchymal or neural crest-like progenitor cell. This single dominant genetic event, occurring against an otherwise quiet genome, sustains uncontrolled proliferation and impaired maturation, and its detection underpins molecular diagnosis. Outcome depends chiefly on stage, primary site, tumour volume, and response to induction chemotherapy; patients with localised, resectable disease that responds well have markedly better survival than those with metastatic disease at presentation, particularly bone or marrow metastases, which carry a poor prognosis.

Exercise-associated hyponatraemia — EAH, exercise-induced hyponatraemia Dehydration and hypernatraemia Exertional heat stroke Other causes of hyponatraemia (SIADH, adrenal insufficiency) Hypoglycaemia Exercise-associated collapse of other cause Point-of-care or laboratory serum sodium measurement Assessment of fluid intake during the event and body-weight change if known Neurological assessment for cerebral oedema Exclusion of other causes of collapse such as heat stroke and hypoglycaemia Monitoring of sodium during correction A dilutional fall in serum sodium developing during or up to a day after prolonged endurance exercise The main mechanism is excessive intake of hypotonic fluid, often compounded by inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone Mild cases may be asymptomatic, while severe cases cause nausea, headache, confusion, seizures and life-threatening cerebral oedema It can be mistaken for dehydration, and giving more hypotonic fluid worsens it Severe symptomatic cases are treated with hypertonic saline, not with additional free water Prevention centres on drinking to thirst rather than overdrinking during endurance events Altered mental state, seizures or signs of cerebral oedema Vomiting with progressive neurological symptoms Pulmonary oedema Rapidly falling or very low serum sodium Assuming dehydration and giving hypotonic fluids that worsen hyponatraemia Confusing it with heat stroke Failing to use hypertonic saline for severe symptomatic cases Encouraging overdrinking as a prevention strategy Exercise-associated hyponatraemia develops when total body water is in excess relative to sodium, chiefly from drinking hypotonic fluid beyond what is lost. Non-osmotic release of antidiuretic hormone during prolonged exercise impairs the ability to excrete the excess water, and failure to mobilise sodium stores contributes. The resulting fall in plasma osmolality drives water into cells, and cerebral oedema produces the dangerous neurological manifestations. Because the problem is water excess rather than sodium deficit, hypotonic fluids aggravate it. Mild cases resolve with fluid restriction, and severe symptomatic cases usually respond to prompt hypertonic saline; delayed recognition with cerebral or pulmonary oedema can be fatal.

Exertional heat stroke — exercise-induced heat stroke Classic (non-exertional) heat stroke Sepsis Serotonin syndrome or neuroleptic malignant syndrome Thyroid storm Exercise-associated hyponatraemia Status epilepticus Immediate core (rectal) temperature measurement Creatine kinase, renal and liver function and coagulation studies Electrolytes including potassium and sodium Assessment for rhabdomyolysis and disseminated intravascular coagulation Exclusion of infection and other causes of hyperthermia A life-threatening emergency defined by a very high core temperature with central nervous system dysfunction arising during strenuous exertion It affects young, fit individuals such as athletes and military recruits, often in hot humid conditions Central nervous system features such as confusion, agitation, seizures or collapse distinguish it from milder heat illness Unlike classic heat stroke, patients may still be sweating Rapid whole-body cooling, ideally by cold-water immersion, is the priority and should not await transfer Complications include rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, disseminated intravascular coagulation and liver injury Very high core temperature with altered consciousness Seizures or coma Evidence of multi-organ dysfunction Hyperkalaemia or rapidly rising creatine kinase Delaying cooling to obtain investigations or arrange transfer Assuming the patient is not heat-struck because they are still sweating Confusing it with exercise-associated hyponatraemia and mismanaging fluids Underestimating rhabdomyolysis and kidney injury Exertional heat stroke occurs when intense muscular heat production during exercise overwhelms the body's capacity to dissipate heat, causing core temperature to rise to a level that injures tissues. Excessive heat denatures proteins and triggers a systemic inflammatory response and endothelial injury, which can progress to multi-organ dysfunction. Muscle breakdown releases myoglobin and potassium, and the combination of hyperthermia, inflammation and hypoperfusion drives rhabdomyolysis, coagulopathy and acute kidney and liver injury. The speed of cooling strongly influences outcome. With immediate aggressive cooling most patients recover fully, but delayed cooling or established multi-organ failure carries a high risk of death or lasting organ damage.

Exertional rhabdomyolysis — exercise-induced rhabdomyolysis, exertional muscle breakdown, effort rhabdomyolysis Acute compartment syndrome Exertional heat stroke Crush injury from other causes Inflammatory or infective myositis Inherited metabolic myopathy (e.g. disorders of glycogen or fatty acid metabolism) Myoglobinuria from drug or toxin exposure Serum creatine kinase, with serial measurement to track the course Renal function and serum electrolytes including potassium, phosphate, and calcium Urinalysis showing a positive dipstick for blood without red cells, indicating myoglobinuria Electrocardiography to detect changes of hyperkalaemia Assessment of hydration status and, where relevant, core temperature for concurrent heat illness Compartment pressure measurement if compartment syndrome is suspected, and workup for an underlying myopathy in recurrent cases The classic triad is muscle pain, weakness, and dark (tea- or cola-coloured) urine following intense or unaccustomed exertion, though not all three are always present The diagnosis rests on a markedly elevated serum creatine kinase, typically many times the upper limit of normal The most serious systemic complication is myoglobinuric acute kidney injury, in which released myoglobin causes pigment nephropathy Dangerous electrolyte derangements include hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, and hypocalcaemia, and hyperkalaemia can precipitate life-threatening arrhythmia Acute compartment syndrome may develop in affected limbs and, conversely, established compartment syndrome can itself cause rhabdomyolysis Contributing factors include heat, dehydration, certain drugs and supplements, sickle cell trait, and recurrent episodes should prompt evaluation for an underlying metabolic myopathy or malignant hyperthermia susceptibility The cornerstone of management is early and aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation to protect the kidneys, alongside correction of electrolyte disturbance and vigilance for compartment syndrome Reduced urine output or rising creatinine indicating acute kidney injury Hyperkalaemia with electrocardiographic changes threatening arrhythmia A tense, painful limb with pain on passive stretch suggesting compartment syndrome Concurrent hyperthermia and altered mental state suggesting exertional heat stroke Under-resuscitating with fluids and allowing preventable myoglobinuric acute kidney injury Interpreting a urine dipstick positive for blood as haematuria when it reflects myoglobinuria Missing evolving compartment syndrome because pain seems in keeping with muscle soreness Failing to investigate recurrent episodes for a metabolic myopathy or malignant hyperthermia susceptibility Exertional rhabdomyolysis occurs when strenuous or unaccustomed muscular activity, often compounded by heat, dehydration, or an underlying metabolic susceptibility, exceeds the energy supply of skeletal muscle and causes myocyte membrane injury. Breakdown of muscle cells releases intracellular contents, including creatine kinase, myoglobin, potassium, and phosphate, into the circulation. Myoglobin filtered by the kidney contributes to acute kidney injury through tubular obstruction, direct tubular toxicity, and renal vasoconstriction, an effect worsened by hypovolaemia. Efflux of potassium and phosphate with sequestration of calcium into damaged muscle produces the characteristic electrolyte pattern, while swelling within fascial compartments can raise pressure enough to cause compartment syndrome and further ischaemic muscle injury. With prompt recognition and aggressive fluid resuscitation, most patients recover fully and renal function usually normalises. Prognosis worsens with severe acute kidney injury, delayed treatment, or compartment syndrome, and recurrent episodes suggest an underlying predisposition that alters long-term counselling and return-to-activity advice.

Exfoliative dermatitis (erythroderma workup) — erythroderma, exfoliative dermatitis, generalised exfoliative dermatitis, red man syndrome Psoriasis (erythrodermic psoriasis) Atopic and other eczemas Drug reaction, including drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and Sezary syndrome Pityriasis rubra pilaris Idiopathic erythroderma and, in neonates, inherited ichthyoses Serial skin biopsies to seek a specific underlying dermatosis or lymphoma Full blood count with blood film and Sezary cell count, plus peripheral blood flow cytometry Renal function, electrolytes, albumin and inflammatory markers to assess metabolic consequences Comprehensive drug history and review of recently introduced medications Assessment for lymphadenopathy and organomegaly with imaging if lymphoma is suspected Cultures of skin and blood if secondary infection or sepsis is suspected Defined as erythema and scaling affecting at least ninety per cent of the body surface, representing a dermatological emergency rather than a single diagnosis The commonest underlying causes are pre-existing dermatoses (notably psoriasis and eczema), drug reactions, and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with a proportion remaining idiopathic Widespread inflammation impairs the skin barrier, causing high-output fluid, protein and heat loss with a risk of hypothermia, dehydration and electrolyte disturbance Peripheral oedema, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly may accompany the skin changes, and high-output cardiac failure can occur in vulnerable patients Clues to the underlying cause include nail and scalp changes suggesting psoriasis, a preceding drug history, or islands of sparing and intense pruritus suggesting lymphoma Repeated skin biopsies over time, together with blood film and lymphocyte studies, help identify Sezary syndrome and other specific causes Secondary infection and sepsis are important complications given the disrupted barrier and thermoregulation Management combines urgent supportive care (fluid balance, warmth, emollients and nutrition) with withdrawal of any culprit drug and treatment directed at the underlying disease Haemodynamic instability, hypothermia or high-output cardiac failure Fluid, electrolyte and protein depletion from barrier failure Sepsis arising from secondary skin infection Features suggesting cutaneous lymphoma such as intense pruritus, lymphadenopathy or atypical circulating lymphocytes A drug reaction with systemic involvement requiring immediate drug withdrawal Treating erythroderma as a diagnosis in itself and failing to search for the underlying cause Underestimating the fluid, protein and temperature losses and the risk of high-output cardiac failure Relying on a single non-diagnostic biopsy rather than repeating biopsies to detect lymphoma Missing a culprit drug or overlooking secondary infection and sepsis Erythroderma results from a massive increase in the rate of epidermal turnover and a generalised inflammatory infiltrate that together produce diffuse erythema and scaling. The widespread cutaneous vasodilatation and loss of the epidermal barrier lead to substantial transepidermal water loss, heat loss and protein loss through desquamated scale, disturbing fluid, electrolyte and temperature homeostasis. Increased cutaneous blood flow can precipitate high-output cardiac failure, while barrier failure predisposes to infection. The underlying trigger differs by cause, ranging from the amplified inflammation of an existing dermatosis or a drug hypersensitivity reaction to malignant T-cell proliferation in cutaneous lymphoma, but the shared final pathway explains the common systemic complications. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause and the patient's comorbidities: erythroderma from a benign dermatosis or a withdrawn drug usually settles with treatment, whereas lymphoma-associated erythroderma carries a poorer outlook, and the acute metabolic complications can be life-threatening in the elderly or frail.

Exploding head syndrome — EHS, episodic cranial sensory shock, snapping of the brain Primary or secondary thunderclap headache Nocturnal seizures, especially of temporal lobe origin Hypnic headache Nightmares or sleep terrors Auditory hallucinations of a psychiatric disorder Sleep-onset (hypnagogic) hallucinations Clinical history distinguishing a painless sensory event from headache Sleep and symptom diary noting the timing relative to sleep onset or waking Polysomnography if the diagnosis is unclear or seizures are suspected Neuroimaging only when atypical features or red flags are present Review of sleep hygiene, stress and sleep deprivation A benign sensory parasomnia in which the patient perceives a sudden, loud imagined noise or a sense of explosion in the head during transitions into or out of sleep The sound may resemble a bang, clash, gunshot or electrical discharge and can be accompanied by a perceived flash of light There is a startle or sense of fright but typically little or no pain, which distinguishes it from headache disorders Episodes are brief and cause abrupt arousal, sometimes with palpitations or a feeling of fear It becomes more common with age and with sleep deprivation or stress Reassurance about the harmless nature of the phenomenon is the mainstay of management Diagnosis is clinical, but recurrent or atypical events may warrant exclusion of nocturnal seizures or other causes Significant pain accompanying the event, suggesting a headache disorder rather than exploding head syndrome Stereotyped events with other features suggesting nocturnal seizures Focal neurological symptoms or signs Progressive change in the frequency or character of episodes Mistaking the event for a serious headache such as thunderclap headache Overlooking nocturnal seizures when events are stereotyped Causing unnecessary anxiety by over-investigating a benign phenomenon Neglecting contributory sleep deprivation and stress Exploding head syndrome is thought to arise from a transient disturbance in the normal shutting-down of brainstem and reticular activity during the wake-to-sleep transition. Rather than a smooth switch, a brief burst of neuronal activity, possibly within auditory pathways, is proposed to generate the perception of a sudden loud sound. It is regarded as a benign phenomenon of the sleep-wake boundary rather than evidence of structural disease. The condition is benign and often self-limiting; episodes tend to wax and wane, and many patients improve simply with reassurance and attention to sleep and stress, without needing medication.

extensor carpi ulnaris subluxation — ECU tendon instability, ECU subluxation, sixth compartment instability Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) tear Distal radioulnar joint instability Extensor carpi ulnaris tendinopathy or tenosynovitis Lunotriquetral ligament injury Ulnar impaction syndrome Pisotriquetral arthritis Ulnar styloid nonunion Dynamic ultrasound during active supination and pronation MRI showing the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon displaced from its groove Plain radiographs to assess the ulnar groove and exclude bony pathology MR arthrography if a concomitant TFCC injury is suspected Comparison examination of the contralateral wrist Diagnostic local anaesthetic infiltration of the sixth compartment Instability of the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon results from disruption of its fibro-osseous subsheath within the groove on the distal ulna. Patients report a painful snap over the ulnar wrist, provoked by forearm supination, wrist flexion and ulnar deviation. The tendon subluxates volarly and ulnarly out of its groove during supination and relocates on pronation. Dynamic ultrasound during active supination and pronation is the investigation of choice to demonstrate the subluxation. Acute subsheath injury may be treated with immobilisation in pronation and slight extension, whereas chronic cases often require subsheath reconstruction. It is a frequently overlooked cause of ulnar-sided wrist pain, especially in racquet and stick sports. Because the extensor carpi ulnaris also acts as a dynamic stabiliser of the distal radioulnar joint, instability may coexist with DRUJ symptoms. Locking or fixed dislocation of the tendon Associated distal radioulnar joint instability Progressive tendon degeneration or attritional rupture Failure to improve after appropriate immobilisation Attributing the snapping solely to a TFCC tear and missing tendon instability. Relying on static imaging, which may appear normal when the tendon is reduced. Immobilising acutely in the wrong forearm position, such as supination rather than pronation. Overlooking the tendon's role in distal radioulnar joint stability. The extensor carpi ulnaris occupies the sixth dorsal compartment, held within a groove on the dorsal-ulnar aspect of the distal ulna by a dedicated fibro-osseous subsheath that is distinct from the overlying extensor retinaculum. Forceful or repetitive supination, palmar flexion and ulnar deviation stress this subsheath, and a tear allows the tendon to escape the groove and snap over the ulnar border. Because the subsheath does not readily heal once torn or attenuated, instability tends to become recurrent, and chronic subluxation can produce tendon degeneration and tenosynovitis. Acute injuries immobilised appropriately can settle, while chronic symptomatic subluxation generally responds well to subsheath reconstruction with return to sport in most patients.

External auditory canal exostoses — surfer's ear, ear canal exostoses Osteoma of the ear canal Cerumen impaction Chronic otitis externa with stenosis Fibrous or soft-tissue canal stenosis Canal tumour Otoscopy demonstrating the characteristic bony narrowing Audiometry if conductive hearing loss is suspected History of cold-water exposure CT of the temporal bone before surgery to define the bony anatomy Assessment for recurrent otitis externa Benign bony outgrowths of the external auditory canal, usually multiple and bilateral, caused by repeated exposure to cold water and wind It is strongly associated with cold-water surfing, diving and swimming, hence the term surfer's ear Many are asymptomatic, but narrowing predisposes to trapped water, wax impaction and recurrent otitis externa Progressive canal occlusion can cause conductive hearing loss A solitary bony lesion is more likely an osteoma, which differs in pathology and distribution Water precautions slow progression, and surgery is reserved for significant obstruction or recurrent infection Recurrent or severe external ear infection Significant conductive hearing loss A solitary or atypical mass suggesting osteoma or neoplasm Complete canal occlusion Confusing multiple exostoses with a solitary osteoma Overlooking recurrent otitis externa driven by water trapping Not advising ear protection to slow progression Underestimating conductive hearing loss from occlusion External auditory canal exostoses are broad-based bony overgrowths arising from the tympanic bone of the canal in response to repeated cold-water and wind exposure. The chronic thermal stimulation is thought to provoke periosteal bone formation, producing progressive concentric narrowing of the bony canal. The narrowed, tortuous canal traps water and cerumen, impairing self-cleaning and predisposing to external ear infection and, when severe, conductive hearing loss. The lesions are benign and slowly progressive; with water precautions and, where needed, surgical canalplasty, symptoms and complications are well controlled.

External-pressure headache — external compression headache, swim-goggle headache, helmet headache Tension-type headache Migraine triggered by external pressure Occipital neuralgia Cervicogenic headache Contact dermatitis or local skin pathology causing pain Clinical diagnosis from the clear relationship to external pressure or traction Examination confirming pain localised to the compressed or tractioned site Investigation only if features are atypical or persist after removing the stimulus Headache caused by sustained external pressure or traction on the scalp or forehead without skin damage The compression form follows a tight band, hat, helmet or swimming goggles pressing on the head The traction form follows sustained pulling, as from tightly tied-back hair Pain is maximal at the site of pressure or traction and generally resolves after the stimulus is removed It can trigger a migraine attack in susceptible individuals Management is simply avoiding or relieving the offending external force Headache persisting well beyond removal of the pressure or traction Focal neurological signs Associated skin breakdown or infection at the site A new or progressive headache pattern unrelated to external force Overlooking a simple mechanical cause and pursuing unnecessary investigation Confusing it with tension-type or cervicogenic headache Missing that it has triggered a migraine in a susceptible person Ignoring recurrent occupational causes such as protective headgear External-pressure headache results from continuous mechanical stimulation of cutaneous nerves and pericranial structures by pressure or traction on the scalp, activating trigeminal and cervical sensory afferents to produce localised pain. It is a benign response to an external physical stimulus rather than intrinsic intracranial pathology, although in migraine-prone individuals the peripheral input can act as a trigger for a full migraine attack. The condition is benign and resolves once the external pressure or traction is removed; recurrence is easily prevented by avoiding the trigger.

Extradural haematoma — EDH, epidural haematoma, extradural haemorrhage Acute subdural haematoma Traumatic intracerebral haemorrhage or contusion Diffuse axonal injury Subarachnoid haemorrhage Depressed skull fracture with underlying injury Urgent non-contrast CT head to confirm the biconvex collection, clot volume, and midline shift CT bone windows to define the associated skull fracture tears the middle meningeal artery, often in younger patients after a blow to the side of the head The textbook lucid interval, where an initial brief loss of consciousness is followed by a period of apparent recovery and then rapid deterioration, is a warning of an expanding arterial collection On CT the haematoma is typically biconvex (lens-shaped) and does not usually cross suture lines because the dura is firmly attached there Deterioration can be abrupt as the clot enlarges, producing a falling conscious level, contralateral weakness, and an ipsilateral dilated pupil from uncal herniation Prompt surgical evacuation of a significant symptomatic clot can be life-saving and, if performed before herniation, is often associated with good recovery Small extradural collections without significant mass effect in a neurologically intact patient may be monitored closely with repeat imaging Venous extradural collections (from a dural sinus or diploic bleed) can evolve more slowly than classic arterial bleeds Because deterioration may be sudden, any patient with a skull fracture and altered consciousness needs urgent imaging and neurosurgical discussion Lucid interval followed by declining consciousness, heralding rapid clot expansion and impending herniation Ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil with contralateral hemiparesis indicating uncal herniation Cushing response (hypertension with bradycardia) signalling raised intracranial pressure Any drop in GCS or new focal deficit after head injury with a temporal fracture Being falsely reassured by the lucid interval and delaying imaging or transfer Underestimating the speed of arterial bleeding and the potential for sudden collapse Failing to correct coagulopathy urgently before or during evacuation Discharging a head-injured patient with a skull fracture without adequate observation An extradural haematoma is a collection of blood between the inner table of the skull and the dura mater. It most often arises when a skull fracture lacerates a meningeal artery, characteristically the middle meningeal artery in the temporal region, producing brisk arterial bleeding that strips the dura from the bone. Because the dura is tightly adherent at sutures, the clot forms a biconvex shape confined by these attachments. Rapid expansion raises intracranial pressure and displaces brain tissue, culminating in transtentorial (uncal) herniation with brainstem compression if not relieved. Outcome is often excellent when a significant clot is evacuated before herniation, since the underlying brain may be relatively undamaged; however, delay to surgery after signs of herniation markedly worsens survival and neurological recovery.

non-cirrhotic portal hypertension / porto-sinusoidal vascular disease Budd-Chiari syndrome Nodular regenerative hyperplasia Schistosomal portal fibrosis Congenital hepatic fibrosis Doppler ultrasound demonstrating portal vein occlusion and cavernomatous collaterals Contrast-enhanced CT or MR portography to map the venous anatomy and biliopathy Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to assess varices portal hypertension, especially in children and young adults, in whom it often presents with well-tolerated variceal bleeding The portal vein is replaced by a network of collateral veins (the portal cavernoma) that develops after chronic occlusion Synthetic liver function is characteristically preserved because the hepatic parenchyma itself is intact Splenomegaly and hypersplenism are common, and
