and shunt or meso-Rex bypass considered in selected patients Acute variceal haemorrhage with haemodynamic compromise Cholangitis or obstructive jaundice from portal biliopathy Extension of thrombus into the mesenteric veins with bowel ischaemia Features of an underlying myeloproliferative or prothrombotic disorder requiring urgent evaluation Mislabelling the portal hypertension as cirrhotic and misjudging prognosis Overlooking an underlying prothrombotic or myeloproliferative disorder Missing portal biliopathy as a cause of cholestasis or recurrent cholangitis Failing to recognise mesenteric extension that threatens bowel viability Extrahepatic portal vein obstruction results from thrombosis of the portal vein, often triggered by local factors such as neonatal umbilical infection, abdominal sepsis or surgery, together with systemic prothrombotic conditions. Following occlusion, a bypassing network of hepatopetal collateral veins develops around the obstructed segment, forming the portal cavernoma. Because the liver parenchyma is not primarily diseased, hepatocellular function is preserved, but presinusoidal portal hypertension drives varices, splenomegaly and, over time, compression of the bile ducts by the collateral network causing portal biliopathy. With preserved liver function and effective control of variceal bleeding, long-term survival is generally good, though portal biliopathy and recurrent bleeding can cause significant morbidity.

extramammary paget disease — EMPD, extramammary Paget's disease Chronic eczema or allergic contact dermatitis Inverse psoriasis Candidal or dermatophyte intertrigo Lichen sclerosus or lichen planus Bowen disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ) Superficial spreading or amelanotic melanoma Hailey-Hailey disease or Bowenoid papulosis Full-thickness or punch skin biopsy with immunohistochemistry (CK7, CK20, GCDFP-15, CDX2, GATA3, uroplakin, HER2, S100/melan-A) Examination of all apocrine-bearing sites and palpation of regional lymph nodes Colonoscopy and anorectal examination for perianal disease Cystoscopy and urine cytology for penoscrotal or periurethral disease Gynaecological examination and pelvic imaging for vulval disease Cross-sectional imaging (CT, MRI or PET) where invasive or nodal disease is suspected Breast examination and mammography, and HER2 testing to inform systemic therapy, where indicated Rare intraepithelial adenocarcinoma of apocrine gland-bearing skin, most often the vulva, and also the perineum, perianal skin, scrotum, penis and axilla. Presents as a chronic, well-demarcated erythematous and eczematous or 'strawberries-and-cream' plaque with itch or burning, frequently misdiagnosed as eczema or dermatophyte infection for years. Classified as primary (intraepidermal cutaneous adenocarcinoma) or secondary (epidermotropic spread from an underlying or adjacent adnexal, anorectal, urothelial or other visceral adenocarcinoma). Perianal and penoscrotal disease carry a higher association with underlying malignancy and warrant directed screening. Histology shows large pale Paget cells with abundant cytoplasm scattered within the epidermis, positive for mucin stains and cytokeratin 7. Immunoprofile aids origin: GCDFP-15 favours primary cutaneous disease, CK20 and CDX2 suggest anorectal origin, and uroplakin or GATA3 point to urothelial origin. Wide local excision, often with Mohs micrographic surgery, is the mainstay, but subclinical multifocal extension leads to frequent positive margins and recurrence. Any dermal nodule or induration suggests invasion and should prompt an adequate-depth biopsy and staging. Palpable dermal nodule or induration suggesting invasive disease Regional lymphadenopathy Symptoms of an associated visceral adenocarcinoma such as rectal bleeding or haematuria Rapid enlargement, ulceration or bleeding of the plaque Persistent anogenital 'eczema' unresponsive to appropriate topical therapy Prolonged empirical treatment as eczema or fungal infection, delaying diagnostic biopsy Failing to screen for an underlying malignancy in perianal or penoscrotal disease Accepting positive surgical margins from subclinical extension, leading to recurrence Missing dermal invasion because of an inadequate-depth biopsy Misinterpreting pagetoid cells as melanoma without a confirmatory immunohistochemistry panel Extramammary Paget disease is an intraepidermal proliferation of malignant glandular (Paget) cells. Primary disease is thought to arise from intraepidermal apocrine or eccrine ductal cells or Toker cell precursors as an adenocarcinoma in situ that may progress to dermal invasion. Secondary disease represents pagetoid epidermotropic spread from an underlying regional adenocarcinoma, such as anorectal or urothelial carcinoma. The neoplastic cells characteristically produce mucin and express cytokeratin 7, and their broader immunohistochemical profile helps distinguish primary from secondary disease and identify the underlying source. Non-invasive primary disease has a good prognosis but a high rate of local recurrence owing to subclinical spread. Dermal invasion, nodal involvement or an associated internal malignancy markedly worsen the outlook.

Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type — ENKTL, nasal NK/T-cell lymphoma, lethal midline granuloma, angiocentric lymphoma, EBV-associated CD56+ NK/T-cell lymphoma Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other destructive midfacial vasculitides Invasive fungal sinusitis such as mucormycosis or aspergillosis Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the sinonasal region Squamous cell carcinoma or other sinonasal malignancy Chronic invasive bacterial infection or cocaine-induced midline destruction Other peripheral T-cell lymphomas involving extranodal sites Deep, representative biopsy avoiding necrotic areas, with immunohistochemistry (CD56, CD3-epsilon, cytotoxic markers) In situ hybridisation for EBV-encoded RNA Plasma or whole-blood EBV DNA quantification MRI of the sinonasal region and skull base to define local extent PET-CT for staging and detection of extranasal disease Bone marrow examination and assessment for haemophagocytic syndrome Most commonly affects the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and palate, causing nasal obstruction, epistaxis, facial swelling, and destructive midfacial ulceration More prevalent in East Asian and Central/South American populations and strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus in essentially all cases Extranasal disease can involve skin, testis, gastrointestinal tract, and soft tissue and generally carries a worse prognosis Tumour cells are usually of NK-cell (or less often cytotoxic T-cell) origin, expressing CD56, cytoplasmic CD3-epsilon, and cytotoxic molecules, with EBV-encoded RNA positivity by in situ hybridisation The classic histology is angiocentric and angiodestructive growth with prominent necrosis, which can render small biopsies non-diagnostic Circulating EBV DNA can serve as a marker of disease burden and treatment response Management commonly combines radiotherapy for localised nasal disease with non-anthracycline, asparaginase-containing chemotherapy regimens Extensive midfacial or orbital destruction threatening vision or the skull base Systemic or disseminated (extranasal) disease with rapid progression Development of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis Airway compromise from nasopharyngeal or palatal involvement Non-diagnostic biopsies because of extensive necrosis, leading to delayed diagnosis Mistaking destructive nasal disease for vasculitis or invasive fungal infection Using anthracycline-based regimens that are relatively ineffective owing to drug efflux Failing to monitor EBV DNA as a marker of response and relapse Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma is an Epstein-Barr virus-driven neoplasm arising most often from natural killer cells and occasionally cytotoxic T-cells. Latent EBV infection contributes to malignant transformation, and the tumour cells characteristically invade and destroy blood vessel walls (angiocentric and angiodestructive growth), producing ischaemic necrosis and the destructive midfacial lesions historically termed lethal midline granuloma. Overexpression of P-glycoprotein and other drug-efflux mechanisms underlies resistance to anthracycline-based chemotherapy, which is why asparaginase-containing regimens and radiotherapy are preferred. Extensive necrosis can make representative sampling difficult. Localised nasal disease treated with combined radiotherapy and asparaginase-based chemotherapy can achieve durable remission, whereas advanced, extranasal, or relapsed disease and secondary haemophagocytosis carry a poor prognosis.

Eyelid papilloma — squamous papilloma of eyelid, eyelid skin tag Seborrhoeic keratosis Verruca vulgaris (viral wart) Basal cell carcinoma of the eyelid Sebaceous gland carcinoma Squamous cell carcinoma or actinic keratosis Intradermal melanocytic naevus Molluscum contagiosum and pyogenic granuloma Slit-lamp and external examination to define margins, lash involvement and surface pattern Dermoscopy to assess vascular and surface features External and anterior-segment photography for documentation and monitoring Excisional biopsy with histopathology for atypical, pigmented or recurrent lesions Assessment of immune status when lesions are multiple or florid Regional lymph node examination if malignancy is suspected Squamous papilloma is one of the commonest benign eyelid lesions, presenting as a skin-coloured, sessile or pedunculated growth, often with a raspberry-like or frond-like surface, frequently along the lid margin. Lesions may be single or multiple; multiple or filiform verrucous papillomas, especially in children or the immunosuppressed, are often viral (human papillomavirus) in origin. The diagnosis is usually clinical, but any pigmented, ulcerated, indurated or rapidly changing eyelid lesion should be regarded as suspicious and biopsied. Involvement of the lid margin and lash line can cause chronic irritation, tear-film disturbance and cosmetic concern; a lesion touching the ocular surface may cause foreign-body sensation. Small asymptomatic papillomas can simply be observed; symptomatic or cosmetically troublesome ones are treated by shave or complete excision, with cautery or cryotherapy for viral lesions. Recurrence is more likely with incomplete excision and with viral papillomas, which may also seed adjacent skin. Loss of eyelashes (madarosis), destruction of the lid margin architecture, or ulceration should prompt suspicion of basal cell or sebaceous carcinoma masquerading as a benign papilloma. Histology after excision is prudent for any lesion with atypical features, since malignant eyelid tumours can closely mimic a benign papilloma. Ulceration, induration, bleeding or a pearly rolled edge suggesting basal cell carcinoma Loss of eyelashes or destruction of lid-margin architecture suggesting sebaceous or basal cell carcinoma Rapid growth, irregular pigmentation or asymmetry Recurrence after apparently complete excision Diffuse or chronic unilateral blepharitis mimicking a benign lesion but concealing sebaceous carcinoma Assuming all verrucous eyelid lesions are benign and missing a malignancy presenting with madarosis or ulceration Incomplete excision of viral papillomas leading to recurrence and local spread Cryotherapy or cautery close to the lid margin causing notching, trichiasis or lash loss Failing to send excised tissue for histology when features are atypical Overlooking immunosuppression in a patient with multiple or recurrent lesions A squamous papilloma is a benign proliferation of the eyelid surface epithelium characterised by acanthosis, hyperkeratosis and papillomatosis over fibrovascular cores. Two overlapping mechanisms operate: chronic actinic and mechanical irritation drives an involutional, non-infective epithelial overgrowth typical of the sessile lesions of older adults, whereas human papillomavirus infection of keratinocytes produces the filiform verrucous lesions, often multiple, seen in younger or immunosuppressed patients. In both, the epithelium folds into finger-like projections supported by vascularised connective-tissue cores, but there is no dermal invasion or cytological malignancy. Benign with an excellent prognosis; complete excision is generally curative. Viral and incompletely excised lesions may recur, and multiple lesions can persist, but there is no threat to vision or life.

Eyelid retraction — lid retraction Thyroid eye disease Contralateral ptosis causing apparent retraction Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome Proptosis from orbital disease Post-surgical or cicatricial retraction Facial nerve palsy (lower lid) Measurement of lid position and margin-reflex distances Thyroid function and thyroid antibody testing Assessment of ocular motility, proptosis and pupil responses Corneal assessment for exposure keratopathy Neuroimaging if a midbrain or orbital cause is suspected An abnormally elevated upper lid or depressed lower lid position exposing sclera, giving a staring appearance Thyroid eye disease is by far the commonest cause and may show upper lid retraction and lid lag on downgaze Upper lid retraction with impaired upgaze and light-near dissociation suggests dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome Other causes include prior lid or orbital surgery, facial nerve palsy affecting the lower lid, and cicatricial changes Retraction causes ocular surface exposure with dryness, irritation and risk of exposure keratopathy Management addresses the underlying cause and protects the ocular surface, with surgical lid lengthening for stable cases Exposure keratopathy or corneal breakdown Optic nerve compromise in thyroid eye disease Neurological signs suggesting a midbrain lesion Rapidly progressive proptosis Overlooking thyroid eye disease as the underlying cause Mistaking contralateral ptosis for retraction Neglecting corneal exposure and surface protection Operating before the underlying disease is stable Eyelid retraction reflects an imbalance between the lid retractors and their antagonists, or mechanical tethering of the lid. In thyroid eye disease, sympathetic overactivity and inflammation and fibrosis of the levator-Muller complex elevate the upper lid, while proptosis compounds scleral show. Neurogenic retraction occurs when dorsal midbrain lesions disinhibit lid elevation. Cicatricial and post-surgical retraction results from scarring that pulls the lid away from the globe. The resulting exposure of the ocular surface predisposes to drying and keratopathy. Prognosis depends on the cause; retraction from active thyroid eye disease may change with disease activity, and surgical correction is reserved for stable disease with generally good functional and cosmetic results.

fabry cardiomyopathy — Anderson-Fabry cardiac disease, alpha-galactosidase A deficiency cardiomyopathy sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy cardiac amyloidosis hypertensive heart disease aortic stenosis with secondary hypertrophy glycogen storage cardiomyopathy (e.g. PRKAG2, Danon disease) cardiac haemochromatosis athlete's heart alpha-galactosidase A enzyme activity (definitive in males) GLA gene sequencing (required in females) plasma or dried blood spot lyso-Gb3 cardiac magnetic resonance with native T1 mapping and late gadolinium enhancement echocardiography with strain imaging for concentric hypertrophy 12-lead ECG and ambulatory monitoring for conduction disease and arrhythmia urinalysis and renal function for associated nephropathy Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient alpha-galactosidase A, leading to globotriaosylceramide accumulation; cardiac involvement is a leading cause of death and may be the only manifestation in later-onset cardiac variants. It is an important mimic of sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and should be considered in any unexplained concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, particularly with a suggestive family history or extracardiac features. Females, as heterozygotes, are not merely carriers and can develop significant and even severe cardiomyopathy owing to X-inactivation, so a family history following an X-linked pattern is a clue. A characteristically low or low-normal T1 on cardiac magnetic resonance reflects sphingolipid storage and is a valuable discriminator from other causes of hypertrophy, which typically show normal or high native T1. Late gadolinium enhancement classically involves the basal inferolateral wall and signals regional fibrosis that predicts arrhythmia and limited response to enzyme therapy. Extracardiac clues include acroparaesthesiae, angiokeratomata, hypohidrosis, cornea verticillata, proteinuric renal disease and early stroke. Diagnosis rests on demonstrating reduced alpha-galactosidase A activity in males and on GLA gene analysis in females, in whom enzyme activity may be normal; plasma lyso-Gb3 supports the diagnosis and monitoring. Enzyme replacement therapy and oral chaperone therapy (for amenable GLA mutations) can stabilise or reduce left ventricular mass, with greatest benefit when started before extensive fibrosis develops. syncope or documented sustained ventricular arrhythmia progressive heart failure with declining systolic function advancing conduction disease or high-grade atrioventricular block extensive basal inferolateral late gadolinium enhancement concurrent rapidly progressive renal impairment or stroke misdiagnosing Fabry cardiomyopathy as sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and missing a treatable cause excluding disease in a symptomatic female on the basis of normal enzyme activity, when GLA testing is required overlooking extracardiac features that would prompt earlier diagnosis starting enzyme therapy after extensive fibrosis, when benefit is limited attributing angina to epicardial coronary disease and missing microvascular dysfunction Deficient lysosomal alpha-galactosidase A activity impairs catabolism of glycosphingolipids, leading to progressive intracellular accumulation of globotriaosylceramide within cardiomyocytes, conduction tissue, valvular tissue, vascular endothelium and smooth muscle. Storage itself accounts for only a fraction of the increased ventricular mass; the accumulated substrate triggers secondary processes of cellular hypertrophy, energetic impairment, inflammation and progressive replacement fibrosis, classically in the basal inferolateral wall. The result is concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with diastolic dysfunction and, later, systolic impairment. Involvement of the conduction system and small-vessel coronary dysfunction produce conduction abnormalities, arrhythmias and angina despite unobstructed epicardial coronary arteries. Cardiac involvement is a principal determinant of survival; disease-modifying therapy started before significant fibrosis can stabilise or regress hypertrophy and improve outlook, whereas advanced fibrosis, heart failure and malignant arrhythmia carry a poor prognosis.

normal Overlooking cornea verticillata that could prompt earlier recognition Failing to screen and counsel at-risk relatives given X-linked inheritance Fabry disease is caused by pathogenic variants in the GLA gene on the X chromosome, which encodes lysosomal alpha-galactosidase A. Deficient enzyme activity prevents cleavage of terminal galactose from globotriaosylceramide (Gb3), causing progressive glycosphingolipid accumulation within lysosomes, most notably in vascular endothelial and smooth muscle cells, renal podocytes and tubular cells, cardiomyocytes, and neurons. This storage triggers endothelial dysfunction, a prothrombotic and pro-inflammatory state, and progressive fibrosis of the kidney, heart, and brain vasculature, producing the multisystem adult phenotype. Untreated classic disease progresses to end-stage renal disease, cardiac complications, and premature stroke, shortening life expectancy. Early initiation of enzyme replacement or chaperone therapy, together with organ-directed supportive care, can slow progression and improve outcomes, though established fibrosis is not reversible.

syndrome refers to pain arising from the synovial zygapophysial joints of the spine. These joints, richly innervated by the medial branches of the dorsal rami, undergo osteoarthritic change (cartilage loss, capsular hypertrophy, osteophytosis, and effusion) as part of the degenerative cascade, frequently alongside disc degeneration. Mechanical loading in extension and rotation together with inflammation of the joint capsule stimulates nociceptors and produces axial pain. Facet hypertrophy can also contribute to lateral recess and foraminal narrowing. Facet-mediated pain typically follows a fluctuating chronic course; many patients are managed conservatively, and those with confirmed facet pain often gain useful, though sometimes temporary, relief from injections or radiofrequency denervation.

(bradycardia, nausea) in children CSF rhinorrhoea or other evidence of skull base and dural breach Associated cervical spine or intracranial injury Focusing on obvious facial injury while missing airway compromise or cervical spine injury Overlooking an orbital floor fracture with entrapment, especially the white-eyed blowout in children Failing to detect and manage CSF leak in fractures extending to the skull base Neglecting occlusion, resulting in malocclusion after fixation Operating before periorbital swelling settles, compromising assessment and fixation Missing retrobulbar haemorrhage, which can cause preventable blindness The facial skeleton is organised into vertical and horizontal buttresses that transmit and dissipate forces of mastication and absorb trauma. Fractures occur when applied force exceeds bone strength, and the pattern reflects the direction and energy of impact and the relative weakness of certain regions such as the orbital floor and the Le Fort lines. High-energy injuries can separate the midface from the skull base along these predictable planes. Associated soft tissue swelling, haemorrhage, and displaced bone fragments can compromise the airway, the orbit and globe, cranial nerves, and the lacrimal and paranasal sinus systems, and disruption near the cribriform plate can breach the dura and cause CSF leak. With accurate reduction and fixation most facial fractures heal with good functional and aesthetic results and restored occlusion. Outcomes are less favourable with delayed treatment, comminution, or associated orbital and skull base injury, where diplopia, enophthalmos, malunion, sensory disturbance, and asymmetry may persist and require secondary correction.

systemic complications Overlooking subtle facial weakness and attributing scapular winging to a local shoulder problem Expecting a markedly raised creatine kinase, which is often only mildly elevated Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy arises from failure to silence the DUX4 gene within the D4Z4 macrosatellite repeat region on chromosome 4q35. In the common type, contraction of the repeat array reduces the normal epigenetic repression of this region, and in the rarer type variants in chromatin-modifying genes have a similar effect. Inappropriate expression of DUX4, a transcription factor normally silent in mature muscle, is toxic to muscle fibres and triggers a cascade of gene activation leading to muscle degeneration. The distinctive facial, scapular, and often asymmetrical pattern of weakness reflects the selective vulnerability of these muscle groups. Progression is usually slow, most patients have a normal lifespan, and a minority eventually require wheelchair support. Severe early-onset disease is associated with a greater burden of weakness and extramuscular complications such as hearing and retinal involvement.

factitial panniculitis — factitious panniculitis, panniculitis artefacta infective panniculitis erythema nodosum pancreatic panniculitis lupus panniculitis traumatic panniculitis alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency panniculitis subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma deep incisional biopsy for histopathology with polariscopy for birefringent foreign material special stains and tissue culture to exclude superimposed infection chemical or spectroscopic analysis of tissue for injected substances where available imaging (ultrasound or MRI) to map injected material and deep involvement screening for exogenous drugs or substances where injection is suspected psychiatric and psychological assessment review of occupational and medication access and any secondary-gain context A panniculitis produced by self-inflicted injury or the injection of foreign material into subcutaneous fat, either as a psychiatric disorder (dermatitis artefacta) or through injection of organic and inorganic substances. Injected materials include drugs (licit and illicit), oils, milk, faeces, povidone, silicone and other foreign substances, each producing characteristic tissue reactions. Lesions typically occur in accessible sites reachable by the dominant hand and may have bizarre, angular or geometric shapes with sharp borders unlike spontaneous panniculitides. A discrepant or evasive history, lesions at varying stages, and failure to fit any recognised inflammatory pattern should raise suspicion. Histology may reveal foreign material, refractile or polarisable particles, lipomembranous change, suppuration or granulomatous foreign-body reaction depending on the agent. Polariscopy of biopsy tissue can demonstrate birefringent foreign material and is a valuable diagnostic aid. Management combines wound care, exclusion of organic disease and infection, and sensitive psychiatric or psychological assessment and support. Direct confrontation is usually counterproductive; a supportive, non-judgemental multidisciplinary approach is preferred. secondary infection, abscess or necrotising soft-tissue infection from injected material systemic toxicity from injected substances (for example oils or drugs) evidence of serious underlying psychiatric illness or risk of self-harm extensive tissue destruction requiring surgical intervention Failing to consider a factitial cause when a panniculitis does not fit any recognised inflammatory pattern. Omitting polariscopy and thus missing diagnostic foreign material. Confronting the patient prematurely, which typically ruptures the therapeutic relationship. Overlooking secondary infection introduced by the self-injury. Treating the skin alone without engaging psychiatric or psychological services. Factitial panniculitis results from mechanical or chemical injury deliberately inflicted on subcutaneous fat, whether by blunt trauma, injection of exogenous substances, or introduction of infective material. The nature of the inflammatory response depends on the agent: oily and organic substances provoke a lipogranulomatous foreign-body reaction with vacuoles and giant cells, particulate or crystalline materials elicit granulomas with polarisable foreign bodies, and injected infective or irritant materials cause suppurative and necrotising panniculitis. Tissue damage releases fatty acids that amplify lobular inflammation. Underlying the physical injury is a psychological or psychiatric driver, ranging from dermatitis artefacta and factitious disorder to secondary gain, which sustains the repetitive self-injury. The cutaneous lesions heal with appropriate wound care once self-injury ceases, but the overall prognosis depends on the underlying psychological or psychiatric condition, and recurrence is common if this is not addressed.

Factitious Disorder — Munchausen syndrome, Factitious disorder imposed on self Malingering with an external incentive Somatic symptom disorder or illness anxiety disorder Conversion (functional neurological) disorder Genuine but elusive organic disease Substance use disorder where drug-seeking predominates Personality disorder presentations Delusional disorder, somatic type Careful objective documentation and corroboration of the clinical course Review and collation of records from multiple institutions within appropriate governance Targeted tests to detect induced pathology, such as toxicology and insulin and C-peptide assays in factitious hypoglycaemia Consistency checks comparing charted and directly measured observations within governance frameworks Psychiatric assessment including personality assessment Safeguarding assessment where the disorder is imposed on another Multidisciplinary case conference Intentional falsification, induction, or exaggeration of physical or psychological signs and symptoms, with deception, in the absence of obvious external reward. Motivation is assumption of the sick role, an internal psychological drive, which distinguishes it from malingering, where the gain is external such as money, drugs, or avoidance of duties. Munchausen syndrome denotes a severe chronic form with pathological lying (pseudologia fantastica), travelling between hospitals (peregrination), and repeated presentations. Factitious disorder imposed on another, formerly Munchausen by proxy, is a form of abuse and a safeguarding emergency. Methods include feigning symptoms, tampering with tests or charts, self-injecting or contaminating wounds, manipulating temperature charts, and inducing hypoglycaemia. Often associated with a healthcare background or knowledge and with personality disorder, particularly borderline traits. Diagnosis rests on demonstrating deception, which is difficult and requires objective evidence rather than merely the absence of organic disease. Confrontation is often counterproductive, and a non-punitive, coordinated, harm-minimisation approach is preferred. Factitious disorder imposed on another child or dependent adult, a safeguarding emergency Self-induced life-threatening pathology such as sepsis, hypoglycaemia, or bleeding Escalating invasive investigation or surgery driven by fabricated symptoms Access to means of self-harm or symptom induction such as medications or syringes Diagnosing factitious disorder merely from the absence of organic findings Premature or aggressive confrontation prompting disengagement and escalation Missing factitious disorder imposed on another and failing to safeguard Iatrogenic harm from repeated invasive testing and surgery Factitious disorder is a psychiatric condition in which the drive to occupy the sick role motivates deliberate simulation or induction of illness. It is not fully explained biologically; psychodynamic formulations emphasise early experiences of illness, trauma, or deprivation, disturbed attachment, and a need for care, control, or attention within the medical system. It is strongly associated with personality pathology, particularly borderline and related traits, and with prior exposure to healthcare environments. The behaviour is intentional, unlike somatic symptom disorder, but the underlying motivation is regarded as a compulsive need beyond straightforward voluntary control, which differentiates it from purely instrumental malingering. The chronic Munchausen form has a poor prognosis with repeated presentations and iatrogenic harm, whereas milder or situational cases and those engaging with psychiatric care may do better; overall outcomes are limited by frequent disengagement.

Complement factor H deficiency — Factor H deficiency, Complement factor H deficiency, CFH deficiency Factor I deficiency Membrane cofactor protein (CD46) abnormalities C3 nephritic factor-mediated C3 glomerulopathy Shiga toxin-associated (typical) haemolytic uraemic syndrome Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura Other causes of thrombotic microangiopathy Primary C3 deficiency C3 and C4 levels (typically low C3 with preserved C4) Factor H antigenic level and functional activity Anti-factor-H autoantibody assay Genetic testing of CFH and related complement regulator genes Renal function, blood film for schistocytes, haptoglobin and platelet count Renal biopsy for C3 glomerulopathy or thrombotic microangiopathy Assessment for encapsulated-organism infection and vaccination status Factor H is the major fluid-phase and surface regulator of the alternative complement pathway; its deficiency leads to uncontrolled complement activation and secondary consumption of C3. Complete deficiency and dysfunctional variants classically cause C3 glomerulopathy, including dense deposit disease, and atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome. A persistently low C3 with a normal or near-normal C4 reflects selective alternative-pathway consumption and is an important clue. Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome from factor H abnormalities presents with microangiopathic haemolysis, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury, often without a diarrhoeal prodrome. There is also an increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms owing to depletion of C3. Variants in the factor H gene and anti-factor-H autoantibodies both cause functional deficiency and must be sought. Complement-directed therapy, particularly terminal-pathway blockade, has transformed management of factor H-related atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome. Factor H genetic variation is also strongly linked to age-related macular degeneration, illustrating the breadth of its regulatory role. Microangiopathic haemolysis with thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury Rapidly declining renal function or oligo-anuria Malignant hypertension complicating thrombotic microangiopathy Nephrotic-range proteinuria in C3 glomerulopathy Invasive infection with encapsulated organisms Overlooking a complement regulatory defect in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome without a diarrhoeal prodrome. Missing anti-factor-H autoantibodies as a treatable cause of functional deficiency. Interpreting a low C3 with normal C4 as nonspecific rather than a marker of alternative-pathway dysregulation. Proceeding to renal transplantation without recognising the high recurrence risk. Neglecting infection prophylaxis when C3 is depleted. Factor H is the principal regulator of the alternative complement pathway, acting both in the fluid phase and on host cell surfaces. It accelerates decay of the alternative-pathway C3 convertase and serves as a cofactor for factor I-mediated cleavage of C3b, thereby protecting host tissues from complement attack. When factor H is deficient or dysfunctional, the alternative pathway is left unchecked, so C3 is continuously activated and consumed, depleting circulating C3 and depositing complement on host surfaces. Endothelial injury from unregulated complement drives thrombotic microangiopathy (atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome), while glomerular C3 deposition produces C3 glomerulopathy. The accompanying fall in C3 also impairs opsonisation, adding a susceptibility to encapsulated-organism infection. Factor H-related atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome carries a high risk of progression to end-stage renal disease and of recurrence after transplantation, though outcomes have improved substantially with complement-blocking therapy; C3 glomerulopathy tends to follow a chronic progressive course.

Complement factor I deficiency — Factor I deficiency, Complement factor I deficiency, CFI deficiency Primary C3 deficiency Factor H deficiency or dysfunction Membrane cofactor protein (CD46) abnormalities C3 nephritic factor-mediated C3 glomerulopathy Other thrombotic microangiopathies Idiopathic systemic lupus erythematosus C3 and C4 levels (low C3 with preserved C4) Factor I antigenic level and functional activity Factor H level and factor B to assess consumption Genetic testing of CFI and related complement genes Renal function, urinalysis and blood film where microangiopathy is suspected Renal biopsy in glomerulopathy or thrombotic microangiopathy Vaccination status and infection history documentation Factor I is a regulatory protease that, with its cofactors, cleaves and inactivates C3b and C4b; its deficiency causes uncontrolled complement activation and secondary consumption of C3. The result is a phenotype resembling C3 deficiency, with recurrent pyogenic infections by encapsulated organisms including invasive neisserial and pneumococcal disease. Secondary depletion of C3 and factor B is characteristic, because unregulated alternative-pathway turnover consumes them. Autoimmune and immune-complex disease, including a lupus-like syndrome and glomerulopathy, can occur. Factor I abnormalities are also a recognised cause of atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and C3 glomerulopathy. A low C3 with a normal C4 points to alternative-pathway dysregulation and should prompt measurement of factor I and factor H. A specific low or dysfunctional factor I level confirms the diagnosis. Management combines vaccination against encapsulated organisms, prompt treatment of infection and, for thrombotic microangiopathy, complement-directed therapy. Invasive infection with encapsulated organisms or meningitis Fulminant sepsis Microangiopathic haemolysis with acute kidney injury Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis Recurrent severe infections in a child Mistaking secondary C3 depletion for primary C3 deficiency without measuring the regulators. Failing to measure factor I and factor H when C3 is low but C4 is normal. Overlooking factor I abnormalities as a cause of atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome. Neglecting vaccination and infection prophylaxis against encapsulated organisms. Attributing recurrent infection to antibody deficiency alone without complement testing. Factor I is a serine protease that regulates complement by cleaving C3b to iC3b and C4b to inactive fragments, using cofactors such as factor H and membrane cofactor protein. Without functional factor I, C3b cannot be inactivated, so the alternative-pathway amplification loop runs unchecked and continuously consumes C3 and factor B. The resulting low circulating C3 impairs opsonisation, producing a susceptibility to encapsulated-organism infection that mirrors primary C3 deficiency. Persistent complement dysregulation on host surfaces can also injure the glomerular endothelium and basement membrane, contributing to atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and C3 glomerulopathy, while defective clearance of immune complexes predisposes to autoimmune phenomena. The infective risk resembles that of C3 deficiency and can be serious, but is substantially reduced by vaccination and prompt antibiotics; renal involvement from associated thrombotic microangiopathy or C3 glomerulopathy is an important determinant of long-term outcome.

without clear benefit or counselling Factor V Leiden results from a guanine-to-adenine substitution that changes an arginine residue at a cleavage site in factor V. Activated protein C normally inactivates factor Va at this site to dampen coagulation; the mutation removes this cleavage site, so factor Va persists and continues to support thrombin generation. This state of activated protein C resistance shifts haemostasis toward clot formation. Because the defect is a gain of prothrombotic function rather than loss of an anticoagulant protein, its per-copy thrombotic risk is lower than for antithrombin, protein C, or protein S deficiency, but its high population frequency makes it the commonest inherited contributor to venous thrombosis. Most heterozygous carriers remain asymptomatic throughout life; overall prognosis is favourable, though thrombotic risk increases with homozygosity, additional thrombophilic defects, and transient provoking factors such as hormonal therapy or surgery.

coagulation and triggers thrombin generation. Congenital deficiency, usually from biallelic mutations in F7, reduces the amount or function of the protein, so extrinsic pathway activation is impaired. Because factor VII participates only in the extrinsic limb, its deficiency prolongs the prothrombin time while leaving the activated partial thromboplastin time normal. The clinical phenotype is notably variable and correlates poorly with the measured factor level, reflecting compensatory features of the coagulation network; some individuals with very low levels bleed little, whereas others bleed significantly, and a subset paradoxically develop thrombosis. Outcome depends on the bleeding phenotype rather than the factor level; many patients have a mild course, while those with severe deficiency are at risk of major bleeding but can usually be managed effectively with targeted factor VII replacement.

transglutaminase that, once activated by thrombin, crosslinks fibrin monomers and incorporates antifibrinolytic proteins into the clot, converting a loose fibrin mesh into a mechanically strong, lysis-resistant structure. In congenital deficiency, usually due to biallelic mutations affecting the A subunit, the initial platelet plug and fibrin clot still form, so standard clotting times are normal, but the clot is not stabilised and disintegrates prematurely. This produces the hallmark of delayed bleeding after an interval of apparent haemostasis. Because factor XIII crosslinking also supports tissue repair and the maintenance of the placenta, its deficiency causes poor wound healing and recurrent miscarriage in addition to a bleeding tendency, and the loss of clot stability predisposes to spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage. With regular factor XIII concentrate prophylaxis the prognosis is generally good and life-threatening bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage, can be largely prevented, whereas untreated severe deficiency carries significant morbidity and mortality.

Faecal impaction — faecal impaction of the rectum, impacted stool, faecaloma Mechanical large-bowel obstruction from stricture or tumour Colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) Sigmoid or caecal volvulus Infective or inflammatory diarrhoea (when overflow is mistaken for true diarrhoea) Obstructing colorectal neoplasm Hirschsprung disease or other neuromuscular colonic disorder in younger patients Pelvic mass causing extrinsic rectal compression Digital rectal examination to confirm rectal loading and assess stool consistency Plain abdominal radiograph to gauge faecal loading and exclude obstruction or free air Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, and thyroid function to identify contributory metabolic causes CT of the abdomen and pelvis where obstruction, perforation, or an underlying mass is suspected Colonoscopy or contrast enema after resolution if an obstructing lesion is possible Review of medication and mobility as contributory factors Faecal impaction is a large, firm, immovable mass of stool in the rectum or colon that cannot be evacuated spontaneously, most often complicating chronic constipation Overflow (spurious) diarrhoea and faecal soiling around an impacted mass are classic and are easily misdiagnosed as simple diarrhoea, leading to inappropriate treatment It is especially common in older, immobile, cognitively impaired, or institutionalised patients and in those on constipating drugs such as opioids and anticholinergics Digital rectal examination revealing a rectum loaded with hard stool is the key bedside diagnostic step; a high impaction may leave an empty rectum despite proximal loading Plain abdominal radiography helps assess the extent of colonic loading and exclude obstruction or perforation Management combines rectal disimpaction (softening enemas or suppositories, and gentle manual disimpaction when needed) followed by oral laxatives and a maintenance bowel regimen Complications include stercoral ulceration, colonic perforation, urinary retention, and, rarely, large-bowel obstruction Prevention through adequate fibre, hydration, mobility, laxatives with opioids, and toileting routines is central to avoiding recurrence Abdominal distension with pain, guarding, or peritonism suggesting perforation Rectal bleeding raising concern for stercoral ulceration or an underlying tumour Features of large-bowel obstruction such as vomiting and absolute constipation Systemic sepsis or signs of ischaemia Acute urinary retention from pelvic pressure Mistaking overflow soiling for infective diarrhoea and prescribing antidiarrhoeal agents Missing a high impaction because the rectum is empty on examination Overlooking an obstructing tumour or stricture as the underlying cause Failing to establish a maintenance regimen, leading to recurrence Forceful disimpaction risking mucosal injury, bleeding, or perforation Faecal impaction develops when colonic transit and rectal evacuation are sufficiently impaired that stool dehydrates and hardens into an immovable mass. Prolonged colonic residence allows excessive water reabsorption, producing progressively firmer stool. Reduced rectal sensation, impaired rectal contractility, weakened pelvic-floor and abdominal effort, and blunted defecatory reflexes, as occur with ageing, neurological disease, immobility, and constipating medications, prevent effective expulsion. The retained mass distends the rectum, and chronic distension further diminishes rectal sensation and the urge to defecate, perpetuating retention. Liquid stool from above may track around the mass, producing overflow incontinence, while sustained pressure on the rectal mucosa can cause stercoral ulceration and, at worst, ischaemic necrosis and perforation. Uncomplicated faecal impaction usually resolves with disimpaction and a maintenance bowel regimen, but it frequently recurs unless underlying causes are corrected; complicated impaction with stercoral ulceration or perforation carries significant morbidity and mortality, particularly in frail older patients.

the picture is atypical Primary familial brain calcification (Fahr disease) is a genetic disorder of symmetrical brain calcification, most commonly autosomal dominant through variants in SLC20A2, PDGFB, PDGFRB, or XPR1 (recessive genes also described) Diagnosis requires exclusion of secondary causes of basal ganglia calcification, above all disorders of calcium-phosphate metabolism such as hypoparathyroidism and pseudohypoparathyroidism Clinical features are variable and include a movement disorder (parkinsonism, dystonia, chorea), cognitive decline, psychiatric symptoms, headache, and important Management is symptomatic, and calcium-phosphate homeostasis should be optimised where relevant New seizures or status epilepticus Rapidly progressive cognitive decline or acute psychiatric crisis Severe or disabling movement disorder Features suggesting a treatable metabolic cause such as symptomatic hypocalcaemia Diagnosing primary (genetic) disease without first excluding secondary metabolic causes, particularly parathyroid disorders Relying on MRI, which can under-detect calcification, rather than CT Interpreting minor age-related pallidal calcification as pathological Overlooking dominant inheritance and the value of family assessment and counselling Primary familial brain calcification is characterised by progressive bilateral calcium deposition in the basal ganglia and other deep brain structures in the absence of a metabolic cause. The recognised genes converge on the neurovascular unit and phosphate homeostasis: SLC20A2 and XPR1 regulate inorganic phosphate transport, while PDGFB and PDGFRB maintain pericyte function and blood-brain barrier integrity. Disruption of phosphate handling and of the barrier is thought to promote mineral deposition within and around small vessel walls, leading to the calcification that underlies the movement, cognitive, and psychiatric manifestations. The course is variable: some gene carriers remain asymptomatic while others develop progressive movement disorder, cognitive decline, and psychiatric disease, and there is no treatment that halts the calcification. Prognosis depends on the extent and rate of neurological involvement.

Failure to Thrive — faltering growth, growth faltering, weight faltering Constitutional growth patterns and familial short stature (not true failure to thrive) Malabsorption (e.g., coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis) Chronic cardiac, respiratory, renal, or gastrointestinal disease Endocrine disorders Chronic or recurrent infection Neglect or psychosocial deprivation Detailed dietary and feeding assessment with observation of a feed Plotting of serial weight, length/height, and head circumference Targeted first-line tests (full blood count, electrolytes, urinalysis) guided by findings Coeliac serology and stool studies when malabsorption is suspected Further specific testing directed by history and examination Failure to thrive describes inadequate physical growth in a young child, most often identified as weight gain that is poor for age or crosses downward through growth chart percentiles over time. A single low measurement is less meaningful than the trajectory of serial measurements plotted on an appropriate growth chart. The traditional split into organic and non-organic causes is artificial; many children have mixed contributors, and inadequate caloric intake is the final common pathway in most cases. The three broad mechanisms are insufficient intake, inadequate absorption or increased losses, and increased energy requirements, and the history usually distinguishes among them. A careful feeding, dietary, developmental, social, and psychosocial history plus observation of a feed often yields more than extensive laboratory testing. Investigations should be guided by clues from the history and examination rather than performed as an indiscriminate panel. Management prioritises adequate catch-up nutrition while addressing any medical, developmental, feeding, and psychosocial factors, often through a multidisciplinary approach. Signs of neglect, abuse, or a threatening environment must be considered, but most children with faltering growth are not victims of maltreatment. Severe or rapidly progressive weight loss or wasting Signs of dehydration or micronutrient deficiency Developmental regression or neurological signs Features suggesting abuse or neglect Symptoms or signs pointing to serious underlying organic disease Diagnosing failure to thrive from a single measurement rather than the growth trend Ordering broad laboratory panels instead of history-directed testing Assuming an organic cause and overlooking feeding technique, caloric adequacy, or psychosocial factors Mislabelling normal constitutional or genetically small children as failing to thrive Growth requires that energy and nutrient intake exceed the demands of maintenance and activity. Faltering growth arises when this balance is disturbed: intake may be insufficient because of feeding difficulties, poor appetite, incorrect feed preparation, or limited food availability; nutrients may be inadequately absorbed or lost through malabsorption, chronic diarrhoea, or vomiting; or requirements may be raised by chronic illness such as cardiac, respiratory, renal, or inflammatory disease. Prolonged deficits deplete energy stores and, if sustained, can impair linear growth and, in severe or early cases, brain development. Psychosocial and caregiving factors frequently interact with these physiological mechanisms. With timely recognition and adequate nutritional rehabilitation most children achieve catch-up growth and do well, but prolonged or severe undernutrition, especially in infancy, can be associated with lasting effects on growth and neurodevelopment.

Falls in the elderly — geriatric falls, recurrent falls, fall risk, falls syndrome Syncope from cardiac arrhythmia, structural heart disease, or vasovagal cause Orthostatic hypotension Transient ischaemic attack or stroke Seizure Vertigo from vestibular disease including benign paroxysmal positional vertigo Mechanical or purely accidental trips related to environment Multifactorial falls assessment including gait, balance, and lower-limb strength testing Orthostatic blood pressure measurement (lying and standing) Medication review focused on psychoactive and hypotensive agents Vision assessment and cognitive screening Cardiac evaluation (ECG and further testing) when syncope is suspected Bone health assessment including fracture risk and consideration of DXA Falls in older adults are usually multifactorial, and each additional risk factor further increases the likelihood of falling A single fall warrants a gait and balance assessment, while recurrent falls or a fall with injury warrant a full multifactorial evaluation Key contributors include muscle weakness, gait and balance disorders, visual impairment, cognitive impairment, environmental hazards, and culprit medications Psychoactive drugs, antihypertensives, and drugs causing orthostatic hypotension are among the most modifiable medication-related risks Always ask about loss of consciousness; syncopal falls point toward cardiac or neurological causes and require separate evaluation Fear of falling is common after a fall and can itself cause activity restriction, deconditioning, and further falls Multicomponent interventions, particularly progressive strength and balance exercise, are the most effective evidence-based prevention strategy Vitamin D repletion in deficient individuals, home hazard modification, and correcting visual and footwear problems reduce fall risk Screen for and manage osteoporosis, since the clinical consequence of falls is largely determined by fracture risk Fall with head injury, especially on anticoagulants, raising concern for intracranial haemorrhage Fall causing fracture or significant soft-tissue injury Fall associated with loss of consciousness or suspected cardiac syncope Long lie on the floor after a fall, with risk of rhabdomyolysis, pressure injury, hypothermia, and dehydration New focal neurological signs suggesting stroke Treating a fall as a simple mechanical accident and not searching for contributing medical causes Overlooking orthostatic hypotension and culprit medications Failing to distinguish a syncopal fall from a mechanical one Ignoring bone health so that fracture risk is left unaddressed Neglecting fear of falling and the resulting deconditioning spiral Safe mobility depends on the integration of sensory input (vision, vestibular function, proprioception), central processing, and effector musculoskeletal responses. Ageing degrades each of these: sensory acuity declines, reaction times lengthen, postural reflexes slow, and sarcopenia reduces the strength needed for recovery. Superimposed disease (neurodegenerative disorders, arthritis, cardiovascular instability), medications, and environmental hazards further erode the margin of safety, so that balance perturbations that a younger person would correct instead result in a fall. Falls are a leading cause of injury, disability, and loss of independence in older people. A fall with fracture, particularly hip fracture, carries substantial morbidity and elevated one-year mortality. Recurrent falls predict functional decline and institutionalisation, but structured multifactorial intervention meaningfully reduces future falls in many patients.

and osteomas can be clinical clues that flag the syndrome before genetic confirmation Rapidly increasing polyp burden or a discrete mass suggesting malignant transformation Symptomatic or enlarging negative APC result excludes polyposis, when MUTYH-associated or other syndromes may be responsible Neglecting upper gastrointestinal and duodenal surveillance after colectomy Underestimating desmoid risk and provoking disease with unnecessary abdominal surgery Failing to arrange cascade testing and paediatric surveillance for at-risk relatives The condition arises from a germline loss-of-function variant in APC, a tumour-suppressor gene central to the Wnt signalling pathway. APC protein normally promotes degradation of beta-catenin, so its loss leads to beta-catenin accumulation and constitutive activation of Wnt target genes that drive crypt-cell proliferation. Somatic inactivation of the second APC allele in colonic epithelium initiates adenoma formation, and further mutations accelerate the well-described adenoma-carcinoma sequence, producing the profuse polyposis and eventual malignancy that define the disorder. Untreated classic disease progresses almost inevitably to colorectal cancer, so timely risk-reducing surgery is decisive for survival. After colectomy, desmoid tumours and upper gastrointestinal malignancy become the leading causes of morbidity and mortality, making lifelong multidisciplinary surveillance essential.

for common-form atrial fibrillation Rare monogenic forms are linked to variants in ion-channel genes (for example KCNQ1, KCNA5, SCN5A) and in genes such as those affecting natriuretic peptide assessment, rate or rhythm control, and treating any underlying disorder Family history-taking and, in selected early-onset cases, genetic evaluation can uncover a treatable inherited substrate Atrial fibrillation at a strikingly young age without acquired risk factors Associated syncope or features suggesting a channelopathy or cardiomyopathy Family history of sudden death or inherited heart disease Rapid ventricular rates causing haemodynamic compromise Overlooking a family history that reframes early-onset atrial fibrillation as inherited Missing an underlying cardiomyopathy or channelopathy heralded by the arrhythmia Assuming a monogenic cause when most familial cases are polygenic Neglecting stroke-risk assessment because the patient is young Familial atrial fibrillation encompasses a spectrum from rare single-gene disorders to common polygenic susceptibility. In monogenic forms, variants that alter atrial ion currents change the action potential and refractoriness, either shortening it to favour re-entry or otherwise destabilising atrial electrical activity, while structural gene variants alter the atrial substrate. In the far more common polygenic form, the cumulative effect of many common variants influences atrial development, electrophysiology and fibrosis, lowering the threshold for triggered activity and re-entrant circuits. Ectopic firing, frequently from the pulmonary vein region, initiates the arrhythmia, which is then sustained by an abnormal atrial substrate. The shared endpoint is disorganised atrial electrical activity with loss of coordinated contraction. Prognosis largely reflects the thromboembolic risk and any underlying structural or electrical heart disease; with appropriate anticoagulation decisions and rhythm or rate control, outcomes are generally favourable, though recurrence is common and an identified inherited substrate may carry additional implications.

arginine vasopressin deficiency to reduce confusion with diabetes mellitus Diagnosis uses a water deprivation test with response to desmopressin, increasingly supported by copeptin measurement Treatment is with desmopressin replacement, with attention to avoiding water intoxication from overtreatment Hypernatraemia and dehydration when access to water is limited Severe symptoms in infancy with poor feeding and failure to thrive Features suggesting a structural pituitary lesion rather than familial disease Hyponatraemia from excessive desmopressin or overhydration Confusing the condition with diabetes mellitus because of the shared name Missing the gradual, progressive childhood onset and attributing symptoms to behaviour Overtreating with desmopressin and precipitating hyponatraemia Failing to distinguish central from nephrogenic or psychogenic causes before treatment Familial central diabetes insipidus arises from mutations in the AVP gene, which encodes the precursor of arginine vasopressin. Most mutations produce a misfolded precursor that accumulates and is thought to be cytotoxic to the magnocellular neurones of the hypothalamus that synthesise the hormone. Progressive loss of these neurones reduces vasopressin secretion from the posterior pituitary, so the kidney cannot concentrate urine; large volumes of dilute urine are produced and compensatory thirst drives high fluid intake. The gradual neuronal loss explains the typical delayed and progressive onset. With reliable desmopressin replacement and free access to water, prognosis is excellent and normal life is expected; the main risks come from dehydration when fluid intake is restricted and from hyponatraemia due to overtreatment.

familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome — FCAS, familial cold urticaria, NLRP3-associated CAPS (mild) Acquired cold contact urticaria Muckle-Wells syndrome Neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease Cryoglobulinaemia and cryofibrinogenaemia Chronic spontaneous urticaria Other hereditary recurrent fevers such as familial Mediterranean fever NLRP3 gene analysis, with NLRP12 testing where the phenotype fits but NLRP3 is negative Generalised (evaporative) cold provocation with monitoring of symptoms and inflammatory markers Local ice-cube contact test to distinguish from acquired cold urticaria Acute-phase reactants measured before and after cold challenge Skin biopsy showing a neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis Baseline audiometry to detect any overlap with Muckle-Wells syndrome Mildest phenotype of the cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome spectrum, usually caused by autosomal dominant gain-of-function NLRP3 variants; a clinically similar NLRP12-associated form (sometimes termed FCAS2) is also recognised. Attacks follow generalised environmental cold exposure rather than direct local contact, typically after a delay of an hour or two, and are often reproducible. Episodes are brief, commonly settling within a day, and comprise a cold-induced urticaria-like rash, fever, chills, arthralgia, conjunctivitis and headache. Unlike acquired cold contact urticaria, the local ice-cube provocation test is negative because it is systemic cooling, not local contact, that provokes symptoms. Symptoms tend to be worse in the evening and can be triggered by air-conditioned or refrigerated environments as well as outdoor cold. Sensorineural hearing loss and amyloidosis are uncommon at this mild end but overlap with Muckle-Wells syndrome can occur, so surveillance remains prudent. Interleukin-1 blockade is highly effective for troublesome disease, alongside practical avoidance of cold exposure. Acute-phase reactants rise during a cold-provoked attack and can help confirm a systemic inflammatory response. Emerging sensorineural hearing loss suggesting progression towards a more severe cryopyrin-associated phenotype Proteinuria raising the possibility of AA amyloidosis Neurological features such as chronic headache or papilloedema that are atypical for the mild phenotype Persistently raised inflammatory markers between cold-provoked attacks Confusing the condition with acquired cold contact urticaria and being misled by a negative local ice-cube test Expecting immediate rather than delayed symptom onset after cold exposure Assuming a negative NLRP3 result excludes the diagnosis without considering NLRP12-associated disease Neglecting audiological and renal surveillance because the phenotype appears mild Gain-of-function NLRP3 variants lower the activation threshold of the cryopyrin inflammasome, which in this phenotype is triggered by a fall in temperature. Cold-induced assembly of the inflammasome activates caspase-1, driving maturation and release of interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-18 and producing a self-limiting burst of neutrophil-rich systemic inflammation. Because the underlying molecular lesion is shared with the more severe cryopyrin-associated syndromes, the mechanism and treatment response mirror those conditions, differing chiefly in the milder degree of constitutive activation and the requirement for a cold stimulus. The prognosis is generally favourable, with cold avoidance and interleukin-1 blockade providing effective control and a low risk of the amyloidosis seen at the severe end of the spectrum. Quality of life can nonetheless be significantly affected in cold climates without treatment.

left ventricular dysfunction and heart failure Sustained or non-sustained ventricular arrhythmia Significant conduction disease suggesting an overlapping or alternative genetic cause Family history of sudden death prompting closer risk stratification Over-interpreting a truncating variant outside the A-band or in low-penetrance regions as clearly causal Failing to counsel carriers about reversible triggers that modulate penetrance Assuming a benign course and under-treating heart failure or arrhythmia Neglecting cascade screening of at-risk relatives Titin is the largest human protein and spans half the sarcomere, acting as a molecular spring that sets passive myocardial stiffness and contributes to sarcomere assembly and mechanosensing. Truncating variants, particularly in the A-band, produce a shortened protein and reduce the amount of functional full-length titin, impairing sarcomere integrity and the myocyte's ability to handle mechanical load. Over time, and often when combined with additional stressors, this leads to progressive ventricular dilatation, contractile dysfunction and interstitial change characteristic of dilated cardiomyopathy. The age-related, stress-modulated penetrance reflects the need for a cumulative insult on top of the genetic predisposition before overt disease develops. Compared with some other genetic cardiomyopathies the prognosis is relatively favourable, with substantial potential for recovery on guideline-directed heart failure therapy, though penetrance, disease progression and arrhythmic risk vary and are worsened by ongoing cardiotoxic exposures.

The predominant Ashkenazi founder variant reduces functional ELP1 in a tissue-specific manner, impairing development and survival of sensory and autonomic neurons. This leads to progressive depletion of neurons in the dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, producing baroreflex failure, defective control of blood pressure, temperature and secretions, reduced pain and temperature sensation, and impaired airway protection. The autonomic crises reflect unbuffered sympathetic surges from this baroreflex and afferent failure. Survival has improved with specialist multidisciplinary care, though morbidity and mortality remain substantial from aspiration, cardiovascular instability, autonomic crises and sudden death. Progressive optic neuropathy, worsening gait ataxia and renal impairment can develop over time.

The resulting retinal ischaemia drives release of angiogenic factors, producing abnormal new vessels, exudation, fibrovascular proliferation and vitreoretinal traction. Traction can drag the macula and vessels temporally and lead to falciform folds and tractional or combined retinal detachment. Prognosis depends heavily on stage: mild peripheral avascularity may never threaten vision, whereas progression to tractional detachment or falciform folds can cause severe, sometimes bilateral, visual loss; early detection and treatment improve outcomes.

the receptor tyrosine-kinase genes KIT or PDGFRA. These variants cause ligand-independent, constitutive activation of the receptor and its downstream proliferative signalling pathways in the interstitial cells of Cajal, the gut pacemaker cells from which GISTs derive. The inherited mutation predisposes to hyperplasia of these cells and to the development of multiple stromal tumours throughout the gastrointestinal tract, often at an earlier age than sporadic disease. The specific germline variant influences tumour distribution, associated phenotypic features and sensitivity to targeted tyrosine-kinase inhibition. Outcome depends on tumour size, mitotic activity, site and resectability; localised tumours may be cured surgically while advanced disease is managed with tyrosine-kinase inhibition. The hereditary predisposition means new tumours can arise over time, so long-term surveillance is required.

mineralocorticoid replacement is generally not required Hypoglycaemia, seizures, or collapse indicating adrenal crisis Prolonged neonatal jaundice with hypoglycaemia Intercurrent illness without stress-dose glucocorticoid cover Failure to recognise deepening hyperpigmentation as a sign of severe glucocorticoid deficiency Expecting salt-wasting and electrolyte disturbance and therefore discounting adrenal insufficiency when they are absent Missing the diagnosis in a hypoglycaemic or persistently jaundiced neonate Adding unnecessary mineralocorticoid replacement Failing to provide stress-dose cover and an emergency plan Familial glucocorticoid deficiency results from failure of the adrenal cortex to respond to ACTH. Mutations in MC2R disable the melanocortin-2 receptor through which ACTH stimulates cortisol synthesis, and mutations in MRAP prevent that receptor from being trafficked to the cell surface; other subtypes affect antioxidant defence or replication pathways in the adrenal. Cortisol production in the zona fasciculata fails while the renin-angiotensin-driven zona glomerulosa continues to make aldosterone. Loss of cortisol feedback drives ACTH to very high levels, causing hyperpigmentation, and leaves the child vulnerable to hypoglycaemia and life-threatening crisis during stress. With early diagnosis, reliable glucocorticoid replacement, and education about sick-day rules and emergency treatment, prognosis is good; the principal danger is unrecognised adrenal crisis, particularly hypoglycaemia in infancy, which can be fatal or cause neurological injury.

a CACNA1A cause Familial hemiplegic migraine is caused by autosomal dominant variants in genes controlling neuronal ion homeostasis: CACNA1A (P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel), ATP1A2 (the astrocytic sodium-potassium ATPase) and SCN1A (a neuronal sodium channel). These variants increase synaptic glutamate availability and neuronal excitability, or impair clearance of potassium and glutamate, lowering the threshold for cortical spreading depression, the slow wave of neuronal and glial depolarisation that underlies migraine aura. The motor weakness reflects spread of this depolarising wave across motor cortex, and the shared final pathway explains why distinct channel and pump defects produce a similar clinical syndrome. Between attacks most patients are neurologically well, and individual episodes, although alarming, are usually fully reversible. Attack frequency and severity vary widely; some CACNA1A-associated cases carry a risk of severe prolonged attacks or progressive cerebellar ataxia, so the outlook depends on the specific genotype and phenotype.
