or cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis Multi-organ dysfunction with hepatic failure and disseminated intravascular coagulation Recurrence of hyperinflammation implying an underlying genetic cause requiring transplantation Attributing the picture to sepsis and missing the diagnosis while the patient deteriorates Waiting for haemophagocytosis on marrow before acting, when it may be absent early and is not required for diagnosis Failing to distinguish primary genetic HLH from secondary causes, which alters the need for transplantation Overlooking central nervous system disease that requires directed therapy Familial haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis results from inherited defects in the machinery that cytotoxic T lymphocytes and natural killer cells use to kill infected or activated target cells. Genes such as PRF1, which encodes the pore-forming protein perforin, and UNC13D, STX11 and STXBP2, which govern the docking, priming and fusion of cytotoxic granules, are required for delivery of the lethal granule contents. When cytotoxicity fails, activated lymphocytes cannot eliminate their targets or contract the immune response, so persistent antigenic (often viral) stimulation drives relentless activation of T cells and macrophages. The resulting cytokine storm, with excessive interferon-gamma and macrophage activation, produces the fever, cytopenias, organ infiltration and haemophagocytosis that define the syndrome. Untreated familial haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis is almost uniformly fatal, but prompt control of hyperinflammation with immunochemotherapy followed by haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offers the chance of long-term survival, with outcome strongly influenced by early diagnosis and the extent of central nervous system involvement.

Familial hyperaldosteronism type 3 (KCNJ5) — FH-III, FH type 3, KCNJ5-related familial hyperaldosteronism, GIRK4 hyperaldosteronism Other familial hyperaldosteronism subtypes (type 1 glucocorticoid-remediable, type 2, type 4 with CACNA1H) Sporadic aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn syndrome) Bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia Apparent mineralocorticoid excess or Liddle syndrome Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (11-beta-hydroxylase or 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency) Renovascular or other secondary hypertension Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio as the screening test, showing high aldosterone with suppressed renin Confirmatory aldosterone suppression testing where the diagnosis is unclear Serum potassium and acid-base assessment for hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis Urinary or plasma hybrid steroids 18-hydroxycortisol and 18-oxocortisol Adrenal CT and, in selected cases, adrenal venous sampling to assess lateralisation KCNJ5 germline genetic testing with cascade family screening A rare autosomal dominant form of primary aldosteronism caused by germline mutations in KCNJ5, which encodes the GIRK4 potassium channel of the adrenal zona glomerulosa Typically presents in childhood with severe, often treatment-resistant hypertension and hypokalaemia Distinct from glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism (familial hyperaldosteronism type 1); it is generally not corrected by dexamethasone and dexamethasone may paradoxically worsen aldosterone secretion in some patients The phenotype is variable, from florid disease with massive bilateral adrenal hyperplasia needing bilateral adrenalectomy to milder disease responsive to mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism Biochemistry shows elevated aldosterone with suppressed renin, and the hybrid steroids 18-hydroxycortisol and 18-oxocortisol are typically raised The mutations impair channel selectivity, causing sodium influx, membrane depolarisation, calcium entry and autonomous aldosterone production Germline genetic testing confirms the diagnosis and informs cascade family screening Severe childhood-onset hypertension resistant to multiple agents Profound or symptomatic hypokalaemia causing arrhythmia or weakness Massive bilateral adrenal enlargement that may require bilateral adrenalectomy Target-organ damage such as left ventricular hypertrophy or stroke from early sustained hypertension Assuming, as in type 1 disease, that dexamethasone will control aldosterone, when it usually does not and can worsen it in this subtype Attributing resistant paediatric hypertension to essential hypertension and missing a monogenic cause Failing to exclude secondary causes of hypokalaemia before genetic testing Overlooking family screening once a KCNJ5 mutation is identified Familial hyperaldosteronism type 3 is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by germline mutations in KCNJ5, which encodes the G-protein-activated inwardly rectifying potassium channel GIRK4 in the adrenal zona glomerulosa. Mutations near the channel selectivity filter cause loss of potassium selectivity and pathological sodium conductance, depolarising the cell, opening voltage-gated calcium channels and raising intracellular calcium. This drives constitutive transcription of aldosterone synthase and autonomous aldosterone hypersecretion independent of the renin-angiotensin system, with resulting sodium retention, potassium wasting and hypertension. The same channel is somatically mutated in many sporadic aldosterone-producing adenomas. Outcome depends on severity: milder cases are controlled with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, whereas florid disease with bilateral hyperplasia may need bilateral adrenalectomy and lifelong steroid replacement; early diagnosis and blood-pressure control limit cardiovascular and renal damage.

Familial hyperaldosteronism type 1 — FH-I, glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism, GRA, CYP11B1/CYP11B2 chimeric gene hyperaldosteronism, dexamethasone-suppressible hyperaldosteronism Aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn syndrome) Bilateral adrenal (idiopathic) hyperaldosteronism Familial hyperaldosteronism types II, III, and IV Apparent mineralocorticoid excess and Liddle syndrome Essential hypertension, particularly resistant hypertension Secondary hyperaldosteronism from renovascular disease Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio with suppressed renin Genetic testing for the chimeric CYP11B1/CYP11B2 gene (long-PCR or Southern blot) Urine or plasma hybrid steroids 18-oxocortisol and 18-hydroxycortisol Serum potassium and acid-base assessment (often only mild hypokalaemia) Cerebral vascular imaging (e.g. MR angiography) to screen for intracranial aneurysms Dexamethasone suppression demonstrating fall in aldosterone (supportive, historically used) Autosomal dominant form of primary aldosteronism caused by a chimeric CYP11B1/CYP11B2 gene, in which aldosterone synthase becomes regulated by adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) rather than the renin-angiotensin system Because aldosterone secretion is ACTH-driven, low-dose glucocorticoid (which suppresses ACTH) corrects the aldosterone excess, giving the alternative name glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism It causes early-onset, often familial, hypertension that can be severe and treatment-resistant, with a high risk of early haemorrhagic stroke from intracranial aneurysms Biochemistry shows a raised aldosterone-to-renin ratio with suppressed renin, and characteristically elevated hybrid steroids (18-oxocortisol and 18-hydroxycortisol) Hypokalaemia is often milder or absent compared with other forms of primary aldosteronism, so normokalaemia does not exclude the diagnosis Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing for the chimeric gene; management uses low-dose glucocorticoid to suppress ACTH and/or mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists, avoiding over-suppression Severe or resistant hypertension presenting in childhood or young adulthood Family history of early haemorrhagic stroke or intracranial aneurysm Marked hypokalaemia or its complications when present Hypertensive end-organ damage at a young age Excluding primary aldosteronism because potassium is normal, when hypokalaemia is often mild in this condition Over-treating with glucocorticoid and causing iatrogenic Cushingoid effects or growth suppression in children Missing the familial nature and failing to screen relatives and assess for intracranial aneurysms Relying on imaging for a nodule and overlooking a genetic, dexamethasone-suppressible cause Familial hyperaldosteronism type 1 arises from unequal crossing over between the highly homologous CYP11B1 (11-beta-hydroxylase) and CYP11B2 (aldosterone synthase) genes, creating a chimeric gene. This fusion places aldosterone synthase activity under the control of the ACTH-responsive CYP11B1 promoter, so aldosterone is produced ectopically in the ACTH-regulated zona fasciculata and is no longer governed by angiotensin II or potassium. The result is inappropriate, ACTH-dependent aldosterone excess causing sodium retention, volume expansion, renin suppression, and hypertension, together with production of the hybrid steroids 18-oxocortisol and 18-hydroxycortisol. Because ACTH drives the process, glucocorticoid suppression of ACTH reduces aldosterone. With early diagnosis and appropriate therapy blood pressure is usually well controlled and cardiovascular and cerebrovascular risk reduced, but undiagnosed disease carries a significant risk of early stroke from ruptured intracranial aneurysms and hypertensive complications. Aneurysm surveillance is advised in affected families.

Familial hyperaldosteronism type 2 — FH-II, CLCN2-related familial hyperaldosteronism, chloride channel ClC-2 hyperaldosteronism, non-glucocorticoid-remediable familial hyperaldosteronism Familial hyperaldosteronism type 1 (glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism) Familial hyperaldosteronism types III (KCNJ5) and IV (CACNA1H) Sporadic aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn syndrome) Bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperaldosteronism Essential and resistant hypertension Other monogenic hypertension syndromes (Liddle syndrome, apparent mineralocorticoid excess) Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio with suppressed renin and confirmatory aldosterone testing CLCN2 gene sequencing and exclusion of the type 1 chimeric gene Serum potassium and acid-base status Adrenal cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI) to identify adenoma or hyperplasia Adrenal venous sampling to assess lateralisation before considering surgery Absence of glucocorticoid-suppressible aldosterone and of type 1 hybrid steroids Autosomal dominant familial primary aldosteronism associated with gain-of-function mutations in CLCN2, encoding the chloride channel ClC-2 in adrenal glomerulosa cells Unlike type 1, it is not glucocorticoid-remediable, so aldosterone excess is not suppressed by dexamethasone and hybrid steroids are not the diagnostic hallmark It presents as familial hypertension from primary aldosteronism, which may be due to adrenal hyperplasia, adenoma, or both, and can appear in childhood or adulthood Biochemistry mirrors other primary aldosteronism with a raised aldosterone-to-renin ratio and suppressed renin, with variable hypokalaemia Diagnosis is clinical and biochemical, supported by CLCN2 testing and by excluding the chimeric gene of type 1; family screening is important Management follows primary aldosteronism principles: mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists for bilateral disease and adrenalectomy for a lateralised aldosterone-producing lesion Early-onset or resistant hypertension with a strong family history Significant hypokalaemia or its complications when present Hypertensive end-organ damage at a young age Lateralising lesion on venous sampling indicating a surgically curable cause Assuming familial hyperaldosteronism will respond to glucocorticoid, as type 1 does, and delaying appropriate therapy Interpreting normokalaemia as excluding primary aldosteronism Proceeding to adrenalectomy without adrenal venous sampling to confirm lateralisation in bilateral disease Not screening hypertensive relatives in an autosomal dominant condition Familial hyperaldosteronism type 2 is linked to germline gain-of-function variants in CLCN2, which encodes the voltage-gated chloride channel ClC-2 expressed in adrenal zona glomerulosa cells. Increased chloride efflux through the mutant channel depolarises the glomerulosa cell membrane, opening voltage-gated calcium channels and raising intracellular calcium, the key signal driving aldosterone synthase expression and aldosterone secretion. This produces autonomous, renin-independent aldosterone excess with sodium retention, volume expansion, and hypertension. Because the mechanism is independent of ACTH, the condition is not glucocorticoid-remediable, in contrast to the chimeric-gene disorder of type 1. With diagnosis and targeted treatment, whether medical therapy for bilateral disease or surgery for a lateralised lesion, blood pressure and cardiovascular risk can be well controlled, whereas undiagnosed aldosterone excess drives hypertensive and cardiovascular complications. Outcome depends on early detection and family screening.

ursodeoxycholic acid, fat-soluble vitamin replacement, and antipruritic measures Vitamin K-responsive coagulopathy with bleeding Progressive itch with sleep disturbance and skin excoriation Growth faltering from malabsorption Evolving chronic liver disease in TJP2-related cases Interpreting a normal GGT as excluding significant cholestasis Missing vitamin K deficiency as a cause of bleeding Overlooking the diagnosis in isolated or consanguineous populations Assuming a uniformly benign outcome despite genotype-dependent progression Familial hypercholanaemia is a genetically heterogeneous condition in which serum bile acid concentrations are elevated without the biochemical hallmarks of biliary obstruction. Reported causes include mutations in TJP2 (tight junction protein 2), which compromises the paracellular barrier of the bile canaliculus; BAAT (bile acid-CoA:amino acid N-acyltransferase), which impairs conjugation of bile acids with glycine and taurine; and EPHX1 (microsomal epoxide hydrolase), affecting hepatocellular bile acid transport. The net effect is disturbed enterohepatic recirculation with raised circulating bile acids, itch, and malabsorption of dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins, characteristically with a low or normal gamma-glutamyl transferase. Many individuals have a benign course with elevated bile acids and manageable symptoms, but pruritus and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency can be troublesome, and certain genotypes (particularly TJP2-related disease) carry a risk of progressive liver injury.

Familial hypercholesterolaemia — FH, familial hypercholesterolemia, LDLR-related hypercholesterolaemia, APOB-related hypercholesterolaemia, PCSK9 gain-of-function hypercholesterolaemia Polygenic hypercholesterolaemia Familial combined hyperlipidaemia Secondary hypercholesterolaemia from hypothyroidism Nephrotic syndrome-related hyperlipidaemia Cholestatic liver disease with lipid elevation Sitosterolaemia Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis Fasting lipid profile with quantification of LDL cholesterol Assessment against Dutch Lipid Clinic Network or Simon Broome diagnostic criteria Genetic testing for LDLR, APOB and PCSK9 variants Exclusion of secondary causes (thyroid function, renal and liver profiles, glucose) Cardiovascular risk assessment and imaging for subclinical atherosclerosis where indicated Cascade screening of first-degree relatives An inherited disorder of markedly elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol from birth, leading to premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease Most commonly caused by loss-of-function variants in the LDL-receptor gene (LDLR), with defective apolipoprotein B (APOB) and gain-of-function PCSK9 variants as further causes Heterozygous FH is common and often underdiagnosed; the rare homozygous form causes very severe hypercholesterolaemia and childhood-onset vascular disease Physical signs include tendon xanthomata (classically of the Achilles and finger extensor tendons), xanthelasma and corneal arcus, though these may be absent Diagnostic tools such as the Dutch Lipid Clinic Network and Simon Broome criteria combine LDL level, clinical signs, personal and family history and genetic testing High-intensity statins are first line, with ezetimibe and PCSK9 inhibitors added to reach LDL targets; homozygous disease may require lipoprotein apheresis and specialist therapies Cascade testing of relatives is highly effective at identifying affected but asymptomatic family members Early, sustained LDL lowering markedly reduces lifetime cardiovascular risk Very high LDL cholesterol, especially with tendon xanthomata Premature coronary or other atherosclerotic disease in the patient or close relatives Childhood presentation or features suggesting homozygous disease Personal or family history of premature sudden cardiac death Attributing very high LDL solely to lifestyle and missing the inherited diagnosis Relying on the presence of xanthomata, which are often absent in younger patients Failing to arrange cascade testing of relatives Under-treating and not escalating therapy to reach LDL targets Overlooking severe homozygous disease presenting in childhood Familial hypercholesterolaemia results from variants that impair clearance of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) from the circulation. Loss-of-function LDL-receptor variants reduce hepatic uptake of LDL particles; defective apolipoprotein B impairs binding of LDL to its receptor; and gain-of-function PCSK9 variants increase degradation of LDL receptors. The common consequence is lifelong elevation of circulating LDL cholesterol, which is deposited in arterial walls to accelerate atherosclerosis and in tendons and skin to form xanthomata. The cumulative cholesterol burden from birth explains the markedly premature coronary and other atherosclerotic disease. Untreated FH substantially shortens life expectancy through premature cardiovascular disease, but early diagnosis and sustained aggressive lipid lowering can bring cardiovascular risk close to that of the general population.

WNK kinases WNK1 and WNK4, regulated by the KLHL3-CUL3 ubiquitin ligase complex, control the activity of the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Disease-causing variants increase WNK signalling, either directly or by impairing degradation of the kinases, which enhances cotransporter activity and boosts distal sodium chloride reabsorption. The resulting volume expansion produces hypertension and suppresses renin. Because more sodium is reabsorbed electroneutrally in the distal convoluted tubule, less sodium reaches the collecting duct for exchange with potassium and hydrogen, reducing potassium and acid secretion and causing hyperkalaemia with hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis. Thiazides reverse the process by blocking the overactive cotransporter. The prognosis is excellent when recognised, because thiazide therapy typically normalises blood pressure and electrolytes; unrecognised disease can lead to complications of chronic hypertension and hyperkalaemia.

This receptor, expressed in the parathyroid glands and renal tubules, normally senses extracellular calcium and suppresses parathyroid hormone secretion and promotes renal calcium excretion as calcium rises. With reduced receptor sensitivity, the set-point for calcium is reset upward, so mild hypercalcaemia persists with inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone, and the kidney avidly reabsorbs calcium, producing the characteristic hypocalciuria. The condition is benign with an excellent prognosis and generally requires no treatment, only recognition and avoidance of inappropriate parathyroid surgery.

familial mediterranean fever — FMF, recurrent hereditary polyserositis, MEFV-associated periodic fever TNF receptor-associated periodic syndrome Mevalonate kinase deficiency (hyper-IgD syndrome) Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome spectrum PFAPA (periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis) syndrome Acute surgical abdomen such as appendicitis or perforated viscus Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease Acute intermittent porphyria Targeted MEFV gene sequencing for pathogenic variants Acute-phase reactants (C-reactive protein, serum amyloid A, fibrinogen) measured during and between attacks Serial urinalysis for proteinuria as amyloidosis surveillance Renal biopsy with Congo red staining when nephrotic-range proteinuria develops SAA1 genotype where available to refine amyloidosis risk stratification Cross-sectional imaging during an attack to document serositis and exclude a surgical cause Caused by pathogenic variants in MEFV encoding pyrin, classically autosomal recessive with founder populations across the eastern Mediterranean (Sephardic and Mizrahi Jews, Armenians, Turks, Arabs); M694V homozygosity carries the most severe phenotype and highest amyloidosis risk. Attacks are short-lived, usually resolving within a few days, and feature fever with self-limiting serositis: sterile peritonitis mimicking an acute abdomen, pleuritis, and less often pericarditis. Acute monoarthritis of a large lower-limb joint and an erysipelas-like erythema over the ankle, foot or shin are characteristic mucocutaneous and articular manifestations. Colchicine taken continuously is the cornerstone of therapy, preventing attacks in most patients and, crucially, preventing systemic AA amyloidosis; adherence rather than dose escalation usually explains apparent failure. Interleukin-1 blockade is reserved for genuinely colchicine-resistant or colchicine-intolerant disease and for established amyloidosis. Subclinical inflammation with persistently raised serum amyloid A can occur between clinically silent intervals and drives amyloid deposition even when attacks seem controlled. Protracted febrile myalgia and exercise-induced lower-limb myalgia are recognised variants that can be mistaken for vasculitis or myositis. A trial of colchicine with a clear symptomatic and biochemical response supports the diagnosis when genetic testing is equivocal. New or increasing proteinuria signalling incipient renal AA amyloidosis An attack that fails to remit within the usual short window, raising concern for true surgical peritonitis or protracted febrile myalgia Breathlessness or haemodynamic compromise suggesting pericardial involvement Persistently elevated inflammatory markers between attacks despite apparent clinical control Recurrent sterile peritonitis leading to unnecessary appendicectomy or laparotomy before the diagnosis is considered Assuming a negative or heterozygous MEFV result excludes the disease, as phenotype does not always follow a simple recessive pattern and not all pathogenic variants are covered by every panel Attributing apparent colchicine failure to true resistance rather than to non-adherence or gastrointestinal intolerance Overlooking silent amyloidosis because attacks are clinically well controlled Pyrin, the product of the MEFV gene expressed predominantly in innate immune cells, normally acts as a sensor that becomes activated when RhoA-mediated pyrin phosphorylation is lost, as occurs with certain bacterial toxins. Gain-of-function variants lower the threshold for assembly of the pyrin inflammasome, leading to caspase-1 activation, unregulated maturation and release of interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-18, and neutrophil-rich serosal inflammation. The episodic nature reflects intermittent triggering superimposed on a lowered inflammatory set point, while chronic overproduction of serum amyloid A during and between attacks underlies reactive AA amyloidosis, the principal determinant of long-term morbidity. With adherent colchicine prophylaxis most patients achieve good control of attacks and normal life expectancy, and the risk of amyloidosis falls substantially. Untreated or poorly controlled disease, particularly with high-risk MEFV and SAA1 genotypes, progresses to renal failure from AA amyloidosis.

Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases — FMF, Hereditary recurrent fever syndromes, Autoinflammatory diseases, Periodic fever syndromes Other hereditary recurrent fever syndromes (TRAPS, HIDS/MKD, FCAS, MWS, NOMID) PFAPA syndrome Systemic-onset juvenile rheumatoid arthritis / adult Still's disease Porphyria Hereditary angioedema Inflammatory bowel disease Gynecologic disorders (in women presenting with recurrent abdominal pain) MEFV genetic testing (severe mutations cluster in exon 10; ~70% of clinically typical FMF have two mutations in trans; expert-curated mutation databases such as Infevers aid interpretation) Acute-phase markers during attacks: elevated ESR, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis (in children), and raised C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, haptoglobin, and serum immunoglobulins Urinalysis (transient albuminuria/hematuria during attacks; persistent proteinuria between attacks should raise concern for amyloidosis) Renal or rectal biopsy to confirm suspected AA amyloidosis Genotype-specific testing for other syndromes: TNFRSF1A (TRAPS), MVK with markedly elevated urinary mevalonate during attacks (HIDS/MKD), NLRP3 (cryopyrinopathies, including testing for somatic mosaicism) Imaging during attacks: chest radiograph (atelectasis/effusion in pleural attacks), upright abdominal radiograph or CT (air-fluid levels, small amount of free fluid) Systemic-onset juvenile rheumatoid arthritis / adult Still's disease Porphyria Hereditary angioedema Inflammatory bowel disease Other monogenic autoinflammatory syndromes FMF is the prototype hereditary autoinflammatory disease: recurrent self-limited fever with serosal, synovial, or cutaneous inflammation, distinguished from autoimmune disease by the relative absence of high-titer autoantibodies or antigen-specific T cells and a predominant role of the innate immune system (Harrison 22e p.2934). Roughly 90% of patients have their first attack by age 20; typical episodes last about 24-72 hours, with arthritic attacks tending to run longer (Harrison 22e p.2934). Over 90% of FMF patients have abdominal (peritoneal) attacks; laparotomy reveals a sterile neutrophil-rich peritoneal exudate, and ascites is rare (Harrison 22e p.2934). Erysipelas-like erythema, a raised erythematous rash typically on the dorsum of the foot, ankle, or lower leg, is the most characteristic skin finding and occurs most often in M694V homozygotes (Harrison 22e p.2934). FMF arthritis is usually monoarticular (knee, ankle, hip) with large sterile neutrophil-rich effusions and little erythema or warmth; radiographic changes are rare even after repeated attacks (Harrison 22e p.2934). The MEFV gene encodes pyrin (~95 kDa); its N-terminal PYRIN domain nucleates the pyrin inflammasome that activates caspase-1, driving IL-1beta and IL-18 secretion and gasdermin-D-mediated pyroptosis (Harrison 22e p.2934). FMF-associated MEFV mutations are gain-of-function, lowering the threshold for pyrin inflammasome activation; severe disease-associated mutations cluster in exon 10, and M694V homozygosity predicts earlier onset and more arthritis, rash, and amyloidosis (Harrison 22e p.2935-2936). The principal hereditary recurrent fever syndromes are differentiated by attack length, ethnicity, and features: TRAPS (TNFRSF1A, dominant, attacks often >7 days, migratory myalgia with overlying erythema, periorbital edema/conjunctivitis), HIDS/MKD (MVK, recessive, painful cervical adenopathy and oral ulcers), and the NLRP3-associated cryopyrinopathies FCAS, MWS, and NOMID (Harrison 22e p.2935-2937). Cryopyrinopathies form a spectrum: FCAS (cold-induced urticaria-like rash, fever, arthralgia, conjunctivitis), MWS (urticarial rash not cold-induced, progressive sensorineural hearing loss), and NOMID/neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease (chronic aseptic meningitis, characteristic arthropathy, rash) (Harrison 22e p.2937). About one-third of clinically typical NOMID patients lack germline NLRP3 mutations but are mosaic for somatic NLRP3 mutations; somatic NLRP3 mosaicism has rarely been reported in Schnitzler's syndrome (middle-age recurrent fever, urticaria, monoclonal IgM gammopathy, abnormal bone remodeling) (Harrison 22e p.2936-2937). PFAPA (periodic fever with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, cervical adenitis) is the most common periodic fever syndrome of childhood, notable for clock-like regularity, familial but non-Mendelian clustering, and a tendency to resolve by early adulthood (Harrison 22e p.2937). Over 60 monogenic autoinflammatory diseases are now recognized, grouped mechanistically into inflammasomopathies (FMF, HIDS, CAPS, PAPA, NLRC4-related), type I interferonopathies (STING-associated vasculopathy, COPA syndrome, Aicardi-Goutieres, CANDLE), and relopathies affecting NF-kB / TNF-induced cell death (Harrison 22e p.2937). Persistent proteinuria between attacks, suggesting developing AA amyloidosis Severe hyperpyrexia or febrile seizures in infants Protracted febrile myalgia lasting several weeks In cryopyrinopathies, sensorineural hearing loss (MWS) or chronic aseptic meningitis and progressive visual/CNS involvement (NOMID) Features of secondary vasculitis (IgA vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa) occurring at increased frequency in FMF Adult-onset relapsing polychondritis, Sweet's syndrome, vasculitis, or myelodysplasia in older men suggesting VEXAS syndrome A positive family history can be elicited in only about half of cases (especially where families are small), so its absence does not exclude FMF; FMF can also occur without known Mediterranean ancestry. Only about 70% of clinically typical FMF patients carry two identifiable MEFV mutations in trans, and many clinical cases have only a single demonstrable mutation, so genetic testing cannot rule out the diagnosis. Certain variants are functional polymorphisms rather than disease-causing: E148Q (common in some Asian populations) often affects overall inflammation more than causing clinical FMF, and TNFRSF1A R92Q and P46L may behave as polymorphisms in TRAPS. Serum IgD elevation is neither sensitive nor specific for HIDS/MKD: disease activity does not track IgD levels, some FMF/TRAPS patients have modestly raised IgD, and some MVK-mutation patients have normal IgD (markedly elevated urinary mevalonate during attacks is more reliable). About one-third of NOMID patients lack germline NLRP3 mutations and require testing for somatic mosaicism, which can be missed on standard germline sequencing. These disorders reflect dysregulated innate immunity rather than adaptive autoimmunity. In FMF, gain-of-function MEFV mutations lower the activation threshold of the pyrin inflammasome; pyrin (via its PYRIN domain and an adaptor) assembles a macromolecular complex that activates caspase-1, producing IL-1beta and IL-18 and triggering gasdermin-D-mediated pyroptosis. Pyrin normally senses bacterial toxins that inactivate RhoA GTPase as part of host defense. The other syndromes map to specific innate pathways: TRAPS arises from misfolding, aggregation, and retention of mutant TNFR1 with ligand-independent kinase activation, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, and proinflammatory cytokine release; HIDS/MKD results from mevalonate kinase deficiency that impairs isoprenoid (geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate) synthesis, mislocalizing and inactivating RhoA and thereby activating the pyrin inflammasome; FCAS/MWS/NOMID arise from NLRP3 (cryopyrin) mutations forming an overactive NLRP3 inflammasome with excess IL-1beta and IL-18. Broader categories include interferonopathies driven by aberrant intracellular nucleic-acid sensing (excess type I interferon) and relopathies that dysregulate NF-kB activation or TNF-induced cell death. Untreated chronic inflammation can lead to systemic AA amyloidosis from deposition of a serum amyloid A fragment. FMF attacks are self-limited and recur with variable frequency over a lifetime; episodes may even be associated with remission during pregnancy. The major determinant of long-term outcome is systemic AA amyloidosis, historically a common and serious complication. Amyloidosis risk is increased by the M694V homozygous genotype, positive family history, the SAA1 genotype, male gender, non-adherence to therapy, and national origin (paralleling infant mortality rate). Among the related syndromes, untreated TRAPS leads to amyloidosis in about 15% of cases, MWS in roughly 25%, while amyloidosis is uncommon in FCAS and is a late complication in NOMID. PFAPA generally has a benign course with resolution by early adulthood. NOMID is the most severe cryopyrinopathy. No formal numeric severity scale is given; the hereditary recurrent fevers are clinically stratified by syndrome (FMF, TRAPS, HIDS/MKD, and the NLRP3-associated spectrum of FCAS [mildest] -> MWS -> NOMID [most severe]) and by attack length, organ involvement, and genotype. In FMF, M694V homozygosity marks more severe disease (earlier onset; higher frequency of arthritis, rash, and amyloidosis). Development of systemic AA amyloidosis defines the severe end of the disease spectrum.

genotype-recommended age Assuming the familial form never involves the adrenal or parathyroid across the MEN2 spectrum Failing to test and counsel at-risk relatives for the dominant RET variant RET encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase essential for the development and function of neural-crest-derived tissues, including thyroid C cells. Activating germline variants cause constitutive, ligand-independent kinase signalling that drives proliferation of parafollicular C cells, progressing from C-cell hyperplasia to medullary thyroid carcinoma. Because the tumour originates from calcitonin-secreting cells, circulating calcitonin rises and serves as a sensitive marker of tumour burden. The particular codon affected determines how strongly the kinase is activated and therefore the aggressiveness and age of onset of the carcinoma, which is why genotype directs the timing of prophylactic thyroidectomy. In the familial form the oncogenic RET signalling is largely confined to the thyroid C cells, without the adrenal or parathyroid involvement seen in other MEN2 subtypes. When prophylactic thyroidectomy is performed early, guided by genotype and before metastatic spread, the outlook is excellent and cure is achievable; prognosis worsens with delayed diagnosis, nodal or distant metastases, and persistently elevated calcitonin.

penetrance, and to offer cascade testing The syndrome usually results from a germline loss-of-function variant in CDKN2A, which encodes two distinct tumour suppressors through alternative reading frames. p16INK4a inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 to hold cells in G1 via the retinoblastoma pathway, while p14ARF stabilises p53 by inhibiting its degradation. Loss of these functions removes key restraints on cell-cycle progression and on the apoptotic response to genomic stress, and when combined with ultraviolet-induced DNA damage in melanocytes this permits the accumulation of mutations that drive melanoma and contributes to pancreatic carcinogenesis. Melanoma risk is high and lifelong, but early detection through surveillance and prompt excision yields excellent outcomes for thin lesions. Pancreatic cancer, when it occurs, carries a poorer prognosis, underscoring the value of risk reduction and, in selected families, pancreatic surveillance.

Fluctuating distortion of the cochlear and vestibular sensory epithelia produces the episodic vertigo and the characteristic fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, which may become fixed and bilateral as the disease progresses. The course is variable and episodic, often with eventual stabilisation of vertigo but a tendency to progressive and sometimes bilateral hearing loss, so familial cases warrant longer-term audiovestibular monitoring.

other genes account for rarer forms Fat is redistributed rather than absent, so patients often show facial, neck, and truncal sparing or accumulation giving a cushingoid or muscular limb appearance Loss of peripheral fat storage capacity produces insulin resistance, hypertriglyceridaemia, hepatic steatosis, acanthosis nigricans, and often early type 2 diabetes Women are frequently recognised more readily than men because muscular, fat-depleted limbs are more conspicuous, and they have high rates of polycystic-ovary-type features Leptin is usually near-normal or only modestly reduced, so leptin (metreleptin) replacement benefits mainly the more leptin-deficient or severely affected patients Management centres on insulin sensitisers, aggressive triglyceride and glucose control, and screening for cardiac and hepatic complications Diagnosis rests on the partial fat-distribution pattern, metabolic profile, family history, and confirmatory genetics Acute pancreatitis from severe hypertriglyceridaemia Conduction disease, arrhythmia, or cardiomyopathy in LMNA mutation carriers Progressive fatty liver disease toward fibrosis Rapidly deteriorating glycaemic control despite treatment Misdiagnosing the truncal fat and rounded face as Cushing syndrome Overlooking limb fat loss in muscular-looking patients, especially men Assuming leptin replacement will help all cases when leptin is often near-normal Neglecting cardiac screening in LMNA-related disease Ascribing the diabetes simply to lifestyle and missing the genetic cause Familial partial lipodystrophy is a dominantly inherited disorder in which subcutaneous adipose tissue in the extremities and gluteal region is progressively lost, most often from mutations in LMNA (lamin A/C, FPLD2) that disrupt the nuclear lamina and adipocyte survival, or in PPARG (FPLD3) that impair adipocyte differentiation. Because the limbs lose their fat-storage capacity while other depots may be spared or expanded, ingested lipid overflows into liver and muscle, generating severe insulin resistance. This produces hypertriglyceridaemia, hepatic steatosis, acanthosis nigricans, and a strong predisposition to insulin-resistant diabetes and, in LMNA disease, associated myopathic and cardiac features. Long-term outlook is governed by metabolic and cardiovascular complications; with proactive control of triglycerides and diabetes and cardiac surveillance in laminopathy many patients do well, though premature cardiovascular disease and pancreatitis remain important risks.

Familial renal glucosuria (SGLT2/SLC5A2) — familial renal glucosuria, FRG, SGLT2, SLC5A2, renal glycosuria Diabetes mellitus Fanconi syndrome (generalised proximal tubulopathy) Gestational glucosuria Glucose-galactose malabsorption (SGLT1 defect, presenting with diarrhoea) Drug-induced glucosuria from SGLT2 inhibitors Laboratory or dipstick artefact Simultaneous blood glucose and urine glucose showing glucosuria with normoglycaemia Oral glucose tolerance test to exclude diabetes HbA1c within the normal range Urinalysis for other proximal tubular markers to exclude Fanconi syndrome Quantification of daily urinary glucose loss where clinically relevant SLC5A2 gene sequencing when confirmation is desired Caused by variants in SLC5A2, encoding the sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT2 in the proximal tubule The hallmark is persistent glucosuria with normal blood glucose and a normal oral glucose tolerance test It is a benign, usually asymptomatic condition discovered incidentally on urinalysis, not a form of diabetes mellitus Inheritance shows co-dominant expression: heterozygotes have mild glucosuria while homozygotes or compound heterozygotes lose larger quantities Rarely, heavy glucose loss is associated with polyuria, mild volume depletion, or enuresis, and occasionally episodic ketosis during fasting or pregnancy No specific treatment is needed; reassurance and confirmation that carbohydrate metabolism is normal are the mainstays The transporter is the pharmacological target of SGLT2-inhibitor drugs, which reproduce a similar glucosuric state therapeutically Coexisting aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, or proteinuria suggesting Fanconi syndrome rather than isolated glucosuria Symptomatic volume depletion or dehydration from heavy glucose loss Fasting or pregnancy-associated ketosis Misdiagnosing the glucosuria as diabetes mellitus and starting unnecessary treatment Failing to distinguish isolated renal glucosuria from generalised Fanconi syndrome Overinvestigating an incidental, harmless finding Not counselling about occasional fasting ketosis or dehydration in heavy losers SGLT2 is a high-capacity, low-affinity sodium-glucose cotransporter on the apical membrane of the early proximal tubule and is responsible for reabsorbing the bulk of filtered glucose. Loss-of-function variants in SLC5A2 lower the renal threshold for glucose, so glucose appears in the urine at normal plasma concentrations. Because systemic glucose handling and insulin secretion are intact, blood glucose remains normal and there is no hyperglycaemia. The degree of glucosuria reflects the residual transporter activity, with homozygous defects producing the largest urinary losses. Downstream SGLT1 in the later proximal tubule reclaims some glucose, limiting total loss and generally keeping the condition clinically silent. The condition is benign with a normal life expectancy and does not progress to renal impairment; most people remain asymptomatic and require no treatment.

Familial sick sinus syndrome (SCN5A/HCN4) — familial sinus node dysfunction, hereditary sick sinus syndrome, SCN5A, HCN4, inherited sinoatrial node disease, familial bradycardia-tachycardia syndrome Acquired degenerative (age-related) sinus node dysfunction Drug-induced bradycardia (beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, antiarrhythmics) Athletic training-related sinus bradycardia and vagotonia Hypothyroidism or other metabolic causes of bradycardia Atrioventricular conduction disease and other inherited arrhythmia syndromes Neurally mediated (vasovagal) syncope 12-lead ECG documenting sinus bradycardia, pauses, or sinoatrial block Ambulatory Holter or extended/implantable loop monitoring to correlate symptoms with rhythm Exercise testing to assess chronotropic competence Echocardiography to evaluate for associated structural disease such as left ventricular non-compaction with HCN4 variants Thyroid function and medication review to exclude reversible causes Genetic testing of an inherited arrhythmia panel with cascade family screening An inherited disorder of sinoatrial node function causing inappropriate sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses or arrest, chronotropic incompetence, and sinoatrial exit block, often presenting earlier in life than acquired degenerative sinus node disease Loss-of-function variants in the cardiac sodium channel gene SCN5A cause an autosomal recessive form that may also feature conduction disease and overlap with other sodium-channelopathies Variants in HCN4, which encodes the pacemaker 'funny' current channel, cause an autosomal dominant form characterised by bradycardia and blunted heart-rate response, sometimes associated with left ventricular non-compaction A bradycardia-tachycardia pattern is common, with atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter alternating with symptomatic pauses Symptoms include fatigue, exertional intolerance, dizziness, presyncope, and syncope; some patients are detected incidentally on ECG Ambulatory monitoring is key to correlating symptoms with bradyarrhythmia, since resting ECG may be normal Permanent pacing is the mainstay for symptomatic bradycardia, and anticoagulation decisions follow standard atrial fibrillation stroke-risk assessment Family screening with ECG and consideration of genetic testing is warranted given the heritable basis Syncope or recurrent presyncope with documented pauses Very long sinus pauses or high-grade sinoatrial or atrioventricular block Bradycardia-tachycardia with thromboembolic risk from atrial fibrillation Family history of sudden death or need for early pacing Associated structural heart disease or additional channelopathy phenotype Attributing symptoms to another cause when resting ECG is normal and failing to arrange prolonged monitoring Overlooking reversible contributors such as rate-limiting drugs or hypothyroidism before implanting a pacemaker Missing associated atrial fibrillation and its stroke risk in the bradycardia-tachycardia phenotype Not recognising the heritable pattern and omitting family screening Failing to look for associated left ventricular non-compaction in HCN4-related disease Familial sick sinus syndrome results from genetically determined impairment of impulse generation and propagation within the sinoatrial node. Loss-of-function variants in SCN5A reduce the cardiac sodium current needed for rapid depolarisation, slowing conduction and depressing nodal and perinodal function, often with recessive inheritance. Variants in HCN4 disturb the hyperpolarisation-activated pacemaker current that sets intrinsic heart rate, producing dominant bradycardia and impaired rate acceleration. The resulting sinus node dysfunction manifests as bradycardia, pauses, exit block, and chronotropic incompetence, frequently accompanied by atrial arrhythmias in a bradycardia-tachycardia pattern. With appropriate pacing for symptomatic bradycardia and management of associated atrial arrhythmias and stroke risk, symptomatic and functional outcomes are generally good; prognosis is influenced by any coexisting conduction disease or structural cardiomyopathy, particularly in SCN5A- and HCN4-related overlap phenotypes.

transforming growth factor beta pathway (TGFBR1, TGFBR2) Dissection can occur at smaller aortic diameters than in sporadic disease, so gene-specific thresholds guide intervention A family history of aortic aneurysm, dissection, or unexplained sudden death is a key clue First-degree relatives warrant screening imaging and genetic counselling Management centres on blood pressure control with beta-blockade and/or angiotensin receptor blockade plus regular aortic surveillance Elective repair is undertaken at gene- and family-specific size thresholds to pre-empt dissection Acute severe chest or back pain suggesting aortic dissection Rapid increase in aortic diameter on surveillance Family history of dissection or sudden death at small aortic size Signs of aortic regurgitation or malperfusion Applying standard sporadic aneurysm size thresholds to genes that dissect at smaller diameters Failing to screen and counsel first-degree relatives Overlooking syndromic aortopathies such as Marfan or Loeys-Dietz syndrome Neglecting long-term surveillance after initial normal imaging Familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection results from inherited defects that impair the integrity of the aortic wall. Variants in smooth-muscle contractile proteins such as ACTA2 and MYH11 weaken the ability of medial smooth-muscle cells to withstand haemodynamic stress, while variants affecting the transforming growth factor beta signalling pathway disturb extracellular matrix homeostasis. The resulting medial degeneration and loss of structural resilience predispose the thoracic aorta to progressive dilatation and to dissection, sometimes at diameters that would be considered low-risk in sporadic disease. With genetic identification, family screening, blood pressure control, and timely prophylactic surgery at gene-specific thresholds, the risk of fatal dissection can be substantially reduced. Prognosis depends on the specific gene involved, some of which confer particularly aggressive disease.

Familial tumoral calcinosis (GALNT3/FGF23/KL) — hyperphosphataemic familial tumoral calcinosis, HFTC, primary tumoral calcinosis, hyperphosphataemia-hyperostosis syndrome Secondary (dystrophic) tumoral calcinosis from chronic kidney disease and hyperphosphataemia Calcinosis of connective tissue disease (dermatomyositis, systemic sclerosis) Synovial or bursal chondromatosis and calcific bursitis Soft-tissue sarcoma or other calcifying mass Gout and calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease Heterotopic ossification Serum phosphate (elevated) with tubular reabsorption of phosphate indices Calcium, parathyroid hormone, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D Intact versus C-terminal FGF23 measurement to reveal excess cleavage in GALNT3/FGF23 disease Radiographs and cross-sectional imaging of periarticular masses Renal function to exclude secondary tumoral calcinosis of chronic kidney disease Sequencing of GALNT3, FGF23, and KL to confirm the genotype The mechanistic mirror image of FGF23-mediated phosphate wasting: here FGF23 signalling is deficient, causing phosphate RETENTION and hyperphosphataemia Autosomal recessive, caused by loss-of-function mutations in GALNT3 or FGF23 (reducing active intact FGF23) or in KL (klotho, the FGF23 co-receptor), all impairing FGF23 action Presents with progressive calcified, lobulated masses in periarticular soft tissues, especially around the hips, shoulders, and elbows Biochemistry shows hyperphosphataemia with increased renal tubular phosphate reabsorption and inappropriately normal or high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D; calcium is usually normal A related overlapping phenotype is the hyperostosis-hyperphosphataemia syndrome with painful diaphyseal bone lesions GALNT3 normally glycosylates and protects intact FGF23; its loss increases cleavage so that intact bioactive FGF23 is low despite high total FGF23 fragments Management aims to lower phosphate through dietary phosphate restriction and phosphate-binding agents, with lesion excision for symptomatic masses Rapidly enlarging or ulcerating calcified masses with secondary infection Painful diaphyseal bone lesions of the hyperostosis variant Functional impairment or nerve compression from large periarticular deposits Vascular or visceral calcification from a persistently high calcium-phosphate product Confusing primary HFTC with the far commoner secondary tumoral calcinosis of renal failure Misinterpreting high total FGF23 as excess activity when intact bioactive FGF23 is actually deficient Excising masses without addressing hyperphosphataemia, leading to recurrence Overlooking the hyperostosis-hyperphosphataemia bone variant as infection or malignancy Hyperphosphataemic familial tumoral calcinosis results from deficient FGF23 signalling. Mutations in FGF23 itself, in GALNT3 (whose O-glycosylation normally protects intact FGF23 from proteolysis), or in KL (encoding klotho, the obligate co-receptor for FGF23) all reduce effective FGF23 action at the kidney. Loss of the normal phosphaturic drive increases proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption, producing hyperphosphataemia, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is inappropriately normal or elevated for the phosphate level, raising the calcium-phosphate product. The resulting supersaturation promotes ectopic calcification in periarticular soft tissue, forming the characteristic lobulated calcified masses, and in some patients a hyperostotic diaphyseal bone reaction. It is the exact counterpart of the FGF23-excess phosphate-wasting rickets syndromes. Course is chronic and progressive with recurrent masses, but phosphate-lowering measures and selective surgical excision can control disease; recurrence after excision is common if hyperphosphataemia is not corrected.

syndrome) Bloom syndrome and Nijmegen breakage syndrome Acquired aplastic anaemia VACTERL association without an underlying repair defect Thrombocytopenia-absent radius syndrome Nutritional or drug-induced macrocytic anaemia Chromosomal breakage analysis with diepoxybutane or mitomycin C as the diagnostic test Fibroblast (skin) breakage testing when blood results are equivocal owing to somatic mosaicism Molecular genetic testing to identify the causative FANC gene and complementation group Full blood count and bone marrow examination with cytogenetics to assess marrow failure and clonal evolution Regular head and neck and gynaecological examination for early squamous malignancy Renal and skeletal imaging and endocrine assessment for associated anomalies A genetically heterogeneous DNA-repair disorder, usually autosomal recessive (with rare X-linked and dominant forms), caused by variants in one of many FANC pathway genes that repair DNA interstrand crosslinks Progressive bone marrow failure typically emerges in the first decade, presenting with cytopenias and often preceded by macrocytosis and thrombocytopenia Congenital anomalies are common but variable, including short stature, radial-ray and thumb defects, cafe-au-lait macules, renal anomalies and microphthalmia There is a very high risk of myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukaemia, and of solid tumours, notably head and neck and gynaecological squamous cell carcinomas at young ages The diagnostic test is a chromosomal breakage study showing excessive chromosomal breakage after exposure to DNA crosslinking agents such as diepoxybutane (DEB) or mitomycin C Somatic mosaicism from reversion in haematopoietic cells can cause false-negative blood breakage tests, so fibroblast testing may be needed Extreme sensitivity to radiation and crosslinking chemotherapy demands markedly modified conditioning and treatment protocols Rapidly falling blood counts or new blasts suggesting evolution to myelodysplastic syndrome or acute leukaemia A new head and neck or anogenital mucosal lesion raising concern for squamous cell carcinoma Severe unexpected toxicity from standard-dose radiotherapy or chemotherapy Signs of severe marrow failure such as life-threatening bleeding or infection Accepting a normal blood breakage test in a suspicious case without pursuing fibroblast testing for mosaicism Administering standard conditioning or chemotherapy doses, causing severe toxicity from the underlying repair defect Attributing isolated congenital anomalies to another syndrome and delaying diagnosis Relaxing cancer surveillance after transplantation despite the continuing solid-tumour risk Fanconi anaemia results from biallelic (or, in the X-linked form, hemizygous) variants in any of numerous genes that cooperate in the Fanconi anaemia/BRCA DNA-repair pathway, which recognises and repairs DNA interstrand crosslinks and helps maintain genomic stability during replication. Failure of this pathway leaves cells unable to resolve crosslink damage, producing chromosomal breakage and instability that drives progressive haematopoietic stem cell attrition (bone marrow failure) and a strong predisposition to leukaemia and squamous carcinomas. The same defect underlies the hypersensitivity of cells to crosslinking agents, which is exploited in the diagnostic breakage assay. Prognosis is guarded and dominated by progressive bone marrow failure and a lifelong, cumulative risk of leukaemia and early-onset solid cancers. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can address marrow failure but does not remove and may increase the risk of later solid tumours, so cancer surveillance must continue lifelong.

Fanconi-Bickel syndrome — FBS, glycogen storage disease type XI, GLUT2 deficiency, SLC2A2 Cystinosis and other causes of renal Fanconi syndrome Other glycogen storage disorders with hepatomegaly and hypoglycaemia Galactosaemia and hereditary fructose intolerance Lowe syndrome and Dent disease Tyrosinaemia type 1 Mitochondrial hepatorenal disease Fasting and postprandial blood glucose to demonstrate the paradoxical pattern Assessment of proximal tubular function including glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate and low-molecular-weight proteinuria Liver imaging and function tests to assess hepatomegaly and glycogen accumulation Skeletal assessment for rickets with measurement of phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D metabolites Genetic testing of SLC2A2 Monitoring of growth and acid-base and electrolyte status A rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in SLC2A2, which encodes the glucose transporter GLUT2 expressed in liver, pancreatic beta cells, intestine and the renal proximal tubule It combines hepatorenal glycogen accumulation with a generalised proximal (Fanconi-type) renal tubulopathy Typical features are hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, a doll-like face and rickets from renal phosphate and bicarbonate wasting A characteristic paradoxical glucose profile is seen: fasting hypoglycaemia together with postprandial hyperglycaemia and glucosuria The proximal tubulopathy produces glycosuria, generalised aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, bicarbonate wasting with proximal renal tubular acidosis and low-molecular-weight proteinuria Growth retardation and rickets often dominate the clinical picture and require attention to phosphate, alkali and vitamin D Massive glucosuria persists despite hypoglycaemia because impaired GLUT2 blocks tubular glucose exit into the blood Symptomatic fasting hypoglycaemia Severe metabolic acidosis or electrolyte disturbance from tubular losses Progressive rickets with skeletal deformity or fracture Significant failure to thrive or dehydration during intercurrent illness Being confused by the paradoxical fasting hypoglycaemia with postprandial hyperglycaemia and misclassifying the glucose disorder Failing to correct phosphate, alkali and vitamin D, leaving rickets undertreated Overlooking the generalised tubulopathy when hepatomegaly dominates the presentation Attributing persistent glucosuria to diabetes rather than proximal tubular glucose loss Fanconi-Bickel syndrome results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in SLC2A2, encoding the facilitative glucose transporter GLUT2. GLUT2 mediates the movement of glucose across the basolateral membrane of hepatocytes, pancreatic beta cells, enterocytes and proximal tubular cells. Its deficiency traps glucose within these cells, causing glycogen accumulation in liver and kidney and disturbing glucose sensing and homeostasis, which manifests as fasting hypoglycaemia with postprandial hyperglycaemia. In the proximal tubule, failure of basolateral glucose exit, together with the intracellular glycogen burden, impairs reabsorptive function broadly, producing a generalised Fanconi syndrome with glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia and bicarbonate wasting, and the consequent phosphate loss and acidosis drive rickets and growth failure. With supportive management of hypoglycaemia, electrolyte and phosphate losses, acidosis and rickets, growth and metabolic control can improve and many patients do reasonably well, although short stature and osteopenia may persist; kidney function is often relatively preserved compared with other proximal tubulopathies.

Fanconi syndrome — renal Fanconi syndrome, proximal tubular dysfunction syndrome, De Toni-Debre-Fanconi syndrome Isolated proximal renal tubular acidosis without full Fanconi features Diabetes mellitus with glycosuria from hyperglycaemia Primary hypophosphataemic rickets Multiple myeloma or other plasma cell dyscrasia Heavy metal or drug-induced tubular toxicity Chronic interstitial nephritis Paired urine and blood glucose to demonstrate glycosuria despite normal glycaemia Serum and urine phosphate, potassium, bicarbonate, and uric acid to document tubular wasting Urine amino acid screen and low-molecular-weight (tubular) protein measurement Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with free light chains to exclude a plasma cell disorder in adults Assessment for underlying causes such as cystinosis, Wilson disease, or nephrotoxic drug exposure Bone imaging or biochemistry when rickets or osteomalacia is suspected Fanconi syndrome is a generalised defect of proximal tubular reabsorption, so multiple solutes normally reclaimed there are lost into the urine at once The hallmark laboratory picture combines glycosuria with normal blood glucose, phosphaturia with hypophosphataemia, aminoaciduria, uricosuria, and a proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis Phosphate and vitamin D handling are disturbed, producing metabolic bone disease that presents as rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults In children the commonest cause is inherited cystinosis, whereas in adults acquired causes such as drugs, heavy metals, and monoclonal light chains predominate Bicarbonate wasting causes a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, and potassium wasting frequently leads to hypokalaemia Recognising the full constellation is important because finding one abnormality (e.g. isolated glycosuria) should prompt a search for the others Treatment is directed at the underlying cause where possible, together with replacement of the wasted solutes: alkali, phosphate, potassium, and active vitamin D as needed Severe hypophosphataemia causing muscle weakness or respiratory compromise Progressive metabolic bone disease with fractures or deformity Evidence of an underlying plasma cell dyscrasia in an adult Declining glomerular filtration suggesting progression of the causative disease Dismissing glycosuria as diabetes without checking blood glucose or looking for other tubular losses Missing an underlying paraproteinaemia in an adult presenting with proximal tubular dysfunction Undertreating the bone disease by giving phosphate without adequate active vitamin D Failing to review the medication list for a reversible tubulotoxic drug Fanconi syndrome results from global dysfunction of the proximal convoluted tubule, the segment responsible for reabsorbing the bulk of filtered glucose, amino acids, phosphate, uric acid, bicarbonate, and low-molecular-weight proteins. When proximal transport fails, all of these are wasted in the urine, giving the characteristic combination of glycosuria with euglycaemia, generalised aminoaciduria, hypophosphataemia, hypouricaemia, proximal renal tubular acidosis from bicarbonate loss, and tubular proteinuria. Impaired proximal conversion of vitamin D and phosphate depletion drive the bone disease. Underlying mechanisms include inherited defects of tubular transporters or metabolism (such as cystinosis or Wilson disease), toxic injury from drugs and heavy metals, and deposition of filtered monoclonal light chains, all of which impair the energy-dependent transport machinery of the proximal tubule. Outlook depends on the cause: reversible drug- or toxin-induced Fanconi syndrome may resolve when the offending agent is removed, while inherited forms such as cystinosis and light-chain-related disease can progress to chronic kidney failure. Early replacement therapy prevents or lessens the associated bone disease and growth impairment.

Farber disease — Farber lipogranulomatosis, acid ceramidase deficiency, ASAH1 deficiency, ceramidase deficiency Juvenile idiopathic arthritis and other inflammatory arthritides Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis and other histiocytic disorders Rheumatoid nodulosis or subcutaneous granuloma annulare Other lysosomal storage disorders with skeletal or visceral involvement Fibromatosis or hyaline fibromatosis syndromes SMA-PME as an allelic ASAH1 phenotype Acid ceramidase enzyme activity assay in leucocytes or fibroblasts ASAH1 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Biopsy of a subcutaneous nodule showing lipogranuloma with lipid-laden macrophages Laryngoscopy and airway assessment for nodular infiltration Brain MRI and neurodevelopmental evaluation in suspected neurovisceral disease Storage/biomarker analysis of ceramide where available Rare autosomal recessive lysosomal disorder from ASAH1 variants causing acid ceramidase deficiency and ceramide accumulation Classic triad is painful, swollen joints with contractures; subcutaneous nodules (lipogranulomas) over joints and pressure points; and a hoarse or weak cry from laryngeal involvement Symptoms typically begin in early infancy and can be mistaken for juvenile idiopathic arthritis Nodular infiltration of larynx and airway causes progressive hoarseness and respiratory difficulty Severity ranges from a severe neurovisceral form with neurological regression to milder forms with predominantly joint and nodule disease Allelic to spinal muscular atrophy with progressive myoclonic epilepsy (SMA-PME), a distinct ASAH1-related phenotype Diagnosis rests on demonstrating deficient acid ceramidase activity and ASAH1 genetic testing; management is largely supportive, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation considered in selected non-neurological cases Progressive hoarseness with stridor or airway compromise Neurological regression indicating a severe neurovisceral phenotype Feeding and respiratory difficulty from laryngeal and pulmonary involvement Rapidly progressive joint contractures with severe pain Misdiagnosing early joint disease as juvenile idiopathic arthritis and delaying metabolic evaluation Overlooking hoarseness as a diagnostic clue to laryngeal storage Not recognising the allelic relationship with SMA-PME Assuming a uniform prognosis across the clinical spectrum Acid ceramidase normally hydrolyses ceramide into sphingosine and free fatty acid within the lysosome. Deficiency of the enzyme leads to lysosomal accumulation of ceramide in many tissues, particularly around joints, subcutaneous tissue, larynx and, in severe forms, the nervous system and viscera. The stored lipid provokes a granulomatous inflammatory response (lipogranulomas) and tissue infiltration that produces the characteristic joint, nodular and laryngeal manifestations, while central nervous system involvement in severe phenotypes drives neurological deterioration. Severe neurovisceral forms are progressive and often fatal in early childhood, whereas milder forms with predominantly joint and nodular disease may survive longer; outcome depends heavily on the degree of neurological and airway involvement.

Fascioliasis — Fasciola hepatica, Fasciola gigantica, sheep liver fluke infection, liver rot, fasciolosis Other liver flukes (Clonorchis, Opisthorchis) in the chronic phase Viral or other hepatitis (acute phase) Pyogenic or amoebic liver abscess Biliary stones and other causes of obstructive jaundice or cholangitis Hypereosinophilic syndromes and other tissue-migrating helminths (e.g. toxocariasis) Hepatic malignancy Serology (antibody detection) as the key test in the acute pre-patent phase Stool microscopy for characteristic large operculated eggs in the chronic phase (with concentration) Bile or duodenal aspirate examination for eggs when stool is negative Full blood count for eosinophilia Liver function tests to assess cholestasis Abdominal ultrasound, CT or MRI showing migratory tracks (acute) or biliary flukes and dilatation (chronic) Fascioliasis is caused by the liver flukes Fasciola hepatica and Fasciola gigantica, primarily parasites of sheep and cattle that also infect humans worldwide, with high-burden foci in the Andes, Nile valley and parts of Asia Humans are infected by eating aquatic plants such as watercress, or drinking water, contaminated with encysted metacercariae The acute (hepatic/migratory) phase reflects larval migration through the liver parenchyma and causes fever, right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly and marked eosinophilia The chronic (biliary) phase occurs once adult flukes reside in the bile ducts, causing biliary colic, obstruction, cholangitis and sometimes obstructive jaundice During the acute phase stool ova are absent because the flukes are not yet egg-laying, so serology is the diagnostic test of choice; eggs appear in stool or bile only in the chronic phase Imaging in the acute phase may show hypodense migratory tracks or nodules in the liver, and eosinophilia is a key clue Triclabendazole is the preferred agent for fascioliasis, and notably praziquantel is ineffective against Fasciola, unlike most other trematode infections Acute cholangitis with fever, jaundice and abdominal pain Obstructive jaundice from adult flukes in the bile ducts Severe acute-phase illness with high fever and marked systemic symptoms Ectopic migration causing lesions outside the hepatobiliary system Failure to respond, given regional triclabendazole resistance concerns Relying on stool microscopy during the acute phase, when eggs are not yet produced, and missing the diagnosis Using praziquantel, which is ineffective against Fasciola, instead of triclabendazole Overlooking dietary exposure such as wild watercress ingestion Mistaking acute-phase hepatic lesions for abscess or malignancy on imaging Not considering treatment failure due to regional drug resistance Ingested metacercariae excyst in the duodenum and the immature flukes penetrate the intestinal wall, cross the peritoneal cavity and burrow through the liver capsule and parenchyma over several weeks, producing necrotic migratory tracks and an intense eosinophilic inflammatory response that underlies the acute phase. The flukes then enter the bile ducts and mature into adults, where they cause chronic mechanical and inflammatory biliary injury, ductal hyperplasia, fibrosis and obstruction. Egg production begins only after maturation, explaining the diagnostic gap in the acute phase. Ectopic migration can rarely deposit flukes in other tissues. Most infections respond well to appropriate anthelmintic therapy with full recovery, but heavy or long-standing chronic infection can cause biliary fibrosis and recurrent cholangitis, and emerging triclabendazole resistance is a growing concern in some regions.

Fasciolopsiasis (Fasciolopsis buski) — Fasciolopsis buski infection, giant intestinal fluke infection, large intestinal fluke disease Fascioliasis (Fasciola hepatica), whose eggs are morphologically similar Other intestinal fluke infection such as heterophyiasis and metagonimiasis Giardiasis and other protozoal enteritis Peptic ulcer disease or functional dyspepsia Protein-losing enteropathy from other causes Intestinal obstruction from other aetiologies Stool microscopy for the large operculated eggs, with concentration techniques Careful egg morphometry to distinguish from Fasciola Full blood count for eosinophilia and anaemia Serum albumin and nutritional assessment in heavy or paediatric infection Abdominal imaging if obstruction is suspected Repeated stool sampling to improve sensitivity Caused by the giant intestinal fluke Fasciolopsis buski, the largest fluke to infect humans, endemic in parts of South and Southeast Asia Acquired by eating raw aquatic plants such as water caltrop, water chestnut and water spinach on which metacercariae encyst Light infection is often silent; heavy infection produces epigastric pain, diarrhoea alternating with constipation, nausea and, in children, malnutrition Very heavy worm burdens can cause intestinal obstruction and a generalised toxic-allergic state with facial and peripheral oedema Diagnosis is by finding the large operculated eggs in stool, which resemble those of Fasciola Praziquantel is the treatment of choice and is highly effective Prevention centres on not eating raw water plants and on improving sanitation, since pigs act as an important reservoir Signs of intestinal obstruction from a heavy worm burden Generalised oedema and ascites indicating a severe toxic-allergic reaction Profound malnutrition and growth failure in children Severe anaemia or protein depletion Confusing Fasciolopsis eggs with those of Fasciola and mislocating the disease to the biliary tract Underestimating worm burden in children presenting mainly with malnutrition Missing intestinal obstruction as a complication of heavy infection Overlooking pigs as a reservoir when advising on control measures Fasciolopsis buski is a large trematode of the small intestine whose life cycle involves freshwater snails and aquatic vegetation. Cercariae released from snails encyst as metacercariae on the surface of water plants; humans and pigs are infected by eating these plants raw or peeling them with the teeth. The larvae excyst in the duodenum and attach to the mucosa of the upper small intestine, where the large flukes cause local inflammation, ulceration and haemorrhage at the attachment sites. Heavy infections mechanically impair digestion and absorption and can obstruct the bowel, while absorption of fluke metabolites is thought to drive a systemic toxic and allergic reaction manifesting as oedema and constitutional upset. Eggs passed in faeces continue the cycle when they reach freshwater. Most infections respond promptly to anthelmintic treatment with full recovery; heavy infections in malnourished children can be debilitating and occasionally fatal if obstruction or profound protein loss is untreated.

different treatment Delaying fracture stabilisation, which increases risk Over-investigating for a confirmatory test rather than supporting the patient Fat embolism syndrome typically follows fractures of long bones or the pelvis, or orthopaedic instrumentation, when marrow fat enters the venous circulation. A mechanical component arises as fat globules occlude pulmonary and systemic capillaries, while a biochemical component follows as circulating free fatty acids are released and produce a toxic inflammatory injury to the pulmonary capillary endothelium. The result is impaired gas exchange resembling acute lung injury, cerebral microembolism causing confusion and reduced consciousness, and dermal capillary involvement producing the characteristic petechiae. Symptoms characteristically appear after a latent interval of roughly one to three days. Most cases are self-limiting with supportive care and resolve over days, but severe presentations with marked respiratory failure or cerebral involvement carry higher morbidity and can be fatal.

Fat necrosis of the breast — fat necrosis, breast fat necrosis, traumatic fat necrosis, post-surgical fat necrosis Breast carcinoma Fibroadenoma or other benign solid lump Breast abscess or infection Haematoma Radial scar or complex sclerosing lesion Duct ectasia with skin change Clinical examination and history for trauma, surgery, or radiotherapy as part of triple assessment Mammography, which may show an oil cyst, calcification, or a suspicious mass Ultrasound to characterise the lesion Core needle biopsy where imaging or clinical features are not clearly benign Magnetic resonance imaging in selected cases when other imaging is indeterminate Interval imaging follow-up when a lesion is presumed benign but not biopsied Fat necrosis is a benign inflammatory response of breast adipose tissue to injury, and it is an important mimic of carcinoma on both examination and imaging There is often a history of trauma, breast surgery, radiotherapy, fat grafting, or anticoagulation, though the precipitating event may be forgotten It can present as a firm, sometimes irregular lump, occasionally with skin tethering, dimpling, or bruising, closely resembling malignancy Imaging appearances assessment with core biopsy is frequently required to reach a confident benign diagnosis An oil cyst with typical features on mammography or ultrasound may be diagnostic and avoid the need for biopsy
