features should be biopsied or excised rather than assumed benign Spiculated mass or suspicious microcalcification that could represent carcinoma Skin tethering or dimpling without a clear benign explanation Discordant triple assessment findings A lesion that enlarges or fails to settle over time Associated axillary lymphadenopathy Assuming a lump is fat necrosis on the basis of trauma history alone and missing a coincidental carcinoma Failing to biopsy imaging features that overlap with malignancy Ignoring discordance between clinical, imaging, and pathological findings Attributing skin tethering to fat necrosis without adequate assessment Not arranging follow-up for a presumed benign but unbiopsied lesion Fat necrosis occurs when adipocytes are damaged by trauma, surgery, radiotherapy, or ischaemia, releasing lipid that triggers a local inflammatory reaction. Macrophages and giant cells engulf the released fat, and the process evolves through acute inflammation, the formation of lipid-laden oil cysts, and eventual fibrosis and dystrophic calcification. The resulting scarring can distort surrounding tissue and tether the skin, while the calcification and architectural change on imaging can closely imitate carcinoma. The variable stage of evolution explains the wide spectrum of clinical and radiological appearances. Fat necrosis is benign with an excellent prognosis; once cancer is excluded, most lesions stabilise, resolve, or persist as an inert scar or oil cyst, and it carries no increased risk of malignancy.

fat pad impingement — Hoffa's syndrome, infrapatellar fat pad impingement, Hoffa's disease Patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee) Chondromalacia patellae and patellofemoral pain syndrome Patellar instability or maltracking Prepatellar or deep infrapatellar bursitis Osgood-Schlatter or Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease in adolescents Medial synovial plica syndrome Localised pigmented villonodular synovitis or intra-articular tumour MRI with fluid-sensitive sequences demonstrating fat pad oedema and impingement Lateral radiograph to assess patella alta and any fat pad calcification or ossification Skyline/Merchant views to evaluate patellar tracking and tilt Dynamic ultrasound of the anterior knee Diagnostic local anaesthetic infiltration of the fat pad Standing alignment views to assess genu recurvatum Arthroscopy for direct visualisation in refractory cases Anterior knee pain localised to either side of the patellar tendon, characteristically aggravated by hyperextension and prolonged standing. The infrapatellar (Hoffa's) fat pad is one of the most richly innervated and vascularised intracapsular structures of the knee, so oedema or impingement is disproportionately painful. Acute Hoffa's disease follows direct trauma or forced hyperextension; the chronic form relates to repetitive extension, patellar maltracking or genu recurvatum. Hoffa's test reproduces pain on pressing the fat pad either side of the tendon as the knee is passively extended from flexion. MRI on fluid-sensitive sequences shows fat pad oedema and may demonstrate superolateral impingement between the patellar tendon and lateral trochlea. Frequently associated with patella alta, patellar maltracking or iatrogenic scarring from previous arthroscopy portals. First-line management is conservative: activity modification, taping to unload the fat pad, and physiotherapy addressing quadriceps control and tracking. Refractory cases may respond to a carefully placed corticosteroid infiltration or arthroscopic resection of hypertrophied/impinging tissue. Rapidly enlarging anterior knee mass suggesting neoplasm rather than benign fat pad hypertrophy Systemic features such as fever, night sweats or weight loss suggesting infection or malignancy True mechanical locking or giving way pointing to meniscal or ligamentous pathology Effusion with warmth and erythema suggesting septic arthritis or inflammatory arthropathy Mislabelling the problem as patellar tendinopathy and prescribing tendon loading, which aggravates impingement. Overlooking underlying patella alta or maltracking that perpetuates symptoms. Poorly placed corticosteroid injection risking fat pad atrophy or tendon weakening. Treating incidental MRI fat pad oedema as clinically significant, or dismissing genuinely symptomatic changes. Forgetting iatrogenic causes related to previous arthroscopy portals. The infrapatellar fat pad is an intracapsular, extrasynovial structure lying deep to the patellar tendon; it is highly vascularised and densely innervated by branches of the femoral, common peroneal and saphenous nerves, making it a potent source of anterior knee pain. Acute trauma or repetitive forced hyperextension provokes haemorrhage and oedema, followed by inflammation, fibrosis and hypertrophy. The enlarged fat pad becomes impinged between the femoral trochlea and the tibia or patellar tendon during terminal extension, and longstanding cases may undergo metaplastic calcification or ossification. Predisposing factors include patella alta, patellar maltracking, genu recurvatum and iatrogenic scarring following arthroscopy. Most patients improve with conservative measures that address patellar tracking and loading. Arthroscopic resection gives good outcomes in refractory impingement, although recurrent scarring can prolong recovery.

Febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome — FIRES, Acute encephalitis with refractory repetitive partial seizures Autoimmune or antibody-mediated encephalitis, including anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis Viral and bacterial meningoencephalitis Other causes of NORSE (paraneoplastic, cryptogenic) Mitochondrial and other metabolic encephalopathies Genetic epileptic encephalopathies such as POLG- and PCDH19-related disease Toxic encephalopathy Continuous EEG monitoring MRI brain, initial and serial Comprehensive CSF analysis including cell count, viral PCR and autoimmune antibodies Serum and CSF autoimmune and paraneoplastic antibody panels Infective screen of blood, CSF and respiratory samples to exclude active infection Metabolic and mitochondrial workup with genetic testing Inflammatory markers and cytokine profiling where available A catastrophic epileptic encephalopathy in previously healthy children, defined by refractory status epilepticus beginning between 24 hours and 2 weeks after a febrile illness, often with fever absent at seizure onset. Considered the paediatric subtype of new-onset refractory status epilepticus (NORSE) with an obligatory preceding febrile infection. Seizures are typically focal with secondary generalisation, extremely frequent and highly drug-resistant, often requiring prolonged anaesthetic coma. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, as extensive investigation usually fails to identify a specific infective or autoimmune cause. Emerging evidence implicates innate immune, cytokine-mediated neuroinflammation, notably the interleukin-1 pathway. Early ketogenic diet and immunotherapy, including interleukin-1 blockade, are increasingly used in the acute phase. Survivors typically enter a chronic phase of drug-resistant epilepsy with cognitive and behavioural impairment. MRI may be normal early and later show mesial temporal and diffuse atrophy, while CSF may show mild pleocytosis. Refractory status epilepticus requiring escalating anaesthesia Autonomic instability and complications of prolonged critical illness Rising intracranial pressure or cerebral oedema Multi-organ complications of prolonged anaesthetic therapy Assuming a treatable central nervous system infection and delaying immunomodulation or ketogenic diet. Labelling the presentation as ordinary febrile status epilepticus and underestimating its severity. Delaying the ketogenic diet, which can be effective but requires setup. Failing to exclude autoimmune encephalitis and metabolic or genetic mimics. Under-recognising the complications of prolonged therapeutic coma. FIRES is thought to be an immune-mediated encephalopathy triggered by a preceding febrile infection in a genetically susceptible child, rather than a direct central nervous system infection. Activation of innate immunity with excessive pro-inflammatory cytokine signalling, particularly the interleukin-1-beta pathway, is proposed to lower seizure threshold and drive self-sustaining status epilepticus and neuronal injury. A vicious cycle of seizures, neuroinflammation and metabolic stress perpetuates the refractory state, with the hippocampus especially vulnerable. Poor overall, with appreciable mortality in the acute phase and a high burden of chronic drug-resistant epilepsy, cognitive impairment and disability among survivors; earlier immunomodulation and ketogenic therapy may improve outcomes.

Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction — FNHTR, Febrile transfusion reaction Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction Bacterial contamination of the component with septic transfusion reaction Transfusion-related acute lung injury Transfusion-associated circulatory overload Underlying infection or sepsis unrelated to transfusion Allergic or anaphylactic transfusion reaction with fever Clerical recheck of patient identity and unit compatibility label Direct antiglobulin test and repeat crossmatch to exclude haemolysis Visual inspection of plasma and urine for haemoglobin Blood cultures from patient and culture of the implicated unit if sepsis suspected Full blood count and film to assess for haemolysis Serum lactate dehydrogenase, bilirubin and haptoglobin to exclude red-cell destruction Defined as a temperature rise of at least 1 degree Celsius to 38 degrees or above, occurring during or within a few hours of transfusion, once other causes are excluded. It is a diagnosis of exclusion; acute haemolysis and bacterial contamination (especially of platelets) must be ruled out before attributing fever to a benign febrile reaction. Two mechanisms operate: recipient antibodies against donor leucocyte antigens (classically in multiparous or multiply transfused patients), and accumulated cytokines released from leucocytes during storage. Universal pre-storage leucoreduction has markedly reduced incidence, particularly the cytokine-driven reactions seen with platelet concentrates. Presents with fever, chills, rigors and sometimes mild dyspnoea; hypotension and shock are not typical and should prompt a search for a more serious reaction. Management is supportive with antipyretics; the transfusion should be stopped and the unit and patient details rechecked while serious causes are excluded. Pre-medication with antipyretics does not reliably prevent recurrence, and routine prophylactic use is discouraged. Recurrent reactions in a patient already receiving leucoreduced components may warrant washed components in selected cases. Fever accompanied by hypotension, loin or back pain suggesting acute haemolysis Rapid onset of high fever with rigors and cardiovascular collapse suggesting bacterial contamination Hypoxia and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates suggesting transfusion-related acute lung injury Haemoglobinuria or dark urine during or after transfusion Disproportionate temperature rise beyond that expected for a benign reaction Assuming fever is benign without excluding acute haemolysis and bacterial contamination first. Relying on prophylactic antipyretics to prevent future reactions when evidence does not support this. Masking an early haemolytic or septic reaction by pre-medicating routinely before transfusion. Failing to recognise that leucoreduced components can still cause reactions, especially via residual cytokines in platelets. Discarding the unit before serious causes have been investigated. Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reactions arise through two overlapping mechanisms. In the antibody-mediated form, recipient anti-leucocyte (anti-HLA or granulocyte-specific) antibodies, generated by prior pregnancy or transfusion, react with residual donor white cells, triggering complement activation and release of endogenous pyrogens. In the storage-lesion form, biologically active cytokines such as interleukin-1, interleukin-6, interleukin-8 and tumour necrosis factor accumulate in the supernatant of cellular components (particularly platelets stored at room temperature) as donor leucocytes degrade, and are passively infused into the recipient where they reset the hypothalamic thermostat. Both pathways converge on a self-limiting inflammatory febrile response without red-cell destruction. The reaction is self-limiting and benign, resolving within hours of stopping the transfusion and giving antipyretics. Its main clinical importance is that it can mask, and must be distinguished from, life-threatening haemolytic or septic reactions.

Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction — FNHTR, febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction, febrile nonhemolytic reaction Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction Bacterial contamination of the component with septic reaction Transfusion-related acute lung injury in its early febrile phase Underlying infection unrelated to transfusion Allergic or anaphylactic reaction with fever Clerical check of patient and unit identity Direct antiglobulin test and inspection of plasma and urine for haemolysis Repeat crossmatch and blood group verification Cultures of patient and implicated unit if sepsis is suspected Full blood count and haemolysis markers to exclude significant red cell destruction One of the most common transfusion reactions, defined by a temperature rise, often with chills or rigors, during or soon after transfusion without haemolysis It is a diagnosis of exclusion, so acute haemolytic reaction and bacterial contamination must be ruled out before attributing fever to a benign febrile reaction Caused either by recipient antibodies reacting with donor leukocytes or by cytokines that accumulate in cellular components during storage Pre-storage leukoreduction of components has markedly reduced its incidence Management is to stop the transfusion, exclude serious causes, and treat symptoms with antipyretics; meperidine may be used for severe rigors A history of prior febrile reactions raises the likelihood of recurrence and may prompt leukoreduced components Because fever can be the first sign of a dangerous reaction, initial evaluation should treat every febrile episode seriously rather than assuming it is benign A temperature rise accompanied by hypotension, back or flank pain, or dark urine suggesting acute haemolysis Rigors with rapid cardiovascular deterioration pointing to bacterial contamination and sepsis Respiratory distress raising concern for TRALI High or persistent fever that does not settle after stopping the transfusion Prematurely labelling fever as benign without excluding haemolysis and sepsis Continuing the transfusion through a febrile episode before serious causes are excluded Routinely premedicating all patients rather than reserving prophylaxis and leukoreduction for those with recurrent reactions Failing to report the reaction, losing the chance to arrange leukoreduced components Febrile non-haemolytic reactions arise through two main mechanisms. In the first, recipient antibodies formed from previous transfusions or pregnancies bind donor leukocytes, triggering complement activation and release of pyrogenic cytokines. In the second, cytokines such as interleukins and tumour necrosis factor accumulate within cellular components, particularly platelets, during storage and are passively infused, producing fever independent of any antibody. Both pathways generate an inflammatory febrile response without red cell destruction, which is why leukoreduction reduces the frequency of these reactions. The reaction itself is self-limiting and benign, resolving with supportive care, but its importance lies in not overlooking a serious reaction that presents identically at onset.

haemolysis High fever with rigors and cardiovascular instability pointing to bacterial contamination Respiratory distress suggesting an alternative serious reaction Fever that is disproportionate or persists after the transfusion is stopped Labelling fever as benign before excluding acute haemolytic and bacterial reactions Restarting the same unit after a febrile reaction without reassessment non-haemolytic reactions arise through two overlapping mechanisms. Recipient antibodies directed against donor leucocyte antigens bind transfused white cells and provoke a cytokine response, while pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukins and tumour necrosis factor generated by residual leucocytes accumulate in the component during storage, particularly in platelet units. When infused, these mediators act on the hypothalamic set point to produce fever and rigors. Febrile seizure — febrile convulsion, fever fit, simple febrile seizure, complex febrile seizure Meningitis or encephalitis Epilepsy with a coincidental febrile illness Rigors or shivering mistaken for a seizure Metabolic disturbance (e.g. hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia) Breath-holding spell Intracranial pathology Assessment to identify and treat the source of fever Blood glucose in any child who is drowsy or slow to recover Lumbar puncture when CNS infection is suspected or the child is very young Electrolytes only when clinically indicated (e.g. dehydration, atypical features) EEG and neuroimaging reserved for complex or recurrent focal features or an abnormal neurological exam A seizure occurring with fever in children roughly 6 months to 5 years of age, without central nervous system infection or a metabolic cause, and not in a child with prior afebrile seizures. Simple febrile seizures are generalised, last under 15 minutes, and do not recur within 24 hours; complex seizures are focal, prolonged, or recur within a day. The diagnosis is clinical, and the main task is to exclude meningitis, encephalitis, and other acute causes of the fever. Routine blood tests, neuroimaging, and EEG are not indicated for simple febrile seizures in an otherwise well child. Lumbar puncture is considered when meningeal signs are present, in very young or incompletely immunised infants, or when the picture is atypical. Most febrile seizures are brief and self-terminating; management centres on reassurance, identifying the febrile illness, and safety advice for parents. Prolonged seizures are treated as status epilepticus with benzodiazepine-based abortive therapy and airway support. Antipyretics improve comfort but do not reliably prevent recurrence, and daily prophylactic anticonvulsants are generally not recommended for simple febrile seizures. Signs of meningitis or encephalitis (neck stiffness, altered consciousness, bulging fontanelle) Prolonged seizure or febrile status epilepticus Focal features, or focal neurological deficit after the seizure Failure to return to baseline alertness within a reasonable period Seizure outside the typical age range or in an unwell, toxic-appearing child Assuming fever excludes meningitis and skipping evaluation in a young or unwell infant Over-investigating a well child after a simple febrile seizure Reassuring families that antipyretics prevent recurrence Starting long-term anticonvulsants for simple febrile seizures unnecessarily Febrile seizures reflect the heightened seizure susceptibility of the developing brain when exposed to fever, likely mediated by fever-associated cytokines (such as interleukin-1 beta), the effect of raised temperature on neuronal excitability, and a genetic predisposition, as demonstrated by strong familial clustering. The rate of temperature rise and the immaturity of the young brain contribute, and in most children the tendency resolves with neurological maturation. The outlook is excellent: most children have normal development and neurological outcome, though about a third experience a recurrence, and the increase in later epilepsy risk is small for simple febrile seizures.

Febrile Urinary Tract Infection in Children — febrile UTI, paediatric pyelonephritis, upper urinary tract infection in children Other sources of occult fever (e.g., bacteraemia, pneumonia) Viral illness with incidental contaminated urine sample Vulvovaginitis or balanitis Appendicitis or other intra-abdominal infection Contaminated specimen giving a false-positive culture Urinalysis or dipstick (leucocyte esterase, nitrites) and microscopy for pyuria Urine culture from an appropriately collected specimen Inflammatory markers and blood culture when systemically unwell Renal and bladder ultrasound Voiding cystourethrography or renal scintigraphy in selected or recurrent cases Fever with a urinary tract infection in a young child usually indicates upper tract involvement (pyelonephritis) and should be taken seriously because of the risk of renal scarring. In infants and preverbal children, features are non-specific, so urinary tract infection must be considered in any young child with unexplained fever. A properly collected urine specimen is essential; contamination from bag or non-clean-catch samples is a frequent source of misleading results. Diagnosis rests on the combination of pyuria and a significant growth of a single uropathogen on culture from an appropriately obtained specimen. Escherichia coli is the predominant pathogen, and prompt appropriate antibiotic treatment reduces the likelihood of renal injury. Imaging, typically renal and bladder ultrasound, is used to detect structural abnormalities, with further studies such as voiding cystourethrography reserved for selected children. Vesicoureteral reflux and other urinary tract abnormalities predispose to recurrent infection and scarring and should be considered, especially after atypical or recurrent infections. Recurrent febrile infections and any resulting renal scarring can contribute to later hypertension and reduced renal function, so follow-up matters. Toxic appearance, signs of sepsis, or haemodynamic instability Very young infant with fever Inability to tolerate oral fluids or oral antibiotics Failure to improve on appropriate treatment Known or suspected urinary tract abnormality or recurrent febrile infections Diagnosing infection from a contaminated bag specimen instead of a properly collected sample Failing to consider urinary tract infection in an infant with unexplained fever Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria as if it were true infection Neglecting follow-up imaging or evaluation after atypical or recurrent febrile infections Most urinary tract infections are ascending: bowel-derived uropathogens, chiefly Escherichia coli, colonise the perineum, ascend the urethra, and multiply in the bladder. When bacteria and inflammation reach the kidney, pyelonephritis develops with fever and systemic signs. Bacterial virulence factors and host factors, including urinary stasis, incomplete bladder emptying, and vesicoureteral reflux that carries infected urine toward the kidney, promote upper tract infection. The inflammatory response within the renal parenchyma can injure tissue and, particularly with delayed treatment or recurrent episodes, lead to permanent scarring. Most children with a promptly treated first febrile urinary tract infection recover fully, but recurrent infections, significant vesicoureteral reflux, or renal scarring carry a risk of long-term complications including hypertension and impaired renal function.

variant or a deletion Microcephaly is a consistent feature and is often the finding that prompts genetic evaluation Characteristic digital anomalies include brachymesophalangy, clinodactyly of the fifth finger, and syndactyly of the toes Gastrointestinal atresias, particularly oesophageal and duodenal atresia, are a hallmark and important surgical concern Learning difficulties are common but many individuals have normal or only mildly reduced intellect Short palpebral fissures and other subtle facial features may be present The combination of microcephaly with digital and gastrointestinal anomalies should raise the diagnosis Diagnosis is by identifying a MYCN variant or a deletion encompassing MYCN on microarray Neonatal oesophageal atresia with aspiration risk requiring urgent surgery Duodenal atresia presenting with bilious vomiting in the newborn Feeding failure and faltering growth related to gastrointestinal anomaly Significant associated cardiac or renal malformation Managing an isolated oesophageal or duodenal atresia without recognising the underlying syndrome Overlooking microcephaly as a diagnostic clue when digital anomalies are subtle Relying on sequencing alone and missing a whole-gene deletion detectable on microarray Assuming intellectual disability is invariable when many individuals have normal cognition Feingold syndrome type 1 arises from haploinsufficiency of MYCN, a transcription factor of the MYC family that drives cell proliferation and is critical during embryonic development of the limbs, gut, brain, and other organs. Reduced MYCN dosage, whether from an intragenic loss-of-function variant or a deletion of the gene, impairs the proliferative programmes it normally coordinates, resulting in microcephaly, the characteristic hand and foot anomalies, and failure of normal luminal development in the gut that produces oesophageal and duodenal atresia. Because the mechanism is loss of one functional copy, the disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, with variable expression among affected individuals. With timely surgical correction of gastrointestinal atresias, the long-term outlook is generally good and lifespan is usually normal; most individuals have normal or mildly reduced intellect, and the microcephaly and digital anomalies are non-progressive, so the principal early risk relates to the neonatal management of the atresias.

feline oesophagus — feline esophagus, transient feline oesophagus, oesophageal ring pattern eosinophilic oesophagitis with fixed concentric rings (ringed oesophagus) gastro-oesophageal reflux disease oesophageal intramural pseudodiverticulosis diffuse oesophageal spasm producing a corkscrew appearance Schatzki ring post-radiation or drug-induced mucosal change normal transient contraction waves on imaging upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with attention to whether rings are transient or fixed distal and proximal oesophageal mucosal biopsies to assess for eosinophilic infiltration barium swallow, which may capture the transient ring pattern ambulatory pH or impedance monitoring for gastro-oesophageal reflux high-resolution manometry if a motility disorder is suspected assessment of atopic history and peripheral eosinophilia where eosinophilic oesophagitis is considered Feline oesophagus refers to the endoscopic or radiographic appearance of transient, fine, concentric circular ridges spanning the oesophageal body, resembling the normal oesophagus of a cat. The rings are produced by transient contraction of the muscularis mucosae and are typically fleeting, appearing and disappearing during endoscopy or on barium swallow. It is strongly associated with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and, importantly, with eosinophilic oesophagitis, and can be seen at the moment of reflux or during belching. Feline oesophagus should be distinguished from the fixed, persistent concentric rings of eosinophilic oesophagitis (trachealisation or a ringed oesophagus), which do not disappear. The finding itself is benign and transient, but its recognition should prompt evaluation for underlying reflux or eosinophilic oesophagitis when the clinical context fits. Because the rings are dynamic, they are easily missed or over-called; correlating with symptoms and taking mucosal biopsies helps clarify the significance. Distal oesophageal biopsies are warranted when dysphagia or food impaction accompanies the appearance, to exclude eosinophilic oesophagitis. No specific treatment is directed at the feline pattern itself; management targets the underlying reflux or eosinophilic disease if present. recurrent food bolus impaction suggesting eosinophilic oesophagitis or stricture progressive dysphagia rather than an incidental transient finding odynophagia or weight loss haematemesis or evidence of mucosal ulceration persistent fixed rings with a narrow-calibre oesophagus Mistaking the transient feline pattern for the fixed rings of eosinophilic oesophagitis, or vice versa. Failing to biopsy the oesophagus in a patient with dysphagia or food impaction and missing eosinophilic oesophagitis. Over-interpreting a normal fleeting contraction as pathological. Not investigating for underlying gastro-oesophageal reflux when the pattern is seen. Attributing dysphagia to the transient rings themselves rather than to the true cause. The feline oesophagus pattern arises from transient contraction of the longitudinally oriented muscularis mucosae of the oesophageal body, throwing the mucosa into fine, closely spaced, transverse concentric folds. These contractions are frequently triggered by gastro-oesophageal reflux events, oesophageal distension or belching, which is why the appearance is dynamic and disappears once the stimulus resolves. The phenomenon reflects heightened or reflex mucosal muscle activity rather than fixed structural remodelling. It is distinguished pathophysiologically from the fixed concentric rings of eosinophilic oesophagitis, in which chronic eosinophilic inflammation drives subepithelial fibrosis and lamina propria remodelling, producing persistent rings and a narrow-calibre oesophagus. Recognition of the transient feline pattern therefore serves mainly as a clue to underlying acid reflux or eosinophilic mucosal disease. The feline oesophagus pattern is itself benign and transient with an excellent prognosis; overall outcome depends entirely on the underlying condition, particularly whether eosinophilic oesophagitis or significant reflux is present and treated.

only the female partner and omitting semen analysis Overlooking silent tubal disease from past infection or endometriosis Failing to address modifiable factors such as weight, smoking, and alcohol before intervention Female fertility requires cyclical hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian function producing a mature oocyte, patent fallopian tubes to allow fertilisation and transport, and a receptive endometrial cavity for implantation. Ovulatory disorders arise from disrupted gonadotrophin secretion: hypothalamic causes (stress, low body weight, excessive exercise, hyperprolactinaemia), polycystic ovary syndrome with anovulation, or premature ovarian insufficiency with follicular depletion. Tubal and peritoneal factors result from scarring and adhesions after pelvic inflammatory disease, endometriosis, or surgery, impairing gamete transport. Uterine factors include fibroids distorting the cavity, intrauterine adhesions, and congenital anomalies that impair implantation. Advancing maternal age reduces both the number and chromosomal quality of remaining oocytes, lowering fecundity and raising miscarriage risk. Prognosis depends heavily on the cause and on ovarian reserve; ovulatory disorders often respond well to induction of ovulation, whereas outcomes decline with maternal age and reduced reserve, and assisted reproduction can help many but not all couples.

despite absent obstruction in a Richter's-type hernia Systemic sepsis or peritonism suggesting perforation of strangulated bowel Confusing a femoral hernia with an inguinal hernia and adopting a conservative approach Missing a small femoral hernia in an obese patient presenting with unexplained bowel obstruction Overlooking a Richter's hernia because bowel obstruction is absent despite strangulation Delaying repair given the disproportionately high strangulation risk A femoral hernia protrudes through the femoral canal, the medial-most compartment of the femoral sheath, below the inguinal ligament. The canal normally contains fat and a lymph node (node of Cloquet) and has an unyielding boundary. Raised intra-abdominal pressure forces peritoneum and abdominal contents through the femoral ring into this confined space. The rigidity and narrowness of the neck predispose trapped contents to incarceration and rapid compromise of blood supply, causing strangulation and bowel ischaemia. The sac may turn upward over the inguinal ligament, mimicking an inguinal hernia. Prompt elective or urgent repair has a good outcome, but the high emergency presentation rate and frequent need for bowel resection mean femoral hernias carry greater morbidity and mortality than inguinal hernias, especially in elderly patients.

coinciding with seizure onset Feeding and respiratory difficulty with profound hypotonia Failure to respond to first-line therapy prompting mechanism-based review Overlooking FGF12 because it is a growth-factor-named gene that actually behaves as a sodium channel modulator Failing to trial sodium-channel blockers despite the gain-of-function mechanism Assuming a primary SCN gene must be responsible when panels are negative Attributing a normal early MRI to a benign prognosis FGF12 encodes fibroblast growth factor homologous factor 1, an intracellular protein that, despite its name, does not act as a secreted growth factor but instead binds the cytoplasmic carboxy-terminal domain of voltage-gated sodium channels. There it modulates channel inactivation and availability, thereby tuning neuronal firing. Pathogenic variants alter this interaction, generally producing a gain-of-function effect that slows inactivation or increases channel availability and raises excitability. Because the defect converges on sodium channel behaviour, the phenotype resembles a primary sodium channelopathy and often responds to sodium-channel-blocking medication, whereas the encephalopathy reflects the impact of aberrant firing on the developing brain. The developmental and epileptic encephalopathy phenotype generally carries significant intellectual disability, though seizures may respond well to sodium-channel-blocking agents given the gain-of-function mechanism, improving seizure burden in some children.

Overlooking it because of its rarity when standard immunofluorescence is only smudgy and polyclonal Fibrillary glomerulonephritis is characterised by organised deposition of Congo-red-negative fibrils, typically around 12 to 24 nanometres in diameter, arranged randomly within the mesangium and glomerular basement membrane. The deposits contain polyclonal immunoglobulin, complement and the chaperone protein DNAJB9, which is abundantly co-deposited and serves as a specific marker; DNAJB9 is thought to participate in misfolding and aggregation of immunoglobulin within the glomerulus. Accumulation of these fibrils disrupts the filtration barrier and incites a variable proliferative or membranoproliferative injury response, producing proteinuria, haematuria and progressive glomerulosclerosis. Associations with autoimmunity, malignancy, hepatitis C and dysproteinaemia are reported but a unifying trigger is not established. Fibrillary glomerulonephritis frequently progresses, with a large proportion of patients reaching end-stage kidney disease within a few years, particularly those with heavy proteinuria and reduced function at diagnosis. Response to immunosuppression is inconsistent, and the disease can recur in transplanted kidneys, though graft loss from recurrence is less common.

Fibro-adipose vascular anomaly — FAVA, Fibroadipose vascular anomaly Intramuscular venous malformation Lymphatic malformation Intramuscular haemangioma Soft-tissue sarcoma Desmoid-type fibromatosis Other PROS lesions such as CLOVES syndrome Contrast-enhanced MRI showing an infiltrative intramuscular fibrofatty lesion with phleboliths and slow-flow channels Doppler ultrasound Biopsy demonstrating fibrofatty replacement of muscle with anomalous vessels PIK3CA mutation testing on lesional tissue Coagulation screen for localised intravascular coagulopathy Nerve conduction studies or assessment where neural involvement is suspected A rare, painful intramuscular lesion characterised by fibrofatty replacement of muscle with associated anomalous slow-flow venous and lymphatic channels. Typically affects children and young adults, most often in the calf and gastrocnemius, the forearm or the thigh. The hallmark is severe, disproportionate pain with a firm intramuscular mass, often accompanied by contracture such as fixed ankle equinus in calf disease. Caused by somatic activating PIK3CA mutations, placing it within the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS). Frequently misdiagnosed as an ordinary venous malformation, but the dense fibrofatty muscle infiltration is distinctive on MRI and histology. MRI shows an infiltrative intramuscular lesion with fibrofatty tissue, phleboliths and abnormal vascular channels. Management includes percutaneous cryoablation, image-guided resection, physiotherapy for contracture, and PI3K/mTOR-targeted therapy such as sirolimus or alpelisib. Involvement of intramuscular nerves can produce neuropathic pain and requires careful surgical planning. Progressive fixed contracture with loss of joint function Severe intractable neuropathic pain Rapid growth raising suspicion of sarcoma Neurovascular compromise of the affected limb Misdiagnosing it as a simple venous malformation and mismanaging the pain and contracture. Failing to recognise it as part of the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum. Inadequate pain control by not addressing nerve involvement. Underestimating the extent of intramuscular infiltration before surgery. Fibro-adipose vascular anomaly is an intramuscular lesion in which normal skeletal muscle is progressively replaced by dense fibrous and adipose tissue intermixed with malformed, predominantly slow-flow venous and lymphatic channels and phleboliths. It arises from somatic mosaic activating mutations in PIK3CA with consequent PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway activation, situating it within the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum. The fibrofatty infiltration and involvement of intramuscular nerves are thought to underlie the characteristically severe pain and the tendency to produce fixed contractures, distinguishing it from a simple intramuscular venous malformation. Fibro-adipose vascular anomaly is benign but causes considerable morbidity from pain and contracture. Targeted therapy, cryoablation and resection can relieve symptoms, though the lesion tends to persist and established contractures may require orthopaedic correction.

more likely Ignoring discordant triple assessment results Over-treating small, asymptomatic, confirmed benign lesions with surgery A fibroadenoma is a benign biphasic tumour arising from the terminal duct lobular unit, in which both the glandular epithelium and the surrounding specialised stroma proliferate. It is regarded as an aberration of normal breast development rather than a true neoplasm, and its growth is influenced by oestrogen, which is why fibroadenomas typically appear during the reproductive years, may enlarge in pregnancy, and tend to involute after the menopause. The well-circumscribed, encapsulated architecture gives the characteristic smooth, freely mobile clinical lump. Malignant change within a fibroadenoma is very rare. Fibroadenomas are benign with an excellent prognosis; many remain stable or regress over time, recurrence after complete excision is uncommon, and the associated increase in future breast cancer risk is minimal except in the uncommon complex subtype.

universal lethality and withholding genetic confirmation that informs recurrence risk Confusing it radiographically with other dumbbell-limb dysplasias such as metatropic dysplasia Overlooking hearing and ophthalmic surveillance in survivors Failing to offer accurate autosomal recessive counselling to parents Fibrochondrogenesis is caused by loss-of-function variants in COL11A1 or COL11A2, which Fibrocystic Breast Change — fibrocystic breast change, fibrocystic breast disease, fibrocystic changes, benign breast change, cystic mastopathy Fibroadenoma Simple or complex breast cyst Breast carcinoma Breast abscess or mastitis Fat necrosis Phyllodes tumour Duct ectasia Clinical breast examination as part of triple assessment Breast ultrasound, preferred in younger women, to characterise cysts and solid lesions Mammography in older women or where malignancy is a concern Fine-needle aspiration or core biopsy of dominant, solid, or suspicious lesions Cyst aspiration for symptomatic relief and cytology of bloodstained fluid Histological assessment to identify proliferative change with atypia where relevant to risk Fibrocystic change is the commonest benign breast condition, presenting with lumpy, nodular, often tender breasts that vary with the menstrual cycle, typically in women of reproductive age Symptoms characteristically worsen in the luteal (premenstrual) phase and improve after menstruation, reflecting hormonal influence on breast tissue Examination often reveals diffuse nodularity or discrete cysts, most prominent in the upper outer quadrants, sometimes with cyclical mastalgia It is better regarded as a physiological change than a disease, and most forms carry no increased breast cancer risk; aspiration is done for symptomatic relief or if the cyst is complex or the fluid is bloodstained Bloodstained cyst aspirate, a residual mass after aspiration, or a rapidly recurring cyst should prompt further evaluation to exclude malignancy Management of cyclical breast pain is largely reassurance and supportive measures such as a well-fitting supportive bra and simple analgesia, with reserved use of specific pharmacological agents for severe refractory pain A new discrete, hard, or fixed lump, or one that does not fluctuate with the cycle, must be investigated rather than attributed to fibrocystic change A new hard, fixed, or irregular lump, or one that persists after aspiration Bloodstained cyst aspirate or spontaneous bloody nipple discharge Rapidly recurring cyst at the same site Skin dimpling, nipple retraction, or overlying skin change Axillary lymphadenopathy or a lump that does not vary with the menstrual cycle Proliferative change with atypia on biopsy indicating elevated cancer risk Attributing a new discrete or suspicious lump to fibrocystic change without triple assessment Ignoring bloodstained aspirate or a residual mass after cyst aspiration Falsely reassuring a patient by labelling all breast lumpiness as benign disease Overlooking proliferative atypical changes that do raise cancer risk Failing to reassess a symptom that does not fluctuate with the menstrual cycle Fibrocystic change reflects an exaggerated but benign response of breast stroma and epithelium to cyclical ovarian hormones. Fluctuating oestrogen and progesterone drive proliferation and involution of the terminal duct-lobular units, producing a spectrum of histological changes including cyst formation, fibrosis (stromal overgrowth), adenosis, and varying degrees of epithelial hyperplasia. Obstruction and dilatation of ducts and lobules generate fluid-filled cysts, while fibrosis produces the palpable nodularity. The hormonal cyclicity explains the premenstrual worsening of pain and swelling and improvement after menstruation. Fibrocystic change is benign and does not, in its common forms, increase breast cancer risk; symptoms often improve with reassurance and simple measures and tend to settle after the menopause. Cysts may recur but are readily managed. Only the minority with proliferative epithelial change and atypia carry an increased future cancer risk and warrant closer surveillance.

Fibrocystic change — Fibrocystic disease, Fibroadenosis, Benign breast change Simple or complex breast cysts Fibroadenoma Sclerosing adenosis presenting as a mass Invasive or in situ carcinoma Cyclical mastalgia without a mass Duct ectasia Fat necrosis Clinical breast examination correlated with menstrual timing Ultrasound of focal or dominant areas Mammography in women of screening age Core biopsy of any discrete or suspicious lesion Cyst aspiration where symptomatic cysts are present Pain chart to document the cyclical pattern of mastalgia Histological grading of the epithelial component when biopsied The commonest benign breast condition, reflecting an aberration of normal development and involution rather than a true disease. Presents with cyclical breast pain, nodularity and lumpiness, typically most marked in the upper outer quadrants and worse premenstrually. Affects women predominantly in the reproductive years, with symptoms usually settling after the menopause. Histology encompasses cysts, apocrine metaplasia, stromal fibrosis, adenosis and variable epithelial hyperplasia. Management is largely reassurance, a well-supporting bra and simple analgesia once malignancy has been excluded by triple assessment. Cancer risk is stratified by the epithelial component: non-proliferative change confers no excess risk, whereas atypical hyperplasia raises risk substantially. Discrete dominant lumps or focal areas warrant imaging and core biopsy rather than being attributed to generalised nodularity. Evening primrose oil and dietary caffeine reduction are commonly tried, though evidence for benefit is limited. A discrete, hard or fixed dominant mass within nodular tissue Bloody or persistent single-duct nipple discharge Skin dimpling, nipple retraction or peau d'orange Histological finding of atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia Progressive non-cyclical pain localised to one site Attributing a discrete dominant lump to generalised nodularity and omitting biopsy Failing to recognise that atypical hyperplasia carries a materially increased cancer risk Labelling the change a 'disease', which causes unnecessary anxiety Overlooking hormone replacement therapy as a cause of persistent symptoms after the menopause Reassuring on the basis of imaging alone when clinical findings are discordant Fibrocystic change results from an exaggerated but physiological response of breast tissue to cyclical ovarian hormones across the reproductive years and to the involutional processes that follow. Relative imbalance in oestrogen and progesterone influence, together with variable local tissue sensitivity, produces a mixture of cyst formation from dilated lobular acini, apocrine metaplasia, fibrous stromal proliferation, adenosis and differing degrees of epithelial hyperplasia. These coexisting elements account for the lumpiness, nodularity and cyclical discomfort, and their proliferative or atypical nature determines any associated increase in subsequent carcinoma risk. The condition is benign and self-limiting, with symptoms typically easing after the menopause. Long-term breast cancer risk depends on the underlying histology, being negligible for non-proliferative change and appreciably higher where atypical hyperplasia is found.

The mutant receptor becomes inappropriately responsive, including to activin, and drives excessive signalling that converts connective-tissue progenitor cells into cartilage and then bone through endochondral ossification. Inflammatory flare-ups, often after tissue injury, seed episodes of heterotopic ossification in muscle, tendon, ligament, and fascia. The accumulating extraskeletal bone bridges joints and restricts the chest wall, producing progressive immobility and life-limiting thoracic insufficiency. The condition is relentlessly progressive, with cumulative loss of mobility and joint ankylosis; median survival is reduced, and thoracic insufficiency from chest-wall ossification is the usual cause of death. Avoiding iatrogenic triggers is central to limiting progression.

response to standard osteomalacia therapy is generally poor Progressive immobilising bone pain and recurrent fractures Detection of a monoclonal gammopathy or macroglobulinaemia Vertebral collapse compromising function Failure to respond to standard osteomalacia therapy, prompting reassessment Mislabelling it as ordinary osteomalacia and treating with vitamin D, which does not correct the matrix defect Not performing bone biopsy with polarised microscopy, the key to diagnosis Overlooking an associated paraproteinaemia that may be driving the bone disease Confusing the coarse radiographic pattern with Paget disease or metastatic infiltration Fibrogenesis imperfecta ossium is a disorder of bone matrix in which osteoblasts lay down collagen in a disorganised, non-lamellar arrangement that fails to mineralise normally, accumulating as abnormal woven bone and excess osteoid. Unlike osteomalacia driven by vitamin D or phosphate deficiency, the mineral-regulating hormones and metabolites are usually normal, and the primary abnormality lies in the collagen fibre organisation itself, evident as loss of normal birefringence on polarised microscopy. The structurally deficient bone is mechanically weak, producing pain and fractures. The occasional association with a monoclonal gammopathy suggests that, in some patients, a circulating paraprotein or marrow disorder may interfere with matrix formation, though the mechanism is incompletely understood. The disorder tends to be progressive and disabling with a variable course; some patients stabilise or improve, particularly if an associated plasma-cell disorder is treated, but overall response to conventional metabolic bone therapy is limited.

fibrolamellar carcinoma — fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma, FLC conventional hepatocellular carcinoma focal nodular hyperplasia hepatic adenoma intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma hepatoblastoma in older children metastatic neuroendocrine tumour hepatic epithelioid haemangioendothelioma multiphase contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen MRI of the liver with hepatobiliary contrast core biopsy with histopathology and immunohistochemistry (including CK7 and CD68) molecular detection of the DNAJB1-PRKACA fusion serum alpha-fetoprotein and other liver tumour markers staging CT of the chest for pulmonary metastases assessment of regional lymph nodes for surgical planning A distinct primary liver carcinoma of adolescents and young adults, typically arising in a non-cirrhotic liver without underlying viral hepatitis or other chronic liver disease. Characterised by the recurrent DNAJB1-PRKACA gene fusion, which is highly specific and increasingly used to confirm the diagnosis. Presents with vague abdominal pain, a palpable mass, weight loss or malaise rather than the decompensation seen in conventional hepatocellular carcinoma. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is usually normal or only mildly raised, distinguishing it from most conventional hepatocellular carcinomas. Histology shows large polygonal eosinophilic tumour cells separated by parallel lamellae of dense collagenous fibrous stroma, giving the tumour its name. Imaging typically reveals a large, well-circumscribed lobulated mass, frequently with a central scar and calcification that can mimic focal nodular hyperplasia. Complete surgical resection, including of resectable nodal or limited metastatic disease, offers the best chance of prolonged survival as the tumour is relatively chemoresistant. Lymph node involvement is common at presentation, so nodal assessment and aggressive surgical clearance are integral to management. large or rapidly enlarging liver mass in a young patient bulky regional lymphadenopathy or biliary obstruction new pulmonary or peritoneal lesions suggesting metastasis features of portal or hepatic venous invasion on imaging constitutional symptoms with progressive weight loss Mistaking the central scar for focal nodular hyperplasia and delaying resection. Excluding malignancy because alpha-fetoprotein is normal. Assuming a cirrhosis-based hepatocellular carcinoma pathway in a young patient with a healthy liver. Under-staging by neglecting regional lymph nodes, which are frequently involved. Relying on systemic chemotherapy as primary treatment given the tumour's relative chemoresistance. Fibrolamellar carcinoma is driven in the great majority of cases by a small deletion on chromosome 19 that generates the chimeric DNAJB1-PRKACA fusion gene. This fusion places the catalytic subunit of protein kinase A under the control of the DNAJB1 promoter, resulting in aberrantly increased and dysregulated protein kinase A activity that promotes tumour cell proliferation and survival. The neoplastic hepatocytes are large and mitochondria-rich, producing the characteristic deeply eosinophilic, oncocytic cytoplasm, and they are separated by abundant parallel bands of lamellar fibrosis produced by an activated stroma. Unlike conventional hepatocellular carcinoma, the tumour arises in an otherwise healthy liver without a background of cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis, and its biology, marker profile and demographic pattern are correspondingly distinct. When completely resected, fibrolamellar carcinoma carries a more favourable outlook than conventional hepatocellular carcinoma, but frequent lymph-node involvement and a high recurrence rate temper long-term survival. Unresectable or metastatic disease responds poorly to systemic therapy and has a guarded prognosis.

Many patients have a benign course, but complications such as dissection, aneurysm rupture, and stroke can be serious; renal disease often responds well to angioplasty, and overall outlook depends on the vascular beds involved.

Fibromyalgia — FM, fibromyalgia syndrome Polymyalgia rheumatica Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthritides) Connective tissue disease (systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjogren's syndrome) Degenerative joint/spine/disk disease Myofascial pain syndromes Bursitis, tendinitis, repetitive strain injuries Hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism Hyperparathyroidism Multiple sclerosis and neuropathic pain syndromes Major depressive disorder Drug-induced myalgia (statins, aromatase inhibitors) Hepatitis C HIV infection Lyme disease Parvovirus B19 infection Epstein-Barr virus infection Routine screen: ESR or CRP, complete blood count, and thyroid-stimulating hormone (results are normal in uncomplicated FM) Guided by history/exam: complete metabolic panel, ANA, anti-SSA/anti-SSB, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP, creatine phosphokinase Viral (e.g., hepatitis C, HIV) and bacterial (e.g., Lyme) serologies when clinically indicated Radiographs used sparingly and only when inflammatory arthritis is suspected; spine MRI reserved for features of inflammatory spine disease or neurologic symptoms Repeat testing is discouraged unless the symptom complex changes Polymyalgia rheumatica Rheumatoid arthritis and spondyloarthritides Systemic lupus erythematosus and Sjogren's syndrome Hypo- or hyperthyroidism and hyperparathyroidism Degenerative joint/spine/disk disease and myofascial pain syndromes Neuropathic pain syndromes and multiple sclerosis Major depressive disorder Statin- or aromatase-inhibitor-induced myalgia Defined by chronic widespread musculoskeletal pain and tenderness, with pain present most of the day on most days for at least 3 months and distributed both above and below the waist, on both sides, and involving the axial skeleton (Harrison 22e p.2963). Beyond pain, patients commonly report fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive dysfunction ("fibro fog"), anxiety, and depression, which may affect function and quality of life as much as or more than the pain itself (Harrison 22e p.2963-2964). Elevated evoked pain sensitivity may be detected clinically by pain on blood-pressure cuff inflation or skin-roll tenderness; a formal tender-point exam applies ~4 kg/m2 of thumbnail pressure (enough to blanch the nail bed) at defined musculotendinous sites (Harrison 22e p.2963). Older ACR criteria required 11 of 18 tender points; newer 2016 criteria abandon tender-point counting and instead use a Widespread Pain Index plus Symptom Severity Score (e.g., WPI >=7 and SSS >=5, or WPI 4-6 and SSS >=9, with generalized pain in at least 4 of 5 regions for >=3 months) (Harrison 22e p.2963-2964). Tenderness is a continuous variable; strict application of a categorical threshold is not required for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2963). Peripheral pain generators such as arthritis, bursitis, tendinitis, neuropathies, joint hypermobility, and scoliosis can trigger and perpetuate the centrally maintained widespread pain of FM (Harrison 22e p.2963). FM is one of the chronic overlapping pain conditions and frequently coexists with myalgic encephalitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, temporomandibular disorder, chronic headaches, irritable bowel syndrome, and interstitial cystitis/painful bladder syndrome, likely sharing central mechanisms (Harrison 22e p.2963). The lifetime prevalence of mood disorders in FM approaches 80%; depression is neither necessary nor sufficient for diagnosis, but screening for depressed mood and anhedonia is important (Harrison 22e p.2964). Symptom onset and flares often cluster around periods of perceived stress, and there is a high prevalence of prior interpersonal or other violence exposure; consider posttraumatic stress disorder where relevant (Harrison 22e p.2964). Some patients meeting FM criteria have a small-fiber neuropathy, and early reports suggest possible autoimmune changes in the peripheral nervous system in subsets of patients (Harrison 22e p.2964). Functional assessment across physical, mental, and social domains is central, since improved function (rather than complete pain elimination) is the principal measure of management success (Harrison 22e p.2964). Pain extending beyond what a known triggering or inflammatory condition could reasonably explain, signaling emergence of central FM-type pain requiring a different management focus Objective inflammatory, neurologic, or systemic findings (abnormal ESR/CRP, focal neurologic deficits) that point toward an alternative or comorbid diagnosis rather than FM Screen-positive major depression with anhedonia, and history suggestive of posttraumatic stress disorder, given high comorbidity and impact on outcome Failing to consider FM, leading to missed or delayed diagnosis since musculoskeletal pain is so common (Harrison 22e p.2964). Over-investigating with repeated laboratory tests or, especially, spine MRI in the absence of inflammatory or neurologic features (Harrison 22e p.2964). Continuing to treat only peripheral or inflammatory pain generators when central FM pain has emerged, instead of addressing central pain processing (Harrison 22e p.2964). Setting complete pain elimination, rather than improved function and quality of life, as the treatment goal (Harrison 22e p.2965). FM is regarded as a disorder in which the central nervous system maintains pain and the other core symptoms. Psychophysical testing shows altered afferent pain processing and impaired descending noxious inhibitory control, producing hyperalgesia and allodynia, and functional MRI demonstrates activation of pain-experiencing brain regions in response to stimuli that are innocuous in unaffected individuals. Pain perception is modulated by emotional and cognitive factors such as catastrophizing and perceived control. Genetic susceptibility appears polygenic, involving pathways that control pain and stress responses, including genes for metabolism, transport, and receptors of serotonin and other monoamines, with some genetic underpinnings shared across chronic pain conditions and overlapping with mood disorders. Peripheral pain generators (e.g., arthritis, bursitis, neuropathy, hypermobility) can serve as triggers that alter central pain processing (Harrison 22e p.2964). FM is a chronic condition with substantial adverse effects on physical and social functioning and on health-related quality of life. Outcomes are best when there is prompt diagnosis, assessment of pain, function, and psychosocial context, patient education, and a partnership-based strategy directed at improving function rather than eliminating pain; illness behaviors such as frequent physician visits are to be discouraged while function-promoting behaviors are encouraged (Harrison 22e p.2964-2965). Severity is captured by the 2016 diagnostic instrument combining the Widespread Pain Index (WPI, range 0-19) and the Symptom Severity Score (SSS, range 0-12, grading fatigue, unrefreshing waking, and cognitive symptoms plus selected somatic items). Diagnosis requires WPI >=7 and SSS >=5, or WPI 4-6 and SSS >=9, with generalized pain in at least 4 of 5 body regions, sustained for at least 3 months; higher WPI and SSS values reflect greater symptom burden (Harrison 22e p.2964).

peel before surgery When blood, pus, or a protein-rich exudate persists in the pleural space, the initial fibrinous layer becomes organised by ingrowth of fibroblasts and capillaries. Instead of resolving, the fibrin matures into dense collagenous tissue that binds the visceral and parietal pleura together as a rigid peel. This inelastic layer mechanically traps the lung, restricts expansion of the hemithorax, and impairs ventilation, and with time it may calcify. The result is a fixed restrictive defect that persists until the constricting rind is surgically removed. If the trapped lung is otherwise healthy, decortication can restore substantial lung expansion and function; outcomes are poorer when there is coexisting parenchymal disease, unresolved infection, or an underlying malignancy.

Cushingoid features Mistaking a ground-glass lesion for a more aggressive tumour and performing unnecessary radical surgery Overlooking associated endocrinopathy in a child presenting with bone disease and cafe-au-lait spots Missing FGF23-mediated hypophosphataemia that worsens bone weakness Attributing all new pain to benign disease and failing to investigate possible sarcomatous change Fibrous dysplasia arises from somatic gain-of-function mutations in the GNAS gene encoding the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G protein, leading to constitutive activation of adenylate cyclase and elevated cyclic AMP in affected cells. Because the mutation occurs after fertilisation, the resulting mosaicism explains the variable and patchy distribution of disease. In bone, the mutation impairs osteoblast differentiation so that normal bone marrow is replaced by disorganised fibrous stroma with immature woven bone. The same signalling defect in endocrine tissue drives autonomous hormone secretion, and lesional cells can produce excess FGF23, causing renal phosphate wasting. Monostotic disease is often mild and stable, whereas extensive polyostotic disease and McCune-Albright syndrome can cause progressive deformity, recurrent fractures, and endocrine morbidity; malignant transformation is rare but serious.

collection timed to microfilarial periodicity (Harrison 22e p.1821) Circulating filarial antigen assays for W. bancrofti (ELISA and rapid lateral-flow); no antigen test available for brugian filariasis (Harrison 22e p.1821) PCR for W. bancrofti and B. malayi DNA in blood (sensitivity equal to or greater than parasitologic methods) (Harrison 22e p.1821) High-frequency ultrasound with Doppler of scrotum/lymph nodes/breast to visualize motile adult worms ('filarial dance sign') (Harrison 22e p.1821) Radionuclide lymphoscintigraphy (mainly a research/lymphedema-assessment tool) (Harrison 22e p.1821) Eosinophilia, elevated serum IgE, and elevated antifilarial antibody (supportive, with extensive helminth cross-reactivity; W. bancrofti- and B. malayi-specific antigen serology has specificity >98%) (Harrison 22e p.1821) Skin snip (incubated in saline/medium; microfilariae emerge in 2-4 h or overnight) or excised nodule for onchocerciasis; Onchocerca-specific antibody assays (Harrison 22e p.1823) Chest x-ray/CT and pulmonary function tests in TPE (restrictive in most, obstructive in half) (Harrison 22e p.1822) Detection of L. loa microfilariae in blood, removal of adult worm from eye/subcutaneous biopsy, or PCR/recombinant-antigen serology for loiasis (Harrison 22e p.1823) Lymphedema of malignancy, postoperative scarring, trauma, chronic edematous states, congenital lymphatic abnormalities (mimic chronic filarial lymphedema) (Harrison 22e p.1821) Asthma and Loffler's syndrome (mimic TPE) (Harrison 22e p.1822) Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss), other systemic vasculitides including periarteritis nodosa, chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, hypereosinophilic syndromes (mimic TPE) (Harrison 22e p.1822) Eight filarial species infect humans, but four cause most symptomatic disease: Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, Onchocerca volvulus, and Loa loa (Harrison 22e p.1819). Filarial disease is characteristically more acute and intense in newly exposed travelers/transmigrants than in lifelong natives of endemic areas; infection usually requires repeated, prolonged exposure to infective larvae (Harrison 22e p.1819). Lymphatic filariasis (W. bancrofti, B. malayi, B. timori) is widely distributed; W. bancrofti affects ~51 million people and B. malayi occurs primarily in eastern India, Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines; humans are the only definitive host for W. bancrofti (Harrison 22e p.1819-1820). Most W. bancrofti is nocturnally periodic (microfilariae scarce by day, increasing at night); blood for microfilaria detection must be timed to the regional periodicity (Harrison 22e p.1819-1821). Common presentations of lymphatic filariasis are asymptomatic/subclinical microfilaremia, hydrocele, acute adenolymphangitis (ADL), and chronic lymphatic disease (lymphedema/elephantiasis) (Harrison 22e p.1820). Genital lymphatic involvement (funiculitis, epididymitis, hydrocele, scrotal elephantiasis) occurs almost exclusively with W. bancrofti, not Brugia (Harrison 22e p.1820). ADL lymphangitis is retrograde (spreads peripherally from the draining node), a feature that distinguishes filarial lymphangitis from ascending bacterial lymphangitis (Harrison 22e p.1820-1821). Dermatolymphangioadenitis (DLA) presents with fever, chills, myalgias, demarcated edematous plaques, and entry lesions (often interdigital) and is frequently misdiagnosed as cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.1820). Obstruction of retroperitoneal lymphatics can rupture renal lymphatics and produce intermittent chyluria, typically most prominent in the morning (Harrison 22e p.1820). On high-frequency ultrasound, live adult worms in dilated lymphatics show a distinctive motion called the 'filarial dance sign'; worms are seen in the spermatic cord in up to 80% of W. bancrofti-infected men (Harrison 22e p.1821). Circulating antigen assays (ELISA and rapid lateral-flow) for W. bancrofti have sensitivities of 93-100% and specificity approaching 100% and detect both microfilaremic and cryptic amicrofilaremic infection; there is currently NO circulating-antigen test for brugian filariasis (Harrison 22e p.1821). Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE) presents with nocturnal paroxysmal cough/wheeze, weight loss, low-grade fever, marked blood eosinophilia (>3000/uL), and very high IgE and antifilarial antibody; microfilariae are cleared from blood by the lungs and are typically NOT found in peripheral blood (Harrison 22e p.1821-1822). Onchocerciasis ('river blindness'), caused by O. volvulus, primarily affects skin, eyes, and lymph nodes; pruritus and a generalized papular rash are most common, and visual impairment is the most serious complication (Harrison 22e p.1822-1823). Sclerosing keratitis (in 1-5% of infected persons) is the leading cause of onchocercal blindness; 'snowflake' punctate keratitis around dying microfilariae is common in younger patients and usually resolves (Harrison 22e p.1823). Onchocercal lymphadenopathy can produce 'hanging groin'; rarely Nakalanga dwarfism and an association with epilepsy/nodding syndrome are seen; blind adults have a 3- to 4-fold higher mortality (Harrison 22e p.1823). Loiasis (Loa loa, the African eye worm) is suggested by transient subconjunctival worm migration and episodic Calabar swellings (evanescent angioedema); microfilariae have a diurnal periodicity peaking ~10:00 a.m.-2:00 p.m. (Harrison 22e p.1823). Wolbachia, an intracellular bacterial endosymbiont present in Brugia, Wuchereria, Mansonella, and Onchocerca, is a target for antifilarial (anti-Wolbachia) therapy (Harrison 22e p.1819, 1824). Sclerosing keratitis, anterior uveitis, chorioretinal lesions, or optic atrophy in onchocerciasis (impending/established blindness) (Harrison 22e p.1823) High Loa loa microfilaremia (>30,000 microfilariae/mL): risk of severe post-treatment encephalopathy with ivermectin or DEC (Harrison 22e p.1822-1823) Loiasis with CNS involvement during treatment of heavy microfilaremia (coma, encephalitis) (Harrison 22e p.1823) Chyluria from retroperitoneal lymphatic obstruction in lymphatic filariasis (Harrison 22e p.1820) Progressive interstitial pulmonary fibrosis in untreated TPE (Harrison 22e p.1822) Seropositivity (antifilarial antibody) cannot be equated with active infection; endemic residents can become sensitized via mosquito exposure without patent infection (Harrison 22e p.1821). Antifilarial antibody/antigen serology has extensive cross-reactivity with other helminths; W. bancrofti antigen tests can be falsely positive in Loa loa infection (Harrison 22e p.1821). Many infected individuals are amicrofilaremic, and travelers are often amicrofilaremic, so a negative blood smear does not exclude filariasis (Harrison 22e p.1821, 1823). Timing of blood collection to the local microfilarial periodicity is critical; mistimed samples miss nocturnally or diurnally periodic microfilariae (Harrison 22e p.1821). DLA is often misdiagnosed as cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.1820). Eosinophilia and elevated IgE are nonspecific (common to many parasitic infections) and are not diagnostic by themselves (Harrison 22e p.1823). For every palpable onchocercal nodule there are an estimated four deeper nonpalpable ones (Harrison 22e p.1823). Filariae are tissue-dwelling nematodes transmitted by mosquitoes or other arthropods; insect-borne infective larvae mature into adult worms that reside in lymphatics (W. bancrofti, Brugia) or subcutaneous tissue (Loa loa, O. volvulus). Adults release microfilariae that circulate in blood or migrate through skin; adults live many years while microfilariae survive 3-36 months. In lymphatic filariasis, pathology results mainly from inflammatory damage caused by ADULT worms (not microfilariae) in afferent lymphatics, with plasma-cell/eosinophil/macrophage infiltration, lymphatic dilation, valve incompetence, and progressive granulomatous reaction and fibrosis (worsened by worm death) leading to obstruction, lymphedema, and elephantiasis; injury is due both to the worm and to host inflammatory response. In contrast, onchocerciasis pathology is elicited by MICROFILARIAE (not adults), causing chronic dermal inflammation/atrophy/fibrosis, fibrous subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomata) around adults, and corneal neovascularization/scarring and intraocular inflammation leading to blindness. In TPE, microfilariae are trapped and cleared by the lungs, provoking allergic/eosinophilic intra-alveolar inflammation that can progress to interstitial fibrosis. Calabar swellings of loiasis are thought to be a hypersensitivity reaction to adult-worm antigens. The Wolbachia endosymbiont contributes to inflammatory reactions (Harrison 22e p.1819-1823). Filarial infections are chronic with potential long-term debilitating effects; adult worms live for many years (W. bancrofti/Brugia >2 decades; O. volvulus up to ~18 years, average ~9). Most microfilaremic persons remain clinically asymptomatic for years, and only a minority progress to acute or chronic disease, but lymphatic damage can become permanent (elephantiasis, hydrocele). In onchocerciasis, visual loss is the most serious outcome and blind adults have a 3- to 4-fold increased mortality. Loiasis, historically considered relatively benign in endemic populations, is now linked to chronic morbidity and increased mortality. TPE responds to therapy but relapses in ~12-25% of cases (sometimes years later); untreated TPE can progress to pulmonary fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.1819-1823). Harrison describes lymphatic filariasis along a clinical spectrum rather than a formal grading: asymptomatic/subclinical microfilaremia, hydrocele, acute adenolymphangitis (ADL)/dermatolymphangioadenitis (DLA), and chronic lymphatic disease (lymphedema progressing to elephantiasis). Onchocerciasis severity is gauged by infection burden (skin/eye involvement increasing with moderate-to-heavy microfilarial load). Loa loa microfilaremia is stratified by treatment risk, with >30,000 microfilariae/mL marking high risk of severe post-treatment encephalopathy (Harrison 22e p.1820-1823).

First bite syndrome — FBS, first-bite pain, post-parapharyngeal surgery pain syndrome Frey syndrome Recurrent or obstructive sialadenitis Temporomandibular joint dysfunction Trigeminal or glossopharyngeal neuralgia Parapharyngeal space tumour Salivary duct calculus with mealtime pain Detailed history establishing the classic first-bite, sour-food-provoked pattern Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the parapharyngeal space and deep parotid to exclude a mass Ultrasound of the salivary glands to exclude obstruction or sialadenitis Review of prior operative records for parapharyngeal or sympathetic chain surgery Sialography or salivary duct assessment if obstruction is suspected Characterised by intense, cramping or spasm-like pain in the parotid region with the first bite or chew of each meal, easing markedly over the next few mouthfuls The pain is worst at the start of eating, provoked most strongly by sour or tart foods, and recurs at the next meal Typically follows surgery in the parapharyngeal space, deep lobe parotid, or upper neck that disturbs cervical sympathetic supply to the parotid It may also be the presenting feature of a parapharyngeal space tumour, so new spontaneous first bite pain warrants imaging The mechanism is loss of sympathetic tone to parotid myoepithelial cells with unopposed parasympathetic supersensitivity, causing painful contraction with initial salivary stimulation Botulinum toxin injected into the parotid gland is the most effective treatment for refractory cases; carbamazepine and other neuropathic agents give variable benefit Symptoms often improve gradually over months as the nervous system adapts New spontaneous first bite pain without prior surgery, suggesting an occult parapharyngeal tumour An associated Horner syndrome indicating sympathetic chain involvement by disease A palpable deep neck or parapharyngeal mass Progressive cranial neuropathies accompanying the pain Dismissing spontaneous (non-surgical) first bite pain and missing a parapharyngeal neoplasm Confusing it with Frey syndrome, which causes sweating rather than pain Attributing the mealtime pain to dental or temporomandibular disease Failing to recognise the characteristic first-bite, sour-food pattern in the history First bite syndrome is attributed to loss of sympathetic innervation to the parotid gland, usually after surgery involving the parapharyngeal space or cervical sympathetic chain. Denervation leaves the parasympathetic supply to the myoepithelial cells relatively unopposed, and these cells become supersensitive. The strong burst of parasympathetic (salivary) stimulation at the first bite of a meal then provokes an exaggerated, painful contraction of the myoepithelial cells. As salivation continues over subsequent bites the stimulus diminishes and the pain subsides, giving the characteristic pattern that repeats at the next meal. The syndrome is benign and tends to lessen in intensity over months to a couple of years, though it may persist. Botulinum toxin provides reliable temporary relief and can be repeated; spontaneous first bite pain resolves once any underlying tumour is treated.

Complex, high, or Crohn's-related fistulae are prone to recurrence and require staged sphincter-preserving strategies, with a persistent risk of continence disturbance.

dermatitis with necrotic keratinocytes and a lichenoid infiltrate, and pigment incontinence accounts for the residual pigmentation The cornerstone of management is identifying and permanently avoiding the responsible drug, with topical corticosteroids for localised disease and supportive care for extensive bullous forms Widespread blistering and skin detachment suggesting generalised bullous fixed body-surface involvement Recurrent episodes indicating continued inadvertent exposure to the culprit drug Failing to elicit the culprit drug so that repeated re-exposure causes recurrent and potentially more severe episodes Mistaking the generalised bullous form for Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis, or vice versa Attributing the residual pigmentation to another cause and missing the diagnosis Overlooking over-the-counter analgesics and sedatives as common triggers Fixed drug eruption is a localised, drug-specific delayed hypersensitivity reaction. Intraepidermal CD8 memory T lymphocytes persist at previously affected sites after an initial episode; on re-exposure to the drug these resident effector-memory cells are rapidly reactivated and release cytokines that damage basal keratinocytes, producing an interface dermatitis with keratinocyte necrosis. Because the memory T cells remain fixed within the epidermis at earlier sites, the eruption characteristically recurs at precisely the same locations. Melanin released from damaged basal cells is taken up by dermal macrophages (pigment incontinence), explaining the persistent grey-brown pigmentation, and widespread activation produces the generalised bullous variant. Localised fixed drug eruption resolves after the drug is stopped, leaving persistent pigmentation but no serious sequelae; the generalised bullous variant carries a more guarded prognosis with a mortality that, although lower than toxic epidermal necrolysis, is not negligible in extensive disease.

FKRP-related dystroglycanopathy — FKRP, LGMD2I, LGMDR9, MDC1C, fukutin-related protein myopathy, alpha-dystroglycanopathy Other limb-girdle muscular dystrophies Dystrophinopathies (Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy) Other dystroglycanopathies (e.g. fukutin, POMT1/2, POMGNT1 related) Other congenital muscular dystrophies including merosin-deficient forms Inflammatory myopathies Metabolic
