dystrophy (MDC1C) with brain and eye involvement The limb-girdle form typically presents with proximal lower-limb and pelvic-girdle weakness, sometimes with calf hypertrophy resembling a dystrophinopathy Serum creatine kinase is usually substantially elevated across the spectrum Inherited in an autosomal recessive manner as one of the alpha-dystroglycanopathies caused by defective glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan Cardiomyopathy and respiratory muscle weakness are important complications even in ambulant patients with the milder phenotype The severe congenital end may include structural brain malformation and eye abnormalities, overlapping with the Walker-Warburg and muscle-eye-brain phenotypes Because cardiac and respiratory involvement can be disproportionate to limb weakness, structured surveillance of the heart and respiratory function is essential Cardiomyopathy or heart failure, which may be out of proportion to limb weakness Respiratory muscle weakness with nocturnal hypoventilation In infants, structural brain malformation, seizures or visual impairment indicating the severe phenotype Loss of ambulation requiring orthopaedic and rehabilitation planning Neglecting cardiac and respiratory monitoring in an ambulant patient with the milder phenotype Mistaking calf hypertrophy and high creatine kinase for a dystrophinopathy without genetic confirmation Assuming normal cognition and vision exclude the diagnosis, since these are only affected at the severe end Not recognising the wide phenotypic range attributable to the same gene FKRP-related dystroglycanopathy is caused by biallelic mutations in FKRP, encoding fukutin-related protein, an enzyme involved in the glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan. Alpha-dystroglycan is a central component of the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex, and its sugar chains bind extracellular-matrix ligands such as laminin to link the muscle-fibre cytoskeleton to the basement membrane. Defective glycosylation weakens this linkage, so the sarcolemma is mechanically vulnerable and undergoes repeated injury and degeneration, producing a dystrophic phenotype. The severity depends on how profoundly glycosylation is impaired, ranging from a relatively mild limb-girdle dystrophy to a severe congenital form in which deficient dystroglycan function also disrupts neuronal migration and eye development. Outcome depends on where on the spectrum a patient sits, from a relatively slowly progressive limb-girdle dystrophy compatible with prolonged ambulation and near-normal lifespan to a severe congenital form with early respiratory and neurological compromise; cardiac and respiratory surveillance materially improves outcomes across the range.

wall movement while underestimating the underlying lung contusion Providing inadequate analgesia, leading to poor ventilation and secretion retention Missing an associated pneumothorax or haemothorax Assuming a stable early gas exchange will remain stable as contusion evolves Excessive fluid administration worsening the pulmonary contusion When several adjacent ribs are each fractured in two or more places, an isolated segment of chest wall loses its bony connection to the rest of the thoracic cage. This segment then moves according to intrapleural pressure rather than muscular effort, producing paradoxical motion that reduces the efficiency of ventilation. More importantly, the force required to cause the injury bruises the lung beneath, and this pulmonary contusion impairs gas exchange, worsening over the first day or two. Pain from the fractures limits chest expansion and coughing, promoting atelectasis and retained secretions, all of which combine to cause hypoxaemia and, in severe cases, respiratory failure. Outcome is largely determined by the severity of the underlying lung contusion and associated injuries. With good analgesia, chest physiotherapy, and respiratory support many patients recover, but extensive contusion and respiratory failure increase morbidity and mortality.

urgent exploration Signs of flexor sheath infection following an open injury (a surgical emergency) Complete loss of active flexion with a retracted tendon needing timely repair before further retraction Devascularised or grossly contaminated wound requiring prompt surgical management Failing to test profundus and superficialis separately and missing a partial or isolated tendon division Overlooking associated digital nerve or vessel injury Damaging or dividing critical pulleys (A2, A4), leading to bowstringing Immobilising rather than starting an appropriate early motion protocol, causing dense adhesions Being too aggressive with rehabilitation and precipitating repair rupture Delaying repair so that tendon retraction complicates later reconstruction Flexor tendons transmit force from forearm muscles to flex the digits and glide within synovial sheaths and beneath a series of annular and cruciate pulleys that hold them close to bone. Laceration divides the tendon and causes proximal retraction of the cut end, particularly when the muscle is contracting at the time of injury. Healing occurs through both intrinsic mechanisms, from tenocytes and synovial nutrition, and extrinsic mechanisms, through ingrowth of surrounding tissue that forms adhesions. Excessive extrinsic healing produces adhesions that restrict glide, while inadequate healing or excessive load risks gap formation and rupture. Within the confined zone II sheath, even small amounts of scarring markedly impair function. Outcome depends on the zone of injury, associated damage, quality of repair, and adherence to rehabilitation. Zone II injuries carry the highest risk of adhesions and stiffness. With sound repair and supervised early motion, many patients regain good function, but adhesions, rupture, and contracture can necessitate tenolysis or staged reconstruction and may leave lasting deficits.

Focal Atrial Tachycardia — Focal AT, Atrial tachycardia, AT Sinus tachycardia (especially when the focus lies high on the crista terminalis near the sinus node, producing a near-sinus P-wave morphology; abrupt onset/offset favors AT) Inappropriate sinus tachycardia AV nodal reentry tachycardia (AVNRT) AV reentry tachycardia using an accessory pathway (AVRT) Atrial flutter / macroreentrant atrial tachycardia (continuous flutter waves, no isoelectric baseline) Multifocal atrial tachycardia (multiple distinct P-wave morphologies) Junctional tachycardia 12-lead ECG to characterize P-wave morphology and the R-P / P-R relationship and to localize the focus Ambulatory/Holter ECG monitoring (nonsustained AT is commonly detected and its prevalence rises with age) Maneuvers to induce AV block (carotid sinus massage, Valsalva, adenosine) to expose buried P waves and to demonstrate that the atrial tachycardia persists despite AV block Assessment for digitalis toxicity and other precipitating illness/drug toxicity when AT with AV block is seen Echocardiography to evaluate for structural heart disease and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy Electrophysiology study with electroanatomic mapping to identify the earliest activation (focal) site, typically prior to catheter ablation Sinus tachycardia (physiologic or inappropriate) Atrial flutter and macroreentrant atrial tachycardia AV-nodal-dependent SVTs (AVNRT, AVRT) Focal AT arises from a discrete atrial site and is driven by one of three mechanisms: abnormal automaticity, triggered activity, or microreentry within diseased atrial tissue; the term 'focal' distinguishes it from typical and atypical (macroreentrant) atrial flutter and does not by itself specify the underlying mechanism (p.1937). It accounts for roughly 10% of paroxysmal SVTs in patients referred for catheter ablation, and may be sustained, nonsustained, paroxysmal, or incessant (p.1937). Because focal AT is not dependent on AV nodal conduction, it does NOT terminate when AV block is induced and the atrial rate is unaffected by AV-nodal blockade — a key feature separating it from AV-nodal-dependent SVTs such as AVNRT and AVRT (p.1937). P waves are typically discrete with an intervening isoelectric baseline (because atrial activation from a single focus occupies only a small part of the cycle), in contrast to the continuous undulating activation of atrial flutter / macroreentrant AT (p.1937). A 'warm-up' phase (gradual acceleration of atrial rate after onset) or a 'cool-down' phase (gradual slowing before termination) favors focal AT with enhanced automaticity over AV-nodal-dependent SVT (p.1937). Foci tend to cluster in areas of complex atrial anatomy — the crista terminalis, valve annuli, atrial septum, and atrial muscle sleeves extending into the thoracic veins (superior vena cava, coronary sinus, pulmonary veins) — and the focus location can often be approximated from P-wave morphology (p.1937). P-wave localization clues: septal foci give a narrower P than sinus; left atrial foci give a monophasic positive P in V1 with negative P in I and aVL; superior foci (SVC, superior pulmonary veins) are positive in II, III, aVF; inferior foci (e.g., coronary sinus ostium) are negative in II, III, aVF (p.1937). Atrial tachycardia WITH AV block is the characteristic arrhythmia of digitalis toxicity, so emergence of AT should prompt consideration of drug toxicity or another underlying illness; sympathetic stimulation promotes AT (p.1937). Incessant focal AT can cause tachycardia-induced (tachycardia-mediated) cardiomyopathy, which is an important reversible cause of LV dysfunction (p.1937). Asymptomatic nonsustained AT seen on monitoring is frequently mislabeled 'SVT' on monitor reports; treatment is NOT recommended for asymptomatic nonsustained AT identified on ECG monitoring (p.1937). Frequent atrial ectopy and nonsustained AT are often precursors to more significant arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter (p.1937). Vagal maneuvers, carotid sinus massage, Valsalva, or AV-nodal-blocking agents (e.g., adenosine) are used diagnostically to create transient AV block and unmask P waves when they are buried in the T wave or QRS (p.1937-1938). Incessant AT — risk of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy Hemodynamic instability with the tachycardia AT with AV block — suggests digitalis toxicity or other underlying illness/drug toxicity Rapid ventricular response causing angina, hypotension, pulmonary edema, or syncope AT as a harbinger of atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter Mislabeling asymptomatic nonsustained AT on a monitor as actionable 'SVT' and over-treating it — treatment is not recommended in this setting (p.1937). Confusing focal AT with sinus tachycardia when the focus is near the sinus node; rely on abrupt onset/offset and subtle P-wave morphology differences (p.1937). Expecting AV-nodal blockade (adenosine, vagal maneuvers) to terminate the tachycardia — it usually only increases AV block while the atrial rhythm continues, since AT is independent of the AV node (p.1937-1938). Overlooking digitalis toxicity or another precipitant when AT presents with AV block (p.1937). Missing reversible tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy as the cause of new LV dysfunction in a patient with incessant AT (p.1937). Focal AT originates from a single discrete atrial site and is caused by abnormal automaticity, triggered activity, or a small reentry circuit in diseased atrial tissue. It may occur in structurally normal hearts or in association with any condition causing atrial fibrosis, including atrial tissue scarred by prior catheter ablation. Zones of fibrosis serve as a nidus for abnormal automaticity arising from injured but partially viable cells, or for microreentry within and at the border of regions of slow conduction. Sympathetic stimulation is a facilitating factor, and the appearance of AT may signal underlying illness or drug toxicity (digitalis being characteristic). The arrhythmia activates the atria from a focal source through only a small portion of the cycle, producing discrete P waves with isoelectric intervals (p.1937). Symptoms vary widely and parallel those of other SVTs. Many nonsustained, asymptomatic episodes require no treatment. The principal adverse outcome is tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy from incessant AT, which is typically reversible once rhythm is controlled. Focal AT is frequently a precursor to atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter; however, the stroke risk and the indications for long-term anticoagulation are not considered equivalent to those of AF/flutter and remain unclear. Catheter ablation targeting the focus is successful in more than 80% of patients (p.1937-1938). No formal grading scale; clinical stratification is by hemodynamic tolerance (stable vs unstable), by burden/pattern (nonsustained vs sustained, paroxysmal vs incessant), and by symptom status (asymptomatic vs symptomatic), since incessant disease carries the risk of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (p.1937).

Focal dermal hypoplasia — Goltz syndrome, Goltz-Gorlin syndrome, PORCN, focal dermal hypoplasia syndrome Incontinentia pigmenti MIDAS/microphthalmia with linear skin defects syndrome Aplasia cutis congenita Nevus lipomatosus superficialis Rothmund-Thomson syndrome Other Blaschko-linear mosaic genodermatoses Molecular genetic testing of PORCN Skin biopsy showing marked dermal thinning with fat approaching the epidermis Skeletal radiographs for osteopathia striata and limb anomalies Ophthalmological examination for colobomata and microphthalmia Dental assessment for enamel and tooth anomalies Multidisciplinary developmental and organ-system evaluation A multisystem ectodermal-mesodermal disorder in which atrophic, linear skin lesions follow the lines of Blaschko Soft, yellow-pink outpouchings of herniated fat through the thinned dermis (fat herniation) are a characteristic cutaneous sign Raspberry-like papillomas around the mouth, anus and vulva, and periungual/mucosal papillomas, are frequent Skeletal defects, classically osteopathia striata on radiographs and limb anomalies such as syndactyly and 'lobster-claw' hands, are common Ocular (colobomata, microphthalmia) and dental anomalies frequently accompany the skin findings X-linked dominant, caused by PORCN mutations; usually lethal in males, so most patients are female and mosaicism explains survival in the few affected males Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, addressing skin, skeletal, ocular and dental problems Significant ocular malformation threatening vision Major limb or skeletal anomaly requiring surgical management Symptomatic internal or gastrointestinal papillomatosis Complications of extensive skin fragility such as infection Focusing on the skin lesions and failing to screen for skeletal, ocular and dental anomalies Misinterpreting fat herniation as a benign lipomatous naevus without recognising the syndrome Overlooking the diagnosis in a rare affected male, in whom mosaicism is expected Not offering genetic counselling given X-linked dominant inheritance and male lethality Focal dermal hypoplasia (Goltz syndrome) is an X-linked dominant disorder caused by mutations in PORCN, which encodes an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane O-acyltransferase required for the palmitoylation and secretion of WNT signalling proteins. WNT signalling is fundamental to the development of skin, bone, eyes, teeth and other structures, so its impairment produces the widespread mesoectodermal defects. The condition is generally lethal in hemizygous males; affected males who survive typically have somatic mosaicism. Random X-inactivation in females creates functional mosaicism, which accounts for the Blaschko-linear distribution of the skin lesions, where dermal connective tissue is hypoplastic and subcutaneous fat herniates through the attenuated dermis. Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the pattern and severity of extracutaneous involvement rather than the skin disease; many affected individuals have a normal lifespan. Ocular, skeletal and dental problems account for most long-term morbidity and often require ongoing multidisciplinary care.

The aberrant arterial supply produces a central fibrous scar containing thick-walled vessels that radiate outward, dividing the lesion into nodules separated by fibrous septa containing malformed ductules. Because the architecture is a reactive rather than clonal neoplastic process, the lesion carries negligible risk of haemorrhage or malignant transformation, in contrast to hepatocellular adenoma. The prognosis is excellent; most lesions remain stable or regress, complications are rare, and there is no meaningful risk of malignant transformation, so intervention is seldom needed.

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis — FSGS, focal glomerulosclerosis, focal sclerosing glomerulonephritis Minimal change disease Membranous nephropathy Diabetic nephropathy Hypertensive nephrosclerosis Collapsing glomerulopathy (a distinct aggressive variant) IgA nephropathy with secondary segmental sclerosis Renal biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy to confirm the segmental sclerosis pattern and variant Quantification of proteinuria by urine protein-to-creatinine or albumin-to-creatinine ratio Serum albumin and lipid profile to characterise the nephrotic state APOL1 genotyping and, in young or familial cases, a podocyte gene panel Serologies and virology to exclude secondary and virus-associated causes (including HIV where relevant) Renal imaging and assessment of nephron mass or obesity to identify an adaptive cause FSGS is a pattern of podocyte injury rather than a single disease, defined by segmental scarring affecting only some (focal) glomeruli on light microscopy Presents most often with nephrotic-range proteinuria, oedema and hypoalbuminaemia, though non-nephrotic proteinuria and microscopic haematuria also occur A practical framework separates primary (podocytopathy, presumed circulating permeability factor), genetic (podocyte and slit-diaphragm gene mutations), secondary/adaptive (hyperfiltration, obesity, reduced nephron mass) and virus/drug-associated forms APOL1 high-risk genotypes markedly increase risk in people of West African ancestry and influence prognosis and treatment response Immunofluorescence is usually negative or shows non-specific segmental IgM and C3 trapping in sclerotic areas; electron microscopy shows diffuse foot-process effacement in primary disease and more segmental effacement in adaptive forms Columbia (tip, cellular, collapsing, perihilar, not-otherwise-specified) histological variants carry differing prognostic and mechanistic implications Immunosuppression/corticosteroids are directed at primary podocytopathy, whereas adaptive/secondary forms are managed with renin-angiotensin blockade and treatment of the underlying driver rather than immunosuppression Rapidly rising creatinine with heavy proteinuria suggesting a collapsing or aggressive course Severe hypoalbuminaemia with anasarca, pleural effusions or thromboembolic complications Acute kidney injury complicating the nephrotic state Signs of an underlying secondary trigger such as advanced obesity, reflux nephropathy or viral infection Labelling all FSGS as primary and giving prolonged immunosuppression when an adaptive or genetic cause is present Missing focal lesions on an inadequate biopsy, since only some glomeruli are affected Overlooking APOL1 risk and genetic testing in young or ancestry-relevant patients Failing to distinguish collapsing glomerulopathy, which behaves far more aggressively Attributing secondary sclerosis (from another glomerular disease) to primary FSGS FSGS represents a common end pathway of injury to the visceral epithelial cell (podocyte). In primary disease a circulating permeability factor is thought to injure podocytes directly, producing widespread foot-process effacement and heavy proteinuria; genetic forms arise from mutations in podocyte cytoskeletal and slit-diaphragm proteins. Adaptive (secondary) FSGS follows glomerular hyperfiltration and increased capillary wall stress from reduced nephron mass, obesity or reflux, causing more limited effacement. Progressive podocyte depletion leaves denuded segments of glomerular basement membrane that adhere to Bowman's capsule and undergo segmental sclerosis, which spreads to involve more glomeruli and drives progressive renal impairment. Outcome depends on the underlying form and, critically, on the degree of proteinuria and its response to therapy. Patients achieving remission of nephrotic-range proteinuria have favourable long-term kidney survival, whereas persistent heavy proteinuria, the collapsing variant and APOL1 high-risk genotypes predict progression to end-stage kidney disease, and primary FSGS may recur after transplantation.

dysphagia Acute onset indicating a new stroke requiring urgent assessment Rapid progression suggesting an expanding lesion or encephalitis Complete inability to manage oral secretions Mistaking the syndrome for a brainstem bulbar palsy and missing the cortical localisation Misinterpreting preserved automatic smiling or crying as intact voluntary function Overlooking aspiration risk because comprehension is preserved Failing to consider the reversible epileptic form in children Foix-Chavany-Marie syndrome arises from bilateral lesions of the anterior operculum, the cortical region overlying the insula that controls voluntary movement of the lower face, tongue, jaw, pharynx, and larynx. Because voluntary corticobulbar control of these muscles is disrupted while the separate pathways mediating automatic and emotionally driven movements (involving limbic and extrapyramidal circuits) remain intact, patients show the striking automatic-voluntary dissociation. The commonest cause is sequential or simultaneous bilateral ischaemic stroke of the opercular cortex, though inflammatory, traumatic, neoplastic, and, in children, epileptic and reversible aetiologies are recognised. Preserved comprehension reflects sparing of language cortex outside the affected motor opercular regions. Outcome depends on the cause and extent of injury; the epileptic childhood form may be reversible, whereas established bilateral opercular strokes often leave persistent anarthria and dysphagia requiring long-term rehabilitation and nutritional support.

Folie à Deux — Shared psychotic disorder, Induced delusional disorder Independent coincident psychosis in both individuals Shared cultural or religious beliefs that are not delusional Coercive control or undue influence Substance-induced psychosis Cognitive impairment or intellectual disability contributing to suggestibility Malingering or shared deception Trauma-related shared beliefs Separate psychiatric assessment of each individual Trial of separation with observation of the belief in the secondary case Collateral history and assessment of relationship dynamics and isolation Assessment of the primary case's underlying disorder Cognitive assessment of the secondary individual Safeguarding assessment for children and dependent adults Organic screen where clinically indicated Transfer of a delusional belief from a dominant, usually psychotic, primary individual to one or more previously well and closely associated people. Classified in ICD as induced delusional disorder; DSM subsumes it within delusional and shared presentations. Typically arises in socially isolated, emotionally close dyads such as spouses, siblings, or a parent and child. The recipient or secondary case is often more suggestible, dependent, or of lower intellectual functioning. Separation of the pair frequently leads to resolution of the delusion in the induced secondary person. The primary individual usually has schizophrenia, delusional disorder, or a mood disorder with psychosis. Recognised variants include folie imposée, folie simultanée, folie communiquée, and folie induite. Shared content is commonly persecutory and is described in convergent detail by both parties. Children or dependent adults sharing the delusion, raising safeguarding concern Delusions driving neglect, refusal of care, or risk to health Persecutory content prompting aggression toward third parties Risk of self-harm or harm arising from acting on the shared belief Treating only the presenting individual and missing the primary inducer Overlooking the safeguarding needs of children in the household Mistaking a shared cultural or religious belief for a delusion Failing to use separation as both a diagnostic and a therapeutic step Folie à deux is understood less as a distinct biological disease than as a psychosocial phenomenon in which a genuine delusion held by a psychotic primary individual is adopted by an intimately associated, usually dependent and isolated, secondary individual. Prolonged close contact, isolation from external reality-testing, and a submissive or suggestible relationship dynamic permit the belief to be internalised. The secondary person typically lacks a primary psychotic illness, which is why physical separation from the inducer commonly extinguishes the shared belief, whereas the primary case requires treatment of the underlying disorder. The induced secondary individual often improves, sometimes markedly, after separation from the primary case, whereas the primary individual's outcome depends on their underlying psychotic illness.

structured reassessment During a normal cycle a dominant follicle matures and ruptures to release the oocyte. If ovulation does not occur, or if the follicle fails to involute afterwards, it continues to secrete fluid and enlarges into a simple cyst lined by granulosa and theca cells. Because the cyst arises from the normal cyclical activity of the ovary, it is termed functional and typically regresses as the hormonal milieu changes across subsequent cycles. The outlook is excellent; most follicular cysts resolve spontaneously without intervention and rarely cause lasting problems.

Inadequate surgical margins leading to local recurrence Follicular dendritic cell sarcoma is a mesenchymal-type neoplasm derived from the follicular dendritic cells that scaffold germinal centres and present antigen to B cells. Clonal proliferation of these stromal cells produces a spindle-cell tumour that retains its immunological markers and characteristically entraps small reactive lymphocytes. The tumour can arise de novo or in association with hyaline-vascular Castleman disease, in which dysplastic follicular dendritic meshworks may represent a precursor state. The distinctive inflammatory pseudotumour-like variant is driven by Epstein-Barr virus and shows a prominent inflammatory background. Although often indolent, the tumour can recur locally and metastasise, particularly when large, deeply sited or cytologically high-grade. Most tumours behave as low-to-intermediate-grade sarcomas that are curable by complete excision, but local recurrence is common and a subset metastasise; large size, deep location, high mitotic rate, necrosis and cytological atypia are associated with more aggressive behaviour and worse outcome.

or lung nodules indicating haematogenous metastasis Rapid nodule growth, fixation, or hoarseness suggesting invasion beyond the capsule Widely invasive or extensively angioinvasive disease on Because tumour cells preferentially enter blood vessels rather than lymphatics, dissemination is predominantly haematogenous, producing distant metastases in lung and bone, sometimes as the presenting feature, while regional nodal involvement is relatively uncommon. Minimally invasive follicular carcinoma has an excellent prognosis approaching that of papillary carcinoma, whereas widely invasive and angioinvasive tumours, older age, and distant metastasis substantially worsen outcome.

pain Features overlapping dissecting cellulitis or hidradenitis suggesting follicular occlusion disease Systemic upset or signs of deep infection Failure to respond, prompting reassessment for resistant organisms or an alternative diagnosis Treating as simple bacterial folliculitis with short antibiotic courses, leading to relapse Failing to recognise tufting as the diagnostic clue Not addressing staphylococcal carriage, allowing recurrence Overlooking overlap with other follicular occlusion disorders Folliculitis decalvans is a primary neutrophilic cicatricial alopecia in which an exaggerated host immune response, frequently associated with Staphylococcus aureus colonisation and possibly a superantigen effect, produces suppurative folliculitis. Sustained neutrophilic inflammation destroys the follicular epithelium and surrounding tissue, and clustering of retained follicles within a shared dilated ostium produces the characteristic tufts. Progressive perifollicular fibrosis leads to permanent follicular loss. The condition is chronic and relapsing; treatment can suppress inflammation and limit spread but cannot restore hair in scarred areas, and prolonged or repeated courses of therapy are often required.

Biphasic reaction recurring hours after apparent recovery Repeated accidental exposures or reactions despite avoidance suggesting inadequate education or hidden allergens Diagnosing allergy from a positive test alone without a supporting history, leading to unnecessary and potentially harmful dietary elimination Relying on antihistamines or steroids for anaphylaxis instead of giving adrenaline promptly Failing to prescribe, or not teaching correct use of, a self-injectable adrenaline device Overlooking cofactors and hidden or cross-contaminating allergens in processed foods and restaurant meals IgE-mediated food allergy arises when sensitisation to dietary protein leads to allergen-specific IgE bound to mast cells and basophils. On re-exposure the allergen cross-links surface IgE, triggering degranulation with release of histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, and other mediators that cause vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, smooth-muscle contraction, and mucus secretion. Non-IgE and mixed mechanisms (e.g. eosinophil- and T-cell-driven) underlie disorders such as eosinophilic oesophagitis and food protein-induced enterocolitis, which produce more delayed, predominantly gastrointestinal disease. Loss of oral tolerance, epithelial barrier dysfunction, and cutaneous sensitisation (notably through eczematous skin) are contributing factors. Milk, egg, wheat, and soy allergy commonly resolve during childhood, whereas peanut, tree nut, fish, and shellfish allergy usually persist for life. With reliable avoidance and prompt access to adrenaline, most patients do well, but unrecognised or undertreated anaphylaxis can be fatal.

gastroenteritis or other viral illness IgE-mediated food allergy or anaphylaxis Surgical abdomen such as intussusception, malrotation with volvulus, or obstruction Inborn errors of metabolism presenting with vomiting and lethargy Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease Necrotising enterocolitis in the neonate Detailed dietary and symptom-timing history, which forms the basis of the diagnosis episodes, which may show neutrophilia or metabolic derangement and are supportive rather than diagnostic Skin-prick or specific IgE testing mainly to identify any coexisting IgE sensitisation in atypical cases Stool examination to exclude infection where relevant Investigations to exclude surgical or metabolic causes when the presentation is atypical A non-IgE-mediated food allergy of infancy and early childhood that causes delayed, predominantly gastrointestinal reactions The hallmark of an acute reaction is profuse, repetitive vomiting beginning typically one to four hours after rice and oats, although many foods can be responsible Because it is non-IgE-mediated, skin-prick tests and specific IgE are typically negative and allergy testing does not confirm the diagnosis Diagnosis is clinical, based on the characteristic history and resolution on removing the food, with a supervised oral food challenge as the reference standard when the diagnosis is unclear Management is strict avoidance of the trigger with dietary elimination, prompt rehydration of acute reactions, and planned supervised reintroduction, and most children outgrow the condition Shock-like presentation with hypotension, marked pallor, and lethargy Severe dehydration with metabolic disturbance Failure to thrive in the chronic form Features suggesting a surgical abdomen Diagnostic uncertainty requiring a challenge in a supervised setting Misdiagnosing severe acute episodes as sepsis and missing the food trigger Expecting positive allergy tests and dismissing the diagnosis when they are negative Failing to identify a grain or other solid-food trigger introduced at weaning Unsupervised food reintroduction that risks a severe reaction Over-restricting the diet and compromising nutrition The disorder is a non-IgE-mediated food allergy in which food proteins provoke an antigen-specific inflammatory response in the gut involving T cells and innate immune activation rather than IgE. The resulting mucosal inflammation increases intestinal permeability and drives fluid shifts, producing the profuse vomiting, diarrhoea, and, in severe cases, the hypovolaemic shock-like presentation. The precise mechanisms remain incompletely understood, but the reaction is reproducible on re-exposure and tends to resolve as tolerance develops with age. The outlook is generally excellent, with most children developing tolerance and outgrowing the condition within the first few years of life, though the timing varies by trigger; acute reactions can be severe but are manageable with prompt rehydration.

Foreign Body Aspiration — airway foreign body, aspirated foreign body, inhaled foreign body Croup or other infectious airway obstruction Asthma or viral wheeze Pneumonia Anaphylaxis with airway compromise Retropharyngeal or peritonsillar abscess Structural airway lesion Chest radiograph including inspiratory and expiratory (or lateral decubitus) views Assessment for asymmetric air entry or localised findings on examination Rigid bronchoscopy for diagnosis and removal Neck radiographs if a laryngotracheal object is suspected Further imaging when diagnosis remains uncertain despite strong suspicion Aspiration of a foreign body is most common in toddlers, who explore with their mouths and have immature airway protective reflexes; food items such as nuts and seeds are frequent culprits. The classic history is a sudden episode of choking, coughing, or gagging in a previously well young child, often while eating or playing with small objects. Clinical presentation varies with the site and degree of obstruction; a lodged object may produce unilateral wheeze, reduced air entry, or persistent cough. A witnessed choking event is a strong clue, but the initial episode can be unwitnessed or followed by a symptom-free interval that leads to delayed diagnosis. Chest radiographs may be normal because most aspirated objects are radiolucent; indirect signs include localised air trapping or hyperinflation, atelectasis, or a persistent infiltrate. Rigid bronchoscopy is the definitive procedure for both confirming and removing an airway foreign body. Complete upper airway obstruction is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate basic choking manoeuvres appropriate to the child's age. Delayed or missed diagnosis can lead to recurrent or persistent pneumonia, bronchiectasis, or chronic lung damage, so a high index of suspicion is important. Complete airway obstruction with inability to cough, speak, or breathe Cyanosis or rapidly progressive respiratory distress Stridor with severe distress suggesting a laryngotracheal foreign body Persistent or recurrent focal pneumonia Altered consciousness from hypoxia Excluding aspiration because the chest radiograph is normal Being falsely reassured by a symptom-free interval after the initial choking event Attributing persistent focal respiratory symptoms to recurrent infection or asthma rather than a retained foreign body Performing blind finger sweeps or inappropriate manoeuvres that may push an object further When a small object is inhaled it may lodge anywhere from the larynx to the distal bronchi, with the site determining the clinical picture. A large object at the larynx or trachea can cause complete or near-complete obstruction and rapid asphyxia. More commonly the object passes into a bronchus, producing partial obstruction: air may move past on inspiration but be trapped on expiration, causing distal hyperinflation, or the airway may become fully blocked, leading to distal atelectasis. Retained material provokes inflammation and, over time, granulation tissue, mucus retention, and secondary infection, which underlie the chronic complications seen with delayed removal. With timely recognition and bronchoscopic removal the outlook is generally excellent, whereas complete obstruction can be rapidly fatal and delayed diagnosis may result in chronic pulmonary complications such as bronchiectasis.

Formiminoglutamic aciduria (FTCD, folate metabolism) — formiminoglutamic aciduria, FIGLU-uria, glutamate formiminotransferase deficiency, formiminotransferase cyclodeaminase deficiency, FTCD deficiency Dietary or malabsorptive folate deficiency (also raises FIGLU excretion) Vitamin B12 deficiency affecting folate-dependent metabolism Other inborn errors of folate metabolism (e.g. MTHFR deficiency) Benign biochemical findings on metabolic screening Coincidental developmental disorder of separate cause Liver disease altering histidine and folate handling Urine organic/amino acid analysis for formiminoglutamate, ideally after a histidine load Serum and red-cell folate and vitamin B12 levels Full blood count and film for megaloblastic or other changes Molecular analysis of the FTCD gene Assessment of dietary folate intake to exclude nutritional cause Developmental assessment where indicated Caused by deficiency of the bifunctional enzyme glutamate formiminotransferase-cyclodeaminase (FTCD), which transfers a formimino group from formiminoglutamate to tetrahydrofolate in the histidine degradation and folate pathways The characteristic biochemical finding is increased urinary excretion of formiminoglutamate (FIGLU), classically enhanced after an oral histidine load Clinical significance is uncertain and probably mild in many cases; reported phenotypes range from apparently benign to variable developmental delay and haematological changes A severe and a mild form have been described, and the disorder is considered one of the more common but least clinically clear-cut inborn errors of folate metabolism Serum folate may be normal or high because the folate-dependent step is blocked downstream, distinguishing it from dietary folate deficiency There is no firmly established specific therapy; folate/folinic acid supplementation has been used empirically Inheritance is autosomal recessive British spelling and paediatric context apply where relevant Significant developmental delay prompting evaluation for other causes Haematological abnormality such as megaloblastic change requiring investigation Assuming pathogenicity and over-treating what may be a benign finding Confusing raised FIGLU excretion from nutritional folate deficiency with the inherited enzyme defect Over-attributing developmental problems to an uncertain biochemical finding Assuming low folate when serum folate is often normal or high Failing to consider vitamin B12 deficiency in the interpretation Histidine is degraded via urocanate and formiminoglutamate (FIGLU), and the final step requires glutamate formiminotransferase to transfer FIGLU's formimino group onto tetrahydrofolate, linking histidine catabolism to one-carbon folate metabolism. Deficiency of the FTCD enzyme blocks this transfer, so FIGLU accumulates and is excreted, particularly after a histidine load, while one-carbon units that would have entered the folate pool are not efficiently captured. Because the block is downstream of folate, circulating folate is often not low, and the overall clinical impact appears variable and frequently mild, which is why the disorder's pathogenicity remains debated. The prognosis is generally thought to be good, with many individuals mildly affected or asymptomatic, though the true clinical significance of the biochemical defect remains uncertain. Management is supportive and empirical.

produce optic atrophy on that side. As the tumour grows it eventually raises intracranial pressure, which is transmitted to the contralateral optic nerve head causing papilloedema; the already-atrophic nerve on the tumour side cannot swell. Involvement of the olfactory tract explains the frequent anosmia. The sequence reflects the interplay between local compressive atrophy and generalised pressure-driven disc swelling. Vision in the atrophic eye is often permanently reduced, but timely resection of the causal tumour can relieve pressure and preserve or improve vision in the fellow eye; overall outcome depends on tumour size and resectability.

Fournier gangrene — Fournier's gangrene, perineal necrotising fasciitis, necrotising fasciitis of the perineum and genitalia, idiopathic gangrene of the scrotum Severe cellulitis or a simple perineal or scrotal abscess Epididymo-orchitis or testicular torsion Strangulated inguinoscrotal hernia Perianal or ischiorectal abscess without necrotising spread Pyoderma gangrenosum or another necrotising dermatosis Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) of adjacent tissues Scrotal or perineal haematoma Blood cultures and tissue or wound cultures (aerobic and anaerobic) to guide antimicrobial therapy Full blood count, renal and liver function, glucose, lactate, and inflammatory markers, with severity scoring where used Coagulation studies and group-and-save in anticipation of surgery Bedside or cross-sectional imaging (ultrasound, plain radiograph, or CT) to detect soft-tissue gas and fascial fluid without delaying surgery Assessment for underlying diabetes or other immunocompromise Intraoperative tissue sampling and histology to confirm necrotising fasciitis and identify the source Fournier gangrene is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening necrotising fasciitis of the perineal, genital, and perianal region, most often affecting men but also occurring in women It is typically polymicrobial and synergistic, involving a mixture of aerobic and anaerobic organisms (such as coliforms, streptococci, staphylococci, and anaerobes like Bacteroides and Clostridium) arising from anorectal, genitourinary, or cutaneous sources Diabetes mellitus is the commonest predisposing condition, and other forms of immunosuppression, alcohol excess, obesity, and local trauma increase risk Early signs (severe pain out of proportion to visible findings, oedema, and erythema) can be deceptively subtle before crepitus, skin discolouration, bullae, foul-smelling discharge, and frank necrosis develop Systemic toxicity and sepsis frequently outpace the visible skin changes because the infection tracks rapidly along fascial planes beneath apparently viable skin It is a clinical diagnosis and a surgical emergency; imaging (showing soft-tissue gas or fascial fluid) must not delay treatment when suspicion is high Management combines aggressive fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and, above all, urgent and often repeated surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue Diversion (urinary or faecal), reconstructive surgery, and adjuncts such as hyperbaric oxygen may be considered, and severity scoring helps gauge prognosis Pain markedly out of proportion to visible skin findings Crepitus, skin discolouration or bullae, and foul-smelling discharge indicating advancing necrosis Systemic features of sepsis or septic shock such as hypotension, tachycardia, and confusion Rapid progression of erythema or induration over hours Any diagnostic delay, as mortality rises sharply without prompt debridement Underestimating early disease because the skin looks relatively benign while infection spreads along deeper fascial planes Delaying surgical debridement to await imaging or a microbiological result Relying on antibiotics alone without adequate and repeated surgical exploration Performing insufficiently extensive initial debridement and not planning early re-look surgery Failing to identify and control the source and to treat underlying diabetes or immunosuppression Fournier gangrene begins when organisms breach the perineal, genital, or perianal tissues, commonly from an anorectal abscess or fistula, a urogenital infection or instrumentation, or a skin breach. A synergistic mix of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria then proliferates, the aerobes promoting anaerobic growth by consuming oxygen and impairing host defences while the combined enzymatic activity (including collagenases, hyaluronidases, and other exotoxins) digests fascia and connective tissue. The infection spreads rapidly along the relatively avascular fascial planes, and an obliterative endarteritis of subcutaneous vessels produces ischaemic necrosis of the overlying skin, gas formation, and the release of toxins that drive a systemic inflammatory response and septic shock. Impaired host defences, as in diabetes and other immunosuppressed states, accelerate this process. Fournier gangrene carries a substantial mortality that rises steeply with delayed surgery, extensive disease, and severe sepsis; early aggressive debridement with intensive supportive care markedly improves survival, though survivors may face major tissue loss requiring reconstruction and long rehabilitation.

Fournier's gangrene — Fournier gangrene, necrotising fasciitis of the perineum, perineal necrotising soft-tissue infection, scrotal gangrene Perianal or ischiorectal abscess without necrosis Scrotal or epididymo-orchitis Simple cellulitis of the perineum Strangulated inguinoscrotal hernia Cutaneous or Bartholin abscess Testicular torsion presenting with acute scrotal pain Severe contact or irritant dermatitis of the groin Pyoderma gangrenosum of the perineum Extensive hidradenitis suppurativa flare Blood cultures and cultures of operative tissue and any discharge Full blood count, renal and liver function, glucose, lactate and coagulation to gauge sepsis severity CT or plain imaging to define the extent of gas and tissue involvement when it will not delay surgery Surgical exploration for definitive diagnosis and debridement Glycaemic assessment and screening for underlying immunosuppression A fulminant necrotising fasciitis of the perineal, genital, and perianal region that constitutes a surgical emergency Usually polymicrobial, mixing aerobic and anaerobic organisms from the gut and skin flora, producing synergistic tissue destruction Diabetes mellitus, obesity, alcohol excess, immunosuppression, and local trauma or anorectal or urogenital infection are major predisposing factors Severe pain, systemic toxicity, and rapidly spreading swelling with skin discolouration, crepitus, or foul-smelling discharge should raise immediate suspicion Diagnosis is clinical and surgical; imaging may show subcutaneous gas but must never delay operative exploration Treatment principles are immediate wide surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue, broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-positives, Gram-negatives, and anaerobes, and haemodynamic resuscitation Repeat debridement is commonly required, and diversion of urine or faeces may be needed to protect the wound Delay in surgery is the strongest driver of mortality, so early recognition and theatre are paramount Rapidly spreading perineal swelling with crepitus or skin necrosis demanding immediate surgical debridement Pain out of proportion to visible findings suggesting deep fascial necrosis Systemic signs of septic shock requiring urgent resuscitation and critical care Subcutaneous gas on examination or imaging indicating gas-forming necrotising infection Mistaking early disease for a simple abscess or cellulitis and delaying theatre Waiting for imaging before surgical exploration in a deteriorating patient Underestimating the extent of necrosis and performing inadequate initial debridement Neglecting planned re-exploration to remove ongoing necrotic tissue Fournier's gangrene is a necrotising infection of the fascial planes of the genitalia, perineum, and perianal area. Mixed aerobic and anaerobic organisms act synergistically, generating enzymes and toxins that thrombose subcutaneous vessels and cause progressive ischaemic necrosis of skin, subcutaneous tissue, and fascia. Bacterial gas production leads to crepitus, and infection tracks rapidly along fascial planes, often outpacing the overlying skin changes, culminating in systemic sepsis and multi-organ failure. Mortality is significant and rises steeply with delayed surgery, extensive disease, advanced age, and multi-organ dysfunction; timely aggressive debridement and organ support improve survival, though survivors often need multiple operations and reconstructive procedures.

PAX6, SLC38A8 and albinism genes Incomplete development of the foveal pit with persistence of inner retinal layers over the fovea, so the normal foveal reflex and avascular zone are absent Commonly presents with reduced acuity and congenital nystagmus, sometimes with mild photophobia OCT is the key investigation, grading the severity of hypoplasia by the extent of persisting inner retinal layers and outer segment lengthening Frequently associated with albinism, aniridia and PAX6-related disease, but can occur in isolation Isolated autosomal recessive foveal hypoplasia has been linked to SLC38A8 mutations, whereas PAX6 disruption underlies aniridia-associated forms Acuity correlates with the grade of hypoplasia and the integrity of the outer retinal layers Colour vision and full-field electroretinography are typically preserved, helping distinguish it from cone dystrophies Progressive visual decline suggesting a coexisting retinal dystrophy rather than stable hypoplasia Associated aniridia mandating monitoring for glaucoma and, in some, screening for WT1-related Wilms tumour risk Systemic or developmental features suggesting a wider PAX6 or contiguous gene syndrome Marked photophobia and absent cone responses pointing to achromatopsia Diagnosing idiopathic congenital nystagmus without OCT and thereby missing the hypoplasia Overlooking associated albinism or aniridia Assuming poor acuity is fixed and neglecting a treatable refractive error Confusing preserved ERG with normality and missing an early cone disorder Foveal hypoplasia reflects arrest of the normal centrifugal migration of inner retinal neurons and the centripetal packing of cone photoreceptors that create the foveal pit and specialised cone mosaic. Genes governing this process, particularly PAX6, and pigment-related pathways in albinism, are critical; when they are disrupted the inner retinal layers fail to withdraw from the fovea and the foveal avascular zone does not form. The immature fovea provides poor central resolution, which impairs the development of steady fixation and drives congenital nystagmus. Because photoreceptor function itself may be relatively intact, electroretinographic responses are often normal. Vision is stable but subnormal, generally correlating with the OCT grade; many individuals retain moderate acuity and benefit from refractive correction and low-vision support.

with a hemispheric contralateral gaze deviation Mistaking Foville for Millard-Gubler by overlooking the conjugate nature of the gaze defect Attributing the facial weakness to a peripheral Bell palsy in isolation Missing an evolving basilar occlusion behind seemingly focal pontine signs Foville syndrome follows a dorsal caudal pontine tegmental lesion supplied by paramedian branches of the basilar artery. The infarct involves the abducens nucleus and the neighbouring paramedian pontine reticular formation, disrupting conjugate horizontal gaze towards the side of the lesion, and the genu of the facial nerve looping around the abducens nucleus, producing ipsilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness. Extension ventrally to the corticospinal fibres in the basis pontis produces contralateral limb weakness. The involvement of the gaze centre rather than the isolated sixth nerve fascicle distinguishes it from Millard-Gubler syndrome, while both share the crossed facial and limb pattern. Limited dorsal pontine infarcts may recover useful gaze and limb function, but the horizontal gaze palsy can persist, and lesions signalling basilar disease carry the risk of progression and a poorer outcome.

options for resistant disease Secondary infection of excoriated, intensely pruritic lesions Significant psychosocial impact from chronic itch in exposed and intimate areas Diagnostic uncertainty requiring biopsy to exclude other follicular disorders Mistaking it for simple folliculitis or eccrine miliaria and treating inappropriately Underestimating the impact of chronic itch and cosmetic concern in intimate sites Expecting a rapid or complete cure from topical therapy Fox-Fordyce disease is thought to begin with keratotic plugging and obstruction of the apocrine sweat-gland duct at its follicular opening. Retained secretion causes the duct to dilate and eventually rupture, releasing its contents into the surrounding dermis and provoking an intensely itchy inflammatory reaction with characteristic perifollicular foamy (lipid-laden) cells. A hormonal influence is suggested by its predominance in women, its variation with the menstrual cycle, and its tendency to improve during pregnancy and after the menopause, though the precise trigger for the initial ductal plugging remains uncertain. Chronic and often persistent, though it tends to improve after the menopause and frequently during pregnancy; treatment controls symptoms with variable success rather than curing the condition.

FOXG1 syndrome affects both sexes and lacks the typical period of normal early development Rapidly decelerating head circumference indicating acquired microcephaly Emerging or poorly controlled seizures Feeding failure, aspiration or faltering growth Severe irritability or sleep disruption affecting the child and family Labelling the child as having cerebral palsy and not pursuing a genetic diagnosis Assuming Rett syndrome requires a female patient and a regression history, thereby missing the congenital FOXG1 variant Overlooking the dyskinetic movement disorder or misattributing it solely to seizures Failing to recognise that FOXG1 duplications cause a distinct, epilepsy-predominant phenotype different from deletions FOXG1 encodes a forkhead-box transcription factor that is a master regulator of early forebrain patterning, controlling telencephalic progenitor proliferation, cortical neuron layering and corpus callosum formation. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants or 14q12 deletions reduce functional protein, disrupting the developmental programme that builds the cerebral cortex and interhemispheric connections. The resulting structural and connectivity abnormalities produce the profound congenital encephalopathy, movement disorder and acquired microcephaly. Because the primary defect is in prenatal brain construction rather than in later synaptic maintenance, the phenotype is congenital rather than regressive. FOXG1 syndrome is a severe lifelong neurodevelopmental disorder with profound intellectual disability, absent speech and limited independent mobility. Life expectancy can be reduced by seizures and respiratory or feeding complications, and care is supportive and multidisciplinary.

Fragile X syndrome — FXS, Martin-Bell syndrome, FMR1-related intellectual disability, marker X syndrome Idiopathic autism spectrum disorder Other X-linked intellectual disability syndromes Sotos syndrome and other overgrowth syndromes Klinefelter syndrome Nonspecific developmental delay of undetermined cause Targeted FMR1 molecular testing with CGG repeat sizing and methylation status clinically indicated Genetic counselling and cascade testing of at-risk relatives Most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and the leading single-gene contributor to autism spectrum disorder Affected boys are typically more severely impaired than girls because of X-linkage, with variable expression in female carriers Characteristic physical features include a long narrow face, prominent forehead and jaw, large protruding ears, and macro-orchidism that becomes evident around puberty Behavioural profile often includes hyperactivity, attention problems, anxiety, hand-flapping, poor eye contact, and tactile defensiveness Connective tissue laxity may produce joint hypermobility, flat feet, and mitral valve prolapse Caused by expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the FMR1 gene leading to loss of the FMRP protein needed for normal synaptic function Repeat number distinguishes normal, intermediate, premutation, and full-mutation alleles, with premutations carrying separate adult risks Diagnosis is confirmed by targeted DNA testing (repeat sizing and methylation analysis) rather than routine karyotype Female premutation carriers face increased risk of primary ovarian insufficiency and reduced fertility Older premutation carriers, particularly men, may develop fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome Recurrence risk in the family is high, making prompt genetic counselling important Emerging seizures or marked behavioural deterioration warrant neurological review Assuming a normal karyotype excludes the diagnosis when specific FMR1 repeat testing is required Overlooking milder or subtle presentations in female carriers Failing to recognise premutation-related adult conditions in relatives Neglecting genetic counselling and cascade screening after diagnosis Fragile X syndrome results from an unstable expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the 5' untranslated region of the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. When the repeat expands beyond the full-mutation threshold, the gene becomes hypermethylated and transcriptionally silenced, so little or no fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP) is produced. FMRP normally regulates translation of numerous messenger RNAs at synapses, and its absence disrupts synaptic maturation and pruning, producing intellectual disability and the behavioural phenotype. Premutation-length repeats are not silenced but generate excess, potentially toxic FMR1 messenger RNA, which underlies the distinct premutation-associated disorders. The repeat tends to expand across generations, particularly through the maternal line, explaining anticipation. Life expectancy is generally normal, but intellectual disability persists lifelong; early behavioural, educational, and speech interventions improve functional outcomes, and severity is typically greater in males than in females.

Frailty syndrome — frailty, frail elderly, physical frailty phenotype, frailty phenotype Depression presenting with fatigue, withdrawal, and weight loss Occult malignancy causing cachexia and functional decline Hypothyroidism or other endocrine disorders Undernutrition from social, dental, or gastrointestinal causes Chronic heart failure or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease limiting activity Anaemia contributing to fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance Comprehensive geriatric assessment across functional, cognitive, psychological, and social domains Objective performance measures such as gait speed, timed up-and-go, and grip strength Nutritional assessment and screening for unintentional weight loss Basic laboratory panel to exclude reversible contributors (anaemia, thyroid dysfunction, renal impairment, vitamin D and B12 status) Medication review to identify drugs contributing to weakness, sedation, or hypotension Frailty is a state of reduced physiological reserve across multiple systems, leaving the patient vulnerable to disproportionate decline after seemingly minor stressors such as an infection, a new drug, or a hospital admission The Fried phenotype describes frailty through five markers: unintentional weight loss, self-reported exhaustion, weakness (low grip strength), slow walking speed, and low physical activity, with three or more indicating frailty The cumulative deficit model quantifies frailty as a frailty index, the proportion of accumulated health deficits, and complements the phenotype approach Frailty is distinct from, though overlapping with, both multimorbidity and disability; a person can be frail without a single dominant diagnosis Simple bedside screens such as gait speed, the timed up-and-go test, and grip strength help identify frailty and predict adverse outcomes Comprehensive geriatric assessment addressing medical, functional, cognitive, psychological, and social domains is the cornerstone of managing frail patients Structured, progressive resistance and balance exercise combined with adequate protein and energy intake can improve or partly reverse frailty Recognising frailty should prompt medication review, attention to nutrition, and realistic, goal-concordant care planning rather than reflex intervention Rapid functional decline or acute loss of independence suggesting an intercurrent illness such as infection or delirium Recurrent falls, especially those causing injury Accelerating unintentional weight loss raising concern for malignancy or severe undernutrition New confusion or fluctuating cognition indicating delirium in a frail patient Equating frailty with chronological age alone and overlooking fit older adults or frail younger ones Missing reversible contributors such as depression, undernutrition, anaemia, or polypharmacy Subjecting frail patients to aggressive investigation or treatment that offers little benefit and risks harm Failing to plan proactively for goals of care before a crisis forces decisions Frailty arises from age-related dysregulation across multiple interacting systems, including chronic low-grade inflammation (raised inflammatory cytokines), sarcopenia and neuromuscular decline, endocrine changes (reduced anabolic hormones and altered cortisol rhythm), and impaired energy metabolism. These changes lower the reserve available to respond to stress, so that a modest insult produces a large, often cascading loss of function. Once physiological reserve falls below a threshold, small perturbations can precipitate falls, delirium, immobility, and dependency, and recovery to baseline becomes slower and less complete. Frailty is a strong independent predictor of falls, hospitalisation, delirium, disability, institutionalisation, and death. Trajectories vary: mild frailty may be stabilised or improved with exercise and nutritional and medical optimisation, while advanced frailty carries high short-term mortality and often signals the need for a palliative, goal-focused approach.

Outlook varies with the severity of cardiac and skeletal involvement; some infants have serious complications early in life, while others survive into childhood and beyond with careful multidisciplinary management, and vision depends on prompt glaucoma treatment.

Freeman-Sheldon syndrome is most often due to dominant variants in MYH3, which encodes embryonic myosin heavy chain expressed in developing skeletal muscle. Disturbed myosin function alters foetal muscle contractility and tone during a key phase of morphogenesis. The resulting reduced and unbalanced foetal movement leads to periarticular fibrosis and fixed contractures, while abnormal tension in the muscles of facial expression and mastication produces the distinctive microstomia, whistling-face appearance and chin dimple. As with other distal arthrogryposes the deformities are largely static rather than progressive. Intellect is usually normal and lifespan is not typically shortened, but affected individuals face repeated surgery for facial and limb deformity, feeding and speech challenges, and meaningful anaesthetic risk; functional outcomes vary with severity of contractures.

Fregoli Syndrome — Fregoli delusion, Fregoli phenomenon Capgras delusion Intermetamorphosis Syndrome of subjective doubles Paranoid schizophrenia with persecutory delusions Delirium Dementia (Alzheimer's or Lewy body type) Temporal lobe epilepsy Structural neuroimaging (MRI brain) to identify right frontotemporal pathology Cognitive and neuropsychological testing including face recognition EEG where seizure activity or delirium is suspected Organic screen bloods (full blood count, metabolic panel, thyroid function, calcium, vitamin B12) Toxicology and substance screen Collateral history to establish onset, content, and progression CSF analysis and autoimmune encephalitis antibodies if atypical or rapidly progressive A delusional misidentification syndrome in which the patient believes that a familiar persecutor is disguising themselves as various strangers encountered in daily life. Characterised by hyperidentification: unfamiliar people are misidentified as one known individual despite no physical resemblance, sometimes described as psychological identity without physical identity. Named after Leopoldo Fregoli, an Italian quick-change stage performer famed for rapid transformations of appearance. Contrasts with the Capgras delusion, in which a familiar person is believed to have been replaced by an impostor. Associated with paranoid schizophrenia but also with right frontal and temporal lobe pathology, dementia, and traumatic brain injury. Usually embedded within persecutory delusions, with the disguised figure experienced as a stalker or persecutor. Neuropsychological accounts implicate dysfunction of face-recognition and familiarity-monitoring networks involving the fusiform and right frontal regions. Late onset, cognitive impairment, or absence of other psychotic features should prompt thorough organic screening. Late-onset misidentification with cognitive decline suggesting neurodegeneration Focal neurological signs pointing to a structural lesion Persecutory content directed at a specific person, raising risk of violence Rapid progression with fluctuating consciousness suggesting encephalitis or delirium Assuming a primary psychiatric cause without excluding organic or neurodegenerative disease Overlooking the risk of violence toward the misidentified persecutor Confusing Fregoli (hyperidentification of strangers as one known person) with Capgras Failing to obtain collateral history that reveals the delusional structure Fregoli syndrome is conceptualised as a disorder of person identification arising from disrupted integration between face-recognition pathways and the affective and mnemonic systems that assign familiarity. Whereas Capgras is linked to loss of the normal autonomic familiarity response, Fregoli is thought to reflect excessive or misattributed familiarity, so that strangers evoke recognition of a known person. Right frontal and temporal dysfunction impairs the monitoring and belief-evaluation processes that would normally reject such misidentifications, allowing the delusion to persist. It occurs both in primary psychotic illness, notably schizophrenia with dopaminergic dysregulation, and in structural or neurodegenerative brain disease. Outcome largely follows the underlying disorder; misidentification in schizophrenia often improves with antipsychotic treatment, whereas that due to neurodegenerative disease tends to persist or progress.

Freiberg disease — Freiberg infraction, osteochondrosis of the metatarsal head Metatarsal stress fracture Morton neuroma Metatarsophalangeal joint synovitis or osteoarthritis Sesamoiditis Inflammatory arthritis Weight-bearing foot radiographs MRI in early disease before radiographic change Clinical assessment of the affected metatarsophalangeal joint Exclusion of stress fracture and neuroma Assessment of foot biomechanics and footwear An osteochondrosis (avascular necrosis) of a metatarsal head, most often the second metatarsal It is the only osteochondrosis more common in females and typically presents in adolescence Presents with forefoot pain, swelling and stiffness of the metatarsophalangeal joint, worse on weight bearing Radiographs show flattening, sclerosis and later collapse and widening of the metatarsal head Repetitive stress and the vulnerability of the metatarsal head blood supply are implicated Early disease is managed conservatively with offloading; advanced disease with joint damage may need surgery Advanced joint collapse and secondary arthritis Features suggesting infection or inflammatory arthritis Severe pain limiting weight bearing Diagnostic uncertainty with stress fracture Confusing it with a metatarsal stress fracture or Morton neuroma Delaying diagnosis until joint collapse Overlooking footwear and biomechanical contributors Not imaging early forefoot pain with MRI when radiographs are normal Freiberg disease is an osteochondrosis in which the subchondral bone of a metatarsal head (usually the second, the longest and most loaded) undergoes avascular necrosis. Repetitive microtrauma and mechanical overload, together with the tenuous blood supply of the metatarsal head, are thought to cause subchondral ischaemia, leading to bone collapse, articular surface flattening and fragmentation. Progressive joint incongruity results in pain, stiffness and secondary osteoarthritis of the metatarsophalangeal joint. Early disease often responds to conservative offloading with a good outcome, whereas advanced collapse can cause persistent pain and metatarsophalangeal arthritis requiring surgery.

second, resulting from interruption of the subchondral blood supply. Repetitive loading and microtrauma across a relatively long or rigid second metatarsal are thought to produce subchondral stress and vascular compromise, leading to necrosis of the articular bone. The subchondral bone subsequently collapses, the metatarsal head flattens and the articular cartilage fissures and fragments. Progressive incongruity of the metatarsophalangeal joint follows, with loose body formation, osteophytosis and secondary degenerative arthritis. Early disease often responds well to offloading and activity modification, but established head collapse and articular fragmentation may progress to metatarsophalangeal osteoarthritis with persistent pain requiring surgical intervention.

fistula or sialocele after parotidectomy Failing to formally map the area with the starch-iodine test before botulinum toxin injection, leading to undertreatment Overlooking congenital Frey syndrome severed parasympathetic secretomotor fibres that originally supplied the parotid gland. After injury (typically parotidectomy) these postganglionic parasympathetic fibres, carried with the auriculotemporal nerve, misdirect and reinnervate the denervated sweat glands and cutaneous blood vessels of the overlying facial skin. Because both pathways are cholinergic, a gustatory stimulus that would normally provoke salivation instead drives sweating and vasodilatation of the skin, producing localised gustatory sweating and flushing in the auriculotemporal distribution. The condition is benign and often improves or stabilises over time; symptoms are reliably controlled with botulinum toxin, although repeat injections are needed as the effect wanes over several months to a year.

Frataxin deficiency impairs mitochondrial energy metabolism and leads to intramitochondrial iron accumulation and oxidative stress. The consequent degeneration affects dorsal root ganglia, dorsal columns, spinocerebellar and corticospinal tracts and the cerebellar dentate nucleus, producing the mixed sensory ataxic and pyramidal syndrome, while mitochondrial dysfunction in cardiac and pancreatic tissue accounts for the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes. Friedreich ataxia is progressive, with most affected individuals losing independent ambulation within one to two decades of onset; cardiomyopathy and its complications are the principal determinants of reduced life expectancy, though there is considerable variability related to repeat length.

Frontometaphyseal dysplasia is caused by gain-of-function variants in FLNA, an X-linked gene encoding filamin A, a cytoskeletal protein that cross-links actin filaments and coordinates cell shape, migration and mechanotransduction. Altered filamin A function disturbs the modelling and remodelling of the skeleton, producing the prominent frontal bony ridge, metaphyseal undermodelling, contractures and progressive spinal deformity. Involvement of the ossicles and middle ear underlies the hearing loss. Because FLNA is X-linked, hemizygous males typically manifest a more severe phenotype, while heterozygous females are protected to a variable degree by X-inactivation, producing the characteristic sex difference across the otopalatodigital spectrum. The prognosis depends on severity and sex, with males often more significantly affected; intelligence is usually normal and life expectancy generally preserved, though scoliosis, contractures, hearing loss and airway or urogenital anomalies contribute to morbidity.
