clefting Overlooking the genetic heterogeneity and the need for tailored counselling Assuming hypertelorism is purely cosmetic without assessing vision and orbital anatomy Frontonasal dysplasia arises from disturbed development of the frontonasal prominence, the midline facial process that gives rise to the forehead, nasal bridge, nasal tip, philtrum, and primary palate. Failure of the medial nasal processes to migrate and merge normally in the midline results in the widened, clefted central face and hypertelorism. Because midline facial and forebrain development are intimately linked, disruption in this region can be accompanied by midline central nervous system anomalies. Several genetic forms are recognised, notably those due to variants in the ALX homeobox genes governing craniofacial midline patterning, though many cases are sporadic and aetiologically heterogeneous. Outcome depends on the extent of facial clefting and, crucially, on any associated brain malformation; isolated milder forms have a good prognosis with staged reconstruction and normal cognition, whereas central nervous system involvement worsens developmental outlook.

Frontotemporal Dementia — FTD, behavioral variant FTD, primary progressive aphasia Alzheimer's disease (FTD has relatively preserved memory and parietal function early; a small percentage of FTD syndromes show Alzheimer's pathology at autopsy) (Harrison 22e p.3486-3487) Progressive supranuclear palsy-Richardson syndrome (PSP-RS) - within the FTD spectrum; falls, vertical supranuclear ophthalmoparesis, axial rigidity (Harrison 22e p.3487) Corticobasal syndrome (CBS) - asymmetric rigidity, dystonia, myoclonus, apraxia, alien limb phenomena (Harrison 22e p.3488) Idiopathic Parkinson's disease - PSP is often confused with PD, but PD does not produce downgaze paresis (Harrison 22e p.3488) Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis / motor neuron disease (FTD-MND overlap) (Harrison 22e p.3486) Structural neuroimaging (MRI) to demonstrate focal frontal/insular/temporal atrophy patterns characteristic of each syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3486) Genetic testing for C9orf72, GRN, and MAPT mutations in suspected familial cases (Harrison 22e p.3486) Molecular (tau) PET imaging shows promise but to date binds robustly only to Alzheimer's-related misfolded tau; amyloid PET may help when negative (Harrison 22e p.3487) Psychiatric disease - depression, idiopathic mania, or acting out: the abulia/blandness of frontal degeneration may be misinterpreted as depression and the disinhibition as mania or acting out; FTD can begin with schizophrenia-like features leading to misdiagnosis of a psychiatric condition (Harrison 22e p.3485, p.209) Other focal frontal lobe causes: head trauma, ruptured aneurysms, hydrocephalus, tumors (metastases, glioblastoma, meningioma) (Harrison 22e p.208) FTD is a group of clinical syndromes united by underlying frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) pathology; like other major neurodegenerative diseases it is considered a disorder of abnormal protein aggregation, with either tau or TDP-43 (transactive response DNA-binding protein of 43 kDa) implicated in most cases (Harrison 22e p.3485). Younger onset than typical Alzheimer's: FTD most often begins in the fifth to seventh decades of life and is nearly as prevalent as Alzheimer's disease in this age group (Harrison 22e p.3485). Three core clinical syndromes are described: the behavioral variant (bvFTD, the most common) and two forms of primary progressive aphasia (PPA) - the semantic and nonfluent/agrammatic variants (Harrison 22e p.3485-3486). bvFTD manifests as social and emotional dysfunction - apathy, disinhibition, compulsivity, loss of empathy, and overeating - often but not always accompanied by deficits in executive control (Harrison 22e p.3486). In semantic variant PPA patients slowly lose the ability to decode word, object, person-specific, and emotion meaning; in nonfluent/agrammatic variant PPA patients develop profound inability to produce words, often with prominent motor speech impairment (Harrison 22e p.3486). Parietal functions such as visuospatial processing and arithmetic calculation are typically unaffected even late in the FTD syndromes, helping distinguish it from Alzheimer's disease (Harrison 22e p.3486). Any of the three syndromes, most often bvFTD, may be accompanied by motor neuron disease (MND), in which case the term FTD-MND is applied; corticobasal syndrome (CBS) and progressive supranuclear palsy-Richardson syndrome (PSP-RS) are also considered part of the FTD clinical spectrum (Harrison 22e p.3486). In contrast to Alzheimer's disease, the cholinergic system is relatively spared in FTD, which accounts for the poor efficacy of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors in this group (Harrison 22e p.3486). Treatment is symptomatic only; there are currently no therapies known to slow progression or improve symptoms, and no disease-modifying treatments have shown efficacy to date (Harrison 22e p.3487). New-onset disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsivity, or altered dietary preference in a middle-aged adult (Harrison 22e p.3486) Progressive language breakdown - loss of word/object meaning or inability to produce words (Harrison 22e p.3486) Emergence of motor neuron disease features in a patient with behavioral or language decline (FTD-MND) (Harrison 22e p.3486) Behavioral variant FTD is frequently mistaken for a primary psychiatric disease - the apathy/blandness can be misread as depression and the disinhibition as mania or acting out; FTD may even begin with schizophrenia-like features and be misdiagnosed as a psychiatric condition. Later age of onset, significant cognitive deficits, or abnormal neuroimaging point to a degenerative process (Harrison 22e p.3485, p.209). Clinical features do not allow reliable prediction of the underlying FTLD molecular subtype (tau vs TDP-43 vs FET) for all syndromes (Harrison 22e p.3487). Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are largely ineffective in FTD because the cholinergic system is relatively spared, unlike Alzheimer's disease (Harrison 22e p.3486). Antipsychotics must be used with caution because FTD is often accompanied by parkinsonism, which they can exacerbate (Harrison 22e p.3487). FTD is linked to frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), characterized by focal atrophy of frontal, insular, and/or temporal cortex; atrophy often begins focally in one hemisphere before spreading to anatomically interconnected cortical and subcortical regions. bvFTD shows medial/orbital frontal cortex and anterior insula degeneration, semantic variant PPA the anterior temporal region, and nonfluent/agrammatic PPA the opercular frontal and precentral gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. Microscopically there is gliosis, microvacuolation, and neuronal loss; the disease is subtyped by the protein composition of neuronal and glial inclusions, which contain either tau or TDP-43 in roughly 90% of patients, with the remaining ~10% showing inclusions containing the FET family of proteins (FUS, Ewing sarcoma protein, TAF-15). Loss of cortical serotonergic innervation is common while the cholinergic system is relatively spared. Misfolded proteins are increasingly recognized to have prion-like/corruptive templating properties that may drive network-rooted patterns of disease spread. Autosomal dominant inheritance is seen in only 10-20% of cases, with mutations in C9orf72 (the most common genetic cause, a noncoding GGGGCC hexanucleotide expansion, presenting as bvFTD with or without MND and overlapping with ALS), GRN/progranulin, and MAPT/tau (Harrison 22e p.3485-3487). Caregivers carry a heavy burden, especially as the illness disrupts core emotional and personality functions. There are currently no therapies known to slow progression or improve symptoms; treatment is symptomatic. For the related PSP-RS within the FTD spectrum, death occurs within 5-10 years of onset (Harrison 22e p.3487). No formal severity grading is given; FTD is categorized by core clinical syndrome - behavioral variant (bvFTD), semantic variant PPA, and nonfluent/agrammatic variant PPA - and by underlying FTLD molecular class (FTLD-tau, FTLD-TDP, FTLD-FET) (Harrison 22e p.3486-3487).

delineate viable from nonviable tissue Inflammatory markers and wound cultures if secondary infection is suspected Frostbite most often affects peripheral and exposed parts such as the fingers, toes, ears, nose, and cheeks, where tissue actually freezes, in contrast to non-freezing cold injuries Severity is graded from superficial injury with numbness and blistering to deep injury involving extremity Deep or extensive frostbite with haemorrhagic blistering and threatened tissue loss Signs of secondary infection, wet gangrene, or systemic sepsis Risk of refreezing, which mandates delaying rewarming until definitively out of the cold Rewarming when refreezing is still possible, which greatly worsens injury Using dry or excessive heat, or rubbing the tissue, causing further damage Performing early debridement or amputation before nonviable tissue has demarcated Treating the local injury while overlooking life-threatening systemic hypothermia Underestimating eventual tissue loss based on the early appearance Neglecting analgesia, tetanus prophylaxis, and prevention of recurrence Frostbite results from tissue freezing when heat loss exceeds the body's ability to maintain local warmth. Extracellular and then intracellular ice crystals form, causing direct mechanical cell damage and osmotic shifts. Vasoconstriction and increased blood viscosity reduce perfusion, and on rewarming there is a reperfusion phase with endothelial damage, inflammatory mediator release, microvascular thrombosis, and progressive dermal ischaemia. This secondary vascular injury and thrombosis, rather than the initial freezing alone, is responsible for much of the eventual tissue loss, which is why final demarcation takes time to declare. Superficial frostbite and frostnip usually recover fully, though long-term cold sensitivity, numbness, and neuropathic symptoms are common. Deep frostbite frequently leads to tissue loss and amputation, but because early appearance overstates the damage, delaying surgery until demarcation improves the extent of salvage. Overall outcome depends on depth, duration of exposure, refreezing, and timeliness of correct rewarming.

Frosted branch angiitis — acute frosted retinal periphlebitis Cytomegalovirus retinitis with vascular sheathing Acute retinal necrosis Behcet retinal vasculitis Systemic lupus or other autoimmune retinal vasculitis Intraocular lymphoma Fluorescein angiography to map leakage, occlusion and ischaemia Infective screen including herpesviruses, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasma and syphilis Autoimmune and systemic vasculitis workup Optical coherence tomography for macular oedema Consideration of intraocular sampling if masquerade is suspected A striking retinal vasculitis in which widespread perivascular sheathing gives the vessels a translucent 'frosted branch' appearance resembling frost on a tree It is a clinical sign rather than a single disease and may be idiopathic or secondary to infection, autoimmune disease or lymphoma The idiopathic form often affects otherwise healthy children and young adults with acute bilateral visual loss Secondary causes include herpesviruses, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasma, syphilis and systemic vasculitis, which must be actively excluded Vascular sheathing predominantly involves the veins but arteries may also be affected The idiopathic form generally responds well to corticosteroids, whereas secondary forms need the underlying cause treated Evidence of an infective cause requiring specific therapy before steroids Severe retinal ischaemia or neovascularisation Features suggesting lymphoma masquerade Profound or progressive bilateral visual loss Treating with corticosteroids before excluding infection Assuming it is always idiopathic and missing lymphoma or systemic vasculitis Overlooking the fellow eye in apparently unilateral cases Failing to monitor for ischaemic complications Frosted branch angiitis reflects intense perivascular inflammation of the retinal vessels, thought in the idiopathic form to be an immune-mediated hypersensitivity response, sometimes following a viral illness. Dense inflammatory cuffing of the vessel walls produces the characteristic sheathing, with associated vascular leakage, macular oedema and, in severe cases, ischaemia. When secondary, the vasculitis is driven by direct infection or by a systemic inflammatory or neoplastic process affecting the retinal vasculature. Visual prognosis is often good in the idiopathic corticosteroid-responsive form, but outcomes in secondary disease depend on the underlying cause and on complications such as ischaemia and macular oedema.

Frozen shoulder — adhesive capsulitis, shoulder contracture, periarthritis of the shoulder Rotator cuff tear or tendinopathy Glenohumeral or acromioclavicular osteoarthritis Calcific tendinitis Posterior shoulder dislocation (locked) Subacromial impingement or bursitis Referred pain from the cervical spine Septic arthritis (if acute, hot, and systemically unwell) Clinical assessment demonstrating global restriction with markedly reduced passive external rotation Plain shoulder radiographs to exclude arthritis, dislocation, or bony lesions Blood glucose or HbA1c given the association with diabetes MRI or ultrasound if a rotator cuff tear or other structural lesion is suspected Thyroid function tests where clinically indicated Characterised by painful, progressive global restriction of shoulder movement with the hallmark loss of passive external rotation, distinguishing it from rotator cuff disease The condition typically evolves through overlapping phases: a painful freezing phase, a stiff frozen phase, and a gradual thawing phase of recovery It most often affects middle-aged patients and is strongly associated with diabetes mellitus, which also predicts a more resistant course May be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to trauma, immobilisation, or shoulder surgery Diagnosis is clinical; radiographs are typically normal and mainly serve to exclude other causes such as arthritis or a locked posterior dislocation Management is largely supportive: analgesia, maintaining movement, physiotherapy, and reassurance about eventual improvement Intra-articular corticosteroid injection can help pain and stiffness, particularly in the early painful phase Refractory cases may be treated with capsular hydrodilatation, manipulation under anaesthesia, or arthroscopic capsular release Constitutional symptoms or a mass suggesting tumour rather than capsulitis Hot, swollen, systemically unwell shoulder raising concern for septic arthritis History of significant trauma with fixed internal rotation suggesting a missed posterior dislocation Rapidly progressive neurological symptoms pointing to an alternative diagnosis Confusing it with a rotator cuff tear by not testing passive external rotation Forcing painful manipulation during the acute inflammatory phase, worsening symptoms Missing an underlying posterior dislocation or arthritis by omitting radiographs Overlooking undiagnosed diabetes in a patient presenting with adhesive capsulitis Frozen shoulder involves inflammation and progressive fibrosis of the glenohumeral joint capsule, particularly the rotator interval and coracohumeral ligament. Fibroblastic proliferation and contracture thicken and tighten the capsule, reducing the intra-articular volume and mechanically limiting movement, with external rotation lost first and most severely. The initial inflammatory, hypervascular stage is painful; as the capsule matures into dense fibrous tissue the pain lessens but stiffness dominates; finally the capsule gradually remodels and mobility returns. The strong association with diabetes and certain endocrine and metabolic states points to a systemic predisposition to abnormal fibrosis. Frozen shoulder is usually self-limiting, with most patients recovering good function over one to three years, though some, particularly those with diabetes, are left with residual stiffness; interventions can shorten symptoms and relieve pain but recovery is generally slow.

Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency — FBPase deficiency, FBP1 deficiency, fructose-1,6-diphosphatase deficiency, hereditary fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency Glycogen storage disease type I (glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency) Hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency) Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency Mitochondrial respiratory chain disorders with lactic acidosis Fatty-acid oxidation defects presenting with hypoglycaemia Sepsis with lactic acidosis Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase deficiency Blood glucose, blood gas and lactate during symptomatic episodes Blood and urine ketones to document accompanying ketosis Urine organic acids, which may show elevated lactate and glycerol-3-phosphate Plasma amino acids and ammonia to help distinguish other causes of metabolic acidosis FBP1 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Enzyme activity assay in liver or leucocytes where genetics are inconclusive Autosomal recessive deficiency of the gluconeogenic enzyme fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBP1 gene) impairs glucose production from precursors such as lactate, glycerol and amino acids Presents with episodes of hypoglycaemia accompanied by lactic acidosis and ketosis, typically triggered by fasting or intercurrent illness First crisis often occurs in the neonatal period or first months of life, sometimes with hyperventilation, hepatomegaly and seizures Between episodes children are usually well and grow normally, distinguishing it from the persistent features of glycogen storage disease Unlike hereditary fructose intolerance, ingestion of fructose or sucrose can precipitate crises but there is no aversion or vomiting reflex, and the defect is in gluconeogenesis rather than fructose metabolism per se Acute treatment uses intravenous glucose to correct hypoglycaemia and clear the lactic acidosis; long-term care emphasises avoidance of prolonged fasting and limiting fructose and sucrose intake Diagnosis is confirmed by FBP1 molecular testing or enzyme assay, supported by the characteristic biochemical pattern during crises Profound hypoglycaemia with severe lactic acidosis in a fasting or unwell infant Hyperventilation, obtundation or seizures during a metabolic crisis Hepatomegaly with rapid clinical deterioration Recurrent hypoglycaemic-acidotic episodes precipitated by fasting or fructose intake Confusing the disorder with hereditary fructose intolerance and mismanaging dietary advice Missing the diagnosis because the child appears entirely well between episodes Failing to measure lactate and ketones during the acute hypoglycaemic episode Allowing prolonged perioperative or illness-related fasting without protective glucose Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase catalyses a key regulatory step of gluconeogenesis, converting fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to fructose-6-phosphate. Its deficiency blocks the synthesis of glucose from lactate, glycerol, amino acids and dietary fructose, so the individual depends on dietary glucose and hepatic glycogen. Once glycogen stores are exhausted during fasting or illness, hypoglycaemia develops together with accumulation of gluconeogenic precursors, producing lactic acidosis; increased fatty-acid oxidation adds ketosis. Fructose and sorbitol loads worsen the metabolic block by trapping phosphate and further inhibiting glucose output. Long-term prognosis is generally good with avoidance of fasting and dietary control, and normal growth and development are usual; however, delayed recognition of severe hypoglycaemic-acidotic crises can be fatal or cause neurological injury.

lowering intraocular pressure early, to endothelial keratoplasty for visually significant oedema Painful bullous keratopathy with recurrent epithelial breakdown Rapid corneal decompensation, particularly after intraocular surgery Marked reduction in endothelial cell density threatening imminent decompensation before planned surgery Corneal infection or ulceration complicating ruptured bullae Failing to assess endothelial reserve before cataract surgery and precipitating decompensation Attributing morning visual blur to other causes and missing early endothelial disease Mistaking guttata alone for visually significant dystrophy when vision loss has another cause Overlooking coexisting glaucoma that worsens corneal oedema Delaying keratoplasty until painful bullae and scarring compromise the surgical outcome Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy is a degenerative disorder of the corneal endothelium, the monolayer of non-dividing cells that pumps fluid out of the stroma to keep the cornea clear. Accelerated endothelial cell loss and the deposition of abnormal extracellular matrix produce guttata (focal thickenings of Descemet membrane). As endothelial cell density falls below the level needed to maintain deturgescence, fluid accumulates in the stroma and epithelium, causing corneal oedema, loss of transparency and eventually painful bullae. Oxidative stress, genetic predisposition and endothelial dysfunction all contribute, and any additional insult such as intraocular surgery can tip a borderline cornea into frank decompensation. Progression is typically slow over years; many patients remain functionally comfortable with conservative measures, and endothelial keratoplasty offers good visual rehabilitation for advanced disease, though transplantation carries risks of rejection and may need to be repeated.

fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis — Fuchs uveitis syndrome, Fuchs heterochromic cyclitis herpetic (herpes simplex or varicella-zoster) anterior uveitis cytomegalovirus anterior uveitis Posner-Schlossman syndrome (glaucomatocyclitic crisis) sarcoid anterior uveitis idiopathic chronic anterior uveitis pigment dispersion syndrome congenital or acquired Horner syndrome causing heterochromia slit-lamp examination for diffuse stellate keratic precipitates and absent synechiae iris transillumination and comparison of iris colour between eyes gonioscopy for fine angle vessels and pigmentation intraocular pressure measurement and glaucoma work-up aqueous polymerase chain reaction for rubella and cytomegalovirus in selected cases optical coherence tomography of the optic nerve and perimetry when glaucoma is suspected cataract assessment and biometry before surgery A chronic, low-grade, usually unilateral anterior uveitis that is characteristically white and painless, often discovered incidentally or when cataract reduces vision. Diffuse, small, stellate keratic precipitates scattered across the whole corneal endothelium, rather than clustered inferiorly, are a hallmark. Iris heterochromia results from stromal atrophy; the affected iris is typically hypochromic and lighter, though in brown irides the loss of the anterior stroma can make it appear darker. Posterior synechiae are characteristically absent even after years of inflammation, an important distinguishing feature. Fine iris and angle vessels are fragile, and a filiform anterior chamber haemorrhage on paracentesis or cataract surgery is the Amsler-Verrey sign. Posterior subcapsular cataract and secondary open-angle glaucoma are the two principal complications. An association with rubella virus, and in some regions cytomegalovirus, is increasingly recognised as an aetiological factor. The inflammation responds poorly to and generally does not warrant long-term topical corticosteroids, which risk steroid-induced pressure rise without altering the course. rising intraocular pressure signalling secondary glaucoma spontaneous hyphaema or unexpected bleeding during surgery atypical bilateral or granulomatous features suggesting an alternative diagnosis rapid visual decline from dense posterior subcapsular cataract Treating the low-grade inflammation with prolonged topical steroids, which add steroid-induced pressure rise without benefit. Overlooking the diagnosis because the eye is white and painless and the patient asymptomatic. Missing early secondary glaucoma, the principal cause of visual loss. Being surprised by intraoperative filiform hyphaema during cataract surgery. Misclassifying the unilateral heterochromia and cataract as another uveitic entity and instituting inappropriate immunosuppression. Fuchs uveitis is a chronic low-grade iridocyclitis characterised by diffuse iris stromal atrophy and depigmentation, mild persistent anterior chamber inflammation and abnormal fragile vasculature in the iris and anterior chamber angle. Progressive atrophy of the iris stroma and pigment epithelium produces the heterochromia and, on transillumination, diffuse thinning. Chronic low-grade inflammation, with lymphocytic infiltration and scattered stellate keratic precipitates, occurs without the fibrinous exudation that produces synechiae in other uveitides, which explains the notable absence of posterior synechiae. Rubella virus, and cytomegalovirus in some populations, has been implicated as a chronic antigenic stimulus. New fragile vessels in the angle and iris account for the tendency to hyphaema with minor trauma or surgery, and chronic trabecular involvement leads to secondary open-angle glaucoma. The prognosis for vision is generally good, with cataract surgery usually well tolerated and effective; the main threat to sight is secondary glaucoma, which can be difficult to control and requires long-term monitoring.

Skeletal survey for dysostosis multiplex Skin examination and biopsy for angiokeratomas Caused by deficiency of alpha-L-fucosidase, leading to accumulation of fucose-containing oligosaccharides, glycolipids, and glycoproteins Presents along a spectrum, from a severe rapidly progressive infantile form to a milder, slowly progressive form with longer survival Progressive neurological decline, coarse facies, dysostosis multiplex, and growth failure are core features Angiokeratoma corporis diffusum, similar to that of Fabry disease, is characteristic, particularly in longer-surviving patients Recurrent infections and dysautonomia with abnormal sweating can occur Urinary oligosaccharide screening reveals fucosylated compounds rather than glycosaminoglycans Diagnosis is confirmed by deficient alpha-L-fucosidase activity and FUCA1 gene testing Progressive developmental regression and spasticity Seizures signalling advancing neurodegeneration Recurrent respiratory infections and failure to thrive Cardiac involvement in more advanced disease Confusing the angiokeratomas with Fabry disease without appropriate enzyme testing Screening only for glycosaminoglycans and missing the oligosaccharide pattern Assuming a uniform severe course despite the wide clinical spectrum Overlooking dysautonomia as part of the disorder Fucosidosis is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in FUCA1, encoding the lysosomal enzyme alpha-L-fucosidase. This enzyme cleaves terminal fucose residues from fucose-containing glycoproteins, glycolipids, and oligosaccharides during their lysosomal degradation. Its deficiency causes accumulation of these fucosylated substrates in tissues throughout the body, including the nervous system, skin, and viscera, with excretion of fucosylated oligosaccharides in the urine. Storage in the central nervous system drives the progressive neurodegeneration, while systemic accumulation produces the coarse features, skeletal changes, and cutaneous angiokeratomas. Residual enzyme activity broadly correlates with the range from severe infantile to attenuated later-onset disease. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Prognosis depends on the phenotype; severe infantile disease progresses rapidly with early mortality, while attenuated forms allow survival into later childhood or adulthood with progressive disability. Management is largely supportive, though haematopoietic stem cell transplantation has been attempted in selected cases.

Fumarase deficiency — fumarase deficiency, fumarate hydratase deficiency, FH deficiency, fumaric aciduria, HLRCC-associated gene (FH) Other TCA-cycle and mitochondrial encephalopathies Other organic acidurias presenting with neonatal encephalopathy Congenital cortical malformation syndromes (e.g. other causes of polymicrogyria) Perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy Congenital infection causing brain malformation Peroxisomal disorders with neonatal hypotonia and seizures Urine organic acids demonstrating marked fumarate elevation Brain MRI for polymicrogyria, open operculum, and other malformations Fumarate hydratase enzyme activity in leucocytes or fibroblasts Molecular analysis of the FH gene Family history and carrier assessment for HLRCC-related tumours Renal imaging surveillance for carrier relatives Caused by deficiency of fumarate hydratase (fumarase, FH), a tricarboxylic acid cycle enzyme that hydrates fumarate to malate, with both mitochondrial and cytosolic isoforms from one gene The recessive biallelic disorder causes a severe neonatal/infantile encephalopathy with hypotonia, seizures, failure to thrive, and characteristic brain malformations such as polymicrogyria and an open operculum The biochemical signature is markedly elevated urinary fumaric acid (fumarate) on organic acid analysis, often with other TCA-cycle intermediates The same gene underlies hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC): heterozygous carriers, including parents, are predisposed to cutaneous and uterine leiomyomas and an aggressive form of renal cell carcinoma Fumarate acts as an oncometabolite, inhibiting 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases and stabilising hypoxia-inducible factor, linking the enzyme defect to tumourigenesis Recognition of a biallelic case has implications for the wider family because of the dominant cancer-predisposition risk in carriers Management of the severe infantile disorder is supportive; carrier relatives warrant tumour surveillance British spelling applies (tumour, leiomyomatosis, paediatric) Severe neonatal encephalopathy with seizures and brain malformation Family history of uterine or cutaneous leiomyomas and renal cell carcinoma indicating HLRCC risk New renal mass in a carrier relative requiring urgent evaluation Progressive failure to thrive and neurological decline in the affected infant Failing to counsel the family about the dominant HLRCC cancer risk after diagnosing a biallelic case Overlooking fumarate on organic acid analysis as a diagnostic clue Attributing the malformation to hypoxic injury rather than a metabolic cause Not arranging renal and dermatological surveillance for carrier relatives Fumarate hydratase catalyses the reversible hydration of fumarate to malate within the citric acid cycle, a step central to mitochondrial energy production. Biallelic loss of function impairs oxidative metabolism and causes fumarate and related intermediates to accumulate and spill into the urine as fumaric aciduria. The resulting bioenergetic failure in the developing brain produces the severe encephalopathy and cortical malformations. Accumulated fumarate also behaves as an oncometabolite: it competitively inhibits 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases and stabilises hypoxia-inducible factor, promoting tumour formation, which is why monoallelic mutation carriers are at risk of leiomyomas and renal cell carcinoma (the HLRCC syndrome). The biallelic infantile disorder carries a poor prognosis with severe neurological impairment and frequent early death. The clinically important legacy for the family is the autosomal dominant HLRCC cancer risk in heterozygous carriers, for whom surveillance can be life-saving.

as a driver Recurrent sensation of abdominal bloating or visible distension not sufficiently explained by another disorder Bloating is the subjective feeling of pressure, whereas distension is a measurable increase in abdominal girth, and they may occur together or separately Symptoms typically worsen through the day and after meals and improve overnight It frequently overlaps with other abdominal bloating and distension arise from a combination of factors including altered handling and perception of intestinal gas, visceral hypersensitivity, abnormal abdominal wall muscle behaviour (an abdomino-phrenic dyssynergia in which the diaphragm descends and the abdominal wall relaxes), and changes in gut microbiota and fermentation. These mechanisms produce the sensation of bloating and, when the abdominal wall protrudes, visible distension, without a defining structural abnormality. Overlap with other functional gut disorders reflects shared gut-brain mechanisms. The condition is benign and often chronic, with symptoms fluctuating; many patients improve when coexisting constipation and dietary triggers are addressed.

Functional constipation — chronic idiopathic constipation Constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome Dyssynergic defecation Secondary constipation (hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, drugs) Colorectal obstruction or stricture Neurological disease affecting the bowel History and examination including rectal examination for evacuation disorder Bloods to exclude metabolic causes such as thyroid dysfunction and hypercalcaemia Colonic transit studies where slow transit is suspected Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion for suspected defecatory disorder Colonoscopy where alarm features or obstruction are suspected Persistent difficult, infrequent or incomplete defecation not attributable to a structural, metabolic or drug cause and not meeting criteria for irritable bowel syndrome Features include straining, hard or lumpy stools, a sense of incomplete evacuation and use of manual manoeuvres It differs from constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome mainly by the absence of predominant abdominal pain Broad mechanisms include normal-transit, slow-transit and evacuation (defecatory) disorders, which guide treatment Secondary causes such as hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, medications and colorectal obstruction must be excluded Management uses fibre and fluid, osmotic and stimulant laxatives, and newer secretagogues or prokinetics for refractory cases Rectal bleeding, anaemia or weight loss New or rapidly progressive constipation in an older patient Features suggesting obstruction Neurological signs suggesting a secondary cause Failing to identify a coexisting defecatory disorder that will not respond to laxatives alone Overlooking secondary metabolic or drug causes Missing alarm features suggesting malignancy Relying on stimulant laxatives without addressing the underlying mechanism Functional constipation encompasses several mechanisms of impaired stool passage in the absence of an identifiable organic cause. Normal-transit constipation reflects perceived difficulty despite normal colonic transit, slow-transit constipation results from reduced colonic propulsive activity, and defecatory disorders arise from impaired coordination of the pelvic floor and anal sphincter during evacuation. Disordered neuromuscular control of the colon and anorectum, sometimes with altered fluid handling, underlies the symptoms, and overlap between mechanisms is common. The condition is chronic but benign, and most patients respond to a stepwise regimen, with defecatory disorders often improving specifically with pelvic floor retraining.

Functional diarrhoea — functional diarrhea Diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome Coeliac disease Microscopic colitis Bile acid diarrhoea Inflammatory bowel disease Chronic infection or malabsorption Coeliac serology and, where indicated, faecal calprotectin Assessment for bile acid diarrhoea in suitable patients Colonoscopy with biopsies to exclude microscopic colitis where appropriate Blood tests for inflammatory, thyroid and malabsorptive causes Stool studies where infection or malabsorption is suspected Recurrent passage of loose or watery stools without predominant abdominal pain or bloating The absence of significant pain distinguishes it from diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome It is a diagnosis made after excluding organic causes of chronic diarrhoea Important mimics include coeliac disease, microscopic colitis, bile acid diarrhoea and inflammatory bowel disease Nocturnal diarrhoea, weight loss or bleeding are not typical and should prompt investigation Management includes dietary review and antidiarrhoeal or bile-acid-binding therapy where appropriate Nocturnal or progressive diarrhoea Weight loss, bleeding or anaemia Onset in an older patient Features suggesting malabsorption or inflammation Missing microscopic colitis, which needs biopsies to diagnose Overlooking bile acid diarrhoea as a treatable cause Attributing organic diarrhoea to a functional cause Failing to exclude coeliac disease Functional diarrhoea is a disorder of gut-brain interaction characterised by accelerated colonic transit and altered secretion and motility without a structural or biochemical cause. Visceral hypersensitivity and disturbed gut-brain signalling contribute, and there is overlap with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome, from which it is separated chiefly by the lack of prominent pain. Because several organic conditions can produce an identical clinical picture, the diagnosis depends on their reasonable exclusion. The condition is benign and often fluctuates over time; symptoms are usually controllable with dietary measures and targeted antidiarrhoeal treatment.

such as weight loss, bleeding, dysphagia, persistent vomiting, or older age at onset warrant endoscopy to exclude malignancy and ulcer Acid suppression is a reasonable first-line therapy, with neuromodulators and prokinetics used for persistent symptoms There is substantial overlap with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and irritable bowel syndrome, and psychological factors commonly modulate symptoms Unintentional weight loss Gastrointestinal bleeding or iron-deficiency anaemia Progressive dysphagia or odynophagia Persistent vomiting or a palpable epigastric mass New dyspepsia in an older patient Failing to recognise and evaluate alarm features before labelling symptoms as functional Repeated normal investigations without addressing the gut-brain nature of the disorder Overlooking Helicobacter pylori as a treatable contributor Escalating acid suppression indefinitely without considering neuromodulators or psychological factors Functional dyspepsia is a disorder of gut-brain interaction without structural disease. Contributing mechanisms include delayed gastric emptying, impaired fundic accommodation to a meal, visceral hypersensitivity to gastric distension and acid, low-grade duodenal inflammation and increased mucosal permeability, and altered central processing of visceral signals. Prior infection, Helicobacter pylori, psychological stress, and genetic predisposition can all contribute, producing symptoms disproportionate to any measurable physiological abnormality. Functional dyspepsia is a benign but often chronic and relapsing condition that can substantially impair quality of life; symptoms fluctuate over time and respond variably to treatment, but there is no increase in serious organic disease.

Functional gait disorder — functional gait disorder, psychogenic gait disorder, functional neurological disorder of gait, astasia-abasia Cerebellar or sensory ataxia Parkinsonism and other hypokinetic neurological disorder in which walking is impaired in a way that is internally inconsistent and incongruent with recognised neurological disease Diagnosis rests on positive clinical signs, not merely on the exclusion of other conditions Characteristic patterns include excessive slowness, buckling of the knees, a cautious walking-on-ice gait, uneconomic postures and sudden lurches with paradoxical preservation of balance Astasia-abasia, with dramatic difficulty standing and walking but better performance when examined on the couch, is a classic presentation Distractibility, with improvement when attention is diverted during tandem or backward walking or dual tasking, is a key positive sign Variability over time and inconsistency between formal testing and spontaneous movement support the diagnosis It often coexists with other functional symptoms, pain, fatigue and psychological stressors, although a trigger is not always identified Objective signs of structural disease such as sustained clonus, fixed weakness with wasting or a sensory level Acute onset with features suggesting stroke or spinal cord compression Progressive deterioration or the emergence of new hard neurological signs Sphincter disturbance or saddle anaesthesia suggesting a cauda equina or cord lesion Making the diagnosis by exclusion alone rather than on positive signs Communicating the diagnosis poorly, which undermines engagement and recovery Assuming a psychological stressor must be present before the diagnosis can be made Over-investigating and reinforcing illness behaviour, or conversely missing comorbid structural disease Functional gait disorder is understood as a disorder of nervous-system functioning rather than of structural damage, in which abnormal self-directed attention, altered expectations and impaired sensorimotor prediction disrupt the normally automatic control of walking. The movements are genuine and are not under voluntary control, but they are potentially reversible, and their inconsistency and distractibility reflect the way that redirecting attention can transiently restore more normal motor patterns. Predisposing, precipitating and perpetuating factors, including psychological ones, may contribute but are not universally present. Outcome is variable; some patients recover substantially, particularly with early diagnosis, a clear positive explanation of the diagnosis and engagement with treatment, while others have a more chronic, disabling course. A confident, transparently explained diagnosis is itself therapeutic, and specialist multidisciplinary rehabilitation with physiotherapy, together with cognitive behavioural therapy where appropriate, offers the best chance of improvement.

Functional heartburn — functional heartburn disorder Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease Reflux hypersensitivity Eosinophilic oesophagitis Oesophageal motility disorder Cardiac chest pain Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, typically normal, with biopsies to exclude eosinophilic oesophagitis Ambulatory pH-impedance monitoring showing normal acid exposure and negative symptom association Oesophageal manometry to exclude a major motility disorder Assessment of psychological comorbidity Review of prior response to acid suppression Retrosternal burning discomfort despite normal oesophageal acid exposure and no correlation between symptoms and reflux events There is no evidence of erosive disease, eosinophilic oesophagitis or a major motility disorder It characteristically responds poorly to acid-suppressing therapy, which helps distinguish it from reflux disease It reflects oesophageal hypersensitivity and altered central pain processing rather than acid injury Diagnosis requires endoscopy and ambulatory reflux monitoring showing physiological acid exposure with a negative symptom association Management uses neuromodulators and psychological therapies rather than escalating acid suppression Dysphagia, weight loss or bleeding suggesting organic disease Chest pain with cardiac features Failure to fit the criteria on objective testing Progressive symptoms Escalating acid suppression that will not help Not performing objective reflux testing before diagnosis Missing eosinophilic oesophagitis Overlooking cardiac causes of chest discomfort Functional heartburn is a disorder of gut-brain interaction in which the sensation of heartburn occurs without pathological acid reflux. Oesophageal hypersensitivity, peripheral and central sensitisation of visceral pain pathways, and psychological factors generate the perception of burning despite normal acid exposure and no temporal link to reflux episodes. Because acid is not driving the symptom, acid suppression is largely ineffective, and treatment targets pain perception instead. The condition is benign but can be persistent and frustrating; symptoms often improve with neuromodulator therapy and psychological approaches once acid-related disease is excluded.

variability) Targeted investigation only to exclude specific mimics suggested by the history Neurophysiology (for example tremor recording with entrainment testing) in selected cases Assessment of comorbid mood, anxiety and other functional symptoms Avoidance of excessive or repeated testing that can reinforce illness beliefs Abnormal movements such as tremor, dystonia, myoclonus, gait disturbance or parkinsonism that are internally inconsistent and incongruent with recognised neurological disease It is a rule-in diagnosis based on positive clinical signs, not merely the absence of another disorder Functional tremor characteristically changes frequency and entrains to the rhythm of a voluntary movement in the other limb Distractibility, variability, suggestibility and a sudden onset are supportive features It sits within the broader category of functional neurological disorder and may coexist with genuine organic disease Clear explanation of the diagnosis and multidisciplinary rehabilitation, including physiotherapy and psychological therapy, are central to management Features that are in fact typical of an organic disorder on review Progressive fixed deficits or abnormal imaging Coexisting organic disease requiring its own treatment Significant psychiatric comorbidity or risk requiring urgent attention Treating it purely as a diagnosis of exclusion rather than demonstrating positive signs Over-investigating and inadvertently reinforcing the disorder Missing coexisting organic disease Communicating the diagnosis poorly, which undermines engagement and recovery Functional movement disorder is understood as a disorder of abnormal motor control and self-agency rather than structural damage, in which movements are generated through mechanisms overlapping with voluntary movement yet experienced as involuntary. Current models emphasise aberrant attention directed to the affected body part, abnormal predictive processing and altered sense of agency, often in the context of predisposing, precipitating and perpetuating psychological and physical factors. The internal inconsistency of the movements reflects their dependence on attention and expectation. Outcomes are variable but early diagnosis, a clear positive explanation and engagement with multidisciplinary therapy are associated with better recovery; long-standing untreated symptoms can be more refractory.

movement disorders Epilepsy where seizures are the presentation Metabolic or toxic encephalopathy Factitious disorder or malingering, in which symptoms are consciously produced Vestibular or orthopaedic causes of gait disturbance Careful neurological examination for positive functional signs such as Hoover sign and give-way weakness Targeted MRI to exclude structural mimics when clinically indicated Video-EEG when functional (dissociative) seizures are suspected Nerve conduction studies and EMG where a neuromuscular cause is considered Assessment for psychological comorbidity and precipitating factors Avoidance of over-investigation that can reinforce illness beliefs Genuine, involuntary neurological symptoms (weakness, movement disorder, sensory or gait disturbance) arising from altered nervous-system functioning rather than structural disease Diagnosis rests on positive rule-in signs of internal inconsistency, not merely on the absence of structural findings Hoover sign, where weakness of voluntary hip extension normalises with contralateral hip flexion against resistance, is a key positive sign of functional leg weakness Symptoms show variability, distractibility, and incongruence with recognised anatomical patterns Often coexists with fatigue, pain, functional (dissociative) seizures, and psychological comorbidity, though a psychological trigger is not required for diagnosis A clear, non-judgemental explanation of the positive diagnosis improves engagement and outcome Management is multidisciplinary rehabilitation, including physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and psychological therapy such as CBT Prognosis improves with early diagnosis, patient understanding, and access to specialist rehabilitation Objective structural signs (fixed reflex asymmetry, an extensor plantar response, true visual field loss) inconsistent with a functional cause Acute presentations that could represent stroke or another emergency Progressive deterioration or new hard neurological signs Persistent diagnostic uncertainty warranting specialist neurological review Diagnosing by exclusion alone rather than identifying positive rule-in signs Equating the disorder with feigning or malingering, which damages the therapeutic relationship Over-investigating and inadvertently reinforcing illness beliefs Missing a coexisting structural disorder, or conversely mislabelling structural disease as functional Functional neurological disorder is understood as a disorder of nervous-system functioning rather than structural damage, in which the brain networks for generating and monitoring movement, sensation, and agency operate abnormally. The symptoms are genuine and involuntary; abnormal attentional focus on the affected body part, altered predictive processing (aberrant internal 'priors'), and an impaired sense of agency are thought to generate and sustain them. Predisposing, precipitating (including physical injury, illness, or psychological stress), and perpetuating factors interact within a biopsychosocial framework. Crucially the symptoms are internally inconsistent, being modifiable by distraction or specific manoeuvres, which reflects intact underlying pathways that are not being accessed normally. Outcome is variable; early, confident diagnosis with a clear explanation and access to multidisciplinary rehabilitation improves recovery, whereas long symptom duration, poor understanding of the diagnosis, and untreated comorbidity predict persistence and disability.

Functional ovarian cyst — Follicular cyst, Corpus luteum cyst, Physiological ovarian cyst Endometrioma Benign ovarian neoplasm such as serous cystadenoma or mature cystic teratoma Ovarian malignancy Tubo-ovarian abscess Ectopic pregnancy Hydrosalpinx or paratubal cyst Polycystic ovarian morphology Transvaginal ultrasound to assess morphology, size and Doppler flow Serum beta-hCG to exclude pregnancy or ectopic and to explain theca lutein cysts Full blood count where haemorrhage is suspected CA-125 interpreted with caution in premenopausal women, ideally within a risk-of-malignancy index or IOTA rules Interval ultrasound to confirm spontaneous resolution Germ-cell and sex-cord tumour markers in young women with complex lesions Functional cysts arise from normal ovulatory physiology; the two principal types are follicular cysts, from failure of a dominant follicle to rupture, and corpus luteum cysts, from failure of the corpus luteum to regress. They are the commonest ovarian cysts in reproductive-age women and the great majority resolve spontaneously over two to three menstrual cycles. Most are asymptomatic but may cause unilateral pelvic pain, menstrual disturbance, or acute pain if rupture or intracystic haemorrhage occurs. A simple, unilocular, anechoic, thin-walled cyst below the usual size threshold in a premenopausal woman is almost always benign and managed expectantly. A corpus luteum cyst may bleed, causing acute pain and occasionally haemoperitoneum, a risk that is heightened in women taking anticoagulants. Ovarian torsion is the key emergency and its likelihood rises with larger cysts. Theca lutein cysts are functional cysts driven by high beta-hCG, seen in molar pregnancy, multiple gestation and ovulation induction. Combined hormonal contraception does not hasten resolution of an existing cyst but reduces the formation of new functional cysts. Acute severe unilateral pain with features of torsion, constituting a surgical emergency Haemodynamic instability or signs of haemoperitoneum from a ruptured haemorrhagic cyst Complex, solid or multilocular morphology or persistence, raising suspicion of neoplasm Any ovarian cyst in a postmenopausal woman, in whom functional cysts should not occur Rapid enlargement or associated ascites Labelling a persistent or complex cyst as functional without confirmatory follow-up imaging. Assuming a cyst in a postmenopausal woman is functional rather than investigating it. Over-reliance on CA-125 in premenopausal women, in whom it is raised by endometriosis, fibroids and pelvic infection. Missing an ectopic pregnancy by not checking beta-hCG in a woman with pain and an adnexal mass. Delaying surgery in suspected torsion while awaiting further imaging. During each cycle a dominant follicle matures under follicle-stimulating and luteinising hormone drive; when such a follicle fails to rupture and continues to accumulate fluid, a follicular cyst forms. After ovulation the corpus luteum normally involutes, and if it instead persists or fills with fluid or blood, a corpus luteum cyst results. These lesions are physiological and hormonally responsive rather than neoplastic, and most involute once the hormonal stimulus wanes. Theca lutein cysts represent bilateral functional enlargement from excessive human chorionic gonadotrophin stimulation. The prognosis is excellent, with the large majority of functional cysts resolving spontaneously and requiring no intervention. Complications such as torsion or haemorrhage are uncommon and readily treatable.

Cardiac arrhythmia causing collapse Panic attacks Movement disorders such as paroxysmal dyskinesia Parasomnias and other sleep disorders Video-EEG telemetry to capture a typical event and confirm the EEG and MRI to assess for coexisting epilepsy or structural disease Serum prolactin interpreted with caution in selected cases Psychological and psychiatric assessment for comorbidity and precipitants seizures include prolonged duration, a fluctuating or waxing-and-waning course, asynchronous or side-to-side movements, pelvic thrusting, and eyes tightly closed with resistance to opening Ictal crying, memory of the event, and rapid recovery without post-ictal confusion may occur, and awareness can be partly retained during bilateral motor activity Video-EEG capturing a typical event with no epileptiform correlate is the diagnostic gold standard Serum prolactin does not rise significantly after dissociative seizures, unlike after many generalised tonic-clonic seizures, though its diagnostic use is limited Epilepsy and dissociative seizures can coexist, complicating the diagnosis Escalating antiepileptic drugs and emergency intubation should be avoided for prolonged 'status' that is actually dissociative Management centres on a clear explanation of the diagnosis and psychological therapy such as CBT within a multidisciplinary framework Features clearly suggesting epilepsy (lateral tongue biting, stereotyped events, post-ictal confusion) or coexisting epilepsy Cardiac symptoms suggesting an arrhythmic cause of collapse Injury, incontinence, or events arising from sleep requiring careful differentiation Persistent diagnostic uncertainty warranting video-EEG at a specialist centre Treating prolonged dissociative seizures as refractory status epilepticus, risking iatrogenic harm from sedation and intubation Diagnosing on semiology alone without video-EEG when the distinction is unclear Overlooking coexisting epilepsy Relying on prolactin as a definitive test Functional (dissociative) seizures are episodes of altered awareness, movement, or behaviour that superficially resemble epileptic seizures but occur without the abnormal, synchronised cortical electrical activity that defines epilepsy. They are understood as involuntary dissociative events in which there is a transient disruption of the normal integration of awareness, emotion, and motor control, often arising in response to internal or external triggers. As with other functional neurological symptoms, a biopsychosocial model applies, with predisposing vulnerabilities, precipitating stressors or trauma, and perpetuating factors; the events are genuine and not consciously feigned. Because cortical electrical activity remains normal, the interictal and ictal EEG shows no epileptiform discharge. Outcome varies; a clear, supportive explanation of the diagnosis alone stops events in some patients, and psychological therapy helps many, but long duration, comorbid psychiatric illness, and coexisting epilepsy are associated with a more persistent course and ongoing disability.

Functional tremor — psychogenic tremor, functional movement disorder - tremor, dissociative tremor Essential tremor Parkinsonian rest tremor Enhanced physiological tremor from anxiety, thyrotoxicosis, or drugs Dystonic tremor Cerebellar (intention) tremor Drug-induced or toxic tremor Bedside examination for distractibility, entrainment, and variability Accelerometry and surface EMG with entrainment and loading tasks in specialist centres Thyroid function tests and a drug review to exclude enhanced physiological tremor MRI or dopamine transporter (DaT) imaging only where an organic parkinsonian or structural cause is genuinely suspected Assessment for psychological comorbidity and precipitants Avoidance of unnecessary repeated investigation The commonest functional movement disorder, often of sudden onset that is maximal at onset with a fluctuating, variable course Distractibility is characteristic: the tremor lessens or disappears when attention is diverted to a complex motor or cognitive task Entrainment is a key positive sign, in which copying a rhythmic tapping movement with the other limb shifts the tremor to match that frequency, or the copied movement cannot be performed Variability in frequency, amplitude, direction, and distribution over time argues against an organic tremor A 'whack-a-mole' phenomenon may occur, in which restraining the tremor in one limb makes it appear elsewhere A coactivation sign, with increased tone from co-contraction of antagonist muscles at tremor onset, is often present Diagnosis is clinical and positive; accelerometry with entrainment testing can support it Management is multidisciplinary: specialist physiotherapy for functional movement disorders, psychological therapy such as CBT, and a clear explanation Coexisting fixed neurological signs suggesting a structural or degenerative disorder Features of parkinsonism such as bradykinesia and rigidity warranting further assessment Rapid progression or systemic illness Persistent diagnostic uncertainty requiring movement-disorder specialist review Diagnosing by exclusion rather than demonstrating positive signs such as entrainment and distractibility Mislabelling an organic tremor as functional, or the reverse Failing to exclude thyrotoxicosis, drugs, or other reversible causes of enhanced tremor Delaying referral to specialist multidisciplinary rehabilitation Functional tremor is a functional movement disorder in which involuntary oscillatory movements arise from abnormal, self-generated motor activity that the patient does not consciously control. Neurophysiological studies suggest the movements share mechanisms with normal voluntary movement, for example they can entrain to an externally paced rhythm and may be preceded by a readiness (Bereitschafts) potential, yet the patient experiences them as involuntary, reflecting a disturbed sense of agency and abnormal attentional focus. As with other functional neurological symptoms, predisposing, precipitating, and perpetuating biopsychosocial factors contribute, and the tremor's variability and distractibility reflect intact underlying motor pathways that are being accessed abnormally. Functional tremor can improve substantially, particularly with early diagnosis and specialist functional-movement physiotherapy combined with psychological therapy, but long duration and entrenched illness beliefs are associated with a poorer, more persistent course.

Fundus albipunctatus — FA, RDH5, RLBP1, retinol dehydrogenase 5 deficiency Retinitis punctata albescens (progressive, with pigmentary degeneration) Other forms of congenital stationary night blindness Oguchi disease Vitamin A deficiency retinopathy Drusen or flecked retina syndromes (for example fundus flavimaculatus) Bietti crystalline dystrophy Prolonged dark adaptometry demonstrating delayed but eventual rod recovery Full-field electroretinography before and after extended dark adaptation Fundus autofluorescence and optical coherence tomography to characterise the white dots and assess structural integrity Colour vision and visual field testing Molecular genetic testing (RDH5 and related visual-cycle genes) Serial assessment to detect any late cone or macular involvement Autosomal recessive form of congenital stationary night blindness, most commonly caused by RDH5 mutations that impair the visual (retinoid) cycle Fundus shows numerous discrete white or yellow-white dots scattered across the retina, sparing the fovea and typically densest in the mid-periphery and posterior pole Night blindness is present from early life; crucially the course is usually stationary, distinguishing it from progressive retinitis punctata albescens The hallmark functional feature is markedly delayed dark adaptation: rod (and often cone) responses are subnormal initially but recover toward normal after a very prolonged period of dark adaptation On standard electroretinography rod responses are reduced, but they improve substantially after extended dark adaptation, reflecting slow regeneration of visual pigment Fundus autofluorescence and optical coherence tomography help characterise the dots and confirm relative structural preservation, in contrast to the degenerative changes of retinitis punctata albescens Management is supportive with reassurance about the stationary course and genetic counselling, though some cases develop late macular or cone dysfunction requiring monitoring Progressive field loss, pigmentary change or acuity decline suggesting retinitis punctata albescens rather than the stationary disorder Late-onset macular dysfunction reducing central acuity Systemic features or malabsorption suggesting acquired vitamin A deficiency Affected siblings requiring screening given recessive inheritance Confusing it with progressive retinitis punctata albescens and giving an incorrectly poor prognosis Recording a reduced rod electroretinogram without repeating it after prolonged dark adaptation and missing the diagnostic recovery Overlooking late cone or macular involvement on follow-up Mistaking the white dots for drusen or a flecked retina dystrophy Fundus albipunctatus is most often caused by recessive mutations in RDH5, which encodes 11-cis retinol dehydrogenase, an enzyme of the retinal pigment epithelium visual cycle. Deficiency slows regeneration of 11-cis retinal and therefore of rhodopsin, so photoreceptors recover very slowly after light exposure, producing night blindness and markedly delayed dark adaptation. Accumulation of retinoid intermediates in the retinal pigment epithelium is thought to underlie the characteristic white dots. Because the photoreceptors themselves are largely preserved, the disorder is usually stationary, unlike the progressive degeneration of retinitis punctata albescens. Generally good, as the disorder is typically stationary with preserved daytime acuity; a minority develop late cone dystrophy or macular changes that can reduce central vision.

Invasive fusariosis — Fusarium infection, disseminated fusariosis, Fusarium solani species complex infection, hyalohyphomycosis due to Fusarium Invasive aspergillosis Disseminated candidiasis Scedosporiosis or lomentosporiosis Mucormycosis Ecthyma gangrenosum from Pseudomonas or other bacterial sepsis Disseminated cutaneous cryptococcosis or other opportunistic mould infections Blood cultures, which are frequently positive in disseminated disease Skin-lesion biopsy for histopathology and fungal culture Fungal biomarkers including serum beta-D-glucan and galactomannan Computed water systems. In hosts with intact immunity infection is usually localised, such as keratitis or onychomycosis, but in profoundly neutropenic or otherwise immunosuppressed patients the fungus invades blood vessels, causing thrombosis, tissue infarction, and haematogenous dissemination. Its ability to sporulate in vivo and release adventitious yeast-like conidia into the bloodstream explains the high rate of positive blood cultures and the widespread cutaneous seeding that typifies disseminated disease. Disseminated fusariosis carries a poor prognosis, driven largely by the degree and persistence of immunosuppression; survival depends heavily on recovery of neutrophil counts, and outcomes are worst in those with persistent neutropenia.

Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase Deficiency — G6PD deficiency, favism, G6PD Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Hereditary spherocytosis Other red cell enzyme defects (e.g. pyruvate kinase deficiency) Unstable haemoglobin disorders Drug- or toxin-induced haemolysis from other causes Neonatal jaundice of other aetiology (ABO/Rh incompatibility, sepsis) Quantitative G6PD enzyme activity assay (repeat after recovery if measured during crisis) Full blood count and reticulocyte count Peripheral blood film for bite cells, blister cells, and Heinz body preparation Markers of haemolysis: bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin Urinalysis for haemoglobinuria Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test to help exclude immune haemolysis The most common human enzyme defect, inherited in an X-linked pattern so that males are predominantly affected while heterozygous females show variable expression. Most individuals are asymptomatic between episodes and present only with acute haemolysis triggered by oxidative stress. Common triggers include certain infections, fava (broad) beans, and oxidant drugs such as some antimalarials, sulphonamides, and nitrofurantoin. Acute haemolysis produces sudden pallor, jaundice, dark urine, and fatigue, typically 1-3 days after exposure to a trigger. It is an important cause of neonatal jaundice, which can be severe and lead to kernicterus if unrecognised. The blood film during a crisis may show bite cells, blister cells, and Heinz bodies, with a rise in reticulocytes. Enzyme activity assay is diagnostic but can be falsely normal during an acute crisis because young reticulocytes have higher enzyme levels, so retesting after recovery is advised. Management centres on avoiding known triggers; acute severe haemolysis may require transfusion, and neonatal jaundice is managed with phototherapy or exchange transfusion as needed. Rapidly falling haemoglobin with haemodynamic compromise Massive haemolysis with haemoglobinuria and acute kidney injury Severe neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia risking kernicterus Marked jaundice with lethargy or poor feeding in a neonate Ongoing exposure to an unrecognised oxidative trigger Interpreting a normal enzyme level during acute haemolysis as excluding the diagnosis Failing to counsel families about drug, food, and infection triggers Underestimating the risk of severe neonatal jaundice and kernicterus Prescribing oxidant medications without checking G6PD status in at-risk populations Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway and generates NADPH, which maintains reduced glutathione in red cells. Deficiency impairs this antioxidant defence, so under oxidative stress haemoglobin is oxidised and denatured, precipitating as Heinz bodies within red cells. These damaged cells are removed by splenic macrophages (producing bite cells) and undergo intravascular haemolysis, resulting in episodic anaemia, jaundice, and haemoglobinuria. Most affected individuals lead normal lives with trigger avoidance; haemolytic episodes are usually self-limiting once the trigger is removed, though neonatal jaundice and rare severe crises can cause serious harm if not promptly managed.

Seizures and cognition often improve with immunotherapy and tumour treatment, but outcome is heavily influenced by the underlying malignancy, and paraneoplastic cases carry a more guarded prognosis.

GABA-enhancing strategies given the underlying inhibitory deficit Overlooking coexisting autistic and behavioural features that need support Failing to consider 15q11-q13 disorders in the differential GABRB3 encodes the beta3 subunit of the GABA-A receptor, a ligand-gated chloride channel that mediates fast synaptic inhibition. Pathogenic variants impair receptor assembly, trafficking, or channel gating, reducing inhibitory chloride currents and shifting the cortical balance towards excitation. This loss of inhibitory tone lowers the seizure threshold and perturbs the developmental maturation of neural circuits, producing epilepsy that ranges from self-limited generalised syndromes to severe encephalopathy. Because the core deficit is reduced GABAergic inhibition, therapies that potentiate GABA-A receptor signalling are mechanistically rational. Milder generalised phenotypes may be well controlled with a good developmental outcome, whereas the developmental and epileptic encephalopathy end carries drug-resistant seizures and significant intellectual disability.

galactocele is a milk-filled retention cyst and is the commonest benign breast lump associated with lactation It typically presents during or shortly after breastfeeding, or on weaning, as a smooth, systemic upset suggesting a lactational abscess A solid residual mass after aspiration Bloodstained aspirate Atypical imaging features or a lump that does not resolve Mistaking a galactocele for an abscess and undertaking unnecessary antibiotics or incision Failing to reassess a mass that persists after aspiration Overlooking the rare possibility of malignancy when features are atypical Assuming any lactational lump is benign without appropriate imaging when uncertain Discouraging breastfeeding unnecessarily A galactocele forms when a lactiferous duct becomes obstructed and milk is retained within a distended, cyst-like space. Obstruction commonly occurs when milk flow changes, such as at weaning or when feeding becomes irregular, allowing stasis and accumulation. Over time the water content of the trapped milk may be reabsorbed, leaving thicker, fatty, or inspissated contents that alter the consistency of the lump and its appearance on imaging. Because the fluid is sterile milk rather than pus, the lesion lacks the inflammatory features of an abscess unless secondary infection supervenes. A galactocele is entirely benign with an excellent prognosis; it usually resolves after aspiration or with conservative management as lactation settles, and breastfeeding can typically continue without harm.

Galactosemia — classic galactosemia, galactosaemia, GALT deficiency Neonatal sepsis of other cause Other causes of neonatal cholestasis and liver failure Tyrosinemia and other hepatorenal metabolic disorders Hereditary fructose intolerance Neonatal hemochromatosis Urea cycle disorders presenting with encephalopathy Newborn screening result and confirmatory GALT enzyme activity assay Quantitative galactose-1-phosphate and molecular genetic testing Liver function tests and coagulation studies Urine for reducing substances (a supportive, non-specific finding) Blood cultures and sepsis evaluation given the risk of E. coli infection Ophthalmological examination for cataracts An autosomal recessive disorder of galactose metabolism; the classic and most severe form results from deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT). Symptoms typically begin in the first days to weeks of life once milk feeding (which contains lactose, a source of galactose) is established. Presenting features include poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, and lethargy, often progressing to liver dysfunction and coagulopathy. Affected neonates are at markedly increased risk of Escherichia coli sepsis, which may be the presenting or dominant feature. Cataracts can develop early owing to accumulation of galactitol in the lens. Diagnosis is supported by newborn screening and confirmed by demonstrating reduced GALT enzyme activity and characteristic metabolite abnormalities; a reducing substance may be found in the urine. The cornerstone of management is strict, lifelong elimination of galactose and lactose from the diet, which reverses the acute toxicity. Despite early dietary treatment, long-term complications such as speech and cognitive difficulties, ataxia, and ovarian insufficiency in females may still occur. Milder variant forms (for example some Duarte variants) may have residual enzyme activity and a more benign course. Signs of Escherichia coli or other Gram-negative sepsis in a jaundiced neonate Acute liver failure with coagulopathy and bleeding Progressive lethargy, poor feeding, and encephalopathy Severe hypoglycaemia or metabolic decompensation Continued galactose exposure delaying recognition and worsening toxicity Treating neonatal sepsis without considering an underlying metabolic disorder such as galactosemia Delaying dietary galactose elimination while awaiting confirmatory results in a decompensating infant Assuming that early dietary treatment fully prevents all long-term complications Overlooking milder variants that may still need dietary attention Failing to arrange ophthalmological and developmental follow-up Deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase blocks the conversion of galactose-1-phosphate to UDP-galactose in the Leloir pathway. Ingested galactose, mainly from lactose in milk, cannot be normally metabolised, so galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in tissues including the liver, kidney, and brain and exerts toxic effects. Excess galactose is also shunted to alternative pathways, generating galactitol, which accumulates in the lens and causes cataract, and galactonate. The metabolite toxicity produces hepatocellular injury, renal tubular dysfunction, and central nervous system effects, and impairs host defences, predisposing to Gram-negative sepsis. Early diagnosis and strict dietary galactose restriction reverse the life-threatening acute manifestations. However, even with good control, a substantial proportion of children experience long-term neurodevelopmental, speech, and motor difficulties, and most affected females develop primary ovarian insufficiency. Variant forms are generally milder.

Gram-negative sepsis in a young infant Progressive liver failure with coagulopathy Encephalopathy or bleeding suggesting decompensation Waiting for newborn screening results before treating a clinically unwell infant Missing associated Gram-negative sepsis, which requires urgent antibiotic treatment Assuming strict dietary control prevents all long-term complications Overlooking the diagnosis when urine glucose oxidase dipstick is negative despite positive reducing substances In the Leloir pathway, dietary galactose is phosphorylated to galactose-1-phosphate, which galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase then converts to glucose-1-phosphate and UDP-galactose. In classic galactosaemia the enzyme is deficient, so galactose-1-phosphate accumulates and, together with galactose and its reduced product galactitol, damages tissues. Galactose-1-phosphate is toxic to hepatocytes and renal tubular cells and interferes with several metabolic processes, while galactitol accumulation in the lens draws in water and produces cataract. The mechanisms of the long-term neurological and ovarian complications remain incompletely understood and are not fully prevented by dietary treatment. A galactose-free diet started early prevents the life-threatening neonatal illness and reverses the acute hepatic, renal and cataract manifestations. However, long-term outcomes remain guarded, with a substantial proportion developing cognitive, speech and motor difficulties, and most females experiencing premature ovarian insufficiency despite adherence.

combined deficiency of both enzymes Three clinical forms are recognised by age at onset: early-infantile, late-infantile, and juvenile/adult, the last being commoner in patients of Japanese ancestry Characteristic features include coarse facial features, a macular cherry-red spot, dysostosis multiplex, and, in the early-infantile form, hydrops fetalis and visceromegaly The juvenile/adult form is Cardiac or renal involvement contributing to deterioration Diagnosing isolated sialidosis or GM1 gangliosidosis and missing the combined deficiency of galactosialidosis Overlooking galactosialidosis as a cause of non-immune hydrops fetalis Failing to consider it in a juvenile/adult progressive myoclonic epilepsy with a cherry-red spot Not recognising the ancestry-related frequency of the juvenile/adult form Cathepsin A (protective protein) forms a lysosomal multienzyme complex with beta-galactosidase and neuraminidase (sialidase), protecting them from premature degradation and enabling their normal activity. In galactosialidosis, biallelic CTSA variants cause loss of this protective function, leading to a secondary combined deficiency of both beta-galactosidase and neuraminidase. Impaired degradation results in lysosomal accumulation of sialylated glycoproteins, oligosaccharides, and glycolipids in neurones and visceral tissues. This storage underlies the neurodegeneration, cherry-red spot, coarse features, skeletal dysostosis, and, in severe forms, the fetal hydrops and organomegaly. Prognosis depends on the form: the early-infantile type is severe and often fatal in infancy, the late-infantile type is intermediate, and the juvenile/adult type is slowly progressive with prolonged survival but accumulating neurological disability.

In the Galeazzi injury a force applied to the distal forearm fractures the distal radial shaft; the resulting radial shortening and angulation disrupt the distal radioulnar joint, tearing its stabilising ligaments or avulsing the ulnar styloid. If the radius is fixed without recognising and addressing the DRUJ, residual instability causes pain, weakness of grip and loss of forearm rotation. With anatomical radial fixation and appropriate DRUJ stabilisation the outcome is generally good; a missed or untreated distal radioulnar joint injury causes chronic pain, weakness and restricted forearm rotation.
