oedematous wall thickening Secondary wall thickening from hepatitis, heart failure, or hypoalbuminaemia Abdominal ultrasound seeking intramural cystic spaces and comet-tail reverberation artefact MRI with MRCP demonstrating the pearl-necklace sign of Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses Contrast-enhanced CT to assess wall thickening and help exclude malignancy Contrast-enhanced or high-resolution ultrasound to characterise indeterminate focal thickening Liver biochemistry to evaluate coexisting biliary or hepatic disease Histological examination of the cholecystectomy specimen for definitive diagnosis Adenomyomatosis is a benign, non-inflammatory hyperplastic change of the gallbladder wall characterised by mucosal proliferation, muscular hypertrophy, and outpouchings of epithelium into the thickened wall known as Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses It is classified by distribution as segmental, fundal (localised), or diffuse, with the segmental form producing a characteristic hourglass narrowing of the gallbladder Most cases are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on ultrasound, cross-sectional imaging, or histology after cholecystectomy performed for other reasons The hallmark imaging finding is intramural cystic spaces (the Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses), with comet-tail reverberation artefact on ultrasound from cholesterol crystals within them and a pearl-necklace appearance on MRCP It frequently coexists with gallstones and chronic cholecystitis, which may account for symptoms attributed to the adenomyomatosis itself The principal clinical challenge is distinguishing focal or segmental adenomyomatosis from gallbladder carcinoma, particularly when there is asymmetrical wall thickening Asymptomatic, confidently benign disease can be managed conservatively with surveillance, whereas cholecystectomy is appropriate for symptomatic disease or when malignancy cannot be excluded MRI with MRCP is the most useful problem-solving investigation when ultrasound leaves diagnostic uncertainty about wall thickening Asymmetric or focal wall thickening with disrupted wall layers suggesting carcinoma Rapidly enlarging lesion or an associated soft-tissue mass New or worsening jaundice or biliary obstruction Regional lymphadenopathy or hepatic invasion on imaging Constitutional symptoms such as weight loss and anorexia Overcalling focal or segmental adenomyomatosis as gallbladder carcinoma, or the reverse, leading to inappropriate management Attributing biliary symptoms to adenomyomatosis when coexisting gallstones or chronic cholecystitis are responsible Failing to use MRI or MRCP to characterise indeterminate wall thickening seen on ultrasound Assuming diffuse wall thickening is always benign without considering diffuse infiltrating carcinoma Neglecting histological review of the resected gallbladder, which provides the definitive diagnosis Adenomyomatosis results from acquired hyperplasia of the gallbladder wall in which the surface epithelium proliferates and invaginates into a hypertrophied muscularis, forming the intramural epithelial-lined diverticula termed Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses. Chronically raised intraluminal pressure, thought to relate to gallbladder dysmotility and functional or mechanical outflow obstruction, is believed to drive both the muscular hypertrophy and the herniation of mucosa into and through the muscle layer. Bile stagnating within the sinuses becomes concentrated and supersaturated, favouring precipitation of cholesterol crystals and small calculi within them; these crystalline deposits generate the comet-tail artefact seen on ultrasound. The overall process is a reactive, proliferative but benign remodelling of the wall rather than a neoplastic or infective one, although the associated stasis and coexisting gallstones contribute to chronic inflammation. In the segmental form, circumferential muscular hypertrophy creates a stricture-like waist that can trap debris in the fundal compartment and further promote stasis. Adenomyomatosis is a benign condition with an excellent prognosis, and asymptomatic disease requires no treatment beyond confident diagnosis; symptomatic patients are cured by cholecystectomy, and although an association with malignancy is debated the lesion itself is not reliably premalignant.

Gallbladder cancer — gallbladder carcinoma, GBC, carcinoma of the gallbladder Cholelithiasis with chronic cholecystitis Benign gallbladder polyp or adenomyomatosis Cholangiocarcinoma involving the biliary tree Hepatocellular carcinoma or hepatic metastases involving the gallbladder fossa Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis mimicking malignancy Pancreatic head carcinoma causing biliary obstruction Abdominal ultrasound as initial imaging for wall thickening, mass, or suspicious polyp Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI with MRCP to assess local invasion, biliary involvement, and nodal or distant spread Serum tumour markers such as CA 19-9 and CEA to support diagnosis and monitoring Histopathological review of the resected gallbladder specimen with attention to depth of wall invasion and margins Staging cross-sectional imaging and, where indicated, diagnostic laparoscopy to exclude peritoneal disease Most cases are adenocarcinomas and are often silent until advanced, so many are found incidentally during or after cholecystectomy performed for presumed benign gallstone disease Chronic gallstones, a large stone burden, and long-standing inflammation are the dominant risk factors; a heavily calcified (porcelain) gallbladder and large gallbladder polyps also raise concern Symptoms when present tend to mimic biliary colic or cholecystitis, or reflect advanced disease with weight loss, jaundice, and a right upper quadrant mass Because early spread to the liver bed and regional nodes is common, tumour depth of invasion into the gallbladder wall strongly determines the extent of surgery needed An unexpected malignancy found on histology after a routine cholecystectomy usually requires re-staging and consideration of a more extensive re-resection Complete surgical resection with adequate margins, often including a wedge of adjacent liver and regional lymphadenectomy, offers the only realistic chance of cure For unresectable or metastatic disease, systemic chemotherapy with gemcitabine-based platinum regimens is the standard backbone, and biliary drainage is used to palliate obstructive jaundice Anatomical association with pancreaticobiliary maljunction and geographic clustering point to both anatomical and environmental contributions to risk Painless jaundice or a palpable right upper quadrant mass suggesting advanced disease Gallbladder wall thickening or a fixed mass on imaging in a patient with weight loss Incidental carcinoma reported after cholecystectomy, mandating urgent re-staging Large or growing gallbladder polyp, particularly over one centimetre Attributing chronic right upper quadrant symptoms solely to benign gallstone disease and missing an underlying tumour Failing to send or carefully review the gallbladder specimen after routine cholecystectomy Not offering re-resection when incidental invasive cancer is identified in an otherwise fit patient Overlooking a suspicious polyp or porcelain gallbladder that warrants prophylactic or definitive surgery Gallbladder cancer usually arises from the mucosal epithelium, most commonly as adenocarcinoma, through a sequence of chronic inflammation, metaplasia, dysplasia, and invasive carcinoma. Prolonged mechanical and inflammatory irritation from gallstones and chronic cholecystitis is thought to drive this progression. The thin gallbladder wall and its lack of a serosa on the hepatic surface allow early direct extension into the adjacent liver and rapid access to lymphatics and the peritoneum, explaining the tendency for early regional nodal and hepatic spread. Outcome depends heavily on stage; tumours confined to the mucosa and found incidentally can have a good prognosis after adequate resection, whereas transmural or node-positive and metastatic disease carries a poor outlook with low long-term survival.

ALP rise often precedes jaundice (p.2731, 2736) AMA (and sp100/gp210 if AMA-negative) for PBC; IgM elevation; serum IgG4 to exclude IgG4 cholangitis; pANCA in PSC; CA 19-9 for cholangiocarcinoma surveillance in PSC (ch.355 p.2711, ch.357 p.2737, ch.87 p.667) Endoscopic brushing of biliary strictures (more accurate than bile cytology alone) in suspected neoplastic stricture, especially in PSC (p.2737) Malignant biliary obstruction (pancreatic head carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, ampullary tumor) - Courvoisier's law: a palpably enlarged gallbladder suggests malignancy rather than stones (p.2736) Functional/vague dyspepsia, eructation, flatulence after fatty meals - common with or without gallstones but not specific for biliary calculi (p.2731) Other postcholecystectomy nonbiliary disorders (reflux esophagitis, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis, irritable bowel syndrome) (p.2734) Two gallstone types: cholesterol stones (>90% in Western countries, contain >50% cholesterol monohydrate) and pigment stones (mainly calcium bilirubinate, <20% cholesterol, split into 'black' and 'brown' types) (p.2728-2729). Cholesterol gallstones arise from three defects: (1) bile supersaturation with cholesterol, (2) accelerated nucleation of cholesterol monohydrate crystals, and (3) gallbladder hypomotility/stasis (p.2729). Black pigment stones associate with chronic hemolysis, alcohol-related cirrhosis, Gilbert's syndrome, cystic fibrosis, and ileal disease/resection/bypass; brown pigment stones form secondary to chronic biliary infection/parasitism with deconjugation of bilirubin (p.2729). Biliary colic is the most specific symptom: a steady (not intermittent) severe ache or fullness in the epigastrium/RUQ radiating to the interscapular area, right scapula, or shoulder, lasting 30 min to 5 h; the word 'colic' is a misnomer (p.2730-2731). 60-80% of asymptomatic gallstones remain asymptomatic over up to 25 years; symptom development is ~2-4% per year (falling to 1-2% later) and yearly complication rate is ~0.1-0.3%, so prophylactic cholecystectomy is not warranted (p.2731). Ultrasound is the procedure of choice for detecting gallstones (>95% accuracy) and can identify stones as small as 1.5 mm using acoustic shadowing criteria (p.2730). Biliary sludge (lecithin-cholesterol liquid crystals, cholesterol monohydrate crystals, calcium bilirubinate, mucin) shifts with posture but does NOT cast an acoustic shadow, distinguishing it from stones; it can be a gallstone precursor (p.2730). Acute cholecystitis usually follows cystic duct obstruction by a stone; Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation) is characteristic, and the triad of sudden RUQ tenderness, fever, and leukocytosis is highly suggestive (p.2732-2733). Charcot's triad (biliary pain, jaundice, spiking fevers with chills) characterizes acute cholangitis; suppurative cholangitis with a completely obstructed duct under pressure causes mental confusion, bacteremia, and septic shock (Reynolds' pentad features) (p.2735). Choledocholithiasis (CBD stones) occurs in ~10-15% of patients with cholelithiasis; incidence rises with age (up to 25% of elderly at cholecystectomy); most are cholesterol stones that migrated from the gallbladder (p.2735). MRCP is the first choice to assess for choledocholithiasis (comparable sensitivity/specificity to ERCP); ERCP is the cholangiogram of choice when intervention is needed and ERCP with sphincterotomy is preferred for both diagnosis and therapy of bacterial cholangitis (p.2736, 2735). PBC: female-predominant (~50 yr median age) autoimmune disease with portal inflammation and necrosis of cholangiocytes in small/medium bile ducts; antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA) present in ~95%; key symptoms are fatigue and pruritus (Harrison 22e ch.355 p.2711). PSC is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease (60-80%, predominantly ulcerative colitis); cholangiography shows multifocal strictures with intervening normal/dilated segments producing a 'beaded' appearance; pANCA positive in ~65% (ch.357 p.2737; ch.355 p.2712). Cholangiocarcinoma is classified as intrahepatic (~20-30%), perihilar (~50-60%), and distal (~20-30%); PSC is a clear risk factor for iCCA and pCCA with a 5-10% lifetime incidence, and is a relative contraindication to liver transplantation (ch.87 p.667; ch.355 p.2712). Gallbladder cancer: cholelithiasis is the major risk factor but <1% of patients with gallstones develop it; polyps >=10 mm are at risk of transformation; early cases are found incidentally at cholecystectomy and symptoms (jaundice, pain, weight loss) indicate advanced disease (ch.87 p.670). Biliary pain persisting beyond 5 h - raises suspicion of acute cholecystitis (p.2731) Fever or chills (rigors) with biliary pain - implies a complication (cholecystitis, pancreatitis, or cholangitis) (p.2731) Charcot's triad (biliary pain, jaundice, spiking fevers/chills) - acute cholangitis (p.2735) Mental confusion, bacteremia, septic shock (suppurative cholangitis) - mortality approaches 100% without prompt drainage (p.2735) Serum bilirubin >=342 micromol/L (20 mg/dL) - suggests neoplastic rather than calculous obstruction (p.2736) Painless jaundice and/or a palpably enlarged gallbladder (Courvoisier) - points to malignancy (p.2736) Sudden transient relief of RUQ pain followed by generalized peritonitis - free gallbladder perforation (~30% mortality) (p.2733) Pruritus preceding jaundice in PBC - indicates severe disease and poor prognosis (ch.355 p.2711) New/rising bilirubin or dominant stricture in PSC - concern for cholangiocarcinoma (ch.355 p.2712; ch.87 p.667) 'Biliary colic' is a misnomer - the pain is steady, not intermittent (p.2731) Vague postprandial dyspepsia, eructation, and flatulence are not specific for gallstones and should not be confused with biliary pain (p.2731) Pigment stones do NOT respond to UDCA dissolution therapy, and stones >10 mm rarely dissolve - only ~10% of symptomatic patients are dissolution candidates with 30-50% recurrence over 3-5 years (p.2731-2732) Jaundice is unusual early in acute cholecystitis; its presence (or bilirubin >5 mg/dL) should prompt suspicion of a CBD stone (p.2732, 2736) Missing Mirizzi's syndrome preoperatively risks CBD injury at surgery (p.2733) AMA is negative in 5-10% of PBC - liver biopsy and sp100/gp210 are needed, and PSC should be excluded by cholangiography (ch.355 p.2711) Every patient diagnosed with sclerosing cholangitis should have serum IgG4 checked to exclude IgG4-associated (secondary) cholangitis, especially without IBD (p.2737) Routine prophylactic cholecystectomy in asymptomatic stones (including young patients and diabetics) is not warranted (p.2731) The carcinoma risk of porcelain gallbladder has been challenged; cholecystectomy is no longer absolute and surveillance is acceptable (p.2734) Bile flow depends on sphincter of Oddi tone and cholecystokinin (CCK)-mediated gallbladder contraction after fatty/amino-acid meals. Gallstones form from abnormal bile composition. Cholesterol stones (>90% in Western countries) require three converging defects: hepatic hypersecretion of cholesterol producing lithogenic/supersaturated bile (driven by obesity, metabolic syndrome, estrogens, rapid weight loss, age, CYP7A1 or MDR3/ABCB4 gene defects, ABCG5/G8 variants), accelerated nucleation of cholesterol monohydrate crystals (excess pronucleating mucin/immunoglobulins vs deficient antinucleating apolipoproteins), and gallbladder hypomotility with stasis (fasting, TPN, pregnancy, octreotide). Pigment stones contain calcium bilirubinate: black stones from chronic hemolysis, cirrhosis, Gilbert's, cystic fibrosis, or ileal disease (enterohepatic bilirubin recycling); brown stones from deconjugation of bilirubin by bacterial beta-glucuronidase in chronically infected/parasitized bile. Symptoms arise when stones obstruct the cystic duct (cholecystitis) or migrate into the CBD (choledocholithiasis) causing biliary obstruction, cholangitis, or gallstone pancreatitis as they pass through the ampulla of Vater. PBC and PSC are chronic cholestatic syndromes from immune-mediated destruction of bile ducts (small/medium ducts in PBC; entire biliary tree in PSC) progressing to biliary cirrhosis and portal hypertension. Most asymptomatic gallstones stay silent (60-80% over up to 25 years); cumulative death risk on expectant management is small. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the gold standard with complications ~4%, conversion ~5%, death rate <0.1%, and bile duct injury 0.2-0.6%; it relieves preoperative symptoms in 75-90%. Acute cholecystitis: ~75% remit medically within 2-7 days but ~25% recur within 1 year and 60% within 6 years; free perforation carries ~30% mortality and suppurative cholangitis approaches 100% mortality without drainage. PSC is progressive with a median survival of 12-18 years regardless of therapy and is a common indication for liver transplantation; small-duct PSC has a significantly better prognosis. PBC: UDCA slows but does not reverse disease; transplantation for decompensated cirrhosis. Cholangiocarcinoma has a 5-year survival of ~10%; gallbladder cancer is curable (5-yr survival 60-90%) only when local and resected (~20% of patients), with median survival 10-12 months in advanced disease (ch.357 p.2731-2737; ch.355 p.2711-2712; ch.87 p.667-670). Stone-based spectrum: asymptomatic gallstones -> biliary colic (cystic duct/CBD obstruction) -> acute cholecystitis -> complications (empyema, hydrops/mucocele, gangrene, perforation, fistula with gallstone ileus, emphysematous cholecystitis, Mirizzi's syndrome). CBD stone (choledocholithiasis) complications: cholangitis (nonsuppurative vs suppurative), obstructive jaundice, gallstone pancreatitis, secondary biliary cirrhosis. Cholangitis severity by Charcot's triad (pain + jaundice + fever/chills) advancing to suppurative cholangitis (adds confusion + septic shock). PBC has four histologic stages from chronic nonsuppurative destructive cholangitis to cirrhosis. PSC: small-duct (better prognosis) vs classic (large-duct) disease. Cholangiocarcinoma classified anatomically as intrahepatic, perihilar, and distal; gallbladder cancer staged as local vs advanced (ch.357 p.2731-2737; ch.355 p.2711; ch.87 p.667-670).

Gallbladder polyp — gallbladder polypoid lesion, polypoid lesion of the gallbladder, cholesterol polyp Adherent gallstone or tumefactive sludge Adenomyomatosis of the gallbladder Gallbladder adenoma Gallbladder adenocarcinoma Metastasis or other rare gallbladder tumour Inflammatory or fibrous polyp Transabdominal ultrasound to measure size, number, and morphology and to detect gallstones Endoscopic ultrasound for detailed characterisation of indeterminate or larger polyps Contrast-enhanced ultrasound or MRI when malignancy is suspected Serial ultrasound surveillance to assess growth of small polyps Liver function tests and CA 19-9 if malignancy is a concern Assessment for primary sclerosing cholangitis in relevant patients A projection from the gallbladder wall found commonly and usually incidentally on ultrasound, most often benign The great majority are non-neoplastic cholesterol polyps or inflammatory or adenomyomatous lesions rather than true neoplasms True adenomas are premalignant, and the main clinical task is stratifying the small risk of malignancy or malignant potential Polyp size is the key risk marker: larger polyps carry a higher likelihood of neoplasia, and a threshold around one centimetre is widely used to prompt consideration of surgery Additional risk features include a solitary sessile polyp, rapid growth on surveillance, older age, coexisting gallstones, and primary sclerosing cholangitis Cholesterol polyps are frequently multiple, small, and pedunculated with an echogenic appearance on ultrasound Management follows a risk-based strategy: cholecystectomy for polyps with concerning features and ultrasound surveillance for small low-risk lesions, with guidelines defining thresholds and intervals A polyp at or above the size threshold that prompts consideration of surgery Documented growth of a polyp during surveillance A solitary sessile polyp or focal wall thickening at the polyp base Older age, coexisting gallstones, or primary sclerosing cholangitis increasing malignant risk Symptoms or biochemical changes suggesting malignancy Mistaking an adherent stone or sludge ball for a fixed polyp Failing to act on a polyp that meets size or growth criteria for surgery Over-treating numerous tiny cholesterol polyps that pose negligible risk Neglecting the heightened malignant risk in primary sclerosing cholangitis Abandoning surveillance of small polyps that warrant continued follow-up Gallbladder polyps are a heterogeneous group of mucosal elevations. Most are pseudopolyps: cholesterol polyps formed by focal accumulation of cholesterol-laden macrophages within the mucosa, inflammatory polyps from chronic inflammation, or localised adenomyomatosis. A minority are true epithelial neoplasms, chiefly adenomas, which can progress through an adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence to gallbladder adenocarcinoma. The probability that a polyp is neoplastic and potentially malignant rises with increasing size and with certain morphological and clinical features, which is why size and growth on serial imaging drive management. Coexisting gallstones and chronic inflammation, as well as conditions such as primary sclerosing cholangitis, further raise the risk of malignancy. Small non-neoplastic polyps have an excellent prognosis and rarely progress, while adenomas and early carcinomas identified and resected promptly can be cured; outcomes are poor once invasive gallbladder carcinoma is advanced, underscoring the value of appropriate risk stratification.

Gallstone ileus — gallstone bowel obstruction, biliary ileus, mechanical obstruction from gallstone Adhesional small bowel obstruction Obstructing small bowel or caecal tumour Incarcerated or strangulated hernia Intussusception Crohn stricture Bezoar-related obstruction Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen (investigation of choice) to show obstruction, ectopic stone, and pneumobilia Abdominal radiograph for signs of obstruction and pneumobilia Full blood count, electrolytes, and renal function to assess dehydration and sepsis Ultrasound to assess the gallbladder and biliary tree where CT is unavailable Serial imaging or examination if the stone is migrating with intermittent symptoms Despite its name, gallstone ileus is a mechanical small bowel obstruction caused by a large gallstone impacting in the gut lumen, not a true paralytic ileus It follows the formation of a cholecystoenteric fistula, usually between an inflamed gallbladder and the duodenum, through which a stone passes into the bowel The stone most often impacts at the narrowest point, the terminal ileum, producing distal small bowel obstruction It characteristically affects older patients, often with comorbidity, and symptoms may be intermittent as the stone tumbles distally before final impaction The classic Rigler triad on imaging is pneumobilia, a mechanical small bowel obstruction, and an ectopic (aberrantly located) gallstone, best appreciated on CT Treatment is surgical relief of the obstruction by enterolithotomy to remove the stone, with the diseased gallbladder and fistula either dealt with at the same operation or later depending on fitness A stone impacting in the duodenum causing gastric outlet obstruction is termed Bouveret syndrome Established small bowel obstruction with distension, vomiting, and absolute constipation requiring urgent surgery Features of bowel ischaemia or perforation (peritonism, systemic sepsis, free gas) Gastric outlet obstruction from a duodenal stone (Bouveret syndrome) Progressive dehydration, electrolyte derangement, and haemodynamic instability in a frail patient Failing to recognise pneumobilia and the ectopic stone on imaging, delaying diagnosis Attempting concurrent cholecystectomy and fistula repair in an unstable or high-risk patient rather than a limited enterolithotomy Not palpating the whole bowel for a second obstructing stone at operation, risking early recurrence Attributing intermittent symptoms to a resolving obstruction and discharging before impaction Underestimating fluid and electrolyte deficits in these often elderly patients Chronic cholelithiasis and recurrent cholecystitis cause dense adhesions between the gallbladder and an adjacent hollow viscus, most often the duodenum. Ongoing inflammation and pressure necrosis create a fistulous communication, allowing a large gallstone to erode directly into the gut. Small stones pass uneventfully, but a stone large enough (typically over about 2.5 cm) can lodge in the bowel and obstruct it, usually at the ileocaecal region where the lumen is narrowest. Air refluxes through the fistula into the biliary tree, producing pneumobilia. The obstruction leads to proximal bowel distension, fluid sequestration, and, if unrelieved, ischaemia and perforation. Mortality is higher than for other causes of small bowel obstruction, largely because patients are elderly with comorbidity and diagnosis is often delayed. Prompt relief of the obstruction gives good results; recurrence from further stones is uncommon, and the need to definitively address the gallbladder and fistula is balanced against operative risk.

Gamekeeper's thumb — skier's thumb, thumb ulnar collateral ligament injury Thumb metacarpophalangeal joint fracture Radial collateral ligament injury of the thumb First carpometacarpal joint injury or osteoarthritis De Quervain tenosynovitis Scaphoid fracture Radiographs to identify an avulsion fracture before stress testing Stress testing of the metacarpophalangeal joint in extension and slight flexion Ultrasound or MRI to detect a Stener lesion or complete tear Assessment of pinch stability and strength Comparison with the uninjured thumb Injury to the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint, causing pain and instability with pinch and grip The acute form (skier's thumb) follows forced abduction of the thumb, classically a fall onto an outstretched hand holding a ski pole The chronic form (the original gamekeeper's thumb) results from repetitive stress A Stener lesion, in which the torn ligament end is displaced superficial to the adductor aponeurosis, prevents healing and needs surgery Careful stress testing assesses instability, ideally after excluding an associated avulsion fracture on radiographs Partial injuries are treated with immobilisation, whereas complete tears and Stener lesions require surgical repair Gross instability indicating a complete tear Suspected Stener lesion requiring surgery Displaced avulsion fracture Chronic instability with developing arthritis Missing a Stener lesion, which will not heal without surgery Performing vigorous stress testing before excluding an avulsion fracture Undertreating a complete tear as a simple sprain Overlooking chronic instability as a source of ongoing weakness Gamekeeper's thumb involves disruption of the ulnar collateral ligament that stabilises the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint against valgus (radially directed) stress during pinch. Acute forced radial deviation tears the ligament, usually at its distal insertion, sometimes with a bony avulsion. If the ligament fully ruptures, its proximal-to-distal recoil can leave the torn end trapped superficial to the adductor aponeurosis (a Stener lesion), which physically blocks healing. Loss of ligament integrity produces instability that impairs pinch strength and, if untreated, leads to chronic instability and arthritis. Partial injuries generally recover well with immobilisation, and surgically repaired complete tears or Stener lesions usually regain good stability and pinch, whereas missed injuries can cause chronic instability and secondary arthritis.

Gamma-glutamylcysteine synthetase deficiency — glutamate-cysteine ligase deficiency, GCL deficiency, gamma-GCS deficiency, GCLC gene Glutathione synthetase deficiency Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency Glutathione reductase deficiency Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Unstable haemoglobin variants Other oxidant-induced haemolytic states Red-cell glutathione concentration measurement Gamma-glutamylcysteine synthetase enzyme activity assay Full blood count, reticulocyte count and blood film for oxidative changes Haemolysis screen with bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin Neurological assessment where indicated Molecular testing of the GCLC gene A rare recessive defect of glutathione synthesis producing an oxidant-sensitive chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia The enzyme catalyses the first, rate-limiting step of glutathione production, so deficiency depletes red-cell glutathione Low glutathione leaves the red cell poorly protected against oxidant stress, and haemolysis may worsen with oxidant drugs or infection Some patients have neurological features such as spinocerebellar degeneration and peripheral neuropathy, reflecting glutathione depletion in other tissues The anaemia is Coombs-negative and the film may show non-specific oxidative changes Diagnosis rests on demonstrating low red-cell glutathione, reduced enzyme activity and a GCLC mutation Management is supportive with folate and transfusion when needed, and above all avoidance of oxidant drugs and foods known to precipitate haemolysis Acute haemolytic crisis triggered by oxidant drug exposure or infection Progressive neurological deterioration in severe deficiency Severe symptomatic anaemia requiring transfusion Aplastic crisis following parvovirus B19 infection Failing to advise strict avoidance of oxidant drugs and foods Confusing the disorder with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency without measuring glutathione Overlooking neurological signs that indicate systemic glutathione depletion Neglecting iron-overload monitoring in transfused patients Gamma-glutamylcysteine synthetase, also called glutamate-cysteine ligase, catalyses the first and rate-limiting step in the synthesis of glutathione, the tripeptide that defends the red cell against oxidative injury. Deficiency lowers red-cell glutathione, leaving haemoglobin and membrane proteins vulnerable to oxidant damage; the resulting chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia is characteristically exacerbated by oxidant stress from certain drugs or infections. Because glutathione is important throughout the body, severe deficiency can also cause neurological dysfunction. The haemolytic anaemia is usually chronic and manageable if oxidant triggers are avoided; prognosis is worse when significant neurological involvement is present.

Gangliocytoma — gangliocytoma, central gangliocytoma, WHO grade 1 neuronal tumour, dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma (Lhermitte-Duclos) Ganglioglioma Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumour Focal cortical dysplasia Pilocytic astrocytoma (cerebellar) Diffuse low-grade glioma Cerebellar medulloblastoma (for the cerebellar variant) Brain MRI to characterise the lesion, including the striated folial pattern of the cerebellar variant Video-EEG when the tumour presents with focal epilepsy Histopathology showing dysplastic ganglion cells without a neoplastic glial component PTEN germline testing when the cerebellar variant or Cowden features are present Screening for Cowden syndrome-associated tumours (breast, thyroid, endometrium) Neuropsychological assessment as part of epilepsy surgery evaluation A benign neuronal tumour (CNS WHO grade 1) composed of mature but dysplastic ganglion (neuronal) cells without a neoplastic glial component Distinguished from ganglioglioma by the absence of a neoplastic glial element Often cortical and supratentorial, and a recognised cause of chronic focal epilepsy The cerebellar variant, dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma (Lhermitte-Duclos disease), is associated with germline PTEN mutation and Cowden syndrome MRI usually shows a well-circumscribed, sometimes calcified lesion; the cerebellar variant has a characteristic striated 'tigroid' folial pattern Surgical resection is generally curative for the typical cortical tumour Recognition of the cerebellar variant should prompt evaluation for Cowden syndrome and its associated cancer risks Drug-resistant seizures affecting quality of life Cerebellar variant causing mass effect, ataxia or obstructive hydrocephalus Features suggesting Cowden syndrome with heightened systemic cancer risk Atypical growth or enhancement suggesting an alternative diagnosis Confusing gangliocytoma with ganglioglioma and misjudging the presence of a neoplastic glial component Failing to test for germline PTEN and diagnose Cowden syndrome in the cerebellar variant Overlooking the diagnosis in long-standing focal epilepsy Incomplete resection of the cerebellar lesion leading to recurrence Gangliocytoma is a benign neuronal tumour formed of clusters of mature but dysplastic ganglion cells set in a stroma of non-neoplastic glial tissue, differing from ganglioglioma in that the glial component is not itself neoplastic. It commonly arises in the cerebral cortex and, when supratentorial, disrupts local circuitry to produce focal epilepsy. The distinctive cerebellar variant, dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma or Lhermitte-Duclos disease, consists of hypertrophic dysplastic ganglion cells expanding the cerebellar folia and is strongly linked to germline PTEN mutation as part of Cowden syndrome, a phakomatosis with increased risk of breast, thyroid and other tumours. Growth is slow and the lesions are essentially non-progressive. Prognosis is excellent, as gangliocytoma is benign and slow-growing; complete resection of a symptomatic cortical tumour is usually curative. The cerebellar variant may recur if incompletely removed, and its main long-term significance lies in the associated Cowden syndrome and lifelong surveillance for related cancers.

Ganglioglioma — ganglioglioma, glioneuronal tumour, WHO grade 1 ganglioglioma, BRAF V600E-mutant ganglioglioma Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumour Pilocytic astrocytoma Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma Diffuse low-grade glioma Focal cortical dysplasia Gangliocytoma Brain MRI with epilepsy protocol to characterise the cystic and solid components Video-EEG to confirm and localise the seizure focus Histopathology demonstrating dysplastic ganglion cells and a glial component BRAF V600E immunohistochemistry or molecular testing CD34 immunostaining, which is frequently positive in glioneuronal tumours Ki-67/MIB-1 index and grading assessment to detect anaplastic change A well-differentiated glioneuronal tumour (usually CNS WHO grade 1) and a common cause of chronic drug-resistant focal epilepsy in children and young adults Composed of both dysplastic neurons (ganglion cells) and a neoplastic glial component Most often cortical and temporal, correlating with its strong association with focal seizures MRI typically shows a circumscribed, often cystic lesion with a mural nodule, variable enhancement and frequent calcification BRAF V600E mutation is common and can be exploited diagnostically and, in selected higher-grade cases, therapeutically Diagnosis rests on recognising the abnormal ganglion cells; a well-formed glial component distinguishes it from lesions of pure neuronal or glial type Complete surgical resection is usually curative and offers a high chance of seizure freedom Drug-resistant seizures with significant impact on quality of life Features of anaplastic transformation such as rapid growth, marked enhancement or oedema New focal neurological deficits suggesting progression Atypical location (e.g. brainstem) complicating resection Failing to identify the neuronal (ganglion cell) component and misclassifying the tumour as a pure glioma Incomplete resection resulting in continued seizures Overlooking anaplastic change in a previously indolent lesion Not testing for BRAF V600E, which carries diagnostic and therapeutic relevance Ganglioglioma is a benign glioneuronal tumour containing a mixture of dysplastic, neoplastic ganglion (neuronal) cells and a neoplastic glial component, usually astrocytic. It commonly arises in the cerebral cortex, most often the temporal lobe, and grows slowly, frequently forming a cyst with a solid mural nodule. Activation of the MAP kinase signalling pathway, most characteristically through the BRAF V600E mutation, is a recurrent molecular event. The disorganised neuronal and glial architecture disrupts cortical circuitry and produces the chronic focal epilepsy that dominates presentation. Rarely the glial component progresses, giving an anaplastic ganglioglioma with more aggressive behaviour. Prognosis is excellent for the typical grade 1 tumour, with complete resection often curative and high rates of long-term seizure freedom. Anaplastic gangliogliomas are uncommon but behave more aggressively and may require adjuvant treatment; BRAF-targeted therapy is an option in selected higher-grade or unresectable cases.

Ganglion cyst — ganglion, synovial cyst, dorsal wrist ganglion, Bible cyst Giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath Lipoma or other benign soft-tissue tumour Extensor tenosynovitis or synovial swelling Carpal boss (osteoarthritic osteophyte) Aneurysm at the volar wrist (near the radial artery) Rarely, a soft-tissue sarcoma Usually diagnosed clinically, aided by transillumination Ultrasound to confirm a cystic lesion, identify an occult ganglion, and assess its relation to vessels and tendons MRI for occult, deep, or atypical swellings and to exclude other soft-tissue lesions Consider vascular imaging for a pulsatile volar wrist mass before any intervention Histology after excision to confirm the diagnosis A ganglion is the commonest soft-tissue swelling of the hand and wrist, presenting as a smooth, firm, rounded lump that may fluctuate in size The most frequent sites are the dorsal wrist (arising from the scapholunate region), the volar wrist, and the flexor tendon sheath of the fingers The cyst contains a viscous, gelatinous mucin and typically transilluminates, which helps distinguish it from a solid mass It arises from a joint capsule or tendon sheath and communicates with the joint through a valve-like stalk, so it is not a true cyst with an epithelial lining Many are painless and diagnosed on appearance alone; discomfort, if present, relates to size, position, or pressure on adjacent structures A small occult dorsal ganglion can cause wrist pain before it becomes visible and may only be found on imaging Reassurance and observation are appropriate for most, as a significant proportion resolve spontaneously Aspiration can relieve symptoms but recurrence is common, and the old practice of striking the cyst is not recommended Surgical excision including the stalk and capsular origin gives the lowest recurrence rate but still carries a risk of recurrence and of scar or stiffness A rapidly enlarging, hard, fixed, or irregular mass suggesting a soft-tissue tumour A pulsatile volar wrist swelling raising the possibility of an aneurysm Neurological symptoms from compression of an adjacent nerve Signs of infection or unexpected features prompting further imaging or biopsy Assuming any wrist lump is a ganglion and missing a tumour or aneurysm Aspirating a volar wrist mass without first excluding a vascular lesion Underestimating recurrence after aspiration or incomplete excision Overlooking an occult dorsal ganglion as a cause of unexplained wrist pain A ganglion forms from mucoid degeneration of the connective tissue of a joint capsule or tendon sheath. Mucin accumulates to form a cyst that connects to the underlying joint via a tortuous, valve-like duct, allowing one-way flow of fluid that fills the cyst. It lacks a true synovial or epithelial lining. Local irritation or minor trauma may contribute, and the fluctuation in size reflects communication with the joint. Ganglia are benign, and a large proportion resolve without treatment; aspiration has a high recurrence rate, and surgical excision reduces but does not eliminate recurrence.

Ganglion wrist — wrist ganglion cyst, synovial ganglion Extensor or flexor tenosynovitis with associated swelling Giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath Lipoma or other benign soft-tissue tumour Carpal boss (osteoarthritic exostosis) Scapholunate instability causing dorsal wrist pain Radial artery aneurysm mimicking a volar ganglion Soft-tissue sarcoma in atypical or rapidly enlarging lesions Diagnosis is usually clinical with transillumination of the cyst Ultrasound to confirm a cystic anechoic lesion and define its relationship to the radial artery MRI for occult dorsal ganglia presenting as unexplained wrist pain or for atypical solid-feeling masses Plain radiographs to assess a carpal boss or associated degenerative change Aspiration demonstrating characteristic clear viscous mucin supports the diagnosis Allen test to document arterial patency before volar intervention Histological examination of any excised atypical lesion Ganglia are the commonest soft-tissue swellings of the wrist and hand, consisting of a mucin-filled cyst arising from a joint capsule or tendon sheath and connected by a pedicle with a one-way valve mechanism. The dorsal wrist ganglion classically arises from the scapholunate interval and may be occult, becoming apparent only on wrist flexion or presenting as unexplained dorsal wrist pain before it is palpable. The volar wrist ganglion typically arises near the radiocarpal or scaphotrapezial joint and lies close to the radial artery, an important consideration before aspiration or excision. Cysts transilluminate, are usually mobile and may fluctuate in size, often enlarging with activity and regressing with rest. A significant proportion resolve spontaneously, so reassurance and observation are entirely appropriate for asymptomatic lesions once the diagnosis is confident. Aspiration is simple but carries a high recurrence rate; surgical excision including the capsular pedicle and stalk offers the lowest recurrence but is not recurrence-free. Allen test assessment of the radial and ulnar arterial supply is prudent before intervention on a volar ganglion adjacent to the radial artery. A firm mass that does not transilluminate, is fixed, or lies in an atypical site warrants imaging to exclude other pathology before it is dismissed as a ganglion. It is thought to arise from mucoid degeneration of periarticular connective tissue and from capsular or tendon-sheath microtrauma, with a pedicle connecting the cyst to the underlying joint. A hypothesised one-way valve at the stalk allows joint fluid to pass into the cyst but not back, explaining fluctuation in size and the tendency to recur if the stalk is not addressed. Benign with an excellent outlook; many resolve without treatment, and although aspiration is frequently followed by recurrence, meticulous surgical excision of the cyst and its stalk achieves durable control in most patients.

neuropathies Attributing progressive palsies to idiopathic causes without excluding malignancy Overlooking cerebrospinal fluid cytology when carcinomatous meningitis is possible Garcin syndrome arises when a pathological process at the base of the skull progressively involves the cranial nerves as they traverse or exit their bony foramina on one side. Most often this is an infiltrative or compressive skull-base malignancy, classically nasopharyngeal carcinoma extending through the skull base, which sequentially compresses or infiltrates multiple cranial nerves. Prognosis is largely that of the underlying cause; when due to an infiltrative skull-base malignancy such as nasopharyngeal carcinoma the outlook is generally guarded, though early identification and directed treatment of the responsible lesion offer the best chance of stabilising the deficits.

Gas Gangrene (Clostridial Myonecrosis) — clostridial myonecrosis Necrotizing fasciitis (including type I polymicrobial and C. perfringens necrotizing fasciitis); distinction from clostridial myonecrosis is made by muscle biopsy (p.1218/1241) Other histotoxic clostridial necrotizing soft tissue infections (C. histolyticum, C. septicum, C. novyi, C. sordellii) (p.1241) Synergistic necrotizing cellulitis / crepitant (crepitus) cellulitis due to mixed anaerobic and aerobic flora (p.gas-forming soft-tissue infections) Fournier's gangrene (C. perfringens with mixed aerobic/anaerobic microbes can cause aggressive type I necrotizing fasciitis or Fournier's gangrene) (p.1239) Clostridial sepsis / bacteremia with myonecrosis (grave prognosis when bacteremia accompanies myonecrosis) (p.1240) Gram stain of a smear of involved tissue (direct examination is of major importance): large gram-positive/gram-variable rods with paucity of leukocytes (p.1242) Surgical exploration with histopathologic examination (widespread tissue destruction, paucity of leukocytes in infected tissue with accumulation of leukocytes in adjacent vessels, gram-positive rods with or without spores) (p.1242) Blood cultures (anaerobic) - obtain when spontaneous gas gangrene is suspected, as bacteremia usually precedes cutaneous manifestations by several hours (p.1242) CT and MRI to define localized vs fascial-plane spread (adjunct only; must not delay surgery) (p.1242) Needle aspiration or punch biopsy may provide an etiologic diagnosis in at least 20% of cases (p.1242) In survivors of C. septicum bacteremia/spontaneous gangrene: aggressive diagnostic workup to rule out gastrointestinal pathology (e.g., colonic malignancy) (p.1241) Gas tracking/dissecting tissue planes from non-clostridial gas-forming processes; note gas gangrene may develop in the ABSENCE of clostridial infection (other gas-producing organisms) (p.crepitus/gas-forming infections) C. perfringens myonecrosis (gas gangrene) is one of the most fulminant gram-positive bacterial infections of humans; it is a true emergency requiring immediate surgical debridement and is invariably fatal if untreated (p.1241). Traumatic gas gangrene presents with sudden onset of excruciating pain at the affected site and rapid development of a foul-smelling wound with thin serosanguineous discharge and gas bubbles; brawny edema and induration give way to cutaneous blisters with bluish to maroon-colored fluid (p.1241). The patient's pain and toxic appearance are characteristically out of proportion to physical findings; the patient may be febrile, apathetic, tachycardic, tachypneic, and may express a feeling of impending doom (p.1218, cross-ref Chap.159). The margin between healthy and necrotic tissue often advances several inches per hour despite appropriate antibiotic therapy; radical amputation remains the single best life-saving intervention (p.1241). Incubation period for traumatic gas gangrene can be as short as 6 h and is usually <4 days (p.1241). Spontaneous (nontraumatic) gas gangrene arises by hematogenous seeding of normal muscle, principally with C. septicum (aerotolerant), C. perfringens, and C. novyi, from a gastrointestinal portal of entry (p.1241). First symptom of spontaneous gas gangrene may be confusion followed by abrupt onset of excruciating pain in the absence of trauma; with fever, these findings should heighten suspicion (p.1242). Gram staining of drainage or tissue biopsy is usually definitive in traumatic disease, showing large gram-positive (or gram-variable) rods, an ABSENCE of inflammatory cells, and widespread soft tissue necrosis (p.1241). CT and MRI help determine whether infection is localized or spreading along fascial planes, but must NOT replace surgical exploration, Gram's staining, and histopathologic examination (p.1242). Emergent thorough surgical debridement with wide resection back to healthy viable muscle and skin is of extreme importance; closure of traumatic wounds or compound fractures should be delayed 5-6 days until sites are certain to be free of infection (p.1242). Pain out of proportion to physical findings - excruciating pain at the affected site (p.1241/1218) Crepitus and gas in the tissues / gas on imaging with rapidly progressive necrosis (p.1241-1242) Tissue margin advancing several inches per hour despite antibiotics (p.1241) Systemic toxaemia: shock, hypotension, multiorgan failure, bacteremia, intravascular hemolysis (p.1241-1242) Foul-smelling serosanguineous wound discharge with bluish/maroon hemorrhagic bullae and brawny induration (p.1241) Spontaneous excruciating pain with confusion and fever and NO obvious portal of entry - suggests spontaneous gas gangrene (correct diagnosis frequently delayed or missed) (p.1242) Feeling of impending doom with apathy, tachycardia, tachypnea (p.1218) Diagnosis depends on clinical signs and symptoms, not solely on bacteriologic findings - 30-80% of open traumatic wounds are contaminated with clostridia and clostridia are isolated equally from suppurative and well-healing wounds (p.1239). In spontaneous gas gangrene the lack of an obvious portal of entry means the correct diagnosis is frequently delayed or missed (p.1242). Adjunctive procedures (CT, MRI) or transport to hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) units must NOT delay emergent surgical debridement (p.1243). The value of HBO remains controversial; HBO inhibits C. perfringens but not the more aerotolerant C. septicum, and blood/macerated muscle inhibit its bactericidal potential in vitro - HBO provides benefit only if surgery and antibiotics precede it (p.1243). Avoid prolonged tourniquet application and surgical closure of contaminated traumatic wounds; patients with compound fractures are at significant risk if the wound is closed surgically (p.1243). C. perfringens remains largely penicillin-susceptible but clindamycin resistance has been reported and is increasing in some regions; C. tertium is resistant to penicillin, cephalosporins, and clindamycin - good anaerobic susceptibility testing matters (p.1242-1243). Development requires an anaerobic environment and wound contamination with clostridial spores or vegetative organisms. Devitalized tissue, foreign bodies, and ischemia lower local oxygen and favor outgrowth. For C. perfringens and C. novyi, trauma must be sufficient to interrupt the blood supply to establish the anaerobic niche; the more aerotolerant C. septicum and C. tertium can seed normal tissue from GI lesions without this. Once established, organisms proliferate and elaborate exotoxins. The major C. perfringens toxins in gas gangrene are alpha toxin (a lethal hemolysin with phospholipase C and sphingomyelinase activity; the major virulence factor) and theta toxin (perfringolysin, a cholesterol-dependent cytolysin). Severe pain, rapid progression, marked tissue destruction, and the characteristic paucity of neutrophils in tissue are largely attributable to alpha-toxin-induced vascular occlusion by heterotypic platelet/neutrophil aggregates (via activation of platelet gpIIb/IIIa). Late cardiovascular collapse reflects theta toxin causing reduced systemic vascular resistance with increased cardiac output ('warm shock') and alpha toxin directly suppressing myocardial contractility, producing profound hypotension (p.1242). Invariably fatal if untreated. When patients become bacteremic the mortality rate exceeds 50%. Spontaneous (nontraumatic) gas gangrene mortality ranges from 67-100% in adults and 59% in children (most childhood deaths within 24 h of onset). Prognosis is more favorable when an extremity is involved (easier debridement) than the trunk or visceral organs. Disease is most likely to progress to shock and death in patients with associated bacteremia and intravascular hemolysis; mortality is highest for patients in shock at diagnosis. Gas gangrene associated with bacteremia represents a later stage with the worst outcomes. Survivors may undergo multiple debridements and face prolonged hospitalization and rehabilitation (p.1242-1243).

gastric bezoar — phytobezoar, trichobezoar, gastric concretion Gastric outlet obstruction from peptic stricture Gastric adenocarcinoma or lymphoma Gastric volvulus Peptic ulcer disease Retained food from gastroparesis without a discrete bezoar Ingested foreign body Superior mesenteric artery syndrome Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy of the underlying mucosa Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen to define size, location and complications Barium meal showing a mottled, freely mobile intraluminal filling defect Gastric emptying study where dysmotility is suspected Full blood count and iron studies if chronic occult blood loss Markers of nutritional depletion Psychiatric assessment where a trichobezoar is confirmed A bezoar is a retained, compacted mass of indigestible material within the gastrointestinal tract, most often lodged in the stomach. Phytobezoars composed of undigested plant fibre are the commonest type; diospyrobezoars from unripe persimmons are particularly hard and refractory to dissolution. Trichobezoars from ingested hair occur almost exclusively in young women with trichotillomania and trichophagia; extension of the mass through the pylorus into the small bowel defines Rapunzel syndrome. Delayed gastric emptying is central to formation, so prior gastric surgery such as vagotomy or partial gastrectomy, diabetic gastroparesis, hypochlorhydria and poor dentition are key predisposing factors. Presentation ranges from vague epigastric fullness, early satiety and halitosis to frank gastric outlet obstruction, mucosal ulceration and bleeding. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is both diagnostic and first-line therapeutic, allowing fragmentation and retrieval under direct vision. Enzymatic or chemical dissolution such as cellulase or cola lavage can soften phytobezoars but is ineffective for trichobezoars, which usually require surgical removal. Always look for a second bezoar or distal migration causing small bowel obstruction after clearing a gastric one. Overlooking a coexisting distal bezoar and precipitating small bowel obstruction after gastric clearance. Missing the underlying psychiatric disorder in trichobezoar, leading to recurrence. Confusing retained food in gastroparesis with a true bezoar, or the reverse. Aggressive endoscopic fragmentation of a large hard phytobezoar without a plan for retrieving the fragments. Bezoar formation reflects an imbalance between the ingestion of poorly digestible material and the stomach's ability to break it down and empty it. Impaired gastric motility and reduced acid-peptic digestion allow fibrous plant residues, hair or medication to aggregate around a nidus that progressively enlarges as further debris and mucus adhere. Tannins and cellulose in certain fruits, notably unripe persimmons, polymerise in an acid environment to produce especially dense, adherent concretions. Hair is resistant to both digestion and peristalsis, so strands become enmeshed within the mucosal folds and mat together over months to years, moulding to the shape of the gastric lumen. The resulting mass causes symptoms through mechanical mass effect, pressure necrosis of the overlying mucosa and obstruction at the pylorus or, if fragments migrate, more distally in the small bowel. Prognosis is generally excellent once the bezoar is removed and the predisposing factor addressed, but recurrence is common if gastroparesis, dietary habits or trichophagia persist.

gastric diverticulum — gastric diverticulum, stomach diverticulum adrenal mass or adenoma on cross-sectional imaging pancreatic pseudocyst or cystic neoplasm para-oesophageal hiatus hernia gastric duplication cyst gastrointestinal stromal tumour or submucosal gastric mass gastric ulcer or malignancy retroperitoneal cyst or lymphadenopathy upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with fundal retroflexion barium meal to demonstrate contrast filling the sac computed tomography with oral contrast to confirm communication with the stomach endoscopic ultrasound to assess wall layers and exclude a submucosal mass cross-sectional imaging to distinguish from adrenal or pancreatic lesions biopsy of the diverticular mucosa if malignancy is suspected Gastric diverticulum is a rare outpouching of the stomach wall, with the great majority being congenital true diverticula located on the posterior wall of the gastric fundus just below the oesophagogastric junction. The characteristic juxta-cardial posterior fundal location and its cystic appearance can mimic an adrenal mass, pancreatic pseudocyst or other retroperitoneal lesion on cross-sectional imaging. Acquired diverticula are less common, usually located in the antrum or prepyloric region, and tend to be pulsion or traction type related to adjacent inflammation, ulcer or prior surgery. Most gastric diverticula are asymptomatic and found incidentally; when symptomatic they cause vague epigastric or postprandial pain, dyspepsia, nausea or a sensation of fullness. Complications, though uncommon, include bleeding from mucosal ulceration within the sac, perforation and, rarely, malignancy arising in the diverticulum. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with retroflexion in the fundus, or barium study, confirms the diagnosis and helps distinguish it from an extrinsic mass. Because it can be mistaken for an adrenal or pancreatic lesion, awareness prevents unnecessary intervention; oral contrast filling the sac on imaging is a helpful clue. Symptomatic or complicated diverticula are treated with surgical resection, increasingly by laparoscopic diverticulectomy, while asymptomatic lesions are managed conservatively. gastrointestinal bleeding or melaena from the sac severe or acute abdominal pain suggesting perforation weight loss or a mass raising concern for malignancy signs of gastric outlet compromise rapidly enlarging or irregular lesion on imaging Misdiagnosing a posterior fundal diverticulum as an adrenal or pancreatic mass and pursuing unnecessary intervention. Failing to retroflex in the fundus at endoscopy and missing the diverticular opening. Attributing non-specific dyspepsia to the diverticulum without excluding commoner causes. Overlooking bleeding or ulceration within the sac as a source of occult blood loss. Not considering malignancy in a symptomatic or atypical diverticulum. Gastric diverticula are either congenital or acquired. Congenital (true) diverticula contain all layers of the gastric wall and typically arise on the posterior fundic wall near the cardia, at a point of relative muscular weakness where the longitudinal and circular muscle layers are deficient and where extraperitoneal support is limited. Acquired diverticula are usually false (pulsion) diverticula, in which mucosa and submucosa herniate through the muscular wall in response to raised intraluminal pressure, or traction diverticula caused by external scarring from adjacent inflammatory processes such as peptic ulcer, pancreatitis or prior surgery; these are more often antral or prepyloric. Retention of food and acid within the sac may lead to mucosal inflammation, ulceration and, rarely, bleeding or perforation. The characteristic posterior juxta-cardial position of congenital diverticula explains why they are readily mistaken for retroperitoneal or adrenal lesions on imaging. The prognosis is excellent for the majority of asymptomatic diverticula managed conservatively, and surgical resection of symptomatic lesions is generally curative. Malignant transformation is rare but carries the prognosis of the underlying tumour.

gastric dumping syndrome — dumping syndrome, rapid gastric emptying, post-gastrectomy dumping postprandial (reactive) hypoglycaemia from other causes insulinoma and other causes of endogenous hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia afferent or efferent loop syndrome after gastric surgery bile-acid or bacterial-overgrowth diarrhoea following surgery carcinoid syndrome and other neuroendocrine tumours causing flushing autonomic dysfunction and postural hypotension anxiety or panic disorder with autonomic symptoms oral glucose challenge with serial glucose and haematocrit measurement gastric emptying scintigraphy to confirm rapid emptying continuous glucose monitoring to capture late postprandial hypoglycaemia modified Sigstad scoring and structured symptom questionnaires upper gastrointestinal endoscopy or contrast study to assess post-surgical anatomy 72-hour fast or supervised testing where insulinoma is suspected tests for bacterial overgrowth or bile-acid malabsorption when diarrhoea predominates A complication of gastric surgery (partial gastrectomy, pyloroplasty, vagotomy) and increasingly of bariatric procedures such as sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass, caused by loss of normal pyloric regulation of gastric emptying. Early dumping occurs within about 15 to 30 minutes of eating and comprises both gastrointestinal (cramping, borborygmi, diarrhoea, bloating) and vasomotor (flushing, palpitations, tachycardia, light-headedness, need to lie down) features. Late dumping occurs one to three hours after a meal and reflects reactive (postprandial) hypoglycaemia, presenting with sweating, tremor, hunger, confusion and palpitations. A carbohydrate-rich meal, particularly rapidly absorbed simple sugars, is the classic trigger for both phases. The modified Sigstad score and an oral glucose challenge with serial glucose and haematocrit measurement help confirm the diagnosis when it is uncertain. First-line management is dietary: small frequent meals, restriction of simple sugars, separation of solids from liquids, and increased soluble fibre or viscosity-modifying agents to slow emptying. Somatostatin analogues are the principal pharmacological option for refractory symptoms, slowing gastric emptying and blunting the vasomotor and hormonal responses; acarbose helps specifically with late dumping. Surgical revision or feeding-tube strategies are reserved for severe, refractory cases after dietary and medical measures have failed. recurrent severe hypoglycaemia causing loss of consciousness, seizures or falls significant unintentional weight loss or malnutrition hypoglycaemic symptoms occurring in the fasting state (pointing away from dumping toward insulinoma) dehydration or syncope from severe vasomotor episodes features suggesting mechanical complications such as afferent loop obstruction Confusing late dumping hypoglycaemia (postprandial) with fasting hypoglycaemia of insulinoma, leading to unnecessary or misdirected investigation. Prescribing rapidly absorbed sugars to treat hypoglycaemic episodes, which perpetuates the cycle rather than resolving it. Overlooking dumping in bariatric surgery patients, in whom it is now a common but under-recognised cause of postprandial symptoms. Escalating to surgery before an adequate trial of dietary measures and somatostatin analogues. Attributing vasomotor symptoms solely to anxiety and missing the temporal relationship to meals. Dumping syndrome arises when ablation or bypass of the pylorus allows rapid, unregulated delivery of hyperosmolar gastric contents into the small intestine. In early dumping, the hyperosmolar load draws fluid from the intravascular compartment into the bowel lumen, causing luminal distension, increased motility and a fall in plasma volume; this, combined with release of vasoactive and incretin gut hormones, produces the gastrointestinal and vasomotor symptoms. In late dumping, rapid absorption of carbohydrate provokes an exaggerated incretin (notably GLP-1) and insulin response; the insulin overshoot outlasts the transient hyperglycaemia and precipitates reactive hypoglycaemia one to three hours after the meal. The two mechanisms frequently coexist in the same patient. Most patients improve substantially with dietary modification, and symptoms often attenuate over months to a few years as the intestine adapts; a minority have persistent, disabling symptoms requiring somatostatin analogues or surgical revision. Late dumping with recurrent hypoglycaemia can be dangerous and warrants prompt, structured management.

gastric outlet obstruction — gastric outlet obstruction, pyloric obstruction, gastroduodenal obstruction gastroparesis and other functional gastric motility disorders peptic ulcer disease with pyloric channel scarring gastric or duodenal adenocarcinoma pancreatic head or periampullary carcinoma superior mesenteric artery (Wilkie) syndrome Crohn disease of the duodenum bezoar, caustic stricture or annular pancreas upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy of any stricture or mass serum electrolytes, renal function and blood gas to characterise metabolic alkalosis contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen to stage malignancy and define anatomy upper gastrointestinal contrast study to demonstrate the level of obstruction gastric emptying study when a functional disorder such as gastroparesis is suspected full blood count and nutritional assessment including albumin Gastric outlet obstruction is a mechanical or functional blockage of gastric emptying at the antrum, pylorus or proximal duodenum, presenting with postprandial vomiting of undigested food, early satiety, bloating and weight loss. In adults, malignancy (pancreatic, gastric antral or duodenal carcinoma) has overtaken peptic ulcer disease as the leading cause, so any new obstruction warrants exclusion of cancer. Chronic vomiting of gastric contents produces a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria, a classic and important electrolyte disturbance to recognise and correct. A succussion splash heard several hours after a meal and a visibly distended stomach are useful bedside signs of retained gastric content. Initial management is nasogastric decompression, correction of dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities, and acid suppression before definitive treatment. Endoscopy with biopsy is central to establishing benign versus malignant aetiology, and cross-sectional imaging defines the extent of any tumour. Benign strictures may respond to endoscopic balloon dilatation, while malignant obstruction is palliated by enteral stenting or surgical gastrojejunostomy depending on prognosis and fitness. In infants, hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is the classic cause, presenting with non-bilious projectile vomiting and a palpable pyloric olive, and is a distinct paediatric entity. haematemesis or melaena indicating bleeding signs of perforation with peritonism and sepsis severe dehydration with metabolic alkalosis and hypokalaemia weight loss, anorexia or a palpable epigastric mass suggesting malignancy aspiration of retained gastric contents Failing to recognise and correct hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis before intervention. Assuming a benign peptic cause and not biopsying to exclude malignancy. Confusing functional gastroparesis with true mechanical obstruction. Inadequate gastric decompression leading to aspiration. Overlooking nutritional depletion that needs correction before definitive treatment. Gastric outlet obstruction results from any process that mechanically narrows or functionally impairs the antropyloric or proximal duodenal outflow tract. Benign mechanical causes include peptic ulcer disease, where acute pyloric channel oedema or chronic fibrotic scarring narrows the lumen, as well as caustic-injury strictures, Crohn disease and rarely bezoars or prolapsing polyps. Malignant causes include distal gastric adenocarcinoma, periampullary and pancreatic head tumours invading or compressing the duodenum, and duodenal tumours. Obstruction leads to retention of ingested food and gastric secretions, progressive gastric dilatation and eventually mucosal ischaemia and atony. Persistent vomiting of hydrochloric-acid-rich gastric fluid produces loss of chloride and hydrogen ions with a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; secondary hypokalaemia and volume depletion drive renal potassium and hydrogen excretion, causing the characteristic paradoxical aciduria. Chronic obstruction also impairs nutrition and causes weight loss. Prognosis depends heavily on aetiology: benign obstruction from peptic disease or a dilatable stricture generally has a good outcome once corrected, whereas malignant obstruction carries the prognosis of the underlying cancer and is often managed palliatively. Prompt correction of fluid and electrolyte derangement is essential to reduce perioperative risk.

Gastric volvulus — volvulus of the stomach, organoaxial volvulus, mesenteroaxial volvulus, gastric torsion Acute gastric dilatation Gastric outlet obstruction from peptic disease or malignancy Large paraoesophageal or hiatus hernia without volvulus Myocardial infarction (given epigastric pain) Acute pancreatitis Small bowel or colonic obstruction Chest and erect abdominal radiographs showing an abnormally sited, distended stomach or intrathoracic gastric bubble CT of the chest and abdomen to confirm rotation, define the axis, and identify a diaphragmatic defect Contrast study demonstrating the site and level of obstruction where the patient is stable Upper GI endoscopy in selected non-emergency cases (with caution) Bloods including lactate and inflammatory markers to detect ischaemia Gastric volvulus is an abnormal rotation of the stomach, classified as organoaxial (around its long axis, more common and often associated with diaphragmatic defects) or mesenteroaxial (around the short axis) The classic Borchardt triad of acute presentation is severe epigastric pain and distension, retching with an inability to vomit, and difficulty passing a nasogastric tube It is frequently associated with a large paraoesophageal or hiatus hernia, diaphragmatic defects, and lax gastric ligaments, and occurs across all ages including infants Acute volvulus is a surgical emergency because rotation can obstruct and strangulate the stomach, leading to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation Chest and abdominal radiographs may show an abnormally positioned, distended gas-filled stomach, and CT confirms the rotation and any associated hernia Initial management of acute presentation is resuscitation and attempted nasogastric decompression, followed by urgent surgery to reduce the volvulus, assess viability, and repair the predisposing defect Chronic or intermittent volvulus causes recurrent postprandial pain, bloating, and early satiety and is easily overlooked Acute presentation with the Borchardt triad indicating a surgical emergency Features of strangulation or ischaemia (severe unremitting pain, haemodynamic instability, rising lactate) Inability to pass a nasogastric tube with progressive distension Signs of gastric perforation with peritonitis and sepsis Mistaking acute volvulus for simple gastric dilatation and delaying surgery Persisting with attempts to pass a nasogastric tube instead of recognising the emergency Failing to assess gastric viability and repair the predisposing hernia or defect at operation Overlooking the diagnosis in a patient with a known large hiatus hernia and vague chronic symptoms Underestimating the severity in elderly patients with atypical or referred pain The stomach is normally anchored by the gastrohepatic, gastrosplenic, gastrocolic, and gastrophrenic ligaments and by its fixation at the oesophagogastric junction and pylorus. Laxity, elongation, or absence of these attachments, or a diaphragmatic defect such as a large paraoesophageal hernia, allows the stomach to rotate abnormally. Rotation of more than around 180 degrees produces a closed-loop obstruction at both the gastro-oesophageal junction and the pylorus. Progressive gaseous and fluid distension raises intragastric pressure and, together with twisting of the mesentery, compromises the blood supply. Unrelieved, this leads to venous congestion, ischaemia, full-thickness necrosis, and perforation with catastrophic sepsis. Prompt reduction and repair of acute volvulus before ischaemia develops carries a good outcome, but delayed diagnosis with strangulation and necrosis is associated with high morbidity and mortality. Chronic volvulus generally does well after elective repair of the underlying defect, with low recurrence when fixation and hernia repair are adequate.

Gastrinoma — gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumour, gastrin-producing islet cell tumour, G-cell tumour Proton pump inhibitor-induced hypergastrinaemia, the commonest cause of a raised gastrin Atrophic gastritis or pernicious anaemia with achlorhydria-driven hypergastrinaemia Retained gastric antrum syndrome after previous gastric surgery Antral G-cell hyperplasia Renal impairment or gastric outlet obstruction raising gastrin Helicobacter pylori-associated hypergastrinaemia Other functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours Fasting serum gastrin, off acid suppression where safe, with concurrent gastric pH or acid output Secretin stimulation test showing a paradoxical rise in gastrin to confirm gastrinoma Chromogranin A as a general neuroendocrine tumour marker Somatostatin receptor PET/CT (DOTATATE) for localisation and staging Endoscopic ultrasound and multiphase CT or MRI, with attention to the duodenum and gastrinoma triangle Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy documenting ulcers, prominent gastric folds and duodenal lesions MEN1 genetic testing with serum calcium, PTH and prolactin Gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumour that causes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome through unregulated hypergastrinaemia and gastric acid hypersecretion Most arise within the gastrinoma triangle, bounded by the junction of the cystic and common bile ducts, the junction of the second and third parts of the duodenum, and the junction of the pancreatic neck and body Duodenal primaries are now recognised as more common than pancreatic; they are often small and multiple, whereas pancreatic gastrinomas tend to be larger with higher metastatic potential Approximately 20 to 30 per cent occur within MEN1, typically as multifocal duodenal tumours that require an individualised surgical approach Malignant behaviour is common, with spread to regional lymph nodes and liver; hepatic metastases are the principal determinant of survival Gastrinomas strongly express somatostatin receptors, so DOTATATE PET is highly sensitive for localisation and staging Fasting serum gastrin must be interpreted with concurrent gastric pH and off proton pump inhibitors where safe, since acid suppression itself raises gastrin Curative resection is achievable for localised sporadic disease, whereas multifocal duodenal MEN1 tumours make cure less likely and management is tailored Complicated peptic ulcer disease with haemorrhage, perforation or gastric outlet obstruction Multiple or distal duodenal or jejunal ulcers, or ulcers refractory to standard therapy Peptic ulceration accompanied by chronic diarrhoea and weight loss Hepatic metastases at presentation Features of MEN1 prompting family screening Measuring gastrin while the patient is taking a proton pump inhibitor, producing misleading elevation Attributing recurrent ulcers to Helicobacter pylori or NSAIDs and missing an underlying gastrinoma Searching only the pancreas and overlooking small duodenal primaries Stopping acid suppression abruptly for testing without safeguards, risking severe ulcer complications Failing to screen for MEN1, which alters surgical strategy and family management Gastrinoma is a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour that autonomously secretes gastrin. Persistent hypergastrinaemia stimulates enterochromaffin-like and parietal cells, driving parietal cell hyperplasia and marked gastric acid hypersecretion. The resulting hyperchlorhydria produces peptic ulceration that is often multiple, distally located or refractory, together with gastro-oesophageal reflux and secretory diarrhoea from acid injury to the small bowel and inactivation of pancreatic enzymes. Tumours arise from gastrin-producing cells of the duodenum or pancreas; in MEN1 biallelic loss of menin underlies the characteristic multifocal duodenal tumours. Malignant potential relates to size, location (pancreatic more than duodenal) and grade, with the liver the principal site of metastasis. Prognosis is largely determined by the presence and extent of hepatic metastases and by tumour grade: localised gastrinoma has favourable long-term survival after resection, whereas diffuse hepatic metastatic disease carries a considerably poorer outlook despite effective acid control.
