neoplasia type 1 such as hypercalcaemia Rapid symptom rebound on stopping acid suppression Attributing hypergastrinaemia to the tumour when it is actually driven by acid-suppressing drugs or atrophic gastritis Dangerously withdrawing acid suppression to test gastrin in a patient at risk of ulcer complications Overlooking multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 and its associated hyperparathyroidism Assuming a single tumour when duodenal gastrinomas are often small and multiple Delaying somatostatin-receptor imaging and missing occult metastatic disease Gastrinoma is a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumour, usually arising in the duodenal wall or pancreas. Autonomous, unregulated gastrin release drives sustained hypersecretion of gastric acid and trophic expansion of the parietal cell mass. The resulting acid load overwhelms mucosal defences, producing severe and recurrent peptic ulceration, while the low intraluminal pH in the small bowel inactivates pancreatic lipase and injures the mucosa, causing diarrhoea and fat malabsorption. A substantial minority occur as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, and a significant proportion behave malignantly with regional nodal and hepatic spread. Effective acid suppression with proton-pump inhibition controls symptoms in most patients, and complete surgical resection of localised sporadic tumours can be curative. Outlook is largely determined by tumour biology and the presence of hepatic metastases, with indolent disease often compatible with prolonged survival.

Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease — GORD, GERD, acid reflux disease Functional heartburn Reflux hypersensitivity Eosinophilic oesophagitis Peptic ulcer disease Cardiac chest pain Oesophageal motility disorder or malignancy Empirical trial of acid suppression for typical symptoms Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy for alarm features or refractory symptoms Ambulatory reflux (pH or pH-impedance) monitoring to confirm reflux and correlate symptoms Oesophageal manometry before anti-reflux surgery Biopsy to assess for Barrett oesophagus or eosinophilic oesophagitis Troublesome symptoms or complications arising from reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus The cardinal symptoms are heartburn and acid regurgitation, and there may be atypical or extra-oesophageal features such as chest pain, chronic cough or laryngeal symptoms It is broadly divided into erosive oesophagitis and non-erosive reflux disease based on endoscopic findings Typical uncomplicated symptoms are often managed empirically with lifestyle measures and acid suppression without initial endoscopy Alarm features such as dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding or anaemia warrant prompt endoscopy Complications include peptic stricture, Barrett oesophagus and, rarely, oesophageal adenocarcinoma Dysphagia or odynophagia Weight loss or gastrointestinal bleeding Iron-deficiency anaemia New symptoms in an older patient or a suspicious mass Attributing symptoms to reflux without confirming it in refractory cases Missing eosinophilic oesophagitis as a cause of reflux-like symptoms and dysphagia Overlooking cardiac causes of chest pain Ignoring alarm features that mandate endoscopy Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease results from excessive reflux of gastric contents across a dysfunctional anti-reflux barrier at the gastro-oesophageal junction. Transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations, a hypotensive sphincter, hiatus hernia and impaired oesophageal clearance allow acidic (and sometimes non-acidic) refluxate to contact the oesophageal mucosa. Prolonged acid exposure injures the mucosa, causing oesophagitis and, over time, metaplastic and stricturing changes, while symptoms also depend on mucosal sensitivity. Most patients achieve good symptom control with lifestyle measures and acid suppression; a minority develop complications such as stricture or Barrett oesophagus that require ongoing surveillance or intervention.

Gastrointestinal Endoscopy — GI endoscopy, EGD, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy, ERCP, endoscopic ultrasound, EUS Melena: distinguish proximal upper-GI bleeding from slow right-colon or small-bowel sources, especially in older patients with slow colonic transit Hematochezia: colonic source vs brisk upper-GI bleed with rapid transit Dyspepsia: gastroesophageal reflux vs peptic ulcer disease vs nonulcer (functional) dyspepsia vs uncommon gastric/esophageal malignancy Colonic dilatation: mechanical obstruction (e.g., malignancy, sigmoid volvulus) vs acute colonic pseudoobstruction Diverticular hematochezia: exclude vascular ectasias, colitis, and colon cancer before attributing bleeding to a diverticulum 24-hour ambulatory pH and impedance monitoring as the most sensitive test for GERD, capturing nonerosive reflux disease that endoscopy may miss MRCP and EUS for bile duct stones (>90% accurate), reserving ERCP for cases needing therapy or high pretest probability Noninvasive H. pylori testing (serology for past/current infection; urea breath test and stool antigen for current infection) before or in lieu of endoscopy in younger patients without alarm features Capsule endoscopy as the typical next test after negative upper and lower endoscopy in suspected small-bowel bleeding (diagnostic yield ~55%), with a patency capsule beforehand if stricture risk exists Plain abdominal radiography (and water-soluble contrast enema or CT) to assess colonic dilatation and differentiate obstruction from pseudoobstruction; neck/chest radiographs before endoscopy for esophageal obstruction with fever, >=24-h impaction, or sharp object Flexible endoscopes generate an electronic video image from a CCD or CMOS chip at the tip, with operator tip-deflection controls, light delivery, and working channels for washing, suction, and accessory passage (Harrison 22e p.2465). Upper endoscopy (EGD) is the best method for examining the upper GI mucosa and is superior to a barium upper-GI series for detecting gastric ulcers and flat lesions such as Barrett's esophagus, while also permitting directed biopsy and therapy (Harrison 22e p.2465). Colonoscopy is the gold standard for imaging the colonic mucosa, reaching the cecum in over 95% of cases, with greater sensitivity than barium enema for colitis, polyps, and cancer; CT colonography rivals it for many polyps and cancers but is less sensitive for flat serrated lesions (Harrison 22e p.2465). For obscure small-bowel bleeding, capsule endoscopy visualizes mucosa beyond the reach of a conventional endoscope but is purely diagnostic; push and balloon-assisted enteroscopy allow deeper intubation with biopsy and therapy (Harrison 22e p.2465-2466). EUS provides the most accurate preoperative local staging of esophageal, pancreatic, and rectal malignancies but does not detect distant metastases beyond its imaging range; it also enables fine-needle aspiration/biopsy and a growing range of therapeutic drainage procedures (Harrison 22e p.2468). Endoscopic stigmata of a peptic ulcer carry prognostic value: a clean-based ulcer has a low (3-5%) rebleeding risk, flat pigmented spots ~10%, adherent clot ~20%, a visible vessel ~40%, and active spurting ~90% (Harrison 22e p.2478-2479). Over 90% of patients with melena bleed proximal to the ligament of Treitz and ~85% with hematochezia bleed from the colon, but massive hematochezia can reflect a brisk upper-GI source with rapid transit, warranting urgent upper endoscopy (Harrison 22e p.2476). Severity of the initial hemorrhage is the most important indicator for urgent endoscopy; falling hematocrit and hemoglobin lag behind the clinical course and are unreliable gauges of acute blood loss (Harrison 22e p.2476). Acute esophageal obstruction from food impaction or a foreign body is an endoscopic emergency; untreated it can lead to esophageal ulceration, ischemia, and perforation, and an underlying web, ring, or stricture is often present (Harrison 22e p.2484-2485). In acute colonic pseudoobstruction (Ogilvie's), the risk of cecal perforation rises when cecal diameter exceeds 12 cm, prompting decompression with intravenous neostigmine or colonoscopy (Harrison 22e p.2487). Charcot's triad (jaundice, abdominal pain, fever) is present in ~70% of ascending cholangitis; the addition of shock and confusion (Reynolds's pentad) signals high mortality and warrants urgent biliary drainage, typically by ERCP (Harrison 22e p.2489). Long-standing GERD confers a roughly sixfold increased risk of Barrett's esophagus versus reflux of under one year; screening EGD should be considered after a chronic (>=10-year) GERD history even when symptoms are mild (Harrison 22e p.2490-2491). Resting hypotension, orthostatic vital-sign change, repeated hematemesis, bloody nasogastric aspirate not clearing with lavage, or transfusion requirement — consider urgent endoscopy within 12-24 h Dyspepsia or reflux with alarm features (weight loss, obstructive symptoms, dysphagia, GI bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia) — perform endoscopy at the outset Esophageal food/foreign-body impaction with hypersalivation and inability to swallow water — endoscopic emergency Reynolds's pentad (Charcot's triad plus shock and confusion) in ascending cholangitis — urgent biliary drainage Cecal diameter exceeding 12 cm in colonic pseudoobstruction — impending perforation Age >70, cirrhosis, coagulopathy, or respiratory/renal failure with GI bleeding — higher rebleeding risk warranting prompt evaluation Relying on hematocrit/hemoglobin to gauge acute bleeding — these lag behind the clinical course Assuming melena always means an upper-GI source or hematochezia always a colonic source — exceptions occur with transit-dependent presentations Performing ERCP indiscriminately in gallstone pancreatitis — only ~20% retain an ampullary/common-bile-duct stone, and initial MRCP/EUS reduces unnecessary ERCP and its adverse events Using endoscopy to diagnose nonerosive reflux disease — it will miss symptomatic reflux without esophagitis Treating a Mallory-Weiss tear bearing a nonbleeding sentinel clot like a peptic ulcer — unlike ulcers, such tears rarely rebleed and need no endoscopic therapy Relying on epinephrine injection alone for ulcer hemostasis — it slows bleeding but is not definitive monotherapy Obtaining radiographic contrast studies before endoscopy in suspected esophageal obstruction — contrast interferes with the subsequent endoscopic procedure Proceeding to endoscopy in marked coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia without correction — hemostatic techniques are limited and correction may itself resolve bleeding Gastrointestinal endoscopy is a diagnostic and therapeutic modality rather than a disease; it directly visualizes mucosal and luminal pathology and adjacent structures (via EUS) and provides access for tissue sampling and intervention. Many of the conditions it manages share a vascular or mechanical basis: peptic ulcers bleed when erosion exposes a submucosal vessel; a Dieulafoy's lesion is an abnormally large-caliber persistent artery running just beneath the epithelium that bleeds through a focal mucosal defect; a Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal rent at the gastroesophageal junction caused by retching/vomiting that can disrupt a submucosal arteriole; colonic diverticular bleeding arises from the nutrient artery at the base of a diverticulum; and vascular ectasias are flat mucosal vascular anomalies (e.g., GAVE/watermelon stomach) that cause slow blood loss. Variceal bleeding reflects portal hypertension. Obstructive syndromes (esophageal food impaction, gastric outlet obstruction, colonic obstruction/pseudoobstruction, biliary obstruction by stone) produce luminal blockage that endoscopy can relieve. Barrett's esophagus represents columnar metaplasia of distal esophageal squamous mucosa driven by chronic acid reflux and is a precursor to adenocarcinoma (Harrison 22e p.2464-2491). Outcomes depend on the underlying condition and endoscopic findings. Most GI bleeding stops spontaneously. Endoscopic therapy of high-risk peptic ulcer stigmata lowers rebleeding to about 5-10%. Endoscopic variceal ligation controls acute esophageal variceal hemorrhage in up to 90% of patients, though chronic eradication therapy prevents long-term rebleeding in only ~50%. A clean-based ulcer carries a low (3-5%) rebleeding risk, permitting early discharge of suitable patients. Post-ERCP pancreatitis is usually mild and self-limited but can be severe. Delayed biliary drainage in ascending cholangitis increases morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.2464-2491). Peptic ulcer rebleeding risk by endoscopic stigmata: clean base 3-5%; flat pigmented spots ~10%; adherent clot ~20%; nonbleeding visible vessel ~40%; active spurting ~90% (Harrison 22e p.2478-2479). Procedural adverse-event risk: bleeding/perforation under 1:1000 for diagnostic EGD, flexible sigmoidoscopy, and colonoscopy, rising to 0.5-5% with therapeutic maneuvers; ERCP carries ~5% pancreatitis risk (up to ~25% in young, anicteric patients with normal ducts) and ~1% post-sphincterotomy bleeding; PEG placement has a 10-15% adverse-event rate (Harrison 22e p.2473-2474).

Gastrointestinal Neuroendocrine Tumors — GI NETs, Carcinoid tumors, Gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, GEP-NETs, Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, Islet cell tumors Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and other nonneuroendocrine pancreatic cancers Irritable bowel syndrome (small-bowel NETs are frequently misattributed to IBS for months to years) Psychiatric illness (insulinoma hypoglycemic symptoms may be mistaken for psychiatric disease) Mixed neuroendocrine-adenocarcinoma tumors (adenocarcinoids) of the appendix Somatostatin-receptor imaging: gallium-68 dotatate (or DOTATOC, copper-64 dotatate) PET, highly sensitive for primaries and metastases Cross-sectional imaging with CT or MRI; endoscopic ultrasound especially for small pancreatic primaries such as insulinomas FDG-PET (often negative in low-grade well-differentiated NETs but positive in higher-grade tumors) Fasting insulin with proinsulin and C-peptide (elevated in insulinoma; proinsulin/C-peptide normal with exogenous insulin) and serum/plasma sulfonylurea levels Fasting serum gastrin (interpret with awareness of PPI and achlorhydria effects) Plasma glucagon (glucagonoma generally >1000 pg/mL), plasma somatostatin, plasma VIP 24-hour urinary or plasma 5-HIAA for carcinoid syndrome (suggestive, not diagnostic; serotonin-rich foods such as salmon and eggs cause false positives) Chromogranin A (neither sensitive nor specific; falsely elevated in renal impairment and with PPI use) Histologic grading with mitotic count and Ki-67 plus chromogranin/synaptophysin immunostaining; vitamin B12 and antiparietal evaluation in type 1 gastric NET with atrophic gastritis Systemic mastocytosis (symptoms can be easily confused with carcinoid syndrome) Other causes of fasting hypoglycemia: severe liver disease, alcoholism, poor nutrition, post-gastric-bypass postprandial hypoglycemia, surreptitious insulin or sulfonylurea use (mimicking insulinoma) Causes of secretory diarrhea mimicking VIPoma: inflammatory bowel disease, short-bowel after small-bowel resection, radiation enteritis, surreptitious laxative/diuretic use Causes of hypergastrinemia other than gastrinoma: proton pump inhibitor use and achlorhydria from chronic atrophic gastritis (mimicking gastrinoma) Drug-induced valvulopathy mimicking carcinoid heart disease: fenfluramine and ergot-containing dopamine agonists (both act via 5-HT2B receptors) GI NETs are broadly grouped by origin into extrapancreatic NETs (historically called carcinoid tumors) and pancreatic NETs; they typically follow a more indolent course than most malignancies but can synthesize peptides, growth factors, and bioactive amines that are ectopically secreted (Harrison 22e p.676). Tumors are classified by differentiation (well vs poorly differentiated) and grade 1-3, which closely correlates with mitotic count and Ki-67 index: grade 1 is <2 mitoses/10 HPF and Ki-67 <3%, grade 2 is 2-20/10 HPF and 3-20%, grade 3 is >20/10 HPF and >20%; poorly differentiated high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas are the most aggressive category (Harrison 22e p.677). Only about 20% of pancreatic NETs are functional (hormone-secreting); the majority are nonfunctional and present incidentally or with mass-related symptoms such as abdominal pain and weight loss (Harrison 22e p.677). The most common functional pancreatic NET is insulinoma, followed by glucagonoma and gastrinoma; somatostatinoma, VIPoma, ACTHoma and others are uncommon (Harrison 22e p.677). Most gastrinomas actually arise in the gastrinoma triangle (bounded by duodenum, pancreas, and confluence of cystic and common bile ducts) rather than the pancreas, and 50-90% of sporadic gastrinomas arise in the duodenum, where they are often small and hard to localize (Harrison 22e p.678). Glucagonoma classically presents with necrolytic migratory erythema (often intertriginous, waxing and waning), glucose intolerance and weight loss; a hypercoagulable state is reported in up to one-third of patients (Harrison 22e p.679). Gastric NETs fall into three types: type 1 (chronic atrophic gastritis, most common, generally benign), type 2 (associated with gastrinoma/ZES), and type 3 (sporadic, normal gastrin, potentially far more aggressive) (Harrison 22e p.680). Small-bowel NETs (most often terminal ileum) arise within the muscularis/submucosa and are notoriously hard to diagnose early; mesenteric fibrosis from serotonin-driven fibroblast proliferation produces a classic calcified spoke-and-wheel mesenteric mass on CT and can cause intermittent obstruction and bowel ischemia (Harrison 22e p.680). Carcinoid syndrome (flushing, watery diarrhea, right-sided valvular heart disease, mesenteric fibrosis) is most associated with small intestine or appendiceal primaries and usually develops only after hepatic metastases or retroperitoneal lesions allow serotonin and vasoactive substances to enter systemic circulation (Harrison 22e p.681). More than 90% of NETs express somatostatin receptors, making somatostatin-analogue PET tracers (gallium-68 dotatate, DOTATOC, copper-64 dotatate) highly sensitive for detecting primaries and metastases (Harrison 22e p.681). Carcinoid heart disease occurs in roughly two-thirds of patients with carcinoid syndrome and is characterized by plaque-like fibrous endocardial thickening classically on the right heart, causing tricuspid regurgitation (nearly universal) plus possible tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary regurgitation, and pulmonary stenosis (Harrison 22e p.683). A minority of NETs arise within inherited syndromes; MEN 1 (menin gene, 11q13) is the most common, and gastrinoma should prompt a family history and assessment for hyperparathyroidism since up to 25% of ZES patients have MEN 1 (Harrison 22e p.676, 678). Carcinoid crisis: life-threatening profound hypotension or hypertension triggered by tumor manipulation during surgery, hepatic artery embolization, radionuclide therapy, exogenous epinephrine, or anesthesia induction Right-sided heart failure from carcinoid heart disease, a major source of morbidity and mortality Severe refractory hypoglycemia from insulinoma causing confusion, coma Mesenteric fibrosis causing intermittent small-bowel obstruction or bowel ischemia Profound watery diarrhea with hypokalemia and dehydration in VIPoma (Verner-Morrison/WDHA syndrome) PPIs and achlorhydria can both raise serum gastrin and confound the diagnosis of gastrinoma Chromogranin A is frequently falsely elevated (renal impairment, PPI use) and is neither sensitive nor specific; assay variability complicates interpretation Elevated 5-HIAA is suggestive but not diagnostic of carcinoid syndrome, with false positives from serotonin-rich foods Somatostatin-receptor PET can be falsely positive (physiologic uptake in the pancreatic uncinate process, sarcoidosis, meningiomas, thyroid goiter/thyroiditis) and falsely negative in higher-grade tumors with lower receptor expression Insulinomas are less reliably avid on somatostatin scintigraphy and are usually small (<2 cm), making EUS the preferred localization tool Insulinoma may be misdiagnosed as psychiatric illness; surreptitious insulin/hypoglycemic-agent use can mimic it Small-bowel NETs are easily missed at colonoscopy due to submucosal location beyond the ileocecal valve and may be misattributed to IBS for years Reduction of serotonin levels does not reverse established carcinoid valvular lesions GI NETs arise from neuroendocrine cells and contain electron-dense neurosecretory granules holding peptides and bioactive amines that can be ectopically secreted. Sporadic pancreatic NETs most frequently harbor MEN1 mutations (about 44%), with frequent mutations in the DAXX/ATRX chromatin-remodeling complex (about 43%) and mTOR-pathway genes (about 15%); recurrent mutations in extrapancreatic NETs are rare, though small-bowel NETs commonly show loss of chromosome 18 and CDKN1B mutations in a minority. In carcinoid syndrome the principal mediator is serotonin (5-HT), synthesized from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase; up to 50% of dietary tryptophan can be diverted into this pathway, which can deplete niacin and produce pellagra-like lesions. Histamine and tachykinins such as substance P also contribute. Serotonin stimulates intestinal secretion and motility and drives fibroblast growth, accounting for mesenteric fibrosis and for valvular fibrosis via activation of 5-HT2B receptors on heart-valve fibroblasts. Right-sided cardiac predominance reflects venous delivery of serotonin from hepatic/retroperitoneal deposits to the right heart, with pulmonary metabolism sparing the left heart. Inherited syndromes (MEN 1, von Hippel-Lindau, neurofibromatosis type 1, tuberous sclerosis) underlie a minority of cases (Harrison 22e p.676-683). NETs are typically more indolent than other malignancies, and both incidence and survival have risen over recent decades (US incidence rose about 6.4-fold from 1973 to 2012; prevalence exceeded 170,000). Prognosis depends strongly on primary site and histologic grade. Median survival for advanced pancreatic NETs rose from roughly 2 years in early SEER analyses to about 4 years more recently, and median survival for well-differentiated advanced small-intestine NETs exceeds 5 years. Appendiceal NETs that are well differentiated and <2 cm have extremely low metastatic risk and excellent prognosis, while metastatic risk rises to about 20-30% for 2-3 cm tumors and is even higher beyond 3 cm. Most rectal NETs are small (<1 cm), well differentiated and rarely metastasize, but up to one-third of 1-2 cm rectal NETs metastasize and >2 cm rectal NETs metastasize in over 70%. Poorly differentiated high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas carry markedly worse prognosis. The natural history is ultimately progressive (Harrison 22e p.677-682). WHO-type histologic classification used in Harrison: well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor grade 1 (low grade, <2 mitoses/10 HPF, Ki-67 <3%); grade 2 (intermediate, 2-20/10 HPF, Ki-67 3-20%); grade 3 (well-differentiated high grade, >20/10 HPF, Ki-67 >20%); and poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma (high grade, >20/10 HPF, Ki-67 >20%), the most clinically aggressive category (Harrison 22e p.677).

gastrointestinal stromal tumour — GIST, gastrointestinal pacemaker cell tumour leiomyoma or leiomyosarcoma of the gut wall schwannoma of the gastrointestinal tract desmoid-type fibromatosis gastrointestinal neuroendocrine tumour solitary fibrous tumour metastatic melanoma to the gut inflammatory fibroid polyp contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis for staging and response assessment endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration or biopsy immunohistochemistry for CD117 (KIT), DOG1, CD34 and SDHB molecular genotyping of KIT and PDGFRA (and BRAF/SDH where indicated) assessment of mitotic count per defined high-power field area by histopathology MRI for rectal or hepatic lesions where CT characterisation is limited FDG-PET for early metabolic response to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy Most common mesenchymal tumour of the gastrointestinal tract, arising from the interstitial cells of Cajal or their precursors, most frequently in the stomach followed by the small intestine. The great majority harbour activating mutations in KIT (CD117) or PDGFRA; immunohistochemistry for CD117 and DOG1 is the diagnostic cornerstone. Small tumours are frequently incidental findings at endoscopy, imaging or surgery for another indication, whereas larger lesions present with occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding, anaemia, abdominal mass or vague discomfort. Risk stratification for malignant behaviour rests on tumour size, mitotic rate and anatomical site rather than a simple benign-versus-malignant dichotomy; small-bowel lesions behave more aggressively than gastric ones of equivalent size. Endoscopic ultrasound shows a hypoechoic mass arising from the muscularis propria (fourth layer) and guides biopsy when tissue is needed; percutaneous biopsy of a resectable lesion is generally avoided owing to rupture and seeding risk. Imatinib and successor tyrosine kinase inhibitors transformed management of advanced disease; response and drug selection are strongly mutation-dependent, and PDGFRA exon 18 D842V tumours are classically imatinib-resistant. Wild-type GIST lacking KIT and PDGFRA mutations includes SDH-deficient tumours (often gastric, paediatric, associated with Carney triad and Carney-Stratakis syndrome) and NF1-associated and BRAF-mutant forms. Complete surgical resection with an intact pseudocapsule and negative margins is the mainstay for localised disease; lymphadenectomy is not routinely required as nodal spread is uncommon except in SDH-deficient tumours. acute gastrointestinal haemorrhage or haemodynamic instability from a bleeding tumour tumour rupture into the peritoneal cavity, markedly increasing recurrence risk rapidly enlarging mass with new pain suggesting high-grade progression signs of bowel obstruction or perforation new hepatic or peritoneal lesions indicating metastatic spread Labelling a GIST as benign on size alone; small tumours can still metastasise and risk is a continuum. Percutaneous biopsy of a readily resectable lesion, risking rupture and peritoneal seeding. Failing to genotype before systemic therapy, leading to use of imatinib in resistant PDGFRA D842V tumours. Misdiagnosing a CD117-negative or DOG1-positive tumour as leiomyoma or schwannoma without full immunohistochemistry. Overlooking SDH-deficient GIST in young patients and its associated syndromic and nodal-spread implications. Gastrointestinal stromal tumours arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal, the pacemaker cells that regulate gut peristalsis, or from their mesenchymal precursors within the wall of the tubular gastrointestinal tract. In most tumours a gain-of-function mutation in the receptor tyrosine kinase KIT drives ligand-independent, constitutive downstream signalling through the RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT pathways, promoting proliferation and survival; a minority are driven by analogous activating mutations in PDGFRA. A distinct subset lacks these mutations and instead shows loss of function of the succinate dehydrogenase complex, producing pseudohypoxic signalling, or is associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 or BRAF mutation. The specific driver dictates both morphology and, critically, sensitivity to tyrosine kinase inhibition, so molecular characterisation is integral to biological understanding and treatment. Prognosis depends chiefly on tumour size, mitotic rate, site and completeness of resection, with small gastric tumours often cured by excision while large small-bowel or ruptured tumours carry substantial recurrence risk. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors have markedly prolonged survival in advanced disease, though outcome varies with the underlying mutation.

gastric emptying study Wireless motility capsule or breath test as alternatives Blood glucose and HbA1c assessment in diabetic patients Review of medications affecting gastric motility Nutritional and electrolyte assessment in severe or chronic disease Gastroparesis is delayed gastric emptying in the absence of mechanical obstruction, presenting with nausea, vomiting, early satiety, bloating, and postprandial fullness The commonest identifiable causes are diabetes mellitus and prior gastric or vagal surgery, but many cases are idiopathic and some follow a viral illness Mechanical obstruction must be excluded, typically by endoscopy, before the diagnosis is made A scintigraphic gastric emptying study of a solid meal is the standard confirmatory test, with wireless motility capsule and breath tests as alternatives Medications that slow gastric emptying, especially opioids and GLP-1 receptor agonists, can cause or worsen symptoms and should be reviewed Management combines dietary modification toward small, low-fat, low-fibre meals with prokinetic and antiemetic therapy Refractory disease may require enteral feeding beyond the stomach, gastric electrical stimulation, or endoscopic pyloric procedures Intractable vomiting with dehydration and electrolyte disturbance Significant weight loss or malnutrition Features suggesting mechanical obstruction or malignancy Marked or unstable glycaemic control complicating diabetic gastroparesis Diagnosing gastroparesis without first excluding mechanical obstruction Overlooking opioids or GLP-1 receptor agonists as reversible contributors Ignoring hyperglycaemia, which acutely delays emptying and undermines treatment Missing alternative diagnoses such as rumination or cyclic vomiting that mimic gastroparesis Gastroparesis arises from impaired neuromuscular coordination of gastric emptying. Injury to the vagus nerve, abnormalities of the interstitial cells of Cajal that pace gastric contractions, smooth muscle dysfunction, and autonomic neuropathy disrupt fundic accommodation, antral contractility, and pyloric relaxation. In diabetes, chronic hyperglycaemia and autonomic neuropathy impair motility, and acute hyperglycaemia itself further slows emptying. The result is retained gastric contents, which produce nausea, vomiting, and impaired nutrient and drug absorption. Gastroparesis is often a chronic, fluctuating condition; many patients achieve reasonable symptom control with diet and medication, but a subset have refractory, disabling symptoms with recurrent hospitalisation and nutritional compromise.

Recovery is often prolonged by intestinal dysmotility and delayed feeding, and outcome is worse when there is complex disease with atresia, perforation, or extensive bowel loss leading to short bowel syndrome.

Severity is mutation dependent, ranging from mild thrombocytopenia to transfusion-dependent anaemia; with supportive care many patients do well, though the associated Down syndrome myeloid disorders require separate specialist management.

suggesting acute neuronopathic (type 2) disease Severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding or profound anaemia Acute bone pain crisis or evidence of avascular necrosis Massive splenomegaly with risk of rupture or hypersplenism Misdiagnosing splenomegaly with cytopenia as a primary haematological malignancy and pursuing unnecessary invasive workup Assuming enzyme replacement therapy will halt neurological progression in neuronopathic forms Overlooking bone disease, which can progress even when visceral parameters improve Failing to offer genetic counselling and carrier testing to at-risk Reduced enzyme activity impairs breakdown of glucocerebroside (glucosylceramide), which accumulates predominantly within the lysosomes of macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system. These engorged macrophages (Gaucher cells) infiltrate the spleen, liver, bone marrow, and, in neuronopathic forms, the nervous system, driving organomegaly, marrow replacement with cytopenias, and skeletal disease. The pattern and severity of residual enzyme activity, influenced by genotype, largely determine whether the phenotype is non-neuronopathic (type 1) or neuronopathic (types 2 and 3). Type 1 disease generally has a good outlook, especially with enzyme replacement or substrate reduction therapy, which reverses much of the visceral and haematological burden. Type 2 carries a poor prognosis with early death, whereas type 3 has an intermediate course with progressive neurological involvement despite treatment of systemic features.

Guillain-Barré syndrome — Nerve conduction studies CSF (albuminocytologic dissociation) Serial vital capacity / NIF Respiratory failure & autonomic instability — monitor FVC, may need ventilation Acute myelopathies, especially with prolonged back pain and sphincter disturbance (p.3620) Diphtheria with early oropharyngeal disturbance (p.3620) Porphyria (clues: abdominal pain, seizures, psychosis) (p.3620) Vasculitic neuropathy (check ESR) (p.3620) Critical illness neuropathy or myopathy (p.3620) Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) in patients with late or recurrent relapses (p.3622) Poliomyelitis and acute flaccid myelitis (wild-type poliovirus, West Nile virus, enterovirus D68, enterovirus A71, Japanese encephalitis virus) (p.3620) Lyme polyradiculitis and other tick-borne paralyses (p.3620) CMV polyradiculitis in immunocompromised patients (p.3620) Botulism (a neuromuscular junction disorder; pupillary reactivity lost early) (p.3620) CSF protein may be normal when symptoms have been present <=48 h and usually rises only by the end of the first week, so a normal early CSF does not exclude GBS (p.3619). A sustained CSF pleocytosis (or counts above the GBS range) should prompt a search for an alternative or concurrent diagnosis such as viral myelitis, HIV, leukemia/lymphoma infiltrating nerves, or neurosarcoidosis (p.3619). Electrodiagnostic abnormalities are mild or absent early and lag behind the clinical course; earliest AIDP findings are prolonged F-wave and distal latencies and reduced CMAP amplitudes (p.3619). Antiganglioside antibodies (e.g., anti-GM1 in AMAN/AMSAN, anti-GQ1b in Miller Fisher) can support specific subtypes (p.3618-3619). Test for HIV in patients with risk factors or CSF pleocytosis (p.3620). Myasthenia gravis (neuromuscular junction disorder) (p.3620) Poisoning with organophosphates, thallium, or arsenic (p.3620) Paralytic shellfish poisoning (p.3620) Severe hypophosphatemia (rare) (p.3620) About 70% of cases follow an acute infection (usually respiratory or GI) by 1-3 weeks; roughly 20-30% are preceded by Campylobacter jejuni, with a similar share after herpesvirus infection (often CMV or EBV) (p.3617). Weakness usually evolves over hours to a few days and is classically ascending (legs more than arms), often first noticed as 'rubbery legs', with tingling dysesthesias in the extremities (p.3617). Facial diparesis occurs in ~50% of patients and lower cranial nerve/bulbar involvement is common; bulbar weakness with difficulty handling secretions can initially be mistaken for brainstem ischemia (p.3617). Pain (neck, shoulder, back, or diffuse spinal pain) is common early, in ~50% of patients, and deep aching muscle pain plus dysesthetic limb pain also occur (p.3617). Large-fiber functions (deep tendon reflexes, proprioception) are affected more severely than cutaneous pain/temperature sensation (p.3617). AMAN and AMSAN are axonal variants associated with anti-GD1a/anti-GM1 antibodies and preceding C. jejuni; AMAN can occur in seasonal outbreaks (e.g., rural China) and is prevalent in China and Mexico (p.3617-3619). Miller Fisher syndrome (~5% of cases) presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia without limb weakness and carries anti-GQ1b antibodies in >90% (p.3617, p.3619). If diagnosis is strongly suspected, treatment should not wait for the characteristic CSF or electrodiagnostic findings to evolve (p.3620). Rapid tempo of progression and severe weakness on admission, plus facial and/or bulbar weakness in the first week, predict the need for mechanical ventilation (up to ~30% of patients require ventilatory support) (p.3617). Bulbar weakness with difficulty handling secretions threatens the airway (p.3617). Autonomic instability — wide blood pressure swings, postural hypotension, and cardiac dysrhythmias — can be fatal and may occur even when limb weakness is otherwise mild (p.3617). Presence of fever or constitutional symptoms at onset casts doubt on the diagnosis and should prompt reconsideration (p.3617). Prominent or early bladder dysfunction, or a sensory level, should raise suspicion for spinal cord disease rather than GBS (p.3617). Corticosteroids have NOT been found effective in GBS and should not be relied on as treatment (p.3621). Treatment timing matters: each day counts, and by ~2 weeks after the first motor symptoms it is unknown whether immunotherapy is still effective; if a patient has reached the plateau, treatment is probably no longer indicated unless severe weakness suggests ongoing immune attack (p.3620). Lack of improvement after a course of IVIg or plasmapheresis is NOT an indication to switch to the other modality, and combining the two is not significantly better than either alone (p.3621). Early CSF and electrodiagnostic studies can be normal/minimal; relying on them to confirm before treating can cause harmful delay (p.3619-3620). Acute flaccid myelitis can closely mimic GBS because sphincter disturbances may be absent (p.3620). GBS is an acute, often fulminant autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy thought to arise from immune responses to non-self antigens (infections, vaccines) that cross-react with peripheral nerve via molecular mimicry, with gangliosides (glycosphingolipids concentrated at sites such as nodes of Ranvier) as likely targets. In AIDP, the demyelinating and most common form, both cellular and humoral mechanisms operate: complement deposits on the outer Schwann cell surface, triggering membrane-attack-complex formation, vesicular myelin disintegration, and macrophage-mediated removal of myelin. The resulting conduction block (with axons left intact) explains the flaccid paralysis and the potential for rapid recovery once remyelination occurs; secondary axonal degeneration in severe cases slows recovery and worsens residual deficit. In the axonal variants (AMAN/AMSAN), IgG and complement deposit at the nodes of Ranvier of motor axons, with anti-GD1a antibodies preferentially targeting motor over sensory roots; low CMAP amplitudes often reflect reversible nodal/paranodal conduction block rather than true axon loss, though severe cases show axonal degeneration (p.3617-3620). About 85% of patients reach full functional recovery within several months to a year, though minor signs (e.g., persistent areflexia) and complaints such as fatigue may remain. Mortality is <5% in optimal settings, usually from secondary pulmonary complications. The outlook is worst with severe proximal motor and sensory axonal damage; other adverse factors are advanced age, a fulminant or severe attack, and delayed treatment. Elevated serum neurofilament light chains and high anti-GM1 titers both correlate with greater axonal involvement and poorer recovery. Between 5 and 10% of typical GBS patients have one or more late relapses, many later reclassified as CIDP (p.3621-3622). Brighton Collaboration case definitions (2011) grade diagnostic certainty in three levels. Level 1 (highest certainty) requires bilateral flaccid limb weakness, decreased/absent reflexes in weak limbs, a monophasic course with onset-to-nadir of 12 h to 28 days followed by plateau, electrophysiology consistent with GBS, cytoalbuminologic dissociation (elevated CSF protein with CSF white cell count <50/microL), and no alternative diagnosis. Lower levels relax the laboratory/electrophysiologic requirements. Parallel criteria exist for Miller Fisher syndrome (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia without limb weakness) (p.3620-3621).

other endocrine disturbance indicating hypothalamic involvement Imaging evidence of a progressive or enhancing mass Dismissing stereotyped inappropriate laughter as behavioural or emotional rather than epileptic Relying on a normal scalp EEG to exclude the diagnosis when the source is deep Failing to image the hypothalamus and missing a causative hamartoma Treating the seizure type generically without addressing the underlying structural lesion Gelastic epilepsy is a semiological description of seizures manifesting as involuntary laughter, most classically generated intrinsically within a hypothalamic hamartoma whose abnormal neurons fire autonomously and recruit hypothalamic and limbic circuits that mediate the motor and affective components of laughter. Gelastic seizures may also originate from cingulate, mesial frontal or temporal cortex when these regions, involved in emotional and motor expression, are the seizure focus. The apparent laughter therefore reflects activation of neural networks subserving the expression of mirth rather than any true emotional experience. Prognosis depends chiefly on the underlying cause. Gelastic seizures from a hypothalamic hamartoma can be drug-resistant and may progress to an epileptic encephalopathy, but targeted surgical, laser ablation or radiosurgical treatment of the lesion can achieve seizure control; gelastic seizures from a resectable cortical focus may also respond to lesion-directed treatment.

Gelatinous drop-like corneal dystrophy — GDLD, familial subepithelial corneal amyloidosis Lattice corneal dystrophy (also amyloid, but stromal) Climatic droplet keratopathy Salzmann nodular degeneration Band keratopathy Other subepithelial corneal deposits Slit-lamp examination of the gelatinous subepithelial nodules Histology or staining demonstrating amyloid where needed TACSTD2 genetic testing Assessment of visual impact and recurrence after treatment Confirmation that amyloidosis is localised to the cornea A rare autosomal recessive dystrophy of subepithelial corneal amyloid deposition, linked to TACSTD2 (M1S1) mutations It is more common in populations of Japanese descent Presents in the first two decades with severe photophobia, watering, foreign-body sensation and progressive visual loss The cornea develops mulberry-like gelatinous subepithelial nodules of amyloid It is a corneal (localised) amyloidosis without systemic amyloid involvement It recurs readily after superficial keratectomy or grafting, often necessitating repeated intervention Rapid visual deterioration Rapid recurrence after surgical removal Severe photophobia and surface breakdown Secondary infective keratitis Confusing it with lattice dystrophy or non-dystrophic surface deposits Underestimating the high recurrence rate after keratectomy or grafting Overlooking the recessive inheritance and relevant ancestry Assuming systemic amyloidosis, which is not part of this condition Gelatinous drop-like corneal dystrophy results from mutations in the TACSTD2 gene, which disrupt tight-junction-related epithelial barrier function. The resulting increased epithelial permeability is thought to allow accumulation of amyloid beneath and within the epithelium, forming the characteristic gelatinous, mulberry-like subepithelial deposits. These deposits scatter light and progressively impair vision, and because the underlying epithelial defect persists, amyloid re-accumulates rapidly after removal, explaining the high recurrence rate. The dystrophy is visually disabling and characteristically recurs after treatment, so many patients require repeated procedures; specialised ocular surface and graft strategies aim to delay recurrence.

early visual loss from confluent subepithelial amyloid Disabling photophobia and surface breakdown Rapid recurrence of deposits after surgical removal Secondary infection of a compromised, highly permeable surface Mistaking subepithelial amyloid nodules for band keratopathy or Salzmann degeneration Expecting durable benefit from superficial keratectomy despite rapid recurrence Overlooking the autosomal recessive inheritance and family risk Failing to recognise the epithelial barrier defect underlying the disease Gelatinous drop-like corneal dystrophy is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the TACSTD2 gene, which encodes a protein important for corneal epithelial tight junction integrity. Loss of normal tight junctions markedly increases epithelial permeability, allowing serum-derived proteins to enter the subepithelial cornea where they aggregate as amyloid. The resulting mulberry-like gelatinous subepithelial nodules progressively opacify and elevate the surface, causing severe photophobia and visual loss from an early age. The underlying barrier defect drives rapid re-accumulation of amyloid after surgical removal. The disorder tends to cause severe visual impairment from an early age and is more visually aggressive than the classic stromal amyloid dystrophies. Surgery can temporarily improve vision, but deposits recur rapidly because of the persistent epithelial barrier defect, often requiring repeated intervention.

Geleophysic dysplasia — ADAMTSL2, FBN1, acromelic dysplasia, geleophysic dwarfism Acromicric dysplasia Weill-Marchesani syndrome Myhre syndrome Mucopolysaccharidoses (storage-like appearance) Pseudohypoparathyroidism/Albright hereditary osteodystrophy Other acromelic dysplasias with short hands Targeted analysis of ADAMTSL2 and FBN1, ideally via a skeletal dysplasia gene panel Skeletal survey demonstrating short tubular bones and cone-shaped epiphyses Echocardiography to assess for progressive valvular disease Airway and respiratory assessment including imaging for tracheal narrowing Abdominal imaging for hepatomegaly Growth monitoring and cardiology follow-up One of the acromelic dysplasias: severe short stature with strikingly short hands and feet and progressive joint stiffness/contractures The characteristic 'happy' or pleasant round facial appearance gives the condition its name (from the Greek for happy face) Progressive cardiac valve disease and airway/tracheal narrowing are the main life-threatening complications Caused by variants in ADAMTSL2 (autosomal recessive) or in a specific region of FBN1 (autosomal dominant), converging on abnormal TGF-beta signalling and microfibril handling Thickened skin, hepatomegaly and recurrent respiratory infections are frequent Radiographs show short tubular bones, cone-shaped epiphyses and a characteristic pattern in the hands Management is supportive with close cardiac and respiratory surveillance; valve and airway disease drive morbidity and mortality Progressive valvular heart disease with signs of cardiac failure Airway compromise or stridor from tracheal or laryngeal narrowing Recurrent severe respiratory infections Rapidly worsening joint contractures limiting function Mistaking the storage-like facies and hepatomegaly for a mucopolysaccharidosis Underestimating progressive cardiac valve involvement that may worsen over time Overlooking silent airway narrowing until acute respiratory compromise occurs Failing to distinguish it from the milder, cardiologically less involved acromicric dysplasia Geleophysic dysplasia arises from disturbance of the extracellular microfibril-transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) system. Recessive variants in ADAMTSL2, a secreted protein that interacts with fibrillin microfibrils, and dominant variants in a particular domain of FBN1 both dysregulate TGF-beta bioavailability and signalling within connective tissue. The resulting abnormal matrix produces the acromelic (distal-limb) shortening, joint contractures, thickened skin, and, importantly, progressive infiltration and fibrosis of cardiac valves and the airway that determine prognosis. Prognosis is guarded because progressive cardiac valve disease and airway narrowing frequently cause serious morbidity and can lead to early death, particularly in severe forms, although milder cases survive into adulthood with supportive care.

Gelsolin Amyloidosis (AGel, Finnish Type) — Meretoja syndrome, Familial amyloidosis, Finnish type, AGel amyloidosis Other causes of corneal lattice dystrophy Other cranial neuropathies including sarcoidosis and idiopathic facial palsy Other hereditary and acquired peripheral neuropathies Cutis laxa of other aetiology Other systemic amyloidoses Sjögren syndrome for the dry eyes Ophthalmological slit-lamp examination for corneal lattice dystrophy GSN gene sequencing Nerve conduction studies and clinical neurological assessment Skin or other tissue biopsy with Congo red staining and typing if the diagnosis is unclear Assessment of renal and cardiac function to gauge systemic involvement Family screening and genetic counselling AGel is an autosomal dominant amyloidosis caused by mutations in the gelsolin gene (GSN), classically Asp187Asn, first described in Finland. The characteristic clinical triad is corneal lattice dystrophy, cranial neuropathy (especially facial) and cutis laxa. Corneal lattice dystrophy is usually the earliest feature, appearing in early adulthood, and may cause visual disturbance and recurrent erosions. A slowly progressive facial neuropathy produces a mask-like drooping face, bulbar symptoms and, later, a peripheral polyneuropathy. The skin becomes lax and prematurely aged, and blepharochalasis can impair vision. Renal and cardiac involvement are usually mild and life expectancy is often near-normal, which distinguishes AGel from most systemic amyloidoses. Diagnosis is clinical in affected kindreds and confirmed by GSN sequencing; management is supportive, including ophthalmic and reconstructive surgery. Progressive facial weakness accompanying corneal disease Corneal erosions threatening vision Bulbar symptoms causing swallowing or speech difficulty New significant proteinuria or cardiac symptoms suggesting atypical systemic burden Dismissing corneal lattice dystrophy as isolated when it heralds a systemic hereditary disease Misdiagnosing the facial neuropathy as idiopathic facial palsy Overlooking the family history Assuming that all amyloidoses share a poor prognosis and over-treating Gelsolin is an actin-binding protein important in cytoskeletal remodelling. Amyloidogenic GSN mutations disrupt calcium binding and expose an abnormal cleavage site, so that aberrant proteolysis generates a fragment that misfolds and forms amyloid fibrils. These deposit preferentially along cranial and peripheral nerves, in the cornea and basement membranes, and in dermal connective tissue, producing the characteristic neuro-ophthalmic and cutaneous phenotype. Visceral deposition is comparatively limited, which explains the relatively benign systemic course, although the disease is nonetheless slowly progressive over decades. The course is slowly progressive over decades with predominantly neuro-ophthalmic and cutaneous morbidity. Life expectancy is usually near-normal, although quality of life is affected by facial palsy, ocular disease and skin laxity.

Generalised eruptive histiocytosis — generalised eruptive histiocytoma, GEH Langerhans cell histiocytosis Benign cephalic histiocytosis Xanthoma disseminatum Juvenile / adult xanthogranuloma Eruptive xanthomas Papular sarcoidosis Secondary syphilis Skin biopsy with histology and immunohistochemistry (CD68, factor XIIIa, CD1a, langerin) Electron microscopy to confirm absence of Birbeck granules where required Fasting serum lipid profile to exclude eruptive xanthoma Clinical and laboratory review to exclude systemic histiocytosis and internal malignancy Full blood count and inflammatory markers Serum protein electrophoresis where an associated dyscrasia is suspected Serial assessment to detect evolution towards a xanthomatous histiocytosis A rare non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis presenting with recurrent crops of numerous symmetrical red-brown papules distributed widely over the trunk, face and proximal limbs. It occurs predominantly in adults but is reported in children, and the eruption appears in successive waves. Lesions are typically monomorphic, non-coalescing papules a few millimetres in diameter that spare or minimally involve mucous membranes. By definition there is no visceral involvement, and the condition is regarded as a purely cutaneous, self-healing histiocytosis. Individual papules tend to resolve spontaneously leaving transient macular hyperpigmentation, though new crops may recur over months to years. Histology shows a monomorphous dermal infiltrate of histiocytes without significant lipidisation, foam cells or Touton giant cells, which are CD68 positive and CD1a and langerin negative. It is widely considered an early or transitional form within the spectrum of cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses and may evolve towards xanthomatous forms such as juvenile xanthogranuloma or xanthoma disseminatum. The diagnosis is partly one of exclusion, requiring differentiation from Langerhans cell histiocytosis and from histiocytoses with systemic involvement. Hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy or cytopenias suggesting a systemic histiocytosis Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss or night sweats Bone pain or lytic lesions raising the possibility of Langerhans cell histiocytosis Rapidly progressive, non-regressing disease Evolution of lesions with features suggesting an alternative malignant histiocytic disorder Making the diagnosis without adequately excluding Langerhans cell histiocytosis and systemic histiocytoses. Mislabelling the eruption as eruptive xanthoma despite normal lipids and absent foam cells on histology. Assuming permanence and over-treating a self-limiting condition. Failing to follow patients for possible evolution towards xanthomatous forms. Confusing recurrent crops with treatment failure. Generalised eruptive histiocytosis is a reactive proliferation of macrophage-derived dermal histiocytes belonging to the non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses. The lesional cells are non-lipidised histiocytes expressing macrophage markers such as CD68 while lacking the Langerhans cell markers CD1a and langerin and Birbeck granules. The characteristic absence of foam cells and Touton giant cells early in the disease, together with the tendency of some cases to acquire xanthomatous features over time, supports the concept that generalised eruptive histiocytosis represents an early, non-lipidised phase of the cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis spectrum that overlaps with benign cephalic histiocytosis, juvenile xanthogranuloma and xanthoma disseminatum. The self-healing crops reflect a self-limited reactive process with clearance of the histiocytic infiltrate rather than a persistent clonal neoplasm. The prognosis is favourable, with a chronic but ultimately self-healing course in which crops of papules regress spontaneously over months to years; a minority of cases evolve into other cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses, and treatment is generally unnecessary.

diffuse malformation of the lymphatic system in which abnormal, dilated lymphatic channels proliferate through multiple organs and tissues, characteristically involving bone, spleen and the thorax. Resistance to thyroid hormone beta — resistance to thyroid hormone beta, RTHbeta, generalised thyroid hormone resistance, Refetoff syndrome, THRB TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma Primary hyperthyroidism (Graves disease) Assay interference or heterophile antibodies Familial dysalbuminaemic hyperthyroxinaemia Thyroid hormone cell-membrane transport defect (MCT8) Thyroid hormone metabolism defect (SBP2) Free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine with a simultaneous non-suppressed TSH Repeat and confirmatory thyroid function tests to exclude assay artefact Alpha-subunit measurement and dynamic testing to distinguish from a TSH-secreting adenoma Pituitary MRI where a TSH-secreting tumour cannot be excluded biochemically Assessment of peripheral markers of thyroid hormone action such as sex hormone-binding globulin THRB gene sequencing Usually autosomal dominant, caused by variants in THRB encoding the beta isoform of the thyroid hormone receptor The characteristic biochemistry is raised free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine with a non-suppressed (normal or mildly elevated) TSH Most patients are clinically euthyroid because the reduced sensitivity is broadly compensated by higher hormone levels Tissue-specific effects can occur: tachycardia and hyperactivity may reflect the intact beta receptor pathway in some tissues alongside resistance in others Goitre, learning difficulties, and attention problems are recognised associations, particularly in children The main differential is a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, which also causes high thyroid hormones with unsuppressed TSH Most patients need no treatment; the priority is to avoid inappropriate antithyroid therapy or thyroidectomy for a misdiagnosis of hyperthyroidism Symptomatic tachyarrhythmia such as atrial fibrillation Growth or neurodevelopmental concerns in an affected child Pituitary mass on imaging suggesting a TSH-secreting adenoma instead Inadvertent thyroid ablation or antithyroid treatment for misdiagnosed hyperthyroidism Treating the raised thyroid hormones as hyperthyroidism and giving antithyroid drugs or thyroidectomy Failing to distinguish the condition from a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma Overlooking assay interference as a simpler explanation for discordant results Not screening first-degree relatives for the dominant condition Thyroid hormone acts through nuclear receptors, of which the beta isoform predominates in the pituitary and liver and mediates negative feedback on TSH secretion. Dominant-negative variants in THRB produce a receptor that binds hormone or DNA poorly yet interferes with the normal receptor, so target tissues expressing the beta receptor are relatively resistant. Because pituitary feedback is blunted, TSH secretion is not suppressed despite high circulating thyroid hormones, and the raised hormone levels represent the compensation needed to achieve near-normal action in resistant tissues. Tissues that rely more on the alpha receptor, such as the heart, remain sensitive and may show features of hormone excess, giving the mixed clinical picture. The persistently non-suppressed TSH is the diagnostic clue that distinguishes the condition from primary hyperthyroidism. Most individuals have a normal life expectancy and remain well without treatment; the principal risk is iatrogenic harm from misdiagnosis, while a minority have persistent cardiac or neurodevelopmental symptoms requiring targeted management.

Genetic Cardiomyopathies — Hereditary cardiomyopathy, Familial cardiomyopathy, Inherited cardiomyopathy, Sarcomeric cardiomyopathy Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (sarcomeric) Dilated cardiomyopathy (e.g., TTN truncating variant) Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy / arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy Restrictive cardiomyopathy (inherited, including DES-related and transthyretin amyloidosis) Left ventricular noncompaction Conduction disease with dilated cardiomyopathy (e.g., LMNA, SCN5A) Inherited metabolic/storage cardiomyopathies (Fabry's, Danon, PRKAG2, carnitine and fatty-acid oxidation defects, mitochondrial syndromes) Detailed multigenerational family history (heart failure, cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, conduction disease, tachyarrhythmias, sudden death, early atrial fibrillation/pacemaker, muscular dystrophy) Two-dimensional and Doppler echocardiography (central to HCM/DCM diagnosis; physical exam and ECG are insensitive for HCM) Electrocardiogram Cardiac MRI for myocardial fibrosis (late gadolinium enhancement) and inflammation Genetic counseling and multigene cardiomyopathy panel testing, with confirmatory variant testing in relatives Endomyocardial biopsy with electron microscopy when a specific diagnosis with therapeutic implications is suspected (e.g., Fabry's lamellar inclusions; not used to diagnose HCM but can exclude infiltrative/metabolic disease) Enzyme activity assay and/or GLA sequencing when Fabry's disease suspected Ambulatory ECG monitoring and exercise testing for nonsustained ventricular tachycardia and outflow gradient provocation Athlete's heart (physiologic hypertrophy that regresses with detraining, with supernormal VO2max >50 mL/kg/min, mild dilation, and normal diastolic function) Hypertensive or aortic valve disease causing secondary LV hypertrophy Infiltrative/storage disease mimicking HCM via pseudohypertrophy (often with short PR interval) Cardiac amyloidosis, particularly transthyretin-variant amyloid causing restrictive physiology Each traditional morphologic form of cardiomyopathy (hypertrophic, dilated, restrictive) can be caused or modified by underlying genetic factors; heritability is well recognized in HCM and present in at least 30% of dilated cardiomyopathy without another clear etiology (p.2003-2004). Most familial cardiomyopathies are autosomal dominant, with occasional autosomal recessive, matrilineal (mitochondrial), and X-linked inheritance; missense and truncating variants are the commonest abnormalities (p.2003). Genetic cardiomyopathy shows age-dependent and incomplete penetrance: the phenotype is rarely present at birth and in some carriers may never manifest; relatives carrying the same variant can differ markedly in severity and progression (p.2004). Penetrance and clinical severity tend to be greater in men for most cardiomyopathies; current therapy is based on phenotype rather than the genetic defect (p.2004). The greatest current utility of genetic testing is to focus and inform family evaluations; it can also provide risk stratification and occasionally identify a treatable disorder such as Fabry's or Gaucher's disease (p.2004). A sarcomere gene variant is found in roughly 40-50% of HCM patients, more often with familial disease and asymmetric septal hypertrophy; about 80% of these involve MYH7 or MYBPC3 encoding the thick myofilament (p.2005). HCM is defined as left ventricular hypertrophy developing without a causative hemodynamic factor (e.g., hypertension, aortic valve disease) or infiltrative/storage disease; prevalence is about 1:500 (p.2005). Outflow tract obstruction is present at rest in about 30% of HCM patients and provoked by exercise in another ~30%; systolic anterior motion of an enlarged anterior mitral leaflet against the hypertrophied septum produces obstruction and posteriorly directed mitral regurgitation (p.2006). Truncating variants in TTN (titin) are the commonest genetic cause of dilated cardiomyopathy, accounting for up to 25% of familial DCM; men with TTN truncating variants typically develop disease about a decade before women (p.2008-2009). DCM is considered present when LVEF is <=0.50 and/or LV diastolic dimension exceeds the 95th percentile predicted for age and sex; some patients have reduced LVEF with minimal dilation (nondilated/minimally dilated cardiomyopathy) (p.2008). Inherited metabolic and storage disorders can mimic HCM by thickening the myocardium with abnormal products ('pseudohypertrophy'), classically with a short PR interval; most are diagnosed in childhood (p.2010). Fabry's disease (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency from GLA variants) can affect female carriers; endomyocardial biopsy shows diagnostic concentric lamellar inclusions on electron microscopy, and diagnosis matters because enzyme replacement can reduce deposits (p.2010). History of cardiac arrest or spontaneous sustained ventricular tachycardia Syncope, particularly nonvagal and occurring with or after exertion Family history of sudden cardiac death at early ages Maximal LV wall thickness >30 mm LV systolic dysfunction with ejection fraction <50% in HCM LV apical aneurysm (especially with apical hypertrophy) Spontaneous nonsustained ventricular tachycardia (>3 beats at rate >120) High late gadolinium enhancement burden on cardiac MRI Pathogenic LMNA or FLNC variants, or right-ventricular cardiomyopathy progressing to LV dysfunction (higher arrhythmic/adverse-event risk) Identifying a variant in a proband to focus family screening requires high certainty the variant is truly pathogenic and not a benign DNA variant. Most identified variants are 'private' to individual families, complicating interpretation; growing recognition that multiple intermediate-effect alleles and polygenic risk influence penetrance and expression. Athlete's heart can mimic mild HCM; distinguishing features include regression with detraining, supernormal exercise capacity, mild dilation, and normal diastolic function. Late gadolinium enhancement on MRI, once attributed to prior viral myocarditis, is now recognized as common in genetic cardiomyopathy. Cardiac glycosides should be avoided in HCM with obstruction because they increase contractility and worsen obstruction. The positive predictive value of most HCM sudden-death risk factors is low, so many patients receiving a defibrillator never receive appropriate device therapy. Endomyocardial biopsy is not used to diagnose HCM itself but may exclude infiltrative/metabolic disease. Many distinct genes are implicated (locus heterogeneity), each with numerous pathogenic variants (allelic heterogeneity). Mutant proteins can interfere with the normal allele via a dominant-negative mechanism, while nonsense/frameshift variants may yield truncated or unstable proteins whose absence causes disease through haploinsufficiency; some genetic DCM combines both effects. Functional gene groups include sarcomeric proteins, Z-disk/cytoskeletal proteins, nuclear membrane proteins, excitation-contraction coupling proteins, metabolic enzymes, mitochondrial DNA, sarcolemmal membrane proteins, and desmosomal proteins. In HCM, sarcomere variants enhance calcium sensitivity, maximal force generation, and ATPase activity, producing abnormal energetics and impaired relaxation; myofibril and myocyte misalignment/disarray occurs, with interstitial fibrosis appearing before overt hypertrophy and focal replacement fibrosis providing arrhythmic substrate, plus microvascular ischemia from thickened intramural vessels. In DCM and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, cytoskeletal, sarcolemmal (dystrophin), nuclear membrane (lamin A/C, emerin), and desmosomal protein defects impair force transmission, mechanical/electrical coupling, and cell survival; desmosomal disruption activates Wnt/beta-catenin and proinflammatory signaling with replacement of myocytes by fat and fibrous tissue, creating arrhythmogenic, sometimes aneurysmal regions. HCM prognosis is better than in early referral-population studies but mortality remains higher than in age-matched individuals without cardiomyopathy; sudden death risk is under 1% per year (about 0.5% per year baseline). Up to 1 in 20 HCM patients progress to overt systolic dysfunction (EF <50%) with or without dilation ('burned out'/end-stage HCM), with increased risk of death from progressive heart failure and sudden death unless transplanted. In DCM and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, prognosis is driven by disease stage and sudden-death risk, which is higher for variants in DES, DSP, DSC2, FLNC, LMNA, PKP2, PLN, RBM20, SCN5A, and TMEM43; progression rate is also gene-dependent, and patients with TTN truncating variants frequently recover with medical therapy. HCM sudden-death risk stratification uses major risk factors (prior cardiac arrest or sustained VT, exertional/nonvagal syncope, family history of sudden cardiac death, LV apical aneurysm, maximal wall thickness >30 mm, LVEF <50%) plus modifying factors (late gadolinium enhancement burden, spontaneous nonsustained VT). The externally validated European Society of Cardiology HCM Risk-SCD calculator integrates age, LV outflow tract gradient, left atrial diameter, maximal wall thickness, syncope, family history, and nonsustained VT to estimate 5-year cardiac-arrest risk: ICD generally advised at >=6%, considered at 4-6%, and not advised at <4%. DCM is defined by LVEF <=0.50 and/or LV diastolic dimension >95th percentile for age and sex.

Geniculate neuralgia — nervus intermedius neuralgia, Hunt neuralgia, facial nerve neuralgia, otalgic neuralgia Glossopharyngeal neuralgia Trigeminal neuralgia Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) Primary otological disease (otitis externa or media) Temporomandibular joint dysfunction Cerebellopontine angle or skull base tumour Referred otalgia from oropharyngeal malignancy Otoscopy and microscopy to exclude middle and external ear disease MRI of the internal auditory meatus and cerebellopontine angle with attention to the facial nerve MR angiography to identify a compressive vascular loop Assessment of the external auditory canal for a triggerable zone Audiometry if hearing symptoms or tinnitus accompany the pain Examination of the oropharynx to exclude referred otalgia from malignancy Produces brief, severe, lancinating pain felt deep within the ear (auditory canal and periauricular region) Attacks may be provoked by touching a trigger zone in the external auditory canal, by swallowing, or by cold stimuli It can be accompanied by autonomic and sensory phenomena such as altered taste, salivation, lacrimation, and tinnitus, reflecting the wider functions of the nervus intermedius The nervus intermedius is the sensory and parasympathetic component of the facial nerve, and geniculate neuralgia is essentially neuralgia of this nerve A viral (herpetic) aetiology is recognised, and it may follow Ramsay Hunt syndrome Diagnosis requires exclusion of other causes of deep ear pain and overlaps clinically with glossopharyngeal and trigeminal neuralgia Management is medical with anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine first; sectioning of the nervus intermedius or microvascular decompression is reserved for refractory cases Vesicles in the ear canal or pinna with facial weakness suggesting Ramsay Hunt syndrome Persistent unilateral otalgia with a normal ear, prompting a search for a head and neck primary Progressive facial weakness or other cranial neuropathies A cerebellopontine angle mass on imaging Attributing deep ear pain to primary ear disease when the ear is normal Failing to consider a herpetic (post-Ramsay Hunt) origin Confusing it with glossopharyngeal neuralgia given the shared deep-ear pain Not excluding referred otalgia from an oropharyngeal malignancy Overlooking a treatable vascular loop or tumour on imaging Geniculate neuralgia is a paroxysmal neuralgia arising from the nervus intermedius, the sensory and parasympathetic division of the facial nerve, whose geniculate ganglion carries sensation from part of the external ear. Ectopic neural discharges, often attributed to vascular compression at the nerve root or to prior herpetic (varicella-zoster) inflammation of the geniculate ganglion, are thought to generate the intense deep-ear pain. Because the nervus intermedius also mediates taste, lacrimation, and salivation, attacks may be accompanied by disturbances of these functions, and its close relationship to the glossopharyngeal and trigeminal systems produces overlapping symptomatology. Geniculate neuralgia is benign but can be highly distressing; many patients respond to anticonvulsant therapy, and surgical sectioning of the nervus intermedius or microvascular decompression offers relief in selected refractory cases.

(hemiepiphysiodesis) or, at maturity, osteotomy Deformity persisting or worsening beyond about seven to eight years of age Marked, severe, or asymmetrical valgus Short stature or disproportion suggesting a dysplasia or metabolic disease Knee pain, patellar instability, or gait disturbance History of trauma, infection, or metabolic disorder affecting the growing bone Over-investigating a normal child during the physiological valgus phase Failing to recognise pathological valgus persisting beyond the expected age Missing rickets, renal disease, or a dysplasia signalled by short stature Overlooking post-traumatic valgus after an apparently minor proximal tibial fracture Deferring guided growth until skeletal maturity, when the opportunity for gentle correction is lost Genu valgum is an inward (valgus) angulation at the knee so that the knees approximate while the ankles separate. It is a normal phase of skeletal maturation, following the earlier varus of infancy, and remodels predictably toward the modest physiological valgus of adulthood. Pathological valgum develops when growth is disturbed: metabolic bone disease such as rickets or renal osteodystrophy softens and deforms the growing bone; skeletal dysplasias alter physeal development; and asymmetric growth after trauma, infection, or a proximal tibial fracture (as in the classic post-fracture valgus) produces localised deformity. Persistent severe valgus laterally displaces the extensor mechanism and predisposes to patellofemoral problems and, in the long term, medial compartment overload. Physiological knock knees resolve spontaneously and carry an excellent prognosis, whereas untreated pathological valgus can progress to fixed deformity, patellofemoral instability, and later degenerative change, though guided growth in the skeletally immature child gives good correction.

The metaphyseal-diaphyseal (Drennan) angle on a standing radiograph helps distinguish physiological bowing from Blount disease Rickets, whether nutritional or hypophosphataemic, is a key metabolic cause and is suggested by short stature, metaphyseal widening, and biochemical abnormalities Management of physiological bowing is reassurance and observation, whereas pathological varus may need bracing, guided growth, or corrective osteotomy Progressive rather than improving deformity, or bowing persisting beyond the expected age Marked asymmetry or unilateral involvement Short stature or disproportion suggesting a skeletal dysplasia or metabolic disease Pain, a lateral thrust on walking, or an abrupt metaphyseal angulation suggesting Blount disease Biochemical or dietary features pointing to rickets Mistaking progressive Blount disease for benign physiological bowing and delaying treatment Overlooking short stature or biochemical clues to rickets or a dysplasia Failing to appreciate the normal varus-to-valgus developmental sequence and over-investigating a normal toddler Not obtaining standing radiographs when the deformity is severe, asymmetrical, or painful Assuming all bowing will resolve and omitting follow-up in atypical cases Genu varum refers to an outward (varus) angulation at the knee so that the legs bow apart. Physiological bow legs reflect the normal alignment of the immature skeleton, partly a carry-over of intrauterine positioning, that remodels predictably toward valgus and then neutral as the child grows and begins to walk. Pathological varus arises when this remodelling is disturbed: in Blount disease abnormal compressive loading suppresses growth at the posteromedial proximal tibial physis, producing progressive tibia vara; in rickets defective mineralisation of the growth plate and metaphysis softens bone that then deforms under weight-bearing. Skeletal dysplasias, physeal injury, and focal growth disturbance are less common structural causes. Physiological bow legs resolve spontaneously with growth and carry an excellent prognosis, whereas pathological varus such as Blount disease or rickets can progress to fixed deformity and early joint degeneration if the underlying cause is not addressed.

Geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) — benign migratory glossitis, erythema migrans (oral), glossitis areata migrans, geographical tongue Oral candidiasis Erythematous (atrophic) lichen
