Oral lesions of lupus erythematosus Clinical diagnosis based on the characteristic migratory appearance Review for associated fissured tongue and any personal or family history of psoriasis or atopy Haematinics (ferritin, vitamin B12, folate) if glossitis or soreness suggests deficiency Candidal swab or smear if fungal infection is suspected Biopsy only in atypical, persistent, or non-migratory lesions to exclude other pathology Photographic documentation to demonstrate the changing pattern A common, benign inflammatory condition of the tongue seen at any age Presents as well-demarcated red areas of depapillation surrounded by slightly raised, serpiginous white or yellowish borders The lesions characteristically change shape and location over days to weeks, giving a migrating map-like appearance Usually asymptomatic, though some patients report soreness or sensitivity to spicy, acidic, or hot foods Frequently coexists with a fissured tongue and has recognised associations with psoriasis and atopy The diagnosis is clinical, based on the characteristic appearance and migratory behaviour, and biopsy is rarely needed There is no malignant potential, and reassurance is the cornerstone of management Symptomatic patients benefit from avoiding trigger foods and, when needed, topical symptomatic measures A fixed, non-migrating red patch that could represent erythroplakia and needs biopsy Persistent soreness with systemic symptoms suggesting nutritional deficiency or another disorder Induration, ulceration, or bleeding not typical of geographic tongue Widespread candidiasis raising concern about immunosuppression Mistaking it for candidiasis and giving unnecessary antifungal treatment Failing to distinguish a fixed red lesion, a possible erythroplakia, from migratory patches Overlooking a treatable nutritional deficiency in a sore tongue Causing undue alarm by suggesting a risk of malignancy where none exists Geographic tongue is a benign inflammatory disorder in which localised loss of the filiform papillae produces smooth red patches, while the advancing margins show a band of inflammatory cells and regenerating epithelium seen clinically as a raised white-yellow border. Histologically the changes resemble those of psoriasis, with collections of neutrophils in the epithelium, and the condition shares associations with psoriasis and atopic disease. The lesions resolve and reappear in new sites, which accounts for the shifting, map-like pattern; the precise trigger is unknown but immune and possibly genetic factors are implicated. The condition is entirely benign with an excellent prognosis; lesions wax and wane over time and may persist for years, but they cause no harm and require no active treatment beyond reassurance and symptomatic relief.

GERD / non-cardiac chest pain — Exclude cardiac cause first Trial of PPI Do not attribute to GERD until ACS excluded Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial ischaemia (must be excluded first given lethal implications) Distal (diffuse) esophageal spasm - dysphagia plus chest pain from abnormal contractions with normal LES relaxation; diagnosed only after commoner causes excluded Hypercontractile (jackhammer) esophagus Peptic esophagitis / esophageal ulcer Eosinophilic esophagitis (especially if dysphagia) Peptic ulcer disease (symptomatic 60-90 min after meals) Functional dyspepsia (postprandial distress and epigastric pain syndromes) Biliary colic / gallbladder disease Pancreatitis Acute aortic syndrome / aortic dissection Pulmonary embolism Pneumothorax Pericarditis (radiation to trapezius ridge, worse supine, relieved leaning forward) Costochondritis / Tietze's syndrome and other musculoskeletal chest-wall causes Cervical radiculitis / cervical disk disease Panic disorder / anxiety state (up to ~10% of ED chest-pain presentations) Esophageal rupture (greatest urgency among noncardiopulmonary causes) Infectious esophagitis (fungal or viral) - more often causes odynophagia than heartburn; ulcerations are numerous, punctate, and diffuse on endoscopy Pneumonia / pleuritis (pulmonary infective cause of chest pain via pleural involvement) Herpes zoster (dermatomal chest pain) 12-lead ECG within 10 min of presentation, with serial ECGs every 30-60 min when ACS suspected; note resting ECG sensitivity for ischaemia is poor (as low as 20%) High-sensitivity cardiac troponin at presentation and repeated (1-3 h hs-assay; 3-6 h conventional) - a rising/falling pattern with a value above the 99th percentile defines MI; a single very low hs-troponin >2-3 h after onset can rule out MI with NPV >99% Validated clinical decision pathways (e.g., HEART, EDACS) combined with serial troponin to risk-stratify and safely discharge low-probability ACS patients Coronary CT angiography or functional stress imaging (nuclear perfusion / stress echo) for intermediate/undetermined risk once life-threatening causes excluded; CTA can also exclude dissection, effusion, and PE Chest radiograph (mediastinal widening, pneumothorax, pneumonia, pulmonary edema) D-dimer to help exclude pulmonary embolism where indicated Upper endoscopy (EGD) - first-line for mucosal lesions, Barrett's detection by color, biopsy of suspicious or atypical findings; erosive esophagitis is found in only ~one-third of GERD patients so a normal EGD does NOT exclude GERD Ambulatory esophageal pH monitoring (24 h, or wireless capsule 48-96 h off acid suppression) - the diagnostic standard for confirming pathologic reflux Combined esophageal pH-impedance testing (on PPI) to identify oesophageal hypersensitivity or nonacid/incompletely controlled acid regurgitation in refractory/atypical symptoms High-resolution esophageal manometry (with FLIP/impedance) - to diagnose motility disorders (achalasia, DES) and assess peristalsis before anti-reflux surgery Barium contrast radiography - higher sensitivity than endoscopy for strictures (especially with a 13-mm barium tablet) and for assessing function/anatomy Pill (medication-induced) esophagitis - solitary deep ulcer at points of luminal narrowing, often near the carina, sparing distal esophagus Eosinophilic esophagitis - edema, rings, linear furrows, white punctate exudate, strictures Distal esophageal spasm and hypercontractile esophagus Achalasia (with stasis esophagitis) Esophageal pain shares a nerve plexus with the heart and esophageal afferents discriminate stimuli poorly, so distention or acid (chemostimulation) is often perceived as pressure-type mid-chest pain radiating to back, arms, or jaw - closely mimicking angina (p.2503-2504). Features that favour an oesophageal rather than cardiac source include pain that is nonexertional, prolonged, meal-related, relieved by antacids, accompanied by heartburn/dysphagia/regurgitation, and that interrupts sleep - but every one of these overlaps with cardiac pain, which must remain the primary consideration (p.2509). Heartburn (pyrosis) is the most common oesophageal symptom and its link to GERD is strong enough that empirical acid-suppression has become accepted management; chest pain and persistent dysphagia are the key exceptions that warrant evaluation rather than empirical treatment (p.2503, p.2510). Gastrointestinal disorders are the single most common cause of nontraumatic chest discomfort, yet fewer than 15% of ED chest-pain presentations turn out to be ACS (p.104). A burning quality suggests acid reflux but can also occur with myocardial ischaemia; conversely oesophageal spasm can produce a severe squeezing pain identical to angina - quality alone never establishes a diagnosis (p.105). Both reflux relief and ischaemia relief overlap with nitroglycerin: oesophageal spasm may be relieved promptly by nitroglycerin just as angina can be, so a nitroglycerin response does not confirm cardiac origin (p.106). Chest wall tenderness on palpation does NOT exclude myocardial ischaemia, and a normal physical exam is not reassuring in unstable ischaemic heart disease (p.106-107). Some patients with acid reflux on pH testing report epigastric/abdominal pain or nausea instead of classic heartburn (atypical GERD) (p.301, ch.48). Visceral hypersensitivity is increasingly recognised as a cofactor in GERD symptom generation, beyond simple mucosal erosion and afferent nerve activation (p.2510). Dysphagia (concerning for oesophageal obstruction - stricture, EoE, or cancer) Odynophagia (suggests infectious or pill esophagitis, or extensive ulceration) Unexplained weight loss Recurrent vomiting Occult or gross gastrointestinal bleeding / anaemia Jaundice Palpable mass or lymphadenopathy Family history of gastro-oesophageal malignancy Nocturnal symptoms Heartburn >5 years' duration, especially age >50, or new dyspepsia age >60 (screen for Barrett's / malignancy by endoscopy) Failure to respond to acid suppression (up to one-third of presumed GERD) Any diagnostic doubt about a cardiac cause - acute exertional/pressure pain, radiation to both arms, diaphoresis, dyspnoea, syncope, hypotension/tachycardia Attributing chest pain to GERD before excluding a cardiac cause - coronary artery disease must be given early consideration because of its potentially lethal implications, and oesophageal pain closely mimics angina. Relying on pain quality, nitroglycerin response, or chest-wall tenderness to distinguish cardiac from oesophageal pain - all overlap and none is reliable; a normal exam and even a normal resting ECG do not exclude ischaemia. Treating a normal endoscopy as ruling out GERD - erosive esophagitis is seen in only about one-third of GERD patients. Overlooking that up to one-third of presumed-GERD patients fail to respond to acid suppression and may have an alternative diagnosis (functional, hypersensitivity, motility, nonacid reflux). Diagnosing distal esophageal spasm or nonspecific manometric abnormalities prematurely - these are made only after GERD, peptic and infectious esophagitis, and cardiac disease are excluded; minor manometric findings are of unclear significance and often coexist with anxiety/depression and IBS. Missing alarm features (dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, bleeding/anaemia) that mandate endoscopy rather than continued empirical therapy. Forgetting that nausea/vomiting and epigastric pain can accompany MI (especially inferior MI via vagal/Bezold-Jarisch reflex) and need not indicate a GI cause. Pathologic reflux arises from anatomic and physiologic failure of the oesophagogastric junction valve - widening of the diaphragmatic hiatus with diminished crural diaphragm function, loss of the intra-abdominal oesophageal segment disabling the flap valve, axial (sliding) hiatus hernia causing LES hypotension, and increased junctional compliance allowing liquid to escape during transient LES relaxations (the belch reflex). Some reflux is physiologic and intertwined with belching, but esophagitis follows excessive reflux plus impaired acid clearance, which depends on peristalsis returning fluid to the stomach and bicarbonate in swallowed saliva neutralising residual acid; impaired peristalsis and reduced salivation therefore prolong acid contact. Mucosal injury is driven by a cytokine-mediated inflammatory pathway rather than purely direct caustic injury. Gastric acid hypersecretion is usually NOT the dominant factor (exceptions: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, severe esophagitis in ~50%); chronic H. pylori gastritis may even be protective by inducing hypoacidity. Pepsin, bile, and pancreatic enzymes also injure the epithelium, and bile persists in refluxate despite acid suppression and is implicated as a cofactor in Barrett's metaplasia and adenocarcinoma. Exacerbating factors include abdominal obesity, pregnancy, gastric hypersecretory states, delayed gastric emptying, disrupted peristalsis, and overeating. Esophageal chest pain itself reflects a shared nerve plexus with the heart and poor discriminative ability of oesophageal afferents (p.2503-2504, p.2509-2510). Most patients in whom an acute cardiopulmonary cause is excluded have a favourable prognosis; in low-risk patients the 30-day major cardiovascular event rate is about 2.5%. However, historically 2-6% of presumed-nonischaemic chest pain patients discharged from the ED were later found to have had a missed myocardial infarction, underscoring the cost of misclassification. For GERD itself, erosive esophagitis and peptic strictures have become rare with potent acid suppression, but Barrett's metaplasia and oesophageal adenocarcinoma have increased; progression of Barrett's to adenocarcinoma is estimated at roughly 0.1-0.5% per year, with obese white men in their sixth decade at greatest risk. High-grade dysplasia in Barrett's carries a high rate of progression and a high prevalence of coexisting unrecognised cancer (p.104, p.2510-2511, ch.85 p.92). GERD spans a spectrum of oesophageal injury: nonerosive reflux disease, erosive esophagitis (graded by antisecretory-responsive severity), peptic stricture, Barrett's metaplasia, and adenocarcinoma. Barrett's dysplasia is staged as low-grade vs high-grade, the latter mandating intervention. For the chest-pain presentation itself, Harrison frames risk by clinical decision pathways categorising patients as low, intermediate, or high probability of ACS using symptoms, age, risk factors, ECG, and serial high-sensitivity troponin (HEART/EDACS scores) (p.107-109, p.2510-2511).

Gerodermia osteodysplastica — GORAB, geroderma osteodysplasticum, Walt Disney dwarfism, wrinkly skin with osteoporosis Autosomal recessive cutis laxa types 1 and 2 De Barsy syndrome Wrinkly skin syndrome (ATP6V0A2-related) Ehlers-Danlos syndromes Osteogenesis imperfecta Progeroid syndromes GORAB sequencing, usually within a cutis laxa gene panel Bone densitometry (DXA) to quantify osteoporosis Skeletal survey for fractures and vertebral changes Skin examination and, where needed, dermal histology for elastic fibre changes Growth monitoring Assessment for fracture-related complications An autosomal recessive cutis laxa disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in GORAB, producing a prematurely aged appearance Lax, wrinkled skin is most marked over the dorsum of the hands and feet and the abdomen, giving a characteristic aged look from infancy Severe osteoporosis leads to fragility fractures, often of the vertebrae and long bones, and can cause vertebral collapse A drooping, jowly facial appearance with a prematurely aged (geroderma) look is typical, sometimes described in older literature by an unflattering eponym Growth is usually mildly reduced and intelligence is typically normal Joint laxity is common but the skin recoils, unlike some other cutis laxa syndromes Management centres on bone protection, fracture prevention and supportive care; there is no specific cure Recurrent fragility fractures or vertebral collapse causing pain or deformity Progressive spinal deformity with neurological compromise Fractures after minimal trauma indicating severe bone fragility Complications of immobility following fractures Mistaking the fragility fractures for non-accidental injury or primary osteogenesis imperfecta Confusing it with other cutis laxa syndromes that lack the severe osteoporosis Overlooking vertebral fractures that may be clinically silent Assuming the aged appearance reflects a systemic progeroid syndrome with shortened lifespan Gerodermia osteodysplastica is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in GORAB, which encodes a Golgi-associated protein involved in intracellular trafficking important for both connective tissue matrix and bone formation. Deficiency disturbs the processing and secretion of extracellular matrix components, weakening dermal elastic tissue to give lax, wrinkled skin, and impairing osteoblast function to produce severe osteoporosis with fragility fractures. The combined connective tissue and skeletal effects account for the prematurely aged appearance alongside the bone disease. Life expectancy is generally normal and intelligence is preserved, but recurrent fractures and progressive osteoporosis cause significant morbidity, so long-term bone health and fracture prevention are the main clinical priorities.

Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker disease (PRNP prion) — GSS, Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker syndrome, familial prion disease, PRNP-related prion disease Sporadic and familial Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease Fatal familial insomnia Hereditary and sporadic degenerative cerebellar ataxias (e.g. spinocerebellar ataxias) Paraneoplastic or immune-mediated cerebellar degeneration Multiple system atrophy Other young-onset dementias with ataxia PRNP gene sequencing to identify the causative mutation MRI brain to assess cerebellar atrophy and exclude alternative pathology Cerebrospinal fluid analysis, including prion-specific assays such as RT-QuIC where available Electroencephalography, though the periodic complexes of classic CJD are often absent Neuropsychological assessment to characterise cognitive decline Detailed family history and pedigree analysis A rare autosomal dominant inherited prion disease caused by mutations in the prion protein gene (PRNP), classically the P102L mutation Typically presents in mid-adult life with slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia as the dominant early feature Cognitive decline and dementia develop later, giving a combined ataxia-dementia picture that distinguishes it from the rapid course of classic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease Progresses more slowly than sporadic CJD, often over several years rather than months Other features may include dysarthria, pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs, gaze abnormalities, and, in some kindreds, prominent lower-limb areflexia Neuropathology is characterised by multicentric amyloid plaques composed of abnormal prion protein No disease-modifying treatment exists; management is supportive with genetic counselling for affected families Progressive ataxia with emerging cognitive decline in a patient with a relevant family history Rapid deterioration suggesting a more aggressive prion phenotype Bulbar involvement compromising swallow and airway Implications for at-risk relatives requiring genetic counselling Mistaking the slowly progressive course for a degenerative ataxia and overlooking a prion cause Failing to take a family history and offer genetic testing and counselling Expecting the EEG and imaging features of classic CJD, which are often absent Not observing appropriate prion precautions for tissue and instruments Attributing early ataxia to a non-hereditary cause Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker disease is an inherited prion disorder in which autosomal dominant mutations in PRNP predispose the normal cellular prion protein to misfold into an abnormal, protease-resistant, self-propagating form. This misfolded protein accumulates and templates further conversion of normal protein, leading to progressive neuronal loss, spongiform change, and the deposition of characteristic multicentric amyloid plaques, particularly in the cerebellum. The prominent cerebellar involvement explains the early ataxia, while cortical spread accounts for the later dementia. The specific PRNP mutation (most often P102L) influences the phenotype and the relatively slow, prolonged clinical course compared with sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. The disease is uniformly progressive and fatal, though the course is characteristically prolonged over several years; no treatment alters the outcome, and care is directed at symptom control and support.

Gerstmann syndrome — angular gyrus syndrome, Gerstmann tetrad Broader aphasic syndromes from dominant parietal or temporal lesions Alexia with or without agraphia Apraxia from parietal disease Confusional state or delirium impairing performance Posterior cortical atrophy Developmental learning disorder in children MRI of the brain focused on the dominant parietal lobe Formal neuropsychological assessment of the four component deficits Vascular imaging and stroke workup where infarction is suspected Cognitive screening for coexisting language and praxis deficits Evaluation for neurodegenerative disease when onset is insidious Assessment for coexisting alexia and aphasia The classic tetrad comprises finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, agraphia, and acalculia It localises to the dominant (usually left) inferior parietal lobule, particularly the angular gyrus Finger agnosia is the inability to name or identify individual fingers on command despite intact sensation Acalculia refers to acquired difficulty with calculation, and agraphia to impaired writing not explained by motor weakness The full tetrad in isolation is uncommon; incomplete forms and associated aphasia or alexia are more typical Common causes include dominant parietal infarction, tumour, and neurodegenerative disease A developmental form is described in children with learning difficulties affecting the same domains Acute onset suggesting a dominant parietal stroke requiring urgent assessment Progressive cognitive decline suggesting a neurodegenerative or neoplastic cause Associated headache or focal signs suggesting a mass lesion Rapid deterioration warranting prompt imaging Expecting the complete tetrad, when partial and mixed presentations are far more common Attributing the deficits to global confusion rather than a focal parietal lesion Missing coexisting aphasia or alexia that alters interpretation Failing to image the dominant hemisphere when the tetrad is recognised Gerstmann syndrome arises from damage to the dominant inferior parietal lobule, especially the angular gyrus and adjacent white matter, a region that integrates the body schema, spatial relationships, language, and numerical processing. Disruption here produces the characteristic combination of finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, agraphia, and acalculia. In adults the usual causes are ischaemic infarction in the middle cerebral artery territory, tumour, or a degenerative process, whereas a developmental variant reflects atypical maturation of the same cortical network. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; deficits from stroke may partially recover with rehabilitation, whereas those from progressive disease tend to worsen, and the developmental form persists but can be supported educationally.

diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome, and certain ethnic backgrounds First-line management is medical nutrition therapy, glucose self-monitoring, and physical activity, with pharmacotherapy added if glycaemic targets are not met Fetal complications include macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, birth trauma, neonatal hypoglycaemia, and polycythaemia Maternal hyperglycaemia drives fetal hyperinsulinaemia, which promotes excessive fetal growth and adiposity Most women return to normal glucose tolerance after delivery, but there is a substantially increased lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes Postpartum glucose testing is essential to detect persistent diabetes and to guide long-term risk reduction Marked fetal macrosomia or polyhydramnios increasing risk of shoulder dystocia and stillbirth Very poor glycaemic control suggesting undiagnosed overt diabetes Coexisting hypertension or pre-eclampsia Reduced fetal movements or non-reassuring fetal surveillance Missing overt pre-existing diabetes by not testing high-risk women in early pregnancy Relying on symptoms, which are usually absent, rather than screening Assuming a normal-sized fetus excludes risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia Failing to arrange postpartum glucose reassessment and long-term follow-up Neglecting neonatal glucose monitoring after delivery Pregnancy is a progressively insulin-resistant state driven by placental hormones such as human placental lactogen, progesterone, and cortisol. Gestational diabetes develops when maternal pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion cannot compensate for this physiological resistance, leading to maternal hyperglycaemia. Glucose crosses the placenta freely and stimulates fetal insulin secretion; the resulting fetal hyperinsulinaemia acts as a growth factor causing macrosomia and, after cord clamping removes the maternal glucose supply, predisposes the neonate to hypoglycaemia. Well-controlled gestational diabetes has an excellent outcome, approaching that of the non-diabetic population. Poor control raises risks of macrosomia, operative delivery, birth trauma, and neonatal metabolic problems. Long term, affected women have a markedly increased risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, and their offspring have higher rates of obesity and glucose intolerance.

Gestational hypertension — pregnancy-induced hypertension, PIH Chronic or pre-existing hypertension Pre-eclampsia White-coat or masked hypertension Secondary hypertension from renal, endocrine (such as phaeochromocytoma or Cushing syndrome), or vascular causes such as coarctation Transient hypertension from pain or anxiety Chronic hypertension with superimposed pre-eclampsia Repeated, correctly measured blood pressure readings, with ambulatory or home monitoring where useful Urinalysis and quantification of protein by protein:creatinine or albumin:creatinine ratio to detect evolving pre-eclampsia Full blood count, liver and renal function, and urate as a baseline and to monitor for progression Placental growth factor-based testing where available to help exclude pre-eclampsia Fetal ultrasound for growth, amniotic fluid volume, and umbilical artery Doppler Cardiotocography for fetal wellbeing when indicated Investigations for secondary hypertension if features are atypical or onset is unusually early Gestational hypertension is new-onset hypertension arising after twenty weeks of gestation in the absence of proteinuria and other features of pre-eclampsia, in a woman previously normotensive It is distinguished from chronic hypertension, present before pregnancy or before twenty weeks, and from pre-eclampsia, which adds proteinuria or maternal organ or uteroplacental dysfunction A substantial proportion of women, particularly those presenting earlier and with higher pressures, progress to pre-eclampsia, so regular surveillance for proteinuria and end-organ features is essential Blood pressure should be confirmed with an appropriately sized cuff and repeated measurement, and severity is graded to guide the threshold for treatment Antihypertensive therapy using agents considered suitable in pregnancy, such as labetalol, nifedipine, or methyldopa, reduces the risk of severe hypertension; the aim is control rather than cure Fetal surveillance with growth scans and assessment of wellbeing is warranted, as hypertensive disorders are associated with fetal growth restriction By definition the hypertension resolves after delivery, generally within the puerperium; persistence beyond around three months postpartum suggests underlying chronic hypertension A history of gestational hypertension confers increased long-term cardiovascular risk and a higher chance of hypertensive disease in future pregnancies, warranting counselling and follow-up New or increasing proteinuria or symptoms of pre-eclampsia such as headache, visual disturbance, or epigastric pain Severe hypertension Evidence of fetal growth restriction or reduced fetal movements Deranged liver, renal, or platelet indices signalling progression to pre-eclampsia Blood pressure that remains uncontrolled despite treatment Labelling hypertension as gestational without excluding proteinuria and pre-eclampsia features Missing progression to pre-eclampsia through infrequent monitoring Misclassifying unrecognised chronic hypertension, present before twenty weeks, as gestational Neglecting fetal growth surveillance Failing to arrange postpartum review and longer-term cardiovascular risk counselling Gestational hypertension represents a maternal cardiovascular response to pregnancy in which systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure rise after mid-gestation without the full systemic endothelial and multiorgan involvement that characterises pre-eclampsia. In many women it reflects an exaggerated haemodynamic and vascular reactivity, and in a subset it is an early or partial expression of the same placental and anti-angiogenic process that culminates in pre-eclampsia, which explains why a proportion progress to overt disease. Because there is as yet no significant glomerular endothelial injury, proteinuria is absent, and by definition there is no evidence of the hepatic, haematological, renal, or neurological dysfunction seen in pre-eclampsia. Delivery removes the placental stimulus and blood pressure returns towards baseline. Isolated gestational hypertension that does not progress generally carries a good outcome with resolution after delivery, but progression to pre-eclampsia worsens the prognosis, and affected women have an elevated lifetime risk of chronic hypertension and cardiovascular disease.

antibody effects on the fetal and neonatal thyroid Pregnancy alters thyroid physiology through oestrogen-driven increases in thyroxine-binding globulin, rising total hormone levels, and hCG-mediated stimulation of the TSH receptor that transiently lowers TSH in the first trimester. Increased renal iodide clearance and placental deiodinase activity raise iodine and hormone demand. Autoimmune thyroid disease may worsen or improve with the shifting immune state of pregnancy, and transplacental passage of TSH-receptor antibodies or antithyroid drugs can affect the fetal thyroid. With appropriate monitoring and treatment, most women with thyroid disease have good maternal and fetal outcomes, but poorly controlled disease increases the risk of miscarriage, pre-eclampsia, growth restriction, and impaired fetal neurodevelopment.

Gestational Trophoblastic Disease — GTD, molar pregnancy, hydatidiform mole, gestational trophoblastic neoplasia Threatened or missed miscarriage Ectopic pregnancy Multiple pregnancy with high hCG Normal early intrauterine pregnancy with bleeding Non-gestational malignancy producing hCG Retained products of conception Quantitative serum hCG, which is often markedly elevated Pelvic ultrasound to assess for molar features and fetal tissue Histological examination of evacuated tissue, with ploidy and immunostaining where needed Serial hCG monitoring after evacuation to detect persistent disease Chest imaging and cross-sectional staging when neoplasia or metastasis is suspected Baseline full blood count, renal, liver and thyroid function given possible hCG-driven thyroid effects Gestational trophoblastic disease is a spectrum of proliferative disorders of placental trophoblast ranging from benign hydatidiform mole to malignant gestational trophoblastic neoplasia including choriocarcinoma A complete mole usually arises from fertilisation of an ovum lacking maternal genetic material and contains no fetal tissue, whereas a partial mole is typically triploid with some fetal parts Classic presentation includes irregular vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy, a uterus large for dates, markedly elevated hCG, and sometimes early or severe hyperemesis or pre-eclampsia before twenty weeks Ultrasound may show a vesicular or snowstorm appearance with absent or abnormal fetal development, and diagnosis is confirmed histologically Uterine evacuation by suction curettage is the treatment for molar pregnancy, followed by structured monitoring of serial hCG to detect persistent disease Persistently elevated or rising hCG after evacuation indicates gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is highly chemosensitive and generally curable even when metastatic Reliable contraception during hCG surveillance is essential because a new pregnancy would obscure the marker used to detect persistent disease Choriocarcinoma can follow any pregnancy, including normal or ectopic, and may present with metastatic symptoms such as haemoptysis or neurological signs Rising or plateauing hCG after evacuation signalling gestational trophoblastic neoplasia requiring urgent oncology referral Heavy vaginal bleeding with haemodynamic compromise Respiratory symptoms or haemoptysis suggesting pulmonary metastases Neurological signs suggesting cerebral metastatic choriocarcinoma Pre-eclampsia, thyrotoxic features, or hyperemesis occurring unusually early in pregnancy Failing to arrange structured hCG follow-up after evacuation Allowing pregnancy during surveillance, which masks persistent disease Missing early or atypical pre-eclampsia and hyperthyroid features as clues to molar pregnancy Not considering choriocarcinoma in a woman with metastatic disease and any recent pregnancy Assuming a benign miscarriage without histological examination of tissue Gestational trophoblastic disease results from abnormal fertilisation and proliferation of trophoblastic tissue. A complete mole typically arises when an anucleate ovum is fertilised and the paternal chromosomes duplicate, giving a diploid androgenetic genome with swollen avascular chorionic villi and no fetus, while a partial mole usually results from dispermic fertilisation producing a triploid conceptus with focal villous change and a nonviable fetus. Excessive trophoblast produces very high hCG. In gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, trophoblast invades the myometrium and vasculature, and choriocarcinoma disseminates haematogenously, favouring the lungs, brain, and liver. Most hydatidiform moles are cured by evacuation alone, and even when gestational trophoblastic neoplasia develops it is one of the most curable malignancies, with excellent survival when managed in specialist centres using chemotherapy guided by prognostic scoring. Outcome depends on prompt diagnosis, adherence to hCG surveillance, and risk stratification, with high-risk and heavily metastatic disease requiring more intensive multi-agent treatment.

or ectopic pregnancy Non-gestational hCG-secreting tumour Uterine arteriovenous malformation Other gynaecological malignancy Pituitary or heterophile sources of a false-positive hCG Serial centre with structured surveillance yields high cure rates Beta-hCG plateau or rise, or new symptoms, after evacuation of a mole Haemoptysis, breathlessness, or neurological features suggesting metastatic choriocarcinoma Heavy uterine or intraperitoneal haemorrhage from vascular tumour High-risk prognostic score requiring urgent multi-agent chemotherapy Not following beta-hCG after molar pregnancy and missing early progression Applying hCG-based monitoring uncritically to placental site tumours, which secrete little hCG Treating high-risk disease with single-agent chemotherapy and inducing resistance Biopsying a highly vascular uterine tumour and provoking major haemorrhage Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia represents persistent or malignant proliferation of trophoblast following a molar or non-molar pregnancy. Invasive mole reflects molar villi penetrating the myometrium, whereas choriocarcinoma is frankly malignant trophoblast without villi that invades vasculature and metastasises early. Placental site and epithelioid trophoblastic tumours arise from intermediate trophoblast, grow more indolently, produce little beta-hCG, and are relatively chemoresistant. Most subtypes secrete beta-hCG in proportion to tumour burden, providing a sensitive marker, and the neoplastic tissue is often highly vascular with a tendency to haemorrhage and, for choriocarcinoma, to spread to lungs, brain, and liver. Most gestational trophoblastic neoplasia is curable, with low-risk disease approaching universal cure and high-risk disease achieving high survival through risk-adapted chemotherapy at specialist centres. Placental site and epithelioid tumours have a less favourable, more surgery-dependent course.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumour — GIST, gastrointestinal stromal tumor, GI stromal tumour Leiomyoma or leiomyosarcoma of the gut Gastrointestinal schwannoma Neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumour Gastric or small-bowel adenocarcinoma or lymphoma Extrinsic compression from an adjacent mass Pancreatic or splenic lesion mimicking a gastric submucosal mass Endoscopy with endoscopic ultrasound to characterise the submucosal lesion and guide sampling Contrast-enhanced CT for staging, size assessment, and detection of liver or peritoneal metastases Immunohistochemistry for KIT (CD117) and DOG1 to confirm the diagnosis Mutational analysis of KIT and PDGFRA to guide targeted therapy and predict response Mitotic count and tumour size assessment for risk stratification The most common mesenchymal tumour of the gastrointestinal tract, thought to arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal, most often in the stomach and next most often in the small intestine Most are driven by activating mutations in the KIT (CD117) or PDGFRA receptor tyrosine kinases, and KIT immunostaining is the diagnostic hallmark Presentation ranges from an incidental finding to vague abdominal discomfort, a palpable mass, or gastrointestinal bleeding from mucosal ulceration On endoscopy they typically appear as a smooth submucosal bulge with normal overlying mucosa, sometimes with central umbilication Malignant potential is estimated mainly from tumour size and mitotic rate together with anatomical site, rather than being simply benign or malignant Surgical resection with negative margins is the mainstay of treatment for localised disease, and routine lymph node dissection is generally unnecessary because nodal spread is rare Tyrosine kinase inhibitors targeting KIT/PDGFRA have transformed management of advanced, metastatic, or high-risk disease and are used in adjuvant and neoadjuvant settings Biopsy should be approached cautiously because of bleeding and rupture risk; endoscopic ultrasound-guided sampling is often preferred when tissue is needed The liver and peritoneum are the usual sites of metastatic spread Large tumour with high mitotic rate indicating high malignant potential and need for oncological management Significant or recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding from an ulcerated tumour Tumour rupture (spontaneous or during biopsy) causing peritoneal dissemination and haemoperitoneum New liver or peritoneal lesions signalling metastatic progression Assuming a submucosal lesion is benign without adequate risk stratification by size and mitotic rate Performing incautious biopsy of a friable tumour and precipitating bleeding or rupture Omitting mutational testing, which can predict poor response to standard targeted therapy Confusing a GIST with other spindle-cell tumours when immunohistochemistry is not performed GISTs originate from or resemble the interstitial cells of Cajal, the pacemaker cells of the gut. Gain-of-function mutations in the KIT proto-oncogene, or less commonly in PDGFRA, produce constitutive receptor tyrosine kinase signalling that drives uncontrolled proliferation. A minority are wild-type for these genes and involve alternative pathways such as succinate dehydrogenase deficiency, which is more common in younger patients and in syndromic disease. Tumours grow as submucosal or intramural masses; larger and more mitotically active lesions have greater potential for haematogenous spread, particularly to the liver and peritoneal surfaces. Small, low-mitotic-rate, completely resected tumours have an excellent outlook, whereas large or mitotically active lesions carry a substantial risk of recurrence and metastasis. Tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy has markedly improved survival in advanced disease, though resistance can develop over time.

dysfunction with aspiration risk Rapid neurological deterioration with new central signs Severe scoliosis or contractures compromising function and respiration Overlooking the characteristic kinky hair as a diagnostic pointer in a child with neuropathy Attributing the picture to a purely peripheral neuropathy and missing the central involvement Delaying nerve biopsy or genetic testing when the phenotype is suggestive Neglecting respiratory and spinal surveillance that guide anticipatory care Giant axonal neuropathy is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in GAN, encoding gigaxonin, an E3 ubiquitin-ligase adaptor that controls the degradation of intermediate filament proteins. Loss of gigaxonin leads to abnormal accumulation and disorganisation of neurofilaments within axons, producing the characteristic focal axonal swellings (giant axons) packed with densely aggregated neurofilaments. This intermediate-filament dysregulation is generalised, disrupting both peripheral and central axons and other filament-rich tissues such as hair, and drives progressive degeneration of the peripheral nerves, cerebellum, corticospinal tracts and cerebral white matter. Giant axonal neuropathy is progressive, with loss of ambulation typically in later childhood or adolescence and death often in the second or third decade from respiratory and bulbar complications; the course and severity vary with the underlying mutation.

in a myxoid to collagenous stroma, distinctive branching pseudovascular (angiectoid) spaces, and scattered floret-like multinucleate giant cells lining those spaces Diffusely CD34-positive, in keeping molecular testing when morphology is ambiguous in a paediatric spindle cell lesion Giant cell fibroblastoma is a fibroblastic tumour driven by the COL1A1-PDGFB fusion, in which the platelet-derived growth factor B gene is placed under a constitutively active collagen promoter, producing autocrine PDGF receptor signalling that fuels proliferation. Because it shares this driver with dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, the two are considered variants of one entity, and tumours can show hybrid or transitional features. The same molecular mechanism that sustains growth also makes the tumour susceptible, when advanced, to PDGF-receptor-directed tyrosine kinase inhibition, as used in unresectable dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans. Giant cell fibroblastoma is locally aggressive but does not usually metastasise, and wide local excision with clear margins is generally curative; incompletely excised tumours recur, sometimes as conventional dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, and only fibrosarcomatous transformation carries appreciable metastatic risk, so complete removal and follow-up are the mainstays.

with adjuvants or wider resection), with RANKL-directed therapy such as denosumab used for unresectable, recurrent or selected cases Rapid growth, marked cortical destruction or a soft-tissue mass suggesting malignant transformation or giant-cell-rich osteosarcoma Pulmonary nodules indicating benign implants or, rarely, metastasis Pathological fracture through the lesion Recurrent disease after previous surgery Assuming a benign label means an indolent course and underestimating local aggressiveness and recurrence Missing giant-cell-rich osteosarcoma or a brown tumour of hyperparathyroidism in the differential Neglecting chest imaging for pulmonary implants Inadequate intralesional curettage without adjuvant treatment leading to high recurrence Giant cell tumour of bone is composed of neoplastic mononuclear stromal cells together with reactive macrophages and abundant osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells. The neoplastic stromal cells, which frequently carry a characteristic H3F3A histone gene mutation, secrete receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL), which recruits and activates the giant cells and drives extensive bone resorption. This produces the expansile, purely lytic epiphyseal lesion that reaches the subchondral bone. The RANKL pathway is the rationale for denosumab therapy. Despite its benign classification the tumour behaves in a locally aggressive manner and can seed benign, slowly growing pulmonary implants. The tumour is benign but locally aggressive, with recurrence after intralesional surgery an important concern; wider resection lowers recurrence at the cost of function. A minority develop pulmonary implants, and malignant transformation, although rare, worsens the outlook considerably.

Giant cell tumour of tendon sheath — localised tenosynovial giant cell tumour, nodular tenosynovitis Ganglion cyst of the digit or tendon sheath Fibroma of the tendon sheath Foreign body granuloma Epidermal inclusion cyst Rheumatoid or gouty tophaceous nodule Glomus tumour when subungual and painful Synovial sarcoma or other soft-tissue sarcoma MRI demonstrating a low-signal mass with gradient-echo blooming from haemosiderin Ultrasound showing a solid hypoechoic mass adjacent to the tendon sheath Plain radiographs to detect pressure erosion of adjacent bone Histopathological confirmation after excision remains the diagnostic standard Immunohistochemistry (for example clusterin and CD68) in equivocal histology Assessment of the mass for transillumination to distinguish from a ganglion Documentation of the tumour's relationship to the flexor sheath and neurovascular bundle The second commonest soft-tissue tumour of the hand after the ganglion, presenting as a firm, slow-growing, painless nodule usually on the volar or lateral aspect of a digit. It represents the localised form of tenosynovial giant cell tumour and is the small-joint counterpart of pigmented villonodular synovitis affecting large joints. The mass is typically firm and does not transilluminate, which helps distinguish it clinically from a ganglion. Lesions are commonest on the radial three digits and frequently overlie or abut the flexor tendon sheath and interphalangeal joints. Longstanding tumours may cause pressure erosion of adjacent bone visible on plain radiographs, though frank bony invasion is unusual. MRI shows characteristic low signal on T1 and T2 sequences with blooming artefact on gradient-echo imaging due to haemosiderin, aiding preoperative planning. Treatment is marginal excision with removal of satellite nodules; incomplete excision is the main driver of the appreciable local recurrence rate. Recurrence is more likely with lesions at the distal interphalangeal joint, those with bony involvement and multilobulated tumours, so careful excision and follow-up are warranted. Rapid enlargement, pain or ill-defined infiltrative margins suggesting a sarcoma Cortical destruction or aggressive bony invasion rather than smooth pressure erosion Recurrent or multinodular disease extending beyond the tendon sheath Neurovascular compromise of the digit from mass effect Mistaking the firm nodule for a ganglion and under-treating it Leaving satellite nodules or intra-articular extension, resulting in recurrence Damaging the digital neurovascular bundle, which is often intimately related to the tumour, during excision Omitting radiographs and missing bony erosion that alters the surgical plan Failing to send tissue for histology, so an unexpected sarcoma is missed Giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath is a benign proliferative lesion of the synovial lining of tendon sheaths, bursae and joints. It is now recognised as a neoplastic process in most cases, frequently driven by a translocation involving the CSF1 gene that leads to overexpression of colony-stimulating factor 1 and recruitment of CSF1-receptor-bearing macrophages (a landscape effect). Histologically it comprises mononuclear stromal cells, multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells, foamy macrophages and haemosiderin-laden cells within a collagenous stroma, forming a well-circumscribed, often lobulated mass adherent to the tendon sheath. Benign with an excellent prognosis after complete marginal excision, but local recurrence is well recognised, particularly with incompletely excised, multilobulated or distal interphalangeal joint lesions; malignant transformation is very rare.

Giardiasis — Giardia lamblia infection, Giardia intestinalis infection, Giardia duodenalis infection, beaver fever Other causes of chronic or malabsorptive diarrhoea (coeliac disease, tropical sprue) Cryptosporidiosis and other protozoal enteritides Bacterial enteritis Lactose intolerance Irritable bowel syndrome Coeliac disease Tropical sprue Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth Inflammatory bowel disease Repeated stool microscopy for cysts and trophozoites Stool antigen detection (ELISA) or PCR for greater sensitivity Duodenal aspirate or biopsy in difficult cases Assessment for malabsorption and nutritional status in chronic disease Evaluation for immunoglobulin deficiency in recurrent or refractory infection A protozoal infection of the small intestine caused by Giardia, acquired by faecal-oral spread of cysts through contaminated water or food, or person to person Highly endemic in India, contributing to childhood diarrhoea, malabsorption and faltering growth Typical illness is prolonged, with foul-smelling greasy diarrhoea, bloating, flatulence, abdominal cramps and weight loss rather than blood or fever Many infections are asymptomatic, and cyst passage can continue in the absence of symptoms, sustaining transmission Chronic infection can cause fat and lactose malabsorption and, in children, nutritional deficiencies and stunting Diagnosis traditionally relies on detecting cysts or trophozoites on repeated stool examination, with stool antigen and PCR tests being more sensitive Because cyst excretion is intermittent, a single negative stool sample does not exclude infection Treatment is with antiprotozoal agents; attention to safe water and hygiene prevents reinfection and outbreaks Severe dehydration or significant weight loss, particularly in young children Malabsorption with nutritional deficiency and growth faltering Persistent or relapsing infection suggesting underlying immunodeficiency Failure to respond to standard therapy, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis Excluding giardiasis on the basis of a single negative stool sample despite intermittent cyst shedding Overlooking it as a treatable cause of chronic diarrhoea and malabsorption Missing underlying immunodeficiency in recurrent or refractory cases Neglecting water and hygiene measures, leading to reinfection or household spread Ingested Giardia cysts excyst in the small intestine and release trophozoites that attach to the duodenal and jejunal mucosa via a ventral adhesive disc. Colonisation causes villous shortening, disruption of the brush-border enzymes and a mucosal inflammatory response, impairing absorption of fats, carbohydrates and other nutrients. This produces the characteristic malabsorptive, non-inflammatory diarrhoea. Trophozoites encyst as they pass down the gut, and the environmentally hardy cysts are excreted to continue the cycle. Most cases respond well to antiprotozoal therapy with full recovery. Untreated or recurrent infection, especially in children, can cause lasting malabsorption and growth impairment, and reinfection is common where sanitation is poor.

Gilbert syndrome — Gilbert's syndrome, constitutional hepatic dysfunction, familial nonhaemolytic jaundice Haemolytic anaemia Crigler-Najjar syndrome (types I and II) Ineffective erythropoiesis Resolving or physiological neonatal jaundice Drug-induced impairment of bilirubin conjugation or uptake Dubin-Johnson and Rotor syndromes (conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia) Fractionated serum bilirubin showing a predominantly unconjugated (indirect) elevation Normal liver enzymes and synthetic function tests Full blood count, reticulocyte count, and blood film to exclude haemolysis Repeat testing to demonstrate fluctuating mild hyperbilirubinaemia, sometimes accentuated by fasting UGT1A1 genotyping in selected or atypical cases A common, benign inherited disorder of bilirubin conjugation causing mild, fluctuating unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinaemia Due to reduced activity of the hepatic enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1), most often from a promoter polymorphism inherited in a recessive pattern Jaundice is typically intermittent and provoked by fasting, intercurrent illness, dehydration, physical stress, or alcohol Liver enzymes, liver synthetic function, and the blood film are normal, and there is no haemolysis, which helps distinguish it from other causes of raised bilirubin The diagnosis is essentially clinical, based on isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with otherwise normal tests and no evidence of haemolysis or liver disease No treatment is needed; reassurance is the mainstay because the condition is harmless and does not progress to liver damage Reduced UGT1A1 activity can impair metabolism of certain drugs (for example irinotecan), which is a clinically relevant consideration It should not be confused with the far more serious Crigler-Najjar syndromes, which cause severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia or abnormal liver enzymes, which point away from Gilbert syndrome to genuine liver or biliary disease Anaemia or a raised reticulocyte count suggesting haemolysis rather than a benign conjugation defect Very high bilirubin levels, especially from infancy, raising concern for Crigler-Najjar syndrome Bilirubin rising with systemic symptoms indicating an alternative serious diagnosis Over-investigating or mislabelling harmless isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia as liver disease Failing to exclude haemolysis, which can also cause unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia Not fractionating bilirubin and therefore missing a conjugated (and more concerning) pattern Overlooking altered metabolism of drugs such as irinotecan in affected patients Gilbert syndrome results from partially reduced activity of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1, the enzyme that conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid to make it water-soluble for biliary excretion. The commonest genetic basis is an expanded TA repeat in the UGT1A1 gene promoter, which lowers enzyme expression. The consequent modest reduction in conjugating capacity produces mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, accentuated when bilirubin load or physiological stress increases, such as during fasting or illness. There is no structural liver disease and no haemolysis, and bilirubin levels usually remain modestly elevated. Excellent. Gilbert syndrome is a lifelong but entirely benign condition that does not cause liver damage or reduce life expectancy, and no specific treatment is required.

absence of attachment loss Review of medications and hormonal or systemic factors Radiographs when needed to exclude bone loss Blood investigations if systemic disease is suspected Gingivitis is reversible inflammation confined to the gingiva without loss of periodontal attachment or bone The cardinal sign is bleeding on gentle probing or brushing, alongside redness, swelling, and loss of the normal stippled contour It is overwhelmingly plaque-induced, so improved oral hygiene and professional cleaning usually reverse it within days to weeks Hormonal changes in pregnancy and puberty, and certain medications, can exaggerate the gingival response to plaque Unlike periodontitis, probing depths remain shallow and there is no true pocketing or attachment loss Untreated gingivitis is a risk state that may progress to periodontitis in susceptible individuals Necrotising gingivitis is a distinct painful form with ulcerated, punched-out interdental papillae and characteristic malodour Persistent gingival inflammation despite good hygiene should prompt consideration of systemic or drug-related causes Spontaneous gingival bleeding or florid enlargement suggesting leukaemia or a bleeding disorder Painful necrotising gingivitis, particularly in immunocompromised patients Gingival changes that fail to resolve with good hygiene, indicating an underlying systemic cause Assuming all gingival inflammation is simple plaque-induced gingivitis and missing early periodontitis Overlooking systemic, hormonal, or drug-related contributors to gingival changes Attributing spontaneous bleeding to local causes when a haematological disorder is present Failing to reinforce oral hygiene, leading to recurrence Plaque-induced gingivitis develops when microbial biofilm accumulates at the gingival margin and triggers a localised host inflammatory response. Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability cause the classic erythema, oedema, and bleeding tendency, while the junctional epithelium remains intact and attachment is preserved, making the condition reversible. If the biofilm persists, the chronic inflammatory infiltrate can, in susceptible hosts and under modifying influences such as hormonal changes, systemic disease, or medications, evolve toward the attachment and bone loss that define periodontitis. Plaque-induced gingivitis is fully reversible with effective plaque control, but if neglected it can act as a precursor to irreversible periodontitis in susceptible people.

Gitelman syndrome — Gitelman's syndrome, familial hypokalaemia-hypomagnesaemia, thiazide-like tubulopathy Bartter syndrome Surreptitious thiazide diuretic use Chronic vomiting Laxative abuse Primary hypomagnesaemia from other causes Primary hyperaldosteronism (distinguished by hypertension) Serum potassium, magnesium, and bicarbonate to define the hypokalaemic, hypomagnesaemic alkalosis Urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio demonstrating hypocalciuria Plasma renin and aldosterone, usually elevated Urine electrolytes and screening for covert diuretic use Genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and for family counselling ECG when significant hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia is present Gitelman syndrome is an inherited tubulopathy that mimics chronic thiazide diuretic use because the defect is in sodium chloride transport in the distal convoluted tubule The distinguishing electrolyte signature is hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis together with hypomagnesaemia and low urinary calcium excretion It usually presents later than Bartter syndrome, often in adolescence or adulthood, with mild symptoms such as cramps, fatigue, tetany, and salt craving Hypocalciuria and hypomagnesaemia are the key features separating it from Bartter syndrome, which typically shows normal or high calcium excretion Blood pressure is normal or low, and renin and aldosterone are elevated as a compensatory response to salt wasting Chondrocalcinosis and joint symptoms can occur, related to chronic magnesium depletion Management principles are generous replacement of potassium and magnesium, liberal salt intake, and sometimes potassium-sparing agents, with magnesium repletion being essential for correcting the hypokalaemia Symptomatic hypomagnesaemia with tetany or seizures Severe hypokalaemia with arrhythmia risk or marked weakness Prolonged QT interval predisposing to dangerous arrhythmia Persistent symptoms despite apparent replacement, suggesting inadequate magnesium correction Attempting to correct hypokalaemia without also replacing magnesium, so the potassium remains refractory Confusing Gitelman with Bartter syndrome by not measuring urinary calcium and serum magnesium Missing surreptitious thiazide use as a mimic of the syndrome Overlooking the diagnosis in a normotensive adult with chronic unexplained hypokalaemic alkalosis Gitelman syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter of the distal convoluted tubule. Impaired sodium chloride reabsorption at this site leads to renal salt wasting and mild volume contraction, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Increased distal sodium delivery combined with secondary hyperaldosteronism promotes potassium and hydrogen secretion, producing hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. The defect enhances calcium reabsorption downstream, giving the characteristic hypocalciuria, while magnesium wasting from altered distal tubular handling causes hypomagnesaemia. The overall picture closely resembles the effect of long-term thiazide therapy. The long-term outlook is generally good, with preserved renal function in most patients, though lifelong electrolyte replacement is required and symptoms can affect quality of life. Correcting magnesium is often the key to stabilising potassium and preventing arrhythmia.
