compromise Status epilepticus in the epilepsy-predominant phenotype Rapid feeding deterioration with aspiration risk Escalating involuntary movements unresponsive to standard therapy Mistaking the dyskinetic phenotype for dyskinetic cerebral palsy and missing the genetic diagnosis Under-recognising a dystonic storm as an emergency requiring escalation and intensive support Focusing only on seizures while neglecting the disabling movement disorder Failing to consider deep brain stimulation in medically refractory dyskinesia GNAO1 encodes Galpha-o, the most abundant G-protein alpha subunit in the mammalian brain, which couples to numerous G-protein-coupled receptors and modulates neurotransmitter release and downstream signalling, including adenylate cyclase and calcium and potassium channel regulation. Disease variants disturb this signalling through loss- or gain-of-function-like effects on the G-protein cycle, perturbing the balance of inhibitory and excitatory transmission in basal ganglia and cortical circuits. This disruption produces both the epileptic and the striking hyperkinetic movement features, and the particular variant helps determine whether epilepsy or movement disorder dominates. Most affected children have significant intellectual disability and persistent movement disorder; life-threatening dyskinetic crises contribute to morbidity, and while deep brain stimulation can markedly reduce refractory movements, cognitive impairment usually persists.

Gnathostomiasis — Gnathostoma spinigerum infection, larva migrans profundus, Yangtze oedema, wandering swelling Cutaneous larva migrans Loiasis (Calabar swellings) Angioedema or urticaria Sparganosis and other migrating tissue helminths Fascioliasis in its migratory phase Other causes of eosinophilic meningitis such as angiostrongyliasis Bacterial or inflammatory panniculitis Full blood count and blood film for eosinophilia Gnathostoma-specific serology Detailed dietary and travel history Cerebrospinal fluid examination (often eosinophilic, sometimes xanthochromic) if neurological involvement is suspected MRI of the brain or spinal cord in neurological disease Histology or identification of a larva if surgically retrieved A food-borne tissue nematode infection caused chiefly by Gnathostoma spinigerum, acquired by eating undercooked freshwater fish, eels, frogs, poultry or snakes Endemic in Southeast Asia, notably Thailand, and increasingly reported from Latin America and among returning travellers The hallmark is intermittent, migratory subcutaneous swellings that move over days, often with overlying erythema, itch or pain Peripheral eosinophilia is common and supports the diagnosis in the right exposure context The larva cannot mature in humans and wanders through tissues, so the most feared complication is invasion of the central nervous system causing eosinophilic meningitis, radiculomyelitis or haemorrhage Serology helps confirm the diagnosis, as recovering the larva is uncommon Treatment uses anthelmintics such as albendazole or ivermectin, sometimes with corticosteroids for the inflammatory reaction; surgical removal is possible if a migrating larva is accessible A dietary history of raw or undercooked freshwater animal flesh is a key diagnostic clue Headache, radicular pain, limb weakness or altered consciousness suggesting central nervous system invasion Signs of intracranial or spinal haemorrhage Ocular involvement threatening vision Rapidly progressive neurological deficit Not eliciting a history of eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish or other flesh Attributing migratory swellings to allergy or angioedema Failing to consider neurognathostomiasis in eosinophilic meningitis from an endemic area Assuming a single course of anthelmintic guarantees cure, as relapse can occur Overlooking the diagnosis in a returning traveller with eosinophilia Human gnathostomiasis follows ingestion of third-stage Gnathostoma larvae in undercooked or raw intermediate hosts such as freshwater fish and other flesh. Humans are accidental hosts in which the larva cannot develop into an adult worm. Instead it penetrates the gut wall and migrates through the liver and other tissues, then wanders through the subcutaneous tissues and, less often, deeper structures. This migration provokes eosinophil-rich inflammation and produces the characteristic shifting swellings. Aberrant migration into the central nervous system causes tracking damage and haemorrhage, giving rise to eosinophilic meningitis and myeloradiculopathy that account for the most serious morbidity. Cutaneous disease is generally benign though it may relapse over months to years, whereas central nervous system gnathostomiasis carries a serious prognosis with a risk of permanent neurological deficit or death.

GNB1 encephalopathy — GNB1, GNB1-related neurodevelopmental disorder, G-protein beta1 encephalopathy, MRD42 GNAO1 encephalopathy STXBP1 and SYNGAP1 encephalopathies GNB5-related disorder Other genetic causes of intellectual disability with epilepsy and movement disorder Chromosomal and copy-number neurodevelopmental disorders Mitochondrial and metabolic encephalopathies Gene panel or whole-exome sequencing to identify the GNB1 variant Electroencephalography where seizures are present, to characterise type Brain magnetic resonance imaging to exclude structural causes Developmental, cognitive, and movement-disorder assessment Feeding, growth, and visual evaluation Haematological review if blood-count abnormalities are noted Caused by usually de novo variants in GNB1, which encodes the beta1 subunit of heterotrimeric G-proteins that relay signals from G-protein-coupled receptors to downstream effectors including ion channels Core features are developmental delay and intellectual disability with hypotonia, and epilepsy occurs in a substantial subset Seizures, when present, are variable in type, including focal, generalised, and infantile spasms, and range from readily controlled to drug-resistant A movement disorder can occur, with dystonia or other involuntary movements, overlapping the broader G-protein-related phenotypes Additional features may include feeding difficulties, growth problems, visual impairment, and, in some, a predisposition to certain haematological abnormalities Because the beta subunit modulates effectors such as G-protein-gated potassium channels, disease reflects disturbed signalling rather than a single channel defect, and antiseizure therapy is broad-spectrum and empirical GNB1 shares mechanistic ground with GNAO1 as a heterotrimeric G-protein subunit disorder, though the phenotypes differ Infantile spasms or drug-resistant seizures with developmental regression Status epilepticus Escalating movement disorder impairing function Significant feeding failure or unexplained haematological abnormality Excluding the diagnosis because it is a signalling protein rather than an ion channel Overlooking the associated movement disorder or haematological features Conflating the phenotype with GNAO1 despite differing clinical patterns Expecting a channel-specific therapy to be available GNB1 encodes the beta1 subunit of heterotrimeric G-proteins, which together with gamma subunits transmits signals from activated G-protein-coupled receptors to effectors including adenylate cyclase, phospholipase C, and G-protein-gated inwardly rectifying potassium channels. The beta-gamma complex is essential for correct assembly and signalling of the G-protein cycle. Pathogenic variants disrupt subunit interactions and downstream signalling, perturbing neuronal excitability and neurotransmission across many circuits. This broad signalling disturbance produces the combination of intellectual disability, hypotonia, epilepsy, and movement disorder, and because the defect is upstream of multiple effectors, treatment cannot target a single channel. Most affected individuals have intellectual disability of variable severity with hypotonia; seizures and movement disorder, when present, add to the burden, and cognitive outcome is generally guarded though heterogeneous.

to exclude a neuropathic cause of foot drop A slowly progressive distal myopathy typically presenting in early adulthood with foot drop and weakness of the tibialis anterior Characteristically spares the quadriceps until late in the disease, a feature that helps distinguish it from many other myopathies Inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and caused by mutations in GNE, the gene for the key enzyme of sialic acid biosynthesis Muscle biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles and cytoplasmic inclusions but characteristically lacks the inflammation of sporadic inclusion body myositis Creatine kinase is usually normal or only modestly raised despite progressive weakness Weakness advances proximally over years and can eventually affect the upper limbs and, later, the hip girdle, with relative sparing of facial and ocular muscles Sialic acid replacement strategies have been investigated experimentally, so accurate genetic diagnosis is important for prognosis, counselling and trial eligibility Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting an inflammatory rather than genetic myopathy Prominent inflammation on biopsy that would favour sporadic inclusion body myositis Respiratory muscle involvement in advanced disease Loss of ambulation requiring mobility and falls assessment Misdiagnosing it as sporadic inclusion body myositis and treating with immunotherapy, which is ineffective Being reassured by a normal creatine kinase and dismissing a genetic myopathy Attributing the foot drop to a peripheral neuropathy without recognising the myopathic pattern Overlooking the characteristic quadriceps sparing that points to the diagnosis GNE myopathy is caused by biallelic mutations in GNE, which encodes the bifunctional enzyme UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 2-epimerase/N-acetylmannosamine kinase that catalyses the rate-limiting steps of sialic acid biosynthesis. Reduced enzyme activity leads to hyposialylation of muscle glycoproteins and glycolipids, which is thought to impair muscle-cell function and promote the accumulation of autophagic and protein aggregates seen histologically as rimmed vacuoles and inclusions. The resulting slow degeneration of muscle fibres produces the characteristic distal-onset, quadriceps-sparing pattern of weakness, although the precise link between hyposialylation and fibre loss is incompletely understood. GNE myopathy is slowly progressive, with many patients losing independent ambulation roughly one to two decades after onset, but life expectancy is usually preserved as respiratory and cardiac involvement are uncommon and generally late.

(overlapping entity) Maternal diabetic embryopathy with facial asymmetry Audiological assessment including brainstem-evoked responses to characterise and quantify hearing loss Ophthalmological upper airway obstruction from severe mandibular hypoplasia or glossoptosis Feeding difficulty and failure to thrive requiring nutritional support Undetected hearing loss threatening speech and language development Unstable cervical vertebral anomalies posing a risk during anaesthesia or manipulation Significant undiagnosed cardiac or renal malformation Attributing developmental delay to the syndrome itself rather than to correctable hearing loss Overlooking the contralateral, less affected side, which frequently has subtle anomalies Failing to screen for cardiac, renal, and vertebral anomalies because attention focuses on the face Assuming a genetic recurrence pattern when most cases are sporadic Neglecting airway assessment before sedation or surgery in infants with mandibular hypoplasia The spectrum is thought to arise from disrupted development of the first and second branchial (pharyngeal) arches and the tissues they give rise to, together with contributions from cranial neural crest cells. A leading hypothesis implicates vascular disruption or haemorrhage in the developing stapedial artery territory early in gestation, leading to variable local tissue loss and hence the striking asymmetry. Because the affected arches contribute to the mandible, external and middle ear, and adjacent facial structures, defects cluster in these regions, while accompanying disturbance of paraxial mesoderm and neural crest migration explains the vertebral, ocular, cardiac, and renal associations. Most cases are sporadic with multifactorial causation. Prognosis depends on the severity and extent of anomalies; many children with milder involvement do well with staged reconstruction and hearing rehabilitation and achieve normal cognition, whereas extensive craniofacial, cardiac, or central nervous system involvement carries greater morbidity.

conduction studies if ulnar neuropathy is suspected Plain radiographs or stress views if bony injury or valgus instability is considered Pain localises to the medial epicondyle and the origin of the wrist flexor-pronator group, aggravated by resisted wrist flexion and forearm pronation Like its lateral counterpart, it is a degenerative tendinopathy of the common flexor origin rather than a true inflammatory epicondylitis It is much less common than tennis elbow and is linked to gripping, throwing, and pronation-loading activities The ulnar nerve lies immediately behind the medial epicondyle ulnar nerve function and check for a positive Tinel sign at the cubital tunnel, as concurrent ulnar neuropathy alters management Management mirrors lateral epicondylitis, centred on load reduction and a progressive eccentric flexor-pronator strengthening programme Steroid injection carries the added risk of ulnar nerve injury and offers only short-term benefit, so it is used cautiously Consider valgus overload and medial collateral ligament pathology in throwing athletes with medial elbow pain Progressive ulnar nerve symptoms with weakness or intrinsic hand muscle wasting Night pain, systemic features, or a mass suggesting infection or tumour Significant trauma or instability raising concern for ligament rupture Persistent symptoms despite appropriate rehabilitation prompting diagnostic review Missing associated ulnar nerve entrapment, which can dominate the clinical picture Injecting corticosteroid without regard to the closely applied ulnar nerve Failing to recognise medial collateral ligament injury in throwing athletes Treating as inflammatory with rest rather than addressing the tendinopathy with loading Golfer's elbow is an overuse tendinopathy of the common flexor-pronator origin at the medial epicondyle, particularly involving pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis. Repetitive flexion, pronation, and valgus loading cause microtrauma and a failed healing response, producing mucoid degeneration and disorganised collagen. Proximity to the ulnar nerve means concurrent nerve irritation is common. Most patients improve with load management and progressive strengthening, though recovery may take months; coexisting ulnar neuropathy or valgus instability tends to worsen outcomes and may need specific treatment.

Gonadoblastoma — gonadoblastoma of dysgenetic gonad, dysgenetic gonadal tumour, in situ germ cell neoplasm of streak gonad Dysgerminoma or other malignant germ cell tumour of the gonad Sex hypogonadism Teratoma or mixed germ cell tumour Karyotype and molecular testing for Y-chromosome material in gonadal dysgenesis or disorder of sex development Serum LH and FSH (typically elevated) with sex-steroid levels (low) Germ cell tumour markers (for example lactate dehydrogenase, alpha-fetoprotein, and beta-hCG) to assess for malignant transformation Pelvic and abdominal imaging to localise gonads and detect a mass Histological examination of removed gonadal tissue to confirm the diagnosis and exclude invasive tumour Assessment for the wider features of the underlying disorder of sex development A tumour composed of both germ cells and sex cord-stromal elements that arises almost exclusively in dysgenetic gonads containing Y-chromosome material Although the lesion itself is amenorrhoea, or features of the underlying disorder of sex development Because of the malignancy risk, prophylactic removal of dysgenetic Y-bearing gonads (gonadectomy) is recommended, with timing individualised to the specific diagnosis Detection of Y-chromosome material on karyotype or molecular testing in a girl with gonadal dysgenesis is the key trigger for considering gonadectomy Identification of Y-chromosome material in a patient with a dysgenetic or streak gonad, indicating malignancy risk and the need to consider gonadectomy A rapidly enlarging pelvic or abdominal mass suggesting invasive germ cell malignancy Rising germ cell tumour markers Signs of metastatic disease such as lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms Failing to karyotype patients with gonadal dysgenesis and therefore missing occult Y-chromosome material that mandates gonadectomy Delaying prophylactic gonadectomy in a Y-bearing dysgenetic gonad and allowing malignant progression Assuming a streak gonad carries no tumour risk irrespective of karyotype Overlooking the diagnosis in a phenotypic female presenting only with primary amenorrhoea Neglecting hormone replacement and the broader care needs of the underlying disorder of sex development after gonadectomy Gonadoblastoma develops in gonads that have failed to differentiate normally (dysgenetic or streak gonads) when Y-chromosome material is present. Genes on the Y chromosome, particularly within the gonadoblastoma region that includes TSPY, are thought to promote survival and abnormal proliferation of germ cells within a disorganised stromal environment, producing a mixed germ-cell and sex cord-stromal lesion. The tumour is regarded as an in situ neoplasm, but the same germ cells can undergo malignant transformation to an invasive germ cell tumour such as dysgerminoma. The dysgenetic gonad itself produces little or no sex steroid, so affected individuals commonly show hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and the phenotype of their underlying disorder of sex development. When dysgenetic Y-bearing gonads are removed before malignant transformation, the outlook is excellent and the risk of invasive germ cell tumour is essentially eliminated; if an invasive tumour has already developed, prognosis depends on tumour type and stage, though dysgerminoma is generally chemosensitive with favourable outcomes.

Gonadotroph (clinically non-functioning) pituitary adenoma — non-functioning pituitary adenoma, NFPA, gonadotroph adenoma, clinically silent gonadotroph tumour Prolactinoma (true prolactin-secreting adenoma) Craniopharyngioma Meningioma of the sellar or suprasellar region Rathke cleft cyst Hypophysitis Metastatic deposit or other sellar mass Pituitary hyperplasia (e.g. from primary hypothyroidism) Pituitary MRI to define tumour size, suprasellar extension and chiasmal or cavernous sinus involvement Full anterior pituitary hormone profile to detect hypopituitarism Serum prolactin, interpreted in the context of possible stalk effect Measurement of FSH, LH and alpha-subunit to characterise gonadotroph output Formal visual field testing (perimetry) when the tumour approaches the optic chiasm Assessment of secondary adrenal and thyroid axes before any surgery The most common type of clinically non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma, usually of gonadotroph lineage, which typically presents through mass effect rather than a hormone excess syndrome Although immunopositive for gonadotropins or their subunits, secretion is usually inefficient and clinically silent, so patients rarely have symptomatic FSH or LH excess Presentation is often with headache, visual field defects (classically bitemporal hemianopia) and features of hypopituitarism from compression of the normal gland Stalk compression can raise prolactin modestly, but this stalk-effect hyperprolactinaemia must be distinguished from a true prolactinoma Many are found incidentally on imaging performed for unrelated reasons (pituitary incidentaloma) Because they are not hormonally driven, medical therapy is of limited benefit and transsphenoidal surgery is the mainstay for symptomatic or growing tumours Pituitary apoplexy from haemorrhage or infarction can be the dramatic first presentation of a previously unrecognised adenoma Progressive or acute visual field loss from chiasmal compression Pituitary apoplexy with sudden severe headache, ophthalmoplegia and collapse Secondary adrenal insufficiency requiring urgent glucocorticoid cover Rapid tumour enlargement or invasion on serial imaging Mistaking stalk-effect hyperprolactinaemia for a prolactinoma and treating with dopamine agonists instead of operating Failing to diagnose and replace secondary adrenal insufficiency before surgery or stress Assuming an incidental pituitary lesion is stable without documenting visual fields and pituitary function Overlooking early apoplexy in a patient with sudden headache and subtle eye signs This is a benign monoclonal tumour arising from pituitary gonadotroph cells. Although the cells often express FSH, LH or the glycoprotein alpha-subunit on immunostaining, they generally secrete these hormones inefficiently and without a recognisable clinical syndrome, hence the label clinically non-functioning. The clinical consequences instead arise from progressive tumour growth: compression of the optic chiasm causes visual field loss, distortion of the pituitary stalk interrupts dopaminergic inhibition and mildly raises prolactin, and destruction or compression of the normal anterior pituitary produces variable hypopituitarism. Sudden haemorrhagic or ischaemic change within the tumour causes pituitary apoplexy. Surgical decompression usually improves visual fields and stabilises the tumour, and many patients do well long term, though hypopituitarism often persists and requires hormone replacement. Residual or recurrent tumour is common enough to warrant lifelong imaging and endocrine surveillance, with radiotherapy considered for progressive remnants.

Gongylonemiasis — Gongylonema pulchrum, gullet worm infection, oral gongylonemiasis Oral larva migrans from other nematodes Aphthous ulceration or other oral mucosal lesions Delusional parasitosis Foreign body in the oral mucosa Herpetic or other viral stomatitis Burning mouth syndrome Careful oral and mucosal examination to locate the serpiginous track or worm Extraction and morphological identification of the worm Histological examination of excised mucosa if the worm fragments Detailed exposure history for beetle, cockroach or contaminated food ingestion Exclusion of other oral mucosal disease by clinical assessment Photographic documentation of the migrating lesion to aid diagnosis Gongylonemiasis is caused by the spirurid nematode Gongylonema pulchrum, a parasite chiefly of grazing mammals that occasionally infects humans Infection follows accidental ingestion of infected intermediate hosts, principally coprophagous beetles and cockroaches, or contaminated food and water The worm characteristically migrates within the mucosa of the mouth, lips, tongue, gums or oesophagus The hallmark is a sensation of a moving thread beneath the oral mucosa, often with local irritation, tingling or discomfort The migrating worm may be visible as a serpiginous track and can sometimes be extracted from the mucosa Diagnosis is made by identifying and removing the worm and confirming its morphology Manual or surgical extraction of the worm is curative; antiparasitic drugs have been used but removal is the mainstay Persistent oral lesions failing to resolve after apparent worm removal Marked local inflammation or secondary infection Diagnostic uncertainty raising concern for oral neoplasia Recurrent symptoms suggesting incomplete extraction Dismissing the crawling sensation as delusional parasitosis without examining the mucosa Incomplete extraction leaving worm fragments and persistent symptoms Failing to take an exposure history for insect ingestion Over-investigating a benign condition once the worm is identified Humans acquire Gongylonema pulchrum by ingesting infected beetles or cockroaches, or food and water contaminated with them. Released larvae penetrate and then migrate within the superficial layers of the oral and oesophageal mucosa, where the thread-like adult worm tunnels through the epithelium. This migration mechanically irritates the mucosa and produces the characteristic crawling or moving sensation and localised inflammation. Because the parasite remains within the upper alimentary mucosa and does not typically disseminate, the illness is usually a benign, localised nuisance rather than a systemic disease. The prognosis is excellent; the infection is benign and self-limited, and removal of the worm results in prompt and lasting resolution of symptoms.

Gonorrhea — gonococcal infection, Neisseria gonorrhoeae Nongonococcal urethritis (C. trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Trichomonas vaginalis, HSV) - clinically often impossible to distinguish from gonococcal urethritis (p.1255-1256) Bacterial cystitis/urinary tract infection versus the urethral syndrome in women presenting with dysuria (p.1256) For the bacteremic stage of DGI: reactive arthritis, acute rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis, erythema nodosum, drug-induced arthritis, and viral infections including hepatitis B and acute HIV infection (p.1257) Suppurative gonococcal arthritis in the absence of symptomatic genital infection cannot be distinguished from septic arthritis caused by other pathogens (p.1257) Meningococcemia, which can produce a dermatitis-arthritis syndrome, purulent monoarthritis, and reactive polyarthritis similar to DGI (p.1058) Acute HIV infection and hepatitis B (viral causes mimicking the bacteremic arthritis-dermatitis stage of DGI) (p.1257) Gram stain of urethral discharge for gram-negative intracellular monococci/diplococci - highly sensitive in symptomatic men, only ~50% sensitive for cervicitis (p.1255, 1257) NAAT (e.g., Aptima Combo 2, Xpert CT/NG, BD ProbeTec, COBAS) on urine, urethral, cervical or self-collected vaginal swabs - more sensitive than culture and co-detects C. trachomatis; point-of-care NAAT with ~30-minute turnaround available (p.1257) Culture on modified Thayer-Martin/selective medium with prompt processing (gonococci do not tolerate drying); single endocervical culture ~80-90% sensitive (p.1257) In MSM, screen rectum and pharynx in addition to urine, since urine alone will miss the majority of cases (p.1257) Blood cultures (Isolator tubes may improve yield; positivity falls after 48 h of illness) and synovial fluid (inoculate into blood culture broth and chocolate agar) in suspected DGI; organisms are seldom recovered from blood and synovial fluid in the same patient (p.1257) Standardized culture is the preferred legal-evidence method in children for suspected sexual abuse; two NAATs targeting different sequences may substitute (p.1257) Total hemolytic complement activity assay in anyone with more than one episode of DGI (p.1255, 1260) Reactive arthritis (joint distribution differs from DGI; skin and genital manifestations also differ) (p.1257) Acute rheumatoid arthritis (p.1257) Sarcoidosis (p.1257) Erythema nodosum (p.1257) Drug-induced arthritis (p.1257) Gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted infection of the epithelium that commonly presents as cervicitis, urethritis, proctitis, or conjunctivitis; if untreated it can cause local complications including endometritis, salpingitis, tuboovarian abscess, bartholinitis, peritonitis, and perihepatitis in women, and periurethritis and epididymitis in men (p.1253). In men, acute urethritis is the most common manifestation, typically after a 2-7 day incubation, with discharge that is initially scant and mucoid but becomes profuse and purulent within a day or two; however, a reservoir of infected men remains asymptomatic (p.1255). About half of women infected with N. gonorrhoeae develop symptoms; many have only minor symptoms (scant cervical discharge, dysuria) and may delay care, so the asymptomatic/minimally symptomatic reservoir is key to ongoing transmission (p.1256). Gram stain of urethral exudate showing gram-negative intracellular monococci and diplococci is highly specific and sensitive in symptomatic men, but is only about 50% sensitive for gonococcal cervicitis, so women should be diagnosed by culture or a nonculture (NAAT) method (p.1257). Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) are now widely used, are more sensitive than culture for both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, allow urine and self-collected vaginal swab testing, and simultaneously detect chlamydial co-infection (p.1257). Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) results from gonococcal bacteremia and most commonly presents as an arthritis-dermatitis syndrome with fever, chills, tenosynovitis, polyarthralgias, and characteristic skin lesions (papules/pustules with a hemorrhagic component, ~5-40, on the extremities) seen in about 75% of patients (p.1257). Menstruation is a risk factor for dissemination and roughly two-thirds of DGI cases occur in women; in about half of affected women symptoms begin within 7 days of onset of menses (p.1257). Persons deficient in terminal complement components (C5-C9) and those receiving the C5-blocking monoclonal antibody eculizumab are predisposed to recurrent neisserial bacteremia; anyone with more than one episode of DGI should be screened for complement deficiency (p.1255, 1260). Ceftriaxone is the recommended first-line agent for uncomplicated gonococcal infection, now at twice the previously recommended dose because mean inhibitory concentrations of current strains have doubled relative to 20 years ago (p.1259). Quinolone-containing regimens and cefixime are no longer recommended as first-line treatment in the United States because of widespread quinolone resistance and rising cefixime MICs (p.1259). Because co-infection with C. trachomatis occurs frequently, concurrent treatment for chlamydia (doxycycline) is recommended whenever chlamydial infection cannot be excluded (p.1259). Disseminated gonococcal infection with the joint-localized suppurative arthritis stage - hospitalization indicated, may need joint aspiration and higher/longer therapy (p.1259) Gonococcal meningitis - rare complication of DGI requiring high-dose IV ceftriaxone for 10-14 days (p.1257, 1260) Gonococcal endocarditis - rare today but historically accounted for about one-quarter of endocarditis cases; requires at least 4 weeks of IV therapy (p.1257, 1260) Ophthalmia neonatorum and adult ocular gonorrhea - prompt recognition and treatment essential, as corneal ulceration may progress to perforation, panophthalmitis and blindness (p.1256-1257) Pelvic inflammatory disease should be considered when cervical infection extends to cause dyspareunia or lower abdominal/back pain (p.1256) Because co-infection with C. trachomatis is frequent, treatment of gonorrhea must include concurrent therapy for chlamydia (doxycycline) whenever chlamydial infection cannot be excluded - omitting this is a key pitfall (p.1259). Azithromycin is no longer recommended as part of the first-line regimen because U.S. gonococcal resistance to azithromycin rose more than sevenfold to 4.7% in 2021 (p.1259). A presumptive diagnosis of gonorrhea cannot be made from gram-negative diplococci on a pharyngeal Gram stain, because commensal Neisseria species are normal pharyngeal flora (p.1257). Gram stain is only ~50% sensitive for gonococcal cervicitis; relying on it in women risks missed diagnoses, so culture or NAAT is required (p.1257). DGI strains often do not incite a local genital inflammatory response and may not cause genital symptoms, so disseminated disease can occur without an obvious mucosal source (p.1254, 1257). Quinolones and cefixime are no longer first-line in the United States due to resistance and rising MICs - using them empirically risks treatment failure (p.1259). Persistent symptoms after a recommended regimen should prompt evaluation for reinfection, a drug-resistant strain, or an alternative diagnosis rather than simple re-treatment; culture and susceptibility testing should be performed (p.1259). Because of high reinfection rates within 6-12 months, persons treated for gonorrhea should be retested at 3 months (p.1259). N. gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative, nonmotile, non-spore-forming, oxidase-positive diplococcus and an exclusively human pathogen; it carries on average three genome copies per coccal unit, and this polyploidy supports a high level of antigenic variation that aids host survival. Pili (fimbriae) mediate initial adherence to nonciliated columnar epithelial cells and enable invasion, transcytosis, genetic competence and transformation; pilus expression is switched off on subculture as a basis for antigenic variation. Opacity-associated protein (Opa) mediates intergonococcal and epithelial adhesion and binds CEACAM receptors, promoting invasion, suppressing CD4+ T-cell activation, and enabling nonopsonic neutrophil phagocytosis. Porin (the most abundant surface protein) forms the basis of serotyping; PorB.1A strains are associated with disseminated infection, resist normal human serum killing, bind complement-inhibitory molecules and may not cause local symptoms, whereas PorB.1B strains usually cause local genital infection. Lipooligosaccharide (LOS) has marked endotoxic activity; sialylation of LOS inhibits classical and alternative complement pathways and reduces neutrophil killing. Iron/zinc scavenging proteins (transferrin-, lactoferrin-, hemoglobin-binding proteins) and IgA1 protease promote survival. Host entry into nonphagocytic cells involves phospholipase C and sphingomyelinase activation with ceramide-mediated apoptosis, and inflammation is driven by LOS and peptidoglycan-induced cytokine release (p.1254-1255). A single recommended ceftriaxone regimen almost always cures uncomplicated urethral, cervical, rectal, or pharyngeal infection, and true treatment failure with a recommended regimen is rare. Symptomatic pharyngeal gonorrhea is harder to eradicate than genital infection. In the preantibiotic era untreated urethritis persisted about 8 weeks. DGI incidence has fallen (from ~0.5-3% of untreated mucosal infections in the 1970s) likely due to a decline in disseminating strains. A dramatic alleviation of arthritis-dermatitis symptoms within 12-24 h of appropriate antibiotics supports a clinical diagnosis of DGI even when cultures are negative. Rising worldwide resistance, including reduced ceftriaxone susceptibility, threatens future treatment efficacy (p.1257-1260). Clinical manifestations span uncomplicated mucosal infection (urethritis, cervicitis, proctitis, pharyngitis, conjunctivitis) versus complicated/disseminated disease. DGI has historically been described in two overlapping stages: a bacteremic stage (higher fever, chills, polyarthralgias, tenosynovitis, and skin lesions) and a joint-localized stage with suppurative (septic) arthritis, though a clear-cut progression is usually not evident (p.1257).

focusing only on the antibody defect Missing associated autoimmune cytopenias or myasthenia gravis Delaying immunoglobulin replacement while investigating the tumour Good syndrome links a tumour of the thymic epithelium to a profound acquired immunodeficiency, although the exact mechanism remains incompletely understood. The abnormal thymic microenvironment is thought to disturb lymphocyte development and tolerance, and bone-marrow precursor abnormalities appear to curtail B-cell production, so that mature B cells become scarce and immunoglobulin levels fall. T-cell numbers and function are also perturbed, producing a combined pattern of susceptibility to both encapsulated bacteria (from the antibody failure) and opportunistic organisms (from the cellular defect). The same immune dysregulation, coupled with the thymoma's known association with autoimmunity, underlies the frequent autoimmune cytopenias and neuromuscular disease. Importantly, the immunodeficiency generally persists after the thymoma is removed. The prognosis is guarded, with higher infection-related mortality than uncomplicated adult antibody deficiency; immunoglobulin replacement and prophylaxis reduce infections, but autoimmune complications and opportunistic infection persist because thymoma resection does not correct the immune defect.

Gordon syndrome sits within the PIEZO2-related distal arthrogryposis spectrum. PIEZO2 encodes a mechanically activated ion channel important for proprioception and touch, and gain-of-function variants disturb sensory feedback and muscle tone during foetal development. Impaired and unbalanced foetal movement permits periarticular fibrosis and joint contracture, giving camptodactyly and clubfoot, while abnormal palatal shelf development produces the cleft palate. The contractures are congenital and static rather than progressive, and the phenotype overlaps with distal arthrogryposis type 5. With cleft repair, feeding support and orthopaedic management the outlook is good; intellect and lifespan are usually normal, though short stature and residual limb deformity may persist and speech may require support after palatal surgery.

malignancy or infection without appropriate biopsy Underestimating the risk of chylothorax when ribs, spine, or thorax are affected Assuming stabilisation is permanent and stopping surveillance too early Attempting isolated surgery without addressing the underlying vascular-lymphatic process, risking recurrence Gorham-Stout disease is characterised by uncontrolled proliferation of vascular and lymphatic endothelial channels within bone that progressively replace and destroy the osseous matrix. The abnormal vessels and associated osteoclastic activity dissolve bone in a relentless, often locally aggressive fashion, though the process does not metastasise. The trigger is not fully understood, but dysregulated lymphangiogenesis and angiogenesis, with increased osteoclast sensitivity to humoral factors, are thought central. When the disease reaches the thoracic cavity or thoracic duct, abnormal lymphatic channels can leak, producing chylous effusions that carry significant morbidity and mortality. The course is unpredictable; disease may stabilise spontaneously or progress relentlessly, and prognosis is generally good when confined to an extremity but markedly worse with thoracic involvement and chylothorax.

Gorlin syndrome — naevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome, NBCCS, basal cell naevus syndrome, PTCH1, Gorlin-Goltz syndrome Sporadic multiple basal cell carcinomas from chronic sun exposure Bazex-Dupre-Christol syndrome Rombo syndrome Trichoepitheliomas of Brooke-Spiegler syndrome Xeroderma pigmentosum with early skin cancers Isolated odontogenic keratocysts Germline molecular genetic testing of PTCH1 and SUFU including deletion/duplication analysis Orthopantomogram or jaw imaging for odontogenic keratocysts Skull and skeletal radiographs for falx calcification and rib or vertebral anomalies Dermatological mapping and biopsy of suspicious skin lesions Baseline and clinically guided brain MRI in young children for medulloblastoma surveillance, favouring non-ionising imaging Cardiac and ovarian ultrasound where fibromas are suspected Autosomal dominant syndrome most often caused by germline loss-of-function variants in PTCH1, a negative regulator of the Sonic hedgehog signalling pathway; SUFU variants are a less common cause Multiple basal cell carcinomas develop from a young age, often on sun-exposed and non-exposed skin, and may number in the many across a lifetime Odontogenic keratocysts of the jaw are an early and characteristic feature, frequently causing swelling or being found incidentally on dental imaging Palmar and plantar pits are a useful clinical clue on close skin examination Skeletal anomalies include bifid or splayed ribs, and calcification of the falx cerebri is commonly seen on skull imaging There is markedly increased radiosensitivity, so diagnostic and therapeutic radiation should be minimised to avoid inducing new basal cell carcinomas in the treatment field Childhood medulloblastoma (desmoplastic subtype) occurs in a minority and is an important early risk, particularly with SUFU variants New neurological signs in a young child raising concern for medulloblastoma Rapidly enlarging or aggressive basal cell carcinoma, particularly around the eyes, nose or ears Expanding jaw swelling or pathological fracture from an odontogenic keratocyst Extensive prior therapeutic radiotherapy given before the diagnosis was recognised Using radiotherapy for basal cell carcinomas and thereby inducing numerous new tumours in the irradiated field Dismissing multiple early-onset basal cell carcinomas as ordinary sun damage Missing palmar and plantar pits and jaw cysts that would prompt the diagnosis Failing to counsel on sun protection and to arrange paediatric medulloblastoma awareness Gorlin syndrome arises from germline inactivating variants in PTCH1 (or less often SUFU), key components of the Sonic hedgehog signalling pathway. PTCH1 normally inhibits the transmembrane protein Smoothened; loss of PTCH1 function releases this inhibition, leading to constitutive hedgehog pathway activation and unchecked proliferation in susceptible tissues. As a tumour-suppressor mechanism, tumour formation follows a somatic second hit. Aberrant hedgehog signalling explains the developmental anomalies and the predisposition to basal cell carcinomas, odontogenic keratocysts and medulloblastoma. The same pathway dependence underlies the therapeutic use of hedgehog pathway inhibitors in advanced disease. Life expectancy is usually near normal, but lifelong burden from recurrent basal cell carcinomas and jaw cysts is considerable and requires ongoing surveillance and treatment. Medulloblastoma in early childhood is the most serious potential complication and drives paediatric monitoring.

Gout — gouty arthritis, monosodium urate crystal arthritis, podagra, urate arthropathy, acute gout Septic arthritis, which must be excluded and can coexist Pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis) Cellulitis Reactive or psoriatic arthritis Trauma or haemarthrosis Acute flare of osteoarthritis Rheumatoid arthritis in polyarticular presentations Joint aspiration with polarised microscopy for negatively birefringent needle-shaped urate crystals and to exclude infection Synovial fluid Gram stain, culture, and cell count Serum urate, interpreted with the timing caveat and repeated once the attack settles Renal function and assessment of cardiovascular and metabolic comorbidity Radiographs for chronic 'punched-out' erosions in longstanding disease Dual-energy CT to detect and characterise urate deposits when the diagnosis is uncertain Ultrasound for the 'double contour' sign of urate over articular cartilage Acute gout classically presents as an abrupt, exquisitely painful monoarthritis, most often of the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra), with redness, swelling, and warmth peaking within hours It is caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in and around joints on a background of chronic hyperuricaemia and urate supersaturation Definitive diagnosis is by joint aspiration and polarised light microscopy showing needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, often seen within phagocytes during an attack Serum urate can be normal or even low during an acute flare, so a normal value does not exclude gout; the level is best measured or repeated once the attack has settled Common triggers and associations include alcohol, purine-rich food and fructose, diuretics, chronic kidney disease, obesity, and the metabolic syndrome Acute attacks are managed with anti-inflammatory therapy, choosing between a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, colchicine, or a corticosteroid according to comorbidity Urate-lowering therapy using a treat-to-target approach (lowering serum urate below the saturation threshold) is indicated for recurrent attacks, tophi, or urate arthropathy, with anti-inflammatory prophylaxis when it is introduced Urate-lowering therapy should not be started or stopped during an acute attack, and any established urate-lowering therapy is continued through a flare rather than interrupted Fever with a hot swollen joint that may represent septic arthritis rather than, or in addition to, gout Rapid polyarticular presentation in a systemically unwell patient Renal impairment or urolithiasis complicating management A tophus with skin ulceration or secondary infection Excluding gout because the serum urate is normal during an acute attack Starting or stopping urate-lowering therapy during an acute flare, which can prolong or precipitate attacks Failing to exclude coexisting septic arthritis in a hot joint Treating a target urate number without a structured treat-to-target strategy and prophylaxis at initiation Overlooking associated cardiovascular, renal, and metabolic disease Sustained hyperuricaemia, arising more often from renal under-excretion than from urate overproduction, leads to supersaturation of extracellular fluid and precipitation of monosodium urate crystals within joints and soft tissues. The crystals are engulfed by resident phagocytes and activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, driving release of interleukin-1 beta and an intense neutrophil-rich inflammatory response that produces the acute attack. Repeated crystal deposition and low-grade chronic inflammation eventually generate tophi and cause structural joint damage. Gout is highly treatable: with effective urate-lowering therapy to target, crystals dissolve, attacks cease, and tophi regress over time; poor adherence or untreated hyperuricaemia, however, leads to recurrent attacks, chronic arthropathy, and progressive joint destruction.

apatite is not identifiable by polarized light alone Synovial fluid leukocyte count and microbial Gram stain and culture to exclude coexisting infection Serum urate (interpreting with awareness it may be transiently normal during a flare) Alizarin red S staining for calcium-containing (apatite, CaOx) crystals; electron microscopy with energy-dispersive analysis, x-ray diffraction, infrared or Raman spectroscopy for definitive apatite identification Plain radiography (erosions with overhanging margins in gout; chondrocalcinosis in CPPD; periarticular calcification in apatite disease) Musculoskeletal ultrasound (double-contour sign) and dual-energy CT for MSU detection In CPPD patients under 50: serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, magnesium, iron, and transferrin, plus screening for familial aggregation and metabolic disease (hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypophosphatasia, hypomagnesemia) Serum creatinine, liver function tests, hemoglobin, WBC count, HbA1c, and lipids at baseline to assess comorbidities and treatment risk Osteoarthritis (pseudoosteoarthritis form of CPPD) Rheumatoid arthritis (chronic tophaceous gout; chronic symmetric synovitis pattern of CPPD) Neuropathic arthropathy (severe destructive CPPD) Erosive osteoarthritis of the fingers (apatite-associated) Spinal stenosis or crowned dens syndrome (CPPD spinal involvement) Gout is a hyperuricemic metabolic disorder in which chronic hyperuricemia leads to supersaturation and deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joints and connective tissue; it typically presents with episodic, intensely painful inflammatory arthritis in middle-aged-to-elderly men and postmenopausal women (Harrison 22e p.2956-2957). The first metatarsophalangeal joint of the great toe (podagra) is involved in 70-90% of cases; other early targets are tarsal joints, ankles, and knees, while finger, wrist, and elbow involvement is more typical of elderly patients or advanced disease (Harrison 22e p.2958). Flares often begin at night or in the early morning and are among the most painful conditions humans experience; affected joints rapidly become warm, red, tender, and swollen, sometimes mimicking cellulitis (pseudocellulitis), and usually subside spontaneously within 1-2 weeks (Harrison 22e p.2958). Definitive diagnosis rests on demonstrating needle-shaped MSU crystals (intracellular and extracellular) showing strong negative birefringence under compensated polarized light; synovial fluid is cloudy with leukocyte counts roughly 5000-75,000/uL (Harrison 22e p.2958-2959). Serum urate may be normal or even low during an acute flare because inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 are uricosuric and can lower it by about 2 mg/dL, so a normal level during a flare does not exclude gout; historical or postflare values are more diagnostically useful (Harrison 22e p.2959). Musculoskeletal ultrasound (double-contour sign over articular cartilage) and dual-energy CT (chemical identification of MSU) aid early diagnosis; plain radiographs in advanced tophaceous gout show well-defined erosions with sclerotic, overhanging margins and soft-tissue masses, though these are absent early (Harrison 22e p.2959). Hyperuricemia is most often due to impaired renal urate excretion (about 90%) rather than overproduction (about 10%); roughly two-thirds of daily uric acid is eliminated renally and one-third through the gut (intestinal uricolysis by gut bacteria) (Harrison 22e p.2957). Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD) is strongly age-related, with prevalence in articular tissues roughly doubling each decade after 60 and reaching nearly 50% in those over 85; most deposition is asymptomatic (Harrison 22e p.2960). Acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) most often affects the knee, then the wrist, and rarely the first MTP joint; episodes tend to last longer than gout flares (weeks to months) and may be accompanied by fever, chills, and elevated acute-phase reactants (Harrison 22e p.2960). Chondrocalcinosis (punctate/linear radiodense deposits in fibrocartilage or hyaline cartilage) supports CPPD; definitive diagnosis requires rhomboid or rod-shaped weakly positively birefringent or nonbirefringent crystals in synovial fluid or tissue (Harrison 22e p.2961). Apatite (basic calcium phosphate) crystals are extremely small and individually visible only by electron microscopy; clumps appear as nonbirefringent globules staining bright red with alizarin red S, and apatite underlies the destructive 'Milwaukee shoulder' of the elderly (Harrison 22e p.2961). Calcium oxalate (CaOx) arthropathy is largely a disease of patients on long-term dialysis, especially with ascorbic acid supplementation, since ascorbate is metabolized to oxalate that is poorly cleared in uremia; the readily recognized crystals are bipyramidal with strong birefringence (Harrison 22e p.2962). Acutely hot, swollen joint where septic arthritis cannot be excluded clinically, mandating synovial fluid Gram stain and culture Fever, chills, and elevated acute-phase reactants during a crystal flare (seen in up to 50% of acute CPPD episodes, occasionally to 40 C), which overlap with infection Hyperuricemia in prepubertal boys, which should prompt evaluation for inherited enzyme defects (HPRT deficiency, PRPP synthetase superactivity) CPPD arthritis in patients under 50, raising concern for an underlying metabolic disorder (e.g., hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypophosphatasia, hypomagnesemia) Progressive destructive large-joint disease (e.g., Milwaukee shoulder) signaling severe apatite-associated joint destruction Assuming a normal serum urate during an acute attack excludes gout; cytokine-mediated uricosuria (e.g., IL-6) can lower it by about 2 mg/dL during flares Failing to exclude infection: bacterial sepsis can coexist with crystals, and crystals do not rule out a septic joint Relying on polarized light microscopy to detect apatite, whose individual crystals require electron microscopy and special stains/techniques Overlooking a secondary metabolic cause when CPPD presents before age 50 Confusing intra-/periarticular apatite calcifications with the linear calcifications of CPPD on radiographs Diagnosing chondrocalcinosis as CPPD without considering calcium oxalate deposition in chronic renal failure as an alternative Chronic hyperuricemia is a prerequisite for gout but not sufficient alone, since only a minority of hyperuricemic individuals ever develop disease. Humans uniquely develop gout spontaneously because of an evolutionary species-wide loss of uricase, the enzyme that converts urate to highly soluble allantoin; at physiologic pH uric acid (pKa about 5.8) exists mainly as ionized urate. An increased urate body pool leads to MSU supersaturation (favored above roughly 6.85 mg/dL) and crystal formation/deposition in joints and connective tissue, modulated by temperature, pH, intra-articular dehydration, cation concentration, and matrix proteoglycans/collagen. Hyperuricemia stems predominantly from impaired renal excretion (about 90%) and less often overproduction (about 10%); overproduction relates to increased cell turnover (hematologic malignancy, psoriasis), chemotherapy, tissue hypoxia, or inherited defects such as PRPP synthetase superactivity or HPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan spectrum). Renal handling involves sodium-dependent apical reabsorption via URAT1/OAT10, basolateral GLUT9 efflux, and intestinal excretion via ABCG2. Acute flares are triggered when MSU crystals are shed from inert deposits and activate resident synovial macrophages, mast cells, and the NLRP3 inflammasome, generating IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-alpha; neutrophil phagocytosis of crystals amplifies inflammation via a respiratory burst. Untreated, growing tophaceous MSU deposits with granulomatous inflammation produce chronic gouty arthritis with erosive deformity. In CPPD, increased cartilage inorganic pyrophosphate (largely from extracellular ATP breakdown, regulated by the ANKH transporter) combines with calcium to form CPP crystals that, like MSU, activate phagocytes and the inflammasome. Apatite deposition occurs in tissue damage (dystrophic), hypercalcemic/hyperparathyroid states (metastatic), connective tissue disease (calcinosis), and chronic renal failure (tumoral calcinosis, calciphylaxis). CaOx deposits accumulate in cartilage, synovium, bone, and viscera in chronic renal failure and primary oxalosis (Harrison 22e p.2956-2962). Typical acute gout flares are self-limited, resolving spontaneously within 1-2 weeks, with symptom-free intercritical intervals; however, untreated recurrent flares over years can progress to chronic gouty arthritis with persistent low-grade synovitis, subcutaneous tophi, deformity, and erosive bony destruction. Gout is associated with multiple cardiometabolic-kidney comorbidities (obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction, stroke, chronic kidney disease, urate nephrolithiasis). Apatite-associated destructive arthropathy (e.g., Milwaukee shoulder) tends to progress indolently but can cause severe pain, instability, and disability requiring joint replacement, and CaOx and chronic CPP arthropathies may progressively destroy joints (Harrison 22e p.2956-2962). Gout is described as a clinical continuum rather than by a formal grading scale: asymptomatic hyperuricemia; acute (episodic) gout flares with intercritical symptom-free intervals; and chronic (tophaceous) gouty arthritis with persistent synovitis, tophi, deformity, and bony destruction. Crystal-induced disease is categorized by pattern as acute (episodic) mono-, oligo-, or polyarthritis; periarticular inflammation (bursitis, tendinitis, enthesitis); tophaceous deposits; chronic destructive or chronic inflammatory arthropathy; a peculiar osteoarthritis-like form; spinal arthritis; and carpal tunnel syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2956-2957).

GRACILE syndrome — growth retardation, aminoaciduria, cholestasis, iron overload, lactic acidosis and early death, BCS1L deficiency, Fellman syndrome, Finnish lactic acidosis with hepatic haemosiderosis Neonatal haemochromatosis (gestational alloimmune liver disease) Other mitochondrial respiratory chain and DNA depletion disorders Congenital lactic acidosis (pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, respiratory chain defects) Zellweger spectrum / peroxisomal disorders Tyrosinaemia type 1 Renal Fanconi syndrome of other cause Blood lactate and lactate/pyruvate ratio Liver function tests, serum bile acids, ferritin and iron studies Urine amino acids demonstrating generalised aminoaciduria Liver biopsy showing cholestasis and iron deposition Respiratory chain enzyme analysis (reduced complex III activity) BCS1L gene sequencing A severe autosomal recessive mitochondrial disorder caused by mutations in BCS1L, first described as a Finnish-heritage disease The acronym captures the phenotype: growth restriction, aminoaciduria, cholestasis, iron overload, lactic acidosis, and early death Presents in the neonatal period with profound, often fatal lactic acidosis and intrauterine growth restriction Hepatic involvement includes cholestasis with iron accumulation (haemosiderosis) resembling neonatal haemochromatosis Renal tubular dysfunction produces a generalised aminoaciduria BCS1L encodes a chaperone required for assembly of complex III of the respiratory chain, so its deficiency impairs oxidative phosphorylation Care is supportive and largely palliative; the Finnish founder (S78G) variant tends to cause the most severe, rapidly lethal form Severe, refractory neonatal lactic acidosis Rapidly progressive liver failure with coagulopathy Marked hepatic iron overload mimicking neonatal haemochromatosis Multiorgan failure with growth restriction in early infancy Mistaking the hepatic iron overload for isolated neonatal haemochromatosis and missing the mitochondrial basis Failing to measure lactate in a sick, growth-restricted neonate Overlooking renal tubular dysfunction as a diagnostic clue Not offering genetic counselling given the autosomal recessive inheritance and founder effect GRACILE syndrome results from biallelic mutations in BCS1L, which encodes a chaperone essential for incorporating the Rieske iron-sulphur protein into complex III of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Impaired complex III assembly disrupts oxidative phosphorylation, causing severe lactic acidosis, and deranges cellular iron handling, leading to hepatic iron overload. The multisystem energy failure manifests as intrauterine growth restriction, cholestatic liver disease, renal tubulopathy with aminoaciduria, and typically death in infancy. The classic Finnish founder mutation produces an especially severe course. The classic Finnish form is usually fatal within days to a few months of birth; milder BCS1L phenotypes with longer survival exist, but overall prognosis is poor and management is largely supportive and palliative.

Granular cell tumour — Abrikossoff tumour, granular cell myoblastoma, granular cell schwannoma, granular cell nerve sheath tumour, GCT Squamous cell carcinoma, when pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia is prominent Histiocytic and xanthomatous lesions Rhabdomyoma and other granular or oncocytic tumours Malignant granular cell tumour Melanoma with granular or oncocytic change Alveolar soft part sarcoma Reticulohistiocytoma Immunohistochemistry for S100 and SOX10 to confirm neural (Schwann-cell) differentiation Adjunctive markers such as CD68, inhibin, calretinin and TFE3 as needed Deep or repeat biopsy when superficial sampling shows only reactive epithelial hyperplasia Assessment of atypical histological features to gauge malignant potential Imaging to define lesion extent and detect multifocal disease at unusual sites Complete excision specimen review to assess margins and exclude malignancy A tumour of Schwann-cell (neural) origin composed of large cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm packed with lysosomes The tongue is the classic site, but it also occurs in the skin, subcutis, breast, gastrointestinal tract, larynx and elsewhere Diffusely and strongly positive for S100 protein and SOX10, together with markers such as CD68 and inhibin, reflecting its neural differentiation Small eosinophilic cytoplasmic granules surrounded by clear haloes (pustulo-ovoid bodies of Milian) are a helpful microscopic clue Overlying pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia of squamous epithelium can be mistaken for squamous cell carcinoma on superficial biopsy The overwhelming majority are benign; a small minority are malignant, defined by features such as necrosis, spindling, high mitotic count, pleomorphism and large size Named after Abrikossoff, who first described the lesion and proposed a muscle origin later revised to Schwann-cell derivation Rapid growth, large size or ulceration suggesting the malignant variant Histological atypia with necrosis, spindling, prominent nucleoli or increased mitoses Regional lymph node or distant metastasis Multiple lesions or visceral involvement requiring broader evaluation Overdiagnosing squamous cell carcinoma because of overlying pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia on a shallow biopsy Mistaking the granular cytoplasm for a histiocytic or xanthomatous process Failing to sample deeply enough to reach the diagnostic granular cells Assuming all lesions are benign and not assessing for malignant histological criteria Overlooking multifocal disease at less typical anatomical sites Granular cell tumour arises from Schwann cells, as supported by consistent S100 and SOX10 expression and ultrastructural features. The characteristic granular cytoplasm reflects the accumulation of autophagic lysosomes rather than true myoblastic differentiation, correcting the original myoblastoma concept. A proportion of cases carry loss-of-function alterations in genes encoding endosomal or lysosomal regulators, consistent with the lysosome-rich phenotype. Most tumours grow slowly and behave in a benign fashion, with only rare examples showing the atypical or malignant features that predict aggressive behaviour. Benign granular cell tumours are cured by complete local excision, with recurrence mainly related to incomplete removal; the rare malignant variant can metastasise to lymph nodes, lung and bone and carries a substantially worse outlook, so recognition of atypical features and adequate resection are important.

Granular cell tumour — Abrikossoff tumour, Granular cell myoblastoma (historical misnomer) Well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma, mimicked by overlying pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia Rhabdomyoma and other granular cell lesions Histiocytic proliferations and xanthoma Schwannoma and other peripheral nerve sheath tumours Fibrous histiocytoma Metastatic carcinoma with granular cytoplasm Malignant granular cell tumour Excisional or incisional biopsy with histological assessment Immunohistochemistry for S100 and SOX10 to confirm Schwann cell origin Periodic acid-Schiff staining with diastase to demonstrate granules Careful pathological review to avoid overcalling overlying epithelial hyperplasia as carcinoma Imaging of the lesion and, for deep or large tumours, of regional structures Assessment against malignancy criteria when clinical or histological features are worrying A tumour of Schwann cell (neural) origin, despite the obsolete term myoblastoma, confirmed by strong S100 and SOX10 positivity The tongue is the single commonest site, followed by skin, subcutis, breast, and the gastrointestinal tract It presents as a small, firm, painless nodule and is more frequent in adults, in women, and in people of African ancestry The tumour cells have abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm packed with lysosomes that are periodic acid-Schiff positive and diastase resistant Pustulo-ovoid bodies of Milian are a helpful cytological clue Overlying pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia can be mistaken for a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma on a superficial biopsy The great majority are benign; a rare malignant variant is defined by features such as large size, necrosis, high mitotic activity, and pleomorphism Conservative complete local excision is the treatment of choice Rapid growth, large size, or a deep-seated location Ulceration, necrosis, or fixation suggesting a malignant variant Local recurrence after excision Regional lymphadenopathy or evidence of metastasis Misdiagnosing overlying pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia as squamous cell carcinoma and undertaking unnecessarily radical surgery Assuming all lesions are benign and overlooking the histological criteria for malignancy Incomplete excision due to the infiltrative, poorly demarcated margins Retaining the outdated myoblastoma label and misattributing a muscle origin Granular cell tumour is a neoplasm of Schwann cell derivation, a lineage established by consistent expression of S100 protein and SOX10 and by ultrastructural findings of abundant autophagic lysosomes. These accumulated lysosomes give the tumour cells their characteristic granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and their strong periodic acid-Schiff positivity that resists diastase digestion. The cells infiltrate between collagen bundles and around nerves and adnexal structures, which explains why margins can be difficult to assess. When the lesion lies immediately beneath a mucosal or epidermal surface it frequently induces marked pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia of the overlying epithelium, a reactive change that closely simulates invasive squamous carcinoma and is a well-recognised source of diagnostic error. Malignant examples are rare and are defined by a constellation of adverse histological features rather than by a single criterion. Most granular cell tumours are benign and are cured by complete excision, with recurrence usually reflecting incomplete removal. The uncommon malignant variant behaves aggressively with a substantial risk of metastasis and a correspondingly poorer outcome.

recurrence Overlooking the autosomal dominant inheritance and failing to counsel family members Granular corneal dystrophy is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the transforming growth factor beta-induced gene (TGFBI). The mutant protein misfolds and accumulates as hyaline deposits within the corneal stroma, appearing as discrete granular opacities separated by clear stroma. Over time deposits enlarge and become more numerous, and superficial deposits can disrupt epithelial adhesion. In the type 2 combined form, the same gene produces both hyaline (granular) and amyloid (lattice) material, giving a mixed histological picture. Progressive accumulation eventually reduces transparency and vision. Vision is often good for many years because clear stroma separates the deposits, but progressive accumulation may eventually require surgery. Deposits commonly recur after keratoplasty, and the combined type 2 form tends to be more visually significant.

generalised disease Confusing subcutaneous GA with rheumatoid nodules and pursuing unnecessary rheumatological work-up Granuloma annulare is characterised histologically by focal degeneration of dermal collagen (necrobiosis) surrounded by a palisaded or interstitial histiocytic and lymphocytic infiltrate, with mucin deposition in the altered dermis. The process is thought to represent a cell-mediated, delayed-type hypersensitivity or macrophage-driven reaction to an as-yet undefined trigger, with cytokine-mediated matrix degradation. Precipitants proposed in individual cases include trauma, infection, insect bites, drugs, and immune dysregulation, and there are reported associations with metabolic and, less commonly, malignant or infective conditions in certain subtypes. Localised granuloma annulare is benign and frequently resolves on its own without scarring, though recurrence is common; the generalised form tends to be more chronic and less responsive to treatment, but it remains a benign condition.

Granuloma faciale — GF, granuloma faciale of the skin, facial granuloma with eosinophilia Sarcoidosis of the skin Discoid lupus erythematosus Cutaneous lymphoma / pseudolymphoma Erythema elevatum diutinum Rosacea and granulomatous rosacea Fixed drug eruption or persistent arthropod reaction Skin biopsy showing leucocytoclastic vasculitis with eosinophils and a Grenz zone Direct immunofluorescence, which may show immunoreactant deposition around vessels Full blood count including eosinophil count Investigations to exclude sarcoidosis or lupus when clinically suggested Dermoscopy to highlight dilated follicular openings and vascular features Histological exclusion of cutaneous lymphoma Presents as one or more well-defined, red-brown to violaceous papules, plaques or nodules, most often on the face of middle-aged adults Prominent, dilated follicular openings (accentuated ostia) over the surface are a helpful clinical clue Despite the name it is a localised chronic fibrosing vasculitis of the skin and is unrelated to systemic granulomatous disease Lesions are usually asymptomatic, persistent and cosmetically bothersome, and sun-exposed facial skin is typically affected Biopsy shows a dense mixed dermal infiltrate rich in eosinophils and neutrophils with a leucocytoclastic vasculitis and a characteristic Grenz zone of uninvolved papillary dermis Later lesions show perivascular fibrosis and haemosiderin deposition reflecting the chronic vascular injury It is often resistant to treatment; options include topical or intralesional corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors, dapsone, laser and surgery Rapid growth, ulceration or atypical features prompting exclusion of cutaneous lymphoma or malignancy Extrafacial or multiple lesions raising diagnostic doubt Failure to respond to standard therapies over prolonged follow-up Diagnostic uncertainty overlapping with systemic granulomatous disease Assuming the name implies systemic granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis Mistaking it clinically for rosacea, lupus or a skin tumour without biopsy Expecting a rapid or durable response, given its refractory nature Overlooking cutaneous lymphoma in the histological differential Granuloma faciale is a chronic, localised leucocytoclastic vasculitis of the skin in which recurrent immune-complex-mediated injury to small dermal vessels drives a persistent, eosinophil- and neutrophil-rich inflammatory infiltrate. Repeated vascular damage leads to fibrinoid change, extravasation of red cells with haemosiderin deposition and, over time, perivascular and dermal fibrosis. A narrow Grenz zone of spared papillary dermis separates the infiltrate from the epidermis. The tendency for sun-exposed facial skin to be affected suggests actinic factors may contribute to its localisation. Granuloma faciale is a benign but persistent and often treatment-resistant condition; lesions rarely resolve spontaneously and tend to recur after treatment, so management is frequently aimed at cosmetic improvement rather than cure.

Granuloma inguinale — donovanosis, Klebsiella granulomatis, Calymmatobacterium granulomatis, granuloma venereum Primary syphilis (painless chancre) Chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi (painful ulcer) Lymphogranuloma venereum Genital herpes simplex Squamous cell carcinoma of the genitalia Cutaneous amoebiasis or other tropical ulcerative infection Genital tuberculosis Tissue crush smear or punch biopsy stained with Giemsa or Wright stain to identify Donovan bodies Histopathology of biopsy to confirm granulomatous inflammation and exclude malignancy Polymerase chain reaction or molecular assay for Klebsiella granulomatis where available Syphilis serology together with dark-field microscopy to exclude a chancre HIV testing and screening for other sexually transmitted infections Nucleic acid amplification testing for gonorrhoea and chlamydia and, where relevant, testing to exclude chancroid Caused by the intracellular bacterium Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium granulomatis) and acquired mainly through sexual contact, with a long and variable incubation period; classically endemic in scattered tropical and subtropical regions The hallmark lesion is a painless, slowly progressive, beefy-red ulcer with a friable granulation-tissue base that bleeds readily on contact Involves the genital and inguinal skin most often; a subcutaneous granulomatous groin swelling (pseudobubo) may mimic, but is not, true suppurative lymphadenopathy Several clinical variants are described, including ulcerogranulomatous, hypertrophic, necrotic, and sclerotic forms Diagnosis rests on demonstrating Donovan bodies, the intracytoplasmic organisms seen within large mononuclear cells on a crush smear or biopsy stained with Giemsa or Wright stain The organism is fastidious and difficult to culture, so diagnosis is largely clinical supported by microscopy, with molecular testing used where available Prolonged antibiotic therapy (for example azithromycin or doxycycline, with macrolide or co-trimoxazole alternatives) is continued until lesions have fully re-epithelialised, and relapse can occur weeks to months later Partner notification and screening for co-existing sexually transmitted infections, including HIV and syphilis, are essential parts of management Extensive tissue destruction or genital mutilation from advanced disease Secondary bacterial infection with spreading cellulitis or systemic sepsis A chronic non-healing lesion raising suspicion of malignant transformation Rare haematogenous dissemination to bone, joints, or viscera Assuming a painless genital ulcer is syphilis and omitting microscopy for Donovan bodies Stopping antibiotics once the ulcer looks improved rather than continuing until full re-epithelialisation, allowing relapse Overlooking concurrent HIV or other sexually transmitted infection Failing to biopsy a chronic non-healing ulcer to exclude malignant change Granuloma inguinale is a chronic, indolent genital ulcerative disease produced by the encapsulated intracellular bacterium Klebsiella granulomatis. Following sexual (and occasionally close non-sexual) contact, the organism invades and multiplies within mononuclear phagocytes of the genital and perineal skin, where it appears as clusters of Donovan bodies. The infected macrophages drive a chronic granulomatous inflammatory response with vascular proliferation, producing the characteristic friable, beefy-red ulcer that enlarges slowly by direct extension and autoinoculation. Because inflammation is subcutaneous rather than nodal, groin swelling reflects granulomatous tissue rather than true lymphadenitis, and long-standing disease can lead to fibrosis, lymphatic obstruction with genital lymphoedema, and destructive scarring. With early and adequately prolonged antibiotic treatment lesions heal well and the outlook is good, but delayed therapy risks progressive tissue destruction, scarring, and genital lymphoedema; relapse can follow apparently successful treatment, so follow-up until complete healing is advised.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis — GPA, Wegener granulomatosis, ANCA-associated vasculitis Microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease Other pulmonary-renal syndromes including lupus Chronic infective sinusitis or invasive fungal disease Sarcoidosis and other granulomatous disorders Malignancy of the upper airway or lung ANCA testing with PR3 and MPO antigen specificity Urinalysis and microscopy for dysmorphic red cells and casts, with renal function monitoring Chest imaging (radiograph and CT) for nodules, cavities, and haemorrhage Tissue biopsy (renal, lung, or ENT) for necrotising granulomatous vasculitis Assessment of upper airway including nasendoscopy and evaluation for subglottic stenosis An ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis with a classic triad of upper airway, lung, and kidney involvement Upper respiratory features include persistent sinusitis, nasal crusting and bleeding, saddle-nose deformity, and subglottic stenosis Pulmonary disease ranges from nodules and cavities to life-threatening alveolar haemorrhage Renal involvement is a pauci-immune, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with an active urinary sediment Most patients are positive for c-ANCA directed against proteinase 3 (anti-PR3) Biopsy shows necrotising granulomatous inflammation with vasculitis; renal biopsy shows crescentic glomerulonephritis with little immune deposition The pulmonary-renal syndrome (diffuse alveolar haemorrhage with glomerulonephritis) is a medical emergency Treatment has induction and maintenance phases using glucocorticoids combined with rituximab or cyclophosphamide, and plasma exchange is considered in severe organ-threatening disease Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage presenting with haemoptysis, hypoxia, and falling haemoglobin Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with rising creatinine requiring urgent immunosuppression and possible plasma exchange Airway compromise from subglottic or tracheal stenosis Ocular involvement such as orbital pseudotumour or scleritis threatening vision Mononeuritis multiplex or central nervous system involvement Treating recurrent sinusitis or nasal symptoms as isolated ENT disease and missing systemic vasculitis Delaying immunosuppression in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, risking irreversible renal failure Assuming a negative ANCA excludes the diagnosis, especially in limited disease Overlooking early alveolar haemorrhage when haemoptysis is minimal Failing to monitor for relapse and treatment-related infection during maintenance Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotising vasculitis of small vessels associated with anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, predominantly against proteinase 3. ANCA activate primed neutrophils, causing degranulation, release of reactive oxygen species and proteases, and endothelial injury, producing pauci-immune (minimal immune complex) inflammation. The disease combines this small-vessel vasculitis with granuloma formation in the respiratory tract. Injury to alveolar capillaries causes diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, and glomerular capillary damage produces crescentic, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Once almost uniformly fatal, the disease now has good remission rates with modern induction therapy, but relapse is common and requires ongoing surveillance. Prognosis is worse with severe renal impairment at presentation and with alveolar haemorrhage; long-term morbidity includes chronic kidney disease and treatment-related complications.
