clinical features indistinguishable from malignancy pending biopsy Caseating granulomas or other findings suggesting tuberculosis Rapidly progressive skin involvement raising concern for inflammatory carcinoma Systemic symptoms suggesting disseminated infection or sarcoidosis Non-resolving disease despite treatment, warranting repeat biopsy Labelling the disease idiopathic without excluding tuberculosis and other infections Relying on fine-needle aspiration and missing the granulomatous architecture or an underlying cancer Undertaking wide surgical excision that heals poorly and tends to recur Overlooking hyperprolactinaemia as a contributing factor Mistaking the presentation for inflammatory breast carcinoma or vice versa Idiopathic granulomatous mastitis is characterised histologically by non-caseating granulomas centred on the breast lobules, formed by epithelioid histiocytes, multinucleate giant cells, and surrounding chronic inflammatory cells. The precise trigger is unknown, but it is thought to represent a localised immune-mediated reaction to extravasated luminal secretions or lobular antigens, sometimes with a contribution from Corynebacterium infection, and it is associated with recent pregnancy, lactation, and hyperprolactinaemic states. The inflammatory process can progress to microabscesses, sinuses, and fistulae. Crucially, the granulomatous appearance is shared with tuberculosis and other infections, so those must be excluded before the label of idiopathic disease is applied. The condition is benign and often eventually self-limiting, but it is notorious for a protracted, relapsing course with recurrent inflammation and sinus formation; most women recover with conservative or medical management, though scarring can result.

treatment of any demodex contribution, avoiding potent topical corticosteroids which aggravate the disease Granulomatous histology that could represent cutaneous tuberculosis or sarcoidosis requiring systemic evaluation Progressive scarring or disfiguring facial involvement Coexisting ocular inflammation threatening vision Failure to respond to appropriate rosacea therapy, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Prescribing potent topical corticosteroids, which characteristically worsen the eruption Misinterpreting necrotising granulomata as proof of tuberculosis without confirmatory microbiology Expecting rapid resolution and stopping treatment prematurely Failing to distinguish it from sarcoidosis and missing systemic disease Granulomatous rosacea is regarded as a granulomatous tissue reaction pattern occurring within the spectrum of rosacea. As in other rosacea subtypes, dysregulation of the innate immune system, an abnormal cutaneous vascular and neurovascular response, and an inflammatory reaction to Demodex mites and their microbial load are thought to contribute. In this variant the inflammatory response organises into dermal epithelioid granulomata around follicular structures, sometimes with central necrosis, producing the characteristic firm papules. The precise trigger for granuloma formation is unclear, and the histological picture can closely resemble that of lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei and cutaneous tuberculosis. Granulomatous rosacea often runs a chronic and relatively treatment-resistant course requiring prolonged therapy, and although many patients eventually improve, residual scarring or persistent papules can occur.

rupture Postmenopausal bleeding with an ovarian mass, mandating endometrial evaluation for hyperplasia or carcinoma Acute abdominal pain and signs of haemoperitoneum from tumour rupture Precocious puberty in a girl with a pelvic mass Recurrent disease presenting years after apparently successful treatment Failing to evaluate the endometrium for hyperplasia or carcinoma driven by oestrogen excess Discharging patients from follow-up too early given the risk of very late recurrence Misclassifying the tumour as an epithelial ovarian cancer and mismanaging it Overlooking rupture as a cause of acute presentation and adverse staging Granulosa cell tumours are sex cord-stromal neoplasms derived from the granulosa cells of the ovarian follicle, often accompanied by a thecal component. They commonly retain the hormonal function of their cell of origin and secrete oestrogen, and sometimes inhibin, which underlies both the clinical syndrome and the useful tumour markers. In the adult type, a characteristic somatic FOXL2 mutation is central to tumorigenesis, and the cells arrange themselves into microfollicular, trabecular, or diffuse patterns, sometimes forming Call-Exner bodies. Unopposed oestrogen stimulation of the endometrium explains the associated hyperplasia and increased risk of endometrial carcinoma. These tumours are indolent but genuinely malignant, with a propensity for local recurrence and spread within the abdomen, sometimes decades after the initial diagnosis. Most adult granulosa cell tumours are diagnosed at an early stage and have a favourable long-term outlook, but their tendency to recur late means survival curves continue to fall over decades; advanced stage and rupture worsen the prognosis. Juvenile tumours are usually cured when confined to the ovary.

granulosa cell tumour — granulosa cell tumor of ovary, GCT thecoma and fibrothecoma Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour diffuse or poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ovary small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcaemic type carcinoid tumour of the ovary endometrioid carcinoma with sex-cord-like pattern metastatic breast carcinoma to the ovary serum inhibin B and anti-Mullerian hormone serum oestradiol transvaginal and abdominal pelvic ultrasound endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopic sampling to assess the endometrium contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of abdomen and pelvis for staging FOXL2 mutation analysis on tumour tissue inhibin, calretinin and SF-1 immunohistochemistry The commonest malignant ovarian sex-cord stromal tumour; oestrogen production drives much of the clinical picture, causing post-menopausal bleeding, endometrial hyperplasia or frank endometrial carcinoma in adults, and isosexual precocious puberty in the juvenile form. Two clinicopathological types exist: the adult type (about 95 per cent) presenting in peri- and post-menopausal women, and the juvenile type presenting in children and young women, distinguished by histology and behaviour rather than simply by age. A somatic FOXL2 missense mutation (C134W) is present in the great majority of adult-type tumours and is a useful diagnostic marker; juvenile-type tumours usually lack it and may harbour other alterations. Inhibin (particularly inhibin B) and anti-Mullerian hormone are valuable serum markers for diagnosis and, importantly, for detecting recurrence during long-term follow-up. Characteristic histology shows Call-Exner bodies, coffee-bean grooved nuclei, and diffuse, trabecular, insular or microfollicular growth patterns; immunohistochemistry is positive for inhibin, calretinin, SF-1 and FOXL2. Most present at an early, confined stage, and surgery is the mainstay; fertility-sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is reasonable in young women with disease apparently limited to one ovary. Late recurrence is characteristic and may occur many years or even decades after initial treatment, mandating prolonged surveillance rather than a fixed short follow-up window. Because oestrogen excess is common, endometrial sampling is essential at diagnosis to exclude concurrent hyperplasia or carcinoma of the endometrium. post-menopausal bleeding with an adnexal mass suggesting concurrent endometrial pathology acute abdomen from tumour rupture with haemoperitoneum rapidly enlarging mass or ascites suggesting higher-stage or aggressive disease recurrent disease presenting years after treatment with rising inhibin or anti-Mullerian hormone signs of virilisation raising concern for an alternative or mixed steroidogenic tumour Assuming a benign course and stopping surveillance early, when recurrence can appear decades later. Failing to sample the endometrium and missing concurrent hyperplasia or carcinoma driven by oestrogen excess. Mistaking the tumour for a poorly differentiated carcinoma or thecoma on limited sampling without inhibin, calretinin and FOXL2 studies. Over-relying on any single tumour marker; inhibin and anti-Mullerian hormone are complementary and neither is perfectly sensitive. Attributing virilisation to a granulosa cell tumour, which is usually oestrogenic, and overlooking a Sertoli-Leydig or steroid cell tumour. Granulosa cell tumours arise from the granulosa cells of the ovarian follicle, part of the sex-cord stromal compartment, often in association with theca cells and fibroblasts. Neoplastic granulosa cells retain the capacity for steroidogenesis and typically secrete oestrogens (and inhibin and anti-Mullerian hormone), producing the hyperoestrogenic clinical syndrome. In the adult type, a recurrent somatic FOXL2 point mutation disrupts a transcription factor essential to granulosa cell identity and folliculogenesis, and is regarded as a driver event. The juvenile type shows different molecular alterations, including changes in the AKT/PI3K and Gs-alpha signalling pathways, correlating with its distinct morphology of luxuriant follicle formation and more mitotically active, atypical cells. Tumours are generally indolent and low-grade, but their steroid output and their tendency to spread locally and recur late reflect ongoing hormonally active, slowly proliferating clones. Overall prognosis is favourable because most adult-type tumours present at an early stage and behave indolently, but late relapse is characteristic and long-term survival falls with advanced stage or recurrence. The juvenile type is usually cured when confined to the ovary, though the rare advanced cases can behave aggressively.

Gratification disorder — infantile gratification behaviour, childhood self-stimulation, infantile masturbation Epileptic seizures, particularly focal seizures with automatisms or absence seizures Paroxysmal dystonia or dyskinesia Abdominal pain or colic and other causes of straining Sandifer syndrome from gastro-oesophageal reflux with posturing Shuddering attacks and other benign paroxysmal movement disorders Tics and motor stereotypies Home video of a typical episode, which is often diagnostic Bedside demonstration that episodes can be interrupted by distraction EEG (ictal if possible) only if seizures are seriously considered, which is normal Confirmation of normal development and a normal neurological examination Examination and urinalysis if a local irritant such as threadworms, vulvovaginitis or dermatitis is suspected as a trigger Neuroimaging and metabolic workup reserved for atypical presentations Gratification disorder is a benign, normal variant of childhood behaviour that is frequently misdiagnosed as seizures, dystonia or abdominal pain It is most common in infants and preschool children, with a recognised peak in girls, though it occurs in both sexes Typical episodes involve stereotyped posturing with adduction and pressure of the thighs, a crossed-leg or rigid posture, or rocking against a firm surface or car seat Accompanying features include a vacant or glazed stare, facial flushing, sweating, grunting, quietening and irregular breathing, followed by relaxation and sometimes sleepiness Awareness is preserved, so the child can usually be distracted or interrupted, and there is no true loss of consciousness, incontinence, tongue-biting or postictal confusion Episodes characteristically occur when the child is bored, tired or unoccupied, such as in a high chair or car seat, and can be stopped by distraction, which is a key diagnostic clue Diagnosis is clinical and greatly aided by a home video; an EEG during an episode is normal and investigations are usually unnecessary Management is reassurance and explanation, as the behaviour is normal and harmless and typically diminishes with age; punishment or excessive attention should be avoided and safeguarding considered only if features are atypical Episodes that cannot be interrupted, or with true loss of awareness or a postictal state Focal neurological signs, developmental delay or regression Atypical features suggesting seizures such as tongue-biting, incontinence or cyanosis Signs of local trauma, genital injury or behavioural indicators raising a safeguarding concern Progressive worsening or the emergence of new event types Misdiagnosis as epilepsy leading to unnecessary EEGs, imaging and antiepileptic drugs Not requesting a home video, which is often diagnostic Overlooking the key clue that episodes stop on distraction Reacting with alarm, punishment or excessive attention, which may reinforce the behaviour Failing to consider and address local irritants or, in atypical cases, safeguarding concerns Gratification behaviour is a normal self-stimulatory activity of early childhood and is not a neurological or psychiatric disorder. The stereotyped movements generate pleasurable sensory feedback, and the associated autonomic features of flushing, sweating and altered breathing reflect physiological arousal rather than epileptic or dystonic activity. There is no cortical epileptic discharge; the behaviour represents normal exploration and self-soothing that diminishes with maturation and with increasing engagement with the environment. The outlook is excellent; it is a benign behaviour that causes no harm and characteristically diminishes with age as the child matures and becomes more occupied, requiring no specific treatment.

Gray baby syndrome (chloramphenicol) — grey baby syndrome, chloramphenicol toxicity in neonates, chloramphenicol grey syndrome, neonatal chloramphenicol toxicity Neonatal sepsis and septic shock Congenital cardiac disease with circulatory collapse Inborn errors of metabolism presenting with acidosis Necrotising enterocolitis Other drug toxicities in the neonate Hypoxic-ischaemic injury Chloramphenicol serum concentration and therapeutic drug monitoring Arterial blood gas for metabolic acidosis and lactate Full blood count (chloramphenicol also causes marrow suppression) Renal and liver function tests Blood cultures and septic screen to exclude infection Continuous cardiovascular monitoring A potentially fatal toxic reaction to chloramphenicol occurring predominantly in neonates, especially preterm infants Features develop over hours to days and include vomiting, poor feeding, abdominal distension, hypothermia and a characteristic ashen-grey skin colour Progresses to hypotension, cyanosis, cardiovascular collapse and metabolic acidosis The syndrome results from accumulation of chloramphenicol due to immature hepatic glucuronidation and reduced renal excretion in the newborn Prevention relies on avoiding chloramphenicol where possible in neonates and, when unavoidable, using reduced dosing with drug-level monitoring Management is immediate cessation of the drug and aggressive supportive care of the circulation and acidosis Extracorporeal removal (for example haemoperfusion or exchange transfusion) may be considered in severe accumulation Older children and adults can also develop toxicity if hepatic metabolism is overwhelmed by excessive dosing Ashen-grey skin with hypotension and poor perfusion Progressive metabolic acidosis and rising lactate Hypothermia and cardiovascular collapse Apnoea or respiratory failure Using standard weight-based dosing without accounting for immature neonatal metabolism Attributing the deterioration to sepsis alone and continuing the drug Failing to monitor chloramphenicol levels when its use is unavoidable Overlooking the concurrent risk of dose-related bone marrow suppression Chloramphenicol is normally inactivated by hepatic conjugation with glucuronic acid and the conjugate is excreted renally. Neonates, particularly premature infants, have immature UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity and reduced glomerular filtration, so unconjugated drug accumulates to toxic concentrations. High levels impair mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and electron transport, reducing cellular energy production, especially in the myocardium and vasculature. The result is myocardial depression, loss of vascular tone, hypotension, tissue hypoxia and lactic (metabolic) acidosis, producing the grey, cyanotic, hypotensive infant. The syndrome is therefore a pharmacokinetic accumulation phenomenon rather than an idiosyncratic or immune reaction. The syndrome carries a high mortality once cardiovascular collapse is established, but early recognition, drug withdrawal and supportive care improve survival. Prevention through cautious neonatal use and monitoring is far more effective than treatment.

Failing to counsel about the progressive nature of the fibrosis and splenomegaly Gray platelet syndrome is caused by biallelic mutations in NBEAL2, a gene required for the biogenesis and retention of alpha-granules in megakaryocytes and platelets. Alpha-granules normally store a large array of proteins involved in haemostasis, wound healing, and inflammation, including von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, platelet factor 4, and growth factors. Without functional NBEAL2 these granules fail to form or retain their cargo, so platelets are released large and agranular, appearing grey on staining, and function poorly. Premature release of granule proteins such as platelet-derived growth factor and transforming growth factor beta into the marrow microenvironment is thought to drive the progressive myelofibrosis that characterises the disorder, while ineffective thrombopoiesis contributes to the thrombocytopenia. The bleeding tendency is usually mild to moderate and manageable, but the outlook is influenced by progressive myelofibrosis and splenomegaly, which can worsen cytopenias over time.

panel to capture the discordant phenotype Obtaining inadequate tissue given the mediastinal fibrosis and diagnostic subtlety Overlooking the young age and bulky mediastinal presentation that should prompt the diagnosis Assuming a favourable Hodgkin-like outcome despite the more resistant biology Grey zone lymphoma occupies a biological continuum between primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma and classic Hodgkin lymphoma, and most cases are thought to derive from a thymic B cell. The tumour cells show a mismatch between appearance and antigen expression, so that cells resembling Reed-Sternberg cells may strongly express B-cell markers, or large pleomorphic cells may variably express the Hodgkin-associated antigens CD15 and CD30. It shares recurrent genetic events with both related entities, particularly amplification of the 9p24 locus that upregulates JAK-STAT signalling and PD-L1/PD-L2, promoting proliferation and immune evasion. This transitional biology explains both the diagnostic difficulty and the intermediate, often more resistant, clinical behaviour. Grey zone lymphoma generally behaves more aggressively and responds less predictably than either primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma or classic Hodgkin lymphoma, so outcomes tend to be poorer; intensive B-cell-directed chemoimmunotherapy offers the best chance of durable remission and checkpoint inhibition may help in the relapsed setting.

Greater trochanteric pain syndrome — GTPS, trochanteric bursitis, gluteal tendinopathy Hip osteoarthritis (groin pain) Lumbar radiculopathy referring to the lateral hip Femoral neck or other stress fracture Iliotibial band syndrome Meralgia paraesthetica Clinical diagnosis from lateral trochanteric tenderness and provocation tests Assessment of hip abductor strength and gait Ultrasound or MRI where gluteal tendon tears or other pathology is suspected Hip and spine assessment to exclude referred causes Radiographs if hip joint or bony pathology is considered Chronic pain and tenderness over the lateral hip at the greater trochanter, often worse lying on the affected side It is now understood to be driven mainly by gluteus medius and minimus tendinopathy rather than isolated bursitis Pain is aggravated by walking, stair climbing, standing on one leg and prolonged sitting with crossed legs It is common in middle-aged and older women and in runners It is usually distinguished from hip joint pathology, which causes groin pain, by the lateral location Load management, targeted exercise and addressing contributing biomechanics are first-line, with injections for selected refractory cases Groin pain or restricted hip rotation suggesting joint pathology Neurological signs suggesting lumbar radiculopathy Features suggesting stress fracture or bone lesion A substantial gluteal tendon tear requiring specific management Attributing it solely to bursitis and overlooking gluteal tendinopathy Confusing it with intra-articular hip disease Missing lumbar spine referral Relying on repeated corticosteroid injections without addressing load and strength Greater trochanteric pain syndrome results predominantly from degenerative and overload changes in the gluteus medius and minimus tendons at their insertion on the greater trochanter, with secondary involvement of the overlying trochanteric bursae. Compressive loads from hip adduction, combined with tensile overload of the tendons, drive tendinopathy and local inflammation. Contributing factors include altered gait, hip abductor weakness, leg-length discrepancy and repetitive activity, which increase load at the lateral hip. The condition is usually self-limiting or manageable with load modification and exercise-based rehabilitation, though symptoms can be persistent and some require injection or, rarely, surgery for tendon tears.

Green nail syndrome — Chloronychia, Pseudomonas nail infection Subungual haematoma Nail plate melanonychia or subungual melanoma Chromogenic mould or fungal onychomycosis (e.g. Aspergillus, Scytalidium) Exogenous staining from dyes, tobacco or topical agents Wilson disease associated blue lunulae Minocycline-induced nail pigmentation Clinical and Wood's light examination for green fluorescence Bacterial culture of subungual debris or nail clipping Nail clipping for mycology to exclude concurrent onychomycosis Dermoscopy of the nail plate to assess pigment distribution Assessment of the affected nail for underlying onycholysis or paronychia Consideration of occupational and wet-work history Presents as a greenish to blue-green discolouration of one or more nails, most often a single fingernail or toenail, caused by colonisation with Pseudomonas aeruginosa producing the pigments pyocyanin and pyoverdine. Almost always develops on a background of pre-existing onycholysis or chronic paronychia, where the detached nail plate creates a moist subungual space favouring bacterial growth. Prolonged immersion in water is the dominant risk factor, so it is common in cleaners, dishwashers, bar staff, healthcare workers and swimmers. The classic triad is green discolouration, proximal chronic paronychia and distolateral onycholysis; the pigment lies within the nail plate rather than beneath it. Wood's light examination may show green fluorescence, and gently trimming or clipping the detached nail confirms the pigment is on the undersurface of the plate. Management centres on keeping the nail dry, clipping away the onycholytic portion and treating with topical antiseptic or dilute acetic acid soaks; systemic therapy is rarely required in the immunocompetent. Although a Pseudomonas colonisation, it is classified as a non-infective nail dyschromia because it reflects surface colonisation of an already-damaged nail rather than an invasive tissue infection. Recurrence is common if the underlying onycholysis or wet-work exposure is not addressed. Green discolouration accompanied by spreading erythema, pain, fever or lymphangitis suggesting invasive soft-tissue infection Onset in an immunocompromised or diabetic patient where systemic Pseudomonas infection is a risk Failure to resolve with drying measures, prompting reconsideration of melanoma or chromogenic fungal infection A single darkening streak or Hutchinson sign that raises concern for subungual melanoma Mistaking the green pigment for a subungual haematoma or melanoma and either over-investigating or under-investigating Treating with topical or oral antifungals on the assumption of onychomycosis without recognising the bacterial cause Failing to address the underlying onycholysis or moisture exposure, leading to relapse Assuming systemic antibiotics are needed in an otherwise well patient when local measures suffice The discolouration arises when Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonises the space created by onycholysis or chronic paronychia. The organism thrives in the warm, moist microenvironment beneath a detached nail plate and elaborates water-soluble pigments, chiefly the blue-green pyocyanin and the yellow-green fluorescent pyoverdine (fluorescein). These diffuse into the ventral nail plate and impart the characteristic green to blue-black hue. There is no true invasion of the nail matrix or bed in the immunocompetent host; the process is essentially a superficial colonisation of already-diseased keratin, which is why it responds to drying measures and removal of the affected plate rather than requiring aggressive systemic antimicrobials. The prognosis is excellent, with most cases resolving once the nail is kept dry and the onycholytic portion is removed. Recurrence is frequent when the underlying onycholysis, paronychia or wet-work exposure persists.

syndrome, which arises from a distinct pattern of GLI3 variant Marked macrocephaly requiring exclusion of hydrocephalus Any developmental regression prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Complex hand or foot malformation significantly affecting function Confusing it with Pallister-Hall syndrome despite the shared GLI3 gene Relying on sequencing alone and missing a whole-gene deletion detectable by microarray Assuming intellectual disability, which is usually absent Overlooking the autosomal dominant recurrence risk when counselling the family Greig cephalopolysyndactyly is caused by loss-of-function variants in GLI3, including whole-gene deletions, chromosomal translocations disrupting the gene, and truncating variants near its ends, all of which reduce the amount of functional protein (haploinsufficiency). GLI3 is the key transcriptional effector of hedgehog signalling, a pathway assembled and processed on the primary cilium, so reduced GLI3 dosage disturbs the ciliary hedgehog signalling that patterns the limbs and skull. This produces the preaxial polysyndactyly, macrocephaly, frontal bossing and hypertelorism characteristic of the condition. The contrast with Pallister-Hall syndrome, caused by truncating variants in the middle of the same gene that favour a repressor form, illustrates how the position and type of GLI3 variant determine the resulting phenotype. The outlook is excellent, with normal life expectancy and usually normal intellect; management centres on surgical correction of the limb anomalies and appropriate genetic counselling.

GRIN1/GRIN2A/GRIN2B-related neurodevelopmental disorder — GRIN1, GRIN2A, GRIN2B, GRIN-related disorder, NMDA-receptor-related encephalopathy Landau-Kleffner syndrome and epilepsy-aphasia spectrum of regression of language skills Electrical status epilepticus in sleep Drug-resistant seizures or status epilepticus Cortical visual impairment or severe movement disorder impairing function Assuming all GRIN variants behave alike when loss- and gain-of-function require different approaches Overlooking electrical status epilepticus in sleep by not recording sleep EEG Using NMDA-modulating agents without knowing the variant's functional direction Attributing the language disorder to hearing or environmental factors alone The genes GRIN1, GRIN2A and GRIN2B encode the GluN1, GluN2A and GluN2B subunits of the NMDA-type ionotropic glutamate receptor, a calcium-permeable channel central to excitatory neurotransmission and synaptic plasticity underlying learning and memory. Pathogenic variants alter receptor assembly, gating or ion permeation, producing either loss-of-function (reduced current) or gain-of-function (excessive or prolonged current) effects. This disturbed glutamatergic signalling disrupts activity-dependent circuit development, generating intellectual disability, epilepsy and movement abnormalities. Because both too little and too much receptor activity are harmful, the direction of the functional change is central to understanding and potentially treating each variant. Outcome ranges from milder speech and learning difficulties to severe intellectual disability with drug-resistant epilepsy, depending on the gene and functional effect of the variant. Language and seizure burden are major determinants of function, and care is individualised and supportive.

progressive neurological deterioration in type 1 Overwhelming infection during immune activation Signs of central nervous system infiltration during the accelerated phase Confusing it with Chediak-Higashi syndrome despite the absence of giant leucocyte granules Failing to distinguish the neurological (type 1) from the immunological (type 2) form, which changes management Delaying treatment of the accelerated phase in type 2 Overlooking the diagnostic hair microscopy findings Griscelli syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in genes governing the docking and transfer of melanosomes and cytotoxic granules. MYO5A (type 1) encodes a motor protein required in melanocytes and neurons; RAB27A (type 2) is essential for both melanosome transfer and the exocytosis of cytotoxic granules by lymphocytes and natural killer cells; MLPH (type 3) links the two in melanocytes only. Consequently, all types share defective pigment distribution, while RAB27A loss additionally impairs cytotoxic granule release, predisposing to haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Type 2 is fatal without treatment of the accelerated phase and definitive haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which can be curative for the immune disease. Type 1 carries a poor neurological prognosis, whereas type 3 has a benign course limited to pigmentary change.

Groove pancreatitis — paraduodenal pancreatitis, cystic dystrophy of the duodenal wall, pancreatic hamartoma of the duodenum, myoadenomatosis Pancreatic head or periampullary adenocarcinoma Duodenal adenocarcinoma Autoimmune pancreatitis Duodenal duplication cyst Cholangiocarcinoma involving the distal bile duct Ampullary neoplasm Contrast-enhanced CT to characterise groove soft tissue, duodenal wall thickening, and cysts MRI with MRCP to assess the biliary and pancreatic ducts and detect intramural cysts Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle biopsy to sample the groove and exclude malignancy Upper endoscopy to inspect the duodenal mucosa and assess luminal narrowing Serum CA 19-9 to help weigh the likelihood of carcinoma Liver function tests to detect biliary obstruction A form of focal chronic pancreatitis centred on the groove between the pancreatic head, the duodenum, and the common bile duct Typically affects middle-aged men with a heavy alcohol history and is often associated with smoking Presents with recurrent upper abdominal pain, postprandial vomiting, and weight loss, sometimes with jaundice from bile duct narrowing Imaging shows sheet-like fibrous tissue in the groove, duodenal wall thickening, and small cysts within the duodenal wall or paraduodenal region Duodenal luminal narrowing and reduced motility from wall oedema and fibrosis can produce a gastric outlet obstruction picture The principal difficulty is distinguishing it from pancreatic head or periampullary carcinoma, which it can closely resemble Management is initially conservative with alcohol and smoking cessation, pain control, and duodenal rest, reserving pancreaticoduodenectomy for intractable symptoms or when malignancy cannot be excluded Features suggesting periampullary or pancreatic carcinoma, such as a discrete enhancing mass or vascular involvement Progressive obstructive jaundice Marked or persistent weight loss with an unexplained mass Gastric outlet obstruction requiring intervention Mistaking the fibrotic groove mass for a resectable or unresectable pancreatic carcinoma Over-reliance on a single biopsy, as sampling error can miss coexisting malignancy Failing to address ongoing alcohol and tobacco use, which perpetuates the disease Attributing all upper gastrointestinal symptoms to the pancreas while overlooking duodenal obstruction Groove pancreatitis is a segmental chronic pancreatitis affecting the anatomical groove bounded by the dorsocranial pancreatic head, the duodenal wall, and the common bile duct. Impaired outflow of pancreatic secretions through the minor papilla and the dorsal duct region, frequently in the setting of alcohol excess and smoking, is thought to provoke inflammation and dense fibrosis in this space, often with cystic change (cystic dystrophy) within the duodenal wall itself. The resulting scar tissue thickens and stiffens the duodenal wall, can narrow the duodenal lumen and distal bile duct, and produces a mass-like appearance that mimics a periampullary neoplasm. Symptoms often improve with abstinence from alcohol and smoking and supportive care, but disease may be relapsing; surgical resection is frequently effective for refractory pain or obstruction and, importantly, confirms the benign nature of the lesion when carcinoma has been a concern.

resembling Darier, Hailey-Hailey, pemphigus, or spongiotic disease Direct immunofluorescence is negative, distinguishing it from the autoimmune pemphigus group It is a benign condition, and management centres on itch control and avoidance of aggravating factors such as heat and sweating Atypical, widespread, or refractory disease prompting consideration of an underlying malignancy Secondary infection of excoriated lesions Severe intractable pruritus disturbing sleep and quality of life Diagnostic uncertainty requiring exclusion of autoimmune blistering disease Confusing it with an autoimmune pemphigus without performing direct immunofluorescence Failing to advise avoidance of heat, sweating, and occlusion that drive flares Overtreating a fundamentally benign, self-limiting condition Missing an underlying systemic illness in atypical or persistent presentations Grover disease is characterised by focal acantholysis and dyskeratosis in the epidermis, producing small blisters and keratotic papules, but unlike pemphigus it is not autoantibody-mediated and direct immunofluorescence is negative. The precise cause is unknown; disruption of the stratum corneum barrier and eccrine duct occlusion related to heat, sweating, xerosis, and ultraviolet exposure are thought to trigger transient loss of keratinocyte cohesion. Occlusion, immobility, and systemic illness commonly precipitate flares, and associations with malignancy and other dermatoses have been reported, though the disorder is fundamentally benign. Grover disease is benign and often self-limiting over weeks to months, though a subset follows a persistent or relapsing course; it does not scar and generally responds to symptomatic measures and avoidance of triggers.

disability, so early recognition matters Management is generic: creatine supplementation to replete the brain, dietary arginine restriction and ornithine supplementation to lower guanidinoacetate production Refractory epilepsy in a child with unexplained developmental delay A progressive extrapyramidal movement disorder Regression or plateauing of development suggesting an untreated metabolic cause An absent creatine peak on MR spectroscopy Failing to consider a treatable creatine disorder in a child with unexplained delay and epilepsy Confusing it with SLC6A8 creatine transporter deficiency, which is not corrected by oral creatine Not measuring guanidinoacetate, which distinguishes GAMT from AGAT deficiency Providing creatine alone without arginine restriction and ornithine to control guanidinoacetate Overlooking normal serum creatinine, which does not exclude cerebral creatine deficiency Creatine is synthesised in two steps: arginine and glycine form guanidinoacetate, which is then methylated by guanidinoacetate methyltransferase to creatine using S-adenosylmethionine. In GAMT deficiency this final step fails, so brain and muscle creatine and phosphocreatine, essential for energy buffering, become depleted, while the precursor guanidinoacetate accumulates. Guanidinoacetate is neurotoxic and epileptogenic, and its build-up together with cerebral creatine deficiency produces the encephalopathy, epilepsy and movement disorder. Treatment aims both to restore creatine and to suppress guanidinoacetate synthesis by limiting arginine and providing ornithine. Outcome depends heavily on timing; presymptomatic or early treatment can allow near-normal development, whereas delayed diagnosis often leaves fixed intellectual disability, though seizures and movement symptoms may still improve.

Gustatory rhinitis — food-induced rhinorrhoea Allergic rhinitis Other non-allergic rhinitis (vasomotor) Cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea Sinonasal disease with postnasal drip Medication-related rhinitis Clinical diagnosis from the clear temporal link to eating Distinguishing it from allergic rhinitis by history and, if needed, allergy testing Exclusion of cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea when discharge is persistent or unilateral Nasal examination to exclude structural or inflammatory disease Review of medications contributing to rhinitis Profuse watery rhinorrhoea triggered soon after eating, especially hot and spicy foods It is a form of non-allergic rhinitis mediated by cholinergic reflexes rather than by allergy Symptoms are predominantly clear nasal discharge without significant itch, sneezing or nasal blockage It is more common in older adults and can be socially troublesome There is no association with specific food allergy, and allergy testing is typically unnecessary Pre-meal use of a topical anticholinergic nasal spray is effective for many patients Unilateral clear discharge raising concern for cerebrospinal fluid leak Associated bleeding, crusting or a mass Systemic or neurological features Failure to respond to appropriate anticholinergic therapy Misdiagnosing it as food allergy and ordering unnecessary tests Overlooking a cerebrospinal fluid leak when discharge is unilateral Failing to offer effective topical anticholinergic treatment Confusing it with other non-allergic rhinitis subtypes Gustatory rhinitis results from a vagally mediated cholinergic reflex in which the act of eating, particularly spicy or hot food, stimulates nasal glandular secretion. Afferent signals from the upper aerodigestive tract provoke parasympathetic efferent activity to the nasal mucosa, driving watery hypersecretion without an allergic or inflammatory basis. Because the mechanism is cholinergic, topical antimuscarinic therapy blocks the glandular response and controls the rhinorrhoea. The condition is benign and readily controlled with pre-meal anticholinergic nasal spray and dietary awareness, though it tends to persist without treatment.

any ganglion when a compressive lesion is present Vascular compromise from ulnar artery thrombosis or aneurysm A mass lesion that may represent a tumour Rapidly progressive intrinsic muscle wasting wrist-level lesion with an elbow-level lesion by not testing dorsal ulnar sensation Overlooking a vascular cause such as hypothenar hammer syndrome Incomplete decompression that does not address all involved zones of the canal The ulnar nerve and its branches can be compressed as they traverse Guyon canal at the wrist between the pisiform and the hook of hamate. Common mechanisms include a space-occupying ganglion, fracture or nonunion of the hook of hamate, thrombosis or aneurysm of the adjacent ulnar artery, and repetitive external compression such as prolonged gripping of handlebars. The level within the canal at which compression occurs determines whether the motor branch, sensory branch or both are affected, and dorsal ulnar sensation is spared because its cutaneous branch arises proximal to the canal. The outlook is good when an identifiable compressive cause such as a ganglion or fracture is treated, though recovery of long-standing intrinsic wasting may be incomplete.

Gynaecomastia — Male breast enlargement, Gynecomastia Pseudogynaecomastia (adipose enlargement) Male breast carcinoma Lipoma of the chest wall Neurofibroma or other benign chest-wall tumour Breast abscess or inflammatory mass Dermoid or sebaceous cyst Metastatic deposit to the male breast Clinical examination of breasts, testes and for signs of systemic disease Serum testosterone, oestradiol, LH and FSH Prolactin, thyroid function and liver and renal function tests Beta-hCG and alpha-fetoprotein if a germ-cell tumour is suspected Testicular ultrasound where a testicular lesion is suspected Breast ultrasound and mammography when malignancy cannot be excluded clinically Core biopsy of any suspicious or eccentric hard mass Benign proliferation of male glandular breast tissue felt as a firm, concentric, often tender disc directly beneath the areola. Must be distinguished from pseudogynaecomastia (fatty enlargement without a glandular disc) and from male breast carcinoma, which is typically hard, eccentric and painless. Physiological forms occur in neonates, at puberty and in older men, and the majority of pubertal cases regress spontaneously within one to two years. Results from a relative excess of oestrogen action over androgen action on breast tissue, whatever the underlying cause. Drugs are a leading cause: examples include spironolactone, digoxin, cimetidine, anti-androgens, some antipsychotics, and recreational agents such as cannabis and anabolic steroids. Pathological causes include hypogonadism, chronic liver disease, chronic kidney disease, thyrotoxicosis and hormone-secreting testicular or adrenal tumours. A careful history for drugs, alcohol and systemic disease with testicular examination is central to the assessment. Management targets the cause; persistent or cosmetically distressing gynaecomastia may be treated medically in the proliferative phase or by surgical excision or liposuction. Hard, eccentric or fixed mass rather than a symmetrical subareolar disc Skin dimpling, nipple retraction, ulceration or bloody nipple discharge Rapid unilateral enlargement in an older man A palpable testicular mass suggesting an oestrogen-secreting tumour Associated axillary lymphadenopathy Mistaking eccentric male breast carcinoma for benign gynaecomastia Failing to examine the testes and missing a hormone-secreting tumour Overlooking a culprit medication or recreational drug in the history Expecting medical therapy to work on long-standing fibrotic disease Labelling fatty pseudogynaecomastia as glandular gynaecomastia without palpating a disc Gynaecomastia arises when the balance between stimulatory oestrogen and inhibitory androgen action on breast tissue shifts in favour of oestrogen, driving proliferation of ductal epithelium and periductal stroma. This may follow increased oestrogen production or peripheral aromatisation, reduced androgen production or action, displacement of oestrogen from binding proteins, or blockade of androgen receptors by drugs. Early (florid) lesions show ductal hyperplasia with loose cellular stroma and are potentially reversible, whereas long-standing disease becomes fibrotic and hyalinised and responds poorly to medical therapy. The physiological peaks of the neonatal period, puberty and older age each reflect transient or age-related alterations in this hormonal balance. Physiological and drug-induced gynaecomastia frequently resolve once the trigger is removed, especially if treated during the early proliferative phase. Long-standing fibrotic disease tends to persist and may require surgery, but the condition itself is benign.

ovarian cancers are split into indolent type 1 (low-grade, KRAS/BRAF/PTEN/PIK3CA mutations) and aggressive type 2 high-grade serous cancers, the latter driven by TP53 loss (about 95%) and BRCA1/2 dysfunction, with growing evidence that many high-grade serous cancers actually originate in the fallopian tube epithelium. Germline BRCA1/2 testing is recommended for all incident epithelial ovarian cancers; lifetime ovarian cancer risk is roughly 39 to 63 percent for BRCA1 and 16.5 to 27 percent for BRCA2, and risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing (ideally before age 40) is highly protective and also lowers subsequent breast cancer risk by about 50 percent. About 70 percent of ovarian cancer patients present at stage III; a markedly elevated serum CA-125 (shed MUC16) is characteristic but not specific, and PET is generally not required for evaluation. Bilateral ovarian masses from metastatic mucin-secreting gastrointestinal cancers are termed Krukenberg tumors; metastatic disease to the ovary also arises from colon, appendix, stomach, and breast primaries, so other malignancies must be considered in the workup. High-risk HPV infection (especially types 16 and 18, also 31, 33, 35, 52, 58) is the primary initiating event in the vast majority of invasive cervical cancers; viral E6 and E7 proteins inactivate p53 and RB respectively, but full transformation requires additional acquired mutations over years. Cervical cancer staging is fundamentally clinical: stage I confined to cervix, stage II into upper vagina/paracervical tissue, stage III to lower vagina or pelvic sidewall, stage IV invading bladder/rectum or distant; MRI better estimates uterine and paracervical soft-tissue extension while CT detects hydronephrosis indicating sidewall disease. Endometrioid endometrial adenocarcinoma is the most common gynecologic malignancy in the United States; unopposed estrogen exposure is the principal risk factor, so obesity, postmenopausal estrogen therapy, estrogen-producing tumors, and tamoxifen (weakly estrogenic in uterine epithelium) all increase risk while progestins are protective. Most women with uterine corpus cancer present with postmenopausal bleeding (or atypical intermenstrual bleeding premenopausally), leading to early-stage detection and high cure rates; about 75 percent are stage I. Routine microsatellite instability (MSI) testing of all endometrial cancers is now standard, because MSI/mismatch-repair-deficient tumors that recur or present advanced are likely to respond to PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint therapy. Gestational trophoblastic disease spans benign hydatidiform mole to choriocarcinoma; complete moles are diploid with entirely paternal genetic material (uniparental disomy, no fetal development), while partial moles are triploid (egg fertilized by two sperm) and may show early fetal development. Trophoblastic disease is exquisitely chemosensitive and monitored by serial serum beta-hCG; even very advanced disease is almost uniformly curable when managed by an expert. Gardasil-9 protects against HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58; vaccination before sexual activity dramatically lowers high-risk infection and dysplasia, but vaccinated women remain at residual risk and still need Pap screening. Ovarian epithelial cancer 5-year survival correlates strongly with stage: roughly 90 to 95 percent stage I, 70 to 80 percent stage II, 25 to 40 percent stage III, and 10 to 15 percent stage IV; prognosis improves with lower histologic grade and BRCA1/2 germline mutation, and complete (R0) cytoreduction yields median survival beyond 60 months versus 28 to 42 months with macroscopic residual disease. Endometrial cancer is usually localized (about 75 percent stage I) with high cure; cervical cancer 5-year survival declines from about 85 percent (stage I) to roughly 7 percent (stage IV). Borderline (low malignant potential) ovarian tumors and ovarian germ cell tumors (including dysgerminoma) are highly curable. Gestational trophoblastic disease is almost uniformly curable, with single-agent therapy curing about 90 percent of low-risk cases. Staging per Table 94-1: Ovarian - I confined to ovary (88-95%), II confined to pelvic organs (70-80%), III intra-abdominal spread to omentum/diaphragm/nodes (20-40%), IV spread outside abdominal cavity/parenchymal/pleural (10-20%); most present as stage IIIC (bulky intraperitoneal or positive nodes). Endometrial - I confined to corpus (>90%), II corpus and cervix (~75%), III outside uterus but within true pelvis (45-60%), IV beyond true pelvis or bladder/rectum (~20%). Cervix - 0 carcinoma in situ (100%), I confined to uterus (85%), II beyond uterus not to pelvic wall (65%), III to pelvic wall and/or lower third vagina or hydronephrosis (35%), IV invading bladder/rectal mucosa or beyond true pelvis (7%). Gestational trophoblastic disease is risk-stratified (low/intermediate/high) by scoring algorithms guiding single- versus multiagent therapy.

suggesting malignancy Rapidly enlarging breast tissue with elevated hCG indicating a hormone-secreting tumour A palpable testicular mass on examination Associated systemic features of significant liver, kidney, or thyroid disease Mistaking fatty pseudogynaecomastia for true glandular tissue and over-investigating Failing to examine the testes and missing a hormone-secreting tumour Overlooking an offending drug as the simplest reversible cause Dismissing a suspicious unilateral mass rather than excluding male breast cancer Gynaecomastia is benign proliferation of the glandular component of the male breast driven by an imbalance between stimulatory oestrogen and inhibitory androgen effects on breast epithelium. This imbalance can arise from decreased androgen production or action (hypogonadism, androgen resistance), increased oestrogen production (testicular or adrenal tumours, hCG-secreting tumours, aromatisation in obesity), or altered clearance and binding of hormones (liver disease, drugs affecting SHBG or steroid metabolism). Physiological forms in the neonate, at puberty, and with ageing reflect transient shifts in this hormonal balance. Over time, early ductal proliferation gives way to fibrosis, which is less responsive to medical treatment. Physiological and drug-related gynaecomastia often resolves once the trigger is removed or with time, particularly in early stages; long-standing fibrotic tissue tends to persist and may require surgical treatment, and prognosis in secondary cases depends on the underlying disorder.

Pubertal gynaecomastia — adolescent gynaecomastia, physiological gynaecomastia of puberty, pubertal breast enlargement in boys Fatty pseudogynaecomastia associated with obesity Drug- or substance-induced gynaecomastia, including anabolic steroids and cannabis Pathological hypogonadism such as Klinefelter syndrome Hormone-secreting tumours (testicular, adrenal, or human-chorionic-gonadotropin-secreting) Systemic disease such as liver or renal impairment or thyrotoxicosis Breast malignancy, rare in adolescents but suggested by a hard eccentric mass Clinical examination of the breasts, testes, and secondary sexual characteristics with pubertal staging Reassurance-based observation with re-examination over several months in typical cases Serum testosterone, luteinising hormone, and follicle-stimulating hormone if hypogonadism is suspected Oestradiol, human chorionic gonadotropin, and dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate if a hormone-secreting tumour is considered Thyroid, liver, and renal function tests to exclude systemic contributors Breast and testicular ultrasound where a discrete mass or testicular abnormality is found Palpable, often tender, firm glandular tissue develops concentrically beneath the areola during mid-puberty and is a common, usually benign finding in adolescent boys It reflects a transient imbalance between oestrogen and androgen action on breast tissue rather than any underlying disease in the great majority of cases True glandular gynaecomastia should be distinguished from fatty pseudogynaecomastia by palpating a discrete rubbery disc of tissue under the nipple The condition is typically self-limiting and resolves spontaneously within months to a couple of years as the hormonal milieu matures Reassurance and observation are the mainstay; medical or surgical intervention is reserved for persistent, large, or distressing cases A careful drug and substance history is essential, as anabolic steroids, cannabis, and certain medications can cause or perpetuate breast enlargement Rapid growth, hard or fixed tissue, eccentric or unilateral masses, or signs of systemic or endocrine disease warrant fuller evaluation A hard, fixed, or eccentric mass, nipple discharge, or skin change suggesting malignancy Rapidly enlarging breast tissue or onset before the expected pubertal window Testicular mass or asymmetry pointing to a hormone-secreting tumour Features of an underlying endocrine or systemic disorder Mistaking fatty pseudogynaecomastia in an obese boy for true glandular enlargement Failing to take a thorough drug and substance history, missing anabolic steroid or cannabis use Over-investigating a typical, self-limiting presentation and causing unnecessary anxiety Dismissing a hard, unilateral, or rapidly growing mass without excluding pathology Overlooking underlying hypogonadism such as Klinefelter syndrome in a boy with small testes Pubertal gynaecomastia arises from a temporary relative excess of oestrogen action over androgen action at the breast during the hormonal fluctuations of puberty. Early in male puberty, peripheral aromatisation of adrenal and testicular precursors can transiently raise oestrogen levels ahead of the full rise in testosterone, and local breast tissue sensitivity to oestrogen stimulates proliferation of ductal and stromal elements. As the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis matures and testosterone secretion becomes dominant, the imbalance corrects and the proliferated tissue usually regresses. Persistent or exaggerated cases may reflect increased aromatase activity, obesity, drug exposure, or, less commonly, an underlying pathological cause of oestrogen excess or androgen deficiency. The outlook is excellent, with the majority of cases resolving spontaneously as puberty progresses; a minority with persistent glandular tissue beyond puberty may seek medical or surgical treatment for cosmetic or psychological reasons.

the OAT gene encoding ornithine aminotransferase, a pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent mitochondrial enzyme that converts ornithine to glutamate semialdehyde. Enzyme deficiency causes ornithine to accumulate in plasma and tissues. Chronically raised ornithine is thought to be toxic to the retinal pigment epithelium and choriocapillaris, producing progressive atrophy of the choroid and outer retina. The condition is progressive, and most patients experience severe visual impairment or blindness by middle age; dietary control of ornithine and pyridoxine supplementation in responsive individuals may slow but not fully arrest the decline.

SLC29A3 disorders Not pursuing genetic testing in a child with hyperpigmented, hypertrichotic indurated skin H syndrome is caused by biallelic mutations in SLC29A3, encoding the equilibrative nucleoside transporter hENT3 that moves nucleosides across intracellular membranes, particularly in lysosomes of macrophages. Loss of transporter function disturbs nucleoside handling and macrophage homeostasis, promoting accumulation and activation of histiocytes. Because the underlying process is a histiocytic infiltration with autoinflammatory features rather than a single cytokine defect, treatment is directed at complications and inflammation as they arise. H syndrome is a chronic multisystem disorder; life expectancy can be relatively preserved but morbidity accrues from progressive skin, endocrine, sensorineural, and organ involvement requiring long-term multidisciplinary care.
