dystrophy and applying the wrong management Overlooking an associated body-focused repetitive behaviour or anxiety disorder Expecting improvement without addressing the causative habit Habit-tic deformity results from chronic mechanical trauma inflicted by the patient on their own proximal nail fold and cuticle, typically by picking or rubbing with an adjacent finger. The repeated injury to the region overlying the matrix produces a series of transverse depressions in the plate as it is laid down, arranged around a central longitudinal groove, so that the nail acquires a rippled, washboard surface. Because the damage is to the soft tissue over the matrix rather than the matrix being intrinsically diseased, the nail can recover fully once the manipulation stops, and the enlarged lunula reflects the ongoing disturbance of the proximal nail unit. The deformity is benign and reversible, and the nail grows out normally once the repetitive trauma stops, although relapse is common if the underlying habit persists and behavioural change can be difficult to sustain.

haemangioblastoma — capillary haemangioblastoma, Lindau tumour metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma pilocytic astrocytoma cerebral or cerebellar metastasis of other origin arteriovenous malformation cavernous malformation reactive angiomatous change cerebellar high-grade glioma contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain and whole spine catheter angiography to define vascular supply and enable embolisation germline VHL gene testing abdominal imaging for renal, adrenal and pancreatic lesions plasma or urinary metanephrines to exclude phaeochromocytoma full blood count for secondary polycythaemia and erythropoietin level dilated retinal examination for retinal haemangioblastoma A highly vascular CNS WHO grade 1 tumour arising most often in the cerebellum, but also the spinal cord, brainstem and retina. The classic imaging pattern is a cyst with an enhancing mural nodule, and MRI frequently shows serpentine flow voids from feeding and draining vessels. Around a quarter of cases occur in von Hippel-Lindau disease, where tumours are often multiple and present at a younger age. A VHL diagnosis mandates screening for retinal haemangioblastomas, clear cell renal cell carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma and pancreatic and endolymphatic lesions. Stromal cells produce erythropoietin, so a minority of patients present with secondary polycythaemia that resolves after resection. Histology shows lipid-laden vacuolated stromal cells within a dense capillary network, and the stromal cells are typically inhibin-alpha positive. Preoperative angiography and embolisation can reduce intraoperative bleeding from these vascular tumours. Metastatic clear cell renal carcinoma is the key mimic and must be excluded, particularly in VHL patients. obstructive hydrocephalus from a posterior fossa lesion acute intratumoural or subarachnoid haemorrhage progressive myelopathy from a spinal cord tumour coexisting phaeochromocytoma causing labile blood pressure mistaking metastatic renal cell carcinoma for haemangioblastoma, especially in VHL failing to screen for von Hippel-Lindau disease and its associated tumours operating without appreciating the vascularity and risk of catastrophic bleeding overlooking an occult phaeochromocytoma before anaesthesia attributing polycythaemia to a primary haematological cause rather than the tumour Haemangioblastoma is a benign, highly vascular neoplasm composed of neoplastic stromal cells and an abundant capillary network. The stromal cell is the tumour cell, and in von Hippel-Lindau disease it carries biallelic inactivation of the VHL tumour suppressor; sporadic tumours also show somatic VHL loss. Loss of functional VHL protein prevents degradation of hypoxia-inducible factors, so HIF-alpha accumulates and constitutively drives transcription of vascular endothelial growth factor and erythropoietin. This produces the exuberant capillary proliferation that characterises the tumour and, through erythropoietin, can cause secondary erythrocytosis. The vacuolated, lipid-rich cytoplasm of the stromal cells reflects this dysregulated hypoxia-response programme. Complete resection of a solitary tumour is usually curative with an excellent outlook, but patients with von Hippel-Lindau disease develop multiple and recurrent lesions over time and require lifelong surveillance.

Haemolytic disease of the newborn — HDN, haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, erythroblastosis fetalis Physiological jaundice Non-immune haemolysis (for example G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis) Sepsis-related jaundice or anaemia Internal haemorrhage (for example cephalohaematoma, intracranial bleed) Non-immune hydrops fetalis Maternal antibody screening and identification antenatally Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test on the neonate Serial bilirubin and haemoglobin measurement Blood group and film of the newborn Antenatal monitoring of fetal anaemia (for example middle cerebral artery Doppler) Immune haemolysis of fetal and neonatal red cells caused by maternal alloantibodies crossing the placenta Rhesus D incompatibility historically caused severe disease; ABO incompatibility is now a common but usually milder cause Other antibodies such as anti-Kell can cause severe disease, partly by suppressing erythropoiesis Antenatally it can cause fetal anaemia and hydrops; postnatally it causes early, rapidly rising jaundice and anaemia The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test on the baby is typically positive in immune haemolysis Routine anti-D prophylaxis has greatly reduced rhesus disease; management includes phototherapy, exchange transfusion and, antenatally, intrauterine transfusion Hydrops fetalis or severe fetal anaemia Rapidly rising bilirubin approaching exchange-transfusion thresholds Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy Severe anaemia causing cardiovascular compromise Underestimating ABO or anti-Kell disease Missing rapidly rising jaundice in the first day of life Overlooking late anaemia after apparent recovery Failing to give appropriate anti-D prophylaxis to at-risk mothers Haemolytic disease of the newborn occurs when maternal IgG alloantibodies, formed against fetal red cell antigens the mother lacks, cross the placenta and bind fetal red cells, leading to their destruction by the reticuloendothelial system. The resulting fetal anaemia can cause high-output failure and hydrops in severe cases. After birth, continued haemolysis produces anaemia and a rapid rise in unconjugated bilirubin, which, if untreated, can cross the immature blood-brain barrier and cause kernicterus. Anti-Kell disease additionally suppresses fetal erythropoiesis. With prophylaxis, antenatal monitoring and modern neonatal treatment, outcomes are usually good, but severe untreated disease can cause hydrops, kernicterus or death, and late anaemia may require follow-up.

Haemophilia — haemophilia A, haemophilia B, factor VIII deficiency, factor IX deficiency, Christmas disease, hemophilia Von Willebrand disease Other clotting factor deficiencies (e.g. factor XI) Vitamin K deficiency or liver disease Disseminated intravascular coagulation Platelet function disorders or thrombocytopenia Non-accidental injury when bruising pattern is unexplained aPTT, prothrombin time, and platelet count as initial screen Specific factor VIII and factor IX activity assays Mixing study to demonstrate factor deficiency versus inhibitor Inhibitor (Bethesda) assay when replacement therapy is failing Von Willebrand factor studies to exclude von Willebrand disease Genetic testing for carrier detection and prenatal diagnosis An X-linked recessive bleeding disorder affecting mainly males; haemophilia A results from factor VIII deficiency and haemophilia B from factor IX deficiency. The two types are clinically indistinguishable and are separated by specific factor assays. Disease severity correlates with residual factor activity: severe disease often presents with spontaneous bleeding, while milder forms bleed mainly after trauma or surgery. Hallmark manifestations are deep bleeding into joints (haemarthrosis) and muscles rather than mucocutaneous bleeding. Screening typically shows a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) with a normal prothrombin time and platelet count. Recurrent joint bleeds lead to chronic synovitis and progressive haemophilic arthropathy if not prevented. Management centres on replacing the deficient clotting factor, with prophylactic regimens preventing bleeds in severe disease and on-demand treatment for acute bleeds. Development of inhibitory antibodies against the replaced factor is a major complication that reduces treatment efficacy. Intracranial haemorrhage is a life-threatening event that warrants immediate factor replacement, and newer therapies such as non-factor agents and gene therapy are changing management. Suspected intracranial haemorrhage (headache, vomiting, altered consciousness, focal signs) Bleeding into the neck, throat, or retroperitoneum threatening the airway or causing large occult loss Compartment syndrome from muscle bleeding Poor response to factor replacement suggesting an inhibitor Significant bleeding after trauma or before surgery without prophylaxis Delaying factor replacement while awaiting imaging in suspected serious bleeding Attributing bleeding solely to trauma and missing an underlying disorder Using aspirin or NSAIDs and intramuscular injections that increase bleeding risk Overlooking inhibitor development when a previously effective factor dose stops working Deficiency of factor VIII or factor IX impairs the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade, reducing generation of activated factor X and thereby the thrombin burst required for a stable fibrin clot. Primary haemostasis (platelet plug formation) is intact, so initial bleeding may stop, but the fibrin clot is inadequate and delayed or recurrent bleeding follows, characteristically into joints and muscles. Repeated haemarthroses cause iron deposition, synovial hypertrophy, and cartilage destruction leading to chronic arthropathy. With modern factor replacement and prophylaxis, life expectancy and quality of life approach normal; outcomes worsen with inhibitor development, chronic arthropathy, and delayed treatment of major bleeds.

Haemophilus and Moraxella Infections — Haemophilus influenzae infection, Hib disease, Nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae, Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid), Moraxella catarrhalis infection Pneumococcal pneumonia and other bacterial pneumonias (clinically indistinguishable from H. influenzae pneumonia) Bacterial meningitis due to other pathogens Acute otitis media due to S. pneumoniae or M. catarrhalis For chancroid: primary syphilis, secondary syphilis (condyloma latum), genital herpes, donovanosis, lymphogranuloma venereum, and folliculitis For H. ducreyi cutaneous ulcers: yaws (Treponema pallidum subsp. pertenue) Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumonia, otitis media, sinusitis, meningitis) Moraxella catarrhalis vs commensal Neisseria species on respiratory culture Haemophilus haemolyticus, a respiratory commensal with identical growth requirements that can be mistaken for H. influenzae Herpes simplex virus and Treponema pallidum in genital ulcer disease Culture from a normally sterile site (blood, CSF, joint, pleural, pericardial fluid, or subdural effusion) is the most reliable means of diagnosing invasive H. influenzae and is needed for susceptibility testing Gram stain of CSF showing gram-negative coccobacilli supports Hib meningitis; predominant gram-negative coccobacilli among abundant neutrophils in sputum suggests nontypeable H. influenzae pneumonia PCR and other DNA-based detection methods, now common in clinical labs Genotypic markers (16S rRNA, superoxide dismutase, outer-membrane protein P6, protein D, fuculose kinase) and whole-genome sequencing to distinguish H. influenzae from H. haemolyticus Pneumatic otoscopy detects middle-ear fluid; tympanocentesis with culture gives etiologic diagnosis of otitis media but is not routine For chancroid: culture of H. ducreyi (requires selective/supplemented media) from the lesion or node aspirate, and PCR; dark-field exam and syphilis serology to exclude T. pallidum and HSV testing of exudate H. influenzae is a small, pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacillus that often stains only faintly with safranin in CSF and sputum, so it is easily overlooked on Gram stain. Aerobic growth of H. influenzae requires both hemin (X factor) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (V factor) and needs preheated blood, so it grows on chocolate agar but not on ordinary (unheated) blood agar. Six capsular serotypes (a-f) exist plus unencapsulated nontypeable strains; type b (Hib) and nontypeable strains are the most clinically important, with Hib being invasive (hematogenous spread) and nontypeable being primarily mucosal pathogens. Maternally acquired anticapsular (anti-PRP) antibody declines from birth to about 6 months; the antibody nadir corresponds to the peak age of type b disease, and systemic Hib disease is unusual after age 6 owing to acquired protective antibody. Hib meningitis primarily affects children under 2 years; subdural effusion is the most common complication and should be suspected when seizures, hemiparesis, or persistent obtundation follow 2-3 days of appropriate therapy. Hib epiglottitis is a life-threatening cellulitis of the epiglottis and supraglottic tissues occurring in an older age group (2-7 years) than other Hib infections; in countries with childhood Hib vaccination it now occurs mainly in adults. Nontypeable H. influenzae is the most common bacterial cause of COPD exacerbations and, in recent years, has caused community-acquired pneumonia more frequently than S. pneumoniae. Nontypeable H. influenzae is one of the three most common causes of childhood otitis media (with S. pneumoniae and M. catarrhalis); clinical clues include recurrent episodes, treatment failure, concomitant conjunctivitis, and bilateral disease. Invasive nontypeable strains causing neonatal/puerperal sepsis after colonizing the female genital tract have been provisionally named Haemophilus quentini (related to but distinct from H. haemolyticus). Moraxella catarrhalis is an unencapsulated gram-negative diplococcus of the respiratory tract; its colonies can be slid intact across the agar surface (the hockey puck sign) and turn pink after 48 h, distinguishing them from commensal Neisseria. M. catarrhalis is the second most common bacterial cause of COPD exacerbations after H. influenzae and accounts for roughly 15-20 percent of acute otitis media cases by middle-ear culture (30-50 percent by molecular detection). Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid, a painful genital ulcer disease; prior chancroid does not confer protection, and H. ducreyi is also an important cause of non-sexually transmitted cutaneous ulcers in children in the South Pacific and Africa. Sore throat and fever rapidly progressing to dysphagia, drooling, and airway obstruction (epiglottitis) - a medical emergency requiring airway maintenance Fever with altered CNS function and nuchal rigidity (which may be absent) in a young child suggesting Hib meningitis Seizures, hemiparesis, or persistent obtundation after 2-3 days of appropriate antibiotics, suggesting subdural effusion Underlying immunosuppression, HIV, cardiopulmonary disease, alcoholism, or cancer in a patient with H. influenzae bacteremia H. influenzae may be missed on Gram stain because it stains only faintly with safranin in CSF and sputum. Ordinary (unheated) blood agar fails to grow H. influenzae, which can lead to false-negative cultures if chocolate agar is not used. Distinguishing H. influenzae from the commensal H. haemolyticus is difficult because they share growth requirements and many H. haemolyticus isolates are now nonhemolytic. M. catarrhalis has historically been overlooked as a pathogen because its colonies resemble those of commensal Neisseria species on respiratory cultures. Approximately 30-40 percent of nontypeable H. influenzae produce beta-lactamase (conferring ampicillin/amoxicillin resistance), and a second mechanism, altered penicillin-binding proteins (beta-lactamase-negative ampicillin-resistant strains), is increasing in Europe and common in Japan. Over 90 percent of M. catarrhalis strains now produce beta-lactamase and are resistant to amoxicillin; macrolide and fluoroquinolone resistance is emerging, notably in Asia. Clinical diagnosis of chancroid is often inaccurate, so laboratory confirmation should be attempted; in HIV-positive patients apparent treatment failure may reflect HSV co-infection. Isolation of M. catarrhalis from expectorated sputum during an exacerbation is suggestive but not diagnostic of it as the cause. Hib strains produce systemic disease by invading the respiratory mucosa and spreading hematogenously to distant sites such as meninges, bones, and joints; the type b polysaccharide capsule (ribosyl-ribitol phosphate) is a key virulence factor that resists opsonization. Nontypeable strains lack a capsule and cause disease by local mucosal invasion (e.g., otitis media via the eustachian tube, lower respiratory infection in COPD), persisting in airways both extracellularly and intracellularly and forming biofilms in the middle ear that resist host clearance and antibiotics; they vary expression of virulence genes by slipped-strand mispairing and phase-variable DNA methylases. M. catarrhalis colonizes the upper airway and infects by contiguous spread, often following a viral upper respiratory infection (e.g., rhinovirus promotes adhesion); it uses multiple adhesins, invades several cell types with an intracellular lymphoid reservoir, and sheds outer-membrane vesicles that deliver beta-lactamase and induce inflammation, potentially protecting co-pathogens such as group A streptococci and H. influenzae. H. ducreyi infects through an epithelial break during sexual contact, producing ulcers with predominantly T-cell infiltrate. The overall mortality of Hib meningitis is about 5 percent with a high morbidity rate; about 6 percent of survivors have permanent sensorineural hearing loss, roughly one-fourth have a significant disability, and up to half have some neurologic sequela such as partial hearing loss or delayed language development when sought carefully. Hib epiglottitis is life-threatening due to risk of acute upper-airway obstruction. Glucocorticoids reduce the incidence of neurologic sequelae in Hib meningitis. Nontypeable strains tend to cause recurrent otitis media and recurrent COPD exacerbations because immunity is strain-specific. M. catarrhalis otitis media and exacerbations are clinically milder (less fever, less red bulging tympanic membrane) than pneumococcal disease, and invasive M. catarrhalis infection is rare. Repeated H. ducreyi infections can occur because infection confers no protection; in HIV-positive patients chancroid healing may be slow and require longer therapy.

Haemorrhoidal thrombosis — thrombosed haemorrhoids, thrombosed prolapsed haemorrhoids, acute haemorrhoidal crisis Isolated perianal haematoma (thrombosed external haemorrhoid) Strangulated full-thickness rectal prolapse Perianal or ischiorectal abscess Anal fissure with sentinel pile Anal or low rectal carcinoma Crohn disease with acute perianal inflammation Pigmented perianal lesion such as melanoma Inspection and gentle digital examination to confirm thrombosed haemorrhoidal tissue Examination under anaesthesia when pain precludes assessment or surgery is planned Proctoscopy once the acute episode settles, to grade residual haemorrhoids Full blood count if bleeding is significant or infection is suspected Assessment for constipation, diarrhoea, or pregnancy as precipitants Histology of excised tissue where appearances are atypical Haemorrhoidal thrombosis is acute clotting within haemorrhoidal tissue, ranging from an isolated thrombosed external haemorrhoid to an acute crisis of thrombosed, prolapsed, and oedematous internal or mixed haemorrhoids The hallmark is sudden severe anal pain with a tense, tender, blue-purple swelling; extensive prolapsed thrombosis produces a circumferential oedematous painful mass at the anal verge It is often precipitated by straining, constipation, diarrhoea, pregnancy, or childbirth Acutely incarcerated, thrombosed, prolapsed internal haemorrhoids may become irreducible and, rarely, progress to ulceration, necrosis, or sepsis Diagnosis is clinical on inspection; painful examination and instrumentation should be deferred or done under anaesthesia in severe cases Most cases settle with conservative care: analgesia, stool softening, warm baths, topical agents, and reduction of oedema, with full assessment once the acute episode resolves Early surgery (excisional haemorrhoidectomy) can be offered for severe or extensive acute thrombosis in suitable patients and gives durable results, but carries risks in the oedematous acute setting The differential includes strangulated rectal prolapse, perianal abscess, and, in immunocompromised patients, a threshold for concern about necrosis and sepsis Necrosis, ulceration, or spreading infection of the thrombosed mass Systemic sepsis, particularly in immunocompromised or diabetic patients Irreducible incarcerated prolapse with compromised viability A pigmented or indurated lesion suggesting malignancy Severe uncontrolled bleeding Confusing incarcerated thrombosed haemorrhoids with strangulated rectal prolapse or abscess Aggressive instrumentation of an acutely painful anus without anaesthesia Simple incision of a clot rather than excision, leading to recurrence and residual tag Underestimating necrosis or sepsis in immunocompromised patients Neglecting to correct constipation, straining, or diarrhoea, allowing recurrence Haemorrhoidal thrombosis develops when blood within the dilated vessels of the haemorrhoidal cushions clots, either from venous stasis and raised pressure or from an acute rise in intra-abdominal and anal pressure that ruptures or occludes vessels. In external thrombosis a discrete clot forms in the subcutaneous plexus below the dentate line. In an acute internal or mixed haemorrhoidal crisis, prolapsed cushions become trapped by sphincter spasm, which impairs venous return, causing progressive engorgement, thrombosis, and marked oedema; the swelling worsens the incarceration in a self-perpetuating cycle. The tense, clotted, oedematous tissue stretches somatically innervated anoderm, producing intense pain, and in severe incarceration the compromised blood supply may lead to mucosal ulceration, necrosis, and, rarely, secondary infection. Most haemorrhoidal thromboses are self-limiting, with pain settling over days to a couple of weeks under conservative care; early excisional surgery in appropriate patients relieves symptoms quickly and reduces recurrence, while severe incarcerated thrombosis with necrosis is uncommon but carries greater morbidity.

Haemorrhoids — piles, haemorrhoidal disease Colorectal carcinoma or rectal polyp causing rectal bleeding Anal fissure (painful bright-red bleeding with sentinel tag) Rectal prolapse (full-thickness circumferential prolapse) Anal or perianal skin tag or hypertrophied anal papilla Anorectal abscess or fistula Inflammatory bowel disease with proctitis Anal carcinoma or anal intraepithelial neoplasia Proctoscopy or anoscopy to visualise and grade internal haemorrhoids Rigid or flexible sigmoidoscopy to inspect the distal bowel Colonoscopy where bleeding is unexplained, atypical, or the patient is at risk of neoplasia Full blood count if bleeding is chronic or heavy, to detect iron-deficiency anaemia Digital rectal examination to exclude a palpable mass and assess sphincter tone Faecal immunochemical testing and further imaging where colorectal cancer must be excluded Haemorrhoids are symptomatic enlargement and distal displacement of the normal anal cushions; the cushions themselves are physiological structures contributing to continence, so their mere presence is not pathological Internal haemorrhoids arise above the dentate line and are typically painless, presenting with bright-red painless bleeding at defecation, mucus discharge, pruritus, and prolapse; external haemorrhoids lie below the dentate line and are somatically innervated, so become painful when thrombosed The Goligher grading of internal haemorrhoids (grade I no prolapse, II prolapse with spontaneous reduction, III prolapse needing manual reduction, IV irreducible) guides management choice Diagnosis rests on inspection, digital rectal examination, and proctoscopy; internal haemorrhoids are usually not palpable and are best seen on proctoscopy or anoscopy First-line management is conservative: increased dietary fibre and fluid, stool softening, avoidance of straining and prolonged toilet sitting, and topical agents for symptom relief Office procedures such as rubber-band ligation are effective for grade I to III disease, while excisional or stapled haemorrhoidectomy and haemorrhoidal artery ligation are reserved for higher-grade or refractory disease Rectal bleeding must never be attributed to haemorrhoids without excluding proximal pathology, particularly colorectal neoplasia, in at-risk patients Pregnancy, chronic constipation with straining, low-fibre diet, and raised intra-abdominal pressure are common contributory factors Change in bowel habit, weight loss, or iron-deficiency anaemia suggesting colorectal malignancy Dark blood, blood mixed within the stool, or a palpable rectal mass Persistent bleeding despite adequate treatment of visible haemorrhoids Severe unremitting anal pain suggesting thrombosis, abscess, or another cause New symptoms in older patients or those with a family history of bowel cancer Attributing rectal bleeding to haemorrhoids without adequately excluding colorectal cancer in at-risk patients Banding external or mixed haemorrhoids below the dentate line, which causes severe pain Overlooking a coexisting fissure or fistula as the true source of symptoms Neglecting to correct constipation and straining, leading to early recurrence Aggressive circumferential excision risking anal stenosis The anal canal contains three main vascular cushions of submucosal connective tissue, smooth muscle (the muscle of Treitz), and arteriovenous communications that contribute to fine continence by sealing the canal. Haemorrhoidal disease develops when these cushions become engorged, hypertrophied, and prolapsed owing to deterioration of the supporting fibromuscular anchoring tissue, allowing distal sliding of the cushions. Repeated straining, prolonged defecation, chronic constipation or diarrhoea, and raised intra-abdominal pressure (as in pregnancy) increase venous congestion and shearing forces. Increased resting anal tone and arteriovenous shunting within the cushions contribute to the bright-red bleeding characteristic of internal haemorrhoids. Progressive fragmentation of the connective tissue and dilatation of the vascular plexus lead to bleeding, prolapse, mucus discharge, and, in external components, thrombosis. Most haemorrhoidal symptoms respond well to conservative measures and office-based procedures, with good long-term control; recurrence can occur, particularly if predisposing factors such as constipation and straining persist, and surgery carries small risks of pain, bleeding, and rarely incontinence or stenosis.

haemothorax — traumatic haemothorax, pleural haemorrhage Simple or malignant pleural effusion Empyema Haemorrhagic pleural effusion not meeting haematocrit criteria (for example malignancy, pulmonary embolism) Pneumothorax or haemopneumothorax Diaphragmatic rupture with herniated abdominal contents Chylothorax Erect chest radiograph Thoracic ultrasound (eFAST) CT thorax, with contrast or angiography if vascular injury is suspected Pleural fluid haematocrit compared with blood haematocrit Full blood count, coagulation screen and group and save or crossmatch Continuous monitoring of chest drain output Echocardiography or CT aortogram if an aortic or cardiac source is suspected Haemothorax is defined by blood in the pleural space; a pleural fluid haematocrit greater than half the peripheral blood haematocrit confirms it. Trauma, whether blunt or penetrating, is the commonest cause; non-traumatic causes include malignancy, thoracic aortic rupture or dissection, pulmonary infarction, anticoagulation and catamenial (thoracic endometriosis) haemothorax. Iatrogenic haemothorax follows central venous line insertion, pleural procedures and cardiothoracic surgery. Initial management combines resuscitation with prompt large-bore chest tube drainage, which also quantifies ongoing blood loss. Surgery (VATS or thoracotomy) is indicated for massive haemothorax (classically more than 1.5 litres drained immediately), ongoing bleeding (for example a persistently high hourly chest-drain output for several hours) or haemodynamic instability. Retained, incompletely drained haemothorax predisposes to empyema and fibrothorax and is best managed by early VATS evacuation. Point-of-care ultrasound (eFAST), erect chest radiograph and CT establish the diagnosis, with CT best for quantifying retained clot. Chest drain output, physiology and imaging together, rather than any single value, should drive the decision to operate. Haemodynamic instability or signs of haemorrhagic shock Massive initial chest drain output or persistently high hourly output Tension physiology (tracheal deviation, distended neck veins, hypotension) Penetrating injury to the cardiac box or a widened mediastinum on imaging Using an inadequate or small-bore drain that fails to evacuate blood and leaves retained clot. Assuming a small effusion on a supine film excludes a significant haemothorax. Delaying surgery in the face of ongoing bleeding while awaiting further imaging. Overlooking non-traumatic causes such as aortic, malignant, catamenial or anticoagulation-related bleeding. Failing to address retained haemothorax early, allowing empyema or fibrothorax to develop. Bleeding into the pleural space arises from injury to chest wall vessels (intercostal or internal mammary arteries), lung parenchyma, the great vessels or heart, or from non-traumatic vascular and pleural pathology. Because the pleura and the moving lung defibrinate blood, a haemothorax often fails to clot completely and can be drained; retained clot, however, organises, while pleural enzymes and mechanical motion may sustain oozing. Large accumulations compress the lung and, if under tension, impair venous return, producing combined hypovolaemic and obstructive compromise. Retained blood is an excellent culture medium and a scaffold for fibroblast proliferation, leading to empyema or a fibrothorax that traps the lung. Outcome depends on the cause and the promptness of drainage; most traumatic haemothoraces resolve well with a chest drain, but delayed or retained haemothorax risks empyema and fibrothorax, and massive haemothorax carries significant mortality.

disease (calcaneal apophysitis) in a skeletally immature patient Calcaneal stress fracture Posterior ankle impingement or an os trigonum Achilles tendon partial tear or ossification Weight-bearing lateral heel radiographs to assess the posterosuperior calcaneal prominence Measurement of parameters such as the parallel pitch lines and Fowler-Philip angle Ultrasound to evaluate the retrocalcaneal bursa and Achilles insertion Magnetic resonance imaging to assess insertional tendinopathy, bursitis and bone oedema Assessment of hindfoot alignment and gastrocnemius-soleus tightness Footwear assessment to identify a rigid heel counter as a contributing factor A prominence of the posterosuperior calcaneus rather than an osteonecrosis or traction apophysitis Affected bone is the calcaneus, specifically its posterosuperior tuberosity behind the Achilles insertion Typically presents in adults, more often women, and is frequently related to rigid, tight-heeled footwear, hence the term pump bump Presents with a firm, tender posterolateral heel bump and pain aggravated by shoe wear, often accompanied by retrocalcaneal bursitis and insertional Achilles tendinopathy The radiographic hallmark is a prominent posterosuperior calcaneal tuberosity, assessed with lines and angles such as the parallel pitch lines and the Fowler-Philip angle The combination of the bony prominence, an inflamed retrocalcaneal bursa and Achilles tendinopathy is often termed Haglund syndrome Local friction between the prominence, the bursa and the Achilles tendon drives the symptoms Management ranges from footwear modification, heel lifts or orthoses and physiotherapy to surgical resection of the prominence for refractory cases as needed Features suggesting an Achilles tendon tear such as a palpable gap or marked weakness of plantarflexion Rest pain, night pain or systemic features raising concern for infection or tumour In an adolescent, posterior heel pain more consistent with calcaneal apophysitis than Haglund deformity Rapidly progressive swelling or erythema suggesting an inflammatory or infective process Attributing all posterior heel pain to the bony prominence and overlooking the associated bursitis and insertional tendinopathy Injecting the region indiscriminately with corticosteroid and risking Achilles tendon weakening or rupture Failing to address footwear and a tight gastrocnemius-soleus complex that perpetuate the friction Confusing the adult deformity with calcaneal apophysitis in a skeletally immature patient Haglund deformity is an enlargement of the posterosuperior prominence of the calcaneal tuberosity that predisposes to mechanical irritation at the back of the heel. The prominent bone lies immediately deep to the retrocalcaneal bursa and adjacent to the insertion of the Achilles tendon. During walking, and particularly when a rigid heel counter compresses the area, the prominence rubs against the bursa and the tendon, producing repetitive friction. This provokes retrocalcaneal bursitis and insertional Achilles tendinopathy, so that the pain of Haglund syndrome arises from the soft-tissue inflammation and tendon degeneration around the bony prominence rather than from the bone itself. A high-arched (cavus) foot posture and a tight Achilles-gastrocnemius complex can accentuate the contact and aggravate symptoms. Most patients improve with footwear modification, offloading and rehabilitation directed at the associated bursitis and Achilles tendinopathy; symptoms can be persistent when conservative measures fail, and surgical resection of the prominence, often with attention to the Achilles insertion, is generally effective in refractory cases.

Hailey-Hailey disease — ATP2C1, benign familial pemphigus, familial benign chronic pemphigus, HHD Darier disease Intertrigo (candidal or bacterial) Inverse psoriasis Pemphigus vegetans Contact dermatitis of the flexures Extramammary Paget disease (persistent unilateral plaque) Skin biopsy showing extensive suprabasal acantholysis ('dilapidated brick wall') Direct immunofluorescence (negative, to exclude pemphigus) ATP2C1 molecular genetic testing Bacterial, fungal, and viral swabs during flares to identify superinfection Family history assessment for dominant inheritance Autosomal dominant disorder caused by variants in ATP2C1, encoding a Golgi calcium/manganese pump (SPCA1) Presents in early adulthood with recurrent flaccid vesicles, erosions, and macerated fissured plaques in the flexures (axillae, groin, neck, inframammary folds) Lesions have a characteristic macerated appearance with painful longitudinal 'ripped-fabric' fissures Friction, sweating, heat, and secondary infection are major aggravating factors Unlike pemphigus it is not autoimmune; direct immunofluorescence is negative Histology shows widespread suprabasal acantholysis giving a 'dilapidated brick wall' appearance Secondary bacterial, candidal, or herpetic infection frequently drives flares and malodour Sudden painful vesicular flare suggesting herpes simplex superinfection Spreading cellulitis or systemic features from bacterial superinfection A persistent, non-healing, or indurated plaque raising concern for squamous carcinoma within chronic lesions Diagnosing recurrent intertrigo or candidiasis and missing the underlying genodermatosis Failing to look for and treat secondary herpetic or bacterial infection during flares Confusing it with autoimmune pemphigus and initiating inappropriate immunosuppression Overlooking rare squamous change in longstanding lesions Hailey-Hailey disease is caused by loss-of-function variants in ATP2C1, encoding SPCA1, a pump that transports calcium and manganese into the Golgi apparatus of keratinocytes. Disturbed intracellular calcium homeostasis impairs the processing and trafficking of proteins needed for desmosomal adhesion, weakening keratinocyte cohesion. The resulting acantholysis is most pronounced in flexural skin subjected to heat, sweat, and friction, which further stress the fragile epidermis. The defect is partial and mosaic in effect, which is why lesions are localised to intertriginous sites rather than generalised. It is a chronic relapsing condition with a benign course that does not affect life expectancy, but recurrent flexural erosions can substantially impair quality of life; symptoms often improve in later life and some patients respond well to measures reducing friction and infection.

Hairy cell leukaemia — HCL, leukaemic reticuloendotheliosis Hairy cell leukaemia variant Splenic marginal zone lymphoma Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia Splenic diffuse red pulp small B-cell lymphoma Other causes of pancytopenia with splenomegaly Myelofibrosis Peripheral blood film review for characteristic cells Flow cytometry showing a characteristic mature B-cell immunophenotype Bone marrow trephine with immunohistochemistry when aspirate is unobtainable BRAF V600E mutation testing Cross-sectional imaging to assess splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy A rare, indolent mature B-cell malignancy that predominantly affects middle-aged and older men Classically presents with pancytopenia, marked splenomegaly and often minimal lymphadenopathy Monocytopenia is characteristic and predisposes to atypical and opportunistic infections Circulating malignant cells show fine cytoplasmic projections, giving the hairy appearance on the blood film Bone marrow is often difficult to aspirate (a dry tap) owing to marrow fibrosis The BRAF V600E mutation is present in almost all cases of classic hairy cell leukaemia It responds very well to purine analogue therapy, with durable remissions Severe neutropenia with fever suggesting serious infection Symptomatic massive splenomegaly or splenic rupture Profound cytopenias causing bleeding or transfusion dependence Features suggesting the more aggressive variant form Attributing pancytopenia to another marrow disorder and missing the diagnosis Interpreting a dry tap as inadequate sampling rather than a clue to the disease Overlooking the more treatment-resistant variant form Failing to consider opportunistic infection in a monocytopenic patient Hairy cell leukaemia is a clonal proliferation of mature B lymphocytes with characteristic cytoplasmic projections. The near-universal BRAF V600E mutation activates the MAP kinase signalling pathway, driving proliferation and survival. The malignant cells infiltrate the bone marrow, spleen (particularly the red pulp) and liver, and induce a reticulin fibrosis that accounts for the frequent dry tap. Marrow infiltration and cytokine effects produce pancytopenia and the characteristic monocytopenia, which underlies the susceptibility to infection. Classic hairy cell leukaemia has an excellent prognosis, with most patients achieving durable remission after purine analogue therapy and a near-normal life expectancy; relapses are usually retreatable.

infection Symptomatic massive splenomegaly or splenic rupture Failure to respond to purine analogue therapy suggesting the variant form Progressive marrow failure with bleeding or transfusion Overlooking monocytopenia as a diagnostic pointer Missing BRAF V600E testing that confirms classic disease and guides targeted therapy Hairy cell leukaemia is a clonal proliferation of mature B lymphocytes with distinctive cytoplasmic projections. The near-universal driver is the activating BRAF V600E mutation, which switches on the RAF-MEK-ERK signalling pathway and promotes survival and characteristic morphology and adhesion properties. Half-and-half nails — Lindsay's nails, Lindsay nails Terry nails Muehrcke lines True leukonychia Uraemic nail pigmentation Normal variant distal nail band Onycholysis with distal discolouration Renal function tests (urea, creatinine, eGFR) Urinalysis for proteinuria and haematuria Assessment for chronic kidney disease and dialysis status Digital pressure (blanch) test to distinguish from Muehrcke lines Examination of all nails for symmetry of the change Full blood count and electrolytes as part of renal workup Half-and-half nails, or Lindsay nails, show a proximal white or dull ground-glass half sharply demarcated from a distal reddish, pink or brown half. The distal band typically occupies from a fifth to a half of the nail length and the transverse border between the two zones is characteristically sharp. The strongest association is with chronic kidney disease and uraemia, and the sign may be found in a substantial proportion of patients on dialysis. The distal darker band does not fade with nail bed pressure, which helps separate it from Muehrcke lines. It is a nail bed change (apparent leukonychia proximally with distal pigmentation) rather than a nail plate abnormality, so it does not migrate distally. The proximal whitening is thought to relate to nail bed oedema while the distal band reflects increased melanin and capillary changes. The sign is asymptomatic and its value is as a marker prompting assessment of renal function. It should be distinguished from Terry nails, where the white zone is more extensive and the distal normal band much narrower. New half-and-half nails in a patient with declining renal function Associated signs of uraemia such as pruritus, nausea or fluid overload Rapid appearance suggesting acute deterioration of kidney function Features overlapping with hepatic disease that might indicate Terry nails instead Confusing half-and-half nails with Terry nails and misdirecting investigation towards liver rather than kidney Mistaking the distal band for Muehrcke lines by not testing whether it blanches Overlooking the sign as a prompt to check renal function Attributing the pigment to trauma or fungal disease Half-and-half nails are an apparent leukonychia in which the proximal portion of the nail bed becomes pale and oedematous, obscuring its normal vascular pink, while the distal portion develops a persistent darker band. The proximal whitening is attributed to oedema of the nail bed, whereas the distal brown-red band is thought to result from a combination of increased melanin deposition, thickening of the capillary walls and the concentration of the vascular bed towards the free edge. These changes are strongly linked to the metabolic and microvascular disturbances of chronic renal failure and uraemia, though the exact trigger for the melanin increase is uncertain. Because the process resides in the bed and its melanin is fixed, the distal band neither blanches with pressure nor migrates as the nail grows, distinguishing it from Muehrcke lines. The nail change is benign and needs no direct treatment, but it commonly signals chronic kidney disease and therefore follows the prognosis of the underlying renal condition. It may persist or fluctuate with the course of the renal impairment.

create a real risk of upper airway obstruction, especially in infancy and around anaesthesia Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, focusing on ophthalmic care, airway safety and dental management Upper airway obstruction from micrognathia and a narrow airway, particularly in infancy Difficult airway during anaesthesia or sedation Visual deprivation from dense congenital cataracts requiring timely management Feeding difficulty with faltering growth in early life Underestimating the airway risk during anaesthesia because of the small mandible Delaying cataract management and risking amblyopia in infancy Confusing the progeroid features with a true progeria and giving inaccurate prognosis Overlooking natal or malformed teeth that can compromise the airway or feeding Hallermann-Streiff syndrome is a congenital disorder of craniofacial and ectodermal development whose precise molecular cause is not fully established, with most cases occurring sporadically. Abnormal development of the first branchial arch derivatives and midline craniofacial structures produces the characteristic dyscephaly, beaked nose, micrognathia and dental anomalies, while disturbed ocular development gives congenital cataracts and microphthalmia. Involvement of ectodermal tissues accounts for the sparse hair and atrophic skin that lend the progeroid appearance. Intelligence is usually normal and many individuals reach adulthood, but airway problems in infancy, feeding difficulties and visual impairment are important sources of morbidity that require proactive management.

dorsiflexion should be compared with the unaffected side Weight-bearing radiographs demonstrate joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, dorsal osteophytes, and periarticular cysts Conservative management uses a stiff-soled or rocker-bottom shoe, a rigid insole to limit painful motion, activity modification, and intra-articular corticosteroid injection Surgical choices depend on disease stage and include dorsal cheilectomy for early impingement and arthrodesis for advanced arthritis, with arthroplasty in selected patients Acutely hot, red, swollen joint suggesting gout, pseudogout, or septic arthritis rather than degenerative disease Systemic features or polyarticular involvement indicating inflammatory arthropathy Rest pain, night pain, or a destructive appearance on imaging and directing treatment to the wrong deformity Performing cheilectomy alone in advanced global arthritis, which fails because the whole joint surface is worn Missing acute gout or infection presenting as a suddenly painful, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint Neglecting footwear and insole modification before considering surgery Overlooking lateral forefoot overload that develops as the patient offloads the stiff great toe Hallux rigidus is degenerative arthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint in which cartilage wear begins dorsally on the metatarsal head, where compressive and shear loads concentrate during dorsiflexion at push-off. Reactive bone forms a dorsal osteophyte on the metatarsal head and often the proximal phalanx, which mechanically blocks dorsiflexion and impinges painfully at the extremes of extension. Over time the wear becomes global with joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis and cyst formation, and the toe becomes progressively stiff. Contributing factors include previous trauma or osteochondral injury, an elevated or long first metatarsal, inflammatory or crystal arthropathy, and possibly a familial predisposition. As dorsiflexion is lost the patient rolls onto the outer border of the foot at toe-off, which can produce lateral forefoot overload and secondary symptoms. Symptoms usually progress slowly with fluctuating pain and increasing stiffness. Many patients are controlled long term with footwear and insole modification and occasional injections. Cheilectomy relieves dorsal impingement well in early to moderate disease, and arthrodesis is a reliable and durable procedure for advanced arthritis that reliably relieves pain at the cost of joint motion. Progression of arthritis after motion-preserving surgery is possible.

bunion surgery Attributing a hot painful joint to the bunion and missing gout, infection, or inflammatory arthritis Hallux valgus is a progressive deformity in which the great toe deviates laterally at the first metatarsophalangeal joint while the first metatarsal drifts medially into varus. As the proximal phalanx pulls into valgus, the medial capsule and collateral ligament stretch and the lateral structures contract, and the sesamoid complex is left behind laterally relative to the metatarsal head. The long flexor and extensor tendons then act eccentric to the joint axis and bowstring across it, generating a deforming force that drives further progression. Intrinsic predispositions such as a mobile or hypermobile first ray, a flat foot, generalised ligamentous laxity, and inherited foot shape combine with extrinsic pressure from narrow, elevated-heel footwear. The exposed medial eminence rubs against the shoe, producing a painful inflamed bursa, while altered load transfer can overload the lesser rays and produce transfer metatarsalgia. Hallux valgus tends to progress slowly over years, and conservative measures relieve symptoms but do not reverse the bony deformity. Appropriately selected surgery corrects alignment and relieves pain in the majority, though recurrence, stiffness, transfer metatarsalgia, or under- or over-correction can occur, and outcomes are poorer when surgery is performed for appearance alone or in the presence of untreated hypermobility or inflammatory disease.

and mallet toe (isolated distal interphalangeal flexion) The second toe is most commonly affected, and the deformity frequently accompanies hallux valgus that crowds the lesser toes A dorsal corn over the prominent proximal interphalangeal joint and an end-of-toe callosity are typical pressure lesions Determining whether the deformity is flexible or fixed is essential, as passively correctable and forefoot alignment Conservative care includes roomy, deep toe-box footwear, silicone toe sleeves or splints, corn padding, and toe-crest orthoses Surgical options range from flexor-to-extensor tendon transfer and extensor lengthening for flexible deformity to proximal interphalangeal joint arthrodesis or resection for fixed deformity Multiple or symmetrical lesser-toe deformities suggesting an underlying neuromuscular disorder or inflammatory arthritis Ulceration or infection of a corn or the toe tip, particularly in diabetes or peripheral vascular disease Signs of digital ischaemia or leading to the wrong choice of procedure Overlooking associated hallux valgus that crowds and deforms the second toe and will cause recurrence if untreated Missing an underlying neuromuscular cause when several toes are involved Neglecting foot perfusion and the diabetic status before operating on the toe Ignoring metatarsophalangeal joint subluxation, so that isolated toe surgery leaves the deformity uncorrected Hammer toe arises from an imbalance between the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the lesser toe that leaves the proximal interphalangeal joint flexed. When the intrinsic muscles fail to stabilise the metatarsophalangeal joint, the long extensor hyperextends that joint while the long flexor and the geometry of the toe pull the proximal interphalangeal joint into flexion. Ill-fitting, tight, or high-heeled footwear that crowds the toes is a major extrinsic contributor, and adjacent hallux valgus commonly displaces and deforms the second toe. Initially the deformity is flexible and passively correctable, but with time capsular and tendon contractures make it rigid. The elevated proximal interphalangeal joint rubs against the shoe to form a painful dorsal corn, and abnormal loading produces callosities at the tip of the toe and beneath the metatarsal head. Flexible hammer toes are often well controlled with footwear and orthotic measures, and soft-tissue surgery corrects them reliably. Fixed deformities respond well to arthrodesis or joint resection with good pain relief, although some residual stiffness, floating toe, recurrence, or malalignment can occur. Outcomes are poorer when an underlying neuromuscular disorder or inflammatory arthritis is not addressed.

Hamstring strain — hamstring muscle injury, pulled hamstring Proximal hamstring tendon avulsion Ischial apophyseal avulsion in adolescents Referred pain from the lumbar spine or sciatic nerve Adductor or other thigh muscle strain Deep vein thrombosis (for posterior leg pain and swelling) Clinical assessment of site, strength and the mechanism of injury Ultrasound or MRI to grade injury and identify tendon or avulsion involvement Assessment for proximal avulsion requiring surgical referral Evaluation of the lumbar spine if referral is suspected Functional testing to guide return to sport One of the commonest sports injuries, typically occurring during high-speed running or sudden stretching of the posterior thigh Patients describe a sudden sharp posterior thigh pain, sometimes with a pop, and difficulty continuing activity The biceps femoris is the most frequently injured of the hamstring muscles in sprinting-type injuries Injuries are graded by severity, and proximal free tendon or bony avulsion injuries behave differently and may need surgery A large proximal avulsion, especially with retraction, warrants prompt orthopaedic assessment Recurrence is common, so structured rehabilitation and graded return to sport are important Proximal avulsion with tendon retraction Large haematoma or neurovascular compromise Adolescent with suspected ischial apophyseal avulsion Posterior leg swelling raising concern for venous thrombosis Missing a proximal tendon avulsion that benefits from early surgery Returning to sport before adequate eccentric strength is restored Overlooking an adolescent ischial apophyseal avulsion Attributing posterior thigh pain to a strain when it is referred from the spine Hamstring strain occurs when tensile load on the muscle-tendon unit exceeds its capacity, usually during the late swing phase of sprinting when the hamstrings contract eccentrically while lengthening. This generates high forces that tear muscle fibres, most often at the musculotendinous junction of the biceps femoris. Stretch-type injuries from combined hip flexion and knee extension tend to involve the proximal free tendon. Incomplete rehabilitation, reduced eccentric strength and scar tissue predispose to the high recurrence rate. Most muscular strains recover with graded rehabilitation, but recovery time varies with grade and site, and recurrence is frequent; proximal avulsions may require surgery for best outcomes.

necrosis indicating severe vascular compromise Features suggesting an underlying connective tissue disease Rapidly progressive sensory or motor loss Persistent severe symptoms despite cessation of exposure Attributing finger blanching to primary Raynaud's without taking an occupational history Missing coexisting carpal tunnel syndrome that also causes numbness Failing to advise on cold protection and smoking cessation Delaying exposure reduction until the disease is advanced and irreversible Repeated transmission of vibration energy to the hand damages digital blood vessels, peripheral nerves and supporting tissues. Vascular injury with endothelial damage and exaggerated sympathetic vasoconstriction produces episodic digital artery closure and finger blanching, while injury to peripheral nerve fibres and mechanoreceptors causes sensory loss; musculoskeletal and joint changes contribute to reduced grip and function. Symptoms may stabilise or partly improve if vibration exposure is stopped early, but well-established vascular and sensorineural changes are often permanent and can continue to affect hand function even after exposure ceases.

Hand-arm vibration syndrome — HAVS, vibration white finger Primary Raynaud phenomenon Secondary Raynaud from connective tissue disease Carpal tunnel syndrome or other entrapment neuropathy Peripheral arterial disease Hypothenar hammer syndrome Detailed occupational history quantifying vibration exposure Assessment and staging of vascular and sensorineural components Cold provocation and vascular testing where available Nerve conduction studies to assess or exclude entrapment neuropathy Exclusion of connective tissue disease causing secondary Raynaud An occupational disorder caused by prolonged use of hand-held vibrating tools, with vascular, neurological and musculoskeletal components The vascular component is an episodic cold-induced blanching of the fingers, a secondary form of Raynaud phenomenon (vibration white finger) The neurological component causes numbness, tingling and reduced dexterity and fine sensation Symptoms are graded by severity using recognised occupational staging scales It is an important prescribed or reportable occupational disease in many jurisdictions Management centres on reducing vibration exposure, keeping warm and stopping smoking, as symptoms may not fully reverse Digital ulceration or critical ischaemia Features suggesting an underlying connective tissue disease Rapidly progressive sensory or motor deficit Asymmetric or unilateral vascular signs suggesting another cause Failing to take a quantified occupational vibration history Attributing symptoms solely to carpal tunnel syndrome Missing an underlying connective tissue disease Not advising exposure reduction and smoking cessation Repeated transmission of vibration from hand-held tools injures the digital vasculature and peripheral nerves. Vascular injury and abnormal sympathetic responses produce exaggerated cold-induced vasospasm and blanching of the fingers, while damage to peripheral nerve fibres and mechanoreceptors causes sensory loss and impaired dexterity. Chronic exposure also affects muscles, joints and bone. The changes reflect cumulative dose, so risk rises with the intensity and duration of vibration exposure. Early vascular changes may improve if exposure stops, but established neurological damage often persists; continued exposure leads to progression and greater disability.

Hand, foot and mouth disease — HFMD, coxsackievirus exanthem, enteroviral vesicular stomatitis Herpetic gingivostomatitis Herpangina Varicella (chickenpox) Aphthous stomatitis Erythema multiforme Contact or vesicular dermatitis Stevens-Johnson syndrome / drug eruption Kawasaki disease in a febrile child with mucocutaneous findings Immunobullous disorders Clinical diagnosis in typical cases without laboratory testing Enterovirus PCR from throat, vesicle or stool samples in severe or atypical disease CSF examination if meningitis or encephalitis is suspected Assessment of hydration status, especially in young children A common, usually self-limiting enteroviral illness of young children caused most often by Coxsackievirus A16 and Enterovirus 71 Characterised by fever with painful oral vesicles/ulcers and a vesicular rash on the hands, feet and often the buttocks Spreads readily by faecal-oral and respiratory routes and by contact with vesicle fluid, causing outbreaks in creches and schools Enterovirus 71 in particular can cause severe neurological complications such as brainstem encephalitis, aseptic meningitis and acute flaccid paralysis Management is supportive, focused on hydration and pain relief for painful oral lesions; antibiotics have no role Poor oral intake from painful mouth ulcers is the commonest reason for medical attention and can lead to dehydration in small children Diagnosis is usually clinical, with PCR or viral culture reserved for severe or atypical cases Good hand hygiene and exclusion of unwell children help limit institutional spread Lethargy, persistent vomiting, ataxia or myoclonic jerks suggesting Enterovirus 71 neurological involvement Signs of severe dehydration from inability to drink Respiratory distress or circulatory collapse indicating brainstem/cardiopulmonary complications Seizures or rapidly declining consciousness Prescribing antibiotics for what is a self-limiting viral illness Underestimating dehydration risk from painful oral ulcers in toddlers Missing early neurological warning signs of Enterovirus 71 disease Confusing severe or atypical rashes with drug reactions or varicella Non-polio enteroviruses (notably Coxsackievirus A16 and Enterovirus 71) enter via the gastrointestinal or respiratory tract, replicate in lymphoid tissue of the pharynx and gut, and produce a viraemia that seeds the skin and oral mucosa, giving the characteristic vesicular enanthem and exanthem. Enterovirus 71 has neurotropic potential and can invade the central nervous system, particularly the brainstem, producing the severe neurological syndromes and, rarely, neurogenic pulmonary oedema and cardiorespiratory collapse. The overwhelming majority of cases resolve within a week to ten days without sequelae. A small subset, particularly Enterovirus 71 infections in young children, develop serious neurological or cardiopulmonary complications that can be fatal or leave lasting deficits.

on passive extension Human bite injuries over the knuckle (fight bite) frequently penetrate the joint and extensor mechanism and are notorious for serious deep infection if underestimated Early localised infections may settle with elevation, splinting, and antibiotics, but established abscesses and closed-space infections require prompt incision and drainage A felon is a closed-space infection of the fingertip pulp that can raise pressure enough to threaten the tissue and requires timely drainage Delayed or inadequate treatment of deep hand infection risks tendon necrosis, stiffness, spread along fascial planes, and permanent loss of function Elevation, splinting in a safe position, and early mobilisation once infection is controlled help preserve hand function Pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis with Kanavel's signs requiring urgent surgical decompression Fight bite over a knuckle with possible joint or extensor tendon penetration Rapidly spreading infection, crepitus, or systemic sepsis suggesting necrotising infection Deep palmar space abscess or infection tracking proximally along fascial planes Signs of tissue necrosis or compartment involvement Underestimating a fight bite and closing or under-treating a wound that has penetrated the joint Incising a herpetic whitlow, which worsens the viral infection Delaying surgical drainage of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis while relying on antibiotics alone Missing a retained foreign body as the source of persistent infection Failing to elevate and splint, leading to persistent oedema and stiffness Overlooking gout or crystal arthropathy masquerading as infection Hand infections usually follow inoculation of bacteria through a break in the skin from trauma, bites, splinters, or nail-care injury. The hand's compartmentalised anatomy - closed pulp spaces, synovial flexor sheaths, web spaces, and deep palmar spaces - confines infection under pressure and allows it to track along defined planes. Rising pressure within closed spaces impairs perfusion and can cause tissue and tendon necrosis. In pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis, pus within the closed synovial sheath compromises the gliding surface and blood supply of the flexor tendon, leading to adhesions and stiffness if not decompressed. Bite wounds introduce mixed oral flora deep into tissues and joints. Superficial infections such as early paronychia treated promptly usually resolve fully. Deep and closed-space infections carry a higher risk of stiffness, contracture, and functional loss, and outcome is closely tied to how quickly drainage and appropriate antibiotics are provided. Untreated flexor sheath and deep space infections can lead to tendon necrosis, amputation, or long-term disability.

Hantavirus infection — hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, HPS, haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, HFRS, VHF Leptospirosis Severe dengue Other viral haemorrhagic fevers (CCHF, Lassa) Bacterial sepsis with ARDS Severe atypical or community-acquired pneumonia Acute glomerulonephritis or other causes of acute kidney injury (for HFRS) Leptospirosis Severe dengue Bacterial sepsis / ARDS Other viral haemorrhagic fevers Hantavirus-specific IgM and IgG serology, which is usually positive by the time of severe illness RT-PCR for viral RNA in early disease and for genotyping Full blood count (looking for haemoconcentration, thrombocytopenia, immunoblasts) and renal function Chest imaging showing bilateral infiltrates and pulmonary oedema in the pulmonary syndrome Exclusion of leptospirosis, dengue, and bacterial sepsis given overlap Rodent-borne viruses acquired mainly by inhaling aerosolised excreta (urine, droppings, saliva) of infected rodents, with exposure often occurring in rural, agricultural, or rodent-infested settings Two main clinical syndromes exist: hantavirus pulmonary (cardiopulmonary) syndrome, seen chiefly in the Americas, and haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, seen across Eurasia The pulmonary syndrome begins with a febrile prodrome of fever and myalgia, then progresses rapidly to a cardiopulmonary phase with capillary leak, pulmonary oedema, and shock Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome evolves through febrile, hypotensive, oliguric, and later polyuric phases, with bleeding tendency and acute kidney injury Haemoconcentration, thrombocytopenia, and the presence of immunoblasts on the blood film are helpful early clues to the pulmonary syndrome Because these are viral haemorrhagic fevers, suspected cases warrant infection-control caution, isolation, and safe specimen handling, though person-to-person spread is limited for most strains Care is supportive with meticulous fluid and haemodynamic management and organ support; there is no widely available specific antiviral, so early recognition and referral to intensive care are vital Rapid onset of dyspnoea, hypoxia, and pulmonary oedema signalling the cardiopulmonary phase Hypotension or shock with rising haematocrit from capillary leak Oliguria, rising creatinine, and bleeding indicating severe renal syndrome Any suspected viral haemorrhagic fever requires isolation, barrier precautions, and public health notification Aggressive fluid resuscitation worsening pulmonary oedema in the cardiopulmonary phase Missing rodent-exposure history in an acutely breathless or febrile patient Confusing the illness with community-acquired pneumonia and delaying intensive supportive care Underestimating the polyuric recovery phase and precipitating dehydration or electrolyte disturbance in HFRS Hantaviruses are enveloped RNA viruses that infect vascular endothelial cells, particularly in the lungs and kidneys, without causing marked direct cell destruction. Instead, the host immune and cytokine response increases capillary permeability. In the pulmonary syndrome this produces non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema and cardiovascular collapse, whereas in haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome the leaky vasculature and renal microvascular injury drive haemorrhage, hypotension, and acute kidney injury with the characteristic sequence of oliguric and polyuric phases. Outcome depends on syndrome and speed of supportive care: the cardiopulmonary syndrome can be rapidly fatal despite intensive care, whereas most patients with haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome recover renal function, though severe strains carry appreciable mortality.

Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome — hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, HPS, HCPS, Sin Nombre virus infection, New World hantavirus infection Community-acquired pneumonia with acute respiratory distress syndrome Influenza and other severe viral respiratory infections Bacterial sepsis with septic shock Leptospirosis with pulmonary haemorrhage Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from primary cardiac disease Plague or other zoonoses with a rodent-exposure history Hantavirus-specific serology for IgM and IgG antibodies RT-PCR on blood for viral RNA in the early phase Full blood count and film looking for thrombocytopenia, left shift, and immunoblasts Chest radiograph and arterial blood gas to characterise bilateral interstitial and alveolar oedema and hypoxaemia Echocardiography and cardiac biomarkers to assess myocardial depression and guide haemodynamic support Lactate and metabolic panel to gauge shock severity Caused by New World hantaviruses (notably Sin Nombre virus in North America and Andes virus in South America) acquired by inhaling aerosolised rodent excreta, classically from deer mice in rural or peridomestic settings A febrile prodrome of fever, myalgia, headache, and gastrointestinal upset lasting several days is followed by an abrupt cardiopulmonary phase with cough, dyspnoea, and rapidly progressive non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema The cardiopulmonary phase reflects a capillary-leak process; hypotension and myocardial depression producing cardiogenic shock carry the highest mortality A characteristic haematological triad supports the diagnosis: thrombocytopenia, left-shifted leucocytosis, and circulating immunoblasts (atypical lymphocytes), often with haemoconcentration Andes virus is distinctive among hantaviruses for documented person-to-person transmission, so respiratory precautions and contact tracing may be warranted in South American cases Care is intensive and supportive with no licensed specific antiviral; early transfer to a centre with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation capability improves survival in refractory cardiogenic shock Diagnosis rests on serology (IgM/IgG) and RT-PCR, and a compatible rodent-exposure history in an endemic region should prompt early consideration Rapid progression from prodrome to breathlessness and hypoxaemia over hours Hypotension with rising lactate signalling impending cardiogenic shock Haemoconcentration with worsening thrombocytopenia indicating severe capillary leak Need for high fractional inspired oxygen or mechanical ventilation Refractory shock potentially requiring extracorporeal membrane oxygenation Attributing the prodrome to a self-limiting viral illness and discharging before the cardiopulmonary phase declares itself Administering large-volume fluid resuscitation, which can worsen pulmonary oedema in a capillary-leak state Overlooking a rural rodent-exposure history that would raise suspicion Failing to arrange early referral to a centre capable of advanced cardiorespiratory support Not considering Andes virus person-to-person spread and appropriate precautions in South American cases Infection follows inhalation of virus shed in the urine, droppings, or saliva of chronically infected rodent reservoirs. The virus targets pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells, and a vigorous host immune response, rather than direct cytopathic injury, increases vascular permeability. The resulting capillary leak floods the alveoli with protein-rich fluid, producing non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, while myocardial dysfunction and reduced cardiac output drive shock. The interplay of profound capillary leak and cardiac depression defines the severe cardiopulmonary phase. The cardiopulmonary phase can be fulminant and case fatality is high in New World hantavirus disease. Patients who survive the first few critical days typically improve rapidly with resolution of the capillary leak and often recover without long-term pulmonary sequelae.

hard metal dermatitis — cobalt-tungsten carbide dermatitis, tungsten carbide worker dermatitis irritant contact dermatitis from coolants and wet work allergic contact dermatitis to nickel or chromate allergic contact dermatitis to biocides or additives in metalworking fluids atopic hand eczema pompholyx (dyshidrotic eczema) psoriasis of the hands contact urticaria to metalworking fluids detailed occupational history of grinding, coolants and materials handled patch testing to cobalt chloride, nickel sulfate and potassium dichromate patch testing to metalworking fluid components and biocides assessment and testing of coolants and gloves used in the workplace skin swabs if secondary infection of eczema is suspected respiratory enquiry with spirometry or peak-flow monitoring if symptomatic chest imaging and specialist referral if hard metal lung disease is suspected Hard metal is a sintered composite of tungsten carbide with a cobalt binder used for cutting tools, drill bits and wear-resistant parts; cobalt is the principal skin sensitiser. Workers in tool grinding, sharpening and manufacture present with hand and forearm eczema, and diamond polishers using cobalt-containing wheels are a classic at-risk group. The dermatitis is usually an allergic contact dermatitis to cobalt, though irritant contact dermatitis from coolants, abrasives and wet work frequently coexists and can be hard to separate. Cobalt allergy commonly occurs together with nickel and sometimes chromate sensitivity, so concurrent reactions on patch testing are frequent. Wet grinding coolants both leach cobalt from the workpiece and act as irritants, increasing skin exposure and barrier damage. The same cobalt exposure can cause hard metal lung disease (giant-cell interstitial pneumonitis) and occupational asthma, so enquire about respiratory symptoms. Patch testing to cobalt chloride, nickel sulfate and potassium dichromate is central to diagnosis; workplace and glove assessment complements it. Management combines cobalt avoidance and substitution, improved coolant hygiene, appropriate gloves and barrier care, and treatment of the eczema. breathlessness or cough suggesting hard metal lung disease or occupational asthma severe or widely spreading eczema with signs of secondary infection rapid recurrence on return to work indicating uncontrolled exposure involvement of multiple co-workers implying a systemic hygiene failure features suggesting systemic contact dermatitis from ingested or inhaled cobalt Attributing the eczema solely to irritation and missing underlying cobalt allergy. Testing only for nickel and overlooking concurrent cobalt and chromate sensitivity. Ignoring respiratory symptoms and failing to consider hard metal lung disease. Assuming gloves are protective without checking permeation and hygiene practices. Overlooking coolant biocides and additives as separate sensitisers or irritants. Hard metal dermatitis is predominantly a delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity to cobalt. Cobalt ions released from the alloy — especially when wet-grinding coolants leach metal from tools — penetrate the epidermis and bind host proteins to form haptens that are processed by Langerhans cells and presented to T lymphocytes; on re-exposure a sensitised T-cell response produces spongiotic eczematous inflammation. Superimposed irritant contact dermatitis is common, driven by coolants, solvents, abrasive dusts and repetitive wet work that damage the stratum corneum barrier, enhance penetration of allergens and lower the threshold for both irritant and allergic reactions. Frequent co-sensitisation to nickel and chromium reflects shared exposures and possibly cross-reactivity. Inhaled cobalt-tungsten carbide particles can additionally provoke immunologically mediated interstitial lung disease and asthma through separate respiratory mechanisms. With cobalt avoidance, improved coolant hygiene and barrier measures the dermatitis often improves, but established cobalt sensitisation is lifelong and eczema may persist or recur if exposure continues. Coexisting respiratory disease worsens the overall outlook and warrants separate management.

Loss of sympathetic outflow on the affected side prevents the normal flushing and sweating response to thermal, exertional, or emotional stimuli, so only the intact contralateral side reddens and perspires, producing the sharply demarcated 'harlequin' appearance. The lesion may be idiopathic, presumed to reflect a focal autonomic neuropathy, or secondary to structural compression or injury of the sympathetic pathway; associated pupillary or Horner findings indicate more extensive autonomic involvement. Idiopathic Harlequin syndrome is benign and usually cosmetically rather than functionally troublesome, often remaining stable or fluctuating over time; the prognosis in secondary cases depends on the underlying structural cause.

transporter defect Assuming all cases are symptomatic, when most are benign screening findings Overlooking precipitating factors such as poor nutrition or intercurrent illness Misinterpreting an neutral amino acid transporter B0AT1 expressed in the intestinal brush border and renal proximal tubule. Impaired transport causes intestinal malabsorption and renal wasting of neutral amino acids, notably tryptophan. Because tryptophan is a precursor for the synthesis of nicotinamide (niacin), its loss can produce a functional niacin deficiency, giving pellagra-like photosensitive dermatitis and neurological features. The unabsorbed amino acids also undergo bacterial degradation in the gut. Adequate dietary protein and niacin supplementation compensate for the losses, and most patients remain asymptomatic because of compensatory absorption of amino acids as small peptides. The great majority of individuals are asymptomatic with a normal life expectancy; symptomatic cases usually respond well to niacin and adequate protein intake and tend to have fewer episodes with increasing age.

nucleotide-gated channel family responsible for the Ih (or funny) current, which activates on membrane hyperpolarisation and stabilises resting membrane potential while shaping dendritic signal
