Alcohol and tobacco are the most significant environmental risk factors and act synergistically when used together; smokeless tobacco is an etiologic agent for oral cancers (Harrison 22e p.610). In Western countries, HPV (predominantly HPV-16) causes over 50% of oropharyngeal cancers (tonsillar bed and base of tongue); these occur in younger patients and carry a better prognosis, especially in nonsmokers (Harrison 22e p.610-611). EBV infection is frequently associated with nasopharyngeal cancer, especially in endemic areas (East Asia, some Mediterranean countries); EBV antibody titers can be used to screen high-risk populations (Harrison 22e p.610). HPV testing should be performed at diagnosis for all patients with oropharyngeal tumors; HPV-related disease has a more favorable AJCC 8th-edition staging (advanced nodal stage can still be equivalent to overall early stage) (Harrison 22e p.611-613). Panendoscopy under anesthesia (laryngoscopy, esophagoscopy, bronchoscopy) with multiple directed biopsies is the definitive staging procedure to establish diagnosis, define extent, and identify second primaries (Harrison 22e p.611). When a head and neck lesion treated initially with antibiotics does not resolve in a short period, further workup is indicated; simply continuing antibiotics may lose the chance for early diagnosis of a malignancy (Harrison 22e p.611). For an enlarged cervical node with no visible primary, diagnose by fine-needle aspiration or lymph node excision; if squamous cell carcinoma, perform panendoscopy with directed biopsies of nasopharynx, tonsil, tongue base, and pyriform sinus (Harrison 22e p.611-612). Most parotid tumors are benign, but about half of submandibular and sublingual tumors and most minor salivary gland tumors are malignant; adenoid cystic carcinoma tends to recur along nerve tracks and metastasize as late as 10-20 years (Harrison 22e p.610-611, 613). Persistent hoarseness requiring referral for indirect laryngoscopy and/or radiographic studies (possible early laryngeal cancer) Non-healing ulcer of the oral cavity Persistent neck mass / cervical lymphadenopathy, especially a solitary, hard, nontender node in an older chronic tobacco user Dysphagia, odynophagia, or decreased tongue mobility Sore throat and/or otalgia, or a head/neck lesion that does not resolve after antibiotics Unilateral serous otitis media, nasal obstruction, or epistaxis (nasopharyngeal cancer); cranial neuropathies from skull base involvement Head and neck symptoms persisting longer than 2-4 weeks Continuing antibiotic treatment for a non-resolving head and neck lesion rather than pursuing workup may delay diagnosis of malignancy (Harrison 22e p.611). Fine-needle aspiration should not be the first diagnostic procedure for a suspicious cervical node when a head and neck primary is suspected; perform a careful ENT exam and biopsy any suspicious mucosal lesion first (Harrison 22e p.4012-type cross-reference, p.611). EGFR overexpression does not reliably predict response to EGFR inhibitors (active in only ~10-15% as single agents); substituting cetuximab for cisplatin in HPV-related cancers has shown inferior survival (Harrison 22e p.611, 613). Retinoid supplements (e.g., cis-retinoic acid) have not been shown to prevent head and neck (or lung) cancer and may increase risk in active smokers (Harrison 22e p.610). About 50% of patients develop hypothyroidism after treatment; thyroid function should be monitored (Harrison 22e p.613). Squamous cell carcinomas arise from the mucosal surfaces of the upper aerodigestive tract. The entire pharyngeal mucosa is exposed to alcohol- and tobacco-related carcinogens, producing field cancerization with risk of premalignant lesions (erythroplakia, leukoplakia) progressing through hyperplasia, dysplasia, and carcinoma in situ to invasive carcinoma. In HPV-negative tumors, p53 mutations are frequent along with mitotic-signaling and Notch pathway alterations and dysregulated cell-cycle control. HPV oncogenes drive carcinogenesis by directly inhibiting the p53 and RB tumor-suppressor genes; HPV-positive tumors carry a distinct mutational signature with frequent PI3K pathway alteration. EGFR is frequently overexpressed and correlates with poor prognosis. EBV is associated with undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma (lymphoepithelioma) (Harrison 22e p.610-611). Poorly differentiated tumors have a worse prognosis than well-differentiated tumors. Overt distant metastases are present in <10% at diagnosis. HPV-related oropharyngeal cancers consistently carry a better prognosis (reflected in a separate, more favorable AJCC 8th-edition staging system), especially in nonsmokers. For localized disease (about one-third of patients), overall 5-year survival is 60-90%, with most recurrences occurring within the first 2 years and usually local. For locally/regionally advanced disease (>50% of patients at presentation), 5-year survival exceeds 50% in many trials (partly due to the increasing fraction of HPV-related tumors); advanced nasopharyngeal cancer treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by concomitant chemoradiotherapy has achieved 5-year survival exceeding 80% in a Southeast Asian study. Patients cured of early-stage tobacco/alcohol-related disease are at greater risk of dying from a second malignancy than from recurrence of the primary (Harrison 22e p.611-613). Clinically categorized into three groups: (1) localized disease (T1-T2 / stage I-II without nodal or distant spread), (2) locally or regionally advanced disease (large primary and/or cervical nodal metastases, lymph-node positive), and (3) recurrent and/or metastatic disease below the neck. Staged by the AJCC TNM system, which varies by anatomic subsite: primary tumors T1-T3 by increasing size with T4 representing invasion of adjacent structures (bone, muscle, root of tongue), and nodes staged by size, number, and laterality. A separate, more favorable staging system applies to HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer in the AJCC 8th edition (Harrison 22e p.611-613).

The obesity paradox: obese HF patients tend to have a more favourable prognosis than those with low or normal BMI (p.1986). post-diuresis pulmonary function tests or cardiopulmonary exercise testing can help (p.1986) Failure to identify and correct a precipitant can leave HF persistent despite adequate treatment; a precipitant is identifiable in 50-90% of admissions (p.1983) Nonpitting oedema unresponsive to escalating diuretics may be lymphoedema, not HF (p.1984) High-output HF (anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, AV shunt, cirrhosis, severe obesity, beriberi) will be missed if not actively considered in predisposed patients (p.1978, p.1982) HFrEF is a progressive disease in which an index injury (e.g. acute MI, chronic pressure/volume overload, genetic or congenital disease) triggers months-to-years of structural and functional cardiovascular remodelling; patients may stay asymptomatic for long periods because compensatory mechanisms are activated that ultimately drive further deterioration. Pressure overload produces concentric hypertrophy and volume overload produces eccentric (dilated) hypertrophy, accompanied by myocyte hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, apoptosis and re-expression of fetal genes. Sustained activation of the sympathetic nervous system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system initially supports cardiac output but becomes maladaptive, causing excessive vasoconstriction, sodium/water retention, electrolyte and renal disturbance, direct myocardial toxicity and arrhythmias; counter-regulatory natriuretic peptides, prostaglandins, bradykinin and nitric oxide are upregulated but inadequate. Therapies that antagonise RAAS and the sympathetic system (RAAS inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, beta blockers) attenuate or reverse remodelling and improve outcomes. Secondary mitral regurgitation arises from ventricular dilatation, sphericity and annular changes, perpetuating a vicious cycle. HFpEF reflects multiple mechanisms beyond diastolic dysfunction (impaired calcium reuptake, vascular stiffness, renal dysfunction, sodium avidity, inflammation related to adiposity, oxidative/nitrosative stress, insulin resistance). The cardiorenal syndrome is driven not only by low forward flow but importantly by systemic venous congestion and raised intra-abdominal/splanchnic pressure, so relief of congestion improves renal function (p.1977-1982). Overall 5-year survival after a HF diagnosis is roughly 50%, and in severe HF 1-year mortality may reach 40%; one in eight U.S. deaths lists HF on the certificate, most dying of progressive HF or sudden cardiac death. After a HF admission, mortality runs from 8-14% at 30 days to 26-37% at 1 year and up to 75% at 5 years, with readmission of 20-25% at 60 days and nearly 50% at 6 months; risk of death rises with each subsequent admission. Independent predictors of adverse outcome include older age, male sex, diabetes, CKD, CAD, advanced NYHA class, a third heart sound or raised JVP, reduced LV (or RV) EF, secondary mitral/tricuspid regurgitation, raised wedge pressure, pulmonary hypertension, low peak VO2, hyponatraemia, hyperuricaemia, worsening renal function, raised troponin/natriuretic peptides and neurohormones, wide QRS/LBBB, atrial fibrillation and ventricular arrhythmia. HFrecEF (recovered EF) generally carries a better prognosis than HFrEF or HFpEF, but withdrawing therapy can cause relapse in up to half within 6 months (p.1976-1977). HFrEF/HFmrEF/HFpEF phenotype by EF: reduced EF (HFrEF) <=40%, mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) 41-49%, preserved EF (HFpEF) >=50%; LVEF >=50% is considered normal systolic function (p.1977-1978, p.1984). NYHA functional class I-IV grades symptoms by the activity that provokes them: class I none with ordinary activity, class II mild symptoms on ordinary exertion, class III symptoms on less-than-ordinary activity, class IV symptoms (or angina) at rest worsening with any activity (p.1982). ACC/AHA stages describe disease progression: stage B asymptomatic ventricular dysfunction, stage C symptomatic HF, stage D advanced/refractory HF with high mortality where transplant or mechanical circulatory support may be considered (p.1987). Killip classification (originally for acute MI) grades pump failure: class I no congestion; class II basal rales, S3 or right-heart congestion; class III pulmonary oedema; class IV cardiogenic shock (SBP <90 mmHg with peripheral vasoconstriction, cyanosis, confusion, oliguria) - historically rising mortality from class I to IV (p.2247).

iron studies for iron deficiency with or without anemia Bronchial asthma or COPD (cardiac asthma can mimic reactive airways disease) Biliary tract disease (right HF with hepatic congestion causes RUQ pain and abnormal liver function tests) Cellulitis arising from chronic dependent edema versus primary skin/soft-tissue infection Cardiac cirrhosis with ascites mimicking primary liver failure Management is driven by clinical phenotype and by left ventricular ejection fraction: HFrEF (LVEF <=40%), HFmrEF (41-49%), and HFpEF (>=50%); the older terms systolic and diastolic heart failure have been abandoned because most patients have both systolic and diastolic abnormalities (Harrison 22e p.1987, 1978). The disease is staged along the ACC/AHA framework: stage A (at risk), stage B (asymptomatic structural/ventricular dysfunction), stage C (symptomatic HF), and stage D (advanced/refractory HF); approach to therapy escalates across these stages (Harrison 22e p.1987). Stage B asymptomatic ventricular dysfunction is treated to facilitate ventricular recovery and prevent progression to clinical HF, whereas stage D carries a high risk of death from sudden death or end-stage pump failure and may prompt consideration of transplant, mechanical circulatory support, or palliative care (Harrison 22e p.1987). The robust randomized-trial evidence base supporting disease-modifying therapy applies to HFrEF (LVEF <=40%); historically HFmrEF and HFpEF management was symptom-focused owing to lack of outcome-improving therapies (Harrison 22e p.1987). Even with effective therapy, patients across all EF categories remain at risk for clinical deterioration, typically from progressive sodium and fluid retention that drives congestive symptoms and acute decompensated HF (Harrison 22e p.1987). Trials of agents that improve outcomes in HFrEF (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta blockers, digoxin, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists) have generally been unsuccessful when exported to HFpEF, with several large trials showing reduced HF hospitalizations but no all-cause mortality benefit (Harrison 22e p.1987-1988). Management of HFpEF has centered on lifestyle modification, control of congestion, rhythm stabilization (especially atrial fibrillation), blood pressure control to guideline targets, and treatment of comorbidities such as obesity, obstructive lung disease, sleep apnea, diabetes/insulin resistance, anemia, iron deficiency, and chronic kidney disease (Harrison 22e p.1987). A favorable signal for spironolactone in HFpEF emerged mainly from the subgroup randomized in the Americas in the TOPCAT trial, supporting only a weak guideline recommendation in selected patients at low risk for hyperkalemia and worsening renal function (Harrison 22e p.1988). The microvascular endothelial inflammation paradigm proposes that comorbidity-driven inflammation impairs nitric oxide signaling and increases myocardial stiffness in HFpEF; trials enhancing NO bioavailability (sildenafil in RELAX, nitrates in NEAT-HFpEF, inorganic nitrite in INDIE-HFpEF) failed to improve functional capacity or quality of life (Harrison 22e p.1988-1989). Approximately one-half of patients with HF have reduced EF and one-half have preserved or mildly reduced EF; classifying by EF matters because of differences in demographics, comorbidities, and treatment response (Harrison 22e p.1978). Acute heart failure (formerly acute decompensated HF) refers to rapid onset or worsening of symptoms; most episodes are decompensations of chronic HF, but roughly 20% are new-onset, occurring with acute coronary syndrome, acute valvular dysfunction, hypertensive urgency, or postcardiotomy syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1976). HF with recovered EF (HFrecEF) is a subgroup whose EF normalizes on therapy; predictors include younger age, shorter HF duration, nonischemic etiology, smaller ventricular volumes, and absence of fibrosis, and withdrawal of disease-modifying therapy can cause recurrence in up to half of patients within 6 months (Harrison 22e p.1977). Acute pulmonary edema with severe dyspnea and pink frothy sputum due to markedly elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure Hypotension with narrow pulse pressure and a rapid, thready pulse indicating severe low-output state Pulsus alternans and an audible S3 gallop signaling severe hemodynamic compromise and adverse prognosis Kussmaul's sign (inspiratory rise in JVP) as a marker of severe biventricular failure and poor outcome Marked elevation of transaminases and lactic acid suggesting cardiogenic shock with severe low output Oliguria from severe reduction in renal blood flow indicating advanced-stage HF Cheyne-Stokes / periodic breathing and central sleep apnea in advanced HF Cardiac cachexia (edema-free weight loss >5% over 12 months) and frailty/sarcopenia in longstanding severe HF Recurrent acute decompensated HF despite optimal therapy heralding advanced (stage D) refractory disease Signs and symptoms of HF are neither sensitive nor specific, so a high index of suspicion is needed, especially in older patients with hypertension, diabetes, or CKD (Harrison 22e p.1985). Right HF with hepatic congestion can elevate transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin and be misdiagnosed as biliary tract disease (Harrison 22e p.1984). Cardiac asthma (wheezing and rhonchi from bronchial congestion) can be mistaken for asthma or COPD and treated inappropriately (Harrison 22e p.1983). Rales may be absent in longstanding HF with chronically elevated wedge pressures because of increased lymphatic drainage, so their absence does not exclude congestion (Harrison 22e p.1983). NYHA functional class correlates poorly with objective measures of cardiac structure (LV size, EF) and function (peak VO2) (Harrison 22e p.1982). Natriuretic peptide levels may be falsely low in obesity and elevated by noncardiac factors (age, female sex, CKD) and other cardiac conditions, limiting interpretation (Harrison 22e p.1985). Lower extremity edema may be absent in acute HF or in younger adults despite marked systemic venous hypertension; unilateral edema suggests DVT, prior trauma, or vein harvest rather than HF (Harrison 22e p.1984). Drugs causing salt/water retention (NSAIDs) or negative inotropy (calcium channel blockers) can precipitate decompensation and should be recognized as provider-related triggers (Harrison 22e p.1983). Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, RAAS inhibitors, and potassium supplements can cause hyperkalemia, particularly with reduced GFR, requiring monitoring (Harrison 22e p.1984-1985). HFrEF is a progressive disorder in which an index event (acute myocardial infarction, chronic pressure or volume overload, inherited or congenital disease) is followed by months to years of cardiovascular remodeling. Concentric hypertrophy reduces wall stress in pressure overload, while eccentric hypertrophy (chamber dilation) occurs in volume overload; remodeling involves myocyte hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, altered calcium handling, fetal gene reexpression, necrosis, apoptosis, and autophagy. Maladaptive activation of the sympathetic nervous system and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system initially supports cardiac output but ultimately produces excessive vasoconstriction, volume retention, electrolyte and renal abnormalities, baroreceptor dysfunction, direct myocardial toxicity, and arrhythmias, with antagonism of these systems shown to attenuate or reverse remodeling and reduce mortality. Counterregulatory vasodilatory hormones (ANP, BNP, prostaglandins, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, nitric oxide) are upregulated; neprilysin inactivates natriuretic peptides and bradykinin, the rationale for angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition. Endothelin, inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6), and reactive oxygen species contribute to remodeling, and the cardiorenal syndrome reflects both reduced forward flow and systemic venous/abdominal congestion. HFpEF pathophysiology is less defined and involves diastolic dysfunction together with vascular stiffness, renal dysfunction, sodium avidity, comorbidity-driven microvascular inflammation, and impaired nitric oxide/cGMP/protein kinase G signaling causing myocardial stiffening (Harrison 22e p.1978-1982, 1989). Overall 5-year survival after a primary-care diagnosis of HF is about 50%, and 1-year mortality may reach 40% in severe HF. After an HF admission, mortality ranges from 8-14% at 30 days to 26-37% at 1 year and up to 75% at 5 years, with readmission rates of 20-25% at 60 days approaching 50% at 6 months; risk of death rises with each subsequent admission. Most deaths are cardiovascular, from progressive pump failure or sudden cardiac death. Independent predictors of adverse outcome include older age, male sex, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, coronary disease, advanced NYHA class, presence of an S3 or elevated JVP, reduced LV/RV ejection fraction, elevated wedge pressure, low cardiac index, reduced peak VO2, pulmonary hypertension, worsening renal function, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, elevated troponin and natriuretic peptides, raised neurohormones, tachycardia, wide QRS/LBBB, atrial fibrillation, and ventricular ectopy. Black patients have higher case-fatality rates and there is regional variation (highest in the US Midwest and rural areas). HFrecEF generally carries a better prognosis than HFrEF or HFpEF. Overall outcomes are improving with guideline-directed therapy and risk-factor control (Harrison 22e p.1976-1977). Two complementary frameworks are used. The NYHA functional classification grades symptom-limiting activity: class I (no limitation), class II (mild; symptoms with ordinary activity), class III (moderate; symptoms with less-than-ordinary activity), and class IV (severe; symptoms at rest worsening with any activity). The ACC/AHA staging is progressive and irreversible: stage A (at risk, no structural disease or symptoms), stage B (structural disease/asymptomatic ventricular dysfunction without symptoms), stage C (structural disease with current or prior symptoms), and stage D (advanced/refractory HF requiring specialized interventions). Patients are additionally phenotyped by ejection fraction: HFrEF (LVEF <=40%), HFmrEF (41-49%), and HFpEF (>=50%) (Harrison 22e p.1982-1983, 1987).

speckle-tracking strain imaging for prognosis Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP) for diagnosis, severity, and prognosis Cardiac MRI for etiology and tissue characterization; cardiac CT/coronary CT angiography when MRI contraindicated; cardiac PET for ischemia/viability and sarcoid inflammation Coronary angiography to exclude reversible ischemic cause Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (peak VO2, VE/VCO2 slope) for transplant/MCS evaluation and unexplained dyspnea Invasive hemodynamics (pulmonary artery catheter; combined right/left heart catheterization to distinguish restriction from constriction) Endomyocardial biopsy in selected cases (myocarditis, amyloidosis, chemotherapy/immunotherapy injury, transplant rejection) Targeted etiologic screening: hemochromatosis, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis; serum free light chains/SPEP, ferritin, ceruloplasmin, ANA, RF, hepatitis C, HIV; three-generation family history and genetic testing for inherited cardiomyopathy Pulmonary embolism (precipitant and elevates BNP) Pulmonary arterial hypertension and right HF Lymphedema (nonpitting edema unresponsive to diuretics) Deep venous thrombosis (unilateral leg edema) Cirrhosis or primary liver failure (ascites) Cardiac amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis (infiltrative mimics) Heart failure is a clinical syndrome of symptoms and signs arising from any structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or ejection; it is the common final pathway for most chronic cardiovascular diseases including hypertension, coronary artery disease, and valvular disease (p.1975). Roughly half of patients with HF have reduced ejection fraction (EF less than or equal to 40%, HFrEF) and about half have preserved (greater than or equal to 50%, HFpEF) or mildly reduced (41-49%, HFmrEF) EF; because most patients have both systolic and diastolic abnormalities, the older terms 'systolic' and 'diastolic' heart failure have been abandoned (p.1977). An EF that recovers to normal on guideline-directed therapy defines HF with recovered EF (HFrecEF); predictors include younger age, shorter HF duration, nonischemic etiology, smaller ventricular volumes, and absence of fibrosis, and withdrawal of therapy can cause symptom and EF recurrence in up to half of patients within 6 months (p.1977). Dyspnea progresses in severity as exertional dyspnea, then orthopnea, then paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, then dyspnea at rest; bendopnea (breathlessness when bending forward) reflects elevated filling pressure, especially with low cardiac output (p.1982). Orthopnea typically occurs within 1-2 minutes of lying down, whereas paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea occurs after prolonged recumbency and may require 30 minutes or more upright for relief; cardiac asthma (wheezing) can mimic primary lung disease (p.1982). An S3 gallop indicates volume overload, suggests severe hemodynamic compromise, and carries negative prognostic significance, whereas an S4 is nonspecific and often reflects hypertensive HFpEF (p.1984). Pulmonary rales may be ABSENT in longstanding HF despite chronically elevated wedge pressures because increased lymphatic drainage prevents alveolar spillage, so a clear chest does not exclude congestion (p.1983, p.1985). Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP) rise with wall stress and aid diagnosis when uncertain, but levels are falsely LOW in obesity and falsely elevated by age, female sex, chronic kidney disease, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism, and pulmonary arterial hypertension (p.1985). Cardiorenal syndrome is driven not only by reduced forward cardiac output but importantly by systemic and abdominal venous congestion; relieving congestion (diuretics or ultrafiltration) often improves renal function (p.1981). High-output HF is rare and usually requires underlying structural heart disease; consider it with severe anemia (often hemoglobin less than or equal to 8 g/dL), arteriovenous fistula, severe obesity, cirrhosis, thyrotoxicosis, end-stage renal disease, or beriberi (p.1982). Iron deficiency (with or without anemia) is common in chronic HF; IV iron (not oral) improves symptoms, exercise capacity, and reduces hospitalizations, though survival benefit is uncertain (p.1985). Q waves with reduced QRS voltage (pseudo-infarct pattern) suggest infiltrative or restrictive cardiomyopathy such as amyloid, and conduction system disease should raise suspicion for cardiac sarcoid or Chagas in the right setting (p.1985). Excluding HF because the lung exam is clear; rales can be absent in chronic HF with chronically elevated wedge pressures. Misreading right-HF hepatic congestion (elevated transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) as biliary tract disease. Misdiagnosing cardiac asthma/bronchial congestion as primary asthma or COPD and treating inappropriately. Over- or under-interpreting natriuretic peptides without accounting for obesity (falsely low) and for age, female sex, CKD, AF, PE, and PAH (falsely elevated). Equating NYHA functional class with objective cardiac structure or function; it correlates poorly with EF and peak VO2. Attributing diuretic-refractory nonpitting edema to HF when it represents lymphedema needing different workup. Failing to seek precipitating factors (identifiable in 50-90% of admissions), such as nonadherence, excess salt/fluid, NSAIDs, negative inotropes, ischemia, arrhythmia, infection, anemia, thyroid disease, or sleep apnea. HFrEF is a progressive disease in which an index event (acute MI, chronic pressure/volume overload, genetic or congenital disease) triggers months to years of cardiovascular remodeling. Pressure overload produces concentric hypertrophy and volume overload produces eccentric hypertrophy; both involve myocyte hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, altered calcium-handling and cytoskeletal proteins, reexpression of fetal genes, and myocyte necrosis, apoptosis, and autophagy, completing a vicious cycle of pump dysfunction and rising wall stress. Compensatory neurohormonal activation of the sympathetic nervous system and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system initially supports output but becomes maladaptive, causing vasoconstriction, sodium and water retention, baroreceptor dysfunction, direct myocardial toxicity, arrhythmia, and adverse remodeling of heart, vessels, and kidneys. Counterregulatory vasodilators (ANP, BNP, prostaglandins, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, nitric oxide) are upregulated and act via guanylate cyclase to promote vasodilation and natriuresis; bradykinin and natriuretic peptides are degraded by neprilysin. Endothelin, inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, IL-6), and reactive oxygen species contribute to remodeling. HFpEF mechanisms are less defined but extend beyond diastolic dysfunction to vascular stiffness, renal dysfunction, sodium avidity, adiposity-related inflammation, oxidative/nitrosative stress, and insulin resistance. Electrical dyssynchrony (LBBB/IVCD), secondary mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, cardiorenal and splanchnic/hepatic congestion, gut microbiome alterations with endotoxemia, and high-output states further drive progression. Overall 5-year survival after HF diagnosis in primary care is about 50%, and 1-year mortality may reach 40% in severe HF. Post-admission mortality ranges from 8-14% at 30 days to 26-37% at 1 year and up to 75% at 5 years, with readmission of 20-25% at 60 days and nearly 50% at 6 months; risk of death rises with each subsequent admission. Most deaths are cardiovascular, from progressive HF or sudden cardiac death. Black patients have higher case-fatality, men higher age-adjusted mortality than women. Independent predictors of adverse outcome include older age, male sex, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, coronary disease, advanced NYHA class, S3 or elevated JVP, reduced LV/RV EF, elevated wedge pressure, low cardiac index and peak VO2, pulmonary hypertension, worsening renal function, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, elevated troponin and natriuretic peptides, elevated neurohormones, widened QRS/LBBB, atrial fibrillation, and ventricular arrhythmias. HFrecEF carries a better prognosis than HFrEF or HFpEF. Overall outcomes are improving with risk-factor treatment and guideline-directed therapies. New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification: Class I, no limitation, ordinary activity causes no undue symptoms; Class II, mild limitation, comfortable at rest but ordinary activity (e.g., carrying heavy packages) causes fatigue, dyspnea, palpitations, or angina; Class III, moderate limitation, comfortable at rest but less-than-ordinary activity (e.g., getting dressed) provokes symptoms; Class IV, severe, symptoms of HF or angina at rest, worsening with any activity. EF-based phenotypes: HFrEF (EF less than or equal to 40%), HFmrEF (41-49%), HFpEF (greater than or equal to 50%). The chapter notes NYHA class correlates poorly with objective measures such as LV size, EF, and peak oxygen consumption.

exposure in a hot environment Core temperature is usually normal or only mildly raised (generally below the threshold used to define heat stroke) and, crucially, mentation remains intact The presence of confusion, agitation, seizures, or any altered mental state signals progression to heat stroke and mandates aggressive cooling Reflects a combination of volume depletion and electrolyte loss from sweating together with cardiovascular strain from peripheral vasodilation Management centres on moving to a cool environment, rest, removing excess clothing, and oral or intravenous rehydration Measuring an accurate core (rectal) temperature is the key step in distinguishing heat exhaustion from early heat stroke Most patients recover rapidly once cooled and rehydrated, and can often be managed without hospital admission Risk factors include poor acclimatisation, high humidity, extremes of age, dehydration, and certain medications that impair thermoregulation Any alteration in mental status (confusion, agitation, seizure, collapse) indicating heat stroke Core temperature at or above the heat stroke threshold Persistent hypotension or failure to improve with cooling and rehydration Signs of end-organ dysfunction such as dark urine, oliguria, or bleeding Relying on peripheral or oral temperature and missing true hyperthermia Assuming intact sweating excludes serious heat illness Overlooking exertional hyponatraemia and giving large volumes of plain water Discharging before mentation and vital signs have clearly normalised Heat exhaustion arises when prolonged heat stress and sweating deplete water and electrolytes while peripheral vasodilation, undertaken to shed heat, redistributes blood volume to the skin. The resulting relative hypovolaemia and reduced central circulating volume produce the characteristic weakness, dizziness, and tachycardia. Thermoregulation is still largely functional, so the core temperature stays normal or only modestly elevated and the central nervous system is spared, which is what separates it from heat stroke, where thermoregulatory failure allows core temperature to climb and causes encephalopathy and multi-organ injury. With prompt removal from the heat, rest, and rehydration the outlook is excellent and full recovery is the norm; the main danger is unrecognised progression to heat stroke, which carries substantial morbidity and mortality.

assess for DIC Creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase - elevated, suggesting EHS/rhabdomyolysis Renal function and calcium/phosphate - evaluate for rhabdomyolysis complications (hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia) Urinalysis - microscopic hematuria, myoglobinuria, granular or red cell casts Blood glucose - hypoglycemia is frequent Lactate - mild acidosis in CHS, marked lactic acidosis in EHS Cardiac biomarkers and ECG - tachyarrhythmias, nonspecific ST-T changes, heat-related ischemia/infarction Toxicologic screening, cranial CT, and CSF analysis if mental status does not improve with cooling Malignant hyperthermia Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Serotonin syndrome Thyroid storm Pheochromocytoma Diabetic ketoacidosis Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (noninfectious) Toxicologic causes of hyperthermia (sympathomimetics, anticholinergic toxidrome, salicylates) Heat-related illnesses span a spectrum from minor syndromes (heat edema, prickly heat, heat syncope, heat cramps) through heat exhaustion to heatstroke, a true medical emergency. Heatstroke is distinguished by the historical/physical triad of heat-stress exposure, CNS dysfunction, and a core temperature above 40.5C (104.9F); some patients with impending heatstroke may initially appear lucid. In contrast to heatstroke, fever reflects intact thermoregulation, whereas heatstroke represents total loss of thermoregulatory control. Heat exhaustion is characterized by preserved thermoregulatory control and CNS function with core temperature usually below 40.5C (105F); more profound CNS impairment should raise concern for heatstroke or another cause. Two clinical forms of heatstroke exist: classic (epidemic) heatstroke (CHS) in older or chronically ill, often medicated, sedentary patients during heat waves (skin frequently hot and dry from ceased sweating), and exertional heatstroke (EHS) in young healthy exercising individuals who are often profusely diaphoretic despite dehydration. Evaporation of skin moisture is the single most efficient mechanism of heat loss but becomes progressively ineffective once relative humidity exceeds 70%; conduction and convection fail once ambient temperature exceeds skin temperature. Many patients are unaware that their medications impair heat tolerance: anticholinergics, phenothiazines, and heterocyclic antidepressants blunt sweating and central thermoregulation, while beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, and various stimulants reduce cutaneous perfusion or increase heat production. Hepatocytes are highly heat sensitive: AST is routinely elevated on presentation in heatstroke, and both AST and ALT can eventually rise to over 100 times normal values. Core-temperature elevation duration directly drives morbidity and mortality; peripheral (non-core) temperature measurement is unreliable, and continuous core monitoring is needed. Heatstroke commonly produces a thermal cardiomyopathy with potentially elevated CVP despite dehydration, plus deceptive noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and basilar rales in a hypovolemic patient. The wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) is a superior environmental heat-load index to the simple heat index because it incorporates radiant heat and wind speed in addition to air temperature and humidity. Acclimatization to heat develops over one to several weeks (lowered sweat threshold, increased sweat volume with lower salt content, plasma volume expansion, lower heart rate with higher stroke volume) and dissipates rapidly within weeks after leaving the hot environment. Core temperature above 40.5C (104.9F) with CNS dysfunction in the setting of heat stress (heatstroke) Persistent or worsening altered mental status, seizures, or failure to improve with cooling Hot, dry, anhidrotic skin in a dehydrated patient (classic heatstroke) Hypotension with widened pulse pressure, tachypnea, and tachyarrhythmia Evidence of rhabdomyolysis (markedly elevated CK, myoglobinuria, oliguria) Coagulopathy / disseminated intravascular coagulation Markedly elevated transaminases indicating hepatic injury Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS, aspiration Heat exhaustion that progresses to heatstroke even after removal from heat stress Treating heat edema with diuretics, which are ineffective and predispose to volume depletion and more serious heat illness. Failing to recognize that heat exhaustion can progress to heatstroke after the patient is removed from heat stress. Relying on peripheral temperature measurements, which are unreliable in heatstroke. Mistaking cold-induced tonic-clonic muscular rigidity during cooling for seizure activity. Misinterpreting an elevated CVP as adequate volume status, since thermal cardiomyopathy and a hyperdynamic circulation can elevate CVP despite significant dehydration. Assuming hemoconcentration is always present in heat exhaustion (it is not), and overlooking that most cases reflect mixed sodium and water depletion. Correcting free water deficits too rapidly, risking an excessive fall in serum osmolality. Overlooking medication and substance contributions (anticholinergics, antipsychotics, stimulants) to impaired thermoregulation. Pursuing the broad infectious/toxic/endocrine differential without simultaneously initiating rapid cooling in suspected heatstroke. The central thermostat in the preoptic nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus orchestrates heat dissipation via autonomic-driven cutaneous vasodilation and diaphoresis. Heat is lost through evaporation, radiation, conduction, and convection; skin blood flow can rise 25-30 fold with compensatory splanchnic and renal vasoconstriction. When heat load overwhelms dissipation, illness results. Heat cramps reflect relative intracellular deficiency of sodium, potassium, and fluid, compounded by copious hypotonic fluid replacement that produces hyponatremia and hypochloremia. Heat exhaustion arises from water depletion, sodium depletion, or both. Heatstroke begins when maintaining perfusion forces peripheral vasoconstriction, which halts cutaneous heat radiation and causes core temperature to rise sharply. Above 42C (107.6F) direct cellular injury occurs: thermosensitive enzymes fail, oxidative phosphorylation uncouples irreversibly, heat-shock proteins and cytokines drive a systemic inflammatory response, and endothelial damage activates the coagulation cascade. Splanchnic shunting causes gut ischemia with endotoxin release that further impairs thermoregulation, potentially progressing to hepatic dysfunction, renal failure, DIC, and fulminant multisystem organ failure. Minor heat syndromes (heat edema, prickly heat, heat syncope, hyperventilation tetany, heat cramps) and heat exhaustion generally resolve favorably with removal from heat, cooling, and fluid/electrolyte repletion; younger, previously healthy heat-exhaustion patients without major laboratory abnormalities often do well, while older patients with comorbidities frequently require inpatient management. Heatstroke prognosis is closely tied to the duration of core-temperature elevation: delayed cooling can lead to severe hepatic dysfunction, permanent renal failure, DIC, and fulminant multisystem organ failure. Heat-related cardiac biomarker elevations and thermal cardiomyopathy may be reversible. Heat waves substantially increase mortality, especially among the elderly and malnourished, and secondary vascular events (strokes, myocardial infarctions) occur at least ten times more often during extreme heat. Severity ladder of heat-related illness: minor heat-emergency syndromes (heat edema, prickly heat/miliaria rubra, heat syncope, hyperventilation tetany) and heat cramps are mild and self-limited; heat exhaustion is intermediate with core temperature usually below 40.5C (105F) and preserved CNS function; heatstroke is the most severe with core temperature above 40.5C (104.9F), CNS dysfunction, and loss of thermoregulation. Heatstroke is further classified as classic (epidemic) heatstroke (CHS - older/chronically ill, sedentary, anhidrotic, milder coagulopathy and lactic acidosis, mild CK rise) versus exertional heatstroke (EHS - younger/healthy, exercising, diaphoretic, with rhabdomyolysis, marked lactic acidosis, acute renal failure, DIC, hypoglycemia/hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia, and hyponatremia).

Heat stroke — heatstroke, exertional heat stroke, classic heat stroke, severe hyperthermia Heat exhaustion without central nervous system dysfunction Sepsis or severe systemic infection with fever Neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin syndrome Malignant hyperthermia Thyroid storm Central nervous system infection such as meningitis or encephalitis Drug toxicity from stimulants or anticholinergics Core temperature measurement, ideally rectal, to confirm severe hyperthermia Electrolytes, renal and liver function tests to assess organ injury Creatine kinase and urinalysis for rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria Coagulation studies and platelets to detect disseminated intravascular coagulation Blood glucose and arterial blood gas for metabolic disturbance Electrocardiogram and cardiac monitoring, with a septic and toxicological screen when the cause is unclear Heat stroke is a life-threatening emergency defined by a markedly raised core temperature, typically above 40 degrees Celsius, together with central nervous system dysfunction It is distinguished from heat exhaustion by the presence of neurological impairment such as confusion, agitation, seizures, or coma Two forms are recognised: classic (non-exertional) heat stroke affecting vulnerable people during heat waves, and exertional heat stroke affecting young, active individuals such as athletes and military recruits Sweating may be present in exertional heat stroke, so absence of dry skin does not exclude the diagnosis Rapid cooling is the priority and takes precedence over detailed investigation; cold-water immersion is the most effective method, particularly for exertional cases Multi-organ complications include rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, liver injury, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and cardiovascular instability The degree and duration of hyperthermia strongly influence outcome, so cooling should begin as early as possible, ideally before or during transport Core temperature above 40 degrees with altered consciousness, seizures, or coma Signs of shock, arrhythmia, or cardiovascular collapse Evidence of rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury Coagulopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation Waiting for laboratory results or transport before starting aggressive cooling Excluding heat stroke because the patient is sweating, which can occur in exertional cases Mistaking heat stroke for simple heat exhaustion and missing the neurological dysfunction Using antipyretics, which are ineffective because the hypothalamic set point is not raised Failing to monitor for and treat rhabdomyolysis, coagulopathy, and organ failure after cooling Heat stroke occurs when heat gain overwhelms the body's ability to dissipate heat, causing core temperature to rise to a level that produces direct thermal injury to cells and tissues. Excessive environmental heat or intense muscular activity generates a heat load that exceeds losses through radiation, convection, and evaporation, especially in hot, humid conditions or when thermoregulation is impaired. The resulting hyperthermia denatures proteins and damages cell membranes, and triggers a systemic inflammatory response and endothelial injury resembling sepsis. This leads to loss of thermoregulatory control, capillary leak, coagulation activation, and progressive multi-organ dysfunction, with the brain being especially vulnerable, producing the characteristic encephalopathy. Outcome depends chiefly on the peak temperature and how quickly cooling is achieved: rapid recognition and cooling greatly improve survival, whereas prolonged severe hyperthermia carries high mortality and a risk of permanent neurological deficit. Multi-organ failure and delayed treatment worsen prognosis, and some survivors have lasting impairment of heat tolerance.

transformation to aggressive lymphoma Heavy chain diseases arise from clonal B cells or plasma cells that carry deletions or mutations in the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene, so that a structurally abnormal, truncated heavy chain is produced which cannot bind light chains and is secreted alone. Each isotype reflects a distinct clinical entity. In alpha heavy chain disease, chronic antigenic stimulation of gut-associated lymphoid tissue, associated with Campylobacter jejuni, is thought to drive a marginal zone lymphoproliferation of the small bowel, which explains why antibiotics can be effective early. Gamma and mu variants represent clonal lymphoplasmacytic proliferations with their own tissue distributions and disease associations. Outcome varies by type and stage; early alpha heavy chain disease may respond to antibiotics, whereas advanced lymphomatous or aggressive disease carries a poorer prognosis and requires lymphoma-directed therapy.

abdominal x-ray for radiopaque arsenic or thallium Idiopathic Parkinson disease (manganese parkinsonism) Alzheimer disease / other neurodegeneration (aluminum association) Iron-deficiency anemia (cadmium-induced anemia unresponsive to iron) Pyelonephritis and other renal disease causing elevated urinary beta-2-microglobulin (overlaps with cadmium nephropathy marker) Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and hearing loss (associations described with lead) The U.S. ATSDR ranks arsenic, lead, mercury, and cadmium as the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 7th most hazardous substances at toxic waste sites; the WHO lists all four among the 10 chemicals of greatest public-health concern globally (Harrison 22e p.3699). Lead and mercury are xenobiotic metals with no clear safe threshold, whereas copper and selenium are essential trace elements that become toxic only at high exposure (Harrison 22e p.3699). Acute arsenic poisoning produces hemorrhagic gastroenteritis with intestinal mucosal necrosis, fluid loss and hypotension, plus delayed cardiomyopathy, acute tubular necrosis, and hemolysis; chronic exposure causes peripheral neuropathy, hyperkeratosis/hyperpigmentation, and cancers of skin, lung, liver (angiosarcoma), bladder, and kidney (Harrison 22e p.3700). Classic arsenic signs include a garlicky breath odor and Mees' lines (transverse white striae on the fingernails); arsenic is radiopaque and may be visible on abdominal x-ray (Harrison 22e p.3700). Cadmium has a biologic half-life of 10-30 years; severe food/water contamination in Japan caused itai-itai (ouch-ouch) disease with painful bone fractures from cadmium-induced bone toxicity (Harrison 22e p.3699-3700). Lead in blood is 95-99% sequestered in red cells, so lead must be measured in whole blood rather than serum; about 15% of an absorbed dose is stored in bone with a half-life >20 years, making bone (KXRF) levels a marker of cumulative exposure (Harrison 22e p.3700). Impairment of childhood IQ from lead occurs with no measurable threshold down to the assay limit of detection (~1 ug/dL); the CDC recommends screening children at about 6 months and intervening if blood lead exceeds 3.5 ug/dL (Harrison 22e p.3700). Chronic metallic mercury vapor exposure produces an intention tremor and mercurial erethism (excitability, memory loss, insomnia, timidity, delirium) -- the historical 'mad as a hatter' picture (Harrison 22e p.3701). Children exposed to mercury in any form may develop acrodynia ('pink disease'): flushing, itching, swelling, tachycardia, hypertension, excessive salivation/perspiration, irritability, weakness, and desquamation of palms and soles (Harrison 22e p.3701). Dimethylmercury is 'supertoxic' -- a few drops absorbed through skin or inhaled can cause fatal cerebellar degeneration (Harrison 22e p.3701). Manganese overexposure (miners, welders, dry-battery workers) causes a parkinsonian syndrome within 1-2 years that, unlike idiopathic Parkinson disease, is nonresponsive to L-dopa (Harrison 22e p.3702). The single most important treatment is recognizing and stopping the exposure; activated charcoal does not bind metals and is of limited value in acute metal ingestion (Harrison 22e p.3699). Acute encephalopathy with convulsions and coma at very high blood lead (>80-120 ug/dL) -- risk of death Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema after acute cadmium or mercury-vapor inhalation Hemorrhagic gastroenteritis with hypotension and delayed cardiomyopathy in acute arsenic poisoning Cardiovascular collapse after acute ingestion of inorganic mercury (lethal dose 10-42 mg/kg) Garlicky breath, Mees' lines, or a gingival 'lead line' indicating significant metal exposure Skin or inhalational exposure to dimethylmercury (supertoxic; minute amounts fatal) Pregnancy exposure to mercury or high maternal bone lead -- risk of severe fetal neurodevelopmental injury Measuring lead in serum instead of whole blood (95-99% of lead is in red cells) (Harrison 22e p.3700). Relying on activated charcoal for metal ingestion -- charcoal does not bind metals (Harrison 22e p.3699); however thallium is an exception, where charcoal interrupts enterohepatic circulation (Harrison 22e p.3702). Attributing high urinary beta-2-microglobulin solely to cadmium -- it also rises in other renal diseases such as pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.3700). Misreading elevated total arsenic from recent seafood (nontoxic organic arsenobetaine/arsenocholine) as toxic inorganic arsenic -- test after 24 h without seafood (Harrison 22e p.3700). Attempting chelation for cadmium poisoning -- chelation is not useful and dimercaprol can worsen cadmium nephrotoxicity (Harrison 22e p.3700). Expecting chelation to improve outcomes in asymptomatic childhood lead exposure -- a large randomized trial showed no benefit on intelligence at BPb 20-40 ug/dL (Harrison 22e p.3700). Mistaking manganese parkinsonism for idiopathic Parkinson disease and expecting an L-dopa response (Harrison 22e p.3702). Metals enter the body chiefly by inhalation of dusts/fumes, ingestion of contaminated food or water (especially via hand-to-mouth activity in children), and sometimes vapor (e.g., mercury) or dermal absorption (organic lead, thallium). Gastrointestinal absorption varies markedly with the chemical form of the metal and host nutritional status. Once absorbed, metals are transported in blood and sequestered in organs such as bone, liver, and kidney, sometimes for years, then excreted mainly by renal and gastrointestinal routes (with minor losses via sweat, saliva, breath, milk, skin, hair, and nails). Toxicity arises from enzyme inhibition, damage to subcellular organelles and DNA, covalent protein modification, generation of reactive oxygen species, and displacement of essential metals from metal-dependent proteins; metals also alter DNA methylation and other epigenetic marks, dysregulating gene and microRNA expression. Many metals bind sulfhydryl (thiol) groups; cadmium and mercury both bind cellular sulfhydryls, cadmium competing with zinc and calcium, and lead interferes with mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, ATPases, and calcium-dependent messengers while enhancing oxidation and apoptosis. Genetic polymorphisms affecting metal binding/transport and nutritional/comorbid factors modify individual susceptibility (Harrison 22e p.3699-3700). Outcome depends on the metal, dose, acuity, and promptness of exposure termination. Acute high-dose poisoning can be fatal (e.g., lead encephalopathy at BPb >120 ug/dL; inorganic mercury ingestion at 10-42 mg/kg; cadmium or mercury-vapor pulmonary edema; dimethylmercury exposure). Many effects of chronic exposure are irreversible or only partly reversible, including peripheral neuropathy, cognitive decline, manganese parkinsonism (L-dopa nonresponsive), itai-itai bone disease, and cadmium-related chronic renal failure for which no effective chelation exists. Cumulative lead burden is an established risk factor for chronic disease, including hypertension, cardiovascular morbidity/mortality, and chronic kidney disease, and prenatal exposure carries lasting offspring neurodevelopmental risk (Harrison 22e p.3699-3702). No single unified grading; severity is metal- and level-specific. Lead: subclinical childhood effects at BPb ~25-60 ug/dL, with IQ impairment down to ~1 ug/dL; clinically apparent neurodevelopmental delay at BPb 40-80 ug/dL; acute impaired neurotransmission/neuronal death at BPb >60-80 ug/dL; acute encephalopathy with convulsions/coma at BPb >80-120 ug/dL. Adult occupational removal at BPb >40 ug/dL (proposed newer target <10 ug/dL, removal if >20 ug/dL). Arsenic lethal dose 120-200 mg in adults, 2 mg/kg in children. Inorganic mercury ingestion lethal at 10-42 mg/kg; organic mercury CNS lesions at >1.7 mg/kg. Thallium severe poisoning after single dose >1 g or >8 mg/kg (Harrison 22e p.3700-3702).

Helicobacter pylori Infection — H. pylori Urea breath test (noninvasive) for active infection and for confirming eradication. Stool (fecal) antigen test (noninvasive) for active infection and eradication confirmation. Endoscopic biopsy with histopathology, including for gastric lymphoma staging. PCR or FISH for the t(11;18) translocation in gastric MALT lymphoma to predict responsiveness to eradication therapy (p.649). H. pylori has a proven etiologic role in peptic ulcer disease; together with NSAID use it is one of the two most common causes of gastroduodenal ulcers (p.302). In dyspeptic patients under 60 with no alarm features, test-and-treat is the recommended initial strategy: assess H. pylori status by fecal (stool) antigen or urea breath testing, and treat those who are positive (p.303). Eradication of H. pylori in patients with bleeding ulcers lowers rebleeding rates to under 5% (p.272). H. pylori is a known driver of gastric cancer; the intestinal subtype of gastric adenocarcinoma is associated with H. pylori infection and atrophic/atopic gastritis (p.646, p.647). Although H. pylori is extremely common (present in roughly half of all humans), gastric cancer develops in only a small subset of those infected, so infection alone is not sufficient (p.646). Treating H. pylori reduces future gastric cancer risk: eradication lowered gastric cancer incidence in people with a first-degree relative who had gastric cancer, and reduced second cancers in patients with prior early-stage gastric cancer (p.646). All patients with gastric lymphoma should have H. pylori status evaluated; if histopathology is negative, confirm with a stool antigen test or urea breath test (p.649). For gastric MALT lymphoma, antibiotic eradication of H. pylori alone is highly effective and is the initial therapy when H. pylori is positive and the t(11;18) translocation assay is negative, producing high response and complete-remission rates (p.649-650). Dyspepsia with alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding/anemia, jaundice, palpable mass or adenopathy, family history of gastroesophageal malignancy) or age over 60 warrants upper endoscopy to exclude malignancy rather than test-and-treat alone (p.302-303). Failure to respond to eradication, or recurrent/refractory symptoms, should prompt further evaluation. PITFALL: PPIs and other acid-suppressing drugs can cause false-negative urea breath and stool antigen tests; acid suppression must be stopped before testing for active H. pylori infection. Confirmation of eradication should be performed 4-6 weeks after completing therapy, not immediately (p.303). Do not rely on a single negative histopathology result in gastric lymphoma; confirm with noninvasive stool antigen or urea breath testing (p.649). NEGATION: Even H. pylori-negative MALT tumors may respond to anti-H. pylori therapy, so a negative test does not preclude a trial of eradication; the t(11;18) translocation identifies a subgroup less likely to respond (p.649-650). NEGATION: H. pylori eradication does NOT worsen GERD symptoms, despite H. pylori infection being associated with a reduced prevalence of GERD (p.302). H. pylori is a flagellated gastric bacterium whose colonization triggers chronic mucosal inflammation. The flagellum lets the organism access the gastric epithelium and is essential for virulence; H. pylori evades innate immunity by producing a flagellin epitope that does not bind TLR5 and tetra-acylated LPS that does not activate TLR4 (p.1009-1010). Adhesion and gastric tropism are mediated by bacterial outer-membrane proteins BabA and SabA interacting with epithelial GM1 ganglioside (p.1009). Chronic H. pylori inflammation, partly via generation of carcinogenic nitrites from dietary nitrates, drives the gastritis-to-cancer sequence and is a recognized cause of peptic ulcer disease, gastric adenocarcinoma (intestinal subtype), and gastric MALT lymphoma; certain higher-virulence strains carry greater cancer risk (p.646). Eradication markedly improves ulcer outcomes (rebleeding falls below 5%). In gastric MALT lymphoma, H. pylori eradication yields high response rates with complete remission in the majority, though time to remission can be prolonged (averaging ~15-16 months in some studies), requiring patient monitoring before declaring non-response (p.272, p.650). Benefit in functional dyspepsia is limited but statistically significant (about a 9% risk reduction vs placebo) (p.302).

sweating, and confirm with CLDN10 testing Hyperthermia and dehydration during heat exposure or febrile illness Severe symptomatic hypokalaemia with arrhythmia risk Corneal damage from chronic dry eyes Failure to thrive from combined salt loss and reduced intake Expecting hypomagnesaemia and being misled by the hypermagnesaemia that distinguishes HELIX Overlooking the extrarenal exocrine features when a tubulopathy dominates the presentation Failing to counsel about heat intolerance and dehydration risk Mistaking the sicca picture for an acquired autoimmune process Claudin-10 is a tight-junction protein that governs paracellular ion permeability. The kidney-relevant isoform (claudin-10b) forms a paracellular sodium pathway in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, and its loss shifts paracellular selectivity towards divalent cations. This impairs paracellular sodium reabsorption, causing renal salt wasting with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, while enhanced paracellular magnesium and calcium transport leads to the characteristic hypermagnesaemia and reduced calcium excretion. In exocrine glands, defective claudin-10 disrupts fluid secretion, explaining hypohidrosis, reduced lacrimation, and xerostomia, and abnormal epidermal barrier function underlies the ichthyosis. The tubulopathy and exocrine features are generally manageable with supportive care and long-term renal function is usually preserved, but chronic sicca symptoms, heat intolerance, and skin involvement require ongoing multidisciplinary attention.

HELLP syndrome — haemolysis elevated liver enzymes low platelets syndrome, HELLP Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia without the full HELLP picture Acute fatty liver of pregnancy Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and haemolytic uraemic syndrome Viral or other acute hepatitis Antiphospholipid syndrome or a systemic lupus flare Acute cholecystitis or other hepatobiliary disease Gestational thrombocytopenia or immune thrombocytopenia Full blood count with platelet count and a blood film for schistocytes Liver function tests including transaminases and bilirubin Markers of haemolysis such as lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin Coagulation screen including fibrinogen to detect disseminated intravascular coagulation Renal function, urate, and quantified proteinuria Blood pressure monitoring and cardiotocography for fetal assessment Hepatic imaging by ultrasound or cross-sectional scanning if a subcapsular haematoma or rupture is suspected HELLP is an acronym for Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets, and is regarded as a severe variant or complication of pre-eclampsia occurring in the late second or third trimester or postpartum Presentation is frequently non-specific, with malaise, nausea and vomiting, and right upper quadrant or epigastric pain; hypertension and proteinuria may be mild or even absent, which can delay recognition The haemolysis is microangiopathic, evidenced by a blood film showing fragmented red cells (schistocytes), a raised lactate dehydrogenase, low haptoglobin, and unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia Classification schemes such as the Tennessee and Mississippi systems grade severity chiefly by the platelet count and the degree of enzyme and haemolysis derangement Serious complications include disseminated intravascular coagulation, placental abruption, acute kidney injury, subcapsular hepatic haematoma with the risk of hepatic rupture, pulmonary oedema, and eclampsia Definitive treatment is delivery; supportive care includes control of severe hypertension, magnesium sulphate for seizure prophylaxis, and judicious fluid and blood-product management Corticosteroids are given for fetal lung maturity when preterm delivery is anticipated, but steroids are not a reliable treatment for the maternal syndrome itself HELLP may develop or worsen after delivery, so vigilant postpartum monitoring is essential, and refractory or atypical cases should prompt consideration of a thrombotic microangiopathy Severe or refractory right upper quadrant pain, or sudden shoulder-tip pain and shock suggesting rupture of a hepatic haematoma A rapidly falling platelet count or evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation Features of eclampsia such as headache, visual disturbance, hyperreflexia, or seizures Acute kidney injury or oliguria Fetal compromise or suspected placental abruption Excluding HELLP because blood pressure or proteinuria is only mildly abnormal or absent Attributing epigastric pain to gastritis or reflux and missing hepatic involvement Relaxing monitoring or discharging too early, as the syndrome can worsen postpartum Overlooking a thrombotic microangiopathy when derangements persist or worsen after delivery Aggressive fluid loading that precipitates pulmonary oedema HELLP shares the origins of pre-eclampsia: deficient trophoblastic remodelling of the spiral arteries leads to placental ischaemia and release of anti-angiogenic factors, endothelial activation, and widespread microvascular dysfunction. Endothelial injury and platelet activation cause deposition of fibrin in small vessels; red cells are mechanically fragmented as they pass through these narrowed, fibrin-laden vessels, producing microangiopathic haemolysis, while platelets are consumed, causing thrombocytopenia. In the liver, fibrin deposition in the sinusoids and periportal areas obstructs flow and produces hepatocellular necrosis, raising transaminases and, in severe cases, generating intrahepatic haemorrhage, subcapsular haematoma, and the potential for capsular rupture. These processes explain both the diagnostic triad and the multiorgan complications. With timely delivery and intensive supportive care most women recover fully within days of birth, but HELLP carries appreciable maternal morbidity and mortality, notably from hepatic rupture, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and stroke, along with raised perinatal risk and an increased chance of hypertensive disease in future pregnancies.

tumours indicating VHL disease Failing to recognise the VHL association and missing multiple or systemic tumours Underestimating the marked vascularity and risk of intraoperative haemorrhage Overlooking secondary polycythaemia as a clue to the diagnosis Mistaking a solitary cerebellar metastasis for haemangioblastoma or vice versa Haemangioblastoma is a benign, highly vascular neoplasm whose neoplastic element is the interstitial stromal cell, set within a rich network of capillaries. It arises most commonly in the cerebellum and also in the brainstem, spinal cord and retina. Inactivation of the VHL tumour-suppressor gene, whether germline in von Hippel-Lindau disease or somatic in sporadic tumours, leads to stabilisation of hypoxia-inducible factors and upregulation of angiogenic and erythropoietic signalling. This drives the characteristic vascularity and, through erythropoietin production, can cause secondary polycythaemia. Cyst formation with a mural nodule is typical, and mass effect on the cerebellum or brainstem produces the clinical features. Prognosis is excellent for solitary sporadic tumours, which are usually cured by complete surgical excision of the mural nodule. Patients with von Hippel-Lindau disease develop multiple lesions over time and require lifelong surveillance, with morbidity arising from recurrent tumours and associated systemic neoplasms.
