This most commonly follows blunt or penetrating scrotal trauma, sometimes with rupture of the tunica albuginea and extrusion of testicular tissue, but it may also arise after surgery, from bleeding into a pre-existing hydrocele, or spontaneously in the presence of a bleeding tendency or tumour. The trapped blood organises over time, and a chronic collection develops a thickened, sometimes calcified wall that can constrict the testis and impair its perfusion and function. With prompt exploration and repair of an associated testicular rupture, testicular salvage rates are good, whereas delayed management or a large chronic haematocele can lead to testicular atrophy or loss; small collections with an intact testis often resolve with conservative care.

Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation — HCT, Bone marrow transplantation, Stem cell transplantation, Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, HSCT Acute GVHD versus conditioning regimen toxicity, drug eruption, or infection as a cause of post-transplant rash, diarrhea, and hepatic dysfunction (biopsy of skin, liver, or gut often needed for confirmation) (Harrison 22e p.917) Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome versus other causes of tender hepatomegaly, jaundice, and fluid retention early after transplant (Harrison 22e p.916) Transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy versus other microangiopathic processes (schistocytes, elevated LDH, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury) (Harrison 22e p.916-917) Idiopathic/diffuse interstitial pneumonia from conditioning toxicity can mimic infectious pneumonia early post-transplant (Harrison 22e p.916) Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia and bronchiolitis obliterans (late, often GVHD-associated) can mimic chronic respiratory infection (Harrison 22e p.916) HLA typing of HLA-A, -B, -C, and -D (and DRB1) to assess donor-recipient matching; AML/ALL candidates should be HLA-typed soon after diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.915, 919) Screening recipients for donor-directed anti-HLA antibodies before transplant, since their presence predicts poor engraftment (Harrison 22e p.917) Chimerism/engraftment documentation by fluorescence in situ hybridization of sex chromosomes (sex-mismatched pairs) or short tandem repeat polymorphism analysis after DNA amplification (Harrison 22e p.916) CD34 antigen quantification or colony-forming unit assays to gauge stem cell dose adequacy (Harrison 22e p.915) PCR monitoring of blood for CMV (and other viral) DNA to guide preemptive therapy (Harrison 22e p.918) Minimal residual disease assessment by multidimensional flow cytometry or molecular methods to refine transplant candidacy in acute leukemia (Harrison 22e p.919) GVHD severity biomarkers including ST2, REG3a, and TNF R1 (Harrison 22e p.917) Many noninfectious conditions can mimic acute GVHD, so histologic confirmation is usually required (Harrison 22e p.917) Post-transplant autoimmune phenomena (autoimmune hemolytic anemia, immune thrombocytopenia) in 3-5% can mimic relapse-related or drug-induced cytopenias (Harrison 22e p.918) Hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) is the umbrella term that has replaced 'bone marrow transplantation,' reflecting that hematopoietic stem cells can be sourced from marrow, growth-factor-mobilized peripheral blood, or umbilical cord blood (Harrison 22e p.914). It is used both to replace a defective but non-malignant lympho-hematopoietic system with a normal donor system and to treat malignancy, the latter by permitting higher myelosuppressive doses and, in allogeneic transplant, by adding an immunologic graft-versus-tumor effect (Harrison 22e p.914). Transplant categories are syngeneic (identical twin, ~1% of cases, no GVHD and no tumor contamination), allogeneic (genetically non-identical donor, risk of GVHD and graft rejection), and autologous (patient's own stored cells, no GVHD/rejection but lacks a graft-versus-tumor effect and may carry contaminating tumor cells) (Harrison 22e p.914-915). The chance any one full sibling is HLA-matched is 1 in 4; the probability a patient has an HLA-identical sibling is 1 - (0.75)^n where n is the number of siblings (Harrison 22e p.915). With registries exceeding 40 million volunteer donors, an HLA-matched unrelated donor can be found for about 60% of patients, with higher rates in Caucasians and lower rates in minorities and people of mixed ancestry; a search and scheduling typically takes 3-4 months (Harrison 22e p.915). Autologous engraftment is reliable when more than 2.5 x 10^6 CD34+ cells/kg are infused; the 5-10% of patients who mobilize poorly with growth factor alone may benefit from plerixafor, a CXCR4 antagonist that releases stem cells from the marrow niche (Harrison 22e p.915). Stem cell homing depends on P- and E-selectin/integrin (e.g., VLA-4) interactions and on niche-derived CXCL12 binding CXCR4 on the stem cell; human HSCs tolerate cryopreservation, enabling autologous storage (Harrison 22e p.914-915). After marrow grafting, granulocytes recover to ~100/uL by about day 16 and ~500/uL by day 22; mobilized peripheral blood speeds recovery by ~1 week while cord blood delays it by ~1 week (Harrison 22e p.916). Innate immunity recovers quickly, but adaptive (T- and B-cell) immunity may take 1-2 years; early T-cell recovery is dominated by infused donor CD8+ T cells with a limited repertoire, with diverse de novo CD4+/CD8+ cells emerging months later (Harrison 22e p.916). Reduced-intensity and nonmyeloablative conditioning rely heavily on the graft-versus-tumor effect; they carry higher relapse but lower transplant-related mortality, favoring older patients and those with comorbidities, whereas high-dose conditioning is preferred when measurable disease is present and the patient can tolerate it (Harrison 22e p.915-916). Evidence for the graft-versus-tumor effect: relapse is lowest in patients who develop acute and chronic GVHD, higher without GVHD, and highest after T-cell-depleted allogeneic or syngeneic grafts; donor lymphocyte infusions can induce remission in post-transplant relapse (Harrison 22e p.916). Worldwide more than 100,000 transplants were performed in 2022, with frequency closely tracking gross national income per capita (Harrison 22e p.914). Tender hepatomegaly, jaundice, ascites, and fluid retention within the first month (peak ~day 16) suggest sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, which carries ~30% mortality and can progress to fatal hepatorenal syndrome (Harrison 22e p.916) Erythematous maculopapular rash, persistent anorexia or diarrhea, and rising bilirubin/transaminases/alkaline phosphatase in the first 3 months point to acute GVHD; grades II-IV require aggressive therapy (Harrison 22e p.917) Schistocytes, elevated LDH, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury about a month post-transplant indicate transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy (Harrison 22e p.916-917) Diffuse fluffy pulmonary infiltrates with alveolar hemorrhage on lavage suggest conditioning-related diffuse alveolar damage rather than infection (Harrison 22e p.916) Failure of marrow function to return, or loss after initial engraftment, signals graft failure/rejection; persistence of host-origin lymphocytes indicates immunologic rejection (Harrison 22e p.917) Fever once the granulocyte count falls below 500/uL prompts broad-spectrum empiric antibacterial therapy because infection risk is so high (Harrison 22e p.918) Community respiratory viruses (RSV, parainfluenza, influenza, metapneumovirus) can be life-threatening or fatal in transplant recipients (Harrison 22e p.918) Premedication is not a reliable solution: in transfusion-related GVHD analogies aside, here the key pitfall is assuming infectious causes for early rash/diarrhea/hepatic dysfunction; acute GVHD typically needs biopsy because many conditions mimic it (Harrison 22e p.917) Grade I acute GVHD is clinically minor, does not affect survival, and does not require treatment; over-treating it adds unnecessary immunosuppression (Harrison 22e p.917) Mobilized peripheral blood gives faster engraftment but, in matched-unrelated-donor transplant, increases chronic GVHD without a compensatory survival advantage (Harrison 22e p.916) No prospective randomized trial has shown that purging autologous grafts of tumor cells reduces relapse or improves survival (Harrison 22e p.915) Standard high-dose conditioning is poorly tolerated if given within 100 days of a first transplant due to cumulative toxicity; reduced-intensity regimens may be needed for graft failure salvage (Harrison 22e p.917) Patients with Fanconi anemia are abnormally sensitive to alkylating agents, so less intensive conditioning must be used (Harrison 22e p.918) Vaccine-preventable antibody titers wane after transplant unless recipients are revaccinated; live vaccines (MMR/MMR-V) are generally avoided until 2 years post-transplant (Harrison 22e p.918) Reinfusing donor stem cells into a patient with immunologic graft rejection is usually futile unless preceded by a second immunosuppressive conditioning regimen (Harrison 22e p.917) A single hematopoietic stem cell can regenerate the entire lympho-hematopoietic system, including red cells, granulocytes, B and T lymphocytes, platelets, and fixed-tissue macrophages (Kupffer cells, alveolar macrophages, osteoclasts, Langerhans cells). Infused cells home to the marrow via selectin/integrin adhesion and CXCL12-CXCR4 signaling. In allogeneic transplant, the central immunologic axis is HLA matching: HLA molecules present antigenic peptides to T cells, so mismatched 'major antigens' provoke strong T-cell reactions while even HLA-matched pairs can react against 'minor' endogenous antigens. Donor T cells reacting against host tissue cause graft-versus-host disease, whereas residual immunocompetent host cells can mediate graft rejection if conditioning is insufficiently immunosuppressive. The same alloreactivity underlies the beneficial graft-versus-tumor effect. Conditioning regimens combine antineoplastic activity, myelosuppression, and (for allogeneic) immunosuppression to eradicate disease and prevent rejection (Harrison 22e p.914-916). Outcomes are highly disease- and stage-dependent (CIBMTR estimates, transplants 2010-2020). Reported approximate 3-year survival: severe combined immunodeficiency ~95% allogeneic; aplastic anemia ~98% allogeneic; thalassemia ~95% allogeneic; AML 57% (first remission) and 53% (second remission); ALL 64% (first remission) and 45% (second remission); CML 71% (chronic phase), 67% (accelerated), 28% (blast crisis); CLL ~64%; myelodysplasia ~50%; multiple myeloma ~80% autologous as initial therapy; non-Hodgkin lymphoma 45% allogeneic / 55% autologous (first relapse/second remission); Hodgkin disease 68% allogeneic / 89% autologous (first relapse/second remission). Matched-unrelated-donor survival now essentially equals matched-sibling survival. Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome carries ~30% mortality; chronic GVHD mortality averages ~15% (range 5-50% by severity). HLA-matched sibling allogeneic transplant carries roughly a 1-3% graft rejection risk and ~15% risk of severe acute GVHD (Harrison 22e p.915-920). Acute GVHD is staged per organ and combined into an overall grade (Harrison 22e p.917). Skin stage 1-4 (rash <25% body surface up to generalized desquamation/bullae); liver stage by bilirubin from 34-51 umol/L [2-3 mg/dL] up to >257 umol/L [>15 mg/dL]; gut stage by diarrhea volume from 500-1000 mL/d up to ileus. Overall grade I (skin 1-2 only) is clinically insignificant; grades II-IV reflect progressively greater organ involvement, worse survival, and need for aggressive therapy. Myelodysplasia transplant timing uses the International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS), with transplant generally reserved for Int-2 or higher (or selected Int-1 with poor features) (Harrison 22e p.919).

Hematopoietic Stem Cells — HSC, blood stem cells, hematopoiesis Deep/next-generation sequencing to detect somatic mutations and clonal hematopoiesis (e.g., DNMT3a, TET2, ASXL1 variant allele fractions) Surface immunophenotyping of stem/progenitor markers (CD34, CD90/Thy-1, CD117/c-Kit, CD133, CD164, CD110/c-Mpl) as described in murine-based studies Every blood cell type and certain tissue-resident cells (e.g., microglia, some macrophages) arise from hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs); catastrophic loss of HSC function leaves a person able to survive only about 2-4 weeks without extraordinary support. The HSC pool is estimated at only about 20,000-200,000 cells, yet it generates hundreds of billions of mature blood cells daily and sustains this output over decades. Stem cells are defined by two cardinal properties: self-renewal (dividing while staying undifferentiated) and differentiation into mature effector cells; loss of either leads to pool exhaustion or to organ failure/neoplasia. A dividing HSC can yield two stem cells, two differentiating cells (symmetric division), or one of each (asymmetric division); this asymmetry lets a small pool produce roughly seven orders of magnitude more mature cells daily. Mature blood cell lifespans vary widely, from hours for neutrophils to a few months for red cells to years for memory lymphocytes, but the durable source is the persistent stem cell pool. HSCs circulate in blood throughout life, but free-circulating time is brief (minutes in the mouse); circulating HSCs remain functional and usable for transplantation. The bone marrow niche (notably perivascular regions near trabecular bone) is both nurturing and constraining: mesenchymal and endothelial cells supply kit ligand and CXCL12, and the niche limits how many stem cells are produced. CXCR4/CXCL12 (SDF1) signaling retains HSCs in marrow; disrupting it (via CXCR4 blockade, CXCL12 cleavage, or receptor downregulation) mobilizes stem cells into blood, enabling collection by leukapheresis rather than operative marrow harvest. Differentiation proceeds along a branching hierarchy (stem cell to multipotent progenitor to lineage-committed precursor to mature cell), with progressive loss of plasticity and, in most lineages, loss of proliferative capacity. Maturation of progenitors into mature cells takes roughly 10-14 days in humans, clinically reflected in the lag between cytotoxic chemotherapy and blood count recovery. HSCs are heterogeneous: individual stem cells can be biased toward particular lineages and differ in proliferation and death responses, so the population behaves as an aggregate. Clonal hematopoiesis: HSCs accumulate roughly 17 somatic mutations per year of life; variant alleles contributing to over 1% of blood cells become nearly universal by age 70, with an inactivating TET2 mutation able to worsen outcomes of some chronic inflammatory conditions. Genetically modifying long-lived HSCs underlies curative cell therapies for cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy and the hemoglobinopathies, including a CRISPR gene-edited approach that suppresses BCL11A to reactivate fetal hemoglobin in beta thalassemia and sickle cell anemia. Complete failure of HSC function (e.g., after a nuclear/radiation accident) predicts survival of only about 2-4 weeks without extraordinary support Expansion of clones carrying 'driver' mutations seen in myelodysplasia and myeloid leukemias, with low-frequency progression to overt neoplastic disease Acquired self-renewal via oncogenic mutation in stem or more mature populations, providing a substrate for leukemia Regulators of mature/progenitor cells do not predict HSC behavior: erythropoietin and G-CSF drive precursor proliferation but do not directly cycle stem cells (G-CSF instead mobilizes HSCs by altering CXCL12 tethering). Deep HSC quiescence and resistance to cytokines make robust in vitro expansion of human HSCs difficult. Assuming leukemia must arise only from normal stem cells is an oversimplification, since less self-renewing mature populations can also be transformed and self-renewal can be acquired by mutation. The classic differentiation hierarchy diagram is a simplification; lineage-biased and intermediate cell states are increasingly recognized. Progenitor (transient amplifying) cells are short-lived and largely lack durable self-renewal, so gene-modifying progenitors rather than true stem cells fails to give lasting benefit. Hematopoiesis originates from a small self-renewing HSC pool. During development, blood production shifts sequentially from the yolk sac (embryonic-hemoglobin red cells and tissue-resident macrophages) to the placenta and intraembryonic sites near the aorta-gonad-mesonephros region, then to fetal liver, and in the second trimester to bone marrow and spleen; HSCs reach marrow via bloodborne transit from fetal liver after long-bone calcification, and proliferation falls sharply soon after birth. HSCs reside in a specialized perivascular/endosteal marrow niche where mesenchymal, endothelial, neural, and other cells provide regulatory signals (kit ligand, CXCL12) governing survival, expansion, and constraint. Trafficking depends on selectins binding CD162/CD44, integrin-mediated firm adhesion (VCAM-1/VLA-4), and CXCL12-CXCR4 plus calcium-sensing receptor signaling. Most HSCs are deeply quiescent and cytokine-resistant, dividing on the order of months to years; quiescence is enforced by high cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors (e.g., p57/CDKN1c blocking the G1-S transition) and niche signals such as angiogenin, IL-18, and angiopoietin 1. Self-renewal preserves any acquired mutation in the durable stem pool, whereas progenitor mutations are largely lost through terminal differentiation; epigenetic regulators (DNMT3a, TET2, ASXL1) are critical for pool homeostasis and for restraining outgrowth of potentially pathogenic clones. In the absence of disease the HSC pool is essentially inexhaustible: serial murine transplants can reconstitute several animals in succession and allogeneic transplant recipients never run out of blood cells over decades, indicating even limiting stem cell numbers suffice. With aging, clonal diversity declines as a small number of expanded clones (estimated 10-20 clones supplying 30-60% of blood cells by age 70) dominate; most such clones are benign, but some carry driver mutations with a low risk of progression to myeloid malignancy.

Semen is derived largely from the seminal vesicles and prostate, and blood can enter it anywhere along the ejaculatory tract, including the prostate, seminal vesicles, ejaculatory ducts, vasa, and posterior urethra. The commonest mechanism is inflammation or infection producing fragile, congested mucosa that bleeds, or iatrogenic trauma after prostate biopsy or instrumentation. self-injury, rhabdomyolysis or exhaustion Reduced consciousness or additional focal deficits suggesting extensive stroke Very high blood glucose indicating a hyperglycaemic emergency Rapid progression suggesting a neoplastic or inflammatory lesion Failing to check blood glucose, thereby missing reversible non-ketotic hyperglycaemic hemiballismus Assuming a functional cause and overlooking an underlying stroke Neglecting measures to prevent injury and exhaustion from violent movements Overlooking the need for secondary stroke prevention once a vascular cause is confirmed Hemiballismus results from disruption of the basal ganglia motor circuit, classically through a lesion of the subthalamic nucleus contralateral to the affected side. Loss of the normal excitatory drive from the subthalamic nucleus to the globus pallidus interna reduces inhibitory basal ganglia outflow, thereby disinhibiting thalamocortical projections and releasing the violent, involuntary proximal movements. Vascular lesions are the commonest cause, but any process damaging the subthalamic nucleus or its connections, including metabolic, neoplastic, infective and inflammatory insults, may be responsible. The outlook is often favourable, particularly for vascular hemiballismus, which frequently settles spontaneously over weeks to months; hyperglycaemia-related cases usually improve once glucose is controlled. Symptomatic treatment with dopamine-receptor blocking or VMAT2-modulating agents can reduce disabling movements. Persistent, intractable cases are uncommon and may occasionally warrant consideration of functional neurosurgery.

difficulty with poor weight gain Unstable cervical vertebral anomalies affecting anaesthetic safety Coexisting significant cardiac or renal malformation Regarding it as purely cosmetic and overlooking functional hearing, airway, and feeding issues Failing to screen for the vertebral, cardiac, and renal associations of the wider spectrum Underestimating progression of asymmetry during facial growth Missing facial nerve involvement Neglecting the psychosocial impact of visible facial asymmetry Hemifacial microsomia is attributed to disturbed development of the first and second branchial arches and adjacent neural crest-derived tissues on one side of the face. A widely cited mechanism is early vascular disruption, such as haemorrhage or ischaemia in the developing stapedial artery territory, causing focal tissue loss that varies with the timing and extent of the insult. This produces graded hypoplasia of the mandibular ramus and condyle, external and middle ear, facial musculature, and overlying soft tissue, with the degree of asymmetry reflecting the severity of the original disruption. Most cases are sporadic and multifactorial, and the phenotype overlaps substantially with the broader oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum. Outcome depends on severity; mild cases require limited intervention and have normal cognition, whereas severe or bilateral involvement demands prolonged multidisciplinary care with staged mandibular and ear reconstruction and hearing rehabilitation.

twitching of muscles innervated by the facial nerve, usually beginning around the eye and spreading over time to the lower face It is typically unilateral and, unlike many other facial movement disorders, can persist during sleep The most common cause is vascular compression of the facial nerve at its root exit zone from the brainstem, often by an ectatic or aberrant artery Secondary causes include tumours, vascular malformations, and demyelinating or other lesions affecting the facial nerve pathway, which imaging helps exclude Contraction of the frontalis and platysma together, or elevation of the eyebrow with eye closure (the 'other Babinski' sign), supports the diagnosis It should be distinguished from blepharospasm, which is bilateral and involves only eye closure, and from facial myokymia and tics MRI, often with vascular sequences, is used to evaluate for a compressive vessel or structural lesion along the nerve Treatment principles include botulinum toxin injections as first-line symptomatic therapy and microvascular decompression surgery for suitable candidates seeking a durable cure Additional cranial nerve deficits or other neurological signs suggesting a structural posterior fossa lesion Rapid progression or bilateral involvement warranting reassessment Facial weakness or sensory change accompanying the spasm Features suggesting a tumour or vascular malformation on imaging Confusing it with bilateral blepharospasm and choosing the wrong treatment approach Failing to image for a compressive vessel or secondary lesion Overlooking the diagnostic clue that spasms may persist during sleep Not recognising post-palsy synkinesis, which can mimic hemifacial spasm Hemifacial spasm is usually caused by pulsatile compression of the facial nerve at its root exit zone from the brainstem, most often by an aberrant or ectatic blood vessel. Chronic compression is thought to cause focal demyelination and ephaptic (cross) transmission between nerve fibres, together with hyperexcitability of the facial motor nucleus, generating spontaneous and spreading involuntary contractions. Secondary cases result from any lesion irritating the nerve along its course, and the pathophysiological common pathway is abnormal facial nerve excitability. Hemifacial spasm is typically chronic and does not resolve spontaneously, but it is not life-threatening; symptoms are well controlled with repeated botulinum toxin injections, and microvascular decompression offers a lasting cure in appropriately selected patients.

Isolated hemihyperplasia — isolated hemihypertrophy, isolated lateralised overgrowth, idiopathic hemihyperplasia Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum Proteus syndrome Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome and vascular overgrowth disorders Neurofibromatosis type 1 with segmental overgrowth Limb hypertrophy from arteriovenous malformation or chronic inflammation Regular abdominal ultrasound surveillance for Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma through the high-risk years Serial serum alpha-fetoprotein measurement for hepatoblastoma detection Molecular testing of the 11p15 imprinting region, preferably on affected tissue given mosaicism Clinical photography and measurement to document and monitor asymmetry Orthopaedic assessment including leg-length evaluation and imaging where indicated Genetic review to exclude a defined overgrowth syndrome The condition is defined by asymmetric overgrowth of one side or region of the body in the absence of another recognised overgrowth syndrome It carries an increased risk of embryonal tumours in childhood, most importantly Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma Because of this tumour predisposition, structured surveillance with regular abdominal ultrasound and measurement of serum alpha-fetoprotein through early childhood is recommended It lies on a molecular spectrum with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and many cases relate to mosaic epigenetic or genetic changes at the imprinted 11p15 region The overgrowth may involve limbs, trunk, or face and can cause leg-length discrepancy requiring orthopaedic assessment Diagnosis is clinical but warrants investigation to exclude a defined syndrome, including molecular testing of the 11p15 region where appropriate, ideally on affected tissue given mosaicism Management combines cancer surveillance, orthopaedic monitoring of asymmetry, and genetic counselling A palpable abdominal mass or haematuria suggesting Wilms tumour A rising alpha-fetoprotein or hepatic mass suggesting hepatoblastoma Rapidly progressive or disproportionate overgrowth suggesting an alternative diagnosis Significant, worsening leg-length discrepancy affecting gait and posture Failing to institute or maintain tumour surveillance during the vulnerable early years Relying on blood-based molecular testing and being falsely reassured when the change is mosaic and tissue-limited Overlooking features that would reclassify the child as having Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome Neglecting orthopaedic follow-up for progressive leg-length discrepancy Isolated hemihyperplasia represents regional overgrowth thought to arise most often from post-zygotic mosaicism, so that a subset of cells carries a growth-promoting genetic or epigenetic alteration while others do not, producing asymmetry. A large proportion of cases involve mosaic disturbances of the imprinted gene cluster on chromosome 11p15, the same region implicated in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, which explains both the overlapping phenotype and the shared predisposition to embryonal tumours such as Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma. The mosaic nature accounts for the variable distribution of overgrowth and for the frequently negative results of testing performed on blood rather than affected tissue. For most children the outlook is good, with the principal risks being childhood embryonal tumours during the surveillance window and the functional impact of limb asymmetry. Early tumour detection through surveillance substantially improves outcomes, and the excess cancer risk falls markedly after early childhood.

Haemobilia — hemobilia, biliary tract haemorrhage Upper gastrointestinal bleeding from peptic ulcer or varices Haemosuccus pancreaticus (bleeding via the pancreatic duct) Bleeding duodenal or ampullary tumour Choledocholithiasis causing obstructive jaundice Aortoenteric fistula Ruptured hepatic tumour into the biliary tree Cross-sectional contrast-enhanced computed tomography, ideally with arterial-phase angiography, to identify a bleeding source or pseudoaneurysm Catheter hepatic angiography, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic through embolisation Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy or side-viewing endoscopy to observe blood issuing from the ampulla of Vater Liver function tests to characterise the obstructive pattern Full blood count, coagulation studies, and crossmatch Abdominal ultrasound to detect ductal clot, dilatation, or an underlying lesion Haemobilia is bleeding into the biliary tree, most often from an abnormal communication between a vessel and a bile duct The classic Quincke triad is right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and gastrointestinal bleeding, although all three features are present in only a minority Iatrogenic and traumatic causes now predominate, including liver biopsy, percutaneous biliary drainage, cholecystectomy, and blunt hepatic trauma Other causes include hepatic artery aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm, tumours, gallstones, and vascular malformations Bleeding may be delayed by days to weeks after the inciting procedure, so a high index of suspicion is needed Blood clots passing through the ampulla can produce biliary colic and transient obstructive jaundice Angiographic transcatheter embolisation is the first-line treatment for significant arterial haemobilia, with surgery reserved for embolisation failure and endoscopic therapy used to relieve biliary obstruction Haemodynamic instability from major arterial bleeding Delayed severe bleeding after recent hepatobiliary intervention or trauma Cholangitis or biliary sepsis complicating obstructing clot Recurrent bleeding after initial control Not considering haemobilia in obscure gastrointestinal bleeding after a recent hepatobiliary procedure Attributing biliary colic and jaundice to stones and missing intraductal clot Overlooking the potentially long delay between the inciting event and the bleed Proceeding to surgery when transcatheter embolisation would suffice Haemobilia arises when a communication forms between the hepatic or cystic arterial circulation (less often the portal or venous system) and the biliary tree, allowing blood to enter the ducts and drain into the duodenum. The commonest triggers are hepatobiliary trauma and instrumentation, which can create a pseudoaneurysm or arteriobiliary fistula that ruptures into a duct. Blood in the biliary tract may clot and intermittently obstruct bile flow, producing colicky pain and jaundice, and then decompress into the gut as melaena or haematemesis, giving the characteristic waxing-and-waning presentation. With modern angiographic embolisation most cases of arterial haemobilia are controlled successfully and the outlook is favourable, although the prognosis worsens with major trauma, underlying malignancy, or delayed recognition.

Hemochromatosis — iron overload, HFE hemochromatosis Secondary (acquired) iron overload from chronic transfusion in hemoglobinopathies/thalassemia (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.821) Other metabolic causes of skin hyperpigmentation: porphyria cutanea tarda, vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, pellagra, malabsorption/Whipple's disease (Harrison 22e p.443) Transferrin saturation (serum iron / total iron-binding capacity) as a key screening test for iron overload (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.805) Serum ferritin to assess body iron stores (Harrison 22e p.805) MRI quantitation of hepatic and cardiac iron stores (Harrison 22e p.2062) Genetic testing for HFE mutations (the gene underlying the common autosomal recessive form) (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.702) Endomyocardial biopsy with Prussian blue iron stain (reserved; not usually needed when MRI is available) (Harrison 22e p.2062) Other causes of restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy; hemochromatosis is listed among restrictive cardiomyopathies but often presents clinically as a dilated cardiomyopathy (Harrison 22e p.2062) Other chronic liver diseases progressing to cirrhosis (alcohol, viral hepatitis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis) (Harrison 22e p.702) Hemochromatosis is variably classified as a metabolic or storage disease; the common autosomal recessive form is related to the HFE gene (Harrison 22e p.2062). Up to 10% of the population is heterozygous for one HFE mutation, so clinical prevalence might be as high as 1 in 500, though observed rates are lower because of limited (incomplete) penetrance (Harrison 22e p.2062). Increased iron in the skin in types 1 and 2 hemochromatosis stimulates melanin pigment production and leads to the classic bronze color (Harrison 22e p.443). Systemic iron overload is diagnosed from serum iron and transferrin saturation, with thresholds noted around >60% in men and >45-50% in women; ferritin and transferrin saturation are the main usable laboratory biomarkers of iron status (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.805). MRI is used to quantitate iron stores in the liver and heart; for cardiac iron overload the diagnosis is made principally by MRI, and endomyocardial biopsy (Prussian blue stain) is not usually needed (Harrison 22e p.2062). When diagnosed early, hemochromatosis can often be managed by repeated phlebotomy to remove iron (Harrison 22e p.2062). Hepcidin-regulating proteins HFE, transferrin receptor 2, and hemojuvelin, whose mutations cause different forms of hemochromatosis, normally contribute to hepcidin upregulation; impaired hepcidin signaling allows excess iron entry into plasma (Harrison 22e p.805). There is no regulated mechanism for iron excretion; physiologic iron loss occurs only through cell desquamation and menses, which is why unregulated absorption produces progressive overload (Harrison 22e p.805). Hemochromatosis (HFE germline mutations) is a recognized risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, typically via cirrhosis (Harrison 22e p.702) Progression to cirrhosis from hepatic iron loading (Harrison 22e p.2062) Cardiomyopathy from cardiac siderosis, which may cause heart failure or arrhythmia (Harrison 22e p.2062) Markedly increased susceptibility to Vibrio vulnificus sepsis (primary sepsis develops most often in patients with cirrhosis or hemochromatosis) (Harrison 22e p.1373) Increased susceptibility to Yersinia (Y. enterocolitica / Y. pseudotuberculosis) septicemia, with iron overload providing accessible iron; iron chelators such as desferrioxamine can precipitate Yersinia infection (Harrison 22e p.1392) Incomplete penetrance: many HFE mutation carriers never develop clinical iron-overload disease, so genotype does not equal phenotype, and additional genetic and environmental factors (e.g., alcohol) modify expression (Harrison 22e p.2062). Hemochromatosis may present clinically as a dilated cardiomyopathy even though it is categorized among restrictive cardiomyopathies (Harrison 22e p.2062). Iron chelation therapy itself (e.g., desferrioxamine) can supply accessible iron to Yersinia and impair neutrophil function, precipitating Yersinia septicemia in iron-overloaded patients (Harrison 22e p.1392). Systemic iron homeostasis is controlled by hepcidin, a hepatocyte-derived peptide that blocks the iron exporter ferroportin, limiting iron flux from duodenal enterocytes, recycling macrophages, and storing hepatocytes. High plasma/liver iron normally raises hepcidin via the BMP-SMAD pathway, with HFE, transferrin receptor 2, and hemojuvelin contributing to hepcidin upregulation. Mutations in these genes (most commonly HFE) lead to inappropriately low hepcidin, increased iron absorption, and rising transferrin saturation. Because no regulated route of iron excretion exists, iron accumulates progressively. When transferrin saturation exceeds ~60%, non-transferrin-bound iron (NTBI) appears in the circulation and is taken up by liver, pancreas, and heart, driving parenchymal injury. In the heart, excess iron deposits in the perinuclear compartment of cardiomyocytes, disrupting intracellular architecture and mitochondrial function (Harrison 22e p.805, p.2062). If diagnosed early, iron overload can often be removed by repeated phlebotomy, and cardiac function can improve with iron removal provided myocyte loss and replacement fibrosis are not too severe. Late disease carries the burden of established cirrhosis (with hepatocellular carcinoma risk) and irreversible cardiac and endocrine damage (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.702).

Hemolytic Anemia — haemolytic anaemia Inherited intracorpuscular defects: hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell, thalassemia; Chap. 103), enzymopathies (G6PD deficiency, pyruvate kinase deficiency, pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase deficiency), membrane-cytoskeleton defects (hereditary spherocytosis) (p.791-792, Table 105-1) Acquired extracorpuscular causes: autoimmune (warm AIHA, cold agglutinin disease, paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria), microangiopathic/mechanical (prosthetic valve, march hemoglobinuria), paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, toxic/drug-induced, infectious (p.792, 801-804, Table 105-1) Familial (atypical) hemolytic-uremic syndrome from inherited dysregulation permitting excessive complement activation (p.799-800) Malaria - the most frequent infectious cause of HA in endemic areas (p.801) Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 causing HUS, more common in children (p.801) Clostridium perfringens sepsis - life-threatening intravascular hemolysis from lecithinase toxin (open wounds, septic abortion, contaminated blood unit) (p.801, Table 105-7) Babesia, and Mycoplasma infection (associated with paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria); viral triggers (EBV, CMV, parvovirus B19, HIV, HCV) of secondary autoimmune HA (p.801-802, Table 105-8) Reticulocyte count - corrected percentage and absolute count (often neglected in initial anemia workup) (p.791) Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin, AST, LDH, haptoglobin (p.791, Table 105-2) Urine for hemoglobinuria/hemosiderinuria and stool/urine urobilinogen when intravascular hemolysis suspected (p.791) Peripheral blood smear for schistocytes (microangiopathy/fragmentation), spherocytes (AIHA, hereditary spherocytosis), bite cells (G6PD), basophilic stippling (lead/P5N deficiency) (p.799-804) Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test - broad-spectrum then specific anti-Ig/anti-C reagents (p.801) Quantitative G6PD assay (screening tests can miss deficiency soon after a hemolytic attack because young high-G6PD reticulocytes mask it); DNA testing and point-of-care tests available (p.799-800) Flow cytometry for CD59-negative red cell population in PNH (p.801, Table 105-7) Donath-Landsteiner antibody for paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria; blood cultures for clostridial septicemia (p.801, Table 105-7) Red cell survival study (51Cr or nonradioactive 15N) as the gold standard for shortened life span; bone marrow (if done) shows erythroid hyperplasia, usually not required (p.791-792) Compensated hemolysis presenting without anemia, mimicking a non-hemolytic state until it decompensates (p.792) Reticulocytosis-driven macrocytosis that can be mistaken for a megaloblastic process (p.791) Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis causing a precipitous hemoglobin fall in a chronic hemolytic patient, mimicking acute worsening of hemolysis (p.792) Coombs-negative AIHA, which can still be severe when a high-affinity antibody opsonizes red cells with few molecules (p.802) Hemolytic anemia (HA) is anemia from increased red-cell destruction with a normal (usually increased) marrow supply; unlike acute blood loss, cells are destroyed within the body rather than physically lost (p.791). Classify by primary etiology (inherited vs acquired), tempo (acute vs chronic), severity, site of hemolysis (intravascular vs extravascular), and mechanism (intracorpuscular vs extracorpuscular defects) (p.791, Table 105-1). Inherited HA generally reflects intracorpuscular defects (hemoglobinopathies, enzymopathies such as G6PD, membrane-cytoskeleton defects); acquired HA generally reflects extracorpuscular factors (autoimmune, microangiopathic/mechanical, toxins, drugs, infection). Exceptions: PNH (inherited-like somatic mutation but acquired) and familial/atypical HUS (p.791-792, Table 105-1). Core clinical sign is jaundice; patients may report dark urine; splenomegaly is common as a preferential site of hemolysis, the liver may enlarge, and pigment gallstones are common with chronic hemolysis (p.791). Laboratory hallmarks: increased reticulocytes (both percentage and the more definitive absolute count), raised MCV with macrocytes/polychromasia on smear, increased unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin and AST, raised LDH, and reduced-to-absent haptoglobin (p.791, Table 105-2). Extravascular hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin and urobilinogen; intravascular hemolysis is signalled by hemoglobinuria (often with hemosiderinuria), free plasma hemoglobin, markedly raised LDH (up to ~10x), and low haptoglobin, with bilirubin only mildly elevated (p.791, Table 105-2). A positive broad-spectrum direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is on its own almost diagnostic of autoimmune HA; the broad reagent detects bound immunoglobulin and/or complement (C3 fragments) on red cells (p.801). Warm AIHA (mostly IgG, optimal 37C) causes predominantly extravascular hemolysis with spherocytes; cold agglutinin disease (mostly IgM anti-I, optimal 4-30C) activates complement causing intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuria plus Kupffer-cell extravascular destruction in the liver (p.801-803, Fig. 105-9, Table 105-8). Compensated hemolysis: a brisk EPO-driven erythropoietic response can fully offset red-cell destruction so an inherited hemolytic condition may present without anemia; it can decompensate in pregnancy, folate deficiency, or renal failure (p.792). Schistocytes (fragmented/helmet cells) on smear indicating microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) - consider TTP, HUS, and DIC; an emergency requiring urgent evaluation (p.799, 801, Table 105-7) Abrupt severe drop in hemoglobin (to as low as 4 g/dL within days) in warm AIHA with jaundice and splenomegaly - a medical emergency (p.801) Acute renal failure - the most serious threat from acute hemolytic attacks in adults (e.g., G6PD-related), and a predictor of poor AIHA outcome (p.799, 801) Hemoglobinuria signalling intravascular hemolysis (mismatched transfusion, PNH, clostridial sepsis, march hemoglobinuria, favism) (p.801, Table 105-7) Evans syndrome (AIHA plus autoimmune thrombocytopenia) signals high-risk disease and may indicate underlying immune deficiency (p.801) Mismatched (usually ABO-incompatible) blood transfusion causing abrupt intravascular hemolysis (p.801, Table 105-7) Clostridium perfringens sepsis causing life-threatening intravascular hemolysis (p.801) Neglecting the reticulocyte count, a key early clue to a hemolytic mechanism (p.791) Screening (semiquantitative) G6PD tests give falsely normal results immediately after a hemolytic attack because the oldest deficient cells are destroyed and young reticulocytes have higher G6PD - use a quantitative assay; female heterozygotes may also be missed (p.799-800) Dismissing Coombs-negative AIHA as not serious - high-affinity antibody can cause severe disease with few bound molecules; false-positive Coombs can follow transfusion, organ transplant, or Ig/anti-lymphocyte products (p.801-802) Assuming an inherited hemolytic disorder always causes anemia - compensated hemolysis can be normo-hemoglobinemic until decompensation (p.792) In cold agglutinin disease, prednisone and splenectomy are ineffective (unlike warm AIHA), and transfused (I-positive) red cells survive no longer than the patient's; the blood bag and patient extremities must be kept warm (p.803) Misattributing favism to fava bean pollen inhalation (it does not cause favism) or to other beans (which are safe) (p.799) The mature red cell loses mitochondria and ribosomes, leaving anaerobic glycolysis (Embden-Meyerhof pathway) as the sole source of ATP and the hexose-monophosphate shunt (via G6PD-generated NADPH and reduced glutathione) as defense against oxidant stress; damaged proteins cannot be replaced, so any metabolic failure ultimately damages the membrane or the cation pump and shortens the ~120-day life span. Senescent or damaged red cells expose band-3 neoantigens, become opsonized, and are phagocytosed by splenic, hepatic, and other macrophages (extravascular hemolysis); this senescence process is accelerated in many HAs. The essential common feature is increased red-cell turnover; when destruction outpaces marrow production, anemia results. Chronic intravascular hemolysis causes iron loss via hemoglobinuria, whereas chronic extravascular hemolysis (especially if transfused) tends toward iron overload and, untreated, secondary hemochromatosis (p.791-792). Transient hemolysis usually has no long-term consequences beyond increased erythropoietic (folate) requirement; recurrent or persistent hemolysis predisposes to pigment gallstones, splenomegaly with hypersplenism (neutropenia/thrombocytopenia), and, with chronic extravascular hemolysis or repeated transfusion, iron overload progressing to secondary hemochromatosis affecting liver and heart. Warm AIHA carries ~5-10% mortality even with appropriate management; predictors of worse outcome/relapse include Evans syndrome, hemoglobin <6 g/dL, acute renal failure, infection, and high-affinity antibody. G6PD-related acute hemolysis generally resolves fully once the trigger is removed and in the absence of comorbidity, with full recovery from renal failure the rule when there is no prior kidney disease (p.792, 799, 801). No single formal grading. Severity is gauged clinically by the hemoglobin level and tempo (mild compensated hemolysis without anemia through to abrupt severe drops to ~4 g/dL in AIHA) and by the site of hemolysis: intravascular hemolysis is signalled by hemoglobinuria, free plasma hemoglobin, LDH up to ~10x normal, and absent haptoglobin, whereas extravascular hemolysis chiefly raises unconjugated bilirubin and urobilinogen. High-risk markers in AIHA include hemoglobin <6 g/dL, acute renal failure, infection, and Evans syndrome (p.791-792, 801, Tables 105-2, 105-7).

Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn — HDN, hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, HDFN, erythroblastosis fetalis Non-immune hydrops fetalis Hereditary red cell membrane or enzyme defects (e.g. spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency) Sepsis-associated haemolysis or jaundice Cephalohaematoma or extravascular blood breakdown causing jaundice Physiological or breast-milk jaundice Twin-to-twin transfusion and other causes of neonatal anaemia Maternal and infant blood group and antibody screening Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test on the newborn Serial total and unconjugated bilirubin measurements Full blood count with reticulocyte count and blood film Fetal middle cerebral artery Doppler to assess for fetal anaemia antenatally Follow-up haemoglobin to detect late anaemia Immune-mediated haemolysis of fetal or neonatal red cells caused by maternal antibodies crossing the placenta and targeting fetal red cell antigens inherited from the father. Rhesus (anti-D) disease was historically the most severe form; ABO incompatibility is now a more common but generally milder cause, and other minor blood-group antibodies can also be responsible. Rh disease typically requires prior maternal sensitisation, so it usually spares the first pregnancy and worsens with subsequent affected pregnancies, whereas ABO disease can affect a first-born. Severe fetal anaemia can cause hydrops fetalis with generalised oedema, effusions, hepatosplenomegaly, and heart failure. In the newborn the dominant problem is rapidly rising unconjugated bilirubin from ongoing haemolysis, which can appear within the first day of life. A positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test on the infant supports immune haemolysis, along with anaemia, reticulocytosis, and a rising bilirubin. Rh disease is largely preventable by giving anti-D immunoglobulin to at-risk Rh-negative mothers to prevent sensitisation. Management ranges from monitoring and phototherapy for hyperbilirubinaemia to exchange transfusion for severe or rapidly rising bilirubin, and intrauterine transfusion for severe fetal anaemia. Late anaemia can develop over the following weeks as haemolysis and marrow suppression continue, so follow-up haemoglobin monitoring is important. Hydrops fetalis with severe anaemia and heart failure Rapidly rising or very high unconjugated bilirubin threatening bilirubin encephalopathy Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (lethargy, poor feeding, hypertonia, abnormal cry) Severe or late anaemia requiring transfusion Underestimating ABO disease because it can affect a first-born and cause significant jaundice Failing to monitor bilirubin closely and intervene before it reaches neurotoxic levels Overlooking late anaemia in the weeks after birth once early jaundice has settled Missing an opportunity for anti-D prophylaxis in an at-risk mother Attributing early jaundice to physiological causes when haemolysis is occurring When fetal red cells carrying a paternally inherited antigen absent in the mother enter the maternal circulation, the mother may form IgG alloantibodies. These IgG antibodies cross the placenta, bind fetal red cells, and cause their destruction, chiefly in the fetal spleen. The resulting anaemia stimulates extramedullary haematopoiesis and, when severe, causes high-output cardiac failure, hepatic dysfunction, hypoalbuminaemia, and hydrops. After birth, loss of placental clearance means the newborn must conjugate the large bilirubin load from continuing haemolysis with an immature liver, producing rapidly rising unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia that risks bilirubin neurotoxicity. With antenatal surveillance, intrauterine transfusion for severe fetal anaemia, and neonatal phototherapy or exchange transfusion, outcomes are generally good. Prophylactic anti-D has dramatically reduced severe Rh disease. Prognosis worsens if severe hyperbilirubinaemia progresses to kernicterus or if profound fetal anaemia and hydrops are untreated.

Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction — AHTR, acute haemolytic reaction, ABO-incompatible transfusion reaction, immediate haemolytic transfusion reaction Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction Bacterial contamination of the transfused unit with septic reaction Transfusion-related acute lung injury Anaphylactic transfusion reaction Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction Non-immune haemolysis from mechanical or thermal red-cell damage Immediate clerical recheck of patient identity, unit label and compatibility documentation Direct antiglobulin test on a post-transfusion sample and repeat ABO grouping and crossmatch on donor and recipient Markers of haemolysis including lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, bilirubin and a blood film Free plasma and urinary haemoglobin to confirm intravascular haemolysis Coagulation screen, fibrinogen and platelet count to detect disseminated intravascular coagulation Renal function and urine output monitoring for acute kidney injury Most severe cases follow ABO-incompatible transfusion, where recipient anti-A or anti-B antibodies bind donor red cells and trigger complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis Classic features are fever, rigors, loin or back pain, a feeling of impending doom, hypotension, and haemoglobinuria appearing early during or soon after transfusion The single most important action is to stop the transfusion immediately, maintain venous access, and provide supportive care with fluids to preserve renal perfusion Disseminated intravascular coagulation and acute kidney injury are the feared complications and drive much of the mortality Most fatal reactions arise from clerical error and misidentification of the patient or sample rather than from any failure of the laboratory crossmatch Send the implicated unit and fresh patient samples back to the laboratory for a clerical recheck, repeat group and crossmatch, and direct antiglobulin test In an anaesthetised or unconscious patient, unexplained hypotension, bleeding from wound sites, and haemoglobinuria may be the only clues Hypotension, rigors and loin pain developing within minutes of starting a transfusion Haemoglobinuria with oliguria signalling evolving acute kidney injury Oozing from cannula and wound sites suggesting disseminated intravascular coagulation Cardiovascular collapse in an anaesthetised patient with unexplained haemoglobinuria Attributing early fever to a benign febrile reaction and continuing the transfusion Failing to perform a clerical recheck, which most often reveals the underlying identification error Overlooking haemoglobinuria and evolving renal impairment in a sedated or ventilated patient Delaying supportive fluid resuscitation while awaiting laboratory confirmation An acute haemolytic transfusion reaction occurs when preformed recipient antibodies bind antigens on transfused donor red cells. In ABO incompatibility, naturally occurring IgM anti-A or anti-B fixes complement efficiently, driving rapid intravascular haemolysis with release of free haemoglobin and red-cell stroma. Complement activation and the resulting cytokine surge produce fever, vasodilatation and hypotension, while procoagulant material triggers disseminated intravascular coagulation. Free haemoglobin and reduced renal perfusion combine to cause acute tubular injury and kidney failure. The severity broadly tracks the volume of incompatible cells infused and the complement-fixing capacity of the antibody involved. Outcome depends on the volume of incompatible blood infused and the speed of recognition; prompt cessation and supportive care are often survivable, but large-volume ABO-incompatible transfusions carry a high risk of disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute kidney injury and death.

Haemolytic uraemic syndrome — HUS, hemolytic uremic syndrome, atypical HUS, aHUS, STEC-HUS Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura Disseminated intravascular coagulation Severe pre-eclampsia / HELLP syndrome Malignant hypertension causing microangiopathy Systemic vasculitis or scleroderma renal crisis Drug-induced thrombotic microangiopathy Full blood count and blood film for schistocytes and thrombocytopenia Haemolysis markers: LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin, and a direct antiglobulin test (expected negative) Renal function, urinalysis, and monitoring of urine output Stool testing and culture for Shiga-toxin-producing organisms ADAMTS13 activity to exclude thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura Complement studies and genetic testing for regulatory protein defects in suspected atypical HUS A thrombotic microangiopathy defined by the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury The typical form follows a Shiga-toxin-producing enteric infection (often E. coli O157:H7), classically preceded by bloody diarrhoea, and predominantly affects children Atypical HUS results from dysregulated activation of the alternative complement pathway, is often familial, and tends to relapse and progress to end-stage renal disease The blood film shows fragmented red cells (schistocytes) with a raised LDH, low haptoglobin, and a negative direct antiglobulin test, indicating mechanical (non-immune) haemolysis Renal involvement dominates the clinical picture, distinguishing HUS from thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, in which neurological features and severe ADAMTS13 deficiency predominate Measuring ADAMTS13 activity helps separate TTP (severely reduced) from HUS (usually normal or only modestly reduced), which is critical because treatments differ Shiga-toxin-associated HUS is largely managed with meticulous supportive care and dialysis when needed, and antibiotics are generally avoided as they may worsen toxin release Complement-mediated atypical HUS responds to terminal complement blockade, which has substantially improved renal and overall outcomes Rapidly progressive acute kidney injury with oliguria or anuria requiring urgent dialysis Severe thrombocytopenia with active bleeding Neurological deterioration raising concern for overlapping TTP or CNS involvement Hyperkalaemia, fluid overload, or refractory hypertension as life-threatening complications of renal failure Confusing HUS with TTP and delaying the correct treatment; ADAMTS13 testing helps distinguish them Giving antibiotics in Shiga-toxin-associated HUS, which may increase toxin release and worsen disease Attributing thrombocytopenia and anaemia to sepsis or DIC without examining the film for schistocytes Failing to consider atypical HUS in relapsing or familial disease and missing the opportunity for complement inhibition Transfusing platelets reflexively, which can aggravate microvascular thrombosis HUS is a thrombotic microangiopathy in which endothelial injury triggers platelet-rich microthrombi in small vessels, especially the renal microvasculature. In Shiga-toxin-associated disease, toxin absorbed from the gut binds glomerular and endothelial cells, causing injury, platelet activation, and microvascular thrombosis. In atypical HUS, uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway, from inherited or acquired defects in complement regulatory proteins, drives endothelial damage. The resulting microthrombi mechanically shear passing red cells (producing schistocytes and haemolysis), consume platelets (causing thrombocytopenia), and obstruct renal perfusion (causing acute kidney injury). Shiga-toxin-associated HUS in children often recovers with supportive care, though a minority sustain chronic kidney damage; atypical, complement-mediated HUS historically carried a high risk of end-stage renal disease and death, but outcomes have improved markedly with complement-blocking therapy.

haemorrhage, which may follow minor or no recognised trauma Airway-threatening neck, throat or retropharyngeal bleeding Compartment syndrome from an expanding muscle haematoma Loss of response to factor replacement suggesting an inhibitor Missing von Willebrand disease as the reason for a low factor VIII level Overlooking an inhibitor when bleeding fails to respond to appropriate replacement Giving intramuscular injections or arterial punctures that provoke deep bleeding Delaying treatment of a suspected head bleed to await imaging or laboratory confirmation Haemophilia A is caused by mutations in F8 on the X chromosome that reduce the activity of coagulation factor VIII, a cofactor that greatly accelerates factor IXa-mediated activation of factor X within the intrinsic tenase complex. Without adequate factor VIII the propagation phase of coagulation is impaired, so thrombin generation on the platelet surface is markedly reduced and the fibrin clot forms slowly and is unstable. Because the initial platelet plug still forms, bleeding is typically delayed and occurs into joints and deep tissues; repeated haemarthroses cause synovial inflammation and progressive destructive arthropathy. With prophylactic replacement or modern non-factor therapies most patients achieve near-normal life expectancy and greatly reduced joint damage, but inhibitor development and established arthropathy remain important sources of morbidity.

Haemophilia B (factor IX, Christmas disease) — haemophilia B, factor IX deficiency, F9, Christmas disease Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) Von Willebrand disease Other vitamin K-dependent factor deficiencies or warfarin effect Acquired factor IX deficiency (rare autoantibodies) Other intrinsic-pathway factor deficiencies (XI, XII) Disseminated intravascular coagulation Activated partial thromboplastin time, prothrombin time and platelet count Mixing study to distinguish factor deficiency from an inhibitor Factor IX activity assay to confirm diagnosis and grade severity Factor VIII assay to differentiate from haemophilia A Factor IX inhibitor assay when replacement response is poor F9 genetic testing for diagnosis and carrier detection An X-linked recessive deficiency of coagulation factor IX from mutations in F9, affecting mainly males with females usually carriers The bleeding phenotype is clinically indistinguishable from haemophilia A, with haemarthroses, deep muscle bleeds and delayed post-traumatic or surgical bleeding It cannot be separated from haemophilia A on clinical grounds or the screening coagulation tests alone; specific factor assays are required The screening pattern is a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time with normal prothrombin time and normal platelet count A specific factor IX assay confirms the diagnosis and grades severity, and a normal factor VIII level distinguishes it from haemophilia A Inhibitor (neutralising alloantibody) development is less common than in haemophilia A but can be associated with allergic or anaphylactic reactions to factor IX Management uses factor IX replacement or non-factor haemostatic therapies and antifibrinolytics, with prophylaxis in severe disease to prevent joint damage Intracranial haemorrhage, sometimes after minimal trauma Airway-threatening neck or throat bleeding Compartment syndrome from an expanding muscle haematoma Allergic or anaphylactic reactions accompanying inhibitor development against factor IX Assuming a haemophilia diagnosis is type A without a specific factor IX assay Missing an inhibitor and its associated allergic reactions when replacement stops working Attributing a low factor IX solely to vitamin K deficiency or anticoagulation without full assessment Giving intramuscular injections that provoke deep bleeding Haemophilia B is caused by mutations in F9 on the X chromosome that reduce the activity of coagulation factor IX, a vitamin K-dependent serine protease. Activated factor IX, with factor VIII as cofactor, forms the intrinsic tenase complex that activates factor X on the platelet surface. Deficiency of factor IX therefore impairs the same propagation step of coagulation as factor VIII deficiency, reducing thrombin generation and producing a slow, unstable clot. As in haemophilia A the initial platelet plug forms normally, so bleeding is delayed and occurs into joints and deep tissues, and recurrent haemarthroses drive progressive arthropathy. With prophylaxis using factor IX or modern non-factor therapy, most patients have near-normal life expectancy and much reduced joint damage, though inhibitors, when they occur, can be complicated by allergic reactions and are harder to manage.

planning Excessive bleeding after surgery or trauma at fibrinolytic-rich sites (oral, nasal, genitourinary) Unexpected postpartum haemorrhage Bleeding disproportionate to the measured factor level Rare inhibitor development, particularly in severely deficient patients after replacement Predicting bleeding risk from the factor XI level, which correlates poorly with clinical bleeding Confusing an isolated prolonged aPTT with a non-bleeding contact-factor deficiency or a lupus anticoagulant Over-transfusing plasma products and risking volume overload or unnecessary exposure Failing to plan haemostatic cover before high-risk procedures at fibrinolytic sites Haemophilia C results from mutations in F11 that reduce the activity of coagulation factor XI, a component of the intrinsic pathway that, once activated, amplifies thrombin generation partly through activation of factor IX. Its role is chiefly in reinforcing and sustaining the clot rather than initiating haemostasis, which explains why bleeding is usually milder and less consistent than with factor VIII or IX deficiency. Because factor XI contributes to protecting clots against fibrinolysis, bleeding is particularly prone to occur at sites rich in local fibrinolytic activity, and the poor correlation between factor level and bleeding suggests additional modifying haemostatic factors. Prognosis is generally good, with many patients only bleeding in response to surgery or trauma, and careful individualised peri-procedural management usually prevents serious bleeding.

Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome — HFRS, Old World hantavirus infection, Hantaan virus infection, Puumala virus infection, nephropathia epidemica, epidemic haemorrhagic fever Leptospirosis with renal involvement Acute glomerulonephritis or other causes of acute kidney injury Sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation Other viral haemorrhagic fevers depending on geography Thrombotic microangiopathy (haemolytic uraemic syndrome or thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura) Acute pyelonephritis Hantavirus serology for IgM and IgG antibodies RT-PCR for viral RNA during the early febrile phase Renal function tests, urinalysis, and quantification of proteinuria and haematuria Full blood count monitoring platelets and haematocrit Coagulation studies to assess for disseminated intravascular coagulation Ultrasound of the kidneys showing enlarged, oedematous kidneys in nephropathia epidemica Caused by Old World hantaviruses (Hantaan, Seoul, Dobrava, and the milder Puumala causing nephropathia epidemica) acquired by inhaling aerosolised rodent excreta across Europe and Asia The classic course progresses through febrile, hypotensive, oliguric, diuretic, and convalescent phases, though milder Puumala infection may not show all stages Capillary leak drives retroperitoneal and renal interstitial oedema, and acute kidney injury with proteinuria and haematuria is the hallmark, distinguishing it from the pulmonary-predominant New World disease Thrombocytopenia, elevated haematocrit from plasma leak, and haemorrhagic manifestations such as conjunctival haemorrhage and petechiae are common Sudden severe lumbar and abdominal pain with blurred or transient myopia is a characteristic clue in Puumala infection Management is supportive with careful fluid and electrolyte balance and renal replacement therapy when needed; some authorities have used ribavirin for severe early Hantaan disease Diagnosis is confirmed by hantavirus serology and RT-PCR, interpreted alongside a rodent-exposure history in an endemic area Progression to anuria or hyperkalaemia requiring urgent renal replacement therapy Shock during the hypotensive phase from capillary leak Significant haemorrhage with worsening thrombocytopenia Overhydration precipitating pulmonary oedema during the oliguric phase Neurological deterioration suggesting central nervous system involvement or severe electrolyte disturbance Missing the diagnosis in the febrile phase before renal features appear Aggressive fluid loading during the oliguric phase, precipitating volume overload Attributing acute kidney injury solely to sepsis or nephrotoxins without considering hantavirus exposure Underestimating the transition to the diuretic phase, risking hypovolaemia and electrolyte loss Overlooking the rodent-exposure or rural travel history Inhaled virus from persistently infected rodent reservoirs infects vascular endothelium, and an immune-mediated increase in vascular permeability produces plasma leakage. In contrast to the pulmonary tropism of New World strains, Old World hantaviruses preferentially injure the renal microvasculature and interstitium, causing acute kidney injury with oliguria followed by a polyuric recovery phase. Platelet consumption and endothelial dysfunction underlie the bleeding tendency, and severity ranges from mild (Puumala) to severe (Hantaan and Dobrava). Puumala-associated nephropathia epidemica is usually self-limiting with full renal recovery, whereas Hantaan and Dobrava infections carry appreciable mortality and greater risk of severe acute kidney injury; most survivors recover normal renal function.

bleeding Aggressive banding or surgery in patients with portal hypertension or coagulopathy Overlooking thrombosis or strangulation as the cause of acute severe pain Haemorrhoids result from abnormal engorgement and downward displacement of the normal anal cushions, which are vascular submucosal structures that contribute to continence. Chronic straining, constipation, and raised intra-abdominal pressure disrupt the supporting connective tissue, allowing the cushions to enlarge, congest, and prolapse. The classical sites are the left lateral, right anterior, and right posterior positions. Bleeding is arteriovenous in origin, giving the characteristic bright red colour. Thrombosis of external components or prolapsed internal haemorrhoids produces acute pain, and long-standing prolapse can cause mucous discharge and pruritus. Most haemorrhoids respond to conservative measures or office procedures with good symptom control, though recurrence is possible. Surgical treatment of advanced disease is effective but may cause post-operative pain and, rarely, incontinence or stenosis.

associated with chronic pancreatitis or a pseudocyst Stopping the workup after a normal standard endoscopy Overlooking a raised amylase as a clue Delaying angiographic embolisation in a patient with a known pseudoaneurysm Haemosuccus pancreaticus occurs when a peripancreatic artery, most commonly the splenic artery, develops a pseudoaneurysm as a result of enzymatic erosion by activated pancreatic secretions, typically in chronic pancreatitis or adjacent to a pseudocyst. Rupture of the pseudoaneurysm into the pancreatic duct allows blood to track along the duct and empty through the ampulla into the duodenum. Because the bleeding decompresses intermittently and its source is deep and remote from the mucosa, standard endoscopy frequently fails to reveal an obvious lesion, and the episodic pattern of pain and haemorrhage reflects transient ductal obstruction by clot. Untreated rupture of a visceral artery pseudoaneurysm carries a substantial mortality, but timely angiographic embolisation controls most cases; the overall outlook is also shaped by the severity of the underlying pancreatic disease.

drainage from unmasked hypovolaemia Respiratory compromise from lung compression and mediastinal shift Features suggesting great-vessel injury as the bleeding source Draining a massive haemothorax without simultaneously restoring blood volume Confusing it with tension pneumothorax by not distinguishing dullness from hyperresonance Failing to recognise ongoing bleeding that mandates surgical exploration Using crystalloid alone rather than blood products in significant haemorrhage Overlooking a great-vessel injury as the source Haemothorax is accumulation of blood in the pleural space, usually from injury to the chest wall vessels (such as intercostal or internal mammary arteries), the lung, or the great vessels. The pleural cavity can hold a large proportion of the circulating blood volume, so bleeding into it causes hypovolaemic shock. At the same time, the collected blood compresses the ipsilateral lung and can shift the mediastinum, impairing ventilation and, when large, venous return. Thus a massive haemothorax produces the dual insult of haemorrhage and respiratory compromise, and the blood must be evacuated while the circulation is restored. Prognosis depends on the rate and source of bleeding and associated injuries. Prompt drainage with adequate transfusion allows recovery in many cases, while massive or ongoing haemorrhage that is not controlled surgically carries high mortality.

Hendra virus infection — Hendra virus disease, HeV infection, equine morbillivirus infection Nipah virus infection Community-acquired or viral pneumonia progressing to acute respiratory distress Viral encephalitis from other causes such as herpes simplex or arboviruses Bacterial meningoencephalitis Influenza and other severe respiratory viral infections Q fever and other zoonoses with an animal-contact history RT-PCR on respiratory secretions, blood, or cerebrospinal fluid in a high-containment laboratory Serology for henipavirus-specific antibodies Cerebrospinal fluid analysis when encephalitis is suspected Neuroimaging with magnetic resonance imaging for encephalitic changes Chest imaging and oxygenation assessment for pneumonitis Liver and renal function tests to gauge systemic involvement A zoonotic henipavirus (closely related to Nipah virus) reported from eastern Australia, with fruit bats (flying foxes) as the natural reservoir Human infection has occurred through close contact with infected horses, which act as an amplifying host after acquiring the virus from bat contamination Presentations range from an influenza-like illness to severe pneumonitis and encephalitis, and a late relapsing encephalitis has been described months to years after the initial infection The clinical overlap with Nipah virus makes henipaviruses a recognised cause of severe febrile encephalitic illness with high case fatality There is no licensed specific antiviral or human vaccine; management is intensive supportive care, and a monoclonal antibody has been used experimentally as post-exposure prophylaxis An equine vaccine is central to prevention by interrupting the horse-to-human transmission chain Diagnosis relies on RT-PCR and serology performed in high-containment laboratories because the virus requires enhanced biosafety handling Altered consciousness, seizures, or focal deficits indicating encephalitis Progressive respiratory failure from severe pneumonitis History of contact with a sick or dead horse in an endemic region Neurological deterioration weeks to years after an initial illness suggesting relapsing encephalitis Any suspected case requiring immediate isolation and notification of public health authorities Failing to elicit a horse-contact history in a patient with severe febrile illness in an endemic area Underestimating the risk of delayed encephalitis after apparent recovery Handling specimens without appropriate high-containment biosafety precautions Delaying notification of veterinary and public health authorities to interrupt the transmission chain Confusing the illness with ordinary community-acquired pneumonia or encephalitis and missing the zoonotic link Hendra virus is a henipavirus maintained in flying-fox reservoirs, which shed virus in urine and other secretions that can contaminate the environment and infect horses. Horses develop severe respiratory and neurological disease and transmit the virus to humans through close contact with respiratory secretions and body fluids. In humans the virus is endotheliotropic and neurotropic, causing systemic vasculitis, pneumonitis, and encephalitis. Persistence within the central nervous system can produce a delayed relapsing encephalitis long after apparent recovery. Human Hendra virus infection is rare but carries a high case fatality, and survivors may suffer neurological sequelae or a late relapsing encephalitis, so long-term follow-up is warranted.

Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) — HSP, IgA vasculitis, anaphylactoid purpura, Henoch-Schonlein syndrome Meningococcaemia / sepsis with purpura Immune thrombocytopenia and other bleeding disorders Haemolytic uraemic syndrome Acute abdomen from other causes (e.g. appendicitis) Other systemic vasculitides Systemic lupus erythematosus Urinalysis for haematuria and proteinuria (repeated over follow-up) Blood pressure measurement Full blood count and coagulation studies to confirm normal platelets and exclude bleeding disorders Renal function and serum albumin Abdominal ultrasound if intussusception or significant gut involvement is suspected Skin or renal biopsy showing IgA deposition in atypical or severe cases The most common small-vessel vasculitis of childhood, typically affecting children 3-10 years, often following an upper respiratory infection. The classic tetrad is palpable purpura (predominantly on the buttocks and lower limbs), arthritis/arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal involvement. The rash is non-thrombocytopenic palpable purpura, distinguishing it from bleeding disorders; platelet count and coagulation are normal. Gastrointestinal involvement causes colicky abdominal pain and can be complicated by intussusception, which is typically ileo-ileal. Renal involvement ranges from isolated microscopic haematuria to nephritis; it is the main determinant of long-term prognosis. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by palpable purpura plus at least one of abdominal pain, arthritis, or renal involvement; biopsy shows IgA deposition when needed. Most cases are self-limiting; management is largely supportive with analgesia and hydration, and corticosteroids are considered for severe abdominal or other significant organ involvement. Prolonged urinalysis and blood pressure monitoring are needed after recovery to detect delayed or progressive nephritis. Severe abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, or signs of intussusception or bowel ischaemia Gastrointestinal bleeding Hypertension, oliguria, heavy proteinuria, or rising creatinine indicating significant nephritis Scrotal pain or swelling (testicular involvement mimicking torsion) Purpura in an unwell, febrile, toxic child raising concern for meningococcaemia Confusing the purpura with a bleeding disorder and missing that platelets are normal Failing to monitor urinalysis and blood pressure after the acute illness, missing delayed nephritis Overlooking intussusception as a cause of worsening abdominal pain Attributing all abdominal pain to HSP and missing a surgical abdomen Henoch-Schonlein purpura is an immune-complex mediated small-vessel vasculitis characterised by deposition of IgA1-containing immune complexes in the walls of small vessels of the skin, gut, joints, and kidney. This triggers a leukocytoclastic vasculitis with neutrophilic infiltration and vessel wall inflammation, producing the palpable purpura and visceral manifestations. In the kidney, mesangial IgA deposition causes a glomerulonephritis histologically similar to IgA nephropathy. A preceding infection or other antigenic trigger is thought to initiate the abnormal IgA response in susceptible children. Most children recover completely within weeks, though relapses can occur; long-term outcome is dictated by renal involvement, with a small proportion developing chronic kidney disease, so renal follow-up is essential.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia — HIT, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and thrombosis, HITT Sepsis-associated or drug-induced thrombocytopenia Disseminated intravascular coagulation Post-transfusion or dilutional thrombocytopenia Immune thrombocytopenia Thrombotic microangiopathy such as TTP or HUS Serial platelet counts with calculation of the 4Ts score Anti-platelet factor 4/heparin immunoassay
