with weight loss indicating heavy infection Lack of response to therapy prompting diagnostic review Confusing the eggs with those of opisthorchiid liver flukes owing to close morphological similarity Missing light infections on a single stool examination Dismissing non-specific gastrointestinal complaints as functional in endemic areas Neglecting the possibility of egg embolisation when unexplained cardiac or neurological features arise Heterophyes heterophyes is a minute heterophyid trematode whose life cycle involves brackish-water snails and euryhaline fish that harbour infective metacercariae. Humans acquire infection by consuming raw, salted or lightly cooked fish. Excysted larvae mature into small adult flukes that nestle deep among the villi of the small intestine, provoking localised mucosal inflammation, villous atrophy and superficial ulceration, which in heavy infection contributes to diarrhoea and mild malabsorption. Eggs deposited in the mucosa can occasionally penetrate lymphatics or vessels and embolise to distant sites such as the myocardium, spinal cord or brain, where they excite granulomatous reactions with potentially grave consequences. Eggs passed in faeces perpetuate the cycle by contaminating water. Intestinal heterophyiasis has an excellent prognosis and clears rapidly with anthelmintic treatment; the uncommon cardiac or neurological ectopic forms carry a far more guarded outlook.

heterotaxy syndrome — situs ambiguus, isomerism, left-right axis malformation situs inversus totalis situs solitus with isolated congenital heart disease asplenia syndrome (right isomerism) polysplenia syndrome (left isomerism) congenitally corrected transposition primary ciliary dyskinesia isolated interrupted inferior vena cava detailed segmental echocardiography including venous and atrial appendage assessment abdominal ultrasound for spleen number, hepatic symmetry and vascular anatomy chest radiograph and cross-sectional imaging for bronchial morphology and situs peripheral blood film for Howell-Jolly bodies indicating functional asplenia cardiac MRI or CT angiography for complex venous and arterial connections twelve-lead ECG and Holter monitoring for conduction disease and heart block genetic evaluation for laterality and ciliopathy genes Heterotaxy describes abnormal arrangement of thoraco-abdominal organs across the left-right axis that is neither normal (situs solitus) nor complete mirror-image (situs inversus), reflecting failure to establish normal asymmetry. It is broadly divided into right atrial isomerism (asplenia, bilateral right-sidedness) and left atrial isomerism (polysplenia, bilateral left-sidedness), each with characteristic cardiac and visceral patterns. Complex congenital heart disease is the rule rather than the exception, so any infant with discordant visceral situs on imaging needs urgent detailed echocardiography. Bronchial and atrial appendage morphology are the most reliable anatomical markers of isomerism, more dependable than spleen number alone. Right isomerism tends to produce severe cyanotic lesions with common atrioventricular canal, single ventricle and anomalous pulmonary venous drainage, often with functional asplenia. Left isomerism is associated with polysplenia, interruption of the inferior vena cava with azygos continuation, biliary atresia and heart block from an abnormal or absent sinus node. Intestinal malrotation is common in both forms, and an apparently well child can present acutely with midgut volvulus. Functional asplenia mandates lifelong sepsis prophylaxis and vaccination, while conduction disease in left isomerism may require pacing. neonatal cyanosis or shock from duct-dependent complex congenital heart disease bilious vomiting suggesting midgut volvulus from associated malrotation fever or overwhelming sepsis in a child with functional asplenia bradycardia or syncope from complete heart block in left isomerism progressive jaundice raising concern for associated biliary atresia Relying on spleen number rather than bronchial and atrial appendage morphology to classify isomerism. Missing intestinal malrotation until the child presents with volvulus. Failing to institute antibiotic prophylaxis and vaccination in functional asplenia. Overlooking inferior vena cava interruption during central line placement or catheterisation. Underappreciating progressive conduction disease in left isomerism. Heterotaxy results from disruption of the molecular pathways that normally break embryonic left-right symmetry. Motile cilia at the primitive node generate leftward nodal flow that is sensed by peripheral immotile cilia, triggering asymmetric activation of the Nodal-Lefty-Pitx2 cascade that instructs sidedness of the heart, gut, spleen and vasculature. When this signalling fails, organ primordia default towards a symmetric or randomised state, so paired structures adopt the same morphology on both sides (isomerism) rather than distinct left and right patterns. Bilateral right-sidedness produces morphologically right structures duplicated (trilobed lungs, eparterial bronchi, absent spleen, midline liver), typically with severe conotruncal and atrioventricular septal defects. Bilateral left-sidedness produces duplicated left structures (bilobed lungs, hyparterial bronchi, multiple spleens, interrupted inferior vena cava) with a tendency to conduction abnormalities. Many cases involve ciliary or laterality gene defects, linking heterotaxy mechanistically to the ciliopathy spectrum. Outcome is dictated by the severity of associated cardiac malformation and, in right isomerism, by the added risk of overwhelming infection from asplenia; right isomerism generally carries the poorer prognosis. Multidisciplinary cardiac surgical staging, malrotation surveillance and infection prophylaxis substantially improve survival though many require complex single-ventricle palliation.

Heterotopic ossification — HO, myositis ossificans, ectopic bone formation Deep vein thrombosis Cellulitis or septic arthritis Fracture or occult bony injury Tumoral calcinosis or soft-tissue calcification Osteosarcoma or other bone tumour Complex regional pain syndrome Serial serum alkaline phosphatase to support diagnosis and monitor activity Triple-phase bone scintigraphy for early and sensitive detection of immature lesions Plain radiographs to characterise and follow established, mineralised bone Ultrasound or CT for further definition and surgical planning Doppler ultrasound and inflammatory markers to exclude thrombosis and infection Heterotopic ossification is the formation of mature lamellar bone within soft tissues where bone does not normally exist, most often around large joints It is common after spinal cord injury, traumatic brain injury, major joint surgery, burns, and severe trauma, typically appearing within weeks to a few months of the inciting event Early presentation can mimic infection or thrombosis, with localised swelling, warmth, erythema, pain, and progressive loss of joint range of motion A markedly raised serum alkaline phosphatase supports early disease but is non-specific and can be normal, so imaging is important Plain radiographs are often normal early; triple-phase bone scan is the most sensitive method for detecting immature heterotopic bone before it is visible on x-ray Maintaining joint range of motion through careful therapy is central to management, alongside prophylaxis in high-risk patients using measures such as NSAIDs and, in selected cases, radiation Bisphosphonates may be used to limit mineralisation of immature lesions as part of medical management Surgical excision is reserved for mature, well-established lesions that significantly limit function, ideally once bone activity has settled to reduce recurrence risk The most disabling consequence is ankylosis of a joint, which can severely impair positioning, mobility, and self-care Presentation mimicking deep vein thrombosis or septic arthritis that must be excluded urgently Rapidly progressive joint ankylosis threatening irreversible loss of function Ossification compressing a peripheral nerve or vessel Skin breakdown or pressure injury developing over a fixed, ossified joint Attributing early swelling and warmth solely to thrombosis or infection and missing the diagnosis Relying on early plain radiographs, which are frequently negative in immature disease Aggressive forced manipulation of the affected joint, which may aggravate the lesion Operating on immature, metabolically active bone, increasing the risk of recurrence Neglecting prophylaxis in high-risk patients such as those with spinal cord or brain injury Heterotopic ossification involves aberrant differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into osteoblasts within soft tissue, driven by a combination of an osteogenic local environment, tissue injury and inflammation, and neurogenic signalling in patients with central nervous system injury. Inflammatory mediators and bone morphogenetic proteins promote the formation of an osteoid matrix that subsequently mineralises into mature bone. The process evolves from an early inflammatory and immature phase through progressive mineralisation to eventual mature lamellar bone. Many lesions stabilise without causing major functional loss, but a significant proportion progress to restrict joint movement, and severe cases cause complete ankylosis. Outcomes are improved by early recognition, preserving range of motion, and appropriately timed prophylaxis or surgery.

Hexokinase deficiency — red-cell hexokinase deficiency, HK1 deficiency, hexokinase 1 deficiency, HK1 gene Pyruvate kinase deficiency Glucose phosphate isomerase deficiency Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Hereditary spherocytosis and membrane disorders Other glycolytic enzymopathies Red-cell hexokinase enzyme assay with reticulocyte-age adjustment Full blood count, reticulocyte count and blood film Red-cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate measurement where available Haemolysis screen with bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin Direct antiglobulin test to exclude immune haemolysis Molecular testing of the HK1 gene A rare autosomal recessive glycolytic enzymopathy causing chronic non-spherocytic, Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia Because hexokinase catalyses the first, rate-limiting step of glycolysis, deficiency can produce clinically significant anaemia even with modest reductions in activity Presentation is often in the neonatal period or infancy with jaundice and anaemia Unlike pyruvate kinase deficiency, red-cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate tends to be low rather than high, subtly shifting the oxygen dissociation curve Some patients have a multisystem phenotype, including HK1-related conditions affecting other tissues, reflecting the gene's broad expression Diagnosis is by reduced red-cell hexokinase activity on assay, interpreted with care because activity is high in young reticulocytes, and HK1 mutation testing Management is supportive with folate, transfusion when required and splenectomy considered in severe transfusion-dependent disease Severe neonatal jaundice risking kernicterus and requiring exchange transfusion Aplastic crisis following parvovirus B19 infection Symptoms of impaired oxygen delivery from a leftward-shifted dissociation curve Transfusional iron overload Misreading a normal-appearing enzyme level that is falsely raised by reticulocytosis Overlooking the low 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate and its effect on oxygen delivery Assuming a membrane disorder when spherocytes are absent Neglecting iron-overload monitoring in transfused patients Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, committing it to glycolysis, the mature red cell's sole source of ATP. As the enzyme catalyses the first and rate-limiting step, reduced activity throttles the whole pathway, lowering ATP production and shortening red-cell survival to cause a chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. Because hexokinase activity is normally highest in young red cells and declines with cell age, the reticulocytosis of haemolysis can partly mask the deficiency on assay, requiring age-adjusted interpretation. Most patients have a chronic compensated or transfusion-supported anaemia; severity depends on residual enzyme activity, and the low 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate may make a given haemoglobin level less well tolerated.

Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state — Glucose, osmolality, electrolytes Venous gas (minimal ketosis) Search for precipitant Profound dehydration — careful fluid/insulin; precipitant often infection Diabetic ketoacidosis (and the DKA/HHS overlap presentation) (p.3216). Other causes of an altered/hyperosmolar sensorium - the differential for hyperosmolar coma includes uremia, nonketotic hyperosmolar states and other metabolic derangements (p.3216, general). Plasma glucose - typically markedly elevated, may be >55.5 mmol/L (1000 mg/dL) (p.3219). Serum osmolality - characteristically >300 mOsm/L (p.3219). Corrected serum sodium - measured Na may be normal or low, but corrected Na (add ~1.6 meq/L for each 5.6 mmol/L [100 mg/dL] rise in glucose) is usually elevated (p.3219). Renal function (BUN/creatinine) - prerenal azotaemia from volume depletion; creatinine typically moderately raised (p.3219). Ketones/beta-hydroxybutyrate - absent or only mild; serum beta-hydroxybutyrate <1.0 mmol/L; any moderate ketonuria is usually due to starvation (p.3219). Acid-base status - acidosis absent or mild; a small anion-gap metabolic acidosis may reflect raised lactic acid (p.3219). Typical patient is an older adult with type 2 diabetes presenting after a several-week prodrome of polyuria, weight loss and falling oral intake, progressing to confusion, lethargy or coma (p.3219). Examination reflects profound dehydration and hyperosmolality: hypotension, tachycardia and altered mental status (p.3219). Features classically ABSENT in HHS that are seen in DKA: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and Kussmaul respirations (p.3219). HHS and DKA lie on a continuum of hyperglycaemia; up to one-third of patients have overlapping features of both (p.3216). Plasma glucose in HHS is usually markedly higher than in DKA and may exceed 55.5 mmol/L (1000 mg/dL) (p.3219). A debilitating condition (e.g. prior stroke, dementia) or a social situation that limits access to water frequently contributes to HHS by impairing water intake (p.3218-3219). Worldwide reported cases of both HHS and DKA are rising for reasons that are not clear (p.3216). HHS carries a substantially higher mortality than DKA (up to ~15% in some series), reflecting older patients, more pronounced dehydration and serious precipitating events with comorbidities (p.3219). Hyperosmolar state must be reversed gradually - too-rapid correction risks worsening neurologic function (p.3219). Precipitant is often a serious concurrent illness - myocardial infarction, stroke, sepsis, pneumonia or other severe infection - which must be actively sought (p.3219). A normal or low measured serum sodium can be falsely reassuring - it must be corrected for hyperglycaemia, after which it is usually elevated and reveals a profound water deficit (p.3219). Mild ketonuria may be present but is typically from starvation, not from ketoacidosis - it should not redirect the diagnosis away from HHS (p.3219). Fever may be absent even when infection is the precipitant; signs of infection should be sought regardless (p.3217, DKA section, applicable to acute hyperglycaemic crises). HHS arises from RELATIVE insulin deficiency combined with inadequate fluid intake. Insulin deficiency drives hepatic glucose overproduction (glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis) and impairs glucose uptake by skeletal muscle. The resulting hyperglycaemia causes an osmotic diuresis with intravascular volume depletion that is worsened by inadequate fluid replacement. The reason ketosis is absent is not fully understood; the insulin deficiency is presumed to be only relative and less severe than in DKA, and some studies show lower counterregulatory hormone and free-fatty-acid levels in HHS than in DKA, with possibly reduced hepatic ketone synthesis or an insulin/glucagon ratio that does not favour ketogenesis. Inflammatory markers (cytokines, C-reactive protein) are elevated in both HHS and DKA (p.3217-3219). Even with appropriate treatment, HHS has a substantially higher mortality rate than DKA, reported up to about 15% in some clinical series. The worse outlook reflects that HHS patients are usually older, have more profound fluid losses and dehydration (developed over days to weeks), are more likely to have mental status changes, and more often have a life-threatening precipitating event with accompanying comorbidities (p.3219). Harrison does not give a graded severity classification specific to HHS (unlike DKA, which is graded mild/moderate/severe by pH, bicarbonate and mental status). HHS is instead defined by marked hyperglycaemia, hyperosmolality (>300 mOsm/L) and the relative absence of ketosis/acidosis, on a continuum with DKA (p.3218-3219).

encephalopathy are present Human herpesvirus 6 (chiefly HHV-6B) is acquired almost universally in early childhood and thereafter remains latent, capable of reactivation under immunosuppression Primary infection in infants causes roseola infantum (exanthem subitum): several days of high fever followed by defervescence and a maculopapular rash as the child improves It is a common cause of febrile amnesia, confusion, seizures, and hyponatraemia MRI in HHV-6 encephalitis characteristically shows medial temporal lobe and limbic signal change, and CSF HHV-6 DNA PCR is usually positive agents active against HHV-6 (such as ganciclovir or foscarnet) are used for significant reactivation disease, particularly encephalitis in the immunocompromised Amnesia, confusion, or seizures with limbic signal change after transplantation Status epilepticus or prolonged febrile seizures Rapidly declining conscious level suggesting encephalitis Severe hyponatraemia accompanying suspected limbic encephalitis Misinterpreting the very high viral loads of chromosomally integrated HHV-6 as active infection and treating unnecessarily Overlooking HHV-6 as a cause of encephalitis and amnesia in the early post-transplant period Attributing all high fever with rash in infants to HHV-6 without considering other exanthems Failing to link HHV-6 reactivation with DRESS and its relapsing course HHV-6 is a betaherpesvirus that infects and replicates in T lymphocytes and establishes lifelong latency in lymphocytes, monocytes, and the central nervous system. Primary infection in infancy produces a viraemic febrile illness; as the immune response develops the fever subsides and a rash may appear. The virus is neurotropic and can invade the limbic system, causing encephalitis when cellular immunity is impaired, as after stem-cell or solid-organ transplantation. Uniquely among human herpesviruses, HHV-6 can integrate its genome into host chromosomal telomeres; when this occurs in a germ cell the integrated virus is inherited in every somatic cell, producing extraordinarily high blood viral loads that do not indicate active replication and can confound diagnosis. Roseola in healthy children is benign and self-limiting; post-transplant HHV-6 limbic encephalitis is serious, with a risk of persistent memory impairment, epilepsy, or death, and outcome depends on prompt antiviral treatment and immune recovery.

hibernating animals use for thermogenesis Typically affects young to middle-aged adults and presents as a slow-growing, painless, mobile mass Favoured sites are the interscapular region, back, neck, axilla, thigh, and mediastinum, mirroring the distribution of brown fat The characteristic cell is a multivacuolated adipocyte with granular, eosinophilic, mitochondria-rich cytoplasm The lesion is highly vascular and often intensely avid on FDG PET, which can lead to a false suspicion of malignancy Recurrent chromosomal rearrangements affect the 11q13-21 region, distinguishing it from ordinary lipoma On MRI it resembles fat but is typically slightly less bright than subcutaneous fat on T1 with prominent internal vascular flow voids Marginal excision is curative and recurrence is not expected Intense metabolic avidity misinterpreted as a malignant or metastatic lesion Rapid growth or infiltration raising concern for a liposarcoma Mediastinal or deep location causing local mass effect Unexpected recurrence after excision prompting review of the diagnosis Over-investigating or over-treating a benign lesion because of striking FDG avidity Confusing multivacuolated cells with the lipoblasts of liposarcoma Underestimating intra-operative vascularity, which can cause troublesome bleeding Failing to consider hibernoma in a fatty mass at a classic brown-fat site Hibernoma is a benign neoplasm recapitulating brown adipose tissue, the specialised thermogenic fat abundant in the fetus and neonate and retained in adults at sites such as the interscapular region, neck, and mediastinum. The tumour cells are packed with mitochondria whose uncoupling protein activity gives the cytoplasm its granular, eosinophilic, multivacuolated appearance and accounts for the high metabolic activity seen on functional imaging. The rich capillary network reflects the high oxygen demand of thermogenic fat. Recurrent structural rearrangements of chromosome 11q13-21, including loss involving the region around the MEN1 locus, are characteristic and separate hibernoma from conventional white-fat lipomas. Despite its vascularity and metabolic avidity, the lesion is entirely benign with no capacity for local aggression or metastasis. Hibernoma is benign with an excellent prognosis; complete marginal excision is curative and local recurrence or malignant transformation does not occur. The main clinical hazard is misinterpretation of its metabolic avidity as malignancy.

Hidradenitis suppurativa — acne inversa, HS, Verneuil's disease Furunculosis or recurrent bacterial abscesses Crohn's disease with cutaneous or perianal involvement Pilonidal disease Cutaneous tuberculosis or actinomycosis in atypical sinus-forming disease Epidermoid or pilonidal cysts Lymphogranuloma venereum in the anogenital region Clinical diagnosis based on characteristic lesions, sites, and recurrence Bacterial swabs of discharging lesions when secondary infection is suspected Imaging such as ultrasound or MRI to map sinus tracts before surgery in extensive disease Screening for associated metabolic disease, including glucose and lipids Assessment for inflammatory bowel disease when gastrointestinal symptoms coexist A chronic, recurrent, inflammatory disease of the apocrine-gland-bearing flexures: axillae, groin, perineum, buttocks, and inframammary folds Presents with painful, deep-seated inflammatory nodules, abscesses, discharging sinus tracts, and eventually rope-like scarring Double-ended (bridged) comedones in affected areas are a helpful diagnostic clue It is a primarily inflammatory, not infective, disease, though secondary bacterial colonisation and infection occur; recurrent painful lesions in typical sites over time define it Strongly associated with obesity, smoking, and metabolic syndrome, and weight loss and smoking cessation are important management measures Severity guides treatment: topical and oral antibacterials for anti-inflammatory effect in milder disease, and biologic immunomodulators, hormonal therapy, or surgery for moderate to severe disease Definitive control of extensive or recurrent disease often requires wide surgical excision of affected tissue rather than incision and drainage alone The condition causes considerable pain, malodour, and psychological distress, and quality of life should be actively assessed Severe systemic infection or sepsis arising from deep abscesses Long-standing chronic sinuses with new induration or non-healing ulceration, raising concern for squamous cell carcinoma Extensive scarring causing contractures or restricted limb movement Severe unremitting pain and profound impairment of quality of life Repeatedly treating flares as simple abscesses with incision and drainage while missing the underlying chronic disease Relying solely on antibacterials and overlooking the inflammatory nature requiring anti-inflammatory or surgical management Neglecting smoking cessation and weight management as core interventions Failing to consider squamous cell carcinoma in chronic non-healing lesions Hidradenitis suppurativa is a chronic inflammatory disorder centred on the hair follicle in apocrine-bearing skin. The primary event is follicular occlusion by hyperkeratosis, leading to follicular dilatation, rupture, and release of keratin and bacteria into the surrounding dermis. This provokes an intense inflammatory response with nodules and abscesses; recurrent inflammation drives formation of epithelialised sinus tracts and progressive scarring. Genetic predisposition, dysregulated innate immunity, hormonal influences, obesity, and smoking all contribute. Although bacteria colonise lesions and secondary infection occurs, the disease is fundamentally inflammatory rather than a primary infection. Hidradenitis suppurativa is a chronic, often progressive disease with a relapsing course; early recognition and treatment can limit scarring, but advanced disease causes substantial morbidity, and long-standing lesions carry a small risk of malignant transformation.

High-altitude cerebral oedema — HACE, high-altitude cerebral edema, altitude cerebral oedema Severe acute mountain sickness without frank encephalopathy Ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke Central nervous system infection such as meningitis or encephalitis Hypoglycaemia or other metabolic encephalopathy Intoxication, hyponatraemia, or dehydration Transient ischaemic attack or migraine with aura Clinical assessment for truncal ataxia (heel-to-toe walking) and mental status change Pulse oximetry to document hypoxaemia Blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia as a cause of altered consciousness Assessment for concurrent high-altitude pulmonary oedema Neuroimaging when available and once evacuated, to exclude alternative intracranial pathology Focused neurological examination for focal deficits suggesting stroke rather than altitude illness High-altitude cerebral oedema is considered the severe, end-stage form of acute mountain sickness and is a neurological emergency The hallmark early sign is truncal ataxia, often with worsening headache, nausea and vomiting, and progressive changes in mental status It usually develops after one or more days at high altitude and is frequently preceded by acute mountain sickness or accompanies high-altitude pulmonary oedema Progression can be rapid, moving from confusion and drowsiness to stupor, coma, and death if untreated Immediate descent is the definitive treatment and should not be delayed; supplemental oxygen and a corticosteroid such as dexamethasone are important adjuncts A portable hyperbaric chamber can temporise when descent is impossible, but it does not replace descent Any traveller with ataxia or altered mental status at altitude should be treated as having cerebral oedema until proven otherwise Ataxia, confusion, or drowsiness in anyone at altitude Rapidly declining level of consciousness or coma Focal neurological deficits suggesting stroke or a structural lesion Coexisting severe pulmonary oedema and hypoxaemia Dismissing ataxia or behavioural change as fatigue or intoxication rather than cerebral oedema Delaying descent to arrange investigations or await improvement Treating with medication or a hyperbaric chamber and then resuming ascent instead of descending Overlooking hypoglycaemia or infection as alternative causes of encephalopathy Failing to look for and manage coexisting pulmonary oedema High-altitude cerebral oedema develops from the effects of hypobaric hypoxia on the brain. Hypoxia triggers cerebral vasodilatation and increased cerebral blood flow, and disturbs the blood-brain barrier, allowing a vasogenic leak of fluid into the brain interstitium. Impaired autoregulation, raised capillary pressure, and inflammatory and free-radical mediated injury contribute to swelling. As oedema accumulates within the rigid skull, intracranial pressure rises, producing the characteristic ataxia, headache, and declining consciousness. The process is closely related to acute mountain sickness and shares mechanisms with high-altitude pulmonary oedema, with which it often coexists, and untreated it can progress to brain herniation. With immediate descent, oxygen, and corticosteroid treatment most patients recover fully, sometimes with residual ataxia that resolves over days. Delay in recognition or treatment can lead to coma and death, and severe cases may leave lasting neurological deficits. Prevention through gradual ascent and prompt response to early acute mountain sickness is key.

High-altitude pulmonary oedema — HAPE, high-altitude pulmonary edema, altitude pulmonary oedema Pneumonia or other lower respiratory tract infection Acute asthma or bronchospasm Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from underlying heart disease Pulmonary embolism High-altitude cerebral oedema or severe acute mountain sickness Pneumothorax or airway obstruction Pulse oximetry showing hypoxaemia disproportionate to the altitude Chest auscultation for crackles and clinical assessment of respiratory distress Chest radiograph, where available, showing patchy non-cardiogenic infiltrates Portable exclude a cardiac cause when in doubt High-altitude pulmonary oedema is a non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema that typically develops within the first few days after a rapid ascent to high altitude, often above around 2500 metres Early features are a decline in exercise tolerance and a dry cough progressing to breathlessness at rest, and later to a productive cough with pink or frothy sputum It is the most common cause of altitude-related death and can coexist with high-altitude cerebral oedema Examination may reveal tachycardia, tachypnoea, crackles, cyanosis, and a low oxygen saturation for the altitude The key intervention is immediate descent to lower altitude, together with supplemental oxygen and rest, which usually produces rapid improvement Where descent is delayed, a portable hyperbaric chamber and pulmonary vasodilator therapy can be used as temporising measures Rapid ascent, heavy exertion, cold, and a previous episode all increase risk, and susceptibility varies between individuals Breathlessness at rest with pink or frothy sputum and severe hypoxaemia Cyanosis, marked tachycardia, and rapidly worsening respiratory distress Coexisting neurological signs such as ataxia or altered consciousness suggesting cerebral oedema Failure to improve despite oxygen when descent has not been possible Attributing early symptoms to a chest infection or simple deconditioning and continuing to ascend Relying on oxygen or medication as a substitute for descent when descent is feasible Missing concurrent high-altitude cerebral oedema in a breathless patient Assuming a normal chest examination excludes early disease Underestimating recurrence risk and advising an unsafe re-ascent profile High-altitude pulmonary oedema is driven by hypoxia at altitude, which causes pulmonary vasoconstriction. In susceptible people this vasoconstriction is exaggerated and uneven, so blood flow is redistributed and some pulmonary capillary beds are exposed to high pressure. The resulting pulmonary hypertension and regional overperfusion damage the alveolar-capillary barrier, producing a high-permeability leak of protein-rich fluid and red cells into the alveoli. This is a non-cardiogenic oedema, occurring with normal left heart function. Impaired alveolar fluid clearance and inflammatory changes contribute, and the accumulation of alveolar fluid worsens gas exchange and hypoxaemia, which further intensifies pulmonary vasoconstriction in a vicious cycle. With prompt descent and oxygen the prognosis is excellent and recovery is usually rapid and complete. Delay in recognition and treatment, or continued ascent, can be rapidly fatal. Individuals with a prior episode remain susceptible and should ascend gradually and consider preventive measures on future trips.

High-altitude retinopathy — altitude retinal haemorrhage Retinal haemorrhage from hypertension or diabetes Valsalva retinopathy Anaemia or blood dyscrasia causing retinal haemorrhage Central retinal vein occlusion Optic disc oedema from other causes Dilated fundus examination documenting haemorrhages and vascular changes Assessment for other features of altitude illness Visual acuity testing, particularly for macular involvement Optical coherence tomography where macular involvement is suspected Exclusion of systemic causes of retinal haemorrhage Retinal changes occurring at high altitude, including dilated tortuous vessels, retinal haemorrhages and disc hyperaemia Most retinal haemorrhages are peripheral and asymptomatic, discovered only on fundoscopy Visual symptoms occur mainly when a haemorrhage involves the macula It is part of the spectrum of high-altitude illness and is more likely with higher altitude, rapid ascent and strenuous exertion Its presence may accompany other altitude illness such as high-altitude cerebral oedema Descent generally leads to resolution of the haemorrhages over weeks Macular haemorrhage with visual loss Coexisting signs of high-altitude cerebral oedema Extensive bilateral haemorrhage Failure of resolution after descent Dismissing extensive retinopathy that may signal serious altitude illness Attributing haemorrhages to altitude without excluding systemic causes Overlooking macular involvement in a symptomatic climber Allowing continued ascent despite significant retinopathy High-altitude retinopathy arises from the retinal vascular response to hypobaric hypoxia. Hypoxia causes retinal vasodilatation and increased retinal blood flow, and raised intracranial and venous pressure together with impaired autoregulation predispose the fragile retinal vessels to leak, producing haemorrhages. The same hypoxic and haemodynamic stresses that drive cerebral involvement in severe altitude illness contribute to the retinal findings, so extensive retinopathy can be a marker of significant altitude stress. Peripheral haemorrhages usually resolve completely after descent with no lasting visual effect, though macular involvement can leave persistent visual deficit.

High ankle sprain — syndesmotic ankle injury, distal tibiofibular syndesmosis injury Lateral ligament ankle sprain Distal fibular (including Maisonneuve) fracture Osteochondral injury of the talus Deltoid ligament injury Ankle impingement Weight-bearing and mortise radiographs assessing tibiofibular clear space and mortise widening Provocation tests (squeeze, external rotation) Assessment of the proximal fibula to exclude a Maisonneuve injury MRI or CT for equivocal or complex injuries Stress imaging where instability is uncertain Injury to the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis, distinct from and higher than the common lateral ligament ankle sprain The usual mechanism is external rotation or forced dorsiflexion of the foot Pain is felt above the ankle joint over the syndesmosis, and weight bearing is often more painful and prolonged than in a lateral sprain Provocation tests such as the squeeze and external rotation tests reproduce the pain Radiographs are assessed for widening of the tibiofibular clear space and associated fractures Unstable injuries require surgical stabilisation, and recovery is generally slower than for lateral sprains Mortise widening or diastasis indicating instability Associated proximal fibular (Maisonneuve) fracture Inability to bear weight with significant deformity Neurovascular compromise Mislabelling it as a simple lateral ankle sprain and under-treating Missing a Maisonneuve fracture by not examining the proximal fibula Failing to detect mortise widening that indicates instability Allowing early full weight bearing on an unstable syndesmosis A high ankle sprain damages the ligaments binding the distal tibia and fibula, chiefly the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament and interosseous membrane, usually through external rotation of the talus that forces the fibula away from the tibia. Disruption of these stabilising structures can allow the ankle mortise to widen, compromising joint congruity and load transmission. The degree of instability determines whether the injury is managed conservatively or surgically, and syndesmotic injuries take longer to heal than lateral ligament sprains because of the loads across the syndesmosis. Stable injuries recover with protected weight bearing and rehabilitation, though more slowly than lateral sprains; unstable injuries do well after appropriate surgical stabilisation but risk long-term stiffness or arthritis if missed.
