the humeral counterpart to the glenoid Bankart lesion and the two together define bipolar bone loss An engaging lesion is one that rotates into and catches on the glenoid rim in abduction and external rotation, driving recurrent instability The glenoid track concept predicts engagement: an off-track lesion extends medial to the glenoid contact zone and needs to be addressed surgically A reverse Hill-Sachs (anteromedial head) occurs after posterior dislocation, classically with seizures or electric shock Small non-engaging lesions are often clinically silent and need no specific treatment CT best characterises the size and orientation for surgical planning Locked or irreducible dislocation from an engaged large defect Reverse lesion suggesting a missed posterior dislocation after seizure Large bipolar bone loss indicating high failure risk for isolated soft-tissue repair Treating instability by labral repair alone while ignoring an off-track Hill-Sachs lesion Missing a reverse Hill-Sachs and the associated posterior dislocation after a seizure Failing to quantify combined glenoid and humeral bone loss Assuming any Hill-Sachs lesion is clinically significant As the humeral head dislocates anteriorly it impacts against the firm anteroinferior glenoid rim, denting the softer posterolateral head. The size, depth and orientation of this defect determine whether it engages the glenoid during functional abduction-external rotation. Combined with glenoid bone loss, an engaging or off-track lesion mechanically perpetuates dislocation despite labral repair, which is why bipolar bone loss guides the choice of procedure. Small non-engaging lesions have an excellent prognosis; larger engaging or off-track lesions require remplissage or bony procedures to prevent recurrent instability, with good stabilisation rates when bone loss is appropriately addressed.

Hip fracture — proximal femoral fracture, fractured neck of femur, femoral neck fracture, intertrochanteric fracture, NOF fracture Pubic ramus or acetabular fracture Greater trochanteric contusion or avulsion Trochanteric bursitis or gluteal tendinopathy Pathological fracture from metastasis or myeloma Osteoarthritis of the hip with acute-on-chronic pain Referred pain from lumbar spine Anteroposterior pelvis and lateral hip radiographs as first-line imaging MRI (or CT) when a fracture is suspected clinically despite normal radiographs (occult fracture) Full blood count, renal function and electrolytes, group and save/crossmatch as part of preoperative workup ECG and assessment of cardiopulmonary fitness for anaesthesia Bone mineral density assessment and metabolic bone screen for secondary fracture prevention Typically follows a low-energy fall in an older, often osteoporotic patient; the leg is characteristically shortened and externally rotated with pain on any movement Fractures are broadly divided into intracapsular (subcapital/transcervical) and extracapsular (intertrochanteric and subtrochanteric), a distinction that governs both blood supply risk and treatment The femoral head's blood supply runs retrograde up the neck, so displaced intracapsular fractures carry a high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union Displaced intracapsular fractures in older patients are usually managed with arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement), whereas undisplaced or young patients' fractures are fixed to preserve the head Extracapsular fractures retain a good blood supply and are typically treated with internal fixation such as a dynamic hip screw or intramedullary device Early surgery (generally within about a day or two) and rapid mobilisation reduce complications; prolonged bed rest causes pressure sores, chest infection, and venous thromboembolism A minority present with subtle or occult fractures and a normal-appearing radiograph; persistent inability to weight-bear warrants MRI or CT Outcome depends heavily on comorbidity and pre-injury mobility; orthogeriatric co-management and bone-health assessment for future fracture prevention are integral Signs of significant blood loss or haemodynamic instability, particularly with subtrochanteric fractures Pathological fracture features (bone destruction, minimal trauma in a younger patient) suggesting malignancy Open fracture or associated neurovascular compromise of the limb Prolonged surgical delay increasing mortality and complication risk in the frail elderly Dismissing a hip fracture because the initial radiograph looks normal, missing an occult fracture Delaying surgery unnecessarily for over-investigation of stable comorbidities Choosing internal fixation for a displaced intracapsular fracture in an older patient, risking avascular necrosis and reoperation Overlooking underlying osteoporosis and failing to institute secondary prevention Hip fractures usually result from a fall onto the greater trochanter in bone weakened by osteoporosis, though high-energy trauma or pathological lesions can cause them at any age. The proximal femur is supplied largely by the medial femoral circumflex artery via retinacular vessels ascending the femoral neck beneath the capsule. Intracapsular fractures may tear these vessels, threatening viability of the femoral head and predisposing to avascular necrosis and non-union, especially when displaced. Extracapsular fractures occur through well-vascularised cancellous bone and heal reliably but can bleed substantially. Immobility after fracture drives systemic decompensation in frail patients. Hip fracture in the elderly carries substantial morbidity and a significant one-year mortality driven by comorbidity; prompt surgery, early mobilisation, orthogeriatric care, and osteoporosis treatment improve functional recovery, though many patients do not regain full pre-injury independence.

hip labral tear — acetabular labral tear, acetabular labrum injury Femoroacetabular impingement without discrete labral tear Early hip osteoarthritis with chondral wear Iliopsoas tendinopathy or internal snapping hip Athletic pubalgia (core muscle injury / sports hernia) Femoral neck stress fracture Ligamentum teres tear Lumbar spine referred pain or spinopelvic imbalance Plain radiographs including standing AP pelvis, Dunn lateral and false-profile views to assess cam/pincer morphology and dysplasia Magnetic resonance arthrography of the hip Diagnostic intra-articular local anaesthetic injection CT with three-dimensional reconstruction for detailed bony morphology and surgical planning Assessment of femoral and acetabular version Dynamic hip examination for impingement and instability Presents with anterior groin pain, often accompanied by mechanical symptoms such as clicking, catching, locking or a sensation of giving way. The C-sign, in which the patient cups the hand over the lateral hip with thumb posterior and fingers into the groin, is a characteristic gesture localising deep intra-articular pain. The anterosuperior labrum is the most frequently torn segment, reflecting the distribution of femoroacetabular contact stress. The flexion-adduction-internal-rotation (FADIR) impingement test is the most sensitive provocation manoeuvre; a positive result reproduces the patient's groin pain. Most symptomatic tears are secondary to an underlying driver: cam or pincer femoroacetabular impingement, acetabular dysplasia, capsular laxity or microinstability, or trauma. Magnetic resonance arthrography is the imaging investigation of choice, and a diagnostic intra-articular local anaesthetic injection that abolishes pain confirms an intra-articular source. Initial management is activity modification and physiotherapy targeting the deep hip stabilisers and lumbopelvic control; arthroscopic labral repair with correction of bony morphology is preferred to debridement where tissue quality allows. Labral preservation restores the suction seal and fluid-film lubrication, so refixation generally outperforms simple excision in appropriately selected hips. Rest pain or night pain unrelieved by position, raising concern for neoplasm or infection Fever or systemic upset suggesting septic arthritis Inability to weight bear after minor trauma, suggesting occult femoral neck fracture Rapidly progressive joint space narrowing indicating a closing window for joint preservation Treating an incidentally imaged tear as the pain source, since asymptomatic labral tears are common on MRI, especially with increasing age. Failing to address the causative cam or pincer morphology, which leads to recurrent tearing after isolated labral surgery. Overlooking acetabular dysplasia and performing rim trimming that further destabilises an already under-covered hip. Attributing all groin pain to the labrum while missing coexisting spinopelvic or lumbar contributions. The acetabular labrum is a horseshoe-shaped fibrocartilaginous rim that deepens the socket, enlarges the articular contact area, and creates a suction seal that maintains intra-articular fluid pressurisation for cartilage nutrition and low-friction load transfer. Tears develop when the seal is repetitively overloaded: cam morphology drives abnormal femoral head-neck contact against the chondrolabral junction during flexion and internal rotation, pincer over-coverage crushes the labrum against the rim, acetabular dysplasia overloads the anterosuperior labrum as a secondary stabiliser, and capsular laxity or trauma imposes shear. Loss of the seal degrades fluid-film lubrication and cartilage nutrition, propagating chondral delamination and progression toward osteoarthritis. Arthroscopic labral repair combined with correction of the underlying bony morphology gives good to excellent medium-term outcomes when performed before significant chondral damage. Established osteoarthritis with joint space narrowing predicts poorer results and a higher rate of conversion to arthroplasty.

Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis — HAEC, Hirschsprung enterocolitis Neonatal sepsis or necrotising enterocolitis Mechanical bowel obstruction (adhesive, anastomotic stricture) Infective gastroenteritis or Clostridioides difficile colitis Anastomotic leak or intra-abdominal abscess after pull-through Residual or transition-zone aganglionosis Internal anal sphincter achalasia Cow's milk protein enterocolitis or food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome Abdominal radiograph for bowel dilatation, air-fluid levels, a rectosigmoid cut-off, pneumatosis or free air Full blood count, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, blood gas and lactate to assess sepsis and dehydration Blood cultures and stool studies including Clostridioides difficile testing Contrast enema to define the transition zone, avoided during acute severe colitis because of perforation risk Rectal suction biopsy for ganglion cells where Hirschsprung disease is not yet confirmed Examination under anaesthesia and anorectal manometry for obstructive causes in recurrent disease Water-soluble contrast study to assess the anastomosis and exclude stricture or leak after surgery The most common and most serious life-threatening complication of Hirschsprung disease, occurring both before and after definitive pull-through surgery. Presents with abdominal distension, explosive foul-smelling and often bloody diarrhoea, fever, vomiting and lethargy, and can progress rapidly to sepsis, toxic megacolon and perforation. It may be the presenting feature of previously undiagnosed Hirschsprung disease in a neonate. Risk factors include long-segment or total colonic aganglionosis, trisomy 21, a prior HAEC episode and delayed diagnosis. Explosive release of gas and stool on digital rectal examination is a classic sign. The cornerstones of management are prompt fluid resuscitation, colonic decompression by rectal irrigation and washouts, bowel rest, and broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic cover. Recurrent HAEC prompts evaluation for mechanical obstruction, residual or transition-zone aganglionosis and internal anal sphincter achalasia. Refractory disease may require intrasphincteric botulinum toxin, anal myectomy or redo pull-through, and a diverting stoma in severe cases. Fever, lethargy, tachycardia and other signs of sepsis or shock Marked abdominal distension with tenderness, guarding or peritonism Bloody, explosive diarrhoea with rapid clinical deterioration Bilious vomiting with features of toxic megacolon Pneumatosis intestinalis or free intraperitoneal air on imaging indicating perforation Attributing distension and diarrhoea to simple gastroenteritis and missing HAEC in a child with, or at risk of, Hirschsprung disease. Delaying rectal decompression and irrigation while awaiting investigations. Performing a contrast enema during acute severe colitis and precipitating perforation. Assuming that a successful pull-through excludes HAEC, as it can occur postoperatively and sometimes years later. Failing to investigate an anatomical or obstructive cause after recurrent episodes. HAEC is a multifactorial inflammatory disorder superimposed on the functional obstruction of aganglionic bowel. Absence of ganglion cells produces tonic contraction and failure of relaxation of the affected segment, causing proximal faecal stasis and distension. Stasis, together with an abnormal intestinal mucin layer, impaired mucosal barrier function, defective innate mucosal immunity including altered secretory IgA and defensins, and intestinal dysbiosis, permits bacterial overgrowth, adherence and translocation across a compromised epithelium. The resulting mucosal invasion and inflammatory cascade drive crypt inflammation and ulceration and, in severe cases, transmural inflammation with the risk of toxic dilatation, perforation and systemic sepsis. With prompt recognition and treatment most episodes resolve, but HAEC remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in Hirschsprung disease; episodes may recur, and severe or delayed-treated disease carries a risk of toxic megacolon, perforation and death.

Hirschsprung Disease — congenital aganglionic megacolon, aganglionosis, Hirschsprung's disease Meconium ileus (often cystic fibrosis) Meconium plug syndrome / small left colon syndrome Anorectal malformation Intestinal atresia or stenosis Functional constipation (in older children) Hypothyroidism-related constipation Rectal suction biopsy for absence of ganglion cells (with acetylcholinesterase staining or calretinin) Contrast (unprepped) enema to identify a transition zone Anorectal manometry in older children Abdominal radiograph showing distal obstruction with dilated proximal bowel Genetic and syndrome evaluation where relevant Caused by absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel, producing a tonically contracted, non-relaxing aganglionic segment and functional obstruction. Most neonates present with delayed passage of meconium beyond 48 hours, abdominal distension, and bilious vomiting. The aganglionic segment extends proximally from the anus for a variable distance; short-segment disease confined to the rectosigmoid is most common and it is more frequent in boys. Associated with Down syndrome and other congenital conditions, and there can be a positive family history. Contrast enema may show a transition zone between the narrow distal aganglionic bowel and dilated proximal colon, but a normal study does not exclude the diagnosis. Anorectal manometry shows failure of the internal anal sphincter to relax with rectal distension. Rectal suction biopsy demonstrating absent ganglion cells with hypertrophied nerve trunks is the diagnostic gold standard. Definitive treatment is surgical resection of the aganglionic segment with a pull-through procedure connecting normally innervated bowel to the anus. Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis is the most serious complication and can present with fever, distension, foul explosive diarrhoea, and sepsis. Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life Bilious vomiting with abdominal distension Fever, explosive foul diarrhoea, and distension suggesting enterocolitis Signs of sepsis, dehydration, or shock Toxic megacolon Attributing neonatal obstruction solely to functional constipation and missing aganglionosis Relying on a normal contrast enema to exclude the diagnosis Overlooking Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis, which can be rapidly fatal Taking a biopsy too close to the anal verge where ganglion cells are normally sparse Missing associated syndromes such as trisomy 21 Failure of the craniocaudal migration of neural crest-derived enteric ganglion cells leaves the distal bowel without submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses. The aganglionic segment cannot relax and remains tonically contracted, while abnormal cholinergic and other innervation adds to the dysmotility. This creates a functional obstruction with proximal dilatation (megacolon) and predisposes to stasis, bacterial overgrowth, and enterocolitis. After definitive pull-through surgery most children do well, though some have ongoing issues such as constipation, soiling, or recurrent enterocolitis; outcome is worse with long-segment or total colonic aganglionosis and with severe enterocolitis.

Hirsutism — excessive terminal hair growth in women, androgen-mediated hair growth Polycystic ovary syndrome / functional ovarian hyperandrogenism Nonclassic and classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (most often 21-hydroxylase deficiency) Ovarian hyperthecosis Androgen-secreting ovarian or adrenal neoplasm Cushing's syndrome Hyperprolactinemia Acromegaly Syndromes of extreme insulin resistance Idiopathic hirsutism / idiopathic hyperandrogenism Obesity-related peripheral androgen overproduction Pregnancy-related hyperandrogenism (hyperreactio luteinalis, thecoma of pregnancy) Drug-induced (androgens, androgenic progestins, minoxidil, phenytoin, diazoxide, cyclosporine, valproic acid) Ovotesticular disorders of sex development Total testosterone (specialty assay) and free/unbound testosterone, calculated from total testosterone and SHBG or measured by LC/tandem mass spectrometry DHEAS to assess adrenal androgen contribution Morning follicular-phase 17-hydroxyprogesterone to screen for 21-hydroxylase deficiency; ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation test if equivocal Dexamethasone androgen-suppression test to broadly distinguish adrenal from ovarian androgen overproduction Overnight 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test with 8 a.m. cortisol when Cushing's syndrome is suspected Prolactin and thyroid function when galactorrhea or other features present CT or MRI to localize a suspected adrenal mass; transvaginal ultrasound for a suspected ovarian mass Note: LH/FSH and ovarian ultrasound have limited diagnostic value for PCOS given pulsatile gonadotropin secretion and low ultrasound specificity Hypertrichosis (androgen-independent generalized hair growth, often drug-induced) Constitutional/ethnic variation in hair distribution mistaken for pathologic hirsutism Hirsutism is defined as excessive growth of terminal (long, coarse, pigmented) hair in an androgen-dependent distribution and affects roughly 10% of reproductive-age women (Harrison 22e p.3137). Most cases are idiopathic or due to androgen excess from polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS); PCOS is the single most common cause of ovarian androgen excess (Harrison 22e p.3137-3140). Hirsutism must be distinguished from hypertrichosis, which is androgen-independent generalized excess vellus/terminal hair often caused by medications such as phenytoin, minoxidil, and cyclosporine (Harrison 22e p.3138). Virilization (deepened voice, breast atrophy, increased muscle bulk, clitoromegaly, increased libido) signals markedly elevated androgens and raises concern for an ovarian or adrenal neoplasm, or hyperthecosis (Harrison 22e p.3138). Sudden onset and rapid progression of hirsutism, especially with virilization, suggests an androgen-secreting tumor and warrants urgent evaluation (Harrison 22e p.3138). The modified Ferriman-Gallwey scale grades nine androgen-sensitive sites from 0 to 4; a normal score is <8, and scores >=8 in most non-Hispanic white and African American women indicate excess androgen-mediated hair growth (Harrison 22e p.3138-3139). Asian and Native American women are less likely to manifest hirsutism even with androgen excess; pustular acne and scalp hair thinning may be the only cutaneous clues (Harrison 22e p.3138). Free (unbound) testosterone is often more informative than total testosterone, because hyperinsulinemia and androgen excess lower SHBG, keeping total testosterone high-normal while unbound testosterone is substantially elevated (Harrison 22e p.3139-3140). Dihydrotestosterone (DHT), formed from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase within the pilosebaceous unit, is the principal mediator of androgen action on the hair follicle; type 2 isoenzyme predominates in hair follicles and type 1 in sebaceous glands (Harrison 22e p.3139). Acanthosis nigricans and skin tags are cutaneous markers of associated insulin resistance in hyperandrogenic women (Harrison 22e p.3138). A BMI >25 kg/m2 (and especially >30) is frequently associated with hirsutism, partly via increased peripheral conversion of androgen precursors to testosterone (Harrison 22e p.3138). After menopause, ovarian estrogen production falls more than androgen production and SHBG declines, increasing the relative proportion of unbound testosterone, which can exacerbate hirsutism (Harrison 22e p.3140). Rapid onset or rapid progression of hirsutism Signs of virilization: voice deepening, clitoromegaly, breast atrophy, increased muscle bulk Total testosterone >12 nmol/L (>3.5 ng/mL) suggesting an androgen-producing tumor DHEAS >18.5 micromol/L (>7000 microg/L) suggesting an adrenal tumor Hypertension, striae, easy bruising, centripetal weight gain suggesting Cushing's syndrome Galactorrhea suggesting hyperprolactinemia Relying on total testosterone alone can miss hyperandrogenism, since low SHBG can keep total levels high-normal while free testosterone is elevated. Assuming shaving increases hair rate or density; it does not. Over-interpreting ovarian ultrasound: polycystic-appearing ovaries also occur in hypothalamic amenorrhea and in women without PCOS, so ultrasound has low specificity and is often unnecessary to diagnose PCOS. Random LH/FSH measurements are unreliable for PCOS because of pulsatile gonadotropin secretion. Mild DHEAS elevations are common in PCOS and do not by themselves indicate an adrenal tumor. Failing to distinguish hirsutism from hypertrichosis, leading to inappropriate hormonal work-up. Underestimating androgen excess in Asian and Native American women, who may show only acne or scalp thinning. Androgens drive differentiation of pilosebaceous units, transforming vellus hairs into terminal hairs and stimulating sebaceous gland development; the total number of follicles is fixed for life, but follicle size and hair type change with androgen exposure and local growth factors. Testosterone, secreted roughly equally by ovaries (LH-driven) and adrenals (ACTH-driven), is a precursor that is converted within the pilosebaceous unit by 5-alpha-reductase to the more potent dihydrotestosterone, the chief local mediator. End-organ sensitivity, genetic and ethnic background, and local growth factors explain why androgen levels correlate only modestly with the amount of hair. Excess androgen also shortens the scalp-hair anagen phase, producing thinning/androgenic alopecia. Hyperinsulinemia and androgen excess suppress hepatic SHBG, raising bioavailable free testosterone. In nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (usually 21-hydroxylase deficiency), impaired cortisol synthesis reduces negative feedback, driving compensatory ACTH-mediated adrenal hyperplasia and accumulation of steroid precursors that are shunted to androgens (Harrison 22e p.3138-3141). Most hirsutism is benign and chronic, reflecting underlying functional androgen excess (commonly PCOS) or idiopathic causes; with treatment, hair growth typically progresses slowly. Even effective therapy yields only modest reduction in hair, with attenuation usually not evident until 4-6 months and maximal effect requiring 9-12 months because of the length of the hair growth cycle. By contrast, rapidly progressive hirsutism with virilization may herald a malignant or otherwise serious neoplasm and carries a prognosis tied to that underlying tumor (Harrison 22e p.3138-3141). Hair growth is quantified objectively with the modified Ferriman-Gallwey scale, scoring nine androgen-sensitive body sites from 0 (no terminal hair) to 4 (frankly virile, male-pattern). A total score <8 is normal in ~95% of non-Hispanic white and African American women; scores >=8 indicate excess androgen-mediated hair growth warranting hormonal evaluation (Harrison 22e p.3138-3139).

Histidinaemia — histidinaemia, histidase deficiency, histidine ammonia-lyase deficiency, HAL deficiency, hyperhistidinaemia Other benign aminoacidaemias identified on newborn screening Secondary histidine elevation from folate status or dietary factors Urea cycle or transport disorders with altered amino acid profiles Renal tubular aminoaciduria Coincidental neurodevelopmental disorder of separate cause Quantitative plasma amino acids showing elevated histidine Urine amino acids and imidazole metabolites with absent/low urocanic acid Skin or sweat urocanic acid testing Histidase enzyme assay (historically in stratum corneum or liver) where confirmation is sought Molecular analysis of the HAL gene Evaluation for an alternative diagnosis if symptoms are present Caused by deficiency of histidase (histidine ammonia-lyase, HAL), the first enzyme of histidine degradation that converts histidine to urocanic acid Now regarded as an essentially benign biochemical condition; historical associations with speech delay and intellectual disability were largely ascription artefacts of the era before newborn screening controls The biochemical signature is raised plasma and urine histidine with reduced or absent urinary urocanic acid, and elevated histidine metabolites (imidazole compounds) in urine Most individuals detected through screening are healthy and require no treatment A sweat/skin test showing absent urocanic acid supports the diagnosis, as urocanic acid is normally abundant in skin and sweat It is important not to attribute unrelated developmental problems to the biochemical finding Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and dietary histidine restriction is not warranted for the benign condition British spelling applies (histidinaemia) Attributing significant developmental or neurological problems to histidinaemia without other evaluation Progressive symptoms suggesting a different, coexisting disorder Unnecessary dietary restriction causing nutritional compromise Treating a benign biochemical finding as a disease requiring dietary therapy Falsely linking developmental delay to the histidine elevation Confusing it with a more serious aminoacidopathy Missing a separate primary diagnosis when symptoms coexist Histidine is normally degraded by histidase, which removes ammonia to form urocanic acid en route to glutamate formation. In histidinaemia, deficient histidase activity causes histidine to accumulate in plasma and urine while urocanic acid, normally produced in liver and skin, is reduced or absent. Because the accumulated histidine and its transamination products (imidazole derivatives) are not appreciably toxic, the condition is now considered a benign inborn variation of metabolism rather than a cause of neurological disease. The prognosis is excellent, as histidinaemia is now recognised as a benign metabolic trait with normal development expected in the great majority. No treatment is generally required.

Histiocytic sarcoma — HS, malignant histiocytosis (historical), true histiocytic sarcoma, CD163-positive histiocytic malignancy Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or anaplastic large cell lymphoma Follicular and interdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma Langerhans cell histiocytosis and Langerhans cell sarcoma Metastatic carcinoma or melanoma Reactive histiocytic proliferations and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma Biopsy with immunohistochemistry showing CD163, CD68 and lysozyme positivity and absence of lymphoid, dendritic and epithelial markers Clonality and molecular studies, including assessment of relationship to any associated lymphoid neoplasm Molecular testing for BRAF and other MAPK-pathway mutations to guide targeted therapy PET-CT and cross-sectional imaging for staging Bone marrow examination and full blood count Exclusion of reactive histiocytic and haemophagocytic conditions A rare aggressive malignancy of cells showing morphological and immunophenotypic features of mature tissue macrophages (histiocytes) May present at nodal, extranodal or disseminated sites, with common involvement of the gastrointestinal tract, skin, soft tissue and lymph nodes Systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss and cytopenias are frequent, and disseminated disease carries a poor outlook The tumour cells are large and pleomorphic and express histiocytic markers such as CD163, CD68 and lysozyme while lacking B-cell, T-cell, dendritic-cell, melanocytic and epithelial markers It can arise in association with, or transform from, other haematological neoplasms such as follicular lymphoma or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, sometimes sharing clonal genetic features Recurrent activating mutations in the MAPK pathway, including BRAF and other kinase genes, occur in a proportion of cases and may offer targeted-therapy opportunities Localised disease may be treated with surgery and radiotherapy, while disseminated disease requires systemic chemotherapy, generally with limited durable success Rapidly progressive disseminated disease with systemic symptoms Bone marrow failure with severe cytopenias Bulky or destructive extranodal masses causing organ compromise Features of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis complicating the disease Central nervous system involvement Misdiagnosing the tumour as anaplastic lymphoma, carcinoma or dendritic-cell sarcoma without a full histiocytic marker panel Failing to recognise clonal relationship to an associated lymphoid neoplasm Overlooking targetable BRAF or other MAPK-pathway mutations Confusing malignant disease with reactive histiocytosis or haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis Underestimating the aggressive behaviour of disseminated disease Histiocytic sarcoma is a clonal proliferation of cells committed to the macrophage/histiocyte lineage, retaining the antigen-expression profile of mature tissue macrophages such as CD163 and CD68. In a subset of cases the tumour is clonally related to a preceding or concurrent lymphoid neoplasm, reflecting a phenomenon of lineage plasticity or transdifferentiation in which a committed lymphoid clone acquires a histiocytic phenotype while sharing molecular hallmarks such as immunoglobulin gene rearrangements. Recurrent activating alterations of the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK (MAPK) signalling pathway drive proliferation in many cases. The malignant histiocytes infiltrate tissues destructively and disseminate widely, producing the aggressive, often treatment-resistant clinical behaviour. Localised histiocytic sarcoma may be controlled with surgery and radiotherapy, but disseminated or high-stage disease is aggressive with poor survival despite chemotherapy; identification of targetable MAPK-pathway mutations offers a potential avenue for improved outcomes in selected patients.

Histoplasmosis — Histoplasma capsulatum infection Tuberculosis (chronic cavitary disease) Sarcoidosis Lymphoma Primary or metastatic lung cancer (asymptomatic pulmonary nodules) Other endemic/dimorphic mycoses: blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis Cavitary tuberculosis (chronic pulmonary histoplasmosis mimics this radiographically and pathologically) Blastomycosis Coccidioidomycosis Paracoccidioidomycosis Talaromycosis Histoplasma antigen detection in urine and serum (and BAL fluid; CSF for CNS disease) Lateral flow antigen point-of-care testing for resource-limited settings Histoplasma serology: immunodiffusion (ID), complement fixation (CF), IgG and IgM enzyme immunoassay (EIA) Fungal culture (BAL fluid, sputum/bronchial washings, blood, bone marrow aspirate; positive in ~75% of PDH and chronic pulmonary disease) Fungal stains/cytopathology or biopsy of affected organ (BAL fluid, bone marrow, liver, adrenal) showing small narrow-budding intracellular yeasts Chest radiograph/CT (pneumonitis, hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, upper-lobe cavitation, calcified nodes) Workup for rare genetic immunodeficiencies of the IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha pathways in healthy individuals presenting with PDH Sarcoidosis Lymphoma Primary lung cancer (asymptomatic controlled nodules found on screening CT in smokers) Metastatic cancer Caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, a thermal dimorphic fungus; H. capsulatum var. capsulatum predominates in North America, while var. duboisii in Africa produces larger yeasts and a clinically distinct disease with frequent skin and bone involvement (p.1692-1693, 1695). Most prevalent endemic mycosis in North America, classically the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys, with foci in Mexico, Central/South America (Brazil), Africa and Asia; soil enriched with bird or bat droppings promotes growth, and disruption aerosolizes microconidia (p.1693). High-exposure, high-attack-rate activities include spelunking (cave exposure), excavation, cleaning chicken coops, demolition/remodeling of old buildings and cutting dead trees (p.1693). Clinical spectrum spans asymptomatic infection to life-threatening illness; severity depends on intensity of exposure, host immune status and underlying lung architecture (p.1693-1694). Acute pulmonary disease appears 1-4 weeks after exposure as a flulike illness (fever, chills, sweats, headache, myalgia, anorexia, dry cough, dyspnea, chest pain), often with hilar/mediastinal adenopathy on chest radiograph (p.1694). Arthralgia/arthritis with erythema nodosum occurs in 5-10% of acute cases and represents an inflammatory response, not extrapulmonary spread; pericarditis may also develop (p.1694). Chronic cavitary pulmonary histoplasmosis occurs in smokers with structural lung disease (e.g., bullous emphysema), with productive cough, dyspnea, low-grade fever, night sweats, weight loss and upper-lobe cavitary infiltrates resembling tuberculosis (p.1694). Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (PDH) involves the reticuloendothelial system - lungs, bone marrow, spleen, liver, adrenal glands and mucocutaneous membranes; common findings are fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia, with possible meningitis, oral/GI ulceration and adrenal insufficiency (p.1694). Fungal culture is the diagnostic gold standard but may take up to 1 month and is often negative in less severe cases; in PDH yield is highest from BAL fluid, bone marrow aspirate and blood (p.1694). Detection of Histoplasma antigen in body fluids is extremely useful for PDH and acute diffuse pulmonary disease (sensitivity >95% in PDH, >80% in severe acute pulmonary disease when both urine and serum are tested); urine is often positive in disseminated disease (p.1694-1695, 1693). Antigen levels correlate with severity in PDH, fall with effective therapy, and a stable or rising level predicts relapse or treatment failure (p.1695-1696). Serology (immunodiffusion, complement fixation, IgG/IgM EIA) is especially useful in immunocompetent patients and for chronic pulmonary disease; IgM appears first and declines, IgG appears later and rises (p.1695). Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (PDH), typically in immunocompromised hosts (~70% of cases), especially AIDS with CD4+ count <200/microliter Acute rapidly fatal PDH with diffuse interstitial/reticulonodular infiltrates, respiratory failure, shock, coagulopathy and multiorgan failure Onset of PDH while on anti-TNF-alpha therapy, methotrexate or other biologic/immunosuppressive agents, or post-transplant immunosuppression CNS involvement: meningitis or focal brain lesions Adrenal insufficiency from adrenal involvement Fibrosing mediastinitis causing superior vena cava syndrome, pulmonary vessel obstruction or airway obstruction (fatal in up to one-third of cases) Large mediastinal masses compressing great vessels, airways or esophagus, or rupturing to form fistulae (e.g., bronchoesophageal) Chronic cavitary histoplasmosis closely mimics cavitary tuberculosis radiographically (upper-lobe infiltrates, cavitation, pleural thickening) and may be misdiagnosed as TB, sarcoidosis, lymphoma or malignancy. Asymptomatic calcified nodules from controlled prior infection may be mistaken for malignancy on screening CT in smokers from endemic areas. Fungal stains may misidentify staining artifacts or other fungal elements as Histoplasma yeasts. Persistent antibodies for several years after infection can cause a false misdiagnosis of active histoplasmosis in a patient with another disease process. ID and CF serology are insensitive early in infection and have reduced sensitivity in immunosuppressed patients, especially organ transplant recipients. Antigen testing cross-reacts with African histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis and rarely aspergillosis. Fibrosing mediastinitis is a chronic fibrotic reaction to past infection, not active disease, and does NOT respond to antifungal therapy. Unlike latent tuberculosis, inactive histoplasmosis does NOT reactivate. Infection follows inhalation of microconidia, the naturally infectious mycelial form; particles 2-4 micrometers reach terminal bronchioles and alveoli where alveolar macrophages engulf them and they transform into small (2-5 micrometer) narrow-budding yeasts, a calcium- and iron-dependent process central to pathogenesis. Yeasts evade the immune system and multiply within resting macrophages, then translocate via phagosomes to draining lymph nodes and spread hematogenously throughout the reticuloendothelial system. Effective cellular immunity develops about 2 weeks after infection, with T-cell interferon-gamma helping macrophages kill the organism; IL-12 and TNF-alpha are essential to cellular immunity. In immunocompetent hosts, organized granulomas contain the organisms and typically fibrose and calcify (calcified lung nodules, mediastinal nodes, hepatosplenic calcifications), and infection confers protective immunity to reinfection. With impaired cellular immunity, infection is not contained and disseminates as progressive disseminated histoplasmosis. Structural lung disease such as emphysema impairs clearance and leads to chronic pulmonary disease with progressive inflammation, necrosis and fibrosis mimicking cavitary tuberculosis (p.1693-1694). Most immunocompetent individuals with low-level exposure are asymptomatic or have a mild, self-limited illness that resolves without therapy; up to 75% of adults in endemic areas have evidence of prior infection without clinical disease. Untreated chronic cavitary disease is slowly progressive. Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis ranges from an acute, rapidly fatal course to a subacute/chronic one and is a devastating illness requiring prompt recognition, particularly in AIDS or anti-TNF therapy. Fibrosing mediastinitis is fatal in up to one-third of cases. Antigen levels track severity and response, with stable or rising levels signaling treatment failure or relapse (p.1693-1696). Clinical forms (Harrison Table 218-1): acute pulmonary, mild to moderate; acute pulmonary, severe with respiratory failure (ARDS); chronic/cavitary pulmonary; progressive disseminated (PDH); and central nervous system disease. Severity is graded by intensity of exposure, host immune status and underlying lung architecture (p.1693-1695).

HIV/AIDS — HIV infection, AIDS, acquired immunodeficiency syndrome Infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus) and acute CMV infection (overlapping mononucleosis-like picture; cross-ref Appendix A1) Acute viral exanthems and other causes of fever with rash (e.g., secondary syphilis, enteroviral exanthem) Streptococcal/viral pharyngitis when sore throat predominates in acute HIV (cross-ref ch.38 p.293) Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis Acute cytomegalovirus infection Secondary syphilis Fourth-generation HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody combination immunoassay with supplemental confirmatory antibody differentiation assay (cross-ref ch.126, Fig.126-1) HIV RNA (plasma viral load) quantification — diagnostic in the early window before antibody, and the key on-treatment monitoring test (cross-ref ch.126; ch.108) CD4+ T-lymphocyte count to stage immunodeficiency and guide opportunistic-infection prophylaxis HIV genotypic resistance testing recommended before starting antiretrovirals (cross-ref ch.126, Fig.126-1) Screening for co-infections (hepatitis B, hepatitis C) prior to immunosuppressive or antineoplastic therapy in HIV-positive patients (cross-ref ch.108 p.745) Drug hypersensitivity reaction with fever and morbilliform rash Autoinflammatory/connective-tissue disease presenting with fever, rash and lymphadenopathy HIV is a retrovirus whose hallmark is progressive depletion of CD4+ T lymphocytes; the resulting immunodeficiency underlies the susceptibility to opportunistic infections and AIDS-defining illnesses (Harrison 22e ch.208, p.1556). Consider acute (primary) HIV infection in a patient presenting with a mononucleosis-like illness: sore throat is reported by roughly half of patients with acute HIV infection, often together with fever, headache, myalgias, lymphadenopathy, anorexia and rash (p.1556; cross-ref ch.38 p.293). The acute retroviral syndrome rash is typically a nonspecific diffuse macular/papular eruption favouring the upper thorax, face and collar region; less commonly urticarial or vesicular lesions occur, and oral or genital ulcers may accompany it (p.1556; cross-ref Appendix A1). After primary infection there is HIV seroconversion, then a usually asymptomatic phase, and ultimately progression to symptomatic HIV disease/AIDS if untreated (cross-ref ch.38 p.297). Three diagnostic markers appear sequentially in primary infection: HIV viral load (RNA) first, then p24 antigen, then HIV antibody; modern fourth-generation Ag/Ab combination assays shorten the window period by detecting p24 antigen before antibody is present (cross-ref ch.126, Fig.126-1). The CD4+ T-cell count stratifies opportunistic-infection risk: as the count falls (notably below ~200 cells/uL) the risk of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex and CMV end-organ disease rises, guiding prophylaxis decisions (p.1556; cross-ref ch.62, ch.108). A nondetectable (suppressed) HIV viral load on antiretroviral therapy is the goal of treatment; sustained viral suppression is the basis of the Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U) principle and of treatment-as-prevention (cross-ref ch.108 p.745). Antiretroviral therapy is recommended for essentially all people with HIV regardless of CD4 count; in patients with concurrent malignancy or other illness, ART should run concurrently with the primary treatment together with appropriate antimicrobial prophylaxis (cross-ref ch.108 p.745). Doses and specific drug regimens are deliberately omitted here; ART is presented only as a principle (combination antiretroviral therapy to achieve durable viral suppression). New CD4+ count below ~200 cells/uL — high risk of Pneumocystis pneumonia and other opportunistic infections; prompts prophylaxis (cross-ref ch.62 p.461) Clinical or radiographic worsening after starting ART suggesting immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), especially with an underlying opportunistic infection such as PML (cross-ref ch.205 p.1490) Features suggesting an AIDS-defining opportunistic process (e.g., focal neurologic deficit from toxoplasmosis or CNS lymphoma; cross-ref ch.30) Adrenal insufficiency precipitated by stress or steroidogenesis-inhibiting drugs in advanced HIV — adrenal involvement is usually subclinical but can become clinically significant (cross-ref ch.49 p.379) Failing to consider acute HIV in a mononucleosis-like illness: although about half of patients with acute HIV infection have a sore throat, in most U.S. settings only about 1% of patients with viral or mononucleosis-like symptoms actually have acute HIV — a negative antibody test early does not exclude it, so check viral load/p24 (cross-ref ch.38 p.293). Relying on antibody testing alone during the window period can miss acute infection before seroconversion; the dashed limit-of-detection and marker sequence (VL, then p24, then Ab) explain false-negative antibody results (cross-ref ch.126, Fig.126-1). Attributing post-ART clinical deterioration to treatment failure rather than recognising IRIS, particularly in patients with a treated or unmasked opportunistic infection (cross-ref ch.205 p.1490). Overlooking subclinical adrenal insufficiency in advanced HIV, which may be unmasked by stress or by drugs that inhibit steroidogenesis (cross-ref ch.49 p.379). HIV is a human retrovirus that infects cells bearing the CD4 receptor together with a chemokine co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4), leading to progressive depletion and dysfunction of CD4+ T lymphocytes (Harrison 22e ch.208, p.1556; co-receptor role cross-ref ch.61 p.448, ch.63). Reverse transcriptase copies the viral RNA genome into DNA that integrates into the host genome, establishing lifelong infection and a latent reservoir. Primary infection produces a burst of high-level viremia (the acute retroviral syndrome) followed by partial immune control and a viral set point, then a prolonged clinically latent phase during which CD4+ T cells are gradually lost. Once CD4+ T-cell counts fall sufficiently, the profound cellular immunodeficiency permits opportunistic infections and AIDS-defining illnesses. The mononuclear phagocyte system can also be infected and serves as a reservoir (cross-ref ch.63 p.461). Untreated HIV infection is progressive and ultimately fatal once advanced immunodeficiency and AIDS-defining illnesses supervene. Effective antiretroviral therapy that achieves a durable nondetectable viral load markedly improves survival and restores immune function; for example, in HIV-positive patients with PML, institution of ART enhances survival, and those with higher CD4 counts (>300/uL) and low or nondetectable HIV viral loads have a better prognosis (cross-ref ch.205, p.1490). Staging is based on the CD4+ T-lymphocyte count, which predicts the spectrum of opportunistic disease: relatively preserved counts carry low opportunistic-infection risk, whereas progressively lower counts (notably <200 cells/uL) define increasing risk for Pneumocystis pneumonia, cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex and CMV disease, with the lowest counts associated with the broadest range of AIDS-defining illnesses (Harrison 22e ch.208, p.1556; opportunistic-infection associations cross-ref ch.62, ch.222, ch.227, ch.235).

species) and confirmed by enzyme assay or HMGCL sequencing Acute management is aggressive intravenous glucose to halt catabolism, with ammonia scavengers and correction of acidosis as needed Long-term care combines avoidance of fasting, moderate protein/leucine restriction and carnitine supplementation Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy and coma Significant hyperammonaemia during an acute crisis Severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis Reye-like hepatic dysfunction with rising transaminases Rapid neurological deterioration during intercurrent illness or fasting Expecting ketosis to accompany hypoglycaemia and being falsely reassured by its absence Misdiagnosing an acute crisis as Reye syndrome and missing the metabolic cause Delaying intravenous glucose while awaiting confirmatory results Overlooking hyperammonaemia as a treatable contributor to encephalopathy Allowing prolonged fasting for procedures or illness without a metabolic emergency plan HMG-CoA lyase catalyses the final step of leucine degradation and the terminal reaction of hepatic ketogenesis, cleaving 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA into acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA. Deficiency blocks both pathways, so during fasting or catabolic stress the liver cannot generate ketone bodies to provide alternative fuel, producing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia once glycogen stores are exhausted. Simultaneously, leucine-derived intermediates and organic acids accumulate, causing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, and secondary inhibition of the urea cycle contributes to hyperammonaemia. The accumulating organic acids and energy failure injure the brain and liver, accounting for the encephalopathic, Reye-like crises. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. With early diagnosis, avoidance of fasting and prompt treatment of crises, many patients do well, but severe or delayed decompensations can cause permanent neurological injury or death, and outcome depends heavily on preventing metabolic crises.

for the 17q12 deletion Caused by heterozygous variants or 17q12 microdeletions affecting HNF1B, a transcription factor governing development of the kidney, pancreas, liver and genital tract The renal phenotype is highly variable, most often bilateral renal cysts or hyperechoic kidneys detected antenatally or in childhood, but also hypoplasia, dysplasia and single kidney The classic association is renal cysts and diabetes (RCAD): a maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY5) coupled with structural kidney disease Extrarenal features include pancreatic hypoplasia with exocrine insufficiency, mechanism Antenatally detected bilateral hyperechoic or cystic kidneys New-onset diabetes with structural kidney disease in a young non-obese patient Progressive decline in renal function towards kidney failure Neurodevelopmental features suggesting a larger 17q12 deletion Excluding the diagnosis because sequencing is normal without testing for a whole-gene deletion Overlooking hypomagnesaemia as a diagnostic clue Assuming diabetes is type 1 or type 2 and missing the MODY5 label affecting management Failing to consider de novo cases in the absence of family history HNF1B (hepatocyte nuclear factor 1-beta) is a transcription factor essential for the normal development and differentiation of the kidney, pancreatic islet and exocrine tissue, biliary tract and Mullerian structures. Loss of one functional copy, through point variants or a 17q12 contiguous gene deletion, causes haploinsufficiency that disrupts nephrogenesis and tubular gene expression, producing cystic, hypoplastic or dysplastic kidneys and impaired tubular handling of magnesium and urate. The same developmental defect in the pancreas leads to beta-cell dysfunction and diabetes (MODY5) with exocrine hypoplasia, and in the genital tract to Mullerian anomalies. The resulting phenotype is therefore a multisystem developmental disorder with prominent structural and functional kidney disease. Outcome is highly variable, ranging from stable mild renal impairment to progression to kidney failure; the combination of diabetes, electrolyte disturbance and structural anomalies requires lifelong multidisciplinary surveillance.

Hodgkin's Lymphoma — Hodgkin disease Inflammatory processes (reactive lymphadenopathy) Infectious mononucleosis Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL) Phenytoin-induced adenopathy Nonlymphomatous malignancies Anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (can mimic HL, especially in older patients) T-cell/histiocyte-rich B-cell lymphoma Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) Reactive/inflammatory lymphadenopathy from infection Adequate biopsy specimen reviewed by an expert hematopathologist (required to establish the diagnosis) Immunohistochemistry: PAX-5, CD15, CD30 (and CD19/CD20, typically low/absent in cHL) PET/CT for anatomic staging (more accurate than marrow biopsy for patchy marrow involvement) Complete blood count with differential Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) Chemistry studies reflecting major organ function, including serum albumin HIV and hepatitis virus testing Careful history (including presence/absence of B symptoms) and physical exam attentive to peripheral nodes, liver, and spleen size; review of comorbidities such as pulmonary disease and congestive heart failure given lung- and heart-toxic chemotherapy Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma Anaplastic large-cell lymphoma T-cell/histiocyte-rich B-cell lymphoma Phenytoin-induced (drug-related) adenopathy Nonlymphomatous malignancies Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL) is a malignancy of mature B lymphocytes and accounts for ~10% of all lymphomas diagnosed each year; most are classical HL (cHL), with nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL (NLPHL) a distinct second subtype (p.868). Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells are diagnostic of cHL: large cells with abundant cytoplasm and bilobed and/or multiple nuclei, comprising <1% of tumor cellularity within a surrounding polyclonal inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, eosinophils, neutrophils, macrophages, plasma cells, fibroblasts, and collagen (p.868-869). By immunohistochemistry HRS cells are often PAX-5 positive but have low to no expression of other B-cell antigens such as CD19 and CD20; they express CD15 and CD30 in 85% and 100% of cases, respectively (p.868). Most patients present with nontender palpable lymphadenopathy, typically in the neck, supraclavicular area, and axilla; more than half have mediastinal adenopathy at diagnosis, sometimes as the initial manifestation (p.869). About one-third of patients present with B symptoms (fevers, night sweats, and/or weight loss); HL can occasionally present as a fever of unknown origin, more common in older patients with mixed-cellularity HL in an abdominal site (p.869). Pel-Ebstein fever describes a pattern of fevers persisting for days to weeks, followed by afebrile intervals and then recurrence (p.869). Pain in lymph nodes on alcohol ingestion and severe unexplained itching (pruritus) are recognized unusual manifestations of HL (p.869). Staging is anatomically based using the Ann Arbor staging system because the disease tends to march from one lymph node group to the next, often contiguous group; staging guides therapy duration and intensity (p.869). PET/CT is used for staging and is more accurate than bone marrow biopsy for assessing bone marrow involvement, which in cHL tends to be patchy and may be missed on a unilateral marrow biopsy (p.869). Cure rates now exceed 85%, and the new central challenge in HL care is late therapy-related toxicity, including a high rate of secondary malignancies and cardiovascular disease (p.868). B symptoms: unexplained weight loss >10% of body weight over the 6 months before staging, persistent or recurrent fever >38°C in the previous month, or recurrent drenching night sweats in the previous month Pel-Ebstein fever (cyclic fever with afebrile intervals) Bulky disease and elevated ESR (>30 with B symptoms; >50 without) marking unfavorable early-stage disease Fever of unknown origin as a presentation, particularly in older patients with mixed-cellularity HL at an abdominal site Superior vena cava syndrome from mediastinal involvement (HL is a recognized cause) The late age peak in the bimodal distribution may be artifactual, attributable to confusion with similar-appearing entities such as anaplastic large-cell lymphoma and T-cell/histiocyte-rich B-cell lymphoma (p.868). Bone marrow involvement in cHL is patchy and can be missed on a unilateral marrow biopsy; PET/CT is more accurate (p.869). Combined-modality therapy in early-stage disease reduces relapse only slightly while increasing late toxicity, with minimal or no improvement in long-term survival; much of the excess risk is attributable to radiotherapy (p.869-870). NLPHL is biologically distinct from cHL and resembles indolent B-cell NHL; its 'popcorn'/L&H cells are CD30- and CD15-negative (unlike HRS cells), so it should not be managed identically to cHL (p.868, 871). Alternative regimens (Stanford V, escalated BEACOPP) have not improved survival over standard therapy in early- or advanced-stage disease and are associated with increased toxicity (p.870). Subdiaphragmatic presentation of cHL is unusual; it is more common in older males (p.869). HL is of B-cell origin. The malignant Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells are large bilobed/multinucleate cells that constitute <1% of the tumor mass; the bulk of the tumor is a surrounding polyclonal inflammatory infiltrate, probably a reaction to cytokines produced by the tumor cells. Immunoglobulin genes in the neoplastic cells are rearranged but not expressed. HRS cells interact with their microenvironment via cell-cell contact and elaboration of growth factors and cytokines, producing a cellular milieu that protects them from host immune attack while supporting their proliferation and survival. 97% of HRS cells in cHL harbor genetic aberrations in the PD-L1 locus on chromosome 9p24.1, causing overexpression of PD-L1 (ligand for the inhibitory PD-1 receptor on immune cells), a mechanism for immune evasion that may also contribute to generalized immune suppression in HL patients. An association with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is suggested: monoclonal/oligoclonal EBV-infected cells are found in 20-40% of HL patients, but a definitive etiologic role is not settled. Viral oncogenesis appears greater in HIV-related cHL, where EBV is detectable in nearly all cases (versus only one-third of non-HIV-associated cHL) and HRS cells express EBV latent membrane protein 1 (LMP-1) with episomal, clonal EBV genomes suggesting direct involvement in early lymphomagenesis (p.868-869). cHL is highly curable and a success story of modern oncology, with cure rates now >85%; the overwhelming majority of patients are cured with chemotherapy alone or combined chemotherapy and radiation. Patients are stratified into early-stage (I/II) versus advanced-stage (III/IV) disease. Early-stage patients have a better prognosis overall and are further classified as favorable or unfavorable. In advanced-stage disease, prognosis is best predicted by the International Prognostic Score (IPS), which assigns 1 point each for male sex, age >45 years, stage IV disease, serum albumin <4 g/dL, hemoglobin <10.5 g/dL, white blood cell count >=15,000/uL, and lymphocyte count <600/uL and/or <8% of WBC count; 5-year progression-free survival ranges from 88% (no risk factors) to 62% (four or more factors), though very few patients carry multiple risk factors. NLPHL tends to have a chronic, relapsing course resembling indolent B-cell NHL, with a 15-year nonrelapse survival of 82% for early-stage disease treated with definitive radiotherapy. A major concern is that in some early-stage series more patients died from late treatment complications than from HL itself (p.868-871). Ann Arbor Staging System: Stage I = single lymph node region or lymphoid structure (e.g., spleen, thymus, Waldeyer's ring); Stage II = two or more node regions on the same side of the diaphragm (mediastinum counts as one site; bilaterally involved hilar nodes constitute stage II); Stage III = node regions/lymphoid structures on both sides of the diaphragm (III1 limited to spleen, splenic hilar, celiac, or portal nodes; III2 adds paraaortic, iliac, or mesenteric nodes); Stage IV = extranodal involvement beyond 'E', more than one extranodal deposit at any location, or any liver/bone marrow involvement. Suffix A = no symptoms; B = unexplained weight loss >10% over 6 months, persistent/recurrent fever >38°C in the previous month, or recurrent drenching night sweats in the previous month; E = localized solitary extralymphatic involvement (excluding liver and bone marrow). Patients are further grouped clinically as early-stage (I/II) versus advanced-stage (III/IV), with early-stage subclassified favorable vs unfavorable and advanced-stage risk-scored by the International Prognostic Score (p.869).

avoiding unnecessary surgery Acute severe distension with concern for perforation or ischaemia Sepsis from bacterial overgrowth, translocation, or line infection during parenteral nutrition Severe malnutrition and dependence on parenteral support Urinary retention or upper tract dilatation from bladder involvement Performing repeated laparotomies for presumed mechanical obstruction that is actually pseudo-obstruction Failing to obtain full-thickness biopsy to distinguish myopathic from neuropathic disease Overlooking urinary tract involvement (megacystis) as part of the same disorder Neglecting bacterial overgrowth and nutritional deficiencies as sources of morbidity Hollow visceral myopathy is a primary disorder of gastrointestinal (and often urinary tract) smooth muscle, in which degeneration, vacuolar change, and replacement fibrosis of the muscle layers impair contractile function. The weakened, poorly contracting muscle cannot generate effective peristalsis, so luminal contents stagnate and the bowel dilates, producing the clinical picture of pseudo-obstruction with megaduodenum and megacystis despite a patent lumen. Stasis promotes small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth and malabsorption, compounding malnutrition. The course is typically chronic and progressive, with morbidity from malnutrition, dependence on parenteral nutrition, and recurrent pseudo-obstructive episodes; prognosis depends on the extent of gut involvement and complications of long-term nutritional support.

Holmes-Adie syndrome — Adie syndrome, Adie's tonic pupil syndrome, Holmes-Adie pupil Pharmacological mydriasis from anticholinergic exposure Compressive third nerve palsy Argyll Robertson pupil of neurosyphilis Ross syndrome Traumatic or ischaemic iris damage Physiological anisocoria Slit-lamp examination for vermiform iris movements and light-near dissociation Dilute pilocarpine test to demonstrate cholinergic supersensitivity Deep tendon reflex assessment Syphilis serology when an Argyll Robertson pupil is a consideration Review of drug and eye-drop exposure to exclude pharmacological mydriasis Autonomic testing where a wider dysautonomia such as Ross syndrome is suspected Combination of a tonic (Adie) pupil with diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes, most often in young adult women The affected pupil is large (mydriatic), reacts poorly and slowly to light, but constricts slowly and tonically to sustained near effort, giving light-near dissociation Vermiform (segmental) movements of the iris margin may be visible on slit-lamp examination Denervation supersensitivity is demonstrated by constriction to dilute pilocarpine that would not affect a normal pupil Usually benign and idiopathic, reflecting damage to the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves Patients may notice anisocoria, photophobia, or difficulty focusing at near from accommodative paresis When accompanied by segmental anhidrosis it overlaps with Ross syndrome Management is reassurance and symptomatic measures; no specific treatment reverses the pupillary abnormality A painful dilated pupil with ptosis or an eye-movement deficit suggesting a compressive third nerve palsy or aneurysm Acute severe headache accompanying the pupillary change Progressive or bilateral involvement with systemic features Signs suggesting neurosyphilis Confusing the tonic pupil with a dangerous third nerve palsy or aneurysmal mydriasis Overlooking light-near dissociation, the key clinical sign Attributing the anisocoria to pharmacological causes without proper testing Missing associated anhidrosis that would indicate Ross syndrome Holmes-Adie syndrome results from postganglionic parasympathetic denervation of the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle, usually from injury to the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves. Acutely the pupil is dilated and poorly reactive; with aberrant reinnervation, fibres originally destined for the ciliary muscle misdirect to the iris sphincter, producing the characteristic slow, tonic constriction to near effort and light-near dissociation. Denervation renders the sphincter supersensitive to dilute cholinergic agonists. The associated hyporeflexia reflects an accompanying degeneration of dorsal root ganglion neurons. The cause is usually unknown, although viral or autoimmune mechanisms have been proposed. Holmes-Adie syndrome is benign; the tonic pupil may remain enlarged or become smaller over years (the 'little old Adie's pupil'), and the main consequences are cosmetic anisocoria and near-vision symptoms rather than serious morbidity.

Holmes tremor — rubral tremor, midbrain tremor, thalamic tremor Parkinsonian rest tremor Essential tremor Cerebellar intention tremor Dystonic tremor Functional tremor MRI of the brain to identify the causative midbrain or thalamic lesion Characterisation of the tremor components (rest, postural, intention) Evaluation for the underlying cause (vascular, demyelinating, traumatic) Assessment of response to a dopaminergic trial in selected cases Referral evaluation for surgical therapy if refractory A disabling low-frequency tremor that is present at rest and worsens with posture and especially with goal-directed movement It is typically irregular and coarse, unlike the more regular tremor of Parkinson disease or essential tremor It results from lesions affecting both the cerebellothalamic and nigrostriatal (dopaminergic) pathways, often in the midbrain or thalamus There is characteristically a delay of weeks to months between the causative lesion and tremor onset Common causes include stroke, trauma, multiple sclerosis and other structural midbrain lesions It is often refractory to drugs, and some patients are considered for deep brain stimulation Progressive brainstem or cerebellar signs A new or enlarging structural lesion Severe disability from the tremor Features suggesting an untreated underlying disease such as multiple sclerosis Mistaking the rest component for Parkinson disease Overlooking the causative lesion by not imaging Expecting a good drug response and not considering surgery Failing to identify and treat an underlying demyelinating or vascular cause Holmes tremor arises from combined disruption of the cerebellothalamocortical outflow and the nigrostriatal dopaminergic system, usually from a single strategically placed lesion in the midbrain, thalamus or their connections. The mixed damage produces a tremor with rest, postural and prominent intention components, and the loss of dopaminergic input explains the rest component and the partial response some patients show to dopaminergic drugs. The delay to onset reflects secondary reorganisation and degeneration after the initial lesion. The tremor is frequently persistent and disabling and often responds poorly to medication, though dopaminergic drugs help some patients and deep brain stimulation can benefit selected refractory cases.

Holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency — HLCS deficiency, early-onset multiple carboxylase deficiency, neonatal biotin-responsive multiple carboxylase deficiency, HLCS Biotinidase deficiency (the late-onset multiple carboxylase deficiency) Isolated propionic, methylmalonic or isovaleric acidaemia Isolated 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency and primary lactic acidoses Neonatal sepsis with lactic acidosis Urea cycle disorders with hyperammonaemia Acrodermatitis enteropathica (for the dermatological picture) Urine organic acids showing the combined carboxylase-deficiency pattern Plasma acylcarnitine profile (raised 3-hydroxyisovaleryl and propionyl species) Blood gas, lactate, glucose and ammonia during crises Serum biotinidase activity to differentiate biotinidase deficiency HLCS gene sequencing or fibroblast carboxylase/enzyme studies Plasma amino acids to assess for secondary elevations Trial of and response to oral biotin as supportive evidence One of the two forms of multiple carboxylase deficiency; the neonatal/early-onset form, caused by biallelic HLCS variants Holocarboxylase synthetase attaches biotin to the four biotin-dependent carboxylases, so deficiency impairs all of them simultaneously Typically presents in the neonatal period with feeding difficulties, lethargy, hypotonia, seizures and severe metabolic acidosis Cutaneous features (erythematous rash, alopecia) and ketolactic acidosis with hyperammonaemia are characteristic Urine organic acids show a combined pattern: 3-hydroxyisovalerate, 3-methylcrotonylglycine, methylcitrate, propionate and lactate Distinguished from biotinidase deficiency, which usually presents later; both are biotin-responsive multiple carboxylase deficiencies Most patients respond well to oral biotin supplementation, though very severe HLCS variants can be partially responsive Confirm by enzyme studies or HLCS sequencing; treat acute crises with fluids, glucose and correction of acidosis alongside biotin Severe ketolactic acidosis with cardiovascular instability in the neonate Encephalopathy with seizures and coma Significant hyperammonaemia during an acute crisis Rapidly progressive skin breakdown with secondary infection Poor or delayed biotin response indicating a severe variant Not starting a biotin trial promptly in an acidotic neonate with a suggestive organic acid pattern Confusing HLCS deficiency with the later-presenting biotinidase deficiency and mismanaging follow-up Attributing the rash to a primary dermatological or nutritional condition Assuming full biotin responsiveness in every case, missing partially responsive severe variants Overlooking hyperammonaemia and lactic acidosis as reversible contributors to encephalopathy Holocarboxylase synthetase covalently links biotin to the apoenzymes of the four biotin-dependent carboxylases: pyruvate carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase, 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase. When the enzyme is deficient, biotinylation fails and all four carboxylases lose activity, disrupting gluconeogenesis, amino acid (leucine, isoleucine, valine) and odd-chain fatty acid catabolism, and fatty acid synthesis. The result is accumulation of lactate, organic acids and ammonia, producing a severe ketolactic metabolic acidosis with hyperammonaemia and multiorgan dysfunction. Because the biochemical defect is in biotin utilisation rather than an absolute lack of the vitamin, pharmacological biotin can drive residual holocarboxylase synthetase activity and restore carboxylase function in most cases. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Most patients respond dramatically to biotin supplementation with resolution of the metabolic and cutaneous features and good long-term outcome, but severely affected neonates with poorly responsive variants may sustain neurological damage or die if treatment is delayed.

Holoprosencephaly — HPE, alobar holoprosencephaly, semilobar holoprosencephaly, lobar holoprosencephaly, SHH, ZIC2, SIX3, TGIF1 Hydranencephaly Severe hydrocephalus with a dilated single-appearing ventricle Septo-optic dysplasia Agenesis of the corpus callosum with interhemispheric cyst Dandy-Walker malformation Arrhinencephaly as an isolated finding Prenatal ultrasound and foetal MRI to assess forebrain cleavage and facial structures Postnatal brain MRI to grade the malformation and detect associated anomalies Karyotype and chromosomal microarray to detect trisomy 13 and other imbalances
