abnormalities, notably trisomy 13, single-gene variants in the sonic hedgehog pathway such as SHH, ZIC2, SIX3, and TGIF1, and environmental factors including maternal diabetes Endocrine dysfunction is common because the hypothalamic-pituitary axis is midline, so diabetes insipidus and other pituitary deficiencies should be sought Clinical features include developmental delay, epilepsy, hypotonia or spasticity, dysautonomia with temperature instability, and feeding difficulty Diagnosis combines prenatal ultrasound and foetal or postnatal MRI with karyotype, microarray, and single-gene testing for counselling Diabetes insipidus with dangerous sodium and fluid disturbance Temperature instability and dysautonomia in the neonatal period Refractory seizures Severe facial malformation with airway or feeding compromise Assuming a normal karyotype excludes a genetic cause when single-gene pathway variants may be responsible Missing hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction, particularly diabetes insipidus, in the neonatal period Mistaking severe hydrocephalus or hydranencephaly for alobar holoprosencephaly on imaging Overlooking the maternal diabetes association during counselling and future pregnancy planning Holoprosencephaly arises from failure of ventral induction and midline patterning of the developing forebrain in early gestation, when the prosencephalon should cleave into paired cerebral hemispheres and lateral ventricles. Disruption of the sonic hedgehog and related signalling pathways, whether from single-gene variants, chromosomal imbalance, or environmental insults such as maternal diabetes, prevents normal separation of midline structures. The result is a spectrum from complete non-cleavage with a monoventricle and fused deep grey nuclei to milder incomplete separation, with parallel disruption of midline facial development. Prognosis correlates with the severity of the malformation. Alobar holoprosencephaly usually results in death in utero or early infancy, whereas milder lobar forms may allow survival with variable degrees of developmental disability, epilepsy, and endocrine dysfunction.

Homocystinuria — classical homocystinuria, cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, CBS deficiency, homocystinuria due to CBS deficiency Marfan syndrome Remethylation defects (e.g. MTHFR deficiency, cobalamin metabolism disorders) Sulphite oxidase / molybdenum cofactor deficiency causing lens dislocation Ehlers-Danlos and other heritable connective-tissue disorders Inherited thrombophilias Plasma total homocysteine (markedly elevated) and plasma amino acids showing raised methionine Urine amino acids and homocysteine measurement Newborn screening for elevated methionine Enzyme assay of cystathionine beta-synthase in fibroblasts and molecular CBS gene testing Pyridoxine responsiveness testing under controlled conditions Ophthalmological assessment for ectopia lentis and DEXA for osteoporosis Classical form results from deficiency of cystathionine beta-synthase, causing accumulation of homocysteine and methionine A Marfanoid habitus with tall stature and arachnodactyly can mimic Marfan syndrome, but lens dislocation here is typically downward whereas in Marfan it is usually upward Downward ectopia lentis, progressive myopia and glaucoma are characteristic ocular features Thromboembolism affecting arteries and veins is the leading cause of morbidity and death and may occur at any age Skeletal involvement includes osteoporosis, scoliosis and a Marfanoid build; intellectual disability and psychiatric disturbance are common Around half of patients respond biochemically to pyridoxine (vitamin B6), which is a key determinant of phenotype severity and management Management principles include a methionine-restricted diet, cysteine supplementation, pyridoxine trial, and folate and vitamin B12 cofactor support, with betaine to promote remethylation of homocysteine Detectable on expanded newborn screening through elevated methionine, allowing early dietary intervention before irreversible damage Acute arterial or venous thromboembolism, including stroke, myocardial or pulmonary events, which may be life-threatening Perioperative period carries a high thrombotic risk requiring specific precautions Acute visual loss from lens dislocation into the anterior chamber or acute glaucoma Undiagnosed young patient with unexplained thrombosis and a Marfanoid appearance Mistaking the condition for Marfan syndrome and overlooking the treatable metabolic cause Failing to distinguish classical CBS deficiency from remethylation defects, in which methionine is low rather than high Not recognising and mitigating the heightened perioperative thrombotic risk Assuming a normal newborn screen excludes the diagnosis in a symptomatic patient, since some cases are missed Classical homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficient cystathionine beta-synthase activity in the transsulphuration pathway. The enzyme normally condenses homocysteine with serine to form cystathionine using pyridoxal phosphate as cofactor. Its deficiency leads to accumulation of homocysteine and its precursor methionine, and reduced downstream cysteine. Elevated homocysteine damages vascular endothelium and interferes with collagen and elastin cross-linking, explaining the thrombotic tendency, lens zonule failure and connective-tissue features. Homocysteine can be partly diverted back to methionine by betaine-dependent remethylation, the basis of betaine therapy. Prognosis depends heavily on pyridoxine responsiveness and on early detection through newborn screening; early treatment can prevent intellectual disability, ectopia lentis and thromboembolism, whereas late or untreated disease carries substantial risk of vascular death and disability.

Hook of hamate fracture — hamate hook fracture Ulnar-sided wrist sprain Triangular fibrocartilage complex injury Pisotriquetral pathology Guyon canal syndrome of other cause Fifth metacarpal base fracture CT of the wrist, the most sensitive test for the fracture Dedicated carpal tunnel or oblique radiographic views Assessment of ulnar nerve and artery function Evaluation of the little and ring finger flexor tendons MRI where soft-tissue or vascular injury is suspected An often-missed fracture presenting with ulnar-sided, hypothenar wrist pain, typically in racquet, bat or club sports The mechanism is usually a direct blow to the hypothenar area, such as from the butt of a club or bat, or a fall Tenderness is localised over the hook of the hamate, and grip may be painful and weak It is frequently missed on standard radiographs, and CT is the most reliable imaging Nearby structures are at risk, including the ulnar nerve and artery and the flexor tendons of the little finger Nonunion is common, and symptomatic cases are often treated by excision of the fractured hook Ulnar nerve or artery compromise Little or ring finger flexor tendon rupture Persistent pain from an established nonunion Missed diagnosis with ongoing grip weakness Relying on standard radiographs and missing the fracture Overlooking ulnar nerve or artery involvement Failing to recognise attritional flexor tendon rupture Attributing persistent ulnar wrist pain to a simple sprain The hook of the hamate projects into the palm and forms part of the ulnar carpal tunnel (Guyon canal) and the origin of hypothenar muscles. A direct blow or repetitive impact fractures the hook, and because it has a relatively tenuous blood supply and is subject to shear from attached ligaments and tendons, healing is often poor, leading to nonunion. Its proximity to the ulnar nerve and artery and to the flexor tendons explains the associated neurovascular symptoms and the risk of attritional tendon rupture. With diagnosis and appropriate treatment, including excision of a symptomatic nonunited hook, outcomes are generally good, whereas missed fractures can cause chronic pain, nerve symptoms and tendon rupture.

Hookworm infection (Ancylostoma/Necator) — ancylostomiasis, necatoriasis, Ancylostoma duodenale infection, Necator americanus infection, uncinariasis Other soil-transmitted helminthiases such as ascariasis and trichuriasis Strongyloidiasis Iron-deficiency anaemia from other causes of chronic blood loss Schistosomiasis Coeliac disease and other malabsorptive states Peptic ulcer disease or other gastrointestinal bleeding Stool microscopy for characteristic hookworm eggs Faecal egg quantification such as Kato-Katz to estimate worm burden Full blood count and film showing microcytic hypochromic anaemia Iron studies including ferritin Serum albumin to assess protein loss Full blood count for peripheral eosinophilia during larval migration Hookworm infection is caused mainly by Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale, soil-transmitted nematodes and a leading cause of iron-deficiency anaemia in the tropics Infective larvae in warm, moist soil penetrate intact skin, classically the feet, producing a localised itchy papulovesicular rash known as ground itch Migrating larvae passing through the lungs can cause a transient cough and wheeze with pulmonary eosinophilia (Loeffler syndrome) Adult worms attach to the small-intestinal mucosa and feed on blood, and the chronic intestinal blood loss produces microcytic hypochromic anaemia and hypoproteinaemia proportional to worm burden Heavy infection in children can impair growth, development and cognition, while in pregnancy it worsens maternal anaemia Diagnosis is by finding the characteristic thin-shelled eggs on stool microscopy, with concentration or quantitative techniques used to estimate burden Albendazole or mebendazole is the mainstay of treatment, alongside iron replacement to correct anaemia Severe symptomatic anaemia with cardiac decompensation Heavy infection in a young child with growth or developmental impairment Anaemia in pregnancy with risk to mother and fetus Marked hypoproteinaemia with oedema Correcting iron-deficiency anaemia without seeking and treating the underlying hookworm burden Overlooking the diagnosis in returning travellers with unexplained eosinophilia Assuming a single deworming dose confers lasting protection where reinfection is ongoing Missing coexisting soil-transmitted helminths Hookworm eggs passed in faeces hatch in warm, moist soil into infective filariform larvae that penetrate the skin, enter the circulation and are carried to the lungs. There they break into the alveoli, ascend the airways, are swallowed, and mature into adults that attach to the small-intestinal mucosa. Using cutting plates or teeth, the adults erode mucosal capillaries and ingest blood, while anticoagulant secretions promote continued oozing from the attachment site. The resulting chronic gastrointestinal blood and protein loss depletes iron stores, causing microcytic hypochromic anaemia and hypoalbuminaemia with oedema when the burden is heavy and dietary iron intake is poor; larval migration through skin and lung accounts for the earlier cutaneous and pulmonary manifestations. Excellent with anthelmintic treatment and iron replacement; anaemia and protein loss are reversible, though reinfection is common in endemic areas without improved sanitation and footwear.

Horseshoe kidney — renal fusion anomaly, horseshoe kidney anomaly, ren arcuatus Crossed fused renal ectopia Pelvic or ectopic kidney Bilateral ureteropelvic junction obstruction of normally positioned kidneys Retroperitoneal mass mimicking an isthmus Malrotated kidney without fusion Nephroptosis Renal ultrasound to identify the isthmus and hydronephrosis CT or MR urography to define anatomy, vasculature, and any obstruction or tumour MAG3 diuretic renogram to assess drainage and differential function Non-contrast CT for suspected calculi Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) if reflux is suspected Urinalysis and culture during infection The commonest renal fusion anomaly, in which the two kidneys are joined, most often at their lower poles, by an isthmus of renal parenchyma or fibrous tissue crossing the midline The isthmus is typically arrested beneath the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent, so the kidney sits lower than normal and its collecting systems and vessels are anomalous Often asymptomatic and found incidentally, but there is an increased risk of ureteropelvic junction obstruction, stone formation, and infection because of high ureteric insertion and impaired drainage Associated with an increased incidence of certain malignancies, including Wilms tumour in children and, in adults, renal and transitional cell tumours, as well as a reported association with retroperitoneal sarcoma of the isthmus The blood supply is highly variable, often with multiple accessory arteries, which is important before any surgery May be associated with other anomalies and syndromes, including Turner syndrome and trisomy 18 Management is directed at complications such as obstruction (pyeloplasty), stones, or tumour; the anomaly itself needs no treatment when asymptomatic Symptomatic ureteropelvic junction obstruction with pain or declining function Recurrent or obstructing calculi with infection A solid mass arising from the isthmus or a renal moiety suggesting malignancy Urosepsis in an obstructed system Failing to map the anomalous and often multiple vessels before surgery on the isthmus or a renal unit Missing an isthmic tumour by not imaging the parenchyma crossing the midline Attributing all flank pain to the anomaly and overlooking a treatable obstruction or stone Overlooking associated syndromic conditions in children A horseshoe kidney forms during early development when the two metanephric masses fuse across the midline, usually at their lower poles, before normal ascent and rotation are complete. As the fused kidney ascends it is halted by the inferior mesenteric artery catching the isthmus, so the kidney remains low and incompletely rotated, with anteriorly directed pelves and high ureteric insertions. These anatomical features impair urinary drainage and predispose to ureteropelvic junction obstruction, stasis, calculus formation, and infection. The variable and often multiple vascular supply reflects the abnormal position and developmental history of the fused kidney. Most horseshoe kidneys are asymptomatic and compatible with normal life expectancy; prognosis worsens only when complications such as obstruction, recurrent stones, infection, or tumour arise, and these are generally manageable with targeted treatment.

Howel-Evans syndrome — tylosis with oesophageal cancer, TOC, RHBDF2, palmoplantar keratoderma with oesophageal cancer Other focal or diffuse hereditary palmoplantar keratodermas without cancer association Acquired keratoderma (mechanical, drug-induced or paraneoplastic) Pachyonychia congenita Palmoplantar keratoderma of Unna-Thost Psoriasis of palms and soles Keratoderma associated with internal malignancy (paraneoplastic acrokeratosis) Molecular genetic testing of RHBDF2 Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy for surveillance and evaluation of symptoms Skin biopsy of palmoplantar lesions where the diagnosis is uncertain Examination of the oral mucosa for leucokeratosis Detailed pedigree and family cancer history Referral for genetic counselling of at-risk relatives A rare autosomal dominant focal palmoplantar keratoderma (tylosis) associated with a very high lifetime risk of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma The keratoderma is typically focal and pressure-related, affecting the soles more than the palms, often with onset in later childhood Oral leucokeratosis (white oral mucosal thickening) may accompany the palmoplantar disease Caused by dominant mutations in RHBDF2 encoding the inactive rhomboid protease iRhom2 The oesophageal cancer risk is the dominant clinical concern and warrants endoscopic surveillance from adulthood A detailed family history is essential, as the malignancy risk clusters in affected kindreds Management combines emollients/keratolytics for the skin with lifelong cancer surveillance and prompt investigation of oesophageal symptoms Dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss or new gastrointestinal symptoms suggesting oesophageal carcinoma Change in an area of oral leucokeratosis Iron-deficiency anaemia or gastrointestinal bleeding A strong family history of oesophageal cancer prompting urgent surveillance Treating the keratoderma as an isolated skin problem and failing to institute oesophageal cancer surveillance Dismissing new swallowing symptoms in an affected individual Not offering genetic testing and counselling to relatives at risk Confusing it with common non-syndromic keratodermas that carry no malignancy risk Howel-Evans syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition caused by gain-of-function mutations in RHBDF2, which encodes iRhom2, a regulator of the enzyme ADAM17 (TACE). ADAM17 controls the shedding and signalling of epidermal growth factor receptor ligands, so the mutations enhance EGFR-pathway signalling and epithelial proliferation. In the palmoplantar epidermis this drives the focal hyperkeratosis (tylosis), while in the oesophageal squamous epithelium the same dysregulated proliferative signalling and impaired wound-healing response markedly increase susceptibility to squamous cell carcinoma. The heightened, lifelong malignancy risk is the defining pathophysiological feature. The keratoderma itself is benign, but the lifetime risk of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma is very high and is the main determinant of prognosis. Outcome depends heavily on early detection through surveillance, since oesophageal cancer diagnosed late carries a poor prognosis.

Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome (severe dyskeratosis congenita) — Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome, HHS, severe dyskeratosis congenita, telomere biology disorder with cerebellar hypoplasia Classic dyskeratosis congenita of later or milder onset Fanconi anaemia and other inherited bone-marrow-failure syndromes Severe combined immunodeficiency with early lymphopenia Coats plus and other telomere-related multisystem disorders Congenital infections causing growth restriction and cerebellar abnormality Cartilage-hair hypoplasia Telomere length measurement in leucocytes Full blood count and bone marrow examination for marrow failure and dysplasia Lymphocyte subset enumeration and immunoglobulin quantification Genetic sequencing of telomere-maintenance genes Neuroimaging to demonstrate cerebellar hypoplasia Chromosomal breakage studies to help exclude Fanconi anaemia Surveillance for malignancy and organ fibrosis over time A severe, early-onset form of dyskeratosis congenita and a telomere biology disorder, presenting in infancy or early childhood The defining combination is intrauterine growth restriction, progressive bone-marrow failure, cerebellar hypoplasia, and immunodeficiency Cerebellar hypoplasia produces developmental delay and ataxia and is a key clue distinguishing it from milder dyskeratosis congenita The mucocutaneous triad of dyskeratosis congenita (abnormal skin pigmentation, nail dystrophy, and oral leucoplakia) may be present but is sometimes absent or evolves later Immunodeficiency spans progressive lymphopenia with B- and natural-killer-cell depletion and impaired T-cell function, adding infection to the marrow-failure risks Very short telomeres for age support the diagnosis, with confirmation by sequencing of telomere-maintenance genes Management is largely supportive with transfusion, infection prevention, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for marrow failure, tempered by heightened toxicity and a lifelong predisposition to malignancy Progressive pancytopenia in an infant with growth restriction Cerebellar signs or ataxia with developmental delay Severe or opportunistic infection from lymphopenia Evolution to myelodysplasia or leukaemia Pulmonary or hepatic fibrosis as a later telomere-disorder complication Attributing pancytopenia to an acquired aplastic process and missing the telomere disorder Using standard-intensity conditioning for transplantation without accounting for heightened tissue fragility Expecting the classic mucocutaneous triad, which may be absent early Overlooking cerebellar hypoplasia as the distinguishing feature Failing to screen for and counsel about lifelong malignancy risk Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome arises from mutations in genes that maintain telomeres, the protective repeats capping chromosome ends, and represents the severe end of the telomere biology disorders. Defective telomere maintenance leads to premature telomere shortening, so highly proliferative tissues exhaust their replicative capacity and cells undergo senescence or death. In the bone marrow this causes progressive aplasia across all lineages, including the lymphocytes needed for immune defence, producing both cytopenias and immunodeficiency. The developing cerebellum and other tissues are likewise vulnerable, giving cerebellar hypoplasia, growth restriction, and the mucocutaneous features of dyskeratosis congenita, while the underlying genomic instability confers a lifelong increased risk of myelodysplasia, leukaemia, and other cancers. The prognosis is poor, with early mortality from marrow failure, infection, and malignancy; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can address the marrow failure but carries increased toxicity in telomere disorders and does not prevent non-haematological complications such as pulmonary or hepatic fibrosis and solid tumours.

Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 1 — HSAN1, HSN1, hereditary sensory neuropathy type 1, SPTLC1-related neuropathy Diabetic and other metabolic sensory neuropathies Leprosy and other infective neuropathies with sensory loss and ulceration Other HSAN subtypes, particularly HSAN2 Amyloid and other acquired small-fibre neuropathies Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease with sensory involvement Alcoholic or nutritional sensory neuropathy Targeted genetic testing of SPTLC1/SPTLC2 and a broader HSAN gene panel Nerve conduction studies confirming an axonal sensory-predominant neuropathy Quantitative sensory and small-fibre testing (e.g. skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density) Plasma deoxysphingolipid measurement where available to support an SPTLC diagnosis Imaging of feet to assess for osteomyelitis or Charcot arthropathy Exclusion of acquired causes (glucose, HbA1c, autoimmune and amyloid screens) Autosomal dominant, adult-onset (usually second to fourth decade) sensory-predominant neuropathy with a length-dependent, distal-to-proximal loss of pain and temperature sensation Most often caused by mutations in SPTLC1 (and the related SPTLC2), subunits of serine palmitoyltransferase, with several other genes implicated Distal sensory loss leads to painless injuries, recurrent foot ulcers, cellulitis, osteomyelitis and acral mutilation with distal amputations if unrecognised Lancinating or burning neuropathic pain is common despite the sensory loss Autonomic involvement is usually milder than in other HSAN subtypes SPTLC mutations cause accumulation of neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids, offering a potential rationale for L-serine supplementation under specialist care Nerve conduction studies show an axonal sensory (and often mild motor) neuropathy; sural nerve biopsy demonstrates loss of small and large fibres Management centres on meticulous foot care, injury and ulcer prevention, and neuropathic pain control Deep foot ulceration with underlying osteomyelitis or spreading infection Charcot neuroarthropathy with acute joint destruction Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting an alternative or superimposed neuropathy Systemic sepsis arising from an infected mutilating injury Attributing painless foot ulcers solely to diabetes or trauma and missing an inherited sensory neuropathy Underestimating neuropathic pain because sensory loss is prominent Neglecting preventive foot care and footwear advice that avert mutilating complications Assuming autonomic features are marked, when in HSAN1 they are typically mild HSAN1 is a dominantly inherited degeneration of peripheral sensory neurons. The commonest cause is mutation in SPTLC1 or SPTLC2, encoding subunits of serine palmitoyltransferase, the enzyme controlling the first step of sphingolipid synthesis. Mutant enzyme acquires altered substrate specificity and generates atypical, neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids that accumulate and preferentially injure long sensory axons, producing a length-dependent axonal sensory neuropathy with variable autonomic and motor involvement. The resulting loss of protective sensation leads to unperceived trauma, ulceration and progressive acral tissue destruction. HSAN1 progresses slowly, and lifespan is usually normal, but morbidity is driven by recurrent ulcers, infections and amputations; disciplined foot care substantially reduces complications and preserves function.

Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 2 — HSAN2, HSN2, hereditary sensory neuropathy type 2, WNK1/HSN2-related neuropathy Other HSAN subtypes, particularly HSAN1 (later onset, dominant) and familial dysautonomia Congenital insensitivity to pain (SCN9A loss-of-function) Leprosy and other infective neuropathies in endemic settings Non-accidental injury when acral wounds are unexplained Diabetic or other acquired sensory neuropathies in older patients Syringomyelia and other central causes of dissociated sensory loss Targeted genetic testing of HSAN2-associated genes (WNK1/HSN2, FAM134B, KIF1A, SCN9A) and gene panels Nerve conduction studies demonstrating absent or markedly reduced sensory responses Skin biopsy or sural nerve biopsy showing loss of sensory fibres Autonomic function testing to gauge the degree of autonomic involvement Imaging of affected limbs to assess osteomyelitis, fractures or joint destruction Exclusion of acquired and infective causes as appropriate Autosomal recessive sensory neuropathy typically presenting in infancy or early childhood, earlier than HSAN1 Caused by mutations in genes including WNK1 (the HSN2 exon/transcript), FAM134B/RETREG1, KIF1A and SCN9A depending on the subtype There is severe, often global loss of all sensory modalities affecting distal limbs, causing painless injuries, ulcers, whitlows and acral mutilation Sensory loss tends to be more diffuse and less strictly length-dependent than in HSAN1, and can involve the trunk Autonomic disturbance is variable and generally less severe than in familial dysautonomia Deep tendon reflexes are reduced or absent and there may be mild distal motor involvement Nerve conduction studies show markedly reduced or absent sensory responses; biopsy reveals loss of myelinated and unmyelinated sensory fibres Management is supportive, focused on protecting insensate limbs, preventing and treating ulcers and infections, and injury education Osteomyelitis or deep infection complicating a painless wound Charcot joints or unrecognised fractures from repeated trauma Corneal injury or ulceration from impaired protective sensation Systemic sepsis from an infected mutilating lesion Mistaking recurrent acral injuries in a child for non-accidental injury and delaying diagnosis Assuming a length-dependent pattern and overlooking the more diffuse sensory loss of HSAN2 Neglecting protective education and foot/hand care that prevent mutilating complications Overlooking corneal and other non-limb sites vulnerable to unperceived injury HSAN2 is a recessively inherited disorder of sensory neuron development and maintenance. Depending on the causative gene, the defect impairs axonal transport, endoplasmic reticulum shaping or sensory neuron survival: for example, the HSN2 nervous-system-specific transcript of WNK1 and mutations in FAM134B/RETREG1, KIF1A or SCN9A each disrupt the integrity of small and large sensory fibres. The result is early, profound loss of cutaneous sensation with relatively variable autonomic involvement, so affected children sustain repeated unperceived trauma leading to ulceration, infection and mutilating acral injury. HSAN2 is a lifelong disorder; the sensory deficit is largely static or slowly progressive, and with vigilant protective care many patients avoid major mutilation, though recurrent injuries, infections and amputations cause significant morbidity.

Hypertensive emergency — BP (both arms), fundoscopy ECG, troponin, renal function CT head if neuro signs Controlled BP reduction; identify target-organ damage Scleroderma renal crisis — accelerated hypertension with AKI, clinically indistinguishable from malignant hypertension; consider in systemic sclerosis, especially diffuse/progressive skin disease, anti-RNA-polymerase-III antibody, or recent glucocorticoid exposure (p.2871). Pheochromocytoma in crisis — catecholamine surge causing paroxysmal severe hypertension (p.2148). Eclampsia / severe pre-eclampsia in a pregnant or peripartum patient (p.2148). Funduscopy for hypertensive end-organ change — arteriolar sclerosis/narrowing, splinter (flame) hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots (nerve-fiber-layer infarcts), hard exudates into the macula, and papilledema (p.227, p.190). CBC with peripheral smear and reticulocytes to detect microangiopathic hemolysis — anemia, schistocytes, reticulocytosis (p.2153-2154). Urinalysis — hematuria, proteinuria, granular/nephritic sediment in renal involvement (p.2153-2154, p.2871). Serum creatinine to detect/track acute kidney injury (p.2153-2154). Once BP is controlled, work-up for secondary hypertension, especially renovascular imaging (p.2148). Cocaine or other vasospastic-drug-induced severe hypertension (can precipitate malignant-phase hypertension) (p.2153-2154). Thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP/HUS) which overlap with the microangiopathic hemolysis seen in malignant hypertension (p.2153-2154). The threshold prompting concern for a crisis is typically a markedly elevated BP, often described as SBP/DBP at or above ~180/100-120 mmHg; however the level alone does not define an emergency — the presence of acute, ongoing end-organ injury does (p.2148). Urgency vs emergency is a functional distinction: an asymptomatic patient without evidence of active end-organ damage has an urgency (manageable with oral agents in the outpatient setting), whereas demonstrable acute target-organ injury makes it an emergency requiring IV therapy with close inpatient/ER supervision (p.2148). Hypertensive urgency is far more common than true emergency; over-treating urgency as if it were an emergency risks harm from excessive BP lowering (p.2148). Certain syndromes — acute aortic dissection, eclampsia or severe pre-eclampsia, and pheochromocytoma in crisis — flag a need for particularly rapid, aggressive BP control compared with other emergencies (p.2148). After the acute BP is brought under control, look for secondary causes of hypertension — renovascular disease in particular is relatively common among patients presenting with a hypertensive emergency (p.2148). Malignant hypertension most often arises in a patient with known, treated hypertension who has stopped taking medications, or who uses vasospastic drugs such as cocaine (p.2153-2154). In acute hypertensive retinopathy, BP must not be lowered precipitously: an abrupt drop risks optic disc infarction and worsening visual loss (p.227). Hypertensive encephalopathy — headache, visual disturbance, nausea/vomiting, seizures, altered consciousness (p.2148). Acute left ventricular failure / pulmonary edema in the setting of severe hypertension (p.2148). Acute kidney failure with severe hypertension (p.2148). Papilledema, retinal hemorrhages or acute visual loss (signs of malignant-phase / hypertensive retinopathy) (p.2153-2154, p.227). Features suggesting a rapid-care syndrome: chest/back pain (aortic dissection), pregnancy with seizures (eclampsia), or paroxysmal catecholamine symptoms (pheochromocytoma) (p.2148). Treating an asymptomatic high BP (urgency) with aggressive IV agents as though it were an emergency, risking harm from over-rapid lowering (p.2148). Aiming for immediate normalization of BP — a controlled reduction rather than normalization is sufficient, followed by transition to oral agents; potent IV vasodilators can overshoot and cause hypotension (p.2148). Lowering BP precipitously in acute hypertensive retinopathy or cerebral involvement, where falling below the autoregulatory range risks optic disc or cerebral infarction (p.227). Missing a treatable secondary cause (notably renovascular disease) by not investigating after acute control (p.2148). Overlooking normotensive scleroderma renal crisis — ~10% present with BP in the normal range and carry a poor outcome (p.2871). Severe, rapidly progressive BP elevation produces mechanical/pressure-related vascular injury that overwhelms protective vascular tone. In malignant hypertension the characteristic lesion is fibrinoid necrosis of small vessels — breakdown of the vessel wall with deposition of eosinophilic fibrin-containing material and a perivascular cellular infiltrate; larger interlobular arteries may show a hyperplastic 'onionskin' proliferative lesion. These changes can obliterate glomeruli and tubular structures, driving progressive kidney failure. Multiple pathways can generate this pressure injury, including activation of the renin-angiotensin system and intense vasospasm from catecholamine release; when endothelial injury is severe enough it triggers microangiopathic hemolysis. Cerebral involvement reflects failure of cerebral blood-flow autoregulation: at extreme pressures autoregulatory limits are exceeded, producing hyperperfusion, vasogenic edema and the encephalopathy/PRES picture — which is also why too-rapid lowering below the autoregulatory range can cause cerebral or optic ischemia (p.2153-2154, p.192, p.227). Untreated malignant-phase hypertension with target-organ injury (papilledema, declining kidney function) historically carried mortality exceeding 50% over 6-12 months, with older reports of >90% one-year mortality before effective drug therapy — hence the term 'malignant'. With effective BP reduction, manifestations of vascular injury including microangiopathic hemolysis and renal dysfunction can improve over time, and current 5-year survival exceeds 50% (p.2153-2154). Hypertensive urgency = markedly elevated BP (e.g., SBP/DBP >=180/100 mmHg) in an asymptomatic patient WITHOUT evidence of acute ongoing end-organ damage — manage with oral agents as outpatient. Hypertensive emergency = comparably high BP WITH evidence of active end-organ injury (encephalopathy, acute LV failure/pulmonary edema, acute kidney failure, retinal hemorrhage/papilledema, dissection, eclampsia, pheochromocytoma crisis) — requires immediate, carefully supervised IV therapy in ER/inpatient setting. Malignant hypertension is the severe phenotype defined by rapidly progressive BP elevation with fibrinoid-necrosis vascular injury, retinal hemorrhages/papilledema, encephalopathy and declining kidney function (p.2148, p.2153-2154).

Verruca vulgaris, the common wart, is typically a sessile, dome-shaped lesion roughly a centimeter across with a hyperkeratotic surface made up of many fine filamentous projections (Harrison 22e p.1525). Plantar warts are endophytic and covered by thick keratin; paring them characteristically uncovers a central core of keratinized debris with punctate bleeding points, which helps distinguish them from corns (Harrison 22e p.1525). Flat warts (verruca plana) are only slightly raised with a velvety, nonverrucous surface, favor the face, arms, and legs, and are frequently spread by shaving (Harrison 22e p.1525). Filiform warts present as papillomatous lesions on a narrow base and are common on the face, neck, and skinfolds (Harrison 22e p.1525). Genital warts start as small papillomas that can enlarge into large fungating lesions; in women they may involve the labia, perineum, perianal skin, and the vaginal, urethral, anal, and cervical mucosa, while in men they often begin in the coronal sulcus and may extend to the penile shaft, scrotum, perianal skin, or urethra (Harrison 22e p.1525). HPV types 16 and 18 are the most intensively studied and are the major risk factors for intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, anus, vulva, and penis (Harrison 22e p.1525). Sexual transmission of HPV is described as the fundamental etiologic factor for cervical cancer (Harrison 22e p.1602). Persistent oral HPV infection, particularly HPV-16, raises the risk of oropharyngeal cancer even without smoking or alcohol use, and the increase appears greater than additive when HPV and smoking coexist; oral HPV is believed to be largely sexually acquired (Harrison 22e p.1601). A highly effective HPV vaccine for selected types is FDA-approved and reduces the incidence of anogenital and cervical carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.1525). The available nonavalent HPV vaccine covers strains 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58; types 6 and 11 cause genital papillomas while the remaining types drive cervical and anal cancer, and reduction of types 16 and 18 alone could theoretically prevent more than 70% of cervical cancers worldwide (Harrison 22e p.1601). Lesions in patients immunosuppressed after solid organ transplantation or with HIV, who carry higher risk of HPV-associated malignancy and warrant monitoring for squamous cell carcinoma and other cutaneous malignancies Anogenital lesions showing histologic features of intraepidermal carcinoma (Bowen's disease) Persistent or growing fungating anogenital masses New oropharyngeal lesions in the setting of persistent HPV-16, particularly with concurrent tobacco use Assuming all warts require aggressive treatment: most resolve spontaneously within 1-2 years in healthy people (Harrison 22e p.1525). Overlooking the malignant potential of oncogenic HPV types and failing to monitor immunosuppressed (transplant or HIV) patients for squamous cell carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.1525). Expecting the HPV vaccine to clear existing infection: it does not appear to affect preexisting infections (Harrison 22e p.1601). Screening cervical cytology more frequently than recommended adds little benefit and can cause harm through unnecessary procedures and overtreatment of transient lesions (Harrison 22e p.1602). Human papillomaviruses are DNA viruses that, like other papillomaviruses, gain entry through breaks in the skin and infect epithelial cells, producing benign cutaneous neoplasms (warts). Keratinized cells are not viable hosts for replication, so the virus targets viable epithelium at cutaneous and mucosal surfaces. More than 100 HPV types exist; certain oncogenic types (notably 16 and 18) integrate into host epithelium and drive intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, anus, vulva, and penis, and persistent oral HPV-16 promotes oropharyngeal carcinoma. Histology of affected sites may show changes of typical warts and/or features of intraepidermal carcinoma (Bowen's disease). The oncogenic potential is markedly amplified in immunosuppressed hosts (Harrison 22e p.1525, p.1601). Most warts in normal (immunocompetent) individuals resolve spontaneously within 1-2 years. However, oncogenic HPV types, especially 16 and 18, can lead to intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, anus, vulva, penis, and oropharynx, with higher risk in immunosuppressed patients. The HPV vaccine is highly effective at preventing persistent strain-specific infection and preneoplastic lesions (cervical or anal intraepithelial neoplasia grades I-III) in individuals not previously infected, though it does not affect established infections (Harrison 22e p.1525, p.1601). HPV-associated cervical and anal disease is described histologically as intraepithelial neoplasia graded I, II, and III (CIN/AIN), reflecting progressive preneoplastic change preceding invasive squamous cell carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.1601).

preoperative bone disease Hungry bone syndrome develops when chronic overstimulation of bone by excess parathyroid hormone, as in long-standing primary or secondary hyperparathyroidism, is suddenly removed, typically by parathyroidectomy but occasionally after other treatments that rapidly lower PTH. During the period of hyperparathyroidism, high bone turnover leaves the skeleton demineralised and primed for repair. Once PTH falls abruptly, bone resorption ceases while bone formation continues, so calcium, phosphate, and magnesium are rapidly deposited into the remineralising skeleton. This net influx into bone outstrips supply, producing the characteristic combination of hypocalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, and hypomagnesaemia that can persist for days to weeks until skeletal mineral demand is met. The syndrome is usually self-limiting once bone mineral demand is satisfied, but recovery can take days to several weeks and occasionally longer, requiring intensive and sustained calcium and vitamin D replacement; with appropriate monitoring and treatment, outcomes are generally good, and identifying at-risk patients preoperatively allows anticipatory management.

The severe neuronopathic form progresses to significant disability and death in childhood or adolescence, whereas the attenuated form is compatible with survival into adulthood with preserved cognition. Enzyme replacement therapy improves somatic outcomes and quality of life but does not address the central nervous system disease with standard delivery.

The mutant protein exerts a toxic gain of function, causing progressive neuronal loss most marked in the medium spiny neurons of the striatum (caudate and putamen), with later cortical involvement. Disruption of basal ganglia circuitry underlies the chorea and other movement abnormalities, while cortical and striatal degeneration drives cognitive and psychiatric decline. Huntington disease is relentlessly progressive over one to two decades from motor onset, leading to severe motor, cognitive, and functional decline. Hurler-Scheie syndrome results from biallelic IDUA variants that leave an intermediate level of residual alpha-L-iduronidase activity, producing a phenotype between the severe and attenuated poles of mucopolysaccharidosis type I. Deficient enzyme activity impairs the stepwise degradation of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate, causing lysosomal accumulation of these glycosaminoglycans throughout connective tissue, cartilage, cornea, heart valves, meninges, and viscera. Progressive substrate storage produces the characteristic multisystem somatic disease, while the greater residual activity compared with Hurler syndrome largely spares the central nervous system. Excess glycosaminoglycan is excreted in the urine. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Survival into adulthood is common, but progressive cardiorespiratory, skeletal, and ocular disease causes significant disability. Enzyme replacement therapy can improve somatic manifestations, though it does not cross the blood-brain barrier or reverse established corneal and skeletal changes.

Hydatid liver cyst — hepatic hydatid disease, hepatic echinococcosis, liver hydatid cyst, cystic echinococcosis of the liver Simple hepatic cyst Pyogenic or amoebic liver abscess Polycystic liver disease Cystic liver neoplasm (cystadenoma or cystadenocarcinoma) Choledochal cyst Caroli disease Abdominal ultrasound to characterise and stage the cyst CT or MRI for anatomical detail, biliary communication, and surgical planning Echinococcal serology (with awareness of false negatives) Full blood count for eosinophilia MRCP or ERCP when biliary communication or obstruction is suspected Chest imaging to exclude concurrent pulmonary hydatid disease Hepatic hydatid disease is caused by the larval stage of Echinococcus granulosus, with dogs as definitive hosts and humans as accidental intermediate hosts, and is endemic in sheep- and cattle-rearing regions The liver is the commonest organ affected, and cysts are frequently asymptomatic for years, presenting as a slowly enlarging right upper quadrant mass or dull ache Ultrasound and CT show a characteristic cyst with a wall, internal daughter cysts, and detached membranes; the Gharbi/WHO classification helps stage activity Serology supports the diagnosis, though false negatives occur, and eosinophilia may be present Diagnostic aspiration is traditionally avoided because of the risk of spillage causing anaphylaxis and peritoneal seeding, although image-guided PAIR is used in selected cases under cover Management options include the PAIR technique (puncture, aspiration, injection of a scolicidal agent, and re-aspiration), surgery, and anthelmintic therapy, chosen by cyst stage, size, and complications Perioperative and periprocedural anthelmintic cover and meticulous protection of the field with scolicidal precautions reduce recurrence and spillage Cyst rupture provoking anaphylaxis or anaphylactic shock, a life-threatening emergency Rupture or communication into the biliary tree causing cholangitis and obstructive jaundice Secondary bacterial infection of the cyst with sepsis Rupture into the peritoneum or thorax with widespread secondary seeding Aspirating or biopsying an undiagnosed cyst and precipitating spillage, seeding, or anaphylaxis Omitting perioperative anthelmintic cover and scolicidal precautions, increasing recurrence Injecting a scolicidal agent when there is biliary communication, risking sclerosing cholangitis Missing associated pulmonary hydatid disease Mistaking a hydatid cyst for a simple cyst or abscess and managing it inappropriately Humans acquire infection by ingesting Echinococcus eggs shed in canine faeces. Embryos penetrate the intestinal wall and travel via the portal circulation, with the liver acting as the first filter and commonest site of lodgement. There the larva develops into a fluid-filled hydatid cyst with three layers: an outer host-derived fibrous pericyst, a middle acellular laminated membrane, and an inner germinal layer that produces protoscolices and daughter cysts. The cyst enlarges slowly and can compress adjacent liver, bile ducts, and vessels. Cyst fluid is highly antigenic, so rupture, whether spontaneous, traumatic, or iatrogenic, can release protoscolices that seed new cysts and trigger a severe allergic or anaphylactic reaction. Communication with the biliary tree can cause cholangitis and obstructive jaundice. The outlook is generally good for uncomplicated cysts treated appropriately, with high cure rates after surgery or PAIR combined with anthelmintic therapy. Recurrence can occur from spillage of viable protoscolices, and prognosis is worse with complications such as anaphylaxis, biliary rupture, or secondary infection.

usually triploid (extra paternal chromosome set) and may contain abnormal foetal or embryonic tissue Pelvic ultrasound may show the classic 'snowstorm' or cluster-of-grapes appearance with theca-lutein cysts of the ovaries Early excessive beta-hCG can provoke hyperemesis, early pre-eclampsia, and hyperthyroid features from cross-reactivity at the TSH receptor Definitive management is suction evacuation of the uterus followed by serial beta-hCG surveillance to detect persistent disease Registration with a trophoblastic disease service and reliable contraception during follow-up are important so rising hCG is not confused with a new pregnancy Complete moles carry a higher risk of progressing to gestational trophoblastic neoplasia than partial moles Heavy or ongoing vaginal haemorrhage with haemodynamic compromise Signs of early severe pre-eclampsia before the usual gestation Features of thyroid storm from very high beta-hCG Respiratory distress suggesting trophoblastic pulmonary embolisation Beta-hCG that plateaus or rises after evacuation, indicating persistent neoplasia Attributing early heavy bleeding or hyperemesis simply to a normal or failing pregnancy and missing molar features Failing to enrol the patient in structured beta-hCG follow-up after evacuation Allowing a new pregnancy during surveillance so that rising hCG masks persistent disease Assuming a partial mole has no malignant potential and abandoning monitoring prematurely Hydatidiform mole is an abnormal pregnancy arising from aberrant fertilisation with an excess of paternal genetic material, producing hydropic swelling of chorionic villi and trophoblastic proliferation. In a complete mole an ovum lacking functional maternal genetic material is fertilised and the paternal genome is duplicated (or two sperm enter), giving diploid androgenetic tissue with no viable foetus. In a partial mole a normal ovum is fertilised by two sperm (or a diploid sperm), giving a triploid conceptus with some foetal tissue and focal villous change. Exuberant trophoblast secretes high levels of beta-hCG, and the abnormal trophoblast retains malignant potential, so a proportion of cases progress to invasive or metastatic trophoblastic neoplasia after evacuation. With timely evacuation and structured beta-hCG surveillance, most molar pregnancies resolve completely and future fertility is usually preserved. A minority progress to gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is highly curable when detected early through follow-up.

Hydranencephaly — hydranencephalus, cystic degeneration of the cerebral hemispheres, in-utero cerebral infarction Severe hydrocephalus with a thin preserved cortical mantle Alobar holoprosencephaly with a monoventricle and fused midline structures Bilateral open-lip schizencephaly Large bilateral porencephaly Massive bilateral subdural collections Severe destructive encephalopathy from congenital infection Brain imaging with ultrasound, CT, or MRI to demonstrate absent hemispheres with a present falx and preserved posterior fossa Prenatal ultrasound and foetal MRI when suspected antenatally Skull transillumination as a supportive bedside finding Evaluation for congenital infection where the cause is uncertain Endocrine assessment for hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction Electroencephalography to characterise seizures A severe destructive disorder in which the cerebral hemispheres are largely absent and replaced by cerebrospinal-fluid-filled sacs, while the falx, brainstem, and cerebellum are relatively preserved It is generally a disruption rather than a primary malformation, usually attributed to bilateral internal carotid territory infarction or a destructive insult after the brain has begun to form The relatively intact brainstem means neonates may initially appear deceptively normal, with preserved brainstem reflexes, sucking, and spontaneous movements Head size may be normal, small, or progressively enlarged, and transillumination of the skull is characteristically strikingly positive It must be distinguished from severe hydrocephalus, in which a rim of compressed cortex persists, and from alobar holoprosencephaly, in which midline structures are fused Later features include developmental failure, irritability, seizures, spasticity, temperature instability, and feeding difficulty Diagnosis is by imaging, with ultrasound, CT, or MRI showing absent hemispheres, a present falx, and preserved posterior fossa structures Progressive macrocephaly with raised intracranial pressure Refractory seizures Temperature instability and autonomic dysfunction Recurrent aspiration and feeding failure Being reassured by an apparently normal early neonatal examination because of preserved brainstem function Mistaking hydranencephaly for severe hydrocephalus and pursuing inappropriate expectations from shunting Confusing it with alobar holoprosencephaly, which has fused midline structures and an absent falx Overlooking hypothalamic dysfunction such as temperature instability and endocrine disturbance Hydranencephaly is thought to result from a destructive vascular event, typically bilateral occlusion or infarction in the internal carotid artery territories, occurring after the cerebral hemispheres have begun to develop. The cortex supplied by these vessels undergoes necrosis and resorption, leaving cerebrospinal-fluid-filled sacs bounded by leptomeninges where the hemispheres should be. Because the posterior circulation is spared, the brainstem, cerebellum, and often the thalami and basal structures are relatively preserved, and the falx cerebri, which forms early, usually remains. Other proposed mechanisms include severe intrauterine infection and profound hypoxic-ischaemic injury. Hydranencephaly carries a very poor prognosis, with most affected infants having profound neurological impairment; many die in infancy, although some survive longer with intensive supportive care. Management is supportive, with shunting sometimes needed for progressive head enlargement.

possibility of erythropoietic protoporphyria Assuming all cases are benign and missing an underlying Epstein-Barr virus associated lymphoproliferative disorder Confusing the vesicles with erythropoietic protoporphyria, in which scarring is usually subtler and porphyrins are abnormal Failing to biopsy atypical or systemic disease, delaying recognition of the lymphoproliferative form Overlooking the need for long-term follow-up in patients with severe or persistent lesions Classic hydroa vacciniforme is a poorly understood photodermatosis in which ultraviolet radiation, chiefly ultraviolet A, provokes epidermal necrosis and a vesicular, scarring reaction in sun-exposed skin, presumed to reflect an abnormal cutaneous response to ultraviolet-induced injury. In contrast, the hydroa vacciniforme-like lymphoproliferative disorder is a distinct Epstein-Barr virus driven proliferation of T or natural killer cells, in which the virus infects lymphocytes that infiltrate the skin and can behave in a locally aggressive or systemic manner. Distinguishing the benign photodermatosis from the virus-associated lymphoproliferative process is therefore central to management. Classic hydroa vacciniforme usually follows a benign course with spontaneous improvement by adolescence, although some scarring may remain; by contrast, the Epstein-Barr virus associated hydroa vacciniforme-like lymphoproliferative disorder carries a more guarded prognosis and requires close specialist monitoring for progression to systemic disease.

Hydrocele — hydrocoele, scrotal hydrocele, processus vaginalis fluid collection Inguinoscrotal hernia Testicular tumour with reactive hydrocele Epididymal cyst or spermatocele Varicocele Haematocele inguinoscrotal hernia, and the testis is often impalpable within a large tension hydrocele In infants, communicating hydroceles arise from a patent processus vaginalis and commonly resolve spontaneously within the first year or two of life Adult hydroceles are usually idiopathic (primary) but may be secondary to underlying pathology such as tumour, infection, trauma, or torsion, so the testis must be assessed Ultrasound is indicated when the testis cannot be palpated or when a secondary cause is suspected, to exclude an underlying testicular tumour A rapidly developing or blood-stained hydrocele after trauma or in a young man should prompt evaluation for testicular malignancy or haematocele Treatment principles include observation for asymptomatic cases, with surgical repair (hydrocelectomy) preferred for large or symptomatic adult hydroceles and aspiration reserved for those unfit for surgery due to high recurrence In children, persistent or symptomatic hydroceles beyond infancy are managed by ligation of the patent processus via an inguinal approach An impalpable testis within the hydrocele, mandating ultrasound to exclude tumour Rapidly enlarging, tense, or blood-stained (haematocele) swelling following trauma A reactive hydrocele masking an underlying testicular malignancy Signs of associated infection or torsion requiring urgent evaluation Assuming a scrotal swelling is a simple hydrocele without confirming a normal underlying testis Aspirating an adult hydrocele as definitive treatment, given the high recurrence and risk of missing tumour Failing to recognise a reactive hydrocele overlying a testicular tumour Confusing a hydrocele with an inguinoscrotal hernia when unable to get above the swelling Operating on infantile hydroceles prematurely before allowing spontaneous resolution A hydrocele results from an imbalance between secretion and absorption of fluid within the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. Congenital (communicating) hydroceles occur when the processus vaginalis fails to obliterate, allowing peritoneal fluid to track into the scrotum. Non-communicating hydroceles arise from excess fluid production or impaired reabsorption by the tunica. Secondary hydroceles develop as a reactive effusion in response to underlying testicular or epididymal disease such as tumour, infection, torsion, or trauma. Chronic large hydroceles may occasionally impair testicular perfusion or spermatogenesis. Infantile communicating hydroceles usually resolve spontaneously; primary adult hydroceles are benign and surgery is generally curative, whereas the outlook of secondary hydroceles depends on the underlying cause.

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension Neurodegenerative dementia (in suspected NPH) Shunt malfunction in a previously treated patient CT or MRI brain to assess ventricular size, the level of obstruction, and periventricular changes MRI with CSF flow studies when aqueductal or outflow obstruction is suspected Head circumference monitoring and cranial ultrasound in infants with an open fontanelle Large-volume lumbar puncture or external drainage trial to predict shunt response in suspected NPH Shunt series and imaging to evaluate suspected shunt malfunction Hydrocephalus reflects an imbalance between cerebrospinal fluid production and absorption or a blockage to its flow, producing ventricular enlargement It is broadly divided into obstructive (non-communicating), where flow is blocked within the ventricular system, and communicating, where absorption at the arachnoid granulations is impaired Acute obstructive hydrocephalus is a neurosurgical emergency presenting with headache, vomiting, reduced consciousness, and papilloedema from rapidly rising intracranial pressure In infants, before fusion of the sutures, features include an enlarging head circumference, bulging fontanelle, splayed sutures, and the sunsetting sign of downward-deviated eyes Normal pressure hydrocephalus classically presents in older adults with the triad of gait apraxia, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence, and gait often improves after CSF drainage Treatment principles include relieving the obstruction where possible and diverting CSF, commonly by ventriculoperitoneal shunting or endoscopic third ventriculostomy for suitable obstructive cases Shunt complications such as infection, blockage, over-drainage, and disconnection are common and should be considered in any shunted patient who deteriorates Imaging helps distinguish true hydrocephalus with raised pressure from ex vacuo ventricular enlargement due to brain atrophy Acute obstructive hydrocephalus with falling conscious level, severe headache, and vomiting requiring emergency CSF diversion Signs of impending herniation from rapidly rising intracranial pressure Rapidly enlarging head with bulging fontanelle and sunsetting eyes in an infant Shunt malfunction or shunt infection presenting with headache, drowsiness, or fever in a shunted patient Mistaking ex vacuo ventriculomegaly from atrophy for treatable hydrocephalus Delaying CSF diversion in acute obstructive hydrocephalus while awaiting further tests Overlooking shunt malfunction as a cause of deterioration in a shunted patient Attributing the NPH triad solely to ageing or dementia and missing a reversible component Hydrocephalus is an abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid within the ventricular system, usually resulting in ventricular dilatation and, when acute, raised intracranial pressure. CSF is produced largely by the choroid plexus, circulates through the ventricles and subarachnoid space, and is absorbed at the arachnoid granulations. Obstruction along this pathway (for example at the aqueduct, fourth ventricular outflow, or by a mass or blood clot) causes non-communicating hydrocephalus, while impaired absorption after haemorrhage, infection, or inflammation causes communicating hydrocephalus. Rising pressure and ventricular expansion compress adjacent white matter and, if unrelieved, can lead to herniation. Prognosis depends on the cause, speed of onset, and timeliness of treatment; well-selected patients do well after CSF diversion, but outcomes are limited by the underlying pathology and by recurrent shunt complications, and untreated acute obstruction can be rapidly fatal.

Hydrofluoric acid exposure — hydrofluoric acid burn, HF acid exposure, hydrofluoric acid poisoning, fluoride burn Other acid or alkali chemical burns Thermal burn Cellulitis or other soft-tissue infection Other causes of acute hypocalcaemia Contact dermatitis or irritant exposure Digital ischaemia from another cause Serum ionised calcium, magnesium and potassium with serial monitoring Electrocardiogram and continuous cardiac monitoring for QT prolongation and arrhythmia Arterial blood gas and renal function in significant exposures Serum fluoride concentration where available Chest radiograph after inhalational exposure Assessment of burn depth, surface area and involved sites Pain is characteristically out of proportion to visible skin changes and may be delayed for hours, especially after exposure to dilute solutions Unlike other acids, the danger is the fluoride ion rather than the hydrogen ion, so injury and systemic toxicity extend well beyond the surface burn Fingertip and nail-bed burns are common and notoriously painful, often with minimal early skin findings Systemic fluoride absorption chelates calcium and magnesium, causing hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia that can precipitate life-threatening arrhythmias Hyperkalaemia from cellular efflux is an additional driver of cardiotoxicity in significant exposures Copious irrigation followed by calcium therapy is the cornerstone of treatment, with topical, local or intra-arterial calcium used depending on site and severity Inhalational and large or concentrated dermal exposures warrant cardiac monitoring and aggressive correction of electrolyte disturbance Any ingestion or large surface-area or high-concentration exposure should prompt early poisons-centre discussion and monitoring for systemic toxicity Ingestion, inhalation or large or high-concentration dermal exposure Severe or worsening pain disproportionate to skin appearance Hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia or hyperkalaemia QT prolongation or ventricular arrhythmia Involvement of the face, airway or extensive body surface area Underestimating severity because the surface burn looks trivial Failing to anticipate and correct hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hyperkalaemia Not instituting cardiac monitoring after significant exposure Treating it like an ordinary acid burn and omitting calcium therapy Discharging a patient with fingertip burns before ensuring adequate pain control and follow-up Hydrofluoric acid is a relatively weak acid, so surface corrosion is often modest, but the fluoride ion penetrates deeply into tissue. There it binds avidly to calcium and magnesium, forming insoluble salts that cause liquefactive necrosis and intense, progressive pain. The resulting fall in ionised calcium and magnesium disrupts cellular function and cardiac conduction, while fluoride also promotes potassium efflux from cells. The combination of hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hyperkalaemia predisposes to ventricular arrhythmias, which are the usual cause of death in serious systemic poisoning. Small dilute dermal burns treated promptly with irrigation and calcium usually heal well, but concentrated, extensive, inhalational or ingested exposures can cause refractory electrolyte disturbance and fatal arrhythmia despite treatment.

Hydrofluoric acid exposure — hydrofluoric acid burn, HF exposure Other acid or alkali chemical burns Thermal burn Cellulitis or other cause of a painful hand lesion Other causes of acute hypocalcaemia Primary cardiac arrhythmia Serial calcium, magnesium and potassium measurement Continuous electrocardiographic monitoring for arrhythmia Assessment of the concentration, route and extent of exposure Renal function and blood gas in significant exposures Evaluation for inhalational injury if vapour was involved Hydrofluoric acid causes both a corrosive burn and systemic toxicity from the fluoride ion, which can be disproportionate to the burn's appearance Pain is often severe and delayed, particularly with more dilute solutions, and skin injury may look deceptively mild initially Fluoride binds calcium and magnesium, causing hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia, and can raise potassium Life-threatening arrhythmias may follow significant dermal, inhalational or ingestion exposure Calcium is the specific treatment, applied topically and given locally or systemically, alongside correction of electrolytes Even relatively small burns from concentrated acid, or larger dilute exposures, can be lethal Large-surface, concentrated, inhalational or ingestion exposure Electrocardiographic changes or arrhythmia Severe or refractory hypocalcaemia Progressive pain despite an unremarkable-looking burn Underestimating injury because the skin looks mild while pain is severe Failing to monitor and aggressively correct calcium and magnesium Missing the arrhythmia risk in seemingly small burns from concentrated acid Neglecting decontamination and specific calcium therapy Hydrofluoric acid penetrates tissue as a relatively non-dissociated acid, then releases fluoride ions that avidly chelate calcium and magnesium. This produces liquefactive tissue injury and profound local and systemic hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia, while fluoride also interferes with cellular enzymes and can cause hyperkalaemia by disrupting membrane function. The electrolyte disturbances destabilise cardiac membranes, explaining the risk of fatal arrhythmia, and the ongoing fluoride effect accounts for the delayed and severe pain. Small dilute exposures managed promptly usually do well, but significant exposures can cause fatal arrhythmia; early calcium therapy and electrolyte correction are decisive for outcome.

Hydrolethalus syndrome — hydrolethalus, HLS, HYLS1, KIF7 Meckel-Gruber syndrome Acrocallosal syndrome Trisomy 13 Pallister-Hall syndrome Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome Hydrocephalus of other causes Detailed antenatal ultrasound and, where appropriate, post-mortem examination Brain imaging to define the midline malformation and hydrocephalus Skeletal radiographs to characterise polydactyly and the occipital defect Karyotype or chromosomal microarray to exclude a chromosomal cause such as trisomy 13 Molecular testing of HYLS1 and KIF7 within a ciliopathy gene panel A lethal ciliopathy characterised by central nervous system malformation, polydactyly and midline facial defects Hydrocephalus or absent midline brain structures with a characteristic keyhole-shaped defect of the occipital bone is typical Polydactyly is usually postaxial in the hands and preaxial (with a duplicated great toe) in the feet Micrognathia, cleft lip or palate and abnormal genitalia are frequent Shows considerable overlap with Meckel-Gruber and acrocallosal syndromes, reflecting shared ciliary and hedgehog pathway biology The Finnish form is caused by variants in HYLS1, while KIF7 variants produce an overlapping phenotype The condition is almost always lethal before or shortly after birth Antenatal findings of hydrocephalus, polydactyly and a midline defect indicating a likely lethal ciliopathy Severe respiratory and neurological compromise at birth A high recurrence risk requiring genetic counselling before future pregnancies Mistaking the condition for isolated hydrocephalus and missing the syndromic diagnosis Confusing it with Meckel-Gruber or acrocallosal syndrome without genetic testing Failing to arrange genetic counselling for the high recurrence risk Overlooking the characteristic keyhole-shaped occipital bone defect Hydrolethalus syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in HYLS1 or, in overlapping cases, KIF7, both of which encode proteins that function at the basal body and primary cilium. Because the primary cilium transduces hedgehog signalling that patterns the neural tube, midline face and limbs, loss of these proteins disrupts development of midline brain structures, producing hydrocephalus or their absence together with the distinctive occipital bone defect. The same disturbance of ciliary hedgehog signalling in the limb bud generates the postaxial and preaxial polydactyly, while impaired midline patterning underlies the facial clefting and micrognathia. The severe, multisystem malformation reflects the central role of the cilium in early embryonic signalling and accounts for the lethal outcome and overlap with other ciliopathies. The condition is almost uniformly lethal in the perinatal period; management is directed at diagnosis, compassionate care and genetic counselling, with a one-in-four recurrence risk in future pregnancies given autosomal recessive inheritance.

Vesicoureteric reflux (non-obstructive dilatation) Ureteric stricture or malignancy Extrinsic compression by pelvic or retroperitoneal masses, or retroperitoneal fibrosis Bladder outlet obstruction (e.g. prostatic enlargement) Physiological dilatation of pregnancy Extrarenal pelvis or parapelvic cyst mimicking dilatation Renal tract ultrasound as first-line to confirm and grade dilatation CT urography or non-contrast CT to identify stones, level, and cause of obstruction Diuretic renography (e.g. MAG3) to distinguish obstructive from non-obstructive dilatation and assess differential function Serum creatinine and electrolytes to assess renal function Urinalysis and culture to detect infection Micturating cystourethrogram in children where reflux is suspected Hydronephrosis is dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces, most often due to obstruction of urinary outflow but sometimes non-obstructive, and it is a radiological finding rather than a diagnosis in itself The clinical priority is to determine whether true obstruction is present, since obstruction threatens renal function, whereas dilatation without obstruction may need only surveillance Causes are classified by level: intraluminal (stones, clots, tumour), mural (pelviureteric junction obstruction, strictures), and extrinsic (pelvic masses, retroperitoneal fibrosis, pregnancy) Acute unilateral obstruction typically causes severe colicky loin-to-groin pain, whereas chronic or bilateral obstruction may be insidious with vague symptoms or present with renal impairment Obstruction combined with infection above the blockage produces an infected, obstructed system (pyonephrosis), a urological emergency requiring urgent drainage and antibiotics Bilateral hydronephrosis or hydronephrosis of a solitary kidney can cause acute kidney injury and post-obstructive changes, and demands prompt relief Antenatally detected hydronephrosis is common and often transient, but significant or persistent dilatation needs postnatal assessment for underlying uropathy and reflux Ultrasound is the first-line investigation, with CT and functional renography used to define the cause, level, and the affected kidney's function and drainage Relief of obstruction is achieved by drainage (ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy) followed by treatment directed at the underlying cause Infected obstructed system (pyonephrosis) with fever, loin pain, and sepsis requiring emergency drainage Bilateral obstruction or obstruction of a solitary kidney causing acute kidney injury Anuria or rapidly rising creatinine indicating significant obstructive nephropathy Severe uncontrolled pain or haemodynamic instability Post-obstructive diuresis after relief, risking fluid and electrolyte disturbance Assuming all dilatation means obstruction and intervening unnecessarily Failing to recognise and urgently drain an infected obstructed system Overlooking bladder outlet obstruction as a cause of bilateral upper tract dilatation Not anticipating and managing post-obstructive diuresis after relieving obstruction Delaying functional imaging so that salvageable renal function is lost When urine outflow is obstructed, pressure builds up proximal to the blockage and is transmitted back to the renal pelvis and calyces, causing them to dilate. Persistently raised intrapelvic and intratubular pressure impairs glomerular filtration and, over time, produces progressive tubular and parenchymal damage with cortical thinning and loss of function. Superimposed infection in a stagnant, obstructed system allows rapid bacterial proliferation and pus accumulation. Non-obstructive hydronephrosis arises where the collecting system is dilated without a pressure gradient, for example vesicoureteric reflux, high urine flow, or a capacious but unobstructed system, and these generally do not damage the kidney. Outcome depends on the cause, the duration and completeness of obstruction, and whether infection intervenes. Prompt relief of acute obstruction usually allows recovery of renal function, but prolonged or severe obstruction leads to irreversible parenchymal loss. Non-obstructive dilatation and much antenatally detected hydronephrosis resolve or remain stable without harm. Infected obstruction is life-threatening if drainage is delayed but recovers well with timely intervention.

Hydrops fetalis — hydrops foetalis, foetal hydrops, immune hydrops, non-immune hydrops fetalis, NIHF Isolated foetal ascites or isolated pleural effusion without generalised hydrops Foetal or neonatal cardiac failure from structural heart disease or arrhythmia Congenital chylothorax or lymphatic malformation Congenital infection such as parvovirus, cytomegalovirus, syphilis, or toxoplasmosis Chromosomal or syndromic disorders including Turner syndrome and trisomies Inherited anaemias such as alpha-thalassaemia major and metabolic storage disorders Maternal blood group and red cell antibody screen to identify alloimmunisation Foetal ultrasound and echocardiography to define effusions, structural anomalies, and rhythm Middle cerebral artery Doppler peak systolic velocity to assess foetal anaemia Karyotype or microarray and, where indicated, targeted genetic and metabolic testing Maternal and neonatal screen for congenital infection Neonatal full blood count, blood film, bilirubin, albumin, and imaging of effusions Hydrops fetalis is defined by abnormal fluid accumulation in two or more foetal compartments, such as ascites, pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, and generalised skin oedema It is classified as immune (from red cell alloimmunisation) or non-immune, and non-immune causes now account for the large majority of cases Immune hydrops results from maternal antibody-mediated haemolysis of foetal red cells, classically anti-D but also other blood group antibodies, causing severe anaemia and high-output cardiac failure Non-immune causes are diverse and include cardiovascular anomalies and arrhythmias, chromosomal and syndromic conditions, thoracic and lymphatic malformations, congenital infection, and inherited anaemias or metabolic disease Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity on Doppler is a key non-invasive marker of foetal anaemia and guides the need for intervention Antenatal management may include intrauterine transfusion for anaemia and treatment of foetal arrhythmia, with planned delivery in a unit able to provide intensive neonatal resuscitation At birth the infant may need respiratory support, drainage of large effusions, correction of anaemia, and careful fluid and cardiovascular management Severe foetal or neonatal anaemia with signs of high-output cardiac failure Large pleural or pericardial effusions causing respiratory or cardiovascular compromise at birth Rapidly progressive hydrops or associated maternal mirror syndrome Hydrops with a lethal underlying anomaly or profound multi-compartment involvement Assuming an immune cause and not pursuing the broad non-immune differential when the antibody screen is negative Failing to identify and treat a reversible cause such as a tachyarrhythmia or parvovirus anaemia Delivering without adequate preparation for complex neonatal resuscitation and effusion drainage Overlooking maternal mirror syndrome, which threatens maternal wellbeing Aggressive fluid resuscitation of the neonate without recognising underlying cardiac failure Hydrops fetalis is the end result of an imbalance between fluid movement out of the vascular space and its return, leading to interstitial fluid accumulation and effusions in multiple compartments. In immune hydrops, maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and destroy foetal red cells, causing severe anaemia, tissue hypoxia, high-output cardiac failure, and hepatic congestion with reduced albumin synthesis. In non-immune hydrops a wide range of mechanisms converge on the same picture: heart failure from structural disease or arrhythmia, obstruction of venous or lymphatic return, hypoproteinaemia, increased capillary permeability, or severe anaemia from causes other than alloimmunisation. Raised central venous pressure, low oncotic pressure, and lymphatic dysfunction combine to drive fluid into the interstitium and body cavities. Prognosis depends strongly on the underlying cause and gestation at presentation: immune hydrops and some treatable arrhythmias or anaemias can respond well to intrauterine and neonatal therapy, whereas hydrops from chromosomal, structural, or metabolic disease often carries a poor outcome. Overall mortality in non-immune hydrops remains high, particularly when it presents early or with a severe underlying condition.

The tubal epithelium continues to secrete fluid, which, unable to escape, accumulates and progressively dilates the tube. The retained fluid is believed to be embryotoxic and can flow retrogradely into the endometrial cavity, both mechanically disturbing and biochemically impairing embryo implantation, which explains the adverse effect of hydrosalpinx on natural and assisted conception. Hydrosalpinx itself is benign but is an important cause of subfertility; addressing the affected tube before in vitro fertilisation restores implantation and pregnancy rates towards those of women without tubal disease.
