atypical sites such as retropharyngeal longus colli tendinitis Hydroxyapatite deposition disease (HADD) is caused by deposition of hydroxyapatite, a basic calcium phosphate crystal, within tendons, bursae, and other periarticular soft tissues Its best-known form is calcific tendinitis, most frequently affecting the rotator cuff (especially the supraspinatus) at the shoulder, but also the hip, elbow, wrist, and around the spine (for example longus colli tendinitis) Patients may be asymptomatic, have a chronic ache, or suffer acute attacks of severe pain when a deposit becomes inflamed or ruptures into an adjacent bursa during the resorptive phase Radiographs show rounded or cloud-like calcific deposits within tendons whose appearance evolves through formative and resorptive phases, and deposits may disappear over time It commonly presents in middle age, can be bilateral, and must be distinguished from an avulsion fracture and from tumoral calcinosis The crystals are non-birefringent and not seen on standard polarised microscopy, so the diagnosis is largely clinical and radiological Management is symptomatic, using rest, anti-inflammatory therapy, physiotherapy, and ultrasound-guided needling (barbotage) or aspiration, with surgery reserved for refractory deposits Acute severe pain with fever mimicking septic arthritis or bursitis Retropharyngeal (longus colli) calcific tendinitis presenting with acute neck pain and dysphagia Rapidly destructive joint changes suggesting a BCP-related destructive arthropathy Mistaking a periarticular calcific deposit for an avulsion fracture Treating self-limiting acute calcific tendinitis as infection Failing to recognise atypical sites such as retropharyngeal longus colli tendinitis Expecting polarised microscopy to reveal the non-birefringent crystals Hydroxyapatite crystals are deposited within tendons and periarticular soft tissue, often at sites of relative hypovascularity or altered cell metabolism such as the rotator cuff. The disease progresses through phases: a quiescent formative phase of crystal accumulation followed by a resorptive phase in which the deposit becomes vascularised and crystals are shed, provoking intense inflammation and acute pain. Rupture of a deposit into a neighbouring bursa produces acute calcific bursitis. Over time deposits may resorb completely, which is why the radiographic appearance changes and symptoms often ultimately settle. The natural history is often favourable, with acute episodes settling and deposits frequently resorbing spontaneously; most patients recover with conservative treatment, although some experience recurrent or persistent symptoms requiring intervention.

immunosuppression in unusually heavy or refractory cases Hymenolepis nana is distinctive because it can complete its cycle entirely within the human intestine. Ingested eggs, or eggs released internally from mature proglottids, hatch and the oncosphere penetrates an intestinal villus to develop into a cysticercoid larva, which then re-enters the lumen and matures into an adult attached to the mucosa. This internal autoinfection lets the worm population expand within a single host without any intermediate stage, so heavy burdens can accumulate, particularly where reinfection from the environment is also ongoing. Mucosal irritation and the metabolic burden of numerous worms underlie the abdominal symptoms and, in children with heavy infection, poor weight gain, while the direct faecal-oral infectivity of the eggs accounts for ready spread in crowded settings. Good; infection responds well to praziquantel, though autoinfection and environmental reinfection can cause persistence or relapse unless treatment and hygiene measures are adequate.

Hymenoptera (bee/wasp) sting anaphylaxis — bee sting anaphylaxis, wasp sting anaphylaxis, insect venom allergy, hornet sting reaction, vespid/apid sting anaphylaxis Anaphylaxis from another allergen (food, drug, latex) Large local reaction or cellulitis at the sting site Vasovagal syncope after a sting Asthma exacerbation or other cause of acute bronchospasm Angioedema of other cause (e.g. ACE-inhibitor related) Systemic mastocytosis Clinical diagnosis of anaphylaxis based on recognised criteria Serial serum tryptase to support a diagnosis of mast cell activation Specific IgE testing and skin testing to the relevant venom (after recovery, via allergy services) In massive envenomation: full blood count, haemolysis markers, creatine kinase, renal and liver function Electrocardiography and monitoring during and after severe reactions Reactions range from local swelling, through large local reactions, to systemic IgE-mediated anaphylaxis, which can be rapidly fatal Anaphylaxis presents with urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, laryngeal oedema, hypotension and gastrointestinal symptoms, often within minutes Intramuscular adrenaline is the first-line, life-saving treatment for anaphylaxis and should not be delayed for antihistamines or corticosteroids Remove a retained bee stinger promptly; the method matters less than speed, as venom continues to be delivered while it remains Massive envenomation from many simultaneous stings can cause a direct toxic reaction with haemolysis, rhabdomyolysis and organ injury, distinct from allergy Biphasic reactions can occur, so a period of observation after apparent recovery is prudent Patients with confirmed venom anaphylaxis should be referred for allergy assessment, prescribed an adrenaline auto-injector, and considered for venom immunotherapy Airway compromise from laryngeal oedema or stridor Severe bronchospasm or hypoxia Hypotension or shock Rapid progression of symptoms after the sting Massive multiple stings with evidence of haemolysis or organ injury Delaying intramuscular adrenaline while giving antihistamines or steroids first Discharging without observation for a possible biphasic reaction Failing to prescribe an adrenaline auto-injector and refer for allergy assessment Mistaking the toxic syndrome of massive envenomation for simple allergy and missing haemolysis or rhabdomyolysis Hymenoptera venoms contain allergenic proteins (such as phospholipase and hyaluronidase) that, in sensitised individuals, cross-link IgE on mast cells and basophils, triggering degranulation and release of histamine and other mediators. This produces the vasodilatation, increased vascular permeability, bronchoconstriction and mucosal oedema of anaphylaxis, which can progress to airway obstruction and distributive shock. Separately, very large numbers of stings can cause a dose-dependent direct toxic syndrome from venom load, with haemolysis, rhabdomyolysis, hepatic and renal injury independent of allergic sensitisation. Anaphylaxis responds well to prompt adrenaline and supportive care, with full recovery expected, though delay increases mortality. Venom immunotherapy substantially reduces the risk of future systemic reactions; massive envenomation carries a higher risk of organ injury.

In sensitised individuals, venom-specific IgE triggers mast-cell and basophil degranulation, producing systemic allergic reactions and anaphylaxis. With very large numbers of simultaneous stings, the direct toxic load of venom can cause haemolysis, muscle breakdown and multi-organ effects even without allergy. Underlying mast-cell disorders can predispose to severe reactions. Most reactions are self-limiting, and even anaphylaxis usually responds well to prompt adrenaline; venom immunotherapy substantially reduces the risk of future severe reactions.

hyper igd syndrome — mevalonate kinase deficiency, HIDS, hyperimmunoglobulinaemia D with periodic fever Familial Mediterranean fever TNF receptor-associated periodic syndrome Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome spectrum PFAPA syndrome Cyclic neutropenia Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis Behcet disease with recurrent orogenital ulceration MVK gene sequencing for biallelic pathogenic variants Urinary organic acids for mevalonic acid, ideally sampled during a febrile attack Serum immunoglobulin D and immunoglobulin A concentrations Mevalonate kinase enzyme activity assay in leucocytes or fibroblasts Acute-phase reactants during and between episodes Urinalysis for proteinuria as amyloidosis surveillance in long-standing disease Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic MVK variants reducing mevalonate kinase activity; partial deficiency produces the hyper-IgD phenotype while near-complete deficiency causes severe mevalonic aciduria with dysmorphism, cataracts, ataxia and developmental delay. Onset is typically in the first year of life, and attacks are frequently precipitated by childhood immunisations, minor infections, physical or emotional stress. The febrile attacks characteristically feature tender cervical lymphadenopathy, prominent abdominal pain with vomiting and diarrhoea, hepatosplenomegaly and arthralgia or arthritis. Painful oral and genital aphthous ulceration together with a polymorphous rash are common mucocutaneous features. Serum immunoglobulin D is often elevated but is neither sensitive nor specific and is frequently normal in young children, so a normal level never excludes the diagnosis. Elevated urinary mevalonic acid excretion during a febrile attack is a useful and more disease-specific pointer than immunoglobulin D. Interleukin-1 blockade is the mainstay for frequent or severe disease; on-demand non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and short corticosteroid courses help milder attacks. Reactive AA amyloidosis is less frequent than in familial Mediterranean fever or TRAPS but can still occur with long-standing uncontrolled inflammation. Coexisting cataracts, developmental regression or ataxia suggesting the severe mevalonic aciduria end of the spectrum Failure to thrive or growth faltering in an infant with recurrent inflammatory attacks New proteinuria indicating possible AA amyloidosis An attack with peritonism severe enough to prompt consideration of a surgical abdomen Excluding the diagnosis because serum immunoglobulin D is normal, particularly in a child under three years of age Failing to sample urinary mevalonic acid during rather than between attacks Overlooking vaccination as a characteristic trigger and mislabelling post-immunisation attacks as adverse reactions Not recognising the continuum with mevalonic aciduria when neurological or ocular features are present Mevalonate kinase catalyses an early step in the mevalonate (isoprenoid and cholesterol) biosynthetic pathway. Reduced enzyme activity, aggravated by the temperature sensitivity of the mutant protein during febrile episodes, limits production of non-sterol isoprenoids required for post-translational prenylation of small GTPases such as RhoA. Deficient geranylgeranylation impairs RhoA-dependent restraint of the pyrin inflammasome, leading to caspase-1 activation and excess interleukin-1 beta. This links the metabolic defect to the autoinflammatory phenotype and explains why blocking interleukin-1 is effective, whereas the accumulation of upstream mevalonic acid itself is a marker rather than the primary driver of inflammation. The hyper-IgD phenotype tends to become less frequent and milder with age, and interleukin-1 blockade markedly improves attack control and quality of life. The severe mevalonic aciduria end of the spectrum carries substantial neurodevelopmental morbidity and higher mortality.

NIH-type score) to gauge probability of the STAT3 form Chest imaging to detect pneumatoceles, bronchiectasis, and fungal colonisation Skeletal and dental assessment for fractures, scoliosis, and retained teeth Hyper-IgE syndrome is a group of primary immunodeficiencies characterised by markedly elevated serum IgE, recurrent skin and lung infections, and often connective tissue or skeletal abnormalities The classic autosomal dominant form results from dominant-negative STAT3 mutations, while autosomal recessive forms (for example DOCK8 deficiency) show overlapping but distinct features The infection pattern is dominated by Staphylococcus aureus skin abscesses that may be surprisingly non-inflamed ('cold' abscesses) and recurrent pneumonias that can leave pneumatoceles Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and other fungal infections are common, reflecting impaired Th17-mediated immunity in the STAT3 form DOCK8 deficiency is distinguished by severe cutaneous viral infections, food allergies, eosinophilia, and a high risk of malignancy Non-immune features of the STAT3 form include a characteristic coarse facial appearance, retained primary teeth, hyperextensible joints, scoliosis, and a tendency to bone fractures Serum IgE is often very high but does not correlate tightly with disease activity, and eosinophilia is frequent Management centres on long-term antistaphylococcal and antifungal prophylaxis, aggressive treatment of infections, and skin care; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can correct the recessive DOCK8 form Recurrent or severe deep-seated infections, including 'cold' abscesses and pneumonia with cavitation, warranting urgent immunological workup Aspergillus or other fungal infection colonising pneumatoceles, risking invasive disease or haemorrhage Severe disseminated viral skin infection in suspected DOCK8 deficiency New or accelerating malignancy, particularly in the recessive form Vascular aneurysms in the STAT3 form Attributing recurrent staphylococcal abscesses to simple atopic dermatitis and missing the underlying immunodeficiency Assuming a very high IgE alone confirms the diagnosis, since it is neither fully sensitive nor specific Overlooking the skeletal, dental, and vascular features that distinguish the STAT3 form Failing to recognise DOCK8 deficiency as a transplantable condition with a different management path Not monitoring pneumatoceles for secondary fungal infection Hyper-IgE syndromes arise from defects in signalling pathways that govern T-helper cell differentiation and epithelial immunity. In the autosomal dominant form, dominant-negative mutations in STAT3 impair the development of Th17 cells and the response to several cytokines, reducing antimicrobial peptide production at skin and mucosal surfaces and blunting the acute inflammatory response, which explains the 'cold' abscesses. STAT3 also influences tissue remodelling and skeletal biology, accounting for the connective tissue, dental, and bony features. Autosomal recessive forms such as DOCK8 deficiency disrupt cytoskeletal function and lymphocyte survival, producing profound susceptibility to cutaneous viruses and severe allergic disease. Dysregulated IgE production and eosinophilia are shared consequences of the altered T-cell cytokine milieu. With sustained prophylaxis and prompt treatment of infections, many patients with the autosomal dominant STAT3 form reach adulthood, though pulmonary complications and vascular aneurysms remain important causes of morbidity. The autosomal recessive DOCK8 form carries a poorer outlook because of severe viral infections and malignancy, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offers the best chance of cure.

to producing IgG, IgA and IgE and to undergo affinity maturation. In the X-linked form, mutations in the gene encoding CD40 ligand on activated T cells prevent effective engagement of CD40 on B cells and other antigen-presenting cells, disrupting both antibody class-switching and cell-mediated immune signalling. Autosomal recessive variants involve CD40 itself or the downstream B-cell enzymes activation-induced cytidine deaminase and uracil-N-glycosylase, which are required for class-switch recombination and somatic hypermutation. Outcome depends on subtype: the autosomal recessive humoral forms generally do well on immunoglobulin replacement, whereas untreated CD40 ligand or CD40 deficiency carries high morbidity from opportunistic infection, liver disease and malignancy, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offering the prospect of cure when performed early.

Pneumocystis prophylaxis Overlooking Cryptosporidium as a cause of chronic diarrhoea and liver disease Missing associated neutropenia Failing to distinguish the combined X-linked form from the milder B-cell-intrinsic recessive forms, which affects prognosis and transplant decisions Hyper-IgM syndromes disrupt immunoglobulin class-switch recombination. In the X-linked form, mutations in the gene for CD40 ligand deprive B cells and antigen-presenting cells of the CD40 signal that activated T cells normally deliver, preventing class switching, germinal centre development, and effective T-cell-dependent activation of macrophages and dendritic cells. Hyperbaric and Diving Medicine — HBO2T, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, decompression sickness, the bends, DCS, cerebral arterial gas embolism, CAGE, diving barotrauma, dysbarism Stroke or transient ischemic attack (can mimic or be mimicked by cerebral arterial gas embolism) Inner ear barotrauma versus vestibulocochlear decompression sickness (both cause sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo) Middle ear barotrauma (should never be invoked to explain post-dive sensorineural hearing loss or true vertigo) Acute coronary syndrome or musculoskeletal injury versus DCS limb pain Other causes of post-dive neurologic symptoms not explained by an alternative mechanism Transcutaneous oximetry (transcutaneous Po2 mapping) around a wound on air and on oxygen at pressure to assess HBO2T suitability Ankle-brachial index and skin perfusion pressure as alternative wound perfusion assessments Carboxyhemoglobin level in suspected CO poisoning (confirms exposure but does not gauge severity or prognosis) Arterial blood-gas analysis for metabolic acidosis in CO poisoning (a marker of poor prognosis) Audiometry / otologic evaluation for suspected inner ear barotrauma Dive profile review combined with clinical examination (there are no useful confirmatory diagnostic tests for DCS) Ischemic stroke / TIA mimicking CAGE Migraine or other transient neurologic events after diving Decompression sickness mimicking CAGE and vice versa (clinically the distinction is unimportant because first aid and definitive management are identical) Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBO2T) means breathing physician-prescribed medical-grade oxygen while the whole body is enclosed in a chamber pressurized to at least 2.0 ATA; most regimens use 2-2.8 ATA for roughly 90-120 minutes per session. At 2.8 ATA, arterial Po2 can theoretically rise above ~2025 mmHg and dissolved plasma oxygen to ~60 mL/L, enough to sustain life without hemoglobin in animal studies, which sharply improves oxygen diffusion through tissues. Even a single HBO2T exposure produces durable cell-signaling effects (on fibroblasts, leukocytes, angiogenesis, antioxidant defenses) that persist for hours after oxygen levels return to baseline, mediated by reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. The UHMS recognizes 15 accepted indications, including air/gas embolism, carbon monoxide poisoning, gas gangrene, crush injury, decompression sickness, problem wounds, intracranial abscess, necrotizing soft tissue infection, refractory osteomyelitis, delayed radiation injury, and sudden sensorineural hearing loss. For chronic problem wounds, candidate selection is often guided by transcutaneous oximetry around the wound while breathing air and oxygen at pressure; in diabetic patients a transcutaneous Po2 threshold of <50 mmHg may be more appropriate than the usual <40 mmHg cutoff. Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with more than 200 times the affinity of oxygen and shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve leftward; HBO2T shortens the COHb half-life to about 21 min at 2.0 ATA versus roughly 5.5 h breathing air at sea level. Admission carboxyhemoglobin levels confirm CO exposure but do NOT reliably predict severity or prognosis; delayed neuropsychological sequelae can appear after days to months of apparent recovery. Ambient pressure increases by 1 atmosphere (101.3 kPa) for every 10.1 m of seawater, so a diver at 20 m experiences about 3 ATA. In diving, the maximum acceptable inspired Po2 is generally considered 1.6 ATA (lower than therapeutic HBO2T pressures) because immersion and exercise raise the risk of oxygen-toxic seizures; helium replaces nitrogen at depth to cut narcosis and gas density. Cerebral arterial gas embolism (CAGE) from pulmonary barotrauma presents within minutes of surfacing with loss of consciousness, confusion, hemiplegia, visual or speech disturbance, and can be mistaken for stroke or TIA by clinicians unfamiliar with diving. Decompression sickness occurs in roughly 1 in 5000-10,000 recreational dives; most cases are mild (limb pain, fatigue, patchy paresthesias), and serious DCS usually appears within 60 min of surfacing. Symptoms beginning more than 24 h after a dive are very unlikely to be DCS unless the diver was subsequently exposed to reduced ambient pressure such as air travel or higher-altitude surface travel. About 25% of adults have a patent foramen ovale; right-to-left shunting (PFO, atrial septal defect, intrapulmonary shunt) lets venous bubbles 'arterialize' and raises the risk of cerebral, spinal cord, inner ear, and skin DCS manifestations. Neurologic symptoms after diving (loss of consciousness, confusion, hemiplegia, visual or speech disturbance) suggesting CAGE or serious DCS — discuss with a diving medicine specialist and consider recompression Spinal cord involvement in DCS (weakness, paralysis, bladder/sphincter dysfunction) which frequently causes permanent disability Pulmonary and cardiovascular DCS manifestations (cough, dyspnea, hypotension, hemoconcentration, coagulopathy) which can be life-threatening Sensorineural hearing loss or true vertigo with nausea, vomiting, nystagmus, ataxia after diving (inner ear barotrauma or vestibulocochlear DCS) Untreated pneumothorax before any hyperbaric exposure (intrapleural gas can expand and tension on decompression) Tonic-clonic seizure during HBO2T or diving from cerebral oxygen toxicity, sometimes preceded by facial twitching, anxiety, and agitation Moderate-to-severe CO poisoning, especially age over 35, prolonged exposure, acidosis, or loss of consciousness Attributing post-dive sensorineural hearing loss or true vertigo to middle ear barotrauma — these point instead to inner ear barotrauma or vestibulocochlear DCS. Misdiagnosing CAGE as a typical stroke or TIA when the clinician is unfamiliar with diving medicine. Relying on admission carboxyhemoglobin level to judge severity or prognosis of CO poisoning. Assuming there is a confirmatory diagnostic test for DCS — diagnosis rests on dive profile, symptom timing, and examination. Treating CAGE/DCS distinction as clinically critical — first aid and definitive management are the same for both. Compressing a patient with an untreated pneumothorax or with gas-trapping lesions such as bullae without careful risk assessment and, for pneumothorax, a patent chest drain. Overstating the risk of pulmonary oxygen toxicity from remote bleomycin exposure; published experience suggests the relationship may have been exaggerated, though recent bleomycin or mitomycin C with pneumonitis warrants careful evaluation. Promoting HBO2T (sometimes with air) as a panacea for unproven indications, general well-being, or anti-aging — practice should be confined to accepted, periodically updated indications. Hyperbaric oxygen exerts effects through both physical mechanisms and biochemical cell signaling. Physically, raising ambient pressure shrinks gas bubbles per Boyle's law and steepens inert-gas diffusion gradients from bubble to tissue to blood and lungs, the basis for treating decompression sickness and arterial gas embolism. The markedly elevated arterial Po2 fully saturates hemoglobin and greatly increases dissolved plasma oxygen, improving diffusion into hypoxic and irradiated tissue. Beyond simple oxygen delivery, intermittent hyperoxia generates reactive oxygen species (superoxide, hydrogen peroxide) and reactive nitrogen species (nitric oxide) that drive cytokine and angiogenic growth-factor production, stimulate fibroblast activity, enhance macrophage bacterial killing, mobilize vasculogenic progenitor cells from marrow, and paradoxically produce anti-inflammatory effects such as reduced leukocyte beta-2 integrin adhesion. Hyperoxia also causes vasoconstriction and an osmotic gradient that reduce tissue edema and is directly toxic or bacteriostatic to anaerobes. In late radiation tissue injury, irradiation produces fibrosis and obliterative endarteritis leaving hypovascular hypoxic tissue (an alternative model emphasizes cytokine-driven fibrosis from oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction); HBO2T's most important benefit is promoting angiogenesis and increasing microvascular density. In carbon monoxide poisoning, CO impairs oxygen carriage, acts as an anesthetic, disrupts cellular oxidative processes, binds heme proteins including cytochrome a/a3, and peroxidizes brain lipids, with brain and heart most vulnerable. In diving, breathing gas at elevated ambient pressure loads inert gas (usually nitrogen) into tissues; if washout during ascent lags the falling ambient pressure, tissues become supersaturated and bubbles form, causing mechanical distortion of tissues and, in the venous circulation, inflammatory and coagulation cascades, endothelial injury, capillary leak, hemoconcentration, and pulmonary vascular obstruction. Barotrauma arises when noncompliant gas-filled spaces fail to equalize with changing ambient pressure. Most HBO2T adverse events are mild and self-limiting, and the therapy is generally safe. For late radiation tissue injury pooled data suggest improved tissue healing and reduced wound dehiscence in jaw osteoradionecrosis. About 70% of indolent problem ulcers are substantially improved or healed 6 months after a course, and meta-analyses report increased complete healing and reduced amputation of diabetic foot ulcers. In CO poisoning the most rigorous trial showed fewer cognitive sequelae at 6 weeks (25% vs 46%) and 12 months (18% vs 32%) with HBO2T, though a Cochrane review found overall evidence insufficient. Survivors of CO poisoning may develop delayed neuropsychological sequelae; risk factors for poor outcome are age over 35, exposure beyond 24 h, acidosis, and loss of consciousness. In diving, CAGE often shows substantial or complete early resolution as bubbles involute, but secondary deterioration or re-embolization can occur. Most DCS cases are mild, but spinal cord DCS frequently causes permanent disability and pulmonary/cardiovascular forms can be fatal. Decompression sickness manifestations (Harrison Table 476-2) are grouped by organ system: musculoskeletal (limb pain); neurologic cerebral (confusion, visual and speech disturbances), spinal (weakness, paralysis, upper motor neuron signs, bladder/sphincter dysfunction, dermatomal sensory disturbance, abdominal/girdle pain), vestibulocochlear (hearing loss, vertigo, ataxia, nausea/vomiting), and peripheral (patchy nondermatomal sensory disturbance); pulmonary (cough, dyspnea); cardiovascular (hemoconcentration, coagulopathy, hypotension); cutaneous (rash, itch); lymphatic (localized soft tissue edema); and constitutional (fatigue, malaise). Most cases are mild; serious DCS usually manifests within 60 min of surfacing.

hypercalcaemia of malignancy — malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia, humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy Primary hyperparathyroidism Thiazide diuretic use Sarcoidosis and other granulomatous disease Vitamin D or vitamin A toxicity Milk-alkali syndrome Thyrotoxicosis or immobilisation Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia Albumin-corrected or ionised calcium with phosphate and magnesium Parathyroid hormone (expected to be suppressed) PTH-related peptide where available 25- and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels Myeloma screen: serum and urine electrophoresis and free light chains Renal function and ECG for QT shortening Imaging to identify or stage the underlying primary Four mechanisms operate: PTH-related peptide secretion (humoral, e.g. squamous cancers, renal and breast), local osteolysis (myeloma, breast), tumour production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (lymphomas and granulomatous processes) and, rarely, ectopic PTH. Endogenous PTH is suppressed in malignancy; a non-suppressed PTH points instead to coexisting primary hyperparathyroidism. Always interpret calcium after correcting for albumin, or measure ionised calcium, because hypoalbuminaemia is common in advanced malignancy and masks true hypercalcaemia. Symptoms follow the classic 'bones, stones, abdominal groans and psychic moans', with polyuria and dehydration driving a vicious cycle of worsening hypercalcaemia. Aggressive isotonic saline rehydration is the immediate priority to restore volume and renal calcium clearance before or alongside specific therapy. Intravenous bisphosphonate (e.g. zoledronic acid) is the mainstay for sustained control but takes two to four days to act; denosumab is an option in bisphosphonate-refractory disease or renal impairment. Calcitonin gives a rapid but short-lived and tachyphylactic reduction, useful as a bridge in severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia while bisphosphonate takes effect. Corticosteroids are effective specifically in vitamin-D-mediated hypercalcaemia (lymphoma, myeloma, granulomatous disease); loop diuretics should be reserved for managing fluid overload, not used routinely to lower calcium. Corrected calcium in the severe range with obtundation or coma Cardiac arrhythmia or markedly shortened QT interval Acute kidney injury from profound dehydration Rapidly progressive drowsiness or delirium Vomiting preventing oral intake and worsening volume depletion Failing to correct calcium for albumin and missing significant hypercalcaemia Administering a bisphosphonate without first restoring intravascular volume Using loop diuretics to force calcium excretion in a still-dehydrated patient Overlooking a non-suppressed PTH indicating concurrent primary hyperparathyroidism Missing myeloma as the underlying cause by not performing a paraprotein screen The predominant driver is systemic PTH-related peptide, which mimics PTH at its receptor to increase osteoclastic bone resorption and renal tubular calcium reabsorption while promoting phosphaturia. Osteolytic metastases and myeloma release calcium locally through cytokine- and RANK-ligand-mediated osteoclast activation, and certain lymphomas convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, enhancing gut calcium absorption. Rising calcium impairs renal concentrating ability, producing polyuria and volume depletion that reduces glomerular filtration and calcium excretion, thereby accelerating the hypercalcaemia in a self-perpetuating loop. Hypercalcaemia of malignancy generally marks advanced disease and is an adverse prognostic sign, with limited survival unless the underlying tumour responds to treatment. The metabolic disturbance itself is usually correctable acutely, but recurrence is common without effective anticancer therapy.

the typical picture is a patient with known malignancy found hypercalcaemic on routine labs, though occasionally hypercalcaemia is the presenting feature of an undiagnosed cancer (p.737). Most malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia runs a relatively acute course, in contrast to the chronic, fluctuating high-normal pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism or occasionally myeloma (p.363). An elevated PTHrP level confirms HHM and is raised in roughly 80% of hypercalcaemic cancer patients; PTH should be suppressed in true HHM (p.738). Features favouring HHM over primary hyperparathyroidism: known malignancy, recent onset, and very high serum calcium levels (p.738). PTHrP shares homology with the first ~13 amino acids of PTH and binds the PTH receptor, explaining the PTH-like biochemical effects on bone and kidney (p.363, 737). Serum free light chains should be checked when myeloma is suspected, since ~3% of myeloma is missed by serum/urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (p.364). Hypercalcaemia of malignancy is one of the few clinical settings where measuring serum 1,25(OH)2D is genuinely useful — it is elevated or inappropriately normal in lymphoma- and granulomatous-mediated hypercalcaemia (p.364). Always confirm true hypercalcaemia first by correcting for albumin (add ~0.8 mg/dL to total calcium per 1.0 g/dL fall in albumin below 4.0 g/dL) to exclude pseudohypercalcaemia (p.363). Markedly elevated calcium (>14 mg/dL / >3.5 mmol/L) with progressive lethargy, stupor or coma (p.363-364, 737) Severe GI involvement — nausea, vomiting, anorexia, peptic ulcer or pancreatitis (p.364) Acute renal failure and volume depletion from hypercalcaemia-induced nephrogenic concentrating defect and polyuria (p.364) Cardiac conduction abnormalities — bradycardia, AV block, QRS widening, short QTc (p.364) Failing to correct calcium for albumin can produce pseudohypercalcaemia or pseudohypocalcaemia and a false diagnosis (p.363). FHH may present with mildly elevated PTH and hypercalcaemia and be mistaken for primary hyperparathyroidism — parathyroid surgery is ineffective in FHH and must be excluded (p.363). Mild hypercalcaemia (10.5-11.9 mg/dL) is often asymptomatic or causes only vague neuropsychiatric or constitutional symptoms, so it may be overlooked (p.363). Ionised calcium measurement is easily distorted by collection technique (e.g. prolonged tourniquet); corrected total calcium is generally preferable (p.363). Up to ~3% of myeloma is undetected by serum/urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation — check free light chains (p.364). In immobilisation-related hypercalcaemia, an unrecognised underlying driver (pHPT, Paget's, myeloma) may coexist and should be sought, especially in older patients (p.363). Calcium balance is governed by PTH and the vitamin D metabolites 1,25(OH)2D and 25(OH)D acting across parathyroid, kidney, intestine and bone. Hypercalcaemia of malignancy arises mainly through three mechanisms. (1) PTHrP overproduction by solid tumours (squamous head/neck, lung, skin; breast; genitourinary; gastrointestinal) — PTHrP mimics PTH at the PTH receptor, raising bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption. (2) Local osteolysis from skeletal metastases (breast, myeloma), where metastatic deposits secrete PTHrP and chemokines driving bone breakdown. (3) Excess 1,25(OH)2D production, notably by lymphomas (and granulomatous disease) via macrophage CYP27B1 converting 25(OH)D to active 1,25(OH)2D, enhancing intestinal calcium absorption. PTHrP induction is linked to PTHLH hypomethylation, hedgehog/Gli signalling, TGF-beta, oncogene activation (e.g. Ras) and p53 loss. In all these malignant mechanisms, the high serum calcium activates the parathyroid CaSR and appropriately suppresses endogenous PTH (p.363, 737). By total serum calcium: mild 10.5-11.9 mg/dL (often asymptomatic); moderate >=12-14 mg/dL; severe >=14 mg/dL (progressive lethargy, stupor or coma, prominent GI symptoms and acute renal failure) (Harrison 22e p.363-364).

hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric acid are characteristic Association with high levels of human chorionic gonadotrophin means it is more common in multiple and molar pregnancies haemodynamic instability Confusion, ataxia, or ophthalmoplegia suggesting Wernicke encephalopathy Refractory vomiting with significant weight loss and inability to maintain any oral intake Severe electrolyte derangement or acid-base disturbance Haematemesis from Mallory-Weiss tears or signs of an alternative serious diagnosis Giving intravenous glucose before thiamine and precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy Attributing all vomiting to pregnancy without excluding molar pregnancy, infection, or metabolic causes Undertreating dehydration and electrolyte loss Overtreating the transient hCG-mediated hyperthyroidism with antithyroid drugs Overlooking the substantial psychological impact and risk of inadequate nutrition The cause is multifactorial. Rising human chorionic gonadotrophin and oestrogen are strongly implicated, explaining the peak in the first trimester and the higher frequency in molar and multiple pregnancies where hCG is elevated. Genetic factors, including variants affecting the appetite-regulating hormone GDF15, and altered gut motility contribute. Protracted vomiting leads to loss of fluid, hydrogen, chloride, and potassium ions, producing dehydration, hypokalaemia, and a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, while starvation drives ketosis and depletes thiamine stores. Most cases settle by the second trimester and, with adequate rehydration and antiemetic therapy, have a good outcome for mother and baby. Severe untreated disease can cause serious maternal complications including Wernicke encephalopathy, and recurrence in subsequent pregnancies is common.

hypereosinophilic cardiomyopathy — Loeffler endocarditis, eosinophilic endomyocardial disease tropical endomyocardial fibrosis idiopathic restrictive cardiomyopathy cardiac amyloidosis cardiac sarcoidosis constrictive pericarditis apical hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with cavity obliteration intracardiac tumour or other cause of ventricular filling defect full blood count with eosinophil quantification and peripheral blood film echocardiography for apical thrombus, cavity obliteration and valve tethering cardiac magnetic resonance with late gadolinium enhancement and thrombus imaging cardiac troponin for active myocardial injury FIP1L1-PDGFRA and other clonal molecular/cytogenetic testing, with bone marrow assessment evaluation for secondary causes of eosinophilia (parasites, drugs, allergy, malignancy, vasculitis) endomyocardial biopsy in selected cases to confirm eosinophilic infiltration Cardiac involvement in the hypereosinophilic syndromes (Loeffler endocarditis) results from sustained eosinophilia of any cause—clonal/myeloproliferative, lymphocytic/reactive, or idiopathic—and is a major source of morbidity and mortality. Disease evolves through three overlapping stages: an early acute necrotic stage, an intermediate thrombotic stage with mural thrombus, and a late fibrotic stage producing a restrictive cardiomyopathy resembling tropical endomyocardial fibrosis. The degree or duration of eosinophilia does not reliably predict cardiac damage, so cardiac surveillance is warranted whenever significant eosinophilia persists. Apical obliteration of one or both ventricles by thrombus, with preserved basal function and characteristic tethering of the atrioventricular valves causing regurgitation, is a hallmark on imaging. Mural thrombus carries a high embolic risk, and systemic or pulmonary thromboembolism may be the presenting event. Cardiac magnetic resonance is valuable for demonstrating endocardial thrombus and subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement, and troponin elevation may flag active myocardial necrosis. Testing for the FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion is essential because such myeloproliferative disease responds dramatically to tyrosine kinase inhibition, whereas reactive and idiopathic forms are treated with corticosteroids and other eosinophil-lowering agents. Anticoagulation is generally required once mural thrombus is present, and surgery (thrombectomy, endocardectomy and valve repair or replacement) may be needed in the fibrotic stage. systemic or pulmonary thromboembolism from intracardiac thrombus acute heart failure or troponin rise indicating active myocardial necrosis large mobile ventricular thrombus on imaging severe atrioventricular valve regurgitation with haemodynamic compromise rapidly progressive restrictive physiology and low-output failure assuming a modest eosinophil count excludes serious cardiac involvement failing to test for FIP1L1-PDGFRA and missing a highly treatable form overlooking apical thrombus and omitting anticoagulation, risking embolism misclassifying the disease as idiopathic restrictive cardiomyopathy or constriction attributing the eosinophilia to a benign cause without excluding clonal or secondary drivers Prolonged elevation of activated eosinophils leads to release of cationic granule proteins—including major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein—that are directly toxic to the endocardium and myocardium. The initial acute stage is characterised by eosinophilic infiltration and myocardial necrosis with an intense inflammatory response. Endocardial injury then promotes mural thrombus formation, particularly at the ventricular apices and along the inflow tracts, during the thrombotic stage. Organisation of thrombus and progressive endomyocardial fibrosis follow, encasing the subvalvular apparatus and obliterating the ventricular cavities. The stiff, scarred endocardium and reduced cavity volume produce restrictive filling, atrioventricular valve regurgitation from leaflet tethering, and ultimately restrictive cardiomyopathy with congestive failure. Outcome depends on the underlying cause and the stage at diagnosis; early eosinophil-lowering therapy (and targeted tyrosine kinase inhibition in FIP1L1-PDGFRA disease) can arrest progression, but established fibrotic restrictive disease with valve involvement carries a poor prognosis and may require surgery.

Hypereosinophilic syndrome — HES, Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome Secondary (reactive) eosinophilia from parasitic infection Drug reaction including DRESS Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis Chronic eosinophilic leukaemia and other myeloid neoplasms Lymphoma (Hodgkin or T-cell) with eosinophilia Allergic or atopic disease and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis Adrenal insufficiency Repeated full blood count with eosinophil quantification and blood film Testing for FIP1L1-PDGFRA and other PDGFRA, PDGFRB and FGFR1 rearrangements Peripheral blood T-cell immunophenotyping and T-cell receptor clonality Serum tryptase, vitamin B12 and IgE Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics Echocardiography, cardiac MRI and troponin Stool and serology for parasites and exclusion of secondary causes Defined by persistent marked eosinophilia (greater than 1.5 x 10^9/L on repeated testing or marked tissue eosinophilia) with end-organ damage and exclusion of secondary causes. Recognised variants include myeloproliferative (often FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion), lymphocytic (an aberrant clonal T-cell population driving interleukin-5), idiopathic and overlap forms. FIP1L1-PDGFRA-positive disease is exquisitely responsive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib. Cardiac involvement (Loffler endocarditis, endomyocardial fibrosis and mural thrombi) is the major cause of morbidity and mortality. Other affected organs include the skin, lungs, gastrointestinal tract and nervous system, with peripheral neuropathy and thromboembolic stroke. Raised serum tryptase and vitamin B12 point towards the myeloproliferative variant. Exclude secondary eosinophilia from parasites, drugs, allergy, malignancy, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and adrenal insufficiency. Corticosteroids are first line for non-PDGFRA disease, with anti-interleukin-5 therapy (mepolizumab) and tyrosine kinase inhibitors as targeted options. Cardiac involvement with heart failure, a new murmur, raised troponin or mural thrombus Thromboembolic events including stroke Rapidly rising eosinophil count with systemic deterioration New focal neurological deficit Missing FIP1L1-PDGFRA, a highly treatable cause, before committing to corticosteroids alone Overlooking cardiac involvement because symptoms lag behind structural damage Failing to exclude Strongyloides before immunosuppression Confusing the syndrome with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis or reactive eosinophilia Hypereosinophilic syndrome is a heterogeneous group of disorders characterised by sustained overproduction of eosinophils that infiltrate and damage tissues through release of granule proteins (major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein), cytokines and pro-thrombotic mediators. In the myeloproliferative variant, clonal expansion is driven by fusion tyrosine kinases, classically FIP1L1-PDGFRA; in the lymphocytic variant an aberrant clonal T-cell population secretes interleukin-5 driving reactive eosinophilia. Cardiac damage evolves through acute necrotic, thrombotic and fibrotic stages, producing restrictive endomyocardial fibrosis. Prognosis has improved markedly with modern targeted therapy: FIP1L1-PDGFRA disease responds excellently to tyrosine kinase inhibitors, while outcome in other variants depends largely on the extent of cardiac and neurological damage.

Hyperhaemolysis syndrome — Hyperhaemolytic transfusion reaction, Bystander haemolysis syndrome Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction Sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis with anaemia Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Aplastic or parvovirus-associated crisis Ongoing haemorrhage Serial haemoglobin demonstrating a fall below the pre-transfusion value Lactate dehydrogenase, bilirubin and haptoglobin confirming brisk haemolysis Reticulocyte count, which may be inappropriately low Direct antiglobulin test and extended antibody identification Urinalysis for haemoglobinuria Review of transfusion history and haemoglobin electrophoresis to quantify remaining donor haemoglobin A severe transfusion reaction, most often seen in sickle cell disease and thalassaemia, in which both transfused and the patient's own red cells are destroyed. The hallmark is a post-transfusion haemoglobin that falls below the pre-transfusion level, so the patient is worse off after being transfused. Markedly raised lactate dehydrogenase, low haptoglobin, haemoglobinuria and often a reticulocytopenia despite severe anaemia are characteristic. Acute and delayed forms are described; the delayed form frequently coincides with an alloantibody response while the acute form may occur without detectable new antibodies. Further transfusion typically worsens haemolysis and should be avoided unless anaemia is immediately life-threatening. Immunosuppression with corticosteroids and immunoglobulin is the mainstay, with complement inhibition and other agents considered in refractory cases. In sickle cell disease it may be mistaken for a painful crisis, delaying recognition and prompting harmful further transfusion. Bystander destruction of autologous cells is thought to involve activated macrophages and complement, extending haemolysis beyond antigen-incompatible cells. Post-transfusion haemoglobin lower than before transfusion Worsening anaemia and haemoglobinuria after each transfused unit Reticulocytopenia in the face of severe anaemia Rapid clinical deterioration in a patient with sickle cell disease Signs of end-organ ischaemia from profound anaemia Giving more blood in response to worsening anaemia and accelerating haemolysis. Mistaking the presentation for a sickle cell painful crisis. Assuming a negative antibody screen excludes the diagnosis, as the acute form may lack new antibodies. Failing to start immunosuppression promptly in a deteriorating patient. Not flagging the patient for specialist input before any future transfusion. Hyperhaemolysis syndrome is characterised by destruction of red cells in excess of the transfused incompatible units, so that autologous cells are also lost. The mechanism is incompletely understood but is thought to involve intense macrophage activation and complement dysregulation triggered by transfusion in a chronically alloimmunised and inflamed host. Activated macrophages destroy both antibody-coated transfused cells and innocent bystander autologous red cells, while suppression of erythropoiesis (a relative reticulocytopenia) compounds the fall in haemoglobin. In the delayed form an anamnestic alloantibody response is often demonstrable, whereas the acute form may occur without new detectable antibodies, suggesting antibody-independent mechanisms. The result is profound, worsening anaemia with brisk intravascular and extravascular haemolysis. The syndrome can be life-threatening, particularly if unrecognised and further transfusion is given, but it often responds to immunosuppression and avoidance of transfusion, with recovery of haemoglobin over days to weeks. Recurrence on re-exposure is a major concern, so future transfusion requires specialist planning.

frequency or severity despite treatment Excluding the diagnosis because serum IgD is normal, which is common in young children Missing the diagnostic window by not collecting urine for mevalonic acid during a febrile attack Confusing frequent early-childhood attacks with recurrent infections and treating with repeated antibiotics Failing to recognise the more severe mevalonic aciduria phenotype in an infant with neurological features Hyper-IgD syndrome lies on the mevalonate kinase deficiency spectrum, caused by biallelic MVK mutations that reduce activity of mevalonate kinase, an enzyme early in the mevalonate (isoprenoid/cholesterol) biosynthetic pathway. Reduced enzyme activity impairs production of downstream non-sterol isoprenoids, particularly geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, which is required for prenylation of small regulatory GTPases. Deficient protein prenylation destabilises inhibitory signals on the innate immune system and enhances NLRP3 inflammasome activation with excess interleukin-1 beta release, producing recurrent inflammatory attacks. Enzyme activity worsens transiently with fever, creating a self-amplifying inflammatory cycle, and profound deficiency produces the severe multisystem phenotype of mevalonic aciduria. Attack frequency in the hyper-IgD end of the spectrum often lessens with age and responds to interleukin-1 blockade, giving a reasonable outlook, whereas severe mevalonic aciduria carries significant neurodevelopmental morbidity and higher mortality, and AA amyloidosis remains a long-term risk in poorly controlled disease.

by protein-containing feeds Persistent hyperammonaemia without an alternative explanation Neurodevelopmental delay or epilepsy despite glycaemic control Mistaking the hyperammonaemia for a urea cycle disorder and instituting inappropriate protein restriction protocols Overlooking protein sensitivity by testing only fasting tolerance Attributing hypoglycaemia to something other than hyperinsulinism because ketones are inappropriately low Assuming good glycaemic control removes all neurodevelopmental and seizure risk Glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH), encoded by GLUD1, catalyses oxidative deamination of glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia in the mitochondrion and is allosterically regulated, being inhibited by GTP and activated by leucine. Gain-of-function mutations reduce GTP inhibition, leaving GDH overactive. In pancreatic beta cells this raises the ratio of ATP generation and triggers inappropriate insulin secretion, especially after a leucine (protein) load, producing hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia. In the liver and elsewhere, increased GDH activity raises ammonia production, giving a persistent hyperammonaemia. The excess ammonia usually remains modest and does not cause the classic urea cycle encephalopathy. With treatment of the hyperinsulinism and avoidance of large protein loads, hypoglycaemia is often manageable and the hyperammonaemia is generally benign; however, there remains an elevated risk of epilepsy and neurodevelopmental difficulties that may not be fully explained by hypoglycaemia alone.

hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis — hyperPP, adynamia episodica hereditaria, Gamstorp disease Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis Paramyotonia congenita Andersen-Tawil syndrome Secondary hyperkalaemia (renal failure, adrenal insufficiency) Myasthenia gravis Guillain-Barre syndrome Serum potassium measured during an attack Electrocardiogram to detect hyperkalaemic changes SCN4A genetic testing Electromyography with long and short exercise (McManis) testing Thyroid function tests to exclude thyrotoxic periodic paralysis Renal and adrenal function to exclude secondary hyperkalaemia Creatine kinase and, where relevant, muscle biopsy Autosomal dominant skeletal muscle sodium channelopathy caused by gain-of-function mutations in SCN4A (Nav1.4). Episodes of flaccid weakness occur with a rising or normal-to-high serum potassium, in contrast to the low potassium of the hypokalaemic form. Attacks are usually shorter and more frequent than in hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, often lasting minutes to a couple of hours. Typical triggers are rest after exercise, fasting, cold exposure and potassium-rich foods. Clinical or electrical myotonia, and overlap with paramyotonia congenita (also SCN4A), point away from the hypokalaemic form. Onset is usually in the first decade, with normal strength between early attacks. Respiratory and bulbar muscles are typically spared, and consciousness is preserved. A fixed progressive proximal myopathy may develop in later life despite fewer acute attacks. Respiratory compromise during a severe attack Cardiac arrhythmia related to hyperkalaemia Rapidly progressive generalised paralysis Findings suggesting a secondary cause of hyperkalaemia Progressive fixed weakness between attacks Confusing it with the hypokalaemic form, in which the potassium direction and treatment are opposite, so misdiagnosis can lead to harmful management. Overlooking myotonia or paramyotonia congenita overlap. Failing to exclude secondary causes of hyperkalaemia before attributing paralysis to the primary channelopathy. Provocative potassium loading carrying a risk of dangerous hyperkalaemia and arrhythmia. Attributing interictal proximal weakness to poor effort rather than an evolving fixed myopathy. Hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis results from gain-of-function mutations in the SCN4A gene encoding the skeletal muscle voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.4. The mutations impair fast inactivation of the channel, producing a persistent inward sodium current that keeps the sarcolemma abnormally depolarised. Sustained depolarisation drives normal sodium channels into an inactivated state, rendering the membrane inexcitable so that action potentials can no longer be generated and the fibre becomes transiently paralysed. A rise in extracellular potassium further depolarises the membrane and precipitates or worsens attacks, whereas manoeuvres that lower potassium or repolarise the membrane tend to abort them. Acute attacks tend to become less frequent with age and life expectancy is normal, but a proportion of patients develop a slowly progressive fixed proximal myopathy over the long term. Trigger avoidance and prophylactic therapy substantially reduce attack frequency.

values <8 suggest tubular resistance/low aldosterone (interpret cautiously) (p.403) Plasma renin activity and aldosterone, with 9-alpha-fludrocortisone response, to characterise hypoaldosteronism (p.403) Pseudohyperkalaemia (factitious hyperkalaemia) — artefactual K+ release during/after venepuncture from fist clenching, marked thrombocytosis/leukocytosis/erythrocytosis with in vitro efflux, cold storage of the sample, or hereditary red-cell membrane transport defects (e.g. SLC4A1/AE1 mutations) (p.401-402) Acute anxiety at venepuncture with respiratory alkalosis causing redistributive (true but transient) hyperkalaemia (p.402) Hyperkalaemia (plasma K+ ≥5.5 mM) occurs in up to 10% of hospitalised patients; severe hyperkalaemia (>6.0 mM) in ~1% and carries significantly increased mortality (p.401). Reduced renal K+ excretion is the single most common underlying cause; transcellular shift and reduced tissue uptake act mainly as acute contributors (p.401). Excess dietary intake alone is a rare cause because the kidney can normally upregulate secretion — but small intake increments can provoke severe hyperkalaemia in susceptible patients (e.g. diabetics with hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism and CKD); occult sources include K+-containing salt substitutes (p.401-402). The ECG changes of hyperkalaemia are notoriously INSENSITIVE, particularly in CKD/ESRD patients — a normal ECG does NOT exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia (p.403). Hyperkalaemia per se impairs renal acid excretion (K+ competes with NH4+ for TALH reabsorption), so it can itself contribute to metabolic acidosis; restoring normokalaemia often corrects this hyperkalaemic acidosis (p.403). Hyperkalaemia can produce a type I Brugada ECG pattern (pseudo-RBBB with coved ST elevation in precordial leads); the hyperkalaemic Brugada sign is distinguished from genetic Brugada syndrome by absent P waves, marked QRS widening and an abnormal QRS axis (p.403). A urine Na+ concentration <20 mM signals that low distal Na+ delivery is limiting K+ excretion, suggesting volume repletion or a loop diuretic may help lower K+ (p.403). Hyperkalaemia is a medical emergency because of its cardiac effects — arrhythmias include sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, slow idioventricular rhythms, VT, VF and asystole (p.402-403). ECG progression as a severity cue: tall peaked T waves (5.5-6.5 mM) -> loss of P waves (6.5-7.5 mM) -> widened QRS (7.0-8.0 mM) -> sine-wave pattern (>8.0 mM), heralding impending VF/asystole (p.403). ECG manifestations mandate urgent treatment; but K+ ≥6.5 mM WITHOUT ECG changes should still be managed aggressively, because ECG findings are an unreliable predictor of cardiac toxicity (p.403-404). Management principle (knowledge): a three-stage sequence — (1) immediately antagonise cardiac effects (IV calcium stabilises the myocardium by raising the action-potential threshold), (2) shift K+ into cells, (3) remove K+ from the body (p.403-404). Secondary hyperkalaemic paralysis — ascending paralysis that can include diaphragmatic paralysis and respiratory failure (p.403). Treating a falsely high K+: failing to exclude pseudohyperkalaemia before intervening (haemolysed sample, fist clenching, extreme thrombo/leuko/erythrocytosis, cold storage) (p.401-402). Relying on a normal/near-normal ECG to exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia — ECG changes are notoriously insensitive, especially in CKD/ESRD (p.403). Forgetting drug and dietary causes: ACEi/ARB/renin inhibitors and mineralocorticoid-receptor blockers (spironolactone, eplerenone, drospirenone) — additive in combination; K+-sparing diuretics and the structurally similar antibiotics trimethoprim and pentamidine block ENaC; NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, calcineurin inhibitors and beta-blockers cause hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism; heparin/LMWH inhibit aldosterone synthesis (p.402). Drugs blocking the RAA axis also blunt the adrenal aldosterone response to a rising K+, compounding the effect (p.402). Anion-gap acidoses (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis) do NOT shift K+ out by the acidosis mechanism, unlike non-anion-gap and respiratory acidoses — so attributing hyperkalaemia to acidosis in these settings can mislead (p.402). Plasma K+ rises when efflux of intracellular K+ outpaces clearance or when renal excretion falls. Acidaemia drives K+ out of cells via effective K+-H+ exchange to buffer extracellular pH — but this shift is seen mainly with non-anion-gap (mineral) and respiratory acidoses; it does NOT occur with the organic anion-gap acidoses (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis). Hyperosmolality (mannitol, hypertonic saline, IVIG, hypertonic glucose without insulin in diabetics) shifts K+ out by solvent drag. Cationic amino acids (lysine, arginine, epsilon-aminocaproic acid) and Na+/K+-ATPase inhibitors (digoxin and related cardiac glycosides from yellow oleander, foxglove, cane-toad bufadienolide; fluoride) cause efflux. Succinylcholine depolarises muscle via upregulated acetylcholine receptors (contraindicated after burns, neuromuscular injury, disuse atrophy, prolonged immobilisation). Impaired excretion arises from blockade of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, reduced distal Na+/flow delivery, hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism, mineralocorticoid resistance, and reduced functioning nephron mass. Cardiotoxicity reflects altered cardiac membrane excitability: mild rises alter repolarisation (T-wave changes), higher levels depress intracardiac conduction (PR/QRS prolongation, P-wave loss, QRS widening, sine wave). (p.401-403) Severe hyperkalaemia (>6.0 mM) is associated with a significantly increased risk of mortality. Cardiac toxicity can progress rapidly to fatal arrhythmia, but is reversible with prompt treatment; hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis frequently corrects once normokalaemia is restored. (p.401, p.403) By plasma K+: hyperkalaemia ≥5.5 mM; severe >6.0 mM (markedly increased mortality). ECG-correlated severity bands: peaked T waves 5.5-6.5 mM; loss of P waves 6.5-7.5 mM; widened QRS 7.0-8.0 mM; sine-wave pattern >8.0 mM. Emergency treatment is triggered by any ECG change or K+ ≥6.5 mM. (p.401, p.403-404)

attacks Hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis is caused by gain-of-function mutations in SCN4A, the gene for the alpha subunit of the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.4. The mutant channels fail to inactivate completely, producing a persistent inward sodium current that keeps the sarcolemma partially depolarised. A modest rise in extracellular potassium further depolarises the membrane, and when depolarisation is sufficient the sodium channels become inactivated and the fibre inexcitable, causing flaccid paralysis. When depolarisation is milder it instead produces repetitive firing experienced as myotonia, explaining the frequent overlap of weakness and stiffness in affected individuals. Attacks tend to be brief and frequent in childhood and often become milder in adult life, and most patients have a normal life expectancy, although some develop a slowly progressive fixed proximal myopathy over time.

SLC30A10 encodes a manganese efflux transporter that exports manganese from hepatocytes into bile and from enterocytes and neurons; its loss causes manganese to accumulate in the liver and brain. SLC39A14 encodes an importer required for hepatic manganese uptake and biliary clearance; its loss paradoxically raises circulating manganese and drives brain deposition while sparing the liver. Excess manganese is neurotoxic to the basal ganglia, producing extrapyramidal features that resemble manganese-induced parkinsonism, and it deposits as a paramagnetic species giving the characteristic T1 basal-ganglia signal. Manganese also upregulates erythropoietin, explaining the polycythaemia, and interacts with iron handling, producing a low-ferritin state. Outcome depends on early diagnosis; chelation and manganese restriction can stabilise or improve neurological and hepatic disease, but delayed treatment risks fixed dystonia and, in SLC30A10 disease, progressive cirrhosis.

homocystinuria rather than isolated hypermethioninaemia Very high sustained methionine warranting prompt clarification of the cause Assuming all isolated hypermethioninaemia is benign and missing AHCY or adenosine kinase deficiency Failing to measure homocysteine and so overlooking classical homocystinuria Not checking S-adenosylmethionine and S-adenosylhomocysteine, which are needed to separate the genetic causes Attributing the finding to diet or liver disease without excluding an inborn error Over-restricting methionine in a benign case, risking essential amino acid deficiency Methionine sits at the head of the transmethylation pathway, being activated to S-adenosylmethionine before serving as the universal methyl donor and then entering the transsulfuration and remethylation cycles. Plasma methionine rises whenever its onward metabolism is impeded or its supply is excessive. Reduced conversion to S-adenosylmethionine, as in MAT I/III deficiency, or a block further along the methylation cycle, as in AHCY, GNMT or adenosine kinase deficiency, causes methionine to accumulate; secondary elevations reflect impaired hepatic handling or high intake. The clinical significance therefore depends entirely on the underlying mechanism, ranging from a harmless finding to a marker of treatable neurological or hepatic disease. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; isolated MAT I/III or GNMT deficiency is generally benign, whereas AHCY and adenosine kinase deficiency and untreated secondary causes carry more serious implications that improve with appropriate treatment.

Extrarenal water loss from gastrointestinal or insensible routes Inadequate water intake in dependent patients Sodium overload from hypertonic fluids or salt ingestion Serum sodium and plasma osmolality with assessment of volume status Urine osmolality and urine volume to characterise water handling Water deprivation testing and response to desmopressin when diabetes insipidus is suspected Hypernatraemia reflects a deficit of water relative to sodium and almost always signifies a problem with water intake or excessive water loss rather than sodium excess Because thirst is a powerful defence, sustained hypernatraemia usually occurs in those who cannot access or request water, such as infants, the elderly, and patients with impaired consciousness The main causes are pure or hypotonic water loss (renal or extrarenal), including diabetes insipidus, and less commonly a gain of sodium Assessment of urine osmolality helps localise the problem: dilute urine in the face of hypernatraemia points to a renal concentrating defect such as diabetes insipidus Clinical features are predominantly neurological, ranging from lethargy and irritability to seizures and coma, reflecting brain cell shrinkage Management principles are to restore water gradually, address ongoing losses, and treat the underlying cause, while calculating and replacing the water deficit Correction of chronic hypernatraemia must be slow because the brain accumulates osmoles to adapt, and rapid rehydration risks cerebral oedema Diabetes insipidus is distinguished into central and nephrogenic forms by the response to desmopressin, which guides treatment Depressed consciousness, seizures, or coma indicating severe hypernatraemia Rapidly rising sodium or profound water deficit Signs of severe volume depletion with haemodynamic compromise Overly rapid correction risking cerebral oedema Correcting chronic hypernatraemia too rapidly and causing cerebral oedema Failing to account for ongoing water losses when calculating replacement Overlooking diabetes insipidus in a patient passing large volumes of dilute urine Assuming hypernatraemia means too much sodium rather than too little water Hypernatraemia results from a relative water deficit that raises plasma osmolality. Normally, a rise in osmolality stimulates thirst and antidiuretic hormone release, restoring water balance; hypernatraemia therefore develops when water is unavailable or the thirst mechanism is impaired, or when water losses overwhelm intake. Losses may be extrarenal (through the gut, skin, or lungs) or renal, the latter including osmotic diuresis and the failure to concentrate urine in diabetes insipidus. Central diabetes insipidus reflects deficient antidiuretic hormone production, whereas the nephrogenic form reflects renal resistance to the hormone. Less commonly, administration or ingestion of excess sodium produces hypernatraemia with volume expansion. The rise in extracellular osmolality draws water out of cells; shrinkage of brain cells produces the neurological manifestations, and the brain's compensatory accumulation of intracellular solutes over time is what makes rapid correction hazardous. Outcome depends heavily on the severity, rate of onset, and underlying condition. Acute severe hypernatraemia and hypernatraemia in critically ill or elderly patients carry significant mortality, largely reflecting the underlying illness. With appropriate identification of the cause and carefully paced water replacement, milder cases generally recover fully, while cautious correction avoids the danger of cerebral oedema.

ataxia or cognitive decline Catabolic triggers such as infection, fasting or the postpartum period precipitating crisis Confusing the hyperornithinaemia with gyrate atrophy and inappropriately focusing on the retina Attributing hepatic dysfunction and coagulopathy to primary liver disease rather than the metabolic disorder Missing the diagnosis in adults with an insidious neurological or psychiatric presentation Failing to look for homocitrulline, the metabolite that anchors the diagnostic triad Ornithine synthesised in the cytosol must be imported into the mitochondrion by the Primary hyperoxaluria type 2 — PH2, primary hyperoxaluria type II, glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase deficiency, GRHPR deficiency, L-glyceric aciduria, GRHPR Primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (AGXT deficiency) Primary hyperoxaluria type 3 (HOGA1 deficiency) Enteric (secondary) hyperoxaluria from fat malabsorption or bariatric surgery Dietary hyperoxaluria from excessive oxalate intake Idiopathic calcium oxalate stone disease Other monogenic stone disorders such as Dent disease and cystinuria Quantitative 24-hour urinary oxalate and glycerate excretion (corrected for surface area in children) Plasma oxalate measurement once glomerular filtration is impaired Renal tract ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis and calculi GRHPR gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis Stone composition analysis where calculi are available Serial estimation of glomerular filtration rate to monitor renal decline Autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase (GRHPR), an enzyme with wide tissue distribution rather than being confined to the liver Biochemical hallmark is raised urinary oxalate accompanied by increased L-glycerate (L-glyceric aciduria), which distinguishes it from the glycolate excess of type 1 and the 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate of type 3 Presents with recurrent calcium oxalate urolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis, often from childhood, though the course is generally milder than type 1 Progression to chronic kidney disease and systemic oxalosis does occur but tends to be slower and less frequent than in type 1 Pyridoxine responsiveness, which benefits a subset of type 1, is not a feature of type 2 Diagnosis rests on quantitative urinary oxalate and glycerate together with GRHPR gene sequencing; historical leucocyte enzyme assay is rarely needed now Management is generic and supportive: vigorous hyperhydration, urinary crystallisation inhibitors such as citrate/alkali, and moderation of dietary oxalate RNA-interference approaches directed at hepatic oxalate production are under evaluation across the primary hyperoxalurias Rapidly falling glomerular filtration rate signalling risk of systemic oxalosis Extrarenal oxalate deposition affecting retina, bone, myocardium or vessels Infantile presentation with early nephrocalcinosis and renal impairment Recurrent obstructing calculi precipitating acute kidney injury Missing the diagnosis by measuring urinary oxalate without also assaying glycerate Assuming type 2 is always benign and omitting long-term renal surveillance Trialling pyridoxine as if the patient had type 1 Allowing dehydration during intercurrent illness, which accelerates crystal formation Loss of glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase activity blocks the conversion of glyoxylate to glycolate and of hydroxypyruvate to D-glycerate. Glyoxylate is instead oxidised by lactate dehydrogenase to oxalate, while hydroxypyruvate is reduced to L-glycerate, producing the characteristic L-glyceric aciduria. Because oxalate cannot be metabolised further and is poorly soluble, calcium oxalate crystals precipitate in the urinary tract, causing stones and nephrocalcinosis. As renal function declines and plasma oxalate rises, calcium oxalate can deposit in bone, retina, heart, vessels and other tissues, producing systemic oxalosis. Renal survival is generally better than in type 1, and many patients maintain function into adulthood, but a proportion progress to kidney failure and systemic oxalosis, so lifelong monitoring is warranted.

there is no enzyme replacement Hepatic lactate dehydrogenase-directed RNA-interference therapy is being studied across the primary hyperoxaluria subtypes Neonatal or early infantile presentation with dense nephrocalcinosis Unexpected decline in glomerular filtration rate despite the usually benign course Recurrent obstructing calculi causing acute kidney injury Evidence of systemic oxalate deposition Overlooking the diagnosis because standard metabolic screens may not report the specific hydroxyglutarate metabolites Assuming the benign reputation guarantees a benign outcome in every patient Attributing recurrent paediatric stones to idiopathic disease without genetic testing Neglecting hydration advice during febrile illness or reduced intake HOGA1 normally cleaves 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate, an intermediate of hydroxyproline catabolism, within the mitochondrion. Its deficiency causes accumulation of 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate and its derivative 2,4-dihydroxyglutarate; the accumulated substrate is thought to be diverted to glyoxylate and then oxidised to oxalate, and loss of a normal inhibitory influence on glyoxylate handling may contribute further. The resulting oxalate overproduction promotes calcium oxalate crystallisation in the urinary tract, causing stones and, less commonly than in the other types, nephrocalcinosis and renal impairment. Overall the most favourable of the primary hyperoxalurias, with preserved renal function in the majority and stone activity that often lessens over time, though occasional progression means continued monitoring is prudent.

disease and anorectal or other structural anomalies when suggested Molecular testing of PIGV and other GPI-anchor pathway genes A congenital disorder of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor biosynthesis, most often from PIGV mutations, with other PIG/PGAP genes implicated Cardinal features are persistently raised serum alkaline phosphatase (hyperphosphatasia), intellectual disability, and seizures The paradoxical hyperphosphatasia arises because alkaline phosphatase, a GPI-anchored enzyme, is shed into the circulation when its anchor is defective Additional features include distinctive facial dysmorphism, brachytelephalangy (short distal phalanges with hypoplastic nails), and variable neurological impairment Some patients have Hirschsprung disease, anorectal or other structural anomalies as part of the phenotypic spectrum The persistently elevated alkaline phosphatase is the biochemical clue that prompts consideration of a GPI-anchor defect rather than bone or liver disease Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, targeting seizures, developmental support, and associated anomalies, as no specific corrective therapy exists Poorly controlled or evolving epilepsy Feeding difficulty or bowel obstruction suggesting Hirschsprung disease Significant developmental regression Structural cardiac or renal anomalies requiring intervention Chasing bone or liver disease to explain the raised alkaline phosphatase and missing the GPI-anchor defect Overlooking the diagnostic significance of persistent hyperphosphatasia in a child with developmental delay and seizures Missing associated Hirschsprung disease or anorectal anomalies Assuming the elevated alkaline phosphatase reflects increased bone turnover requiring treatment The GPI anchor tethers numerous proteins to the outer cell membrane. PIGV and related genes encode enzymes in the GPI biosynthetic pathway; loss-of-function mutations impair anchor assembly, so GPI-anchored proteins are either misprocessed or released rather than retained at the cell surface. Alkaline phosphatase is a GPI-anchored ectoenzyme, so a defective anchor causes it to be secreted into plasma, producing the characteristic hyperphosphatasia. Disruption of other GPI-anchored proteins essential for neuronal function underlies the intellectual disability and seizures, while developmental roles of affected proteins explain the dysmorphism, digital anomalies, and structural malformations. The disorder therefore links a striking laboratory finding to a neurodevelopmental syndrome through a shared membrane-anchoring defect. Prognosis is determined by the severity of neurological impairment and associated malformations; many affected individuals have lifelong intellectual disability and epilepsy, and management remains supportive since no disease-modifying therapy is established.
