Symptomatic hyponatraemia / SIADH — Serum & urine osmolality, urine Na⁺ Volume status assessment Correct slowly (osmotic demyelination risk) Hypovolaemic: GI losses (vomiting, diarrhoea, tube drainage) and insensible loss (sweating, burns) with inadequate replacement — urine Na+ typically <20 mM (p.390). Hypovolaemic renal: thiazide diuretics, mineralocorticoid/aldosterone deficiency (primary adrenal insufficiency, hypoaldosteronism), salt-losing nephropathies (reflux nephropathy, interstitial nephropathies, post-obstructive uropathy, medullary cystic disease, recovery phase of ATN) — urine Na+ typically >20 mM (p.390-391). Osmotic/solute-driven hypovolaemic: glycosuria, ketonuria (starvation, diabetic or alcoholic ketoacidosis), bicarbonaturia (RTA, metabolic alkalosis) (p.391). Cerebral salt wasting (subarachnoid haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, craniotomy, encephalitis, meningitis) (p.391). Hypervolaemic: congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, and acute or chronic renal failure (the latter uniquely with raised urine Na+) (p.391). Euvolaemic: SIAD, moderate-to-severe hypothyroidism, secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary disease (glucocorticoid deficiency) (p.391). Low solute intake: beer potomania (alcoholics whose sole nutrient is beer) and nutrient-restricted/extreme vegetarian diets — urine osmolality <100-200 mOsm/kg, urine Na+ <10-20 mM (p.391-392). SIAD causes: malignancy (especially small-cell lung carcinoma — 75% of malignancy-associated SIAD; ~10% present with Na+ <130 mM), pulmonary disease (pneumonia, TB, abscess, pleural effusion), CNS disease (tumour, subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis, encephalitis, head trauma, hydrocephalus), drugs, and transient causes (pain, nausea, stress, endurance exercise, general anaesthesia) (p.391-392). Pseudohyponatraemia — hyponatraemia coexisting with normal/increased plasma tonicity, from extreme hyperlipidaemia or hyperproteinaemia (p.393). Hyperglycaemia-related ('true') hyponatraemia — plasma Na+ falls ~1.6-2.4 mM per 100 mg/dL rise in glucose; resolves after correcting hyperglycaemia (p.393). Serum osmolality, converted to effective osmolality/tonicity by subtracting urea (in mg/dL divided by 2.8) — true hyponatraemia has effective osmolality <275 mOsm/kg; this also excludes pseudohyponatraemia (p.393). Serum glucose — to identify and correct hyperglycaemic (translocational) hyponatraemia (p.393). Serum uric acid — low (<4 mg/dL) in SIAD physiology, often high in volume depletion (p.393). Serum K+, BUN/creatinine — hyperkalaemia suggests adrenal insufficiency/hypoaldosteronism; raised urea/creatinine suggests renal cause (p.393). Thyroid, adrenal and pituitary function testing, including a cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test to assess primary adrenal insufficiency, in the appropriate setting (p.393). Urine osmolality — <100 mOsm/kg suggests primary polydipsia; >400 mOsm/kg indicates dominant AVP excess; intermediate values suggest multifactorial physiology (p.393). Urine Na+ — <20-30 mM suggests hypovolaemia; >30 mM suggests SIAD, but values overlap, especially in the elderly (p.393). Urine K+ — to calculate the urine-to-plasma electrolyte ratio, useful for predicting response to fluid restriction (p.393). Demonstration that plasma Na+ corrects after isotonic saline hydration is the diagnostic gold standard for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia (p.393). Imaging — chest CT in smokers/high-risk patients (screening CXR can miss small-cell lung carcinoma); CNS imaging where a central cause is suspected (p.393). Pseudohyponatraemia from severe hyperlipidaemia/hyperproteinaemia: measured Na+ is low but plasma tonicity is normal or high; exclude by measuring serum osmolality (p.393). Hyperglycaemic hyponatraemia: a translocational, true hyponatraemia driven by glucose-induced water efflux that corrects once glucose is lowered (p.393). Hyponatraemia (plasma Na+ <135 mM) is very common, affecting up to ~22% of hospitalised patients (p.390). The absolute plasma Na+ concentration says nothing about a patient's volume status, which must be assessed separately for both diagnosis and management (p.390). Hyponatraemia is almost always driven by excess circulating AVP and/or increased renal sensitivity to AVP combined with free-water intake; the main exception is hyponatraemia from low solute intake (p.390). Diagnostically subdivide by ECF volume into hypovolaemic, euvolaemic, and hypervolaemic groups based on clinical history and volume status (p.390). In hypovolaemic patients, a urine Na+ <20 mM predicts a brisk rise in plasma Na+ with isotonic saline, because AVP falls and a water diuresis ensues (p.391). Serum uric acid helps discriminate: SIAD is typically associated with low uric acid (<4 mg/dL), whereas hypovolaemic hyponatraemia is often hyperuricaemic (p.391, p.393). Thiazides can mimic SIAD and do not impair urinary concentrating ability, so AVP retains full effect; defer diagnosing SIAD until 1-2 weeks after stopping the thiazide (p.391, p.393). The 48-hour mark distinguishes acute from chronic hyponatraemia and is decisive for how aggressively/cautiously sodium may be corrected (p.392). Cerebral salt wasting (a rare hypovolaemic cause linked to intracranial disease) responds to aggressive salt-and-water repletion, so distinguishing it from SIAD is critical because their management diverges (p.391). Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia is a medical emergency: nausea/headache/vomiting can rapidly progress to seizures, brainstem herniation, coma and death (p.392). Acute hyponatraemia can cause normocapnoeic or hypercapnoeic respiratory failure, typically from non-cardiogenic 'neurogenic' pulmonary oedema with normal wedge pressure; resulting hypoxia amplifies neurological injury (p.392). Premenopausal women are far more likely than men to develop encephalopathy and severe neurological sequelae (p.392). Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia (>8-10 mM in 24 h or >18 mM in 48 h) risks osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), classically central pontine myelinolysis — presenting days later with para-/quadriparesis, dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, 'locked-in' syndrome, or reduced consciousness (p.393). ODS can occur even with appropriately slow correction in high-risk patients: alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, and liver transplantation (p.393). Plasma Na+ <125 mM is the threshold at which chronic hyponatraemia commonly becomes overtly symptomatic (nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures) (p.392). Iatrogenic settings for acute hyponatraemia: postoperative premenopausal women given hypotonic fluids, glycine irrigation (TURP/uterine surgery), colonoscopy prep, recent thiazide initiation (Table 56-2, p.392). MDMA ('Ecstasy'/'Molly') causes potent thirst and AVP induction leading to severe acute hyponatraemia; exercise-associated (endurance/marathon) hyponatraemia is another acute setting (p.392). Hypovolaemic patients may appear clinically euvolaemic, with only a low urine Na+ to reveal the cause (p.390). Hyponatraemia is frequently multifactorial, especially when severe — evaluate every source of excess AVP (volume status, drugs, nausea, pain) rather than settling on one (p.393). Failing to exclude pseudohyponatraemia/hyperglycaemia before correcting; check serum osmolality and glucose first (p.393). The 93%-water assumption used by ion-sensitive electrodes makes plasma Na+ falsely low in extreme hyperlipidaemia/hyperproteinaemia (p.393). Urine Na+ values overlap substantially between SIAD and hypovolaemia (particularly in the elderly); the saline-challenge response is the definitive discriminator (p.393). Diagnosing SIAD in a patient on thiazides — defer the SIAD label until 1-2 weeks after stopping the drug (p.393). Distinguishing cerebral salt wasting from SIAD is critical because management differs (salt repletion vs fluid restriction) (p.391). Hyponatraemia reflects a relative excess of body water to sodium, almost always from increased circulating AVP (or heightened renal AVP sensitivity) together with free-water intake. Volume status modulates AVP release: hypovolaemia raises AVP at any given osmolality, and 'hypervolaemic' arterial underfilling (heart failure, cirrhosis) triggers neurohumoral activation that likewise elevates AVP, causing water retention. In hypovolaemia, AVP-mediated V2-receptor water reabsorption plus free-water intake lowers Na+. In hypervolaemic oedematous states (CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), total-body Na+ rises but water rises proportionally more; reduced arterial filling drives the AVP response. In euvolaemic hyponatraemia, SIAD is the commonest cause: free-water intake persists at osmolalities below the normal thirst threshold, with patients subclinically volume-expanded (so-called 'AVP escape' limits distal tubular transport, preserving a modestly hypervolaemic steady state). Four AVP-secretion patterns occur in SIAD: erratic unregulated secretion (~1/3 of patients), failure to suppress at low osmolality, a 'reset osmostat', and a subset with undetectable AVP (gain-of-function V2-receptor mutations causing 'nephrogenic' SIAD). At the brain level, hyponatraemia causes water to move down the osmotic gradient from hypotonic ECF into cells, producing cellular swelling and cerebral oedema within the rigid skull; acute encephalopathy results when volume-regulatory mechanisms (CSF shunting, efflux of Na+/K+/Cl-) are overwhelmed. In chronic hyponatraemia, brain cells extrude organic osmolytes (creatine, betaine, glutamate, myoinositol, taurine), a process largely complete within 48 h, which mitigates but does not abolish symptoms (p.390-392). Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia carries high risk of severe neurological injury and death; encephalopathy is more severe in premenopausal women. The degree of hyponatraemia is an important prognostic indicator in hypervolaemic states, reflecting the intensity of neurohumoral activation. Chronic hyponatraemia, even when judged 'asymptomatic', is associated with subtle gait and cognitive deficits (reversible with correction), increased risk of falls, and an increased fracture risk due to neurological dysfunction and reduced bone density — so safe correction is warranted even without overt symptoms. Osmotic demyelination from overcorrection can produce permanent disabling neurological deficits (p.392-393). By volume status: hypovolaemic (total body water down, total body Na+ down more), euvolaemic/no oedema (total body water up, Na+ near-normal), and hypervolaemic (total body water up markedly, Na+ up) — Fig. 56-5, p.391. By chronicity: acute hyponatraemia is <48 h (osmolyte extrusion incomplete, higher cerebral-oedema risk) and chronic is >48 h (osmolytes largely extruded, lower acute symptom risk but higher ODS risk on correction), p.392. By tonicity: true hypotonic hyponatraemia has effective osmolality <275 mOsm/kg, distinct from pseudohyponatraemia (normal/high tonicity) and hyperglycaemic translocational hyponatraemia, p.393. Symptomatic threshold for chronic disease is generally plasma Na+ <125 mM (p.392). SIAD diagnostic features include euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia, inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osmolality typically >400 mOsm/kg / not maximally dilute), urine Na+ >30 mM, low serum uric acid (<4 mg/dL), and absence of thyroid/adrenal dysfunction, diuretics, hypovolaemia or hypervolaemia (p.391, p.393).

excess of water compared with sodium, usually driven by impaired water excretion The diagnostic approach begins by confirming true hypotonic hyponatraemia, then assessing volume status and measuring cause treated wherever possible Correction must be gradual in chronic hyponatraemia because overly rapid rises in sodium risk osmotic demyelination, whereas acute symptomatic hyponatraemia with severe neurological signs warrants prompt but controlled correction with hypertonic saline Exclude pseudohyponatraemia and hyperglycaemia-related dilution before attributing a low sodium to a water-handling disorder Seizures, marked confusion, or reduced consciousness indicating severe or acute hyponatraemia Rapid onset of symptoms suggesting acute cerebral oedema Signs of raised intracranial pressure Overly rapid correction risking osmotic demyelination Correcting chronic hyponatraemia too quickly and precipitating osmotic demyelination Diagnosing SIADH without excluding hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, and volume depletion Giving isotonic saline in SIADH, which can paradoxically worsen the sodium Overlooking a drug or occult malignancy as the driver of persistent SIADH Hyponatraemia develops when water intake exceeds the kidney's ability to excrete free water, diluting plasma sodium. Antidiuretic hormone is central: when its release is appropriate (as in volume depletion or reduced effective circulating volume in heart failure and cirrhosis) or inappropriate (as in SIADH), water is retained and urine remains concentrated. In SIADH, ADH is secreted or acts independently of osmotic and volume signals, so the kidney retains water despite plasma hypotonicity; patients are clinically euvolaemic because the retained water distributes across body compartments and mild volume expansion promotes natriuresis. The fall in plasma osmolality drives water into brain cells, and the resulting cerebral oedema accounts for the neurological features. In chronic hyponatraemia the brain adapts by extruding solutes, which is why rapid correction can dehydrate neurons and cause osmotic demyelination. Mild chronic hyponatraemia is often well tolerated but is associated with falls, cognitive impairment, and worse outcomes in the underlying illness. Acute severe hyponatraemia can be life-threatening from cerebral oedema, while inappropriately rapid correction can cause devastating osmotic demyelination. With cause-directed treatment and appropriately paced correction most patients recover, and SIADH prognosis largely follows that of its underlying cause.

hypophosphataemic rickets — phosphopenic rickets, vitamin D-resistant rickets nutritional vitamin D-deficiency rickets vitamin D-dependent rickets types 1 and 2 Fanconi syndrome and renal tubular acidosis tumour-induced osteomalacia (acquired) Dent disease chronic kidney disease with renal osteodystrophy hypophosphatasia serum phosphate, calcium, alkaline phosphatase and PTH 25-hydroxy and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D urinary phosphate with tubular reabsorption of phosphate (TmP/GFR) urine calcium-to-creatinine ratio to identify HHRH intact FGF23 wrist and knee radiographs for cupping, fraying and widened physes genetic panel (PHEX, FGF23, DMP1, ENPP1, SLC34A3) and renal ultrasound Hypophosphataemic rickets is a group of disorders in which chronic hypophosphataemia from renal phosphate wasting impairs growth-plate and bone mineralisation, causing rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults. Most forms are FGF23-mediated: X-linked (PHEX, the commonest), autosomal dominant (FGF23) and autosomal recessive (DMP1, ENPP1); the main non-FGF23 form is hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH, SLC34A3). The hallmark biochemistry is low serum phosphate, normal calcium, normal or low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and raised alkaline phosphatase, with PTH normal or only mildly raised, contrasting with the high PTH of calcipenic rickets. Children show leg bowing, genu varum or valgum, short stature, delayed walking, a rachitic rosary, craniotabes and dental abscesses, without hypocalcaemic features. The key distinction from nutritional rickets is normal calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D with hypophosphataemia and phosphaturia, and a lack of response to standard vitamin D ('vitamin D-resistant'). HHRH is set apart by appropriately raised 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and hypercalciuria and responds to phosphate alone, since active vitamin D can worsen hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis. FGF23-mediated forms are treated with oral phosphate plus active vitamin D, or increasingly with burosumab for the X-linked type. Early diagnosis and sustained treatment optimise linear growth and reduce deformity, though orthopaedic correction may be needed for residual bowing. nephrocalcinosis or renal impairment progressive skeletal deformity craniosynostosis with raised intracranial pressure recurrent dental abscesses failure to thrive or severe growth failure labelling as nutritional rickets and treating with plain vitamin D alone missing hypercalciuria in HHRH and worsening it with calcitriol overlooking acquired causes such as tumour-induced osteomalacia in older children and adults treatment-related nephrocalcinosis and hyperparathyroidism not measuring urinary phosphate to confirm renal wasting Normal mineralisation of the growth plate and osteoid depends on an adequate phosphate supply. In these disorders renal phosphate wasting produces chronic hypophosphataemia and defective mineralisation. In the FGF23-mediated forms, excess or overactive FGF23 downregulates proximal tubular sodium-phosphate cotransporters and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase, so calcitriol fails to rise appropriately. In HHRH, a defect in the NaPi-IIc cotransporter (SLC34A3) causes primary phosphate wasting with a compensatory, appropriate rise in calcitriol, driving intestinal calcium absorption, hypercalciuria and suppressed PTH. The final common consequence is accumulation of unmineralised osteoid at the growth plate (rickets) and in mature bone (osteomalacia). With early and sustained treatment growth and deformity improve, but some residual short stature and orthopaedic problems commonly persist into adulthood.

hypercalcaemia and nephrocalcinosis Dental assessment documenting premature loss of primary teeth Caused by mutations in ALPL encoding tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, with severe forms not be dismissed as unimportant Clinical severity spans a wide spectrum from lethal perinatal disease with almost unmineralised bone to mild adult disease with fractures and early tooth loss Premature and craniosynostosis Enzyme replacement therapy (asfotase alfa) has transformed outcomes for severe paediatric disease Bisphosphonates and other antiresorptives are generally avoided because they are pyrophosphate analogues and may worsen the condition Perinatal or infantile respiratory failure from an unmineralised, poorly compliant chest Vitamin B6-responsive seizures in an infant with a low alkaline phosphatase Symptomatic hypercalcaemia with nephrocalcinosis and renal impairment Craniosynostosis with raised intracranial pressure in infantile disease Ignoring a low alkaline phosphatase as a laboratory artefact rather than a diagnostic clue Giving bisphosphonates, which can aggravate the mineralisation defect Supplementing with high-dose vitamin D reflexively, risking worsening hypercalcaemia Misclassifying severe perinatal disease as osteogenesis imperfecta Hypophosphatasia results from deficient activity of tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, an enzyme that normally hydrolyses inorganic pyrophosphate at the mineralising surface of bone and teeth. Because inorganic pyrophosphate is a potent inhibitor of hydroxyapatite crystal formation, its accumulation blocks normal mineralisation, producing rickets and osteomalacia despite adequate calcium and phosphate. Accumulation of pyridoxal-5-phosphate impairs vitamin B6 delivery to the brain and can cause seizures in severe forms, while phosphoethanolamine accumulates and is excreted in the urine. The perinatal and infantile forms were historically often lethal, but enzyme replacement therapy has markedly improved survival and skeletal outcome; milder childhood and adult forms have a good prognosis with attention to fractures, dental health and pain.

Hypopituitarism — panhypopituitarism, Sheehan syndrome Pituitary adenoma (mass on MRI may be indistinguishable from lymphocytic hypophysitis) Craniopharyngioma, Rathke's cyst, meningioma, germinoma, glioma, ependymoma Pituitary metastases (breast, lung, colon) and lymphoma/leukemia Empty sella syndrome Primary (target-organ) endocrine failure as opposed to central deficiency Tuberculosis involving the pituitary/hypothalamus Fungal infection (histoplasmosis) and opportunistic fungal infection in AIDS Parasitic infection (toxoplasmosis) Pneumocystis jirovecii Tertiary syphilis Low target-organ hormone with low or inappropriately normal trophic hormone (e.g., low free thyroxine with low/inappropriately normal TSH = secondary hypothyroidism; low testosterone without elevated gonadotropins = hypogonadotropic hypogonadism) Dynamic/provocative testing of pituitary reserve GH reserve: insulin-induced hypoglycemia, arginine, glucagon, l-dopa, GHRH, or macimorelin; AGHD defined by peak GH response to hypoglycemia <3 ug/L ACTH/cortisol reserve: most reliably assessed during insulin-induced hypoglycemia; CRH stimulation and cosyntropin (synthetic ACTH) testing also used Pituitary MRI or CT to identify mass, hemorrhage, stalk deviation, or empty sella; age-matched IGF-1 as an index of GH therapeutic response Lymphocytic and granulomatous hypophysitis Sarcoidosis Hemochromatosis Histiocytosis X (Langerhans cell histiocytosis) Amyloidosis Checkpoint-inhibitor immunotherapy hypophysitis Deficient production of one or more anterior pituitary trophic hormones produces the clinical features of hypopituitarism; most adult cases are acquired (Harrison 22e p.2992). With pituitary compression or destruction, trophic hormone failure usually occurs sequentially: GH first, then FSH, LH, TSH, and ACTH last; in children growth retardation is often the presenting feature, in adults hypogonadism is the earliest symptom (Harrison 22e p.2992). Clinical manifestations depend on which hormones are lost and the degree of deficiency: GH deficiency causes growth disorders in children and abnormal body composition in adults; gonadotropin deficiency causes menstrual disorders/infertility/loss of secondary sexual characteristics; TSH deficiency causes hypothyroidism; ACTH deficiency causes secondary adrenal insufficiency; PRL deficiency causes failure of lactation (Harrison 22e p.2996). Secondary adrenal insufficiency from ACTH deficiency causes hypocortisolism with relative preservation of mineralocorticoid production (unlike primary adrenal failure) (Harrison 22e p.2996). Pituitary apoplexy is an endocrine emergency: acute intrapituitary hemorrhage/infarction presenting with severe headache, meningeal signs, bilateral visual changes, ophthalmoplegia, and in severe cases cardiovascular collapse and loss of consciousness (Harrison 22e p.2993). Lymphocytic hypophysitis occurs most often in postpartum women, presents with hyperprolactinemia and an MRI mass resembling an adenoma, and may be transient or permanent; it should be considered before unnecessary surgery in a postpartum woman with a new pituitary mass (Harrison 22e p.2993). Up to 20% of patients receiving CTLA-4 inhibitor immunotherapy (e.g., ipilimumab) develop hypophysitis; PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) can also cause it, sometimes with delayed presentation (Harrison 22e p.2993). Patients on glucocorticoid replacement require careful dose escalation (stress dosing) during acute illness, dental procedures, trauma, and hospitalization (Harrison 22e p.2996). Pituitary apoplexy: an endocrine emergency that may cause severe hypoglycemia, hypotension/shock, CNS hemorrhage, and death; severe ophthalmoplegia or progressive visual loss indicates need for urgent surgical decompression Secondary adrenal insufficiency / adrenal crisis: hypocortisolism that can precipitate life-threatening shock, especially during stress, illness, surgery, or trauma Acute severe headache with meningeal signs, bilateral visual changes, or loss of consciousness in a patient with known/suspected pituitary mass Critical sequencing pitfall: in suspected combined deficiency, glucocorticoid replacement must be started BEFORE thyroid hormone, because giving thyroxine first can accelerate cortisol clearance and precipitate an adrenal crisis in a patient with unrecognized secondary adrenal insufficiency (Harrison 22e p.3133). Insulin-induced hypoglycemia testing must be performed cautiously in suspected adrenal insufficiency (enhanced susceptibility to hypoglycemia/hypotension) and is contraindicated in active coronary artery disease or known seizure disorders (Harrison 22e p.2996). Lymphocytic hypophysitis may be radiologically indistinguishable from a pituitary adenoma and should be considered in a postpartum woman with a new pituitary mass before surgery is undertaken (Harrison 22e p.2993). Radiation-induced and brain-injury-related hypopituitarism develops insidiously over 5-15 years (and in 25-40% after brain injury), so long-term periodic endocrine follow-up is required even after apparently successful treatment (Harrison 22e p.2993). Empty sella patients usually have normal pituitary function, but hypopituitarism may develop insidiously (Harrison 22e p.2994). Impaired synthesis or secretion of one or more anterior pituitary trophic hormones (GH, FSH, LH, TSH, ACTH, PRL), and sometimes posterior pituitary AVP. Causes are developmental/genetic (transcription factor mutations such as PROP1, PIT-1, TPIT, midline defects) or, more commonly in adults, acquired from compressive mass effect of tumors or from local pituitary/hypothalamic traumatic, autoimmune, inflammatory, infiltrative, or vascular damage. The same processes may impair hypothalamic hormone production with secondary pituitary failure. With progressive compression/destruction, hormone loss is typically sequential (GH > FSH > LH > TSH > ACTH) (Harrison 22e p.2992). Hormone replacement is usually safe and effective at maintaining homeostasis when it mimics physiologic secretion. However, long-standing pituitary damage carries an increased mortality rate, primarily from cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease; adult hypopituitarism is associated with an approximately threefold increase in cardiovascular mortality versus age- and sex-matched controls. Prior head/neck irradiation is an additional determinant of increased mortality, especially from cerebrovascular disease. Lymphocytic hypophysitis may resolve with recovery of pituitary function after glucocorticoid treatment depending on extent of damage; hypopituitarism is common after apoplexy (Harrison 22e p.2996).

Hypoplastic left heart syndrome — HLHS Critical aortic stenosis Interrupted aortic arch Critical coarctation Other duct-dependent systemic circulation lesions Neonatal sepsis or metabolic collapse Antenatal and postnatal echocardiography Assessment of ductal patency and atrial communication Blood gas and lactate for perfusion Pre- and post-ductal saturations Multidisciplinary congenital cardiac evaluation A spectrum of severe underdevelopment of the left heart structures, including the left ventricle, mitral and aortic valves and ascending aorta The systemic circulation is duct-dependent, so infants collapse as the arterial duct closes Presentation is with poor perfusion, shock and acidosis in the first days of life, often with only mild cyanosis initially Survival before repair depends on maintaining ductal patency with prostaglandin and balancing pulmonary and systemic blood flow Management is either staged single-ventricle palliation (Norwood pathway) or transplantation It is one of the most serious forms of congenital heart disease and may be detected antenatally Circulatory collapse as the duct closes Rising lactate and acidosis indicating poor systemic perfusion A restrictive atrial septum causing severe pulmonary congestion Signs of inadequate systemic output despite treatment Mistaking early collapse for sepsis and not starting prostaglandin Over-oxygenating and increasing pulmonary flow at the expense of systemic perfusion Missing a restrictive atrial septum Underestimating the need for early specialist transfer In hypoplastic left heart syndrome the left ventricle cannot support the systemic circulation because of hypoplasia and inflow/outflow obstruction. Systemic perfusion depends on right ventricular output crossing the arterial duct, while pulmonary venous return must cross an atrial communication. As the duct constricts after birth, systemic output falls, producing shock and metabolic acidosis. The parallel circulation makes the balance between pulmonary and systemic flow critical, and excessive pulmonary flow can paradoxically worsen systemic perfusion. Without intervention the condition is fatal; with staged surgical palliation or transplantation many children survive, though with significant long-term morbidity and the need for lifelong specialist care.

evaluate testicular androgen production when a synthetic defect is suspected Pelvic ultrasound to assess internal genital structures in ambiguous presentations A congenital anomaly in which the achieve a normal cosmetic and functional result, usually undertaken in early childhood Isolated distal hypospadias in an otherwise normally virilised boy generally does not require an extensive endocrine workup Proximal hypospadias with unilateral or bilateral cryptorchidism, suggesting a disorder of sex development requiring urgent assessment Any genital ambiguity or a bifid scrotum accompanying the hypospadias Features suggestive of salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia in a virilised infant Impaired urinary stream or difficulty voiding related to meatal position Permitting neonatal circumcision, thereby removing foreskin tissue that is valuable for later repair Failing to evaluate proximal hypospadias with cryptorchidism as a possible disorder of sex development Overlooking congenital adrenal hyperplasia in an infant with atypical genitalia and its salt-wasting risk Missing associated chordee, which must be corrected to achieve a straight, functional penis Subjecting isolated distal hypospadias to an unnecessarily extensive endocrine investigation During male genital development, androgen-driven fusion of the urethral folds progresses from proximal to distal to form the penile urethra and close the ventral shaft. Hypospadias results when this tubularisation is incomplete, leaving the urethral meatus proximal to its normal position and often accompanied by a ventral tethering of tissue (chordee) and a defect in foreskin formation. The defect reflects inadequate or mistimed androgen action, or disturbance of the developmental signalling that guides urethral closure. When hypospadias is proximal and severe or occurs with undescended testes, it more often signals a broader disturbance of sexual differentiation, whereas isolated distal disease usually represents a localised developmental anomaly. Distal hypospadias has an excellent outcome after repair, with good cosmetic and functional results; more proximal forms may require staged or complex reconstruction and carry a higher rate of complications such as fistula or stricture, but most children ultimately achieve satisfactory urinary and sexual function.

hyposplenism — asplenia, functional hyposplenism, splenic hypofunction Sickle cell disease and other haemoglobinopathies causing autosplenectomy Coeliac disease and inflammatory bowel disease Myeloproliferative and other haematological neoplasms Autoimmune disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis Amyloidosis and other infiltrative disease Prior splenic irradiation or splenic embolisation Other primary immunodeficiencies causing recurrent encapsulated organism infection Peripheral blood film for Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells and Pappenheimer bodies Pitted (pocked) red cell count by interference-contrast microscopy or flow cytometry to quantify function Abdominal ultrasound or cross-sectional imaging to assess splenic size or absence Coeliac serology such as tissue transglutaminase antibodies Haemoglobinopathy screen where relevant Autoimmune and, where indicated, immunoglobulin and vaccine-response studies Full blood count to characterise associated cytopenias or thrombocytosis Encompasses anatomical asplenia (surgical or congenital) and functional hyposplenism, in which the spleen is present but underperforms Sickle cell disease is the classic cause of autosplenectomy, while coeliac disease is the commonest non-haematological cause and merits a low threshold to test for Other causes include inflammatory bowel disease, autoimmune disease such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis, amyloidosis, infiltration, splenic irradiation, graft-versus-host disease and advancing age The peripheral blood film shows Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells, acanthocytes, Pappenheimer bodies and often thrombocytosis; a pitted or pocked red cell count quantifies residual function The cardinal danger is overwhelming post-splenectomy infection from encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b and meningococcus), which can be fulminant with high mortality There is also increased susceptibility to severe malaria, babesiosis and Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis following dog bites Prevention rests on immunisation against encapsulated organisms and influenza, long-term antibiotic prophylaxis, and a patient-held alert card with standby emergency antibiotics Any fever in an asplenic or hyposplenic patient is a medical emergency demanding immediate empirical antibiotics and urgent assessment Fever, rigors or any flu-like illness that may herald overwhelming sepsis Rapidly progressive shock with disseminated intravascular coagulation Recent dog bite with malaise, raising the possibility of Capnocytophaga sepsis Travel to a malarial area with febrile illness Failing to vaccinate and provide prophylaxis in functional hyposplenism, such as coeliac disease, because the spleen is anatomically present Delaying empirical antibiotics in a febrile asplenic patient while awaiting investigations Poor timing of vaccination around planned splenectomy, reducing the immune response Neglecting to issue an alert card, standby antibiotics and clear patient education Assuming a single course of vaccination confers durable lifelong protection without planned boosting The spleen filters the blood and provides key immune functions: macrophages of the red pulp remove senescent and abnormal red cells and clear opsonised and poorly opsonised encapsulated bacteria, while the white pulp supports antibody production including protective IgM from marginal-zone B cells. When splenic tissue is absent or its microcirculation and macrophage function are impaired, these roles are lost. Incomplete clearance of red cell inclusions produces the characteristic blood-film changes, and defective clearance of encapsulated organisms together with reduced specific antibody leaves the patient vulnerable to rapidly progressive bacteraemia. In functional hyposplenism the mechanism varies with the cause, from microvascular occlusion and repeated infarction in sickle cell disease to reticuloendothelial blockade, congestion or infiltration in other disorders. With appropriate immunisation, antibiotic prophylaxis and patient education the risk of serious infection is substantially reduced, though it persists lifelong. Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection carries a high mortality when treatment is delayed, so prompt recognition is decisive.

Hypothalamic hamartoma — HH, hamartoma of the tuber cinereum, hypothalamic hamartoma with gelastic seizures Hypothalamic or optic pathway glioma Craniopharyngioma Other suprasellar mass lesions Idiopathic central precocious puberty Temporal or frontal lobe epilepsy from other causes Tuberous sclerosis or other structural epileptogenic lesions Brain MRI with dedicated hypothalamic views to characterise a non-enhancing grey-matter-isointense mass Endocrine evaluation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis for precocious puberty Electroencephalography and video-EEG to characterise gelastic and other seizures Neuropsychological assessment for cognitive and behavioural comorbidity Genetic evaluation where a syndromic association such as Pallister-Hall is suspected Serial imaging to confirm lesion stability and exclude neoplasm A congenital, non-neoplastic malformation of disorganised but mature neurons and glia arising in the region of the tuber cinereum and mammillary bodies The classic presentation combines gelastic (laughing) seizures with central precocious puberty Gelastic seizures often begin in infancy and can be subtle, sometimes dismissed as normal laughter Sessile lesions with a broad intrahypothalamic attachment are more strongly associated with intractable epilepsy, while pedunculated lesions more often present with precocious puberty Over time an epileptic encephalopathy can develop, with additional seizure types, cognitive decline and behavioural disturbance including aggression MRI shows a non-enhancing mass isointense to grey matter that does not change over time, helping distinguish it from a tumour Precocious puberty is treatable hormonally, and drug-resistant seizures may respond to surgical, laser or radiosurgical approaches targeting the lesion Progressive epileptic encephalopathy with cognitive regression and behavioural deterioration Drug-resistant seizures affecting development and quality of life Signs of a growing or enhancing mass suggesting an alternative neoplastic diagnosis Endocrine disturbance beyond precocious puberty indicating wider hypothalamic dysfunction Mistaking early gelastic seizures for normal or emotional laughter and delaying diagnosis Misinterpreting the lesion as a neoplasm and pursuing unnecessary oncological management Attempting to control intractable seizures with medication alone when disconnection or ablation is more effective Overlooking central precocious puberty as a clue when seizures dominate the presentation Hypothalamic hamartoma is a congenital heterotopic mass of intrinsically epileptogenic neuronal and glial tissue located at the tuber cinereum. Intralesional small GABAergic-type neurons can fire autonomously, generating seizures within the lesion itself, which then propagate through hypothalamic and limbic networks to produce gelastic and other seizures. The lesion's disruption of hypothalamic regulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis drives central precocious puberty, and some cases are associated with somatic GLI3 pathway variants or with syndromic disorders such as Pallister-Hall syndrome. Precocious puberty is generally well controlled with hormonal therapy. The epilepsy outlook depends on lesion type and size: some remain mild, but sessile intrahypothalamic lesions can produce a progressive epileptic encephalopathy, and in these cases targeted surgical, laser ablation or radiosurgical treatment offers the best chance of seizure control and cognitive stabilisation.

Hypothermia and Peripheral Cold Injuries — Accidental hypothermia, Primary accidental hypothermia, Secondary hypothermia, Frostbite, Peripheral cold injury, Chilblain, Pernio, Trench foot, Immersion foot, Nonfreezing cold injury Hypoglycemia Hypothyroidism / myxedema coma Adrenal insufficiency and hypopituitarism Sepsis (hypothermia is a poor prognostic sign) Drug or ethanol intoxication / overdose Diabetic ketoacidosis and other metabolic acidoses Uremia CNS injury (cerebrovascular accident, subarachnoid hemorrhage, hypothalamic lesion, spinal cord injury) Shapiro syndrome (agenesis of corpus callosum with episodic hypothermia) Continuous core temperature monitoring, ideally esophageal (lower third); rectal/bladder as ancillary ECG (look for J/Osborn wave, bradydysrhythmias, atrial and ventricular arrhythmias) Arterial blood gas read uncorrected for temperature Serum potassium (prognostic in arrest), glucose, electrolytes, renal function Coagulation studies, fibrinogen, and platelet count (interpret with caution) Hematocrit (artificially elevated by cold) and white-cell count Bedside echocardiography and end-tidal CO2 to confirm perfusion status For frostbite: angiography, fluorescence microangiography, technetium-99 / pyrophosphate bone scan, or MR angiography to assess tissue viability and demarcation Cold-induced ileus with rectus abdominis spasm mimicking an acute abdomen Areflexia attributed to hypothermia masking a spinal cord lesion J (Osborn) waves misinterpreted as an injury current / ischemia Trench/immersion foot bullae indistinguishable from frostbite Shaking rigors of infection mistaken for shivering Accidental hypothermia is defined as an unintentional fall in core temperature below 35C (95F); at this threshold the compensatory mechanisms that conserve heat begin to fail. Primary hypothermia follows direct cold exposure of a previously healthy person, while secondary hypothermia complicates a systemic illness or injury and carries a much higher mortality. Core temperature cannot be reliably predicted from the clinical picture, so confirmation requires direct measurement; a probe in the lower third of the esophagus with continuous monitoring is preferred because rectal and bladder readings lag behind true core changes. Severity grading by core temperature: mild 35C to 32.2C (initial tachycardia then bradycardia, shivering, apathy, dysarthria, impaired judgment, cold diuresis); moderate 32.2C to 28C (declining consciousness, pupillary dilation, paradoxical undressing, atrial/ventricular arrhythmias, J-wave changes, loss of protective airway reflexes); severe below 28C (coma, loss of cerebrovascular autoregulation, maximal risk of ventricular fibrillation and asystole, apnea, poikilothermia). Vital signs are difficult to interpret without the core temperature: respiratory rate should be low because CO2 production declines, so persistent hyperventilation suggests a CNS lesion or organic acidosis, and tachycardia out of proportion to temperature suggests secondary causes such as hypoglycemia, hypovolemia, or toxin overdose. Paradoxical undressing (inappropriate removal of clothing in response to cold stress) is a classic maladaptive behavior; cold-induced ileus and rectus abdominis spasm can mimic or mask an acute abdomen, and confusion or combativeness resolves faster with rewarming than with chemical or physical restraint. The J (Osborn) wave at the QRS-ST junction supports the diagnosis and is frequently misread by automated ECG software as an injury current. Laboratory values are systematically distorted by cold: hematocrit rises about 2% per 1C drop (masking anemia), white-cell sequestration and marrow suppression can mask infection, and coagulation tests run at 37C appear deceptively normal despite a genuine in-vivo coagulopathy, so platelet and fresh-frozen-plasma transfusion is ineffective for the cold-induced coagulopathy. Arterial blood gases should NOT be temperature-corrected; an uncorrected pH of 7.42 and PCO2 of 40 mmHg reflect appropriate ventilation and acid-base balance at any core temperature, and overzealous hyperventilation is a common error given depressed CO2 production. Frostbite occurs when tissue temperature falls below 0C (32F): ice-crystal formation distorts cellular architecture, endothelial damage produces microvascular thrombosis, and after thawing there is progressive dermal ischemia, arteriovenous shunting, edema, and superficial necrosis, with mummification and demarcation taking weeks to months. Frostbite always produces a sensory deficit (light touch, pain, or temperature); superficial frostbite causes anesthesia and erythema without tissue loss, whereas vesiculation with surrounding edema/erythema indicates deeper injury and hemorrhagic vesicles signal severe microvascular damage that may lead to amputation. Chilblain (pernio) is a nonfreezing injury from repetitive damp-cold exposure above freezing, most common in young women with a history of Raynaud phenomenon, producing erythema, edema, pruritus, then plaques, blue nodules, and ulcerations on the dorsa of hands and feet. Trench foot / immersion foot results from repetitive wet-cold exposure above freezing; feet are initially cyanotic, cold, and edematous, with bullae progressing to ulceration and liquefaction gangrene, and survivors may have hyperhidrosis, cold sensitivity, and painful ambulation for years. Core temperature below 28C (severe): coma, maximal risk of ventricular fibrillation and asystole Potassium >12 mmol/L during resuscitation indicates widespread cell lysis and grave prognosis Core temperature <10-12C, pH <6.5, or fibrinogen <0.5 g/L may preclude continued resuscitation Hypothermia complicating sepsis is a poor prognostic sign Asphyxia preceding cooling (e.g., avalanche burial) is the strongest negative predictor of survival Hemorrhagic vesicles or persistent cyanosis after rewarming in frostbite (risk of amputation, compartment syndrome) Frostbite with rhabdomyolysis and completely frozen extremities Correcting arterial blood gases for temperature; the uncorrected values guide management Overzealous hyperventilation despite depressed CO2 production, dangerously raising pH Applying direct heat to extremities in chronic severe hypothermia, which causes peripheral vasodilation and core 'afterdrop' Transfusing platelets or fresh-frozen plasma for the cold coagulopathy (ineffective, as the defect is temperature-dependent enzyme inhibition) Deep insertion of central venous catheters or pulmonary artery catheters into the cold heart, which can precipitate refractory arrhythmias or perforation Trusting coagulation tests or hematocrit at face value (assays run at 37C; hematocrit falsely elevated) Premature termination of frostbite thawing because reperfusion is intensely painful Repeated dosing of drugs (e.g., digoxin, insulin) that are ineffective while cold but become toxic during rewarming Heat is lost by radiation (55-65%), conduction (10-15%, markedly increased in cold water), convection (increased with wind), respiration, and evaporation. The preoptic anterior hypothalamus orchestrates thermoregulation: the immediate autonomic defense releases norepinephrine, raises muscle tone, and triggers shivering to increase the basal metabolic rate, while cutaneous cold reception drives reflex vasoconstriction; prolonged cold also stimulates the thyroid axis. When these defenses are overwhelmed, hypothermia first stimulates and then progressively depresses every organ system. In peripheral freezing injury, tissue freezing causes ice-crystal formation that destroys cellular architecture; endothelial damage leads to stasis and microvascular thrombosis, and after thawing progressive dermal ischemia, arteriovenous shunting, rising tissue pressures, edema, and necrosis develop. Nonfreezing injuries (chilblain, trench/immersion foot) arise from neuronal and endothelial damage caused by repetitive cold exposure above the freezing point. Outcome depends heavily on whether hypothermia is primary or secondary, the precipitating cause, and the presence of asphyxia. Secondary hypothermia complicating systemic illness carries much higher mortality, and hypothermia with sepsis is a poor prognostic sign. Because cold itself is protective, survival has been reported after cardiac arrest times exceeding 7 hours, and intact neurologic recovery has occurred at extremely low core temperatures; the patient is not dead until warm and dead. Markers of a grave prognosis during resuscitation include potassium >12 mmol/L (cell lysis), pH <6.5, fibrinogen <0.5 g/L, and core temperature <10-12C, while preceding asphyxia (avalanche) is the most important negative predictor. The HOPE score uses six covariates to predict which arrested hypothermic patients may benefit from extracorporeal life support. Frostbite sequelae often persist as paresthesia, thermal misperception, and hyperhidrosis, with delayed nail deformities, cutaneous carcinomas, and epiphyseal damage in children. Hypothermia is graded by core temperature: Mild = 35C (95F) to 32.2C (90F); Moderate = below 32.2C (90F) to 28C (82.4F); Severe = below 28C (82.4F). Frostbite is classified as superficial (anesthesia and erythema, no tissue loss) versus deep (vesiculation, hemorrhagic vesicles, possible amputation); an alternative scheme grades by the proximal extent of presenting cyanosis: grade 1 none, grade 2 distal phalanx, grade 3 to the metacarpophalangeal joint, grade 4 proximal to the MP joint.

Hypothyroidism — Hashimoto thyroiditis, underactive thyroid Hyperthyroidism / thyrotoxicosis (opposite end of thyroid dysfunction; thyroiditis can pass through both phases) Sick euthyroid (nonthyroidal illness) syndrome Secondary (central) hypothyroidism from hypopituitarism or hypothalamic disease Multinodular goiter or thyroid carcinoma (asymmetric Hashimoto goiter may mimic these) Primary thyroid lymphoma (rare, strongly associated with pre-existing autoimmune thyroiditis) Depression and dementia (overlapping fatigue, poor concentration, slowing) Serum TSH as the primary screening test (most sensitive for primary disease) Free/unbound T4 to confirm clinical hypothyroidism when TSH is elevated (T3 measurement is not indicated) TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies to establish autoimmune etiology Lipid panel (cholesterol, triglycerides), creatine phosphokinase, and full blood count for associated abnormalities Anterior pituitary function testing when central hypothyroidism is suspected (after excluding drug effect and sick euthyroid syndrome) Thyroid ultrasound to distinguish heterogeneous Hashimoto echotexture from true nodules warranting FNA Depression Dementia Nephrotic syndrome (edema, hyperlipidemia) Chronic fatigue states Anemia of other cause In iodine-sufficient regions the most common causes are autoimmune disease (Hashimoto's thyroiditis) and iatrogenic injury (treatment of hyperthyroidism); iodine deficiency remains a leading cause worldwide (p.3027). Biochemical hallmark of primary hypothyroidism is an elevated TSH with a low unbound (free) T4; a normal TSH excludes primary, but not secondary/central, disease (p.3030-3031). Subclinical hypothyroidism is biochemical thyroid hormone deficiency (raised TSH, usually still-normal free T4) with few or no symptoms; overt hypothyroidism typically corresponds to TSH >10 mIU/L with a low free T4 (p.3029, p.3032). Symptoms (descending frequency) include tiredness/weakness, dry skin, cold intolerance, hair loss, poor concentration and memory, constipation, and modest weight gain with poor appetite (the weight gain is mainly fluid retention in myxedematous tissue) (p.3028-3029). Signs include dry coarse skin, cool extremities, nonpitting puffiness of face/hands/feet (myxedema), diffuse alopecia with thinning of the outer eyebrow, bradycardia, peripheral edema, and delayed relaxation of tendon reflexes (p.3028-3029). TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies are present in >95% of autoimmune hypothyroidism and confirm the etiology once hypothyroidism is established (p.3030). Onset is usually insidious, so patients may only recognize symptoms once euthyroidism is restored; Hashimoto's patients may present with goiter (irregular, firm) rather than hypothyroid symptoms (p.3029-3030). Associated laboratory abnormalities include raised creatine phosphokinase, elevated cholesterol and triglycerides, and a normocytic or macrocytic anemia, which generally resolve with thyroxine replacement (p.3030). Autoimmune hypothyroidism clusters with other autoimmune disorders, particularly vitiligo, pernicious anemia, Addison's disease (Schmidt's syndrome), type 1 diabetes, and the autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes (p.3030). Myxedema coma — the severe end of untreated hypothyroidism: reduced level of consciousness (sometimes seizures), hypothermia (can reach 23 C), with 20-40% mortality despite treatment; almost always in the elderly and often precipitated by infection, cold, sedatives, or acute cardiopulmonary events. Hypoventilation with hypoxia and hypercapnia, plus hypoglycemia and dilutional hyponatremia, in profound hypothyroidism. Impaired adrenal reserve in profound hypothyroidism (consider co-existing adrenal insufficiency before/with thyroid replacement). Neonatal/congenital hypothyroidism — risk of permanent neurologic damage if treatment is delayed, mandating neonatal screening. Significant pericardial or other serous effusions, conductive deafness, or carpal tunnel/entrapment syndromes as manifestations of severe disease. Central (secondary) hypothyroidism is missed if TSH is used alone: in pituitary/hypothalamic disease TSH may be low, normal, or even slightly raised, so a low free T4 is needed to make the diagnosis and TSH cannot be used to monitor therapy. A normal TSH excludes primary but NOT secondary/central hypothyroidism. T4 alone is an inferior screening test because it will not detect subclinical hypothyroidism; T3 is normal in ~25% of patients and is not indicated. An elevated TSH with normal/high free T4 in a patient on adequate levothyroxine usually reflects poor adherence (taking medication only shortly before testing), not a TSH-secretion disorder. Confirm that a raised TSH is sustained over ~3 months before treating subclinical hypothyroidism. TSH should not be relied on in the months immediately after radioiodine for Graves' disease (it stays suppressed); use unbound T4 instead. External rewarming in myxedema coma can precipitate cardiovascular collapse, and hypotonic fluids can worsen hyponatremia. Hypothyroidism is deficient thyroid hormone action, most often from primary thyroid failure. In autoimmune (Hashimoto's) disease, T cell-mediated lymphocytic infiltration with germinal-center formation, follicular atrophy, oxyphil metaplasia, and fibrosis progressively destroy the gland; atrophic thyroiditis represents its fibrotic end stage. As function declines there is a compensated phase in which a rising TSH maintains hormone levels (subclinical hypothyroidism); later free T4 falls and TSH rises further, producing overt disease. Susceptibility reflects genetic factors (HLA-DR3/DR4/DR5, PTPN22, CTLA-4) and environmental factors including high iodine intake. TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies are markers; up to 20% of patients have TSH-receptor-blocking antibodies that prevent TSH binding and can cause thyroid atrophy and, by transplacental passage, transient neonatal hypothyroidism. Increased dermal glycosaminoglycan deposition traps water, producing nonpitting myxedema (Harrison 22e p.3029-3030). With levothyroxine replacement and dose titration to a normal TSH, prognosis is excellent and most laboratory and clinical abnormalities resolve, though full symptomatic relief may take months and about 10-15% report persistent symptoms despite biochemical euthyroidism. Untreated congenital hypothyroidism causes permanent neurologic damage, and myxedema coma still carries a 20-40% mortality independent of T4 and TSH levels (Harrison 22e p.3031-3032). Spectrum from subclinical hypothyroidism (raised TSH, normal free T4, few/no symptoms) to overt/clinical hypothyroidism (raised TSH usually >10 mIU/L with low free T4 and symptoms); myxedema coma represents the severe, life-threatening end. Etiologically classified as primary (thyroidal), secondary/central (pituitary or hypothalamic), congenital, or transient (Harrison 22e p.3027-3032).

Hypovolemic / haemorrhagic shock — Identify bleeding source Crossmatch Resuscitate GI bleed / occult haemorrhage Distributive shock (e.g. sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic, adrenal crisis) - high cardiac output, low SVR, warm peripheries (pp.2310-2311) Cardiogenic shock - low output but with elevated CVP/PCWP and raised JVP (p.2311, p.2313) Obstructive shock (tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection) - low output with raised filling pressures/JVP (p.2311) Mixed shock - more than one mechanism coexisting (e.g. hypovolemic plus septic) (p.2311) Serial serum lactate for diagnosis, risk stratification and to gauge response to resuscitation - elevated lactate/lactic acidosis correlates with worse outcome (p.2314) Haemoglobin/haematocrit - reduced in haemorrhagic loss, but may be normal early in active bleeding before haemodilution occurs (pp.2313, 850-851) Coagulation profile (PT, PTT, INR) as part of the undifferentiated shock workup, relevant before/around transfusion (p.2313) Arterial or venous blood gas to quantify the degree of metabolic acidosis (p.2313) Urine electrolytes with FENa/FEUrea, which may indicate hypovolaemia or reduced effective circulating volume (p.2313) Point-of-care ultrasound (RUSH/ACES/SESAME protocols): a collapsible IVC at end-expiration in a spontaneously breathing patient and focused views of abdomen/pelvis suggest reduced intravascular volume and can identify intra-abdominal haemorrhage (pp.2314, 2336-2337) Dynamic fluid-responsiveness assessment - passive leg raise, or >12% stroke-volume/pulse-pressure variation in suitable mechanically ventilated patients - to predict response to volume (p.2315) Pregnancy test (to detect ruptured ectopic pregnancy as a haemorrhagic source) (p.2313, p.2310) Localising signs of occult internal bleed: Grey Turner sign (flank ecchymosis) and Cullen sign (umbilical ecchymosis) suggest retro-/intraperitoneal haemorrhage; rectal exam may reveal GI bleeding (pp.851, 2313) Cardiogenic shock - shares cool peripheries and narrow pulse pressure (low output) but is distinguished by raised JVP, peripheral oedema, an S3/S4 gallop and pulmonary crackles, indicating high filling pressures rather than volume depletion (p.2313, pp.2336-2337) Obstructive shock - low-output state but typically with an elevated JVP; tamponade (pulsus paradoxus, raised JVP, low-voltage ECG with electrical alternans) and tension pneumothorax (absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation) mimic the hypoperfusion of hypovolemia (p.2313) Distributive shock unmasked after fluid loss (e.g. adrenal insufficiency with aldosterone-deficient hypovolaemia) (pp.2310-2311) Hypovolemic shock is haemodynamically a low-output state: reduced cardiac output and oxygen delivery driven by low preload, with a compensatory rise in systemic vascular resistance and low CVP and PCWP from depleted intravascular volume (p.2311). Divide causes into haemorrhagic (external/trauma or internal, most often upper or lower GI bleeding) and non-haemorrhagic fluid loss (profuse vomiting/diarrhoea; renal losses such as osmotic diuresis in DKA or diabetes insipidus; skin losses from severe burns or Stevens-Johnson syndrome) (p.2311). On examination it presents as a cold, low-output shock: cool/clammy peripheries, narrow pulse pressure, delayed capillary refill and a reduced JVP (<8 cm) - the heart is 'empty' - in contrast to the warm peripheries and wide pulse pressure of distributive shock (pp.2312-2313, p.2335). Tachycardia and tachypnoea are early compensatory signs, but hypotension may be a late finding; younger patients in particular can compensate for an extended period before blood pressure falls (pp.2312-2313). Signs of vascular instability appear once roughly 25% of blood volume is lost; the usual sympathetic compensation (tachycardia, vasoconstriction, regional flow shift) fails beyond ~30% loss, and loss of >40% (>2 L in an average adult) produces overt shock (confusion, dyspnoea, diaphoresis, hypotension, tachycardia) (pp.850-851). Among hypovolemic causes, haemorrhage is the most common; non-haemorrhagic GI, renal and skin fluid losses are also recognised causes (p.2311). Overt features of severe blood-volume loss (>40%): confusion, dyspnoea, diaphoresis, hypotension and tachycardia indicating critical vital-organ hypoperfusion needing immediate volume replacement (pp.850-851) New altered mental status or new oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h) - signs the compensatory mechanisms have been overwhelmed (decompensated shock) (p.2312) Occult bleeding sites - retroperitoneal haemorrhage, long-bone fracture haematoma, intra-abdominal/intrapleural bleeding - that may not be externally apparent (pp.851, 2315) Elevated shock index (HR/SBP >0.9) flagging critical bleeding and likely transfusion need in haemorrhagic shock (p.2313) Compensated shock can present with a normal blood pressure: relying on an absolute SBP/MAP threshold misses early shock, since young patients may maintain pressure with tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure and only a mildly raised lactate before decompensating (pp.2312-2313). Do not be falsely reassured by tachycardia without hypotension, nor exclude shock because the heart rate is normal - patients on nodal-blocking drugs or with conduction disease may have a blunted or absent tachycardic response (pp.2312-2313). A normal initial haemoglobin/haematocrit does NOT exclude significant active haemorrhage; values fall only later as haemodilution develops, and the haematocrit does not reflect the true volume lost early on (pp.2313, 850-851). Misclassifying low-output shock: an elevated JVP, peripheral oedema, gallop or crackles point to cardiogenic/obstructive rather than hypovolemic shock and warn against indiscriminate large-volume resuscitation (pp.2313, 2336-2337). Over-resuscitation is harmful - targeted, reassessed fluid therapy is the goal rather than maximal volume (pp.2336-2337). Estimates of external blood loss at a bloody scene are often overestimated, while large internal bleeds may be clinically inapparent - examine carefully for localising signs (p.851). Hypovolemic shock arises when a fall in intravascular volume reduces preload, lowering stroke volume and cardiac output and therefore systemic oxygen delivery; CVP and PCWP are low and systemic vascular resistance rises as a compensatory response (p.2311). Inadequate oxygen delivery forces cells into anaerobic metabolism, so pyruvate is converted to lactate with markedly less ATP generation; failure of ATP-dependent ion pumps disrupts ionic and pH homeostasis, and calcium influx activates phospholipases/proteases causing cell swelling and death, with leaked intracellular contents driving inflammation and microvascular injury (p.2310). In acute haemorrhage, hypovolaemia dominates first and threatens high-flow organs (brain, kidneys); the haemoglobin is initially normal and only falls over hours as fluid shifts from the extravascular to the intravascular space (haemodilution), so the haematocrit does not reflect the volume lost early on (pp.850-851). Hypovolemic shock carries a lower mortality than septic or cardiogenic shock, which have the highest death rates among shock types (p.2311). Organ dysfunction in early (compensated) shock is often reversible if perfusion and oxygen delivery are restored, but untreated shock progresses through a decompensated phase to an irreversible phase with permanent multisystem organ dysfunction and death (pp.2311-2312). Harrison frames severity along the shock continuum (compensated/pre-shock to decompensated to irreversible) (pp.2311-2312) and, for haemorrhage, by the fraction of blood volume lost rather than an ATLS Class I-IV table (not present in this source): vascular instability emerges at about 25% loss; compensation fails beyond ~30% (postural hypotension and tachycardia); and loss of >40% (>2 L in an average adult) produces overt hypovolemic shock with confusion, dyspnoea, diaphoresis, hypotension and tachycardia (pp.850-851). The shock index (HR/SBP; normal 0.5-0.7) is a bedside severity marker, with values >0.9 indicating critical bleeding and likely transfusion need (p.2313).

Neonatal hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy — HIE, perinatal asphyxia encephalopathy Neonatal sepsis or meningitis Inborn errors of metabolism Neonatal stroke Intracranial haemorrhage Neuromuscular disorders Drug effects or withdrawal Cord and early blood gases and assessment of the perinatal history Amplitude-integrated or conventional EEG for background activity and seizures MRI of the brain to define injury pattern and prognosis Investigations to exclude infection and metabolic causes Multi-organ assessment (renal, hepatic, cardiac, coagulation) Brain injury in the term or near-term newborn resulting from a perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic insult Severity is graded clinically (for example by the Sarnat stages) from mild irritability to severe coma with absent reflexes Features include altered tone and consciousness, poor feeding, abnormal primitive reflexes and seizures Therapeutic hypothermia started within the first hours improves outcomes in moderate to severe cases meeting criteria It is important to exclude and treat other causes of neonatal encephalopathy such as infection, metabolic disease and stroke MRI and amplitude-integrated or standard EEG help characterise injury and prognosis Moderate to severe encephalopathy meeting cooling criteria (time-critical) Refractory seizures or status epilepticus Multi-organ dysfunction Deep or extensive injury on MRI Missing the narrow window for therapeutic hypothermia Attributing all neonatal encephalopathy to hypoxia-ischaemia without excluding mimics Overlooking subclinical seizures detectable on EEG Neglecting multi-organ complications Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy follows an interruption of oxygen delivery and blood flow to the brain around the time of birth. The initial insult causes primary energy failure with cell depolarisation, and after partial recovery a delayed secondary energy failure ensues over hours, driven by excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, inflammation and apoptosis, which extends the injury. This latent interval is the rationale for therapeutic hypothermia, which slows the injurious cascade. Patterns of injury depend on the severity and duration of the insult and on regional vulnerability of the immature brain. Mild encephalopathy often has a good outcome, whereas moderate to severe disease carries significant risk of death or long-term disability including cerebral palsy, epilepsy and cognitive impairment; therapeutic hypothermia improves survival free of disability.

are no visible clinical signs Overheating or allowing temperature instability, which can worsen brain injury Offering firm prognosis too early before EEG and MRI findings are available Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy results from a perinatal reduction in cerebral blood flow and oxygen delivery. The acute insult causes primary energy failure with anaerobic metabolism, lactic acidosis, and failure of ion pumps, leading to cytotoxic oedema and early cell death. After partial recovery of oxygenation and perfusion there is a latent phase, followed by delayed secondary energy failure driven by excitotoxicity from excess glutamate, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and inflammatory and apoptotic cascades over the subsequent hours to days. This delayed injury provides the therapeutic window during which cooling can reduce neuronal loss. The pattern of injury depends on the severity and duration of the insult, with the basal ganglia, thalamus, and perirolandic cortex affected in acute profound events and watershed regions in prolonged partial insults. Outcome depends on the severity and pattern of injury: mild encephalopathy usually has a favourable outcome, whereas moderate and severe HIE carry substantial risk of death or long-term disability including cerebral palsy, cognitive impairment, and epilepsy. Therapeutic hypothermia improves survival free of disability in eligible infants, but severe injury on EEG and MRI predicts poor neurodevelopmental outcome.

involvement Recurrent respiratory infections Rapid neurodevelopmental decline Misdiagnosing it as a mucopolysaccharidosis and being misled by near-normal urinary glycosaminoglycans Overlooking the diagnostic value of raised plasma lysosomal enzyme activity Attributing coarse facies at birth to congenital hypothyroidism alone Failing to distinguish severe ML II from the milder ML III phenotype I-cell disease results from deficiency of the enzyme UDP-N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, encoded (alpha/beta subunits) by GNPTAB. This enzyme adds the mannose-6-phosphate recognition marker that normally directs newly synthesised lysosomal hydrolases to the lysosome. Without the marker, multiple enzymes are instead secreted into the extracellular space, so lysosomes are depleted of hydrolases and undigested substrates accumulate as characteristic inclusion bodies within cells. The biochemical signature is therefore paradoxical: low intracellular lysosomal enzyme activity but high activity of the same enzymes in plasma. Widespread lysosomal dysfunction produces severe multisystem storage disease. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The disorder is severe and progressive, with cardiorespiratory complications commonly limiting survival to early childhood. Management is supportive, as no established disease-modifying therapy exists.

this distribution difference is a key way to separate the two (p.2555-2556). Granulomas (noncaseating, in all bowel-wall layers) are characteristic of Crohn's but are found less often on mucosal biopsy than on surgical resection specimens, so their absence does not exclude Crohn's (p.2556). On biopsy, distorted/branching crypt architecture and basal plasmacytosis/lymphoid aggregates indicate chronicity and help distinguish IBD from acute self-limited or infectious colitis (p.2556). Faecal calprotectin and lactoferrin correlate with histologic inflammation, help predict relapse, and can detect pouchitis; they are used to distinguish active inflammation from IBS or bacterial overgrowth (p.2556-2557). Distal/proctitis-limited UC can paradoxically present with constipation due to slowed proximal transit despite distal inflammation (p.2557). In severely ill UC patients serum albumin falls quickly; leukocytosis can occur but is not a specific marker of disease activity (p.2557). Toxic megacolon - transverse or right colon dilated >6 cm with loss of haustration during a severe attack; surgical emergency, can be precipitated by electrolyte abnormalities and narcotics (p.2557) Perforation - the most dangerous local complication; signs of peritonitis may be masked by glucocorticoids; mortality of perforation complicating toxic megacolon is ~15% (p.2557) Toxic colitis with deep ulceration - bowel may perforate without first dilating (p.2557) Massive haemorrhage (occurs in ~1% of UC patients) (p.2557) High-spiking fever in Crohn's suggesting intraabdominal abscess (p.2557) Colonic stricture that prevents colonoscope passage - presume malignant until proven otherwise (indication for surgery) (p.2557) Before escalating immunosuppression in a presumed flare, exclude superimposed infection - C. difficile and CMV colitis can mimic or complicate IBD; diagnosis requires negative stool studies (culture, C. difficile toxin, ova and parasites) and, for CMV, identification of intranuclear inclusions on mucosal biopsy (p.2557, p.2560). A first 'flare' of bloody diarrhoea may actually be an infectious colitis (e.g., Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, C. difficile, amoebic) - infection should be excluded before diagnosing IBD; Campylobacter and others can also reactivate established UC (p.2559-2560). Granulomas are frequently absent on mucosal biopsy even in Crohn's, so their absence does not rule it out (p.2556). Effective medical therapy can normalise mucosal appearance and create apparent skip areas in UC, mimicking Crohn's distribution; biopsy normal-appearing mucosa (p.2555-2556). Extensive perianal lesions in a patient labelled UC should raise suspicion for Crohn's instead (p.2557). In patients on glucocorticoids, peritoneal signs of perforation may be blunted/absent (p.2557). An impassable colonic stricture should be presumed malignant rather than benign inflammatory (p.2557). IBD is a chronic idiopathic inflammatory disease of the GI tract regarded as a dysregulated, inappropriate immune response to the endogenous commensal microbiota (with or without an autoimmune component) in a genetically susceptible host. Homeostasis among the gut microbiota, intestinal epithelial cells, and mucosal immune system is normally maintained by regulatory pathways (e.g., FoxP3 T-regulatory cells); environmental factors (smoking, antibiotics, enteropathogens, diet) acting on genetic susceptibility (>240 GWAS loci, ~20% of risk explained; rare single-gene defects such as IL10/IL10R in very-early-onset disease) disrupt this balance and produce sustained inflammation. UC is a mucosal/superficial-submucosal disease, while Crohn's is transmural with fissuring and fistula/stricture formation (p.2551-2556). Toxic megacolon occurs rarely; about 50% of acute dilations resolve with conservative management, but those that do not require urgent colectomy. Perforation complicating toxic megacolon carries ~15% mortality. Risk of colorectal cancer rises with duration and extent of colitis (historically ~2% at 10 yr, 8% at 20 yr, 18% at 30 yr, though rates have fallen with better inflammation control and surveillance; still ~1.5-2x the general population). Extensive long-standing colitis carries the highest cancer risk. Strictures occur in ~5% of UC patients. Up to one-third of IBD patients develop at least one extraintestinal manifestation (p.2557-2563, p.2570). Montreal classification of UC severity (Harrison Table 337-4, p.2557): S0 clinical remission (no symptoms); S1 mild = up to 4 stools/day +/- blood, no systemic illness, normal ESR; S2 moderate = 4 or more stools/day with minimal systemic toxicity; S3 severe = 6 or more bloody stools/day plus pulse >=90/min, temperature >=37.5 C, haemoglobin <10.5 g/dL, and ESR >=30 mm/h. (These severe-disease physiologic thresholds mirror the classic Truelove-Witts criteria for acute severe colitis.) Montreal extent: E1 proctitis, E2 left-sided (distal to splenic flexure), E3 extensive/pancolitis. Crohn's is categorised by the Vienna/Montreal classification (Table 337-5, p.2558) by age at diagnosis (A), location ileal/colonic/ileocolonic/upper (L), and behaviour nonstricturing-nonpenetrating/stricturing/penetrating (B) with a perianal modifier.

abdominal pain on average at least 1 day/week over the prior 3 months plus at least two of being related to defecation, a change in stool frequency, or a change in stool form, with onset at least 6 months earlier. Rome IV is stricter than Rome III: it requires pain at least weekly and dropped 'discomfort' as a qualifying symptom; painless diarrhoea or constipation alone does NOT meet criteria. Abdominal pain is mandatory for the diagnosis; it is typically episodic and crampy, often worsened by eating or emotional stress and relieved by passing flatus or stool. Subtype by predominant stool form: IBS-C (constipation), IBS-D (diarrhoea), and IBS-M (mixed) — but subtypes are unstable, with about three-quarters of patients changing subtype and ~29% switching between IBS-C and IBS-D over a year. Onset is usually before age 45 and IBS is two to three times more common in women, who make up ~80% of severe cases. Symptoms commonly overlap with other functional disorders (fibromyalgia, headache, backache, genitourinary symptoms) and with functional dyspepsia, suggesting a shared, more extensive digestive disorder. Bloating and a subjective sense of excess gas are common, but most patients actually generate a normal volume of intestinal gas and instead have impaired gas transit/tolerance and proximal reflux of gas. Malnutrition is exceedingly rare in IBS and the pain almost always occurs only during waking hours, so sleep disruption from pain is unusual. First appearance of symptoms in old age Progressive course from the time of onset Rectal bleeding Persistent diarrhoea after a 48-hour fast Nocturnal diarrhoea Steatorrhoeal stools Anaemia, elevated sedimentation rate, or leukocytes/blood in stool Stool volume >200-300 mL/day Family history of colorectal malignancy (lowers threshold for thorough evaluation) Treating IBS as a diagnosis of exclusion only and over-investigating: few tests are needed when symptoms are typical and alarm features are absent, and unnecessary investigations may be costly and even harmful. Missing organic disease in higher-risk patients: older age, rapidly progressive symptoms, or alarm features should prompt a thorough work-up to exclude IBD, coeliac disease and colorectal cancer rather than labelling as IBS. Attributing bloating to excess gas when most patients produce a normal gas volume but have impaired gas transit. Over-interpreting an abnormal hydrogen breath test, which can be positive simply from rapid small-bowel transit and does not reliably predict treatment response. IBS is a multifactorial functional bowel disorder with no structural lesion. Proposed mechanisms include altered GI motor activity (e.g., exaggerated postprandial and distention-evoked colonic contractions, increased high-amplitude propagating contractions with rapid transit in IBS-D), visceral hypersensitivity (lower thresholds to rectal balloon distention with sparing of somatic pain pathways), and disordered brain-gut interaction with central neural dysregulation (greater activation of mid-cingulate and prefrontal cortices on functional imaging). Psychological factors (anxiety, depression, somatization, prior physical/sexual abuse) modulate pain thresholds, and genetic factors such as serotonin transporter (SERT) polymorphisms are implicated. Peripheral contributors include low-grade mucosal immune activation with mast cells, lymphocytes and proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1beta, TNF), upregulated TRPV1 sensory channels, increased intestinal permeability ('leaky gut', chiefly in IBS-D and post-infectious IBS), gut dysbiosis (reduced microbial diversity, fewer Bifidobacterium/Faecalibacterium, more Enterobacteriaceae), abnormal serotonin pathways with increased enterochromaffin-cell serotonin in IBS-D, and bile acid malabsorption in up to ~25% of IBS-D. Harrison classifies IBS by predominant bowel pattern under Rome IV into IBS-C (predominant constipation), IBS-D (predominant diarrhoea), and IBS-M (mixed constipation and diarrhoea); these subtypes are noted to be unstable over time. Overall symptom severity ranges from mild to severe with significant quality-of-life impairment, but no formal graded severity score is specified.
