favoured over hypertensive ICH when there is a prodrome and altered mental status before any bleed (p.3455) Brain tumour presenting with haemorrhage (p.3455) ICH typically presents as abrupt-onset focal deficit; compared with ischaemic stroke, headache is more common, but imaging is still required to distinguish the two (p.3453). Putaminal haemorrhage damages the adjacent internal capsule, so contralateral hemiparesis is the sentinel sign, often with the eyes deviated away from the side of the weakness (p.3454). Thalamic haemorrhage produces a prominent all-modality contralateral sensory deficit and characteristic ocular signs from inferior extension into the upper midbrain (e.g. eyes deviated down-and-in 'looking at the nose', poorly reactive unequal pupils, vertical-gaze palsy) (p.3454). Pontine haemorrhage causes rapid deep coma with quadriplegia, decerebrate rigidity and reactive 'pinpoint' (~1 mm) pupils (p.3454). Cerebellar haemorrhage classically gives occipital headache, repeated vomiting and gait ataxia; in mild cases gait ataxia may be the only sign (p.3454). Lobar haemorrhage symptoms mirror the lobe involved: occipital → hemianopia, left temporal → aphasia and confusion, parietal → hemisensory loss, frontal → arm weakness (p.3454). Seizures are uncommon at presentation but occur in roughly 6-15% of patients within the first 3 days (p.3453). Lumbar puncture is generally unnecessary and should usually be avoided in ICH because focal signs and raised ICP make it potentially herniation-inducing (p.3455). ICH accounts for about 10% of all strokes, with disproportionately high incidence in Asian and Black populations (p.3453). 'Spot sign' on CTA/post-contrast CT - associated with increased haematoma expansion, higher mortality and lower likelihood of favourable outcome (p.3455) Haematoma expansion: about a third of patients (even without coagulopathy) have significant expansion within the first day; anticoagulant-related bleeds may keep enlarging for 24-48 h (p.3454) Progressive decline in consciousness with headache and vomiting signalling rising ICP; deterioration may continue over 24-96 h from perihaematoma oedema (p.3453-3454) Cerebellar haemorrhage with depressed consciousness or obstructive hydrocephalus, or radiographic hydrocephalus - high risk of rapid brainstem-compression deterioration requiring immediate neurosurgical evaluation (p.3454) Signs of herniation (stupor/coma, dilated fixed pupil, decerebrate rigidity) (p.3453-3454) Intraventricular extension of blood - substantially increases morbidity and may cause hydrocephalus (p.3454) Cerebellar haemorrhage can deteriorate precipitously from brainstem compression or obstructive hydrocephalus; immediate surgical evacuation before severe brainstem compression may be lifesaving, and hydrocephalus from a cerebellar haematoma should generally be managed by definitive evacuation rather than ventricular drainage alone (p.3454). Haemorrhage outside the typical deep hypertensive sites, or in a non-hypertensive patient, should prompt a search for other causes (amyloid angiopathy, tumour, vascular malformation, vasculitis, coagulopathy) rather than being assumed hypertensive (p.3454). Conflating hypertensive encephalopathy/PRES with hypertensive ICH leads to inappropriately aggressive BP lowering - hypertensive encephalopathy warrants less aggressive reduction (p.3455). ICP is often normal even with large ICHs, so it cannot be assumed; conversely induced hyperventilation can cause ischaemia and should be limited to acute resuscitation only (p.3456). Glucocorticoids are not recommended for treating ICH (p.3456). In ICH on antiplatelet drugs without thrombocytopenia, platelet transfusion showed no benefit and possible harm (p.3456). Despite the presence of haemorrhage, venous sinus thrombosis is an indication for anticoagulation to relieve venous hypertension (p.3455). Hypertensive ICH usually results from spontaneous rupture of a small (~30-100 microns) penetrating artery deep in the brain, with chronic hypertension producing vascular injury preferentially at the basal ganglia (especially putamen), thalamus, cerebellum and pons. The clot may stay small or enlarge to compress adjacent tissue and cause herniation; dissection into the ventricles markedly increases morbidity and can produce hydrocephalus. Most hypertensive bleeds evolve over 30-90 minutes, whereas anticoagulant-related bleeds may keep expanding for 24-48 h. By ~48 h macrophages begin phagocytosing the haemorrhage at its surface, and over 1-6 months it resolves to a slit-like glial-scarred cavity with haemosiderin-laden macrophages. In cerebral amyloid angiopathy, arteriolar degeneration with amyloid deposition in cortical vessel walls causes single and recurrent lobar haemorrhages, the commonest cause of lobar bleeding in the elderly (p.3453-3454). Overall, about 35-45% of patients die within the first month, and roughly 40% with a hypertensive ICH die, though survivors can achieve good to complete recovery because peri-haematoma tissue is displaced rather than infarcted and often regains function as the clot resorbs over months. The validated ICH Score stratifies mortality and outcome but should not be used to precisely prognosticate an individual, since withholding early aggressive care risks a self-fulfilling prophecy of poor outcome. Deep pontine haemorrhage with coma usually ends in death or a locked-in state, but small bleeds are compatible with survival; in cerebellar haemorrhage, full recovery is common if the deep cerebellar nuclei are spared (p.3453-3456). ICH Score (Hemphill et al., Stroke 2001) - validated grading scale for mortality/outcome stratification, summing five factors: age >=80 (1 pt), haematoma volume >=30 cc (1 pt), intraventricular haemorrhage present (1 pt), infratentorial origin (1 pt), and Glasgow Coma Scale 13-15 (0), 5-12 (1) or 3-4 (2); total 0-6 (p.3455-3456).

and examination, including family history and age of onset, to separate inherited from acquired disease Skin biopsy where the diagnosis is unclear Targeted investigation for underlying malignancy or systemic disease when adult-onset acquired ichthyosis is suspected Biochemical or genetic testing to define specific subtypes (for example steroid sulfatase assessment in suspected X-linked disease) Neonatal monitoring of hydration, temperature, and electrolytes in severe congenital forms Ichthyosis describes a group of disorders of cornification characterised by persistent, generalised dry, scaly skin, most of which are inherited, though acquired ichthyosis also occurs Ichthyosis vulgaris is the commonest form, presenting with fine scaling that spares the flexures, associated hyperlinear palms, and a strong link to atopy and filaggrin mutations X-linked recessive ichthyosis affects males and produces larger, darker (dirty-brown) scales, and may be associated with corneal opacities and, in some, cryptorchidism Congenital ichthyoses can present dramatically at birth, including the collodion baby encased in a taut membrane and, at the severe end, the harlequin phenotype Acquired ichthyosis appearing in an adult without a childhood history should prompt a search for underlying malignancy (notably lymphoma), metabolic, autoimmune, or nutritional disease, or a drug cause Management is largely supportive, centred on regular emollients, keratolytics or humectants to reduce scale, and gentle skin care, with systemic retinoid therapy reserved for severe congenital forms under specialist care Neonates with severe congenital ichthyosis are at risk of dehydration, temperature instability, infection, and, with a constricting collodion membrane, feeding and breathing difficulty Genetic counselling and accurate classification through clinical, and where needed genetic, assessment are valuable for families Severe congenital ichthyosis in a neonate with impaired thermoregulation, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and infection risk Constricting collodion or harlequin membrane restricting respiration, feeding, or limb perfusion New adult-onset acquired ichthyosis signalling possible underlying malignancy or systemic disease Signs of secondary skin infection in a compromised barrier Ectropion, eclabium, or ocular exposure requiring protective ophthalmic care in severe forms Overlooking adult-onset acquired ichthyosis as a marker of underlying malignancy or systemic disease Attributing chronic scaling simply to dry skin or eczema without considering an ichthyosis Under-treating with insufficient emollient use, allowing scale and fissuring to persist Failing to anticipate dehydration and infection risk in affected neonates Neglecting genetic counselling and accurate subtyping for affected families The ichthyoses share a defect in the formation or shedding of the stratum corneum, resulting in accumulation of scale and an impaired epidermal barrier. In ichthyosis vulgaris, loss-of-function mutations in filaggrin reduce production of the protein that aggregates keratin filaments and generates natural moisturising factors, causing retention hyperkeratosis and barrier dysfunction. X-linked ichthyosis stems from steroid sulfatase deficiency, leading to cholesterol sulfate accumulation that impairs corneocyte shedding. The congenital autosomal recessive ichthyoses involve mutations affecting lipid processing and cornified envelope formation. Across subtypes, the disrupted barrier drives increased water loss, compensatory hyperproliferation, and inflammation, with the specific molecular defect determining scale pattern and severity. Most common inherited ichthyoses, such as ichthyosis vulgaris and X-linked ichthyosis, are lifelong but manageable with regular skin care and compatible with normal life expectancy; severe congenital forms carry significant neonatal risk and lifelong burden, while acquired ichthyosis often improves when the underlying cause is treated.

Ichthyosis hystrix — ichthyosis hystrix Curth-Macklin type, porcupine skin, KRT1 Epidermolytic ichthyosis (bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma) Epidermal naevus and systematised epidermolytic naevus Lamellar ichthyosis Erythrokeratodermia variabilis Pityriasis rubra pilaris Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis Skin biopsy showing marked hyperkeratosis and abnormal keratinocyte differentiation Electron microscopy for perinuclear keratin shells (Curth-Macklin type) Molecular genetic testing of KRT1 and related keratin genes Family history and pedigree analysis Assessment of palmoplantar involvement and function Screening for secondary infection of fissured hyperkeratosis A descriptive term for severe hyperkeratotic disorders producing thick, spiny, verrucous scale that resembles porcupine quills The Curth-Macklin type is an autosomal dominant condition caused by variants in KRT1 (keratin 1) Unlike epidermolytic ichthyosis, the Curth-Macklin form typically lacks widespread blistering despite prominent hyperkeratosis Lesions may be generalised or arranged in a linear or systematised naevoid pattern following the lines of Blaschko when the disorder is mosaic A severe palmoplantar keratoderma is frequently present and can cause functional impairment Diagnosis is clinical and histological; electron microscopy classically shows perinuclear shells of keratin filaments, and molecular testing can identify the KRT1 variant Management is supportive with intensive emollients and keratolytics, and oral retinoids may reduce the burden of hyperkeratosis in severe disease Extensive barrier failure with recurrent infection and fluid or temperature dysregulation Disabling palmoplantar keratoderma with deep painful fissures Rapid change in an established lesion suggesting alternative pathology Signs of secondary cutaneous or systemic infection Assuming all severe keratin-related ichthyoses blister and overlooking the non-blistering Curth-Macklin type Not recognising a systematised naevoid variant as a mosaic form of the disorder Neglecting the disabling palmoplantar component Underusing emollients and keratolytics before considering systemic therapy Ichthyosis hystrix of the Curth-Macklin type is caused by variants in KRT1, which encodes keratin 1, a component of the suprabasal keratin intermediate filament network. The variants disrupt normal filament assembly, producing aggregated perinuclear keratin shells and abnormal terminal differentiation of keratinocytes. This leads to gross retention hyperkeratosis with the characteristic spiny, verrucous scale, while the specific filament defect accounts for the relative absence of the fragility and blistering seen in classical epidermolytic ichthyosis from other keratin variants. The disorder is lifelong and can be physically and cosmetically disabling, but with sustained emollient and keratolytic care, and retinoids where appropriate, many patients achieve worthwhile reduction in scale.

Cumulative ultraviolet exposure and skin ageing are the principal contributors, with a possible genetic predisposition. The result is scattered focal areas of reduced epidermal melanisation on chronically photodamaged skin. The condition is benign, stable and permanent, with individual macules persisting indefinitely; it carries no health risk and is purely a cosmetic issue.

Unlike narcolepsy type 1 it is not associated with loss of hypocretin (orexin) signalling. Proposed contributors include enhanced activity of endogenous substances that promote sleep or potentiate inhibitory GABA-A neurotransmission, together with disturbed regulation of the sleep-wake and circadian systems, which could explain the prolonged, deep and unrefreshing sleep with pronounced sleep inertia. The disorder is usually chronic and stable, though spontaneous improvement occurs in a minority; symptoms are often only partially controlled by wake-promoting medication, and residual sleepiness and sleep inertia can substantially affect function.

disorder of raised intracranial pressure in the absence of a mass lesion, hydrocephalus, infection or venous sinus thrombosis. The mechanism is incompletely understood but is thought to involve impaired cerebrospinal fluid absorption and possibly increased production, together with cerebral venous and metabolic factors linked to obesity. The elevated pressure is transmitted along the optic nerve sheaths, obstructing axoplasmic flow at the optic disc and producing papilloedema. Persistent disc swelling leads to progressive optic nerve fibre loss and irreversible visual field constriction if the pressure is not controlled. With weight loss and medical therapy, most patients have a good visual outcome, but a subset, particularly those with fulminant disease or poor adherence, suffer permanent optic atrophy and visual field loss; the condition can be chronic and relapsing and headaches may persist despite controlled pressure.

It is considered immune-mediated, with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate and variable fibrosis affecting the extraocular muscles, lacrimal gland, orbital fat or apex. The inflammation and mass effect produce pain, proptosis and restricted motility, and some cases overlap with, or are later reclassified as, IgG4-related disease or a defined systemic inflammatory disorder. Many cases respond rapidly to corticosteroids, but relapse is common and some require steroid-sparing immunosuppression or radiotherapy; sclerosing variants can cause lasting fibrosis and dysfunction.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis — Cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis, IPF, Idiopathic UIP Fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease (notably rheumatoid arthritis and systemic sclerosis) Fibrotic nonspecific interstitial pneumonia Asbestosis and other pneumoconioses Drug-induced pulmonary fibrosis Combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema Chronic fibrotic sarcoidosis HRCT thorax with supine and prone acquisitions to identify a UIP pattern Full pulmonary function tests including transfer factor (restrictive defect with reduced DLCO) Autoimmune serology (antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, myositis panel) to exclude connective tissue disease Serum precipitins and a detailed environmental and occupational exposure history Six-minute walk test with oximetry to document exertional desaturation Surgical or transbronchial lung cryobiopsy when the HRCT pattern is indeterminate and the multidisciplinary team advises Echocardiography to screen for pulmonary hypertension The most common idiopathic interstitial pneumonia; typically presents after the age of 60 with a male and ex-smoker predominance. Progressive exertional breathlessness and a dry cough with bibasal fine end-inspiratory 'Velcro' crackles and finger clubbing are characteristic. Diagnosis rests on a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern on HRCT: subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, and absence of features suggesting an alternative diagnosis. Multidisciplinary team discussion integrating clinical, radiological and, where required, histological data is the diagnostic reference standard. Antifibrotic therapy slows the decline in forced vital capacity but does not reverse established fibrosis. Acute exacerbations, defined by rapid worsening with new ground-glass change over fibrosis, carry a very high mortality. Actively screen for and manage comorbidities: gastro-oesophageal reflux, pulmonary hypertension, coexisting emphysema, obstructive sleep apnoea and lung cancer. Refer eligible patients early for lung transplantation assessment and for pulmonary rehabilitation and palliative symptom support. Rapidly worsening breathlessness with new widespread ground-glass change over fibrosis suggesting an acute exacerbation Resting or exertional hypoxaemia Clinical signs of right heart failure or pulmonary hypertension Haemoptysis or a new pulmonary mass raising concern for lung cancer Rapid decline in forced vital capacity Mislabelling fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis or connective tissue disease-ILD as IPF and missing a treatable or removable cause Attributing crackles and breathlessness to cardiac disease and delaying HRCT Using combination immunosuppression as for other interstitial pneumonias, which is harmful in IPF Overlooking coexisting pulmonary hypertension, emphysema or lung cancer Failing to discuss transplantation and palliative symptom control early Repetitive micro-injury to ageing alveolar epithelium in genetically susceptible individuals provokes aberrant wound healing rather than a primarily inflammatory response. Dysregulated epithelial-fibroblast crosstalk drives fibroblast and myofibroblast proliferation with excessive extracellular matrix deposition, producing fibroblastic foci, irreversible architectural distortion and honeycombing that is subpleural and basal in distribution. idiopathic restrictive cardiomyopathy — primary restrictive cardiomyopathy, non-infiltrative restrictive cardiomyopathy constrictive pericarditis cardiac amyloidosis cardiac sarcoidosis cardiac haemochromatosis Fabry and other storage cardiomyopathies endomyocardial fibrosis / hypereosinophilic cardiomyopathy hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with restrictive physiology echocardiography with Doppler and tissue Doppler for restrictive filling and biatrial enlargement cardiac magnetic resonance with tissue characterisation to exclude infiltration and pericardial disease simultaneous or careful right and left heart catheterisation to distinguish restriction from constriction serum free light chains and amyloid work-up including consideration of endomyocardial biopsy genetic testing and family screening where familial disease is suspected natriuretic peptides for severity and follow-up cross-sectional imaging (CT) for pericardial thickening or calcification Idiopathic restrictive cardiomyopathy is defined by restrictive ventricular physiology with impaired filling and raised filling pressures, near-normal wall thickness and normal or only mildly reduced systolic function, in the absence of an identifiable infiltrative, storage or endomyocardial cause. Biatrial enlargement that is often marked, in the setting of non-dilated and non-hypertrophied ventricles, is a characteristic morphological signature. Predominant right-sided congestion with elevated jugular venous pressure, ascites and oedema frequently dominates the clinical picture and can be mistaken for hepatic or renal disease. The most important and difficult distinction is from constrictive pericarditis, because the latter is surgically curable; ventricular interdependence, respiratory variation in filling and pericardial features must be sought. It is essentially a diagnosis of exclusion, so amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, haemochromatosis, Fabry disease and endomyocardial disease must be actively ruled out before the label is applied. A subset is familial, associated with sarcomeric gene mutations (including troponin I) and may overlap phenotypically with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, warranting family screening and genetic counselling. Atrial fibrillation and thromboembolism are common owing to atrial dilatation and stasis, and contribute substantially to morbidity. Management is largely supportive, with cautious diuresis to relieve congestion while avoiding excessive preload reduction that compromises the already limited stroke volume. syncope or presyncope suggesting arrhythmia or critically limited output refractory right heart failure with progressive ascites and cachexia thromboembolic event or intracardiac thrombus features suggesting a treatable mimic such as constrictive pericarditis or amyloidosis rising filling pressures with worsening functional class despite therapy failing to exclude surgically curable constrictive pericarditis before labelling disease idiopathic applying the diagnosis without excluding infiltrative and storage causes over-diuresis that precipitates a fall in cardiac output and renal impairment missing familial disease and the opportunity for family screening underestimating thromboembolic risk in dilated, fibrillating atria The ventricular myocardium becomes abnormally stiff and non-compliant, so that even small increases in volume produce large increases in ventricular pressure. Systolic contraction and ventricular cavity size are relatively preserved, but impaired diastolic relaxation and compliance raise atrial and venous pressures, driving pulmonary and systemic congestion. Chronically elevated atrial pressures cause progressive biatrial dilatation while the ventricles remain non-dilated and of near-normal thickness. In familial disease, sarcomeric protein mutations alter myofilament function and calcium handling; in sporadic disease, variable interstitial fibrosis and myocyte disarray contribute to the stiff-ventricle physiology. The fixed limitation of ventricular filling ultimately caps cardiac output and, over time, may be accompanied by pulmonary hypertension and low-output heart failure. Prognosis is variable but often unfavourable once symptomatic heart failure develops, with progression to low-output failure and a significant risk of thromboembolism and arrhythmia; selected patients, particularly children and those with progressive disease, are considered for cardiac transplantation.

IgG4-Related Disease — IgG4-RD, IgG4-related systemic disease, Type 1 (IgG4-related) autoimmune pancreatitis, Lymphoplasmacytic sclerosing pancreatitis, Mikulicz's disease Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (mimicked by type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis) Primary sclerosing cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma (mimicked by IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis) Sjogren's syndrome (Mikulicz's disease presentation) Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (when destructive sinus/middle-ear/nasopharyngeal lesions occur) Lymphoma and other causes of lymphadenopathy or pseudotumor Riedel's thyroiditis and fibrosing variant of Hashimoto's thyroiditis Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis Idiopathic membranous glomerulonephropathy Orbital pseudotumor / orbital myositis from other causes Serum IgG4 concentration (commonly elevated, but normal in ~30% of histologically proven cases; usually measured by nephelometry). Awareness of the prozone effect: very high serum IgG4 can yield spuriously low/normal nephelometric values, correctable by serum dilution; failure to detect dramatic elevations misses the subset at greatest risk for multiorgan disease and end-organ injury. Cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI) to map multiorgan involvement and detect subclinical or incidental disease. MRI of brain/orbits for pachymeningeal thickening and enhancement or enlarged extraocular muscles in CNS/orbital disease. Tissue biopsy with immunohistochemical staining for IgG4 and IgG, quantifying IgG4+ plasma cells per high-power field and the IgG4:total IgG ratio. Malignancy (carcinoma, lymphoma) presenting as a tumefactive mass Sarcoidosis Granulomatosis with polyangiitis Sjogren's syndrome Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis and inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm A fibroinflammatory disorder whose hallmark is a tendency to form tumefactive (mass-like) lesions that frequently mimic malignancy; initial misdiagnosis as cancer is extremely common. Protean and multisystem: can affect virtually any organ, with predilection for pancreas, biliary tree, major salivary glands (submandibular, parotid), periorbital/lacrimal tissues, kidneys, lungs, lymph nodes, and retroperitoneum; meninges, aorta, prostate, thyroid, pericardium, and skin are also described. Regarded as a variable-vessel vasculitis because it can target arteries and veins of any size, with venous involvement (obliterative phlebitis) being a particular hallmark. Typical patient is a middle-aged to elderly man (male-to-female ratio about 2:1), contrasting with classic autoimmune diseases that favor young women; head-and-neck (orbit, lacrimal, salivary) disease has a sex ratio closer to 1:1. Usually presents subacutely; most patients lack fever or marked C-reactive protein elevation even with multiorgan disease. Substantial weight loss can occur, often from exocrine pancreatic failure. Mikulicz's disease (lacrimal, parotid, and submandibular gland enlargement), once thought to be a Sjogren's subset, is one of the most common presentations of IgG4-RD. Allergic features are common: atopy, eczema, asthma, nasal polyps, sinusitis, and modest peripheral eosinophilia. Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis classically shows a diffusely enlarged 'sausage-shaped' pancreas with loss of normal lobularity; 20-50% of patients present with acute glucose intolerance and a pancreatic mass mimicking adenocarcinoma. Diagnosis requires correlation of clinical, serologic, radiologic, and pathologic findings; pathology alone is never sufficient, and biopsy is often done mainly to exclude malignancy. Renal involvement (tubulointerstitial nephritis) is strongly associated with hypocomplementemia; membranous glomerulonephropathy is a less common renal manifestation that must be distinguished from idiopathic disease. Clinical course is variable: disease may relapse and remit within a given organ, accumulate new organ involvement over time, or be found incidentally on imaging. Disease can evolve over months, years, or even decades before an organ becomes symptomatic enough to prompt medical attention. New tumefactive mass mimicking cancer in pancreas, salivary gland, orbit, lung, or other organ. Obstructive jaundice from pancreatic or biliary involvement (undiagnosed/undertreated sclerosing cholangitis can lead to hepatic failure within months). Ureteral entrapment, hydronephrosis, postobstructive uropathy, and renal atrophy from retroperitoneal fibrosis. Aortic involvement causing aneurysm or dissection. Anterior pituitary hormone deficiency and/or central diabetes insipidus from hypothalamic-pituitary involvement. Spinal cord compression, cranial nerve palsies, or radiculopathy from hypertrophic pachymeningitis. Destructive bone lesions of sinuses, head, and middle ear mimicking granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Persistently rising serum IgG4 concentrations signaling risk of clinical flare and serious organ involvement. Coronary arteritis (wall thickening, periarterial encasement, stenosis, calcification, aneurysm/ectasia) in longstanding disease with high IgG4 and biomarker levels. Treating the disease as purely IgG4-antibody-mediated; the IgG4 molecule is largely noninflammatory and may be counterregulatory rather than a primary driver. Excluding the diagnosis because serum IgG4 is normal: ~30% of histologically proven cases have normal levels, and retroperitoneal fibrosis (often advanced/fibrotic at presentation) frequently shows normal IgG4. Missing markedly elevated IgG4 because of the prozone effect on nephelometry; suspect this when results are normal despite strong clinical features and re-test with dilution. Relying on pathology alone for diagnosis; histopathology, while characteristic, is essentially never diagnostic by itself and must be interpreted with clinical, serologic, and radiologic data. Mistaking tumefactive lesions for malignancy and proceeding to major resections (e.g., Whipple procedure, thyroidectomy) before the correct diagnosis is recognized. Histologic features such as intense neutrophilic infiltration, leukocytoclasis, granulomatous inflammation, multinucleated giant cells, or fibrinoid necrosis are uncommon in IgG4-RD and argue against the diagnosis. Assuming serum IgG4 reliably tracks disease activity; correlations are imperfect, levels often do not fully normalize, and remissions can occur with persistently elevated levels. IgG4-RD is characterized by a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells, a distinctive storiform (woven-mat / basket-weave) pattern of fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis reflecting vascular tropism, and a mild-to-moderate tissue eosinophilia. The infiltrate combines B cells (organized in germinal centers, with IgG4+ CD19/CD138 plasma cells radiating outward) and a more diffusely distributed, predominant population of CD4+ T cells. Despite the disease's name, the IgG4 molecule itself is not thought to directly drive injury in most organs: IgG4 undergoes Fab-arm exchange, binds antigen weakly, and has low affinity for Fc receptors and C1q, making it a generally noninflammatory immunoglobulin that may even play a counterregulatory role. A unique oligoclonally expanded CD4+ cytotoxic T cell, abundant at tissue sites, secretes interferon-gamma, TGF-beta, and interleukin-1 (driving storiform fibrosis) as well as perforin, granzymes A/B, and granulysin (mediating cytotoxicity), and appears to be a major disease driver. Oligoclonal plasmablast expansions in blood, with continuous B-cell/plasmablast antigen presentation, are thought to support these profibrotic, tissue-injuring CD4+ cytotoxic T cells. Course is generally subacute but can cause major morbidity and organ failure. Aggressive disease may rapidly produce end-stage liver disease, permanent pancreatic exocrine and endocrine (diabetes) impairment, renal atrophy, aortic dissection or aneurysm, and destructive sinonasal lesions. Some manifestations (e.g., IgG4-related lymphadenopathy) can remain indolent and asymptomatic for years. Even with apparently effective immunosuppression, renal atrophy is a frequent sequel to tubulointerstitial nephritis, and end-organ fibrotic damage may be irreversible if diagnosis is delayed. Relapses are common, including in patients with persistently normal IgG4 levels. No formal numeric severity score is given. Practical stratification distinguishes vital/organ-threatening involvement (e.g., pancreas, biliary tree/liver, kidneys, aorta, sinonasal destruction, pituitary, meninges) requiring prompt treatment from indolent manifestations (e.g., asymptomatic lymphadenopathy) amenable to watchful waiting with close monitoring; classification of disease itself relies on correlation of clinical, serologic, radiologic, and pathologic findings (ACR/EULAR classification criteria are referenced).

An aberrant immune response leads to infiltration of the bile duct walls by IgG4-positive plasma cells and lymphocytes, accompanied by storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis. This transmural inflammation thickens the duct wall and narrows the lumen, producing single or multiple strictures anywhere along the biliary tree, though the intrapancreatic distal bile duct is most often affected, frequently in association with autoimmune pancreatitis. The condition typically responds rapidly and completely to corticosteroids with resolution of strictures and jaundice; relapse is common in systemic IgG4-related disease and may require maintenance therapy, and untreated or refractory disease can progress to secondary biliary cirrhosis.

Fulminant papilloedema can cause rapid-onset blindness and constitutes an emergency (p.229). Inaccurate CSF opening-pressure readings at lumbar puncture are a common pitfall (p.229). Failing to exclude a dural venous sinus thrombosis before attributing raised pressure to IIH (p.229). Mistaking buried optic disc drusen (pseudopapilloedema) for true papilloedema, prompting an unnecessary work-up (p.229). Assuming a normal fundus excludes the diagnosis; IIH can occur without funduscopic changes, so formal perimetry is still warranted (p.117). Raised CSF pressure without a space-occupying lesion, occurring in the setting of obesity, female sex, and occasionally pregnancy; partial obstruction of the cerebral venous sinuses is found in a small number of cases (p.117). Stenosis at the transverse-sigmoid sinus junction is commonly present, providing the rationale for venous sinus stenting (p.229). Vitamin A excess is a recognised cause of pseudotumor cerebri (p.3379). Headache often improves within weeks of starting medical therapy (p.117). However, unremitting papilloedema leads to progressive peripheral field loss and optic atrophy, and fulminant cases can cause rapid blindness, so visual loss is the feared outcome that drives urgent intervention (p.229).

Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion through loss of the shared beta-1 chain of the interleukin-12 and interleukin-23 receptors Loss of the immunoglobulin and lymphocyte profile to rule out the condition Interleukin-12 and interleukin-23 share a common receptor beta-1 subunit encoded by IL12RB1, and this subunit is essential for both the interstitial space between epithelium and endothelium is the dominant site, but alveolar epithelium and endothelial (airway and vessel) cells also drive pathogenesis (p.2259). No single piece of data is diagnostic on its own; a confident ILD diagnosis requires the combined weight of clinical, laboratory, PFT, imaging and (when obtained) histopathologic findings, ideally reviewed in a multidisciplinary conference of pulmonologists, rheumatologists, radiologists and pathologists (pp.2259-2260). Fine end-inspiratory bibasal crackles described as sounding like Velcro being pulled apart are characteristic of fibrotic ILD such as IPF and may be one of the earliest signs (pp.2200, 2261). Egophony, whispered pectoriloquy and bronchial breath sounds suggest alveolar filling (e.g. pneumonia) rather than interstitial fibrosis (IPF); their absence helps distinguish fibrotic crackles from consolidation (p.2200). Age strongly shifts pretest probability: IPF is most common in patients over 60 and rare under 50, whereas sarcoidosis, CTD-ILD, LAM and pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically present between ages 20 and 40 (p.2260). On HRCT, apical-predominant interstitial thickening favours NSIP, whereas a basal and subpleural/dependent predominance favours IPF (p.2211). A dry cough can be the most prominent symptom of IPF; some patients (even with extensive disease) report no dyspnoea at all (p.2261). HRCT is now standard of care in initial ILD evaluation and can be diagnostic for IPF in the right clinical context, sparing the patient a lung biopsy (p.2262). BAL findings can point to specific entities: eosinophilia >25% suggests chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, fat globules in macrophages suggest lipoid pneumonia, and serial bloody lavage indicates diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (p.2262). A close relative with an idiopathic interstitial pneumonia is among the strongest risk factors for IPF; up to ~20% of pulmonary fibrosis is familial, and diverse IIP subtypes (IPF, NSIP, DIP) can run in the same family (p.2261). Acute exacerbation of IPF - acute (<30 days) onset of respiratory distress and hypoxaemia in a patient with underlying fibrosis, not explained by infection or heart failure; reported mortality >85% (p.2265) Acute interstitial pneumonia (Hamman-Rich) - acute respiratory distress and hypoxaemia with >50% mortality within 6 months (p.2265) Haemoptysis suggesting diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (Goodpasture's, GPA) or LAM - warrants urgent evaluation (p.2261) Honeycombing or extensive fibrosis on HRCT indicating advanced disease and worse prognosis (p.2262) Signs of advanced disease: cyanosis, digital clubbing and cor pulmonale (p.2262) Rapidly progressive ILD in anti-Jo-1-positive inflammatory myopathy (p.2266) A declining FVC on serial testing, which signals elevated mortality risk (p.2261) Attributing all wheezing to asthma - wheeze can reflect heart failure or other airway narrowing; conversely wheeze is uncommon in ILD but does occur in sarcoidosis, HP and eosinophilic GPA (pp.2200, 2262). Forgetting that a UIP pattern on biopsy is not unique to IPF - it also occurs in CTD (e.g. RA-associated) ILD (p.2260). Misreading acute ILD presentations as pneumonia, COPD exacerbation or heart failure, since acute ILD is unusual (p.2260). Treating presumed IPF with immunosuppression - this has been shown to increase morbidity and mortality in IPF (p.2263). Relying on PFT pattern to diagnose HP - HP can be restrictive or obstructive, so the pattern is not diagnostic (p.2229). Over-relying on HP serum precipitin panels - they cover a limited antigen set and frequently give false negatives, and a positive IgG alone does not confirm HP (p.2230). Confusing HP granulomas with sarcoidosis - HP granulomas are loose/poorly formed and peribronchiolar, whereas sarcoid granulomas are well-formed; caseating granulomas should prompt a search for infection (pp.2230, 2264). Assuming CTD must be apparent - ILD can precede other CTD features by years or be the sole manifestation (pp.2261, 2265). Diagnosing IPF without excluding a treatable mimic - heart failure, infection (e.g. PCP) and malignancy must be considered first (p.2260). ILDs are characterised by remodelling of the interstitium with variable degrees of inflammation and fibrosis, but alveolar epithelial and endothelial cell injury is also central to pathogenesis. The idiopathic interstitial pneumonias (IIPs) are the most common group. In IPF the histologic hallmark is a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern: subpleural reticulation with honeycomb change and fibroblast foci (subepithelial collections of myofibroblasts and collagen) alternating with preserved normal alveolar architecture, producing temporal and spatial heterogeneity. NSIP shows more uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis with honeycombing usually absent and fibroblast foci rare. Genetic studies show that a substantial fraction of familial and even sporadic/idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has a genetic basis: a MUC5B promoter variant (present in ~20% of Caucasians, 35-45% of IPF patients) confers an approximately sixfold risk, and variants in telomere-length genes (TERT, TERC, RTEL1) and surfactant protein genes (SFTPA2) are also implicated. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is an immune-mediated response to inhaled antigens small enough to reach distal airways and alveoli, driven by dysregulated TH1/TH17 responses with precipitating IgG and innate (Toll-like receptor/MyD88) signalling; chronic HP shares the MUC5B variant with IPF (pp.2259-2266; 2228-2229). Prognosis varies widely by ILD subtype and disease extent. IPF carries a poor prognosis (~50% survival at 3-5 years; pre-antifibrotic-era life expectancy 3-5 years from diagnosis). Idiopathic NSIP is comparatively favourable (>80% 5-year survival), with cellular NSIP doing better than fibrosing NSIP. Reported subtype mortality includes RB-ILD ~25% at 7 years and systemic sclerosis-associated ILD ~20-30% at 10 years; sarcoidosis mortality is generally low but state-dependent. RB-ILD usually has prolonged survival with death from progressive ILD rare. AIP has >50% 6-month mortality with frequent recurrences, though survivors can recover substantial lung function. Acute exacerbations of fibrotic ILD carry very high mortality (>85%). In CTD-ILD, a UIP pattern and more extensive fibrosis (e.g. in RA) predict reduced survival. Chronic fibrotic HP can mirror IPF in radiology and prognosis (pp.2260, 2262-2266; 2229). Harrison frames ILD pattern recognition rather than a single numeric severity score. ILDs are first split into known cause (occupational e.g. asbestosis/silicosis; drug-induced e.g. amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, methotrexate, bleomycin; systemic/CTD-associated; granulomatous including HP) versus unknown cause (idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, plus rarer entities such as LAM, PAP, PLCH, sarcoidosis). The idiopathic interstitial pneumonias are further classified (per the ATS/ERS consensus) into chronic fibrosing (IPF, idiopathic NSIP), smoking-related (RB-ILD, DIP), and acute/subacute (COP, acute interstitial pneumonia, lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia). The UIP pattern (subpleural, basal reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis) defines IPF, while NSIP shows more ground-glass and rare honeycombing. HP is now classified as nonfibrotic versus fibrotic (replacing the older acute/subacute/chronic terminology). Disease severity is gauged by extent of fibrosis/honeycombing on HRCT, degree of PFT (FVC/DLCO) impairment and its rate of decline, and presence of pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale (pp.2259-2266; 2229).

iliotibial band friction syndrome — iliotibial band syndrome, ITB friction syndrome, lateral runner's knee Lateral meniscal tear Patellofemoral pain syndrome Biceps femoris tendinopathy Popliteus tendinopathy Lateral collateral ligament injury Proximal tibiofibular joint pathology Common peroneal nerve entrapment or referred lumbar pain Primarily a clinical diagnosis based on history and provocation testing MRI showing oedema and thickening deep to the iliotibial band at the lateral epicondyle and excluding intra-articular pathology Ultrasound of the region for dynamic assessment, band thickness and fluid Running and gait biomechanical analysis Hip abductor strength testing Lower limb alignment assessment for genu varum and foot posture Radiographs to exclude other lateral knee pathology in atypical presentations The commonest cause of lateral knee pain in runners and cyclists, and an overuse rather than traumatic injury. Pain is well localised to the lateral femoral epicondyle and is typically provoked near early flexion around foot strike during running. Symptoms worsen with downhill running and a lengthened stride, ease with rest, and reliably recur on resuming activity. Noble's compression test over the lateral epicondyle during extension and Ober's test for iliotibial band tightness support the diagnosis. Weak hip abductors with increased hip adduction and internal rotation, genu varum, excessive foot pronation and a sudden training-load increase are key risk factors. Current understanding favours compression of a richly innervated fat and connective tissue layer beneath the band rather than a true friction or bursal mechanism. Management is conservative: relative rest and load management, hip abductor and gluteal strengthening, and correction of gait and biomechanics. Point tenderness over the epicondyle rather than the joint line helps distinguish it from lateral meniscal or patellofemoral pathology. Locking, catching or effusion suggesting intra-articular meniscal or chondral pathology Lateral joint line tenderness with positive meniscal provocation rather than epicondylar tenderness Neurological symptoms such as foot drop or paraesthesia suggesting common peroneal nerve involvement Rest or night pain and systemic features suggesting infection or neoplasm Focusing on stretching the band while neglecting hip abductor strengthening and gait correction. Misdiagnosing the condition as lateral meniscal pathology, or the reverse. Failing to identify and correct training errors, leading to recurrence. Repeated corticosteroid injection without addressing the underlying biomechanics. Assuming the iliotibial band can be meaningfully lengthened by stretching alone. The iliotibial band is a thickened longitudinal reinforcement of the fascia lata extending from the tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus to Gerdy's tubercle on the anterolateral tibia. During repetitive knee flexion and extension the posterior fibres of the band shift relative to the lateral femoral epicondyle, and near early flexion they compress a well-innervated, vascular layer of fat and connective tissue against the epicondyle. Repetitive compression, rather than a true friction or bursal process, produces local inflammation and pain. Contributing biomechanical factors include hip abductor weakness that increases hip adduction and internal rotation, genu varum, and training errors such as a rapid increase in mileage or downhill running, all of which raise the compressive load on the tissue deep to the band. The great majority respond to load management and correction of biomechanical and strength deficits over weeks to months; recurrence relates to inadequate rehabilitation or unaddressed training errors, and surgery is rarely required.

Iliotibial band syndrome arises when repetitive knee flexion and extension causes the distal iliotibial band to compress the underlying highly vascular and innervated connective and fatty tissue against the lateral femoral epicondyle, particularly around thirty degrees of flexion. This produces local inflammation and pain. Hip abductor weakness, training overload, downhill running and lower-limb malalignment predispose to the condition. It was historically attributed to friction of the band moving back and forth over the epicondyle. The outlook is good with conservative management and correction of training and biomechanical factors, though the condition tends to recur if these factors are left unaddressed.

indispensable structural subunit of Polycomb Repressive Complex 2, the assembly that, through its catalytic partner EZH2, deposits the repressive mark H3K27me3 to keep developmental genes Pathogenic SUZ12 variants destabilise the complex and impair its methyltransferase activity, weakening repression of genes that drive growth and proliferation. The consequent loss of transcriptional restraint produces generalised overgrowth, advanced skeletal maturation and disordered neurodevelopment, and because Weaver, Cohen-Gibson and Imagawa-Matsumoto syndromes all disable this single complex, they present with strongly overlapping clinical features. Data are limited by rarity, but the picture resembles the wider PRC2 overgrowth group, with persistent overgrowth and intellectual disability of variable severity; life expectancy is not clearly reduced without malignancy, and care centres on developmental support, orthopaedic monitoring and tumour vigilance.

Imerslund-Grasbeck syndrome — IGS, selective vitamin B12 malabsorption with proteinuria, megaloblastic anaemia 1, CUBN, AMN Pernicious anaemia and juvenile pernicious anaemia Transcobalamin deficiency Intrinsic factor deficiency (hereditary) Nutritional vitamin B12 deficiency Other causes of childhood megaloblastic anaemia (folate deficiency) Chronic ileal disease causing B12 malabsorption CUBN and AMN molecular genetic testing Serum vitamin B12 with plasma homocysteine and methylmalonic acid Full blood count and blood film for megaloblastic anaemia Urinalysis and quantification of low-molecular-weight proteinuria Intrinsic factor antibody and gastric studies to exclude pernicious anaemia Bone marrow examination when needed Consider it in a child with megaloblastic anaemia and low serum B12 who also has mild, benign proteinuria Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in CUBN (cubilin) or AMN (amnionless), which together form the cubam receptor for intrinsic factor-B12 complex in the terminal ileum The receptor defect blocks ileal absorption of the intrinsic factor-B12 complex, causing selective B12 malabsorption Cubilin also mediates renal tubular protein reabsorption, so tubular (low-molecular-weight) proteinuria is a characteristic feature, especially with CUBN variants Typical onset is in infancy or early childhood with anaemia, failure to thrive, recurrent infection and sometimes neurological signs Lifelong parenteral B12 corrects the anaemia and neurological features; the proteinuria persists but is generally benign Intrinsic factor level and gastric parietal cell function are normal, distinguishing it from pernicious anaemia The Schilling test historically showed malabsorption not corrected by intrinsic factor, reflecting the ileal receptor defect Neurological features of B12 deficiency such as regression or subacute combined degeneration Severe symptomatic anaemia in infancy Recurrent infection from associated cytopenias Failure to thrive Overlooking the diagnosis when proteinuria is dismissed as unrelated Attributing B12 deficiency to diet or pernicious anaemia without testing absorption or genetics Relying on oral B12, which cannot bypass the ileal receptor defect reliably Assuming the proteinuria signifies progressive renal disease Imerslund-Grasbeck syndrome is a selective inherited defect of vitamin B12 absorption. The cubam receptor, formed by cubilin (CUBN) and amnionless (AMN), mediates endocytosis of the intrinsic factor-B12 complex at the brush border of terminal ileal enterocytes. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in either gene disable this receptor, so dietary B12 that has bound intrinsic factor cannot be taken up, producing systemic B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anaemia and, if prolonged, neurological dysfunction. Because cubilin is also expressed in the renal proximal tubule where it reclaims filtered proteins, its deficiency additionally causes low-grade tubular proteinuria. Bypassing the absorptive defect with parenteral B12 restores cobalamin status. Lifelong parenteral B12 fully corrects the anaemia and prevents neurological complications, giving an excellent outlook; the accompanying proteinuria usually remains mild and non-progressive.

Familial iminoglycinuria — iminoglycinuria, familial renal iminoglycinuria, hyperglycinuria with iminoaciduria, proline glycine hydroxyproline transporter defect, SLC36A2 Physiological neonatal iminoglycinuria before transporter maturation Isolated hyperglycinuria (a related partial transport defect) Generalised aminoaciduria of renal Fanconi syndrome Non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia (a plasma, not urinary transport, disorder) Secondary aminoaciduria from tubular toxins or heavy metals Hydroxyprolinaemia and other imino acid metabolic disorders Urine amino acid chromatography showing raised glycine, proline and hydroxyproline Plasma amino acids to confirm normal circulating levels Assessment of other tubular functions to exclude generalised Fanconi syndrome Family studies, as the trait segregates in relatives SLC36A2 (and modifier gene) sequencing where confirmation is desired Repeat testing beyond infancy if the pattern was found in a young neonate A benign inherited trait of impaired proximal renal tubular reabsorption of the imino acids proline and hydroxyproline together with glycine The main gene is SLC36A2 (the PAT2 transporter), with SLC6A20, SLC6A19 and SLC6A18 acting as modifiers of the phenotype Diagnosed by the characteristic urinary pattern of increased glycine, proline and hydroxyproline with normal plasma levels Essentially asymptomatic and usually an incidental laboratory finding of no clinical consequence Newborns physiologically excrete imino acids and glycine until tubular transporters mature at around six months, so the pattern is normal in early infancy Older weak associations with conditions such as stones or neurological problems reflect ascertainment bias rather than causation No treatment is needed; the key task is reassurance and avoiding overinvestigation It should not be confused with hyperglycinaemia or with generalised aminoaciduria of Fanconi syndrome Accompanying glycosuria, phosphaturia or proteinuria suggesting generalised tubular dysfunction rather than isolated iminoglycinuria Raised plasma glycine indicating a systemic disorder such as non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia Growth failure or acidosis pointing to a tubulopathy Persistence attributed to disease when the finding is a benign trait Interpreting the neonatal physiological pattern as a pathological transport defect Confusing urinary iminoglycinuria with plasma hyperglycinaemia and initiating inappropriate workup Pursuing extensive investigation or treatment for a benign incidental finding Overlooking a broader Fanconi syndrome when other solutes are also being lost Reabsorption of glycine and the imino acids proline and hydroxyproline from the glomerular filtrate depends on a set of proximal tubular transporters, chiefly the proton-coupled amino acid transporter PAT2 encoded by SLC36A2, with contributions from additional transporters that also handle these substrates. When transporter function is reduced, filtered glycine, proline and hydroxyproline are incompletely reabsorbed and appear in excess in the urine while remaining normal in plasma. Because these amino acids are non-essential and the losses are modest, there is no metabolic deficiency or tissue consequence, so the trait is clinically silent. The prognosis is excellent; iminoglycinuria is a lifelong but harmless trait with no impact on health, growth or life expectancy.

immature teratoma — immature teratoma of ovary, malignant teratoma mature cystic teratoma with torsion yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumour dysgerminoma mixed germ cell tumour ovarian neuroectodermal tumour small round blue cell tumours involving the ovary carcinosarcoma of the ovary serum alpha-fetoprotein serum beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin serum lactate dehydrogenase pelvic ultrasound and MRI to characterise the mass CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging histological grading of the primary tumour and any peritoneal implants beta-hCG and AFP monitoring during follow-up A malignant ovarian germ cell tumour of children and young women, defined by the presence of immature (usually neuroepithelial) tissue, in contrast to the common benign mature cystic teratoma. Grading is based on the quantity of immature neuroepithelium, and a widely used two-tier scheme divides tumours into low grade and high grade, which guides the need for chemotherapy. Serum alpha-fetoprotein may be mildly elevated, and a markedly raised level should prompt a search for a yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumour component within a mixed germ cell tumour. Typical presentation is a rapidly enlarging, often large, solid or mixed solid-cystic adnexal mass in an adolescent or young woman, sometimes complicated by torsion or rupture. Fertility-sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with surgical staging is the standard operation, since the disease is usually unilateral and preserving the uterus and contralateral ovary is a priority in this young population. Adjuvant platinum-based combination chemotherapy is highly effective for higher-grade or advanced disease, and many low-grade, stage-confined tumours can be managed with surgery and surveillance alone. Peritoneal and lymph node deposits should be assessed for grade, and mature glial implants on the peritoneum (gliomatosis peritonei) are typically benign and do not by themselves worsen the prognosis. Growing teratoma syndrome, the enlargement of mature teratomatous masses during or after chemotherapy with normal markers, requires surgical excision rather than more chemotherapy. rapidly enlarging pelvic mass in an adolescent or young woman markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein suggesting a yolk sac component acute abdomen from torsion or rupture enlarging masses during chemotherapy with normalising markers suggesting growing teratoma syndrome peritoneal or nodal deposits containing immature elements Confusing an immature teratoma with a benign mature cystic teratoma on imaging and undertreating it. Overlooking a coexisting yolk sac tumour when alpha-fetoprotein is markedly raised. Grading the primary but neglecting to grade peritoneal implants, which independently affects management. Treating growing teratoma syndrome with further chemotherapy instead of surgical excision. Performing unnecessarily radical surgery in a young woman when fertility-sparing resection with staging is appropriate. Immature teratomas are germ cell tumours arising from a totipotent germ cell that differentiates along all three embryonic germ layers but, unlike mature teratoma, retains variable amounts of immature, embryonal-type tissue. The immature component is most often primitive neuroectoderm forming neuroepithelial rosettes and tubules, and the amount of this tissue determines tumour grade and malignant potential. As a germ cell neoplasm of the young ovary, it grows rapidly and can seed the peritoneum; implants may be immature (worsening prognosis) or may mature over time into benign glial nodules. Some tumours coexist with other germ cell elements such as yolk sac tumour, accounting for occasional marker elevation. The tendency of residual disease to differentiate into mature tissue under chemotherapy underlies the growing teratoma syndrome and the general principle that grade of both primary and implants dictates management. With fertility-sparing surgery and, where indicated, platinum-based chemotherapy, cure rates are high, particularly for low-grade and early-stage disease; prognosis worsens with higher grade, advanced stage and the presence of immature peritoneal implants.

The quantity of this immature neuroepithelium underlies the histological grading system, with higher grades reflecting greater immaturity and more aggressive potential. Because the tumour arises from a germ cell, it may coexist with other germ-cell elements, and any yolk sac component can raise serum alpha-fetoprotein. Mature glial implants on the peritoneum (gliomatosis peritonei) represent differentiation of tumour tissue and, when entirely mature, carry a benign course, whereas immature implants indicate genuine dissemination. Depends heavily on grade and stage; low-grade, early-stage tumours have an excellent outlook, and higher-grade or advanced disease responds well to chemotherapy so that cure remains common, often with fertility preserved.

Two defining myositis-specific antibodies: anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR; a seronegative subgroup also exists. Anti-HMGCR disease is associated with prior statin exposure, but occurs without statins, particularly in younger patients, and weakness progresses despite drug withdrawal. Persistence or progression of weakness after stopping a statin distinguishes immune-mediated necrotising myopathy from self-limited toxic statin myopathy. Muscle biopsy shows scattered necrotic and regenerating fibres with sparse inflammatory infiltrate, sarcolemmal MHC-I upregulation and membrane-attack-complex deposition on capillaries and non-necrotic fibres. Anti-SRP disease tends to be more severe, treatment-resistant and may involve the myocardium; anti-HMGCR disease often responds well to intravenous immunoglobulin. Dysphagia is common and an early marker of disease severity. An underlying occult malignancy should be considered, particularly in older and seronegative patients. Dysphagia with aspiration risk Respiratory muscle weakness and falling respiratory reserve Cardiac involvement, particularly in anti-SRP disease Rapidly progressive generalised weakness Features suggesting an underlying malignancy Misattributing persistent weakness to self-limited statin myopathy when it is in fact anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy. Interpreting the sparse inflammatory infiltrate on biopsy as a muscular dystrophy and overlooking complement and MHC-I markers. Failing to recognise the seronegative subgroup when standard antibody testing is negative. Omitting cardiac assessment and malignancy screening. Undertreating anti-SRP disease, which typically needs early aggressive immunosuppression. Immune-mediated necrotising myopathy is a humorally driven idiopathic inflammatory myopathy in which antibodies, rather than a T-cell-rich infiltrate, are thought to be directly pathogenic. Circulating anti-signal-recognition-particle (anti-SRP) and anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme-A-reductase (anti-HMGCR) antibodies target antigens expressed on the myofibre surface, with antibody titres broadly tracking disease activity. Complement is activated on the sarcolemma and capillaries, generating membrane-attack complex and leading to repeated cycles of myofibre necrosis and regeneration. Because regenerating fibres re-express HMGCR, which is upregulated by statins, statin exposure is thought to prime and sustain the anti-HMGCR response in genetically susceptible individuals, so autoimmunity continues even after the drug is withdrawn. The course is typically chronic and frequently treatment-refractory, especially with anti-SRP antibodies, requiring prolonged combination immunotherapy and carrying a high relapse rate on tapering. Anti-HMGCR disease often responds well to intravenous immunoglobulin, whereas untreated disease may lead to fixed proximal weakness and disability.

immune thrombocytopenia — ITP, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura pseudothrombocytopenia due to EDTA-induced platelet clumping drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia hypersplenism myelodysplasia or other marrow failure and infiltration thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or haemolytic uraemic syndrome heparin-induced thrombocytopenia gestational thrombocytopenia full blood count and blood film to confirm true isolated thrombocytopenia and exclude clumping or blasts HIV and hepatitis C serology immunoglobulin levels antinuclear antibody and autoimmune screen Helicobacter pylori testing direct antiglobulin test where there is coexisting anaemia (to detect Evans syndrome) bone marrow examination in atypical presentations or older patients ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion, defined by isolated thrombocytopenia with an otherwise normal full blood count and blood film and no alternative explanation. It is mediated by antiplatelet autoantibodies that cause accelerated splenic destruction of platelets and also impair megakaryocyte platelet production. It may be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and lymphoma, HIV, hepatitis C, Helicobacter pylori, drugs or common variable immunodeficiency. Bleeding is typically mucocutaneous, with petechiae, purpura, epistaxis and menorrhagia, and the risk of serious internal bleeding correlates only loosely with the platelet count. Childhood ITP is usually acute and self-limiting, often following a viral illness, whereas adult ITP more often runs a chronic course. Bone marrow examination is not required in typical cases but is considered where features are atypical, before splenectomy, or in older patients to exclude myelodysplasia. Treatment (corticosteroids with or without intravenous immunoglobulin) is reserved for significant bleeding or a very low count, and many patients can safely be observed. Second-line options include thrombopoietin receptor agonists, rituximab and splenectomy, and the therapeutic aim is a safe haemostatic count rather than a normal platelet count. headache, vomiting or focal neurology suggesting intracranial haemorrhage gastrointestinal bleeding such as melaena or haematemesis extensive wet purpura with mucosal (buccal or gingival) bleeding gross haematuria profound thrombocytopenia accompanied by active bleeding missing pseudothrombocytopenia and treating a spurious low count caused by EDTA-dependent clumping over-treating asymptomatic mild thrombocytopenia rather than observing failing to look for secondary causes such as HIV, hepatitis C, lupus or a lymphoproliferative disorder expecting platelet transfusion to be effective outside life-threatening bleeding, when transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed overlooking myelodysplasia in an older patient with apparently isolated thrombocytopenia ITP arises from a loss of immune tolerance to platelet surface antigens, generating IgG autoantibodies directed chiefly against the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa and Ib/IX complexes. Antibody-coated platelets are recognised by Fc receptors on splenic and hepatic macrophages and cleared prematurely, shortening platelet lifespan. The same autoantibodies and dysregulated T-cell responses also act on megakaryocytes to impair platelet production, so the marrow response is inappropriately blunted rather than compensatory. Cytotoxic T lymphocytes and abnormalities of regulatory T-cell function contribute to the sustained autoimmune process, and in secondary ITP an underlying infection, lymphoproliferative disorder, autoimmune disease or drug drives the antiplatelet response. The overall outlook is good; most children remit spontaneously within weeks to months, and although adult disease is frequently chronic it is usually manageable, with serious haemorrhage being uncommon.

the syndromic and cytogenetic clues Not requesting cytogenetics, thereby missing the diagnostic centromeric instability Assuming the presence of B cells excludes a significant antibody deficiency Attributing the facial and developmental features to an unrelated syndrome Overlooking the epigenetic basis and the possible need for transplantation in severe cases ICF syndrome is an inherited disorder of DNA methylation. In the commonest form, biallelic loss-of-function variants in the DNA methyltransferase DNMT3B, or in the related factors ZBTB24, CDCA7 or HELLS, impair methylation of satellite repeat DNA in pericentromeric heterochromatin. The resulting hypomethylation destabilises these regions, producing the characteristic centromeric chromosomal rearrangements, and disturbs the regulated gene-expression programmes needed for normal lymphocyte development and terminal B-cell differentiation. Consequently, although B cells may be present, they fail to mature into effective antibody-secreting cells, giving hypogammaglobulinaemia and a predominantly humoral immunodeficiency, with variable T-cell involvement and the associated developmental and facial features. Prognosis depends on the severity of the antibody deficiency and any T-cell involvement; recurrent infection can be life-limiting, but immunoglobulin replacement improves outcome and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be considered where cellular immunity is severely affected.

on immunofluorescence Overlooking the diagnosis because of its rarity in a nephrotic patient Immunotactoid glomerulopathy results from glomerular deposition of immunoglobulin that organises into hollow microtubular structures, usually 30 to 50 nanometres in diameter, aligned in parallel arrays within the mesangium and capillary walls. The deposits are commonly monoclonal, reflecting an underlying clonal B-cell or plasma-cell population that produces an immunoglobulin prone to crystalline or microtubular self-assembly. Accumulation disrupts the glomerular filtration barrier and triggers a proliferative or membranoproliferative injury pattern, causing proteinuria, haematuria and progressive glomerulosclerosis. The association with lymphoproliferative disease and paraproteinaemia underpins the rationale for treating the causative clone. Renal outcome is closely tied to identification and treatment of the underlying clone; clone-directed therapy can stabilise or improve renal function, whereas untreated disease tends to progress. Because of the strong haematological association, prognosis also depends on the behaviour of the associated lymphoproliferative disorder.

presenting with chest pain, arrhythmia, or heart failure, which can be rapidly fatal Severe immune colitis with profuse diarrhoea, dehydration, and risk of bowel perforation Pneumonitis with hypoxia and progressive breathlessness Adrenal crisis from unrecognised hypophysitis or adrenal insufficiency, and other severe events such as neurological or hepatic toxicity Attributing new symptoms to infection or cancer progression and missing an immune-related cause Delaying corticosteroids in severe toxicity while awaiting further tests Overlooking endocrine toxicity and failing to replace deficient hormones, risking adrenal crisis Assuming toxicity cannot occur because therapy was stopped weeks or months earlier Immune checkpoint inhibitors release the normal brakes on T-cell activation by blocking inhibitory pathways such as CTLA-4 and the PD-1/PD-L1 axis. This enhances antitumour immunity but also reduces self-tolerance, allowing activated T cells, autoantibodies, and inflammatory cytokines to attack normal tissues. The resulting immune-related adverse events reflect off-target autoimmune inflammation that can involve the skin, gut, liver, endocrine glands, lungs, heart, kidneys, nervous system, and other organs, with severity ranging from mild to fatal. Most immune-related adverse events are reversible with prompt recognition, drug interruption, and immunosuppression, but severe events such as myocarditis, colitis with perforation, or pneumonitis carry significant mortality, and some endocrine effects are permanent.

colostogram and cross-table lateral radiography help define the anatomy before definitive repair Signs of intestinal obstruction (abdominal distension, bilious vomiting) requiring urgent decompression and surgical review Meconium in the urine indicating a rectourinary fistula and risk of urinary contamination Associated cardiac or renal anomalies that may destabilise the neonate before surgery Failure to identify any perineal opening in a distended infant, mandating prompt surgical decompression Missing the diagnosis when a perineal fistula allows some meconium to pass, giving false reassurance Attempting a primary perineal repair on a high lesion without a protective colostomy Overlooking associated VACTERL anomalies, particularly cardiac and renal lesions Underestimating the long-term need for bowel management and continence follow-up Imperforate anus results from abnormal development of the hindgut and its separation from the urogenital sinus during early embryogenesis, so the terminal rectum fails to descend and open normally onto the perineum. The rectal pouch commonly ends blindly or communicates through a fistula with the urinary system, vagina, or perineal skin. The relationship of the pouch to the levator ani and external sphincter complex, together with the degree of sacral and spinal development, determines whether continence structures are adequate and largely predicts functional outcome. Outcomes vary with the type of malformation: low lesions with good sphincter and sacral development often achieve near-normal continence, while high or cloacal lesions carry higher rates of faecal incontinence and constipation requiring long-term bowel management. Associated anomalies significantly influence overall morbidity.

bulging bluish membrane at the introitus Pelvic (often transabdominal or perineal) ultrasound to demonstrate haematocolpos and haematometra Magnetic resonance imaging where the level or nature of urinary tract malformations An imperforate hymen is a persistent membrane that completely occludes the vaginal opening, and it is the commonest obstructive anomaly of the female genital tract The classic adolescent presentation is primary amenorrhoea with cyclical lower abdominal or pelvic pain, because menstrual blood cannot escape and accumulates behind the obstruction Retained blood distends the vagina (haematocolpos) and may extend to the uterus (haematometra), producing a lower abdominal mass and, at times, urinary retention from pressure on the urethra or bladder Secondary sexual characteristics are normal because ovarian function and the endocrine axis are intact, distinguishing it from causes of primary amenorrhoea due to hormonal failure On inspection the hymen typically bulges as a tense, bluish membrane, and a rectal or abdominal examination may reveal a pelvic mass of retained blood It can occasionally present in neonates as a mucocolpos from mucus accumulation driven by maternal oestrogen, seen as a bulging introital membrane Definitive treatment is surgical incision of the membrane, classically a cruciate incision, to release the retained blood and restore patency, ideally performed electively rather than as an emergency Aspiration alone should be avoided because it risks introducing infection into a closed collection of blood Acute urinary retention or severe pain from a large obstructing collection Features suggesting a more proximal or complex obstruction rather than a simple imperforate hymen Signs of infection within a retained blood collection A pelvic mass of uncertain nature requiring urgent imaging Overlooking imperforate hymen in an adolescent with cyclical pain and primary amenorrhoea by not inspecting the introitus Confusing it with a transverse vaginal septum, which sits higher and needs different surgical planning Aspirating the collection rather than performing formal incision, risking infection Attributing normal pubertal development plus amenorrhoea to hormonal causes and missing an obstructive anomaly Failing to arrange renal tract imaging for associated urinary anomalies The hymen represents the junction between the sinovaginal bulbs and the urogenital sinus and normally becomes perforate before or around birth. When canalisation fails, a complete membrane persists across the vaginal introitus. Before menarche this is usually silent, but once ovulatory cycles begin, endometrial shedding produces menstrual blood that cannot drain. Blood collects first in the vagina (haematocolpos) and then in the uterus (haematometra), and with time can reflux along the tubes (haematosalpinx). The expanding collection causes cyclical pain and a pelvic mass and may compress the urethra or rectum. Because the ovaries and hormonal axis are unaffected, pubertal development proceeds normally despite the absence of visible menstruation. The outlook after timely surgical release is excellent, with restoration of normal menstruation and preservation of fertility; delayed diagnosis can allow complications such as endometriosis from retrograde menstruation or, rarely, infection of the retained blood.

children away from school or nursery until lesions have crusted or treatment has been under way for the recommended period Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a recognised complication following certain streptococcal strains, so watch for signs such as dark urine or oedema Recurrent impetigo warrants consideration of staphylococcal carriage and decolonisation Rapidly spreading erythema, pain out of proportion, or systemic toxicity suggesting cellulitis or a deeper, necrotising infection Widespread tender blistering and skin peeling in a young child indicating staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome Features of eczema herpeticum such as punched-out erosions and systemic upset in an atopic patient Dark urine, facial oedema, or hypertension after infection suggesting post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis Missing an underlying dermatosis such as scabies or eczema that will drive recurrence if untreated Failing to recognise eczema herpeticum and treating presumed impetigo with antibiotics alone Overusing topical antibiotics and promoting resistance Neglecting infection-control advice, allowing continued spread among household and school contacts Impetigo is a superficial bacterial infection of the epidermis caused predominantly by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, alone or together. Organisms colonise and then invade skin whose barrier has been breached by minor trauma, bites, or pre-existing dermatoses. In bullous disease, staphylococcal exfoliative toxins cleave desmoglein-1 in the superficial epidermis, causing intraepidermal separation and blister formation. The host inflammatory response and serous exudate dry to form the typical crusts. Certain nephritogenic streptococcal strains can trigger immune-complex-mediated post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Impetigo generally responds well to treatment and often heals without scarring, though it can recur, particularly with staphylococcal carriage or an untreated underlying skin condition; serious sequelae are uncommon but include post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
