commonest reasons for orthopaedic referral in childhood and is usually a normal variant that provokes more parental than functional concern The three anatomical levels responsible are the foot (metatarsus adductus), the leg (internal tibial torsion), and the hip (increased femoral anteversion), and each predominates at a characteristic age Metatarsus adductus dominates in infancy, internal tibial torsion in the toddler, and femoral anteversion in the older preschool and early school child A systematic rotational profile with the foot progression angle localises the level of the deformity and guides counselling The great majority of cases are physiological, symmetrical, painless, and resolve spontaneously as the skeleton matures Reassurance and periodic observation are the mainstays, and orthotics, special shoes, braces, and exercises do not alter the natural history Surgery is exceptional and reserved for severe, persistent, functionally significant torsional deformity in the older child Progressive deformity rather than the expected improvement with growth Marked asymmetry or unilateral in-toeing Pain, limp, or functional limitation Neurological signs suggesting cerebral palsy or another neuromuscular disorder Short stature or dysmorphism suggesting a skeletal dysplasia Treating a benign variant with ineffective braces, cables, or special footwear Failing to localise the level of the deformity with a proper rotational profile Overlooking asymmetry, pain, or neurological signs that point to a pathological cause Recommending surgery prematurely before natural derotation is complete Providing reassurance without arranging follow-up when the presentation is atypical In-toeing is a symptom rather than a single disease, describing an inwardly directed foot progression angle during gait that arises from rotational alignment at one or more levels of the lower limb. Most commonly it reflects the normal sequence of skeletal maturation, in which fetal internal torsion of the tibia and high femoral anteversion gradually derotate through childhood; a lag in this process leaves a residual inward rotation. At the foot, medial deviation of the metatarsals in metatarsus adductus contributes. Pathological in-toeing is uncommon and is largely confined to neuromuscular conditions such as cerebral palsy, in which spasticity and failure of physiological derotation maintain the inward gait. The outlook is excellent, with spontaneous resolution in the overwhelming majority as the tibia and femur derotate with growth, and normal function without arthritic consequence is the expected outcome for physiological in-toeing.

Incisional hernia — ventral incisional hernia, post-operative hernia Divarication of the recti Recurrent primary ventral hernia at another site Seroma or haematoma at the operative site Abdominal wall defects with a narrow neck carry a higher risk of incarceration and strangulation than broad-necked defects Very large hernias may result in loss of abdominal domain, where returning contents to the associated with the hernia Skin breakdown or ischaemia over a large or rapidly enlarging hernia Systemic sepsis or peritonism from strangulated bowel Performing suture-only repair of a sizeable defect and accepting a high recurrence risk Failing to optimise obesity, diabetes, and smoking before elective repair Underestimating loss of domain and precipitating abdominal compartment syndrome at repair Overlooking a small tender defect that is at high risk of strangulation An incisional hernia develops when the musculo-aponeurotic layers of a healed surgical wound fail to maintain their integrity, allowing peritoneum and abdominal contents to protrude beneath the intact skin. Impaired wound healing, whether from infection, ischaemia, raised intra-abdominal pressure, technical factors, or patient factors such as obesity, diabetes, and malnutrition, weakens the fascial repair. Over time the defect enlarges and the sac expands, sometimes housing much of the abdominal contents. Narrow-necked defects can trap and strangulate bowel, while very large defects lead to loss of domain and altered abdominal wall mechanics. Recurrence rates are higher than for primary hernias but are substantially reduced by mesh repair and by optimising risk factors. Large hernias with loss of domain require specialised techniques and carry greater perioperative risk, while emergency presentation with strangulation increases morbidity.

or bulbar deterioration Misdiagnosing it as treatment-resistant polymyositis and prolonging futile immunosuppression Being reassured by a normal creatine kinase into excluding a myopathy Overlooking the diagnostic finger-flexor and quadriceps weakness pattern Failing to recognise and manage dysphagia and aspiration risk Sporadic inclusion body myositis is a slowly progressive myopathy with combined inflammatory and degenerative features. Endomysial T-cell infiltration and up-regulation of major histocompatibility complex on muscle fibres coexist with a degenerative process marked by rimmed vacuoles and intracellular accumulation of misfolded proteins, including beta-amyloid, phosphorylated tau, TDP-43, and p62. The relative contribution of autoimmunity and protein mishandling remains debated, but the degenerative component is thought to explain the characteristic treatment resistance and the selective, progressive involvement of finger flexors and quadriceps. The condition progresses slowly but relentlessly over years, leading to significant disability, dependence on mobility aids, and swallowing difficulties; life expectancy is relatively preserved but quality of life declines with functional loss.

Incontinentia pigmenti — IKBKG, NEMO, Bloch-Sulzberger syndrome, IP Neonatal herpes simplex or bullous impetigo (vesicular stage) Epidermolytic ichthyosis and other blistering genodermatoses Linear and whorled naevoid hypermelanosis Hypomelanosis of Ito (late hypopigmented stage) Epidermal naevi (verrucous stage) IKBKG molecular genetic testing (including the common deletion) Skin biopsy showing stage-dependent features including eosinophilic spongiosis or dermal pigment incontinence Full blood count for peripheral eosinophilia in the neonatal period Urgent paediatric ophthalmology review with retinal examination and fluorescein angiography Neuroimaging and EEG if neurological symptoms occur Dental assessment for tooth anomalies X-linked dominant disorder caused by variants in IKBKG (NEMO); usually lethal in males in utero, so it predominantly affects females Skin lesions evolve through four classic stages along Blaschko lines: vesicular, verrucous, hyperpigmented (whorled/swirled), and atrophic/hypopigmented The blistering first stage in a neonate can be mistaken for infection, and there is often a peripheral eosinophilia Associated dental anomalies (peg or missing teeth), alopecia, and nail dystrophy are common Ocular involvement includes a retinal vasculopathy that can cause retinal detachment and blindness if not detected Neurological complications (seizures, stroke-like episodes, developmental delay) may occur, mainly in the neonatal period Diagnosis rests on characteristic staged skin findings, Blaschkoid distribution, and IKBKG genetic testing Retinal neovascularisation or detachment threatening vision Neonatal seizures or stroke-like neurological events Extensive vesicular eruption mistaken for, or complicated by, infection Developmental regression requiring neurological evaluation Mistaking the neonatal vesicular stage for herpes or bacterial infection and delaying diagnosis Failing to arrange prompt retinal screening, risking preventable visual loss Overlooking the diagnostic significance of Blaschko-linear lesions and eosinophilia Not counselling about X-linked inheritance and male lethality for family planning Incontinentia pigmenti is caused by loss-of-function variants in IKBKG, encoding NEMO, an essential regulatory component of the NF-kappaB signalling pathway. NF-kappaB activation protects cells from apoptosis and coordinates inflammatory responses, so cells that carry the mutation on the active X chromosome are prone to death and to abnormal inflammatory signalling. Random X-inactivation produces a mosaic of affected and unaffected cells, explaining the Blaschko-linear pattern of skin lesions and the variable multisystem involvement. The histological hallmark of 'pigment incontinence', with melanin dropping from damaged basal keratinocytes into the dermis, gives the disorder its name. The skin manifestations are generally self-limiting and evolve to subtle residual changes, and most affected females have a normal lifespan; overall prognosis is determined largely by the presence and severity of ocular and neurological involvement.

Indeterminate cell histiocytosis — indeterminate dendritic cell tumour, ICH Langerhans cell histiocytosis Juvenile / adult xanthogranuloma Generalised eruptive histiocytosis Rosai-Dorfman disease Reticulohistiocytosis Cutaneous involvement by leukaemia or lymphoma Mastocytosis Skin biopsy with immunohistochemistry (CD1a, S100, langerin/CD207, CD68) Electron microscopy to confirm absence of Birbeck granules where diagnosis is uncertain Molecular testing for ETV3-NCOA2 fusion and BRAF / MAP kinase pathway mutations where available Full blood count and blood film to screen for associated haematological malignancy Bone marrow examination if a myeloid or lymphoid neoplasm is suspected Serum protein electrophoresis and lactate dehydrogenase Imaging to assess for nodal or visceral involvement in extensive disease A rare histiocytic proliferation whose lesional cells share the immunophenotype of Langerhans cells (CD1a positive) yet lack langerin (CD207) and Birbeck granules, placing them at an indeterminate position between Langerhans cells and dermal dendrocytes. It usually presents in adults as solitary or multiple asymptomatic red-brown to yellowish papules, plaques or nodules on the trunk, limbs, face or neck. The disease is most often confined to the skin, but mucosal, nodal and rare visceral involvement have been described. Lesions may appear in crops and can persist, progress or occasionally regress spontaneously, so the course is variable. Histology shows a dermal infiltrate of histiocytes that are CD1a and S100 positive but langerin negative, and electron microscopy characteristically lacks Birbeck granules. An association with haematological malignancies, particularly myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms including chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia and low-grade B-cell lymphomas, has been reported and warrants haematological review. Some cases harbour clonal kinase-pathway alterations, including translocations involving the ETV3-NCOA2 fusion and BRAF or other MAP kinase pathway mutations, supporting a neoplastic basis in a subset. It should be distinguished from Langerhans cell histiocytosis, which is langerin positive with Birbeck granules, and from the CD1a-negative non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses. Cytopenias, monocytosis or abnormal blood film suggesting an associated myeloid neoplasm Lymphadenopathy, organomegaly or systemic symptoms suggesting nodal or visceral disease Rapidly progressive or ulcerating lesions Coexisting or subsequent diagnosis of leukaemia or lymphoma Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss or night sweats Misclassifying it as Langerhans cell histiocytosis on the basis of CD1a positivity without testing for langerin or Birbeck granules. Failing to screen for an associated haematological malignancy at diagnosis and during follow-up. Assuming a uniformly benign course given the variable and sometimes neoplastic behaviour. Overlooking molecular testing that may guide targeted therapy in progressive disease. Confusing it with the CD1a-negative non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses and thereby misdirecting management. Indeterminate cell histiocytosis is a proliferation of so-called indeterminate dendritic cells, which display a hybrid immunophenotype expressing the Langerhans cell markers CD1a and S100 but, crucially, lacking langerin (CD207) and the ultrastructural Birbeck granules that define mature Langerhans cells. These cells are thought to correspond to a precursor or transitional dendritic cell that has not fully differentiated along the Langerhans cell pathway, or to a dermal dendritic cell that has acquired CD1a expression. While historically regarded as reactive, the identification of clonal molecular alterations in a proportion of cases, including the ETV3-NCOA2 gene fusion and activating mutations of the MAP kinase pathway such as BRAF, indicates that at least some cases are genuinely neoplastic. The reported co-occurrence with myeloid and lymphoid malignancies further supports a clonal, potentially shared-progenitor relationship in a subset of patients. The prognosis is variable and depends on the extent of disease and any associated haematological malignancy; purely cutaneous disease may remain stable, progress or occasionally regress, whereas cases linked to leukaemia or lymphoma follow the course of the underlying neoplasm.

enteropathy Recurrent genetic alterations, including STAT3-JAK2 fusions in some CD4-positive cases, have been described Management is generally conservative given the indolent course, with careful surveillance for the uncommon transformation to a more aggressive lymphoma Change to rapidly progressive symptoms suggesting transformation to aggressive lymphoma Development of a mass lesion, bowel obstruction or perforation Systemic B symptoms with rising lactate dehydrogenase Refractory malabsorption with severe weight loss or nutritional compromise Misdiagnosing the condition as inflammatory bowel disease or coeliac disease and delaying recognition Overtreating an indolent process with aggressive chemotherapy Confusing it with the aggressive intestinal T-cell lymphomas that require intensive therapy Attributing lack of response to a gluten-free diet to poor adherence rather than reconsidering the diagnosis Failing to maintain surveillance for transformation This disorder reflects a clonal expansion of mature small T lymphocytes that home to the gastrointestinal mucosa, producing a persistent but slowly proliferating infiltrate within the lamina propria. Unlike the aggressive intestinal T-cell lymphomas, the cells lack marked epitheliotropism, cytological atypia and destructive behaviour, and the proliferation fraction is low, accounting for the indolent, chronic-relapsing course. The neoplastic cells are commonly CD8-positive cytotoxic-type or, less often, CD4-positive T cells, and recurrent molecular lesions such as STAT3-JAK2 fusions can activate JAK-STAT signalling in a subset. Although generally stable over many years, a minority of cases can undergo transformation to a higher-grade lymphoma. The disorder generally follows a protracted, indolent course over many years with a good outlook, but it is typically persistent and difficult to eradicate, and a small proportion of cases transform to a more aggressive lymphoma, which requires vigilant long-term surveillance.

Infant dyschezia — Functional infant dyschezia, Infant straining Functional constipation (stools are hard rather than soft) Anorectal malformation or anal stenosis Anal fissure with painful defecation Hirschsprung disease Cow's milk protein allergy Infantile colic Sandifer syndrome or reflux-related posturing Clinical examination including inspection of the perineum and anal position and patency Documentation of stool consistency (soft stool supports the diagnosis) Serial growth and weight monitoring Digital rectal examination if a structural anomaly or Hirschsprung disease is suspected Contrast studies or rectal suction biopsy reserved for suspected Hirschsprung disease or anatomical anomaly A benign functional disorder of young infants, typically under nine months, marked by prolonged screaming, crying and straining with facial reddening that precedes passage of a soft stool. The episodes reflect failure to coordinate a Valsalva effort with relaxation of the pelvic floor and anal sphincter, not obstruction or hard stool. The stool that is eventually passed is soft or normal in consistency, which is the key feature distinguishing dyschezia from constipation. Crying stops immediately once the stool is passed, and the infant is otherwise well and thriving. It is a Rome IV functional gastrointestinal disorder of infancy; the diagnosis is clinical from a typical history in a well infant. Reassurance and parental education are the mainstay; no medication or dietary change is required. Rectal or digital stimulation and suppositories should be avoided as they may create a harmful conditioned response and delay learning of normal defecation. Symptoms resolve once the infant learns to coordinate defecation, usually within a few weeks. Passage of hard stools, or delayed passage of meconium at birth suggesting constipation or Hirschsprung disease Faltering growth, abdominal distension or bilious vomiting Blood in the stool Abnormal anal position, an imperforate or stenotic anus, or an absent anal wink on examination Symptoms beginning after nine months of age or persisting well beyond infancy Misdiagnosing the condition as constipation and prescribing laxatives despite the stools being soft. Recommending rectal stimulation or suppositories, which can establish a conditioned dependence. Overlooking an anorectal anomaly by omitting inspection of the perineum. Failing to reassure parents, prompting unnecessary investigation and anxiety. Confusing the straining with pain arising from an anal fissure. Infant dyschezia arises from immaturity of the coordination between the rise in intra-abdominal pressure generated by the infant through crying, straining and Valsalva, and the reflex relaxation of the pelvic floor and external anal sphincter required to permit stool passage. Because the infant cannot yet synchronise these events, effective evacuation is delayed and considerable straining and crying occur, even though the stool is soft and the rectum is not obstructed. There is no structural, neuromuscular or metabolic abnormality; the phenomenon represents normal maturation of the defecation reflex and resolves as the infant learns the appropriate coordination. Excellent; a self-limiting condition that resolves spontaneously within weeks to a few months as the infant matures and learns to coordinate defecation, with no long-term sequelae.

Infant Gastro-oesophageal Reflux Disease — infant GORD, infant GERD, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease in infancy Physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux (normal regurgitation) Cow's milk protein allergy Pyloric stenosis (with projectile non-bilious vomiting) Overfeeding Infection (including urinary tract infection) Intestinal obstruction or malrotation (particularly with bilious vomiting) Clinical assessment with growth monitoring (usually sufficient) Trial of cow's milk protein elimination when allergy is suspected Upper gastrointestinal contrast study to assess anatomy if obstruction or malrotation is a concern Oesophageal pH or impedance monitoring in selected complex cases Endoscopy when oesophagitis or another mucosal complication is suspected It is essential to distinguish physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux, which is common and benign in healthy infants, from reflux disease, in which reflux causes troublesome symptoms or complications. Effortless regurgitation or posseting in a thriving, comfortable infant (the happy spitter) is normal and typically improves as the infant matures and begins to sit and take solids. Reflux disease is suggested by poor weight gain, feeding refusal or distress, persistent irritability, back-arching with feeds, or respiratory symptoms attributable to reflux. Diagnosis is largely clinical from the history and examination; investigations are reserved for atypical presentations, complications, or diagnostic uncertainty. First-line management uses conservative measures such as optimising feeding volume and technique, thickened feeds where appropriate, and positioning advice consistent with safe sleep guidance. A trial of cow's milk protein elimination is reasonable when allergy is suspected, since it can mimic or coexist with reflux disease. Acid-suppressing medication is not appropriate for uncomplicated physiological reflux and should be limited to infants with clear evidence of reflux disease. Warning features such as bilious or forceful vomiting, gastrointestinal bleeding, or onset of vomiting after six months point away from simple reflux and toward an alternative diagnosis. Bilious vomiting or haematemesis Forceful or projectile vomiting suggesting pyloric stenosis Faltering growth or feeding refusal Onset of vomiting after six months or persistence beyond infancy Systemic signs such as fever, lethargy, or a bulging fontanelle Treating benign physiological reflux with acid suppression or unnecessary investigation Missing an alternative diagnosis such as pyloric stenosis or malrotation presenting with vomiting Overlooking cow's milk protein allergy as a mimicking or coexisting cause Recommending positioning that conflicts with safe sleep advice Gastro-oesophageal reflux occurs when gastric contents pass back into the oesophagus, largely through transient relaxations of the lower oesophageal sphincter. Reflux is especially common in infancy because of a short oesophagus, a predominantly liquid and high-volume diet, frequent recumbency, and immaturity of the antireflux barrier. In most infants this is physiological and self-resolving. Reflux disease develops when refluxate causes oesophageal mucosal injury and pain, impairs feeding and growth, or reaches the airway to provoke respiratory symptoms. Contributing factors include delayed gastric emptying and, in some infants, cow's milk protein allergy that produces overlapping symptoms. Physiological reflux resolves in the great majority of infants during the first year to eighteen months as the infant matures; reflux disease also generally improves with time and appropriate management, though some infants with underlying conditions require more prolonged treatment.

infantile acropustulosis — acropustulosis of infancy, infantile acropustulosis of Kahn scabies with active infestation dyshidrotic (pompholyx) eczema transient neonatal pustular melanosis erythema toxicum neonatorum bullous impetigo or staphylococcal pustulosis palmoplantar pustulosis hand, foot and mouth disease skin scrapings and dermoscopy to exclude active scabies pustule smear cytology (Tzanck-type preparation) showing neutrophils with or without eosinophils Gram stain and bacterial culture of pustule contents to exclude infection potassium hydroxide microscopy to exclude dermatophyte or candidal pustules full blood count with differential where peripheral eosinophilia is queried skin biopsy in atypical or persistent cases examination and treatment history review of household contacts for scabies Characterised by recurrent crops of intensely pruritic vesiculopustules on the palms, soles and lateral aspects of the hands and feet in infants and toddlers. Lesions appear in episodic waves lasting one to two weeks, then clear, with symptom-free intervals of several weeks before the next crop. The intense itch is disproportionate to the modest number of lesions and often causes marked irritability and disturbed sleep. A strong association exists with preceding scabies, and the condition is thought in many cases to be a persistent hypersensitivity reaction after treated infestation. Cytology of a pustule shows a predominance of neutrophils, sometimes with eosinophils, and no organisms, helping to distinguish it from infection. The disorder is self-limiting and tends to resolve by two to three years of age with progressively less frequent and milder episodes. Potent topical corticosteroids and oral antihistamines reduce itch and inflammation during flares; dapsone is reserved for severe refractory disease. Persistent acral pustules should always prompt reassessment for active scabies in the child and close contacts before attributing them to acropustulosis. burrows, family itch or persistent lesions indicating untreated active scabies fever, spreading erythema or crusting suggesting secondary bacterial infection failure to enter remission between crops, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis widespread or systemic pustulation raising concern for other pustular disorders significant sleep disruption and distress requiring escalation of symptom control failing to look for and treat active scabies in the child and contacts misinterpreting sterile pustules as bacterial infection and giving repeated unnecessary antibiotics under-treating the severe pruritus, leading to excoriation and secondary infection confusing recurrent crops with an evolving neonatal pustular condition rather than a distinct entity reaching for dapsone before optimising topical corticosteroids and antihistamines Infantile acropustulosis is a benign, recurrent, sterile pustular dermatosis of unknown precise cause. It is characterised histologically by intraepidermal or subcorneal pustules filled with neutrophils, often admixed with eosinophils, without evidence of infection. A widely accepted view is that in a substantial proportion of cases the disorder represents a prolonged id-type or hypersensitivity response of the infant skin following scabies infestation, even after the mites have been successfully eradicated, with the acral skin showing an exaggerated inflammatory reactivity. The episodic, self-limiting nature and eventual spontaneous resolution suggest maturation of immune regulation with age. There is no systemic involvement and the pustules are consistently sterile on culture. The prognosis is excellent; the condition is entirely benign and self-limiting, with flares becoming less frequent and less severe over time and complete resolution usually by around two to three years of age.

Infantile Colic — colic, excessive infant crying, baby colic Cow's milk protein allergy Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease Infection (including urinary tract infection or otitis media) Feeding difficulties or underfeeding Incarcerated hernia, intussusception, or other acute abdominal cause Corneal abrasion, hair tourniquet, or other occult source of pain Thorough history and full physical examination (colic is clinical and one of exclusion) Growth assessment to confirm normal weight gain Targeted tests only if history or examination suggests an organic cause Trial of maternal or infant dietary modification when cow's milk protein allergy is suspected Urinalysis if infection is a concern Infantile colic describes recurrent, prolonged episodes of inconsolable crying and fussiness in an otherwise healthy, well-fed, and thriving young infant. It is often characterised by the rule of threes: crying for more than about three hours a day, on more than three days a week, for more than three weeks, though clinical judgement matters more than strict criteria. Episodes commonly cluster in the late afternoon and evening and may be accompanied by drawing up of the legs, a flushed face, and clenched fists. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, established when a careful history and thorough examination reveal no underlying organic cause and growth is normal. Typical onset is in the first few weeks of life, with peak intensity around six weeks and spontaneous resolution by around three to four months of age. The cause is not fully understood and is likely multifactorial, involving normal developmental crying, gut and feeding factors, and infant-caregiver interaction. Management centres on parental reassurance, education about the benign and self-limiting nature, soothing techniques, and support for exhausted caregivers. Because the crying is intense and distressing, clinicians should assess caregiver stress and coping and be alert to the risk of frustration-related harm such as abusive head trauma. Poor weight gain or failure to thrive Fever or signs of systemic illness Vomiting (especially bilious), blood in stool, or abdominal distension Lethargy, abnormal tone, or an unwell appearance Signs of possible non-accidental injury or a caregiver at breaking point Labelling crying as colic without excluding organic causes or confirming normal growth Missing a serious acute condition such as intussusception or infection presenting as excessive crying Overmedicalising a benign condition or making unnecessary formula changes Neglecting caregiver distress and the associated risk of abusive head trauma Infantile colic does not have a single established mechanism and is best understood as excessive crying at the upper end of the normal developmental crying curve, which peaks in early infancy. Proposed contributors include transient gastrointestinal factors such as immature motility, gas, or feeding-related discomfort, alterations in the gut microbiome, cow's milk protein sensitivity in a subset of infants, heightened infant sensitivity or difficult temperament, and stress within the infant-caregiver relationship. In most infants no pathological process is identified, and the self-limited course paralleling normal maturation supports a developmental rather than a disease-based explanation. Infantile colic is benign and self-limiting, resolving spontaneously by around three to four months of age in most infants, with no adverse effect on long-term growth or development.

and then occlusion or penalisation, and surgical alignment is undertaken early once vision is equalised to give the best chance of binocular cooperation Distinguish it from pseudoesotropia, in which prominent epicanthal folds or a broad nasal bridge give a false appearance of esotropia despite a symmetrical corneal light reflex and no shift on cover testing Absent red reflex or leukocoria suggesting retinoblastoma or cataract Limitation of abduction suggesting a sixth nerve palsy rather than infantile esotropia Associated neurological signs, developmental delay or papilloedema New-onset esotropia in an older child, or esotropia with diplopia, suggesting raised intracranial pressure Progressive or variable deviation accompanied by systemic or neurological features Mistaking pseudoesotropia for true esotropia, or the reverse, by not checking the corneal light reflex and cover test Missing an underlying sensory cause such as retinoblastoma by omitting a dilated fundus examination Failing to detect and treat amblyopia before surgery Confusing infantile esotropia with an abducens palsy by not testing abduction, for example with the doll's-head manoeuvre Delaying referral and surgery beyond the window for developing binocular cooperation Infantile esotropia is a disorder of early binocular development. Ocular misalignment during the critical period of visual maturation prevents normal development of binocular fusion and stereopsis and disrupts cortical binocular connections, giving rise to the associated motor phenomena of dissociated vertical deviation, latent nystagmus and oblique muscle dysfunction. The precise cause is uncertain and probably multifactorial, reflecting a primary defect in the neural control of ocular alignment and binocularity rather than a simple mechanical or refractive problem; there is a genetic predisposition and an increased incidence with prematurity and neurological impairment. With early amblyopia treatment and timely surgical alignment, satisfactory ocular alignment is usually achievable, although high-grade stereopsis is often not fully attained. Some children require more than one procedure and need long-term follow-up for recurrence, dissociated vertical deviation and amblyopia.

Infantile haemangioma — Strawberry naevus, Strawberry haemangioma, Infantile capillary haemangioma Congenital haemangioma (RICH, NICH or PICH) Capillary malformation (port-wine stain) Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma or tufted angioma Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary haemangioma) Infantile fibrosarcoma or other soft-tissue tumour Venous or lymphatic malformation Nasal glioma or encephalocoele for midline facial lesions Clinical diagnosis in most cases, with serial photographic documentation of growth Doppler ultrasound showing a high-flow, high-vessel-density soft-tissue mass MRI for deep, segmental or syndromic lesions and airway assessment GLUT1 immunohistochemistry on biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain Echocardiography and aortic arch imaging if PHACE is suspected Abdominal ultrasound for hepatic haemangiomas when five or more cutaneous lesions are present Ophthalmology and ENT/airway review as dictated by lesion site Most common benign tumour of infancy; usually absent or only a faint precursor mark at birth, then rapid proliferation over the first weeks to months. GLUT1 immunopositivity is the diagnostic hallmark and distinguishes it from congenital haemangiomas and vascular malformations. Follows a stereotyped natural history: proliferative phase, plateau, then slow spontaneous involution over several years. Segmental facial lesions warrant evaluation for PHACE association; lumbosacral or perineal segmental lesions for LUMBAR/PELVIS/SACRAL associations. Beard-distribution lesions raise concern for subglottic airway involvement presenting with biphasic stridor. Beta-blocker therapy (propranolol) is first-line for problematic lesions; ulceration is the commonest complication and cause of pain. Periocular lesions threaten vision through induced astigmatism, amblyopia or visual-axis occlusion. Five or more cutaneous haemangiomas should prompt abdominal imaging to exclude hepatic involvement. Periocular location threatening the visual axis Beard-distribution or symptomatic airway lesion with stridor Segmental facial lesion suggesting PHACE (posterior fossa, arterial, cardiac and eye anomalies) Ulceration, bleeding or secondary infection Multiple lesions with hepatic involvement risking high-output cardiac failure Assuming all birthmarks behave alike and missing the distinction from malformations, which do not involute. Under-appreciating rapid proliferative growth and delaying treatment of periocular or airway lesions. Failing to investigate segmental lesions for PHACE or LUMBAR associations. Overlooking anaemia or heart failure in extensive hepatic involvement. Attributing persistent ulceration purely to infection rather than to the lesion itself. Infantile haemangioma is a benign proliferation of endothelial cells expressing the erythrocyte-type glucose transporter GLUT1, a marker shared with placental microvasculature. Proliferation is driven by immature endothelial and pericyte populations with upregulated angiogenic signalling (VEGF, basic fibroblast growth factor) and hypoxia-related pathways. The beta-adrenergic system modulates growth, which explains the response to beta-blockade through vasoconstriction, downregulation of angiogenic drive and promotion of endothelial apoptosis. After the proliferative phase the tumour involutes, with progressive replacement of vascular tissue by fibrofatty stroma. The great majority involute spontaneously with a good cosmetic outcome, although residual telangiectasia, fibrofatty tissue or atrophic scarring may persist. Timely beta-blocker therapy improves outcomes in high-risk or function-threatening lesions.

During the proliferative phase there is rapid, disorganised angiogenesis with plump endothelial cells forming densely cellular masses; hypoxia-driven and angiogenic signalling pathways, including vascular endothelial growth factor mechanisms, are implicated. The great majority of infantile haemangiomas are benign and resolve substantially over the first several years of life, often with little residual change; however, high-risk lesions can cause functional impairment, disfigurement, ulceration, or, rarely, life-threatening complications, and timely treatment improves these outcomes.

vitamin D signalling. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations abolish this degradation, so active vitamin D metabolites persist and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D remains inappropriately normal or elevated. Unopposed vitamin D action increases intestinal calcium absorption and bone resorption, producing hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria, and suppressed parathyroid hormone. The excess filtered calcium promotes nephrocalcinosis and stone formation. Because the defect is one of clearance, disease is often unmasked when exogenous vitamin D (as supplements or sunlight) increases substrate, explaining the classic onset after infant prophylaxis. With early recognition, withdrawal of vitamin D, and calcium moderation, acute hypercalcaemia resolves and children usually thrive; long-term prognosis depends on the extent of nephrocalcinosis and any resulting renal impairment.

A substantial proportion is driven by activating mutations in PDGFRB, a receptor tyrosine kinase that promotes myofibroblastic proliferation, and the gene can be involved in both familial and sporadic forms. Lesions typically display a distinctive biphasic architecture, with nodules of mature spindled myoid cells at the periphery surrounding a more cellular, primitive zone containing thin-walled branching vessels. Solitary and multicentric disease without visceral involvement has an excellent outlook, with frequent spontaneous regression. Generalised disease with visceral involvement carries a higher risk of morbidity and mortality, particularly in the neonatal period, though many still improve with supportive care.

that arises in the absence of any congenital vertebral anomaly or identifiable neuromuscular disease. Its cause is uncertain, with proposed contributions from intrauterine moulding and postnatal positioning as well as asymmetric growth of the immature spine. Because it develops during the period of most rapid spinal and pulmonary growth, progressive curves can restrict thoracic volume and impair lung development, producing thoracic insufficiency. A subset of apparently idiopathic infantile curves in fact harbour an intraspinal abnormality such as a Chiari malformation, syrinx, or tethered cord, which is why magnetic resonance imaging is important before attributing the deformity to a purely idiopathic cause. Many infantile curves, especially those with a low rib-vertebral angle difference, resolve spontaneously with a good outcome, whereas progressive early-onset curves can become severe and threaten pulmonary development, making early identification and growth-friendly management essential.

Infantile Spasms — West syndrome, epileptic spasms, salaam attacks Benign non-epileptic myoclonus of infancy Sandifer syndrome (dystonic posturing with reflux) Exaggerated startle response or hyperekplexia Infantile colic Other early-onset epileptic encephalopathies (e.g. Ohtahara syndrome) Tonic seizures of other origin Urgent EEG, ideally capturing sleep, to identify hypsarrhythmia MRI brain to detect structural or malformative causes Skin examination and evaluation for tuberous sclerosis Metabolic and genetic testing to establish an underlying aetiology Developmental assessment to document baseline and progress Fundoscopy and ophthalmological review where indicated An age-specific epileptic encephalopathy of infancy, with onset usually in the first year of life and peaking around 4-8 months. Spasms are brief, often symmetrical contractions producing sudden flexion or extension of the trunk and limbs, typically occurring in clusters especially on waking. The full West syndrome triad comprises epileptic spasms, the EEG pattern of hypsarrhythmia, and arrest or regression of development. Developmental regression or loss of previously acquired skills, including loss of social smile or visual attention, is a crucial and sometimes early sign. Spasms are frequently mistaken for colic, startle, or normal infant movements, causing dangerous delays in diagnosis. An urgent EEG is essential; hypsarrhythmia is a chaotic, high-amplitude, disorganised interictal pattern that supports the diagnosis. Many cases have an identifiable underlying cause such as a structural brain abnormality, tuberous sclerosis, genetic or metabolic disease, or perinatal injury, so investigation for aetiology is important. Rapid initiation of effective treatment is critical, as prompt control of spasms and resolution of hypsarrhythmia is associated with better developmental outcomes. New clusters of spasms in an infant require urgent EEG and prompt treatment (EMERGENCY) Developmental regression or loss of acquired milestones Hypsarrhythmia on EEG Delay between symptom onset and treatment, which worsens prognosis Signs suggesting an underlying structural, metabolic, or genetic disorder Evolution to other seizure types or epileptic encephalopathy Dismissing spasms as colic, reflux, or benign startle and delaying EEG Failing to appreciate developmental regression as a warning sign Not pursuing a thorough search for an underlying cause Delaying initiation of effective therapy, which reduces the chance of good outcome Under-recognising subtle spasms occurring in clusters around sleep transitions Infantile spasms represent an age-dependent epileptic encephalopathy in which diverse insults to the developing brain converge on a common electroclinical expression. Structural, genetic, metabolic, or acquired abnormalities disrupt the maturing cortical and subcortical networks during a vulnerable developmental window, producing the hypersynchronous discharges seen as hypsarrhythmia and the characteristic spasms. The ongoing epileptic activity itself further disrupts normal brain development, contributing to the associated cognitive and developmental regression. Prognosis is variable and strongly influenced by the underlying cause and by how quickly spasms and hypsarrhythmia are controlled; delayed treatment and identifiable structural or genetic causes are associated with worse developmental outcomes, while prompt effective therapy in previously normal infants offers the best chance of favourable development.

Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities — Nosocomial infections, Health care-associated infections, HAI, Hospital-acquired infections Community-acquired infection (onset within 48-72 h of admission) Asymptomatic bacteriuria versus true catheter-associated urinary tract infection Noninfectious causes of fever or organ dysfunction in the critically ill Drug-related or transfusion-related complications mimicking infection Asymptomatic bacteriuria mistaken for symptomatic urinary tract infection (especially in the elderly with nonspecific confusion) Colonization with multidrug-resistant organisms misread as active infection Ventilator-associated events that are noninfectious complications of mechanical ventilation Laboratory-based surveillance supplemented by clinical chart review by infection preventionists Whole genome sequencing as the gold standard for establishing clonality and detecting plasmid-borne resistance genes during outbreak investigation Molecular typing of bacterial/fungal (less commonly viral) isolates to confirm an outbreak PCR or culture screening for Candida auris in patients transferred from long-term care facilities (isolate pending results) Interferon-gamma release assay (preferred over tuberculin skin test) for preemployment tuberculosis screening of health care personnel Targeted water testing for Legionella pneumophila in facilities with prior nosocomial cases Dedicated public health laboratory testing (nasopharyngeal swabs/washes, conjunctival swabs) for strain identification when novel influenza such as H5N1 is suspected, as commercial multiplex PCR panels are insufficient Aspiration pneumonitis without bacterial infection Postoperative inflammatory fever Thrombotic or chemical phlebitis at vascular access sites Infections appearing within the first 48-72 hours of admission are generally regarded as community-acquired (or attributed to a transferring institution); those arising afterward are considered health care-associated (nosocomial). Patient-related vulnerabilities to nosocomial infection include indwelling invasive devices, immune deficiency (congenital or acquired), renal insufficiency, diabetes, and other major comorbidities. Disruption of a patient's own microbiota by antibiotics or other drugs promotes colonization with multidrug-resistant organisms; colonized patients then act as silent reservoirs for transmission to others and to the environment. Colonization pressure (the proportion of patients on a ward who are colonized) is itself a risk factor for the spread of resistant organisms. Catheter-associated bloodstream infections roughly triple the risk of in-hospital death; central lines are foreign objects in direct contact with the bloodstream and each handling is a potential contamination event. Ventilator-associated pneumonia occurs in up to 10% of mechanically ventilated patients and can prolong ventilation and ICU stay or be fatal. Clostridioides difficile infection is both the most frequent cause of health care-associated diarrhea and the most frequent hospital-acquired infection in the United States; recent antibiotic exposure is the most common precipitant. Alcohol-based hand gel and standard hospital cleaners do NOT kill C. difficile spores or inactivate norovirus, so handwashing with soap and water plus sporicidal (e.g., bleach) cleaning is required. Candida species account for the vast majority of health care-associated fungal infections; antifungal prophylaxis can select for non-albicans species such as Candida glabrata. Candida auris is a multidrug-resistant, environment-adapted pathogen that survives long periods on surfaces and is resistant to some standard disinfectants, requiring select agents and strict contact precautions. Tap water is not sterile; waterborne organisms such as Legionella pneumophila and nontuberculous mycobacteria colonize plumbing biofilm, favored by low disinfectant levels, warm temperatures, and stagnation. Apart from pregnant patients, asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterized patients should generally not be cultured or treated; in the elderly nonspecific symptoms like confusion are often unrelated to bacteriuria, and overtreatment drives a cycle of escalating antimicrobial use and resistance. Surveillance infection rates are expressed as standardized infection ratios (observed infections divided by predicted infections), benchmarked through the CDC National Healthcare Safety Network. New bloodstream infection in a patient with a central venous catheter (markedly elevated in-hospital mortality) Nosocomial diarrhea progressing toward toxic megacolon in C. difficile colitis A single case of nosocomial Legionnaires disease, which should trigger a full investigation Suspected active tuberculosis requiring immediate airborne precautions Identification of Candida auris, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, or other high-priority multidrug-resistant organisms requiring coordinated containment Presentation of a returning traveler with possible viral hemorrhagic fever (Ebola, Marburg) Culturing and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterized patients, then re-testing for 'clearance', fueling a cycle of escalating antimicrobial use and resistance. Relying on alcohol-based hand gel against C. difficile spores or norovirus, which it does not eliminate. Failing to remove indwelling urinary catheters and central lines promptly when no longer needed, the principal driver of these preventable device infections. Overlooking that patients already colonized with C. difficile on admission are by far the most likely to develop infection during the stay. Missing exogenous transmission of Candida auris because it resists some standard disinfectant cleaners and recontaminates surfaces rapidly. Treating commercial multiplex respiratory PCR results as adequate to exclude or identify novel influenza strains such as H5N1. Hospitalized patients are exposed to pathogens from other patients, visitors, staff, and the inanimate environment. Health care personnel carry multidrug-resistant organisms between patients on hands or shared equipment (stethoscopes, portable imaging machines); spread also occurs via contaminated plumbing, person-to-person respiratory routes, or contamination of food, water, and medications. Antibiotic exposure disrupts the host microbiota, permitting colonization with resistant organisms; colonized but immunocompromised patients, or those whose barriers are breached by surgery or invasive devices, then develop infection either from their own flora or from cross-transmitted pathogens. Invasive devices (urinary catheters, central venous catheters, endotracheal tubes) create direct portals of entry, bypassing normal defenses. Resistant organisms frequently colonize the gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts and can establish enduring environmental reservoirs, with potential horizontal transfer of resistance genes between co-colonizing strains. Health care-associated infections are a substantial source of morbidity and mortality in hospitalized patients, frequently caused by antimicrobial-resistant organisms that prolong hospital stays and worsen outcomes. Catheter-associated bloodstream infections triple in-hospital mortality risk, and ventilator-associated pneumonia can be fatal or prolong ICU stay. Multidrug-resistant organism infections are associated with higher morbidity, higher mortality, and added costs; globally about 1.27 million deaths were attributed to antibiotic-resistant infections in 2019. After years of decline from prevention efforts, device-related and other nosocomial infection rates rose during the COVID-19 pandemic. C. difficile colitis spans a clinical spectrum from mild diarrhea to life-threatening toxic megacolon. Pathogen transmission risk is operationally classified by route into contact, droplet, and airborne precautions (per WHO and CDC); some conditions (e.g., concurrent varicella and SARS-CoV-2) warrant combined precautions. Airborne isolation requires a negative-pressure room with at least 12 air changes per hour, exhausted outdoors or through a HEPA filter, with respirator use; protective (positive-pressure, HEPA-filtered) isolation is used for highly susceptible patients such as those with prolonged neutropenia or stem cell transplants to exclude mold spores.

Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms — Campylobacteriosis, Campylobacter jejuni enteritis, Campylobacter enteritis, Campylobacter fetus infection Salmonella gastroenteritis Shigellosis Yersinia enterocolitica enteritis Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli infection Typhoid fever (when fever is the sole early manifestation) Acute appendicitis (versus C. jejuni pseudoappendicitis) Ulcerative colitis Crohn's disease Salmonella enteritis Shigella dysentery Yersinia enterocolitica infection Enterohemorrhagic E. coli colitis Early typhoid fever Stool culture on Campylobacter-specific selective media (diagnostic gold standard) Species-specific real-time PCR (more sensitive than culture) Culture-independent diagnostic tests / antigen detection (may detect nonviable organisms and give false positives) MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for species identification Gram or Wright stain of fecal smear for vibrioid morphology; phase-contrast or dark-field microscopy for darting motility Fecal leukocyte/erythrocyte examination Peripheral leukocyte count (reflects inflammatory severity) Blood cultures (note: low metabolic activity can make Campylobacter bacteremia hard to detect) Ulcerative colitis Crohn's disease Acute appendicitis Campylobacters are motile, non-spore-forming, curved (vibrio-like) gram-negative rods that are microaerophilic, and the genus was split off from Vibrio in 1973; over 20 species now span the genera Campylobacter, Arcobacter, and Helicobacter (Harrison 22e p.1304). C. jejuni is the dominant diarrheal pathogen, accounting for roughly 80-90% of recognized illness in this group, while C. fetus is the principal cause of extraintestinal/systemic disease (Harrison 22e p.1304). Undercooked poultry is the leading source in developed countries (30-70% of cases); other routes include unpasteurized milk, untreated water, infected pets, contaminated seafood, foreign travel, and oral-anal sexual contact (Harrison 22e p.1304). Enteritis typically begins 2-4 days after exposure (range 1-7 days) and is often preceded 12-48 h by a prodrome of fever, headache, myalgia, and malaise (Harrison 22e p.1304-1305). Visibly bloody stool occurs in about 10% of adult cases; most patients presenting for care have 10 or more bowel movements on the worst day, and cramping abdominal pain may be the most prominent feature (Harrison 22e p.1305). C. jejuni can produce pseudoappendicitis, and isolated fever can be the only early sign, mimicking the onset of typhoid fever; myocarditis and pericarditis have been seen, especially in young men, and febrile young children may have convulsions (Harrison 22e p.1305). C. fetus has a tropism for vascular sites, causing endocarditis, mycotic aneurysm, and septic thrombophlebitis; its protective S-layer resists complement-mediated killing and opsonization, enabling bacteremia and antigenic variation (Harrison 22e p.1305). About 90% of bacteremic cases are due to C. jejuni and C. fetus in roughly equal numbers, despite C. jejuni being far more common overall (Harrison 22e p.1305). The two major postinfectious sequelae are reactive arthritis (up to 2.5% of cases, no HLA-B27 association, averaging about 3.2 joints, knees most often) and Guillain-Barre syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1305). Sialylated lipopolysaccharide on certain C. jejuni strains drives molecular mimicry against axonal cell-surface molecules; Campylobacter is estimated to trigger 20-40% of all Guillain-Barre cases despite occurring in only ~1 per 1000-2000 infections (Harrison 22e p.1305). Diagnosis rests on culture on Campylobacter-selective fastidious media (the gold standard), with species-specific real-time PCR being more sensitive; MALDI-TOF identifies species, and Gram/Wright fecal smears or dark-field microscopy may reveal vibrioid forms with characteristic darting motility (Harrison 22e p.1305-1306). Infection with C. jejuni in low- and middle-income countries, even when asymptomatic, is associated with childhood stunting (short stature) and a distinctive microbiome signature (Harrison 22e p.1304). High fever Grossly bloody or severe diarrhea Symptoms persisting beyond one week or worsening Signs of sepsis, meningitis, or endovascular infection (suggesting C. fetus) Septic abortion or infection during pregnancy (often leads to fetal death) Septic thrombophlebitis (suggests C. fetus) Immunocompromise, diabetes, liver disease, or extremes of age (risk of severe/recurrent extraintestinal disease) Neurologic symptoms suggesting Guillain-Barre syndrome or its Miller Fisher variant following infection Labeling inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn's) before excluding Campylobacter and related infections, since presentations and biopsy findings can overlap and Campylobacter enteritis is far more common in young adults (Harrison 22e p.1306). Assuming a negative stool culture excludes Campylobacter, as these fastidious organisms are missed without selective media or techniques (Harrison 22e p.1306). Over-interpreting culture-independent test positivity, which may reflect nonviable bacteria and can be falsely positive, unlike culture which usually implies active or recent infection (Harrison 22e p.1306). Treating commensal oral organisms (C. sputorum, C. concisus) as pathogens, since they rarely have pathogenic significance (Harrison 22e p.1306). Missing C. fetus bacteremia because of its low metabolic activity in standard blood culture media (Harrison 22e p.1306). Overlooking that not every patient with enteritis benefits from antimicrobials, and that antimotility agents can prolong symptoms and have been associated with toxic megacolon and death (Harrison 22e p.1306). Campylobacters survive in the gastrointestinal mucous layer of food animals and pets and reach humans mainly via undercooked/contaminated food or animal contact. In C. jejuni enteritis the jejunum, ileum, and colon are injured; biopsy shows a nonspecific acute inflammatory reaction with neutrophils, monocytes, and eosinophils in the lamina propria plus epithelial damage, mucus loss, glandular degeneration, and crypt abscesses. Strain motility and adherence favor disease, whereas classic entero- and cytotoxins (including cytolethal distending toxin) seem not to drive tissue injury; tissue invasion and occasional bacteremia indicate clinically significant invasion. C. fetus pathogenesis is better defined: nearly all clinical isolates bear a proteinaceous S-layer capsule-like structure conferring resistance to complement and opsonization, allowing bacteremia and seeding of extraintestinal sites, while antigenic switching of S-layer proteins contributes to chronicity and recurrence in compromised hosts. Protective immunity is incompletely understood but appears antibody-dependent and may be short-lived without continuous exposure (Harrison 22e p.1304-1305). Almost all patients recover fully from Campylobacter enteritis, spontaneously or with therapy; the rare deaths are linked largely to volume depletion. Symptoms persist beyond one week in 10-20% of patients seeking care, and clinical relapses occur in 5-10% of untreated patients. Some patients develop reactive arthritis or Guillain-Barre syndrome. Systemic C. fetus infection is far more often fatal than infection with related species, with overall reported bacteremia mortality around 12%; outcome depends on how promptly appropriate therapy begins. Otherwise healthy hosts usually survive C. fetus infection without sequelae, whereas compromised hosts often suffer recurrent and/or life-threatening disease (Harrison 22e p.1306). Three patterns of extraintestinal infection are described: (1) transient bacteremia in a normal host with enteritis, which is benign and needs no specific treatment; (2) sustained bacteremia or focal infection in a normal host, arising from enteritis and responding well to antimicrobials; and (3) sustained bacteremia or focal infection in a compromised host, in which enteritis may not be apparent and prompt, possibly prolonged, therapy is required (Harrison 22e p.1305).

Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms — Anaerobic bacterial infections, Mixed aerobic-anaerobic infection, Polymicrobial anaerobic infection, Bacteroides fragilis infection, Non-clostridial anaerobic infection Aerobic abscess (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus), which can also produce deep abscesses and lung abscess without an anaerobic component Chemical pneumonitis / Mendelson syndrome (acid aspiration) versus bacterial aspiration pneumonia Foreign-body aspiration with obstruction and atelectasis versus bacterial aspiration pneumonia Simple parapneumonic effusion (e.g., pneumococcal) versus anaerobic empyema Necrotizing pneumonia, bronchopleural fistula with purulent effusion, and pneumatocele in the lung-abscess differential Group A streptococcal necrotizing fasciitis versus mixed aerobic-anaerobic (polymicrobial) necrotizing fasciitis Malignancy or granulomatous disease mimicked by cervicofacial actinomycosis ('lumpy jaw') Staphylococcus aureus abscess or lung abscess (no anaerobic component) Group A streptococcal necrotizing fasciitis (more rapid, 1-3 day progression) Pneumococcal pneumonia with parapneumonic effusion Gram stain of pus/sputum showing a mixed bacterial population, especially when routine culture is negative or grows only streptococci or a single aerobe such as E. coli Anaerobic culture from normally sterile sites (blood, pleural/peritoneal fluid, CSF, sterile-site aspirates or biopsies); samples from mouth, nose, vagina, or feces are unacceptable due to commensal contamination Air-free syringe collection capped and placed in anaerobic transport media with rapid transport; liquid/tissue specimens preferred over swabs Pleural fluid analysis (WBC count, LDH, pH) to distinguish empyema from a simple parapneumonic effusion Imaging (chest x-ray/CT) showing dependent-segment consolidation or cavitary abscess; cross-sectional imaging for intraabdominal/pelvic abscess and for typhlitis bowel-wall thickening (>4 mm) Referral to a reference laboratory for susceptibility testing in serious, refractory, or prolonged-therapy infections (brain abscess, meningitis, joint infection, osteomyelitis, prosthetic joint infection, endocarditis) Chemical pneumonitis from gastric acid aspiration (Mendelson syndrome) Foreign-body airway obstruction Malignancy or granulomatous disease mimicked by chronic actinomycotic 'lumpy jaw' Most clinically relevant anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis, Prevotella melaninogenica, Fusobacterium nucleatum) are relatively aerotolerant rather than strict obligate anaerobes; obligate anaerobes are killed by oxygen at or above roughly 0.5%, whereas facultative anaerobes grow with or without oxygen (Harrison 22e p.1371). Anaerobes dominate the normal mucocutaneous microbiota, accounting for about 99.0-99.9% of cultivable organisms, with concentrations ranging from ~10^3/mL in the nose to ~10^12/mL in gingival crevices and colon; the lower GI tract is the major reservoir (anaerobe-to-aerobe ratio ~1000:1) (Harrison 22e p.1371-1372). Infections are typically polymicrobial, commonly yielding three to six species, and occasionally more than 10 species from a single suppurative site; the etiologic organisms mirror the neighboring resident microbiota (Harrison 22e p.1372-1373). Bacteroides fragilis, though only ~0.5-1% of the colonic microbiota, is the anaerobe most often isolated from intraabdominal infections and bacteremia; its zwitterionic capsular polysaccharide A (PSA) is the principal virulence factor driving abscess formation via a TLR2-dependent cytokine/chemokine response (IL-8, IL-17, TNF-alpha) (Harrison 22e p.1373). Anaerobic gram-negative endotoxin (lipid A) is roughly 100-1000 times less biologically potent than aerobic gram-negative endotoxin, which helps explain why DIC, purpura, and septic shock are less frequent in anaerobic gram-negative bacteremia; Fusobacterium LPS is an exception and contributes to the severity of Lemierre's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1373). A putrid/foul-smelling discharge is considered suggestive of anaerobic infection but is a late finding present in only about 30-50% of cases, so its absence does not exclude anaerobes (Harrison 22e p.1374). Sterile pus paradox: an abscess that yields no growth on routine culture but shows teeming organisms on Gram stain strongly suggests anaerobes that failed to grow because of inadequate transport/culture technique (Harrison 22e p.1373-1378). Anaerobes are recovered in up to ~30% of brain abscesses, ~20% of epidural abscesses, and ~10% of subdural empyemas, but rarely cause meningitis; brain abscesses from contiguous (otogenic, odontogenic, sinus) spread are the most likely to involve anaerobes (Harrison 22e p.1375). Bacterial aspiration pneumonia evolves indolently over days to weeks, distinguishing it from chemical pneumonitis (e.g., Mendelson syndrome from acid aspiration), which develops within 4-6 hours and can produce a bilateral chest x-ray 'whiteout' within 8-24 hours (Harrison 22e p.1375). Empyema fluid characteristics (mean WBC ~55,000 cells/mL, LDH >1000 IU/L, pH <7.2, loculations, thick pleural peel) contrast sharply with a simple parapneumonic effusion (mean WBC ~5000 cells/mL, LDH >200 IU/L, pH ~7.4) (Harrison 22e p.1376). Aspiration pneumonia/lung abscess localizes to dependent segments: basilar lower-lobe segments if aspiration occurred upright, and posterior upper-lobe (usually right) or superior lower-lobe segments if supine (Harrison 22e p.1375-1376). Clostridium septicum bacteremia, often arising via neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis), is strongly associated with underlying malignancy, particularly colon cancer (Harrison 22e p.1376).
