Clostridium septicum bacteremia signaling possible occult colon malignancy B. fragilis-group bacteremia indicating underlying colonic pathology (neoplasia, diverticulitis) and carrying high untreated mortality Submitting specimens from heavily colonized sites (mouth, nose, vagina, feces) or expectorated sputum for anaerobic culture, which yields uninterpretable results from commensal contamination Dismissing an infection as 'sterile' when routine culture is negative despite a Gram stain teeming with organisms, missing inadequate anaerobic transport/culture Prior antibiotic therapy reducing the cultivability of anaerobes and masking the diagnosis Using agents with no useful anaerobic activity (aminoglycosides, monobactams, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) and attributing nonresponse to other causes; failure to respond to such agents itself suggests an anaerobic etiology Treating gas in tissue or a putrid odor as pathognomonic for anaerobes; gas can be produced by aerobes and putrid odor appears in only 30-50% of cases Overlooking that right-lower-quadrant pain and tenderness are absent in nearly half of typhlitis cases (and may be absent entirely in patients on glucocorticoids) Relying on antibiotics alone without surgical debridement of devitalized tissue and drainage of large abscesses Anaerobic infection requires an anaerobic microenvironment with a lowered oxidation-reduction potential, which arises directly from tissue ischemia, trauma, surgery, or a perforated viscus, or is established and maintained by co-infecting facultative organisms that consume local oxygen. Disease typically follows breakdown of a mucosal barrier (intestinal perforation, ischemia, surgery) or direct inoculation (bite wounds, trauma), seeding normally sterile tissue with commensal organisms. The resulting infections are usually polymicrobial, with facultative and obligate anaerobes acting synergistically: facultative organisms create and sustain the reduced-oxygen environment, short-chain fatty acids and succinic acid impair phagocyte clearance, certain organisms supply growth factors to others (e.g., oral diphtheroids producing vitamin K needed by P. melaninogenica), and tissue damage promotes spread. Virulence factors include adhesins/fimbriae (P. gingivalis, B. fragilis pili, F. nucleatum as a bridging coaggregator), exoproteins such as P. gingivalis collagenase, and capsular polysaccharides. The B. fragilis capsular polysaccharide complex, particularly the zwitterionic PSA, is the most studied factor; its charged repeating-unit motif drives abscess formation by stimulating peritoneal macrophages (via TLR2) to release IL-8, IL-17, and TNF-alpha, recruiting PMNs that adhere to ICAM-1-upregulated mesothelial cells to form the abscess nidus, with T-cell IL-17/IFN-gamma also required (Harrison 22e p.1372-1373). Manifestations of severe sepsis and DIC are unusual in purely anaerobic infection, and septic shock is less common with B. fragilis than with aerobic gram-negative bacillary bacteremia. Nonetheless, isolation of a B. fragilis-group organism from blood indicates serious underlying infection with an untreated mortality rate of about 60%; case-fatality rises with advancing age (reported >66% in patients over 60), with isolation of multiple species, and with failure to surgically remove the focus. Reported relative mortality has been suggested to vary by species (B. thetaiotaomicron > P. distasonis > B. fragilis). Anaerobic endocarditis, though rare, carries significant mortality (~21-43%). Noma is highly lethal without treatment (70-90%). Recovery from empyema may take several months, particularly without surgical intervention (Harrison 22e p.1374, 1377-1378). No single formal grading scheme; severity is judged by anatomic site, extent, and systemic involvement. Localized/indolent processes (chronic sinusitis, periodontal disease, indolent anaerobic cellulitis) contrast with severe, life-threatening forms (Ludwig's angina with airway compromise, noma, Lemierre's syndrome, necrotizing fasciitis/Fournier gangrene, brain abscess, B. fragilis-group bacteremia, endocarditis). Antibiotic selection is guided empirically by infection location, severity, and local resistance patterns; reference-laboratory susceptibility testing is reserved for serious, refractory, or prolonged-therapy infections (Harrison 22e p.1374-1379).

Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species — Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, Burkholderia cepacia complex infection, Melioidosis, Glanders, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia infection, Pseudomallei infection, Ecthyma gangrenosum (Pseudomonas) Other gram-negative bacterial pneumonia and sepsis (clinically often indistinguishable from P. aeruginosa) Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (can also produce ecthyma-gangrenosum-like lesions) Tuberculosis (chronic cavitary melioidosis mimic) Pyogenic meningitis of other bacterial etiology (CSF profile of Pseudomonas meningitis is nonspecific) Polymicrobial osteomyelitis from trauma or decubitus ulcers Aspergillosis and mucormycosis (can produce ecthyma-gangrenosum-like lesions) Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus species causing malignant/necrotizing otitis externa Tuberculosis mimicked by chronic pulmonary melioidosis Other gram-negative enterocolitis mimicked by Pseudomonas enterocolitis / Shanghai fever Sputum Gram stain showing predominant polymorphonuclear leukocytes plus culture positive for P. aeruginosa supports acute pneumonia rather than colonization Multiplex PCR platforms on respiratory and blood samples identify P. aeruginosa earlier than classical culture Technetium-99 bone scan as the gold standard for malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa MRI and bone scan for puncture-wound foot osteomyelitis; needle aspiration usually yields the diagnosis Deep bone biopsy before treating presumed P. aeruginosa osteomyelitis in trauma or decubitus settings to confirm its causative role Blood cultures plus echocardiographic/clinical signs for endocarditis (blood cultures often negative in vertebral osteomyelitis unless endocarditis coexists) Mandatory laboratory susceptibility testing before using newer beta-lactam/beta-lactamase-inhibitor agents or cefiderocol against MDR/XDR strains Fluid overload mistaken for pneumonia on CT in ventilated patients (contributes to overdiagnosis of HAP/VAP) The pseudomonads are a heterogeneous group of non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative bacteria now split across three medically important genera: Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas; most cause disease opportunistically, the exceptions being the primary pathogens B. pseudomallei and B. mallei. P. aeruginosa rarely causes infection without a breach in host defenses; disease typically requires compromised immunity, mucosal trauma, physiologic derangement, or antibiotic-mediated suppression of normal flora, so most infections cluster in intensive care units. On primary culture P. aeruginosa is identified by a yellow to dark-green or bluish pigment, a shiny gun-metal colony sheen, a characteristic fruity odor, failure to ferment lactose on MacConkey agar, and a positive oxidase reaction; cystic fibrosis isolates may appear mucoid from overproduction of alginate. Ecthyma gangrenosum is the distinctive skin lesion of P. aeruginosa bacteremia, occurring almost exclusively in markedly neutropenic patients and those with AIDS; lesions begin pink, darken to purple, then become black and necrotic, and histologically are due to vascular invasion teeming with bacteria. P. aeruginosa keratitis is a medical emergency because it can progress over roughly 48 hours to involve the entire cornea with opacification and even perforation; it is strongly associated with contact lenses, especially the extended-wear type. Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa most often occurs in elderly diabetics and can extend to cranial nerve palsies (most commonly cranial nerve VII) or cavernous sinus thrombosis; the ESR is invariably elevated, often 100 mm/h or more. Hot-tub folliculitis, toe-web infection, and the green-nail syndrome (pyocyanin diffusing into the nail bed of a Pseudomonas paronychia) are characteristic community skin manifestations; whirlpools, spas, and pools are common sources, and folliculitis is usually self-limited. Vertebral osteomyelitis and sternoclavicular septic arthritis are uncommon but characteristic complications in people who inject drugs; Pseudomonas osteomyelitis of the foot typically follows a puncture wound through a sneaker, mainly in children, often with negative blood cultures. Melioidosis (B. pseudomallei) is geographically restricted chiefly to Southeast Asia and northern Australia (with cases in India and China); the organism is a facultative intracellular pathogen acquired from soil and water that can cause latent infection presenting long after exposure. Melioidosis can mimic tuberculosis with chronic cough, fever, hemoptysis, night sweats, and cavitary upper-lobe disease, and may also present as skin ulceration with lymphangitis and regional lymphadenopathy or as high-mortality septicemia. Burkholderia cepacia complex can cause the rapidly fatal cepacia syndrome (respiratory distress plus septicemia) in cystic fibrosis; B. cenocepacia in particular is a barrier to lung transplantation, with relatively high one-year mortality. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is an opportunist whose emergence requires major disruption of host flora, classically broad-spectrum cephalosporin or carbapenem therapy; distinguishing colonization from true infection in ventilated, non-neutropenic patients is a recurring clinical dilemma. Ecthyma gangrenosum in a neutropenic or AIDS patient suggesting P. aeruginosa bacteremia Rapidly progressive corneal opacification/perforation indicating sight-threatening Pseudomonas keratitis (medical emergency) Severe lancinating ear pain with granulation tissue in a diabetic, plus cranial nerve palsy, signaling malignant otitis externa Hypothermia or shock in P. aeruginosa bacteremia (marker of severe illness) Cepacia syndrome: rapidly fatal respiratory distress with septicemia in cystic fibrosis Hemoptysis, night sweats, and cavitary disease in a patient from an endemic region suggesting melioidosis with systemic spread Overdiagnosing HAP/VAP: positive sputum, endotracheal aspirate, or PCR results may reflect tracheobronchial colonization, endotracheal-tube biofilm, or simple tracheobronchitis rather than true pneumonia; clinical judgment is essential. In trauma- or decubitus-associated osteomyelitis, infection is often polymicrobial and the causative role of P. aeruginosa can be overstated without a deep bone biopsy. Treating S. maltophilia or P. aeruginosa pulmonary cultures as infection when they may represent colonization, especially in non-neutropenic patients; unnecessary therapy promotes resistance. Assuming community sputum cultures prove community-acquired P. aeruginosa pneumonia in patients prone to airway colonization by multiple bacterial strains. Empirically relying on first-line antipseudomonal agents in settings where susceptibility is below 80%, or on the newer agents/cefiderocol without susceptibility testing given unpredictable resistance mechanisms. Failing to remove indwelling foreign bodies (urinary catheters, stents, stones, central lines) — relapse of UTI or bacteremia may be due to the retained device or ongoing obstruction rather than antibiotic resistance. Not recognizing that melioidosis can present long after travel to an endemic area due to latent intracellular infection. P. aeruginosa possesses an unusually large arsenal of putative virulence factors, yet few are individually proven to drive human disease, and there is great redundancy. Adhesins (pili, flagellin/flagellar cap binding mucins, LPS outer core binding CFTR to aid internalization, and alginate in mucoid strains) mediate colonization, with adhesion strongest to injured cell surfaces. A type III secretion system injects toxins (ExoS or ExoU, ExoT, ExoY) into host cells, allowing evasion of phagocytes; strains secreting ExoU are associated with higher mortality. A type II secretion system releases diffusible toxins including exotoxin A, multiple proteases (which degrade host cytokines and chemokines), and phospholipases. Rhamnolipids, pyocyanin, and hydrocyanic acid further injure tissue and can cause neutrophil death. Inflammatory responses to lipid A and flagellin via Toll-like receptors (principally TLR4 and TLR5) are required for defense but, when florid, contribute to sepsis and septic shock. In chronic infection (cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, diffuse panbronchiolitis) defective mucociliary clearance and mucus stasis select for P. aeruginosa, which adapts over time by losing pili and flagella, losing the O side chain of LPS (becoming complement-sensitive), and overproducing mucoid exopolysaccharide, dampening the host response and enabling decades of persistence with attenuated virulence factor production. B. pseudomallei survives within neutrophils and macrophages, aided by a polysaccharide capsule and a type III secretion system, and provokes a florid inflammatory response. B. cepacia complex organisms bind lung mucus and possess potent LPS that drives lung inflammation. S. maltophilia virulence is limited, with disease largely a host inflammatory response to LPS and flagellin; its hallmark is broad intrinsic antibiotic resistance via efflux pumps and the L1 and L2 beta-lactamases. P. aeruginosa carries high attributable mortality and is among the most feared pathogens in neutropenic patients. Historical crude bacteremia mortality exceeded 50%, with more recent attributable mortality of about 28 to 44% depending on adequacy and timing of treatment and underlying disease severity. Pneumonia mortality has been reported at 40 to 80%, though the fraction attributable to underlying disease is uncertain, and VAP outcomes are poor. Chronic airway infection (e.g., cystic fibrosis) is rarely eradicated and is the leading contributor to respiratory failure and death in CF. Pseudomonas endovascular infection in people who inject drugs is more indolent than S. aureus endocarditis and is more often curable when right-sided. Melioidosis septicemia carries high mortality, with rates as high as 44% reported in Thailand. B. cenocepacia infection has relatively high one-year mortality after lung transplantation. S. maltophilia pneumonia/bacteremia can cause septic shock, with a severe high-mortality form described in neutropenic patients. No single formal severity score is presented. Resistance is graded as multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) P. aeruginosa, with extremely high MDR rates reported from eastern/southern Europe, Latin America, India, and China, especially in ICUs. Carbapenemase production is highlighted as the most threatening resistance mechanism. The B. cepacia cepacia syndrome denotes a rapidly fatal severe phenotype. Melioidosis spans a clinical spectrum from asymptomatic infection through localized abscesses and pneumonia to high-mortality disseminated septicemic disease.

Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria — HACEK endocarditis, HACEK group infections, Fastidious gram-negative bacterial infections, Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella infections Viridans group streptococcal endocarditis (also subacute, culture-positive, common in dental-source disease) Enterococcal endocarditis Culture-negative endocarditis (Bartonella, Coxiella burnetii, Tropheryma whipplei) when blood cultures are sterile Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis when the course is more acute Septic arthritis/osteomyelitis from Staphylococcus aureus in children (where K. kingae may have surpassed S. aureus as a leading cause) Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection when ecthyma gangrenosum-like skin lesions are present (Aeromonas) Neisseria meningitidis sepsis (K. kingae bacteremia can produce a similar petechial rash) Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection (Aeromonas can cause indistinguishable ecthyma gangrenosum) Other gram-negative bacteremic pneumonias (Achromobacter xylosoxidans bacteremia, similar high mortality) Other causes of culture-negative or slow-growing endocarditis Blood cultures with notification of the laboratory that a HACEK organism is suspected; modern automated systems (e.g., BACTEC) usually yield growth within the first week 16S rRNA gene amplification (PCR) of blood or cardiac valve specimens for culture-negative or fastidious cases MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry performed directly on colonies for rapid, accurate species identification Echocardiography to detect valvular vegetations (seen in up to 85% of HACEK endocarditis) Real-time PCR of blood or joint fluid for Kingella kingae; inoculation of synovial fluid into aerobic blood culture bottles to improve recovery In vitro antimicrobial susceptibility testing, including Etest, given slow growth and possible undetected beta-lactamase; susceptibility testing is essential for the miscellaneous multidrug-resistant gram-negative organisms Noninfective embolic disease and vasculitis (HACEK endocarditis frequently presents with embolic, vascular, and immunologic phenomena such as cerebrovascular accidents, mycotic aneurysms, and immune-complex glomerulonephritis that may mimic primary vasculitic or thromboembolic disorders) Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (rare HUS following bloody diarrhea has been linked to Aeromonas, but HUS itself is the differential) HACEK is an acronym for a group of fastidious, slow-growing gram-negative bacteria that require a carbon-dioxide-enriched atmosphere and do not grow on routine enteric media such as MacConkey agar: Haemophilus species, Aggregatibacter (formerly Actinobacillus) species, Cardiobacterium species, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella kingae. These organisms normally colonize the oral cavity; invasive disease characteristically follows a recent dental procedure or nasopharyngeal infection in a patient with underlying valvular heart disease or prosthetic valves. A positive HACEK blood culture is strongly predictive of underlying infective endocarditis, with an overall positive predictive value around 60%, though this varies sharply by organism (e.g., 62-100% with Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans bacteremia versus only 0-6% with Eikenella bacteremia). HACEK organisms cause roughly 0.8-6% of infective endocarditis cases, most often due to Aggregatibacter species, Haemophilus species, and Cardiobacterium hominis; the aortic and mitral valves are most commonly affected. Compared with non-HACEK endocarditis, HACEK endocarditis occurs in younger patients and is more frequently associated with embolic, vascular, and immunologic manifestations; systemic embolization is common (major emboli in roughly 28-71% of cases) and vegetations are seen on echocardiography in up to 85% of patients. Kingella kingae behaves differently from the other HACEK organisms: more than half of K. kingae infections are bone and joint infections, oropharyngeal colonization peaks in the first 3 years of life and is higher in daycare-attending children, and it can be transmitted child-to-child and cause outbreaks; K. kingae bacteremia can present with a petechial rash resembling Neisseria meningitidis sepsis. Capnocytophaga canimorsus and C. cynodegmi are endogenous to the dog and cat mouth; infection often follows a dog or cat bite (or exposure without a bite), and asplenia, glucocorticoid use, and alcohol abuse predispose to severe sepsis with shock and DIC, classically with a petechial rash progressing to purpura and gangrene. Pasteurella multocida colonizes the respiratory and GI tracts of domestic animals (oropharyngeal colonization 50-90% in cats, 50-70% in dogs) and is transmitted by bites, scratches, or licking; most human infections are skin and soft tissue, and almost two-thirds are caused by cats. Aeromonas can produce ecthyma gangrenosum (hemorrhagic vesicles with a rim of erythema and central necrosis/ulceration) resembling lesions of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, and is associated with water exposure, floods, and other hydrologic disasters (along with Shewanella and Chromobacterium). Diagnostic recovery of HACEK organisms is improved by alerting the microbiology laboratory; most cultures turn positive within the first week with modern systems (e.g., BACTEC), and prolonged incubation has not been shown to increase recovery of clinically significant isolates. Molecular methods aid diagnosis: 16S rRNA gene amplification (PCR) on blood or cardiac valve tissue and MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry on colonies increase the accuracy and speed of HACEK identification; real-time PCR and inoculation of synovial fluid into aerobic blood culture bottles enhance recovery of K. kingae in culture-negative cases. Chromobacterium violaceum causes rare but often fatal soft tissue infections and metastatic abscesses, occurring especially in children with defective neutrophil function such as chronic granulomatous disease. Systemic embolization (cerebral and other major emboli are common in HACEK endocarditis) Congestive heart failure complicating endocarditis (reported in roughly 19-50% of Haemophilus HACEK cases) Mycotic aneurysm formation Petechial/purpuric rash with sepsis after a dog or cat bite in an asplenic, alcohol-abusing, or glucocorticoid-treated patient (Capnocytophaga canimorsus, may progress to shock, DIC, and gangrene) Petechial rash with bacteremia mimicking meningococcemia (Kingella kingae) Necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis after water/wound exposure (Aeromonas; very high mortality with myonecrosis) Sepsis with metastatic abscesses in a child with defective neutrophil function (Chromobacterium violaceum) Because of slow growth, antimicrobial susceptibility testing may be difficult and beta-lactamase production may go undetected; resistance is most common in Haemophilus and Aggregatibacter species. Prolonged blood-culture incubation has not been shown to improve recovery of clinically significant HACEK isolates, so relying on extended incubation alone may delay diagnosis—molecular methods may be needed. Failing to alert the microbiology laboratory that a fastidious HACEK organism is suspected can compromise recovery and identification. Eikenella corrodens is resistant to clindamycin, metronidazole, and aminoglycosides, so empirical regimens chosen for typical gram-negatives may fail. Many miscellaneous gram-negative organisms (Achromobacter, Elizabethkingia/Chryseobacterium, Chromobacterium, Aeromonas) are frequently multidrug-resistant—Elizabethkingia/Chryseobacterium are typically resistant to carbapenems while Aeromonas can produce carbapenemases—so therapy must be guided by susceptibility testing rather than assumptions. Capnocytophaga canimorsus infection may be missed when there is exposure without an obvious scratch or bite, and severe disease can occur in patients without an apparent wound. HACEK organisms are commensals of the human oral cavity. Disruption of the oral mucosa (dental procedures, nasopharyngeal infection, periodontal disease) allows transient bacteremia; in patients with damaged native valves or prosthetic material, the slow-growing organisms seed and form valvular vegetations, producing a typically subacute, indolent endocarditis. Their fastidious, CO2-dependent slow growth accounts for delayed culture positivity and difficulty in susceptibility testing (including underdetection of beta-lactamase). The remaining fastidious and miscellaneous gram-negative organisms in this chapter act largely as opportunists: animal-mouth flora (Pasteurella multocida, Capnocytophaga canimorsus) inoculated through bites/scratches/licking, environmental and waterborne organisms (Aeromonas, Shewanella, Chromobacterium violaceum, Achromobacter xylosoxidans) introduced through wounds or contaminated fluids, and nosocomial nonfermenters (Elizabethkingia/Chryseobacterium, Rhizobium radiobacter, Alcaligenes faecalis) associated with contaminated fluids, indwelling devices, and immunocompromised hosts. Overall prognosis in both native-valve and prosthetic-valve HACEK endocarditis is excellent and significantly better than endocarditis caused by non-HACEK pathogens; one case-control study found significantly lower 1-year mortality than viridans group streptococcal endocarditis. Mortality associated with HACEK endocarditis in older series ranged from about 28 to 71% depending on the cohort. By contrast, several miscellaneous organisms carry high mortality: Pasteurella multocida invasive disease up to ~30% despite therapy, Achromobacter xylosoxidans bacteremia up to ~67%, Aeromonas sepsis ~25% in immunocompromised adults and >90% with myonecrosis, Chryseobacterium indologenes up to ~50%, and Elizabethkingia anophelis bloodstream infection ~18%. No formal grading system; clinical severity is stratified by site and host factors. HACEK endocarditis runs a typically subacute course (more aggressive with Kingella kingae) with severity marked by embolic, vascular, and immunologic complications, heart failure, and mycotic aneurysm. For the miscellaneous organisms, severity escalates with immunocompromise, asplenia, cirrhosis, malignancy, diabetes, neutrophil dysfunction, and extremes of age, and with deep/invasive presentations such as bacteremia, necrotizing fasciitis, myonecrosis, and septic shock with DIC.

anatomic approach is the key to diagnosis: the level and physical appearance of the lesion (epidermis, dermis, subcutaneous fat, fascia, or muscle) together with location, time course, travel/animal-bite history, age, comorbidities, and lifestyle narrow the differential (Harrison 22e p.1049-1052). Because the avascular epidermis is protected mainly by the stratum corneum, any breach (burns, bites, abrasions, foreign bodies, ulcers, surgery, primary dermatologic disease) lets bacteria reach deeper structures (Harrison 22e p.1049). Edema with purple bullae, ecchymosis, and cutaneous anesthesia signals loss of vascular integrity and mandates exploration of deep structures for necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis (Harrison 22e p.1049). Unexplained fever plus disproportionate soft-tissue pain and tenderness, even without overt cutaneous inflammation, should raise high suspicion for a deep necrotizing infection and prompt early diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1049). Vesicular lesions reflect viral proliferation within the epidermis (e.g., varicella with crops of 'dewdrop' vesicles, dermatomal herpes zoster preceded by pain, HSV around lips or genitals, coxsackievirus A16 hand-foot-mouth); rickettsialpox produces a crusted black eschar after mite-bite inoculation of Rickettsia akari (Harrison 22e p.1049-1050). Crusted golden-brown lesions suggest impetigo: impetigo contagiosa from S. pyogenes (linked to poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis but NOT rheumatic fever) and bullous impetigo from S. aureus; MRSA impetigo epidemics have been reported (Harrison 22e p.1051). A focused exposure history points to the organism in cellulitis: cat/dog bites (Pasteurella multocida, also S. intermedius, Capnocytophaga), freshwater lacerations (Aeromonas hydrophila), Gulf of Mexico/Atlantic saltwater or raw seafood in cirrhosis (Vibrio vulnificus), fish/swine handling (Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae), and aquariums/swimming pools (Mycobacterium marinum) (Harrison 22e p.1050-1052). Cultures are frequently unrevealing in cellulitis: even needle aspiration of the leading edge or punch biopsy is positive in only about 20% of cases, suggesting low bacterial numbers and a toxin/inflammatory-mediator effect (Harrison 22e p.1052). Erysipelas (S. pyogenes) shows abrupt fiery-red swelling with sharply demarcated indurated margins (classically along the nasolabial fold), rapid spread, and intense pain; desquamation follows at 5-10 days (Harrison 22e p.1052). Imaging (plain films, CT, MRI) helps localize abscess or detect gas in tissue but may show only nonspecific soft-tissue swelling; notably, gas is usually absent in necrotizing fasciitis and myonecrosis caused by group A Streptococcus or MRSA, so a negative gas finding does not exclude fulminant infection (Harrison 22e p.1053). Hospital admissions for skin and soft tissue infections rose ~27% from 2000-2004, largely due to emergence of the USA300 MRSA clone (Harrison 22e p.1049). Pyomyositis (usually S. aureus, common in the tropics) typically has no portal of entry and begins at the exact site of blunt trauma or muscle strain; PVL-producing MRSA pyomyositis has occurred in U.S. children (Harrison 22e p.1053). Disproportionate pain and tenderness with unexplained fever and minimal skin findings Edema with purple/violaceous bullae, ecchymosis, skin sloughing, or cutaneous anesthesia Rapidly progressing lesion with brawny edema, dark-red or bluish/maroon/black skin discoloration Systemic toxicity, shock, multiorgan failure, or renal impairment preceding shock (streptococcal necrotizing fasciitis/TSS) Scrotal/perineal swelling extending to abdominal wall or legs (Fournier gangrene) Postpartum or post-abortion woman with little/no fever, no purulent discharge, refractory hypotension, marked edema/effusions, hemoconcentration, and a very high WBC count (Clostridium sordellii infection - often rapidly fatal) Halophilic Vibrio infection that is as fulminant as necrotizing fasciitis with seawater/raw-seafood exposure, especially in cirrhosis Relying on absence of gas to exclude necrotizing fasciitis/myonecrosis - gas is usually absent with group A Streptococcus or MRSA Sending home patients with severe pain and fever after misdiagnosing early necrotizing fasciitis as thrombophlebitis and giving only analgesia Trusting negative imaging or biopsy (negative in ~80% of deep infections) to rule out fulminant infection Using empirical vancomycin against Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, which is unusually vancomycin-resistant among gram-positive organisms Confusing SSSS with TEN without frozen-section evaluation of the cleavage plane Letting hyperbaric oxygen delay or substitute for surgical debridement when debridement is indicated Infection localizes according to skin anatomy. The epidermis is avascular and relies on the stratum corneum as a mechanical barrier; disruption permits bacterial entry, and hair follicles act as portals for normal flora (Staphylococcus) or exogenous organisms (Pseudomonas in hot-tub folliculitis). The rich subpapillary capillary plexus mediates inflammatory signs and allows metastatic seeding (Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, palpable purpura in endocarditis; cutaneous lesions of disseminated fungal, gonococcal, Salmonella, Pseudomonas/ecthyma gangrenosum, meningococcal, and staphylococcal infection) and access to the bloodstream. Bacteria such as S. pyogenes spread laterally via lymphatics, producing rapidly extending erysipelas, and subsequent lymphatic obstruction causes flaccid epidermal edema. Excess cytokines or bacterial toxins amplify these responses, causing leukostasis, venous occlusion, and edema; loss of vascular integrity produces purple bullae and cutaneous anesthesia indicative of deep necrotizing infection. In necrotizing fasciitis, infection extends along fascial planes and through venous channels and lymphatics, with dermal-papillary vessel thrombosis and progression to friable, bluish/black skin and systemic toxicity. Group A streptococcal and clostridial muscle infection can produce acute rhabdomyolysis with markedly elevated creatine phosphokinase. Toxin biology drives several syndromes: exfoliatin (phage group II S. aureus) cleaves the stratum corneum in staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome, while PVL-producing MRSA can cause necrotizing fasciitis and pyomyositis, and TSST-1/enterotoxins underlie shock in toxic shock syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1049-1053). Outcome ranges from benign and self-limited (e.g., hot-tub folliculitis, though rare bacteremia and shock have occurred) to rapidly fatal. Necrotizing fasciitis with no defined portal of entry carries high mortality, and survivors often require repeated surgery including amputation. Clostridium sordellii infection (postpartum, post-abortion, or black-tar-heroin injection) is often fatal with rapid death. Mpox case-fatality (1-10%) is lower than smallpox, and TEN carries higher mortality than SSSS. Delay in surgical debridement significantly increases mortality in fulminant infections (Harrison 22e p.1050-1053). Clinically stratified by depth and aggressiveness rather than a single formal score: (1) superficial epidermal/follicular infections (vesicular, crusted, folliculitis); (2) dermal/lymphatic spread (erysipelas, cellulitis - subdivided into purulent cellulitis [MSSA/MRSA, focal abscess source] versus nonpurulent cellulitis [S. pyogenes, rapidly spreading, lymphangitis/fever]); and (3) deep, life-threatening necrotizing infections of fascia and muscle (necrotizing fasciitis, gas gangrene/myonecrosis, pyomyositis), signaled by systemic inflammatory response, shock, and multiorgan failure (Harrison 22e p.1052-1053).

Infectious Arthritis — septic arthritis, bacterial arthritis, pyogenic arthritis, joint infection Crystal-induced arthritis (gout, pseudogout) - can clinically mimic and may coexist with septic arthritis Cellulitis Bursitis Acute osteomyelitis Hemarthrosis or fracture Monoarticular flare of rheumatoid arthritis Reactive/postinfectious arthritis Acute rheumatic fever Osteoarthritis Gonococcal disseminated infection presenting as arthritis-dermatitis (versus true septic monoarthritis) Meningococcemia with dermatitis-arthritis or purulent monoarthritis Poncet's disease (reactive polyarthritis of disseminated tuberculosis, with no organisms in the joint) Viral arthritides (parvovirus B19, rubella, hepatitis B, arboviruses) Postinfectious/reactive arthritis following enteric or chlamydial infection Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid cell count, differential, Gram stain, and culture (obtain before antibiotics) Synovial fluid examination for crystals to exclude/identify coexistent gout or pseudogout Blood cultures (positive in up to 50-70% of S. aureus infections) Inoculation of synovial fluid into blood-culture bottles to improve yield for fastidious organisms Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) and MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for partially treated or culture-negative cases Sonication of explanted prosthetic material to disrupt biofilm and improve culture yield Plain radiographs; ultrasound for hip effusion; CT/MRI for sacroiliac, sternoclavicular, and spinal joint infection Mucosal cultures (endocervical/urethral, rectal, oropharyngeal) and urine NAAT when gonococcal arthritis is suspected Synovial tissue biopsy and culture for suspected mycobacterial or fungal arthritis Crystal-induced arthritis (gout, pseudogout) Rheumatoid arthritis flare Reactive arthritis / serum sickness Hemarthrosis, fracture, or foreign body Ischemic necrosis and osteoarthritis Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are the most common causes of infectious arthritis, though mycobacteria, spirochetes, fungi, and viruses can also seed joints. Acute bacterial infection can rapidly destroy articular cartilage, so every inflamed joint warrants prompt evaluation; cartilage degradation can begin within about 48 hours. Roughly 90% of acute septic arthritis presents in a single joint, most often the knee, then the hip, and less often shoulder, wrist, or elbow. In IV drug users, infections of the spine, sacroiliac joints, and sternoclavicular joints are more common than those of the appendicular skeleton. Acute bacterial infection typically causes mono- or oligoarthritis; subacute/chronic monoarthritis suggests mycobacterial or fungal disease, and acute polyarthritis suggests viral, immunologic (endocarditis, rheumatic fever, DGI), or underlying rheumatoid disease. Synovial fluid Gram stain is positive in roughly 30-50% of cases overall; organisms are seen on smear in nearly three-quarters of S. aureus and streptococcal infections but only 30-50% of gram-negative and other bacterial infections. Synovial fluid cultures are positive in over 90% of nongonococcal bacterial arthritis cases, but in gonococcal arthritis synovial cultures are frequently negative and blood cultures positive in fewer than 45%. Disseminated gonococcal infection most commonly presents as an arthritis-dermatitis syndrome with fever, chills, hemorrhagic pustular rash, tenosynovitis, and migratory arthritis; women are 2-3 times more likely than men to develop DGI, with peak risk during menses and pregnancy. Lyme disease causes arthritis in up to 60% of untreated persons; serologic IgG to B. burgdorferi is positive in over 90% of Lyme arthritis, and NAAT detects Borrelia DNA in synovial fluid in about 85%. Tuberculous arthritis is usually a chronic granulomatous monoarthritis of large weight-bearing joints (hips, knees, ankles); synovial fluid acid-fast staining is positive in under one-third of cases but synovial tissue culture is positive in about 90%. Parvovirus B19 causes polyarthritis or polyarthralgia in about 60% of infected women and 10% of children; rubella, mumps, hepatitis B, and arboviruses (Zika, chikungunya, Ross River) are other notable viral causes. Prosthetic joint infection complicates roughly 0.5-2% of total joint replacements and is more common after knee than hip arthroplasty; indolent infection with coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium, enterococci, or diphtheroids may persist for months to years without constitutional symptoms. Acutely inflamed joint - treat as a medical emergency given rapid cartilage destruction Narrowing of joint space and bony erosions on radiographs indicate advanced infection and poor prognosis Septic arthritis of the hip, especially in young children, threatens viability of the femoral head and is best managed surgically Polyarticular involvement or absent fever in rheumatoid, renal, hepatic, or immunosuppressed patients can mask infection Failure of repeated needle aspiration to clear effusion, lower synovial WBC, and sterilize cultures signals need for arthroscopic or open drainage Serum procalcitonin is only about 50% sensitive and must not be used to rule out infectious arthritis. Elevated synovial protein and lactate dehydrogenase with depressed glucose are nonspecific and not required for diagnosis. Failing to test synovial fluid for crystals can miss coexisting infection and crystal disease, which can occur together. Relying on synovial fluid culture in suspected gonococcal arthritis is misleading, since cultures are often negative; mucosal-site cultures and NAAT are needed. Coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium, or diphtheroids in a prosthetic joint may represent indolent true infection rather than contamination, so semiquantitative culture and careful aspiration technique are important. Cellulitis, bursitis, and osteomyelitis can mimic septic arthritis; preserved passive range of motion and less-than-circumferential swelling help distinguish them. Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) are typically elevated but nonspecific. Bacteria reach the joint hematogenously, from a contiguous bone or soft-tissue focus, or by direct inoculation during surgery, injection, bite, or trauma. In hematogenous infection, organisms escape from synovial capillaries, which lack a limiting basement membrane, and within hours provoke neutrophilic infiltration of the synovium. Neutrophils and bacteria enter the joint space and bacteria adhere to articular cartilage. Cartilage degradation begins within about 48 hours owing to increased intraarticular pressure, release of proteases and cytokines from chondrocytes and synovial macrophages, and invasion of cartilage by bacteria and inflammatory cells. Synovial proliferation forms a pannus over the cartilage, and thrombosis of inflamed synovial vessels develops; abscesses may extend into synovium, cartilage, and subchondral bone. S. aureus surface adhesins promote cartilage adherence and endotoxins drive chondrocyte-mediated cartilage breakdown. Gonococcal arthritis-dermatitis and viral arthritides are believed to be largely immune-mediated, reflecting reaction to circulating organisms and immune-complex deposition rather than direct joint invasion. Prompt systemic antibiotics with timely joint drainage can prevent cartilage destruction, postinfectious degenerative arthritis, joint instability, and deformity, so outcome depends heavily on early recognition and adequate decompression. Radiographic joint-space narrowing and bony erosions indicate advanced disease and a poorer outcome. Gonococcal and Lyme arthritis generally respond well to therapy, and most reactive arthritis resolves within about 6 months, though recurrent disease is more common after chlamydial urethritis. Untreated Lyme arthritis leaves about 10% with chronic erosive synovitis, and certain viral arthropathies (e.g., parvovirus B19) occasionally become chronic. No single formal grading system; synovial fluid cell count guides likelihood and severity. Normal synovial fluid contains fewer than 180 cells/uL (predominantly mononuclear). Acute bacterial infection averages about 100,000 cells/uL (range roughly 25,000-250,000/uL) with over 90% neutrophils. Crystal-induced, rheumatoid, and other noninfectious inflammatory arthritides usually show under 30,000-50,000 cells/uL. Mycobacterial and fungal infections typically show 10,000-30,000 cells/uL with 50-70% neutrophils. Gonococcal DGI synovial fluid usually contains only 10,000-20,000 leukocytes/uL, whereas true gonococcal septic arthritis contains over 50,000/uL.

Infectious Complications of Bites — bite wound infection, animal bite infection, human bite infection, dog bite, cat bite, clenched-fist injury, fight bite, rat-bite fever, seal finger Rat-bite fever versus Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Lyme disease, leptospirosis, and secondary syphilis (p.1143) Localized bite-wound cellulitis versus tissue damage from snake envenomation, which can mimic infection (p.1145) Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) as a late consequence of cat bites/scratches (p.1143) Inflammatory tissue necrosis from venomous snake envenomation, which can be difficult to distinguish from secondary infection (p.1145) Gram's stain and aerobic culture of all infected wounds; anaerobic cultures when abscess, devitalized tissue, or foul-smelling exudate is present (p.1144) Notify the microbiology laboratory when fastidious organisms such as Eikenella corrodens are suspected in human bites (p.1144) White blood cell count, and blood cultures if systemic infection is suspected (p.1144) Radiographs of penetrating wounds to assess fracture or retained foreign body such as a tooth fragment (p.1144) Hand-surgery consultation for hand injuries to evaluate tendon, nerve, and muscular involvement (p.1144) For suspected Capnocytophaga sepsis, prolonged blood-culture incubation (up to 14 days); organisms may be seen within polymorphonuclear leukocytes on Wright-stained peripheral smears (p.1143) Traumatic soft-tissue injury, crush injury, and laceration without infection Local envenomation reaction Bite-wound flora generally mirrors the oropharyngeal flora of the biting animal, though organisms from soil, the victim's and animal's skin, and animal feces may also contribute (p.1142). Dogs account for about 80% of animal bites; roughly 15-20% of dog bites become infected, whereas more than half of cat bites and scratches become infected (p.1142-1143). Cat bites carry a higher infection risk than dog bites because narrow sharp canine teeth inoculate deeply, predisposing to septic arthritis and osteomyelitis, especially with punctures over or near a joint of the hand (p.1143). Dog-bite infection typically appears 8-24 h after injury with pain and cellulitis plus purulent, sometimes foul-smelling discharge; the bite-to-symptom interval is notably shorter for cat bites (p.1143). Pasteurella multocida, a small gram-negative coccobacillus from feline oral flora, causes the majority of cat-bite infections and tends to advance rapidly, sometimes within hours (p.1143). Capnocytophaga canimorsus following dog bites (or licking of open wounds) can cause fulminant sepsis, DIC, and renal failure, particularly in asplenic, immunosuppressed, or hepatically impaired hosts; this thin gram-negative rod is hard to grow on solid media and may need up to 14 days to grow on blood culture (p.1143). Human bites become infected more often than other animal bites (~10-15%); clenched-fist ('fight bite') injuries are especially serious because deep hand structures including bone, joint, and tendon are inoculated (p.1144). Eikenella corrodens is a fastidious organism particularly associated with clenched-fist injuries; the microbiology laboratory should be alerted when it is suspected (p.1144). Rat-bite fever (Streptobacillus moniliformis in the US; Spirillum minor 'sodoku' mainly in Asia) characteristically manifests after the initial wound has healed; streptobacillary disease causes fever, migratory arthralgias, and a maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles (p.1143). Aquatic exposures matter: alligator or piranha bites may harbor Aeromonas hydrophila, while shark, moray eel, and barracuda bites are associated with marine Vibrio species (p.1143). Old World monkey (Macaca) bites can transmit B virus (Macacine herpesvirus 1), a cause of serious CNS infection; nonhuman primate bites otherwise resemble human bites (p.1143). Seal, walrus, and polar bear bites can cause 'seal finger,' a chronic suppurative infection attributed to Mycoplasma species such as M. phocacerebrale (p.1143). Asplenia, hepatic dysfunction, or immunosuppression after a dog bite raising concern for fulminant Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis with DIC and renal failure (p.1143) Clenched-fist ('fight bite') injury over the metacarpophalangeal joints with possible joint, tendon, or bone involvement (p.1144) Systemic features: fever, lymphangitis, lymphadenopathy, or signs of bacteremia, meningitis, or endocarditis (p.1143) Rapidly advancing inflammation within hours suggesting Pasteurella infection (p.1143) Suspicious human-bite wounds prompting evaluation for domestic or child abuse (p.1144) Bites posing rabies risk, requiring contact with public-health authorities (p.1144) Underestimating infection risk in cat bites, whose deep punctures seed joints and bone despite small surface wounds (p.1143) Missing occult joint/tendon involvement in clenched-fist injuries because patients often present only after frank infection develops (p.1144) Failing to consider rat-bite fever when illness appears after the original wound has already healed (p.1143) Inadequate anaerobic culture when devitalized tissue or foul-smelling exudate is present (p.1144) Not alerting the lab to fastidious organisms (e.g., Eikenella, Capnocytophaga) that require special or prolonged culture conditions (p.1143-1144) Primary closure of high-risk wounds (e.g., cat puncture wounds, wounds >12 h old on a limb or >24 h old on the face), which raises infection risk (p.1144) Bite injuries inoculate the victim's tissues with the biting animal's oral flora plus environmental and cutaneous organisms, producing a typically polymicrobial mix of aerobes and anaerobes. Deep puncture wounds (cat canines, clenched-fist injuries) drive organisms into joints, tendons, and bone, predisposing to septic arthritis and osteomyelitis. Local spread produces cellulitis with purulent discharge, while seeding can lead to systemic disease (bacteremia, meningitis, brain abscess, endocarditis). Impaired lymphatic drainage (e.g., post-mastectomy limb) or immunocompromise (glucocorticoids, SLE, leukemia, cirrhosis, splenectomy) facilitates dissemination, and Capnocytophaga can incite DIC and renal failure in such hosts (p.1142-1144). Most localized bite-wound infections resolve with appropriate wound care and treatment, but a significant minority become severe or life-threatening. Septic arthritis and osteomyelitis prolong the course. Capnocytophaga sepsis can be fulminant in susceptible hosts. Streptobacillary rat-bite fever was frequently fatal in the preantibiotic era and may be complicated by endocarditis, myocarditis, meningitis, pneumonia, and multi-organ abscesses (p.1142-1145). Human-bite wound infection risk stratifies by depth: approximately 2% for superficial wounds versus over 25% for deep wounds such as clenched-fist injuries. Human bites are categorized as occlusional injuries (from actual biting) or clenched-fist ('fight bite') injuries (fist striking teeth), the latter being more common and more serious owing to inoculation of deep hand structures (p.1144).

Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV) — EBV infection, glandular fever CMV infection (the most common cause of heterophile-negative mononucleosis; older age, longer fever, exudative pharyngitis uncommon) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Acute HIV infection (diffuse rash, oral/genital ulcers, aseptic meningitis) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Toxoplasmosis (less splenomegaly; exposure to cats or raw meat) (Harrison 22e p.1511) HHV-6 infection (older age at presentation) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Streptococcal pharyngitis (no splenomegaly, less fatigue) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Viral hepatitis (higher aminotransferase levels) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Rubella (maculopapular rash, no splenomegaly) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Lymphoma (fixed, nontender lymph nodes) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Drug reaction, most often to phenytoin, carbamazepine, sulfonamides, or minocycline (can occur at any age) (Harrison 22e p.1511) CMV mononucleosis (heterophile-negative) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Acute (primary) HIV infection (Harrison 22e p.1511) Toxoplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.1511) HHV-6 infection (Harrison 22e p.1511) Streptococcal pharyngitis (Harrison 22e p.1511) Viral hepatitis (Harrison 22e p.1511) Rubella (Harrison 22e p.1511) Heterophile antibody test (titer >=40 diagnostic with compatible symptoms and atypical lymphocytes), or the more sensitive commercial Monospot test (~75% sensitive, ~90% specific vs EBV-specific serology) (Harrison 22e p.1511) EBV-specific serology: IgM and IgG anti-VCA, anti-EBNA, and (less useful for routine diagnosis) anti-early antigen (EA-D, EA-R) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Peripheral blood examination for atypical lymphocytes and CBC (leukocytosis, possible neutropenia/thrombocytopenia) (Harrison 22e p.1509) Liver function tests (aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) (Harrison 22e p.1509) EBV DNA detection by PCR in blood or CSF (useful when serology is equivocal, in CNS lymphoma in AIDS, and for monitoring lymphoproliferative disease); throat or blood culture is NOT helpful because EBV persists for life in the oropharynx and B cells (Harrison 22e p.1511) Lymphoma (fixed, nontender nodes; atypical lymphocytes) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Drug-induced mononucleosis-like reaction (phenytoin, carbamazepine, sulfonamides, minocycline) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is the cause of heterophile-positive infectious mononucleosis (IM), classically marked by the triad of fever, sore throat (pharyngitis), and lymphadenopathy, together with atypical lymphocytosis (Harrison 22e p.1508). EBV is spread mainly by contact with oral secretions (saliva); by adulthood >90% of individuals are seropositive. IM is typically a disease of young adults, while in young children primary infection is usually asymptomatic or a mild pharyngitis (Harrison 22e p.1508-1509). The incubation period in young adults is about 4-6 weeks, often preceded by a 1-2 week prodrome of fatigue, malaise, and myalgia before fever, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy appear (Harrison 22e p.1509). Lymphadenopathy (most often posterior cervical, tender, symmetric, not fixed) and pharyngitis are most prominent in the first 2 weeks, whereas splenomegaly is more prominent during the second and third weeks (Harrison 22e p.1509). Lymphadenopathy and fever are the most common signs (each in >90%), with pharyngitis/tonsillitis in ~82% and splenomegaly in ~51%; tonsillar exudate can resemble streptococcal pharyngitis (Harrison 22e p.1509). Characteristic laboratory features: leukocytosis peaking at the second-to-third week with >10% atypical lymphocytes (enlarged cells with abundant cytoplasm, predominantly CD8+ T cells), often with mild neutropenia and thrombocytopenia (Harrison 22e p.1509). Abnormal liver function (mildly elevated aminotransferases and alkaline phosphatase) occurs in >90% of cases, with hyperbilirubinemia in about 40% (Harrison 22e p.1509). The heterophile (and the somewhat more sensitive Monospot) test is the standard diagnostic test in children and adults; heterophile antibodies do not interact with EBV proteins. Tests are positive in ~40% in week 1 and 80-90% by week 3, so repeat testing may be needed if performed early (Harrison 22e p.1511). Heterophile antibodies are often absent in children under 5 years, the elderly, and patients with atypical presentations; in these cases EBV-specific serology should be used (Harrison 22e p.1511). EBV-specific serology pattern: IgM antibody to viral capsid antigen (VCA) is most useful for acute IM (present only during the first 2-3 months); IgG anti-VCA persists for life and indicates past exposure; antibodies to EBNA appear late (3-6 weeks after symptom onset) and persist for life (Harrison 22e p.1511). Most cases of IM are self-limited; most patients have symptoms for 2-4 weeks, but nearly 10% have fatigue persisting for 6 months or more (Harrison 22e p.1509). EBV is associated with several malignancies, including Burkitt's lymphoma (~90% of African cases, ~15% of US cases), anaplastic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (uniformly EBV-associated in southern China), gastric carcinoma (the most common EBV-associated malignancy worldwide), Hodgkin's lymphoma (especially mixed-cellularity type), and various T-/NK-cell and CNS lymphomas; EBV-driven lymphoproliferative disease occurs in immunodeficient and transplant patients (Harrison 22e p.1509-1511). Large epidemiologic data show a strong association of EBV with multiple sclerosis; one study of over a million military personnel found a 32-fold higher MS risk after primary EBV infection, though the causal role still requires further research (Harrison 22e p.1508, 1511). Splenic rupture (occurs in <0.5% of cases, more common in males; may present as abdominal pain, referred shoulder pain, or hemodynamic compromise) - a leading cause of the rare deaths from IM (Harrison 22e p.1510) Upper-airway obstruction from tonsillar/adenoidal hypertrophy or epiglottic/pharyngeal/uvular edema (Harrison 22e p.1510) CNS complications (meningitis, encephalitis, cerebellar ataxia, cranial nerve palsies especially CN VII, Guillain-Barre syndrome, transverse myelitis) - usually within the first 2 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1510) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Coombs-positive, cold agglutinins to red-cell i antigen, ~2% of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1510) Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, severe cytopenias (red-cell aplasia, severe granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, pancytopenia) (Harrison 22e p.1510) Fulminant hepatitis, myocarditis/pericarditis, pneumonia with pleural effusion (Harrison 22e p.1510) Fatal IM in patients with X-linked lymphoproliferative disease or other primary immunodeficiencies - and rarely in patients with no obvious preexisting immune defect (Harrison 22e p.1510) Ampicillin/penicillin rash pitfall: about 95% of patients with infectious mononucleosis given ampicillin develop a rash; classically a macular rash followed penicillin-derivative use, although more recent studies suggest EBV-associated rashes may occur at similar frequency with or without penicillin exposure, and these rashes are not predictive of future penicillin reactions (Harrison 22e p.1509, 1513). Heterophile/Monospot tests are often falsely negative early in illness (positive in only ~40% during week 1) and are unreliable in children under 5, the elderly, and atypical presentations - repeat testing or EBV-specific serology may be required (Harrison 22e p.1511). False-positive Monospot results are more common in connective tissue disease, lymphoma, viral hepatitis, and malaria (Harrison 22e p.1511). Culture of EBV from throat washings or blood does NOT diagnose acute infection because the virus persists lifelong in the oropharynx and B cells (Harrison 22e p.1511). Glucocorticoids are NOT indicated for uncomplicated IM and may predispose to bacterial superinfection (Harrison 22e p.1512). Acyclovir has had no significant clinical impact on IM in controlled trials (Harrison 22e p.1512). Persistent EBV infection is NOT a cause of chronic fatigue syndrome; antibody titers in such patients are not significantly different from healthy seropositive adults and EBV DNA is not elevated (Harrison 22e p.1510-1511). EBV, a herpesvirus, is transmitted in saliva and infects oropharyngeal and salivary epithelium plus B lymphocytes (including tonsillar-crypt lymphocytes directly), then disseminates via the bloodstream. Proliferation of EBV-infected B cells alongside reactive T cells enlarges lymphoid tissue. During acute IM up to 1 in 100 peripheral B cells is infected (falling to 1-50 per million after recovery), and there is an inverted CD4+/CD8+ ratio with large clonal CD8+ T-cell expansions (up to 40% directed against EBV antigens). The EBV receptor on B cells is CD21 (the C3d complement receptor); HLA class II is a co-receptor for B-cell entry, while epithelial entry uses ephrin A2. Memory B cells (not epithelial cells) are the lifelong reservoir. Cellular immunity (NK cells, cytotoxic T cells recognizing EBNAs and LMPs) is more important than humoral immunity in control; if T-cell immunity is impaired, infected B cells may proliferate, and in EBV-associated tumors LMP-1 mimics TNF-receptor-family signaling (e.g., CD40) to drive growth (Harrison 22e p.1508-1509). Most cases of IM are self-limited and resolve over 2-4 weeks; deaths are very rare and are most often due to CNS complications, splenic rupture, upper-airway obstruction, or bacterial superinfection. Nearly 10% of patients have fatigue persisting for 6 months or more. Disease severity correlates with blood CD8+ T-cell and EBV DNA levels. Most neurologic complications resolve without sequelae. The risk of EBV-positive Hodgkin's lymphoma is significantly increased in young adults for several years after EBV-seropositive IM (Harrison 22e p.1509-1511).

infective panniculitis — infectious panniculitis, septic panniculitis erythema nodosum erythema induratum / nodular vasculitis pancreatic panniculitis lupus panniculitis traumatic panniculitis factitial panniculitis subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma deep incisional biopsy for histopathology with special stains (Gram, Ziehl-Neelsen, PAS, Grocott) tissue culture for bacteria, mycobacteria and fungi from a deep specimen blood cultures and inflammatory markers full blood count and assessment of immune status (including HIV testing where relevant) imaging (ultrasound or MRI) to define the extent of deep infection or abscess polymerase chain reaction or molecular assays for fastidious organisms review of injections, travel, animal exposure and immunosuppressive therapy An inflammation of subcutaneous fat caused directly by microbial infection, encompassing bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal and, rarely, parasitic organisms. It should be suspected when panniculitis is accompanied by fever, systemic upset, immunosuppression, ulceration, abscess formation or a suppurative, draining quality. Immunocompromised patients (including those on biologics, chemotherapy or corticosteroids, and diabetics) are at particular risk and may show atypical or opportunistic organisms. Histology characteristically shows a mixed septal and lobular panniculitis with neutrophils, sometimes suppuration, necrosis and, in mycobacterial or fungal disease, granulomas. Special stains (Gram, Ziehl-Neelsen, PAS, Grocott) and, crucially, tissue culture of a deep biopsy are needed because organisms may be sparse. So-called bottom-heavy inflammation, deep dermal and subcutaneous extension, vascular proliferation and interstitial neutrophils are histological clues that favour an infective cause. Empirical broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy may be required in the septic patient while cultures are pending, then narrowed to the identified organism. A deep incisional biopsy sent for both histology and microbiology, rather than a superficial punch, is the single most useful diagnostic step. sepsis with fever, hypotension or rapidly spreading induration necrotising soft-tissue infection requiring urgent surgical debridement immunosuppression with atypical or disseminated infection fluctuance, discharge or abscess formation requiring drainage failure to improve on empirical antibiotics, suggesting mycobacterial, fungal or resistant organisms Treating an infective panniculitis as a sterile inflammatory panniculitis with immunosuppression, worsening the infection. Relying on a superficial biopsy that misses deep organisms and yields negative cultures. Omitting tissue culture and special stains when only routine histology is requested. Underestimating atypical organisms in immunocompromised patients. Missing an evolving necrotising infection that requires surgical rather than purely medical management. Infective panniculitis arises when micro-organisms reach the subcutaneous fat, either by direct inoculation through trauma or injection, by contiguous spread from overlying skin or deeper structures, or haematogenously in bacteraemic or immunocompromised hosts. Microbial proliferation and released enzymes and toxins damage adipocytes and vasculature, and the host mounts a predominantly neutrophilic and, for intracellular organisms such as mycobacteria and fungi, granulomatous inflammatory response. Fat necrosis, abscess formation and septal and lobular inflammation follow. The pattern and intensity of the reaction depend on the organism and the immune competence of the host, so immunosuppressed patients may show attenuated inflammation yet abundant organisms. Prognosis depends on the organism, host immune status and timeliness of treatment; most immunocompetent patients recover fully with appropriate antimicrobial therapy, whereas deep, necrotising or opportunistic infections in immunocompromised hosts carry appreciable morbidity and mortality.

chronic infertility itself is non-infective) Mumps orchitis as a historical cause of testicular damage and male infertility Transvaginal and abdominal pelvic ultrasound for uterine/adnexal pathology and antral follicle count (ovarian reserve) Ovulation assessment: urinary LH detection kits or serum progesterone ~7 days after ovulation Hysterosalpingogram (HSG) or saline infusion sonogram to assess tubal patency and intrauterine pathology Ovarian reserve testing: day 2-3 serum FSH and estradiol plus anti-mullerian hormone (AMH) and antral follicle counts Endocrine tests in irregular menses: serum TSH, prolactin, total and free testosterone Semen analysis after 2-7 days abstinence (count, motility, morphology, volume, pH); CFTR testing in congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens Preconception genetic carrier screening based on ethnicity/family history Endometriosis presenting with pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea overlapping other gynecologic disease Fibroid-related symptoms mimicking other uterine pathology Anovulation from systemic endocrine disease (thyroid, prolactin) Infertility is defined as failure to conceive after 12 months of unprotected intercourse; global prevalence is roughly 17.5%, affecting an estimated 48-72 million couples (Harrison 22e p.3149). Primary infertility describes couples who have never conceived, whereas secondary infertility follows at least one prior pregnancy; about 85% of couples conceive within 12 months and 95% within 24 months (Harrison 22e p.3149). Female-only factors account for roughly 30-40% of cases, male-only factors 40-50%, combined factors 20-30%, and unexplained infertility up to about 30% - so a complete workup of BOTH partners is recommended (Harrison 22e p.3149-3150). Fecundability falls steeply with maternal age: compared with women aged 30-31, it is reduced about 14% at 34-35, 53% at 40-41, and 59% at 42-44 years, largely from oocyte meiotic chromosomal errors; a comparable decline is NOT seen in men under 50 (Harrison 22e p.3149). Evaluation is generally started after 12 months of trying, but after only 6 months if the female partner is over 35 and immediately if she is over 40 (Harrison 22e p.3150). The fertile window is about 5-6 days before ovulation; intercourse every 1-2 days during this interval maximizes the chance of conception. A basal body temperature rise confirms ovulation has already occurred and therefore cannot be used prospectively to time intercourse (Harrison 22e p.3151). Long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARC; IUDs and subdermal implants) are the most effective reversible methods, rivaling sterilization, with high continuation and satisfaction rates, making them a good choice even for adolescents and nulliparous women (Harrison 22e p.3153-3154). Combined estrogen-progestin contraceptives reduce the risk of endometrial cancer (about 50%) and ovarian cancer (about 40%) and help regulate cycles and reduce menorrhagia, dysmenorrhea and hyperandrogenism (Harrison 22e p.3153). Unintended pregnancies arise mainly from non-use or inconsistent use rather than method failure; methods requiring daily or coitus-related use fail more often than LARC and permanent methods (Harrison 22e p.3152-3153). Emergency contraception should be offered to any woman who requests it up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse and should NOT be delayed for a pregnancy test or exam; the copper IUD is the most effective option and ulipristal acetate the most effective oral agent (Harrison 22e p.3154). Lactation can provide effective contraception during the first 6 postpartum months only if breastfeeding is exclusive and menses have not resumed, with failure rates as low as 0.5-1.5 per 100 women-years (Harrison 22e p.3154). Female partner over 40 years - evaluate immediately rather than waiting Azoospermia or severe oligospermia (<5 million/mL) - requires genetic and endocrine evaluation Smoker aged 35 or older using >=15 cigarettes/day - USMEC category 4 contraindication to estrogen-containing contraception History of venous thromboembolism, known thrombogenic mutations, stroke, or ischemic heart disease - avoid estrogen-containing contraceptives Migraine with aura - contraindication to combined hormonal contraception Current breast cancer - contraindication to hormonal contraception Recurrent pregnancy loss - consider sperm DNA fragmentation assay Treating only one partner - both must be evaluated because male, female, and combined factors are common. Using basal body temperature to time intercourse prospectively; the temperature rise only confirms ovulation has already happened. Over-relying on HSG positive findings - its positive predictive value for tubal occlusion is low even though its negative predictive value is high. Performing routine sperm-antibody testing, scrotal ultrasound, diagnostic laparoscopy, postcoital test, endometrial biopsy, thrombophilia, immunologic testing, or karyotype as part of the initial infertility workup - these are NOT indicated routinely. Attempting tubal repair/reconstruction with hydrosalpinx or prior tubal infection - low success and increased ectopic risk; salpingectomy of hydrosalpinges actually improves subsequent IVF outcomes. Routine screening for familial thrombotic disorders before prescribing hormonal contraception is not recommended. Withholding or delaying emergency contraception to obtain a pregnancy test or exam, or withholding it from overweight/obese women. Assuming individual abnormal semen parameters predict infertility - none alone is predictive; risk rises with multiple abnormalities. Conception requires ovulation of a competent oocyte, patent fallopian tubes, a receptive uterus, and adequate sperm delivery and function; disruption at any step causes infertility. Female causes include tubal damage (often from pelvic inflammatory disease, endometriosis, prior surgery, or salpingitis isthmica nodosum), uterine factors (fibroids distorting the cavity, congenital mullerian anomalies, intrauterine scarring), ovulatory dysfunction (PCOS, diminished ovarian reserve, premature ovarian insufficiency), and endocrine disturbance (hypothyroidism, hyperprolactinemia). Age-related decline reflects accumulating meiotic chromosomal errors in the oocyte after 35. Male causes include anatomic/obstructive problems (vasectomy, infection, congenital absence of the vas), endocrine causes (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, hyperprolactinemia, morbid obesity, certain drugs and exogenous testosterone suppressing spermatogenesis), sexual dysfunction, and primary testicular/genetic defects (Klinefelter syndrome, Y-chromosome microdeletions). Hormonal contraception works through negative feedback: continuous estrogen suppresses FSH and follicular development while continuous progestin suppresses the LH surge and ovulation, thickens cervical mucus, thins/alters the endometrium, and impairs tubal motility; progestin-only and levonorgestrel-IUD effects rely mainly on cervical mucus thickening and endometrial thinning. Copper IUDs act as a spermicide that also impairs fertilization and implantation (Harrison 22e p.3149-3154). About 85% of couples not using contraception conceive within one year and 95% within two years, but success of fertility treatment depends strongly on the female partner's age, ovarian reserve, smoking, BMI, and race; advanced maternal age (>35) raises aneuploidy risk and advanced paternal age (>40) is linked to adverse offspring outcomes. IVF carries an overall low complication risk, with multiple pregnancy being the main hazard and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome reduced by careful monitoring and GnRH (rather than hCG) triggering. Infertility causes substantial psychological stress, but the condition and its treatment do not appear to produce long-term psychological sequelae (Harrison 22e p.3149-3152). Contraceptive choice is guided by the U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria (USMEC, adapted from WHO): Category 4 = unacceptable health risk (e.g., smoker >=35 years with >=15 cigarettes/day, acute DVT or prior VTE at high recurrence risk, stroke or thrombogenic mutations, complicated valvular disease, current breast cancer, migraine with aura, uncontrolled hypertension >=160/100); Category 3 = theoretical/proven risks outweigh benefits (e.g., smoker >=35 with <15 cigarettes/day, controlled or moderate hypertension, certain enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants, rifampin/rifabutin, some HIV regimens, bariatric malabsorptive surgery); Category 2 = benefits generally outweigh risks (e.g., obesity alone). Method effectiveness ranges from highly effective sterilization and LARC (>99%) to less reliable barrier and fertility-awareness methods (Harrison 22e p.3152-3153).

periaortic inflammation Overlooking ureteric entrapment and obstructive uropathy Failing to consider IgG4-related disease as an underlying cause Not excluding an infective (mycotic) aneurysm before superimposed on aneurysmal degeneration. Transmural lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, medial destruction, and adventitial fibrosis thicken the wall and generate a periaortic inflammatory mass that can entrap the ureters and bowel. The process shares features with chronic periaortitis and, in some cases, IgG4-related disease, and the inflammation contributes to pain, systemic symptoms, and adhesion of adjacent structures. Repair of the aneurysm carries the usual operative considerations, and the periaortic inflammation often regresses afterwards; where an underlying inflammatory or IgG4-related process persists, immunosuppression and surveillance are added. Overall prognosis after treatment is generally good, though ureteric involvement may need separate management.
