consider patency capsule first) CT enterography or MR enterography (MR preferred in young patients/serial imaging to avoid radiation) Pelvic MRI for perianal/ischiorectal fistulas and abscesses Small-bowel ultrasound and intestinal ultrasound for assessing activity and mucosal healing MRCP (or ERCP) when primary sclerosing cholangitis is suspected Serologic markers ASCA and pANCA (limited clinical utility; less helpful than clinical factors) Diverticulitis Ischemic colitis Radiation colitis/enteritis Collagenous / lymphocytic (microscopic) colitis Diversion colitis Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome NSAID-induced colitis Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-related colitis Drug/chemical colitis (phosphosoda, gold, mycophenolate mofetil, cocaine, oral contraceptives) Neoplasia (lymphoma, carcinoma of colon/ileum, carcinoid, metastatic disease, familial polyposis) Appendicitis IBD is a chronic, idiopathic inflammatory disease of the GI tract; ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease (CD) are its two major types (Harrison 22e p.2551). UC is a mucosal disease that almost always involves the rectum and extends proximally in continuity, without intervening areas of uninvolved (skip) mucosa; ~40-50% have disease limited to rectum/rectosigmoid and ~20% have pancolitis (Harrison 22e p.2555). CD can affect any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus, is segmental with skip areas, and characteristically spares the rectum (unlike UC); the terminal ileum is involved in ~90% of those with small-intestinal disease (Harrison 22e p.2556). CD is a transmural process producing fistulas, strictures, abscesses and an endoscopic/radiographic 'cobblestone' appearance, whereas UC inflammation is limited to mucosa and superficial submucosa except in fulminant disease (Harrison 22e p.2555-2556). Noncaseating granulomas are a characteristic histologic feature of CD but are found less often on mucosal biopsy than on surgical resection specimens; UC shows crypt distortion, basal plasmacytosis, cryptitis and crypt abscesses (Harrison 22e p.2556). Major UC symptoms are diarrhoea, rectal bleeding, tenesmus, mucus passage and crampy abdominal pain; severe pain is not prominent in UC, whereas CD ileocolitis classically causes right-lower-quadrant pain and diarrhoea, sometimes mimicking acute appendicitis (Harrison 22e p.2556-2557). Perianal disease (perirectal fistulas, fissures, abscesses, anal stenosis, skin tags) occurs in about one-third of CD patients and points away from UC; extensive perianal lesions in apparent UC should suggest CD (Harrison 22e p.2556, p.2557). Faecal calprotectin and faecal lactoferrin are neutrophil-derived markers that correlate with histologic inflammation, help distinguish IBD from irritable bowel syndrome, predict relapse and detect pouchitis; calprotectin is more sensitive for ileocolonic/colonic than isolated ileal inflammation (Harrison 22e p.2557, p.2558). Distinguishing UC from CD is impossible initially in up to 15% of cases (indeterminate colitis); ~5% of resection specimens cannot be classified due to overlapping features (Harrison 22e p.2559). Up to one-third of IBD patients have at least one extraintestinal manifestation; some parallel bowel activity (erythema nodosum, peripheral arthritis, episcleritis) while others run an independent course (pyoderma gangrenosum, ankylosing spondylitis, sacroiliitis, uveitis, PSC) (Harrison 22e p.2561-2563). Smoking has opposite associations in the two diseases: it may be protective in UC (OR 0.58) but is a risk factor for CD (OR 1.76); prior appendectomy with confirmed appendicitis is protective against UC but not CD (Harrison 22e p.2551-2552). Patients with long-standing extensive colitis (UC or Crohn's colitis) have an increased risk of colonic dysplasia and carcinoma; surveillance colonoscopy with multiple biopsies is the standard of care (Harrison 22e p.2612-2613). Toxic megacolon (transverse or right colon diameter >6 cm with loss of haustration in a severe attack) - may be precipitated by electrolyte abnormalities and narcotics; risk of perforation Perforation - most dangerous local complication; peritoneal signs may be masked by glucocorticoids; mortality of perforation complicating toxic megacolon is ~15% Massive GI haemorrhage Bowel obstruction from fibrostenotic stricture (CD) Intraabdominal or pelvic abscess and fistula formation (CD); high-spiking fever suggests abscess Stricture impassable to the colonoscope - presume malignant until proven otherwise New or worsening dysplasia/carcinoma on surveillance in long-standing colitis Failing to exclude infective colitis (especially C. difficile, Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli, CMV) and amebiasis before diagnosing or escalating treatment of IBD - infection can both mimic IBD and trigger relapse (Harrison 22e p.2559-2561). In UC, biopsies of normal-appearing mucosa are usually abnormal, so multiple biopsies should be taken from apparently uninvolved proximal and distal mucosa; effective medical therapy can also create pseudo-skip areas (Harrison 22e p.2555). Peritoneal signs of perforation may be absent or subtle in patients on glucocorticoids (Harrison 22e p.2557). A colonic stricture impassable with the colonoscope should be presumed malignant until proven otherwise (Harrison 22e p.2557). Extensive perianal lesions in apparent UC should raise suspicion for Crohn's disease (Harrison 22e p.2557). Wireless capsule endoscopy must be avoided when a small-bowel stricture is suspected because of the risk of capsule retention (Harrison 22e p.2558). Serologic tests (ASCA, pANCA) have variable predictive value and unclear clinical usefulness for distinguishing or predicting IBD (Harrison 22e p.2559). Pyoderma gangrenosum and ankylosing spondylitis run a course independent of bowel disease and do not reliably improve with colectomy (Harrison 22e p.2561-2562). IBD is regarded as an inappropriate, dysregulated mucosal immune response to the endogenous commensal microbiota (with or without an autoimmune component) in a genetically susceptible host, shaped by environmental factors. Homeostasis among the commensal microbiota, intestinal epithelial cells and mucosal immune cells is disrupted, producing chronic inflammation. More than ~240 genetic loci (e.g. NOD2, ATG16L1, IL23R, IL12B, IL10, XBP1) contribute incrementally and affect pathways of innate immunity, autophagy/unfolded-protein response, adaptive immunity and inflammation/healing; ~two-thirds are shared between CD and UC. Dysbiosis (e.g. expansion of adherent/invasive E. coli, loss of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii) and defective oral (mucosal) tolerance lead to unrestrained CD4+ T-cell (TH1/TH2/TH17) and innate immune activation, with a self-perpetuating cytokine cascade (IL-1, IL-6, IL-12, IL-23, TNF) driving fibrogenesis, leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage. TH1-driven transmural granulomatous inflammation resembles CD; TH2-type superficial mucosal inflammation resembles UC. Roughly 5-10% of patients have familial disease and only ~20% of disease risk is currently explained by known genetics (Harrison 22e p.2551-2555). IBD is a lifelong chronic disease with a relapsing-remitting course; only ~15% of UC patients present initially with severe disease. Massive haemorrhage occurs in ~1% of UC patients and toxic megacolon is rare (about 50% of acute dilations resolve with conservative management, the remainder requiring urgent colectomy). In CD the inflammatory process tends to evolve toward a fibrostenotic obstructing pattern or a penetrating fistulous pattern; intestinal obstruction occurs in ~40%, intraabdominal/pelvic abscesses in 10-30%, and free perforation in 1-2%. Long-standing extensive colitis carries an increased colorectal cancer risk (UC meta-analysis figures of ~2% at 10 years, 8% at 20 years, 18% at 30 years, though rates have fallen with better inflammation control and surveillance; overall colorectal cancer rates remain ~1.5-2 times the general population). CD and UC cancer risks are probably equivalent for similar extent and duration. Associated PSC carries a 7-10% risk of cholangiocarcinoma (Harrison 22e p.2557-2563, p.2612-2613). Ulcerative colitis is graded by the Montreal classification of extent (E1 proctitis; E2 left-sided/distal UC, distal to splenic flexure; E3 extensive/pancolitis, proximal to splenic flexure) and severity (S0 clinical remission; S1 mild: <=4 stools/day with or without blood, no systemic illness, normal ESR; S2 moderate: >=4 stools/day with minimal systemic toxicity; S3 severe: >=6 bloody stools/day, pulse >=90/min, temperature >=37.5C, haemoglobin <10.5 g/100 mL, ESR >=30 mm/h). Crohn's disease is classified by the Vienna and Montreal systems by age at diagnosis (A1/A2/A3), location (L1 ileal, L2 colonic, L3 ileocolonic, L4 upper/foregut) and behaviour (B1 nonstricturing-nonpenetrating, B2 stricturing, B3 penetrating), with a 'p' modifier for perianal disease (Harrison 22e p.2557-2558).

for kinase fusions Confusing it with IgG4-related disease, which has overlapping histology but different management Assuming ALK negativity excludes a targetable driver, since ROS1 and NTRK fusions occur Underestimating the epithelioid variant because of its deceptively inflammatory appearance Attributing constitutional symptoms to infection rather than the tumour itself Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour is a clonal neoplasm of myofibroblastic cells, most often driven by a fusion involving the ALK receptor tyrosine kinase that leads to constitutive kinase activation and cell proliferation. In ALK-negative cases, alternative kinase fusions such as those involving ROS1 or NTRK play an equivalent oncogenic role. Most inflammatory myofibroblastic tumours are cured by complete excision, though local recurrence occurs in a minority and distant metastasis is rare; the epithelioid inflammatory myofibroblastic sarcoma variant behaves more aggressively, and ALK inhibition offers durable responses in unresectable or metastatic ALK-positive disease.

Serum creatine kinase (CK) is the most sensitive laboratory marker of muscle destruction; a markedly elevated CK (e.g. >2000 U/L) is almost always due to a myopathy, and CK is always elevated in uncontrolled PM and markedly elevated (usually >10x normal) in IMNM (Harrison 22e p.2910-2912). DM rash includes the heliotrope rash (violaceous eyelid discoloration with periorbital edema), Gottron sign and Gottron papules over extensor joint surfaces, V-sign (anterior neck/chest), shawl sign (posterior neck/shoulders), nail-bed telangiectasias, and subcutaneous calcium deposits; a heliotrope rash with Gottron papules and dilated nailfold capillaries is diagnostic for DM (Harrison 22e p.2910-2911). Myositis-specific antibodies (MSAs) help define subtypes: DM (anti-Mi-2, anti-TIF1-gamma, anti-MDA5, anti-NXP-2, anti-SAE); IMNM (anti-HMGCR, anti-SRP); ASyS (antisynthetase antibodies, most commonly anti-Jo-1); IBM (anti-cN-1A) (Harrison 22e p.2909-2914). EMG/nerve conduction studies help localize the lesion to muscle but are nonspecific for cause; muscle MRI shows edema, atrophy, or fatty replacement and can show subtype-specific patterns (e.g. IBM spares the rectus femoris while involving vastus medialis/lateralis) (Harrison 22e p.2910-2914). A muscle biopsy is often required to distinguish myopathies when there is no characteristic DM rash or MSA, and should be performed in every case of suspected PM to exclude IBM and other causes; biopsy a clinically affected but not too-weak muscle (e.g. MRC grade 4/5) to avoid sampling only end-stage muscle (Harrison 22e p.2910-2911). Patients with severe muscle pain, subjective weakness, and fatigue but normal strength/function on exam are not likely to have an IM; consider polymyalgia rheumatica in older patients with raised ESR/CRP but normal CK and EMG, and fibromyalgia when the lab workup is normal (Harrison 22e p.2911). Overlap syndrome describes an IM associated with another connective tissue disease (scleroderma, MCTD, Sjogren syndrome, SLE, rheumatoid arthritis); overlap syndromes are usually responsive to immunotherapy, except Sjogren syndrome with coexisting IBM (Harrison 22e p.2912). DM, PM, ASyS, and IMNM are typically responsive to immunotherapy with high-dose glucocorticoids as first-line; IBM does NOT typically respond to any known immunotherapy and is managed with physical/occupational and swallowing therapy (Harrison 22e p.2915-2916). Dermatomyositis rash (heliotrope rash, Gottron sign/papules) - adult-onset DM carries ~15% malignancy risk within the first 2-3 years; enhanced cancer vigilance especially with anti-TIF1-gamma (89% specificity, 70% sensitivity for cancer-associated DM) Anti-MDA5 antibodies - palmar rash, severe ischemic skin ulceration, and rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (also frequent in amyopathic DM) Dyspnea from ILD, bronchopneumonia, alveolitis, or ventilatory muscle weakness Dysphagia and dysarthria (aspiration risk; common in IBM and seen in DM/IMNM) Myocarditis / cardiac disease (poor prognostic feature) Markedly elevated CK (e.g. >2000 U/L) - almost always indicates a myopathy IBM is frequently misdiagnosed and is distinguished from PM by distal/asymmetric weakness with predilection for finger/wrist flexors and quadriceps in patients >50, normal or only mildly elevated CK, and being essentially steroid-refractory and unresponsive to any known immunotherapy - so a normal CK should alert clinicians to the possibility of IBM Many older series of 'PM' likely actually included patients with IBM, IMNM, or muscular dystrophies with inflammation, biasing reported treatment response and cancer-risk data Perifascicular atrophy (the classic DM biopsy finding) is present in perhaps only 50% of DM patients; MxA immunostaining is diagnostically more sensitive and highly specific Rimmed vacuoles may be absent in up to 20-30% of IBM biopsies; mitochondrial abnormality (ragged-red/COX-negative fibers) and p62 inclusions help distinguish IBM from PM in such cases Anti-HMGCR myopathy does NOT improve when statins are stopped (unlike common toxic statin myopathy) and can occur in statin-naive children/young adults, mimicking limb-girdle muscular dystrophy IBM EMG can show large-amplitude long-duration motor units that may be misinterpreted as neurogenic but actually reflect chronicity of the myopathy Muscle biopsy should sample a clinically affected but not too-weak muscle (e.g. MRC 4/5); biopsying an end-stage muscle yields non-diagnostic tissue The inflammatory myopathies are immune-mediated muscle diseases with distinct mechanisms by subtype. DM microvasculopathy and skin/muscle damage are increasingly attributed to type I interferon (IFN)-mediated toxicity, most likely IFN-beta, rather than the older model of antibody/complement-mediated capillary destruction with watershed ischemia; immunoglobulin deposition on endothelium is largely absent and complement deposition may be secondary, and there is increasing evidence MSAs are directly pathogenic (e.g. anti-Mi-2 entering myonuclei to inhibit the CHD4/NuRD complex). PM is heterogeneous with poorly understood pathogenesis; its infiltrate is predominantly CD8+ T cells and macrophages in endomysial, perimysial, and perivascular regions. IMNM shows multifocal necrotic and regenerating fibers with few inflammatory cells; it does not appear primarily complement-driven (complement inhibition failed in anti-HMGCR and anti-SRP disease), anti-HMGCR antibodies may bind sarcolemmal receptor causing acetyl-CoA and lipid accumulation, and anti-SRP antibodies appear directly causal. ASyS resembles DM histologically but with more perifascicular necrosis and HLA-DR (MHC-II) expression suggesting gamma-IFN rather than type I IFN drive. IBM combines adaptive immune attack (highly differentiated CD8+CD57+ KLRG1+ T cells invading non-necrotic MHC-I/II-expressing fibers, plus a relatively specific autoantibody) with degenerative features including rimmed vacuoles, beta-sheet amyloid inclusions, p62/LC3 aggregates and ER stress/autophagy, mitochondrial abnormality (ragged-red and COX-negative fibers), and extrusion of TDP-43 from myonuclei; whether damage is primarily immune or a secondary neurodegenerative process is unclear. In the absence of malignancy, DM prognosis is generally favorable with 5-year survival of 70-93%; poor prognostic features (DM and PM) are increased age, associated ILD, cardiac disease, and late or previously inadequate treatment. Most PM patients improve with immunotherapy but usually require lifelong treatment. IMNM varies by subtype: anti-HMGCR myopathy is often responsive to IVIG monotherapy, whereas anti-SRP and seronegative IMNM are much harder to treat and need aggressive immunotherapy; increased cancer incidence may exist in anti-HMGCR myopathy. ASyS patients mostly respond but disease can be difficult to treat (especially with ILD, where early rituximab is warranted) with no apparent increased malignancy risk. IBM is slowly progressive and not typically responsive to immunotherapy; most patients require a scooter or wheelchair within ~10-15 years of symptom onset, with no known increased malignancy risk. Harrison does not provide a formal numeric severity grading scale for the inflammatory myopathies. Disease is characterized instead by clinical subtype (DM, PM, IMNM, ASyS, IBM), pattern and degree of weakness (graded clinically, e.g. MRC strength), serum CK elevation, presence of organ involvement (ILD, myocarditis, dysphagia), associated malignancy, and responsiveness to immunotherapy. Treatment intensity (first-line high-dose glucocorticoids; early second-line agents for severe weakness, organ involvement such as myocarditis/ILD, steroid-complication risk, or IMNM) reflects severity stratification in practice.

Influenza — flu COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2) respiratory illness Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection Human metapneumovirus infection Parainfluenza virus infection Rhinovirus / common cold Adenovirus infection Acute bronchitis SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) Respiratory syncytial virus Human metapneumovirus Parainfluenza virus Adenovirus Rhinovirus Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (e.g., S. pneumoniae) RT-PCR molecular testing of respiratory secretions (most sensitive and specific; multiplex respiratory panels available) Rapid antigen-based diagnostic test for influenza viral protein in nasopharyngeal secretions Viral isolation by cell culture in a reference laboratory (gold standard but insensitive/slow) Direct or indirect fluorescent antibody detection of virus-infected cells in nasal secretions Chest radiograph for all patients with suspected pneumonia Acute exacerbation of COPD Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis Decompensated cardiovascular disease presenting with fever and dyspnea Influenza presents with an abrupt febrile illness: fever, myalgias, fatigue, sore throat, headache, and cough (Harrison 22e p.1576). Influenza A viruses are the most virulent for humans and cause most severe disease, though type B viruses (Victoria lineage) also cause substantial morbidity; type A is subdivided by hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) surface protein subtypes (Harrison 22e p.1576). Two type A subtypes (H1N1 and H3N2) and one type B lineage (Victoria) cause annual seasonal epidemics, which occur in winter in temperate regions (Harrison 22e p.1576, p.1579). Influenza pneumonia has an unusually high rate of complication by bacterial superinfection, with staphylococcal and streptococcal pneumonia occurring in as many as 10% of cases in some series (Harrison 22e p.1576). Antiviral treatment of influenza is effective only when given early in the course of illness; baloxavir marboxil is approved for acute uncomplicated flu when started within 2 days of onset (Harrison 22e p.1537, p.1580). Antibiotics do NOT improve the outcome of uncomplicated viral respiratory infection in otherwise healthy people, but influenza can be complicated by secondary bacterial infection that does warrant antibacterials (Harrison 22e p.1537). Annual vaccine reformulation is required because antigenic drift (point mutations in HA and NA) causes antigenic divergence; an occasional antigenic mismatch can render a vaccine component of negligible efficacy (Harrison 22e p.1538). Secondary bacterial pneumonia complicating influenza, classically caused by S. aureus (including MRSA, with risk of necrotizing pneumonia) and S. pneumoniae/S. pyogenes Severe or fatal primary viral pneumonia, particularly in elderly patients, nursing-home residents, immunocompromised persons, and very young children Hypoxia or respiratory failure requiring supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation Avian/zoonotic strains (e.g., H5N1, H7N9) with high mortality and pandemic potential, especially with relevant exposure history RT-PCR is extremely sensitive: viral genome can persist in nasal secretions for weeks after an infection resolves, so a positive test may reflect a recently resolved rather than a currently acute infection, and laboratory contamination can produce false positives (Harrison 22e p.1537). Rapid diagnostic tests have the highest positive predictive value when applied to high-risk, appropriately seasonal samples; indiscriminate testing lowers predictive value (Harrison 22e p.1537). Adamantanes (amantadine, rimantadine) should not be relied upon: widespread resistance has occurred in many currently circulating influenza A viruses (Harrison 22e p.1580). Antiviral therapy started late is of limited benefit, as it is effective mainly when given early in the course (Harrison 22e p.1537). Influenza is a single-stranded, segmented, negative-sense RNA genome virus of the family Orthomyxoviridae, with four (sero)types: A, B, C, and D. Influenza A and C infect multiple species; B infects humans almost exclusively; D primarily infects cattle and is not known to infect humans. Influenza A is subdivided into 18 hemagglutinin (H) and 11 neuraminidase (N) surface-protein subtypes. Two distinct mechanisms drive antigenic variation: antigenic drift (accumulation of point mutations in the HA and NA molecules) produces the gradual divergence underlying annual epidemics and requires new vaccines each year; antigenic shift, enabled by the segmented genome allowing reassortment between two viruses co-infecting one host, can produce a major novel virus and a pandemic. Type B viruses mutate less frequently than type A, probably reflecting their near-exclusive human host range. Many highly pathogenic strains circulate in aquatic birds; pigs, which carry both avian and human receptors, can serve as a mixing vessel for reassortment that makes zoonotic viruses more fit for human replication (Harrison 22e p.1576). Uncomplicated influenza in otherwise healthy adults is generally self-limited, and antiviral therapy started early shortens illness. Severe and even fatal pneumonia occurs particularly in elderly patients, nursing-home residents, immunocompromised persons, and very young children. Bacterial superinfection complicates as many as 10% of influenza pneumonia cases in some series. Pandemics caused by novel viruses occur on average every 20-30 years (Harrison 22e p.1576, p.1538).

Inguinal hernia — groin hernia, indirect inguinal hernia, direct inguinal hernia Femoral hernia Inguinal lymphadenopathy Saphena varix Hydrocele or encysted hydrocele of the cord Lipoma of the cord or groin Undescended or ectopic testis Femoral artery aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm Psoas abscess Clinical examination in standing and supine positions with cough impulse assessment Ultrasound of the groin when the diagnosis is uncertain or the swelling is not clinically obvious CT or MRI in complex, recurrent, or occult hernias Herniography in selected occult cases (rarely used now) Baseline bloods and lactate if strangulation or obstruction is suspected Presents as a groin swelling that appears or enlarges on standing, coughing, or straining and often reduces on lying flat Indirect hernias travel down the inguinal canal along the spermatic cord and lie lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, while direct hernias push forward through a weakness in the posterior canal wall medial to those vessels A hernia arising below and lateral to the pubic tubercle suggests a femoral hernia, whereas one above and medial to it suggests an inguinal hernia; this landmark helps distinguish the two Reducibility, cough impulse, and whether the swelling can be controlled at the deep ring are key clinical assessments Loss of cough impulse with a tense, tender, irreducible lump raises concern for obstruction or strangulation Indirect hernias are the commonest groin hernia in both sexes and across all ages, reflecting a persistent processus vaginalis Elective repair, most commonly tension-free mesh repair (open Lichtenstein or laparoscopic), is the definitive treatment; watchful waiting may be reasonable for small, minimally symptomatic hernias in selected patients Chronic cough, constipation, bladder outflow obstruction, and heavy lifting raise intra-abdominal pressure and should be sought as contributing factors Tense, tender, irreducible groin lump with loss of cough impulse indicating incarceration or strangulation (surgical emergency) Features of bowel obstruction (colicky pain, distension, vomiting, absolute constipation) with an irreducible hernia Overlying skin erythema, systemic sepsis, or rising lactate suggesting strangulated ischaemic bowel Sudden severe pain in a previously reducible hernia Mislabelling a femoral hernia as inguinal and underestimating its higher strangulation risk Attributing a groin lump to a hernia without excluding lymphadenopathy, saphena varix, or vascular causes Forcible reduction of a strangulated hernia, which can reduce non-viable bowel into the abdomen (reduction en masse) Failing to identify and address contributing causes of raised intra-abdominal pressure Delaying surgery in an irreducible, tender hernia and missing evolving strangulation An inguinal hernia is protrusion of abdominal contents through the inguinal canal. Indirect hernias pass through the deep (internal) inguinal ring into the canal, often through a patent processus vaginalis, and may descend into the scrotum. Direct hernias bulge forward through an attenuated posterior wall of the canal (Hesselbach's triangle) as a result of acquired weakness of the transversalis fascia. Raised intra-abdominal pressure and weakened abdominal wall connective tissue promote herniation. As a hernia enlarges the neck may narrow relative to the sac, predisposing to incarceration (irreducibility) and strangulation, in which the blood supply to trapped bowel is compromised, leading to ischaemia and, if untreated, perforation. Elective repair has a good outcome with low recurrence after tension-free mesh techniques. Emergency presentation with strangulation carries substantially higher morbidity and mortality, particularly if bowel resection is required in an elderly or comorbid patient.

Inherited Defects of Membrane Transport — Amino acid transport defects, Cystinuria, Lysinuric protein intolerance, Citrullinemia type 2, Citrin deficiency, Hartnup disease, Cystinosis, SLC transporter disorders Other causes of urolithiasis (calcium, uric acid, struvite stones) versus cystine stones Classic urea cycle defects versus the hyperammonemia of lysinuric protein intolerance and citrin deficiency Dietary niacin deficiency versus Hartnup disease as a cause of pellagra Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis versus the fatty liver seen in citrullinemia type 2 Other inherited causes of renal Fanconi syndrome versus nephropathic cystinosis Quantitative urinary amino acid analysis (selective overexcretion of cystine, lysine, arginine, ornithine in cystinuria; distinguishes heterozygotes from homozygotes) Urinary nitroprusside test and microscopy for hexagonal cystine crystals in acidified, concentrated, chilled urine Plasma and urine amino acids (low plasma lysine/arginine/ornithine with increased urinary excretion and orotic acid in lysinuric protein intolerance) Genetic sequencing: SLC3A1/SLC7A9 (cystinuria), SLC7A7 (lysinuric protein intolerance), SLC25A13 (citrin deficiency, on hyperammonemia panels), SLC6A19 or CTLRN/collectrin (Hartnup disease), CTNS including deletion analysis (cystinosis) During acute citrin deficiency attacks: ammonia, citrulline, arginine, glutamine, and red-cell galactose-1-phosphate Slit-lamp corneal examination and white-blood-cell cystine content for cystinosis Dietary niacin deficiency producing pellagra (mimics Hartnup disease but lacks neutral aminoaciduria) Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis on liver histology (mimics citrin deficiency) Other (non-cystine) urinary tract calculi These disorders arise from defects in solute-carrier (SLC) family transporters; tissue distribution of the affected transporter and presence or absence of redundant transporters determine which organs (notably brain and sensory organs) are involved. Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive defect of apical brush-border transport in the proximal renal tubule and small intestine, impairing reabsorption of the dibasic amino acids cystine, lysine, arginine, and ornithine; only poorly soluble cystine causes clinical disease through stone formation. Cystine stones account for roughly 1-2% of all urinary calculi and about 4-5% of stones in children; suspect cystinuria when typical hexagonal crystals appear in acidified, concentrated, chilled urine or with a positive nitroprusside test. Two cystinuria variants exist: type A (SLC3A1, a membrane glycoprotein) and type B (SLC7A9, the b0,+ transporter); the SLC3A1 glycoprotein aids correct processing of the b0,+ transporter, explaining why two different genes cause similar disease. Lysinuric protein intolerance is a basolateral (not luminal) transport defect (SLC7A7, y+LAT transporter) affecting lysine, arginine, and ornithine but sparing cystine, with secondary impairment of the urea cycle and characteristic episodic hyperammonemia after protein loads or infection. Citrullinemia type 2 (citrin deficiency, SLC25A13) reduces cytoplasmic aspartate available for the urea cycle and impairs the malate-aspartate NADH shuttle; affected individuals often spontaneously prefer protein/fat-rich foods and avoid carbohydrates, since carbohydrate-driven cytoplasmic NADH worsens the defect. Hartnup disease is an autosomal recessive defect of the neutral/aromatic amino acid transporter B0AT1 (SLC6A19), which requires collectrin in kidney and ACE2 in intestine for surface expression; symptoms reflect tryptophan and consequent niacin deficiency. In Hartnup disease only a minority of carriers of the transport defect become symptomatic, indicating that clinical expression depends on additional environmental and nutritional factors. Cystinosis (CTNS gene; lysosomal cystine/proton transporter cystinosin) causes intralysosomal cystine accumulation and crystal formation; cystine crystals in the cornea on slit-lamp examination are an important diagnostic clue. Cystinosis has three forms graded by residual transporter function: classic nephropathic (renal Fanconi syndrome with rickets in infancy, progressing to renal failure), juvenile nephropathic (proteinuria leading slowly to kidney failure), and ocular nonnephropathic (photophobia from corneal crystals as the only manifestation). Citrin deficiency can present in infancy as neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis with failure to thrive and dyslipidemia, or in adulthood (typically ages 20-50) with recurrent hyperammonemic neuropsychiatric episodes resembling hepatic encephalopathy. Most inherited amino acid transport defects are autosomal recessive; exceptions include certain neuronal/synaptic-vesicle glutamate transporter disorders (e.g., SLC1A2, SLC1A3, SLC17A8) that are autosomal dominant. Episodic hyperammonemia with altered mental status, seizures, or coma in lysinuric protein intolerance or citrin deficiency (risk of cerebral edema and death) Recurrent urolithiasis progressing to obstructive uropathy and renal insufficiency in cystinuria Infantile renal Fanconi syndrome with rickets in nephropathic cystinosis (progression to renal failure by about age 10 without treatment) Pellagra-like rash with neurologic relapse in Hartnup disease provoked by fever, sunlight, stress, or sulfonamides Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, severe osteoporosis, or pancreatitis as adult presentations of lysinuric protein intolerance Attributing pellagra solely to dietary niacin deficiency and missing Hartnup disease; neutral aminoaciduria distinguishes the two and does not occur in dietary deficiency. Expecting elevated glutamine as in classic urea cycle defects in citrin deficiency, where glutamine is often low or normal during attacks. Failing to recognize that cystinuria heterozygotes (especially type B) can have increased cystine excretion and may form stones, so quantitative measurement is needed. Overlooking that only a minority of individuals with the Hartnup transport defect become symptomatic, so genotype does not equal disease. Missing the carbohydrate-driven decompensation in citrin deficiency, where high sugar intake (and triggers such as acetaminophen, surgery, or alcohol) precipitates attacks. Membrane transporters of the solute-carrier (SLC) superfamily move amino acids, peptides, sugars, ions, vitamins, water, and other molecules across plasma membranes and organelle membranes. Inherited loss of a transporter produces disease whose organ pattern depends on the transporter's tissue distribution and whether redundant transporters exist. In cystinuria, defective apical proximal-tubule and intestinal transport of dibasic amino acids leads to massive cystine excretion; because cystine is poorly soluble, it precipitates and forms stones. In lysinuric protein intolerance, a basolateral transport defect traps arginine inside cells and secondarily impairs the urea cycle, with proposed nitric-oxide-mediated immune dysfunction. In citrin deficiency, the mitochondrial aspartate-glutamate carrier defect limits cytoplasmic aspartate for argininosuccinate synthesis and impairs the malate-aspartate NADH shuttle, so a cytoplasmic NADH excess (worsened by carbohydrate) drives metabolic decompensation and hyperammonemia. In Hartnup disease, loss of the neutral amino acid transporter B0AT1 causes renal and intestinal malabsorption of tryptophan, producing functional niacin deficiency and pellagra-like features. In cystinosis, a defective lysosomal cystine/proton transporter causes intralysosomal cystine accumulation and crystal deposition throughout tissues, with the kidney (Fanconi syndrome, progressive renal failure) and cornea most prominently affected. Prognosis is disorder-specific. Cystinuria can cause recurrent stones and occasional progression to renal failure requiring transplantation. Citrin deficiency, untreated, leads to death from cerebral edema within a few years in most symptomatic patients, but liver transplantation halts progression and normalizes biochemistry. In nephropathic cystinosis, life span was under 10 years before cystine-depleting therapy and transplantation; with current management affected individuals can survive into their late forties with satisfactory quality of life, though many still progress to end-stage renal disease and develop late multisystem complications. Cystinosis is graded by residual transporter function into classic nephropathic (most severe, infantile Fanconi syndrome and early renal failure), juvenile nephropathic (proteinuria with slower decline to renal failure), and ocular nonnephropathic (photophobia from corneal crystals only). Cystinuria homozygotes excrete 2400-7200 micromol (600-1800 mg) cystine daily versus the maximum urinary solubility of roughly 1200 micromol/L (300 mg/L) at physiologic pH 4.5-7.0.

misdiagnosed in urea cycle defects presenting with hepatic dysfunction Quantitative plasma amino acid analysis (ion-exchange or LC/tandem MS) Urine organic acid analysis by GC/MS Plasma acylcarnitine profile by tandem mass spectrometry Plasma ammonia and plasma glutamine measurement in suspected urea cycle defects Urine orotic acid to differentiate OTC from CPS-1 and NAGS deficiency Total plasma homocysteine and methionine for the homocystinurias Urine organic acid analysis to identify homogentisic acid in alkaptonuria Enzyme assay on cells/tissues or confirmatory DNA testing Newborn screening (blood phenylalanine, methionine) with confirmatory metabolic testing for positive screens Gastrointestinal disorders, food allergies, and behavioral problems are common misdiagnoses in milder urea cycle defects with protein aversion and recurrent vomiting Acquired hyperammonemia from liver disease of any cause, organic acidemias, or fatty acid oxidation defects can mimic urea cycle defects Marfan syndrome can mimic the marfanoid habitus and lens dislocation of classic homocystinuria Disorders of amino acid metabolism are individually rare (roughly 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 200,000) but collectively affect around 1 in 4000 newborns, and nearly all are inherited as autosomal recessive traits. Conditions are generally named for the compound that accumulates to highest concentration: aminoacidopathies show excess of the parent amino acid, whereas organic acidemias accumulate downstream catabolic products. Some defects (e.g., sarcosinemia, cystathioninuria, hyperlysinemia) are clinically benign, while at the opposite extreme complete ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is lethal in the untreated neonate. Classic phenylketonuria results from deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase activity; untreated infants are normal at birth but develop microcephaly, progressive intellectual disability, seizures, hypopigmentation, eczema, and a characteristic mousy odor from phenylacetate. Classic homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency) typically presents at 3-5 years with dislocated optic lenses, intellectual disability in about half, marfanoid habitus, and osteoporosis, with total plasma homocysteine usually above 100 micromol/L. Alkaptonuria (homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency) may be unrecognized until midlife; urine darkens on standing or with alkali, and ochronotic pigment deposits cause degenerative arthritis, scleral and ear pigmentation, and later aortic stenosis. Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is X-linked and the most common urea cycle defect; heterozygous females can become symptomatic when mutant hepatocytes predominate due to random X-inactivation. Plasma citrulline helps localize urea cycle defects: it is low or undetectable in proximal defects (NAGS, CPS-1, OTC) and markedly elevated in citrullinemia type 1 (argininosuccinate synthase deficiency). Urine orotic acid is increased only in ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency among the proximal urea cycle defects, distinguishing it from CPS-1 and N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency. Diagnosis relies on plasma amino acid analysis, urine organic acid analysis (GC/MS), and plasma acylcarnitine profile (tandem MS), confirmed by enzyme assay or DNA testing. Some metabolic disorders remain asymptomatic until adulthood, declaring themselves only when fasting or severe stress demands full activity of the affected pathway. In maternal phenylketonuria, uncontrolled maternal phenylalanine levels before and during pregnancy increase fetal risk of congenital defects, microcephaly, intellectual disability, and growth retardation regardless of fetal genotype. Neonate with refusal to feed and lethargy progressing to coma (classic urea cycle defect presentation at 1-4 days of life) Hyperammonemia precipitated by systemic corticosteroids or chemotherapy, which can be fatal in previously asymptomatic individuals of any age Postpartum behavioral change, stupor, or coma in a female (possible decompensated OTC deficiency from fasting and stress) Life-threatening coronary, renal, or cerebral arterial thrombosis in a young patient with homocystinuria Aortic stenosis developing in alkaptonuria, especially after age 60, from pigment deposition in heart valves Milder variants of homocystinuria may be missed by newborn methionine screening. Heterozygous females with X-linked OTC deficiency can be overlooked because symptoms depend on the proportion of mutant hepatocytes from random X-inactivation. Adult-onset metabolic decompensation can be triggered by involuntary fasting, severe stress, corticosteroids, or chemotherapy and may be mistaken for primary GI, allergic, behavioral, or hepatic disease. Hyperhomocysteinemia has many acquired causes (B6/folate/B12 deficiency, aging, smoking, renal failure, hypothyroidism, leukemias, and certain drugs such as methotrexate, nitrous oxide, and isoniazid) that must be distinguished from inherited homocystinuria. An abnormal newborn screen in an infant may actually reflect a maternal metabolic disorder (e.g., glutaric acidemia type 1, methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency, primary carnitine deficiency, fatty acid oxidation defect). Each amino acid has a unique degradative pathway that recycles its nitrogen and carbon for synthesis of other amino acids, carbohydrates, and lipids. An enzymatic block causes accumulation of compounds upstream of the lesion; what accumulates depends on the site of the block, reversibility of proximal reactions, and availability of alternative metabolic runoff pathways. In phenylketonuria, accumulated phenylalanine competitively inhibits transport of other amino acids needed for protein and neurotransmitter synthesis, reduces myelin synthesis while increasing its degradation, impairs norepinephrine and serotonin formation, and inhibits tyrosinase causing hypopigmentation. In homocystinuria, defective cystathionine beta-synthase or impaired remethylation of homocysteine to methionine raises homocysteine, which produces endothelial dysfunction and acts as an atherogenic and thrombophilic agent. In urea cycle defects, ammonia generated from protein nitrogen cannot be cleared, so ammonia and glutamine accumulate causing direct neuronal toxicity and brain edema. In alkaptonuria, deficient homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase leads to urinary excretion of homogentisic acid and deposition of its oxidized pigment in connective tissue (ochronosis). Clinical manifestations of many of these conditions can be prevented or mitigated when diagnosis is early and appropriate management (e.g., dietary protein/amino acid restriction or vitamin supplementation) is started promptly; for phenylketonuria, treatment must begin before 2 weeks of age to prevent intellectual disability, and children detected and treated at birth show none of the classic abnormalities. Untreated classic disorders carry severe outcomes, including lethality of complete neonatal OTC deficiency and early vascular morbidity/mortality in homocystinuria. Alkaptonuria progresses slowly to disabling ochronotic arthritis and later cardiac valve disease. Severity is largely biochemical and enzyme-activity dependent: complete enzyme deficiencies (e.g., classic urea cycle defects) present catastrophically in the neonatal period, whereas partial/residual-activity variants may remain asymptomatic until adulthood and declare during fasting or stress. For phenylketonuria, dietary restriction is generally instituted when blood phenylalanine exceeds 360 micromol/L, with a target maintenance range of 120-360 micromol/L for life.

reduce relapse risk Excessive daytime sleepiness with witnessed apnoeas suggesting untreated sleep apnoea Suicidal ideation associated with comorbid depression Escalating hypnotic or alcohol use to induce sleep Severe sleep deprivation impairing safety, such as while driving Reaching for hypnotics as first-line rather than offering cognitive behavioural therapy Relying on sleep hygiene advice alone, which is rarely sufficient Missing obstructive sleep apnoea or restless legs as the true cause Overlooking caffeine, alcohol, and stimulant contributions Failing to recognise and treat comorbid depression or anxiety Insomnia disorder is conceptualised through a model of hyperarousal, in which heightened cognitive, emotional, and physiological arousal impairs the normal sleep process. Predisposing traits, precipitating stressors, and perpetuating behaviours and beliefs (such as excessive time in bed and worry about sleep) interact, with dysregulation of arousal and sleep-wake regulatory systems maintaining the condition over time. Insomnia disorder often becomes chronic and relapsing, particularly when perpetuating behaviours and beliefs are established, but cognitive behavioural therapy produces durable improvement in most patients. Prognosis is better with early behavioural treatment and management of comorbidities, and worse with long-term hypnotic reliance and untreated psychiatric or medical contributors.

Interferon-gamma pathway defect — MSMD, Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, IFN-gamma/IL-12 axis defect HIV/AIDS and other causes of acquired T-cell deficiency with mycobacterial disease Severe combined immunodeficiency and combined immunodeficiencies Chronic granulomatous disease Anti-interferon-gamma autoantibody syndrome (an acquired phenocopy) Disseminated tuberculosis or non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection in an immunocompetent host Genetic testing of the IL-12/interferon-gamma axis (IFNGR1, IFNGR2, IL12B, IL12RB1, STAT1 and related genes) Functional assays of interferon-gamma production and receptor signalling Flow cytometry for interferon-gamma receptor expression Cultures and molecular identification of mycobacterial and Salmonella species Testing for anti-interferon-gamma autoantibodies to exclude the acquired phenocopy Imaging to define the extent of disseminated infection Defects of the interferon-gamma/IL-12 axis cause Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (MSMD), a selective vulnerability to weakly virulent mycobacteria Affected individuals develop disseminated infection with environmental (non-tuberculous) mycobacteria and with the BCG vaccine strain, as well as an increased risk of severe tuberculosis and salmonellosis The underlying problem is failure of the cytokine circuit by which macrophages and T/NK cells communicate to control intracellular pathogens, involving genes such as IFNGR1, IFNGR2, IL12B, IL12RB1, and STAT1 IL-12 produced by macrophages normally drives lymphocytes to secrete interferon-gamma, which in turn activates macrophages to kill intracellular organisms; breaking this loop cripples defence against mycobacteria The clinical severity depends on the specific defect, ranging from complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency with severe early disseminated disease to partial defects with milder, more localised infection Because the immune defect is narrow, patients are typically not broadly susceptible to the wide range of pathogens seen in combined immunodeficiencies Complete receptor defects respond poorly to interferon-gamma therapy, whereas partial or IL-12-axis defects may benefit from adjunctive interferon-gamma alongside prolonged antimycobacterial treatment Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is considered for severe complete defects, though outcomes can be challenging Disseminated mycobacterial or salmonella infection requiring urgent diagnosis and prolonged therapy Disseminated BCG infection following vaccination (BCG and other live vaccines must be avoided) Severe complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency presenting with overwhelming early infection Recurrent or unusually severe intracellular infection prompting immunological evaluation Administering BCG or other live vaccines before recognising the defect, risking disseminated vaccine-strain infection Stopping antimycobacterial therapy too early, since prolonged and sometimes lifelong treatment may be needed Assuming a broad immunodeficiency and missing the selective nature of the defect Overlooking the acquired anti-interferon-gamma autoantibody syndrome as a phenocopy in adults Expecting interferon-gamma therapy to help in complete receptor deficiency This group of disorders disrupts the interferon-gamma-dependent axis that controls intracellular pathogens. Following ingestion of mycobacteria, macrophages secrete IL-12, which acts on T cells and natural killer cells (via the IL-12 receptor) to induce production of interferon-gamma. Interferon-gamma then signals through its receptor and the JAK-STAT1 pathway to activate macrophages, enhancing their capacity to kill ingested organisms and to form protective granulomas. Mutations at any point in this circuit, in the interferon-gamma receptor chains, IL-12 or its receptor, or STAT1, impair macrophage activation and granuloma formation, leaving weakly virulent mycobacteria and Salmonella able to disseminate. The narrow, well-defined nature of the defect explains the characteristic selective infection susceptibility. Prognosis depends heavily on the molecular defect: complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency carries a poor outlook with severe, recurrent disseminated disease that responds poorly to cytokine therapy, whereas partial receptor and IL-12-axis defects often have a much better prognosis with prolonged antimycobacterial treatment and, where appropriate, adjunctive interferon-gamma.

distance or divergence-excess deviation (use prolonged occlusion and plus lenses) Overlooking a small refractive error, including myopia, that affects control Mistaking a constant sensory exotropia for the benign intermittent form Operating too early or on poorly documented control, risking consecutive esotropia Failing to monitor stereopsis and control over time Intermittent exotropia reflects an imbalance between an excessive tonic divergence position of the eyes and the fusional convergence mechanisms that normally maintain alignment. When fusional convergence is adequate the eyes stay straight; when fusional control is overcome, by fatigue, illness, inattention, bright light or dissociation under monocular or distance conditions, the latent exophoria becomes a manifest exotropia. The precise cause is not fully understood but involves anatomical and innervational factors and the balance between accommodative convergence and the resting divergent position. Over time control may deteriorate, with a longer duration of manifest deviation, suppression of the deviating eye and possible progression to a constant exotropia. The prognosis is generally good: many children maintain useful binocular vision and stereopsis, and surgery achieves satisfactory alignment in most, although under- and over-correction and recurrence occur and repeat surgery is sometimes needed. Binocular outcomes are best when good control and stereoacuity are preserved before intervention.

internal impingement shoulder — posterosuperior glenoid impingement, throwers shoulder SLAP (superior labral) tear Articular-sided partial rotator cuff tear from other causes Anterior glenohumeral microinstability Subacromial (external) impingement syndrome Biceps tendinopathy Suprascapular neuropathy Posterior labral tear MR arthrography to demonstrate articular-sided cuff fraying and posterosuperior labral pathology Standard MRI to assess cuff, labrum and any cysts Assessment and quantification of glenohumeral internal rotation deficit Evaluation of scapular kinematics and posture Examination for anterior microinstability including apprehension and relocation testing Diagnostic arthroscopy with dynamic assessment in abduction and external rotation for refractory cases Internal impingement describes contact between the articular (undersurface) fibres of the posterosuperior rotator cuff and the posterosuperior glenoid labrum when the arm is abducted and maximally externally rotated. It characteristically affects overhead athletes such as throwers, tennis players and swimmers, who present with posterior shoulder pain in the late cocking phase. Although a degree of posterosuperior contact is physiological in abduction and external rotation, it becomes pathological when repetitive, causing articular-sided cuff fraying and posterosuperior labral damage. Glenohumeral internal rotation deficit from posteroinferior capsular tightness is a central contributing factor and a key rehabilitation target. Scapular dyskinesis and subtle anterior microinstability shift the contact zone and aggravate the impingement, so assess the whole kinetic chain. It is distinct from classic external subacromial impingement; the pain is posterior and provoked in the abducted externally rotated position rather than on forward elevation. First-line management is non-operative, emphasising posterior capsular stretching, scapular control and correction of throwing mechanics. Surgery is reserved for refractory cases and addresses the specific pathology found, such as debridement of articular-sided cuff fraying and labral treatment, rather than routine subacromial decompression. Progressive weakness suggesting a significant or full-thickness rotator cuff tear Features of frank instability with recurrent subluxation Infraspinatus wasting suggesting suprascapular nerve involvement or a paralabral cyst Night and rest pain unrelated to activity raising concern for other pathology Misdiagnosing it as external subacromial impingement and performing an inappropriate acromioplasty. Neglecting glenohumeral internal rotation deficit and scapular dyskinesis, the principal reversible drivers. Interpreting the physiological posterosuperior contact seen on imaging as pathological in an asymptomatic athlete. Overlooking associated anterior microinstability that perpetuates the impingement. During the late cocking phase of overhead activity the abducted, maximally externally rotated humerus brings the articular surface of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus into contact with the posterosuperior glenoid rim and labrum. When repetitive, this normally protective contact produces shear and compressive loading that frays the undersurface of the cuff and damages the posterosuperior labrum. A tight posteroinferior capsule causes glenohumeral internal rotation deficit and a posterosuperior shift of the humeral rotation point, increasing the peel-back force on the biceps-labral complex and the degree of contact. Concurrent anterior capsular laxity or microinstability and scapular malposition further increase external rotation and posterior contact. The result is a self-perpetuating cycle of articular-sided partial cuff tearing, labral injury and pain that limits throwing performance. Most overhead athletes improve with a structured programme addressing posterior capsular tightness, scapular control and throwing mechanics, though return to the pre-injury level of high-demand throwing is not guaranteed. Refractory structural lesions may require arthroscopic treatment, with variable rates of return to elite performance.

brainstem Attributing the adduction failure to a medial rectus palsy and missing the internuclear localisation Overlooking myasthenia, which can perfectly mimic an INO and fluctuate Failing to image the spinal cord and brain fully when demyelination is suspected Missing an accompanying skew deviation or one-and-a-half syndrome that changes localisation The medial longitudinal fasciculus carries signals from abducens internuclear neurones in the pons upward to the contralateral medial rectus subnucleus of the oculomotor nucleus, coordinating conjugate horizontal gaze. A lesion of the fasciculus interrupts this yoking so that the adducting eye fails to move while the abducting eye develops a dissociated nystagmus, thought to reflect an adaptive increase in innervation. In younger patients the commonest cause is a demyelinating plaque of multiple sclerosis, while in older patients small-vessel brainstem infarction predominates; tumour, Wernicke encephalopathy, and drug toxicity are less common causes. Demyelinating INO frequently improves or resolves over weeks, whereas ischaemic INO has a variable outcome depending on infarct size; residual adduction lag and diplopia may persist and reflect the underlying cause more than the sign itself.

Allowing the duct to close before prostaglandin is started Overlooking subaortic obstruction that complicates surgical planning Failing to test for 22q11.2 deletion, with its calcium, immune and irradiated blood product implications Interrupted aortic arch is an extreme conotruncal and arch anomaly in which a segment of the aortic arch is absent, leaving no luminal continuity between the proximal and distal aorta. Perfusion of the lower body and any arch vessels beyond the interruption depends entirely on right-to-left flow through the arterial duct. While the duct remains open the circulation is balanced, but as the duct constricts after birth lower-body perfusion falls abruptly, causing profound metabolic acidosis, renal and gut hypoperfusion and cardiovascular collapse. An almost invariable ventricular septal defect and frequent posterior malalignment causing subaortic obstruction shape the intracardiac haemodynamics and pulmonary overcirculation. The lesion, particularly type B, is closely linked to 22q11.2 microdeletion. Untreated the condition is rapidly fatal once the duct closes, but with prostaglandin stabilisation and surgical repair survival is good, although recurrent arch obstruction and residual subaortic stenosis may require reintervention.

intersection syndrome distal — distal intersection syndrome, EPL-ECRL/ECRB intersection tenosynovitis Proximal intersection syndrome De Quervain tenosynovitis Extensor pollicis longus tenosynovitis or impending rupture Dorsal wrist ganglion Scapholunate pathology or dorsal wrist impingement Wartenberg syndrome (superficial radial nerve irritation) Second carpometacarpal or carpal boss pathology Ultrasound demonstrating peritendinous fluid at the extensor pollicis longus crossover MRI showing oedema and tenosynovitis at the crossover distal to Lister's tubercle Plain radiographs to exclude bony causes and prior distal radius fracture Clinical Finkelstein test to help differentiate de Quervain tenosynovitis Dynamic assessment for crepitus on wrist and thumb motion Diagnostic local anaesthetic infiltration Distal intersection syndrome is a tenosynovitis occurring where the extensor pollicis longus crosses over the extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, distal to Lister's tubercle. It is much less common and more distal than the classic proximal intersection syndrome, which occurs where the first-compartment muscles cross the radial wrist extensors. Pain, swelling and sometimes crepitus localise to the dorsal wrist around Lister's tubercle rather than the more proximal forearm. The extensor pollicis longus is at risk because it angulates sharply around Lister's tubercle, where friction and tenosynovitis can precede attritional rupture. Ultrasound or MRI shows peritendinous oedema and fluid at the crossover point of the extensor pollicis longus with the radial wrist extensors. First-line management is activity modification, splinting and anti-inflammatory measures, with corticosteroid injection used cautiously given the rupture risk. Signs of impending or actual extensor pollicis longus rupture, such as loss of thumb retropulsion History of distal radius fracture with new dorsal wrist pain Failure to respond to appropriate conservative care Rapidly progressive swelling suggesting infection or inflammatory arthropathy Confusing it with the more common proximal intersection syndrome or de Quervain tenosynovitis. Injecting corticosteroid carelessly and risking extensor pollicis longus rupture. Missing an impending tendon rupture, especially after distal radius fracture. Mislocalising the pathology proximally in the forearm. At the dorsal wrist the extensor pollicis longus turns sharply around Lister's tubercle and crosses superficial to the second-compartment radial wrist extensors, the extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis. Repetitive wrist and thumb motion generates friction at this distal crossover, producing a peritendinous tenosynovitis with oedema and, at times, crepitus. Persistent inflammation combined with the sharp angulation of the tendon around the tubercle can compromise the extensor pollicis longus and predispose it to attritional rupture, analogous to the rupture seen after distal radius fracture. The condition is usually self-limiting and responds well to conservative measures, though delayed recognition risks extensor pollicis longus attrition and rupture.

chemical cystitis Urinalysis and urine culture to exclude infection Urine cytology and cystoscopy where malignancy is a concern, particularly with haematuria Bladder diary documenting frequency, voided volumes, and symptom pattern Validated symptom and pain questionnaires to assess severity and monitor response Cystoscopy, with or without hydrodistension, to identify Hunner lesions Imaging to exclude stones or other structural pathology when indicated Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome is a chronic condition of bladder or pelvic pain perceived to relate to the bladder, accompanied by urinary urgency and frequency, in the absence of infection or other identifiable cause Pain characteristically worsens as the bladder fills and is relieved by voiding, a pattern that helps distinguish it from overactive bladder It is far more common in women and frequently coexists with other chronic pain and functional conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia, and chronic pelvic pain Diagnosis is essentially clinical and one of exclusion, requiring that infection, malignancy, stones, and other bladder pathology be ruled out Cystoscopy may be normal or may reveal Hunner lesions, whose presence defines a distinct phenotype that responds to lesion-directed treatment Management is stepwise, beginning with education, dietary trigger avoidance, stress and pain management, and pelvic floor physical therapy Oral and intravesical therapies form later steps, and Hunner lesions are specifically treated by fulguration or resection Refractory disease may be considered for neuromodulation or, rarely, major reconstructive surgery, reserved for carefully selected severe cases New haematuria, especially in older patients or smokers, must trigger evaluation for bladder cancer rather than being ascribed to the syndrome Visible or microscopic haematuria requiring exclusion of bladder cancer New or changing symptoms in an older patient or smoker Persistent sterile pyuria warranting exclusion of tuberculosis or malignancy Abnormal urine cytology Rapidly worsening or atypical pain suggesting an alternative diagnosis Repeatedly treating for infection despite negative cultures Missing bladder cancer by attributing haematuria to the syndrome Failing to identify and treat Hunner lesions, which need specific therapy Escalating to invasive surgery before conservative and behavioural measures are exhausted Overlooking coexisting pelvic floor dysfunction and other chronic pain conditions The mechanism is incompletely understood and probably multifactorial. A leading hypothesis is a defective bladder urothelial glycosaminoglycan (GAG) layer, which normally protects the underlying tissue; increased permeability allows urinary solutes such as potassium to penetrate the urothelium and irritate sensory nerves and detrusor muscle. Mast cell activation, neurogenic inflammation, and up-regulation of sensory pathways contribute to chronic pain and central sensitisation. In the Hunner lesion subtype there is a demonstrable inflammatory bladder wall change, whereas non-lesion disease is dominated by neuropathic and functional pain mechanisms, explaining the frequent overlap with other chronic pain disorders. The condition is chronic and typically follows a relapsing and remitting course; it is rarely progressive but can significantly impair quality of life. Many patients gain meaningful symptom control with a multimodal, stepwise approach, and the Hunner lesion subtype often responds well to lesion-directed therapy. A minority with severe refractory disease may ultimately require advanced interventions.

bladder malignancy Persistent sterile pyuria warranting exclusion of tuberculosis or carcinoma in situ New neurological symptoms or a suspected neurogenic bladder Escalating opioid use and worsening disability Diagnosing the syndrome without excluding infection, carcinoma in situ, and gynaecological causes Treating repeatedly for presumed infection despite negative cultures Overlooking pelvic floor dysfunction, which is a key and treatable contributor Escalating to irreversible surgery before exhausting conservative and intravesical options The cause of interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome is not fully understood and is probably multifactorial. A leading hypothesis is that a defective urothelial glycosaminoglycan (GAG) mucous layer allows urinary solutes such as potassium to penetrate the bladder wall, provoking sensory nerve activation, mast cell recruitment, and neurogenic inflammation. Chronic activation leads to central and peripheral sensitisation, upregulated bladder afferents, and, in some patients, mucosal inflammation with Hunner lesions. The condition is chronic and often relapsing rather than curable; many patients achieve meaningful symptom control with a stepwise multimodal approach, though the Hunner-lesion phenotype behaves differently and a minority with refractory disease may ultimately require major reconstructive or ablative surgery.

tissue disease requiring systemic management A temporally related culprit drug that should be reviewed and withdrawn Systemic symptoms suggesting active or progressive autoimmune disease Atypical the eruption persists despite topical therapy Confusing it histologically with granuloma annulare and missing the systemic associations Not recognising the rope sign as a clue to the diagnosis Interstitial granulomatous dermatitis is considered a reactive inflammatory pattern rather than a specific disease. It is thought to reflect immune-complex deposition within small dermal vessels and the interstitium, triggering a histiocytic response to altered dermal collagen. Histiocytes accumulate between collagen bundles and palisade around foci of degenerate collagen, sometimes with admixed neutrophils and nuclear dust. This process is frequently linked to circulating immune complexes in autoimmune connective tissue disease, and an identical pattern can be induced by certain drugs, supporting the concept of a shared reactive mechanism to a range of systemic immunological triggers. The skin lesions often fluctuate with the activity of the associated disease and may resolve when a culprit drug is withdrawn or the underlying disorder is controlled, though the eruption can be persistent or recurrent; the overall outlook is largely determined by the associated systemic condition.

Interstitial keratitis — IK, non-ulcerative stromal keratitis, syphilitic interstitial keratitis Herpetic stromal (disciform) keratitis Bacterial or fungal keratitis with stromal infiltrate Acanthamoeba keratitis Corneal graft rejection with stromal vascularisation Peripheral ulcerative keratitis from systemic vasculitis Stromal deposits from corneal dystrophy Slit-lamp examination documenting stromal oedema, infiltrate, and deep or ghost vessels Syphilis serology (treponemal and non-treponemal tests) Tuberculosis testing (interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test and chest imaging) Lyme serology and other targeted infective workup based on exposure history Audiovestibular assessment when Cogan syndrome is suspected Systemic inflammatory and vasculitis screen when an autoimmune cause is considered A non-ulcerative inflammation of the corneal stroma with intact epithelium, usually representing an immune response to a systemic infection rather than direct corneal infection Congenital syphilis is the classic cause, typically bilateral and part of the Hutchinson triad (interstitial keratitis, notched incisors, and sensorineural deafness) Active disease shows stromal oedema, cellular infiltration, and deep stromal vascularisation; when vessels lose their blood column they leave residual ghost vessels Cogan syndrome links interstitial keratitis with vestibuloauditory dysfunction and may herald a systemic vasculitis Other infective associations include tuberculosis, Lyme disease, leprosy, and herpes simplex or zoster (which more often cause unilateral disease) Chronic sequelae include stromal scarring, thinning, and lipid keratopathy, with vision reduced by scarring and irregular astigmatism Management combines treatment of the underlying systemic cause with topical corticosteroids to control stromal inflammation, and later keratoplasty for dense scarring Identifying and treating the systemic cause is essential, so serological and systemic workup should accompany ocular treatment Associated vestibuloauditory symptoms suggesting Cogan syndrome and possible systemic vasculitis Evidence of active systemic infection such as syphilis or tuberculosis requiring urgent treatment Progressive stromal thinning with perforation risk Dense central scarring causing significant visual loss Treating the cornea without identifying and treating the underlying systemic infection Missing Cogan syndrome and the risk of systemic vasculitis when hearing symptoms coexist Confusing immune stromal inflammation with active infective keratitis Overlooking congenital syphilis in a child with bilateral disease and systemic stigmata Interstitial keratitis is an inflammation of the corneal stroma in which the epithelium and endothelium are typically spared and there is no primary ulceration. It usually reflects an immune (often antigen-driven or hypersensitivity) reaction to a systemic infection such as syphilis, tuberculosis, Lyme disease, or a viral agent, rather than active replication of organisms within the cornea. Inflammatory cells infiltrate the stroma, causing oedema and the ingrowth of deep stromal vessels. When inflammation subsides the vessels may empty, leaving ghost vessels, and the stroma is left scarred and sometimes thinned or laden with lipid. The resulting opacity and irregular astigmatism impair vision. Active inflammation usually settles with treatment of the underlying cause and topical corticosteroids, but residual stromal scarring, ghost vessels, and irregular astigmatism can leave lasting visual impairment. Dense central scarring may ultimately require keratoplasty.

Intestinal atresia (jejunoileal/colonic) — jejunal atresia, ileal atresia, jejunoileal atresia, colonic atresia, apple-peel atresia, Christmas-tree deformity Meconium ileus Malrotation with midgut volvulus Hirschsprung disease Duodenal atresia or stenosis Meconium plug syndrome or small left colon Incarcerated inguinal hernia causing obstruction Abdominal radiograph to count dilated loops and gauge the level of obstruction Water-soluble contrast enema to assess a microcolon and exclude colonic atresia or meconium ileus Upper gastrointestinal contrast study when malrotation cannot be excluded Prenatal ultrasound review for dilated bowel loops and polyhydramnios Screening for cystic fibrosis given overlap with meconium ileus Assessment of bowel length at operation to anticipate short-bowel risk Congenital interruption of the intestinal lumen producing neonatal obstruction, most commonly in the jejunum and ileum and less often in the colon Jejunoileal atresia is largely attributed to a late intrauterine mesenteric vascular accident rather than a primary failure of recanalisation The more distal the atresia, the greater the number of dilated loops and air-fluid levels; proximal jejunal atresia gives few dilated loops Classified into types I (membrane), II (fibrous cord), IIIa (V-shaped mesenteric gap), IIIb (apple-peel/Christmas-tree), and IV (multiple atresias) The apple-peel (type IIIb) variant features a proximal atresia with the distal bowel coiled around a single perfusing vessel and carries higher morbidity Bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and failure to pass meconium in a neonate should prompt urgent evaluation for atresia Treatment is surgical resection of the atretic segment with primary anastomosis, often tapering the dilated proximal bowel to restore peristalsis Bilious vomiting in a neonate, which must be treated as a surgical emergency until proven otherwise Abdominal tenderness, discoloration, or distension suggesting ischaemia or perforation Signs of associated volvulus compromising bowel viability Extensive atresia threatening inadequate residual bowel length Rapid deterioration with sepsis or peritonitis Delaying laparotomy in a neonate with bilious vomiting while awaiting non-urgent tests Overlooking a second, more distal atresia at operation (multiple atresias) Anastomosing grossly dilated proximal bowel without tapering, risking functional obstruction Failing to measure remaining bowel length and anticipate nutritional needs Attributing distal obstruction solely to atresia and missing coexisting cystic fibrosis Jejunoileal atresia is thought to result from a localised intrauterine mesenteric vascular insult (for example volvulus, intussusception, or a strangulated segment) that devitalises a portion of already-formed bowel, which is then resorbed, leaving an atretic gap and a variable mesenteric defect. This contrasts with duodenal atresia, which reflects failed recanalisation of the solid embryonic cord. The proximal bowel becomes dilated, hypertrophied, and dysmotile, while the distal bowel is small and unused. Colonic atresia is rarer and follows a similar vascular mechanism. Extensive or apple-peel patterns may leave a foreshortened bowel and predispose to short-bowel syndrome. Isolated single atresias repaired promptly have excellent outcomes, whereas apple-peel and multiple atresias, or those complicated by extensive bowel loss, may lead to short-bowel syndrome and prolonged parenteral nutrition dependence. Overall survival with modern neonatal surgical and nutritional care is high.

intestinal duplication cyst — enteric duplication cyst, alimentary tract duplication mesenteric or omental cyst choledochal cyst cystic lymphangioma ovarian cyst Meckel diverticulum cystic teratoma pancreatic pseudocyst abdominal ultrasound to demonstrate the gut-signature double-wall sign contrast-enhanced CT to define anatomy and relationship to bowel MRI, particularly for thoracic and spinal involvement technetium-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy for ectopic gastric mucosa contrast luminal studies to assess communication spinal imaging when a thoracic duplication is identified histopathology of the resected specimen Duplications are spherical (cystic, commoner) or tubular structures that arise on the mesenteric border of the native bowel and share a common muscular wall and blood supply with it. The ileum is the single most frequent site, but duplications can occur anywhere from the oral cavity to the anus; most are non-communicating with the true lumen. The epithelial lining is typically alimentary mucosa, and ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue is common, predisposing to peptic ulceration and gastrointestinal bleeding. Ultrasound shows the classic 'gut signature' or double-wall sign — an inner echogenic mucosa with an outer hypoechoic muscular rim — which strongly suggests the diagnosis. Presentation is usually in infancy or early childhood with a palpable mass, obstruction, or bleeding, but incidental adult diagnosis is well recognised. Complications include bowel obstruction, volvulus, intussusception (the cyst acting as a lead point), and pain from distension or intracystic haemorrhage. Thoracic and thoraco-abdominal (oesophageal) duplications are frequently associated with vertebral anomalies and a persistent connection to the spinal canal, in keeping with the split-notochord theory. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan can localise ectopic gastric mucosa when bleeding is the presenting feature. gastrointestinal haemorrhage suggesting ectopic gastric mucosa features of bowel obstruction, volvulus, or intussusception acute abdomen from perforation or intracystic haemorrhage respiratory compromise from a thoracic duplication new solid or nodular components raising concern for rare malignant change in adults mistaking the cyst for another abdominal cystic lesion and overlooking its shared wall with native bowel failing to resect adjacent bowel when the shared blood supply precludes simple enucleation, leading to incomplete removal overlooking ectopic gastric mucosa as the source of occult bleeding missing an associated spinal or vertebral anomaly in thoracic duplications attempting enucleation of a long tubular duplication and leaving retained mucosa Intestinal duplications are congenital malformations whose precise embryogenesis is uncertain; leading theories include aberrant recanalisation of the gut lumen, persistence of embryonic diverticula, partial twinning, and the split-notochord hypothesis for the thoracic and thoraco-abdominal forms associated with vertebral defects. The lesion invariably lies on the mesenteric aspect of the adjacent alimentary tract, shares a common muscular coat and mesenteric blood supply, and is lined by gastrointestinal-type epithelium. Ectopic gastric mucosa, present in a substantial minority, secretes acid that ulcerates the lining or adjacent bowel and produces haemorrhage or perforation; ectopic pancreatic tissue may also occur. Progressive accumulation of secretions within a non-communicating cyst causes mass effect, obstruction, or a lead point for intussusception or volvulus. Prognosis is excellent following complete surgical excision, which is curative. Malignant transformation is rare and largely confined to lesions presenting in adulthood.
