is supported by demonstrating enteric protein loss, for example with faecal alpha-1-antitrypsin clearance Management is a low-fat diet enriched with medium-chain triglycerides that bypass the lymphatics, with treatment of any underlying secondary cause Severe hypoalbuminaemia with anasarca and serous effusions Recurrent or serious infection from immunoglobulin and lymphocyte depletion Chylous ascites or chylothorax Features suggesting an underlying malignancy or cardiac cause of secondary disease Attributing hypoalbuminaemia to renal or hepatic causes without considering enteric protein loss Missing patchy lymphangiectasia when only a single biopsy site is sampled Overlooking a secondary cause such as cardiac disease or malignancy Failing to substitute medium-chain triglycerides and monitor fat-soluble vitamins Intestinal lymphangiectasia is characterised by dilatation of the lymphatic channels of the small-bowel mucosa and submucosa, which may be a primary congenital anomaly or secondary to obstruction of lymphatic flow by cardiac disease, malignancy, infection or fibrosis. The dilated, incompetent lymphatics leak or rupture into the bowel lumen, causing loss of protein-rich lymph containing albumin, immunoglobulins and lymphocytes. This produces a protein-losing enteropathy with hypoalbuminaemia and consequent oedema, hypogammaglobulinaemia with susceptibility to infection, and lymphopenia, while impaired lymphatic transport of long-chain fats causes fat malabsorption. Primary disease is usually controlled but not cured by lifelong dietary modification; secondary disease may resolve if the underlying cause is treated, and prognosis then depends largely on that condition.

Intestinal malrotation — malrotation, midgut malrotation, malrotation with volvulus Duodenal atresia or stenosis Jejunoileal atresia Necrotising enterocolitis Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (non-bilious vomiting) Incarcerated hernia causing obstruction Upper gastrointestinal contrast series to locate the duodenojejunal junction Abdominal ultrasound to assess superior mesenteric vessel orientation and look for a whirlpool sign Plain abdominal radiograph, which may show a paucity of distal gas or a double-bubble pattern Blood gas and lactate to detect metabolic acidosis suggesting bowel ischaemia Baseline bloods and cross-match in preparation for emergency laparotomy Arises from incomplete rotation and fixation of the midgut, leaving a narrow mesenteric base that predisposes to twisting (volvulus) The classic presentation is a previously well neonate who develops sudden bilious vomiting, which must be treated as a surgical emergency until proven otherwise Bilious vomiting in an infant should trigger urgent imaging because midgut volvulus can infarct the entire small bowel within hours The upper gastrointestinal contrast study is the key investigation, showing an abnormally positioned duodenojejunal junction and a corkscrew or spiral appearance if volvulus is present Ultrasound may reveal an inverted relationship of the superior mesenteric artery and vein or a whirlpool sign of twisted mesentery Abnormal peritoneal (Ladd) bands can cross and obstruct the duodenum even without volvulus, producing intermittent obstructive symptoms The definitive operation is the Ladd procedure: untwisting the volvulus, dividing Ladd bands, broadening the mesenteric base, and placing the bowel in a non-rotated position, usually with appendicectomy Some children present later in life with intermittent, vague abdominal pain or feeding difficulty rather than acute obstruction Bilious vomiting in a neonate or infant, which mandates emergency evaluation for midgut volvulus Abdominal distension, tenderness, or rectal bleeding suggesting established bowel ischaemia Rapidly worsening metabolic acidosis or haemodynamic instability indicating strangulated midgut requiring immediate laparotomy Any delay in diagnosis, as the whole midgut can become necrotic within a few hours of volvulus Dismissing bilious vomiting as feed intolerance or reflux and delaying imaging Assuming a normal plain radiograph excludes malrotation or volvulus Failing to arrange emergency surgery once volvulus is suspected while awaiting further tests Overlooking older children with intermittent symptoms in whom malrotation is still possible During normal development the midgut herniates, rotates counterclockwise around the superior mesenteric artery, and returns to the abdomen with broad mesenteric fixation. In malrotation this process is incomplete, so the caecum sits abnormally and the mesenteric root is short and narrow. This narrow pedicle allows the midgut to twist around the superior mesenteric vessels, compromising blood supply and causing ischaemia, while abnormal fibrous bands may simultaneously compress the duodenum and produce obstruction. When volvulus is corrected before ischaemia sets in, outcomes are excellent with low recurrence after a Ladd procedure. Delayed presentation with extensive bowel infarction can necessitate massive resection, leading to short bowel syndrome and long-term nutritional dependence, and carries significant mortality.

Intestinal Nematode (Roundworm) Infections — soil-transmitted helminths, Ascaris, hookworm, Strongyloides Strongyloides midepigastric pain resembles peptic ulcer disease, except it is aggravated by food ingestion (p.1816) Heavy trichuriasis with bloody/mucoid diarrhea may resemble inflammatory bowel disease (p.1818) Intestinal/biliary ascariasis may present as a surgical acute abdomen mimicking acute appendicitis in endemic areas (p.1815) Strongyloides hyperinfection-associated gram-negative sepsis, pneumonia, or meningitis can dominate or be mistaken for primary bacterial infection (p.1817) Hookworm rhabditiform larvae in non-fresh stool must be differentiated from Strongyloides larvae (p.1816) Stool microscopy for characteristic ova and parasites: Ascaris eggs (~65 x 45 um), hookworm eggs (~40 x 60 um, species indistinguishable by light microscopy), Trichuris lemon-shaped eggs (~50 x 20 um) (p.1815-1818) Strongyloides: rhabditiform larvae (~250 um, short buccal cavity) on stool microscopy; single stool detects only ~one-third of uncomplicated cases, so serial examinations and agar plate method improve sensitivity; duodenojejunal aspirate/biopsy; ELISA serum antibody serology (sensitive for uncomplicated infection); in dissemination, filariform larvae in stool, sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage, or surgical drainage fluid (p.1817) Enterobius: eggs are NOT found in stool - diagnose with morning cellulose acetate tape applied to the perianal region (eggs oval, ~55 x 25 um, flattened on one side) (p.1818) Ascaris lung phase: larvae detectable in sputum or gastric aspirates before eggs appear in stool; chest imaging showing transient rounded infiltrates (Loffler's syndrome) (p.1815) PCR of stool worm DNA (increasing use, mostly research/some clinical) for species-level diagnosis (p.1815-1818) Abdominal imaging: plain film for masses of worms in obstruction; ultrasound and ERCP for pancreaticobiliary Ascaris (ERCP can also extract worms) (p.1815) Hookworm disease bloodwork: hypochromic microcytic anemia, sometimes eosinophilia or hypoalbuminemia (p.1816) Inflammatory bowel disease (heavy trichuriasis) (p.1818) Peptic ulcer disease (strongyloidiasis epigastric pain) (p.1816) Acute appendicitis / surgical acute abdomen (intestinal or biliary ascariasis) (p.1815) More than one billion people worldwide are infected with one or more intestinal nematode species; they are most common where sanitation and fecal-waste disposal are inadequate, especially resource-limited tropical and subtropical regions, but are seen with increasing frequency among immigrants and refugees to developed countries (p.1814). The major intestinal roundworms are Ascaris lumbricoides, the hookworms (Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale, A. ceylanicum), Strongyloides stercoralis, Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), and Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) (p.1815). Ascaris, Trichuris, and the hookworms require a soil phase for development, whereas S. stercoralis and E. vermicularis can be transmitted directly from person to person (p.1814). Because most helminths cannot fully complete their life cycle within the same human host, heavy adult-worm burdens require repeated exposure; clinical disease (versus asymptomatic/subclinical infection) generally develops only with repeated exposure and is typically related to infection intensity (p.1814). Eosinophilia and elevated serum IgE are features of many helminth infections, the latter particularly when the life cycle involves tissue migration (Ascaris, Strongyloides, hookworms) (p.1814). Ascaris larval migration through the lungs (~9-12 days after egg ingestion) can cause an irritating nonproductive cough, substernal discomfort, eosinophilia, and transient rounded pulmonary infiltrates - eosinophilic pneumonitis (Loffler's syndrome) (p.1815). Heavy Ascaris infection can cause small-bowel obstruction by a bolus of entangled worms (more common in children with narrow lumens), sometimes complicated by perforation, intussusception, or volvulus; an adult worm migrating into the biliary tree can cause biliary colic, cholecystitis, cholangitis, pancreatitis, or rarely intrahepatic abscess (p.1815). In highly endemic areas, intestinal and biliary ascariasis can rival acute appendicitis as a cause of surgical acute abdomen (p.1815). The major consequence of chronic hookworm infection is iron deficiency; symptoms are minimal if iron stores are adequate, but undernourished individuals develop progressive iron-deficiency anemia and hypoproteinemia (fatigue, weakness, dyspnea). Hookworm disease requires the combination of heavy worm burden, prolonged duration, and inadequate iron intake (p.1816). Hookworm larvae may cause a pruritic maculopapular rash (ground itch) at the skin penetration site; hypochromic microcytic anemia, sometimes with eosinophilia or hypoalbuminemia, is characteristic of hookworm disease (p.1816). S. stercoralis is distinguished by its ability - unique among helminths except Capillaria - to complete its life cycle and replicate within a human host (autoinfection), so infection can persist for decades without further exogenous exposure (p.1816). Larva currens, a rapidly advancing (up to ~10 cm/h) pruritic serpiginous skin eruption, is pathognomonic of strongyloidiasis; recurrent urticaria, often on the buttocks, is the most common cutaneous manifestation (p.1816). Impaired cell-mediated immunity - especially high-dose glucocorticoid therapy, and less commonly other immunosuppressants or HTLV-1 infection - can trigger Strongyloides hyperinfection with massive larval numbers, leading to colitis/enteritis/malabsorption and disseminated disease (CNS, skin, peritoneum, liver, kidneys) (p.1817). Disseminated strongyloidiasis is often complicated by gram-negative bacteremia, pneumonia, or meningitis from enteric flora translocating through disrupted mucosal barriers; eosinophilia is often ABSENT in severely infected patients (p.1817). Even asymptomatic strongyloidiasis must be treated because of the potential for later hyperinfection and fatal dissemination; Strongyloides serology should be performed before starting glucocorticoids or solid-organ transplantation in patients with prior potential exposure, especially with eosinophilia (p.1817). Most Trichuris (whipworm) infections are asymptomatic, but heavy infections may cause anemia and bloody/mucoid diarrhea resembling inflammatory bowel disease; massive infection in children can cause rectal prolapse from protracted tenesmus (p.1818). Enterobius (pinworm) is more common in temperate climates than the tropics; perianal pruritus, worse at night when gravid females emerge, is the cardinal symptom, and eosinophilia is uncommon (p.1818). Disseminated strongyloidiasis - particularly in patients with unsuspected infection who are taking glucocorticoids - has a HIGH mortality rate (p.1817) Strongyloides hyperinfection with gram-negative sepsis, pneumonia, or meningitis from enteric flora translocation (p.1817) Eosinophilia is often ABSENT in severe/disseminated strongyloidiasis, removing a reassuring marker (p.1817) Complete intestinal obstruction with perforation, intussusception, or volvulus from a heavy Ascaris worm bolus (p.1815) Biliary Ascaris causing cholangitis, pancreatitis, or intrahepatic abscess (p.1815) Failing to screen for and treat asymptomatic strongyloidiasis before glucocorticoids or solid-organ transplantation - asymptomatic infection must still be treated because of the risk of later hyperinfection and fatal dissemination (p.1817) Relying on eosinophilia to exclude strongyloidiasis - it is often absent in severe/disseminated disease (p.1817) Using routine stool ova-and-parasite microscopy to diagnose pinworm - Enterobius eggs are not passed in feces; perianal cellulose acetate tape is required (p.1818) Single stool examination for Strongyloides detects only about one-third of uncomplicated cases (p.1817) Misidentifying hookworm rhabditiform larvae (in non-fresh stool) as Strongyloides (p.1816) Intestinal nematodes are nonsegmented roundworms ranging from ~1 mm to many centimeters. Ascaris and the hookworms have life cycles involving migration through the heart and lungs before maturing in the intestine (larvae penetrate alveoli, ascend the bronchial tree, are swallowed, and reach the small bowel). Ascaris adults live in the small-intestinal lumen and females are extraordinarily fecund (>200,000 eggs/day); eggs are highly environmentally resistant and become infective after maturation in warm, moist soil. Hookworm adults attach to the small-bowel mucosa using buccal teeth (Ancylostoma) or cutting plates (Necator), invade submucosa, and ingest blood and villous tissue, producing iron-deficiency anemia; filariform larvae penetrate skin. S. stercoralis filariform larvae penetrate skin or mucous membranes, migrate via blood to the lungs and then the small intestine, where parthenogenetic adult females embed in the mucosa; rhabditiform larvae can transform directly into filariform larvae that re-penetrate the colonic wall or perianal skin to drive ongoing autoinfection - which can amplify into hyperinfection and dissemination under immunosuppression. Trichuris adults embed their thin anterior portions in colonic/cecal mucosa with no pulmonary larval passage. Enterobius adults dwell in the cecum; gravid females migrate nocturnally to the perianal skin to deposit eggs, which become infective within hours and spread by hand-to-mouth (autoinfection from scratching) and retroinfection. (p.1814-1818) Intestinal nematode infections are not usually fatal but contribute to malnutrition, impaired physical and cognitive development, and diminished work capacity, particularly in children with marginal nutritional status. Significant protective immunity does not appear to develop in humans. The major exception is strongyloidiasis: autoinfection allows decades-long persistence, and in immunocompromised hosts hyperinfection and dissemination can be fatal (high mortality, especially with unrecognized infection on glucocorticoids). (p.1814, p.1816-1817) Harrison does not provide a formal severity classification for intestinal nematode infections; severity correlates with infection intensity (worm burden) and host factors. Disease ranges from asymptomatic/subclinical light infection to clinical disease with heavy burden (e.g., Ascaris bowel/biliary obstruction; hookworm iron-deficiency anemia/hypoproteinemia; Trichuris dysentery and rectal prolapse). For Strongyloides, the spectrum is uncomplicated strongyloidiasis vs. hyperinfection (amplified autoinfection, larvae confined largely to the normal migration route) vs. disseminated strongyloidiasis (larvae in CNS, skin, peritoneum, liver, kidneys). (p.1814-1817)

uncertain reproducibility Features of complete or worsening intestinal obstruction Enterocolitis with sepsis, particularly where Hirschsprung disease coexists Failure to thrive or severe malnutrition Bowel ischaemia or perforation from chronic distension Confidently diagnosing or excluding the condition despite substantial interobserver variability in histology Missing coexisting Hirschsprung aganglionosis in the distal segment Proceeding to resection when conservative management would suffice Interpreting inadequate or superficial biopsies as definitive Intestinal neuronal dysplasia is a form of enteric dysganglionosis in which ganglion cells are present but abnormally organised. In the classic type B pattern there is hyperplasia of the submucosal (and myenteric) plexus with giant ganglia, increased ganglion cell numbers, and ectopic neurons within the lamina propria and around submucosal vessels, together with abnormal acetylcholinesterase activity. This disordered innervation impairs coordinated peristalsis, producing a functional obstruction that clinically resembles Hirschsprung disease despite the presence of ganglion cells. Many children improve over time with conservative bowel management, and outcome depends on the extent of disease and whether aganglionosis coexists; the uncertain diagnostic criteria complicate prognostication.

leukocytosis, normochromic normocytic anemia (~50%), hypoalbuminemia (~33%) Amebic serology and PCR to exclude amebic liver abscess In CAPD-associated peritonitis, dialysate cell count with differential (cloudy fluid with >100 WBC/uL, >50% neutrophils, or >50% PMN with shortened dwell time) and concentrated dialysate culture in blood-culture bottles Needle aspiration under CT guidance for culture in suspected infected pancreatic necrosis Acute pancreatitis without infected necrosis (sterile inflammation producing fever and leukocytosis) Chemical peritonitis from a ruptured gastric ulcer in the absence of significant bacterial load Malignant ascites or metastatic intraabdominal malignancy Congestive heart failure, systemic lupus erythematosus, and lymphedema as noncirrhotic settings reported with PBP Intraperitoneal infection follows disruption of a normal anatomic barrier (ruptured appendix, diverticulum, or ulcer; ischemic, tumor-related, or inflammatory bowel wall weakening; or leakage from adjacent pancreatitis or pelvic inflammatory disease), and evolves in two sequential stages: peritonitis first, then abscess formation if the patient survives untreated. Primary (spontaneous) bacterial peritonitis (PBP) in adults occurs chiefly with cirrhotic ascites, develops in up to about 10% of cirrhotic patients, and is thought to arise from hematogenous spread when impaired hepatic filtration and altered portal flow allow organisms to seed and multiply in ascitic fluid. A peritoneal-fluid count of more than 250 polymorphonuclear leukocytes/uL is diagnostic of PBP; this threshold does not apply to secondary peritonitis. Normal peritoneal fluid contains under 300 WBC/uL (mainly mononuclear) and protein under 30 g/L. PBP is typically caused by a single organism (often enteric gram-negative bacilli such as E. coli, but increasingly gram-positive cocci and ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae); recovery of multiple organisms including anaerobes should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis and a search for a secondary source. Fever is the most common manifestation of PBP (up to 80%), but abdominal pain and peritoneal signs may be absent; nonlocalizing features such as malaise, encephalopathy, jaundice, or unexplained acute kidney injury in a cirrhotic with ascites should also trigger diagnostic paracentesis. Yield of peritoneal-fluid culture is improved by inoculating about 10 mL directly into a blood-culture bottle, and simultaneous blood cultures should be drawn because bacteremia frequently accompanies PBP; samples are best obtained before antibiotics. Secondary peritonitis results from spillage from an intraabdominal viscus and yields a mixed flora dominated by facultative gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes, especially with a colonic source; early death is driven by gram-negative bacillary sepsis and circulating endotoxin. The bacterial burden of a perforation depends on site: a ruptured gastric ulcer (if not achlorhydric) causes mainly low-pH chemical irritation with a low bacterial load, whereas leaked colonic contents (pH 7-8, ~10^11 anaerobes/g feces) cause intense infection from heavy bacterial load. Bacteroides fragilis, though only about 0.5% of normal colonic flora, is the anaerobe most frequently isolated from intraabdominal infections and abscesses and the most common anaerobic bloodstream isolate; its zwitterionic capsular polysaccharide (polysaccharide A) drives abscess localization via a CD4+ T-cell-dependent host response. Of all intraabdominal abscesses, about 74% are intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal (non-visceral); most intraperitoneal abscesses arise from fecal spillage (e.g., an inflamed appendix), and diverticular abscesses are the least likely to rupture. The liver is the organ most subject to abscess; biliary tract disease is now the most common source (formerly ruptured appendicitis), and pylephlebitis (suppurative portal vein thrombosis) is another route of seeding. Half of liver-abscess patients lack hepatomegaly, right-upper-quadrant tenderness, or jaundice, so liver abscess can present as fever of unknown origin, especially in the elderly. Hypermucoviscous (hypervirulent) Klebsiella pneumoniae causes a distinctive community-acquired syndrome of liver abscess with bacteremia and metastatic infection of the eye(s) and lung(s), originally described in Southeast Asia and now emerging in North America and elsewhere. Splenic abscess is rare but frequently fatal if untreated and often diagnosed late (at autopsy in about 37% of one series); hematogenous spread predominates, with bacterial endocarditis the most common associated infection and streptococci then S. aureus the usual isolates. More than 75% of perinephric and renal abscesses now arise from ascending urinary tract infection rather than hematogenous seeding; concomitant obstructing nephrolithiasis is the most important risk factor (renal stones in 20-60% of perinephric abscess cases). Inflammation triggers an early influx of polymorphonuclear leukocytes followed by a prolonged phase of mononuclear cell migration, with the leukocyte phenotype shaped by resident-cell chemokine synthesis. In primary (spontaneous) bacterial peritonitis, a diseased liver with altered portal circulation impairs the normal filtration function, allowing hematogenous organisms to seed ascites; cirrhosis-related defects (low peritoneal complement, diminished PMN opsonic and phagocytic capacity, gut dysbiosis with overgrowth of Enterobacteriaceae, reduced Paneth cell defensins, decreased motility, and portal-hypertensive enteropathy) promote bacterial translocation. Secondary peritonitis follows direct viscus spillage; an early containment phase produces a fibrin- and PMN-rich exudate, and severity reflects whether spillage is chemically irritant (acidic gastric contents) or heavily bacterial (colonic contents). If overt gram-negative sepsis does not prove fatal, the host walls off persisting organisms and PMNs in a fibrous capsule to form an abscess; B. fragilis is uniquely able to induce abscesses, with its zwitterionic capsular polysaccharide A stimulating peritoneal macrophages (TNF-alpha, ICAM-1) and CD4+ T lymphocytes that secrete leukoattractant cytokines, while the alternative complement pathway and fibrinogen also participate. PBP carries substantial morbidity and mortality, reflecting its concentration among patients with advanced liver disease; reported in-hospital mortality was about 17.6% in a 2018 US cohort, and another series found 23% mortality at 30 days and 37% at 90 days. PBP recurs frequently, with up to 70% of patients experiencing recurrence within 1 year. Patients with PBP usually respond to appropriate antibiotics within 72 h, and delayed therapy increases mortality. In secondary peritonitis, early death is attributable to gram-negative bacillary sepsis and endotoxemia, and the urgency and success of source control - rather than the choice of empiric antibiotics - drive survival odds. Pyogenic liver abscess mortality averaged about 15% despite treatment. Splenic and perinephric abscesses are frequently fatal when diagnosis is delayed, so early diagnosis is the most important determinant of outcome. No single formal severity score is given; the text frames disease along the peritonitis-to-abscess continuum and stratifies risk by setting. PBP is graded operationally by ascitic-fluid PMN count (>250/uL diagnostic) and by markers of advanced liver disease (serum creatinine, BUN, total bilirubin, Child-Turcotte-Pugh score) that identify highest-risk and worst-prognosis patients. Secondary and abscess-related infection severity is stratified clinically as community-acquired mild-to-moderate disease versus critically ill or health care-associated infection, which guides anticipated flora and management intensity.

They represent a spectrum from low-grade dysplasia to invasive carcinoma, following an adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence. Main-duct involvement reflects more extensive, higher-grade disease with greater malignant potential, whereas branch-duct lesions are generally lower risk. Mucin extrusion from a patulous papilla may be seen endoscopically. Prognosis is excellent for resected non-invasive lesions, but invasive IPMN carries a prognosis related to the associated carcinoma; appropriate surveillance and timely resection are key.

An intraductal papilloma is a benign proliferation of ductal epithelium supported by fibrovascular cores that projects into the lumen of a breast duct. Its delicate, highly vascular fronds are fragile and bleed easily, which accounts for the characteristic bloodstained or serous nipple discharge, and the growth may partially obstruct the duct producing localised dilatation. Solitary central lesions are generally isolated benign growths, whereas multiple peripheral papillomas represent a more diffuse proliferative process associated with a modestly increased risk of concurrent or subsequent malignancy, so histological confirmation is important to detect any atypia. A solitary intraductal papilloma is benign and generally cured by duct excision with an excellent prognosis, whereas multiple peripheral papillomas or lesions with atypia warrant closer surveillance because of their higher associated risk of malignancy.

Rising oestrogen and progesterone metabolites impair hepatocellular bile acid transport in genetically susceptible women, many of whom carry heterozygous variants in canalicular transporter genes such as ABCB4 (MDR3), ABCB11 (BSEP), or ATP8B1. Reduced canalicular excretion raises circulating bile acids, causing maternal pruritus; transplacental passage of elevated bile acids is implicated in fetal complications including arrhythmia, preterm birth, and sudden intrauterine death, with risk rising steeply at very high maternal bile acid concentrations. The condition characteristically resolves after delivery. Maternal prognosis is excellent with resolution of pruritus and biochemistry after delivery, though recurrence in future pregnancies is common; the main determinant of outcome is fetal, with planned delivery and bile-acid-guided monitoring aimed at reducing the risk of stillbirth.

mesenchymal neoplasm characterised by the production of copious mucoid, hyaluronic acid-rich matrix by scattered fibroblast-like cells. The tumour is driven by post-zygotic activating missense mutations in GNAS, which encodes the alpha subunit of a stimulatory G protein; constitutive signalling through this pathway alters fibroblast behaviour and matrix production. Because the same somatic GNAS mutation can affect skeletal progenitor cells, the lesion shares its molecular basis with fibrous dysplasia, and when the two coexist the combination is termed Mazabraud syndrome. The tumour grows by expansion within the muscle, remaining well demarcated and hypovascular, which accounts for its fluid-like imaging characteristics and its indolent, non-metastasising behaviour. The chief diagnostic challenge is separating it, and especially its more cellular variant, from myxoid soft tissue sarcomas. Intramuscular myxoma is benign with an excellent prognosis, and marginal excision is generally curative with only rare local recurrence. Recognition of associated fibrous dysplasia in Mazabraud syndrome is important, as those bony lesions carry their own morbidity.

In the calcaneus it typically occupies the neutral triangle, the region of sparse trabeculae, and is usually an incidental finding. Radiographs show a well-defined lucent lesion with a thin sclerotic rim, frequently containing a central focus of dystrophic calcification producing a target or cockade appearance. CT demonstrating fat attenuation (negative Hounsfield values) and MRI showing signal that follows subcutaneous fat on all sequences and suppresses with fat saturation are effectively diagnostic. The Milgram staging reflects natural involution: stage 1 viable fat, stage 2 partial fat necrosis with calcification, and stage 3 extensive necrosis with cyst formation, calcification and ossification. Advanced involuted lesions may become cystic and calcified and mimic a simple bone cyst or bone infarct. Most lesions require no treatment; curettage and grafting are reserved for persistent pain or fracture risk. Malignant transformation to liposarcoma is exceedingly rare and remains debated. Aggressive imaging features such as cortical destruction or ill-defined margins Soft-tissue extension beyond the bone Rapid interval growth New or escalating pain localised to the lesion Loss of the characteristic fatty signal or attenuation Confusing the lesion with a simple bone cyst or the normal calcaneal pseudocyst and intervening unnecessarily Misreading an involuted, calcified stage 3 lesion as an aggressive process Failing to obtain fat-specific imaging that would establish the diagnosis non-invasively Overtreating an asymptomatic incidental lesion Intraosseous lipoma is a benign neoplasm composed of lobules of mature adipocytes that replace the medullary bone and its haematopoietic marrow. Its behaviour is characterised by a tendency to spontaneous involution, described in the Milgram stages: initially viable fat, then progressive fat necrosis with dystrophic calcification, and finally cystic degeneration with reactive ossification, which explains the variable and sometimes confusing imaging appearance. The calcaneal predilection is attributed to the biomechanically determined region of sparse trabeculae, and the fatty composition gives the lesion its characteristic low CT attenuation and fat-matched MRI signal that permit confident non-invasive diagnosis. The prognosis is excellent; the lesion is benign, frequently involutes spontaneously and rarely requires intervention.

early for prematurity risk or too late with ongoing fetal hypoxia Overlooking congenital infection or aneuploidy in early symmetrical restriction The commonest pathway is uteroplacental insufficiency, in which inadequate trophoblastic remodelling of the spiral arteries produces a poorly perfused placenta with reduced capacity to deliver oxygen and nutrients. The fetus adapts by redistributing cardiac output to preserve the brain, heart, and adrenals at the expense of the abdominal viscera and peripheral tissues, producing asymmetrical growth and oligohydramnios from reduced renal perfusion. Progressive hypoxaemia and acidaemia manifest as deteriorating Doppler indices and, ultimately, cardiovascular decompensation. Other cases stem from fetal chromosomal or structural abnormalities, congenital infection, or maternal disease reducing substrate supply. Outcome depends on the underlying cause, the severity and gestation at onset, and the timeliness of surveillance and delivery. Early-onset severe placental disease carries the greatest risk of stillbirth and neonatal morbidity, whereas late-onset restriction is often milder but still increases perinatal risk. Survivors have higher rates of neurodevelopmental impairment and of adult cardiovascular and metabolic disease, underscoring the importance of careful monitoring and appropriately timed birth.

Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma is a rare aggressive B-cell neoplasm in which malignant cells remain confined within the lumina of small vessels rather than forming tumour masses. The cells are thought to lack surface adhesion and homing molecules required to exit the vasculature, so they accumulate intraluminally and occlude capillaries, arterioles, and venules. This produces widespread microvascular obstruction and ischaemic dysfunction of affected organs, most often the central nervous system and skin, and in the Asian-type variant the marrow, liver, and spleen with an associated haemophagocytic syndrome. The absence of masses and lymphadenopathy accounts for the elusive, multisystem presentation. Untreated disease is rapidly fatal, but prompt recognition and anthracycline-based combination immunochemotherapy, with central nervous system-directed treatment where appropriate, can achieve remission in a substantial proportion of patients.

acute haemorrhage Neonatal intraventricular haemorrhage in the preterm infant arises from the germinal matrix, a highly vascular and metabolically active region near the caudate that is present until around term. Its capillaries are structurally immature and fragile, and the region has limited autoregulatory support, so it is vulnerable to rupture when cerebral blood flow or venous pressure fluctuates. Contributing factors include pressure-passive cerebral circulation, swings in arterial pressure, hypercarbia and hypoxia, coagulopathy, and rapid volume shifts. Bleeding may remain confined to the germinal matrix or rupture into the ventricular system, and when it obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow it causes post-haemorrhagic ventricular dilatation. Associated venous congestion can lead to periventricular haemorrhagic infarction of the surrounding white matter, the most severe pattern. Outcome is closely linked to grade: low-grade haemorrhage confined to the germinal matrix or with minimal intraventricular blood often has a good neurodevelopmental outcome, whereas high-grade haemorrhage with ventricular dilatation or parenchymal infarction carries a substantial risk of cerebral palsy, cognitive impairment, and post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus. Prematurity and coexisting complications also influence long-term prognosis.

Intussusception — intestinal invagination, bowel telescoping, ileocolic intussusception Gastroenteritis Incarcerated hernia Malrotation with volvulus Appendicitis Henoch-Schonlein purpura with bowel involvement Constipation or other causes of colicky pain Abdominal ultrasound (target/doughnut sign) as first-line imaging Abdominal radiograph to look for obstruction or free air Air or contrast enema (diagnostic and therapeutic in stable children) Full blood count and electrolytes to assess dehydration Assessment for an underlying lead point in older or atypical cases The most common cause of intestinal obstruction in infants and toddlers, typically between 6 months and 3 years, in which one segment of bowel telescopes into the adjacent distal segment. The classic triad is intermittent colicky abdominal pain (with drawing up of the legs), vomiting, and red currant jelly stool, but all three are present in only a minority. Between painful episodes the infant may appear well or lethargic; lethargy can be a prominent and misleading feature. A sausage-shaped mass may be palpable, often in the right upper quadrant, with an empty right lower quadrant. Most cases are ileocolic and idiopathic, sometimes following a viral illness with hypertrophied Peyer patches acting as a lead point. Ultrasound is the diagnostic investigation of choice, showing a target or doughnut sign on cross-section. In a stable child without peritonitis or perforation, non-operative reduction with an air or contrast enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Surgery is required when enema reduction fails, or when there is perforation, peritonitis, shock, or a pathological lead point. Signs of peritonitis or a rigid, tender abdomen Free air on radiograph indicating perforation Shock, marked lethargy, or haemodynamic instability Bilious vomiting and abdominal distension indicating established obstruction Fever with toxic appearance suggesting bowel ischaemia or sepsis Waiting for the full classic triad, which is often incomplete, and delaying diagnosis Attributing marked lethargy to another cause and missing intussusception Attempting enema reduction in a child with peritonitis, perforation, or shock Failing to consider a pathological lead point in older children or recurrent cases A proximal segment of bowel (the intussusceptum) invaginates into the lumen of the adjacent distal segment (the intussuscipiens), dragging its mesentery with it. This compromises venous and lymphatic drainage, producing bowel wall oedema and engorgement; the mixture of sloughed mucosa, blood, and mucus produces the characteristic red currant jelly stool. Progressive swelling obstructs the lumen and, if unrelieved, arterial compromise leads to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation. In infants a lead point is usually hypertrophied lymphoid tissue, whereas older children more often have a pathological lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum or polyp. With early diagnosis and reduction the outlook is excellent; delay increases the risk of ischaemia, resection, and complications, and a proportion recur after non-operative reduction.

intussusception Waiting for the full classic triad, which delays diagnosis and reduction Attempting enema reduction in the presence of peritonitis or perforation Failing to consider a pathological lead point in older children and recurrent cases Under-resuscitating a dehydrated child before attempting reduction Intussusception occurs when a proximal segment of bowel (the intussusceptum) invaginates into the lumen of the contiguous distal segment (the intussuscipiens), dragging its mesentery with it. The commonest ileocolic form is usually idiopathic, frequently preceded by a viral infection that causes hypertrophy of ileal lymphoid tissue serving as a lead point. Progressive telescoping compresses the mesenteric vessels, producing venous congestion, mucosal oedema, and bleeding that gives rise to the redcurrant-jelly stool; if unrelieved, arterial compromise leads to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation. In older children an anatomical lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum, duplication cyst, polyp, or tumour is more often responsible. Early diagnosis with prompt enema reduction resolves most idiopathic cases with excellent outcomes, though a minority recur. Delayed presentation with ischaemic or necrotic bowel requires operative reduction or resection and carries higher morbidity.

or a third nerve palsy masquerading as simple age-related ptosis Overlooking coexisting dermatochalasis or brow ptosis Attributing pseudoptosis from enophthalmos to true ptosis Failing to document levator function before surgery Involutional ptosis results from stretching, thinning or disinsertion of the levator palpebrae superioris aponeurosis from the tarsal plate, an age-related degenerative change also promoted by chronic eyelid rubbing, prior surgery and contact lens use. Because the levator muscle itself remains strong, levator function is preserved, but the weakened aponeurotic attachment fails to hold the lid elevated, producing a low lid margin and elevation of the skin crease as the crease is pulled upward. The condition is benign and progressive, and surgical repair of the aponeurosis is very effective and durable because levator function is retained.

Iodine deficiency — iodine deficiency disorders, endemic goitre, endemic cretinism Autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto or Graves) Sporadic non-toxic goitre and thyroid nodules Congenital iodine concentration for assessing population and individual status Thyroid ultrasound to characterise goitre or nodules Neonatal thyroid screening where available Developmental and neurological assessment in affected children Iodine deficiency is the leading preventable cause of goitre and of acquired intellectual disability worldwide It occurs in regions with iodine-poor soil and water, historically including large parts of the Himalayan and sub-Himalayan belt of India, and salt iodisation is the mainstay of control Deficiency in pregnancy is the most serious consequence, causing impaired fetal brain development and, in severe cases, endemic cretinism The clinical spectrum ranges from diffuse or nodular goitre to hypothyroidism, growth and developmental delay, and neurological deficits The population iodine status is assessed by median urinary iodine concentration rather than by individual blood tests Rapid correction of longstanding deficiency, or excess iodine, can occasionally provoke thyroid dysfunction, so replacement is at physiological population levels Neurological damage sustained in fetal life and infancy is largely irreversible, making prevention through adequate maternal intake essential Deficiency in pregnancy threatening fetal neurodevelopment Large goitre causing airway or oesophageal compression Overt hypothyroidism, especially in infants where it threatens development Signs of endemic cretinism requiring urgent public health and clinical action Relying on individual blood iodine levels rather than urinary iodine for status assessment Overlooking maternal iodine adequacy in pregnancy Assuming a goitre is always autoimmune and missing endemic iodine deficiency Causing iodine-induced thyroid dysfunction through excessive supplementation Iodine is an essential substrate for the synthesis of the thyroid hormones thyroxine and triiodothyronine. When dietary intake is inadequate, reduced hormone production lowers feedback inhibition and raises thyroid-stimulating hormone, driving thyroid hyperplasia and goitre as a compensatory response; over time nodularity and, if compensation fails, hypothyroidism develop. Thyroid hormone is critical for normal neuronal migration and myelination in the developing brain, so maternal and early-life deficiency impairs neurodevelopment irreversibly, producing the cognitive and neurological features of iodine deficiency disorders, including cretinism in severe endemic areas. Goitre and hypothyroidism from deficiency can improve with adequate iodine intake, but neurodevelopmental damage from fetal and early-life deficiency is largely permanent, underscoring prevention.

Autoantibody panels (including anti-enterocyte and endocrine autoantibodies) Blood glucose, thyroid function, and other endocrine screening Small-bowel biopsy showing autoimmune enteropathy Full blood count and haemolysis screen for autoimmune cytopenias IPEX syndrome is an X-linked disorder caused by mutations in FOXP3, the master transcription factor for regulatory T cells Loss of functional regulatory T cells leads to severe, early-onset systemic autoimmunity affecting multiple organs The classic triad is severe enteropathy with intractable watery diarrhoea, early-onset endocrinopathy (especially neonatal type 1 diabetes and thyroiditis), and eczematous dermatitis It typically presents in male infants and can be rapidly life-threatening from malabsorption, failure to thrive, and metabolic derangement Additional autoimmune features include haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, nephropathy, and hepatitis Infections may occur, partly reflecting the underlying immune dysregulation and partly the intensive immunosuppression used to control the disease The autoimmune enteropathy often shows characteristic small-bowel histology with villous atrophy and does not respond to dietary exclusion alone Treatment relies on immunosuppression (for example calcineurin inhibitors and sirolimus) to control disease, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offering the only definitive cure Intractable diarrhoea with dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and failure to thrive as a neonatal emergency Neonatal or early-onset diabetes with metabolic decompensation Severe autoimmune cytopenias or nephropathy Live vaccines should be avoided given the immune dysregulation and immunosuppressive therapy Overwhelming infection during intensive immunosuppression Attributing intractable infantile diarrhoea to food allergy and missing autoimmune enteropathy Overlooking a monogenic cause of neonatal diabetes in a boy with multi-organ autoimmunity Delaying genetic testing and transplant referral in a critically ill infant Giving live vaccines during immunosuppression Confusing IPEX with APECED, which is autosomal recessive, AIRE-related, and presents later IPEX syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in FOXP3 on the X chromosome, the transcription factor essential for the development and function of CD4-positive CD25-positive regulatory T cells. Without functional regulatory T cells, peripheral tolerance collapses and autoreactive effector T cells drive widespread tissue-specific autoimmunity. The resulting immune attack on the gut epithelium, endocrine organs (pancreatic islets, thyroid), skin, blood cells, and kidneys produces the characteristic multi-organ autoimmune phenotype. Because the defect is one of immune regulation rather than a simple failure of host defence, the dominant problem is aggressive autoimmunity from early infancy, though secondary infection is common. Untreated IPEX is frequently fatal in infancy or early childhood from enteropathy, metabolic complications, and infection; immunosuppression can achieve temporary control, but haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, ideally undertaken early, provides the best prospect of long-term survival.

Pancreatic pseudocyst Chronic obstructive pancreatitis with duct dilatation Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm MRI with MRCP to assess ductal communication, cyst morphology, and main duct calibre Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration for cyst fluid and mural nodule assessment Cyst fluid CEA (elevated in mucinous lesions) and cytology Cyst fluid Main-duct and mixed types carry a substantially higher risk of high-grade dysplasia and invasive carcinoma than branch-duct disease Branch-duct lesions communicate with the main duct and are frequently multifocal, often found incidentally as cystic lesions A classic endoscopic finding of main-duct disease is a patulous, mucin-extruding ampulla (the fish-mouth papilla) Worrisome features and high-risk stigmata (as in the international consensus and European guidelines) drive decisions between surveillance and resection High-risk stigmata include obstructive jaundice with a pancreatic head cyst, an enhancing mural nodule of significant size, and marked main pancreatic duct dilatation Worrisome features include cyst growth, thickened enhancing cyst walls, smaller mural nodules, an abrupt duct calibre change with distal atrophy, and raised CA 19-9 Management ranges from periodic imaging surveillance for low-risk branch-duct lesions to surgical resection for main-duct disease and lesions with high-risk features Obstructive jaundice attributable to a cystic head lesion An enhancing mural nodule of significant size or a solid component Marked dilatation of the main pancreatic duct New-onset diabetes, weight loss, or rapid cyst growth Positive or high-grade atypical cytology on aspiration Misclassifying a mucinous cyst as a benign serous cystadenoma or pseudocyst Under-recognising main-duct involvement and its high malignant potential Discontinuing surveillance prematurely, as risk persists and can increase over time Attributing main duct dilatation to chronic pancreatitis and missing an IPMN Over-reliance on cyst size alone rather than the full set of worrisome and high-risk features Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms are proliferations of mucin-secreting columnar epithelium that grow within and dilate the pancreatic ductal system. Excess mucin production and papillary epithelial growth obstruct the ducts, producing cystic dilatation of branch ducts, diffuse or segmental dilatation of the main duct, or both. These lesions progress through a spectrum from low-grade dysplasia to high-grade dysplasia and, ultimately, invasive adenocarcinoma, following an adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence. The malignant potential correlates with the ductal compartment involved and with morphological features such as mural nodules, main duct dilatation, and epithelial subtype, with pancreatobiliary and intestinal subtypes behaving differently. Branch-duct lesions without worrisome features generally have a low short-term risk of malignancy and can be safely surveyed, whereas main-duct and mixed lesions carry a high risk of harbouring or progressing to invasive cancer; outcomes after resection depend on whether invasive carcinoma is present and on its stage and subtype.

endothelial dystrophy Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome and other anterior segment dysgenesis Iris melanoma or naevus Peripheral anterior synechiae from chronic angle-closure or uveitis Traumatic or surgical
