that migrates across the angle and onto the iris Typically unilateral and affecting middle-aged women, presenting with corneal oedema, iris changes, or secondary glaucoma The three overlapping clinical variants are essential (progressive) iris atrophy, Chandler syndrome, and Cogan-Reese (iris naevus) syndrome Essential iris atrophy shows marked iris thinning, hole formation, corectopia (pupil displacement), and pseudopolycoria Chandler syndrome is dominated by endothelial change and corneal oedema with relatively mild iris atrophy Cogan-Reese syndrome features pigmented iris nodules on the abnormal endothelial-lined membrane Specular microscopy shows characteristic ICE cells with a dark-light reversal (epithelial-like) appearance of the endothelium Management targets the two main problems: corneal oedema (medical measures then endothelial keratoplasty) and secondary angle-closure glaucoma (medical, laser, or surgical, often with drainage devices) Progressive secondary glaucoma with optic nerve damage and field loss Corneal decompensation with worsening oedema and visual loss Rapidly advancing iris destruction and corectopia Features suggesting iris melanoma rather than the benign nodules of Cogan-Reese syndrome Mistaking ICE syndrome for Fuchs or posterior polymorphous dystrophy, which are usually bilateral Underestimating the aggressive, often refractory secondary glaucoma Confusing Cogan-Reese iris nodules with iris melanoma Attributing unilateral corneal oedema to primary endothelial dystrophy without gonioscopy and specular microscopy Iridocorneal endothelial syndrome is characterised by an acquired abnormality of the corneal endothelium, whose cells take on epithelial-like proliferative and migratory behaviour. These abnormal endothelial cells and an accompanying basement-membrane-like layer proliferate across the trabecular meshwork and over the anterior iris surface. Contraction of this membrane produces peripheral anterior synechiae, angle closure, iris stretching with corectopia, iris hole formation, and, in the Cogan-Reese variant, pigmented iris nodules. Blockage of the trabecular meshwork by the membrane and synechiae raises intraocular pressure, causing secondary glaucoma, while endothelial dysfunction leads to corneal oedema. The condition is typically unilateral and slowly progressive. The syndrome is slowly progressive and often difficult to control, with secondary glaucoma frequently requiring surgery and a tendency for corneal decompensation over time. Endothelial keratoplasty can restore corneal clarity, but glaucoma commonly limits the long-term visual outcome.

Iron Deficiency Anemia — IDA Anemia of inflammation (anemia of chronic disease) - the second most common anemia worldwide, due to functional iron deficiency; a diagnosis of exclusion usually occurring with an inflammatory disorder such as cancer or infection (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450). Thalassemia trait - microcytosis with normal-to-high ferritin and serum iron; red cells are more homogeneous in volume with a low/normal RDW (Harrison 22e p.450, p.767). Mixed forms (combined absolute and functional iron deficiency) (Harrison 22e p.767). Other nutritional anemias - vitamin B12 and folate deficiency (megaloblastic, macrocytic); may coexist with and mask iron deficiency in malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.765). Sideroblastic anemia (rare) as a cause of microcytic hypochromic red cells (Harrison 22e p.~). Serum ferritin (mainstay; <30 µg/L diagnostic, sensitivity 92% / specificity 98%); note ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and may rise severalfold in inflammation (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450). Transferrin saturation (serum iron/TIBC); iron-restricted erythropoiesis at <15-20% (Harrison 22e p.765). Serum iron (reduced, but diurnal fluctuation prevents use as a single test) (Harrison 22e p.765). MCV and RDW from the CBC (MCV <80 fL when established; RDW often elevated reflecting anisocytosis) (Harrison 22e p.765). Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) - increased in iron deficiency; sTfR/log ferritin ratio >2 favors iron deficiency (Harrison 22e p.766, p.767). Reticulocyte hemoglobin content (CHr, reduced) and percentage of hypochromic red cells (%HYPO, increased >6%), reflecting iron availability days to months before testing (Harrison 22e p.766, p.767). Serum hepcidin (low/undetectable in absolute deficiency; not routinely measured, reference values not standardized) (Harrison 22e p.766, p.767). Absence of stainable iron in bone marrow remains the gold standard, although it is rarely needed and unacceptably invasive (Harrison 22e p.765). Endoscopy and/or radiographic imaging to identify the cause - essential in males and postmenopausal females to rule out malignancy or other severe bleeding sources (Harrison 22e p.765, p.~). Anemia of inflammation / chronic disease (functional iron deficiency from high hepcidin: low serum iron and transferrin saturation with NORMAL-to-HIGH ferritin) (Harrison 22e p.764, p.767). Thalassemia trait (microcytic but with normal-to-high ferritin and iron, and a low/normal RDW) (Harrison 22e p.450, p.767). Classic blood picture is a microcytic, hypochromic anemia (MCV <80 fL in established disease), but microcytosis can be ABSENT in early iron deficiency or masked by liver disease or concomitant folate/B12 deficiency (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450). Low serum ferritin is the mainstay of absolute iron deficiency, reflecting depleted stores; ferritin <30 µg/L has high sensitivity and specificity (92% and 98%) and can be used as a single diagnostic test (Harrison 22e p.765). Transferrin saturation (serum iron/TIBC) measures iron available for erythropoiesis; erythropoiesis becomes iron-restricted at values <15-20% (Harrison 22e p.765). Anemia develops only in the LATE stage because the erythron is relatively spared compared with heart and skeletal muscle, which become iron-depleted earlier; slow progression plus compensation means anemia is often undetected, especially in the young, until hemoglobin falls below ~8 g/dL (Harrison 22e p.765). Clinical clues include pica (compulsive ingestion of nonnutritive substances such as ice, soil, or clay), nail fragility and koilonychia, hair loss, cheilosis, atrophic glossitis, and dysphagia from esophageal webs (Plummer-Vinson syndrome) (Harrison 22e p.765; Koilonychia association noted p.~). Even symptomatic isolated iron deficiency WITHOUT anemia matters: suboptimal myocyte, cardiomyocyte, and neuron function can cause fatigue, irritability, poor concentration, restless legs syndrome, and reduced exercise capacity (Harrison 22e p.765). Severe iron-deficiency anemia may be accompanied by thrombocytosis, due to prevalent megakaryocyte commitment of the common erythroid-platelet progenitor when iron is insufficient (Harrison 22e p.766). Serum hepcidin is low/undetectable in absolute iron deficiency (maximizing dietary iron absorption) but elevated in inflammation and in IRIDA (TMPRSS6 mutations) (Harrison 22e p.766). Inadequate therapeutic response (no reticulocytosis after 1 week, or <1 g/dL hemoglobin rise after 2 weeks of iron therapy) should prompt a search for the cause: noncompliance, ongoing blood loss, or malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.766). Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia in any adult (with the possible exception of a premenopausal, multiparous woman) MANDATES thorough endoscopic and/or radiographic visualization of the entire large bowel - right (ascending) colon cancer causes insidious blood loss and often presents as IDA (Harrison 22e p.~, colorectal cancer chapter). Imaging and endoscopy to trace the cause are essential in males and postmenopausal females to rule out malignancy or other severe causes of bleeding (Harrison 22e p.765). Hemoglobin falling below ~8 g/dL or otherwise severe anemia (Harrison 22e p.765). Myelophthisic blood smear (nucleated red cells, teardrop cells, immature white cells) suggesting marrow infiltration mandates marrow examination - a competing cause of anemia to recognize (Harrison 22e p.450). Classic microcytosis/hypochromia can be ABSENT in early iron deficiency, in elderly patients, or when masked by concomitant folate/B12 deficiency or liver disease - do not exclude IDA on a normal MCV alone (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450). Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant; normal or high ferritin during inflammation can mask coexisting iron deficiency (Harrison 22e p.450). Serum iron alone is unreliable as a single test due to diurnal variation (Harrison 22e p.765). Treating IDA without investigating the cause can miss occult GI malignancy; isolated symptomatic iron deficiency without anemia should not be underestimated (Harrison 22e p.764, p.765). Biomarkers other than ferritin and transferrin saturation are limited by poor standardization and accessibility (Harrison 22e p.766). Iron supply becomes inadequate for needs through excessive demand, insufficient intake, defective absorption, or blood loss; multiple causes frequently co-occur, especially in the elderly and in multimorbidity (Harrison 22e p.764). In ISOLATED iron deficiency, stores are depleted while hemoglobin is still normal; when iron remains sufficient for erythropoiesis, red cells are normochromic/normocytic with decreased ferritin (<15-30 µg/L). As transferrin saturation falls <15-20%, iron supply to erythropoiesis is insufficient and cells become hypochromic and microcytic, the classic feature of iron-deficiency anemia (Harrison 22e p.764). Iron deficiency is ABSOLUTE when stores are exhausted and FUNCTIONAL when erythropoiesis is iron-restricted but stores are adequate or even increased. Low hepcidin in iron deficiency maximizes dietary absorption; TMPRSS6 mutations cause hereditary iron-refractory IDA (IRIDA) with reduced absorption and oral-iron refractoriness. In inflammation, high hepcidin sequesters iron into stores, producing functional iron deficiency with low serum iron and transferrin saturation despite elevated ferritin; absolute and functional deficiency often coexist (IBD, CKD, aging). Beyond anemia, heart, muscle, and brain are affected; immune response may be blunted as lymphocytes require iron during the metabolic burst (Harrison 22e p.764). Iron deficiency and IDA are highly treatable with iron replacement. Oral iron usually requires at least ~3 months of therapy to restore hemoglobin and replenish stores and prevent early recurrence; inadequate response (no reticulocytosis at 1 week or <1 g/dL hemoglobin rise at 2 weeks) should prompt a search for noncompliance, ongoing blood loss, or malabsorption. Prognosis ultimately depends on the underlying cause (e.g., occult GI malignancy) rather than the anemia itself (Harrison 22e p.766). Harrison describes a continuum rather than a formal grading scale: (1) isolated/absolute iron deficiency with depleted stores (ferritin <15-30 µg/L) but NORMAL hemoglobin and normochromic-normocytic cells; (2) iron-restricted erythropoiesis once transferrin saturation falls <15-20%, with hypochromic microcytic cells; (3) overt iron-deficiency anemia. Severe anemia is generally taken as hemoglobin <=8 g/dL (the threshold at which anemia commonly becomes detectable and at which rapid IV correction is considered) (Harrison 22e p.764-766).

Iron poisoning — iron overdose, iron toxicity, ferrous sulfate poisoning Other corrosive or caustic ingestions Acute gastroenteritis of infective cause Other causes of high anion-gap metabolic acidosis Paracetamol or other hepatotoxic ingestion Sepsis with shock Serum iron level, ideally timed to peak absorption Abdominal radiograph for radiopaque tablets Arterial blood gas with anion gap and lactate Liver function tests and coagulation profile to track hepatic injury Full blood count, electrolytes, renal function, and glucose Toxicity relates to the amount of elemental iron ingested, not the total salt weight, so the specific preparation must be identified The classic course has recognised stages: early GI toxicity, a deceptive latent phase of apparent improvement, then shock and metabolic acidosis, hepatic failure, and finally late gastric scarring and outlet obstruction Early severe vomiting, diarrhoea, and haematemesis reflect direct corrosive injury to the gut mucosa Do not be misled by the quiescent second phase; serious systemic toxicity can still evolve after the patient seems to settle Radiopaque tablets may be visible on an abdominal radiograph and can confirm ingestion and guide decontamination Whole-bowel irrigation is the preferred decontamination method for significant ingestions, as activated charcoal does not bind iron Deferoxamine is the specific chelating antidote, indicated for systemic toxicity, shock, significant acidosis, or high serum iron levels A high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, hypotension, and progressive hepatic injury mark severe poisoning requiring urgent chelation and intensive support Haematemesis or melaena indicating corrosive GI injury Hypotension, shock, or lethargy signalling systemic toxicity High anion-gap metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate Evidence of hepatic injury or coagulopathy Persistent or worsening symptoms after the apparent latent phase Calculating dose from tablet weight rather than elemental iron content Discharging a patient during the deceptive latent phase before systemic toxicity manifests Giving activated charcoal, which does not adsorb iron Delaying deferoxamine in a patient with shock, acidosis, or high iron levels In overdose, free iron overwhelms the body's binding capacity (transferrin) and circulates unbound. It is directly corrosive to the gastrointestinal mucosa, causing haemorrhagic gastroenteritis and fluid loss. Absorbed free iron is a potent catalyst of free-radical formation and disrupts mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, causing cellular injury most prominently in the liver, along with a high anion-gap metabolic (lactic) acidosis. Iron-induced vasodilatation, increased capillary permeability, and myocardial depression produce shock. Healing of the corrosive gastric injury can later cause strictures and gastric outlet obstruction. Small ingestions causing only GI upset usually resolve, but severe poisoning with shock, acidosis, and hepatic failure carries significant mortality; early recognition, decontamination, and deferoxamine chelation greatly improve survival, though late gastric strictures may still occur.

Irritable bowel syndrome — IBS, spastic colon Coeliac disease Inflammatory bowel disease Microscopic colitis Bile acid diarrhoea Colorectal cancer Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth Symptom-based diagnosis using recognised criteria Coeliac serology Faecal calprotectin where inflammatory bowel disease is a concern Full blood count and inflammatory markers Colonoscopy or further imaging when alarm features are present A disorder of gut-brain interaction defined by recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation and associated with a change in stool frequency or form It is subclassified by predominant bowel habit into constipation-predominant, diarrhoea-predominant, mixed and unclassified types It is a positive clinical diagnosis based on symptom criteria with limited targeted testing, not merely a diagnosis of exclusion Alarm features such as weight loss, rectal bleeding, anaemia, older age of onset or a family history of bowel cancer warrant investigation Coeliac serology and, where indicated, faecal calprotectin help exclude coeliac disease and inflammatory bowel disease Management combines dietary measures, symptom-directed pharmacotherapy and psychological therapies Rectal bleeding or iron-deficiency anaemia Unintentional weight loss New symptoms in an older patient Family history of colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease Nocturnal symptoms waking the patient Treating it purely as a diagnosis of exclusion and over-investigating Missing coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease presenting similarly Ignoring alarm features Overlooking the role of psychological factors and the gut-brain axis in management Irritable bowel syndrome is a disorder of gut-brain interaction in which altered gastrointestinal motility, visceral hypersensitivity, changes in the gut microbiota, low-grade mucosal immune activation, and disturbed central processing of visceral signals combine to produce pain and altered bowel habit. Bidirectional signalling along the gut-brain axis, often modulated by stress and psychological factors, amplifies visceral perception. There is no structural or biochemical abnormality that defines the condition, which is characterised instead by its symptom pattern. The condition is chronic and relapsing but benign, and most patients achieve worthwhile symptom control with an individualised combination of diet, medication and psychological approaches.

Irukandji syndrome — Carukia barnesi sting, Irukandji jellyfish envenomation, irukandji, cubozoan catecholamine syndrome Acute coronary syndrome Phaeochromocytoma crisis or sympathomimetic toxidrome Box jellyfish (Chironex) envenomation Acute abdomen or renal colic Decompression illness in a diver Subarachnoid haemorrhage given severe pain and hypertension Electrocardiography for ischaemia and arrhythmia Serial cardiac troponin and echocardiography for stress cardiomyopathy Blood pressure monitoring for hypertensive emergency Chest imaging for pulmonary oedema Electrolytes, renal function and glucose Caused by small cubozoans (classically Carukia barnesi); the initial sting is often trivial or barely noticed After a delay of roughly 20-40 minutes, patients develop severe generalised pain, especially in the back, chest and abdomen, with muscle cramps A striking catecholamine surge produces sweating, agitation, hypertension, tachycardia, nausea, vomiting and a sense of impending doom Serious complications include hypertensive emergency, myocardial dysfunction (stress cardiomyopathy) and potentially fatal pulmonary oedema Vinegar is applied to the sting site to inactivate undischarged nematocysts, but the syndrome is driven by systemic venom effects rather than local injury Management principles are aggressive analgesia, antiemetics, and control of hypertension and cardiac dysfunction with monitoring in a high-dependency setting There is no specific antivenom; treatment is supportive and directed at the hyperadrenergic state and its cardiac consequences Severe or refractory hypertension with end-organ features Evidence of myocardial injury or pulmonary oedema Progressive dyspnoea or hypoxia Altered consciousness or neurological deficit Haemodynamic instability Discharging early after a trivial-looking sting before the delayed systemic syndrome has been excluded Failing to anticipate and monitor for venom-induced cardiomyopathy and pulmonary oedema Providing inadequate analgesia for what is often extreme pain Overlooking hypertensive emergency requiring controlled blood pressure reduction The venom of Irukandji-type jellyfish triggers a massive endogenous release of catecholamines, producing a delayed systemic syndrome disproportionate to the minor local sting. Sympathetic overactivity causes severe pain, hypertension, tachycardia and diaphoresis, while catecholamine excess can injure the myocardium, producing a stress (takotsubo-type) cardiomyopathy with left ventricular dysfunction. Cardiac failure and capillary changes can lead to acute pulmonary oedema, and the profound autonomic activation accounts for the anxiety and feeling of doom that characterise the syndrome. Most cases resolve over hours to a couple of days with supportive care, but a minority develop life-threatening cardiac failure or pulmonary oedema, and deaths have occurred, so cardiac monitoring is essential.

Ischaemic colitis — colonic ischaemia Acute mesenteric ischaemia (small bowel) Infective colitis Inflammatory bowel disease Diverticulitis Colorectal malignancy Pseudomembranous colitis CT of the abdomen with contrast Colonoscopy showing segmental changes (avoided if peritonitis) Blood tests including lactate and inflammatory markers Stool studies to exclude infection Assessment for a precipitating low-flow or thrombotic cause The commonest form of intestinal ischaemia, usually a transient, non-occlusive reduction in colonic perfusion Presents with sudden crampy abdominal pain followed by bloody diarrhoea, typically in older patients Watershed areas such as the splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction are most vulnerable It is usually self-limiting, unlike acute mesenteric ischaemia of the small bowel, which is a surgical emergency CT may show colonic wall thickening, and colonoscopy shows segmental mucosal changes Most cases resolve with supportive care, but gangrenous or fulminant colitis needs surgery Peritonitis or signs of transmural infarction Rising lactate, acidosis or systemic toxicity Right-sided (isolated) ischaemic colitis, which behaves more aggressively Failure to improve, suggesting gangrene or stricture Confusing it with acute mesenteric ischaemia and delaying surgery when the small bowel is involved Mistaking it for infective colitis or inflammatory bowel disease Underestimating isolated right colonic ischaemia Performing colonoscopy in a patient with peritonitis Ischaemic colitis results from a temporary compromise of colonic blood flow that is insufficient to meet metabolic demand, most often non-occlusive and related to a low-flow state, with the poorly collateralised watershed regions most affected. Mucosal injury ranges from reversible superficial changes to transmural infarction. Precipitants include hypotension, hypovolaemia, cardiac failure, vasoconstrictors and, in younger patients, causes such as vasculitis, thrombophilia, cocaine use and strenuous exertion. Most transient cases resolve within days with supportive care; gangrenous or fulminant colitis carries significant mortality, and some develop a chronic segment or stricture.

ischaemic hepatitis — shock liver, hypoxic hepatitis Acute viral hepatitis Paracetamol or other drug-induced hepatotoxicity Acute Budd-Chiari syndrome Hepatic infarction Autoimmune hepatitis flare Acute biliary obstruction Heat stroke-related liver injury Serial liver function tests demonstrating the rapid rise and fall in transaminases Serum lactate dehydrogenase with calculation of the ALT-to-LDH ratio Echocardiography and assessment of cardiac output Arterial blood gas and lactate Coagulation profile and renal function Viral hepatitis and paracetamol screen to exclude alternatives Doppler assessment of the hepatic vessels where outflow obstruction is suspected Ischaemic hepatitis, or shock liver, is diffuse hepatocellular injury caused by inadequate oxygen delivery to the liver rather than by a primary hepatic disease. Cardiac failure with hepatic venous congestion is the most frequent setting, while circulatory shock, severe hypoxaemia and sepsis are other important precipitants. The biochemical hallmark is a massive, abrupt rise in serum transaminases that peaks quickly and then falls rapidly once perfusion is restored. A markedly elevated lactate dehydrogenase with a low ALT-to-LDH ratio helps distinguish it from acute viral hepatitis. Mild jaundice, a transient coagulopathy and acute kidney injury commonly accompany the transaminase spike. The diagnosis is clinical and biochemical, and liver biopsy, rarely needed, shows centrilobular zone 3 necrosis. Management is directed entirely at restoring haemodynamics and treating the underlying cardiac or circulatory disorder rather than the liver itself. A precipitating haemodynamic event is not always overt, and cardiac failure can cause the picture without a documented episode of hypotension. Progressive rise in bilirubin and INR after transaminases have peaked, suggesting evolving liver failure Persistent shock or refractory hypotension Encephalopathy or other features of acute liver failure Concurrent multi-organ dysfunction Misdiagnosing the transaminase spike as acute viral or drug-induced hepatitis and missing the haemodynamic cause. Waiting for a documented episode of hypotension, which may be absent in congestive cardiac failure. Focusing on hepatic management rather than urgently correcting the underlying circulatory problem. Attributing the accompanying acute kidney injury to a separate process. Hepatocytes in the centrilobular zone, acinar zone 3, lie furthest from the incoming oxygenated blood and are the most metabolically active, making them exquisitely sensitive to hypoxia. Ischaemic hepatitis develops when oxygen delivery falls below hepatic demand through reduced cardiac output, systemic hypotension, passive venous congestion, arterial hypoxaemia or a combination of these. Congestive cardiac failure is especially important because raised central venous pressure produces hepatic congestion that both lowers effective perfusion pressure and sensitises the parenchyma, so that even a modest fall in output precipitates injury. The resulting zone 3 necrosis releases large quantities of intracellular enzymes, generating the characteristic transaminase and lactate dehydrogenase surge, and a reperfusion component may follow restoration of flow. Because the insult is typically brief and the hepatic architecture is preserved, enzymes normalise rapidly and function usually recovers once the circulation is corrected. The liver injury itself usually resolves quickly once perfusion is restored, but overall prognosis is poor and is driven by the severity of the underlying cardiac, circulatory or respiratory illness.

Ischaemic colitis — ischemic colitis, colonic ischaemia, colonic ischemia Acute mesenteric ischaemia (small bowel) Infective (bacterial) colitis Inflammatory bowel disease, especially Crohn colitis Diverticular haemorrhage or diverticulitis Colorectal malignancy Pseudomembranous (Clostridioides difficile) colitis CT of the abdomen and pelvis to assess segmental wall thickening and exclude perforation Colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy showing segmental mucosal injury with an abrupt transition zone Serum lactate and inflammatory markers to gauge severity and detect possible gangrene Stool studies to exclude infective causes when the picture is atypical Cardiac and vascular assessment to identify a precipitating low-flow state The commonest form of intestinal ischaemia, usually affecting older adults and typically arising from a transient, non-occlusive fall in colonic perfusion rather than a fixed arterial blockage Classic presentation is sudden mild crampy left-sided abdominal pain followed within a day by the passage of bloody or maroon stool, with only modest blood loss The watershed zones (splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction) are most vulnerable, while the rectum is usually spared because of its dual blood supply CT often shows segmental bowel-wall thickening, and colonoscopy is the key diagnostic test showing segmental oedema, haemorrhage, and mucosal ulceration with an abrupt transition to normal mucosa Most cases are non-gangrenous and settle with supportive care: bowel rest, intravenous fluids, and correction of any precipitating hypoperfusion Right-sided (isolated right colon) involvement carries a worse prognosis and should raise concern for coexisting acute mesenteric ischaemia Distinguish from infective colitis and inflammatory bowel disease; the segmental distribution and rapid resolution favour an ischaemic cause Recognised triggers include hypotension, cardiac or vascular surgery, dehydration, hypercoagulable states, and certain drugs such as vasoconstrictors Peritonism, fever, marked leucocytosis, or rising lactate suggesting gangrenous colitis and impending perforation Isolated right-sided colonic involvement, which may signal concurrent acute mesenteric ischaemia Persistent bleeding, haemodynamic instability, or failure to improve on supportive care Development of a colonic stricture with obstruction during recovery Assuming rectal sparing excludes colonic ischaemia, or mistaking segmental ischaemic changes for inflammatory bowel disease Delaying surgical review when signs of transmural necrosis are present Overlooking a precipitating hypoperfusion event that will otherwise recur Failing to recognise that isolated right colon disease may reflect small-bowel mesenteric ischaemia needing urgent vascular evaluation Ischaemic colitis results from a temporary reduction in blood flow to a colonic segment, most often a low-flow (non-occlusive) event superimposed on the marginal circulation of watershed areas. Reduced perfusion injures the mucosa first, producing oedema, submucosal haemorrhage, and superficial ulceration. In most patients reperfusion allows healing, but persistent or severe ischaemia can progress to transmural (gangrenous) necrosis with perforation or, later, to fibrotic stricture. It is usually a disease of small vessels and systemic hypoperfusion rather than a large-artery occlusion, which distinguishes it from acute mesenteric ischaemia. Non-gangrenous ischaemic colitis usually resolves within a few days with conservative management and has a good outcome. Gangrenous disease requiring surgery carries substantial mortality, and right-sided involvement predicts a worse course. A minority develop chronic segmental colitis or a stricture.

Ischemic Heart Disease — IHD, Chronic Coronary Disease, Chronic Coronary Syndrome, Coronary Artery Disease, Stable Angina Pectoris Aortic stenosis with severe LVH causing subendocardial ischemia and angina without coronary atherosclerosis (Harrison 22e p.2091) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Harrison 22e p.2093) Aortic regurgitation and pulmonary hypertension as causes of angina-like chest discomfort (Harrison 22e p.2093) Microvascular angina / abnormal cardiac nociception in patients with ischemic-type chest pain but no flow-limiting epicardial obstruction, more common in women (Harrison 22e p.2093) Vasospastic (variant) angina due to coronary spasm (Harrison 22e p.2091, 2093) Pericarditis (suggested by discomfort radiating to the trapezius) (Harrison 22e p.2092) Esophageal/gastrointestinal disease and musculoskeletal chest wall pain (Harrison 22e p.2093-2094) Fasting lipid panel (total, LDL, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, lipoprotein(a)) (Harrison 22e p.2094) Glucose / hemoglobin A1c, creatinine, hematocrit; urinalysis including microalbuminuria; thyroid function if indicated (Harrison 22e p.2094) High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (1-3 mg/L is an independent risk marker, most useful for reclassifying intermediate-risk patients) (Harrison 22e p.2094) Resting 12-lead ECG (Harrison 22e p.2094) Chest x-ray for cardiac enlargement, ventricular aneurysm, or heart failure signs (Harrison 22e p.2094) Exercise treadmill ECG stress testing (sensitivity about 75%) (Harrison 22e p.2094-2095) Stress myocardial perfusion imaging (thallium-201 or 99m-technetium sestamibi SPECT) or PET (N-13 ammonia, rubidium-82) with exercise or pharmacologic (adenosine, dobutamine) stress (Harrison 22e p.2095) Stress echocardiography and cardiac MR stress testing (Harrison 22e p.2095-2096) Coronary artery calcium scoring (Agatston score) by EBCT/MDCT as adjunctive, not primary screening (Harrison 22e p.2095-2097) Coronary CT angiography for intermediate pretest probability and plaque assessment (Harrison 22e p.2097) Invasive coronary arteriography (with FFR/iwFR) per ISCHEMIA-informed indications (Harrison 22e p.2097-2098) Aortic stenosis (subendocardial ischemia) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Pericarditis Esophageal disease Chest wall / musculoskeletal pain reproducible on palpation IHD reflects an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand; the dominant cause is atherosclerotic narrowing of one or more epicardial coronary arteries reducing regional myocardial perfusion (Harrison 22e p.2090). Anginal discomfort is classically described as heaviness, pressure, squeezing, smothering or choking rather than frank pain, is crescendo-decrescendo, typically lasts 2-5 minutes, and may be signaled by a clenched fist over the sternum (Levine's sign) (Harrison 22e p.2092). Anginal pain may radiate to either shoulder, both arms (especially the ulnar forearm/hand), back, interscapular region, neck, jaw, teeth, or epigastrium; it is rarely localized below the umbilicus or above the mandible (Harrison 22e p.2092). Radiation to the trapezius muscles is NOT typical of myocardial ischemia and points more toward pericarditis; this is a useful discriminating feature (Harrison 22e p.2092). Anginal equivalents (dyspnea, nausea, fatigue, faintness) and atypical presentations are more common in women, the elderly, and patients with diabetes mellitus, in whom angina may not relate strictly to provoking factors (Harrison 22e p.2093). A resting 12-lead ECG may be entirely normal in typical angina; ST-T and LVH changes are suggestive but nonspecific, whereas dynamic ST-T changes appearing with an anginal episode and resolving afterward are more specific (Harrison 22e p.2094). A stenosis must reduce epicardial luminal diameter by about 50% to limit flow augmentation on demand, and by roughly 80% before resting flow falls; beyond that, small further reductions cut flow dramatically (Harrison 22e p.2091). Reversible ischemic injury occurs within roughly 20 minutes of total occlusion (without collaterals); occlusion beyond 20 minutes leads to myocardial necrosis (Harrison 22e p.2091). The Canadian Cardiovascular Society class grades angina severity and the New York Heart Association class grades functional limitation (Harrison 22e p.2093). An ischemic stress-ECG response is flat or downsloping ST depression >0.1 mV lasting >0.08 s; upsloping or junctional ST changes are not diagnostic, and a test failing to reach 85% of age/sex-predicted maximal heart rate is nondiagnostic (Harrison 22e p.2094-2095). Chest wall tenderness, pain reproduced by palpation, or pain localizable with a single fingertip makes a myocardial ischemic origin unlikely (Harrison 22e p.2093-2094). Most patients who die suddenly from IHD do so from ischemia-induced ventricular tachyarrhythmias (Harrison 22e p.2092). Angina occurring with less exertion than before, at rest, or awakening the patient from sleep (features of an unstable syndrome) (Harrison 22e p.2093) Angina accompanied by symptoms or signs of heart failure, pulmonary edema, transient third heart sound, or mitral regurgitation (Harrison 22e p.2092, 2097) Inability to exercise beyond 6 minutes / stage II of the Bruce protocol (Harrison 22e p.2097) Ischemia at low workload, >=0.2 mV ST depression, or ST depression persisting >5 minutes after exercise (Harrison 22e p.2097) A fall in systolic blood pressure >10 mmHg during exercise or exercise-induced ventricular tachyarrhythmia (Harrison 22e p.2096-2097) Large or multiple perfusion defects, increased lung tracer uptake, or a fall in LV ejection fraction during stress imaging (Harrison 22e p.2097) Reduced resting LV ejection fraction (<0.40) (Harrison 22e p.2097) Sudden cardiac death may be the unheralded presenting manifestation of IHD (Harrison 22e p.2092) Relying on coronary artery calcium as the primary screening test or sole basis for therapeutic decisions; it is adjunctive only (Harrison 22e p.2092). Interpreting a stress ECG without accounting for pretest probability; false positives rise in low-probability patients (e.g., asymptomatic men <40, premenopausal women without risk factors) and in those on digitalis/antiarrhythmics, with conduction disturbances, LVH, resting ST-T abnormalities, or abnormal potassium (Harrison 22e p.2095). Assuming a negative stress ECG excludes CAD; sensitivity is only about 75%, though it makes three-vessel or left main disease unlikely (Harrison 22e p.2095). Circumflex-territory disease may yield a false-negative stress test because the posterolateral wall is poorly represented on the surface 12-lead ECG (Harrison 22e p.2095). Coronary arteriography images only the lumen and can miss severe non-luminal (remodeled, outwardly bulging) atherosclerosis (Harrison 22e p.2097). Missing atypical/anginal-equivalent presentations in women, the elderly, and patients with diabetes (Harrison 22e p.2093). Overlooking that about 25% of acute MI survivors never come to medical attention yet share the same adverse prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2092-2093). Myocardial oxygen demand (MVO2) is governed by heart rate, contractility, and wall tension, while supply depends on oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood and coronary blood flow (predominantly diastolic). Coronary resistance resides mainly in prearteriolar (R2) and arteriolar/capillary (R3) microvascular beds, which normally dilate to match demand (metabolic regulation and autoregulation). Atherosclerosis of epicardial arteries, driven by endothelial dysfunction from high LDL, smoking, hypertension, and diabetes, produces subintimal plaques; plaque rupture or erosion exposes contents to blood, triggering platelet activation/aggregation and the coagulation cascade with fibrin deposition and thrombus formation. As proximal stenoses worsen, distal resistance vessels dilate maximally and flow becomes pressure-dependent, so increased demand (exertion, emotion, tachycardia) precipitates ischemia. Ischemia causes regional contractile dysfunction (hypokinesis to dyskinesis), impaired relaxation, a metabolic shift to anaerobic lactate production with falling intracellular pH and high-energy phosphate depletion, membrane dysfunction with potassium leak and cytosolic calcium rise, characteristic ECG repolarization changes, and electrical instability. The subendocardium is most vulnerable to underperfusion (Harrison 22e p.2090-2092). Principal prognostic determinants are age, left ventricular function, the location and severity of coronary stenoses, and the severity/activity of ischemia. Recent-onset or unstable angina, early post-MI angina, angina poorly responsive to therapy, and angina with heart failure all carry increased risk. Elevated LV end-diastolic pressure/volume and reduced ejection fraction signal poor prognosis. Left main (>50% diameter) or proximal LAD obstruction carries greater risk than right or circumflex lesions because more myocardium is jeopardized. With any obstructive disease, mortality rises sharply when LV function is impaired; the larger the established necrosis, the poorer the prognosis. Conversely, patients with chest discomfort but normal LV function and normal coronary arteries have an excellent prognosis, as do those completing stage III of the Bruce protocol with a normal perfusion scan or negative stress echo. Greater number/severity of risk factors (advanced age >75, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, morbid obesity, peripheral/cerebrovascular disease, prior MI), elevated CRP, extensive coronary calcification, and increased carotid intimal thickening all worsen prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2097). Angina severity is graded by the Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) functional classification (Class I: angina only with strenuous/rapid/prolonged exertion; Class II: slight limitation of ordinary activity; Class III: marked limitation with ordinary activity such as walking 1-2 blocks; Class IV: inability to perform any physical activity without discomfort, angina may be present at rest). Functional impact is described by the New York Heart Association (NYHA) classification (Classes I-IV) (Harrison 22e p.2093).

may evolve to abscess or hemorrhagic infarct) Brain abscess CNS infection-related vasculitis (syphilis, tuberculosis, fungal, bacterial, zoster meningitis) Finger-stick blood glucose - one of only two tests (with brain imaging) truly required before IV thrombolysis ECG and continuous cardiac telemetry to detect atrial fibrillation or recent MI; ambulatory monitoring if AF not captured inpatient Echocardiography (transthoracic/transoesophageal); bubble-contrast study to detect right-to-left shunt / PFO Carotid duplex ultrasound and transcranial Doppler (can also detect microemboli) CT/MR perfusion imaging to define the penumbra and select late-window candidates MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging - most sensitive for acute infarction, especially in the posterior fossa, and detects new infarction after TIA Catheter cerebral angiography (gold standard for stenosis/vasculopathy; reserved for when noninvasive studies are inadequate) Secondary-prevention workup: lipid profile, ESR, FBC, electrolytes, renal function, coagulation (PT/PTT); selective thrombophilia/vasculitis screen in young or cryptogenic cases Seizure with postictal (Todd's) paralysis - an observer history of no convulsive onset usually excludes seizure, but ongoing complex partial seizures can mimic stroke Migraine, including acephalgic migraine even without prior history; sensory/motor deficits migrate slowly over minutes and may cross vascular territories Metabolic encephalopathy (fluctuating mental status, typically without focal signs) Hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia (check finger-stick glucose before thrombolysis) Intracranial tumour Stroke is a clinical diagnosis: abrupt-onset focal neurologic deficit from a vascular cause; imaging is used to support it and to separate ischemia from hemorrhage (p.3427). Time-is-brain: with complete arterial occlusion, neurons die within roughly 4-10 minutes; flow <16-18 mL/100 g/min infarcts within an hour, while 18-20 mL/100 g/min causes reversible ischemia unless prolonged (p.3439). The ischemic penumbra is reversibly dysfunctional tissue around the infarct core; it is the target of reperfusion and can be visualized as a perfusion-diffusion (or CT-perfusion) mismatch (p.3439). A useful triage rule of thumb is that a deficit maximal at onset (or one that remits) favors ischemia, whereas a depressed conscious level, very high initial blood pressure, or progressive worsening favors hemorrhage - though no clinical feature reliably separates them, so CT is required (p.3440). The public FAST acronym (Facial weakness, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time) captures common stroke features and emphasizes time-sensitivity; about 85% of ischemic stroke patients have hemiparesis (p.3428). Stroke onset is timed from when the patient was last seen well, not when found; wake-up strokes default to bedtime, though advanced imaging may still allow treatment selection (p.3441). Cerebellar infarction can masquerade as labyrinthitis with vertigo and vomiting; accompanying head/neck pain should prompt suspicion of vertebral dissection, and even small cerebellar edema can obstruct CSF and compress the brainstem (p.3440). Roughly 30% of ischemic strokes remain cryptogenic despite thorough evaluation (p.3443). Painful neck or head pain preceding stroke in a young patient (under ~60) suggests arterial dissection (p.3445). Disabling deficit (NIHSS >5) - candidate for thrombolysis and/or thrombectomy; act fast Suspected large-vessel occlusion (ICA terminus, M1/M2, basilar) - candidate for mechanical thrombectomy Cerebellar infarct with declining consciousness or new brainstem signs - impending herniation/hydrocephalus needing emergency decompression Large hemispheric (malignant MCA) infarct - 5-10% develop space-occupying edema peaking on day 2-3, may need hemicraniectomy Painful neck/Horner's or recent neck trauma/manipulation - suspect arterial dissection Multifocal deficits with fever - suspect septic emboli from endocarditis Treating a stroke mimic as stroke: a postictal (Todd's) paralysis, acephalgic migraine, or hypoglycaemia can convincingly imitate acute stroke - always confirm glucose and seek an observer history of convulsive onset. Mislabelling cerebellar stroke as benign labyrinthitis and missing life-threatening brainstem compression / hydrocephalus. Omitting the embolic-source workup (carotid, heart) after a lacunar-appearing infarct, since a large-vessel source can present as a small-vessel syndrome. A normal early CT does not exclude infarction; CT may be only subtly abnormal acutely and the hyperdense MCA sign is specific but seen in only ~20% of MCA occlusions (DWI-MRI is far more sensitive). Over-attributing stroke to a patent foramen ovale, which is present in ~15% of the general population and is often incidental. Aggressively lowering blood pressure acutely can reduce pressure-dependent collateral flow and worsen the penumbra; permissive hypertension is generally allowed early. Distinguish benign reperfusion petechial haemorrhage within an infarct from frank haemorrhagic transformation with mass effect. Acute occlusion of an intracranial artery reduces regional cerebral blood flow; the resulting deficit depends on collateral supply, occlusion site, and systemic pressure. Energy failure from loss of glucose and oxygen halts ATP-dependent ion pumps, causing depolarization, sodium and calcium influx, excess synaptic glutamate, and excitotoxicity with reactive oxygen species that damage membranes and DNA, followed by an innate inflammatory response. Fever and hyperglycaemia (glucose >200 mg/dL) worsen the injury. Mechanistically, ischemic stroke arises by three routes (the basis of TOAST-style classification): (1) embolic occlusion of a large intracranial vessel - either cardioembolic (e.g., atrial fibrillation, mural thrombus, valvular disease) or artery-to-artery from carotid/aortic-arch plaque; (2) in-situ thrombosis of small penetrating arteries from lipohyalinosis or microatheroma, producing lacunar (small-vessel) infarcts; and (3) hypoperfusion from flow-limiting stenosis of a major extracranial or intracranial vessel, producing watershed/border-zone ischemia. Cardioembolism causes ~20%, large-artery/carotid atherosclerosis ~10%, and small-vessel disease ~20% of ischemic strokes (p.3439, p.3443-3446). Stroke is the second leading cause of death worldwide; outcome hinges on time to reperfusion ('time-is-brain'). For large-vessel occlusion, the chance of a good outcome falls steeply with delay - the odds of a good result exceed 3 if groin puncture for thrombectomy is within 2 h but fall to about 2 by 8 h, and over 80% do well if the vessel opens within 1 h of arrival versus about one-third at 6 h. In pooled thrombectomy trials ~46% achieved functional independence (modified Rankin 0-2) versus ~26.5% with medical care, with a mortality benefit. Small-vessel (lacunar) strokes generally recover more rapidly and completely than large-vessel strokes, though some stutter or leave severe disability. Without secondary prevention the annual risk of a further stroke after atherothrombotic stroke/TIA is about 8-10%; symptomatic intracranial atherosclerosis and untreated symptomatic carotid stenosis each carry ~15% per year. Care in a dedicated stroke unit followed by rehabilitation improves neurologic outcome and reduces mortality (p.3427, p.3441-3442, p.3445-3446). Severity is graded clinically by the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS). A disabling deficit (NIHSS >5) flags potential eligibility for thrombolysis/endovascular therapy, whereas minor non-disabling stroke (NIHSS 0-5) may be managed with aspirin or short-term dual antiplatelet therapy. Mechanism-based (TOAST-style) classification - cardioembolic, large-artery atherosclerosis (carotid/intracranial), small-vessel/lacunar, other defined cause, and cryptogenic (~30%) - drives secondary prevention. Carotid disease is further classed as symptomatic vs asymptomatic and by degree of stenosis, with risk rising with stenosis severity except for near-occlusions, which carry lower risk (p.3440-3441, p.3443, p.3445).

ischiofemoral impingement — ischiofemoral impingement syndrome, quadratus femoris impingement Proximal hamstring tendinopathy Deep gluteal syndrome with sciatic nerve entrapment Ischiogluteal bursitis Hip osteoarthritis Lumbar radiculopathy Piriformis syndrome Femoral neck or ischial stress fracture MRI of the pelvis with measurement of the ischiofemoral and quadratus femoris spaces MRI assessment of quadratus femoris oedema, tears or fatty atrophy Dynamic ultrasound of the ischiofemoral interval Image-guided diagnostic local anaesthetic injection into the quadratus femoris Radiographs to assess coxa valga and proximal femoral morphology Assessment of femoral version by CT or MRI Presents with deep posterior hip, buttock or groin pain that may radiate distally, characteristically worsened by hip extension, adduction and external rotation. Pain is typically reproduced during the terminal stance phase of a long stride; the long-stride walking test provokes symptoms whereas short strides relieve them. Oedema, and in chronic cases fatty infiltration, of the quadratus femoris muscle on MRI is the hallmark imaging finding. Narrowing of both the ischiofemoral space (between lateral ischium and lesser trochanter) and the quadratus femoris space supports the diagnosis. It is more common in women, related to a wider pelvis, coxa valga and increased femoral anteversion. Secondary causes include hip instability, proximal femoral or ischial malunion, prior arthroplasty and space-occupying lesions. First-line management is activity modification, physiotherapy to correct pelvic mechanics, and an image-guided local anaesthetic and corticosteroid injection into the quadratus femoris, which is also diagnostic. Refractory cases may be treated by lesser trochanter resection or endoscopic decompression, addressing any underlying morphology or instability. Progressive sciatic neurological deficit, indicating significant nerve involvement Rest pain or night pain suggesting a neoplasm around the ischium or proximal femur A palpable soft-tissue mass narrowing the space Bilateral symptoms with systemic features prompting a search for an underlying disease Interpreting a narrowed ischiofemoral space in isolation as diagnostic, since space narrowing occurs in asymptomatic individuals and must be correlated with quadratus femoris signal change and clinical findings. Relying on neutral-position static MRI, which can miss impingement that only occurs dynamically in extension and adduction. Mislabelling the condition as piriformis syndrome or a simple hamstring strain. Ignoring associated femoral version or instability, leading to persistent symptoms after isolated soft-tissue treatment. The ischiofemoral space is bounded by the lateral cortex of the ischial tuberosity and the medial and posterior aspect of the lesser trochanter, and transmits the quadratus femoris muscle. Congenital or acquired narrowing of this corridor causes dynamic entrapment of quadratus femoris, particularly during hip extension combined with adduction and external rotation, when the space narrows further. Contributing factors include coxa valga, an increased femoral neck-shaft angle or anteversion, prominence of the ischium or lesser trochanter, hip instability, and post-traumatic or post-surgical malalignment. Repeated impingement produces muscle oedema, tears and eventually fatty atrophy, and may irritate the adjacent hamstring origin and sciatic nerve. Many patients improve with conservative measures and image-guided injection, particularly when a reversible mechanical driver is present. Surgical decompression or lesser trochanter resection gives good reported outcomes in carefully selected refractory cases.

fracture rather than apophysitis Inability to bear weight or acute severe pain after an inversion injury Rest pain, night pain or systemic features suggesting infection or tumour Persistent unilateral symptoms not settling with conservative treatment Mistaking the normal obliquely oriented apophysis for an avulsion fracture, or vice versa Overlooking a Jones fracture, which requires different management and has a risk of nonunion Failing to consider infection when there is swelling, warmth or systemic upset Prolonged immobilisation when graded activity modification would suffice Iselin disease is a traction apophysitis of the secondary ossification centre at the base of the fifth metatarsal, the site of insertion of the peroneus brevis tendon. During the period when this apophysis is developing, repetitive traction from the peroneus brevis, particularly during running, jumping and side-to-side cutting movements, stresses the cartilaginous bone-tendon junction. The repeated microtrauma causes inflammation, and the apophysis may appear enlarged or fragmented on imaging. Because the apophysis lies obliquely, roughly parallel to the long axis of the metatarsal, it can be mistaken for an avulsion fracture, which instead produces a transverse lucent line. The condition resolves once the apophysis fuses at skeletal maturity. The prognosis is excellent; symptoms are self-limiting and resolve as the apophysis fuses at skeletal maturity, with activity modification and offloading controlling pain and no long-term sequelae expected.

characterised by impaired secretion of corticotropin from the pituitary corticotrophs while the other anterior pituitary hormones remain intact, resulting in secondary adrenal insufficiency with glucocorticoid deficiency but preserved mineralocorticoid function. Acquired cases most often reflect autoimmune corticotroph destruction as in lymphocytic hypophysitis, including that triggered by immune checkpoint inhibitor drugs; congenital cases result from mutations in TBX19 (TPIT), a transcription factor essential for pro-opiomelanocortin expression in corticotrophs, or from defects in pro-opiomelanocortin processing. Because aldosterone is regulated by the renin-angiotensin system rather than ACTH, salt and potassium handling is largely maintained, and the absence of ACTH excess explains the lack of hyperpigmentation. Excellent with appropriate glucocorticoid replacement and sick-day dosing education; the main danger is unrecognised or under-treated adrenal crisis, and checkpoint-inhibitor-induced deficiency is typically permanent and requires lifelong replacement.

Because it may represent a limited or early form of large-vessel vasculitis, some cases evolve into a recognised systemic disease over time. With surgical repair of the affected segment and appropriate immunosuppression when active inflammation persists, outcomes are generally favourable, but ongoing surveillance is essential because new aneurysms and dissection can develop elsewhere in the aorta.

to the diagnosis Attributing symptoms solely to concurrent medication such as proton-pump inhibitors The gamma-subunit encoded by FXYD2 modulates the activity of the basolateral sodium-potassium ATPase in the distal convoluted tubule, the main site of active transcellular magnesium reabsorption. A dominant-negative variant impairs correct routing or function of the ATPase, reducing the electrochemical gradient that drives apical magnesium entry through TRPM6. The result is defective distal magnesium reabsorption and renal magnesium wasting. As in Gitelman syndrome, reduced distal tubular sodium chloride handling promotes compensatory proximal sodium and calcium reabsorption, producing the associated hypocalciuria. Because the defect is confined to distal magnesium handling, calcium deposition and progressive nephron loss do not occur. The condition is generally benign with a normal life expectancy and preserved renal function; symptoms are controlled with lifelong magnesium supplementation, though complete biochemical correction is often not achievable.

between normosmic disease and Kallmann syndrome Assuming the deficiency is permanent and not reassessing for the possibility of reversal Overlooking neonatal signs (micropenis, cryptorchidism) that offer an early diagnostic clue Not screening for other pituitary deficits before concluding the defect is isolated Isolated GnRH deficiency arises from failure of the hypothalamic GnRH pulse generator, either from deficient GnRH synthesis or secretion or from defective signalling at the pituitary GnRH receptor. Without adequate pulsatile GnRH stimulation, the pituitary secretes insufficient LH and FSH, so the gonads are not driven to produce sex steroids or gametes, resulting in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with absent or arrested puberty. In the normosmic form the olfactory system develops normally, unlike Kallmann syndrome where a shared developmental defect impairs migration of both olfactory and GnRH neurons. Numerous causative genes affect GnRH neuronal function, the kisspeptin and neurokinin B signalling pathways, and receptor activity, and the incomplete penetrance and occasional later reversibility indicate that the defect is one of axis regulation rather than fixed structural loss. Secondary sexual development and, in many cases, fertility can be achieved with appropriate hormonal and gonadotropin therapy; a subset of patients experience reversal of the deficiency, but untreated disease leaves patients hypogonadal with associated bone loss and infertility.

deficiency Neonatal hypoglycaemia, prolonged jaundice, or micropenis suggesting hypopituitarism Rapidly declining growth velocity crossing centiles Features of an intracranial mass such as headache or visual disturbance Evidence of additional pituitary hormone deficiencies Confusing it with growth hormone insensitivity by not measuring IGF-1 and growth hormone together Overlooking additional pituitary deficiencies that need replacement Missing an underlying structural lesion by omitting pituitary imaging Attributing short stature to constitutional delay without adequate testing Not recognising anti-growth-hormone antibodies as a cause of poor response in certain genetic subtypes Isolated growth hormone deficiency arises when the somatotroph axis fails to produce adequate growth hormone while other anterior pituitary functions remain intact. Genetic causes include mutations in the growth hormone gene (GH1) or the growth-hormone-releasing-hormone receptor (GHRHR), and acquired cases follow structural, inflammatory, or idiopathic hypothalamic-pituitary disease. Because growth hormone drives hepatic IGF-1 production and skeletal growth, its deficiency lowers IGF-1 and slows linear growth, and in infancy the loss of growth hormone's counter-regulatory action can cause hypoglycaemia. Unlike growth hormone insensitivity, the receptor and downstream signalling are intact, so exogenous growth hormone restores IGF-1 and promotes growth. With timely growth hormone replacement the growth outlook is good and many children reach a height within the normal range; prognosis worsens when treatment is delayed or when the deficiency is part of broader pituitary disease.

high anion-gap acidosis Status epilepticus from primary epilepsy Capillary and laboratory glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia as a seizure cause Arterial blood gas with lactate and anion-gap assessment neuroimaging if the cause is unclear The classic acute overdose triad is refractory seizures, severe high anion-gap metabolic (lactic) acidosis and coma Seizures typically begin within an hour or two of a significant ingestion and are often resistant to standard anticonvulsants Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is the specific antidote and usually terminates the seizures when benzodiazepines alone fail Suspect isoniazid in any patient being treated for tuberculosis who presents with unexplained seizures and profound acidosis The lactic acidosis is driven largely by seizure activity but also by impaired lactate metabolism, and it may persist until seizures are controlled Benzodiazepines act synergistically with pyridoxine and are the first-line anticonvulsant while pyridoxine is prepared Chronic therapeutic use can cause a separate spectrum of toxicity including peripheral neuropathy (prevented by pyridoxine) and hepatotoxicity If the ingested amount is unknown and seizures are present, empirical pyridoxine is given, with dosing guided by the poisons centre Recurrent or refractory seizures unresponsive to benzodiazepines Severe or persistent high anion-gap lactic acidosis Coma or need for airway protection Rhabdomyolysis or acute kidney injury after prolonged seizure activity Ingestion by a patient on antituberculous therapy with unknown quantity Persisting with standard anticonvulsants without giving pyridoxine Failing to consider isoniazid in tuberculosis patients presenting with seizures Attributing the acidosis solely to seizures and undertreating the underlying cause Not securing sufficient pyridoxine, which may be needed in substantial quantity Overlooking chronic hepatotoxicity and neuropathy in long-term therapeutic users Isoniazid inhibits the enzyme that regenerates the active form of pyridoxine (pyridoxal-5-phosphate) and also complexes directly with pyridoxine, depleting this essential cofactor. Because pyridoxal-5-phosphate is required for synthesis of the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid, its depletion reduces central inhibition and precipitates seizures. Sustained seizure activity, together with impaired conversion of lactate to pyruvate, produces a severe high anion-gap lactic acidosis. Restoring pyridoxine replenishes the cofactor and allows gamma-aminobutyric acid synthesis to resume, which is why it controls the otherwise refractory seizures. With early pyridoxine and benzodiazepines to control seizures and correct the acidosis, most patients recover fully; delayed treatment with prolonged seizures and profound acidosis is associated with significant morbidity and mortality.

Isopropanol poisoning — isopropyl alcohol poisoning, rubbing alcohol ingestion Methanol poisoning Ethylene glycol poisoning Ethanol intoxication Diabetic or alcoholic ketoacidosis Other causes of coma with a raised osmolar gap Serum osmolality and calculation of the osmolar gap Anion gap and blood gas (acidosis characteristically absent) Serum and urine ketones and glucose Isopropanol and acetone levels where available Assessment for gastritis and haemodynamic compromise Isopropanol causes central nervous system depression that is typically deeper and longer than an equivalent amount of ethanol It produces ketosis without a significant metabolic acidosis, because it is metabolised to acetone rather than to an organic acid There is a raised osmolar gap but characteristically a normal anion gap, distinguishing it from methanol and ethylene glycol Acetone on the breath and ketonaemia with a near-normal glucose are useful clues Gastritis with haematemesis and hypotension can occur after large ingestions Management is largely supportive, with haemodialysis reserved for severe or refractory cases Deep coma or airway compromise Hypotension or gastrointestinal bleeding after large ingestion A significant metabolic acidosis, which should prompt reconsideration of methanol or ethylene glycol Co-ingestion of other toxic alcohols Assuming a high-anion-gap acidosis and misclassifying it as methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning Overlooking the deep, prolonged sedation and airway risk Attributing ketosis solely to diabetes Failing to reconsider the diagnosis if acidosis develops Isopropanol is absorbed rapidly and metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to acetone. Both the parent alcohol and acetone are central nervous system depressants, accounting for the prominent and prolonged sedation. Because acetone is a ketone rather than an organic acid, the result is ketosis with a raised osmolar gap but without the severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis seen with methanol and ethylene glycol. Direct mucosal irritation causes the associated haemorrhagic gastritis. With supportive care most patients recover fully; serious outcomes relate to profound central nervous system depression, aspiration, haemorrhagic gastritis or very large ingestions.

acidosis, ketosis, hyperammonaemia, hypoglycaemia and cytopenias such as neutropenia and thrombocytopenia Elevated isovalerylcarnitine (C5) on acylcarnitine profile and isovalerylglycine in urine confirm the diagnosis Management principles are leucine (protein) restriction, and conjugation of the toxic metabolite using glycine and carnitine supplementation to enhance excretion, plus aggressive treatment of catabolism Readily identified on newborn screening through elevated C5 acylcarnitine, allowing pre-symptomatic treatment Acute metabolic decompensation with severe acidosis and encephalopathy is an emergency Hyperammonaemia contributing to altered consciousness during crises Sepsis-like collapse in a neonate that is actually metabolic decompensation Severe neutropenia with risk of overwhelming infection during acute illness Missing the diagnostic sweaty-feet odour or attributing the presentation to sepsis Neglecting glycine and carnitine conjugation therapy that enhances detoxification Under-treating catabolic stress during intercurrent illness Overlooking neutropenia and infection risk during acute crises Isovaleric acidemia is an autosomal recessive defect of isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase, an enzyme of the leucine degradation pathway. Deficiency causes isovaleryl-CoA and its derivatives (isovaleric acid, isovalerylglycine, isovalerylcarnitine and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid) to accumulate. Isovaleric acid is responsible for the characteristic odour and, together with the other metabolites, produces metabolic acidosis and is toxic to the central nervous system and bone marrow. Accumulated organic acids also secondarily impair the urea cycle, contributing to hyperammonaemia. Conjugation of isovaleryl-CoA with glycine and carnitine forms non-toxic, readily excreted products, which is exploited therapeutically. With newborn screening and early treatment many patients have a favourable outcome and normal development; the chronic intermittent form is often milder, but untreated acute neonatal disease can be fatal or cause neurological damage, and outcome depends on preventing and promptly treating decompensations.

Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) — CBC + film (isolated thrombocytopenia) Exclude secondary causes Major bleeding / very low platelets need urgent treatment Drug-induced thrombocytopenia (e.g., quinine, sulfonamides, vancomycin; classic drug-dependent antibodies react with platelet antigens only when drug is present) (p.922-923) Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) - associated with thrombosis rather than bleeding, nadir rarely <20,000/uL; use 4T scoring (p.923) Congenital/inherited thrombocytopenia (e.g., autosomal dominant macrothrombocytopenia) (p.922, p.965 algorithm) Pseudothrombocytopenia from platelet clumping (EDTA-dependent) - redraw in sodium citrate or heparin (p.922, p.965 algorithm) Evans syndrome - combined autoimmune hemolytic anemia with ITP (perform direct antiglobulin/Coombs test if anemia present) (p.924) HIV infection - can cause immune thrombocytopenia early; late HIV causes pancytopenia with decreased/dysplastic platelet production (p.922) Hepatitis C virus infection - recognized cause of secondary ITP (p.924) Infectious mononucleosis - immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (p.922) Systemic infection with gram-negative bacteria or COVID-19 - thrombocytopenia that may be associated with DIC (p.922) Helicobacter pylori - association with ITP is unclear but appears to have a geographic distribution (p.924) CBC with peripheral blood smear review to confirm isolated thrombocytopenia and exclude clumping/schistocytes (p.922, p.924) HIV and hepatitis C testing to evaluate for secondary ITP (p.924) Serologic testing for SLE (p.924) Serum protein electrophoresis and immunoglobulin levels (to detect hypogammaglobulinemia or monoclonal gammopathy) (p.924) Selective testing for IgA deficiency (p.924) H. pylori testing depending on clinical circumstance (p.924) Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test if anemia present, to detect Evans syndrome (p.924) Bone marrow examination reserved for patients with unexplained additional findings or failure to respond to initial therapy (p.924) Microangiopathic hemolytic anemias (TTP, DIC) - distinguished by schistocytes/fragmented red cells on smear (p.922, p.965 algorithm) Hypersplenism/splenomegaly (e.g., chronic liver disease) causing platelet sequestration (p.922) Bone marrow production failure - low platelet count with absence of large young platelets on smear (p.916, p.922) ITP is an acquired disorder of immune-mediated platelet destruction, with possible additional inhibition of platelet release from megakaryocytes (p.924). In children ITP is usually acute, often follows an infection, and is self-limited; in adults it tends to be chronic, though some adults remit spontaneously within months of diagnosis (p.924). It is largely a diagnosis of exclusion: characterized by mucocutaneous bleeding and a low (often very low) platelet count with otherwise normal peripheral blood cells and smear (p.924). Presentation is either with ecchymoses/petechiae or with thrombocytopenia found incidentally on a routine CBC (p.924). Mucocutaneous bleeding may include oral mucosal, gastrointestinal, or heavy menstrual bleeding; rarely life-threatening (including CNS) bleeding occurs (p.924). Wet purpura (blood blisters in the mouth) and retinal hemorrhages may herald life-threatening bleeding (p.924, p.922). Petechiae are pinpoint, nonblanching hemorrhages that signal decreased platelet number rather than platelet dysfunction, and first appear in dependent areas of increased venous pressure (ankles/feet in an ambulatory patient) (p.922). Serologic (antiplatelet antibody) testing is generally not helpful because of low sensitivity and specificity of current tests (p.924). The peripheral smear may show large platelets with otherwise normal morphology, reflecting young/rapidly turned-over platelets (p.924, p.916). Wet purpura (oral blood blisters) - may herald life-threatening bleeding (p.924, p.922) Retinal hemorrhages - may herald life-threatening bleeding (p.924) Active mucosal, GI, or CNS bleeding (p.924) Very severe thrombocytopenia (<5000/uL) or signs of impending bleeding (p.924) Treating presumed ITP without excluding secondary causes (HIV, HCV, SLE, drugs) (p.924). Relying on antiplatelet antibody serology - low sensitivity/specificity makes it unhelpful for diagnosis (p.924). Missing pseudothrombocytopenia from EDTA-induced platelet clumping, which produces a falsely low automated count; confirm on smear and redraw in citrate/heparin (p.922, p.916). Overlooking Evans syndrome - failing to do a Coombs test when anemia accompanies thrombocytopenia (p.924). Failing to take a careful drug/herbal/OTC history, since drugs are the most common cause of thrombocytopenia (p.922). ITP results from immune-mediated destruction of antibody-coated platelets by the reticuloendothelial system, and possibly impaired platelet release from megakaryocytes. Primary ITP has no identifiable cause; secondary ITP is associated with an underlying disorder such as autoimmune disease (notably SLE) or infection (HIV, hepatitis C). Childhood ITP commonly follows a viral infection through immune mechanisms and usually resolves spontaneously (Harrison 22e p.922, p.924). Childhood ITP is usually acute and almost always resolves spontaneously. Adult ITP is more often chronic, though some adults remit spontaneously within months. Patients with platelet counts >30,000/uL appear not to have increased mortality related to the thrombocytopenia, so diagnosis does not mandate treatment (Harrison 22e p.924). Harrison does not give a formal grading scale. Practical thresholds noted: platelet counts >30,000/uL are not associated with increased mortality; ~5000-10,000/uL is the level needed to maintain microvascular integrity; severe thrombocytopenia is cited as <5000/uL for treatment-decision purposes (Harrison 22e p.922, p.924).

to exclude ischaemic chest pain Functional lumen imaging or reflux monitoring in selected cases Presents with dysphagia and non-cardiac chest pain, often with a sensation of food sticking peroral endoscopic myotomy considered in selected refractory cases The finding may be an incidental manometric pattern in some patients with few symptoms Chest pain indistinguishable from cardiac ischaemia Progressive dysphagia or weight loss suggesting obstruction or malignancy Food impaction requiring urgent endoscopy Coexisting outflow obstruction that changes management Treating the manometric label rather than correlating with symptoms Overlooking oesophagogastric junction outflow obstruction driving the hypercontractility Confusing it with distal spasm, which has abnormal contraction timing rather than excessive vigour Attributing chest pain to the oesophagus before excluding cardiac disease Jackhammer oesophagus is a hypercontractile motility disorder in which the smooth-muscle segment of the oesophagus generates abnormally forceful, high-amplitude, and often repetitive contractions. The mechanism is incompletely understood but is thought to involve excessive cholinergic drive and altered inhibitory neural control, sometimes as a compensatory response to distal outflow resistance at the oesophagogastric junction. The exaggerated contractile force is captured on high-resolution manometry as a very high distal contractile integral and correlates with episodes of chest pain and dysphagia. The natural history is variable; many patients respond to pharmacological and neuromodulatory therapy, while a subset have persistent symptoms, and a minority evolve towards a spastic achalasia phenotype.

jackhammer oesophagus — hypercontractile oesophagus, hypercontractile peristalsis distal (diffuse) oesophageal spasm type III (spastic) achalasia oesophagogastric junction outflow obstruction gastro-oesophageal reflux disease cardiac ischaemic chest pain functional chest pain and oesophageal hypersensitivity eosinophilic oesophagitis high-resolution oesophageal manometry with distal contractile integral quantification upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to exclude mucosal, structural and obstructing lesions timed barium oesophagram to assess emptying and outflow functional lumen imaging probe (FLIP) to evaluate oesophagogastric junction distensibility ambulatory pH-impedance monitoring for reflux cardiac evaluation to exclude ischaemia provocative testing (multiple rapid swallows, solid test meal) during manometry Defined on high-resolution manometry (Chicago Classification) by at least two swallows with markedly elevated distal contractile integral above the hypercontractile threshold, with preserved peristaltic sequence. The exaggerated contractions may involve repetitive or multi-peaked waves and can include vigorous contraction of the lower oesophageal sphincter, distinguishing it from diffuse spasm where contractions are premature rather than merely vigorous. Chest pain and dysphagia are the dominant complaints; a proportion of patients are minimally symptomatic and the manometric finding is incidental. Always exclude obstruction at the oesophagogastric junction, as outflow resistance (including early achalasia or a tight fundoplication) can provoke a compensatory hypercontractile pattern. Coexisting gastro-oesophageal reflux and oesophageal hypersensitivity are common and should be actively assessed and treated. Smooth-muscle relaxants and neuromodulators (tricyclics, other visceral analgesics) form first-line therapy; peppermint oil may reduce contractile vigour. Endoscopic botulinum toxin injection can give temporary relief, and peroral endoscopic myotomy is reserved for refractory, clearly symptom-correlated disease. The diagnosis carries prognostic uncertainty because some patients progress to spastic achalasia, so follow-up manometry may be warranted if symptoms evolve. progressive dysphagia or weight loss suggesting evolving achalasia or mechanical obstruction chest pain requiring urgent exclusion of acute coronary syndrome food bolus impaction or inability to manage secretions manometric evidence of impaired oesophagogastric junction relaxation indicating an obstructive process rapid symptom progression in an older patient raising concern for malignant pseudo-obstruction Diagnosing jackhammer oesophagus without excluding oesophagogastric junction outflow obstruction that can secondarily drive hypercontractility. Assuming that severe manometric findings mandate invasive therapy in a patient who is minimally symptomatic. Overlooking coexistent reflux and hypersensitivity as treatable contributors to chest pain. Failing to repeat manometry when symptoms evolve, thereby missing progression to spastic achalasia. Attributing chest pain to the manometric abnormality before cardiac disease has been excluded. Jackhammer oesophagus is a hypercontractile disorder of the oesophageal smooth-muscle segment defined by excessively vigorous peristaltic contractions, quantified by an abnormally high distal contractile integral. The peristaltic sequence remains intact, distinguishing it from the premature contractions of distal spasm. The underlying mechanism is thought to involve an imbalance favouring excitatory cholinergic drive over inhibitory nitrergic input to the oesophageal musculature, sometimes compounded by asynchronous or prolonged contraction of the longitudinal and circular muscle layers and hypertrophy of the muscularis. In a subset, hypercontractility is a secondary or compensatory response to distal outflow obstruction at the oesophagogastric junction. Oesophageal hypersensitivity contributes substantially to symptom generation, which explains the frequent dissociation between manometric severity and clinical severity. Outcomes are variable and often benign, with many patients stable or improving on medical therapy and neuromodulation; symptom severity correlates poorly with manometric findings. A minority progress to spastic achalasia or have refractory symptoms, and response to myotomy is less predictable than in classic achalasia.

It is a contiguous-gene disorder in which haploinsufficiency of multiple dosage-sensitive genes produces the multisystem phenotype. Loss of FLI1, a transcription factor required for normal megakaryocyte and platelet development, underlies the Paris-Trousseau thrombocytopenia, while loss of other genes contributes to the cardiac, craniofacial and neurodevelopmental features. Larger deletions tend to be associated with more extensive involvement. Outlook is largely determined by the severity of the congenital heart disease and the bleeding tendency, both of which are important early causes of morbidity; the thrombocytopenia persists lifelong and requires bleeding precautions, particularly around surgery. With cardiac correction and appropriate developmental support, many children survive into adulthood with variable intellectual disability.

metaphyseal chondrodysplasia results from dominant activating variants in PTH1R, which encodes the receptor shared by parathyroid hormone and PTH-related peptide. Constitutive, ligand-independent receptor signalling mimics persistent PTH and PTHrP action. In the growth plate, PTHrP signalling normally delays chondrocyte hypertrophy; its unregulated activation disrupts the orderly transition of proliferating to hypertrophic chondrocytes, producing the disorganised, expanded metaphyses. A severe dysplasia with marked short stature and deformity; the biochemical calcium disturbance may cause nephrocalcinosis and renal complications over time, but the metaphyseal changes tend to remodel toward maturity. Multidisciplinary metabolic and orthopaedic care is required.
