care is supportive, centred on seizure control, airway protection and management of raised intracranial pressure A safe and effective vaccine exists and is incorporated into immunisation programmes in endemic Indian districts, making prevention the cornerstone of control MRI often shows characteristic bilateral thalamic lesions, sometimes with haemorrhage, which supports the diagnosis Confirmation relies on detecting JEV-specific IgM in cerebrospinal fluid or serum by capture ELISA Rapidly declining consciousness or coma indicating severe encephalitis and need for critical care Status epilepticus or repeated seizures Signs of raised intracranial pressure or brainstem involvement (abnormal breathing, pupillary changes) Progressive respiratory compromise requiring airway protection and ventilation Attributing acute encephalitis syndrome to JE without confirmatory serology and missing treatable causes such as herpes encephalitis Overlooking the diagnosis outside the classic transmission season or in adults in newly endemic areas Failing to protect the airway and control seizures early in a deteriorating patient Neglecting vaccination and vector-control opportunities in endemic districts Japanese encephalitis virus is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus maintained in an enzootic cycle between Culex mosquitoes and amplifying vertebrate hosts, chiefly pigs and water birds. Humans are incidental dead-end hosts. Following a mosquito bite the virus replicates locally and in regional lymph nodes, producing a viraemia that may seed the central nervous system across the blood-brain barrier. Neuronal infection and the accompanying inflammatory response cause neuronal death particularly in the thalamus, basal ganglia, brainstem and cerebral cortex, accounting for the movement disorders and depressed consciousness seen clinically. Symptomatic encephalitis carries substantial mortality, and a large proportion of survivors are left with lasting neurological or psychiatric sequelae including motor deficits, movement disorders, cognitive impairment and epilepsy. Outcome is worse at the extremes of age and with delayed presentation.

Once detached, the tendon retracts proximally to a degree determined by whether its vincular blood supply and the fibro-osseous pulleys remain attached; greater retraction jeopardises the tendon's nutrition and complicates repair. Early surgical repair or reattachment generally restores good function, but delayed diagnosis, significant retraction or chronic injury can necessitate more complex reconstruction with poorer outcomes.

Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome — JLNS, KCNQ1, KCNE1, cardio-auditory syndrome, congenital deafness with long QT Romano-Ward long QT syndrome without deafness Acquired QT prolongation from drugs or electrolyte disturbance Seizure disorder or epilepsy misattributed to a primary neurological cause Vasovagal or reflex syncope Other syndromic congenital sensorineural hearing loss Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and other inherited arrhythmias Twelve-lead ECG with corrected QT measurement, the key diagnostic test Audiometry including auditory brainstem response to confirm profound hearing loss Ambulatory ECG and exercise testing to capture arrhythmia and QT behaviour Serum electrolytes to exclude reversible causes of QT prolongation Molecular genetic testing of KCNQ1 and KCNE1 and cascade screening of relatives Combines profound congenital sensorineural hearing loss with a markedly prolonged QT interval on the ECG Caused by biallelic mutations in KCNQ1 (or less often KCNE1), which encode subunits of a potassium channel; inheritance is autosomal recessive The same channel is needed for endolymph production in the inner ear and for cardiac repolarisation, explaining the combined phenotype Presents with syncope, seizures or sudden collapse triggered by exertion, emotion or startle, reflecting torsades de pointes Any deaf child with unexplained syncope, seizures or a family history of sudden death must have an ECG to look for QT prolongation Heterozygous carriers may have isolated long QT (Romano-Ward pattern) without deafness Cardiac risk is high and untreated patients face a substantial risk of sudden cardiac death, so cardiology referral is urgent Syncope, seizures or cardiac arrest, particularly during exertion, emotion or sudden noise Family history of sudden unexplained death or long QT syndrome Documented torsades de pointes or very prolonged corrected QT interval Exposure to QT-prolonging medications that could precipitate arrhythmia Not performing an ECG in a deaf child with syncope or seizures and missing the cardiac diagnosis Misdiagnosing arrhythmic collapse as epilepsy and delaying cardiac treatment Prescribing QT-prolonging medications, which can precipitate fatal arrhythmia Overlooking the recessive inheritance and failing to screen at-risk relatives Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in KCNQ1 or KCNE1, subunits forming the slow delayed-rectifier potassium current channel. In the stria vascularis of the inner ear this current is essential for secreting potassium-rich endolymph; its loss disrupts the endocochlear potential and causes profound congenital sensorineural deafness. In cardiac myocytes the same current contributes to repolarisation, so its loss prolongs the action potential and the QT interval, predisposing to torsades de pointes ventricular arrhythmia, syncope and sudden death. The recessive combined phenotype requires two defective alleles, whereas single-allele defects tend to cause isolated long QT syndrome. Untreated the syndrome carries a high risk of sudden cardiac death from malignant arrhythmia, but prognosis improves substantially with beta-blockade, avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs, and consideration of an implantable defibrillator, alongside hearing rehabilitation for the profound deafness.

underlying sleep disorder Overusing alcohol or hypnotics, which can fragment sleep and delay adaptation Jet lag disorder results from a temporary mismatch between the endogenous circadian clock, Because the clock naturally runs slightly longer than a day, delaying it (westward travel) is usually easier than advancing it (eastward travel). Jet lag is self-limiting and resolves as the circadian clock entrains to the new time zone, typically over several days depending on the number of time zones crossed and direction of travel; well-timed light and melatonin can shorten the adjustment.

central to signalling downstream of numerous cytokines. Many patients survive into adulthood with consistent prophylaxis and prompt treatment of infections, but chronic lung damage, fungal superinfection of pneumatoceles, and vascular aneurysms are important sources of long-term morbidity and can be life-threatening.

Johanson-Blizzard syndrome is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in UBR1, which encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase of the N-end rule pathway that targets specific proteins for degradation by the proteasome. Loss of UBR1 function disturbs regulated protein turnover, and the acinar cells of the exocrine pancreas are especially vulnerable, undergoing destruction and fatty or fibrotic replacement that produces early and severe exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. The same developmental disturbance affects craniofacial, ectodermal, endocrine and other structures, giving the hypoplastic nasal alae, aplasia cutis of the scalp, hearing loss, hypothyroidism, dental and genitourinary anomalies and variable developmental delay. Management is supportive, centred on enzyme replacement, nutrition and treatment of the associated endocrine and sensory deficits. With early pancreatic enzyme replacement, nutritional support and treatment of hypothyroidism and hearing loss, growth and development can improve; long-term outcome depends on the severity of malabsorption, endocrine involvement and any associated malformations and developmental impairment.

suggesting failure of union Confusing a proximal tuberosity avulsion (pseudo-Jones) with a true Jones fracture Permitting early weight-bearing that promotes non-union Failing to recognise chronic stress-fracture features on radiographs Not counselling athletes about the option and benefits of early fixation The proximal fifth metatarsal has a zonal blood supply, and the metaphyseal-diaphyseal Fractures in this relatively poorly perfused region heal slowly and are prone to delayed and non-union, in contrast to the well-vascularised tuberosity where avulsion fractures unite readily. Tensile and bending forces transmitted through the lateral border of the foot during adduction or inversion, or accumulated microdamage from repetitive loading, exceed the bone's capacity to remodel, producing an acute fracture or a chronic stress fracture. True zone 2 Jones fractures have notable rates of delayed and non-union owing to their watershed blood supply, whereas proximal tuberosity avulsions generally heal uneventfully; surgical fixation improves and speeds union in high-demand patients.

more than thirty causative genes encode proteins of the primary cilium and basal body Because it is a ciliopathy, extra-neurological involvement is common and defines subtypes, including retinal dystrophy, nephronophthisis or cystic renal disease, hepatic fibrosis, and polydactyly The CEP290 and NPHP1 genotypes carry higher risk of renal disease, while TMEM67 is associated with hepatic fibrosis, guiding organ-directed surveillance Cognitive outcome is variable and many children have moderate impairment, so early developmental support and multidisciplinary follow-up are important Prenatal suspicion may arise from vermian abnormality on foetal imaging, and diagnosis is confirmed by the molar tooth sign on postnatal MRI plus molecular testing Neonatal apnoea and irregular breathing requiring respiratory monitoring Progressive renal impairment from nephronophthisis leading to end-stage kidney disease Deteriorating vision from retinal dystrophy Signs of portal hypertension or hepatic decompensation from fibrosis Attributing neonatal apnoea and hypotonia to birth asphyxia and missing the underlying malformation Failing to recognise the molar tooth sign on suboptimal or non-dedicated posterior fossa imaging Not screening for renal, hepatic, and retinal disease that may present years after the neurological diagnosis Assuming a uniform prognosis despite wide genotype and phenotype variability Joubert syndrome is a disorder of the primary cilium and basal body (a ciliopathy). Pathogenic variants in genes encoding ciliary transition-zone and axonemal proteins disrupt ciliary signalling that guides mid-hindbrain patterning and axonal decussation. The resulting failure of cerebellar vermis development and abnormal crossing of superior cerebellar peduncle and corticospinal fibres produce the characteristic mid-hindbrain malformation seen as the molar tooth sign. The same ciliary dysfunction in the retina, renal tubule, and biliary tract accounts for the frequently associated multi-organ features. Prognosis depends on the degree of neurological impairment and the extent of renal, hepatic, and retinal involvement. Many individuals survive into adulthood with variable cognitive and motor disability, but progressive kidney or liver disease can substantially affect life expectancy.

junctional ectopic tachycardia — JET, His bundle tachycardia atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia focal atrial tachycardia ectopic atrial tachycardia in infancy accelerated junctional rhythm ventricular tachycardia with narrow QRS twelve-lead ECG and rhythm strip seeking atrioventricular dissociation with ventricular rate exceeding atrial rate atrial electrogram recording via temporary epicardial wires in the postoperative patient continuous telemetry to monitor rate, dissociation and haemodynamic effect serum electrolytes including potassium, magnesium and calcium core temperature monitoring in the postoperative period echocardiography to assess ventricular function and structural substrate JET is a narrow-complex tachycardia arising from enhanced automaticity of the atrioventricular junction or proximal His bundle, characteristically with atrioventricular dissociation and a ventricular rate exceeding the atrial rate. The postoperative form is a feared complication of paediatric cardiac surgery, especially repairs near the atrioventricular node such as ventricular septal defect and tetralogy of Fallot correction. A rarer congenital form presents in infancy, is often incessant and can lead to tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy and carries a familial tendency. The QRS is usually narrow and identical to sinus conduction unless rate-related aberrancy or pre-existing bundle branch block is present. Retrograde ventriculoatrial conduction may occasionally produce 1 to 1 association, mimicking other supraventricular tachycardias and obscuring the diagnosis. Cornerstones of postoperative management include avoiding hyperthermia, minimising catecholamines, correcting electrolytes and inducing mild hypothermia. Because the mechanism is abnormal automaticity, direct-current cardioversion is ineffective, though atrial pacing faster than the junctional rate can restore atrioventricular synchrony. Loss of the atrial contribution to ventricular filling makes JET poorly tolerated in the vulnerable early postoperative period. haemodynamic deterioration in the early postoperative period from loss of atrioventricular synchrony incessant tachycardia leading to tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy in infants very high junctional rates unresponsive to first-line measures escalating inotrope and catecholamine requirement aggravating the arrhythmia signs of low cardiac output syndrome after congenital heart surgery Attempting direct-current cardioversion for an automatic rhythm that will not respond. Failing to recognise atrioventricular dissociation and misclassifying JET as another supraventricular tachycardia. Aggravating the arrhythmia with escalating catecholamines and permissive hyperthermia in the postoperative child. Overlooking retrograde 1 to 1 conduction that masks the diagnosis. Neglecting electrolyte correction and temperature control as primary therapeutic levers. JET is caused by abnormal enhanced automaticity of tissue in the atrioventricular junction or proximal His bundle, which discharges more rapidly than the sinus node and drives the ventricles independently, producing atrioventricular dissociation with a faster ventricular than atrial rate. In the postoperative setting, mechanical trauma, oedema, suture lines and stretch near the conduction system combine with high circulating catecholamines, hyperthermia and electrolyte shifts to provoke this automatic focus. The congenital form reflects an intrinsic abnormality of junctional automaticity presenting in early life. Because activation originates at or below the node, ventricular depolarisation follows the normal His-Purkinje route and the QRS remains narrow unless conduction is otherwise disturbed. Postoperative JET is usually transient and resolves within a few days with supportive measures, though it increases perioperative morbidity. The congenital form is more difficult to control and, if incessant, may cause cardiomyopathy, but responsiveness to modern rhythm control and ablation has improved outcomes.

management is supportive with wound care and nutritional support Airway involvement with stridor or respiratory compromise from laryngeal granulation tissue Extensive skin loss with sepsis, fluid, and electrolyte disturbance in a neonate Failure to thrive and severe anaemia from chronic wounds and poor intake Rapid deterioration in the severe generalised subtype, which carries high infant mortality Failing to identify the severe generalised subtype early, delaying appropriate supportive and palliative planning Overlooking airway involvement heralded by perioral and perinasal granulation tissue Neglecting nutritional support, dental care, and anaemia management Mistaking neonatal junctional disease for infection Assuming a uniform prognosis rather than recognising the wide spectrum of severity The dermo-epidermal junction is held together by hemidesmosomes and their associated anchoring filaments, which span the lamina lucida of the basement membrane and connect basal keratinocytes to the underlying lamina densa. Laminin-332 and collagen XVII (the bullous pemphigoid antigen 180) are key structural components of this adhesion complex. In junctional epidermolysis bullosa, biallelic mutations reduce or abolish these proteins, weakening adhesion so that the skin separates within the lamina lucida under minimal mechanical stress. The same proteins are important in mucosal epithelia and in tooth enamel formation, which explains the mucosal involvement and enamel defects. The most severe subtypes cause extensive skin and mucosal loss with a high risk of infection, fluid loss, and airway compromise in infancy. Outlook varies markedly by subtype: the severe generalised form carries high mortality in infancy from sepsis, respiratory involvement, and failure to thrive, whereas milder junctional variants are compatible with survival into adulthood with chronic blistering and extracutaneous complications.

inflammatory bowel disease Juvenile ankylosing spondylitis is an axial spondyloarthritis in which HLA-B27-associated immune dysregulation, with prominent involvement of the interleukin-23/interleukin-17 pathway, drives inflammation at entheses, sacroiliac joints and the spine. Enthesitis and osteitis are followed by reparative new bone formation, which over time can produce syndesmophytes, joint fusion and progressive loss of spinal and sacroiliac mobility. Because the skeleton is still growing, hip and axial involvement in childhood can have particularly significant functional and structural consequences. Juvenile-onset disease tends to have more peripheral and hip involvement than adult-onset ankylosing spondylitis and can progress to significant axial disease and disability over years. Early diagnosis, physiotherapy and TNF inhibition improve symptom control and may limit structural progression.

Juvenile Dermatomyositis — JDM, juvenile dermatomyositis Muscular dystrophy Systemic lupus erythematosus / overlap connective tissue disease Viral or post-viral myositis Polymyositis Hypothyroid or metabolic myopathy Spinal muscular atrophy or other neuromuscular disorders Serum muscle enzymes (creatine kinase, aldolase, LDH, transaminases) MRI of muscle to identify inflammation and guide biopsy site Nailfold capillaroscopy Myositis-specific and myositis-associated autoantibodies Muscle biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain Electromyography in selected cases The most common inflammatory myopathy of childhood, characterised by proximal muscle weakness together with distinctive skin changes. Look for the heliotrope rash (violaceous discolouration of the upper eyelids) and Gottron papules over the knuckles, elbows, and knees. Weakness is typically symmetrical and proximal, so children struggle to climb stairs, rise from the floor, or lift their arms overhead. Nailfold capillary changes (dilated, dropout, or tortuous loops) are a useful bedside clue and correlate with disease activity. Calcinosis of skin and soft tissues is a late complication, more likely when treatment is delayed or inadequate. Unlike adult dermatomyositis, an underlying malignancy is rarely associated in children. A small vessel vasculopathy can affect the gastrointestinal tract, potentially causing ulceration, bleeding, or perforation. Early diagnosis and adequate immunosuppression improve outcomes and reduce the risk of chronic disability and calcinosis. Severe dysphagia or nasal regurgitation indicating pharyngeal muscle involvement with aspiration risk Respiratory muscle weakness or interstitial lung disease causing hypoventilation Gastrointestinal vasculopathy with abdominal pain, bleeding, or perforation Rapidly progressive weakness or inability to protect the airway Extensive skin ulceration reflecting severe vasculopathy Attributing subtle proximal weakness to clumsiness or normal fatigue and delaying diagnosis Assuming normal muscle enzymes exclude the disease, as they can be near-normal in some children Under-treating early disease and thereby increasing the risk of calcinosis Overlooking dysphagia and aspiration risk when pharyngeal muscles are involved Juvenile dermatomyositis is an immune-mediated systemic vasculopathy affecting small vessels of skeletal muscle, skin, and other organs. Complement-mediated injury to the capillary endothelium leads to capillary dropout, ischaemia, and perifascicular muscle fibre atrophy. Interferon-driven inflammation and immune complex deposition contribute to ongoing muscle and skin damage, producing the characteristic weakness and rash. With prompt, adequate immunosuppression many children achieve remission and regain function; delayed or insufficient treatment increases the risk of chronic disease, calcinosis, and long-term disability. A monocyclic course carries the best prognosis.

Juvenile fibroadenoma — Cellular fibroadenoma, Giant juvenile fibroadenoma Benign phyllodes tumour Ordinary adult fibroadenoma Pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia forming a mass Virginal (juvenile) breast hypertrophy Breast hamartoma Tubular or lactating adenoma Secretory carcinoma (rare in adolescents) Clinical breast examination with documentation of size and asymmetry Breast ultrasound as first-line imaging in adolescents Core needle biopsy to characterise the fibroepithelial lesion Histology assessing stromal cellularity, atypia and architecture MRI in very large lesions to plan excision Follow-up imaging to confirm stability or excision completeness Multidisciplinary review if phyllodes tumour cannot be excluded A variant of fibroadenoma occurring predominantly in adolescents and young women, characterised by increased stromal cellularity and epithelial hyperplasia. Tends to grow more rapidly and reach a larger size than the common adult fibroadenoma; large lesions are termed giant juvenile fibroadenoma. Presents as a firm, mobile, painless mass that may cause obvious breast asymmetry, skin stretching and dilated overlying veins. Rapid growth can compress and displace surrounding normal breast tissue rather than invading it. Ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice in this young age group, showing a well-defined solid mass. The principal differential on core biopsy is a benign phyllodes tumour, which juvenile fibroadenoma can closely resemble. Treatment is enucleation or excision, preserving the developing breast and nipple where possible; the outlook is excellent. Despite alarming size and rapid growth, it is entirely benign with negligible malignant potential. Very rapid enlargement with skin compromise or ulceration Histological features raising the possibility of a phyllodes tumour Stromal overgrowth or mitotic activity on biopsy Recurrence after excision Skin changes or fixity atypical for a benign lesion Misclassifying a benign phyllodes tumour as juvenile fibroadenoma on limited biopsy Delaying excision of a large lesion and allowing further distortion of the developing breast Performing overly aggressive surgery that damages the breast bud or nipple in an adolescent Confusing the lesion with virginal breast hypertrophy Assuming rapid growth implies malignancy and causing unnecessary alarm Juvenile fibroadenoma is a benign biphasic fibroepithelial tumour arising from the hormone-responsive stroma of the terminal duct lobular unit, most likely reflecting an exaggerated proliferative response to the hormonal milieu of adolescence. It differs from the ordinary adult fibroadenoma in its greater stromal cellularity and its pericanalicular growth pattern with florid, sometimes gynaecomastoid, epithelial hyperplasia. This heightened cellular activity drives the characteristic rapid enlargement and large size, yet the stroma lacks the atypia, mitotic activity, leaf-like architecture and overgrowth that define a phyllodes tumour, so the lesion remains benign. Juvenile fibroadenoma is benign with an excellent prognosis after complete excision, and malignant transformation is not a feature. Recurrence is uncommon, though further fibroadenomas may develop elsewhere in the breast over time.

Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis — JIA, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile chronic arthritis Septic arthritis and osteomyelitis Reactive and post-infectious arthritis (including acute rheumatic fever) Leukaemia and other malignancy presenting with bone or joint pain Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue diseases Inflammatory bowel disease-associated arthritis Non-inflammatory causes such as trauma, hypermobility, and benign limb pains Full blood count, ESR, and C-reactive protein Antinuclear antibody (informs uveitis risk) and rheumatoid factor HLA-B27 in suspected enthesitis-related arthritis Slit-lamp ophthalmological examination for uveitis screening Joint imaging (ultrasound or MRI) to assess synovitis and effusion Ferritin, triglycerides, and fibrinogen if macrophage activation syndrome is suspected The most common chronic rheumatic disease of childhood, defined by arthritis beginning before 16 years of age and persisting for at least 6 weeks, with other causes excluded. It is a heterogeneous group of subtypes, including oligoarticular, polyarticular, systemic, enthesitis-related, and psoriatic forms, each with distinct features and prognosis. Arthritis presents with joint swelling, morning stiffness or gelling, and limited movement, often with less pain than expected; young children may present with limp or refusal to use a limb. Oligoarticular JIA is the most common subtype, typically affecting large joints in young girls and carrying a significant risk of chronic anterior uveitis. Uveitis is frequently asymptomatic, so regular ophthalmological slit-lamp screening is essential to prevent visual loss, particularly in young ANA-positive children. Systemic JIA features prominent extra-articular disease with quotidian high fever, an evanescent salmon-coloured rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and serositis. The diagnosis is clinical and one of exclusion; laboratory tests support rather than confirm it, and inflammatory markers may be normal in oligoarticular disease. A serious complication of systemic JIA is macrophage activation syndrome, a form of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis that can be rapidly fatal. Management principles combine anti-inflammatory therapy, disease-modifying agents, and increasingly biologic therapy, alongside physiotherapy to preserve joint function and growth. Features of macrophage activation syndrome (persistent fever, falling cell counts, very high ferritin, hepatic dysfunction) Findings suggesting malignancy such as severe night pain, cytopenias, or systemic decline A hot, acutely swollen joint with fever suggesting septic arthritis Visual symptoms or complications of uveitis Systemic features such as high spiking fever with serositis Missing asymptomatic uveitis by omitting scheduled slit-lamp screening Overlooking leukaemia in a child with bone pain and abnormal counts before starting steroids Failing to recognise early macrophage activation syndrome in systemic JIA Attributing a single hot joint to JIA and missing septic arthritis JIA results from immune dysregulation leading to chronic inflammation of the synovium. In most subtypes, an aberrant adaptive immune response with T-cell activation and autoantibody production drives synovial proliferation (pannus), which can erode cartilage and bone and disturb the growth of nearby physes. Systemic JIA is instead an autoinflammatory condition driven predominantly by the innate immune system and proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1 and interleukin-6, accounting for its prominent systemic features and its predisposition to macrophage activation syndrome. Outcome varies by subtype; many children with oligoarticular disease do well, while polyarticular and systemic forms may follow a more persistent course, and modern therapy has substantially improved remission rates and reduced long-term joint damage. Uveitis and macrophage activation syndrome remain important causes of morbidity.

the skin and deeper tissues. Early inflammation with lymphocytic infiltration and endothelial activation is followed by fibroblast activation and excessive deposition of collagen and extracellular matrix, producing progressive sclerosis. In linear and en coup de sabre forms the fibrotic process can extend into fascia, muscle, bone and, on the face, adjacent structures, so that involvement over a growing limb or the developing face leads to atrophy, contracture and growth disturbance rather than the internal organ fibrosis seen in systemic sclerosis. Early immunosuppression during the active phase improves outcomes and reduces long-term morbidity.

Juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia — JMML Infection causing reactive monocytosis/hepatosplenomegaly (for example viral) Other myeloproliferative or myelodysplastic disorders Noonan-syndrome-associated myeloproliferative disorder (often transient) Infantile leukaemoid reactions Langerhans cell histiocytosis Full blood count and film showing monocytosis and immature cells Bone marrow examination with cytogenetics (including monosomy 7 assessment) RAS-pathway mutation analysis (PTPN11, NRAS, KRAS, NF1, CBL) Assessment for neurofibromatosis type 1 and Noonan syndrome Exclusion of infective mimics An aggressive clonal myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm of early childhood Presents with hepatosplenomegaly, monocytosis, leucocytosis, cytopenias and often a rash It is driven by dysregulation of the RAS pathway, with mutations in PTPN11, NRAS, KRAS, NF1 or CBL There are associations with neurofibromatosis type 1 and Noonan syndrome (the latter can cause a self-limiting JMML-like disorder) Hypersensitivity of myeloid progenitors to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor is characteristic Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the main curative treatment for most cases Rapidly rising white cell count and organomegaly Progressive cytopenias with bleeding or infection Respiratory compromise from leukaemic infiltration Transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia Mistaking a viral illness with hepatosplenomegaly for JMML and vice versa Overlooking an underlying RASopathy (NF1, Noonan) Delaying referral for transplantation Assuming all RAS-mutant infantile disease is aggressive Juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia arises from constitutive activation of the RAS signal transduction pathway in a haematopoietic stem cell, through mutations in genes such as PTPN11, NRAS, KRAS, NF1 or CBL. This hyperactive signalling makes myeloid progenitors hypersensitive to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor, driving excessive proliferation of monocytes and granulocytes that infiltrate the spleen, liver, skin and lungs. The clonal proliferation with dysplasia produces the mixed myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative picture and, untreated, is rapidly progressive. Untreated JMML is rapidly fatal in most children; allogeneic stem cell transplantation cures many, though relapse occurs, and certain CBL- and Noonan-associated forms may follow a milder or self-resolving course.

Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy — JME, Janz syndrome Other idiopathic generalised epilepsies (childhood or juvenile absence epilepsy) Progressive myoclonic epilepsies Focal epilepsy with secondary generalisation Benign physiological (hypnagogic) myoclonus Non-epileptic movements or tics Psychogenic non-epileptic events EEG, ideally including a recording after sleep deprivation and on awakening Photic stimulation during EEG to elicit a photoparoxysmal response MRI brain, mainly to exclude structural or progressive causes in atypical cases Detailed history focusing on early-morning jerks and provoking factors Metabolic or genetic testing when a progressive myoclonic epilepsy is suspected A common idiopathic (genetic) generalised epilepsy syndrome, usually beginning in adolescence. The defining seizure type is myoclonic jerks, typically of the arms and shoulders, occurring soon after waking. Most patients also have generalised tonic-clonic seizures, and a subset have absence seizures. Early morning clumsiness, such as dropping objects like a toothbrush or cup, is a classic historical clue that is often overlooked. Seizures are strongly provoked by sleep deprivation, alcohol, and sometimes photic stimulation. The interictal EEG characteristically shows generalised polyspike-and-wave discharges, and a photoparoxysmal response may be seen. Development and intelligence are typically normal, and neuroimaging is usually unremarkable. Seizures are generally well controlled with appropriate broad-spectrum treatment, but the condition usually requires long-term therapy as relapse on withdrawal is common; certain narrow-spectrum antiseizure medicines can worsen it. Progressive cognitive decline or neurological deterioration suggesting a progressive myoclonic epilepsy Focal neurological signs or focal features on EEG or imaging Seizures worsening after starting treatment (possible inappropriate narrow-spectrum drug) Frequent generalised tonic-clonic seizures or status epilepticus Recurrent seizures driven by unrecognised sleep deprivation or non-adherence Missing the diagnosis by not asking specifically about early-morning myoclonic jerks Misclassifying generalised seizures as focal and selecting a drug that aggravates myoclonus and absences Underestimating the impact of sleep deprivation, alcohol, and poor adherence on seizure control Attempting early withdrawal of treatment and precipitating relapse Overlooking coexisting absence seizures JME is a genetically determined generalised epilepsy involving abnormal thalamocortical network excitability and synchronisation rather than a focal structural lesion. Inherited susceptibility, likely polygenic in most cases, produces a lowered threshold for generalised epileptiform discharges. The characteristic myoclonus and generalised seizures arise from these hyperexcitable cortico-thalamic circuits, and the strong link with the sleep-wake transition reflects state-dependent changes in cortical excitability. Prognosis for seizure control is favourable with suitable therapy and lifestyle measures, and cognition is preserved, but JME is generally a lifelong tendency; most patients relapse if medication is stopped, so long-term or indefinite treatment is often needed.

and spreads submucosally into the nasopharynx, nasal cavity, pterygopalatine fossa, and potentially the orbit and intracranial compartment Examination reveals a firm reddish mass in the nasopharynx or clinical and imaging picture Preoperative angiography with embolisation of feeding vessels reduces intraoperative haemorrhage Surgical excision, endoscopic or open depending on extent, is the mainstay, with radiotherapy reserved for extensive or unresectable intracranial disease Recurrent or profuse epistaxis that can be life-threatening from this highly vascular tumour Biopsy in the clinic setting risking uncontrolled haemorrhage and generally to be avoided Intracranial or orbital extension threatening vision or neurological structures Rapid enlargement or cranial nerve involvement requiring urgent specialist management Performing an outpatient biopsy of a vascular nasopharyngeal mass and precipitating severe bleeding Dismissing recurrent epistaxis in an adolescent male as trivial Underestimating tumour extent by omitting cross-sectional imaging and angiography Inadequate resection leaving residual tumour at the skull base with subsequent recurrence Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a histologically benign tumour composed of a fibrous stroma interspersed with numerous thin-walled vascular channels that frequently lack a complete muscular coat, which explains the tendency to torrential bleeding. It typically originates around the sphenopalatine foramen and pterygopalatine fossa and grows submucosally along natural pathways, expanding into the nasopharynx and nasal cavity and eroding bone to reach the orbit, infratemporal fossa, and skull base. Its almost exclusive occurrence in adolescent males has prompted the hypothesis of hormonal (androgen) sensitivity influencing growth. Although histologically benign, the tumour is locally aggressive and prone to recurrence when incompletely excised; complete removal, aided by preoperative embolisation, gives good long-term control, while extensive skull-base or intracranial disease is more difficult to eradicate and may require radiotherapy.

Overlooking early hearing loss that warrants audiological follow-up Attributing the very high alkaline phosphatase to liver disease rather than bone turnover Delaying antiresorptive treatment that can alter the disease trajectory Juvenile Paget disease is caused by biallelic inactivating mutations in TNFRSF11B, which encodes osteoprotegerin, a decoy receptor that normally binds RANKL and prevents it from activating RANK on osteoclast precursors. Without functional osteoprotegerin, RANKL signalling is unopposed, leading to greatly increased osteoclast formation and activity. Coupled to this is a compensatory surge in osteoblastic bone formation, so the skeleton undergoes extremely rapid but disorganised remodelling. The resulting woven, mechanically weak bone produces widespread deformity, bowing, fractures, and skull enlargement, and the very high turnover is mirrored by strikingly raised alkaline phosphatase. Untreated disease causes progressive deforming bone disease, fractures, and deafness with substantial disability, but antiresorptive therapy can markedly reduce turnover and improve the clinical course, making early diagnosis important.

juvenile plantar dermatosis — forefoot dermatitis, sweaty sock dermatitis tinea pedis with web-space and instep involvement allergic contact dermatitis to footwear components such as rubber or chromate atopic dermatitis of the feet palmoplantar psoriasis pitted keratolysis hereditary or acquired palmoplantar keratoderma dyshidrotic (pompholyx) eczema potassium hydroxide microscopy and fungal culture of scale to exclude tinea pedis patch testing when footwear allergic contact dermatitis is suspected bacterial swab if secondary infection or pitted keratolysis is considered clinical assessment for atopic stigmata elsewhere on the skin skin biopsy only in atypical or treatment-resistant cases examination of footwear and sock materials as part of history review for koebnerising psoriasis at other sites such as nails and scalp Presents in prepubertal children as symmetrical, shiny, glazed erythema with fissuring over the weight-bearing forefoot and plantar surfaces of the great toes. The instep and the interdigital web spaces are characteristically spared, a pattern that helps distinguish it from tinea pedis and allergic contact dermatitis. Occlusive synthetic footwear and socks with alternating sweating and rapid drying are central to the process, hence the descriptive term sweaty sock dermatitis. It is often painful rather than itchy, with a smooth glazed cracked-porcelain appearance and painful fissures that impair walking. There is an association with atopy, and many affected children have a personal or family history of eczema, asthma or hay fever. Management centres on reducing occlusion and friction with breathable leather or open footwear, cotton socks, emollients and greasy barrier ointments. Potassium hydroxide microscopy and fungal culture should be negative and are useful to exclude tinea, which typically involves the web spaces and instep. The condition tends to settle around puberty, so reassurance about eventual spontaneous resolution is an important part of counselling. web-space maceration or unilateral disease suggesting tinea rather than juvenile plantar dermatosis spreading vesiculation or oozing indicating secondary bacterial infection nail pitting, onycholysis or plaques elsewhere pointing to psoriasis onset outside the typical prepubertal age range prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis severe painful fissuring limiting mobility and quality of life misdiagnosing it as tinea pedis and prescribing prolonged antifungals that do not help overlooking the diagnostic sparing of the instep and web spaces relying on potent topical corticosteroids alone rather than addressing footwear occlusion and friction failing to reassure families that resolution around puberty is expected missing coexisting atopic dermatitis or early psoriasis Juvenile plantar dermatosis is a friction and moisture-related dermatitis of the weight-bearing plantar skin, thought to arise from repeated cycles of hyperhydration and rapid dehydration within occlusive modern footwear and synthetic socks. Sweat is trapped against the skin during activity, then evaporates quickly, and this alternating wetting and drying, combined with mechanical friction on pressure-bearing surfaces, disrupts the stratum corneum barrier of the forefoot. The resulting impaired barrier produces the glazed, fissured appearance. An atopic tendency predisposes to the disorder through an inherently compromised epidermal barrier, and the condition is not primarily allergic or infective, although secondary irritant and, occasionally, contact factors may aggravate it. The condition is benign and self-limiting, characteristically improving and resolving spontaneously around puberty. Symptoms fluctuate with footwear and activity, and consistent barrier and footwear measures usually control discomfort in the interim.

Early detection of organ involvement and timely immunosuppressive and vasoactive therapy improve outcomes, though the disease can be chronic and disabling.

Juvenile xanthogranuloma — JXG, naevoxanthoendothelioma Langerhans cell histiocytosis Spitz naevus Mastocytoma / solitary mastocytosis Benign cephalic histiocytosis Dermatofibroma Molluscum contagiosum Xanthoma associated with hyperlipidaemia Skin biopsy with histology and immunohistochemistry (CD68, factor XIIIa, CD1a, langerin) Slit-lamp ophthalmological examination when ocular symptoms or multiple lesions in young children Full blood count and blood film to screen for juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia in at-risk infants Examination for café-au-lait macules and features of neurofibromatosis type 1 Serum lipid profile to exclude hyperlipidaemic xanthoma when clinically indicated Imaging (ultrasound, MRI) if visceral or central nervous system involvement is suspected Dermoscopy showing the characteristic setting-sun or clouds pattern as an adjunct The commonest non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis of childhood, typically presenting in infancy as one or a few firm yellow-orange to reddish-brown papules or nodules on the head, neck or upper trunk. Solitary lesions predominate; most appear within the first year of life and a proportion are congenital. The majority are cutaneous and self-limiting, involuting spontaneously over months to a few years, often leaving atrophy or hyperpigmentation. Ocular involvement, most often unilateral iris disease, is the commonest extracutaneous site and may cause spontaneous hyphaema, glaucoma or visual loss; young children with skin lesions warrant ophthalmological vigilance. An association with neurofibromatosis type 1 and, in a subset, with juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia (the classic triple association) should prompt review of café-au-lait macules and full blood count. Histology shows a dermal infiltrate of foamy histiocytes with characteristic Touton giant cells; lesions are CD68 and factor XIIIa positive but CD1a and langerin (CD207) negative, distinguishing them from Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Systemic or visceral disease (liver, lung, central nervous system) is rare and occurs mainly in infants with multiple cutaneous lesions. Reassurance and observation suffice for uncomplicated skin disease; intervention is reserved for symptomatic ocular or systemic involvement. Recommending disfiguring excision of a lesion destined to involute spontaneously. Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a benign proliferative disorder of the mononuclear phagocyte system, classified among the non-Langerhans cell (so-called C group / cutaneous) histiocytoses. The lesional cell is a dermal dendrocyte-derived histiocyte that accumulates lipid to produce the characteristic foamy, xanthomatous appearance despite normal serum lipids. The infiltrate is composed of histiocytes expressing macrophage markers such as CD68, CD163 and factor XIIIa but lacking the Langerhans cell markers CD1a and langerin, and Touton giant cells with a wreath of nuclei surrounding a central eosinophilic cytoplasm and a peripheral foamy rim are typical. The proliferation is thought to represent a reactive granulomatous response of dermal dendrocytes rather than a clonal neoplasm in most cases, which accords with its usual self-limiting behaviour and spontaneous involution as lipidised histiocytes are cleared. The cutaneous prognosis is excellent, with most solitary lesions involuting spontaneously over months to a few years leaving little or no residual change. Ocular and systemic disease carries greater morbidity and requires specialist management, but life-threatening visceral involvement is uncommon.

HIV co-infection worsens response and relapse risk Prolonged fever with massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia requiring urgent diagnosis and treatment Severe anaemia, bleeding or intercurrent bacterial infection from marrow suppression, which can be fatal Failure to respond to therapy or relapse, especially with HIV co-infection Emergence of post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis, signalling a transmission reservoir Attributing prolonged fever with splenomegaly to malaria or typhoid and missing visceral leishmaniasis in endemic areas Overlooking HIV co-infection, which alters treatment response and relapse risk Failing to recognise post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis as a source of ongoing transmission Delaying treatment while awaiting invasive confirmation when serology and clinical picture are diagnostic Sandfly bites inoculate Leishmania promastigotes, which are taken up by macrophages and transform into amastigotes that multiply within the mononuclear phagocyte system. The parasite disseminates to the spleen, liver and bone marrow, driving reticuloendothelial hyperplasia that produces organomegaly and, through hypersplenism and marrow infiltration, the characteristic pancytopenia. A vigorous but non-protective humoral response causes hypergammaglobulinaemia, while impaired cell-mediated immunity permits unchecked parasite proliferation and progressive, potentially fatal systemic disease. With prompt, effective antileishmanial therapy most patients recover fully, and liposomal amphotericin B has markedly improved outcomes in India. Untreated disease is nearly always fatal, and prognosis is poorer in the very young, malnourished, and those with HIV co-infection or advanced disease.

During development, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons originate in the olfactory placode and migrate along the olfactory nerve fibres to reach the hypothalamus. In Kallmann syndrome, mutations affecting the genes that guide this migration disrupt both the olfactory pathway and the arrival of GnRH neurons in the hypothalamus. The resulting deficiency of hypothalamic GnRH leads to reduced pituitary secretion of luteinising and follicle-stimulating hormones and consequent hypogonadism, while the shared developmental defect explains the coexisting impairment of smell. With appropriate hormone replacement, secondary sexual characteristics and bone health can be maintained, and fertility is frequently achievable with gonadotropin or pulsatile GnRH therapy; a minority experience reversal of the hypogonadism.

Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma — KHE, Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma of infancy Tufted angioma Infantile haemangioma Kaposi sarcoma Infantile fibrosarcoma Angiosarcoma Venous or lymphatic malformation Biopsy showing characteristic infiltrative spindled vascular lobules with D2-40 positivity Full blood count demonstrating marked thrombocytopenia Coagulation profile with low fibrinogen, raised D-dimer and prolonged clotting times Contrast-enhanced MRI delineating an ill-defined infiltrative enhancing mass crossing tissue planes Doppler ultrasound Baseline and serial monitoring during sirolimus therapy Locally aggressive, borderline vascular tumour of infancy that infiltrates tissue planes but does not metastasise. Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma is an infiltrative vascular neoplasm composed of coalescing lobules and sheets of spindled endothelial cells forming slit-like, crescentic vessels reminiscent of Kaposi sarcoma, intermingled with abnormal lymphatic channels (D2-40 positive) and microthrombi. The disorganised vasculature and abnormal endothelium trap and activate platelets, triggering intralesional platelet aggregation, profound thrombocytopenia and secondary consumptive coagulopathy, together termed the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. Activating GNA14 mutations and dysregulated angiogenic and lymphangiogenic signalling drive growth, and mTOR pathway activity provides the rationale for sirolimus. Mortality can be significant when the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon complicates large or deep lesions, but sirolimus-based therapy has markedly improved outcomes. Residual fibrosis, chronic pain and lymphoedema may persist.

kawasaki disease incomplete — Incomplete Kawasaki disease, Atypical Kawasaki disease Viral exanthems such as measles, adenovirus, enterovirus and Epstein-Barr virus Streptococcal and staphylococcal toxin-mediated disease, including scarlet fever, toxic shock and scalded skin syndrome Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (paediatric inflammatory multisystem syndrome) Stevens-Johnson syndrome and drug hypersensitivity reactions including DRESS Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis Other systemic infections such as leptospirosis Mercury exposure (acrodynia) Serial echocardiography to assess coronary artery dimensions using body-surface-area-adjusted z-scores Full blood count showing anaemia and later thrombocytosis, with ESR and CRP Serum albumin, sodium and liver enzymes Urinalysis for sterile pyuria Electrocardiogram for arrhythmia, ischaemia and a baseline recording Cultures, serology and viral studies to exclude infective mimics N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide as an adjunctive supportive marker Incomplete Kawasaki disease should be considered in any child with prolonged unexplained fever and fewer than the required number of principal clinical criteria, particularly in infants. Infants under about six months of age are at highest risk of both incomplete presentation and coronary artery aneurysms, so the threshold for evaluation and treatment should be low. The principal features may appear sequentially rather than together: bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection, oral mucosal changes with cracked red lips or strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, extremity changes with erythema and oedema followed by periungual peeling, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Supportive laboratory findings — markedly raised inflammatory markers, anaemia, a rising platelet count in the second week, sterile pyuria, transaminitis, hypoalbuminaemia and hyponatraemia — strengthen the diagnosis when clinical criteria are incomplete. Echocardiography is central: coronary artery dilatation or aneurysm supports the diagnosis and mandates treatment even when full clinical criteria are absent. Timely immunoglobulin therapy, ideally within the first ten days of illness, substantially reduces the risk of coronary artery aneurysms. Perineal desquamation and erythema or reactivation at a previous BCG scar site are useful supportive clues. Incomplete Kawasaki disease belongs in the differential of fever of unknown origin and of a prolonged, viral-seeming illness that fails to settle. Coronary artery dilatation or aneurysm on echocardiography Myocarditis, heart failure or circulatory shock (Kawasaki disease shock syndrome) Persistent or recrudescent fever despite immunoglobulin, indicating treatment resistance Young infants with prolonged fever and marked irritability Features suggesting macrophage activation syndrome Waiting for all classic criteria before treating and thereby delaying immunoglobulin beyond the optimal window Attributing prolonged fever to a self-limiting viral illness and missing incomplete disease, especially in infants Being falsely reassured by a normal initial echocardiogram, as coronary changes may evolve later Overlooking supportive laboratory criteria that would justify treatment Failing to recognise immunoglobulin resistance requiring escalation of therapy Kawasaki disease is a self-limiting, medium-vessel systemic vasculitis of childhood with a striking predilection for the coronary arteries; the incomplete form shares identical pathology but presents with insufficient clinical criteria to meet the classic case definition. An infectious or environmental trigger is thought to provoke an aberrant, dysregulated immune response in a genetically susceptible child, driving neutrophilic and then mononuclear infiltration of the arterial wall. Inflammation destroys the media and internal elastic lamina, weakening the vessel and predisposing to dilatation and aneurysm formation, most importantly in the coronary tree, where subsequent thrombosis, stenosis or rupture accounts for the principal morbidity and mortality. With prompt immunoglobulin therapy the great majority of children recover fully, whereas untreated or delayed disease carries a substantial risk of coronary artery aneurysms. Such aneurysms are the leading cause of long-term morbidity and may lead to thrombosis, myocardial ischaemia or sudden death.

Kawasaki Disease Shock Syndrome — KDSS, Kawasaki shock syndrome, Kawasaki disease with shock Toxic shock syndrome (staphylococcal or streptococcal) Septic shock Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis with macrophage activation Severe adenoviral or other viral infection Drug reaction with systemic involvement Echocardiography to assess coronary arteries and ventricular function Inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) Full blood count with attention to platelets and anaemia Serum albumin, sodium, and liver function tests Cardiac biomarkers (troponin, natriuretic peptides) Blood cultures and infection screen to exclude sepsis and toxic shock Coagulation studies A severe presentation of Kawasaki disease in which children develop haemodynamic instability and hypotension requiring fluid resuscitation or inotropic support. It should be considered in a child with features of Kawasaki disease (prolonged fever, mucocutaneous changes, conjunctival injection, extremity changes, rash, cervical lymphadenopathy) who also appears shocked. Compared with classic Kawasaki disease, shock syndrome is more often associated with incomplete presentations, greater systemic inflammation, and a higher risk of coronary artery involvement. Laboratory markers tend to show more intense inflammation, lower platelet counts, and evidence of consumptive or capillary-leak processes. These children are more likely to be initially resistant to intravenous immunoglobulin and may need additional immunomodulatory therapy. The overlap with toxic shock syndrome and septic shock frequently leads to diagnostic delay, so a high index of suspicion is essential. Prompt echocardiography is important because of the elevated risk of coronary artery aneurysms and myocardial dysfunction. Timely treatment of the underlying vasculitis, in addition to circulatory support, is key to reducing coronary complications. In the shock variant, an exaggerated inflammatory response with high circulating cytokine levels produces vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, and increased vascular permeability with capillary leak. The combination of impaired cardiac contractility and fluid shifts out of the intravascular space results in hypotension and organ hypoperfusion, superimposed on the vasculitic damage that threatens the coronary arteries. With early recognition and treatment most children recover, but the shock variant carries a higher rate of coronary artery abnormalities, myocardial dysfunction, and immunoglobulin resistance than classic disease, so outcomes depend on prompt immunomodulation and cardiac follow-up.

epileptic encephalopathy KCNQ2 encephalopathy is caused by pathogenic variants, frequently dominant-negative or gain- and loss-of-function missense changes, in KCNQ2 encoding the Kv7.2 potassium channel subunit. Kv7.2 combines with Kv7.3 to generate the M-current, a slow potassium current that stabilises the resting membrane potential and limits repetitive firing. Disruption of this current increases neuronal excitability in the neonatal brain, producing early tonic seizures and a severe epileptic encephalopathy, in contrast to the milder self-limited phenotype seen with less disruptive variants. Outcome varies with the underlying variant: many children with the encephalopathy form have intellectual disability and persistent epilepsy, though seizures may improve over the first years. Early recognition and use of sodium-channel-blocking therapy can improve seizure control in responsive cases.

sleep-related hypermotor phenotype and failing to counsel relatives Mislabelling nocturnal hypermotor seizures as parasomnias KCNT1 encodes Slack (KNa1.1), a sodium-activated potassium channel that contributes to the slow afterhyperpolarisation and shapes the timing and adaptation of neuronal firing. Pathogenic variants are predominantly gain-of-function, producing constitutively increased potassium current. Although greater potassium conductance might be expected to dampen activity, in affected networks it disrupts normal firing patterns and inhibitory balance, promoting the intense multifocal or frontal-predominant seizures seen clinically. The gain-of-function mechanism underlies the rationale for quinidine, which partially blocks the channel, though its clinical utility has proven variable. The migrating focal seizure phenotype generally has a poor outcome with refractory seizures and severe developmental impairment, whereas the sleep-related hypermotor phenotype varies from relatively mild to disabling, sometimes with significant psychiatric and cognitive comorbidity.

or bulbar deterioration Progressive respiratory muscle weakness Failing to institute cardiac surveillance and offer timely pacing for conduction block Mistaking the ophthalmoplegia for myasthenia gravis Overlooking treatable associated endocrinopathies Not recognising that Pearson syndrome in a survivor may evolve into Kearns-Sayre syndrome Kearns-Sayre syndrome usually results from a single large-scale deletion of mitochondrial DNA arising during oogenesis or early embryogenesis, so it is generally sporadic. The deletion removes genes encoding subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation chain and mitochondrial transfer RNAs, impairing energy production. Heteroplasmic distribution of deleted genomes across tissues, with a bias toward post-mitotic high-energy-demand organs such as extraocular muscle, retina, cardiac conduction tissue, brain and endocrine glands, explains the characteristic multisystem phenotype. The condition is progressive and multisystem; prognosis is largely determined by cardiac conduction disease, which can cause sudden death and is mitigated by surveillance and pacing. Life expectancy is reduced, with care focused on supportive and organ-specific management.

Keloid — keloid scar, keloidal scar Hypertrophic scar (raised but confined to the wound edges and tends to regress) Dermatofibroma Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans Foreign-body granuloma Cutaneous manifestation of sarcoidosis in a scar Nodular presentation of acne keloidalis nuchae on the occipital scalp Diagnosis is clinical based on history and morphology Skin biopsy only when an alternative or malignant process is suspected, recognising that biopsy itself may stimulate keloid growth Photographic documentation to monitor size and response to treatment A keloid is firm, rubbery, and shiny, and crucially extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound, distinguishing it from a hypertrophic scar that stays within the wound margins Lesions often itch or feel tender and may continue to enlarge over months to years rather than regressing Predilection sites include the earlobes, presternal chest, shoulders, upper back, and jawline Risk is higher in people with darker skin phototypes, in younger patients, and where there is a family history Even minor triggers such as ear piercing, acne, vaccination, or surgery can precipitate lesions in predisposed individuals Prevention matters: minimise tension on wounds, avoid unnecessary elective procedures in prone sites, and counsel high-risk patients before piercings or cosmetic surgery Treatment is often multimodal and includes intralesional anti-inflammatory injection, pressure or silicone therapy, and carefully planned surgery combined with adjuvant measures to reduce recurrence Surgical excision alone carries a high recurrence rate and can produce a larger keloid, so it should be paired with adjuvant therapy Rapid growth, ulceration, bleeding, or fixation suggesting a fibrosarcomatous tumour rather than a keloid Recurrent or aggressive lesions in a scar raising the possibility of dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans Functional impairment or contracture over a joint or the ear requiring specialist input Excising a keloid without adjuvant therapy, which commonly produces a larger recurrence Failing to distinguish a keloid from a self-limiting hypertrophic scar and over-treating Performing elective cosmetic procedures or piercings in high-risk patients without counselling Overlooking the symptom burden of itch and pain and treating only for appearance Keloids arise from dysregulated wound healing in which the normal resolution of the proliferative phase fails and fibroblasts remain persistently activated. Overexpression of profibrotic mediators, notably transforming growth factor-beta, drives excessive and disorganised deposition of thick, hyalinised collagen bundles that extend into surrounding normal dermis. Reduced apoptosis of fibroblasts, altered mechanotransduction from wound tension, and a genetic predisposition all contribute. Unlike hypertrophic scars, keloids do not remodel and regress over time, reflecting a sustained imbalance between collagen synthesis and breakdown. Keloids are chronic and prone to recurrence; some stabilise with combined therapy, but complete and permanent resolution is difficult, and lesions frequently recur after excision unless adjuvant treatment is used. They do not spontaneously involute in the way hypertrophic scars often do.

There are no upper motor neuron signs, which helps distinguish it from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis Sensory involvement can be demonstrated electrophysiologically even when clinically subtle, detecting the expanded CAG repeat in the androgen receptor gene Progressive dysphagia with aspiration and weight loss Choking episodes or compromised airway protection Rapid deterioration suggesting an alternative or superimposed diagnosis Emergence of upper motor neuron signs prompting reconsideration of ALS Misdiagnosing it as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and giving an unduly poor prognosis Overlooking the endocrine and metabolic features that support the diagnosis Underestimating aspiration risk from bulbar involvement Not offering genetic counselling to at-risk male relatives and carrier daughters Kennedy disease is a polyglutamine disorder caused by an expanded CAG repeat in the androgen receptor gene on the X chromosome. The elongated polyglutamine tract renders the mutant, ligand-bound androgen receptor prone to misfolding and nuclear accumulation, which is toxic to lower motor neurons in the brainstem and spinal cord and to dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons. The androgen-dependent toxicity explains why the phenotype is expressed in males and why partial androgen insensitivity features accompany the neuronopathy. The disorder progresses slowly over many years, and life expectancy is often near normal, though bulbar weakness can lead to aspiration and disability; mobility and swallowing decline gradually and management is supportive.

Kenny-Caffey syndrome — KCS, Kenny-Caffey syndrome type 1 (TBCE), Kenny-Caffey syndrome type 2 (FAM111A), hypoparathyroidism with medullary stenosis Sanjad-Sakati (hypoparathyroidism-retardation-dysmorphism) syndrome Autoimmune or surgical hypoparathyroidism with unrelated skeletal disease DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome with hypoparathyroidism Osteopetrosis and other sclerosing bone dysplasias Pseudohypoparathyroidism / Albright hereditary osteodystrophy Vitamin D-related rickets or osteomalacia Serum calcium, phosphate, magnesium and albumin with corrected calcium Intact parathyroid hormone level (inappropriately low or undetectable relative to hypocalcaemia) Skeletal survey to demonstrate cortical thickening, medullary stenosis and delayed fontanelle closure 25-hydroxyvitamin D and renal function to contextualise mineral metabolism Molecular genetic testing of TBCE and FAM111A with pedigree-based family screening Ophthalmological assessment for microphthalmia and refractive error A rare inherited disorder combining hypoparathyroidism with a distinctive skeletal dysplasia and proportionate short stature Skeletal features include thickened long-bone cortices with narrowing (stenosis) of the medullary cavity, delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle, and slender tubular bones Two genetically distinct forms exist: an autosomal recessive type from TBCE variants (often with intellectual disability, seen in Middle Eastern populations) and an autosomal dominant type from FAM111A variants Hypoparathyroidism presents as hypocalcaemia that may manifest with tetany, carpopedal spasm, or seizures, especially in infancy Ophthalmic abnormalities such as small eyes and hyperopia and recurrent infections may accompany the phenotype The TBCE-related form overlaps with hypoparathyroidism-retardation-dysmorphism (Sanjad-Sakati) syndrome, reflecting shared molecular pathology Diagnosis rests on the combination of biochemical hypoparathyroidism, characteristic radiographic bone changes, and confirmatory genetic testing Acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany, laryngospasm or seizures requiring urgent correction Neonatal or infantile presentation with failure to thrive and recurrent infections Prolonged QT interval on the ECG from hypocalcaemia Signs of raised intracranial pressure or CNS complications Attributing infantile seizures to primary epilepsy rather than checking calcium and parathyroid status Overlooking the diagnosis when skeletal radiographic clues are subtle or misread as osteopetrosis Failing to distinguish the recessive and dominant forms, which affects inheritance counselling Aggressive calcium and vitamin D therapy precipitating hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis if unmonitored Kenny-Caffey syndrome is a monogenic disorder of bone development and parathyroid function. The autosomal recessive form arises from loss-of-function variants in TBCE, which encodes a tubulin-folding cofactor essential for microtubule assembly, disturbing intracellular trafficking and organ development including the parathyroid glands. The autosomal dominant form results from variants in FAM111A, a protein implicated in genome maintenance and possibly parathyroid and skeletal morphogenesis. The net effect is defective or absent parathyroid tissue causing hypoparathyroidism with consequent hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia, together with abnormal endochondral and cortical bone growth producing medullary stenosis, cortical thickening, and short stature. Prognosis depends on the severity of hypocalcaemia control and any associated intellectual impairment or infections, which are more prominent in the recessive TBCE-related form. With careful lifelong management of calcium and vitamin D metabolism, biochemical stability is achievable, though short stature and skeletal changes persist.

keratoacanthoma — KA, molluscum sebaceum Invasive squamous cell carcinoma Nodular basal cell carcinoma Hypertrophic actinic keratosis Verruca vulgaris (viral wart) Giant molluscum contagiosum Amelanotic melanoma Merkel cell carcinoma or deep fungal infection Excisional biopsy that includes the deep base to allow assessment for invasion Dermoscopy showing central keratin and peripheral white circles or looped vessels Review of immunosuppression status and drug history including BRAF inhibitors Assessment for multiplicity and family history to identify a syndromic cause Mismatch repair immunohistochemistry and colonoscopy when Muir-Torre syndrome is suspected Regional lymph node examination if invasive squamous cell carcinoma is confirmed Presents as a rapidly growing, dome-shaped, flesh-coloured nodule with a central keratin-filled crater, typically on sun-exposed skin of older, fair-skinned patients. Classically follows a triphasic natural history of rapid proliferation, a stationary phase and then spontaneous involution over months, often leaving a depressed scar. Widely regarded as a well-differentiated variant of squamous cell carcinoma that cannot be reliably distinguished from invasive disease on clinical or histological grounds. Complete excision with a deep margin is generally preferred, because superficial or partial biopsy may miss an invasive squamous cell carcinoma at the base. Multiple lesions suggest a syndrome: Ferguson-Smith type (multiple self-healing), Grzybowski type (eruptive) or Muir-Torre syndrome with sebaceous neoplasms and visceral malignancy. Associations include ultraviolet exposure, immunosuppression, trauma and BRAF inhibitor therapy. Dermoscopy typically shows a central keratin mass with surrounding white structures and looped vessels. Histology shows a central keratin plug with buttressing (lipping) epidermal edges and a glassy, well-differentiated keratinocyte proliferation. Ulceration, induration or continued rapid growth without the expected involution Lesions on the lip, ear or in a periungual or mucosal site, where malignant behaviour is more likely Occurrence in an immunosuppressed patient Recurrence after treatment or perineural symptoms Multiple or eruptive lesions suggesting an underlying syndrome or malignancy Assuming a lesion is benign and observing it, thereby missing an invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Relying on a superficial shave or partial biopsy that fails to sample the tumour base. Overlooking Muir-Torre syndrome in patients with multiple or atypical lesions. Failing to consider drug-induced lesions in patients on BRAF inhibitor therapy. Keratoacanthoma arises from a neoplastic proliferation of keratinocytes, thought to originate from the follicular infundibulum, driven largely by ultraviolet-induced DNA damage and, in some cases, immunosuppression, trauma or drug exposure such as BRAF inhibitors. The proliferative phase produces the characteristic crateriform nodule, while a cell-mediated immune response is believed to underlie the spontaneous involution seen in many lesions. Because the proliferation shares molecular and morphological features with well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma, the two exist on a continuum. Although many lesions involute spontaneously, they leave scars and cannot be reliably distinguished from invasive squamous cell carcinoma, so complete excision is recommended and generally curative, with an excellent outcome.

and to monitoring progression Management is staged: spectacles or soft lenses early, rigid gas-permeable or specialty contact lenses for irregular astigmatism, corneal collagen cross-linking to arrest progression, and keratoplasty for advanced scarring or intolerance to lenses Acute corneal hydrops causes sudden pain, redness, and reduced vision from a break in Descemet membrane allowing aqueous into the stroma Sudden pain, marked visual loss, and corneal oedema suggesting acute hydrops Rapidly progressive steepening in young patients requiring urgent cross-linking assessment Corneal scarring or lens intolerance indicating need for keratoplasty referral Repeatedly changing spectacle prescriptions instead of recognising an underlying ectasia Overlooking eye rubbing as a modifiable driver of progression Delaying cross-linking in demonstrable progression, allowing avoidable visual loss Mistaking acute hydrops for infective keratitis Keratoconus is a progressive, non-inflammatory ectasia in which the cornea thins and steepens into a conical shape, producing irregular astigmatism and myopia. The stromal thinning reflects disorganisation of collagen lamellae and altered enzyme activity with increased degradation of the corneal matrix. Mechanical stress from chronic eye rubbing and an association with atopy and certain systemic syndromes are recognised contributors. As the cone advances, the apex scars and Descemet membrane may rupture, precipitating acute hydrops with corneal oedema. Progression is most rapid in younger patients and often stabilises with age; timely cross-linking can halt deterioration, and most patients achieve good functional vision with lenses, though a minority need corneal transplantation.

Keratolytic winter erythema — Oudtshoorn skin, Oudtshoorn disease, erythrokeratolysis hiemalis Peeling skin syndrome Erythrokeratodermia variabilis Palmoplantar exfoliative dermatitis of other cause Dyshidrotic (pompholyx) eczema Tinea manuum or pedis Acral peeling from contact or irritant dermatitis Skin biopsy showing a band of parakeratosis with subcorneal or intracorneal separation Family history and pedigree analysis for autosomal dominant inheritance Molecular studies of the chromosome 8 regulatory duplication where available Mycological examination to exclude dermatophyte infection Patch testing if contact dermatitis is considered Clinical photography to document the seasonal cyclical pattern An autosomal dominant disorder of keratinisation first characterised in Afrikaner families around Oudtshoorn in South Africa Characterised by cyclical palmoplantar erythema with centrifugal peeling of the stratum corneum, producing annular collarettes of desquamation Symptoms classically worsen in cold winter weather and improve in summer, hence the name It is associated with duplications in a regulatory region on chromosome 8 affecting expression of CTSB (cathepsin B) Affected skin shows recurrent superficial peeling that can extend beyond the palms and soles, sometimes with hyperhidrosis Diagnosis is clinical, based on the recurrent annular peeling and seasonal pattern with a supportive family history; biopsy shows a distinctive band of parakeratosis with underlying separation Management is supportive with emollients and keratolytics; some patients benefit from oral retinoids in severe disease Widespread desquamation with barrier failure and secondary infection Painful fissuring impairing hand or foot function Atypical persistent lesions not following the seasonal pattern, prompting reconsideration of diagnosis Signs of secondary bacterial infection in peeling areas Misdiagnosing recurrent peeling as tinea and prescribing repeated antifungals Overlooking the seasonal history that is central to recognition Failing to note the autosomal dominant family history Escalating to systemic therapy before optimising emollient and keratolytic care Keratolytic winter erythema is linked to non-coding genomic duplications on chromosome 8 that upregulate cathepsin B, a lysosomal cysteine protease active in keratinocyte differentiation and cornified-envelope turnover. Increased proteolytic activity is thought to promote premature and disordered breakdown of the stratum corneum, so the cornified layer separates and peels in a centrifugal, annular fashion. Environmental cold appears to trigger or accentuate the cycles of erythema and desquamation, explaining the striking seasonal variation. The condition is benign, tending to improve after childhood and adolescence, with a chronic relapsing but non-scarring course punctuated by winter exacerbations.

later fibrosis Ophthalmological assessment including slit-lamp examination for corneal changes Trichoscopy of the scarring alopecia Bacterial swabs where secondary infection is suspected Family with keratolytics and emollients, treatment of secondary inflammation and infection, and ophthalmology input for ocular involvement Progressive corneal disease threatening vision Extensive rapidly progressive scarring alopecia Recurrent secondary infection of inflamed follicular lesions Features suggesting the broader IFAP phenotype Not recognising the shared MBTPS2 basis and overlap with IFAP syndrome Mistaking early disease for ordinary keratosis pilaris and missing the scarring alopecia Neglecting ophthalmological surveillance for corneal disease Delaying anti-inflammatory measures that might limit follicular scarring Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans is usually caused by variants in MBTPS2, encoding a membrane-bound zinc metalloprotease required for regulated intramembrane
