Disturbed function impairs follicular keratinisation, producing spiny follicular plugs, while chronic perifollicular inflammation gradually destroys hair follicles to give a scarring (cicatricial) alopecia. Because the same gene underlies IFAP syndrome, the two conditions represent an allelic spectrum with overlapping cutaneous and ocular features. The follicular keratoses may improve after puberty, but the associated scarring alopecia is permanent; visual prognosis depends on the extent of corneal involvement.

Keratosis pilaris — KP, follicular keratosis, keratosis pilaris Lichen nitidus Follicular eczema Folliculitis Phrynoderma (vitamin A deficiency) Lichen spinulosus Milia or comedones Keratosis pilaris atrophicans variants Clinical diagnosis, generally requiring no investigation Dermoscopy showing coiled hairs and keratin plugs within follicular openings Assessment for associated atopic dermatitis and ichthyosis vulgaris Skin biopsy only in atypical presentations, showing follicular hyperkeratosis with a keratin plug Consideration of an underlying syndrome when atrophy or scarring is prominent (keratosis pilaris atrophicans) An extremely common, benign disorder of follicular keratinisation producing rough, gritty, keratotic follicular papules with a goose-flesh texture Classically affects the extensor upper arms, thighs, buttocks, and cheeks in a symmetrical distribution Often accompanied by perifollicular erythema; a variant with prominent redness and atrophy affects the face (keratosis pilaris rubra and atrophicans) Strongly associated with atopic dermatitis and ichthyosis vulgaris and tends to run in families with an autosomal dominant tendency Frequently improves with age and is usually worse in winter and in dry skin Caused by a keratin plug occluding the follicular opening, sometimes trapping a coiled hair Usually asymptomatic and cosmetic, with a clinical diagnosis that seldom needs a biopsy Management is symptomatic with regular emollients and keratolytics (urea, lactic acid, salicylic acid) and gentle exfoliation, and topical retinoids for resistant cases, with realistic expectations Prominent facial erythema with scarring loss of the eyebrows suggesting a syndromic form (keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans) Atrophy or scarring that may cause permanent hair loss Atypical, inflammatory, or rapidly evolving lesions prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Over-treating a benign, cosmetic condition and causing irritation Mistaking the atrophic facial variants for a scarring alopecia or another condition Failing to recognise associated atopy or ichthyosis vulgaris Promising cure rather than control Keratosis pilaris results from excessive or abnormal keratinisation of the hair-follicle infundibulum, so that a keratin plug forms and occludes the follicular opening, sometimes enclosing a coiled or trapped hair. The plug produces the palpable, rough papule, while surrounding low-grade inflammation gives the perifollicular erythema. The disorder is constitutional and often familial, and its association with atopic dermatitis and ichthyosis vulgaris reflects a shared tendency to disordered keratinisation and impaired epidermal barrier function; the atrophic facial variants involve additional follicular inflammation and scarring. Benign and chronic but tends to improve over time, often lessening markedly by adulthood; treatment controls rather than cures, and lesions recur if therapy is stopped.

Keratosis pilaris atrophicans — keratosis pilaris atrophicans faciei, ulerythema ophryogenes, atrophoderma vermiculatum, keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans spectrum Ordinary keratosis pilaris Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans and IFAP syndrome Lichen spinulosus Acne vulgaris (for the facial variants) Discoid lupus erythematosus (for scarring facial lesions) Folliculitis Skin biopsy showing follicular hyperkeratosis, perifollicular inflammation and dermal fibrosis Assessment for associated syndromes (Noonan, cardiofaciocutaneous) including cardiac and developmental review Molecular genetic testing guided by phenotype (e.g. RASopathy genes, MBTPS2) Trichoscopy and dermoscopy of affected areas Family history and pedigree analysis Clinical photography to monitor scarring and erythema A group of related disorders in which follicular keratosis is accompanied by inflammation that heals with atrophic scarring, distinguishing it from ordinary keratosis pilaris Ulerythema ophryogenes affects the eyebrows and lateral cheeks with follicular papules, erythema and later loss of the outer eyebrows Atrophoderma vermiculatum causes a distinctive worm-eaten (honeycomb) pitted scarring of the cheeks, usually beginning in childhood Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans is the most severe variant, with widespread spiny follicular keratosis and scarring alopecia Some cases occur in isolation while others are associated with syndromes such as Noonan and cardiofaciocutaneous syndromes or with MBTPS2-related disease Diagnosis is clinical, supported by biopsy showing follicular hyperkeratosis, perifollicular inflammation and dermal fibrosis; genetic testing is guided by the phenotype Management is supportive with emollients and keratolytics, anti-inflammatory measures for the erythema, and cosmetic treatment such as laser for residual redness once inflammation settles Progressive scarring alopecia suggesting the severe decalvans variant Dysmorphic, cardiac or developmental features indicating an associated RASopathy Rapidly progressive facial scarring Secondary infection of inflamed follicular lesions Dismissing early disease as ordinary keratosis pilaris and missing the scarring potential Overlooking an associated RASopathy such as Noonan or cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome Using ablative cosmetic treatments while active inflammation persists Failing to recognise the continuum with keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans and IFAP syndrome Keratosis pilaris atrophicans encompasses several disorders sharing abnormal follicular keratinisation with a significant inflammatory component. Keratotic plugging of follicles is accompanied by perifollicular inflammation that, unlike simple keratosis pilaris, damages the follicle and surrounding dermis and heals with atrophy and scarring, hence the eyebrow loss, honeycomb facial atrophy or scarring alopecia depending on the variant. Genetic contributions vary, ranging from isolated dominant traits to association with RASopathies such as Noonan and cardiofaciocutaneous syndromes and with MBTPS2-related keratinisation disorders at the severe end of the spectrum. The inflammatory phase and follicular keratosis often improve after puberty, but any atrophic scarring, eyebrow loss or scarring alopecia is permanent; overall prognosis depends on whether an underlying syndrome is present.

Kernicterus — bilirubin encephalopathy, chronic bilirubin encephalopathy, acute bilirubin encephalopathy Neonatal sepsis or meningitis Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy Inborn errors of metabolism causing encephalopathy Neonatal seizures of other cause Hypoglycaemic or electrolyte-related encephalopathy Other causes of neonatal hypertonia or abnormal movements Serial total and unconjugated bilirubin, interpreted against age-in-hours nomograms Albumin level and bilirubin-to-albumin ratio to gauge binding reserve Haemolysis workup (blood group, direct antiglobulin test, blood film, reticulocytes) Auditory brainstem response testing for auditory neuropathy MRI showing characteristic basal ganglia signal changes in established disease Evaluation for contributing factors such as sepsis, acidosis, and prematurity Kernicterus refers to the neurological injury caused by deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the brain, classically in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei. It is a preventable complication of severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and represents the chronic, permanent form of bilirubin neurotoxicity. Acute bilirubin encephalopathy evolves through phases: early lethargy, hypotonia, and poor feeding, followed by hypertonia with backward arching (retrocollis and opisthotonus), high-pitched cry, and fever, and later apnoea, seizures, and coma. The classic chronic tetrad includes choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (or auditory neuropathy), impaired upward gaze, and dental enamel dysplasia. Only unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin that is not bound to albumin can cross the blood-brain barrier, so free bilirubin and factors lowering albumin binding increase risk. Prematurity, haemolysis, sepsis, acidosis, hypoalbuminaemia, and certain drugs that displace bilirubin heighten vulnerability at any given bilirubin level. Prevention rests on identifying and monitoring at-risk newborns, timely phototherapy, and exchange transfusion when bilirubin approaches neurotoxic thresholds. Once established, chronic bilirubin encephalopathy is largely irreversible, underscoring the importance of early recognition and treatment of hyperbilirubinaemia. Structured predischarge risk assessment and follow-up of jaundiced newborns reduce the incidence of this now-rare but devastating condition. Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy: lethargy or hypertonia, retrocollis/opisthotonus, high-pitched cry, poor feeding Bilirubin approaching or exceeding exchange transfusion thresholds for the infant's age and risk Apnoea, seizures, or coma in a severely jaundiced newborn Rapidly rising bilirubin, especially with haemolysis, sepsis, or acidosis Jaundice in a preterm or unwell infant where binding reserve is reduced Interpreting bilirubin values without reference to the infant's age in hours and risk factors Underestimating neurotoxic risk in preterm, acidotic, hypoalbuminaemic, or septic infants at lower bilirubin levels Delaying phototherapy or exchange transfusion while bilirubin rises Missing early, subtle neurological signs of acute encephalopathy Discharging a jaundiced newborn without adequate follow-up and risk assessment Unconjugated bilirubin is normally tightly bound to albumin and does not enter the brain. When the bilirubin load overwhelms albumin binding capacity, or binding is reduced by acidosis, hypoalbuminaemia, prematurity, or competing substances, free unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier. It is neurotoxic, being preferentially deposited in and damaging the basal ganglia (notably the globus pallidus and subthalamic nuclei), the brainstem auditory and oculomotor nuclei, hippocampus, and cerebellum. Bilirubin impairs mitochondrial function and neuronal signalling, causing acute dysfunction and, if sustained, permanent neuronal loss and gliosis with the characteristic clinical sequelae. Acute bilirubin encephalopathy may be partly reversible if bilirubin is lowered promptly, but progression to chronic kernicterus produces permanent, often severe disability including movement disorder, hearing loss, and gaze abnormalities. Because the condition is largely preventable, prognosis hinges on timely detection and treatment of severe hyperbilirubinaemia.

Keratitis-ichthyosis-deafness (KID) syndrome — KID syndrome, GJB2, connexin 26, keratitis-ichthyosis-deafness syndrome Erythrokeratodermia variabilis Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma / other bacterial infection Rapidly extending erythroderma with barrier failure in infancy Attributing recurrent skin or mucosal infection to poor hygiene rather than the intrinsic immune/barrier defect diagnosis when the deafness or ocular features precede overt skin change KID syndrome results from usually dominant, often de novo mutations in GJB2, the gene encoding connexin 26. Connexins assemble into gap-junction channels that allow direct intercellular exchange of small molecules and ions; the disease-causing mutations act in a dominant fashion that disturbs channel gating and epidermal and cochlear cell communication. The resulting defect impairs epidermal differentiation and keratinocyte homeostasis, producing hyperkeratosis and a compromised barrier, disrupts inner-ear function causing sensorineural deafness, and affects the corneal epithelium leading to keratitis with neovascularisation. Impaired barrier and immune function predispose to infection and, over time, to keratinocyte malignancy. KID syndrome is a lifelong, progressive condition; vision may deteriorate from keratitis and deafness is usually permanent. The most serious long-term concern is a substantially increased risk of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, so continued surveillance is essential.

wrist pain, stiffness, swelling, reduced grip strength and limited wrist extension The radiographic hallmark is early sclerosis (increased density) of the lunate, progressing to fragmentation, loss of grip and wrist motion suggesting carpal disintegration Bilateral or atypical presentation prompting consideration of an underlying systemic cause of osteonecrosis Attributing persistent wrist pain to a soft-tissue strain and missing early sclerosis on plain films Relying on normal early radiographs and failing to obtain magnetic resonance imaging when suspicion is high Overlooking negative ulnar variance as a contributing mechanical factor Underestimating carpal collapse and applying joint-preserving surgery when salvage is more appropriate Kienbock disease is an osteonecrosis of the lunate in which the bone loses its blood supply and undergoes progressive death, collapse and fragmentation. The cause is regarded as multifactorial, combining interruption of the tenuous intraosseous and extraosseous vascular supply with mechanical overload. A relatively short ulna (negative ulnar variance) is commonly present and is believed to increase compressive stress on the lunate, while repetitive loading and single or repeated microtrauma may precipitate ischaemia. As the necrotic bone weakens it fractures and collapses, altering carpal mechanics, producing proximal migration of the capitate and rotation of the scaphoid, and ultimately leading to secondary degenerative arthritis of the wrist. Outcome depends on the stage at presentation; early disease treated with offloading or joint-levelling procedures may preserve function, whereas advanced lunate collapse and carpal disruption tend to progress to degenerative wrist arthritis with lasting stiffness and reduced grip.

Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease — histiocytic necrotising lymphadenitis, Kikuchi disease, Kikuchi's disease, Kikuchi-Fujimoto lymphadenitis Lymphoma (Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin) Tuberculous and other granulomatous lymphadenitis Systemic lupus erythematosus lymphadenopathy Reactive or viral lymphadenitis (including infectious mononucleosis) Metastatic carcinoma to cervical nodes Adult-onset Still disease Excisional lymph node biopsy showing paracortical necrosis, karyorrhexis, and histiocytes without neutrophils Full blood count and film often showing leucopenia with atypical lymphocytes Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) and lactate dehydrogenase Autoimmune screen including antinuclear antibody to assess for associated lupus Investigations to exclude tuberculosis and other infective causes Cross-sectional imaging if lymphoma is a concern A benign, self-limiting cause of cervical lymphadenopathy, classically in young women of Asian descent Presents with tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, and sometimes night sweats, weight loss, and a maculopapular rash Leucopenia with atypical lymphocytes is a common laboratory clue The main clinical importance is that it mimics lymphoma and tuberculous lymphadenitis, and it can be confused with lupus lymphadenopathy on histology Diagnosis rests on excisional lymph node biopsy showing paracortical necrosis with abundant histiocytes and karyorrhectic debris and a characteristic absence of neutrophils There is a recognised association with systemic lupus erythematosus, which may precede, coincide with, or follow the lymphadenitis Management is supportive with analgesia and antipyretics; corticosteroids are reserved for severe or recurrent disease Persistent or progressive lymphadenopathy raising concern for lymphoma Development of features of systemic lupus erythematosus Prolonged high fever or systemic deterioration Rare aseptic meningitis or other extranodal involvement Misdiagnosing it as lymphoma on histology and initiating unnecessary treatment Failing to consider or later screen for systemic lupus erythematosus Relying on fine-needle aspiration, which is often non-diagnostic, rather than excisional biopsy Mistaking the necrosis for tuberculous lymphadenitis Prescribing antibiotics for a non-infective, self-limiting condition Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is a self-limiting histiocytic necrotising lymphadenitis of uncertain cause, thought to represent an exuberant T-cell and histiocyte-mediated immune response, possibly triggered by a viral or other infectious agent in a genetically predisposed individual. Affected lymph nodes show paracortical zones of coagulative necrosis populated by proliferating histiocytes, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and CD8-positive T lymphocytes, with prominent karyorrhectic (apoptotic) debris and a striking paucity of neutrophils and plasma cells. The same mechanisms of immune dysregulation link it to systemic lupus erythematosus. The condition is benign and usually resolves spontaneously over several weeks to a few months; recurrence occurs in a minority, and patients warrant follow-up for the possible later emergence of systemic lupus erythematosus.

killian jamieson diverticulum — Killian-Jamieson diverticulum, proximal lateral cervical oesophageal diverticulum Zenker (pharyngo-oesophageal) diverticulum thyroid nodule or cyst on imaging lateral cervical (branchial) cyst cricopharyngeal bar or achalasia parathyroid cyst or adenoma laryngocoele cervical oesophageal duplication cyst barium swallow with lateral and oblique cervical views to define sac position relative to the cricopharyngeus upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to inspect the ostium and exclude mucosal disease neck ultrasound, which may first detect the lesion adjacent to the thyroid cross-sectional imaging (computed tomography of the neck) to clarify anatomy before intervention high-resolution manometry to assess upper sphincter function laryngoscopic assessment of vocal cord function before any planned surgery A Killian-Jamieson diverticulum is a pulsion outpouching that herniates through the Killian-Jamieson space, an anterolateral muscular gap in the proximal cervical oesophagus just below the cricopharyngeus and lateral to the longitudinal muscle insertion. It is much less common than a Zenker diverticulum and arises below rather than above the cricopharyngeus, which is the key anatomical distinction. On barium swallow it projects anterolaterally (more often on the left) below the upper oesophageal sphincter, whereas a Zenker diverticulum arises posteriorly above the sphincter. Most are small and asymptomatic; larger ones may cause dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, cough or a palpable neck fullness. The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in close relationship to the diverticular neck, so surgical or endoscopic treatment carries a real risk of vocal cord palsy. Because of the nerve relationship, endoscopic septotomy (as used for Zenker) is generally avoided or approached with great caution, and open transcervical diverticulectomy is often preferred for symptomatic lesions. It may be discovered incidentally during thyroid ultrasound as a cystic or mixed lesion abutting the thyroid, and can be mistaken for a thyroid nodule. Cricopharyngeal dysfunction and raised intraluminal pressure are thought to contribute, so myotomy considerations may apply as in other pulsion diverticula. progressive dysphagia with weight loss recurrent aspiration or pneumonia new hoarseness or vocal cord palsy indicating recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement signs of perforation such as neck pain, crepitus or fever after instrumentation rapidly enlarging neck mass Misidentifying the sac as a thyroid nodule on ultrasound and subjecting it to inappropriate biopsy. Applying a standard endoscopic Zenker septotomy and injuring the adjacent recurrent laryngeal nerve. Confusing it with a Zenker diverticulum because the anatomical distinction below versus above the cricopharyngeus is not appreciated. Attempting fine-needle aspiration of a presumed thyroid lesion and causing perforation or infection. Overlooking coexisting cricopharyngeal dysfunction that may need to be addressed. The Killian-Jamieson diverticulum is a pulsion (false) diverticulum containing mucosa and submucosa but lacking a muscular wall, herniating through the Killian-Jamieson triangle. This is a muscular weak point in the anterolateral wall of the proximal cervical oesophagus, bounded by the oblique fibres of the cricopharyngeus superiorly and the longitudinal and circular muscle of the oesophagus, located just distal to the cricopharyngeus and inferior to the recurrent laryngeal nerve entry. Elevated intraluminal pressure, often related to incoordination or spasm of the upper oesophageal sphincter and cricopharyngeal dysfunction, drives mucosal herniation through this defect. Because the sac lies below the sphincter and adjacent to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, it differs anatomically and surgically from the posteriorly located, supra-sphincteric Zenker diverticulum. Small asymptomatic diverticula have an excellent prognosis and can be observed, while symptomatic lesions generally respond well to surgical diverticulectomy. The principal prognostic concern is iatrogenic recurrent laryngeal nerve injury during treatment.

Kimura disease — eosinophilic lymphogranuloma, Kimura's disease, eosinophilic hyperplastic lymphogranuloma Angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia (epithelioid haemangioma) Lymphoma, particularly Hodgkin and T-cell types Langerhans cell histiocytosis Salivary gland tumour or reactive lymphadenopathy Parasitic infection with eosinophilia IgG4-related disease Excisional or core biopsy of the mass for histology showing lymphoid follicles and eosinophilic infiltration Full blood count with differential documenting peripheral eosinophilia Serum total IgE, which is characteristically very high Urinalysis and renal function to detect associated nephrotic syndrome or proteinuria Cross-sectional imaging (ultrasound or MRI) to define extent and lymph node involvement Exclusion of parasitic infection and lymphoma where clinically indicated A chronic inflammatory disorder typically affecting young to middle-aged men of Asian descent Presents with painless subcutaneous nodules or masses in the head and neck, often with regional lymphadenopathy and salivary gland involvement Marked peripheral blood eosinophilia and strikingly elevated serum IgE are characteristic Renal involvement, particularly nephrotic syndrome, occurs in a notable minority and should be actively sought Histology shows lymphoid follicles with germinal centres, dense eosinophilic infiltration with eosinophilic microabscesses, and proliferation of postcapillary venules Distinct from angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia, which is more superficial and occurs in a different demographic Benign but frequently relapses after excision; corticosteroids and other systemic immunosuppression are used for extensive or recurrent disease Nephrotic-range proteinuria indicating renal involvement Rapidly enlarging or systemic lymphadenopathy suggesting lymphoma Constitutional symptoms such as fever and weight loss requiring exclusion of malignancy Airway compromise from large head and neck masses Confusing it with angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia, a distinct entity Failing to check for renal involvement and missing associated nephrotic syndrome Attributing the mass to malignancy without histological confirmation, or vice versa Assuming surgical excision is curative when relapse is common Overlooking the diagnosis in a patient with unexplained eosinophilia and raised IgE Kimura disease is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory condition of unknown cause, possibly reflecting an aberrant T-helper-2 driven allergic or autoimmune response. There is exuberant reactive lymphoid proliferation with well-formed germinal centres accompanied by heavy eosinophil recruitment, elevated IgE, and proliferation of small blood vessels within affected soft tissue and lymph nodes. Cytokines such as interleukin-4 and interleukin-5 are thought to promote the eosinophilia and IgE production. The immune dysregulation may also injure the glomerulus, accounting for the associated nephrotic syndrome. Kimura disease is benign and does not undergo malignant transformation, but it is characterised by a chronic, relapsing course with frequent recurrence after excision; associated nephrotic syndrome influences long-term outcome.

evaluation, including in-vitro/caffeine-halothane contracture testing where available Cardiac and respiratory assessment and monitoring of scoliosis A rare congenital myopathy caused predominantly by anaesthesia is undertaken Creatine kinase is often mildly to moderately elevated and electromyography shows a myopathic pattern Muscle biopsy findings are variable and may show non-specific myopathic changes, cores, or fibre-type disproportion, so genetics are important for confirmation Diagnosis integrates the myopathy, the recognisable dysmorphic phenotype, and RYR1 genetic testing, with formal malignant hyperthermia (in-vitro contracture) testing where available Any planned anaesthesia, given the high risk of triggering a malignant hyperthermia crisis Personal or family history of an unexplained anaesthetic reaction, rigidity, or hyperthermia Respiratory muscle weakness or progressive scoliosis compromising ventilation Episodes of rhabdomyolysis or exertional hyperthermia Cardiac symptoms warranting evaluation Failing to recognise malignant hyperthermia susceptibility before surgery and using triggering agents Not ensuring dantrolene and a trigger-free anaesthetic technique are available for affected patients Attributing the dysmorphic features to another syndrome and missing the underlying RYR1 myopathy Assuming a normal or non-specific muscle biopsy excludes the diagnosis without genetic testing Omitting family screening and anaesthetic counselling for at-risk relatives King-Denborough syndrome is most often caused by variants in RYR1, the gene encoding the skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor, the calcium-release channel of the sarcoplasmic reticulum that is central to excitation-contraction coupling. Abnormal channel function disturbs regulated calcium release, impairing muscle contraction and producing a congenital myopathy, while the same channel abnormality renders muscle liable to uncontrolled calcium release and hypermetabolic crisis on exposure to triggering anaesthetic agents, the basis of malignant hyperthermia susceptibility. The associated dysmorphic and skeletal features form part of the recognisable syndromic phenotype. The myopathy itself is usually slowly progressive and compatible with prolonged ambulation and a reasonable lifespan, but the malignant hyperthermia susceptibility poses a serious perioperative risk; with recognition, trigger avoidance, and availability of dantrolene, life-threatening anaesthetic crises are largely preventable.

genitourinary anomalies, recurrent infections, and later obesity are associated systemic features Caused by haploinsufficiency of EHMT1 at chromosome 9q34.3, from either a subtelomeric microdeletion or an intragenic EHMT1 variant EHMT1 encodes a histone methyltransferase, placing Kleefstra syndrome among the chromatin-modification (epigenetic machinery) disorders Diagnosis uses chromosomal microarray to detect the 9q34.3 deletion, with EHMT1 sequencing when the array is normal Behavioural or developmental regression or catatonia-like state in adolescence or adulthood New seizures requiring evaluation Significant congenital heart disease needing cardiology management Recurrent or severe infection prompting immune assessment Mistaking the facial features and hypotonia for Down syndrome and not pursuing microarray Assuming a normal microarray excludes the diagnosis when an intragenic EHMT1 variant may be responsible Failing to anticipate and monitor for adolescent or adult regression and psychiatric change Overlooking associated cardiac or renal anomalies that need screening Kleefstra syndrome is caused by haploinsufficiency of EHMT1, which encodes euchromatic histone methyltransferase 1, an enzyme that dimethylates histone H3 lysine 9 to establish repressive chromatin marks and silence target genes. Reduced EHMT1 activity, whether from a 9q34.3 deletion or an intragenic variant, dysregulates transcriptional programmes controlling neuronal development and function, producing intellectual disability, hypotonia, speech impairment, and behavioural features. Contiguous deletions removing neighbouring genes can add to the systemic and dysmorphic phenotype. Intellectual disability and speech impairment are lifelong and most individuals require ongoing support, with the additional long-term concern of possible regression or psychiatric deterioration in later life. Systemic complications are managed as they arise, and multidisciplinary care optimises function and wellbeing.

intoxication or withdrawal Focal temporal or frontal epilepsy Encephalitis or another structural hypothalamic lesion Narcolepsy Detailed episode history and a sleep diary documenting the recurrent pattern Polysomnography and multiple sleep latency testing, ideally comparing periods within and between episodes MRI brain to exclude a hypothalamic or thalamic structural lesion Screening for Behavioural changes such as hyperphagia and, in some patients, disinhibited hypersexuality occur during episodes Between episodes sleep, cognition, mood and behaviour return to normal It most often begins in adolescence with a male predominance, and episodes are frequently triggered by infection or alcohol The disorder is typically self-limiting, with episodes becoming less frequent and eventually resolving over years Diagnosis rests on the recurrent stereotyped pattern after excluding other medical, neurological and psychiatric causes Focal neurological signs or persistent deficits between episodes A first episode in later adulthood or an atypical, non-remitting course Fever, meningism or other features of central nervous system infection Evidence of a structural hypothalamic lesion on imaging Dismissing episodes as psychiatric illness or malingering in an adolescent Missing an encephalitic or structural cause at first presentation Failing to counsel about the episodic, self-limiting nature and about safety during episodes Over-investigating between episodes when examination is normal The cause of Kleine-Levin syndrome is not established, but the episodic nature and the frequent infective trigger suggest a transient, possibly immune-mediated or inflammatory disturbance affecting hypothalamic and thalamic circuits that regulate sleep, appetite and behaviour. Functional imaging during episodes has shown reduced activity in thalamic and other regions, supporting a reversible functional disturbance rather than a fixed structural lesion. The natural history is generally favourable, with episodes tending to shorten and become less frequent over several years before remitting, although the unpredictability of relapses causes considerable disruption to education and work.

Klinefelter syndrome — 47,XXY, XXY syndrome, seminiferous tubule dysgenesis Other causes of primary hypogonadism Kallmann syndrome and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism Marfan syndrome (for tall stature) Fragile X syndrome (for learning difficulties) Constitutional tall stature Karyotype to confirm the diagnosis and define any mosaicism or higher-grade aneuploidy Testosterone with luteinising and follicle-stimulating hormone measurement Semen analysis when fertility is a concern Bone density assessment given osteoporosis risk Metabolic screening for glucose intolerance and dyslipidaemia Most common sex chromosome aneuploidy in males, caused by one or more extra X chromosomes, typically a 47,XXY karyotype Often unrecognised until adolescence or adulthood, when hypogonadism and infertility prompt evaluation Characteristic features include tall stature with long legs, small firm testes, reduced facial and body hair, and gynaecomastia Testicular failure produces low testosterone with elevated gonadotrophins and, usually, azoospermia Learning difficulties, particularly with language and executive function, are common though intelligence is usually within the normal range Testosterone replacement supports pubertal development, bone health, and wellbeing but does not restore fertility Sperm retrieval techniques can occasionally allow biological fatherhood in selected men Associated with an increased risk of osteoporosis, metabolic syndrome, venous thromboembolism, and certain tumours Untreated hypogonadism leading to osteoporosis and fragility fractures Increased risk of venous thromboembolism Mediastinal germ cell tumours and a raised risk of male breast cancer Significant psychosocial and educational difficulties requiring support Delaying diagnosis by attributing tall stature and learning issues to other causes Overlooking hypogonadism and its long-term skeletal and metabolic consequences Assuming complete infertility without offering fertility counselling and sperm retrieval options Not screening for associated metabolic and thromboembolic risks Klinefelter syndrome results from the presence of one or more supernumerary X chromosomes in a phenotypic male, most commonly a single extra X producing a 47,XXY karyotype, arising from meiotic nondisjunction in either parent. The additional X chromosome material leads to progressive seminiferous tubule fibrosis and hyalinisation, causing primary testicular failure with impaired spermatogenesis and reduced testosterone production, while Leydig cell dysfunction raises luteinising and follicle-stimulating hormone levels. Extra X-linked gene dosage, including genes escaping X-inactivation, is thought to underlie the tall stature, cognitive profile, and other systemic features. Higher-grade aneuploidies produce more severe phenotypes. Life expectancy is close to normal, and with testosterone replacement and multidisciplinary support most men lead full lives, though infertility is usual and comorbidity risk is increased.

Klippel-Feil syndrome — Klippel-Feil sequence, congenital cervical vertebral fusion, cervical vertebral fusion syndrome, KFS Wildervanck (cervico-oculo-acoustic) syndrome Spondylocostal and spondylothoracic dysostoses Oculo-auriculo-vertebral (Goldenhar) spectrum Isolated congenital scoliosis Acquired cervical fusion from juvenile arthritis MURCS association Cervical spine radiographs including flexion-extension views to detect fusion and instability Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine to assess the cord and craniocervical junction Audiological assessment for hearing loss Echocardiography to screen for congenital heart disease Renal ultrasound to detect urinary tract anomalies Assessment for scoliosis and Sprengel deformity Results from failure of normal segmentation of the cervical vertebrae, producing congenital fusion of two or more cervical segments The classic clinical triad is a short neck, a low posterior hairline, and restricted neck movement, though not all features are present in every case Fusion may be limited to a single level or extensive, and the clinical severity varies accordingly Associated anomalies are common and include scoliosis, Sprengel deformity, hearing loss, and cardiac and renal malformations Neurological risk arises because fused segments concentrate stress on adjacent mobile levels, predisposing to instability and cord injury It may occur in isolation or as part of broader spectrums such as the oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum Wildervanck syndrome is a related presentation adding sensorineural deafness and Duane retraction anomaly, seen chiefly in females Neurological signs suggesting cervical cord compression or myelopathy Craniocervical or segmental instability increasing the risk of catastrophic cord injury New or progressive weakness, numbness, or sphincter disturbance High anaesthetic risk from restricted neck movement and potential instability Significant undiagnosed cardiac or renal malformation Overlooking cervical instability and clearing patients for contact sport or manipulation Failing to anticipate a difficult airway from restricted neck extension Missing associated hearing, cardiac, and renal anomalies Not recognising Wildervanck syndrome when deafness and Duane anomaly coexist Attributing new neurological symptoms to unrelated causes rather than adjacent-level stress Klippel-Feil syndrome originates from a disturbance of somite segmentation and resegmentation in the cervical region during early embryogenesis, so that adjacent vertebrae fail to separate and instead fuse. This defective segmentation of the paraxial mesoderm produces the shortened, immobile cervical spine and low hairline, and the same developmental window overlaps with the formation of the ear, heart, kidneys, and scapula, accounting for the associated anomalies. Some familial forms are linked to variants in genes governing segmentation and mesodermal patterning, while many cases are sporadic. The fused rigid segments alter cervical biomechanics, transferring load to neighbouring mobile levels and creating a long-term risk of degenerative change and instability. Many individuals with limited fusion lead normal lives, but extensive fusion or associated instability carries a lifelong risk of neurological injury and degenerative disease, and activities with high cervical impact are generally discouraged.

comprises a capillary malformation (port-wine stain), venous and/or lymphatic malformation, and limb overgrowth, usually affecting one lower limb Persistent embryonic lateral (marginal) veins and deep selected severe cases Signs of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism arising from venous anomalies Evidence of arteriovenous fistulae or high-output cardiac features suggesting Parkes-Weber syndrome Severe or recurrent bleeding from vascular malformations or gastrointestinal/pelvic involvement Recurrent cellulitis or rapidly worsening limb function and deformity Failing to distinguish Klippel-Trenaunay (low-flow) from Parkes-Weber (high-flow) disease, which changes management Overlooking localised intravascular coagulopathy and thromboembolic risk before procedures Neglecting orthopaedic surveillance for progressive limb-length discrepancy and scoliosis Intervening on anomalous superficial veins without confirming adequate deep venous drainage Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome is largely driven by somatic mosaic activating variants in PIK3CA, which encodes the catalytic subunit of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase. Because the variant arises after fertilisation, only a proportion of cells are affected, producing the segmental and asymmetric pattern of disease. Constitutive activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway promotes tissue growth and abnormal vascular development, giving rise to the combined capillary, venous and lymphatic malformations and the overgrowth of soft tissue and bone. Anomalous and persistent embryonic veins contribute to venous hypertension and thrombotic risk. The disorder is sporadic and not inherited. Most affected individuals have a normal life expectancy, but chronic pain, venous insufficiency, orthopaedic problems and recurrent infections cause significant long-term morbidity. Thromboembolic complications and, in some, extensive malformations are the principal serious risks, and targeted pathway inhibitors offer benefit in severe disease.

dysfunction of the anterior temporal lobes and amygdalae, structures central to assigning emotional and biological significance to sensory stimuli. Loss of amygdala function disconnects perception from appropriate emotional appraisal, producing tameness and loss of fear (placidity), indiscriminate oral and sexual exploration, and an inability to attach meaning to what is seen despite intact primary vision. Lifelong multidisciplinary surveillance mitigates avoidable complications.

Koilonychia develops when the normal transverse and longitudinal curvature of the nail is lost or reversed, producing a flattened or upturned, concave plate. A thin, soft plate is more easily deformed by the ordinary pressures of daily use, and reduced availability of iron, which is required for the keratinisation and structural integrity of the nail, is thought to contribute in deficiency states. Softening from repeated exposure to water, solvents, or oils has a similar mechanical effect, while in infancy the nail is naturally thin and pliable, explaining the transient physiological form that corrects itself as the plate matures. The physiological form of childhood resolves spontaneously, and acquired koilonychia usually improves once the cause, particularly iron deficiency, is corrected, although the flattened nail only normalises gradually as new plate grows out.

The aberrant vessel typically courses behind the oesophagus, and the diverticulum with its associated ligamentum arteriosum can complete a vascular ring encircling the trachea and oesophagus. Haploinsufficiency disturbs this epigenetic regulation, affecting neuronal development and function and producing the intellectual disability, hypotonia, epilepsy, and characteristic facial features. The recurrent deletion is facilitated by a common inversion polymorphism of the region carried by a parent, which places the chromosome at increased risk of the non-allelic homologous recombination that generates the deletion. Lifespan is generally not shortened, and the outlook is defined by lifelong intellectual disability of variable degree together with the sociable temperament that is typical of the condition; epilepsy is often manageable, and most individuals make developmental progress with appropriate educational and therapeutic support, though independent living is usually limited.

Koro — Genital retraction syndrome, Shook yang Panic disorder or acute anxiety Psychotic disorder with somatic delusion Body dysmorphic disorder Substance intoxication or withdrawal Depressive disorder with somatic preoccupation Genuine urological or endocrine pathology Temporal lobe epilepsy or organic brain disease in secondary koro Careful history including cultural context and precipitants Mental state examination for psychosis and mood disorder Physical and genital examination to exclude organic pathology and to reassure Substance and toxicology screen Endocrine and metabolic bloods if an organic cause is suspected Neuroimaging or EEG only where secondary organic koro is suspected Collateral and cultural-informant history Culture-bound syndrome of acute anxiety or panic that the genitals (penis, or vulva and nipples in women) are retracting into the body, with a feared outcome of death. Reported predominantly in South and East Asia, with well-documented epidemic or mass outbreaks. The patient may use physical means to prevent retraction, such as clamps, string, or having others hold the organ. Acute onset with intense autonomic anxiety; in the classical epidemic form it is usually short-lived. Distinguish culturally sanctioned epidemic koro from koro-like symptoms secondary to psychiatric or organic disease. In epidemic cases the belief is often overvalued rather than frankly delusional, and reassurance and education are central. Secondary koro can occur within psychotic disorders, depression, substance use, and neurological disease. Self-inflicted genital injury from attempts to prevent retraction Underlying psychosis, severe depression, or suicidal ideation Features suggesting organic brain disease in sporadic cases A genuine urological emergency mislabelled as koro Dismissing distress as merely cultural and failing to treat comorbid anxiety or psychosis Missing self-inflicted genital trauma Overlooking a secondary organic or psychotic cause in sporadic cases Imposing a purely Western delusional framework on a culturally normative fear Koro is best understood as a culturally shaped anxiety syndrome in which culturally transmitted beliefs about genital loss and mortality interact with acute autonomic arousal. In the classical epidemic form, shared cultural models and social contagion generate an overvalued fear of genital retraction with a florid panic response, often precipitated by sexual guilt or perceived transgression. Sympathetic activation can produce genuine cremasteric contraction and smooth-muscle changes that the individual misinterprets as retraction, reinforcing the fear. Secondary or sporadic koro reflects the same cognitive theme emerging from an underlying psychotic, affective, substance-related, or organic disorder. Epidemic, culturally sanctioned koro typically resolves rapidly with reassurance and abatement of the outbreak, whereas secondary koro follows the course of the underlying psychiatric or organic disorder.

window for transplantation Overlooking peripheral neuropathy as a supportive diagnostic clue Krabbe disease is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in GALC, encoding the lysosomal enzyme Deficient activity impairs degradation of galactolipids found in myelin, notably galactosylceramide, and leads to accumulation of the cytotoxic metabolite psychosine (galactosylsphingosine). Psychosine is toxic to oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells, causing widespread loss of myelin-forming cells and demyelination of the central and peripheral nervous system. Stem cell transplantation offers benefit mainly when performed in presymptomatic infants, and once symptoms are established the outlook remains poor.

ovarian surgery is largely palliative or diagnostic Bilateral solid ovarian masses in a woman with weight loss or gastrointestinal symptoms Ascites and rapid clinical deterioration suggesting disseminated malignancy New virilisation or abnormal uterine bleeding from stromal hormone production Evidence of an occult gastric or colorectal primary on investigation Mistaking bilateral ovarian masses for a primary ovarian cancer and omitting a search for the primary Overlooking a small or asymptomatic gastric primary because the ovarian disease dominates Failing to use immunohistochemistry to confirm the metastatic nature and origin Attributing hormonal symptoms to a benign functioning tumour rather than luteinised metastatic stroma A Krukenberg tumour represents ovarian metastasis of a mucin-producing signet-ring cell adenocarcinoma, classically from the stomach. Tumour cells are thought to reach the ovaries chiefly by lymphatic and haematogenous spread, and possibly transcoelomic seeding, where they proliferate within and stimulate the ovarian stroma. The reactive proliferation of ovarian stromal cells, sometimes with luteinisation, is a defining histological feature and can drive hormone production. Because the ovaries provide a receptive stromal environment, metastatic deposits often grow into sizeable bilateral masses that may dominate the clinical picture even when the primary lesion is small or clinically silent. Generally poor, as the tumour signifies disseminated metastatic carcinoma; survival is usually measured in months and depends on the primary tumour and the extent of spread.

krukenberg tumour — Krukenberg tumor, metastatic signet-ring cell carcinoma of ovary primary ovarian mucinous carcinoma primary signet-ring stromal tumour of the ovary other metastatic carcinomas to the ovary (colorectal, breast, pancreatobiliary) primary ovarian carcinoid or goblet cell adenocarcinoma of appendiceal origin sclerosing stromal tumour sex-cord stromal tumour with luteinised stroma lymphoma involving the ovary upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy colonoscopy and assessment of the appendix bilateral breast examination and mammography CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis to identify the primary and disease extent immunohistochemistry panel including CK7, CK20, CDX2 and ovarian markers serum tumour markers such as CA19-9, CEA and CA125 pelvic ultrasound demonstrating bilateral solid adnexal masses A Krukenberg tumour is a metastatic ovarian carcinoma characterised by mucin-filled signet-ring cells set in a cellular, often sarcomatoid-appearing ovarian stroma, and by definition is a secondary rather than a primary ovarian tumour. The stomach is the commonest primary site, followed by the colon, appendix, breast and other gastrointestinal sources; the gallbladder, biliary tree and cervix are less frequent origins. Ovarian involvement is bilateral in the large majority of cases, an important clue that an apparently ovarian mass is in fact metastatic. It often affects women younger than those with primary ovarian carcinoma, and may occasionally present before the primary tumour is recognised. The stroma can be hormonally active, producing oestrogen or androgen, so patients may present with abnormal uterine bleeding or virilisation in addition to a mass. Immunohistochemistry helps confirm a gastrointestinal origin, with signet-ring cells typically expressing cytokeratin 20 and CDX2 and often being negative or only focally positive for cytokeratin 7 and characteristically negative for markers of primary ovarian epithelium. Whenever bilateral solid ovarian masses with signet-ring morphology are found, a diligent search for an occult gastrointestinal or breast primary, including upper and lower endoscopy, is mandatory. Management is directed at the underlying disseminated malignancy; oophorectomy is usually palliative and the overall outlook is poor. bilateral solid ovarian masses, which strongly suggest metastatic rather than primary disease signet-ring cell histology on ovarian sampling new virilisation or abnormal uterine bleeding from hormonally active stroma weight loss, dyspepsia or gastrointestinal bleeding pointing to a gastric or colonic primary widespread peritoneal disease and ascites indicating advanced malignancy Mistaking a Krukenberg tumour for a primary ovarian mucinous carcinoma and failing to search for the true primary. Stopping the work-up after ovarian surgery without endoscopic evaluation of the stomach and bowel. Overlooking a small or early gastric primary that may be clinically silent when the ovarian metastasis presents first. Misattributing virilisation or bleeding to a primary sex-cord tumour rather than hormonally active metastatic stroma. Assuming unilateral disease excludes a Krukenberg tumour, since a minority are unilateral. The Krukenberg tumour represents metastatic spread to the ovary of a mucin-producing adenocarcinoma, most often gastric, in which malignant epithelial cells accumulate intracytoplasmic mucin that displaces the nucleus to give the signet-ring appearance. Metastasis is thought to occur predominantly by lymphatic and haematogenous routes, and possibly transcoelomic spread, which helps explain the frequent bilaterality and the involvement of ovaries even without gross peritoneal disease. A striking feature is the reactive proliferation of ovarian stroma around the infiltrating tumour cells; this stroma may undergo luteinisation and secrete steroid hormones, producing oestrogenic or androgenic effects. Because the ovary provides a hormonally responsive, vascular environment, it is a favoured site for such metastases, particularly in premenopausal women. The prognosis is generally poor because the tumour reflects disseminated metastatic carcinoma, and survival is measured in months for most patients, being influenced chiefly by the site, stage and treatability of the primary tumour.

fluid overload Missing occult infection because the usual signs of fever and inflammation are blunted Kwashiorkor is a form of severe acute malnutrition in which protein deficiency is relatively greater than energy deficiency. Reduced hepatic synthesis of albumin lowers plasma oncotic pressure, and this, together with increased capillary permeability, sodium retention, and oxidative stress, produces the characteristic oedema. Loss of immune competence, gut mucosal atrophy, and micronutrient deficiencies compound the picture, and metabolic adaptation to starvation makes the child vulnerable to hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, and dangerous fluid and electrolyte shifts during treatment. With careful staged nutritional rehabilitation and treatment of infection, recovery is possible, but mortality is high when complications such as sepsis, hypoglycaemia, or refeeding are not anticipated and managed.

Kyasanur Forest disease — KFD, monkey fever, Kyasanur forest disease virus infection Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever Severe dengue Leptospirosis Severe malaria Scrub typhus and other rickettsial infections Other viral encephalitides (for the neurological phase) Dengue haemorrhagic fever Leptospirosis Scrub typhus Severe malaria Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever RT-PCR for KFD viral RNA during the early viraemic phase KFD-specific IgM and IgG serology in the later course Full blood count, liver function, and coagulation studies to assess severity CSF examination and neuroimaging if the neurological second phase is suspected Exclusion of dengue, malaria, leptospirosis, and scrub typhus given the endemic overlap in India A tick-borne flaviviral haemorrhagic fever endemic to India, first recognised in the Kyasanur forest of Karnataka and now reported across several Western Ghats states Transmitted mainly by Haemaphysalis ticks, with monkeys serving as amplifying hosts, so the disease clusters among forest workers, farmers, and people with rural forest exposure Illness typically begins abruptly with high fever, severe headache, myalgia, and prostration, often with conjunctival injection and gastrointestinal symptoms A haemorrhagic phase with bleeding from gums, nose, or gut and thrombocytopenia may develop, and a subset of patients experience a biphasic course with a later neurological phase The second phase, after an afebrile interval, can bring meningoencephalitic features such as headache, tremor, and altered mentation Laboratory clues include leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and raised transaminases; diagnosis is confirmed by RT-PCR early and serology later, handled with appropriate biosafety Management is supportive; a vaccine has been used in endemic districts of Karnataka, and tick-bite avoidance is central to prevention Mucosal or gastrointestinal bleeding with progressive thrombocytopenia Return of fever with neurological features such as altered mentation, tremor, or meningism marking the second phase Hypotension, dehydration, or signs of multi-organ involvement Severe hepatic derangement or coagulopathy indicating a complicated course Attributing a forest-exposed febrile patient's illness to dengue or malaria and missing KFD in an endemic Western Ghats setting Interpreting the afebrile interval as recovery and discharging before the neurological second phase declares itself Neglecting biosafety precautions when handling blood and specimens from a suspected haemorrhagic fever Overlooking occupational and vaccination history in patients from endemic districts Kyasanur Forest disease virus is an RNA flavivirus transmitted to humans through the bite of infected hard ticks, with monkeys acting as amplifying hosts during epizootics. After inoculation the virus disseminates and infects multiple organs, producing viraemia with a systemic inflammatory response, increased vascular permeability, and haemorrhagic manifestations together with cytopenias and hepatic involvement. In some patients the virus involves the central nervous system during a second phase, producing meningoencephalitis. Most patients recover with supportive care, though the illness can be severe with haemorrhagic and neurological complications and a meaningful case-fatality rate; the biphasic form with encephalitis tends to have a more protracted recovery.

kyrle disease — hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis in cutem penetrans, Kyrle's disease reactive perforating collagenosis perforating folliculitis prurigo nodularis hypertrophic lichen planus keratosis pilaris and other follicular keratoses multiple keratoacanthomas perforating granuloma annulare skin biopsy of an intact keratotic papule to demonstrate the epidermal invagination, parakeratotic plug and perforation renal function tests and estimated glomerular filtration rate fasting glucose and glycated haemoglobin liver function tests serum calcium, phosphate and albumin thyroid function tests urinalysis for proteinuria A perforating dermatosis characterised by large keratotic papules and nodules with a central horny plug, typically on the lower limbs, and often only mildly pruritic compared with other perforating disorders. Classically described in adults with chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus or hepatic dysfunction, overlapping clinically with acquired perforating dermatosis. Lesions may coalesce into verrucous plaques and characteristically follow a Koebner (isomorphic) distribution along scratch lines. Histology shows a keratotic plug filling an epidermal invagination with a parakeratotic column and focal perforation through the epidermis, with basophilic connective-tissue debris in the plug. In classic Kyrle disease the perforating channel is said not to specifically eliminate collagen or elastic fibres, distinguishing it from reactive perforating collagenosis and elastosis perforans serpiginosa, though overlap is common. Diagnosis rests on correlating the clinical picture (keratotic plugged papules on legs of a patient with renal or metabolic disease) with the perforating histology. Treatment mirrors other acquired perforating dermatoses: emollients, keratolytics, topical or oral retinoids, phototherapy, and control of the underlying systemic disease. A rare familial form with childhood onset and no systemic association is described, but most cases are acquired in adulthood. presentation without recognised renal, hepatic or metabolic disease, warranting systemic evaluation features suggesting secondary infection of excoriated lesions rapid enlargement of a solitary nodule raising concern for keratoacanthoma or squamous cell carcinoma intractable pruritus indicating uncontrolled uraemia or hyperglycaemia labelling any leg-predominant perforating eruption as Kyrle disease without histological correlation, given substantial overlap with other perforating dermatoses overlooking the need to screen for chronic kidney disease, diabetes and hepatic dysfunction mistaking a coalescent verrucous plaque for a viral wart or squamous neoplasm sampling a superinfected or excoriated lesion, which distorts the characteristic histology Kyrle disease is regarded by many authorities as a variant within the acquired perforating dermatosis spectrum. The primary abnormality is thought to be a focal disturbance of epidermal keratinisation producing a keratotic plug and a clone of abnormally differentiating keratinocytes that accelerates upward, breaching the basement membrane and perforating the epidermis. Basophilic degenerate connective-tissue debris accumulates within the plug and is eliminated transepidermally. In acquired cases, metabolic derangements of uraemia, diabetes and hepatic disease, together with microangiopathy and repetitive scratch-induced trauma (Koebnerisation), are believed to trigger the aberrant keratinisation and perforation. The course is chronic with a tendency to relapse; individual lesions may resolve leaving scars or hyperpigmentation, and overall activity generally parallels control of the underlying systemic disease.

Labyrinthine concussion — inner ear concussion, cochleovestibular concussion, post-traumatic labyrinthine dysfunction Temporal bone fracture, otic-capsule sparing or violating Perilymph fistula Traumatic benign paroxysmal positional vertigo Ossicular chain disruption causing conductive loss Post-concussion syndrome or central vestibular injury Tympanic membrane perforation Acoustic trauma from an associated blast Pure-tone audiometry to document the pattern and degree of hearing loss High-resolution CT of the temporal bone to exclude fracture Tympanometry to assess middle-ear and ossicular status Videonystagmography with positional testing Vestibular-evoked myogenic potentials MRI of the brain if central injury is suspected Follows head trauma, often a temporal-bone or occipital impact, without a visible fracture of the otic capsule Presents with sensorineural hearing loss, frequently in the higher frequencies, together with tinnitus and vertigo or imbalance beginning soon after the injury Vertigo may be constant at first and then settle, or may present as positional vertigo if otoconia are dislodged (traumatic BPPV) The mechanism is an energy or pressure wave transmitted through the skull to the membranous labyrinth and hair cells, causing microscopic damage without frank bony disruption It is a diagnosis of exclusion - temporal-bone fracture, perilymph fistula, ossicular disruption, and central brain injury must be ruled out Management is largely supportive, with vestibular rehabilitation for persistent imbalance and repositioning manoeuvres for traumatic BPPV, while hearing loss is often permanent High-resolution CT of the temporal bone and audiometry are central to distinguishing it from fracture and conductive causes Progressive or fluctuating hearing loss suggesting a perilymph fistula Otorrhoea or clear fluid leak raising concern for a CSF fistula Facial nerve weakness Focal neurological deficit or deteriorating conscious level Vertigo accompanied by severe or worsening headache Attributing all post-traumatic dizziness to concussion and missing a perilymph fistula or temporal-bone fracture Overlooking traumatic BPPV, which is readily treated with repositioning manoeuvres Failing to obtain baseline audiometry, which is important both clinically and medicolegally after head injury Missing a co-existing CSF leak or facial nerve injury A blow to the head transmits kinetic energy through the skull to the fluid-filled inner ear even when the bony otic capsule stays intact. The resulting pressure wave and shearing forces damage the delicate cochlear and vestibular hair cells and their supporting structures, and may dislodge utricular otoconia into the semicircular canals. Cochlear injury produces sensorineural hearing loss, classically affecting higher frequencies, together with tinnitus, while vestibular injury causes vertigo and disequilibrium. Because the damage is at the cellular level rather than a gross fracture, imaging is frequently normal, and the diagnosis rests on the temporal relationship to trauma and on exclusion of other injuries. Vertigo and imbalance often improve over weeks to months through central compensation and vestibular rehabilitation, but sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus are frequently permanent.

Lactate dehydrogenase deficiency — LDH deficiency, LDH-A subunit deficiency, LDH-B subunit deficiency, LDHA gene, LDHB gene McArdle disease and other glycogen storage myopathies Phosphofructokinase deficiency Phosphoglycerate mutase deficiency Fatty-acid oxidation disorders causing exertional rhabdomyolysis Statin- or drug-induced myopathy Analytical interference causing a spuriously low LDH Serum and red-cell lactate dehydrogenase activity with isoenzyme analysis Forearm ischaemic exercise test assessing the lactate response Creatine kinase and myoglobin during exertional symptoms Full blood count and blood film to confirm the absence of haemolysis Skin assessment for the associated erythematosquamous lesions Molecular testing of the LDHA or LDHB genes A recessive enzyme defect that, unusually among glycolytic disorders, characteristically does not cause haemolytic anaemia Deficiency of the muscle (M/A) subunit produces exercise intolerance and exertional myoglobinuria, resembling a glycogenoses-type myopathy A dermatological phenotype with erythematosquamous skin lesions has been described with M-subunit deficiency The subunit composition differs between tissues, so red cells tolerate the defect while muscle does not, explaining the paradoxical absence of haemolysis A characteristic laboratory clue is a very low or absent serum LDH activity, which may be an incidental finding on routine biochemistry Diagnosis is confirmed by isoenzyme analysis and enzyme assay, with LDHA or LDHB mutation testing Management centres on avoiding the strenuous exertion that provokes rhabdomyolysis; specific treatment for the red cell is not required as haemolysis is absent Exertional rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria and risk of acute kidney injury Recurrent disabling muscle cramps limiting activity Extensive or ulcerating skin lesions requiring dermatological input Pregnancy complications reported in M-subunit deficiency Expecting a haemolytic anaemia and being misled when it is absent Dismissing an incidentally low serum LDH as artefact without considering the diagnosis Not testing the lactate response to exercise in a patient with exertional symptoms Overlooking the associated skin manifestations Lactate dehydrogenase interconverts pyruvate and lactate, regenerating the NAD+ needed to sustain anaerobic glycolysis under conditions of high energy demand. The enzyme is a tetramer of M (A) and H (B) subunits combined in tissue-specific ratios. In the red cell, alternative routes for NAD+ regeneration mean that deficiency does not appreciably shorten survival, so haemolysis is characteristically absent; in skeletal muscle, however, loss of the M subunit impairs anaerobic energy supply during exertion and predisposes to cramps, exercise intolerance and rhabdomyolysis. Prognosis is generally good; because haemolysis is absent, morbidity relates to muscle symptoms and skin involvement, which are usually manageable with avoidance of heavy exertion.

Lactational Mastitis — lactational mastitis, puerperal mastitis, breastfeeding mastitis, postpartum mastitis Breast abscess Blocked (plugged) duct without infection Engorgement Inflammatory breast carcinoma (especially if non-lactating or non-resolving) Candidal nipple or ductal infection causing pain Galactocele Clinical diagnosis is usually sufficient; investigations are reserved for atypical or non-resolving cases Breast milk culture and sensitivity where infection is severe, recurrent, hospital-associated, or unresponsive to first-line antibiotics Breast ultrasound to identify or exclude an abscess when a fluctuant or non-resolving mass is present Needle aspiration of a suspected abscess for both diagnosis and drainage with culture of the aspirate Consideration of biopsy and specialist referral if inflammatory changes fail to resolve, to exclude malignancy Lactational mastitis is an inflammatory, usually infective, condition of the breast in a breastfeeding woman, presenting with a tender, hot, erythematous, wedge-shaped area often accompanied by fever and flu-like malaise It typically begins with milk stasis from ineffective or infrequent drainage, which then becomes secondarily infected, most often by Staphylococcus aureus entering through a cracked or damaged nipple Continued effective milk removal is the cornerstone of treatment; breastfeeding from the affected side should continue and is safe for the infant Supportive measures include frequent feeding or expression, correcting attachment and positioning, warmth before feeds and cold after for comfort, adequate hydration, rest, and simple analgesia Antibiotics active against Staphylococcus aureus are indicated when symptoms are severe, systemic, or fail to improve within a short period of conservative management, or when a nipple fissure is infected A localised fluctuant, non-resolving mass suggests a breast abscess, which requires drainage by needle aspiration or incision alongside antibiotics Failure to improve with appropriate treatment should prompt consideration of an abscess or, in a non-lactating or persistent case, inflammatory breast cancer Prevention centres on good breastfeeding technique, ensuring full drainage, avoiding abrupt weaning, and prompt attention to nipple trauma Recurrent mastitis warrants review of feeding technique and evaluation for a persistent focus or underlying breast pathology A fluctuant or non-resolving mass indicating breast abscess requiring drainage Systemic sepsis with high fever, rigors, tachycardia, or hypotension Failure to respond to appropriate antibiotics and milk drainage within a few days Persistent inflammatory changes, skin thickening, or peau d'orange raising concern for inflammatory breast cancer Overlying skin breakdown or rapidly spreading erythema Advising cessation of breastfeeding, which worsens stasis and prolongs the illness Failing to recognise and drain a breast abscess, treating with antibiotics alone Overlooking inflammatory breast cancer in non-lactating or persistent presentations Not addressing the underlying poor attachment or drainage, leading to recurrence Delaying antibiotics when systemic or severe features are present Inadequate or infrequent milk drainage leads to milk stasis and rising intraductal pressure, causing milk to leak into the surrounding stroma and provoke a local inflammatory response. Nipple trauma, commonly from poor latch, provides a portal of entry for skin flora, predominantly Staphylococcus aureus, so the stagnant milk becomes a culture medium and infection is established. If untreated, the localised infection can organise into a walled-off collection of pus, forming a breast abscess. The wedge-shaped distribution reflects involvement of a segment of the ductal-lobular system. Most cases resolve quickly with effective milk removal and, when needed, appropriate antibiotics, and breastfeeding can continue throughout. Delayed or inadequate treatment increases the risk of abscess formation, which then requires drainage. Recurrence is uncommon when feeding technique is optimised, and the majority of women recover fully without lasting effect on lactation.

Lafora disease (progressive myoclonic epilepsy, EPM2A/NHLRC1) — Lafora body disease, EPM2A, NHLRC1, progressive myoclonic epilepsy type 2, malin/laforin deficiency Unverricht-Lundborg disease (EPM1) Mitochondrial disease including MERRF Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses Sialidosis (cherry-red spot myoclonus syndrome) Juvenile Huntington disease Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy Molecular genetic testing of EPM2A and NHLRC1 EEG to document background slowing, generalised and occipital discharges, and photosensitivity Skin biopsy for periodic acid-Schiff-positive Lafora bodies when genetics are inconclusive Brain MRI to exclude structural causes and assess for atrophy Metabolic and mitochondrial screening to exclude other progressive myoclonic epilepsies Lafora disease is a severe autosomal recessive progressive myoclonic epilepsy caused by biallelic variants in EPM2A (laforin) or NHLRC1 (malin) It typically begins in previously healthy adolescents with myoclonus, occipital and generalised seizures including visual seizures, and progressive cognitive decline The hallmark is relentless deterioration into dementia, worsening intractable myoclonus, and dependency, unlike the milder course of Unverricht-Lundborg disease Diagnosis is confirmed by molecular genetic testing; historically periodic acid-Schiff-positive Lafora bodies (polyglucosan inclusions) are demonstrated in skin (eccrine duct) or other tissues EEG shows progressive background slowing with generalised and occipital epileptiform discharges and photosensitivity Treatment is symptomatic with anti-myoclonic and antiseizure medication; sodium-channel-blocking agents can worsen myoclonus and should generally be avoided Genetic counselling and early palliative planning are important given the poor prognosis Rapidly worsening myoclonus and seizures becoming refractory to treatment Progressive dementia and loss of independence in a previously healthy teenager Aspiration, immobility, or status epilepticus signalling advanced disease Deterioration after introduction of sodium-channel-blocking antiseizure drugs Confusing Lafora disease with the more treatable Unverricht-Lundborg disease, giving falsely reassuring prognosis Prescribing sodium-channel-blocking agents that aggravate myoclonus Attributing early cognitive decline to psychiatric illness or medication Delaying genetic confirmation and counselling in a suspected progressive myoclonic epilepsy Lafora disease results from defective regulation of glycogen synthesis. Laforin (a glycogen phosphatase) and malin (an E3 ubiquitin ligase) normally act together to control glycogen branching and chain length. Loss of either protein leads to synthesis of abnormally long, poorly branched, and hyperphosphorylated glycogen that is insoluble and precipitates as polyglucosan Lafora bodies. These inclusions accumulate in neurones and other tissues, driving neuronal dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and progressive neurodegeneration that manifests as the characteristic progressive myoclonic epilepsy and dementia. Lafora disease is relentlessly progressive, with escalating myoclonus, refractory seizures, and dementia leading to profound disability and death typically within about a decade of onset.

Lagophthalmos — incomplete eyelid closure Facial nerve palsy Thyroid eye disease with proptosis or retraction Cicatricial eyelid shortening Proptosis from orbital disease Nocturnal lagophthalmos Floppy eyelid syndrome Measurement of the closure gap and assessment of blink Corneal examination with fluorescein for exposure keratopathy Assessment of the Bell phenomenon and corneal sensation Evaluation for facial nerve palsy or orbital cause Thyroid assessment where relevant Incomplete closure of the eyelids, leaving the ocular surface exposed and at risk of drying The commonest cause is facial (seventh nerve) palsy weakening the orbicularis oculi Nocturnal lagophthalmos, exposure from proptosis or lid retraction, and cicatricial lid shortening are other causes A protective upward rotation of the globe on attempted closure (Bell phenomenon) helps guard the cornea Exposure keratopathy, ranging from punctate staining to ulceration, is the main threat to sight Management centres on intensive ocular surface lubrication and protection, with surgical measures for persistent cases Corneal ulceration or thinning Reduced corneal sensation compounding exposure risk (neurotrophic component) Absent Bell phenomenon Progressive or severe exposure with visual loss Underestimating exposure risk when corneal sensation is also reduced Relying on infrequent lubrication in significant lagophthalmos Overlooking nocturnal lagophthalmos as a cause of morning irritation Failing to protect the eye during the recovery phase of facial palsy Lagophthalmos occurs when the eyelids cannot fully appose, whether from weakness of the orbicularis oculi (as in facial nerve palsy), mechanical factors such as proptosis or lid retraction, or cicatricial shortening of the lids. Failure of the normal blink and closure leaves the interpalpebral cornea and conjunctiva exposed, so the tear film evaporates and the surface dries. Without an effective Bell phenomenon or protective measures, exposure leads to epithelial breakdown, keratopathy and potential ulceration or perforation. With diligent lubrication and protection the cornea can be preserved, and many neurogenic cases improve as the palsy recovers; persistent or severe exposure may need surgical lid procedures to protect sight.

Laing distal myopathy (MYH7) — MPD1, Laing early-onset distal myopathy, MYH7-related distal myopathy, myosin heavy chain 7 distal myopathy Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and other causes of distal neurogenic foot drop Myotonic dystrophy Other distal myopathies (Udd/tibial, Welander, Markesbery-Griggs) Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy with foot extensor weakness Chronic acquired distal neuropathy Congenital myopathies with distal predominance Serum creatine kinase (usually normal or mildly raised) Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to confirm a myopathic, non-neurogenic process Muscle biopsy with histochemistry and immunohistochemistry Muscle MRI to define the pattern of selective muscle involvement Targeted MYH7 sequencing or a distal myopathy gene panel Baseline and periodic cardiac evaluation with ECG and echocardiography Caused by pathogenic variants in MYH7, the gene encoding slow/beta-cardiac myosin heavy chain, with autosomal dominant inheritance Typically an early-onset distal myopathy, often beginning in childhood or adolescence, though onset can extend into adulthood Weakness starts in the anterior compartment of the lower legs, producing foot drop and weakness of great-toe and ankle dorsiflexion, classically with a 'hanging big toe' sign Finger extensor and neck flexor weakness commonly follow, while progression is slow and many
