normal or only mildly elevated and electromyography shows a myopathic pattern Muscle biopsy may show fibre-type disproportion, type 1 fibre predominance, and sometimes cores or hyaline bodies, but findings can be non-specific so genetic confirmation is important Diagnosis rests on the characteristic distal weakness distribution combined with MYH7 genetic testing Symptoms or signs of cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia given the MYH7 association Rapidly progressive or asymmetric weakness suggesting an alternative diagnosis Respiratory muscle involvement with reduced vital capacity Prominent dysphagia or bulbar features atypical for Laing myopathy Mistaking the foot drop for a peripheral neuropathy and missing the myopathic cause Assuming normal creatine kinase excludes a myopathy Over-interpreting non-specific biopsy changes without genetic confirmation Neglecting cardiac screening given the MYH7 gene's cardiac role Laing distal myopathy is caused by dominant variants in MYH7, which encodes the slow/beta-cardiac myosin heavy chain expressed in type 1 skeletal muscle fibres and cardiac muscle. Mutant myosin impairs the assembly and function of the thick filament of the sarcomere, disturbing contraction of predominantly slow-twitch fibres. This selectively affects muscles rich in type 1 fibres, accounting for the early anterior lower-leg and neck flexor involvement, and the shared gene explains the potential for associated cardiac disease. Progression is typically slow, and most patients retain independent walking well into adulthood, though distal weakness gradually extends more proximally over decades; life expectancy is usually normal unless significant cardiac or respiratory involvement develops.

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome — LEMS, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, myasthenic syndrome of Lambert-Eaton Myasthenia gravis Inflammatory or metabolic myopathy Motor neuron disease Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy Botulism (also a presynaptic disorder) Guillain-Barre syndrome Serum antibodies against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels Repetitive nerve stimulation at low and high frequency and post-exercise testing CT of the chest and, if negative, FDG-PET to search for small-cell lung cancer Interval tumour surveillance imaging when initial screening is negative but risk is high SOX1 antibodies as a marker supporting an underlying small-cell lung cancer Single-fibre electromyography in equivocal neuromuscular transmission cases A presynaptic disorder of neuromuscular transmission caused by antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels that reduce acetylcholine release Presents with proximal limb weakness, especially the legs, together with autonomic features such as dry mouth, constipation, and erectile dysfunction Strength may transiently improve with sustained or repeated effort (post-exercise facilitation), and depressed reflexes can augment after exercise Ocular and bulbar symptoms are usually milder than in myasthenia gravis, though some overlap occurs About half of cases are paraneoplastic, most often linked to small-cell lung cancer, and may precede the tumour diagnosis Repetitive nerve stimulation shows a low baseline compound muscle action potential with decrement at low frequency and marked increment at high frequency or after exercise Treatment addresses any underlying tumour and enhances acetylcholine release; immunotherapy is used for symptom control A validated screening score helps stratify the likelihood of underlying small-cell lung cancer and guides surveillance Any new diagnosis should trigger a directed search for occult malignancy, especially small-cell lung cancer Weight loss, haemoptysis, or a smoking history increasing suspicion of underlying tumour Progressive bulbar or respiratory weakness requiring monitoring of airway and ventilation Severe autonomic failure causing symptomatic hypotension or gastrointestinal stasis Misdiagnosing LEMS as myasthenia gravis and missing the search for lung cancer Stopping tumour surveillance too early after an initially negative chest scan Overlooking autonomic symptoms that are an important diagnostic clue Failing to appreciate post-exercise facilitation on examination and electrophysiology Attributing proximal weakness to a primary myopathy without neuromuscular junction testing In LEMS, IgG autoantibodies target P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels on the presynaptic motor nerve terminal. Reduced calcium influx during depolarisation diminishes the quantal release of acetylcholine, so the endplate potential often fails to reach threshold at rest, causing weakness. Repeated activity allows calcium to accumulate in the terminal, temporarily augmenting release and improving strength, which explains facilitation. The same antibodies act on autonomic ganglia and terminals, producing cholinergic autonomic failure. In paraneoplastic cases the tumour expresses calcium channels that trigger the cross-reactive immune response. Symptoms often improve with treatment of any underlying cancer and with therapies that enhance acetylcholine release; the overall outlook is dominated by the associated malignancy when present, whereas non-paraneoplastic disease tends to follow a more indolent, manageable course.

swallow and airway protection Positive calcium-channel antibodies indicating high likelihood of underlying malignancy Severe autonomic instability Rapid progression of generalised weakness reflexes as a peripheral neuropathy Overlooking drugs that further impair neuromuscular transmission Not recognising respiratory involvement early Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome results from autoantibodies directed against presynaptic voltage-gated P/Q-type calcium channels at the motor nerve terminal and in autonomic nerve endings. Reduced calcium influx during the nerve action potential impairs the quantal release of acetylcholine, weakening neuromuscular transmission and producing muscle weakness and autonomic dysfunction. Because more calcium accumulates in the terminal with repeated rapid firing, sustained or high-frequency activity transiently boosts transmitter release, explaining the characteristic post-exercise facilitation of strength and reflexes. In paraneoplastic cases, small-cell lung cancer expresses the same calcium channels, triggering the cross-reactive antibody response. Symptomatic and immunomodulatory treatment often improves strength, and non-paraneoplastic disease may be well controlled long term; in paraneoplastic cases the neurological syndrome frequently improves with successful tumour treatment, though overall prognosis is dominated by the underlying cancer.

Lamellar ichthyosis — TGM1, transglutaminase-1 deficiency, autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis, LI Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma Harlequin ichthyosis (severe end of spectrum) X-linked ichthyosis Netherton syndrome Ichthyosis vulgaris Acquired ichthyosis from systemic disease Molecular genetic testing including TGM1 and other congenital ichthyosis genes Skin biopsy showing marked orthohyperkeratosis with a normal or thickened granular layer In vitro transglutaminase-1 activity assay where available Ophthalmology assessment for ectropion and corneal exposure Assessment of thermoregulation and hydration, particularly in neonates Prenatal or carrier genetic testing for at-risk families A form of autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis, most often caused by variants in TGM1 encoding transglutaminase-1, with several other causative genes Typically presents at birth as a collodion baby encased in a taut, shiny membrane that sheds over the first weeks Evolves into large, plate-like, dark brown adherent scales with relatively little underlying erythema, contrasting with the erythrodermic phenotype Ectropion and eclabium are common and cause chronic ocular exposure problems Scalp scarring alopecia, palmoplantar keratoderma, and reduced sweating with heat intolerance are frequent Sits on a clinical spectrum with congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma; some patients show overlapping features Management centres on topical emollients and keratolytics, with oral retinoids for severe disease Neonatal dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and temperature instability in the collodion phase Corneal exposure and ulceration from severe ectropion Heat intolerance and hyperthermia from impaired sweating Secondary skin infection of fissured skin Assuming all collodion babies have lamellar ichthyosis when the membrane can precede several distinct disorders Overlooking heat intolerance from anhidrosis, risking hyperthermia in warm environments or exercise Neglecting ophthalmic monitoring for ectropion-related corneal damage Failing to counsel on the recessive inheritance and recurrence risk Lamellar ichthyosis most commonly arises from deficiency of transglutaminase-1, an enzyme that cross-links structural proteins to form the cornified cell envelope and covalently attaches lipids to the envelope surface. Loss of enzyme activity prevents formation of a normal cornified envelope and disrupts the lipid scaffold of the stratum corneum, impairing the permeability barrier and desquamation. Compensatory hyperproliferation and retention of corneocytes produce the characteristic thick, plate-like scaling. Other causative genes (including those for lipid transport and processing) can produce overlapping phenotypes within the autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis spectrum. It is a lifelong disorder; after the vulnerable collodion period most patients stabilise into chronic generalised scaling that requires continuous skin care, with visual and thermoregulatory complications influencing overall morbidity.

LMNA laminopathy with dilated cardiomyopathy and muscular dystrophy — LMNA-related dilated cardiomyopathy, cardiolaminopathy, lamin A/C cardiomyopathy, Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (LMNA), limb-girdle muscular dystrophy 1B Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy from EMD (emerin) and other genes Other genetic dilated cardiomyopathies with conduction disease (including desmin and SCN5A) Myotonic dystrophy with cardiac conduction involvement Sarcoglycanopathies and other limb-girdle muscular dystrophies Cardiac sarcoidosis or other infiltrative conduction-system disease Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy LMNA sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, often within a cardiomyopathy or muscular dystrophy gene panel 12-lead ECG and ambulatory (Holter) monitoring to detect conduction disease and ventricular arrhythmia Echocardiography and cardiac MRI to assess ventricular function and myocardial fibrosis Serum creatine kinase, electromyography and, where needed, muscle biopsy for the neuromuscular phenotype Baseline and serial respiratory function testing given diaphragmatic and spinal involvement Arrhythmic risk stratification to guide the timing of defibrillator implantation Cascade genetic testing and cardiac screening of at-risk relatives Caused by variants in LMNA, which encodes the nuclear envelope proteins lamin A and C; the same gene underlies a spectrum including dilated cardiomyopathy, Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy and limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 1B The neuromuscular phenotype often features humeroperoneal or limb-girdle weakness with early, prominent joint contractures (elbows, Achilles tendons and spine) and rigid spine, sometimes preceding overt cardiac symptoms Cardiac disease characteristically begins with conduction-system involvement, such as atrioventricular block and atrial arrhythmias, and progresses to dilated cardiomyopathy with heart failure LMNA cardiolaminopathy carries a high risk of malignant ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death, which can occur even before or out of proportion to left ventricular dysfunction Because of this arrhythmic risk, guidelines set a lower threshold for implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement rather than a pacemaker alone, taking account of risk markers such as non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, atrioventricular conduction delay, non-missense variants and male sex Lifelong cardiac surveillance with ECG, ambulatory monitoring and cardiac imaging (echocardiography and cardiac MRI) is essential, and competitive or intense exertion is generally discouraged There is no cure; management is multidisciplinary and supportive, combining heart failure and device therapy, contracture and respiratory care, and cascade genetic screening of relatives Syncope, presyncope or documented non-sustained ventricular tachycardia signalling high arrhythmic risk High-grade atrioventricular block or symptomatic bradyarrhythmia Rapidly declining left ventricular function or decompensated heart failure Family history of sudden cardiac death in a gene-positive relative Respiratory insufficiency from diaphragmatic weakness Implanting a pacemaker alone for conduction disease when a defibrillator is warranted because of the sudden-death risk Underestimating arrhythmic risk in patients with preserved or only mildly reduced ejection fraction Focusing on the neuromuscular weakness and under-recognising the life-threatening cardiac involvement Failing to arrange cascade screening, leaving at-risk relatives unprotected Permitting intense or competitive exercise despite the arrhythmic risk LMNA encodes lamins A and C, intermediate filament proteins that form the nuclear lamina underlying the inner nuclear membrane. This meshwork provides mechanical support to the nucleus, organises chromatin and regulates gene expression and mechanotransduction. Pathogenic variants weaken the lamina and disturb these functions, rendering mechanically stressed tissues such as cardiac and skeletal muscle particularly vulnerable. In the heart this produces fibrosis and disease of the conduction system and myocardium, leading to arrhythmia, conduction block and dilated cardiomyopathy, while skeletal muscle involvement causes weakness and the early contractures characteristic of the Emery-Dreifuss and limb-girdle phenotypes. Prognosis in LMNA disease is dominated by the cardiac phenotype: conduction disease and dilated cardiomyopathy tend to progress, and the substantial risk of ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death makes early defibrillator protection central to reducing mortality. With timely device therapy, heart failure management and cardiac surveillance, outcomes can be improved, though the neuromuscular component contributes to cumulative disability.

success by seizure control alone rather than language recovery Delaying immunomodulatory or steroid therapy in resistant cases with ongoing regression Landau-Kleffner syndrome is an epileptic encephalopathy in which intense epileptiform activity, markedly activated during non-REM sleep, disrupts the function of language-related cortical networks, particularly perisylvian regions. Continuous or near-continuous spike-wave discharges through slow-wave sleep are thought to interfere with the sleep-dependent consolidation and maturation of language and other higher functions, producing acquired aphasia and cognitive-behavioural regression even when overt seizures are few. The underlying cause is often unknown, with genetic and immune contributions implicated in some cases. Seizures, when present, usually remit by adolescence, but language and cognitive outcomes are variable and a significant proportion of children have persistent language or learning difficulties. Earlier recognition and effective suppression of the sleep-activated discharges are associated with better language recovery.

Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis — LCH, histiocytosis X, eosinophilic granuloma, Hand-Schuller-Christian disease, Letterer-Siwe disease Osteomyelitis or Ewing sarcoma (for bone lesions) Leukaemia or lymphoma Neuroblastoma with bony metastases Seborrhoeic or atopic dermatitis (for skin lesions) Other histiocytic disorders (e.g. haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, juvenile xanthogranuloma) Chronic infection (e.g. tuberculosis) Biopsy with immunohistochemistry for CD1a and CD207 (langerin) BRAF V600E and broader MAPK pathway mutation testing Skeletal imaging survey (radiographs and/or PET) to map bone lesions Assessment of risk organs: liver and spleen imaging, full blood count, liver function Endocrine evaluation and MRI of the pituitary/hypothalamus if diabetes insipidus is suspected Baseline evaluation for pulmonary and CNS involvement when indicated A clonal proliferative disorder of Langerhans-type dendritic cells that can range from a single isolated lesion to widespread multisystem disease. Bone is the most commonly involved site, often presenting as a painful lytic lesion, classically in the skull but also in other flat and long bones. Skin involvement can mimic seborrhoeic dermatitis or a persistent scaly, petechial rash, particularly in infants. Diabetes insipidus from pituitary or hypothalamic involvement is a characteristic endocrine manifestation and may be the presenting feature. Risk organ involvement (liver, spleen, and bone marrow) identifies higher-risk multisystem disease with greater mortality. Diagnosis rests on biopsy showing characteristic cells expressing CD1a and CD207 (langerin); Birbeck granules may be seen on electron microscopy. Many cases harbour activating mutations in the MAPK pathway, most commonly BRAF V600E, which has therapeutic implications. Treatment ranges from observation or local therapy for single-system disease to systemic chemotherapy for multisystem or risk-organ disease. Risk-organ (liver, spleen, marrow) involvement indicating high-risk multisystem disease Cytopenias suggesting marrow infiltration Polyuria and polydipsia indicating diabetes insipidus from CNS/pituitary disease Rapidly progressive multisystem disease in an infant Neurodegenerative CNS involvement causing progressive neurological decline Mistaking the infantile skin rash for simple seborrhoeic dermatitis and delaying diagnosis Overlooking diabetes insipidus as an early or isolated manifestation Assuming a solitary lytic bone lesion is infection or a benign cyst without biopsy Failing to assess for risk-organ involvement, which changes treatment intensity and prognosis Langerhans cell histiocytosis is now understood as a myeloid neoplasm driven by activating mutations of the MAPK/ERK signalling pathway, most often BRAF V600E, in dendritic cell precursors. Constitutive pathway activation causes accumulation of pathological CD1a-positive, langerin-positive histiocytes that, together with eosinophils and other inflammatory cells, form granulomatous infiltrates. These lesions destroy local tissue (such as lytic bone lesions) and, when disseminated, impair function of organs including the liver, spleen, marrow, and pituitary. Single-system disease, especially isolated bone lesions, often has an excellent prognosis and may even regress; multisystem disease with risk-organ involvement carries higher mortality. Survivors are at risk of long-term sequelae such as diabetes insipidus, other endocrinopathies, orthopaedic problems, and neurodegeneration.

immunosuppression is reserved for symptomatic cytopenias or transfusion dependence Anaemia, including a pure red cell aplasia pattern, and thrombocytopenia may accompany the neutropenia Severe neutropenia with recurrent or life-threatening infection Transfusion-dependent anaemia or symptomatic pancytopenia Rapidly rising lymphocyte count or transformation to an aggressive phenotype Constitutional symptoms suggesting an alternative aggressive lymphoproliferative disorder Assuming a modest large granular lymphocytosis is reactive without checking clonality Overlooking STAT3 mutation testing that can clarify a borderline diagnosis Attributing neutropenia solely to rheumatoid arthritis or its drugs Treating asymptomatic patients who could simply be monitored T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukaemia arises from a clonal expansion of mature cytotoxic (usually CD8 positive) T lymphocytes. Chronic antigen-driven stimulation is thought to trigger the expansion, which then escapes normal apoptotic control through constitutive activation of the JAK/STAT signalling pathway, frequently driven by acquired activating mutations in STAT3. The persistent cytotoxic clone suppresses granulopoiesis and erythropoiesis in the marrow and, together with autoimmune mechanisms, produces the neutropenia, anaemia and thrombocytopenia that dominate the clinical picture. The strong link with rheumatoid arthritis reflects the shared background of dysregulated immune activation. Most patients have an indolent disease with prolonged survival, and morbidity relates mainly to infection from neutropenia; a minority have refractory cytopenias or, rarely, aggressive transformation.

Laron syndrome (GH receptor / GH insensitivity) — Laron dwarfism, growth hormone insensitivity syndrome, GHR mutation, primary IGF-1 deficiency Isolated growth hormone deficiency IGF-1 gene or IGF-1 receptor defects Constitutional delay of growth and puberty Small-for-gestational-age short stature without catch-up Hypothyroidism causing growth failure Other skeletal dysplasias or syndromic short stature Chronic systemic illness or malnutrition Basal growth hormone (high or normal) and IGF-1 (low) IGF-1 generation test, which fails to raise IGF-1 after growth hormone IGF binding protein-3 and acid-labile subunit levels GHR gene sequencing and testing of downstream signalling genes where indicated Fasting glucose monitoring for hypoglycaemia in infants Bone age and growth velocity assessment Usually autosomal recessive growth hormone insensitivity, most often from growth hormone receptor (GHR) mutations, causing severe postnatal growth failure The defining biochemistry is high or normal circulating growth hormone with low IGF-1 that fails to rise after growth hormone administration Clinical features include proportionate short stature, frontal bossing, a depressed nasal bridge, small genitalia, and a high-pitched voice Fasting hypoglycaemia is common in infancy because IGF-1 deficiency and altered fuel handling impair glucose maintenance Because the defect lies downstream of growth hormone, growth hormone replacement is ineffective; recombinant IGF-1 is the specific treatment for growth and metabolic benefit Populations with Laron syndrome show notably low rates of diabetes and cancer, illustrating the growth hormone/IGF-1 axis in growth and proliferation It contrasts with isolated growth hormone deficiency, where growth hormone itself is low and replacement works Diagnosis rests on the growth pattern, the high-GH/low-IGF-1 profile with a failed IGF-1 generation test, and GHR genetics Recurrent fasting or nocturnal hypoglycaemia in infancy Severe growth failure crossing centiles downward Signs of hypoglycaemic seizure or encephalopathy Marked developmental or feeding difficulties in an affected infant Giving growth hormone replacement, which fails because the defect is downstream Misdiagnosing the condition as isolated growth hormone deficiency without checking IGF-1 response Overlooking infantile hypoglycaemia as a presenting feature Ignoring the diagnostic value of the IGF-1 generation test Failing to distinguish GHR defects from IGF-1 or IGF-1-receptor defects Laron syndrome is a state of growth hormone insensitivity in which growth hormone is secreted normally or in excess but cannot act, most commonly because of loss-of-function mutations in the growth hormone receptor (GHR). Growth hormone normally binds its hepatic receptor to stimulate IGF-1 production, which mediates most of its growth-promoting effects; when the receptor is defective, IGF-1 generation fails despite high growth hormone levels. The resulting profound IGF-1 deficiency produces severe postnatal growth failure and characteristic craniofacial features, while loss of IGF-1's metabolic actions contributes to fasting hypoglycaemia in early life. Because the block is at or beyond the receptor, only IGF-1 replacement, not growth hormone, restores signalling. Untreated individuals have marked short stature but often a favourable metabolic profile with low rates of diabetes and malignancy; recombinant IGF-1 improves growth, though final height usually remains below average.

Larsen syndrome — FLNB, filamin B disorder Atelosteogenesis (also FLNB-related) Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita Ehlers-Danlos syndromes with joint instability Desbuquois dysplasia Otopalatodigital spectrum disorders Recessive Larsen-like syndromes Skeletal survey documenting joint dislocations, accessory carpal ossification, and spinal anomalies Cervical spine imaging including flexion-extension views to assess kyphosis and instability FLNB molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Airway and respiratory assessment for tracheomalacia before anaesthesia Echocardiography where cardiac involvement is suspected Audiological assessment for hearing loss Characterised by congenital dislocations of large joints, notably bilateral knee dislocations, together with hip and elbow dislocations and severe talipes The dominant form is caused by variants in FLNB encoding filamin B, a cytoskeletal protein regulating chondrocyte function; rarer recessive Larsen-like phenotypes have distinct causes A characteristic flat facial appearance with a depressed nasal bridge, prominent forehead, and widely spaced eyes aids recognition Hand findings include cylindrical, spatulate fingers and, radiographically, an accessory carpal ossification centre Cervical spine abnormalities with kyphosis and instability are a critical hazard that can cause myelopathy and complicate airway management Additional features may include cleft palate, hearing loss, and, in some, cardiac and respiratory (tracheomalacia) involvement Diagnosis integrates the pattern of congenital joint dislocations and facial features with FLNB molecular testing Cervical kyphosis or instability with myelopathy, particularly around anaesthesia Airway compromise from tracheomalacia or cervical involvement Neurological deterioration from spinal cord compression Respiratory distress in infancy Overlooking cervical kyphosis and instability, risking cord injury during airway management Reducing knee or hip dislocations without recognising the underlying syndrome and its spinal risks Failing to assess for tracheomalacia before anaesthesia Confusing it with arthrogryposis without appropriate radiographic and genetic evaluation Larsen syndrome most often results from dominant variants in FLNB, which encodes filamin B, a cytoskeletal protein that cross-links actin and regulates signalling and mechanical responses in chondrocytes. Disturbed filamin B function alters chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation and the development of joints, ligaments, and the vertebral column. This produces the hallmark congenital large-joint dislocations, ligamentous laxity, cervical spine anomalies, and characteristic craniofacial and hand features. FLNB variants underlie a spectrum of skeletal disorders ranging from Larsen syndrome to more severe atelosteogenesis phenotypes. With careful orthopaedic and spinal management, intelligence and lifespan are generally normal, but untreated cervical instability can cause devastating neurological injury, and joint dislocations and foot deformity require staged surgical and physiotherapy management.

hoarseness to benign causes without laryngoscopy Missing advanced supraglottic tumours that present without early voice change Underestimating impending airway compromise in a patient with stridor Neglecting the functional impact of treatment on voice and swallowing when counselling patients Laryngeal carcinoma arises from the squamous epithelium lining the supraglottis, glottis, or subglottis. Chronic carcinogen exposure from tobacco smoke and alcohol produces field change with progressive dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, and invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Behaviour depends on subsite anatomy: the true vocal cords have limited lymphatic drainage so glottic tumours cause early hoarseness but spread to nodes late, whereas the richly lymphatic supraglottis allows earlier cervical nodal metastasis. Local extension can involve cartilage, paraglottic and pre-epiglottic spaces, and adjacent hypopharynx. Early glottic cancers have high cure and voice-preservation rates, whereas advanced or node-positive supraglottic and subglottic tumours carry poorer prognosis; overall outcome depends on stage, subsite, and treatment response.

endoscopy Attributing feeding-related symptoms solely to reflux and delaying definitive assessment Overlooking associated congenital anomalies that alter management Underestimating aspiration risk and permitting unmodified oral feeding in a symptomatic infant A laryngeal cleft results from failure of the posterior cricoid lamina and the tracheo-oesophageal septum to fuse during embryogenesis, leaving an abnormal midline communication between the airway posteriorly and the digestive tract. The deficient partition removes the normal separation that protects the airway during swallowing, so liquids and secretions spill directly into the larynx and trachea. The degree of aspiration and respiratory compromise parallels the depth of the cleft, ranging from occasional aspiration with a shallow interarytenoid defect to life-threatening soiling of the airway and recurrent pneumonia with an extensive cleft reaching the carina. Shallow clefts often do well with conservative feeding and reflux management, and repaired clefts generally have a good outcome, but deep laryngotracheo-oesophageal clefts carry substantial morbidity and mortality, especially where associated anomalies coexist.

bulky papillomas before anaesthesia Laryngeal papillomas are the airway expression of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, in which human papillomavirus, predominantly the low-risk genotypes 6 and 11, infects the respiratory epithelium and drives proliferation of the basal squamous cells. Juvenile-onset disease is thought to result from vertical transmission during passage through an infected birth canal, whereas adult acquisition is less clearly defined. The virus persists within apparently normal-looking mucosa, which explains the characteristic tendency to recur after removal. Lesions cluster at squamociliary junctions and produce friable, frond-like growths that add mass to the vocal folds and, when bulky, obstruct the airway; rarely the process spreads distally or undergoes malignant change. The course is unpredictable and often chronic with repeated recurrences, and some childhood cases eventually remit spontaneously, but aggressive multifocal or distally spreading disease carries significant morbidity and a small but important risk of malignant transformation.

and a tracheostomy is best avoided as it may promote distal spread Malignant transformation is uncommon but recognised, particularly with certain HPV types or after irradiation, so persistent or atypical lesions warrant biopsy Progressive stridor and airway obstruction from bulky laryngeal disease requiring urgent airway management Distal spread into the trachea and bronchi indicating aggressive disease Features suggesting malignant transformation such as a firm, ulcerated, or rapidly enlarging lesion Rapid recurrence needing frequent surgical intervention Aggressive surgery that damages the vocal cords and causes scarring or web formation Performing a tracheostomy that may encourage distal tracheobronchial spread Assuming benignity and not biopsying atypical or persistent lesions Overlooking airway compromise in a child presenting only with a hoarse cry Laryngeal papillomatosis results from infection of the respiratory epithelium by human papillomavirus, most often types 6 and 11, which drives proliferation of squamous epithelium into finger-like papillary fronds supported by fibrovascular cores. Lesions favour the transition zones between squamous and ciliary epithelium, so the vocal cords are commonly affected. In children the virus is usually acquired at birth from an infected maternal genital tract, and the immature or immunologically naive host tends to develop multiple, recurrent lesions. Latent virus in adjacent normal-looking mucosa underlies the persistent recurrence after removal, and lesions may seed distally in the airway. The course is unpredictable and marked by recurrence; juvenile disease may require many procedures over years before eventual regression around puberty in some children, while adult disease is often more limited, and although malignant change is rare it is an important long-term consideration.

epiglottitis, life-threatening airway obstruction Hoarseness persisting beyond a few weeks, particularly in a smoker, requires laryngeal visualisation to exclude malignancy Stridor or respiratory difficulty, especially in a child, suggesting airway compromise or epiglottitis Hoarseness persisting beyond a few weeks in a smoker raising concern for laryngeal cancer Associated dysphagia, weight loss, haemoptysis or a neck mass Rapidly worsening symptoms with drooling and toxaemia Attributing persistent hoarseness to simple laryngitis and delaying laryngoscopy in a smoker Overlooking laryngopharyngeal reflux as a driver of chronic symptoms Underestimating airway risk in a child with laryngeal inflammation Failing to address vocal misuse and continued irritant exposure Laryngitis is inflammation of the laryngeal mucosa, especially the vocal folds. In acute laryngitis, viral (or sometimes bacterial) infection produces mucosal hyperaemia and oedema that increase the mass and stiffness of the vocal folds, disturbing their vibratory pattern and causing hoarseness. In chronic laryngitis, sustained irritation from voice overuse, tobacco smoke, gastric reflux or persistent infection leads to ongoing mucosal changes such as oedema, thickening and keratosis. In children, the narrow subglottis means that inflammatory swelling can significantly compromise the airway. Acute laryngitis usually resolves within days to a couple of weeks with conservative measures, whereas chronic laryngitis requires removal of the underlying irritant for improvement; persistent hoarseness always warrants exclusion of a serious cause.

laryngopyocele with pain, fever, and rapidly enlarging swelling threatening the airway Progressive stridor or dyspnoea from a large internal component Rapid or unilateral enlargement without a pressure-related occupation Assuming a laryngocele is purely idiopathic and missing an obstructing saccular tumour in an adult Draining a laryngopyocele without addressing the underlying sac and airway risk Underestimating the external component and planning an inadequate approach Failing to warn wind players or glassblowers about the aggravating role of raised intralaryngeal pressure A laryngocele is an air-containing dilatation of the laryngeal saccule, the small blind-ending pouch that arises from the anterior ventricle between the true and false vocal folds. Persistently raised pressure within the larynx, or narrowing of the saccular opening, allows air to distend the saccule while maintaining its communication with the airway. If it stays medial to the thyrohyoid membrane it remains internal; if it herniates through the membrane alongside the superior laryngeal neurovascular bundle it becomes external. Because a saccular obstruction can also produce a fluid-filled saccular cyst, an important consideration is a coexisting mucosal neoplasm at the saccular opening, particularly in adults. Surgical excision is usually curative with a low recurrence rate, and the outlook is excellent provided any underlying obstructing neoplasm is identified and treated and infective complications are avoided.

Laryngomalacia — floppy larynx, congenital laryngeal stridor, soft larynx Vocal cord paralysis Subglottic stenosis Vascular ring or other extrinsic airway compression Laryngeal web, cyst, or haemangioma Tracheomalacia Acquired causes of stridor such as croup or foreign body Flexible awake laryngoscopy Assessment of feeding and growth Pulse oximetry or sleep study if obstruction or apnoea is suspected Bronchoscopy or airway endoscopy to exclude synchronous lesions in severe or atypical cases Evaluation for gastro-oesophageal reflux when contributory Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of chronic stridor in infants and results from collapse of soft, immature supraglottic structures during inspiration. The typical presentation is inspiratory stridor that begins in the first weeks of life, worsens with feeding, crying, agitation, or lying supine, and improves when the infant is calm or prone. In most infants the condition is mild and self-limiting, with symptoms peaking in the early months and resolving as the airway matures, usually within the first one to two years. Flexible laryngoscopy in the awake infant is the diagnostic gold standard, demonstrating the characteristic dynamic supraglottic collapse. Gastro-oesophageal reflux commonly coexists and can aggravate symptoms, so it is often addressed as part of management. Feeding difficulty, choking or coughing with feeds, and poor weight gain indicate more significant disease and warrant closer evaluation. Severe disease with significant obstruction, apnoea, or failure to thrive may require surgical intervention such as supraglottoplasty. Persistent or atypical stridor should prompt evaluation for additional or synchronous airway lesions. Cyanosis, apnoea, or significant desaturation Marked work of breathing or worsening obstruction Feeding difficulty with choking, aspiration, or failure to thrive Stridor that is severe, progressive, or atypical for laryngomalacia Life-threatening obstructive episodes Assuming all infant stridor is laryngomalacia and missing another airway lesion Underestimating severity by not assessing feeding, growth, and oxygenation Overlooking a synchronous second airway abnormality Failing to recognise and manage contributing gastro-oesophageal reflux In laryngomalacia the supraglottic tissues, including the epiglottis and aryepiglottic folds, are excessively soft and poorly supported, and there is often associated neuromuscular immaturity affecting airway tone and coordination. During inspiration the negative airway pressure draws these floppy structures inward, causing dynamic collapse over the laryngeal inlet and producing turbulent airflow and inspiratory stridor. The obstruction is worse when airflow demand or negative pressure increases, such as with crying, feeding, or agitation, and lessens with maturation as the tissues become firmer and neuromuscular control improves. Coexisting reflux can worsen supraglottic oedema and symptoms. The outlook is excellent for the majority, in whom mild laryngomalacia resolves spontaneously as the airway matures; a minority with severe disease require surgery, which is generally effective.

Lassa fever — Lassa virus infection, Lassa haemorrhagic fever, VHF Severe malaria Typhoid (enteric) fever Other viral haemorrhagic fevers (Ebola, CCHF) Severe bacterial sepsis Leptospirosis Severe dengue Severe malaria Typhoid fever Ebola virus disease Bacterial sepsis RT-PCR for Lassa virus RNA in early illness, performed under strict biosafety Lassa-specific IgM and IgG serology and antigen detection where available Full blood count, liver and renal function, and coagulation studies to gauge severity Exclusion of malaria and typhoid, which are common and treatable co-considerations in endemic regions All sampling coordinated with the laboratory and public health authorities under enhanced biosafety A viral haemorrhagic fever endemic to West Africa, caused by an arenavirus, with the multimammate rat as the natural reservoir; humans are infected through contact with rodent excreta or contaminated food Onset is typically gradual with fever, malaise, headache, sore throat, and retrosternal or muscular pain, which makes early distinction from other febrile illnesses difficult Many infections are mild or subclinical, but severe cases progress to bleeding, facial and neck oedema, pleural and pericardial effusions, encephalopathy, and shock Sensorineural hearing loss is a characteristic and often permanent complication, sometimes occurring during recovery Person-to-person and nosocomial transmission through body fluids is well recognised, so isolation, barrier precautions, and safe specimen handling are essential It is especially severe in pregnancy, with high maternal and fetal mortality, particularly in the third trimester This is a medical emergency and a notifiable disease; ribavirin is used and is most effective when started early, alongside intensive supportive care Mucosal bleeding, facial or neck oedema, or effusions indicating severe disease Encephalopathy, seizures, or rapidly rising transaminases Hypotension, shock, or signs of multi-organ failure Any suspected case requires immediate isolation, barrier nursing, and notification because of high nosocomial transmission risk, with pregnancy signalling especially high risk Delaying isolation and barrier precautions, exposing staff and other patients to nosocomial spread Attributing the gradual febrile onset solely to malaria or typhoid and missing Lassa in an endemic or travel context Starting antiviral therapy too late, when its benefit is greatest early in the illness Overlooking evolving hearing loss and failing to counsel about this recognised sequela Lassa virus is an enveloped RNA arenavirus that, after exposure to rodent excreta or infected body fluids, replicates in multiple organs and suppresses innate immune responses. Widespread infection of endothelial cells and immune dysregulation lead to impaired vascular integrity and platelet dysfunction rather than large-scale tissue necrosis, producing capillary leak, oedema, and haemorrhage. Hepatic, adrenal, and endothelial involvement, together with a poorly controlled inflammatory response, drive progression to shock and multi-organ failure in severe cases. Most infections are mild, but hospitalised severe cases carry a high case-fatality rate, worse with delayed treatment, bleeding, and organ failure; survivors may be left with permanent sensorineural hearing loss, and pregnancy is associated with markedly poorer maternal and fetal outcomes.

Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults — LADA, latent autoimmune diabetes of adults, type 1.5 diabetes, slowly progressive autoimmune diabetes Type 2 diabetes mellitus Classic type 1 diabetes mellitus Maturity-onset diabetes of the young Ketosis-prone diabetes Secondary diabetes from pancreatic disease Drug- or steroid-induced hyperglycaemia Islet autoantibody testing, particularly anti-GAD dysfunction Lipid profile and assessment of features of insulin resistance to help differentiate from type 2 diabetes Periodic reassessment of beta-cell reserve to anticipate insulin requirement A type 2 diabetes shows early failure of oral agents or unexpectedly rapid progression to insulin dependence Anti-GAD antibodies are the most commonly positive marker and support the diagnosis There may be an association with other organ-specific autoimmune conditions such as thyroid disease Recognition matters because these patients progress to insulin requirement and benefit from monitoring Unexplained weight loss suggesting advancing insulin deficiency Coexisting autoimmune disorders such as adrenal or thyroid disease Assuming all adult-onset diabetes is type 2 and missing the autoimmune nature Delaying insulin when oral agents are clearly failing Not testing autoantibodies in a leaner adult with atypical type 2 diabetes Overlooking associated autoimmune endocrine disease Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults is an autoimmune diabetes in which immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells proceeds more slowly than in classic childhood type 1 diabetes. Circulating islet autoantibodies, most often against glutamic acid decarboxylase, reflect this ongoing autoimmune process. Because residual beta-cell function persists at diagnosis, patients initially maintain some endogenous insulin secretion and may be controlled without insulin, but progressive loss of beta-cell mass leads to eventual insulin dependence. The disorder shares genetic and immunological features with type 1 diabetes while its adult onset and initial non-insulin-requiring course cause frequent misclassification as type 2 diabetes. Patients generally progress to insulin dependence over months to years as beta-cell function declines; with timely recognition and appropriate transition to insulin, glycaemic control and complication risk can be managed similarly to other forms of diabetes, and monitoring for associated autoimmune conditions is advisable.

Latent nystagmus — fusion maldevelopment nystagmus syndrome, manifest latent nystagmus Congenital (infantile) nystagmus syndrome Acquired gaze-evoked nystagmus Spasmus nutans Peripheral or central vestibular nystagmus Periodic alternating nystagmus Orthoptic assessment of ocular alignment and fusion Careful acuity testing that avoids full occlusion (using a fogging lens) Documentation of the nystagmus with each eye fixating Assessment for associated infantile esotropia and dissociated vertical deviation Eye-movement recording where diagnostic doubt persists A conjugate horizontal jerk nystagmus that appears or intensifies when one eye is occluded, now termed fusion maldevelopment nystagmus syndrome The fast phase beats toward the viewing (uncovered) eye, reversing direction depending on which eye fixates It is strongly associated with early disruption of binocular vision, such as infantile esotropia and dissociated vertical deviation When some nystagmus is present even with both eyes open it is called manifest latent nystagmus Covering one eye to measure visual acuity can worsen the nystagmus and falsely reduce the measured acuity Recognition matters mainly to avoid misinterpreting it as a sign of intracranial disease Vertical or purely torsional nystagmus suggesting central disease Associated neurological signs New onset in an older child or adult Optic atrophy or other afferent pathway signs Underestimating acuity by fully occluding one eye during testing Mistaking it for acquired nystagmus and ordering unnecessary imaging Missing the associated infantile strabismus and amblyopia Confusing manifest latent nystagmus with congenital nystagmus syndrome Latent nystagmus arises from maldevelopment of binocular fusion during early infancy, typically in the context of infantile strabismus, which disturbs the normal cortical monocular motion processing that underlies gaze holding. Monocular occlusion unbalances this system and elicits a jerk nystagmus whose fast phase beats toward the fixating eye. The condition reflects a developmental abnormality of the visual motion pathways rather than an acquired brainstem or cerebellar lesion. The condition itself is benign and stable; visual outcome depends on the associated strabismus and amblyopia, which should be managed on their own merits.

Latent tuberculosis infection — LTBI, latent TB, TB infection Active pulmonary tuberculosis (must be excluded) Prior BCG vaccination causing tuberculin reactivity Non-tuberculous mycobacterial sensitisation Old healed tuberculosis on imaging without active disease Subclinical active tuberculosis Non-tuberculous mycobacterial exposure causing test cross-reactivity BCG-related tuberculin positivity Tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay to detect infection Symptom screening and chest radiography to exclude active tuberculosis HIV testing given its major impact on reactivation risk Assessment for other risk factors such as diabetes, immunosuppressive therapy and silicosis Sputum evaluation if any features suggest active disease Latent tuberculosis infection is a state of persistent immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis without clinical, radiological or bacteriological evidence of active disease People with LTBI are asymptomatic and non-infectious, but carry a lifetime risk of reactivation into active tuberculosis, greatest in the first two years after infection Diagnosis relies on the tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assays, both of which detect immune sensitisation but cannot distinguish latent from active disease Active tuberculosis must always be excluded, by symptom screening and chest imaging, before treating someone for latent infection Reactivation risk is markedly increased by HIV, anti-TNF therapy, organ transplantation, silicosis, diabetes, malnutrition and other immunosuppressive states TB preventive treatment substantially reduces the risk of progression, using rifamycin- or isoniazid-based short-course regimens without specifying doses India's NTEP prioritises TB preventive treatment for household contacts of pulmonary TB, people living with HIV and other high-risk groups as part of the End TB strategy Any symptoms or imaging findings suggesting active tuberculosis, which changes management entirely Recent close contact with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis, especially in children under five Planned immunosuppression such as anti-TNF therapy or transplantation Coexisting HIV infection markedly raising reactivation risk Starting preventive treatment without first excluding active tuberculosis, risking monotherapy of active disease and resistance Interpreting a positive test as active disease when it only indicates infection Overlooking preventive treatment in eligible high-risk contacts and people living with HIV Ignoring the reduced sensitivity of immune-based tests in severe immunosuppression After inhalation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, most immunocompetent individuals mount a cell-mediated immune response that contains the organism within granulomas, where bacilli persist in a dormant, metabolically quiescent state. This equilibrium between host immunity and bacillary persistence defines latency, and there is likely a spectrum from complete eradication to subclinical infection. When immunity wanes or is suppressed, dormant bacilli can resume replication, breaching the granuloma and producing active, potentially transmissible disease. The tuberculin and interferon-gamma tests measure the memory T-cell response to mycobacterial antigens rather than the presence of live bacilli. Most people with latent infection never develop active disease, but progression risk is highest soon after infection and in the immunocompromised; TB preventive treatment substantially lowers this risk and is central to India's elimination goals.

Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) — tennis elbow, lateral epicondylalgia, common extensor origin tendinopathy, lateral elbow tendinopathy Radial tunnel syndrome (posterior interosseous nerve entrapment) Radiocapitellar osteoarthritis Cervical radiculopathy (C6 or C7) Posterolateral rotatory instability of the elbow Osteochondral or plica pathology of the radiocapitellar joint Referred pain from the shoulder Clinical provocative tests (resisted wrist extension, Cozen's test, Mill's test) Ultrasound to confirm common extensor tendinopathy or a tear MRI in refractory or diagnostically unclear cases Plain radiographs to assess the joint and exclude calcification or arthritis Nerve conduction studies if radial tunnel syndrome or radiculopathy is suspected Lateral elbow pain arising from the common extensor origin, chiefly extensor carpi radialis brevis Despite the '-itis' name it is a degenerative tendinopathy (angiofibroblastic tendinosis) from overuse, not primary inflammation Provoked by gripping and wrist and finger extension; pain is reproduced by resisted wrist extension and by Cozen's test Tenderness is typically just distal and anterior to the lateral epicondyle Diagnosis is largely clinical, with ultrasound or MRI reserved for uncertain or refractory cases Often self-limiting; management is load modification, avoiding aggravating grip activity, and progressive or eccentric loading with physiotherapy Corticosteroid injection may give short-term relief but is associated with poorer longer-term outcomes and possible tendon harm, so it is used cautiously Counterforce bracing, and shockwave therapy in resistant cases, may help Neurological symptoms suggesting nerve entrapment or cervical radiculopathy Night pain, systemic upset or a mass suggesting other pathology Locking or instability implying intra-articular derangement Failure to respond, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis Treating as inflammatory and relying on rest or repeated steroid injections rather than progressive loading Corticosteroid injection giving short-term relief but poorer long-term outcomes Missing radial tunnel syndrome, which can mimic or coexist Overlooking the cervical spine as a source of referred pain Lateral epicondylitis is an overuse tendinopathy of the common extensor origin at the lateral humeral epicondyle, predominantly involving extensor carpi radialis brevis. Repetitive gripping and wrist extension generate cumulative tensile load that exceeds the tendon's repair capacity. Histology shows angiofibroblastic degeneration with disorganised collagen, increased ground substance and neovascularisation, and a notable absence of inflammatory cells, so it is best regarded as a tendinosis rather than a true '-itis'. Chronic change reflects a failed healing response at the enthesis. The majority recover within a year with load management and rehabilitation, although symptoms can be prolonged; a minority with refractory disease may need shockwave therapy or, rarely, surgery.

Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome — Wallenberg syndrome, posterior inferior cerebellar artery syndrome, PICA syndrome, lateral bulbar syndrome Medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome Vestibular neuronitis or acute peripheral vertigo Cerebellar infarction or haemorrhage Demyelinating plaque of the brainstem in multiple sclerosis Vertebral artery dissection presenting with posterior circulation ischaemia Brainstem neoplasm or metastasis Diffusion-weighted MRI of the brainstem to confirm acute dorsolateral medullary infarction MR or CT angiography of the vertebrobasilar system to dorsolateral medulla, most often due to intracranial vertebral artery disease rather than a discrete posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion The hallmark is a crossed sensory pattern: ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature over the face with contralateral loss over the trunk and limbs Vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and nystagmus reflect vestibular nucleus involvement and are frequently the presenting complaint Ipsilateral Horner syndrome (partial ptosis, miosis, facial anhidrosis) arises from disruption of the descending sympathetic fibres Dysphagia, hoarseness, and reduced gag reflex follow nucleus ambiguus involvement and carry a genuine aspiration risk Ipsilateral limb and gait ataxia occur from inferior cerebellar peduncle and cerebellar involvement, and intractable hiccups may be prominent Motor power is characteristically preserved because the pyramidal tract lies ventromedially and is spared Progressive drowsiness or new long-tract signs suggesting brainstem or cerebellar swelling with mass effect Silent aspiration with subsequent pneumonia in an apparently mild presentation Vertebral artery dissection with risk of recurrent embolism or basilar extension Central vertigo mistaken for benign peripheral disease and discharged Attributing isolated vertigo and vomiting to a peripheral labyrinthine cause and missing the stroke Allowing oral feeding before a formal swallow assessment and precipitating aspiration Overlooking a subtle ipsilateral Horner syndrome that would localise the lesion Assuming preserved limb power excludes a significant brainstem infarct The syndrome follows ischaemia of the dorsolateral medulla oblongata, a territory supplied by penetrating branches of the intracranial vertebral artery and the posterior inferior cerebellar artery. Because vertebral disease is the usual culprit, the infarct straddles several closely packed structures: the spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract (ipsilateral facial sensory loss), the crossed spinothalamic tract (contralateral body sensory loss), the vestibular nuclei (vertigo and nystagmus), the nucleus ambiguus (dysphagia and hoarseness), the descending sympathetic pathway (Horner syndrome), and the inferior cerebellar peduncle (ipsilateral ataxia). The medial position of the corticospinal tract explains the preservation of limb strength, producing the classic dissociated, crossed clinical picture. Many patients recover functional swallowing and gait over weeks to months, though disabling ataxia, persistent dysphagia, or central neuropathic facial pain can remain; overall outcome is generally more favourable than for medial or ventral brainstem strokes.

cause and discharged New long-tract or bulbar signs suggesting medial extension Attributing acute vertigo and hearing loss to a peripheral labyrinthine cause and missing the stroke Overlooking a subtle Horner syndrome that helps localise the lesion Confusing lateral pontine with lateral medullary syndrome when auditory signs are not sought Assuming preserved limb power excludes a significant brainstem infarct Lateral pontine syndrome follows ischaemia of the lateral pontine tegmentum and adjacent cerebellum, supplied chiefly by the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, a branch of the basilar artery. The infarct affects the facial nucleus and nerve (ipsilateral facial weakness), the vestibulocochlear nucleus and often the labyrinthine artery territory (vertigo and ipsilateral hearing loss), the trigeminal nucleus and crossing spinothalamic tract (ipsilateral facial and contralateral body sensory loss), the middle cerebellar peduncle (ipsilateral ataxia), and the descending sympathetic fibres (Horner syndrome). The medial location of the corticospinal tract usually spares limb strength, giving a crossed brainstem picture analogous to Wallenberg syndrome but at pontine level and with prominent auditory involvement. Vertigo and facial weakness often improve over weeks, but ipsilateral hearing loss may be permanent and cerebellar ataxia can persist; outcome is generally favourable unless the infarct is large or heralds basilar disease.

Latex allergy — natural rubber latex allergy, latex hypersensitivity, NRL allergy Irritant contact dermatitis from gloves or hand hygiene Type IV allergic contact dermatitis to rubber accelerator chemicals Anaphylaxis from perioperative drugs, antiseptics (chlorhexidine), or antibiotics Food-related latex-fruit cross-reactive allergy Idiopathic urticaria or angioedema Serum latex-specific IgE testing Skin prick testing with a standardised latex extract where available Patch testing for suspected delayed contact dermatitis to rubber chemicals Serum tryptase during a suspected acute systemic reaction Supervised glove-use or challenge testing in specialist settings when the diagnosis is uncertain IgE-mediated (type I) reactions to natural rubber latex proteins range from contact urticaria to rhinoconjunctivitis, asthma, and anaphylaxis, and are distinct from irritant or allergic contact dermatitis from rubber-processing chemicals Healthcare workers, patients with spina bifida or urogenital anomalies, and those with repeated surgical or catheter exposure are at highest risk owing to frequent mucosal and cutaneous contact Powdered gloves historically amplified sensitisation because latex allergen adsorbed to cornstarch became airborne, so a shift to powder-free low-protein or non-latex gloves has markedly reduced new cases The latex-fruit syndrome reflects cross-reactivity between latex proteins and plant allergens, so patients may also react to banana, avocado, kiwi, and chestnut Diagnosis combines a compatible history with skin testing and serum latex-specific IgE; a validated skin test extract may not be uniformly available, making the history and in-vitro testing important Reactions can occur through skin, mucosal, inhalational, or parenteral routes, and intraoperative anaphylaxis may be the presenting event when latex is contacted internally Cornerstones of care are strict avoidance, a latex-safe environment for procedures, medical-alert identification, and a self-injectable adrenaline device for those with systemic reactions Type IV allergic contact dermatitis from rubber accelerators (e.g. thiurams, carbamates) presents as delayed eczema and is confirmed by patch testing, not by IgE tests Intraoperative or procedural anaphylaxis with hypotension or bronchospasm requiring immediate intramuscular adrenaline and removal of all latex sources Progressive airway or respiratory symptoms after mucosal or inhalational latex exposure Systemic reaction in a high-risk patient (spina bifida, multiple surgeries) not previously identified as latex-allergic Recurrent reactions despite avoidance suggesting unrecognised hidden latex exposure Confusing delayed contact dermatitis from rubber chemicals with true IgE-mediated latex allergy Failing to arrange a latex-safe environment for surgery or dental and radiological procedures Overlooking cross-reactive foods in the latex-fruit syndrome Not counselling the patient to carry medical-alert identification and an adrenaline device Type I latex allergy results from IgE sensitisation to water-soluble proteins in natural rubber harvested from Hevea brasiliensis. Repeated cutaneous, mucosal, or airborne exposure drives production of latex-specific IgE bound to mast cells and basophils; re-exposure cross-links this IgE and triggers mediator release causing urticaria, bronchospasm, and anaphylaxis. Airborne allergen bound to glove powder facilitates respiratory sensitisation. Structural homology between latex proteins (e.g. hevein-related and profilin allergens) and plant proteins accounts for cross-reactivity in the latex-fruit syndrome. A separate delayed, T-cell-mediated contact dermatitis is caused not by latex protein but by rubber-manufacturing chemicals. With reliable avoidance and a latex-safe healthcare environment, most patients avoid further reactions and occupational sensitisation often improves after exposure ceases. Unrecognised sensitisation, however, can lead to severe or fatal perioperative anaphylaxis.

Latrodectism (widow spider envenomation) — black widow spider bite, widow spider envenomation Acute abdomen from a surgical cause Other spider or arthropod envenomation Tetanus Hypocalcaemic or metabolic tetany Sympathomimetic toxidrome Clinical diagnosis from the bite history and characteristic spasms Assessment of vital signs for autonomic disturbance Exclusion of a surgical abdomen where abdominal rigidity dominates Basic bloods and electrolytes to exclude metabolic mimics Cardiac monitoring in severe autonomic involvement Envenomation by widow spiders causes painful muscle cramps and spasm that spread from the bite site to the abdomen, back and limbs Severe abdominal rigidity can mimic an acute surgical abdomen Autonomic features such as hypertension, tachycardia, sweating and restlessness are common The local bite may be surprisingly minor despite intense systemic symptoms Most cases are managed with analgesia and supportive care, with antivenom reserved for severe envenoming The characteristic pattern of diffuse painful spasms with autonomic upset helps distinguish it from other bites Severe uncontrolled hypertension or chest pain Respiratory distress Priapism or marked autonomic instability Symptoms in very young, elderly or pregnant patients Mistaking the abdominal rigidity for a surgical emergency and operating Underestimating pain severity despite a minor-looking bite Overlooking autonomic complications Using antivenom without weighing hypersensitivity risk Widow spider venom contains alpha-latrotoxin, which binds presynaptic nerve terminals and triggers massive release of neurotransmitters including acetylcholine and noradrenaline, followed by depletion. This excessive neurotransmission produces sustained muscle contraction, pain and autonomic overactivity. The systemic syndrome of cramping pain and autonomic disturbance reflects this widespread presynaptic effect rather than local tissue destruction. The condition is rarely fatal and symptoms usually settle over hours to a few days; antivenom can shorten severe episodes but carries a risk of hypersensitivity.

from other basement membrane dystrophy Stromal scarring from prior keratitis Reis-Bucklers and Thiel-Behnke anterior stromal dystrophies Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with retroillumination to identify (type I) is autosomal dominant and caused by mutations in the TGFBI gene on chromosome 5q31, part of the TGFBI dystrophy cluster Amyloid deposits stain with Congo red and show apple-green birefringence and dichroism under polarised light Recurrent corneal erosions are frequent early in the disease and can dominate the symptomatic picture before vision declines Progressive stromal haze between the lattice lines eventually reduces vision as deposits coalesce over decades Type II lattice dystrophy (Meretoja syndrome) is a systemic gelsolin amyloidosis with cranial and peripheral neuropathy, facial mask-like features, and cutis laxa in addition to sparse corneal lattice lines Management is largely supportive with lubrication and treatment of erosions, with phototherapeutic keratectomy or lamellar/penetrating keratoplasty for advanced visual loss Recurrence of deposits within a corneal graft over time is characteristic and should be anticipated when counselling Rapidly progressive visual loss suggesting dense confluent stromal amyloid Systemic features of cranial or peripheral neuropathy indicating gelsolin type II amyloidosis Severe or non-healing epithelial defects raising concern for secondary infection Recurrence of deposits in a corneal graft threatening the visual result Attributing recurrent erosions to trauma or dry eye and missing the underlying dystrophy Failing to recognise systemic features that point to Meretoja gelsolin amyloidosis Not counselling patients about the near-inevitable recurrence of deposits after grafting Overlooking the shared TGFBI origin with granular dystrophy when interpreting mixed phenotypes Lattice corneal dystrophy results from the abnormal deposition of amyloid within the corneal stroma. In the classic autosomal dominant form, mutations in the transforming growth factor beta-induced gene (TGFBI) produce an abnormal protein that misfolds and aggregates as amyloid fibrils, forming the branching lattice lines and intervening haze. In the systemic type II variant (Meretoja syndrome), mutations in the gelsolin gene lead to widespread amyloid deposition affecting the cornea, cranial and peripheral nerves, and skin. Amyloid accumulation progressively disrupts stromal transparency and undermines epithelial adhesion, producing recurrent erosions and gradual loss of vision. Vision typically declines slowly over decades, with recurrent erosions often preceding visual loss. Keratoplasty can restore clarity but amyloid deposits frequently recur in the graft, and the systemic type II form carries additional neurological morbidity.

Lattice degeneration — lattice retinal degeneration, peripheral lattice degeneration Other peripheral retinal degenerations such as snailtrack degeneration, paving-stone (cobblestone) degeneration and white-without-pressure Peripheral chorioretinal atrophy or old chorioretinitis scarring Retinal holes or breaks from other causes Peripheral retinoschisis Pigmented lesions such as congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium Peripheral chorioretinal changes of high myopia Dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral indentation to examine the peripheral retina Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with a wide-field or three-mirror lens to characterise lesions and their margins Wide-field fundus imaging to document extent and to monitor over time Examination of the fellow eye given the frequent bilaterality OCT where available to assess associated retinoschisis or subclinical detachment Assessment for a symptomatic break, including Shafer's sign and subretinal fluid, if new symptoms develop The commonest clinically significant peripheral retinal degeneration predisposing to retinal breaks, more frequent in myopic eyes and often bilateral Appears as sharply demarcated, circumferentially oriented, spindle-shaped areas of retinal thinning, usually anterior to the equator, often crossed by a network of white sclerosed vessels (the lattice) with pigment clumping and yellow-white flecks Overlying the lesion the vitreous is liquefied, while at its margins there is exaggerated, firm vitreoretinal adhesion, and it is this combination that predisposes to tears Two break types occur: atrophic round holes within the lesion, which are more common, lower risk and often seen in younger myopes, and tractional tears at the posterior or lateral margins during posterior vitreous detachment, which carry a higher detachment risk Although common in the general population, only a minority of eyes with lattice ever develop retinal detachment, so routine prophylactic treatment of asymptomatic lattice is generally not recommended Prophylactic laser retinopexy or cryotherapy is considered in higher-risk situations, for example symptomatic tears, the fellow eye of a patient who has had a retinal detachment, or before intraocular surgery in selected cases Patients should be counselled about retinal detachment symptoms such as flashes, new floaters and a field defect and advised to seek urgent review if these occur New flashes, a shower of floaters or a field defect suggesting a retinal tear or detachment Subretinal fluid extending from a break Tobacco dust (Shafer's sign) in the vitreous A tractional tear at the margin of a lattice lesion, particularly during acute posterior vitreous detachment Over-treating asymptomatic lattice with prophylactic laser when the evidence does not support routine intervention Failing to examine the full peripheral retina with indentation and so missing lattice or an associated break Neglecting to examine the fellow eye Providing inadequate detachment-symptom safety-netting to patients with known lattice Assuming laser retinopexy abolishes all future detachment risk Lattice degeneration is characterised by focal thinning of the inner retinal layers with an overlying pocket of liquefied vitreous and abnormally strong vitreoretinal adhesion at the margins of the lesion. Sclerosis and hyalinisation of retinal vessels crossing the lesion produce the characteristic white branching lattice pattern, while disturbance of the retinal pigment epithelium gives the pigmentary changes. Atrophic round holes may develop within the thinned retina. The principal risk arises during posterior vitreous detachment, when dynamic traction transmitted to the firm marginal adhesions can tear the retina at the edge of a lattice lesion, allowing liquefied vitreous to enter the subretinal space and produce a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. Most eyes with lattice degeneration remain stable and never develop retinal detachment, so the overall prognosis is good. Risk is higher in high myopes and in the fellow eye of a patient who has already suffered a detachment, and outcomes are favourable when breaks are detected and treated promptly.

Long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency — LCHAD deficiency, LCHADD, HADHA deficiency, mitochondrial trifunctional protein alpha-subunit deficiency, long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency Generalised mitochondrial trifunctional protein deficiency (alpha and beta subunit involvement) Very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II and translocase deficiencies Other causes of infantile cardiomyopathy or hepatopathy Inherited retinal dystrophies and peripheral neuropathies of other cause Sepsis or metabolic acidosis in a decompensating infant Plasma acylcarnitine profile showing raised long-chain hydroxyacylcarnitines (e.g. C16-OH, C18:1-OH) Urine organic acids seeking 3-hydroxydicarboxylic aciduria Blood glucose, ketones, ammonia, lactate and liver function during illness Ophthalmological assessment and electroretinography for retinopathy, and nerve conduction studies for neuropathy HADHA molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Echocardiography and creatine kinase during acute decompensation Caused by HADHA variants affecting the alpha subunit of the mitochondrial trifunctional protein, which carries the long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase activity; the common c.1528G>C variant is characteristic Distinctive complications not seen in most other oxidation defects are progressive pigmentary retinopathy and peripheral neuropathy Carrying an affected fetus is strongly associated with maternal acute fatty liver of pregnancy and HELLP syndrome Newborn screening shows elevated long-chain hydroxyacylcarnitines, notably 3-hydroxytetradecanoylcarnitine (C16-OH) and related hydroxy species Acute presentations include hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy, hepatic dysfunction and rhabdomyolysis, overlapping with generalised trifunctional protein deficiency Management combines long-chain fat restriction with medium-chain triglyceride substitution, avoidance of fasting and an emergency regimen during illness Regular ophthalmological surveillance is needed because retinopathy can progress despite metabolic control Maternal acute fatty liver of pregnancy or HELLP syndrome prompting testing of the infant Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy or cardiomyopathy Rhabdomyolysis with pigmenturia and acute kidney injury risk Progressive visual loss or neuropathic symptoms indicating chronic complications Not testing the neonate after maternal acute fatty liver of pregnancy or HELLP syndrome Overlooking retinopathy or neuropathy because acute metabolic control appears adequate Using unrestricted long-chain fat instead of medium-chain triglyceride substitution Permitting fasting for procedures without a glucose-containing infusion The mitochondrial trifunctional protein is a membrane-bound complex that catalyses three sequential steps of long-chain fatty-acid beta-oxidation; isolated LCHAD deficiency reflects selective loss of the 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase activity of its alpha subunit. Blocked long-chain oxidation impairs energy supply to heart, muscle and liver during fasting and stress and prevents hepatic ketogenesis, while accumulation of long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl metabolites is thought to be toxic and to underlie the retinopathy and neuropathy. Transplacental passage of these hydroxy intermediates from an affected fetus is implicated in the maternal liver disease of pregnancy. Early screen-detected diagnosis and dietary management improve survival and reduce acute crises, but retinopathy and neuropathy may progress over time, so long-term morbidity remains a concern even with good metabolic control.

Lead nephropathy — saturnine nephropathy, lead-induced kidney disease Other chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathies (analgesic, aristolochic acid) Hypertensive nephrosclerosis Gouty (urate) nephropathy of other cause Chronic kidney disease of other aetiology Cadmium or other heavy-metal nephropathy Blood lead level and exposure history Assessment of renal function, urate and blood pressure Lead-mobilisation (chelation) test for body burden where indicated Urinalysis and markers of tubular dysfunction Occupational and environmental exposure assessment Chronic kidney disease caused by prolonged lead exposure, producing a chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy It is classically associated with hyperuricaemia and gout (saturnine gout) and with hypertension Acute high-dose exposure in children can cause a reversible proximal tubulopathy (Fanconi-type) with lead inclusion bodies Sources include occupational exposure, old lead paint and pipes, contaminated traditional remedies and illicit alcohol Blood lead reflects recent exposure; body burden may be assessed with a chelation-mobilisation test where available Management is removal from exposure and treatment of hypertension, with chelation for significant lead burden Progressive chronic kidney disease with ongoing exposure Features of systemic lead toxicity (neurological, anaemia) Severe hypertension Childhood exposure with encephalopathy Overlooking lead as a cause of chronic kidney disease with gout and hypertension Failing to take an occupational and environmental exposure history Relying only on blood lead, which reflects recent rather than cumulative exposure Not addressing ongoing exposure sources Lead nephropathy results from accumulation of lead in renal tubular cells, where it impairs mitochondrial and enzymatic function and, with chronic exposure, causes tubulointerstitial fibrosis and progressive chronic kidney disease. Lead also reduces renal urate excretion, producing hyperuricaemia and gout, and contributes to hypertension, which further damages the kidney. In acute childhood poisoning, lead causes a proximal tubular dysfunction with characteristic intranuclear inclusion bodies that is often reversible. Removing exposure and controlling hypertension can stabilise renal function, and acute childhood tubulopathy may reverse, but established chronic interstitial fibrosis is irreversible.

with ciliopathy features), so systemic evaluation may be warranted Systemic features suggesting an associated ciliopathy (renal impairment, neurological or developmental signs) Rapidly progressive In RPE65-related disease, for example, the retinal pigment epithelium cannot regenerate the chromophore needed to restore light sensitivity to photoreceptors, so phototransduction fails and photoreceptors degenerate. Other causative genes impair photoreceptor ciliary transport, guanylate cyclase signalling, or outer-segment structure. The common consequence is early and severe loss of rod and cone function, reflected in a profoundly abnormal electroretinogram and progressive retinal degeneration. Vision is severely impaired from infancy and most genotypes are progressive, though some are relatively stable; the prognosis is being transformed for RPE65-related disease by gene therapy, and genotype-specific trials are altering outlook for other subtypes.

'LHON-plus' phenotype Continued smoking or alcohol exposure accelerating visual loss Misdiagnosing it as atypical optic neuritis and giving prolonged unhelpful immunosuppression Failing to counsel on maternal inheritance and the risk to relatives Overlooking modifiable triggers such as smoking and alcohol in carriers Not recognising the disc appearance can mimic true papilloedema early on Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is caused by pathogenic point mutations in mitochondrial DNA that impair complex I of the respiratory chain, reducing ATP production and increasing oxidative stress. Retinal ganglion cells, particularly the small fibres of the papillomacular bundle, are exquisitely dependent on mitochondrial energy and are preferentially vulnerable. Energy failure and oxidative damage trigger dysfunction and then apoptotic loss of these ganglion cells, producing the characteristic central visual loss and subsequent optic atrophy. Incomplete penetrance and the male bias reflect the influence of mitochondrial heteroplasmy, nuclear modifiers, hormonal factors, and environmental triggers. Most patients suffer severe and permanent bilateral central visual loss, although a minority recover useful vision, most commonly those with the m.14484 mutation and younger patients; avoidance of smoking and excess alcohol and emerging gene and pharmacological therapies may modify outcomes.
