supportive and palliative, with the emphasis on accurate diagnosis, postmortem confirmation and genetic counselling Foetal hydrops and cystic hygroma indicating a lethal course Severe pulmonary hypoplasia incompatible with postnatal survival Progressive antenatal akinesia and polyhydramnios Recurrence in subsequent pregnancies given autosomal recessive inheritance Failing to distinguish the lethal form from the survivable Escobar variant when counselling Not securing genetic confirmation, leaving recurrence risk uncertain Overlooking the autosomal recessive one-in-four recurrence risk Missing the opportunity for postmortem examination to guide future pregnancies Lethal multiple pterygium syndrome is caused by severe loss of function in genes encoding subunits of the foetal acetylcholine receptor, most often CHRNG (gamma subunit) but also CHRNA1 and CHRND. Complete failure of foetal neuromuscular transmission abolishes foetal movement during a critical developmental period. The profound akinesia produces multiple joint contractures, webbing across the flexed joints, pulmonary hypoplasia from absent breathing movements, and impaired lymphatic drainage manifesting as cystic hygroma, hydrops and generalised oedema. The completeness of the receptor defect explains why this form is lethal in utero or shortly after birth, in contrast to the survivable Escobar variant. The prognosis is uniformly poor, with death occurring in utero or in the early neonatal period; care is supportive and palliative, and the priority is establishing a genetic diagnosis to inform recurrence risk and prenatal options.

Leukocyte adhesion deficiency — LAD, LAD-1, leucocyte adhesion deficiency Chronic granulomatous disease Congenital or cyclic neutropenia Chediak-Higashi syndrome Other neutrophil functional disorders Glanzmann thrombasthenia (for the bleeding seen in LAD-3) Flow cytometry for CD18 and CD11 expression on neutrophils (reduced or absent in LAD-1) Full blood count demonstrating marked neutrophil leucocytosis Genetic testing (ITGB2 for LAD-1, SLC35C1 for LAD-2, FERMT3 for LAD-3) Neutrophil adhesion and chemotaxis functional assays Assessment of sialyl-Lewis X expression and blood group testing where LAD-2 is suspected Platelet aggregation studies when LAD-3 is considered Leukocyte adhesion deficiency is a group of autosomal recessive disorders in which neutrophils cannot adhere to and migrate across the vascular endothelium to reach sites of infection The most common form, LAD-1, results from defects in the beta-2 integrin common chain (CD18), impairing firm adhesion of leucocytes A cardinal clinical clue is delayed separation of the umbilical cord accompanied by omphalitis in the newborn period Recurrent bacterial and fungal soft-tissue infections occur characteristically without pus formation, because neutrophils fail to enter the tissues A persistently high blood neutrophil count (marked leucocytosis) is typical, since neutrophils remain in the circulation rather than migrating out Severe gingivitis, periodontitis, and poor wound healing are frequent features LAD-2 involves defective fucosylation of selectin ligands and is associated with the Bombay blood group and developmental abnormalities, while LAD-3 combines adhesion failure with a bleeding tendency due to impaired integrin activation in platelets Management includes aggressive treatment of infections and antimicrobial prophylaxis, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offering cure in severe LAD-1 Delayed umbilical cord separation with omphalitis in a neonate requiring urgent evaluation Severe soft-tissue or invasive infection without pus formation requiring prompt antimicrobial therapy Life-threatening sepsis given the severe impairment of neutrophil migration Live vaccines and non-irradiated blood products should be approached cautiously, especially peri-transplant Bleeding episodes in suspected LAD-3 Interpreting the high neutrophil count as ongoing bacterial infection rather than a diagnostic clue to impaired migration Expecting pus and abscess formation and being falsely reassured by its absence Missing the neonatal sign of delayed cord separation Failing to distinguish the LAD subtypes, which differ in associated features and management Delaying transplant referral in severe LAD-1 Leukocyte adhesion deficiency arises from defects in the adhesion cascade that normally allows leucocytes to roll along, firmly adhere to, and transmigrate across activated endothelium. In LAD-1, mutations in ITGB2 reduce or abolish the shared CD18 subunit of the beta-2 integrins, so neutrophils cannot form the firm adhesion needed to exit the bloodstream, leaving tissues undefended despite abundant circulating neutrophils. LAD-2 results from a defect in GDP-fucose transport that impairs synthesis of sialyl-Lewis X, the selectin ligand required for rolling, and also causes the rare Bombay phenotype and neurodevelopmental problems. LAD-3 stems from defective inside-out signalling (kindlin-3/FERMT3) that prevents activation of integrins on both leucocytes and platelets, combining infection susceptibility with a Glanzmann-like bleeding disorder. Severe LAD-1 with very low CD18 expression carries a high risk of early fatal infection unless corrected by haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, whereas moderate phenotypes with partial expression can survive longer with vigilant infection control; LAD-2 tends to have a milder infectious course dominated by developmental issues, and LAD-3 combines infection and bleeding risks.

Leukocyte Chemotactic Factor 2 Amyloidosis (ALECT2) — ALECT2 amyloidosis, LECT2 amyloidosis AL (immunoglobulin light-chain) amyloidosis AA amyloidosis Other hereditary amyloidoses such as fibrinogen and apolipoprotein A-I types Diabetic and hypertensive nephropathy Other tubulointerstitial diseases Other causes of chronic kidney disease with modest proteinuria Renal biopsy with Congo red staining showing interstitial and glomerular amyloid Amyloid typing by mass spectrometry, which is essential to identify LECT2 Serum free light chains and immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis Serum amyloid A and C-reactive protein to exclude AA amyloidosis Renal function and quantified proteinuria Liver function tests and hepatic imaging SAP scintigraphy to assess organ burden ALECT2 is caused by deposition of leukocyte chemotactic factor 2, a protein of largely wild-type sequence, rather than by a classic amyloidogenic mutation. It is a common cause of renal amyloidosis in specific populations, notably people of Mexican or Hispanic, Punjabi, First Nations, Native American and Egyptian ancestry. The kidney is the dominant target, typically producing slowly progressive chronic kidney disease with only sub-nephrotic proteinuria, which is lighter than in AL or AA amyloidosis. The liver is the second most commonly affected organ, and incidental hepatic ALECT2 is sometimes found at biopsy or resection. Amyloid characteristically deposits in the renal cortical interstitium and glomeruli. A homozygous common polymorphism in the LECT2 gene is associated, but the disease is not inherited in a classic Mendelian pattern. There is no specific antifibril therapy, so management is supportive with attention to chronic kidney disease and its complications. Accurate typing by mass spectrometry is essential, as ALECT2 is easily misclassified. Progressive chronic kidney disease with disproportionately mild proteinuria in a patient of at-risk ancestry Unexplained hepatic amyloid found on biopsy Declining renal function without an obvious alternative cause Misclassifying as AL or AA amyloidosis without mass spectrometry typing Discounting amyloid because proteinuria is only sub-nephrotic Overlooking the diagnosis outside the classically affected ethnic groups Giving inappropriate chemotherapy on the assumption of AL amyloidosis Leukocyte chemotactic factor 2 is a hepatically synthesised protein involved in inflammation and tissue repair. In ALECT2 the essentially wild-type protein deposits as amyloid, with a strong ancestral predisposition suggesting genetic susceptibility linked to a common LECT2 polymorphism rather than a destabilising point mutation. Fibrils accumulate preferentially in the renal interstitium and glomeruli, and in the liver, producing indolent organ dysfunction. Because proteinuria is characteristically modest despite significant renal impairment, the disease can be clinically silent until chronic kidney disease is advanced. The mechanisms triggering deposition of the normal-sequence protein remain incompletely defined. ALECT2 is generally indolent, but renal involvement tends to progress slowly to end-stage kidney disease over years. There is no proven disease-specific therapy, so outcomes depend on chronic kidney disease management and on renal replacement or transplantation.

Leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and lactate (LBSL, DARS2) — LBSL, DARS2-related leukoencephalopathy, mitochondrial aspartyl-tRNA synthetase leukoencephalopathy, leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and elevated lactate Other mitochondrial leukoencephalopathies and MELAS-spectrum disorders Multiple sclerosis and other inflammatory demyelination Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency (dorsal column involvement) Hereditary spastic paraplegia with white matter change Leukoencephalopathy with brainstem involvement from other tRNA synthetase defects Adult-onset vanishing white matter disease and other genetic leukoencephalopathies Brain and spinal cord MRI to demonstrate the selective tract involvement and cord signal change Proton MR spectroscopy to detect elevated lactate within affected white matter DARS2 sequencing, including analysis for the common intronic splice variant and a second pathogenic allele Nerve conduction and somatosensory evoked potentials to characterise dorsal-column and peripheral involvement Blood and CSF lactate as supportive metabolic markers Leukodystrophy or mitochondrial gene panel if targeted DARS2 testing is inconclusive An autosomal recessive leukoencephalopathy caused by variants in DARS2, which encodes mitochondrial aspartyl-tRNA synthetase The MRI pattern is highly specific: selective involvement of particular tracts rather than the whole white matter, including the cerebral white matter with sparing of the U-fibres, the pyramidal tracts and dorsal columns of the spinal cord, and defined brainstem tracts such as the medial lemniscus, superior and inferior cerebellar peduncles and the medullary pyramids Proton MR spectroscopy typically shows raised lactate within the abnormal white matter, an important confirmatory clue Onset ranges from infancy to adulthood; the common presentation is slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia with spasticity and dorsal-column sensory loss causing impaired proprioception and a positive Romberg sign Deterioration or acute worsening can be provoked by minor head trauma, febrile illness or other stressors in some patients Diagnosis rests on the combination of the selective tract pattern, elevated white-matter lactate on spectroscopy and biallelic DARS2 variants; a common intronic splice variant is frequently paired with a second allele There is no specific treatment, so care is supportive and multidisciplinary, with physiotherapy, mobility aids and management of spasticity and sensory ataxia Acute neurological deterioration following minor head trauma or febrile illness Rapidly progressive weakness or bulbar dysfunction requiring reassessment Severe sensory ataxia with recurrent falls and injury Cognitive decline or seizures suggesting more extensive disease Missing the diagnosis by not appreciating the selective tract pattern and treating it as non-specific white matter change Failing to perform MR spectroscopy and thereby overlooking the elevated white-matter lactate Mislabelling the presentation as multiple sclerosis and exposing the patient to unnecessary immunotherapy Not testing for the common intronic DARS2 variant, which can be missed by some assays Overlooking the risk of stress- or trauma-related deterioration when counselling patients LBSL is caused by biallelic variants in DARS2, which encodes the mitochondrial enzyme that charges transfer RNA with aspartate for mitochondrial protein synthesis. Reduced enzyme activity, often driven by a leaky intronic splice-site variant that lowers the amount of correctly spliced transcript, impairs translation of mitochondrially encoded respiratory-chain subunits in neural tissue. The resulting energy deficit and mitochondrial dysfunction selectively affect long myelinated tracts with high metabolic demand, producing the distinctive pattern of tract-specific white-matter signal change and the elevated lactate seen on spectroscopy. The course of LBSL is variable but usually slowly progressive, with gradually worsening ataxia, spasticity and dorsal-column dysfunction; some patients remain mildly affected for many years, while early-onset cases can be more severe. Episodic decline after stressors and cumulative disability influence outcome, and life expectancy is often relatively preserved in milder phenotypes.

combines the characteristic imaging triad with SNORD118 sequencing, remembering that variants affect a non-coding RNA gene and may be missed by analyses focused on protein-coding regions Management is largely neurosurgical and supportive, with consideration of surgical drainage or resection of symptomatic enlarging cysts and control of seizures and raised pressure Signs of raised intracranial pressure from an enlarging cyst requiring urgent neurosurgical review New focal deficit or rapid neurological deterioration Status epilepticus or poorly controlled seizures Progressive cognitive decline with loss of independence Attributing the calcification to a congenital infection and not pursuing the genetic diagnosis Confusing the disorder with Coats plus by failing to look for the systemic features that distinguish CTC1 disease Missing SNORD118 variants because sequencing was targeted only at protein-coding genes Underestimating the tendency of cysts to enlarge and cause delayed mass effect Overlooking treatable contributors such as seizures while focusing on the imaging findings Labrune syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in SNORD118, a gene encoding the box C/D small nucleolar RNA U8, which is involved in the processing and maturation of ribosomal RNA. Disturbed ribosomal RNA biogenesis is thought to render cerebral small blood vessels vulnerable, producing a progressive microangiopathy with vascular wall thickening, calcification and breakdown of the blood-brain barrier. The resulting chronic tissue injury generates the leukoencephalopathy, dystrophic calcification and progressively enlarging fluid-filled cysts that together define the disorder, while the disease remains restricted to the central nervous system. The course of Labrune syndrome is variable and often slowly progressive, punctuated by episodes related to cyst enlargement or seizures; outcome depends on lesion location, the rate of cyst growth and the success of neurosurgical intervention. Some patients stabilise for long periods, whereas others accumulate neurological disability over time.

leukostasis — symptomatic hyperleucocytosis, leucostasis Pneumonia or neutropenic sepsis Pulmonary embolism Tumour lysis syndrome Intracranial haemorrhage or ischaemic stroke Hyperviscosity syndrome from a paraprotein Acute respiratory distress syndrome from other causes Disseminated intravascular coagulation Full blood count with white-cell differential and blast percentage Blood film for blasts and features of leukaemia Coagulation screen with fibrinogen and D-dimer for DIC Urea, electrolytes, urate, phosphate and calcium for tumour lysis Arterial blood gas (interpreted with awareness of leucocyte artefact) Chest radiograph and CT head where neurological signs are present Lactate dehydrogenase and rapid confirmatory bone marrow or immunophenotyping A medical emergency of symptomatic hyperleucocytosis, most often in acute myeloid leukaemia (especially monocytic and myelomonocytic subtypes) with very high blast counts, or in the blast phase of chronic myeloid leukaemia. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia causes leukostasis less readily at any given count because lymphoblasts are smaller and less adhesive than myeloblasts. The dominant clinical picture is pulmonary (dyspnoea, hypoxia, diffuse infiltrates) and neurological (confusion, headache, visual change, stupor), reflecting microcirculatory obstruction in lung and brain. Early mortality is high, so urgent cytoreduction with hydroxycarbamide and/or prompt induction chemotherapy, together with leucapheresis in selected unstable patients, should not be delayed. Tumour lysis syndrome and disseminated intravascular coagulation frequently coexist and must be anticipated and managed concurrently. Red-cell transfusion should be avoided or minimised until the white-cell count is controlled, because it raises whole-blood viscosity and can precipitate clinical deterioration. Platelet transfusion, in contrast, does not appreciably raise viscosity and may be given to reduce the risk of intracranial haemorrhage. Beware spurious laboratory results from metabolically active leucocytes: pseudohyperkalaemia, artefactually low arterial oxygen ('leucocyte larceny') and spurious hypoglycaemia. Hypoxaemic respiratory failure Altered mental status or focal neurological deficit Intracranial haemorrhage Priapism Rapidly rising blast count with clinical deterioration Transfusing red cells before cytoreduction and worsening leukostasis Trusting an artefactually low arterial oxygen tension caused by leucocyte oxygen consumption Delaying cytoreductive therapy while awaiting definitive diagnosis Failing to anticipate and manage concurrent tumour lysis syndrome and DIC Misinterpreting pseudohyperkalaemia and administering unnecessary or harmful treatment A greatly elevated count of large, poorly deformable and adhesive myeloid blasts increases blood viscosity and plugs the microcirculation. Blasts compete with tissues for oxygen, adhere to and damage the endothelium, and release cytokines that promote further leucocyte-endothelial interaction and local hypoxia. The lungs and central nervous system are most vulnerable, producing hypoxaemic respiratory failure and neurological dysfunction; endothelial injury, coagulation activation and concurrent tumour lysis add the risks of haemorrhage, disseminated intravascular coagulation and metabolic derangement. Leukostasis carries a high risk of early death from respiratory or cerebral complications and intracranial haemorrhage; prompt cytoreduction improves survival. Longer-term outcome is determined by the biology and treatment response of the underlying leukaemia.

physiotherapy and biofeedback, digital massage, and muscle-relaxation or neuromodulation strategies Overlaps with other functional pelvic floor and defecatory disorders Rectal bleeding, weight loss, older patient without a prior functional history Labelling anorectal pain as functional without excluding structural or neoplastic disease Overlooking coexisting dyssynergic defecation amenable to biofeedback Repeated ineffective surgery for presumed fissure or haemorrhoids Underestimating the contribution of psychological stress and pelvic floor tension Levator ani syndrome is thought to arise from chronic spasm and tension of the pelvic floor muscles, particularly the puborectalis and levator ani, producing a persistent aching or pressure sensation high in the rectum. often described as sitting on a ball It falls within the Rome classification of functional anorectal pain, distinguished from proctalgia fugax (brief fleeting episodes) by its longer duration, typically lasting twenty minutes or more The defining physical sign is tenderness on posterior traction of the puborectalis during digital rectal examination, often more pronounced on the left It is a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring the elimination of structural and inflammatory causes of anorectal pain such as abscess, fissure, thrombosis, malignancy, and coccygeal pathology Pain is frequently worse with prolonged sitting and may be relieved by walking or lying down, and can be associated with pelvic-floor dysfunction and dyssynergic defecation The Rome framework separates highly likely such as digital massage, warm baths, electrogalvanic stimulation, and muscle relaxation techniques It commonly coexists with other functional gastrointestinal and pelvic-floor disorders and with psychological stressors, warranting a holistic approach Rectal bleeding, weight loss, or a palpable mass suggesting malignancy Fever or localised swelling suggesting abscess Progressive neurological symptoms or saddle anaesthesia New severe pain of abrupt onset with structural findings Pain unresponsive to treatment with evolving alarm features Diagnosing levator syndrome without adequately excluding structural or malignant causes Overlooking coexisting dyssynergic defecation that is amenable to biofeedback Attributing pain solely to haemorrhoids and performing unnecessary anal surgery Neglecting the psychological and gut-brain dimension of the disorder Repeated invasive investigations for a functional disorder once alarm features are excluded Levator syndrome is understood as a disorder of chronic spasm and tension in the pelvic-floor musculature, particularly the levator ani and puborectalis. Sustained or dysregulated contraction of these muscles, often in the setting of pelvic-floor dyssynergia, produces ischaemic, aching pain referred to the rectum and perineum. Central and peripheral sensitisation, abnormal pain processing, and the interplay of stress and anxiety contribute to symptom persistence, in keeping with a disorder of gut-brain and pelvic-floor interaction. There is no structural lesion; rather, heightened muscle tone, tenderness of the puborectalis, and impaired relaxation during defecation underlie the symptoms, which may be exacerbated by prolonged sitting and by dyssynergic straining. Levator syndrome is benign but often chronic and relapsing; a substantial proportion of patients improve with biofeedback, physiotherapy, and reassurance, though symptoms can persist and fluctuate, and response is generally better when puborectalis tenderness is present and pelvic-floor dyssynergia is addressed.

controlled congenital adrenal hyperplasia) and from familial testotoxicosis Most childhood Leydig cell tumours are benign, and testis-sparing surgery is often possible, with orchidectomy reserved for larger or suspicious lesions A distinct testicular mass or asymmetric enlargement in a boy with signs of androgen excess Histological features suggesting malignancy (more common in adults than children), such as large size, necrosis, or vascular invasion Rapidly progressive virilisation with markedly elevated testosterone Persistence or recurrence of hormonal signs after surgery, suggesting residual or recurrent tumour Mistaking the tumour for familial testotoxicosis or Leydig cell hyperplasia and thereby missing a resectable mass Failing to examine and image the testes in a boy with gonadotropin-independent precocity Overlooking testicular adrenal rest tissue of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which mimics a tumour but responds to glucocorticoid control Performing orchidectomy when testis-sparing surgery would suffice for a benign lesion Not confirming gonadotropin independence with a stimulation test before attributing signs to a central cause A Leydig cell tumour arises from the testosterone-producing interstitial cells of the testis (or the analogous hilus cells of the ovary) and commonly retains steroidogenic activity, secreting androgens autonomously and sometimes aromatising them to oestrogens. The resulting sex-steroid excess is independent of pituitary gonadotropin drive, so the axis is suppressed and the clinical picture is one of precocious pseudopuberty rather than true, centrally mediated puberty. In boys this manifests as virilisation with an enlarged or nodular testis, whereas oestrogen production can cause gynaecomastia. The principal differential considerations are conditions that expand or stimulate Leydig cells without a true neoplasm, such as hyperplasia from chronic gonadotropin or LH-receptor stimulation, testicular adrenal rest tumours in congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and the activating LH-receptor disorder of familial testotoxicosis. The great majority of Leydig cell tumours in childhood are benign, and removal (often testis-sparing) reverses the hormonal effects with an excellent outcome; malignant behaviour is uncommon in children but requires more extensive surgery and surveillance when present.

Leydig cell tumour of the testis — Leydig cell tumor, interstitial cell tumour of the testis, testicular Leydig cell tumour Germ cell tumour of the testis Sertoli cell tumour Leydig cell hyperplasia precocious puberty in a boy Marked hormonal disturbance with new gynaecomastia in an adult Assuming a hormonally active mass is benign without assessing malignancy-associated histological features Overlooking bilateral testicular adrenal rest tumours in congenital adrenal hyperplasia and mistaking them for neoplasm Proceeding to orchidectomy for a small benign lesion where testis-sparing surgery was feasible Failing to investigate gynaecomastia or precocious puberty as a clue to a functioning tumour Leydig cell tumours arise from the interstitial Leydig cells that normally produce testosterone under luteinising hormone stimulation. Neoplastic Leydig cells may retain steroidogenic activity and secrete androgens or, through peripheral or intratumoral aromatisation, oestrogens, producing the endocrine syndromes seen clinically. Excess oestrogen can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and impair spermatogenesis, contributing to gynaecomastia and infertility. The majority of Leydig cell tumours are benign and cured by surgical excision, with resolution or improvement of hormonal effects; malignant Leydig cell tumours, more frequent in adults, respond poorly to chemotherapy and radiotherapy and carry a guarded prognosis once metastatic.

are directed against leucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1 (LGI1), a protein secreted by neurons that bridges presynaptic ADAM23 and postsynaptic ADAM22 to regulate synaptic excitability and AMPA-receptor Antibody-mediated disruption of this signalling increases neuronal excitability within the temporal lobes and basal ganglia, producing seizures, and impairs limbic circuits underlying memory. The response is usually not tumour-driven but is strongly linked to specific HLA types. Prompt immunotherapy often improves seizures and cognition, but delayed treatment is associated with persistent memory impairment and medial temporal atrophy. suggesting a further primary cancer Radiation-field second malignancy after prior therapeutic irradiation Excluding the diagnosis because family history is limited, since de novo variants and incomplete pedigrees are frequent Using therapeutic radiotherapy without weighing the heightened risk of radiation-induced tumours Overlooking a second primary by attributing new symptoms solely to a prior cancer Failing to offer cascade testing and paediatric surveillance to at-risk relatives The syndrome results from a heterozygous germline loss-of-function variant in TP53, the gene encoding the p53 protein that acts as a master regulator of the cellular response to DNA damage. Structured surveillance improves early detection and survival, but the diversity and aggressiveness of tumours mean prognosis remains guarded and lifelong monitoring is required.

functional or sleep disturbance Rapidly changing or ulcerating lesions requiring re-biopsy Assuming an association with systemic amyloidosis, which does not apply to this keratin-derived form Failing to address the itch-scratch cycle that perpetuates the deposits Confusing it with lichen simplex chronicus or hypertrophic lichen planus without biopsy Overlooking familial cases and their inheritance In lichen amyloidosis the amyloid deposits are of keratinocyte origin. Chronic friction and scratching are thought to injure basal keratinocytes, which undergo apoptosis (filamentous degeneration) and shed cytokeratin that is then converted, with the help of dermal cells, into amyloid deposited in the papillary dermis. The keratin-derived nature of the amyloid explains why the disease remains confined to the skin without systemic organ involvement, and the persistence of the itch-scratch cycle continuously supplies degenerate keratin, perpetuating and enlarging the deposits. Benign but chronic and often refractory; it poses no systemic threat, but the itch and cosmetic appearance persist and lesions recur while scratching continues.

treatment (topical corticosteroids, occasionally phototherapy) is reserved for symptomatic or cosmetically troublesome disease Widespread or generalised eruption that fails to remit and warrants reassessment Features suggesting lichen scrofulosorum, prompting evaluation for underlying tuberculosis Nail dystrophy or mucosal change suggesting overlap with lichen planus Confusing the pinpoint papules with keratosis pilaris or plane warts Overlooking the Koebner phenomenon as a helpful diagnostic feature Failing to distinguish it from lichen scrofulosorum, which mandates a tuberculosis workup Lichen nitidus is an inflammatory dermatosis in which a focal, cell-mediated response involving T-lymphocytes and histiocytes targets the epidermis, producing the characteristic sharply circumscribed papular infiltrate. The precise trigger is unknown, and although it shares a lichenoid tissue reaction with lichen planus, the two are usually considered separate conditions. The dense but tiny granulomatous focus, held between elongated rete ridges, corresponds to the minute shiny papule seen clinically, and the tendency to Koebnerise reflects an antigen-independent response to local trauma. Benign, typically resolving spontaneously over months to a few years without scarring, although the course can occasionally be more protracted.

treatable inflammatory scarring alopecia Confusing it with discoid lupus, which differs in management and immunofluorescence Sampling a burnt-out scarred centre rather than the active edge on biopsy Underestimating the symptom burden of itch and pain that should guide treatment intensity Lichen planopilaris is a T-cell-mediated inflammatory disorder in which a lichenoid lymphocytic infiltrate targets the follicular epithelium, particularly the bulge region housing the follicular stem cells. Destruction of these stem cells and of the sebaceous glands leads to permanent follicular loss with perifollicular fibrosis. It is considered a follicular expression of lichen planus, and loss of follicular immune privilege as well as altered peroxisome-proliferator-activated receptor signalling have been implicated, but the end result is irreversible cicatricial alopecia. Lichen planopilaris follows a chronic, unpredictable course; treatment can reduce symptoms and slow progression but cannot regrow hair in scarred areas, and disease may reactivate after periods of quiescence.

erosive oral or genital disease is painful and warrants monitoring Nail involvement can cause ridging and, if severe, scarring with pterygium formation, while scalp disease (lichen planopilaris) causes scarring alopecia Consider a lichenoid drug eruption when a similar rash follows introduction of a new medication, and screen for hepatitis C where locally relevant Treatment centres on topical corticosteroids for cutaneous and localised mucosal disease, with phototherapy or systemic immunomodulators for widespread or resistant cases Long-standing erosive oral or genital lichen planus carries a small risk of malignant transformation and should be followed up Erosive oral or genital disease with non-healing or indurated areas suggesting malignant change Scarring alopecia or nail destruction indicating a need for prompt treatment to limit permanent damage Rapidly extensive eruption suggesting a drug cause requiring medication review Severe painful mucosal disease impairing eating or causing significant morbidity Overlooking a lichenoid drug reaction and continuing the causative medication Failing to examine the mouth, genitalia, nails, and scalp for additional sites of involvement Not monitoring erosive oral or genital disease for malignant change Attributing scarring alopecia to non-scarring causes and delaying treatment Lichen planus is a T-cell-mediated inflammatory disorder in which cytotoxic CD8 T lymphocytes target basal keratinocytes, apparently in response to an altered self-antigen. The resulting band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction produces the characteristic histological features of basal cell degeneration, a saw-tooth epidermal profile, hypergranulosis, and apoptotic keratinocytes (Civatte bodies). Pigment released from damaged basal cells accounts for the post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation often seen, particularly in darker skin. Triggers can include certain drugs (lichenoid reactions) and, in some populations, hepatitis C infection. Cutaneous lichen planus is often self-limiting, frequently resolving within one to two years but leaving post-inflammatory pigmentation; mucosal, nail, and scalp forms tend to be chronic, and erosive mucosal disease requires long-term surveillance for malignant transformation.

Lichen Sclerosus — lichen sclerosus et atrophicus, LS, balanitis xerotica obliterans (penile form) Vulval or penile lichen planus Morphea (extragenital plaques can look similar) Vitiligo or genital scarring Skin biopsy to confirm diagnosis in atypical cases and to exclude malignancy in suspicious areas Screening or a low threshold for testing for associated autoimmune disease, such as intensely itchy or sore It is commonest in postmenopausal women and prepubertal girls, but also occurs in men, where it can affect the glans and foreskin In women the vulva may show loss of architecture with resorption of the labia minora, clitoral hood adhesions, and introital narrowing, often in a figure-of-eight distribution around the vulva and anus In boys and men it can cause a tight, non-retractile foreskin (phimosis) and meatal narrowing Extragenital lesions appear as white atrophic patches, classically on the trunk, and are usually asymptomatic Long-term topical anti-inflammatory therapy and regular emollient use are the mainstays, aiming to control symptoms and reduce scarring and malignant risk There is a recognised, though modest, increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma at affected genital sites, so persistent, thickened, ulcerated, or non-healing areas need biopsy Arrange long-term follow-up to monitor for scarring, functional problems, and malignant change, and address sexual and urinary dysfunction sympathetically Persistent thickened, warty, ulcerated, or non-healing areas suggesting squamous cell carcinoma and requiring biopsy Progressive scarring causing urinary obstruction or inability to retract the foreskin Significant introital stenosis interfering with micturition or intercourse New fixed nodule or enlarging lesion at a chronically affected site Symptoms unresponsive to adequate treatment, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis Dismissing genital symptoms as thrush or non-specific irritation and delaying diagnosis Under-treating with only intermittent or weak topical therapy, allowing progressive scarring Failing to biopsy persistent or changing lesions and missing early malignancy Overlooking the condition in men and children, in whom presentation differs Neglecting the psychological and sexual impact of chronic genital disease Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis thought to have an autoimmune basis, with associations to other autoimmune conditions and to specific autoantibodies in some patients. The characteristic histology shows epidermal atrophy, hyperkeratosis, a homogenised (hyalinised) upper dermis with loss of normal elastic fibres, and a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate beneath this zone. Genetic predisposition, hormonal influences, local trauma or the Koebner phenomenon, and possibly infective triggers have all been implicated. Chronic inflammation and scarring drive the architectural distortion, and sustained epithelial disturbance underlies the small risk of malignant transformation. Lichen sclerosus is typically a chronic relapsing condition; symptoms and inflammation can be well controlled with maintenance therapy, but architectural scarring is often permanent and lifelong surveillance is advised because of the small risk of genital squamous cell carcinoma.

Lichen simplex chronicus (vulval) — lichen simplex chronicus, vulval lichen simplex, neurodermatitis, squamous cell hyperplasia of the vulva Lichen sclerosus Lichen planus Psoriasis of the vulva Contact or irritant dermatitis Candidal or dermatophyte infection Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia Extramammary Paget disease Clinical examination for lichenification, excoriation, and features of an underlying dermatosis Vulval biopsy for atypical, unilateral, or treatment-resistant lesions Skin swabs or scrapings to exclude candidal or dermatophyte infection Patch testing where allergic contact dermatitis is suspected Assessment for atopy and systemic causes of pruritus Vulval lichen simplex chronicus is a reactive skin change produced by a persistent itch-scratch cycle rather than a primary disease in its own right The dominant symptom is relentless itch, often worse at night and during stress, which drives rubbing and scratching that in turn thickens the skin and perpetuates the itch Chronic scratching produces lichenification, seen as thickened, leathery skin with accentuated skin markings, often with excoriations and variable pigment change It commonly arises on a background of an underlying trigger such as atopic or contact dermatitis, a pre-existing dermatosis, or environmental irritants, which should be sought and treated Diagnosis is usually clinical, but biopsy is indicated when the appearance is atypical, unilateral, or fails to respond, to exclude a specific dermatosis or neoplasia Management aims to break the itch-scratch cycle with generic measures: avoiding irritants, restoring the skin barrier with emollients, potent topical anti-inflammatory treatment for flares, and addressing nocturnal scratching Identifying and treating any underlying dermatosis or allergen is essential to prevent relapse Persistent, non-resolving, or ulcerated areas require re-biopsy because chronic vulval skin disease can rarely harbour intraepithelial neoplasia A persistent unilateral plaque, ulcer, or nodule requiring biopsy to exclude neoplasia Failure to respond to appropriate anti-inflammatory treatment Progressive architectural change suggesting lichen sclerosus rather than simple lichenification New pigmented or bleeding lesion Treating the lichenification without identifying and correcting the underlying itch trigger, leading to relapse Missing an underlying lichen sclerosus or intraepithelial neoplasia by not biopsying atypical or resistant areas Under-treating with weak topical preparations so the itch-scratch cycle continues Ignoring nocturnal scratching, which sustains the process Overlooking contact allergens or irritants from hygiene products Lichen simplex chronicus is the end result of repeated mechanical trauma to the skin from chronic rubbing and scratching. An initial pruritic stimulus, whether an underlying dermatosis, irritant contact, dryness, or psychological stress, provokes scratching that damages the epidermis and stimulates further itch through nerve and inflammatory mediators, establishing a self-sustaining itch-scratch cycle. Persistent trauma leads to epidermal thickening (acanthosis and hyperkeratosis) and dermal changes that clinically appear as lichenification. The condition is therefore secondary and reactive, and lasting improvement depends on interrupting the cycle and removing the provoking cause. The condition usually improves well once the itch-scratch cycle is broken and any underlying trigger is treated, but it is prone to relapse if irritants recur or scratching resumes, so ongoing skin care is often needed.

reconsideration of ILVEN or linear lichen planus Progressive nail destruction Atypical widespread or bilateral distribution requiring biopsy Mistaking it for linear lichen planus or ILVEN, which run or environmental) provokes a T-lymphocyte-mediated reaction directed against a mosaic population of epidermal cells carrying a somatic mutation acquired during embryogenesis. Because these mutant clones are distributed along the developmental lines of Blaschko, the resulting lichenoid inflammation produces the characteristic linear band. The interface and sometimes spongiotic inflammation, often extending around adnexal structures deep in the dermis, damages the epidermis and disturbs pigmentation, accounting for the papules and the frequent residual hypopigmentation. Excellent; most cases resolve spontaneously within months to about a year, although post-inflammatory hypopigmentation and nail changes may take longer to normalise.

suggesting a drug cause Review of temporal relationship between drug introduction, withdrawal and improvement Autoimmune serology to help exclude lupus in photodistributed cases Assessment of mucosae and nails to compare with idiopathic lichen planus Patch testing in selected cases to support identification of the culprit A drug-induced eruption that clinically and histologically mimics idiopathic lichen planus, with violaceous flat-topped papules and plaques Compared with classic lichen planus it tends to be more widespread and symmetrical, may favour sun-exposed sites, and Wickham striae and mucosal involvement are often less prominent There is characteristically a latent period of weeks to months between starting the drug and the onset of the eruption, which can hamper recognition responsible drug together with topical or, if extensive, systemic corticosteroids and symptomatic measures Extensive or erythrodermic involvement requiring urgent assessment Painful or erosive mucosal disease impairing function Eruption associated with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy needing oncology liaison Failure to improve after drug withdrawal, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Failing to recognise the long latent period and therefore not linking the eruption to a drug Mistaking it for idiopathic lichen planus and missing the treatable drug cause Expecting rapid clearance and stopping investigation prematurely Overlooking newer agents such as checkpoint inhibitors as triggers Lichenoid drug eruption is a T-cell-mediated interface reaction in which a drug or its metabolite triggers a cytotoxic lymphocytic attack on basal keratinocytes. The resulting band-like (lichenoid) infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction, with basal cell degeneration and apoptotic keratinocytes (Civatte bodies), reproduces the histological pattern of lichen planus. The drug is thought to act as a hapten or to alter self-antigens so that basal keratinocytes are recognised as foreign, and the relatively long latent period reflects the time required for sensitisation. Damage to basal cells releases melanin that is taken up by dermal macrophages, accounting for the prominent residual pigmentation. The eruption usually resolves after the responsible drug is stopped, although clearance may take several weeks to months and often leaves lasting hyperpigmentation; recurrence follows re-exposure to the culprit drug.

Liddle syndrome — pseudoaldosteronism, ENaC gain-of-function, SCNN1B, SCNN1G, epithelial sodium channel disorder Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) Apparent mineralocorticoid excess (HSD11B2 deficiency) Glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism (familial hyperaldosteronism type 1) Cushing syndrome with mineralocorticoid effect Renovascular or other secondary hypertension Licorice ingestion or exogenous mineralocorticoid effect Plasma renin activity and aldosterone (both suppressed) Serum potassium and bicarbonate to document hypokalaemic alkalosis Aldosterone-to-renin ratio to exclude primary hyperaldosteronism Assessment of therapeutic response to ENaC blockade versus aldosterone antagonism Screening for licorice and exogenous mineralocorticoids Molecular genetic testing of SCNN1B and SCNN1G Liddle syndrome is an autosomal dominant cause of early-onset, low-renin hypertension caused by gain-of-function variants in the beta or gamma subunits of the epithelial sodium channel (SCNN1B, SCNN1G) The variants disrupt channel removal from the collecting-duct membrane, so ENaC remains constitutively active regardless of aldosterone The typical picture is hypertension with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis, and characteristically both renin and aldosterone are suppressed It behaves like a mineralocorticoid excess state but there is no excess hormone, hence the older term pseudoaldosteronism Because the defect is at the sodium channel itself, an ENaC-blocking potassium-sparing diuretic (amiloride or triamterene) is effective, whereas an aldosterone-receptor antagonist is not Dietary salt restriction complements pharmacological ENaC blockade Consider it in young patients with resistant hypertension, hypokalaemia and a suppressed renin and aldosterone, especially with a supportive family history Severe or resistant hypertension in a young person Profound hypokalaemia with muscle weakness or arrhythmia End-organ damage from long-standing untreated hypertension Strong family history of early hypertension or premature stroke Treating with an aldosterone-receptor antagonist, which is ineffective because the defect is downstream of the receptor at the channel Misdiagnosing it as primary hyperaldosteronism despite the suppressed aldosterone Overlooking the diagnosis in young hypertensive patients without checking renin and aldosterone Failing to screen and counsel first-degree relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance Liddle syndrome is driven by activating variants in the SCNN1B or SCNN1G genes that encode the beta and gamma subunits of the epithelial sodium channel in the distal nephron. These variants typically delete or alter a cytoplasmic motif that is normally recognised by the ubiquitin ligase machinery, so the channel is not internalised and degraded and instead accumulates at the apical membrane. The result is excessive, aldosterone-independent sodium reabsorption with parallel renal loss of potassium and hydrogen ion, generating volume expansion, hypertension, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. The expanded volume and raised pressure suppress renin release and therefore aldosterone secretion, giving the paradoxical combination of a mineralocorticoid-excess phenotype with low aldosterone. With ENaC-blocking therapy and salt restriction, blood pressure and potassium usually normalise and long-term outlook is good; untreated disease carries the cardiovascular and renal risks of chronic hypertension.

Ligamentum flavum hypertrophy — ligamentum flavum thickening, hypertrophic ligamentum flavum, yellow ligament hypertrophy Ossification of the ligamentum flavum, particularly in the thoracic spine Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament Degenerative disc herniation or bulge causing anterior canal compromise Facet joint hypertrophy or synovial cyst compressing the lateral recess Epidural lipomatosis narrowing the canal Spondylolisthesis with dynamic instability Vascular claudication as a cause of exertional leg symptoms MRI of the affected spinal region to measure ligamentum flavum thickness and grade canal and recess stenosis CT to demonstrate any calcification or ossification and bony anatomy for surgical planning Standing and flexion-extension radiographs to assess dynamic instability and spondylolisthesis Upright or axially loaded MRI where dynamic stenosis is suspected but supine imaging is equivocal Ankle-brachial pressure index or vascular studies to exclude peripheral arterial disease Electrophysiological studies where a peripheral neuropathy or radiculopathy needs clarification The ligamentum flavum connects adjacent laminae and is normally rich in elastin, giving it its characteristic recoil; hypertrophy reflects loss of elastic fibres with fibrosis and increased collagen rather than simple thickening It is a major posterior contributor to degenerative spinal canal stenosis, combining with disc bulging and facet hypertrophy to produce the trefoil-shaped canal of lumbar stenosis The thickened ligament buckles and infolds into the canal during extension and axial loading, producing a dynamic component to stenosis that worsens on standing and walking and eases on flexion This dynamic behaviour underlies neurogenic claudication, with the shopping-trolley sign and relief on sitting or leaning forward It should be distinguished from ossification of the ligamentum flavum, a distinct entity that predominantly affects the thoracic spine and can cause myelopathy, particularly in East Asian populations and in association with diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis MRI shows the thickened low-signal ligament indenting the dorsolateral thecal sac, and the degree of thickening correlates with the severity of canal narrowing Definitive treatment of symptomatic stenosis is surgical decompression to remove the hypertrophied ligament, with conservative measures reserved for milder disease Progressive myelopathy with hyperreflexia and gait disturbance, especially with thoracic ossification Cauda equina syndrome with saddle anaesthesia and bladder or bowel dysfunction Rapidly progressive or profound lower-limb weakness New or nocturnal back pain with systemic features suggesting infection or malignancy rather than degenerative stenosis Relying on supine MRI alone and underestimating dynamic stenosis that only manifests on standing or extension Confusing neurogenic with vascular claudication and missing peripheral arterial disease Overlooking thoracic ossification of the ligamentum flavum as a cause of myelopathy Attributing all symptoms to ligamentum flavum thickening when a synovial cyst, disc herniation or instability is the dominant lesion Ligamentum flavum hypertrophy is a degenerative process in which chronic mechanical stress and low-grade inflammation drive fibrosis of the normally elastic ligament. Repetitive loading, disc-height loss and segmental instability increase strain on the ligament and stimulate fibroblasts through transforming growth factor beta and other profibrotic mediators, leading to loss of elastic fibres, disorganised collagen deposition, scarring and sometimes calcification or ossification. Reduced disc height also allows the ligament to buckle and infold into the canal rather than stretch. The combined static bulk and dynamic buckling narrow the central canal and lateral recesses, compressing neural elements and, with axial loading and extension, producing intermittent ischaemia of the cauda equina or nerve roots that manifests as neurogenic claudication. Symptomatic degenerative stenosis due to ligamentum flavum hypertrophy tends to progress slowly, and surgical decompression reliably relieves neurogenic claudication in appropriately selected patients, although established myelopathy from thoracic ossification recovers less predictably.

Light chain deposition disease — LCDD, monoclonal light chain deposition disease, Randall-type monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease Diabetic nodular glomerulosclerosis Renal amyloidosis (Congo-red positive) Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Myeloma cast nephropathy Immunotactoid glomerulopathy Fibrillary glomerulonephritis Renal biopsy with immunofluorescence showing monoclonal light-chain restriction and electron microscopy showing granular deposits Congo-red staining to exclude amyloid Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation Serum free light chains and the free light-chain ratio Bone marrow examination for a plasma-cell clone and to assess for myeloma Skeletal survey or cross-sectional imaging and calcium where myeloma is suspected A monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease in which non-organised, non-amyloid monoclonal light chains (most often kappa) deposit along basement membranes Presents commonly with proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, hypertension and progressive renal impairment, frequently with nodular glomerulosclerosis on biopsy Deposits are Congo-red negative and lack the fibrillar or microtubular organisation of amyloid and immunotactoid disease Immunofluorescence shows monoclonal light-chain restriction along glomerular and tubular basement membranes; electron microscopy shows granular, punctate electron-dense deposits Reflects an underlying plasma-cell or B-cell clone, so a monoclonal gammopathy workup is mandatory, and it may accompany myeloma It falls within the spectrum of monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance when the clone is small but nephrotoxic Treatment is clone-directed therapy for the paraprotein-related disease alongside renin-angiotensin blockade and supportive care Features of overt multiple myeloma such as hypercalcaemia, anaemia or bone lesions Rapidly progressive renal impairment Coexisting cardiac or hepatic light-chain deposition Nephrotic syndrome with thromboembolic risk Mistaking nodular glomerulosclerosis for diabetic nephropathy without immunofluorescence Confusing it with amyloidosis when Congo-red staining is not performed Failing to identify and treat the underlying clone Overlooking small but nephrotoxic clones within the monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance spectrum Not screening for concurrent cast nephropathy and myeloma Light chain deposition disease arises from a clonal plasma-cell or B-cell population that secretes a monoclonal light chain with physicochemical properties favouring tissue deposition rather than fibril formation. The light chains deposit as granular, non-Congophilic material along the glomerular and tubular basement membranes and in the mesangium, where they stimulate mesangial matrix production and nodular expansion resembling diabetic glomerulosclerosis. Tubular basement membrane deposition contributes to tubulointerstitial injury. The result is progressive proteinuria, nodular glomerulosclerosis and declining renal function; because the causative clone may be small, the systemic tumour burden can be modest even when renal damage is substantial. Renal and overall outcome depend on the underlying clone and its response to clone-directed therapy; suppression of the pathogenic light chain can stabilise or improve renal function, whereas advanced renal impairment at diagnosis and coexisting myeloma predict worse outcomes. Extra-renal deposition, particularly cardiac, further worsens prognosis, and the disease may recur after transplantation if the clone is not controlled.

Lightning injury — lightning strike injury, keraunopathy, lightning-related injury High-voltage electrical injury Cardiac arrest from primary arrhythmia or ischaemia Blunt polytrauma from a fall or blast Seizure with postictal deficit Acute stroke Syncope or collapse of other cause Continuous cardiac monitoring and electrocardiography to detect arrhythmia and conduction abnormality Cardiac biomarkers where myocardial injury is suspected Serum creatine kinase and renal function to assess for muscle injury, recognising it is usually less severe than in high-voltage injury Trauma assessment with imaging directed at possible blunt injuries Otoscopic examination for tympanic membrane rupture and audiological review Ophthalmological assessment for cataract and other ocular injury, and neurological evaluation of persistent deficits The chief cause of immediate death is cardiac arrest, as the massive brief current can depolarise the entire myocardium and produce asystole; a secondary respiratory arrest from medullary paralysis may outlast the cardiac standstill Because primary arrest may be reversible, lightning casualties warrant a 'reverse triage' approach in which apparently lifeless victims are resuscitated first Keraunoparalysis is a transient limb paralysis, often of the legs, with cold, mottled, pulseless extremities that usually resolves over hours Lichtenberg figures are transient, fern-like or feathering skin markings that are effectively pathognomonic of a lightning strike and fade within a day or two Most of the current flashes over the body surface rather than passing deeply, so extensive deep tissue destruction and severe myoglobinuria are less typical than in high-voltage electrical injury Tympanic membrane rupture, cataracts, autonomic disturbance, and a range of neurological and neuropsychological sequelae are recognised complications Emergency management prioritises resuscitation and cardiac monitoring, with assessment for associated blunt trauma from the blast or a fall and evaluation of the eyes and ears Cardiac arrest or significant arrhythmia requiring immediate resuscitation and monitoring Respiratory arrest persisting after return of cardiac activity Depressed consciousness or focal neurological deficit Evidence of major associated blunt trauma from blast or fall Applying conventional triage and deprioritising an apparently dead lightning victim who could be resuscitated Stopping ventilation once a pulse returns, when persistent respiratory arrest still requires support Expecting the deep tissue destruction and severe rhabdomyolysis pattern of high-voltage injury and mismanaging fluids accordingly Overlooking tympanic, ocular, or occult traumatic injuries while focused on the cardiac presentation Lightning delivers an extremely high-voltage current over a very short duration, and much of it passes over the body surface as a flashover rather than through deep tissues, which distinguishes its injury pattern from that of sustained high-voltage electrical contact. The instantaneous current can act as a massive countershock that depolarises the myocardium and causes asystole; cardiac automaticity may then resume while the respiratory centre remains paralysed, so ongoing ventilation can be life-saving. Neurological effects include transient autonomic and vascular dysregulation producing keraunoparalysis. The characteristic skin ferning (Lichtenberg figures) reflects a transient electrical effect on cutaneous vessels rather than a true burn. Blast effect and secondary trauma from being thrown add to the injury burden. Prognosis hinges on whether cardiac and respiratory arrest are promptly and effectively treated; those who survive the initial event and receive early resuscitation can recover well, though a proportion are left with chronic neurological, cognitive, or autonomic sequelae. Keraunoparalysis and the cutaneous markings themselves are transient.

Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy — LGMD, sarcoglycanopathy, calpainopathy, dysferlinopathy Becker and Duchenne muscular dystrophies Inflammatory myopathies Metabolic and mitochondrial myopathies Spinal muscular atrophy Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy Congenital and myofibrillar myopathies Serum creatine kinase measurement Next-generation sequencing gene panel for limb-girdle muscular dystrophy Muscle biopsy with immunohistochemistry for specific structural proteins Muscle MRI to characterise the pattern of muscle involvement Electrocardiography and echocardiography for cardiomyopathy Pulmonary function testing for respiratory muscle weakness A genetically diverse group of muscular dystrophies unified by predominantly proximal weakness of the shoulder and pelvic girdles, with both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive forms Autosomal recessive subtypes are generally more common and include calpainopathy, dysferlinopathy, and the sarcoglycanopathies Onset ranges from childhood to adulthood, typically with difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, and lifting the arms Serum creatine kinase is usually elevated, sometimes markedly, especially in the recessive subtypes Some subtypes carry a significant risk of cardiomyopathy or respiratory muscle involvement, which guides surveillance Dysferlinopathy characteristically presents with distal calf involvement and very high creatine kinase in young adults Diagnosis increasingly relies on next-generation sequencing panels, complemented by muscle biopsy with protein immunostaining and imaging Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, with physiotherapy, aids to mobility, and cardiac and respiratory monitoring targeted to the subtype Symptoms of cardiomyopathy or conduction disturbance in cardiac-associated subtypes Declining respiratory function or nocturnal hypoventilation Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting an inflammatory or alternative cause Dysphagia or aspiration risk Acute rhabdomyolysis with very high creatine kinase and dark urine Grouping all cases together and missing subtype-specific cardiac or respiratory risks Overlooking a treatable inflammatory myopathy that can mimic the phenotype Failing to pursue genetic confirmation, which is essential for prognosis and counselling Attributing a very high creatine kinase solely to exercise in dysferlinopathy Neglecting cardiac surveillance in subtypes with known cardiomyopathy risk The limb-girdle muscular dystrophies result from variants in a wide range of genes encoding proteins essential to muscle-fibre structure and function, including components of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (such as the sarcoglycans), membrane-repair proteins (dysferlin), enzymes (calpain-3), and nuclear and glycosylation-related proteins. Loss of these proteins impairs sarcolemmal stability, membrane repair, or muscle-fibre maintenance, leading to repeated fibre injury, necrosis, and progressive replacement of muscle by fat and connective tissue. The predominant involvement of proximal girdle muscles produces the characteristic pattern of weakness, while the specific protein defect determines any associated cardiac or respiratory involvement. Prognosis varies widely by subtype, from slowly progressive forms compatible with a near-normal lifespan to more severe childhood-onset disease with early loss of ambulation. Cardiac and respiratory involvement in certain subtypes are the principal determinants of survival, underscoring the value of precise genetic diagnosis.

Limbic encephalitis — autoimmune limbic encephalitis, paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis, LE Herpes simplex and other viral encephalitis Status epilepticus and other seizure disorders Rapidly progressive dementia including prion disease Wernicke encephalopathy and metabolic encephalopathies CNS lymphoma or other neoplastic infiltration Primary psychiatric illness Serum and cerebrospinal fluid neuronal antibody panels (surface and intracellular antigens) Brain MRI focused on the medial temporal lobes Lumbar puncture for cell count, protein, oligoclonal bands, and to exclude infection EEG for seizures and encephalopathic patterns Whole-body CT and FDG-PET to search for an underlying malignancy, with repeat surveillance if negative Age- and antibody-directed tumour screening (e.g. pelvic imaging for ovarian teratoma in NMDA-receptor disease) An inflammatory syndrome of the medial temporal lobes presenting subacutely with short-term memory loss, confusion, psychiatric change, and seizures It may be paraneoplastic (driven by an underlying cancer) or a primary autoimmune process, and identifying the antibody helps predict the association with tumour Antibodies to intracellular antigens (e.g. Hu, Ma2) carry a strong cancer association and respond less well to immunotherapy, whereas surface-antigen antibodies (e.g. LGI1, NMDA receptor, GABA-B) often respond better LGI1 antibody encephalitis characteristically causes faciobrachial dystonic seizures and hyponatraemia NMDA-receptor encephalitis often affects younger patients with psychiatric onset, movement disorders, autonomic instability, and reduced consciousness, and is associated with ovarian teratoma Brain MRI typically shows increased T2/FLAIR signal in the medial temporal lobes, and CSF may show a lymphocytic pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands A thorough search for an occult malignancy is essential and may need repeating over time if initial screening is negative Early immunotherapy and treatment of any underlying tumour improve outcome, so prompt recognition matters Subacute encephalopathy warrants urgent workup for autoimmune and paraneoplastic causes alongside exclusion of infective encephalitis Positive onconeural or surface antibodies mandate a directed and, if negative, repeated search for occult cancer Refractory seizures or status epilepticus requiring urgent management Autonomic instability or reduced consciousness (notably in NMDA-receptor encephalitis) needing intensive monitoring Failing to start empirical aciclovir while herpes simplex encephalitis remains possible Not searching thoroughly, or repeatedly, for an occult tumour after a negative initial screen Missing faciobrachial dystonic seizures as a treatable clue to LGI1 antibody disease Attributing early psychiatric presentations solely to a primary psychiatric disorder Delaying immunotherapy while awaiting antibody results in a clinically compatible case Limbic encephalitis results from an immune attack, often antibody-mediated, directed at neuronal antigens concentrated in the limbic system, particularly the hippocampi and amygdalae. In paraneoplastic disease, a systemic tumour expresses neuronal antigens that trigger a cross-reactive immune response; antibodies against intracellular antigens mark a T-cell-mediated, less reversible process, whereas antibodies against neuronal surface proteins (such as NMDA receptor, LGI1, CASPR2, and GABA-B receptor) are considered directly pathogenic and more treatment-responsive. Inflammation of limbic structures produces the memory, behavioural, and seizure manifestations. Outcome depends on the antibody and cause: surface-antigen syndromes and prompt immunotherapy often allow substantial recovery, whereas classic paraneoplastic encephalitis with intracellular-antigen antibodies tends to respond poorly and is dominated by the underlying malignancy.

hippocampal sclerosis, contributing to mixed dementia Amyloid biomarkers are typically negative when it occurs in isolation, which helps distinguish it from Alzheimer's disease A neuropathological staging scheme tracks TDP-43 spread from the amygdala to the hippocampus and then the middle frontal gyrus Subacute or rapidly progressive amnesia suggesting autoimmune limbic encephalitis Seizures or fluctuating consciousness Focal neurological signs indicating an alternative structural cause Onset in a much younger patient than expected for this age-related entity Assuming all late-life amnestic dementia is Alzheimer's disease and not considering this entity, especially in amyloid-negative patients Interpreting negative amyloid biomarkers as excluding a neurodegenerative cause of memory loss of abnormally phosphorylated TDP-43 protein within limbic structures, beginning in the amygdala and spreading to the hippocampus and neocortex, often accompanied by hippocampal sclerosis. This proteinopathy disproportionately affects the oldest old and produces a predominantly amnestic syndrome. It is a distinct entity from Alzheimer's disease but frequently coexists with it, and the combination of pathologies tends to accelerate cognitive decline. This is a slowly progressive dementia; when it occurs in isolation the course tends to be more indolent than Alzheimer's disease, but coexisting Alzheimer or vascular pathology worsens the outlook. It is a neuropathologically defined entity, so definitive confirmation remains post-mortem, and management is supportive with attention to safety, function and carer support.

Postulated mechanisms include autoimmune-mediated microvascular injury and inflammation, with possible roles for cutaneous mosaicism and, in some, antecedent trauma or infection as triggers; contiguous involvement of underlying structures accounts for the bony atrophy and neurological findings. The disease often becomes inactive over years but leaves permanent atrophy and asymmetry; early immunosuppression can limit progression, while neurological and ocular involvement determine additional morbidity.

Lipodermatosclerosis is a sclerosing panniculitis driven by chronic venous insufficiency. Sustained venous hypertension leads to capillary proliferation, leakage of fibrinogen and red cells into the dermis, and localised tissue ischaemia and hypoxia. Fibrin cuffs around capillaries, activation of leucocytes and release of proteolytic and profibrotic mediators cause progressive fat necrosis followed by fibrosis of the subcutis and dermis. Over time the affected lower leg becomes woody and constricted, and the compromised skin is prone to ulceration. The condition is chronic and progressive if venous hypertension is untreated, but consistent compression and management of venous disease can relieve pain, halt progression and reduce ulceration; established sclerosis and skin changes are only partially reversible.

lipoedema — lipohyperplasia dolorosa, painful fat syndrome primary or secondary lymphoedema generalised obesity with bilateral lipohypertrophy chronic venous insufficiency Dercum disease (adiposis dolorosa) hypothyroid myxoedema systemic oedema from cardiac, renal or hepatic disease familial multiple symmetrical lipomatosis clinical assessment of distribution, tenderness, bruising and Stemmer sign lymphoscintigraphy where lymphoedema or lipo-lymphoedema is suspected venous duplex ultrasonography to exclude venous disease dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry or bioimpedance for body composition thyroid, renal, hepatic and cardiac evaluation to exclude systemic causes high-resolution ultrasound of subcutaneous tissue to gauge fat thickness A disorder of symmetrical, disproportionate subcutaneous adipose accumulation affecting the buttocks, hips and legs and sometimes the arms, occurring almost exclusively in women. Onset or worsening clusters around periods of hormonal change, notably puberty, pregnancy and the menopause, pointing to an oestrogen-related influence. The feet are characteristically spared, producing an abrupt cuff or bracelet at the ankle, in contrast to lymphoedema which typically involves the foot. The affected tissue is tender and painful, and patients bruise easily owing to increased capillary fragility. The Stemmer sign is negative in early disease and the swelling is non-pitting, helping to separate it from lymphoedema. The disproportion is resistant to dietary energy restriction and generalised weight loss, which reduce visceral and upper-body fat while sparing the affected depots. Longstanding lipoedema may cause secondary lymphatic overload, producing lipo-lymphoedema with foot involvement and a positive Stemmer sign. It is frequently misdiagnosed as simple obesity, causing considerable psychological distress and inappropriate blame for perceived dietary failure. new pitting oedema and a positive Stemmer sign indicating secondary lymphatic failure skin breakdown, recurrent cellulitis or lymphorrhoea disabling pain or mobility loss features of a coexisting eating disorder or severe psychological distress rapidly progressive or asymmetrical swelling prompting reassessment of the diagnosis labelling the condition as simple obesity and attributing failure to lose the affected fat to poor adherence confusing it with lymphoedema and applying the wrong management emphasis overlooking evolution into lipo-lymphoedema when the foot becomes involved neglecting the pain, bruising and psychological burden that define the patient experience expecting bariatric or dietary weight loss alone to resolve the disproportion Lipoedema is characterised by hyperplasia and hypertrophy of subcutaneous adipose tissue in a symmetrical, gynoid distribution that spares the trunk, hands and feet. The precise mechanism is incompletely understood, but proposed contributors include a hormonally modulated adipose disorder, microangiopathy with increased capillary permeability and fragility (accounting for pain and bruising), altered adipocyte and extracellular matrix behaviour, and a hereditary predisposition given frequent familial clustering. In early disease lymphatic transport is preserved, but progressive adipose expansion mechanically overloads the lymphatics and may culminate in secondary lymphatic insufficiency (lipo-lymphoedema). Chronic inflammation within the expanded fat and low-grade tissue oedema are thought to sustain symptoms. Lipoedema is a chronic, often slowly progressive condition that is not corrected by diet alone; conservative measures such as compression, exercise and complex decongestive therapy control symptoms, and liposuction can achieve durable reduction of affected fat in selected patients. Progression to lipo-lymphoedema worsens the outlook if untreated.

management is supportive as no specific therapy exists Progressive airway compromise from laryngeal and pharyngeal infiltration Seizures related to temporal lobe involvement Feeding or swallowing difficulty from tongue and oropharyngeal deposition Corneal or ocular involvement threatening vision Attributing lifelong hoarseness to recurrent laryngitis rather than recognising it as an early sign of the disease Confusing the hyaline deposits with amyloid, which requires Congo red staining and clinicopathological correlation to distinguish Overlooking the diagnosis in a child with unexplained scarring, beaded eyelid papules and a husky voice Failing to image the brain and missing epilepsy-associated temporal lobe calcification Not offering genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive condition Lipoid proteinosis is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in ECM1, which encodes extracellular matrix protein 1, a glycoprotein important in basement membrane structure, dermal homeostasis and regulation of growth factors and collagen organisation. ECM1 deficiency disrupts the dermo-epidermal junction and perivascular connective tissue, leading to progressive deposition of amorphous, periodic acid-Schiff-positive hyaline material composed of excess basement membrane components and disordered collagen around blood vessels, adnexa and at the epidermal-dermal interface. This infiltration thickens and stiffens the skin and mucosae, while similar deposition and dystrophic calcification within the brain, particularly the amygdala, account for the neurological and neuropsychiatric features. Lipoid proteinosis generally follows a benign, slowly progressive course with a normal life expectancy, though hoarseness, cutaneous scarring and neurological features such as epilepsy may persist lifelong. Airway compromise is uncommon but can require intervention, and the overall outlook is determined largely by the extent of laryngeal and neurological involvement.

Lipoma — Benign lipomatous tumour, Simple lipoma Atypical lipomatous tumour and well-differentiated liposarcoma Angiolipoma and spindle cell lipoma Hibernoma Epidermoid or sebaceous cyst Nodular fasciitis or other benign soft tissue proliferation Myxoid soft tissue tumour when myxoid change is present Lipoblastoma in a young child Ultrasound as a first-line assessment of a superficial soft tissue lump MRI with fat-saturated sequences to confirm uncomplicated fat and exclude worrying features Image-guided core biopsy for deep, large, or radiologically atypical lesions MDM2 amplification testing by FISH when atypical lipomatous tumour is a consideration Cross-sectional imaging of the affected compartment to define depth and relationship to muscle Histological examination of the excised specimen to confirm the diagnosis The commonest soft tissue tumour, composed of mature white adipocytes, typically presenting as a soft, mobile, painless subcutaneous mass Most are superficial and small; marginal excision is reserved for symptomatic, enlarging, or cosmetically troublesome lesions Any deep or rapidly growing fatty mass should be imaged and, if atypical, biopsied before excision rather than simply shelled out Rapid growth, size beyond roughly ten centimetres, or a deep or intramuscular location Pain, fixation to deeper structures, or overlying skin change Thick or nodular septa, non-fatty enhancing components, or incomplete fat suppression on MRI Recurrence after previous excision New neurological or vascular symptoms from local mass effect Assuming any fatty lump is a simple lipoma and shelling out a deep mass that proves to be an atypical lipomatous tumour Failing to image deep or large lesions before intervention Overlooking multiple lipomas as a clue to an underlying syndrome Mistaking myxoid or spindle cell change for malignancy, or vice versa, without molecular confirmation A lipoma is a benign clonal neoplasm of mature adipocytes rather than a simple overgrowth of normal fat. The majority are solitary, well-circumscribed, and enclosed by a thin fibrous capsule, arising most often in the subcutaneous tissue of the trunk, neck, and proximal limbs. A large proportion harbour clonal chromosomal rearrangements, most frequently involving the high-mobility group gene HMGA2 at 12q13-15, which drives adipocyte proliferation while preserving terminal differentiation, so the cells remain cytologically bland. The key biological distinction is from atypical lipomatous tumour and well-differentiated liposarcoma, which show amplification of MDM2 and CDK4 on 12q and carry a risk of dedifferentiation and local recurrence; this molecular separation, rather than morphology alone, underpins modern classification and management. Simple lipomas are benign with an excellent prognosis and rarely recur after complete marginal excision. The principal clinical task is to identify the minority of fatty masses that are in fact atypical lipomatous tumours, since these carry a risk of local recurrence and, in certain sites, dedifferentiation.
