intervention is reserved for the rare case causing significant obstruction or refractory arrhythmia Very bulky deposits causing right atrial inflow obstruction or superior vena cava compromise Refractory atrial arrhythmias attributable to the septal infiltration Imaging features atypical for fat that raise concern for a true neoplasm Rapid growth prompting reassessment of the benign diagnosis Misinterpreting benign FDG avidity as malignancy and pursuing unnecessary biopsy or surgery Confusing the deposit with an atrial tumour or thrombus Failing to note the characteristic sparing of the fossa ovalis that confirms the diagnosis Attributing unrelated symptoms to an incidental, asymptomatic septal deposit Lipomatous hypertrophy of the atrial septum is an overgrowth of adipose tissue, including metabolically active brown fat, within the interatrial septum. Because the fossa ovalis contains little fat, it is characteristically spared, so the deposit expands the muscular septum above and below it to create the classic dumbbell shape. The tissue is hyperplastic rather than neoplastic, which explains its benign course, but the brown-fat element takes up glucose and can appear avid on FDG imaging, mimicking malignancy. Extensive deposits may bulge into the right atrium, interfere with the adjacent conduction tissue, and predispose to supraventricular arrhythmias. The condition is benign and generally carries an excellent prognosis, with most patients remaining asymptomatic and requiring only reassurance and recognition of its characteristic imaging appearance.

or new pain in a previously indolent lipomatous lesion Neurological, bony, or soft-tissue symptoms suggesting atypical metastases from myxoid liposarcoma Recurrent retroperitoneal disease compromising adjacent organs Mistaking a well-differentiated liposarcoma for a benign lipoma without MDM2 testing Sampling only the fatty component and missing a coexisting dedifferentiated area on biopsy Staging myxoid liposarcoma with chest imaging alone and overlooking extrapulmonary metastases Underestimating the local recurrence risk of retroperitoneal disease and the need for meticulous margins Applying a single management approach across the biologically diverse subtypes Liposarcoma encompasses several distinct entities. Well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcomas are driven by supernumerary ring or giant marker chromosomes containing amplified 12q13-15 material, leading to overexpression of MDM2 and CDK4 that inactivates p53-mediated control and drives the cell cycle; dedifferentiation represents progression to a non-lipogenic high-grade component. Myxoid liposarcoma is a translocation-associated tumour defined by a FUS-DDIT3 fusion gene that produces an aberrant transcription factor impairing adipocytic differentiation. Pleomorphic liposarcoma, by contrast, has a complex, unstable karyotype without a defining recurrent alteration, explaining its high-grade, aggressive phenotype. Prognosis varies markedly by subtype, grade, size, and site: well-differentiated tumours have an excellent survival but recur locally, retroperitoneal dedifferentiated disease carries a high recurrence risk, myxoid tumours have an intermediate course dependent on round-cell content, and pleomorphic liposarcoma has the poorest outlook.

missed injuries lead to chronic pain and midfoot arthritis Foot compartment syndrome with tense swelling and disproportionate pain Plantar ecchymosis accompanying a midfoot injury Vascular compromise of the foot Instability missed on non-weight-bearing films Relying on non-weight-bearing films and missing subtle diastasis Dismissing significant midfoot pain as a simple sprain Overlooking evolving foot compartment syndrome Failing to recognise the significance of the fleck sign The tarsometatarsal joints are stabilised by their bony architecture, particularly the recessed base of the second metatarsal locked between the cuneiforms, and by strong plantar and interosseous ligaments including the Lisfranc ligament. An axial or twisting force on a plantarflexed foot, or a direct crush, disrupts these restraints and allows the metatarsal bases to displace, usually dorsally and laterally. Even subtle diastasis reflects loss of the midfoot's stabilising arch, and if left unreduced the resulting incongruity and instability progress to painful post-traumatic arthritis and arch collapse. Anatomical reduction with stable fixation offers the best outcome; non-anatomical reduction or missed instability commonly results in post-traumatic midfoot arthritis, deformity and chronic pain.

malformation pattern and gradient combined with targeted or panel-based molecular genetic testing Drug-resistant epilepsy including infantile spasms causing developmental regression Recurrent aspiration and failure to thrive from bulbar dysfunction Progressive respiratory compromise in severe forms Facial dysmorphism suggesting Miller-Dieker syndrome that warrants microarray testing Confusing classic lissencephaly with cobblestone lissencephaly, which has different genetics and eye and muscle involvement Overlooking subcortical band heterotopia in a mother of an affected child, missing X-linked DCX inheritance Failing to arrange microarray testing when facial features suggest Miller-Dieker syndrome Underestimating the anteroposterior gradient as a clue to the causative gene Lissencephaly results from failure of the tangential and radial migration of neurons from the germinal zones to the developing cortical plate during the first half of gestation. Variants in genes that regulate the microtubule cytoskeleton and motor-driven nucleokinesis, most notably LIS1 and DCX, impair neuronal movement so that neurons arrest before reaching their proper cortical layers. The cortex becomes abnormally thick and disorganised with few or no gyri, and the anteroposterior gradient of severity reflects the particular gene involved. Disrupted cortical architecture underlies the profound epilepsy and neurodevelopmental impairment. Prognosis is generally poor in severe classic lissencephaly, with profound intellectual disability, refractory epilepsy, and often shortened survival due to respiratory and feeding complications. Milder pachygyria and band heterotopia can be associated with better cognitive and seizure outcomes.

Listeriosis — Listeria monocytogenes infection Other causes of community-acquired bacterial meningitis (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae, group B streptococcus) (p.1228, Chap.143) Fungal or tuberculous meningitis (low CSF glucose with mononuclear pleocytosis can mimic Listeria) (p.1228, Chap.143) Brain abscess or other space-occupying CNS infection (Listeria abscess) (p.1228) Other bacteraemic/septic illnesses presenting with fever without a focus (p.1228) Blood cultures (note positive only ~half the time in pregnancy) (p.1229) CSF culture and Gram stain (may show gram-positive rods, but often no organisms or misleading gram-positive cocci/diplococci/diphtheroids) (p.1228-1229) Culture of normally sterile sites: amniotic fluid, placental tissue, fetal tissue (p.1229) Multiplex PCR panel on CSF (includes L. monocytogenes as a target) (p.1229) MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for rapid isolate identification (p.1229) MRI brain (superior to CT for neurolisteriosis and rhombencephalitis) (p.1228) Selective enrichment medium (PALCAM Listeria Selective Agar or Oxford Agar) for non-sterile specimens / outbreak work-up (p.1229) Whole-genome sequencing for outbreak investigation (p.1229) Primary or metastatic CNS malignancy (Listeria brain abscess may be misdiagnosed as tumour) (p.1228) Neoplasia / haematologic malignancy presenting with fever (also a risk factor and prognostic comorbidity) (p.1228) Listeriosis is acquired almost always via foodborne transmission; implicated foods are refrigerated ready-to-eat items (deli/delicatessen meats, hot dogs), soft cheeses made with raw/unpasteurised milk, unpasteurised dairy, raw produce (packaged salad, sprouts, enoki mushrooms, cantaloupe, caramel apples, frozen vegetables) and pate/meat spreads (p.1227-1228). Major risk groups for invasive disease are pregnant women and their neonates, older adults (risk rises with each decade over age 59), and immunocompromised persons (impaired cellular immunity from haematologic malignancy, transplant, HIV, glucocorticoids/immunosuppressants, or TNF-alpha inhibitors) (p.1227-1228). Bacteraemia without a focus is the most common manifestation of invasive listeriosis; presents with fever, chills, myalgias and arthralgias sometimes preceded by nausea/diarrhoea (p.1228). Neurolisteriosis is the second most common invasive manifestation; in a French cohort 84% of neurolisteriosis cases presented as meningoencephalitis (meningitis plus altered mental status, seizures, or focal findings) (p.1228). Compared with other bacterial meningitides, CSF pleocytosis and neutrophil predominance are typically LESS pronounced; ~60-75% have CSF WBC <1000/uL and only ~30-40% have low CSF glucose, so normal-ish CSF does not exclude Listeria (p.1228). Empiric bacterial-meningitis cover (ceftriaxone + vancomycin) does NOT cover Listeria; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage in patients >50 years old or with comorbid/immunocompromising disease (Chap.143, p.140372 / p.1122). Rhombencephalitis (brainstem/cerebellar encephalitis) disproportionately affects otherwise healthy older adults, classically biphasic (fever and headache, then asymmetric cranial nerve palsies, ataxia, tremor, hemiparesis or hemisensory deficits); nearly half develop respiratory failure (p.1228). MRI is superior to CT for diagnosis of neurolisteriosis, including rhombencephalitis (p.1228). Diagnosis is by isolation from a normally sterile site (blood, CSF, amniotic fluid, placental or fetal tissue); blood cultures are positive only about half the time in pregnant women, and CSF multiplex PCR panels and MALDI-TOF aid rapid identification (p.1229). Pregnant women usually have only mild flulike illness and rarely develop neurolisteriosis or death, yet transmit infection transplacentally to the fetus with high fetal morbidity; prepartum antibiotics started >=1 day before delivery improve the chance of a healthy infant (p.1228-1229). In invasive disease virtually all patients are hospitalised and 18% die; consider listeriosis acquired in hospital and investigate hospital-provided food when a hospitalised (especially immunocompromised) patient develops new symptoms (p.1227-1228). TMP-SMX given as Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis (e.g. in HIV or transplant recipients) also helps prevent listeriosis (p.1229). Signs of meningitis with altered mental status, seizures or focal neurologic deficits (meningoencephalitis) (p.1228) Brainstem/cerebellar signs - asymmetric cranial nerve palsies, ataxia, tremor, hemiparesis, hemisensory deficits (rhombencephalitis), with respiratory failure in nearly half (p.1228) Fever or signs of fetal distress in a pregnant woman (meconium-stained amniotic fluid, abnormal fetal heart rate) (p.1229) Multiorgan failure and monocytopenia (<200 cells/uL) - markers associated with death (p.1228) Cephalosporins are NOT effective against L. monocytogenes; standard empiric meningitis cover (ceftriaxone +/- vancomycin) misses Listeria, so ampicillin must be added empirically in patients >50 years or with comorbid/immunocompromising disease (p.1229, Chap.143 p.140372). Febrile gastroenteritis form is rarely diagnosed because Listeria is not detected by routine stool cultures or rapid stool tests, and stool culture is NOT indicated in evaluating invasive listeriosis (p.1227, p.1229). Gram-variable appearance as cocci, diplococci or diphtheroids can obscure the diagnosis; Listeria must be distinguished from other gram-positive rods, especially diphtheroids (p.1227, p.1229). Relatively bland CSF (WBC often <1000/uL, frequently no organisms on Gram stain, only ~30-40% with low glucose) can falsely reassure - do not exclude Listeria meningitis on CSF profile alone (p.1228). Brain abscess due to Listeria may be misdiagnosed as primary or metastatic malignancy; CSF can be normal when abscess occurs without concurrent meningitis (p.1228). Adjunctive dexamethasone is associated with reduced survival in neurolisteriosis and should be avoided; it is also not recommended for established Listeria meningitis (p.1229, Chap.143). Treatment failures have been reported with meropenem despite in vitro susceptibility, and TMP-SMX resistance occurs - perform susceptibility testing if TMP-SMX is considered (p.1229). Testing/treatment is NOT indicated for an asymptomatic person who ate a recalled product, even if they have risk factors (p.1229). L. monocytogenes is a ubiquitous, nonsporulating, facultatively anaerobic gram-positive rod (showing small zones of beta-haemolysis and characteristic tumbling motility) that lives in soil and decaying vegetation and can grow at refrigerator temperatures as low as 4 C and tolerate low-pH/high-salt environments. Infection follows ingestion of contaminated food; the infectious dose is likely very low in the severely immunocompromised, and raised gastric pH (e.g. from proton-pump inhibitors) probably promotes gut survival. After transcytosis across the intestinal epithelium the organism spreads via mesenteric lymph nodes and bloodstream to its target organs (liver and spleen) and can cross the blood-brain barrier and the placenta. Virulence factors include internalins (InlA, InlB) for invasion of nonphagocytic cells, listeriolysin O and phospholipases for escape from the phagocytic vacuole, and ActA for actin-based cell-to-cell spread that evades antibodies and complement. Iron promotes growth, explaining the association of listeriosis with iron-overload states such as haemochromatosis. Host defence is predominantly cell-mediated (interferon-gamma, TNF-alpha, and CD8+ T cells), accounting for the predilection for those with impaired cellular immunity. (p.1227) Invasive listeriosis carries substantial mortality: 18% of reported cases die and virtually all are hospitalised. In a large French (MONALISA) cohort the 3-month mortality was 46% for bacteraemia and 30% for neurolisteriosis; death was associated with multiorgan failure, neoplasia, worsening of preexisting comorbidities, monocytopenia (<200 cells/uL), older age and female sex, and (for neurolisteriosis) a positive blood culture and adjunctive dexamethasone use. Nearly half of neurolisteriosis survivors have long-term neurologic impairment. In pregnancy-associated disease, fetal/neonatal outcomes are poor: in a cohort of 107 pregnancies 24% ended in fetal loss, 45% in premature birth and only ~5% had a normal delivery and postpartum course; overall 3% of 189 live-born infants died. (p.1228-1229) No formal severity score. Harrison frames the clinical spectrum from non-invasive self-limited febrile gastroenteritis in healthy persons to invasive listeriosis (bacteraemia without a focus, neurolisteriosis [meningoencephalitis, cerebritis, focal abscess, rhombencephalitis], focal infections, and pregnancy-associated/neonatal disease [granulomatosis infantiseptica, early-onset sepsis, late-onset meningitis]). Severity is judged clinically by syndrome, with prognostic markers including multiorgan failure and monocytopenia. (p.1227-1229)

Lithium-associated nephropathy — lithium nephropathy, lithium-induced nephrotoxicity, lithium-associated chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (lithium) Other chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathies (analgesic, aristolochic acid) Central diabetes insipidus Primary polydipsia Hypertensive nephrosclerosis Obstructive uropathy with polyuria Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (given microcysts) Serum lithium level and review of cumulative exposure and duration Renal function trend and estimated glomerular filtration rate Urine osmolality with a water-deprivation and desmopressin assessment for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus Urinalysis and quantification of proteinuria Renal ultrasound or MRI, which may show microcysts Renal biopsy in selected cases to confirm chronic tubulointerstitial disease Long-term lithium therapy causes a chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy with slowly progressive renal impairment Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is the earliest and commonest renal effect, with polyuria, polydipsia and impaired urinary concentration Biopsy typically shows tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis and characteristic distal tubular and collecting-duct microcysts Lithium enters collecting-duct principal cells via the epithelial sodium channel and interferes with aquaporin-2 water channels, causing resistance to antidiuretic hormone Nephrotoxicity relates to cumulative dose and duration, so the decision to continue lithium must balance renal risk against psychiatric benefit Distinguish chronic nephropathy from acute lithium toxicity, which can cause acute kidney injury and neurotoxicity, sometimes requiring dialysis Management centres on drug withdrawal and supportive care where feasible, careful monitoring, and adequate hydration, with a specialist mental-health discussion before stopping Acute lithium toxicity with neurological features and acute kidney injury Severe hypernatraemia from uncontrolled nephrogenic diabetes insipidus Rapidly declining renal function suggesting an additional insult Volume depletion precipitating lithium accumulation and toxicity Stopping lithium abruptly without psychiatric input, risking relapse of mood disorder Attributing polyuria to primary polydipsia rather than nephrogenic diabetes insipidus Allowing volume depletion or NSAID use that precipitates lithium toxicity Assuming renal impairment will reverse fully once the drug is withdrawn Confusing lithium microcysts with polycystic kidney disease on imaging Lithium is freely filtered and reabsorbed in the proximal tubule and enters collecting-duct principal cells through the epithelial sodium channel. Within these cells it disrupts signalling and downregulates aquaporin-2 water channels, impairing the antidiuretic response and producing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Chronic exposure injures the distal nephron and collecting ducts, driving tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis and the formation of distal tubular and collecting-duct microcysts, which correlate with progressive loss of glomerular filtration. Some patients also develop a distal renal tubular acidification defect and, less commonly, proteinuria. The cumulative burden of exposure determines the degree of irreversible chronic damage. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and early functional changes are often partly reversible if lithium is stopped, but established interstitial fibrosis and reduced glomerular filtration may be irreversible and can progress even after discontinuation, occasionally to end-stage kidney disease. Careful monitoring and shared decision-making about continuing therapy improve long-term renal outcomes.

Lithium toxicity — lithium poisoning, lithium overdose, lithium intoxication Serotonin syndrome or neuroleptic malignant syndrome Other causes of encephalopathy (metabolic, infective) Cerebellar stroke or other structural lesion Sepsis with delirium Other drug intoxications causing tremor and confusion Serial serum lithium levels to track trend rather than a single value Serum electrolytes, urea, and creatinine to assess renal function ECG for T-wave changes, QT effects, and arrhythmia Thyroid function, as chronic use affects the thyroid Assessment for precipitants such as dehydration and interacting medications Lithium has a narrow therapeutic window, and toxicity is usually neurological - tremor, hyperreflexia, ataxia, dysarthria, agitation, confusion, and in severe cases seizures and coma Distinguish acute, acute-on-chronic, and chronic toxicity, as chronic toxicity produces serious neurological features at lower serum levels and is more likely to cause lasting harm Serum levels correlate poorly with severity in chronic toxicity because lithium distributes slowly into tissues including the central nervous system Common precipitants of chronic toxicity include dehydration, renal impairment, and interacting drugs such as thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and NSAIDs There is no antidote; management centres on generous isotonic fluid resuscitation to restore volume and promote renal elimination Activated charcoal does not bind lithium, but whole-bowel irrigation may help after ingestion of sustained-release preparations Haemodialysis is the definitive means of removal and is indicated for severe neurological features, renal failure, or very high levels, with rebound rises possible afterwards requiring repeat treatment Chronic toxicity can leave a permanent cerebellar and neurological deficit (the syndrome of irreversible lithium-effectuated neurotoxicity) Seizures, marked confusion, or reduced consciousness Severe neurological signs at only modestly raised levels, suggesting chronic toxicity Acute kidney injury impairing lithium clearance Cardiac arrhythmia or significant ECG changes Persistent or rebound rises in level after initial treatment Relying on a single serum level and underestimating chronic toxicity with a modest number Giving activated charcoal, which does not adsorb lithium Overlooking interacting drugs and dehydration that precipitated the toxicity Delaying haemodialysis in severe or chronic toxicity, risking permanent neurological damage Lithium is a monovalent cation handled by the kidney similarly to sodium, so states that reduce renal perfusion or increase sodium reabsorption (volume depletion, diuretics, renal impairment) reduce its clearance and raise levels. It moves slowly across cell membranes, accumulating intracellularly and particularly in the central nervous system, which explains the delay between serum levels and clinical effect and the persistence of neurotoxicity. Intracellularly it interferes with neurotransmission and second-messenger systems. Lithium also impairs renal concentrating ability, causing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus that promotes dehydration and a vicious cycle of rising concentration. Acute overdose in a lithium-naive patient often does well with fluids and, if needed, dialysis, whereas chronic toxicity carries a higher risk of prolonged or permanent neurological (especially cerebellar) impairment; outcome depends on severity, renal function, and timeliness of dialysis.

Little League elbow — medial epicondyle apophysitis, medial elbow overuse injury in throwers Osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum Ulnar collateral ligament injury Ulnar neuritis Medial epicondylitis (in adults) Elbow fracture Clinical assessment of medial elbow tenderness and throwing history Radiographs, including comparison views, for apophyseal widening or avulsion MRI where soft-tissue or osteochondral injury is suspected Assessment of throwing mechanics and workload Evaluation of ulnar nerve function A spectrum of overuse injury to the medial elbow in skeletally immature throwing athletes, centred on the medial epicondyle apophysis Repetitive valgus stress during the throwing motion causes traction injury at the medial epicondyle Presents with medial elbow pain during and after throwing, sometimes with reduced throwing velocity and control Severe cases can produce avulsion of the medial epicondyle apophysis It is strongly linked to excessive pitching volume, and pitch-count and rest guidelines are central to prevention Management is relative rest from throwing, mechanics correction and graded return, with surgery for significant displaced avulsion Displaced medial epicondyle avulsion Locking or mechanical symptoms suggesting osteochondritis dissecans with loose bodies Ulnar nerve symptoms Persistent pain despite rest Allowing continued throwing through pain Missing capitellar osteochondritis dissecans as a coexisting lateral injury Overlooking a displaced avulsion needing surgery Not addressing pitch counts and throwing mechanics Little League elbow results from repetitive valgus forces generated during overhead throwing, which place traction on the medial structures of the immature elbow, particularly the medial epicondyle apophysis where the flexor-pronator muscles and ulnar collateral ligament attach. The growth cartilage is weaker than the adjacent tendon and ligament, so repetitive stress causes apophysitis and, when overload is severe, apophyseal separation or avulsion. Lateral compressive forces can additionally injure the capitellum in the same throwing mechanism. With early recognition and rest most young throwers recover fully, but continued overload risks apophyseal avulsion and longer-term elbow problems; adherence to workload limits is protective.

livedo reticularis — livedo racemosa (pathological variant), cutis marmorata Cutis marmorata (physiological livedo) Livedo racemosa secondary to systemic disease Livedoid vasculopathy Erythema ab igne Cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita Reticulate erythema of connective tissue disease Cholesterol embolisation syndrome Antiphospholipid antibody testing (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I antibodies) Autoimmune screen including antinuclear antibodies and ANCA Cryoglobulins and complement levels Deep skin biopsy taken from the centre of the pale area Screening for an embolic source and a thrombophilia workup Neuroimaging when Sneddon syndrome is suspected A net-like, reticular violaceous mottling of the skin caused by altered flow within the dermal vascular network. The physiological form (cutis marmorata) produces complete, symmetrical rings that reverse with warming and is common and benign in infants and young women. Livedo racemosa, by contrast, shows broken, irregular, asymmetrical rings that persist on warming and signals an underlying vasculopathy. Livedo racemosa is an important cutaneous marker of Sneddon syndrome (with cerebrovascular events) and of antiphospholipid syndrome. Secondary causes include vasculitis such as polyarteritis nodosa, cholesterol embolisation, calciphylaxis, hyperviscosity, cryoglobulinaemia and certain drugs. Reversibility with warming and the regularity of the pattern help separate the benign from the pathological forms. When biopsy is needed it should be deep and taken from the pale centre of the network rather than the blue rim, where the culprit vessel is more likely to be sampled. Neurological symptoms such as stroke or transient ischaemic attack suggesting Sneddon syndrome Skin ulceration or necrosis Systemic features of vasculitis or embolic disease A fixed, irregular racemosa pattern that does not resolve with warming Dismissing pathological livedo racemosa as benign cutis marmorata. Taking a superficial or peripherally placed biopsy that misses the affected vessel. Failing to test for antiphospholipid syndrome in a young patient presenting with livedo and stroke. Attributing drug-induced or embolic livedo to a primary skin disorder. The reticular pattern reflects the cone-shaped territories supplied by ascending dermal arterioles: deoxygenated blood pooling in the venous plexus at the periphery of each cone produces the bluish reticulate network. Anything that reduces inflow or increases stasis at the cone periphery accentuates the pattern, including vasospasm, luminal obstruction from thrombosis, emboli or hyperviscosity, and inflammatory vessel-wall disease. In the physiological form the change is purely vasomotor and reverses with warming, whereas in pathological livedo racemosa fixed vascular occlusion or wall damage produces a persistent, irregular pattern. The physiological form is entirely benign, whereas the prognosis of pathological livedo depends on the underlying disorder, with thrombotic risk in antiphospholipid and Sneddon syndromes being of particular concern.

Livedoid vasculopathy — livedoid vasculitis, atrophie blanche, segmental hyalinizing vasculopathy, PURPLE (painful purpuric ulcers with reticular pattern of the lower extremities) Cutaneous small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis Venous stasis ulceration and lipodermatosclerosis Antiphospholipid syndrome Cryoglobulinaemia Polyarteritis nodosa (cutaneous) Pyoderma gangrenosum Skin biopsy showing hyaline fibrin thrombi with minimal vessel-wall inflammation Thrombophilia screen (including antiphospholipid antibodies and relevant clotting factor abnormalities) Autoimmune and connective-tissue disease serology Cryoglobulins and, where indicated, hepatitis serology Assessment of venous insufficiency with duplex studies Wound swab if secondary infection of ulcers is suspected A chronic thrombo-occlusive disorder of dermal vessels presenting with painful purpuric macules and recurrent ulcers of the lower legs, ankles, and feet Healing leaves characteristic atrophie blanche: smooth, porcelain-white stellate scars ringed by telangiectasia and pigmentation Pain is often disproportionate to the visible lesions and is a prominent, disabling feature It is primarily a vasculopathy driven by intravascular thrombosis, not a true inflammatory vasculitis, so histology shows hyaline thrombi and fibrin with little primary vessel-wall inflammation Frequently associated with thrombophilic and prothrombotic states, and screening for these is important Disease is typically chronic with a seasonal (summer) flare pattern in many patients Management is directed at reducing thrombosis and improving blood flow, using antithrombotic and other vasoactive approaches alongside wound care Detection of an underlying thrombophilia or antiphospholipid syndrome requiring specialist management Rapidly progressive or extensive ulceration with severe pain Secondary infection of chronic ulcers Features suggesting an alternative systemic vasculitis or connective-tissue disease Mislabelling it as an inflammatory vasculitis and relying on immunosuppression rather than antithrombotic therapy Failing to screen for thrombophilia and antiphospholipid syndrome Confusing atrophie blanche scarring with simple venous stasis change Underestimating the severity of pain and its impact on function Livedoid vasculopathy results from occlusion of dermal microvessels by fibrin thrombi rather than from primary inflammatory destruction of vessel walls. Hypercoagulable and prothrombotic tendencies promote intravascular thrombosis, causing localised ischaemia and infarction of the skin. The resulting tissue hypoxia produces the painful purpura and punched-out ulcers, and healing of these infarcts yields the sclerotic, avascular white scars of atrophie blanche surrounded by reactive telangiectasia. Because the process is occlusive, any inflammatory infiltrate is usually secondary, and identifying and treating underlying thrombophilia is central to control. Livedoid vasculopathy is a chronic, relapsing condition with recurrent painful ulceration and progressive atrophie blanche scarring; outcomes improve when an underlying prothrombotic state is identified and treated, though many patients experience persistent disease.

Liver haemangioma — hepatic haemangioma, cavernous haemangioma of the liver, hepatic cavernous haemangioma, liver hemangioma Focal nodular hyperplasia Hepatic adenoma Hepatocellular carcinoma Hypervascular liver metastasis Simple hepatic cyst Angiosarcoma (rare) Contrast-enhanced CT showing peripheral nodular discontinuous enhancement with centripetal fill-in MRI with heavily T2-weighted sequences for a characteristically bright lesion Ultrasound (often a well-defined hyperechoic lesion) as an initial or incidental finding Labelled red-cell scintigraphy in selected diagnostically uncertain cases Coagulation screen and platelet count if a very large lesion raises concern for consumptive coagulopathy Interval imaging surveillance for indeterminate or enlarging lesions Hepatic haemangioma is the commonest benign liver tumour and is usually an incidental finding on imaging in an asymptomatic patient Most are small and require no treatment; large (giant) lesions may cause dull right upper quadrant discomfort, early satiety, or a mass effect Contrast imaging shows a characteristic pattern of peripheral nodular enhancement with progressive centripetal fill-in on CT or MRI, which is typically diagnostic MRI demonstrates a markedly hyperintense lesion on heavily T2-weighted sequences, helping to confirm the diagnosis non-invasively Percutaneous biopsy is generally avoided because of the theoretical risk of bleeding and because imaging is usually diagnostic Management is overwhelmingly conservative with reassurance and, for uncertain or enlarging lesions, surveillance; intervention is reserved for significant symptoms, diagnostic doubt, or complications Kasabach-Merritt syndrome, a consumptive coagulopathy, is a rare association with very large lesions, chiefly in infants Spontaneous or traumatic rupture with intraperitoneal haemorrhage and haemodynamic instability (rare but life-threatening) Consumptive coagulopathy (Kasabach-Merritt syndrome) with a very large lesion Rapid enlargement or atypical imaging raising doubt about the benign diagnosis Severe, progressive symptoms from a giant lesion causing mass effect Performing percutaneous biopsy of a suspected haemangioma and risking haemorrhage Misinterpreting the lesion as a metastasis or hepatocellular carcinoma and subjecting the patient to unnecessary intervention Over-treating small asymptomatic lesions that only need reassurance Attributing unrelated abdominal symptoms to a small incidental haemangioma Overlooking coagulopathy in a patient with a very large lesion A hepatic haemangioma is a benign vascular malformation composed of multiple dilated, blood-filled vascular channels lined by a single layer of endothelium and separated by thin fibrous septa. It is thought to be congenital in origin, enlarging by ectasia rather than by cellular proliferation, and its growth can be influenced by hormonal factors such as pregnancy and oestrogen exposure. Blood flow through the lesion is slow, which underlies the characteristic delayed centripetal enhancement on imaging. Very large lesions can trap and consume platelets and clotting factors, producing the Kasabach-Merritt consumptive coagulopathy, and rarely a superficial lesion may bleed after trauma. The prognosis is excellent; most haemangiomas remain stable, cause no symptoms, and never require treatment, with an extremely low risk of complications. Even large lesions usually behave benignly, and surgical resection of genuinely symptomatic or complicated lesions gives good long-term results.

Liver Transplantation — Orthotopic liver transplantation, OLT, Hepatic allograft transplantation, Living-donor liver transplantation Posttransplant graft dysfunction: rejection vs biliary obstruction vs primary graft nonfunction vs vascular compromise (portal vein or hepatic artery thrombosis) vs drug hepatotoxicity vs recurrent primary disease vs viral hepatitis/CMV — these are clinically and biochemically difficult to distinguish, often requiring biliary imaging and percutaneous liver biopsy. Recurrent primary biliary cholangitis vs chronic rejection (histologically nearly indistinguishable; a florid inflammatory bile duct lesion favors recurrent PBC but is not specific). Recurrent autoimmune hepatitis or sclerosing cholangitis vs rejection or posttransplant bile duct injury. MELD/MELD-Na/MELD-3.0 score calculation (bilirubin, albumin, sodium, creatinine, INR) for allocation and prognosis; PELD for children under 12. Serum bilirubin and aminotransferases — most reliable, though nonspecific, indicators of allograft rejection. Percutaneous liver biopsy and radiographic visualization of the biliary tree to differentiate causes of graft dysfunction. Donor screening: hemodynamic stability, oxygenation, absence of infection/abdominal trauma/hepatic dysfunction; serologic testing for HBV, HCV, HIV (infected organs now used selectively with matching and informed consent). Recipient cardiopulmonary evaluation (especially age >70) to exclude ischemic cardiac disease; assessment of pulmonary artery pressure and intrapulmonary shunting. anti-HBs titer monitoring (threshold ~100 mIU/mL) to guide HBIg dosing in hepatitis B recipients. Orthotopic transplantation (native liver removed, donor organ placed in the same anatomic site) is the preferred and technically most advanced approach; 1-year survival has risen from roughly 30% in the 1970s to over 90% today, attributed more to better patient selection and timing than to technical or immunologic advances alone. Optimal timing matters: the disease should be advanced enough that medical options are exhausted, yet the procedure performed early enough to allow success. Better pretransplant clinical status predicts higher posttransplant survival. Allocation of deceased-donor organs is driven by the MELD score (bilirubin, albumin, sodium, creatinine, INR, plus a female adjustment), a continuous scale from 6 to 40 in which higher values indicate greater illness severity; it replaced the older Child-Turcotte-Pugh-based scheme and reduced waiting-list mortality. Status 1 (highest priority) is reserved for acute liver failure and for early posttransplant catastrophes such as primary graft nonfunction and hepatic artery thrombosis, superseding the MELD score. Liver recipients with MELD scores below 15 have higher posttransplant mortality than comparable patients who remain on the waiting list, so transplant at very low MELD offers limited benefit. HLA tissue typing is NOT required for liver transplantation, and preformed cytotoxic HLA antibodies do not preclude the procedure; ABO compatibility and organ size are the key matching considerations. Tacrolimus has supplanted cyclosporine as primary immunosuppression; it is 10-100 times more potent, but nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity (tremor, seizures, hallucinations, psychosis, coma) are its principal adverse effects. Cyclosporine and tacrolimus should not be combined because of overlapping nephrotoxicity. Both calcineurin inhibitors are metabolized by cytochrome P450 IIIA: enzyme inducers (phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, rifampin) lower drug levels, while inhibitors (azoles, macrolides, verapamil, diltiazem, ritonavir) raise them. Sirolimus is avoided early posttransplant because it impairs wound healing and is associated with increased hepatic artery thrombosis in the first 30 days; its antiproliferative effect makes it attractive in recipients with prior or current malignancy such as HCC. Infection timing follows a predictable pattern: conventional postoperative infections (pneumonia, wound, urinary, line, intraabdominal) dominate the first month, after which opportunistic pathogens (CMV, herpesviruses, Aspergillus, Candida, Cryptococcus, mycobacteria, Pneumocystis, Toxoplasma, Nocardia, Legionella, Listeria) predominate as immunosuppression takes its toll. Long-term HBIg prophylaxis transformed transplantation for chronic hepatitis B; without prophylaxis hepatitis B almost always recurs, but indefinite/long-term HBIg (often combined with high-barrier oral antivirals such as entecavir or tenofovir) reduces reinfection and mortality, yielding outcomes indistinguishable from non-HBV indications. Direct-acting antiviral (DAA) agents against HCV have markedly improved both pre- and posttransplant outcomes, allowing pretransplant clearance of viremia (sometimes delaying or obviating transplant) and high sustained virologic response rates in allograft HCV infection. Acute liver failure with impending cerebral edema — a transplant emergency requiring rapid donor identification before life-threatening complications set in. Fever, right upper quadrant pain, and falling bile pigment/volume with rising bilirubin and aminotransferases — suggest acute allograft rejection. Fibrosing cholestatic hepatitis (marked hyperbilirubinemia and prolonged prothrombin time out of proportion to modest aminotransferase rises) in recurrent hepatitis B — rapidly progressive liver failure. Postoperative intraperitoneal bleeding raising intraabdominal pressure and reducing renal blood flow — reversible with laparotomy to evacuate clot and ligate the bleeding site. New opportunistic infection beyond the first postoperative month in an immunosuppressed host demands prompt recognition and treatment. Severe portopulmonary hypertension (mean pulmonary artery pressure >35 mmHg) or severe hypoxemia from right-to-left intrapulmonary shunts (PO2 <50 mmHg) — relative contraindications signaling high operative risk. Treating acute rejection with pulse glucocorticoids in HCV-infected recipients risks triggering severe recurrent allograft hepatitis C (though DAAs now mitigate this concern). Cyclosporine and tacrolimus must not be co-administered because of overlapping nephrotoxicity and because tacrolimus reduces cyclosporine clearance. Prior extensive biliary/hepatobiliary surgery complicates transplantation and is a relative contraindication, so biliary diversion has been largely abandoned in sclerosing cholangitis candidates. Cholangiocarcinoma recurs almost invariably; only highly selected stage I/II patients after neoadjuvant chemoradiation should be considered. Eradicating HCV before transplant can lower the MELD score and paradoxically reduce allocation priority in patients who still need a graft for ongoing decompensation. Advanced age alone is no longer an absolute contraindication, but in patients over 70 a thorough cardiac and comorbidity workup is mandatory. Relying on short-term (2 months or less) HBIg, preoperative vaccination, or interferon alone is ineffective for preventing hepatitis B recurrence; long-term prophylaxis is required. End-stage liver disease produces portal hypertension, coagulopathy (prolonged prothrombin time, thrombocytopenia), and a hyperdynamic high-cardiac-output circulatory state; transplantation replaces the failing organ and rapidly reverses the hyperdynamic state. The graft is vulnerable to immunologic and ischemic injury. Acute cellular rejection arises 1-2 weeks postoperatively from a T-cell-mediated response, with histology showing a mixed portal infiltrate, bile duct injury, and endothelialitis. Chronic rejection produces progressive cholestasis, vascular lesions (intimal fibrosis, subintimal foam cells, fibrinoid necrosis), and ductopenia (vanishing bile duct syndrome). Calcineurin inhibitors act on the calcium-dependent T-cell signal transduction pathway to block lymphokine (IL-2/3/4, TNF-alpha) gene activation. Ischemic injury during harvesting underlies primary graft nonfunction; preservation in University of Wisconsin solution (rich in lactobionate and raffinose) extends tolerable cold-ischemic time. ABO-mismatched grafts (e.g., group O liver into a group A or B recipient) can cause transient passenger-lymphocyte autoimmune hemolytic anemia that resolves once recipient marrow repopulates the graft. One-year survival is now about 85-90%, and 5-year survival exceeds 60%. Outcome correlates strongly with pretransplant status: patients still working or only partially disabled achieve roughly >85% 1-year survival; those needing continuous in-hospital care about 70%; those requiring ICU life support about 50%. High pretransplant disease severity (MELD >25) and high-risk features (malignancy, fulminant hepatitis, age >65, concurrent renal failure, respirator dependence, portal vein thrombosis, prior portacaval shunt or multiple right-upper-quadrant operations) reduce survival to about 60% at 1 year and 35% at 5 years. Survival after retransplantation for primary graft nonfunction is about 50%. Failures within the first 3 months are mainly technical, infectious, or hemorrhagic; later failures stem from infection, rejection, or recurrent disease (malignancy, viral hepatitis, return to alcohol use). Renal failure (18% at 5 years, 25% at 10 years) and cardiovascular disease are leading causes of late mortality. Allocation and prognosis use the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score, a continuous scale from 6 to 40 (values above 40 counted as 40) derived from serum bilirubin, albumin, sodium, creatinine, and INR with a female adjustment; higher scores indicate greater illness severity. Variants include MELD-Na (2016) and MELD-3.0 (2023). PELD is used for candidates under 12. Status 1 (acute liver failure, primary graft nonfunction, hepatic artery thrombosis) supersedes MELD. The older Child-Turcotte-Pugh score (encephalopathy, ascites, bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time) has been replaced for allocation. MELD exception points are granted (e.g., for HCC) via the National Liver Review Board.

LMNA cardiomyopathy — lamin A/C cardiomyopathy, LMNA-related dilated cardiomyopathy, laminopathy cardiomyopathy, LMNA dilated cardiomyopathy with conduction disease Idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy of other genetic cause (for example titin) Cardiac sarcoidosis Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy Myocarditis with conduction disease Progressive cardiac conduction defect (SCN5A) Other muscular dystrophies with cardiac involvement Serial 12-lead ECGs to detect evolving conduction disease and atrial arrhythmia Ambulatory ECG monitoring for non-sustained ventricular tachycardia Echocardiography to assess chamber size and systolic function Cardiac MRI to quantify function and detect myocardial fibrosis Genetic testing of LMNA with cascade family screening Creatine kinase and neurological assessment where skeletal myopathy is suspected Caused by variants in LMNA, encoding the nuclear envelope proteins lamin A and C, and characterised by dilated cardiomyopathy with prominent conduction system disease The typical sequence is early atrioventricular conduction disturbance and atrial arrhythmia, followed by ventricular arrhythmia and progressive left ventricular dysfunction It carries a notably high risk of malignant ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death, which can precede or exceed the degree of pump failure Because sudden death may occur even with only mildly reduced ejection fraction, defibrillator implantation is considered at a lower threshold than in many other cardiomyopathies Skeletal muscle involvement (Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy or limb-girdle patterns) may coexist, reflecting the wider laminopathy spectrum Recognised high-risk markers include non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, male sex, non-missense variants, and progressive reduction in ejection fraction Family screening is essential given autosomal dominant inheritance and the arrhythmic risk in relatives Non-sustained or sustained ventricular tachycardia High-grade atrioventricular block or need for pacing at a young age Progressive fall in left ventricular ejection fraction Family history of sudden death or LMNA-confirmed disease Applying standard ejection-fraction-based defibrillator thresholds and underestimating arrhythmic risk Attributing early conduction disease to benign causes and missing the underlying laminopathy Overlooking coexisting skeletal muscle involvement Failing to screen relatives who may harbour the variant and face sudden-death risk Lamins A and C form a meshwork underlying the inner nuclear membrane that provides structural support to the nucleus and regulates gene expression and mechanotransduction. Pathogenic LMNA variants weaken this nuclear lamina, rendering cardiomyocytes and their conduction-system counterparts vulnerable to mechanical stress and abnormal signalling. This leads to progressive fibrosis and cell loss, first affecting the atria and the specialised conduction tissue, causing conduction block and atrial arrhythmia, and later the ventricular myocardium, producing chamber dilatation, systolic dysfunction and a substrate for re-entrant ventricular arrhythmia. The disproportionate arrhythmic and conduction burden relative to the degree of ventricular impairment is the defining clinical hallmark. LMNA cardiomyopathy is among the more aggressive inherited cardiomyopathies, with high rates of malignant arrhythmia, progressive heart failure and sudden death; outcome is improved by early rhythm surveillance, defibrillator therapy in high-risk patients, and heart failure management, with transplantation for end-stage disease.

Loiasis (Loa loa filariasis) — loiasis, Loa loa infection, African eye worm, Calabar swellings, loa loa filariasis Onchocerciasis Lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia species) Other causes of angio-oedema or urticaria Gnathostomiasis and other migratory helminths Cutaneous larva migrans Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia Daytime (midday) peripheral blood film for sheathed microfilariae Full blood count documenting eosinophilia Quantification of Loa loa microfilarial density before treatment Filarial serology or antigen/antibody testing where available Slit-lamp or direct examination if a worm is visible in the eye Molecular (PCR) assays for species confirmation where accessible Caused by the filarial nematode Loa loa, transmitted by the day-biting Chrysops (mango or deer) fly in the rainforests of West and Central Africa The classic features are transient, localised, non-pitting angio-oedematous 'Calabar swellings', often around joints, and the sensation or sight of an adult worm migrating across the subconjunctiva of the eye Peripheral eosinophilia is typically prominent, and symptoms are often more marked in expatriates and visitors than in endemic residents Diagnosis rests on detecting sheathed microfilariae with daytime (midday) periodicity on a stained blood film, reflecting the vector's daytime biting Adult worms may be identified during their migration across the eye or under the skin Treatment options include diethylcarbamazine (which targets microfilariae and adult worms) and albendazole, with careful attention to microfilarial load High Loa loa microfilarial loads carry a risk of severe encephalopathy when treated with certain antifilarial drugs, so the burden must be assessed before therapy Very high microfilarial load, given the risk of treatment-associated encephalopathy Neurological deterioration or encephalopathy during antifilarial therapy Renal involvement or severe systemic hypersensitivity reactions Starting antifilarial treatment without first measuring the microfilarial load and considering encephalopathy risk Timing the diagnostic blood film incorrectly and missing the daytime-periodic microfilariae Co-treating without recognising overlap with onchocerciasis or lymphatic filariasis in co-endemic regions Attributing Calabar swellings to simple allergy in a returning traveller Loiasis is caused by infection with the filarial worm Loa loa. Infective larvae are deposited when an infected Chrysops fly takes a blood meal; the larvae mature into adult worms that migrate through subcutaneous and connective tissues over years. Adult females release sheathed microfilariae that circulate in the peripheral blood with a diurnal periodicity matching the daytime feeding of the vector, allowing onward transmission. Host immune and hypersensitivity responses to migrating adults and their products produce the transient inflammatory Calabar swellings and eosinophilia, while migration across the bulbar conjunctiva gives the classic 'eye worm'. Heavy microfilaraemia is largely asymptomatic itself but becomes clinically important because rapid microfilarial killing during treatment can trigger severe inflammatory reactions, including encephalopathy. Loiasis is generally a chronic, non-fatal infection with a good prognosis when managed carefully; the principal danger is treatment-related severe reactions, especially encephalopathy in heavily microfilaraemic individuals.

Lobomycosis — Lacazia loboi, Loboa loboi, lacaziosis, Jorge Lobo disease, keloidal blastomycosis Keloid or hypertrophic scar Chromoblastomycosis Cutaneous leishmaniasis Lepromatous leprosy Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans or other cutaneous tumours Other subcutaneous mycoses (e.g. paracoccidioidomycosis) Skin biopsy with fungal stains showing chains of yeast cells joined by tubular bridges Direct microscopy of tissue scrapings for the characteristic yeast cells Clinical and exposure history (forest/riverine work, dolphin contact) Assessment of lesion extent and margins to plan excision Exclusion of other subcutaneous mycoses and leprosy Molecular identification where available given inability to culture Lobomycosis is a chronic cutaneous and subcutaneous fungal infection caused by the uncultivated organism Lacazia loboi, endemic to the humid tropics of the Amazon basin and Central/South America It occurs in rural forest and riverine workers and has also been reported in dolphins, with rare dolphin-to-human transmission Infection follows traumatic inoculation of the organism into the skin; there is no evidence of person-to-person spread The characteristic lesions are slowly growing, firm, shiny keloid-like nodules and plaques, typically on exposed cooler sites such as the ears, limbs and face Lesions are usually painless but may itch; they spread by local extension and autoinoculation over years while sparing internal organs Diagnosis is made histologically by finding chains of uniform, thick-walled yeast-like cells linked by tubular bridges; the organism cannot be cultured in vitro Treatment is difficult: surgical excision of localised lesions is preferred, and antifungal drugs alone are generally disappointing, so wide excision with clear margins is often required Rapid change, ulceration or induration in a long-standing lesion raising concern for malignant transformation Extensive or multifocal disease limiting surgical options Involvement of functionally or cosmetically critical sites Recurrence after excision Diagnostic uncertainty with a cutaneous malignancy Mistaking lesions for keloid and delaying biopsy and diagnosis Expecting antifungal drugs alone to be curative Incomplete excision leading to recurrence Attempting culture and being misled by its failure to grow Overlooking malignant change in chronic, altering lesions Lacazia loboi is thought to reside in soil, vegetation or aquatic environments and is introduced into the dermis through minor trauma. The organism proliferates as yeast-like cells within the dermis, provoking a granulomatous response, and spreads slowly by contiguous extension and by autoinoculation from scratching. Because it does not disseminate haematogenously or invade viscera, disease remains confined to the skin and subcutaneous tissue, producing progressively enlarging fibrotic, keloid-like nodules. The inability to culture the fungus reflects its obligate in vivo growth and has limited understanding of its biology. Lobomycosis is indolent and non-life-threatening but chronic and disfiguring; localised lesions may be cured by complete excision, whereas extensive disease tends to recur and responds poorly to medical therapy, and rare malignant transformation is reported in long-standing lesions.

Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity — LAST, local anaesthetic toxicity, systemic local anaesthetic poisoning Vasovagal syncope or simple faint during a block High or total spinal anaesthesia Primary cardiac arrhythmia or ischaemic event Anaphylaxis to an injected agent or additive Hyperventilation or panic reaction Adrenaline effect from an epinephrine-containing solution Continuous ECG and cardiovascular monitoring for arrhythmia and conduction abnormality Pulse oximetry and capnography to confirm oxygenation and ventilation Arterial blood gas to assess acidosis and guide resuscitation Serial electrolytes and glucose during prolonged resuscitation Plasma local anaesthetic level where available (rarely used acutely) Occurs when plasma levels of local anaesthetic rise excessively, usually from inadvertent intravascular injection or absorption from a large or repeated dose Classic progression moves from early neurological signs (perioral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste, agitation, dysarthria) to seizures, then to cardiovascular collapse, but atypical or delayed presentations are common Cardiac toxicity can appear with little warning, especially with more lipophilic and potent agents such as bupivacaine, and may manifest as conduction block, arrhythmia, or refractory arrest Immediate priorities are stopping the injection, calling for help, securing the airway with oxygenation, and controlling seizures while avoiding large doses of propofol in the unstable patient Lipid emulsion therapy (intravenous lipid rescue) is the specific antidote and should be started early alongside high-quality resuscitation During arrest, resuscitation is often prolonged; cardiopulmonary bypass or extracorporeal support may be needed and efforts should not be abandoned prematurely Prevention relies on aspiration before injection, incremental dosing, use of a test dose, ultrasound guidance, and staying within weight-based maximum limits Standard-dose adrenaline may be less effective and vasopressin is generally avoided; arrhythmias are managed while lipid rescue takes effect Seizure activity or rapidly declining consciousness after a regional block Cardiovascular collapse, malignant arrhythmia, or cardiac arrest following local anaesthetic administration Refractory hypotension or wide-complex rhythms unresponsive to standard measures Progressive symptoms after a large-volume or repeated injection suggesting rising systemic levels Attributing early neurological symptoms to anxiety and continuing injection Delaying lipid emulsion until after prolonged, unsuccessful resuscitation Abandoning resuscitation too early despite the potential for good recovery Exceeding weight-based maximum doses or omitting aspiration and incremental dosing Using large sedative doses that worsen cardiovascular instability Local anaesthetics block voltage-gated sodium channels. When systemic concentrations become excessive, they also disrupt cardiac and central nervous system membrane excitability and interfere with cardiac ion channels, mitochondrial energy production, and myocardial fatty acid metabolism. The central nervous system is affected first because inhibitory pathways are suppressed before excitatory ones, producing an excitatory phase followed by global depression. Cardiac effects include impaired conduction, reduced contractility, and malignant arrhythmias. More potent, lipid-soluble agents bind cardiac tissue avidly, making toxicity harder to reverse. Lipid emulsion is thought to act as a circulating sink that sequesters drug away from tissue and to support myocardial energetics. With early recognition, prompt lipid emulsion therapy, and sustained high-quality resuscitation, many patients recover fully; delayed treatment or severe bupivacaine-related arrest carries a higher risk of death or hypoxic injury.

Localised Amyloidosis — Localised AL amyloidosis, Organ-limited amyloidosis, Focal amyloidosis Systemic AL amyloidosis Malignancy at the affected site such as bladder or laryngeal carcinoma Chronic inflammatory or granulomatous lesions Other benign masses Lymphoproliferative disease for orbital and conjunctival lesions Sarcoidosis Biopsy of the lesion with Congo red staining and amyloid typing by mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry Serum free light chains and serum and urine immunofixation to exclude a systemic clone SAP scintigraphy to confirm the absence of systemic deposits Bone marrow examination if a systemic clone is suspected Site-specific imaging and endoscopy Echocardiography with renal and liver function to exclude systemic organ involvement Localised amyloidosis is confined to a single organ or site without systemic deposition, and is most often of immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) type produced by a local clone of plasma cells or B-cells. Frequently affected sites include the urinary tract (especially the bladder), larynx, tracheobronchial tree, skin, conjunctiva or orbit, and gastrointestinal tract. Presentation reflects the site, with painless haematuria in bladder disease, hoarseness in laryngeal disease, and wheeze or haemoptysis in airway disease. Unlike systemic AL amyloidosis, there is usually no significant circulating monoclonal protein and no risk to vital organs such as the heart or kidney. Progression to systemic amyloidosis is uncommon, so the prognosis is generally excellent. Management is local, using endoscopic or surgical excision, local radiotherapy, or watchful waiting, rather than systemic chemotherapy. A thorough evaluation to exclude underlying systemic disease is mandatory before labelling amyloid as localised. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is a distinct organ-limited beta-amyloid form affecting the cerebral vasculature. Features suggesting systemic disease such as proteinuria, cardiac symptoms or a significant serum monoclonal protein Rapid local growth or bleeding Airway compromise from laryngeal or tracheal disease Recurrent obstruction Assuming localised disease without excluding systemic amyloidosis Giving systemic chemotherapy inappropriately for organ-limited disease Missing a co-existing malignancy at the biopsy site Failing to type the amyloid and presuming it is AL In localised AL amyloidosis a small clone of plasma cells or B-lymphocytes resident within the affected tissue secretes amyloidogenic immunoglobulin light chains that misfold and deposit as fibrils in situ. Because the clone and the deposition are confined to that site, there is no meaningful systemic light-chain excess and other organs are spared. The deposits form tumour-like masses or diffuse infiltration that disrupt local function, for example by obstructing or ulcerating the urinary tract or by stiffening the vocal cords. The reasons for the localised behaviour of the clone are incompletely understood, but the process rarely disseminates. Localised amyloidosis carries an excellent prognosis with rare progression to systemic disease. Local recurrence can occur and may require repeat local treatment, but organ-threatening systemic complications are unusual.

Locked-in syndrome — ventral pontine syndrome, de-efferented state, pseudocoma, cerebromedullospinal disconnection Coma from bilateral hemispheric or brainstem dysfunction Persistent vegetative or minimally conscious state Severe Guillain-Barre syndrome with total paralysis Myasthenic or other neuromuscular crisis Akinetic mutism from bifrontal lesions Deep sedation or neuromuscular blockade in critical care MRI with diffusion imaging demonstrating ventral pontine infarction MR or CT angiography confirming basilar artery occlusion or stenosis Electroencephalography showing preserved reactive background to confirm awareness Assessment of vertical eye movements and blinking to establish communication and awareness Electrolyte and osmolality review where central pontine myelinolysis is possible Nerve conduction studies where a neuromuscular mimic is suspected Most often caused by extensive infarction of the ventral pons from basilar artery thrombosis, damaging the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts bilaterally The patient is quadriplegic and anarthric but fully conscious and aware, with preserved cognition Communication is typically possible only through vertical eye movements and blinking, which are mediated by spared midbrain structures The reticular activating system is preserved, so the sleep-wake cycle and awareness remain intact, distinguishing it from coma It must be actively distinguished from coma, persistent vegetative state, and severe Guillain-Barre syndrome Other causes include central pontine myelinolysis, pontine haemorrhage, and rarely advanced neuromuscular disease Early recognition allows a communication code to be established and appropriate supportive and rehabilitative care to begin Failure to recognise preserved awareness and misdiagnosis as coma or vegetative state Evolving basilar thrombosis requiring urgent recanalisation consideration Respiratory failure demanding airway protection and ventilatory support Rapid osmotic shifts precipitating or worsening central pontine myelinolysis Mistaking a fully aware patient for being comatose and communicating inappropriately at the bedside Overlooking preserved vertical gaze as the key sign of retained consciousness Delaying recognition of basilar occlusion amenable to intervention Correcting hyponatraemia too rapidly and inducing osmotic demyelination Locked-in syndrome results from bilateral interruption of the ventral pons, classically through basilar artery occlusion causing infarction of the basis pontis. The corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres are destroyed, abolishing voluntary movement of the limbs and lower cranial musculature and producing quadriplegia and anarthria. Crucially, the dorsal pontine tegmentum containing the reticular activating system is spared, so consciousness and cognition are retained, and supranuclear pathways for vertical gaze and blinking in the midbrain remain intact, providing the only avenue for voluntary responses. The disconnection of efferent motor output from an intact conscious brain gives the characteristic de-efferented state. Mortality is high in the acute basilar occlusion phase, and most survivors remain severely disabled, though some regain limited movement and many retain a meaningful quality of life with communication aids; recovery is generally slow and incomplete.

Loeffler endocarditis — Loffler endocarditis, eosinophilic endomyocardial disease, eosinophilic endomyocarditis, hypereosinophilic restrictive cardiomyopathy Endomyocardial fibrosis (tropical) Other restrictive cardiomyopathies such as cardiac amyloidosis Constrictive pericarditis Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis with cardiac involvement Infective endocarditis with intracardiac thrombus or vegetation Cardiac tumour or apical thrombus of other cause Full blood count and blood film confirming and quantifying eosinophilia Echocardiography for apical thrombus, endomyocardial thickening, valve involvement and restrictive filling Cardiac MRI for thrombus, inflammation and endomyocardial fibrosis Investigation of the cause of eosinophilia (clonal markers, secondary causes, parasitic and allergic screens) Endomyocardial biopsy in selected cases Cardiac biomarkers and assessment of embolic complications A form of eosinophilic endomyocardial disease occurring in the setting of persistent hypereosinophilia, leading to a restrictive cardiomyopathy Despite the name, it is a non-infective inflammatory and fibrotic process rather than infective endocarditis Cardiac involvement evolves through an acute necrotic phase, a thrombotic phase and a late fibrotic phase with endomyocardial scarring Mural thrombus within the ventricular apices and along the inflow tract predisposes to systemic embolism Fibrosis and thrombus can tether the atrioventricular valves and obliterate the ventricular cavities, producing restrictive physiology and valvular regurgitation Underlying causes of the eosinophilia include primary (clonal) and secondary hypereosinophilic syndromes, and it overlaps with tropical endomyocardial fibrosis Treatment targets the eosinophilia (for example corticosteroids and cause-specific therapy) alongside heart failure management, anticoagulation for thrombus and surgery for advanced valvular or fibrotic disease Cardiac MRI is valuable for detecting thrombus, inflammation and the characteristic endomyocardial fibrosis Signs of heart failure with restrictive physiology in a patient with marked eosinophilia Systemic embolic event from intracardiac thrombus Rapidly progressive valvular regurgitation or cavity obliteration Very high or rising eosinophil count with cardiac symptoms Mistaking it for infective endocarditis because of the name Overlooking mild eosinophilia and failing to link it to the cardiac picture Missing apical mural thrombus and the consequent need for anticoagulation Delaying treatment of the eosinophilia until irreversible fibrosis has developed Not investigating the underlying cause of the hypereosinophilia Loeffler endocarditis results from sustained hypereosinophilia in which activated eosinophils infiltrate the endomyocardium and release toxic granule proteins. These damage the endocardium and myocardium, initiating an acute necrotic and inflammatory phase. Endocardial injury then promotes mural thrombus formation, and over time organising thrombus and reactive fibrosis produce dense endomyocardial scarring. The resulting stiff, non-compliant ventricles impair filling to cause restrictive cardiomyopathy, while fibrosis and thrombus involving the subvalvular apparatus lead to atrioventricular valve regurgitation and apical cavity obliteration. Systemic embolism from mural thrombus is an important complication. Outcome depends on early control of the eosinophilia and the extent of endomyocardial fibrosis; treatment during the earlier phases can limit damage, whereas established fibrotic restrictive disease carries a poor prognosis with heart failure and embolic risk.

Loeys-Dietz syndrome — LDS, TGFBR1-related aortopathy, TGFBR2-related aortopathy, TGF-beta signalling vasculopathy Marfan syndrome Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome Arterial tortuosity syndrome Familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, hypermobile type Transthoracic echocardiography with aortic root measurement Head-to-pelvis CT or MR angiography to map arterial tortuosity and aneurysms Molecular genetic testing of the TGF-beta pathway aortopathy gene panel Slit-lamp examination to confirm absence of ectopia lentis and assess other ocular features Cervical spine imaging for instability before intervention or anaesthesia Skeletal review for scoliosis, pectus deformity, and club foot Autosomal dominant connective-tissue disorder caused by pathogenic variants in genes of the TGF-beta signalling pathway, most often TGFBR1 and TGFBR2, and also SMAD3, TGFB2, and TGFB3 Characterised by arterial tortuosity and aneurysms that can affect the aorta and its branches well beyond the aortic root The triad of arterial tortuosity, hypertelorism, and a bifid or broad uvula/cleft palate is a classic clinical clue Aneurysms tend to dissect at smaller diameters and younger ages than in Marfan syndrome, so surveillance and surgical thresholds are more aggressive Whole-arterial-tree imaging from head to pelvis is recommended because aneurysms are not confined to the aortic root Ectopia lentis is characteristically absent, which helps distinguish it from Marfan syndrome Craniofacial, skeletal, and cutaneous features overlap with Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, so genetic testing guides definitive classification Management combines medical aortic protection (beta-blockers and/or angiotensin-receptor blockers), close imaging surveillance, and earlier prophylactic vascular surgery Acute severe chest, back, or abdominal pain suggesting arterial dissection or rupture Aneurysm growth or an aortic diameter reaching the individualised surgical threshold Aneurysms in cerebral or visceral arteries detected on surveillance imaging Signs of cervical spine instability, especially peri-operatively Pregnancy complications given the heightened maternal dissection risk Applying Marfan aortic surgical thresholds, which are too conservative for Loeys-Dietz syndrome Imaging only the aortic root and missing distal or branch-vessel aneurysms Overlooking cervical spine instability before intubation or surgery Confusing it with Marfan syndrome despite the absence of ectopia lentis Underestimating the maternal vascular risk during pregnancy Loeys-Dietz syndrome arises from variants that disturb transforming growth factor beta signalling within the vascular wall. Paradoxically, despite loss-of-function receptor variants, downstream TGF-beta signalling is upregulated, driving abnormal extracellular matrix remodelling and smooth-muscle cell dysfunction. The result is a fragile, tortuous arterial tree with a propensity to aneurysm formation and dissection throughout the aorta and its branches. The same signalling disturbance underlies the craniofacial, skeletal, and connective-tissue features, and the widespread vascular fragility explains the elevated risk of rupture at relatively small vessel diameters. Prognosis has improved substantially with recognition, aggressive imaging surveillance, medical aortic protection, and earlier surgery, but the widespread and aggressive arterial disease still carries meaningful risk of dissection and rupture. Outcomes vary with the causative gene and the extent of vascular involvement.

Loin pain haematuria syndrome — LPHS, Loin pain-haematuria syndrome Nephrolithiasis or crystalluria Nutcracker syndrome (left renal vein compression) Thin basement membrane disease or IgA nephropathy Ureteropelvic junction obstruction Renal or urothelial malignancy Renal papillary necrosis Medullary sponge kidney or musculoskeletal loin pain Urinalysis and microscopy for dysmorphic red cells and casts Urine culture and cytology CT urography for stones, obstruction and masses Doppler or cross-sectional venography for nutcracker phenomenon Cystoscopy to localise bleeding and exclude bladder pathology Glomerular screen (complement, autoimmune serology, protein quantification) Renal biopsy to exclude glomerulonephritis A diagnosis of exclusion: severe recurrent loin pain with macroscopic or microscopic haematuria and no identifiable urological or glomerular cause. It predominantly affects young women. Pain may be unilateral or bilateral, is often severe and disproportionate to findings, and may be triggered by minor events. Extensive imaging and cystoscopy are needed to exclude stones, obstruction, tumour and vascular anomalies. Renal biopsy may show C3 deposition in arteriolar walls or glomerular basement membrane abnormalities, but is often near-normal and mainly serves to exclude glomerulonephritis. There is a strong association with psychological distress and analgesic dependence, so multidisciplinary pain management is central. Actively exclude nutcracker syndrome and thin basement membrane disease as mimics. Invasive options such as nerve blocks, renal denervation, autotransplantation and nephrectomy are last resort with inconsistent and often disappointing results. Features suggesting malignancy such as a mass or unexplained weight loss Signs of urinary obstruction or infection with sepsis New proteinuria, red-cell casts or rising creatinine suggesting glomerulonephritis Escalating opioid requirement and dependence Making the diagnosis without adequately excluding treatable causes such as stones, nutcracker syndrome and glomerulonephritis Escalating opioids without a multidisciplinary pain strategy Proceeding to nephrectomy or autotransplantation with unrealistic expectations and risk of contralateral recurrence Dismissing the patient as functional and missing evolving organic disease The mechanism is poorly understood and probably heterogeneous. Proposed contributors include a renal microvascular or glomerular abnormality allowing red cells to escape into tubules with tubular obstruction and capsular distension, abnormally thick or thin glomerular basement membranes, complement (C3) deposition in vessel walls, intrarenal vascular spasm, and crystalluria causing microtrauma. Altered central pain processing and visceral hypersensitivity are increasingly recognised components, and by definition no obstructing, neoplastic, infective or defined glomerular cause is found. It is a chronic and often debilitating condition with a relapsing course; pain diminishes over time in some patients, but many endure years of symptoms and invasive interventions frequently fail to provide durable relief.

Loin pain-haematuria syndrome — loin pain haematuria syndrome, LPHS, loin pain-hematuria syndrome Urolithiasis or microlithiasis Glomerulonephritis (e.g. IgA nephropathy) Nutcracker syndrome (renal vein compression) Urothelial or renal malignancy Chronic or recurrent pyelonephritis Ureteric obstruction or clot colic Coagulopathy or anticoagulant-related bleeding Urinalysis, microscopy for dysmorphic red cells and casts, and culture CT urography and ultrasound to exclude stones, tumour, and obstruction Cystoscopy and, where indicated, ureteroscopy to localise bleeding and exclude urothelial lesions Doppler or cross-sectional venous imaging to exclude nutcracker phenomenon Coagulation screen and renal function tests Renal biopsy to exclude glomerular disease when clinically warranted A diagnosis of exclusion characterised by severe, often disabling, unilateral or bilateral loin pain accompanied by haematuria in the absence of an identifiable structural, infective, or glomerular cause Predominantly affects young to middle-aged women Haematuria may be macroscopic or microscopic and is often intermittent; the pain is frequently out of proportion to objective findings The condition is defined only after thorough exclusion of stones, tumour, infection, glomerular disease, clotting disorders, and vascular causes such as nutcracker syndrome Renal biopsy may show non-specific findings such as C3 deposition or thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, but is mainly used to exclude other pathology Management is challenging and centres on multidisciplinary chronic pain control; invasive and ablative procedures have unpredictable and often disappointing results Careful psychological assessment and support are integral, without dismissing the pain as non-organic Features suggesting malignancy, such as a mass, weight loss, or persistent unexplained macroscopic haematuria Signs of obstruction, infection, or sepsis requiring urgent intervention Escalating opioid requirements and dependence New proteinuria or declining renal function pointing to an alternative diagnosis Labelling a patient with the syndrome before adequately excluding treatable structural, glomerular, or vascular causes Escalating to irreversible surgery such as nephrectomy or renal denervation with unpredictable benefit Dismissing the pain as purely psychogenic and failing to provide multidisciplinary support Overlooking nutcracker syndrome, which can mimic the presentation but is potentially treatable The cause of loin pain-haematuria syndrome is poorly understood and probably heterogeneous. Proposed mechanisms include abnormalities of the glomerular basement membrane allowing red cells to escape into tubules, where they may form microcrystals or casts that provoke tubular obstruction and pain; intrarenal vascular or microvascular abnormalities; and abnormal pain processing or sensitisation. Because no single consistent lesion is found, the syndrome is best regarded as a clinical entity defined by its symptom complex once other renal and urological diseases have been rigorously excluded. The natural history is variable; some patients improve or remit over time, but many experience a chronic relapsing course with substantial impact on quality of life, and durable relief from invasive interventions is inconsistent.
