Long QT syndrome — LQTS, congenital long QT syndrome, acquired long QT, prolonged QT interval Acquired QT prolongation from drugs or electrolyte disturbance Other inherited arrhythmia syndromes such as Brugada syndrome and catecholaminergic polymorphic VT Vasovagal or other non-cardiac syncope Epilepsy Short QT syndrome (opposite repolarisation abnormality) Structural causes of ventricular arrhythmia 12-lead ECG with accurate rate-corrected QT measurement, repeated as needed Electrolyte panel including potassium, magnesium, and calcium Review of all medications for QT-prolonging agents Exercise or ambulatory ECG to unmask latent QT prolongation and assess dynamics Genetic testing and family screening when a congenital syndrome is suspected Echocardiography to exclude structural heart disease LQTS is characterised by prolongation of the rate-corrected QT interval on ECG and a predisposition to the polymorphic ventricular tachycardia torsades de pointes It may be congenital, from ion-channel gene mutations, or acquired, most often from QT-prolonging drugs and electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, and hypocalcaemia Presentations range from an incidental ECG finding to palpitations, syncope, seizures, or sudden cardiac death, frequently triggered by exertion, emotion, or auditory stimuli depending on the genotype The QT interval must be corrected for heart rate, and serial or exercise ECGs may be needed because the interval can be borderline at rest A careful family history of syncope, seizures, or premature sudden death supports a congenital cause Management of acquired LQTS centres on withdrawing offending drugs and correcting electrolytes; congenital LQTS is often managed with beta-blockade and activity modification An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is considered for survivors of cardiac arrest or those with high-risk features despite therapy Torsades is treated acutely with magnesium, correction of precipitants, and measures to raise the heart rate, with defibrillation if it degenerates to a sustained unstable rhythm MEDICAL EMERGENCY: torsades de pointes, which may cause syncope and can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest Syncope or seizures in a patient with a prolonged QT, indicating a high risk of malignant arrhythmia Family history of sudden cardiac death at a young age Marked QT prolongation compounded by multiple QT-prolonging drugs or profound electrolyte disturbance Failing to correct the QT for heart rate or missing intermittent prolongation on a single resting ECG Overlooking cumulative QT effects when several QT-prolonging drugs or electrolyte disturbances coexist Attributing syncope or seizures to a neurological cause without measuring the QT Neglecting family screening once a congenital syndrome is diagnosed The QT interval reflects the duration of ventricular repolarisation. In congenital LQTS, mutations affecting cardiac potassium, sodium, or calcium channels delay repolarisation by reducing outward current or increasing inward current, prolonging the action potential. This heterogeneous prolongation favours early afterdepolarisations that can trigger torsades de pointes. Acquired LQTS most often results from drugs that block the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current or from electrolyte disturbances that impair repolarisation. Bradycardia and pauses further lengthen the QT and can precipitate pause-dependent torsades. With recognition, avoidance of QT-prolonging triggers, and appropriate therapy including beta-blockade or a defibrillator, prognosis is generally favourable; risk of sudden death rises with greater QT prolongation, prior syncope or arrhythmia, and specific high-risk genotypes.

Longitudinal melanonychia — melanonychia striata, longitudinal pigmented band, melanonychia Benign melanocytic activation (racial, drug-induced, traumatic, inflammatory) Nail matrix naevus Subungual melanoma Subungual haematoma (usually non-longitudinal and moves out with growth) Fungal or bacterial pigmentation (for example Pseudomonas or dematiaceous fungi) Pigmentation from systemic disease or endocrinopathy Exogenous staining of the nail Onychoscopy (dermoscopy of the nail) to assess the pattern and regularity of pigmented lines Assessment for Hutchinson sign and periungual pigment spread Nail matrix biopsy for histology of a suspicious or changing band Photographic documentation to monitor change over time Review of drug history and examination of other nails and skin Mycology or microbiology if an infective pigment source is suspected Longitudinal melanonychia is a brown-to-black pigmented band running lengthwise along the nail, caused by increased melanin deposition within the plate It has many benign causes, including racial or ethnic pigmentation (often multiple nails in darker skin), melanocytic activation, drugs, trauma, and benign naevi The crucial task is to separate benign bands from those arising from a subungual melanoma, especially when a single nail is involved in a fair-skinned adult Worrying features can be remembered with the ABCDEF guide (age and ethnicity, band characteristics, change, digit involved, extension of pigment, family or personal history) Hutchinson sign, spread of pigment onto the proximal or lateral nail fold, is an important warning sign for melanoma, though a pseudo-Hutchinson sign can mislead Onychoscopy helps by showing regular parallel lines in benign activation versus irregular, variably coloured lines with disrupted parallelism in melanoma A suspicious band requires a nail matrix biopsy for histology, as pigment alone cannot reliably distinguish benign from malignant A single broad, irregular, or widening band in an adult, particularly of the thumb, index finger, or great toe Hutchinson sign with pigment extending onto the nail folds Variegated colour, blurred borders, or loss of parallelism on onychoscopy Associated nail dystrophy, bleeding, or a nodule suggesting invasive melanoma Rapid change in the width or colour of an established band Reassuring a patient without biopsy when a single band shows suspicious features Relying on pigment colour alone rather than pattern, change, and histology Misinterpreting a pseudo-Hutchinson sign or, conversely, dismissing a true one Assuming multiple bands in darker skin are always benign without examining each nail Delaying matrix biopsy for fear of nail deformity in a potentially malignant lesion Longitudinal melanonychia occurs when melanin is deposited into the developing nail plate by melanocytes in the nail matrix, producing a pigmented streak that grows out along the length of the nail. The pigment may reflect simple activation of matrix melanocytes without an increase in their number, as seen with racial pigmentation, drugs, trauma, or inflammation, or a true increase in melanocytes such as a benign naevus or, importantly, a melanoma. Because a malignant melanocytic proliferation in the matrix can present in exactly the same way as a benign band, the pattern, regularity, and behaviour of the pigment, rather than its mere presence, guide the assessment. Most bands are benign and require only monitoring, but subungual melanoma carries a serious prognosis that worsens with delayed diagnosis, so appropriately timed biopsy of suspicious lesions is critical to outcome.

Loose anagen syndrome — LAS, loose anagen hair syndrome, LAHS Telogen effluvium, with club hairs, older patients and a trigger history Alopecia areata, which is patchy with exclamation-mark hairs Short anagen syndrome Hair-shaft disorders causing fragility such as trichorrhexis nodosa Trichotillomania Gentle hair-pull test extracting numerous anagen hairs Light microscopy (trichogram) showing sheathless anagen roots with ruffled cuticles Trichoscopy for solitary yellow dots and black granular structures Assessment for associated ectodermal or syndromic features Reassurance-based follow-up to document improvement with age A disorder mainly of young children in which anagen hairs are poorly anchored and can be pulled out painlessly with little force It typically presents in fair-haired girls aged around two to six with sparse, dull, unruly hair that seems never to need cutting and does not grow long The hair-pull test easily extracts numerous anagen hairs, and light microscopy shows anagen roots lacking sheaths with a ruffled proximal cuticle and a distorted floppy-sock appearance Trichoscopy may show rectangular black granular structures and solitary yellow dots It is non-scarring with preserved follicular ostia, and hair anchorage tends to improve as the child grows It is usually sporadic, though familial cases with autosomal dominant inheritance and associations with certain genetic syndromes are described No specific treatment is required beyond gentle hair care and reassurance, as the condition generally improves spontaneously through childhood Features suggesting an associated genetic syndrome such as dysmorphism or ectodermal defects Progressive loss or scarring, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Onset or persistence into adulthood requiring exclusion of other causes Misinterpreting easily pulled hairs as alopecia areata or an effluvium Overlooking associated syndromic features in familial cases Subjecting children to unnecessary treatment for a self-limiting condition Failing to perform trichogram microscopy, which is the key diagnostic test Loose anagen syndrome results from defective anchorage of the hair shaft within the follicle owing to abnormal or premature keratinisation of the inner root sheath, so that cohesion between the shaft and the surrounding sheaths is impaired and anagen hairs are easily and painlessly extracted. Mutations affecting the companion-layer and inner-root-sheath keratin, including K6HF (KRT75), have been implicated. Because the follicles are structurally intact and not destroyed, the process is non-scarring and anchorage typically strengthens with maturity. The condition is benign and non-scarring, with hair anchorage and density generally improving spontaneously as the child grows, although hair may remain somewhat sparse or slow-growing.

Loricrin keratoderma — Vohwinkel syndrome variant with ichthyosis, mutilating keratoderma with ichthyosis, LOR Vohwinkel syndrome due to GJB2 (connexin 26) with deafness Mal de Meleda Olmsted syndrome Other mutilating keratodermas Bart-Pumphrey syndrome Diffuse epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma Molecular genetic testing of LOR Skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis with retained nuclei (parakeratosis) in the stratum corneum Examination for pseudo-ainhum and starfish keratoses Audiological assessment to distinguish from connexin-related Vohwinkel syndrome Family history and pedigree analysis Assessment of foot and hand function An autosomal dominant disorder of keratinisation caused by variants in LOR, which encodes loricrin, a major protein of the cornified cell envelope Presents as a mutilating (Vohwinkel-like) palmoplantar keratoderma combined with a generalised ichthyosis The palmoplantar keratoderma typically has a honeycomb surface and may show starfish-shaped keratoses over the knuckles Constricting fibrous bands (pseudo-ainhum) can form around digits and threaten autoamputation Unlike classic connexin-related Vohwinkel syndrome, the loricrin variant is associated with ichthyosis rather than sensorineural deafness Diagnosis is clinical, supported by biopsy showing hyperkeratosis with retained nuclei and by LOR molecular testing Management is supportive with keratolytics, emollients and foot care, oral retinoids for severe keratoderma, and surgical release of constricting bands where necessary Constricting bands (pseudo-ainhum) risking digital autoamputation Deep secondary infection of fissured keratoderma Rapid or asymmetrical change raising concern for malignant transformation Severe functional impairment of hands or feet Confusing it with connexin-related Vohwinkel syndrome and overlooking the associated ichthyosis Missing early pseudo-ainhum before irreversible digital constriction Failing to arrange audiology to distinguish the two forms of mutilating keratoderma Delaying surgical release of constricting bands Loricrin keratoderma arises from frameshift variants in LOR that alter loricrin, the principal structural protein of the cornified cell envelope. The mutant protein carries an abnormal carboxy-terminal extension with a nuclear localisation signal, causing it to be mistargeted to the nucleus rather than incorporated correctly into the cornified envelope. Defective envelope assembly impairs the epidermal barrier and terminal differentiation, producing generalised ichthyosis and a thick mutilating palmoplantar keratoderma, with chronic fibrosis around digits generating pseudo-ainhum. The disorder is lifelong; with keratolytic and emollient care, retinoids and timely surgical release of constricting bands most patients preserve function, though pseudo-ainhum and disability can complicate severe disease.

Louse-borne relapsing fever — LBRF, epidemic relapsing fever, Borrelia recurrentis infection, spirochaetal fever Tick-borne relapsing fever Malaria Typhus and other rickettsioses Leptospirosis Typhoid fever Viral haemorrhagic fever in relevant epidemiological settings Yellow fever Thick and thin peripheral blood films during fever showing numerous spirochaetes PCR of blood for Borrelia recurrentis where available Full blood count for thrombocytopenia and anaemia Liver enzymes and bilirubin Coagulation studies given the bleeding tendency Examination of clothing for body lice to support the diagnosis Caused by Borrelia recurrentis and transmitted by the human body louse; infection follows crushing of the louse so that its coelomic fluid contaminates broken skin or mucosae rather than the bite itself Epidemic in conditions of overcrowding, poverty, cold and poor hygiene, and re-emerging among refugees and migrants travelling from endemic regions of the Horn of Africa After an incubation of about a week there is sudden high fever, rigors, severe headache, myalgia and prostration lasting several days, followed by a crisis and an afebrile interval before relapse Compared with the tick-borne form it typically causes fewer relapses, often only one or two, but tends to be more severe with a higher untreated mortality Jaundice, a bleeding tendency with petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly and neurological involvement are prominent features of severe disease Diagnosis is made by demonstrating abundant spirochaetes on a Giemsa- or Wright-stained peripheral blood film taken during fever A single dose of an appropriate antibiotic can be curative, but the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after treatment is frequent and can be life-threatening, so patients must be closely monitored Severe Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction with hyperpyrexia, rigors and hypotension after the first dose Jaundice with a marked bleeding tendency Neurological deterioration or meningism Myocarditis or circulatory collapse Occurrence in a crowded refugee or migrant population indicating epidemic potential Underestimating the severity and life-threatening potential of the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction Not examining blood films during fever, missing the abundant spirochaetes Failing to recognise the diagnosis in migrants from endemic regions Neglecting delousing and public-health control measures Confusing it with malaria and delaying appropriate antibiotics and monitoring Borrelia recurrentis is a spirochaete confined to humans and spread by the body louse. Once inoculated it proliferates to produce intense spirochaetaemia driving the febrile episode. Host antibody responses clear the dominant antigenic variant, but antigenic variation allows escape variants to expand and cause relapse, though fewer cycles occur than in the tick-borne disease. Heavy spirochaetal loads and the associated inflammatory response cause hepatic dysfunction with jaundice, thrombocytopenia and bleeding, splenic enlargement and neurological involvement. Antibiotic-induced mass lysis of spirochaetes releases inflammatory mediators, producing the often severe Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction with abrupt rigors, hyperpyrexia and haemodynamic instability. Louse-borne relapsing fever is more severe than the tick-borne form and untreated epidemics carry high mortality, but prompt antibiotic treatment is very effective; the main early hazard of treatment is the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, which itself can be fatal without supportive care.

Low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma — LGFMS, Evans tumour, hyalinizing spindle cell tumour with giant rosettes, FUS-CREB3L2 sarcoma, low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma (FUS-CREB3L2) Desmoid-type fibromatosis Perineurioma and other benign nerve sheath tumours Sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcoma (which shares MUC4 expression and fusions) Low-grade myxofibrosarcoma Neurofibroma and schwannoma Solitary fibrous tumour Cellular myxoma MUC4 immunohistochemistry as the key diagnostic screen FISH or molecular testing for FUS and CREB3L2/CREB3L1 rearrangements Panel to exclude nerve sheath tumours and fibromatosis (S100, SOX10, beta-catenin) MRI to define the deep soft-tissue mass and plan resection Staging chest imaging given the risk of late pulmonary metastasis Long-term imaging surveillance because recurrence and metastasis can occur years later A deceptively bland-looking sarcoma that, despite its innocuous histology, has genuine metastatic potential, often after a long interval Typically presents as a painless deep soft-tissue mass in the trunk, limbs or limb girdles of young to middle-aged adults Histology shows alternating fibrous and myxoid zones with bland spindle cells arranged in whorls and characteristic arcades of small curvilinear vessels The great majority carry a FUS-CREB3L2 gene fusion, with a smaller proportion showing FUS-CREB3L1 or EWSR1-CREB3L1 Strong and diffuse MUC4 immunohistochemical expression is a highly sensitive and specific diagnostic marker The hyalinizing spindle cell tumour with giant rosettes is a morphological variant within the same entity, featuring collagen rosettes Because the cells look benign, the diagnosis is easily missed unless MUC4 staining or molecular testing is applied Late local recurrence or distant metastasis, often to the lungs, sometimes after many years Increasing size or deep fixation of a previously stable mass Areas of increased cellularity or higher-grade transformation within the tumour Incomplete excision margins predisposing to recurrence Misinterpreting the bland cytology as a benign fibrous or nerve sheath lesion Omitting MUC4 staining, which readily distinguishes it from benign mimics Discontinuing surveillance too early and missing late metastasis Confusing it with sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcoma, which overlaps molecularly and by MUC4 Underestimating malignant potential because of the low mitotic rate Low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma is a fibroblastic malignancy defined by a recurrent gene fusion, most often FUS-CREB3L2, which joins an RNA-binding protein gene to a transcription-factor gene and deregulates downstream transcriptional programmes. This single driver produces a tumour of monotonous, cytologically bland spindle cells set in alternating collagenous and myxoid matrix. The fusion upregulates expression of MUC4, providing a reliable diagnostic marker, and although proliferation is low the tumour retains the capacity for late local recurrence and distant metastasis, underscoring its fully malignant nature. Although low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma grows slowly and looks histologically bland, it can recur locally and metastasise, characteristically to the lungs and sometimes decades after initial treatment; complete wide excision offers the best chance of cure, and prolonged follow-up is essential because the risk of late relapse persists.

Lowe syndrome — oculocerebrorenal syndrome, oculocerebrorenal syndrome of Lowe, OCRL, Lowe oculocerebrorenal syndrome Dent disease 2 (OCRL) Cystinosis and other causes of renal Fanconi syndrome Galactosaemia (cataract with metabolic disease) Congenital infection causing cataract and neurological impairment Other inherited proximal tubulopathies Mitochondrial disease with multisystem involvement Ophthalmological examination for congenital cataract and glaucoma Assessment of proximal tubular function including low-molecular-weight proteinuria, aminoaciduria, phosphate, bicarbonate and urinary calcium Genetic testing of OCRL Developmental and neurological evaluation, with brain imaging where indicated Serial kidney function and growth monitoring Slit-lamp examination of the mother to detect carrier lens opacities An X-linked multisystem disorder affecting males, caused by loss-of-function variants in OCRL, which encodes a phosphatidylinositol phosphatase Defined by a triad of eye, brain and kidney involvement: congenital cataracts, neurological impairment and a renal proximal tubulopathy Congenital bilateral cataracts are present from birth and glaucoma may develop, so early ophthalmological assessment is essential Neurological features include neonatal hypotonia, developmental delay, intellectual disability and, in some, behavioural problems and seizures The kidney phenotype is a proximal (Fanconi-type) tubulopathy with low-molecular-weight proteinuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, bicarbonate wasting and hypercalciuria OCRL variants also underlie Dent disease 2, and the two conditions represent a phenotypic spectrum of the same gene Female carriers are usually asymptomatic but may show characteristic lenticular opacities on slit-lamp examination Untreated congenital cataract threatening visual development, or rising intraocular pressure Failure to thrive and growth failure from tubulopathy and acidosis Progressive decline in kidney function Seizures or significant electrolyte and acid-base disturbance Delaying cataract surgery and vision support, harming neurodevelopmental outcome Failing to recognise and treat the Fanconi-type tubulopathy and its metabolic consequences Not appreciating the OCRL spectrum linking Lowe syndrome and Dent disease 2 Overlooking carrier detection in the mother by slit-lamp examination Lowe syndrome is caused by loss of function of OCRL, which encodes an inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatase that regulates phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate at the Golgi, endosomes and primary cilium. Disrupted phosphoinositide metabolism impairs membrane trafficking, actin cytoskeletal organisation and endocytosis in multiple tissues. In the proximal tubule this compromises receptor-mediated endocytosis of filtered proteins, producing low-molecular-weight proteinuria and a generalised Fanconi-type tubulopathy; in the developing lens and brain the same trafficking defects lead to congenital cataract and neurodevelopmental impairment. The overlap with Dent disease 2 reflects a shared molecular basis with differing severity of extrarenal involvement. Lowe syndrome is a chronic multisystem condition; the proximal tubulopathy and, later, progressive chronic kidney disease, together with visual and neurodevelopmental impairment, determine outcome, and life expectancy is reduced though many survive into adulthood with supportive care.

Loxoscelism (recluse spider envenomation) — brown recluse spider bite, necrotic arachnidism Bacterial skin and soft-tissue infection or abscess Necrotising fasciitis Cutaneous anthrax or other necrotic infections Pyoderma gangrenosum Vasculitis or other causes of skin necrosis Serial wound examination and documentation of lesion evolution Full blood count and haemolysis markers where systemic illness is suspected Coagulation studies and renal function in suspected viscerocutaneous loxoscelism Urinalysis for haemoglobinuria Microbiological assessment to exclude infective mimics Recluse spider bites can cause a locally necrotic skin lesion (cutaneous loxoscelism) and, less often, a systemic (viscerocutaneous) illness The lesion often evolves over days from an erythematous area to a central blister and then a dark eschar with surrounding pallor and redness Systemic loxoscelism can include haemolysis, disseminated intravascular coagulation and acute kidney injury, more often in children Definitive diagnosis is difficult because the spider is rarely captured and many necrotic lesions are wrongly blamed on spiders Most cutaneous lesions heal with supportive wound care alone Because presentation overlaps with infection, careful reassessment is needed before attributing necrosis to a spider Haemolysis, dark urine or falling haemoglobin Features of disseminated intravascular coagulation or acute kidney injury Rapidly spreading necrosis or systemic sepsis suggesting necrotising infection Systemic illness in a child Diagnosing a spider bite for any necrotic ulcer without a confirmed exposure Missing a necrotising soft-tissue infection masquerading as loxoscelism Overlooking systemic haemolysis, especially in children Performing early aggressive surgery on an evolving lesion Recluse spider venom contains sphingomyelinase D, which damages cell membranes and activates complement and neutrophils, producing local dermonecrosis and, when venom effects are systemic, intravascular haemolysis and a coagulopathy. The characteristic necrotic ulcer results from vascular injury, thrombosis and inflammatory tissue destruction at the bite site. Systemic loxoscelism reflects widespread red-cell membrane injury and immune activation. Most cutaneous cases heal over weeks with supportive care, though large lesions may scar; systemic loxoscelism is uncommon but can be serious, particularly in children.

LRBA deficiency — LRBA, LPS-responsive beige-like anchor protein deficiency, CVID with autoimmunity and enteropathy CTLA4 haploinsufficiency Common variable immunodeficiency IPEX and IPEX-like syndromes Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS) Very-early-onset inflammatory bowel disease of other genetic cause Activated PI3K-delta syndrome Flow cytometry for LRBA protein expression in lymphocytes Lymphocyte subsets and regulatory T-cell enumeration with CTLA-4 expression studies Serum immunoglobulins and specific antibody responses Autoantibody screen and direct antiglobulin test for autoimmune cytopenias LRBA gene sequencing for biallelic loss-of-function variants Endoscopy with biopsy and chest imaging for enteropathy and interstitial lung disease Combines early-onset immune dysregulation with immunodeficiency, typically presenting in childhood with severe autoimmunity, enteropathy, lymphoproliferation and recurrent infection Autoimmune cytopenias, chronic diarrhoea with an inflammatory bowel disease-like enteropathy and endocrinopathies such as type 1 diabetes and thyroid disease are common Hypogammaglobulinaemia with poor vaccine responses frequently develops, so cases are often initially labelled common variable immunodeficiency The mechanism converges on CTLA-4, because LRBA loss accelerates CTLA-4 degradation, so the phenotype closely resembles CTLA4 haploinsufficiency Granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease and organ-infiltrating lymphocytic disease can occur Inheritance is autosomal recessive, from biallelic loss-of-function variants in LRBA CTLA4-Ig fusion therapy (abatacept) is effective because it substitutes for the reduced CTLA-4 signalling, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is curative in severe disease Diagnosis rests on reduced or absent LRBA protein by flow cytometry together with biallelic variants Severe autoimmune cytopenia with life-threatening anaemia or bleeding Refractory enteropathy with malnutrition and growth failure Rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease Lymphoproliferation or organomegaly raising concern for malignant transformation New endocrine crisis such as diabetic ketoacidosis or adrenal insufficiency Settling on a diagnosis of common variable immunodeficiency and not pursuing genetic and protein testing Treating the enteropathy as ordinary inflammatory bowel disease Overlooking the shared CTLA-4 mechanism and the resulting response to targeted therapy Missing associated endocrinopathies until they present in crisis Delaying definitive treatment until multi-organ autoimmune damage is established LRBA (lipopolysaccharide-responsive beige-like anchor protein) is an intracellular trafficking protein that protects CTLA-4 from lysosomal degradation and recycles it back to the cell surface. In its absence, CTLA-4 is degraded excessively, so regulatory T cells cannot deliver the inhibitory signal that normally restrains effector T-cell activation. The resulting loss of peripheral tolerance produces widespread autoimmunity and lymphocytic organ infiltration, mirroring CTLA4 haploinsufficiency, while impaired B-cell survival and differentiation lead to progressive hypogammaglobulinaemia and infection susceptibility. Because the defect ultimately reduces functional CTLA-4, replacing that signal is therapeutically effective. Untreated disease is severe and often life-limiting from autoimmune and infective complications, but recognition allows targeted CTLA4-Ig therapy and, where indicated, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, both of which substantially improve outcome.

Ludwig angina — Ludwig's angina, submandibular space infection, bilateral submandibular cellulitis Peritonsillar or parapharyngeal abscess Submandibular sialadenitis or salivary gland abscess Deep neck space abscess from other sources Angioedema of the floor of mouth and neck Cervical lymphadenitis with cellulitis Sublingual haematoma (for example after anticoagulation) Early airway assessment and continuous monitoring, taking priority over imaging Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck to define spread and detect any collection or mediastinal extension Full blood count, inflammatory markers and blood cultures Culture and sensitivity of any pus obtained at drainage Orthopantomogram or dental assessment to identify the causative tooth Blood glucose and screening for diabetes or immunosuppression Ludwig angina is a rapidly spreading cellulitis of the floor of the mouth involving the submandibular, sublingual and submental spaces bilaterally The great majority arise from dental infection, especially of the lower molar teeth whose roots relate to the mylohyoid line It produces a tense, brawny, tender swelling of the upper neck and floor of mouth that does not usually fluctuate, since it is a cellulitis rather than a discrete abscess The tongue is pushed upward and backward, causing drooling, difficulty swallowing, muffled speech and a serious threat to the airway Infection is typically polymicrobial with mixed aerobic and anaerobic mouth organisms The overriding priority is airway management, as swelling can rapidly cause life-threatening obstruction Treatment combines securing the airway, high-dose intravenous antibiotics and surgical decompression or drainage together with removal of the dental source Contrast CT delineates the extent of spread and any collection but must never delay airway assessment in a deteriorating patient Any sign of airway compromise (stridor, drooling, inability to swallow secretions, respiratory distress) constituting an airway emergency Rapidly progressive neck swelling and inability to protrude the tongue Features of spreading sepsis, high fever and haemodynamic instability Chest pain, dyspnoea or widened mediastinum suggesting descending mediastinitis Trismus limiting mouth opening and airway access Underestimating the speed of airway deterioration and delaying definitive airway management Waiting for fluctuation before intervening, when the process is a cellulitis without a drainable abscess early on Sending an unstable patient for prolonged imaging instead of prioritising the airway Overlooking and failing to treat the underlying dental source Missing spread to the mediastinum in a patient who is not improving Ludwig angina begins most often as an odontogenic infection of the mandibular molars. Because the roots of the second and third molars lie below the attachment of the mylohyoid muscle, infection spreads into the submandibular space and then communicates with the sublingual and submental spaces, involving all three bilaterally. The result is a rapidly advancing cellulitis of the floor of the mouth with dense inflammatory oedema rather than a localised abscess. Swelling of the sublingual tissues elevates and displaces the tongue posteriorly, while induration of the submandibular region narrows the oropharyngeal airway. Untreated, infection can extend along fascial planes to the parapharyngeal and retropharyngeal spaces and into the mediastinum, and airway obstruction or sepsis can be fatal. With early airway control, prompt intravenous antibiotics and timely surgical drainage the outlook is good, but delay in securing the airway or in treatment can lead to fatal airway obstruction, descending mediastinitis or sepsis.

Lumbar disc herniation — prolapsed intervertebral disc, slipped disc, herniated nucleus pulposus, lumbar disc prolapse, sciatica Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication Facet joint or sacroiliac joint referred pain Piriformis syndrome or extraspinal sciatic nerve entrapment Hip osteoarthritis or trochanteric bursitis Peripheral neuropathy or diabetic amyotrophy Spinal tumour or infection when red flags are present MRI of the lumbar spine when symptoms are severe, persistent, or progressive Plain radiographs to assess alignment and exclude other bony pathology Nerve conduction studies and EMG in equivocal cases or to exclude peripheral neuropathy CT or CT myelography where MRI is contraindicated Targeted diagnostic selective nerve-root block to confirm the symptomatic level Most herniations occur posterolaterally at L4/5 and L5/S1, compressing the traversing nerve root and producing dermatomal leg pain (sciatica) Leg pain typically exceeds back pain and follows a dermatomal distribution: L5 to the dorsum of the foot and great toe, S1 to the sole and lateral foot The straight-leg-raise (Lasegue) test reproduces radicular pain within roughly 30 to 70 degrees of elevation, and a positive crossed straight-leg-raise is highly specific Motor, reflex, and sensory findings localise the level: an absent ankle jerk suggests S1, while weak great-toe dorsiflexion suggests L5 Symptoms are typically aggravated by sitting, coughing, sneezing, or the Valsalva manoeuvre The natural history is largely favourable, with most radiculopathy settling within weeks to a few months as the herniation resorbs, so initial management is conservative MRI is reserved for persistent, severe, or progressive symptoms or when injection or surgery is contemplated, because asymptomatic disc bulges are common Management includes analgesia, activity modification, physiotherapy, and nerve-root or epidural injection; discectomy is considered for refractory pain or significant neurological deficit Saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction, or bilateral sciatica indicating possible cauda equina syndrome and mandating urgent MRI Progressive or severe motor weakness such as a foot drop Constitutional symptoms suggesting malignancy or infection Rushing to image or operate on radiculopathy that would resolve spontaneously Missing an evolving cauda equina syndrome by not asking about bladder, bowel, and saddle symptoms Over-attributing symptoms to an incidental disc bulge seen on MRI Overlooking a far-lateral herniation that compresses the exiting rather than the traversing root A lumbar disc herniation occurs when the gelatinous nucleus pulposus displaces through a tear or weakness in the surrounding annulus fibrosus. The displaced material, together with accompanying inflammatory mediators, irritates and compresses the adjacent nerve root, causing radicular pain and dermatomal sensory, motor, or reflex changes. Posterolateral herniations most often affect the traversing root at that level, whereas far-lateral (foraminal) herniations tend to compress the exiting root. Chemical radiculitis from inflammatory cytokines can generate pain even without marked mechanical compression, and gradual resorption of extruded disc material underlies the frequently favourable natural course. The outlook is generally excellent: the majority of patients improve substantially within six to twelve weeks with conservative care, and surgery for persistent radiculopathy provides faster relief of leg pain, although longer-term outcomes often converge with non-operative treatment.

Lumbar disc prolapse — prolapsed intervertebral disc, herniated lumbar disc, slipped disc, lumbar disc herniation, sciatica from disc prolapse Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication Cauda equina syndrome from other causes Spinal infection (discitis, epidural abscess) or vertebral osteomyelitis Spinal or metastatic tumour Peripheral neuropathy or diabetic amyotrophy Hip osteoarthritis or greater trochanteric pain referring to the leg Piriformis syndrome MRI of the lumbar spine as the imaging modality of choice when indicated Detailed neurological examination for the affected root (motor, sensory, reflexes) Straight-leg-raise and femoral stretch tests to localise root tension Urgent MRI if cauda equina syndrome is suspected Inflammatory markers and further imaging if infection or malignancy is a concern Presents with low back pain followed by radicular leg pain (sciatica) that typically radiates below the knee in a dermatomal pattern and is worsened by coughing, sneezing, or sitting Most prolapses occur at L4/5 and L5/S1, affecting the L5 and S1 nerve roots respectively; the level is inferred from the pattern of pain, weakness, sensory loss, and reflex change A positive straight-leg-raise (or its variants) reproduces radicular pain and supports nerve-root tension from a disc lesion The great majority settle with conservative management: reassurance, maintained activity, analgesia, and physiotherapy, as most herniations resorb over weeks to months Cauda equina syndrome from a large central prolapse is a surgical emergency and must be actively excluded in every patient Imaging (MRI) is reserved for persistent or severe symptoms, progressive neurological deficit, or when surgery is being considered, since asymptomatic disc bulges are common Surgery (discectomy) is considered for intractable radicular pain unresponsive to conservative care, significant or progressive motor weakness, or cauda equina compression Isolated back pain without leg symptoms is usually not due to a surgically treatable disc prolapse SURGICAL EMERGENCY: cauda equina syndrome (saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction, bilateral leg symptoms) requires urgent MRI and decompression Progressive or severe motor weakness (e.g. foot drop) indicating significant root compression Features suggesting infection or malignancy (fever, weight loss, night pain, history of cancer) New neurological deficit with structural back pain in the presence of trauma or osteoporosis Failing to screen for and act on cauda equina syndrome Ordering MRI too early and over-treating incidental disc bulges that do not explain the symptoms Attributing pure axial back pain to a disc prolapse amenable to discectomy Prolonged bed rest, which worsens outcomes compared with maintained activity The intervertebral disc comprises a gelatinous nucleus pulposus contained by the fibrous annulus fibrosus. With age and repetitive loading the annulus weakens and fissures, allowing nuclear material to bulge or herniate, usually posterolaterally where the annulus is thinnest and the posterior longitudinal ligament offers least support. The herniated fragment compresses and inflames the traversing or exiting nerve root, producing radicular pain, and inflammatory mediators from the nucleus contribute to root irritation. A large central herniation can compress the cauda equina. Over time herniated material often shrinks through dehydration and resorption, correlating with symptom resolution. The natural history is favourable, with most patients improving substantially within weeks to a few months as the herniation resorbs; surgery gives faster relief of radicular pain in selected cases but does not clearly improve very long-term outcome, and recurrence or residual back pain can occur.

Lumbar spinal stenosis — LSS, central canal stenosis, lateral recess stenosis, neurogenic claudication Vascular (arterial) claudication from peripheral arterial disease Lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy Diabetic or other peripheral neuropathy Hip or knee osteoarthritis Trochanteric bursitis or other referred hip pathology Peripheral nerve entrapment MRI of the lumbar spine as the investigation of choice Standing and flexion-extension radiographs to assess instability or degenerative spondylolisthesis CT or CT myelography where MRI is contraindicated Ankle-brachial pressure index and vascular studies to exclude arterial claudication Nerve conduction studies and EMG if peripheral neuropathy is suspected Typically affects older adults and reflects degenerative narrowing of the central canal, lateral recesses, or neural foramina The hallmark symptom is neurogenic claudication: bilateral buttock, thigh, and calf discomfort, heaviness, or paraesthesiae brought on by standing and walking Symptoms are characteristically relieved by lumbar flexion, such as sitting, leaning forward on a shopping trolley, or cycling, because flexion enlarges the canal Walking downhill (which extends the spine) tends to worsen symptoms whereas bending forward or walking uphill eases them, a useful contrast with vascular claudication Vascular claudication is relieved simply by stopping and standing still and is associated with diminished peripheral pulses, unlike neurogenic claudication which requires postural flexion for relief Neurological examination is often normal at rest, and deficits may only emerge after a provocative period of walking MRI is the investigation of choice, and standing or extension imaging can reveal dynamic compression not apparent when supine Initial management is conservative (activity modification, physiotherapy, analgesia, epidural steroid injection); decompressive surgery is considered for disabling or progressive symptoms New saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, or faecal incontinence suggesting cauda equina syndrome and mandating urgent MRI Rapidly progressive bilateral leg weakness Constitutional features such as weight loss, fever, or night pain suggesting malignancy or infection Mistaking neurogenic for vascular claudication, or vice versa, and instituting the wrong management Attributing symptoms to imaging findings when incidental degenerative narrowing is common in the asymptomatic elderly Overlooking coexisting hip osteoarthritis as a cause of buttock and leg pain Missing an evolving cauda equina syndrome Lumbar spinal stenosis arises from progressive degenerative narrowing of the spinal canal and its lateral recesses and neural foramina. A combination of intervertebral disc bulging, facet joint hypertrophy, thickening and buckling of the ligamentum flavum, and sometimes degenerative spondylolisthesis reduces the space available for the cauda equina and exiting nerve roots. The compression is dynamic: spinal extension during standing and walking further narrows the canal and compromises neural blood flow, producing the characteristic exertional leg symptoms, whereas flexion enlarges the canal and relieves them. Venous congestion and transient ischaemia of the compressed nerve roots are thought to underlie the claudicant pattern. Many patients have a stable or slowly progressive course and can be managed conservatively for years; decompressive surgery gives good relief of leg symptoms in appropriately selected patients, although back pain and other degenerative changes may persist.

an SUV >2.5 is highly suspicious for malignancy, with false negatives in lesions <8 mm, diabetes, and slow-growing tumours (p.620) MRI of the brain for metastases (and to assess brachial plexus in superior sulcus tumours); recommended in SCLC staging where brain metastases are present in ~10% of asymptomatic patients (p.620-621) EBUS/EUS-guided or invasive mediastinal staging (mediastinoscopy, thoracoscopy) since one-quarter to one-half of NSCLC patients have mediastinal nodal metastases at diagnosis (p.620-621) Repeat thoracentesis if the first is negative in suspected malignant pleural effusion; spinal MRI/CT and lumbar puncture if cord compression or leptomeningeal disease is suspected (p.620-621) Immunohistochemistry panel to confirm neuroendocrine differentiation (CD56/NCAM, synaptophysin, chromogranin, INSM1) and to distinguish primary lung from metastatic adenocarcinoma (TTF-1, napsin-A) (p.616) Routine labs suggesting metastatic spread: anaemia, and elevated alkaline phosphatase, GGT, transaminases, and calcium (p.619) Paraneoplastic syndromes can mimic metastatic disease and, if unrecognised, lead to inappropriate palliative rather than curative treatment (p.619) Benign causes of SVC obstruction (central venous catheters, pacemaker/defibrillator leads, aortic aneurysm, thyromegaly, thrombosis, fibrosing mediastinitis from prior radiation/histoplasmosis/Behcet) now account for at least 40% of SVC syndrome cases (p.585) Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy with periostitis can produce bone pain and a positive bone scan that mimics skeletal metastasis (p.619) Histology splits into small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) and three non-small-cell types (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell, large-cell) grouped as NSCLC; these four account for about 90% of epithelial lung cancers and the SCLC/NSCLC distinction drives entirely different natural history and management (p.616). SCLC and NSCLC behave very differently: SCLC is more strongly tobacco-associated, harbours TP53 and RB1 mutations in roughly 90% of cases, and presents with extensive-stage disease in 60-70% of patients (p.617, p.622). Adenocarcinoma is now the most common subtype as smoking has declined, and predominates in never-smokers/light smokers, women, and younger adults (<60); squamous and small-cell types remain the most tobacco-linked (p.616). Within NSCLC, distinguishing squamous from nonsquamous is critical for therapy; 'non-small-cell carcinoma, not otherwise specified' is no longer an acceptable diagnosis, and immunohistochemistry (TTF-1/napsin-A for adeno, p40/p63 for squamous) resolves ambiguous small biopsies (p.616). About two-thirds of new US lung cancer diagnoses occur in former smokers or never-smokers; roughly one in five women and one in 12 men with lung cancer have never smoked, so a never-smoking history does not exclude the diagnosis (p.614). Smoking cessation benefits patients even after a lung cancer diagnosis (better overall survival, fewer treatment side effects, improved quality of life), yet about 30% continue to smoke after diagnosis (p.614-615). A normal chest x-ray does not exclude lung cancer: chronic cough with or without haemoptysis in a current/former smoker with COPD aged 40 or older warrants thorough investigation even with a normal CXR (p.618). Tissue sampling is mandatory to confirm diagnosis in all suspected cases; a core biopsy is preferred over FNA to provide enough material for molecular and PD-L1 testing (p.620). Central lesions (squamous, small-cell, endobronchial carcinoids) are best reached by bronchoscopy, whereas peripheral lesions (adenocarcinoma, large-cell) favour transthoracic biopsy (p.620). PET should never be used alone to diagnose lung cancer or confirm mediastinal/metastatic involvement; tissue confirmation is always required, and false positives occur with infection and granulomatous disease such as tuberculosis (p.620). Chronic cough with or without haemoptysis in a smoker/former smoker with COPD aged 40+, even with a normal chest x-ray (p.618) A persistent pneumonia without constitutional symptoms that fails to clear after repeated antibiotic courses (p.618) Superior vena cava syndrome: neck/facial swelling, dilated neck and chest-wall collateral veins, plethora worse when supine; cerebral or laryngeal oedema signals a poorer prognosis and demands urgent evaluation (p.585-586) Tracheal obstruction from a superior mediastinal mass is the one immediately life-threatening complication and needs emergent therapy (p.586) Pancoast/superior sulcus tumour: shoulder pain radiating in the ulnar distribution of the arm with destruction of the first and second ribs (p.619) Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis, enophthalmos) from sympathetic chain involvement, often coexisting with Pancoast syndrome (p.619) Spinal cord compression symptoms (pain, weakness, paralysis, urinary retention) requiring urgent spinal imaging (p.621) Symptomatic hypercalcaemia (nausea, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, thirst, altered mental status) as the most common life-threatening metabolic complication, usually from squamous cell carcinoma (p.619) Weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight, a poor prognostic sign (p.619) Treating a non-resolving pneumonia with further antibiotics rather than investigating risks losing the chance at early cancer diagnosis (analogous principle stated for head/neck cancer p.611; applied to lung p.618). Mistaking a paraneoplastic syndrome for metastatic disease and switching to palliative care when the patient may still be curable; many paraneoplastic syndromes resolve with successful tumour treatment (p.619). Relying on PET alone for diagnosis or staging without tissue confirmation, given false positives from infection/granulomatous disease and false negatives in small or indolent lesions (p.620). Accepting a negative TTF-1 as excluding a lung primary; a negative TTF-1 does not rule out lung cancer (p.616). Stopping at a single negative thoracentesis in suspected malignant effusion, or a single negative lumbar puncture in suspected leptomeningeal disease, when a repeat is warranted (p.620-621). Overly rapid correction of SIADH-related hyponatraemia (including with tolvaptan) can cause irreversible neurologic injury; patients with ectopic ANP may worsen unless sodium intake is increased (p.619). In screening, ignoring lead-time bias, length-time bias and overdiagnosis can overstate apparent survival benefit; LDCT also carries a very high false-positive rate (about 96% of positive screens were false positives in NLST) (p.617-618). Lung cancer arises from respiratory epithelium (bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli). Environmental carcinogens, chiefly tobacco smoke, drive transformation of bronchoepithelial cells, modulated by polymorphisms in carcinogen-metabolising genes (e.g. CYP1A1). Cancers accumulate gain-of-function oncogene mutations and loss-of-function tumour-suppressor mutations; allelic loss on chromosome 3p occurs very early, even in histologically normal smoke-damaged epithelium. NSCLC adenocarcinomas are frequently driven by targetable oncogenic alterations (EGFR ~10-35%, KRAS ~15-25%, ALK rearrangement 3-7%, plus BRAF, HER2, MET, RET, ROS1, NTRK), whereas nearly 90% of SCLCs carry TP53 and RB1 mutations. Clinical manifestations stem from the primary lesion, local/regional invasion, distant metastases, or paraneoplastic syndromes. Paraneoplastic endocrine effects reflect ectopic hormone secretion: PTH-related peptide (squamous cell) causing hypercalcaemia, ADH or atrial natriuretic peptide (SCLC) causing hyponatraemia, and ectopic ACTH (SCLC, pulmonary carcinoids) causing Cushing-type biochemistry. (p.615-619) Outcome is closely tied to stage at diagnosis, but over half of patients present with locally advanced or metastatic disease. In NSCLC, about 15% have localised disease amenable to curative surgery or radiotherapy, roughly a quarter have local/regional disease that may or may not be curable, and about half have metastatic disease at diagnosis. SEER data (2022) show a 5-year survival of about 63% for localised disease. Extrathoracic metastases are found at autopsy in >50% of squamous, ~80% of adenocarcinoma/large-cell, and >95% of SCLC cases. SCLC is highly likely to present extensive-stage (60-70%). Adenocarcinoma pattern carries prognostic weight: lepidic-predominant is favourable, acinar/papillary intermediate, and solid or micropapillary poor; adenocarcinoma in situ and minimally invasive adenocarcinoma achieve essentially 100% 5-year disease-free survival after complete resection. Weight loss >10%, and thrombotic disease complicating cancer, are poor prognostic signs. (p.616, p.619, p.621-622) NSCLC: TNM (8th edition, effective 2018; 9th edition expected 2024). T by size/invasion - T1 <=3cm (T1a <=1, T1b >1-2, T1c >2-3), T2 >3-5cm or visceral pleura/main bronchus/atelectasis (T2a >3-4, T2b >4-5), T3 >5-7cm or chest wall/pericardium/phrenic nerve invasion or same-lobe satellite nodule, T4 >7cm or invasion of mediastinum/heart/great vessels/trachea/oesophagus/spine/carina or different ipsilateral-lobe nodule. N: N0 none, N1 ipsilateral peribronchial/hilar/intrapulmonary, N2 ipsilateral mediastinal/subcarinal, N3 contralateral mediastinal/hilar or any scalene/supraclavicular. M: M1a contralateral-lobe nodule or pleural/pericardial nodule/malignant effusion, M1b single distant metastasis to one organ, M1c multiple metastases. SCLC: dual classification recommended - the Veterans Administration two-stage system (limited-stage = confined to ipsilateral hemithorax within a tolerable radiation port, including contralateral supraclavicular nodes, recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement and SVC obstruction; extensive-stage = overt metastatic disease, or cardiac tamponade/malignant effusion/bilateral parenchymal involvement) plus the TNM system, with TNM preferred for the rare apparent stage I SCLC. (p.620-622)

lunotriquetral instability — lunotriquetral ligament injury, LT dissociation Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) tear Ulnar impaction syndrome Extensor carpi ulnaris tendinopathy or subluxation Pisotriquetral arthritis Midcarpal instability Distal radioulnar joint pathology Hamate or triquetral fracture PA, lateral and clenched-fist radiographs assessing Gilula arcs and carpal alignment Lateral view to detect a VISI pattern with abnormal scaphoid flexion and capitolunate angulation MRI or MR arthrography of the lunotriquetral ligament and TFCC Wrist arthroscopy for definitive diagnosis and grading Assessment of ulnar variance Fluoroscopic dynamic motion study Contralateral comparison views Lunotriquetral instability arises from injury to the lunotriquetral interosseous ligament, causing ulnar-sided wrist pain and a sense of clunking. It may occur in isolation, often after a fall on the extended, radially deviated and pronated wrist, or as part of a reverse perilunate (progressive perilunar) injury. The Reagan ballottement test and the Kleinman shear test reproduce pain and abnormal motion at the lunotriquetral interval. When secondary stabilisers also fail, the lunate follows the scaphoid into flexion, producing a volar intercalated segment instability (VISI) posture. Static radiographs are often normal; a break in the smooth proximal Gilula arcs or a lunotriquetral step-off is suggestive. Ulnar impaction syndrome frequently coexists and should be assessed, as positive ulnar variance may need addressing. Arthroscopy is the reference standard for confirming and grading the tear when imaging is inconclusive. Features of a progressive perilunate injury or dislocation Fixed VISI deformity indicating chronic complete disruption Associated ulnar impaction with lunate or triquetral chondral change Neurovascular compromise after a high-energy injury Overlooking associated ulnar impaction and treating the ligament in isolation. Interpreting normal static radiographs as excluding instability. Missing a reverse perilunate injury pattern. Confusing lunotriquetral instability with a primary TFCC tear. The lunotriquetral interosseous ligament, strongest volarly, tightly couples the lunate and triquetrum within the proximal carpal row. Disruption, whether traumatic or degenerative and often associated with ulnar impaction, uncouples this linkage. With loss of the palmar lunotriquetral ligament and secondary volar stabilisers, the triquetrum extends while the lunate, still tethered to the scaphoid, is drawn into flexion, generating a VISI collapse pattern. The resulting abnormal midcarpal kinematics produce pain, clicking and reduced load tolerance on the ulnar side of the wrist. Isolated partial injuries often respond to non-operative care, whereas complete or chronic instability may require repair, reconstruction or lunotriquetral arthrodesis, with outcomes influenced by coexisting ulnar impaction.

tetracyclines and other systemic agents while avoiding potent topical corticosteroids Necrotising facial granulomata requiring exclusion of tuberculosis before immunosuppression Rapidly progressive or ulcerating lesions atypical for the condition Periocular involvement threatening the eyelids or ocular surface Development of disfiguring scarring during the active phase Being misled by the caseating histology into diagnosing tuberculosis without supporting microbiology Using potent topical corticosteroids, which tend to aggravate the eruption Delaying treatment and allowing avoidable scarring to It is characterised by dermal granulomatous inflammation, classically epithelioid granulomata with central caseation-like necrosis, arising in a symmetrical facial distribution. Although the historical name and the necrotising histology suggested a tuberculid, no consistent link to mycobacterial infection has been demonstrated, and tuberculin reactions and mycobacterial studies are typically negative. It is now considered an idiopathic granulomatous reaction pattern, possibly related to a follicular or perifollicular process, and is discussed alongside granulomatous rosacea as part of a shared spectrum. The tendency to scar reflects destruction of dermal structures by the granulomatous infiltrate. The disorder is self-limiting and usually resolves spontaneously over one to two years, but it frequently leaves permanent pitted or depressed scars, and treatment often produces only modest benefit.

in systemic lupus erythematosus and is a major determinant of morbidity and long-term outcome in the disease It can present across a spectrum from asymptomatic urinary abnormalities to nephrotic syndrome or rapidly progressive nephritic disease Kidney biopsy is the cornerstone of assessment, classifying disease into histological classes that directly guide the intensity of treatment The proliferative classes (particularly diffuse involvement) carry the greatest risk of progression and generally require intensive immunosuppression Low complement levels and rising anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies often accompany active renal disease and can herald flares Screening urinalysis and quantification of proteinuria at intervals is essential in all lupus patients because early nephritis is frequently silent Treatment is divided into an induction phase to control active inflammation and a maintenance phase to prevent relapse, alongside general measures such as blood pressure control and reduction of proteinuria Antiphospholipid antibodies can cause a thrombotic microangiopathy that contributes to renal injury independent of immune-complex nephritis Rapidly rising creatinine with an active nephritic sediment suggesting proliferative or crescentic disease Nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema Features of thrombotic microangiopathy such as haemolysis and thrombocytopenia Signs of severe extrarenal lupus or infection complicating immunosuppression Relying on serology alone without biopsy to determine the class and intensity of treatment Missing silent early nephritis by not performing regular urinalysis in lupus patients Overlooking antiphospholipid-related thrombotic microangiopathy as a cause of worsening function Stopping maintenance therapy prematurely and precipitating a relapse Lupus nephritis results from deposition of immune complexes and autoantibodies within the glomerulus, driving complement activation and inflammatory injury. Circulating and in-situ immune complexes, including those containing anti-DNA antibodies, localise in the mesangium, subendothelial, and subepithelial regions, and the site of deposition largely determines the clinical and histological pattern. Subendothelial and mesangial deposits provoke inflammatory, proliferative lesions with a nephritic picture, whereas predominantly subepithelial (membranous) deposits produce heavy proteinuria with less inflammation. Complement consumption, cytokine release, and recruitment of inflammatory cells damage the glomerular capillaries, and in severe forms crescents develop. Chronic activity leads to glomerulosclerosis, tubulointerstitial scarring, and progressive loss of function. Concurrent antiphospholipid antibodies may add a thrombotic microangiopathic component. Outcome has improved substantially with modern immunosuppression, but proliferative lupus nephritis still carries a meaningful risk of progression to end-stage kidney disease, especially with delayed treatment, high chronicity on biopsy, persistent proteinuria, or frequent relapses. Adherence, blood pressure control, and reduction of proteinuria strongly influence long-term renal survival.

facial disfigurement or lipoatrophy Misdiagnosing subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma as benign lupus panniculitis Taking a biopsy that is too shallow to sample the fat lobules adequately Attributing new depressed scars to injections or trauma rather than recognising the panniculitis Overlooking coexisting systemic lupus and its organ complications Lupus panniculitis is an autoimmune, predominantly lobular inflammation of subcutaneous fat that forms part of the spectrum of cutaneous lupus erythematosus. A T-lymphocyte-driven immune response targets the deep dermis and fat lobules, producing hyaline necrosis of adipocytes, lymphoid aggregates, mucin deposition and lymphocytic vascular injury. Repeated bouts of fat inflammation and necrosis are followed by fibrosis and loss of fat volume, accounting for the characteristic depressed atrophic scars. It may occur alone or in association with discoid or systemic lupus, reflecting a shared loss of immune tolerance. The condition tends to run a chronic, relapsing course; inflammation usually responds to antimalarials but residual lipoatrophy and scarring are frequently permanent and cosmetically distressing. Prognosis worsens if there is coexisting active systemic lupus or if an underlying lymphoma has been mistaken for it.

(DNMT3A-related) Malan syndrome (NFIX-related) Fragile X syndrome Other histone-modification-related intellectual disability syndromes Exome or genome sequencing, or a targeted overgrowth/intellectual macrocephaly, tall stature, and neurodevelopmental difficulties It is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SETD2, a histone methyltransferase gene responsible for trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 36 Intellectual disability, autism spectrum features, and speech and language delay are prominent Obesity and advanced bone age may accompany the tall stature and macrocephaly It sits within the differential of Sotos and related overgrowth syndromes and is usually distinguished by molecular testing rather than clinical features alone Diagnosis is established by exome or genome sequencing, or a targeted overgrowth/intellectual disability panel Management is supportive and anticipatory, focusing on developmental, educational, and behavioural interventions with surveillance of function Emergence of features suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis Anchoring on a clinical diagnosis of Sotos syndrome and not extending genetic testing to SETD2 Assuming overgrowth syndromes are clinically distinguishable when molecular testing is usually required Underestimating the autism spectrum and language needs that benefit from targeted intervention Omitting genetic counselling regarding autosomal dominant, commonly de novo, inheritance Luscan-Lumish syndrome is an overgrowth disorder within the group of chromatin-modification syndromes. It results from germline heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SETD2, which encodes a histone methyltransferase that catalyses trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 36, an epigenetic mark that regulates transcription, splicing, and DNA repair. Reduced SETD2 activity disturbs these chromatin-dependent gene-expression programmes during development, giving rise to generalised overgrowth, macrocephaly, and neurodevelopmental impairment. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, and reported cases are frequently de novo. As with other genes in this pathway, distinct classes of SETD2 variant have been linked to different clinical presentations. The condition is not known to shorten lifespan for most individuals, and the outlook is governed principally by the severity of intellectual disability and autism spectrum features. Early and sustained developmental and educational support optimises functional outcomes.

alone Echocardiography defines the size and severity of both the defect and the valve lesion and guides the treatment strategy Modern management often combines percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty for suitable valves with device or surgical closure of the atrial septal defect Progressive right heart failure from combined volume and pressure loading Development of pulmonary hypertension and shunt reversal New atrial fibrillation with haemodynamic deterioration or embolic risk Severe mitral stenosis with a valve unsuitable for balloon valvuloplasty Missing coexisting mitral stenosis because the atrial defect masks its classic symptoms and signs Attributing all findings to an isolated atrial septal defect and overlooking the valve lesion Closing the atrial septal defect without addressing significant mitral stenosis, abruptly raising left atrial pressure Failing to assess mitral valve suitability before planning balloon valvuloplasty In Lutembacher syndrome coexisting mitral stenosis and an atrial septal defect interact haemodynamically. Mitral stenosis obstructs left atrial emptying and raises left atrial pressure; the atrial septal defect then allows this pressurised blood to shunt into the right atrium, so left atrial pressure is partly relieved and the pulmonary venous congestion typical of isolated mitral stenosis may be attenuated. The trade-off is a larger left-to-right shunt than the defect alone would produce, imposing a volume load on the right atrium and ventricle and increasing pulmonary blood flow, which over time can lead to right heart dilatation, atrial arrhythmia, and pulmonary hypertension. With timely treatment of both the valve lesion and the septal defect the outlook is generally good, but untreated disease can progress to right heart failure, atrial arrhythmia, and pulmonary hypertension.

standard blood counts may give clues (cytopenias) Fibromyalgia Chronic fatigue syndrome Allergic reaction to tick saliva Peripheral spondyloarthropathy / juvenile idiopathic arthritis (for the arthritis presentation) Caused by spirochetes of the Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato group (also called Borreliella spp.), transmitted by Ixodes ricinus complex ticks; B. burgdorferi sensu stricto is the predominant cause in the United States, while B. afzelii, B. garinii, and B. bavariensis also occur in Europe and Asia. (p.1448-1449) Staged illness: stage 1 (early localized) presents with erythema migrans (EM); stage 2 (early disseminated) may follow with secondary skin lesions, neurologic involvement (meningitis, cranial neuritis, radiculoneuritis), carditis with atrioventricular block, and migratory musculoskeletal pain; stage 3 (late/persistent) typically manifests as intermittent arthritis and, rarely, chronic encephalopathy, polyneuropathy, or acrodermatitis. (p.1448-1449) EM begins after an incubation period of roughly 3-32 days as a red macule or papule at the bite site that expands into a large annular lesion, often with a bright red outer border and partial central clearing; common sites include the thigh, groin, and axilla, and the lesion is warm but usually not painful. (p.1451) Approximately 20% of patients do NOT develop the characteristic EM skin lesion, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis. (p.1451) Cardiac involvement occurs in about 8% of patients within weeks of onset; the most common abnormality is fluctuating atrioventricular block (first-degree, Wenckebach, or complete heart block), and most cardiac involvement lasts only a few weeks. (p.1451) About 15% of untreated patients develop frank neurologic abnormalities after weeks to months; the typical U.S. pattern is fluctuating meningitis with facial palsy (cranial neuritis, often the facial nerve, sometimes bilateral) and peripheral radiculoneuropathy. CSF in U.S. neuroborreliosis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis (~100 cells/uL) with elevated protein and normal or slightly low glucose. (p.1451) In Europe and Asia the characteristic first neurologic sign is radicular pain followed by CSF pleocytosis (meningopolyneuritis or Bannwarth's syndrome), often without meningeal or encephalitic signs. (p.1451) Lyme arthritis (stage 3) develops in about 60% of untreated U.S. patients months after onset; the typical pattern is intermittent oligoarticular attacks in large joints, especially the knees. Joint fluid white cell counts range widely (500-110,000/uL, average ~25,000/uL), mostly neutrophils, and rheumatoid factor and ANA tests are usually negative. (p.1451) Most patients experience early symptoms during summer, reflecting transmission by nymphal Ixodes ticks; the tick must usually remain attached for at least about 24 hours for transmission of B. burgdorferi. (p.1449-1450) Lyme disease is the most common vector-borne infection in the United States and Europe; in the U.S. more than 30,000 cases are reported annually but true cases are estimated at about 476,000 per year. (p.1450) Posttreatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS) affects roughly 10% of treated patients (reported figures vary widely) with persistent subjective pain, neurocognitive symptoms, or fatigue; there is NO evidence these symptoms reflect active infection, and randomized trials show repeated antibiotic courses do not help and are not recommended. (p.1451-1453) Reinfection can occur after EM treated with antibiotics because the immune response after early infection is not protective; however, patients who develop an expanded immune response over months (e.g., those with Lyme arthritis) have protective immunity for years and rarely become reinfected. (p.1454) Maternal-fetal transmission of B. burgdorferi appears to occur rarely if at all; standard therapy is recommended for pregnant women. (p.1453) No Lyme disease vaccine is currently commercially available; the previously marketed vaccine was discontinued by its manufacturer. (p.1454) High-degree (third-degree) atrioventricular block or PR interval >0.3 s in carditis, warranting IV therapy and cardiac monitoring Severe objective neurologic abnormalities (e.g., meningitis, encephalitis, severe neuroborreliosis) Optic nerve involvement in children from inflammation or raised intracranial pressure, which may lead to blindness Borrelial encephalomyelitis/leukoencephalitis (rare, mainly B. garinii in Europe) with spastic paraparesis and bladder dysfunction Rare fatal pancarditis or cardiomegaly Suspected tick-borne co-infection (e.g., babesiosis, anaplasmosis, Powassan virus), which can cause severe or fatal illness, especially in the very young or elderly Assuming a negative serologic test excludes acute Lyme disease - serology may be negative during the first several weeks (early seronegativity), so diagnosis of early Lyme disease is clinical Missing the diagnosis because of atypical EM morphology or because ~20% of patients never develop EM Relying on a positive IgM result alone in illness lasting more than 2 months - such an isolated IgM is likely false-positive and should not support the diagnosis Misusing or misinterpreting IgM Western blots, a recognized cause of incorrect Lyme diagnoses in patients with other illnesses Using serology as a screening test in patients with nonspecific pain or fatigue (low pretest probability), where a false-positive result is more likely than a true-positive Interpreting persisting seropositivity (including VlsE C6 and IgM responses, which can persist for years after therapy) as evidence of active, recent, or recurrent infection Treating persistent subjective symptoms as active infection - 'chronic Lyme disease' equated with chronic B. burgdorferi infection is a misnomer, and repeated/prolonged antibiotic courses lack benefit and carry documented harm Using PCR positivity in joint fluid to judge active infection or adequacy of therapy, since DNA may persist for weeks after spirochetal killing B. burgdorferi is a fastidious microaerophilic spirochete with an unusually small genome and more than 100 predicted lipoproteins, mostly plasmid-encoded and displayed on the outer membrane to interact with host and tick. It expresses outer-surface protein A (OspA) in the tick midgut and upregulates OspC during migration to the salivary gland, where OspC binds the tick salivary protein Salp15 (required for mammalian infection). After injection into skin the organism downregulates OspC and upregulates the antigenically variable VlsE lipoprotein, then may migrate outward to produce EM and spread hematogenously or via lymphatics to skin, nervous system, heart, and joints. Its only known virulence factors are surface proteins that attach to host proteins, integrins, glycosaminoglycans, or glycoproteins (e.g., plasminogen binding aids tissue spread; complement regulators such as Factor H protect against lysis; decorin-binding proteins bind collagen-associated decorin, possibly explaining alignment with collagen fibrils). The host mounts innate and adaptive responses producing proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IFN-gamma) and opsonizing antibodies; immune mechanisms eventually control disseminated infection even without antibiotics, though spirochetes may persist in localized niches for years. Postinfectious (antibiotic-refractory) Lyme arthritis is not due to persistent infection (culture and PCR of synovium are uniformly negative after antibiotics) but to a dysregulated, excessive proinflammatory response with very high IFN-gamma, host genetic factors (HLA-DRB1*0401, TLR1 1805GG polymorphism), and autoimmune responses to vascular and extracellular matrix autoantigens. Response to treatment is best when given early in the disease; later treatment remains effective but the convalescent period may be longer. Eventually most patients recover with minimal or no residual deficits. Even without antibiotics, innate and adaptive immunity usually control disseminated infection within weeks to months, though untreated spirochetes may persist in localized niches for years. A small percentage develop persistent postinfectious arthritis or, rarely, chronic encephalopathy or polyneuropathy, and about 10% have PTLDS, which usually improves over months but may last years. Staged clinical classification per Harrison: Stage 1 - early localized infection (erythema migrans at the bite site). Stage 2 - early disseminated infection (secondary annular skin lesions, neurologic involvement such as meningitis/cranial neuritis/radiculoneuritis/peripheral neuritis, carditis with atrioventricular nodal block, and migratory musculoskeletal pain). Stage 3 - late/persistent infection (intermittent or persistent arthritis, and rarely chronic encephalopathy, polyneuropathy, or acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans). For diagnostic/testing purposes, the American College of Physicians algorithm stratifies by pretest probability: high (EM - treat empirically without serology), intermediate (e.g., oligoarticular arthritis - test and treat if positive), and low (nonspecific symptoms - neither test nor treat).
