Lymphangioma circumscriptum — Microcystic lymphatic malformation, Superficial lymphatic malformation Macrocystic lymphatic malformation Venous malformation Angiokeratoma Herpes simplex or zoster with grouped vesicles Molluscum contagiosum Acquired cutaneous lymphangiectasia from lymphatic obstruction Clinical and dermoscopic assessment showing lacunae and frogspawn-like vesicles Skin biopsy showing dilated papillary dermal lymphatics MRI to define the deep cisternal component and overall extent Ultrasound PIK3CA mutation testing in selected cases Assessment for secondary infection when the lesion is inflamed The most common cutaneous (microcystic) lymphatic malformation, now classified as a superficial lymphatic malformation. Presents as clusters of clear, translucent, thick-walled vesicles likened to frogspawn, often with haemorrhagic red-black vesicles when blood enters. Commonly affects the proximal limbs, limb girdles, axillae, trunk and oral cavity or tongue. Frequently connected to deeper, larger lymphatic cisterns beneath the skin, which explains the high recurrence after superficial treatment. Prone to recurrent leakage of clear lymph, oozing, bleeding and secondary cellulitis. Usually congenital or appearing in early childhood, though it can present later in life. MRI helps define the depth of the deeper cisternal component before intervention. Treatment options include sclerotherapy, ablative laser and excision of the deep component, but recurrences are common. Recurrent cellulitis or sepsis arising within the malformation Persistent lymph leakage with skin breakdown New firm nodularity in longstanding lymphoedema, raising concern for lymphangiosarcoma Extensive lesions causing functional impairment Treating only the visible surface vesicles and ignoring the deep cisterns, which guarantees recurrence. Misdiagnosing grouped haemorrhagic vesicles as herpes infection. Underestimating the extent without MRI before surgery. Overlooking recurrent cellulitis as a driver of long-term morbidity. Lymphangioma circumscriptum is a superficial (microcystic) lymphatic malformation in which dilated lymphatic channels form thin-walled vesicles within the papillary dermis. These superficial cisterns typically communicate with larger, muscular-walled lymphatic cisterns in the deeper dermis and subcutis that are disconnected from the normal lymphatic system; rhythmic contraction of the deep cisterns transmits pressure to the surface vesicles. Failure to address the deep component underlies the characteristic recurrence. As with other lymphatic malformations, many lesions harbour somatic PIK3CA-pathway activation, and communication with dermal capillaries accounts for the intermittent haemorrhagic appearance. The condition is benign but chronic and notoriously recurrent after treatment unless the deep cisternal component is addressed. Complications are mainly recurrent infection, leakage and cosmetic concern.

Lymphatic malformation — Lymphangioma, Cystic hygroma, Macrocystic/microcystic lymphatic malformation Venous malformation Infantile haemangioma Thyroglossal or branchial cyst for cervical lesions Teratoma Kaposiform lymphangiomatosis Combined lymphaticovenous malformation Ultrasound distinguishing macrocystic from microcystic disease Contrast-enhanced MRI (T2-bright cysts with fluid-fluid levels after bleeding) Antenatal ultrasound and, where indicated, fetal karyotyping Aspiration and analysis of cyst fluid when the diagnosis is unclear PIK3CA mutation testing Airway assessment with nasendoscopy or imaging for cervicofacial lesions Slow-flow malformation of dysplastic lymphatic channels, classified as macrocystic, microcystic or combined. Macrocystic lesions are soft, transilluminant and often cervicofacial or axillary (historically termed cystic hygroma); microcystic lesions are ill-defined and infiltrative. Somatic activating PIK3CA mutations underlie most lesions, placing them within the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum. Sudden enlargement typically follows intralesional bleeding or infection. Superficial microcystic mucosal or cutaneous lesions produce characteristic clear or blood-filled vesicles resembling frogspawn. Sclerotherapy is first-line for macrocystic disease; microcystic disease is harder to treat and sirolimus is increasingly used. Large cervicofacial lesions can compromise the airway and may require antenatal airway planning such as an EXIT procedure. Antenatally detected cystic hygroma is associated with chromosomal abnormalities such as Turner syndrome and with other structural anomalies. Lymphatic malformation results from abnormal embryonic development of lymphatic channels that fail to establish normal connections with the venous system, producing dilated, endothelium-lined cystic spaces filled with lymph. Most sporadic lesions carry somatic activating mutations in PIK3CA, driving PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling and abnormal lymphatic endothelial growth. Because the channels drain poorly they are prone to stasis, intralesional haemorrhage and infection, which cause abrupt and sometimes dramatic enlargement. Prognosis depends on site and type. Well-defined macrocystic lesions respond well to sclerotherapy, whereas diffuse microcystic and cervicofacial disease tends to recur and cause chronic morbidity, although mTOR inhibition has improved control.

Lymphoedema — lymphedema, lymphatic oedema, primary lymphoedema, secondary lymphoedema Chronic venous insufficiency and venous oedema Deep vein thrombosis Systemic causes of oedema (cardiac, renal, hepatic, hypoalbuminaemia) Lipoedema Dependent or immobility-related oedema Myxoedema Clinical assessment including Stemmer sign and limb circumference or volume measurement Lymphoscintigraphy to confirm lymphatic dysfunction when the diagnosis is unclear Duplex ultrasound to exclude venous disease or thrombosis Cross-sectional imaging to identify malignancy or nodal obstruction in secondary cases Evaluation for filariasis in endemic regions Results from impaired lymphatic drainage causing accumulation of protein-rich interstitial fluid and progressive limb swelling Primary forms arise from congenital or inherited lymphatic maldevelopment, while secondary forms follow damage from surgery, radiotherapy, malignancy, infection, or trauma Worldwide, filarial infection is the leading cause of secondary lymphoedema, whereas in high-income settings cancer treatment predominates Early swelling is soft and pitting but becomes non-pitting and fibrotic over time, with skin thickening and a positive Stemmer sign at the base of the toes The distribution characteristically includes the dorsum of the foot and toes, helping distinguish it from other causes of limb swelling Diagnosis is largely clinical; lymphoscintigraphy can confirm lymphatic dysfunction when the cause is uncertain Cornerstone management is complete decongestive therapy with skin care, manual lymphatic drainage, compression, and exercise Meticulous skin hygiene reduces recurrent cellulitis, which itself further damages lymphatics and worsens the oedema Features of cellulitis (spreading erythema, warmth, fever) requiring prompt treatment Rapidly progressive or unilateral swelling raising concern for underlying malignancy New or changing cutaneous lesions suggesting lymphangiosarcoma in longstanding lymphoedema Sudden painful swelling that could indicate concurrent deep vein thrombosis Confusing lymphoedema with venous oedema or lipoedema and applying inappropriate treatment Applying compression without first excluding significant arterial disease Overlooking an underlying malignancy in new unilateral limb swelling Neglecting skin care, allowing recurrent cellulitis that accelerates progression Lymphoedema develops when lymphatic transport capacity is exceeded by the lymphatic load, leading to accumulation of protein-rich fluid in the interstitium. In primary disease the lymphatic vessels or nodes are congenitally hypoplastic, aplastic, or dysfunctional. In secondary disease, previously normal lymphatics are obstructed or destroyed by surgery, radiotherapy, tumour infiltration, recurrent infection (notably filariasis), or trauma. Stagnant protein draws further fluid osmotically and incites chronic inflammation, fibrosis, adipose deposition, and skin changes, creating a self-reinforcing cycle. Impaired local immune surveillance predisposes to recurrent cellulitis. Lymphoedema is generally a chronic, progressive condition without cure, but sustained decongestive therapy and compression can control swelling, preserve function, and reduce complications. Poor adherence, recurrent infection, and untreated underlying causes worsen the outlook, and rarely longstanding disease can undergo malignant change.

Lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome is an autosomal dominant primary lymphatic disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in the transcription factor FOXC2, which is essential for normal development of lymphatic valves and vessels. The resulting valvular dysfunction leads to lymphatic reflux and impaired drainage, producing lower-limb lymphoedema, and the same developmental disturbance affects venous valves (accounting for varicose veins) and eyelash follicles (distichiasis). FOXC2 also contributes to eyelid, palatal and cardiac development, explaining the associated anomalies. The condition is chronic but generally compatible with a normal lifespan; lymphoedema is manageable with sustained conservative care, and distichiasis is treatable, though recurrent infection, progressive swelling and any associated cardiac disease influence long-term outcome.

Lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia — LIP, Lymphoid interstitial pneumonia Pulmonary MALT lymphoma and other lymphoproliferative disease Follicular bronchiolitis Cellular nonspecific interstitial pneumonia Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Sarcoidosis Lymphangioleiomyomatosis or Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome as cystic mimics Pneumocystis or other opportunistic infection in the immunocompromised HRCT thorax to characterise ground-glass change and cysts Autoimmune serology and a Sjögren work-up including anti-Ro/La antibodies and Schirmer test HIV testing and serum immunoglobulins with electrophoresis Surgical lung biopsy with immunohistochemistry and clonality studies to exclude lymphoma Bronchoalveolar lavage typically showing lymphocytosis Pulmonary function tests with transfer factor A rare, largely benign lymphoproliferative interstitial process classified among the idiopathic interstitial pneumonias but usually secondary to an underlying disorder. Strongly associated with Sjögren syndrome, other connective tissue diseases, HIV infection (especially in children), common variable immunodeficiency and autoimmune thyroid disease. Presents insidiously with cough and breathlessness, sometimes with systemic or autoimmune features. The HRCT hallmark is diffuse ground-glass opacity with scattered thin-walled perivascular cysts; centrilobular nodules and septal thickening are also seen. Histology shows a dense polyclonal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate expanding the alveolar septa. Peribronchiolar lymphoid infiltration with air trapping is thought to produce the characteristic thin-walled cysts. The course is variable; many patients stabilise or improve with treatment of the underlying disorder, but some progress to fibrosis or, uncommonly, transform to lymphoma.

Lymphomatoid granulomatosis reflects an Epstein-Barr virus-driven proliferation of B-cells that occurs when T-cell immune surveillance is deficient. EBV-infected atypical B-cells accumulate and invade the walls of small and medium vessels (angiocentric and angiodestructive growth), producing ischaemic necrosis within affected organs, most prominently the lung. A prominent reactive T-cell infiltrate accompanies the relatively sparse malignant B-cells. The number of EBV-positive B-cells and the degree of necrosis define the histological grade, and higher-grade lesions represent a form of EBV-positive large B-cell lymphoma, explaining the spectrum from indolent to aggressive behaviour. Outcome is variable and grade-dependent: low-grade disease may respond to immune-modulating therapy and occasionally regresses with immune restoration, whereas high-grade disease behaves as an aggressive lymphoma requiring immunochemotherapy.

confined to the skin. The prognosis is excellent with a normal life expectancy in most patients, but lifelong surveillance is warranted because a subset develop an associated lymphoma over time.

Labelling a microsatellite-unstable tumour as Lynch syndrome without excluding MLH1 promoter methylation Relying solely on family history criteria and missing carriers who do not meet Amsterdam or Bethesda thresholds Overlooking endometrial and other extracolonic risks by focusing only on the colon Failing to arrange cascade testing of relatives once a germline variant is confirmed The syndrome stems from a germline defect in the DNA mismatch-repair system, which normally corrects base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops that arise during replication. When the remaining functional allele is lost in a somatic cell, repair fails and errors accumulate, most conspicuously in repetitive microsatellite sequences, producing the microsatellite instability that characterises these tumours. The resulting hypermutable state generates numerous mutations in growth-regulatory genes, accelerating carcinogenesis and also creating neoantigens that make the tumours responsive to immune checkpoint blockade. Cancer risk is high but gene-dependent, being greatest for MLH1 and MSH2 and lower for MSH6 and PMS2. Colonoscopic surveillance markedly reduces colorectal cancer mortality, and mismatch-repair-deficient tumours often respond well to immune checkpoint inhibitors, so outcomes are frequently favourable when the diagnosis is recognised.

y+LAT1 transporter, which mediates efflux of the cationic amino acids lysine, arginine and ornithine across the basolateral membrane of enterocytes and renal tubular cells. Defective transport impairs intestinal absorption and promotes renal loss of these amino acids, lowering their plasma concentrations. Because arginine and ornithine are urea-cycle intermediates, their deficiency limits ureagenesis and leads to hyperammonaemia, especially after protein intake. The disorder also disturbs macrophage and immune function, contributing to the systemic features such as pulmonary alveolar proteinosis and haematological abnormalities. With protein restriction, citrulline supplementation and ammonia control, metabolic stability and growth can be maintained, but multisystem complications such as pulmonary alveolar proteinosis and renal or immune involvement affect long-term outcome. Prognosis varies with the severity of these systemic manifestations.

Missing the diagnosis in infants by not measuring enzyme activity in unexplained hepatosplenomegaly and failure to thrive Mislabelling later-onset disease as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease or familial hypercholesterolaemia Overlooking adrenal insufficiency in the infantile form Delaying enzyme replacement therapy in rapidly progressive infantile disease Lysosomal acid lipase hydrolyses cholesteryl esters and triglycerides taken up by cells through lipoprotein endocytosis, releasing free cholesterol and fatty acids for cellular use. Complete or near-complete deficiency causes massive lysosomal accumulation of cholesteryl esters and triglycerides in liver, spleen, intestine, adrenal glands and macrophages, producing the fulminant multi-organ infantile Wolman phenotype; partial deficiency causes the slower cholesteryl ester storage disease phenotype. Impaired liberation of free cholesterol disrupts cholesterol homeostasis, driving compensatory synthesis and the characteristic dyslipidaemia, while progressive tissue storage leads to hepatic failure or, in milder disease, fibrosis and premature atherosclerosis. Untreated infantile Wolman disease is almost uniformly fatal within the first months of life, whereas the later-onset form is more indolent; enzyme replacement therapy substantially improves survival and hepatic and metabolic outcomes across the spectrum.

Lysosomal Storage Diseases — Lysosomal system diseases, LSDs, Tay-Sachs disease, Fabry disease, Gaucher disease, Niemann-Pick disease, Mucopolysaccharidoses, Pompe disease, Lysosomal acid lipase deficiency, LALD, Krabbe disease, CLN2 Batten disease, Alpha-mannosidosis Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (mimicked by late-onset Pompe disease) Idiopathic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (about 1-3% have Fabry disease) Idiopathic stroke at 35-50 years (about 2-5% carry GLA mutations) Idiopathic renal failure in males (about 5% have GLA mutations) Cryptogenic cirrhosis / nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (childhood/adult-onset LALD) Familial hyperlipidemia (LALD) Parkinson disease (associated with GBA1 carriage) Acute appendicitis or renal colic (Fabry abdominal pain can mimic these) Enzyme assay in nucleated cells, serum/plasma, or leukocytes specific to the suspected disorder Molecular/genetic testing: whole GBA1 sequencing is the standard for Gaucher (enzyme testing has poor sensitivity for heterozygote detection) Slit-lamp examination for corneal and lenticular lesions to support a Fabry diagnosis Decreased acid beta-glucosidase activity (0-20% of normal) in nucleated cells establishes Gaucher disease; the enzyme is normally absent from bodily fluids Markedly reduced acid sphingomyelinase activity (1-10% of normal) in nucleated cells confirms Niemann-Pick A/B Confirmation of specific enzyme deficiency in Morquio (GALNS vs acid beta-galactosidase) before therapy Gene sequencing to confirm CLN2 given overlap among the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses Newborn screening (now includes MPS I and, in many states, Pompe disease) Bone imaging / nuclear scan in Gaucher bone crises (localized absent uptake of pyrophosphate agents indicates acute bone infarction) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Fabry cardiac variant) Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (late-onset Pompe) Cryptogenic/idiopathic cirrhosis (childhood/adult-onset LALD) Other neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (significant clinical overlap with CLN2) Lysosomes are subcellular organelles holding specific hydrolases that process or degrade proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates and lipids; there are more than 50 distinct lysosomal storage diseases (now also called lysosomal system diseases), grouped by the predominant accumulated material. Consider an LSD in the differential when a patient has unexplained neurologic, renal or muscular degeneration, or unexplained hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, cardiomyopathy, or skeletal dysplasias/deformities; physical findings are disease-specific and diagnosis is confirmed by enzyme assay or genetic testing. Nearly all LSDs are autosomal recessive, with notable exceptions: Hunter disease (MPS II), Danon disease and Fabry disease are X-linked, and two autosomal dominant conditions exist (Parry-type CLN from DNAJC5 mutations, and frontotemporal dementia/CLN11 from GRN/progranulin mutations). Tay-Sachs disease (total hexosaminidase A deficiency) is carried by roughly 1 in 30 Ashkenazi Jews; the infantile form features macrocephaly, loss of motor skills, an exaggerated startle reaction and a macular cherry-red spot, with carrier screening recommended in this population. Fabry disease (X-linked, alpha-galactosidase A deficiency) presents with angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis, corneal and lenticular opacities, debilitating episodic burning pain of the hands and feet (acroparesthesia), and progressive renal, cardiac and cerebrovascular disease; angiokeratomas are punctate, dark red to blue-black, do not blanch and cluster in the 'bathing suit area' between umbilicus and knees. Gaucher disease (acid beta-glucosidase deficiency, GBA1) is classified by CNS involvement: type 1 is nonneuronopathic with hepatosplenomegaly and bone disease, type 2 is a severe progressive CNS disease causing death by about 2 years, and type 3 has variable CNS and visceral disease; early CNS signs in type 3 may be limited to supranuclear lateral gaze palsy. GBA1 mutations, whether heterozygous or homozygous, substantially raise the lifetime risk of Parkinson disease. Niemann-Pick types A and B reflect acid sphingomyelinase deficiency: type A has early onset with rapid CNS deterioration, while type B is later/variable with hepatosplenomegaly, cirrhosis, and lethal progressive pulmonary disease (foam cells in alveoli, lymphatics and pulmonary arteries); Niemann-Pick C is a separate disorder from NPC1/NPC2 defects in cholesterol/sphingolipid transport. Pompe disease (acid alpha-glucosidase/acid maltase deficiency, GAA) is the only LSD causing primary glycogen storage; the classic infantile form has hypotonia, cardiomyopathy and hepatosplenomegaly with near-total enzyme deficiency, whereas late-onset forms resemble a limb-girdle myopathy and may not have cardiomyopathy. Lysosomal acid lipase deficiency (LIPA mutations) spans infantile Wolman syndrome (failure to thrive, vomiting, hepatosplenomegaly; median death about 3.7 months) and childhood/adult-onset cholesterol ester storage disease (elevated liver enzymes, microvesicular fatty liver, cryptogenic cirrhosis); neither variant causes primary CNS disease and statins do not halt the underlying tissue pathology. CLN2 (neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis type 2, TPP1/tripeptidyl peptidase 1 deficiency) usually begins at age 2-4 years with seizures, ataxia, myoclonus and vision loss, progressing to severe disability and death around age 12; it is the only NCL with a specific approved treatment. Alpha-mannosidosis (MAN2B1 biallelic loss of function) accumulates mannose-rich oligosaccharides and causes intellectual disability, incapacitating skeletal changes, immunodeficiency, ataxia, hearing loss, neurodegeneration and psychosis. Macular cherry-red spot with macrocephaly and exaggerated startle in an infant (infantile Tay-Sachs) Splenic infarction in Gaucher disease that can present as an acute abdomen Gaucher 'bone crisis' with excruciating localized pain, sometimes erythema, fever and leukocytosis, representing acute bone infarction Pulmonary hypertension or alveolar Gaucher cell accumulation (uncommon but life-threatening, more common in splenectomized females) Vertebral collapse and avascular necrosis (femoral head) with potential spinal cord involvement in Gaucher disease Infantile-onset LALD presenting as a medical emergency with severe failure to thrive, vomiting and hepatosplenomegaly Fetal hydrops in severe MPS VII (Sly), which can cause stillbirth or perinatal demise Progressive pulmonary disease with dyspnea and hypoxemia in Niemann-Pick type B Respiratory insufficiency requiring ventilation in late-onset Pompe disease Treating the disease nosology as fixed discrete entities is misleading: each LSD is heuristic and clinically expresses a continuous spectrum from severe to attenuated forms. Angiokeratomas of Fabry disease can be easily overlooked and also occur in several other rare LSDs, so they are not specific. Fabry abdominal pain may be mistaken for appendicitis or renal colic, delaying diagnosis. Enzyme testing has poor sensitivity for Gaucher heterozygote detection; molecular GBA1 sequencing is required. In Niemann-Pick, hepatic or bone marrow transplantation has produced more complications than expected (recurrent hepatic disease from ASM-deficient myeloid repopulation after liver transplant, or failure to clear hepatocyte sphingomyelin after BMT/HSCT). Enzyme replacement therapy does not cross the blood-brain barrier and does not directly treat CNS disease (e.g., MPS I, MPS II); HSCT has not succeeded against CNS disease in MPS II. Statins lower hypercholesterolemia in LALD but do not alter the underlying progressive tissue (e.g., liver) pathology. Late cardiac and respiratory complications of MPS I (obstructive breathing, cardiomyopathy, valve disease) can emerge even after successful HSCT, so lifelong follow-up is required. Morquio variants A and B require confirmation of the specific enzyme deficiency because approved enzyme therapy (elosulfase alfa) applies only to MPS IVA. Lysosomal biogenesis requires ongoing synthesis of lysosomal hydrolases, membrane proteins and new membranes; lysosomes form by fusion of trans-Golgi network vesicles with late endosomes, and progressive acidification creates a pH gradient that drives pH-dependent dissociation of receptors from ligands and activates the hydrolases. Lysosomes are part of the lysosome/autophagy/mitophagy system regulated by mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of transcription factors TFEB/TFE3, which balances anabolic and catabolic pathways; this regulation is disrupted to varying degrees in tissues affected by specific LSDs. Defects at any biosynthetic step can impair enzyme function: oligosaccharide remodeling in the Golgi (including the mannose-6-phosphate lysosomal targeting ligand), membrane sorting signals, phosphorylation, sulfation, additional proteolysis and heteromer assembly are all critical, and abnormalities in these shared processes can produce multiple simultaneous enzyme/protein deficiencies. The final common pathway is accumulation of specific macromolecules within tissues and cells that normally carry a high flux of those substrates; most deficiencies arise from point mutations or rearrangements at a single hydrolase/subunit locus, though some mutations affecting targeting, active sites, macromolecular assembly or trafficking impair several hydrolases at once. Substrate buildup distorts lysosomes and may exert pharmacologic effects, notably activation of innate immune responses. Some substrates are made within the tissue of pathology, while others are delivered exogenously (LDL receptor-mediated uptake in Fabry and LALD; phagocytosis in Gaucher type 1). The threshold hypothesis holds that disease emerges below a certain level of residual enzyme activity, and that activity can be challenged by changes in substrate flux from genetic background, cell turnover, recycling or metabolic demand, so a given residual level may suffice in some tissues but not others. Prognosis varies enormously across and within disorders, each spanning a spectrum from severe to attenuated forms. Infantile Tay-Sachs is fatal in infancy; juvenile-onset Tay-Sachs causes death by 10-15 years. In Fabry disease, death results from cardiovascular, renal or cerebrovascular disease; renal insufficiency, cardiac fibrosis and stroke are irreversible, so early therapy offers the best chance to slow life-threatening complications, and heart disease is the most common life-threatening manifestation in females while renal then cardiovascular disease predominates in males. Gaucher type 2 leads to death by about 2 years, while type 1 and type 3 are highly variable. Niemann-Pick type B can progress to death in adolescence or early adulthood from hepatic or pulmonary disease. Infantile Pompe is rapidly progressive with death typically in the first year without treatment. Infantile-onset LALD is fatal by about 1 year (median 3.7 months) untreated, and untreated childhood/adult-onset LALD progresses to early cirrhosis (mean about age 13) and early-adulthood atherosclerosis. Early infantile Krabbe presents around 4 months and progresses rapidly to death at a mean of about 18 months. CLN2 progresses to severe disability with most children wheelchair-bound in late childhood, death at a mean of about 12 years, and survival beyond adolescence rare. Within individual diseases, severity is typically stratified by age of onset and CNS involvement. Examples: Tay-Sachs is divided into infantile, juvenile-onset and adult-onset forms. MPS I is graded as Hurler (MPS I H, severe with neurodegeneration), Hurler-Scheie (MPS I H/S, intermediate, severe somatic disease without major neurologic decline), and Scheie (MPS I S, later-onset without neurologic involvement). Gaucher disease is classed as type 1 (nonneuronopathic), type 2 (acute severe CNS), and type 3 (variable subacute/chronic CNS). Niemann-Pick distinguishes type A (early-onset, progressive CNS), type B (later, variable, with an A/B variant having slowly progressive CNS involvement), and the separate type C. LALD ranges from infantile-onset (Wolman) to childhood/adult-onset (cholesterol ester storage disease). Pompe and Krabbe are divided into early/infantile and later-onset variants.

Lysozyme Amyloidosis (ALys) — ALys amyloidosis, Hereditary lysozyme amyloidosis AL (immunoglobulin light-chain) amyloidosis Other hereditary amyloidoses (fibrinogen, apolipoprotein A-I, transthyretin) AA amyloidosis Other causes of gastrointestinal bleeding or hepatosplenomegaly Sjögren syndrome for the sicca features Other causes of nephrotic syndrome Biopsy of affected tissue (gut, liver or kidney) with Congo red staining Amyloid typing by mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry LYZ gene sequencing Cross-sectional imaging of the liver and spleen to assess size and rupture risk Renal function and quantified proteinuria Full blood count and clotting studies given the bleeding risk Serum free light chains and immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis ALys is a rare autosomal dominant amyloidosis caused by mutations in the lysozyme gene (LYZ). It is characteristically multi-visceral, with prominent involvement of the kidney, liver, spleen and gastrointestinal tract. Spontaneous and potentially life-threatening haemorrhage is a hallmark, with reports of hepatic and splenic rupture and gastrointestinal bleeding. Sicca symptoms of dry eyes and mouth and cutaneous petechiae are recognised features. Renal involvement is common but often slowly progressive, with nephrotic syndrome developing over years. Cardiac and neurological involvement are typically mild or absent, which helps distinguish ALys from ATTR. Diagnosis rests on tissue typing and LYZ sequencing; there is no specific antifibril therapy, so management is supportive and directed at complications. Acute abdominal pain with haemodynamic compromise suggesting hepatic or splenic rupture Gastrointestinal haemorrhage Rapidly enlarging liver or spleen Progressive proteinuria and renal decline Mistyping as AL amyloidosis and exposing patients to chemotherapy Underestimating the risk of spontaneous organ rupture Attributing sicca symptoms to Sjögren syndrome without considering amyloid Relying on single-organ transplantation to remove the amyloid source Lysozyme is a bacteriolytic enzyme secreted by macrophages, Paneth cells and various epithelia. Amyloidogenic variants destabilise the folded protein, promoting partial unfolding, aggregation and deposition of lysozyme-derived amyloid fibrils in the extracellular matrix of viscera. Deposition is widespread but shows particular avidity for the gastrointestinal tract, liver, spleen and kidney, where infiltration weakens tissue integrity and predisposes to haemorrhage and organ dysfunction. Because lysozyme is produced by many cell types, the amyloid source cannot be removed by transplantation of a single organ, and deposition continues over decades in a slowly progressive fashion. The disorder is generally slowly progressive, with survival often measured in decades, but life-threatening visceral haemorrhage from organ rupture is the principal cause of acute mortality.

treatment is symptomatic and multidisciplinary Progressive dysphagia with aspiration risk Severe spasticity or dystonia impairing mobility and safety Respiratory or bulbar decline in advanced disease Attributing the diverse features to separate diagnoses rather than recognising the SCA3 spectrum Assuming a subtype without gene-specific confirmation Missing the characteristic bulging eyes and faciolingual fasciculations as diagnostic clues Neglecting anticipation and genetic counselling for at-risk relatives Machado-Joseph disease (SCA3) is a polyglutamine disorder caused by expansion of the CAG repeat in the ATXN3 gene. Ataxin-3 normally functions as a deubiquitinating enzyme involved in protein quality control; the expanded polyglutamine tract confers a toxic gain of function, promoting misfolding, aggregation, and formation of neuronal intranuclear inclusions that impair the ubiquitin-proteasome system and cellular homeostasis. Neurodegeneration affects the cerebellum and its connections, brainstem and cranial nerve nuclei, basal ganglia, spinal motor and sensory pathways, and peripheral nerves, accounting for the wide phenotypic range. Repeat length correlates inversely with age at onset, underlying anticipation. The disease is progressive over one to several decades with steadily accumulating disability; life expectancy is reduced, usually as a consequence of bulbar dysfunction and respiratory complications, although progression rate varies with subtype.

Macrocephaly-capillary malformation — Macrocephaly-capillary malformation (M-CM), Megalencephaly-capillary malformation (MCAP), Macrocephaly-cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita Other PROS conditions such as CLOVES and Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome Sturge-Weber syndrome Proteus syndrome Sotos syndrome and other overgrowth syndromes Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome Isolated cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita Brain MRI for megalencephaly, polymicrogyria, ventriculomegaly and tonsillar herniation Serial head circumference and growth measurements Echocardiography and arrhythmia screening Skeletal assessment for asymmetry and limb-length discrepancy PIK3CA mutation testing on affected tissue, since blood may be mutation-negative in mosaic disease Developmental and neurological assessment A congenital overgrowth syndrome within the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS). Combines macrocephaly or megalencephaly with a midline facial capillary malformation and often reticulate or patchy capillary staining of the trunk and limbs. Caused by somatic mosaic activating PIK3CA mutations. Additional features include body asymmetry (hemihypertrophy), syndactyly or polydactyly, connective-tissue laxity, developmental delay and hypotonia. Neuroimaging may show megalencephaly, ventriculomegaly, polymicrogyria and cerebellar tonsillar herniation. There is a risk of progressive hydrocephalus and a Chiari-like malformation from ongoing brain overgrowth. Cardiac arrhythmia has been reported and warrants baseline and periodic assessment. Requires multidisciplinary neurodevelopmental, orthopaedic and neurosurgical follow-up. Signs of raised intracranial pressure or progressive hydrocephalus Symptomatic Chiari-like malformation Cardiac arrhythmia Significant or progressive limb-length discrepancy and asymmetry Seizures Testing blood rather than affected tissue for the mosaic PIK3CA mutation and being falsely reassured by a negative result. Attributing macrocephaly to a benign familial cause and missing megalencephaly. Overlooking an evolving Chiari-like malformation or hydrocephalus. Failing to arrange multidisciplinary developmental support. Macrocephaly-capillary malformation is one of the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum disorders, arising from postzygotic somatic mosaic activating mutations in PIK3CA that constitutively activate the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway and drive excessive cellular growth and proliferation in affected tissues. The mosaic distribution explains the segmental and asymmetric overgrowth, capillary malformations and brain overgrowth (megalencephaly) with cortical malformations such as polymicrogyria. Progressive brain and skull growth can secondarily cause ventriculomegaly, hydrocephalus and cerebellar tonsillar ectopia. The condition is associated with variable developmental delay and neurological complications; prognosis depends on the severity of the brain malformation and overgrowth, and lifelong multidisciplinary surveillance is required.

Macrophage Activation Syndrome — MAS, secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, secondary HLH Primary (familial) haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis Sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation Flare of the underlying rheumatic disease Systemic infection (EBV and other viruses, intracellular pathogens) Malignancy, particularly lymphoma or leukaemia Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) Serum ferritin (very high levels are characteristic and trended for response) Full blood count to detect evolving cytopenias Fibrinogen, D-dimer, and full coagulation profile Fasting triglycerides Liver function tests and lactate dehydrogenase Soluble interleukin-2 receptor (soluble CD25) and natural killer cell function where available Bone marrow aspirate to look for haemophagocytosis when the diagnosis is uncertain A life-threatening hyperinflammatory state, considered a form of secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, characterised by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and T cells. It most commonly complicates rheumatic conditions, especially systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, but can be triggered by infection or malignancy. Suspect it when a child with an underlying inflammatory disease develops persistent high fever, worsening general condition, and hepatosplenomegaly. A characteristic and counterintuitive clue is falling blood counts (cytopenias) and a paradoxically falling or normalising ESR despite active inflammation. Markedly elevated ferritin is a hallmark laboratory feature and useful for both suspicion and monitoring. Other typical findings include high triglycerides, low fibrinogen, deranged liver function, and coagulopathy, sometimes with overt bleeding. Bone marrow examination may show haemophagocytosis, but a normal marrow does not exclude the diagnosis and treatment should not be delayed for it. This is a medical emergency requiring rapid immunosuppression to interrupt the cytokine storm before multi-organ failure develops. Rapidly progressive multi-organ dysfunction from cytokine storm (EMERGENCY) Persistent high fever with deteriorating clinical state Falling cell counts across multiple lineages Falling fibrinogen with rising ferritin and clinical bleeding Neurological involvement: seizures, altered consciousness Progression toward disseminated intravascular coagulation or shock Being falsely reassured by a falling or normal ESR, which can accompany the low fibrinogen of MAS Interpreting the picture solely as a disease flare or sepsis and delaying specific treatment Waiting for bone marrow confirmation of haemophagocytosis before starting therapy Underappreciating how quickly the condition can progress to coagulopathy and organ failure Not monitoring ferritin and blood counts closely to track response MAS results from defective downregulation of the immune response, with impaired cytotoxic function of natural killer cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes. This allows persistent activation and proliferation of T cells and well-differentiated macrophages (histiocytes), which phagocytose blood cells and release a flood of pro-inflammatory cytokines. This cytokine storm produces sustained fever, cytopenias from marrow phagocytosis and suppression, hepatic dysfunction, coagulopathy resembling disseminated intravascular coagulation, and progressive multi-organ damage. MAS carries significant mortality if unrecognised, but early aggressive immunosuppression can be life-saving and many children recover; outcome depends on prompt diagnosis, control of the trigger, and reversal of organ dysfunction before it becomes irreversible.

the tumour and controlled prolactin Failing to exclude drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia and macroprolactinaemia before imaging Overlooking coexisting hypopituitarism, particularly cortisol deficiency, before treatment A macroprolactinoma is a benign monoclonal tumour of pituitary lactotroph cells that autonomously secretes prolactin. High circulating prolactin suppresses hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone pulsatility, lowering LH and FSH and causing hypogonadism and galactorrhoea. As the tumour enlarges beyond the sella it compresses adjacent structures, causing headache, optic chiasm compression with visual field defects, and, by disrupting the pituitary stalk or gland, hypopituitarism. Because prolactin secretion is under dominant inhibitory dopaminergic control, dopamine agonists both suppress hormone output and reduce tumour bulk. Most macroprolactinomas respond well to dopamine agonists with normalisation of prolactin, restoration of gonadal function and significant tumour shrinkage; long-term outcome is generally favourable, though some tumours are resistant or require surgery, and lifelong monitoring is usual.

Macular amyloidosis — macular cutaneous amyloidosis, macular amyloidosis Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation Notalgia paraesthetica Ashy dermatosis / erythema dyschromicum perstans Lichen amyloidosis birefringence Management focuses on reducing friction and itch by stopping vigorous rubbing and using topical corticosteroids, keratolytics, and phototherapy, generally with modest results Atypical overlap with notalgia paraesthetica Assuming a link to systemic amyloidosis, which does not apply Macular amyloidosis, like the lichen form, involves deposition of keratin-derived amyloid in the papillary dermis. Repeated friction and scratching are believed to injure basal keratinocytes, which degenerate and release cytokeratin that is transformed into amyloid. Associated release of melanin into the dermis (pigment incontinence) accounts for the grey-brown discolouration and the rippled appearance. Because the amyloid originates from epidermal keratin rather than immunoglobulin, the process stays localised to the skin and carries no systemic risk, while ongoing friction sustains and extends the deposits. Benign and chronic; there is no systemic risk, but the pigmentation is persistent and often only partly responsive to treatment, tending to recur while friction continues.

features suggesting an underlying mucopolysaccharidosis rather than isolated corneal disease Corneal thinning increasing the risk of perforation or surgical complication Endothelial dysfunction contributing to oedema and graft failure risk Assuming autosomal dominant inheritance and missing the recessive pattern and family risk Failing to exclude systemic mucopolysaccharidosis when stromal clouding is present Underestimating corneal thinning and endothelial involvement before surgery Mistaking diffuse haze for scarring from previous inflammation Macular corneal dystrophy is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CHST6 gene encoding a corneal N-acetylglucosamine-6-O-sulfotransferase. Defective sulfation of keratan sulfate leads to accumulation of abnormal, poorly soluble glycosaminoglycan within keratocytes, the extracellular stroma, and the endothelium. This deposition, together with diffuse clouding of the intervening stroma, spreads from limbus to limbus and through the full corneal thickness, progressively degrading transparency. Because the defect involves a systemic sulfation pathway that is clinically confined to the cornea, deposits accumulate throughout the stroma rather than in discrete islands. Macular dystrophy tends to progress earlier and more severely than other stromal dystrophies, often requiring keratoplasty by early adulthood. Grafts can restore useful vision, though recurrence in the graft is possible over time.

hole with signs of retinal detachment requiring urgent surgical assessment Sudden worsening or new peripheral field loss suggesting an associated detachment Bilateral or fellow-eye symptoms indicating risk to the only good eye Traumatic hole with other posterior segment injury Confusing a pseudohole or lamellar hole with a full-thickness hole without OCT confirmation Delaying referral so that a small, highly repairable hole enlarges and chronifies Overlooking a coexisting retinal detachment in a myopic eye Setting unrealistic expectations for visual recovery in long-standing holes An idiopathic full-thickness macular hole develops when tangential and anteroposterior traction from the perifoveal vitreous acts on the fovea during posterior vitreous detachment. This traction elevates and then dehisces the foveal tissue, creating a full-thickness defect with surrounding cuff of subretinal fluid and cystic change. Progressive stages run from foveal detachment and pseudocyst through to an established round hole. Secondary holes may follow blunt trauma or the mechanical stresses of high myopia, where posterior staphyloma adds traction. Modern vitrectomy with membrane peeling closes the large majority of idiopathic holes, and visual improvement is best when the hole is small and of short duration; large, chronic, or myopic holes have lower closure rates and more limited recovery.

macular telangiectasia — MacTel, idiopathic juxtafoveal telangiectasia, parafoveal telangiectasia Diabetic maculopathy with parafoveal microaneurysms Branch retinal vein occlusion with macular telangiectasia Coats disease and other exudative retinal telangiectasias Age-related macular degeneration with neovascularisation Radiation retinopathy Adult-onset foveomacular vitelliform dystrophy Macular hole or pseudohole causing metamorphopsia Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography for retinal cavitation and ellipsoid zone integrity Fluorescein angiography demonstrating deep temporal parafoveal telangiectasia and late leakage Optical coherence tomography angiography to map deep capillary plexus abnormalities and detect neovascularisation Fundus autofluorescence showing loss of the normal foveal masking by macular pigment Macular pigment optical density measurement Blue-light or confocal imaging of refractile crystalline deposits Microperimetry to quantify parafoveal scotomata Type 2 (idiopathic perifoveal) is by far the most common form, presenting in middle age with gradual bilateral blurring, metamorphopsia and difficulty reading despite a relatively preserved distance acuity early on. The perifoveal telangiectatic vessels are frequently subtle on ophthalmoscopy; the diagnosis often rests on characteristic optical coherence tomography and fluorescein angiographic findings rather than the visible fundus appearance. A loss of retinal transparency with a greyish sheen temporal to the fovea, right-angled venules and refractile crystalline deposits at the inner retinal surface are classic type 2 signs. Optical coherence tomography shows hyporeflective inner and outer retinal cavities and, importantly, disruption of the ellipsoid zone without correspondingly large fluid accumulation. Depletion of the parafoveal Muller cells and macular pigment is a central feature, and macular pigment optical density imaging can reveal a characteristic parafoveal loss. Fluorescein angiography demonstrates deep telangiectatic capillaries that leak in the late phase, typically temporal to the fovea, but this leakage does not respond to the anti-angiogenic or laser strategies used for other exudative maculopathies. Type 2 is subdivided into a non-proliferative stage and a sight-threatening proliferative stage in which subretinal neovascularisation grows from the deep retinal circulation. Type 1 (aneurysmal telangiectasia) is usually unilateral, males predominate, and it behaves more like a congenital retinal vascular anomaly with exudation akin to Coats disease. New or worsening metamorphopsia with subretinal fluid suggesting progression to the proliferative neovascular stage Sudden central visual loss from subretinal haemorrhage Development of a full-thickness macular hole Rapidly enlarging pigment plaque or disciform scar involving fixation Marked exudation or a retinal detachment in suspected type 1 (aneurysmal) disease Mistaking the subtle telangiectasia and leakage for diabetic maculopathy and applying focal laser or anti-angiogenic injections that are ineffective in non-proliferative disease. Interpreting late fluorescein leakage as an indication for treatment when it does not correlate with treatable exudation in type 2. Overlooking the diagnosis when distance acuity is preserved and the fundus appears near-normal, delaying recognition of the ellipsoid zone loss on optical coherence tomography. Failing to distinguish the neurodegenerative type 2 from the vascular malformation type 1, which have different natural histories and management. Attributing reading difficulty and metamorphopsia to early cataract or refractive error rather than examining the macula in detail. Macular telangiectasia type 2 is now understood primarily as a neurodegenerative disorder of the macula in which the Muller glial cells, which maintain retinal architecture and the blood-retinal barrier and sequester macular pigment, are progressively depleted in the parafoveal region. Loss of these glial cells produces retinal cavitation, photoreceptor (ellipsoid zone) disruption and secondary abnormalities of the deep retinal capillary network that manifest as the visible telangiectasia; the vascular changes are therefore considered a consequence rather than the primary event. Impaired retinal handling of serine and glycine metabolism has been implicated, and reduced circulating serine with accumulation of neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids is associated with the condition. In the proliferative stage, ischaemia and glial loss permit neovascular complexes to invade from the deep capillary plexus into the subretinal space, causing haemorrhage, exudation and disciform scarring. Type 1 disease, by contrast, reflects a developmental telangiectatic and aneurysmal malformation of the retinal capillaries with breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier and lipid exudation. Non-proliferative type 2 typically causes slow, progressive parafoveal visual decline over years with relatively preserved distance acuity until late, whereas the proliferative stage can cause rapid central loss from neovascular haemorrhage and scarring. Anti-angiogenic therapy is reserved for the proliferative neovascular stage and does not benefit the non-proliferative leakage; overall central vision often remains functional for reading tasks for a prolonged period.

Madarosis — eyelash loss, eyebrow and eyelash loss Chronic blepharitis Alopecia areata or other alopecias Hypothyroidism Eyelid malignancy (for example basal or sebaceous cell carcinoma) Trichotillomania Leprosy (in endemic settings) Examination of the lid margin, skin and pattern of hair loss Assessment for scarring versus non-scarring loss Thyroid function tests where indicated Biopsy of any suspicious lid margin lesion Investigation for systemic or dermatological causes as directed by the history Loss of eyelashes, and sometimes eyebrows, which is a sign rather than a disease in itself Causes are broad: local lid disease, dermatological conditions, systemic disease, drugs, trauma and psychiatric causes Chronic blepharitis is a common local cause, while alopecia areata and cicatricial alopecias affect the follicles Loss of the lateral third of the eyebrows is a classic sign of hypothyroidism and of leprosy Trichotillomania and factitious causes should be considered, especially with irregular patchy loss A lid margin lesion with associated madarosis raises concern for eyelid malignancy A localised lid margin lesion with lash loss suggesting malignancy Scarring loss indicating follicle destruction Systemic features suggesting endocrine or infiltrative disease Rapidly progressive or asymmetric loss Overlooking an eyelid malignancy causing localised lash loss Missing hypothyroidism with lateral eyebrow loss Not distinguishing scarring from non-scarring loss Failing to consider trichotillomania Madarosis results from any process that damages or destroys the eyelash (and eyebrow) follicles or disrupts the hair cycle. Non-scarring loss occurs with conditions such as alopecia areata, telogen effluvium, hypothyroidism and drug effects, where follicles are preserved and regrowth is possible. Scarring (cicatricial) loss follows chronic inflammation, cicatrising skin disease or infiltrating eyelid tumours that destroy the follicles, causing permanent loss. Identifying whether the loss is scarring or non-scarring guides the search for cause and the likelihood of regrowth. Prognosis depends on the cause: non-scarring loss often recovers when the underlying condition is treated, whereas scarring loss and tumour-related loss are permanent.

underlying skeletal dysplasia that warrants genetic evaluation Mistaking early Madelung deformity for a simple wrist sprain and missing its progression Failing to release the Vickers ligament, allowing continued tethering after bony surgery Not recognising the association with SHOX-related short stature (dyschondrosteosis) Operating on skeletally immature bone without addressing the physeal tether Madelung deformity results from a localised dysplasia and premature growth arrest of the volar-ulnar quadrant of the distal radial physis. Continued growth of the dorsal-radial portion of the physis, combined with tethering by a thick anomalous volar ligament (Vickers ligament) running from the radius to the lunate, produces progressive volar and ulnar angulation of the distal radial joint surface. Relative overgrowth of the ulna leads to dorsal ulnar prominence and carpal triangulation. Many cases are genetically determined through SHOX haploinsufficiency, as seen in Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis, which links the wrist deformity to a wider skeletal dysplasia. Progression tends to occur during skeletal growth and then stabilises at maturity; early ligament release with physiolysis can halt progression in the growing child, while corrective osteotomy in the mature wrist reliably improves pain and appearance, although some loss of rotation may persist.

Madelung disease (multiple symmetric lipomatosis) — multiple symmetric lipomatosis, MSL, Launois-Bensaude syndrome, benign symmetric lipomatosis Cushing syndrome (dorsocervical and supraclavicular fat pads) Familial multiple lipomatosis (discrete encapsulated lipomas) Obesity with prominent cervical fat Liposarcoma or other soft-tissue tumour Lymphoma or other neck/mediastinal mass Dercum disease (adiposis dolorosa) Angiolipomatosis CT or MRI of the neck and thorax to map fat deposits and assess compression Liver function tests and markers reflecting chronic alcohol use Fasting glucose/HbA1c and lipid profile for associated metabolic disturbance Nerve conduction studies if neuropathy is suspected Evaluation for mitochondrial disease where clinically indicated Cortisol testing to exclude Cushing syndrome when the picture is ambiguous Characterised by symmetric, non-encapsulated masses of adipose tissue around the neck, shoulders, and upper trunk, producing a 'horse-collar' or pseudoathletic appearance Predominantly affects middle-aged men and is strongly associated with chronic heavy alcohol use Distinct from lipodystrophy in that fat accumulates abnormally rather than being lost, though the lower limbs may appear relatively fat-depleted Some cases are linked to mitochondrial dysfunction (including MERRF-associated mutations), suggesting impaired brown-fat metabolism The accumulating tissue resembles brown adipose tissue with defective catecholamine-driven lipolysis Neck and mediastinal fat deposition can cause compressive symptoms such as dysphagia, dyspnoea, or airway compromise An associated peripheral or autonomic neuropathy is common, and metabolic disturbances including insulin resistance may coexist Diagnosis rests on the characteristic symmetric fat distribution and imaging; alcohol cessation is advised and debulking surgery is used for compression or cosmesis Airway compromise, stridor, or dyspnoea from cervical/mediastinal fat Progressive dysphagia from oesophageal compression Rapid growth or atypical features raising concern for malignancy Superior vena cava or vascular compression Mistaking the fat distribution for Cushing syndrome or simple obesity Overlooking airway or oesophageal compression from neck deposits Failing to recognise the strong association with chronic alcohol use Assuming the masses are discrete encapsulated lipomas amenable to simple excision Missing an associated neuropathy or mitochondrial disorder Madelung disease is a disorder of abnormal proliferation and accumulation of adipose tissue in a symmetric distribution around the neck, nape, shoulders, and upper trunk. The affected fat has features of brown adipose tissue with impaired catecholamine-stimulated lipolysis, so it expands unchecked rather than being mobilised. Mitochondrial dysfunction, including mutations associated with MERRF and heavy alcohol exposure, is implicated in disrupting normal adipocyte metabolism. Unlike the lipodystrophies, the primary problem is pathological fat gain in specific depots; the growing masses are cosmetically disfiguring and can compress the airway, oesophagus, and vascular structures, while an associated neuropathy and metabolic disturbance may accompany the condition. Madelung disease is benign but often progressive and disfiguring; alcohol cessation may slow growth, and surgical debulking relieves compression and improves appearance, though recurrence is common and any associated neuropathy or metabolic disease persists.

suggesting transformation to chondrosarcoma Neurological symptoms that may indicate an associated intracranial tumour A rapidly enlarging or bleeding vascular lesion Systemic features suggesting an associated visceral neoplasm Managing it as simple enchondromatosis and neglecting surveillance for the broader malignancy risk Giving inherited recurrence-risk counselling for what is a sporadic mosaic disorder Overlooking the vascular lesions that define the syndrome and its higher risk Failing to investigate new neurological or systemic symptoms for associated neoplasms Maffucci syndrome shares its origin with Ollier disease in post-zygotic somatic mosaic gain-of-function variants of IDH1 or IDH2. The broader mutational burden is thought to underlie the higher risk of malignant transformation and of non-skeletal tumours compared with Ollier disease. Morbidity arises from skeletal deformity, fractures and vascular lesions, but the defining concern is a substantially increased lifetime risk of malignancy, both chondrosarcoma and other tumours, mandating lifelong multi-system surveillance.
