vision Growth failure and anaemia from renal disease Cerebellar signs indicating central nervous system involvement Attributing early visual loss to isolated retinal disease and missing the progressive nephropathy Overlooking subtle cone-shaped epiphyses on hand radiographs Failing to monitor renal concentrating ability so that nephronophthisis is recognised late Not distinguishing it from other nephronophthisis-related ciliopathies without genetic testing Mainzer-Saldino syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in intraflagellar transport genes, particularly IFT140 and IFT172, whose products carry cargo along the primary cilium. Impaired ciliary transport disturbs the specialised sensory cilia of retinal photoreceptors, the primary cilia of renal tubular epithelium and the signalling that governs epiphyseal cartilage, producing the retinal dystrophy, nephronophthisis and cone-shaped phalangeal epiphyses respectively. The same ciliary dependence in the cerebellum accounts for the ataxia seen in some individuals. The condition therefore sits within the wider group of nephronophthisis-related ciliopathies, sharing mechanisms with Senior-Loken and Jeune syndromes while showing milder skeletal change than the short-rib thoracic dysplasias. Renal failure typically develops during childhood or adolescence and requires dialysis or transplantation, while visual loss from retinal dystrophy is variable but may be severe; overall outlook is largely determined by the renal course.

Maisonneuve fracture — proximal fibular fracture with syndesmotic injury, Maisonneuve ankle injury, high fibular fracture with mortise instability Isolated ankle fracture (Weber A or B pattern) Isolated medial malleolus fracture Isolated syndesmotic (high ankle) sprain Proximal fibular fracture from direct trauma Weber C ankle fracture Common peroneal nerve injury Full-length tibia and fibula radiographs in addition to a dedicated ankle series Ankle mortise view assessing the medial clear space for widening Stress or weight-bearing views to demonstrate syndesmotic instability CT to evaluate the adequacy of syndesmotic reduction Examination and documentation of common peroneal nerve function A proximal fibular fracture combined with disruption of the interosseous membrane and syndesmosis and a medial ankle injury (either a medial malleolus fracture or a deltoid ligament rupture) An external-rotation force drives energy up the interosseous membrane, exiting proximally in the fibula The proximal fibula must be palpated in every ankle injury; proximal tenderness or a medial injury with a widened mortise mandates imaging of the whole leg The ankle mortise may be widened at the medial clear space despite an apparently isolated medial malleolar injury Treatment focuses on restoring the mortise and stabilising the syndesmosis with a screw or suture-button construct; the proximal fibular fracture itself is usually not fixed The injury is easily missed when the proximal fibula is neither examined nor imaged Assess and document common peroneal nerve function at the fibular neck Common peroneal nerve injury at the fibular neck Unrecognised syndesmotic instability A widened mortise indicating an unstable ankle Open injury requiring urgent management Failing to examine and image the proximal fibula in an ankle injury Treating an apparently isolated medial malleolus fracture without recognising syndesmotic instability Malreduction of the syndesmosis during fixation Overlooking a common peroneal nerve injury A pronation-external rotation force at the ankle is transmitted proximally through the interosseous membrane. As the talus externally rotates, the syndesmosis and interosseous membrane tear and the energy exits as a fracture of the proximal fibula, while the medial restraint fails either as a deltoid ligament rupture or a medial malleolus fracture. The result is an unstable ankle mortise despite an intact distal fibula, and the key to a good outcome is anatomical reduction of the syndesmosis rather than the proximal fracture. With anatomical restoration of the mortise and adequate syndesmotic fixation the outcome is generally good; malreduction of the syndesmosis is the strongest predictor of pain and post-traumatic arthritis.

Majeed syndrome — chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis with congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia, LPIN2 deficiency, LPIN2, lipin-2 associated autoinflammation Sporadic chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO) DIRA Infective osteomyelitis Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia of other cause Sweet syndrome from other triggers SAPHO syndrome Genetic testing for LPIN2 mutations Radiographs and MRI for multifocal osteomyelitis and periosteal reaction Full blood count and blood film showing microcytic dyserythropoietic anaemia Bone marrow examination demonstrating dyserythropoiesis Acute-phase reactants during flares Skin biopsy of neutrophilic dermatosis lesions A recessive autoinflammatory disease caused by loss-of-function mutations in LPIN2, encoding the lipid-regulating enzyme lipin-2 Classic triad is chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia, and a neutrophilic dermatosis Bone disease begins in early childhood with recurrent painful, sterile inflammatory bone lesions and periosteal reaction The anaemia is microcytic and dyserythropoietic, sometimes requiring transfusion, and reflects abnormal red cell production Skin involvement typically resembles Sweet syndrome (neutrophilic dermatosis) or pustulosis Growth impairment and recurrent fevers accompany the bone and marrow disease Interleukin-1 blockade is generally more effective than tumour necrosis factor inhibition and can control the inflammatory features Severe anaemia requiring transfusion support Extensive bone involvement causing deformity or growth arrest Failure to thrive with persistent systemic inflammation Development of complications from chronic transfusion such as iron overload Treating recurrent bone lesions as infective osteomyelitis with prolonged antibiotics Overlooking the associated anaemia as unrelated iron deficiency Choosing tumour necrosis factor inhibition when interleukin-1 blockade is generally more effective Failing to test for LPIN2 in a child with CRMO and unexplained anaemia Majeed syndrome results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in LPIN2, which encodes lipin-2, an enzyme involved in lipid metabolism and control of inflammation. Deficiency of lipin-2 dysregulates lipid handling in myeloid cells and enhances inflammasome activation, leading to excess interleukin-1 production. This drives sterile neutrophilic inflammation in bone (chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis) and skin, while associated effects on erythropoiesis produce a congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia. The central role of interleukin-1 explains the therapeutic benefit of IL-1 blockade. Majeed syndrome is a chronic disease of childhood; with interleukin-1 blockade the inflammatory bone and skin disease can be well controlled, though anaemia and growth effects may persist and require additional support.

Major depressive disorder — MDD, major depression, clinical depression, unipolar depression Bipolar disorder in a depressive phase Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) Adjustment disorder with depressed mood Grief and bereavement reactions Hypothyroidism and other endocrine or metabolic disorders Substance-induced or medication-induced mood disorder Depression in the context of a neurocognitive disorder (pseudodementia) Structured suicide risk assessment Standardised symptom rating scales to gauge severity and track response Thyroid function testing Full blood count and metabolic panel to exclude anaemia and other medical contributors Vitamin B12 and folate where clinically indicated Substance use screening Diagnosis requires a sustained period (at least around two weeks) of either persistently low mood or loss of interest/pleasure, together with several additional symptoms causing significant distress or functional impairment Associated features commonly include disturbed sleep, appetite or weight change, fatigue, poor concentration, psychomotor slowing or agitation, feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, and recurrent thoughts of death Always screen actively for suicidal ideation, intent, and plan, and ask about prior attempts and access to means Screen for a past manic or hypomanic episode before starting an antidepressant, because an unrecognised bipolar diathesis can be destabilised Exclude medical and substance-related contributors such as hypothyroidism, anaemia, and medication effects before attributing symptoms solely to a primary mood disorder Management principles combine evidence-based psychotherapy (such as cognitive behavioural therapy or interpersonal therapy) with antidepressant pharmacotherapy, typically first-line SSRIs, chosen by side-effect profile and comorbidity Antidepressant benefit is often delayed by several weeks, adherence should be reinforced, and treatment is generally continued well beyond symptom remission to reduce relapse Severe, psychotic, treatment-resistant, or high-suicide-risk presentations may warrant combination pharmacotherapy, augmentation, or electroconvulsive therapy Active suicidal ideation with plan, intent, or access to means Psychotic features such as mood-congruent delusions or hallucinations Profound self-neglect, refusal of food or fluids, or catatonia Rapid deterioration or emerging manic symptoms after starting an antidepressant Starting an antidepressant without screening for a prior manic or hypomanic episode Underestimating suicide risk or failing to reassess it during treatment Stopping antidepressants too early once mood improves, increasing relapse risk Attributing symptoms to depression while missing an underlying medical cause such as hypothyroidism Judging non-response before an adequate dose and duration of treatment Major depressive disorder is understood as a multifactorial condition arising from interactions among genetic vulnerability, dysregulation of monoamine neurotransmission (serotonin, noradrenaline, and dopamine), and disturbance of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis stress responses. Contemporary models also emphasise impaired neuroplasticity and neurotrophic signalling, altered function in limbic and prefrontal circuits, and the role of chronic stress and adverse life events acting on a predisposed individual. Major depressive disorder is frequently recurrent; many patients respond to treatment but relapse risk rises with each subsequent episode and with residual symptoms. Prognosis is generally better with early treatment, good adherence, and psychosocial support, and worse with comorbid substance use, chronic medical illness, and untreated recurrent episodes.

Mal de debarquement syndrome — MdDS, disembarkment syndrome, sickness of disembarkment Vestibular migraine Persistent postural-perceptual dizziness Peripheral vestibular disorders (e.g. vestibular neuritis, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo) Central neurological causes of imbalance Ordinary motion sickness or transient post-voyage unsteadiness Anxiety-related dizziness Detailed clinical history linking onset to a period of passive motion Neurological and vestibular examination to exclude central and peripheral disease Audiometry and vestibular function testing where a peripheral cause is suspected Brain imaging (MRI) if focal neurological features or atypical presentation Assessment for migraine and psychological contributors Characterised by a persistent sensation of rocking, swaying, or bobbing that continues after returning to stable ground following passive motion, most often a sea voyage or long flight The perceived self-motion is typically relieved, at least temporarily, by re-exposure to passive motion such as driving a car Unlike motion sickness, there is usually no nausea or vertigo, and the dominant complaint is the internal sense of movement Diagnosis is clinical and requires exclusion of vestibular, neurological, and other causes of imbalance Symptoms lasting only days after travel are common and self-limiting; the syndrome proper is diagnosed when the rocking persists for weeks or longer Vestibular rehabilitation and habituation strategies are central to management, and stress or fatigue tends to aggravate symptoms It is thought to reflect a failure of the brain to readapt from the motion-adapted state back to a stable environment Focal neurological signs suggesting a central lesion True rotational vertigo, hearing loss, or tinnitus pointing to a vestibular disorder Progressive or asymmetric symptoms atypical for MdDS Severe functional impairment or associated mood disturbance Confusing MdDS with ordinary motion sickness or peripheral vertigo Failing to note the characteristic relief with re-exposure to motion Missing vestibular migraine or persistent postural-perceptual dizziness as alternatives Under-recognising the impact of stress, fatigue, and anxiety on symptoms Mal de debarquement syndrome is understood as a disorder of central vestibular adaptation. During sustained passive motion the brain adapts its internal model of self-motion and postural control; on return to a stable environment this adaptation normally reverses quickly, but in MdDS the maladaptive state persists, so the person continues to perceive rocking or swaying. Re-exposure to motion transiently restores the adapted state and eases symptoms, which supports a central sensory reweighting mechanism rather than peripheral vestibular dysfunction. Many cases that follow travel resolve spontaneously within days to weeks, but a proportion become persistent and can wax and wane over months to years; vestibular rehabilitation and habituation help, though a subset have a chronic, relapsing course.

Mal de Meleda — keratosis palmoplantaris transgrediens of Siemens, Meleda disease, SLURP1 Other diffuse hereditary palmoplantar keratodermas (e.g. Vörner/Unna-Thost) Loricrin keratoderma (Vohwinkel variant) Olmsted syndrome Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome Huriez syndrome Acquired keratoderma from inflammatory or infective causes Molecular genetic testing of SLURP1 Skin biopsy showing orthohyperkeratosis with acanthosis Mycological and bacterial swabs for secondary infection Clinical examination for pseudo-ainhum and digital constriction Nail assessment for associated dystrophy Family history and pedigree analysis A rare autosomal recessive transgredient palmoplantar keratoderma originally described on the Adriatic island of Mljet (Meleda) Caused by biallelic variants in SLURP1, which encodes a secreted lymphocyte antigen-6 protein modulating cholinergic signalling and keratinocyte differentiation The keratoderma extends beyond the palms and soles onto the dorsa of the hands and feet (the transgredient pattern), often with a well-demarcated erythematous border Progressive constricting bands (pseudo-ainhum) can develop around digits and may lead to autoamputation Associated features include hyperhidrosis with malodour, secondary fungal and bacterial infection, nail changes and perioral erythema Diagnosis is clinical, supported by the family history and SLURP1 molecular testing Management is supportive with keratolytics, emollients, oral retinoids in severe disease, meticulous foot care and treatment of secondary infection Constricting fibrous bands (pseudo-ainhum) risking digital autoamputation Deep secondary infection or cellulitis of macerated acral skin Rapidly progressive or asymmetrical thickening raising concern for malignant change Severe functional impairment of hands or feet Missing the transgredient spread onto dorsal skin that distinguishes it from common diffuse keratodermas Overlooking early pseudo-ainhum that is amenable to intervention before autoamputation Failing to treat the secondary fungal and bacterial colonisation that worsens odour and maceration Not offering genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder Mal de Meleda is caused by loss-of-function variants in SLURP1, encoding secreted Ly-6/uPAR-related protein 1, which acts on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors to regulate keratinocyte proliferation, differentiation and apoptosis and to modulate skin inflammation. Deficiency disturbs the balance of epidermal proliferation and terminal differentiation in acral skin, producing a thick, diffuse transgredient keratoderma. Accompanying hyperhidrosis and barrier disruption predispose to maceration, malodour and secondary infection, while chronic inflammation and fibrous constriction can create pseudo-ainhum. The keratoderma is lifelong and tends to progress through childhood; with diligent skin and foot care most patients maintain function, but pseudo-ainhum, recurrent infection and disability can complicate severe cases.

Malakoplakia — malacoplakia, Michaelis-Gutmann body disease, von Hansemann histiocyte disease Genitourinary or gastrointestinal malignancy Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis Tuberculosis or other chronic granulomatous infection Inflammatory pseudotumour Other chronic inflammatory or infective plaques Whipple disease when the gut is involved Biopsy for histology demonstrating von Hansemann macrophages and Michaelis-Gutmann bodies Special stains (von Kossa for calcium, Perls for iron, periodic acid-Schiff) to highlight the inclusions Urine and tissue cultures, commonly yielding coliform organisms Cystoscopy or endoscopy to characterise mucosal plaques Cross-sectional imaging to define the extent of organ involvement Assessment of immune status and screening for underlying malignancy Malakoplakia is a rare chronic granulomatous inflammatory condition arising from defective macrophage killing of bacteria, most often coliforms such as Escherichia coli It most commonly affects the urinary tract, particularly the bladder, but can involve the kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, skin and other organs It is strongly associated with immunosuppression, chronic infection, malignancy and debilitated states Cystoscopically it appears as soft yellow-brown mucosal plaques or nodules The diagnostic histological hallmark is the Michaelis-Gutmann body, a laminated calcified inclusion within large macrophages (von Hansemann cells) Management combines prolonged antibiotics that concentrate intracellularly, such as fluoroquinolones or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, with reduction of immunosuppression where possible Surgical excision may be required for large, obstructive or destructive lesions Obstructive uropathy or renal impairment from urinary tract lesions Mass lesions mimicking or coexisting with malignancy Systemic infection in an immunosuppressed patient Progressive or destructive organ involvement Mistaking mass-forming lesions for malignancy without biopsy Choosing antibiotics that do not penetrate macrophages well Overlooking and failing to reduce contributory immunosuppression Underestimating the risk of urinary obstruction and renal damage Malakoplakia is thought to arise from a defect in the intracellular killing and digestion of phagocytosed bacteria, typically coliform organisms, by macrophages. Incompletely degraded bacterial fragments accumulate within these cells, and mineralisation of the residual material with calcium and iron produces the characteristic laminated Michaelis-Gutmann bodies. The resulting collections of engorged macrophages form the soft plaques and nodules seen clinically. Because the underlying problem is impaired bacterial clearance, the condition is closely linked to immunosuppression and chronic infection, and can produce mass-like or obstructive lesions in affected organs. Localised disease often responds to prolonged intracellularly active antibiotics and control of predisposing factors, but extensive or renal involvement, particularly in immunosuppressed patients, carries a worse outlook and may require surgery.

Malan syndrome — Sotos syndrome 2, NFIX-related overgrowth syndrome, Malan overgrowth syndrome Sotos syndrome (NSD1-related) Weaver syndrome (EZH2-related) Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome (DNMT3A-related) Marfan syndrome and related connective tissue disorders Fragile X syndrome Other transcription- or chromatin-related overgrowth syndromes Exome or genome sequencing, or a targeted overgrowth/intellectual disability gene panel Chromosomal microarray to exclude copy number causes of overgrowth and developmental delay MRI of the brain where neurological signs or macrocephaly warrant imaging Ophthalmological assessment for strabismus and optic atrophy Developmental and behavioural evaluation Skeletal and cardiovascular assessment given the marfanoid habitus This is an overgrowth-with-intellectual-disability syndrome characterised by tall stature, macrocephaly, and a recognisable facial appearance including a long, narrow face and prominent forehead It is caused by variants in NFIX, a transcription factor gene; the overgrowth phenotype arises from a distinct molecular mechanism to that producing the separate, unrelated Marshall-Smith syndrome caused by other NFIX variants Developmental delay and intellectual disability are typical, and behavioural features such as anxiety and autistic traits are common A slender, marfanoid habitus with long limbs may prompt consideration of connective tissue disorders Ophthalmological anomalies including strabismus and optic atrophy are recognised associations Diagnosis is confirmed by molecular genetic testing, often through genome or exome sequencing or a targeted overgrowth panel, having considered Sotos syndrome in the differential There is no specific treatment; care is anticipatory and multidisciplinary, addressing development, behaviour, vision, and skeletal and cardiovascular surveillance as clinically indicated Rapidly increasing head circumference or neurological signs suggesting intracranial pathology Features suggesting aortic root dilatation or other cardiovascular involvement in a marfanoid child Significant regression of skills prompting re-evaluation Progressive visual loss from optic atrophy Confusing the disorder with Sotos syndrome and stopping testing at NSD1 Attributing the marfanoid habitus to a primary connective tissue disorder and missing the overgrowth syndrome Overlooking anxiety and autistic features that benefit from targeted support Assuming NFIX variants always cause the same phenotype, when they may instead cause Marshall-Smith syndrome Malan syndrome is a chromatin- and transcription-related overgrowth disorder caused by heterozygous variants in NFIX, which encodes a nuclear factor I transcription factor involved in regulating cell proliferation and differentiation during development, including in brain and skeletal tissue. Loss-of-function variants that reduce functional NFIX dosage disturb the tightly controlled transcriptional programmes governing growth, producing the characteristic tall stature, macrocephaly, and neurodevelopmental features. Notably, a separate class of NFIX variants causes the clinically distinct Marshall-Smith syndrome, illustrating how different molecular consequences at one locus generate divergent phenotypes. Most cases arise de novo and inheritance, when relevant, is autosomal dominant. Prognosis relates chiefly to the degree of intellectual disability and any associated medical complications; lifespan is not clearly reduced in most individuals. Ongoing developmental, educational, and behavioural support improves function, and surveillance addresses ophthalmological and skeletal issues as they arise.

Male infertility — male factor infertility, male subfertility, impaired male fertility Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism (pituitary or hypothalamic) Primary testicular failure including Klinefelter syndrome Varicocele Obstructive azoospermia including congenital absence of the vas deferens Retrograde or failed ejaculation Exogenous androgen or anabolic steroid use suppressing spermatogenesis Repeated semen analysis performed to standard laboratory criteria Hormonal profile including FSH, LH, testosterone, and prolactin Scrotal examination and ultrasound to detect varicocele or obstruction Karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion analysis in severe cases Post-ejaculatory urinalysis when retrograde ejaculation is suspected A male factor contributes to roughly half of couples presenting with infertility, so both partners should be evaluated in parallel from the outset Semen analysis is the cornerstone investigation and should be repeated because of considerable biological variability before conclusions are drawn Abnormalities are described in terms of sperm concentration, motility, and morphology, with azoospermia, oligozoospermia, and asthenozoospermia denoting the main patterns Causes are grouped into pre-testicular (hypothalamic-pituitary and hormonal), testicular (primary spermatogenic failure), and post-testicular (obstruction or ejaculatory disorders) Endocrine evaluation with gonadotrophins and testosterone helps localise the problem; low gonadotrophins suggest a central cause whereas high FSH indicates primary testicular failure Varicocele is a common and potentially correctable cause, and reversible contributors such as heat, smoking, alcohol, obesity, and certain drugs should be sought Azoospermia should be characterised as obstructive or non-obstructive, since surgical sperm retrieval with assisted reproduction can achieve fatherhood in many cases Genetic evaluation, including karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing, is indicated in severe oligozoospermia or non-obstructive azoospermia Azoospermia requiring prompt distinction between obstructive and non-obstructive causes Signs of a pituitary mass such as visual field loss or headache with low gonadotrophins Bilateral testicular atrophy or gynaecomastia suggesting significant endocrine or genetic disease A testicular mass discovered during fertility evaluation, raising concern for malignancy Investigating and treating only the female partner while overlooking male factor contribution Drawing conclusions from a single abnormal semen analysis without repeat testing Missing exogenous androgen or anabolic steroid use as a reversible cause of azoospermia Failing to offer genetic counselling before assisted reproduction in men with genetic causes Male fertility depends on the integrity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, on spermatogenesis within the seminiferous tubules driven by FSH and intratesticular testosterone, and on an unobstructed ductal system allowing sperm transport and ejaculation. Pre-testicular disease reflects deficient gonadotrophin stimulation (hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism from pituitary or hypothalamic disorders, hyperprolactinaemia, or exogenous androgen use). Testicular causes include genetic conditions such as Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, prior orchitis, chemotherapy or radiation, and varicocele-related impairment of the testicular thermal and vascular environment. Post-testicular causes include congenital absence or acquired obstruction of the vas deferens, ejaculatory duct obstruction, retrograde ejaculation, and antisperm antibodies. The final common pathway is a reduction in the number or function of sperm reaching the oocyte. Outcome depends on the cause; hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism and obstruction are often correctable, varicocele repair may improve parameters in selected men, and even severe spermatogenic failure can frequently be overcome by surgical sperm retrieval combined with assisted reproductive techniques.

Malignancy (B-symptoms) — Imaging directed to site Biopsy/histology LDH, blood film Persistent unexplained B-symptoms warrant urgent workup Hodgkin lymphoma (classical) - nontender cervical/supraclavicular/axillary nodes, frequent mediastinal involvement (Harrison 22e p.869) Non-Hodgkin lymphoma - nodal and extranodal disease; B symptoms part of staging (Harrison 22e p.860) Acute or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (can produce generalised adenopathy and constitutional symptoms) (Harrison 22e p.476) Richter transformation of CLL - rapidly progressive focal adenopathy with night sweats, fever, weight loss and high LDH (Harrison 22e p.897) Metastatic carcinoma to nodes (head/neck, lung, breast, thyroid, GI primaries) (Harrison 22e p.477) Germ-cell tumour (retroperitoneal nodes in young men) (Harrison 22e p.477) Occult solid tumours presenting with involuntary weight loss - GI/hepatobiliary, lung, breast, genitourinary, ovarian, prostate (Harrison 22e p.317) Infectious mononucleosis (EBV or CMV) - generalised adenopathy with constitutional symptoms (Harrison 22e p.476) Tuberculosis - can cause unilateral mediastinal adenopathy and mesenteric lymphadenitis mimicking lymphoma, with night sweats and weight loss (Harrison 22e p.477) Histoplasmosis - unilateral paratracheal node involvement that can mimic lymphoma in endemic regions (Harrison 22e p.477) Toxoplasmosis - generalised reactive adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.476) HIV / AIDS - generalised lymphadenopathy and a recognised lymphoma risk factor (Harrison 22e p.476, p.903) Excisional biopsy of the largest abnormal node is preferred; fine-needle aspiration should NOT be the first procedure as it usually yields insufficient tissue and delays diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.478) Serum protein electrophoresis to detect a monoclonal paraprotein (Harrison 22e p.903) Serum beta2-microglobulin and LDH - independent prognostic markers in NHL (Harrison 22e p.903) CBC with differential, comprehensive metabolic/liver panel, uric acid and calcium (Harrison 22e p.317, p.904) ESR and CRP as part of the constitutional-symptom / weight-loss workup (Harrison 22e p.316, p.869) Contrast CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging; FDG-PET/CT preferred for aggressive lymphomas and Hodgkin lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.904) Bone marrow biopsy where indicated; lumbar puncture if CNS-risk histology or neurologic features (Harrison 22e p.903-904) HIV and hepatitis B and C serology - risk factors for NHL and relevant to hepatitis B reactivation risk (Harrison 22e p.904) Cervical node ultrasound long-to-short axis ratio (<2.0 favours malignancy) where head/neck cancer is suspected (Harrison 22e p.478) Age/sex/risk-appropriate cancer screening (e.g. faecal occult blood, colonoscopy, mammography) and abdominal ultrasound in occult-malignancy weight-loss workup (Harrison 22e p.318) Sarcoidosis - mediastinal/hilar adenopathy and constitutional symptoms (Harrison 22e p.477) Systemic lupus erythematosus and mixed connective tissue disease - generalised adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.476) Drug-induced (phenytoin/diphenylhydantoin and others) lymphadenopathy, including DRESS/DIHS with eosinophilia and extensive adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.193, p.476) Castleman disease, Kikuchi histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis, Rosai-Dorfman disease, angioimmunoblastic lymphadenopathy, IgG4-related disease (Harrison 22e p.476) B symptoms are formally defined for lymphoma staging (the Ann Arbor 'B' suffix) as unexplained fever (>38C), drenching night sweats, and/or unexplained weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight over the 6 months before diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.861, p.869). The tempo of symptoms helps separate aggressive from indolent lymphoma: rapid symptomatic progression and the presence of B symptoms suggest a more aggressive process (Harrison 22e p.903). Among malignancies, lymphoma is by far the commonest cause of malignancy-related fever of unknown origin, and the fever can precede any palpable lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.193). About one-third of patients with classical Hodgkin lymphoma present with B symptoms; Hodgkin disease can even present as a fever of unknown origin, more often in older patients with abdominal mixed-cellularity disease (Harrison 22e p.869). Pel-Ebstein fever (cyclical fever lasting days to weeks alternating with afebrile intervals) is a rare but classic Hodgkin lymphoma presentation (Harrison 22e p.869). Node character matters: lymphomatous nodes tend to be large, firm, rubbery, mobile, symmetric and non-tender, whereas metastatic carcinoma nodes are typically hard, non-tender and fixed to surrounding tissue (Harrison 22e p.477). Supraclavicular and scalene node enlargement is always abnormal and warrants prompt evaluation; a left supraclavicular node (Virchow node) classically reflects a gastrointestinal primary, but lung, breast, testis and ovarian cancers also seed these nodes (Harrison 22e p.477). Examination in suspected lymphoma should systematically cover all peripheral nodal sites plus Waldeyer ring, liver and spleen size, effusions/ascites, and testicular, breast or skin involvement, since any of these can change staging and management (Harrison 22e p.903). Enlarged intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal nodes are usually malignant (lymphoma, or germ-cell tumour in young men), in contrast to the largely benign causes of cervical adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.477). Half of all cancer patients lose some weight and up to 20% of cancer deaths are attributable directly to cachexia; malignancy that declares itself through marked weight loss generally carries a poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.317). Supraclavicular or scalene adenopathy - always abnormal, biopsy promptly (Harrison 22e p.477-478) Solitary hard non-tender cervical node in an older tobacco user - prompt biopsy after ENT mucosal assessment (Harrison 22e p.478) Node size >2 cm with an abnormal chest x-ray in younger patients - predicts malignant/granulomatous biopsy yield (Harrison 22e p.521) Hard fixed nodes, or firm mobile generalised adenopathy suggestive of lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.478) Airway, oesophageal or SVC compression from thoracic adenopathy (cough/wheeze, hoarseness, dysphagia, facial/arm/neck swelling) (Harrison 22e p.520) Enlarged intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal nodes (usually malignant) (Harrison 22e p.477) Involuntary weight loss >=5% over 6 months prompting structured malignancy workup (Harrison 22e p.358) Do NOT give glucocorticoids for undiagnosed lymphadenopathy - their lympholytic effect can obscure lymphoma, leukaemia and Castleman disease and delay/disrupt diagnosis (the rare exception is life-threatening pharyngeal obstruction from Waldeyer-ring tissue in mononucleosis) (Harrison 22e p.521). Fine-needle aspiration is inadequate for an initial lymphoma diagnosis - obtain an excisional/core biopsy; FNA is reserved for thyroid nodules and confirming relapse of a known cancer (Harrison 22e p.478). Antibiotics are NOT indicated for lymphadenopathy unless there is strong evidence of bacterial infection (Harrison 22e p.521). Localized-versus-generalized adenopathy has limited discriminatory value because many causes produce either pattern; do not over-rely on it (Harrison 22e p.476). In primary care most lymphadenopathy is benign (>two-thirds nonspecific/URI, <1% malignant) and needs only short-interval follow-up - but persistent or enlarging nodes must be re-evaluated and biopsied (Harrison 22e p.476, p.521). If a head-and-neck primary is suspected behind a solitary cervical node, perform a careful ENT exam and biopsy any suspicious mucosal lesion first before excising the node (Harrison 22e p.478). B symptoms in lymphoma are cytokine-mediated systemic effects of the tumour rather than direct mass effects. In classical Hodgkin lymphoma the malignant Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells are rare within a tumour mass that is largely a polyclonal inflammatory infiltrate reacting to tumour-derived cytokines; this inflammatory milieu drives constitutional symptoms and contributes to the generalised immune suppression seen in these patients. Involuntary weight loss in malignancy reflects a combination of anorexia, sarcopenia and a cytokine-driven cachexia syndrome. (Harrison 22e p.316, p.869) Lymphoma prognosis is stage- and biology-dependent. For NHL the International Prognostic Index uses five factors (age >=60, elevated LDH, ECOG performance status >=2, Ann Arbor stage III/IV, and >1 extranodal site); for DLBCL treated with R-CHOP, 0 factors gives ~94% 4-year survival versus ~53% with 3-5 factors. Across lymphomas, decreased outcome is associated with B symptoms, advanced stage, elevated LDH and bulky disease (e.g. lymph-node mass >7 cm). In occult solid malignancy, presentation through significant involuntary weight loss generally carries a very poor prognosis, whereas when no cause is found after thorough workup the prognosis is comparatively favourable. (Harrison 22e p.317, p.861, NHL prognosis section) Ann Arbor staging (stages I-IV) with suffix A (no systemic symptoms) or B (presence of B symptoms: fever >38C, drenching night sweats, or weight loss >10% body weight over preceding 6 months); suffix E for localized extralymphatic extension. B-symptom status (the A/B designation) and stage drive prognosis and therapy. (Harrison 22e p.861, p.869)

malignant acanthosis nigricans — paraneoplastic acanthosis nigricans, acanthosis nigricans maligna Benign obesity/insulin-resistance-related acanthosis nigricans Drug-induced acanthosis nigricans (nicotinic acid, systemic corticosteroids, oestrogens, protease inhibitors) Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis of Gougerot-Carteaud Endocrinopathy-associated acanthosis nigricans (HAIR-AN syndrome, acromegaly, Cushing syndrome) Dowling-Degos disease Pellagra and other nutritional dermatoses affecting flexures Terra firma-forme dermatosis / retention hyperkeratosis Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy, given the leading association with gastric adenocarcinoma CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis to identify an occult primary and to stage disease Tumour markers as directed by suspected primary (CEA, CA 19-9, CA-125) Skin biopsy demonstrating papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis with minimal hyperpigmentation Fasting glucose, HbA1c and insulin to exclude insulin-resistance-related disease Colonoscopy and faecal occult blood testing when a lower gastrointestinal primary is suspected PET-CT when conventional imaging is unrevealing Abrupt onset and rapid extension of symmetrical velvety, hyperpigmented plaques in flexures (neck, axillae, groin) in a non-obese, often older adult should prompt an urgent malignancy search. Overwhelmingly associated with intra-abdominal adenocarcinoma; gastric carcinoma accounts for the majority, with pancreatic, colorectal, hepatobiliary and ovarian primaries also reported. Mucosal and mucocutaneous involvement (oral cavity, lips, conjunctiva, anogenital) and periorbital or palmar disease are far more frequent than in the benign obesity-related form. Commonly coexists with other paraneoplastic signs, notably tripe palms (palmar acanthosis) and the sign of Leser-Trelat, reflecting a shared growth-factor mechanism. Pruritus is frequently marked, in contrast to the largely asymptomatic insulin-resistance-associated variant. The eruption may precede, accompany or follow diagnosis of the tumour and characteristically parallels the malignancy, regressing with successful treatment and recurring with relapse. Weight loss rather than obesity, together with rapid progression over weeks to months, helps distinguish it clinically from the common benign insulin-resistance type. New extensive acanthosis nigricans in a non-obese adult over 40 Rapid progression with mucosal involvement and unexplained weight loss Concurrent tripe palms or eruptive seborrhoeic keratoses Marked pruritus with associated systemic symptoms Attributing new acanthosis nigricans to obesity and missing an underlying tumour Failing to examine the mucosae and palms or to look for the sign of Leser-Trelat Assuming a normal initial endoscopy excludes malignancy when clinical suspicion is high Overlooking recurrence of the skin signs as a marker of tumour relapse Malignant acanthosis nigricans is thought to arise from tumour-secreted growth factors that stimulate epidermal proliferation. Transforming growth factor alpha (TGF-alpha), which is structurally similar to epidermal growth factor and binds the epidermal growth factor receptor on keratinocytes, is considered central, with contributions from fibroblast growth factor and insulin-like growth factor 1. This drives keratinocyte and fibroblast hyperproliferation producing papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis, while relatively modest increases in melanin account for the hyperpigmented appearance. The parallel course with tumour burden supports a humoral, growth-factor-mediated aetiology rather than local insulin-receptor activation as seen in benign disease. The prognosis reflects the underlying malignancy, which is frequently an advanced, aggressive adenocarcinoma with short median survival. Cutaneous lesions may improve or regress following effective tumour treatment.

Malignant glaucoma — aqueous misdirection, aqueous misdirection syndrome, ciliary block glaucoma, malignant glaucoma (aqueous misdirection) Pupillary-block angle closure (relieved by patent iridotomy) tighten the zonule and pull the lens back, together with pressure-lowering and anti-inflammatory therapy, and aqueous suppressants Laser disruption of the anterior hyaloid, sometimes with the posterior capsule, can re-establish forward aqueous flow, and refractory cases require vitrectomy to relieve the block Miotics tend to worsen the condition and should be avoided, whereas cycloplegics help A uniformly shallow or flat chamber after intraocular surgery despite a patent iridotomy Rising pressure with progressive chamber flattening requiring urgent intervention Failure to distinguish it from a suprachoroidal haemorrhage, which needs very different management Worsening after miotic treatment given in the mistaken belief it is pupillary block Treating it as pupillary block and giving miotics, which aggravate the misdirection Missing a suprachoroidal haemorrhage or choroidal effusion as the cause of the flat chamber Repeating an iridotomy when one is already patent instead of addressing the hyaloid block Delaying vitrectomy in medically unresponsive cases Failing to treat the fellow eye's angle-closure risk that predisposed to the original condition Malignant glaucoma, or aqueous misdirection, is thought to result from an abnormal anteriorly displaced relationship between the ciliary processes, lens equator, and anterior vitreous face, which diverts aqueous posteriorly into or behind the vitreous body instead of forward into the anterior chamber. Trapped aqueous raises pressure in the vitreous compartment and pushes the lens-iris diaphragm forward, producing uniform shallowing or flattening of the entire anterior chamber and secondary angle closure. A ciliary-block or hyaloid element impedes normal forward aqueous movement. Because the mechanism is behind the iris, a patent peripheral iridotomy does not relieve it, and interventions that draw the diaphragm backward or open the hyaloid pathway are needed to break the cycle. With prompt recognition many eyes respond to cycloplegic and medical therapy or to laser hyaloidotomy, but the condition can be difficult to control and may need vitrectomy; delayed or misdirected treatment risks persistent flat chamber, corneal decompensation, and glaucomatous visual loss.

Malignant hyperthermia — MH, malignant hyperpyrexia, anaesthetic-induced hypermetabolic crisis Inadequate anaesthesia or analgesia with sympathetic response Sepsis or systemic inflammatory response Thyroid storm or phaeochromocytoma crisis Neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin syndrome Equipment-related rebreathing or exhausted carbon dioxide absorbent Environmental or iatrogenic hyperthermia Continuous capnography and core temperature monitoring to detect the crisis early Arterial blood gas showing combined respiratory and metabolic acidosis Serial potassium, creatine kinase, and myoglobin to track rhabdomyolysis Coagulation studies to detect disseminated intravascular coagulation Later in-vitro contracture testing and RYR1 genetic analysis for confirmation A pharmacogenetic hypermetabolic crisis triggered by volatile anaesthetics and depolarising neuromuscular blockers in susceptible individuals The earliest and most sensitive sign is an unexplained rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide despite increased ventilation, often with tachycardia and mixed acidosis Masseter or generalised muscle rigidity, rapidly rising temperature, and dark urine from myoglobin are later features; hyperthermia is frequently a late rather than early sign Immediate management is to stop triggering agents, call for help and the emergency supply of dantrolene, hyperventilate with high-flow oxygen, and switch to a non-triggering technique Dantrolene is the specific antidote and should be given without delay and repeated until the hypermetabolic state resolves Supportive care includes active cooling, treating hyperkalaemia and arrhythmias, correcting acidosis, and maintaining urine output to protect against myoglobinuric renal injury Susceptibility is largely inherited (commonly RYR1 gene variants) and is linked to certain myopathies; a family or personal history should prompt a trigger-free anaesthetic Confirmatory testing uses the in-vitro contracture (caffeine-halothane) test with genetic testing, and survivors should be counselled and referred to an MH unit Rapidly rising end-tidal carbon dioxide with tachycardia and rigidity indicating an evolving MH crisis Severe hyperthermia with mixed acidosis and hyperkalaemia threatening arrhythmia and arrest Cardiac arrhythmia or arrest during or after a triggering anaesthetic Dark urine and rising creatine kinase signalling rhabdomyolysis and renal risk Attributing rising carbon dioxide or tachycardia to light anaesthesia and delaying diagnosis Failing to have dantrolene immediately available or delaying its administration Confusing an isolated masseter spasm with a full crisis or, conversely, dismissing it entirely Neglecting active cooling and management of hyperkalaemia and myoglobinuria Not counselling the patient and family or arranging specialist referral after recovery Malignant hyperthermia results from abnormal regulation of skeletal muscle calcium, most often due to mutations affecting the ryanodine receptor (RYR1) that controls calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. On exposure to volatile agents or succinylcholine, uncontrolled calcium release produces sustained muscle contraction and a massive increase in aerobic and anaerobic metabolism. This drives rapid carbon dioxide and heat generation, oxygen consumption, lactic acidosis, ATP depletion, and eventually muscle breakdown with hyperkalaemia, myoglobinaemia, and rhabdomyolysis. Dantrolene reduces calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and interrupts the cycle. Mortality has fallen dramatically with early recognition and prompt dantrolene, but delayed treatment can lead to disseminated intravascular coagulation, renal failure, and death; survivors and relatives require testing and lifelong trigger avoidance.

the CACNA1S calcium channel that triggers it. The abnormal channel is hypersensitive, so on exposure to volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine it releases uncontrolled calcium into the myoplasm. Sustained high calcium drives continuous muscle contraction and a runaway increase in aerobic and anaerobic metabolism, generating heat, carbon dioxide and lactate, depleting adenosine triphosphate, and causing membrane breakdown with rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia and acidosis. With early recognition, prompt dantrolene and modern supportive care the mortality of an acute crisis is now low, and susceptible individuals can undergo safe anaesthesia using trigger-free agents, but an unrecognised or untreated crisis remains rapidly fatal.

Epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures (KCNT1) — EIMFS, malignant migrating partial seizures of infancy, MMPSI, migrating partial epilepsy of infancy, KCNT1 migrating focal seizures SCN2A, SCN1A, and SCN8A developmental and epileptic encephalopathies Other KCNT1-related epilepsy phenotypes SLC12A5 (KCC2) related epilepsy TBC1D24-related epileptic encephalopathy Structural or metabolic epilepsies of infancy Ohtahara syndrome and early myoclonic encephalopathy Prolonged video electroencephalography to demonstrate migrating independent multifocal ictal patterns Epilepsy gene panel or whole-exome sequencing, with KCNT1 a priority target Brain magnetic resonance imaging to exclude structural causes and document acquired changes Metabolic screen to exclude treatable mimics Electrocardiography and cardiac review before and during any quinidine trial Developmental and growth monitoring including head circumference A severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy of early infancy, most often caused by gain-of-function variants in KCNT1, which encodes the sodium-activated potassium channel Slack The defining feature is near-continuous focal seizures that migrate independently between multiple cortical regions and between hemispheres, seen dramatically on video electroencephalography Seizure onset is typically in the first six months of life, often within the first weeks, with rapidly escalating frequency Development arrests or regresses with seizure onset, leading to profound impairment, acquired microcephaly, and loss of visual and social responsiveness Other genes, including SCN2A, SCN1A, SCN8A, SLC12A5, and TBC1D24, can cause the same clinical syndrome, so it is genetically heterogeneous Seizures are characteristically drug-resistant; quinidine has been trialled to target the KCNT1 gain-of-function channel but with inconsistent benefit and a need for cardiac monitoring There is significant morbidity and mortality, including a raised risk of sudden unexpected death, so supportive multidisciplinary care and family counselling are central Near-continuous migrating seizures with developmental arrest in early infancy Acquired microcephaly and loss of previously attained skills Cardiac conduction changes during quinidine therapy Features suggesting elevated sudden unexpected death in epilepsy risk Expecting a reliable quinidine response when benefit is variable and requires cardiac monitoring Assuming KCNT1 is the only cause and stopping the genetic workup Overlooking treatable metabolic mimics early in the presentation Neglecting family counselling about prognosis and sudden unexpected death risk Epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures is most commonly driven by gain-of-function variants in KCNT1, encoding the sodium-activated potassium channel Slack that shapes the slow afterhyperpolarisation and neuronal firing patterns. Enhanced channel activity disrupts the normal control of excitability and inhibitory balance, generating multiple independent seizure foci that migrate across the cortex. The relentless multifocal ictal activity impairs the developing brain, producing the characteristic developmental arrest and regression. Because the syndrome can also arise from sodium-channel and other genes, the migrating seizure phenotype reflects a final common pathway of severely disordered early network excitability. The syndrome generally carries a poor prognosis, with drug-resistant seizures, profound developmental impairment, and significant mortality including sudden unexpected death, though occasional milder courses are reported.

patient to a benign neurofibroma and delaying investigation Relying on S100 positivity, which is often only focal, without additional markers such as loss of H3K27me3 Sampling a benign area of a large plexiform lesion and missing the malignant component Underestimating the extent of nerve involvement and achieving inadequate margins Failing to consider prior radiotherapy as a predisposing factor in sporadic-appearing tumours Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour is an aggressive sarcoma showing nerve sheath (usually Schwann cell) differentiation. In neurofibromatosis type 1 it typically arises through malignant progression of a plexiform neurofibroma, driven by biallelic loss of the NF1 tumour-suppressor gene, subsequent loss of CDKN2A, and inactivation of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (through SUZ12 or EED mutation). Loss of PRC2 function results in global loss of histone H3 lysine-27 trimethylation, deregulating gene expression and promoting a high-grade phenotype. Sporadic and radiation-associated tumours accumulate analogous alterations, and the resulting cells display variable, often incomplete, Schwannian marker expression. Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour is an aggressive sarcoma with substantial recurrence and metastatic risk; prognosis depends on tumour size, grade, resectability, and setting, and neurofibromatosis type 1-associated and large or incompletely resected tumours generally carry a worse outcome.

malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour — neurofibrosarcoma, malignant schwannoma, neurogenic sarcoma benign neurofibroma or plexiform neurofibroma cellular or ancient schwannoma synovial sarcoma fibrosarcoma and myxofibrosarcoma leiomyosarcoma spindle cell melanoma dedifferentiated liposarcoma contrast-enhanced MRI of the primary site to assess nerve of origin and local extent FDG PET-CT to identify malignant transformation and guide biopsy image-guided core or open incisional biopsy of the most active focus immunohistochemistry including S100, SOX10 and H3K27me3 staging CT of the thorax for pulmonary metastases molecular assessment for NF1, CDKN2A and PRC2 alterations clinical and genetic assessment for underlying neurofibromatosis type 1 Roughly half of cases arise in neurofibromatosis type 1, typically from malignant transformation of a pre-existing plexiform neurofibroma; the remainder are sporadic or radiation-associated. A rapidly enlarging, newly painful mass in a known NF1 plexiform neurofibroma is the classic warning of transformation and warrants urgent imaging and biopsy. FDG PET-CT is valuable for distinguishing malignant transformation from a benign neurofibroma and for directing biopsy to the most metabolically active focus. Loss of nuclear H3K27me3 on immunohistochemistry, reflecting PRC2 (SUZ12/EED) inactivation, is a useful diagnostic adjunct, though not entirely specific. S100 and SOX10 staining is typically patchy or lost, unlike the diffuse positivity seen in benign nerve sheath tumours. Wide surgical resection with negative margins is the cornerstone of treatment; the tumour is relatively resistant to radiotherapy and chemotherapy. Radiation-associated tumours may arise years to decades after therapeutic irradiation and carry a particularly poor outcome. The lung is the dominant site of distant metastasis, so staging chest imaging is mandatory. rapid enlargement of a previously stable neurofibroma new persistent or nocturnal pain within a known nerve sheath lesion progressive neurological deficit referable to the involved nerve hard, fixed mass with rapid growth over weeks mistaking malignant transformation for a benign neurofibroma and delaying biopsy sampling error from a non-representative biopsy of a heterogeneous mass assuming radiotherapy or chemotherapy will substitute for inadequate surgical margins overlooking a second occult tumour or NF1 diagnosis in a young patient interpreting H3K27me3 loss in isolation as definitive without correlating morphology The tumour originates from Schwann cell or perineurial lineage of the peripheral nerve. In neurofibromatosis type 1, biallelic loss of the NF1 tumour suppressor drives dysregulated RAS-MAPK signalling within a plexiform neurofibroma, and stepwise acquisition of further hits, notably inactivation of CDKN2A and of the polycomb repressive complex 2 components SUZ12 or EED, precipitates high-grade transformation. Loss of PRC2 function causes global loss of the repressive histone mark H3K27me3, promoting aberrant transcription and a spindle-cell sarcoma with fascicular architecture, nuclear pleomorphism and brisk mitotic activity. Sporadic and post-irradiation tumours converge on similar molecular pathways without a germline NF1 defect. Outcome is guarded, with high rates of local recurrence and distant metastasis and a substantial risk of death; large size, high grade, truncal location, incomplete resection and an NF1 background all worsen survival.

malignant pleural effusion — MPE, metastatic pleural effusion Parapneumonic effusion or empyema Tuberculous pleuritis Effusion secondary to pulmonary embolism Transudative effusion from heart failure or hepatic hydrothorax Benign asbestos-related pleural effusion Chylothorax (for example from lymphoma) Paramalignant effusion from lymphatic obstruction or post-obstructive pneumonia rather than direct pleural involvement Diagnostic pleural aspiration with cytology, protein, LDH, pH and glucose Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax with abdomen and pelvis for staging Thoracic ultrasound to assess pleural nodularity, septations and guide sampling Image-guided or local anaesthetic thoracoscopic pleural biopsy Immunohistochemistry and molecular studies on pleural tissue or fluid Assessment of lung re-expansion after drainage to detect trapped lung Prognostic scoring (LENT or PROMISE) alongside performance status assessment A malignant pleural effusion indicates disseminated or advanced malignancy and generally portends a poor prognosis. Lung and breast carcinoma account for the majority; lymphoma, ovarian and gastric cancers and mesothelioma are other important causes, and a proportion arise from an unknown primary. Effusions are typically exudative by Light's criteria and are frequently blood-stained; a massive effusion with mediastinal shift towards the effusion suggests a central obstructing tumour or mesothelioma. Low pleural fluid pH and glucose correlate with higher tumour burden, poorer pleurodesis success and shorter survival. Pleural fluid cytology confirms malignancy in only around 60 percent of cases, with sensitivity higher in adenocarcinoma and low in mesothelioma. When cytology is negative, image-guided or thoracoscopic pleural biopsy provides tissue for diagnosis and molecular characterisation. Definitive management aims at symptom control through therapeutic aspiration, talc pleurodesis or an indwelling pleural catheter, guided by patient preference and the presence of trapped lung. Prognostic scores such as LENT and PROMISE help select the least burdensome yet most durable management strategy. Rapid re-accumulation with breathlessness at rest Massive effusion with contralateral mediastinal shift Ipsilateral or absent mediastinal shift suggesting trapped lung or central airway obstruction Features of superior vena cava obstruction Signs of pleural infection complicating an indwelling catheter Relying on a single negative cytology to exclude malignancy. Attempting pleurodesis in a trapped lung, which is likely to fail. Draining a large effusion too rapidly and precipitating re-expansion pulmonary oedema. Mislabelling a paramalignant effusion, which may respond to systemic therapy, as directly malignant. Not offering an indwelling pleural catheter to patients with limited prognosis or a non-expandable lung. Malignant effusions form when tumour involves the pleura, most often through haematogenous or lymphatic metastasis to the parietal and visceral pleura or by direct invasion. Pleural tumour increases capillary and mesothelial permeability, elaborates vascular endothelial growth factor and other mediators, and obstructs the lymphatic stomata and mediastinal lymphatics that normally drain the pleural space. The combination of increased fluid formation and impaired lymphatic reabsorption produces a progressive exudate. Extensive visceral pleural tumour or fibrosis may prevent the lung re-expanding after drainage (trapped lung), which strongly influences the choice between pleurodesis and an indwelling catheter. Survival is generally measured in months and varies markedly with tumour type and fluid characteristics, being worse with low pleural fluid pH or glucose and poor performance status; mesothelioma and lung primaries carry the poorest outlook, whereas breast cancer and haematological malignancies may respond to systemic therapy.

effusion Overlooking the potential for tumour seeding along biopsy or drain tracts Failing to document occupational exposure for medico-legal and compensation purposes Asbestos fibres retained in the pleura, particularly amphibole types, cause chronic inflammation, oxidative injury, and genetic damage to mesothelial cells over many years. Loss of tumour-suppressor function and accumulated somatic mutations drive malignant transformation of the mesothelium. The tumour then spreads diffusely along the pleural surfaces, forming a thickened rind that encases the lung, invades the chest wall, diaphragm, and mediastinal structures, and commonly produces a recurrent exudative and often bloody effusion. malignant spinal cord compression — MSCC, metastatic spinal cord compression, malignant epidural spinal cord compression Benign disc prolapse or degenerative canal stenosis Epidural abscess or discitis Spinal epidural haematoma Leptomeningeal metastasis or intramedullary metastasis Radiation myelopathy Transverse myelitis or other inflammatory myelopathy Pathological vertebral fracture without cord compression Urgent whole-spine MRI with and without contrast CT of the spine to assess bony stability and for surgical planning CT staging of chest, abdomen and pelvis to identify primary and disease extent Prostate-specific antigen and myeloma screen where primary is unknown Image-guided or surgical biopsy when the diagnosis of malignancy is not established Bloods including calcium, renal and liver function Bone scintigraphy or PET for disease mapping Progressive or unremitting back pain, often thoracic, band-like or worse on lying, coughing or straining, frequently precedes neurological signs by days to weeks and should trigger urgent whole-spine imaging. The thoracic spine is the commonest site; multiple non-contiguous levels are present in up to a third of patients, so imaging must cover the entire spine, not just the symptomatic region. Breast, lung, prostate, myeloma and renal malignancies account for most cases; MSCC is the presenting feature of cancer in a substantial minority. Whole-spine MRI is the investigation of choice and should be obtained within 24 hours of suspicion (sooner if neurology is progressing). Start high-dose corticosteroid (dexamethasone) with gastroprotection immediately on suspicion unless contraindicated—but withhold if untreated lymphoma is likely and tissue is needed, as steroids can lyse tumour and obscure diagnosis. Ambulatory and continent status at presentation is the strongest predictor of functional outcome, underscoring the value of treating before deficits are established. Definitive treatment is decompressive surgery (favoured for good performance status, single-level disease, spinal instability or radioresistant tumour) or radiotherapy; the choice depends on histology, prognosis and stability. Nurse the patient flat with neutral spine alignment and log-roll until spinal stability is confirmed, and provide venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and bladder care. New or progressive limb weakness or gait disturbance Sensory level or saddle anaesthesia Bladder or bowel dysfunction (a late and ominous sign) Severe, progressive or nocturnal thoracic spinal pain Rapidly evolving neurological deficit over hours Waiting for neurological signs before imaging in a cancer patient with new back pain Imaging only the symptomatic level and missing higher or lower compressions Giving corticosteroids before biopsy when lymphoma is the likely cause Overlooking spinal instability and mobilising the patient prematurely Attributing bladder dysfunction to opioids or immobility rather than to cord or cauda equina compromise Metastatic tumour, most often within a vertebral body, expands into the epidural space and compresses the thecal sac and cord (or cauda equina below the conus). Direct mechanical pressure is compounded by venous plexus obstruction causing vasogenic cord oedema, and by arterial compromise producing ischaemia and, ultimately, infarction. Vertebral collapse or retropulsed bone or tumour fragments may add an element of instability and further canal compromise. The progression from reversible oedema to irreversible infarction explains why outcome is time-critical and why neurological deficit, once fixed, seldom recovers. Neurological outcome hinges on the deficit at the time treatment starts: patients ambulant at presentation usually remain so, whereas established paraplegia rarely reverses. Overall survival is governed by the underlying malignancy and its treatability rather than the compression itself.

splinting, since allowing the joint to flex even briefly resets the healing process Skin maceration or pressure necrosis from an ill-fitting or overtightened splint Missing volar subluxation that requires surgical rather than splint treatment Overlooking the development of a secondary swan-neck deformity A mallet finger arises from disruption of the terminal extensor tendon at its insertion on the dorsal base of the distal phalanx, either through a tendinous avulsion or through a dorsal avulsion fracture. Loss of active extensor input leaves the flexor digitorum profundus unopposed, so the distal phalanx rests in flexion. Over time the disrupted balance of the extensor mechanism can shift force proximally through the central slip and lateral bands, hyperextending the proximal interphalangeal joint and producing a secondary swan-neck posture. Outcomes are generally good with early continuous splinting; delayed presentation or interrupted splinting commonly leaves a small residual extension lag that is usually well tolerated functionally.

before surgery Inflammatory markers or serology only if inflammatory arthritis is suspected A mallet toe is an isolated flexion deformity of the distal interphalangeal joint, with the flexion) and claw toe (metatarsophalangeal hyperextension plus flexion of both interphalangeal joints) It most often affects the longest lesser toe, typically the second, where the toe tip is while a fixed one needs joint resection or fusion Conservative care includes deep-toe-box footwear, toe caps or crest pads to relieve tip pressure, and callus management Surgical treatment uses flexor tenotomy for flexible deformity and distal interphalangeal arthrodesis or resection for fixed deformity Ulceration or infection at the toe tip, particularly in diabetes or peripheral vascular disease suggesting exostosis or, rarely, tumour Failing to test flexibility and performing joint resection when a simple flexor tenotomy would suffice Missing an underlying bony lesion such as subungual exostosis as the cause of tip pain Overlooking ulceration or ischaemia at the toe tip in the neuropathic or vasculopathic foot Attributing an isolated distal deformity to a broader claw or hammer toe pattern and over-treating Neglecting footwear correction so that pressure recurs after treatment Mallet toe is a flexion deformity confined to the distal interphalangeal joint, produced by an imbalance favouring the long flexor tendon across that joint while the more proximal joints remain in neutral alignment. It is commonly precipitated by chronic pressure from footwear that is too short or too shallow, so that the longest toe is repeatedly forced into flexion, and by minor trauma. Over time the flexor tendon and joint capsule contract, converting an initially flexible deformity into a fixed one. The buckled distal phalanx concentrates load at the toe tip, producing a painful end-of-toe corn or callosity, subungual pressure changes, and occasionally ulceration, particularly where sensation or perfusion is impaired. Because the deformity is distal and isolated, associated metatarsophalangeal subluxation and generalised clawing are typically absent. Mallet toe generally responds well to simple measures. Flexible deformity is often corrected by flexor tenotomy with reliable relief of tip pain, and fixed deformity does well with distal interphalangeal arthrodesis or resection. Recurrence is uncommon when appropriate footwear is maintained, though tip numbness, mild residual deformity, or persistent nail changes can occur.

with haemodynamic instability Features suggesting Boerhaave perforation such as severe chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema, or sepsis Rebleeding after initial haemostasis Bleeding in a patient with
