Overlooking coexisting varices or portal hypertension that raise the bleeding risk Assuming all tears are benign and not applying endoscopic haemostasis to actively bleeding lesions A Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal and submucosal laceration at or just below the gastro-oesophageal junction produced by a sudden rise in intra-abdominal and intragastric pressure, most often during forceful retching or vomiting. The abrupt pressure gradient across the junction stretches and splits the mucosa longitudinally, disrupting submucosal vessels and causing bleeding. A hiatus hernia is thought to predispose by accentuating the pressure differential across the herniated segment, and the tear characteristically remains confined to the mucosa, distinguishing it from the transmural rupture of Boerhaave syndrome. The outlook is excellent for most patients, as bleeding is self-limiting and the mucosal tear heals rapidly; rebleeding is uncommon and is more likely with coagulopathy or portal hypertension, where the prognosis is correspondingly poorer.

Malnutrition and Nutritional Assessment — Protein-calorie malnutrition, Protein-energy malnutrition, Undernutrition Sarcopenia (progressive generalized loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength; screened with SARC-F) Sarcopenic obesity Cachexia of chronic disease (malignancy, organ failure) Frailty syndrome Dehydration / fluid shifts mimicking weight change Micronutrient deficiency states Validated risk-screening tools: Malnutrition Screening Tool, Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST), Nutritional Risk Screening 2002, Mini Nutritional Assessment, Subjective Global Assessment Anthropometrics: serial body weight (without shoes/heavy garments), BMI, calf circumference, mid-upper arm circumference; height estimated by arm span or knee-height caliper when needed Body composition: bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA, portable), dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA), air displacement plethysmography, and opportunistic CT/MRI muscle measurement Laboratory: complete blood count with differential (screen for iron, B12, folate, vitamin C deficiencies), C-reactive protein for inflammation, specific micronutrient levels Indirect calorimetry for resting energy expenditure; 24-h urine urea nitrogen and nitrogen balance to gauge catabolism and protein adequacy (normal renal/hepatic function required) Functional tests: handgrip strength, Sit-to-Stand test, 6-Meter Walk Test, Clinical Frailty Scale, SARC-F Nutrition-focused physical examination for edema, subcutaneous fat and muscle loss; diet history including oral supplements, enteral and parenteral intake Edema or fluid overload masking true weight loss (dry weight estimation may be needed) Hypoalbuminemia from systemic inflammation, hepatic or renal insufficiency, protein-losing enteropathy, or corticosteroid use rather than nutrition itself Low BUN/creatinine from renal or hepatic disease falsely suggesting reduced muscle mass Hypocholesterolemia related to acute illness rather than malnutrition per se Malnutrition affects roughly 30-50% of hospitalized patients, with the exact prevalence varying by clinical setting, underlying diagnosis, and the diagnostic criteria applied (Harrison 22e p.2615). The 2019 GLIM (Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition) consensus requires at least one phenotypic criterion (nonvolitional weight loss, low BMI, or reduced muscle mass) PLUS at least one etiologic criterion (reduced food intake/assimilation, or disease burden/inflammation) to diagnose malnutrition (Harrison 22e p.2616). Severity grading in GLIM is determined by the phenotypic criterion: moderate (stage 1) malnutrition is 5-10% weight loss within 6 months (or 10-20% beyond 6 months), and severe (stage 2) is >10% within 6 months (or >20% beyond) (Harrison 22e p.2616). Patients at any BMI can be malnourished; overweight or obese individuals may have sarcopenic obesity from muscle loss, and conversely being underweight does not by itself equal malnutrition (Harrison 22e p.2617). Handgrip strength is among the more clinically useful functional measures because it is easy to perform and helps identify which patients are most likely to benefit from individualized nutritional support (Harrison 22e p.2617). Patients with apparently adequate oral intake may still be at risk of malnutrition when chronic gastrointestinal disease compromises nutrient assimilation or absorption (Harrison 22e p.2617). A 5-10% loss of body weight over 6 months is clinically relevant, while >10% loss over the same period is considered severe (Harrison 22e p.2617). Albumin and prealbumin are negative acute-phase reactants and fall with injury, disease, or inflammation; they have poor sensitivity and specificity for malnutrition, though they retain value for predicting clinical outcomes (Harrison 22e pp.2617-2618). C-reactive protein is a positive acute-phase reactant useful for confirming inflammation, with the chapter noting supportive thresholds of mild 3.0-9.9 mg/L, moderate 10-50 mg/L, and severe >50 mg/L (Harrison 22e p.2616). Calf circumference is a practical, valid estimate of skeletal muscle mass that requires less training than mid-upper arm circumference, with ethnicity-specific reference ranges that should be adjusted for BMI extremes (Harrison 22e p.2618). When inflammation is severe, nutrition care tends to be supportive only; at low-to-moderate inflammation, nutrition care may be therapeutic and improve clinical outcomes (Harrison 22e pp.2615-2616). Calf circumference, BMI, and other GLIM parameters make malnutrition diagnosis feasible even in the outpatient/ambulatory setting where dietitian access may be limited (Harrison 22e p.2617). Nonvolitional weight loss >10% within 6 months (or >20% beyond 6 months) indicating severe malnutrition BMI <18.5 kg/m2 in adults <70 years (or <20 if >=70 years) indicating severe malnutrition by GLIM Severe acute inflammatory state with negative nitrogen balance and elevated resting energy expenditure Low handgrip strength predicting poorer clinical outcomes Hypocholesterolemia (<120 mg/dL) developing during hospitalization, linked to worse outcomes Reduced food intake/assimilation (<=50% of energy requirement for >1 week, any reduction >2 weeks, or chronic GI condition impairing absorption) Relying on albumin or prealbumin to diagnose malnutrition or judge response to nutrition therapy; they reflect inflammation, hepatic/renal status, hydration, and other factors and have poor specificity (Harrison 22e pp.2617-2618). Assuming a normal or high BMI excludes malnutrition; sarcopenic obesity and muscle loss can occur at any BMI (Harrison 22e p.2617). Overlooking edema, which can mask true weight loss unless dry weight is estimated (Harrison 22e p.2617). Using BUN/creatinine, total lymphocyte count, cholesterol, creatinine-height index, cytokines, ECG, recall-antigen skin testing, or urine 3-methylhistidine as malnutrition indicators; the chapter lists these as NOT recommended for diagnosis (Harrison 22e pp.2618-2619). Comparing malnutrition prevalence across studies without accounting for differences between diagnostic tools, which yield incomparable rates (Harrison 22e p.2616). Failing to recognize prolonged pre-admission decreases in intake when an acute event is superimposed on chronic disease (Harrison 22e p.2617). Malnutrition arises from an imbalance between nutrient intake/assimilation and metabolic demand, and acute or chronic inflammation is now recognized as central to its pathophysiology. Inflammatory mediators raise resting energy expenditure, promote anabolic resistance and muscle catabolism, and cause anorexia that further reduces intake. Severe acute inflammation (e.g., critical illness, sepsis, burns, trauma, closed head injury) may be superimposed on a mild-to-moderate chronic inflammatory state (e.g., malignancy, COPD, congestive heart failure, chronic renal disease, chronic GI disease). The resulting deficits impair wound healing, immune function, and organ function. Because albumin and prealbumin behave as negative acute-phase reactants, the inflammatory milieu also distorts these traditional nutrition biomarkers (Harrison 22e pp.2615-2617). Malnutrition is associated with poor wound healing, compromised immunity, and impaired organ function, leading to longer hospital stays, more readmissions, higher mortality, and increased health care costs. Severe inflammation may limit nutritional interventions to a supportive rather than therapeutic role, and the associated malnutrition can diminish the effectiveness of medical therapies. Robust evidence indicates that a multipronged approach to malnutrition intervention reduces mortality and holds promise for improving quality of life, so timely diagnosis and treatment are important (Harrison 22e pp.2615, 2618). GLIM severity grading by phenotypic criteria. Stage 1 (moderate): weight loss 5-10% within 6 months or 10-20% beyond 6 months; BMI <20 (<70 years) or <22 (>=70 years); mild-to-moderate muscle mass deficit. Stage 2 (severe): weight loss >10% within 6 months or >20% beyond 6 months; BMI <18.5 (<70 years) or <20 (>=70 years); severe muscle mass deficit. WHO/NIH BMI categories: <18.5 underweight, 18.5-24.9 desirable, 25.0-29.9 overweight, >=30 obese (Harrison 22e pp.2616-2617).

Malonic aciduria (malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency) — MLYCD deficiency, malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency, malonic acidaemia, combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria (distinct entity) Methylmalonic and other classic organic acidaemias Fatty acid oxidation disorders with cardiomyopathy and hypoglycaemia Combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria (ACSF3-related), a distinct entity Mitochondrial disease presenting with cardiomyopathy Glycogen storage disorders with hypoglycaemia Other causes of infantile hypotonia with developmental delay Urine organic acids showing elevated malonic acid and the malonic to methylmalonic acid ratio Plasma acylcarnitine profile MLYCD molecular genetic testing Echocardiography for cardiomyopathy Blood glucose, blood gas and ketone measurement during illness Neuroimaging and developmental assessment A rare organic aciduria caused by deficiency of malonyl-CoA decarboxylase (MLYCD), which converts malonyl-CoA to acetyl-CoA and regulates fatty acid synthesis and oxidation Presents in infancy or childhood with developmental delay, hypotonia, seizures and cardiomyopathy Metabolic decompensation with hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis and ketosis can occur, sometimes triggered by fasting or illness The biochemical hallmark is elevated urinary malonic acid, often with a raised malonic to methylmalonic acid ratio Cardiomyopathy is an important feature and a major determinant of outcome Management centres on avoiding fasting, a modified diet and supportive metabolic care; carnitine supplementation may be used adjunctively Diagnosis is supported by urine organic acids and acylcarnitine profile and confirmed by MLYCD molecular testing Acute metabolic decompensation with hypoglycaemia and acidosis Signs of heart failure from cardiomyopathy New or worsening seizures Cardiac arrhythmia Confusing malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency with the distinct combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria Overlooking cardiomyopathy, which drives prognosis Failing to prevent catabolism during intercurrent illness Misreading a mildly abnormal organic acid profile without confirmatory genetics Malonyl-CoA decarboxylase converts malonyl-CoA to acetyl-CoA. Malonyl-CoA both provides substrate for fatty acid synthesis and inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1, the gatekeeper of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation. Loss of the enzyme causes malonyl-CoA accumulation, which impairs long-chain fatty acid oxidation and disturbs the balance of energy metabolism, particularly in heart and brain. Accumulated malonic acid is excreted in urine, giving the characteristic organic aciduria, while impaired energy supply underlies the cardiomyopathy, neurological features and susceptibility to metabolic crises. Outcome is variable and strongly influenced by the severity of cardiomyopathy; with dietary management and avoidance of fasting, some children stabilise, but significant cardiac or neurological disability can persist.

mesenteric artery/vein relationship Volvulus twists the bowel around the superior mesenteric vessels, threatening ischaemia and loss of the entire midgut within hours Treatment of volvulus is urgent laparotomy with counterclockwise detorsion and a Ladd procedure to broaden the mesenteric base Bilious vomiting in a neonate or infant, mandating emergency assessment for volvulus Abdominal distension with tenderness, guarding, or discoloration indicating ischaemia Blood per rectum, a late and ominous sign of bowel infarction Haemodynamic instability, acidosis, or rising lactate Rapid clinical deterioration where imaging should not delay laparotomy Dismissing bilious vomiting as benign feed intolerance and delaying imaging or surgery Awaiting non-urgent tests in a compromised infant instead of proceeding to laparotomy Relying on a normal abdominal radiograph to exclude volvulus Misinterpreting a normally positioned duodenojejunal junction variant and overlooking subtle malrotation Failing to perform appendicectomy and full Ladd manoeuvres, leaving the patient at future risk During normal development the midgut herniates, rotates 270 degrees counterclockwise around the superior mesenteric artery, and returns to the abdomen with broad retroperitoneal fixation of the duodenojejunal junction and caecum. In malrotation this sequence is arrested or aberrant, so the mesenteric root remains narrow and points of fixation are abnormal, often with peritoneal (Ladd) bands tethering the caecum across the duodenum. The narrow pedicle allows the midgut to twist around the superior mesenteric vessels, producing both luminal obstruction and vascular compromise; sustained torsion leads to venous congestion, arterial occlusion, and infarction of bowel supplied by the superior mesenteric artery. When volvulus is recognised and untwisted promptly the outcome is usually excellent, but delayed diagnosis can lead to massive bowel loss, short-bowel syndrome, or death. Elective Ladd procedure for asymptomatic malrotation carries low risk and prevents future volvulus.

generated by chronic infection or autoimmune inflammation. Persistent antigenic drive, exemplified by Helicobacter pylori in the stomach, sustains T-cell-dependent proliferation of marginal-zone B cells; early in the disease this dependence explains why eradicating the antigenic stimulus can lead to regression. The overall prognosis is excellent with prolonged survival; early gastric disease often achieves durable remission after H. pylori eradication, while t(11;18)-positive tumours are less likely to respond to eradication but usually remain localised, and the main adverse event is transformation to aggressive large B-cell lymphoma.

Mammary duct ectasia — Duct ectasia, Plasma cell mastitis Periductal mastitis Intraductal papilloma Ductal carcinoma in situ presenting with discharge or calcification Invasive carcinoma causing nipple retraction Paget's disease of the nipple Breast abscess Galactorrhoea from hyperprolactinaemia Triple assessment with examination, ultrasound and mammography Assessment of discharge for single- versus multiple-duct and colour Mammography to characterise secretory calcification and exclude malignancy Ultrasound of any subareolar mass or dilated duct Core biopsy of a discrete or suspicious mass Ductography or ductoscopy in selected discharge cases Serum prolactin and thyroid function if galactorrhoea is suspected Dilatation and shortening of the major subareolar (lactiferous) ducts, usually affecting peri- and postmenopausal women. Classic presentation is thick, cheesy, multicoloured nipple discharge (creamy, green or brown) from multiple ducts, often bilateral. Slit-like or transverse nipple retraction may develop as periductal fibrosis shortens the ducts and can mimic malignant retraction. A firm subareolar mass or thickening can form and, with associated calcification, may raise concern on mammography. Distinct from periductal mastitis, which affects younger smokers, although the two overlap within the duct ectasia-periductal mastitis spectrum. Coarse, rod-like ('needle-shaped') secretory calcifications aligned toward the nipple are a characteristic benign mammographic feature. Most cases need only reassurance once malignancy is excluded; total duct excision is reserved for troublesome discharge or recurrent problems. Blood-stained single-duct discharge should not be assumed to be duct ectasia and warrants investigation for papilloma or carcinoma. Blood-stained or single-duct nipple discharge A hard, irregular or fixed subareolar mass Fine pleomorphic or branching microcalcification rather than coarse secretory calcification Eczematous or ulcerated nipple change suggesting Paget's disease Progressive unilateral nipple retraction with skin distortion Assuming all nipple retraction is malignant, or conversely dismissing malignant retraction as benign ectasia Failing to distinguish benign coarse secretory calcification from suspicious pleomorphic microcalcification Attributing blood-stained single-duct discharge to ectasia without excluding papilloma or carcinoma Confusing duct ectasia with periductal mastitis and mismanaging the younger smoker Overlooking hyperprolactinaemia when discharge is milky and bilateral Mammary duct ectasia is a benign involutional process in which the large subareolar ducts dilate and fill with inspissated proteinaceous and lipid-rich secretions. Stagnant secretions may leak into the periductal tissue, provoking a chronic inflammatory reaction rich in plasma cells and macrophages (giving the alternative term plasma cell mastitis) and progressive periductal fibrosis. This fibrosis shortens the ducts, producing nipple retraction, while the retained secretions calcify to form the characteristic coarse ductal calcifications. The condition sits at the involutional end of the duct ectasia-periductal mastitis spectrum and is more prevalent with advancing age. Duct ectasia is a benign, self-limiting condition that does not increase breast cancer risk. Symptoms often settle spontaneously, and surgery, when required for persistent discharge or retraction, is generally curative.

fracture Missing a second (often condylar) fracture after identifying the first Failing to recognise malocclusion as a key diagnostic sign Underestimating infection risk in fractures communicating with the oral cavity Overlooking airway risk in bilateral anterior fractures Prolonged rigid immobilisation of condylar fractures leading to stiffness or ankylosis Neglecting to document inferior alveolar nerve deficit before intervention The mandible is a mobile, U-shaped bone whose weaker regions - the condylar neck, angle (often at an unerupted third molar), and parasymphysis - are prone to fracture. Because it forms a ring-like structure articulating at both temporomandibular joints, force at one point is frequently transmitted to produce a second fracture elsewhere. Displacement is influenced by the pull of the muscles of mastication, which can distract or override fracture segments depending on their orientation (favourable versus unfavourable patterns). Fractures through tooth-bearing segments breach the oral mucosa, creating a contaminated, effectively open injury, and disruption of the inferior alveolar nerve within the canal causes lower lip and chin numbness. Most mandibular fractures heal well with restored occlusion and function when reduction and fixation are appropriate, and many condylar fractures do well with conservative management. Poorer outcomes - malunion, malocclusion, nonunion, infection, temporomandibular joint stiffness or ankylosis, and persistent nerve numbness - are associated with delayed treatment, inadequate reduction, open contaminated fractures, or prolonged immobilisation.

pancreatitis Progressive skeletal deformity and joint contractures limiting function Rapidly advancing progeroid features in the more severe MADB form Poorly controlled insulin-resistant diabetes Mistaking the disorder for isolated familial partial lipodystrophy and missing the skeletal features Overlooking acro-osteolysis on hand radiographs Failing to distinguish the milder LMNA type from the more severe ZMPSTE24 type Neglecting metabolic screening for diabetes and hypertriglyceridaemia Not arranging genetic confirmation and counselling Mandibuloacral dysplasia is a laminopathy-spectrum disorder caused by biallelic mutations in LMNA, which encodes the nuclear-lamina proteins lamin A/C, or in ZMPSTE24, the metalloprotease that cleaves prelamin A to mature lamin A. Defective lamin processing destabilises the nuclear envelope, impairing the function and survival of mesenchymal-derived tissues including bone and adipocytes. This produces the characteristic mandibular and acral skeletal defects, progeroid connective-tissue changes, and loss of subcutaneous fat. As with other lipodystrophies, reduced fat-storage capacity drives ectopic lipid deposition, insulin resistance, acanthosis nigricans, and a tendency to hypertriglyceridaemia and diabetes. Prognosis varies with subtype and severity; the LMNA-related type A tends to be milder with a partial lipodystrophy phenotype, whereas the ZMPSTE24-related type B is more severe and progeroid, and long-term outlook is shaped by metabolic and skeletal complications.

forms part of the U5 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein of the major spliceosome, the molecular machine that removes introns from pre-messenger RNA. Loss-of-function variants reduce the amount of functional protein (haploinsufficiency), impairing efficient and accurate splicing during a critical window of embryonic development. Tissues derived from the neural crest, which give rise to much of the facial skeleton and ears, appear particularly sensitive to this reduction, producing the characteristic mandibulofacial dysostosis. Concurrent disturbance of neuronal proliferation is thought to underlie the microcephaly and intellectual disability, while disrupted patterning of the foregut and other structures accounts for the oesophageal and cardiac anomalies. Outcome is highly variable and is driven chiefly by the severity of airway compromise, feeding difficulty and cardiac disease in infancy; with coordinated multidisciplinary care these can often be managed, after which intellectual ability determines longer-term function across a wide spectrum from mild to severe impairment.

primary immunodeficiency Over-attributing a patient's recurrent infections to MBL deficiency and stopping the workup prematurely Treating a common benign polymorphism as a serious primary immunodeficiency Failing to look for a co-existing, more clinically important immune defect Interpreting a single low MBL level without a functional lectin pathway assessment Mannose-binding lectin is a circulating pattern-recognition molecule of the innate immune system that binds carbohydrate arrays on microbial surfaces and activates the lectin pathway of complement through MBL-associated serine Common polymorphisms in the MBL2 gene reduce the amount of functional, correctly oligomerised protein, lowering lectin-pathway activity. Because this pathway provides an antibody-independent first line of defence, deficiency may leave a window of increased vulnerability, particularly in infancy or when other arms of immunity are compromised; however, redundancy with the classical and alternative complement pathways and with adaptive immunity means most deficient individuals remain healthy. The great majority of individuals with low mannose-binding lectin are healthy and have a normal outlook; any excess infection risk is modest and mainly emerges in combination with immune immaturity, another immune defect, or immunosuppression.

Mansonelliasis (Mansonella filariasis) — Mansonella perstans, Mansonella ozzardi, Mansonella streptocerca, Mansonella filariasis Lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia species) Onchocerciasis Loiasis Other causes of eosinophilia such as strongyloidiasis and toxocariasis Allergic and hypersensitivity disorders Reactive or inflammatory arthropathy Peripheral blood films (including concentration techniques) for microfilariae Skin snip examination for M. streptocerca microfilariae Full blood count to detect eosinophilia Species identification of microfilariae by morphology or molecular methods Screening for co-infection with other filariae, particularly Loa loa before treatment Serological or antigen tests where available to support diagnosis Mansonelliasis is a filarial infection caused by Mansonella species (M. perstans, M. ozzardi, M. streptocerca) transmitted by biting midges and blackflies It is endemic across parts of sub-Saharan Africa, and the Caribbean and Latin America, often coexisting with other filariases Most infections are asymptomatic or cause mild, non-specific complaints, so the parasite is frequently an incidental finding When symptomatic, features may include itching, transient swellings, arthralgia, serous-cavity involvement and, with M. streptocerca, skin changes Peripheral eosinophilia is common and may be the clue that prompts investigation Diagnosis rests on detecting microfilariae in blood or skin, depending on species; M. perstans and M. ozzardi produce blood microfilariae while M. streptocerca is found in skin Treatment differs by species and often involves agents such as diethylcarbamazine or ivermectin, with doxycycline used against Wolbachia-harbouring species Marked eosinophilia with systemic symptoms warranting exclusion of other pathology Co-infection with Loa loa raising the risk of treatment-related reactions Serositis or effusions attributable to the parasite Persistent symptoms despite therapy suggesting alternative or additional diagnoses Attributing all symptoms to Mansonella when co-infection with other filariae is common Treating without first excluding heavy Loa loa co-infection Missing the diagnosis because microfilariae require the correct sampling method and timing Over-treating an incidental, asymptomatic infection Mansonella infection begins when infective larvae are inoculated by biting midges (Culicoides) or blackflies during a blood meal. The larvae mature into adult worms that reside in serous cavities, mesentery or subcutaneous tissue depending on the species, and release microfilariae into the blood or skin. Many species harbour Wolbachia endosymbiotic bacteria that contribute to inflammatory responses. Because the parasite provokes relatively little tissue reaction in most hosts, infection is often clinically silent; symptomatic disease reflects localised inflammatory and hypersensitivity responses to the worms and microfilariae, frequently accompanied by eosinophilia. The prognosis is generally very good, as most infections are benign and asymptomatic; symptomatic disease usually responds to appropriate species-directed therapy, though clearance of adult worms can be slow.

leukaemic non-nodal variant as aggressively as classic disease Overlooking TP53 status, which should influence treatment choice Failing to consider gastrointestinal involvement, which is common even when asymptomatic Mantle cell lymphoma arises from a mature B cell of the follicle mantle zone, generally before germinal-centre transit. The defining event is the t(11;14) translocation, which places the CCND1 gene under the control of the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer and leads to constitutive overexpression of cyclin D1, dysregulating the cell cycle at the G1-S transition. The transcription factor SOX11 is commonly expressed and contributes to the tumour phenotype. Additional genomic lesions affecting DNA-damage response and cell-cycle pathways, notably TP53 and CDKN2A alterations, drive more aggressive blastoid disease. The tumour disseminates widely, colonising the mantle zones of follicles and infiltrating nodes, spleen, marrow, blood and the gastrointestinal tract. Classic mantle cell lymphoma is generally incurable with a relapsing course, though modern chemoimmunotherapy, HSCT and targeted agents have improved survival; blastoid morphology, high Ki-67 and TP53 abnormalities predict poor outcomes, whereas the leukaemic non-nodal SOX11-negative variant can follow an indolent course.

Map-dot-fingerprint dystrophy — epithelial basement membrane dystrophy, Cogan microcystic dystrophy, anterior basement membrane dystrophy Recurrent corneal erosion from prior trauma Meesmann corneal dystrophy Dry eye disease Epithelial infectious keratitis (during an acute erosion) Other anterior corneal dystrophies Slit-lamp examination, including retroillumination, for the characteristic patterns Fluorescein staining to identify epithelial defects during erosions Corneal topography if irregular astigmatism affects vision History focused on recurrent erosion episodes Exclusion of infection during an acute painful episode The commonest anterior corneal dystrophy, involving abnormal epithelial basement membrane Slit-lamp examination shows map-like patches, dot-like microcysts and fingerprint lines in the epithelium Many patients are asymptomatic, but it is a leading cause of recurrent corneal erosion syndrome Recurrent erosions cause episodes of sharp pain, watering and photophobia, classically on waking It can transiently blur vision and cause irregular astigmatism Management targets recurrent erosions with lubrication and, if needed, procedures such as epithelial debridement or stromal micropuncture Signs of infective keratitis complicating an erosion Persistent or non-healing epithelial defect Significant visual loss from irregular astigmatism or scarring Frequent disabling erosion episodes Missing an infective keratitis during an acute erosion Overlooking the dystrophy as the underlying cause of recurrent erosions Under-treating erosions and allowing recurrent episodes Attributing visual blur solely to refractive error Map-dot-fingerprint dystrophy is characterised by abnormal production and organisation of the epithelial basement membrane, with reduplicated membrane and intraepithelial cysts. Poor adhesion of the corneal epithelium to this faulty basement membrane predisposes to recurrent breakdown, so the epithelium detaches, producing recurrent corneal erosions. The abnormal membrane and microcysts create the characteristic map, dot and fingerprint patterns and can distort the overlying epithelial surface. The dystrophy is benign and often asymptomatic; recurrent erosions can be troublesome but are usually controllable, and vision is generally preserved.

Maple Syrup Urine Disease — MSUD, branched-chain ketoaciduria, BCKD deficiency Neonatal sepsis Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy Urea cycle disorders Organic acidemias Nonketotic hyperglycinemia Other causes of neonatal encephalopathy and seizures Newborn screening result and confirmatory plasma amino acid profile (elevated leucine, presence of alloisoleucine) Urine organic acids and detection of branched-chain ketoacids Molecular genetic testing of the BCKD complex genes Blood gas, glucose, ammonia, and ketone assessment during crises Neuroimaging if cerebral oedema is suspected An autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, impairing breakdown of the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine. The classic severe form presents in the first week of life with poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, and worsening encephalopathy after protein feeding begins. Neurological signs may include fluctuating tone, dystonic posturing, a boxing or bicycling movement pattern, and progression to seizures and coma. The urine, sweat, or cerumen may carry a characteristic sweet, maple-syrup or burnt-sugar odour. Leucine and its ketoacid accumulation is the principal driver of neurotoxicity and cerebral oedema. Newborn screening detects elevated branched-chain amino acids; diagnosis is confirmed by the plasma amino acid pattern (notably raised leucine and the presence of alloisoleucine) and molecular testing. Acute management centres on halting protein intake, promoting anabolism with adequate energy, and rapidly lowering branched-chain amino acid levels, with dialysis or haemofiltration in severe crises. Long-term treatment is a carefully monitored diet restricting branched-chain amino acids while providing enough protein and energy for growth. Intercurrent illness, fasting, or catabolic stress can precipitate metabolic crises even in previously stable, treated children. Rapidly progressive encephalopathy with lethargy, abnormal movements, and coma in a neonate Signs of cerebral oedema and raised intracranial pressure Metabolic crisis precipitated by intercurrent illness or fasting Marked elevation of leucine requiring emergency clearance Seizures or apnoea in a decompensating infant Mistaking early presentation for neonatal sepsis and delaying metabolic evaluation Not recognising the characteristic sweet odour as a diagnostic clue Continuing protein feeds during an acute crisis instead of stopping them and driving anabolism Underestimating how rapidly catabolic stress can trigger dangerous decompensation Failing to establish sick-day plans and long-term dietary monitoring A defect in the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex blocks the oxidative decarboxylation of the ketoacids derived from leucine, isoleucine, and valine. As a result these branched-chain amino acids and their corresponding ketoacids accumulate in blood, urine, and tissues. Leucine and its ketoacid are particularly neurotoxic, disturbing neurotransmitter balance, cerebral amino acid transport, and cellular osmolarity, which produces cerebral oedema and encephalopathy. During catabolic states, endogenous protein breakdown releases further branched-chain amino acids, precipitating acute, potentially life-threatening metabolic decompensation. Outcome depends on how quickly the diagnosis is made and metabolic control is achieved; early treatment and avoidance of crises support near-normal development, whereas repeated or severe decompensations and prolonged high leucine levels risk permanent neurological damage. Lifelong dietary management and prompt sick-day protocols are essential.

Marasmus — severe wasting, protein-energy malnutrition (non-oedematous), energy malnutrition Kwashiorkor and marasmic-kwashiorkor Wasting from chronic infection such as tuberculosis or HIV Malabsorptive disorders Malignancy and other chronic wasting illnesses Congenital or metabolic disease causing failure to thrive Anthropometry with weight-for-height and mid-upper-arm circumference Blood glucose and body temperature to detect hypoglycaemia and hypothermia Electrolytes including potassium, magnesium, and phosphate Screening for underlying and intercurrent infection Assessment for micronutrient deficiencies and anaemia Marked wasting of muscle and subcutaneous fat gives an emaciated, wizened appearance with an apparently large head and loose skin folds Unlike kwashiorkor there is no oedema, and the child is often alert but irritable and ravenously hungry It results from severe, prolonged deficiency of total energy intake, frequently compounded by chronic infection or feeding difficulties It remains a significant problem among food-insecure young children in India and other low-resource settings Hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, and infection are common and dangerous accompaniments Assessment relies on anthropometry, especially low weight-for-height and reduced mid-upper-arm circumference Nutritional rehabilitation must be gradual to avoid refeeding complications Hypoglycaemia and hypothermia in a severely wasted child Signs of sepsis, which may be subtle Circulatory compromise from severe dehydration Refeeding-related electrolyte shifts during nutritional rehabilitation Refeeding too rapidly and precipitating refeeding syndrome or cardiac failure Failing to detect and correct hypoglycaemia and hypothermia early Overlooking an underlying chronic infection such as tuberculosis Rehydrating aggressively and causing fluid and electrolyte imbalance Marasmus is a form of severe acute malnutrition dominated by deficiency of overall energy intake. The body adapts to prolonged starvation by mobilising fat and muscle for fuel, lowering metabolic rate, and preserving visceral protein and albumin, which is why oedema is characteristically absent. Depletion of energy stores leads to profound wasting, immune suppression, gut mucosal atrophy, and impaired thermoregulation and glucose homeostasis. As with other forms of severe malnutrition, the depleted state creates vulnerability to hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, infection, and to metabolic disturbance during refeeding. Gradual nutritional rehabilitation with treatment of infection allows recovery, but delayed presentation, sepsis, or mismanaged refeeding carry a high mortality, and prolonged early malnutrition can impair growth and development.

corticosteroids requiring urgent escalation Delaying treatment while pursuing an assumed tumour diagnosis Confusing it with monophasic acute disseminated encephalomyelitis and under-treating Omitting The variant carries a guarded prognosis, historically often fatal within months, though aggressive modern immunotherapy has allowed survival and partial recovery in some patients.

which a ptotic upper eyelid elevates on movement of the jaw, classically when the mouth opens or the jaw moves to the opposite side Reflects anomalous connections between the motor branch of the trigeminal nerve supplying the pterygoid muscles and the levator palpebrae superioris Usually unilateral and present from birth, often noticed during bottle or breast feeding as the lid flickers with involve levator disinsertion with frontalis suspension, sometimes bilaterally for symmetry Amblyopia from ptosis, anisometropia or strabismus needing prompt treatment A large or cosmetically and socially troublesome wink causing functional impact Associated ophthalmoplegia or pupil signs suggesting a third nerve process Fatigable ptosis raising the possibility of myasthenia Correcting the ptosis without addressing the synkinetic levator, leaving a persistent wink Missing associated amblyopia, anisometropia or strabismus Failing to observe feeding or jaw movement and overlooking the diagnosis Confusing it with aberrant third nerve regeneration Marcus Gunn jaw-winking is a congenital trigemino-oculomotor synkinesis caused by aberrant innervation, in which fibres of the motor division of the trigeminal nerve destined for the pterygoid muscles are misdirected to the levator palpebrae superioris. As a result, activation of the jaw muscles simultaneously produces contraction of the levator, so the ptotic lid rises when the mouth opens or the jaw deviates. The baseline ptosis reflects the abnormal levator innervation, and the synkinetic elevation is an involuntary, stimulus-linked movement. Because the anomaly is at the level of nerve wiring, the winking is not abolished by conventional levator-strengthening surgery alone. The synkinesis is stable and benign, and outcomes are generally good when amblyopia is managed and surgery is appropriately selected, though residual asymmetry or persistence of the wink can occur if the synkinetic levator is not addressed.

individualised to body size and family history Activity advice usually restricts high-intensity isometric exercise, competitive contact sport, and heavy lifting to reduce aortic wall stress Sudden severe chest, back, or abdominal pain suggesting acute aortic dissection Rapidly enlarging aortic root or diameter approaching the surgical threshold New aortic regurgitation or signs of cardiac failure Sudden painless visual loss suggesting retinal detachment or acute lens dislocation Symptoms of pneumothorax such as acute breathlessness and pleuritic pain Attributing tall marfanoid habitus to Marfan syndrome without excluding homocystinuria, which needs different management Relying on a single aortic measurement rather than tracking the trend over time Overlooking non-aortic vascular and ocular complications during follow-up Failing to offer cascade family screening and genetic counselling Assuming a normal childhood echocardiogram excludes future aortic disease Marfan syndrome results from loss of normal fibrillin-1, a glycoprotein that assembles into microfibrils forming the scaffold of elastic fibres in the aorta, suspensory ligament of the lens, skin, and periosteum. Deficient or abnormal microfibrils weaken these connective tissues and also dysregulate transforming growth factor beta signalling, since microfibrils normally sequester latent TGF-beta. Excess TGF-beta activity contributes to progressive weakening and dilatation of the aortic media, degeneration of the zonular fibres causing lens subluxation, and overgrowth of the long bones. The combined structural and signalling defects explain the cardiovascular, ocular, skeletal, and dural manifestations. With regular cardiovascular surveillance, medical aortic protection, and timely prophylactic surgery, life expectancy now approaches that of the general population. Untreated aortic disease carries a high risk of dissection and premature death, so adherence to monitoring and lifestyle advice is critical.

to infection by marine organisms such as Vibrio species, so wound care, tetanus prophylaxis and vigilance for infection are essential A small number of syndromes are rapidly life-threatening (Chironex cardiotoxicity, Irukandji cardiac failure, tetrodotoxin paralysis from blue-ringed octopus, sea snake neuro/myotoxicity), so resuscitation and monitoring come first Specific antivenoms exist for a few marine species (box jellyfish, stonefish, sea snake); most stings are managed supportively Cardiovascular collapse or arrhythmia after a jellyfish sting Progressive paralysis or respiratory failure Delayed severe systemic syndrome after a trivial sting (Irukandji) Spreading soft-tissue infection or systemic sepsis Compartment syndrome or extensive necrosis around a puncture wound Applying a single decontamination method to all jellyfish stings rather than species-appropriate treatment Rinsing cnidarian stings with fresh water or rubbing them, provoking further nematocyst discharge Missing retained spine fragments and marine wound infection during follow-up Focusing on local wound care while overlooking rapidly evolving systemic toxicity Marine venoms are delivered by two main mechanisms. Cnidarians (jellyfish, anemones, corals) fire nematocysts that inject venom on contact, with effects ranging from local pain and dermatitis to systemic cardiotoxicity or catecholamine-driven syndromes. Venomous fish, stingrays, sea urchins and cone snails introduce venom through spines, barbs or a radular tooth, causing intense local pain, tissue injury and, in some species, systemic neurotoxic or cardiovascular effects. Many fish and echinoderm venoms are heat-labile proteins, explaining the benefit of hot-water immersion, whereas cnidarian nematocyst discharge is influenced by osmotic and chemical changes, which underpins species-specific decontamination. Most marine envenomations cause self-limiting local pain and heal well with first aid and wound care. A minority of species cause life-threatening systemic toxicity, where outcome depends on prompt resuscitation, appropriate decontamination and, where available, species-specific antivenom.

and repair creates an environment of persistent inflammation, sustained cellular proliferation and impaired local immune surveillance within scarred, poorly vascularised tissue. Over a prolonged latent period, accumulated genetic damage in chronically regenerating keratinocytes, together with the tumour-permissive inflammatory milieu and relative isolation of the scar from immune effector cells, drives malignant transformation, most often to squamous cell carcinoma. Prognosis depends on tumour type, differentiation, depth of invasion and nodal status; well-differentiated lesions detected early can be cured by excision, but nodal metastasis, notably with burn-scar carcinomas, markedly worsens outcome.

respiratory involvement in later disease Markesbery-Griggs myopathy is a myofibrillar myopathy caused by dominant variants in LDB3, which encodes the Z-band alternatively spliced PDZ-motif protein (ZASP). ZASP stabilises the sarcomeric Z-disc through interactions with alpha-actinin and other cytoskeletal proteins. Mutant ZASP disrupts Z-disc integrity, leading to disintegration of myofibrils, streaming of Z-disc material, and abnormal aggregation of cytoskeletal proteins including desmin. This myofibrillar disorganisation produces progressive muscle weakness and, because the same proteins are important in cardiac muscle and nerve, predisposes to associated cardiomyopathy, conduction disease, and neuropathy. Skeletal muscle weakness progresses slowly over years, but overall prognosis depends heavily on associated cardiac involvement; unrecognised cardiomyopathy or conduction disease can be life-limiting, making cardiac surveillance central to management.

pathogenic variants in ARSB, causing deficiency of arylsulfatase B (also called N-acetylgalactosamine-4-sulfatase). This enzyme is required for the lysosomal degradation of dermatan sulfate, so its deficiency leads to accumulation of dermatan sulfate within lysosomes of connective tissue, cartilage, bone, cornea, heart valves, and meninges. The resulting multisystem storage produces the characteristic skeletal, ocular, and cardiac disease. Because heparan sulfate metabolism is unaffected and the brain is relatively spared, cognition is typically normal despite severe somatic involvement. Excess dermatan sulfate is excreted in the urine. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and residual enzyme activity correlates broadly with disease severity. Outlook varies widely with disease severity; rapidly progressive forms cause early cardiorespiratory and skeletal complications, while attenuated forms allow survival into adulthood. Enzyme replacement therapy improves endurance and some somatic manifestations but does not reverse established skeletal or corneal disease.

ulcer is a painful ischaemic skin ulcer caused by subcutaneous arteriolosclerosis, arising almost exclusively in patients with long-standing, often poorly controlled arterial hypertension and frequently coexisting type 2 diabetes It characteristically affects the dorsolateral aspect of the lower leg or the region overlying the Achilles tendon, and is bilateral in a substantial proportion of cases The pain is severe and disproportionate to ulcer size; lesions begin as a livid or purpuric patch that rapidly breaks down into a necrotic ulcer with an irregular, often serpiginous, advancing border Peripheral pulses are typically preserved and the ankle-brachial index is normal, which helps distinguish it from large-vessel atherosclerotic arterial ulceration Diagnosis rests on subintimal proliferation It is frequently mistaken for pyoderma gangrenosum, and inappropriate immunosuppression may worsen the wound and delay correct treatment Management centres on optimising blood pressure control, meticulous wound care with debridement of necrotic tissue, and adequate analgesia, while avoiding strongly vasoconstricting agents where feasible Early split-skin grafting, sometimes aided by negative-pressure wound therapy, can markedly reduce pain and accelerate healing Rapidly enlarging necrotic ulcer with pain out of proportion to its appearance Signs of secondary wound infection or systemic sepsis Features suggesting calciphylaxis, such as renal failure or dialysis dependence with painful skin necrosis Exposure of deep structures such as tendon within the wound base Misdiagnosing the ulcer as pyoderma gangrenosum and treating with immunosuppression Attributing the ulcer to large-vessel arterial disease despite normal pulses and ankle pressures Providing inadequate analgesia for a characteristically severe pain Taking a superficial biopsy that fails to sample the deep arteriolar pathology Relying on strongly vasoconstricting antihypertensive agents that may impair skin perfusion The primary lesion in Martorell ulcer lies in the subcutaneous small arteries and arterioles, which develop medial hypertrophy and calcification together with subintimal (myointimal) proliferation as a consequence of chronic arterial hypertension and diabetic microvascular disease. Progressive luminal narrowing of these vessels critically reduces dermal and subcutaneous perfusion, so that a comparatively minor rise in local tissue pressure or trivial trauma produces a cutaneous infarct. Because the occlusive process is confined to the microcirculation, the large conduit arteries remain patent and pulses are preserved, yet the ischaemic skin necroses and ulcerates, extending as the surrounding arterioles are progressively compromised. Martorell ulcers are typically slow to heal and intensely painful, but with good blood pressure control, meticulous wound care and early skin grafting many will heal; recurrence and involvement of the contralateral leg are common.

early activation of an institutional protocol streamlines product delivery Ongoing uncontrolled haemorrhage with haemodynamic instability requiring emergency surgical or interventional haemostasis Refractory hypocalcaemia with cardiovascular compromise during rapid transfusion Rising potassium with electrocardiographic changes Persistent coagulopathy despite balanced product resuscitation, suggesting DIC or hyperfibrinolysis Over-reliance on crystalloid resuscitation, worsening dilutional coagulopathy and tissue oedema Neglecting patient and fluid warming, allowing hypothermia-driven coagulopathy Forgetting to monitor and replace ionised calcium during rapid citrate exposure Continuing fixed high-ratio product delivery after bleeding is controlled rather than switching to laboratory-guided replacement Massive haemorrhage and its replacement produce a combination of dilutional and consumptive coagulopathy: clotting factors and platelets are lost with bleeding and diluted by crystalloid and red cell replacement. Hypoperfusion drives metabolic acidosis and, together with infusion of cold products, causes hypothermia; both impair enzymatic clotting and platelet function. Citrate load from banked products chelates ionised calcium and magnesium, further impairing coagulation and cardiac contractility, while potassium leaked from stored red cells can accumulate. The result is a self-perpetuating cycle of bleeding, impaired haemostasis, and shock unless actively interrupted. Outcome depends chiefly on control of the bleeding source and speed of resuscitation; early balanced transfusion, prevention of the lethal triad, and timely antifibrinolytic therapy improve survival, whereas delayed correction of coagulopathy and shock markedly increases mortality.

Massive transfusion coagulopathy — Dilutional coagulopathy, Coagulopathy of massive transfusion Disseminated intravascular coagulation Trauma-induced coagulopathy Pre-existing anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy Inherited bleeding disorder unmasked by haemorrhage Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction with coagulopathy Hyperfibrinolysis Full blood count with platelet count Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time Fibrinogen concentration Viscoelastic testing such as thromboelastography or rotational thromboelastometry Ionised calcium, temperature and arterial blood gas for the lethal triad D-dimer and fibrin degradation products where disseminated intravascular coagulation is suspected A bleeding tendency arising during large-volume resuscitation, driven by dilution and consumption of clotting factors and platelets, hypothermia, acidosis and hypocalcaemia. The lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy is self-reinforcing and a leading cause of death in major haemorrhage. Stored red cells contain little functional platelet or coagulation factor activity, so replacing large blood losses with red cells alone dilutes haemostasis. Fibrinogen is often the first factor to fall to critical levels and requires early replacement with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate. Modern major haemorrhage protocols favour balanced ratios of red cells, plasma and platelets and early empirical treatment before laboratory results return. Point-of-care viscoelastic testing can guide targeted component therapy and reduce unnecessary transfusion. Correcting hypothermia and acidosis is essential because clotting enzymes function poorly when cold and acidotic. In trauma, an early consumptive coagulopathy of trauma-induced coagulopathy coexists with and precedes purely dilutional effects. Diffuse microvascular oozing from wounds, puncture sites and mucosa Critically low fibrinogen during ongoing haemorrhage Core hypothermia with worsening bleeding Severe metabolic acidosis in a bleeding patient Ionised hypocalcaemia during rapid transfusion Resuscitating with red cells and crystalloid alone and neglecting plasma, platelets and fibrinogen. Waiting for laboratory results before treating in the face of active major haemorrhage. Ignoring hypothermia and acidosis while transfusing components. Overlooking hypocalcaemia from citrate during rapid transfusion. Failing to consider trauma-induced coagulopathy and hyperfibrinolysis as distinct contributors. Massive transfusion coagulopathy is a multifactorial failure of haemostasis during and after large-volume blood replacement. As shed blood is replaced with red cell concentrates and crystalloid, platelets and coagulation factors are progressively diluted while ongoing bleeding and clot formation consume them. Concurrent hypothermia slows the kinetics of coagulation enzymes and impairs platelet function, and metabolic acidosis from hypoperfusion further inhibits the coagulation cascade and accelerates fibrinogen breakdown. Citrate-induced hypocalcaemia reduces calcium-dependent clotting reactions and myocardial performance. In trauma an endogenous trauma-induced coagulopathy, driven by tissue injury, shock, endothelial activation and hyperfibrinolysis, is superimposed on these dilutional and metabolic derangements. Together these processes produce diffuse microvascular bleeding that compounds the original haemorrhage. Outcome depends on rapid haemorrhage control and correction of the lethal triad; established coagulopathy with hypothermia and acidosis carries high mortality. Structured major haemorrhage protocols with balanced component ratios and goal-directed therapy improve survival.

constellation of disturbances that accompanies replacement of a large proportion of the circulating blood volume within hours. Coagulopathy develops through dilution and consumption of clotting factors and platelets, compounded by fibrinolysis and by the underlying tissue injury. Stored components are anticoagulated with citrate, which binds ionised calcium and can produce hypocalcaemia that impairs both coagulation and myocardial contractility. Cold components lower core temperature, and the resulting hypothermia slows the enzymatic clotting cascade and platelet function. Tissue hypoperfusion generates a metabolic acidosis, and together hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy form a self-reinforcing lethal triad. Outcome is largely determined by the underlying cause of haemorrhage and the speed of control, but timely correction of coagulopathy, calcium, temperature and acidosis within a structured major haemorrhage protocol improves survival.

Most patients achieve good symptom control with trigger avoidance and mediator-directed therapy and have a normal life expectancy; prognosis is less favourable when there is an underlying advanced clonal mast cell disorder.

Mast cell leukaemia has a poor prognosis with short median survival in many series, though newer KIT-targeted agents and transplantation may improve outcomes in selected patients.

Loss of maspardin is thought to disturb endosomal sorting and membrane homeostasis in neurons, leading to a diffuse neurodegenerative process. This affects the corticospinal tracts, cerebral white matter (with the characteristic thin corpus callosum), cerebellum and basal ganglia, producing the combination of spastic paraparesis, dementia and mixed cerebellar and extrapyramidal features that defines the syndrome. MAST syndrome progresses slowly but is a multisystem neurodegenerative disorder, and over years affected individuals develop increasing motor disability and dementia with substantial dependence.

Mastocytosis — mast cell disease, systemic mastocytosis Carcinoid syndrome (exclude with 24-h urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid) Pheochromocytoma (exclude with 24-h urine/plasma metanephrines) Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (autosomal dominant extra copies of the alpha-tryptase gene at TPSAB1; elevated baseline serum tryptase with multisystem mast cell activation symptoms) Recurrent IgE-mediated or idiopathic anaphylaxis (usually presents with urticaria, angioedema and/or bronchospasm, which are not typical manifestations of anaphylaxis in SM) Basal (baseline) serum tryptase as a noninvasive screen before bone marrow biopsy Bone marrow biopsy with mast cell morphology, immunophenotype (CD25, CD2, CD30), and KIT D816V mutation testing for systemic disease Skin biopsy to confirm diffuse cutaneous and bullous mastocytosis subvariants 24-h urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (carcinoid) and metanephrines (pheochromocytoma) to exclude mimics Bone densitometry, bone scan, or skeletal survey (osteoporosis is increased and may cause pathologic fractures) CT scan or endoscopy and neuropsychiatric evaluation as directed by presentation Carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhea) Pheochromocytoma (flushing, tachycardia, vascular collapse) Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia Idiopathic or IgE-mediated anaphylaxis Mastocytosis is defined by accumulation of clonally expanded mast cells in tissues (skin, bone marrow, liver, spleen, gut); mast cell expansion is most readily identified in skin and/or bone marrow (p.2819). More than 90% of patients carry a somatic gain-of-function KIT D816V mutation in the stem cell factor receptor gene (p.2819). Classification recognizes cutaneous mastocytosis (with variants), systemic mastocytosis (SM, five variants), and mast cell sarcoma; cutaneous mastocytosis is the most common diagnosis in children and is usually diagnosed within the first year of life (p.2819-2820). Systemic mastocytosis denotes involvement of an extracutaneous site, most often bone marrow; indolent systemic mastocytosis (ISM) accounts for >70% of adult patients and is associated with a normal life expectancy (p.2820). Cutaneous lesions of maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (MPCM, also called urticaria pigmentosa) are reddish-brown macules, papules, or plaques that urticate and become erythematous on rubbing or trauma (Darier's sign) (p.2820). Clinical manifestations of SM reflect release of bioactive mast cell mediators plus tissue infiltration: intermittent urticaria, flushing, tachycardia and vascular collapse, gastric acid hypersecretion, crampy lower abdominal pain, and diarrhea (p.2820). Anaphylaxis in mastocytosis is most commonly triggered by Hymenoptera stings and NSAIDs; symptom flares may also follow alcohol, temperature change, stress, and mast cell-interactive opioids (p.2820). A basal serum tryptase level is a useful noninvasive test to consider before bone marrow biopsy; total serum tryptase >20 ng/mL is a minor diagnostic criterion for SM (p.2821). Diagnosis of SM requires tissue confirmation (lesional/bone marrow biopsy): one major plus one minor, or three minor criteria. Major = multifocal dense mast cell aggregates (>15 mast cells per aggregate) in extracutaneous tissue; minor = spindled/atypical morphology, aberrant CD25/CD2/CD30 phenotype, activating KIT mutation, or tryptase >20 ng/mL (p.2821). Patients with recurrent mast cell activation (especially anaphylaxis with hypotensive syncope) who carry KIT D816V but do not meet full SM criteria are termed monoclonal mast cell activation syndrome (p.2821). Anaphylaxis with rapid, life-threatening vascular collapse (most often after Hymenoptera stings or NSAIDs) Hypotensive syncope from mast cell activation C findings of aggressive disease: cytopenias, hepatomegaly with ascites and impaired liver function, splenomegaly with hypersplenism, malabsorption with hypoalbuminemia and weight loss, or osteolytic skeletal lesions with pathologic fractures Circulating atypical mast cells suggesting mast cell leukemia Atopy is not increased in mastocytosis compared with the general population (p.2819). Imatinib is not effective in most cases because the KIT D816V mutation confers resistance (p.2821). Osteoporosis alone without osteolytic lesions does not satisfy the C-finding skeletal criterion for aggressive SM (p.2821). SM cannot be confirmed on clinical and laboratory grounds alone; tissue diagnosis is required (p.2821). Anaphylaxis in SM typically lacks the urticaria, angioedema, and bronchospasm seen in IgE-mediated or idiopathic anaphylaxis (p.2821). Baseline serum tryptase elevation must be interpreted with caution where hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (extra TPSAB1 copies) coexists (p.2821). Mastocytosis is a clonal mast cell disorder driven by somatic gain-of-function mutations in the KIT (stem cell factor receptor) gene, with KIT D816V present in >90% of patients. The mutation produces ligand-independent KIT activation and clonal mast cell proliferation/accumulation in skin, bone marrow, liver, spleen, and gut. KIT mutations occur across all forms of SM and in lesional skin of some children with cutaneous disease; additional mutations (TET2, SRSF2, ASXL1, RUNX1) seen in other hematologic neoplasms can appear in advanced SM variants. Disease manifestations arise from release of bioactive mast cell mediators acting locally and distally, tissue infiltration by mast cells, and the tissue response to that infiltrate; mast cell-mediated fibrosis may affect liver, spleen, and bone marrow but not gastrointestinal tissue or skin (p.2819-2820). Prognosis is variant-dependent. Life expectancy is normal for cutaneous mastocytosis and most ISM; progression from ISM to a more advanced form is uncommon (~5% lifetime risk). In SM-AHNMD, outcome is determined by the associated non-mast cell hematologic disorder. SSM carries an intermediate prognosis. Aggressive SM and mast cell leukemia have a poor prognosis, and mast cell leukemia is invariably fatal at present. In infants and children with cutaneous disease, visceral involvement is usually absent and spontaneous resolution before adolescence is common; progression from cutaneous mastocytosis to ISM occurs in ~10% of children, especially with high mast cell burden or hematologic abnormalities (p.2820). Consensus classification: Cutaneous mastocytosis (CM) - maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (MPCM/urticaria pigmentosa), solitary mastocytoma of skin, diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis. Systemic mastocytosis (SM) - indolent SM (ISM, >70% of adults, normal life expectancy), smoldering SM (SSM; >=2 B findings, no C findings: high mast cell burden with marrow infiltration >30%, basal tryptase >200 ng/mL, and/or KIT D816V VAF >10%, dysmyelopoiesis, organomegaly), SM with associated clonal hematologic non-mast cell lineage disease (SM-AHNMD), aggressive SM (ASM; >=1 C finding - cytopenias, hepatic dysfunction with ascites, hypersplenism, malabsorption with weight loss, osteolytic fractures), mast cell leukemia (MCL, rarest, invariably fatal). Mast cell sarcoma (MCS) is a rare invasive solid mast cell tumor (Tables 366-1, 366-2; p.2820).

Acute mastoiditis — acute coalescent mastoiditis, mastoid abscess, suppurative mastoiditis Severe acute otitis media without true mastoid coalescence Postauricular lymphadenitis or infected sebaceous cyst Suppurating postauricular lymph node from scalp infection Furunculosis of the external canal with periauricular swelling Histiocytosis or malignancy involving the temporal bone Otitis externa with surrounding cellulitis Contrast-enhanced CT of the temporal bone to assess air cell coalescence and abscess formation MRI with venography when intracranial extension or sinus thrombosis is suspected Otoscopy for sagging canal wall, drum changes and discharge Culture and sensitivity of ear or abscess pus to guide antibiotics Full blood count and inflammatory markers to gauge severity and monitor response Audiometry once the acute phase settles to document hearing Usually arises as a complication of acute otitis media when infection spreads into the air cell system of the mastoid and pus fails to drain Suspect it when a child with a middle ear infection develops worsening pain, fever and swelling behind the ear despite treatment The classic sign is a boggy, tender postauricular swelling that pushes the pinna forward and downward, often obliterating the retroauricular groove Otoscopy commonly shows sagging of the posterosuperior canal wall and a bulging or discharging drum Progressive breakdown of the bony walls between air cells (coalescence) distinguishes surgical disease from simple mastoid mucosal inflammation seen in every acute otitis media Contrast CT of the temporal bone defines the extent of coalescence, subperiosteal abscess and any early intracranial extension Management combines aggressive parenteral antibiotics with drainage; cortical mastoidectomy is indicated when there is a subperiosteal abscess, no response to medical therapy, or a suspected complication Pus should be sent for culture, and common organisms include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus and Pseudomonas in chronic cases Headache, high fever, neck stiffness or altered consciousness suggesting meningitis or brain abscess (intracranial spread is an emergency) Swelling and tenderness over the sigmoid sinus region with swinging fever pointing to lateral sinus thrombophlebitis Neck swelling and torticollis suggesting a Bezold abscess tracking into the neck Facial nerve weakness or vertigo indicating deeper temporal bone involvement Rapid clinical deterioration or failure to respond to intravenous antibiotics Attributing postauricular swelling to simple lymphadenopathy and delaying imaging Assuming any mastoid opacity on imaging equals surgical mastoiditis without correlating clinical signs and bony coalescence Under-treating with oral antibiotics when parenteral therapy and drainage are required Missing evolving intracranial complications by not reassessing the non-improving patient Overlooking that the pinna is pushed forward, mistaking the picture for external ear pathology The mastoid air cells are continuous with the middle ear, so mucosal inflammation accompanies most episodes of acute otitis media. Mastoiditis develops when purulent material is trapped because the aditus ad antrum becomes blocked by oedema, allowing pressure and infection to build within the air cells. Persistent suppuration decalcifies and destroys the thin bony septa between cells, which fuse into an abscess cavity (coalescent mastoiditis). Pus may then track outward through the cortex to form a subperiosteal abscess, along fascial planes into the neck (Bezold abscess), or inward toward the dura, sigmoid sinus and posterior/middle cranial fossae, producing serious intracranial complications. With early recognition, appropriate antibiotics and timely surgical drainage the outlook is good and hearing is usually preserved, but delayed treatment allows intracranial and intratemporal complications that carry significant morbidity and can be life-threatening.

recurrence-risk counselling Missing the infantile diagnosis because early hypotonia is non-specific Underestimating the raised psychiatric risk in maternal UPD15 cases The Prader-Willi region at 15q11-q13 contains paternally expressed genes that are silenced on the maternal chromosome. In maternal uniparental disomy 15 both chromosome 15s come from the mother, so there is no paternal contribution and the paternally expressed genes are not transcribed, producing Prader-Willi syndrome. This uniparental disomy most often results from rescue of an initial trisomy 15 through loss of the paternal chromosome, which is why it is associated with advanced maternal age; the same clinical picture can also follow a paternal deletion or an imprinting defect. With early diagnosis, growth-hormone therapy, and strict dietary and behavioural management, outcomes have improved, but morbid obesity and its complications remain the main threat to health and life expectancy, and a higher rate of psychiatric illness is noted in the uniparental disomy subtype.

Mature cystic teratoma of the ovary — dermoid cyst, benign cystic teratoma, ovarian dermoid Endometrioma Haemorrhagic ovarian cyst Ovarian fibroma or other solid stromal tumour Mucinous cystadenoma Immature (malignant) teratoma Struma ovarii Pedunculated uterine leiomyoma Transvaginal ultrasound to identify fat, hair, and the Rokitansky nodule Pelvic MRI with fat-suppression sequences when imaging is equivocal Tumour markers (CA125, AFP, beta-hCG, LDH) mainly to help exclude a malignant germ-cell component Doppler assessment of ovarian blood flow if torsion is suspected Histological examination of the excised specimen to confirm maturity of all elements Thyroid function testing if a struma ovarii component is suspected Commonest ovarian germ-cell tumour and the most frequent ovarian neoplasm in young women of reproductive age; usually benign Contains mature tissue derived from all three germ layers, so cut sections typically reveal sebaceous material, hair, and sometimes teeth or cartilage Often an incidental finding; when symptomatic it causes vague pelvic discomfort, a palpable mass, or presents acutely with torsion Ultrasound features are characteristic, including echogenic mural nodules (Rokitansky protuberance), fat-fluid levels, and dense shadowing from hair and sebum Torsion is the most common complication because of the fatty content and long pedicle; rupture spills irritant sebaceous material and provokes chemical peritonitis Malignant transformation is rare and almost always squamous cell carcinoma arising in the ectodermal component, seen mainly in older women with larger lesions Ovarian cystectomy with preservation of normal ovarian tissue is the usual fertility-sparing approach; bilateral disease occurs in a minority May rarely trigger anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis, so a paraneoplastic neurological presentation should prompt a search for a dermoid Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with nausea suggesting ovarian torsion Signs of chemical peritonitis following cyst rupture Rapid enlargement or solid vascularised areas raising concern for malignant transformation New neuropsychiatric or seizure symptoms suggesting associated anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis Attributing acute pain solely to the mass and missing torsion, which threatens ovarian viability Rupturing the cyst intraoperatively and spilling contents, provoking granulomatous peritonitis Assuming all teratomas are benign and overlooking an immature or malignantly transformed component Failing to consider a dermoid as the cause of a paraneoplastic encephalitis A mature cystic teratoma arises from a single germ cell that undergoes parthenogenetic development after the first meiotic division, generating well-differentiated tissues from ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Ectodermal elements usually predominate, which is why skin, sebaceous glands, hair follicles, and neural tissue are conspicuous, giving the lesion its dermoid character. The tumour is typically a unilocular cyst lined by squamous epithelium and filled with keratin and sebum, with a raised nodule (the Rokitansky protuberance) from which hair, teeth, and other solid tissues project. Because the components are mature, the lesion behaves benignly, with complications arising chiefly from its physical bulk and fatty content rather than from invasive growth. Excellent for the great majority, which are benign and cured by complete cystectomy; recurrence is uncommon and usually reflects a new primary. Prognosis worsens markedly if squamous carcinoma has developed within the lesion, particularly when detected late.

May-Hegglin anomaly — MYH9-related disorder, Macrothrombocytopenia with Dohle-like bodies, May-Hegglin anomaly Immune thrombocytopenia Bernard-Soulier syndrome Other MYH9-related syndromes (Epstein, Fechtner, Sebastian) Grey platelet syndrome Type 2B or platelet-type von Willebrand disease with macrothrombocytopenia Congenital macrothrombocytopenias (for example ACTN1, TUBB1, GP1BA/B) Pseudothrombocytopenia from platelet clumping Full blood count with mean platelet volume and manual platelet estimate Peripheral blood film for giant platelets and neutrophil Dohle-like inclusions Immunofluorescence staining for MYH9 protein distribution in neutrophils MYH9 gene sequencing Audiometry to detect sensorineural hearing loss Urinalysis and renal function for proteinuria and nephropathy Ophthalmological assessment for cataract An autosomal dominant disorder within the MYH9-related disease spectrum caused by mutations in the gene for non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA. Defined by the triad of macrothrombocytopenia, characteristic Dohle-like leucocyte inclusion bodies and generally mild bleeding. The pale-blue cytoplasmic inclusions in neutrophils are aggregates of mutant myosin and can be confirmed by immunofluorescence for MYH9 protein. Platelets are large or giant, and automated counters often underestimate the count by miscategorising platelets as red cells, so a manual film review is essential. Many patients are asymptomatic or have only mild mucocutaneous bleeding disproportionately milder than the platelet count suggests. The wider MYH9 spectrum (Epstein, Fechtner, Sebastian syndromes) may add sensorineural deafness, nephropathy and cataract, which can appear over time. Bleeding management uses antifibrinolytics and desmopressin for minor procedures, reserving platelet transfusion for major haemorrhage. Genotype broadly predicts risk of non-haematological features, guiding surveillance for renal and auditory complications. Significant haemorrhage after major surgery, trauma or delivery Progressive proteinuria or renal impairment indicating MYH9 nephropathy Progressive sensorineural hearing loss Severe unexplained thrombocytopenia prompting inappropriate immunosuppression or splenectomy Visual deterioration from cataract Misdiagnosing the macrothrombocytopenia as immune thrombocytopenia and treating with steroids, immunoglobulin or splenectomy. Accepting a falsely low automated platelet count without manual film review. Overlooking the Dohle-like inclusions or dismissing them as reactive change in sepsis. Failing to screen for the renal, auditory and ocular features of the wider MYH9 spectrum. Transfusing platelets unnecessarily in a patient with mild bleeding and preserved platelet function. May-Hegglin anomaly is one phenotype of MYH9-related disease, caused by heterozygous mutations in MYH9, which encodes non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA. This cytoskeletal motor protein is essential for cytokinesis, cell shape and migration, and for the terminal stages of megakaryocyte maturation and proplatelet formation. Mutant myosin disrupts orderly platelet release, yielding reduced numbers of abnormally large platelets, and aggregates within neutrophil cytoplasm to form the Dohle-like inclusion bodies. Because myosin IIA is also expressed in the cochlea, kidney podocytes and ocular lens, certain mutations additionally cause the sensorineural deafness, glomerular nephropathy and cataract seen across the MYH9 disease spectrum. Platelet function is largely preserved, explaining bleeding that is milder than the platelet count implies. Isolated May-Hegglin anomaly carries an excellent prognosis with normal life expectancy and usually only mild bleeding. Long-term outlook depends on the specific MYH9 mutation and the development of renal, auditory or ocular complications, which warrant lifelong monitoring.
