compromise (phlegmasia) Recurrent thrombosis despite adequate anticoagulation Signs of pulmonary embolism An extrinsic pelvic mass causing the compression Treating left iliofemoral DVT with anticoagulation alone and missing the underlying compression Relying on duplex alone, which visualises the iliac veins poorly Under-recognising the syndrome in young women with left leg swelling Failing to use intravascular ultrasound and thereby underestimating the degree of stenosis May-Thurner syndrome arises from the anatomical position of the right common iliac artery crossing over and compressing the left common iliac vein against the fifth lumbar vertebra. Repetitive arterial pulsation and mechanical compression cause endothelial injury and the development of intraluminal venous spurs or webs, producing a fixed venous stenosis. This impairs venous outflow from the left leg, causing venous hypertension and greatly increasing the risk of left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis, which may present acutely or lead to chronic post-thrombotic sequelae. With recognition and treatment of the underlying compression by stenting, alongside thrombus removal and anticoagulation, outcomes are good with high stent patency; untreated compression predisposes to recurrent thrombosis and post-thrombotic syndrome.

Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome — MRKH syndrome, müllerian aplasia, congenital absence of the uterus and vagina Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY, absent or scant pubic hair, testes, absent uterus) Transverse vaginal septum Imperforate hymen with haematocolpos Isolated distal vaginal agenesis with an intact uterus Cervical agenesis or dysgenesis with a functioning uterus Gonadal dysgenesis (e.g., Turner or Swyer syndrome) Functional hypothalamic or constitutional causes of primary amenorrhoea with normal anatomy Karyotype to confirm 46,XX and exclude androgen insensitivity and gonadal dysgenesis Pelvic ultrasound and, definitively, pelvic MRI to assess uterine remnants, functioning endometrium and vaginal length Renal tract imaging (ultrasound and MR urogram) for associated anomalies Serum FSH, LH and oestradiol (expected normal) and serum testosterone to distinguish androgen insensitivity Spinal and skeletal imaging where vertebral or Klippel-Feil anomalies are suspected Audiological assessment and echocardiography in atypical or MURCS presentations Ovarian reserve assessment (antral follicle count and anti-müllerian hormone) if assisted reproduction is planned MRKH is congenital aplasia of the uterus and the upper (proximal) two-thirds of the vagina resulting from müllerian (paramesonephric) duct agenesis in a phenotypically normal 46,XX woman with functioning ovaries. It is the second most common cause of primary amenorrhoea after gonadal dysgenesis and typically presents in adolescence with primary amenorrhoea despite normal breast and pubic-hair development. Because the ovaries develop independently of the müllerian ducts and function normally, secondary sexual characteristics, cyclical hormone production and ovulation are preserved, with normal gonadotrophins and oestradiol. Examination shows normal external genitalia with a short, blind-ending vaginal dimple or pouch and an absent or rudimentary uterus. Type 1 (typical, isolated) is symmetrical uterovaginal aplasia with normal fallopian tubes and no extragenital anomaly; Type 2 (atypical) and the MURCS association add renal, skeletal (vertebral, Klippel-Feil) and, less often, cardiac and auditory anomalies. Renal tract anomalies such as unilateral renal agenesis and ectopic or horseshoe kidney occur in a substantial proportion, so upper urinary tract imaging is mandatory. First-line creation of a functional vagina is non-surgical self-dilation (Frank technique); vaginoplasty (Vecchietti, McIndoe, Davydov or bowel) is reserved for those who fail or decline dilation. Ovulation is intact, so genetic parenthood is achievable through oocyte retrieval with gestational surrogacy and, increasingly, uterus transplantation; functioning endometrium in a rudimentary horn can rarely cause cyclical pain and haematometra. Cyclical or progressive pelvic pain from an obstructed functioning uterine remnant or haematometra requiring surgical excision Undiagnosed renal anomaly such as a solitary or ectopic kidney affecting anaesthetic and surgical planning Severe psychological distress, low mood or suicidal ideation following the diagnosis Skeletal anomalies causing spinal deformity or, in MURCS, cardiac lesions needing evaluation Confusing MRKH with complete androgen insensitivity, when pubic and axillary hair with a 46,XX karyotype distinguish MRKH and gonadal management differs entirely Omitting renal tract imaging and missing a clinically important solitary or ectopic kidney Overlooking a functioning rudimentary uterine horn as a treatable cause of cyclical pain Proceeding to surgical vaginoplasty before offering first-line dilation therapy Neglecting the profound psychological impact and failing to arrange specialist counselling and peer support MRKH arises from failure of development of the müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts during embryogenesis, when these ducts would normally fuse and canalise to form the uterus, cervix and upper two-thirds of the vagina; the result is aplasia or hypoplasia of these structures, while the lower vagina, derived from the urogenital sinus, persists as a short pouch. Ovaries and fallopian tubes develop from separate lineages that are independent of the müllerian ducts, so ovarian endocrine and germ-cell function is retained and the karyotype is 46,XX with a normal female hormonal milieu. The aetiology is heterogeneous and largely sporadic, with familial clustering in some kindreds suggesting polygenic or multifactorial inheritance and implicating genes that govern müllerian duct and mesodermal development. The frequent coexistence of renal and skeletal anomalies reflects the shared intermediate-mesoderm origin of the urogenital and axial skeletal systems, which underlies the MURCS association. Life expectancy is normal and, with vaginal dilation or vaginoplasty, satisfactory sexual function is achievable for most women. Fertility requires assisted reproduction with surrogacy or uterus transplantation, and the long-term outcome is strongly influenced by psychological support around the diagnosis.

menstruation Undiagnosed associated renal anomaly affecting overall health Significant psychological distress requiring dedicated support Diagnostic uncertainty needing distinction from androgen insensitivity or a disorder of sex development Confusing MRKH with androgen insensitivity by not checking karyotype and hormone profile Failing to screen for associated renal and skeletal anomalies Missing a functioning rudimentary uterine horn causing cyclical obstructed pain Neglecting the psychological impact and support needs of the diagnosis Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome results from failure of development of the mullerian (paramesonephric) ducts, which normally form the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina. The defect leaves absent or rudimentary uterine structures and a shortened or absent upper vagina, while the lower vagina, derived separately, and the external genitalia are normal. Because ovarian tissue arises independently and is unaffected, the ovaries function normally with a 46,XX karyotype, producing normal secondary sexual characteristics. With dilation or surgery a functional vagina can usually be achieved, and psychological support is central to long-term wellbeing.

Mannose-binding lectin deficiency — MBL deficiency, mannan-binding lectin deficiency, MBL2 deficiency Antibody deficiencies (for example IgA deficiency or common variable immunodeficiency) Complement component deficiencies affecting other pathways Other causes of recurrent childhood respiratory infection Secondary immunodeficiency from immunosuppression or malignancy Normal variation in a healthy individual with incidental low MBL Serum mannose-binding lectin level and functional lectin pathway assay MBL2 genotyping where clinically indicated Broader immune workup (immunoglobulins, specific antibody responses, complement pathways) to exclude a more significant coexisting defect Assessment of infection frequency and severity in clinical context Review of concurrent immunosuppressive factors Mannose-binding lectin is a pattern-recognition protein that initiates the lectin pathway of complement by binding carbohydrate structures on microbial surfaces Low MBL levels are common in the general population, arising from polymorphisms in the MBL2 gene, and many people with low levels are entirely healthy MBL deficiency is therefore best regarded as a susceptibility factor or disease modifier rather than a strong stand-alone immunodeficiency Any increased infection risk is generally modest and most apparent in infancy, when adaptive immunity is still developing, or when combined with another immune defect or immunosuppression Reported associations include recurrent respiratory infections in young children and a greater burden of infection in patients undergoing chemotherapy or with other coexisting deficiencies The organisms involved are typically pyogenic bacteria, reflecting impaired complement-mediated opsonisation Diagnosis relies on measuring serum MBL levels and, where relevant, MBL2 genotyping, while interpreting results cautiously in the light of the high population prevalence of low levels There is no specific replacement therapy in routine use; management is supportive, with attention to vaccination, prompt treatment of infections, and evaluation for additional or more significant immune defects Recurrent or severe infection that is disproportionate to isolated MBL deficiency, prompting a search for an additional immune defect Serious infection during chemotherapy or other immunosuppression where MBL deficiency may compound risk Invasive pyogenic infection needing prompt treatment Recurrent infection in infancy warranting follow-up as adaptive immunity matures Over-attributing recurrent infections to MBL deficiency and stopping the workup prematurely, missing a more important coexisting defect Treating an incidental low MBL level in a healthy person as a clinically significant disease Failing to interpret MBL levels against the high population prevalence of low values Neglecting standard vaccination and infection-prevention measures Assuming a specific replacement therapy exists when management is essentially supportive Mannose-binding lectin is a serum collectin that recognises repeating sugar patterns on the surface of many microorganisms. On binding, it activates associated serine proteases (MASPs) to trigger the lectin pathway of complement, promoting opsonisation and clearance of pathogens independently of antibody. Common MBL2 polymorphisms reduce circulating MBL levels or impair its function, modestly weakening this early, antibody-independent arm of innate defence. Because other complement pathways and adaptive immunity usually compensate, the clinical impact is limited in most individuals; susceptibility becomes more evident when MBL deficiency coexists with immaturity of the immune system, immunosuppression, or another immune defect. The prognosis for isolated MBL deficiency is generally excellent, as most affected individuals have no significant clinical consequences; the main relevance is as a modifier that can worsen outcomes when combined with immune immaturity, immunosuppression, or another immunodeficiency.

the c.985A>G (p.Lys304Glu) allele predominates in populations of northern European ancestry The defective enzyme cannot dehydrogenate medium-chain (C6-C10) acyl-CoA substrates, so beta-oxidation stalls once glycogen stores are exhausted during fasting or intercurrent illness Classic decompensation is hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with lethargy, vomiting and encephalopathy, often after a period of poor feeding or a viral illness Newborn screening detects a characteristic acylcarnitine profile with elevated octanoylcarnitine (C8) and a raised C8:C10 ratio Urine organic acids during crisis show medium-chain dicarboxylic aciduria with inappropriately low ketones Cornerstone of management is avoidance of prolonged fasting, an emergency regimen with oral or intravenous glucose during illness, and prompt presentation when unwell Many diagnosed on screening remain asymptomatic if fasting is avoided, but sudden unexpected death and Reye-like presentations occurred historically before screening Reduced consciousness or seizures with documented hypoketotic hypoglycaemia Vomiting and refusal to feed during intercurrent illness in a known or at-risk infant Hyperammonaemia or hepatic dysfunction suggesting metabolic decompensation Apparent life-threatening event or sudden unexpected collapse in a young infant Attributing hypoglycaemia to a simple viral illness and missing the underlying oxidation defect Expecting ketosis to accompany hypoglycaemia, when the hallmark is that ketones are inappropriately low Allowing prolonged fasting for procedures or investigations without a glucose-containing infusion Assuming an asymptomatic screen-detected infant needs no emergency plan Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase catalyses the first, rate-limiting dehydrogenation step of mitochondrial beta-oxidation for medium-chain fatty acyl-CoA esters. When the enzyme is deficient, fatty acids cannot be fully oxidised to supply acetyl-CoA and hepatic ketone bodies during fasting, so tissues that depend on ketones and fatty-acid-derived energy are compromised and hypoglycaemia develops once hepatic glycogen is depleted. Accumulating medium-chain acyl-CoA intermediates are diverted to carnitine esters and dicarboxylic acids, and the shortage of acetyl-CoA impairs ureagenesis, producing hyperammonaemia in severe crises. With newborn screening, education on fasting avoidance and a written emergency regimen, the long-term outlook is excellent and most individuals develop normally. Risk of morbidity and death concentrates in the first decompensation, so prevention and early recognition are decisive.

symptoms and rhabdomyolysis risk Severe rhabdomyolysis with markedly elevated creatine kinase and pigmenturia Acute kidney injury following an episode of myoglobinuria Fixed muscle contractures or severe cramps during exertion Dismissing exertional symptoms as deconditioning and missing the diagnosis for years Performing an ischaemic forearm test with a tourniquet when a non-ischaemic protocol is safer and adequate Advising complete avoidance of activity rather than encouraging graded aerobic conditioning Overlooking the risk of acute kidney injury during rhabdomyolysis McArdle disease is caused by deficiency of myophosphorylase, the muscle isoform of glycogen phosphorylase encoded by PYGM, which initiates glycogen breakdown by cleaving glucose units from glycogen in skeletal muscle. Without functional enzyme, muscle cannot mobilise its glycogen stores to fuel anaerobic and early aerobic exercise, so ATP generation fails during intense or sustained activity, producing cramps, contractures, and fatigue. Because glycolysis downstream cannot be fed from glycogen, blood lactate does not rise normally with exercise. Energy-depleted muscle fibres are prone to injury and breakdown, causing rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria. The 'second wind' reflects the delayed availability of blood glucose and free fatty acids as alternative fuels once the circulation delivers them to working muscle. Life expectancy is usually normal and most patients remain functional with lifestyle adaptation; the principal risks are recurrent rhabdomyolysis and consequent acute kidney injury, and a minority develop fixed muscle weakness with age.

contributor to bone disease Assuming precocious puberty is centrally driven and giving inappropriate GnRH-analogue therapy McCune-Albright syndrome results from an activating variant in GNAS occurring after fertilisation, producing a mosaic distribution of affected cells; a germline variant would be lethal, which explains why the condition arises only as somatic mosaicism. The variant renders the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G protein constitutively active, leading to unregulated adenylate cyclase activity and elevated intracellular cyclic AMP. In hormone-responsive endocrine tissues this drives autonomous hormone secretion independent of normal control, while in bone-forming cells it produces the fibrous dysplasia lesions. The pattern and severity of disease reflect which tissues carry the variant and in what proportion. Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the extent and location of affected tissues, ranging from mild monostotic disease to severe polyostotic bone disease with multiple endocrinopathies. Malignant transformation of fibrous dysplasia is rare, and most morbidity relates to skeletal complications and hormonal excess, which are managed rather than cured.

excluding Bardet-Biedl syndrome, which shares the MKKS gene and emerges later Mistaking hydrometrocolpos for other pelvic masses and delaying decompression Overlooking associated renal or cardiac anomalies Failing to arrange long-term retinal and renal surveillance McKusick-Kaufman syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in MKKS, which encodes a chaperonin-like protein that helps assemble the BBSome, a complex trafficking membrane proteins into and along the primary cilium. Impaired ciliary function during development disturbs the patterning and morphogenesis of the genital tract, limbs and heart, producing hydrometrocolpos, postaxial polydactyly and congenital heart disease. Because the same gene, when more severely affected, causes Bardet-Biedl syndrome type 6, the two disorders lie on a continuum: the additional Bardet-Biedl features of retinal dystrophy, obesity, renal disease and learning difficulties depend on wider ciliary dysfunction and typically appear only with time, which is why the diagnosis may need revision during follow-up. With timely decompression of hydrometrocolpos and management of any cardiac lesion the early outlook is good, but if the phenotype evolves into Bardet-Biedl syndrome the long-term prognosis follows that of the retinal and renal disease.

standard donor blood without recognising the McLeod phenotype, risking alloimmune reactions Attributing the movement disorder solely to Huntington disease and missing the X-linked pattern Failing to screen for cardiomyopathy in a patient labelled as a pure movement disorder Assuming a normal chorein result excludes neuroacanthocytosis, since McLeod syndrome requires XK and Kell testing McLeod syndrome arises from pathogenic variants in the XK gene on the X chromosome, which encodes a membrane transport-related protein that is covalently linked to the Kell glycoprotein on the red-cell surface. Loss of XK weakens the erythrocyte membrane, producing acanthocytes and the McLeod blood-group phenotype with depressed Kell antigen expression. The same protein is expressed in brain, muscle and heart, and its deficiency drives striatal neurodegeneration, skeletal myopathy, peripheral neuropathy and a dilated cardiomyopathy, giving the characteristic multisystem picture. McLeod syndrome is a slowly progressive multisystem disorder; neurological disability accrues over years, but cardiac involvement with cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia is a leading cause of morbidity and premature death, so cardiac surveillance is central to care.

agents such as bedaquiline and linezolid, delivered under programmatic support India's NTEP provides free universal drug-susceptibility testing and standardised drug-resistant TB regimens, with active follow-up to improve adherence and outcomes Rifampicin resistance on molecular testing requiring urgent switch to a drug-resistant TB pathway Extensive or progressive disease with respiratory compromise Emergence of additional resistance (pre-XDR or XDR) narrowing treatment options Public health emergency of transmission of resistant strains, especially in congregate or HIV settings Adding a single new drug to a failing regimen, which amplifies resistance Delaying drug-susceptibility testing and treating empirically as drug-susceptible disease Under-recognising drug toxicities such as QT prolongation and peripheral neuropathy during monitoring Neglecting adherence support and contact tracing, allowing transmission Drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis arises from spontaneous chromosomal mutations in genes encoding drug targets or activating enzymes, for example rpoB mutations conferring rifampicin resistance and katG or inhA mutations conferring isoniazid resistance. Selective pressure from inadequate drug exposure, poor adherence, or malabsorption allows resistant mutants to become the dominant population. Sequential accumulation of mutations produces multidrug and extensively drug-resistant strains. These resistant organisms can be transmitted directly to new hosts, so resistance is propagated both by acquisition during treatment and by primary transmission within communities. Outcomes have improved substantially with all-oral shorter regimens containing newer agents, but MDR-TB still carries higher treatment failure, relapse and mortality than drug-susceptible disease, with worse outcomes as resistance broadens or when treatment is delayed.

Measles (Rubeola) — rubeola Rubella (German measles) - milder, no cough, with posterior auricular/suboccipital lymphadenopathy Kawasaki disease Infectious mononucleosis (atypical lymphocytosis, in contrast to the leukopenia common in measles) Roseola (exanthem subitum) - rash appears after fever subsides Scarlet fever Rocky Mountain spotted fever Enterovirus or adenovirus infection Drug sensitivity/eruption Rubella Infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus) Roseola/exanthem subitum (HHV-6/HHV-7) Scarlet fever Rocky Mountain spotted fever Enterovirus (echovirus, coxsackievirus) infection Adenovirus infection Early meningococcemia or rickettsial infection (morbilliform before petechiae/purpura) Detection of measles virus-specific IgM in a single serum or oral fluid specimen is diagnostic of acute infection Fourfold or greater rise in measles virus-specific IgG between acute- and convalescent-phase sera Note timing pitfall: IgM may not be detectable until 4-5 days after rash onset (false-negatives if drawn too early) and usually falls to undetectable within 4-8 weeks Reverse-transcription PCR for measles virus RNA (sensitive/specific; can genotype and distinguish wild-type from vaccine strain) Virus isolation in cell culture from respiratory secretions, nasopharyngeal/conjunctival swabs, blood, or urine Direct detection of giant cells in respiratory secretions, urine, or biopsy tissue Neutralization tests (highly correlated with protective immunity but expensive and laborious) Kawasaki disease Drug eruption / drug sensitivity Acute graft-versus-host disease Caused by measles virus, a paramyxovirus; transmitted primarily by respiratory droplets and, less commonly, by small-particle aerosols that can remain suspended in air, making it highly transmissible (Harrison 22e p.1639). Incubation is ~10 days to fever onset and ~14 days to rash onset; this period may be shorter in infants and longer (up to 3 weeks) in adults (Harrison 22e p.1640). Classic prodrome is fever and malaise beginning ~10 days after exposure, followed by the three Cs: cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, increasing in severity over ~4 days (Harrison 22e p.1640). Koplik's spots (bluish-white ~1 mm dots surrounded by erythema on the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars) are pathognomonic, appear ~2 days before the rash, and fade with rash onset (Harrison 22e p.1641). The exanthem is an erythematous maculopapular rash beginning behind the ears and on the neck/hairline, spreading cephalocaudally to face, trunk, arms, and then legs/feet by the end of the second day; it fades in the same order and may desquamate, especially in undernourished children (Harrison 22e p.1641). Care is largely supportive; vitamin A is recommended for children with measles and can markedly reduce morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.1641). Two doses of live attenuated measles vaccine (commonly as MMR or MMRV) are highly protective; ~85% develop protective antibody after one dose at 9 months and ~95% at 12 months (Harrison 22e p.1642). Post-exposure human immunoglobulin within 72 h usually prevents infection and, given up to 6 days after exposure, can still prevent or modify disease in susceptible high-risk contacts (Harrison 22e p.1642). Endemic transmission was eliminated in the United States in 2000, but outbreaks recur from imported cases amplified in under- and unvaccinated communities; vaccine hesitancy and pandemic-related disruption of immunization programs have driven a global resurgence (Harrison 22e p.1638, p.1369). Pneumonia - secondary bacterial bronchopneumonia or measles giant cell pneumonitis (the latter in immunocompromised persons); recurrence or persistence of fever after the rash suggests secondary bacterial infection Acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup) with risk of airway obstruction, particularly in young children Post-measles encephalomyelitis (~1 in 1000 cases) within 2 weeks of rash onset with fever, seizures, and neurologic abnormalities - thought to be autoimmune Measles inclusion body encephalitis (MIBE) - rare, fatal, in those with defective cellular immunity, months after infection Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) - slowly progressive, fatal, 5-15 years after infection (mostly in those infected at <2 years) Diarrhea worsening undernutrition Absent or delayed rash in immunocompromised or severely undernourished children with impaired cellular immunity - associated with a high case-fatality rate Patients are contagious before recognizable disease appears, which undermines isolation measures; nosocomial transmission in waiting rooms, hospitals, and physicians' offices is well recognized. Clinical diagnosis is difficult during the prodrome, when the rash is attenuated by passively acquired antibody or prior immunization, when the rash is absent/delayed in immunocompromised or severely undernourished children, and in low-incidence regions. Measles virus-specific IgM may be falsely negative if serum is obtained too early (within the first few days of rash onset). Persons with impaired cellular immunity may not develop the characteristic rash, may develop giant cell pneumonitis, and have a high case-fatality rate. There is no specific antiviral therapy; ribavirin benefit has not been conclusively demonstrated in trials. The 1998 report hypothesizing an MMR-autism link was a misinterpreted temporal association, has been refuted by numerous studies, and was retracted - there is no causal link. Measles virus is deposited in the respiratory tract, oropharynx, or conjunctivae, then proliferates locally in dendritic cells and lymphocytes and spreads to draining lymph nodes. It enters the bloodstream by budding from infected lymphocytes, producing a viremia that disseminates infection throughout the body (respiratory epithelium, lymphatic tissue, spleen, lung, thymus, liver, skin). Signs and symptoms appear 8-12 days after infection as virus replicates in target organs and the host immune response develops; the characteristic rash is itself a consequence of the cellular immune response. TH1 (interferon-gamma) responses are essential for viral clearance and later TH2 (interleukin-4) responses drive protective antibody. Paradoxically, measles induces a state of immunosuppression lasting weeks to months that depresses responses to unrelated antigens, reduces the magnitude and diversity of pre-existing antibody ("immune amnesia"), and increases susceptibility to secondary bacterial and viral infections, accounting for much measles-related morbidity and death. Most persons recover and develop long-term (generally lifelong) protective immunity. Case-fatality varies with age at infection, nutritional and immunologic status, vaccine coverage, and access to care. In most developed countries the case-fatality rate is 0.01-0.1%, but in endemic areas of sub-Saharan Africa it may be 5-10% or higher, and in refugee camps and internally displaced populations rates have reached 20-30%. Previously vaccinated persons who become infected have less severe disease and significantly lower mortality. Measles still causes more than 100,000 deaths per year worldwide. Harrison does not give a formal grading scale. Severity is driven by host and population factors: severe or fatal disease occurs in those with impaired/deficient T-lymphocyte (cellular) immunity and in malnourished/undernourished children (e.g., vitamin A deficiency), among whom the rash may be absent and giant cell pneumonitis and high case-fatality occur; pregnant women, immunocompromised persons, and infants <1 year are at risk of severe measles and are prioritized for immunoglobulin prophylaxis.

Measles inclusion body encephalitis — MIBE, measles inclusion-body encephalitis, subacute measles encephalitis, immunosuppressive measles encephalitis Herpes simplex and other viral encephalitides in the immunocompromised Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis Cerebral toxoplasmosis or CNS lymphoma Metabolic or drug-related encephalopathy Autoimmune or paraneoplastic encephalitis Detection of measles virus RNA by PCR or antigen in cerebrospinal fluid or brain tissue Brain biopsy showing intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies with immunostaining for measles antigen MRI of the brain to identify cortical and subcortical signal change Electroencephalography, often showing focal epileptiform activity rather than the periodic complexes of SSPE Assessment of immune status including HIV testing, CD4 count, and chemotherapy or transplant history Measles exposure and immunisation history of the patient and close contacts A subacute encephalitis caused by persistent measles virus infection of the brain occurring specifically in immunocompromised patients It is seen in children and adults with impaired cell-mediated immunity, such as leukaemia and lymphoma, chemotherapy, HIV, or transplantation Unlike SSPE, the latent interval is short, typically weeks to a few months after measles exposure or infection, and the illness may lack a preceding rash Presentation is with altered mental status, focal neurological deficits, and, very characteristically, refractory focal seizures including epilepsia partialis continua Because antibody responses are blunted by immunosuppression, cerebrospinal fluid measles antibody may be low or absent, unlike the high titres of SSPE Diagnosis rests on detecting measles virus RNA or antigen and viral inclusions in brain tissue, supported by imaging, since serology is unreliable in these hosts The prognosis is poor; there is no established effective therapy, and prevention through avoiding measles exposure and ensuring immunity in contacts is essential Refractory focal seizures or epilepsia partialis continua in an immunocompromised patient Progressive decline in conscious level or new focal deficits Recent measles exposure or infection in a severely immunosuppressed host Status epilepticus or rapid neurological deterioration Excluding measles because CSF antibody is low, when the immunosuppressed host cannot mount a strong response Confusing MIBE with SSPE despite their different time course, immune context, and EEG findings Failing to obtain brain tissue or molecular testing when serology is unrevealing Overlooking measles exposure in an immunocompromised patient with new refractory seizures Measles inclusion body encephalitis develops when the measles virus persists and replicates within the central nervous system of a host whose cell-mediated immunity is too impaired to clear it. In contrast to subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, where a defective virus smoulders for years and provokes intense antibody production, here the immunosuppressed brain permits relatively active viral replication over a much shorter period with only a weak immune response. Neurones and glia contain intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies packed with viral nucleocapsids, and there is neuronal loss with comparatively little inflammatory infiltrate because the immune response is suppressed. The rapidly progressive cortical involvement produces the characteristic intractable focal seizures and focal deficits, and the blunted humoral response explains why CSF measles antibody is often unhelpful for diagnosis. The outlook is poor, with most patients deteriorating over weeks to months and high mortality; survival and any recovery depend heavily on restoring immune function, and no antiviral regimen is reliably effective.

or night pain Features suggesting infection: fever, intravenous drug use, immunosuppression, and severe night pain Significant trauma or possible osteoporotic fracture, and inflammatory features such the intervertebral discs, facet joints, ligaments, and paraspinal muscles, without a single identifiable lesion in most cases. Age-related disc and facet degeneration, muscular strain, and altered movement patterns contribute. Pain is influenced by biomechanical factors together with central pain processing and psychosocial factors, which can drive the transition from acute to chronic pain. The majority of acute episodes improve substantially within a few weeks, but recurrences are common and a minority develop persistent disabling chronic pain, strongly influenced by psychosocial factors.

oligohydramnios from renal disease Meckel-Gruber syndrome is a severe ciliopathy caused by biallelic variants in genes encoding proteins of the ciliary transition zone and basal body. Loss of normal primary cilium function disrupts developmental signalling across multiple organs during embryogenesis, producing central nervous system malformation (typically an occipital encephalocele), cystic dysplasia of the renal collecting system, ductal plate malformation of the liver, and limb patterning defects manifesting as polydactyly. The renal enlargement reduces amniotic fluid, and the consequent oligohydramnios impairs lung development. Meckel-Gruber syndrome is uniformly lethal, with death occurring before birth or within the neonatal period, chiefly from pulmonary hypoplasia and renal failure. Management is directed at prenatal diagnosis, compassionate perinatal care, and genetic counselling for recurrence risk.

Meconium Aspiration Syndrome — MAS, meconium aspiration Neonatal pneumonia or sepsis Transient tachypnoea of the newborn Respiratory distress syndrome (in less mature infants) Persistent pulmonary hypertension from other causes Air-leak syndromes Congenital heart disease Chest radiograph for patchy infiltrates, hyperinflation, and air leaks Pulse oximetry (pre- and post-ductal) and blood gas analysis Echocardiography to assess for pulmonary hypertension Sepsis screen when infection cannot be excluded Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring Respiratory distress in a newborn born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid, when meconium is aspirated into the airways around the time of birth. It occurs mainly in term and post-term infants and is associated with fetal distress and intrauterine hypoxia. Affected infants may be meconium-stained, have distress from birth with tachypnoea and recession, and show a barrel-shaped, hyperinflated chest. The chest radiograph typically shows patchy or coarse infiltrates with areas of hyperinflation and atelectasis, and air leaks are common. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn frequently complicates the syndrome and contributes to severe hypoxaemia. Routine intrapartum suctioning of the airway and routine tracheal suction of vigorous meconium-stained infants are no longer recommended. Non-vigorous infants born through meconium may need resuscitation, and management is largely supportive with oxygen and respiratory support. Severe cases may require mechanical ventilation, surfactant, inhaled nitric oxide for pulmonary hypertension, and occasionally extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Air leaks such as pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum are important and potentially sudden complications. Severe or refractory hypoxaemia despite respiratory support Large pre- to post-ductal saturation gradient suggesting pulmonary hypertension Sudden deterioration indicating pneumothorax or other air leak Signs of hypoxic-ischaemic injury to other organs Escalating ventilatory requirements or shock Performing routine intrapartum or tracheal suctioning that is no longer recommended Underestimating the risk of pneumothorax and missing a sudden air leak Failing to recognise coexisting persistent pulmonary hypertension Overlooking associated hypoxic-ischaemic injury to other organs Delaying escalation of respiratory support in rapidly deteriorating infants Intrauterine stress and hypoxia can provoke passage of meconium into the amniotic fluid and gasping that draws it into the airways. Aspirated meconium causes mechanical airway obstruction with a ball-valve effect producing air trapping and air leaks, a chemical pneumonitis with inflammation, and inactivation of surfactant. These changes cause ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxaemia, and, combined with hypoxia-driven pulmonary vasoconstriction, promote persistent pulmonary hypertension with right-to-left shunting. Most infants with mild to moderate disease recover with supportive care, but severe disease complicated by persistent pulmonary hypertension or air leaks carries significant morbidity and mortality; survivors may have transient respiratory sequelae.

hyperosmolar contrast enema Overlooking evolving meconium peritonitis when abdominal calcification is present In meconium ileus, deficient CFTR chloride channel function reduces luminal fluid secretion and, together with abnormal pancreatic enzyme delivery, produces meconium that is dehydrated, viscid, and adherent. This inspissated meconium obstructs the distal ileum, causing proximal small-bowel dilatation and an unused microcolon distally. In complicated disease, the heavy, obstructed loops may twist (volvulus), lose their blood supply, become atretic, or perforate in utero, spilling sterile meconium into the peritoneum and producing meconium peritonitis with dystrophic calcification. With prompt relief of obstruction, outcomes for the bowel are generally good, but overall prognosis is dominated by the underlying cystic fibrosis and its pulmonary and pancreatic manifestations. Complicated meconium ileus carries higher perioperative morbidity but survival with modern care remains favourable.

Medial collateral ligament injury — MCL sprain, medial collateral ligament tear, tibial collateral ligament injury Medial meniscal tear ACL injury (unhappy triad) Pes anserine bursitis Medial patellofemoral ligament injury after patellar dislocation Physeal injury in skeletally immature patients Valgus stress testing at 0 and 30 degrees MRI to grade the tear and detect associated injuries Radiographs to exclude fracture and detect Pellegrini-Stieda calcification or physeal injury Stress radiographs in skeletally immature patients to distinguish physeal fracture The most commonly injured knee ligament, typically from a valgus force to the lateral knee Graded I-III by the degree of medial laxity on valgus stress at 30 degrees of flexion Pain and tenderness localise along the medial joint line and femoral or tibial attachment The great majority of isolated MCL injuries heal without surgery owing to the ligament's good blood supply Valgus laxity in full extension implies a more severe injury with cruciate or capsular involvement Part of the 'unhappy triad' alongside ACL and medial meniscus injury A Pellegrini-Stieda lesion (calcification at the femoral origin) can follow chronic proximal MCL injury Valgus laxity in full extension indicating combined ligamentous injury Multiligament injury or knee dislocation Physeal fracture mimicking ligament injury in children Assuming an isolated MCL injury when valgus laxity in extension signals a combined injury Missing a paediatric distal femoral physeal fracture that mimics MCL laxity Overlooking a concurrent ACL or meniscal tear Immobilising rigidly when early protected motion aids healing The superficial MCL is the primary restraint to valgus stress. A laterally directed blow or valgus load stretches or tears its fibres, most often at the femoral origin. Because the ligament is extra-articular with a rich blood supply, isolated tears typically heal with conservative management; combined injury to the cruciates or posteromedial corner produces greater instability and worse healing. Isolated MCL injuries of all grades usually recover well with bracing and rehabilitation; outcomes are less predictable when the injury is combined with cruciate or posteromedial corner damage.

collateral ligament injury in throwing athletes Medial epicondylitis is an overuse tendinopathy of the common flexor-pronator origin at the medial humeral epicondyle, arising from repetitive wrist flexion, forearm pronation and gripping loads, as in golf and throwing or racquet sports. As with other chronic tendinopathies the pathology is degenerative, with disorganised collagen, mucoid change and neovascularisation and little inflammation, reflecting failed tendon healing under repetitive load. The proximity of the ulnar nerve within the cubital tunnel means concurrent ulnar neuropathy is not uncommon. Most improve with load management and progressive rehabilitation, although recovery may be slow; coexisting ulnar neuropathy or ligament injury can complicate the course.

or the distal vertebral artery Presents as a classic crossed picture: contralateral limb weakness with ipsilateral tongue deviation Contralateral hemiparesis spares the face because the lesion lies towards the pons threatening consciousness and airway Vertebral dissection with risk of recurrent posterior circulation embolism Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting an evolving basilar territory event Confusing the facial-sparing hemiparesis with a hemispheric stroke and misdirecting imaging Overlooking ipsilateral tongue deviation that localises the lesion to the medial medulla Missing evolving bilateral infarction that can precipitate respiratory failure Assuming intact pain and temperature sensation excludes a brainstem stroke Medial medullary infarction results from ischaemia in the paramedian territory supplied by penetrating branches of the anterior spinal artery and distal vertebral artery. Three vertically oriented midline structures are affected: the pyramid carrying the corticospinal tract (contralateral limb weakness with facial sparing), the medial lemniscus (contralateral loss of dorsal-column sensation), and the emerging hypoglossal nerve fibres and nucleus (ipsilateral tongue weakness with deviation to the paretic side). Because the spinothalamic tract and the lateral medullary structures lie outside this territory, pain and temperature sensation and cranial nerves nine and ten are generally spared, giving the characteristic dissociated, crossed deficit. Unilateral cases often show meaningful motor recovery with rehabilitation, but bilateral or extensive infarcts causing quadriparesis and bulbar failure carry a substantially worse outcome.

Medial tibial stress syndrome — shin splints, tibial periostitis Tibial stress fracture Chronic exertional compartment syndrome Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome Tendinopathy of tibialis posterior or soleus Nerve entrapment causing exertional leg pain Clinical diagnosis from the diffuse posteromedial tibial tenderness Plain radiographs, often normal, to exclude other bony pathology MRI or bone scan where stress fracture needs to be distinguished Assessment of training load, footwear and biomechanics Compartment pressure testing if exertional compartment syndrome is suspected Exercise-induced pain along the posteromedial border of the tibia, typically over a diffuse length rather than a focal point Pain characteristically eases with rest early on but can become more persistent with continued activity It is an overuse injury common in runners, dancers and military recruits, often after a change in training load or surface A key differential is tibial stress fracture, which causes more focal tenderness and pain, and chronic exertional compartment syndrome Tenderness is spread over several centimetres of the distal medial tibia, unlike the pinpoint tenderness of a stress fracture Management centres on relative rest, load modification, addressing biomechanical and training factors, and graded return Focal tenderness and night or rest pain suggesting stress fracture Neurovascular symptoms suggesting compartment syndrome or arterial entrapment Failure to improve with appropriate load management Features suggesting bone pathology other than stress injury Missing a progressing tibial stress fracture Overlooking chronic exertional compartment syndrome as the true cause Returning to full training too quickly Failing to correct biomechanical and training-load factors Medial tibial stress syndrome represents a bone-stress and periosteal overload injury along the posteromedial tibia, sitting on a continuum that can progress to tibial stress fracture. Repetitive loading exceeds the bone's capacity to remodel, producing periosteal and cortical stress and traction from the muscles attaching along the tibial border. Contributing factors include training errors, poor footwear, hard surfaces and biomechanical abnormalities such as overpronation, which concentrate load on the medial tibia. The condition usually resolves with load modification and correction of contributing factors, though recovery can be slow and recurrence is common if training errors persist.

after other causes have been excluded Signs of gastrointestinal bleeding pointing to another diagnosis Diagnosing MALS from an incidental coeliac indentation on imaging in an asymptomatic patient Failing to perform respiratory-phase imaging to demonstrate dynamic compression Overlooking other treatable causes of chronic abdominal pain before intervention Attributing all postoperative symptom relief to arterial rather than neural decompression In median arcuate ligament syndrome, a low-lying or hypertrophied median arcuate ligament (the fibrous arch connecting the diaphragmatic crura) compresses the proximal coeliac artery and the surrounding coeliac neural plexus. The compression is dynamic, tightening during expiration as the artery rides upward. Symptoms are attributed both to a degree of foregut ischaemia or flow limitation and, importantly, to irritation of the compressed coeliac plexus, which may explain the disproportionate, meal-related pain despite generally rich collateral mesenteric circulation. Outcomes after ligament release are variable but often favourable in carefully selected patients, particularly younger patients with classic postprandial pain and confirmed dynamic compression; symptom persistence can occur when the diagnosis is misapplied.

split or canal running down the centre of the nail, most often the thumb Fine ridges angle outwards from the central groove towards the sides, producing the classic inverted fir-tree or Christmas-tree pattern An enlarged lunula is a frequently associated feature It commonly affects both thumbs symmetrically and can wax and wane over time Repetitive trauma or pressure on the proximal nail fold is thought to contribute, and it overlaps clinically with habit-tic deformity It is a benign condition, and the diagnosis is usually made clinically from the characteristic pattern Management is conservative, centring on avoiding trauma and protecting the nail, as many cases improve spontaneously though relapse is common A persistent groove localised to one nail with a swelling over the proximal fold suggesting a myxoid cyst Features of scarring nail disease such as lichen planus that require specific treatment Atypical or destructive change inconsistent with a benign central dystrophy Evidence of significant self-injurious behaviour requiring psychological support Confusing it with a myxoid cyst, which needs different management of the underlying cyst Overlooking a contributory habit or repetitive trauma Over-treating a benign, self-limiting condition Assuming permanent cure when the course is typically relapsing and remitting Median canaliform dystrophy is thought to arise from a temporary defect in nail formation at the centre of the matrix, producing a longitudinal split or canal down the middle of the plate with oblique ridges branching towards the edges. The cause is not fully understood, but repetitive trauma or pressure transmitted to the proximal nail matrix is considered an important contributor, which is why it overlaps with self-induced habit-tic deformity. Because the matrix is disturbed rather than destroyed, the change is generally reversible and can fluctuate, with the nail capable of recovering a normal surface once any trauma ceases. Median canaliform dystrophy is benign and often improves spontaneously, particularly when trauma is avoided, but it characteristically fluctuates and may recur, and complete permanent resolution cannot be guaranteed.

Median rhomboid glossitis — central papillary atrophy of the tongue Geographic tongue Erythematous candidosis elsewhere on the tongue Squamous cell carcinoma or other tongue neoplasm (if indurated) Vitamin deficiency glossitis Lingual thyroid or other midline swelling Clinical diagnosis from the characteristic midline site and appearance Mycological assessment for Candida where indicated Review of predisposing factors (smoking, inhaled steroids, immune status) Biopsy if there is induration, ulceration or diagnostic doubt A well-demarcated rhomboid or oval area of papillary atrophy in the midline of the tongue dorsum, just anterior to the circumvallate papillae It is usually asymptomatic and found incidentally, appearing smooth, red and depapillated There is a strong association with Candida colonisation, and it is often regarded as a form of chronic mucosal candidosis Smoking, denture use, inhaled corticosteroids and immunosuppression are recognised associations A matching (kissing) lesion on the opposing palate suggests more extensive candidal involvement Management includes antifungal therapy where Candida is implicated and addressing predisposing factors Induration, ulceration or a mass suggesting malignancy Failure to respond to antifungal treatment Associated widespread candidosis suggesting immunosuppression Rapid change in the lesion Mistaking an indurated lesion for the benign condition and missing carcinoma Overlooking the candidal association and predisposing factors Confusing it with geographic tongue Failing to examine the opposing palate for a kissing lesion Median rhomboid glossitis is a localised area of atrophy of the filiform papillae in the midline dorsal tongue. Although historically attributed to a developmental defect, it is now strongly linked to chronic Candida colonisation of the site, with the yeast contributing to the persistent papillary atrophy. Local factors that favour candidal overgrowth, such as smoking, corticosteroid inhalers and immunosuppression, promote the lesion, and the condition is considered a chronic candidal-associated process rather than a primary invasive infection. The condition is benign; it often improves with antifungal treatment and control of predisposing factors, though the depapillated area may persist.

vena caval obstruction or airway compromise from a bulky mass Markedly elevated tumour markers indicating aggressive non-seminomatous disease Rapid growth with distant metastases at presentation a seminoma when a raised alpha-fetoprotein indicates non-seminomatous disease Overlooking a testicular primary and mislabelling the tumour as extragonadal Not considering Klinefelter syndrome in a young man with a mediastinal germ cell tumour Primary mediastinal germ cell tumours are believed to originate from primordial germ cells that became arrested in the mediastinum during their embryonic migration along the midline. These pluripotent cells can give rise to the full spectrum of germ cell tumours, from mature teratoma through seminoma to malignant non-seminomatous types such as yolk sac tumour, embryonal carcinoma, and choriocarcinoma. Malignant elements secrete alpha-fetoprotein or beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin, which serve as diagnostic and monitoring markers. The association with Klinefelter syndrome implicates the extra X chromosome in the pathogenesis of mediastinal disease in affected young men. Mediastinal seminoma has an excellent prognosis with chemotherapy and radiotherapy, whereas primary mediastinal non-seminomatous tumours carry a poorer outlook than their gonadal counterparts and require intensive chemotherapy with resection of residual masses.

B-cell lymphoma derives from a specialised thymic medullary B cell, giving it a distinct gene-expression signature that overlaps substantially with classic Hodgkin lymphoma. Recurrent genetic events, notably gains and amplifications of the 9p24 region, upregulate JAK-STAT signalling and the programmed death-ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2, promoting proliferation and immune evasion within the tumour microenvironment. Constitutive NF-kappaB activation further supports cell survival. The neoplasm grows as sheets of large clear cells within the anterior mediastinum, accompanied by fine compartmentalising fibrosis, and tends to spread locally to adjacent thoracic structures before distant dissemination. With intensive chemoimmunotherapy the majority of patients achieve durable remission and cure, and outcomes in young patients are generally favourable; checkpoint inhibition offers meaningful salvage in relapsed or refractory disease, though bulky presentation and treatment-related toxicity remain concerns.

Mediastinal mass — mediastinal tumour, paediatric mediastinal mass Lymphoma (Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin) Germ cell tumour (including teratoma) Neuroblastoma, ganglioneuroblastoma, or ganglioneuroma Foregut duplication or bronchogenic cyst Thymic lesions and reactive or infective lymphadenopathy Chest radiograph followed by CT or MRI to localise and characterise the mass MRI of the spine for posterior masses to assess intraspinal extension Tumour markers such as alpha-fetoprotein and beta-hCG for germ cell tumours, and urinary catecholamine metabolites for neuroblastoma Tissue sampling by the safest feasible route, with bone marrow examination where relevant Airway assessment and echocardiography before anaesthesia in large anterior masses The likely diagnosis is best predicted by which mediastinal compartment is involved, so localisation to the anterior, middle, or posterior mediastinum guides the differential Anterior masses often reflect the 'terrible T's', notably lymphoma and germ cell tumours; posterior masses in children are frequently neurogenic tumours such as neuroblastoma Middle mediastinal lesions include lymphadenopathy, foregut duplication cysts, and bronchogenic cysts Many masses are found incidentally on chest imaging, but they can cause cough, wheeze, stridor, superior vena cava obstruction, or dysphagia through mass effect A large anterior mediastinal mass is a serious anaesthetic hazard because it can compress the airway and great vessels, particularly when the child lies supine Whenever possible a tissue diagnosis should be obtained by the least invasive and safest route, and general anaesthesia may need to be avoided in high-risk airway compression Investigation includes cross-sectional imaging, and, depending on suspected pathology, tumour markers and marrow or nodal sampling Neurogenic posterior tumours require spinal imaging to detect intraspinal (dumbbell) extension that may threaten the cord A large anterior mediastinal mass causing airway or great-vessel compression, which is a critical anaesthetic emergency and can cause cardiorespiratory collapse under sedation or when supine Superior vena cava obstruction with facial swelling, distended veins, and respiratory distress Stridor, orthopnoea, or inability to lie flat indicating significant tracheal compression Posterior tumour with intraspinal extension threatening spinal cord compression Inducing general anaesthesia in a child with a large anterior mass without assessing airway and cardiovascular compression risk Delaying diagnosis of superior vena cava obstruction or airway compromise Failing to image the spine in posterior neurogenic tumours and missing cord compression Pursuing an invasive biopsy when a diagnosis could be obtained more safely by markers or peripheral sampling A mediastinal mass is any space-occupying lesion within the mediastinum, and its nature relates strongly to the compartment of origin because different tissues predominate in each. Anterior lesions arise from thymic, lymphoid, germ cell, or thyroid tissue; middle lesions from lymph nodes, the airway, and foregut-derived cysts; and posterior lesions largely from neural tissue along the sympathetic chain. Symptoms result mainly from compression or invasion of adjacent structures such as the trachea, bronchi, great vessels, oesophagus, and spinal cord, and systemic effects may occur with malignant or hormonally active tumours. Prognosis depends entirely on the underlying pathology, ranging from excellent for benign cysts and localised resectable tumours to highly variable outcomes for lymphomas and neuroblastoma, which depend on stage, histology, and biology. Early recognition of airway compromise is critical to avoid procedure-related mortality.

Underestimating the technical difficulty of resecting a mass densely adherent to great vessels Mediastinal teratomas are thought to arise from primordial germ cells that fail to complete their migration and become mislocated within the mediastinum during embryogenesis. These pluripotent cells give rise to tissues derived from all three germ layers, so the resulting mass typically contains a mixture of ectodermal skin and hair, mesodermal fat and cartilage, and endodermal glandular elements, accounting for the characteristic heterogeneous imaging appearance with fat and calcification. Mature teratomas are well differentiated and benign, but tumours containing immature tissue or other malignant germ cell components behave more aggressively and may secrete tumour markers. Completely resected mature teratomas have an excellent prognosis and are effectively cured, whereas immature or malignant germ cell tumours require multimodality treatment and carry a more guarded outlook.

cause New headache with onset over the age of 50 Not taking a thorough medication history including over-the-counter and non-headache analgesics Overlooking opioid and combination-analgesic overuse as major drivers Escalating acute treatment instead of recognising and treating the overuse Failing to start preventive therapy and support around withdrawal, increasing the risk of relapse Assuming that persistent headache after withdrawal is still medication overuse and missing a secondary cause Medication-overuse headache develops in predisposed individuals with a primary headache disorder through medication-induced changes in central pain processing. Chronic exposure to acute headache drugs is thought to cause neuroadaptive changes, including sensitisation of trigeminal and central pain pathways, altered descending pain modulation, receptor changes in serotonergic and opioid systems, and cortical hyperexcitability, which lower the threshold for headache. The result is a self-perpetuating cycle in which increasing medication use drives more frequent headache. Genetic and behavioural factors, including dependence-related mechanisms, contribute, and the disorder characteristically reverses after withdrawal. With withdrawal of the overused medication and optimisation of preventive treatment, a large proportion of patients improve substantially and revert to their underlying episodic pattern, usually within weeks to a couple of months. Relapse is common, however, so ongoing education and limitation of acute-medication use are needed.

The enlarged platelets and modestly reduced counts reflect abnormal megakaryocyte fragmentation rather than peripheral destruction. The condition is usually benign with a normal life expectancy and minimal bleeding, and its main clinical importance lies in correct recognition to avoid unnecessary investigation and treatment.

Local replication at the inoculation site produces the characteristic necrotic eschar (tache noire) through focal vasculitis and dermal necrosis, while dissemination causes a generalised small-vessel vasculitis analogous to other spotted fever rickettsioses. Endothelial injury increases vascular permeability and activates coagulation, producing the rash and, in severe cases, organ dysfunction affecting the brain, kidneys and lungs. The majority of cases resolve fully with timely doxycycline, but the severe malignant form carries appreciable mortality, especially in older or comorbid patients, so early empirical treatment is important.

considering an underlying fatty acid oxidation defect MCAD deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder, usually due to a common ACADM gene variant, that impairs the beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids. During fasting the body normally shifts to oxidising fatty acids for energy and generating ketones for the brain; when medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase is deficient, this pathway stalls, so energy production fails and ketogenesis is inadequate. Glucose is consumed without adequate fat-derived backup, producing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia. Accumulated medium-chain fatty acids and their carnitine and glycine conjugates are toxic and contribute to encephalopathy and hepatic dysfunction. Secondary carnitine depletion is common. With diagnosis (especially via newborn screening) and simple preventive measures the prognosis is excellent and most individuals remain healthy; however, an unrecognised metabolic crisis can cause sudden death or permanent neurological injury, so the main determinant of outcome is prevention of fasting-induced decompensation.

AP-1 mediates clathrin-dependent sorting of transmembrane cargo between the trans-Golgi network and endosomes. Disrupted AP-1 function impairs the correct trafficking and localisation of the copper-transporting ATPases ATP7A and ATP7B, producing a mixed copper-handling defect that biochemically overlaps both Menkes and Wilson disease. The same trafficking failure perturbs epidermal keratinocyte differentiation, enterocyte function, myelination, and neuronal development, generating the combined dermatological, gastrointestinal, auditory, neurological, and cognitive phenotype. A chronic multisystem disorder; early enteropathy can be life-threatening, while survivors face progressive hearing loss, neuropathy, and variable cognitive impairment, with liver involvement contributing to long-term morbidity.

Inheritance is autosomal dominant, with slowly progressive chronic kidney disease and characteristically bland urine showing little or no proteinuria or haematuria. UMOD (uromodulin) disease typically causes hyperuricaemia and early-onset gout, often preceding renal impairment. Cysts are few, small and corticomedullary and are frequently absent, so the historical name is a misnomer and the diagnosis is not made on imaging. Kidneys are normal or small in size and imaging is usually non-specific. Distinguish it from nephronophthisis, which is autosomal recessive, causes end-stage disease in childhood or adolescence and has retinal, hepatic and skeletal associations. Diagnosis rests on family history, clinical phenotype and genetic testing; biopsy shows tubulointerstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy. Management is supportive, progressing over decades to end-stage renal disease requiring renal replacement or transplantation. Rapidly declining renal function Uraemic symptoms indicating advanced chronic kidney disease Refractory or tophaceous gout Extrarenal features suggesting an alternative genetic syndrome Expecting imaging cysts to confirm the diagnosis when they are often absent Confusing autosomal recessive nephronophthisis with autosomal dominant ADTKD Missing UMOD disease in young patients presenting with gout and chronic kidney disease Overlooking the family history because of variable expression Medullary cystic kidney disease belongs to a group of autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial diseases caused by mutations in genes expressed in the distal nephron. UMOD mutations cause misfolding and intracellular retention of uromodulin within thick ascending limb cells, provoking endoplasmic reticulum stress and tubular injury, whereas MUC1 frameshift mutations generate a toxic mucin-1 neoprotein; HNF1B and REN mutations account for further cases. The common pathway is progressive tubulointerstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy with relatively bland urine, and corticomedullary cysts, when present, are a secondary and inconstant feature. The disease progresses slowly over decades, with most affected individuals reaching end-stage renal disease in adulthood; transplantation is successful because the condition does not recur in the graft.

the precalyceal segments of the collecting ducts within the renal pyramids are cystically dilated, producing a sponge-like cut surface. The stagnant urine within these ectatic ducts, combined with frequently coexisting metabolic tubular abnormalities such as hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia and impaired distal urinary acidification, favours crystal precipitation, medullary nephrocalcinosis and recurrent calcium stone formation. Urinary stasis also predisposes to infection. Although the defect is structural and lifelong, glomerular function is generally maintained because the process is confined to the distal tubular architecture. The long-term outlook is generally good, with renal function usually preserved; morbidity arises chiefly from recurrent stones and infections, which are reduced by metabolic evaluation, high fluid intake and correction of underlying tubular abnormalities.

Because it does not originate from follicular epithelium, it neither takes up iodine nor produces thyroglobulin, so calcitonin and CEA serve as its markers and radioactive iodine has no role. Sporadic tumours and the hereditary MEN2 syndromes are both driven by activating RET proto-oncogene mutations; germline RET mutations cause the familial forms and, in MEN2, associate with phaeochromocytoma and, in MEN2A, primary hyperparathyroidism. Outcome depends heavily on stage: node-negative disease confined to the thyroid can be cured surgically, whereas extensive nodal or distant metastasis and short calcitonin/CEA doubling times predict poorer survival.

Long-term survivors frequently experience treatment-related neurocognitive, endocrine and growth sequelae.

counsel about the autosomal dominant inheritance Meesmann epithelial corneal dystrophy is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the cornea-specific keratin genes KRT12 and KRT3. These keratins form the intermediate filament cytoskeleton of the corneal epithelium, and mutations weaken epithelial cell integrity. The fragile epithelium develops numerous small intraepithelial cysts containing degenerated cellular material, and the compromised cells are prone to breakdown. disease Failing to recognise the X-linked inheritance when counselling and screening families Assuming carrier females are unaffected Delaying surgical referral for an enlarging aneurysm Meester-Loeys syndrome is an X-linked heritable connective-tissue aortopathy caused by loss-of-function variants in BGN, encoding biglycan. Biglycan is a small leucine-rich proteoglycan of the extracellular matrix that helps organise collagen and elastic fibres and modulates transforming growth factor beta signalling in the arterial wall. Deficiency of functional biglycan weakens the structural integrity of the aortic media and dysregulates growth-factor signalling, predisposing to aortic root and more widespread arterial dilatation, tortuosity, aneurysm and dissection. The same matrix disturbance produces the skeletal and connective-tissue features. Because the gene is X-linked, hemizygous males are generally affected more severely than heterozygous females. Prognosis is dominated by the risk of aortic aneurysm and dissection, which can be life-threatening, particularly in males; structured surveillance, medical therapy and timely surgery substantially improve outcome.

a subset arises from variants in GLIALCAM (HEPACAM), which can produce both recessive disease and a remitting dominant form Presents in infancy with macrocephaly that develops within the first year, often the earliest and most striking sign Early motor and cognitive development is often near-normal, with slow deterioration of gait, ataxia, and spasticity over years Seizures are common and may be precipitated by minor head trauma; epilepsy is a frequent feature Cognitive decline is usually mild and late relative to the severity of the white-matter changes on imaging MRI shows diffusely swollen, abnormal cerebral white matter with characteristic subcortical cysts, typically in the anterior temporal and frontoparietal regions The dominant GLIALCAM-related variant may show improving imaging and a milder, sometimes reversible course Diagnosis rests on the combination of macrocephaly, the typical MRI pattern, and confirmatory genetic testing; there is no disease-modifying therapy Acute neurological deterioration or seizures following minor head trauma Rapidly progressive loss of ambulation or bulbar function Status epilepticus Signs of raised intracranial pressure disproportionate to the known chronic swelling Attributing infantile macrocephaly to benign familial causes and delaying imaging Interpreting the extensive MRI white-matter change as indicating imminent severe cognitive collapse, which is usually late Missing the distinct improving-imaging pattern of the dominant GLIALCAM variant Overlooking head-trauma-precipitated seizures as a recognised feature Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts is a disorder of brain water and ion homeostasis. MLC1 and GlialCAM are proteins expressed at astrocytic end-feet and cell-cell contacts, where they regulate ion and water flux (including chloride channel activity via ClC-2) across the blood-brain and glial-limiting barriers. Defective function impairs the astrocytic handling of fluid, leading to chronic intramyelinic and extracellular oedema. Histologically the white matter is vacuolated, with splitting of myelin lamellae, and fluid accumulates to form the subcortical cysts and diffuse swelling characteristic of the disease. The classic recessive form follows a slowly progressive course over years to decades, with preserved cognition until late and gradual loss of motor function; the dominant GLIALCAM-related form is milder and may partially remit. Life expectancy varies but many patients survive into adulthood.
