giving incorrect recurrence-risk counselling Megalencephaly-capillary malformation syndrome is part of the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum and results from post-zygotic mosaic activating variants in PIK3CA, which constitutively activate the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway. Excessive signalling promotes unregulated growth and proliferation, producing brain overgrowth (megalencephaly with cortical malformation such as polymicrogyria), segmental somatic overgrowth, and vascular anomalies. Because the mutation is mosaic, disease burden and distribution depend on when and where the variant arose during development. Outcome is variable and largely determined by the severity of brain involvement, with many individuals having developmental delay, epilepsy, and a risk of hindbrain herniation requiring neurosurgical monitoring. Somatic overgrowth and vascular features are managed supportively, and targeted pathway inhibition is being explored for severe disease.

Megaloblastic Anemias — Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia, Cobalamin deficiency anemia, Folate deficiency anemia, Pernicious anemia Megaloblastic anemia from antifolate/antimetabolite drugs (methotrexate, pyrimethamine, trimethoprim; hydroxyurea, cytarabine, mercaptopurine, thioguanine, AZT) (Harrison 22e p.780, p.790) Orotic aciduria (responds to uridine) (Harrison 22e p.780, p.790) Thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anemia (SLC19A2 transporter defect; may have diabetes, deafness, ringed sideroblasts) (Harrison 22e p.780, p.790) Megaloblastic changes in acute myeloid leukemia and myelodysplasia (refractory to folate/cobalamin) (Harrison 22e p.780, p.790) Macrocytosis without true megaloblastic change: alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, myelodysplasia, myeloma/paraproteinemia, aplastic anemia, smoking (Harrison 22e p.790) Serum cobalamin (ELISA or competitive-binding luminescence assay); note IF antibodies can cause falsely normal results in up to 50% of pernicious anemia cases (Harrison 22e p.788) Serum methylmalonic acid (raised in cobalamin deficiency sufficient for anemia/neuropathy; fluctuates in renal failure) (Harrison 22e p.788, p.789) Serum homocysteine (raised in early cobalamin and folate deficiency but nonspecific) (Harrison 22e p.789) Serum folate and red cell folate (red cell folate reflects body stores; false-normal after transfusion or with high reticulocytes) (Harrison 22e p.789) Serum gastrin (raised in pernicious anemia) and pepsinogen I (low) (Harrison 22e p.785, p.789) Intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies; gastric endoscopy/biopsy (Harrison 22e p.786, p.789) Bone marrow examination in selected severely anemic patients (Harrison 22e p.784) Transglutaminase antibodies to exclude gluten-induced enteropathy in folate deficiency (Harrison 22e p.789) Myelodysplasia (megaloblastoid marrow may mimic megaloblastic anemia and, in severe cases, accumulation of blasts may mimic acute myeloid leukemia) (Harrison 22e p.785) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (a weakly positive direct antiglobulin test due to complement from ineffective erythropoiesis can lead to a false diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.785) Other causes of macrocytosis: alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, pregnancy (Harrison 22e p.790) Megaloblastic anemias share a defect in DNA synthesis affecting rapidly dividing marrow cells, producing characteristic morphology with a hypercellular marrow and ineffective erythropoiesis (Harrison 22e p.780). The usual cause is deficiency of cobalamin (vitamin B12) or folate, but the picture can also arise from genetic or acquired abnormalities of their metabolism or from DNA-synthesis defects unrelated to either vitamin (Harrison 22e p.780). Body cobalamin stores (about 2-3 mg) are large enough to last 3-4 years if intake stops, whereas folate stores (about 10 mg total, mostly hepatic) suffice for only 3-4 months, so severe folate deficiency can develop rapidly (Harrison 22e p.780, p.781). Cobalamin is made only by microorganisms; the sole human source is animal-derived food, so strict vegans are at risk of dietary deficiency (Harrison 22e p.781, p.786). Pernicious anemia, the dominant cause of severe cobalamin deficiency in Western countries, is gastric atrophy with severe lack of intrinsic factor; median onset is age 70-80, it clusters with other organ-specific autoimmune diseases (thyroid disease, vitiligo, type 1 diabetes, Addison disease), and gastric output of acid, pepsin, and intrinsic factor is severely reduced with raised serum gastrin and low pepsinogen I (Harrison 22e p.785, p.786). Cobalamin deficiency can cause neurologic disease (subacute combined degeneration) with demyelination of posterior and lateral spinal columns, peripheral neuropathy, optic atrophy, and cerebral changes including dementia and psychosis; patients (more often male) present with paresthesias, weakness, or gait difficulty, often with positive Romberg and Lhermitte signs (Harrison 22e p.783). Peripheral blood shows oval macrocytes with marked aniso-poikilocytosis, an MCV usually >100 fL (unless coexisting microcytosis), and hypersegmented neutrophils (more than five nuclear lobes) (Harrison 22e p.784). In a nonanemic patient, a few macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils may be the only clue to underlying deficiency, and serum cobalamin may be borderline; supporting tests include MMA, IF/parietal-cell antibodies, and serum gastrin (Harrison 22e p.783, p.784). Periconceptional folic acid reduces neural tube defects (anencephaly, meningomyelocele, encephalocele, spina bifida) by roughly 80%; the lower the maternal folate, the greater the fetal risk (Harrison 22e p.783). Older patients with iron deficiency should also be assessed for cobalamin deficiency and vice versa, since coexistence is common (15-20% over age 60) and iron deficiency may blunt the macrocytosis (Harrison 22e p.789). Removal of 1.2 m or more of terminal ileum, total gastrectomy, fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum) infestation, and intestinal stagnant-loop syndrome are recognized malabsorptive causes of cobalamin deficiency (Harrison 22e p.786, p.787). Neurologic signs of subacute combined degeneration: loss of proprioception/vibration, positive Romberg and Lhermitte signs, ataxic/spastic gait, hyperreflexia (Harrison 22e p.783) Cerebral involvement: dementia, depression, psychosis, cognitive impairment, visual impairment from optic atrophy (Harrison 22e p.783) Nonanemic patient with neurologic/psychiatric features and low or borderline serum cobalamin (deficiency must be actively confirmed) (Harrison 22e p.783) Severe thrombocytopenia (rarely <40 x 10^9/L) with bruising (Harrison 22e p.783, p.784) Marked marrow blast accumulation in severe cases mimicking acute leukemia (Harrison 22e p.785) Intrinsic-factor antibodies can produce falsely normal serum cobalamin in up to 50% of pernicious anemia patients tested by certain assays — a normal level does not exclude pernicious anemia when clinical suspicion is strong (Harrison 22e p.788). Giving large doses of folic acid before excluding/correcting cobalamin deficiency can allow cobalamin neuropathy to progress despite hematologic response (Harrison 22e p.789, p.790). Serum folate falls with recent poor diet but rises in severe cobalamin deficiency (methylfolate trap) and in stagnant-loop syndrome, so it can mislead (Harrison 22e p.789). Mildly elevated MMA and/or homocysteine occur in up to 30% of healthy volunteers and in 15% of elderly with normal cobalamin, so cutoffs and clinical significance are uncertain (Harrison 22e p.789). Coexisting iron deficiency may mask macrocytosis; the term 'megaloblastoid' is best avoided as it refers to myelodysplastic change refractory to vitamin therapy (Harrison 22e p.785, p.789). A weakly positive direct antiglobulin test from ineffective erythropoiesis can be misread as autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Harrison 22e p.785). The common defect is impaired DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells. In folate or cobalamin deficiency, conversion of deoxyuridine monophosphate (dUMP) to deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP) fails because the folate coenzyme 5,10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate, needed for this step, becomes scarce. The shortage of dTTP precursor slows DNA replication, leaving single-stranded breaks; an alternative theory invokes misincorporation of uracil into DNA. Cobalamin is a cofactor for two reactions: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and the methionine-synthase-mediated methylation of homocysteine to methionine, which also requires 5-methyl-THF. In cobalamin deficiency, 5-methyl-THF accumulates in plasma while intracellular THF (the substrate for folate polyglutamate formation) falls — the methylfolate trap (THF starvation) — explaining high serum folate but low cell folate, and why the anemia of cobalamin deficiency can respond to large folic acid doses. Death of nucleated red cells in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) produces unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, raised LDH, raised urine urobilinogen, and reduced haptoglobins (Harrison 22e p.782, p.783, p.785). With regular treatment of pernicious anemia, life expectancy is normal in women; men historically had slightly reduced life expectancy due to a higher incidence of gastric carcinoma, with current data unavailable. Neurologic recovery depends on duration before treatment, and a therapeutic trial of at least 3 months may be needed to judge improvement in neuropsychiatric cases. Untreated severe deficiency causes progressive anemia, neurologic deterioration, and infertility (Harrison 22e p.783, p.786). Severity is gauged by the degree of anemia and parallels the morphologic changes; marrow involvement is described as severe, intermediate, mild, or early. In megaloblastic anemia due to cobalamin deficiency the serum cobalamin is usually <74 pmol/L (100 ng/L), with 74-148 pmol/L (100-200 ng/L) regarded as borderline; the more severe the deficiency, the lower the level, and very low levels occur with spinal cord involvement even without anemia (Harrison 22e p.785, p.788).

Megalocornea — anterior megalophthalmos Primary congenital glaucoma (buphthalmos) Keratoglobus High axial myopia Marfan and other connective tissue disorders (for lens subluxation) Anterior megalophthalmos as part of a syndrome Measurement of corneal diameter and intraocular pressure Assessment for corneal clarity and Descemet tears (to exclude glaucoma) Lens and zonule assessment Refraction Family history and, where appropriate, genetic evaluation A non-progressive, bilaterally symmetrical enlargement of the cornea with a normal intraocular pressure The corneal diameter is enlarged beyond the normal range while the cornea remains clear It is most often X-linked recessive, so it predominantly affects males The crucial differential is primary congenital glaucoma (buphthalmos), which is distinguished by raised pressure, corneal oedema and progression Associated features can include high myopia, lens subluxation, cataract and pigment dispersion Management is largely refractive and monitoring, with attention to lens-related complications later in life Raised intraocular pressure or corneal oedema indicating glaucoma Progressive corneal enlargement Lens subluxation or cataract Features of an underlying connective tissue disorder Mistaking it for primary congenital glaucoma and vice versa Overlooking later lens subluxation or cataract Attributing reduced vision solely to refractive error Missing an associated systemic disorder Megalocornea is a developmental enlargement of the cornea, thought to result from either an oversized optic cup or failure of the developing anterior segment to close normally, producing a large but structurally clear cornea with a deep anterior chamber. In the common X-linked form it is caused by mutations affecting anterior segment development. Unlike buphthalmos, the enlargement is not driven by raised intraocular pressure, so the cornea stays clear; however, the enlarged anterior segment can be associated with zonular weakness leading to lens subluxation and cataract. Megalocornea itself is benign and non-progressive with generally good vision when refractive error is corrected; later lens complications may need intervention.

megalopapilla — megalopapilla, abnormally large optic disc Glaucomatous optic disc cupping Optic nerve coloboma Morning glory disc anomaly Physiological large cup Peripapillary staphyloma Optic disc pit Tilted disc syndrome Stereoscopic disc examination and disc photography to assess rim integrity Optical coherence tomography of the disc and retinal nerve fibre layer Intraocular pressure measurement to exclude glaucoma Automated perimetry to document any enlarged blind spot and exclude glaucomatous loss Measurement of disc diameter and cup-to-disc ratio Neuroimaging when a basal encephalocoele or midline anomaly is suspected A congenital anomaly defined by an abnormally large optic disc, conventionally with a horizontal or vertical diameter of roughly 2.1 mm or more. Two forms are described: a common form with generalised disc enlargement and a large but round cup, and a form with a superotemporal or inferonasal enlargement resembling a coloboma. The enlarged cup produces a raised cup-to-disc ratio that can be mistaken for glaucomatous cupping. The neuroretinal rim remains healthy and of normal colour, and the cup shape is typically round and central rather than notched. Frequently bilateral and usually associated with normal or near-normal visual acuity. May show an enlarged blind spot on perimetry but generally without progressive glaucomatous field loss. Distinguished from glaucoma by a normal intraocular pressure, an intact rim, and a stable, non-progressive course. Rarely associated with midline anomalies such as basal encephalocoele, so imaging is considered when other features are present. Progressive cup enlargement or neuroretinal rim thinning suggesting coexisting glaucoma Raised intraocular pressure with a suspicious disc Midline facial anomalies or features suggesting basal encephalocoele Development of a glaucomatous or arcuate visual field defect over time Misdiagnosing the large physiological cup as glaucomatous cupping and starting pressure-lowering therapy unnecessarily. Failing to appreciate that the neuroretinal rim is intact when interpreting a high cup-to-disc ratio. Overlooking coexisting glaucoma in a large disc by assuming all cupping is congenital. Neglecting to consider a midline encephalocoele in atypical or syndromic presentations. Megalopapilla reflects a congenital enlargement of the scleral canal and optic nerve head, resulting in an abnormally large disc with a correspondingly large optic cup. The normal complement of retinal ganglion cell axons is distributed across a wider canal, so the cup-to-disc ratio increases while the neuroretinal rim tissue remains structurally and functionally intact. Because the enlargement is a primary developmental variant of canal size rather than a loss of axons, there is no progressive excavation or rim thinning as seen in glaucoma. The larger disc surface projects a correspondingly larger blind spot, but ganglion cell function and the visual field are otherwise typically preserved. Megalopapilla is a stationary developmental variant with an excellent visual prognosis and normal acuity in most cases. Recognising it prevents overdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment for glaucoma.

MEGDEL syndrome — SERAC1 deficiency, 3-methylglutaconic aciduria with deafness, encephalopathy and Leigh-like syndrome, MEGD(H)EL syndrome, 3-methylglutaconic aciduria type IV / SERAC1-related Other causes of 3-methylglutaconic aciduria (Barth syndrome, TMEM70 defect, DNAJC19-related disease) Leigh syndrome from other nuclear or mitochondrial DNA mutations Neonatal mitochondrial hepatopathies Dystonic cerebral palsy in a child with sensorineural hearing loss Congenital or acquired causes of neonatal hypoglycaemia with liver dysfunction Other progressive encephalopathies with movement disorder Urine organic acids demonstrating persistent 3-methylglutaconic aciduria SERAC1 gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis Brain MRI to document evolving basal ganglia (putaminal) and Leigh-like changes Audiological assessment for sensorineural hearing loss Liver function tests and glucose monitoring in the neonatal period Blood and CSF lactate as markers of mitochondrial dysfunction Autosomal recessive disorder caused by SERAC1 mutations affecting a protein involved in phospholipid remodelling and cholesterol trafficking at the mitochondria-associated membranes The acronym captures the core features: 3-Methylglutaconic aciduria, Deafness (sensorineural), Encephalopathy, and Leigh-like disease Neonates often have transient hepatic dysfunction and hypoglycaemia in the newborn period that resolves, followed by developmental regression and a dystonia-spasticity movement disorder Persistent 3-methylglutaconic aciduria on urine organic acids is the biochemical hallmark and a key screening clue in an infant with deafness and encephalopathy Brain MRI evolves to show basal ganglia (especially putaminal) changes in a Leigh-like pattern, correlating with the extrapyramidal movement disorder Diagnosis combines the biochemical and MRI findings with SERAC1 sequencing; management is supportive, including hearing rehabilitation and movement-disorder care Neonatal hypoglycaemia with hepatic dysfunction requiring urgent stabilisation Developmental regression with an emerging severe dystonic movement disorder Progressive sensorineural deafness affecting communication and development Acute neurological deterioration during intercurrent illness Attributing transient neonatal liver disease and hypoglycaemia to sepsis or perinatal stress and missing the metabolic diagnosis Not testing urine organic acids, thereby overlooking the diagnostic 3-methylglutaconic aciduria Labelling the child as dystonic cerebral palsy without investigating a progressive mitochondrial disorder Failing to identify and rehabilitate sensorineural hearing loss early MEGDEL syndrome results from biallelic SERAC1 mutations. SERAC1 localises to mitochondria-associated endoplasmic reticulum membranes and participates in phosphatidylglycerol remodelling, a step needed for mature cardiolipin synthesis, and in intracellular cholesterol trafficking. Disturbed phospholipid composition impairs mitochondrial membrane function and oxidative metabolism, producing the multisystem picture of neonatal hepatopathy and hypoglycaemia, sensorineural deafness, and a progressive Leigh-like encephalopathy with dystonia. The disrupted mitochondrial lipid metabolism underlies the characteristic and persistent 3-methylglutaconic aciduria. MEGDEL syndrome is a progressive disorder; the neonatal hepatopathy and hypoglycaemia are often transient, but the neurological course leads to significant intellectual and motor disability with a disabling dystonia and deafness, and life expectancy is reduced. Care is supportive and multidisciplinary.

newborn Assuming intellectual disability when cognition is often relatively preserved Meier-Gorlin syndrome results from variants in components of the origin recognition complex and other pre-replication complex proteins that license origins of DNA replication before each cell division. Airway and feeding difficulties in infancy are the main early risks.

meige lymphoedema — lymphoedema praecox, hereditary lymphoedema type II Milroy disease (congenital hereditary lymphoedema type I) lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome (FOXC2) lymphoedema tarda with onset after 35 years secondary lymphoedema from infection, malignancy or trauma lipoedema chronic venous insufficiency systemic oedema from cardiac, renal or hepatic disease lymphoscintigraphy to demonstrate impaired lymphatic transport detailed family pedigree and targeted genetic testing venous duplex ultrasonography to exclude venous disease MR or CT lymphangiography for anatomical assessment slit-lamp ophthalmic examination to exclude distichiasis thyroid, renal, hepatic and cardiac evaluation to exclude systemic oedema The most common form of primary lymphoedema, defined by onset around puberty and before the age of 35 years, hence the alternative term lymphoedema praecox. It shows a clear female predominance and typically presents as bilateral, often asymmetrical, lower-limb swelling. Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant with variable penetrance and expressivity, so an affected first-degree relative supports the diagnosis. It is distinguished from Milroy disease, which is congenital, type I and classically linked to FLT4 (VEGFR3) mutations, whereas Meige disease presents later and is genetically heterogeneous. By definition Meige disease is isolated lymphoedema; the presence of distichiasis points instead to FOXC2-related lymphoedema-distichiasis and warrants ophthalmic examination. The Stemmer sign is positive and the swelling begins distally before ascending, becoming progressively less pitting over time. As with all chronic lymphoedema, recurrent cellulitis is common and both worsens and is worsened by the underlying lymphatic failure. Lymphoscintigraphy confirms impaired lymphatic transport and helps exclude a secondary cause when onset is unusually asymmetrical or abrupt. recurrent cellulitis with systemic sepsis new violaceous or haemorrhagic cutaneous nodules suggesting angiosarcoma rapidly progressive or newly asymmetrical swelling prompting exclusion of malignancy syndromic features such as distichiasis, ptosis or yellow nails indicating an alternative diagnosis skin ulceration or lymphorrhoea labelling all pubertal-onset lymphoedema as isolated Meige disease without checking for distichiasis or other syndromic features failing to take a family history and thereby missing the hereditary pattern confusing early presentation with lipoedema undertreating cellulitis and accelerating lymphatic damage attributing swelling to venous disease and delaying appropriate lymphatic management Meige lymphoedema arises from a constitutional abnormality of the peripheral lymphatic vessels, most often hypoplasia or aplasia of the collecting lymphatics, which becomes clinically manifest around puberty. The peripubertal timing suggests a hormonal trigger that unmasks marginal lymphatic reserve. Deficient lymphatic drainage causes accumulation of protein-rich interstitial fluid, and the resulting chronic inflammation drives adipose deposition and dermal fibrosis in the same self-perpetuating manner seen across primary lymphoedema. The condition is genetically heterogeneous, and it must be separated from defined single-gene entities such as FOXC2-related lymphoedema-distichiasis and GJC2-associated disease, which have distinct features and inheritance. Meige lymphoedema is a lifelong condition, but with compression, skin care, exercise and infection prevention most patients maintain good limb function and a favourable quality of life. The outlook worsens with recurrent cellulitis and advanced fibrosis, and the small long-term risk of angiosarcoma persists.

Meige syndrome — cranial dystonia, blepharospasm-oromandibular dystonia, Brueghel syndrome Isolated blepharospasm Hemifacial spasm Tardive dyskinesia or tardive dystonia Functional facial movements Facial tics Temporomandibular joint disorder (for jaw symptoms) Clinical diagnosis from the characteristic combination of signs Medication history to identify drug-induced tardive syndromes MRI of the brain if features suggest a secondary cause Assessment of functional impact on vision, speech and eating Evaluation for sensory tricks supporting a dystonic diagnosis A segmental cranial dystonia combining blepharospasm with oromandibular dystonia affecting the jaw, tongue and lower face Blepharospasm causes involuntary forced eyelid closure that can be functionally blinding Oromandibular dystonia produces involuntary jaw opening or closing, lip and tongue movements, and can impair speech and eating It typically begins in mid to late adult life and is more common in women Sensory tricks (geste antagoniste) such as touching the face may transiently relieve the spasms Botulinum toxin injection into the affected muscles is the mainstay of treatment Rapid progression or additional neurological signs suggesting secondary dystonia History of dopamine-receptor-blocking drug use Functional blindness from severe blepharospasm Marked speech or swallowing impairment Mistaking bilateral cranial dystonia for unilateral hemifacial spasm Overlooking a tardive syndrome from previous neuroleptic exposure Underestimating the functional impact of severe blepharospasm Failing to recognise sensory tricks that confirm dystonia Meige syndrome is a focal or segmental dystonia of the cranial muscles arising from dysfunction within basal ganglia motor circuits and their control of facial and jaw musculature. As in other dystonias, abnormal patterns of muscle co-contraction produce sustained or repetitive involuntary movements, and altered sensorimotor integration underlies both the dystonic postures and the benefit from sensory tricks. Most cases are idiopathic, though secondary cranial dystonia can follow certain drug exposures or brain lesions. The condition is usually chronic, but repeated botulinum toxin treatment provides substantial symptomatic relief for most patients and can preserve function.

ovarian tumour, ascites, and a pleural effusion, all of which resolve after the tumour is removed The classic tumour is an ovarian fibroma, though thecomas, Brenner tumours, and granulosa cell tumours radiological picture indistinguishable from disseminated ovarian malignancy A markedly raised CA-125 heightening concern for cancer A large pleural effusion causing breathlessness or respiratory compromise Any histological or cytological feature suggesting true malignancy Misdiagnosing the syndrome as advanced ovarian malignancy and instituting inappropriate treatment Placing undue reliance on a raised CA-125 to infer malignancy Failing to obtain fluid cytology to confirm the benign nature of the effusions Not recognising that resolution of effusions after surgery supports the diagnosis A benign solid ovarian tumour, most commonly a fibroma, becomes associated with the accumulation of ascitic fluid and a pleural effusion. The fluid is thought to arise from transudation or leakage from the surface of the tumour or its lymphatics into the peritoneal cavity, from where it passes to the pleural space through diaphragmatic lymphatic channels and defects. Because the effusions are secondary to the presence of the tumour rather than to malignant spread, they resolve once it is excised. The prognosis is excellent; because the tumour is benign, complete surgical removal cures the condition and leads to full resolution of the ascites and pleural effusion.

antioxidant supplements while avoiding agents that impair respiratory-chain function Acute stroke-like episode with encephalopathy, seizures or status epilepticus requiring urgent neurological support New or decompensating cardiomyopathy or cardiac conduction block Rapidly rising lactic acidosis with metabolic decompensation Exposure to mitochondrial toxins that may precipitate deterioration Misdiagnosing stroke-like episodes as conventional ischaemic stroke and overlooking the underlying mitochondrial disease Testing only blood, where the m.3243A>G mutation may be undetectable or at low level; urine or muscle sampling improves yield Using agents that impair mitochondrial function, which can trigger decompensation Attributing hearing loss, diabetes or short stature to unrelated causes rather than recognising a unifying maternal disorder MELAS results from a defect of oxidative phosphorylation, most often the m.3243A>G substitution in the mitochondrial transfer RNA(Leu) gene, which impairs mitochondrial protein synthesis and reduces the activity of respiratory-chain complexes. Because mitochondrial DNA is maternally transmitted and present in many copies per cell, a mixture of mutant and normal genomes (heteroplasmy) exists, and disease appears only once the mutant proportion exceeds a tissue-specific threshold. Energy-demanding tissues such as brain, muscle and the endocrine pancreas are preferentially affected. The stroke-like episodes are thought to reflect a combination of neuronal hyperexcitability, an angiopathy of small cerebral vessels with dysfunctional mitochondria in endothelium and smooth muscle, and a mismatch between metabolic demand and impaired energy supply rather than true thromboembolic occlusion. MELAS is a progressive multisystem disorder; recurrent stroke-like episodes tend to accumulate neurological disability, dementia and, in many patients, a shortened lifespan, though the course is highly variable and depends on mutant load and organ involvement.

Melasma — chloasma, mask of pregnancy, melasma faciei Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation following acne or dermatitis Solar lentigines and other photo-induced pigmentation Drug-induced pigmentation Ochronosis (which can be exogenous, from overuse of hydroquinone) Riehl's melanosis / pigmented contact dermatitis Naevus of Ota or acquired dermal melanocytosis Primarily a clinical diagnosis supported by dermoscopy Wood's lamp examination to help assess pigment depth Skin biopsy only in atypical or treatment-resistant cases Review of hormonal and drug history as part of assessment Presents as symmetrical, poorly defined brown to grey-brown patches on sun-exposed facial skin, typically the cheeks, forehead, upper lip, and chin It is far more common in women and in people with darker skin phototypes, and often follows pregnancy or hormonal exposure Recognised patterns are centrofacial, malar, and mandibular; a similar eruption can also occur on the forearms Wood's lamp examination can help gauge the depth of pigment, with epidermal pigment enhanced and dermal pigment less so, which influences treatment expectations Ultraviolet and visible light, including screen and heat exposure, are major drivers, so broad-spectrum photoprotection with a tinted (iron-oxide-containing) product is the cornerstone of care Combination topical lightening agents and gentle chemical peels can help, but aggressive procedures risk post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, especially in darker skin Review and, where feasible, stop contributory hormonal exposures such as combined oral contraception Set realistic expectations: recurrence is common and lifelong sun protection and maintenance are usually needed Asymmetric, irregular, or evolving pigmented lesions raising concern for melanoma rather than melasma Rapidly darkening or nodular change within a pigmented area Paradoxical darkening or blue-black discolouration suggesting exogenous ochronosis from prolonged skin-lightening use Neglecting visible-light protection and relying only on conventional UV sunscreen Provoking post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation with overly aggressive peels or lasers in darker skin Causing exogenous ochronosis through prolonged, unsupervised use of skin-lightening agents Promising a permanent cure rather than emphasising control and maintenance Melasma reflects an acquired disorder of localised hyperpigmentation in which functionally hyperactive melanocytes deposit excess melanin in the epidermis, dermis, or both. Ultraviolet and visible light, hormonal influences (pregnancy, oestrogen), and a genetic predisposition upregulate melanogenic signalling, while an altered dermal environment with solar elastosis, increased vascularity, and a disrupted basement membrane allows pigment to drop into the dermis. This basement-membrane damage helps explain the chronic, relapsing nature and the resistance of dermal pigment to topical therapy. Melasma is typically chronic and relapsing; pregnancy-related disease may fade after delivery, but many patients experience persistence or recurrence, and long-term photoprotection with maintenance therapy is usually required to sustain improvement.

Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome — MRS, orofacial granulomatosis with facial palsy, Miescher cheilitis (monosymptomatic form) Angio-oedema (allergic, hereditary, or ACE-inhibitor related) Orofacial granulomatosis secondary to Crohn disease Sarcoidosis Contact or allergic cheilitis Cheilitis glandularis Recurrent isolated Bell palsy Cutaneous or oral lymphoma infiltration Labial or oral mucosal biopsy seeking non-caseating granulomas Faecal calprotectin, and gastrointestinal endoscopy where Crohn disease is suspected Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and chest imaging to screen for sarcoidosis Patch testing and dietary/allergen assessment for contactants such as cinnamon and benzoates C1 esterase inhibitor level and complement studies to exclude hereditary angio-oedema MRI of the facial nerve if palsy is atypical or fails to recover Classically a triad of recurrent orofacial oedema, recurrent (often alternating) peripheral facial nerve palsy, and a fissured (scrotal/plicated) tongue, though the complete triad is uncommon Most patients present with only one or two features, and the lip swelling (granulomatous cheilitis of Miescher) is frequently the first and most persistent sign Facial swelling is typically non-pitting, painless, and initially transient but tends to become firm and permanent with recurrent attacks Lip biopsy may show non-caseating granulomas, but a normal histology does not exclude the diagnosis The condition sits within the spectrum of orofacial granulomatosis and can overlap with Crohn disease and sarcoidosis, which should be considered particularly in younger patients Facial palsy may precede, accompany, or follow the swelling and can be recurrent, mimicking repeated Bell palsy Management is largely supportive and anti-inflammatory (intralesional or systemic corticosteroids); refractory persistent lip swelling may be reduced with reduction cheiloplasty Systemic features (weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, respiratory symptoms) suggesting Crohn disease or sarcoidosis Progressive or incomplete recovery of facial palsy raising concern for a compressive or neoplastic lesion Rapidly evolving airway or tongue swelling suggesting angio-oedema rather than granulomatous oedema Unilateral fixed mass rather than diffuse recurrent swelling Misdiagnosing recurrent orofacial oedema as allergic angio-oedema and treating only with antihistamines Assuming a normal lip biopsy excludes the diagnosis, since granulomas are patchy Overlooking underlying Crohn disease or sarcoidosis, especially in children and young adults Treating recurrent facial palsy as simple Bell palsy without recognising the wider syndrome Attributing the fissured tongue to poor hygiene rather than a syndromic feature The syndrome is characterised by non-caseating granulomatous inflammation affecting the orofacial soft tissues, with lymphoedema and perivascular granulomas obstructing lymphatic drainage and producing recurrent, eventually persistent, oedema. The facial nerve is thought to be compromised by granulomatous or oedematous swelling within its bony canal, producing lower motor neurone palsy that may recur. The underlying trigger is unclear but is presumed to be an aberrant delayed-type immune response, possibly to dietary, dental, or microbial antigens, and the disorder overlaps mechanistically with other granulomatous conditions such as Crohn disease and sarcoidosis. The fissured tongue is regarded as a developmental/constitutional feature associated with the syndrome rather than a granulomatous lesion. The course is chronic and relapsing; early oedema is transient but repeated attacks can lead to permanent disfiguring lip swelling. Facial palsy often recovers but may be incomplete after recurrent episodes. The syndrome itself is benign, though associated systemic granulomatous disease influences the overall outlook.

Melnick-Needles syndrome (FLNA) — MNS, osteodysplasty, FLNA, Melnick-Needles osteodysplasty Otopalatodigital syndrome (FLNA spectrum) Frontometaphyseal dysplasia (FLNA spectrum) Osteogenesis cheeks, micrognathia and a high forehead Radiographs show characteristic ribbon-like (wavy) ribs, S-shaped bowing of the long bones, and irregular cortices Marked X-linked sex difference: heterozygous females typically survive with the characteristic phenotype, whereas hemizygous males are usually severely affected and the condition is frequently lethal in males Skeletal features include a small contribute to morbidity Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, with respiratory and airway monitoring, orthopaedic care and hearing assessment, alongside genetic counselling Respiratory compromise from a small thorax or airway narrowing, especially in neonates Severe presentation in a male fetus or infant, which is often life-threatening Urinary tract obstruction threatening renal function Significant cardiac anomaly Failing to place the disorder within the FLNA otopalatodigital spectrum and appreciate its X-linked inheritance Underestimating the perinatal severity and lethality in affected males Overlooking extraskeletal airway, renal or cardiac complications Attributing the bowed bones and abnormal ribs to osteogenesis imperfecta without genetic confirmation Melnick-Needles syndrome results from gain-of-function variants in the X-linked FLNA gene encoding filamin A, a cytoskeletal actin-cross-linking protein integral to cell shape, migration and mechanical signalling in developing bone and connective tissue. Disordered filamin A activity yields grossly abnormal bone modelling, producing the wavy ribbon-like ribs, bowed long bones with irregular cortices and the characteristic facial gestalt. The strong sex bias reflects X-linked inheritance: heterozygous females survive with the full phenotype because of X-inactivation mosaicism, whereas hemizygous males, lacking a normal allele, generally have severe, often lethal disease. Involvement of the airway, urinary tract and heart underlies the extraskeletal complications that determine outcome. Prognosis differs sharply by sex: affected females usually survive into adulthood with the characteristic phenotype and variable morbidity, whereas affected males typically have severe disease that is frequently lethal in the perinatal period.

discrepancy or deformity, often beginning in adulthood Overlying soft-tissue changes such as fibrosis, contractures, oedema, and skin thickening can accompany the bony disease Somatic mosaic mutations, notably in MAP2K1 and related pathway genes, have been implicated in the endosteal and soft-tissue components Management is symptomatic, addressing pain and function, with orthopaedic surgery reserved for disabling deformity or contracture New rapidly enlarging mass or pain raising concern for a surface osteosarcoma Progressive contracture or neurovascular compromise of a limb Significant limb-length discrepancy or deformity in a growing child Severe intractable pain limiting function Mistaking the flowing hyperostosis for an aggressive surface bone tumour and vice versa Assuming the condition is purely osseous and overlooking disabling soft-tissue fibrosis and contracture Expecting a hereditary pattern when the disorder is typically sporadic and mosaic Undertaking extensive surgery that may be complicated by recurrence and poor soft-tissue healing Melorheostosis is characterised by localised, progressive hyperostosis affecting the cortex of long bones and adjacent soft tissues. It is generally sporadic and non-hereditary, and recent work has identified somatic mosaic mutations, including activating changes in MAP2K1 within the MAP-kinase pathway, in affected lesional tissue, with other genetic changes reported in the endosteal component. Enhanced local signalling drives excess bone formation confined to affected regions, often distributed along a sclerotome, producing the characteristic asymmetrical flowing cortical thickening. Associated fibrosis and contracture of surrounding soft tissue contribute to the pain and functional limitation. The condition is benign and slowly progressive with a normal lifespan, but it can cause chronic pain, joint contracture, and functional impairment; outcomes depend on lesion location and the degree of soft-tissue involvement.

disease) Immunoglobulin-positive patterns point to infection, autoimmune disease or a monoclonal gammopathy, so a paraprotein screen is essential in adults C3-dominant staining with scanty immunoglobulin indicates dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, sometimes with C3 nephritic factor or complement gene abnormalities Clinical presentation spans nephrotic syndrome, nephritic features with haematuria, or a mixed picture, frequently with persistently low serum complement Treatment targets the underlying cause: eradicate infection, treat autoimmune disease or the paraprotein-producing clone, and consider complement-directed therapy in refractory C3 glomerulopathy Crescentic transformation with rapidly progressive renal impairment Nephrotic syndrome with thromboembolic complications Persistently low complement with systemic features suggesting active autoimmune or cryoglobulinaemic disease Detection of a monoclonal protein indicating an underlying haematological clone Treating the pattern as a single entity instead of pursuing the immune-complex versus complement cause Failing to screen adults for a monoclonal gammopathy driving the disease Overlooking chronic infection as a reversible trigger Assuming normal complement excludes the diagnosis Giving broad immunosuppression in complement-mediated disease without addressing the pathway dysregulation The MPGN pattern results from deposition of immune complexes or complement components in the mesangium and subendothelial space, which activates complement and recruits inflammatory cells. Mesangial cells proliferate and interpose their cytoplasm between the endothelium and the glomerular basement membrane while laying down new basement membrane material, producing the characteristic double-contour appearance. In immune-complex disease the trigger is chronic antigenaemia from infection, autoimmunity or a monoclonal immunoglobulin; in C3 glomerulopathy uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway, from acquired autoantibodies (such as C3 nephritic factor) or inherited regulator defects, drives predominant C3 deposition, with dense osmiophilic transformation of the basement membrane in dense deposit disease. The MPGN pattern is often chronic and progressive, with a substantial proportion reaching end-stage kidney disease, though outcome is strongly influenced by the underlying cause and its treatment. Dense deposit disease and crescentic forms carry a poorer prognosis, and both immune-complex and complement-mediated disease can recur after transplantation.

interferon-gamma and interleukin-12 production after stimulation Flow cytometry for interferon-gamma receptor and interleukin-12 receptor beta-1 surface expression and STAT1 phosphorylation Targeted or panel-based genetic sequencing of the known MSMD genes Mycobacterial and Salmonella cultures with species identification and drug-susceptibility testing Testing for anti-interferon-gamma neutralising autoantibodies to exclude the acquired phenocopy Assessment for HIV and other secondary immunodeficiency Imaging to define the extent of disseminated infection and organ involvement A group of inherited disorders in which defects along the interleukin-12/interleukin-23 to interferon-gamma circuit cripple the immune response to intracellular pathogens, leaving affected individuals uniquely vulnerable to weakly virulent mycobacteria The hallmark is disseminated or recurrent infection with the BCG vaccine strain, non-tuberculous (environmental) mycobacteria, and non-typhoidal Salmonella, often in an otherwise healthy-looking child Disease severity tracks the underlying genetic lesion: complete receptor defects present in infancy with overwhelming, poorly granuloma-forming disease, whereas partial defects present later with more contained, granulomatous illness Severe reactions to BCG immunisation (BCGitis or disseminated BCGosis) in a previously well infant should trigger evaluation for this pathway Susceptibility to intramacrophage organisms including certain fungi (histoplasma, coccidioides), and in some genotypes an added vulnerability to severe viral infection, may accompany the mycobacterial phenotype Diagnosis rests on functional testing of the interferon-gamma axis together with molecular genetic confirmation, as several distinct genes converge on the same clinical picture Management combines prolonged, tailored antimicrobial therapy against the offending organism with adjunctive interferon-gamma in receptor-competent forms, and consideration of haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for the most severe complete defects Disseminated illness following BCG vaccination in an infant Recurrent or multifocal non-tuberculous mycobacterial or non-typhoidal Salmonella infection A family history of childhood death from disseminated mycobacterial disease Failure of poorly formed granulomas with progressive organ infiltration in complete defects Concurrent severe viral or intracellular fungal infection suggesting a broader signalling defect Attributing severe BCG or environmental mycobacterial disease to poor technique or contamination rather than an underlying host defect Stopping antimicrobial therapy too early, as relapse is common while the immune defect persists Giving live BCG or other live vaccines before the diagnosis is excluded in a suggestive family Assuming a normal routine immunology screen excludes the disorder, since antibody and lymphocyte counts are typically normal Overlooking the acquired anti-interferon-gamma autoantibody syndrome as a treatable adult mimic The control of intracellular pathogens such as mycobacteria and Salmonella depends on a self-reinforcing loop between phagocytes and lymphocytes. Infected macrophages and dendritic cells release interleukin-12 and interleukin-23, which act on natural killer and T cells to drive production of interferon-gamma; that interferon-gamma in turn binds its receptor on the phagocyte, signals through the JAK-STAT1 pathway, and switches on the microbicidal machinery needed to kill the organism. Inherited defects at any node of this circuit (the interferon-gamma receptor chains, STAT1, the interleukin-12/23 subunit or its receptor, and several regulatory or transcription-factor genes) interrupt the loop, so phagocytes fail to be fully activated and organisms of low intrinsic virulence persist and spread. The depth of the defect determines whether granulomas form poorly and disease disseminates or whether infection remains comparatively localised. Outcome depends heavily on genotype: partial defects and interleukin-12/23-pathway lesions often do well with prolonged antimicrobial therapy and adjunctive interferon-gamma, whereas complete interferon-gamma receptor defects carry a poor prognosis with recurrent life-threatening infection unless haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is undertaken, itself difficult in the face of active infection.

Menetrier disease (hyperplastic gastropathy) — hyperplastic gastropathy, giant hypertrophic gastritis, protein-losing hypertrophic gastropathy, Menetrier's disease Zollinger-Ellison syndrome with hypertrophic gastric folds Gastric lymphoma including mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma Infiltrative gastric adenocarcinoma (linitis plastica) Hypertrophic lymphocytic gastritis Gastric involvement by sarcoidosis or eosinophilic gastritis Polyposis syndromes affecting the stomach Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy demonstrating enlarged folds, with deep (well or jumbo) biopsies to sample the full mucosal thickness Serum albumin and total protein to document the protein-losing state Cross-sectional imaging to assess fold thickness and help exclude malignancy Gastric acid studies typically showing hypochlorhydria Testing for cytomegalovirus, particularly in children Stool alpha-1 antitrypsin clearance to confirm gastrointestinal protein loss Fasting serum gastrin to exclude a gastrinoma Characterised by giant, cerebriform rugal folds in the gastric body and fundus that typically spare the antrum Foveolar (mucous cell) hyperplasia with cystic dilatation of glands and loss of parietal cells produces a thickened, boggy mucosa and excess mucus secretion A protein-losing gastropathy causes hypoalbuminaemia, which may present with peripheral oedema and anasarca Acid output is characteristically reduced (hypochlorhydria or achlorhydria) because of parietal cell loss Overexpression of transforming growth factor-alpha (TGF-alpha) with excessive epidermal growth factor receptor signalling is implicated in the adult form In children the disorder is frequently self-limiting and associated with cytomegalovirus infection Management is largely supportive, with a high-protein diet and protein replacement; anti-epidermal growth factor receptor antibody therapy has been used in refractory adult disease and gastrectomy is reserved for severe or premalignant cases The adult form carries an increased long-term risk of gastric adenocarcinoma, so surveillance is prudent Progressive weight loss, anaemia, or a focal mass raising concern for underlying malignancy Severe hypoalbuminaemia with anasarca and effusions Biopsy or imaging features overlapping with infiltrative carcinoma or lymphoma Persistent bleeding or obstructive symptoms Taking superficial biopsies that miss the diagnosis because the characteristic changes lie deep within the mucosa Attributing hypoalbuminaemia to hepatic or renal disease and overlooking a protein-losing gastropathy Failing to distinguish giant folds from malignant infiltration or a gastrinoma Neglecting surveillance for gastric cancer in long-standing adult disease Menetrier disease is a rare hyperplastic gastropathy in which marked expansion of surface mucous (foveolar) cells with cystic gland dilatation and progressive loss of acid-secreting parietal cells thickens the gastric body and fundus into giant folds. Excessive epidermal growth factor receptor activation, driven by overexpression of transforming growth factor-alpha, is thought to underlie the mucous cell hyperplasia and to suppress acid secretion in the adult form, whereas the paediatric form is often triggered by cytomegalovirus. The abnormal mucosa is leaky, allowing plasma proteins to escape into the gastric lumen, which produces a protein-losing gastropathy with hypoalbuminaemia and dependent oedema. The adult form is usually chronic and may be complicated by disabling protein loss and an elevated risk of gastric adenocarcinoma, whereas the childhood form associated with cytomegalovirus is typically self-limiting and resolves over weeks to months.

(vestibular schwannoma) Autoimmune inner ear disease Perilymph fistula Pure tone audiometry to document fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss Tests of vestibular function such as caloric testing and video head impulse testing Electrocochleography and other specialised tests where available MRI of the internal auditory meatus to exclude a vestibular schwannoma Blood tests to exclude alternative causes when clinically indicated Characterised by a triad of episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, often with a sense of aural fullness Vertigo attacks typically last from minutes to hours, distinguishing them from the seconds-long spells of positional vertigo Hearing loss initially affects lower frequencies and fluctuates, but tends to become permanent and progressive over time Usually begins unilaterally, though the second ear can become involved in a proportion of patients The underlying disorder is endolymphatic hydrops, an increase in endolymph volume within the membranous labyrinth Management principles include dietary salt restriction, diuretics and vestibular sedatives for acute attacks, with lifestyle measures to reduce triggers Escalating options for intractable disease range from intratympanic therapy to surgical procedures such as endolymphatic sac decompression or labyrinthine ablation Sudden drop attacks (Tumarkin crises) can cause falls without warning and pose an injury risk Progressive unilateral hearing loss with tinnitus raising concern for vestibular schwannoma Neurological signs suggesting a central cause Sudden severe sensorineural hearing loss requiring urgent assessment Recurrent drop attacks causing injury Diagnosing Meniere's without excluding a retrocochlear lesion such as acoustic neuroma Confusing it with vestibular migraine, which can present similarly Overusing vestibular sedatives beyond acute attacks and impairing compensation Underestimating the psychosocial and safety impact of unpredictable attacks Meniere's disease is attributed to endolymphatic hydrops, an abnormal accumulation of endolymph that distends the membranous labyrinth. Impaired production, circulation or absorption of endolymph, potentially involving the endolymphatic sac, raises pressure within the scala media. Episodic rupture or dysfunction of the membranes allows mixing of endolymph and perilymph, disturbing the ionic environment of the sensory hair cells and producing acute vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus. Repeated insults cause progressive damage to cochlear and vestibular structures, leading to permanent hearing loss and vestibular hypofunction. The course is variable and unpredictable, with clustered attacks and remissions; vertigo often diminishes over years as vestibular function declines, but hearing loss tends to be progressive and permanent.

Meningioma — meningeal tumour, dural-based tumour Dural metastasis Solitary fibrous tumour / haemangiopericytoma Schwannoma (at skull base sites) Dural-based lymphoma or granulomatous disease Extra-axial abscess or empyema MRI brain or spine with contrast to characterise the extra-axial dural-based mass and dural tail CT to assess associated hyperostosis, calcification, or bony erosion Serial imaging to monitor growth of incidental or conservatively managed lesions Histopathology and grading after biopsy or resection Vascular imaging when preoperative embolisation of a highly vascular tumour is considered Meningiomas are the most common primary intracranial tumours and are usually slow-growing and benign, arising from the meningeal covering of the brain and spinal cord Many are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on imaging performed for other reasons When symptomatic, features depend on location and result from gradual compression, producing focal deficits, seizures, or symptoms of raised intracranial pressure They are more common in women and their growth can be influenced by hormonal factors; some carry hormone receptors On imaging they are typically well-defined, extra-axial, dural-based, avidly and homogeneously enhancing masses, often with a dural tail and sometimes adjacent bony change Small asymptomatic meningiomas are frequently managed by surveillance imaging, reserving intervention for growth or symptoms Symptomatic or enlarging tumours are usually treated by surgical resection, with radiotherapy or radiosurgery for residual, recurrent, higher-grade, or surgically inaccessible lesions Although most are low grade, a minority are atypical or malignant with a greater tendency to recur, so histological grading guides follow-up Rapid growth or atypical imaging features suggesting a higher-grade tumour Progressive neurological deficit, new seizures, or cranial nerve compromise Signs of raised intracranial pressure from a large lesion with oedema and mass effect Acute deterioration from peritumoural oedema or, rarely, haemorrhage Assuming every dural-based enhancing mass is a benign meningioma without considering metastasis or other lesions Over-treating small, stable, asymptomatic incidental tumours Underestimating the recurrence risk of atypical or malignant subtypes Overlooking peritumoural oedema as a treatable cause of symptoms Meningiomas arise from meningothelial (arachnoid cap) cells of the meninges and are therefore extra-axial, growing outside the brain parenchyma and compressing it from the surface. They are typically slow-growing and attached to the dura, and their growth can distort adjacent brain, cranial nerves, and vessels, provoke surrounding oedema, and erode or hyperostose overlying bone. Symptoms arise from mass effect at the specific location rather than infiltration. Most are histologically low grade, but atypical and anaplastic variants show more aggressive behaviour and higher recurrence rates. Prior cranial irradiation and certain genetic conditions increase risk. Most meningiomas are benign and, when completely resected, have an excellent prognosis with low recurrence; incompletely removed, atypical, or malignant tumours recur more often and may need adjuvant radiotherapy and closer surveillance.

Meningococcal Disease — meningococcemia, Neisseria meningitidis infection Other causes of bacterial meningitis (presentation of meningococcal meningitis is indistinguishable unless an associated petechial/purpuric rash or gram-negative diplococci are present) (p.1248-1249) Differential of chronic meningococcemia: bacterial endocarditis, acute rheumatic fever, Henoch-Schonlein purpura, infectious mononucleosis, disseminated gonococcal infection, immune-mediated vasculitis (p.1248-1249) Viral infections (enteroviruses, influenza and other respiratory viruses, measles, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, parvovirus) - most patients presenting with a petechial/purpuric rash have a viral infection (p.1248) Pneumococcal, streptococcal, staphylococcal, or other gram-negative bacterial sepsis (p.1248) Blood culture for confirmation and public health investigation (positive in up to ~75% of cases); avoid media containing sodium polyanethol sulfonate, which may inhibit meningococcal growth, and avoid delay in transport (p.1249) Real-time PCR of whole blood increases diagnostic yield by more than 40% and may remain positive for several days after antibiotics (p.1249) Lumbar puncture for CSF in suspected meningitis (unless contraindicated); CSF Gram stain is up to ~80% sensitive, CSF culture sensitivity ~90%, plus PCR where available; CSF latex agglutination antigen testing is insensitive and should be replaced by molecular diagnosis (p.1249) Inflammatory markers (WBC count, C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, ESR) may support the diagnosis but can be normal or low in rapidly progressive disease and do not exclude it (p.1249) Severe septicemia laboratory findings: hypoglycemia, acidosis, hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia, anemia, coagulopathy (p.1249) Measure total hemolytic complement activity to assess for complement deficiency in patients with recurrent disease, particularly non-B capsular groups (p.1247) Protein C or S deficiency (including post-varicella protein S deficiency) (p.1248) Platelet disorders (e.g., idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, drug effects, bone marrow infiltration) (p.1248) Henoch-Schonlein purpura, connective tissue disorders, and trauma (including nonaccidental injury in children) (p.1248) Neisseria meningitidis most commonly causes asymptomatic nasopharyngeal colonization; invasive disease is rare and usually presents as either bacterial meningitis or meningococcal septicemia (p.1244). A nonblanching petechial or purpuric rash develops in over 80% of cases, but it is often absent early in the illness and may begin as a blanching maculopapular or urticarial eruption indistinguishable from common viral rashes before becoming petechial/purpuric over hours; some patients, including those with overwhelming sepsis, have no rash at all (p.1248). In the most severe cases large purpuric lesions develop (purpura fulminans) with signs of peripheral ischemia (p.1248). Roughly 30-50% present with a meningitis syndrome alone, up to 40% of meningitis patients also have features of septicemia, and meningococcal septicemia alone accounts for up to 20% of cases (p.1248). In fulminant disease death may occur within hours of the first symptoms; early septicemic symptoms are nonspecific and influenza-like (fever, headache, myalgia, vomiting, abdominal pain) (p.1248). In children, hypotension is a late sign; they more commonly present with compensated shock (tachycardia, poor peripheral perfusion, normal blood pressure) (p.1248). Terminal complement component (C5-9), properdin or factor D deficiency, and treatment with complement inhibitors such as eculizumab, increase the risk of meningococcal disease (up to ~600-fold) and may cause recurrent attacks (p.1247). Chronic meningococcemia is rarely recognized and presents as recurrent episodes of petechial rash with fever, joint pain/arthritis, and splenomegaly, with bacteremia that characteristically clears without treatment then recurs (p.1248-1249). Tobacco smoking (and passive smoke exposure) is an important risk factor that damages the nasopharyngeal epithelium and increases both carriage and invasive disease (p.1247). Immunization is regarded as the only rational approach to prevention at a population level; chemoprophylaxis of close contacts aims to eradicate carriage of the invasive strain (p.1250-1253). A nonblanching (petechial or purpuric) rash in a febrile patient should be treated as a medical emergency suggestive of meningococcal disease (p.1248) Purpura fulminans / large purpuric lesions with peripheral ischemia (p.1248) Signs of shock: tachycardia, poor peripheral perfusion, tachypnea, oliguria, cold mottled extremities, limb pain (hypotension is a late sign in children) (p.1248) Reduced level of consciousness, agitation, or confusion (decreased cerebral perfusion or raised intracranial pressure) (p.1248) Features of raised intracranial pressure: reduced consciousness, relative bradycardia and hypertension, focal neurologic signs, abnormal posturing, unequal/dilated/poorly reactive pupils (p.1248) Rapid progression - death may occur within hours of first symptoms in fulminant cases (p.1248) A normal or low WBC count and inflammatory markers do not exclude meningococcal disease and may occur in rapidly progressive disease (p.1249) The rash may be absent early or absent altogether (including in overwhelming sepsis), and may initially appear blanching/viral before becoming petechial or purpuric (p.1248) Most patients with a petechial/purpuric rash and fever do NOT have meningococcal disease - fewer than 10% of children (and in some settings under 1%) with this presentation are found to have it, so most have a viral cause (p.1248) Lumbar puncture should generally be avoided in meningococcal septicemia because positioning may critically compromise circulation in hypovolemic shock; it is also contraindicated with raised intracranial pressure, uncorrected shock, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, respiratory insufficiency, local infection, or ongoing convulsions (p.1249) A normal CT brain scan does not exclude raised intracranial pressure in meningococcal meningitis (p.1249) CSF latex agglutination antigen testing and urinary antigen testing are insensitive; throat-swab identification has limited diagnostic value because N. meningitidis is normal nasopharyngeal flora (p.1249) Postmeningococcal reactive (immune-complex) disease arising ~4-10 days after onset (rash, arthritis, iritis, pericarditis/polyserositis with fever) can be mistaken for relapse and lead to unnecessarily prolonged antibiotics; it resolves spontaneously (p.1249) Aggressive fluid resuscitation with unbuffered electrolyte solutions was found to increase mortality in febrile African children (p.1249-1250) N. meningitidis colonizes the human nasopharynx, then in a susceptible individual may invade the mucosa into the bloodstream, usually within a few days of acquisition. The polysaccharide capsule is a key virulence factor providing resistance to phagocytosis; acapsular strains rarely cause invasive disease. During growth meningococci shed outer-membrane blebs containing lipopolysaccharide (LPS, endotoxin), which binds CD14/TLR4 to trigger an inflammatory cascade (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, PAI-1 and others). Disease severity relates to both endotoxin levels and the magnitude of the inflammatory response. Endothelial injury is central to meningococcemia, causing increased vascular permeability (capillary leak with hypovolemia, tissue and pulmonary edema), altered vascular tone, loss of thromboresistance, intravascular coagulation, and myocardial dysfunction. Procoagulant activation with tissue factor upregulation, downregulation of anticoagulant pathways (loss of thrombomodulin/protein C receptors; reduced antithrombin III, protein C, protein S, tissue factor pathway inhibitor) and impaired thrombolysis from high PAI-1 produce purpura fulminans and skin/limb infarction. Shock results from hypovolemia plus myocardial depression (hypoxia, metabolic derangements such as hypocalcemia, cytokines). Bacteria reaching the meninges provoke a local cytokine-driven inflammatory response that can cause cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure (p.1247-1248). About 10% of patients with meningococcal disease die despite antimicrobial therapy and intensive care. Fulminant meningococcemia is more likely to cause death or ischemic skin loss than meningitis alone. Factors associated with poorer prognosis include shock; extremes of age (infancy and old age) and adolescence; coma; purpura fulminans; disseminated intravascular coagulation; thrombocytopenia; leukopenia; absence of meningitis; metabolic acidosis; low antithrombin and protein S/C levels; high PAI-1; and a low ESR or C-reactive protein. The Glasgow Meningococcal Septicaemia Prognostic Score (GMSPS) performs well for severity assessment, though scoring systems do not direct specific interventions; the management priority remains recognition and urgent treatment of compromised airway, breathing, or circulation. Most patients improve rapidly with appropriate antibiotics and supportive care. Complications include scarring after purpuric skin necrosis (~10%, sometimes requiring skin grafting), amputation in 1-2% of survivors after peripheral ischemia or compartment syndrome, hearing loss (~5%), neurologic complications (~7%), chronic pain, and psychological/psychosocial sequelae (p.1249-1250). Clinical spectrum spans asymptomatic nasopharyngeal carriage, occult bacteremia, localized/focal infection (pneumonia, arthritis, osteomyelitis, pericarditis, conjunctivitis), meningitis, and meningococcal septicemia, with chronic meningococcemia as a relapsing form. The Glasgow Meningococcal Septicaemia Prognostic Score (GMSPS) is used for severity assessment. Fulminant meningococcemia with purpura fulminans and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (overwhelming meningococcal sepsis) represents the most severe end of the spectrum (p.1244, p.1248-1249).

partial meniscectomy is reserved for irreparable tears Meniscus preservation is important because meniscectomy increases contact stress and the long-term risk of osteoarthritis Degenerative tears in older knees with early arthritis often respond as well to conservative management and rehabilitation as to arthroscopic surgery A truly locked knee unable to fully extend, suggesting a displaced bucket-handle tear needing prompt surgery Acute tense haemarthrosis suggesting a significant associated injury such as an ACL rupture Hot, swollen, systemically unwell knee raising concern for septic arthritis Signs of associated ligamentous instability or fracture Performing meniscectomy on a degenerative tear in an arthritic knee that would do as well with rehabilitation Removing repairable peripheral tissue rather than attempting repair, accelerating arthritis Missing a locked knee from a displaced bucket-handle tear Overlooking a concurrent ACL injury that leaves the meniscal repair at risk of re-tear The menisci are fibrocartilaginous, wedge-shaped structures that deepen the tibial articular surface, distribute load, absorb shock, and contribute to joint stability and lubrication. A twisting force on a weight-bearing flexed knee shears the meniscus between the femoral and tibial condyles, producing longitudinal, radial, horizontal, or complex tears; a longitudinal tear whose free fragment displaces into the notch forms a bucket-handle lesion that can block extension. With age the meniscal tissue degenerates and tears more readily under low loads. Only the peripheral third has a blood supply capable of healing, so the location of a tear largely determines whether repair or excision is appropriate. Loss of meniscal tissue raises articular contact pressures and predisposes to degenerative change. Peripheral tears repaired successfully can restore durable meniscal function, while small stable tears may settle with conservative care; extensive meniscectomy relieves mechanical symptoms but increases the long-term likelihood of osteoarthritis, and degenerative tears in already arthritic knees have a more limited response to surgery.

Shear and compressive forces on a rotating flexed knee, or cumulative degeneration, tear the collagen architecture in vertical, horizontal, radial, flap or bucket-handle patterns. Peripheral repairable tears in stable knees heal well; degenerate tears often improve with rehabilitation, and outcomes after meniscectomy are limited by the long-term risk of accelerated osteoarthritis, especially with larger resections.

moves copper across the enterocyte basolateral membrane and delivers it within cells to copper-dependent enzymes. The defect traps dietary copper in intestinal and renal cells while depriving other tissues, so despite total-body copper accumulation in some sites, functional copper deficiency dominates. Menopause and Postmenopausal Hormone Therapy — Menopause, Perimenopause, Postmenopausal hormone therapy, Climacteric, Menopausal transition Pregnancy as a cause of amenorrhea in perimenopausal women (unintentional pregnancy rate in the forties rivals that of adolescents) Premature ovarian insufficiency / primary ovarian insufficiency when ovarian failure occurs well before the usual age Thyroid dysfunction or other endocrine causes of menstrual irregularity and vasomotor-like symptoms Uterine structural lesions (leiomyomata, endometrial polyps, hyperplasia or carcinoma) presenting as abnormal/heavy bleeding Other age-related conditions causing midlife mood, sleep, cognitive, or sexual complaints not attributable to ovarian senescence Menstrual cycle history as the principal STRAW+10 criterion for staging reproductive aging, with biomarkers as supportive criteria FSH measurement: random level >25 IU/L is characteristic of the late menopausal transition; day-3 levels <20, 20 to <30, and >=30 IU/L indicate good, fair, and poor pregnancy likelihood respectively Estradiol levels, recognizing that FSH and estradiol are imperfect diagnostic indicators in still-menstruating perimenopausal women due to marked intraindividual variability Anti-mullerian hormone and inhibin B as additional markers of reproductive aging Transvaginal ultrasound (with saline enhancement) to detect leiomyomata or polyps when bleeding is abnormal Endometrial aspiration/biopsy to identify hyperplastic or premalignant changes when menorrhagia or abnormal bleeding occurs Bone mineral density assessment and FRAX 10-year fracture risk estimation to guide osteoporosis decisions; 25-hydroxyvitamin D level >=50 nmol/L considered sufficient for bone maintenance Thyroid disease producing vasomotor-like flushing and menstrual change Anxiety or panic disorder mimicking hot flashes Endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma presenting as abnormal bleeding rather than physiologic transition Medication effects or other causes of secondary amenorrhea Menopause is the permanent cessation of menstruation from loss of ovarian follicular function and is diagnosed retrospectively after 12 months of amenorrhea; the average age in U.S. women is about 51 years. Perimenopause is the transition preceding menopause when fertility wanes and cycles become irregular, typically beginning 2-8 years before the final menses (mean duration about 4 years); smoking advances the transition by roughly 2 years. Perimenopause is marked by 'irregularly irregular' hormone levels rather than the consistently high FSH and low estradiol of established menopause; intermenstrual intervals often shorten (by about 3 days) due to an accelerated follicular phase. FSH rises before LH during the transition, attributed to loss of inhibin and estrogen feedback; after menopause estradiol falls markedly while estrone is relatively preserved through peripheral aromatization of adrenal and ovarian androgens. Vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, night sweats), irregular bleeding, and vaginal dryness are strongly attributable to the transition; sleep disturbance has moderate supporting evidence, while mood swings, memory/concentration changes, incontinence, and sexual dysfunction are not clearly caused by ovarian aging alone. Nearly 60% of women in one U.S. study reported hot flashes in the 2 years before their final menses; symptom intensity, frequency, duration, and quality-of-life impact are highly variable. Estrogen therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor and genitourinary symptoms; randomized trial data suggest hormone therapy reduces menopausal symptoms by roughly 65-90%. The 'timing hypothesis' holds that estrogen may slow early atherosclerosis but adversely affect advanced lesions, so women initiating hormone therapy early after menopause may differ in cardiovascular outcome from those starting many years later. Primary prevention of cardiovascular disease should NOT be considered an expected benefit of hormone therapy; an increased stroke risk and a small early increase in coronary risk should be weighed. A 1-year absence of spontaneous menses reliably indicates ovulation has ceased, but natural menstrual pattern cannot be assessed while a woman is taking oral contraceptives. Estrogen reduces bone turnover and resorption; postmenopausal estrogen (with or without a progestogen) increases spine bone density by about 4-6% and hip density by about 2-3%, with WHI showing roughly a 33% reduction in hip fractures. Unopposed estrogen markedly raises endometrial cancer risk; adding a progestogen opposes this effect and can even reduce endometrial cancer risk, which is why estrogen-only therapy is reserved for women without a uterus. Unexplained or undiagnosed vaginal bleeding requires evaluation to exclude endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma before attributing it to the transition An acute coronary event or stroke while on hormone therapy mandates immediate discontinuation of therapy New or worsening vasomotor symptoms accompanied by features suggesting thromboembolism, given the increased VTE risk with oral estrogen Heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) in perimenopause warrants evaluation for uterine disorders rather than assumption of benign cause Symptoms or signs of estrogen-dependent malignancy in a woman considering or using hormone therapy Observational studies overstated cardiovascular benefit because women choosing hormone therapy tend to be healthier and more health-conscious (healthy-user confounding); randomized trials did not confirm the benefit. Relying on a single FSH or estradiol value to diagnose perimenopause in a menstruating woman is unreliable given extreme intraindividual variability. Prescribing unopposed estrogen to a woman with an intact uterus markedly raises endometrial cancer and atypical hyperplasia risk; a progestogen is needed for endometrial protection. Attributing midlife mood, cognitive, urinary, or sexual complaints to menopause when evidence does not support ovarian aging as the principal cause. Counseling should emphasize absolute rather than relative risk measures, since absolute risks rise with age even when relative risks are similar. Apparent excess breast cancer detection in early hormone therapy users may partly reflect more frequent screening mammography rather than a true biologic effect. Assuming the cardiovascular and other effects of one formulation/route apply to all, since transdermal estrogen may carry lower thrombotic and gallbladder risk than oral estrogen. Ovarian mass and fertility decline sharply after age 35 and more steeply during perimenopause as the pool of primary follicles, depleting since before birth, runs down. Altered folliculogenesis and reduced inhibin secretion cause FSH to rise; the propensity for anovulatory cycles produces a relatively hyperestrogenic, hypoprogestagenic milieu that may underlie the increased perimenopausal incidence of endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma, uterine polyps, and leiomyomata. With transition into menopause, estradiol falls markedly while estrone is comparatively preserved through peripheral aromatization of adrenal and ovarian androgens; FSH rises more than LH owing to loss of inhibin plus estrogen feedback. Exogenous estrogen lowers LDL and raises HDL cholesterol by about 10-15% and favorably affects lipoprotein(a), LDL oxidation, and endothelial function, but it also raises triglycerides, promotes coagulation (factor VII, prothrombin fragments, fibrinopeptide A), and elevates C-reactive protein, providing a mechanistic basis for both potential benefits and thrombotic/inflammatory harms. Most peri- and postmenopausal symptoms are self-limited though variable in duration and intensity. In the WHI, many risks and benefits of hormone therapy dissipated within 5-7 years after stopping, though some persisted: with estrogen-progestin an elevated breast cancer risk continued over long follow-up and a reduced hip fracture risk and reduced endometrial cancer risk persisted; with estrogen alone the breast cancer risk reduction became significant on extended follow-up. Estrogen-progestin carried an overall unfavorable global benefit-risk profile that did not vary by 10-year age group, whereas estrogen-only therapy had a roughly neutral profile overall with a more favorable balance in younger women (relative risks for the global index of about 0.84, 0.99, and 1.17 in ages 50-59, 60-69, and 70-79). Over extended follow-up estrogen alone was associated with reduced all-cause mortality in women aged 50-59 (notably those with bilateral oophorectomy), while estrogen-progestin showed elevated breast cancer risk and a suggestion of increased breast cancer mortality. The Stages of Reproductive Aging Workshop +10 (STRAW+10) system stages reproductive aging using menstrual cycle characteristics as principal criteria (e.g., persistent >=7-day differences in consecutive cycle length in the early transition; an interval of amenorrhea of >=60 days in the late transition) with endocrine markers (FSH, AMH, inhibin B, antral follicle count) as supportive criteria, spanning reproductive, menopausal transition (perimenopause), and postmenopause stages around the final menstrual period.

primary amenorrhea is rare (<1% of women), whereas roughly 3-5% of women have at least 3 months of secondary amenorrhea in a given year.
