Menstrual function depends on coordinated signaling among four compartments - hypothalamus, pituitary, ovary, and uterus/outflow tract - linked by feedback loops involving GnRH, the gonadotropins FSH and LH, and the ovarian products estradiol, progesterone, and the inhibins (inhibin A and B). Disorders divide into outflow-tract/uterine problems and ovulatory disorders. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism arises when anatomic, genetic, or functional disturbances impair hypothalamic GnRH output or pituitary responsiveness, producing low estrogen with normal or low LH/FSH; in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, energy deficit and stress raise CRH, suppress GnRH, and lower TRH input, with leptin and hypothalamic kisspeptin/neurokinin B/dynorphin signaling transducing metabolic and stress cues to the GnRH pulse generator. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (ovarian insufficiency) removes negative feedback, raising FSH and LH. In PCOS, abnormal GnRH pulsatility elevates LH and drives ovarian androgen output, and insulin resistance in muscle and fat further augments insulin-stimulated ovarian androgen production; frequent anovulation yields irregular menses and unopposed estrogen effect on the endometrium. Pelvic pain shares mechanisms with abdominal pain - parietal peritoneal inflammation, hollow-viscus obstruction, vascular compromise (e.g., ovarian torsion), and abdominal-wall pain - and may be referred from extrapelvic sources. Primary dysmenorrhea is mediated chiefly by prostaglandin pathways causing intense uterine contractions, reduced blood flow, and peripheral nerve hypersensitivity, with PG-independent mediators such as platelet-activating factor also contributing. Endometriosis reflects ectopic endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus that respond to hormonal stimulation. Outcome depends on cause. Many causes of functional hypothalamic amenorrhea are reversible with restoration of energy balance, though bone density may not fully recover with hormone replacement alone. Amenorrhea of any cause is usually associated with chronically low estrogen, carrying risk to bone and cardiovascular health if untreated. PID untreated risks infertility and ectopic pregnancy, and subclinical PID remains a major worldwide cause of these complications. PCOS carries elevated long-term risk of metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnea, steatotic liver disease, and a two- to sixfold increase in endometrial hyperplasia/cancer from chronic anovulation; symptoms often improve with age, with most women regaining regular menses and normal androgens by the fourth decade. POI is associated with additional health problems and infertility, though oocyte donation has high success. Ectopic pregnancy with tubal rupture can be fatal. Abnormal uterine bleeding is categorized etiologically by the PALM-COEIN system (structural causes: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia; non-structural: Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified). PCOS is diagnosed by the updated Rotterdam criteria (2023 international guidelines): two of three among irregular menses (fewer than 8 per year), clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (>=20 antral follicles or ovarian volume >=10 cm3 in one ovary) or elevated AMH, yielding hyperandrogenic and non-hyperandrogenic phenotypes. Pelvic pain is classified as acute versus chronic and cyclic versus noncyclic to guide evaluation. Endometriosis is staged by laparoscopy.

The majority of cases resolve with conservative measures and removal of the precipitating compression, and pregnancy-related cases usually settle after delivery. A minority with persistent axonal injury develop chronic dysaesthesia that may require injection therapy or surgical decompression or neurectomy.

purely sensory neuropathy Proceeding to surgery before an adequate trial of conservative therapy and a confirmatory nerve block The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is a purely sensory nerve derived from the L2 and L3 roots that supplies the skin of the anterolateral thigh. As it courses toward the thigh it passes near the anterior superior iliac spine and beneath, through, or over the inguinal ligament, where its relatively fixed and angulated path makes it vulnerable to mechanical compression or stretch. Increased intra-abdominal pressure or local tension from obesity, pregnancy, tight garments, or postoperative scarring compresses the nerve, causing focal demyelination and axonal irritation that produce the characteristic burning dysaesthesia and numbness. Because the nerve carries no motor fibres, there is no weakness or reflex change, and the deficit is confined to a well-defined cutaneous patch. Most cases are benign and resolve or substantially improve with conservative measures, particularly weight loss and removing constrictive pressure; refractory cases may respond to nerve blocks, and surgical decompression or neurectomy is reserved for the few with persistent disabling symptoms.

Mercury poisoning — mercurialism, mercury toxicity, hydrargyria Essential or other causes of tremor Primary psychiatric or neurodegenerative disease Other heavy metal poisoning Peripheral neuropathy of other cause Acute corrosive ingestion of other agents Acute kidney injury from other nephrotoxins Blood mercury (more useful for recent organic exposure) and urinary mercury (for elemental and inorganic exposure) Renal function and urinalysis to detect tubular injury Neurological and neuropsychological assessment Chest imaging in acute vapour inhalation for pneumonitis Exposure history covering occupation, dental amalgam handling, and dietary fish intake The clinical picture depends on the chemical form: elemental mercury vapour, inorganic mercury salts, and organic mercury (such as methylmercury) each cause distinct patterns Inhaled elemental mercury vapour, seen in industries such as chloralkali and instrument work, chiefly affects the central nervous system and can cause an acute chemical pneumonitis at high concentrations Chronic elemental and inorganic exposure produces the classic triad of tremor, gingivostomatitis and neuropsychiatric changes ('erethism') with irritability, shyness and memory impairment Ingested inorganic mercury salts are corrosive, causing gastrointestinal burning and haemorrhage and acute kidney injury Organic methylmercury, the cause of environmental epidemics from contaminated fish, targets the nervous system with sensory disturbance, ataxia, visual field constriction and hearing loss, and crosses the placenta to harm the developing fetus Diagnosis uses blood and urine mercury levels, with the appropriate specimen depending on the form of exposure, interpreted with the exposure history Management centres on removing exposure and supportive care, with a chelating agent used in significant inorganic or elemental poisoning under specialist advice, while chelation is less effective for organic mercury Acrodynia (pink disease) is a distinctive reaction to mercury seen particularly in children, with painful pink extremities, irritability and desquamation MEDICAL EMERGENCY: acute high-level vapour inhalation causing respiratory distress and chemical pneumonitis Corrosive ingestion of inorganic salts with gastrointestinal haemorrhage and shock Acute kidney injury Pregnancy with organic mercury exposure given the risk of fetal neurological harm Using the wrong specimen (for example relying on blood levels for chronic elemental exposure) Expecting chelation to reverse established organic mercury neurotoxicity Attributing neuropsychiatric change to primary psychiatric illness without an exposure history Overlooking dietary fish as a source of methylmercury Missing the risk to the fetus in exposed pregnant women Mercury binds avidly to sulfhydryl groups, disrupting numerous enzymes and cellular proteins. Lipophilic elemental vapour and organic mercury readily cross the blood-brain barrier (and placenta), producing neuronal injury and the neurological and neuropsychiatric features, while inorganic salts concentrate in and damage the renal tubules and are locally corrosive to the gut. Oxidative stress and immune-mediated renal effects contribute to the tissue damage. Removal from exposure often allows gradual improvement of inorganic and elemental effects, but severe neurological injury, especially from organic methylmercury, may be permanent, and prenatal exposure can cause lasting developmental impairment.

(including lymphoblastic and other small round cell infiltrates) Basal cell carcinoma, particularly nodular type Amelanotic melanoma Cutaneous metastasis from other neuroendocrine primaries Poorly with negativity for TTF-1 helping exclude metastatic small-cell lung carcinoma Early regional nodal spread is common, so sentinel lymph node biopsy is central to staging even in clinically node-negative disease Management combines wide local excision (or Mohs micrographic surgery) with adjuvant radiotherapy, and immune-checkpoint inhibition has transformed treatment of advanced disease sun-exposed skin of an older or immunosuppressed patient Palpable regional lymphadenopathy suggesting nodal metastasis In-transit cutaneous satellite lesions indicating aggressive lymphatic spread Systemic symptoms or imaging findings suggesting distant metastatic disease New aggressive skin tumour in a transplant recipient or other profoundly immunosuppressed individual Mistaking the bland-looking nodule for a benign cyst or lipoma and delaying biopsy Failing to perform immunohistochemistry to distinguish it from metastatic small-cell lung carcinoma and other small round cell tumours Omitting sentinel lymph node biopsy in clinically node-negative disease and thereby understaging Underestimating aggressiveness in immunosuppressed patients or attributing rapid growth to a benign process Merkel cell carcinoma is an aggressive cutaneous neuroendocrine malignancy that arises through two convergent routes. In roughly the majority of cases in many populations, clonal integration of Merkel-cell polyomavirus into the host genome, together with truncating mutations of the viral large T antigen, drives persistent expression of viral oncoproteins that inactivate tumour-suppressor pathways such as retinoblastoma protein signalling. The alternative route is chronic ultraviolet damage producing a very high burden of somatic mutations, typically in virus-negative tumours. Both pathways yield a proliferation of small cells with neuroendocrine differentiation that infiltrate the dermis, invade lymphatics readily, and metastasise early to regional nodes and beyond. The strong influence of immune surveillance explains both the excess incidence in immunosuppression and the notable responsiveness to checkpoint blockade. Merkel cell carcinoma is aggressive with a substantial risk of nodal and distant metastasis; outcome is strongly stage-dependent, being relatively favourable for small localised node-negative lesions but poor once regional or distant spread occurs. Immunosuppression worsens prognosis, while immune-checkpoint inhibition has meaningfully improved survival in advanced disease.

MERRF syndrome — Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibres, m.8344A>G, MT-TK, MERRF Other progressive myoclonic epilepsies such as Unverricht-Lundborg and Lafora disease MELAS and overlap mitochondrial syndromes Sialidosis and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis Spinocerebellar ataxias with myoclonus Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy Coeliac-associated or paraneoplastic cerebellar ataxia Resting and post-exercise blood lactate and pyruvate Electroencephalography to characterise generalised epileptiform and photosensitive discharges Brain MRI, which may show cerebellar and brainstem atrophy or basal ganglia calcification Targeted molecular testing for m.8344A>G with heteroplasmy quantification in appropriate tissue Skeletal muscle biopsy for ragged-red fibres and respiratory-chain enzymology Audiometry and nerve conduction studies for associated deafness and neuropathy The defining tetrad is myoclonus, generalised epilepsy, cerebellar ataxia and a myopathy with ragged-red fibres on muscle biopsy Most cases are due to the maternally inherited m.8344A>G point mutation in the MT-TK gene encoding the mitochondrial transfer RNA for lysine As with other mitochondrial tRNA disorders, heteroplasmy and a threshold effect explain the variable severity and age of onset across a maternal lineage Additional features may include sensorineural deafness, optic atrophy, peripheral neuropathy, dementia and multiple symmetrical lipomatosis of the neck and trunk Elevated resting or exercise-induced lactate supports the diagnosis but is neither universal nor specific Myoclonus is frequently stimulus-sensitive and can be difficult to control; some anticonvulsants worsen mitochondrial function and are best avoided Muscle histochemistry shows ragged-red fibres that are typically cytochrome c oxidase deficient, reflecting the tRNA translation defect Poorly controlled myoclonic seizures or status epilepticus Rapid neurological deterioration or new cardiorespiratory compromise Cardiac conduction abnormality or cardiomyopathy on surveillance Metabolic decompensation with rising lactic acidosis Labelling the disorder an idiopathic progressive myoclonic epilepsy without pursuing mitochondrial testing Relying on blood alone for genetic testing, since low-level heteroplasmy may be missed Prescribing anticonvulsants that impair respiratory-chain or mitochondrial function Overlooking cardiac and audiological involvement that warrants surveillance MERRF is caused by a mitochondrial tRNA mutation, usually m.8344A>G in MT-TK, that impairs mitochondrial translation and thereby the synthesis of respiratory-chain subunits, reducing oxidative phosphorylation capacity. The mutation is maternally inherited and heteroplasmic, so clinical expression depends on the proportion of mutant genomes and the energy threshold of each tissue. Neurons of the cerebellum, brainstem and cerebral cortex, together with skeletal muscle, are especially vulnerable to the resulting energy deficit, producing the characteristic myoclonus, seizures, ataxia and myopathy. Accumulation of abnormal mitochondria beneath the sarcolemma gives the ragged-red appearance on trichrome staining. MERRF is slowly progressive with a broad spectrum of severity; many patients have a normal early childhood before symptoms emerge, but accumulating myoclonus, ataxia and dementia can be disabling, and lifespan may be reduced in severely affected individuals.

mesenteric cyst — mesenteric lymphangioma, chylolymphatic cyst omental cyst intestinal duplication cyst ovarian cyst pancreatic pseudocyst hydatid cyst cystic mesothelioma choledochal cyst abdominal ultrasound to characterise the cyst and its septa contrast-enhanced CT to define anatomy and vascular relationships MRI for soft-tissue characterisation and surgical planning analysis of aspirated fluid for chyle versus serous content histopathology with endothelial and mesothelial immunohistochemical markers diagnostic laparoscopy in equivocal cases Mesenteric cysts are rare intra-abdominal cysts arising within the mesentery, most commonly in the small bowel mesentery and particularly the ileum. The de Perrot classification groups them by origin into lymphatic, mesothelial, enteric, urogenital, dermoid, and non-pancreatic pseudocyst types, with lymphatic (lymphangiomatous) lesions predominating. Many are asymptomatic incidental findings; symptomatic lesions cause abdominal distension, vague pain, or a palpable mass. The classic Tillaux sign is a mass that moves freely in a plane perpendicular to the axis of the mesentery but is restricted along it. Complications include torsion, intracystic haemorrhage, infection, rupture, and bowel obstruction, any of which can produce an acute abdomen. Ultrasound and CT typically show a thin-walled, well-defined, fluid-filled lesion; internal septation or chylous fluid suggests a lymphatic origin. Complete surgical excision is the treatment of choice and may require resection of intimately adherent bowel to ensure clearance. Chylous ascites can accompany or follow lymphatic cysts and complicate surgical management. acute abdomen from torsion, intracystic haemorrhage, or rupture features of bowel obstruction rapid enlargement or systemic signs suggesting infection development of chylous ascites solid or thickened components raising concern for cystic mesothelioma misinterpreting a large cyst as free ascites on imaging confusing the lesion with an ovarian cyst in female patients incomplete excision of a lymphatic cyst leading to recurrence underestimating the need for adjacent bowel resection when the cyst is inseparable from the mesenteric vessels overlooking postoperative chylous leak after excision of a lymphatic cyst Mesenteric cysts are benign lesions most often thought to result from proliferation of ectopic or maldeveloped lymphatic tissue that fails to establish communication with the normal lymphatic system, leading to progressive accumulation of lymph or chyle. Other histogenetic origins account for the mesothelial, enteric, and urogenital variants, reflecting entrapped embryonic tissues within the mesenteric leaves. The cyst enlarges as fluid accumulates, exerting mass effect on adjacent bowel and mesenteric vessels; because the lesion lies between the mesenteric leaves it can twist on its pedicle, bleed, become infected, or rupture. The lining varies with origin — endothelial in lymphatic cysts and mesothelial in mesothelial cysts — a distinction confirmed histologically and with immunohistochemistry. Prognosis is excellent after complete excision, with cure and low recurrence. Incomplete removal of lymphatic lesions may be followed by recurrence.

Acute mesenteric ischemia — CT angiography (mesenteric) Lactate Urgent surgical/vascular review Pain out of proportion to exam — time-critical Chronic mesenteric ischaemia / intestinal angina (postprandial pain, weight loss, fear of eating) Ischaemic colitis (notably after elective or emergent aortic repair) Gastrointestinal malignancy (must be excluded in chronic presentations) Superior mesenteric artery syndrome (duodenal compression after weight loss/immobilisation) Median arcuate ligament syndrome (celiac artery compression) Thin-cut (1 mm or thinner) CT angiography is the gold standard for detecting mesenteric arterial occlusive (embolic/thrombotic) disease and for assessing bowel; venous-phase imaging detects mesenteric venous thrombosis with diffuse bowel-wall thickening and splanchnic thrombus (p.2588-2589). Mesenteric duplex ultrasound is a sensitive/specific screening tool; a high SMA peak flow velocity carries ~80% positive predictive value, and a negative duplex virtually excludes mesenteric ischaemia (test must be done fasting) (p.2588). Leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis and lactic acidosis support advanced ischaemia but may be absent in reversible ischaemia and cannot reliably distinguish reversible ischaemia from frank necrosis (p.2589). ECG and echocardiogram may help identify an embolic cardiac source but must not delay surgical therapy (p.2588). Hypercoagulability workup in suspected mesenteric venous thrombosis (e.g. factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation, protein C/S or antithrombin deficiency, antiphospholipid syndrome) (p.2587, 2589). Colonoscopy if ischaemic colitis is suspected, to grade mucosal injury (p.2589). Acute intestinal obstruction (mechanical or strangulated bowel) Other noninflammatory causes of abdominal pain such as biliary colic and neoplasia Inflammatory abdominal conditions: pancreatitis, cholecystitis, appendicitis, diverticulitis, peptic ulcer, inflammatory bowel disease Severe, acute, non-remitting abdominal pain that is strikingly out of proportion to physical findings is the most common complaint in arterial acute mesenteric ischaemia, present in about 95% of cases; pain precedes signs because ischaemia begins in the mucosa and progresses outward to the serosa (p.2588). About half of acute mesenteric ischaemia cases are embolic, lodging in the mid-to-distal SMA just past the middle colic artery origin; emboli commonly arise from atrial fibrillation, recent MI, soft atherosclerotic plaque, infective endocarditis, valvular heart disease, or recent cardiac/vascular catheterisation (p.2587). Acute-on-chronic thrombotic ischaemia (about 25-30% of cases) occurs at sites of severe atherosclerotic narrowing of the SMA or celiac artery, typically in patients with pre-existing mesenteric atherosclerosis who may have had prior chronic mesenteric ischaemia (p.2587, 2588). Embolic disease is suggested by older patients with a predisposing cardiac source (AF, prior embolic event, recent infective endocarditis), whereas thrombotic disease suggests underlying atherosclerosis with possible prior intestinal angina (p.2588). Chronic mesenteric ischaemia classically presents as recurrent dull, crampy, postprandial epigastric pain ('intestinal angina') with fear of eating and weight loss; chronic diarrhoea may occur and symptoms typically last 6-12 months before diagnosis (p.2587-2588). Mesenteric venous thrombosis tends to present more vaguely and subacutely with non-specific abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, distension, mild-to-moderate tenderness and dehydration, making it easy to under-recognise (p.2589). The decision to operate in suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia is often based on a high index of suspicion from history and examination despite normal laboratory results (p.2588). Pain out of proportion to examination with a high-risk cardiac source (AF, recent MI, endocarditis) — embolic acute mesenteric ischaemia until proven otherwise Later signs of peritonitis and cardiovascular collapse indicate established transmural infarction Blood per rectum, marked distension or obtundation in a critically ill/shocked patient (suggests non-occlusive ischaemia) Rising lactate / metabolic acidosis is a late marker and its absence does not exclude ischaemia Treating pain out of proportion to examination as benign — early ischaemia produces severe pain with deceptively unremarkable abdominal signs because injury starts in the mucosa (p.2588). Waiting for abnormal labs before acting — lactate and acidosis are late and may be normal in reversible ischaemia or even necrosis; the operative decision is often made on clinical suspicion despite normal results (p.2588-2589). Overlooking non-occlusive ischaemia in obtunded/critically ill patients where examination findings are absent or obscured by the underlying illness (p.2589). Missing the vaguer, subacute presentation of mesenteric venous thrombosis (non-specific pain, nausea, distension) (p.2589). Failing to perform mesenteric duplex while fasting — bowel gas obscures flow and the post-prandial vasodilatory response (p.2588). Intestinal ischaemia occurs when splanchnic perfusion fails to meet the bowel's metabolic demand, producing ischaemic tissue injury. The gut is supplied by the celiac artery, SMA and IMA with extensive collateralisation between major trunks and mesenteric arcades; protective responses include this collateral network, autoregulation of flow and the ability to increase oxygen extraction. Watershed colonic zones with inherently lower flow are Griffiths' point (splenic flexure) and Sudeck's point (descending/sigmoid colon), the commonest sites of colonic ischaemia. The splanchnic bed can receive up to 30% of cardiac output. Occlusive ischaemia results from an embolus or progressive thrombosis in a major mesenteric artery (over 75% of emboli are cardiac in origin and lodge in the SMA distal to the middle colic artery). Chronic intestinal angina generally requires progressive stenosis of two of the three major vessels. Non-occlusive ischaemia is driven by disproportionate mesenteric arteriolar vasospasm in response to severe physiological stress such as shock; untreated, early mucosal stress ulceration progresses to full-thickness injury. Mesenteric venous thrombosis is usually precipitated by a hypercoagulable state. (p.2587-2588) Acute mesenteric ischaemia carries a high mortality, roughly 50-80% at presentation (with the acute arterial form quoted at over 50%); it is one of the most challenging diagnoses, and the single most important determinant of survival is the timeliness of diagnosis and treatment. Endovascular stenting for chronic mesenteric ischaemia has about an 80% long-term success rate. (p.2587-2588) Harrison classifies intestinal ischaemia into chronic mesenteric ischaemia (CMI) and acute mesenteric ischaemia (AMI). Acute mesenteric vascular insufficiency is subdivided into (1) arterio-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia — further split into arterial embolus (~50%) and arterial thrombosis (~25-30%, often acute-on-chronic), (2) non-occlusive/vasospastic mesenteric ischaemia (~20%, vasospasm or hypoperfusion), and (3) mesenteric venous thrombosis (<10%). Ischaemic colitis mucosal injury is graded as mild (minimal erythema), moderate (pale ulceration extending into muscularis), or severe (black/green discoloration with full-thickness necrosis). (p.2587-2589)

Mesenteric Vascular Insufficiency — Intestinal ischemia, Mesenteric ischemia, Chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI), Acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI), Intestinal angina, Nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia (NOMI), Mesenteric venous thrombosis, Ischemic colitis Gastrointestinal malignancy (must be excluded in CMI before intervention) Peptic ulcer disease and other causes of epigastric/postprandial pain Biliary colic / biliary tract disease Acute pancreatitis Inflammatory bowel disease (ischemic colitis is commonly confused with IBD) Acute intestinal obstruction (especially strangulated obstruction with vascular insufficiency) Infectious colitis Infectious gastroenteritis CT angiography with thin (1-mm or finer) cuts, including venous phase for venous thrombosis (gold standard) Fasting mesenteric duplex ultrasound (screening; SMA peak velocity) Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy (to exclude malignancy in CMI and assess colonic mucosa in ischemic colitis) Abdominal CT and abdominal ultrasound Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram (to identify embolic source such as atrial fibrillation; should not delay surgery) Laboratory markers: leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis, lactic acidosis (support advanced ischemia but do not reliably distinguish reversible ischemia from necrosis) Hypercoagulability workup in mesenteric venous thrombosis Inflammatory bowel disease Diverticular disease / diverticulitis Colonic neoplasm Peptic ulcer disease Biliary tract disease Intestinal ischemia arises when splanchnic perfusion cannot meet the metabolic demands of the gut; it is broadly divided into chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI) and acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI), with the latter carrying a high mortality (~50-80%) and depending critically on early diagnosis and prompt intervention (p.2586). AMI is mechanistically categorized into three patterns: arterio-occlusive (embolic or thrombotic), nonocclusive (vasospastic/hypoperfusion), and mesenteric venous thrombosis (p.2587). Roughly half of AMI cases are embolic, with emboli typically lodging in the mid-to-distal superior mesenteric artery (SMA) just beyond the origin of the middle colic artery; about 25-30% are acute-on-chronic thrombosis on preexisting mesenteric atherosclerosis (p.2586-2587). The hallmark of acute arterial mesenteric ischemia is severe, abrupt, nonremitting abdominal pain that is strikingly out of proportion to physical examination findings, present in roughly 95% of cases (p.2588). Pain is disproportionate to exam because ischemia begins in the mucosal layer and advances outward toward the serosa, so peritoneal signs and cardiovascular collapse are late developments (p.2588). CMI classically presents with insidious, recurrent dull crampy postprandial epigastric pain ('intestinal angina'), fear of eating, and consequent weight loss, often over 6-12 months, in a malnourished patient with other signs of atherosclerosis (p.2587). CT angiography with 1-mm or thinner cuts is the gold-standard diagnostic test for both acute and chronic mesenteric arterial occlusive disease; a venous-phase study aids detection of mesenteric venous thrombosis (p.2587-2588). Fasting mesenteric duplex ultrasound is a useful screening tool: a high SMA peak flow velocity carries about an 80% positive predictive value, and a negative duplex study virtually excludes mesenteric ischemia (p.2587). In suspected AMI the decision to operate is frequently driven by a high index of suspicion from history and exam despite normal laboratory values, and surgical consultation should not be delayed (p.2588). Mesenteric venous thrombosis (<10% of cases) tends to be associated with hypercoagulable states; documented inherited thrombophilia warrants long-term anticoagulation (p.2587, p.2588-2589). Severity of ischemic colonic mucosal injury is graded by colonoscopy from mild (minimal erythema) to moderate (pale ulcerations extending into muscularis) to severe (black/green discoloration indicating full-thickness necrosis) (p.2589). Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings Blood per rectum / bloody stools Peritonitis and cardiovascular collapse (late findings indicating advanced ischemia) Leukocytosis with metabolic/lactic acidosis suggesting advanced ischemia or necrosis Black or green colonic mucosal discoloration on colonoscopy indicating full-thickness necrosis Atrial fibrillation, recent myocardial infarction, or infective endocarditis in a patient with acute abdominal pain (embolic source) Anchoring on a benign cause and underestimating severity because abdominal pain is markedly out of proportion to a relatively unremarkable exam (p.2588). Waiting for abnormal laboratory values before acting; lactate, leukocytosis, and acidosis may be normal early or fail to distinguish reversible ischemia from necrosis (p.2588-2589). Performing mesenteric duplex without fasting, since bowel gas obscures flow and the postprandial vasodilation response (p.2587). Mistaking ischemic colitis for inflammatory bowel disease (p.2589). Overlooking nonocclusive ischemia in obtunded, critically ill patients in whom physical findings are obscured by the underlying illness (p.2589). Failing to recognize that the proximal jejunum may be spared in SMA embolism while the rest of the small bowel to the transverse colon becomes ischemic, leading to incomplete bowel assessment (p.2589). The intestine is perfused by the celiac artery, superior mesenteric artery (SMA), and inferior mesenteric artery (IMA), with extensive collateralization through the mesenteric arcades; small-bowel collaterals converge at the duodenum and pancreatic bed, while colonic collaterals meet at the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) and the descending/sigmoid colon (Sudeck's point), the watershed zones most prone to colonic ischemia. The splanchnic bed can receive up to ~30% of cardiac output, and protective mechanisms include abundant collaterals, autoregulation of flow, and the capacity to increase oxygen extraction. Occlusive ischemia results from embolic or thrombotic interruption of a major mesenteric artery (emboli, originating from the heart in >75% of cases, preferentially lodge in the SMA distal to the middle colic origin); development of chronic intestinal angina generally requires significant stenosis of two of the three major vessels, with SMA involvement most concerning. CMI reflects failure to mount the normal postprandial hyperemic increase in intestinal blood flow, analogous to cardiac angina, due to atherosclerotic narrowing of the SMA and/or celiac origins. Nonocclusive ischemia represents disproportionate mesenteric arteriolar vasospasm in response to severe physiologic stress such as shock; if untreated, early mucosal stress ulceration progresses to full-thickness injury. Mesenteric venous thrombosis arises from inherited or acquired hypercoagulable states (p.2587). Acute mesenteric ischemia carries a mortality rate exceeding 50% and is among the most challenging diagnoses; the timeliness of diagnosis and treatment is the single most important determinant of survival. Chronic mesenteric ischemia managed with revascularization has favorable long-term outcomes, with endovascular stenting associated with about an 80% long-term success rate. Outcomes hinge on early recognition before progression to full-thickness bowel necrosis and peritonitis (p.2587-2588). Ischemic colonic mucosal injury is graded by colonoscopy: mild = minimal mucosal erythema; moderate = pale mucosal ulcerations with extension into the muscular layer; severe = severe ulcerations with black or green mucosal discoloration consistent with full-thickness bowel-wall necrosis. Mechanically, mesenteric ischemia is classified as chronic (CMI) versus acute (AMI), and AMI is subclassified as arterio-occlusive (embolic or thrombotic), nonocclusive (vasospastic/hypoperfusion), or mesenteric venous thrombosis (p.2587, p.2589).

absence of infarction Not investigating for an underlying thrombophilia or malignancy after the acute event Mesenteric venous thrombosis occurs when thrombus obstructs venous outflow from the bowel, most commonly in the superior mesenteric vein. Impaired venous drainage raises intestinal capillary and interstitial pressure, producing bowel wall oedema, arterial inflow compromise, and progressive congestion. If flow is not restored, transmural ischaemia and infarction ensue, with translocation of bacteria, peritonitis, and sepsis. It is usually driven by hypercoagulable states (primary thrombophilia, malignancy) or local factors such as portal hypertension, abdominal sepsis or inflammation, and recent surgery. The extent of collateral drainage and the speed of thrombus propagation determine whether ischaemia remains reversible. When diagnosed before infarction and treated promptly with anticoagulation, mesenteric venous thrombosis has a better prognosis than acute arterial mesenteric ischaemia. Delayed diagnosis with established bowel necrosis carries high morbidity and mortality, and recurrence risk depends on the underlying prothrombotic cause and duration of anticoagulation.

Inhaled asbestos fibres, particularly amphibole types, are retained in tissues and provoke chronic inflammation, oxidative injury, and DNA damage over many years, leading to malignant transformation. The tumour characteristically grows as a diffuse rind along serosal surfaces, encasing the lung and invading the chest wall, diaphragm, and mediastinum. Histological subtypes range from epithelioid through biphasic to the more aggressive sarcomatoid form. Prognosis is generally poor with limited long-term survival; the epithelioid subtype, early stage, and good performance status favour longer survival, while sarcomatoid histology and advanced disease predict rapid progression.

vomiting, diuretic, or laxative use Metabolic alkalosis is a primary rise in serum bicarbonate with a compensatory increase in carbon dioxide from reduced ventilation Understanding it requires separating the process that generates the alkalosis from the factors that allow the kidney to maintain it Urine chloride is the single most useful test for classification, dividing cases into chloride-responsive (low urine chloride) and chloride-resistant (high urine chloride) forms Chloride-responsive alkalosis, from vomiting, nasogastric suction, or diuretics, is accompanied by volume and chloride depletion and corrects with saline and potassium repletion Chloride-resistant alkalosis reflects mineralocorticoid excess or severe potassium depletion and does not respond to saline, so the underlying disorder must be treated Hypokalaemia both contributes to and is worsened by alkalosis, and the two often need correcting together Maintenance of the alkalosis depends on factors such as volume contraction, chloride depletion, potassium depletion, and mineralocorticoid activity that impair renal bicarbonate excretion Severe alkalaemia can cause neuromuscular irritability, arrhythmias, and reduced tissue oxygen delivery, and may need more aggressive correction Severe alkalaemia causing tetany, seizures, or cardiac arrhythmia Profound hypokalaemia with muscle weakness or arrhythmia risk Marked volume depletion with haemodynamic compromise Hypertension with hypokalaemic alkalosis suggesting mineralocorticoid excess Giving saline to a chloride-resistant alkalosis that will not respond Failing to measure urine chloride and thereby misclassifying the disorder Neglecting concurrent potassium and magnesium deficits that perpetuate the alkalosis Overlooking surreptitious vomiting or diuretic use as the underlying cause Metabolic alkalosis arises when there is a net gain of bicarbonate or a loss of hydrogen ions, but its persistence depends on the kidney's inability to excrete the excess bicarbonate. Normally the kidney can excrete a large bicarbonate load rapidly, so an alkalosis is only sustained when a maintenance factor is present. Generation occurs through loss of acid from the upper gastrointestinal tract or the kidney, or from a gain of alkali. Maintenance results from conditions that increase renal bicarbonate reabsorption, including reduced effective circulating volume, chloride depletion, potassium depletion, and excess mineralocorticoid activity, all of which enhance sodium and bicarbonate reabsorption and hydrogen secretion. In chloride-responsive states, volume and chloride depletion drive the maintenance and are corrected by saline; in chloride-resistant states, ongoing mineralocorticoid excess or profound potassium loss sustains the alkalosis despite adequate volume. Most cases resolve readily once the generating cause is removed and the maintenance factors (volume, chloride, and potassium depletion) are corrected. Chloride-resistant forms require treatment of the underlying disorder and may persist otherwise. Severe alkalaemia is dangerous but usually reversible with appropriate management, and overall outcome is governed by the underlying condition.

Metabolic encephalopathy — Electrolytes, glucose, calcium Renal & liver panel, ammonia ABG Reversible — correct the derangement Dementia and pre-existing cognitive impairment - the major predisposing condition; at least two-thirds of delirium occurs in patients with underlying dementia, and the two coexist and overlap (p.183). Dementia with Lewy bodies - fluctuating course, prominent visual hallucinations and parkinsonism can closely mimic hyperactive delirium (p.183). Nonconvulsive status epilepticus and recurrent seizures with prolonged postictal confusion (p.185). Focal stroke or haemorrhage in nondominant (right) parietal lobe or medial dorsal thalamus - rare structural cause of an acute confusional state (p.184-185). Hypertensive encephalopathy / posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) and eclampsia (p.184, p.190). Diffuse neoplastic disease - multiple brain metastases, diffuse glioma, CNS lymphoma, carcinomatous meningitis (p.184). Postoperative encephalopathy from a shower of microemboli, particularly after cardiac/cardiopulmonary bypass surgery (p.2348). Acute primary psychiatric disturbance, depression and catatonia - must be distinguished, particularly from the quiet hypoactive subtype (p.184). Systemic infections - urinary tract infection, pneumonia and other respiratory infections, skin/soft tissue infection and frank sepsis; a UTI precipitating acute confusion in an elderly patient with baseline dementia is a classic scenario (p.184). CNS infections - bacterial meningitis, encephalitis (including herpes simplex) and brain abscess; less common causes but high morbidity/mortality if missed (p.184). Sepsis-associated ('septic') encephalopathy - diffuse cytokine-mediated brain dysfunction occurring in the majority of patients with sepsis and multiorgan failure (p.184, p.2348-2349). Severe systemic infections causing coma - septicaemia, typhoid fever, malaria (including cerebral malaria), Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (p.190). Complete blood count and full electrolyte panel including magnesium and phosphorus (p.185). Serum/urine toxicology screen - performed earlier in younger patients (p.185). TSH and free T4, and serum cortisol for suspected endocrinopathy (p.185). Vitamin levels - B12, folate, thiamine (p.185). EEG - essential when seizures are suspected or when no cause is found after initial workup; shows nonspecific diffuse symmetric slowing in encephalopathy, frontal high-voltage slow or triphasic waves in metabolic (e.g., hepatic) coma, and can reveal nonconvulsive status epilepticus (p.184-185, p.190). Brain imaging - MRI with diffusion and gadolinium is the preferred study (CT often used first for speed/availability) to exclude structural causes; note imaging is frequently unrevealing in pure metabolic delirium (p.185, p.189-190). Lumbar puncture (after neuroimaging) when CNS infection, autoimmune, inflammatory or neoplastic disease is suspected, or in any delirium with a negative workup (p.185, p.190). Inflammatory and autoimmune serologies - ESR, ANA, complement, p-/c-ANCA, and paraneoplastic/autoimmune encephalitis panels in serum and CSF when indicated (p.185). ECG and infectious serologies (RPR, HIV; fungal/viral if high suspicion) as second-tier tests (p.185). Anticholinergic, opioid, sedative-hypnotic and other prescription drug toxicity, and drugs of abuse (alcohol, opiates, MDMA/ecstasy, GHB, ketamine/PCP, cocaine, 'bath salts', synthetic cannabinoids) (p.184). Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal - to be considered in all delirium including the elderly, since even modest daily drinkers can withdraw on admission (p.184). Poison/toxin exposure - carbon monoxide, ethylene glycol, inhalants, pesticides (p.184). Endocrinopathies - hyper- or hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, adrenal insufficiency / Addisonian crisis (p.184, p.190). Hypothermia and hyperthermia (p.184, p.190). Global cerebral hypoperfusion from hypotension - heart failure, septic shock, severe dehydration or anaemia (p.184-185). Autoimmune and paraneoplastic disorders - CNS vasculitis, cerebral lupus, autoimmune encephalitis (anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis shows a characteristic 'extreme delta brush' EEG) (p.184, p.190). Sedative drug overdose mimicking structural brainstem disease or even brain death (e.g., barbiturates) - toxic causes must be excluded before diagnosing brain death (p.189). Delirium is an acute, relatively rapid decline in cognition (hours to days) that characteristically fluctuates; the cardinal neuropsychological deficit is inattention, though memory, executive function, visuospatial skills and language are variably affected (p.181-182). It is a purely clinical bedside diagnosis. The validated Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) requires (1) acute onset with fluctuating course and (2) inattention, plus either (3) disorganized thinking or (4) altered level of consciousness (p.184). Recognize two ends of a spectrum: a hyperactive subtype (classic example: delirium tremens, with agitation, hallucinations, tremor, autonomic instability) and a hypoactive subtype (e.g., benzodiazepine intoxication, with apathy and psychomotor slowing); hypoactive cases are frequently overlooked, especially on wards and in the ICU (p.182). Bilateral asterixis and multifocal myoclonus on motor exam are non-focal signs that, while nonspecific, usually point to a metabolic or toxic encephalopathy / drug intoxication rather than a structural lesion (p.184, p.190). A simple bedside test of attention is forward digit span: healthy adults manage 5-7 digits, while a span of 4 or fewer suggests an attentional deficit; many delirious patients can repeat only 3 or fewer (p.184). Worsening in the evening (sundowning) is typical but not required; because the course fluctuates, a single morning assessment can be falsely reassuring and serial examinations are needed (p.184). About one-third of delirium cases are drug-related, especially agents with anticholinergic or sedative properties, narcotics and benzodiazepines; nearly any drug can precipitate delirium in a predisposed patient (p.184). Delirium can act as a 'stress test for the brain' - a minor insult (UTI, elective surgery, hospitalization) that unmasks delirium in a previously well person should prompt later outpatient screening for an unrecognized underlying neurodegenerative or cerebrovascular disorder (p.183). The MMSE is unreliable in delirium because tasks such as spelling 'world' backward and serial subtraction are corrupted by the underlying attentional deficit (p.184). New focal neurologic deficit, meningismus, fever or papilloedema - point away from a simple metabolic cause toward a structural, infectious or raised-ICP process needing urgent imaging/LP (p.184, p.189-190). Suspected nonconvulsive status epilepticus - if suspicion is high, EEG should be obtained immediately as it is treatable and easily missed in a fluctuating patient (p.185). Sodium <125 mmol/L (especially if acute) causing confusion, and <119 mmol/L acutely associated with coma and convulsions (p.188-189). In-hospital delirium carries a 25-33% mortality (comparable to sepsis) and a roughly fivefold higher mortality in following months - it signals serious underlying illness, not a benign transient state (p.182). Delirium in the ICU should be regarded as organ dysfunction on a par with liver, kidney or heart failure, and is associated with worse outcomes (p.182, p.2348). Treating the symptoms of delirium pharmacologically while neglecting the underlying cause merely prolongs the confused state and can mask important diagnostic clues (p.185). Missing nonconvulsive status epilepticus - its fluctuating presentation mimics ordinary delirium, and only EEG will reveal it (p.185). Diagnosing delirium without knowledge of the patient's cognitive baseline, so that dementia or long-standing depression is mistaken for an acute confusional state - collateral history is essential (p.184). Overlooking the quiet hypoactive subtype, which is commonly missed and may be wrongly attributed to depression or sedation (p.182, p.2348). Attributing coma to incidental imaging findings (small subdural, old stroke) when the true cause is intoxication; a normal CT does not exclude an anatomic lesion, and most coma/confusion is metabolic or toxic in origin (p.190). Forgetting that the severity of metabolic encephalopathy depends on how rapidly the derangement developed, so a 'mildly' abnormal value reached acutely can produce marked impairment (p.188-189). Diagnosing brain death without first excluding sedative/toxic causes (e.g., barbiturates) that can mimic its findings (p.189). Delirium reflects diffuse rather than focal brain dysfunction; the attentional deficit localizes broadly to brainstem, thalamus, prefrontal cortex and parietal lobes, and most cases arise from widespread cortical and subcortical disturbance rather than a single lesion. Acetylcholine deficiency is thought to be central (explaining the potency of anticholinergic drugs), with additional roles for excess dopamine, proinflammatory mediators and individual susceptibility. The concept is that of an insult acting on a vulnerable, low-reserve brain. For most metabolic causes (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperosmolarity, hypercapnia, hypercalcaemia, hepatic and renal failure) the brain shows little or no structural damage and the effects are largely reversible, attributed to impaired energy supply, altered ion fluxes across neuronal membranes and neurotransmitter abnormalities. In hepatic encephalopathy, raised ammonia is proposed to drive astrocytic glutamine synthesis and osmotic swelling, mitochondrial energy failure, reactive nitrogen/oxygen species, increased inhibitory GABA tone and 'false' neurotransmitters, with chronic disease producing diffuse astrocytosis. Uraemic encephalopathy is multifactorial (urea itself is not the cause): accumulated neurotoxins, catecholamine depletion, altered glutamate/GABA tone, raised brain calcium and blood-brain-barrier disruption. Importantly, the degree of neurologic change in metabolic encephalopathies depends heavily on the rapidity with which the serum derangement develops, not just its absolute level. In sepsis-associated encephalopathy, circulating inflammatory mediators (TNF, IL-1, IL-2, IL-6) appear to cause diffuse cerebral dysfunction that is not simply explained by the metabolic derangements of organ failure (p.183, p.188-189, p.2348-2349). Once viewed as benign and transient, delirium is now recognized as a marker of serious illness with substantial morbidity and mortality: in-hospital mortality is roughly 25-33% (similar to sepsis), and delirious patients have about a fivefold higher mortality in the ensuing months versus matched non-delirious inpatients, plus longer stays, more nursing-home discharge, higher readmission and recurrent episodes. Most metabolic and toxic encephalopathies are reversible with no or minimal structural brain damage, and drug/toxin-induced coma typically resolves fully provided hypoxia or severe hypotension has not occurred. However, some episodes persist for weeks to months or longer, delirium can cause lasting cognitive decline, and lingering effects (ranging from amnesia for the episode to PTSD-like re-experiencing) are common. Sepsis-associated encephalopathy severe enough to cause coma carries a mortality approaching 50%, though this mainly reflects severity of the underlying critical illness rather than the encephalopathy itself (p.182, p.188-189, p.2349). No formal grading scale is described; severity is gauged clinically by the level of consciousness (a continuum from hyperarousal through lethargy to coma) and by the depth of the attentional deficit (e.g., forward digit span). The EEG correlates with severity, showing progressive generalized background slowing as the encephalopathy deepens (p.184, p.190).

well toddler Combined central and peripheral neurological signs Rapid cognitive or psychiatric deterioration in older patients Feeding and swallowing difficulty with aspiration risk Being misled by pseudodeficiency alleles that lower measured enzyme activity without causing disease Attributing early behavioural or psychiatric changes in adults to a primary psychiatric disorder Missing the peripheral neuropathy that helps distinguish it from other leukodystrophies Delaying assessment for disease-modifying therapy until symptoms are advanced Metachromatic leukodystrophy results from biallelic pathogenic variants in ARSA, encoding the lysosomal enzyme arylsulfatase A, which desulfates sulfatide (cerebroside sulfate). Deficient activity causes sulfatides to accumulate within lysosomes of myelin-forming cells (oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells) and other tissues. Juvenile and adult forms progress more slowly and variably. Presymptomatic or very early treatment with stem cell transplantation or gene therapy offers the best chance of altering the course, but symptomatic disease responds poorly.

only arylsulfatase A and diagnosing isolated metachromatic leukodystrophy while missing the combined deficiency Overlooking the somatic and dermatological clues (coarse features, ichthyosis, dysostosis) that point away from an isolated leukodystrophy Attributing the neuropathy solely to a central process and not testing nerve conduction Failing to recognise the multisystem nature when planning surveillance and supportive care In multiple sulfatase deficiency, biallelic variants in SUMF1 impair the formylglycine-generating enzyme that performs a post-translational modification essential for the catalytic activity of every sulfatase. As a result all sulfatases are simultaneously deficient, so sulfated substrates accumulate across multiple pathways: sulfatides build up in myelin (as in metachromatic leukodystrophy), glycosaminoglycans accumulate (as in mucopolysaccharidoses), and cholesterol sulfate accumulates in skin (as in X-linked ichthyosis). The combined storage produces central and peripheral demyelination alongside the somatic, skeletal, and dermatological features of the overlapping disorders. The disorder is progressive with a poor prognosis, especially in neonatal and late-infantile presentations, which typically lead to severe disability and early death; later-onset forms progress more slowly but remain relentless. No disease-modifying treatment is currently available.

Metagonimiasis (intestinal fluke) — Metagonimus yokogawai infection, Yokogawa's fluke, minute intestinal fluke infection, heterophyid intestinal fluke disease Heterophyiasis and other heterophyid intestinal fluke infection Fasciolopsiasis and other intestinal trematode disease Giardiasis and other protozoal enteritis Opisthorchiasis or clonorchiasis (from egg morphology overlap) Irritable bowel syndrome or functional dyspepsia Chronic bacterial or viral gastroenteritis Stool microscopy for ova and parasites with concentration techniques Repeated stool examination given intermittent and low egg output Full blood count for eosinophilia Careful egg morphometry to distinguish from other small trematode eggs Imaging or echocardiography only if ectopic (cardiac or cerebral) disease is suspected Serology where available to support the diagnosis One of the smallest human intestinal flukes, acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish carrying metacercariae, particularly in East Asia Light infection is usually asymptomatic; heavier burdens cause colicky abdominal pain, intermittent diarrhoea, nausea and lethargy Adult flukes attach to the mucosa of the small intestine and provoke local inflammation and mild malabsorption Diagnosis relies on finding small operculated eggs in stool that closely resemble those of Opisthorchis, Clonorchis and other heterophyids Rarely, eggs or flukes enter the circulation and embolise to the heart or brain, causing ectopic disease Praziquantel is highly effective and the treatment of choice Prevention centres on avoiding raw freshwater fish and improving sanitation to reduce egg contamination Neurological deficit or seizures suggesting cerebral egg embolisation Cardiac symptoms raising concern for myocardial involvement Persistent diarrhoea with weight loss and evidence of malabsorption Failure to respond to treatment, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Misidentifying the eggs as those of opisthorchiid liver flukes because of near-identical morphology Overlooking light infections when only a single stool sample is examined Attributing non-specific gastrointestinal symptoms to functional disease in endemic settings Failing to consider ectopic embolisation when unexplained cardiac or neurological signs appear Metagonimus yokogawai is a minute intestinal trematode whose life cycle passes through freshwater snails and then freshwater fish, in which infective metacercariae encyst. Humans and other fish-eating animals acquire infection by consuming raw or undercooked fish. The larvae excyst in the small intestine and mature into tiny adult flukes that burrow among the villi of the jejunum, causing localised mucosal inflammation, villous flattening and superficial ulceration. Heavy infection can impair absorption and produce chronic diarrhoea. Occasionally eggs deposited in the mucosa penetrate vessels and are carried to distant organs such as the myocardium or central nervous system, where they excite a granulomatous reaction. Eggs excreted in faeces continue the cycle by contaminating freshwater. Prognosis is excellent for intestinal disease, which resolves promptly with anthelmintic therapy; the rare ectopic cardiac or cerebral forms can be serious depending on the site affected.

Overlooking a tight gastrocnemius that maintains forefoot overload Failing to recognise transfer metatarsalgia following hallux surgery or with a short or elevated ray Neglecting fat pad atrophy and footwear factors in older patients Metatarsalgia arises when load beneath the lesser metatarsal heads exceeds what the forefoot soft tissues can tolerate, causing pain, inflammation, and protective callosity. Normal forefoot loading depends on even metatarsal length and alignment, a mobile first ray that shares weight, an adequate plantar fat pad, and balanced toe function. Disturbance of any of these concentrates pressure: a tight gastrocnemius increases forefoot load throughout stance, hallux valgus or hallux rigidus shifts weight laterally, lesser-toe clawing or hammering plantarflexes the metatarsal heads, and a long or plantarflexed metatarsal bears excess load. Distal migration or atrophy of the protective plantar fat pad, common with age, removes cushioning. When one ray is shortened, elevated, or surgically altered, adjacent rays absorb the redistributed force, producing transfer metatarsalgia. The result is localised or diffuse plantar forefoot pain that reflects the specific mechanical derangement. Most mechanical metatarsalgia responds well to identifying and correcting the underlying cause with footwear, orthoses, calf stretching, and activity modification. Outcomes are good when contributing deformity is addressed, whereas symptoms persist or recur if the mechanical driver, such as a tight gastrocnemius or uncorrected toe deformity, is overlooked. Focal causes have their own prognosis and may require targeted intervention.

Metatarsus adductus — metatarsus varus, forefoot adduction, MTA, hooked forefoot Clubfoot (congenital talipes equinovarus) with associated hindfoot equinus and varus Skewfoot (serpentine foot) with forefoot adduction plus hindfoot valgus Residual forefoot adduction following treated clubfoot Metatarsus primus varus contributing to juvenile hallux valgus Internal tibial torsion producing an in-toeing appearance without a true foot deformity Neuromuscular forefoot deformity in conditions such as cerebral palsy Clinical assessment of forefoot flexibility and the heel bisector angle to grade severity Examination of the hindfoot to exclude equinus and confirm a supple heel Hip examination, with ultrasound or radiography where developmental dysplasia is suspected Standing or simulated weight-bearing foot radiographs reserved for rigid or atypical deformity Assessment of the contralateral foot and lower-limb rotational profile Neurological examination to exclude an underlying neuromuscular cause in rigid or asymmetrical cases The commonest congenital foot deformity of infancy, thought to reflect intrauterine moulding, giving a foot that curves inward at the forefoot while the hindfoot stays neutral The forefoot is adducted and sometimes supinated, producing a C-shaped or bean-shaped lateral border with a prominent base of the fifth metatarsal The heel bisector line normally passes through the second or third toe web; in metatarsus adductus it points more laterally toward the third to fifth toes, grading severity Flexibility is the key clinical distinction: most feet can be passively abducted past the midline (mild) or to the midline (moderate), and only rigid feet resist correction The vast majority resolve spontaneously without any intervention, so reassurance and observation are appropriate for flexible feet There is a recognised association with developmental dysplasia of the hip, so the hips should always be examined and imaged if clinically indicated Serial casting or reverse-last footwear is reserved for feet that remain rigid or fail to improve, and surgery is rarely needed A rigid deformity that cannot be passively corrected, suggesting a structural rather than positional cause Associated hindfoot equinus or varus indicating clubfoot rather than isolated forefoot adduction Concurrent signs of hip dysplasia such as limited abduction or leg-length discrepancy Progressive, painful, or markedly asymmetrical deformity, or features suggesting an underlying neuromuscular disorder Mistaking metatarsus adductus for clubfoot by overlooking the normal, supple hindfoot Failing to examine the hips and thereby missing coexisting developmental dysplasia Overtreating flexible feet that would have resolved with simple observation Delaying casting in the rare truly rigid foot, when earlier intervention is more effective Confusing the condition with skewfoot, in which uncorrected hindfoot valgus needs recognition Metatarsus adductus is a transverse-plane deformity in which the metatarsals deviate medially at the tarsometatarsal joints while the hindfoot remains in normal alignment, distinguishing it from clubfoot which also involves hindfoot equinus and varus. It is generally regarded as a positional or packaging deformity resulting from crowding in utero, although imbalance of the medial soft tissues and abnormal insertion of the tibialis anterior or posterior have been implicated in more rigid forms. The medial soft tissues and the abductor hallucis may be tight, and in persistent cases bony adaptation of the medial cuneiform and metatarsal bases can develop, but the subtalar and ankle joints are typically unaffected. The outlook is excellent, as most flexible cases correct spontaneously within the first year or two of life; even moderate deformity usually responds well to serial casting, and long-term function and comfort are rarely impaired.

Metatropic dysplasia — TRPV4, metatropic dwarfism, hyperplastic dysplasia Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita Kniest dysplasia Diastrophic dysplasia Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia (Kozlowski type) Morquio syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis IV) Fibrochondrogenesis Full skeletal survey to document platyspondyly, dumbbell long bones and metaphyseal flaring TRPV4 molecular genetic testing (targeted or via a skeletal dysplasia panel) Flexion-extension cervical spine imaging to assess atlantoaxial instability Whole-spine imaging and monitoring for progressive kyphoscoliosis Respiratory and sleep assessment where thoracic or cervical involvement threatens ventilation Caused by gain-of-function variants in TRPV4, a calcium-permeable cation channel; most cases are autosomal dominant, frequently arising de novo The name reflects a 'changing' body proportion: relatively long trunk with short limbs at birth that evolves into a short trunk as progressive kyphoscoliosis develops A small coccygeal skin-covered 'tail' overlying an elongated coccyx is a characteristic and highly suggestive external feature Radiographs show severe platyspondyly with dumbbell-shaped shortened long bones due to marked metaphyseal flaring Progressive kyphoscoliosis and cervical spine instability (odontoid hypoplasia, atlantoaxial subluxation) are the dominant clinical problems Presents with a large joints that appear prominent, contractures, and restricted movement; joint hypermobility may coexist The TRPV4 channelopathy spectrum overlaps other skeletal dysplasias (spondylometaphyseal dysplasia Kozlowski type) and neuropathies, so phenotype varies widely Cervical myelopathy or atlantoaxial instability threatening the spinal cord Rapidly progressive kyphoscoliosis with thoracic insufficiency and respiratory compromise New neurological deficit in limbs suggesting cord compression Neonatal respiratory distress in severe early-presenting forms Overlooking cervical instability before sedation, anaesthesia or manipulation, risking cord injury Attributing the changing body proportions to a different evolving dysplasia and missing the diagnosis Failing to recognise the coccygeal appendage as a diagnostic clue Underestimating the pace of scoliosis progression and delaying orthopaedic referral Metatropic dysplasia results from gain-of-function variants in TRPV4, which encodes a widely expressed calcium-permeable transient receptor potential channel important in chondrocyte and osteoblast signalling. Abnormal channel gating disturbs endochondral ossification, producing severe platyspondyly and dumbbell-shaped long bones with exuberant metaphyseal flaring. The progressive nature reflects worsening vertebral collapse and kyphoscoliosis over time, which transforms an initially long trunk into a short trunk. Cervical instability arises from odontoid hypoplasia and ligamentous laxity, posing a risk of cord compression. Outcome depends on severity: milder cases have near-normal survival with orthopaedic morbidity, whereas severe forms cause significant respiratory and neurological compromise from thoracic restriction and cervical instability. Lifelong spinal surveillance is required.

Methanol poisoning — methyl alcohol poisoning, wood alcohol poisoning, methanol toxicity Ethylene glycol poisoning Diabetic ketoacidosis Lactic acidosis from other causes Salicylate poisoning Uraemia and other high anion-gap acidoses Serum methanol and formate levels where available Arterial blood gas and calculated anion gap Serum osmolality with calculated osmolal gap Serum electrolytes, urea, creatinine, and glucose Fundoscopy and formal visual assessment for optic involvement Methanol itself is relatively inert; toxicity comes from hepatic metabolism to formaldehyde and then formic acid, which produces severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis and target-organ injury There is a characteristic latent period of hours (longer if ethanol is co-ingested) before symptoms appear, so early presentation can look deceptively mild Visual symptoms are a hallmark - blurred vision, photophobia, a snowfield or blizzard-like whiteout, and potentially permanent blindness from optic nerve injury Look for a wide anion-gap metabolic acidosis together with a raised osmolal gap; the osmolal gap falls as methanol is metabolised while the anion gap rises Fomepizole is the preferred antidote as it inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase and blocks formation of toxic metabolites; ethanol is an alternative competitive substrate where fomepizole is unavailable Folinic acid (or folic acid) is given to accelerate metabolism of formic acid to carbon dioxide and water Haemodialysis removes methanol and formate and corrects acidosis, and is indicated in severe acidosis, visual impairment, renal failure, or high methanol levels Consider methanol in any unexplained high anion-gap acidosis with visual complaints, particularly after consumption of illicit or adulterated spirits Visual disturbance or reduced acuity signalling optic nerve toxicity and impending blindness Severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis Reduced consciousness, seizures, or coma Rising anion gap with a narrowing osmolal gap indicating ongoing conversion to toxic metabolites Consumption of illicit or home-distilled alcohol in a cluster of patients Being falsely reassured by the asymptomatic latent period, especially with co-ingested ethanol Waiting for a confirmatory methanol level before starting antidote in a strongly suggestive case Overlooking the diagnosis when the osmolal gap has already normalised late in the course Failing to arrange haemodialysis for severe acidosis or visual symptoms Methanol is oxidised by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde, which is rapidly converted by aldehyde dehydrogenase to formic acid. Formic acid is the principal toxin: it inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, causing cellular hypoxia and lactate accumulation, and produces a profound high anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Formate is directly toxic to the retina and optic nerve, causing oedema and demyelination that can lead to irreversible blindness, and can injure the basal ganglia (putaminal necrosis). Because the parent alcohol elevates serum osmolality, an early osmolal gap precedes the later anion-gap acidosis. Outcome depends on the interval to treatment and the depth of acidosis at presentation; early antidote and dialysis can be curative, but delayed treatment risks permanent blindness, neurological deficits, and death.

Methaemoglobinaemia — methemoglobinemia, MetHb, acquired methaemoglobinaemia, congenital methaemoglobinaemia Sulfhaemoglobinaemia Carbon monoxide poisoning Cyanotic congenital heart disease Hypoxaemic respiratory failure Shock or peripheral cyanosis from low cardiac output Co-oximetry to quantify the methaemoglobin fraction Arterial blood gas alongside pulse oximetry to demonstrate the saturation suspected Occurs when haemoglobin iron is oxidised from the ferrous to the ferric state, producing methaemoglobin that cannot bind oxygen and shifts the dissociation curve so remaining oxygen is and tending toward the mid-80s while arterial blood gas calculates a normal partial pressure of oxygen Co-oximetry, not standard oximetry or blood gas calculation, is required to measure the methaemoglobin fraction directly Acquired causes predominate and include oxidant drugs and chemicals such as topical and local anaesthetics, dapsone, nitrites and nitrates, and aniline compounds Congenital forms arise from cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency or from haemoglobin M variants and are usually better tolerated because of chronic adaptation First-line treatment of significant symptomatic acquired disease is methylene blue, which is ineffective and potentially harmful in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, where exchange transfusion or ascorbic acid may be considered Symptomatic hypoxia with high methaemoglobin levels causing altered consciousness, seizures, arrhythmia, or cardiovascular collapse, which is an emergency Cyanosis unresponsive to high-flow oxygen Suspected methaemoglobinaemia in a patient with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, where methylene blue is hazardous Rapidly rising levels after a large oxidant exposure Trusting pulse oximetry or a calculated blood gas saturation instead of measuring methaemoglobin by co-oximetry Persisting with oxygen alone when cyanosis fails to respond Giving methylene blue in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, risking haemolysis and worsening Failing to identify and stop the causative oxidant exposure Haemoglobin normally keeps its iron in the reduced ferrous state, which binds oxygen; a small fraction is continually oxidised to the ferric methaemoglobin form and reduced again, mainly by the cytochrome b5 reductase (NADH-dependent) system. Methaemoglobinaemia develops when oxidative stress from drugs or chemicals overwhelms this reducing capacity, or when the reductase enzyme or the globin chain is congenitally abnormal. Ferric haem cannot carry oxygen, and its presence increases the oxygen affinity of the remaining ferrous haem, impairing oxygen delivery to tissues. The NADPH-dependent methaemoglobin reductase pathway becomes relevant therapeutically because methylene blue acts through it, which is why it fails when glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is deficient. Acquired disease usually resolves well once the offending agent is removed and, where needed, methylene blue is given; congenital reductase deficiency is generally compatible with normal life, whereas very high acute levels can be fatal without prompt treatment.

Methionine adenosyltransferase I/III deficiency — MAT I/III deficiency, MAT deficiency, hepatic methionine adenosyltransferase deficiency, S-adenosylmethionine synthetase deficiency, isolated persistent hypermethioninaemia, MAT1A Classical homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency), which also raises methionine but with homocystinuria Glycine N-methyltransferase deficiency S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency Adenosine kinase deficiency Hypermethioninaemia secondary to liver disease or high methionine/protein intake Tyrosinaemia type 1 with secondary hypermethioninaemia Plasma amino acids demonstrating isolated raised methionine Plasma total homocysteine to exclude homocystinuria S-adenosylmethionine and S-adenosylhomocysteine measurement to distinguish related disorders Liver function tests to exclude hepatic causes MAT1A gene sequencing for confirmation Brain MRI in the rare cases with neurological signs to assess for demyelination Caused by variants in MAT1A affecting the liver-specific isoenzymes (MAT I and MAT III) that convert methionine to S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) The commonest cause of isolated persistent hypermethioninaemia and a frequent incidental finding on newborn screening Most individuals are clinically well; the biochemical abnormality is usually benign and does not require intervention Reduced SAM production, with an elevated methionine but normal or low SAM, helps separate it from GNMT deficiency where SAM is high A distinctive boiled-cabbage or sulphurous breath odour may occur from dimethyl sulfide when methionine is very high Rare individuals with severe biallelic disease can develop neurological signs and central demyelination, attributed to SAM deficiency Inheritance is usually autosomal recessive for the severe forms and autosomal dominant for the common mild elevation Where treatment is considered in severe cases it is generic, such as a moderately methionine-restricted diet or SAM supplementation Emerging neurological signs or developmental regression suggesting a severe biallelic form with demyelination Very high plasma methionine sustained over time Failure of methionine to normalise, prompting search for an alternative diagnosis Coexisting hepatic dysfunction pointing to a different or additional cause Mislabelling isolated hypermethioninaemia as classical homocystinuria and imposing unnecessary treatment Failing to check homocysteine and SAM/SAH, which are needed to place the disorder correctly Over-restricting methionine in a well child, risking deficiency of an essential amino acid Assuming all cases are benign without excluding the rare severe form when neurological signs appear Methionine adenosyltransferase catalyses the first step of methionine metabolism, forming S-adenosylmethionine, the principal biological methyl donor. MAT1A encodes the isoenzymes expressed mainly in the liver; when their activity is reduced, methionine is not efficiently converted and accumulates in blood, while hepatic SAM formation falls. Because MAT II activity in other tissues is preserved, most methylation reactions continue and patients are typically asymptomatic. In the uncommon severe forms, marked SAM deficiency in the nervous system is thought to impair myelin methylation reactions, giving rise to demyelination and neurological features. The great majority have an entirely benign course with normal development and lifespan; only the rare severe biallelic forms carry a risk of neurological impairment, which may improve with dietary or SAM treatment.

and lethargy, often during catabolic illness Characteristic acylcarnitine finding is elevated 3-hydroxyisovalerylcarnitine (C5-OH), which flags it on screening Urine organic acids show raised Metabolic acidosis with hyperammonaemia and encephalopathy during illness Hypoglycaemia with lethargy in a catabolic child Severe carnitine depletion with hypotonia or cardiac concern Reye-like deterioration during intercurrent infection or fasting Recurrent unexplained vomiting and decompensation Over-treating or over-restricting asymptomatic screen-positive infants given the low penetrance Failing to consider maternal 3-MCC deficiency when a healthy infant screens positive Missing symptomatic decompensation by assuming the condition is always benign Overlooking secondary carnitine depletion Allowing prolonged perioperative or illness-related fasting without an emergency plan 3-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase is a biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme that catalyses a step in the degradation of leucine, converting 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA to 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA. Deficiency, from defects in either the alpha (MCCC1) or beta (MCCC2) subunit, blocks leucine catabolism so that 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA is diverted to 3-methylcrotonylglycine and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid, which accumulate and are excreted. The conjugation of these metabolites with carnitine and glycine can deplete free carnitine. Although the biochemical defect is consistent, clinical expression is highly variable and often benign, so it is regarded as a condition of low and unpredictable penetrance. During catabolic stress a minority develop a Reye-like metabolic crisis with acidosis and hyperammonaemia. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The great majority of individuals identified are asymptomatic with a normal outlook; a minority experience metabolic crises, and with fasting avoidance and carnitine supplementation the prognosis is generally good.

with vitamin B12 (hydroxocobalamin), so a cofactor trial is standard Chronic management principles are a protein-restricted diet limiting propiogenic amino acids, carnitine supplementation and avoidance of catabolism, with metronidazole sometimes used to reduce gut propionate production Detectable through newborn screening by elevated C3 acylcarnitine, prompting confirmatory testing Acute metabolic decompensation with severe high-anion-gap acidosis is a life-threatening emergency Hyperammonaemia with encephalopathy accompanying an acidotic crisis Rapid deterioration during intercurrent illness, fasting or increased protein catabolism Progressive renal impairment or acute basal ganglia injury with a new movement disorder Attributing an acidotic, unwell neonate to sepsis and delaying metabolic investigation Failing to trial and document vitamin B12 responsiveness Overlooking evolving chronic kidney disease during long-term follow-up Under-treating catabolism during intercurrent illness, allowing preventable decompensation Methylmalonic acidemia results from a block in the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, a step catalysed by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase using adenosylcobalamin. This reaction lies on the final common pathway for catabolism of the branched-chain amino acids isoleucine and valine, methionine, threonine, odd-chain fatty acids and cholesterol side chains. Enzyme deficiency or impaired cofactor synthesis causes methylmalonic acid and related organic acids to accumulate, producing severe metabolic acidosis. These metabolites inhibit ureagenesis (causing secondary hyperammonaemia) and mitochondrial energy metabolism, are toxic to bone marrow and renal tubules, and injure the basal ganglia during decompensation. Prognosis varies by subtype; cobalamin-responsive forms generally do better, whereas mutase-deficient disease carries significant risk of recurrent metabolic crises, chronic kidney disease and neurological injury, and severe cases may require kidney or combined liver-kidney transplantation. Early screening detection and meticulous metabolic control improve outcomes.
