impairment, ataxia or visual loss suggesting mevalonic aciduria Failure to thrive with recurrent crises in infancy Signs of macrophage activation syndrome during a severe flare Excluding the diagnosis because serum IgD is normal Missing the raised urinary mevalonic acid by sampling only between attacks Overlooking the risk of secondary amyloidosis with chronic inflammation Failing to distinguish the severe (mevalonic aciduria) form, which needs broader multisystem care Mevalonate kinase deficiency results from biallelic variants in MVK that reduce the activity of mevalonate kinase, an enzyme of the isoprenoid biosynthetic pathway downstream of HMG-CoA reductase. Impaired production of non-sterol isoprenoids, particularly geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, disrupts prenylation of small GTPases and activates the inflammasome, driving excess interleukin-1 beta release. The degree of residual enzyme activity determines whether the phenotype is the milder periodic fever (hyper-IgD) syndrome or severe mevalonic aciduria. The milder periodic fever form tends to improve with age but can be complicated by secondary amyloidosis if inflammation is poorly controlled. Mevalonic aciduria carries a poor prognosis with significant neurodevelopmental disability and early mortality; IL-1 blockade can substantially reduce flare frequency.

alongside supportive care Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and cataracts and progressive neurological impairment can occur in severe cases British spelling applies (hyperimmunoglobulinaemia, tumour) Severe recurrent inflammatory crises with dehydration and systemic compromise Progressive neurological deterioration, ataxia, or developmental regression Failure to thrive with hepatosplenomegaly in infancy Visual impairment from cataract formation Attributing recurrent fevers to infection alone and missing an autoinflammatory metabolic cause Not sampling urine organic acids during a crisis when mevalonic acid excretion peaks Overlooking the neurodevelopmental and ophthalmological complications of severe disease Failing to anticipate vaccination or infection as attack triggers Mevalonate kinase phosphorylates mevalonate, an early committed step in the biosynthesis of cholesterol and non-sterol isoprenoids. Severe deficiency causes mevalonic acid to accumulate and be excreted in large amounts, while downstream isoprenoid products, including those needed for protein prenylation (such as geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate), are relatively depleted. Reduced prenylation of small regulatory proteins is believed to activate inflammasome-driven interleukin-1 production, explaining the recurrent autoinflammatory fevers. The combination of substrate accumulation and deficient isoprenoid end-products underlies both the systemic inflammation and the neurodevelopmental and dysmorphic features of the severe form. The severe mevalonic aciduria form carries significant morbidity and mortality, with recurrent crises, neurological impairment, and failure to thrive, whereas the milder periodic fever phenotype has a better outlook. Interleukin-1-directed therapy has improved control of inflammatory attacks.

MGAT2-CDG (CDG-IIa) — MGAT2, GnT-II deficiency, N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase II deficiency, congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIa, CDG-IIa Other type II CDG subtypes (e.g. TMEM165-CDG, B4GALT1-CDG, COG-complex CDG, SLC35A2-CDG) Type I CDG subtypes when the transferrin pattern is ambiguous Chromosomal and other syndromic causes of dysmorphism with developmental delay Primary immunodeficiency with recurrent infection Inherited coagulation disorders Mitochondrial disease in infancy Transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry demonstrating a type II pattern MGAT2 molecular genetic testing N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase II enzyme activity assay Coagulation profile and immunoglobulin levels Neuroimaging and electroencephalography Skeletal survey and dysmorphology assessment A prototypical N-linked type II CDG caused by deficiency of Golgi N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase II, which blocks conversion of hybrid to complex N-glycans Presents in infancy with dysmorphism, developmental delay, hypotonia and seizures rather than the peripheral neuropathy and cerebellar hypoplasia characteristic of type I disease Recurrent infections and a bleeding tendency reflect hypoglycosylation of immune and coagulation proteins Skeletal and facial dysmorphic features are common, and gastrointestinal problems may occur Because the defect is in glycan processing, transferrin isoelectric focusing shows a type II pattern (increased mono- and asialotransferrin from truncated antennae) Management is supportive and multidisciplinary; no specific dietary or enzyme therapy alters the underlying defect Confirmed by MGAT2 sequencing supported by enzyme assay in leucocytes or fibroblasts Recurrent or severe infections suggesting significant immune dysfunction Unexplained bleeding from coagulation factor hypoglycosylation Progressive encephalopathy or refractory seizures Failure to thrive with multi-organ involvement Assuming a type II transferrin pattern excludes CDG when the clinical picture differs from classic PMM2-CDG Failing to distinguish type I from type II defects, which alters the candidate gene list Overlooking immunodeficiency and bleeding risk in perioperative planning Interpreting an isolated enzyme result without molecular confirmation MGAT2 encodes N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase II, a Golgi enzyme that adds a second N-acetylglucosamine branch during maturation of N-glycans from hybrid to biantennary complex structures. Deficiency arrests processing after the oligosaccharide has already been transferred to protein, so the glycan chains are structurally truncated rather than absent. This defines a type II disorder, distinguishable from type I assembly defects by the transferrin isoform pattern on isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry. Truncated complex glycans impair function of many secreted and membrane glycoproteins, producing the multisystem phenotype. MGAT2-CDG causes significant and lasting neurodevelopmental disability; life expectancy is variable and depends on the severity of infections, bleeding and other systemic complications. There is no treatment that corrects the enzymatic defect.

directly by flow cytometry Missing cryptosporidial infection and evolving sclerosing cholangitis Giving live vaccines or non-irradiated blood products before diagnosis MHC class II deficiency results from loss-of-function variants in the transcriptional regulators that drive HLA class II gene expression, most often CIITA, RFX5, RFXAP or RFXANK, rather than from defects in the HLA loci themselves. Without these regulators, class II molecules are not expressed on antigen-presenting cells, so peptides cannot be presented to CD4 T cells; positive selection of CD4 thymocytes fails, causing profound CD4 lymphopenia, and mature CD4 cells cannot be activated. The lack of effective CD4 help cripples antibody production and cell-mediated immunity, yielding a combined immunodeficiency with susceptibility to a broad range of viral, bacterial, fungal and protozoal pathogens. The natural history is poor with early mortality from infection and hepatobiliary disease; allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offers the only cure but survival is lower than for several other combined immunodeficiencies, underlining the value of early diagnosis.

Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia — MAHA Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (including atypical) Disseminated intravascular coagulation Malignant hypertension Pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome Disseminated malignancy or mechanical valve haemolysis Blood film for schistocytes and platelet count Direct antiglobulin test (negative in MAHA) Coagulation screen and fibrinogen to assess for DIC Renal function and blood pressure Cause-specific tests (ADAMTS13, complement studies, pregnancy assessment) A mechanical (non-immune) haemolysis in which red cells are fragmented as they pass through abnormal small vessels The blood film hallmark is schistocytes (red cell fragments) with features of haemolysis and often thrombocytopenia The direct antiglobulin test is negative, distinguishing it from immune haemolysis It is a syndrome, not a single disease, and the key task is to identify the underlying cause Thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP, haemolytic uraemic syndrome) are urgent causes requiring specific treatment Other causes include disseminated intravascular coagulation, malignant hypertension, pre-eclampsia/HELLP, disseminated cancer and mechanical heart valves Thrombocytopenia with neurological or renal features suggesting a thrombotic microangiopathy Rapidly rising creatinine Pregnancy with hypertension and haemolysis (HELLP) Evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation Missing thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, a medical emergency, by delaying ADAMTS13 testing and plasma exchange Attributing MAHA to immune haemolysis despite a negative antiglobulin test Overlooking pregnancy-related causes Failing to search systematically for the underlying cause Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia results from physical shearing of red cells within the microcirculation or across abnormal surfaces. In thrombotic microangiopathies, platelet-rich or fibrin thrombi partially occlude small vessels, and red cells passing through are fragmented into schistocytes. Similar fragmentation occurs across fibrin strands in disseminated intravascular coagulation, in vessels damaged by malignant hypertension or vasculitis, or across prosthetic valves. Because the process is mechanical, the antiglobulin test is negative, and consumption of platelets is common in thrombotic causes. Prognosis depends entirely on the cause; thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is rapidly fatal untreated but responds to prompt plasma exchange, whereas other causes require treatment of the underlying process.

Microcornea — small cornea Microphthalmos or nanophthalmos Anterior segment dysgenesis syndromes Congenital glaucoma (which enlarges the cornea, the opposite finding) Sclerocornea Syndromic associations (for example with cataract or coloboma) Measurement of corneal diameter and axial length to distinguish from microphthalmos Refraction and cycloplegic assessment Gonioscopy and intraocular pressure for glaucoma risk Assessment for associated ocular and systemic anomalies Amblyopia evaluation in children A congenitally small cornea (reduced horizontal diameter) in an eye that is otherwise of relatively normal size It is distinct from microphthalmos, in which the whole globe is small, and from nanophthalmos The cornea is usually clear and often flatter than normal, tending toward hyperopia It may be isolated or associated with other anterior segment anomalies and syndromes There is an increased long-term risk of angle-closure and other glaucoma Management centres on refractive correction, amblyopia treatment and lifelong glaucoma surveillance Signs of angle-closure or other glaucoma Associated cataract, coloboma or dysgenesis Amblyopia in childhood Syndromic features Confusing microcornea with microphthalmos Overlooking the elevated glaucoma risk Neglecting amblyopia management Missing associated anterior segment or systemic anomalies Microcornea arises from arrest of corneal growth in the fifth month of gestation or from overgrowth of the surrounding optic cup rim, producing a cornea of reduced diameter. The small, often flat cornea reduces refractive power, typically causing hyperopia, and the associated crowded anterior segment anatomy predisposes to angle-closure glaucoma. It can occur in isolation or as part of anterior segment dysgenesis and various systemic syndromes, reflecting shared developmental pathways. Isolated microcornea generally has good vision with refractive correction; the main long-term concern is glaucoma, and prognosis worsens with associated anomalies.

excision, leading to recurrence Ignoring perineural symptoms that signal deep nerve involvement Microcystic adnexal carcinoma is a malignant adnexal tumour displaying dual follicular and sweat-duct (eccrine) differentiation. It is characterised by a striking zonation: the superficial portion comprises bland keratin-filled microcysts and small basaloid nests, while the deeper portion consists of infiltrating cords and ductal structures set in a dense sclerotic stroma. The tumour extends far beyond its apparent clinical borders, tracks along nerves (perineural invasion), and may invade underlying muscle, cartilage, and bone. This discrepancy between an indolent appearance and aggressive infiltrative local behaviour underlies both the frequent misdiagnosis on superficial biopsy and the high rate of local recurrence when margins are inadequate. The tumour rarely metastasises but is notorious for extensive subclinical local infiltration and perineural spread, giving a high local recurrence rate after conventional excision; margin-controlled surgery substantially reduces recurrence, and long-term follow-up is required.

Many infants respond to early androgen therapy with satisfactory penile growth and can expect adequate adult size and function; the overall outlook is dictated by the underlying cause, with fertility potential depending on whether the defect is central, gonadal, or in androgen action.

Microphthalmia and anophthalmia — MAC spectrum, microphthalmia-anophthalmia-coloboma, SOX2, OTX2, clinical anophthalmia Isolated coloboma at the milder end of the MAC spectrum Cryptophthalmos and other eyelid or orbital malformations Congenital cystic eye or orbital cyst Phthisis bulbi from an acquired process mimicking a small eye Nanophthalmos and posterior microphthalmos with a normal external appearance Syndromic associations such as CHARGE syndrome Detailed ophthalmic examination and measurement of axial length by ocular biometry Orbital and cranial imaging (ultrasound, CT or MRI) to confirm the presence and size of ocular tissue Systemic and neurodevelopmental assessment, including for pituitary and brain anomalies Chromosomal and molecular genetic testing including SOX2 and OTX2 Assessment of the fellow eye and orbit to guide prosthetic and reconstructive planning Microphthalmia is an abnormally small, disorganised eye, whereas anophthalmia is the complete absence of ocular tissue; the two lie on a continuous spectrum Both often coexist with coloboma as part of the microphthalmia-anophthalmia-coloboma (MAC) spectrum Presentation ranges from an obviously small or absent eye to a clinically normal-looking eye with reduced axial length (nanophthalmos or posterior microphthalmos) Frequently syndromic, with SOX2 and OTX2 among the most important causative genes, and association with chromosomal and multisystem disorders Can be caused by genetic, chromosomal or environmental (including gestational infective and teratogenic) factors, so a broad aetiological workup is needed True clinical anophthalmia is confirmed only when imaging shows no ocular tissue, as a rudimentary globe may be hidden Early involvement of ocularists and orbital specialists supports socket and facial growth in severe cases Bilateral severe microphthalmia or anophthalmia implying profound visual impairment Associated neurological, endocrine or systemic anomalies requiring urgent evaluation Progressive orbital or facial asymmetry from impaired socket growth Family history indicating a heritable cause needing genetic counselling Diagnosing anophthalmia clinically without imaging to exclude hidden rudimentary ocular tissue Overlooking associated brain, pituitary or systemic anomalies Delaying socket expansion and prosthetic management, impairing orbital and facial development Assuming a normal-appearing eye excludes posterior microphthalmos without biometry Microphthalmia and anophthalmia arise from disturbance of early eye morphogenesis. Normal eye formation depends on outgrowth of the optic vesicle from the developing forebrain and its invagination to form the optic cup, guided by a network of transcription factors including SOX2 and OTX2. Mutations in these developmental genes, chromosomal abnormalities, or environmental insults during embryogenesis can halt or distort this process, so the eye fails to grow to normal size (microphthalmia) or fails to develop at all (anophthalmia). Because the same signalling controls closure of the optic fissure, coloboma frequently coexists, and because these genes act in other tissues, associated brain, pituitary and systemic anomalies are common. Visual prognosis depends on the severity and laterality of the malformation, ranging from useful vision in mild unilateral microphthalmia to no vision in bilateral anophthalmia; in severe cases the focus shifts to promoting orbital and facial growth with expanders and prostheses, and overall outcome is strongly influenced by associated systemic conditions.

suggesting diffuse alveolar haemorrhage Progressive sensorimotor deficits from mononeuritis multiplex Oliguria or dialysis-requiring acute kidney injury Widespread purpura with systemic deterioration Delaying biopsy and treatment while awaiting ANCA serology in a deteriorating patient Failing to distinguish MPA from anti-GBM disease, which alters urgency and use of plasma exchange Overlooking alveolar haemorrhage when haemoptysis is minimal but haemoglobin falls Attributing pauci-immune crescentic nephritis to another cause without checking ANCA Microscopic polyangiitis is a systemic pauci-immune small-vessel vasculitis within the ANCA-associated spectrum. Circulating anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies prime and activate neutrophils, which adhere to and degranulate against endothelium, releasing reactive oxygen species and proteolytic enzymes that produce necrotising inflammation of capillaries, venules, and arterioles. In the kidney this yields a focal segmental necrotising and crescentic glomerulonephritis with minimal immunoglobulin deposition, and in the lung it can cause alveolar capillaritis with haemorrhage. Unlike granulomatosis with polyangiitis, granuloma formation is characteristically absent. Prompt immunosuppression induces remission in most patients, but many are left with chronic kidney disease and some progress to end-stage renal failure. Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage and advanced renal impairment at presentation predict worse outcomes.

Microspherophakia — spherophakia Weill-Marchesani syndrome Marfan syndrome and other causes of ectopia lentis Homocystinuria Isolated ectopia lentis Primary angle-closure glaucoma of other cause Slit-lamp assessment of lens size, shape and position Refraction demonstrating lenticular myopia Gonioscopy and intraocular pressure for angle-closure risk Assessment for systemic features of Weill-Marchesani or other syndromes Family history and genetic evaluation where indicated A developmental anomaly in which the crystalline lens is small and abnormally spherical The increased lens curvature causes marked lenticular myopia The spherical lens and weak zonules predispose to lens subluxation and to pupillary-block glaucoma It may be isolated or part of Weill-Marchesani syndrome and other connective tissue disorders Pupillary block can be paradoxically worsened by miotic drugs and improved by cycloplegics, which is important for management Careful glaucoma management and lens surgery in selected cases are the mainstays Acute angle-closure (pupillary block) glaucoma Lens subluxation or dislocation Worsening pressure after miotic use Systemic features of a connective tissue syndrome Giving miotics for glaucoma, which worsen pupillary block in spherophakia Missing associated Weill-Marchesani or homocystinuria Overlooking lens subluxation Attributing high myopia solely to axial length Microspherophakia results from arrested lens development leaving a small, highly curved (spherical) lens with attenuated or abnormal zonules. The increased curvature produces high myopia, and the lax zonules allow the lens to move anteriorly. Anterior movement of the spherical lens can obstruct the pupil, causing pupillary-block angle-closure glaucoma; miotics worsen this by relaxing the zonule and allowing further forward lens movement, whereas cycloplegics tighten the zonule and pull the lens back. Zonular weakness also predisposes to frank lens subluxation. With appropriate refractive correction and glaucoma management the prognosis can be reasonable, but recurrent pupillary block and lens dislocation may necessitate surgery and carry risk to vision.

Giardiasis HIV enteropathy Cytomegalovirus enterocolitis Stool microscopy with chromotrope (modified trichrome) staining for spores Calcofluor white or immunofluorescent staining of faecal smears Molecular PCR with species identification Small-bowel biopsy with electron microscopy when stool testing is inconclusive HIV testing and CD4 count Urine, corneal scrapings or other specimens when dissemination is suspected Microsporidia are spore-forming, obligate intracellular organisms now classified with the fungi, transmitted by ingesting or inhaling environmentally resistant spores Enterocytozoon bieneusi and Encephalitozoon intestinalis are the commonest species causing chronic, watery, non-bloody diarrhoea and wasting in people with advanced HIV The infection came to prominence as an AIDS-defining cause of intractable diarrhoea before widespread antiretroviral therapy Encephalitozoon species can disseminate beyond the gut to cause keratoconjunctivitis, sinusitis, hepatitis, nephritis and encephalitis, unlike the largely enteric E. bieneusi Diagnosis relies on detecting the small spores in stool or biopsy using chromotrope-based (modified trichrome) stains that colour the spores pinkish-red against a pale background, or with calcofluor and immunofluorescence Albendazole is effective against Encephalitozoon species, whereas E. bieneusi responds poorly and is better managed with fumagillin where available Immune reconstitution with antiretroviral therapy is the most important measure for durable resolution in HIV-associated disease Chronic dehydrating diarrhoea with severe wasting in advanced HIV Visual symptoms suggesting microsporidial keratoconjunctivitis Features of disseminated disease such as renal, hepatic or neurological involvement Failure of enteric symptoms to settle despite species-directed therapy Missing the tiny spores because routine stool microscopy lacks a chromotrope or fluorescent stain Treating all species with albendazole and expecting response, when Enterocytozoon bieneusi responds poorly Overlooking extraintestinal sites such as the eye in disseminated Encephalitozoon infection Neglecting antiretroviral therapy, without which relapse is likely Microsporidia are unicellular, obligate intracellular organisms that infect host cells by explosively everting a coiled polar tubule, through which the sporoplasm is injected into the cytoplasm. Intracellular multiplication culminates in the release of resistant spores that are shed in stool, urine or respiratory secretions and transmit infection. In the gut, infection of enterocytes causes villous atrophy, epithelial disarray and malabsorption with a secretory diarrhoea. Effective control depends on cell-mediated immunity, so heavy chronic infection and dissemination to eye, sinuses, liver, kidney and central nervous system occur predominantly in profound immunosuppression such as advanced HIV. In immunocompetent hosts infection is usually mild and self-limiting; in advanced HIV it can be chronic and disabling, though outcomes improved markedly with immune reconstitution and species-directed therapy.

intestinal transplantation Antenatal or early genetic diagnosis is valuable given the severity and lifelong nutritional dependence Profound dehydration and haemodynamic instability from massive fluid loss in the neonatal period Severe electrolyte and acid-base derangement requiring intensive correction Failure of diarrhoea to abate on complete bowel rest, indicating a secretory process Emerging cholestatic liver disease during long-term parenteral nutrition Mistaking the persistent secretory diarrhoea for infection and delaying biopsy and genetic testing Attributing the picture to feed intolerance and repeatedly changing formulas rather than investigating for a congenital enteropathy Failing to obtain electron microscopy, which is often required to identify the diagnostic inclusions Overlooking parenteral-nutrition-associated cholestasis and catheter-related complications during long-term care Microvillus inclusion disease arises from defective apical trafficking within the enterocyte. Loss-of-function variants in MYO5B (and less often STX3 or STXBP2) disrupt the myosin Vb-mediated recycling of apical membrane and transporter proteins to the brush border. The result is failure to assemble a normal apical microvillus surface, with brush-border components mislocalised into cytoplasmic vesicles and microvillus inclusions. Because functional transporters and the absorptive surface are lost, the intestine cannot reabsorb fluid and electrolytes, producing a severe secretory diarrhoea that continues even when enteral feeds are withheld. The classic early-onset form carries a guarded prognosis with lifelong dependence on parenteral nutrition and its complications; intestinal or combined transplantation offers the main prospect of enteral autonomy. Milder late-onset phenotypes may be managed with prolonged nutritional support.

middle lobe syndrome — right middle lobe syndrome, Brock syndrome endobronchial carcinoma or carcinoid tumour broncholithiasis obstructing the middle lobe bronchus aspirated foreign body non-tuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary infection bronchiectasis from other causes extrinsic nodal compression from sarcoidosis, tuberculosis or malignancy recurrent aspiration or asthma-related mucus plugging chest CT with attention to the middle lobe bronchus, nodes and bronchiectasis flexible bronchoscopy to exclude obstruction and obtain samples sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage for bacteria, mycobacteria and fungi cytology or biopsy of any endobronchial lesion pulmonary function testing and assessment for asthma evaluation for impaired mucociliary clearance or immunodeficiency in recurrent disease tuberculin or interferon-gamma release testing where granulomatous disease is suspected Middle lobe syndrome denotes recurrent or chronic collapse, consolidation or bronchiectasis of the right middle lobe, and by extension the lingula. Anatomical predisposition is central: the right middle lobe bronchus is long and narrow, arises at an acute angle, and is surrounded by a collar of lymph nodes, with relatively poor collateral ventilation to the lobe. It is classified into obstructive forms (endobronchial tumour, broncholith, extrinsic nodal compression, foreign body) and non-obstructive forms (recurrent infection, asthma, impaired clearance). In adults, a persistently collapsed middle lobe must prompt exclusion of an endobronchial neoplasm before it is assumed to be benign. In children and non-smokers, asthma, recurrent infection and impaired mucociliary clearance are common non-obstructive causes. Presentation includes chronic cough, recurrent focal pneumonia, wheeze and haemoptysis, or it may be an incidental radiographic finding. The lateral chest radiograph shows a characteristic thin, wedge-shaped opacity overlying the cardiac shadow; CT delineates bronchiectasis, volume loss and any obstructing lesion. Bronchoscopy is central to excluding an obstructing lesion and obtaining microbiological and cytological samples; non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection (the 'Lady Windermere' pattern) is an important association. haemoptysis or an endobronchial lesion suggesting malignancy persistent lobar collapse in an adult smoker systemic features such as weight loss or night sweats recurrent pneumonia confined to the same lobe despite treatment progressive bronchiectasis with worsening sputum burden Assuming benign disease and omitting bronchoscopy in an adult with a persistently collapsed middle lobe. Overlooking non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection as both cause and consequence of the syndrome. Missing a small obstructing broncholith or foreign body on low-resolution imaging. Attributing recurrent focal pneumonia to simple community infection without pursuing the anatomical explanation. Proceeding to resection without adequately characterising and treating a reversible infective or inflammatory cause. The right middle lobe is anatomically vulnerable: its bronchus is comparatively long and slender, branches at an acute angle from the bronchus intermedius, and is encircled by hilar and interlobar lymph nodes, while collateral ventilation from adjacent lobes is limited because the lobe is largely surrounded by fissures. Any process that narrows the bronchus — an endobronchial tumour, broncholith, aspirated foreign body, or extrinsic compression by enlarged nodes — readily produces atelectasis with impaired clearance and post-obstructive infection. In non-obstructive disease, recurrent infection, asthma or ciliary and clearance defects lead to mucus retention and repeated inflammation; because collateral ventilation cannot easily re-expand the lobe, atelectasis persists and a cycle of infection, inflammation and bronchial wall damage ensues, culminating in bronchiectasis and chronic volume loss. Non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection may both result from and perpetuate this process, classically in the middle lobe and lingula. Non-obstructive disease often improves with treatment of infection, airway inflammation and clearance, whereas established bronchiectasis or an obstructing lesion may require targeted therapy or surgical resection; outcome is generally good once malignancy is excluded and the underlying cause addressed.

Migraine — Clinical diagnosis (POUND criteria) Neuroimaging only if red flags New focal deficit, thunderclap onset, or fever → exclude secondary cause Tension-type headache - the main differential; distinguished by being completely featureless (no nausea/vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia, throbbing or aggravation with movement), whereas migraine has one or more of these (p.3471). Cluster headache and other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (p.3462). Acephalgic migraine / typical aura without headache - recurrent neurologic symptoms with little or no headache (p.3464). Vestibular migraine - common, underdiagnosed cause of episodic vertigo lasting minutes to hours, sometimes without headache (p.3464). Migraine with brainstem aura (formerly basilar/basilar-type migraine) (p.3464). Medication-overuse headache complicating an underlying migraine tendency (p.115-116). Bacterial/viral meningitis - acute severe headache with stiff neck and fever; can be mistaken for migraine because pounding headache, photophobia, nausea and vomiting are shared cardinal features, and there is often striking accentuation of pain on eye movement; lumbar puncture is mandatory (p.113-114). Migraine is a clinical diagnosis in patients with a normal examination and no other reasonable cause for headache (Table 441-3, p.3466). A headache diary aids diagnosis and quantifies disability and attack frequency (p.3462). The Migraine Disability Assessment Score (MIDAS) is a validated tool to grade disability (p.3465). CT or MRI of the brain (equally sensitive as initial screen for intracranial pathology) is indicated for an abnormal neurologic examination or recent-onset headache; lumbar puncture may additionally be required when a benign cause cannot otherwise be established (p.113). General acute-headache workup may include palpation of cranial arteries, assessment of the cervical spine, blood pressure and urine examination, and funduscopy with intraocular pressure measurement (p.113). Subarachnoid hemorrhage / ruptured aneurysm, AVM or intraparenchymal hemorrhage - thunderclap headache maximal in under 5 min lasting over 5 min, stiff neck without fever; CT may rarely be normal so LP may be needed (p.114). Brain tumor - intermittent deep dull aching, may worsen with exertion or position change and cause nausea/vomiting; vomiting preceding headache by weeks is highly characteristic of posterior fossa tumors (p.114). Temporal (giant cell) arteritis - dull/boring headache with superimposed stabbing pains, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, polymyalgia, fever, weight loss in patients over ~50; migraineurs may report relief with prednisone, confounding interpretation of treatment response (p.114-115). Acute angle-closure glaucoma - prostrating headache with nausea/vomiting beginning with severe eye pain; red eye with a fixed, mid-dilated pupil (p.115). Transient ischemic attack / vertebrobasilar insufficiency - acute homonymous visual symptoms with fogging/graying and positive phenomena that can mimic migraine aura (p.230). Ischemic stroke - migraine can mimic stroke even without prior migraine history, especially acephalgic migraine (p.3429). Migraine is the second most common cause of headache and the leading neurologic cause of disability worldwide; over a 1-year period it affects roughly 15% of women and 6% of men (p.3462). An attack classically evolves through three phases - premonitory (prodrome), headache, and postdrome - and only about 20-25% of patients also experience an aura phase (p.3462). Premonitory symptoms (yawning, sleepiness, fatigue, cognitive 'fog', mood change, neck discomfort, polyuria/polydipsia, food cravings) can begin hours to days before the pain; some apparent 'triggers' such as light sensitivity may actually be part of this early phase rather than true precipitants (p.3462). Postdromal tiredness, poor concentration and mild neck discomfort can persist for hours and occasionally up to a day after the pain settles (p.3462). Simplified diagnostic criteria require repeated attacks of headache lasting 4-72 h with a normal examination and no other reasonable cause, plus at least 2 of (unilateral, throbbing, aggravated by movement, moderate/severe) and at least 1 of (nausea/vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia) (Table 441-3, p.3466). Cranial autonomic symptoms (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, periorbital swelling, ptosis) can occur in migraine - even in children - and may be mistaken for sinus disease, leading to overdiagnosis of sinusitis and inappropriate treatment (p.114). Migraine is a brain disorder, not a 'vascular headache'; vascular changes when present are secondary, driven by cranial parasympathetic activation, and treatment response cannot be predicted by vascular effects (p.114). The vast majority of patients presenting with severe headache have a benign cause, most often migraine; brain tumor is a rare cause of isolated headache and an even rarer cause of severe pain (p.114). Migraineurs do not encounter more stress than headache-free people; the problem is overresponsiveness to changes in stress, and they are characteristically sensitive to environmental/sensory stimuli, failing to habituate easily (p.3462, p.3508). Vertigo can be a prominent migraine feature - about one-third of patients referred for vertigo/dizziness have a primary diagnosis of migraine (vestibular migraine) (p.3464). Sudden-onset (thunderclap) headache or first/worst-ever severe headache (p.114). Vomiting that precedes the headache (p.114). Subacute worsening over days or weeks (p.114). Pain induced by bending, lifting or cough (p.114). Pain that disturbs sleep or is present immediately on awakening (p.114). New headache in a patient with a known systemic illness (e.g., malignancy) (p.114). Onset after age 55 (p.114). Fever or unexplained systemic signs (p.114). Abnormal neurologic examination (p.114). Pain with local tenderness, e.g., over the temporal artery (p.114). Mistaking migraine-related cranial autonomic symptoms for sinusitis, leading to overdiagnosis and inappropriate sinus treatment (p.114). Misdiagnosing meningitis as migraine (or vice versa) because pounding headache, photophobia, nausea and vomiting overlap - hence LP is mandatory when fever and stiff neck are present (p.113-114). Attributing a steroid-responsive headache in an elderly patient to giant cell arteritis when migraine (far more prevalent in the elderly) also improves with prednisone (p.115). Treating headache from a reawakened migraine syndrome (e.g., after otologic or endodontic procedures) without first addressing the primary problem - the headache stays refractory until the cause is treated (p.113). Failing to recognize acephalgic migraine, which can present de novo even after age 65 and is easily confused with stroke; the sensory/motor deficit migrates slowly across a limb over minutes (versus seconds in stroke) (p.3429). Continuing acute analgesics while starting a preventive - a common cause of treatment failure and of medication-overuse headache (p.115-116). Migraine is understood as a brain disorder of sensory processing rather than a primary vascular disease. The characteristic sensory sensitivity is attributed to dysfunction of monoaminergic and other sensory-control systems in the brainstem and hypothalamus. The key nociceptive pathway is the trigeminovascular system: trigeminal innervation of large intracranial vessels and dura, with terminals that, when activated, release vasoactive neuropeptides - notably calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) - at vascular terminals and within the trigeminal nucleus. Second-order neurons of the trigeminocervical complex (caudal trigeminal nucleus extending into the upper cervical dorsal horns, receiving C1-C2 input) decussate and project via the quintothalamic tract to ventrobasal and posterior thalamic nuclei, with additional projections to periaqueductal gray and hypothalamus that exert descending antinociceptive modulation; the dorsal raphe nucleus, locus coeruleus, parabrachial nucleus and rostroventromedial medulla are implicated in this modulation. Serotonin (5-HT) is involved - triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists (some also 5-HT1F) and ditans are selective 5-HT1F agonists - and dopamine contributes, with dopamine-receptor hypersensitivity in migraineurs. Functional imaging shows hypothalamic activation in the premonitory phase and persistent dorsolateral pontine (including locus coeruleus) activation during attacks and in chronic migraine, with lateralization correlating with the side of head pain. Genetic study of familial hemiplegic migraine implicates ion channels (CACNA1A/Cav2.1 P/Q calcium channel in FHM1 ~50%; ATP1A2 Na-K ATPase in FHM2 ~20%; SCN1A sodium channel in FHM3), suggesting altered membrane excitability predisposes to aura. The slowly advancing visual scotoma with luminous (fortification) edges is recognized as a marker of spreading cortical depression associated with migraine (p.3462-3464, p.3379). Patients should understand that migraine is an inherited tendency to headache that can be modified and controlled by lifestyle measures and medication but not eradicated. Except on some occasions in women taking oral estrogens or contraceptives, migraine is not associated with serious or life-threatening illness (p.3464). Migraine is nonetheless the most common neurologic cause of disability worldwide (p.3462). Recognized complications (ICHD-3) include status migrainosus, persistent aura without infarction, migrainous infarction, and migraine aura-triggered seizure; migraine may also progress to chronic migraine (Table 441-1, p.3463). Overuse of acute analgesics can transform episodic migraine into refractory medication-overuse headache; many patients improve after withdrawal, though residual headache often persists reflecting the underlying primary disorder (p.115-116). ICHD-3 (IHS 2018) classifies migraine into migraine without aura, migraine with aura (typical aura with/without headache, migraine with brainstem aura, hemiplegic migraine including FHM1-3 and sporadic, retinal migraine), chronic migraine, complications of migraine (status migrainosus, persistent aura without infarction, migrainous infarction, migraine aura-triggered seizure), probable migraine, and episodic syndromes that may be associated with migraine (cyclical vomiting, abdominal migraine, benign paroxysmal vertigo/torticollis, infantile colic, vestibular migraine). Chronic migraine is defined as migraine on 8 or more days per month with at least 15 total headache days per month (Table 441-1, p.3463; p.3462). Disability is graded by MIDAS: Grade I 0-5, Grade II 6-10, Grade III 11-20, Grade IV over 20 (Fig. 441-4, p.3466).

Miliaria — heat rash, prickly heat, sweat rash, miliaria rubra, miliaria crystallina Folliculitis Acute eczema or contact dermatitis Candidal intertrigo in flexures Viral exanthem or drug eruption Neonatal erythema toxicum or transient neonatal pustular melanosis Grover's disease (transient acantholytic dermatosis) in adults Diagnosis is clinical, based on morphology and a history of heat, occlusion, or fever Skin swab if secondary bacterial infection (pustular miliaria) is suspected Investigations are seldom required, and biopsy is reserved for atypical or persistent cases Assessment of the environment and clothing or dressing practices, especially in infants and bedridden patients Miliaria arises from blockage of eccrine sweat ducts, so it favours hot, humid conditions, febrile illness, occlusion, and overdressing, and is common in neonates and in the newly bedridden The subtype reflects the depth of duct obstruction: crystallina shows tiny clear, easily ruptured superficial vesicles; rubra produces itchy or prickly erythematous papulovesicles; and the deeper profunda presents as firm, skin-coloured papules Typical sites are areas of occlusion and friction such as the trunk, flexures, and skin under clothing or dressings In infants it commonly affects the neck, groin, and axillae and is easily provoked by warm environments and heavy wrapping The cornerstone of management is cooling and reducing sweating: a cooler environment, loose breathable clothing, and avoiding occlusion, which allow the ducts to reopen It is generally self-limiting once the provoking heat and occlusion are removed, and specific drug treatment is rarely needed Widespread deep miliaria can impair sweating and predispose to heat intolerance and, in extreme heat, heat exhaustion Secondary bacterial infection (miliaria pustulosa) can complicate the picture if lesions are scratched or persist Extensive deep (profunda) involvement impairing sweating with symptoms of heat intolerance or heat exhaustion Signs of secondary bacterial infection such as pustules, increasing pain, or spreading erythema Systemic upset or fever suggesting an alternative or complicating diagnosis Failure to settle after removing heat and occlusion, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Treating with occlusive creams or heavy dressings that worsen duct blockage Overwrapping or overdressing infants and perpetuating the rash Mistaking pustular miliaria with secondary infection for a primary bacterial folliculitis or vice versa Overlooking impaired thermoregulation in extensive deep disease during hot conditions Miliaria results from obstruction of the eccrine sweat ducts, which causes sweat to leak into the surrounding skin rather than reach the surface. Keratin plugging of the duct, often aggravated by an overgrowth of skin flora producing occlusive material, blocks flow at varying levels. The level of the block determines the clinical form: obstruction within the stratum corneum causes the superficial vesicles of crystallina, blockage within the epidermis produces the inflammatory papulovesicles of rubra, and obstruction at the dermo-epidermal junction gives the deeper papules of profunda. The extravasated sweat provokes local inflammation and the sensation of prickling, while widespread duct blockage can compromise thermoregulation. Miliaria is benign and typically resolves quickly once overheating and occlusion are addressed; recurrence is common with repeated heat exposure, and only extensive deep disease or secondary infection causes significant problems.

Milk-alkali syndrome — calcium-alkali syndrome, milk alkali syndrome, Burnett syndrome Primary hyperparathyroidism Malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia Vitamin D intoxication Sarcoidosis and other granulomatous diseases Thiazide-induced hypercalcaemia Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone, the latter suppressed in milk-alkali syndrome Venous blood gas or bicarbonate demonstrating a metabolic alkalosis Renal function and electrolytes A careful history of calcium, antacid and supplement intake Serum phosphate and vitamin D to exclude other causes of hypercalcaemia Renal imaging for nephrocalcinosis if the exposure has been chronic A triad of hypercalcaemia, metabolic alkalosis and acute kidney injury caused by ingesting large amounts of calcium together with absorbable alkali Historically from milk and antacids taken for peptic ulcer; now more often from calcium carbonate used for osteoporosis prevention, dyspepsia or as a phosphate binder Increasingly recognised in older women and in patients with chronic kidney disease, who handle a calcium load less well It presents with symptoms of hypercalcaemia such as nausea, vomiting, polyuria and confusion, alongside features of volume depletion and renal impairment Hypercalcaemia causes renal vasoconstriction and a natriuresis that worsens volume depletion, which further impairs calcium excretion in a self-reinforcing cycle Unlike primary hyperparathyroidism, parathyroid hormone is appropriately suppressed and the acid-base picture is a metabolic alkalosis rather than acidosis Nephrocalcinosis may develop with prolonged exposure Management is to stop the calcium and alkali and restore volume with intravenous fluids, after which the hypercalcaemia and renal function usually improve Severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia with marked confusion or arrhythmia risk Significant acute kidney injury or oliguria Profound volume depletion Persisting hypercalcaemia after intake has stopped, suggesting another cause Not asking about over-the-counter calcium supplements and antacids Misdiagnosing as hyperparathyroidism despite a suppressed PTH and an alkalosis Overlooking the syndrome in CKD patients taking calcium-based phosphate binders Failing to correct volume depletion promptly A high intake of calcium plus absorbable alkali raises the serum calcium, which acts on the calcium-sensing receptor to reduce sodium and water reabsorption, producing a natriuresis and volume depletion. Hypercalcaemia also causes renal afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, lowering the glomerular filtration rate. The fall in filtration and in circulating volume reduces excretion of both calcium and bicarbonate, so calcium and alkali accumulate, generating a metabolic alkalosis that perpetuates the hypercalcaemia. Alkalosis itself enhances distal tubular calcium reabsorption, closing the self-reinforcing loop, and prolonged hypercalcaemia can lead to calcium deposition within the kidney. Usually reversible once the calcium and alkali are withdrawn and volume is restored, though repeated or prolonged episodes can leave residual chronic kidney disease and nephrocalcinosis.

motor neurone facial palsy for a peripheral Bell palsy in isolation Overlooking the contralateral hemiparesis and missing the brainstem localisation Failing to recognise an evolving basilar occlusion The infarct or haemorrhage damages the intrapontine fascicles of the facial and abducens nerves as they course towards their exit, producing ipsilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness and a lateral rectus palsy, together with the descending corticospinal fibres in the basis pontis, producing contralateral hemiparesis with facial sparing on the weak side. Because the cranial nerve deficits are ipsilateral and the limb weakness contralateral, the picture is that of a caudal alternating hemiplegia; extension towards the paramedian pontine reticular formation can add an ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy. Isolated small ventral pontine infarcts may show useful recovery of limb power and facial function, but larger lesions or those heralding basilar thrombosis carry a poor prognosis with risk of progression to a locked-in state.

The prognosis is generally excellent, with most patients recovering fully over weeks to months, though those with overlapping Guillain-Barre features may have a more prolonged course.

syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by variants in DHODH, which encodes dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, a mitochondrial enzyme catalysing a rate-limiting step in de novo pyrimidine With airway stabilisation, feeding support, hearing rehabilitation, and staged craniofacial and limb reconstruction, most affected individuals have normal intellect and a reasonable functional outcome, the main early risk being airway compromise.

Milroy disease is a chronic lifelong condition but is compatible with normal life expectancy; with consistent conservative lymphoedema management most patients maintain good limb function, though recurrent cellulitis and progressive skin changes are the main sources of morbidity.

superimposed on a destroyed joint Large recurrent haemorrhagic effusions Mistaking the large, low-inflammatory effusion for a benign process, or conversely over-diagnosing sepsis Failing to detect the BCP crystals because they are non-birefringent Overlooking the massive rotator cuff tear that drives the deformity Assuming a standard arthroplasty will behave as it would in routine osteoarthritis, when cuff deficiency alters the options and outcome In Milwaukee shoulder, basic calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) crystals within the joint are phagocytosed by synovial lining cells, which respond These enzymes degrade articular cartilage and the rotator cuff tendons; the resulting cuff deficiency allows the humeral head to migrate superiorly, and continued crystal shedding perpetuates enzyme release and progressive joint destruction. and cardiac arrhythmia Failure to thrive and dehydration unresponsive to mineralocorticoid replacement Respiratory compromise in the systemic form mimicking cystic fibrosis Confusing it with adrenal insufficiency and giving mineralocorticoid, which is ineffective because resistance lies downstream Missing transient or secondary pseudohypoaldosteronism due to infant urinary tract infection or obstruction Mislabelling the systemic form as cystic fibrosis on the basis of a raised sweat chloride Failing to distinguish salt-wasting type 1 from hypertensive type 2 (Gordon syndrome) Mineralocorticoid resistance encompasses the pseudohypoaldosteronism syndromes, in which the distal nephron fails to respond to aldosterone despite elevated hormone levels. In the autosomal dominant renal form of type 1, heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in NR3C2 (the mineralocorticoid receptor) blunt renal sodium reabsorption. In the autosomal recessive systemic form, mutations in the epithelial sodium channel subunits abolish sodium transport across multiple aldosterone-responsive epithelia including kidney, colon, sweat and salivary glands, and lung. Impaired sodium reabsorption drives salt wasting, volume depletion and secondary activation of renin and aldosterone, while reduced electrogenic sodium uptake impairs potassium and hydrogen secretion, producing hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis. Type 2 (Gordon syndrome) instead reflects overactive distal sodium chloride reabsorption from mutations in the WNK-kinase pathway. The autosomal dominant renal form of type 1 is generally mild and tends to improve with age as dietary sodium intake rises, whereas the recessive systemic form requires lifelong aggressive salt supplementation and carries greater morbidity; with careful electrolyte management most patients grow and develop normally.

Minimal Change Nephrotic Syndrome (Child) — minimal change disease, MCNS, idiopathic nephrotic syndrome of childhood, steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis Membranous nephropathy Post-infectious or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Lupus nephritis Congenital nephrotic syndrome (in infants) Secondary nephrotic syndrome (e.g. Henoch-Schonlein, infection-related) Urinalysis and quantification of proteinuria (protein:creatinine ratio or 24-hour protein) Serum albumin, lipid profile, and renal function Serum complement (C3, C4) Autoimmune serology when secondary causes are suspected Assessment for infection and, in selected cases, screening for thrombosis Renal biopsy in atypical presentations or steroid resistance Minimal change disease accounts for the large majority of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in children, most commonly presenting between about 1 and 6 years of age. The defining features are heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and hyperlipidaemia. Oedema is typically dependent and periorbital and can progress to generalised swelling with ascites and pleural effusions. Most children are steroid-responsive, and a favourable response to corticosteroids is both diagnostic and therapeutic in the typical age group. Renal biopsy is generally reserved for atypical features such as age under 1 or over 10 years, persistent hypertension, gross haematuria, low complement, impaired renal function, or steroid resistance. Children are at increased risk of infection, particularly spontaneous bacterial peritonitis from encapsulated organisms, because of urinary immunoglobulin losses. A hypercoagulable state develops from urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins, increasing the risk of venous and arterial thrombosis. Relapses are common, and some children become frequent relapsers or steroid-dependent, requiring steroid-sparing agents. Signs of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (fever, abdominal pain, tenderness) Features of venous or arterial thrombosis, including limb swelling, respiratory compromise, or neurological signs Hypovolaemic shock during aggressive diuresis Severe respiratory distress from large pleural effusions or ascites Steroid resistance or deteriorating renal function suggesting a more aggressive lesion Missing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis because ascitic signs can be subtle in an oedematous child Overlooking thrombosis risk during periods of heavy proteinuria and diuresis Assuming all childhood nephrotic syndrome is minimal change and delaying biopsy in atypical cases Over-diuresing and precipitating hypovolaemia in a child with low intravascular volume A poorly understood immune dysregulation, involving circulating permeability factors and T-cell mediated signalling, injures the glomerular podocytes. On light microscopy the glomeruli appear normal, but electron microscopy reveals diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes. Loss of the size- and charge-selective filtration barrier permits massive albumin leakage into the urine, producing hypoalbuminaemia, reduced oncotic pressure, oedema, and compensatory hepatic lipoprotein synthesis causing hyperlipidaemia. Children with steroid-sensitive minimal change disease generally have an excellent long-term renal prognosis, though many experience relapses over several years before remitting; steroid-resistant disease, often reflecting focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, carries a higher risk of progression to chronic kidney disease.

parallel course alongside the common hepatic duct. The stone and the surrounding inflammatory reaction compress the adjacent common hepatic duct extrinsically, obstructing bile flow and causing jaundice. Persistent pressure and chronic inflammation can erode the wall separating the gallbladder from the bile duct, producing a cholecystobiliary fistula of varying size; in advanced disease the stone may migrate into the common duct. The dense inflammation and distorted anatomy in Calot's triangle obscure normal landmarks and predispose to iatrogenic bile duct injury during cholecystectomy. With timely recognition and appropriate surgery the outlook is generally good, but the syndrome carries a higher risk of bile duct injury and operative complications than routine gallstone disease, and the associated gallbladder carcinoma, if present, worsens prognosis considerably.

Misophonia — Selective sound sensitivity syndrome, Sound-rage Hyperacusis with reduced tolerance to sound loudness Phonophobia with fear or anxiety about specific sounds Tinnitus-related distress Obsessive-compulsive disorder Anxiety disorders Autism spectrum sensory sensitivities Post-traumatic reactions to specific sounds Detailed clinical history of triggers, reactions, and impairment Validated questionnaires such as the Misophonia Questionnaire or the Amsterdam Misophonia Scale Audiological assessment including audiometry and loudness discomfort levels to exclude hyperacusis Screening for anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and autistic traits Assessment of functional and relational impact ENT or audiology referral where auditory pathology is suspected Mood and risk assessment where aggression or guilt is prominent A strong, disproportionate aversive emotional and physiological reaction, typically anger, disgust, or anxiety, to specific trigger sounds that are often human-generated. Common triggers include chewing, lip-smacking, slurping, breathing, sniffing, pen-clicking, and keyboard tapping. The reaction includes autonomic arousal, an urge to escape, irritability or rage, and sometimes aggression, frequently followed by guilt. Onset is often in childhood or adolescence, and early triggers frequently involve family members. It is not currently a formal DSM-5-TR or ICD-11 disorder but is increasingly recognised, and should be distinguished from hyperacusis (loudness intolerance) and phonophobia (fear of sound). Causes significant functional and relational impairment, with avoidance of shared meals and social situations. High comorbidity is seen with anxiety, obsessive-compulsive traits, and sometimes attention-deficit or autistic traits. Management is largely psychological, particularly cognitive-behavioural therapy with coping and sound-based strategies, and no established pharmacotherapy exists. Aggression or violence toward others during trigger exposure Severe avoidance causing social or occupational collapse or nutritional impact Comorbid depression with suicidal ideation Self-harm related to the distress Confusing misophonia with hyperacusis or phonophobia and mismanaging accordingly Dismissing it as mere irritability or fussiness Overlooking comorbid anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, or autistic traits Recommending indefinite avoidance, which can reinforce the response Misophonia is proposed to reflect abnormal salience and connectivity between the auditory system and limbic, autonomic, and interoceptive networks, such that specific learned trigger sounds evoke exaggerated activation of the anterior insula and associated emotional-processing regions, with heightened autonomic responses. Enhanced functional connectivity between auditory cortex and salience and limbic structures, together with conditioned associations formed early in life, is thought to underlie the automatic aversive response. It is distinct from peripheral auditory pathology, since audiometric function is typically normal, and it is best regarded as a disorder of emotional and attentional processing of sound rather than of hearing itself. Misophonia tends to be chronic, but cognitive-behavioural approaches and coping and sound strategies can meaningfully reduce distress and functional impact, although complete resolution is uncommon.

management is largely supportive with cofactor and antioxidant cocktails, avoidance of mitochondrial toxins, and treatment of organ-specific complications Certain metabolic markers may appear on newborn screening, but most mitochondrial disorders are not reliably detected by standard screening Stroke-like episodes with encephalopathy, seizures and lactic acidosis (as in MELAS) Acute metabolic decompensation with severe lactic acidosis Rapidly progressive encephalopathy, respiratory failure or brainstem dysfunction in Leigh syndrome Cardiac conduction block (e.g. in Kearns-Sayre) with risk of sudden death, and status epilepticus Excluding the diagnosis on the basis of a normal blood lactate, which can be intermittent Using medications toxic to mitochondria (e.g. valproate in some contexts, certain antivirals) without caution Failing to screen for treatable organ complications such as cardiac conduction disease and endocrinopathy Overlooking maternal inheritance and the implications of heteroplasmy for family counselling Mitochondrial diseases arise from impaired oxidative phosphorylation, the process by which the electron transport chain generates ATP. Because mitochondria contain their own DNA encoding some respiratory chain subunits, while most subunits and assembly factors are nuclear-encoded, disease can follow maternal, autosomal or X-linked inheritance. Mutations reduce ATP production and may increase reactive oxygen species and lactate. Tissues with high energy demand are preferentially affected, and in mitochondrial DNA disorders the mixture of normal and mutant genomes within cells (heteroplasmy) and a threshold of mutant load determine which tissues manifest disease and how severely, explaining the marked clinical variability. Prognosis is highly variable, ranging from severe fatal infantile encephalopathy to slowly progressive or relatively stable adult disease, depending on the genetic defect, mutant load and organs involved; most forms are progressive with no cure, and management aims to preserve function and prevent decompensation.

Prognosis is generally poor, with many infants dying of liver failure or neurological disease in the first years of life; liver transplantation may help isolated hepatic forms but does not address neurological involvement and carries a worse outcome when extrahepatic disease is present.

Prognosis varies by subtype and gene: severe infantile hepatocerebral and encephalomyopathic forms often carry a poor outlook with early mortality, whereas some myopathic forms are more slowly progressive, and outcome depends heavily on the specific genetic defect and organ involvement.

care is supportive, with management of dystonia, spasticity, and neuropsychiatric symptoms Rapid loss of ambulation from progressive spasticity and dystonia Severe dystonic crisis requiring urgent management Marked neuropsychiatric deterioration with safety concerns Progressive visual loss from optic atrophy Failing to recognise the diagnostic MRI iron pattern and pursuing broader neurology unnecessarily Attributing the peripheral neuropathy to a separate cause rather than the same disorder Overlooking the neuropsychiatric component of the phenotype Not excluding treatable mimics such as Wilson disease before settling on the diagnosis MPAN belongs to the NBIA group and is caused by variants in C19orf12, which encodes a small protein localised to mitochondrial membranes and implicated in lipid homeostasis and mitochondrial function. Loss of normal protein function disturbs mitochondrial and lipid metabolism in vulnerable neurons, leading to progressive neurodegeneration accompanied by pathological iron deposition in the basal ganglia, particularly the globus pallidus and substantia nigra. The neuropathology characteristically shows axonal spheroids and alpha-synuclein-positive Lewy-body-like inclusions in addition to iron, linking the disorder to both iron-accumulation and synucleinopathy mechanisms. This produces the mixed clinical picture of upper motor neuron, extrapyramidal, and peripheral nerve involvement with optic atrophy. A progressive neurodegenerative disorder leading to increasing motor and cognitive disability over years to decades; no treatment halts progression and care is supportive.

loss with a maternal inheritance pattern The mitochondrial 12S ribosomal RNA gene MT-RNR1 forms part of the mitochondrial ribosome. The m.1555A>G variant alters the RNA so that it more closely resembles the bacterial ribosomal binding site targeted by aminoglycosides, increasing drug binding and impairing mitochondrial protein synthesis. Because cochlear hair cells are highly dependent on oxidative metabolism, this susceptibility renders them vulnerable to aminoglycoside-induced injury, producing sensorineural hearing loss. Even without drug exposure some carriers develop progressive loss, reflecting a milder underlying deficit in mitochondrial function; the mitochondrial genome is inherited exclusively through the maternal line, explaining the pattern of transmission. Aminoglycoside-triggered loss is typically severe and irreversible, but the disorder is highly preventable through drug avoidance; baseline and progressive loss are managed with amplification or cochlear implantation.

isolated LCHAD deficiency is a common subtype Presents across a spectrum from severe neonatal cardiomyopathy and hypoketotic hypoglycaemia to a milder later-onset phenotype with episodic rhabdomyolysis and a progressive peripheral neuropathy Fasting or intercurrent illness precipitates hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, liver dysfunction and metabolic decompensation LCHAD deficiency is distinctively associated with a progressive pigmentary retinopathy and peripheral neuropathy not usually seen in other fatty-acid oxidation defects Carrying an affected fetus is linked to maternal HELLP syndrome and acute fatty liver of pregnancy, so a maternal obstetric history is an important clue Blood acylcarnitines show elevated long-chain hydroxyacylcarnitines, detectable on newborn screening Management centres on avoidance of fasting, a low long-chain-fat diet with medium-chain triglyceride substitution, and prompt glucose during catabolic stress Neonatal cardiomyopathy with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and collapse Acute rhabdomyolysis with risk of renal impairment during illness or exertion Arrhythmia or cardiac decompensation during metabolic crises Maternal HELLP syndrome or acute fatty liver of pregnancy prompting evaluation of the infant Missing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia by not measuring ketones alongside glucose Failing to consider the diagnosis in a mother with HELLP or acute fatty liver of pregnancy Overlooking the evolving retinopathy and neuropathy that distinguish LCHAD/MTP deficiency Allowing prolonged fasting or high long-chain-fat intake that precipitates decompensation The mitochondrial trifunctional protein is a hetero-octamer of alpha (HADHA) and beta (HADHB) subunits that performs the last three enzymatic steps of long-chain fatty-acid beta-oxidation: long-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase, long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD) and long-chain 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase activities. Deficiency blocks energy production from long-chain fats, so during fasting or illness tissues cannot generate adequate ATP or ketones, producing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and accumulation of toxic long-chain hydroxyacyl intermediates. These intermediates injure the heart, skeletal muscle, liver, peripheral nerves and retina. Reduced fatty-acid oxidation in the fetus and placenta also underlies the associated maternal liver disease of pregnancy. The severe neonatal cardiomyopathic form carries high mortality, whereas milder phenotypes may be managed with diet and fasting avoidance; however, progressive retinopathy and peripheral neuropathy can cause long-term morbidity even with good metabolic control.

calcification is a degenerative process in which calcium and phosphate are deposited within the fibrous annulus of the mitral valve, sharing mechanisms with atherosclerosis and with the disordered The rigid, calcified ring loses its normal systolic contraction and can prevent adequate leaflet coaptation, producing regurgitation, while heavy calcium extending onto the leaflet bases narrows the inflow and mimics rheumatic mitral stenosis. Underestimating the difficulty of achieving a durable repair of the malformed apparatus In a mitral arcade the normal delicate chordal support of the mitral leaflets is replaced by direct or near-direct insertion of the papillary muscles into a thickened fibrous ridge running along the free edge of the leaflets. This tethering fixes the leaflets in a curtain-like or hammock configuration that limits their excursion and prevents proper coaptation, so blood flow across the valve is obstructed and, or, the valve leaks.
