Mitral Regurgitation — MR Aortic stenosis (basally-radiating MR murmur from posterior leaflet prolapse/flail can be confused with AS) (p.2054) Mitral stenosis (a brief early-diastolic LA-LV gradient with rapid filling sound and mid-diastolic rumble in pure severe MR can masquerade as MS) (p.2053-2054) Ventricular septal defect and other causes of a holosystolic murmur Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) with Doppler to define mechanism and severity (jet width/area, regurgitant volume, regurgitant fraction, effective regurgitant orifice area, LV volumes/EF, LA/LV size, chordal integrity, annular calcification) (p.2053) Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) for greater anatomic detail (p.2053-2054) Estimation of pulmonary artery systolic pressure from the tricuspid regurgitation jet velocity (p.2053) Exercise (stress) echocardiography to assess exercise capacity and dynamic change in MR severity, PA pressures, and biventricular function when clinical and resting findings disagree (p.2053) Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) for quantitative regurgitant measures when TTE is discordant or insufficient (noted as not widely available) (p.2052-2053) ECG (LA enlargement, possible RA enlargement with pulmonary hypertension, AF, eccentric LVH) (p.2053) Chest X-ray (LA/LV enlargement, pulmonary venous congestion, Kerley B lines, mitral/annular calcification; asymmetric pulmonary edema possible in acute MR) (p.2053-2054) Left and right heart catheterization with contrast ventriculography and coronary angiography when noninvasive findings are discrepant or to identify coronary disease before surgery (p.2053, p.2056) Distinguish primary (degenerative) MR, where the leaflets and/or chordae are themselves abnormal, from secondary (functional) MR, where leaflets and chordae are usually normal and regurgitation is driven by LV/LA remodeling, annular dilation, papillary muscle displacement, dyssynchrony, or leaflet tethering; assessment, treatment, and prognosis differ significantly between the two (p.2052). The characteristic murmur of chronic severe MR is a holosystolic, plateau-configuration systolic murmur of at least grade III/VI, most prominent at the apex and radiating to the axilla (p.2053-2054). Murmur radiation reflects jet direction: with posterior leaflet prolapse/flail the eccentric anteriorly-directed jet strikes the LA wall near the aortic root and the murmur radiates to the base (can mimic aortic stenosis), whereas anterior leaflet prolapse/flail directs the jet and murmur toward the axilla (p.2054). Ruptured chordae tendineae may give the systolic murmur a cooing or 'seagull' quality; a flail leaflet may produce a musical murmur (p.2054). The murmur of chronic MR not due to MVP is intensified by isometric handgrip and reduced during the strain phase of Valsalva (decreased LV preload) (p.2054). In acute severe MR the murmur is early in timing and decrescendo, ending well before S2, reflecting the rapidly rising LA pressure and diminishing LV-LA gradient — in contrast to the holosystolic plateau murmur of chronic MR (p.2053-2054). Because EF rises in severe MR when LV function is normal, even a modest fall in EF (below 60%) reflects significant contractile dysfunction (p.2052-2053). Atrial fibrillation is almost invariably present once the LA dilates significantly in chronic severe MR; LA enlargement and AF support the diagnosis on ECG (p.2053). 'MR begets MR': LA enlargement tensions the posterior leaflet pulling it away from the orifice, and LV dilation increases regurgitation, enlarging LA and LV further in a vicious cycle (p.2052). With post-MI papillary muscle rupture the posteromedial papillary muscle is involved far more often than the anterolateral muscle because of its single blood supply (p.2052). Acute severe MR is a surgical emergency: papillary muscle rupture post-MI or leaflet destruction/perforation in infective endocarditis can cause sudden pulmonary edema and hemodynamic collapse, requiring urgent stabilization and emergent surgery (p.2052, p.2055-2056) Acute pulmonary edema, hypotension with narrow pulse pressure, and prominent signs of pulmonary congestion with a non-displaced apex point to acute severe MR (p.2053) Onset of palpitations or atrial fibrillation in chronic severe MR (p.2053) Late-onset right heart failure with hepatic congestion, ankle edema, distended neck veins, ascites, and secondary tricuspid regurgitation, indicating pulmonary vascular disease and pulmonary hypertension (p.2053) Falling LVEF (to 60% or below) or rising LV end-systolic dimension (40 mm or more), even when asymptomatic, signals contractile dysfunction warranting surgical referral (p.2053, p.2056) In secondary MR the severity can be underappreciated by echocardiographic/Doppler techniques, and lesser degrees of regurgitation may carry relatively greater prognostic weight (p.2053). An S3 in MR may reflect rapid LV filling, but in ischemic or dilated cardiomyopathy an S3 may instead signify ventricular dysfunction (p.2054). Because EF is artifactually elevated in severe MR with normal myocardium, a 'low-normal' EF may already represent meaningful contractile dysfunction (p.2052-2053). Routine surgical valve repair for significant secondary MR due to dilated cardiomyopathy has NOT been shown to improve long-term survival versus optimal guideline-directed medical therapy, especially in the era of quadruple HFrEF therapy (p.2056). Direct oral anticoagulants should NOT be used if moderate or severe rheumatic mitral stenosis coexists, and are NOT approved for mechanical prosthetic valves (p.2055). A presystolic murmur is not ordinarily heard with isolated MR (p.2054). MR can arise from disease of any of the five components of the mitral apparatus: leaflets, annulus, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles, and subjacent myocardium (p.2052). MR reduces resistance to LV emptying (lowers afterload); the LV decompresses into the LA during ejection, so initial compensation is more complete LV emptying. Over time LV volume rises as regurgitation worsens and contractile function deteriorates, and forward cardiac output falls; LV compliance is often increased so LV diastolic pressure does not rise until late (p.2052-2053). The regurgitant volume varies directly with LV systolic pressure and the size of the regurgitant orifice (influenced by LV and annular dilation and leaflet morphology). LA compliance governs the clinical picture: in acute severe MR the regurgitant volume enters a normal-sized, noncompliant LA so LA and pulmonary venous pressures rise sharply with a prominent v wave and pulmonary edema is common; in chronic severe MR the LA enlarges and becomes more compliant, buffering pressure so pulmonary congestion is initially less prominent and fatigue from low forward output predominates (p.2053). Chronic secondary MR results from annular dilation, ventricular remodeling, papillary muscle displacement, and leaflet tethering (e.g., after MI, in dilated cardiomyopathy once LV end-diastolic dimension reaches ~6 cm, or atrial functional MR from chronic AF with annular dilation) (p.2052). Chronic mild-to-moderate isolated MR is well tolerated and usually asymptomatic. Chronic severe MR tends to be progressive ('MR begets MR') and, when secondary, severity correlates inversely with prognosis, with adverse outcome tied to the degree of LV remodeling and myocardial dysfunction (p.2052-2053). With surgery, repair carries substantially lower risk than replacement; a 2023 STS database analysis reported mean perioperative mortality of about 1.16% (under 0.5% in patients younger than 65) for repair of primary MR, durable repair is feasible in up to 95% of degenerative cases at high-volume centers, and reoperation runs about 1% per year over the first 10 years. In ischemic MR with severely impaired LV function (EF below 30%), surgical risk is higher, recovery of LV performance is incomplete, and long-term survival is reduced (p.2055-2056). Chronic severe MR (Doppler/CMR quantitative criteria) is defined by a regurgitant volume of at least 60 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction of at least 50%, and effective regurgitant orifice area of at least 0.40 cm2 (p.2053). ACC/AHA disease staging (Stages B, C1, C2, D) is applied: Stage C is asymptomatic severe MR (C1 normal LV systolic function with LVEF above 60% and ESD below 40 mm; C2 LV systolic dysfunction with LVEF at or below 60% or ESD at or above 40 mm) and Stage D is symptomatic severe MR (p.2054-2055).

Mitral Stenosis — MS Mitral regurgitation (may have an apical diastolic flow murmur, but it begins slightly later, S1 is soft or absent, and there is no opening snap; LV enlargement is common) (p.2049) Severe aortic regurgitation with an Austin Flint murmur (apical mid-diastolic murmur not intensified in presystole and softened by amyl nitrite/arterial vasodilators) (p.2049) Tricuspid stenosis (rare without MS; its diastolic murmur increases with inspiration and the jugular venous y descent is delayed) (p.2049-2050) Atrial septal defect (RV enlargement and increased pulmonary vascularity, but no LA enlargement or Kerley B lines, with fixed splitting of S2) (p.2050) Left atrial myxoma (obstructs LA emptying causing a positional diastolic murmur; often with systemic features such as weight loss, fever, anemia, emboli, elevated IgG/IL-6) (p.2050) Infective endocarditis with large vegetations is itself a recognized (uncommon) cause of left ventricular inflow obstruction mimicking MS (p.2048) Transthoracic echocardiography with color flow and spectral Doppler for mitral inflow velocities, peak/mean gradients, mitral orifice area, leaflet calcification and restriction, and suitability for percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy (p.2049) Transesophageal echocardiography when TTE is inadequate, and specifically to exclude left atrial thrombus before commissurotomy (p.2049) Exercise (stress) echocardiography to assess mean mitral diastolic gradient, PA pressures, and RV function when clinical and resting hemodynamic findings are discrepant (p.2049) ECG showing left atrial enlargement (P-wave changes), and right axis deviation/RV hypertrophy when severe pulmonary hypertension supervenes (p.2049) Chest X-ray showing straightening of the left cardiac border, prominent main PAs, upper-lobe pulmonary venous dilation, an enlarged LA, and Kerley B lines when mean LA pressure exceeds about 20 mmHg (p.2049) Left and right heart catheterization when clinical and noninvasive findings are discrepant; CT coronary angiography to screen for coronary disease before valve surgery (p.2050) Congenital mitral valve stenosis (parachute valve, cor triatriatum) (p.2048) Severe mitral annular calcification with extension onto the leaflets (p.2048) Systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis involving the valve (p.2048) Left atrial myxoma (p.2048) Rheumatic fever is the leading cause of mitral stenosis; pure or predominant MS occurs in roughly 40% of patients with rheumatic heart disease and a history of rheumatic fever (p.2048). Although declining in temperate, middle- to high-income climates, MS remains a major problem in low-income countries, especially sub-Saharan Africa, India, Southeast Asia, and Oceania (p.2048). Auscultation classically reveals an accentuated first heart sound (S1), an opening snap (OS) of the mitral valve heard best in expiration at or just medial to the apex, followed by a low-pitched rumbling diastolic murmur heard best at the apex in the left lateral recumbent position (p.2049). The A2-to-opening-snap interval varies inversely with severity of MS: a shorter interval indicates more severe stenosis (p.2049). In patients in sinus rhythm, the diastolic murmur often reappears or becomes louder during atrial systole (presystolic accentuation) (p.2049). Development of persistent atrial fibrillation often marks a turning point in the patient's course and is associated with acceleration of symptom progression (p.2048). Echocardiography (TTE with Doppler) provides mitral orifice area, transvalvular gradients, leaflet calcification/restriction, and suitability for percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy; TEE is especially indicated to exclude LA thrombus before intervention (p.2049). Mitral valve area 1-1.5 cm2 denotes severe MS; an LA pressure of about 25 mmHg is needed to maintain normal cardiac output when the orifice falls below 1.5 cm2 (p.2048-2049). Atrial fibrillation, which accelerates symptom progression and markedly increases thromboembolic risk (p.2048) Systemic embolization (incidence 10-20%), more frequent with AF, age over 65, and reduced cardiac output; may be the presenting feature even in mild MS (p.2049) Hemoptysis from rupture of pulmonary-bronchial venous connections due to pulmonary venous hypertension (p.2048) Pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure (hepatomegaly, ankle edema, ascites, pleural effusion) (p.2048-2049) Recurrent pulmonary emboli, sometimes with infarction, an important late cause of morbidity and mortality (p.2048) Decompensation precipitated by tachycardia, fever, severe anemia, paroxysmal AF, thyrotoxicosis, exertion, or pregnancy (p.2048) In pregnancy, increased blood volume, cardiac output, and tachycardia can raise the transmitral gradient and cause pulmonary edema or tachyarrhythmias, with the immediate postpartum period a time of particular concern due to rapid volume shifts (p.3900) When cardiac output is markedly reduced, the typical auscultatory findings including the diastolic rumble may be undetectable (silent MS) and may reappear only as compensation is restored (p.2049) Systemic embolization may be the presenting feature in otherwise asymptomatic patients with only mild MS (p.2049) The Graham Steell murmur of pulmonic regurgitation can be indistinguishable from aortic regurgitation, though it may increase with inspiration and is accompanied by a loud, often palpable P2 (p.2049) A history of rheumatic carditis is increasingly rare and often cannot be elicited (p.2048) In normal adults the mitral valve orifice area is 4-6 cm2. Significant obstruction occurs when the orifice is reduced to less than about 2 cm2, so blood can only flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle if propelled by an abnormally elevated left atrioventricular pressure gradient, the hemodynamic hallmark of MS. When the orifice is below 1.5 cm2 (severe MS), an LA pressure of about 25 mmHg is required to maintain normal cardiac output. Elevated pulmonary venous and PA wedge pressures reduce pulmonary compliance and cause exertional dyspnea. Because tachycardia shortens diastole proportionately more than systole, an increased heart rate (including rapid AF) augments the transvalvular gradient and further elevates LA pressure. Chronic LA pressure elevation leads to LA enlargement, predisposing to AF and to thrombus formation (particularly in the LA appendage) with risk of systemic embolization. Pulmonary hypertension develops from passive backward transmission of elevated LA pressure, reactive pulmonary arteriolar constriction (the so-called second stenosis), interstitial edema of small pulmonary vessels, and, at end stage, obliterative pulmonary vascular changes; severe pulmonary hypertension produces RV enlargement, secondary tricuspid and pulmonic regurgitation, and right-sided heart failure (p.2048-2049). In temperate climates the latent period between the initial attack of rheumatic carditis and symptomatic MS is generally about two decades, with disability typically beginning in the fourth decade. Historical studies before surgical valvotomy showed that once a patient became seriously symptomatic, the disease progressed inexorably to death within 2-5 years. Onset of persistent AF generally marks acceleration of symptom progression (p.2048). Severity is graded by mitral valve area. The normal orifice is 4-6 cm2; significant obstruction begins below about 2 cm2. A valve area below 1.5 cm2 is termed severe MS (with an LA pressure of about 25 mmHg required to maintain normal cardiac output), and an area below 1 cm2 is very severe, at which cardiac output is subnormal at rest. Echocardiographic measurement of mitral orifice area and transvalvular gradient is the basis for grading; commissurotomy is generally indicated for symptomatic patients with valve area below about 1 cm2/m2 body surface area or below 1.5 cm2 in normal-sized adults (p.2048-2051).

mitral valve arcade — anomalous mitral arcade, hammock mitral valve Parachute mitral valve Congenital mitral stenosis with supravalvar mitral ring Rheumatic mitral valve disease Mitral valve prolapse Cleft mitral valve or atrioventricular septal defect Ischaemic or dysplastic papillary muscle dysfunction Transthoracic echocardiography with focused subvalvar apparatus imaging Transoesophageal and 3D echocardiography Cardiac MRI Cardiac catheterisation with transvalvar pressure measurement Electrocardiography Screening for associated Shone-complex left-heart obstructive lesions Anomalous mitral arcade, or hammock valve, is a rare congenital dysplasia in which the papillary muscles attach directly to the leaflet free edge through a bridging band of fibrous tissue, obliterating the normal chordae. It causes mixed mitral dysfunction, with regurgitation from restricted coaptation and stenosis from limited leaflet opening. It often forms part of the congenital mitral dysplasia spectrum and may coexist with parachute valve, supravalvar mitral ring and subaortic stenosis within Shone complex. Echocardiography shows papillary muscles displaced towards the annulus with a hammock-like subvalvar apparatus and thickened, immobile leaflet edges. It is distinguished from parachute mitral valve, in which chordae converge on a single papillary muscle, whereas the arcade shows direct muscular or fibrous attachment to the leaflet margin. Because chordal shortening tethers the leaflet tips while the body may still billow, the appearance should not be mistaken for prolapse. Surgical repair is difficult owing to the deficient subvalvar apparatus, and valve replacement is sometimes required. Heart failure or pulmonary oedema from severe mitral dysfunction Pulmonary hypertension Failure to thrive in infants Atrial arrhythmia with haemodynamic compromise Confusing arcade with parachute valve or rheumatic disease Missing associated Shone-complex lesions Mistaking tethered leaflet tips with a billowing body for prolapse Underestimating the stenosis component when regurgitation dominates the clinical picture The lesion results from abnormal development of the mitral tension apparatus in which the interchordal spaces fail to form. The papillary muscles insert directly onto the free margin of the anterior leaflet, or a continuous fibrous arcade bridges the papillary muscle tips along the leaflet edge, so that discrete chordae are effectively absent. The resulting tethering restricts leaflet excursion, producing regurgitation through failure of coaptation and stenosis through limited diastolic opening. The abnormality lies within the wider spectrum of congenital mitral valve dysplasia and commonly accompanies other left-heart obstructive lesions. Outcome depends on severity and associated lesions; mild disease may remain stable for years, but significant mixed mitral disease often needs repair or replacement, and the deficient subvalvar apparatus makes durable repair difficult.

Mitral Valve Prolapse — MVP, Systolic click-murmur syndrome, Barlow's syndrome, Floppy-valve syndrome, Billowing mitral leaflet syndrome Other causes of primary mitral regurgitation Rheumatic mitral valve disease (chordae thickened but not fused in MVP, unlike rheumatic disease) Innocent or functional systolic murmurs Angina pectoris (when atypical chest pain is present) ECG (often normal; may show biphasic or inverted T waves in leads II, III, aVF and supraventricular or ventricular premature beats) Transthoracic echocardiography to identify abnormal leaflet position and prolapse and define the >=2 mm displacement criterion Color flow and continuous-wave Doppler to assess associated MR and estimate severity Three-dimensional echocardiography and cardiac MRI for more precise LV volumes and detection of papillary muscle fibrosis/late gadolinium enhancement Transesophageal echocardiography when detailed anatomy is needed and for intraoperative or transcatheter procedural guidance Exercise testing (often with rest and immediate poststress TTE) to assess functional capacity, LV/RV function, dynamic MR, and pulmonary pressures Left ventriculography during catheterization (rarely necessary) MVP is a clinically variable syndrome arising from diverse pathologic mechanisms affecting the mitral valve apparatus, commonly excessive or redundant leaflet tissue associated with myxomatous degeneration and increased glycosaminoglycan concentrations (p.2057). It is the most common abnormality leading to primary mitral regurgitation and to mitral valve repair surgery, and in North America is now the most common cause of isolated severe MR requiring surgery (p.2057-2058). MVP is more common in women than men and typically presents between ages 15 and 30 with a generally benign course; in older patients (>50 years, often men) MR tends to be more severe because of chordal rupture (p.2058). The posterior leaflet is usually more affected than the anterior, the annulus is often dilated, and elongated, redundant, or ruptured chordae tendineae frequently cause or contribute to regurgitation (p.2058). The hallmark auscultatory finding is a mid- or late nonejection systolic click occurring 0.14 s or more after S1, often followed by a high-pitched mid-late systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur best heard at the apex, sometimes described as whooping or honking (p.2058). Dynamic auscultation aids diagnosis: standing, the strain phase of Valsalva, and any maneuver decreasing LV volume make the click and murmur occur earlier, whereas squatting and isometric exercise (increasing LV volume) delay the click-murmur complex and may make it disappear (p.2058). Murmur radiation depends on the leaflet involved: posterior leaflet prolapse directs the jet anteriorly with radiation toward the base, while anterior leaflet involvement directs the jet posteriorly with radiation to the axilla and back (p.2058). A useful echocardiographic definition is systolic displacement of the belly of the mitral leaflets by at least 2 mm into the left atrium above the plane of the mitral annulus in the parasternal long-axis view (p.2058). Chest pain in MVP is often substernal, prolonged, and unrelated to exertion, and only rarely resembles angina pectoris (p.2058). Most patients are asymptomatic and remain so for life; the disease may progress slowly over years to decades or worsen abruptly from chordal rupture or endocarditis (p.2058). MVP can occur as a rare sequel to acute rheumatic fever, in ischemic heart disease, in various cardiomyopathies, and in about 20% of patients with ostium secundum atrial septal defect (p.2058). Severe MR with depressed LV systolic function (highest risk for sudden death) Flail leaflet, which carries an excess risk of sudden death and usually accompanies severe MR High-grade ventricular ectopy with inferior-apical T-wave abnormalities, high-density premature ventricular complexes at rest, mitral annular disjunction, and papillary muscle fibrosis on cardiac MRI Syncope or light-headedness from arrhythmias Transient ischemic attacks from emboli due to endothelial disruption on the valve Features suggesting infective endocarditis in patients with MR and/or leaflet thickening Relying on a static exam can miss MVP; the click and murmur are dynamic and shift with maneuvers that alter LV volume (Valsalva/standing exaggerate, squatting/isometrics diminish them). Presentations vary: some patients have a mid-systolic click without a murmur, others a murmur without a click, and still others both at different times. The eccentric MR jet typical of MVP makes effective regurgitant orifice area and regurgitant volume difficult to assess with standard techniques. Atypical, prolonged, non-exertional chest pain may be misattributed to coronary disease and is often difficult to evaluate. Sudden death and significant arrhythmias can occur even in patients with normal LV size and function, so apparently low-risk patients are not entirely without risk. MVP results from myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve apparatus with excessive or redundant leaflet tissue and markedly increased glycosaminoglycan content. In many cases the cause is unknown, but some forms are genetically determined; reduced type III collagen production has been implicated, and electron microscopy shows fragmentation of collagen fibrils. Genome-wide association work has identified multiple genetic loci (candidate genes include LMCD1, SPTBN1, LTBP2, TGFB2, NMB, and ALPK3), and associations with LMNA, FLNC, and FLNA that are often expressed as cardiomyopathies. The posterior leaflet is typically more affected, the annulus is often dilated, and elongated, redundant, or ruptured chordae contribute to regurgitation. Prolapse may impose excessive stress on the papillary muscles, producing localized ischemia, infarction, and replacement fibrosis that can serve as a nidus for ventricular arrhythmias (visible as late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI even without coronary disease). Chordal rupture along with progressive annular dilation and calcification worsen regurgitation, placing further stress on the diseased apparatus in a self-perpetuating cycle (p.2057-2058). The clinical course is most often benign, and the majority of patients remain asymptomatic for their entire lives. In many the condition progresses gradually over years to decades, while in others it worsens rapidly from chordal rupture or endocarditis. Sudden death is a very rare complication, occurring most often with severe MR and depressed LV systolic function but possible even with normal LV size and function; a small high-risk subset has high-grade ventricular ectopy with characteristic imaging features, and patients with a flail leaflet carry an excess sudden-death risk (p.2058). Severity is anchored on the associated mitral regurgitation, ranging from a benign isolated systolic click with mild posterior-leaflet prolapse to severe MR from chordal rupture and leaflet flail. Echocardiographic prolapse is defined as >=2 mm systolic displacement of the leaflet belly into the left atrium above the annular plane (parasternal long-axis), with Doppler used to grade MR severity (p.2058).

Mittelschmerz — mid-cycle pain, ovulation pain, ovulatory pain, midcycle ovulatory pain Ectopic pregnancy Acute appendicitis Ovarian torsion Ruptured ovarian cyst Pelvic inflammatory disease Endometriosis Urinary or serum pregnancy test to exclude early or ectopic pregnancy Transvaginal ultrasound to assess the ovaries and exclude a cyst, torsion, or free fluid Full blood count and inflammatory markers if an infective or inflammatory cause is being considered Urinalysis to help exclude urinary tract infection or renal tract pathology Menstrual symptom diary correlating pain with the timing of ovulation Presents as recurrent unilateral lower abdominal or pelvic pain occurring around the middle of the menstrual cycle, roughly coinciding with ovulation Pain classically alternates sides between cycles depending on which ovary ovulates, and typically lasts from a few hours up to a couple of days The discomfort is usually mild to moderate and self-limiting, sometimes accompanied by light spotting or a small amount of physiological vaginal discharge It is fundamentally a clinical diagnosis of exclusion made from a characteristic cyclical history in an otherwise well woman Correlating symptoms with a menstrual diary and confirming the timing relative to ovulation supports the diagnosis and reassures the patient Management is generally conservative with reassurance and simple analgesia; suppression of ovulation with a combined oral contraceptive abolishes the pain in troublesome cases A positive pregnancy test in a woman with mid-cycle-type pain should always prompt exclusion of ectopic pregnancy rather than attribution to mittelschmerz A positive pregnancy test with pain, raising the possibility of ectopic pregnancy Signs of peritonitis, haemodynamic instability, or a tender palpable mass Fever or systemic upset suggesting infection rather than physiological pain Progressive, severe, or atypical pain that does not follow the expected mid-cycle pattern Attributing pain to mittelschmerz and thereby missing an ectopic pregnancy, torsion, or appendicitis Failing to confirm the cyclical mid-cycle pattern before making the diagnosis Over-investigating a clear, characteristic history in an otherwise well woman Overlooking that ovulation pain cannot occur when ovulation is suppressed, prompting a review of alternative causes The pain is attributed to the physiological events of ovulation. Rapid stretching of the ovarian capsule by the enlarging dominant follicle, followed by rupture of the follicle, releases follicular fluid together with a small quantity of blood into the peritoneal cavity. This fluid irritates the adjacent peritoneum and may provoke localised contraction of the fallopian tube and surrounding smooth muscle, producing transient unilateral pain on the side of the ovulating ovary. Mittelschmerz is a benign, self-limiting condition with an excellent outlook; symptoms resolve within a day or two each cycle and are readily controlled by ovulation suppression when they interfere with daily life.

immunosuppression Overlooking the very high creatine kinase as a clue to a dysferlinopathy Assuming a purely distal disorder, when proximal limb-girdle phenotypes share the same gene Attributing early calf weakness to a neuropathy rather than a myopathy Miyoshi myopathy is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in DYSF, the gene encoding dysferlin, a membrane protein concentrated at the disease-modifying strategies that lower toxic nucleosides are handled in specialist centres Intestinal pseudo-obstruction or perforation from diverticular disease Severe malnutrition and cachexia requiring nutritional rescue Aspiration from dysphagia and gastroparesis Rapidly progressive neuropathy causing loss of ambulation Misdiagnosing the cachexia and gastrointestinal symptoms as an eating disorder or functional gut disorder Overlooking the diagnosis because the leukoencephalopathy is often clinically silent Attributing ophthalmoplegia to an isolated ocular myopathy rather than the systemic disease Not measuring plasma nucleosides, the most accessible and specific biochemical clue MNGIE is caused by recessive loss-of-function mutations in TYMP, the gene encoding cytosolic thymidine phosphorylase. Without this enzyme, the pyrimidine nucleosides thymidine and deoxyuridine accumulate in blood and tissues. The resulting imbalance of the mitochondrial deoxyribonucleotide pool disturbs mitochondrial DNA replication, causing depletion, multiple deletions and point mutations and thereby a secondary failure of oxidative phosphorylation. The smooth muscle of the gut, peripheral nerves, extraocular muscles and cerebral white matter are particularly affected, producing the visceral myopathy and dysmotility, neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia and leukoencephalopathy that define the disorder. MNGIE is a progressive, life-limiting disorder; the relentless gastrointestinal dysmotility and cachexia are major contributors to morbidity and premature death, typically in early to mid adulthood without disease-modifying therapy.

Both disruptive/vascular and genetic mechanisms are implicated: proposed hypoxic-ischaemic interruption of the developing rhombencephalic vascular supply (associated with misoprostol exposure and, historically, chorionic villus sampling) and, less commonly, defined genetic causes. The end result is absent or deficient innervation of the muscles of facial expression and the lateral recti, on a background of rhombencephalic maldevelopment. Most cases are sporadic. Facial diplegia is permanent, but smile-reanimation surgery (such as gracilis free-muscle transfer) and strabismus surgery can improve function and appearance.

Modic changes — vertebral endplate signal changes, vertebral endplate marrow changes, Modic endplate changes Infective spondylodiscitis or vertebral osteomyelitis Metastatic marrow infiltration or myeloma Traumatic or insufficiency endplate fracture Seronegative spondyloarthropathy with Andersson lesions or corner inflammation Haemangioma or focal fatty marrow of the vertebral body Neuropathic (Charcot) spinal arthropathy Calcium pyrophosphate or crystal-related endplate change MRI including T1, T2 and fat-suppressed sequences to classify the change and assess the disc and marrow Contrast-enhanced MRI when infection or tumour is a concern Radiographs to demonstrate disc-space narrowing and endplate sclerosis Inflammatory markers and blood cultures if spondylodiscitis is suspected Image-guided biopsy or aspiration where infection or malignancy must be excluded Provocative discography only in selected cases when confirming a discogenic pain source Modic changes are MRI signal changes in the vertebral endplate and adjacent subchondral marrow that accompany degenerative disc disease, most often in the lower lumbar spine Type 1 represents oedema and fibrovascular marrow, appearing low on T1 and high on T2, and is the type most strongly associated with active low back pain and can enhance with contrast Type 2 represents fatty marrow replacement, appearing high on T1 and iso- to slightly hyperintense on T2, and is generally regarded as a more stable, less painful state Type 3 represents subchondral bony sclerosis, appearing low on both T1 and T2 and corresponding to endplate sclerosis on radiographs The types are dynamic and can convert into one another over time or coexist as mixed patterns, reflecting an evolving degenerative and reparative process The key differential for a painful type 1 change is infective spondylodiscitis; Microfractures and increased permeability of the endplate allow mechanical overload and biochemical exposure of subchondral marrow to disc material, provoking a local inflammatory and reparative response. In the acute type 1 pattern there is oedema, granulation tissue and fibrovascular marrow with an inflammatory infiltrate; over time this may resolve into type 2 fatty marrow replacement or type 3 subchondral sclerosis. Proposed drivers include mechanical stress, an autoimmune reaction to sequestered nucleus pulposus, and a contested hypothesis of low-grade colonisation by anaerobic skin organisms, though the changes are classified as a degenerative endplate and marrow phenomenon rather than an infective process. Associated inflammatory mediators sensitise nociceptive fibres in the endplate and outer disc, linking type 1 changes in particular to low back pain. Modic changes are common incidental findings whose clinical significance is variable; type 1 changes correlate best with low back pain and may fluctuate or convert to the more quiescent type 2, and their presence is only one modest factor in the overall prognosis of degenerative disc disease.

the young comprises several monogenic disorders in which a mutation in a single gene critical to pancreatic beta-cell development or function impairs insulin secretion. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, so an affected parent transmits the condition to roughly half of offspring, producing diabetes across successive generations at a young age. Unlike type 1 diabetes, there is no autoimmune beta-cell destruction, and unlike type 2 diabetes, obesity and insulin resistance are not central. Different causative genes give distinct clinical pictures, ranging from mild stable hyperglycaemia due to an altered glucose-sensing threshold, to progressive insulin secretory failure with risk of the usual diabetes complications. Prognosis varies by subtype: the mild glucose-sensing form is typically stable with low complication risk and may need no treatment, whereas transcription-factor subtypes are progressive and can develop classic microvascular and macrovascular complications if hyperglycaemia is uncontrolled; accurate genetic diagnosis enables tailored, often simpler, management.

associated limb and chest wall anomalies Attributing feeding difficulty solely to prematurity or reflux Moebius syndrome is best understood as a disruption sequence affecting the developing brainstem, live vaccines before the immune defect is excluded Failing to consider X-linked inheritance in an affected male Underestimating the variability in severity between patients Moesin belongs to the ezrin-radixin-moesin family of proteins that tether the cortical actin cytoskeleton to the cell membrane and thereby govern cell shape, membrane dynamics, and movement. In lymphocytes this linkage is required for the cytoskeletal rearrangements underlying migration through tissues, adhesion, and the formation of the immunological synapse during activation. Loss of moesin impairs these processes, so lymphocytes migrate and proliferate poorly and fail to survive in normal numbers, producing a combined lymphopenia of T, B, and natural killer cells. The defective leucocyte trafficking and activation leave the host prone to recurrent bacterial and viral infections, with herpesvirus reactivation reflecting the weakened cellular immunity. The prognosis is variable; some patients stabilise or improve on supportive treatment with immunoglobulin replacement and prophylaxis, while those with severe, persistent immunodeficiency may require haematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

deficiency by checking uric acid Molybdenum cofactor is a pterin-based cofactor synthesised through a multistep pathway (involving MOCS1, MOCS2 and gephyrin) that is essential for the activity of the The most damaging consequence is loss of sulphite oxidase, which normally converts sulphite to sulphate in cysteine catabolism; sulphite accumulates and is directly neurotoxic, while S-sulphocysteine builds up and may act as an excitotoxin. The classic neonatal form is usually devastating, with profound neurodevelopmental impairment and early death. Type A (MOCS1) disease may respond to early substrate replacement therapy, so prognosis can improve markedly when treatment is started before irreversible brain injury; type B and other genetic forms currently lack specific treatment.

anticoagulation or surgery Overlooking an underlying thrombophilia in recurrent or migratory cases Not addressing modifiable precipitants such as tight garments Mondor disease is a localised thrombophlebitis affecting the superficial veins that drain the breast and adjacent chest wall. Thrombosis of the vein, together with an inflammatory reaction in and around the vessel wall, converts the vein into a firm, tender, palpable cord. As the process organises and the vein retracts, traction on the overlying skin produces the characteristic linear groove or dimple. The trigger is often venous stasis or endothelial injury from trauma, surgery, or compression, in keeping with the classic contributors to thrombosis, though a proportion of cases have no identifiable cause. Mondor disease is benign and self-limiting, with the thrombosed cord typically resolving spontaneously over a few weeks with conservative measures, and recurrence is uncommon.

persistent lesions, or those combined with vascular birthmarks (phakomatosis pigmentovascularis), may occasionally signal an inborn error such as GM1 gangliosidosis or a mucopolysaccharidosis Aberrant lesions over unusual sites such as the shoulders or face overlap with naevus of Ito and naevus of Ota Lesions mistaken for bruising that raise safeguarding concerns, requiring careful documentation Extensive or persistent melanocytosis with dysmorphic features or organomegaly suggesting a lysosomal storage disease An associated vascular malformation indicating phakomatosis pigmentovascularis Atypical siting or nodular change prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Mistaking the blue-grey patch for a bruise and misattributing it to non-accidental injury Investigating or treating typical, self-limiting lesions unnecessarily Missing an underlying metabolic disorder in extensive, persistent melanocytosis Overlooking overlap with naevus of Ito or Ota when lesions occur at unusual sites During embryogenesis melanocytes derived from the neural crest normally migrate to the epidermis, but in dermal melanocytosis some are arrested within the dermis. Light scattering by this deep melanin produces the blue-grey colour, and most lesions involute as the ectopic melanocytes gradually disappear during childhood. Extensive or persistent lesions can rarely accompany lysosomal storage diseases, in which impaired clearance is thought to allow the melanocytosis to persist. Typical lumbosacral lesions are benign and usually fade by mid-childhood without treatment; aberrant, extensive or syndrome-associated lesions may persist and occasionally point to underlying systemic disease.

Monilethrix — beaded hair, moniliform hair, KRT81, KRT83, KRT86, DSG4 Pseudomonilethrix (an artefactual beading) Pili torti Trichorrhexis nodosa Netherton syndrome (trichorrhexis invaginata) Trichothiodystrophy Keratosis pilaris atrophicans / other follicular keratoses with alopecia Light microscopy of plucked or cut hairs showing regular beading Trichoscopy (dermoscopy) demonstrating the regularly bent, beaded shafts Molecular genetic testing of KRT81, KRT83, KRT86 and DSG4 Scalp examination for follicular keratosis and pattern of alopecia Family history and pedigree analysis Skin biopsy of scalp where the diagnosis is uncertain A hair-shaft disorder in which hairs show regular beading, with elliptical nodes and narrowed internodes, and fracture at the constrictions Presents with sparse, short, brittle hair and patchy alopecia, often with prominent follicular keratosis (keratosis pilaris), especially on the occiput and nape Onset is typically in infancy or early childhood after normal lanugo is shed Most cases are autosomal dominant due to mutations in hair-cortex keratin genes (KRT81, KRT83, KRT86); a recessive form is caused by DSG4 mutations Diagnosis is confirmed by light microscopy of hair showing the characteristic beaded (moniliform) shafts Severity varies and some improvement may occur with age, during summer, or in pregnancy Management is supportive with gentle hair care, emollients/keratolytics for follicular hyperkeratosis, and avoidance of trauma; oral retinoids have been tried in severe cases Extensive alopecia causing significant psychosocial distress Associated features suggesting a broader ectodermal or syndromic disorder Secondary infection or inflammation of hyperkeratotic follicles Atypical hair-shaft findings prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Mistaking the alopecia for alopecia areata or tinea and missing the diagnostic hair-shaft beading Failing to examine hairs microscopically, which is the key diagnostic step Confusing genuine monilethrix with artefactual pseudomonilethrix Aggressive cosmetic or chemical hair treatment that worsens breakage Monilethrix is usually an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the type II hair-cortex keratin genes KRT81, KRT83 and KRT86; a rarer autosomal recessive form results from mutations in DSG4 encoding desmoglein 4. These genes are essential for normal assembly of the keratin intermediate-filament network and cell adhesion within the hair cortex. The mutations produce periodic weakness along the hair shaft, giving alternating nodes (of normal calibre) and internodes (constricted, medulla-deficient segments). The narrowed internodes are mechanically fragile and fracture readily, so hairs break before reaching any length, producing the clinical picture of short, sparse, brittle hair with follicular hyperkeratosis. Monilethrix is a chronic condition, but it is compatible with normal health and often improves spontaneously with age, in summer months, or during pregnancy. Complete resolution is uncommon and hair fragility tends to persist, though severity fluctuates.

Mpox (Monkeypox) & Poxvirus Infections — mpox, monkeypox, molluscum contagiosum Varicella (Harrison 22e p.1519) Herpes simplex virus infection (Harrison 22e p.1519) Syphilis (anogenital mpox lesions may resemble STIs) (Harrison 22e p.1519) Gonorrhea (Harrison 22e p.1519) Chlamydia (Harrison 22e p.1519) Papillomavirus infection (Harrison 22e p.1519) Yaws (Harrison 22e p.1519) Cutaneous anthrax (particularly with parapoxvirus infections) (Harrison 22e p.1519) Smallpox (variola) - distinguished from mpox classically by absence of lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.1519) Varicella (Harrison 22e p.1519) Herpes simplex virus (Harrison 22e p.1519) Syphilis and other STIs (gonorrhea, chlamydia) in anogenital presentations (Harrison 22e p.1519) Yaws (Harrison 22e p.1519) Papillomavirus infection (Harrison 22e p.1519) Cutaneous anthrax (with parapoxvirus infections) (Harrison 22e p.1519) Malaria (tanapox initially presents with very high fever and may be mistaken for malaria in endemic areas) (Harrison 22e p.1519) Nucleic acid (molecular) testing is the most common diagnostic tool: PCR assays for non-variola orthopoxvirus (NVO), orthopoxvirus generic, generic mpox, and mpox clade II; sequencing for full isolate characterization (Harrison 22e p.1519). Multiplex assays combining NVO- and MPXV-specific targets, and clade-specific testing (U.S. Government and Public Health Laboratories), are available (Harrison 22e p.1519). Viral culture: orthopoxviruses grow well in standard clinical tissue culture; parapoxviruses are difficult to isolate (primary cells best); MCV cannot be cultured (Harrison 22e p.1519). Electron microscopy: characteristic large brick-shaped particles on negative stain for orthopoxvirus, yatapoxvirus, or MCV; parapoxviruses show an ovoid structure with crisscross spicules (Harrison 22e p.1519). Histopathology of biopsy: MCV shows classic Henderson-Patterson bodies (Harrison 22e p.1519). Serology can demonstrate orthopoxvirus reactivity but most assays cannot distinguish between orthopoxvirus species due to broad antigenic similarity (Harrison 22e p.1519). Classic mpox/smallpox prodrome: fever first, followed days later by rash; other prodromal features include malaise, sore throat, and headache (Harrison 22e p.1519). Lymphadenopathy is a key historical feature distinguishing mpox (present) from smallpox (absent) in endemic countries (Harrison 22e p.1519). Classic systemic orthopoxvirus rash evolves through macular, papular, vesicular, and pustular phases (the pustular stage with central umbilication), each stage lasting 2-3 days, with lesions in the same anatomic location typically at the same stage of development (Harrison 22e p.1519). Classic distribution is diffuse, well-circumscribed, and centrifugal: lesions more prominent on face and extremities (including palms and soles) than on the trunk; lesions are painful as they emerge and become pruritic in later stages (Harrison 22e p.1519). In the 2022 clade IIb outbreak, transmission was primarily through close, intimate (e.g., sexual) contact and predominantly affected gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (MSM) (Harrison 22e p.1518). Clade IIb mpox often departed from the classic picture: rash was frequently the first or only sign (prodrome absent or concurrent), lesions were often localized to the anogenital region, smaller, fewer (often <10), and could be at different stages at the same anatomic site (Harrison 22e p.1519). Up to 50% of those diagnosed during the 2022 outbreak in the U.S. context were also living with HIV (Harrison 22e p.1518). Molluscum contagiosum (MCV) has a classic pearly appearance that may umbilicate as it matures, with little surrounding inflammation and painless lesions that persist for months but gradually regress over 6-12 months (Harrison 22e p.1519). The infectious period for orthopoxvirus infections lasts from symptom onset until all lesions have crusted, the crusts have separated, and fresh healthy skin has formed underneath; lesion scabs contain viable virus (Harrison 22e p.1518). Two distinct MPXV clades exist: Clade I (formerly Congo Basin, Central Africa) causes a higher proportion of severe disease than Clade II (formerly West African); Clade II subdivides into IIa (endemic West Africa) and IIb (spread worldwide in 2022) (Harrison 22e p.1517). Severe immunocompromise (advanced HIV with CD4 <200 cells/mm3, especially <50; organ transplantation) predisposes to severe, disseminated, prolonged mpox with numerous large coalescing or necrotic lesions and multi-organ involvement (GI tract, liver, lungs, brain) (Harrison 22e p.1519). Ocular involvement: eye pain, redness, vision changes/loss, periorbital swelling, blepharitis, conjunctivitis, keratitis - can result in vision loss (Harrison 22e p.1519). Neurologic complications: encephalitis, myelitis - severe headache, neck pain, altered mentation, focal deficits (Harrison 22e p.1519). Myopericarditis: dyspnea or palpitations with elevated cardiac biomarkers and ECG changes (Harrison 22e p.1519). Mucosal complications affecting alimentation, urination, or defecation due to painful or obstructive lesions; may lead to strictures, edema, and severe lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.1519). Most deaths have occurred predominantly among people with advanced HIV and CD4 <50 cells/mm3 (Harrison 22e p.1519). Do not assume a classic systemic presentation: during the 2022 clade IIb outbreak rash was often the first/only sign with prodrome absent, lesions localized to the anogenital area, smaller, fewer (<10), and could be at different stages at the same site - contrary to the classic rule that lesions in the same location are at the same stage (Harrison 22e p.1519). Anogenital mpox lesions can be mistaken for common STIs (gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis); up to 10% of mpox patients may be coinfected with an STI, so a positive STI test does not exclude mpox (Harrison 22e p.1519). Characteristic lesions plus exposure history narrow the differential, but laboratory testing is required to confirm the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1519). Distinguish mpox from varicella (VZV), herpes simplex, and syphilis - overlapping vesiculopustular/anogenital presentations are a recognized diagnostic trap (Harrison 22e p.1519). MCV cannot be cultured, so reliance on culture for diagnosis of molluscum is futile; biopsy (Henderson-Patterson bodies) or clinical/EM findings are needed (Harrison 22e p.1519). Poxviruses are large double-stranded DNA viruses that replicate entirely in the cytoplasm. Orthopoxvirus infection (variola, MPXV) is thought to involve systemic spread from the inoculation site to local lymph nodes, seeding of lymphoreticular tissue, and then symptomatic (febrile) viremia with viral skin tropism; disease severity reflects how well innate immune and interferon responses control early infection. Immunocompetent hosts develop lesions (often at the exposure site) about 1 week after exposure, progressing through staged phases over 7-14 days with scabbing and resolution by 14-21 days after rash onset. In severe immunocompromise (e.g., advanced HIV with CD4 <200 cells/mm3, organ transplantation), MPXV spread/growth goes unchecked, producing wide dissemination with large confluent lesions persisting for months and additional organ involvement. Most other poxvirus infections (e.g., parapoxviruses, MCV) involve only local viral growth at the inoculation site; yatapoxvirus (tanapox) pathogenesis is poorly understood (Harrison 22e p.1518). In immunocompetent hosts most poxvirus infections are self-limited, resolving in weeks (or months for molluscum contagiosum). Exceptions are the generalized orthopoxvirus infections caused by MPXV and variola, which carry higher case-fatality. In unvaccinated individuals smallpox mortality is up to 30%; MPXV mortality is approximately 1.4-10% (clade I), ~1% (clade IIa), and <1% (clade IIb). Immunocompromised hosts may have more severe orthopoxvirus and parapoxvirus disease (severe mpox, progressive vaccinia, eczema vaccinatum, severe borealpox) with higher mortality, or atypical presentations (e.g., giant orf). In advanced HIV, effective antiretroviral therapy is essential to favorable outcomes. MCV can be diffuse in the immunocompromised, and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) has been associated with recrudescence of MCV. Poxvirus reinfections are seldom reported (Harrison 22e p.1521). Mpox ranges from typical self-limited disease (immunocompetent, including HIV with CD4 >200 cells/mm3, generally without increased severity) to severe mpox. Severe manifestations include ocular infection, neurologic complications (encephalitis, myelitis), myopericarditis, obstructive mucosal disease, and uncontrolled viral replication with disseminated/necrotic lesions and multi-organ involvement, occurring chiefly in severely immunocompromised patients (advanced HIV, organ transplantation). Clade I causes a higher proportion of severe disease than clade II (Harrison 22e p.1519).

against the underlying clone to remove the pathogenic protein and preserve kidney function, and disease can recur after transplantation if the clone persists Rapidly progressive renal impairment threatening dialysis dependence Nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia Features suggesting systemic amyloidosis or evolving overt malignancy Recurrence of disease in a kidney transplant Dismissing a small monoclonal protein as benign despite unexplained kidney disease Not performing a renal biopsy to define the specific lesion Failing to confirm that the renal deposits match the circulating paraprotein Transplanting the kidney without controlling the underlying clone, risking recurrence Monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance describes kidney injury caused by a monoclonal immunoglobulin or its fragments secreted by a small, non-malignant B-cell or plasma-cell clone. Despite a low tumour burden, the abnormal protein has physicochemical properties that make it nephrotoxic: it may deposit in glomerular or tubular basement membranes, form organised fibrils or crystals, aggregate within proximal tubular cells, or activate complement, depending on its structure. These mechanisms produce a spectrum of glomerular and tubulointerstitial lesions. Because damage stems from the protein rather than tumour bulk, effective treatment must suppress the clone that produces it. Kidney outcome depends on early recognition and effective clone-directed therapy; timely treatment can stabilise or improve renal function, whereas delayed diagnosis often leads to irreversible kidney failure, and the disease may recur after transplantation if the clone is not controlled.

A clonal mast cell population, frequently harbouring the KIT D816V mutation, is present but the burden and features fall short of the diagnostic threshold for systemic mastocytosis. These clonal mast cells are prone to activation and mediator release, producing episodic symptoms such as flushing, hypotension and anaphylaxis, often with an identifiable trigger such as insect venom. Prognosis is generally favourable with mediator-directed therapy and anaphylaxis management, though patients remain at risk of severe reactions and require monitoring for progression.

monocular elevation deficiency — double elevator palsy, monocular elevation deficit Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles Brown syndrome, which limits elevation only in adduction (key distinction) Inferior rectus restriction from thyroid eye disease or an orbital floor fracture with entrapment Congenital superior-division third nerve palsy Superior oblique overaction and other causes of vertical strabismus Skew deviation and supranuclear vertical gaze disturbance Congenital ptosis with an apparent (pseudo) motility defect Forced duction testing for inferior rectus restriction and force generation testing Orthoptic assessment across all positions of gaze with measurement of head posture Assessment of Bell's phenomenon and saccadic velocities Cycloplegic refraction and amblyopia evaluation Distinguishing true ptosis from pseudoptosis by rechecking lid height on fixation with the affected eye Orbital CT or MRI if restriction from trauma, thyroid disease or a mass is suspected Neuro-imaging if a supranuclear cause is suspected A unilateral limitation of elevation of one eye in all horizontal positions, affecting the action of both elevators (superior rectus and inferior oblique), hence the older term double elevator palsy Usually congenital: the affected eye is hypotropic in the primary position and the patient adopts a chin-up head posture to maintain binocular single vision Ptosis or pseudoptosis is common; true ptosis occurs in roughly half of cases, and pseudoptosis from the hypotropic globe resolves when the eye elevates to fixate Three mechanisms are recognised: restriction of the inferior rectus (positive forced duction, the commonest), primary elevator weakness (superior rectus and inferior oblique paresis), and a supranuclear cause Forced duction and force generation testing differentiate a tight (restrictive) inferior rectus from a paretic cause and guide the choice of operation If the patient fixates with the affected hypotropic eye, the sound eye shows a secondary hypertropia; a preserved Bell's phenomenon points to a supranuclear or paretic rather than restrictive mechanism Marcus Gunn jaw-winking and other synkineses should be excluded when ptosis is present Surgical choice depends on mechanism: inferior rectus recession for restriction and a Knapp procedure (transposition of the horizontal recti towards the superior rectus) for elevator weakness An acquired (rather than congenital) elevation deficit suggesting orbital, neurological or thyroid pathology Signs of an orbital floor fracture with inferior rectus entrapment, including recent trauma and an oculocardiac reflex Pupillary involvement or other neurological signs suggesting a third nerve or midbrain lesion Amblyopia in a young child requiring prompt treatment Confusing the condition with Brown syndrome, which limits elevation only in adduction Operating on ptosis before correcting the hypotropia, when pseudoptosis may resolve once the eye is realigned Omitting forced ductions and thereby missing a restrictive inferior rectus, leading to the wrong operation Overlooking amblyopia in the hypotropic eye Assuming every case is paretic and missing a supranuclear cause by not checking Bell's phenomenon Monocular elevation deficiency is a heterogeneous condition characterised by defective elevation of one eye. The commonest mechanism is a restrictive, tight inferior rectus (fibrosis) that mechanically prevents elevation; alternatively there may be a primary paresis of the elevator muscles (superior rectus and inferior oblique) or, less often, a supranuclear lesion of the elevation pathway in the pretectal region, in which case Bell's phenomenon is preserved. Many cases are congenital and may fall within the congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder spectrum. The resulting hypotropia in the primary position drives the compensatory chin-up head posture and, where the visual axes are not aligned, amblyopia of the affected eye. Congenital cases are non-progressive, and surgery to correct the hypotropia and abnormal head posture, combined with amblyopia treatment and ptosis repair where needed, generally gives good functional and cosmetic outcomes. Some limitation of elevation typically persists.

amblyopia threatening visual development in a child An unexplained macular lesion found on examination requiring further assessment Diplopia developing where none was present, indicating loss of suppression Overlooking the small deviation on standard cover testing and labelling the patient orthotropic Missing coexisting amblyopia in the non-fixating eye Attempting to eliminate the small residual angle surgically and inducing intractable diplopia Failing to correct anisometropia that underlies the condition Monofixation syndrome reflects a compromise in binocular sensory function in which a small central suppression scotoma develops in one eye to eliminate diplopia and confusion, while peripheral retinal correspondence and fusion are retained. This produces a stable small-angle deviation. Recognised triggers include anisometropia (unequal refraction), a small unilateral macular lesion, and residual misalignment after correction of a larger childhood strabismus. Because high-grade central stereopsis is lost but peripheral fusion persists, stereoacuity is reduced but not abolished, and the patient retains a degree of comfortable binocular vision. Monofixation syndrome is a stable and often favourable sensory state that provides peripheral fusion and gross stereopsis; many patients remain comfortably aligned long term, although associated amblyopia needs monitoring and the small deviation may occasionally decompensate.

settings Mononeuritis multiplex arises from multifocal damage to individual peripheral nerves, most classically through occlusion or inflammation of the vasa nervorum (nerve ischaemia) in systemic or Ischaemic infarction of nerve fascicles produces predominantly axonal loss in the territories supplied by affected vessels, explaining the patchy, asymmetric deficits. Other mechanisms include direct infiltration, compression at multiple sites, immune-mediated demyelination, and metabolic injury as in diabetes. The random distribution reflects the scattered nature of the underlying microvascular or infiltrative lesions. Outcome depends on the underlying cause and the speed of treatment; vasculitic cases can recover substantially if immunosuppression is started before extensive axonal infarction, but delayed treatment or severe systemic disease leaves persistent deficits.

Because the radius and ulna are coupled proximally through the annular ligament and the proximal radioulnar joint, ulnar deformity displaces the radial head from its articulation with the capitellum. Restoring anatomical ulnar length and curvature is therefore essential, as residual ulnar malalignment leaves the radial head subluxed or dislocated. The dislocating radial head can also stretch or injure the posterior interosseous nerve as it passes around the radial neck. Anatomical restoration of ulnar length and alignment usually re-establishes radiocapitellar congruity with a good outcome; missed dislocation, ulnar malreduction or nerve injury worsen the result.

ulcer is thought to be an autoimmune peripheral ulcerative keratitis in which an immune response against corneal stromal antigens leads to progressive destruction. Autoantibodies and cell-mediated inflammation recruit neutrophils and activate collagenolytic and proteolytic enzymes from the limbal vessels and adjacent conjunctiva, degrading peripheral corneal stroma. The ulcer advances circumferentially and centrally with a characteristic undermined edge, and the sclera is spared. Progressive stromal melting can lead to marked thinning, irregular astigmatism, and perforation. Because the process is inflammatory rather than infective, treatment is directed at suppressing the immune response. The limited unilateral form in older patients often responds to treatment, whereas the bilateral aggressive form can be relentless, causing severe thinning, perforation, and significant visual loss despite immunosuppression.

Underestimating the risk of complications when advising conservative management The foramen of Morgagni is a small anterior triangular gap between the sternal and costal muscular origins of the diaphragm, where the superior epigastric vessels pass. A congenital weakness or failure of muscular fusion at this point leaves a retrosternal defect through which abdominal contents, carried within a peritoneal sac, can herniate into the thorax. Raised intra-abdominal pressure from obesity, pregnancy, constipation, or exertion promotes progressive herniation, which is why many cases only become apparent in adult life. Herniated omentum or bowel is usually asymptomatic but can become obstructed, incarcerated, or strangulated. The outlook after elective repair is excellent with low recurrence, whereas emergency presentation with incarceration or strangulation carries higher morbidity, which is the rationale for repairing even asymptomatic hernias.

abnormal development of the optic nerve head and surrounding neuroectodermal and mesodermal tissues. The result is a large, funnel-shaped excavation of the disc with a central glial remnant, a raised pigmented peripapillary ring and anomalous radiating retinal vessels. Because these structures develop alongside midline forebrain and vascular elements, the anomaly is frequently accompanied by midline brain defects, hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction and cerebral arterial anomalies such as moyamoya. Vision in the affected eye is usually poor and often does not improve, and serous detachment can worsen it; systemic outcome depends on the associated central nervous system, vascular and endocrine anomalies.

Morphea — localised scleroderma, circumscribed scleroderma, morphoea Systemic sclerosis (must be distinguished as it involves internal organs) Lichen sclerosus (can coexist and overlap clinically) Eosinophilic fasciitis Scleredema and scleromyxoedema Chronic graft-versus-host disease with sclerodermatous features Lipodermatosclerosis and post-radiation fibrosis Skin biopsy, ideally deep enough to assess dermis, subcutis, and fascia, to confirm the diagnosis and subtype Clinical assessment for systemic sclerosis features, with autoantibody testing where indicated Imaging (including MRI) in linear or deep disease to define extent and detect muscle, bone, or CNS involvement Ophthalmology and neurology review for craniofacial linear disease Serial mapping or scoring of lesions to monitor activity and progression Morphea is a localised sclerosing disorder of the skin that, unlike systemic sclerosis, spares the internal organs and is not accompanied by Raynaud phenomenon or sclerodactyly Early plaques are erythematous or violaceous and indurated, evolving into firm, waxy, ivory-coloured centres often surrounded by a lilac inflammatory ring that signals active disease Subtypes include circumscribed (plaque) morphea, generalised, linear, and deep forms, each with different distribution and complication profiles Linear morphea in children can cross joints and, when it affects the limbs or face, may impair growth, cause contractures, or produce the en coup de sabre pattern on the forehead Facial and periorbital linear disease warrants assessment for underlying neurological and ophthalmological involvement Treatment aims to halt inflammation during the active phase, since established sclerosis and atrophy are difficult to reverse; options range from topical and phototherapy approaches to systemic immunomodulation in extensive or deep disease Physiotherapy and monitoring for joint contractures are important in linear and deep subtypes Distinguish morphea from systemic sclerosis clinically and, if needed, serologically, to avoid unnecessary alarm and inappropriate investigation Craniofacial linear morphea (en coup de sabre / Parry-Romberg) with neurological symptoms, seizures, or eye involvement Rapidly extending or deep lesions crossing joints and threatening contractures Growth disturbance or limb length discrepancy in affected children Extensive generalised disease causing functional impairment Diagnostic uncertainty where systemic sclerosis cannot be confidently excluded Confusing morphea with systemic sclerosis and triggering unnecessary anxiety or investigation Missing the active inflammatory (lilac ring) phase when treatment is most effective Underappreciating growth and contracture risk in paediatric linear disease Failing to screen for neurological and ocular involvement in craniofacial disease Assuming established sclerosis will respond to anti-inflammatory therapy Morphea is an immune-mediated fibrosing process in which an initial inflammatory phase, characterised by a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate and endothelial activation, is followed by excessive deposition of collagen in the dermis and, in deeper subtypes, the subcutis and fascia. Dysregulated production of pro-fibrotic cytokines and growth factors drives fibroblasts to lay down dense, thickened collagen bundles, with loss of adnexal structures and normal fat. Vascular changes and, in some cases, autoimmune associations contribute. The result is progressive induration and, later, atrophy; when fibrosis extends across joints or affects growing tissues in children, functional and cosmetic sequelae follow. Many plaque-type lesions eventually become inactive over several years, leaving pigmentary change and atrophy, whereas linear and deep subtypes, particularly in children, carry a higher risk of lasting functional and cosmetic sequelae; early treatment of the inflammatory phase improves outcomes.

dysplasia without measuring glycosaminoglycans Missing Morquio B because of overlap with GM1 gangliosidosis phenotypes Assuming normal urinary keratan sulfate excludes the diagnosis in older patients Morquio syndrome is caused by deficiency of enzymes needed to degrade keratan sulfate. In type A, biallelic GALNS variants cause deficiency of N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase; in type B, GLB1 variants cause deficiency of beta-galactosidase. The resulting block in keratan sulfate (and, in type A, also chondroitin-6-sulfate) degradation leads to lysosomal accumulation, which disproportionately affects cartilage and bone and produces the distinctive spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia. Because keratan sulfate is concentrated in cartilage and cornea rather than the brain, intelligence is characteristically normal. Excess keratan sulfate is excreted in the urine, though levels can normalise with age. Both subtypes are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Intelligence is preserved and survival into adulthood is usual, but skeletal complications, especially cervical instability and restrictive respiratory disease, cause significant morbidity and can be life-threatening if unrecognised. Enzyme replacement therapy is available for type A and may improve endurance and some somatic features.

plantar interdigital nerve rather than a genuine tumour. The nerve is irritated where it passes beneath the deep transverse intermetatarsal ligament, and the third web space is especially vulnerable where medial and lateral plantar nerve contributions converge. Repetitive dorsiflexion in narrow footwear causes chronic compression and traction, leading to perineural fibrosis, endoneurial oedema and thickening of the nerve, which generate the characteristic neuritic pain. Many patients improve with footwear modification and injection, and surgical excision gives good relief, though it carries a risk of a recurrent stump neuroma and a permanent patch of sensory loss between the toes.

Morvan syndrome is an autoimmune disorder in which antibodies against the voltage-gated potassium channel complex, most often the CASPR2 protein, disrupt neuronal excitability. CASPR2 is expressed at juxtaparanodal regions of peripheral nerves and within limbic and thalamic circuits, so loss of its function produces both continuous peripheral motor nerve firing and central nervous system dysfunction. The result is peripheral nerve hyperexcitability with neuromyotonia, autonomic overactivity, and an encephalopathy dominated by intractable insomnia and fluctuating cognition. A subset is paraneoplastic, driven by thymoma, which sustains the aberrant immune response. With immunotherapy and removal of any associated tumour many patients improve substantially, but relapses occur and paraneoplastic cases carry the prognosis of the underlying malignancy. Autonomic instability can be life-threatening during the acute phase.

Mosaic variegated aneuploidy syndrome — MVA, MVA syndrome, BUB1B-related mosaic variegated aneuploidy, mosaic variegated aneuploidy syndrome 1 Constitutional mismatch repair deficiency Fanconi anaemia and other chromosome-breakage syndromes Nijmegen breakage syndrome Primary microcephaly syndromes without aneuploidy Seckel syndrome and microcephalic primordial dwarfism Other cancer-predisposition syndromes presenting in early childhood Cytogenetic karyotyping of multiple cells to demonstrate variegated mosaic aneuploidy Molecular genetic testing of BUB1B, CEP57, and TRIP13 MRI of the brain to assess microcephaly and posterior fossa anomalies such as Dandy-Walker malformation Tumour surveillance imaging, particularly abdominal ultrasound for Wilms tumour Ophthalmological examination for cataract and other anomalies Developmental assessment and, where relevant, EEG for seizures The defining laboratory feature is constitutional mosaic aneuploidy, with different cells carrying gains or losses of various chromosomes (variegated), typically involving a substantial proportion of cells on cytogenetic study Clinically it presents with severe microcephaly, pre- and postnatal growth restriction, and developmental delay There is a strong predisposition to childhood cancers, particularly Wilms tumour, rhabdomyosarcoma, and leukaemia, reflecting genome instability The most recognised cause is biallelic variants in BUB1B, which encodes BUBR1, a core component of the mitotic spindle assembly checkpoint; other causes include CEP57 and TRIP13 Additional features can include Dandy-Walker malformation and other brain anomalies, cataracts and other eye abnormalities, and seizures Diagnosis combines cytogenetic demonstration of multiple aneuploidies across cells with molecular confirmation of the causative gene Management is supportive with heightened tumour surveillance, since early detection of embryonal tumours is central to care An abdominal mass, haematuria, or other features suggesting Wilms tumour or another embryonal malignancy Pancytopenia or other haematological abnormalities suggesting leukaemia Rapidly enlarging head or signs of raised intracranial pressure New seizures or acute neurological deterioration Dismissing an isolated aneuploid cell on karyotype without recognising the pattern of variegated mosaic aneuploidy Failing to institute tumour surveillance and thereby missing early, treatable embryonal tumours Overlooking posterior fossa malformations on neuroimaging Not recognising the autosomal recessive inheritance and its implications for recurrence risk The syndrome is a chromosome-instability disorder arising, in its classic form, from biallelic loss-of-function variants in BUB1B, which encodes BUBR1, an essential protein of the spindle assembly checkpoint. This checkpoint normally delays progression through mitosis until all chromosomes are correctly attached to the spindle, preventing missegregation. When checkpoint function is impaired, chromosomes are distributed unequally to daughter cells, generating the characteristic mosaic pattern of gains and losses across many different chromosomes. The resulting aneuploidy and genomic instability drive the growth failure, microcephaly, neurodevelopmental impairment, and the marked predisposition to embryonal tumours. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The prognosis is generally guarded, reflecting the combination of severe growth and neurodevelopmental impairment and a high risk of early childhood malignancy. Outcomes depend substantially on the specific genotype and on whether tumours are detected and treated early through surveillance.

suggesting migraine or other pathology Giving preventive medication after symptoms are already established, when it is less effective Overlooking an underlying vestibular disorder or migraine in atypical cases Ignoring sedation from antihistamine or anticholinergic drugs in those who must remain alert Failing to advise simple positional and visual strategies alongside medication Motion sickness is attributed to a mismatch between the movement information the brain receives from the vestibular apparatus, the visual system, and proprioceptors, and the pattern it expects from prior experience. This sensory conflict is processed in the vestibular and brainstem pathways and activates the emetic centres, producing autonomic features such as pallor, sweating, salivation, and nausea culminating in vomiting. A classic example is reading in a moving vehicle, where the eyes signal a stable scene while the vestibular system detects motion. Repeated exposure allows central adaptation and habituation. Motion sickness resolves once the provoking motion ceases and susceptibility often lessens with habituation; it is benign, though it can be disabling during travel and, in prolonged exposure such as at sea, may cause dehydration.

outpouchings Pulmonary function tests including flow-volume loops Sputum microbiology in recurrent infection Assessment for associated bronchiectasis and connective tissue disease A rare condition of marked dilatation of the trachea and main bronchi (tracheobronchomegaly) due to atrophy or deficiency of elastic and smooth-muscle tissue in the airway wall Redundant airway mucosa herniates between and bronchial diameters on CT above defined thresholds, alongside the typical clinical picture Bronchoscopy shows a widened, flaccid airway with mucosal outpouchings between cartilaginous rings
