and attributing recurrent infection to ordinary bronchiectasis without noting the megatrachea Failing to measure airway diameters on CT Missing the diagnostic clue of tracheal diverticulosis and a corrugated airway Not addressing dynamic airway collapse contributing to poor secretion clearance Mounier-Kuhn syndrome is characterised by atrophy or congenital deficiency of the elastic fibres and smooth muscle of the tracheal and bronchial walls, which causes progressive dilatation of these large airways. The weakened wall allows the mucous membrane to bulge outward between the cartilage rings, forming diverticula and giving a scalloped contour, and the flaccid airway collapses excessively during expiration and coughing. This dynamic collapse and enlargement impair the effectiveness of cough and mucociliary clearance, leading to retained secretions, recurrent infection, and secondary bronchiectasis. Most cases are considered congenital, and associations with connective tissue disorders have been described. The course is variable; some patients remain relatively stable with airway clearance and prompt treatment of infections, while others develop progressive bronchiectasis and respiratory impairment, and prognosis is largely determined by the extent of secondary lung damage.

Movement Disorders (Tremor, Chorea, Dystonia) — essential tremor, Huntington disease, dystonia, chorea Parkinson's disease (rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia) — see parkinsons_disease Progressive supranuclear palsy (axial rigidity, vertical gaze palsy, early falls) Multiple-system atrophy and corticobasal syndrome (asymmetric akinesia, rigidity, dystonia, myoclonus, alien limb) Orthostatic tremor (high-frequency low-amplitude leg tremor, shakiness on standing relieved by sitting/walking) Drug-induced/tardive dyskinesia from D2-blocking agents Sydenham's chorea / post-streptococcal autoimmune chorea Sydenham's chorea following group A streptococcal infection (acute rheumatic fever) Other post-infectious or autoimmune (paraneoplastic) chorea and movement disorders Genetic testing for the CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion when Huntington's disease is suspected Serum ceruloplasmin (low), 24-h urinary copper (elevated), slit-lamp exam for Kayser-Fleischer rings, and liver copper to evaluate for Wilson's disease in any young patient with unexplained chorea, dystonia, tremor or parkinsonism Echocardiography when chorea suggests acute rheumatic fever (>50% have carditis); anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B titers for preceding streptococcal infection MRI brain to assess for basal ganglia and other structural/degenerative changes Wilson's disease (copper accumulation; young patient with chorea, dystonia, parkinsonism or tremor) Drug-induced movements from dopamine-receptor blockers (tardive dyskinesia, acute dystonia) Functional (psychogenic) movement disorder Hyperthyroidism (fine tremor; chorea rare) Movement disorders are classified as hypokinetic (poverty of movement, e.g. parkinsonism with rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia) versus hyperkinetic (excess movement, e.g. chorea, dystonia, tremor); the rest tremor and cogwheel rigidity of Parkinson's disease are extrapyramidal signs distinct from the action tremor of essential tremor (Harrison 22e p.3508; cf. p.197 ch.31). Essential tremor is an action/postural tremor; a key pitfall is mislabeling it as Parkinson's disease, but Parkinson tremor is characteristically a rest tremor accompanied by cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia, whereas essential tremor lacks these and worsens with sustained posture or movement (Harrison 22e p.3508). Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant degenerative disorder producing the triad of chorea, psychiatric/behavioral disturbance (mood, anxiety, psychosis), and progressive dementia; the unpredictable choreic movements give the gait a characteristic dancing quality (Harrison 22e p.3508; gait described p.~3535 ch.32; HD as autosomal-dominant dementia p.198 ch.31). Dystonia is defined as sustained muscle contractions producing repetitive twisting movements and abnormal posture; it often has a genetic basis, but new asymmetric dystonia—particularly involving gait—in a younger adult may be an early sign of Parkinson's disease (Harrison 22e p.3508; cf. gait chapter p.~3535). Sydenham's chorea (a manifestation of acute rheumatic fever after group A streptococcal infection) is the prototypical post-infectious chorea: it occurs mainly in females after a prolonged latent period, affects especially the head (darting tongue movements) and upper limbs, may be generalized or hemichoreic, and is frequently accompanied by emotional lability or obsessive-compulsive traits; >50% of patients presenting with chorea have carditis, so echocardiography is warranted (Harrison 22e p.3508; ch. on rheumatic fever p.~2992). Tardive dyskinesia is a drug-induced hyperkinetic disorder seen with chronic exposure to antipsychotics and other agents that block the D2 dopamine receptor, and is a common cause of stereotypic movement and gait disturbances (Harrison 22e p.3508). New chorea, dystonia, tremor or parkinsonism in an adolescent or young adult — exclude Wilson's disease (treatable; look for Kayser-Fleischer rings, low ceruloplasmin, high urinary copper) before manifestations become irreversible Chorea with autosomal dominant family history plus psychiatric change and cognitive decline — consider Huntington's disease Acute chorea (especially in a young female) — evaluate for acute rheumatic fever and carditis with echocardiography Abnormal movements in a patient on long-term antipsychotics/D2 blockers — recognize tardive dyskinesia and acute dystonic reactions Misdiagnosing essential (action) tremor as Parkinson's disease, or vice versa — Parkinson tremor is a rest tremor with cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia Failing to test for Wilson's disease in a young patient with new movement disorder; Wilson's may present with chronic hepatitis long before neurologic signs or Kayser-Fleischer rings appear Overlooking carditis in a patient presenting with chorea (Sydenham's), since chorea may be the sole or delayed manifestation of rheumatic fever Not recognizing drug-induced/tardive movements from D2-blocking medications Movement disorders arise predominantly from dysfunction of the basal ganglia (striatum = caudate plus putamen) and their cortical and thalamic connections, which modulate motor output rather than directly generating it; disruption of these circuits yields either hypokinetic syndromes (parkinsonism) or hyperkinetic syndromes (chorea, dystonia, tremor). Huntington's disease is caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat (autosomal dominant) with degeneration of the striatum. Wilson's disease results from impaired copper excretion with copper accumulation in liver and brain. Tardive dyskinesia reflects chronic blockade of striatal D2 dopamine receptors (Harrison 22e p.3508; basal ganglia/striatum anatomy p.~199-200 ch.31). Prognosis is disorder-specific. Essential tremor is typically slowly progressive and non-degenerative. Huntington's disease is relentlessly progressive and degenerative. Wilson's disease can improve substantially with prompt diagnosis and copper-chelating treatment before end-stage manifestations become irreversible. Sydenham's chorea is usually self-limited, with choreiform movements resolving within about 6 weeks, occasionally up to 6 months, though associated obsessive-compulsive or emotional symptoms may persist longer (Harrison 22e p.3508; Wilson p.~2713 ch.355; chorea p.~2992). No single unified severity scale spans all movement disorders; assessment is disorder-specific and functional. Chorea, for example, ranges from movements evident only on careful examination in mild cases to inability to perform activities of daily living in severe cases (Harrison 22e p.3508).

Intimal thickening from smooth muscle cell proliferation and luminal narrowing reduce anterior circulation flow, prompting the growth of fragile lenticulostriate and leptomeningeal collateral networks that give the smoky angiographic appearance. cord atrophy correlates more strongly) (p.3583) T1 imaging for 'black holes' (markers of irreversible demyelination and axonal loss) (p.3583) Visual, somatosensory, brainstem-auditory, and motor evoked potentials (p.3583-3584) Workup to exclude mimics in suspected MS: ESR, serum B12, antinuclear antibodies, and treponemal antibody (p.3585) NMOSD (anti-AQP4) and MOGAD - consider with bilateral/severe optic neuritis or severe transverse myelitis (p.3584) ADEM - consider with hyperacute or postinfectious presentation (p.3584) Tumefactive demyelination mimicking a primary or metastatic brain tumor (p.3584, 3589) Sarcoidosis, Sjogren's syndrome, SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, vasculitis (p.3584-3585) Vitamin B12 deficiency, hereditary leukodystrophies, CADASIL, MELAS (p.3585) MS is defined by lesions disseminated in both time and space: plaques arise at different times and in anatomically separate CNS sites (p.3577). Typical onset is age 20-40 (slightly later in men); women are affected roughly three times as often as men (p.3577). The most common presenting symptoms are sensory loss (~37%) and optic neuritis (~36%), followed by limb weakness (~35%) and paresthesias (p.3577). Optic neuritis usually causes monocular reduced acuity, dimness, and color desaturation, with periorbital pain worsened by eye movement and an afferent pupillary defect; uveitis is uncommon and should prompt thought of sarcoidosis or lymphoma (p.3577). A bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia (impaired adduction with nystagmus of the abducting eye, from a medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion) is particularly suggestive of MS; related gaze findings include horizontal gaze palsy and the 'one-and-a-half' syndrome (p.3578). Lhermitte's symptom is a neck-flexion-induced electric-shock sensation radiating down the spine/legs; it is not specific to MS and can occur with other cervical cord disease such as spondylosis (p.3578). Uhthoff's symptom (heat sensitivity) is transient worsening of neurologic symptoms with elevated core temperature (hot shower, exercise, fever) and reflects temperature-dependent conduction block rather than a true new lesion (p.3578). Exercise-induced weakness is characteristic; weakness is of upper-motor-neuron type with spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses, though a tendon reflex can occasionally be lost if a plaque disrupts the afferent reflex arc (p.3578). Paroxysmal symptoms (tonic spasms, paroxysmal dysarthria/ataxia, sensory bursts) are brief (10 s-2 min), frequent (5-40/day), without altered consciousness, and self-limited; they arise from spontaneous discharges at the edges of demyelinated plaques (p.3578). Trigeminal neuralgia, hemifacial spasm, or glossopharyngeal neuralgia in a young patient, or with bilateral/atypical features or objective sensory loss, should raise suspicion of MS involving the cranial nerve root entry zone (p.3578). Fatigue is experienced by most patients and is the leading cause of work-related disability in MS; depression affects about half of patients (p.3578). On MRI, MS plaques are oriented perpendicular to the ventricular surface (Dawson's fingers) reflecting perivenous demyelination; lesions >6 mm in the corpus callosum, periventricular white matter, brainstem, cerebellum, or cord are especially helpful diagnostically (p.3583). A central vein sign within plaques on susceptibility-weighted (T2*) imaging supports an MS diagnosis (p.3583). Two or more discrete CSF oligoclonal bands not present in paired serum are found in >90% of MS patients; bands may be absent at onset and increase over time (p.3583). Evoked potential abnormalities occur in 80-90% of MS patients; a marked latency delay (rather than reduced amplitude or distorted waveform) is what suggests demyelination, and EPs are most informative when testing a clinically uninvolved pathway (p.3583-3584). Most MRI-visible lesions and most early disease activity in MS are clinically silent—bursts of focal inflammation on serial MRI far exceed the relapse rate (p.3583). Even relapse-free RRMS patients undergo subtle 'silent progression,' and disability accumulation is now attributed mainly to progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA) rather than incomplete recovery from relapses (RAW), across RRMS, SPMS, and PPMS (p.3578-3580). A radiologically isolated syndrome (RIS) is incidental MRI evidence of MS in an asymptomatic person; clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) is a first demyelinating event at high risk for MS (p.3577-3580). Distinguish a true relapse from a pseudoexacerbation driven by raised ambient temperature, fever, or infection - glucocorticoids are inappropriate for a pseudoexacerbation (p.3585). Features atypical for MS that should prompt an alternative diagnosis: symptoms confined to posterior fossa/craniocervical junction/spinal cord; onset <15 or >60 years; progressive course from onset; never any visual, sensory, or bladder symptoms; or atypical MRI/CSF/EP findings (p.3584). Symptoms rare/uncommon in MS that favor another diagnosis: aphasia, parkinsonism, chorea, isolated dementia, severe muscle atrophy, peripheral neuropathy, episodic loss of consciousness, fever, headache, seizures, or coma (p.3584). Bilateral and/or severe optic neuritis or severe transverse myelitis should raise NMOSD, MOGAD, or GFAP autoimmunity rather than MS (p.3584). Uveitis is uncommon in MS and should suggest sarcoidosis or lymphoma (p.3577). Intense inflammatory swelling can produce a mass lesion mimicking tumor (tumefactive MS), sometimes requiring brain biopsy (p.3584, 3589). Do not over-diagnose MS from a single isolated event or from MRI white-matter lesions alone - the diagnosis requires dissemination in space and time (clinical, MRI, or CSF evidence) per the McDonald criteria, and there is no single confirmatory test (p.3582-3583). A pseudoexacerbation from heat/fever/infection (Uhthoff phenomenon) can mimic a relapse but reflects transient conduction block, not a new lesion; treating it as a relapse with steroids is inappropriate (p.3578, 3585). Failing to distinguish NMOSD, MOGAD, and GFAP autoimmunity from MS - clues are bilateral/severe optic neuritis, severe longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (>=3 vertebral segments), brain MRI lesions that are non-destructive/cloud-like and can fully resolve, and CSF pleocytosis greater than in MS with neutrophils/eosinophils and oligoclonal bands in <20% (p.3584, 3590). ADEM should be considered for hyperacute or postinfectious demyelinating presentations rather than assuming a first MS attack (p.3584). MS-associated genetic variants (including HLA-DRB1*1501) lack the sensitivity and specificity to be used for diagnosis (p.3581). Highly restricted CNS oligoclonal antibodies are characteristic of MS but their specific antigenic targets differ between patients and their pathogenic role is uncertain - they aid diagnosis, not mechanistic certainty (p.3581). Lhermitte's symptom and trigeminal neuralgia are not specific to MS and occur with other cervical cord/cranial nerve pathology (p.3578). MS is an autoimmune CNS disease producing chronic inflammation, demyelination, gliosis (sclerotic plaques) and neuronal/axonal loss (p.3577). New lesions begin with perivenular cuffing by T cells and macrophages and blood-brain-barrier (BBB) disruption with a preserved vessel wall (unlike vasculitis); cytotoxic CD8 cells line the leading edge, B cells infiltrate, myelin-specific autoantibodies coat degenerating myelin, and complement is activated (p.3581). Sharply demarcated demyelination is the hallmark; axons are relatively spared early but can be destroyed in highly inflammatory lesions, and partial remyelination produces 'shadow plaques' (p.3581). Cumulative axonal/neuronal loss drives irreversible disability (up to ~70% of corticospinal axons lost in MS paraplegia) via demyelination-related loss of trophic support, ion-channel redistribution, and dying-back axonopathy (p.3581). Progressive MS features more diffuse microglial activation, chronic active (slowly expanding) plaques with microglia at a leading edge behind an intact BBB, cortical/subpial plaques poorly seen on MRI, and meningeal ectopic lymphoid follicles linked to subpial cortical demyelination (p.3581-3582). Physiologically, demyelination causes conduction block (hyperpolarization from exposed potassium channels) and conduction slowing; temperature and metabolic changes worsen block, explaining heat- and fever-related fluctuations (p.3582-3583). Susceptibility is polygenic with the strongest signal at HLA-DRB1*1501 (~10% of risk), and EBV seroconversion appears a near-universal prerequisite, plausibly via molecular mimicry between EBV peptides and myelin autoantigens (p.3580-3581). The clinical course is highly variable. RRMS accounts for ~90% of cases with attacks evolving over days to weeks and substantial early recovery; PPMS (~10%) declines steadily from onset, begins later (mean ~40 years), has a more even sex ratio, and accrues disability faster (p.3578-3580). In the pretreatment era, by 15 years after onset only ~20% had no functional limitation and one-third to one-half of relapsing patients had progressed to SPMS needing ambulatory assistance, with ~80% reaching that level by 25 years; the prior RRMS-to-SPMS conversion rate of ~3%/year has fallen to <1%/year in the high-efficacy-therapy era (p.3579, 3588). Favorable prognostic features (pretreatment data): optic neuritis or sensory onset, fewer than two relapses in the first year, and minimal impairment at 5 years; adverse predictors: older onset age, male sex, greater disability, and motor signs in the first year. About <10% have a benign variant that never produces disability even untreated (p.3588). Pregnancy: fewer attacks during gestation (especially the third trimester) but more in the first 3 months postpartum, with the overall pregnancy-year course unchanged (p.3588). Course-based subtypes: relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS, ~90%), secondary progressive MS (SPMS, always evolves from RRMS), and primary progressive MS (PPMS, ~10%); 'relapsing MS (RMS)' covers all relapsing patients and 'active progressive MS' denotes SPMS/PPMS with ongoing relapses or new MRI lesions (p.3578-3579). Neurologic impairment is graded with the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS), 0 (normal) to 10 (death), built from Functional Status (FS) subscores; EDSS <3.5 generally indicates normal walking and little disability, whereas EDSS >4.0 indicates gait-impaired progressive (SPMS/PPMS) disease. An EDSS >=4 plus a motor FS score >=2 supports an SPMS diagnosis (p.3579-3580, 3585). Fulminant clinical variants include Marburg's (acute fulminant) MS, tumefactive MS, and Balo's concentric sclerosis (p.3589).

5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate to 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, the methyl donor required for the vitamin B12-dependent remethylation of homocysteine to methionine. When the enzyme is severely deficient, this methyl supply fails, so homocysteine accumulates and is excreted (homocystinuria) while methionine and S-adenosylmethionine, needed for methylation in the nervous system, fall. Caused by autosomal dominant gain-of-function variants in NLRP3 encoding cryopyrin; de novo variants and somatic mosaicism both occur. The rash is a neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis: migrating wheals that burn or sting rather than itch, are not relieved by antihistamines and are not consistently cold-provoked. Progressive sensorineural hearing loss is a hallmark and a key reason for early recognition, as it can be halted by timely treatment. Recurrent low-grade fever, fatigue, conjunctivitis, headache and large-joint arthralgia accompany the cutaneous features. Reactive AA amyloidosis, presenting with proteinuria and progressive renal impairment, is the most serious long-term complication. Interleukin-1 blockade produces a rapid and often dramatic response and can prevent progression of both hearing loss and amyloidosis when started early. A raised neutrophil count and persistently elevated acute-phase reactants with serum amyloid A are typical even between overt flares. Somatic mosaicism of NLRP3 can produce the phenotype despite a negative conventional germline genetic test. Early and sustained interleukin-1 blockade controls inflammation, preserves hearing and markedly reduces the risk of amyloidosis, allowing a good quality of life. Delayed treatment risks irreversible deafness and renal failure from amyloidosis.

can be overlooked in the mucolipidosis/mucopolysaccharidosis differential Diagnosis rests on MCOLN1 molecular testing supported by suggestive biochemistry; management is supportive and multidisciplinary rather than disease-modifying Progressive rather than static loss of vision or motor skills, indicating a neurodegenerative process Corneal clouding in an infant that mandates urgent metabolic and genetic evaluation Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia with markedly raised gastrin prompting achlorhydria workup Developmental regression signalling advancing neurological disease Attributing early hypotonia and developmental delay to cerebral palsy and missing the progressive storage disorder Overlooking the diagnosis because the classic storage-disease features of organomegaly and coarse facies are absent Not recognising raised gastrin and iron-deficiency anaemia as diagnostic pointers Delaying ophthalmological review so that treatable contributors to visual loss are not addressed Mucolipidosis type IV results from loss-of-function mutations in MCOLN1, encoding mucolipin-1 (TRPML1), a transient receptor potential cation channel located in late endosomes and lysosomes. Impaired channel function disrupts lysosomal calcium and iron handling, membrane trafficking, and autophagosome-lysosome fusion, so heterogeneous lipids and mucopolysaccharide-like material accumulate within enlarged storage vacuoles. Neurons, retinal cells, and gastric parietal cells are particularly vulnerable, producing the combination of neurodevelopmental impairment, retinal degeneration, corneal clouding, and achlorhydria with reactive hypergastrinaemia. The disorder is slowly progressive; most affected individuals never develop speech beyond a few words and reach a developmental plateau in childhood, with visual function declining to severe impairment or blindness by early adulthood. Life expectancy can extend into adulthood with supportive care, though severe neurological disability persists.

Mucopolysaccharidosis — MPS, mucopolysaccharidoses, glycosaminoglycan storage disorders Other lysosomal storage disorders such as the oligosaccharidoses and mucolipidoses GM1 gangliosidosis with coarse features and skeletal changes Skeletal dysplasias from other causes Congenital hypothyroidism with coarse features Multiple sulfatase deficiency Urinary glycosaminoglycan quantification and electrophoresis as a screening step Specific lysosomal enzyme assays to identify the subtype Molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and guide counselling Skeletal survey to demonstrate dysostosis multiplex and assess spine stability Echocardiography, audiology, ophthalmology, and airway assessment for multisystem involvement A group of lysosomal storage disorders caused by deficiency of specific enzymes needed to degrade glycosaminoglycans (mucopolysaccharides), leading to their accumulation in tissues and excretion in urine Most subtypes are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner; the notable exception is MPS II (Hunter syndrome), which is X-linked recessive Shared features across many subtypes include coarse facial features, short stature, joint stiffness or contractures, hepatosplenomegaly, and dysostosis multiplex on radiographs Corneal clouding is prominent in several subtypes (for example MPS I and MPS VI) but characteristically absent in MPS II and in the neuronopathic MPS III Neurocognitive decline is a major feature of severe MPS I, MPS II, and especially MPS III (Sanfilippo), whereas MPS IV (Morquio) primarily affects the skeleton with preserved intellect Cardiac valve disease, airway narrowing, hearing loss, and carpal tunnel syndrome are common and progressive complications Cervical spine instability and cord compression are important risks, particularly in Morquio syndrome Enzyme replacement therapy exists for several subtypes, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can benefit selected patients, most notably severe MPS I when performed early Signs of cervical spine instability or spinal cord compression Progressive airway obstruction or obstructive sleep apnoea Cardiac valve disease or heart failure Rapid neurocognitive regression in neuronopathic subtypes Missing early disease because features can be subtle in infancy and evolve over time Overlooking cervical spine risk before anaesthesia or intubation Assuming enzyme replacement will reverse neurological or advanced skeletal disease Not recognising the X-linked inheritance of MPS II when counselling families The mucopolysaccharidoses arise from deficiency of one of the lysosomal enzymes required for the stepwise degradation of glycosaminoglycans such as dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate, keratan sulfate, and chondroitin sulfate. Incomplete breakdown leads to progressive accumulation of partially degraded glycosaminoglycans within lysosomes across many tissues, including connective tissue, cartilage, bone, cornea, heart valves, airways, and the central nervous system. This storage produces the progressive, multisystem, and often neurodegenerative phenotypes. The specific enzyme deficiency and the glycosaminoglycans that accumulate determine the clinical subtype. Prognosis varies widely by subtype and severity. Severe neuronopathic forms progress to early disability and death, while attenuated forms are compatible with longer survival. Enzyme replacement and, for selected patients, stem cell transplantation can slow somatic disease, but established skeletal and neurological damage is often irreversible and does not fully respond to enzyme therapy.

Mucormycosis — zygomycosis, rhinocerebral mucormycosis Aspergillosis Scedosporiosis (Scedosporium species) Fusariosis (Fusarium species) Dematiaceous (brown-pigmented) mold infections Entomophthoromycosis (Basidiobolus and Conidiobolus) Bacterial orbital cellulitis / cavernous sinus thrombosis (Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci, gram-negative species) Rhinoscleroma (Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis) Tolosa-Hunt syndrome Aspergillosis (septate mold, may co-infect with Mucorales) Scedosporiosis Fusariosis Dematiaceous mold infection Entomophthoromycosis (Basidiobolus, Conidiobolus) Bacterial orbital cellulitis / cavernous sinus thrombosis (S. aureus, streptococci, gram-negatives) Rhinoscleroma (Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis) Biopsy with histopathologic examination (most sensitive/specific; PAS or H&E staining) Culture from a sterile site (needle aspirate, tissue biopsy, pleural fluid) for definitive species identification; tissue sectioned NOT homogenized, incubated at both room temperature and 37C CT of the chest (best method to define extent of pulmonary disease; may detect infection before chest x-ray) MRI of head/sinuses (more sensitive ~80% than CT for orbital and CNS extension) Endoscopy and/or surgical exploration with biopsy of suspected areas; blind biopsy of normal-appearing sinus tissue when suspicion is high Mucorales-specific PCR (useful but no FDA-approved assay) Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (painful ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, headache, cavernous sinus inflammation; lacks progression) Mucormycosis is a group of life-threatening infections caused by fungi of the order Mucorales (subphylum Mucoromycotina); it is highly invasive and relentlessly progressive, with morbidity/mortality higher than many other infections (Harrison 22e p.1717). Rhizopus oryzae and R. delemar (family Mucoraceae) are by far the most common causes in the Western Hemisphere; Apophysomyces elegans is a notable cause in India and Mucor irregularis in China (Harrison 22e p.1718). Five well-defined clinical syndromes: rhino-orbital-cerebral, pulmonary, cutaneous, gastrointestinal, and disseminated; specific host defects predispose to specific syndromes (diabetes/DKA to rhino-orbital-cerebral; leukemia/HSCT to pulmonary) (Harrison 22e p.1718). Rhino-orbital-cerebral disease is the most common form worldwide; early symptoms are nonspecific (eye/facial pain, facial numbness) progressing to conjunctival suffusion, blurry vision, proptosis, and chemosis (Harrison 22e p.1718-1719). Biopsy with histopathology is the most sensitive and specific modality: wide (>=6-30 microm), thick-walled, ribbon-like, ASEPTATE hyphae branching at RIGHT angles, in contrast to thinner, septate, acute-angle-branching Aspergillus/Fusarium/Scedosporium (Harrison 22e p.1719). Mucorales are best visualized with periodic acid-Schiff or H&E; methenamine silver may NOT stain them optimally (Harrison 22e p.1719). Tissue for culture should be cut into sections and placed in the center of culture media, NOT homogenized, because homogenization kills the long filamentous hyphae and lowers culture yield; the lab should be alerted when mucormycosis is suspected (Harrison 22e p.1720). It is important to distinguish mucormycosis from aspergillosis because treatments differ: polyenes for Mucorales versus expanded-spectrum triazoles for most septate molds; voriconazole is the first-line treatment for aspergillosis but EXACERBATES mucormycosis in animal models (Harrison 22e p.1719-1720). Rhino-orbital-cerebral involvement with a black necrotic eschar and/or painful necrotic ulceration of the hard palate (late finding indicating extensive, well-established angioinvasive infection) is a surgical emergency requiring urgent debridement. Bilateral proptosis, chemosis, vision loss, and ophthalmoplegia (contralateral eye involvement) suggest cavernous sinus thrombosis and are ominous. Hyperglycemia or DKA with sinusitis and possible orbital extension, even without a known diabetes history, should raise high suspicion (presentation may be the first recognition of diabetes, often unmasked by recent glucocorticoids). Necrotizing fasciitis from cutaneous mucormycosis (mortality approaching 80%) and necrotic skin lesions from hematogenous dissemination. Disseminated disease (most lethal form), seen with antifungal prophylaxis breakthrough and in highly immunocompromised patients. Misperception that mucormycosis is always rapidly progressive; rate of progression is in fact highly variable (days to a year or more). Cultures are positive in fewer than half of cases, and up to half of cases are diagnosed only at autopsy; a negative culture does NOT exclude the diagnosis. Standard tissue homogenization for culture kills the filamentous Mucorales and lowers yield; tissue must be sectioned and not homogenized, and the lab alerted. Imaging underestimates disease: sinus CT may look like ordinary bacterial sinusitis, and bony erosion into the orbit is rarely seen on CT even when clinically present. Treating with voriconazole (first-line for aspergillosis) can exacerbate mucormycosis; distinguish the two molds because preferred treatments differ, and consider dual infection in highly compromised patients. Delaying treatment of the underlying malignancy until mucormycosis is 'cured' is a common error; antifungals provide only a holding action until near-normal immunity is restored, and untreated underlying disease is the typical primary driver of death. Iron administration and liberal blood transfusion (free iron from hemolysis) should be avoided as iron exacerbates infection. Therapy should not be delayed for diagnostic confirmation: when suspicion is reasonable, empirical lipid polyene therapy should be started early because earlier polyene therapy improves survival. Mucorales are ubiquitous environmental fungi to which humans are constantly exposed; they cause invasive, angioinvasive infection primarily in hosts with uncontrolled diabetes, phagocytic defects (neutropenia or high-dose corticosteroids), and/or elevated free iron, which supports fungal growth in serum and tissue. Iron-overloaded end-stage renal failure patients treated with the iron chelator deferoxamine had high risk of rapidly fatal disseminated disease, because deferoxamine acts as a fungal xenosiderophore that delivers iron directly to the Mucorales. In diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), acidosis dissociates iron from sequestering proteins (enhancing fungal survival/virulence) and the ketoacid beta-hydroxybutyrate upregulates host and fungal receptors that increase fungal adherence and tissue penetration; however the majority of diabetic patients with mucormycosis are NOT acidotic on presentation. Even without acidosis, hyperglycemia raises risk via hyperglycation of iron-sequestering proteins, upregulation of the host receptor GRP78 (which binds Mucorales and enables tissue penetration), poorly characterized phagocytic defects, and enhanced expression of the Mucorales-specific invasin CotH (which binds GRP78). Blood vessel thrombosis and tissue necrosis impair antifungal penetration to the site of infection. (Harrison 22e p.1717-1718) Overall mortality remains high though it has declined with earlier initiation of effective antifungal therapy; outcome is often driven by progression of the underlying predisposing condition. Necrotizing fasciitis from cutaneous disease carries mortality approaching 80%, gastrointestinal disease progressing to perforation has extremely high mortality, and widely disseminated disease exceeds 90% mortality. In contrast, isolated nonnecrotizing cutaneous mucormycosis treated with prompt aggressive surgical debridement has a favorable prognosis and low mortality. Rate of progression is highly variable (days to a year or more), not invariably rapid. (Harrison 22e p.1717-1720) Harrison classifies mucormycosis by clinical syndrome rather than a numeric severity score: rhino-orbital-cerebral, pulmonary, cutaneous (ranging from isolated nonnecrotizing cutaneous disease with favorable prognosis to necrotizing fasciitis), gastrointestinal, and disseminated/miscellaneous disease, with mortality rising steeply from localized cutaneous disease to disseminated disease (>90%). (Harrison 22e p.1718-1720)

Mucous cyst of the finger — digital mucous cyst, distal interphalangeal ganglion Heberden node of distal interphalangeal osteoarthritis Dorsal wrist or digital ganglion arising elsewhere Giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath Epidermal inclusion cyst Gouty tophus at the distal interphalangeal joint Subungual or periungual tumour deforming the nail Rheumatoid nodule Diagnosis is clinical from the typical site, translucency and associated nail groove Plain radiographs of the digit to demonstrate distal interphalangeal osteoarthritis and osteophytes Ultrasound to confirm a cystic lesion and its joint connection when uncertain MRI reserved for atypical or recurrent lesions Transillumination of the cyst at the bedside Assessment of overlying skin integrity to plan soft-tissue cover Microbiological sampling if there is discharge or suspected secondary infection A mucous cyst is a ganglion arising from the distal interphalangeal joint and is intimately associated with underlying osteoarthritis of that joint. It typically presents in older adults as a small, dome-shaped, translucent swelling on the dorsum of the finger between the DIP joint and the nail fold. Compression of the germinal nail matrix by the cyst commonly produces a longitudinal groove or ridge in the nail plate, a useful diagnostic clue. An osteophyte at the DIP joint is almost always present and is considered a key driver; addressing it at surgery reduces recurrence. Progressive attenuation of the overlying skin risks spontaneous rupture and a direct communication to the joint, creating a portal for septic arthritis or osteomyelitis. Management ranges from observation to surgical excision with osteophyte debridement; excision that includes the joint pedicle and osteophyte offers the most durable results. When skin over the cyst is thin or ulcerated, a local rotation or advancement flap may be needed to achieve stable soft-tissue cover. Repeated aspiration or needling is associated with recurrence and carries a risk of introducing infection into the DIP joint, so it is generally discouraged. Skin breakdown or discharge with signs of septic arthritis or osteomyelitis of the distal interphalangeal joint Cellulitis or ascending infection of the digit Rapidly enlarging or atypical solid mass suggesting alternative pathology Marked nail plate destruction raising concern for a subungual tumour Repeatedly needling or aspirating the cyst, risking recurrence and inoculation of the DIP joint Failing to remove the associated osteophyte, the principal cause of recurrence Not recognising thin or ulcerated overlying skin that requires flap cover rather than simple closure Overlooking an established communication with the joint that predisposes to septic arthritis Attributing a nail deformity to a primary nail disorder rather than matrix compression by the cyst A digital mucous cyst is a ganglion of the distal interphalangeal joint that develops in the setting of osteoarthritis. Marginal osteophytes and degenerative capsular changes are thought to promote herniation of mucin-rich synovial fluid through a capsular defect, forming a mucin-filled pseudocyst connected to the joint by a pedicle. The cyst tracks dorsally between the extensor terminal tendon and the collateral structures towards the nail fold, where pressure on the germinal matrix disturbs nail growth. As with other ganglia the lesion lacks a true epithelial lining and recurs if the underlying joint communication and osteophyte are not addressed. Benign but linked to progressive distal interphalangeal osteoarthritis; surgical excision with osteophyte removal gives good durable results, whereas simple aspiration frequently recurs and the associated arthritis continues to progress.

mucous membrane pemphigoid — cicatricial pemphigoid, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid bullous pemphigoid pemphigus vulgaris erosive lichen planus epidermolysis bullosa acquisita linear IgA bullous dermatosis paraneoplastic pemphigus Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis (chronic ocular sequelae) perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence (linear IgG/IgA/C3 at the basement-membrane zone) lesional biopsy for histopathology (subepithelial split with mixed infiltrate) indirect immunofluorescence on salt-split skin (epidermal vs dermal binding) serum ELISA/immunoblot for BP180, BP230 and laminin-332 antibodies slit-lamp ophthalmological assessment and conjunctival forniceal measurement nasendoscopy and laryngoscopy for upper-airway involvement age-appropriate malignancy screening when anti-laminin-332 antibodies are detected A heterogeneous group of subepithelial autoimmune blistering diseases with a predilection for mucous membranes and a marked tendency to scar. The oral mucosa is most frequently involved (desquamative gingivitis is a common presenting sign), followed by ocular, nasopharyngeal, oesophageal, laryngeal and anogenital sites. Ocular disease progresses through chronic conjunctivitis, subconjunctival fibrosis, symblepharon, forniceal shortening, entropion, trichiasis and ultimately corneal opacification and blindness. Autoantibodies target multiple basement-membrane antigens, most commonly BP180 (particularly its C-terminus) and laminin-332; anti-laminin-332 disease carries an association with underlying malignancy. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional mucosa showing linear IgG, IgA and/or C3 along the basement-membrane zone is the diagnostic cornerstone; sensitivity rises with multiple biopsies. The Nikolsky sign may be positive; healing with scarring distinguishes it clinically from bullous pemphigoid, which typically heals without scars. Management is stratified by site and severity; high-risk (ocular, laryngeal, oesophageal, severe oral) disease warrants aggressive systemic immunosuppression to prevent irreversible scarring. A multidisciplinary approach involving dermatology, ophthalmology, ENT, oral medicine and gastroenterology is essential for organ-threatening disease. ocular involvement with progressive symblepharon or forniceal shortening threatening sight laryngeal or supraglottic disease causing stridor or airway compromise oesophageal stricture with dysphagia and risk of aspiration or malnutrition anti-laminin-332 antibodies signalling possible occult malignancy rapidly progressive scarring despite first-line therapy Attributing desquamative gingivitis to poor oral hygiene or dental disease and delaying immunofluorescence biopsy. Taking the biopsy from an ulcerated (rather than perilesional) site, yielding a false-negative direct immunofluorescence. Overlooking asymptomatic early ocular disease because cutaneous involvement is minimal or absent. Failing to screen for malignancy when laminin-332 antibodies are identified. Under-treating so-called low-risk oral disease that later extends to high-risk sites. Mucous membrane pemphigoid results from autoantibodies, predominantly IgG and IgA, directed against structural components of the epithelial basement-membrane zone, chiefly the BP180 (type XVII collagen) antigen and laminin-332 (epiligrin), and less often BP230, type VII collagen and the integrin beta-4 subunit. Antibody binding activates complement and recruits inflammatory cells, causing dermo-epidermal separation within the lamina lucida. Unlike bullous pemphigoid, the inflammatory infiltrate and cytokine milieu at mucosal sites drive a fibrotic reparative response, so repeated cycles of blistering and healing produce progressive submucosal scarring. The predilection for particular target antigens correlates loosely with clinical phenotype, and anti-laminin-332 reactivity is linked to paraneoplastic disease. The condition is chronic and relapsing; with early aggressive immunosuppression, scarring can often be arrested, but established fibrosis is irreversible and untreated organ-threatening disease may lead to blindness, airway stenosis or oesophageal stricture.

Muehrcke lines — Muehrcke's lines, Muehrcke bands Mees lines (true transverse leukonychia) Beau lines (transverse grooves) Half-and-half (Lindsay) nails Terry nails True punctate or transverse leukonychia Transverse traumatic leukonychia Serum albumin and total protein Renal function and urinalysis for proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome Liver function tests Full nutritional assessment Blanch test with digital pressure to confirm bed origin Review of recent chemotherapy or systemic illness Muehrcke lines are paired transverse white bands running parallel to the lunula across the nail, classically separated by strips of normal pink nail. They are an apparent leukonychia arising in the nail bed, not the plate, so the bands do not move distally as the nail grows and disappear when the nail bed is compressed or a tourniquet is applied. The classic association is hypoalbuminaemia, particularly nephrotic syndrome, and the lines may resolve if the serum albumin normalises. They are also described with chemotherapy, malnutrition, chronic liver disease and other systemic illnesses that lower albumin or disturb nail bed vasculature. Because the abnormality is in the bed rather than the plate, blanching with pressure is a useful bedside test that distinguishes them from true leukonychia and from Mees lines. Mees lines, by contrast, are true plate leukonychia that do migrate distally and are linked to arsenic and thallium poisoning and severe systemic insults. Muehrcke lines are asymptomatic and are a clinical sign to investigate rather than a disease to treat. They typically affect several nails symmetrically, most often the second, third and fourth fingers. Newly appearing lines in the context of unexplained weight loss or systemic illness Associated heavy proteinuria or oedema suggesting nephrotic syndrome Signs of decompensated liver disease alongside the nail changes Coexisting features that might instead indicate Mees lines and heavy-metal exposure Confusing Muehrcke lines with Mees lines and missing heavy-metal poisoning, or vice versa Failing to perform the blanch test that distinguishes bed-based from plate-based whiteness Treating the nail sign rather than investigating the underlying cause Assuming the lines will migrate out with the nail, which they do not Muehrcke lines are a form of apparent leukonychia, meaning the whiteness originates in the nail bed rather than in the keratin of the nail plate. The prevailing explanation is a localised oedematous or vascular change in the nail bed, associated with hypoalbuminaemia, that alters the way light is transmitted through the normally translucent plate and produces the appearance of pale transverse bands. Because the plate itself is structurally normal, the bands remain fixed in position while the nail grows and vanish transiently when pressure empties the underlying vascular bed. When the provoking state, most commonly a low serum albumin, is corrected, the abnormal transmission of light resolves and the lines fade. This mechanism cleanly separates them from true leukonychia, in which the plate keratin is abnormal and the white mark migrates distally. Muehrcke lines are themselves benign and often reversible, fading when the underlying hypoalbuminaemia or systemic illness is corrected. Their significance lies in flagging the underlying disorder, whose prognosis they follow.

osteonecrosis) Tarsal navicular stress fracture Midfoot (talonavicular or naviculocuneiform) osteoarthritis Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction Inflammatory arthritis of the midfoot Charcot not spontaneously reconstitute and tends to progress The altered mechanics predispose to talonavicular and naviculocuneiform degenerative change Management ranges from orthoses, offloading and activity modification to arthrodesis for advanced or refractory disease as needed Progressive navicular collapse with fixed hindfoot deformity Established talonavicular or naviculocuneiform arthritis with persistent pain Features suggesting Charcot neuroarthropathy in a patient with peripheral neuropathy Rapidly worsening pain or swelling prompting exclusion of infection or another destructive process Confusing the progressive adult disease with the benign, self-limiting childhood Kohler disease Expecting a flatfoot and overlooking the characteristic paradoxical hindfoot varus Mistaking the fragmentation for a simple navicular stress fracture Delaying recognition of secondary midfoot arthritis until deformity is fixed Mueller-Weiss syndrome is an osteonecrosis of the tarsal navicular in the mature skeleton, thought to result from a combination of abnormal loading and impaired vascularity of the bone. Disordered ossification or delayed maturation of the navicular is believed to leave it mechanically vulnerable, and abnormal distribution of load across the midfoot then concentrates compressive stress on its lateral portion. The resulting subchondral insufficiency and osteonecrosis lead to lateral compression, fragmentation and a characteristic comma-shaped deformity of the navicular. As the lateral navicular collapses, the talar head is displaced and the hindfoot paradoxically drifts into varus rather than the valgus seen with typical medial column failure, and secondary degeneration of the surrounding tarsal joints follows. Unlike the self-limiting childhood Kohler disease, adult Mueller-Weiss disease tends to progress; conservative measures may control symptoms for a time, but many patients ultimately develop midfoot arthritis and deformity that require arthrodesis, with outcomes depending on the extent of collapse and secondary joint involvement.

development Developmental delay warranting additional evaluation Progressive craniofacial deformity requiring surgical revision Diagnosing Saethre-Chotzen syndrome clinically without molecular pressure monitoring in bicoronal cases Muenke syndrome is caused by a specific gain-of-function change in fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (the P250R substitution) that increases ligand-independent or ligand-enhanced receptor signalling. The heightened FGFR3 activity in the coronal suture drives premature osteogenic differentiation and suture fusion. The same receptor is expressed in the cochlea, which accounts for the associated sensorineural hearing loss, and its wide expression contributes to the marked variability in expression, including non-penetrant carriers. Outcome ranges from unaffected carriers to children needing craniofacial surgery; cognition is usually normal or only mildly affected, but unrecognised hearing loss can compromise development, so audiological follow-up is important.

Progressive metabolic derangement with insulin resistance Failure to thrive with cardiac decompensation in infancy Overlooking constrictive pericarditis as the cause of hepatomegaly and ascites in a child with growth failure Failing to institute tumour surveillance for Wilms tumour and other neoplasms Mistaking the disorder for Silver-Russell or Seckel syndrome given overlapping growth restriction Missing the emergence of metabolic and endocrine complications in later childhood and adulthood Mulibrey nanism is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in TRIM37, which encodes a peroxisomal and nuclear E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in protein turnover, chromatin regulation, and cell proliferation control. Prognosis is largely dictated by cardiac involvement, and constrictive pericarditis can cause progressive heart failure that may require pericardiectomy. With cardiac management and tumour surveillance many individuals survive into adulthood, though short stature and endocrine complications persist.

Mullerian duct cyst — mullerian duct cyst, paramesonephric duct cyst, midline prostatic cyst Prostatic utricle cyst, which is midline and communicates with the urethra Seminal vesicle cyst, which is laterally placed Ejaculatory duct cyst Prostatic retention cyst Cystic prostatic neoplasm Zinner syndrome when renal agenesis is present Pelvic MRI to confirm the midline location and characterise the contents Transrectal ultrasound for size and relationship to the prostate and ejaculatory ducts Cyst fluid analysis, where absence of spermatozoa favours a mullerian rather than utricle or ejaculatory duct origin Semen analysis if infertility is present Cross-sectional imaging to exclude solid components or malignancy Renal imaging to assess for associated anomalies A midline cystic remnant of the paramesonephric (mullerian) duct, situated in or above the prostate near the midline It does not communicate with the urethra and does not contain spermatozoa, in contrast to a prostatic utricle cyst Often asymptomatic and found incidentally; larger cysts may cause voiding symptoms, perineal pain, ejaculatory dysfunction, haematospermia or infertility It typically presents in the third to fourth decades as the cyst enlarges, unlike utricle cysts, which more often present in childhood Its midline position distinguishes it from laterally placed seminal vesicle cysts MRI and transrectal ultrasound define the midline location and the relationship to the verumontanum Small asymptomatic cysts are observed, whereas symptomatic cysts may be aspirated, marsupialised or excised Solid components or rapid growth suggesting rare malignant transformation Infection or abscess formation Obstructive voiding symptoms or infertility Recurrent haematospermia Confusing a mullerian duct cyst with a prostatic utricle cyst, when fluid spermatozoa and urethral communication help distinguish them Mislabelling a midline cyst as a lateral seminal vesicle cyst Overlooking rare malignant change in long-standing cysts Attributing symptoms to benign prostatic enlargement Mullerian duct cysts arise from incomplete regression of the paramesonephric ducts, which in males normally involute under the influence of anti-mullerian hormone, leaving only the prostatic utricle and the appendix testis. A retained segment can dilate into a midline cyst behind the prostate that lies above the verumontanum and, unlike the utricle, does not open into the prostatic urethra. Benign with a favourable outcome; most remain asymptomatic and symptomatic lesions respond well to drainage or excision, with only rare reports of malignancy arising within long-standing cysts.

Attributing the nodules to gouty tophi without biopsy Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis is a systemic histiocytic disorder in which histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells with characteristic ground-glass eosinophilic cytoplasm infiltrate the synovium, skin, and other tissues. Overexpression of proinflammatory cytokines, particularly tumour necrosis factor and interleukin-1 and interleukin-6, and osteoclast-activating pathways (including RANK ligand signalling) drives the aggressive, erosive joint destruction. The infiltrating cells are of monocyte-macrophage lineage. The frequent association with malignancy and autoimmune disease suggests an aberrant reactive immune process rather than a purely clonal neoplasm. The skin lesions may eventually regress, but untreated joint disease can progress rapidly to severe, disabling arthritis mutilans; overall outlook is heavily influenced by any associated malignancy.

nephrectomy is reserved for the rare complications of a very large lesion, symptoms, hypertension, or diagnostic uncertainty (concern for malignancy) Any abnormality of the contralateral solitary functioning kidney New-onset hypertension attributable to the dysplastic kidney Enlarging or solid components within the lesion raising concern for malignancy Respiratory or renal compromise suggesting bilateral disease in the neonate Confusing multicystic dysplastic kidney with severe hydronephrosis and mismanaging accordingly Neglecting thorough evaluation and follow-up of the contralateral kidney Performing unnecessary nephrectomy on a lesion that would involute Overlooking rare malignant transformation or a coexisting tumour Multicystic dysplastic kidney is a severe form of renal dysplasia thought to result from an early developmental insult, such as complete ureteric or ureteropelvic obstruction/atresia, that disrupts the normal inductive interaction between the ureteric bud and the metanephric blastema. The affected kidney develops as a disorganised collection of non-communicating cysts with dysplastic stroma and cartilage and no functioning nephron mass. Because the collecting system does not connect, the unit produces no urine and typically involutes over time. Unlike hydronephrosis, there is no central dilated pelvis draining the cysts. For unilateral disease with a normal contralateral kidney the outlook is generally excellent, with progressive involution and good overall renal function; prognosis depends chiefly on the health of the contralateral kidney, and rare complications such as hypertension are the main reasons for intervention.

multifocal atrial tachycardia — MAT, chaotic atrial tachycardia atrial fibrillation atrial flutter with variable conduction frequent atrial premature complexes with wandering atrial pacemaker focal atrial tachycardia sinus tachycardia with premature atrial beats atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia twelve-lead ECG demonstrating three or more P-wave morphologies with an isoelectric baseline arterial blood gas analysis to assess hypoxaemia and acid-base status serum potassium and magnesium concentrations theophylline level where the drug is in use chest imaging to evaluate underlying pulmonary disease echocardiography to assess right heart size, pulmonary pressures and left ventricular function MAT is defined by an irregular atrial tachycardia with at least three distinct P-wave morphologies and varying PP, PR and RR intervals at a rate above 100 per minute. It is strongly associated with decompensated chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and other causes of hypoxaemia and pulmonary hypertension. An isoelectric baseline between clearly discernible P waves distinguishes MAT from atrial fibrillation, which lacks organised atrial activity. Other precipitants include theophylline toxicity, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, sepsis and the postoperative state. Treatment centres on correcting the underlying pulmonary and metabolic disturbance rather than on antiarrhythmic drugs. Magnesium and potassium repletion can reduce ectopy even when baseline levels appear within the reference range. Beta-blockers are effective for rate control but are frequently limited by bronchospastic disease, so a non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker is often preferred. Direct-current cardioversion is ineffective because the mechanism is enhanced automaticity from multiple foci rather than reentry. severe hypoxaemia or respiratory failure driving the arrhythmia haemodynamic instability from a rapid ventricular response theophylline toxicity requiring urgent management profound electrolyte depletion features of decompensated cor pulmonale or right heart failure Misdiagnosing MAT as atrial fibrillation and pursuing rate or rhythm strategies aimed at the wrong mechanism. Attempting electrical cardioversion, which does not work for an automatic multifocal rhythm. Prescribing non-selective beta-blockers in bronchospastic disease and worsening respiratory status. Overlooking magnesium deficiency because the serum level appears normal. Focusing on antiarrhythmic therapy while neglecting the underlying hypoxaemia and metabolic derangement. MAT results from abnormal automaticity or triggered activity arising from multiple ectopic atrial foci, producing P waves of differing morphology and timing. It typically occurs in the setting of atrial stretch, hypoxaemia, catecholamine excess and metabolic derangement, conditions epitomised by decompensated chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with right atrial enlargement and elevated pulmonary pressures. Fluctuating autonomic tone, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and drugs such as theophylline and beta-agonists further destabilise atrial membrane potentials and promote ectopic firing. Because the arrhythmia is driven by automatic foci rather than a fixed reentrant circuit, it does not respond to cardioversion and resolves chiefly with correction of the underlying disturbance. MAT itself is rarely dangerous, but it signals serious underlying illness and its prognosis reflects the severity of the associated pulmonary or systemic disease. The arrhythmia usually resolves once the precipitating condition is treated.

multifocal choroiditis — multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis, MCP punctate inner choroidopathy presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome ocular sarcoidosis ocular tuberculosis syphilitic chorioretinitis birdshot chorioretinopathy primary vitreoretinal lymphoma masquerade fundus fluorescein angiography to characterise lesions and detect choroidal neovascularisation indocyanine green angiography showing hypofluorescent spots optical coherence tomography for sub-retinal fluid, neovascular membranes and outer retinal disruption fundus autofluorescence to map active and atrophic lesions chest imaging and interferon-gamma release assay to exclude tuberculosis and sarcoidosis serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and syphilis serology visual field testing for blind spot enlargement and scotomata Typically affects young to middle-aged, moderately myopic women and is often bilateral though frequently asymmetric. Fundoscopy shows multiple small, round, yellow-grey lesions at the level of the choroid and retinal pigment epithelium in the posterior pole and mid-periphery that evolve into punched-out atrophic scars with pigmented margins. When accompanied by anterior chamber and vitreous inflammation it is termed multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis, distinguishing it from the non-inflammatory punctate inner choroidopathy. Choroidal neovascular membranes are a major sight-threatening complication and a common cause of central visual loss. It is an important cause of the enlarged blind spot syndrome and can produce photopsia and progressive scotomata. Infective mimics, especially ocular tuberculosis, sarcoidosis and syphilis, must be excluded before attributing lesions to idiopathic disease. Active inflammatory lesions respond to corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression, whereas choroidal neovascularisation is treated with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy. Optical coherence tomography and fundus autofluorescence help distinguish active inflammatory lesions from inactive atrophic scars and detect new neovascular activity. sudden central visual loss or metamorphopsia suggesting choroidal neovascularisation rapidly progressive or confluent lesions threatening the fovea features suggesting an infective cause such as tuberculosis or syphilis unilateral progressive vitritis in an older patient raising concern for masquerade lymphoma Diagnosing idiopathic disease without excluding tuberculosis, sarcoidosis and syphilis. Missing a choroidal neovascular membrane as the cause of new central visual symptoms. Confusing inflammatory reactivation with a new neovascular membrane, leading to inappropriate therapy. Overlooking a masquerade syndrome such as vitreoretinal lymphoma in older or atypical patients. Treating with corticosteroids alone in aggressive disease when steroid-sparing immunosuppression is needed. Multifocal choroiditis is considered an idiopathic inflammatory disorder within the spectrum of white dot syndromes, in which an aberrant immune response targets the outer retina, retinal pigment epithelium and choriocapillaris. Focal collections of lymphocytes accumulate at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium and inner choroid, producing the characteristic discrete lesions. Repeated or ongoing inflammation disrupts Bruch's membrane and the retinal pigment epithelium, leaving punched-out chorioretinal scars and predisposing to the ingrowth of choroidal neovascular membranes through the breaks in Bruch's membrane. An autoimmune reaction against retinal or retinal pigment epithelial antigens, in a genetically susceptible host, is the leading hypothesis, and the disorder frequently coexists with intraocular inflammation in the anterior chamber and vitreous. Visual outcome is variable and depends largely on foveal involvement and the development of choroidal neovascularisation; many retain good vision with prompt control of inflammation and neovascular activity, but recurrent disease and macular scarring can cause permanent central loss.

antibodies are negative Failing to search adequately for conduction block outside common entrapment sites Multifocal motor neuropathy is an immune-mediated disorder of motor axons in which antibodies, frequently against the GM1 ganglioside enriched at the node of Ranvier, disrupt nodal sodium-channel clusters and paranodal architecture. This produces persistent focal conduction block along motor fibres while sensory fibres are spared, generating the pattern of weakness confined to individual nerve territories without sensory loss. Many patients maintain function with regular intravenous immunoglobulin, though the disorder is usually chronic and requires ongoing treatment; progressive axonal loss can cause slowly accumulating disability over years.

SELENON encodes selenoprotein N, an endoplasmic reticulum protein involved in redox regulation and calcium handling, and its loss impairs protection against oxidative stress and calcium homeostasis in muscle. RYR1 encodes the skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor, the calcium-release channel of the sarcoplasmic reticulum central to excitation-contraction coupling; variants disturb calcium release and can also confer malignant hyperthermia susceptibility. In both, focal areas of mitochondrial depletion and disrupted oxidative metabolism form the multiple minicores seen histologically, and the resulting impaired contraction produces weakness, with axial and respiratory muscles particularly affected in the SELENON-related form. Many patients remain ambulant with slow progression, but respiratory muscle involvement, especially in the SELENON-related form, can lead to ventilatory failure requiring support and is a major determinant of prognosis; proactive respiratory and orthopaedic surveillance improves outcomes.

Multinodular goitre — MNG, nodular goitre, multinodular goiter, toxic multinodular goitre, Plummer disease Solitary thyroid nodule or thyroid adenoma Differentiated thyroid carcinoma (papillary or follicular) Graves disease with diffuse goitre Thyroiditis (Hashimoto or subacute) Thyroglossal cyst or other midline neck mass Lymphoma of the thyroid Serum TSH with free T4/T3 to define thyroid status Neck ultrasound to map nodules and identify suspicious features Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology of dominant or sonographically suspicious nodules Radioisotope thyroid scan when autonomy or a toxic nodule is suspected Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI without iodinated contrast where feasible) for retrosternal extension and airway assessment Flow-volume loops or laryngoscopy to assess airway and vocal cord function before surgery Typically presents as a painless, gradually enlarging anterior neck swelling that moves upward on swallowing, reflecting attachment to the thyroid cartilage Most patients are euthyroid, but longstanding disease can develop autonomous nodules and progress to a toxic (hyperfunctioning) goitre with thyrotoxic features Retrosternal extension may cause tracheal or oesophageal compression, producing dyspnoea, stridor, or dysphagia, and Pemberton sign (facial congestion on raising the arms) suggests thoracic inlet obstruction Ultrasound is the first-line imaging to characterise nodules; a dominant or suspicious nodule should be sampled by fine-needle aspiration to exclude malignancy Thyroid function tests and, where autonomy is suspected, a radionuclide uptake scan help distinguish hot (autonomous) from cold nodules Surgical management is usually total or near-total thyroidectomy for compressive symptoms, cosmetic concern, suspected malignancy, or toxicity not controlled medically Sudden painful enlargement of a single nodule often represents haemorrhage into a cyst rather than malignant change Stridor, orthopnoea, or acute airway compromise from tracheal compression Rapid enlargement, fixation, hoarseness, or cervical lymphadenopathy suggesting malignancy Symptoms of severe thyrotoxicosis or impending thyroid storm in a toxic goitre Superior vena cava obstruction features from a large retrosternal goitre Assuming all nodular goitres are benign and omitting cytology of a dominant or suspicious nodule Overlooking retrosternal extension and airway narrowing before anaesthesia Failing to render a toxic goitre biochemically controlled before surgery, risking perioperative thyrotoxic crisis Not documenting preoperative vocal cord status, obscuring the cause of any postoperative hoarseness Missing postoperative hypocalcaemia or recurrent laryngeal nerve injury after total thyroidectomy A multinodular goitre develops through cycles of thyroid follicular hyperplasia and involution, driven by relative iodine deficiency, fluctuating TSH stimulation, and heterogeneous growth responses among follicular cells. Over time the gland becomes structurally heterogeneous, with colloid nodules, cystic degeneration, haemorrhage, fibrosis, and calcification. Some clones of cells acquire autonomous function independent of TSH, which can lead to subclinical or overt hyperthyroidism (toxic multinodular goitre). Progressive enlargement, particularly with retrosternal growth, can compress the trachea and oesophagus and displace or narrow the airway. The outlook is generally good; benign euthyroid goitres often remain stable or are cured by thyroidectomy, and toxic goitres respond to definitive treatment. Recurrence can occur after subtotal resection, and lifelong thyroid hormone replacement is expected after total thyroidectomy.
