Mycobacterium xenopi is a slow-growing, thermophilic scotochromogenic mycobacterium that thrives in hot-water systems, its principal reservoir. Inhalation of aerosols leads to pulmonary infection predominantly in hosts with structural lung disease, producing cavitary or fibronodular changes. Because the organism colonises water systems and instruments, it is frequently isolated as a contaminant or coloniser, and clusters of positive cultures may represent pseudo-outbreaks rather than disease. Disseminated infection is uncommon and occurs with significant immunosuppression. Reported mortality is relatively high, though this partly reflects the burden of underlying comorbidity. The prognosis of M. xenopi pulmonary disease is guarded, with relatively high mortality that is influenced strongly by coexisting lung disease and comorbidity. Response to treatment is variable and the best regimen remains uncertain, so outcomes are less favourable than for M. kansasii.

Mycoplasma genitalium infection — Mycoplasma genitalium, M. genitalium, Mgen, MG Chlamydia trachomatis urethritis or cervicitis Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection Trichomonas vaginalis infection Ureaplasma or other genital mollicute infection Urinary tract infection Non-infective (mechanical or chemical) urethritis Herpes simplex urethritis Nucleic acid amplification testing of first-void urine (men) or vaginal, endocervical, or urine samples (women) Reflex molecular testing for 23S rRNA macrolide-resistance mutations on positive specimens Concurrent nucleic acid amplification testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea Microscopy of urethral or genital smears to document urethritis or cervicitis where available Test of cure by nucleic acid amplification testing several weeks after completing treatment Screening for other sexually transmitted infections including HIV and syphilis Mycoplasma genitalium is a small, slow-growing, cell-wall-deficient bacterium and an established sexually transmitted cause of non-gonococcal urethritis in men and cervicitis in women Many infections are asymptomatic; when symptomatic, men typically report dysuria and urethral discharge while women may have discharge, intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, or pelvic pain It is an important cause of persistent or recurrent non-gonococcal urethritis after treatment for presumed chlamydia and is linked to cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease Diagnosis relies on nucleic acid amplification testing because the organism is extremely difficult to culture; lacking a cell wall, it is not seen on Gram stain Wherever possible, positive samples should undergo testing for macrolide-resistance-mediating mutations to guide therapy, given rapidly rising macrolide resistance First-line treatment is often azithromycin (frequently as an extended regimen) in macrolide-susceptible infection, with doxycycline commonly used to lower bacterial load beforehand Moxifloxacin is reserved for macrolide-resistant or persistent infection, and treatment failure with escalating resistance is an increasing problem Test of cure and partner notification are recommended, and routine screening of asymptomatic people is discouraged to limit resistance selection Features of pelvic inflammatory disease such as pelvic pain, adnexal tenderness, or fever Persistent or recurrent urethritis despite appropriate first-line therapy suggesting antimicrobial resistance Signs of epididymo-orchitis in men Repeated treatment failure indicating multidrug-resistant infection needing specialist input Treating with azithromycin without resistance-guided testing, which can select for macrolide resistance Assuming persistent non-gonococcal urethritis is chlamydia and not testing for Mycoplasma genitalium Screening asymptomatic individuals, which drives unnecessary treatment and resistance Omitting test of cure and partner notification, allowing reinfection and onward transmission Mycoplasma genitalium is among the smallest self-replicating bacteria and lacks a rigid cell wall, which renders it invisible on Gram stain and intrinsically resistant to cell-wall-active antibiotics such as beta-lactams. It is transmitted sexually and attaches to and glides along genital and urethral epithelial surfaces by means of a specialised terminal adhesion organelle, provoking a local inflammatory response that manifests as urethritis, cervicitis, or endometrial and tubal inflammation. Because it grows slowly and fastidiously, infection tends to be indolent and persistent, and its capacity to acquire mutations in the 23S ribosomal RNA gene (conferring macrolide resistance) and in topoisomerase genes (conferring fluoroquinolone resistance) underlies the growing difficulty in achieving cure. Susceptible infections usually respond to appropriate antibiotics, but rising macrolide and emerging fluoroquinolone resistance make persistent and recurrent infection increasingly common; untreated or inadequately treated disease may contribute to pelvic inflammatory disease and associated reproductive sequelae.

Mycoplasma Infection — Mycoplasma pneumoniae, atypical pneumonia, walking pneumonia Chlamydia (Chlamydophila) pneumoniae community-acquired pneumonia Legionella species pneumonia Streptococcus pneumoniae and other bacterial community-acquired pneumonia Viral respiratory tract infection / pneumonia Chlamydophila pneumoniae pneumonia Legionella pneumonia Viral atypical pneumonia Respiratory PCR for M. pneumoniae (sensitivity 65-90%, specificity 90-100%) - allows rapid early diagnosis Paired acute- and convalescent-phase serology (IgM and IgG) by enzyme-linked immunoassay; a single acute sample is inadequate because antibodies may not develop until ~2 weeks Respiratory culture on special media (sensitivity <=60%, specificity 100%) - not recommended for routine diagnosis as it may take weeks Chest radiography Cerebrospinal fluid PCR for extrapulmonary (CNS) infection Macrolide-resistance testing by culture and/or PCR when resistance is suspected Asthma / reactive airway disease (wheezing overlap) Drug-induced or herpes-associated erythema multiforme major (overlapping with Mycoplasma-associated SJS/MIRM) M. pneumoniae pneumonia is also called Eaton agent pneumonia, primary atypical pneumonia, and 'walking' pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1465). Onset of pneumonia is usually gradual over several days; the most common presenting symptom is cough, which is typically nonproductive, though headache, malaise, chills, and fever are noted in the majority of patients (Harrison 22e p.1465). Pneumonia develops in only 3-13% of infected individuals; upper respiratory illness is far more common, with an estimated incidence up to 20 times that of pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1465). Wheezes or rales are detected in about 80% of patients with M. pneumoniae pneumonia, but in many patients pneumonia can be diagnosed only by chest radiography (Harrison 22e p.1465). The most common radiographic pattern is peribronchial pneumonia with thickened bronchial markings, streaks of interstitial infiltration, and subsegmental atelectasis; segmental or lobar consolidation is not uncommon (Harrison 22e p.1465). Clinical presentation does not reliably distinguish M. pneumoniae pneumonia from other causes of community-acquired pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1465). Many patients with extrapulmonary M. pneumoniae disease do not have respiratory disease (Harrison 22e p.1465). Hematologic manifestations include hemolytic anemia, aplastic anemia, cold agglutinins, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and hypercoagulopathy; when anemia occurs it generally develops in the second or third week of illness (Harrison 22e p.1466). Erythema multiforme major (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) is the most clinically significant skin eruption associated with M. pneumoniae and appears to occur more commonly with M. pneumoniae than with other infectious agents; in M. pneumoniae-induced rash and mucositis (MIRM)/reactive infectious mucocutaneous eruption (RIME) there may be minimal cutaneous involvement with prominent mucosal disease (Harrison 22e p.1466, p.591). M. pneumoniae has been implicated as a likely etiologic agent in 5-7% of cases of encephalitis (Harrison 22e p.1465). Diagnosis is most sensitively and rapidly made by combining PCR of respiratory tract secretions with serologic testing of paired acute- and convalescent-phase samples (Harrison 22e p.1466). M. pneumoniae is the most frequently detected 'atypical' organism in adult community-acquired pneumonia; older pooled data gave a prevalence of about 22.7%, and more recent (2002-2015) analyses gave about 7.2% (Harrison 22e p.1465). Neurologic manifestations: meningoencephalitis, encephalitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, aseptic meningitis, transverse myelitis, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, cerebrovascular thromboembolic events, acute psychosis, cerebellar ataxia, cranial neuropathy Severe mucocutaneous disease: erythema multiforme major / Stevens-Johnson syndrome / MIRM Hemolytic anemia, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hypercoagulopathy Disseminated infection (septic arthritis, meningitis, osteomyelitis), especially in hypogammaglobulinemic / humorally immunodeficient patients Community-acquired pneumonia failing to respond to a penicillin or cephalosporin Because mycoplasmas lack a cell wall, beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins and cephalosporins) are ineffective; consider M. pneumoniae particularly when community-acquired pneumonia fails to respond to these agents (Harrison 22e p.1464-1465). M. pneumoniae lacks a cell wall and is therefore not visible on Gram stain (Harrison 22e p.1466). Measurement of cold agglutinin titers is no longer recommended for diagnosis because the findings are nonspecific and specific M. pneumoniae assays are now available (Harrison 22e p.1466). A single acute-phase serum sample is not adequate for diagnosis, and IgM antibody can persist for up to 1 year, so its presence may indicate recent rather than acute infection - paired samples are needed (Harrison 22e p.1466). Little evidence supports the commonly held belief that M. pneumoniae is an important cause of otitis media, with or without bullous myringitis (Harrison 22e p.1465). A test of cure for eradication is not suggested, because appropriate antibiotics do not appear to shorten the duration of detection by culture or PCR (Harrison 22e p.1466). Ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin are not recommended for M. pneumoniae owing to high MICs and poor experimental performance, in contrast to respiratory fluoroquinolones (Harrison 22e p.1466). Mycoplasmas are prokaryotes of the class Mollicutes, the smallest organisms capable of independent replication; they lack a cell wall and are bound only by a cell membrane, which explains the inactivity of beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins and cephalosporins) against them. M. pneumoniae is generally an extracellular pathogen that attaches to ciliated respiratory epithelial cells via a complex terminal organelle using interactive adhesins and accessory proteins. Tissue injury is thought to be mediated by production of hydrogen peroxide and an ADP-ribosylating and vacuolating cytotoxin similar to pertussis toxin. Lacking a cell wall, mycoplasmas lack cell-wall-derived innate immune stimulators (lipopolysaccharide, lipoteichoic acid, peptidoglycan), but membrane lipoproteins act through Toll-like receptors (primarily TLR2). Innate immunity provides most lung defense, cellular immunity may be immunopathogenic, and humoral immunity protects against dissemination; patients with humoral immunodeficiency are prone to disseminated disease (arthritis, meningitis, osteomyelitis). Extrapulmonary manifestations may arise from disseminated infection, postinfectious autoimmune phenomena (e.g., Guillain-Barre syndrome), or possibly an ADP-ribosylating toxin (Harrison 22e p.1464-1466). M. pneumoniae pneumonia is generally self-limited, with symptoms usually resolving within 2-3 weeks of onset even without treatment; appropriate antimicrobial therapy significantly shortens the duration of clinical illness. Infection uncommonly results in critical illness and only rarely in death. Long-term recurrent wheezing or reactive airway disease may follow resolution of acute pneumonia, and a possible link to asthma is under investigation. Immunity following severe infection is more protective and longer-lasting than after mild infection, and genuine second attacks of pneumonia are reported infrequently (Harrison 22e p.1465). No formal severity classification is given for Mycoplasma infection; M. pneumoniae illness is generally graded clinically from mild self-limited upper respiratory illness through pneumonia to severe/refractory or critical disease, with macrolide resistance and extrapulmonary involvement marking more severe courses (Harrison 22e p.1464-1466).

Mycosis Fungoides — MF, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, CTCL Chronic eczema or atopic dermatitis Psoriasis and parapsoriasis Drug eruptions and chronic contact dermatitis Tinea corporis and other superficial dermatoses Erythroderma of other causes (for the erythrodermic variant) Other cutaneous lymphomas and lymphomatoid conditions Skin biopsy, often repeated, with immunohistochemistry and T-cell receptor gene rearrangement (clonality) studies Peripheral blood examination including flow cytometry for circulating atypical (Sezary) cells Full staging with lymph node assessment and imaging (such as CT or PET-CT) in advanced disease Lactate dehydrogenase and other bloods to help gauge tumour burden Lymph node biopsy where nodal involvement is suspected Mycosis fungoides is the commonest form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and usually runs an indolent course over years, evolving classically through patch, plaque, and tumour stages Early patches are erythematous, finely scaly, and often persistent in sun-protected sites such as the buttocks and trunk (the bathing-trunk distribution), frequently mimicking eczema or psoriasis for years before diagnosis A high index of suspicion is warranted for atypical, treatment-resistant, or variably shaped chronic dermatitis in an adult, particularly with poikilodermatous change Diagnosis often requires multiple biopsies over time, since early histology can be subtle and non-specific; T-cell clonality studies and immunophenotyping support the diagnosis Staging assesses skin (patch/plaque/tumour or erythroderma), lymph nodes, blood, and viscera, and drives both prognosis and treatment intensity Skin-directed therapies (topical agents, phototherapy, radiotherapy) are used for early-stage disease, while advanced or transformed disease requires systemic and specialist haemato-oncological management Sezary syndrome is the leukaemic, erythrodermic variant, characterised by widespread redness, circulating atypical (Sezary) cells, and lymphadenopathy, and carries a poorer prognosis Large-cell transformation, tumour-stage disease, and extracutaneous spread mark a more aggressive course and warrant prompt reassessment Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma is a malignancy: persistent, atypical, or treatment-resistant chronic dermatitis in an adult should prompt biopsy and specialist referral Development of tumours, ulceration, or rapid progression suggesting large-cell transformation Erythroderma with circulating atypical cells indicating Sezary syndrome Lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or systemic symptoms suggesting extracutaneous spread Signs of secondary infection or sepsis in extensively involved or eroded skin Labelling persistent atypical dermatitis as eczema or psoriasis for years and delaying biopsy Relying on a single non-diagnostic biopsy to exclude the diagnosis Overlooking Sezary syndrome as a cause of adult erythroderma Undertreating early disease or, conversely, overtreating indolent disease with aggressive therapy Missing large-cell transformation or extracutaneous progression during follow-up Mycosis fungoides is a malignant proliferation of skin-homing mature memory T-helper lymphocytes, typically expressing a CD4-positive phenotype with characteristic loss of certain T-cell surface antigens. The neoplastic cells display epidermotropism, migrating into the epidermis and forming intraepidermal collections (Pautrier microabscesses), a histological hallmark. A clonal T-cell receptor rearrangement can often be demonstrated. Over time, accumulating genetic and epigenetic alterations, altered cytokine signalling, and impaired antitumour immunity allow progression from patches and plaques to tumours, large-cell transformation, and dissemination to blood, nodes, and organs, as seen in advanced disease and Sezary syndrome. Early patch- and plaque-stage mycosis fungoides is often indolent with a life expectancy close to normal, but prognosis worsens markedly with tumour-stage disease, large-cell transformation, nodal or visceral involvement, and Sezary syndrome; ongoing surveillance is needed because progression can occur after years of stable disease.

Mycotic (infective) aneurysm — infective aneurysm, infected aneurysm, microbial arteritis with aneurysm, Salmonella aortitis, Staphylococcus aureus aortitis Degenerative (atherosclerotic) aneurysm Inflammatory aortic aneurysm Non-infectious aortitis Contained aneurysm rupture Perivascular abscess or retroperitoneal infection Penetrating aortic ulcer Multiple blood cultures before starting antimicrobials CT angiography for aneurysm morphology and periaortic gas or fluid PET or labelled white-cell imaging in diagnostically uncertain cases Echocardiography to assess for infective endocarditis as a source Inflammatory markers and full blood count Intraoperative tissue and pus samples for microbiological culture Refers to an infected arterial aneurysm, not a fungal one; most cases are bacterial Salmonella species and Staphylococcus aureus are the most common causative organisms Presents with fever, localised pain, and a tender, often rapidly enlarging pulsatile mass Imaging may show a saccular, lobulated, or rapidly growing aneurysm with periaortic gas, fluid, or soft tissue Positive blood cultures with a new or expanding aneurysm strongly support the diagnosis Rupture risk is high and the process can progress quickly, so it is a surgical emergency Treatment combines urgent surgical or endovascular repair with prolonged targeted antimicrobial therapy Sudden severe pain or haemodynamic collapse indicating rupture Rapidly enlarging aneurysm on serial imaging Sepsis with a pulsatile, tender mass Periaortic gas suggesting aggressive infection Attributing a rapidly enlarging aneurysm to degeneration and missing infection Starting antimicrobials before obtaining blood cultures Delaying surgical referral in a febrile patient with a tender pulsatile mass Underestimating the duration of antimicrobial therapy needed after repair A mycotic (infective) aneurysm forms when microorganisms infect and destroy the arterial wall. Bacteria reach the vessel through haematogenous seeding of the vasa vasorum, septic embolism (as in endocarditis), contiguous spread from adjacent infection, or direct inoculation. Organisms such as Salmonella, with its affinity for atherosclerotic and diseased intima, and Staphylococcus aureus incite suppurative inflammation that weakens and digests the wall, producing a rapidly expanding, often saccular aneurysm. The infected, structurally compromised wall is prone to early rupture and life-threatening haemorrhage. Mycotic aneurysm carries high mortality, particularly if rupture occurs, but prompt combined surgical or endovascular repair and prolonged targeted antimicrobial therapy substantially improve survival. Relapse of infection and graft complications require long-term follow-up.

myelinated retinal nerve fibres — medullated nerve fibres, myelinated nerve fibre layer Cotton wool spots Retinal infiltrates or exudates Chorioretinal scarring Retinoblastoma or astrocytic hamartoma (in children) Branch retinal artery occlusion with retinal whitening Optic disc drusen with peripapillary changes Combined hamartoma of the retina and RPE Dilated fundoscopy and fundus photography documenting the feathery-edged patch Optical coherence tomography showing hyper-reflective thickening of the nerve fibre layer Automated perimetry to map any associated scotoma or enlarged blind spot Cycloplegic refraction to detect associated high myopia Amblyopia assessment in children, including visual acuity and fixation testing Fundus autofluorescence or fluorescein angiography where the diagnosis is uncertain Appear as white or greyish-white patches with characteristic feathery, striated borders following the retinal nerve fibre bundle orientation. Most commonly located at or contiguous with the optic disc margin, most often superiorly or inferiorly, and may obscure the underlying retinal vessels. Represent aberrant myelination of retinal ganglion cell axons anterior to the lamina cribrosa, where myelin normally stops. Usually an incidental, benign and non-progressive finding compatible with normal vision when isolated. Extensive peripapillary myelination can produce a corresponding scotoma or enlarged blind spot on perimetry. A recognised triad exists of unilateral extensive myelinated fibres, high axial myopia and dense amblyopia that responds poorly to treatment. Rarely associated with neurofibromatosis and other neurocutaneous or developmental disorders. Acquired myelinated fibres are uncommon but reported, sometimes following optic nerve or retinal insult. Apparent progression or new appearance of myelination, which is atypical and warrants investigation Associated dense amblyopia and high myopia in a child requiring prompt management Features suggesting an alternative infiltrative or vascular lesion masquerading as myelin Systemic signs suggesting neurofibromatosis or other syndromic association Mistaking myelinated fibres for cotton wool spots or retinal infiltrates and pursuing an unnecessary systemic work-up. In children, confusing extensive lesions with retinoblastoma or a retinal hamartoma. Failing to detect and treat the associated high myopia and deprivation amblyopia early. Assuming the amblyopia will respond fully to occlusion, leading to unrealistic expectations. Myelination of the anterior visual pathway normally proceeds from the lateral geniculate body towards the eye and halts at the lamina cribrosa before birth, so that the retinal nerve fibre layer remains unmyelinated. Myelinated retinal nerve fibres result from oligodendrocytes, or oligodendrocyte-like cells, aberrantly present within the retina depositing myelin around ganglion cell axons anterior to the lamina cribrosa. The opaque myelin sheaths scatter light, producing the white feathery patches and obscuring the underlying vasculature. The myelin itself does not usually impair conduction, but dense peripapillary or macular involvement can create field defects, and when combined with high myopia it contributes to a deprivation-type amblyopia that is characteristically refractory. Isolated myelinated retinal nerve fibres are benign and stable with an excellent visual prognosis. When part of the myopia–amblyopia triad, the visual outcome is poor and often resistant to conventional amblyopia therapy.

Myelodysplastic syndrome — MDS, myelodysplasia, myelodysplastic syndromes, preleukaemia Aplastic anaemia (especially hypoplastic MDS) Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency causing megaloblastic dysplasia Acute myeloid leukaemia Myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative overlap syndromes (e.g. CMML) Reactive dysplasia from alcohol, copper deficiency, or drugs Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria Full blood count, reticulocytes, and careful blood film review for dysplastic changes Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with blast count and assessment of dysplasia and ring sideroblasts Cytogenetic analysis and targeted molecular/next-generation sequencing panels Serum erythropoietin level to predict response to erythropoiesis-stimulating agents B12, folate, and copper levels to exclude reversible mimics Flow cytometry and PNH clone testing when the picture overlaps with marrow failure A group of clonal stem cell disorders defined by ineffective haematopoiesis, producing peripheral cytopenias despite a marrow that is usually normocellular or hypercellular Typically affects older adults, often presenting with symptomatic anaemia; neutropenia and thrombocytopenia may also occur, sometimes with recurrent infection or bleeding The paradox of low blood counts with a busy marrow reflects intramedullary apoptosis of dysplastic precursors Diagnosis rests on morphological dysplasia in one or more lineages, blast percentage, and cytogenetic or molecular abnormalities; ring sideroblasts and specific mutations (e.g. SF3B1) carry prognostic meaning Risk stratification with scoring systems that weight blast count, cytogenetics, and depth of cytopenias guides both prognosis and treatment intensity Lower-risk disease is managed supportively with transfusions, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, and iron chelation when transfusion burden is high; an isolated 5q deletion responds well to lenalidomide Higher-risk disease is treated with hypomethylating agents, and allogeneic stem cell transplant offers the only potential cure for suitable patients Progression to acute myeloid leukaemia is a defining risk, greatest in high-risk categories with excess blasts and adverse cytogenetics Rising blast percentage or new adverse cytogenetics signalling transformation to acute leukaemia Severe neutropenia with fever requiring urgent treatment for sepsis Profound thrombocytopenia with clinically significant bleeding Rapidly worsening pancytopenia demanding urgent haematology review and transplant assessment Diagnosing MDS without excluding reversible causes of dysplasia such as B12 or folate deficiency, copper deficiency, alcohol, or recent chemotherapy Failing to obtain cytogenetics and molecular testing, which are central to risk stratification Undertreating iron overload in chronically transfused patients Overlooking an isolated 5q deletion that has a favourable, targeted treatment Missing the transition to acute leukaemia by not repeating marrow assessment when counts deteriorate MDS arises from an acquired mutation in a haematopoietic stem cell that gains a clonal growth advantage. Accumulating mutations in genes governing RNA splicing, epigenetic regulation, transcription, and signalling produce disordered maturation. Precursors are produced abundantly but undergo excessive apoptosis within the marrow, so mature cells are released ineffectively, giving cytopenias in the face of a cellular marrow. Over time the clone may acquire further mutations and expand, with rising blast counts marking transformation towards acute myeloid leukaemia. Prior chemotherapy or radiotherapy can cause therapy-related MDS, which typically carries adverse cytogenetics. Outcomes vary widely by risk category: lower-risk patients may live many years with supportive care, whereas high-risk disease carries short survival and a substantial chance of progression to acute myeloid leukaemia. Allogeneic transplant is the only curative option but is limited by age and comorbidity.

median survival >=10 years; M component in <30%) (p.888) Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia / other IgM monoclonal gammopathies (p.883) Primary (AL) amyloidosis (p.883, Ch.117) POEMS syndrome (polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, M-protein, skin changes; MRI spine/pelvis for marrow infiltration and cord/root compression (p.889, Table 116-2) Serum viscosity if IgM, high IgA, or serum M component >7 g/dL (p.889, Table 116-2) Abdominal fat-pad aspirate for amyloid in selected cases (p.889, Table 116-2) Metastatic carcinoma with lytic bone lesions (e.g. breast) (p.887) Other causes of hypercalcemia of malignancy (PTHrP-mediated); myeloma must be specifically excluded with serum free light chains as ~3% are missed by serum/urine electrophoresis (Ch.57, p.349-350 region) Other causes of marrow-infiltrative normocytic anemia in the elderly (p.886) MGUS or smoldering myeloma misclassified as active disease without myeloma-defining events (p.887) Bone pain is the most common presenting symptom, affecting nearly 70% of patients; lesions are purely lytic (osteoblast suppression by DKK-1), so a radioisotope bone scan is LESS useful than plain radiography (p.886-887). Serum alkaline phosphatase is typically NORMAL despite extensive bony disease because osteoblastic activity is suppressed (p.889). Myeloma bone lesions are classically 'punched-out' lytic lesions (e.g. skull); diffuse osteopenia may also occur (p.887-889). A reduced or negative anion gap may be a clue: the cationic M protein causes chloride retention; an associated pseudohyponatremia reflects reduced serum water from the high protein load (p.887). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is characteristically elevated (p.889). Urine dipstick is unreliable for light chains and the heat test for Bence Jones protein is falsely negative in ~50% of light-chain myeloma; a 24-h urine and serum free light chains are needed (p.888-889). About 20% of myelomas secrete only light chains; <1% are truly non-secretory (M protein undetectable even by serum free light chain assay) (p.884, p.888-889). Median age at diagnosis is ~69 years; uncommon under age 40; nearly twice the incidence in Black versus White populations; male predominance (p.885). Susceptibility to infection is driven by hypogammaglobulinemia (of the non-M-component immunoglobulins), impaired antibody responses to polysaccharide antigens, and granulocyte/complement/T-cell dysfunction (p.886). Most common infections are pneumonia (S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae) and pyelonephritis/UTI (E. coli and other gram-negatives) (p.886). Renal light-chain cast nephropathy, light chain deposition disease, and AL amyloidosis are at least partially reversible with effective antimyeloma therapy (p.887). Patients are prone to acute kidney injury when dehydrated or after iodinated contrast; NSAIDs and hypercalcemia further worsen renal function (p.887). Plasma cell leukemia (>2000 circulating plasma cells/microL) is rare (~1%) but disproportionately frequent in IgD (12%) and IgE (25%) myeloma (p.889). Spinal cord compression from vertebral collapse or plasmacytoma - radicular pain, loss of bowel/bladder control (oncologic emergency) (p.887) Symptomatic hypercalcemia - lethargy, weakness, confusion, AKI (p.886-887) Acute kidney injury, especially with dehydration, contrast, NSAIDs, or hypercalcemia (p.887) Hyperviscosity syndrome - headache, visual disturbance, mucosal bleeding, somnolence, heart failure, retinopathy; symptoms above ~4 cP, most common with IgM > IgG3 > IgA (p.887) Sepsis / serious bacterial infection (recurrent infection is the presenting feature in ~25%) (p.886) Pathologic fracture (p.887) Relying on urine dipstick (detects albumin, not light chains) or the Bence Jones heat test (false-negative ~50%) to exclude light-chain myeloma - use 24-h urine immunofixation and serum free light chains (p.888-889). Excluding myeloma in hypercalcemia of malignancy without serum free light chains - ~3% of myeloma is missed by serum/urine electrophoresis with immunofixation. Ordering a radionuclide bone scan instead of skeletal radiography/CT/PET-CT - lytic lesions lack osteoblastic activity and may be missed (p.887). Misreading a normal alkaline phosphatase as evidence against bone disease (p.889). Interpreting hyponatremia at face value - it is often pseudohyponatremia from high serum protein (p.887). Labeling all monoclonal proteins as myeloma - M components occur in many neoplastic, autoimmune, and reactive conditions and require myeloma-defining events for the diagnosis (p.883, p.887). Failing to distinguish MGUS/smoldering myeloma from active myeloma; active disease requires marrow clonal plasmacytosis (and/or plasmacytoma) plus a myeloma-defining event (CRAB or a malignancy biomarker). Multiple myeloma is a malignant proliferation of a single plasma-cell clone. Myeloma cells adhere to bone marrow stromal cells and extracellular matrix, triggering cytokine loops (IL-6, IGF-1, VEGF) and signaling (Ras/Raf/MAPK, PI3K/Akt, PKC) that drive growth, survival, drug resistance, and migration. Osteoclast-activating factors (RANK ligand, MIP-1alpha, IL-1, lymphotoxin, TNF, VEGF) increase bone resorption while DKK-1 suppresses osteoblasts, producing purely lytic bone disease, hypercalcemia, fractures, and cord compression. The immune microenvironment is remodeled (expansion of MDSCs, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, TH17; suppression of effective antimyeloma T/B/NKT responses). Recurrent cytogenetic events include hyperdiploidy (trisomies) in ~half, and 14q32 IGH translocations [t(11;14), t(4;14), t(14;16)] in the rest, plus del13q, 1q amplification/1p deletion, and del17p; KRAS/NRAS are the most frequently mutated genes (~20% each), with TP53, DIS3, FAM46C, BRAF in 5-10%. No single unifying mutation exists; subclonal heterogeneity present at diagnosis drives genomic evolution. All myeloma is preceded by MGUS (p.883-885). Serum beta-2-microglobulin is the single most powerful survival predictor; combined with albumin it defines the 3-stage International Staging System (ISS): Stage I (b2M <3.5 mg/L, albumin >=3.5 g/dL) median survival ~62 months; Stage II ~44 months; Stage III (b2M >5.5 mg/L) ~29 months. High LDH, circulating plasma cells, high labeling index, and poor performance status indicate worse outcome. Cytogenetic risk: high-risk = del(17p) (>=20% clonality)/TP53 mutation, t(4;14)/t(14;16)/t(14;20) with 1q gain or 1p deletion, biallelic/del1p with 1q gain, and high b2M with normal creatinine (~20-25% of patients, expected survival 3-4 years); standard-risk includes t(11;14), del(13), hyperdiploidy (~75-80%, survival 8-10+ years). del(13q) and t(11;14) are NOT high-risk markers. MGUS progresses ~1%/yr; SMM higher (high-risk SMM ~76% at 5 years). Solitary plasmacytomas carry median survival >=10 years. The Durie-Salmon system is no longer used (p.888-889). Diagnosis (IMWG, Table 116-1): clonal marrow plasma cells (or biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) PLUS >=1 myeloma-defining event. CRAB end-organ damage: hyperCalcemia (>2.75 mmol/L or >0.25 mmol/L above ULN); Renal insufficiency (CrCl <40 mL/min or creatinine >177 micromol/L [>2 mg/dL]); Anemia (Hb <100 g/L or >20 g/L below LLN); Bone lesions (>=1 lytic lesion on radiograph/CT/PET-CT). SLiM biomarkers of malignancy (any one): clonal marrow plasma cells >=60%; involved:uninvolved serum free light chain ratio >=100; >1 focal lesion (>=5 mm) on MRI. Staging severity: International Staging System (ISS) I-III by serum beta-2-microglobulin and albumin; cytogenetic high-risk vs standard-risk further stratifies (R-ISS combines ISS with high-risk cytogenetics and LDH). MGUS = M protein <30 g/L, marrow plasma cells <10%, no myeloma-defining events; smoldering myeloma = M protein >=30 g/L (or urine >=500 mg/24h) and/or marrow plasma cells 10-60%, no myeloma-defining events (p.887-889).

giant cells and tubular injury Presentation is typically acute or subacute kidney injury, sometimes precipitated by dehydration, hypercalcaemia, infection, contrast or nephrotoxic drugs Urine dipstick underestimates the proteinuria because it detects albumin rather than the predominant light-chain (Bence Jones) protein Diagnosis rests on serum free light-chain assay, serum and urine electrophoresis with immunofixation, and confirmation of the plasma-cell clone Management combines rapid reduction of the pathogenic light chain by clone-directed therapy for the paraprotein-related disease with correction of precipitating factors and supportive care Severe or dialysis-requiring acute kidney injury Hypercalcaemic crisis compounding renal failure Very high free light-chain burden Concurrent infection, sepsis or hyperviscosity Relying on urine dipstick, which misses Bence Jones proteinuria Missing precipitants such as dehydration, hypercalcaemia, contrast and loop diuretics Delaying clone-directed therapy while awaiting biopsy in clear-cut cases Confusing cast nephropathy with light chain deposition disease or amyloidosis Giving nephrotoxic drugs that worsen cast formation In multiple myeloma a plasma-cell clone secretes large amounts of monoclonal free light chains that are filtered by the glomerulus and delivered to the distal nephron. There they co-aggregate with Tamm-Horsfall (uromodulin) protein secreted by the thick ascending limb, forming dense, waxy, often fractured casts that obstruct tubular flow and incite an inflammatory and giant-cell reaction with tubular epithelial injury. Obstruction and back-pressure reduce glomerular filtration, producing acute kidney injury, while direct proximal tubular toxicity of light chains adds further damage. Volume depletion, hypercalcaemia, loop diuretics, contrast and nephrotoxins promote cast formation by concentrating light chains and reducing flow, explaining common precipitants. Renal recovery depends on the speed and depth of light-chain reduction and on the degree of established tubular and interstitial damage at diagnosis; early, effective clone-directed therapy offers the best chance of renal recovery and improved survival. Extensive cast formation with fibrosis and a delayed light-chain response predict dialysis dependence.

glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency with granulocyte dysfunction Diabetes-associated neutrophil dysfunction Other causes of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis Acquired myeloperoxidase deficiency due to myelodysplasia, drugs or heavy-metal exposure Peroxidase cytochemical stain on the blood film showing absent neutrophil activity Automated analyser peroxidase channel demonstrating absent granulocyte peroxidase Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry or nitroblue tetrazolium test, normal results excluding chronic granulomatous disease MPO gene sequencing Fasting glucose and glycated haemoglobin to detect coexisting diabetes Fungal cultures and imaging when invasive candidiasis is suspected Neutrophil bactericidal and functional assays if the phenotype is atypical The commonest inherited neutrophil enzyme defect, yet most affected individuals are clinically asymptomatic because alternative oxygen-dependent and oxygen-independent killing mechanisms compensate Caused by variants in the MPO gene and inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, producing either complete or partial enzyme deficiency Myeloperoxidase generates hypochlorous acid and other reactive halogen species from hydrogen peroxide and chloride within the phagolysosome, a potent microbicidal system The defect is frequently discovered incidentally when peroxidase-based automated haematology analysers flag absent neutrophil and eosinophil peroxidase activity Clinically significant infection is uncommon, but there is a recognised predisposition to invasive candidiasis, including Candida sepsis, particularly when diabetes mellitus coexists The NADPH oxidase respiratory burst is intact, which distinguishes myeloperoxidase deficiency from chronic granulomatous disease on nitroblue tetrazolium or dihydrorhodamine testing Most individuals need no specific treatment, so management focuses on prompt recognition and treatment of fungal infection in those at risk Invasive or disseminated candidiasis, especially in a person with diabetes Deep fungal infection or Candida bloodstream infection Severe or recurrent infection suggesting an additional or alternative immune defect Unexplained absence of neutrophil peroxidase in the context of active infection Misinterpreting an incidental analyser flag as myelodysplasia or a laboratory artefact Confusing myeloperoxidase deficiency with chronic granulomatous disease despite the normal respiratory burst Assuming that every inherited neutrophil defect is clinically significant Overlooking coexisting diabetes that heightens candidal risk Failing to consider acquired myeloperoxidase deficiency in the setting of myelodysplasia Myeloperoxidase is a haem-containing enzyme stored in the azurophilic (primary) granules of neutrophils and in monocyte lysosomes. After phagocytosis it is discharged into the phagosome, where it uses hydrogen peroxide generated by the NADPH oxidase respiratory burst together with chloride to form hypochlorous acid and related reactive species that kill ingested microbes. Inherited deficiency removes this halogenation system, but killing mediated by hydrogen peroxide itself, defensins and other granule constituents remains largely intact, which explains the generally mild phenotype. Killing of fungi, particularly Candida hyphae, is more dependent on the myeloperoxidase system, accounting for the specific vulnerability to invasive candidiasis, an effect amplified by hyperglycaemia. The great majority of individuals have a normal life expectancy with no excess infection burden, so the overall prognosis is excellent; clinically important risk is largely confined to invasive fungal infection in those with concurrent diabetes or additional immune compromise.

monitor sensorineural hearing loss Urinalysis and renal function tests to screen for nephropathy Ophthalmological assessment for cataract An autosomal dominant disorder caused by MYH9 mutations affecting non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA, presenting with macrothrombocytopenia The blood film shows large or giant platelets together with pale blue Dohle-like cytoplasmic inclusions in neutrophils The historical eponyms (May-Hegglin, Sebastian, Fechtner, Epstein) are now recognised as one disease spectrum defined by the MYH9 gene Extra-haematological features may include progressive sensorineural deafness, presenile cataract, and nephropathy that can advance to renal failure The thrombocytopenia is often mild and the bleeding tendency modest, so the low platelet count is frequently discovered incidentally Automated counters may undercount the giant platelets and overstate the severity, so film review is essential Diagnosis combines macrothrombocytopenia with leucocyte inclusions on immunofluorescence for myosin IIA and MYH9 sequencing Progressive proteinuria or declining renal function heralding nephropathy Rapidly progressive hearing loss requiring audiological intervention Significant bleeding disproportionate to the platelet count, prompting review of the diagnosis Unnecessary immunosuppression or splenectomy after misdiagnosis as immune thrombocytopenia Misdiagnosing the condition as immune thrombocytopenia and giving steroids, immunoglobulin, or splenectomy Relying on automated platelet counts that miss giant platelets Failing to screen for and monitor renal, auditory, and ocular involvement Overtreating a mild, incidentally found thrombocytopenia MYH9-related disorder results from mutations in MYH9, which encodes the heavy chain of non-muscle myosin IIA, a cytoskeletal motor protein expressed in platelets, leucocytes, cochlea, lens, and kidney. In megakaryocytes, defective myosin IIA disrupts the cytoskeletal remodelling required for orderly proplatelet formation, so platelets are released as fewer, abnormally large cells, producing macrothrombocytopenia. In neutrophils, the mutant protein aggregates into cytoplasmic inclusions visible as Dohle-like bodies. The same protein is essential in other tissues, so its dysfunction can cause sensorineural hearing loss, cataract, and a glomerular nephropathy, with the pattern and severity of extra-haematological involvement varying by the specific mutation. The haematological course is usually benign with only a modest bleeding tendency, but long-term prognosis is shaped by extra-haematological complications, particularly progressive nephropathy and hearing loss in susceptible genotypes.

constriction or effusion causing haemodynamic compromise Progressive airway stenosis or restrictive respiratory failure Exuberant fibrotic response following surgery or cardiac catheterisation Uncontrolled hypertension or evolving cardiovascular disease Proceeding to elective surgery or catheterisation without anticipating the exaggerated fibrotic response Attributing progressive stiffness results from recurrent heterozygous variants in SMAD4 that stabilise the protein and enhance transforming growth factor beta and bone morphogenetic protein signalling. Because the underlying tendency is to fibrose, tissue injury from surgery or instrumentation can trigger disproportionate scarring, a key consideration in management. The condition is progressive and can be life-limiting, with cardiovascular and respiratory fibrosis being the principal threats; outcomes are worsened by the exaggerated scarring that may follow interventions, so a cautious, multidisciplinary approach is essential.

clinical patterns include furuncular (boil-like), wound (traumatic), migratory (creeping), and cavity/body-orifice forms Furuncular myiasis is classically caused by the human botfly (Dermatobia hominis) in the Americas and the tumbu fly (Cordylobia anthropophaga) in sub-Saharan Africa Dermatobia eggs are carried to skin by biting insects (phoresis), whereas tumbu fly eggs are laid on soil or drying laundry and larvae penetrate contact skin The typical furuncular lesion is a painful nodule with a central punctum that intermittently discharges serosanguineous fluid; patients often describe movement or a sensation of crawling A central breathing pore that bubbles, and sometimes a visible larval tip, help confirm the diagnosis; occlusion can bring the larva to the surface Wound and cavity myiasis (e.g. screwworm) can be aggressively tissue-destructive and occurs in neglected wounds, orifices or debilitated patients Treatment is removal of the larva (occlusion and extraction or minor surgical removal), wound care, and tetanus/antibiotic cover for secondary infection where indicated Aggressive wound or cavity (e.g. nasal, orbital, aural) myiasis with rapid tissue destruction Screwworm infestation requiring prompt eradication and public health notification Secondary cellulitis, abscess or signs of systemic sepsis Involvement of the eye, sinuses or central structures threatening deep spread Infestation in a neglected, debilitated or cognitively impaired patient Rupturing or fragmenting the larva during extraction, leaving parts that provoke a foreign-body reaction Misdiagnosing furuncular myiasis as a simple boil and incising without recognising the larva Underestimating aggressive wound or cavity myiasis and its capacity for deep destruction Neglecting tetanus prophylaxis and secondary infection management Failing to notify authorities for obligate parasites such as screwworm where reportable Fly larvae invade host tissue by species-specific routes: some deposit larvae directly, some lay eggs transferred by biting arthropods, and others deposit eggs on soil or clothing from which larvae penetrate intact or broken skin. The larva develops within the dermis or a wound, feeding on tissue and exudate while maintaining a respiratory opening at the skin surface. Local host inflammation produces a furuncle-like nodule in obligate skin-dwelling species, whereas facultative or obligate wound feeders such as screwworm can burrow and destroy tissue extensively. Secondary bacterial infection frequently complicates the lesion. Furuncular myiasis is generally benign and resolves completely once the larva is removed, whereas wound and cavity myiasis, especially screwworm, can cause serious tissue destruction and requires urgent intervention; secondary infection is the main complication.

Myocardial bridging — myocardial bridge, coronary muscle bridge, intramural coronary artery, tunnelled coronary artery Obstructive coronary atherosclerosis Coronary vasospasm Anomalous coronary artery origin or course Microvascular angina Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with demand ischaemia Non-cardiac chest pain Coronary angiography demonstrating systolic compression with diastolic relaxation Coronary CT angiography showing the intramyocardial segment Intravascular imaging or physiological indices to assess functional significance in selected cases Stress testing or perfusion imaging to document inducible ischaemia Echocardiography to exclude hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Electrocardiogram during symptoms A segment of an epicardial coronary artery, usually the mid left anterior descending, dips into the myocardium and is compressed during systole Angiography shows systolic narrowing that relaxes in diastole, the milking effect, since most coronary perfusion occurs in diastole The overwhelming majority are benign incidental findings with a favourable natural history Symptomatic cases may report exertional chest pain, and rarely arrhythmia or ischaemic events are attributed to deep or long bridges Diastolic flow disturbance and a persistent early-diastolic delay in relaxation can occasionally impair perfusion Tachycardia shortens diastole and can unmask or worsen symptoms by reducing perfusion time Most patients need reassurance only; medical therapy that reduces contractility and heart rate is first-line, with intervention reserved for refractory, well-documented ischaemia Documented exertional ischaemia attributable to a deep or long bridge Ventricular arrhythmia associated with the bridged segment Persistent symptoms despite optimal rate and contractility control Ischaemic event in a young patient without atherosclerotic risk factors Overtreating an incidental bridge and attributing unrelated chest pain to it Using nitrates, which can worsen systolic compression and symptoms Failing to control heart rate, allowing tachycardia to shorten diastolic perfusion time Ignoring coexisting fixed atherosclerotic disease proximal to the bridge Myocardial bridging occurs when a portion of an epicardial coronary artery, most often the mid left anterior descending, takes an intramuscular course so that overlying myocardium compresses it during systole. Because coronary perfusion is predominantly diastolic, the systolic compression is usually of little consequence, which explains why most bridges are benign. In deeper or longer bridges the compression can persist into early diastole and a phase lag in vessel re-expansion may transiently reduce flow, and tachycardia further curtails diastolic filling time. Local wall stress at the bridge entrance may also predispose the proximal segment to atherosclerosis. The net functional effect ranges from none in the great majority to occasional demand ischaemia in a minority. The natural history is generally benign with normal life expectancy in the majority; adverse events are rare and largely confined to deep, long bridges or those with proven ischaemia.

cortical, subcortical, spinal, or peripheral origin helps guide investigation and treatment Post-hypoxic action myoclonus (Lance-Adams syndrome) can follow cardiac arrest and cerebral hypoxia Treatment principles combine correcting any underlying cause with symptomatic antimyoclonic agents chosen according to the presumed generator Myoclonus with declining consciousness suggesting a serious metabolic, toxic, or hypoxic encephalopathy Rapidly progressive myoclonus with cognitive decline raising concern for prion disease or an autoimmune encephalitis Myoclonus following cardiac arrest, which may indicate severe hypoxic brain injury Myoclonus as part of a status myoclonicus or in the context of status epilepticus requiring urgent treatment Failing to search for and correct a reversible metabolic or drug-induced cause Misclassifying myoclonus as tremor, tics, or seizures and mismanaging it Overlooking a serious progressive cause such as prion disease or autoimmune encephalitis Not localising the myoclonus neurophysiologically, leading to poorly targeted therapy Myoclonus results from abnormal, excessive neuronal discharge that can arise at several levels of the nervous system. Cortical myoclonus reflects hyperexcitability of the sensorimotor cortex and often coexists with epilepsy; subcortical and brainstem forms arise from deeper generators; and spinal and peripheral forms originate in the cord or nerve. Loss of normal inhibitory control, frequently involving impaired GABAergic and serotonergic mechanisms, allows brief synchronous muscle discharges. Underlying processes include metabolic derangement, drugs and toxins, neurodegeneration, hypoxia, and epilepsy. Prognosis is dictated by the underlying cause. Myoclonus due to reversible metabolic or drug causes typically resolves once the trigger is corrected, whereas myoclonus from neurodegenerative, prion, or severe hypoxic injury carries a poor outlook. Symptomatic treatment can meaningfully reduce disability in many chronic cases even when the cause cannot be cured.

Myoclonus-dystonia — myoclonus-dystonia syndrome, DYT11, SGCE, epsilon-sarcoglycan deficiency, M-D, alcohol-responsive myoclonic dystonia Essential tremor and other tremor syndromes Primary (isolated) dystonias such as DYT1 Progressive myoclonic epilepsies and other myoclonus syndromes Tic disorders including Tourette syndrome Functional (psychogenic) jerks Cortical myoclonus from other neurological disease SGCE molecular genetic testing, interpreted with attention to maternal imprinting Neurophysiological studies (EMG with back-averaging) to characterise the myoclonus as subcortical EEG to distinguish myoclonic epilepsy Brain MRI, expected to be normal, to exclude structural or degenerative causes Serum copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude Wilson disease when the picture is atypical Most commonly caused by variants in SGCE (epsilon-sarcoglycan), inherited autosomal dominantly with maternal imprinting, so penetrance depends on parent of origin (usually manifest only when inherited from the father) Core phenotype combines lightning-like myoclonic jerks, predominantly of the upper body and arms, with milder dystonia (often cervical dystonia or writer's cramp) Onset is typically in childhood or adolescence, and the myoclonus is usually the more disabling feature A characteristic and well-recognised feature is marked, if temporary, improvement of myoclonus with alcohol, which can lead to alcohol misuse Psychiatric comorbidity is common, including anxiety, obsessive-compulsive features, and depression The disorder is non-degenerative with normal cognition and structural imaging, and course is generally benign and non-progressive Symptomatic treatment may target myoclonus and dystonia; deep brain stimulation is an option in severely affected, refractory cases Diagnosis is supported by the clinical picture and family history and confirmed by SGCE molecular testing, keeping imprinting in mind when interpreting inheritance Development of alcohol dependence driven by self-medication of myoclonus Severe psychiatric symptoms including suicidal ideation Atypical progression, cognitive decline, or additional neurological signs suggesting another diagnosis Disabling myoclonus or dystonia refractory to medical therapy Misinterpreting the inheritance by ignoring maternal imprinting and wrongly excluding the diagnosis in an unaffected carrier parent Overlooking or inadvertently reinforcing alcohol misuse arising from symptom self-treatment Labelling the jerks as tics or a functional disorder without neurophysiology or genetic testing Failing to address the frequently associated psychiatric comorbidity Myoclonus-dystonia is most often caused by loss-of-function variants in SGCE, encoding epsilon-sarcoglycan, a transmembrane protein widely expressed in neurons including cerebellar Purkinje cells and monoaminergic neurons. SGCE is maternally imprinted, so only the paternally inherited allele is normally expressed, which explains why the disorder typically manifests when the variant is inherited from the father. Deficiency of epsilon-sarcoglycan is thought to disrupt cerebellothalamocortical and striatal network function, producing subcortical myoclonus and dystonia without neurodegeneration, consistent with the normal cognition and imaging. The condition is generally benign and non-progressive, compatible with a normal lifespan and preserved cognition, though myoclonus and dystonia can cause functional and social disability and psychiatric comorbidity may be significant. Selected refractory patients benefit from deep brain stimulation.

a subset show FUS rearrangement Occurs across a wide age range in the limbs, limb girdles and trunk, with morphology ranging from epithelioid to spindled cells in a myxoid or hyaline stroma Malignancy is chiefly determined by cytological atypia, and malignant tumours (myoepithelial carcinoma) may recur and metastasise Parachordoma is now regarded as part of the myoepithelial tumour spectrum rather than a separate entity Marked nuclear atypia indicating myoepithelial carcinoma Rapid growth, large size or infiltrative margins Local recurrence after excision Distant metastasis, most often to lung and bone, in malignant tumours Confusing myoepithelioma with extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma or chordoma on limited sampling Relying on a single marker rather than demonstrating the characteristic dual immunophenotype Underrecognising malignancy because architecture can appear deceptively bland despite atypia Overlooking SMARCB1 loss, which can mimic other INI1-deficient tumours Assuming an EWSR1 rearrangement points to Ewing sarcoma rather than a myoepithelial tumour Soft-tissue myoepithelioma is defined by differentiation towards myoepithelial cells, which normally combine epithelial and contractile (myoid) properties, explaining the dual immunophenotype of keratins, S100 and myoid markers. Many tumours are driven by EWSR1 gene fusions, in which a strong promoter is joined to a transcription-factor partner to deregulate gene expression, while a minority use FUS as the alternative partner. The genetic drivers overlap with those of other EWSR1-associated soft-tissue tumours, and the degree of nuclear atypia rather than the specific fusion best predicts clinical behaviour. Benign myoepitheliomas and mixed tumours are generally cured by complete excision, though local recurrence can follow incomplete removal; malignant myoepithelial carcinomas, defined largely by significant cytological atypia, carry a real risk of recurrence and metastasis, and paediatric malignant tumours in particular may behave aggressively.

for contributing conditions including thyroid dysfunction, vitamin deficiency, and sleep disturbance Blood tests such as inflammatory markers where inflammatory or systemic disease is considered Myofascial pain syndrome is a regional pain disorder characterised by myofascial trigger points, which are hyperirritable spots within a palpable taut band of skeletal muscle Pressing a trigger point reproduces the patient's familiar pain and refers it in a characteristic, reproducible pattern that does not follow dermatomal boundaries A local twitch response, elicited by snapping palpation or needling of the taut band, supports the diagnosis, which is fundamentally clinical It is distinguished from fibromyalgia, which is a widespread pain disorder with diffuse tender points rather than regional referring trigger points Perpetuating factors such as poor posture, ergonomic strain, muscle overload, and underlying structural or psychological stressors should be identified and corrected Core treatment is manual and physical therapy including trigger-point release, stretching, spray-and-stretch techniques, and posture and activity correction Trigger-point injection or dry needling can deactivate stubborn points, and botulinum toxin injection is used for selected refractory cases Addressing sleep, mood, and contributing chronic conditions improves durability of the response, and long-term management emphasises self-directed exercise Constitutional features such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats suggesting infection or malignancy Progressive neurological deficit indicating a radicular or cord lesion rather than muscular pain Sudden severe pain or a mass suggesting an alternative acute pathology Pain unresponsive to appropriate myofascial treatment prompting review of the diagnosis Mislabelling widespread fibromyalgia as regional myofascial pain, or vice versa Treating trigger points while ignoring the posture, ergonomic, or structural factors that perpetuate them Relying on passive treatments and medication without an active exercise programme Overlooking sleep disturbance, mood, and stress that maintain chronic muscle pain Repeated needling of trigger points without addressing the underlying cause Myofascial trigger points are thought to develop where sustained or repetitive muscle overload leads to localised areas of contracted sarcomeres and a taut band. A widely cited model proposes excessive acetylcholine release at dysfunctional motor endplates, producing sustained contraction, local ischaemia and energy crisis, and accumulation of sensitising biochemical mediators. This lowers the local pain threshold, sensitises peripheral nociceptors, and, through convergence in the dorsal horn, generates referred pain and contributes to central sensitisation when the process becomes chronic. Acute myofascial pain from an identifiable overload often resolves well when the trigger points are treated and perpetuating factors corrected. Chronic cases with central sensitisation and unaddressed contributing factors can be persistent, but most patients improve with an active, multimodal rehabilitation approach.

complications drive morbidity, systematic cardiac and respiratory surveillance is central to management Cardiac conduction block, arrhythmia or heart failure, which can be life-threatening and may precede weakness Respiratory muscle weakness with nocturnal hypoventilation Rapid functional decline suggesting an aggressive subtype Sudden cardiac events in the patient or affected relatives Focusing on the skeletal weakness and failing to screen for the potentially fatal cardiac disease Mislabelling it as a limb-girdle dystrophy and missing the diagnostic aggregate pathology Overlooking coexisting peripheral neuropathy or respiratory involvement Assuming a single gene, when the group is genetically heterogeneous and needs broad testing Myofibrillar myopathies are caused by mutations in genes encoding proteins of the sarcomeric Z-disc and its associated cytoskeletal network, including desmin, alpha-B-crystallin, myotilin, ZASP and filamin C. These proteins maintain the structural integrity and mechanical linkage of the myofibrils and the intermediate-filament scaffold that connects sarcomeres to the sarcolemma and organelles. When they are defective, the Z-disc disintegrates and misfolded proteins, particularly desmin, accumulate as insoluble aggregates that disrupt myofibrillar architecture, mitochondrial positioning and protein-quality-control pathways. The resulting mechanical and metabolic failure of the fibre produces progressive weakness, and because several of these proteins are also essential in cardiac muscle, cardiomyopathy and conduction disease are frequent. Prognosis varies with the causative gene, but progression is usually slow for the skeletal weakness while cardiac and respiratory complications are the main determinants of morbidity and mortality, so outcomes are substantially improved by early detection and treatment of heart and respiratory involvement.

anti-VEGF therapy is the mainstay of treatment Myopic traction maculopathy, including foveoschisis, results from inward traction on a stretched, non-compliant retina overlying a staphyloma and may progress to macular hole and detachment Dome-shaped macula and peripapillary changes such as myopic conus, peripapillary atrophy and tilted disc are recognised associated features that can complicate glaucoma assessment OCT is essential for detecting neovascularisation, foveoschisis, macular hole and dome-shaped macula, and OCT-angiography aids detection of myopic choroidal neovascularisation Because early myopic neovascularisation is very treatable, patients benefit from education about warning symptoms and often Amsler grid monitoring New metamorphopsia, a central scotoma or sudden drop in central vision suggesting neovascularisation or subretinal haemorrhage Flashes, floaters or a field defect suggesting retinal detachment, to which high myopes are predisposed Progressive distortion suggesting foveoschisis advancing towards a macular hole Fresh subretinal haemorrhage at the fovea Attributing reduced vision solely to refractive error and missing treatable myopic choroidal neovascularisation Misinterpreting myopic disc and peripapillary changes, leading to over- or under-diagnosis of glaucoma Overlooking foveoschisis on clinical examination when OCT would reveal it Failing to examine the peripheral retina for breaks in a high myope Confusing myopic neovascularisation with neovascular AMD, which differs in lesion size, behaviour and treatment response Pathological myopia is characterised by excessive axial elongation of the eye and development of a posterior staphyloma, an outpouching of the wall of the globe. Progressive mechanical stretching thins the retina, retinal pigment epithelium, Bruch's membrane and choroid, producing chorioretinal atrophy and breaks in Bruch's membrane known as lacquer cracks. These breaks together with the attenuated choroid predispose to myopic choroidal neovascularisation and subsequent scarring (Fuchs spot). Over the rigid, non-compliant posterior pole, persistent vitreoretinal and epiretinal traction on a stretched retina causes myopic traction maculopathy and foveoschisis, which may progress to full-thickness macular hole and retinal detachment. The combination of atrophy, neovascularisation and traction accounts for the central visual loss. Myopic maculopathy is a leading cause of irreversible central visual impairment in high myopia and tends to progress with age and increasing axial length. Nonetheless, early detection and prompt anti-VEGF treatment of myopic choroidal neovascularisation gives a relatively favourable visual outcome compared with untreated disease.

Myosin storage myopathy — Hyaline body myopathy, MYH7-related myosin storage myopathy Laing distal myopathy (MYH7) Myofibrillar myopathies (desmin, myotilin) Scapuloperoneal muscular dystrophy Limb-girdle muscular dystrophies Nemaline and cap myopathy Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy MYH7 gene sequencing Muscle biopsy with slow-myosin immunostaining and electron microscopy Serum creatine kinase Electrocardiography and echocardiography, with cardiac MRI if needed Electromyography Muscle MRI to define the selective involvement pattern Respiratory function testing Caused by mutations in MYH7 encoding slow or beta-cardiac myosin heavy chain, typically within the distal light-meromyosin rod domain. The pathological hallmark is subsarcolemmal hyaline bodies of accumulated slow myosin that are eosinophilic on haematoxylin and eosin and stain strongly for slow-myosin ATPase. Weakness ranges from a scapuloperoneal to a limb-girdle distribution, often with prominent scapular and foot-dorsiflexor involvement. Cardiomyopathy, whether hypertrophic or dilated, may coexist because of the shared MYH7 gene and warrants active surveillance. Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant, with recessive and de novo cases described. Onset ranges from childhood to adulthood, with generally slow progression. Clinically and genetically it overlaps with Laing distal myopathy and MYH7-related cardiomyopathies. New arrhythmia, syncope or symptoms of heart failure Progressive respiratory muscle weakness Family history of sudden cardiac death Failing to screen for and monitor cardiomyopathy. Mistaking hyaline bodies for other protein aggregates without slow-myosin immunostaining. Overlooking the clinical overlap with Laing distal myopathy. Not offering cascade cardiac and neurological screening to relatives. MYH7 encodes the slow beta-myosin heavy chain expressed in type 1 skeletal fibres and in myocardium. Mutations, frequently in the rod domain, impair thick-filament assembly and stability, so myosin aggregates into hyaline bodies within type 1 fibres and sarcomeric contraction is disrupted. Because the same isoform is expressed in the heart, a cardiomyopathy may accompany the skeletal phenotype. Skeletal weakness is generally slowly progressive with ambulation preserved for many years. The overall outlook is strongly influenced by any associated cardiomyopathy, making cardiac surveillance essential.

the immature cellular centre mimics a sarcoma histologically Management is usually conservative with observation, as the lesion matures and often partially regresses without excision A mass without peripheral maturation raising concern for extraskeletal osteosarcoma Continued growth beyond the expected maturation window Central rather than peripheral dense mineralisation on imaging Absence of any traumatic history with atypical imaging features Misinterpreting the cellular immature centre on early biopsy as a sarcoma Reversing the zonal reasoning and mistaking it for extraskeletal osteosarcoma Excising a lesion prematurely before maturation, increasing recurrence risk Imaging too early before diagnostic peripheral ossification has developed Myositis ossificans traumatica is a benign, reactive proliferation of fibroblasts, cartilage and bone within soft tissue, most often triggered by a single injury or repetitive microtrauma. Local tissue damage initiates a proliferative fibroblastic response that undergoes progressive metaplastic differentiation into cartilage and then bone. The lesion matures in a centripetal, zonal fashion, with the peripheral rim ossifying first and most completely, while the centre remains cellular and immature early in the course. Over weeks to months the whole lesion becomes better demarcated and ossified, and it may shrink. Myositis ossificans is benign and self-limiting, typically maturing and stabilising over several months, often with partial resorption. Excision, if required for symptoms, is best delayed until the lesion is mature to reduce recurrence, and the outlook is excellent.

or safe mobility Adverse response to depolarising neuromuscular blockade during anaesthesia Mistaking it for myotonic dystrophy and missing the systemic surveillance the latter requires, or vice versa Confusing the warm-up phenomenon of myotonia congenita with the paradoxical cold-worsened myotonia of paramyotonia congenita Overlooking the transient exercise-induced weakness of Becker myotonia and labelling it a fixed myopathy Not warning about depolarising muscle relaxants and other anaesthetic triggers of severe myotonia Myotonia congenita results from loss-of-function mutations in CLCN1, the gene encoding the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated chloride channel ClC-1. This channel carries most of the resting membrane conductance and normally stabilises the sarcolemma after an action potential. When chloride conductance is reduced, potassium that accumulates in the transverse tubules during activity depolarises the membrane more readily, producing runs of repetitive after-discharges experienced as delayed muscle relaxation, or myotonia. The autosomal dominant form reflects a dominant-negative effect on the dimeric channel, whereas the recessive form arises when both alleles are severely impaired, and the transient warm-up improvement reflects redistribution of ions with repeated activity. Myotonia congenita is a non-progressive, non-dystrophic disorder compatible with a normal lifespan, and although stiffness can be functionally limiting it often stabilises or improves in adulthood and usually responds to antimyotonic therapy.
