DMPK for DM1 and CCTG in CNBP for DM2) that are transcribed into RNA containing long repeat tracts. These toxic RNA transcripts accumulate in the nucleus and sequester RNA-binding proteins, particularly muscleblind-like proteins, disrupting the normal alternative splicing of many downstream genes. The resulting misregulated splicing of ion-channel, insulin-receptor, and other transcripts produces myotonia, progressive muscle degeneration, and the wide-ranging systemic features. Repeat instability during transmission enlarges the expansion across generations, underlying the phenomenon of anticipation. Prognosis depends on the type and severity: DM1 tends to be more severe than DM2, and the congenital form carries high neonatal morbidity and mortality. Cardiac conduction disease and respiratory failure are the leading causes of premature death, so lifelong cardiac and respiratory surveillance is central to care.

Myotubular myopathy — X-linked myotubular myopathy, X-linked centronuclear myopathy, XLMTM Spinal muscular atrophy type 1 Congenital myotonic dystrophy Other centronuclear myopathies (DNM2, BIN1, RYR1) Congenital myasthenic syndromes Infantile-onset Pompe disease Prader-Willi syndrome Congenital muscular dystrophies MTM1 sequencing with deletion and duplication analysis Muscle biopsy with histochemistry (NADH, SDH, PAS) Serum creatine kinase (usually normal or mildly raised) Nerve conduction studies and electromyography Overnight oximetry and capnography with respiratory function assessment Cranial and muscle imaging where indicated Genetic counselling and carrier testing of the mother X-linked recessive congenital myopathy caused by MTM1 mutations encoding myotubularin, a phosphoinositide phosphatase regulating membrane trafficking and excitation-contraction coupling. Affected male neonates present with profound hypotonia, respiratory failure frequently requiring immediate ventilatory support, and feeding difficulty. Macrocephaly, a long face, external ophthalmoplegia and undescended testes are characteristic supportive features. Muscle biopsy shows small rounded fibres with central nuclei resembling fetal myotubes, with central aggregation of oxidative enzyme activity on NADH and SDH staining. Antenatal clues include polyhydramnios, reduced fetal movements and increased birth length. Female carriers are usually asymptomatic but may show variable weakness through skewed X-inactivation. Milder and later-onset MTM1 phenotypes are increasingly recognised and should not be excluded by survival beyond infancy. Belongs to the centronuclear myopathy family alongside autosomal DNM2- and BIN1-related forms. Neonatal respiratory failure requiring ventilation Recurrent aspiration and feeding failure Apnoea or hypoventilation Hepatic peliosis or haemorrhage, a recognised MTM1 association Unexplained bleeding complications Attributing neonatal hypotonia solely to central causes and missing a primary myopathy. Being falsely reassured by a normal creatine kinase. Overlooking hepatic haemorrhage or peliosis as a cause of sudden deterioration. Failing to test and counsel the carrier mother and at-risk female relatives. Assuming survival beyond infancy excludes an MTM1 diagnosis. MTM1 encodes myotubularin, a lipid phosphatase that dephosphorylates phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphate and its 3,5-bisphosphate, regulating endosomal membrane trafficking, autophagy and the triad structures responsible for excitation-contraction coupling. Loss of function disorganises T-tubules and triad positioning, impairs calcium release and arrests myofibre maturation, so nuclei persist centrally in a manner reminiscent of fetal myotubes and severe congenital weakness results. Classic severe disease historically carries high early mortality from respiratory failure, although survival is improving with ventilatory and nutritional support and milder variants run a more favourable course. Gene-directed therapies are under active investigation.

Myxoedema coma — TFTs, cortisol ECG, electrolytes (Na↓) IV thyroxine + hydrocortisone; treat precipitant Sick euthyroid syndrome confounding thyroid function tests in a critically ill or hypothermic patient (p.3769). Adrenal insufficiency / hypopituitarism, which independently increase susceptibility to hypothermia and may coexist (p.3768). Hashimoto's encephalopathy - a steroid-responsive syndrome with TPO antibodies, myoclonus and EEG slow-wave activity (relationship to hypothyroidism not established) (p.3030). Sepsis should be actively suspected as a precipitant; hypothermia obscures fever and leukocytosis, and infectious rigors may be mistaken for shivering (p.3032, p.3769). Pneumonia as a respiration-impairing precipitant (p.3032). Arterial blood gas to detect hypoxia and hypercapnia from hypoventilation (p.3032). Glucose to detect contributing hypoglycemia (p.3032). Septic screen / cultures, since infection is a common precipitant and is masked by hypothermia (p.3032, p.3769). Core temperature measurement (may be very low, down to ~23 degrees C) (p.3032). Environmental / accidental hypothermia from cold exposure, drugs (ethanol, sedatives, antipsychotics, antidepressants), or malnutrition (p.3768). Hypoglycemia from insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents, which itself causes hypothermia via neuroglycopenic hypothalamic effects (p.3768). Myxedema coma carries a 20-40% mortality despite intensive care, and outcome does not correlate with the degree of T4 or TSH abnormality (p.3032). It occurs almost exclusively in the elderly, often in winter, and may arise either in a known hypothyroid patient with poor treatment adherence or in someone not previously diagnosed (p.3032). Hypothermia in myxedema can be profound, reaching as low as 23 degrees C (74 degrees F) (p.3032). Reduced consciousness is the hallmark and may be accompanied by seizures, alongside the usual signs of hypothyroidism (p.3032). A distinguishing examination clue in hypothyroidism is a deep tendon reflex (e.g., Achilles) whose relaxation phase is prolonged out of proportion to the contraction phase (p.3769). Hypothyroidism, especially extreme as in myxedema coma, is a recognised endocrine cause of hypothermia by reducing metabolic rate and impairing thermogenesis and behavioural responses (p.3768). Bradycardia, reduced myocardial contractility and stroke volume, and pericardial effusion (up to ~30% of hypothyroid patients) reflect the cardiac depression that underlies the haemodynamic picture (p.3030). Carotene accumulation can give the skin a yellow tinge, and nonpitting (myxedematous) tissue swelling distinguishes the oedema from pitting fluid overload (p.3029-3030). Reduced level of consciousness with seizures in a hypothyroid patient (p.3032). Profound hypothermia (toward 23 degrees C) (p.3032). Hypoventilation with hypoxia/hypercapnia signalling impending respiratory failure (p.3032). Severe dilutional hyponatremia and hypoglycemia (p.3032). An identifiable precipitant such as infection, MI, CHF, GI bleeding, cerebrovascular accident, or respiratory-depressant drugs (p.3032). Sedatives, anesthetics, and antidepressants can precipitate or worsen myxedema coma, and impaired drug metabolism means standard doses may accumulate (p.3032). Hypothermia masks fever and leukocytosis, so infection can be missed; rigors may be misread as shivering (p.3769). Giving parenteral levothyroxine to a euthyroid hypothermic patient is potentially hazardous, so clinical/historical evidence of hypothyroidism should be sought first (p.3769). Sick euthyroid syndrome can confound thyroid function tests in the acutely ill patient (p.3769). Long-standing thyroid hormone deficiency depresses the metabolic rate and thermogenesis, producing hypothermia, bradycardia, and reduced myocardial contractility. Dermal accumulation of glycosaminoglycans traps water, giving nonpitting myxedematous swelling. In myxedema coma, hypoventilation is central to pathogenesis: it leads to hypoxia and hypercapnia (CO2 retention). Dilutional hyponatremia (reduced renal perfusion with inappropriate vasopressin) and hypoglycemia further contribute. There is impaired adrenal reserve in profound hypothyroidism, and impaired peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion (p.3032; p.3768). Mortality remains 20-40% even with intensive treatment, and prognosis is independent of the measured T4 and TSH levels. Hypothermia associated with concurrent sepsis is a poor prognostic sign (p.3032, p.3769).

adrenal insufficiency with steroids Aggressive active external rewarming that precipitates vasodilatory collapse Overcorrecting hyponatraemia too rapidly Missing the precipitating infection or Severe thyroid-hormone deficiency slows metabolic rate and thermogenesis, producing hypothermia, and depresses respiratory drive with carbon-dioxide retention. A precipitating stress such as infection or sedation tips the decompensated patient into obtundation and multi-organ dysfunction. Even with modern intensive care, mortality remains substantial; outcome depends on prompt recognition, early hormone replacement and treatment of the precipitating illness.

With repeated recurrence, tumours often increase in grade and cellularity, acquiring greater metastatic potential, most commonly to the lungs. Prognosis relates chiefly to grade and adequacy of excision; low-grade tumours rarely metastasise but recur locally, whereas high-grade tumours carry a significant metastatic risk, and repeated recurrence with grade progression worsens the outlook.

later with episodic hyperammonaemia and neurocognitive symptoms The key distinguishing feature is its responsiveness to carglumic acid, a synthetic N-acetylglutamate analogue that restores CPS1 activity Low or absent orotic aciduria helps separate proximal urea cycle defects (NAGS, CPS1) from OTC deficiency Confirm with NAGS gene sequencing and by demonstrating a therapeutic response to carglumic acid Acute management is emergency ammonia lowering (dialysis if needed) with carglumic acid, nitrogen scavengers, arginine and protein restriction Neonatal hyperammonaemic coma requiring emergency ammonia removal Cerebral oedema from severe hyperammonaemia Rapidly rising ammonia with encephalopathy at any age Decompensation triggered by catabolic illness, high protein load or surgery Failure of ammonia to fall despite standard scavenger therapy (prompting carglumic acid) Not distinguishing NAGS from CPS1 deficiency and thereby missing a treatable disorder Failing to trial carglumic acid, which is specifically effective in NAGS deficiency Overlooking the low orotic acid clue that points to a proximal urea cycle defect Delaying emergency ammonia lowering while awaiting confirmatory genetics Assuming carglumic acid is equally effective in all urea cycle disorders N-acetylglutamate synthase catalyses formation of N-acetylglutamate from glutamate and acetyl-CoA. N-acetylglutamate is the essential allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1), the enzyme that initiates the urea cycle by incorporating ammonia into carbamoyl phosphate. In NAGS deficiency the activator is not produced, so CPS1 remains inactive and the urea cycle cannot begin, leading to accumulation of ammonia. Because the block is at the very first step, downstream intermediates such as citrulline and arginine are low, and carbamoyl phosphate is not diverted into pyrimidine synthesis, so orotic acid excretion stays low (mirroring CPS1 deficiency and contrasting with OTC deficiency). Uniquely, the missing activator can be replaced pharmacologically by carglumic acid, which reactivates CPS1. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. NAGS deficiency is one of the few urea cycle disorders with a specific pharmacological treatment; with early diagnosis and carglumic acid therapy long-term metabolic control and outcome can be excellent, whereas delayed treatment of severe neonatal hyperammonaemia risks permanent neurological injury.

to reassure and exclude neoplasia Cervical cytology and human papillomavirus testing as part of routine screening A nabothian cyst is a benign mucus-filled retention cyst on the cervix formed when the opening of an endocervical gland becomes covered by squamous epithelium during normal metaplasia They are extremely common, usually multiple, and almost always asymptomatic incidental findings on speculum examination or pelvic imaging Typical appearance is one or more smooth, translucent or yellowish-white raised nodules on the ectocervix, often over the transformation zone They require no treatment when characteristic and asymptomatic, and reassurance is the mainstay of management On ultrasound they appear as well-defined cystic spaces within the cervix and can occasionally be large or deep, prompting unnecessary concern if misinterpreted Rarely, very large or numerous deep cysts (so-called tunnel clusters) can be mistaken on imaging for a cervical neoplasm, so correlation with the benign clinical picture is important Intervention such as marsupialisation or excision is only considered if a cyst is unusually large, symptomatic, or the diagnosis is uncertain Cervical screening should continue as normal, since nabothian cysts themselves carry no malignant potential Atypical, rapidly enlarging, or irregular cervical lesion that could represent malignancy Abnormal bleeding, particularly postcoital or postmenopausal, warranting further assessment Deep or extensive cystic change on imaging that raises the question of adenoma malignum Abnormal cervical screening results Over-investigating or excising a characteristic asymptomatic cyst unnecessarily Misinterpreting deep or clustered cysts on imaging as cervical malignancy Attributing abnormal bleeding to a nabothian cyst and failing to exclude other cervical pathology Neglecting routine cervical screening because a benign cyst is present The cervix undergoes continuous squamous metaplasia at the transformation zone, where columnar endocervical epithelium is progressively replaced by squamous epithelium. When advancing squamous epithelium grows over the mouth of a mucus-secreting endocervical gland, the gland's outflow is obstructed and mucus is retained, distending it into a smooth cyst. The process is entirely physiological and benign, and the cysts have no relationship to infection or malignancy. Their main clinical relevance is avoiding misdiagnosis, since deep or clustered cysts can superficially resemble other cervical lesions on imaging. Nabothian cysts are benign with an excellent prognosis, requiring no treatment in the vast majority of cases and carrying no risk of malignant transformation.

Naegeli-Franceschetti-Jadassohn syndrome — NFJS, KRT14, keratin 14, Naegeli syndrome Dermatopathia pigmentosa reticularis (allelic KRT14 disorder) Incontinentia pigmenti (which has preceding inflammatory/vesicular stages) Dyskeratosis congenita Franceschetti-Jadassohn variants / other reticulate pigmentary disorders Dowling-Degos disease Other hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasias Molecular genetic testing of KRT14 Examination for absent dermatoglyphics (fingerprint loss) Skin biopsy showing pigment incontinence without significant inflammation Assessment of sweating and heat tolerance Dental and nail evaluation Family history and pedigree analysis An ectodermal dysplasia characterised by reticulate (net-like) hyperpigmentation that, unusually, is not preceded by an inflammatory or vesicular stage Absent or markedly reduced dermatoglyphics (loss of fingerprints) is a distinctive and helpful sign Diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma and reduced sweating (hypohidrosis) with consequent heat intolerance are typical Dental anomalies, including yellow-brown discolouration and early tooth loss, and nail dystrophy are common Autosomal dominant; caused by mutations in KRT14 encoding keratin 14 The reticulate pigmentation tends to fade with age, in contrast to some other pigmentary genodermatoses Management is supportive with emollients/keratolytics, heat-avoidance measures for hypohidrosis, and dental care Hyperthermia or heat intolerance from hypohidrosis, particularly in infancy Severe early dental disease requiring intervention Functionally limiting palmoplantar keratoderma Features suggesting an alternative diagnosis with systemic risk (e.g. dyskeratosis congenita) Confusing it with incontinentia pigmenti, which has vesicular and verrucous stages preceding pigmentation Overlooking the diagnostically useful absence of fingerprints Failing to warn about heat intolerance and to advise cooling measures Not distinguishing it from the allelic dermatopathia pigmentosa reticularis Naegeli-Franceschetti-Jadassohn syndrome is an autosomal dominant ectodermal dysplasia caused by mutations in KRT14, which encodes keratin 14, a basal keratinocyte intermediate-filament protein that pairs with keratin 5 to maintain the mechanical integrity of the basal epidermis. The disease-causing mutations affect the non-helical head domain of keratin 14 and are thought to disturb keratin-network function and increase basal keratinocyte apoptosis, with resultant transfer of melanin/pigment into the dermis producing the reticulate hyperpigmentation. The same defect disturbs the development of epidermal appendages, giving hypohidrosis (from reduced or abnormal sweat glands), palmoplantar keratoderma, nail dystrophy, dental abnormalities and the absence of dermatoglyphics. (Mutations in KRT14 that abolish the protein instead cause the allelic dermatopathia pigmentosa reticularis.) The condition is compatible with a normal lifespan and general health; the reticulate pigmentation characteristically fades with age. The main ongoing issues are heat intolerance from hypohidrosis, keratoderma and dental problems, all of which are manageable with supportive measures.

naevus anaemicus — nevus anemicus, pharmacological naevus Naevus depigmentosus Vitiligo Ash-leaf macule of tuberous sclerosis Pityriasis alba Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation Hypopigmented segmental lesions of mosaicism Diascopy demonstrating disappearance of the lesion margin under glass pressure Rubbing or warming test showing surrounding erythema that spares the lesion Wood's lamp examination confirming absence of pigmentary accentuation Examination for café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, and other features of neurofibromatosis type 1 Dermoscopy showing reduced or absent background vascular erythema Skin biopsy (rarely required) confirming normal melanocytes and vasculature A congenital vascular anomaly rather than a true pigmentary disorder, appearing as a pale, well-demarcated macule or patch usually on the upper trunk. The pallor is functional and reflects a localised hypersensitivity of dermal vessels to catecholamines causing persistent vasoconstriction, not a deficiency of melanin. Diascopy (pressure with a glass slide) causes the lesion to blend indistinguishably with the surrounding blanched skin, confirming the vascular basis. Rubbing or warming the area produces reactive erythema in the normal surrounding skin but not within the naevus, sharply outlining the lesion. Wood's lamp examination does not accentuate the border, because there is no melanin abnormality, helping distinguish it from hypomelanotic lesions. Injection of an alpha-adrenergic blocker or heating abolishes the pallor, underscoring the pharmacological (catecholamine-mediated) mechanism. It is associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 and may be an early cutaneous marker, and can also co-occur with tuberous sclerosis and phacomatosis pigmentovascularis. The lesion is stable throughout life and of cosmetic significance only. Multiple café-au-lait macules or neurofibromas suggesting associated neurofibromatosis type 1 Coexisting vascular and pigmentary naevi indicating phacomatosis pigmentovascularis Features of tuberous sclerosis accompanying the lesion Any progressive change, which would be atypical for this stable congenital anomaly Misinterpreting the pallor as a hypomelanotic or depigmenting disorder and pursuing unnecessary pigmentary work-up Omitting diascopy and the rub test, which are the simplest confirmatory bedside manoeuvres Expecting Wood's lamp accentuation and doubting the diagnosis when none occurs Failing to examine for neurofibromatosis type 1 when a naevus anaemicus is identified Attempting active treatment of an inherently stable, benign vascular anomaly Naevus anaemicus is a congenital functional vascular defect in which the cutaneous blood vessels within a circumscribed area exhibit exaggerated sensitivity to circulating and locally released catecholamines. This heightened alpha-adrenergic responsiveness maintains the affected vessels in a state of near-permanent vasoconstriction, reducing local blood flow and producing the characteristic pallor against normally perfused surrounding skin. The vessels are structurally normal, and there is no abnormality of melanocytes, melanin, or vessel number; the phenomenon is therefore pharmacological rather than anatomical or pigmentary. Evidence for this mechanism includes the abolition of pallor by intradermal alpha-adrenergic blockade, by warming, and by physical trauma that would normally provoke a vasodilatory flare, and its persistence despite normal vascular architecture. Because there is no melanin defect, the lesion neither fluoresces abnormally under Wood's lamp nor blanches distinctly on diascopy. Naevus anaemicus is entirely benign and permanent, remaining stable throughout life with no risk of malignant transformation. Its main clinical value is as a potential early cutaneous marker prompting evaluation for neurofibromatosis type 1.

naevus depigmentosus — naevus achromicus, nevus depigmentosus Segmental vitiligo Ash-leaf macule of tuberous sclerosis Naevus anaemicus Hypomelanosis of Ito Pityriasis alba Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation Piebaldism Wood's lamp examination showing off-white rather than chalky-white fluorescence Dermoscopy demonstrating faint, ill-defined pigment network with irregular borders Skin biopsy with electron microscopy showing normal melanocyte numbers and abnormal melanosomes (rarely needed) Neurocutaneous evaluation and neuroimaging if systematised or associated with neurological signs Ophthalmological and developmental assessment when pigmentary mosaicism is extensive Serial photography to confirm stability over time A congenital, stable, well-demarcated hypopigmented (not depigmented) macule or patch that is usually solitary and often noted at or shortly after birth. Three clinical patterns are recognised: an isolated localised form, a segmental or dermatomal form, and a rarer systematised (whorled/blaschkoid) form. Under Wood's lamp the lesion appears off-white or dull rather than the chalky bright-white accentuation seen in vitiligo, reflecting reduced but not absent melanin. The lesion is stable relative to body growth and does not spread or repigment, with borders that are frequently serrated or irregular. Melanocyte numbers are normal or only slightly reduced; the defect lies in abnormal melanosome morphology and impaired transfer to keratinocytes. Overlying hair may be hypopigmented within the patch, a helpful supportive sign. Multiple or systematised lesions warrant evaluation for associated neurocutaneous or developmental abnormalities. Differentiation from a single ash-leaf macule of tuberous sclerosis is critical, as management and prognosis differ substantially. Multiple hypopigmented macules with seizures or developmental delay suggesting tuberous sclerosis Progressive enlargement or new depigmentation inconsistent with a stable congenital naevus Extensive systematised lesions accompanied by neurological or skeletal abnormalities Associated ocular or dental anomalies indicating a broader mosaic syndrome Confusing a solitary lesion with an ash-leaf macule and either missing or wrongly attributing tuberous sclerosis Misdiagnosing it as segmental vitiligo and prescribing futile depigmentation-targeted therapy Expecting Wood's lamp to show the bright accentuation typical of vitiligo and thereby doubting the diagnosis Failing to recognise systematised forms as pigmentary mosaicism warranting further assessment Reassuring about stability without documenting the lesion photographically at baseline Naevus depigmentosus is best regarded as a localised functional defect of pigmentation rather than an absence of melanocytes. Electron microscopy demonstrates a normal or near-normal number of melanocytes containing aggregated, abnormally structured melanosomes and reduced melanosome transfer to surrounding keratinocytes; the melanocytes show stunted dendrites. The result is a stable region of hypomelanosis in which some residual pigment remains, distinguishing it clinically and on Wood's lamp from the total melanocyte loss of vitiligo. The mosaic segmental and blaschkoid distributions are thought to reflect post-zygotic somatic mutation affecting a clone of melanocytic precursors, producing pigmentary mosaicism along the lines of Blaschko. Because the underlying melanocytes are present and viable, the lesion neither progresses nor responds to the immunomodulatory therapies used for vitiligo. Naevus depigmentosus is a benign, lifelong, and stable condition of purely cosmetic significance in the localised form, with no risk of malignant change. The main clinical importance lies in correctly distinguishing it from tuberous sclerosis and vitiligo to avoid unnecessary anxiety and treatment.

LSM >12 kPa associated with cirrhosis) Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) blood test (ELF >=9.8 increased risk; >11.8 suspect cirrhosis) Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) and cT1 for refined risk stratification Abdominal ultrasound / cross-sectional imaging for steatosis Workup to exclude other causes: viral hepatitis serologies, autoimmune markers, iron/copper studies, alpha-1 antitrypsin Screening for T2DM; assessment of metabolic syndrome components Liver biopsy - historical gold standard for staging, reserved for indeterminate/discordant NITs, diagnostic uncertainty, or suspected concurrent chronic hepatitis (limited by sampling and observer variability) Alcohol-associated liver disease (histologically can be indistinguishable; alcohol intake must be excluded) Autoimmune hepatitis (note ~20% of steatotic liver disease patients have a positive ANA) Medication/drug-associated steatosis or steatohepatitis Wilson disease, hemochromatosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Steatotic liver disease (SLD) is the most common cause of chronic liver disease in the US and worldwide; metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and steatohepatitis (MASH) now replace the older terms NAFLD and NASH, with ~98% population overlap (Harrison 22e p.2700-2701). Diagnosis of MASLD requires hepatic steatosis plus little/no alcohol intake (<20 g/d women, <30 g/d men) and at least one cardiometabolic risk factor (overweight/obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance/T2DM) (Harrison 22e p.2700, 2703). Most patients are asymptomatic; MASLD is typically detected incidentally via raised ALT or steatosis on imaging done for other reasons (Harrison 22e p.2702-2703). Disease spans a dynamic, potentially reversible spectrum: simple steatosis (MASL) -> steatohepatitis (MASH) -> fibrosis -> cirrhosis/HCC; chronic steatohepatitis is the primary driver of fibrosis, and fibrosis severity is the chief predictor of liver-related morbidity/mortality (Harrison 22e p.2700-2701, 2704). FIB-4 (age, AST, ALT, platelets) is the recommended first-line noninvasive score with excellent negative predictive value: FIB-4 <1.3 = low risk (manage in primary care), >=2.67 = moderate/high risk warranting a secondary test (elastography or ELF) (Harrison 22e p.2704-2705). T2DM is the strongest risk factor for MASLD acquisition, fibrosis progression, and HCC; the MASLD-T2DM relationship is bidirectional, so patients with MASLD should be screened for T2DM (Harrison 22e p.2703). Foundational treatment is lifestyle modification with weight loss: ~5% weight loss improves steatosis, while >10% improves MASH and can reverse fibrosis; cardiovascular risk reduction and treatment of metabolic comorbidities apply to all patients (Harrison 22e p.2706). Statins are safe across the MASLD spectrum and indicated for dyslipidemia given high cardiovascular risk; reluctance to use them is not supported by evidence of liver harm (Harrison 22e p.2707). FIB-4 >=2.67 (moderate/high risk for advanced fibrosis - needs secondary testing/specialist referral) Fibrosis stage >=F2 = 'at-risk MASH' with increased risk of further progression and adverse liver outcomes Persistently elevated AST and ALT Stigmata of advanced disease: spider angiomata, palmar erythema, splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, clubbing, ascites, encephalopathy Features of decompensation/end-stage disease: jaundice, ascites, variceal hemorrhage Clinical/radiologic suspicion of cirrhosis or ELF >11.8 Failing to exclude significant alcohol intake and other chronic liver diseases (viral, autoimmune, iron/copper overload, alpha-1 antitrypsin) before attributing steatosis to MASLD. Assuming normal liver enzymes exclude MASLD - they do not; normal ALT 'reference ranges' are inflated by including people with undiagnosed liver disease. Relying on liver tests for staging - aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, albumin, and PT may all be completely normal even with significant disease. MASLD can occur in lean individuals (BMI <25, or <23 in Asians), especially with truncal/visceral adiposity, so a normal BMI does not exclude it. FIB-4 has reduced accuracy in patients >65 and <35 years and is a less robust predictor in T2DM, so a secondary noninvasive test is needed in these groups. Liver biopsy is limited by sampling error, inter/intraobserver variability (worse with cores <2 cm), and gives only a static snapshot of disease activity. MASLD arises from imbalance between energy intake and expenditure: excess caloric intake, reduced physical activity, and limited peripheral adipose expansion drive visceral adiposity, insulin resistance, and metabolic dysfunction. Hepatocyte triglyceride accumulates from increased free fatty acid delivery (dietary uptake, adipose lipolysis, de novo lipogenesis), impaired fatty acid disposal, or impaired triglyceride export; triglyceride storage itself is relatively safe, so steatosis per se does not damage the liver but is a biomarker of metabolic dysfunction. When adaptive mechanisms are overwhelmed, lipotoxicity from dysfunctional lipid handling injures and kills hepatocytes, producing steatohepatitis (MASH) with inflammation and ballooned hepatocytes. Repeated/protracted MASH triggers regenerative responses that become maladaptive, promoting progressive fibrosis (replacement of functional parenchyma by scar) and primary liver cancer; cirrhosis represents futile repair. Heritable factors (e.g., PNPLA3, TM6SF2, MBOAT7 variants), epigenetic influences, gut microbiota alterations, and environmental factors (high-fat/high-sugar diets) modify susceptibility (Harrison 22e p.2701-2702). Variable and stage-dependent. The 10-year probability of liver-related morbidity/mortality is negligible with steatosis alone, so this group is managed conservatively. Fibrosis severity is the primary predictor of outcome: average fibrosis progression is roughly one stage every 14 years in steatosis versus one stage every 7 years in MASH; once at stage >=F2 ('at-risk MASH') the risk of further progression and bad outcomes rises. Once MASLD-related cirrhosis develops, progression to decompensation runs 3-20% per year and annual primary liver cancer incidence can reach 1-2% per year, prompting biannual HCC surveillance and variceal screening. Cirrhosis can regress, and MASLD outcomes after liver transplantation are generally good in well-selected patients, though comorbid diabetes, obesity, and CVD limit candidacy and disease may recur post-transplant. MASLD is also a premalignant condition increasing risk of primary and extrahepatic malignancy even in noncirrhotic livers (Harrison 22e p.2701, 2704, 2708). Histopathologic/fibrosis staging spectrum: simple steatosis (MASL) -> steatohepatitis (MASH) -> fibrosis -> cirrhosis. Fibrosis stages F0 (none), F1 (minimal), F2 (significant), F3 (advanced/bridging), F4 (cirrhosis, further stratified into compensated and decompensated). 'At-risk MASH' = MASH with fibrosis stage >=F2. Noninvasive risk stratification: FIB-4 <1.3 low risk, >=1.3 intermediate, >=2.67 moderate/high; secondary tests VCTE <8 kPa low / 8-12 intermediate / >12 high, ELF <7.7 low / 7.7-9.8 intermediate / >9.8 high (Harrison 22e p.2704-2705).

regulate proteolytic activity within the stratum corneum. Its deficiency is thought to impair the water-barrier properties of the cornified layer, so that acral skin absorbs water abnormally and swells and whitens on immersion, and terminal keratinocyte processing is disturbed to give a diffuse transgredient keratoderma. The compromised barrier and associated hyperhidrosis favour secondary microbial colonisation and malodour. The condition is benign and non-progressive; with regular keratolytic and emollient care and attention to secondary infection, most patients maintain good function and quality of life.

Early mortality relates chiefly to airway compromise; those who survive the neonatal period with secure airway and feeding generally have normal intellect and function reasonably well with staged craniofacial and hand reconstruction.

napkin dermatitis — nappy rash, diaper dermatitis candidal (monilial) dermatitis with satellite pustules seborrhoeic dermatitis involving the folds and scalp infantile or napkin psoriasis atopic dermatitis with secondary napkin involvement acrodermatitis enteropathica or acquired zinc deficiency Langerhans cell histiocytosis perianal streptococcal dermatitis or bullous impetigo skin swab and microscopy or culture for Candida when folds are involved or satellite lesions present bacterial swab for suspected streptococcal or staphylococcal secondary infection serum zinc and alkaline phosphatase if an acrodermatitis-like periorificial and acral eruption coexists skin biopsy for persistent, erosive or petechial eruptions to exclude histiocytosis stool assessment when chronic diarrhoea is driving an erosive irritant pattern blood glucose and immune screen where recurrent or refractory candidiasis suggests underlying immunodeficiency patch testing in older children with suspected allergic contact dermatitis to wipes or fragrances Irritant contact dermatitis is the commonest form, sparing the inguinal and gluteal skin folds because the convex surfaces in contact with the napkin bear the brunt of friction, moisture and irritants. Fold involvement is the key clue that the picture is no longer simple irritant dermatitis and points to candidal infection, seborrhoeic dermatitis, or intertrigo. Candidal napkin dermatitis characteristically shows beefy-red confluent erythema with peripheral scaling and satellite papules and pustules extending into the folds. Prolonged skin wetness raises pH and activates faecal proteases and lipases, so the mainstay of prevention is frequent changing, gentle cleansing and a barrier preparation. Jacquet erosive dermatitis is a severe irritant form with punched-out ulcers and raised papulonodules, seen with chronic diarrhoea or infrequent changing. A napkin eruption that is erosive, purpuric, ulcerated or unresponsive to standard care should raise suspicion of Langerhans cell histiocytosis, zinc deficiency or child neglect. Perianal streptococcal disease and staphylococcal folliculitis can mimic or complicate napkin dermatitis and should be considered with a well-demarcated painful perianal erythema. Low-potency topical corticosteroid for short courses helps inflammatory cases, but potent fluorinated steroids under occlusion of the napkin risk atrophy and granuloma gluteale infantum. erosive, ulcerated or purpuric lesions suggesting Langerhans cell histiocytosis rather than simple irritant rash periorificial and acral dermatitis with diarrhoea and alopecia indicating zinc deficiency failure to respond to appropriate barrier and antifungal treatment systemic upset, spreading cellulitis or blistering suggesting invasive bacterial infection features raising concern for neglect such as a severe untreated eruption with poor general care treating fold-involving candidal dermatitis as pure irritant rash and omitting an antifungal prescribing potent fluorinated corticosteroids under napkin occlusion, causing atrophy or granuloma gluteale infantum missing acrodermatitis enteropathica by not examining periorificial and acral sites overlooking Langerhans cell histiocytosis in an erosive, petechial or treatment-resistant eruption attributing all perianal erythema to irritation and missing perianal streptococcal disease Napkin dermatitis is predominantly an irritant contact dermatitis arising from the occluded, humid microenvironment beneath a nappy. Sustained contact with urine and faeces increases skin hydration and surface pH, which in turn activates faecal proteolytic and lipolytic enzymes that degrade the stratum corneum barrier. Friction against the napkin, maceration and repeated wetting-drying cycles compound the barrier disruption, allowing irritants and microbes to penetrate. Overgrowth of Candida albicans from the gastrointestinal tract frequently supervenes on damaged skin, and secondary bacterial colonisation may occur. Underlying inflammatory dermatoses such as seborrhoeic dermatitis, atopic eczema and psoriasis can localise to or be exacerbated within the napkin area because of the Koebner phenomenon and occlusion. Simple irritant napkin dermatitis resolves rapidly with barrier protection and improved hygiene and clears completely once nappies are discontinued. Recurrence is common while in nappies, and persistent or atypical eruptions require reassessment for an alternative underlying diagnosis.

(orexin)-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, most likely through an autoimmune process in genetically susceptible individuals carrying HLA-DQB1*06:02. Hypocretin normally stabilises wakefulness and suppresses inappropriate REM sleep; its deficiency destabilises the sleep-wake switch, producing daytime sleepiness and the intrusion of REM features such as cataplexy into wakefulness. Type 2 has preserved hypocretin levels and a less well-defined mechanism. Narcolepsy is a lifelong disorder, but symptoms can usually be controlled well enough with treatment and behavioural measures to allow good function. It carries important safety implications for driving and work, and untreated disease significantly impairs quality of life, mood, and daytime performance.

The deficiency is believed to be autoimmune, occurring in genetically susceptible individuals carrying HLA-DQB1*06:02, sometimes after immune triggers. Loss of hypocretin signalling destabilises the boundaries between wake and REM sleep, producing sleepiness and intrusion of REM phenomena such as cataplexy, sleep paralysis and dream-like hallucinations into wakefulness. The preserved hypocretin signalling is thought to explain the absence of cataplexy, while residual instability of wake-REM regulation produces the sleepiness and sleep-onset REM periods. Narcotic bowel syndrome — opioid-induced gastrointestinal hyperalgesia Centrally mediated abdominal pain syndrome Opioid-induced constipation with pain Structural intra-abdominal disease Chronic pancreatitis Opioid withdrawal (during treatment) Careful opioid and pain history documenting the dose-pain relationship Targeted investigation to exclude structural disease rather than repeated testing Assessment of psychological comorbidity and functional impact Planning of a structured opioid withdrawal programme Review of previous investigations to avoid duplication A paradoxical worsening of chronic abdominal pain with continued or escalating opioid use The pain increases as opioid doses rise, in contrast to the expected analgesic effect It is a form of opioid-induced hyperalgesia affecting the gut and is distinct from simple opioid-induced constipation It should be suspected when abdominal pain persists or worsens despite high or increasing opioid doses without another explanation The key intervention is a planned, supported withdrawal of opioids, often with adjunctive medication and psychological support Pain typically flares transiently during withdrawal before improving, which must be anticipated and explained New alarm features suggesting organic disease Signs of a surgical abdomen Severe psychological distress complicating withdrawal Escalating opioid requirements without benefit Escalating opioids in response to worsening pain Attributing the pain to undiagnosed structural disease and operating Not preparing the patient for the transient flare during withdrawal Failing to provide psychological and multidisciplinary support Narcotic bowel syndrome is a manifestation of opioid-induced hyperalgesia, in which chronic opioid exposure produces neuroplastic changes that paradoxically enhance pain sensitivity. Mechanisms include activation of pronociceptive pathways, central sensitisation and glial activation, so that escalating opioids further amplify rather than relieve visceral pain. Opioid effects on gut motility may compound symptoms, but the defining feature is the worsening pain with increasing opioid dose, which resolves only when opioids are withdrawn. Pain usually improves substantially after supported opioid withdrawal, though relapse is common if opioids are resumed; long-term success depends on a multidisciplinary approach.

phenotype New seizures or encephalopathy Progressive visual loss impairing safety and function Cardiorespiratory compromise during metabolic stress Excluding a mitochondrial disorder because lactate is normal, which is common in NARP Failing to recognise the NARP-Leigh continuum and its dependence on heteroplasmy level Attributing retinitis pigmentosa to an isolated retinal dystrophy and missing of ATP synthase (respiratory-chain complex V). The mutations impair proton flux through the enzyme and reduce ATP generation while altering mitochondrial membrane potential. Because the gene is mitochondrial, inheritance is maternal and the mutation is heteroplasmic, so the phenotype depends on the mutant load within energy-dependent tissues. Neurons of the peripheral nerves, cerebellum and retina, which have high and sustained energy requirements, are preferentially affected, producing the neuropathy, ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa. At very high mutant proportions the same defect causes the more severe maternally inherited Leigh phenotype. NARP tends to run a slowly progressive course with episodic worsening during metabolic stress; visual, sensory and cerebellar disability accumulate over time, and prognosis is worse at high mutant loads where a Leigh-type picture may supervene.

haematoma requires prompt drainage because untreated it can cause septal cartilage necrosis, perforation, and a saddle-nose deformity It is important to establish the pre-injury shape of the nose, often with a photograph, to judge post-traumatic deformity accurately Reduction, when needed, is best performed either within the first few hours before swelling develops or after several days once swelling subsides but before the fracture sets, generally within about two weeks Persistent deformity or nasal obstruction after healing may need later formal septorhinoplasty rather than early manipulation Clear rhinorrhoea after nasal trauma should raise concern for a CSF leak from an associated skull base or cribriform injury Septal haematoma requiring urgent drainage to prevent cartilage necrosis Clear rhinorrhoea suggesting a CSF leak from skull base or cribriform injury Telecanthus, medial canthal disruption, or features of a naso-orbito-ethmoid fracture Uncontrolled epistaxis or signs of a more extensive midface fracture Failing to examine the septum and missing a septal haematoma Relying on plain radiographs, which rarely change management Attempting reduction during peak swelling, giving an inaccurate result Delaying reduction beyond the window in which the fracture can be manipulated Overlooking an associated naso-orbito-ethmoid or skull base injury Not documenting the pre-injury appearance, leading to unrealistic expectations The prominent, relatively thin nasal bones and the cartilaginous septum are readily displaced by frontal or lateral trauma. Lateral forces tend to displace the nasal bones to one side, while frontal impact can flatten and splay the bones and buckle the septum. Bleeding into the subperichondrial space of the septum forms a septal haematoma, which strips the perichondrium from the cartilage and deprives it of its blood supply; the resulting ischaemia and any superimposed infection can destroy the cartilage, leading to septal perforation and loss of dorsal support (saddle deformity). Higher-energy injuries may extend into the naso-orbito-ethmoid region or the skull base. Most isolated nasal fractures heal well, and timely closed reduction gives good cosmetic and functional results in many patients. A proportion are left with residual deformity or nasal obstruction that may require later septorhinoplasty. The main preventable adverse outcome is the saddle-nose deformity and septal perforation that follow an undrained septal haematoma.

underlying inflammation Overlooking associated asthma and aspirin sensitivity Nasal polyps are pedunculated masses of oedematous, chronically inflamed sinonasal mucosa, most often stemming from Ongoing mucosal inflammation, frequently eosinophil-rich, causes fluid accumulation within the lamina propria, and gravity together with impaired lymphatic drainage encourages the mucosa to prolapse into the nasal cavity as polyps. Contributing factors include chronic rhinosinusitis, allergy, aspirin sensitivity and, in children, cystic fibrosis. The antrochoanal polyp arises from maxillary sinus mucosa, passes through its ostium and enlarges into the choana and nasopharynx. Nasal polyps are benign but tend to be chronic and recurrent, particularly in association with asthma and aspirin sensitivity; symptoms are usually controllable with combined medical and surgical management, though repeated treatment is often needed.

cocaine use remains active Overlooking systemic vasculitic involvement that requires urgent medical management A nasal septal perforation develops when the mucoperichondrium is disrupted on both sides of the septum and the intervening cartilage or bone, deprived of its blood and nutrient supply, necroses and is lost. Iatrogenic injury during septal surgery, repetitive digital trauma, and the intense vasoconstriction produced by cocaine or overused topical decongestants all compromise mucosal perfusion. Inflammatory and granulomatous diseases such as vasculitis, and infiltrative malignancy, destroy the septal framework directly. Once a perforation is established, turbulent airflow across its edges causes drying, crusting, and repeated mucosal breakdown, which tends to enlarge the defect and produces the characteristic crusting, bleeding, whistling, and obstruction. Many small perforations remain stable and are well controlled with conservative measures or a septal button, and carefully selected defects can be repaired successfully, but the outlook worsens when the cause is an ongoing destructive vasculitis, infection, cocaine use, or malignancy.

nasolacrimal drainage system canalises from the eye toward the nose, and the last segment to open is the distal duct at the valve of Hasner. Failure of this membrane to perforate produces a functional obstruction so that tears and mucus cannot drain, causing epiphora and stagnation within the sac that predisposes to secondary infection. Retained secretions may distend the sac to form a dacryocele, and bacterial colonisation can progress to acute dacryocystitis, occasionally with surrounding cellulitis. The outlook is excellent, with most cases resolving spontaneously during the first year; probing is highly successful when required, and only a minority need intubation, balloon dilatation, or dacryocystorhinostomy.

epithelial lining of the nasopharynx, typically in the recess of the fossa of Rosenmuller near the Eustachian tube opening. Malignant transformation is closely linked to latent Epstein-Barr virus infection, together with genetic susceptibility and environmental exposures such as diets rich in preserved salted foods and nitrosamines. The tumour tends to spread submucosally and infiltrate early, obstructing the Eustachian tube to cause middle ear effusion, and eroding through the skull base foramina to involve cranial nerves and the cavernous sinus. Its rich lymphatic drainage leads to early and often bilateral cervical lymph node metastasis, and distant spread to bone, lung and liver can occur. Outcome depends heavily on stage at presentation; early disease treated with radiotherapy has a favourable prognosis, whereas advanced disease with skull base invasion or distant metastasis carries a poorer outlook, and the frequently late presentation makes vigilance for early signs important.

Navajo neurohepatopathy — NNH, MPV17-related hepatocerebral mitochondrial DNA depletion, Navajo neuropathy, MPV17 deficiency Other hepatocerebral mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes (DGUOK, POLG, MPV17-related non-Navajo) Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathies Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome Wilson disease with neurological features Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis Leukodystrophies of other cause Liver function tests, serum bile acids, and lactate/pyruvate Nerve conduction studies and electromyography documenting sensorimotor neuropathy Brain MRI to demonstrate leukoencephalopathy Liver biopsy with quantitative mitochondrial DNA content showing depletion Respiratory chain enzyme analysis in liver or muscle MPV17 gene sequencing An autosomal recessive disorder of the Navajo (Diné) population caused by a founder mutation in MPV17, producing a hepatocerebral mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome Combines progressive liver disease with a severe sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy and central white-matter involvement (leukoencephalopathy) Neuropathy leads to distal weakness, sensory loss, painless injuries, acral mutilation, and corneal anaesthesia with recurrent ulceration Hepatic presentations range from infantile liver failure to a slowly progressive childhood cirrhosis Metabolic decompensation may be accompanied by lactic acidosis reflecting impaired oxidative phosphorylation Diagnosis rests on the ethnic background, characteristic neurological and hepatic features, quantitative mitochondrial DNA depletion in liver, and MPV17 sequencing Management is supportive; liver transplantation may be considered for hepatic failure but does not arrest the progressive neurological disease Acute infantile liver failure with coagulopathy and lactic acidosis Corneal anaesthesia leading to unnoticed ulceration and visual loss Progressive acral mutilation from sensory loss and painless injury Rapid neurological deterioration or encephalopathy Attributing painless injuries or mutilation to non-accidental causes rather than a sensory neuropathy Expecting liver transplantation to halt neurological progression Missing corneal anaesthesia and failing to protect the eye Overlooking mitochondrial disease when liver dysfunction and neuropathy coexist Navajo neurohepatopathy is caused by biallelic mutations in MPV17, which encodes an inner mitochondrial membrane protein needed to maintain the deoxyribonucleotide pool and mitochondrial DNA. Loss of function leads to depletion of mitochondrial DNA in the liver and nervous system, impairing oxidative phosphorylation in tissues with high energy demand. The result is progressive hepatocellular injury alongside a demyelinating/axonal sensorimotor neuropathy and leukoencephalopathy, with lactic acidosis during metabolic stress. A founder MPV17 variant underlies the disorder in the Navajo population. The prognosis is poor: the infantile hepatic form may cause early liver failure and death, and even in the more slowly progressive childhood form the neurological disability advances relentlessly; liver transplantation does not correct the neuropathy or leukoencephalopathy.

Naxos disease — JUP-related cardiocutaneous syndrome, plakoglobin cardiocutaneous syndrome, Naxos syndrome, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with woolly hair and palmoplantar keratoderma Arrhythmogenic appear in childhood, before the cardiac disease becomes evident The cardiomyopathy resembles arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, with fibrofatty replacement, ventricular arrhythmia and risk of sudden death, typically emerging by adolescence The recognisable skin and hair phenotype offers an early clue to identify individuals at future cardiac risk Cardiac management mirrors arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, including exercise restriction, antiarrhythmic therapy and a defibrillator for high-risk patients It clusters in families from Naxos and other Greek islands and Mediterranean regions, reflecting founder effects A related recessive desmoplakin cardiocutaneous condition, Carvajal syndrome, features a more left-dominant cardiomyopathy Syncope or sustained ventricular arrhythmia in a child or young adult with the cutaneous phenotype Progressive heart failure Family history of sudden death, especially in consanguineous or founder-population families Documented ventricular tachycardia of right ventricular origin Regarding the woolly hair and keratoderma as purely cosmetic and missing the cardiac risk Failing to institute cardiac surveillance before symptoms appear Confusing it with dominant arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and overlooking recessive inheritance and family risk Permitting intense exercise, which accelerates the cardiomyopathy Not distinguishing it from the desmoplakin-related Carvajal syndrome Naxos disease is caused by recessive variants in JUP, which encodes plakoglobin, a component of the desmosomes and adherens junctions that mechanically couple cells. Because plakoglobin is expressed in both cardiac muscle and the epidermis, its dysfunction weakens cell-cell adhesion in both tissues. In the heart, impaired desmosomal integrity under mechanical stress leads to myocyte death and fibrofatty replacement, creating an arrhythmogenic substrate akin to arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. In the skin and hair follicles, defective adhesion produces the woolly hair and palmoplantar keratoderma that characterise the syndrome. The cutaneous features are benign, but the associated arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy is progressive and carries a significant risk of ventricular arrhythmia, heart failure and sudden death; early recognition through the skin phenotype allows timely cardiac surveillance and risk reduction.

Drowning / submersion injury — near drowning, near-drowning, submersion injury, drowning, immersion injury Primary cardiac arrest or arrhythmia precipitating submersion Seizure disorder causing the submersion event Traumatic injury, including cervical spine injury from diving Intoxication with alcohol or drugs contributing to the event Hypoglycaemia or other metabolic cause of collapse Acute respiratory distress syndrome from another cause Pulse oximetry and arterial blood gas to assess oxygenation and acid-base status Chest radiograph to detect aspiration and evolving pulmonary oedema Core temperature measurement to identify and grade hypothermia Electrocardiogram and cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia Blood glucose, electrolytes, and a toxicology screen where relevant Imaging of the cervical spine and head when trauma is suspected Drowning is defined as respiratory impairment from submersion or immersion in liquid, and modern terminology discourages older labels such as near drowning, wet, dry, and secondary drowning in favour of describing outcome and severity The primary insult is hypoxia, so early and effective ventilation and oxygenation are the most important interventions and rescue breathing should begin as soon as possible The historical distinction between wet and dry drowning and between fresh and salt water is of little practical importance; management is dictated by hypoxia and its consequences The mammalian diving reflex, more pronounced in children and in cold water, can support survival after prolonged submersion, so aggressive resuscitation is justified Pulmonary injury with surfactant washout and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema can evolve over hours, so symptomatic patients need a period of observation even if they initially look well Hypothermia frequently accompanies submersion and both complicates resuscitation and may offer neuroprotection, so cold arrested patients warrant prolonged efforts Consider precipitating factors such as seizure, arrhythmia, intoxication, trauma including cervical spine injury, and hypoglycaemia Apnoea, cardiac arrest, or persistent severe hypoxaemia after rescue Deteriorating respiratory status with worsening pulmonary oedema over hours Altered consciousness or neurological signs indicating hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury Associated severe hypothermia or suspected cervical spine injury Discharging an initially well-appearing patient without observing for delayed pulmonary oedema Overemphasising fresh versus salt water instead of treating hypoxia Prematurely stopping resuscitation in a cold, submerged patient who may still recover Neglecting cervical spine precautions when diving or trauma is possible Failing to identify a precipitating cause such as seizure, arrhythmia, or intoxication In drowning, submersion leads to breath-holding and then, as hypoxia and hypercarbia develop, involuntary inspiration and aspiration of liquid or laryngospasm. The central problem is hypoxaemia. Aspirated water and the associated washout and dysfunction of surfactant collapse alveoli, increase permeability, and cause ventilation-perfusion mismatch and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, which may progress over subsequent hours. Systemic hypoxia damages the brain, heart, and other organs, and prolonged arrest can lead to hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy. Only small volumes are typically aspirated, and the once-emphasised electrolyte and haemolytic differences between fresh and salt water are rarely clinically significant. Concurrent hypothermia and the diving reflex modify the physiological response and can influence survival. Prognosis is determined mainly by the duration of submersion and hypoxia and the response to initial resuscitation. Brief submersion with prompt effective rescue often has an excellent outcome, whereas prolonged submersion with prolonged resuscitation and persistent coma carries a high risk of death or severe neurological disability. Cold-water submersion, particularly in children, occasionally allows good recovery after remarkably long submersion times.

granulomatous dermatosis presenting as well-demarcated plaques with a yellow-brown, atrophic, waxy centre and a raised violaceous border Most commonly affects the pretibial skin (shins), usually bilaterally, and is more frequent in women Prominent telangiectasia and a shiny, atrophic surface through which underlying vessels are visible are characteristic Classically associated with diabetes mellitus, though it occurs in non-diabetic individuals and its course does not track tightly with glycaemic control Ulceration, often precipitated by minor trauma, is a common and troublesome complication Histology shows layered ('palisaded') necrobiotic collagen degeneration with granulomatous inflammation throughout the dermis Long-standing lesions carry a small risk of squamous cell carcinoma developing within them Chronic non-healing ulceration with signs of secondary infection Nodular growth or induration within a long-standing plaque suggesting squamous cell carcinoma Newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus uncovered during evaluation Rapidly enlarging or atypical lesions requiring reassessment Assuming tight glycaemic control will clear the skin lesions Biopsying pretibial lesions without anticipating poor wound healing and ulceration Overlooking malignant transformation in a chronic non-healing plaque Confusing it with granuloma annulare or stasis dermatitis and mismanaging accordingly Necrobiosis lipoidica is a granulomatous disorder characterised by degeneration ('necrobiosis') of dermal collagen with surrounding palisaded granulomatous inflammation. Microangiopathy with vessel-wall thickening and altered collagen, plus immune-complex-mediated vascular injury, are thought to compromise dermal blood supply and connective-tissue integrity, producing the atrophic, telangiectatic plaques. Although strongly linked with diabetes mellitus and its microvascular disease, the association is not absolute and glycaemic control does not reliably alter the skin lesions, indicating that additional immune and vascular mechanisms contribute. Necrobiosis lipoidica is chronic and often persistent; lesions may slowly enlarge and can ulcerate, treatment responses are variable, and only a minority resolve spontaneously, with squamous cell carcinoma a rare long-term complication.

Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma — NXG, necrobiotic xanthogranuloma with paraproteinaemia Necrobiosis lipoidica Xanthelasma and other periorbital xanthomas Sarcoidosis Granuloma annulare Cutaneous involvement by lymphoma or plasma cell disorder Erdheim-Chester disease Rheumatoid nodule Skin biopsy with histology showing necrobiosis, cholesterol clefts and Touton giant cells Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation to detect a monoclonal paraprotein Serum free light chain assay Bone marrow examination when a plasma cell or lymphoproliferative disorder is suspected Full blood count, renal profile and serum calcium as myeloma screen Complement studies and cryoglobulins where indicated Ophthalmological assessment for periorbital and ocular complications A rare chronic non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis of adults presenting as indurated yellow to violaceous plaques and nodules that characteristically ulcerate and develop atrophic, telangiectatic centres. The periorbital region is the most frequently affected site, though the trunk and limbs are also involved; periorbital disease may be complicated by ectropion, scarring and ocular inflammation. A strong association with monoclonal gammopathy, most often IgG kappa, is a defining feature and may precede or follow the skin disease by years. It is linked to underlying or subsequent lymphoproliferative and plasma cell disorders, including multiple myeloma and other B-cell dyscrasias, mandating long-term haematological surveillance. Histology shows extensive palisading and diffuse xanthogranulomatous inflammation with broad zones of necrobiosis (hyaline collagen degeneration), numerous Touton and foreign-body giant cells and cholesterol clefts. Cholesterol clefts and lymphoid aggregates within the necrobiotic zones help distinguish it from necrobiosis lipoidica and other palisading granulomas. Complement abnormalities, cryoglobulinaemia and low C1 esterase inhibitor levels have been described in some patients. Management is directed at the underlying paraproteinaemia; alkylating and other systemic immunomodulatory agents are used, and disfiguring or ulcerated lesions may require specialist care. Detection of a monoclonal paraprotein or rising paraprotein level indicating an evolving plasma cell dyscrasia Anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment or bone pain suggesting multiple myeloma Periorbital ulceration, ectropion or ocular inflammation threatening vision Lymphadenopathy or organomegaly suggesting lymphoproliferative disease Extensive ulceration with secondary infection Confusing it histologically and clinically with necrobiosis lipoidica and missing the associated paraproteinaemia. Failing to perform and repeat serum protein electrophoresis, since the gammopathy may appear years after the skin disease. Attributing periorbital plaques to ordinary xanthelasma and overlooking the systemic implications. Neglecting long-term haematological monitoring after an initially negative myeloma screen. Aggressive surgery on ulceration-prone lesions that heal poorly and may recur. Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma is a xanthogranulomatous histiocytic disorder in which lipid-laden macrophages, Touton and foreign-body giant cells accumulate within the dermis and subcutis, producing broad bands of collagen necrobiosis interspersed with cholesterol clefts and lymphoplasmacytic aggregates. Its consistent association with a monoclonal paraprotein, usually IgG kappa, has led to the hypothesis that circulating immunoglobulin, potentially acting as an antibody with lipoprotein-binding activity or forming immune complexes, drives a granulomatous foreign-body-type reaction to lipid within tissue. The resulting chronic granulomatous inflammation degrades dermal collagen and elastic tissue, giving the characteristic atrophic, telangiectatic and ulcerating plaques. The frequent coexistence of, or progression to, plasma cell and lymphoproliferative disorders underscores that the cutaneous disease is a marker of an underlying clonal immunoglobulin-producing process. The cutaneous disease is chronic, progressive and relapsing, and while the skin lesions themselves are not life-threatening, prognosis is governed by the associated haematological disorder, which may evolve into multiple myeloma or lymphoma over many years and necessitates indefinite surveillance.

improvement It belongs to the family of necrolytic erythemas that includes necrolytic migratory erythema and nutritional deficiency dermatoses Biopsy shows psoriasiform hyperplasia with upper epidermal pallor, necrosis of keratinocytes and parakeratosis, overlapping with other necrolytic erythemas Management combines treatment of the underlying hepatitis C with correction of zinc and other nutritional deficiencies Undiagnosed chronic hepatitis C with progression to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma Extensive erosions with secondary bacterial infection Failure to respond, prompting reassessment for glucagonoma or other cause Features of decompensated liver disease Treating it as recalcitrant psoriasis or eczema without testing for hepatitis C Not checking or replacing zinc despite its therapeutic value Confusing it with necrolytic migratory erythema and missing a glucagonoma, or vice versa Overlooking progression of underlying chronic liver disease Necrolytic acral erythema is a necrolytic erythema most consistently linked to chronic hepatitis C virus infection. Its pathogenesis is thought to involve metabolic and nutritional disturbances associated with liver disease, particularly zinc deficiency and abnormalities of amino-acid, albumin and fatty-acid metabolism, which impair epidermal keratinocyte integrity. The nutrient-deprived upper epidermis undergoes necrolysis with the characteristic pallor, vacuolisation and parakeratosis. The frequent response to zinc supplementation supports a central role for micronutrient deficiency in genetically or hepatically susceptible individuals. Lesions can be chronic and refractory to topical therapy alone but often improve substantially with zinc repletion and successful antiviral treatment of hepatitis C; long-term outcome is influenced by the course of the underlying liver disease.

possible, with somatostatin analogues and amino-acid, zinc and fatty-acid repletion Weight loss, new diabetes and rash together, pointing to glucagonoma Venous thromboembolism, which is common and potentially fatal in the glucagonoma syndrome Evidence of metastatic neuroendocrine disease at diagnosis Severe malnutrition with extensive skin breakdown and secondary infection Repeatedly treating the rash as eczema, psoriasis or candidiasis and missing the underlying tumour Not measuring glucagon and amino acids in a suggestive migratory erosive eruption Overlooking the high risk of venous thrombosis in affected patients Attributing all cases to a tumour and ignoring nutritional or hepatic causes of a similar picture Necrolytic migratory erythema is most often a paraneoplastic manifestation of a glucagon-secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour. Sustained hyperglucagonaemia promotes catabolism with depletion of amino acids, and the resulting hypoaminoacidaemia, together with deficiencies of zinc and essential fatty acids, is thought to impair epidermal integrity. Nutrient-starved keratinocytes in the upper epidermis undergo necrolysis, producing the characteristic superficial necrosis, vacuolisation and crusting. Similar changes can arise in non-tumour states of malnutrition, malabsorption or liver disease that share these deficiencies. When a glucagonoma is localised and resected the rash and metabolic disturbances usually resolve, but many tumours have already metastasised at diagnosis, which worsens the outlook; nutritional and somatostatin-based measures can improve the skin and symptoms even when cure is not possible.

Necrotising enterocolitis — NEC Spontaneous intestinal perforation Neonatal sepsis with ileus Malrotation with volvulus Hirschsprung enterocolitis Milk protein intolerance Anal fissure or swallowed maternal blood (for bloody stool) Abdominal radiographs for pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas and free air Full blood count, inflammatory markers and blood culture Blood gas, glucose and coagulation studies Serial abdominal examination and, where used, abdominal ultrasound Surgical review for advanced or deteriorating disease A serious neonatal gastrointestinal emergency of bowel inflammation and necrosis, predominantly affecting preterm infants Presents with feed intolerance, abdominal distension, bloody stools, bilious aspirates and systemic instability Prematurity and formula feeding increase risk, while human breast milk is protective The abdominal radiograph may show pneumatosis intestinalis, and portal venous gas or free air indicate advanced disease The modified Bell staging system grades severity from suspected disease to established and advanced perforation Management ranges from bowel rest, gastric decompression and antibiotics to surgery for perforation or deterioration Pneumoperitoneum indicating perforation Rapid clinical deterioration with shock or disseminated intravascular coagulation Abdominal wall erythema or a fixed mass Portal venous gas or extensive pneumatosis Continuing feeds despite early warning signs Missing perforation by not repeating imaging in a deteriorating baby Confusing spontaneous intestinal perforation with necrotising enterocolitis Underestimating the risk of later strictures after recovery Necrotising enterocolitis is a multifactorial disorder in which immaturity of the preterm gut, in combination with enteral feeding, an abnormal microbial colonisation pattern and mucosal ischaemia, triggers an exaggerated inflammatory response and breakdown of the intestinal barrier. Bacterial translocation across the compromised mucosa amplifies inflammation, leading to variable bowel-wall necrosis, gas within the bowel wall (pneumatosis) and, in severe cases, full-thickness necrosis with perforation and peritonitis. Although bacteria contribute, it is regarded as a distinct inflammatory-ischaemic disease of the immature gut rather than a simple infection. Outcome varies with severity; medical disease often resolves, but advanced disease carries significant mortality and long-term risks including short bowel syndrome, strictures and neurodevelopmental impairment.

Necrotising sialometaplasia — necrotizing sialometaplasia Squamous cell carcinoma Mucoepidermoid carcinoma or other salivary malignancy Traumatic ulcer Deep fungal or other infective ulcer Ulceration from vasculitis or other systemic disease Incisional biopsy with experienced histopathological assessment History of preceding local trauma, injection or surgery Clinical follow-up to confirm spontaneous healing Exclusion of malignancy and infective causes on histology A benign, self-limiting inflammatory condition of minor salivary glands that clinically and histologically mimics malignancy It most often presents as a sudden crater-like ulcer of the hard palate, sometimes bilateral The lesion is important chiefly because it can be mistaken for squamous cell carcinoma or a salivary malignancy Preceding local ischaemic insults such as trauma, injection, surgery or smoking are commonly identified Histology shows lobular necrosis with squamous metaplasia of ducts while preserving the lobular architecture Recognition avoids unnecessary radical surgery, as the lesion heals spontaneously over weeks Failure to heal within the expected weeks Histological features favouring malignancy on expert review Progressive enlargement or induration Associated systemic features suggesting another cause Misinterpreting the clinical or histological picture as carcinoma and performing radical surgery Failing to obtain expert histopathology review Overlooking a preceding ischaemic insult in the history Not arranging follow-up to confirm healing Necrotising sialometaplasia is thought to result from ischaemic injury to the minor salivary glands, most often in the palate, following vascular compromise from trauma, local anaesthetic injection, surgery, pressure or smoking. The ischaemia causes acinar necrosis, and reparative squamous metaplasia of the salivary ducts follows. This combination of necrosis and metaplasia can closely resemble malignancy both clinically and microscopically, but the preserved lobular architecture indicates a benign reactive process. The condition is benign and self-limiting, healing spontaneously over several weeks without specific treatment.

Necrotizing Enterocolitis — NEC, necrotising enterocolitis Neonatal sepsis with ileus Spontaneous intestinal perforation Malrotation with midgut volvulus Hirschsprung enterocolitis Infectious gastroenteritis Milk protein intolerance / allergic colitis Supine and lateral decubitus or cross-table lateral abdominal radiographs for pneumatosis, portal gas, or free air Full blood count (looking for neutropenia, thrombocytopenia) and inflammatory markers Blood culture and blood gas with lactate Serum electrolytes and glucose, coagulation studies Abdominal ultrasound to assess bowel wall perfusion and free fluid The most common acquired gastrointestinal emergency of the newborn, occurring mainly in preterm, low-birth-weight infants and usually within the first weeks after birth. Presentation ranges from feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, and bloody stools to systemic signs such as lethargy, temperature instability, apnoea, and shock. The pathognomonic radiographic sign is pneumatosis intestinalis (intramural gas); portal venous gas and free intraperitoneal air are more ominous findings. Prematurity is the dominant risk factor; enteral feeding, particularly with formula, and intestinal dysbiosis are contributory, while human milk is protective. Initial management is medical: stop enteral feeds, decompress the bowel with a nasogastric tube, give intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics, and provide supportive care. Serial abdominal radiographs and clinical review guide progression; free air on imaging indicates perforation and the need for surgery. Surgical options include peritoneal drainage or laparotomy with resection of necrotic bowel, sometimes with a stoma. The Bell staging system grades severity from suspected to advanced disease with perforation and is used to guide management. Extensive resection can leave short bowel syndrome with long-term dependence on parenteral nutrition. Free intraperitoneal air indicating perforation Portal venous gas Persistent metabolic acidosis or rising lactate Thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, or evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation Abdominal wall erythema, fixed mass, or clinical deterioration despite medical therapy Attributing early nonspecific signs to feeding intolerance and delaying evaluation Advancing enteral feeds too rapidly in vulnerable preterm infants Missing a subtle pneumoperitoneum on a single supine film Underestimating rapid clinical deterioration and delaying surgical consultation Overlooking strictures that can develop weeks after apparent recovery Necrotizing enterocolitis reflects a multifactorial injury to the immature intestine. An excessive inflammatory response of the immature gut mucosa, altered microbial colonisation, ischaemia or impaired mucosal perfusion, and enteral substrate combine to cause mucosal injury, bacterial translocation, and gas production within the bowel wall. Progression leads to full-thickness necrosis, perforation, peritonitis, and systemic inflammatory response with sepsis and shock. Outcome depends on gestational age and severity; mild disease often resolves with medical management, but advanced disease requiring surgery carries substantial mortality and long-term morbidity including strictures, short bowel syndrome, and adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes.
