Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome — NAS, neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome, NOWS Neonatal sepsis or infection Hypoglycaemia Hypocalcaemia or other electrolyte disturbance Hyperthyroidism (neonatal thyrotoxicosis) Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy Central nervous system haemorrhage or injury Serial standardised withdrawal scoring (e.g. modified Finnegan) or function-based assessment Maternal history of substance use and prescribed medications Toxicology testing of infant urine, meconium, or other matrices where appropriate Blood glucose monitoring Electrolytes and calcium if clinically indicated Sepsis screen when infection cannot be excluded A constellation of withdrawal signs in a newborn following intrauterine exposure to substances, most commonly opioids, that the infant is no longer receiving after birth. Signs typically involve central nervous system irritability, autonomic disturbance, and gastrointestinal dysfunction. Common features include tremors, high-pitched crying, poor sleep, irritability, hypertonia, sweating, sneezing, nasal stuffiness, feeding difficulty, vomiting, and loose stools. The timing of onset depends on the substance and its half-life; short-acting opioids produce earlier withdrawal, while longer-acting agents may delay onset for days. Standardised scoring tools are used to assess severity and guide whether pharmacological treatment is needed. First-line care emphasises supportive, non-pharmacological measures such as a low-stimulation environment, swaddling, gentle handling, and rooming-in with the mother. The Eat, Sleep, Console approach focuses on the infant's function rather than symptom counts alone. When supportive care is insufficient, opioid-based pharmacological treatment is used with gradual weaning; polysubstance exposure and breastfeeding considerations should also be addressed. Seizures attributable to withdrawal Severe feeding intolerance with dehydration or poor weight gain Excessive weight loss or failure to thrive Marked autonomic instability or persistent high scores despite supportive care Signs suggesting an alternative serious diagnosis such as sepsis or hypoglycaemia Difficulty consoling with escalating pharmacological requirements Relying on medication before optimising non-pharmacological, function-focused care Excessive handling and stimulation that worsen the infant's symptoms Overlooking polysubstance exposure, which alters the withdrawal course Missing concurrent problems such as sepsis or hypoglycaemia Inconsistent scoring between assessors leading to inappropriate treatment decisions Neglecting maternal support, breastfeeding counselling, and social care coordination During pregnancy, drugs that cross the placenta reach the fetus and lead to physiological dependence, particularly with opioids acting on central opioid receptors. After delivery the sudden loss of transplacental drug supply removes this stimulation, producing a hyperexcitable state affecting the central and autonomic nervous systems and the gastrointestinal tract. The resulting neurotransmitter imbalance manifests as the characteristic irritability, autonomic instability, and feeding disturbance; the pattern and timing vary with the specific agent, dose, and its pharmacokinetics. Acute withdrawal is usually self-limited and manageable, and most infants recover well with appropriate supportive and, when needed, pharmacological care; longer-term neurodevelopmental outcomes are influenced more by the broader social and environmental context, so coordinated family support and follow-up are important.

Neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy belongs to the Zellweger spectrum of peroxisome biogenesis disorders, in which recessive mutations in PEX genes prevent the normal assembly of functional peroxisomes. Because the organelle itself is defective, the many enzymatic functions it houses are lost together: beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids fails so these accumulate, alpha-oxidation of phytanic acid is impaired, bile acid synthesis is incomplete, and plasmalogen biosynthesis is deficient. The combined biochemical disturbance disrupts membrane and myelin formation and produces toxic lipid accumulation, leading to the progressive leukodystrophy, adrenocortical dysfunction, hepatic disease and multisystem involvement that characterise the disorder. Neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy is progressive with a poor prognosis; although milder than classic Zellweger syndrome, most affected children have severe neurodevelopmental impairment and shortened survival, with outcome depending on residual peroxisomal function.

counselling parents about the high recurrence risk and need for specialist care in future pregnancies Confusing alloimmune with maternal autoimmune thrombocytopenia, which differ in mechanism and management Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia occurs when the foetus inherits a platelet antigen from the father that is absent in the mother. Foetal platelets crossing into the maternal circulation stimulate production of maternal IgG alloantibodies, which then cross the placenta and bind foetal and neonatal platelets bearing the target antigen. These opsonised platelets are removed by the reticuloendothelial system, producing severe thrombocytopenia. Because IgG transfer and sensitisation can occur early, a first pregnancy may be affected and haemorrhage, including intracranial bleeding, can develop before birth. The mother remains unaffected because her own platelets lack the antigen, which is why she has a normal platelet count. Most affected neonates recover as maternal antibody levels fall and platelet counts normalise over days to a few weeks. Prognosis is excellent in the absence of intracranial haemorrhage, but antenatal or neonatal intracranial bleeding can cause death or lasting neurological disability. Subsequent pregnancies are typically as severe or more severe and warrant specialist antenatal management.

transient forms often relate to chromosome 6q24 abnormalities and may relapse later in life Some KCNJ11 mutations cause the DEND syndrome with developmental delay, epilepsy and neonatal diabetes, reflecting KATP channels in neural tissue Urgent genetic testing is essential because the result directly changes treatment and prognosis Diabetic ketoacidosis or severe dehydration in a young infant requiring emergency stabilisation Neurological features such as developmental delay or seizures suggesting a DEND-type presentation Failure to thrive or intractable hyperglycaemia needing rapid diagnostic clarification Associated syndromic features indicating a broader multisystem disorder Assuming any infantile diabetes is type 1 and committing to lifelong insulin without genetic testing Missing the opportunity to transition sulfonylurea-responsive cases off insulin Overlooking neurodevelopmental features that indicate a KATP channel syndrome Failing to plan follow-up for transient neonatal diabetes that can relapse in later life In beta cells the ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channel links glucose metabolism to insulin release; rising ATP normally closes the channel, depolarising the cell and triggering secretion. Activating mutations in KCNJ11 or ABCC8 hold the channel open, preventing depolarisation and impairing insulin release, yet high-affinity sulfonylureas can close the channel independently of ATP and restore secretion. Prognosis varies by genotype: many KATP channel cases achieve excellent control on sulfonylureas with potential neurodevelopmental benefit, transient forms may remit though relapse is common, while syndromic and INS-related forms carry a more guarded outlook.

Transient hypoglycaemia corrected promptly usually has an excellent outcome, but severe, prolonged or recurrent hypoglycaemia, especially with symptoms, carries a risk of neurodevelopmental injury.

Neonatal Hypoglycaemia — low blood sugar in newborn, hypoglycaemia of the newborn, neonatal low glucose Sepsis Neonatal seizures from other causes Hypocalcaemia or other electrolyte disturbance Congenital hyperinsulinism Panhypopituitarism or cortisol deficiency Inborn errors of metabolism Confirmatory laboratory plasma glucose Critical sample during hypoglycaemia (insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ketones, free fatty acids) when persistent Serum electrolytes and calcium Sepsis screen if clinically indicated Metabolic screen (ammonia, lactate, acylcarnitine profile) in recurrent or refractory cases Low blood glucose is common in the transitional period after birth as the newborn adapts from continuous placental glucose supply to intermittent feeding. Infants at highest risk include those of diabetic mothers, large- or small-for-gestational-age babies, preterm infants, and any newborn who is stressed, cold, or septic. Signs are often subtle and non-specific: jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, temperature instability, apnoea, or seizures; many affected infants appear asymptomatic. At-risk and symptomatic infants should be screened with bedside glucose testing, with low values confirmed on a laboratory sample given the imprecision of point-of-care meters. Early and frequent feeding is the first-line measure; infants who cannot maintain adequate glucose or who are symptomatic require intravenous dextrose. Symptomatic hypoglycaemia with a documented low glucose that resolves when glucose is normalised (Whipple triad) warrants investigation and treatment. Persistent or recurrent hypoglycaemia beyond the first days of life suggests an underlying disorder such as hyperinsulinism, endocrine deficiency, or an inborn error of metabolism. The clinical concern is that prolonged or severe low glucose can injure the developing brain, so prevention and prompt correction are priorities. Seizures, apnoea, or coma Persistent hypoglycaemia despite feeding and initial glucose infusion High glucose infusion requirement suggesting hyperinsulinism Recurrent hypoglycaemia beyond the transitional period Associated hypotonia, poor feeding, or encephalopathy Treating an isolated low bedside meter reading without confirming on a laboratory sample or clinical context Assuming all at-risk infants are symptomatic, or dismissing subtle signs as normal newborn behaviour Failing to investigate hypoglycaemia that persists or recurs beyond the first days of life Overlooking hyperinsulinism when a high rate of glucose infusion is needed to keep glucose normal After the cord is cut, the newborn loses its steady maternal glucose supply and must mobilise hepatic glycogen, activate gluconeogenesis, and use alternative fuels such as ketones and lactate, processes driven by a surge in counter-regulatory hormones and a fall in insulin. When glycogen stores are limited (prematurity, growth restriction), glucose demand is high (stress, sepsis, hypothermia), or insulin secretion is excessive (infant of a diabetic mother, hyperinsulinism), this adaptation fails and blood glucose falls. Because the neonatal brain depends heavily on glucose, inadequate supply combined with immature ketogenesis in some infants places the brain at risk. Brief, promptly treated transitional hypoglycaemia in an otherwise well infant usually has an excellent outcome, whereas severe, prolonged, symptomatic, or recurrent hypoglycaemia carries a risk of long-term neurodevelopmental impairment.

Neonatal ichthyosis-sclerosing cholangitis syndrome — NISCH syndrome, ichthyosis-sclerosing cholangitis, CLDN1 deficiency, claudin-1 deficiency, neonatal sclerosing cholangitis with ichthyosis Biliary atresia Primary sclerosing cholangitis of other cause Alagille syndrome Other neonatal sclerosing cholangitis (e.g. DCDC2-related) Ichthyosis syndromes without hepatic disease Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis Liver function tests and gamma-glutamyl transferase (characteristically raised) Serum bile acids and fractionated bilirubin Cholangiography (MRCP or intraoperative) showing irregular sclerosing bile ducts Liver biopsy demonstrating ductular reaction, cholangitis, and fibrosis Dermatological assessment and skin examination for ichthyosis and hypotrichosis CLDN1 gene sequencing A rare autosomal recessive syndrome combining scalp and skin ichthyosis with neonatal sclerosing cholangitis, caused by mutations in CLDN1 encoding claudin-1 Cholestasis presents in the neonatal period with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and a raised gamma-glutamyl transferase, unlike low-GGT inherited cholestases Cholangiography demonstrates an irregular, beaded intrahepatic biliary tree typical of sclerosing cholangitis Characteristic features include a scaly (ichthyotic) skin, scalp hypotrichosis or scarring alopecia, and sometimes oligodontia and dental anomalies Claudin-1 is a tight-junction protein of biliary epithelium and skin; its loss disrupts the epithelial barrier in both organs Diagnosis integrates the dermatological and cholestatic features with cholangiographic findings and CLDN1 sequencing Management is supportive with ursodeoxycholic acid, fat-soluble vitamins, and skin care, with liver transplantation for progressive biliary cirrhosis Progressive biliary cirrhosis with portal hypertension Vitamin K-dependent coagulopathy in the cholestatic neonate Recurrent cholangitis with fever and worsening jaundice Failure to thrive from fat and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption Overlooking the diagnostic significance of coexisting ichthyosis and scalp involvement in a cholestatic infant Confusing the cholangiographic appearance with biliary atresia Assuming a low GGT, which does not fit and can delay the correct diagnosis Neglecting fat-soluble vitamin supplementation and skin care Neonatal ichthyosis-sclerosing cholangitis (NISCH) syndrome is caused by biallelic mutations in CLDN1, which encodes claudin-1, an integral tight-junction protein maintaining paracellular barriers in the biliary epithelium and epidermis. Loss of claudin-1 disrupts these junctions, producing an ichthyotic skin phenotype and a sclerosing cholangitis in which bile leaks across a defective canalicular/ductular barrier and provokes biliary inflammation, strictures, and progressive fibrosis. The combination of high-GGT neonatal cholestasis with ichthyosis and scalp involvement is characteristic. The sclerosing cholangitis is usually progressive, and many children develop biliary cirrhosis requiring liver transplantation over time; the cutaneous features persist but are managed supportively, and outcome depends chiefly on the hepatic course.

Neonatal intraventricular haemorrhage — germinal matrix haemorrhage, IVH of prematurity Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy Neonatal seizures of other cause Metabolic derangement (hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance) Sepsis or meningitis Other intracranial haemorrhage (subdural, subarachnoid) Cranial ultrasound for diagnosis, grading and serial monitoring Measurement of head circumference and fontanelle assessment Coagulation studies and full blood count MRI where parenchymal injury or prognosis needs clarification Monitoring for post-haemorrhagic ventricular dilatation Bleeding arising from the fragile germinal matrix, chiefly in preterm infants, with risk inversely related to gestation and birth weight Most haemorrhages occur within the first few days of life It is graded from small germinal matrix or intraventricular bleeding to large haemorrhage with ventricular dilatation or parenchymal involvement Presentation ranges from clinically silent to a catastrophic decline with bulging fontanelle, seizures and shock Cranial ultrasound is the mainstay of diagnosis and surveillance in at-risk infants Post-haemorrhagic ventricular dilatation and parenchymal (grade IV) involvement carry the greatest risk of adverse outcome Rapid neurological deterioration with a tense fontanelle Progressive post-haemorrhagic ventricular dilatation Parenchymal (grade IV) involvement Seizures or cardiovascular collapse Assuming a normal neurological examination excludes haemorrhage Failing to monitor for evolving ventricular dilatation Overlooking modifiable haemodynamic factors that propagate bleeding Not arranging neurodevelopmental follow-up after high-grade haemorrhage In preterm infants the germinal matrix is a highly vascular, metabolically active region with fragile, poorly supported vessels. Immature cerebral autoregulation means fluctuations in cerebral blood flow and pressure, from hypotension, hypercapnia, ventilation or handling, are transmitted to these vessels and cause them to rupture. Blood may remain localised to the matrix or extend into the ventricles, and large haemorrhages can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow causing ventricular dilatation, or be accompanied by venous infarction of adjacent white matter, which underlies the neurological sequelae. Low-grade haemorrhages often have a good outcome, whereas high-grade haemorrhage with parenchymal involvement or progressive ventricular dilatation carries a substantial risk of cerebral palsy and developmental impairment.

Neonatal jaundice — neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia, jaundice of the newborn, physiological jaundice, icterus neonatorum Rh or ABO haemolytic disease G6PD deficiency and other red cell enzyme/membrane defects Sepsis or congenital infection Biliary atresia and other causes of neonatal cholestasis Hypothyroidism Breastfeeding and breast-milk jaundice Cephalohaematoma or extensive bruising Total and conjugated (direct) serum bilirubin, interpreted against age in hours Transcutaneous bilirubinometry for screening Blood group and direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test on infant and mother Full blood count, reticulocyte count, and blood film G6PD assay where clinically indicated Thyroid function and septic screen when suggested by the picture Assessment for cholestasis (e.g. pale stools, dark urine) when direct bilirubin is raised Visible yellow discolouration of skin and sclerae from raised serum bilirubin, extremely common in newborns and usually due to unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinaemia. Physiological jaundice appears after the first 24 hours, peaks around days 3-5 in term infants, and resolves without harm; it reflects normal neonatal bilirubin handling. Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is always pathological and demands urgent evaluation, commonly for haemolysis. Key pathological causes include blood-group incompatibility (Rh, ABO), G6PD deficiency, sepsis, and other haemolytic conditions. Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia is never physiological and requires investigation for cholestasis, notably biliary atresia, which needs early surgery. Breastfeeding-associated (early, from inadequate intake) and breast-milk (later, prolonged) jaundice are common benign patterns once other causes are excluded. Management depends on bilirubin level plotted against age in hours and risk factors; phototherapy is first-line and exchange transfusion is reserved for dangerously high or rapidly rising levels. The feared complication is bilirubin-induced neurological dysfunction (acute encephalopathy progressing to kernicterus), which is preventable with timely treatment. Jaundice within the first 24 hours of life Rapidly rising bilirubin or a level near the exchange-transfusion threshold Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy: lethargy, poor feeding, hypotonia progressing to hypertonia, high-pitched cry, arching Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, pale stools, and dark urine suggesting biliary atresia Prolonged jaundice beyond two weeks (term) or three weeks (preterm) requiring evaluation Dismissing jaundice in the first 24 hours as physiological Failing to fractionate bilirubin and missing cholestasis / biliary atresia Assessing jaundice by clinical appearance alone rather than measured bilirubin against age-specific thresholds Overlooking dehydration from inadequate feeding as a contributor in early breastfeeding jaundice Not investigating jaundice that persists beyond the expected period Newborns have increased bilirubin production from a high red cell mass with shorter red cell lifespan, combined with immature hepatic conjugation (low UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity) and enhanced enterohepatic recirculation of bilirubin. These factors produce transient physiological unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Pathological jaundice arises when production is excessive (haemolysis, extravasated blood), conjugation or uptake is impaired, or excretion is obstructed (cholestasis). Unbound unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and can cross the blood-brain barrier, depositing in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei to cause neurotoxicity. Most neonatal jaundice is benign and resolves without sequelae; with appropriate monitoring and treatment, kernicterus is largely preventable, but untreated severe hyperbilirubinaemia can cause permanent neurological injury.

neonatal onset multisystem inflammatory disease — NOMID, CINCA syndrome, chronic infantile neurological cutaneous and articular syndrome Muckle-Wells syndrome Familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome Deficiency of the interleukin-1 receptor antagonist Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis of very early onset Congenital (TORCH) infection Neonatal sepsis or congenital bacterial meningitis Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome and other interferonopathies NLRP3 gene analysis with deep or next-generation sequencing to detect somatic mosaicism Cerebrospinal fluid examination for raised opening pressure and sterile pleocytosis Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain for leptomeningeal enhancement and ventricular changes Pure-tone audiometry and serial ophthalmological assessment including fundoscopy for papilloedema Skeletal radiographs demonstrating epiphyseal and physeal overgrowth Acute-phase reactants with serum amyloid A and urinalysis for amyloidosis surveillance Most severe phenotype of the cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome spectrum, caused by gain-of-function NLRP3 variants that are frequently de novo and often present as somatic mosaicism. Presents in the neonatal period with a near-continuous migratory urticarial rash, in contrast to the episodic attacks of the milder phenotypes. Chronic aseptic meningitis produces raised intracranial pressure, chronic headache, papilloedema, optic atrophy, sensorineural hearing loss and, if untreated, developmental delay. A characteristic deforming arthropathy with bony overgrowth of the epiphyses, especially of the patella and long-bone growth plates, is highly suggestive and can be radiographically distinctive. Dysmorphic features evolve, including frontal bossing, saddle-shaped nose and macrocephaly, together with growth failure. Reactive AA amyloidosis is a serious late complication of poorly controlled disease. Early interleukin-1 blockade transforms the natural history and can prevent irreversible neurological, ophthalmological and auditory damage. Cerebrospinal fluid typically shows a raised opening pressure with a sterile neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis. Signs of raised intracranial pressure such as papilloedema, bulging fontanelle or persistent vomiting Progressive visual or hearing loss indicating ongoing neurosensory damage Developmental regression or seizures Proteinuria signalling renal AA amyloidosis Concluding the diagnosis is excluded by a negative germline NLRP3 test when somatic mosaicism has not been sought Misinterpreting the sterile neutrophilic cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis as bacterial meningitis Delaying interleukin-1 blockade and allowing irreversible neurosensory injury to accumulate Overlooking the diagnostic value of the characteristic epiphyseal bony overgrowth on imaging Highly activating NLRP3 variants cause near-constitutive assembly of the cryopyrin inflammasome with minimal need for any trigger, driving continuous caspase-1 activation and overwhelming secretion of interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-18. The resulting unremitting innate immune activation produces persistent multisystem inflammation: neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis, chronic aseptic leptomeningitis with raised intracranial pressure, cochlear and optic nerve damage, and a growth-plate arthropathy with disordered endochondral ossification and epiphyseal overgrowth. Somatic mosaicism, in which the activating variant is present in only a proportion of cells, is common and can yield a negative conventional germline test despite classic disease. Without treatment the disorder causes progressive neurological, visual and auditory disability, deforming arthropathy and a shortened lifespan. Early interleukin-1 blockade substantially improves outcome and can preserve neurosensory function, though damage sustained before treatment is often irreversible.

Ophthalmia neonatorum — ophthalmia neonatorum, neonatal conjunctivitis, gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum, chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis Gonococcal conjunctivitis Chlamydial conjunctivitis Other bacterial conjunctivitis (for example Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci, Gram-negative organisms) Herpes simplex virus conjunctivitis or keratitis Chemical conjunctivitis from topical prophylaxis Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction with secondary infection (dacryocystitis) Congenital glaucoma presenting with tearing and a cloudy cornea Gram stain of conjunctival exudate looking for Gram-negative intracellular diplococci suggesting gonococcus Bacterial culture of conjunctival swabs, including chocolate agar for Neisseria gonorrhoeae with antimicrobial susceptibility testing Nucleic acid amplification testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae Chlamydial-specific specimen collection sampling conjunctival cells for detection of the intracellular organism Viral testing for herpes simplex when vesicles, keratitis, or systemic features are present Maternal and partner screening for sexually transmitted infections to identify the source and guide treatment Ophthalmia neonatorum is conjunctivitis in the first month of life, classically acquired as the infant passes through an infected birth canal The two most important sexually transmitted causes are Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, alongside other bacteria, herpes simplex virus, and chemical irritation Timing offers a clue: chemical conjunctivitis appears within the first day or two, gonococcal disease typically within the first few days, and chlamydial disease usually toward the end of the first week or later Gonococcal ophthalmia is a sight-threatening emergency because it can rapidly cause corneal ulceration, perforation, and blindness, and it characteristically produces a hyperacute, profuse purulent discharge Chlamydial ophthalmia is generally milder with mucopurulent discharge but is the commonest infective cause and can be accompanied by chlamydial pneumonitis Diagnosis combines Gram stain and culture with nucleic acid amplification testing of conjunctival specimens to distinguish gonococcal, chlamydial, and other causes Gonococcal disease requires systemic treatment with a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone plus saline irrigation, while chlamydial disease requires systemic macrolide therapy, as topical treatment alone is inadequate Because it reflects maternal infection, management must include testing and treatment of the mother and her partners, and antenatal screening is the key preventive measure Hyperacute copious purulent discharge with marked lid oedema suggesting gonococcal infection Corneal haze, ulceration, or clouding indicating sight-threatening keratitis Systemic features such as poor feeding, lethargy, or respiratory signs suggesting disseminated gonococcal infection or chlamydial pneumonitis Vesicular skin or eye lesions or encephalopathic features raising concern for neonatal herpes simplex Attributing a purulent neonatal eye to harmless chemical or blocked-duct causes and missing gonococcal disease Relying on topical antibiotics alone for gonococcal or chlamydial infection, which require systemic therapy Failing to test for and treat coexisting infection (for example both gonorrhoea and chlamydia) and to consider chlamydial pneumonitis Neglecting to investigate and treat the mother and her sexual partners Overlooking herpes simplex, which needs antiviral rather than antibacterial treatment Ophthalmia neonatorum arises when pathogens colonising the maternal genital tract contaminate the neonatal conjunctiva, most often during vaginal delivery, though ascending infection after membrane rupture can also occur. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is especially virulent: it can penetrate intact corneal epithelium, and its intense neutrophilic response with copious purulent exudate can rapidly progress to corneal ulceration and perforation. Chlamydia trachomatis, an obligate intracellular organism, infects conjunctival epithelial cells to produce a more subacute follicular or papillary conjunctivitis and may seed the nasopharynx and lungs, causing an afebrile pneumonitis. Chemical conjunctivitis, by contrast, is a transient self-limiting irritant reaction to topical prophylaxis rather than an infection. With prompt recognition and appropriate systemic treatment the outlook is excellent, but delayed treatment of gonococcal ophthalmia can lead to corneal perforation and permanent blindness, and untreated chlamydial infection may be complicated by pneumonitis; antenatal screening and neonatal ocular prophylaxis have greatly reduced severe outcomes.

Neonatal polycythaemia — neonatal polycythemia, hyperviscosity of the newborn Dehydration causing haemoconcentration Sepsis (as a cause of similar non-specific symptoms) Congenital heart disease Hypoglycaemia of other cause Capillary sampling artefact overestimating haematocrit Confirmatory venous haematocrit Blood glucose (hypoglycaemia is common) Bilirubin monitoring Assessment of hydration and perfusion Evaluation for underlying cause and for complications where symptomatic An abnormally high haematocrit in the newborn, conventionally a venous value above the mid-sixties percent The clinical concern is hyperviscosity, which impairs microcirculatory flow Causes include placental transfusion (delayed cord clamping, twin-to-twin transfusion), intrauterine hypoxia and maternal diabetes Many infants are asymptomatic; symptoms are non-specific and include plethora, lethargy, poor feeding, jitteriness and hypoglycaemia Capillary samples overestimate haematocrit, so a venous sample is needed to confirm Partial exchange transfusion is considered for symptomatic infants with significant polycythaemia, alongside hydration and treating hypoglycaemia Neurological signs such as seizures or marked lethargy Features of necrotising enterocolitis or renal compromise Respiratory distress suggesting cardiopulmonary involvement Severe symptomatic hyperviscosity Acting on a capillary rather than venous haematocrit Overlooking hypoglycaemia in a polycythaemic infant Attributing symptoms to polycythaemia without excluding sepsis Treating asymptomatic mild polycythaemia unnecessarily Neonatal polycythaemia results from either increased red cell transfusion to the fetus or newborn (as with delayed cord clamping, cord stripping or twin-to-twin transfusion) or increased fetal red cell production in response to chronic intrauterine hypoxia (as in growth restriction, maternal diabetes or maternal smoking). As the haematocrit rises, blood viscosity increases disproportionately, impairing flow through the microcirculation and reducing oxygen and glucose delivery to tissues. This underlies complications affecting the brain, gut, kidneys and metabolic status, and increases the risk of hypoglycaemia and jaundice. Asymptomatic infants generally do well with hydration and monitoring; symptomatic hyperviscosity, particularly with end-organ effects, carries a less certain neurodevelopmental prognosis.

Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome — hyaline membrane disease, RDS, surfactant deficiency disease, respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn Transient tachypnoea of the newborn Neonatal pneumonia or early-onset sepsis (especially group B streptococcus) Meconium aspiration syndrome Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn Congenital heart disease Air-leak syndromes (pneumothorax) Chest radiograph to assess the reticulogranular pattern and lung volumes Arterial or capillary blood gas to quantify hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis Pulse oximetry and continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring Blood culture and inflammatory markers when sepsis cannot be excluded Blood glucose and electrolyte monitoring Echocardiography if congenital heart disease or pulmonary hypertension is suspected A disease of surfactant deficiency affecting mainly preterm infants; incidence rises steeply as gestational age falls, being greatest below about 28 weeks. Distress typically begins at or soon after birth with tachypnoea, grunting, nasal flaring, intercostal and subcostal recession, and cyanosis that worsen over the first hours to days. Chest radiograph classically shows a diffuse fine reticulogranular (ground-glass) pattern with air bronchograms and low lung volumes. Antenatal maternal corticosteroids given before anticipated preterm delivery accelerate lung maturation and markedly reduce incidence and severity. Exogenous surfactant replacement, delivered into the airway, is a cornerstone of treatment and improves oxygenation and survival. Early nasal continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) helps maintain functional residual capacity and can reduce the need for intubation and mechanical ventilation. Maternal diabetes, male sex, second-born twins, caesarean delivery without labour, and perinatal asphyxia increase risk, whereas chronic intrauterine stress and prolonged rupture of membranes may reduce it. Untreated disease tends to worsen for about 2-3 days before recovery begins, often heralded by a spontaneous diuresis. Rapidly escalating oxygen or ventilatory requirement Sudden deterioration suggesting pneumothorax or other air leak Persistent hypoxaemia despite surfactant and respiratory support (possible pulmonary hypertension) Apnoea, bradycardia, or signs of impending respiratory failure Hypotension and poor perfusion suggesting shock or sepsis Assuming RDS in a term or near-term infant without considering sepsis, aspiration, or cardiac causes Over-oxygenation, which increases the risk of retinopathy of prematurity and oxidative lung injury Delaying surfactant or CPAP in an infant who is deteriorating Failing to recognise a tension pneumothorax as the cause of abrupt worsening Not administering antenatal corticosteroids when preterm birth is anticipated Immature type II pneumocytes produce insufficient pulmonary surfactant, so alveolar surface tension is high. This causes progressive diffuse atelectasis, reduced lung compliance, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Hypoxaemia and hypercapnia with acidosis follow, and pulmonary vascular resistance may remain elevated with right-to-left shunting. Epithelial injury and protein-rich exudate form the hyaline membranes that give the disease its historical name, further impairing gas exchange. With antenatal steroids, surfactant, and modern respiratory support, survival is high, particularly in more mature preterm infants; outcome worsens with decreasing gestational age and with complications such as air leak, intraventricular haemorrhage, and progression to bronchopulmonary dysplasia.

Neonatal Seizures — seizures in the newborn, neonatal convulsions, newborn fits Jitteriness or benign neonatal sleep myoclonus Apnoea of other cause Hypoglycaemia or electrolyte disturbance Meningitis or encephalitis Intracranial haemorrhage or perinatal stroke Inborn errors of metabolism and vitamin-responsive epilepsies EEG or amplitude-integrated EEG monitoring Blood glucose, electrolytes, calcium, and magnesium Cranial imaging (ultrasound and MRI) Lumbar puncture and sepsis evaluation when infection is possible Metabolic and genetic testing in unexplained or refractory cases Seizures in the newborn period are usually a symptom of an acute underlying brain insult rather than a chronic epilepsy, so the priority is to find and treat the cause. Presentations are often subtle: repetitive eye deviation or blinking, lip-smacking or chewing, cycling or boxing limb movements, and apnoea, in addition to clonic or tonic activity. Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy is the most common cause; other important causes include stroke, intracranial haemorrhage, infection, metabolic disturbances, and inborn errors of metabolism. Because clinical signs are unreliable and electroclinical dissociation is common, EEG or amplitude-integrated EEG monitoring is central to accurate diagnosis. Immediate workup should exclude readily treatable causes such as hypoglycaemia and electrolyte abnormalities, correcting these before escalating anticonvulsant therapy. Non-epileptic movements like jitteriness can mimic seizures but are stimulus-sensitive, suppressible by gentle restraint, and lack autonomic or ocular features. Neuroimaging and, where appropriate, lumbar puncture and metabolic or genetic testing help establish aetiology and guide prognosis. Pyridoxine-dependent and other vitamin-responsive epilepsies should be considered when seizures are refractory to standard agents. Status epilepticus or very frequent recurrent seizures Seizures refractory to first-line therapy Encephalopathy with depressed consciousness and abnormal tone Signs of meningitis or sepsis Focal neurological deficits suggesting stroke or a structural lesion Relying on clinical observation alone and missing electrographic-only seizures Mistaking jitteriness or benign myoclonus for seizures and over-treating Escalating anticonvulsants before correcting hypoglycaemia or electrolyte abnormalities Failing to consider vitamin-responsive epilepsies in seizures resistant to standard drugs The immature neonatal brain is intrinsically more excitable because excitatory glutamatergic circuits mature earlier than inhibitory GABAergic systems, and GABA can be depolarising early in development. An acute insult, most often hypoxia-ischaemia, disrupts energy metabolism and ion gradients, leading to neuronal depolarisation and synchronised, excessive electrical discharges. Metabolic derangements, structural lesions, infection, or genetic and metabolic disorders lower the seizure threshold further. Frequent dissociation between electrical seizures and visible clinical signs reflects this immaturity and underlies the need for electrographic monitoring. Outcome depends largely on the underlying cause and the severity of any brain injury; seizures due to transient metabolic disturbances often resolve well, whereas those from severe hypoxic-ischaemic injury, major structural lesions, or certain genetic-metabolic disorders carry a higher risk of epilepsy and neurodevelopmental impairment.

Neonatal sepsis — sepsis neonatorum, newborn sepsis, early-onset neonatal sepsis, late-onset neonatal sepsis, EOS, LOS Transient tachypnoea of the newborn Respiratory distress syndrome Congenital heart disease with poor perfusion Inborn errors of metabolism Neonatal encephalopathy / birth asphyxia Congenital viral infection (e.g. herpes simplex, cytomegalovirus) Blood culture before starting antibiotics Complete blood count with differential and immature-to-total neutrophil ratio C-reactive protein and/or procalcitonin, ideally serially Lumbar puncture with CSF cell count, protein, glucose and culture Urine culture (more relevant in late-onset disease) Chest radiograph if respiratory signs are present Blood glucose, electrolytes and blood gas to assess metabolic status A systemic bacterial (occasionally fungal or viral) infection in the first 28 days of life, conventionally split into early-onset (within roughly the first 72 hours, often maternally acquired) and late-onset (after 72 hours, frequently nosocomial or community-acquired). Signs are notoriously nonspecific: temperature instability (fever or hypothermia), poor feeding, lethargy or irritability, respiratory distress, apnoea, tachycardia, and abdominal distension. Group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli dominate early-onset disease; coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, and Gram-negative organisms are common in late-onset disease, especially in preterm infants with indwelling lines. Maternal risk factors include prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, maternal fever, and GBS colonisation without adequate intrapartum prophylaxis. Blood culture is the diagnostic gold standard; a lumbar puncture should be considered because meningitis frequently coexists and may be missed. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics must be started promptly after cultures because deterioration can be rapid; the regimen is later narrowed to culture results. Supportive care (thermoregulation, respiratory and haemodynamic support, glucose management) is as important as antimicrobials. A low threshold for treatment is appropriate given nonspecific signs, but antibiotics are stopped early when cultures remain negative and the infant is well. Septic shock: poor perfusion, hypotension, prolonged capillary refill Apnoea or worsening respiratory failure requiring support Bulging fontanelle, seizures, or other signs suggesting meningitis Petechiae, purpura, or bleeding suggesting disseminated intravascular coagulation Persistent hypoglycaemia or profound metabolic acidosis Attributing nonspecific signs to prematurity or feeding issues and delaying evaluation Omitting a lumbar puncture and missing coexisting meningitis Relying on a single normal inflammatory marker to exclude sepsis early in the illness Failing to remove or consider infected central venous catheters in late-onset disease Neonates are relatively immunocompromised, with immature innate and adaptive defences, low immunoglobulin levels, and impaired neutrophil function. Organisms reach the infant by ascending or intrapartum transmission from the maternal genital tract in early-onset disease, or from the postnatal environment and invasive devices in late-onset disease. Once bloodstream invasion occurs, bacterial products trigger a systemic inflammatory response with cytokine release, endothelial injury, capillary leak, and impaired perfusion that can progress to septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and multi-organ dysfunction. The immature blood-brain barrier and limited containment of infection predispose to meningitis. Outcome depends on gestational age, organism, and speed of treatment; prompt therapy usually leads to recovery, but meningitis, shock, and prematurity carry higher mortality and risk of neurodevelopmental sequelae.

Neoplasms of the Lung — Lung cancer, Bronchogenic carcinoma, Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC), Pulmonary carcinoma Persistent or recurrent pneumonia unresponsive to antibiotics Metastatic carcinoma to the lung from an extrapulmonary primary Malignant pleural mesothelioma (CK5/6, calretinin, WT-1 positive, distinguishing it from adenocarcinoma) Pulmonary carcinoid tumor (neuroendocrine, often central/endobronchial) Benign solitary pulmonary nodule (granuloma, hamartoma) Tuberculosis and other granulomatous disease (false-positive FDG-PET uptake; can mimic malignant nodules) Postobstructive pneumonia from an underlying endobronchial tumor Lung abscess from tumor cavitation Parapneumonic pleural effusion mimicking malignant effusion Chest CT and FDG PET, preferably integrated PET-CT, for anatomic staging and detection of mediastinal nodal and extrathoracic metastases Tissue biopsy: fiberoptic bronchoscopy with bronchial/transbronchial biopsy, image-guided percutaneous core biopsy, or EBUS-guided biopsy; core biopsy preferred for adequate molecular material Mediastinal nodal assessment by EBUS- or EUS-guided biopsy, mediastinoscopy, mediastinotomy, thoracoscopy, or thoracotomy Next-generation sequencing (multigene panel) for driver oncogenes and PD-L1 immunohistochemistry reported as tumor proportion score (TPS) Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) 'liquid biopsy' when tissue is limited or inaccessible MRI brain for suspected brain metastases (most effective method) and for superior sulcus tumors to assess brachial plexus involvement Immunohistochemistry: TTF-1 and napsin-A for adenocarcinoma (TTF-1 positive in over 70%, napsin-A in over 90% of primary lung adenocarcinomas), p40/p63 for squamous; neuroendocrine markers (CD56/NCAM, synaptophysin, chromogranin, INSM1) for SCLC Thoracentesis with cell block for suspected malignant pleural effusion (repeat if first sample negative) Spinal CT/MRI for suspected cord compression; brain/spine MRI plus lumbar puncture for suspected leptomeningeal disease Physiologic evaluation: spirometry (FEV1), DLCO, and cardiopulmonary exercise testing (VO2max) before surgical resection Sarcoidosis and other granulomatous disorders Benign pulmonary nodules (hamartoma, hamartochondroma) Pulmonary metastases from non-lung primaries Mesothelioma Paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes mimicking primary neurologic disease Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide and in the United States; over half of patients present with locally advanced or metastatic disease at diagnosis. Tobacco smoking accounts for roughly two-thirds of lung cancer deaths globally, but about 65% of new U.S. diagnoses are now in former smokers or never-smokers; one in five women and one in twelve men diagnosed have never smoked. The WHO divides epithelial lung cancers into four major types: small-cell carcinoma (SCLC) and three non-small-cell types (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell, large-cell). Together these account for about 90% of epithelial lung cancers; adenocarcinoma is now the most common subtype. Separating SCLC from NSCLC and, within NSCLC, squamous from nonsquamous histology is essential because natural history and management differ markedly; a generic diagnosis of 'non-small-cell carcinoma, not otherwise specified' is no longer acceptable. A chronic cough with or without hemoptysis in a current or former smoker with COPD aged 40 or older warrants thorough evaluation for lung cancer even with a normal chest x-ray; a persistent pneumonia unresponsive to repeated antibiotics also requires workup. Tissue sampling is required to confirm diagnosis in all suspected cases; a core biopsy is preferred over fine-needle aspiration to provide adequate material for molecular and PD-L1 testing. Central, endobronchial lesions (squamous cell, small-cell, carcinoid) are more readily reached by bronchoscopy, whereas peripheral lesions (adenocarcinoma, large-cell) are more amenable to transthoracic biopsy. Driver oncogenes (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, RET, NTRK, BRAF, MET, HER2, KRAS) are enriched in nonsquamous NSCLC and define distinct molecular cohorts; nearly 90% of SCLCs carry TP53 and RB1 mutations. Paraneoplastic syndromes are common, especially with SCLC, and may be the presenting feature or first sign of recurrence; they can mimic metastatic disease and lead to inappropriately palliative rather than curative management. Hypercalcemia from ectopic PTH-related peptide is the most common life-threatening metabolic complication of malignancy and occurs primarily with squamous cell carcinoma. On FDG PET, a standardized uptake value (SUV) above 2.5 is highly suspicious for malignancy, but PET must never be used alone to diagnose cancer, nodal involvement, or metastasis because of false positives (infection, granulomatous disease such as tuberculosis) and false negatives (lesions under 8 mm, slow-growing tumors, diabetes). Adenocarcinoma in situ and minimally invasive adenocarcinoma (solitary lesions 3 cm or less with pure or predominant lepidic growth and 5 mm or less invasion) achieve near 100% 5-year disease-free survival after complete resection. Hemoptysis in a smoker over 40 with chronic cough Hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement) or superior vena cava syndrome Pancoast/superior sulcus presentation: shoulder pain radiating in ulnar distribution with destruction of first/second ribs, often with Horner syndrome Signs of cord compression: pain, weakness, paralysis, urinary retention Weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight (poor prognostic sign) Hypercalcemia with nausea, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, altered mental status Symptomatic brain metastases (headache, nausea/vomiting, seizures, focal deficits) or pathologic fractures/bone pain A normal chest x-ray does not exclude lung cancer in a high-risk symptomatic smoker. Negative TTF-1 does not exclude a pulmonary primary; TTF-1 is also positive in neuroendocrine and thyroid tumors. PET-CT cannot establish a tissue diagnosis: false positives occur with tuberculosis/granulomatous and infectious disease and false negatives with sub-8 mm, slow-growing, or carcinoid/well-differentiated tumors. Paraneoplastic syndromes may be mistaken for metastatic disease, risking inappropriate palliative rather than curative treatment. A single negative thoracentesis does not exclude a malignant effusion; repeat sampling is essential. Diagnosing on small biopsy/cytology specimens may blur squamous-versus-nonsquamous distinction; repeat biopsy is advised in advanced disease for adequate molecular and PD-L1 testing. Low-dose CT screening carries a high false-positive rate (false-positive rate about 96% among positive screens in NLST), with attendant risks of overdiagnosis, unnecessary procedures, and radiation exposure. Inhaled environmental carcinogens, principally those in tobacco smoke, drive transformation of bronchoepithelial cells to a malignant phenotype. Susceptibility is modulated by polymorphisms in carcinogen-metabolizing genes (e.g., CYP1A1) and by genetic loci affecting nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and telomerase (5p15, 6p21, 15q25). Tumorigenesis reflects accumulation of gain-of-function mutations in oncogenes and loss-of-function mutations in tumor-suppressor genes, with the sequence differing by histologic type. Adenocarcinomas frequently harbor targetable driver alterations: activating receptor tyrosine kinase mutations (EGFR, HER2/ERBB2, MET), intracellular signaling mutations (KRAS, BRAF), and chromosomal rearrangements activating ALK, ROS1, RET, and NTRK. Squamous tumors may show FGFR1 amplification, DDR2 mutations, PIK3CA mutations/PTEN loss, and BRAF/MET alterations. Inactivated tumor suppressors include TP53, RB1, RASSF1A, CDKN2A/B, LKB1 (STK11), and FHIT; allelic loss on chromosome 3p occurs very early, even in histologically normal smoke-damaged epithelium. Clinical manifestations arise from central/endobronchial growth (cough, hemoptysis, wheeze, postobstructive pneumonia), peripheral growth (pleural/chest-wall pain, dyspnea, cavitation), regional intrathoracic spread (recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy with hoarseness, phrenic nerve palsy, Horner syndrome, Pancoast syndrome, superior vena cava syndrome, pericardial/lymphatic involvement), distant metastasis, or paraneoplastic mechanisms. Outcome is strongly stage-dependent. For NSCLC by the eighth-edition TNM system, 5-year overall survival ranges from roughly 90% for the earliest (stage IA1) disease down to about 10% for stage IVB; SEER data report a 5-year survival of about 63% for localized NSCLC. Lepidic-predominant adenocarcinoma has a favorable prognosis, acinar and papillary intermediate, and solid-predominant and micropapillary patterns poor. SCLC is more aggressive: 60-70% present with extensive-stage disease, and even in limited-stage SCLC median survival is roughly 12-20 months historically. Weight loss over 10% of body weight and thrombotic complications of malignancy are poor prognostic signs. Extrathoracic metastases are found at autopsy in over 50% of squamous, about 80% of adenocarcinoma/large-cell, and over 95% of SCLC cases. NSCLC is staged with the eighth-edition (2018) TNM system: T1 (3 cm or less; subdivided T1a 1 cm or less, T1b over 1 to 2 cm, T1c over 2 to 3 cm), T2 (over 3 to 5 cm or visceral pleura/main bronchus involvement/atelectasis; T2a over 3 to 4 cm, T2b over 4 to 5 cm), T3 (over 5 to 7 cm or invasion of chest wall/pericardium/phrenic nerve or satellite nodule in same lobe), T4 (over 7 cm or invasion of mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, recurrent laryngeal nerve, esophagus, vertebra, carina, or separate nodule in a different ipsilateral lobe). Nodes: N0 none, N1 ipsilateral peribronchial/hilar/intrapulmonary, N2 ipsilateral mediastinal/subcarinal, N3 contralateral mediastinal/hilar or scalene/supraclavicular. Metastasis: M1a contralateral nodule or pleural/pericardial nodule/malignant effusion, M1b single extrathoracic metastasis, M1c multiple extrathoracic metastases. SCLC is commonly classified by the two-stage Veterans Administration system: limited-stage (confined to ipsilateral hemithorax within a tolerable radiation port) versus extensive-stage (overt metastatic disease). Physiologic operability thresholds: FEV1 over 2 L or over 80% predicted suggests tolerance of pneumonectomy; FEV1 over 1.5 L suggests adequate reserve for lobectomy; VO2max under 15 mL/kg/min predicts higher postoperative risk; contraindications to thoracic surgery include FEV1 under 1 L, resting PCO2 over 45 mmHg, DLCO under 40%, severe pulmonary hypertension, and recent myocardial infarction.

Neovascular glaucoma — NVG, rubeotic glaucoma, haemorrhagic glaucoma, thrombotic glaucoma Primary acute angle-closure glaucoma Inflammatory (uveitic) glaucoma with anterior segment vessels Chronic angle-closure glaucoma from other causes Fuchs heterochromic uveitis with fine iris vessels Intraocular tumour causing secondary glaucoma Post-traumatic or ghost cell glaucoma with a red painful eye Undilated slit-lamp examination and gonioscopy to detect early rubeosis and angle new vessels Applanation tonometry to gauge the pressure rise Dilated fundus examination and retinal imaging or fluorescein angiography to identify the ischaemic driver Carotid Doppler or vascular imaging when ocular ischaemic syndrome is suspected Assessment and control of systemic diabetes and cardiovascular risk factors B-scan ultrasonography when media opacity obscures the retina A severe secondary glaucoma driven by new vessel growth on the iris (rubeosis iridis) and in the drainage angle in response to retinal ischaemia The commonest underlying causes are ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion, proliferative diabetic retinopathy, and ocular ischaemic syndrome from carotid disease Early rubeosis begins as fine vessels at the pupillary margin and angle before spreading; careful undilated gonioscopy and iris examination detect it before pressure rises A fibrovascular membrane initially blocks the open angle, then contracts to pull the peripheral iris forward, producing progressive synechial (secondary) angle closure Late presentation is with a painful red eye, very high intraocular pressure, corneal oedema, and poor vision, often with ectropion uveae from membrane contraction Management targets the ischaemic drive with panretinal photocoagulation and anti-VEGF injection, alongside topical pressure-lowering agents and control of pain and inflammation Once the angle is extensively closed, drainage surgery with a tube or trabeculectomy, or a cyclodestructive procedure, is usually needed to control pressure Identifying and treating the underlying retinal or carotid ischaemia is essential and may require systemic and vascular assessment New iris or angle vessels signalling active retinal ischaemia that demands urgent treatment before the angle closes Painful red eye with very high pressure and corneal oedema requiring emergency care An ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion or proliferative diabetic retinopathy known to precede rubeosis Ocular ischaemic syndrome pointing to significant carotid disease and systemic vascular risk Dilating the pupil before examining for early rubeosis and missing angle new vessels Treating the pressure alone without addressing the underlying retinal or carotid ischaemia Relying on anti-VEGF injection, whose effect is temporary, without definitive panretinal photocoagulation Delaying treatment until the angle has already closed synechially Overlooking ocular ischaemic syndrome and an underlying carotid stenosis Neovascular glaucoma results from chronic retinal ischaemia, which triggers release of vascular endothelial growth factor and other angiogenic mediators into the aqueous. These stimulate growth of a fibrovascular membrane over the iris surface and across the trabecular meshwork. In the early open-angle phase this membrane physically covers and obstructs the meshwork, raising pressure while the angle still appears open on gonioscopy. As the membrane matures its myofibroblasts contract, dragging the peripheral iris anteriorly to form peripheral anterior synechiae and everting the pupil margin (ectropion uveae), which produces progressive synechial angle closure. The combination of outflow obstruction and secondary angle closure causes marked pressure elevation, corneal oedema, pain, and optic-nerve damage. Prognosis depends on how early the neovascular drive is treated; caught at the rubeosis stage, panretinal photocoagulation and anti-VEGF therapy may regress vessels and preserve the angle, but established synechial closure often leaves a difficult-to-control eye with poor visual potential, and some eyes become painful and blind despite treatment.

Nephrocalcinosis — renal calcinosis, medullary nephrocalcinosis, cortical nephrocalcinosis, renal parenchymal calcification Medullary sponge kidney Distal renal tubular acidosis Primary hyperparathyroidism and other hypercalcaemic states Primary or enteric hyperoxaluria Sarcoidosis and vitamin D excess Acute cortical necrosis or chronic pyelonephritis for the cortical pattern Papillary calcification of medullary origin Renal ultrasound, supplemented by CT, to confirm and characterise a medullary versus cortical pattern Serum calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone Serum and urine pH, bicarbonate and electrolytes to assess for distal renal tubular acidosis 24-hour urine calcium, oxalate and citrate Serum vitamin D and, where indicated, angiotensin-converting enzyme for sarcoidosis Urinalysis and renal function tests Nephrocalcinosis is generalised deposition of calcium salts within the renal parenchyma, distinct from discrete calculi in the collecting system The medullary pattern is far more common and usually reflects a disorder of calcium handling The classic medullary causes are hyperparathyroidism, distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis and medullary sponge kidney Further medullary causes include hypervitaminosis D, sarcoidosis, milk-alkali syndrome and primary hyperoxaluria Cortical nephrocalcinosis is rarer and follows acute cortical necrosis, chronic glomerulonephritis or severe pyelonephritis It is often found incidentally on imaging; ultrasound shows echogenic medullary pyramids in the medullary pattern Management is directed at the underlying metabolic cause rather than at the calcification itself Distal renal tubular acidosis is suggested when nephrocalcinosis accompanies a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis with an inappropriately alkaline urine, and is treated with alkali replacement Progressive chronic kidney disease from an untreated underlying disorder Severe hypercalcaemia with acute kidney injury Nephrocalcinosis in a child suggesting primary hyperoxaluria or an inherited tubulopathy Superimposed stones causing obstruction Confusing nephrocalcinosis, which is parenchymal, with nephrolithiasis in the collecting system Failing to search for a treatable metabolic cause such as distal renal tubular acidosis or hyperparathyroidism Missing primary hyperoxaluria in a child, in whom it is progressive and serious Attributing renal impairment to the calcification rather than the underlying disease Nephrocalcinosis denotes deposition of calcium, as oxalate or phosphate, diffusely through the renal tissue, most often in the medulla. Medullary deposition arises when there is an increased filtered calcium load, impaired urinary acidification or reduced inhibitor activity, as in hyperparathyroidism, distal renal tubular acidosis (where alkaline urine and hypocitraturia favour calcium phosphate precipitation), medullary sponge kidney with stasis in dilated collecting ducts, and states of hypercalcaemia or hyperoxaluria. Cortical nephrocalcinosis instead follows destructive processes such as acute cortical necrosis or chronic infection, where calcium is laid down in devitalised tissue as dystrophic calcification. The renal outlook depends on the underlying cause and how early it is treated; some tubulopathies stabilise with alkali therapy, whereas primary hyperoxaluria and progressive hypercalcaemic disorders can lead to established renal failure.

dehydration in an infant with lethargy or seizures Recurrent unexplained fevers and failure to thrive in a young child Obstructive uropathy or hydronephrosis from chronic high-volume output Rapid labelling disease hereditary In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus the principal cells of the collecting duct fail to respond to vasopressin. X-linked disease results from loss-of-function mutations in AVPR2, the gene for the V2 vasopressin receptor, so hormone binding cannot trigger the intracellular signalling that normally inserts water channels into the apical membrane. Autosomal forms result from mutations in AQP2, the aquaporin-2 water channel itself, impairing its trafficking or function. Either defect prevents water reabsorption, producing large volumes of inappropriately dilute urine, a tendency to hypernatraemia and dehydration, and compensatory polydipsia. With early diagnosis, reliable access to water and volume-reducing measures, growth and development are usually preserved, but repeated episodes of severe hypernatraemic dehydration in infancy can cause lasting neurological injury.

nephrogenic systemic fibrosis — nephrogenic fibrosing dermopathy, NSF Systemic sclerosis and morphoea Scleromyxoedema Scleroedema Eosinophilic fasciitis Chronic graft-versus-host disease with sclerodermatous features Lipodermatosclerosis of chronic venous disease Deep incisional (including fascia) skin biopsy showing fibrocyte proliferation, thickened collagen bundles and mucin Renal function including eGFR to confirm and stage kidney impairment Review of gadolinium contrast exposure history, agent type and dose Immunohistochemistry for CD34 highlighting spindle-cell fibrocytes Autoimmune serology to help exclude systemic sclerosis and related disorders Serum protein electrophoresis to exclude a paraproteinaemia mimicking scleromyxoedema An acquired fibrosing disorder of skin and internal organs occurring almost exclusively in patients with severe renal impairment exposed to gadolinium-based contrast agents Presents with symmetrical, progressive woody induration of the skin, most often on the lower limbs and forearms, with brawny hyperpigmentation and a cobblestoned, peau d'orange surface Fibrosis leads to painful joint contractures and marked loss of mobility, and yellow scleral plaques may be seen in younger patients Characteristically the face is spared, an important clue distinguishing it from scleroderma and scleromyxoedema Risk is greatest with high-risk (linear, less stable) gadolinium agents, higher doses and repeated exposures in patients with an eGFR below about thirty or on dialysis, including those with acute kidney injury Diagnosis combines the clinical picture with a deep skin biopsy showing spindle-cell proliferation with CD34-positive fibrocytes and thickened collagen, correlated with clinicoradiological criteria Prevention is paramount: avoid or minimise high-risk contrast agents in advanced renal disease and prefer more stable macrocyclic agents; established disease is difficult to treat and may improve if renal function is restored Rapidly progressive skin thickening with developing joint contractures Systemic fibrosis causing restrictive lung disease or cardiac involvement Diaphragmatic involvement leading to respiratory compromise Profound loss of mobility with dependency and risk of complications of immobility Administering high-risk gadolinium agents to patients with advanced renal disease without recognising the risk Mistaking the condition for systemic sclerosis and overlooking the characteristic sparing of the face Taking too superficial a biopsy and missing the diagnostic deep dermal and fascial fibrosis Failing to obtain a contrast exposure history in a dialysis patient with new skin induration Assuming a single, low-dose exposure carries no risk in severe renal impairment Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is triggered by exposure to gadolinium-based contrast agents in the setting of markedly reduced renal clearance, which prolongs circulation of gadolinium and permits dissociation of the metal from its chelate (transmetallation), particularly with less stable linear agents. Retained gadolinium deposits in tissues and, together with uraemia and possibly other cofactors, is thought to recruit circulating CD34-positive, procollagen-positive bone-marrow-derived fibrocytes into the skin and other organs. These cells, driven by profibrotic cytokines such as transforming growth factor-beta, proliferate and deposit excess collagen and mucin, producing progressive dermal and systemic fibrosis that can involve muscle, lungs, heart and diaphragm. The course is typically chronic and progressive with substantial disability from contractures and immobility, and systemic fibrosis contributes to mortality in severe cases. Some patients stabilise or improve when renal function recovers, for example after successful transplantation, but established fibrosis often persists.

Nephrolithiasis — Kidney stone disease, Renal calculi, Urolithiasis, Renal stones Acute cholecystitis (right ureteropelvic-junction stone) Acute appendicitis (stone at right pelvic brim) Acute diverticulitis (stone at left pelvic brim) Bacterial cystitis (ureterovesical-junction stone causing urgency/frequency) Acute pyelonephritis (obstructing stone with proximal infection) Musculoskeletal pain Herpes zoster Duodenal ulcer Abdominal aortic aneurysm Gynecologic conditions Ureteral stricture Ureteral obstruction by blood clot or sloughed papilla Extraluminal ureteral compression (typically gradual onset, not true colic) Acute pyelonephritis (an obstructing stone with proximal infection can present this way) Bacterial cystitis (ureterovesical stone causes urgency/frequency with red and white cells in urine but a negative urine culture) Noncontrast helical CT (gold standard; detects stones as small as 1 mm and uric acid stones) Renal ultrasound (avoids radiation, shows hydronephrosis, but insensitive for ureteral stones) Plain abdominal radiograph (KUB) (may miss ureteral/renal stones and gives no obstruction information) Urinalysis with sediment examination for red/white cells and crystals (calcium oxalate dihydrate = bipyramidal; cystine = hexagonal) Urine culture if infection is suspected Serum electrolytes (for hypokalemia/RTA), creatinine, calcium, phosphorus, uric acid PTH and 25-hydroxy vitamin D when serum/urine calcium is elevated or high/low-normal At least two 24-h urine collections on usual diet (volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium, pH, creatinine; supersaturation when available) Stone composition analysis of any passed or retrieved stone Acute cholecystitis Acute appendicitis Acute diverticulitis Abdominal aortic aneurysm Duodenal ulcer Herpes zoster Gynecologic conditions Musculoskeletal pain Calcium oxalate stones are by far the most common type (~75%), followed by calcium phosphate (~15%), uric acid (~8%), struvite (~1%), and cystine (<1%); many stones are mixtures and contain protein matrix (Harrison 22e p.2448). Identifying the stone type is clinically important because it informs prognosis and the choice of preventive strategy; patients should be encouraged to retrieve and submit passed stones for composition analysis (Harrison 22e p.2451-2452). The two classic acute presentations are renal colic and painless gross hematuria; symptom onset reflects a stone moving into the ureter and gives no clue as to when the stone actually formed, since stone growth is typically clinically silent over weeks to years (Harrison 22e p.2450). Pain radiation depends on stone location: an upper ureteral stone may radiate anteriorly, while a lower ureteral stone may radiate to the ipsilateral testicle (men) or labium (women); a ureterovesical-junction stone can cause urinary urgency and frequency (Harrison 22e p.2450). Absence of hematuria does not exclude a stone, particularly when urine flow is completely obstructed (Harrison 22e p.2450). Noncontrast helical CT is the gold-standard imaging test: it detects stones as small as 1 mm and visualizes uric acid stones that are traditionally considered radiolucent on plain films (Harrison 22e p.2450). Urine pH governs solubility of several stone types: uric acid stones form at pH consistently <=5.5, calcium phosphate stones are favored at pH >=6.5, and cystine is more soluble at higher pH; calcium oxalate stone risk is not influenced by urine pH (Harrison 22e p.2450). Urine citrate is the most clinically important natural inhibitor of calcium-containing stones; metabolic acidosis (including from high animal-flesh intake) lowers citrate excretion by enhancing its tubular reabsorption (Harrison 22e p.2448, 2449). Dietary calcium restriction is counterproductive: higher dietary calcium intake lowers stone risk by binding intestinal oxalate and reducing urinary oxalate, whereas low calcium intake increases stone risk and may lower bone density (Harrison 22e p.2449). Two 24-h urine collections on the patient's usual diet are the cornerstone of preventive evaluation, measuring volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium, pH, and creatinine; two collections are needed because of substantial day-to-day variability (Harrison 22e p.2451-2452). Urinary risk factors (calcium, oxalate, citrate) are continuous variables with no valid normal/abnormal cutoff; dichotomizing them is misleading and arbitrary thresholds should be avoided (Harrison 22e p.2449, 2452). Pure uric acid stones can be recognized by their low Hounsfield units on CT, helping distinguish stone composition non-invasively (Harrison 22e p.2452). UTI in the setting of an obstructing stone is a urologic emergency ('pus under pressure') requiring urgent restoration of drainage via ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy Complete urinary obstruction by a stone (hematuria may be absent) Stone measuring >=6 mm or anatomic abnormality (low probability of spontaneous passage) Intractable pain unresponsive to analgesia Staghorn or multiple bilateral stones (suggest cystinuria or struvite/infection stones) Infection (struvite) stones, which if untreated can lead to end-stage renal disease Assuming a normal urinalysis (no hematuria) rules out a stone, which is false especially with complete obstruction Recommending low dietary calcium, which actually increases stone risk and harms bone density Using arbitrary normal/abnormal thresholds for urine calcium, oxalate, or citrate when risk is continuous Basing the preventive regimen on a single 24-h urine collection despite large day-to-day variability Mistaking a preexisting residual stone for a new stone when baseline imaging was suboptimal, leading to unnecessary changes in therapy Misattributing flank/abdominal pain to a stone and missing cholecystitis, appendicitis, diverticulitis, AAA, or an occlusive vascular event Failing to recognize that symptom onset does not indicate when the stone formed Stones form when urine becomes supersaturated with lithogenic solutes, i.e., when the concentration product exceeds the solubility product. Most people's urine is supersaturated for one or more crystal types, but crystallization inhibitors (notably urine citrate) prevent continuous stone formation. Recent biopsy data have shifted the paradigm for stone initiation: calcium phosphate deposits in the renal interstitium, hypothesized to begin at the thin limb of the loop of Henle, then extends to and erodes through the papillary epithelium, forming Randall's plaque on which most calcium oxalate stones grow. Tubular plugs of calcium phosphate may initiate calcium phosphate stones. Thus stone formation can begin years before a stone is clinically detectable. Higher urine calcium (from greater GI absorption and/or bone turnover) and higher urine oxalate (largely dietary, with higher dietary calcium reducing GI oxalate absorption) raise calcium oxalate/phosphate risk, while low urine citrate removes a key inhibitor (Harrison 22e p.2448-2450). Although renal colic is reported as among the worst pain patients experience, nephrolithiasis is rarely fatal. More than half of first-time stone formers have a recurrence within 10 years, but recurrence of most or all stone types can be prevented with careful evaluation and targeted, often lifelong, intervention. Untreated infection (struvite) stones can have devastating consequences and progress to end-stage renal disease, and repeated obstruction and instrumentation (e.g., in cystinuria) can reduce GFR. Primary hyperoxaluria can cause intraparenchymal calcium oxalate deposition leading to renal failure (Harrison 22e p.2448, 2450, 2451). No formal grading; clinical risk stratification rests on likelihood of spontaneous passage (stone size and location, e.g., >=6 mm or anatomic abnormality favoring intervention) and on presence of emergency features such as obstruction with superimposed infection.

Early features reflect impaired urinary concentration: polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia and secondary enuresis, often with salt wasting Growth retardation and anaemia can be disproportionate to the (Joubert syndrome), liver fibrosis and skeletal changes Blood pressure is often normal until late, unlike many other progressive nephropathies Progressive decline toward kidney failure requiring planning for kidney replacement therapy Marked polyuria with dehydration and electrolyte disturbance Visual symptoms suggesting associated retinal degeneration Neurological signs suggesting a syndromic ciliopathy such as Joubert syndrome Expecting enlarged kidneys and dismissing the diagnosis when ultrasound shows normal-sized echogenic kidneys Missing the diagnosis in a child with unexplained polyuria, anaemia and growth failure Failing to screen for retinal and neurological extrarenal manifestations Attributing early salt wasting and polyuria to a primary concentrating defect without considering nephronophthisis Nephronophthisis is an inherited ciliopathy in which variants in NPHP genes disrupt proteins (nephrocystins) that localise to the primary cilium, basal body and cell junctions of renal tubular epithelial cells. Impaired ciliary signalling and planar cell polarity disturb tubular development, cell adhesion and repair, leading to a chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy with tubular basement membrane disruption, interstitial fibrosis and small corticomedullary cysts. Because the concentrating mechanism is affected early, the disease presents with polyuria and salt wasting before progressing to fibrosis and kidney failure. The same ciliary dysfunction in other organs accounts for the associated retinal, cerebellar, hepatic and skeletal syndromes. Nephronophthisis is progressive and typically leads to kidney failure, with the age of onset varying by subtype (infantile, juvenile and adolescent forms); the juvenile form commonly reaches kidney failure in the teenage years. Outcome after transplantation is generally good as the disease does not recur in the graft.

Abrupt adult-onset nephrotic syndrome with markedly elevated cholesterol suggests a podocytopathy such as minimal change disease, which is often preceded by upper respiratory infection, allergy or immunisation (p.2358).
