Nephrotic-range proteinuria without oedema, with rapid renal function loss, raises HIV-associated nephropathy (collapsing glomerulopathy, a severe treatment-resistant FSGS variant), more common in patients of African ancestry (p.2358). Heavy proteinuria with new haematuria suggesting renal vein thrombosis (p.384) Rapidly declining renal function with very heavy proteinuria and no oedema suggesting collapsing glomerulopathy/HIVAN (p.2358) Cellulitis or ulceration from ruptured oedema bullae (p.2358) Hoarseness from vocal cord oedema or scrotal/penile oedema obstructing urinary flow (p.2358) Assuming any nephrotic-range proteinuria equals classic nephrotic syndrome — heavy proteinuria can occur without hypoalbuminaemia/oedema (p.385). Relying on dipstick alone — it misses light chains, so myeloma-associated overflow proteinuria can be overlooked; total protein:creatinine ratio is not specific for albumin (p.385, p.2357). Equating subnephrotic albuminuria with absence of significant glomerular disease — focal disease causes lower albuminuria yet can be significant (p.2357). Misreading biopsy-proven FSGS as a single entity — primary podocytopathic FSGS, secondary/adaptive FSGS, and post-GN healing scars are distinct (p.2356, p.2398). Nephrotic syndrome reflects increased glomerular permeability to plasma proteins. Minimal change disease causes diffuse fusion (effacement) of podocyte foot processes producing predominantly 'selective' albumin loss, whereas immune-complex disruption of the basement membrane and slit diaphragms yields 'nonselective' loss of albumin and larger proteins. Hypoalbuminaemia results from urinary loss plus increased proximal-tubule catabolism of filtered albumin, exceeding hepatic synthesis (a hypercatabolic, negative-nitrogen-balance state). Oedema arises from renal sodium retention and reduced plasma oncotic pressure; perceived reduction in effective intravascular volume activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, AVP and the sympathetic nervous system, and filtered proteases can directly activate the epithelial Na channel (ENaC) in principal cells, promoting further salt/water retention. Hyperlipidaemia/hypercholesterolaemia reflect increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis. Notably, hypertension is uncommon in primary kidney diseases causing nephrotic syndrome (p.385). Hereditary nephrotic syndrome can result from podocyte slit-diaphragm gene mutations (nephrin NPHS1, podocin NPHS2); APOL1 risk variants predispose to FSGS, with disease expression triggered by a 'second hit' of infection/inflammation damaging podocytes and glomerular endothelium (p.2357-2358). Glomerular proteinuria in diabetes typically appears after years of small-vessel disease (hence frequent coexistent retinopathy) and predicts progression to nephrotic syndrome and renal failure; the rate of progression is faster with hypertension, obesity and poor glucose control. Diffuse glomerular involvement (most glomeruli) makes nephrotic syndrome likely, whereas focal disease (<50% of glomeruli) tends to give subnephrotic albuminuria. In membranous nephropathy, ~70% of primary cases are anti-PLA2R associated. Collapsing glomerulopathy (HIVAN) is a severe, treatment-resistant FSGS variant. Quartan malarial nephropathy responds poorly to therapy (p.2356-2358). Albuminuria categories (Ch.55 Fig.55-3): moderately increased 30-300 mg/d or mg/g (formerly microalbuminuria); severely increased 300-3500 mg/d or mg/g (formerly macroalbuminuria); nephrotic range >3500 mg/d or mg/g. Full nephrotic syndrome defined by the triad of oedema, hypoalbuminaemia (<3.5 g/dL) and proteinuria >3.5 g/d, usually with lipid abnormalities (high LDL, low HDL, lipiduria) (p.385, p.2357).

Nephrotic syndrome (paediatric) — childhood nephrotic syndrome, idiopathic nephrotic syndrome, minimal change disease, paediatric nephrotic syndrome Acute glomerulonephritis (nephritic syndrome) Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis Membranous nephropathy (uncommon in children) Henoch-Schonlein purpura nephritis Systemic lupus erythematosus nephritis Congenital nephrotic syndrome in infants Oedema from cardiac, hepatic, or nutritional causes Urinalysis and quantification of proteinuria (urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or timed collection) Serum albumin, total protein, and lipid profile Renal function and electrolytes Full blood count Complement levels and autoimmune serology when nephritic features are present Renal biopsy in atypical or steroid-resistant cases Defined by the tetrad of heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and hyperlipidaemia. In children it is most often idiopathic, and minimal change disease is the predominant histology, especially in preschool children. Oedema is the usual presenting feature, typically starting periorbitally and becoming generalised with dependent swelling and sometimes ascites. Most childhood cases are steroid-responsive, so an empirical corticosteroid trial is standard first-line therapy without initial biopsy in the typical age group. Renal biopsy is reserved for atypical features: older or very young age, gross haematuria, hypertension, impaired renal function, or steroid resistance. Children are at increased risk of infection (notably pneumococcal peritonitis) from urinary immunoglobulin loss, and of thromboembolism from a hypercoagulable state. Supportive care includes sensible salt restriction, careful management of oedema, and attention to nutrition and infection prevention including vaccination. Relapses are common; the pattern of response guides classification into steroid-sensitive, frequently relapsing, steroid-dependent, or steroid-resistant disease. Fever with abdominal pain suggesting spontaneous bacterial peritonitis Signs of thromboembolism (limb swelling, respiratory distress, neurological signs) Hypertension, gross haematuria, or reduced renal function suggesting a nephritic process Severe hypovolaemia from rapid fluid shifts, or tense ascites and respiratory compromise Steroid resistance prompting reassessment and biopsy Attributing oedema to another cause and missing proteinuria on urinalysis Overlooking infection or thrombosis, the major acute complications Missing atypical features that warrant biopsy rather than empirical steroids Aggressive diuresis precipitating hypovolaemia and thrombosis in an intravascularly depleted child Injury to the glomerular filtration barrier, particularly the podocytes and their slit diaphragms, increases permeability to plasma proteins, producing heavy albuminuria. In minimal change disease, light microscopy is near-normal and electron microscopy shows diffuse podocyte foot process effacement, implicating a circulating permeability factor and immune dysregulation. Urinary protein loss lowers serum albumin, reducing plasma oncotic pressure and, together with secondary sodium retention, causing oedema. The liver increases lipoprotein synthesis in response to low oncotic pressure, producing hyperlipidaemia. Loss of immunoglobulins and complement factors predisposes to infection, and loss of anticoagulant proteins with raised procoagulants predisposes to thrombosis. Children with steroid-sensitive minimal change disease generally have a good long-term renal outcome despite frequent relapses; steroid resistance, often from focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, carries a higher risk of progression to chronic kidney disease.

Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care — Neurologic critical care, Neurocritical care disorders, ICU neurologic complications Diffuse/metabolic encephalopathy: organ failure (hepatic, renal), drug overdose, sedative/analgesic effect, electrolyte disturbance (hyponatremia, hypoglycemia), hypoxia-ischemia, hypercarbia Focal/structural lesions: ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke, traumatic brain injury with intracranial hematoma, tumor, abscess, subdural/epidural hematoma Basilar artery thrombosis causing brainstem ischemia (may mimic generalized seizures with extensor posturing) Nonconvulsive status epilepticus presenting as unexplained decreased consciousness Wernicke's disease in any disoriented at-risk patient Sepsis-associated encephalopathy Bacterial meningitis presenting as global encephalopathy Encephalitis (including herpes simplex virus in immunosuppressed transplant patients) CNS opportunistic infection in transplant patients (Nocardia, Toxoplasma, aspergillosis, CMV, HHV-6, varicella, JC virus PML) Noncontrast CT as the initial study for hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, and tissue shifts; hyperdense basilar artery sign suggests thrombus MRI including diffusion-weighted imaging for acute ischemic stroke and laminar cortical injury after hypoxia-ischemia CT/MR angiography or venography for arterial occlusion or cerebral venous thrombosis EEG to detect nonconvulsive status epilepticus and characterize metabolic slowing or burst-suppression/myoclonic status Lumbar puncture to exclude infection/inflammation (after neuroimaging in coma); elevated opening pressure may indicate venous sinus thrombosis ICP monitoring (ventriculostomy preferred as it allows CSF drainage; parenchymal device for small ventricles or coagulopathy) Serum electrolytes (especially sodium, calcium), glucose, renal and hepatic function, CBC, coagulation studies; toxicology screen in unexplained encephalopathy Somatosensory evoked potentials (N20) and neuron-specific enolase for post-arrest prognostication Carboxyhemoglobin measurement for suspected carbon monoxide poisoning Bubble study (agitated saline echocardiography) to evaluate right-to-left shunt after embolic infarction in transplant patients Sedative/analgesic or polypharmacy-induced delirium misattributed to depression Postcardiac bypass microembolic encephalopathy Calcineurin inhibitor (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) neurotoxicity / PRES, possible even at normal drug levels Checkpoint inhibitor immune encephalitis and CAR-T neurotoxicity Posthypoxic myoclonus / myoclonic status epilepticus after cardiac arrest Korsakoff amnestic state evolving from Wernicke's disease Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) equals mean arterial pressure (MAP) minus intracranial pressure (ICP); the general targets in neurocritical care are ICP below 20 mmHg and CPP at or above 60 mmHg (Harrison 22e p.2345). Cerebral autoregulation normally keeps cerebral blood flow constant across a wide MAP range, but in severe brain injury it can be lost, making flow directly pressure-dependent so that hypotension causes ischemia and hypertension causes hyperperfusion (Harrison 22e p.2343-2344). Cerebral blood flow rises with hypercapnia/acidosis and falls with hypocapnia/alkalosis, which is the basis for short-term hyperventilation to lower ICP; the effect is short-lived (hours) due to interstitial buffering, and abrupt discontinuation can cause rebound ICP elevation (Harrison 22e p.2344, p.2345). In altered consciousness, the first task is to separate a diffuse/metabolic process from a focal/structural one; prominent focal signs such as pupillary asymmetry, hemiparesis, gaze palsy, or visual field deficit suggest a structural lesion and mandate urgent neuroimaging (Harrison 22e p.2344). After cardiac arrest, poor-prognosis indicators include absent pupillary light reflex or extensor/absent motor response to pain at days 5-7, bilateral absence of the N20 somatosensory evoked potential component, a burst-suppression or nonreactive EEG, and a markedly elevated neuron-specific enolase (NSE), but sedation, metabolic derangements, and hypothermia confound these signs (Harrison 22e p.2346). Osmotic demyelination syndrome (formerly central pontine myelinolysis) is typically precipitated by rapid correction of hyponatremia or hyperosmolar states, presenting days later with quadriplegia and pseudobulbar palsy; corrective sodium changes should be limited to roughly 8 mmol/L per 24 h and 15 mmol/L per 48 h (Harrison 22e p.2348-2349). Wernicke's disease is a thiamine-deficiency emergency; only about one-third of patients show the classic triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and global confusion, and IV glucose can precipitate or worsen it, so thiamine must precede glucose in at-risk patients (Harrison 22e p.2349). Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) reflects hyperperfusion/vasogenic edema favoring posterior (occipital) regions; the rate of blood pressure rise rather than the absolute value is the key risk factor, and the syndrome is not always reversible or strictly posterior (Harrison 22e p.2349-2350). Sepsis-associated encephalopathy is a diffuse brain dysfunction without focal findings, occurs in the majority of patients with sepsis and multiorgan failure, and is not simply explained by metabolic derangements; cytokines such as TNF and interleukins are implicated (Harrison 22e p.2348). Critical illness polyneuropathy is the most common PNS complication of prolonged critical illness and sepsis; it is a distal axonal sensorimotor neuropathy and should be suspected when a patient fails to wean from the ventilator despite resolving sepsis (Harrison 22e p.2351). Persistent neuromuscular junction weakness in the ICU is almost always drug-related, most often from nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents (pancuronium, vecuronium, rocuronium, cisatracurium) and potentiated by aminoglycosides; recovery is full once the drug is cleared (Harrison 22e p.2351-2352). In PNS weakness, intubation should be considered when maximal inspiratory force falls below -25 cmH2O or vital capacity is under 1 L, and the decision should be clinical rather than waiting for oxygen desaturation or CO2 retention (Harrison 22e p.2351). (suggests critical illness neuropathy/myopathy or prolonged neuromuscular blockade) Performing lumbar puncture before neuroimaging in a comatose or profoundly encephalopathic patient Delaying empiric antibiotics for suspected bacterial meningitis while awaiting diagnostic studies Attributing the hypoactive confusional state of microembolic encephalopathy after cardiac surgery to depression or sedative delirium Giving IV glucose before thiamine in malnourished/alcoholic patients, precipitating or worsening Wernicke's disease Correcting hyponatremia too rapidly and triggering osmotic demyelination syndrome Assuming normal serum calcineurin inhibitor levels exclude drug-induced PRES or neurotoxicity Prolonged or unmonitored use of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers leading to persistent blockade or thick-filament myopathy (use lowest effective dose with peripheral nerve stimulator monitoring) Using glucocorticoids for ICP in head trauma or ischemic/hemorrhagic stroke, where they are not indicated (reserved for vasogenic edema from tumor or abscess) Sustained or aggressive hyperventilation, which can worsen cerebral ischemia and cause rebound ICP on discontinuation Life-threatening neurologic illness in the critically ill arises from primary lesions anywhere along the neuraxis or as a consequence of systemic disorders (hepatic failure, multiorgan failure, cardiac arrest). The unifying goal is preventing secondary brain injury from ischemia, hemorrhage, edema, herniation, and elevated ICP. Brain edema is vasogenic (fluid crossing an incompetent blood-brain barrier) and/or cytotoxic (cellular swelling and death); clinically significant edema usually combines both and can raise ICP and cause tissue shifts. Inadequate oxygen/glucose delivery triggers the ischemic cascade: excitatory amino acid (glutamate) release, calcium and sodium influx, protease/lipase activation, lipid peroxidation, free-radical membrane injury, cytotoxic edema, and necrotic cell death; an alternative apoptotic pathway occurs without edema and is often not seen on imaging. Penumbra denotes still-salvageable ischemic tissue. Secondary insults (hypotension, hypoxia, fever, seizures, hyperglycemia) worsen the cascade. The skull tolerates little added volume, so once intracranial compliance is exhausted, small volume increases sharply raise ICP, lower CPP, and provoke ischemia; ischemia-driven autoregulatory vasodilation can paradoxically further raise blood volume and ICP, creating a vicious cycle. Outcome depends heavily on the underlying disorder and on prevention of secondary injury. After hypoxia-ischemia, recovery may be full if circulation is restored within 3-5 minutes, while longer insults often cause permanent damage; the brain tolerates pure hypoxia better than combined hypoxia-ischemia. Reliable post-arrest prognostication requires sufficient observation time, and hypothermia/sedation delay when predictors become valid; some patients awaken after a week or longer, so premature withdrawal risks a self-fulfilling prophecy. Sepsis-associated encephalopathy carries roughly 50% mortality when severe enough to cause coma, though this mainly reflects underlying illness severity; the encephalopathy usually improves substantially with successful treatment, but long-term cognitive dysfunction is increasingly recognized, especially in older survivors. Critical illness polyneuropathy and thick-filament critical illness myopathy generally recover spontaneously if the patient survives, though recovery may take weeks to months and some residual weakness can persist. Prolonged neuromuscular blockade causes no permanent damage and resolves once the agent clears. Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 8 or less defines severe traumatic brain injury and is a key criterion for ICP monitoring (Harrison 22e p.2345). Operational neurocritical care targets include ICP below 20 mmHg and CPP at or above 60 mmHg, with stepwise escalation of therapy for sustained ICP above 20-25 mmHg; CAR-T cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity severity track with degree of fever, CRP, and ferritin elevation.

Nervus intermedius neuralgia — intermedius neuralgia, nervus intermedius neuralgia of Wrisberg, facial nerve sensory neuralgia Geniculate neuralgia Glossopharyngeal neuralgia Trigeminal neuralgia Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) Primary otological disease (otitis externa or media) Cerebellopontine angle tumour Referred otalgia from a head and neck malignancy Otoscopy and microscopy to exclude external and middle ear disease MRI of the internal auditory meatus and cerebellopontine angle focused on the facial nerve MR angiography to detect a compressive vascular loop Testing of the external auditory canal for a triggerable zone Examination of the pharynx and larynx to exclude referred otalgia from malignancy Audiometry if hearing symptoms accompany the pain Causes brief paroxysms of severe pain felt deep in the ear canal, sometimes radiating to the auricle, soft palate, or over the face A trigger zone in the posterior wall of the external auditory canal is characteristic, with attacks provoked by touching the canal or by swallowing Because the nervus intermedius carries taste, lacrimal, and salivary fibres, attacks may be associated with altered taste, lacrimation, or salivation It is closely related to, and often used synonymously with, geniculate neuralgia, both reflecting neuralgia of the sensory division of the facial nerve A varicella-zoster (herpetic) origin is recognised and it may follow Ramsay Hunt syndrome Diagnosis requires exclusion of primary ear disease, glossopharyngeal and trigeminal neuralgia, and structural posterior fossa lesions First-line treatment is anticonvulsant medication such as carbamazepine; microvascular decompression or nervus intermedius section is reserved for refractory cases Auricular vesicles with facial weakness suggesting Ramsay Hunt syndrome Persistent unilateral otalgia with a normal ear prompting a search for a head and neck primary A cerebellopontine angle mass on imaging Progressive facial nerve weakness or additional cranial neuropathies Attributing deep-ear pain to primary ear disease when the ear is normal Not distinguishing it from, or conflating it with, glossopharyngeal neuralgia Overlooking a herpetic (post-Ramsay Hunt) aetiology Failing to exclude referred otalgia from an occult malignancy Missing a treatable vascular loop or posterior fossa lesion on imaging Nervus intermedius neuralgia is a paroxysmal pain disorder of the nervus intermedius, the sensory and parasympathetic branch of the facial nerve. Its sensory fibres, relaying via the geniculate ganglion, supply a small area of the external auditory canal and auricle, which explains the deep-ear pain. Ectopic, hyperexcitable neural activity, attributed to vascular compression at the root entry zone or to prior herpetic inflammation of the ganglion, generates the lancinating paroxysms. The nerve's parasympathetic and taste functions account for accompanying lacrimation, salivation, and gustatory disturbance during attacks, and its anatomical intimacy with the facial, glossopharyngeal, and trigeminal nerves produces overlapping presentations. The condition is benign but distressing; many patients respond to anticonvulsant therapy, and surgical decompression or sectioning of the nervus intermedius provides relief in selected refractory cases.

biallelic loss-of-function variants in SPINK5, which encodes the serine protease inhibitor LEKTI Classic triad of congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, a specific hair shaft defect (trichorrhexis SPINK5 genetic testing supported by absent LEKTI staining on immunohistochemistry Neonatal hypernatraemic dehydration and thermoregulatory instability from barrier failure Sepsis or recurrent severe skin and systemic infections Failure to thrive and growth faltering Signs of systemic toxicity from absorbed topical agents (particularly calcineurin inhibitors) Misdiagnosing it as recalcitrant atopic dermatitis and delaying genetic evaluation Applying topical calcineurin inhibitors over large areas of impaired barrier, risking systemic absorption and toxicity Sampling only scalp hair and missing the diagnostic shaft defect best seen in eyebrows Underestimating fluid, electrolyte, and infection risk in the erythrodermic neonate Netherton syndrome results from loss of function of the LEKTI protein, a multidomain serine protease inhibitor expressed in the granular and uppermost spinous layers of the epidermis. Without LEKTI, kallikrein-related peptidases (notably KLK5 and KLK7) are unrestrained, leading to premature and excessive degradation of corneodesmosomes and detachment of the stratum corneum. The result is a profoundly defective epidermal barrier with abnormal desquamation. Unchecked protease activity also drives proinflammatory and pro-allergic signalling, producing the severe atopic phenotype, elevated IgE, and susceptibility to cutaneous infection. It is a lifelong condition; the neonatal period carries the highest mortality risk from dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and infection, after which the phenotype tends to stabilise into ichthyosis linearis circumflexa with persistent atopy, though quality of life and growth remain affected.

Neuroblastoma — neuroblastic tumour Wilms tumour Rhabdomyosarcoma Lymphoma or leukaemic infiltration Phaeochromocytoma Ewing sarcoma / other small round blue cell tumours Hepatoblastoma or other abdominal masses Urinary catecholamine metabolites (HVA and VMA) Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) of the primary site MIBG scintigraphy for functional imaging and metastasis detection Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy for marrow involvement Tumour biopsy for histology and biology including MYCN status Full blood count, renal and liver function, lactate dehydrogenase and ferritin The most common extracranial solid tumour of childhood and the most common malignancy of infancy, arising from primitive sympathetic neural crest cells. It can occur anywhere along the sympathetic chain; the adrenal medulla and paraspinal abdomen are the most frequent primary sites. An abdominal primary often presents as a firm, irregular mass that crosses the midline, distinguishing it from Wilms tumour. Presentation is highly variable and may include systemic upset, bone pain, proptosis with periorbital bruising ('raccoon eyes') from orbital metastases, or a paraspinal mass causing cord compression. Distinctive paraneoplastic features include opsoclonus-myoclonus (dancing eyes, dancing feet) and secretory diarrhoea from vasoactive intestinal peptide. Most tumours secrete catecholamines, so urinary homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) are useful markers. Behaviour spans a remarkable spectrum, from spontaneous regression in infants (including stage MS/4S disease) to aggressive, widely metastatic disease. MYCN amplification is a key adverse biological marker that upstages risk and intensifies therapy. Risk stratification integrating age, stage, histology, and genetics guides treatment ranging from observation or surgery to intensive multimodal therapy. Signs of spinal cord compression from a paraspinal (dumbbell) tumour Rapidly progressive or widely metastatic disease Periorbital bruising and proptosis suggesting orbital metastases Severe secretory diarrhoea from a VIP-secreting tumour Systemic deterioration with bone pain and marrow failure Confusing it with Wilms tumour when it presents as an abdominal mass Missing spinal cord compression from a paraspinal component Overlooking opsoclonus-myoclonus as a paraneoplastic clue to occult tumour Failing to obtain MYCN status, which changes management Assuming all disease is aggressive and over-treating low-risk or regressing tumours Neuroblastoma develops from neural crest-derived precursors of the sympathetic nervous system, giving rise to a spectrum from undifferentiated neuroblastoma to more mature ganglioneuroblastoma and benign ganglioneuroma. Tumour behaviour is strongly governed by biology: MYCN amplification, segmental chromosomal changes, and DNA ploidy correlate with aggressiveness, while some infant tumours undergo differentiation or apoptosis and regress spontaneously. Outcome is extremely variable: low-risk and infant disease (including 4S/MS) often has excellent survival and may regress, whereas high-risk disease with MYCN amplification or widespread metastases has a much poorer prognosis despite intensive therapy.

leptomeningeal melanocytes Management is generic and supportive: neuroimaging surveillance, treatment of hydrocephalus and seizures, and oncological referral if melanoma develops Signs of raised intracranial pressure or rapidly enlarging head circumference New seizures, focal deficit or cranial nerve palsy Developmental regression Any feature suggesting central nervous system melanoma Focusing only on cutaneous naevi and not arranging early MRI in high-risk patients Delaying imaging until after infancy when myelination reduces sensitivity for melanin Attributing hydrocephalus to other causes and missing leptomeningeal melanosis Underestimating the melanoma risk in symptomatic disease Neurocutaneous melanosis results from a post-zygotic activating variant, most commonly in NRAS, occurring in a neural-crest melanocyte precursor early in embryogenesis. The affected clone gives rise both to large or multiple congenital melanocytic naevi in the skin and to an excess of melanocytes that populate the leptomeninges. Proliferation of these leptomeningeal melanocytes can impair cerebrospinal fluid flow, producing hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure, and may undergo malignant transformation into central nervous system melanoma. The shared NRAS driver explains the concurrence of extensive cutaneous pigmentation and intracranial melanocytic disease. Prognosis varies widely: asymptomatic children may remain well, but symptomatic leptomeningeal disease carries a guarded outlook, and the development of central nervous system melanoma is associated with a poor prognosis despite treatment.

Neurocysticercosis — NCC, CNS cysticercosis, cerebral cysticercosis Tuberculoma Cerebral toxoplasmosis Pyogenic or fungal brain abscess Primary or metastatic brain tumour Other parasitic CNS lesions (e.g. hydatid cyst) CNS tuberculosis Toxoplasma encephalitis in immunocompromised patients Primary CNS neoplasm Vasculitic or demyelinating lesions MRI brain to characterise cyst stage, detect a scolex and assess perilesional oedema CT to identify calcified lesions Serological antibody testing (e.g. EITB) as supportive evidence Ophthalmological examination to exclude ocular cysts before therapy CSF studies and assessment for hydrocephalus in suspected extraparenchymal disease Central nervous system infection by larval Taenia solium and one of the leading causes of acquired epilepsy in India and other endemic regions Seizures are the most frequent presentation, typically from a single or few degenerating parenchymal cysts Clinical features depend on cyst number, location and stage, ranging from asymptomatic calcified lesions to disabling neurological disease Extraparenchymal disease (intraventricular, subarachnoid or racemose forms) can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow and cause hydrocephalus, and behaves more aggressively MRI and CT are central to diagnosis; the finding of a cyst with a visible scolex is highly characteristic, and calcified lesions indicate old, dead cysts Antiparasitic therapy is combined with corticosteroids to blunt the inflammatory reaction to dying cysts, with antiseizure medication for those presenting with seizures Treatment must be individualised: viable parenchymal cysts, calcified lesions and intraventricular cysts are managed differently, and some forms need neurosurgical intervention Fundoscopy or ophthalmic assessment is advised before antiparasitic treatment to exclude ocular cysts New-onset or breakthrough seizures, including status epilepticus, requiring urgent management Signs of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus from intraventricular disease, a neurosurgical emergency Rapid neurological deterioration precipitated by inflammation when antiparasitic therapy is started Focal deficits, altered consciousness or signs of stroke from subarachnoid vasculitis Giving antiparasitic drugs without corticosteroid cover, risking severe inflammatory worsening and seizures Treating without first excluding ocular or intraventricular cysts, where drug-induced inflammation is dangerous Assuming all ring-enhancing brain lesions are neurocysticercosis and missing tuberculoma or tumour Overlooking hydrocephalus as a cause of deterioration in extraparenchymal disease Ingested Taenia solium eggs release oncospheres that reach the brain and develop into cysticerci. Viable cysts in the parenchyma may remain quiescent, but immune-mediated degeneration releases antigens that provoke perilesional inflammation and oedema, generating seizures and focal deficits. As cysts die they may calcify, and these calcified foci can remain epileptogenic. In the ventricles and subarachnoid space, cysts and the associated inflammation can block cerebrospinal fluid pathways, producing raised intracranial pressure and hydrocephalus, while subarachnoid (racemose) disease may cause arachnoiditis and vasculitis. Solitary parenchymal cysts often resolve with good seizure control and a favourable outcome, though some patients develop chronic epilepsy from residual calcified lesions. Extraparenchymal, subarachnoid and heavy-burden disease carries a worse prognosis with risk of hydrocephalus, recurrent complications and higher mortality.

high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma with widespread metastases Severe hormonal effects such as refractory hypoglycaemia from an insulinoma Carcinoid heart disease with right-sided valve involvement in metastatic midgut tumours Assuming a normal-appearing indolent tumour is benign and underestimating metastatic potential Failing to prevent carcinoid crisis with somatostatin analogue cover before surgery or interventions Managing high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma as if it were an indolent tumour Overlooking an associated hereditary syndrome that alters surveillance and family screening Neuroendocrine tumours originate from cells of the diffuse neuroendocrine system distributed throughout the body, which share the capacity to synthesise and secrete peptide hormones and biogenic amines. Well-differentiated tumours retain hormone production and receptor expression, including somatostatin receptors that are exploited for imaging and therapy, and generally grow slowly. Functioning tumours produce clinical syndromes through hormone excess, such as serotonin in carcinoid syndrome or insulin, gastrin, and other peptides from pancreatic tumours. Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinomas lose these features and behave aggressively with rapid proliferation and early metastasis. Some tumours occur within hereditary syndromes such as multiple endocrine neoplasia. Prognosis varies widely by grade, differentiation, site, and stage; well-differentiated low-grade tumours can be compatible with prolonged survival even with metastases, whereas poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinomas have an aggressive course and poor outcome.

management is symptomatic Severe or disabling generalised chorea or dystonia Bulbar dysfunction with dysphagia and aspiration risk Status dystonicus in advanced disease Rapid functional decline or new significant cognitive or psychiatric change Diagnosing Huntington disease on clinical grounds without pursuing NBIA imaging and FTL testing when the huntingtin expansion is negative Overlooking a low serum ferritin as a diagnostic clue Failing to obtain iron-sensitive MRI sequences that reveal the deep grey-matter iron and cavitation Not recognising the dominant inheritance and missing the opportunity for family counselling Neuroferritinopathy is caused by dominant variants in FTL, the gene for the ferritin light chain, most commonly small insertions that disrupt the carboxy-terminus of the protein. The abnormal ferritin has impaired capacity to sequester iron safely, so iron and abnormal ferritin aggregates accumulate within neurons and glia, particularly in the basal ganglia and cerebellar dentate nuclei. The resulting iron-mediated oxidative stress and inclusion formation drive progressive neurodegeneration, and advanced disease may lead to tissue cavitation within the affected deep grey-matter structures. The disorder is slowly progressive over years to decades, with worsening movement disorder and eventual loss of independence, although cognition is often comparatively spared. Prognosis and rate of progression vary between affected individuals and families.

Neurofibromatosis — NF1, NF2, von Recklinghausen disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, neurofibromatosis type 2 Legius syndrome (cafe-au-lait macules without neurofibromas) McCune-Albright syndrome Schwannomatosis Constitutional mismatch repair deficiency Multiple lipomatosis Clinical assessment against established diagnostic criteria, supported by NF1 or NF2 molecular testing when needed Ophthalmological examination including slit-lamp for Lisch nodules and optic pathway assessment Magnetic resonance imaging for suspected central or peripheral nervous system tumours Blood pressure monitoring for hypertension including phaeochromocytoma and renal artery stenosis Audiological evaluation and brain imaging for suspected NF2 Neurofibromatosis type 1 is diagnosed clinically using criteria that include multiple cafe-au-lait macules, skinfold freckling, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, optic pathway glioma, characteristic bony lesions, and an affected first-degree relative Cafe-au-lait macules and axillary or inguinal freckling are usually the earliest features in NF1 Optic pathway gliomas are a recognised childhood complication and warrant ophthalmological and imaging surveillance Plexiform neurofibromas can be disfiguring and carry a risk of malignant transformation Neurofibromatosis type 2 is distinct, typically presenting with bilateral vestibular schwannomas causing hearing loss, tinnitus, and balance problems NF1 is caused by mutations in the NF1 gene encoding neurofibromin, a tumour suppressor regulating RAS signalling; NF2 involves the NF2 gene encoding merlin Both are autosomal dominant with high penetrance, variable expressivity, and a high de novo mutation rate Learning difficulties, hypertension, and skeletal complications such as scoliosis are common in NF1 New or rapidly enlarging, painful, or firm masses suggesting malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour and needing urgent evaluation Visual changes indicating optic pathway glioma progression Hypertension that may reflect phaeochromocytoma or renovascular disease Progressive hearing loss or neurological signs from vestibular schwannomas or other tumours in NF2 Attributing multiple cafe-au-lait macules alone to NF1 without considering mimics such as Legius syndrome Failing to institute malignancy surveillance for changing plexiform neurofibromas Overlooking hypertension and its treatable secondary causes Missing NF2 in a young adult with unilateral or bilateral hearing loss Neurofibromatosis type 1 is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NF1 gene, which encodes neurofibromin, a GTPase-activating protein that downregulates RAS signalling; loss of neurofibromin increases RAS-pathway activity and predisposes to tumour formation in neural crest-derived tissues. Neurofibromatosis type 2 results from mutations in the NF2 gene encoding merlin (schwannomin), another tumour suppressor, leading characteristically to schwannomas and meningiomas. Both disorders are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner but frequently arise de novo, and tumour development typically follows a second somatic hit inactivating the remaining normal allele, consistent with the two-hit tumour suppressor model. Most people with NF1 have a good quality of life, but morbidity and reduced life expectancy relate to tumour complications, particularly malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours and vascular disease; NF2 prognosis depends on the burden and location of nervous system tumours.

Neurofibromatosis type 2 — NF2, NF2-related schwannomatosis, merlin deficiency, central neurofibromatosis, bilateral vestibular schwannoma syndrome Neurofibromatosis type 1 Schwannomatosis (SMARCB1/LZTR1) without vestibular tumours Sporadic unilateral vestibular schwannoma Multiple meningiomatosis without NF2 Von Hippel-Lindau disease (other inherited tumour predisposition) Meningioma predisposition from prior cranial irradiation Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain (including internal auditory meati) and whole spine Molecular genetic testing of the NF2 gene, with tumour testing where mosaicism is suspected Pure-tone audiometry and speech discrimination testing with serial monitoring Brainstem auditory evoked responses to assess auditory pathway function Ophthalmological examination for juvenile cataract and retinal lesions Baseline neurological and dermatological assessment for schwannomas and skin tumours The hallmark of the condition is bilateral vestibular schwannomas, which typically present with progressive sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance in adolescence or early adulthood It is a distinct disorder from neurofibromatosis type 1: NF2 is dominated by schwannomas, meningiomas, and ependymomas rather than the neurofibromas, café-au-lait macules, and Lisch nodules of NF1 Additional tumours include cranial and spinal meningiomas, spinal and peripheral nerve schwannomas, and intramedullary or cauda equina ependymomas A characteristic ophthalmological clue is juvenile posterior subcapsular or cortical cataract, which may predate tumour diagnosis The disorder is caused by loss-of-function variants in the NF2 tumour suppressor gene, which encodes merlin (schwannomin); it is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern but a large proportion of cases are de novo and mosaicism is common Management is delivered through specialist multidisciplinary teams, using serial MRI surveillance of the brain and spine and audiological monitoring Treatment prioritises hearing preservation; the anti-VEGF agent bevacizumab can shrink vestibular schwannomas and improve hearing in selected cases, alongside microsurgery, stereotactic radiosurgery, and auditory implantation Rapidly progressive hearing loss or brainstem compression from an enlarging vestibular schwannoma New or worsening myelopathy or radiculopathy from spinal tumours Raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus from large posterior fossa lesions Facial nerve dysfunction or lower cranial nerve palsies indicating local tumour progression Mislabelling the disorder as NF1 and expecting neurofibromas and café-au-lait macules rather than schwannomas and meningiomas Treating a young person's vestibular schwannoma as sporadic and failing to image the contralateral side and spine Overlooking mosaicism, which can give falsely reassuring blood genetic testing and complicate counselling Delaying referral to a specialist centre, where hearing-preservation and multidisciplinary planning materially affect outcome The disorder results from inactivating germline variants in the NF2 gene on chromosome 22, which encodes merlin (also called schwannomin), a cytoskeletal linker protein that normally suppresses cell proliferation by regulating contact inhibition and several growth-signalling pathways. Loss of functional merlin, following a second somatic hit in Schwann cells, meningeal cells, and ependymal cells, removes this brake and predisposes to multiple nervous-system tumours. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with high penetrance, though many patients harbour de novo variants and somatic mosaicism, which influences severity and the recurrence risk offered during counselling. The condition is chronic and progressive, with morbidity driven by cumulative tumour burden, hearing loss, and the risks of surgery near critical neural structures. Early diagnosis, expert multidisciplinary surveillance, and hearing-preservation strategies have improved outcomes, but the disorder shortens life expectancy on average and disease is generally more aggressive when it presents in childhood.

(BPH, stricture) Diabetic cystopathy Cauda equina syndrome Multiple sclerosis or other demyelinating disease Spinal cord injury or compression Pelvic surgery-related denervation Video-urodynamic studies to assess detrusor pressure, compliance, and sphincter coordination Renal function tests and upper tract imaging (ultrasound) to monitor for hydronephrosis Post-void residual measurement Urinalysis and culture for infection surveillance Neurological evaluation and imaging directed at the underlying condition Periodic surveillance for bladder stones and, where relevant, malignancy in long-term catheterised patients Neurogenic bladder describes bladder dysfunction due to disease or injury of the nervous system, with the pattern depending on the level of the neurological lesion Suprapontine and suprasacral (upper motor neuron) lesions typically cause a spastic, overactive detrusor, often with detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, whereas sacral or peripheral (lower motor neuron) lesions cause a flaccid, areflexic, poorly emptying bladder Common causes include spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, spina bifida, diabetes mellitus, Parkinson's disease, stroke, and cauda equina lesions The paramount goal of management is protection of the upper urinary tracts, because high storage pressures and detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia can cause hydronephrosis and renal failure Video-urodynamics is central to characterising bladder behaviour, storage pressures, and sphincter coordination to guide safe management Clean intermittent catheterisation is a cornerstone for bladders that do not empty adequately, reducing residual urine and infection risk while preserving the upper tracts Management principles combine measures to lower storage pressure and improve emptying, such as antimuscarinics, intradetrusor botulinum toxin, catheterisation regimens, and, in selected cases, augmentation or diversion surgery Patients are at risk of recurrent urinary infection, stones, and, in high spinal cord injuries, autonomic dysreflexia triggered by bladder distension High detrusor storage pressures or detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia threatening the upper tracts and renal function New or progressive hydronephrosis and rising creatinine Autonomic dysreflexia in high spinal cord injury, a potentially life-threatening emergency triggered by bladder overdistension Urosepsis in an obstructed or poorly draining neurogenic bladder Acute cauda equina syndrome presenting with retention and neurological deficit Focusing on continence while neglecting upper tract protection and storage pressures Failing to recognise and treat detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia Not anticipating autonomic dysreflexia during bladder distension or instrumentation in high spinal injuries Inadequate surveillance for renal deterioration, stones, and infection Treating overactivity with antimuscarinics without ensuring adequate emptying Normal micturition depends on coordinated control between the pontine micturition centre, spinal pathways, and sacral (S2-S4) reflexes governing the detrusor and urethral sphincter. Neurological lesions disrupt this coordination in patterns determined by lesion level. Upper motor neuron lesions above the sacral cord release the sacral reflex from higher inhibition, producing detrusor overactivity and often detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, in which the sphincter contracts against a contracting bladder, generating dangerously high pressures. Lower motor neuron or peripheral lesions abolish the reflex arc, producing an acontractile, flaccid bladder with retention and overflow. Sustained high intravesical pressure and incomplete emptying threaten the upper tracts and predispose to infection and stones. With structured management focused on low-pressure storage, adequate emptying, and regular upper tract surveillance, many patients maintain renal function and continence; neglected high-pressure bladders carry a significant risk of progressive renal impairment and recurrent complications.

Neuroimaging in Neurologic Disorders — Neuroimaging, CT and MRI in neurology, Brain and spine imaging Ring-enhancing lesion: cerebral abscess versus high-grade glioma or metastasis (restricted central diffusion favors abscess) Restricted diffusion in medial temporal lobe: herpes simplex encephalitis versus acute infarction versus other limbic inflammatory processes Multiple low-signal SWI foci: cerebral amyloid angiopathy versus chronic hypertensive microbleeds versus hemorrhagic metastases versus diffuse axonal injury Focal arterial narrowing/wall enhancement: atherosclerosis versus primary CNS vasculitis versus reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome Noncontrast CT for acute hemorrhage, trauma, and acute mental-status change MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging for suspected ischemia, encephalitis, or abscess CT angiography or gadolinium-enhanced/time-of-flight MR angiography for vascular assessment Vessel wall MR imaging to characterize arteriopathies and vasculitis Perfusion CT or perfusion MRI/ASL to assess core versus penumbra and tumor vascularity CT myelography for failed-back syndrome, CSF fistula localization, and meningeal/arachnoid cysts FDG-PET and amyloid/tau PET ligands for oncologic staging and neurodegenerative evaluation Estimated GFR before contrast in at-risk patients MRI is generally more sensitive than CT for lesions of the central and peripheral nervous system, whereas CT is faster and the pragmatic first choice for uncooperative patients and for suspected acute stroke, hemorrhage, or acute intracranial/spinal trauma (Harrison 22e p.3383). Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is the single most sensitive technique for detecting acute cerebral or spinal cord ischemia, with restricted diffusion (high DWI signal) appearing in infarction of less than about 7 days; it also lights up encephalitis, abscess, and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (Harrison 22e p.3383, 3389). CT is superior to MRI for fine osseous detail and is preferred for the initial workup of conductive hearing loss and skull/spine bone lesions, while MRI better detects bone-marrow infiltrative processes that CT may miss (Harrison 22e p.3383). On unenhanced CT, denser structures such as bone or acute blood appear bright (high attenuation), whereas water, air, and soft tissue appear dark; this is why acute hemorrhage and bone are well seen on noncontrast CT (Harrison 22e p.3383-3384). Iodinated contrast highlights vascular structures and blood-brain barrier defects; in the normal CNS only vessels and structures lacking a blood-brain barrier (pituitary, choroid plexus, dura) enhance (Harrison 22e p.3384). Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) is highly sensitive to blood, calcium, and air and is the sequence of choice for microhemorrhages seen in amyloid angiopathy, hypertension, hemorrhagic metastases, traumatic brain injury, and thrombotic states (Harrison 22e p.3387-3388). FLAIR suppresses the bright CSF signal of T2 imaging, improving detection of edematous/water-containing lesions adjacent to CSF spaces such as periventricular plaques and cortical lesions (Harrison 22e p.3387). Gadolinium-based contrast does not cause contrast-induced nephropathy, but linear (group 1/3) agents can cause nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in patients with severe renal impairment; macrocyclic (group 2) agents are far safer and preferred in at-risk patients (Harrison 22e p.3388-3389). Perfusion imaging that shows a region of prolonged mean transit time with preserved cerebral blood volume identifies tissue at risk (ischemic penumbra) that may be salvageable, distinct from infarcted core where blood volume and flow are reduced (Harrison 22e p.3390). CTA and gadolinium-enhanced MRA have largely replaced catheter angiography, which is now reserved for cases needing fine small-vessel detail or planned interventional therapy (Harrison 22e p.3383). Vessel wall MR imaging is a high-resolution technique that interrogates the arterial wall itself and helps distinguish atherosclerosis, primary CNS vasculitis, and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3390). Amyloid PET can be positive in up to about 25% of cognitively normal older adults, so a positive scan does not by itself diagnose Alzheimer disease; tau PET appears more specific (Harrison 22e p.3392). Acute change in mental status, new focal deficit, or head/spine trauma warranting urgent noncontrast CT Suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage (CT then CTA, with lumbar puncture if CT negative) Severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min per 1.73 m2) or dialysis raising concern for nephrogenic systemic fibrosis with linear gadolinium agents Prior severe contrast (anaphylactoid) reaction, with eightfold higher recurrence risk for gadolinium Ferromagnetic implants (some aneurysm clips, non-conditional pacemakers/defibrillators) or ocular metallic foreign body before MRI Suspected spinal block or elevated intracranial pressure before myelography/lumbar puncture Reliance on shellfish or iodine allergy to predict contrast reactions is unreliable; the strongest predictor is a prior contrast reaction (about fivefold risk), plus atopy/asthma and other drug/food allergies (Harrison 22e p.3385). Premedication regimens shorter than 4-5 hours have no demonstrated efficacy and do not guarantee prevention of contrast reactions (Harrison 22e p.3387). Bicarbonate and acetylcysteine have not shown protection over normal saline against contrast-associated AKI in recent meta-analyses (Harrison 22e p.3385). MRA has lower spatial resolution than catheter angiography, is insensitive to slow flow, and may not distinguish near-complete from complete occlusion or detect small-vessel vasculitis/distal vasospasm (Harrison 22e p.3390). Brain gadolinium deposition (dentate nuclei, globus pallidus) occurs even with normal renal/hepatic function, is dose-dependent and greater with linear agents, but to date has no proven neurotoxic histologic correlate (Harrison 22e p.3387-3388). The MR magnet is always on; ferromagnetic missile injuries and torqued implants can be fatal, so rigorous screening of patients and staff is mandatory (Harrison 22e p.3389). Patient motion degrades MRI; uncooperative patients should be sedated or imaged with CT, and children under ~8 years often require monitored anesthesia (Harrison 22e p.3389). Iodinated contrast should be avoided before planned radioactive iodine thyroid therapy because it reduces radioisotope uptake (Harrison 22e p.3387). Neuroimaging techniques exploit differing physical tissue properties. CT reconstructs a cross-sectional map of x-ray attenuation: dense tissue (bone, acute clot) attenuates heavily and appears bright, while water and air appear dark. MRI maps the distribution and relaxation behavior of (mainly hydrogen) protons placed in a strong static magnetic field and excited by radiofrequency pulses; T1 relaxation is the time for ~63% of protons to return toward equilibrium and T2 the time for ~63% to dephase. Manipulating pulse timing (TR and TE) yields T1-weighted images (fat and subacute hemorrhage bright; CSF/edema dark) or T2-weighted images (CSF/edema/demyelination/infarct bright). Gray matter contains roughly 10-15% more water than white matter, providing intrinsic contrast. Pathology such as infarction, abscess, and dense tumor restricts microscopic water motion, producing high DWI signal. Iodinated and gadolinium contrast agents reveal blood-brain barrier breakdown by tumor, infarct, or infection. Flow phenomena underlie MR angiography, and regional changes in oxy/deoxyhemoglobin underlie the BOLD signal of functional MRI (Harrison 22e p.3383-3392). As a diagnostic modality, neuroimaging itself is generally safe. Contrast-associated acute kidney injury from iodinated contrast is rare, usually transient with creatinine returning toward baseline within 1-2 weeks, and most strongly associated with preexisting severe renal insufficiency; gadolinium does not cause it. Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis from linear gadolinium agents in severe renal failure is rare (reported incidence ~0.19-4% in GFR <30) but can be severely disabling with multiorgan fibrosis. Severe allergic reactions are uncommon (~0.04% with nonionic iodinated agents; gadolinium severe reactions exceedingly rare). Radiation-induced malignancy from diagnostic CT is felt to be minimal but is dose-dependent (Harrison 22e p.3384-3389). Contrast-associated acute kidney injury is defined per KDIGO criteria within 48 h of contrast: absolute serum creatinine rise >=0.3 mg/dL (>26.4 micromol/L), a >=50% (>=1.5-fold) increase over baseline, or urine output <=0.5 mL/kg per h for at least 6 h. Renal-risk stratification for contrast uses eGFR, with <30 mL/min per 1.73 m2 carrying the greatest evidence for risk (normal >=90 mL/min per 1.73 m2) (Harrison 22e p.3384-3386).

particularly antipsychotics, or to abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy in Parkinson's disease The cardinal features are hyperthermia, generalised lead-pipe muscular rigidity, altered mental status and autonomic instability Creatine kinase is characteristically markedly elevated, reflecting muscle injury, and rhabdomyolysis with renal failure may follow Onset is typically slow, over days, in contrast to the rapid onset of serotonin syndrome Reflexes are usually normal or reduced (hyporeflexia) with rigidity, unlike the hyperreflexia and clonus of serotonin syndrome Risk factors include high-potency agents, rapid dose escalation, parenteral administration, dehydration and agitation Management is immediate withdrawal of the causative drug (or reinstatement of dopaminergic therapy if withdrawal-related), aggressive cooling, fluids and supportive care Specific pharmacological treatments include dantrolene to reduce muscle rigidity and dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine Severe hyperthermia Rhabdomyolysis with rising creatine kinase and acute kidney injury Autonomic instability with labile blood pressure or arrhythmia Progressive decline in consciousness Respiratory compromise from chest wall rigidity Confusing it with serotonin syndrome and missing the distinguishing slow onset and hyporeflexia Failing to consider it after abrupt withdrawal of Parkinson's medication Overlooking antiemetic dopamine antagonists as a cause Restarting the causative antipsychotic too soon after recovery Attributing hyperthermia and rigidity to infection alone Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is thought to result from acute central dopamine deficiency caused by blockade of D2 dopamine receptors (or by sudden loss of dopaminergic stimulation when Parkinson's medication is stopped). Reduced dopaminergic activity in the hypothalamus impairs thermoregulation, producing hyperthermia, while blockade in the basal ganglia and related motor pathways causes the severe generalised rigidity. The sustained muscle contraction generates heat and causes muscle breakdown with a very high creatine kinase, risking rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury. Loss of central autonomic regulation produces labile blood pressure, tachycardia, diaphoresis and fluctuating consciousness. The slow evolution and the pattern of rigidity with hyporeflexia help distinguish it from serotonin syndrome. With prompt drug withdrawal and intensive supportive care most patients recover over one to two weeks, but the condition can be fatal from hyperthermia, renal failure or cardiorespiratory complications. Cautious, delayed reintroduction of antipsychotics, preferably a lower-potency agent, is needed if treatment must resume.

Neuromyelitis Optica — NMO, NMOSD, Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, Devic's disease, Devic disease Multiple sclerosis (especially opticospinal MS subtype in Asian/African ancestry, which can itself be AQP4-seropositive and represent NMOSD) MOG antibody-associated disease (AQP4-negative cases) Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis Idiopathic or postinfectious transverse myelitis Neurosarcoidosis Systemic autoimmune myelopathy (SLE, Sjögren's syndrome, Behcet's disease) Spinal cord infarction (longitudinally extensive anterior cord syndrome) Viral myelitis (e.g., herpes simplex virus type 2 causing recurrent myelitis) Tuberculous CNS involvement HIV-associated myelopathy Serum AQP4-IgG testing using a cell-based assay (strongly recommended detection method) MOG-IgG testing in AQP4-seronegative patients Spinal cord MRI to demonstrate longitudinally extensive (>=3 segment) gray matter-centered lesions Brain MRI to detect area postrema, periependymal brainstem, diencephalic, or cloud-like hemispheric lesions Optic nerve MRI (T2/gadolinium-enhancing lesion over >half optic nerve length or chiasm) Lumbar puncture for CSF pleocytosis, cell differential, and oligoclonal bands Screening for coexisting systemic autoimmune disease Multiple sclerosis MOG antibody-associated disease Neurosarcoidosis Systemic lupus erythematosus / Sjögren's-associated myelopathy Paraneoplastic optic neuropathy/myelopathy Spinal cord infarction NMO is an aggressive antibody-mediated inflammatory CNS disorder defined by recurrent attacks of optic neuritis and myelitis; the broader term NMOSD captures partial forms and cases with additional CNS involvement (Harrison p.3590). Strongly female-predominant (women:men roughly 9:1), with a mean onset around age 40 but possible at any age (Harrison p.3590). Optic neuritis in NMO can be bilateral and cause severe vision loss, a pattern uncommon in MS; myelitis is often severe, transverse, and longitudinally extensive spanning three or more contiguous vertebral segments (Harrison p.3590). Unlike MS, NMO rarely follows a progressive course; accumulated disability results from attack-related injury rather than progression (Harrison p.3590). Brain MRI is not invariably normal: lesions may involve the area postrema (intractable hiccups or vomiting), hypothalamus (sleep disorder or endocrinopathy), or cerebral hemispheres; large hemispheric lesions can be asymptomatic, show a 'cloud-like' appearance, be non-destructive, and resolve completely (Harrison p.3590). Spinal cord lesions are focal enhancing areas of swelling and tissue destruction over three or more segments and are centered on the gray matter on axial imaging (Harrison p.3590). CSF typically shows greater pleocytosis than MS, sometimes with neutrophils and eosinophils in acute cases, while oligoclonal bands are uncommon (present in fewer than 20% of patients) (Harrison p.3590-3591). A highly specific serum autoantibody against the water channel aquaporin-4 (AQP4) is present in about 90% of patients and is diagnostic when paired with a typical clinical presentation (Harrison p.3590). In a subset of AQP4-negative cases, autoantibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) are found (Harrison p.3591). Up to 40% of NMO patients have a coexisting systemic autoimmune disorder (e.g., SLE, Sjögren's syndrome, p-ANCA vasculitis, myasthenia gravis, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, mixed connective tissue disease) - a feature distinguishing it from MS (Harrison p.3591). Symptomatic onset may follow acute infection with varicella-zoster virus, Epstein-Barr virus, HIV, or tuberculosis; rare cases are paraneoplastic (breast, lung, or other cancers) (Harrison p.3592). Asian and African ancestry populations are disproportionately affected, with the highest reported prevalence in Martinique; among white populations MS is far more common than NMO (Harrison p.3591). Bilateral simultaneous optic neuritis with severe vision loss Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis spanning three or more vertebral segments Intractable hiccups, nausea, or vomiting (area postrema syndrome) Cervical myelitis threatening respiratory failure Acute brainstem or diencephalic syndrome (e.g., symptomatic narcolepsy, hypothalamic dysfunction) Recurrent attacks, since more than half of untreated AQP4-seropositive patients relapse within 1 year Assuming a normal brain MRI excludes NMO - characteristic area postrema, periependymal brainstem, diencephalic, and cloud-like hemispheric lesions can be present (Harrison p.3590). Conflating NMO with MS: bilateral severe optic neuritis, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, marked CSF pleocytosis, and frequent absence of oligoclonal bands favor NMO (Harrison p.3590). Relying on oligoclonal bands, which are present in fewer than 20% of NMO patients (Harrison p.3590-3591). Overlooking that NMO frequently coexists with systemic autoimmune disease, unlike MS (Harrison p.3591). Failing to recognize AQP4-negative disease, where MOG antibodies may be present and where seronegative NMOSD requires both optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive myelitis to meet criteria (Harrison p.3591-3592). NMO is an autoimmune astrocytopathy driven by autoantibodies against the water channel aquaporin-4 (AQP4), which is concentrated on astrocyte foot processes apposed to endothelium and at paranodal regions near nodes of Ranvier. Pathology shows loss of AQP4 staining with antibody and complement deposition, astrocyte cytolysis, thickened vessel walls, demyelination, and inflammation. AQP4 antibodies are likely pathogenic, since passive transfer reproduces disease features in animals; both complement fixation and antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity contribute to astrocyte injury, and TH17 proinflammatory T cells recognizing an immunodominant AQP4 epitope may also participate. A thymic B-cell population that constitutively expresses AQP4 normally interacts with AQP4-specific T cells to maintain tolerance, and impairment of this interaction may contribute. During acute myelitis attacks, CSF levels of IL-6 and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) are markedly elevated, reflecting active inflammation and astrocyte injury (Harrison p.3590-3591). NMO is typically a relapsing disease; a monophasic course occurs in fewer than 10% of patients and is somewhat more likely in AQP4-antibody-negative individuals. Untreated disease is severely disabling: historically about one-third of patients developed respiratory failure from cervical myelitis, and by 8 years roughly 60% were blind and more than half had permanent limb paralysis. AQP4-seropositive patients carry a high relapse risk (more than half relapse within 1 year if untreated). Long-term outcomes have substantially improved with the advent of attack and relapse therapies, with reported 5-year survival rising from about 68-75% around 1999 to 91-98% by 2017 (Harrison p.3590-3591). No formal severity grading; diagnosis follows the 2015 International Consensus Diagnostic Criteria for NMOSD, which stratify by AQP4-IgG status. AQP4-IgG-positive disease requires at least one core clinical characteristic, a positive AQP4-IgG test, and exclusion of alternatives. AQP4-IgG-negative or unknown-status disease requires at least two core characteristics (one of which must be optic neuritis, acute myelitis with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, or area postrema syndrome), dissemination in space, fulfillment of additional MRI requirements, a negative or unavailable AQP4-IgG test, and exclusion of alternatives. Core clinical characteristics: optic neuritis, acute myelitis, area postrema syndrome, acute brainstem syndrome, symptomatic narcolepsy/acute diencephalic syndrome with typical MRI lesions, and symptomatic cerebral syndrome with typical brain lesions (Harrison p.3591, Table 456-1).

cerebellar atrophy Ophthalmological assessment and electroretinography for retinal degeneration, with electron microscopy of tissue where genetics are inconclusive The neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses are a group of inherited, mostly autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorders characterised by accumulation of autofluorescent lipopigment (ceroid and lipofuscin) in neurones and other cells The classical phenotype combines progressive dementia, seizures, myoclonus, motor decline, and (in most childhood forms) visual failure from retinal degeneration Subtypes are classified by causative gene (CLN1-CLN14) and traditionally by age at onset into infantile, late-infantile, juvenile, and adult forms Age at onset guides the differential: for example CLN1 often infantile, CLN2 late-infantile, and CLN3 juvenile (Spielmeyer-Vogt) with early visual loss Ultrastructural inclusion patterns (granular osmiophilic deposits, curvilinear bodies, fingerprint profiles) historically help characterise subtypes Enzyme replacement therapy is available for CLN2 (TPP1) deficiency, making early recognition of that subtype particularly important Diagnosis now rests principally on molecular genetics rather than a genetically heterogeneous group with different onsets and prognoses Delaying genetic testing while relying solely on historical electron microscopy The neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses are lysosomal disorders in which defects in a range of genes disrupt lysosomal degradation and autophagy. Several subtypes involve deficient soluble lysosomal enzymes (such as palmitoyl-protein thioesterase in CLN1 and tripeptidyl peptidase 1 in CLN2), while others affect transmembrane or membrane-associated proteins of the lysosome and endoplasmic reticulum. Impaired turnover leads to intralysosomal accumulation of autofluorescent ceroid-lipofuscin storage material. Neurones, being long-lived and metabolically demanding, are especially vulnerable, and progressive neuronal loss with retinal degeneration produces the characteristic combination of dementia, epilepsy, motor decline, and blindness. Most childhood-onset forms are progressive and life-limiting, leading to dementia, blindness, and loss of motor function, though rate of decline varies by subtype; disease-modifying enzyme replacement can slow progression in CLN2 disease.

intranuclear inclusions within neurones, glia and cells of many other tissues, including the skin. The disorder is generally slowly progressive over years, though the course and rate vary widely between individuals; episodic encephalopathy, accumulating cognitive decline and autonomic involvement contribute to disability, and management is supportive.

Neuropathic pain — nerve pain, neurogenic pain, neuralgia Nociceptive musculoskeletal pain Inflammatory or ischaemic pain Complex regional pain syndrome Fibromyalgia and centralised pain states Myofascial pain syndrome Vascular claudication mimicking limb pain Detailed sensory examination mapping the distribution and testing for allodynia and hyperalgesia Nerve conduction studies and electromyography where a peripheral nerve or root lesion is suspected Screening questionnaires such as DN4 or painDETECT to support recognition Targeted investigation of the underlying cause, for example glycaemic testing, imaging of the spine, or metabolic screening Quantitative sensory testing or skin biopsy for small-fibre assessment in selected cases Neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system and is distinct from nociceptive pain caused by ongoing tissue damage Typical descriptors are burning, shooting, electric-shock, or stabbing pain, often with numbness, and it characteristically maps to a recognisable neuroanatomical distribution Hallmark abnormal sensory findings include allodynia, where a normally non-painful stimulus causes pain, and hyperalgesia, an exaggerated response to a painful stimulus Common causes span diabetic and other polyneuropathies, postherpetic neuralgia, trigeminal neuralgia, radiculopathy, post-stroke central pain, spinal cord injury, and chemotherapy-induced neuropathy Screening tools such as the DN4 or painDETECT can support recognition, but diagnosis rests on history, distribution, and confirmatory sensory examination First-line pharmacological principles favour gabapentinoids, tricyclic antidepressants, and serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, with topical agents for localised pain and opioids generally avoided as first choice A multimodal, multidisciplinary approach combining medication, physical therapy, psychological strategies, and treatment of the underlying cause gives the best results Interventional options such as nerve blocks and neuromodulation may help selected patients with refractory pain Realistic goals centre on partial pain reduction and improved function and sleep rather than complete pain relief Progressive motor weakness, sphincter disturbance, or saddle anaesthesia suggesting cord or cauda equina compression Rapidly worsening deficit implying an evolving compressive or inflammatory lesion Systemic features such as weight loss or night pain raising concern for malignancy or infection New severe pain with fever suggesting an infective or inflammatory neurological process Treating neuropathic pain with conventional analgesics or NSAIDs alone, which are usually ineffective Escalating opioids for a pain type that responds poorly to them and carries dependence risk Missing a serious underlying cause such as cord compression or malignancy Setting an expectation of complete pain relief rather than functional improvement Neglecting the psychological and sleep dimensions that amplify chronic neuropathic pain Neuropathic pain results from maladaptive changes throughout the nervous system after nerve injury or disease. Damaged neurons develop ectopic and spontaneous discharge and altered ion-channel expression, producing peripheral sensitisation. In the dorsal horn, increased excitability, loss of inhibitory interneuron function, and glial activation drive central sensitisation and wind-up. Structural and functional reorganisation extends to the brain, and descending modulatory pathways may shift toward facilitation of pain. These changes together explain the spontaneous pain, allodynia, and hyperalgesia that persist beyond any ongoing tissue injury. Neuropathic pain is often chronic and only partially responsive to treatment, but many patients achieve meaningful reductions in pain intensity and improved function with a structured multimodal approach. Prognosis is better when a reversible underlying cause is identified and treated early.

Neuropathic ulcer — neurotrophic ulcer, mal perforans, trophic ulcer Arterial (ischaemic) ulcer Diabetic foot ulcer with a neuroischaemic component Venous leg ulcer Infected ulcer with underlying osteomyelitis Charcot neuroarthropathy with ulceration Malignant ulcer such as a Marjolin ulcer Plantar callus or verruca without true ulceration Testing of protective sensation with a monofilament and of vibration or quantitative sensory thresholds Ankle-brachial index, toe pressures and duplex to assess perfusion Plain radiograph and MRI to detect osteomyelitis or Charcot changes Wound or deep tissue culture and inflammatory markers if infection is suspected Blood glucose and glycated haemoglobin, vitamin B12 and other tests to identify the cause of neuropathy Nerve conduction studies where the underlying cause is unclear Neuropathic ulcers develop over pressure-bearing areas in patients with sensory, and often autonomic and motor, peripheral neuropathy, where loss of protective sensation allows repetitive unnoticed trauma They are classically painless, punched-out ulcers rimmed by callus, located over weight-bearing sites such as the metatarsal heads, plantar surface and heel, the plantar lesion being termed mal perforans Diabetes mellitus is the commonest cause worldwide, but leprosy, alcohol-related and nutritional neuropathies including B12 deficiency, hereditary sensory neuropathies and tabes dorsalis are also recognised Motor neuropathy causes intrinsic muscle wasting and foot deformity such as clawing and prominent metatarsal heads, which increase focal pressure, while autonomic neuropathy produces dry, fissured skin prone to breakdown Peripheral pulses are usually present and the foot is often warm and well perfused, distinguishing a purely neuropathic from an ischaemic ulcer Assessment includes testing protective sensation with a monofilament and vibration, inspecting for deformity and callus, and evaluating perfusion to detect any coexisting arterial disease Management centres on offloading pressure with total-contact casting, therapeutic footwear or orthoses, regular debridement of callus and wound, infection control and treatment of the underlying cause Charcot neuroarthropathy should be considered in a warm, swollen, deformed neuropathic foot, as it can coexist with or mimic infection Signs of deep infection or osteomyelitis such as the ability to probe to bone, purulent discharge or systemic features A warm, swollen, deformed foot suggesting Charcot neuroarthropathy Spreading cellulitis or systemic sepsis New ischaemic changes indicating superimposed arterial disease Overlooking coexisting arterial disease in an apparently neuropathic ulcer Providing inadequate offloading so the ulcer persists Missing underlying osteomyelitis Confusing Charcot neuroarthropathy with infection or vice versa Failing to investigate non-diabetic causes of neuropathy, or assuming that painlessness excludes serious infection Sensory neuropathy removes the pain that normally prompts a person to offload an injured area, so repetitive mechanical stress at pressure points goes unrecognised and produces callus, subkeratotic haemorrhage and eventual tissue breakdown. Motor neuropathy weakens the intrinsic foot muscles and alters the architecture of the foot, redistributing load onto the metatarsal heads and other prominences and raising focal plantar pressures. Autonomic neuropathy reduces sweating, leaving dry, fissured skin and altering local blood flow through arteriovenous shunting. Together these deficits generate a chronic ulcer over a pressure point that will not heal, and will recur, unless the mechanical load is redistributed. With effective offloading and management of the underlying cause, neuropathic ulcers often heal, but recurrence is high because the neuropathy is usually irreversible, and deep infection can threaten the limb.

Neurosarcoidosis — neurological sarcoidosis, CNS sarcoidosis, sarcoid neuropathy Tuberculous or fungal meningitis CNS lymphoma or leptomeningeal carcinomatosis Multiple sclerosis and other demyelinating disease IgG4-related disease and other granulomatous vasculitides Idiopathic hypertrophic pachymeningitis Neuro-Behcet and neurosyphilis Contrast-enhanced brain and spinal MRI to map meningeal and parenchymal involvement Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, and exclusion of infection and malignancy Serum and CSF angiotensin-converting enzyme with awareness of limited sensitivity and specificity Whole-body imaging such as CT chest and FDG-PET to find accessible extraneural biopsy sites Tissue biopsy demonstrating non-caseating granulomas with special stains and cultures to exclude infection Cranial neuropathy is the commonest presentation, with facial nerve palsy the classic finding, often bilateral Basal meningeal involvement favours the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, causing diabetes insipidus and other endocrine deficits Presentations are protean and include aseptic meningitis, myelopathy, seizures, hydrocephalus, and peripheral neuropathy Only a minority have isolated neurological disease; most have systemic sarcoidosis providing an accessible biopsy target Contrast MRI often shows leptomeningeal enhancement, dural masses, or parenchymal and spinal cord lesions Diagnosis rests on demonstrating non-caseating granulomas while rigorously excluding infection and lymphoma Corticosteroids are first-line, with steroid-sparing immunosuppression and anti-TNF agents for refractory disease Acute hydrocephalus or raised intracranial pressure from meningeal disease Hypothalamic-pituitary failure with hyponatraemia or adrenal insufficiency Rapidly progressive myelopathy with sphincter involvement Diagnostic uncertainty where lymphoma or infection has not been excluded Diagnosing neurosarcoidosis on imaging alone without histological or robust supportive evidence Missing coexisting infection because granulomas can occur in tuberculosis and fungal disease Under-treating and allowing relapse when corticosteroids are tapered too quickly Overlooking neuroendocrine dysfunction in basal meningeal involvement Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disorder in which an exaggerated cell-mediated immune response leads to non-caseating epithelioid granulomas. When the nervous system is affected, granulomatous inflammation tends to concentrate around the basal meninges and perivascular spaces, spreading along Virchow-Robin spaces into brain parenchyma, cranial nerves, the hypothalamic-pituitary region, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. The inflammatory infiltrate and secondary vasculopathy produce the diverse neurological syndromes seen, and chronic meningeal involvement can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow to cause hydrocephalus. Many patients respond to corticosteroids, but the course is often chronic or relapsing and some develop fixed neurological deficits; parenchymal and spinal disease and hydrocephalus carry a less favourable outlook.
