The mutant protein is prone to aberrant conformational change and polymerisation, so that molecules link together and are retained within the endoplasmic reticulum of neurones, forming intracytoplasmic inclusions known as Collins bodies. The resulting protein overload and neuronal dysfunction cause progressive encephalopathy; the extent of polymerisation and inclusion burden, determined by the particular mutation, correlates with the age of onset and disease severity, ranging from a later-onset dementia to an early, severe encephalopathy with epilepsy. The disorder is progressive, and prognosis depends strongly on the mutation, with earlier-onset forms causing severe encephalopathy and epilepsy and later-onset forms a slower dementia; management is supportive, including seizure and myoclonus control and genetic counselling.

neutropenic enterocolitis — typhlitis, neutropenic colitis, ileocaecal syndrome Acute appendicitis Clostridioides difficile / pseudomembranous colitis Ischaemic colitis Cytomegalovirus colitis Gastrointestinal graft-versus-host disease Intra-abdominal abscess Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome) Full blood count confirming neutropenia and assessing platelets Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis Blood cultures Stool for Clostridioides difficile toxin and enteric pathogens Serum lactate and venous blood gas Coagulation screen Serial abdominal examination with erect and supine abdominal radiographs if perforation is suspected A necrotising inflammation of the caecum and right colon (typhlitis) occurring in profound neutropenia, classically after intensive chemotherapy for acute leukaemia and in the post-transplant setting. The characteristic clinical triad is fever, right iliac fossa pain and neutropenia, often with watery or bloody diarrhoea, nausea and abdominal distension. CT of the abdomen is the imaging modality of choice, showing circumferential bowel-wall thickening (typically greater than four millimetres), caecal distension, pericolic fat stranding and, in severe disease, pneumatosis intestinalis. Colonoscopy and contrast enema should be avoided because of the high risk of perforation in inflamed, friable, neutropenic bowel. Management is predominantly conservative: bowel rest, nasogastric decompression if obstructed, intravenous fluids, and broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-negative organisms and anaerobes, with antifungal cover added for persistent fever. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and correction of thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy support recovery, which closely tracks neutrophil count recovery. Surgery is reserved for defined indications: free perforation, uncontrolled gastrointestinal haemorrhage, persistent obstruction, or clinical deterioration despite maximal medical therapy. Distinguish from Clostridioides difficile colitis and acute appendicitis, and continue treatment until both symptoms resolve and neutropenia recovers, as relapse can occur with subsequent chemotherapy cycles. Peritonitis or radiological free intraperitoneal air Significant gastrointestinal haemorrhage Haemodynamic instability or septic shock Pneumatosis intestinalis on imaging Rising lactate or persistent deterioration despite therapy Performing colonoscopy or contrast enema and precipitating perforation Delaying broad-spectrum antibiotics while awaiting imaging or cultures Operating for presumed appendicitis when conservative management is appropriate Failing to add antifungal cover for persistent fever Stopping treatment once the patient is afebrile while still neutropenic Chemotherapy-induced mucosal injury combines with profound neutropenia to breach the bowel's defences, most severely in the caecum, whose distensibility and relatively poor blood supply predispose it to injury. Loss of mucosal integrity allows intramural invasion by gut flora—Gram-negative bacilli, anaerobes and fungi such as Candida—producing oedema, transmural inflammation, haemorrhage and necrosis. The absence of an effective neutrophil response permits unchecked bacterial proliferation and translocation, driving bacteraemia and sepsis; progressive wall necrosis may culminate in pneumatosis and perforation. Outcome is closely tied to neutrophil recovery; with prompt supportive care and antimicrobials many patients recover fully. Perforation, uncontrolled haemorrhage or full-thickness necrosis markedly worsen prognosis and carry a high mortality.

treatment of secondary infection, and surgery for troublesome or extensive lesions New-onset or refractory seizures Progressive neurological deficit or developmental regression Recurrent abscess or deep infection within the naevus Progressive scoliosis or skeletal deformity Mistaking the naevus for ordinary acne and missing the segmental hamartomatous pattern Overlooking neurological or skeletal associations in extensive or facial disease Underestimating the tendency to recurrent inflammation and secondary infection Neglecting ophthalmological screening for cataract and anterior-segment anomalies Naevus comedonicus syndrome arises from a post-zygotic mosaic variant, with activating NEK9 variants described, affecting a clone of follicular keratinocytes during embryogenesis. This produces a hamartomatous malformation of the pilosebaceous unit in which rudimentary follicles fail to form normal hair and sebaceous structures and instead retain keratin, giving the characteristic comedo-like plugs distributed along the lines of Blaschko. Secondary inflammation, cyst formation and bacterial infection can complicate the lesion. When the mosaic clone extends to neuroectodermal, ocular and skeletal progenitors, the associated central nervous system, ocular and skeletal malformations of the syndrome develop. The cutaneous lesion is benign but often cosmetically and symptomatically troublesome, and prognosis overall depends on the severity of any neurological, ocular or skeletal involvement, which determines the need for long-term multidisciplinary care.

Naevus depigmentosus — nevus depigmentosus, naevus achromicus, achromic naevus Vitiligo, particularly the segmental type Naevus anaemicus Ash-leaf macule of tuberous sclerosis Hypomelanosis of Ito Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation Pityriasis alba Idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis Wood-lamp examination showing off-white rather than chalky-white change Dermoscopy of the patch Diascopy to exclude naevus anaemicus Examination for other features of tuberous sclerosis or mosaic disorders Skin biopsy only rarely, when the diagnosis is uncertain A congenital or early-onset, well-defined, off-white hypopigmented (not fully depigmented) patch that is stable in relative size and does not progress Often has a serrated or block-like/segmental configuration and remains fixed in its distribution Distinguished from vitiligo, which shows chalky-white complete depigmentation and tends to spread, and in which Wood-lamp accentuation is far more stark Differentiated from naevus anaemicus, a vascular anomaly that vanishes with diascopy and lacks true pigment loss Reflects a functional melanocyte defect with normal or slightly reduced melanocyte numbers but impaired melanosome transfer It is benign; management is reassurance, with cosmetic camouflage and photoprotection of the pale area if desired The patch grows in proportion to the child rather than extending independently Multiple ash-leaf macules or other features suggesting tuberous sclerosis Segmental depigmentation that is spreading, raising the possibility of vitiligo An extensive whorled or streaky pattern with systemic features suggesting hypomelanosis of Ito Misdiagnosing it as vitiligo, or vice versa Overlooking tuberous sclerosis when hypopigmented macules are multiple Confusing it with naevus anaemicus by omitting diascopy Attempting active repigmentation of a stable developmental lesion Naevus depigmentosus is a mosaic developmental defect in which melanocytes are present in normal or slightly reduced numbers but function abnormally, with defective melanosome formation and impaired transfer of melanosomes to keratinocytes. Melanin is therefore reduced rather than absent, producing hypopigmentation rather than the complete depigmentation of vitiligo. Because it is a fixed developmental anomaly, the lesion remains stable throughout life. The lesion is benign, stable and permanent, enlarging only in proportion to body growth, and carries no health risk beyond its cosmetic effect.

Naevus of Ito — nevus of Ito, naevus fuscoceruleus acromiodeltoideus, acromiodeltoid dermal melanocytosis Mongolian spot (congenital dermal melanocytosis) Naevus of Ota Blue naevus Bruise or resolving haematoma Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation Congenital melanocytic naevus Dermoscopy to confirm the dermal melanocytic pattern Full skin examination to detect a coexisting naevus of Ota Serial photography to monitor stability Wood-lamp examination to confirm the pigment is dermal Biopsy of any nodular or atypical area to exclude melanoma Blue-grey dermal melanocytic pigmentation over the shoulder, supraclavicular, scapular and deltoid region, following the posterior supraclavicular and lateral brachial cutaneous nerves Analogous to naevus of Ota but affecting the shoulder girdle rather than the face, and without ocular involvement May coexist with an ipsilateral naevus of Ota in the same individual The pigment is dermal, so it shows no Wood-lamp accentuation and topical agents are ineffective More common in Asian populations and in females Pigment-specific laser is the mainstay of treatment where cosmetic improvement is desired Malignant transformation is very rare but has been reported, so persistent change warrants review Development of a nodule or focal change suggesting melanoma Rapid growth or ulceration within the lesion New symptoms such as bleeding or persistent tenderness Mistaking the blue-grey patch for a persistent bruise Attempting to treat dermal pigment with topical lightening agents Failing to look for a coexisting naevus of Ota Overlooking a rare melanoma developing within the naevus As in naevus of Ota, the lesion results from melanocytes of neural crest origin that fail to complete their migration to the epidermis and remain within the dermis. Naevus of Ota — nevus of Ota, oculodermal melanocytosis, naevus fuscoceruleus ophthalmomaxillaris Mongolian spot (congenital dermal melanocytosis) Naevus of Ito Blue naevus Melasma Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation Minocycline or other drug-induced pigmentation Congenital melanocytic naevus Ophthalmic examination with intraocular pressure and glaucoma screening Dermoscopy to characterise the dermal pigment pattern Serial photography to monitor for change Biopsy of any nodular or clinically suspicious area to exclude melanoma Neuroimaging if leptomeningeal melanosis or neurological features are suspected Unilateral, mottled blue-grey to brown pigmentation in the distribution of the ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) divisions of the trigeminal nerve Frequently involves the sclera, conjunctiva and other ocular structures (oculodermal melanocytosis), and ipsilateral glaucoma can develop, so ophthalmology review is important More common in individuals of Asian and African descent and in females; it may be present at birth or first appear around puberty The pigment is dermal, so it is not accentuated by Wood lamp and topical lightening agents are ineffective Pigment-specific Q-switched or picosecond lasers are the treatment of choice for the cutaneous component Rarely, melanoma may arise within cutaneous, uveal or leptomeningeal melanocytes, so new nodules or visual change require prompt assessment Bilateral involvement is uncommon but recognised and warrants consideration of associated conditions A new nodule, thickening or focal change suggesting cutaneous or uveal melanoma Rising intraocular pressure or visual disturbance indicating glaucoma Neurological symptoms raising concern for leptomeningeal melanocytosis Rapid extension or ulceration of the pigmented area Overlooking the need for ophthalmic review and glaucoma screening Attempting to treat the dermal pigment with topical lightening agents Missing an evolving melanoma within the lesion or eye Confusing it with a Mongolian spot or acquired melasma During embryogenesis melanocytes derived from the neural crest normally migrate to the epidermis, but in naevus of Ota some are arrested within the dermis. These entrapped, melanin-producing dermal melanocytes scatter light to give a characteristic blue-grey (Tyndall) hue, and their distribution follows the ophthalmic and maxillary trigeminal branches. The same melanocytic population can involve ocular tissues, accounting for scleral pigmentation and the associated glaucoma and, rarely, melanoma risk. The naevus is benign and persists lifelong if untreated, with good cosmetic improvement achievable using pigment-specific lasers; the main long-term concerns are glaucoma and a small risk of ocular or cutaneous melanoma.

Naevus sebaceus of Jadassohn — nevus sebaceus, naevus sebaceus, sebaceous naevus, organoid naevus Aplasia cutis congenita Juvenile xanthogranuloma Epidermal (keratinocytic) naevus Solitary mastocytoma clinical surveillance, and consideration of complete excision where there is cosmetic concern or a suspicious secondary growth New nodule, ulceration or bleeding within the plaque suggesting a secondary malignancy Rapid change in a long-stable lesion Extensive lesions with seizures or developmental delay indicating a neurocutaneous syndrome Ocular or skeletal anomalies in association with a large naevus Assuming any secondary growth is malignant when benign trichoblastoma is far more common Failing to reassess a lesion that changes in adulthood Not screening for systemic involvement when the naevus is extensive Excising purely for a low malignancy risk without discussing that benign tumours predominate Naevus sebaceus of Jadassohn is a mosaic organoid hamartoma resulting from a post-zygotic activating variant in the RAS-MAPK pathway, most often HRAS and occasionally KRAS, arising in an epidermal progenitor during development. The affected clone produces disordered overgrowth of the epidermis together with sebaceous glands, abortive hair follicles and apocrine structures, giving the lesion its organoid character and its distribution along the lines of Blaschko. Persistent RAS-pathway activation drives the pubertal thickening of the lesion and predisposes to the development of secondary benign and, less commonly, malignant appendageal tumours over the patient's lifetime. Isolated naevus sebaceus has an excellent prognosis; the main long-term consideration is the modest risk of secondary tumours, predominantly benign, so periodic surveillance or elective excision is reasonable, while extensive lesions require assessment for associated syndromic disease.

phenotype A postural component suggesting a cerebrospinal-fluid-pressure disorder Papilloedema, visual symptoms or pulsatile tinnitus Focal neurological deficit, seizures or a thunderclap onset Age over fifty with scalp tenderness or jaw claudication Fever, neck stiffness or immunocompromise Accepting the diagnosis without excluding cerebrospinal-fluid-pressure disorders or venous thrombosis Overlooking giant cell arteritis in an older patient Allowing medication-overuse headache to develop during treatment Assuming a migrainous phenotype rules out a secondary cause The mechanism of new daily persistent headache is unclear. Proposed contributors include a post-infectious or post-inflammatory state with persistent cytokine activation, cervical or ligamentous factors, and disordered central pain processing. Because the abrupt, unremitting pattern can also be produced by disorders of cerebrospinal fluid pressure or venous drainage, these secondary processes must be excluded before the primary label is applied. Outcome is variable: some patients remit spontaneously over months, while a persisting subgroup proves refractory to preventive treatment; the prognosis is better when a treatable secondary cause is identified.

Nicotine Addiction — Tobacco dependence, Tobacco use disorder, Nicotine dependence, Cigarette addiction Other substance use disorders (alcohol use disorder, stimulant use) Caffeine use/dependence Primary mood or anxiety disorders presenting with cravings or restlessness Cannabis use via vaping devices (refillable pods may aerosolize marijuana oils) Structured history of total daily frequency of all nicotine products used (cigarettes, cigars, roll-your-own, vaping, oral pouches/snuff) Duration of regular use, prior quit experiences, and current interest in quitting Markers of addiction intensity: episodes per day, spacing through the day, and use within 30 minutes of waking Biomarkers of smoke-toxicant exposure (markedly lower in exclusive e-cigarette users than in cigarette smokers) Withdrawal-related irritability and restlessness mimicking primary anxiety or depressive disorders Chronic cough from smoking-related mucous hyperplasia mimicking other causes of chronic productive cough Addiction is established when nicotine in any form (combusted or heated tobacco, oral pouches, or vaped nicotine/nicotine salt) is used with sufficient intensity for a sufficient duration; addicted users self-titrate the frequency and intensity of use to achieve psychoactive effects and avoid withdrawal. The diagnosis is clinical and hinges on loss of control over the next use of a nicotine product, evidenced by daily use, high number of episodes per day, use shortly after waking, craving during abstinence, and prior failed quit attempts. The clinically important metric is the cumulative frequency of any nicotine dosing across all products used, not the specific product source, because it is dosing frequency that creates and sustains addiction. Nicotine itself causes relatively little disease (notably pregnancy complications); the majority of disease burden comes from repetitive exposure to the carcinogens and toxicants carried with nicotine in various products, which addiction drives by compelling multiple daily exposures. Withdrawal symptoms intensify with longer abstinence as blood nicotine falls and detaches from receptors, and these symptoms can persist for roughly 4-6 weeks. Acidic aerosols (cigarettes and nicotine salt vaping devices) reduce airway irritation, permit deep inhalation, and produce rapid arterial nicotine rises reaching the brain, making them more addictive than products with slower delivery. Cancer risk rises linearly with the number of cigarettes per day and logarithmically with duration of smoking; relative risk of lung cancer in current smokers ranges roughly 13-28 across age groups. Cigarette smoking accounts for about 80% of COPD, about 90% of peripheral vascular disease in nondiabetics, about 50% of aortic aneurysms, about 24% of coronary artery disease, and about 11% of strokes. Smoking induces the cytochrome P450 system, which can lower serum levels of drugs such as warfarin; conversely, levels may rise during hospitalization when a patient stops smoking, an important consideration for narrow-therapeutic-index agents. About 40% of cigarette smokers die prematurely from smoking unless they quit; the population still smoking has shifted toward socially disadvantaged groups, and prevalence has declined more slowly in those over 40 who are most likely to develop disease. 'Lower tar/nicotine' filtered cigarettes do not reduce real exposure because smokers compensate by altering puffing behavior or number smoked; ventilation-hole designs lower only machine-measured yields, not delivered toxicants. Several genes are associated with nicotine addiction (some reducing nicotine clearance, others increasing dependence likelihood or depression risk), but the large declines in smoking since the mid-1950s indicate non-genetic factors dominate population trends. Continued smoking during chemotherapy or radiation, associated with poorer outcomes and reduced survival Smoking in pregnancy: premature rupture of membranes, abruptio placentae, placenta previa, preterm delivery, small-for-gestational-age, increased perinatal mortality and sudden infant death syndrome Dual use of e-cigarettes and combusted cigarettes, which negates toxicant-reduction benefits High-frequency use of noncombusted inhaled nicotine products in patients who never used combusted tobacco Multiplicative cardiac risk when smoking is combined with hypertension or elevated lipids Higher vascular graft occlusion rates in smokers after bypass surgery Assuming cigars or pipe tobacco are lower-risk: most cigars are now made like cigarettes and most pipe tobacco is used for roll-your-own, so risks are similar; clinicians should ask about and not recommend them. Treating 'low tar/nicotine' cigarettes as safer; compensatory smoking negates any benefit and design changes have raised adenocarcinoma rates. Focusing only on cigarettes and missing cumulative nicotine intake from vaping, oral pouches, and other products when assessing addiction intensity. Overlooking smoking-induced cytochrome P450 changes when adjusting drug doses around hospitalization or discharge. Dismissing patients not currently interested in quitting; many still attempt cessation in the subsequent year and benefit from a clear personalized message. Equating exclusive e-cigarette use (lower toxicant exposure) with cessation of addiction, since persistent nicotine dependence and relapse risk remain. Nicotine reaching the brain reversibly binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors that are highly active in networks mediating mood, reward, joy, and excitement. With sustained high exposure, nicotinic receptors are upregulated on brain cells, so that for most people daily use is required to maintain the addicted state. As blood nicotine falls between doses, nicotine detaches from receptors and addicted individuals no longer feel 'normal,' producing a compulsive drive for the next dose. The strength and speed of addiction depend on dosing frequency and on the arterial nicotine concentration reaching the brain, which varies by product. Unprotonated (freebase) nicotine, favored at alkaline pH, is absorbed readily across mucosa but is airway-irritating at high concentration; addictive products use mildly acidic aerosols in the mouth to limit irritation and permit deep inhalation, after which alveolar pH shifts toward blood pH (~7.4), rapidly liberating absorbable unprotonated nicotine and driving fast arterial rises to the brain. Cessation produces substantial reversible benefit: risk of a second coronary event falls within 6-12 months, and first myocardial infarction and coronary death rates decline within 2-4 years; after about 15 years of abstinence cardiovascular risk approaches that of never-smokers. Cancer risk declines relative to continued smoking after about 4 years, but a roughly three- to fourfold excess lung cancer risk persists even 20 years after quitting. Small-airway changes in young smokers reverse after 1-2 years of abstinence; in established airflow obstruction cessation mainly slows further decline rather than restoring lung function. Quitting is typically cyclical with multiple attempts: about 70-80% of smokers want to quit and over half try in a given year, but only about 6% remain abstinent at 6 months and about 3% at 2 years; systemwide tracking and assistance can raise 12-month abstinence to as high as 25%. No formal grading is presented; addiction intensity is gauged clinically by cumulative daily dosing frequency across all products, spacing of use through the day, use within 30 minutes of waking, craving during abstinence, and history of failed quit attempts.

Niemann-Pick type C is mechanistically distinct: variants in NPC1 or NPC2 disrupt the intracellular transport of unesterified cholesterol and other lipids out of the late endosomal/lysosomal compartment, leading to lipid accumulation, neuronal dysfunction, and secondary sphingomyelin storage. All forms are inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. Type A is uniformly severe with death typically in early childhood. Type B has a more favourable course with survival into adulthood, though pulmonary and hepatic disease may limit outcomes. Type C is progressive and variable, with age of onset strongly influencing survival; disease-modifying and supportive therapies can slow but not cure neurological decline.

Nipah virus infection — NiV, Nipah encephalitis, Nipah virus disease Japanese encephalitis and other viral encephalitides Herpes simplex encephalitis Cerebral malaria Bacterial or tuberculous meningoencephalitis Scrub typhus with CNS involvement Leptospirosis with meningoencephalitis Autoimmune encephalitis Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis Severe sepsis with encephalopathy RT-PCR of throat/nasal swabs, CSF, urine and blood in a biosafe reference laboratory Nipah-specific IgM and IgG serology by ELISA MRI brain, which may show disseminated small cortical and subcortical lesions CSF examination when safe, typically showing lymphocytic pleocytosis Chest imaging if respiratory involvement is suspected A highly lethal zoonotic paramyxovirus (henipavirus) whose natural reservoir is fruit bats (Pteropus species) In India transmission has been linked to consumption of date-palm sap contaminated by bat secretions and to close contact with infected patients, with documented person-to-person and nosocomial spread Presents as rapidly progressive encephalitis with fever, headache, altered mental status and often prominent brainstem signs; management is supportive with rigorous infection control Strict barrier precautions, patient isolation and contact tracing are essential because human-to-human transmission drives outbreaks It is classified as a priority pathogen of pandemic potential requiring immediate public-health notification Diagnosis uses RT-PCR on respiratory secretions, CSF, urine or blood, and serology (IgM/IgG ELISA), performed in high-containment laboratories Rapidly deteriorating consciousness or brainstem dysfunction signalling life-threatening encephalitis Any respiratory distress raising concern for airborne/droplet transmissibility and severe disease Cluster of cases or contact with a confirmed case, mandating immediate isolation and outbreak response Autonomic instability or seizures requiring critical-care support Failing to institute isolation and barrier precautions early, allowing nosocomial and family transmission Delaying notification to public-health authorities during a suspected cluster Attributing the illness to more common encephalitides and not sending appropriate high-containment testing Underestimating the risk to healthcare workers during aerosol-generating procedures Nipah virus is an enveloped RNA henipavirus that infects endothelium and neurons. After spillover from fruit bats (directly, via contaminated food, or from intermediate hosts such as pigs), the virus causes a systemic vasculitis with endothelial infection, syncytium formation, thrombosis and microinfarction, particularly in the central nervous system. This vasculitic and direct neuronal injury produces the severe encephalitis, while pulmonary endothelial and epithelial infection can cause acute respiratory distress. The capacity of the virus to persist may underlie relapsing or delayed-onset encephalitis in some survivors. Nipah virus disease is one of the most lethal human encephalitides, with case fatality frequently exceeding half of symptomatic cases. Survivors may be left with persistent neurological impairment, and a minority develop relapsing or late-onset encephalitis months to years later.

Nipple adenoma — Florid papillomatosis of the nipple, Erosive adenomatosis of the nipple Paget's disease of the nipple Intraductal papilloma Tubular carcinoma Syringomatous adenoma of the nipple Nipple eczema or dermatitis Subareolar sclerosing duct hyperplasia Squamous cell carcinoma of the nipple Clinical examination of the nipple-areola complex Ultrasound of the retroareolar region Mammography as part of triple assessment Punch or excisional biopsy of the nipple lesion Histopathology with assessment of the myoepithelial layer Immunohistochemistry for myoepithelial markers (p63, smooth muscle myosin) Cytology of any nipple discharge A benign proliferation of the lactiferous ducts within the nipple, presenting as erosion, crusting, ulceration or a palpable nipple nodule. Frequently accompanied by serous or blood-stained discharge from the nipple surface. Clinically and macroscopically mimics Paget's disease of the nipple, making biopsy essential for diagnosis. Failure of an eroded nipple lesion to heal, requiring biopsy to exclude Paget's disease Associated deep breast mass or suspicious microcalcification Blood-stained discharge with atypical cytology Histological loss of the myoepithelial layer suggesting malignancy Coexisting invasive or in situ carcinoma in the specimen Mistaking the lesion for Paget's disease and vice versa without biopsy Misinterpreting the pseudoinfiltrative pattern as tubular carcinoma on histology Treating a persistent eroded nipple as eczema and delaying biopsy Incomplete excision leading to local recurrence Failing to sample the specimen adequately and missing coexistent malignancy Nipple adenoma is a benign tumour arising from the collecting ducts of the nipple, characterised by a compact proliferation of ductal epithelial and myoepithelial cells forming adenotic and papillary structures. The proliferating ductal tissue may erode the overlying epidermis, producing the surface ulceration and discharge that clinically resemble Paget's disease. Retention of a continuous myoepithelial cell layer around the proliferating tubules is the key feature confirming benignity and distinguishing the lesion from invasive carcinoma, although sclerosis and epithelial crowding can create a worrying pseudoinfiltrative appearance. Nipple adenoma is benign and complete excision is curative, with recurrence uncommon and generally attributable to incomplete removal. It carries no intrinsic malignant potential, although rare coexistent carcinoma should be excluded.

Nitrogen narcosis — inert gas narcosis, rapture of the deep, narcosis Oxygen toxicity (central nervous system effects) Carbon dioxide retention (hypercapnia) Hypoxia Contaminated breathing gas (e.g. carbon monoxide) Hypothermia impairing cognition Early decompression illness affecting the nervous system Clinical recognition based on depth and the reversibility of symptoms on ascent Review of the dive profile, depth reached, and breathing gas used Assessment for other causes of impaired consciousness at depth (gas contamination, hypercapnia) Analysis of the breathing gas mixture where contamination is suspected Post-dive neurological assessment to confirm full recovery and exclude decompression illness An impairment of higher mental function caused by the anaesthetic effect of nitrogen breathed under increased pressure at depth Onset and severity increase with depth; effects usually become noticeable at moderate depths and intensify progressively as the diver goes deeper Symptoms resemble alcohol intoxication, with euphoria, impaired judgement and reasoning, slowed reactions, overconfidence, and reduced attention The key feature is that it is fully and rapidly reversible on ascent to shallower depth, leaving no lasting deficit The main danger is behavioural, as impaired judgement at depth can lead to fatal errors rather than direct physiological harm Using helium-based breathing mixtures for deep dives reduces or avoids the narcotic effect Prevention rests on limiting depth, careful dive planning, and adequate training and experience Severe impairment at depth threatening safe diving behaviour Failure of symptoms to resolve fully on ascent, suggesting an alternative diagnosis Concurrent features of oxygen toxicity or gas contamination Loss of consciousness or seizure while diving Underestimating impaired judgement and continuing to descend Attributing narcosis symptoms to another cause and failing to ascend Assuming tolerance develops, when susceptibility remains at depth Overlooking coexisting hypercapnia or gas contamination that worsens narcosis Nitrogen narcosis reflects the anaesthetic action of inert gases dissolved in nervous tissue at raised partial pressure. As a diver descends, the partial pressure of the nitrogen in the breathing gas rises in proportion to depth, and the increasing amount of dissolved nitrogen interferes with neuronal signalling in a manner analogous to inhaled anaesthetics, producing dose-dependent central nervous system depression. Because the effect depends on the gas partial pressure and no structural injury occurs, it resolves promptly and completely once the diver ascends and the partial pressure falls. Nitrogen narcosis is entirely reversible and leaves no residual deficit once the diver ascends; its significance lies in the risk of impaired judgement causing accidents at depth rather than any lasting physiological harm.

Nocardiosis — Nocardia infection, Actinomycetoma (Nocardia) Lymphocutaneous (sporotrichoid) presentation overlaps with Sporothrix schenckii and Mycobacterium marinum infection (p.1360). Mycetoma differential: actinomycetoma (filamentous bacteria, e.g., Nocardia), eumycetoma (fungal), and botryomycosis (cocci/bacilli, often Staphylococcus aureus) are difficult to separate clinically and require granule microscopy, culture, or biopsy (p.1361). Ocular nocardiosis (keratitis, scleritis, endophthalmitis) cannot be distinguished from other ocular infections by signs and symptoms alone (p.1360). Sporothrix schenckii (sporotrichosis) for lymphocutaneous disease Mycobacterium marinum for lymphocutaneous disease Eumycetoma (fungal mycetoma) for actinomycetoma Botryomycosis (often Staphylococcus aureus) for actinomycetoma Other causes of pulmonary nodules/cavitation and ring-enhancing brain lesions in immunocompromised hosts (e.g., fungi, mycobacteria, toxoplasmosis as discussed in brain abscess context) Sputum or pus microscopy for branching beaded Gram-positive filaments plus modified (weak-acid) acid-fast staining; organisms may also take up silver stains (p.1360-1361). Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid or lung biopsy when sputum smears are negative, as they frequently are in pulmonary nocardiosis (p.1361). Selective media (colistin-nalidixic acid agar, modified Thayer-Martin agar, or buffered charcoal-yeast extract agar) for mixed-flora specimens; avoid mycobacterial decontamination procedures, which can kill nocardiae; alert the laboratory to incubate cultures for prolonged periods (up to 2-4 weeks) (p.1361). Species/complex identification by MALDI-TOF or genomic sequencing (16S rRNA, secA1, hsp65, or gyrB), with antimicrobial susceptibility testing (ideally CLSI broth dilution); susceptibility testing requires experience because nocardiae grow slowly and clump (p.1361). Granule examination in mycetoma: wash suspect particles in saline, examine microscopically, and culture; culture is the most reliable way to identify the causative organism (p.1361). Contrast-enhanced CNS imaging (MRI preferred, with IV gadolinium more sensitive than CT) in all patients with non-cutaneous/non-ocular nocardiosis to detect occult brain abscess (p.1360-1362). Testing for underlying immunodeficiency in patients lacking typical risk factors, including HIV testing; test for chronic granulomatous disease in children and adults with nocardiosis who have no major risk factor (p.1359, p.1362). Pulmonary or cerebral malignancy/metastases presenting as nodules, masses, or ring-enhancing lesions Nocardiosis is usually an opportunistic infection occurring primarily in hosts with impaired defenses, especially defects in cell-mediated immunity and specific phagocyte function; typical risk factors include solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, systemic corticosteroids or Cushing syndrome, other immunosuppressive therapy, and HIV infection (p.1358-1359). Pulmonary disease is the usual portal after inhalation of fragmented mycelia; onset is typically subacute over days to weeks (more acute in the severely immunocompromised), with prominent cough producing thick non-malodorous purulent sputum, fever, anorexia, and malaise (p.1359). Typical chest imaging shows infiltrates, nodules, and masses in one or more lobes, and nodules frequently cavitate; pleural effusion or empyema occurs in about one-third of cases, occasionally without lung involvement (p.1359). Dissemination occurs in up to one-third of patients with pneumonia, most often to the CNS and to skin/subcutaneous tissues; virtually any organ can be involved (p.1359-1360). CNS involvement occurs in up to two-thirds of disseminated cases; brain imaging classically shows one or more ring-enhancing, multilobulated lesions, and multiple abscesses are seen in two-thirds of patients (p.1360). Diagnosis starts with examining sputum or pus for branching, beaded, Gram-positive filaments (~1 um wide, up to 50 um long) that fragment into apparent cocci/coccobacilli; most nocardiae are modified (weak) acid-fast (e.g., modified Kinyoun, modified Ziehl-Neelsen, Fite-Faraco) (p.1360-1361). Primary cutaneous nocardiosis follows transcutaneous inoculation (often thorn/gardening injury) and takes three forms: cellulitis, lymphocutaneous (sporotrichoid) syndrome, or actinomycetoma; N. brasiliensis is the usual cause of skin-limited and lymphocutaneous disease and of actinomycetoma (p.1358, p.1360). Nocardiosis tends to remit and relapse; without definitive treatment, pulmonary disease characteristically follows a course of remissions and exacerbations over weeks to months, and prolonged therapy (months) is required (p.1359, p.1362-Table 179-1). CNS dissemination: brain abscess may be clinically silent, so absence of neurologic symptoms does not exclude it - one-third of patients with CNS involvement have no CNS symptoms and one-fourth have no apparent pulmonary disease at presentation (p.1360). Disseminated nocardiosis carries a higher mortality than localized pulmonary disease, especially with CNS involvement (p.1362). Nocardiosis in a patient without a major risk factor should prompt evaluation for an undiagnosed immunologic defect, including HIV and chronic granulomatous disease (p.1359, p.1362). Failing to image the brain: because brain abscess may be asymptomatic, all patients with pulmonary or systemic nocardiosis should have contrast-enhanced CNS imaging (MRI preferred) regardless of neurologic symptoms (p.1360, p.1362). Missing the diagnosis on smear: sputum smears are frequently negative in pulmonary nocardiosis, and the modified (weak) acid-fast technique must be used or organisms may be overlooked; standard mycobacterial decontamination can kill nocardiae (p.1360-1361). Cultures lost to short incubation: nocardiae grow slowly (colonies up to 2 weeks, characteristic appearance up to 4 weeks), so the laboratory must be informed to incubate cultures for prolonged periods (p.1361). Overcalling colonization or contamination: Nocardia can colonize the respiratory tract in bronchiectasis/structural lung disease, and isolation from a respiratory specimen does not always indicate infection; blood culture isolates may be contaminants in low-risk patients without clinical disease (p.1361). Adjunctive topical corticosteroids should NOT be given to patients with nocardial keratitis (p.1362). Nocardia species are saprophytic, filamentous, aerobic Gram-positive bacteria ubiquitous in soil, water, and decaying organic matter; their cell walls contain mycolic acids and trehalose (Mycobacteriales order), and they are weakly (modified) acid-fast and catalase positive. Pulmonary and systemic disease follow inhalation of fragmented bacterial mycelia, while primary cutaneous and ocular disease follow direct inoculation. Most immunocompetent people clear inhaled nocardiae without disease; invasive infection is favored by impaired host defenses. Innate and adaptive responses, with neutrophils and macrophages central to antinocardial defense (underscored by the frequency of nocardiosis in chronic granulomatous disease), normally control the organism. Nocardiae have evolved mechanisms to survive within phagocytes, including neutralization of oxidants and prevention of phagosome-lysosome fusion and phagosome acidification; neutrophils limit but do not efficiently kill them. The characteristic pathology is an abscess with neutrophilic infiltration and prominent necrosis, with little fibrosis/encapsulation, whereas actinomycetoma shows granulomatous inflammation with sinus tract formation. (p.1358-1359) With appropriate treatment, mortality for localized pulmonary nocardiosis is less than 10%. Disseminated disease carries a higher mortality, especially with CNS involvement. Primary cutaneous and ocular disease often respond to therapy. Mortality from actinomycetoma is exceedingly low, but patients often suffer substantial morbidity, disfigurement, disability, and/or stigmatization. Prolonged therapy is required and disease tends to relapse, so secondary prophylaxis is considered by some experts for patients who remain at high risk after completing antimicrobial therapy. (p.1362) Disease is categorized clinically and by host status to guide therapy duration: pulmonary/systemic disease in hosts with intact defenses versus deficient defenses, CNS disease, primary cutaneous disease (cellulitis, lymphocutaneous), osteomyelitis/arthritis/laryngitis/sinusitis, actinomycetoma, and keratitis - longer courses for immunocompromised and CNS disease, with indefinite therapy considered in some AIDS patients with CD4 below 200/uL or chronic granulomatous disease (p.1362). [Durations noted as classification context only; not dosing guidance.]

Nocturnal Enuresis — bedwetting, nighttime wetting, sleep enuresis Urinary tract infection Constipation with secondary bladder dysfunction Diabetes mellitus or diabetes insipidus Overactive bladder or other daytime voiding dysfunction Obstructive sleep apnoea Psychosocial stressors (particularly in secondary enuresis) Urinalysis to screen for infection and glucosuria Assessment of bowel habits for constipation Bladder diary of daytime symptoms and voiding pattern Blood glucose if polyuria or other features suggest diabetes Renal or bladder imaging only when structural or neurological pathology is suspected Nocturnal enuresis is involuntary voiding during sleep in a child old enough to be expected to have night-time bladder control, generally around five years and older. It is classified as primary when the child has never achieved a sustained period of night-time dryness and secondary when wetting returns after at least six months of dryness. Monosymptomatic enuresis involves night-time wetting alone, whereas non-monosymptomatic enuresis is accompanied by daytime lower urinary tract symptoms such as urgency, frequency, or daytime wetting. Common contributing factors include a family history, delayed maturation of arousal and bladder control, reduced overnight bladder capacity, and relative overnight excess of urine production. Most primary monosymptomatic enuresis is not caused by serious disease, and evaluation is mainly history, examination, and urinalysis to exclude infection and glycosuria. Secondary enuresis or associated daytime symptoms warrant closer evaluation for causes such as urinary tract infection, constipation, diabetes, or psychosocial stress. First-line management emphasises reassurance, education, and behavioural measures, with the enuresis alarm being the most effective long-term intervention for motivated families. Constipation frequently coexists and, when treated, wetting often improves, so bowel habits should always be assessed. New-onset (secondary) enuresis with weight loss, polyuria, or polydipsia Daytime incontinence, straining, or a poor urinary stream Recurrent urinary tract infections Neurological signs or spinal abnormalities Significant behavioural change or evidence of psychosocial distress or abuse Treating the child punitively or blaming the child for an involuntary problem Overlooking coexisting constipation as a contributor Failing to distinguish monosymptomatic from non-monosymptomatic enuresis before choosing therapy Missing an underlying cause of secondary enuresis such as infection or diabetes Night-time continence depends on the balance between overnight urine production, bladder storage capacity, and the ability to either suppress bladder contractions during sleep or wake in response to a full bladder. Enuresis arises when this balance fails: some children produce a relatively large volume of urine at night, some have a smaller functional bladder capacity or overactive bladder, and many have a high arousal threshold so a full or contracting bladder does not wake them. These factors, strongly influenced by genetic predisposition and developmental maturation, often coexist. Constipation can reduce functional bladder capacity and provoke bladder overactivity, and secondary enuresis may reflect an acquired medical or psychosocial trigger. Primary monosymptomatic enuresis has a high rate of spontaneous resolution with age, and treatment can accelerate dryness; the outlook is generally excellent, though relapses can occur and cases with daytime symptoms may need more prolonged management.

Chronic antigenic and immune stimulation, including autoimmune conditions and hepatitis C virus infection in a proportion of cases, is thought to promote clonal outgrowth. The tumour cells display heterogeneous marginal-zone, monocytoid and plasmacytic morphology and may harbour recurrent mutations affecting NF-kappaB signalling and marginal-zone differentiation. By definition the disease lacks the defining splenic or extranodal features of the other marginal zone lymphomas, although secondary spread to bone marrow or blood can occur. The disease usually follows an indolent course with prolonged survival, though it is generally considered to have a somewhat less favourable outcome than extranodal MALT lymphoma; the principal adverse event is transformation to aggressive large B-cell lymphoma.

most commonly involving an MYH9-USP6 fusion. This fusion places USP6 under an active promoter, producing a self-limited burst of proliferation that characteristically resolves, which explains the rapid growth followed by spontaneous regression. The lesion arises in relation to fascia and is composed of spindled myofibroblasts in a loose myxoid or collagenous background with cleft-like spaces, extravasated erythrocytes and scattered giant cells. Its brisk mitotic activity and cellularity can closely imitate a sarcoma. Nodular fasciitis is benign and self-limiting, frequently regressing spontaneously and cured by simple excision when removed. Recurrence is very rare, and a recurrence should raise doubt about the original diagnosis.

diffuse or T-cell-rich architecture carry a higher risk of relapse and transformation A rapidly enlarging or fixed nodal mass suggesting transformation to aggressive large B-cell lymphoma New B symptoms, bulky disease or extranodal spread after an indolent course Discordant histology between sites on staging imaging warranting re-biopsy Rising lactate dehydrogenase with clinical deterioration Misclassifying the tumour as classic Hodgkin lymphoma and thereby selecting inappropriate therapy Relying on fine-needle aspiration, which cannot demonstrate the diagnostic nodular architecture Overlooking a variant (diffuse or T-cell-rich) growth pattern that predicts higher relapse risk Failing to re-biopsy a discordant or rapidly growing node and missing transformation Assuming cure after early remission and abandoning long-term follow-up The tumour arises from a germinal-centre B cell that has undergone clonal transformation, giving rise to the characteristic large LP (popcorn) cell with a multilobated nucleus. Unlike classic Hodgkin lymphoma, these cells preserve much of the mature B-cell transcriptional programme and continue to express B-cell antigens and surface immunoglobulin machinery. They reside within expanded nodular meshworks of follicular dendritic cells surrounded by small reactive B lymphocytes and a rosetting rim of T cells. This retained B-cell identity underlies both the CD20 positivity that makes the tumour amenable to anti-CD20 targeting and the propensity, in some cases, to progress to a diffuse aggressive large B-cell lymphoma. Early-stage disease has an excellent long-term outlook with high cure rates, but the indolent behaviour is offset by a tendency to late relapse and a small but real risk of transformation to aggressive large B-cell lymphoma, which worsens prognosis and mandates long-term surveillance.

should be addressed Nodular regenerative hyperplasia is thought to result from heterogeneous hepatic blood flow: obliteration or injury of small portal venules leads to atrophy of poorly perfused The altered intrahepatic vascular resistance and obliterative portal venopathy generate presinusoidal portal hypertension while hepatocellular function is relatively spared, distinguishing it from cirrhosis. Prognosis is generally more favourable than cirrhosis because hepatocellular function is preserved, and outcome is largely determined by control of portal-hypertensive complications and the course of any associated systemic disease.

enforce hearing protection and noise control at source Excessive acoustic energy causes mechanical and metabolic injury to the outer hair cells of the cochlea, initially at the basal turn that encodes bright-light exposure combined with melatonin is used to reinforce entrainment New circadian disruption with neurological or cognitive decline suggesting a central cause Severe daytime impairment with occupational or safety risk Coexisting untreated mood disorder or suicidal ideation Features suggesting a structural hypothalamic or pineal lesion Mislabelling the drifting pattern as simple insomnia and prescribing hypnotics Giving melatonin at the wrong circadian time, which can fail to entrain or even worsen misalignment Not recognising total blindness as the key predisposing factor Overlooking the need for sustained, correctly timed treatment The suprachiasmatic nucleus generates an intrinsic rhythm that is on average slightly longer than 24 hours and is normally reset each day, mainly by light reaching the retina. When this entraining signal is absent, as in total blindness, or is ineffective, the clock runs free at its own period and sleep-wake timing drifts later day by day. Melatonin, secreted by the pineal gland under circadian control, provides a complementary timing signal that can be supplied exogenously to help re-entrain the rhythm. With correctly timed melatonin or a melatonin-receptor agonist, and light therapy in sighted patients, many achieve entrainment and stable sleep, though relapse is common if treatment timing lapses, and management is a long-term commitment.

When this entrainment fails, most often because blindness removes photic input to the pacemaker, the sleep-wake rhythm free-runs on its own longer-than-24-hour cycle, drifting out of and back into phase with the environment. The disorder tends to be chronic, but appropriately timed melatonin or a melatonin-receptor agonist, and light where vision permits, can achieve and maintain entrainment in many patients.

non arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy — NAION, non-arteritic AION Arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy from giant cell arteritis Optic neuritis Compressive optic neuropathy Diabetic papillopathy Central retinal vein occlusion with disc oedema Papilloedema from raised intracranial pressure Infiltrative optic neuropathy Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein and platelet count to exclude giant cell arteritis Blood pressure assessment including consideration of nocturnal hypotension Fasting glucose or glycated haemoglobin and a fasting lipid profile Optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer Automated perimetry to document the field defect Screening for obstructive sleep apnoea where clinically suggested Neuroimaging with magnetic resonance imaging if the presentation is atypical Most common acute optic neuropathy in patients over 50; typically painless, sudden, monocular loss often noticed on waking. An inferior altitudinal visual field defect is the classic pattern, though any nerve-fibre-bundle defect may occur. The structural predisposition is a small, crowded optic disc with a small or absent physiological cup, the so-called disc at risk, best appreciated in the fellow eye. Vasculopathic risk factors predominate: hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea and nocturnal hypotension. At onset the disc shows segmental or diffuse hyperaemic oedema with peripapillary splinter haemorrhages, later resolving to sectoral pallor. A relative afferent pupillary defect is present unless there is bilateral or previous fellow-eye involvement. There is no proven effective treatment; the essential immediate step is to exclude an arteritic (giant cell arteritis) cause. Fellow-eye involvement occurs in a meaningful minority over subsequent years, so vascular risk-factor modification is advised. Symptoms of giant cell arteritis such as jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, new headache or polymyalgia rheumatica Pain on eye movement suggesting optic neuritis rather than ischaemia Progressive rather than static visual loss suggesting a compressive or infiltrative cause Simultaneous bilateral involvement warranting urgent systemic evaluation Failing to exclude giant cell arteritis and thereby missing a treatable, sight-threatening arteritic cause Misattributing the presentation to optic neuritis in an older vasculopathic patient Not screening for obstructive sleep apnoea and modifiable vascular risk factors Assuming corticosteroids provide benefit, for which evidence is lacking The disorder results from transient hypoperfusion or non-perfusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries supplying the laminar and prelaminar anterior optic nerve head. In a structurally crowded disc with little room for swelling, the initial ischaemic insult produces axonal oedema that raises tissue pressure within the confined scleral canal, creating a compartment-like effect that compresses capillaries and propagates further ischaemia. The process is neither embolic nor inflammatory in most cases, distinguishing it from arteritic and retinal arterial occlusive disease. Visual acuity commonly stabilises after the acute event and a proportion of patients show modest spontaneous improvement. Recurrence in the same eye is uncommon, but fellow-eye involvement occurs in roughly one in six to one in five patients over several years.

Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma — NHL Hodgkin's lymphoma (distinguished by Reed-Sternberg cells) Reactive follicular hyperplasia (major differential for follicular lymphoma on biopsy) Lymphoid leukemias (CLL/SLL, ALL), plasma cell disorders (multiple myeloma) Other causes of lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or B-symptom-like constitutional illness Infectious mononucleosis / EBV infection and other viral lymphadenopathies Reactive lymphadenopathy from systemic infection Multicentric Castleman's disease (HHV-8), which causes diffuse lymphadenopathy with fever, malaise, and weight loss mimicking lymphoma B symptoms Adequate tissue biopsy reviewed by an expert hematopathologist (follicular lymphoma and Burkitt's lymphoma can be diagnosed on morphology; immunophenotyping required) (Harrison 22e p.860, 863) Complete blood count, routine chemistries, liver function tests, uric acid, calcium Serum protein electrophoresis (to detect monoclonal paraproteins) Serum LDH and serum beta-2-microglobulin (prognostic) (Harrison 22e p.860) CT scan of chest, abdomen, and pelvis (essential for staging, especially indolent lymphomas) (Harrison 22e p.861) FDG-PET (preferred for aggressive lymphomas such as DLBCL and Burkitt's, and to assess suspected transformation of indolent disease) (Harrison 22e p.861) Bone marrow biopsy Lumbar puncture in lymphoblastic, Burkitt's, and DLBCL with positive marrow biopsy or CNS-risk presentations (Harrison 22e p.861) Screening for HIV and hepatitis B and C at diagnosis (risk factors and risk of HBV reactivation with therapy) (Harrison 22e p.861) Autoimmune disease with lymphadenopathy (e.g., Sjögren's syndrome, SLE, rheumatoid arthritis) Reactive follicular hyperplasia Sarcoidosis and other causes of constitutional symptoms with adenopathy NHLs are cancers of mature B, T, and NK cells; ~90% are of B-cell origin. They are distinguished from Hodgkin's lymphoma by the absence of the Reed-Sternberg cell and differ from HL in biology, natural history, and the more variable prognosis (Harrison 22e p.857). Clinically, NHL is grouped by behavior: indolent/slow-growing (e.g., follicular lymphoma, the most common indolent NHL), aggressive (DLBCL, the most common subtype overall, ~one-third of cases), and highly aggressive/most rapidly growing (Burkitt's lymphoma, doubling time <24 h). Mantle cell lymphoma is intermediate-grade (Harrison 22e p.857, 862). The duration and pace of symptoms help distinguish aggressive from indolent disease, as does the presence or absence of 'B' symptoms — fevers, drenching night sweats, and unexplained weight loss (>10% of body weight over the 6 months before diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.860-861). Most common presentation of follicular lymphoma is new, painless lymphadenopathy at multiple sites; most patients lack elevated LDH or B symptoms. Asymptomatic indolent disease should be observed, as treating asymptomatic patients does not improve survival (Harrison 22e p.863-864). Serum LDH and serum beta-2-microglobulin are important independent prognostic factors in NHL and should be measured at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.860). Aggressive lymphomas (DLBCL, Burkitt's) are potentially curable with combination chemotherapy, whereas most indolent lymphomas are very responsive to therapy but not ultimately curable in the vast majority of cases except in localized early-stage disease (Harrison 22e p.862-863). Burkitt's lymphoma is highly aggressive (doubling time <24 h) — treatment must be initiated quickly and the tumor carries a high risk of tumor lysis syndrome; TLS is most often associated with treatment of Burkitt's lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.862, 1014) Rapid growth of lymph nodes with new B symptoms in known indolent (follicular) lymphoma suggests histologic transformation to DLBCL (~3% per year) (Harrison 22e p.864) Disease involving paranasal sinuses, testes, breast, kidneys, adrenal glands, or epidural space — and highly aggressive histologies like Burkitt's — carries increased risk of CNS dissemination (Harrison 22e p.861) Concerning neurologic signs/symptoms warrant lumbar puncture for CNS involvement (Harrison 22e p.860) 'Double-hit' high-grade B-cell lymphoma (concurrent MYC and BCL2 rearrangements) has an extremely poor prognosis (median OS ~12-18 months) (Harrison 22e p.862-863) Diagnosis requires an adequate tissue sample interpreted by an expert hematopathologist; an inadequate or unrepresentative specimen risks misclassification (e.g., missing coexisting DLBCL within follicular lymphoma or confusing lymphoma with reactive follicular hyperplasia) (Harrison 22e p.860, 863). The Ann Arbor anatomic staging system is less useful in NHL than in Hodgkin's lymphoma because NHL disseminates widely rather than in an ordered stepwise fashion; histology and the IPI matter more than stage (Harrison 22e p.861). Treating asymptomatic indolent (follicular) lymphoma does not improve survival — appropriate patients should be observed rather than treated immediately (Harrison 22e p.864). Failing to anticipate and prevent tumor lysis syndrome before treating rapidly proliferating Burkitt's lymphoma can be life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.862). A residual mass on CT after therapy may represent treated fibrosis rather than active disease; PET can help distinguish, but end-of-treatment PET should be delayed (preferably 6-8 weeks after chemotherapy) to avoid false positives (Harrison 22e p.861). NHLs arise from mature B, T, or NK lymphocytes, with ~90% being B-cell neoplasms; transformation typically requires several genetic events. Characteristic chromosomal translocations create fusion or deregulated oncogenes: t(14;18) with BCL2 overexpression in follicular lymphoma (>85% of cases, necessary but not sufficient for transformation); MYC rearrangement at 8q24 in >95% of Burkitt's lymphoma (most often t(8;14) fusing MYC to IgH); and t(11;18) (API2-MLT) in MALT lymphoma. Gene-expression profiling subdivides DLBCL into germinal-center B-cell (GCB)-like and activated-B-cell (ABC)-like subtypes with differing prognoses. Several NHLs are linked to chronic antigenic stimulation or infection-driven immune dysregulation, and immunodeficiency states strongly predispose to (often EBV-associated) lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.857-863). Prognosis is highly variable and driven more by histology and clinical parameters than by anatomic stage. Overall 5-year survival for NHL is ~74%. The International Prognostic Index (IPI; age >=60, elevated LDH, ECOG performance status >=2, Ann Arbor stage III/IV, and >1 extranodal site) is the best predictor for aggressive NHL: 5-year overall survival ~73%, 51%, 43%, and 26% for 0-1, 2, 3, and 4-5 risk factors. With R-CHOP, ~65-70% of DLBCL patients are cured. The FLIPI predicts follicular lymphoma outcome; most FL patients live 15-20 years but the disease is generally not curable (except localized early-stage), and Burkitt's lymphoma is curable in ~80-90% when treated promptly and correctly (Harrison 22e p.857, 861-862). WHO (WHO-HAEM5) classification of lymphoid malignancies categorizes NHL by cell of origin (mature B-cell vs mature T/NK-cell neoplasms) and entity. Anatomic extent is described by the Ann Arbor staging system (Stage I-IV, with suffix A/B for absence/presence of B symptoms). Prognostic stratification uses the International Prognostic Index (IPI) for aggressive NHL and the FLIPI for follicular lymphoma; follicular lymphoma is also graded I-III by centroblasts per high-power field (Harrison 22e p.857-862).

Non-ossifying fibroma — Fibroxanthoma, Metaphyseal fibrous defect, Fibrous cortical defect Fibrous dysplasia Chondromyxoid fibroma Aneurysmal bone cyst Simple (unicameral) bone cyst Desmoplastic fibroma Osteofibrous dysplasia Giant cell tumour (in the skeletally mature) Plain radiographs, which are usually diagnostic on their own MRI reserved for atypical appearances or diagnostic uncertainty CT to assess cortical thinning and fracture risk in large lesions Clinical assessment for cafe-au-lait macules and other features of neurofibromatosis type 1 or Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome Interval follow-up radiographs to confirm expected regression and ossification Biopsy only in genuinely atypical lesions, since it is not required for classic ones One of the most common incidental bone lesions of childhood and adolescence, typically found in the metaphysis of long bones about the knee (distal femur, proximal and distal tibia). The small purely cortical form is termed a fibrous cortical defect, whereas the larger lesion extending into the medullary cavity is called a non-ossifying fibroma; they represent a spectrum of the same process. Radiographs show an eccentric, cortically based, well-defined lucent lesion with a thin sclerotic scalloped or grape-cluster margin and its long axis parallel to the shaft. It is a classic do-not-touch or leave-me-alone lesion; imaging is diagnostic and biopsy of a typical lesion is unnecessary. Most lesions regress spontaneously and ossify from the diaphyseal side with skeletal maturation, becoming uncommon after early adulthood. Large lesions occupying more than roughly half the transverse diameter of the bone carry a risk of pathological fracture and may warrant curettage and grafting. Multiple non-ossifying fibromas with extraskeletal features (cafe-au-lait macules, learning difficulty, hypogonadism, ocular and cardiovascular anomalies) constitute Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome. An association with neurofibromatosis type 1 should be considered when lesions are multiple. Pain in the absence of a pathological fracture Rapid or unexpected enlargement of the lesion Cortical breach or an associated soft-tissue mass Size approaching the threshold for pathological fracture in a weight-bearing bone Atypical location such as the axial skeleton or a flat bone Performing an unnecessary biopsy of a radiographically classic lesion Misinterpreting a benign lesion as an aggressive or malignant tumour Underestimating the fracture risk of a large lesion in a weight-bearing bone Overlooking a syndromic association when lesions are multiple Non-ossifying fibroma is a benign, developmental, non-neoplastic fibrous lesion rather than a true tumour, believed to arise near the physis and to migrate away from the growth plate into the metaphysis and diaphysis as the bone lengthens. Histologically it consists of a cellular proliferation of bland spindle-shaped fibroblasts arranged in a storiform (whorled) pattern, admixed with lipid-laden foam cells, scattered multinucleated osteoclast-type giant cells and haemosiderin deposition, accounting for the alternative name fibroxanthoma. The lesion is self-limiting and resolves through progressive ossification and remodelling, so that most examples heal spontaneously by the end of the second decade. The prognosis is excellent, with spontaneous resolution the rule and a very low recurrence rate after curettage of large or fractured lesions. Malignant potential is essentially absent.

arise from the neuroendocrine cells of the pancreatic islets but do not release hormones in amounts sufficient to produce a recognisable clinical syndrome. Because they are hormonally silent, they typically remain undetected until they grow large enough to cause local effects or metastasise, most often to regional lymph nodes and the liver. Their biological behaviour spans a spectrum from indolent, well-differentiated tumours to aggressive, poorly differentiated carcinomas, largely reflected in histological grade and stage. A meaningful minority occur in the context of hereditary syndromes, particularly multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, which favours multifocal disease. Prognosis depends chiefly on grade and stage; small, well-differentiated, resectable tumours have an excellent outlook, whereas high-grade or metastatic disease carries a considerably poorer prognosis, though indolent metastatic tumours may still be compatible with prolonged survival.

outcome is often poor Central apnoea requiring ventilatory support in the neonate Intractable seizures and burst-suppression progressing to status Rapidly deteriorating consciousness with profound hypotonia Progressive microcephaly and developmental arrest Family history of unexplained neonatal deaths Interpreting a raised plasma glycine without a paired CSF sample and missing the diagnostic ratio Mistaking secondary (ketotic) hyperglycinaemia of an organic acidaemia for true NKH Blood contamination of CSF invalidating the CSF glycine measurement Assuming valproate is safe, when it can worsen hyperglycinaemia and should be avoided Overlooking transient neonatal hyperglycinaemia, which resolves and does not need lifelong therapy Nonketotic hyperglycinaemia arises from impaired activity of the glycine cleavage system, a mitochondrial multienzyme complex (comprising the P-protein/GLDC, T-protein/AMT, H-protein/GCSH and a lipoamide dehydrogenase) that degrades glycine. Loss of function causes glycine to accumulate in body fluids and especially the central nervous system. Excess glycine acts both as an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brainstem and spinal cord, causing apnoea and hypotonia, and as a co-agonist at excitatory NMDA glutamate receptors in the forebrain, driving seizures and neuronal injury. The elevated CSF glycine relative to plasma reflects central overproduction/accumulation and is the diagnostic signature. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The severe neonatal form carries a poor prognosis with high early mortality and profound intellectual disability, intractable epilepsy and spasticity in survivors; attenuated forms have a milder course, and genotype and residual enzyme activity are the main determinants.

they are histologically identical Most are asymptomatic and regress or ossify spontaneously with skeletal maturity, so no treatment is needed Large lesions occupying a substantial portion of the bone width may carry a pathological fracture risk and warrant follow-up or fixation Multiple lesions with cafe-au-lait macules and other features raise the possibility of Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome Large lesion occupying more than half the bone diameter with fracture risk Aggressive or ill-defined margins atypical for a benign fibrous lesion Persistent pain in the absence of fracture, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Multiple lesions with extraskeletal features suggesting a syndrome Performing unnecessary biopsy of a classic incidental lesion that could be diagnosed radiographically Overlooking fracture risk in a large lesion of a weight-bearing bone Failing to recognise multiple lesions as a possible syndromic association Confusing it with more aggressive fibro-osseous lesions on limited imaging Non-ossifying fibroma is a benign fibrous developmental lesion rather than a true neoplasm, arising in the metaphysis of growing bone. It is composed of spindle-shaped fibroblastic cells arranged in a storiform pattern, admixed with osteoclast-type giant cells and foamy lipid-laden macrophages. The lesion represents a localised failure of normal ossification at the metaphysis and characteristically migrates towards the diaphysis and involutes as the skeleton matures, often filling in with reactive bone. The eccentric cortical location and thin sclerotic rim reflect its slow, non-aggressive growth. Non-ossifying fibroma is benign and self-limiting, with the overwhelming majority resolving spontaneously by early adulthood and requiring no intervention. Outcomes are excellent, and treatment is reserved for the uncommon large lesion at fracture risk.

Strongly associated with connective tissue disease, particularly systemic sclerosis, polymyositis/dermatomyositis and Sjögren syndrome, and may be its first manifestation. Idiopathic NSIP is a diagnosis of exclusion made only after a thorough search for connective tissue disease, drug exposure and hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Two histological subtypes exist: cellular (predominantly inflammatory, better prognosis) and fibrotic (worse prognosis). HRCT shows bilateral, symmetrical, basal-predominant ground-glass opacity with fine reticulation and traction bronchiectasis; relative subpleural sparing is characteristic. Honeycombing is absent or minimal, which helps distinguish NSIP from the UIP pattern of IPF. Temporal uniformity on histology, with all areas of the same apparent age, contrasts with the spatial and temporal heterogeneity of UIP. Unlike IPF, disease commonly responds to corticosteroids with or without steroid-sparing immunosuppression. Rapid clinical decline or an acute exacerbation Features of associated connective tissue disease requiring systemic treatment, such as scleroderma renal or cardiac involvement Progressive hypoxaemia Clinical signs of pulmonary hypertension Labelling disease as idiopathic without a thorough connective tissue disease and exposure work-up Confusing fibrotic NSIP with UIP, leading to incorrect prognosis and management Withholding immunosuppression that could benefit inflammatory disease Missing antisynthetase syndrome presenting initially as interstitial lung disease NSIP is characterised by a temporally uniform interstitial process combining varying proportions of chronic inflammation and interstitial fibrosis that preserves the underlying alveolar architecture, lacking the fibroblastic foci and honeycombing of UIP. In many patients it represents a pulmonary manifestation of systemic autoimmune disease, in which immune-mediated alveolar septal injury and repair produce diffuse septal thickening and ground-glass change. Cellular NSIP has an excellent outlook with treatment, whereas fibrotic NSIP behaves intermediately between cellular NSIP and IPF, and a subset progresses despite therapy.

GJB2, is a gap-junction protein expressed in the supporting cells and fibrocytes of the cochlea. Connexins assemble into intercellular channels that permit potassium and small-molecule movement, supporting recycling of potassium away from hair cells back to the endolymph and maintaining the endocochlear potential. Loss-of-function variants disrupt this gap-junction network, impairing potassium homeostasis and cochlear amplification, which produces sensorineural hearing loss without structural malformation. Because the deficit lies within the cochlear support apparatus rather than the auditory nerve, the phenotype is a pure cochlear sensorineural loss. The hearing loss is usually stable over time, and because the auditory nerve and central pathways are intact, most children achieve good outcomes with early amplification or cochlear implantation and structured habilitation.
