GATA2 evaluation when myelodysplasia coexists Malignancy presenting as painless cervical or intrathoracic adenopathy Hot-tub lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis-type reaction to NTM rather than invasive infection) NTM (also termed atypical, environmental, or mycobacteria other than tuberculosis) are ubiquitous in soil and water and refer to mycobacteria other than M. tuberculosis and its close relatives and M. leprae; over 199 species are recognized (p.1414). Most NTM cause human disease only when host defense is impaired (e.g., bronchiectasis) or breached by inoculation (liposuction, trauma, cardiac surgery); human-to-human transmission is rare and occurs almost exclusively in cystic fibrosis (p.1414). Pulmonary disease is by far the most common form in North America and is highly associated with pulmonary epithelial defects but NOT with systemic immunodeficiency; disseminated disease instead denotes significant immune dysfunction such as advanced HIV (p.1414, 1416). Pulmonary MAC most commonly presents in the 6th-7th decade in women with months to years of nagging intermittent cough and fatigue; pulmonary NTM in a tall, thin woman with chest-wall abnormalities is termed 'Lady Windermere syndrome' (p.1416). Pulmonary MAC affects older nonsmoking white women more than men (onset ~60 years); such patients tend to be taller and thinner with high rates of scoliosis, mitral valve prolapse, and pectus anomalies (p.1416). Male smokers with upper-lobe cavitary disease tend to carry the same single MAC strain indefinitely, whereas nonsmoking women with nodular bronchiectasis carry several MAC strains simultaneously that change over the disease course (p.1416). M. kansasii can produce a clinical syndrome strongly resembling tuberculosis with hemoptysis, chest pain, and cavitary lung disease (p.1416). Disseminated MAC (or M. kansasii) in advanced HIV is now uncommon in North America owing to effective prophylaxis and improved HIV treatment; when common, the portal of entry was the bowel with spread to bone marrow and bloodstream (p.1415). Disseminated NTM is often indolent and progressive over weeks to months with malaise, fever, weight loss, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and anemia; blood cultures may be negative even though involved organs carry heavy organism burdens, sometimes with grossly impaired granulomatous response (p.1415). Isolated cervical lymphadenopathy is the most common form of NTM infection in young children in North America (usually MAC); the swelling is firm and relatively painless with few systemic signs and is often diagnosed inadvertently at biopsy for suspected malignancy (p.1416). Children with isolated cervical or intrathoracic NTM infection do NOT commonly have underlying immune defects and usually do NOT go on to develop other opportunistic infections (p.1416). Cutaneous NTM usually requires a break in the skin; rapidly growing NTM (M. abscessus, M. fortuitum, M. chelonae) cause outbreaks via contaminated surgical instruments/injections, with painful erythematous draining subcutaneous nodules typically WITHOUT fever or systemic symptoms (p.1416). M. marinum (fish tanks, pools, fish handling) causes 'fish-tank granuloma' and can spread up the arm in a sporotrichoid pattern; M. ulcerans causes painless Buruli ulcer via the toxin mycolactone (p.1416). 'Hot-tub lung' is a pulmonary hypersensitivity reaction to NTM (most often MAC) growing in underchlorinated water, distinct from true pulmonary or disseminated infection (p.1415). For susceptibility testing, only MAC testing for clarithromycin and M. kansasii testing for rifampin is indicated; few data support other in vitro susceptibility tests, and MAC isolates not previously exposed to macrolides are almost always susceptible (p.1417). Disseminated involvement of two or more organs without an iatrogenic cause (prompts IFN-gamma/IL-12 pathway genetic investigation) Disseminated NTM with bacterial/viral infections plus conical/peg/missing teeth or abnormal hair pattern in males (suggests NEMO/IKBKG NF-kB defect, possibly with immunoglobulin defects) Mycobacterial disease with myelodysplasia (investigate GATA2 deficiency) Disseminated MAC and rapidly growing NTM with other opportunistic infections (e.g., Talaromyces), especially in East Asian women (anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies) Infected indwelling IV catheters/lines (M. abscessus, M. fortuitum from contaminated water) requiring catheter removal Not all NTM isolations, especially from the lung, reflect disease or require treatment; distinguishing colonization/contamination from true infection requires an appropriate clinical and radiographic setting (nodules, bronchiectasis, cavities) plus repeated isolation per American Thoracic Society criteria (p.1417). The single most critical and sensitive step in diagnosis is simply to suspect NTM and request the correct, separately processed mycobacterial smears, cultures, and dedicated blood culture media; many cases go undiagnosed because the appropriate test was never ordered (p.1416-1417). M. gordonae is frequently recovered from respiratory samples but is almost never a pathogen (p.1417). PPD does not differentiate NTM from M. tuberculosis well; intermediate (~10 mm) reactions overlap, BCG cross-reacts, but large reactions (>15 mm) most commonly signify TB (p.1416-1417). Slow-growing NTM typically do NOT proliferate in routine blood culture media, so suspicion and correct bottles are essential; biopsy isolation is strong evidence but laboratory contamination does occur (confirm with organisms on stained sections) (p.1417). NTM are ubiquitous environmental organisms (soil and water) with specific niches (e.g., M. simiae in aquifers, M. fortuitum in pedicure baths, M. immunogenum in metalworking fluids). Because exposure is essentially universal yet disease is rare, normal host defenses are strong and significant disease implies a specific susceptibility. Mycobacteria are phagocytosed by macrophages, which release IL-12; IL-12 activates T and NK cells (via STAT4) to secrete IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages/neutrophils (via STAT1) and upregulates TNF-alpha, forming a positive IFN-gamma/IL-12 feedback loop critical for mycobacterial control. Disseminated NTM correlates with declining CD4+ T cells (advanced HIV, idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia), TNF-alpha inhibitors (which impair granuloma formation), Mendelian mutations in the IFN-gamma/IL-12 pathway (IFNG, IFNGR1, IFNGR2, STAT1, GATA2, ISG15, IRF8, IL-12A, IL-12RB1, IL-12RB2, CYBB, IKBKG/NEMO and others), or neutralizing anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies. Only ~70% of non-HIV disseminated cases have a genetic diagnosis. In contrast, the best-recognized substrate for pulmonary NTM is bronchiectasis (cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, STAT3 hyper-IgE/Job's syndrome, idiopathic), but the mechanism by which bronchiectasis predisposes to locally destructive yet non-systemic disease is unknown (p.1414-1415). NTM cause chronic infections evolving slowly over weeks to years, so emergent therapy before diagnosis and speciation is rarely needed. Treatment is complex, often poorly tolerated, and potentially toxic; inadequate single-drug therapy is almost always associated with emergence of resistance and relapse. Pulmonary MAC therapy is prolonged, generally continued for 12 months after culture conversion (typically at least 18 months total). The typical lag between symptom onset and diagnosis is about 5 years in older women (p.1416-1418). American Thoracic Society criteria for pulmonary NTM diagnosis: growth of NTM from two of three sputum samples (regardless of smear), OR a positive bronchoalveolar lavage sample (regardless of smear), OR a lung parenchymal biopsy with granulomatous inflammation or mycobacteria on section plus NTM on culture, in an appropriate clinical and radiographic setting. Isolation of NTM from blood or organ biopsy in a compatible clinical setting is considered diagnostic. NTM are categorized as rapidly growing (<7 days) versus slowly growing (>=7 days) (p.1417).

mycobacteria from water and soil are inhaled and establish infection in a susceptible airway. The main predisposing factor is impaired local defence from structural lung disease such as bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cystic fibrosis, or prior tuberculosis, rather than systemic immunodeficiency. The organisms provoke a granulomatous inflammatory response that produces either upper-lobe cavitation resembling tuberculosis or a nodular-bronchiectatic pattern with tree-in-bud change, particularly in the right middle lobe and lingula. Prognosis varies by species and phenotype: M. kansasii responds well to rifampicin-based therapy, nodular-bronchiectatic MAC is often controllable though relapse and reinfection are common, and fibrocavitary or M. abscessus disease carries a worse outlook with lower cure rates. The majority of cases result from germline missense variants in PTPN11, which encodes the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP2. intraocular pressure stays within the normal statistical range. Damage is thought to arise from a combination of pressure-dependent stress on a susceptible optic nerve head and pressure-independent factors, particularly impaired optic-nerve blood flow from vascular dysregulation, systemic and nocturnal hypotension, and possibly a low cerebrospinal-fluid pressure that increases the translaminar pressure gradient. Many eyes progress slowly, and lowering intraocular pressure substantially reduces the rate of visual field deterioration, but a subset with marked vascular dysregulation or recurrent disc haemorrhages progress despite treatment and risk central visual loss.

notalgia paraesthetica — notalgia paresthetica, posterior ramus sensory neuropathy of the back brachioradial pruritus macular or lichen amyloidosis postinflammatory hyperpigmentation from another dermatosis tinea or other localised cutaneous infection contact or atopic dermatitis thoracic radiculopathy or herpes zoster-related neuropathic itch cutaneous T-cell lymphoma presenting as a persistent patch clinical examination mapping the itch to a thoracic dermatomal distribution thoracic spine imaging to assess degenerative or structural change when clinically indicated skin biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain or to exclude amyloid and other dermatoses screening for features of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A in selected patients dermoscopy to characterise the pigmented patch assessment of posture and musculoskeletal contributors review for coexisting neuropathic itch syndromes such as brachioradial pruritus A sensory neuropathy of the dorsal rami of thoracic spinal nerves presenting as a localised, chronically itchy patch on the upper or mid back, usually just medial to the scapula. The hallmark is a well-circumscribed area of pruritus often accompanied by burning, tingling or a localised hyperpigmented patch from chronic rubbing and scratching. The hyperpigmentation is secondary to chronic friction and postinflammatory change rather than a primary pigmentary disorder, and biopsy may show amyloid deposition. The distribution corresponds to the posterior rami of thoracic dermatomes, most often in the T2 to T6 range. Symptoms may improve transiently with cooling or capsaicin and are typically resistant to conventional antihistamines, reflecting the neuropathic mechanism. An association with degenerative changes of the thoracic spine and with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A has been described. It is closely analogous to brachioradial pruritus, which affects the dorsolateral forearm through a comparable neuropathic mechanism. Diagnosis is clinical; the key is to recognise the neuropathic nature and avoid an exhaustive search for primary skin disease. an evolving, indurated or ulcerated plaque that could represent cutaneous malignancy associated neurological deficit or radicular pain suggesting significant spinal pathology features suggesting multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A such as relevant family history or endocrine symptoms rapidly spreading or systemic symptoms inconsistent with a localised neuropathic itch treating the hyperpigmented patch as a primary pigmentary or infective dermatosis and missing the neuropathic cause prescribing sedating antihistamines that are ineffective for neuropathic itch overlooking an association with thoracic spine disease or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A attributing a persistent solitary patch to notalgia without considering cutaneous lymphoma when atypical Notalgia paraesthetica is attributed to dysfunction of the posterior primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves supplying sensation to the paravertebral skin of the back. Proposed mechanisms include entrapment or compression of these cutaneous nerve branches as they pass through the paraspinal musculature at a near right angle, and irritation associated with degenerative thoracic spine disease. The resulting neuropathic itch and dysaesthesia provoke chronic rubbing and scratching, which produce the characteristic hyperpigmented, sometimes lichenified patch; histology may reveal dermal amyloid deposition thought to be secondary to the chronic friction rather than a primary amyloidosis. The condition is benign but typically chronic and relapsing, with symptoms that can be controlled but often persist over years. Treatment directed at the neuropathic mechanism and reduction of scratching improves symptoms and the associated pigmentation.

These rami take an angulated course through the paraspinal musculature, where they are thought to be vulnerable to compression or irritation, frequently in association with degenerative or postural changes of the thoracic spine. The resulting neuropathy generates a chronic neuropathic itch and dysaesthesia confined to the nerve's cutaneous territory. Persistent scratching and rubbing produce secondary skin changes, notably a localised hyperpigmented lichenified patch, and amyloid may deposit in the chronically traumatised skin. Because the itch is neurogenic rather than inflammatory, conventional anti-itch therapy is largely ineffective. The condition is benign but often chronic and relapsing; symptoms may be controlled with neuropathic therapy and by addressing spinal or postural contributors, though complete and lasting resolution can be difficult to achieve.

myocardial necrosis requiring urgent admission, monitoring, and antithrombotic therapy Refractory or recurrent ischaemic pain despite optimal medical therapy Haemodynamic instability, cardiogenic shock, or acute heart failure Sustained ventricular arrhythmia or high-grade conduction block New mechanical complications such as acute mitral regurgitation Interpreting any raised troponin as type 1 infarction without considering type 2 injury or non-ischaemic causes Mislabelling an NSTEMI as STEMI or vice versa and applying the wrong reperfusion pathway Relying on a single early troponin or ECG to exclude infarction Delaying dual antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy while awaiting angiography in eligible patients NSTEMI most commonly arises from rupture or erosion of a coronary plaque with partially occlusive thrombus, or from severe fixed stenosis with superimposed thrombosis, producing prolonged ischaemia sufficient to cause myocyte necrosis. Because flow is reduced rather than completely and persistently interrupted, injury is often subendocardial and the ECG lacks persistent ST elevation. Distal embolisation of platelet-fibrin material and dynamic vasoconstriction contribute. Type 2 infarction reflects an imbalance between oxygen supply and demand (for example from tachyarrhythmia, anaemia, hypotension, or hypertensive crisis) without acute plaque rupture. Outcomes depend on infarct size, coronary anatomy, left ventricular function, and comorbidities; timely risk-based invasive management and secondary prevention improve survival, though NSTEMI carries meaningful medium- and long-term mortality, sometimes exceeding STEMI over the longer term because of older age and comorbidity burden.

Numb chin syndrome — mental neuropathy, mental nerve neuropathy Metastatic malignancy (breast, prostate) or lymphoma/leukaemia Leptomeningeal or skull-base disease Dental or mandibular local pathology / trauma Mandibular osteomyelitis Sickle cell disease (vaso-occlusion) Multiple sclerosis or other trigeminal pathology MRI of the brain, skull base and mandible with attention to the trigeminal/mental nerve pathway Orthopantomogram and dental assessment Investigation for systemic malignancy (imaging, tumour markers) where a cause is not evident Cerebrospinal fluid analysis if leptomeningeal disease is suspected Full blood count and film if leukaemia is considered Numbness of the chin and lower lip in the distribution of the mental (or inferior alveolar) nerve It is an important red-flag sign because it is frequently caused by underlying malignancy Recognised causes include metastatic breast and prostate cancer, lymphoma and leukaemic infiltration, and it may herald relapse Benign causes exist (dental or local trauma, mandibular osteomyelitis, sickle cell disease), but malignancy must be excluded The lesion may be at the mandible (mental nerve) or more proximally at the skull base or leptomeninges Investigation targets the whole nerve pathway and a search for systemic malignancy Known or suspected malignancy (new numb chin may signal metastasis or relapse) Associated other cranial neuropathies Systemic symptoms of malignancy Progressive or bilateral involvement Dismissing chin numbness as dental without excluding malignancy Failing to image the entire nerve pathway including the skull base Overlooking it as a marker of cancer relapse Not considering leptomeningeal disease Numb chin syndrome arises from injury to the mental nerve or its parent inferior alveolar/mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, anywhere from the leptomeninges and skull base to the mandibular canal and mental foramen. Malignant causes act by perineural spread, mandibular or leptomeningeal metastasis, or direct compression, which is why the sign so often reflects cancer. Benign local processes injure the nerve within the mandible. The chin and lip sensory loss reflects the terminal cutaneous territory of the affected nerve. Prognosis is driven by the underlying cause; when due to malignancy it often signifies advanced or recurrent disease and a poor outlook, whereas benign causes may resolve.

temporal artery in an older patient Not examining the skin and skull beneath the painful zone Escalating systemic analgesics without considering targeted local treatment Nummular headache is thought to be a disorder of the terminal twigs of the scalp sensory nerves, producing pain and sensory disturbance restricted to a small, well-defined territory of the epicranial tissues. The sharply localised, fixed area of tenderness and dysaesthesia points to a peripheral, extracranial focus rather than referred or intracranial pain, although central sensitisation may contribute to its persistence. The condition is usually benign; many patients have a chronic but stable course, and symptoms often respond to simple analgesia, gabapentinoids or local injection therapy when troublesome.

nursemaids elbow — Pulled elbow, Radial head subluxation Supracondylar fracture of the humerus Radial head or radial neck fracture Clavicle fracture presenting as a reluctant-to-use arm in a toddler Elbow dislocation Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis involving the elbow Non-accidental injury Torus or buckle fracture of the distal forearm Clinical diagnosis alone in classic presentations, with no imaging required Elbow radiographs in anteroposterior and lateral views if atypical features, swelling or failed reduction Comparison views of the contralateral elbow where there is diagnostic uncertainty Ultrasound in selected uncertain cases Assessment for non-accidental injury where the history is inconsistent or the injury unexplained Observation of spontaneous, pain-free arm use after reduction as confirmation of success Nursemaid's elbow is a subluxation of the radial head beneath the annular ligament and is the commonest elbow injury of early childhood, most often in toddlers and pre-school children. The classic mechanism is a sudden longitudinal (axial) pull on a pronated, extended forearm, such as lifting or swinging a child by the hand or arm. The child typically holds the arm slightly flexed and pronated against the body and declines to use it, yet is otherwise settled with no swelling or deformity. The absence of swelling, bruising, focal bony tenderness or deformity helps distinguish it from a fracture. When the history and examination are classic, with no bony tenderness or swelling, radiographs are not required before attempting reduction. Reduction is achieved by supination-flexion or by hyperpronation of the forearm; a palpable click is often felt and the child usually resumes normal use within minutes. If the mechanism is atypical, there is significant swelling, or reduction fails, radiographs should be obtained to exclude a fracture such as a supracondylar or radial neck injury. Recurrence is common until the radial head and annular ligament mature, so carers should be advised against pulling the child by the hand or wrist. Significant swelling, bruising, deformity or focal bony tenderness suggesting a fracture An inconsistent, absent or implausible mechanism raising concern for non-accidental injury Neurovascular compromise of the limb Failure to regain normal use after appropriate reduction attempts Fever, erythema or warmth around the joint suggesting infection Attempting reduction when swelling or deformity suggests an unrecognised fracture Assuming every toddler who will not use an arm has a pulled elbow and thereby missing a supracondylar fracture Failing to consider non-accidental injury when the history is inconsistent Neglecting to counsel carers on prevention, leading to recurrence Obtaining radiographs in every case when the presentation is classic and reduction straightforward Nursemaid's elbow arises when sudden axial traction is applied to an extended, pronated forearm, causing the annular ligament that encircles the radial neck to slip proximally over the head of the radius and become partially interposed within the radiohumeral joint. In young children the radial head is relatively small and incompletely ossified and the annular ligament is thin and lax, which permits this displacement; the trapped ligament produces pain and reluctance to use the arm while the joint itself remains structurally intact. As the radial head enlarges and the ligament strengthens with growth, the anatomy no longer permits the ligament to slip, and the condition ceases to recur. The prognosis is excellent; reduction is usually rapid and complete with immediate return of function and no long-term sequelae. Recurrence during the toddler years is common, but the tendency resolves with skeletal maturation.

rapid progression despite conventional therapy Mistaking the tumour for ordinary poorly differentiated squamous carcinoma and not requesting NUT testing Overlooking the diagnosis in older adults or non-midline sites where it is less expected Interpreting focal keratinisation as evidence of a more differentiated, less aggressive carcinoma Failing to preserve tissue for molecular confirmation when the initial impression is a small round cell tumour Attributing weak or patchy NUT staining to a negative result without confirmatory molecular studies NUT carcinoma is driven by a balanced rearrangement of the NUTM1 gene, most commonly generating a BRD4-NUT fusion in which a bromodomain protein is joined to nuclear protein in testis. The fusion protein sequesters histone-modifying machinery and drives aberrant chromatin acetylation across large genomic regions, locking cells in a proliferative, undifferentiated state and preventing terminal squamous maturation. This single genetic event is sufficient to produce a highly aggressive epithelial malignancy, and the resulting dependence on chromatin readers and acetylation underpins interest in bromodomain and histone-deacetylase directed therapies. NUT carcinoma is one of the most aggressive human solid tumours, with rapid local progression, early metastasis and generally short survival despite multimodality treatment; long-term survival is uncommon, although outcomes may be marginally better for non-thoracic primaries amenable to complete surgical resection combined with radiotherapy, and targeted agents remain investigational.

Nutcracker syndrome — renal vein compression syndrome, left renal vein entrapment, renal nutcracker syndrome Glomerular causes of haematuria (e.g. IgA nephropathy, thin basement membrane disease) Urolithiasis causing loin pain and haematuria Urothelial or renal malignancy Loin pain-haematuria syndrome Pelvic congestion syndrome from other cause Varicocele of primary venous incompetence Doppler ultrasound of the left renal vein to assess flow velocities and compression CT or MR venography to demonstrate the compressed segment and anatomy Retrograde venography with renocaval pressure gradient measurement in equivocal cases Urinalysis to confirm haematuria and quantify proteinuria (including orthostatic testing) Cystoscopy to lateralise bleeding to the left ureteric orifice when macroscopic haematuria is present Exclusion of glomerular disease with appropriate renal workup Caused by compression of the left renal vein, most often the anterior (classic) type where it is squeezed between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta, or the posterior type where a retroaortic left renal vein is compressed between the aorta and vertebral column Nutcracker phenomenon describes the anatomical compression on imaging; nutcracker syndrome denotes compression that produces symptoms Typical features are left-sided haematuria (micro- or macroscopic), left flank or abdominal pain, and orthostatic proteinuria In men it may cause a left varicocele and in women pelvic congestion symptoms owing to raised gonadal vein pressure Tends to occur in slender individuals with little retroperitoneal fat, and symptoms may worsen with upright posture or exertion Diagnosis integrates Doppler ultrasound, cross-sectional venous imaging, and, when needed, venography with pressure gradient measurement Management ranges from conservative observation (many young patients improve with growth and weight gain) to left renal vein transposition, stenting, or other surgical options for severe disease Severe or recurrent macroscopic haematuria causing anaemia or clot retention Progressive proteinuria or evidence of renal impairment Debilitating flank or pelvic pain unresponsive to conservative measures Features suggesting an alternative serious cause such as malignancy Diagnosing the syndrome from imaging compression alone without correlating symptoms (over-diagnosis of an incidental phenomenon) Missing a coexisting glomerular cause of haematuria Placing an endovascular stent prematurely in a young patient likely to improve conservatively Overlooking the posterior (retroaortic) variant on imaging Nutcracker syndrome results from mechanical compression of the left renal vein along its course to the inferior vena cava. In the anterior variant the vein is entrapped in the narrowed angle between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta; in the posterior variant a retroaortic vein is compressed between the aorta and the spine. Compression raises pressure within the left renal vein and its tributaries, causing venous congestion, development of collaterals, and rupture of thin-walled veins into the collecting system, which produces haematuria. Raised pressure transmitted to the gonadal vein underlies varicocele in men and pelvic congestion in women. Many younger patients improve spontaneously as retroperitoneal fat increases with growth, and conservative management is often sufficient; those with severe, persistent symptoms generally respond well to renal vein transposition or endovascular stenting, though stent-related complications can occur.

nutritional optic neuropathy — deficiency optic neuropathy, nutritional amblyopia Toxic optic neuropathy Leber hereditary optic neuropathy Dominant optic atrophy Compressive optic neuropathy or chiasmal lesion Demyelinating optic neuritis Maculopathy such as occult macular dystrophy Serum vitamin B12 with folate and red-cell folate Thiamine and serum copper with caeruloplasmin Full blood count and blood film looking for macrocytosis Magnetic resonance imaging to exclude a compressive or chiasmal lesion Automated perimetry and colour vision testing Optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer Mitochondrial DNA testing for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy where suspected Presents with bilateral, symmetric, painless and slowly progressive visual loss with a central or centrocaecal scotoma and prominent dyschromatopsia. Key deficiencies include vitamin B12, folate, thiamine, pyridoxine, riboflavin and copper, often on a background of protein-calorie malnutrition. Important settings are chronic alcohol misuse, bariatric surgery, malabsorption, highly restrictive diets and famine, and combined nutritional and toxic injury is common. Red-green colour vision is disturbed early and disproportionately to the level of acuity. The disc is normal or mildly hyperaemic early and develops temporal pallor as the papillomacular bundle atrophies. Pupillary light responses are relatively preserved and a relative afferent pupillary defect is absent when involvement is symmetric. Early recognition and repletion, including empirical thiamine in at-risk patients, can reverse or arrest visual loss. A hereditary mitochondrial optic neuropathy such as Leber hereditary optic neuropathy can mimic the picture and should be considered. Rapidly progressive or markedly asymmetric loss, prompting reconsideration of a compressive or other cause Accompanying neurological signs or features of Wernicke encephalopathy Failure to improve after adequate nutritional repletion Coexisting toxic exposure that may accelerate the injury Attributing loss to alcohol alone without measuring B12 and folate Overlooking a coexisting toxic contribution to the neuropathy Delaying thiamine replacement in at-risk or alcohol-dependent patients Failing to consider copper deficiency, for example after bariatric surgery or with excess zinc intake The small-calibre fibres of the papillomacular bundle have exceptionally high metabolic demand and depend on efficient mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. B-group vitamins act as cofactors in the enzymatic pathways generating cellular energy, so their deficiency impairs adenosine triphosphate production, disrupts axonal transport and myelin maintenance, and increases oxidative stress. These fibres are therefore selectively vulnerable, producing the characteristic central and centrocaecal field loss, with copper deficiency causing an analogous metabolic injury. The outcome is variable and depends on the duration of deficiency; vision may recover substantially with early repletion. Prolonged, untreated deficiency leads to optic atrophy and permanent visual impairment.

Nutritional Rickets — rickets, vitamin D deficiency rickets, calcipenic rickets Hypophosphataemic (vitamin D-resistant) rickets Vitamin D-dependent rickets (types 1 and 2) Renal osteodystrophy from chronic kidney disease Hypophosphatasia Osteogenesis imperfecta Skeletal dysplasias and physiologic bowing Serum calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase 25-hydroxyvitamin D level Parathyroid hormone Renal function and, where indicated, urine calcium and phosphate Wrist or knee radiographs for metaphyseal changes 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in atypical or treatment-resistant cases A disorder of defective mineralisation of growing bone, most commonly due to deficiency of vitamin D and/or dietary calcium. Risk factors include exclusive breastfeeding without vitamin D supplementation, darker skin pigmentation, limited sun exposure, and prematurity. Skeletal signs include widening of the wrists and ankles, a rachitic rosary at the costochondral junctions, frontal bossing, delayed fontanelle closure, and bowing of the legs once weight-bearing begins. Non-skeletal features can include delayed motor milestones, hypotonia, growth faltering, and increased susceptibility to fractures. Severe hypocalcaemia may present with tetany, carpopedal spasm, or seizures, especially in infants. Biochemistry classically shows low or low-normal calcium and phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase, raised parathyroid hormone, and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Radiographs of the wrist or knee reveal metaphyseal cupping, fraying, and widening of the growth plate. Treatment replaces vitamin D and ensures adequate dietary calcium, with biochemical and radiological healing confirming response. Prevention through routine vitamin D supplementation in infancy is highly effective, and failure to respond should prompt evaluation for inherited or renal forms. Hypocalcaemic seizures, tetany, or laryngospasm Cardiomyopathy associated with severe hypocalcaemia or vitamin D deficiency Pathological fractures Failure to respond to appropriate vitamin D and calcium therapy Progressive deformity or signs suggesting an inherited or renal cause Attributing bowed legs solely to physiologic causes and missing biochemical rickets Overlooking dietary calcium deficiency as a cause even when vitamin D is adequate Failing to investigate inherited or renal rickets when there is no response to treatment Not providing routine vitamin D supplementation to exclusively breastfed infants Vitamin D deficiency reduces intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate, lowering their availability for bone mineralisation. The falling calcium stimulates parathyroid hormone secretion (secondary hyperparathyroidism), which mobilises calcium from bone and promotes renal phosphate wasting. The combination of low calcium-phosphate product and PTH-driven bone resorption leaves the expanding cartilage of the growth plate and newly formed osteoid unmineralised, producing the soft, deformable bones and characteristic metaphyseal changes of rickets. With adequate treatment, biochemical recovery occurs within weeks and radiographic healing over months; most deformities remodel in young children, though severe or late-treated cases may leave residual bowing.

O-mannosylation disorder (dystroglycanopathy-spectrum glycosylation defect) — dystroglycanopathy, alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation disorder, O-mannosylation defect, POMT1/POMT2/POMGNT1/FKTN/FKRP/LARGE-related CDG, muscle-eye-brain / Walker-Warburg spectrum Merosin-deficient and other congenital muscular dystrophies Spinal muscular atrophy and other infantile hypotonia causes N-linked CDGs with neuromuscular features Other causes of cobblestone lissencephaly and structural brain malformation Congenital myopathies and myotonic dystrophy Metabolic myopathies with raised creatine kinase Serum creatine kinase measurement Muscle biopsy with immunostaining for glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan Molecular genetic testing of the dystroglycanopathy gene panel Brain MRI for cortical malformation, cerebellar and brainstem anomalies Ophthalmological assessment for structural eye involvement Respiratory and cardiac evaluation as part of muscular dystrophy surveillance A group of glycosylation disorders affecting O-mannosylation of alpha-dystroglycan, presenting as congenital muscular dystrophy with variable brain and eye involvement The clinical spectrum spans Walker-Warburg syndrome and muscle-eye-brain disease at the severe end to milder limb-girdle muscular dystrophy phenotypes Severe forms combine congenital muscular dystrophy with cobblestone (type II) lissencephaly, cerebellar and brainstem malformations, and ophthalmological anomalies Serum creatine kinase is typically markedly elevated, reflecting muscle involvement, in contrast to the usual N-linked CDGs Standard serum transferrin isoelectric focusing is usually normal because these are O-linked defects, so a normal transferrin test does not exclude them Muscle biopsy shows dystrophic change with reduced glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan on immunostaining; many genes are involved (e.g. POMT1, POMT2, POMGNT1, FKTN, FKRP, LARGE) Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, addressing motor, respiratory, feeding, visual and neurological needs Congenital hypotonia with contractures and respiratory compromise Structural brain malformation with seizures or profound developmental delay Progressive loss of motor milestones or ambulation Severe visual impairment from ocular malformation Excluding a glycosylation disorder because transferrin testing is normal in these O-linked defects Not measuring creatine kinase in a hypotonic infant with suspected CDG Overlooking cardiac and respiratory surveillance in the muscular dystrophy phenotype Assuming a single gene when the dystroglycanopathies are genetically heterogeneous Alpha-dystroglycan requires a specialised O-mannose-linked glycan to bind extracellular matrix proteins such as laminin and anchor the sarcolemma and basement membranes. Defects in the enzymes and glycosyltransferases that build this O-mannosyl glycan disrupt the link between the cytoskeleton and matrix, causing muscle fibre injury and impaired neuronal migration. The result is a dystroglycanopathy, with congenital muscular dystrophy and, in severe cases, malformations of cortical development and the eye. Because the defect is in O-linked rather than N-linked glycosylation, conventional transferrin screening is characteristically normal. Prognosis ranges widely: Walker-Warburg and muscle-eye-brain phenotypes carry high early mortality and severe disability, whereas milder limb-girdle dystroglycanopathies may permit prolonged ambulation and survival into adulthood. Respiratory and cardiac complications influence long-term outcome.

Obesity — overweight Hypothyroidism — may cause weight gain but is rarely the sole cause of severe obesity; check TSH (and free thyroxine for rare secondary hypothyroidism) in any patient presenting with obesity (Harrison 22e p.3185, 3188) Cushing's syndrome / endogenous hypercortisolism — suggested by spontaneous bruising, livid striae, myopathy and marked centripetal fat distribution; confirmed via 24-h urinary free cortisol or dexamethasone suppression (Harrison 22e p.3185) Hypothalamic obesity — from tumors (e.g., craniopharyngioma), inflammatory masses, or severe head injury disrupting hypothalamic energy-balance centres, often with anterior/posterior pituitary dysfunction and short history of hyperphagia (Harrison 22e p.3185) Insulinoma — weight gain driven by frequent eating to avoid hypoglycemia (Harrison 22e p.3185) Polycystic ovarian syndrome — secondary cause/association meriting evaluation (Harrison 22e p.3188) Monogenic / syndromic obesity — leptin or leptin-receptor deficiency, POMC, PCSK1, MC4R, SIM1, BDNF/TrkB, SH2B1 mutations; syndromes such as Prader-Willi, Bardet-Biedl, Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy/pseudohypoparathyroidism, Cohen's, Carpenter's, Alström's, Tubby (Harrison 22e p.3183–3185) Drug-induced weight gain — insulin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, glucocorticoids, antipsychotics (clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone), lithium, antidepressants (tricyclics, MAOIs, paroxetine, mirtazapine), antiepileptics (valproate, gabapentin, carbamazepine) (Harrison 22e p.3188) BMI calculation plus waist circumference (surrogate for visceral fat; measure horizontally above the iliac crest, particularly when BMI ≤35) and/or waist-to-hip ratio (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187) Fasting lipid profile (total, LDL, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides), chemistry panel, glycated haemoglobin, and blood pressure in all patients (Harrison 22e p.3187) TSH ± free thyroxine to evaluate for hypothyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3185, 3188) 24-h urinary free cortisol or dexamethasone suppression test when Cushing's syndrome is suspected (Harrison 22e p.3185) Genetic testing in severe early-onset obesity (up to ~20% of children with severe obesity have chromosomal abnormalities or highly penetrant mutations) (Harrison 22e p.3183) Very muscular body habitus — BMI may overestimate body fat (Harrison 22e p.3181) Peripheral edema from NSAIDs or calcium channel blockers — increases weight without increasing body fat (Harrison 22e p.3188) Obesity is defined as a state of excess adipose tissue mass that adversely affects health; because direct measurement of fat mass is impractical in routine clinical practice, the body mass index (BMI = weight/height² in kg/m²) is used as a proxy (Harrison 22e p.3181). WHO BMI classes: underweight <18.5; normal 18.5–24.9; overweight 25–29.9; obesity ≥30 kg/m². AACE/ACE management staging further subdivides obesity into class I (30.0–34.9), class II (35.0–39.9), and class III / extreme obesity (≥40) with correspondingly higher disease risk (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187). BMI-based cutoffs were derived largely from white Western populations; adverse outcomes occur at lower BMI in other ethnic groups, so lower thresholds and ethnic-specific waist-circumference cutpoints (e.g., South Asians/Chinese, Japanese) are recommended (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187). Fat distribution matters independent of overall BMI: a waist-to-hip ratio >0.9 in women and >1.0 in men, and excess abdominal (visceral) adiposity, are independently associated with type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, metabolic syndrome, and cardiovascular disease (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187). Energy balance is under homeostatic control by the hypothalamus, which integrates the adipose-derived hormone leptin (rises with fat stores, falls fast with caloric restriction) with gut signals — GLP-1, CCK, GIP, PYY, oxyntomodulin, ghrelin — plus pancreatic insulin and amylin (Harrison 22e p.3181–3182). Insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinemia is one of the earliest and most prominent biochemical abnormalities of obesity, is worse with central adiposity, and underlies/precedes many adverse cardiometabolic consequences (Harrison 22e p.3186). Two leading (not mutually exclusive) hypotheses link obesity to insulin resistance: adipose-tissue inflammation (macrophage accumulation around dying adipocytes), and ectopic lipid deposition once safe adipose storage capacity is exceeded — with stronger human data supporting the ectopic-fat / limited-storage mechanism (Harrison 22e p.3186). Obesity care begins with sensitive, non-stigmatizing language and an obesity-focused history covering diet, physical activity, sleep, stress, contributing factors, complications, and the patient's readiness/motivation to change (Harrison 22e p.3187–3188). Short history of hyperphagia and rapid weight gain with signs of anterior/posterior pituitary dysfunction — suggests hypothalamic damage from tumor, inflammation, or head injury (Harrison 22e p.3185) Spontaneous bruising, livid striae, proximal myopathy, marked centripetal fat — suggests Cushing's syndrome rather than common obesity (Harrison 22e p.3185) Severe early-onset obesity in childhood with intense hyperphagia/food-seeking — prompts screening for monogenic/syndromic causes (Harrison 22e p.3183–3185) Severe hypertriglyceridemia secondary to insulin resistance — risk of pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.3186) Treating BMI alone: BMI only reflects body size, not body composition, fat distribution, health, or quality of life — not all patients with a high BMI need treatment, and BMI overestimates fat in very muscular individuals (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187, 3190). Applying white-Western-derived BMI cutoffs uniformly: adverse outcomes occur at lower BMI in other ethnic groups, and ethnic-specific (e.g., Asia-Pacific) thresholds should be used (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187). Overlooking that severe hypothyroidism is rarely the sole cause of severe obesity, yet thyroid function should still always be checked (Harrison 22e p.3185). Mistaking the lower GH response to provocative testing in common obesity for a structural hypothalamic-pituitary lesion (Harrison 22e p.3186). Assuming a specific macronutrient ratio is key: weight loss depends primarily on total caloric reduction and adherence, not on the proportion of carbohydrate, fat, or protein (Harrison 22e p.3190). Using stigmatizing language ('obesity', 'morbid obesity', 'fatness') rather than neutral terms ('weight', 'excess weight', 'unhealthy weight'), which leaves patients feeling judged (Harrison 22e p.3188). Initiating lifestyle change before assessing readiness, which leads to frustration and may hamper future efforts (Harrison 22e p.3188). Adipose tissue evolved to store excess calories as triglyceride in unilocular lipid droplets and release free fatty acids and glycerol when needed. In an obesogenic environment (abundant energy-dense palatable food, larger portions, reduced physical activity), chronic energy intake exceeding expenditure — even by as little as ~7 kcal/day sustained over years — produces a cumulative excess of adipose triglyceride. Genetic factors strongly determine individual susceptibility (twin studies show adiposity tracks with biological, not adoptive, family), acting largely through the brain's control of food intake. Body weight is homeostatically defended by the hypothalamus, which integrates the adipose hormone leptin (whose fall below an individual's habitual level is a powerful drive to eat) with gut hormones (GLP-1, CCK, GIP, PYY, oxyntomodulin, ghrelin) and pancreatic insulin/amylin. Within the arcuate nucleus, leptin stimulates POMC neurons (whose products α-/β-MSH act via MC4R in the paraventricular nucleus to reduce intake and raise energy expenditure) and inhibits orexigenic AGRP/NPY/GABA neurons. Leptin defends strongly against fat loss but responds weakly to fat excess ("leptin resistance"), explaining why rising leptin does not prevent obesity. As obesity develops, the earliest abnormality is insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinemia, worse with central fat; this arises from adipose-tissue inflammation and/or ectopic lipid deposition in liver and muscle once safe adipose storage capacity is exceeded (the human data favouring the ectopic-fat mechanism, as illustrated by lipodystrophy). Insulin resistance/hyperinsulinemia then predisposes to the metabolic, endocrine, and cardiovascular complications of obesity (Harrison 22e p.3181–3186). Obesity is a serious, highly heterogeneous chronic disease that increases morbidity and mortality across many organ systems. The number and severity of complications generally rise with increasing BMI, and excess abdominal/visceral fat confers added cardiometabolic risk. As BMI rises by 5 kg/m², cancer mortality increases by ~10%; in some countries obesity has overtaken smoking as the leading risk factor for cancer. People with obesity have increased morbidity and mortality from atherothrombotic vascular disease (coronary artery disease, stroke) even without diabetes, and are at increased risk of heart failure (especially diastolic dysfunction) and atrial fibrillation. Modest, sustained weight loss (an initial goal of ~8–10% over 6 months) improves obesity-related complications and quality of life; some complications, including type 2 diabetes (e.g., the DiRECT trial showed remission in nearly half of participants with intensive low-energy dietary intervention), can substantially improve or remit with weight loss (Harrison 22e p.3186–3187, 3190). BMI-based (kg/m²): underweight <18.5; healthy/normal weight 18.5–24.9; overweight 25.0–29.9; obesity class I 30.0–34.9 (high disease risk); obesity class II 35.0–39.9 (very high risk); extreme/class III obesity ≥40 (extremely high risk). Risk is refined by excess abdominal fat (ethnic-specific waist-circumference cutpoints; waist-to-hip ratio >0.9 women / >1.0 men). Disease-staging systems augment BMI: the AACE/ACE staging (stage 0 = no complications; stage 1 = mild-moderate complications; stage 2 = at least one severe complication) and the Edmonton Obesity Staging System (EOSS, grades 0–4 across medical, functional, and psychological domains, independent of BMI) (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187–3188).

obesity increases the mechanical load on the respiratory system through chest wall and abdominal fat, reducing lung volumes and respiratory compliance and increasing the work of breathing. Combined with blunted central ventilatory responsiveness to carbon dioxide and, in most patients, coexisting upper airway obstruction during sleep, this leads to chronic alveolar hypoventilation. Sustained carbon dioxide retention drives renal bicarbonate retention, which further blunts the ventilatory drive. Chronic hypoxaemia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction and, over time, pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular failure. Positive airway pressure therapy and weight reduction improve gas exchange, symptoms, and survival; untreated disease carries high morbidity and mortality from respiratory failure and cor pulmonale.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder is typically chronic with waxing and waning severity, but many patients achieve substantial improvement with exposure and response prevention and adequate pharmacotherapy. Early onset, poor insight, and comorbidity are associated with a more persistent course.

intrinsic liver disease Gallstone disease or biliary obstruction Serum bile acid measurement, ideally with serial monitoring of peak levels Liver function tests including transaminases and bilirubin surveillance, recognising that routine monitoring poorly predicts sudden stillbirth Obstetric cholestasis is a pregnancy-specific liver disorder characterised by pruritus and raised bile acids, typically presenting in the second half of pregnancy The hallmark symptom is generalised itching, often severe and worse at night, classically involving the palms and soles, in the absence of a primary skin rash Diagnosis rests on elevated serum bile acids with or without raised transaminases once other causes of itch and abnormal liver function are excluded The main concern is fetal rather than maternal, as high bile acid concentrations are associated with an increased risk of stillbirth, preterm birth, and meconium-stained liquor The risk of stillbirth rises with the degree of bile acid elevation, so severity is graded on peak bile acid levels and guides timing of delivery Ursodeoxycholic acid is commonly used to relieve maternal itching, though its effect on fetal outcome is limited, and vitamin K may be considered if there is prolonged clotting from fat malabsorption Symptoms and biochemistry resolve after delivery, but the condition recurs in a high proportion of future pregnancies and with oestrogen-containing contraception Persistent abnormal liver function after delivery should prompt investigation for underlying hepatobiliary disease Markedly elevated bile acids indicating higher stillbirth risk and need for planned delivery Coexisting features of pre-eclampsia or HELLP suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis Jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, or severe pruritus in pregnancy without checking bile acids and liver function Failing to exclude pre-eclampsia, HELLP, and acute fatty liver in a woman with abnormal liver tests Over-reliance on cardiotocography to predict a sudden stillbirth it cannot reliably foresee Not grading severity by bile acid level to guide timing of delivery Overlooking persistent postpartum liver dysfunction that signals underlying disease Obstetric cholestasis reflects impaired hepatocellular secretion and enterohepatic circulation of bile acids in genetically susceptible women, in whom the high oestrogen and progesterone levels of pregnancy reduce the function of bile acid transport proteins. This leads to accumulation of bile acids in the maternal circulation, causing pruritus, and their transfer across the placenta is thought to underlie the fetal risks, with high concentrations having arrhythmogenic and vasoconstrictive effects that may contribute to sudden fetal death. Cholestasis can also impair absorption of fat-soluble vitamins including vitamin K. For the mother the condition is usually self-limiting and resolves promptly after birth, though it recurs frequently in later pregnancies and with oestrogen exposure. The principal concern is the fetus, and careful monitoring of bile acid levels with timely delivery reduces perinatal risk; failure of liver function to normalise postpartum should prompt further hepatological assessment.

pelvic floor dysfunction, or both. Mechanical contributors include an anterior rectocele that traps stool, internal rectal intussusception, enterocele, and sigmoidocele; functional contributors include paradoxical puborectalis contraction (anismus), impaired rectal propulsion, and reduced rectal sensation. Chronic straining aggravates prolapse and perineal descent, creating a self-perpetuating cycle. The disorder overlaps with mucosal prolapse syndromes and pelvic organ prolapse. Symptoms often improve with conservative measures and biofeedback where dyssynergia predominates; results of surgery for structural lesions are variable, and recurrence or persistent symptoms are common, so careful patient selection matters.

Recurrent cycles of desaturation-reoxygenation and arousal drive sympathetic activation, surges in blood pressure, oxidative stress, and systemic inflammation, which over time contribute to cardiovascular and metabolic disease. With consistent adherence to positive airway pressure and weight management, symptoms and quality of life usually improve markedly and cardiovascular risk is reduced; poorly controlled or untreated disease carries substantial long-term cardiovascular, metabolic, and accident-related morbidity.

parenteral copper supplementation has limited proven benefit once connective-tissue disease is established Bladder diverticulum rupture presenting as acute abdomen or urosepsis Symptomatic arterial aneurysm or dissection from vascular fragility Recurrent complicated urinary tract infection with obstruction Severe orthostatic hypotension causing syncope and injury Mislabelling the connective-tissue phenotype as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and missing the underlying copper-transport defect Overlooking the diagnostic occipital exostoses on imaging Assuming copper supplementation will reverse established connective-tissue disease Failing to monitor the urinary tract for diverticula and obstructive complications Occipital horn syndrome arises from partial-loss-of-function variants in ATP7A, an X-linked gene encoding a copper-transporting P-type ATPase that delivers copper to the secretory pathway and exports it from enterocytes. Because some residual transporter activity is preserved, the phenotype is milder than the near-complete loss seen in classic Menkes disease. Impaired copper delivery limits the activity of copper-dependent cuproenzymes; reduced lysyl oxidase function in particular disrupts cross-linking of collagen and elastin, producing the lax skin, joint laxity, bladder diverticula, vascular tortuosity, and the characteristic occipital exostoses. Deficiency of other cuproenzymes such as dopamine beta-hydroxylase contributes to autonomic features, while relative sparing of central copper delivery explains the comparatively preserved neurodevelopment. Life expectancy is substantially better than in classic Menkes disease, with survival into adulthood; morbidity stems from connective-tissue complications such as bladder diverticula, hernias, autonomic dysfunction, and occasional vascular events.

another disorder when it reflects trigeminocervical convergence Occipital neuralgia is caused by irritation, entrapment, or injury of the greater, lesser, or third occipital nerves, which arise from the upper cervical (chiefly C2) roots. Compression as the nerve passes through the suboccipital muscles and fascia, degenerative change or instability of the upper cervical spine, or local trauma provoke ectopic discharges and pain referred throughout the nerve's cutaneous territory over the posterior scalp. Convergence of upper cervical and trigeminal afferents in the trigeminocervical complex explains why pain may also be felt in frontal and periorbital regions. Refractory cases can be helped by neurostimulation or surgical decompression, and any underlying cervical pathology should be addressed.

there is no established treatment to reverse the macular dysfunction Unexplained progressive central visual loss with a normal fundus that risks being dismissed as non-organic Asymmetric or unilateral presentation prompting exclusion of an optic neuropathy Rapid deterioration warranting prompt multifocal electroretinography and OCT Affected relatives who may benefit from screening given frequent dominant inheritance Diagnosing non-organic or functional visual loss because the fundus, angiography and full-field electroretinogram are normal Relying on full-field electroretinography alone and omitting multifocal or focal macular testing Overlooking subtle foveal ellipsoid zone disruption on optical coherence tomography Confusing it with an optic neuropathy in asymmetric cases Occult macular dystrophy is an inherited cone dysfunction confined to the central macula, commonly caused by mutations in RP1L1, a gene expressed in photoreceptors and important for outer-segment structure and function. The disorder selectively impairs the central cone photoreceptors while sparing the peripheral retina, so the standard full-field electroretinogram, which reflects the whole retina, remains normal, whereas the focal macular and multifocal electroretinogram are abnormal. Corresponding subtle disruption of the foveal ellipsoid and interdigitation zones on optical coherence tomography reflects the localised photoreceptor dysfunction, with a normal fundus and normal angiography throughout. Central acuity declines slowly and progressively over years to a moderate low-vision level, while peripheral vision, colour vision and night vision are typically preserved.

frequent low-molecular-weight agents include isocyanates, colophony solder flux and certain wood dusts Serial peak flow monitoring recorded several times a day at and away from work is a practical and valuable tool for confirming a work relationship Early diagnosis matters because prolonged continued exposure after symptoms begin predicts persistent asthma even after removal Complete removal from the causative agent, rather than simply reducing exposure, gives the best chance of recovery A confident diagnosis has major implications for the worker's livelihood, so objective confirmation should be sought before advising job change Consider workplace surveillance and review of coworkers, since others exposed to the same agent may also be affected Acute severe bronchospasm following a major irritant exposure or spill Progressive symptoms despite continued exposure indicating risk of fixed airflow obstruction Nocturnal attacks or falling peak flows suggesting poorly controlled disease Features of anaphylaxis with certain protein allergens such as latex Attributing symptoms to ordinary asthma and failing to take an occupational history Advising reduced rather than complete removal from a sensitising agent Relying on symptoms alone without objective serial lung function data Delaying diagnosis so that airway changes become irreversible Overlooking coexisting occupational rhinitis, which often precedes asthma Sensitiser-induced occupational asthma develops through immunological sensitisation to an inhaled workplace agent, often IgE-mediated for high-molecular-weight proteins, leading to airway inflammation, bronchial hyper-responsiveness and reversible airflow obstruction on re-exposure. Outcome depends heavily on how quickly the diagnosis is made and exposure stopped; early cessation gives a good chance of improvement, whereas prolonged exposure before removal is associated with persistent asthma and airway hyper-responsiveness that may not fully resolve.

occupational contact urticaria — work-related contact urticaria, occupational immediate contact reaction allergic contact dermatitis irritant contact dermatitis protein contact dermatitis physical urticarias such as cholinergic or pressure urticaria chronic spontaneous urticaria unrelated to work angio-oedema from other causes contact reaction to airborne irritants detailed occupational history correlating symptoms with specific tasks and materials open and closed (use) application testing on intact and lightly abraded skin skin-prick testing to suspected allergens including latex and foods specific serum IgE to latex, foods and relevant occupational proteins patch testing to exclude concurrent allergic contact dermatitis workplace assessment of materials, gloves and safety data sheets peak-flow or spirometry if associated respiratory symptoms are reported Contact urticaria is an immediate (wheal-and-flare) reaction appearing within minutes of skin contact with a causative agent and usually resolving within hours, in contrast to the delayed course of allergic contact dermatitis. It is classified into immunological (IgE-mediated, often with potential for systemic reactions) and non-immunological (direct mast-cell mediator release without prior sensitisation) forms. Natural rubber latex is a classic immunological occupational cause, particularly in healthcare and laboratory workers wearing powdered gloves; foods are important in catering and food-handling trades. The contact urticaria syndrome describes a spectrum from localised wheals through generalised urticaria to rhinoconjunctivitis, asthma and, at worst, anaphylaxis, so hands-first symptoms can herald systemic risk. Common occupational triggers include latex, foodstuffs (fish, meat, flour, fruits, vegetables), animal proteins and dander, plants, ammonium persulfate in hairdressing, and some preservatives and fragrances. Protein contact dermatitis is a related entity presenting as a chronic eczematous dermatitis with immediate flares on re-exposure, typically in food handlers. Diagnosis relies on careful history plus open and closed application (use) tests, skin-prick testing and specific IgE where appropriate, performed with resuscitation facilities available for potent allergens. Management is avoidance and substitution (for example switching to low-protein powder-free or non-latex gloves), barrier measures, and provision of emergency treatment for those at risk of systemic reactions. history of generalised urticaria, angio-oedema or anaphylaxis after contact associated rhinoconjunctivitis, wheeze or breathlessness suggesting systemic involvement reactions to latex in a healthcare worker with potential for cross-reactive food allergy rapidly spreading wheals beyond the contact site symptoms during high-exposure tasks in workers with known potent-allergen contact Overlooking the diagnosis because wheals have faded by the time of assessment. Failing to recognise localised contact urticaria as a warning of potential anaphylaxis. Performing provocation tests to potent allergens without resuscitation facilities. Confusing protein contact dermatitis with ordinary irritant hand eczema. Neglecting cross-reactivity, such as latex-fruit syndrome, when advising on avoidance. In immunological contact urticaria, prior sensitisation generates allergen-specific IgE bound to cutaneous mast cells; on re-exposure the allergen cross-links IgE, triggering mast-cell degranulation with release of histamine and other mediators that cause the immediate wheal-and-flare response and, when absorption is sufficient, systemic mediator release and anaphylaxis. In non-immunological contact urticaria no prior sensitisation is required: agents such as certain preservatives, fragrances and plant substances act directly on cutaneous vessels and mast cells, sometimes via non-antibody mediators, producing localised wheals that rarely generalise. In protein contact dermatitis, repeated exposure to high-molecular-weight proteins produces a combined immediate hypersensitivity and eczematous reaction. A damaged or eczematous skin barrier enhances penetration of the offending agent and amplifies reactions. Symptoms usually settle promptly once the causative agent is identified and avoided, and localised non-immunological reactions carry a good outlook. Immunological cases, especially latex allergy, may persist and carry an ongoing risk of systemic reactions if exposure continues.

Occupational and Environmental Lung Disease — pneumoconiosis, silicosis, asbestosis Asbestosis vs other causes of diffuse interstitial fibrosis (IPF/UIP) (Harrison 22e p.2234) Chronic beryllium disease vs sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.2234) Silicosis (complicated/PMF) vs coal worker's pneumoconiosis and progressive massive fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2234) Acute silicosis vs pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (Harrison 22e p.2234) Acute farmer's lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis) vs influenza or community-acquired pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.2234) Occupational asthma / RADS vs nonoccupational asthma and COPD (Harrison 22e p.2234) Acute farmer's lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis from thermophilic actinomycete spores) presenting 4-8 h after exposure with fever, chills, malaise, cough, and dyspnea can mimic influenza or pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.2234) Acute silicosis with profuse miliary infiltration may radiographically resemble miliary infectious processes (Harrison 22e p.2234) Pre- and post-shift spirometry (change in FEV1) to detect acute bronchoconstriction (Harrison 22e p.2234) Chest radiograph graded by the ILO International Classification of Radiographs of Pneumoconioses (Harrison 22e p.2234) CT and high-resolution CT (HRCT) - more sensitive than radiograph for lung opacities, pleural thickening, and interstitial change (Harrison 22e p.2234) Pulmonary function testing (restrictive pattern with reduced lung volumes and diffusing capacity in fibrosing disease) (Harrison 22e p.2234) Skin prick testing or specific IgE for immediate hypersensitivity (e.g., flour antigens in bakers) (Harrison 22e p.2234) Specific IgG precipitating antibody titers for hypersensitivity pneumonitis agents (e.g., pigeon antigen in bird handlers) (Harrison 22e p.2234) Beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT) for beryllium sensitization (Harrison 22e p.2234) Fiberoptic bronchoscopy with transbronchial lung biopsy (e.g., to diagnose chronic beryllium disease); occasionally video-assisted thoracoscopic surgical biopsy for definitive diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2234) Chronic beryllium disease closely mimics sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.2234) Aluminum and titanium dioxide exposure can produce a sarcoid-like reaction in lung tissue (Harrison 22e p.2234) Asbestosis mimics idiopathic and other diffuse interstitial fibroses (Harrison 22e p.2234) Hard-metal (tungsten carbide/cobalt) exposure can cause giant cell interstitial pneumonitis (Harrison 22e p.2234) A detailed occupational and environmental exposure history is the single most important step; include hobbies, home characteristics, secondhand smoke, and proximity to traffic/industry, plus short- and long-term exposures in the distant past (Harrison 22e p.2234). Inorganic/organic dust exposure characteristically causes interstitial lung disease with a restrictive pattern and reduced diffusing capacity, whereas dusts/chemicals causing occupational asthma or COPD produce airway obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2234). A drop in FEV1 measured before vs after a work shift can detect an acute occupational bronchoconstrictive response (Harrison 22e p.2234). Radiographic pattern hints at etiology: small rounded opacities suggest silicosis or coal worker's pneumoconiosis, while small linear/irregular opacities suggest asbestosis (Harrison 22e p.2234). Asbestos exposure causes a spectrum of disease: pleural plaques and benign effusions (marking exposure only), asbestosis (interstitial fibrosis), bronchogenic lung cancer, and pleural/peritoneal mesothelioma (Harrison 22e p.2234). Pleural plaques indicate past asbestos exposure but, by themselves, imply only exposure and not pulmonary impairment (Harrison 22e p.2234). Smoking and asbestos exposure interact more than additively, producing lung cancer risk greater than the sum of each factor; mesothelioma risk is NOT associated with smoking (Harrison 22e p.2234). Silicosis raises the risk of mycobacterial (including M. tuberculosis), atypical mycobacterial, and fungal infection because silica impairs alveolar macrophage function; treatment of latent TB is given for a longer duration in these patients (Harrison 22e p.2234). Eggshell calcification of hilar nodes (seen in up to ~20% of cases) is a characteristic radiographic clue to silicosis (Harrison 22e p.2234). Acute (accelerated) silicosis from very heavy exposure (e.g., sandblasting in confined spaces, denim sandblasting, artificial-stone countertop fabrication) can resemble pulmonary alveolar proteinosis with a 'crazy paving' HRCT pattern and may progress despite stopping exposure (Harrison 22e p.2234). Chronic beryllium disease mimics sarcoidosis (noncaseating granulomas); the distinguishing feature is a beryllium-specific cell-mediated (delayed hypersensitivity) immune response demonstrated by the beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT) (Harrison 22e p.2234). Caplan syndrome is the combination of pneumoconiotic nodules and seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, first described in coal miners and later in silicosis (Harrison 22e p.2234). Documented mesothelioma in a patient with occupational/environmental asbestos exposure may be compensable, as >80% of mesotheliomas are associated with asbestos exposure (Harrison 22e p.2234). Mesothelioma may follow relatively short asbestos exposures (<=1-2 years) with latency up to ~40 years - a thorough exposure history is essential (Harrison 22e p.2234) Lung cancer after asbestos exposure has a minimum latency of ~15-19 years from first exposure (Harrison 22e p.2234) Progressive massive fibrosis (PMF), occurring in complicated silicosis and CWP, causes severe lung function deficits and is associated with premature mortality; PMF is rising at an alarming rate in the Appalachian coal belt (Harrison 22e p.2234) Active tuberculosis risk is increased in silicosis (Harrison 22e p.2234) Acute silicosis can be severe and progressive even after exposure ceases (Harrison 22e p.2234) Failing to take an occupational/environmental exposure history is the cardinal pitfall - the etiologic link to occupation is missed unless specifically sought, e.g., asking about beryllium exposure in a patient labeled as having sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.2234) The ILO radiographic classification, though useful for screening populations, is problematic for the individual worker: rounded-opacity disease may look extensive on film with minimal functional impairment, whereas linear/irregular opacities (asbestosis) may lead to underestimation of impairment until late (Harrison 22e p.2234) In early chronic beryllium disease both chest imaging and pulmonary function tests may be normal (Harrison 22e p.2234) Attributing dust-related chronic bronchitis/COPD solely to occupation without accounting for cigarette smoking, whose effect is generally additive (Harrison 22e p.2234) Overlooking that talc and vermiculite may be contaminated with asbestos, conferring fibrosis, lung cancer, and mesothelioma risk (Harrison 22e p.2234) Combat-related embedded metal fragments (shrapnel) in veterans may contain beryllium and serve as an unrecognized exposure source (Harrison 22e p.2234) Disease depends on the chemical/physical properties of the inhaled agent, which determine dose and site of deposition: water-soluble gases (ammonia, SO2) are absorbed in proximal airways causing irritation/bronchoconstriction, while less-soluble gases (NO2, phosgene) reach bronchioles/alveoli causing chemical pneumonitis. Particles >10-15 micrometres deposit in the nose/throat; particles <10 micrometres reach below the larynx, with coarse-mode (~2.5-10 micrometres, crustal elements like silica) depositing high in the tracheobronchial tree, fine-mode (<2.5 micrometres, from combustion/high-temperature processes) dominating surface area for toxin delivery to lower airways, and ultrafine (<0.1 micrometres, nanoparticles) potentially entering the circulation. Asbestos fibers induce fibrosis through oxidative injury from reactive oxygen species generated by surface transition metals and by phagocytosing cells. Silica causes alveolar macrophage dysfunction (predisposing to infection) and has immunoadjuvant properties (predisposing to autoimmune connective tissue disease). Beryllium drives a CD4+ T-cell-mediated granulomatous inflammation, with susceptibility strongly linked to HLA-DP alleles bearing glutamic acid at position 69 of the beta chain. (Harrison 22e p.2234) Outcome varies by exposure and disease. Pleural plaques alone do not imply impairment. Simple silicosis and simple CWP are often present without significant functional impairment, but nodular fibrosis can progress even after exposure ceases, coalescing into complicated disease and PMF, which carries severe functional deficits and premature mortality. Acute silicosis may be severe and progressive despite stopping exposure. No specific therapy exists for asbestosis (supportive care as for any diffuse interstitial fibrosis); newly diagnosed cases usually reflect exposures from many years earlier. Asbestos exposure carries excess lung cancer risk (latency ~15-19 years) and mesothelioma risk (latency up to ~40 years). (Harrison 22e p.2234) Silicosis and coal worker's pneumoconiosis are categorized as simple (small rounded opacities, usually without functional impairment) versus complicated (nodules >=1 cm) which can progress to progressive massive fibrosis (PMF, conglomerate masses >1 cm with restrictive and obstructive impairment). Acute (accelerated) silicosis is distinguished from chronic silicosis by very heavy short-duration exposure and an alveolar-proteinosis-like presentation. Occupational asthma is divided into immunologic (high- vs low-molecular-weight stimuli, with a latency period) and irritative (reactive airway dysfunction syndrome, RADS) forms. (Harrison 22e p.2234)

disease Progressive rather than stable visual loss prompting reassessment for a retinal dystrophy Marked asymmetry of findings requiring exclusion of other pathology Failure to thrive or dysmorphism suggesting a broader syndrome Overlooking the diagnosis in a boy with nystagmus because skin and hair look normal Missing carrier status in the mother by not examining her iris and fundus Failing to check for syndromic albinism when there is bruising or infection Attributing poor acuity solely to nystagmus and neglecting foveal hypoplasia Ocular albinism type 1 arises from mutations in the X-linked GPR143 gene, whose product regulates melanosome maturation and size within the retinal pigment epithelium and other melanocytes. Loss of function leads to abnormal, enlarged melanosomes and deficient ocular melanin, chiefly affecting the eye while skin and hair are relatively spared. Reduced retinal pigment impairs normal foveal development (foveal hypoplasia) and disturbs the guidance cues that determine crossing of ganglion cell axons at the chiasm, causing excessive decussation and misrouting. The combined effects produce nystagmus, subnormal acuity, iris transillumination and defective binocular vision. Female carriers show mosaic features owing to random X-inactivation. Vision is subnormal but usually stable, with acuity commonly in the low-vision range; most individuals function well with refractive correction, tints and low-vision support.

fornix shortening or corneal involvement indicating aggressive disease Oesophageal or laryngeal mucosal involvement risking stricture and airway compromise Corneal ulceration or perforation from surface failure Acute worsening after ocular surgery signalling a disease flare Attributing chronic conjunctival inflammation to dry eye and missing early cicatrisation Relying on topical therapy alone when systemic immunosuppression is required Operating on lids or the ocular surface during active inflammation and precipitating a flare Overlooking a drug-induced pseudopemphigoid pattern from chronic topical medication Failing to screen for extraocular mucosal disease that carries its own morbidity Ocular cicatricial pemphigoid is an autoimmune type II hypersensitivity disorder in which autoantibodies are directed against components of the epithelial basement membrane zone of mucous membranes. Antibody and complement deposition triggers chronic subepithelial inflammation and activation of fibroblasts, leading to progressive subconjunctival fibrosis and scarring. This cicatrisation destroys goblet cells and accessory lacrimal tissue, shortens the fornices and produces symblepharon, while lid malposition and trichiasis further damage the ocular surface. Loss of limbal stem cells and severe aqueous and mucin deficiency culminate in corneal keratinisation, scarring and blindness. Without systemic immunosuppression the disease tends to progress relentlessly to bilateral blindness, but early control of inflammation can arrest scarring and preserve vision; established cicatricial damage is generally irreversible.

causing rubeosis Carotid Doppler ultrasonography, and where indicated CT or MR angiography, to assess carotid stenosis Fluorescein angiography to demonstrate delayed arm-to-retina and arteriovenous transit and patchy choroidal filling Gonioscopy to detect angle neovascularisation and intraocular pressure measurement Dilated fundus examination for mid-peripheral haemorrhages and vascular changes exposure to bright light Anterior segment signs include episcleral congestion, a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil, iris and angle neovascularisation (rubeosis) and, in some, flare and low intraocular
