life-threatening condition, mandating carotid imaging and vascular risk management to reduce stroke and cardiac mortality Management principles combine treatment of the carotid disease and systemic risk factors with panretinal photocoagulation and anti-VEGF for neovascularisation and control of neovascular glaucoma Iris or angle neovascularisation heralding neovascular glaucoma Critical carotid stenosis carrying a high risk of stroke Rapidly progressive visual loss from worsening ischaemia Systemic features suggesting giant cell arteritis in an older patient Misdiagnosing the retinopathy as an ordinary central retinal vein occlusion and missing the underlying carotid disease Overlooking the systemic (stroke and cardiac) mortality risk and failing to refer for vascular assessment Being falsely reassured by a normal or low intraocular pressure despite florid angle neovascularisation Not considering giant cell arteritis in an older patient with ocular ischaemia Delaying panretinal photocoagulation or anti-VEGF until neovascular glaucoma is established Ocular ischaemic syndrome results from chronic hypoperfusion of the eye, most often due to severe stenosis or occlusion of the ipsilateral internal or common carotid artery, and less commonly ophthalmic artery or aortic arch disease. Reduced ocular perfusion pressure causes chronic ischaemia of the retina, choroid and anterior segment. Retinal and anterior segment hypoxia stimulates release of vascular endothelial growth factor, driving neovascularisation of the iris, angle and retina that can progress to neovascular glaucoma. Ischaemia of the ciliary body reduces aqueous production, which can paradoxically keep intraocular pressure low despite angle neovascularisation. Persistent hypoperfusion leads to progressive retinal and optic nerve damage. The visual prognosis is generally guarded, particularly once neovascularisation or neovascular glaucoma develops, and the syndrome carries a substantial risk of stroke and cardiovascular death, so systemic vascular management is as important as ocular treatment.

Ocular neuromyotonia — ONM Superior oblique myokymia Cyclic oculomotor palsy Thyroid eye disease with restriction Myasthenia gravis (fatigable diplopia) Decompensating phoria Detailed history of prior cranial radiotherapy or sellar disease MRI of the brain, orbits and cavernous sinus to exclude compression or recurrence Orthoptic assessment during and between attacks Acetylcholine-receptor antibody testing to exclude myasthenia when relevant Paroxysmal involuntary sustained contraction of one or more extraocular muscles causing episodic diplopia Classically follows sellar or parasellar radiotherapy, often months to years later Any of the ocular motor nerves may be affected, producing a transient strabismus in the field of the involved muscle Attacks are often triggered by sustained eccentric gaze and last seconds to minutes Between attacks ocular alignment may be normal, which can lead to misdiagnosis Membrane-stabilising agents that reduce neuronal excitability are the usual treatment New or progressive structural lesion on imaging Additional cranial nerve involvement Signs of tumour recurrence in a previously irradiated field Features suggesting myasthenia (fatigability, ptosis, bulbar signs) Missing the diagnosis because alignment is normal between attacks Attributing episodic diplopia to myasthenia without antibody or imaging workup Overlooking a history of prior radiotherapy Confusing sustained deviation with the shimmering oscillopsia of superior oblique myokymia Ocular neuromyotonia is attributed to impaired membrane stability and spontaneous or triggered discharges within an ocular motor nerve, frequently after radiation-induced or compressive injury that alters axonal excitability. The abnormal firing produces sustained contraction (tonic spasm) of the muscles supplied by the affected nerve, generating an intermittent deviation and diplopia, particularly after maintained eccentric gaze. The condition is benign for vision and often responds well to membrane-stabilising therapy, though symptoms can persist for years and may recur if treatment is stopped.

Chronic ultraviolet damage, alongside cofactors such as human papillomavirus infection, immunosuppression, and older age, induces mutations in limbal epithelial stem cells, the presumed cells of origin at the interpalpebral limbus. Disordered proliferation begins as partial-thickness dysplasia, advances to full-thickness carcinoma in situ while the basement membrane remains intact, and, if the basement membrane is breached, becomes invasive squamous cell carcinoma with potential for deeper ocular and, less commonly, regional spread. The intraepithelial phases are typically indolent and amenable to topical therapy, whereas invasion signifies a more serious tumour requiring definitive surgical management. Most intraepithelial disease is controlled with complete excision or topical therapy and carries an excellent prognosis, though recurrence is not uncommon after narrow-margin surgery; invasive squamous cell carcinoma has a more guarded outlook with risk of ocular invasion and, rarely, regional or distant spread.

oculocutaneous albinism — OCA, albinism Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome Chediak-Higashi syndrome Ocular albinism (X-linked, GPR143) Griscelli syndrome Waardenburg syndrome type II Menkes disease Phenylketonuria-related hypopigmentation Comprehensive ophthalmological assessment including visual acuity, nystagmus evaluation, and fundoscopy for foveal hypoplasia Visual evoked potentials demonstrating chiasmal misrouting Molecular genetic panel testing (TYR, OCA2, TYRP1, SLC45A2 and syndromic genes) Full blood count and platelet aggregation studies where Hermansky-Pudlak or Chediak-Higashi is suspected Peripheral blood film for giant granules in neutrophils (Chediak-Higashi) Regular dermatological surveillance with dermoscopy for cutaneous malignancy A genetically heterogeneous group of autosomal recessive disorders of melanin biosynthesis affecting skin, hair, and eyes, with OCA1 (tyrosinase/TYR), OCA2 (OCA2/P gene), OCA3 (TYRP1), and OCA4 (SLC45A2) accounting for most cases. OCA1A reflects complete tyrosinase deficiency with lifelong white hair, milky skin, and translucent blue-grey irides, whereas OCA1B (yellow variant) permits some pigment accumulation with age. The ocular phenotype is the diagnostic core: congenital nystagmus, foveal hypoplasia, reduced visual acuity, iris transillumination, and photophobia occur across all subtypes. Misrouting of the optic nerve fibres at the chiasm, with excessive decussation, is a defining neuro-ophthalmic feature demonstrable on visual evoked potentials. Cutaneous melanin deficiency confers a markedly increased lifetime risk of actinic damage, squamous and basal cell carcinoma, and melanoma, mandating lifelong sun protection. Syndromic albinism must be excluded: Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (bleeding diathesis, pulmonary fibrosis, ceroid deposition) and Chediak-Higashi syndrome (immunodeficiency, giant granules) are life-limiting mimics. TYR mutations remain heat-sensitive in the temperature-sensitive variant, producing darker hair at cooler acral sites analogous to the Siamese-cat pattern. Skin and hair colour vary widely between and within subtypes and ethnic backgrounds, so ocular signs rather than degree of cutaneous pigment guide diagnosis. Easy bruising or bleeding suggesting Hermansky-Pudlak platelet dysfunction Recurrent severe infections or a hyperinflammatory (accelerated) phase indicating Chediak-Higashi syndrome Progressive respiratory decline from pulmonary fibrosis in Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome New, changing, or ulcerated cutaneous lesion suspicious for skin cancer Neurological deterioration pointing to a syndromic or alternative diagnosis Assuming visible skin or hair pigment excludes albinism, when ocular features are the true diagnostic key Missing syndromic albinism by failing to enquire about bleeding, infection, or pulmonary symptoms Under-emphasising lifelong photoprotection and skin cancer surveillance in darker-skinned patients Confusing OCA with X-linked ocular albinism, which spares the skin and affects mainly males Neglecting low-vision aids and educational support, thereby compounding avoidable disability Oculocutaneous albinism results from mutations that reduce or abolish melanin synthesis within otherwise structurally normal melanocytes. In OCA1 the defect lies in tyrosinase, the rate-limiting enzyme catalysing the conversion of tyrosine to dopaquinone; complete deficiency (OCA1A) yields no melanin, while partial activity (OCA1B) permits limited pigment. Other subtypes disrupt melanosomal proteins that regulate melanosome pH, maturation, and tyrosinase trafficking: the OCA2 (P) protein and SLC45A2 (MATP) influence melanosomal acidification and enzyme processing, and TYRP1 stabilises tyrosinase and directs eumelanin synthesis. The resulting hypomelanosis affects the developing eye, where melanin is required for normal foveal development and correct routing of retinal ganglion cell axons; its absence produces foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus, and abnormal chiasmal decussation. In the skin, absent melanin removes the natural photoprotective shield, accelerating ultraviolet-induced mutagenesis and photoageing. Isolated oculocutaneous albinism is compatible with a normal lifespan, though visual impairment is lifelong and non-progressive, and diligent photoprotection substantially reduces the otherwise high risk of skin malignancy. Syndromic forms such as Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi carry a markedly worse prognosis owing to bleeding, pulmonary, or immunological complications.

Oculodentodigital dysplasia — GJA1, ODDD, oculodentoosseous dysplasia, connexin-43 disorder Other syndromic syndactylies (e.g. Apert syndrome) Hallermann-Streiff syndrome Hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (dental and craniofacial features) Craniofacial-digital syndromes Leukodystrophies (for the neurological features) Isolated congenital glaucoma or microphthalmia GJA1 sequencing to confirm the diagnosis Ophthalmic assessment including intraocular pressure and screening for glaucoma Hand and skeletal radiographs to characterise syndactyly and bone changes Dental assessment for enamel hypoplasia and tooth anomalies Neurological evaluation and brain MRI where neurological features are present Family evaluation given autosomal dominant inheritance A recognisable pattern of ocular, dental and digital anomalies caused by variants in GJA1, encoding the gap junction protein connexin-43 The hand hallmark is type III syndactyly, characteristically fusion of the fourth and fifth fingers, sometimes with camptodactyly Ocular features include microphthalmia, microcornea and a narrow palpebral fissure, with a risk of glaucoma Enamel hypoplasia and small, malformed teeth are typical, alongside a thin nose with hypoplastic alae and a narrow nasal bridge Usually autosomal dominant; neurological problems including spasticity and white matter changes can emerge, sometimes progressively The combination of syndactyly, small eyes and dental anomalies with a distinctive nose is highly suggestive Management is supportive with ophthalmic surveillance (including for glaucoma), dental care and monitoring for neurological features Raised intraocular pressure or established glaucoma threatening vision Progressive spasticity, gait disturbance or other neurological decline Significant visual impairment from microphthalmia or associated anomalies Functional impairment of the hands from severe syndactyly Missing glaucoma because intraocular pressure is not routinely monitored Treating the syndactyly in isolation without recognising the broader syndrome Overlooking evolving neurological features that may appear years after diagnosis Failing to examine and counsel apparently mildly affected relatives Oculodentodigital dysplasia is caused by variants in GJA1, which encodes connexin-43, a component of gap junctions that permit direct intercellular communication. Impaired connexin-43 channel function disrupts coordinated signalling between cells in developing eyes, teeth, digits, bone and neural tissue. This explains the pleiotropic phenotype of microphthalmia and glaucoma risk, enamel hypoplasia, syndactyly and craniofacial features, as well as the later neurological manifestations attributable to disturbed gap-junction communication in the central nervous system. Life expectancy is generally normal, but vision is at risk from glaucoma and ocular anomalies, and a subset develop progressive neurological problems, so long-term ophthalmic and neurological follow-up is advisable.

evolving palsy warrants imaging even if the pupil is initially spared Pupil involvement, especially with acute severe pain Signs of raised intracranial pressure or reduced conscious level Progression or additional cranial nerve involvement Bilateral involvement or evolving deficits Falsely reassuring pupil sparing in an incomplete or evolving palsy Delaying angiography in a pupil-involving palsy Attributing the palsy to diabetes without imaging when features are atypical Missing aberrant regeneration that indicates a chronic compressive cause The pupillary parasympathetic fibres travel superficially on the oculomotor nerve and derive their blood supply from surface vessels, so external compression (from an aneurysm, tumour or uncal herniation) tends to involve the pupil early. In contrast, microvascular ischaemia from diabetes or hypertension damages the central fascicles while sparing the peripheral pupillomotor fibres, producing a pupil-sparing palsy. Compression of the nerve as it passes near the posterior communicating artery or through the cavernous sinus and superior orbital fissure accounts for the classic anatomical patterns. Outcome depends on the cause; microvascular palsies commonly recover over weeks to a few months, whereas compressive palsies depend on timely treatment of the underlying lesion, and a ruptured aneurysm is life-threatening.

Oculopalatal tremor — symptomatic palatal tremor, oculopalatal myoclonus Essential palatal tremor Other acquired pendular nystagmus (for example demyelinating) See-saw nystagmus Downbeat or other central nystagmus Brainstem or cerebellar tremor syndromes MRI of the brainstem showing hypertrophic olivary degeneration Examination of the palate and eyes for synchronous rhythmic movement History of a preceding brainstem or cerebellar lesion Neuro-ophthalmological assessment of the nystagmus and oscillopsia Investigation of the underlying causative lesion if not already known A symptomatic tremor combining rhythmic palatal movement with a synchronous pendular, often vertical, nystagmus It develops months after a lesion in the brainstem or cerebellum affecting the triangle of Guillain and Mollaret The delay to onset corresponds to the development of hypertrophic degeneration of the inferior olive The pendular nystagmus causes oscillopsia and is frequently the most disabling symptom for vision Unlike essential palatal tremor, it typically persists during sleep and is not primarily associated with an ear click MRI characteristically shows enlargement and increased signal of the inferior olive Disabling oscillopsia impairing vision New or progressive brainstem or cerebellar signs An undiagnosed underlying lesion requiring evaluation Features suggesting an alternative progressive disorder Confusing it with benign essential palatal tremor despite the nystagmus and persistence in sleep Overlooking the typical delayed onset after a brainstem lesion Missing hypertrophic olivary degeneration on imaging Underestimating the visual disability from oscillopsia Oculopalatal tremor arises after a lesion interrupts the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway (the Guillain-Mollaret triangle), leading to transsynaptic hypertrophic degeneration of the inferior olivary nucleus. The abnormal, hypertrophied olive develops rhythmic oscillatory activity that drives synchronous rhythmic movements of the palate and the eyes, producing pendular nystagmus. The characteristic delay of months between the causative lesion and symptom onset reflects the time course of olivary hypertrophy. The tremor and pendular nystagmus tend to persist and are often difficult to treat; some patients gain partial benefit from medication for the nystagmus, but the underlying olivary change is irreversible.

Significant weight loss or malnutrition Choking episodes indicating unsafe swallowing Ptosis obscuring vision and impairing safe mobility Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting an alternative diagnosis Mistaking the ptosis and ophthalmoplegia for myasthenia gravis and giving inappropriate treatment Underestimating the aspiration risk from progressive dysphagia Overlooking the family history given the autosomal dominant late-onset pattern Neglecting nutritional assessment as swallowing deteriorates Failing to consider the diagnosis in older adults presenting with isolated ptosis Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy is caused by a modest expansion of a GCN repeat in PABPN1, which lengthens the polyalanine tract of the poly(A)-binding protein nuclear 1. The mutant protein misfolds and aggregates into intranuclear inclusions within muscle-fibre nuclei, disturbing RNA processing and polyadenylation. The selective vulnerability of the levator palpebrae, pharyngeal, and later proximal limb muscles produces the characteristic combination of progressive ptosis, dysphagia, and eventual limb-girdle weakness. Aggregate accumulation over decades accounts for the late onset and slow progression. Progression is slow and life expectancy is often near normal, but dysphagia-related complications such as aspiration and malnutrition are the principal threats to health. Proactive swallowing management and timely surgical intervention improve quality of life and reduce aspiration risk.

from remnants of the dental lamina and is lined by a distinctive keratinising epithelium whose basal cells show intrinsic proliferative activity, giving it a more neoplastic-like behaviour than ordinary odontogenic cysts. Growth occurs by mural expansion and extension through cancellous bone rather than by hydrostatic pressure alone, and small satellite cysts and epithelial islands within the fibrous capsule act as sources of recurrence if left behind. Inactivation of the PTCH1 tumour-suppressor gene in the sonic hedgehog pathway underlies both sporadic lesions and the multiple keratocysts of the naevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome. Individual cysts are benign and treatable, but recurrence is common, particularly after simple enucleation, so prolonged follow-up is essential; the prognosis is influenced by the treatment method and, in syndromic patients, by the tendency to form new cysts over time.

sinusitis, particularly when symptoms are refractory to standard rhinological treatment A foul smell or taste and unilateral purulent discharge are characteristic clues pointing to a dental origin collaboration with ENT Spread beyond the sinus with orbital swelling, visual changes, or signs of intracranial extension Features suggesting invasive fungal sinusitis in immunocompromised or diabetic patients Persistent unilateral disease or a mass raising suspicion of malignancy Systemic sepsis from an odontogenic infection extending into deep spaces Treating recurrent unilateral maxillary sinusitis medically while missing the dental cause Overlooking an oroantral communication after upper molar extraction Failing to test the vitality of upper posterior teeth adjacent to the sinus Neglecting displaced roots or implants within the sinus as a persistent nidus Odontogenic sinusitis develops when the integrity of the barrier between the maxillary posterior teeth and the sinus floor is breached, allowing bacteria and inflammatory products to enter the sinus. This may follow periapical or periodontal infection extending through thin or dehiscent bone, an oroantral communication created during extraction, or displacement of roots, foreign material, or implants into the sinus. The resulting mixed, often anaerobic, infection disrupts mucociliary clearance and can obstruct the ostiomeatal complex, perpetuating sinus inflammation. Because the driver is dental, the process persists until the source is eliminated. Prognosis is good when the dental cause is identified and treated, with resolution of sinus symptoms; failure to address the source leads to persistent or recurrent sinusitis and occasional serious complications.

oesophageal hypomotility — ineffective oesophageal motility, hypocontractile oesophagus, absent contractility achalasia (particularly when sphincter relaxation is impaired) systemic sclerosis and other connective-tissue disease oesophagopathy gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with secondary peristaltic dysfunction diabetic or other autonomic neuropathy affecting the oesophagus hypothyroidism-related dysmotility medication or opioid-induced hypomotility oesophageal involvement by amyloidosis or a myopathic process high-resolution oesophageal manometry with bolus-transit or impedance assessment upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsies to exclude mucosal disease and eosinophilic oesophagitis ambulatory pH-impedance monitoring to quantify reflux burden timed barium oesophagram assessing clearance and emptying connective-tissue disease serology (antinuclear and scleroderma-associated antibodies) thyroid function tests and glycaemic assessment gastric emptying study when a diffuse gut dysmotility is suspected Encompasses a spectrum from ineffective oesophageal motility, defined on high-resolution manometry by a high proportion of weak or failed swallows, to absent contractility where no effective peristalsis is present with normal sphincter relaxation. Strongly associated with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease because poor peristaltic clearance prolongs acid contact time and predisposes to severe reflux and its complications. Absent contractility with a poorly relaxing sphincter should prompt evaluation for achalasia; when relaxation is normal it may reflect an end-stage or scleroderma-type pattern. Systemic sclerosis characteristically produces a hypomotile smooth-muscle oesophagus with a patulous, hypotensive lower sphincter, and oesophageal involvement is often an early feature of the disease. Symptoms include dysphagia (often to solids and worse when supine), heartburn and regurgitation; some patients are asymptomatic despite marked manometric abnormality. Management centres on aggressive acid suppression and reflux precautions rather than prokinetics, as available prokinetic agents have limited efficacy on the aperistaltic oesophagus. Anti-reflux surgery must be approached with caution because a partial (rather than complete) fundoplication is usually preferred to avoid precipitating dysphagia in a poorly clearing oesophagus. Screen for an underlying connective-tissue disease, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism or a myopathic/neuropathic process when hypomotility is severe or of recent onset. progressive dysphagia with weight loss suggesting stricture, malignancy or evolving achalasia features of systemic sclerosis such as Raynaud phenomenon, skin tightening or telangiectasia recurrent aspiration or nocturnal respiratory symptoms from reflux and retention severe erosive oesophagitis, ulceration or peptic stricture on endoscopy anaemia or gastrointestinal bleeding Relying on prokinetic drugs, which rarely restore effective peristalsis in a severely hypomotile oesophagus. Performing a complete (360-degree) fundoplication in a poorly clearing oesophagus and thereby causing intractable dysphagia. Missing an underlying connective-tissue disease, especially systemic sclerosis, in a patient presenting with reflux and dysphagia. Failing to distinguish absent contractility with impaired sphincter relaxation (achalasia) from that with normal relaxation. Underestimating reflux burden and its complications because peristaltic failure prolongs acid exposure. Oesophageal hypomotility results from failure of the smooth-muscle segment to generate contractions of adequate vigour and coordination to clear a bolus. The defect may lie in the myenteric neurons, in cholinergic excitatory signalling, or in the smooth muscle itself. In systemic sclerosis, progressive smooth-muscle atrophy and fibrosis of the distal two-thirds of the oesophagus, together with incompetence of the lower oesophageal sphincter, produce weak or absent peristalsis and severe reflux. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy, hypothyroidism, amyloidosis and certain medications can produce similar hypocontractility. The common physiological consequence is impaired bolus transit and defective acid clearance, which drives reflux disease and, when severe, oesophageal retention and dysphagia. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause: idiopathic ineffective motility is often stable and managed by reflux control, whereas the hypomotility of systemic sclerosis tends to be progressive and predisposes to severe reflux disease, stricture and Barrett's oesophagus. Absent contractility is generally irreversible, so treatment aims to control reflux and preserve nutrition rather than restore peristalsis.

oesophageal web — esophageal web, cervical oesophageal web, Plummer-Vinson web Schatzki ring (distal oesophageal mucosal ring) peptic stricture from gastro-oesophageal reflux eosinophilic oesophagitis with rings or strictures cricopharyngeal bar or dysfunction extrinsic compression (cervical osteophyte, aberrant vessel, thyroid mass) oesophageal carcinoma or post-cricoid malignancy oropharyngeal (transfer) dysphagia of neuromuscular origin barium swallow with dedicated lateral and anteroposterior cervical oesophageal views full blood count with iron studies (ferritin, transferrin saturation) to detect iron-deficiency anaemia upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with careful inspection of the cervical oesophagus oesophageal biopsies where eosinophilic oesophagitis or a mucocutaneous disorder is suspected high-resolution oesophageal manometry if a motility disorder is considered evaluation for occult blood loss and coeliac disease when iron deficiency is unexplained An oesophageal web is a thin, eccentric mucosal membrane composed of squamous epithelium and lamina propria, typically arising from the anterior wall of the cervical (upper) oesophagus just below the cricopharyngeus. Most webs are asymptomatic incidental findings; symptomatic webs cause intermittent, non-progressive solid-food dysphagia because they only partially occlude the lumen. The classic association is Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Brown-Kelly) syndrome: a cervical web with iron-deficiency anaemia and dysphagia, seen predominantly in middle-aged women. Barium swallow with careful lateral views of the cervical oesophagus is more sensitive than endoscopy, which can rupture a thin web before it is recognised. Webs differ from Schatzki rings by location (cervical versus distal), circumferentiality (webs are usually partial and eccentric, rings circumferential) and histology (webs are squamous-lined only). Simple mechanical disruption during endoscopy or through-the-scope balloon or bougie dilatation is usually curative, and correction of underlying iron deficiency should accompany treatment in Plummer-Vinson syndrome. Plummer-Vinson syndrome carries an increased long-term risk of post-cricoid and upper oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, warranting surveillance awareness. Multiple or lower webs, or webs with mucosal fragility, should raise suspicion of an associated dermatological or immune disorder such as epidermolysis bullosa or a mucocutaneous blistering condition. progressive rather than intermittent dysphagia, suggesting stricture or malignancy weight loss, odynophagia or anorexia raising concern for carcinoma haematemesis or evidence of significant gastrointestinal blood loss a neck mass or hoarseness suggesting post-cricoid or laryngeal malignancy recurrent aspiration or an inability to manage secretions Missing a thin cervical web on endoscopy because it is inadvertently disrupted or lies just below the upper sphincter before careful inspection. Failing to investigate and correct underlying iron deficiency, so that dysphagia recurs. Attributing all dysphagia to the web without excluding a coexisting motility disorder or malignancy. Overlooking the malignancy risk in Plummer-Vinson syndrome and omitting appropriate follow-up. Confusing a web with a Schatzki ring and mislocating or mistreating the lesion. An oesophageal web is a protrusion of normal mucosa (stratified squamous epithelium over vascular connective tissue of the lamina propria) into the lumen, without a muscular component, producing a shelf-like partial obstruction. In the cervical oesophagus the aetiology is often idiopathic but is strongly linked to chronic iron deficiency, where impaired iron-dependent oxidative enzyme activity in rapidly regenerating mucosal cells is thought to promote atrophy and abnormal epithelial healing with web formation. Webs may also be congenital, or acquired secondary to chronic mucosal injury from gastro-oesophageal reflux, eosinophilic oesophagitis, graft-versus-host disease, mucocutaneous blistering disorders (epidermolysis bullosa, cicatricial pemphigoid, lichen planus) or prior caustic or radiation injury. The partial luminal narrowing impedes passage of a solid bolus while liquids pass freely, explaining the characteristic intermittent solid dysphagia. The prognosis is excellent for isolated webs, which usually resolve with simple dilatation and correction of iron deficiency, though recurrence can occur. Patients with Plummer-Vinson syndrome require awareness of a heightened long-term risk of upper aerodigestive squamous cell carcinoma.

Oesophagostomiasis — Oesophagostomum infection, esophagostomiasis, nodular worm disease, Dapaong tumour Intestinal tuberculosis with an ileocaecal mass Crohn's disease and other inflammatory bowel disease Colonic or caecal carcinoma Amoeboma or other infective mass lesion Appendicular or other intra-abdominal abscess Other tissue-invasive helminth infection with eosinophilia Cross-sectional imaging or ultrasound demonstrating bowel wall nodules or an abdominal mass Full blood count showing marked eosinophilia Histopathology of excised or biopsied nodules identifying the larvae Stool microscopy, recognising that eggs and larvae may be absent Colonoscopy with biopsy when malignancy or inflammatory bowel disease is considered Inflammatory markers and assessment for abscess formation Caused by Oesophagostomum species, nodular worms of the large bowel, with human disease concentrated in parts of West Africa, notably northern Togo and Ghana Acquired by ingesting infective larvae from soil or contaminated food and water, the larvae burrowing into the intestinal wall The hallmark is formation of inflammatory nodules or abscesses in the colonic wall, which may coalesce into a palpable abdominal mass The classic uninodular presentation, the Dapaong tumour, is a painful abdominal wall or intra-abdominal mass, while multinodular disease causes diffuse colitis-like symptoms Presentations include abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss and a palpable mass, often with marked eosinophilia Diagnosis relies on imaging showing bowel wall nodules and on histology of excised or biopsied lesions; larvae may not appear in the stool Treatment is with a benzimidazole anthelmintic such as albendazole, with surgical drainage or excision for large nodules or abscesses A large or enlarging abdominal mass raising concern for malignancy or abscess Signs of intestinal obstruction or perforation Systemic sepsis from a secondarily infected nodule Persistent symptoms after treatment prompting reassessment Mistaking a nodular mass for colonic carcinoma, tuberculosis or Crohn's disease Relying on stool examination, which is frequently negative in tissue-dwelling disease Overlooking the diagnosis in travellers or residents from endemic West African foci Failing to drain or excise large abscesses in addition to giving anthelmintic therapy Oesophagostomum species are nematodes related to hookworms whose natural hosts include primates, pigs and ruminants. Humans acquire infection by ingesting infective larvae from contaminated soil, food or water. In the intestine the larvae invade the wall of the colon and terminal ileum, where they encyst and provoke an intense inflammatory reaction. The host response forms characteristic granulomatous nodules and abscesses around the developing larvae, which may remain solitary as a large tumour-like mass or occur as multiple smaller nodules producing a colitis-like picture. Some larvae complete development, emerge into the lumen and mature into adult worms in the large bowel, while others remain trapped and die within the nodules. The inflammatory nodules account for the palpable masses, abdominal pain and, when they erupt or become secondarily infected, for abscess formation and local complications. Prognosis is generally good with anthelmintic treatment and, where needed, surgical management of nodules; complications such as large abscesses or obstruction increase morbidity but are usually treatable.

Ogilvie syndrome (acute colonic pseudo-obstruction) — acute colonic pseudo-obstruction, ACPO, colonic ileus Mechanical colonic obstruction from tumour, stricture or volvulus Toxic megacolon from colonic and caecal diameter CT abdomen or water-soluble contrast enema to exclude mechanical obstruction Electrolytes including potassium, magnesium, calcium and phosphate Thyroid function and review of the drug chart for opioids and anticholinergics Serial examination and imaging to monitor caecal diameter Presents with massive colonic distension, abdominal pain and often reduced bowel sounds in the absence of a mechanical obstructing lesion Typically occurs in hospitalised or postoperative patients and those with serious systemic illness, trauma or electrolyte disturbance Imaging shows marked dilatation of the caecum and right colon, and the risk of ischaemia and perforation rises sharply as caecal diameter increases A mechanical obstruction and toxic megacolon must be excluded before making the diagnosis, often with water-soluble contrast or CT Initial management is supportive with correction of electrolytes, review of opioids and other contributing drugs, and bowel rest with decompression Neostigmine or decompression for Ogilvie is used when conservative measures fail and there is no perforation or ischaemia, with colonoscopic decompression as an alternative Serial abdominal examination and imaging are essential to detect impending caecal perforation early Progressive caecal dilatation approaching diameters associated with perforation Peritonism, fever or rising inflammatory markers suggesting ischaemia or perforation Marked tenderness localised to the right iliac fossa over the caecum Haemodynamic instability or rising lactate Assuming mechanical obstruction and failing to consider a functional cause, or vice versa Giving neostigmine when perforation or ischaemia is present or unexcluded Neglecting to correct electrolyte disturbances and reduce opioids Underestimating caecal diameter and missing impending perforation Ogilvie syndrome is a massive dilatation of the colon without a mechanical cause, arising from an imbalance in autonomic innervation of the colon. Excess sympathetic tone and reduced parasympathetic (sacral) drive impair colonic motility, particularly in the distal colon, producing a functional obstruction and gross proximal dilatation that is most pronounced in the caecum and right colon. It is precipitated by severe illness, surgery, trauma, metabolic and electrolyte disturbances and drugs that impair motility such as opioids. As the caecum has the largest diameter and thinnest wall, rising wall tension there threatens ischaemia and perforation. With prompt recognition and treatment most cases resolve without surgery, but delayed diagnosis complicated by caecal ischaemia or perforation carries a high mortality.

Oguchi disease — Oguchi's disease, SAG, GRK1, arrestin deficiency, congenital stationary night blindness with Mizuo-Nakamura phenomenon Other forms of congenital stationary night blindness Fundus albipunctatus Retinitis pigmentosa and progressive rod-cone dystrophies Vitamin A deficiency retinopathy Retinitis punctata albescens Enhanced S-cone syndrome Fundus examination in light- and dark-adapted states to demonstrate the Mizuo-Nakamura phenomenon Prolonged dark adaptometry showing delayed rod recovery Full-field electroretinography before and after extended dark adaptation Fundus autofluorescence and optical coherence tomography to exclude degeneration Molecular genetic testing for SAG and GRK1 mutations Visual field testing to confirm preservation Rare autosomal recessive form of congenital stationary night blindness caused by mutations in SAG (arrestin) or GRK1 (rhodopsin kinase), genes needed to deactivate rhodopsin after light exposure The pathognomonic sign is the Mizuo-Nakamura phenomenon: a golden-yellow or metallic sheen of the fundus in the light-adapted state that reverts to a normal colour after prolonged dark adaptation Patients report lifelong, non-progressive night blindness with normal daytime acuity and colour vision Dark adaptometry shows a characteristic profile in which rod sensitivity recovers only after a very prolonged period of distinguished from progressive rod-cone dystrophies, as Oguchi disease is stationary with preserved acuity Management is supportive with reassurance about the stationary course, advice regarding night vision, and genetic counselling Documented progression of field loss or acuity decline, which is inconsistent with the diagnosis and suggests a degenerative disorder Pigmentary retinopathy or bone-spicule change indicating retinitis pigmentosa instead Onset of night blindness in adulthood pointing to an acquired cause Affected siblings warranting screening given recessive inheritance Overlooking the Mizuo-Nakamura phenomenon by examining the fundus only in the light-adapted state Misdiagnosing the disorder as progressive retinitis pigmentosa Interpreting the reduced rod electroretinogram without repeating it after prolonged dark adaptation Confusing it with fundus albipunctatus, which shows white dots and a different mechanism Oguchi disease arises from recessive mutations in SAG (S-antigen/arrestin) or GRK1 (rhodopsin kinase), proteins that normally quench activated rhodopsin so that rods can recover after light exposure. Defective deactivation leaves rods persistently desensitised following illumination, producing profound but non-progressive night blindness and abnormally slow dark adaptation. The abnormal state of the rod photoreceptors and their outer segments underlies the Mizuo-Nakamura phenomenon, in which the light-adapted retina takes on a golden sheen that disappears after prolonged darkness. The condition is stationary and non-progressive; daytime vision remains normal throughout life and only night vision is impaired, so the overall visual prognosis is good.

syndrome (infantile spasms) Neonatal seizures from hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy Pyridoxine-dependent and other vitamin-responsive epilepsies Inborn errors of metabolism presenting with neonatal neurotransmitter disorder is suspected Onset is very early, usually within the first weeks to three months of life, with frequent tonic spasms occurring both awake and asleep The defining EEG hallmark is a burst-suppression pattern present in both wakefulness and sleep Causes are heterogeneous, including structural brain malformations and pathogenic variants in genes such as STXBP1, KCNQ2, SCN2A and ARX Development is severely impaired from onset, and seizures are typically drug-resistant It may evolve into West syndrome and later into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome as the child grows Structural imaging is essential because malformations of cortical development are a frequent underlying cause Distinguishing it from early myoclonic encephalopathy rests on the predominant seizure type and the state-dependence of the EEG pattern Refractory tonic spasms with persistent burst-suppression in early infancy Failure to respond to pyridoxine trial when a vitamin-responsive cause is possible Evidence of a progressive metabolic disorder Rapid developmental arrest from birth Failing to trial vitamin-responsive treatments before concluding refractoriness Overlooking a subtle malformation of cortical development on early imaging Confusing it with early myoclonic encephalopathy by not characterising the predominant seizure type Not pursuing genetic testing, which increasingly identifies a specific cause Ohtahara syndrome is an early infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy in which severe disruption of neuronal networks in the immature brain produces continuous epileptic activity. The underlying causes, whether structural malformations of cortical development or pathogenic variants affecting synaptic transmission and ion channels, converge on profound cortical hyperexcitability and impaired inhibition. This generates the persistent burst-suppression pattern and frequent tonic spasms, while the same widespread dysfunction arrests brain development from the outset. The prognosis is generally very poor, with high early mortality, severe intellectual and motor disability in survivors, and frequent evolution to West and then Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Outcome is strongly influenced by the underlying cause.

Olecranon bursitis — student's elbow, miner's elbow, elbow bursitis, olecranon bursopathy Septic olecranon bursitis Gout or pseudogout Rheumatoid nodule or rheumatoid arthritis Olecranon fracture or other elbow trauma Cellulitis of the elbow Triceps insertional tendinopathy Bursal aspiration with fluid cell count, Gram stain and culture Polarised light microscopy of the aspirate for crystals is suspected Ultrasound to characterise the fluid collection Swelling over the point of the elbow from inflammation of the superficial olecranon bursa Causes include repetitive pressure and friction, direct trauma, crystal arthropathy such as gout, and infection The key clinical task is distinguishing septic from aseptic bursitis Warmth, marked erythema, fever, disproportionate pain and an overlying skin breach favour a septic bursa Aspiration with fluid sent for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystal microscopy is central when infection is suspected Aseptic bursitis is generally managed conservatively with avoidance of pressure, and aspiration if symptomatic Corticosteroid injection is reserved for stubborn aseptic cases and avoided when infection is possible because of complication risk Septic bursitis requires antibiotics and sometimes drainage Fever, spreading erythema and disproportionate pain suggesting septic bursitis or cellulitis An overlying skin breach or immunosuppression increasing infection risk Features of systemic sepsis Failure to settle, raising suspicion of infection or underlying disease Injecting corticosteroid into a bursa that may be infected Failing to aspirate and analyse fluid when infection is possible Missing gout as an underlying cause Attributing a fracture-related swelling to simple bursitis The olecranon bursa is a superficial sac over the extensor aspect of the elbow that reduces friction between the skin and the olecranon. Repetitive pressure or leaning on the elbow, a direct blow, or systemic conditions such as gout and rheumatoid arthritis can provoke bursal inflammation and effusion. Because it is superficial, the bursa is prone to becoming infected, commonly through a breach in the overlying skin and most often with skin flora such as staphylococci. Distinguishing this septic process from aseptic inflammation is the central diagnostic challenge. Aseptic bursitis usually settles with conservative care, although it can recur with continued pressure; septic bursitis generally resolves with prompt antibiotics and drainage but may need repeated aspiration.

Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis — oligoarticular JIA, oligo JIA, pauciarticular JIA, persistent and extended oligoarthritis Septic arthritis and osteomyelitis Reactive or post-viral arthritis Lyme arthritis in endemic areas Haemarthrosis or trauma Malignancy (leukaemia, neuroblastoma) causing joint or bone pain Other JIA subtypes including enthesitis-related arthritis Antinuclear antibody to stratify uveitis risk Inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein), which may be normal or only mildly raised Joint ultrasound or MRI to confirm synovitis and count and film to help exclude malignancy Rheumatoid factor and HLA-B27 to help distinguish other subtypes Defined under the ILAR framework as arthritis affecting four or fewer joints in the first six months, subclassified into persistent (never more than four joints) and extended (spreading to five or more thereafter) forms Typically affects young girls, often with a positive antinuclear antibody, and commonly involves large joints such as the knee and ankle asymmetrically The chief long-term threat is chronic anterior uveitis, which is frequently insidious and asymptomatic (white eye) yet sight-threatening Regular slit-lamp surveillance is essential, with the highest uveitis risk in young, antinuclear-antibody-positive girls with early disease onset A swollen, warm but often surprisingly non-tender knee with a limp and morning stiffness is a common presentation Limb-length discrepancy and localised overgrowth can occur because chronic inflammation accelerates growth at the affected joint First-line treatment is NSAIDs and intra-articular corticosteroids, with methotrexate reserved for persistent or extended disease and uveitis Painless progressive visual loss or band keratopathy indicating chronic uveitis complications Fever, severe pain or systemic upset suggesting infection or malignancy Nocturnal bone pain and cytopenias raising concern for leukaemia Rapid spread to many joints suggesting extended or polyarticular evolution Relying on the child to report eye symptoms, when sight-threatening uveitis is frequently asymptomatic Assuming normal inflammatory markers exclude active arthritis Missing limb-length discrepancy and consequent gait or postural problems Failing to reassess for extension of joint involvement over time Overlooking infection or malignancy in an atypical monoarthritis Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is a chronic, immune-mediated synovitis in which T-cell-driven inflammation of the synovial membrane produces effusion, pannus formation and, if untreated, cartilage and bone damage. The strong association with antinuclear antibody positivity and chronic anterior uveitis suggests shared autoreactivity between synovial and uveal tissue. Chronic hyperaemia around an inflamed joint can stimulate the adjacent growth plate, producing localised overgrowth and limb-length inequality, while unchecked synovitis eventually causes erosive joint damage in the extended subtype. The persistent form often has a favourable articular outcome, whereas the extended form carries a higher risk of erosive joint damage and disability. Uveitis, if undetected, can cause cataract, glaucoma and permanent visual loss, making ophthalmic surveillance the key determinant of long-term outcome.

oligodendroglioma — oligodendroglial tumour, IDH-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted glioma IDH-mutant astrocytoma glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype clear cell ependymoma central neurocytoma dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumour small cell glioblastoma cerebral metastasis contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain with perfusion and spectroscopy CT to demonstrate calcification IDH1 and IDH2 mutation testing 1p/19q codeletion analysis to confirm the diagnosis TERT promoter and CDKN2A status tissue diagnosis by resection or stereotactic biopsy neuropsychological and seizure assessment at baseline Diagnosis now requires both an IDH1 or IDH2 mutation and whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion; without codeletion the tumour is not an oligodendroglioma regardless of morphology. It is a tumour of adults with a predilection for the cerebral cortex and subcortical white matter, most often frontal. Seizures are the commonest presenting feature and may precede diagnosis by years, reflecting the tumour's cortical, slow-growing nature. Calcification is frequent and is well seen on CT, an unusual and helpful feature among diffuse gliomas. Classic histology shows monotonous cells with perinuclear haloes, the fried-egg artefact, and a delicate chicken-wire capillary network. The 1p/19q codeletion predicts sensitivity to alkylating chemotherapy and to combined chemoradiotherapy, underpinning a relatively favourable outcome. Graded as CNS WHO grade 2 or grade 3, with grade 3 showing brisk mitoses, microvascular proliferation or necrosis, and CDKN2A homozygous deletion portends worse behaviour. Even grade 3 oligodendroglioma generally outperforms IDH-mutant astrocytoma of comparable grade. clinical or radiological signs of raised intracranial pressure new or progressive focal neurological deficit status epilepticus or escalating seizure frequency new nodular enhancement suggesting higher-grade transformation diagnosing oligodendroglioma on morphology alone without confirming 1p/19q codeletion mistaking the fried-egg halo, a fixation artefact, for a specific diagnostic finding overlooking calcified cortical lesions on MRI that are obvious on CT assuming all IDH-mutant gliomas share the same prognosis and treatment underestimating higher-grade transformation when enhancement appears Oligodendroglioma is a diffusely infiltrating glioma defined molecularly by an early IDH1 or IDH2 mutation together with combined whole-arm loss of chromosomes 1p and 19q, typically arising from an unbalanced translocation. The mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase produces the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate, which inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases and drives a hypermethylator phenotype that reprogrammes gene expression. TERT promoter mutation and, frequently, CIC and FUBP1 mutations accompany the codeletion. The resulting neoplastic cells infiltrate cortex and white matter while retaining an indolent tempo, and higher-grade transformation is marked by increased proliferation, microvascular proliferation, necrosis and CDKN2A loss. Among diffuse gliomas the outlook is relatively favourable, with prolonged survival particularly in grade 2 disease, and the 1p/19q codeletion predicts chemosensitivity; nonetheless the tumour remains incurable and eventually progresses.

Oligospermia — oligozoospermia, low sperm count, reduced sperm concentration Varicocele Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism or hyperprolactinaemia Prior cryptorchidism or testicular injury Chromosomal abnormality or Y-chromosome microdeletion Gonadotoxic exposure including anabolic steroids, chemotherapy, or heat Partial ejaculatory duct obstruction Idiopathic spermatogenic impairment Repeat semen analysis by WHO methodology after a standardised abstinence interval Endocrine profile including testosterone, luteinising hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and prolactin Scrotal and, where indicated, transrectal ultrasound to detect varicocele or ductal pathology Karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion analysis in severe oligospermia Assessment of reversible lifestyle and occupational factors Post-ejaculatory urine examination if a component of retrograde ejaculation is suspected Cystic-fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator gene testing when ductal or seminal-vesicle abnormalities are found Oligospermia denotes a sperm concentration below the lower reference limit of the WHO semen-analysis framework and is a description, not a diagnosis in itself At least two properly collected semen samples, taken after a defined period of abstinence and analysed by WHO methods, are needed before drawing conclusions because output varies considerably over time Causes are best organised as pre-testicular (endocrine), testicular (spermatogenic), and post-testicular (partial obstruction or ejaculatory) so that the evaluation is systematic A hormonal profile of testosterone, luteinising hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and prolactin helps localise the problem; a raised follicle-stimulating hormone signals impaired spermatogenesis Varicocele is a common and potentially correctable contributor and should be sought on scrotal examination and confirmed on ultrasound if in doubt Modifiable factors such as heat exposure, obesity, smoking, alcohol, anabolic steroids, and certain medications should be identified and addressed Where numbers remain too low for natural or intrauterine conception, assisted reproduction with intracytoplasmic sperm injection offers an effective route to fatherhood Severe oligospermia warrants karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing before assisted conception because of the genetic implications for offspring A testicular mass identified during scrotal examination or on ultrasound Symptoms or signs of a pituitary lesion such as visual disturbance or headache Very low sperm counts with markedly raised follicle-stimulating hormone indicating severe spermatogenic failure Sudden deterioration in a previously normal count prompting a search for a new insult Drawing conclusions from a single semen sample despite the wide biological variability Neglecting a systematic pre-testicular, testicular, and post-testicular approach Missing a correctable varicocele or endocrine cause Proceeding to assisted conception in severe cases without genetic testing and counselling Overlooking a partial retrograde or obstructive component reducing the count A reduced sperm concentration results from disturbance at one or more levels of male reproductive function. Pre-testicular causes are endocrine, with deficient gonadotropin drive (as in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism or hyperprolactinaemia) reducing the hormonal stimulation of the testis. Testicular causes involve the seminiferous epithelium itself and include varicocele, prior cryptorchidism, chromosomal or Y-microdeletion defects, gonadotoxic exposures, and idiopathic spermatogenic failure, typically accompanied by a compensatory rise in follicle-stimulating hormone. Post-testicular causes reflect partial obstruction of the excurrent ducts or ejaculatory dysfunction that reduces the number of sperm reaching the ejaculate. In many men the cause is multifactorial or remains unexplained despite full assessment. The outlook depends on the underlying cause and severity; correctable factors such as varicocele, endocrine deficiency, or gonadotoxin exposure may improve counts, while many couples achieve pregnancy through assisted reproduction even when the concentration remains low.

The mosaic origin explains the asymmetric distribution and the absence of vertical transmission. Prognosis depends on lesion number, size and site; morbidity comes from deformity, limb-length discrepancy and fracture, while the principal serious concern is malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma, warranting lifelong surveillance.

Olmsted syndrome — TRPV3, mutilating palmoplantar keratoderma with periorificial keratotic plaques, MGP-1 Vohwinkel syndrome (mutilating keratoderma) Mal de Meleda Papillon-Lefevre syndrome Pachyonychia congenita Acrodermatitis enteropathica Pityriasis rubra pilaris with palmoplantar involvement Skin biopsy showing massive orthohyperkeratosis, acanthosis and psoriasiform change Molecular genetic testing of TRPV3 and related genes Assessment and monitoring of digital constriction bands and function Ophthalmological and oral examination for periorificial and mucosal involvement Surveillance biopsy of chronic or ulcerated plaques for malignant change Pain assessment and multidisciplinary evaluation Defined by the combination of a severe, mutilating, bilateral palmoplantar keratoderma with sharply demarcated periorificial keratotic plaques (around the mouth, nose, eyes, anus and genitalia) The keratoderma is often intensely painful and can be transgredient, with constricting bands and pseudo-ainhum threatening digits Onset is usually in infancy or early childhood with progressive thickening Most cases result from dominant gain-of-function mutations in TRPV3, a keratinocyte cation channel; recessive and other genetic forms exist Associated features may include alopecia, nail dystrophy, oral leucokeratosis and, over time, a risk of squamous cell carcinoma within affected skin Severe itch, pain and functional disability are prominent and difficult to manage Management is supportive with emollients/keratolytics, oral retinoids, pain control and surgery for constricting bands; TRPV3-directed and other targeted therapies are under investigation Progressive pseudo-ainhum threatening digital viability New, ulcerated or non-healing lesion within keratoderma suggesting squamous cell carcinoma Uncontrolled pain or itch causing severe disability Secondary infection of fissured or eroded plaques Failing to recognise the diagnostic periorificial plaques and treating as isolated keratoderma Neglecting early release of constricting bands, risking digital loss Underestimating pain and itch, which are central to morbidity Overlooking malignant transformation in long-standing plaques Olmsted syndrome is most often caused by dominant gain-of-function mutations in TRPV3, which encodes a transient receptor potential vanilloid cation channel expressed in keratinocytes and involved in temperature sensing, epidermal barrier formation, keratinocyte proliferation and hair growth. Overactivity of the mutant channel increases calcium influx and drives excessive keratinocyte proliferation and abnormal differentiation, together with dysregulated apoptosis and sensory-nerve signalling that generates the marked pain and itch. The result is a severe, mutilating palmoplantar keratoderma with periorificial plaques; chronic hyperproliferation and inflammation also underlie the long-term risk of squamous cell carcinoma. Recessive and phenocopy forms involving other genes have been described. Olmsted syndrome is a chronic, often progressive and disabling disorder; the keratoderma rarely resolves and can be mutilating, and there is a long-term risk of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Pain and functional impairment are major and lifelong, though targeted therapies offer emerging hope.

omphalomesenteric duct remnant — vitelline duct remnant, omphalomesenteric duct anomaly urachal remnant or patent urachus umbilical granuloma Meckel diverticulum umbilical hernia omphalitis patent vitellointestinal fistula versus enterocutaneous fistula umbilical dermoid abdominal and umbilical ultrasound sinogram or fistulogram to define a patent tract technetium-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy for ectopic gastric mucosa contrast luminal studies to demonstrate communication with bowel MRI for complex or ambiguous anatomy histopathology of the excised remnant The omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct normally connects the embryonic midgut to the yolk sac and involutes in early gestation; incomplete obliteration yields a spectrum of remnants. Meckel diverticulum is by far the commonest remnant, arising when the intestinal end persists; a patent duct, umbilical sinus, vitelline cyst, umbilical polyp, or fibrous band represent other patterns. A completely patent duct presents in the neonate with enteric or faecal discharge from the umbilicus, whereas a persisting fibrous band predisposes to volvulus and internal herniation. An umbilical polyp is a firm, bright-red mucosal nodule of retained gastrointestinal epithelium that does not respond to silver nitrate, unlike an umbilical granuloma. A vitelline cyst forms when both ends of the duct obliterate but a central patent segment traps secretions. Ectopic gastric mucosa within a remnant can ulcerate and bleed, and a technetium-99m pertechnetate scan helps localise it. Persistent umbilical discharge demands distinction from a urachal remnant, which drains urine rather than enteric content. Symptomatic remnants and persistent bands are managed by surgical excision, including division of the band to prevent obstruction. bilious vomiting or obstruction suggesting volvulus around a persistent band gastrointestinal or umbilical bleeding indicating ectopic gastric mucosa persistent enteric or faecal umbilical discharge signs of peritonitis from perforation or strangulation prolapse of bowel mucosa through a patent duct confusing a vitelline remnant with a urachal anomaly by not distinguishing enteric from urinary discharge treating an umbilical polyp as a granuloma with repeated silver nitrate application overlooking ectopic gastric mucosa as a source of occult bleeding failing to divide an asymptomatic band discovered incidentally, leaving a future obstruction risk incomplete excision leaving residual mucosa at the umbilicus During early development the omphalomesenteric duct links the yolk sac to the primitive midgut and normally regresses as the placenta takes over nutrition. Failure of this involution leaves a remnant whose clinical form depends on which portion persists and whether it remains patent. Persistence of the intestinal end produces a Meckel diverticulum; a fully patent lumen creates an entero-umbilical fistula; obliteration of the ends with a patent centre yields a vitelline cyst; and a fibrous cord may persist as a band tethering the bowel to the umbilicus. Retained mucosa is frequently gastrointestinal and may include ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue, whose acid secretion causes ulceration and bleeding. A persistent band or the mesodiverticular vessels provide a fixed point around which small bowel can twist, producing volvulus or internal herniation. Prognosis is excellent after complete excision of the remnant. Untreated persistent bands carry an ongoing risk of obstruction, and unrecognised ectopic mucosa may bleed.
