changes Serological (Ov-16) antibody or antigen testing PCR assays on skin snips for species confirmation Assessment for Loa loa co-infection in co-endemic areas before treatment Caused by the filarial nematode Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by the bite of Simulium blackflies that breed in fast-flowing rivers, hence 'river blindness' Chronic infection produces intensely itchy dermatitis, altered skin pigmentation ('leopard skin'), skin atrophy, and firm subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomas) housing adult worms Microfilariae migrating to the eye cause keratitis, iritis, chorioretinitis, and optic atrophy, leading to progressive and potentially irreversible blindness The endosymbiotic bacterium Wolbachia within the worm drives much of the inflammatory response, making doxycycline for Wolbachia a useful adjunct that also sterilises adult female worms Diagnosis is classically by skin snips examined for emerging microfilariae, supported by nodule examination and antigen/antibody or PCR testing Ivermectin is the mainstay microfilaricidal treatment and the basis of mass drug administration control programmes, given repeatedly as it does not reliably kill adult worms Ivermectin can precipitate a severe reaction in patients heavily co-infected with Loa loa, so loiasis must be considered in co-endemic areas before treatment Ocular involvement threatening progressive or irreversible visual loss Severe Mazzotti reaction after microfilaricidal treatment Risk of severe reaction if ivermectin is given with high Loa loa co-infection Extensive sight-threatening keratitis or optic atrophy Giving ivermectin without excluding heavy Loa loa co-infection in co-endemic regions Expecting a single course of ivermectin to cure infection despite persistence of adult worms Underestimating the sight-threatening potential of ocular microfilariae Failing to anticipate and manage the Mazzotti reaction after treatment Onchocerciasis results from infection with Onchocerca volvulus. Infective larvae are introduced by biting Simulium blackflies and mature into adult worms that reside coiled within fibrous subcutaneous nodules. Adult females release large numbers of microfilariae that migrate through the skin, connective tissue, and eye. Most disease is driven not by the live microfilariae but by the inflammatory reaction to dying microfilariae and to their endosymbiotic Wolbachia bacteria, which provoke dermal and ocular inflammation. In the eye, repeated microfilarial death causes punctate then sclerosing keratitis, anterior uveitis, and posterior segment damage, culminating in blindness. In the skin, chronic inflammation produces pruritus, depigmentation, and atrophy. Killing microfilariae abruptly, as with treatment, can intensify this inflammatory response (the Mazzotti reaction). With repeated ivermectin therapy and vector control, transmission and morbidity can be greatly reduced; however, established ocular damage and optic atrophy are irreversible, and untreated chronic infection remains a leading infective cause of blindness.

Salivary gland oncocytoma — Oxyphilic adenoma, Oncocytic adenoma Warthin tumour Oncocytic carcinoma Acinic cell carcinoma Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (oncocytic variant) Oncocytic metaplasia or nodular oncocytosis Metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (clear-cell variant) Pleomorphic adenoma Fine-needle aspiration cytology Ultrasound of the gland Technetium pertechnetate scintigraphy (uptake is supportive but non-specific) MRI or CT to define extent Immunohistochemistry with antimitochondrial antibody Exclusion of metastatic renal cell carcinoma when clear-cell morphology is present A rare benign tumour composed almost entirely of oncocytes: large cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm packed with mitochondria. It most often affects the parotid in older adults and presents as a well-circumscribed, encapsulated, painless mass. Unlike Warthin tumour, the classic oncocytoma lacks a lymphoid stroma, which is the key distinguishing histological feature. Like Warthin tumour, oncocytes are avid for technetium pertechnetate, so scintigraphy is not discriminating between the two. Diffuse or multifocal oncocytosis of the gland may coexist and can make complete separation of tumour from background difficult. A clear-cell variant, due to intracytoplasmic glycogen, can mimic metastatic clear-cell renal carcinoma and warrants careful exclusion. Immunohistochemistry with antimitochondrial antibody highlights the oncocytic cytoplasm and supports the diagnosis. The principal diagnostic task is to distinguish it from oncocytic carcinoma, which shows infiltration, necrosis and increased mitoses. Rapid growth or new pain Facial nerve weakness Infiltrative margins or tumour necrosis suggesting oncocytic carcinoma Regional lymphadenopathy Fixation to skin or deep tissues Confusing oncocytoma with Warthin tumour or oncocytic carcinoma on limited material Mistaking the clear-cell variant for metastatic renal cell carcinoma Sampling background oncocytic metaplasia rather than the lesion itself Relying on technetium avidity to distinguish it from Warthin tumour Salivary gland oncocytoma results from clonal proliferation of oncocytes, epithelial cells that accumulate vast numbers of morphologically and often functionally abnormal mitochondria. The oncocytic phenotype reflects a compensatory mitochondrial hyperplasia thought to relate to acquired defects in mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, and its frequency increases with age; a history of prior irradiation is recognised in some cases. The tumour forms an encapsulated nodule of solid or organoid nests and cords of oncocytes with granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and round nuclei. Because oncocytic metaplasia is common in ageing salivary tissue, oncocytoma exists on a continuum with focal and diffuse oncocytosis, and the abundant mitochondria account for both the tinctorial appearance and the radionuclide avidity. Prognosis is excellent, as the tumour is benign and complete excision is curative. The main clinical importance lies in reliably distinguishing it from oncocytic carcinoma and from metastatic renal carcinoma.

Oncologic Emergencies — tumor lysis syndrome, superior vena cava syndrome SVCS in a young man with a mediastinal mass: lymphoma versus primary mediastinal germ cell tumor (Harrison 22e p.585) Cauda equina syndrome: low back pain, saddle sensory loss, rectal/bladder dysfunction, sexual impotence and absent reflexes from compression of nerve roots forming the cauda equina (Harrison 22e p.589) Abrupt stroke-like onset of headache, nausea, vomiting and focal deficit in brain metastasis usually indicates hemorrhage into the metastasis (melanoma, germ cell and renal cell tumors bleed readily) (Harrison 22e p.590) Pyogenic epidural abscess or vertebral tuberculosis can mimic malignant spinal cord compression (Harrison 22e p.589) SVCS: chest radiograph (superior mediastinal widening, usually right-sided), CT thorax (most reliable mediastinal view; 'hot quadrate' hepatic hotspot sign suggests SVC obstruction), MRI (100% sensitivity/specificity but supine positioning may be difficult in dyspneic patients) (Harrison 22e p.586) Spinal cord compression: neurologic exam and plain spine films first (earliest finding is the 'winking owl' sign of pedicle erosion; plain films are insensitive), then full-length spinal MRI (procedure of choice); myelography reserved for poor or unobtainable MRI (Harrison 22e p.589) Brain metastases/raised ICP: gadolinium-enhanced MRI is superior to CT and more sensitive for meningeal involvement and small posterior-fossa lesions (Harrison 22e p.590) TLS pretreatment evaluation in at-risk patients: complete blood count, serum chemistry (electrolytes, creatinine, calcium, phosphate, uric acid) and urinalysis; follow plasma rather than serum potassium when pseudohyperkalemia is suspected; sonography/CT of kidneys and retroperitoneum if baseline renal function is abnormal (Harrison 22e p.593) A urinary uric acid to urinary creatinine ratio >1 supports acute hyperuricemic nephropathy; <1 suggests renal failure of other cause (Harrison 22e p.593) Spinal cord compression mimics: osteoporotic vertebral collapse, disk disease, radiation myelopathy, neoplastic leptomeningitis, benign tumors, epidural hematoma and spinal lipomatosis (Harrison 22e p.589) About 20% of vertebral collapse (especially in older patients and postmenopausal women) is due to osteoporosis rather than cancer (Harrison 22e p.589) Benign causes of SVCS: aortic aneurysm, thyromegaly, thrombosis, and fibrosing mediastinitis from prior irradiation, histoplasmosis or Behcet's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.585) Pseudohyperkalemia from high leukocyte/platelet counts (cell lysis after blood draw) can falsely elevate potassium in TLS; no ECG abnormalities are present (Harrison 22e p.593) Pseudohypoglycemia from glucose consumption in the test tube with hyperleukocytosis, myeloproliferative disease or CSF treatment (Harrison 22e p.593) Emergencies in cancer fall into three groups: pressure/obstruction from a space-occupying lesion (structural-obstructive), metabolic or hormonal problems (paraneoplastic), and treatment-related complications (Harrison 22e p.585). Superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS) reflects SVC obstruction with severe reduction of venous return from head, neck and upper extremities; lung cancer (especially small-cell and squamous) accounts for ~85% of malignant cases, and in young adults lymphoma is a leading cause (Harrison 22e p.585). Benign causes of SVCS are increasing with intravascular device use (central catheters, pacemaker/defibrillator leads) and now account for at least 40% of cases (Harrison 22e p.585). SVCS typically presents with neck and facial swelling (especially periorbital), dyspnea, cough, dilated neck veins, collateral chest-wall veins, cyanosis and facial plethora that worsens when supine; bending forward or lying down aggravates symptoms (Harrison 22e p.585). The diagnosis of SVCS is clinical; the most significant chest radiograph finding is widening of the superior mediastinum (most often right-sided), and CT provides the most reliable mediastinal anatomy (Harrison 22e p.586). Malignant spinal cord compression (MSCC) is compression of cord and/or cauda equina by an extradural tumor mass; spinal cord compression occurs in 5-10% of cancer patients and is the first manifestation of malignancy in ~10% (Harrison 22e p.588). Localized back pain and tenderness is the most common initial symptom of spinal cord compression, often present for days to months before neurologic findings; it characteristically worsens when supine, unlike disk-disease pain (Harrison 22e p.588-589). The thoracic spine is the most common site of cord compression (70%), followed by lumbosacral (20%) and cervical (10%); lung, breast and prostate cancers are the most frequent offenders (Harrison 22e p.588). Treatment of spinal cord compression is more often successful in patients still ambulatory and with sphincter control at initiation; patients whose exam suggests compression should receive dexamethasone immediately and undergo MRI (Harrison 22e p.589). Full-length spinal MRI is the imaging procedure of choice for cord compression and is as good as or better than myelography plus post-myelogram CT (Harrison 22e p.589). About 25% of cancer patients die with intracranial metastases; lung and breast cancer and melanoma metastasize to brain most often, and brain metastases present features of an expanding intracranial lesion: headache, nausea, vomiting, behavioral change, seizures and focal progressive deficits (Harrison 22e p.589-590). Dexamethasone is the best initial treatment for all symptomatic patients with brain metastases and raised intracranial pressure (Harrison 22e p.590). Hypercalcemia is the most common paraneoplastic syndrome, and SIADH is the most common cause of hyponatremia among cancer patients (both detailed in Chaps. 98 and 422/393) (Harrison 22e p.592). Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is characterized by hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia and hypocalcemia from destruction of large numbers of rapidly proliferating cells; acidosis may develop and acute renal failure occurs frequently (Harrison 22e p.593). TLS is most often associated with treatment of Burkitt's lymphoma, ALL, AML and other rapidly proliferating lymphomas, and usually occurs during or shortly (1-5 days) after chemotherapy; risk correlates with tumor burden and high LDH (>1500 U/L) (Harrison 22e p.593). Recognition of risk and prevention are the most important steps in TLS management; the standard preventive approach is allopurinol plus aggressive hydration (Harrison 22e p.593). Febrile neutropenia is the clinical presentation of fever with <1500 granulocytes/uL; it is a key treatment-related emergency in cancer patients (Harrison 22e p.575). SVCS with cerebral and/or laryngeal edema, proptosis, glossal/laryngeal edema, obtundation or postural hypotension carries poorer prognosis and requires urgent evaluation and early stenting (Harrison 22e p.585-586) Tracheal obstruction from a superior mediastinal mass is the one potentially life-threatening complication of SVCS and demands emergent therapy; cardiac arrest or respiratory failure can occur, particularly with sedatives or general anesthesia (Harrison 22e p.585-586) Cancer patient with back pain plus a crescendo pain pattern, Lhermitte's sign, or pain aggravated by cough/Valsalva/recumbency should be evaluated for cord compression as quickly as possible (Harrison 22e p.589) Loss of bowel or bladder control, autonomic dysfunction (decreased anal tone, distended bladder, absent anal wink/bulbocavernosus reflex) signals significant cord involvement and is an unfavorable prognostic feature (Harrison 22e p.588) Hyperkalemia in TLS with renal failure can rapidly become life-threatening, causing ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death (Harrison 22e p.593) Acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis) is potentially lethal and may be masked by nonspecific symptoms attributed to cancer or therapy (Harrison 22e p.593) Febrile neutropenia (fever with <1500 granulocytes/uL) is a treatment-related emergency requiring prompt management (Harrison 22e p.575) A normal chest radiograph is still compatible with the diagnosis of SVCS if other characteristic findings are present (Harrison 22e p.586) A normal appearance of plain spine films does not exclude cancer; plain films are insensitive for cord compression (Harrison 22e p.589) Vertebral collapse is not a reliable indicator of tumor since ~20% of collapses are osteoporotic (Harrison 22e p.589) After SVC stenting, the prompt increase in venous return may precipitate heart failure and pulmonary edema (Harrison 22e p.586) Urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate is no longer recommended in TLS: although it increases uric acid solubility, a high pH decreases solubility of xanthine, hypoxanthine and calcium phosphate, potentially increasing intratubular crystallization (Harrison 22e p.593) Rasburicase is contraindicated in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, and it causes ex vivo degradation of uric acid in the test tube giving spuriously low levels unless samples are cooled immediately (Harrison 22e p.594) Pseudohyperkalemia in TLS shows no ECG abnormalities; plasma rather than serum potassium should be followed (Harrison 22e p.593) Arterial blood gas oxygen tension can be spuriously low in hyperleukocytosis due to oxygen consumption by white cells; pulse oximetry is the most accurate measure of oxygenation (Harrison 22e p.591) Oncologic emergencies arise by three mechanisms (Harrison 22e p.585). Structural-obstructive emergencies result from a space-occupying lesion: in SVCS, malignant tumor or thrombosis obstructs the superior vena cava, reducing venous return from head, neck and upper limbs; in malignant spinal cord compression, an expanding extradural tumor (usually metastasis to vertebral body or pedicle, or paravertebral extension through the intervertebral foramen) mechanically injures axons and myelin and compromises blood flow, causing ischemia/infarction; raised intracranial pressure results from brain metastases and surrounding edema, sometimes with hemorrhage or CSF obstruction causing hydrocephalus and herniation (Harrison 22e p.585-590). Metabolic/hormonal (paraneoplastic) emergencies include hypercalcemia, SIADH-related hyponatremia, lactic acidosis and hypoglycemia (Harrison 22e p.592-593). Treatment-related TLS occurs when cytotoxic killing of a large rapidly proliferating tumor releases intracellular contents: nucleic acid turnover raises uric acid which precipitates in the acidic renal tubules; released phosphate causes hyperphosphatemia with reciprocal hypocalcemia and calcium-phosphate nephrocalcinosis; and massive cell destruction releases potassium causing hyperkalemia, which in renal failure can cause fatal ventricular arrhythmias (Harrison 22e p.593). In SVCS, mortality relates to the underlying cause rather than to caval obstruction itself, and clinical improvement occurs in most patients (sometimes via collateral circulation); SVCS recurs in 10-30% (Harrison 22e p.586). For spinal cord compression, tumor histology is an important determinant of recovery and survival, and rapid onset/progression of signs and symptoms are poor prognostic features; treatment is more often successful in ambulatory patients who retain sphincter control (Harrison 22e p.589). Brain metastases frequently cause major symptoms, disability and early death (Harrison 22e p.590). Lactic acidosis in cancer carries a poor prognosis regardless of treatment, and cancer patients with malignant cells on pericardial cytology have very poor survival (Harrison 22e p.587, 592). Despite aggressive prophylaxis, TLS with oliguric/anuric renal failure may still occur and often requires renal replacement therapy (Harrison 22e p.594). Spinal cord compression management uses the NOMS framework (Memorial Sloan Kettering): Neurologic assessment (degree of epidural compression, myelopathy, functional radiculopathy), Oncologic assessment (tumor radiosensitivity), Mechanical assessment (spinal stability), and Systemic factors (extent of disease and comorbidities determining tolerance of therapy) (Harrison 22e p.589-590). TLS risk is stratified by tumor burden, renal function, hyperuricemia and high LDH (>1500 U/L); a high-risk management algorithm escalates from hydration and allopurinol to recombinant urate oxidase/rasburicase and hemodialysis based on serum uric acid, creatinine, potassium, phosphate and symptomatic hypocalcemia thresholds (Harrison 22e p.593-594).

One-and-a-half syndrome — Fisher one-and-a-half syndrome, paralytic pontine exotropia Isolated horizontal gaze palsy without internuclear component Bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia Myasthenia gravis with complex ophthalmoplegia Combined multiple ocular motor nerve palsies from skull base disease Progressive supranuclear gaze disorders Thyroid eye disease with restrictive limitation MRI of the pons and brainstem to localise the lesion MRI of the brain and cord for demyelinating disease Vascular imaging and stroke workup in older patients Cerebrospinal fluid examination for oligoclonal bands where relevant Acetylcholine receptor antibodies to exclude myasthenia Assessment for associated facial nerve involvement There is a complete horizontal gaze palsy to one side (the 'one') combined with an internuclear ophthalmoplegia on the other side (the 'half') In practice the only preserved horizontal movement is abduction of the contralateral eye, which often shows nystagmus The lesion damages the ipsilateral paramedian pontine reticular formation or abducens nucleus together with the adjacent medial longitudinal fasciculus The abducting eye may sit in exotropia in primary position, termed paralytic pontine exotropia Vertical eye movements and convergence are typically spared because their pathways lie outside the affected pontine region Common causes are pontine infarction, demyelination, and less often haemorrhage or tumour The addition of a facial nerve palsy from involvement of the adjacent facial colliculus produces the 'eight-and-a-half syndrome' Acute presentation with additional brainstem signs indicating infarction or haemorrhage Progressive course suggesting a pontine mass Reduced consciousness or long-tract signs implying extensive brainstem damage New facial weakness indicating spread to the facial colliculus Misreading the preserved abduction as normal gaze and underestimating the deficit Failing to recognise the combined gaze palsy and internuclear ophthalmoplegia as a single localising lesion Overlooking an accompanying facial palsy that broadens the localisation Not imaging urgently when an acute vascular cause is likely A single paramedian pontine lesion damages the abducens nucleus or paramedian pontine reticular formation on one side, abolishing all conjugate horizontal gaze toward that side, and simultaneously involves the neighbouring medial longitudinal fasciculus, which produces an internuclear ophthalmoplegia affecting adduction of the ipsilateral eye on gaze to the opposite side. The combined result is that the affected eye cannot move horizontally at all, while the other eye can only abduct. Ischaemia is the leading cause in older patients and demyelination in younger patients, with haemorrhage and neoplasm accounting for a minority. Outcome depends on the underlying cause; ischaemic and demyelinating lesions often improve with partial recovery of horizontal movement over weeks to months, though a residual exotropia and diplopia may remain.

Onychogryphosis — onychogryphosis, ram's horn nail, ram's-horn nail, onychogryposis Onychomycosis with gross nail thickening Pachyonychia congenita and other hereditary thickening disorders Psoriatic nail with marked subungual hyperkeratosis Subungual tumour distorting the plate Post-traumatic nail dystrophy Chronic pressure changes from ill-fitting footwear Clinical assessment of mobility, self-care ability, and footwear Peripheral vascular examination including pulses in elderly patients Nail clipping for mycology to identify coexisting fungal infection Assessment of diabetic and neuropathic status where relevant Radiograph if an underlying bony abnormality or exostosis is suspected Onychoscopy to help distinguish deformity from primary infection Onychogryphosis is a grossly thickened, opaque, curved nail that grows into a ram's-horn or oyster-shell shape, most often affecting the great toenail It is largely a disorder of the elderly, driven by neglect, poor mobility, ill-fitting footwear, and repeated minor trauma The nail typically deviates to one side and shows transverse ridges reflecting irregular, uneven growth Peripheral vascular disease and any condition limiting a person's ability to reach and cut their nails predispose to it It is often mistaken for fungal disease, but the deformity is primarily one of shape and bulk rather than infection, although secondary onychomycosis may coexist Conservative management involves regular chiropody, mechanical thinning and reduction of the plate, and attention to footwear Definitive treatment for a recurrent painful nail is surgical avulsion with matrix ablation to prevent regrowth Underlying peripheral arterial disease or diabetes raising the risk of ulceration and infection A painful, discharging, or ulcerated nail suggesting secondary infection or pressure necrosis Sudden change in a long-standing deformed nail that could hide a tumour Signs of ischaemia in the affected digit requiring vascular assessment Labelling the deformity as purely fungal and relying on antifungals alone Neglecting the vascular and diabetic status before considering nail surgery Underestimating the role of poor self-care and footwear in recurrence Overlooking a subungual tumour hidden beneath the hypertrophic plate Onychogryphosis develops when the nail matrix produces plate at an uneven rate across its width, so that one side grows faster than the other and the nail progressively curves and twists as it thickens. Chronic low-grade trauma, pressure from footwear, impaired peripheral circulation, and simple failure to trim the nail all contribute to the disordered growth, and the accumulating layers become hard, opaque, and heaped up. The condition is self-perpetuating because the deformed plate can no longer be cut or worn down normally, allowing the characteristic hypertrophic, hooked shape to develop over months to years. Onychogryphosis is a chronic, recurrent condition that responds to regular mechanical care but tends to return unless the matrix is ablated, and prognosis is closely tied to the patient's mobility, circulation, and ongoing foot care.

Onycholysis — nail plate separation, detached nail, onychomadesis distalis Nail psoriasis with associated pitting and subungual hyperkeratosis Onychomycosis (distal-lateral subungual fungal infection) Traumatic or occupational nail bed damage Contact irritant or allergic reactions to nail cosmetics and adhesives Thyroid dysfunction (hyperthyroidism) Drug-induced photo-onycholysis Subungual tumour lifting the plate Careful history for trauma, wet work, cosmetics, and photosensitising medication Nail clipping and subungual scrapings for mycology to confirm or exclude fungal infection Onychoscopy (dermoscopy of the nail) to characterise the pattern and margin of separation Thyroid function tests when a systemic cause is suspected Swab of the subungual space if greenish discolouration suggests Pseudomonas Assessment for cutaneous psoriasis or other skin disease elsewhere on the body Onycholysis is separation of the nail plate from the underlying nail bed, usually starting distally or laterally and creating a whitish or yellowish air-filled space It is a sign, not a diagnosis, so the priority is to identify the underlying cause rather than simply treat the loosened nail Psoriasis is a very common cause and is often accompanied by pitting, oil-drop discolouration, and subungual hyperkeratosis Repeated mechanical or chemical trauma, including aggressive manicuring and prolonged wet work, is a frequent and overlooked trigger Thyroid dysfunction, especially hyperthyroidism, can produce distal separation known as Plummer's nail Photo-onycholysis follows exposure to certain photosensitising drugs (for example tetracyclines and some psoralens) after sunlight and typically affects several nails The exposed nail bed loses its protective seal and becomes vulnerable to secondary colonisation by yeasts and Pseudomonas, the latter giving a greenish tinge Management is directed at the cause, keeping the nail short and dry, minimising trauma and wet exposure, and treating any secondary infection Separation confined to a single nail with an underlying mass, suggesting a subungual tumour Associated pigmentation or bleeding raising the possibility of subungual melanoma Rapidly spreading discolouration or pain indicating secondary infection Persistent unexplained onycholysis unresponsive to removal of obvious triggers Assuming all onycholysis is fungal and prescribing antifungals without confirmatory mycology Overlooking a photosensitising drug when several nails are affected after sun exposure Failing to recognise a single stubborn separated nail as a marker of an underlying tumour Encouraging cleaning under the nail, which extends the space and worsens the separation Onycholysis arises when the bonds anchoring the keratinised nail plate to the epithelium of the nail bed are disrupted, so that the plate lifts away and an air-filled space forms beneath it. The separation may be driven by inflammatory disease of the nail bed such as psoriasis, by repeated mechanical or chemical injury, by a phototoxic reaction to circulating drugs, or by systemic influences such as altered thyroid hormone levels. Once the seal between plate and bed is broken, keratin debris, moisture, and micro-organisms accumulate in the subungual space, and secondary colonisation with yeasts or Pseudomonas can perpetuate the problem and alter the colour of the nail. Onycholysis usually resolves once the underlying cause is corrected and the nail is allowed to grow out attached, but recovery is slow because it depends on outgrowth of new plate, and persistent triggers such as psoriasis or continued trauma lead to relapse.

Onychomadesis — nail shedding, proximal nail separation, onychomadesis Beau lines (partial matrix arrest on the same spectrum) Traumatic nail avulsion Severe bullous disorders affecting the nail (for example epidermolysis bullosa or drug reactions) Onychomycosis with proximal involvement Nail shedding in severe psoriasis or lichen planus Idiopathic periodic shedding History for recent febrile illness, viral infection (including hand, foot and mouth disease), or chemotherapy Examination of all nails to determine single versus multiple involvement Estimation of the timing of the insult from the level of separation Screening for systemic or metabolic disease if no clear trigger is found Review of recent medications, particularly cytotoxic agents Mycology if fungal infection is a consideration Onychomadesis is complete, full-thickness separation of the nail plate beginning at the proximal end, which can progress to shedding of the whole nail It represents the severe end of the same spectrum as Beau lines, both reflecting temporary arrest of nail matrix activity When several nails are affected it usually follows a systemic insult such as a febrile illness, chemotherapy, or a major metabolic disturbance It is a well-recognised sequel of hand, foot and mouth disease, appearing weeks after the acute infection has resolved A single affected nail more often reflects local trauma to that matrix The timing of the causative event can be estimated from the position of the separation and the rate of nail growth It is generally self-limiting, and a new nail grows to replace the shed plate once matrix function recovers, so reassurance is central to management Widespread nail shedding pointing to a significant systemic illness or drug reaction Mucocutaneous blistering or a severe drug eruption requiring urgent evaluation Signs of secondary infection of the exposed nail bed Recurrent shedding suggesting cyclical systemic disease or ongoing exposure Alarming the patient rather than reassuring them when the cause is a self-limited illness Failing to link post-viral nail shedding to a preceding hand, foot and mouth disease episode Overlooking a serious systemic cause when many nails shed simultaneously Neglecting protection of the exposed nail bed, allowing secondary infection Onychomadesis is caused by a complete but temporary halt in nail matrix activity, so that for a period no nail plate is produced and the newly forming proximal plate is disconnected from the older distal plate. When matrix function resumes, the new plate grows out and pushes off the detached older nail, which is shed. The insult may be systemic, such as a high fever, viral infection, cytotoxic drug, or metabolic upheaval that transiently diverts the matrix from plate production, or local trauma affecting a single digit; the more severe or prolonged the arrest, the more complete the separation compared with the partial groove of a Beau line. Onychomadesis is usually self-limiting, and a new nail regrows over several months once the matrix recovers, with a good outcome provided the underlying trigger is transient and any secondary infection is prevented.

Opioid-induced constipation — OIC Functional constipation Dyssynergic defecation Secondary constipation (hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia) Bowel obstruction Other drug-induced constipation Clinical history linking constipation to opioid use Assessment of stool pattern and abdominal and rectal examination Exclusion of obstruction and metabolic causes where indicated Review of the full medication list for other constipating drugs Assessment of response to laxatives before escalating therapy Constipation that develops or worsens on starting or increasing opioid therapy, with hard stools, straining and incomplete evacuation Unlike many opioid effects, it does not reliably diminish with continued use (little tolerance develops) It is a very common and often under-treated adverse effect that limits opioid therapy and quality of life It is a component of the broader opioid-induced bowel dysfunction, which also includes reflux, bloating and cramping Stimulant and osmotic laxatives are used first-line, with peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonists for refractory cases It is distinct from narcotic bowel syndrome, in which the problem is worsening pain rather than constipation Features suggesting bowel obstruction or faecal impaction with overflow Severe abdominal pain or distension Rectal bleeding or weight loss Failure to respond to appropriate laxative therapy Failing to co-prescribe laxatives when starting opioids Expecting tolerance to the constipating effect to develop Confusing it with narcotic bowel syndrome Missing faecal impaction with overflow diarrhoea Opioid-induced constipation results from opioid action on mu-opioid receptors in the enteric nervous system of the gut wall. This reduces propulsive peristalsis, increases non-propulsive tone and fluid absorption, and impairs the defecatory reflex, producing hard, infrequent stools and difficult evacuation. Because these peripheral gut receptors do not develop the tolerance seen with central analgesic effects, the constipation tends to persist throughout opioid therapy. Peripherally acting antagonists relieve it by blocking these gut receptors without reversing central analgesia. With appropriate laxatives and, where needed, peripherally acting antagonists, constipation is usually controllable, allowing continued analgesia; it persists as long as opioids are taken.

Opioid overdose — Clinical (pinpoint pupils, ↓RR) Trial of naloxone Respiratory depression — naloxone + airway support Cholinergic (muscarinic/nicotinic) poisoning — also causes miosis plus a depressed physiologic state (p.3748) Sedative-hypnotic / GABAergic poisoning (alcohols, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, GHB) — depressed state, distinguished as naloxone-unresponsive (p.3748) Sympatholytic poisoning (alpha-2 agonists e.g. clonidine, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, cardiac glycosides) (p.3747) Other causes of coma including hypoglycemia (reversed by dextrose) (p.3748) Blood/urine toxicology can confirm a suspected diagnosis but must not delay clinical management (p.3690) ECG to detect QT prolongation (e.g. methadone), which can cause sudden death (p.3733) Chest imaging for noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS, a recognized complication of opioid poisoning (p.3749) In IV users, screen for blood-borne infection (hepatitis B, HIV) and bacterial complications (meningitis, osteomyelitis, abscesses, endocarditis) (p.3733) Hypoglycemia (responds to dextrose, mimics opioid coma) (p.3748) Benzodiazepine intoxication (responds to flumazenil) (p.3748) The classic overdose picture is shallow/slow respirations, miosis, bradycardia, hypothermia, and stupor or coma; toxicology can confirm but immediate management is clinical (p.3690). Pinpoint pupils are characteristic, BUT mydriasis (dilated pupils) appears once significant cerebral anoxia supervenes — dilated pupils do not exclude opioid toxicity in a deteriorating patient (p.3690). Hypoxia, not the drug itself, is what kills: in opioid and sedative-hypnotic poisoning, vital-sign changes are secondary to CNS depression or consequent hypoxemia and do not appear until consciousness is markedly reduced (grade 3-4 depression) (p.3748). Aspiration pneumonia is common in overdose because of loss of the gag reflex (p.3733). Opioids generally do NOT cause seizures, except in polydrug use, with meperidine, with high-dose tramadol, or in the newborn (p.3690). Fentanyl and its derivatives may require severalfold higher reversal doses than other opioids, and adulteration of illicit fentanyl with xylazine markedly worsens respiratory suppression (p.3689, p.3733). Prompt reversal of altered mental status and vital signs within minutes of IV naloxone is virtually diagnostic of opioid poisoning (alongside dextrose for hypoglycemia and flumazenil for benzodiazepine intoxication) (p.3748). Fluoroquinolones commonly cause false-positive opiate urine screens; rapid urine drug screens are screening-only, prone to false results, and miss agents such as kratom (p.3748). When naloxone has only a limited effect, suspect a co-ingested sedative — most commonly a benzodiazepine, which has caused fatal overdoses in combination with buprenorphine (p.3691). Dilated pupils in a suspected opioid overdose suggest cerebral anoxia has already occurred (p.3690) Re-sedation: naloxone lasts only a few hours while most opioids (especially methadone, sustained-release/'toxic time-bomb' formulations) last far longer (p.3691, p.3747) Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS (p.3749) Methadone-associated QT prolongation and sudden death (p.3733) Necrosis and limb-loss risk with fentanyl-xylazine injection (p.3733) Do not assume normal-sized or dilated pupils exclude opioids — mydriasis does NOT occur until significant brain anoxia supervenes (p.3690). Significant vital-sign abnormalities do NOT occur in opioid poisoning until there is a marked decrease in level of consciousness, so early near-normal vitals are falsely reassuring (p.3748). A negative urine drug screen does NOT rule out opioid toxicity (concentration too low, or agent such as kratom not detected); opiate screens also give false positives (e.g. fluoroquinolones) (p.3748). Primary buprenorphine overdose is nearly impossible because it is a partial agonist with increasing antagonist activity at higher doses; failure to respond to naloxone should prompt search for a co-ingested sedative (p.3690-3691). Be sure a patient is not also withdrawing from alcohol or sedatives, which may be more dangerous to manage than opioid withdrawal (p.3733). Opioids act mainly through the mu receptor (also kappa, delta, nociceptin/orphanin), all G protein-coupled, inhibiting the cAMP system and opening GIRK potassium channels to hyperpolarize and silence neurons. Life-threatening respiratory depression results from opioid-induced insensitivity of brainstem (medullary) respiratory neurons to rising carbon dioxide; analgesia and respiratory depression are mediated by receptors in the periaqueductal grey and medulla oblongata. Untreated, progression goes to respiratory and then cardiovascular collapse and death (p.3733, p.3690). Potentially lethal but rapidly reversible if respiratory depression is recognized and supported; untreated overdose progresses to respiratory and cardiovascular collapse and death. Opioid use disorder is chronic and relapsing, and most patients relapse during or after detoxification (p.3690, p.3691). Some opioid intoxications can leave delayed diffuse white-matter injury producing a persistent coma syndrome (p.232). Harrison frames poisoning severity by physiologic state (Tables 470-1/470-2): opioids produce a 'depressed' physiologic state (decreased pulse, BP, respiratory rate, temperature, neuromuscular activity, with miosis). Severity is graded by depth of CNS/physiologic depression (grades 1-4); marked vital-sign abnormalities indicate grade 3-4 depression (p.3747-3748). Note: opioid WITHDRAWAL is a separate 'stimulated' syndrome — onset 8-10 h after the last dose with lacrimation, rhinorrhea, yawning and sweating, progressing to gooseflesh, nausea/vomiting, myalgia, hyperpnea, hyperthermia, hypertension, mydriasis over a 7-10 day acute course (p.3690).

Opioid-Related Disorders — Opioid use disorder, Opioid addiction, Opioid dependence, Opioid intoxication, Opioid withdrawal, Opioid overdose Concurrent sedative-hypnotic (benzodiazepine) overdose or withdrawal, which may coexist and be more dangerous to manage Alcohol intoxication or withdrawal in a polydrug user Stimulant co-intoxication (cocaine/methamphetamine), including combined 'speedball' use Other causes of coma with respiratory depression (CNS structural lesion, metabolic encephalopathy) before miosis-based diagnosis is confirmed Blood or urine toxicology to confirm a suspected opioid diagnosis (management must not wait for results) ECG for QT-interval monitoring, particularly with methadone or in overdose Arterial/clinical assessment of respiratory status and gag reflex (aspiration pneumonia risk in overdose) Liver function tests when considering opioid-antagonist relapse-prevention therapy (most providers avoid it if LFTs exceed about three times normal) Screening for blood-borne infection (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV) in people who inject Toxic megacolon from severe opioid-induced constipation mimicking primary abdominal catastrophe MPTP-induced parkinsonism from contaminated illicitly synthesized meperidine, mimicking idiopathic Parkinson disease Orthostatic hypotension from opioid-related histamine release mimicking other causes of hypotension DSM-5 (2022) replaced the older terms dependence and addiction with opioid use disorder, opioid intoxication, and opioid withdrawal; the disorder is defined as repeated use over a 12-month period causing problems in two or more domains (tolerance, withdrawal, using larger amounts than intended, craving, and continued use despite adverse consequences) (Harrison 22e p.3688). The mu receptor is the receptor most clinically relevant to opioid effects; mu actions include analgesia, euphoric reinforcement, cough and appetite suppression, decreased respiration, decreased GI motility, sedation, and hormonal changes, while kappa activation tends to produce dysphoria and psychotic symptoms (Harrison 22e p.3689). An opioid 'high' occurs only when the rate of rise in dopamine is fast, so rapid routes such as smoking and intravenous injection produce a 'rush' whereas oral and transdermal routes give analgesia/sedation without the euphoric high (Harrison 22e p.3689). Opioid overdose is recognized clinically by shallow, slow respirations, pupillary miosis (mydriasis appears only after significant brain anoxia), bradycardia, hypothermia, and stupor or coma; immediate management is based on clinical criteria rather than waiting for toxicology (Harrison 22e p.3690). Fentanyl overdose may require roughly twice the reversal-agent dose needed for other opioids, and reversal antagonists are short-acting relative to most opioids, so re-sedation can occur after an initial response (Harrison 22e pp.3688, 3690). Adding xylazine (a nonopioid veterinary sedative) to illicit fentanyl markedly worsens respiratory suppression and is associated with tissue necrosis and increased risk of limb amputation in people who inject (Harrison 22e p.3690). Opioids generally do not cause seizures except in unusual situations: polydrug use with meperidine, high-dose tramadol, or the newborn (Harrison 22e p.3690). Withdrawal risk has a strong genetic component (up to ~50% related to functional polymorphisms), including a mu-opioid receptor variant conferring threefold higher affinity for opioids and beta-endorphin; epigenetic methylation may compensate by reducing mu-receptor numbers (Harrison 22e p.3689). Methadone can prolong the QT interval (rates reported as high as ~16% above non-methadone injecting patients) and has caused sudden death; QT monitoring is relevant during overdose and maintenance (Harrison 22e pp.3690, 3691). Heroin users are frequently polydrug users (alcohol, sedatives, cannabinoids, stimulants); none substitute for opioids but they have additive effects, so concurrent alcohol or sedative withdrawal (which can be more dangerous) must be excluded before managing opioid withdrawal (Harrison 22e p.3690). Buprenorphine's partial agonism means escalating doses shift toward antagonist activity, so primary buprenorphine overdose is nearly impossible, but high doses can precipitate withdrawal in patients on full agonists such as morphine or methadone (Harrison 22e pp.3690-3691). Most opioid-using individuals meet more than three diagnostic criteria, so reducing the DSM threshold from three to two problem areas did not change measured disease rates (Harrison 22e p.3688). Shallow/slow respirations with pinpoint miosis, bradycardia, hypothermia, and stupor or coma indicating life-threatening overdose Mydriasis in a suspected overdose suggesting significant brain anoxia has supervened Limited or absent response to standard reversal dosing, prompting suspicion of fentanyl, high antagonist requirement, or concurrent benzodiazepine overdose Loss of gag reflex with aspiration pneumonia risk Skin necrosis or limb compromise suggesting xylazine-adulterated fentanyl use Septic complications of injection use such as meningitis, osteomyelitis, or organ abscesses Administering so much antagonist that opioid withdrawal is precipitated, rather than targeting reversal of respiratory depression Assuming a single antagonist dose is sufficient, since antagonists last only a few hours while most opioids persist longer, risking re-sedation (close monitoring/continuous antagonism often needed) Overlooking concurrent benzodiazepine or alcohol/sedative involvement when reversal has only limited effect Misjudging dose in naive or infrequent users because actual ingested potency is hard to estimate, especially with fentanyl derivatives Forgetting that buprenorphine and methadone themselves can be misused and that buprenorphine can precipitate withdrawal in fentanyl- or high-dose-methadone-dependent patients Opioid receptors (mu, kappa, delta, nociceptin/orphanin) are G protein-linked and coupled to the cyclic AMP (cAMP) second-messenger system and to G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium channels (GIRKs); receptor binding increases potassium permeability, hyperpolarizes neurons, and inhibits action potentials, producing analgesia, sedation, and reinforcement. Reinforcing euphoria is mediated through the mesolimbic dopaminergic pathway from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens, where opioids indirectly raise dopamine by inhibiting GABAergic interneurons; the subjective high requires a fast rate of dopamine change. Tolerance and withdrawal arise from adaptive upregulation of the cAMP-PKA-CREB cascade in locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons after chronic mu-receptor inhibition: sustained inhibition triggers compensatory increases in cyclic AMP enzyme activity, so abrupt opioid cessation produces unopposed noradrenergic overactivity and withdrawal symptoms; this model underlies the use of alpha2-agonists to suppress that activation. PKA-driven phosphorylation of CREB also induces genes such as tyrosine hydroxylase and BDNF, the latter implicated in long-term neuroplastic changes (Harrison 22e pp.3689-3690). Opioid use disorder is a chronic, relapsing condition; most patients tend to relapse during or after detoxification, and stopping use is far easier than preventing relapse. Long-term relapse prevention requires combined pharmacologic and psychosocial approaches. Medication-free inpatient/outpatient programs have poor 1- to 5-year outcomes compared with pharmacotherapy, except for residential programs lasting roughly 6-18 months. Untreated potentially lethal overdose progresses to respiratory and cardiovascular collapse and death. Globally the World Drug Report attributes the greatest burden of drug-related morbidity and mortality to opioid misuse; in 2022 over 76,000 US overdose deaths involved opioids, with rates accelerating due to high-potency fentanyl derivatives and stimulant co-use (Harrison 22e pp.3688, 3691-3692). Withdrawal time course (heroin): symptoms begin ~8-10 h after the last dose, with early lacrimation, rhinorrhea, yawning, and sweating; later stages bring restless sleep, weakness, chills, piloerection ('cold turkey'), nausea/vomiting, muscle aches, involuntary movements, hyperpnea, hyperthermia, and hypertension. Acute withdrawal lasts ~7-10 days, followed by a protracted abstinence phase of ~26-30 weeks (hypotension, bradycardia, hypothermia, mydriasis, blunted respiratory CO2 responsiveness). Tolerance/withdrawal can develop within ~6-8 weeks of chronic daily use. Plasma half-lives vary widely: ~2.5-3 h for morphine, >22 h for methadone, minutes for fentanyl-related opioids, and longest for buprenorphine/metabolites (Harrison 22e pp.3689-3690).

Opioid toxidrome — opioid toxicity, opioid overdose syndrome Sedative-hypnotic or alcohol intoxication Clonidine or other central sympatholytic overdose Pontine haemorrhage or other brainstem lesion (for pinpoint pupils) Hypoglycaemia or other metabolic coma CNS infection Clinical recognition and response to a trial of opioid antagonist Oxygenation and ventilation assessment, including capnography where available Blood glucose and basic metabolic screen to exclude mimics Chest imaging if pulmonary oedema or aspiration is suspected Consideration of co-ingestants such as paracetamol in combination products The classic triad is depressed consciousness, respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils Respiratory depression is the immediate life threat and the target of resuscitation Naloxone, an opioid antagonist, reverses toxicity and is titrated to restore adequate ventilation rather than full alertness Miosis may be absent with certain agents or co-ingestants, so its absence does not exclude opioid toxicity Long-acting or sustained-release opioids and potent synthetic opioids may need repeated doses or an infusion of antagonist Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema and aspiration are recognised complications Inadequate ventilation or hypoxia Recurrent toxicity after initial antagonist, suggesting a long-acting agent Signs of aspiration or pulmonary oedema Coma with an uncertain airway Excluding opioid toxicity because pupils are not pinpoint Giving a single antagonist dose for a long-acting opioid and missing recurrence Overzealous antagonist dosing precipitating severe withdrawal Overlooking co-ingested paracetamol in combination analgesics The opioid toxidrome results from agonism at mu-opioid receptors in the central nervous system, depressing the brainstem respiratory drive and level of consciousness and causing pupillary constriction. Hypoventilation leads to hypercapnia and hypoxia, which are the principal causes of death. The duration and severity depend on the agent's potency and pharmacokinetics, so long-acting and highly potent synthetic opioids can outlast a single dose of antagonist and cause recurrent toxicity. With timely airway and ventilatory support and opioid antagonist, recovery is usually rapid and complete; death results mainly from unrecognised respiratory failure or complications such as aspiration and hypoxic brain injury.

Non-opioid causes of altered consciousness such as hypoglycaemia or head injury Sepsis or other acute medical illness in an injecting drug user Comorbid depression or anxiety driving misuse Urine toxicology confirming opioid and other substance use Assessment of withdrawal severity with a standardised scale Screening for blood-borne viruses and injection-related infection Liver function and general medical assessment Screening for comorbid psychiatric disorders and suicide risk Review of prescription monitoring data where available The disorder is a problematic pattern of opioid use, whether of prescribed analgesics or illicit opioids such as heroin, leading to clinically significant impairment or distress with impaired control, craving, and continued use despite harm Intoxication features include pinpoint pupils, drowsiness, slurred speech, and, dangerously, respiratory depression, which is the principal cause of death in overdose Withdrawal is intensely unpleasant but not usually life-threatening, with features such as dilated pupils, sweating, gastrointestinal upset, muscle aches, yawning, and piloerection Opioid agonist therapy with long-acting agents is the evidence-based cornerstone of treatment and substantially reduces mortality and illicit use Antagonist treatment is an option for motivated, detoxified patients, while overdose reversal with an opioid antagonist is a life-saving emergency intervention Take-home overdose-reversal medication and harm-reduction measures should be offered to patients and, where appropriate, their families Injecting use carries risks of blood-borne virus transmission, endocarditis, and skin and soft-tissue infection, so screening and preventive care are essential Comorbid mental illness, chronic pain, and social instability are common and should be addressed within an integrated treatment plan Respiratory depression or reduced consciousness indicating overdose requiring immediate reversal Features of endocarditis, sepsis, or deep soft-tissue infection in injecting users High overdose risk following loss of tolerance, such as after detoxification or release from custody Suicidal ideation or intent Abrupt discontinuation of opioids or detoxification without maintenance planning, which raises overdose risk Failing to offer take-home overdose-reversal medication Undertreating pain or comorbid mental illness, perpetuating illicit use Overlooking the sharply increased overdose risk after periods of abstinence Stigmatising attitudes that deter engagement with treatment Opioid use disorder results from repeated stimulation of mu-opioid receptors, producing potent dopaminergic reward signalling and rapid neuroadaptation in reward, stress, and executive-control circuits. Tolerance and physical dependence develop through receptor and second-messenger adaptations, and withdrawal reflects rebound noradrenergic overactivity, particularly from the locus coeruleus, while genetic, psychiatric, and environmental factors modulate vulnerability and relapse. Opioid use disorder is a chronic, relapsing condition with substantial mortality, largely from overdose, but agonist maintenance treatment markedly improves survival, retention in care, and function. Prognosis is better with sustained maintenance treatment, psychosocial support, and social stability, and worse with continued injecting, polysubstance use, and disengagement from care.

Opisthorchiasis (Opisthorchis liver fluke) — Opisthorchis viverrini infection, Opisthorchis felineus infection, cat liver fluke, Southeast Asian liver fluke, opisthorchiid liver fluke disease Clonorchiasis (Clonorchis sinensis), which is clinically and morphologically very similar Fascioliasis and other biliary trematode infection Cholelithiasis and choledocholithiasis with biliary colic Ascending bacterial cholangitis Cholangiocarcinoma or other hepatobiliary malignancy Recurrent pyogenic (oriental) cholangitis Stool microscopy for ova and parasites, ideally with concentration and repeated samples Serology or antigen detection where available to support diagnosis in light infection Full blood count for eosinophilia and liver function tests Abdominal ultrasound for biliary dilatation, gallbladder sludge and ductal wall changes MRCP or CT when malignancy or complicated biliary disease is suspected Endoscopic examination of bile with cytology if cholangiocarcinoma is a concern Acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish (often as fermented or pickled fish dishes) that carry metacercariae; highly endemic across parts of Southeast Asia and eastern Europe Most light infections are asymptomatic; heavier or chronic infection causes right upper quadrant discomfort, dyspepsia, hepatomegaly and features of biliary irritation Chronic infection is a recognised risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma, making it one of the few parasitic causes of a defined human cancer Diagnosis rests on finding characteristic operculated eggs in stool, which are difficult to distinguish from other opisthorchiid and heterophyid eggs on morphology alone Peripheral eosinophilia is common, and imaging may show intrahepatic ductal dilatation, gallbladder sludge and biliary wall thickening Praziquantel is the treatment of choice and is highly effective against the adult flukes Public health control depends on discouraging consumption of raw freshwater fish and on sanitation to interrupt egg contamination of water bodies Progressive jaundice, weight loss and a biliary mass suggesting cholangiocarcinoma Fever with rigors and right upper quadrant pain indicating ascending cholangitis Biliary obstruction with worsening liver dysfunction Recurrent cholangitis or intrahepatic stone formation Assuming eradication removes cancer risk; malignancy can develop years after treatment in previously heavily infected patients Misidentifying eggs as heterophyid or other opisthorchiid species because of overlapping morphology Missing light infections on a single stool sample and prematurely excluding the diagnosis Attributing biliary symptoms solely to gallstones and overlooking coexistent fluke infection in endemic populations Opisthorchis species are small liver flukes whose life cycle involves freshwater snails as first intermediate hosts and cyprinid fish as second intermediate hosts. Humans and other fish-eating mammals become definitive hosts when they ingest infective metacercariae in raw or inadequately cooked fish. The larvae excyst in the duodenum, ascend the biliary tree through the ampulla, and mature into adult flukes residing in the intrahepatic bile ducts and gallbladder. Long-standing mechanical irritation and the fluke's secretions drive chronic inflammation, epithelial hyperplasia, periductal fibrosis and cholestasis; sustained biliary injury with proliferative and dysplastic change underlies the strong association with cholangiocarcinoma. Eggs passed in bile reach the intestine and are excreted in faeces, continuing the cycle when they contaminate freshwater. Uncomplicated infection responds well to anthelmintic treatment with resolution of symptoms, but chronic heavy infection carries a serious long-term risk of cholangiocarcinoma and biliary complications, for which the outlook is poor.

Opitz G/BBB syndrome (MID1) — MID1, X-linked Opitz G/BBB syndrome, Opitz-Frias syndrome, hypertelorism-hypospadias syndrome Autosomal dominant Opitz G/BBB syndrome (22q11.2 region) 22q11.2 deletion syndrome CHARGE syndrome Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome Other midline malformation syndromes Isolated hypospadias with hypertelorism Swallowing assessment and airway evaluation for laryngo-tracheo-oesophageal cleft Echocardiography for congenital heart disease Renal and genital imaging and evaluation of anal anatomy Brain MRI and developmental assessment Targeted MID1 sequencing or a gene panel or exome sequencing, with chromosomal microarray to exclude 22q11.2 deletion A disorder of midline development in which the X-linked form is caused by MID1 variants and affects males more severely The cardinal features are hypertelorism (widely spaced eyes) and hypospadias in males A laryngo-tracheo-oesophageal cleft can cause swallowing difficulty, recurrent aspiration and respiratory problems in infancy Additional midline anomalies include cleft lip and palate, imperforate anus and congenital heart defects Developmental delay and intellectual disability are variable and often mild to moderate Caused by variants in MID1, encoding a microtubule-associated E3 ubiquitin ligase; carrier females typically show only hypertelorism Aspiration and airway involvement are the main early clinical threats Recurrent aspiration or respiratory distress from an airway or oesophageal cleft Feeding failure and faltering growth Haemodynamically significant congenital heart disease Airway compromise requiring urgent intervention Missing a laryngo-tracheo-oesophageal cleft in an infant with recurrent aspiration Not distinguishing the X-linked MID1 form from the 22q11.2-associated autosomal dominant form Overlooking the diagnosis when only hypertelorism is present in a carrier mother Attributing feeding problems to reflux alone without airway assessment MID1 encodes a microtubule-associated protein of the TRIM/RBCC family that functions as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, regulating the turnover of the catalytic subunit of protein phosphatase 2A and thereby influencing microtubule dynamics and signalling during midline morphogenesis. Loss-of-function variants disturb this regulation, impairing the fusion and development of ventral midline structures in the face, larynx, heart, abdomen and genitalia. The result is the constellation of hypertelorism, laryngo-tracheo-oesophageal cleft, hypospadias and other midline defects, with variable neurodevelopmental impact. Because MID1 is X-linked, males are affected while carrier females usually show only hypertelorism. Outcome depends largely on the severity of the laryngo-tracheo-oesophageal cleft and cardiac anomalies; with surgical management of midline defects many children do well, though neurodevelopmental outcome is variable. Care is multidisciplinary and supportive.

Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome — opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome, OMS, dancing eyes-dancing feet syndrome, Kinsbourne syndrome Cerebellar ataxia of infective, toxic, or metabolic cause Other encephalomyelitis Cross-sectional imaging of chest, abdomen, and pelvis to search for neuroblastoma or other tumour Metabolic tumour imaging and urinary catecholamine metabolites in children in adults, including for small-cell lung and breast carcinoma Characterised by opsoclonus (chaotic, involuntary, multidirectional saccades), myoclonus, and cerebellar ataxia Behavioural disturbance, irritability, and sleep disruption are common, especially in children In children it is strongly associated with neuroblastoma, so cross-sectional and metabolic tumour imaging is mandatory In adults it may be parainfectious or paraneoplastic, notably with small-cell lung and breast carcinoma Opsoclonus persists during eye closure and sleep, helping distinguish it from other abnormal eye movements First-line immunotherapy uses corticosteroids or corticotropin with intravenous immunoglobulin, escalating to rituximab or other agents in refractory disease In paraneoplastic cases, removal or treatment of the underlying tumour is central to management Failure to identify an occult neuroblastoma or other tumour on initial screening Severe ataxia or myoclonus impairing safety and function Progressive encephalopathy or developmental regression in children Relapse after apparent recovery suggesting undertreated disease or occult tumour Failing to search repeatedly for an occult tumour when initial imaging is negative Mistaking opsoclonus for nystagmus or a functional disorder Under-treating, as inadequate immunotherapy is linked to relapse and long-term sequelae Overlooking behavioural and developmental effects that require broader support Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome is an immune-mediated disorder affecting brainstem and cerebellar circuits that control eye movements and coordination. Loss of inhibitory control over the saccadic burst neurons, thought to involve dysfunction of omnipause and fastigial-cerebellar pathways, produces the chaotic saccades of opsoclonus, while cerebellar involvement generates myoclonus and ataxia. The immune response is frequently triggered by an occult tumour, classically neuroblastoma in children through cross-reacting antineural immunity, or by preceding infection; a defined single antibody is often not identified. Many patients, especially children, improve with immunotherapy and tumour treatment, but relapses and residual cognitive, behavioural, or motor deficits are common, and outcome in paraneoplastic adult cases depends on the underlying malignancy.

distinguish pseudopapilloedema (no true leakage) from genuine disc swelling Neuroimaging when true papilloedema cannot be confidently excluded on clinical and ultrasound grounds Acellular calcified prompting unnecessary investigation if not recognised Superficial drusen appear as glistening, refractile bodies at the disc margin, whereas buried drusen produce an elevated disc with blurred margins but no true swelling Features favouring pseudopapilloedema over true papilloedema include an absent central cup, anomalous branching vessels, a lumpy disc contour and the lack of hyperaemia, exudates or nerve fibre layer oedema obscuring vessels Most patients are asymptomatic, but drusen can cause progressive visual field defects, typically arcuate or nasal, and an enlarged blind spot
