tomography can directly visualise buried drusen and has become a preferred imaging modality Management is largely observation with monitoring of visual fields, and rare complications such as choroidal neovascularisation or anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy require specific attention Progressive visual field loss attributable to the drusen Sudden visual loss suggesting anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy Subretinal fluid or haemorrhage indicating peripapillary choroidal neovascularisation Any doubt about coexisting true papilloedema, which mandates exclusion of raised intracranial pressure Misinterpreting pseudopapilloedema as true papilloedema and subjecting the patient to unnecessary lumbar puncture and imaging Conversely, assuming disc elevation is drusen and missing coexisting raised intracranial pressure Failing to monitor visual fields in an asymptomatic patient and overlooking progressive loss Not recognising a treatable complication such as choroidal neovascularisation Assuming absence of visible superficial drusen excludes buried drusen, which need ultrasound or OCT to detect Optic disc drusen are calcified concretions that accumulate within the prelaminar optic nerve head, thought to arise from disturbed axonal metabolism and impaired axoplasmic transport in a congenitally crowded disc with a small scleral canal. Degenerating axonal mitochondria and extruded material undergo progressive calcification over time, which is why drusen are frequently buried in childhood and become more superficial and visible with age. The crowded, drusen-laden disc can mechanically compress adjacent nerve fibres, producing slowly progressive visual field defects, and the compromised vascular supply predisposes to ischaemic optic neuropathy and, rarely, peripapillary choroidal neovascularisation. Most patients retain good central vision throughout life, but slowly progressive peripheral field loss is common and irreversible; central vision is usually only threatened by uncommon complications such as ischaemic optic neuropathy or choroidal neovascularisation.

optic disc pit — optic pit, congenital optic disc pit Central serous chorioretinopathy Optic nerve coloboma Morning glory disc anomaly Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment involving the macula X-linked retinoschisis Glaucomatous acquired pit of the optic nerve Vitreomacular traction syndrome Optical coherence tomography of the macula and optic nerve head Fundus fluorescein angiography to exclude active RPE leakage Automated perimetry for arcuate or centrocaecal field defects Fundus autofluorescence to map the extent of serous detachment Serial fundus photography to monitor pit and maculopathy OCT angiography to exclude a secondary choroidal neovascular membrane A congenital, usually unilateral, greyish oval or round excavation of the optic disc, most often located in the inferotemporal quadrant. Discs harbouring a pit are frequently larger than normal, and the pit may be accompanied by a peripapillary crescent or halo. The major sight-threatening complication is optic disc pit maculopathy, a serous macular detachment often with an inner and outer retinoschisis-like separation. Fluid in maculopathy is thought to originate from vitreous or cerebrospinal fluid tracking through the pit rather than from a classic RPE leak. Fluorescein angiography typically shows late hyperfluorescence of the pit but, importantly, no active leakage into the subretinal fluid. Optical coherence tomography is the key investigation, demonstrating schisis-like intraretinal splitting and subretinal fluid communicating with the pit. Temporal pits are more likely to develop maculopathy than nasal or central pits. Vitrectomy with gas tamponade, sometimes combined with internal limiting membrane peel or laser to the temporal disc margin, is the mainstay for persistent maculopathy. New central metamorphopsia or blurring indicating evolving maculopathy Progressive serous macular detachment on serial OCT Marked reduction in best-corrected visual acuity Features suggesting acquired glaucomatous pitting with raised intraocular pressure Mistaking optic pit maculopathy for central serous chorioretinopathy and delaying appropriate surgical referral. Assuming subretinal fluid arises from an RPE leak; fluorescein typically shows no active leak, misleading the unwary. Confusing a congenital pit with an acquired glaucomatous pit and missing coexisting raised intraocular pressure. Underestimating the chronicity of maculopathy fluid, which may resorb slowly even after successful surgery. An optic disc pit represents a localised herniation of dysplastic retina into a defect in the lamina cribrosa, regarded as part of the optic disc coloboma spectrum arising from imperfect closure of the fetal fissure. The pit is a discontinuity in the normal disc architecture through which the subarachnoid space and vitreous cavity may communicate with the intraretinal and subretinal spaces. In optic pit maculopathy, fluid, believed to derive from liquefied vitreous or cerebrospinal fluid, tracks through the pit and dissects into the retina, producing a schisis-like inner separation and an overlying serous detachment. Persistent traction and fluid accumulation lead to photoreceptor damage and progressive central visual loss. An isolated pit without maculopathy is compatible with normal lifelong vision. Once maculopathy develops, untreated cases frequently progress to poor central acuity, though surgical repair can restore useful vision in a substantial proportion.

optic nerve coloboma — optic disc coloboma, coloboma of the optic nerve head Morning glory disc anomaly Optic disc pit Peripapillary staphyloma Optic disc hypoplasia Megalopapilla Glaucomatous optic disc cupping Tilted disc syndrome Dilated fundus examination and fundus photography to map the coloboma Optical coherence tomography of the disc, peripapillary retina and macula B-scan ultrasonography or MRI where a colobomatous cyst is suspected Systemic evaluation including renal ultrasound and cardiac/ENT assessment for syndromic associations Genetic testing (e.g. PAX6, and panels for CHARGE/papillorenal syndrome) Visual field testing and electrophysiology to quantify functional deficit Results from defective closure of the embryonic fetal (choroidal) fissure, producing a sharply demarcated, bowl-shaped white excavation that characteristically involves the inferonasal disc. The excavation is decentred inferiorly, in contrast to the morning glory anomaly in which the abnormality is central and the disc is surrounded by a raised annulus. May occur in isolation or extend inferonasally as a chorioretinal coloboma, and can be unilateral or bilateral. Autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity is described, including mutations affecting the PAX6 and other developmental genes. Associated with systemic syndromes, notably CHARGE syndrome, renal coloboma (papillorenal) syndrome and morning glory-related conditions. Retinal detachment is an important complication, often related to a break within colobomatous retina or the fragile intercalary membrane. Visual acuity is variable and difficult to predict from disc appearance alone, ranging from near normal to severely reduced. A relative afferent pupillary defect and corresponding field loss may accompany larger colobomas. Sudden reduction in vision or new floaters suggesting retinal detachment Bilateral colobomas or associated microphthalmos indicating a syndromic disorder Signs of CHARGE association (choanal atresia, cardiac or ear anomalies) Proteinuria or renal impairment raising suspicion of papillorenal syndrome Confusing a coloboma with the morning glory anomaly, which alters both prognosis and syndromic associations. Overlooking systemic disease, particularly renal and cardiac anomalies, by not screening for associated syndromes. Attributing the excavation to glaucoma and treating intraocular pressure unnecessarily. Missing an evolving retinal detachment because the colobomatous anatomy obscures the break. Optic nerve coloboma is a congenital dysplasia resulting from incomplete or abnormal closure of the embryonic fetal fissure, which normally seals during the fifth to seventh week of gestation along the inferonasal aspect of the developing optic cup and stalk. Failure of fusion leaves a defect through which mesodermal and neuroectodermal tissue is deficient, creating an excavated, glial-lined depression at the disc that may extend contiguously into the choroid and retina. The thin intercalary membrane overlying the coloboma is prone to breaks, predisposing to serous or rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. Because closure defects reflect broader disturbances in ocular and systemic morphogenesis, colobomas frequently accompany multisystem developmental syndromes. Visual outcome is highly variable and depends on the extent of the coloboma and macular involvement; some patients retain good acuity while others have marked impairment. The lifelong risk of retinal detachment warrants ongoing surveillance.

Optic nerve hypoplasia — ONH, hypoplastic optic disc, optic disc hypoplasia Optic atrophy of other causes Optic disc coloboma or morning glory anomaly Megalopapilla with pseudo-small disc appearance Tilted disc syndrome Delayed visual maturation Cortical visual impairment Leber congenital amaurosis MRI of the brain, orbits and pituitary region Full endocrine evaluation including cortisol, thyroid, growth hormone and prolactin axes OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer where cooperation allows Visual evoked potentials and electrophysiology Cycloplegic refraction and orthoptic assessment Developmental and paediatric review A leading cause of congenital visual impairment, characterised by an abnormally small optic disc with a reduced complement of retinal ganglion cell axons The classic double-ring sign is a pale, small disc surrounded by a ring of pigment marking where the normal disc margin should lie May be unilateral or bilateral; vision ranges from near normal to severe impairment, often with nystagmus in bilateral cases Frequently associated with midline brain defects and hypopituitarism, forming part of septo-optic dysplasia Endocrine assessment is essential because unrecognised cortisol or thyroid deficiency can be life-threatening in infancy Neuroimaging with MRI evaluates the optic nerves, chiasm, septum pellucidum and pituitary Risk factors include young maternal age and gestational exposures, though most cases are sporadic Neonatal hypoglycaemia or adrenal crisis from unrecognised hypopituitarism Prolonged jaundice, micropenis or growth failure suggesting endocrine deficiency Diabetes insipidus indicating hypothalamic involvement Developmental regression or seizures suggesting broader brain malformation Temperature instability pointing to hypothalamic dysfunction Failing to arrange endocrine assessment and missing dangerous hormone deficiencies Assuming unilateral disease excludes systemic associations Overlooking the double-ring sign and misdiagnosing optic atrophy Not imaging the brain to identify midline and pituitary anomalies Optic nerve hypoplasia results from a deficiency of retinal ganglion cell axons, arising either from failure of adequate axon generation or from excessive regression during development. Because optic nerve development is intimately linked with midline forebrain and hypothalamic-pituitary formation, the same developmental disturbance often produces associated midline brain malformations and pituitary dysfunction. The small disc has fewer nerve fibres, and the surrounding retinal pigment epithelium and lamina cribrosa create the double-ring appearance. Visual deficit reflects the degree of axonal deficiency, while the systemic consequences depend on the extent of hypothalamic-pituitary and midline involvement. Visual outcome varies widely from good to severely impaired and is generally stable, but overall prognosis and safety hinge on timely recognition and treatment of associated endocrine deficiencies.

Optic neuritis — ON, retrobulbar neuritis, papillitis, optic nerve inflammation, demyelinating optic neuritis Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (arteritic and non-arteritic) Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder MOG-antibody-associated optic neuritis Compressive optic neuropathy from tumour or aneurysm Toxic, nutritional, or hereditary (Leber) optic neuropathy Central retinal artery occlusion and other causes of acute visual loss Assessment of visual acuity, colour vision, and relative afferent pupillary defect Visual field testing (commonly shows a central scotoma) Contrast MRI of the brain and orbits to assess the nerve and demyelinating lesions Aquaporin-4 and MOG antibody testing in atypical or severe cases OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer to monitor atrophy; bloods/lumbar puncture where an infective or inflammatory cause is suspected Typically presents in a young adult (more often female) with subacute unilateral visual loss developing over hours to days, accompanied by pain worse on eye movement A relative afferent pupillary defect is present, and colour vision (especially red desaturation) is impaired out of proportion to acuity In retrobulbar neuritis the optic disc looks normal at onset ('the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing'), whereas papillitis shows a swollen disc It is commonly the presenting or an associated feature of multiple sclerosis, so demyelination should be considered MRI of the brain and orbits with contrast assesses the optic nerve and detects demyelinating white-matter lesions that predict multiple sclerosis risk Vision usually recovers spontaneously over weeks; intravenous corticosteroids speed recovery but do not change final visual outcome Atypical features (bilateral, no pain, poor recovery, severe disc swelling) should prompt consideration of neuromyelitis optica, MOG-associated disease, or an infective/compressive cause Bilateral simultaneous, severe, or poorly recovering visual loss suggesting neuromyelitis optica or a non-demyelinating cause Absence of pain or a progressive course pointing to a compressive or ischaemic optic neuropathy Systemic features suggesting infection, sarcoidosis, or vasculitis Older patient with headache and jaw claudication — exclude giant cell arteritis as a cause of ischaemic optic neuropathy Attributing every acute optic neuropathy to demyelination and missing arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy in older patients Assuming steroids improve the final visual outcome rather than just the speed of recovery Overlooking neuromyelitis optica or MOG disease in atypical or severe cases that need different management Failing to counsel on and investigate the associated risk of multiple sclerosis Optic neuritis is inflammation and demyelination of the optic nerve, most commonly immune-mediated and associated with multiple sclerosis. An inflammatory, often T-cell-driven process attacks the myelin sheath of optic nerve axons, disrupting conduction and causing loss of visual acuity, colour vision, and contrast. Because conduction rather than the axon itself is initially affected, remyelination allows substantial recovery, though repeated or severe attacks cause axonal loss and permanent deficits with optic atrophy. Antibody-mediated variants (aquaporin-4 in neuromyelitis optica, MOG antibody disease) and infective or granulomatous causes produce similar inflammation through different mechanisms. Most patients with typical demyelinating optic neuritis recover good vision over several weeks regardless of steroid use, though some residual colour and contrast deficits and a risk of future multiple sclerosis remain.

of the oral cavity and neck with biopsy of the lesion CT or MRI to assess local extent, bony invasion, and nodal disease Chest imaging and PET-CT for distant staging and second primaries Examination under anaesthesia and panendoscopy where indicated to map extent and exclude synchronous tumours Dental assessment and nutritional evaluation before treatment Most oral cavity cancers are squamous cell carcinomas driven by tobacco in all its forms, betel or areca nut chewing, and heavy alcohol use, which act synergistically It typically presents as a persistent ulcer, red or white patch, lump, or non-healing sore in the mouth, often with pain, bleeding, or loose teeth as disease advances Any oral lesion that fails to heal within a few weeks should be biopsied rather than treated repeatedly as trauma or infection Premalignant lesions such as leukoplakia, erythroplakia, and oral submucous fibrosis carry malignant potential and warrant monitoring and biopsy Cervical lymph node metastasis markedly affect speech, swallowing, and appearance, so multidisciplinary rehabilitation and dental assessment before radiotherapy are important A mouth ulcer or lesion that fails to heal within a few weeks A firm, fixed, or enlarging cervical lymph node Unexplained loosening of teeth, numbness, or difficulty moving the tongue Persistent oral bleeding, pain, or difficulty swallowing with weight loss Repeatedly treating a persistent oral ulcer as trauma or infection without biopsy Neglecting to examine and image the cervical lymph nodes Overlooking premalignant lesions that require surveillance Failing to arrange dental and rehabilitation input before and after treatment Oral squamous cell carcinoma arises from the mucosal lining of the oral cavity through cumulative genetic damage caused by carcinogens in tobacco, areca nut, and alcohol. This produces field cancerisation with premalignant changes such as leukoplakia and erythroplakia that can progress through dysplasia to invasive carcinoma. The tumour invades local structures including muscle, bone, and nerves, and spreads readily to regional cervical lymph nodes; distant metastasis occurs later. Chronic mucosal irritation and conditions such as oral submucous fibrosis further predispose to malignant change. Prognosis depends on stage, tumour thickness, and nodal status; early localised tumours have good cure rates, whereas nodal metastasis, deep invasion, and advanced stage substantially reduce survival and increase recurrence.

Oral candidiasis — oral thrush, oral candidosis, candidal stomatitis, moniliasis Oral leukoplakia and other keratotic white lesions Lichen planus and lichenoid reactions Geographic tongue for the atrophic form Chemical or thermal mucosal burns Mucosal manifestations of anaemia or nutritional deficiency Oral swab, smear, or oral rinse for microscopy and culture Biopsy for adherent white patches to assess hyperplastic candidiasis and dysplasia Blood glucose and screening for diabetes Haematinics (iron, folate, B12) where atrophic or recurrent disease Evaluation for immunodeficiency, including HIV, in unexplained or severe cases Oral candidiasis is usually an opportunistic infection by Candida species, most often Candida albicans, and typically signals a local or systemic predisposing factor The pseudomembranous form (thrush) shows white curd-like plaques that wipe off to reveal an erythematous, sometimes bleeding, base Erythematous (atrophic) candidiasis presents as a red, sore mucosa or a depapillated tongue, and is common under dentures or after antibiotics Angular cheilitis at the mouth corners frequently coexists and reflects candidal and bacterial colonisation with local moisture Denture stomatitis appears as erythema confined to the denture-bearing palatal mucosa and relates to poor denture hygiene and continuous wear Common predisposing factors include inhaled or systemic corticosteroids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, xerostomia, diabetes, and immunosuppression Management combines antifungal therapy with correction of the underlying cause, including denture hygiene and control of dry mouth Chronic hyperplastic candidiasis presents as an adherent white patch that will not rub off and carries a small malignant potential warranting biopsy Unexplained or severe oral candidiasis in a previously healthy adult raising suspicion of undiagnosed HIV or other immunodeficiency Chronic hyperplastic candidiasis with dysplasia and potential for malignant transformation Extension into the oesophagus with dysphagia suggesting significant immunosuppression Treating recurrent candidiasis without seeking and correcting the underlying predisposing factor Assuming an adherent white patch is thrush when it is hyperplastic candidiasis or leukoplakia needing biopsy Overlooking denture hygiene and continuous wear as the driver of denture stomatitis Missing an immunocompromising condition in unexplained or florid infection Candida species are common oral commensals kept in check by intact mucosal defences, salivary factors, and the resident microbiota. Disruption of this balance allows overgrowth and conversion to an invasive hyphal form that adheres to and penetrates the epithelium. Local factors such as denture coverage, dry mouth, and topical steroids, together with systemic factors such as antibiotics, immunosuppression, diabetes, and nutritional deficiency, create the conditions for opportunistic infection. The clinical pattern (pseudomembranous, erythematous, or hyperplastic) reflects the host state and chronicity rather than different organisms. Most acute candidiasis responds well to antifungal treatment when predisposing factors are corrected, but recurrence is common if the underlying cause persists, and chronic hyperplastic lesions require monitoring for dysplasia.

Oral-facial-digital syndrome — orofaciodigital syndrome, OFD syndrome, OFD1, OFD type I (Papillon-Leage-Psaume) Joubert syndrome and related disorders Pallister-Hall syndrome Ellis-van Creveld syndrome Meckel-Gruber syndrome Mohr syndrome (OFD type II) versus other OFD subtypes Isolated cleft palate with limb anomaly Detailed dysmorphology and oral examination to document tongue, frenula, and palatal anomalies Radiographs of the hands and feet to characterise digital malformations Brain MRI for callosal, cerebellar, and posterior fossa anomalies including the molar tooth sign Renal ultrasound to detect polycystic or cystic kidney disease Molecular genetic testing including OFD1 and a ciliopathy gene panel Developmental assessment where intellectual disability is present A group of ciliopathies defined by malformations of the oral cavity, face, and digits, with several distinct subtypes differing in inheritance and associated features Oral findings include lobulated or bifid tongue with hamartomas, multiple frenula, cleft palate or lip, and dental anomalies Facial features may include hypertelorism, a broad or bifid nasal tip, and micrognathia, while digital anomalies include brachydactyly, syndactyly, clinodactyly, and polydactyly Type I is X-linked dominant, caused by OFD1 variants and typically lethal in males, and is frequently associated with polycystic kidney and intracerebral cysts As a ciliopathy it overlaps with Joubert syndrome and other disorders, and the OFD1 gene product localises to the centriole and basal body of the primary cilium Diagnosis integrates the oral-facial-digital pattern with imaging of brain and kidneys and molecular confirmation for subtype classification and counselling Progressive polycystic kidney disease leading to renal failure Significant central nervous system malformation with neurological impairment or seizures Airway or feeding compromise from severe oral and palatal malformation Male fetal or neonatal loss suggesting an X-linked dominant lethal genotype Classifying an affected child into the wrong OFD subtype and giving inaccurate prognostic and recurrence advice Overlooking the ciliopathy association with progressive renal cystic disease requiring long-term surveillance Missing subtle central nervous system malformation without dedicated brain imaging Attributing oral hamartomas or extra frenula to isolated dental problems Oral-facial-digital syndromes are ciliopathies in which defective primary cilium and basal body function disrupts developmental signalling that patterns midline craniofacial structures, the palate and tongue, and the limbs. The prototypic type I results from variants in OFD1, encoding a centriolar and basal body protein; because the gene is X-linked, hemizygous males are usually not viable while heterozygous females show variable manifestations owing to X-inactivation. Impaired ciliary signalling in the kidney predisposes to cystic renal disease, and in the developing brain it contributes to callosal, cerebellar, and other midline malformations. Prognosis varies by subtype and organ involvement. Many females with type I have a normal or near-normal lifespan but may develop progressive polycystic kidney disease, while central nervous system malformation and severe systemic involvement worsen the outlook in some subtypes.

transformation Non-homogeneous, speckled, or verrucous lesions and any red component, indicating higher malignant potential Ulceration, induration, or a developing mass suggesting transformation to carcinoma High-risk sites such as the floor of mouth and ventrolateral tongue Presence of moderate to severe epithelial dysplasia on biopsy Labelling a white patch as benign without biopsy or follow-up Assuming absence of symptoms means absence of risk Sampling only a homogeneous area and missing dysplasia in a red or nodular component Failing to address tobacco, areca nut, and alcohol use that perpetuate the lesion Leukoplakia reflects an alteration in the oral epithelium in which increased keratin production and epithelial thickening scatter light to produce a white appearance that does not rub off. Chronic exposure to carcinogens such as tobacco and areca nut drives genetic and epigenetic changes in basal keratinocytes, which may manifest histologically as hyperkeratosis with or without epithelial dysplasia. Dysplastic change represents disordered maturation and cellular atypia that can accumulate over time, and lesions with higher grades of dysplasia carry a greater likelihood of progressing to invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Many lesions remain stable or regress after risk factors are removed, but a proportion undergo malignant transformation, and the risk rises with non-homogeneous appearance, high-risk sites, and higher grades of dysplasia, making long-term surveillance important.

Oral lichen planus — OLP Oral lichenoid drug or contact reaction Chronic graft-versus-host disease Mucous membrane pemphigoid Pemphigus vulgaris Lupus erythematosus of the mucosa Oral leukoplakia or dysplasia Clinical assessment of distribution and morphology Biopsy with histopathology, and direct immunofluorescence to exclude immunobullous disease Review of medications and dental materials for lichenoid triggers Long-term surveillance for malignant change, especially in erosive disease Assessment for cutaneous or other mucosal lichen planus A chronic immune-mediated mucosal disorder presenting with bilateral, often symmetrical, white striae, plaques, atrophic or erosive lesions The reticular form with lacy white Wickham striae is frequently asymptomatic, whereas erosive and atrophic forms cause pain and burning The buccal mucosa, tongue and gingivae are commonly involved, and desquamative gingivitis may be the presenting feature A lichenoid reaction that is clinically similar can be caused by drugs, dental materials or graft-versus-host disease There is a small but recognised risk of malignant transformation, so long-term monitoring is advised Topical corticosteroids are the mainstay for symptomatic disease, with other immunomodulators for refractory cases Non-homogeneous, indurated or non-healing areas suggesting dysplasia or carcinoma Rapidly changing or ulcerated lesions Widespread erosive disease impairing nutrition Features suggesting immunobullous disease requiring different management Not distinguishing lichen planus from a lichenoid drug or contact reaction Missing an immunobullous disorder presenting as desquamative gingivitis Failing to monitor for malignant transformation Overlooking coexisting skin or genital lichen planus Oral lichen planus is a T-cell-mediated chronic inflammatory condition in which cytotoxic T lymphocytes target basal keratinocytes of the mucosal epithelium, producing basal cell damage and a band-like subepithelial lymphocytic infiltrate. The resulting epithelial changes create the characteristic striae, atrophy and erosions. Similar lichenoid reactions can be triggered by drugs, contact with dental restorative materials or systemic graft-versus-host disease, reflecting a shared final immunological pathway. The condition is chronic with relapses and remissions; symptoms are usually controllable, but erosive forms carry a small long-term risk of malignant transformation requiring surveillance.

Oral squamous cell carcinoma — oral cancer, oral SCC, mouth cancer, squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity Traumatic ulcer Recurrent aphthous ulceration Oral leukoplakia or erythroplakia without invasion Chronic infective ulcers such as tuberculosis or syphilis Erosive lichen planus Salivary gland or other oral malignancy Incisional biopsy of the lesion for histological diagnosis and grading Examination and imaging of the neck for lymph node involvement Cross-sectional imaging (CT, MRI) to assess local extent and staging Assessment for distant metastasis and synchronous primaries Multidisciplinary evaluation for treatment planning Oral squamous cell carcinoma is the most common malignancy of the oral cavity and often presents as a non-healing ulcer, lump, or persistent red or white patch Classic worrying features are an indurated ulcer with rolled margins, fixation to underlying tissue, and failure to heal beyond two to three weeks Tobacco in all forms, areca nut, and alcohol are the dominant risk factors and act synergistically The lateral and ventral tongue and the floor of mouth are high-risk sites, though any oral surface can be affected Early lesions may be painless, so any persistent oral abnormality warrants a high index of suspicion and referral Cervical lymphadenopathy, especially firm or fixed nodes, may indicate regional metastatic spread Definitive diagnosis requires biopsy, and staging guides treatment involving surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy as appropriate Prognosis depends heavily on stage at diagnosis, underscoring the value of early detection and opportunistic screening Any oral ulcer or lesion persisting beyond two to three weeks requires urgent specialist referral to exclude cancer Induration, fixation, rolled margins, or spontaneous bleeding of a lesion Unexplained firm or fixed cervical lymphadenopathy Persistent unexplained pain, numbness, loosening of teeth, or difficulty swallowing Attributing a persistent ulcer to trauma or denture irritation and delaying biopsy Reassurance because a lesion is painless, since early cancers are often symptomless Failing to examine and palpate the neck for nodal disease Overlooking the risk of second primaries in a field-changed mucosa Oral squamous cell carcinoma develops through the accumulation of genetic and epigenetic alterations in oral keratinocytes, typically driven by chronic exposure to carcinogens such as tobacco, areca nut, and alcohol. Many tumours arise within or adjacent to potentially malignant disorders such as leukoplakia or erythroplakia, progressing through increasing grades of epithelial dysplasia to carcinoma in situ and then invasive disease when malignant cells breach the basement membrane. The invasive tumour infiltrates local tissue, can destroy bone, and spreads via lymphatics to cervical nodes, with distant metastasis in advanced disease. Field change means the whole mucosa is at risk of further primaries. Outcome is strongly stage-dependent, with early localised disease carrying a favourable prognosis, whereas advanced tumours with nodal involvement have substantially poorer survival and higher morbidity from treatment.

Oral submucous fibrosis — OSMF, oral submucosal fibrosis Scleroderma with orofacial involvement Oral leukoplakia or erythroplakia Oral lichen planus Radiation-induced fibrosis Squamous cell carcinoma Clinical assessment of mouth opening and fibrous bands Biopsy to confirm fibrosis and exclude dysplasia or carcinoma Detailed habit history of areca nut and tobacco use Regular surveillance for malignant change Assessment of nutritional status and anaemia where relevant A chronic progressive fibrosing disease of the oral mucosa strongly linked to areca (betel) nut chewing Patients develop burning on eating spicy food, blanching and stiffening of the mucosa and progressive limitation of mouth opening Palpable fibrous bands in the buccal mucosa and a rigid, pale mucosa are characteristic It is a recognised oral potentially malignant disorder with a significant risk of squamous cell carcinoma It is most prevalent in South and South-East Asian populations and their diaspora Management includes strict habit cessation, medical measures to improve mouth opening and surgery for severe trismus, with lifelong cancer surveillance Development of a non-healing ulcer, red patch or mass suggesting carcinoma Rapidly worsening trismus Induration or dysplasia on biopsy Weight loss or difficulty maintaining nutrition Failing to counsel firmly on areca nut and tobacco cessation Overlooking malignant transformation during follow-up Confusing early disease with lichen planus or leukoplakia Underestimating the functional impact of progressive trismus Oral submucous fibrosis is driven chiefly by arecoline and other alkaloids in areca nut, which stimulate fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis while reducing collagen breakdown, leading to excessive deposition of dense fibrous tissue in the lamina propria and submucosa. Chronic inflammation and juxta-epithelial hyalinisation cause progressive mucosal stiffening and trismus, and epithelial atrophy with altered turnover increases susceptibility to malignant transformation. The result is an irreversible fibrotic and potentially premalignant state. The fibrosis is largely irreversible and progressive if the habit continues; cessation and treatment can improve symptoms, but the elevated lifelong risk of oral cancer necessitates ongoing surveillance.

Orbital apex syndrome — Jacod syndrome, orbital apex-optic canal syndrome Superior orbital fissure syndrome without optic nerve involvement Cavernous sinus syndrome Tolosa-Hunt granulomatous inflammation Orbital cellulitis or subperiosteal abscess Thyroid eye disease with apical crowding Idiopathic orbital inflammatory disease Orbital tumour or metastasis MRI of the orbit and skull base with contrast CT of the orbit and paranasal sinuses to assess bone and sinus disease Nasoendoscopy and biopsy where invasive fungal infection is suspected Inflammatory markers and infection screen Blood glucose and immune status assessment Visual field testing and assessment of the afferent pupillary pathway Characterised by ophthalmoplegia from involvement of the third, fourth, and sixth cranial nerves together with visual loss from optic nerve involvement The distinguishing feature from superior orbital fissure syndrome is the addition of optic neuropathy, since the optic canal lies at the apex Sensory loss follows the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, and proptosis may be present with an orbital mass A relative afferent pupillary defect and reduced acuity or colour vision reflect the optic nerve component Common causes include invasive infection such as mucormycosis and aspergillosis, tumour, and inflammatory disease Aggressive fungal orbital apex infection must be considered urgently in diabetic or immunocompromised patients Imaging of the orbit and skull base is essential to define the responsible lesion Rapidly progressive signs in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient suggesting invasive fungal infection needing emergency management Acute visual loss requiring urgent evaluation of the optic nerve Signs of orbital cellulitis or abscess Features of malignant infiltration of the skull base Failing to recognise optic nerve involvement that distinguishes it from superior orbital fissure syndrome Delaying diagnosis of invasive fungal infection in an at-risk patient Attributing the picture to inflammation and giving steroids before excluding infection and tumour Underestimating the urgency of associated visual loss The orbital apex is the crowded posterior region of the orbit where the superior orbital fissure and the optic canal converge, transmitting the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery alongside the ocular motor nerves, the ophthalmic trigeminal branches, and sympathetic fibres. A lesion here compresses or infiltrates these structures, combining an ophthalmoplegia and trigeminal sensory disturbance with an optic neuropathy that causes visual loss. Responsible processes include invasive fungal and bacterial infection, neoplasm, granulomatous and other inflammatory disease, trauma, and vascular lesions. Prognosis depends heavily on the cause and speed of treatment; invasive infection carries high morbidity and mortality without prompt intervention, whereas inflammatory causes may respond to treatment, though optic nerve damage can leave permanent visual loss.

Orbital blowout fracture — orbital floor fracture, blowout fracture Orbital rim or complex facial fracture Traumatic extraocular muscle palsy without entrapment Retrobulbar haemorrhage Globe rupture or other ocular trauma Orbital cellulitis (if delayed presentation with swelling) CT of the orbits and facial bones Full ophthalmic assessment to exclude globe injury Assessment of ocular motility, diplopia and enophthalmos Testing of infraorbital nerve sensation Monitoring for the oculocardiac reflex, especially in children A fracture of the orbital wall, most often the floor or medial wall, from blunt trauma without fracture of the orbital rim Features include periorbital bruising, diplopia, restricted eye movements (especially vertical), enophthalmos and infraorbital numbness Vertical diplopia from inferior rectus tethering is typical, and pain or nausea on upgaze suggests muscle entrapment In children a white-eyed blowout fracture with muscle entrapment and marked oculocardiac reflex is a surgical emergency CT of the orbit defines the fracture and any herniated or entrapped tissue Many fractures are managed conservatively, with surgery for significant entrapment, enophthalmos or persistent diplopia White-eyed blowout fracture with entrapment and bradycardia in a child (surgical emergency) Signs of globe rupture or retrobulbar haemorrhage with visual loss Non-resolving diplopia or significant enophthalmos A relative afferent pupillary defect indicating optic nerve injury Missing a paediatric trapdoor entrapment that needs urgent surgery Overlooking an associated globe injury Attributing early diplopia solely to swelling and not reassessing Failing to warn against nose-blowing, which can cause orbital emphysema An orbital blowout fracture occurs when blunt force raises intra-orbital pressure or buckles the orbital walls, fracturing the thin floor or medial wall while sparing the sturdier rim. Orbital fat and the inferior rectus or its surrounding tissue can prolapse or become entrapped in the fracture, causing restricted motility and diplopia, while loss of orbital volume support leads to enophthalmos. Injury to the infraorbital nerve produces cheek and upper-lip numbness. In children the more elastic bone can snap shut and trap muscle (a trapdoor mechanism), causing ischaemia and a marked oculocardiac reflex. Many blowout fractures do well with conservative care and resolution of early diplopia; timely surgery for entrapment or significant volume change gives good outcomes, whereas delayed treatment of paediatric entrapment risks permanent motility problems.

Orbital cellulitis — postseptal cellulitis, post-septal cellulitis, orbital infection Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis Idiopathic orbital inflammation (orbital pseudotumour) Thyroid eye disease Cavernous sinus thrombosis Orbital tumour or rhabdomyosarcoma in children Allergic or traumatic periorbital oedema Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbit, sinuses, and brain to detect abscess and sinus disease Assessment of visual acuity, colour vision, pupil reactions, and eye movements Blood cultures and inflammatory markers Swabs/cultures of any discharge or drained material Ophthalmology and ENT review; consider MRI if intracranial extension is suspected A sight- and life-threatening infection of the orbital tissues behind the orbital septum, most often spreading from adjacent (especially ethmoid) sinusitis Key features distinguishing it from preseptal cellulitis are painful or restricted eye movements (ophthalmoplegia), proptosis, and pain on eye movement Systemic signs of fever and malaise accompany a red, swollen, tender lid; a relative afferent pupillary defect signals optic nerve compromise Reduced visual acuity, colour vision loss, or an afferent pupillary defect indicate optic nerve threat and demand emergency intervention Commonest in children and frequently caused by Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, and Haemophilus species, sometimes anaerobes Urgent contrast CT of the orbit and sinuses identifies subperiosteal or orbital abscess and sinus involvement Requires admission and prompt intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, with surgical drainage of abscesses or sinuses when needed Emergency — threatens vision (optic nerve compression) and life (cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, intracranial abscess) Reduced acuity, impaired colour vision, or a relative afferent pupillary defect indicate imminent optic nerve damage Restricted or painful eye movements and proptosis distinguishing it from benign preseptal cellulitis Bilateral involvement, drowsiness, or cranial nerve palsies suggesting cavernous sinus or intracranial spread Mistaking sight-threatening orbital cellulitis for benign preseptal cellulitis and failing to assess eye movements and optic nerve function Delaying CT imaging and abscess drainage Treating as an outpatient rather than admitting for intravenous therapy Overlooking the underlying sinusitis that needs concurrent treatment Orbital cellulitis is infection of the soft tissues posterior to the orbital septum. Infection most commonly extends directly from the paranasal sinuses (particularly the ethmoid, separated from the orbit only by the thin lamina papyracea), but can also arise from trauma, dacryocystitis, dental infection, or haematogenous spread. Inflammation and oedema within the confined bony orbit raise pressure, displace the globe forward (proptosis), impair extraocular muscle function, and can compress or ischaemically injure the optic nerve. Spread posteriorly risks cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, and intracranial abscess. With prompt intravenous antibiotics and timely drainage the outlook is good, but delay can lead to permanent visual loss, intracranial complications, and death.

Orbital myositis — idiopathic orbital myositis, myositic orbital inflammation, extraocular muscle myositis, inflammatory orbital myositis Thyroid eye disease (tendon-sparing muscle enlargement) Idiopathic orbital inflammation of other patterns Orbital cellulitis Carotid-cavernous fistula Orbital metastasis or lymphoma involving muscle Systemic vasculitis or IgG4-related orbital disease Orbital CT or MRI demonstrating enlargement of the affected muscle with tendon involvement Assessment of ocular motility, diplopia, and pain on eye movement Visual acuity, colour vision, and pupil assessment to exclude optic-nerve involvement Bloods including inflammatory markers, thyroid function and autoantibodies, and serum IgG4 to exclude mimics ANCA and systemic workup where vasculitis or systemic disease is suspected Biopsy in atypical, recurrent, or steroid-unresponsive cases An inflammatory disorder of one or more extraocular muscles, usually considered a myositic subtype of idiopathic orbital inflammation Typical presentation is with acute painful diplopia, pain worsened by eye movement, redness over the involved muscle insertion, and restricted motility It is frequently unilateral and often affects a single muscle, most commonly a horizontal rectus On orbital imaging the affected muscle is enlarged with characteristic involvement of the tendon, in contrast to the tendon-sparing enlargement of thyroid eye disease Injection and swelling are often most marked over the insertion of the inflamed muscle Most cases respond briskly to systemic corticosteroids, with relief of pain and improvement in movement, though recurrence can occur Atypical, recurrent, bilateral, or treatment-resistant cases warrant investigation and sometimes biopsy to exclude specific inflammations, IgG4-related disease, vasculitis, and lymphoma The key clinical distinction from thyroid eye disease is the pain, tendon involvement, and usually single-muscle pattern Poor or absent response to corticosteroids suggesting an alternative diagnosis such as lymphoma Bilateral or recurrent myositis pointing to a systemic or IgG4-related cause Signs of optic-nerve compromise or marked proptosis Features suggesting infection or a carotid-cavernous fistula rather than sterile inflammation Confusing it with thyroid eye disease by overlooking the pain and tendon involvement Mistaking it for orbital cellulitis and treating with antibiotics alone Attributing a poor steroid response to underdosing rather than reconsidering the diagnosis Failing to investigate recurrent or bilateral disease for a systemic cause Missing IgG4-related disease or vasculitis underlying the myositis Orbital myositis is inflammation localised to the extraocular muscles, with an infiltrate of lymphocytes and other inflammatory cells causing the muscle belly and, characteristically, its tendon of insertion to swell. The inflamed, oedematous muscle contracts and moves poorly, producing pain on eye movement, diplopia, and restriction, while overlying congestion causes redness at the insertion. It is regarded as a form of idiopathic orbital inflammation confined to muscle, and some cases fall within the IgG4-related disease spectrum or accompany systemic inflammatory disorders. The immune-mediated nature explains the typically rapid response to corticosteroids, whereas persistent or recurrent inflammation can lead to fibrosis with fixed restriction. The prognosis is generally good, with most single-muscle cases responding promptly to corticosteroids, but recurrences are common and repeated or chronic inflammation may cause muscle fibrosis with persistent diplopia and restriction needing further treatment.

Idiopathic orbital inflammation — orbital pseudotumour, idiopathic orbital inflammatory syndrome, nonspecific orbital inflammation, orbital inflammatory pseudotumour Thyroid eye disease Orbital cellulitis Orbital lymphoma or other neoplasm IgG4-related orbital disease Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other systemic vasculitides Sarcoidosis or carotid-cavernous fistula Ruptured dermoid cyst causing inflammation Orbital CT or MRI to define the pattern and extent of inflammation and exclude a discrete mass Assessment of visual acuity, colour vision, and pupils to detect optic-nerve involvement Bloods including inflammatory markers, and serum IgG4, with ANCA and thyroid function to exclude mimics Orbital biopsy in atypical, recurrent, bilateral, or steroid-unresponsive disease Systemic evaluation for sarcoidosis, vasculitis, or lymphoproliferative disease when indicated Monitoring of response and relapse during and after corticosteroid treatment A benign, non-infective inflammatory process of the orbit with no identifiable local or systemic cause, and a diagnosis reached largely by exclusion It classically presents with acute, painful proptosis, periorbital swelling and redness, chemosis, and restricted eye movements with diplopia Any orbital structure may be involved, giving subtypes such as myositic, lacrimal (dacryoadenitis), anterior, apical, and diffuse patterns Involvement of the orbital apex can threaten vision through optic-nerve compression Imaging shows inflammatory infiltration that may involve muscles including their tendons, the lacrimal gland, or diffuse orbital fat, without a discrete mass A characteristically rapid and dramatic response to systemic corticosteroids supports the diagnosis, though relapse on withdrawal is common Atypical, bilateral, recurrent, or steroid-unresponsive cases require biopsy and workup to exclude lymphoma, specific inflammations, and IgG4-related disease It is distinguished from thyroid eye disease, which is usually less painful and spares muscle tendons, and from orbital cellulitis, which is infective Reduced acuity or colour vision suggesting apical optic-nerve compression Failure to respond promptly to corticosteroids, raising suspicion of lymphoma or specific inflammation Bilateral or recurrent disease pointing to a systemic or IgG4-related cause Rapidly progressive proptosis with severe pain and congestion Labelling an orbital mass idiopathic without excluding lymphoma and specific inflammations by biopsy Mistaking it for orbital cellulitis and giving antibiotics alone, or vice versa Attributing a poor steroid response to inadequate dosing rather than an alternative diagnosis Overlooking IgG4-related disease and systemic vasculitis as underlying causes Missing apical involvement threatening the optic nerve Idiopathic orbital inflammation is a polymorphous inflammatory infiltrate of orbital tissues, comprising lymphocytes, plasma cells, and variable fibrosis, that occurs without an identifiable infective, neoplastic, or systemic autoimmune cause. The inflammation may target any orbital component, producing the myositic, dacryoadenitis, anterior, apical, or diffuse patterns, and the resulting swelling and mass effect cause pain, proptosis, congestion, and restriction of eye movement. Some cases represent part of the IgG4-related disease spectrum. The condition is thought to be immune-mediated, which underlies its responsiveness to corticosteroids, but the tendency to relapse and to develop fibrosis reflects an ongoing dysregulated inflammatory drive. Most patients respond rapidly to corticosteroids with resolution of pain and swelling, but relapses are frequent on tapering, and some develop chronic fibrosis with persistent restriction, proptosis, or visual loss; refractory cases may need steroid-sparing immunosuppression or radiotherapy.

Orbital varix — orbital venous varix Orbital lymphatic malformation (lymphangioma) Arteriovenous or carotid-cavernous fistula Other orbital vascular lesions Orbital tumour causing proptosis Thyroid eye disease CT or MRI with and without Valsalva or in a dependent position Assessment of positional proptosis clinically Imaging to detect phleboliths and to exclude a fistula Evaluation of optic nerve function if compromise is suspected Vascular imaging where a high-flow lesion must be excluded A distensible venous malformation of the orbit that enlarges with raised venous pressure The hallmark is positional or Valsalva-induced proptosis, appearing or worsening on bending, straining or the Valsalva manoeuvre It may be asymptomatic or cause intermittent proptosis, pain and, occasionally, acute thrombosis or haemorrhage Imaging with the patient performing Valsalva, or in a dependent position, demonstrates the distending lesion Enophthalmos can occur when the varix is decompressed and the orbit is at rest Many are observed, with intervention reserved for significant symptoms, thrombosis or visual compromise Acute painful proptosis suggesting thrombosis or haemorrhage Optic nerve compromise with visual loss Rapid enlargement Features suggesting a high-flow vascular lesion Missing the diagnosis by imaging only at rest without a distending manoeuvre Confusing it with a lymphatic malformation or a fistula Overlooking acute thrombosis or haemorrhage as a cause of sudden proptosis Underestimating the bleeding risk of surgical intervention An orbital varix is a low-flow venous malformation consisting of dilated, thin-walled venous channels that communicate with the orbital venous system. Because these channels distend under increased venous pressure, manoeuvres that raise it (bending forward, straining, Valsalva) cause the varix to fill and produce proptosis, which reverses at rest. Stagnation within the malformation predisposes to thrombosis, and thin vessel walls can bleed, causing acute pain and proptosis; chronic changes may leave enophthalmos from orbital fat atrophy. Most orbital varices are benign and can be observed; complications such as thrombosis or haemorrhage are usually self-limiting, and intervention for symptomatic lesions carries a risk of significant bleeding.

Idiopathic granulomatous orchitis — granulomatous orchitis, idiopathic granulomatous orchitis, non-specific granulomatous orchitis Germ cell tumour of the testis Testicular lymphoma Tuberculous orchitis or epididymo-orchitis Other infective granulomatous orchitis (e.g. fungal, brucellosis) Sarcoidosis involving the testis Chronic bacterial epididymo-orchitis Scrotal ultrasound to characterise the mass and assess the epididymis Serum AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH (typically normal) to help assess for germ cell tumour Urinalysis, culture, and tests for tuberculosis and other infections Investigations for sarcoidosis when clinically suggested Radical inguinal orchidectomy with histology when malignancy cannot be excluded Histopathological review to confirm non-specific granulomatous inflammation Idiopathic granulomatous orchitis is a rare non-infective inflammatory condition that characteristically mimics a testicular tumour, usually in middle-aged men It presents as a firm, sometimes tender, testicular mass or diffuse enlargement, often with a preceding history of trauma or infection Germ cell tumour markers are normal, but this does not reliably distinguish it from a testicular tumour, so malignancy remains the primary concern Ultrasound findings are non-specific and may resemble a neoplasm, and the diagnosis is frequently only made on histology after orchidectomy It is a diagnosis of exclusion once specific granulomatous causes such as tuberculosis, other infections, and sarcoidosis have been considered Because a tumour cannot be confidently excluded preoperatively, many patients undergo radical inguinal orchidectomy, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic Where diagnosis can be established without radical surgery, anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive treatment may be considered, but tumour must first be excluded Features indistinguishable from a testicular tumour on examination and imaging Rapidly enlarging or hard testicular mass Systemic symptoms suggesting tuberculosis or malignancy Constitutional upset or nodal enlargement raising concern for lymphoma Assuming a benign inflammatory cause and delaying exclusion of a testicular tumour Relying on normal tumour markers to rule out malignancy Failing to exclude tuberculosis and other specific granulomatous causes before labelling it idiopathic Attempting conservative management before a tumour has been confidently excluded Idiopathic granulomatous orchitis is thought to represent an autoimmune or hypersensitivity reaction to extravasated sperm antigens, sometimes following trauma, infection, or obstruction that breaches the blood-testis barrier. The exposed germ cell antigens provoke a granulomatous inflammatory response within the seminiferous tubules and interstitium, with destruction of the tubules and formation of a firm mass. By definition, no specific infective organism or systemic granulomatous disease is identified, and the resulting swelling can closely imitate a testicular neoplasm. The condition itself is benign, but because it cannot be reliably distinguished from malignancy preoperatively, the affected testis is often removed; once a tumour is excluded and specific causes treated, the prognosis is good, though the involved testis is frequently rendered non-functional by the inflammation.

Orf (ecthyma contagiosum) — orf virus, ecthyma contagiosum, contagious pustular dermatitis, scabby mouth, parapoxvirus infection Milker's nodule (pseudocowpox, another parapoxvirus) Cutaneous anthrax Pyogenic granuloma Atypical mycobacterial or sporotrichoid skin infection Cutaneous tularaemia or other zoonotic ulcers Squamous cell carcinoma or keratoacanthoma in persistent lesions Detailed occupational and animal-contact history Polymerase chain reaction for parapoxvirus DNA from lesion material Electron microscopy of lesion scrapings showing ovoid parapoxvirus particles Skin biopsy for histology when malignancy or another diagnosis is suspected Bacterial swab and culture if secondary infection is suspected Assessment of immune status in atypical, giant, or persistent lesions A zoonotic parapoxvirus infection acquired by direct contact with infected sheep and goats or contaminated fomites, and an occupational hazard of farmers, shepherds, abattoir workers, and vets Presents as one or a few solitary lesions, usually on the fingers or hands, evolving through recognised stages from a papule to a targetoid nodule and finally a regressing crust The history of animal contact, particularly around lambing or after bottle-feeding lambs, is the key diagnostic clue Regional lymphadenopathy and a low-grade constitutional upset may accompany the lesion; secondary bacterial infection can occur It is usually a clinical diagnosis; confirmation is by electron microscopy, PCR, or biopsy when the presentation is atypical The infection is self-limiting in immunocompetent people and resolves over several weeks without scarring, so treatment is largely supportive Immunocompromised patients may develop large, persistent, or progressive giant orf lesions requiring intervention Large, rapidly enlarging, or persistent giant lesions suggesting immunocompromise Features of secondary bacterial infection or spreading cellulitis A non-healing lesion raising concern for malignancy or an alternative diagnosis such as anthrax Systemic upset out of proportion to a simple localised lesion Mistaking orf for a bacterial abscess and performing unnecessary incision or prescribing antibiotics Failing to elicit the animal-contact history and pursuing invasive investigations Overlooking a persistent lesion that may actually be malignant or a different zoonosis Not recognising that immunocompromised hosts can develop atypical giant orf needing active management Orf is caused by the orf virus, a parapoxvirus of the Poxviridae family that infects the epithelium of sheep and goats, producing crusted lesions around their mouths and udders. Humans are infected through breaks in the skin during handling of animals or contaminated material, and the virus replicates locally in keratinocytes. The lesion progresses through characteristic morphological stages as viral replication and the host inflammatory and immune responses evolve, producing a nodule with a distinctive targetoid appearance before regressing. The virus encodes immunomodulatory proteins, including a viral vascular endothelial growth factor homologue that drives the vascular, granulation-like histology. Immunity is incomplete, so reinfection is possible. In healthy people orf is self-limiting and resolves spontaneously over about six weeks with little or no scarring; immunocompromised patients may have prolonged or giant lesions that need specific therapy such as topical or destructive treatments.

Organophosphate / cholinergic poisoning — Clinical cholinergic toxidrome Plasma/RBC cholinesterase Atropine + pralidoxime; airway/secretion control Carbamate insecticide poisoning (aldicarb, carbaryl, propoxur) — same cholinergic mechanism (p.3712) Other acetylcholinesterase inhibitors: medicinal agents neostigmine, physostigmine, tacrine (p.3712) Muscarinic agonists: bethanechol, pilocarpine, and muscarine-containing mushrooms (Boletus, Clitocybe, Inocybe spp.) (p.3712) Nicotine / tobacco and lobeline (nicotinic agonists) (p.3712) Opioid poisoning (also causes miosis and physiologic depression) (p.3705) Cholinesterase activity in plasma and red cells is <50% of normal in acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning (p.3712) ECG — may show bradycardia and atrioventricular block (p.3706) EMG/nerve conduction studies in delayed neuropathy — early repetitive firing of CMAPs and decrement on repetitive nerve stimulation; later, axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy (p.3610) Guillain-Barré syndrome / acute flaccid paralysis — organophosphate, thallium and arsenic poisonings are listed in the GBS differential (p.3620) Botulism and myasthenia gravis (neuromuscular junction disorders in the acute paralysis differential) (p.3620) Paralytic shellfish poisoning, ciguatera, type E botulism and tetrodotoxin poisoning — organophosphate poisoning is in their shared differential (ciguatera chapter) Belongs to the depressed physiologic state / cholinergic toxidrome; miosis is common and is most pronounced in opioid and cholinergic poisoning, distinguished from other depressant syndromes by muscarinic and nicotinic signs (p.3705). Muscarinic features: seizures, excessive secretions (lacrimation, salivation, bronchorrhoea and wheezing, diaphoresis), and increased bowel/bladder activity with nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, and incontinence of faeces and urine (p.3712). Nicotinic features: hypertension, tachycardia, muscle cramps, fasciculations, weakness, and paralysis — note these oppose the muscarinic picture, so vital signs can be mixed (p.3712). Death is usually due to respiratory failure (p.3712). Organophosphates and carbamates can produce bradycardia and atrioventricular block on ECG (p.3706). Organophosphate (and amanita/mushroom) poisoning can present as acute, often systemic-compromising diarrhoea (p.46/Acute Diarrhea chapter). Organophosphates can cause a delayed organophosphate-induced neuropathy: early generalised weakness from neuromuscular blockade, then an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy ensues (p.3610). Bronchorrhoea, wheezing and excessive secretions with progression to respiratory failure — the usual cause of death (p.3712) Nicotinic weakness, fasciculations and paralysis (p.3712) Seizures (p.3712) Bradycardia / atrioventricular block (p.3706) Vital signs may be discordant: muscarinic effects cause bradycardia while nicotinic stimulation can cause hypertension and tachycardia, so a 'normal' or mixed heart rate does not exclude poisoning (p.3712). Organophosphates are 'toxic time-bombs' requiring metabolic activation, so a patient may be initially well or minimally symptomatic and deteriorate later (p.3704). Cholinesterase activity is <50% of normal in acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning — a key confirmatory threshold not to overlook (p.3712). Organophosphate (and carbamate) insecticides, and nerve agents such as sarin, soman, tabun and VX, inhibit acetylcholinesterase, leading to accumulation of synaptic acetylcholine at both muscarinic and nicotinic cholinergic receptor sites; the resulting overstimulation produces the combined muscarinic, nicotinic and CNS toxidrome. Organophosphates are 'toxic time-bombs' in that they may require metabolic activation, so onset of toxicity can be delayed. Separately, organophosphates bind and inhibit neuropathy target esterase, with axonal degeneration of the gracile fasciculus and corticospinal tracts producing a delayed sensorimotor polyneuropathy. (p.3610, p.3712, p.3704) Death is usually due to respiratory failure (p.3712). Outcome and reversibility of any poisoning depend on the functional reserve of the individual or target organ, influenced by age and preexisting disease (p.3704). Harrison grades poisoning by degree of physiologic depression rather than by a disease-specific scale: grade 1 — arousable by voice/touch, can converse and follow commands; grade 2 — responds to pain but not voice, brainstem reflexes intact; grade 3 — unresponsive to pain, brainstem reflexes depressed, decreased respirations and temperature; grade 4 — flaccid paralysis with absent brainstem reflexes and respirations and decreased cardiovascular vital signs (p.3705).

poisoning is always trivial and omitting close respiratory monitoring Organophosphates and carbamates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, preventing the breakdown of acetylcholine at muscarinic, nicotinic and central synapses. The resulting accumulation of acetylcholine overstimulates cholinergic receptors, producing the mixed muscarinic and nicotinic cholinergic crisis. Organophosphate-enzyme bonds can undergo 'ageing', becoming permanent and refractory to oxime reactivation, whereas carbamate inhibition spontaneously reverses. Excess cholinergic activity at the neuromuscular junction first causes fasciculations, then depolarising blockade and weakness, while central accumulation drives seizures and depressed consciousness. With early airway control, adequate atropinisation and oxime therapy, many patients recover fully, though severe poisoning, delayed presentation or intermediate syndrome may require prolonged ventilation; mortality is driven mainly by respiratory failure and aspiration.

undiagnosed carrier and precipitating a crisis Ornithine transcarbamylase is a mitochondrial enzyme that combines carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline, the second step of the urea cycle. Its deficiency, caused by mutations in the X-linked OTC gene, blocks ureagenesis and causes waste nitrogen to accumulate as ammonia. Because the block is proximal, carbamoyl phosphate builds up and is diverted into the pyrimidine synthesis pathway, generating excess orotic acid excreted in urine. Ammonia is neurotoxic, producing glutamine accumulation, astrocyte swelling and cerebral oedema. Females show a spectrum of severity determined by the pattern of X-chromosome inactivation in hepatocytes. Neonatal-onset disease in boys is severe and, without rapid control of hyperammonaemia, carries a high risk of death or lasting neurodevelopmental impairment; later-onset and carrier presentations vary widely, and outcome depends on prompt recognition and management of crises, with liver transplantation offering definitive correction in selected patients.

which proteins localising to the basal body and primary cilium fail to support normal ciliary structure and signalling. In the midline structures of the developing face, the branchial arches and the limb buds, disrupted ciliary hedgehog signalling produces the clefting and lobulation of the tongue and lip, the hypertelorism and nasal anomalies, and the polysyndactyly with hallucal duplication that define the group. Type II (Mohr syndrome) follows autosomal recessive inheritance and is distinguished within the group by the combination of these oral and digital features with conductive hearing loss, separating it from the X-linked type I caused by variants in the ciliary gene OFD1. Most affected individuals have normal intellect and a good functional outcome with multidisciplinary craniofacial, dental and audiological care; prognosis is chiefly influenced by the presence and severity of any brain malformation.

and tongue muscles, arising from disordered motor control within the basal ganglia circuits and their connections, with abnormal inhibition and excessive co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles. This produces involuntary, patterned, often task-related movements of the masticatory and lower facial musculature. It may be idiopathic (primary) or secondary to dopamine-receptor-blocking drugs, neurodegenerative disorders, or structural lesions. The characteristic sensory trick, which temporarily reduces the dystonia through sensorimotor modulation, is a hallmark of dystonic disorders. Oromandibular dystonia is usually chronic; primary forms rarely remit but respond to repeated botulinum toxin injections combined with oral agents and appliances, allowing reasonable function. Secondary and drug-induced forms may improve if the underlying cause is addressed.

mmHg, or diastolic of at least 10 mmHg, within three minutes of standing Symptoms include light-headedness, dizziness, visual dimming, weakness, and falls on standing, but many older adults are causes, including antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates, alpha-blockers, and drugs with anticholinergic or vasodilating effects Volume depletion from dehydration, bleeding, or diuretics should always management comes first: gradual position change, adequate fluid and salt intake where appropriate, compression garments, avoiding large meals and alcohol, and reviewing culprit drugs A large accompanied by chest pain, palpitations, or signs of cardiac disease Evidence of significant volume loss such as gastrointestinal bleeding Recurrent falls attributable to postural drops Severe, treatment-resistant orthostatic hypotension suggesting advanced autonomic failure Measuring standing blood pressure only once and missing delayed orthostatic drops Overlooking medications as the reversible cause Failing to consider volume depletion or occult bleeding Aggressively treating supine hypertension in ways that worsen orthostatic symptoms Not recognising post-prandial hypotension as a distinct contributor to falls On standing, gravity shifts blood to the lower body, and normally baroreceptor-mediated reflex increases in heart rate and vascular tone maintain cerebral perfusion. Ageing blunts baroreflex sensitivity and reduces cardiac and vascular compensatory responses. Orthostatic hypotension develops when these mechanisms fail, either because of impaired autonomic reflexes (neurogenic causes) or because of reduced circulating volume or vasodilating and blood-pressure-lowering drugs (non-neurogenic causes). The resulting transient cerebral hypoperfusion produces symptoms and predisposes to falls and syncope. Orthostatic hypotension is common in older adults and is associated with falls, syncope, reduced quality of life, and higher cardiovascular and overall mortality. Many cases improve substantially once contributing medications are withdrawn, volume is restored, and non-pharmacological measures are applied, though neurogenic forms can be chronic and challenging.

Orthostatic tremor — primary orthostatic tremor, orthostatic tremor, shaky legs syndrome, POT Essential tremor Parkinson's disease and other parkinsonian syndromes Cerebellar ataxia and other gait disorders Anxiety-related unsteadiness Peripheral neuropathy or vestibular imbalance Functional (psychogenic) unsteadiness Surface electromyography of the leg muscles demonstrating the characteristic high-frequency, highly coherent tremor, which is the key diagnostic investigation Clinical assessment comparing symptoms on standing with those on sitting and walking MRI brain where a secondary or structural cause is suspected DAT imaging where coexisting parkinsonism is suspected (orthostatic-tremor-plus) Assessment for peripheral neuropathy and vestibular dysfunction Review of medication and metabolic contributors to unsteadiness Presents with a subjective feeling of unsteadiness on standing still that is promptly relieved by sitting, walking or leaning on support The tremor is a high-frequency oscillation (characteristically about 13 to 18 Hz) of the legs and trunk that is often not visible but may be palpable or audible on auscultation over the leg muscles Patients describe a fear of falling when standing still, although actual falls are relatively uncommon early on The high frequency is highly specific and is best confirmed with surface electromyography Symptoms are absent when the legs are unloaded and appear within seconds of standing It most often affects older adults and is more common in women It is under-recognised and frequently misattributed to anxiety or a non-specific balance disorder Rapidly progressive unsteadiness or frequent falls suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis Associated parkinsonism, ataxia or focal signs indicating a secondary cause Early prominent autonomic failure Onset in a young patient, which is atypical Missing the diagnosis because the tremor is not visible; palpation, auscultation and surface EMG are needed Misattributing symptoms to anxiety or a primary balance disorder Failing to distinguish primary orthostatic tremor from orthostatic-tremor-plus syndromes with parkinsonism Overlooking the characteristic relief on sitting or walking within the history Primary orthostatic tremor is characterised by a highly synchronous, high-frequency oscillation affecting the weight-bearing leg and trunk muscles, thought to originate from a central generator that may involve the brainstem and cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuits. The tremor appears only when the legs are loaded during standing and resolves once that load is removed, producing the characteristic relief on sitting or walking. Its remarkable frequency and its high coherence between different muscles distinguish it from other tremors. Primary orthostatic tremor is usually slowly progressive and, although it can be disabling because of the persistent fear of falling and limited standing tolerance, it is not life-shortening. Response to pharmacotherapy is often partial and may wane over time, and selected refractory patients have been treated with deep brain stimulation. Practical measures such as using a stool or walking to relieve symptoms help maintain function.

os acromiale — unfused acromial apophysis, acromial ossicle Acute acromial fracture Subacromial impingement syndrome from other causes Rotator cuff tear Acromioclavicular joint osteoarthritis Calcific tendinitis of the shoulder Stress fracture of the acromion Distal clavicular osteolysis Axillary lateral radiograph to demonstrate and classify the unfused segment Outlet (scapular Y) and anteroposterior views to assess the subacromial arch CT to define fragment size, bony margins and any degenerative change at the synchondrosis MRI to evaluate the rotator cuff, marrow oedema across the synchondrosis and bursal changes Diagnostic local anaesthetic injection into the synchondrosis to confirm it as the pain source Dynamic ultrasound to assess fragment mobility and cuff integrity Os acromiale is failure of fusion of one or more acromial ossification centres, which normally unite in early adult life. It is frequently an incidental, asymptomatic finding and is bilateral in a substantial proportion of affected individuals. Classified by the site of the unfused segment: pre-acromion, meso-acromion, meta-acromion and basi-acromion, with the meso-acromion type being the most common and most often symptomatic. An axillary lateral radiograph is the key view; on a standard anteroposterior film the ossicle can be mistaken for the acromioclavicular joint or missed entirely. A mobile fragment can be pulled inferiorly by the deltoid during contraction, dynamically narrowing the subacromial space and producing secondary impingement. It is associated with rotator cuff pathology, and both should be assessed together when planning treatment. Do not confuse an os acromiale with an acute acromial fracture; smooth, corticated, symmetrical margins favour the congenital ossicle. Caution is needed at arthroscopic subacromial decompression, as aggressive resection of an unstable fragment can destabilise the deltoid origin. Acute onset after trauma with sharp margins suggesting a true acromial fracture rather than a congenital ossicle Progressive rotator cuff weakness indicating a significant associated tear Marrow oedema with destructive change raising concern for infection or tumour Deltoid dysfunction following prior surgery to the region Missing the ossicle by omitting an axillary lateral view or misreading it as the acromioclavicular joint. Mistaking a congenital os acromiale for an acute fracture and vice versa. Performing standard acromioplasty that destabilises the fragment and deltoid origin without addressing the synchondrosis. Failing to recognise and treat a coexisting rotator cuff tear. The acromion develops from several ossification centres that typically coalesce by the third decade. Os acromiale results when one or more of these centres fails to fuse, leaving a segment joined to the remaining acromion by fibrocartilaginous or fibrous tissue rather than bone. Symptoms arise when this synchondrosis becomes mobile or degenerate: motion at the pseudarthrosis generates pain, and traction by the deltoid, whose fibres insert on the mobile fragment, can tilt it inferiorly to reduce the subacromial outlet and cause dynamic impingement of the underlying cuff. Chronic instability of the segment may also provoke reactive changes at the synchondrosis and contribute to adjacent rotator cuff tendinopathy or tearing. Asymptomatic os acromiale requires no treatment and carries an excellent prognosis. Symptomatic cases often respond to conservative management, while persistent instability may require fixation with bone grafting or fragment excision, with outcomes influenced by fragment size and the state of the associated rotator cuff.

nerve Rest or night pain or a destructive lesion suggesting infection or tumour Progressive locking or triggering of the great toe indicating significant flexor hallucis longus pathology Overlooking coexistent flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy that will continue to cause symptoms if not addressed Attributing posterior ankle pain to the Achilles tendon and missing posterior impingement Assuming an os trigonum seen on imaging is the cause of pain without confirming it clinically or with an injection Missing a fracture of the ossicle or posterior talar process after an acute injury Failing to modify the provocative activity or technique, leading to recurrence The os trigonum forms from a separate ossification centre behind the talus that fails to fuse with the posterolateral talar process; when it does fuse it forms a prominent Stieda process. During extreme plantarflexion, as in ballet en pointe or a footballer striking a ball, the ossicle or prominent process is compressed between the posterior tibial margin and the calcaneus, pinching the intervening soft tissues and producing posterior impingement pain. Repetitive forced plantarflexion causes inflammation across the synchondrosis or a stress reaction, and can fracture or displace the ossicle. Because the flexor hallucis longus tendon passes through its fibro-osseous tunnel immediately medial to the ossicle, the same mechanism frequently irritates that tendon, producing coexistent flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy with pain on great-toe flexion and, sometimes, triggering. The result is a syndrome of activity-related deep posterior ankle pain in individuals who load the ankle in plantarflexion. Many athletes improve with a period of activity and technique modification, physiotherapy, and sometimes an image-guided injection, allowing return to sport or dance. When conservative treatment fails, excision of the os trigonum, whether arthroscopic or open, with release of the flexor hallucis longus if involved, reliably relieves symptoms and generally permits return to full activity, with the arthroscopic approach offering quicker recovery.
