severe pain Confusing the condition with Sinding-Larsen-Johansson syndrome at the inferior patellar pole Failing to address extensor mechanism tightness that perpetuates apophyseal traction Recommending prolonged complete rest rather than graded activity modification Osgood-Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity, the apophysis onto which the patellar tendon inserts. Repetitive, forceful quadriceps contraction during running and jumping transmits tension through the patellar tendon to the developing tuberosity at a time when the apophysis is still partly cartilaginous and mechanically weak. This repeated microtrauma causes small avulsive injuries, inflammation and heterotopic ossification within the distal patellar tendon and apophysis, producing the characteristic prominence and fragmentation. Rapid adolescent growth, with relative tightness of the extensor mechanism, increases the traction load. The condition typically settles as the tuberosity ossifies and the apophysis fuses, although a separate ossicle can persist and remain a source of pain. The prognosis is favourable; symptoms are self-limiting and usually resolve as the tubercle ossifies and the apophysis fuses, though a prominent tubercle or persistent ossicle may cause residual discomfort with kneeling in a minority of patients.

adjacent structures Assessment of cellularity, mitotic rate and atypia to assign typical, atypical or malignant category A rare tumour of uncertain differentiation, typically presenting as a small, uniform round to ovoid cells arranged in cords and nests within a fibromyxoid stroma, surrounded by an incomplete peripheral shell of lamellar bone Frequently expresses S100 protein, often with the diagnosis Divided into typical, atypical and malignant categories based on cellularity, mitotic activity and nuclear features The peripheral bony rim is characteristic but not always present, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis High cellularity, brisk mitotic activity or necrosis indicating a malignant tumour Rapid growth or large size Local recurrence after excision Metastatic spread in malignant examples Excluding the diagnosis when the peripheral bone shell is absent Mistaking the tumour for myoepithelioma or extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma given overlapping S100 positivity Underestimating malignant potential in highly cellular or mitotically active tumours Confusing prominent ossification with a primary bone-forming neoplasm Failing to use PHF1 molecular testing in histologically ambiguous cases Ossifying fibromyxoid tumour is a mesenchymal neoplasm whose precise line of differentiation remains unsettled, though frequent S100 expression suggests a partly neural or cartilaginous phenotype. Most cases are defined by rearrangement of the PHF1 gene, which encodes a component of a Polycomb-like chromatin-regulatory complex, leading to deregulated gene transcription. The distinctive shell of metaplastic lamellar bone at the tumour periphery gives the lesion its name, and the degree of cellularity and mitotic activity, rather than the specific fusion, governs whether a tumour behaves in a benign or malignant manner. Typical ossifying fibromyxoid tumours behave in a benign or borderline fashion and are usually cured by complete excision, although local recurrence can follow incomplete removal; atypical and malignant variants carry a higher risk of recurrence and, in the malignant group, of metastasis, so accurate grading and clear margins are important.

Osteoarthritis — OA, degenerative joint disease Inflammatory arthritis (suggested by prolonged morning stiffness and involvement of many joints) Bursitis (anserine bursitis medial/distal to the knee; trochanteric bursitis lateral to the hip) Iliotibial band syndrome Internal derangement of the knee (anterior cruciate ligament or meniscal tear), especially after acute injury Septic arthritis (consider when synovial fluid white count is elevated/inflammatory) No blood tests are routinely indicated unless symptoms or signs suggest inflammatory arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2953). Synovial fluid examination is often more helpful diagnostically than x-ray; a white count >1000/uL suggests inflammatory arthritis, gout, or pseudogout, the latter two confirmed by crystals (Harrison 22e p.2953). Radiographs are not routinely indicated; order only when pain and findings are atypical of OA or when pain persists after effective treatment. Imaging findings correlate poorly with pain, and x-rays may be normal in early disease (insensitive to cartilage loss) (Harrison 22e p.2953). MRI is not indicated in the diagnostic workup; meniscal tears and cartilage/bone lesions are common both in OA and in older persons without joint pain, and MRI findings rarely warrant a change in therapy (Harrison 22e p.2953). Gout and pseudogout (crystal arthritis; suggested by synovial fluid white count >1000/uL with identifiable crystals) Rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory arthritides Fibromyalgia (noninflammatory pain amplification) OA is the most common type of arthritis and a leading cause of disability in the elderly; prevalence rises strikingly with age, being uncommon before 40 and highly prevalent after 60 (Harrison 22e p.2949). Joint involvement is characteristic: hips, knees, first MTP joint, cervical/lumbosacral spine, and in the hands the DIP, PIP, and thumb base; the wrist, elbow, and ankle are usually spared (Harrison 22e p.2949). Joint pain is primarily activity-related early on, coming on during or just after use and resolving with rest; as disease progresses pain becomes continuous and may be bothersome at night (Harrison 22e p.2952). Morning stiffness, when present, is usually brief (<30 min), in contrast to the prolonged stiffness (hours) of inflammatory arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2952). Hand OA produces bony enlargement of the DIP joints (Heberden's nodes) and PIP joints (Bouchard's nodes) (Harrison 22e p.2949). On hip examination, OA can be detected by loss of internal rotation on passive movement (Harrison 22e p.2953). Mechanical symptoms (buckling, catching, locking) are common in knee OA and need further evaluation for internal derangement only when they follow an acute knee injury (Harrison 22e p.2952). Osteophytes are an important radiographic hallmark of OA, along with joint-space narrowing reflecting cartilage loss (Harrison 22e pp.2952-2953). Prominent nocturnal pain in the absence of end-stage OA merits a distinct workup (Harrison 22e p.2953). Prolonged morning stiffness with many joints affected suggests inflammatory arthritis rather than OA (Harrison 22e p.2952). Mechanical symptoms (buckling, catching, locking) developing after an acute knee injury warrant evaluation for internal derangement (Harrison 22e p.2952). Distinguish OA from rheumatoid (and other inflammatory) arthritis, crystal arthritis (gout/pseudogout), and septic arthritis; prolonged morning stiffness, systemic features, and an inflammatory synovial fluid white count point away from OA. Do not rely on radiographs to gauge symptom severity: x-ray changes correlate poorly with pain, and films may be normal in early disease. Many persons with x-ray or MRI evidence of OA have no joint symptoms, so structural findings alone do not establish symptomatic OA. Back pain and neck pain are not tied to x-ray findings of spinal OA and are evaluated separately. OA is joint failure in which all joint structures undergo pathologic change. The pathologic hallmark is focal, initially nonuniform loss of hyaline articular cartilage, accompanied by thickening and sclerosis of the subchondral bony plate, marginal osteophyte outgrowth, stretching of the articular capsule, variable synovitis, and weakness of muscles bridging the joint (meniscal degeneration occurs in knees). Disease begins with joint injury when protective mechanisms (joint capsule/ligaments, bridging muscle, sensory afferents, underlying bone, and synovial-fluid lubrication via hyaluronic acid and lubricin) fail. Cartilage shows depletion of aggrecan and loss/unfurling of type 2 collagen, losing compressive stiffness; chondrocytes shift toward catabolism, producing matrix-degrading enzymes (MMPs, ADAMTS-5). Local inflammation (including mechanoinflammation), with cytokines, alarmins/DAMPs, and growth factors (BMP-2, TGF-beta drive osteophytes; VEGF drives vascular invasion), accelerates progression. Risk reflects the balance between joint vulnerability (age, female sex, genetics such as GDF5, prior damage, malalignment, bridging-muscle weakness, high bone density) and joint loading (obesity, occupational/repetitive use, major injury) (Harrison 22e pp.2949-2952). OA is a chronic, generally progressive disorder of the elderly whose high prevalence and impact on physical function make it a leading cause of disability. Severely malaligned knees may be destined to progress regardless of other risk factors, whereas weight loss greater than 10% of body weight reduces cartilage loss and, in most affected persons, alleviates pain (Harrison 22e pp.2949-2952). Harrison's chapter 383 does not present a single formal grading scale; OA is characterized clinically along a spectrum from early, episodic activity-related pain with brief morning stiffness to advanced/end-stage disease with continuous and nocturnal pain. The chapter references the WOMAC index as a patient-reported outcome measure of pain, stiffness, and function (Harrison 22e p.2952).

leading to local recurrence Osteoblastoma is a benign osteoblastic neoplasm composed of osteoid and woven bone deposited by plump osteoblasts within a richly vascular stroma. Although its cellular make-up resembles osteoid osteoma, it lacks the self-limited behaviour of that lesion, being larger and capable of progressive, sometimes locally aggressive, growth. Unlike osteoid osteoma it excites comparatively little reactive sclerosis and produces less prostaglandin-driven nocturnal pain. The aggressive subtype shows epithelioid osteoblasts and more permeative growth, creating overlap with osteosarcoma that demands careful histological and radiological correlation. Most osteoblastomas are cured by complete surgical removal, though incompletely excised lesions may recur locally. The aggressive variant has a higher recurrence rate and requires closer follow-up, and its distinction from osteosarcoma is critical to outcome.

Disruption of the osteochondral unit produces bone oedema, cyst formation and, if the fragment separates, an unstable lesion or loose body. Persistent altered joint mechanics cause pain and can progress to ankle osteoarthritis. Small stable lesions often improve with non-operative care; larger, cystic or unstable lesions have more guarded outcomes, and surgical results decline with lesion size, chronicity and revision surgery.

Osteochondritis dissecans — OCD, osteochondral lesion, osteochondritis dissecans of the knee, juvenile osteochondritis dissecans Meniscal tear Chondral (cartilage) injury without a bony fragment Loose body from another cause such as synovial chondromatosis Spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee Patellofemoral pain syndrome In the elbow, capitellar Panner disease in a younger child Plain radiographs including tunnel or notch views to detect the crescentic lucency and any loose body Magnetic resonance imaging to assess cartilage integrity and stage fragment stability Assessment for fluid tracking behind the fragment on imaging as a sign of instability Computed tomography to define the bony bed when planning surgery Examination for a joint effusion, mechanical symptoms and localised tenderness Comparison with the contralateral joint and evaluation of physeal status A focal disorder of subchondral bone and overlying articular cartilage that may separate as an osteochondral fragment, distinct from a diffuse osteonecrosis or apophysitis Most commonly affects the knee, classically the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle, and also the capitellum and the talar dome Occurs in adolescents and young adults; juvenile disease with open physes generally has a better prognosis than adult-onset disease Presents with poorly localised activity-related joint pain, and with mechanical symptoms such as catching, locking or giving way once a fragment becomes unstable The radiographic hallmark is a crescentic radiolucent line demarcating an osteochondral fragment from the underlying bone Fragment stability is the central determinant of management and prognosis and is best assessed on magnetic resonance imaging A stable lesion with intact overlying cartilage may heal with offloading, whereas an unstable fragment or a loose body usually requires surgery Management spans activity modification and immobilisation for stable juvenile lesions through to fixation, drilling or fragment removal and cartilage restoration as needed Mechanical locking or a palpable loose body indicating an unstable, detached fragment A recurrent tense effusion suggesting an unstable lesion or intra-articular derangement Progressive articular surface collapse or established secondary arthritis Adult-onset disease with a large lesion carrying a higher risk of poor healing Assuming a lesion is stable without magnetic resonance imaging assessment of the overlying cartilage Missing a detached loose body as a cause of intermittent locking Confusing capitellar disease in a young child (Panner disease) with adolescent osteochondritis dissecans Under-treating an unstable fragment and allowing progressive articular damage Osteochondritis dissecans is a focal disturbance of the subchondral bone in which a segment of bone and its overlying articular cartilage may lose structural continuity with the parent bone. Although the precise cause is debated, repetitive microtrauma and localised ischaemia of the subchondral bone are thought to be central, sometimes with a contribution from disordered ossification of the epiphysis in the growing skeleton. The affected subchondral bone weakens and a demarcation line develops; if the overlying cartilage remains intact the lesion may be stable and heal, but progressive separation can leave the fragment partially attached (a flap) or fully detached as an intra-articular loose body. Once the fragment is unstable the articular surface becomes incongruent, causing mechanical symptoms and predisposing to secondary degenerative change. Stable lesions in skeletally immature patients often heal with conservative management, whereas unstable fragments, loose bodies and adult-onset lesions have a poorer capacity to heal and carry an increased long-term risk of osteoarthritis if the articular surface is not restored.

Osteochondroma — Osteocartilaginous exostosis, Exostosis Parosteal osteosarcoma Periosteal (juxtacortical) chondroma Secondary peripheral chondrosarcoma Subungual exostosis Bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation (Nora lesion) Myositis ossificans Plain radiographs to demonstrate the surface lesion and its relationship to the joint CT to confirm corticomedullary continuity with the host bone MRI to measure cartilage cap thickness and detect any soft-tissue mass Clinical assessment and family history to identify hereditary multiple exostoses Vascular imaging or angiography when a vascular complication such as pseudoaneurysm is suspected Comparison with prior imaging to document growth after skeletal maturity The most common benign bone tumour, typically arising from the metaphysis of long bones about the knee and the proximal humerus and pointing away from the adjacent joint. The pathognomonic feature is continuity of both the cortex and the medullary cavity of the lesion with those of the host bone, best demonstrated on CT or MRI. It may be pedunculated (stalked) or sessile (broad-based) and grows only until skeletal maturity; continued growth thereafter is a warning sign. Complications include mechanical impingement, formation of an overlying bursa, fracture of a pedunculated stalk, and compression of adjacent nerves or vessels, including popliteal pseudoaneurysm. The cartilage cap is thin in adults; a cap thicker than roughly 1.5 to 2 cm on MRI raises concern for transformation to secondary peripheral chondrosarcoma. Hereditary multiple exostoses is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by EXT1 or EXT2 mutations, producing multiple lesions, short stature and forearm deformity with a higher risk of malignant transformation. Malignant transformation occurs in roughly 1 per cent of solitary lesions but is appreciably more frequent in hereditary multiple exostoses. Symptomatic lesions or those suspected of transformation are excised, taking the cartilage cap and overlying perichondrium to minimise recurrence. Pain or documented growth after skeletal maturity Cartilage cap thicker than about 2 cm on MRI A new or enlarging soft-tissue mass overlying the lesion Irregular, lucent or destructive areas developing within a previously stable lesion Sudden neurovascular symptoms suggesting compression or pseudoaneurysm Mistaking a thick cartilage cap for a benign feature and missing early chondrosarcomatous transformation Overlooking the diagnosis of hereditary multiple exostoses and its familial and malignancy implications Incomplete excision leaving perichondrium and cap, leading to recurrence Failing to recognise vascular injury such as popliteal artery pseudoaneurysm from a stalked lesion Osteochondroma is a cartilage-capped bony projection arising on the external surface of a bone, regarded as a developmental lesion in which a fragment of physeal cartilage herniates through a defect in the perichondrial ring of Ranvier, separates from the growth plate and continues to grow by endochondral ossification. Because it originates from the physis, the lesion enlarges only during skeletal growth and characteristically maintains corticomedullary continuity with the parent bone. Biallelic inactivation of the tumour suppressor genes EXT1 or EXT2, which encode glycosyltransferases required for heparan sulfate biosynthesis, disrupts the diffusion gradients of signalling molecules that regulate chondrocyte proliferation; germline EXT mutations underlie hereditary multiple exostoses, while sporadic solitary lesions harbour somatic EXT alterations. Solitary osteochondroma has an excellent prognosis, with recurrence occurring mainly after incomplete excision of the cartilage cap. Malignant transformation is uncommon overall but is an important long-term consideration, particularly in hereditary multiple exostoses.

fibro-osseous proliferation confined largely to the cortex of the tibia, and less often the fibula. The lesion is composed of a bland fibroblastic stroma containing irregular trabeculae of woven bone that, in contrast to fibrous dysplasia, are lined by prominent osteoblasts. It is developmentally and biologically linked to adamantinoma, and lesions exist along a continuum from pure osteofibrous dysplasia through OFD-like adamantinoma to classic adamantinoma, defined by the extent of an epithelial component. Cortical weakening produces the characteristic anterior bowing of the tibia. Osteofibrous dysplasia is benign and frequently stabilises or regresses around skeletal maturity, but it recurs readily after excision in young children. Its principal significance lies in its relationship to adamantinoma, which mandates careful histological assessment and follow-up.

Perinatal presentation with a small deformed thorax and multiple in-utero fractures suggesting a lethal form Attributing fractures solely to abuse, or conversely dismissing genuine inflicted injury as OI, without appropriate multidisciplinary assessment Relying on sclerae colour alone, as blue sclerae are non-specific and may be absent in some types Overlooking hearing loss and dental disease, which need proactive surveillance Failing to monitor for basilar invagination in progressively deforming disease Osteogenesis imperfecta is a heritable disorder of connective tissue in which abnormal type I collagen, the principal protein of bone matrix, leads to reduced bone mass and mechanical fragility. Most patients carry dominant variants in COL1A1 or COL1A2; null variants reduce the amount of otherwise normal collagen and cause milder disease, whereas variants that distort the collagen triple helix produce a more severe dominant-negative effect. Rarer recessive forms disrupt genes involved in collagen folding, post-translational modification, or bone mineralisation. The resulting defective matrix impairs bone strength and also affects other collagen-rich tissues such as sclera, dentine, and the middle ear ossicles. Prognosis spans from a near-normal lifespan and function in mild type I disease to perinatal lethality in type II. Severe deforming forms carry lifelong mobility limitation, and outcome is strongly influenced by respiratory reserve and craniocervical complications.

interosseous calcification Spinal fractures or scoliosis compromising function Biopsying or resecting hyperplastic callus mistaken for osteosarcoma, which can itself provoke more callus Expecting blue sclerae or dentinogenesis imperfecta and discounting OI when they are absent Overlooking the diagnostic triad of callus, interosseous calcification, and metaphyseal band on imaging Failing to test IFITM5 because collagen gene studies are normal OI type V is caused by a recurrent point mutation in the 5' untranslated region of IFITM5, which creates a new upstream start codon and adds five amino acids to the BRIL protein expressed by osteoblasts. BRIL participates in bone mineralisation, and the mutant protein disturbs normal osteoblast function and matrix mineralisation, producing brittle bones without the type I collagen abnormality of classic OI. The altered bone biology manifests as an exaggerated reparative response, generating hyperplastic callus, and abnormal soft-tissue mineralisation such as calcification of the forearm interosseous membrane and a characteristic dense metaphyseal band. Bone histology shows a distinctive mesh-like (irregular) lamellar pattern. The result is increased fracture risk with these unique radiological and clinical hallmarks. Skeletal fragility is lifelong but generally responsive to fracture management and antiresorptive therapy; forearm rotation may remain limited, and the main avoidable harm comes from misdiagnosing hyperplastic callus as tumour.

Osteoid osteoma — osteoid osteoma, benign osteoblastic nidus lesion Osteoblastoma (larger, more aggressive, less reactive sclerosis) Brodie abscess (subacute osteomyelitis) Stress fracture Osteomyelitis of other cause Ewing sarcoma or other primary bone malignancy Bone island (enostosis) Thin-section CT to identify and localise the nidus Plain radiographs showing a lucent nidus with surrounding sclerosis MRI to assess marrow and soft-tissue oedema, though it may overestimate aggressiveness Bone scintigraphy showing focal intense uptake (double-density sign) Correlation of symptom pattern with response to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs Histological confirmation when the diagnosis is uncertain or tissue is obtained at ablation A small benign bone-forming tumour, by definition under about two centimetres, most common in children and young adults and predominating in males The hallmark is well-localised pain that is characteristically worse at night and relieved dramatically by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs Typically arises in the cortex of long bones, especially the femur and tibia, with the proximal femur a classic site Imaging shows a small radiolucent nidus surrounded by dense reactive sclerosis; CT is the best modality to demonstrate the nidus Spinal lesions may present with painful scoliosis, the lesion sitting on the concave side of the curve The nidus produces prostaglandins, which explains both the nocturnal pain and its striking response to prostaglandin-inhibiting drugs Treatment options include conservative management with NSAIDs, since many lesions eventually resolve, or radiofrequency ablation for persistent symptoms Rapid growth or a lesion larger than expected suggesting osteoblastoma or malignancy Progressive painful scoliosis or neurological signs from a spinal lesion Atypical imaging with cortical destruction or a soft-tissue mass Failure of pain to respond to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, prompting reconsideration Mistaking the reactive sclerosis for osteomyelitis or malignancy and missing the small nidus Overlooking a spinal osteoid osteoma as the cause of painful scoliosis in an adolescent Relying on MRI alone, which can exaggerate surrounding oedema and suggest aggression Incomplete ablation or excision of the nidus leading to persistent pain Osteoid osteoma is a benign osteoblastic neoplasm consisting of a small central nidus of woven bone and osteoid set in vascular connective tissue, encircled by a zone of dense reactive sclerosis in the surrounding bone. The nidus is richly innervated and expresses high levels of cyclooxygenase enzymes, generating prostaglandins that mediate the intense, often nocturnal pain and the vasodilatation seen in the lesion. The prostaglandin dependence accounts for the characteristic relief with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. The tumour has limited growth potential, does not metastasise, and may involute spontaneously over years. The outlook is excellent; the lesion is benign and does not metastasise, symptoms often settle with medical treatment or spontaneous involution, and targeted ablation is usually curative with low recurrence. Malignant transformation does not occur.

osteomalacia — adult rickets, defective bone mineralisation osteoporosis Paget's disease of bone renal osteodystrophy metastatic bone disease or multiple myeloma polymyalgia rheumatica (proximal myopathy mimic) primary hyperparathyroidism fibromyalgia serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase 25-hydroxyvitamin D and PTH renal profile with urine phosphate and tubular reabsorption of phosphate (TmP/GFR) plain radiographs seeking Looser zones coeliac serology and markers of malabsorption intact FGF23 where unexplained phosphate wasting is suspected transiliac bone biopsy with tetracycline labelling in diagnostic uncertainty Osteomalacia is impaired mineralisation of newly formed osteoid in the mature skeleton; the childhood equivalent, affecting the growth plate, is rickets. The commonest cause worldwide is vitamin D deficiency (nutritional, malabsorption, limited sunlight); hypophosphataemia and mineralisation inhibitors are important non-calcipenic causes. Classic biochemistry is low or low-normal calcium, low phosphate, raised alkaline phosphatase, raised PTH and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Diffuse bone pain with a proximal myopathy (waddling gait, difficulty rising from a chair) is characteristic, often with bony tenderness on sternal or tibial pressure. Looser zones (pseudofractures) on the compression side of long bones, pubic rami, scapula and ribs are a near-pathognomonic radiological feature. Distinguish calcipenic forms (vitamin D or calcium deficiency, high PTH) from phosphopenic forms (renal phosphate wasting, FGF23-mediated) as treatment differs fundamentally. Transiliac bone biopsy after tetracycline double-labelling showing increased osteoid thickness and prolonged mineralisation lag time is the gold standard but rarely required. Hypocalcaemia and hypophosphataemia may worsen transiently when repletion begins ('hungry bone'), so monitor biochemistry during treatment. symptomatic hypocalcaemia (tetany, seizures, prolonged QT interval) insufficiency fractures, particularly of the femoral neck severe proximal weakness causing recurrent falls unexplained renal phosphate wasting raising suspicion of tumour-induced osteomalacia underlying malabsorption such as coeliac disease or previous bariatric surgery attributing symptoms to osteoporosis or fibromyalgia and missing osteomalacia assuming normal serum calcium excludes the diagnosis failing to seek an underlying malabsorptive cause not distinguishing calcipenic from phosphopenic mechanisms before treatment giving vitamin D alone when renal phosphate wasting is the primary problem Mature bone is continually remodelled, with osteoblasts laying down unmineralised osteoid that is subsequently mineralised by deposition of calcium and phosphate as hydroxyapatite. In osteomalacia this mineralisation step fails or lags, so accumulating unmineralised osteoid weakens the skeleton. The dominant mechanism is inadequate availability of calcium and phosphate at the mineralising front, most often from vitamin D deficiency (reduced intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal phosphate loss). Other routes include chronic hypophosphataemia from renal phosphate wasting (FGF23 excess, Fanconi syndrome), renal failure with impaired 1-alpha-hydroxylation, hypophosphatasia (low tissue-non-specific alkaline phosphatase), and inhibitors of mineralisation such as aluminium, fluoride and some bisphosphonates. Prognosis is excellent when the underlying deficiency is corrected, with bone pain and proximal myopathy usually resolving over weeks to months. Established skeletal deformity or fractures may leave residual disability.

benign dysplasia Rising tumour markers or abnormal bone biochemistry indicating an alternative diagnosis Pathological fracture, which would be unexpected and warrant reassessment Mistaking the axial sclerosis for osteoblastic metastases and subjecting patients to unnecessary cancer investigation Confusing it with osteopetrosis and expecting marrow failure or fracture risk Overlooking the normal bone biochemistry that supports a benign diagnosis Failing to recognise the autosomal dominant pattern within a family Osteomesopyknosis is a benign heritable sclerosing bone dysplasia characterised by increased bone density restricted to the axial skeleton, particularly the vertebrae, pelvis, and proximal femora. The precise molecular basis is not firmly established, but the pattern reflects a localised disturbance of the balance between bone formation and resorption favouring accrual of dense trabecular bone in axial sites, with sparing of the appendicular skeleton and skull. Because bone modelling and marrow function are otherwise preserved, there is no medullary compromise, and calcium homeostasis and bone-turnover biochemistry remain normal. The condition therefore behaves as a radiologically striking but clinically indolent finding, in contrast to the diffuse and complication-prone sclerosis of osteopetrosis. Excellent; it is a benign, non-progressive condition with a normal life expectancy and no risk of marrow failure or nerve compression, with symptoms limited to mild back pain.

in adults hematogenous disease most often involves the vertebral column, whereas in children long bones are seeded (Harrison 22e p.1061). The clinically decisive distinction is not a fixed duration but the presence or absence of bone necrosis (sequestra): acute osteomyelitis without necrosis can generally be cured with antimicrobials alone, while chronic osteomyelitis with sequestra requires combined surgical debridement (Harrison 22e p.1062). Back pain is the leading symptom of vertebral osteomyelitis (>85%), and the location maps to the level of infection (lumbar ~60%, thoracic ~30%, cervical ~10%); only about half of patients are febrile, partly because of analgesic use (Harrison 22e p.1062). ESR and CRP are markedly more useful than the leukocyte count for screening: CRP is elevated in essentially all and ESR in ~98% of vertebral osteomyelitis cases, whereas leukocytosis and neutrophilia have sensitivities of only ~65% and ~40% (Harrison 22e p.1062). In patients without sepsis syndrome, antibiotics should be withheld until a pathogen is documented (by blood culture, bone biopsy, or aspirated pus), because pretreatment markedly lowers culture yield and an established microbiologic diagnosis guides therapy (Harrison 22e p.1062-1063). MRI is the diagnostic gold standard for vertebral osteomyelitis and should be obtained urgently when neurologic impairment is present to detect epidural abscess or exclude disk herniation; 18F-FDG PET is the alternative when MRI is contraindicated or implants/multifocal disease are suspected (Harrison 22e p.1062). A primary focus is found in only about half of hematogenous cases; common sources are the urinary tract, skin/soft tissue, intravascular catheters, and the endocardium, and endocarditis is identified in roughly 10% overall (and in ~50% of viridans streptococcal cases) (Harrison 22e p.1061-1062). Implanted foreign material creates a zone of local immunodeficiency and a host-protein-coated surface that promotes staphylococcal adherence and biofilm formation, so device-related bone and joint infection generally cannot be cured by antimicrobials alone (Harrison 22e p.1062, 1066). Brodie's abscess is a subacute form occurring mainly in young males, presenting with pain (~98%) and swelling (~53%) in the tibia or femur, with a median diagnostic delay of about 3 months; localized unexplained tibial/femoral pain in a young patient warrants imaging (Harrison 22e p.1064). Subacute or chronic vertebral disease is typically caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Brucella in endemic regions, and by low-virulence organisms (coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium acnes) in implant-associated infection; tuberculous spondylitis preferentially involves the thoracic spine (about two-thirds of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1062). Synovial fluid analysis is central to diagnosing periprosthetic joint infection: leukocyte thresholds of ~1700/uL (knee) and ~4200/uL (hip) are about 90% sensitive and specific, and alpha-defensin is highly specific but limited by cost and sensitivity, so it should confirm rather than screen (Harrison 22e p.1066). Chronic osteomyelitis can reactivate decades later; recurrence after a symptom-free interval exceeding 70 years has been described, most often in elderly patients with S. aureus disease acquired in the preantibiotic era (Harrison 22e p.1063-1064). New or progressive neurologic deficit (radiculopathy, weakness, sensory loss, bowel/bladder dysfunction, paralysis) suggesting spinal epidural abscess, present in about one-third of vertebral cases Cervical or thoracic spinal involvement and S. aureus etiology, identified risk factors for severe neurologic deficit Persistent or rising CRP, persistent pain, or sepsis syndrome indicating undrained abscess or treatment failure Persistent pain after CRP normalization, suggesting mechanical complication such as severe osteonecrosis or spinal instability requiring orthopedic evaluation Sinus tract, wound-healing impairment, or implant loosening signaling deep device-related infection Starting empiric antibiotics before obtaining cultures in a non-septic patient, which markedly lowers culture yield and obscures the microbiologic diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1062-1063). Relying on plain radiographs or the leukocyte count in acute disease, both of which have low sensitivity; normal radiographs do not exclude acute osteomyelitis (Harrison 22e p.1062). Using follow-up MRI to judge treatment response in uncomplicated cases, since radiologic improvement correlates poorly with clinical healing; imaging follow-up is reserved for pyogenic complications (Harrison 22e p.1063). Misinterpreting a three-phase bone scan or 18F-FDG PET within ~1 year of surgery, when ongoing bone remodeling produces nonspecific uptake (Harrison 22e p.1064, 1066). Assuming antimicrobials alone will cure device-associated osteomyelitis or PJI; without appropriate surgery such therapy is generally only suppressive (Harrison 22e p.1061, 1067). Dismissing coagulase-negative staphylococci or Cutibacterium acnes as contaminants, when in the setting of an implant or prolonged bacteremia they may be the true low-virulence pathogens (Harrison 22e p.1062). Failing to consider tuberculous or brucellar disease in patients from or traveling to endemic regions, where subacute/chronic vertebral osteomyelitis predominates (Harrison 22e p.1063-1065). Osteomyelitis is infection of bone reached by microorganisms via one of three routes. In hematogenous disease, circulating organisms seed the metaphyses of long bones in children and the vertebral column in adults; because the adult intervertebral disk is avascular, organisms enter through the segmental arteries supplying the adjacent endplates and then spread into the disk, producing the characteristic involvement of two contiguous vertebrae and the intervening disk. Alternative routes include retrograde seeding through the prevertebral venous plexus and direct inoculation during spinal surgery, epidural procedures, or trauma. Contiguous-focus disease follows bone trauma or surgery, with wound infection after sternotomy, open-fracture repair, or prosthetic-joint placement. Vascular-insufficiency/neuropathic disease, most often in poorly controlled diabetes, arises from progressively deep foot infection driven by ischemia of skin, soft tissue, and bone combined with motor, sensory, and autonomic neuropathy. Foreign material is highly vulnerable: host proteins such as fibronectin coat the device, favoring staphylococcal adherence and biofilm formation that resists phagocytosis and antibiotics. Failure of timely or adequate therapy leads to bone necrosis (sequestra) and progression to chronic osteomyelitis with sinus tracts and soft-tissue destruction (Harrison 22e p.1061-1066). Prognosis depends on early diagnosis, presence of bone necrosis, and whether an implant is involved. Acute hematogenous vertebral and long-bone osteomyelitis without sequestra or hardware can usually be cured with antimicrobials alone; a randomized trial in pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis reported ~91% cure at one year with no difference between 6- and 12-week regimens. Failure of adequate treatment, open fractures, and unaddressed implant infection drive progression to chronic osteomyelitis with sinus tracts and soft-tissue damage. In fracture-related infection, implant-retention success falls with chronicity (about 86-100% in early, 82-89% in delayed, and ~67% in late infection). In periprosthetic joint infection, implant retention offers >80% infection-free survival only when the infection is acute, the implant is stable, the pathogen is susceptible to a biofilm-active agent, and the soft tissues are intact; in patients with severe comorbidity, lifelong suppressive therapy may be the chosen goal rather than cure (Harrison 22e p.1063-1067). No single accepted comprehensive scheme exists. Osteomyelitis is categorized by pathogenesis (hematogenous, contiguous, vascular insufficiency/neuropathic), by course (acute versus subacute/chronic, with the presence or absence of sequestra being the decisive feature), and by location (long bone, vertebral, periarticular). The Cierny-Mader staging system classifies long-bone disease by anatomic extent, host physiologic class (systemic and local compromise of immunity, metabolism, and vascularity), and radiographic findings, and is used mainly to guide surgical management. Implant-associated disease is further classified by timing relative to surgery (e.g., early/acute, delayed, late), and periprosthetic joint infection is grouped for therapeutic decisions as acute hematogenous, early postinterventional, or chronic (Harrison 22e p.1061, 1066).

osteopathia striata — Voorhoeve disease, osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis osteopoikilosis melorheostosis osteopetrosis sclerotic bone metastases engelmann diaphyseal dysplasia healing rickets with metaphyseal lines plain radiography of long bones and pelvis for striation pattern skull radiography or CT for cranial sclerosis in syndromic cases bone scintigraphy to demonstrate absent increased uptake audiometry when cranial nerve involvement is suspected AMER1 gene sequencing in syndromic presentations serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase to exclude metabolic bone disease Osteopathia striata is a sclerosing bone dysplasia defined radiologically by fine linear longitudinal striations in the metaphyses and diaphyses of long bones and a fan-like pattern in the iliac wings. Isolated osteopathia striata (Voorhoeve disease) is usually an asymptomatic incidental radiographic finding of no clinical consequence. When combined with cranial sclerosis it forms an X-linked disorder caused by AMER1 (WTX) mutations, typically more severe in affected males and often lethal or with major anomalies in hemizygous males. Females with osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis characteristically have macrocephaly, cranial nerve compression with hearing loss, and cleft palate. The striations run parallel to the long axis of the bone and do not disturb bone modelling or cause pathological fracture in the isolated form. It is one of the classic mixed sclerosing bone dysplasias and may coexist with osteopoikilosis and melorheostosis. Bone scintigraphy is typically normal, helping distinguish it from active sclerotic processes such as metastasis or osteomyelitis. Recognition matters chiefly to avoid unnecessary investigation of an incidental benign pattern. progressive hearing loss or other cranial neuropathy suggesting foraminal narrowing macrocephaly with developmental concern in an infant severe skeletal or visceral anomalies in a male fetus or neonate unexpected sclerotic lesions with abnormal tracer uptake prompting reappraisal Mistaking incidental striations for sclerotic metastases and initiating an oncological work-up. Overlooking associated cranial sclerosis and its neurological consequences by imaging long bones alone. Failing to offer genetic counselling once the X-linked syndromic form is recognised. Confusing the linear striations with the rounded foci of osteopoikilosis. Attributing hearing loss to unrelated causes rather than foraminal stenosis. The isolated form is a sporadic or benign developmental anomaly of endochondral ossification in which longitudinal columns of persistent dense trabecular bone produce the characteristic striations without disturbing overall bone architecture. The syndromic osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis results from loss-of-function mutations in AMER1, which encodes a negative regulator of the canonical Wnt/beta-catenin signalling pathway central to osteoblast activity. Loss of this brake enhances Wnt signalling and osteoblastic bone formation, producing the striations in long bones together with sclerotic overgrowth of the skull base and vault. The X-linked pattern and X-inactivation account for the milder mosaic phenotype in females and the severe or lethal presentation in hemizygous males. Isolated osteopathia striata is benign with a normal life expectancy and requires no treatment; the syndromic form carries morbidity from cranial nerve compression and craniofacial anomalies and may be lethal in affected males.

The skull-base overgrowth encroaches on foramina, accounting for the cranial neuropathies. Affected females generally have a good prognosis with intellect usually preserved, though cranial-nerve complications may accrue over time; affected males can have severe multisystem disease that is frequently lethal in the prenatal or neonatal period.

optic nerve involvement Failing to distinguish osteoclast-intrinsic from osteoclast-poor forms, which affects transplant suitability Osteopetrosis results from failure of osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, most often due to defects in the machinery that acidifies the resorption lacuna, such as the proton pump subunit encoded by TCIRG1 or the chloride channel encoded by CLCN7. Without effective resorption, bone remodelling is disrupted and immature, poorly organised, densely mineralised bone accumulates. This encroaches on the marrow cavity, causing cytopenias and extramedullary haematopoiesis, narrows cranial foramina to compress nerves, and produces bone that is dense yet mechanically brittle. Some forms reflect defective osteoclast differentiation rather than function, which influences whether transplantation is likely to help. Untreated severe infantile osteopetrosis is often fatal in early childhood from marrow failure and infection, whereas transplantation can be curative in suitable osteoclast-intrinsic forms. The dominant adult form is compatible with a normal lifespan but carries fracture, osteomyelitis, and nerve-compression morbidity.

Reduced antagonism tips the balance towards osteoblastic activity in discrete foci, producing scattered islands of compact lamellar bone within the spongiosa. These enostosis-like foci concentrate near the ends of long bones and around the pelvis and short tubular bones, remain metabolically quiet, and do not disturb the overall bone architecture, explaining the asymptomatic incidental presentation and the absence of scintigraphic uptake. The skeletal condition is benign and does not shorten life or cause meaningful disability; the main risk is diagnostic confusion with malignancy leading to unnecessary investigation, and prognosis is excellent once the diagnosis is recognised.

osteopenia (low bone density) is a T-score of -1.0 to -2.5 and is a risk factor for developing osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3291). A fragility fracture (hip or vertebral) by definition establishes osteoporosis and warrants treatment, regardless of the T-score; patients presenting with hip or spine fractures by definition have osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3291, p.3298). Osteoporosis is most common among postmenopausal women, but ~30% of fragility fractures occur in men; secondary osteoporosis arises from other underlying diseases (Harrison 22e p.3291). >50% of fractures, including hip fractures, among postmenopausal women occur in individuals with osteopenia rather than densitometric osteoporosis, because that population is much larger - hence the shift toward absolute fracture-risk assessment (Harrison 22e p.3291). FRAX and the Garvan Fracture Risk Calculator estimate 10-year probability of hip or major osteoporotic fracture by combining age, sex, and clinical risk factors with or without BMD, and inform country-specific intervention thresholds distinct from diagnostic thresholds (Harrison 22e p.3291, p.3298). Glucocorticoids are the most common cause of medication-induced osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3296). Any fracture (excluding fingers, toes, face, skull) in a woman aged >50 or a man aged >60 should trigger investigation for osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3293). Vertebral fracture (even asymptomatic) is a major sign of skeletal fragility and markedly increases risk of subsequent fracture, especially within the first 12-24 months (imminent fracture risk) Significant height loss (>4 cm) suggesting occult vertebral fracture Hip fracture - high mortality (20-25% die within the year) and major loss of independence More chronic severe pain after vertebral fracture should raise suspicion of multiple myeloma or other underlying bone condition Failing to exclude secondary causes of osteoporosis (e.g. myeloma, hyperparathyroidism, thyrotoxicosis, Cushing's, malabsorption/celiac, hypogonadism, mastocytosis) before attributing low bone mass to primary disease, particularly in patients with fractures or unexpectedly low Z-scores. Excluding a patient from osteoporosis evaluation simply because a fracture was traumatic - patients with osteoporosis are also more likely to sustain traumatic fractures, and any fracture warrants skeletal assessment. Relying solely on BMD, which can underestimate fragility (microarchitectural deterioration not captured) and is falsely elevated in the spine by osteoarthritic bone spurs/spondylosis; small slim people show falsely low DXA values. Fewer than 20% of fracture patients are investigated or treated for osteoporosis within 6 months; postfracture care remains fragmented. Drug holidays are appropriate to consider for oral/IV bisphosphonates but should be avoided for denosumab and anabolic agents because of more rapid offset. Osteoporosis is reduced bone strength leading to skeletal fragility and fractures; BMD alone underestimates fragility because microarchitectural deterioration and component misalignment also contribute. A low peak bone mass (genetic, hormonal, nutritional) may underlie disease, with superimposed age-related and extrinsic changes in bone remodeling. In adults remodeling (not modeling) predominates and serves to repair microdamage and supply calcium. Estrogen deficiency drives bone loss by (1) activating new remodeling sites and (2) creating an imbalance favoring resorption over formation: loss of estrogen increases RANKL and reduces osteoprotegerin, increasing osteoclast formation/recruitment, while shortening osteoblast life span and prolonging osteoclast longevity/activity. Trabecular bone (80% of surface area) is preferentially affected, so vertebral fractures are the earliest skeletal consequence. Estrogen also regulates remodeling in men. Heritability of BMD is ~50-80%; LRP5 activating mutations cause high bone mass and inactivating mutations cause osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3293-3295). Lifetime osteoporotic fracture risk for a 50-year-old Caucasian woman is ~50% and ~25% for a man; lifetime hip fracture probability ~14% (women) and ~5% (men), roughly half for African Americans. Hip fractures carry high morbidity and mortality with 20-25% of patients dying within the year (higher among men and African Americans), and ~30% of survivors requiring long-term care, many never regaining prior independence. A first fracture exponentially increases risk of further fracture, especially in the first year; almost 20% of women sustain a second fracture within 2 years (Harrison 22e p.3291-3293). WHO densitometric categories: normal (T-score >= -1.0), osteopenia/low bone density (T-score -1.0 to -2.5), osteoporosis (T-score <= -2.5 at lumbar spine, femoral neck, or total hip). Presence of a fragility fracture (notably hip or vertebral) defines established/clinical osteoporosis regardless of T-score. Absolute fracture risk (FRAX/Garvan 10-year hip and major osteoporotic fracture probability) is increasingly used alongside or instead of T-score for treatment decisions (Harrison 22e p.3291, p.3297-3298).

malignant tumour of mesenchymal cells that produce osteoid or immature bone. It typically arises in the metaphysis of rapidly growing long bones, explaining its predilection for the knee region in adolescence during the growth spurt. The tumour destroys normal bone while laying down disorganised neoplastic osteoid, lifts and stimulates the periosteum, and breaks through the cortex to form a soft-tissue mass. Prognosis depends principally on the presence of metastases at diagnosis and the tumour's response to chemotherapy; with modern combined chemotherapy and surgery many patients with localised, chemosensitive disease achieve long-term survival, whereas metastatic or chemoresistant disease carries a substantially worse outlook.

of the skin lining the external auditory canal. Breakdown of the canal's protective barrier, through excess moisture, mechanical trauma, cerumen removal, or altered pH, allows bacterial or fungal overgrowth. The resulting inflammation causes oedema, discharge and narrowing of the canal, producing pain and conductive hearing loss when the lumen is occluded. In malignant otitis externa, infection (typically Pseudomonas) spreads from the soft tissue into the temporal bone and skull base, causing progressive osteomyelitis and potential cranial nerve involvement. Uncomplicated otitis externa usually resolves with topical treatment and ear care, but malignant otitis externa is potentially life-threatening and requires prolonged systemic therapy and close monitoring.

sodium fluoride may be used to stabilise active disease Rapidly progressive or asymmetrical sensorineural loss prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Vertigo or disequilibrium suggesting labyrinthine or alternative pathology Sudden deterioration or facial nerve symptoms after stapes surgery requiring urgent review Unilateral pulsatile tinnitus or other features that raise concern for a vascular or retrocochlear lesion Overlooking otosclerosis when the drum looks normal and attributing the loss to wax or effusion Failing to counsel about the small risk of dead ear and sensorineural loss with stapes surgery Missing a coexisting sensorineural (cochlear) component that limits surgical benefit Not recognising the Carhart notch as a bone conduction artefact rather than true cochlear loss Otosclerosis is a primary disorder of endochondral bone of the otic capsule in which foci of normal lamellar bone are resorbed and replaced by irregular, highly cellular and vascular spongy bone that later matures into dense sclerotic bone. deformity with a rotational profile Overtreating benign infantile out-toeing with unnecessary orthoses Overlooking associated patellofemoral maltracking that may need attention Out-toeing describes an outwardly directed foot progression angle during walking, produced by external rotational alignment at the hip, tibia, or foot. In the infant it commonly reflects a residual external rotation contracture of the hip capsule from intrauterine position, which stretches out with ambulation. In the older child it usually arises from external tibial torsion or reduced femoral anteversion (relative retroversion), representing variation in the normal course of skeletal derotation. Unlike internal torsion, external tibial torsion often progresses with growth. Pathological out-toeing is important to recognise because hip disorders such as a slipped capital femoral epiphysis characteristically hold the limb in external rotation. Physiological out-toeing generally carries a good prognosis, with infantile hip contractures resolving after walking begins; external tibial torsion is less predictable and may persist or progress, occasionally warranting correction for symptoms.

responders Exogenous gonadotrophin stimulation, followed by an hCG or agonist trigger, produces multiple corpora lutea that secrete large amounts of vasoactive mediators, principally vascular endothelial growth factor. hCG amplifies this response, which is why an established pregnancy prolongs and worsens the syndrome. VEGF-driven increases in vascular permeability allow protein-rich fluid to shift from the intravascular compartment into the peritoneal, and sometimes pleural, spaces. This produces ascites, intravascular volume depletion, haemoconcentration, and a hypercoagulable state, which in severe cases lead to oliguria, electrolyte disturbance, thromboembolism, and multi-organ compromise. Most cases are mild and self-limiting, resolving as hCG levels fall, typically within one to two weeks unless pregnancy sustains the process. Severe and critical OHSS, though uncommon, can be life-threatening from thromboembolism, renal failure, or respiratory compromise, but with prompt supportive care and thromboprophylaxis outcomes are generally good. Preventive strategies have markedly reduced the incidence of severe disease.

Protein-rich fluid leaks from the circulation into the peritoneal, pleural, and occasionally pericardial spaces, producing ascites, effusions, and intravascular volume depletion. The resulting haemoconcentration and stasis, compounded by the hypercoagulable state of stimulation and early pregnancy, predispose to thromboembolism, while reduced renal perfusion causes oliguria and electrolyte disturbance. Ongoing hCG stimulation, including from an implanting pregnancy, sustains and worsens the process. Most cases are mild to moderate and resolve spontaneously, particularly when not compounded by pregnancy. Severe and critical OHSS can be life-threatening through thromboembolism, renal failure, and respiratory compromise, but outcomes are generally good with timely supportive care and thromboprophylaxis.

ovarian androgen output with a GnRH agonist, insulin-sensitising strategies, and bilateral oophorectomy in postmenopausal women when malignancy must be excluded or symptoms are severe Rapid onset or signs suggesting coexisting Cushing syndrome Labelling the presentation as polycystic ovary syndrome despite disproportionately severe virilisation and testosterone elevation Failing to exclude an androgen-secreting tumour before attributing symptoms to hyperthecosis Neglecting the associated insulin resistance and its cardiometabolic implications Expecting a polycystic appearance on imaging when the ovaries are typically enlarged and solid Ovarian hyperthecosis is a non-neoplastic disorder in which islands of luteinised theca-type cells are distributed throughout the ovarian stroma and secrete androgens, chiefly testosterone. Unlike the follicle-based dysfunction of polycystic ovary syndrome, the androgen excess here arises from these stromal luteinised cells, whose activity is amplified by hyperinsulinaemia; insulin and insulin-like growth factor stimulate ovarian theca and stromal cells to produce androgens, creating a self-reinforcing link between insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism. The resulting high circulating testosterone produces the virilising features. Because the androgen source is diffuse ovarian stroma rather than a discrete mass, imaging typically shows bilaterally enlarged solid ovaries rather than a tumour. The condition itself is benign, but it causes considerable distress from virilisation and carries the metabolic consequences of associated insulin resistance, including increased cardiometabolic risk. Androgen suppression or oophorectomy can control hyperandrogenism, and addressing insulin resistance improves the broader metabolic profile.

fallopian tube, twists on its pedicle and compromises its blood supply, threatening ovarian viability It classically presents with sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain, often colicky and associated intervention, usually laparoscopic detorsion with conservation of the ovary, is preferred over oophorectomy even when the ovary looks dusky, as tissue often recovers The classic error is delay: repeated observation while awaiting imaging or normalisation of pain risks irreversible ischaemic loss of the ovary Intermittent torsion produces recurrent self-limiting episodes of pain and warrants evaluation before a definitive infarction occurs Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with an adnexal mass, mandating urgent assessment to preserve the ovary Persistent pain with peritonism suggesting ischaemia or necrosis Haemodynamic instability raising concern for haemorrhage or a ruptured ectopic Signs of sepsis suggesting necrotic or infected adnexa Recurrent episodic pain indicating intermittent torsion needing prompt surgical evaluation Excluding torsion because Doppler shows preserved arterial flow Delaying surgery for repeated imaging or observation while ischaemia progresses Performing oophorectomy on a dusky ovary that would recover after simple detorsion Failing to consider torsion in premenarchal girls and pregnant women Missing intermittent torsion by attributing recurrent pain to functional cysts When the ovary or adnexa rotates about the infundibulopelvic and utero-ovarian ligaments, the lower-pressure venous and lymphatic drainage is occluded first, producing congestion and marked ovarian oedema and enlargement. Continued or tightening rotation eventually compromises arterial inflow, leading to ischaemia, haemorrhagic infarction, and necrosis. Because arterial flow may persist longer than venous outflow owing to the thicker arterial wall and dual blood supply, viability can be maintained for a variable period, defining a window in which detorsion can salvage the ovary. When detorsion is performed promptly the ovary usually recovers function even if it appeared ischaemic at surgery, and future fertility is generally preserved. Delayed diagnosis leads to infarction requiring oophorectomy and loss of that ovary's function; recurrence can occur, and oophoropexy may be considered in selected cases such as recurrent torsion or a normal ovary in a child.

Overactive bladder — OAB, Urge syndrome, Detrusor overactivity syndrome Urinary tract infection or bacterial cystitis Bladder carcinoma or carcinoma in situ Bladder pain syndrome / interstitial cystitis Bladder outlet obstruction with secondary detrusor overactivity Neurogenic detrusor overactivity from spinal or cerebral disease Polyuria from diabetes, diuretics or excessive fluid intake Bladder calculus or foreign body Frequency-volume bladder diary over several days Urinalysis and urine culture to exclude infection and haematuria Post-void residual measurement by bladder ultrasound Urine cytology when carcinoma in situ is suspected Validated symptom and quality-of-life questionnaires Urodynamic study in refractory, complex or pre-surgical cases Cystoscopy where haematuria, pain or malignancy risk is present Overactive bladder is a symptom syndrome defined by urinary urgency, usually with frequency and nocturia, with or without urgency incontinence, in the absence of infection or other identifiable pathology. Urgency, the sudden compelling desire to void that is difficult to defer, is the cornerstone symptom and distinguishes overactive bladder from the normal, deferrable urge to pass urine. Detrusor overactivity on urodynamics is a related but separate concept; many patients with overactive bladder symptoms show no involuntary contractions, and the diagnosis remains clinical. A bladder diary quantifying frequency, voided volumes, urgency episodes and fluid intake is the single most useful assessment tool and guides behavioural therapy. First-line treatment is conservative: fluid and caffeine modification, bladder training and pelvic floor muscle training, before considering pharmacotherapy. Pharmacological options include antimuscarinic agents and beta-3 adrenergic agonists; antimuscarinic anticholinergic load should be minimised in older and cognitively vulnerable patients. Refractory cases may respond to intradetrusor botulinum toxin injection, percutaneous or sacral neuromodulation, always after excluding significant post-void residual and other pathology. New or persistent overactive bladder symptoms in an older patient, or symptoms with visible haematuria, mandate exclusion of bladder carcinoma or carcinoma in situ before ascribing them to overactive bladder. Visible haematuria accompanying storage symptoms Persistent sterile pyuria or recurrent proven infection Significant post-void residual or palpable bladder suggesting retention New neurological signs, back pain or lower limb symptoms suggesting a neurological cause Rapidly progressive symptoms or bladder pain suggesting malignancy or bladder pain syndrome Starting antimuscarinic therapy without excluding a large post-void residual, risking precipitation of retention Labelling symptoms as overactive bladder without excluding infection, haematuria or malignancy Ignoring cumulative anticholinergic burden and cognitive risk in elderly patients Overlooking modifiable contributors such as caffeine, excessive evening fluids or constipation Failing to recognise bladder pain syndrome, in which pain rather than urgency drives frequency Overactive bladder reflects a disturbance of the storage phase of the micturition cycle in which afferent and efferent control of the detrusor is dysregulated. Proposed mechanisms include a myogenic component, with increased spontaneous detrusor activity and enhanced coupling between smooth muscle cells, and a neurogenic component, with heightened afferent signalling and reduced central inhibition of the voiding reflex. Urothelial and suburothelial signalling abnormalities, involving altered release of acetylcholine, ATP and other mediators and up-regulated receptor sensitivity, augment sensory input from the bladder wall. The net effect is a perception of urgency at low bladder volumes, often accompanied by phasic involuntary detrusor contractions during filling. Contributing factors include ageing, bladder outlet obstruction, metabolic and neurological disease, and pelvic floor dysfunction, but in most patients no single structural cause is identified. Overactive bladder is a chronic, fluctuating condition rather than a curable one, but the majority of patients achieve meaningful symptom control and improved quality of life with a stepped combination of behavioural measures, pharmacotherapy and, where needed, minimally invasive therapies. Symptom relapse after stopping treatment is common.

convert the Rh-associated glycoprotein into an abnormally permeable cation-conducting pore, greatly increasing monovalent cation flux across the red-cell membrane. Net cation and water gain overhydrate and swell the cell, lowering its haemoglobin concentration and producing the characteristic stomatocyte morphology with associated loss of the membrane protein stomatin. The fragile, overhydrated cells undergo premature destruction, causing a chronic haemolytic anaemia; as with related disorders, splenectomy is hazardous because it predisposes to thrombosis. The chronic haemolytic anaemia is usually moderate and compatible with a good quality of life, but the major avoidable hazard is post-splenectomy thrombosis, and iron overload requires monitoring.

overlap myositis — overlap syndrome myositis, connective-tissue-disease-associated myositis Isolated polymyositis or dermatomyositis Immune-mediated necrotising myopathy Inclusion body myositis Systemic sclerosis with primary myopathy Systemic lupus erythematosus myositis Drug-induced or hypothyroid myopathy Fibromyalgia and steroid myopathy Serum creatine kinase and muscle enzymes Extended myositis and overlap antibody panel (anti-Jo-1 and other synthetases, anti-PM/Scl, anti-U1-RNP, anti-Ku) Antinuclear and extractable-nuclear-antigen antibodies High-resolution CT of the chest and pulmonary function tests with gas transfer Nailfold capillaroscopy Electromyography and muscle MRI or biopsy Echocardiography to assess for pulmonary hypertension Inflammatory myopathy arising alongside another defined connective tissue disease, or defined by an overlap-associated autoantibody, rather than as isolated myositis. The antisynthetase syndrome is a key subset, marked by anti-Jo-1 or other anti-tRNA-synthetase antibodies (anti-PL-7, anti-PL-12, anti-EJ, anti-OJ, anti-KS). Its clinical cluster comprises myositis, interstitial lung disease, non-erosive arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, mechanic's hands and fever, though not all features are present together. Anti-PM/Scl antibodies define a scleroderma-myositis overlap with sclerodactyly, Raynaud and calcinosis, and generally carry a favourable, steroid-responsive course. Anti-U1-RNP points to mixed connective tissue disease, while anti-Ku indicates another overlap phenotype. Muscle weakness is often milder than in classic polymyositis or dermatomyositis, and creatine kinase may be only modestly raised. Interstitial lung disease is the principal driver of morbidity and mortality and can be the presenting or dominant feature. There is a female predominance and a chronic relapsing course requiring long-term immunosuppression. Progressive breathlessness or rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease Pulmonary hypertension Dysphagia with aspiration risk Features suggesting an underlying malignancy New cardiac symptoms Overlooking interstitial lung disease, which may dominate the presentation while muscle symptoms are mild. Attributing arthritis solely to rheumatoid disease and missing the overlap. Missing overlap antibodies when only a limited myositis panel is requested. Underestimating disease when creatine kinase is normal or only mildly elevated. Failing to reassess for pulmonary hypertension over time. Overlap myositis is an autoimmune inflammatory myopathy that occurs within the immune dysregulation of a broader connective tissue disease and is closely linked to specific autoantibodies. In the antisynthetase syndrome, antibodies target aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, and it is proposed that these enzymes, upregulated and exposed in regenerating muscle and injured lung epithelium, act as autoantigens that sustain a self-amplifying response involving both antibody and T-cell mechanisms. Anti-PM/Scl and anti-U1-RNP overlaps share features of scleroderma and lupus-spectrum disease, with vasculopathy, complement activation and cytokine-driven fibrosis contributing to the muscle, skin and lung manifestations. Outcome is variable and largely determined by the presence and severity of interstitial lung disease; anti-PM/Scl overlap is relatively favourable, whereas some antisynthetase phenotypes carry a poorer prognosis. The disease typically follows a chronic relapsing course needing sustained immunosuppression.

Shared genetic susceptibility and dysregulated adaptive immunity generate autoantibodies and tissue inflammation spanning several disorders, sometimes marked by antibodies such as anti-PM/Scl or anti-Ku that associate with combined phenotypes. The resulting clinical picture blends the vasculopathy, fibrosis, synovitis, and myositis of the component diseases, and organ involvement reflects the summed pathology. Outcome is determined by the combination and severity of component diseases and their organ involvement; some overlaps behave indolently while others, particularly those with significant lung, cardiac, or renal disease, carry substantial morbidity. Tailored immunosuppression can control inflammation across the overlapping conditions.

dysgenetic or Y-bearing tissue Progressive inappropriate virilisation or feminisation after sex assignment Delayed or absent puberty indicating gonadal insufficiency Assuming imaging can distinguish ovotestis from other gonads without histology Overlooking coexisting congenital adrenal hyperplasia as a cause of ambiguity Removing potentially functional gonadal tissue congruent with the sex of rearing Neglecting the malignancy risk of retained Y-bearing or dysgenetic components Ovotesticular disorder of sex development arises when the bipotential gonad differentiates into both ovarian and testicular tissue within the same person. In 46,XX cases this can follow cryptic or translocated SRY, gain-of-function in the testis-promoting pathway (for example SOX9 duplication) or as-yet-undefined mechanisms that allow partial testis determination without a Y chromosome. The mixed gonadal tissue secretes a variable combination of testosterone and anti-mullerian hormone, so internal ducts and external genitalia develop along an intermediate path determined locally by the dominant tissue on each side. The result is a spectrum of ambiguity, and gonadal segments with testicular or dysgenetic elements can predispose to germ cell tumours. Outcomes depend on gonadal function preserved after surgery, the assigned sex and psychosocial support; fertility has occasionally been reported, particularly from the ovarian component. Malignancy risk in retained testicular or dysgenetic tissue necessitates lifelong awareness and surveillance.

unexplained acute kidney injury to progressive chronic kidney disease, sometimes with nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis Enteric hyperoxaluria arises because unabsorbed fatty acids bind calcium, leaving free oxalate to be absorbed in the colon Management addresses the cause: drug withdrawal and supportive care in toxin-related cases, dietary oxalate restriction and calcium supplementation with bile-acid handling in enteric disease, and specific therapy for primary hyperoxaluria Rapidly progressive or dialysis-requiring acute kidney injury with widespread crystal deposition Systemic oxalosis with extrarenal crystal deposition in advanced disease Suspected ethylene glycol poisoning with metabolic acidosis and an osmolar gap Recurrent nephrolithiasis with declining renal function suggesting primary hyperoxaluria Overlooking oxalate nephropathy as a cause of unexplained acute kidney injury Failing to take a bariatric-surgery, malabsorption or supplement history Missing primary hyperoxaluria in patients with recurrent stones and early renal failure Not recognising ethylene glycol poisoning as an acute cause Assuming standard dialysis adequately clears the systemic oxalate load Oxalate is an end-product of metabolism that is renally excreted, and when plasma and tubular oxalate rise, calcium oxalate supersaturates and precipitates as crystals within the tubular lumina. These birefringent crystals obstruct and directly injure tubular epithelial cells, triggering inflammasome activation, interstitial inflammation and fibrosis, which drive acute kidney injury and, with sustained exposure, progressive chronic damage and nephrocalcinosis. Hyperoxaluria may be primary, from inherited defects of hepatic glyoxylate metabolism causing endogenous overproduction, or secondary, from enhanced enteric absorption in fat malabsorption, high oxalate or ascorbic-acid intake, or acute overproduction as in ethylene glycol poisoning. Declining renal function further impairs oxalate clearance, creating a self-amplifying cycle of systemic oxalate accumulation. Outcome depends on the cause and the crystal and fibrosis burden at diagnosis; reversible or treatable causes may allow partial renal recovery, whereas heavy crystal deposition with interstitial fibrosis and untreated ongoing hyperoxaluria often progresses to end-stage kidney disease. Primary hyperoxaluria carries a particularly poor renal prognosis without disease-specific treatment, and dialysis alone poorly clears oxalate.

generalised seizure, which is especially dangerous underwater Warning symptoms of CNS toxicity may include visual disturbance, tinnitus, nausea, twitching (notably facial), irritability, and dizziness, though a seizure can occur without warning The pulmonary form develops with prolonged exposure to elevated oxygen and causes retrosternal burning, cough, and progressive reduction in lung function Management is to remove or reduce the excess oxygen exposure promptly, after which the effects are largely reversible A convulsion in the water risks drowning, so prevention through oxygen exposure limits is critical Susceptibility varies between individuals and is increased by factors such as carbon dioxide retention and immersion Seizure occurring underwater, with a high risk of drowning Progressive respiratory symptoms with declining lung function Persisting neurological deficit after the event, suggesting an alternative diagnosis Coexisting decompression illness or gas contamination Exceeding recommended oxygen exposure limits on enriched gas mixtures Assuming a warning aura always precedes a seizure Confusing CNS oxygen toxicity with nitrogen narcosis or decompression illness Overlooking carbon dioxide retention, which lowers the seizure threshold Oxygen toxicity is caused by excessive generation of reactive oxygen species when tissues are exposed to a high partial pressure of oxygen that overwhelms antioxidant defences. In the central nervous system, high oxygen partial pressure disturbs neuronal excitability and can trigger seizures, typically after relatively short high-level exposures. In the lungs, more prolonged hyperoxia injures the alveolar-capillary membrane and airway epithelium, producing inflammation, tracheobronchial irritation, and impaired gas exchange. Both forms depend on the dose and duration of oxygen exposure and are largely reversible once exposure is curtailed. Both central nervous system and pulmonary oxygen toxicity are generally reversible once the excessive oxygen exposure is stopped; the principal danger is a seizure occurring underwater leading to drowning rather than lasting toxicity itself.

E2 for degradation. Either defect raises circulating and tissue prostaglandin E2, which promotes periosteal new bone formation, soft-tissue and dermal proliferation and vascular changes. The primary disease is benign and self-limiting, typically progressing over years before stabilising, with morbidity from bone and joint pain and cosmetic skin changes rather than reduced life expectancy; recognising and excluding secondary causes is what matters most for outcome.

It is a lifelong condition without effect on life expectancy, but the painful plantar keratoderma often causes chronic disability and reduced mobility; management is supportive, focused on mechanical offloading, keratolysis, and pain control.
