Page kidney — Page phenomenon, Perinephric compression hypertension Renovascular hypertension from renal artery stenosis Essential hypertension Other secondary hypertension (phaeochromocytoma, primary aldosteronism) Renal artery or vein thrombosis after trauma Acute kidney injury of another cause after trauma or a procedure Renal malignancy causing hypertension Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease Contrast CT or MRI of the kidneys showing the compressing collection and compressed parenchyma Renal ultrasound with Doppler Plasma renin activity and aldosterone Renal function and electrolytes Blood pressure profiling or ambulatory monitoring Coagulation screen if anticoagulated or with spontaneous haematoma Isotope renography for differential function where intervention is considered Renin-mediated hypertension caused by external compression of the renal parenchyma, usually by a subcapsular or perinephric haematoma. It is named after Irvine Page, who reproduced hypertension experimentally by wrapping animal kidneys in cellophane. Common triggers include trauma (including sporting injury), renal biopsy, anticoagulation, extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy, tumour and cysts. Compression reduces intrarenal perfusion and activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system in a mechanism analogous to Goldblatt hypertension. It may present acutely after trauma or a procedure, or as unexplained or resistant hypertension months to years later. Cross-sectional imaging with CT or MRI demonstrates the compressing collection and the compressed parenchyma. Blockade of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is a rational first-line therapy, while acute or refractory cases may need drainage, evacuation or rarely nephrectomy. Small acute haematomas may resolve spontaneously with improvement in blood pressure. Severe or accelerated hypertension with end-organ damage Expanding haematoma with haemodynamic compromise Deteriorating renal function An underlying malignancy as the compressing lesion Overlooking Page kidney as a reversible cause of secondary or resistant hypertension after trauma, biopsy or lithotripsy Attributing post-procedural hypertension to essential hypertension Premature nephrectomy when drainage or medical therapy would suffice Failing to recognise a malignant compressing lesion Page kidney results from external compression of the kidney by a subcapsular or perinephric collection, most often a haematoma but sometimes a urinoma, tumour or cyst, which raises intraparenchymal pressure and compresses the renal microvasculature. The resulting reduction in renal blood flow is sensed as hypoperfusion and activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system in a manner analogous to Goldblatt one-kidney hypertension. Angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction and aldosterone-driven sodium retention produce systemic hypertension, which can persist while the compressing lesion and secondary parenchymal ischaemia and fibrosis remain. The outlook is often good, with hypertension resolving as an acute haematoma reabsorbs or after drainage or evacuation; chronic compression with established parenchymal fibrosis may cause persistent hypertension requiring long-term therapy or intervention.

Paget-Schroetter syndrome — Effort thrombosis, Primary axillosubclavian vein thrombosis Secondary upper-limb deep vein thrombosis from a central venous catheter, pacemaker or malignancy Superior vena cava obstruction Lymphoedema of the arm Cellulitis Arm oedema from cardiac failure Muscle strain or rotator cuff injury Neurogenic or arterial thoracic outlet syndrome Duplex ultrasound of the upper-limb veins Contrast venography, often as a prelude to thrombolysis CT or MR venography with provocative arm positioning Chest and thoracic outlet imaging for a cervical rib or bony anomaly Thrombophilia screen in selected patients Assessment for occult malignancy when features suggest secondary thrombosis Dynamic positional imaging to demonstrate extrinsic compression after clot clearance Primary (effort) thrombosis of the axillary-subclavian vein, representing the venous form of thoracic outlet syndrome. Typically affects young, healthy, muscular individuals after repetitive or strenuous upper-limb activity such as throwing, weightlifting or swimming, usually in the dominant arm. Presents with sudden arm swelling, heaviness, cyanotic discolouration and dilated superficial collateral veins over the shoulder and chest wall. The underlying cause is venous compression within the costoclavicular space by the first rib, the subclavius and anterior scalene muscles and the costoclavicular ligament, with repetitive endothelial trauma and thrombosis. Duplex ultrasound is first-line; contrast, CT or MR venography with the arm in provocative positions confirms extrinsic compression. Contemporary management combines early catheter-directed thrombolysis with first-rib resection and thoracic outlet decompression to address the anatomical cause. It must be distinguished from secondary upper-limb deep vein thrombosis related to central venous catheters or malignancy, which is more common overall. A thrombophilia screen may be considered in selected patients, but the primary abnormality is mechanical. Phlegmasia cerulea dolens with massive swelling, cyanosis and threatened limb viability. Signs of pulmonary embolism, which can complicate upper-limb deep vein thrombosis. Rapidly progressive swelling with neurological or arterial compromise. Features suggesting an underlying malignancy in apparent secondary thrombosis. Failure to improve or early re-thrombosis after anticoagulation. Treating with anticoagulation alone and ignoring the underlying mechanical compression, leading to recurrence and post-thrombotic morbidity. Delaying venography and thrombolysis beyond the window when the clot is still amenable. Failing to image in provocative positions and thereby missing dynamic compression once the vein is recanalised. Mislabelling effort thrombosis as a simple muscle strain in an athlete. Overlooking a cervical rib or other bony anomaly on the affected side. Repetitive hyperabduction and extension of the arm compress the subclavian vein as it passes through the narrow costoclavicular space, bounded by the first rib, clavicle, subclavius muscle, costoclavicular ligament and anterior scalene. Chronic mechanical trauma produces intimal hyperplasia, perivenous fibrosis and venous wall injury which, combined with stasis during compression, triggers thrombosis by completing Virchow's triad. The dominant arm is usually affected because of greater muscular hypertrophy and activity. Untreated, residual stenosis and fibrosis perpetuate obstruction, driving collateral formation and post-thrombotic symptoms. With prompt thrombolysis and thoracic outlet decompression most young patients regain a patent vein and return to full activity, whereas delayed or anticoagulation-only treatment leaves a significant minority with post-thrombotic arm symptoms and activity limitation.

bone-specific ALP may be raised when total ALP is normal in single-site disease Bone formation marker P1NP (reflects disease activity; can be used instead of total ALP) Bone resorption markers (serum/urine N-telopeptide or C-telopeptide) Serum calcium and phosphate (normal in Paget's disease) CT for assessment of possible fracture; MRI to assess possible sarcoma, giant cell tumor, or metastatic disease Bone biopsy for definitive diagnosis of suspected malignancy Note: serum osteocalcin is NOT always elevated and is NOT recommended for diagnosis or management Familial bone disorders that clinically and radiographically resemble Paget's disease with more severe, earlier-onset presentation: juvenile Paget's disease (familial idiopathic hyperphosphatasia, TNFRSF11B/osteoprotegerin deletion), familial expansile osteolysis, expansile skeletal hyperphosphatasia, and early-onset Paget's disease (TNFRSF11A/RANK mutations) Inclusion body myopathy with Paget's disease and frontotemporal dementia (IBMPFD; valosin-containing protein mutation) Sarcoma, giant cell tumor, or metastatic disease producing focal changes in or near pagetic bone A localized bone-remodeling disorder affecting widespread, noncontiguous areas of the skeleton; initiated by overactive osteoclastic resorption followed by compensatory osteoblastic new bone formation, producing a disorganized mosaic of woven and lamellar bone (p.3311). Most patients are asymptomatic; diagnosis is often made incidentally from an elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) on routine blood chemistry or an abnormal skeletal radiograph obtained for another indication (p.3311, p.3312-3313). Serum calcium and phosphate levels are normal in Paget's disease; isolated/raised ALP with normal calcium is the characteristic biochemical picture (p.3314). Sites most commonly involved are the pelvis, vertebral bodies, skull, femur, and tibia; familial early-onset cases often have numerous active sites (p.3313). The most common presenting symptom is pain, which may arise from increased bony vascularity, expanding lytic lesions, fractures, bowing, or deformity; long-bone bowing causes gait abnormalities and secondary osteoarthritis of hip or knee (p.3313). Skull involvement may cause headaches, frontal bossing, increased head size, and narrowing of cranial foramina leading to hearing loss (cochlear nerve damage from temporal bone involvement), cranial nerve palsies, and platybasia with risk of brainstem compression (p.3313). For most patients, serum total ALP remains the test of choice for both diagnosis and assessing response to therapy; bone resorption markers (N-telopeptide, C-telopeptide) fall more rapidly with treatment than ALP (p.3313). Radionuclide 99mTc bone scans are less specific but more sensitive than standard radiographs for identifying sites of active skeletal lesions (p.3313). New pain in a long-standing pagetic lesion - suggests sarcomatous (most often osteosarcoma) transformation, although neoplasms arising from pagetic bone are rare (<0.5%) High-output cardiac state and cardiac enlargement from extensive arteriovenous shunting when large portions (15-35%) of the skeleton are involved with high disease activity (e.g., ALP four times above normal); overt high-output heart failure is relatively rare and usually requires concomitant cardiac pathology Platybasia (softening of the skull base) with risk of brainstem compression; spinal cord compression from bone enlargement or vascular steal syndrome Fractures, typically in long bones at areas of active or advancing lytic lesions (common at femoral shaft and subtrochanteric regions) Discovery of hypercalcemia (even with immobilization) should prompt a search for another cause of hypercalcemia Assuming an isolated raised ALP is benign - it can be the only clue to asymptomatic Paget's disease and warrants workup (radiograph plus bone scan). A symptomatic patient with progression at a single site may have a normal total ALP but an increased bone-specific ALP. Using serum osteocalcin to diagnose or monitor disease - it is not always elevated and is not recommended. Attributing hypercalcemia to Paget's disease/immobilization - normal calcium and phosphate are expected, so hypercalcemia should prompt a search for another cause. Starting bisphosphonate therapy without ensuring adequate calcium and vitamin D intake first - very active bone formation with rapid resorption suppression can precipitate hypocalcemia or mild secondary hyperparathyroidism. The principal abnormality is increased number and activity of osteoclasts, which are large, increased 10- to 100-fold in number, and contain many nuclei (up to 100 vs 3-5 in normal osteoclasts), creating a sevenfold rise in resorptive surfaces. Contributing mechanisms include osteoclast precursor hypersensitivity to 1,25(OH)2D3, hyperresponsiveness to RANK ligand (RANKL), increased RANKL expression by marrow stromal cells, increased IL-6 (raising precursor recruitment), increased c-fos expression, and overexpression of the antiapoptotic oncogene Bcl-2. Osteoblasts are recruited to resorption sites and lay down large amounts of new bone matrix, so turnover is high and bone mass is normal or increased (not reduced) unless there is concomitant calcium/vitamin D deficiency. The process passes through an initial osteolytic phase (prominent resorption and hypervascularization, seen radiographically as an advancing lytic wedge or 'blade of grass' lesion), an active mixed phase replacing lamellar bone with haphazard woven bone (marrow may be replaced by fibrous tissue), and a final sclerotic ('burned-out') phase of hard, dense, less vascular mosaic bone; all three phases may coexist at different sites. Etiology remains unknown but evidence supports both genetic (family history in 15-25%; familial syndromes linked to TNFRSF11B/osteoprotegerin, TNFRSF11A/RANK, profilin 1, valosin-containing protein, and the common SQSTM1/p62 mutation) and viral (paramyxovirus-like inclusions and viral mRNA in osteoclasts) contributions (p.3311-3313). Most patients are asymptomatic and have a benign course; for unclear reasons the prevalence and severity are decreasing and the age of diagnosis is increasing. Effective potent antiresorptive (bisphosphonate) therapy can normalize bone turnover and is associated with an apparently decreasing incidence of sarcoma. Serious complications - fractures, deformity, secondary osteoarthritis, neurologic compromise (hearing loss, cranial nerve palsies, cord/brainstem compression), high-output cardiac state, and rare (<0.5%) malignant transformation (usually osteosarcoma) - drive morbidity. Whether early therapy prevents late complications remains to be determined; deformities may take many years to manifest (p.3312-3314). Harrison does not give a formal staging system. Disease activity is gauged by the extent of skeletal involvement and the degree of bone-turnover marker elevation (notably total ALP, with ALP roughly four times above normal cited as marking high activity and cardiovascular risk when 15-35% of the skeleton is involved). Pathologically the disease evolves through three phases that may coexist: an osteolytic phase, an active mixed (woven-bone) phase, and a final sclerotic 'burned-out' phase (p.3313-3314).

pagets disease of bone — osteitis deformans, Paget disease of bone osteoblastic metastases (prostate or breast) primary bone tumour including osteosarcoma fibrous dysplasia osteomalacia or hyperparathyroidism multiple myeloma sclerosing bone dysplasias total and bone-specific alkaline phosphatase serum calcium, phosphate and liver function tests plain radiographs of affected regions radionuclide bone scan to define extent CT or MRI if malignancy or nerve compression is suspected 25-hydroxyvitamin D (corrected before intravenous bisphosphonate) audiometry where the skull is involved Paget's disease is a focal disorder of accelerated, disorganised bone remodelling, with greatly increased osteoclastic resorption followed by disordered osteoblastic new bone that is expanded but structurally weak. It is frequently asymptomatic and found incidentally through a raised alkaline phosphatase or an abnormal radiograph, most often affecting the pelvis, femur, spine, skull and tibia. Symptoms include bone pain, deformity (bowing, skull enlargement, increasing hat size), pathological fracture, secondary osteoarthritis and warmth over affected bone. Biochemistry typically shows a markedly raised total and bone-specific alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium and phosphate and normal other liver enzymes. Radiographs show cortical thickening, coarse trabeculation, mixed lytic and sclerotic areas (osteoporosis circumscripta in the skull) and bone expansion; an isotope bone scan best defines disease extent. Complications include deafness from otic capsule involvement, cranial nerve compression, spinal stenosis, rarely high-output cardiac failure in extensive disease, and osteosarcoma. Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates, typically a single potent intravenous infusion, are the mainstay and produce prolonged biochemical remission. Treatment is directed at symptoms, complications or planned surgery at an affected site, and response is monitored using alkaline phosphatase. new severe or unremitting pain or a soft-tissue mass suggesting sarcomatous transformation pathological fracture neurological deficit from cord or nerve compression rapidly progressive deformity high-output cardiac failure in extensive disease attributing an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase to liver disease missing sarcomatous change when the character of pain alters failing to correct vitamin D deficiency before intravenous bisphosphonate, risking hypocalcaemia over-treating asymptomatic disease without complications confusing sclerotic Paget's disease with osteoblastic metastases The primary abnormality is a marked increase in the number, size and activity of osteoclasts, which show characteristic nuclear inclusions; genetic factors (notably SQSTM1 mutations) and possible environmental triggers contribute. Intense focal resorption is followed by exuberant but disorganised osteoblastic new bone formation, producing a chaotic mosaic of woven and lamellar bone that is hypervascular, enlarged and mechanically weak. This accounts for deformity, fracture, high blood flow with local warmth, and the greatly elevated bone-turnover markers. Disease usually remains confined to the initially affected sites rather than spreading to new bones. Prognosis is generally good, with bisphosphonates giving durable biochemical remission and symptom control; sarcomatous transformation is rare (under one per cent) but carries a poor outcome.

post-traumatic bleeding Heavy menstrual bleeding causing anaemia Bleeding disproportionate to a normal routine coagulation screen Dismissing a bleeding history because routine coagulation tests are normal Failing to request specific PAI-1 activity testing Confusing it with alpha-2-antiplasmin or factor XIII deficiency Not providing antifibrinolytic cover for surgery or menorrhagia Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1, encoded by SERPINE1, is the primary serpin that restrains tissue-type and urokinase-type plasminogen activators, thereby limiting plasmin generation and fibrinolysis. In its deficiency, plasminogen activation proceeds unchecked, so fibrin clots are lysed prematurely and haemostatic plugs are not maintained. Because clot formation itself is normal, bleeding is characteristically delayed and follows a haemostatic challenge. The phenotype is generally milder and more provocation-dependent than in classic coagulation factor deficiencies. The disorder is usually mild and provocation-dependent, and antifibrinolytic cover around haemostatic challenges generally gives excellent outcomes. Serious bleeding is uncommon in the absence of significant trauma or surgery.

Painful legs and moving toes syndrome — painful legs moving toes, PLMT Restless legs syndrome Peripheral neuropathy with neuropathic pain Complex regional pain syndrome Dystonia or myoclonus of the foot Functional movement disorder Clinical diagnosis from the combination of leg pain and continuous toe movements Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to identify peripheral nerve or root injury Imaging of the lumbosacral spine or plexus where a lesion is suspected Assessment of neuropathic pain features Exclusion of restless legs syndrome by history A syndrome of deep, poorly localised pain in the leg accompanied by continuous involuntary writhing or flexion-extension movements of the toes or foot The pain usually dominates the clinical picture and the movements may be only partially suppressible It often follows injury to peripheral nerves, roots or the cauda equina, though many cases are idiopathic An analogous painful arms and moving fingers variant is recognised in the upper limb The movements persist during rest and may reduce but not always disappear in sleep It is frequently refractory, and management focuses on neuropathic pain control with variable success Progressive weakness or sensory loss suggesting an evolving lesion New cauda equina or radicular signs Severe intractable pain Rapidly progressive or asymmetric neurological features Confusing it with restless legs syndrome, which has an urge to move relieved by movement Overlooking a treatable peripheral nerve or root lesion Focusing on the movements rather than the dominant pain Expecting complete resolution and under-supporting the patient Painful legs and moving toes syndrome is thought to result from aberrant reorganisation of sensory input after peripheral nerve, root or plexus injury, generating abnormal central processing that produces both neuropathic pain and disordered motor output to the toes. The exact generator is uncertain and may involve spinal and supraspinal reorganisation, which is why the movements can be difficult to localise or suppress. In idiopathic cases no antecedent lesion is identified despite a similar clinical picture. The syndrome tends to be chronic and often treatment-resistant, with the pain being the most disabling component; some patients gain partial relief from neuropathic pain treatments.

indicating a destructive arthropathy Systemic features (rash, serositis, cytopenias) pointing to lupus or another connective tissue disease Fever with monoarthritis where septic or crystal arthritis must be excluded Dismissing the diagnosis because examination and imaging are normal between attacks Failing to check autoantibodies and therefore missing patients at high risk of progression to rheumatoid arthritis Confusing recurrent attacks with gout without joint aspiration or urate measurement Delaying DMARD consideration in seropositive patients with frequent flares Palindromic rheumatism is an episodic inflammatory arthropathy in which transient synovial and periarticular inflammation produces recurrent short-lived attacks without cumulative joint destruction. It is widely regarded as an abortive or early form of rheumatoid arthritis, and autoantibodies such as rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are frequently present, reflecting shared autoimmune mechanisms. During attacks there is neutrophil-rich synovial inflammation that resolves without pannus formation or erosion, but persistent autoimmunity in seropositive individuals can eventually give way to sustained synovitis and conversion to established rheumatoid arthritis or, less often, other connective tissue disease. Between attacks patients are usually asymptomatic with no lasting joint damage, but a substantial proportion, especially those with positive autoantibodies, progress to rheumatoid arthritis or another chronic inflammatory disease over time.

insufficiency Airway compromise from laryngeal anomalies Imperforate anus requiring surgical management Missing neonatal hypopituitarism and adrenal insufficiency, which can be fatal Attempting resection of a hypothalamic hamartoma without recognising its benign, malformative nature Overlooking a bifid epiglottis on airway assessment Confusing it with Greig cephalopolysyndactyly despite the shared GLI3 basis Pallister-Hall syndrome results from heterozygous truncating variants in GLI3, typically in the middle third of the gene, that generate a shortened protein biased towards its transcriptional repressor form. GLI3 is the principal transcriptional effector of hedgehog signalling, a pathway that is assembled and processed on the primary cilium, so the disorder is intimately linked to ciliary biology. During development the resulting imbalance of hedgehog output disturbs patterning of the hypothalamus, limbs, larynx and hindgut, producing the hypothalamic hamartoma, central or postaxial polydactyly, bifid epiglottis and anorectal and renal anomalies. The contrasting effect of GLI3 loss-of-function variants elsewhere in the gene explains why Greig cephalopolysyndactyly is allelic yet clinically distinct. With recognition and management of endocrine and airway problems the outlook is generally good and intellect is usually normal; the hypothalamic hamartoma is benign and malformative, though associated seizures can be difficult to control.

diaphragmatic hernia Undiagnosed congenital heart disease causing cardiorespiratory compromise Refractory seizures Severe feeding difficulty with aspiration and failure to thrive Excluding the diagnosis on a normal blood karyotype because the isochromosome is lost from lymphocytes Failing to test fibroblasts or buccal cells, the tissues most likely to reveal the mosaic Attributing the pigmentary changes to an unrelated skin disorder Underestimating the risk of associated diaphragmatic hernia and cardiac anomalies Pallister-Killian syndrome results from mosaic tetrasomy 12p, most often due to a supernumerary isochromosome composed of two copies of the short arm of chromosome 12, giving four copies of 12p in affected cells. The extra genetic material causes an imbalance of dosage-sensitive genes during development. Because the isochromosome is unstable and tends to be lost from rapidly dividing tissues such as blood, the mosaicism is often confined to fibroblasts and other tissues, which accounts for the diagnostic difficulty and the tissue-dependent detection. Outcome is variable and correlates with the tissue distribution of the mosaicism; many affected children have profound intellectual disability and significant medical needs, and severe cases with diaphragmatic hernia have high early mortality. Those surviving infancy generally live into childhood or beyond with major disability.

Impaired chromatin remodelling disturbs keratinocyte proliferation, differentiation and genomic stability, producing the diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma and the scleroatrophic changes of the distal limbs with nail hypoplasia. The same disturbance predisposes the affected skin to malignant transformation, accounting for the characteristically early and aggressive squamous cell carcinomas that dominate the prognosis. Skin and nail changes are chronic but stable; prognosis is dominated by the lifelong risk of aggressive squamous cell carcinoma, which can metastasise and be fatal, making early detection through surveillance essential.

Underestimating the functional disability and its psychosocial impact Palmoplantar pustulosis is an inflammatory disorder centred on the acrosyringium, the intra-epidermal portion of the sweat duct, of palmar and plantar skin, where accumulation of neutrophils forms the characteristic sterile pustules. It is thought to represent an autoinflammatory process with prominent innate immune involvement, including neutrophils and the interleukin-17 and interleukin-36 pathways. Nicotine and its effects on acrosyringeal sweat glands and immune signalling are strongly implicated, which fits the striking association with smoking, and the frequent overlap with psoriasis suggests shared inflammatory mechanisms. Chronic and relapsing over years and often refractory to treatment; smoking cessation and appropriate therapy improve control, but complete and lasting clearance is difficult to achieve.

Panayiotopoulos syndrome — Early-onset benign childhood occipital epilepsy, Self-limited epilepsy with autonomic seizures Gastroenteritis or cyclical vomiting syndrome Migraine and its variants Syncope Encephalitis, considered during prolonged autonomic status Late-onset (Gastaut) occipital epilepsy Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes Structural or symptomatic occipital epilepsy EEG including a sleep recording MRI brain if features are atypical or the examination is abnormal Blood glucose and basic metabolic screen during an acute event ECG to exclude cardiac syncope or arrhythmia Lumbar puncture if encephalitis is suspected during prolonged status Developmental assessment A common self-limited focal epilepsy of early childhood dominated by autonomic seizures, especially emesis. Onset is typically 3 to 6 years; seizures are infrequent but often prolonged, amounting to autonomic status epilepticus. A typical event comprises nausea, retching and vomiting with pallor, eye deviation and impaired responsiveness, frequently arising from sleep and sometimes progressing to a hemiconvulsion or generalised convulsion. Additional autonomic features include pupillary changes, incontinence, hypersalivation and cyanosis. Interictal EEG classically shows multifocal, shifting spikes, often occipital, but the distribution is variable and the EEG may be normal. Neurological examination, development and neuroimaging are normal. Because seizures are infrequent, long-term daily medication is often unnecessary and a rescue plan for prolonged seizures is central to management. Prognosis is excellent, with spontaneous remission within a year or two of onset. Autonomic status epilepticus with a seizure lasting beyond thirty minutes Focal neurological deficit or abnormal development An atypical or fixed occipital lesion on imaging Recurrent seizures deviating from the expected benign course Misdiagnosing prolonged autonomic seizures as encephalitis, gastroenteritis or syncope. Over-treating an essentially benign, infrequent-seizure condition with long-term medication. Failing to provide a rescue plan for prolonged seizures. Confusing it with late-onset (Gastaut) occipital epilepsy, which causes visual seizures and follows a different course. Panayiotopoulos syndrome is regarded as a benign, maturation-dependent focal epilepsy reflecting a diffuse, age-related cortical hyperexcitability with a predilection for autonomic networks. The prominent emetic and autonomic features are attributed to epileptic activation of central autonomic networks, particularly insular and anterior regions, while the shifting, often posterior EEG foci indicate widespread rather than fixed epileptogenicity that resolves with brain maturation. Excellent: the disorder is self-limited with remission usually within one to two years of onset and normal long-term cognitive and neurological outcome, although a minority later develop other seizure types.

rather than a simple anatomical variant Unexplained weight loss or steatorrhoea Assuming the anomaly is the cause of abdominal pain when it is merely an incidental and common finding Proceeding to endoscopic intervention without objective evidence of recurrent pancreatitis Overlooking coexisting genetic, metabolic, or biliary causes of recurrent pancreatitis Underestimating the procedural risk of post-ERCP pancreatitis when intervening on the minor papilla Pancreas divisum results from failure of the embryonic dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts to fuse, so that the bulk of exocrine secretion from the dorsal anlage drains through the accessory (Santorini) duct and the minor papilla, while only the small ventral segment drains through the main (Wirsung) duct and the major papilla. The proposed mechanism for symptoms is relative outflow obstruction: the minor papilla may be too small to accommodate the secretory volume of the dorsal duct, producing raised intraductal pressure, ductal distension, and recurrent pancreatitis in a susceptible minority. Because most individuals with this anatomy never develop symptoms, additional factors such as minor papilla stenosis or genetic susceptibility are thought necessary for clinical disease. As an isolated anatomical variant the outlook is excellent and no treatment is required; in the minority with recurrent pancreatitis, endoscopic therapy of the minor papilla helps some patients but responses are inconsistent, and a subset progress to chronic pancreatitis.

Pancreatic Cancer — pancreatic adenocarcinoma Chronic pancreatitis Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor Acinar cell carcinoma Colloid carcinoma Medullary carcinoma Adenosquamous carcinoma Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) Mucinous cystic neoplasm Metastasis to the pancreas (renal, breast, lung, urothelial carcinoma, melanoma, lymphoma) Dual-phase contrast-enhanced CT using a pancreas-cancer protocol (arterial and portal venous phases) to assess tumor-vessel relationships, resectability, and staging Abdominal ultrasonography (often first imaging in the jaundiced patient) MRI 18F-glucose PET to detect occult metastatic disease Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) with EUS-guided core needle biopsy of pancreatic lesions Tru-Cut core needle biopsy (preferred over fine-needle aspiration) for histologic diagnosis; percutaneous biopsy for liver/lymph node lesions Next-generation sequencing for genomic alterations (including KRAS) and microsatellite status Serum CA19-9 (drawn after bilirubin normalizes), CEA, and CA125 Staging laparoscopy (selectively, before or at definitive surgery) Chronic pancreatitis (can be difficult to distinguish from adenocarcinoma and is itself a risk factor) Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor Mucinous cystic neoplasm and IPMN Metastatic disease to the pancreas from other primaries The classic presentation of cancer arising in the head of the pancreas is 'painless' jaundice; jaundice is visually detectable once bilirubin exceeds ~2 mg/dL and may be accompanied by pruritus from bile salt skin deposition (p.672). Pain, when present, is typically mid-epigastric and 'boring' with radiation to the back (from retroperitoneal invasion of the splanchnic nerve plexus) and may be worsened by eating or lying flat (p.672). A palpable, non-tender gallbladder in the setting of biliary obstruction is Courvoisier's sign (p.672). Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis and combined deep venous plus arterial thromboses (Trousseau's syndrome) can occur; metastatic disease is frequently associated with a hypercoagulable state requiring anticoagulation (p.672-674). New-onset diabetes (especially with concomitant weight loss) or unexplained worsening of type 2/type 3c diabetes, or rising HbA1c/hyperglycemia in the preceding 1-2 years, may signal underlying pancreatic cancer (p.671-672). CA19-9 is best drawn after the bilirubin has normalized because biliary obstruction itself elevates CA19-9; CA125 can help in the 8-15% of Lewis-antigen non-secretors who have undetectable CA19-9 (p.674). Cigarette smoking is the greatest environmental risk factor, accounting for an estimated 25-30% of cases, with risk persisting at least 10 years after cessation (p.671). Histologic/cytologic tissue diagnosis is essential and also enables molecular testing (next-generation sequencing for KRAS and other alterations) and microsatellite status determination, which increasingly guide therapy (p.674). Signs of late-stage disease include a left supraclavicular Virchow's node and a periumbilical Sister Mary Joseph's nodule indicating peritoneal metastases (p.672-673). Painless obstructive jaundice (classic for head-of-pancreas tumor) Palpable non-tender gallbladder with obstruction (Courvoisier's sign) Unintentional weight loss with loss of muscle mass New-onset diabetes, especially with concomitant weight loss Mid-epigastric boring pain radiating to the back Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis / venous or arterial thrombosis (Trousseau's syndrome) Left supraclavicular Virchow's node or periumbilical Sister Mary Joseph's nodule (late disease) Light/clay-colored stools and steatorrhea Drawing CA19-9 while bilirubin is elevated falsely raises the level, since biliary obstruction itself elevates CA19-9 (p.674). 8-15% of patients are Lewis-antigen non-secretors with undetectable CA19-9, so a normal CA19-9 does not exclude disease; CA125 may help in this group (p.674). Even high-grade PanIN precursor lesions are not detectable by current imaging, limiting early detection (p.672). For average-risk individuals with no predisposing factors there is currently no recommended screening (p.671). Whether diabetes causes or is caused by pancreatic cancer is not clearly established (p.671). Fine-needle aspiration cytology is acceptable but less preferred than core (Tru-Cut) biopsy, which yields adequate tissue for molecular testing (p.674). Biliary stenting is not necessarily warranted if upfront surgery is planned, but is required (where medically indicated) before neoadjuvant systemic therapy (p.674). Ductal adenocarcinoma is the most common and most lethal exocrine pancreatic neoplasm, characterized by infiltrating desmoplastic stromal reaction and arising in the head, body, or tail. Most cancers arise from pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN, graded 1-3 in a progression model), with genetic alterations accumulating as PanIN grade increases; some arise from noninvasive cystic precursors (e.g., IPMN). The mutational landscape is dominated by four commonly altered genes: KRAS (mutated in 90-95%, primarily codon 12), p16/CDKN2A (inactivated in >90% of invasive tumors), TP53 (~75%), and DPC4/SMAD4 (~50%); BRCA2 is mutated in 3.5-10%. A 'KRAS wildtype' subset (more common in patients under 55) may harbor actionable BRAF mutations, oncogenic fusions (NRG-1, NTRK1-3), or microsatellite instability (p.672). Pancreatic cancer is the most lethal human cancer, with an overall 5-year survival of about 13% (up from 3% in 1975). SEER estimates 5-year survival of ~44% for localized disease, ~16% for regional disease, and ~3.2% for metastatic disease. Late presentation is common, only about 10-20% of tumors are resectable, and the disease is the third leading cause of cancer mortality in the U.S. and projected to become the second by 2030 (p.671-672). Staged by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system. Clinically also categorized by extent of disease and therapeutic approach: resectable (~10-20%), borderline resectable/locally advanced, and metastatic (p.674).

Pancreatic panniculitis — enzymatic panniculitis, pancreatic fat necrosis, subcutaneous fat necrosis of pancreatic disease Erythema nodosum Erythema induratum / nodular vasculitis Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency panniculitis Infective panniculitis Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa Subcutaneous fat necrosis of other cause Deep incisional biopsy of a fresh nodule including subcutaneous fat Serum lipase and amylase Cross-sectional pancreatic imaging (CT or MRI) to identify pancreatitis or tumour Full blood count for peripheral eosinophilia Tumour markers and further evaluation if pancreatic carcinoma is suspected Serum calcium and inflammatory markers Presents as tender, erythematous to violaceous subcutaneous nodules, classically on the lower legs but also thighs, buttocks and trunk Nodules may soften, ulcerate and discharge an oily brown viscous material as liquefied fat is released It signals underlying pancreatic disease, most often acute or chronic pancreatitis but also pancreatic carcinoma (especially acinar cell type) Skin lesions can precede recognition of the pancreatic disorder, so unexplained leg nodules warrant pancreatic evaluation The triad of panniculitis, polyarthritis and eosinophilia (PPP syndrome) carries a worse prognosis Biopsy shows a lobular panniculitis with pathognomonic anucleate 'ghost' adipocytes and basophilic saponification of fat by calcium salts Treatment is directed at the underlying pancreatic disease; the skin improves as the pancreatic process is controlled Panniculitis with polyarthritis and eosinophilia (PPP syndrome), which is associated with high mortality Nodules arising without an obvious cause, raising suspicion of occult pancreatic carcinoma Features of severe acute pancreatitis with systemic compromise Extensive ulceration with secondary infection Dismissing recurrent leg nodules as ordinary erythema nodosum and missing the pancreatic cause Failing to search for an occult pancreatic tumour when pancreatitis is absent Sampling too superficially to demonstrate the diagnostic saponified ghost adipocytes Overlooking accompanying arthritis and eosinophilia that portend a worse course Pancreatic panniculitis results from release of pancreatic enzymes, principally lipase, amylase and trypsin, into the circulation during pancreatic inflammation or from an enzyme-secreting tumour. These enzymes reach the subcutaneous fat and hydrolyse triglycerides, liberating free fatty acids that combine with calcium to form insoluble soaps (saponification). This enzymatic fat necrosis destroys adipocytes, leaving characteristic anucleate ghost cells with thick shadowy walls and basophilic granular calcium deposits, surrounded by a mixed inflammatory infiltrate within the fat lobules. Outcome depends heavily on the underlying pancreatic disease: lesions accompanying self-limiting pancreatitis resolve as the pancreas recovers, whereas panniculitis linked to pancreatic carcinoma or the PPP syndrome carries a poor prognosis. Skin nodules often heal with atrophic hyperpigmented scars.

pancreatic head mass Rapid weight loss or a rapidly enlarging mass Hepatic or nodal metastases at presentation High-grade histology with an elevated Ki-67 index Features suggesting MEN1 Interpreting a raised pancreatic polypeptide as diagnostic when it is non-specific and rises in other conditions Mistaking the tumour for pancreatic adenocarcinoma and withholding appropriate neuroendocrine-directed therapy Assuming non-functioning implies benign, thereby underestimating malignant potential Omitting Ki-67 grading, which is central to prognosis and treatment selection Failing to consider MEN1 in younger patients or those with other endocrine tumours Pancreatic polypeptidoma is a well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour arising from pancreatic polypeptide (F) cells, which are concentrated in the head and uncinate process. Although the tumour oversecretes pancreatic polypeptide, this hormone does not generate a recognisable clinical syndrome, so the tumour is grouped clinically with non-functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours and typically declares itself through local growth or metastasis rather than a hormonal effect. Elevated circulating pancreatic polypeptide therefore serves chiefly as a biochemical marker. As with other pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, tumorigenesis may be sporadic or occur within MEN1 through loss of menin, and behaviour is graded by proliferative activity. Prognosis depends on tumour grade and stage: localised, well-differentiated tumours resected completely have a favourable outlook, whereas high-grade or metastatic disease carries a worse prognosis, though often a more indolent course than pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

Pancreatic pseudocyst — pseudocyst of the pancreas, pancreatic fluid collection, post-pancreatitis pseudocyst Cystic pancreatic neoplasm (serous or mucinous cystadenoma, intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm) Acute peripancreatic fluid collection or walled-off necrosis Pancreatic abscess Mesenteric or omental cyst Duplication cyst or choledochal cyst Pancreatic pseudoaneurysm Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen to characterise the collection and its wall Endoscopic ultrasound with fluid aspiration for amylase, CEA, and cytology to exclude a neoplasm Serum amylase and lipase and liver function tests MRCP or ERP to assess pancreatic ductal anatomy and communication before drainage Ultrasound for follow-up of size in conservatively managed cysts A pancreatic pseudocyst is a persistent, encapsulated collection of pancreatic fluid that develops weeks after acute or chronic pancreatitis, or after pancreatic trauma Unlike a true cyst it lacks an epithelial lining and is bounded by a wall of fibrous and granulation tissue, requiring around four weeks to mature Common presentations include persistent or recurrent upper abdominal pain, a palpable epigastric mass, early satiety, nausea, and failure to recover after an episode of pancreatitis A raised serum amylase and high amylase within aspirated fluid support the diagnosis and help distinguish it from a cystic neoplasm Contrast CT and endoscopic ultrasound define the collection, its relation to the stomach and duodenum, and any ductal communication Many small, asymptomatic pseudocysts resolve spontaneously and can be observed, whereas large, symptomatic, enlarging, or complicated collections need drainage Drainage is increasingly endoscopic (transmural cystgastrostomy or cystduodenostomy), with surgical internal drainage or percutaneous approaches reserved for selected cases In older patients or those without a clear pancreatitis history, a cystic pancreatic neoplasm must be excluded before assuming a pseudocyst Sudden severe pain, expanding mass, or gastrointestinal bleeding suggesting pseudoaneurysm erosion or rupture Fever, rigors, and systemic sepsis indicating an infected pseudocyst Progressive gastric outlet or biliary obstruction from a large cyst Rapid clinical deterioration suggesting free rupture into the peritoneal cavity Mistaking a cystic pancreatic neoplasm for a pseudocyst and draining rather than resecting it Draining a collection before the wall has matured, increasing the risk of leakage and failure Overlooking an associated pseudoaneurysm, so that drainage precipitates torrential bleeding Ignoring underlying pancreatic ductal obstruction, leading to recurrence after drainage Delaying treatment of an infected pseudocyst presenting with sepsis Pancreatic pseudocysts arise when pancreatic ductal disruption, from acute inflammation, chronic pancreatitis, or trauma, allows enzyme-rich secretions to leak and collect in or around the pancreas. The surrounding tissue reacts, and over several weeks an inflammatory capsule of fibrous and granulation tissue forms, producing a mature pseudocyst without a true epithelial lining. Persistent communication with the pancreatic duct maintains the collection. Enlargement can compress adjacent structures, and complications develop when the cyst becomes infected, erodes into a vessel to form a pseudoaneurysm or bleed, or ruptures into the peritoneum or an adjacent viscus. Small uncomplicated pseudocysts frequently resolve without intervention, and drainage of symptomatic collections has good outcomes. Prognosis worsens with complications such as haemorrhage from a pseudoaneurysm, infection, or rupture, and recurrence is more likely when underlying ductal disease or chronic pancreatitis is not addressed.

ALT - ALT >3x ULN supports gallstone aetiology (Harrison 22e p.2745) Serum triglycerides - to detect hypertriglyceridaemic cause (levels usually >1000 mg/dL) (Harrison 22e p.2744, p.2748) Serum calcium - to detect hypercalcaemic cause and to monitor for hypocalcaemia (~25% of patients) (Harrison 22e p.2744-2745) Hematocrit - hemoconcentration >44% is a severity marker (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746) Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) at admission and 48 h - rising BUN predicts mortality (Harrison 22e p.2745, p.2748) White cell count - leukocytosis 15,000-20,000/uL is common (Harrison 22e p.2745) MRI/MRCP - more sensitive than CT for mild pancreatitis, necrosis, choledocholithiasis and ductal abnormalities (Harrison 22e p.2739) EUS - useful for occult microlithiasis/biliary cause and choledocholithiasis; best performed ~4 weeks after resolution to find predisposing lesions (Harrison 22e p.2741) Contrast-enhanced CT - to assess necrosis and local complications when not improving, ideally at 3-5 days (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746) C-reactive protein - severity marker during hospitalization (thresholds >100 mg/L reported) (Harrison 22e p.2748) Diabetic ketoacidosis - abdominal pain with raised TOTAL amylase mimics pancreatitis, but lipase is often NOT elevated and pancreatic imaging is normal (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746) Perforated peptic ulcer - can raise serum/ascitic amylase (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745) Acute cholecystitis / biliary colic - amylase may be raised; pain is more right-sided/epigastric and ileus is usually absent (Harrison 22e p.2745) Mesenteric ischemia/infarction - can raise ascitic-fluid amylase (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745) Intestinal obstruction - can raise ascitic-fluid amylase; differentiated by crescendo-decrescendo pain and obstruction pattern on CT (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745) Diagnosis requires 2 of 3: typical epigastric pain radiating to the back, serum lipase/amylase >=3x ULN, or characteristic findings on cross-sectional imaging (Harrison 22e p.2745). Lipase is more pancreas-specific than amylase and is the single best enzyme to measure; it stays elevated longer (7-14 days) whereas amylase often normalises by 3-7 days (Harrison 22e p.2740, p.2745). Gallstones and alcohol together account for ~80-90% of cases; gallstones are the single most common cause (30-60%), alcohol the second (15-30%) (Harrison 22e p.2744). ALT >3x ULN strongly points to a gallstone aetiology in acute pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2745). Abdominal ultrasound is the recommended initial imaging study, chiefly to assess for gallstones and bile-duct dilation; contrast CT is best deferred to ~3-5 days if the patient is not improving and is usually not needed in the first 48-72 h (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746). Persistent organ failure (>48 h) is the most important determinant of severity; if SIRS has resolved by 24 h, organ failure or necrosis is unlikely to develop (Harrison 22e p.2746, p.2748). Hemoconcentration (hematocrit >44%) and a rising BUN are early warning signs of more severe disease and higher mortality (Harrison 22e p.2745-2748). Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising) and Grey Turner's sign (flank discoloration) are rare but signal severe necrotizing/hemorrhagic disease (Harrison 22e p.2745). Persistent organ failure >48 h (respiratory, cardiovascular or renal) - hallmark of severe disease (Harrison 22e p.2746) Modified Marshall organ-failure signs: systolic BP <90 mmHg, HR >130/min, PaO2 <60 mmHg, or creatinine >2.0 mg/dL (Harrison 22e p.2748) BISAP score >=3 - increased in-hospital mortality (Harrison 22e p.2748) APACHE II >=8 at 24 h (Harrison 22e p.2748) Hemoconcentration (hematocrit >44%) and rising/admission BUN - predict severe disease and mortality (Harrison 22e p.2745-2748) Persistent SIRS at 24 h - predisposes to organ failure and necrosis (Harrison 22e p.2746, p.2748) Pancreatic necrosis on CT - greatest mortality risk (3-10% with single-organ failure, ~50% with multiorgan failure) (Harrison 22e p.2747) Hypoxemia (PaO2 <=60 mmHg) - may herald ARDS (Harrison 22e p.2745) Cullen's sign / Grey Turner's sign - severe necrotizing/hemorrhagic pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2745) Ascending cholangitis (sepsis + biliary obstruction) complicating gallstone pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2748) Enzyme magnitude does NOT track severity - degree or serial trend of lipase/amylase does not correlate with how severe the pancreatitis is (Harrison 22e p.2745). Serum amylase can be falsely normal or low in hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis, masking the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745). Amylase is non-specific - raised in salivary, tubo-ovarian, pulmonary, malignant and other conditions, and spuriously high in acidemia/DKA (arterial pH <=7.32) without true pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2740, p.2745). Lipase can be mildly elevated in renal failure, and >3x ULN can occur in hepatobiliary/GI malignancy, sepsis, cirrhosis, SLE, head injury, chronic alcoholism, diabetes and post-ERCP without pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2740). Routine/early CT (within 72 h) is overused and usually unnecessary, especially in mild disease; necrosis may not be visible until several days in (Harrison 22e p.2746-2747). Prophylactic antibiotics are NOT recommended, even in severe or necrotizing pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2746, p.2749). Enzyme levels may be normal if blood is drawn 2-5 days after onset or if the underlying problem is chronic rather than acute pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2740). Acute pancreatitis is thought to begin with autodigestion: intracellular premature activation of trypsin (via lysosomal cathepsin B colocalising with digestive zymogens) within acinar cells, which then activates other proteolytic and lipolytic enzymes (chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, phospholipase A2). A second phase recruits and sequesters leukocytes/macrophages, amplifying intrapancreatic inflammation, and a third phase results from activated enzymes and cytokines acting on distant organs, producing edema, hemorrhage, vascular damage, fat necrosis and coagulation/cellular necrosis. Release of bradykinin, vasoactive substances and histamine drives vasodilation, increased vascular permeability and edema, and can culminate in SIRS, ARDS and multiorgan failure. Pathologically the spectrum runs from interstitial (perfusion preserved, self-limited) to necrotizing pancreatitis (perfusion interrupted). Genetic susceptibility/modifier variants include PRSS1 (cationic trypsinogen), SPINK1, CFTR, CTRC, CASR and CLDN2, all converging on control of intrapancreatic trypsin activity (Harrison 22e p.2744-2745). Overall mortality is low (~1%) and median hospital stay ~4 days; most cases are mild and self-limited within 3-7 days. Interstitial pancreatitis (90-95% of admissions) carries low mortality, whereas necrotizing pancreatitis (5-10%) drives most deaths. In necrotizing disease the median prevalence of organ failure exceeds 50% (slightly higher with infected vs sterile necrosis); mortality is 3-10% with single-organ failure but approaches 50% with multiorgan failure. Patients with only extrapancreatic necrosis fare better than those with pancreatic parenchymal necrosis. About 25% of patients have a recurrence, most commonly from alcohol or gallstones (Harrison 22e p.2747, p.2749). Revised Atlanta classification (Banks et al., Gut 2013). PHASES: early (<2 weeks; severity judged clinically, not by morphology) and late (>2 weeks; imaging for local complications). SEVERITY: (1) Mild - no local complications and no organ failure (most interstitial cases; self-limited 3-7 days); (2) Moderately severe - transient organ failure (resolves <48 h) and/or local or systemic complications without persistent organ failure; (3) Severe - persistent organ failure >48 h in >=1 organ system (respiratory, cardiovascular, renal; defined by modified Marshall score >=2). MORPHOLOGY: two types - interstitial (parenchymal enhancement, no necrosis) vs necrotizing (lack of parenchymal enhancement and/or peripancreatic necrosis); local collections - acute pancreatic fluid collection and pseudocyst (interstitial, pseudocyst usually >4 wk) vs acute necrotic collection (ANC) and walled-off necrosis (WON, usually >4 wk, encapsulated). SEVERITY SCORES/MARKERS: BISAP >=3 (BUN >25 mg/dL, Impaired mental status/GCS<15, SIRS >=2/4, Age >60, Pleural effusion); APACHE II >=8 at 24 h; SIRS >=2 of 4 (temp <36 or >38C, HR >90, RR >20 or PCO2 <32, WCC >12,000 or <4000 or >10% bands); hematocrit >44%; admission BUN >20 mg/dL; persistent organ failure >=48 h, and pancreatic/extrapancreatic necrosis as in-hospital markers. Ranson criteria are a traditional severity index (referenced contextually).

pancreatoblastoma — pancreatic blastoma, infantile pancreatic carcinoma Neuroblastoma (adrenal or retroperitoneal) Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas Acinar cell carcinoma Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour Wilms tumour or other retroperitoneal mass Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the pancreas Pancreatic metastasis of another paediatric tumour Serum alpha-fetoprotein at baseline and serially Abdominal ultrasound followed by contrast-enhanced CT or MRI for local extent and vascular involvement CT of the chest for pulmonary metastases Core or open biopsy for histological confirmation when upfront resection is not planned Testing for Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis where clinically indicated Assessment of exocrine and endocrine pancreatic function Baseline audiometry and renal function before platinum-based chemotherapy The commonest pancreatic neoplasm of childhood, typically presenting in the first decade as a large, often palpable upper abdominal mass. Histologically defined by acinar differentiation with distinctive squamoid nests (squamoid corpuscles), and it may also show endocrine and ductal elements. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is elevated in a substantial proportion and is a useful marker for monitoring response and relapse. Associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, in which it may be congenital, and with familial adenomatous polyposis through the APC/Wnt-beta-catenin pathway. Abnormalities of chromosome 11p15 and activation of Wnt/beta-catenin signalling are the principal molecular drivers. Complete surgical resection is the mainstay of cure, and neoadjuvant chemotherapy can downstage large or initially unresectable tumours. Symptoms are frequently nonspecific (mass, abdominal pain, weight loss), and obstructive jaundice is less common than in adult pancreatic cancer. Metastases occur most often to the liver, regional lymph nodes, and lungs. Obstructive jaundice or duodenal obstruction from a pancreatic head mass Rapid abdominal distension or pain suggesting haemorrhage into the tumour Rising alpha-fetoprotein after resection, indicating recurrence Features of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome prompting tumour surveillance Mistaking pancreatoblastoma for the commoner neuroblastoma or for a solid pseudopapillary neoplasm without adequate histology. Proceeding to a mutilating upfront resection when neoadjuvant chemotherapy could render a large tumour resectable with less morbidity. Overlooking an underlying Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis. Interpreting alpha-fetoprotein without accounting for the high physiological levels of infancy. Pancreatoblastoma arises from pluripotent pancreatic precursor cells and recapitulates the embryonic pancreas, characteristically showing acinar differentiation together with squamoid nests (corpuscles) and variable endocrine and ductal components. The dominant molecular alteration is activation of the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway, with frequent involvement of the APC/beta-catenin axis and nuclear beta-catenin accumulation; abnormalities at the imprinted 11p15.5 locus link the tumour to Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, while germline APC loss links it to familial adenomatous polyposis. Alpha-fetoprotein production reflects the tumour's primitive, partly hepatoid differentiation. Tumours are often large and encapsulated at presentation and spread to regional lymph nodes, liver, and lungs. Completely resected, localised pancreatoblastoma has a good prognosis, whereas unresectable, recurrent, or metastatic disease carries a considerably poorer outlook despite chemotherapy.

Panic attack / anxiety — Diagnosis of exclusion — rule out ACS/PE first ECG normal Do not anchor on anxiety until cardiac/pulmonary emergencies excluded Hyperventilation syndrome (respiratory alkalosis) — itself a diagnosis of exclusion (p.376) Generalized anxiety disorder and somatization presenting with palpitations or pseudo-syncope (p.161, p.291) Vasovagal syncope precipitated by fear/stress/anxiety (distinguished by accompanying hypotension +/- bradycardia, unlike psychogenic pseudo-syncope) (p.161) Cataplexy / narcolepsy as a cause of episodic collapse (consciousness preserved) (p.161) Persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) and chronic subjective dizziness, in which anxiety disorders are common comorbidities (p.165) Resting 12-lead ECG, with serial tracings, to exclude arrhythmia and ischemia in palpitations/chest discomfort (p.291); note hyperventilation in panic can itself produce nonspecific ST-segment and T-wave abnormalities (p.107) Ambulatory rhythm monitoring (Holter, event/loop recorder, implantable loop recorder, or mobile cardiac outpatient telemetry) for infrequent recurrent palpitations (p.291) Arterial blood-gas analysis when hyperventilation suspected: shows respiratory alkalosis with hypocapnia (Paco2 ~15-30 mmHg) but no hypoxemia (p.376) Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial ischemia (aching, heavy, squeezing retrosternal discomfort) (p.103) Pulmonary embolism (chest discomfort, sinus tachycardia, ECG axis shift/S1Q3T3) (p.107) Supraventricular or ventricular tachyarrhythmia and atrial fibrillation (palpitations) (p.291) Thyrotoxicosis / hyperthyroidism (palpitations, hyperdynamic state) (p.291, p.376) Pheochromocytoma (catecholamine-driven palpitations, hyperdynamic cardiovascular state) (p.291) Hypoglycemia (tremor, palpitations, anxiety, diaphoresis, hunger, paresthesias from autonomic activation) (p.161) Systemic mastocytosis; stimulant/drug effects (caffeine, cocaine, amphetamines, cannabis, ethanol); post-COVID syndrome — as causes of palpitations (p.291) Up to ~10% of patients presenting to emergency departments with acute chest discomfort have an underlying panic disorder or a related condition (p.104). Psychiatric/emotional chest discomfort is variable in duration (fleeting to prolonged), often felt as chest tightness and breathlessness with a sense of panic or impending doom, and may be retrosternal; situational triggers and a prior history of panic attacks or depression support the diagnosis (p.103). A psychiatric cause for palpitations is favoured when the sensation is reported as lasting longer (>15 min) and is accompanied by additional symptoms, in contrast to most arrhythmic causes (p.291). Panic attacks can arise out of sleep and must be distinguished from parasomnias and other nocturnal events (p.215). Apparent (psychogenic) loss of consciousness can occur in panic disorder and related conditions; suspect it in patients who faint frequently without prodrome, are rarely injured despite repeated falls, and have no concurrent hemodynamic change (no hypotension/bradycardia) during the event (p.161). Normocapnia together with hypoxemia in a hyperventilating patient is a warning sign that may herald impending respiratory failure — do not assume benign anxiety (p.376) High-risk syncope features that argue against a psychogenic cause: new chest discomfort, dyspnea, exertional or supine syncope, palpitations preceding syncope, structural/coronary heart disease (p.161) Chest discomfort with features of an acute cardiopulmonary catastrophe (ACS, acute aortic syndrome, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, pericarditis with tamponade) must be excluded first (p.105) Anchoring on anxiety/panic prematurely: because attacks mimic ACS, PE, arrhythmia, thyrotoxicosis, pheochromocytoma and hypoglycemia, organic emergencies must be excluded — panic disorder and the hyperventilation syndrome are diagnoses of exclusion (p.105, p.376). Misreading hyperventilation-related nonspecific ST-segment/T-wave changes as evidence of ischemia (or vice versa) (p.107). When ruling in a hyperventilation/psychiatric cause, still exclude pulmonary embolism, coronary artery disease and hyperthyroidism (p.376). Acute attacks are commonly accompanied by hyperventilation; the resulting hypocapnia (Paco2 often 15-30 mmHg) produces an acute respiratory alkalosis without hypoxemia, which underlies many of the somatic symptoms (paresthesia, circumoral numbness, chest-wall tightness, dizziness, air hunger, and rarely tetany) and can perpetuate the disorder. Catecholaminergic/hyperadrenergic activation contributes to palpitations and the hyperdynamic sensation (Harrison 22e p.376, p.291).

Panic disorder — panic attacks disorder, episodic paroxysmal anxiety Cardiac arrhythmia or acute coronary syndrome Hyperthyroidism and other endocrine disturbances Phaeochromocytoma Hypoglycaemia Substance intoxication or withdrawal, including caffeine, stimulants, and alcohol Other anxiety disorders such as generalised anxiety disorder or social anxiety disorder Vestibular or respiratory disorders presenting with dizziness or breathlessness Electrocardiogram to exclude arrhythmia in appropriate presentations Thyroid function testing Blood glucose measurement during symptomatic episodes Substance and caffeine use screening Standardised anxiety rating scales to gauge severity and monitor response The core feature is recurrent, unexpected surges of intense fear or discomfort that peak within minutes, accompanied by prominent physical symptoms such as palpitations, chest tightness, breathlessness, sweating, trembling, dizziness, and a sense of impending doom Diagnosis also requires persistent worry about further attacks or a maladaptive change in behaviour to avoid them, distinguishing the disorder from isolated panic attacks Many patients present first to emergency or cardiology services convinced they are having a heart attack, so a compassionate explanation of the mind-body link is central to engagement Exclude medical mimics before settling on the diagnosis, including arrhythmia, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycaemia, phaeochromocytoma, asthma, and caffeine or stimulant effects Agoraphobic avoidance frequently develops as patients begin to avoid places or situations from which escape might feel difficult during an attack First-line management combines cognitive behavioural therapy, including interoceptive exposure and breathing retraining, with SSRIs or SNRIs as pharmacological options Benzodiazepines may give rapid relief but carry dependence and rebound risks, so they are generally reserved for short-term or adjunctive use rather than maintenance Reassurance, psychoeducation about the self-limiting nature of attacks, and reduction of stimulants can markedly reduce anticipatory anxiety Syncope, sustained chest pain, or objective signs suggesting a primary cardiac event Emerging suicidal ideation, particularly with comorbid depression Escalating benzodiazepine or alcohol use to self-manage symptoms Severe agoraphobic avoidance causing housebound behaviour and functional collapse Repeated extensive medical investigations that reinforce illness beliefs rather than addressing the anxiety Relying on long-term benzodiazepines and creating dependence Missing comorbid depression and its associated suicide risk Underdosing or prematurely stopping SSRIs before an adequate therapeutic trial Overlooking caffeine, stimulants, or withdrawal states as drivers of attacks Panic disorder is thought to arise from dysregulation of fear-processing circuits, particularly hypersensitivity of the amygdala and brainstem structures involved in the alarm and respiratory response, with contributions from serotonergic, noradrenergic, and GABAergic dysfunction. A heritable predisposition interacts with heightened sensitivity to internal bodily cues (interoceptive conditioning) and catastrophic misinterpretation of benign somatic sensations, which perpetuates the cycle of fear and physiological arousal. Panic disorder tends to run a chronic, fluctuating course, but a substantial proportion of patients achieve marked improvement or remission with adequate treatment. Prognosis is better with early intervention and engagement in cognitive behavioural therapy, and worse when agoraphobia, depression, or substance misuse is comorbid or when treatment is delayed.

Panner disease — osteochondrosis of the capitellum, capitellar osteochondrosis, osteonecrosis of the humeral capitellum, Panner's disease Osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum Medial epicondyle apophysitis (little league elbow) Radial head or neck fracture Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis of the elbow Juvenile idiopathic arthritis of the elbow Radiocapitellar plica or synovitis Anteroposterior and lateral elbow radiographs showing capitellar fragmentation and sclerosis Comparison views of the contralateral elbow to gauge normal ossification Magnetic resonance imaging to assess the articular cartilage and distinguish from osteochondritis dissecans Assessment of elbow range of motion and any fixed flexion contracture Inflammatory markers if infection or inflammatory arthritis is suspected Follow-up imaging to confirm reossification of the capitellum A true osteonecrosis of the capitellum affecting its developing ossification centre, not a traction apophysitis Affected bone is the capitellum of the distal humerus at the lateral elbow Typically affects young children, roughly five to ten years of age, often in the dominant throwing arm Presents with dull lateral elbow pain, stiffness and a mild flexion contracture, worse with throwing or weight-bearing on the arm The radiographic hallmark is irregularity, fragmentation and sclerosis of the capitellar ossification centre, sometimes with later reossification It should be distinguished from osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum, which occurs in older adolescents and can produce loose bodies Unlike osteochondritis dissecans, Panner disease usually involves the whole ossific nucleus and tends to reconstitute with growth Management is conservative with rest, activity modification and avoidance of throwing, with physiotherapy to restore motion as needed Mechanical locking or catching suggesting a loose body and osteochondritis dissecans rather than Panner disease Progressive fixed flexion contracture or loss of motion Systemic features or joint effusion raising concern for infection or inflammatory arthritis Persistent symptoms in an older adolescent, which favour osteochondritis dissecans with poorer prognosis Confusing Panner disease with capitellar osteochondritis dissecans, which has a different age group and worse outlook Allowing continued throwing, which perpetuates loading of the healing capitellum Missing an alternative diagnosis such as infection when an effusion or systemic features are present Failing to arrange follow-up imaging to confirm reossification Panner disease is an osteochondrosis of the capitellum in which the ossification centre of the lateral distal humerus undergoes ischaemic change during childhood. Repetitive valgus and compressive loading of the immature elbow, particularly from throwing or upper limb weight-bearing, is thought to disturb the blood supply to the developing capitellum. This produces necrosis, fragmentation and sclerosis of the ossific nucleus, followed by revascularisation and reossification as growth continues. Because the process typically affects the entire ossification centre in a skeletally immature child and remodels with growth, it is generally self-limiting, in contrast to capitellar osteochondritis dissecans in older adolescents, which involves a focal osteochondral fragment and carries a higher risk of loose bodies and residual joint incongruity. Panner disease generally carries a favourable prognosis; the capitellum usually reossifies and remodels with growth once the elbow is rested, and most children recover full or near-full function without long-term joint damage.

Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration — PKAN, PANK2, NBIA type 1, Hallervorden-Spatz syndrome, neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation type 1 Other NBIA subtypes (PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration, BPAN, aceruloplasminaemia, neuroferritinopathy) Wilson disease Juvenile Huntington disease Dopa-responsive dystonia and other early-onset dystonias Mitochondrial disorders with basal ganglia involvement Secondary pallidal injury from hypoxia or manganese exposure Brain MRI including iron-sensitive sequences to demonstrate the eye-of-the-tiger sign and pallidal iron PANK2 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Ophthalmological assessment including electroretinography for pigmentary retinopathy Serum copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude Wilson disease Serum ferritin and caeruloplasmin to help distinguish other NBIA subtypes Most common form of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA), inherited autosomal recessively through biallelic PANK2 variants Classic early-onset form presents in childhood with gait disturbance, dystonia, rigidity, and pigmentary retinopathy, progressing over years Atypical later-onset form has slower progression with prominent speech and neuropsychiatric features and less retinopathy Oromandibular and limb dystonia can be severe and may lead to status dystonicus, a neurological emergency The pathognomonic MRI finding is the eye-of-the-tiger sign: a central region of T2 hyperintensity within surrounding hypointensity in the globus pallidus, reflecting focal gliosis amid iron deposition Iron-sensitive MRI sequences (T2*/gradient-echo/susceptibility-weighted imaging) accentuate the pallidal iron and support the NBIA diagnosis Management is symptomatic, targeting dystonia and spasticity with oral agents, botulinum toxin, and in selected refractory cases deep brain stimulation Diagnosis is confirmed by PANK2 molecular testing in the setting of the characteristic clinical and imaging picture Status dystonicus with unremitting severe dystonia causing pain, hyperthermia, or rhabdomyolysis Acute swallowing failure with aspiration risk Rapid loss of ambulation or new bulbar dysfunction Self-injury from severe oromandibular dystonia Mistaking the eye-of-the-tiger appearance for another basal ganglia lesion or dismissing subtle pallidal iron on standard sequences Failing to obtain iron-sensitive MRI sequences that reveal the diagnostic iron deposition Overlooking status dystonicus as an emergency requiring prompt escalation Not screening for Wilson disease, a treatable mimic, before settling on an NBIA diagnosis Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in PANK2, encoding a mitochondrial pantothenate kinase that catalyses the first, rate-limiting step of coenzyme A biosynthesis from vitamin B5. Impaired coenzyme A synthesis is thought to disrupt lipid and energy metabolism and to allow accumulation of cysteine-containing substrates that chelate iron, driving oxidative damage. The net effect is progressive iron deposition and neurodegeneration concentrated in the globus pallidus, producing the extrapyramidal features and the characteristic pallidal imaging changes. The classic childhood-onset form is progressive, with most patients losing independent ambulation within years of onset, whereas the atypical form advances more slowly over decades. Life expectancy is reduced, largely from complications of severe dystonia and immobility.

PAPA syndrome — pyogenic arthritis, pyoderma gangrenosum and acne syndrome, PSTPIP1-associated inflammatory disease, PSTPIP1, CD2 binding protein 1 disorder Septic arthritis Juvenile idiopathic arthritis Idiopathic pyoderma gangrenosum Severe nodulocystic acne without systemic disease Other PSTPIP1-associated syndromes (e.g. PAMI) Behcet disease Genetic testing for PSTPIP1 mutations Synovial fluid analysis and culture demonstrating sterile neutrophilic arthritis Acute-phase reactants during flares Skin biopsy of pyoderma gangrenosum lesions Joint imaging to assess destructive arthritis Wound swabs to exclude secondary infection of skin ulcers An autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disease caused by mutations in PSTPIP1, which regulates the pyrin inflammasome Classic triad is recurrent sterile pyogenic arthritis, pyoderma gangrenosum, and severe cystic acne Joint disease often begins in childhood with recurrent, destructive, sterile arthritis triggered by minor trauma Pyoderma gangrenosum and severe nodulocystic acne tend to become more prominent from adolescence Aspirated joint fluid is sterile and neutrophil-rich, reflecting an autoinflammatory rather than infective arthritis Interleukin-1 and tumour necrosis factor directed biologics are the main therapies, with variable individual response The skin lesions can pathergically worsen after surgery or trauma, so aggressive surgical debridement should be approached cautiously Rapidly progressive destructive arthritis threatening joint integrity Enlarging pyoderma gangrenosum ulcers with secondary infection Pathergy with wound breakdown after surgery or trauma Systemic inflammatory response requiring escalation of therapy Treating sterile pyogenic arthritis as septic and pursuing repeated invasive intervention Aggressively debriding pyoderma gangrenosum, which can provoke pathergy and worsen ulcers Assuming acne is cosmetic and missing the wider autoinflammatory diagnosis Not testing for PSTPIP1 in a child with recurrent sterile arthritis and skin disease PAPA syndrome arises from dominant mutations in PSTPIP1 (also called CD2 binding protein 1), a protein that interacts with pyrin to regulate inflammasome activity. Mutations enhance PSTPIP1 binding to pyrin, promoting inappropriate inflammasome assembly and excess interleukin-1 beta production. The resulting sterile neutrophilic inflammation targets joints, skin, and pilosebaceous units, producing pyogenic arthritis, pyoderma gangrenosum, and cystic acne. Because both interleukin-1 and tumour necrosis factor contribute to the inflammation, biologics against these cytokines are used therapeutically. PAPA syndrome is a chronic relapsing disease; biologic therapy can control inflammation and limit joint and skin damage, but responses vary and established joint destruction or skin scarring may persist.

Papillary fibroelastoma — cardiac papillary fibroelastoma, CPF, papillary fibroelastoma of the valve, fibroelastic papilloma Infective endocarditis vegetation Non-bacterial thrombotic (marantic)
