valvular mass Cardiac MRI in selected cases to further characterise the lesion Blood cultures and inflammatory markers to help exclude infective endocarditis Neuroimaging when cerebral embolism is suspected Coronary assessment if there are features of coronary embolism Histological confirmation of the excised specimen The most common primary tumour of the cardiac valves and a leading benign valvular tumour, typically small and arising on valve surfaces It has a characteristic frond-like, sea-anemone appearance with multiple papillary arms attached by a short stalk The aortic valve is the most frequent site, followed by the mitral valve, and lesions are usually single Many are found incidentally on echocardiography performed for other reasons The principal clinical hazard is embolism, which can cause stroke, transient ischaemic attack, coronary embolism with angina or myocardial infarction, or peripheral events The mobile tumour or associated thrombus on its surface is the embolic source, so mobility on imaging is an important risk marker Transoesophageal echocardiography best characterises the lesion, and it must be distinguished from vegetation and thrombus Surgical excision, usually with valve preservation, is considered for symptomatic, left-sided, or highly mobile tumours because of embolic risk Stroke or transient ischaemic attack attributable to the lesion Coronary embolism causing angina or myocardial infarction Highly mobile left-sided tumour with high embolic potential Peripheral or systemic embolic events Mistaking the lesion for an infective vegetation and initiating unnecessary prolonged antibiotics Underestimating embolic risk in mobile left-sided lesions Confusing it with benign Lambl's excrescences or valvular thrombus Assuming an incidental finding is harmless without weighing embolic potential Papillary fibroelastoma is a benign avascular tumour of the endocardial surface, most often on the valves. It consists of a branching core of dense connective tissue rich in elastic fibres, covered by a layer of endothelium, giving the multiple frond-like papillary projections that resemble a sea anemone when immersed in fluid. The clefts between the fronds promote stasis and deposition of platelet-fibrin thrombus. Because the tumour and any adherent thrombus are mobile and exposed to flow, fragments can detach and embolise; left-sided lesions on the aortic or mitral valve threaten the cerebral, coronary, and systemic circulations. The tumour itself is benign and surgical excision is generally curative with a good outlook and low recurrence; the main determinant of prognosis is the embolic complications that occur before treatment.

Papillary muscle rupture — post-infarction papillary muscle rupture Post-infarction ventricular septal rupture Free wall rupture with tamponade Acute ischaemic mitral regurgitation without rupture Infective endocarditis with chordal rupture Spontaneous chordal rupture in degenerative valve disease Urgent echocardiography, often transoesophageal Assessment of coronary anatomy Haemodynamic monitoring for cardiogenic shock Electrocardiogram and cardiac biomarkers confirming infarction Prompt cardiac surgical assessment A mechanical complication of acute myocardial infarction causing sudden severe mitral regurgitation It typically occurs a few days after infarction and presents with abrupt pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock The posteromedial papillary muscle is more vulnerable because it has a single coronary blood supply The murmur may be soft or absent despite severe regurgitation because of rapid pressure equalisation Echocardiography (often transoesophageal) is diagnostic, showing a flail leaflet and severe regurgitation It is a surgical emergency; temporising measures include afterload reduction and mechanical circulatory support Acute pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock after recent infarction A new severe mitral regurgitation, even with a soft murmur Haemodynamic instability requiring urgent support Multiorgan hypoperfusion Being falsely reassured by a soft or absent murmur Confusing it with post-infarction ventricular septal rupture Delaying surgery in a deteriorating patient Attributing shock solely to left ventricular dysfunction Papillary muscle rupture results from ischaemic necrosis of a papillary muscle following myocardial infarction, most often affecting the posteromedial muscle owing to its single-vessel supply. Complete or partial rupture disrupts the subvalvular apparatus, producing an acutely flail mitral leaflet and torrential mitral regurgitation. Because the left atrium and ventricle cannot accommodate the sudden volume, pressures equalise rapidly, causing flash pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock, and the murmur may therefore be unimpressive despite catastrophic haemodynamics. Without surgery mortality is very high; emergency valve surgery, supported by mechanical circulatory support and revascularisation, offers the best chance of survival though operative risk is substantial.

Papillary renal cell carcinoma — papillary RCC, pRCC, chromophil renal cell carcinoma Clear cell renal cell carcinoma Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma Collecting duct carcinoma Metanephric adenoma Fumarate hydratase-deficient renal cell carcinoma MiT family translocation renal cell carcinoma Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to characterise and stage the mass Renal mass biopsy where it will guide management Immunohistochemistry and, where indicated, fumarate hydratase staining Genetic assessment when hereditary features or syndromic signs are present Chest imaging and baseline bloods for staging of larger tumours The second most common subtype of renal cell carcinoma after clear cell disease Often appears as a hypovascular renal mass, enhancing less avidly than clear cell tumours on contrast imaging Frequently multifocal and bilateral, more so than other subtypes Traditionally divided into type 1 and type 2, with type 2 generally behaving more aggressively Hereditary forms include hereditary papillary renal carcinoma (MET) and hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (fumarate hydratase) A fumarate hydratase-deficient tumour should prompt genetic assessment because of its aggressive nature Localised low-grade disease generally carries a good prognosis after surgery High-grade or type 2 histology, especially fumarate hydratase-deficient tumours Locally advanced or metastatic disease at presentation Cutaneous or uterine leiomyomas suggesting a hereditary syndrome Rapid growth of a previously indolent lesion Assuming a hypovascular mass is benign because it enhances poorly Overlooking multifocal or contralateral tumours Missing a hereditary syndrome in a young patient with an aggressive type 2 tumour Applying clear cell prognostic assumptions to papillary disease Papillary renal cell carcinoma arises from the epithelium of the proximal or distal tubule and is characterised by papillary or tubulopapillary growth, often with foamy macrophages and haemosiderin. Type 1 tumours are frequently associated with gains of chromosomes 7 and 17 and, in hereditary cases, activating MET mutations. Type 2 tumours are more heterogeneous and include fumarate hydratase-deficient cancers linked to hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer, which pursue an aggressive course. The relatively poor vascularity explains the characteristically modest enhancement on imaging. Localised, low-grade type 1 tumours generally have a favourable prognosis after surgery; higher-grade type 2 and fumarate hydratase-deficient tumours carry a worse outlook with a greater risk of metastasis.

thyroid carcinoma arises from follicular epithelial cells and is defined by distinctive nuclear changes produced by constitutive activation of the MAPK signalling cascade, most commonly through the BRAF V600E mutation or RET/PTC gene rearrangements. These oncogenic drivers promote proliferation while cells retain many features of thyroid differentiation, including iodine handling and thyroglobulin production, which underpins the utility of radioactive iodine and thyroglobulin monitoring. The tumour characteristically invades intrathyroidal lymphatics, giving multifocal disease and early spread to regional cervical lymph nodes, whereas distant haematogenous metastasis is comparatively uncommon. Prognosis is generally excellent, especially in younger patients with intrathyroidal disease, where long-term survival is the norm; older age, extrathyroidal extension, large tumour size, and distant metastases are the main adverse factors.

immunopositivity for cytokeratins (notably CK18) helps distinguish it from other pineal tumours Behaviour is variable and it has a notable tendency to recur locally despite treatment Management combines maximal safe resection with radiotherapy considered for residual or recurrent disease Acute obstructive hydrocephalus with raised intracranial pressure Progressive dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) signs and impaired consciousness Local recurrence on surveillance imaging Features suggesting dissemination along the neuraxis Misclassifying it as an ependymoma or pineal parenchymal tumour without cytokeratin staining Underestimating the strong tendency to local recurrence and relaxing surveillance Overlooking a coexisting germ cell tumour by not checking tumour markers Delaying relief of obstructive hydrocephalus Papillary tumour of the pineal region is a rare neuroepithelial neoplasm believed to originate from specialised ependymocytes of the subcommissural organ within the pineal region. It forms a circumscribed mass with a characteristic mixture of papillary structures, in which epithelial-like cells surround fibrovascular cores, and more densely cellular solid areas. The tumour cells express cytokeratins, a feature that helps separate it from pineal parenchymal tumours and ependymomas. Grading is imprecise but corresponds to CNS WHO grade 2 or 3, and the lesion is characterised clinically by a marked propensity for local recurrence. Its midline pineal location readily obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow and compresses the dorsal midbrain. Prognosis is intermediate and difficult to predict, being limited chiefly by a high rate of local recurrence even after resection and radiotherapy. Extent of resection influences outcome, and long-term surveillance is required because recurrences may occur years after initial treatment.

Papilloedema is passive swelling of the optic nerve head produced by raised intracranial pressure transmitted along the subarachnoid space surrounding the optic nerve. The elevated pressure impedes axoplasmic flow within the retinal ganglion cell axons at the optic disc, causing them to become distended, along with venous congestion and leakage that produce the characteristic disc appearance. Because the mechanism is mechanical rather than primarily ischaemic or inflammatory, central acuity is often spared until late. Persistently raised pressure eventually causes axonal loss and secondary optic atrophy. Vision can be preserved if the underlying cause of raised intracranial pressure is treated promptly, but delayed or chronic papilloedema leads to optic atrophy and permanent visual field loss.

Cathepsin C activates a range of serine proteases stored in immune and inflammatory cells, including neutrophil elastase, cathepsin G and granzymes. Its deficiency impairs neutrophil and immune-cell function, reducing the ability to control bacteria at the gingival margin and skin, which produces aggressive periodontitis and heightened susceptibility to pyogenic infection. In the epidermis, disturbed protease-mediated regulation of keratinocyte differentiation contributes to the diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma. The combined immune and epidermal effects explain the characteristic skin-and-gum phenotype. The keratoderma is chronic but manageable; the major morbidity is early loss of the dentition, which intensive periodontal care and dental preservation can mitigate. With attention to infection risk, general prognosis is good, although recurrent pyogenic infection and periodontal disease persist.

parachute mitral valve — parachute mitral valve deformity, single papillary muscle mitral valve Supravalvar mitral ring Anomalous mitral arcade Cor triatriatum Rheumatic mitral stenosis Congenital mitral valve dysplasia Double-orifice mitral valve Transthoracic echocardiography with short-axis papillary muscle count and Doppler inflow gradients Transoesophageal and 3D echocardiography Cardiac MRI Cardiac catheterisation Aortic arch imaging to screen for Shone-complex lesions Electrocardiography for right ventricular hypertrophy and left atrial enlargement Parachute mitral valve has all chordae inserting into a single dominant papillary muscle, producing subvalvar inflow obstruction and congenital mitral stenosis. It is the classic component of Shone complex alongside supravalvar mitral ring, subaortic stenosis and coarctation, so the other three lesions should always be sought. Obstruction occurs at the interchordal level, so the mitral orifice can look adequate while flow is restricted between crowded chordae. Parasternal short-axis imaging shows a single papillary muscle with limited leaflet opening and a narrow subvalvar funnel. A true parachute with one papillary muscle is distinguished from a parachute-like asymmetric valve, which has two papillary muscles, one of them hypoplastic. Symptoms track the gradient and include dyspnoea, poor feeding and pulmonary hypertension in infants. Surgery is technically difficult; splitting the papillary muscle or fenestrating chordae may relieve obstruction, but replacement is sometimes required. Severe pulmonary hypertension Heart failure or failure to thrive in infancy Severe inflow gradient with low cardiac output Coexisting critical left-heart outflow obstruction Overlooking subvalvar obstruction when the annulus and orifice appear normal Failing to identify associated Shone-complex lesions Confusing the lesion with supravalvar mitral ring or cor triatriatum Assuming a successful repair is durable when restenosis is common In a true parachute mitral valve all chordae tendineae converge and insert into a single papillary muscle, while in the parachute-like asymmetric variant they insert into one dominant papillary muscle with a hypoplastic second muscle. The interchordal spaces are markedly reduced, so blood entering the left ventricle must pass through the crowded, narrowed spaces between chordae, generating functional stenosis at the subvalvar level even when the annular orifice appears normal. The lesion frequently coexists with other left-heart obstructive anomalies as part of Shone complex, compounding the inflow and outflow obstruction. Isolated mild parachute valve may be well tolerated, but significant stenosis, especially within Shone complex, carries higher surgical risk and a tendency to residual or recurrent obstruction requiring reintervention.

Paracoccidioidomycosis — Paracoccidioides brasiliensis, Paracoccidioides lutzii, South American blastomycosis, Lutz-Splendore-Almeida disease, PCM Pulmonary tuberculosis (frequently co-exists and mimics the chronic form) Histoplasmosis and other endemic dimorphic mycoses Oral or laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma Leishmaniasis (mucocutaneous) Lymphoma or other causes of generalised lymphadenopathy in the juvenile form Sarcoidosis Direct microscopy of sputum, mucosal scrapings or aspirated pus with potassium hydroxide preparation for multiple-budding yeasts Fungal culture on appropriate media (slow-growing) with demonstration of dimorphism Histopathology of biopsy material with special fungal stains showing the pilot's-wheel yeast Serology by immunodiffusion or complement fixation for diagnosis and follow-up Chest imaging to characterise the pulmonary infiltrates and fibrosis Screening for co-existing tuberculosis and for HIV in atypical or severe presentations Endemic to humid rural areas of Central and South America, especially Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela and Argentina, and typically affects male agricultural workers exposed to soil Caused by the thermally dimorphic fungi Paracoccidioides brasiliensis and P. lutzii, acquired by inhalation of conidia; the acute/subacute (juvenile) form and the chronic (adult) form behave very differently The chronic adult form is dominated by pulmonary disease with mucocutaneous lesions of the mouth, gums and oropharynx, often with a characteristic mulberry-like haemorrhagic stippling The acute juvenile form presents with prominent reticuloendothelial involvement: generalised lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and marrow involvement, and is more aggressive Microscopy of pus, sputum or tissue classically shows the multiple-budding 'pilot's wheel' or 'Mickey Mouse' yeast form, which is diagnostic Serology (immunodiffusion, complement fixation) supports diagnosis and helps monitor treatment response and relapse Prolonged therapy with azole antifungals is standard for most cases, with amphotericin-based therapy reserved for severe or disseminated disease and long consolidation required to prevent relapse Progressive dyspnoea and respiratory compromise from advanced pulmonary fibrosis Laryngeal or tracheal involvement threatening the airway Disseminated juvenile-type disease with marrow failure or extensive lymphadenopathy Central nervous system or adrenal involvement Relapse or deterioration on treatment suggesting inadequate duration or immunosuppression Misdiagnosing the chronic form as tuberculosis or cancer and delaying antifungal therapy Stopping treatment when symptoms resolve rather than continuing prolonged consolidation, leading to relapse Overlooking co-existing tuberculosis, which can worsen if only one condition is treated Failing to recognise adrenal insufficiency arising from adrenal involvement Not screening for underlying immunosuppression in unusually severe disease Paracoccidioidomycosis follows inhalation of airborne conidia of Paracoccidioides species from contaminated soil in endemic zones. At body temperature the fungus converts to its pathogenic multiply-budding yeast form and establishes a primary pulmonary focus, which may remain latent for years or decades before reactivating, often when cell-mediated immunity wanes. A vigorous granulomatous response tends to contain infection in the chronic adult form, whereas an inadequate Th1 response permits lymphohaematogenous dissemination in the acute juvenile form. Chronic pulmonary involvement produces progressive fibrosis, and mucosal seeding gives rise to the destructive oral and laryngeal lesions. With prolonged antifungal therapy most patients improve, but chronic pulmonary fibrosis and mucosal scarring can leave permanent disability; the acute juvenile and disseminated forms carry higher mortality, and relapse is common if treatment is stopped early.

some tumours secrete predominantly noradrenaline or dopamine Somatostatin receptor PET (DOTATATE) is highly sensitive, particularly for SDHB-related and metastatic disease, complementing MIBG and cross-sectional imaging Preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade, established before any beta-blockade, is mandatory for secretory tumours to prevent intraoperative hypertensive crisis Hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia or catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy Rapid tumour growth, local invasion or metastatic disease (SDHB association) New cranial neuropathies from an enlarging skull-base or neck tumour Symptoms provoked by anaesthesia, biopsy or tumour manipulation without prior blockade Family history of paraganglioma or phaeochromocytoma indicating a hereditary syndrome Biopsying or operating on a secretory tumour without excluding catecholamine excess and without alpha-blockade, precipitating a hypertensive crisis Giving beta-blockade before adequate alpha-blockade, causing unopposed alpha vasoconstriction Assuming head and neck paragangliomas are always non-secretory and omitting biochemical screening Not offering germline genetic testing, thereby missing hereditary and malignancy risk Relying on histology alone to predict malignancy, which is defined by the presence of metastasis Paragangliomas arise from neural crest-derived chromaffin or glomus cells of the autonomic paraganglia. Sympathetic paraganglia along the paravertebral and para-aortic chains may synthesise and release catecholamines, producing the adrenergic syndrome, whereas parasympathetic paraganglia of the head and neck rarely secrete and instead cause symptoms through local mass effect. A large fraction are driven by germline mutations, most often in the succinate dehydrogenase complex genes; loss of SDH function causes succinate accumulation and a pseudohypoxic state that stabilises hypoxia-inducible factors and promotes tumorigenesis. Malignancy is defined by the presence of metastases at sites where paraganglia are not normally found. Benign, completely resected paragangliomas have an excellent prognosis, but metastatic disease, which is more frequent with SDHB mutations, reduces survival although its course can still be prolonged; lifelong surveillance is required because of multifocal and recurrent disease.

tumours Head and neck paragangliomas are neuroendocrine tumours derived from paraganglia of the parasympathetic nervous system distributed along the carotid, jugulotympanic and vagal territories. In contrast to their sympathetic abdominal and adrenal counterparts, most are non-chromaffin and do not oversecrete catecholamines. A large fraction are hereditary, driven by germline mutations in succinate dehydrogenase complex subunit genes such as SDHD, SDHB, SDHC, SDHAF2 and SDHA, which impair mitochondrial complex II and stabilise hypoxia-inducible factors, promoting a pseudohypoxic, pro-angiogenic state and slow tumour growth. Chronic hypoxia, for example at high altitude, can also enlarge the carotid body. Much of the morbidity arises from local mass effect on adjacent cranial nerves and great vessels. Most head and neck paragangliomas are slow-growing and benign, and long-term control is achievable with surgery, radiotherapy or surveillance; however cranial nerve deficits may result from the tumour or its treatment, and SDHB-related tumours carry a higher risk of metastatic spread, so lifelong follow-up is warranted.

species in Africa and the Americas Infection follows eating raw, undercooked or pickled freshwater crabs or crayfish, or in some regions raw meat of paratenic hosts, containing infective metacercariae After ingestion the larvae penetrate the gut and diaphragm and produce migratory subcutaneous swellings before settling in the lungs to form parasitic cysts The pulmonary syndrome mimics tuberculosis: chronic cough, chest pain and haemoptysis with rusty-brown or blood-streaked sputum, often in an otherwise well patient Ectopic (extrapulmonary) disease is important, particularly cerebral paragonimiasis, which can cause seizures, focal deficits and space-occupying lesions Diagnosis rests on finding the characteristic operculated eggs in sputum or stool, supported by serology, eosinophilia and imaging showing cysts, ring shadows or pleural effusion Praziquantel is the treatment of choice for paragonimiasis, with corticosteroid cover considered in cerebral disease to limit inflammatory reaction Neurological features (seizures, focal deficit, raised intracranial pressure) suggesting cerebral paragonimiasis Massive or persistent haemoptysis Large pleural effusion or empyema causing respiratory compromise Diagnostic confusion with tuberculosis leading to inappropriate anti-TB therapy Extensive or multiorgan ectopic disease Treating the patient as smear-negative tuberculosis and overlooking lung fluke eggs in sputum Relying on a single sputum sample, which may miss eggs Not considering cerebral paragonimiasis in an endemic patient with seizures Neglecting dietary counselling, allowing reinfection from raw crab or crayfish Omitting corticosteroid cover in cerebral disease where an inflammatory reaction to dying flukes is a concern Ingested metacercariae excyst in the small intestine, penetrate the intestinal wall into the peritoneal cavity, and migrate through the diaphragm into the pleural space and lungs, where paired adult flukes become enclosed in fibrous cysts that communicate with bronchioles. Eggs are coughed up and either expectorated or swallowed and passed in stool. Local inflammation, cyst formation and rupture into airways produce the chronic cough and haemoptysis, while pleural involvement causes effusion. Aberrant migration of larvae to the brain, subcutaneous tissue, abdomen or other sites produces ectopic disease, with cerebral involvement being the most serious. Pulmonary paragonimiasis usually responds well to anthelmintic therapy with a good outlook, but cerebral and other ectopic disease can leave lasting neurological deficits, and misdiagnosis as tuberculosis often delays effective treatment.

Paralytic shellfish poisoning (saxitoxin) — PSP, saxitoxin poisoning, shellfish neurotoxin poisoning, red tide shellfish poisoning Tetrodotoxin (pufferfish) poisoning Ciguatera poisoning Neurotoxic or amnesic shellfish poisoning Guillain-Barre syndrome or botulism Blue-ringed octopus envenomation Scombroid poisoning (though this is histaminic rather than paralytic) Clinical diagnosis based on shellfish ingestion and characteristic neurology Continuous respiratory monitoring and serial forced vital capacity Pulse oximetry and arterial blood gases for ventilatory failure Electrocardiography and cardiac monitoring Electrolytes and baseline bloods to exclude alternative causes Toxin assay of shellfish or biological samples where available, and public health notification Follows ingestion of bivalve shellfish that have accumulated saxitoxins from toxic dinoflagellate blooms (red tides) Symptoms typically begin within minutes to an hour with perioral and facial paraesthesiae and tingling of the extremities Progresses to ataxia, dysarthria, limb weakness and, in severe cases, ascending flaccid paralysis with respiratory failure As with other sodium-channel toxins, consciousness is characteristically preserved throughout the paralysis There is no antidote; management is supportive with airway protection and mechanical ventilation until toxin clearance Early gastrointestinal decontamination may be considered soon after ingestion in a protected airway The toxins are heat-stable, so cooking does not make contaminated shellfish safe Progressive limb, bulbar or respiratory muscle weakness Declining respiratory function or oxygen saturation Rapid symptom onset after a large ingestion Inability to swallow or protect the airway Cluster of cases suggesting a contaminated batch requiring public health action Assuming thorough cooking removes the risk, as the toxins are heat-stable Underestimating progression from paraesthesiae to respiratory failure Mistaking preserved consciousness for a mild or non-organic presentation Failing to notify public health authorities to prevent further poisonings Saxitoxin and related paralytic shellfish toxins are produced by marine dinoflagellates and concentrated in filter-feeding bivalves. After ingestion, the toxins bind voltage-gated sodium channels on excitable membranes, blocking sodium conductance and inhibiting nerve and muscle action potentials. This causes early sensory disturbance followed by progressive flaccid paralysis, including of respiratory muscles, which is the principal life threat. The toxins are heat-stable and are not destroyed by normal cooking, and central nervous system function is relatively spared, so consciousness is retained despite paralysis. With prompt recognition and ventilatory support through the critical period, recovery is usually complete within days; untreated severe cases can be fatal from respiratory failure, particularly where advanced support is unavailable.

Paramyotonia congenita is caused by gain-of-function mutations in SCN4A, encoding the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.4. The mutant channels show impaired or slowed inactivation, and this defect is temperature sensitive so that cooling exaggerates the persistent sodium current. Incomplete inactivation produces sustained membrane depolarisation, which at moderate levels causes repetitive firing perceived as myotonia and, when depolarisation becomes severe, inactivates the remaining channels to render the fibre inexcitable and weak. Because the abnormality worsens with sustained activity and with cold, patients experience the characteristic paradoxical, cold-sensitive myotonia followed by weakness rather than the warm-up improvement of chloride channelopathies. Paramyotonia congenita is a non-progressive disorder compatible with a normal lifespan, and although cold-triggered stiffness and weakness can be disabling in cold climates or occupations, symptoms are usually manageable with trigger avoidance and antimyotonic therapy.

than repeating surveillance Delaying immunotherapy and tumour treatment while awaiting antibody results Expecting full neurological recovery once the cancer is treated Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration arises when a systemic tumour expresses antigens also present in cerebellar neurons, most notably Purkinje cells. The immune response mounted against the tumour cross-reacts with these neuronal antigens, producing an immune-mediated attack on the cerebellum. Antibodies such as anti-Yo, anti-Hu, anti-Ri, and anti-Tr/DNER serve as diagnostic markers of specific antigen-tumour associations, while cytotoxic T-cell mechanisms are believed to drive the neuronal destruction in antibodies targeting intracellular antigens. Progressive, often irreversible loss of Purkinje cells underlies the clinical picture, explaining why cerebellar atrophy appears on later imaging and why neurological recovery is usually incomplete even when the tumour is treated. Neurological outcome is generally poor because Purkinje cell loss is largely irreversible; treatment of the tumour and immunotherapy may halt progression but rarely restores function, and prognosis is heavily influenced by the underlying cancer.

Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) is the archetypal antibody, with small-cell lung carcinoma found in the large majority of cases. Anti-CV2/CRMP5 disease may add chorea, optic neuritis and peripheral neuropathy to the picture. Brainstem involvement produces vertigo, nystagmus, diplopia, dysarthria and dysphagia, and can threaten respiration. Autonomic involvement is common and may manifest as gastrointestinal pseudo-obstruction from enteric neuronal loss, orthostatic hypotension or cardiac dysrhythmia. Neurological symptoms usually antedate the cancer diagnosis and the underlying tumour is often small and limited-stage. Response to immunotherapy is generally poor; prompt treatment of the tumour offers the best chance of neurological stabilisation. CSF is usually inflammatory (pleocytosis, raised protein, oligoclonal bands) even when MRI is normal. respiratory failure or bulbar compromise from brainstem involvement autonomic instability with cardiac dysrhythmia gastrointestinal pseudo-obstruction rapidly progressive multifocal neurological deficit newly identified malignancy requiring urgent staging Attributing multifocal neurological signs to cerebral metastases rather than a paraneoplastic process. Discontinuing the tumour search after an initial negative imaging screen. Underestimating autonomic involvement, which can be life-threatening. Delaying oncological treatment while awaiting a neurological response to immunotherapy. Tumour cells (most often small-cell lung carcinoma) express intracellular onconeural antigens such as HuD that are normally restricted to neurons. The resulting immune response is dominated by antigen-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes that infiltrate multiple levels of the neuraxis, producing perivascular inflammation, microglial nodules and neuronal loss in cortex, brainstem, cerebellum, spinal cord, dorsal root ganglia and autonomic ganglia. The detected antibodies (anti-Hu, anti-CV2/CRMP5, anti-amphiphysin) are useful diagnostic markers but are largely not directly pathogenic, which accounts for the poor reversibility. Neurological prognosis is generally poor; deficits often persist even when the tumour is controlled, although the disease may stabilise with effective oncological treatment. Paradoxically, anti-Hu-associated small-cell lung carcinoma is sometimes detected at a limited stage and may show relatively favourable tumour control.

Anti-LGI1 disease produces faciobrachial dystonic seizures and hyponatraemia and is often non-paraneoplastic, though thymoma may occur. Anti-GABA-B encephalitis presents with prominent early seizures and is strongly linked to small-cell lung carcinoma. MRI typically shows unilateral or bilateral medial temporal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, and CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein and oligoclonal bands. The syndrome frequently antedates the tumour diagnosis by months, so a negative initial cancer screen warrants periodic re-screening. refractory or non-convulsive status epilepticus rapidly progressive decline in consciousness or coma autonomic instability (especially with NMDAR antibodies) severe symptomatic hyponatraemia identification of an underlying malignancy requiring urgent staging Misdiagnosing as herpes simplex encephalitis and missing the paraneoplastic search. An immune response directed against a tumour that ectopically expresses neuronal antigens cross-reacts with limbic structures (hippocampi, amygdala, cingulate and insular cortex), producing inflammation and neuronal loss. Two mechanistic groups exist: antibodies against intracellular onconeural antigens (Hu/ANNA-1, Ma2, CV2/CRMP5, amphiphysin) are markers of a predominantly cytotoxic T-cell mediated process that is poorly reversible, whereas antibodies against neuronal cell-surface or synaptic proteins (NMDAR, LGI1, GABA-B, AMPAR, CASPR2) are directly pathogenic, disrupt receptor function or clustering, and are potentially reversible with immunotherapy. Cell-surface antibody syndromes often improve substantially with tumour treatment and immunotherapy, whereas intracellular onconeural antibody-associated disease tends to leave persistent cognitive deficits. Overall outcome is governed by the antibody type and the stage and treatability of the underlying tumour.

Tumour-related immune dysregulation drives production of autoantibodies against a broad panel of antigens, characteristically the plakin family proteins envoplakin and periplakin, together with desmogleins and other desmosomal and hemidesmosomal components. This wide antigen targeting explains the polymorphous mucocutaneous picture, combining intraepidermal acantholysis with interface (lichenoid) inflammation. Both humoral and cell-mediated mechanisms contribute, and antibody or cytotoxic attack on respiratory epithelium can produce bronchiolitis obliterans, contributing to high mortality. Prognosis is generally poor, with high mortality driven by the underlying malignancy, sepsis, and respiratory failure from bronchiolitis obliterans; skin disease may improve if a benign tumour is fully removed but often remains refractory.

paraneoplastic retinopathy — cancer-associated retinopathy, melanoma-associated retinopathy retinitis pigmentosa and other inherited retinal dystrophies acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR) non-paraneoplastic autoimmune retinopathy toxic or drug-induced retinopathy vitamin A deficiency retinopathy retinal vascular occlusion compressive or inflammatory optic neuropathy full-field electroretinography to characterise photoreceptor versus ON-bipolar dysfunction serum anti-retinal antibody panel (anti-recoverin, anti-alpha-enolase and others) optical coherence tomography of the outer retinal layers fundus autofluorescence imaging automated perimetry for scotomata and field constriction whole-body FDG-PET/CT and CT chest for occult malignancy dermatological review and imaging for melanoma when MAR is suspected Cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) causes subacute, painless, usually bilateral though often asymmetric visual loss with photosensitivity, shimmering photopsiae, ring scotomata and impaired colour vision. Melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR) typically arises in a patient with known cutaneous melanoma and presents with night blindness and shimmering photopsiae with relatively preserved acuity. CAR is most often linked to small-cell lung carcinoma and to gynaecological and breast cancers, with anti-recoverin and anti-alpha-enolase antibodies. MAR is caused by antibodies against retinal ON-bipolar cells (including TRPM1) and correlates with metastatic melanoma. The full-field electroretinogram is the key test: CAR shows reduced a- and b-waves (photoreceptor dysfunction) whereas MAR shows a selectively reduced b-wave with a preserved a-wave, producing an electronegative waveform. The fundus is frequently normal early, with later arteriolar attenuation, retinal pigment epithelial mottling and optic disc pallor. In CAR the visual symptoms may precede the cancer diagnosis, prompting a systemic malignancy search. Response to immunosuppression is generally limited and visual recovery is often incomplete. rapidly progressive bilateral visual loss a known or newly suspected melanoma or lung carcinoma constitutional symptoms suggesting occult malignancy electronegative electroretinogram indicating bipolar cell dysfunction Mistaking the presentation for retinitis pigmentosa and missing the paraneoplastic cause. Being falsely reassured by a normal-appearing fundus in the early stages. Failing to order electroretinography, which is central to the diagnosis. Overlooking a history of melanoma in a patient presenting with night blindness. Circulating antibodies directed against retinal antigens shared by the tumour trigger photoreceptor or bipolar cell injury. In cancer-associated retinopathy, antibodies against recoverin and alpha-enolase promote calcium-dependent photoreceptor apoptosis. In melanoma-associated retinopathy, antibodies against ON-bipolar cell antigens such as TRPM1 impair signal transmission from photoreceptors to bipolar cells, explaining the selective b-wave loss on electroretinography. The resulting outer retinal and bipolar dysfunction produces progressive, often irreversible visual impairment. Visual prognosis is often poor; cancer-associated retinopathy tends to be progressive, while melanoma-associated retinopathy is more variable. Tumour treatment and immunosuppression have limited efficacy in restoring vision.

paraneoplastic sensory neuronopathy — subacute sensory neuronopathy, Denny-Brown syndrome Sjogren syndrome-associated sensory ganglionopathy platinum (cisplatin/oxaliplatin) chemotherapy neurotoxicity pyridoxine (vitamin B6) toxicity vitamin B12 or vitamin E deficiency chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (sensory variant) hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy tabes dorsalis serum and CSF anti-Hu (ANNA-1) and paraneoplastic antibody panel nerve conduction studies and EMG demonstrating a sensory ganglionopathy pattern anti-Ro/La antibodies and Schirmer test to assess for Sjogren syndrome whole-body FDG-PET/CT and CT chest for occult malignancy MRI spine looking for posterior column T2 hyperintensity vitamin B12 and vitamin B6 levels CSF analysis for pleocytosis and oligoclonal bands Subacute, often asymmetric and multifocal sensory loss that is non-length-dependent, affecting the face, trunk and proximal limbs as well as the distal extremities. Failing to screen for Sjogren syndrome, the principal non-paraneoplastic cause. Not pursuing small-cell lung carcinoma when anti-Hu antibodies are positive. Overlooking a drug or vitamin cause such as platinum agents or pyridoxine excess. An immune response against intracellular onconeural antigens (most often HuD, expressed by small-cell lung carcinoma) targets the sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglia. Cytotoxic T-cell mediated inflammation and neuronal destruction within the ganglia produce a ganglionopathy affecting both large and small fibres. Because the primary sensory cell body is destroyed, deficits are non-length-dependent and largely irreversible, and secondary degeneration of the central posterior columns and peripheral sensory axons follows. Recovery of sensory function is usually poor because the ganglion neurons are destroyed; the realistic therapeutic goal is stabilisation through treatment of the underlying tumour. Functional outcome is often limited by persistent sensory ataxia.

1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in suspected lymphoma Serum sodium and osmolality with paired urine osmolality and urine sodium for SIADH Plasma ACTH, urine-free cortisol, high-dose (8 mg) dexamethasone suppression test, and inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH stimulation (>3:1 central:peripheral ACTH ratio suggests pituitary source) Serum glucose with insulin, IGF-II, and IGF-II/IGF-I ratio (>10:1 suggestive) for tumor hypoglycemia Serum phosphorus, FGF23, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D for oncogenic osteomalacia; octreotide scan to localize tumor Hematocrit, red cell mass, and serum erythropoietin for erythrocytosis Compression ultrasonography/impedance plethysmography (venography if equivocal) for DVT; ventilation-perfusion scan, chest radiograph, ECG, and ABG for suspected pulmonary embolism Functional imaging (CT, MRI, PET, octreotide scintigraphy) to localize hormone-producing tumors, particularly when endocrine features precede cancer diagnosis Hypercalcemia of primary hyperparathyroidism Exogenous glucocorticoid (iatrogenic) Cushing's syndrome Drug-induced or volume-depletion hyponatremia Insulinoma or factitious hypoglycemia (vs IGF-II tumor hypoglycemia) Paraneoplastic syndromes are disorders accompanying benign or malignant tumors that are NOT due to direct mass effect, invasion, or metastasis; neuroendocrine tumors such as small-cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) and carcinoids are especially common sources, and these syndromes are more common than generally appreciated (Harrison 22e p.736). Hormones may be eutopic (from normal tissue of origin) or ectopic (atypical source); ectopic expression is often quantitative rather than absolute and is characterized by defective feedback regulation (e.g., ectopic ACTH) and release of large, unprocessed precursor peptides such as POMC (Harrison 22e p.736). The three most common paraneoplastic endocrine syndromes are hypercalcemia from PTHrP overproduction, hyponatremia from excess vasopressin (SIADH), and Cushing's syndrome from ectopic ACTH (Harrison 22e p.737). Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (HHM) occurs in up to 20% of cancer patients, is most often caused by PTHrP, and favoring features over primary hyperparathyroidism are known malignancy, recent onset, and very high calcium; PTH is suppressed and an elevated PTHrP is raised in roughly 80% of hypercalcemic cancer patients (Harrison 22e p.737-738). HHM produces hypercalciuria and hypophosphatemia like hyperparathyroidism, but is typically accompanied by metabolic alkalosis rather than the hyperchloremic acidosis of hyperparathyroidism; lymphomas can cause hypercalcemia via 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D rather than PTHrP (Harrison 22e p.737-738). Ectopic vasopressin causes SIADH in at least half of SCLC patients; hyponatremia with low serum osmolality occurs alongside an inappropriately normal or high urine osmolality, and intake of free water (oral or IV) can rapidly worsen the hyponatremia (Harrison 22e p.738). Ectopic ACTH accounts for 10-20% of Cushing's syndrome; SCLC is the leading cause, followed by bronchial and thymic carcinoids; plasma ACTH is usually >22 pmol/L (>100 pg/mL) and urine-free cortisol is typically more than 2-4 times normal (Harrison 22e p.738-739). Ectopic ACTH Cushing's differs from pituitary disease: less weight gain/centripetal fat (brief exposure plus cachexia), but prominent fluid retention, hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, glucose intolerance, and hyperpigmentation from MSH within the POMC precursor (Harrison 22e p.739). Most ectopic ACTH sources fail to suppress with high-dose dexamethasone (8 mg suppresses ~80% of pituitary adenomas but fails in ~90% of ectopic cases), though bronchial and other carcinoids are notable exceptions that may show pituitary-like feedback (Harrison 22e p.739). Non-islet-cell tumor hypoglycemia is driven by IGF-II precursor; serum IGF-II may not be markedly elevated, but an IGF-II/IGF-I ratio greater than 10:1 is suggestive, and the responsible tumor is usually large (>10 cm) and clinically apparent (Harrison 22e p.739-740). Oncogenic (tumor-induced) osteomalacia from FGF23 (phosphatonin) presents with low serum phosphorus, renal phosphate wasting, low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, but NORMAL serum calcium and PTH; it is usually caused by benign mesenchymal tumors and reverses with tumor resection (Harrison 22e p.739-741). Among paraneoplastic hematologic syndromes (erythrocytosis, granulocytosis, thrombocytosis, eosinophilia), red/white/platelet elevations are usually self-limited and asymptomatic; by far the most consequential hematologic abnormality in cancer patients is hypercoagulability (Harrison 22e p.740). Migratory or recurrent thrombophlebitis can be the initial manifestation of cancer; peripheral venous thrombosis coexisting with visceral carcinoma, especially pancreatic cancer, is termed Trousseau's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.741). Markedly elevated calcium (>3.5 mmol/L [>14 mg/dL]) with fatigue, altered mentation, polyuria, dehydration, or arrhythmias (short ST/QT, bundle branch block, bradyarrhythmia) Severe hyponatremia (Na <115 meq/L) or any hyponatremia with confusion, depressed mental status, or seizures Profound hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis and hypertension in ectopic ACTH; opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, mycoses) are a frequent cause of death Increased venous thromboembolism risk in ectopic ACTH and in cancer generally; migratory/recurrent thrombophlebitis or clot in an unusual site New atypical clinical or metabolic findings in a known cancer patient should prompt consideration of a paraneoplastic syndrome Markedly elevated eosinophils (>5000/uL) causing dyspnea, wheezing, and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates Attributing atypical metabolic or neurologic findings to the malignancy or its treatment and overlooking a paraneoplastic syndrome Confusing HHM with primary hyperparathyroidism; PTH should be suppressed and acid-base pattern differs (alkalosis in HHM vs hyperchloremic acidosis in hyperparathyroidism) Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia, which can precipitate central pontine myelinolysis; correction should be gradual (about 0.5-1 meq/L per hour) Excluding ectopic ACTH on the basis of high-dose dexamethasone suppression alone, since bronchial/thymic carcinoids can suppress like pituitary adenomas; conversely a suppressed ACTH indicates an ACTH-independent cause Relying on serum IGF-II levels, which may be normal in tumor hypoglycemia because assays may miss IGF-II precursors (use the IGF-II/IGF-I ratio) Over-relying on D-dimer in cancer patients, where it is less predictive of DVT and rises with age without thrombosis Pursuing extensive cancer work-up after a first unprovoked thrombophlebitis or PE in a patient without cancer; targeted evaluation is reserved for refractory, unusual-site, or migratory/recurrent clots Neoplastic cells, particularly those of neuroendocrine origin (SCLC, carcinoids), secrete peptide hormones, cytokines, and growth factors or induce antibody production, altering endocrine, hematologic, and other systems independently of tumor bulk. Most ectopic hormone production reflects cellular dedifferentiation with derepression of developmental gene programs (epigenetic changes, altered microRNA expression); genetic rearrangements bringing a hormone gene under aberrant regulatory control are a rare alternative mechanism. HHM arises chiefly from tumor PTHrP, which binds the PTH receptor to mimic hyperparathyroidism (driven by PTHLH hypomethylation, hedgehog/Gli, TGF-beta, Ras activation, p53 loss); lymphomas may instead convert 25-OH vitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. SIADH results from ectopic vasopressin (often with co-expressed oxytocin) causing water retention and dilutional hyponatremia. Ectopic ACTH comes from unregulated POMC expression, with release of large biologically inactive fragments plus small amounts of active ACTH; very high cortisol overwhelms renal 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type II, allowing cortisol to act at mineralocorticoid receptors and produce severe hypokalemia. IGF-II precursor (from loss of 11p15 imprinting) causes hypoglycemia by acting on insulin/IGF-I receptors and suppressing GH and insulin. FGF23 forms a ternary complex with klotho and renal FGF receptors to reduce phosphate reabsorption and inhibit 1-alpha-hydroxylation. Hematologic syndromes are mediated by ectopic erythropoietin (erythrocytosis); G-CSF, GM-CSF, IL-6 (granulocytosis); IL-6/thrombopoietin (thrombocytosis); IL-5 (eosinophilia); and poorly defined procoagulants/cytokines (hypercoagulability). Endocrine paraneoplastic syndromes can cause substantial morbidity and may be the presenting clue to an occult malignancy; treatment of the underlying tumor is the mainstay but rarely alters overall survival or cancer progression. Hematologic cell-count syndromes are generally self-limited and asymptomatic, but thrombocytosis can mark advanced-stage disease and poorer prognosis. Hypercoagulability is the most consequential hematologic complication, and oncogenic osteomalacia and several endocrinopathies can reverse with successful tumor resection; checkpoint-inhibitor-associated endocrinopathies are generally irreversible and require lifelong hormone replacement. No single formal severity scale; severity is gauged by the magnitude and acuity of the biochemical derangement (e.g., calcium level and rate of rise, sodium level [Na <115 meq/L denotes severe hyponatremia], eosinophil count >5000/uL). For venous thromboembolism risk during chemotherapy, the Khorana risk score (Harrison Table 98-3) stratifies patients using cancer type, therapy, blood counts, and body mass index.

Paraphimosis — entrapped foreskin, irreducible retracted foreskin, trapped prepuce Preputial or penile oedema from another cause, such as insect bite or allergic angio-oedema Balanoposthitis Penile cellulitis Penile tourniquet syndrome from an encircling hair or thread Contact dermatitis Penile lymphoedema Clinical diagnosis by inspection of the retracted foreskin and constricting ring Assessment of glans colour and capillary refill to gauge perfusion Blood glucose, given the association of recurrent balanoposthitis with diabetes Swab if secondary infection is suspected Review of recent instrumentation or catheter history A urological emergency in which a retracted foreskin cannot be returned over the glans, forming a constricting band behind the corona The trapped prepuce and glans become progressively oedematous and painful, and delayed reduction risks arterial compromise, ischaemia, and necrosis of the glans Commonly iatrogenic, when the foreskin is retracted for catheterisation, cystoscopy, or cleaning and is not replaced afterwards Prompt manual reduction is the priority - reduce the oedema with sustained compression and adjuncts such as cold or osmotic agents, then push the glans back while drawing the foreskin forward Adequate analgesia or a penile block greatly aids reduction, and the goal is to relieve the constricting ring as quickly as possible If manual reduction fails, a dorsal slit or emergency circumcision is performed to release the constriction Elective circumcision may be offered later to prevent recurrence, and staff should always replace a retracted foreskin after any procedure A dusky, dark, or blistering glans indicating ischaemia Absent capillary refill of the glans Severe unremitting pain Signs of necrosis or systemic sepsis Failure of manual reduction Failing to recognise it as an emergency and delaying reduction Retracting a foreskin for catheterisation or examination and forgetting to replace it, the commonest iatrogenic cause Attempting reduction without adequate analgesia and without first reducing the oedema Confusing paraphimosis (foreskin stuck retracted) with phimosis (foreskin that cannot be retracted) Missing early ischaemic changes of the glans Paraphimosis develops when a tight foreskin is retracted behind the glans and left there. The constricting preputial ring first obstructs venous and lymphatic return from the distal penis, producing progressive oedema of the glans and inner prepuce. This swelling tightens the ring further in a vicious cycle, and if it is not relieved the rising tissue pressure eventually compromises arterial inflow, threatening ischaemia and necrosis of the glans. Management centres on breaking this cycle by reducing the oedema and returning the foreskin to its normal position before irreversible damage occurs. Excellent when reduced promptly; the outlook worsens sharply with delay, when tissue ischaemia and glans necrosis can occur, so time to reduction is critical.

Paraquat poisoning — paraquat toxicity, herbicide poisoning, gramoxone poisoning Corrosive ingestion from other agents Other lethal pesticide ingestions (organophosphate, aluminium phosphide) Acute respiratory distress syndrome from other causes Acute interstitial pneumonitis Caustic oesophageal injury Plasma or urine paraquat level and the urine dithionite qualitative test Serial renal and liver function tests Arterial blood gas and serial chest imaging to track evolving lung injury Full blood count and electrolytes Prognostic assessment using plasma concentration versus time since ingestion A highly lethal herbicide with no effective antidote; even small deliberate ingestions of concentrated solution are frequently fatal It concentrates in and selectively destroys the lungs, causing progressive pulmonary oedema, haemorrhage, and then relentless fibrosis over days to weeks Early features include painful corrosive burns to the mouth, throat, and oesophagus, vomiting, and abdominal pain Oxygen supplementation should generally be avoided or minimised, as high oxygen tension accelerates free-radical lung injury; supplemental oxygen is reserved for severe, refractory hypoxaemia Immediate gastrointestinal decontamination with an adsorbent such as activated charcoal or Fuller's earth is a priority if the patient presents very early Enhanced elimination (haemoperfusion or haemodialysis) and immunosuppression with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide have been tried, but none reliably alters the poor outcome Acute kidney injury and hepatic injury commonly precede the delayed, usually fatal, pulmonary fibrosis Plasma paraquat concentration plotted against time since ingestion helps estimate prognosis and guide the intensity of intervention Ingestion of concentrated solution or any large deliberate ingestion Early acute kidney injury, which predicts high toxin burden and poor outcome Progressive hypoxaemia and radiographic lung changes Extensive oropharyngeal and oesophageal corrosive burns Rising plasma paraquat level for the time since ingestion indicating a lethal exposure Giving liberal supplemental oxygen, which accelerates oxidative lung injury Delaying adsorbent decontamination in an early presentation Offering false reassurance during the deceptively stable early period before lung failure Underestimating lethality and under-treating the psychosocial and palliative needs of the patient Paraquat undergoes cyclical reduction and oxidation (redox cycling), generating large amounts of superoxide and other reactive oxygen species that deplete NADPH and cause lipid peroxidation and cell death. It is actively taken up and concentrated by alveolar epithelial (type I and II) cells, making the lung the primary target: an early destructive phase of alveolitis and haemorrhagic oedema is followed by an obliterative pulmonary fibrosis. The kidneys and liver, which also accumulate the compound, sustain acute injury, and high oxygen tensions worsen the oxidative damage. Prognosis is generally poor and dose-dependent; ingestion of concentrated formulation is usually fatal, with death from multi-organ failure early or from progressive pulmonary fibrosis over subsequent days to weeks, and no treatment has been shown to reliably improve survival.

Parasomnia — parasomnias, NREM parasomnia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, RBD, sleepwalking, night terrors Nocturnal (frontal-lobe) epilepsy Obstructive sleep apnoea with confusional arousals Nocturnal panic attacks Periodic limb movement disorder Dissociative or psychogenic nocturnal episodes Nocturnal delirium in the elderly Detailed history from patient and bed partner, including timing within the night and degree of recall Video polysomnography with expanded EEG montage to capture events and exclude seizures Neurological assessment and, where indicated, dopaminergic imaging when REM sleep behaviour disorder is suspected Screening for coexisting sleep apnoea as a trigger for arousals Review of medications and substances that can provoke parasomnias Parasomnias are undesirable physical or experiential events that intrude on sleep and are broadly divided by the sleep stage from which they arise into non-REM (NREM) and REM types NREM disorders of arousal (confusional arousals, sleepwalking, night terrors) typically occur in the first third of the night during deep slow-wave sleep, with the person appearing awake but confused and having little or no recall REM sleep behaviour disorder involves loss of the normal muscle atonia of REM sleep, so patients physically act out vivid, often violent dreams and can injure themselves or a bed partner REM sleep behaviour disorder is strongly associated with, and may precede by years, neurodegenerative alpha-synucleinopathies such as Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies NREM parasomnias are common and usually benign in children, tending to resolve with age, whereas new-onset events in adults warrant more careful evaluation Triggers that deepen or fragment sleep, including sleep deprivation, alcohol, fever, stress, and certain medications, can precipitate NREM events Management prioritises sleep hygiene, safety-proofing the bedroom, and removal of precipitants; pharmacological treatment is reserved for frequent, dangerous, or distressing episodes Nocturnal frontal-lobe seizures can mimic parasomnias and should be considered when events are stereotyped, very frequent, or occur repeatedly within a single night Dream enactment with violent behaviour suggesting REM sleep behaviour disorder and possible underlying neurodegeneration New-onset complex nocturnal behaviour in an adult without childhood history Stereotyped, repetitive episodes clustering within one night raising suspicion of nocturnal seizures Episodes causing injury to the patient or bed partner Mislabelling nocturnal seizures as benign parasomnia and delaying appropriate neurological workup Failing to counsel patients with REM sleep behaviour disorder about future neurodegenerative risk and bedroom safety Overlooking obstructive sleep apnoea as the arousal trigger driving NREM events Attempting to forcibly wake a sleepwalker, which may increase agitation and injury risk Parasomnias reflect incomplete or dysregulated transitions between wakefulness and sleep states rather than a single disease. In NREM disorders of arousal, partial awakening from slow-wave sleep leaves motor and autonomic systems active while consciousness and memory circuits remain asleep, producing complex behaviours without awareness; a genetic predisposition and any factor that increases slow-wave sleep or arousal frequency raises the risk. REM sleep behaviour disorder results from failure of the brainstem circuits that normally impose skeletal muscle atonia during REM sleep, allowing dream enactment; the underlying neuronal dysfunction is closely linked to synucleinopathy neurodegeneration. Other parasomnias, such as sleep-related eating or nightmare disorder, arise from analogous state-boundary instability. Most childhood NREM parasomnias are benign and remit spontaneously; adult NREM events can often be controlled by addressing precipitants, while REM sleep behaviour disorder tends to persist and carries an appreciable long-term risk of evolving neurodegenerative disease.

Parathyroid adenoma — primary hyperparathyroidism, PHPT, solitary parathyroid adenoma, hyperfunctioning parathyroid adenoma Malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia (PTH-related peptide or bony metastases) Parathyroid hyperplasia (four-gland disease) Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia Tertiary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease Vitamin D intoxication or granulomatous disease (e.g. sarcoidosis) Parathyroid carcinoma Serum calcium (corrected or ionised), phosphate, and intact PTH 24-hour urinary calcium to help exclude familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia Vitamin D level and renal function assessment Neck ultrasound and technetium-99m sestamibi scintigraphy for localisation 4D-CT or selective venous sampling in reoperative or non-localising cases Bone density (DXA) scan and renal imaging for end-organ effects The commonest cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is a single hyperfunctioning adenoma, with hyperplasia and, rarely, carcinoma accounting for the remainder Many patients are asymptomatic and detected on incidental hypercalcaemia; classical symptoms are summarised as bones, stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans The biochemical hallmark is hypercalcaemia with an inappropriately non-suppressed or elevated parathyroid hormone level Chronic disease can cause nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, osteoporosis or osteitis fibrosa cystica, peptic ulceration, and pancreatitis Localisation before surgery combines neck ultrasound with sestamibi scintigraphy, and 4D-CT is useful when these are discordant or negative Minimally invasive (focused) parathyroidectomy is favoured when a single adenoma is confidently localised, often guided by intraoperative parathyroid hormone measurement Consider familial and syndromic disease (MEN 1, MEN 2A, familial hyperparathyroidism) in young patients or those with multigland involvement Severe hypercalcaemia with confusion, dehydration, arrhythmia, or hypercalcaemic crisis requiring urgent treatment Very high calcium with a palpable neck mass or markedly elevated PTH raising suspicion of parathyroid carcinoma Renal impairment or obstructing calculi from longstanding disease Pathological fractures from advanced skeletal involvement Attributing hypercalcaemia to an adenoma without excluding familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, in whom surgery is inappropriate Relying on a single localising study and missing an ectopic (mediastinal or intrathyroidal) gland Overlooking four-gland hyperplasia and performing an inadequate focused exploration Failing to recognise MEN syndromes, leading to incomplete treatment and missed associated tumours Not monitoring for postoperative hypocalcaemia, including hungry bone syndrome after severe disease A parathyroid adenoma is a benign clonal proliferation of chief cells that secretes parathyroid hormone autonomously, independent of the normal negative feedback from serum calcium. Excess PTH increases osteoclastic bone resorption, enhances renal tubular calcium reabsorption while promoting phosphate excretion, and stimulates renal activation of vitamin D, which raises intestinal calcium absorption. The net result is hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia. Sustained bone resorption reduces bone density, and the filtered calcium load promotes renal stone formation and, over time, renal impairment. Surgical removal of a solitary adenoma is curative in the great majority, with normalisation of calcium and PTH and improvement in bone density and stone risk over time. Outcomes are excellent when a single gland is correctly identified; multigland disease or missed ectopic glands increases the risk of persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism.

subtract when albumin is high) Intact PTH by two-site assay - the key second test that separates PTH-dependent from PTH-independent disorders Serum phosphorus (low/low-normal in pHPT; elevated in some hypocalcemic states) Serum magnesium (hypo- or severe hypermagnesemia impairs PTH) Serum creatinine / renal function Serum 25(OH)D - useful in both hyper- and hypocalcemia to assess vitamin D stores Serum 1,25(OH)2D - useful in hypercalcemia (increased/inappropriately normal in granulomatous disease or lymphoma) and suspected vitamin D resistance PTHrP level when hypercalcemia of malignancy is suspected with suppressed PTH Serum free light chains / SPEP-UPEP with immunofixation to exclude multiple myeloma Calcium/creatinine clearance ratio (<0.01 suggests FHH); 24-hour urinary fractional calcium excretion (>0.02 supports pHPT) Genetic sequencing of CASR, GNA11, AP2S1 for definitive FHH diagnosis when urine studies are inconclusive; genetic testing for syndromic/hereditary pHPT (MEN, CDC73) ECG (hypercalcemia: bradycardia, AV block, QRS widening, short QTc; hypocalcemia: QTc prolongation) Pseudohypercalcemia (e.g., calcium-binding IgM in Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia) and pseudohypocalcemia (low albumin from malnutrition, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis; gadoversetamide MRI contrast) - artifactual values requiring albumin correction before workup Sarcoidosis and other granulomatous disease - 1,25(OH)2D-mediated hypercalcemia Lymphoma (B cell, cutaneous T cell/Sezary) - extrarenal 1,25(OH)2D Thyrotoxicosis, Paget's disease, immobilization - increased bone resorption mimicking parathyroid hypercalcemia Thiazides, lithium, vitamin A, foscarnet, teriparatide, aromatase inhibitors - drug-induced hypercalcemia Acute pancreatitis, rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis, burns - hypocalcemia from tissue injury / hyperphosphatemia Respiratory or metabolic alkalosis - hypocalcemia from increased calcium binding to albumin Primary hyperparathyroidism (pHPT) and malignancy are the two most common causes of hypercalcemia; the diagnostic split hinges on the PTH level (Harrison 22e p.3271). pHPT is almost always a benign neoplastic disorder of the parathyroids (adenoma or hyperplasia) producing PTH that is not appropriately suppressed by the elevated calcium; parathyroid carcinoma is a rare cause (Harrison 22e p.3271). In hypercalcemia, an elevated or 'inappropriately normal' PTH with elevated calcium and low/low-normal phosphorus is almost always pHPT; because of PTH's phosphaturic action, pHPT hypercalcemia is often accompanied by low/frankly low serum phosphate (Harrison 22e p.3271). A suppressed PTH in the face of hypercalcemia means the process is independent of the parathyroid glands and is most often malignancy; many solid tumors secrete PTHrP, which mimics PTH at its receptor on bone and kidney (Harrison 22e p.3271). Hypercalcemia from lymphoma or granulomatous disease (e.g., sarcoidosis, tuberculosis) is driven by extrarenal macrophage CYP27B1 conversion of 25(OH)D to 1,25(OH)2D; in such cases 1,25(OH)2D is increased or inappropriately normal (Harrison 22e p.3271). Classic chronic hypercalcemia (months to years, fluctuating between high-normal and just above normal) is most often pHPT or FHH, occasionally multiple myeloma; malignancy-associated hypercalcemia usually has a more acute course (Harrison 22e p.3271). Mild hypercalcemia (10.5-11.9 mg/dL) is largely asymptomatic; symptoms ('stones, bones, groans') include nephrolithiasis, reduced bone density / bone pain or pathologic fractures with long-standing hyperparathyroidism, constipation/nausea/vomiting/anorexia/peptic ulcer/pancreatitis, plus fatigue, proximal weakness, hyporeflexia, and neuropsychiatric changes (Harrison 22e p.3271). Hypocalcemia is differentiated by whether PTH is low (hypoparathyroidism) or high (secondary hyperparathyroidism); a low or 'inappropriately low' PTH with hypocalcemia establishes hypoparathyroidism, whereas an elevated PTH points to the vitamin D axis or primary small-bowel calcium malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.3271). In adults, hypoparathyroidism most commonly results from inadvertent damage to all four parathyroid glands during thyroid or parathyroid surgery; autoimmune endocrinopathy accounts for about a quarter of cases (Harrison 22e p.3271). Neuromuscular irritability of hypocalcemia is detected by Chvostek's sign (perioral twitch on tapping the facial nerve) and the more specific Trousseau's sign (carpal spasm after inflating a BP cuff above systolic for 3 min); paresthesias of fingers, toes, and circumoral region are typical (Harrison 22e p.3271). Because PTH is the main minute-by-minute defense against hypocalcemia, hypoparathyroidism can produce profound, life-threatening hypocalcemia, whereas vitamin D deficiency causes less severe hypocalcemia since the parathyroids mount a compensatory PTH rise (at the expense of bone) (Harrison 22e p.3271). Impaired PTH secretion may be secondary to magnesium deficiency (via intracellular effects); hypomagnesemic hypocalcemia will not correct until magnesium is repleted (Harrison 22e p.3271). Hungry bone syndrome after parathyroidectomy is a recognized cause of post-operative hypocalcemia with high PTH (Harrison 22e p.3271). Moderate-to-severe hypercalcemia (>=12-14 mg/dL) with progressive lethargy, stupor, or coma Hypercalcemia with acute renal failure and volume depletion from polyuria Hypercalcemic ECG changes: bradycardia, AV block, QRS widening, short QTc Severe hypocalcemia causing seizures, carpopedal spasm, bronchospasm, or laryngospasm Hypocalcemic QTc prolongation with risk of ventricular tachyarrhythmia (Torsade) and sudden death Tetany (positive Trousseau's sign / carpal spasm) signaling impending neuromuscular crisis New severe hypocalcemia after thyroid or parathyroid neck surgery (damage to all four glands), especially in patients with prior malabsorption Syndromic pHPT with a jaw tumor (CDC73 mutation) carrying ~30% lifetime risk of parathyroid carcinoma Failing to correct calcium for albumin before launching a workup - low albumin can mask true hypercalcemia and falsely suggest hypocalcemia (Harrison 22e p.3271). Mistaking FHH for pHPT: FHH can present with mildly elevated PTH and hypercalcemia, but parathyroid surgery is ineffective; a calcium/creatinine clearance ratio <0.01 and family history of mild asymptomatic hypercalcemia or repeated failed neck surgeries should prompt CASR/GNA11/AP2S1 testing (Harrison 22e p.3271). Overlooking lithium therapy, which raises the CaSR set point and can cause hyperparathyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3271). Not repleting magnesium in hypocalcemia: hypomagnesemia impairs PTH secretion and the hypocalcemia will not correct until magnesium is restored (Harrison 22e p.3271). Chvostek's sign is nonspecific - present in ~10% of normal individuals; Trousseau's sign is the more definitive marker of neuromuscular irritability (Harrison 22e p.3271). Attributing hypercalcemia of immobilization solely to bed rest - an unrecognized resorptive process (pHPT, Paget's, myeloma) may be the real driver, especially in older patients (Harrison 22e p.3271). When tetany accompanies alkalosis, a second cause of impaired calcium homeostasis is usually present (Harrison 22e p.3271). Ectopic PTH secretion, unlike pHPT, does not fluctuate with correction of calcium because it is not under CaSR control (Harrison 22e p.3271). Extracellular calcium is held in a narrow range (~8.5-10.5 mg/dL) by feedback among the parathyroids, kidney, bone, and intestine. A fall in ECF calcium is sensed by the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) on parathyroid chief cells, triggering PTH release; PTH increases bone calcium resorption, distal-tubule reabsorption of filtered calcium, and renal proximal-tubule 1,25(OH)2D production, and 1,25(OH)2D in turn raises intestinal calcium absorption. Hypercalcemia arises from derangements of this loop: PTH-dependent overproduction (pHPT due to adenoma/hyperplasia, rarely carcinoma; tertiary hyperparathyroidism; ectopic PTH; FHH and CaSR-altering states such as lithium), or PTH-independent mechanisms (PTHrP-secreting tumors, lytic skeletal metastases, extrarenal 1,25(OH)2D production in granulomatous disease/lymphoma, vitamin D intoxication, increased bone resorption from thyrotoxicosis/Paget's/immobilization, and calcium overload e.g. milk-alkali). Hypocalcemia results from low PTH (hypoparathyroidism: surgical, autoimmune, infiltrative, genetic, CaSR-activating, or magnesium-related) or high PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency, renal failure, intestinal malabsorption, or PTH resistance/pseudohypoparathyroidism). Low calcium increases neuromuscular irritability (Harrison 22e p.3271). Mild, asymptomatic hypercalcemia (commonly pHPT detected incidentally in settings with routine calcium screening) carries a benign short-term course, whereas advanced pHPT can cause severe skeletal disease (osteitis fibrosa cystica). Hypoparathyroidism, because PTH is the chief minute-by-minute defense against hypocalcemia, can be profound, debilitating, and life-threatening, while vitamin D-deficiency hypocalcemia is typically milder owing to compensatory PTH secretion (at the expense of bone). Severe hypercalcemia (coma, renal failure, arrhythmia) and severe hypocalcemia (seizures, laryngospasm, Torsade) are medical emergencies (Harrison 22e p.3271). Hypercalcemia severity (Harrison 22e p.3271): mild 10.5-11.9 mg/dL (largely asymptomatic); moderate >=12-14 mg/dL; severe >=14 mg/dL (progressive lethargy, stupor, coma, prominent GI symptoms, acute renal failure). Hypocalcemia severity ranges from asymptomatic (mild/chronic) to moderate-severe with paresthesias, positive Chvostek's/Trousseau's signs, through severe with seizures, carpopedal spasm, broncho-/laryngospasm, and QTc prolongation with arrhythmia risk.

for persistent disease, are central to management Severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia or hypercalcaemic crisis with dehydration, confusion, and cardiac effects A palpable neck mass accompanying primary hyperparathyroidism Very high PTH and calcium far exceeding the usual adenoma range Local recurrence, hoarseness, or distant metastasis indicating malignant behaviour Mistaking carcinoma for a benign adenoma intraoperatively and rupturing the capsule, causing tumour seeding Attributing very high calcium and PTH with a palpable mass to a simple adenoma Relying on histology alone for diagnosis when features overlap with atypical adenoma Overlooking a germline CDC73 mutation and the associated familial syndrome Parathyroid carcinoma is a rare malignancy of the parathyroid chief cells that secretes excessive parathyroid hormone, driving severe hypercalcaemia through increased bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption, and vitamin D-mediated intestinal calcium absorption. A substantial proportion of tumours show inactivation of the CDC73 (HRPT2) tumour-suppressor gene, with germline mutations causing the hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome and predisposing to malignancy. Distinguishing carcinoma from atypical adenoma is challenging histologically and rests on unequivocal invasion of the capsule or vessels, invasion of adjacent structures, or metastasis, so the diagnosis is sometimes confirmed only when the disease recurs or spreads. Complete initial en-bloc resection offers the best outcome, but the tumour tends to recur locally and metastasise late; morbidity and mortality are driven largely by uncontrolled hypercalcaemia rather than tumour bulk.

Paratubal cyst — paraovarian cyst, hydatid of Morgagni, broad ligament cyst Ovarian follicular or functional cyst Hydrosalpinx Peritoneal inclusion cyst Endometrioma Cystadenoma Ovarian neoplasm Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrating a cyst separate from a normal ovary Application of the split sign to confirm the ovary is distinct from the cyst Magnetic resonance imaging to localise larger or complex cysts Tumour markers where features are atypical Surgical and histological assessment when excision is undertaken Thin-walled cysts lying within the broad ligament or mesosalpinx, between the fallopian tube and the ovary, and separate from ovarian tissue They arise from embryological remnants, either mesonephric (Wolffian) or paramesonephric (Müllerian) in origin The hydatid of Morgagni is a small pedunculated paramesonephric remnant that hangs near the fimbrial end of the tube Most are asymptomatic and found incidentally at imaging or surgery, appearing as simple unilocular cysts On ultrasound, demonstrating that the cyst is separate from a normal ipsilateral ovary is the key to diagnosis Larger cysts may cause pressure symptoms or undergo torsion, sometimes taking the adjacent tube or ovary with them Management ranges from expectant observation for small simple cysts to surgical excision for symptomatic, enlarging, or atypical lesions Torsion involving the cyst, tube, or ovary presenting with acute pain Rapid growth or solid vascular components suggesting a rare neoplastic change in the wall A large cyst causing significant pressure symptoms Features that cannot confidently be distinguished from ovarian malignancy Mistaking a paratubal cyst for an ovarian cyst and misdirecting management Failing to recognise torsion involving the adjacent tube or ovary Overlooking the rare borderline or neoplastic change that can arise in the cyst wall Unnecessary intervention for small, asymptomatic, clearly benign cysts Paratubal cysts develop from vestigial embryological structures in the broad ligament. Remnants of the mesonephric duct system, or of the paramesonephric duct that gives rise to the tube, persist and accumulate clear serous fluid to form a cyst. Because they lie alongside but outside the ovary, they retain a simple thin-walled structure; the pedunculated hydatid of Morgagni represents a paramesonephric remnant at the fimbrial end and is prone to torsion on its narrow stalk. Paratubal cysts are benign with an excellent outlook; simple cysts require little or no intervention, and surgical removal is curative when symptoms or diagnostic uncertainty warrant it.

preserved early, distinguishing it from progressive supranuclear palsy where downgaze is prominently affected Signs of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus requiring urgent neurosurgical assessment A pineal or tectal mass on imaging needing prompt oncological and surgical evaluation Rapidly progressive gaze failure with headache and papilloedema New reduced consciousness suggesting acute aqueduct obstruction Confusing the syndrome with progressive supranuclear palsy, which characteristically affects downgaze Missing early hydrocephalus that is treatable if recognised Overlooking contain the rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus and the posterior commissure fibres that mediate vertical gaze, together with the pretectal olivary nuclei serving the Prognosis depends entirely on the cause; relief of hydrocephalus or treatment of a tumour can improve the eye signs, while some patients retain a chronic upgaze limitation and pupillary abnormality.
