other cause Full blood count and film looking for giant alpha-granule-containing platelets Bone marrow examination for dysplastic micromegakaryocytes Cytogenetic analysis and array CGH to define the 11q deletion FLI1 status assessment within the deleted region Platelet function testing Echocardiography and developmental/dysmorphology assessment for Jacobsen syndrome features A congenital thrombocytopenia arising from deletion of the distal long arm of chromosome 11 (11q), which removes one copy of the megakaryocytic transcription factor FLI1 It is the haematological component of Jacobsen syndrome, which also features dysmorphism, cardiac defects, and intellectual disability The blood film characteristically shows a subset of platelets containing giant alpha-granules (fused granules) The bone marrow contains an increased number of small, immature, dysplastic micromegakaryocytes Thrombocytopenia is often present from birth and may improve somewhat during childhood, though anomalies should be actively sought Diagnosis combines the giant alpha-granule finding, marrow micromegakaryocytes, and cytogenetic or molecular demonstration of the 11q deletion Significant bleeding from thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction, especially in neonates Serious congenital cardiac defects associated with Jacobsen syndrome Feeding, growth, or developmental concerns requiring multidisciplinary input Perioperative haemorrhage requiring platelet support Treating the low count as immune thrombocytopenia and missing the underlying chromosomal deletion Failing to investigate for associated Jacobsen syndrome anomalies once the deletion is identified Overlooking the giant alpha-granule clue on the blood film Assuming normal platelet function once the count recovers, despite a persistent qualitative defect Paris-Trousseau syndrome results from hemizygous loss of FLI1, an ETS-family transcription factor essential for megakaryocyte differentiation, as part of a terminal 11q deletion (Jacobsen syndrome). Reduced FLI1 dosage disrupts the transcriptional programme of megakaryopoiesis, producing dysplastic micromegakaryocytes and a subpopulation of platelets with abnormally fused giant alpha-granules that do not release their contents normally. The result is thrombocytopenia with impaired platelet function; because the deletion spans multiple contiguous genes, the haematological defect coexists with the developmental features of Jacobsen syndrome. The thrombocytopenia often partially improves during childhood, but a functional platelet defect and the systemic features of Jacobsen syndrome determine overall prognosis, which varies with the extent of associated anomalies.

Attempting complete surgical cure of diffuse fistulae rather than selective control Neglecting orthopaedic management of limb-length discrepancy Parkes-Weber syndrome is a congenital fast-flow vascular anomaly in which a limb bears a capillary malformation together with numerous microscopic and macroscopic arteriovenous fistulae, causing direct arterial-to-venous shunting throughout the affected extremity. Many patients carry germline RASA1 variants within the capillary malformation-AVM spectrum, disrupting RAS-MAPK control of vascular differentiation. The persistent high-flow shunting drives limb overgrowth, venous hypertension and, when substantial, high-output cardiac strain; this fast-flow physiology is the key contrast with the slow-flow Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome. Prognosis depends on the extent of arteriovenous shunting; limited disease may be managed conservatively, but extensive fistulae can cause progressive limb morbidity, ulceration and cardiac strain. High-flow lesions are difficult to cure and often require staged, palliative interventions with long-term follow-up.

Parkinson's Disease — PD, parkinsonism Atypical parkinsonism: multiple-system atrophy (MSA) - cerebellar (MSA-c) and Parkinson (MSA-p) types Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) - parkinsonian and Richardson variants Corticobasal syndrome (CBS) Dementia with Lewy bodies / PD with dementia Secondary parkinsonism: drug-induced, tumor, infection, vascular, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, trauma, liver failure, toxins (carbon monoxide, manganese, MPTP, cyanide, hexane, methanol, carbon disulfide) Essential tremor (high-frequency 6-10 Hz symmetric postural tremor with prominent kinetic component) Wilson's disease Huntington's disease (especially the juvenile Westphal variant) Dopa-responsive dystonia (DRD) Spinocerebellar ataxias and neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (e.g., PANK-associated neurodegeneration) Infection-related secondary parkinsonism (basal ganglia damage from CNS infection) Post-influenza / postencephalitic parkinsonism (historical association with the influenza A epidemic); new-onset PD has been reported following SARS-CoV-2 infection, which can also worsen existing PD features Dopamine-system imaging with PET or SPECT (reduced, asymmetric striatal/posterior-putamen uptake); not routinely required Metabolic basal ganglia/thalamus imaging (18F-deoxyglucose) - may help distinguish atypical parkinsonism (decreased GPi with increased thalamic activity, the reverse of PD) MRI - to evaluate for vascular/structural causes and atypical features (e.g., midbrain 'hummingbird sign' in PSP, putaminal rim change or pontine 'hot cross bun' sign in MSA); transcranial sonography or special MRI protocols may detect increased SNc iron Alpha-synuclein seeding amplification assay (SAA) on CSF or skin - high sensitivity and specificity, can distinguish PD from other parkinsonisms (currently mainly research use) Genetic testing - selective use for strong family history, early onset (<40 years), or particular ethnic backgrounds (GBA1, LRRK2, SNCA, etc.); monogenic forms account for ~5% of cases (~15% including GBA1 variants) Serum/urinary copper studies to exclude Wilson's disease, which is treatable with copper chelators Drug-induced parkinsonism - most commonly dopamine-blocking neuroleptics, and also metoclopramide (a neuroleptic agent used for GI problems), tetrabenazine, calcium channel blockers (flunarizine, cinnarizine), amiodarone, and lithium Vascular parkinsonism (stroke affecting the SNc may closely resemble PD) Toxin-induced parkinsonism (carbon monoxide or manganese damaging the globus pallidus resemble atypical parkinsonism with poor levodopa response) Tumor and normal-pressure hydrocephalus Atypical parkinsonism (MSA, PSP, CBS) Essential tremor Dopa-responsive dystonia PD is the second most common age-related neurodegenerative disease after Alzheimer's; mean age of onset ~60 years, lifetime risk ~3% in men and ~2% in women, though cases can occur in the twenties or younger, particularly with a pathogenic gene mutation (p.3493). Cardinal motor features are bradykinesia, rest tremor, rigidity, and gait dysfunction with postural instability; additional motor features include freezing of gait, micrographia, masked facies (hypomimia), reduced eye blinking, drooling, soft voice (hypophonia), and dysphagia (p.3493-3494). Parkinsonism (bradykinesia with rigidity and/or tremor) combined with rest tremor, asymmetry of motor impairment, and a good levodopa response is much more likely to predict the correct pathologic diagnosis; with these U.K. Brain Bank Criteria, PD can be confirmed pathologically in >90% of patients (p.3495). Levodopa is the gold standard symptomatic therapy; almost all PD patients improve, and failure to respond to an adequate trial of levodopa should cause the diagnosis to be questioned (p.3501). Dopamine-system imaging (PET/SPECT) typically shows reduced, asymmetric striatal uptake, most pronounced in the posterior putamen with relative sparing of the caudate; it is useful when the diagnosis is uncertain but is not routinely required (p.3495-3496). Among forms of parkinsonism, PD is the most common (~75% of cases) (p.3495). Early speech and gait impairment with early falls, lack of rest tremor, and lack of motor asymmetry - suggests atypical parkinsonism Poor or no response to an adequate trial of levodopa - suggests atypical or secondary parkinsonism Exposure to neuroleptics - suggests drug-induced parkinsonism Onset before age 40 years - consider a genetic form of PD, Wilson's disease, or dopa-responsive dystonia Liver disease - consider Wilson's disease or non-Wilsonian hepatolenticular degeneration Hallucinations and dementia preceding or as the first/early feature - suggests dementia with Lewy bodies Diplopia, impaired vertical gaze, slow saccades with impaired downgaze - suggests PSP Prominent orthostatic hypotension or prominent cerebellar signs - suggests MSA Diagnosing PD on two of three cardinal features alone carries a ~24% postmortem error rate; rest tremor, motor asymmetry, and a good levodopa response markedly improve diagnostic accuracy (p.3495). Drug-induced parkinsonism is the most common secondary parkinsonism and is easily missed - remember that metoclopramide, used for GI symptoms, is a neuroleptic, and that calcium channel blockers (flunarizine, cinnarizine), tetrabenazine, amiodarone, and lithium can also be responsible (p.3497). Wilson's disease must be actively excluded because progression can be prevented with copper chelators (p.3497). Dopamine-system imaging cannot separate PD from atypical parkinsonism, since striatal dopamine depletion occurs in both (p.3496). Some genetic forms of PD (e.g., certain LRRK2 cases) may occur without Lewy bodies, and MPTP toxicity causes parkinsonism typically without Lewy bodies (p.3496, p.3498). Pathologic hallmarks are degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), reduced striatal dopamine, and intraneuronal alpha-synuclein-staining inclusions in cell bodies and axons (Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites; collectively Lewy pathology). Lewy pathology can also affect cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis of Meynert, noradrenergic neurons of the locus coeruleus, serotonergic raphe neurons, and the olfactory system, cerebral hemispheres, spinal cord, and peripheral autonomic nervous system, accounting for nonmotor features. Pathology may begin in the peripheral autonomic nervous system, GI tract, olfactory system, or dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and spread sequentially (Braak staging), giving rise to 'body-first' versus 'brain-first' concepts. In the basal-ganglia network, dopamine denervation leads to increased firing of the subthalamic nucleus (STN) and globus pallidus interna (GPi), excessive inhibition of the thalamus, reduced cortical motor activation, and the emergence of parkinsonian features. Pathogenesis involves an interacting network of oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, protein aggregation, excitotoxicity, and inflammation; a 'double hit' of genetic susceptibility plus an environmental insult has been proposed (p.3493-3494, p.3498-3500). PD is progressive. Levodopa prolongs independence and employability, improves quality of life, and increases life span, but chronic treatment with ongoing disease progression is associated in most patients with motor complications - response fluctuations ('on'/'off', wearing-off, on-off phenomenon) and dyskinesias. As the disease advances, nondopaminergic features that respond poorly to levodopa emerge - falling, freezing, autonomic dysfunction, sleep disorders, and dementia - and these (especially falls and dementia) are the primary source of disability and the main reason for hospitalization and nursing home placement in advanced PD. Atypical parkinsonisms generally follow a more aggressive course than classic PD (p.3496-3497, p.3501). Harrison does not present a single formal severity grading; clinical diagnostic confidence is staged by the MDS Clinical Diagnostic Criteria into 'clinically established PD' and 'clinically probable PD', which combine core motor parkinsonism with supportive criteria, absolute exclusion criteria, and red flags. Disease evolution is commonly framed by the emergence of levodopa-related motor complications and levodopa-unresponsive nondopaminergic features in advanced PD (p.3495-3496, p.3501).

Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria — PCH, Donath-Landsteiner haemolytic anaemia Cold agglutinin disease Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency haemolysis Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia Donath-Landsteiner test Direct antiglobulin test (often positive for complement only) Full blood count, reticulocytes and haemolysis markers Urinalysis for haemoglobinuria History of recent viral infection An uncommon cold-antibody haemolytic anaemia causing acute intravascular haemolysis after cold exposure It is most often seen in children following a viral infection and is usually self-limiting The causative Donath-Landsteiner antibody is a biphasic IgG that binds red cells in the cold and fixes complement on rewarming The antibody classically has specificity for the P antigen Presentation is with fever, back or abdominal pain, pallor and passage of dark (haemoglobinuric) urine Management is supportive with keeping warm and transfusion if needed; most childhood cases resolve spontaneously Severe acute anaemia with haemodynamic compromise Massive intravascular haemolysis with renal impairment Recurrent episodes suggesting an underlying disorder Very dark urine with rapidly falling haemoglobin Confusing it with cold agglutinin disease (different antibody and mechanism) Not requesting the Donath-Landsteiner test Failing to keep the patient warm during care and transfusion Overlooking haemoglobinuria as a sign of intravascular haemolysis Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria is mediated by the Donath-Landsteiner antibody, a biphasic IgG autoantibody usually directed at the P antigen. In the cooler peripheral circulation the antibody binds red cells and fixes early complement components; when the cells return to the warmer central circulation, the complement cascade completes, causing intravascular haemolysis and haemoglobinuria. It frequently follows a viral illness, particularly in children, and the transient antibody explains the self-limiting course. The post-viral childhood form is usually acute and self-limiting with an excellent prognosis; chronic or recurrent disease is rarer and may relate to an underlying condition.

(provoked by sudden movement), non-kinesigenic (spontaneous, often with alcohol or caffeine as triggers), and exercise-induced forms Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia commonly begins in childhood or adolescence, causes brief frequent attacks, and is frequently linked to PRRT2 gene mutations Paroxysmal non-kinesigenic dyskinesia tends to cause longer, less frequent attacks and is associated with PNKD (MR-1) gene mutations Paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia is provoked by sustained exertion and can be associated with GLUT1 deficiency, which has important dietary treatment implications Consciousness is preserved during attacks, which helps distinguish these disorders from epileptic seizures Kinesigenic forms are often strikingly responsive to low-dose anticonvulsant therapy, whereas non-kinesigenic forms respond less predictably and rely on trigger avoidance Secondary paroxysmal dyskinesias can occur with multiple sclerosis, stroke, metabolic disturbance, and other structural or acquired causes, which should be excluded Impaired awareness during episodes suggesting seizures rather than dyskinesia Fixed or progressive neurological deficits between attacks New onset in later adult life pointing to a secondary cause Developmental delay or refractory attacks suggesting an underlying metabolic disorder Misclassifying attacks as epilepsy or as functional without careful history of triggers and preserved awareness Missing GLUT1 deficiency in exercise-induced cases where dietary therapy would help Overlooking a secondary cause in later-onset disease Assuming poor treatment response before trying appropriate agents in kinesigenic forms Paroxysmal dyskinesias are episodic disorders of movement control involving basal ganglia and related motor circuits, with a strong genetic basis in the primary forms. Mutations in PRRT2 affect a synaptic protein and underlie many kinesigenic cases, PNKD (MR-1) mutations underlie the non-kinesigenic form, and SLC2A1 mutations causing GLUT1 deficiency impair glucose transport into the brain and produce exercise-induced attacks. The shared theme is transient, trigger-dependent dysfunction of neuronal excitability and motor network output rather than fixed structural damage, with normal function between events. Primary kinesigenic disease often responds well to treatment and may improve with age, giving a favourable outlook; non-kinesigenic and exercise-induced forms are more variable, though recognition of GLUT1 deficiency allows targeted dietary management with meaningful benefit.

paroxysmal dyskinesia secondary — secondary paroxysmal dyskinesia, symptomatic paroxysmal dyskinesia Primary (genetic) paroxysmal kinesigenic and non-kinesigenic dyskinesias Focal motor seizures and frontal lobe epilepsy Episodic ataxias Tonic spasms of multiple sclerosis Hyperekplexia and startle syndromes Functional (psychogenic) paroxysmal movement disorder Tics MRI brain and spinal cord for demyelination or structural lesions Serum glucose (including for non-ketotic hyperglycaemia) and HbA1c Serum calcium, phosphate, magnesium and parathyroid hormone EEG, ideally ictal, to exclude epilepsy Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and oligoclonal bands where demyelination suspected Genetic testing (e.g. PRRT2) when a primary disorder remains possible Autoimmune and paraneoplastic antibody screen in selected cases Secondary paroxysmal dyskinesias are episodic, self-limiting attacks of chorea, dystonia, athetosis or ballism arising from an identifiable acquired cause rather than a primary genetic channelopathy. Multiple sclerosis is a classic cause, producing brief, stereotyped paroxysmal dystonic or dyskinetic attacks, often precipitated by movement. Other causes include stroke and basal ganglia lesions, non-ketotic hyperglycaemia, hypoparathyroidism and other calcium disturbances, and central nervous system infection. Attacks are classified by trigger: kinesigenic (movement-induced), non-kinesigenic (spontaneous) and exertion-induced, mirroring the phenomenology of primary forms. Consciousness is preserved throughout and there is no ictal EEG correlate, helping distinguish attacks from focal seizures. A secondary cause is suggested by later age at onset, atypical or prolonged attacks, interictal neurological signs and abnormal neuroimaging. Kinesigenic secondary forms, like their primary counterparts, often respond well to low-dose sodium-channel-blocking anticonvulsants. The cornerstone of management is identifying and treating the underlying disorder, which may abolish the attacks. First presentation of demyelinating disease requiring urgent neurological evaluation New focal neurological deficit indicating stroke or a structural lesion Severe hyperglycaemia or profound hypocalcaemia needing urgent correction Features suggesting central nervous system infection or encephalitis Prolonged or increasingly frequent attacks with interictal deficits Misdiagnosing attacks as epileptic seizures and committing to inappropriate long-term antiepileptic strategy. Labelling episodes as functional without excluding demyelination, structural lesions or metabolic causes. Overlooking non-ketotic hyperglycaemia or hypocalcaemia as readily reversible triggers. Assuming a primary genetic disorder in a late-onset or atypical presentation. Failing to reassess for multiple sclerosis when paroxysmal attacks are the initial manifestation. Secondary paroxysmal dyskinesias arise when an acquired lesion or metabolic disturbance intermittently destabilises basal ganglia or related motor circuits, producing transient, self-terminating episodes of abnormal movement. In demyelinating disease, ephaptic transmission across demyelinated fibres in the basal ganglia, thalamus or their connections is thought to generate the brief, movement-triggered paroxysms. Structural lesions of the striatum or thalamus, and metabolic derangements such as hyperglycaemia or hypocalcaemia, transiently alter neuronal excitability and striatal output. The episodic nature, preserved consciousness and absence of an EEG correlate distinguish these movement paroxysms from epileptic seizures, reflecting a subcortical rather than cortical generator. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; attacks often resolve or improve markedly once a metabolic derangement is corrected or the primary disorder is treated. Kinesigenic secondary forms are frequently well controlled with low-dose anticonvulsants, whereas outlook otherwise tracks that of the causative disease.

Paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia — PED, paroxysmal exertion-induced dyskinesia Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia Paroxysmal non-kinesigenic dyskinesia Dopa-responsive dystonia Exercise-induced cramps or myopathy Functional (psychogenic) paroxysmal movements Genetic testing for SLC2A1 (GLUT1) and PRRT2 Paired cerebrospinal fluid and blood glucose to assess for GLUT1 deficiency Detailed characterisation of triggers and episode semiology MRI of the brain to exclude structural causes Trial of ketogenic diet where GLUT1 deficiency is confirmed Episodes of dystonia or choreoathetosis brought on by sustained or prolonged physical exertion, typically affecting the exercised limbs Attacks come on after minutes of continuous exercise rather than at the sudden onset of movement, distinguishing it from the kinesigenic form An important cause is glucose transporter type 1 (GLUT1) deficiency due to SLC2A1 mutations, which is treatable with a ketogenic diet GLUT1-related cases may also have epilepsy, developmental problems and a low cerebrospinal fluid glucose relative to blood The paroxysmal dyskinesia spectrum overlaps genetically with PRRT2-related disorders Recognising a GLUT1 cause is critical because dietary therapy can dramatically improve symptoms Associated seizures or developmental delay suggesting GLUT1 deficiency Progressive fixed neurological deficit Onset with atypical features suggesting a structural lesion Frequent disabling attacks affecting daily function Failing to test for GLUT1 deficiency and missing a diet-responsive cause Confusing it with the kinesigenic form triggered by sudden movement Mislabelling episodes as functional without genetic and metabolic workup Overlooking coexisting epilepsy in GLUT1-related disease Paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia is a paroxysmal movement disorder in which prolonged exertion triggers transient involuntary movements without loss of consciousness. A major mechanism is impaired glucose transport across the blood-brain barrier from GLUT1 deficiency, so that sustained metabolic demand during exercise outstrips brain glucose supply and precipitates dyskinesia. Other cases relate to channel and synaptic-protein abnormalities within the broader paroxysmal dyskinesia and PRRT2 spectrum, reflecting episodic dysfunction of basal ganglia motor control. Prognosis is generally good, especially when a treatable cause such as GLUT1 deficiency is identified and managed with diet; many other cases are controllable and non-progressive.

Why the disorder shows its characteristic near-universal sensitivity to indometacin remains incompletely understood but may relate to the drug's effects on prostaglandin-mediated vascular tone and intracranial pressure. With an adequate indometacin trial most patients gain complete relief; the episodic form may remit for long periods, while the chronic form usually requires ongoing preventive therapy, and prolonged indometacin use needs monitoring for gastrointestinal and renal effects.

strong therapeutic response to sodium-channel blockers that can confirm the diagnosis Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia is most often due to heterozygous loss-of-function variants in PRRT2 on chromosome 16, which encodes a presynaptic transmembrane protein that regulates neurotransmitter release through interactions with SNARE proteins and with voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels. Reduced PRRT2 function increases neuronal excitability, so a sudden movement or startle can trigger paroxysmal, self-limited abnormal basal-ganglia output experienced as brief dyskinesia. The shared molecular basis explains the clinical overlap with benign familial infantile seizures and hemiplegic migraine, and the marked benefit from sodium-channel blockade reflects stabilisation of this hyperexcitable state. PKD is a benign, non-degenerative condition; attacks frequently respond dramatically to low-dose sodium-channel-blocking therapy and often diminish or remit with age, so long-term outlook is favourable.

Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria — PNH, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria Aplastic anaemia Myelodysplastic syndrome Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemias (TTP/HUS) Other causes of intravascular haemolysis Inherited haemolytic anaemias Peripheral blood flow cytometry for GPI-anchored proteins (CD55/CD59) and FLAER to identify and size the PNH clone Full blood count, reticulocytes, and blood film Markers of intravascular haemolysis: LDH, haptoglobin, and urinary haemosiderin Direct antiglobulin test (typically negative) to exclude immune haemolysis Bone marrow examination with cytogenetics to assess for aplastic anaemia or myelodysplasia Imaging for suspected venous thrombosis, particularly abdominal veins An acquired clonal stem cell disorder in which red cells lack complement-regulating surface proteins and undergo intravascular haemolysis The classic clinical triad is complement-mediated haemolytic anaemia, a strong tendency to thrombosis, and variable degrees of bone marrow failure Haemoglobinuria is often most noticeable in the first morning urine, reflecting overnight complement activation, though continuous low-grade haemolysis is the rule Thrombosis, frequently at unusual sites such as hepatic (Budd-Chiari), portal, mesenteric, or cerebral veins, is the leading cause of death and is disproportionate to the degree of thrombocytopenia Free haemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, producing smooth-muscle-related symptoms such as abdominal pain, dysphagia, fatigue, and erectile dysfunction PNH is closely linked to aplastic anaemia and myelodysplasia, and clones can emerge from a failing marrow, so screening is warranted in these settings Diagnosis is made by flow cytometry demonstrating deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins (such as CD55 and CD59), often using the FLAER reagent, rather than older lysis tests Terminal complement inhibition markedly reduces haemolysis and thrombotic risk; anticoagulation is used for thrombotic events, and allogeneic transplant is reserved for marrow failure or refractory disease, with vaccination against encapsulated organisms before complement blockade Acute venous thrombosis, especially Budd-Chiari or other intra-abdominal or cerebral vein thrombosis Severe haemolytic exacerbation with profound anaemia or acute kidney injury Progressive pancytopenia indicating evolving marrow failure Meningococcal or other encapsulated-organism sepsis in patients receiving complement inhibition Not screening for a PNH clone in patients with unexplained intravascular haemolysis, aplastic anaemia, or myelodysplasia Attributing thrombosis solely to other risk factors and missing the underlying complement-mediated cause Relying on outdated lysis-based tests instead of flow cytometry for diagnosis Starting terminal complement inhibition without meningococcal vaccination and infection counselling Overlooking iron and folate needs or the nitric-oxide-related symptoms that drive morbidity PNH arises from an acquired somatic mutation in the PIGA gene within a haematopoietic stem cell, impairing synthesis of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor. As a result, the affected clone and its progeny lack GPI-anchored surface proteins, including the complement regulators CD55 and CD59 that normally protect cells from complement attack. Unprotected red cells are lysed by activated complement, producing chronic intravascular haemolysis with haemoglobinaemia and haemoglobinuria. Complement activation and free haemoglobin also promote platelet activation and consume nitric oxide, driving a marked prothrombotic state and smooth-muscle dystonia. The clone typically expands in the context of marrow injury, explaining its association with aplastic anaemia. Historically PNH carried substantial mortality, largely from thrombosis and marrow failure, but terminal complement inhibitors have greatly reduced haemolysis and thrombotic events and improved survival towards that of the general population; outcomes still depend on the degree of underlying marrow failure and access to therapy.

Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria — Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, PNH, Marchiafava-Micheli syndrome Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Aplastic anaemia Myelodysplastic syndrome Other causes of intravascular haemolysis including microangiopathy Hereditary haemolytic anaemias Inherited or acquired thrombophilia with venous thrombosis March or exertional haemoglobinuria Peripheral blood flow cytometry with FLAER and GPI-linked marker antibodies on multiple lineages Markers of intravascular haemolysis: lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, reticulocytes and bilirubin Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test, characteristically negative Urinalysis for haemoglobinuria and haemosiderinuria Full blood count and bone marrow examination to assess for marrow failure or myelodysplasia Cross-sectional or Doppler imaging where thrombosis is suspected Iron studies, as chronic urinary iron loss can cause deficiency Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria is an acquired clonal disorder caused by a somatic PIGA mutation in a haematopoietic stem cell, leading to loss of the GPI-anchored complement regulators CD55 and CD59. Absence of CD55 and CD59 leaves red cells exposed to unregulated complement, producing chronic intravascular Coombs-negative haemolysis with haemoglobinuria. The classic triad is intravascular haemolysis, a marked thrombotic tendency and a degree of bone marrow failure. Thrombosis, often at unusual sites such as the hepatic (Budd-Chiari), portal or cerebral veins, is the leading cause of death. Smooth-muscle dystonia from nitric oxide scavenging by free haemoglobin causes abdominal pain, dysphagia, erectile dysfunction and fatigue disproportionate to anaemia. There is a close relationship with aplastic anaemia and myelodysplastic syndrome, and a PNH clone may emerge in that setting. Diagnosis rests on flow cytometry demonstrating GPI-anchor-deficient cells, using fluorescent aerolysin (FLAER) and antibodies to GPI-linked proteins. Terminal complement blockade markedly reduces haemolysis and thrombotic risk but mandates meningococcal vaccination beforehand because of the resulting terminal-pathway deficiency. New or worsening abdominal pain suggesting hepatic or mesenteric vein thrombosis Neurological deficit or headache suggesting cerebral venous thrombosis Breathlessness or hypoxia suggesting pulmonary embolism or pulmonary hypertension Rapidly falling blood counts indicating evolving marrow failure Fever in a patient on terminal complement blockade, given meningococcal risk Excluding the diagnosis because the direct antiglobulin test is negative, when Coombs-negativity is expected. Overlooking paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria in unexplained venous thrombosis at unusual sites. Failing to screen for a PNH clone in aplastic anaemia or myelodysplastic syndrome. Starting terminal complement blockade without prior meningococcal vaccination and counselling. Attributing fatigue and smooth-muscle symptoms solely to the degree of anaemia rather than to nitric oxide depletion. Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria results from a somatic mutation in the X-linked PIGA gene within a haematopoietic stem cell, impairing synthesis of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor. Blood cells derived from this clone lack all GPI-anchored surface proteins, including the complement regulators CD55 (decay-accelerating factor) and CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis). Without these regulators, red cells cannot restrain the alternative pathway or the membrane attack complex on their surface, so complement lyses them, producing chronic intravascular haemolysis that worsens during complement-activating stresses such as infection. Liberated free haemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, causing smooth-muscle dystonia and promoting platelet activation, which, together with complement-mediated effects, underlies the characteristic thrombophilia. Clonal expansion is often favoured in the context of immune-mediated marrow failure. The natural history is variable and can span many years, but thrombosis and progressive marrow failure are the principal causes of death; terminal complement inhibition has substantially improved survival and quality of life, and allogeneic stem cell transplantation remains the only curative option in selected cases.

aplastic anaemia or myelodysplasia Missing iron deficiency from chronic urinary haemoglobin and haemosiderin loss Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria arises from an acquired somatic mutation in the X-linked PIGA gene within a haematopoietic stem cell, so it is a clonal but non-inherited disorder. PIGA is required for the first step in synthesis of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor that tethers many proteins to the cell surface. Loss of GPI anchoring strips the affected cells of the complement-regulatory proteins CD55 and CD59, which normally protect them from complement attack. Unopposed activation of the alternative complement pathway on red cells causes chronic intravascular haemolysis, releasing free haemoglobin that depletes nitric oxide and drives smooth-muscle dystonia and pulmonary hypertension. The PIGA-mutant clone often expands in the setting of immune-mediated marrow injury (as in aplastic anaemia), and complement activation on platelets and endothelium underlies the characteristic thrombotic tendency. The course is variable and can be chronic; thrombosis remains the major cause of mortality, but complement C5 inhibition has substantially improved survival and quality of life, and marrow failure or clonal evolution influences the long-term outlook.

Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardias — PSVT, AV nodal reentry tachycardia, AVNRT, AV reciprocating tachycardia, AVRT, Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome related SVT Atrioventricular nodal reentry tachycardia (AVNRT) Orthodromic AV reciprocating tachycardia (concealed or manifest AP) Atypical AVNRT (long R-P, P wave between QRS complexes) Focal atrial tachycardia Atrial flutter Atrial fibrillation Permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia (PJRT) from a slowly conducting septal AP Junctional ectopic / accelerated junctional rhythm Continuous ECG monitoring during the episode and during vagal/pharmacologic maneuvers (the response can establish the mechanism) 12-lead ECG during tachycardia (P-wave timing and morphology, pseudo-r' in V1, pseudo-S in inferior leads) and during sinus rhythm (delta wave, short PR) Echocardiography to exclude Ebstein's anomaly, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy associated with APs, or tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy Invasive electrophysiology study to define mechanism and to assess whether an AP can support rapid antegrade conduction (risk stratification) Ambulatory monitoring or exercise testing to look for abrupt loss of preexcitation suggesting a lower-risk pathway (not completely reliable) Ventricular tachycardia (especially versus antidromic AVRT or PSVT with aberrancy, wide-complex tachycardia) Sinus tachycardia Lateral or inferior wall myocardial infarction Q waves (mimicked by negative delta waves of left-sided or diaphragmatic accessory pathways) Bundle branch block pattern (mimicked by preexcitation: right-sided AP gives LBBB-like V1, left-sided AP gives RBBB-like V1) PSVT here refers to sustained supraventricular tachycardias that depend on the AV node: AVNRT, junctional tachycardia, AV reciprocating tachycardia (AVRT) using an accessory pathway, and preexcited tachycardias (Harrison 22e p.1938). AVNRT is the most common form of PSVT, accounting for roughly 60% of cases referred for catheter ablation, typically presenting in the second to fourth decades and more often in women (Harrison 22e p.1939). AVNRT mechanism is reentry within the AV node and perinodal atrium, made possible by dual conduction pathways; the typical form uses a slowly conducting pathway (right inferior nodal extension) for the antegrade limb and the fast pathway as the exit (Harrison 22e p.1939). In typical AVNRT atrial and ventricular activation are near-simultaneous, so the P wave falls during, just before, or just after the QRS and is hard to see — often appearing as a pseudo-r' in V1 and pseudo-S waves in leads II, III, and aVF (Harrison 22e p.1939). Simultaneous atrial and ventricular contraction drives atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve, producing cannon A waves and a fluttering neck sensation; elevated venous pressure can release natriuretic peptides causing post-tachycardia diuresis (Harrison 22e p.1939). Unlike atrial tachycardias, maneuvers or drugs that block the AV node terminate AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT, because the AV node is part of the reentry circuit (Harrison 22e p.1939). Accessory pathways occur in about 1 in 1500-2000 people; most patients have structurally normal hearts, but APs are associated with Ebstein's anomaly and certain hypertrophic cardiomyopathies including PRKAG2 mutations, Danon's disease, and Fabry's disease (Harrison 22e p.1940). Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is defined as ventricular preexcitation during sinus rhythm (short PR <0.12 s, delta wave, widened QRS) plus episodes of PSVT (Harrison 22e p.1940). Orthodromic AVRT is the most common AP-mediated PSVT: the wavefront goes antegrade down the AV node/His-Purkinje and returns retrograde up the AP, giving a narrow (or aberrant) QRS with the P wave always following the QRS, never simultaneous with it (Harrison 22e p.1941). Concealed accessory pathways conduct only retrograde (ventricle to atrium), so no preexcitation is seen in sinus rhythm, yet SVT can still occur (Harrison 22e pp.1940-1941). Antidromic AVRT and bystander AP conduction produce preexcited (wide-complex) tachycardias that can be indistinguishable from monomorphic VT; the presence of preexcitation in sinus rhythm suggests the diagnosis (Harrison 22e pp.1941-1942). Junctional ectopic tachycardia arises from automaticity within the AV node, is rare in adults, and is more often seen as an incessant tachycardia in children, especially perioperatively after congenital heart surgery (Harrison 22e p.1940). Hemodynamic instability with hypotension, loss of consciousness, or respiratory distress Preexcited atrial fibrillation presenting as a very irregular wide-complex tachycardia Accessory pathway with shortest preexcited R-R interval <250 ms during AF (about 25% of preexcitation-causing APs), associated with higher risk of ventricular fibrillation and sudden death Wide-complex tachycardia that cannot be confidently distinguished from VT (manage as VT until proven otherwise) Rapid SVT in the elderly precipitating angina, pulmonary edema, hypotension, or syncope Administering AV nodal-blocking agents (verapamil, diltiazem, beta blockers, adenosine, amiodarone) during preexcited AF is contraindicated, as slowing the AV node without slowing the AP can accelerate ventricular rate and precipitate ventricular fibrillation (Harrison 22e p.1942). Gradual loss of AP conduction with rising sympathetic tone on exercise testing does not reliably indicate a low-risk pathway, because it can simply reflect shortening AV nodal conduction time (Harrison 22e p.1942). Adenosine itself can precipitate atrial fibrillation in up to ~15% of patients, which is hazardous in WPW where AF may cause hemodynamic instability (Harrison 22e p.1942). Adenosine is contraindicated after cardiac transplantation due to denervation hypersensitivity and may aggravate bronchospasm (Harrison 22e p.1942). Negative delta waves from left-sided or diaphragmatic/paraseptal APs can mimic Q waves of lateral or inferior myocardial infarction (Harrison 22e p.1940). Left free wall APs may show minimal or absent preexcitation on the 12-lead ECG because of the distance from the sinus node, so preexcitation can be missed (Harrison 22e p.1940). PJRT and atypical AVNRT both produce long R-P tachycardias that can be difficult to distinguish from atrial tachycardia without an invasive EP study (Harrison 22e p.1941). PSVTs in this group are AV node-dependent. AVNRT is a reentrant circuit within the compact AV node and perinodal atrium enabled by dual pathways: a slowly conducting pathway (usually the right inferior nodal extension running toward the coronary sinus floor) and a faster pathway near the His bundle, allowing a self-sustaining loop. Accessory pathways are congenital muscular connections that bridge atrium and ventricle across the fibrous AV rings owing to incomplete partitioning during development; they most often lie at the left free wall, followed by posteroseptal, right free wall, and anteroseptal sites. Antegrade conduction over an AP produces ventricular preexcitation (short PR, delta wave, wide QRS), with QRS/delta morphology determined by pathway location. AVRT reentry circulates between the AV node/His-Purkinje system and the AP (orthodromic when antegrade over the node and retrograde over the AP, antidromic when reversed). Junctional ectopic tachycardia is due to abnormal automaticity within the AV node rather than reentry (Harrison 22e pp.1938-1942). In patients without structural heart disease, AVNRT is not life-threatening though it may cause significant symptoms. Catheter ablation of the slow AV nodal pathway is curative in over 95% of cases, with a risk of AV block requiring permanent pacing in under 1%. For accessory pathways, ablation efficacy is around 95% (varies by location) with serious complications in under 3% and procedural mortality under 1 in 1000. Risk of cardiac arrest in symptomatic preexcitation patients is roughly 2 per 1000 adults and likely higher in children. Adults with asymptomatic preexcitation have an estimated sudden death risk of about 1 per 1000 patient-years, while children carry a higher risk of around 2 per 1000 patient-years (Harrison 22e pp.1939-1942). No formal severity grading scale; risk is stratified clinically by hemodynamic stability and, for accessory pathways, by the capacity for rapid antegrade conduction. A shortest preexcited R-R interval <250 ms during atrial fibrillation marks a high-risk pathway predisposing to ventricular fibrillation and sudden death (Harrison 22e p.1942).

paroxysms through unrecognised triggering care activities Undertreating hyperthermia and hypertension, allowing secondary injury Abruptly stopping controlling medication and precipitating rebound storms Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity follows severe brain injury and reflects a loss of the normal inhibitory control that higher centres exert over spinal and brainstem sympathetic circuits. One influential model proposes that injury disconnects descending inhibitory pathways, leaving excitatory spinal circuits disinhibited, so that ordinarily non-noxious stimuli provoke exaggerated, paroxysmal sympathetic discharges (an 'excitatory-to-inhibitory ratio' disturbance). The result is episodic surges of sympathetic outflow producing tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, sweating, and motor posturing, often with allodynia-like sensitivity to stimulation. The paroxysms subside as recovery progresses, but sustained autonomic and metabolic stress can aggravate secondary brain injury. The presence of paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity is associated with more severe brain injury, longer intensive care and hospital stays, and worse short-term outcomes; the paroxysms themselves usually diminish over weeks to months as the brain recovers, although some autonomic features may persist.

Many cases are idiopathic and maturational, improving as the nervous system develops, while some are linked to channelopathies or to structural lesions of the midbrain and its vertical-gaze pathways. The down-beating saccades on attempted downgaze reflect preserved attempts to overcome the tonic upward drive. The idiopathic form usually improves over months to a few years, though some children have residual ataxia or cognitive and language difficulties; prognosis of secondary cases depends on the underlying cause.

associated neurological or ocular disease that requires specific management Failing to recognise the overlap with localised scleroderma and its implications for systemic assessment Parry-Romberg syndrome is a progressive hemifacial atrophy considered part of the localised scleroderma spectrum. Although the cause is not fully established, an immune-mediated, inflammatory process is favoured, potentially with neurovascular or trophic contributions, leading to progressive loss of dermal, subcutaneous, muscular, and occasionally osseous tissue confined largely to one side of the face. The inflammatory activity tends to be self-limited over months to years, after which atrophy stabilises, but the accumulated tissue loss produces lasting asymmetry. Its overlap with linear scleroderma 'en coup de sabre' supports a shared sclerodermatous mechanism, and associated central nervous system and ocular findings suggest the process can extend beyond the skin. The disease typically progresses over a period of years and then stabilises, leaving fixed facial asymmetry of variable severity. Prognosis for function is generally good once the active phase resolves, though neurological or ocular complications can cause lasting morbidity, and reconstructive surgery in the stable phase can substantially improve appearance.

Organised inflammatory exudate accumulates as a snowbank over the inferior pars plana and ora serrata, while cellular aggregates form snowballs in the vitreous. Persistent inflammation and breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier drive cystoid macular oedema and occasionally peripheral retinal neovascularisation. The condition overlaps with the demyelinating spectrum, hence its association with multiple sclerosis. The course is typically chronic and relapsing; vision is generally preserved when cystoid macular oedema is controlled, although complications such as cataract, glaucoma and retinal detachment may reduce the final outcome.

shoulder or musculoskeletal problem and delaying diagnosis Attributing patchy weakness to a single radiculopathy Overlooking phrenic or long thoracic involvement Failing to consider a hereditary (SEPT9) cause in recurrent or familial cases Assuming a uniformly rapid and complete recovery Parsonage-Turner syndrome is an immune-mediated inflammatory disorder of the brachial plexus and its branches. An aberrant immune response, frequently triggered by a preceding infection, vaccination, surgery, or physical stress, produces multifocal inflammation and secondary axonal damage of individual nerve fascicles. This patchy involvement explains why weakness does not follow a single nerve or root territory and why certain nerves such as the long thoracic, suprascapular, and anterior interosseous are preferentially affected. Nerve constrictions and hourglass-like fascicular changes have been demonstrated on imaging and at surgery. The severe early pain reflects the acute inflammatory phase, after which axonal loss produces the weakness and wasting. Most patients recover useful function over months to a few years, though recovery can be slow and incomplete, with residual weakness, fatigue, or scapular winging; recurrence is uncommon in the idiopathic form.

transfusion Abrupt severe anaemia with reticulocytopenia in a patient with chronic haemolysis (aplastic crisis) Progressive anaemia in an immunocompromised patient suggesting persistent infection Foetal hydrops, ascites, or abnormal Doppler indicating severe foetal anaemia Signs of high-output cardiac failure from profound anaemia Assuming a patient is no longer infectious once the rash appears, when contagiousness is greatest before the exanthem Relying on IgM serology in immunocompromised patients who may not mount an antibody response, missing the need for DNA PCR Overlooking small non-enveloped DNA virus transmitted by respiratory droplets, transfusion, and vertically across the placenta. It binds the P blood-group antigen (globoside) expressed on erythroid precursors and infects and lyses them, transiently halting red-cell production in the marrow. In healthy people the resulting brief drop in reticulocytes is clinically silent, and the rash and arthropathy that follow are immune-complex mediated as antibody develops. Where red-cell survival is already shortened by chronic haemolysis, this pause in erythropoiesis causes an abrupt fall in haemoglobin (aplastic crisis). When neutralising antibody cannot be generated, as in immunosuppression, infection persists and causes chronic pure red cell aplasia. In the foetus the combination of a short red-cell lifespan and rapid erythroid expansion makes severe anaemia, cardiac failure, and hydrops possible. Most immunocompetent infections are self-limiting with full recovery, arthropathy usually resolving over weeks to months; aplastic crisis recovers as immunity develops, immunoglobulin usually corrects persistent red cell aplasia, and foetal outcome depends on gestation and timely intrauterine transfusion.

Parvovirus Infections — Parvovirus B19 infection, B19V infection, Erythema infectiosum, Fifth disease, Slapped-cheek disease, Human bocavirus infection Other viral exanthems (B19V rash is difficult to distinguish clinically; laboratory confirmation is advised when a definite diagnosis is needed, such as in pregnancy) Rheumatoid arthritis (B19V polyarthropathy can mimic it, and rheumatoid factor may be present) Other causes of nonimmune hydrops fetalis Other causes of transient aplastic crisis or red cell aplasia Other respiratory viral infections (for HBoV1, which presents like other viral RTIs with fever, cough, wheezing) Co-infection with Plasmodium has been suggested to contribute to severe anemia in young children with malaria B19V IgM by indirect enzyme immunoassay - detectable at the time of rash in erythema infectiosum and by the third day of TAC; may persist about 3 months or longer B19V IgG - detectable by the seventh day of illness and persists for life, marking immunity; seroconversion or a fourfold or greater rise on paired sera taken 2 weeks apart is diagnostic of acute infection IgG avidity testing and epitope-type-specific (ETS) EIA to distinguish acute from past infection B19V DNA by PCR in serum (or amniotic fluid), with quantitative PCR preferred because low-level DNA can persist for months to years even in healthy people Bone marrow examination showing giant pronormoblasts and absent/scant erythroid precursors in TAC or PRCA In suspected fetal infection: maternal serology in exposed seronegative mothers, with regular monitoring if positive, and PCR of amniotic fluid or tissue Rheumatoid arthritis (clinical and serologic overlap with B19V polyarthropathy syndrome) Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (B19V can be associated with thrombocytopenia) Parvovirus B19 (B19V) has a narrow tropism for erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow, which underlies most of its clinical effects on red cell production. Most B19V infections are asymptomatic or cause only a mild nonspecific illness; the characteristic disease, erythema infectiosum (fifth disease, slapped-cheek disease), occurs mainly in children 3-12 years old. Transmission is primarily respiratory and occurs before the onset of rash or arthralgia; once the rash appears the child is no longer infectious and can return to school. In adults the classic slapped-cheek appearance is usually absent; instead they often present with arthralgia, with or without a macular rash. Arthropathy occurs in roughly 50% of infected adults, is more common in women, tends to be symmetrical and involves small joints of the hands (sometimes ankles, knees, wrists), and can mimic rheumatoid arthritis with detectable rheumatoid factor. In patients dependent on rapid red cell turnover (hemolytic disorders, hemoglobinopathies, red cell enzymopathies, autoimmune hemolytic anemia), B19V is the predominant cause of transient aplastic crisis (TAC). Bone marrow in TAC and pure red cell aplasia shows characteristic giant pronormoblasts with absent or scarce erythroid precursors; in a sickle-cell patient, reticulocytopenia with acute worsening anemia is diagnostic without marrow examination. Chronic B19V infection causing pure red cell aplasia (PRCA)/persistent anemia is a treatable cause of anemia in immunocompromised hosts and is important to recognize because effective immunoglobulin therapy exists. Individuals genetically lacking the blood group P antigen (globoside) are naturally resistant to B19V infection because that antigen is a required receptor. Detection of B19V DNA in tissue by PCR alone does not establish causation, since viral DNA can persist in healthy tissues for decades; quantitative PCR and serologic correlation are needed. Human bocavirus 1 (HBoV1) is a separate human parvovirus causing upper and lower respiratory tract infection in young children (peak ~2 years) and infecting nearly all children before age 5. An immune-mediated rash can appear in chronically infected immunocompromised patients after immunoglobulin administration, due to antigen-antibody complexes in skin. Severe to life-threatening anemia with a low reticulocyte count in a patient with a known hemolytic disorder (transient aplastic crisis) Persistent anemia with reticulocytopenia and extremely high serum B19V DNA titers in an immunocompromised patient (pure red cell aplasia) Maternal B19V infection before gestational week 20, given the risk of fetal loss and hydrops fetalis Nonimmune hydrops fetalis with gross edema and severe fetal anemia (B19V causes an estimated 10-20% of such cases) Hemophagocytic syndrome occasionally precipitated by B19V Interpreting tissue B19V DNA detected by PCR as proof of active disease - viral DNA persists in healthy tissues for decades, so PCR alone in tissue should not establish a B19V etiology. Presence of B19V DNA in synovium does not prove a causal role in arthritis, since healthy individuals also harbor viral DNA in synovia. In TAC and chronic infection, classic immune-mediated symptoms (rash, arthralgia) are often absent, making the diagnosis easy to miss in immunocompromised or hemolytic patients. Relying on qualitative PCR for HBoV1 in respiratory secretions can misattribute etiology, since HBoV1 DNA may persist for weeks to months after acute infection. Serology may be negative or only weakly positive in immunodeficient patients with PRCA, so quantitative serum DNA is needed. B19V is a small nonenveloped single-stranded DNA virus (genus Erythroparvovirus) that replicates in erythroid progenitor cells. Cell entry depends on the unknown primary receptor recognized by VP1u and, at a later step, the blood group P antigen (globoside); people lacking P antigen are naturally resistant. Infection produces high-titer viremia (up to ~10^12-10^14 particles/mL at the peak) and virus-induced cytotoxicity that halts red cell production. In immunocompetent hosts with normal hematopoiesis the arrest of erythropoiesis is transient with only a minimal fall in hemoglobin, resolving as neutralizing antibody is produced. In hosts with increased erythropoiesis (e.g., hemolytic anemia) the same arrest precipitates a transient aplastic crisis; in those who fail to mount neutralizing antibody (immunocompromised hosts or the fetus) lytic infection persists and chronic anemia/PRCA develops. The classic rash and arthropathy of erythema infectiosum are immune-mediated, beginning 2-3 weeks after infection as the IgM response peaks. B19V can also enter nonpermissive cells (B cells, monocytes, endothelial cells) by antibody-dependent enhancement and persist as DNA for life in many tissues (heart, liver, kidney, synovium, brain, bone), generally without disease. Most B19V infections are self-limited. Erythema infectiosum and B19V-associated arthropathy generally resolve spontaneously, though joint symptoms may recur for weeks to months. Transient aplastic crisis is, by definition, transient: anemia resolves once cytopathic infection of erythroid progenitors ceases, and lifelong immunity follows. Chronic anemia/PRCA in immunocompromised hosts is treatable and can be cured or ameliorated with immunoglobulin. Risk of fetal loss is highest (excess risk roughly 9%) when maternal infection occurs before gestational week 20 and is very low thereafter; most fetal infections resolve spontaneously, B19V does not appear to be teratogenic, and rare reports of eye damage, CNS abnormalities, and congenital anemia exist. Clinical spectrum of B19V infection (per Table 202-1): fifth disease in healthy children (IgM and IgG positive, viral load >10^4 IU/mL); polyarthropathy syndrome in healthy adults; transient aplastic crisis in patients with increased erythropoiesis (often >10^12 IU/mL, rapidly decreasing); persistent anemia/pure red cell aplasia in immunodeficient or immunosuppressed patients (often >10^12 IU/mL, typically >10^6 untreated); and hydrops fetalis/congenital anemia in fetuses of mothers infected before 20 weeks.

Pasteurellosis — Pasteurella multocida infection, animal-bite cellulitis, Pasteurella soft-tissue infection Staphylococcal or streptococcal wound cellulitis Capnocytophaga canimorsus infection after a dog bite Bartonella henselae cat-scratch disease Anaerobic or polymicrobial bite-wound infection Necrotising soft-tissue infection Erysipeloid in occupationally exposed patients Culture of wound exudate or aspirated pus, informing the laboratory of the animal-bite context Blood cultures where systemic infection is suspected Gram stain of exudate showing Gram-negative coccobacilli Plain radiography of the affected part to detect osteomyelitis or a retained foreign body such as a tooth fragment Inflammatory markers to gauge severity Cross-sectional imaging or surgical exploration for suspected deep-space hand infection Caused by Pasteurella multocida, a Gram-negative coccobacillus that is a common commensal in the mouths of cats and dogs, and usually acquired through animal bites or scratches, particularly from cats Soft-tissue infection develops strikingly rapidly, often within hours of a cat bite, with intense pain, erythema, swelling and a serosanguinous or purulent discharge The speed of onset helps distinguish it from staphylococcal and streptococcal wound infections, which typically evolve more slowly Deep hand bites are prone to spread to tendon sheaths, joints and bone, causing tenosynovitis, septic arthritis and osteomyelitis, so hand wounds warrant careful assessment Non-bite disease, including respiratory infection and, in vulnerable hosts, bacteraemia and meningitis, can follow close animal contact without an obvious wound Co-amoxiclav is a standard choice because it covers Pasteurella together with the other mouth flora and skin organisms in bite wounds; notably many oral agents such as flucloxacillin and first-generation cephalosporins have poor activity against Pasteurella Wound management, thorough irrigation, consideration of leaving bite wounds open, and assessment of tetanus and rabies risk are integral to care Deep hand or joint involvement with signs of tenosynovitis or septic arthritis Rapidly spreading infection or features suggesting a necrotising process Systemic sepsis or suspected bacteraemia Meningitis or respiratory infection in a vulnerable host Underlying immunosuppression, asplenia or chronic liver disease predisposing to invasive disease Choosing an antibiotic such as flucloxacillin or a first-generation cephalosporin with poor Pasteurella activity for a bite wound Underestimating a small cat-bite puncture that has inoculated organisms deep into tissue Missing early tenosynovitis or joint involvement in hand bites Neglecting tetanus and rabies risk assessment Assuming systemic disease cannot occur without an obvious bite wound Pasteurella multocida is inoculated into tissue when an animal bites or scratches, or when saliva contaminates an existing wound. The organism produces virulence factors, including a polysaccharide capsule and endotoxin, that provoke a brisk acute inflammatory response, accounting for the characteristically rapid onset of pain, erythema and swelling. Because bites deposit organisms deep in tissue, infection can track along tendon sheaths and reach joints and bone, and in hosts with impaired defences, chronic liver disease or immunosuppression the organism may invade the bloodstream and seed distant sites such as the meninges, respiratory tract and prosthetic material. Most localised bite-associated Pasteurella infections resolve well with appropriate antibiotics and wound care, but deep hand infections can cause lasting functional impairment, and invasive disease such as bacteraemia or meningitis carries significant mortality, particularly in comorbid patients.

age. Around a fifth of cases result from an unbalanced Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 13, and a smaller proportion from mosaicism. The surplus chromosome 13 material disrupts embryonic development, particularly midline structures of the brain and face, producing holoprosencephaly and associated craniofacial defects, along with cardiac, renal, and limb malformations. The severity of central nervous system and cardiac anomalies underlies the very high mortality. Prognosis is very poor, with most infants dying in the first days to weeks of life and few surviving beyond the first year, typically with profound disability; mosaic forms may have a better outlook.

Underlying malalignment and dysplasia (shallow trochlea, patella alta, lateralised tubercle) lower the threshold for dislocation and for recurrence, while impaction of the patella against the lateral femoral condyle can shear off osteochondral fragments. Most first-time dislocations recover with rehabilitation, but recurrence is common in young patients with dysplasia; surgical stabilisation reduces recurrence when anatomical risk factors are addressed.

patellar instability — patellofemoral instability, recurrent patellar dislocation, patellar subluxation Anterior cruciate ligament rupture, which also causes acute haemarthrosis after a twisting injury Meniscal tear Patellar or quadriceps tendon rupture Isolated osteochondral fracture without persistent instability Patellofemoral pain syndrome or chondromalacia patellae Medial synovial plica syndrome Referred hip pathology such as a slipped capital femoral epiphysis in adolescents Radiographs including skyline/Merchant views for patellar tilt, subluxation and osteochondral fragments MRI to assess the site of medial patellofemoral ligament tear, chondral injury and the characteristic bone bruise pattern CT or MRI measurement of the tibial tubercle to trochlear groove distance and grading of trochlear dysplasia Assessment of patella alta using the Insall-Salvati or Caton-Deschamps index Rotational profile assessment of femoral anteversion and tibial torsion Beighton score to assess generalised ligamentous laxity Lateral patellar dislocation is by far the usual direction, typically caused by a twisting valgus force on a flexed knee or a direct medial blow. A first-time dislocation often reduces spontaneously as the knee extends, and a tense haemarthrosis is common. The medial patellofemoral ligament is the primary passive restraint to lateral translation and is almost invariably torn in first dislocation. Key anatomical risk factors are trochlear dysplasia, patella alta, an increased tibial tubercle to trochlear groove distance, and rotational malalignment or ligamentous laxity. A positive apprehension test and a J-sign on active extension support the diagnosis of maltracking and instability. Always exclude an osteochondral fracture of the medial patellar facet or lateral femoral condyle after dislocation. First-time dislocation without a loose body is usually treated conservatively with bracing and physiotherapy targeting the vastus medialis obliquus and hip. Recurrent instability may require medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction, with bony procedures such as tibial tubercle osteotomy or trochleoplasty for underlying dysplasia. A locked knee or mechanical block suggesting a displaced osteochondral fragment or loose body An irreducible dislocation or gross deformity Neurovascular compromise following a high-energy injury A tense haemarthrosis with fat globules indicating an osteochondral fracture Medial or multidirectional dislocation suggesting an iatrogenic cause or connective tissue disorder Missing an osteochondral fracture on initial radiographs after the patella has relocated. Attributing the haemarthrosis solely to an anterior cruciate ligament injury and overlooking patellar dislocation. Reconstructing the medial patellofemoral ligament without addressing underlying bony malalignment, leading to failure. Overtightening a ligament graft, causing medial overload and stiffness. Neglecting hip and core weakness during rehabilitation. Patellar stability depends on the interplay of static restraints (the medial patellofemoral ligament, trochlear geometry and patellar shape), dynamic restraints (the quadriceps, especially the vastus medialis obliquus) and overall limb alignment. Lateral dislocation occurs when a valgus and external rotation force acts on a flexed, weight-bearing knee, overcoming the medial soft tissues and tearing the medial patellofemoral ligament from its femoral or patellar attachment. Predisposing morphology - trochlear dysplasia with a shallow or convex trochlea, patella alta with late trochlear engagement, a laterally positioned tibial tubercle, rotational malalignment and generalised laxity - lowers the force threshold for displacement and drives recurrence. Each event risks osteochondral shear injury and progressive patellofemoral chondral wear. Many first-time dislocators do well with conservative treatment, but recurrence is common in young patients with dysplastic anatomy. Surgical stabilisation, particularly ligament reconstruction combined with correction of bony risk factors, has a high success rate in reducing redislocation.

shockwave and other adjuncts may help resistant cases Sudden pain with loss of active knee extension suggesting tendon rupture Night pain, systemic upset or a mass suggesting other pathology Locking or giving way suggesting intra-articular derangement Failure to progress despite appropriate loading Prescribing complete rest instead of progressive tendon loading Intratendinous corticosteroid injection with its attendant rupture risk Over-interpreting imaging change that can occur in pain-free tendons Ignoring the wider kinetic chain and training-load errors Patellar tendinopathy results from repetitive energy-storage loading of the extensor mechanism, as in jumping and deceleration, most often affecting the deep posterior fibres at the inferior pole of the patella. Cumulative overload exceeds the tendon's adaptive repair capacity, producing degenerative change with disorganised collagen, increased ground substance, neovascularisation and neural ingrowth, and little classic inflammation, hence tendinosis. A continuum model describes progression from reactive tendinopathy through disrepair to degenerative tendinopathy depending on the balance of load and recovery. Often responsive to a structured loading programme, but rehabilitation may take many months and symptoms can be persistent or recurrent, particularly if training load is not managed.

pathology Labelling all anterior knee pain as chondromalacia and relying on rest alone Neglecting hip and gluteal strengthening and focusing only on the knee Missing patellar instability, referred hip pathology, or tumour Rushing return to sport without addressing training load and biomechanics Patellofemoral pain arises from excessive or maldistributed stress across the patellofemoral joint. Imbalance in the forces controlling patellar tracking, weakness of the quadriceps and hip abductors, dynamic valgus, and altered lower-limb alignment concentrate load on the retropatellar and peripatellar tissues. Repetitive overload of richly innervated subchondral bone and soft tissue, rather than cartilage damage alone, generates pain. Many improve with structured rehabilitation, but symptoms can be persistent or recurrent in a substantial minority, particularly if strength and biomechanical deficits are not corrected; long-term association with patellofemoral osteoarthritis is debated.

Patellofemoral pain syndrome — anterior knee pain, runner's knee Patellar tendinopathy Chondromalacia patellae or early osteoarthritis Patellar instability or subluxation Plica syndrome Referred pain from the hip Osgood-Schlatter or Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease in adolescents Clinical assessment of pain reproduction and patellar tracking Evaluation of hip and quadriceps strength and lower-limb biomechanics Radiographs if structural abnormality, instability or arthritis is suspected MRI reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected internal derangement Assessment of training load and footwear Diffuse peripatellar or retropatellar pain aggravated by activities that load the flexed knee, such as stairs, squatting and running Pain after prolonged sitting with the knee bent (the theatre sign) is characteristic It is one of the commonest causes of knee pain in active adolescents and young adults, especially women Contributing factors include abnormal patellar tracking, muscle imbalance, weakness of the hip and quadriceps, and training overload It is a clinical diagnosis, and imaging is used mainly to exclude other pathology Structured physiotherapy focusing on hip and quadriceps strength and load management is the mainstay of treatment True locking or giving way suggesting internal derangement or instability Significant effusion Night pain or systemic features suggesting other pathology Focal tendon or bony tenderness pointing to an alternative diagnosis Over-investigating with imaging for a clinical diagnosis Neglecting hip and proximal muscle strengthening Missing patellar instability or internal derangement Advising rest alone rather than active rehabilitation Patellofemoral pain syndrome is a multifactorial overuse condition in which altered load distribution across the patellofemoral joint irritates pain-sensitive structures. Malalignment or maltracking of the patella, weakness or imbalance of the quadriceps and hip abductors and external rotators, and excessive or rapidly increased loading all contribute to abnormal patellofemoral stress. The pain arises from the richly innervated subchondral bone, synovium and peripatellar soft tissues rather than from cartilage, which is aneural. Most patients improve with a sustained rehabilitation programme, though symptoms can be persistent or recurrent, particularly if underlying strength and biomechanical factors are not addressed.

Patent Ductus Arteriosus — PDA, persistent ductus arteriosus Ventricular septal defect Aortopulmonary window Venous hum (an innocent continuous murmur) Coronary or systemic arteriovenous fistula Truncus arteriosus Peripheral pulmonary stenosis murmur Echocardiography to confirm the ductus and assess shunt magnitude and left heart size Chest radiograph for cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings in large shunts Electrocardiogram for left ventricular volume overload Assessment of pulse character and pulse pressure Monitoring of respiratory status and feeding in preterm infants Persistence of the fetal ductus arteriosus beyond the normal postnatal closure period allows shunting between the aorta and pulmonary artery; it is especially common in preterm infants. Because aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary pressure once pulmonary resistance falls, the shunt is left-to-right, increasing pulmonary blood flow and left heart volume load. The classic sign is a continuous machinery murmur beneath the left clavicle, though in neonates only a systolic component may be audible. A large shunt produces bounding peripheral pulses and a wide pulse pressure from diastolic runoff into the pulmonary circulation. In preterm infants a significant ductus can worsen respiratory distress, contribute to heart failure, and is associated with complications such as necrotising enterocolitis and intraventricular haemorrhage. In some duct-dependent congenital heart lesions the ductus is essential for survival, and a prostaglandin infusion is used to keep it open until definitive intervention. Closure of an isolated symptomatic ductus may use pharmacological prostaglandin inhibitors in preterm infants or transcatheter/surgical closure in others. Echocardiography confirms the ductus, estimates shunt size, and assesses left heart dilation and pulmonary pressures. A large, longstanding, unrepaired ductus risks pulmonary vascular disease and eventual shunt reversal. Worsening heart failure or respiratory deterioration in a preterm infant with a significant ductus Abrupt cardiovascular collapse in a neonate with a duct-dependent lesion as the ductus closes Signs of poor systemic perfusion from diastolic runoff (weak distal perfusion, oliguria, feeding intolerance) Development of pulmonary hypertension or shunt reversal in a large longstanding ductus Necrotising enterocolitis or intraventricular haemorrhage associated with a large shunt Failing to recognise that some critical congenital heart lesions depend on ductal patency, and inadvertently allowing the ductus to close Misinterpreting a benign venous hum as a pathological continuous murmur Underestimating the contribution of a significant ductus to a preterm infant's respiratory difficulty Overlooking the wide pulse pressure and bounding pulses that signal a large shunt Delaying closure of a haemodynamically significant duct until pulmonary vascular disease develops The ductus arteriosus normally constricts and closes after birth in response to rising oxygen tension and falling circulating prostaglandins. When it remains patent, the postnatal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance establishes a left-to-right shunt from the aorta to the pulmonary artery throughout the cardiac cycle. This increases pulmonary blood flow and volume-loads the left atrium and left ventricle, while diastolic runoff from the aorta lowers diastolic pressure and can compromise systemic and coronary perfusion. A large chronic shunt raises pulmonary pressures and can lead to pulmonary vascular remodelling and shunt reversal over time. An isolated ductus closed in a timely fashion has an excellent outlook. In preterm infants outcome depends heavily on the associated prematurity complications. A large duct left untreated risks irreversible pulmonary vascular disease and a poorer prognosis.

without other vascular risk factors Frequently accompanied by an atrial septal aneurysm, and the combination increases the likelihood that the PFO is the culprit for stroke Linked with migraine, especially migraine with aura, and with decompression illness in divers and platypnoea-orthodeoxia in selected patients Detected by transthoracic or transoesophageal echocardiography with an agitated-saline bubble study, ideally combined with a Valsalva manoeuvre to provoke shunting Percutaneous device closure reduces recurrent stroke in carefully selected younger patients with an otherwise unexplained (cryptogenic) stroke and a high-risk PFO Cryptogenic ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism in a younger patient Recurrent embolic events despite antithrombotic therapy Platypnoea-orthodeoxia with hypoxaemia that worsens on sitting or standing A large shunt with an associated atrial septal aneurysm in the context of unexplained stroke Attributing a stroke to a PFO without excluding atrial fibrillation and other embolic sources first Performing a bubble study without an adequate Valsalva, so a shunt is missed Offering closure to older patients whose stroke is more likely due to conventional vascular disease Confusing a PFO with a true secundum atrial septal defect, which has different management The foramen ovale is a physiological right-to-left channel in fetal life; after birth the rise in left atrial pressure normally holds the flap of septum primum against septum secundum, and the two fuse. When fusion is incomplete a potential channel persists. Because left atrial pressure usually exceeds right, the flap stays shut, but a transient reversal of the interatrial pressure gradient, for example during straining, coughing, or the release phase of a Valsalva manoeuvre, can open the channel and allow right-to-left flow. This permits venous thrombus or other material to bypass the pulmonary filter and enter the systemic circulation, the mechanism of paradoxical embolism; an associated atrial septal aneurysm increases septal mobility and the propensity to shunt. Most patent foramina are benign and never cause problems, but in those with a cryptogenic stroke and a high-risk PFO, appropriate device closure or antithrombotic therapy substantially reduces the risk of recurrent stroke.
