MFN2-related Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2A; OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy) presenting as neurodegeneration Microglia, the brain's resident innate immune and antigen-presenting cells, arise from primitive yolk-sac macrophages that seed the CNS before the blood-brain barrier forms and are sustained largely by self-renewal rather than by replenishment from the circulation; under some conditions peripherally derived macrophages can become microglia-like and replace damaged cells. Microglia sculpt and prune synapses via classical complement proteins (C1q, C3) and complement receptors; in Alzheimer's disease, excess beta-amyloid drives C1q/C3 tagging of synapses that are then eliminated by CR3-expressing microglia, and knockout of C1q or C3 can rescue some neurodegenerative pathology in models. Genetic data link innate immunity to neurodegeneration: more than half of genes implicated in Alzheimer's GWAS involve innate immune/microglial processes, and loss-of-function mutations in the microglial receptor TREM2 increase Alzheimer's risk up to roughly fourfold. Around 10% of frontotemporal degeneration cases are due to heterozygous granulin (GRN) mutations causing progranulin haploinsufficiency; progranulin is a neurotrophic factor essential for lysosomal function and microglial homeostasis. Activated microglia (via IL-1alpha, TNF, and C1q) can convert astrocytes to a reactive, neurotoxic (A1) phenotype that loses phagocytic capacity and damages neurons and oligodendrocytes through complement, nitric oxide, and free radicals; astrocytes are non-cell-autonomous contributors across MS, AD, PD, and ALS. The glymphatic system uses periarterial CSF inflow through aquaporin-4-rich astrocyte foot processes to clear interstitial solutes and debris; clearance accelerates during sleep, and in models sleep deprivation increased beta-amyloid plaque accumulation while aquaporin-4 knockout reduced interstitial flow. Harrison proposes a prion-based reclassification of neurodegenerative disease in which host proteins (PrP, Abeta, tau, alpha-synuclein, SOD1, possibly huntingtin) adopt self-propagating, beta-sheet-rich conformations that template normal precursor protein and spread between synaptically connected neurons. The prion concept holds that the transmissible agents of kuru, CJD, scrapie, and BSE are devoid of nucleic acid and composed of host-encoded protein; AD is framed as a 'double-prion' disease in which both Abeta and tau prions coexist. Late onset of inherited neurodegenerations, despite lifelong expression of the mutant protein, is attributed to age-dependent decline in protein quality-control/clearance mechanisms, consistent with the view that these are disorders of the aging nervous system. Toxic small oligomers, rather than the mature plaques, tangles, and inclusion bodies, are increasingly viewed as the harmful species; visible aggregates may represent a relatively protective sequestration of toxic protein. Impaired autophagy and lysosomal handling are central to neurodegeneration; GBA (glucocerebrosidase) mutations underlie about 5% of Parkinson's disease and 8-9% of dementia with Lewy bodies, with bidirectional inhibition between alpha-synuclein and glucocerebrosidase. Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons and 3D cerebral organoids model human neurodevelopmental disease (microcephaly, lissencephaly/Miller-Dieker, fragile X, Rett, Timothy syndrome) and confirmed Zika virus tropism for human neural progenitor (radial glia) cells as the cause of congenital microcephaly. Progressive, age-related cognitive or motor decline suggesting an underlying self-propagating proteinopathy Family history with high penetrance (e.g., GRN mutations highly penetrant for FTD) prompting genetic evaluation Rapidly progressive dementia raising concern for a transmissible prion disease Microcephaly with developmental delay and intractable epilepsy in neurodevelopmental disorders Assuming that macroscopic aggregates (plaques, tangles, inclusion bodies) directly cause neuronal dysfunction; toxic soluble oligomers may be the harmful species and sequestration may be protective. Viewing microglia and astrocytes as merely secondary scavengers; genetic evidence places them as primary drivers of many neurodegenerative conditions. Treating the resting-versus-activated microglial dichotomy as adequate; single-cell data reveal extensive, functionally heterogeneous states. Over-extrapolating from rodent models; several human organoid findings (e.g., outer radial glia defects in Miller-Dieker syndrome) were not seen in mice, and some iPSC findings require replication before confidence. Accepting unproven microbiome-seeding hypotheses (e.g., bacterial Curli triggering Parkinson's) as established; no proven microbiome-modulating therapy yet exists for any brain disease. Therapeutic targeting of broadly acting systems (e.g., complement) risks off-target toxicity and loss of homeostatic functions such as physiologic synaptic pruning. This foundational chapter frames nervous-system disease around several converging mechanisms rather than a single illness. (1) Neuroimmunology/neuroinflammation: microglia and brain macrophages (yolk-sac-derived innate immune cells) and astrocytes are active, non-passive participants that prune synapses through complement, present antigen, secrete cytokines and trophic factors, and can shift between homeostatic and tissue-damaging states; crosstalk among microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes produces non-cell-autonomous pathology in MS, AD, PD, and ALS. (2) Myelin biology: oligodendrocytes maintain saltatory conduction and provide metabolic/neuroprotective support to axons, with activity-dependent (adaptive) myelination. (3) Waste clearance: the glymphatic system and meningeal lymphatic-like vessels clear interstitial solutes and aggregated proteins, with sleep-dependent and age-dependent modulation via aquaporin-4. (4) The microbiome can influence brain disease through molecular mimicry, immune modulation, circulating bacterial metabolites, enteric neural signaling, and possible prion-like seeding (e.g., the unproven hypothesis that E. coli Curli templates alpha-synuclein). (5) Protein aggregation and prion biology: misfolded, self-propagating proteins (Abeta, tau, alpha-synuclein, PrP, SOD1, TDP-43, expanded-polyglutamine huntingtin) spread trans-synaptically; toxic oligomers, defective ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy-lysosome clearance, mitochondrial dynamics (fission/fusion via Drp1, MFN1/2, OPA1; mitophagy via PINK1/parkin), and retromer (VPS35/VPS26/VPS29) dysfunction all contribute to neuronal death. (6) Stem cell biology: iPSCs and cerebral organoids reproduce early human brain-development disorders and enable disease modeling and drug screening. As a mechanistic overview the chapter does not give a single prognosis. It frames many neurodegenerative diseases as relentlessly progressive disorders of the aging nervous system driven by self-propagating prion-like proteins, while emphasizing that emerging understanding of complement, microglial, lysosomal/autophagy, mitochondrial, and prion-clearance pathways offers new and rational therapeutic targets (e.g., anti-C1q and anti-TREM2 antibody trials, progranulin-directed and gene/protein-replacement strategies) and new hope for prevention, treatment, and repair.

from colonization or laboratory contamination when fungi are recovered from culture (Harrison 22e p.1690) Chronic cavitary pulmonary mycosis versus cavitary tuberculosis (Harrison 22e p.1690) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis versus invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in differing host settings (Harrison 22e p.1688) Mycobacterial infection (notably tuberculosis), which shares granulomatous histology and intramacrophagic survival with endemic dimorphic fungi (Harrison 22e p.1689) Salmonellosis and other intramacrophagic pathogens that exploit the same IL-12/IFN-gamma defects as intramacrophagic fungi (Harrison 22e p.1689) Histopathology with PAS and GMS stains, plus H&E to assess granuloma, angioinvasion, and necrosis (Harrison 22e p.1690) Calcofluor white staining with fluorescence microscopy for fungi in fluid specimens (Harrison 22e p.1690) Lysis-centrifugation blood culture to increase sensitivity for Candida and less common fungi such as Histoplasma (Harrison 22e p.1690) MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for detection and speciation of cultured fungi (Harrison 22e pp.1690-1691) Antigen and serologic assays: cryptococcal polysaccharide antigen, Histoplasma antigen, Coccidioides antibody, galactomannan (BAL preferred), and serum beta-D-glucan (Harrison 22e p.1691) T2 magnetic resonance assay for Candida in whole blood (Harrison 22e p.1691) India ink stain of CSF, diagnostic for cryptococcosis (Harrison 22e p.1690) Neoplasia and other causes of granulomatous or necrotizing tissue reaction (H&E-defined granuloma, angioinvasion, necrosis are nonspecific without organism identification) (Harrison 22e p.1690) Sarcoidosis and other granulomatous conditions in patients predisposed to cryptococcosis (Harrison 22e p.1688) Human fungal disease has risen sharply with the AIDS pandemic, broad antibacterial use, cytotoxic chemotherapy, biologic/precision-medicine immunosuppressants, and solid-organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (Harrison 22e p.1687). Mycoses are categorized clinically as mucocutaneous versus deep-organ disease, and epidemiologically as endemic versus opportunistic; mucocutaneous disease causes morbidity but is rarely fatal, whereas deep-organ disease is often severe with high mortality (Harrison 22e p.1687). Endemic fungi are environmentally acquired and not part of normal flora, typically causing self-limited disease in immunocompetent hosts but severe illness when immunity is impaired; opportunistic fungi such as Candida and Aspergillus are commensal or ubiquitous and invade when host defenses fail (Harrison 22e p.1687). Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic demonstration of the fungus invading tissue together with culture from the specimen; a positive culture from blood or tissue can instead reflect colonization or laboratory contamination depending on organism and site (Harrison 22e p.1690). PAS and Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) are the principal fungal stains; Candida (unlike most fungi) is visible on Gram-stained tissue, and a positive India ink stain of CSF is diagnostic for cryptococcosis (Harrison 22e p.1690). The most reliable antigen/serologic tests are Coccidioides antibody, Histoplasma antigen, and cryptococcal polysaccharide antigen; galactomannan (best in BAL fluid) aids aspergillosis diagnosis but has frequent false negatives during antifungal prophylaxis and false positives with other fungi (Harrison 22e p.1691). The serum beta-D-glucan assay has a high negative predictive value for invasive candidiasis but lacks specificity, and T2 magnetic resonance is FDA-approved for detecting Candida in blood (Harrison 22e p.1691). Inherited CARD9 deficiency is the only known primary immunodeficiency that produces fungus-specific susceptibility without predisposition to other infections, autoimmunity, allergy, or cancer, causing chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, CNS Candida/Aspergillus/phaeohyphomycete infection, and deep dermatophytosis (Harrison 22e p.1688). Antifungal host defense is compartmentalized: IL-17-producing lymphoid cells protect mucosal surfaces against Candida invasion, neutrophils control invasive Aspergillus and Candida, and the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis with activated macrophages controls intramacrophagic fungi such as Cryptococcus, Pneumocystis, and endemic dimorphic fungi (Harrison 22e pp.1688-1689). AIDS predisposes to mucosal but not invasive candidiasis (reflecting IL-17 dependence), whereas vaginal candidiasis arises with antibiotic use rather than AIDS or IL-17-targeted biologics, highlighting the protective role of the vaginal microbiota (Harrison 22e p.1689). Chronic granulomatous disease, caused by NADPH-oxidase subunit mutations impairing neutrophil superoxide generation, carries roughly a 40% lifetime risk of invasive aspergillosis; Aspergillus nidulans is seen almost exclusively in this condition (Harrison 22e pp.1688-1689). Early initiation of appropriate antifungal therapy is a key determinant of outcome in candidemia, aspergillosis, and mucormycosis, alongside source control (catheter removal in candidemia, abscess drainage, surgical debridement in mucormycosis) and immune reconstitution (Harrison 22e p.1691). Profound or prolonged neutropenia, allogeneic HSCT, or high-dose glucocorticoids portend invasive mold disease (aspergillosis, mucormycosis) and invasive candidiasis (Harrison 22e pp.1688-1689) Diabetic ketoacidosis as a setting for rhinocerebral/sinopulmonary mucormycosis (Harrison 22e p.1688) Advanced AIDS with low CD4 counts predisposing to intramacrophagic and mucosal mycoses (Harrison 22e p.1689) Delay in appropriate antifungal therapy in candidemia, aspergillosis, or mucormycosis, which worsens outcome (Harrison 22e p.1691) Failure to achieve source control (retained central venous catheter in candidemia, undrained abscess, undebrided necrotic sinus tissue in mucormycosis) (Harrison 22e p.1691) Emerging drug-resistant species: azole/echinocandin-resistant Candida glabrata, Candida auris, and azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus (Harrison 22e p.1687) Treating a positive fungal culture as proof of infection when it may represent colonization or contamination, depending on organism and anatomic site (Harrison 22e p.1690) Relying on galactomannan for aspergillosis without accounting for frequent false negatives under antifungal prophylaxis and false positives from other fungi (Harrison 22e p.1691) Interpreting a beta-D-glucan result without recognizing its lack of specificity despite a high negative predictive value (Harrison 22e p.1691) Attempting to identify fungi reliably on H&E alone, which defines tissue reaction but is insufficient for speciation (Harrison 22e p.1690) Overlooking that fluconazole and echinocandins lack activity against molds (and echinocandins against Cryptococcus and endemic dimorphic fungi), and that voriconazole/echinocandins do not cover Mucorales (Harrison 22e pp.1691-1692) Failing to monitor drug levels where pharmacokinetics are variable (e.g., itraconazole capsules, voriconazole with CYP2C19 polymorphism) (Harrison 22e pp.1691-1692) Not recognizing that emerging immunomodulatory biologics (IL-17/IL-23 inhibitors, BTK inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, anti-TNF, SYK inhibitors) create predictable, compartment-specific fungal risk (Harrison 22e pp.1688-1689) Fungi are eukaryotes classified morphologically as yeasts (round/budding single cells), molds (filamentous hyphae at both room temperature and in tissue, e.g., Aspergillus, Mucorales, dermatophytes), and dimorphic fungi (yeast or spherical structures in tissue but filamentous forms in the environment). Candida produces both yeast and pseudohyphal forms in tissue except C. glabrata and C. auris, which form only yeasts; Cryptococcus exists only as yeast. Deep-organ infection by molds and endemic dimorphic fungi follows inhalation, whereas commensal Candida invades from mucocutaneous colonization in the gut or skin. Antifungal immunity centers on the C-type lectin receptor/SYK/CARD9 signaling pathway, which recognizes fungal polysaccharides and drives proinflammatory mediator release, leukocyte recruitment, inflammasome activation, and Th17 differentiation. Protection is site- and pathogen-specific: at mucosa, IL-17A/IL-17F and IL-22 from Th17, Tc17, gamma-delta T, and innate lymphoid cells stimulate epithelial antimicrobial peptide production and barrier repair (STAT3-dependent); against invasive molds and Candida, recruited neutrophils assemble the six-subunit NADPH oxidase to generate superoxide for fungal killing; against intramacrophagic fungi, IL-12-producing macrophages activate STAT4 in T cells to release IFN-gamma, which signals through STAT1 (with TNF-alpha and GM-CSF) to enable intracellular killing. Defects at any node, whether inherited (e.g., IL17F/IL17RA/IL17RC/TRAF3IP2, STAT3, STAT1, CARD9, NADPH oxidase subunits, IL12RB1, IFNGR1/2, IRF8, GATA2) or pharmacologic/acquired (IL-17/IL-23 biologics, BTK inhibitors, glucocorticoids, anti-TNF agents, JAK inhibitors, anti-IFN-gamma or anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies), produce predictable, compartment-specific fungal susceptibility (Harrison 22e pp.1687-1689). Outcome hinges on host immune status, the fungus and site involved, timeliness of appropriate therapy, source control, and immune reconstitution. Mucocutaneous mycoses cause morbidity but are rarely fatal, whereas deep-organ infections are frequently severe with high mortality. Before amphotericin B, cryptococcal meningitis and other disseminated mycoses were nearly always fatal. A favorable prognosis in opportunistic mycoses depends substantially on restoring host immunity, for example neutrophil recovery, tapering of immunosuppression, or starting combination antiretroviral therapy in AIDS (Harrison 22e pp.1687, 1691). Classified by anatomic depth (mucocutaneous infections, which are rarely fatal, versus deep-organ infections, which are severe and often highly fatal) and by epidemiologic category (endemic versus opportunistic). Severity within these groups is further modulated by host immune competence, the implicated fungus, and the involved tissue (Harrison 22e p.1687).

Patulous eustachian tube — patulous ET, PET, abnormally patent eustachian tube, patulous auditory tube Superior semicircular canal dehiscence Obstructive eustachian tube dysfunction Meniere's disease Middle-ear effusion Temporomandibular joint dysfunction Palatal or middle-ear myoclonus Third-window lesions producing conductive-type autophony Tympanometry during quiet and forced respiration to detect breathing-related pressure swings Pure-tone audiometry to exclude other causes of aural symptoms Nasoendoscopy of the eustachian tube orifice Otoscopy observing tympanic membrane movement synchronous with breathing High-resolution CT of the temporal bone to exclude superior canal dehiscence Nutritional and weight assessment, including recent weight loss or GLP-1 agonist use The eustachian tube stays abnormally open at rest instead of remaining closed and opening only briefly on swallowing or yawning The cardinal symptom is autophony - patients hear their own voice, and often their own breathing, unnaturally loudly in the affected ear Breathing-synchronous tinnitus or aural fullness that fluctuates with the respiratory cycle is characteristic Symptoms typically improve or resolve on lying down, bending forward, or lowering the head, as venous engorgement of the tubal mucosa closes the lumen, and worsen when upright or after exertion Strongly associated with weight loss, including rapid loss from illness, bariatric surgery, or GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy, as well as dehydration, pregnancy, and oestrogen use Otoscopy may show a tympanic membrane that moves medially and laterally with respiration, and tympanometry can demonstrate pressure swings synchronous with breathing Reassurance and explanation are the mainstay, as the condition is benign and often self-limiting; correcting dehydration or weight loss and using measures to plump the tubal lining help selected patients It is frequently mistaken for obstructive eustachian tube dysfunction, and inappropriate ventilation-tube insertion can make the autophony worse Persistently unilateral symptoms with a possible nasopharyngeal mass, requiring exclusion of tumour Rapidly progressive or profound hearing loss Associated neurological signs Sound- or pressure-induced vertigo suggesting superior canal dehiscence rather than a patulous tube Mislabelling it as obstructive eustachian tube dysfunction and inserting a ventilation tube, which usually fails and can worsen autophony Overlooking recent weight loss, GLP-1 agonist use, or dehydration as the trigger Not recognising the improvement on lying down as a key diagnostic clue Missing a nasopharyngeal lesion in a persistently unilateral case The eustachian tube is normally closed at rest, opening momentarily during swallowing or yawning to equalise middle-ear pressure. In a patulous tube the lumen remains open, so sound and airflow from the nasopharynx pass directly into the middle ear, producing autophony and breathing-synchronous symptoms. The usual mechanism is loss of the peritubal soft-tissue and mucosal bulk that normally keeps the tube collapsed, as occurs with weight loss, dehydration, or reduction of the fat around Ostmann's pad. Lying down or lowering the head increases venous congestion of the tubal mucosa, which closes the lumen and relieves symptoms, accounting for the strongly positional pattern. Often benign and self-limiting, especially when a reversible precipitant such as dehydration or recent weight loss is corrected; a minority have persistent troublesome autophony that may require procedural intervention.

to status epilepticus New developmental regression or behavioural deterioration during a cluster Fever-triggered clustering in a young girl resembling Dravet syndrome Marked affective or fear semiology raising diagnostic uncertainty Assuming Dravet syndrome and stopping after a negative SCN1A result without testing PCDH19 Overlooking the diagnosis in an affected girl with an apparently unaffected carrier father Underestimating the intensity of acute clusters and undertreating them Attributing behavioural features solely to epilepsy rather than the underlying disorder PCDH19-related epilepsy arises from variants in the X-linked PCDH19 gene, which encodes protocadherin-19, a cell-adhesion molecule involved in neuronal migration and network formation. The unusual sex-limited pattern is explained by cellular interference: random X-inactivation in heterozygous females produces a mosaic of cells with and without functional protocadherin-19, disrupting cell-cell communication, whereas hemizygous males express a uniform population and are usually spared. This mosaic disruption of neuronal connectivity underlies the fever-sensitive seizure clusters and the associated cognitive and behavioural features. Seizure clusters are often severe in early childhood but frequently diminish or remit with age, so the epilepsy prognosis is generally more favourable than in Dravet syndrome. Cognitive and behavioural outcomes vary widely, from normal development to significant intellectual disability and autistic features.

Hirschsprung disease requiring urgent surgical management Respiratory compromise from combined central and peripheral neuromuscular involvement Feeding difficulty and aspiration risk Progressive weakness or loss of motor milestones Treating the Waardenburg, Hirschsprung and neurological features as unrelated rather than recognising a single SOX10 disorder Overlooking the peripheral neuropathy when central dysmyelination is evident, or vice versa Missing Hirschsprung disease as a cause of neonatal obstruction or refractory constipation Attributing hearing loss and pigmentary changes to isolated Waardenburg syndrome without pursuing the broader phenotype Failing to provide genetic counselling, including for de novo dominant variants PCWH is caused by heterozygous variants in SOX10, a transcription factor that governs the development, migration and differentiation of neural crest cells and their derivatives, including melanocytes, enteric ganglia, and both Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes. Disruption of SOX10 function impairs multiple neural crest lineages simultaneously: defective melanocyte and inner-ear development produces the Waardenburg pigmentary and auditory features, failed enteric ganglion formation causes Hirschsprung disease, and impaired Schwann cell and oligodendrocyte function produces combined peripheral demyelinating neuropathy and central dysmyelination. Certain variants that escape nonsense-mediated decay are thought to exert dominant-negative effects, contributing to the severe combined phenotype. PCWH is a severe, multisystem disorder and prognosis depends on the combined burden of neurological, enteric and sensory involvement; the central and peripheral myelin disease contributes to significant motor and developmental disability. Early surgical management of Hirschsprung disease and coordinated supportive care influence outcome, but the overall course is serious.

does not apply to suspected acute DVT (p.2159-2160) Wells point-score clinical decision rule to stratify pretest probability (validated in ambulatory, not hospitalized, patients); low/low-to-moderate probability with normal D-dimer can avoid imaging (p.2159) BNP / NT-proBNP as markers of RV myocardial stretch (p.2160) ECG looking for S1Q3T3 (specific but insensitive) and T-wave inversion in V1-V4 from RV strain (p.2160) Chest x-ray signs: focal oligemia (Westermark's sign), peripheral pleural-based density (Hampton's hump, from infarction), enlarged right descending pulmonary artery (Palla's sign); often normal (p.2160) Echocardiography to assess RV dysfunction and to detect mimics (MI, tamponade, aortic dissection); usually normal in PE so not a reliable rule-out (p.2161) Compression venous ultrasonography for DVT (loss of vein compressibility) (p.2160) Ventilation/perfusion lung scan as second-line when IV contrast cannot be given (p.2161) MR pulmonary angiography / MR venography when CT or ultrasound is unsuitable (p.2161) RV-to-LV diameter ratio >1 on chest CT as a marker of RV enlargement (p.2161) Acute coronary syndrome (massive PE can give substernal pain mimicking MI) Aortic dissection Pericardial tamponade Pneumothorax / rib fracture Asthma / COPD exacerbation Ruptured Baker's cyst, muscle strain, and postthrombotic syndrome/venous insufficiency (mimic DVT) PE is the 'great masquerader' because its symptoms and signs are nonspecific; unexplained breathlessness is the most common symptom (p.2159). Suspect occult PE when a patient with congestive heart failure or pneumonia fails to improve as expected on standard treatment (p.2159). Pleuritic chest pain typically reflects a small, peripherally lodged embolus near pleural nerves, whereas massive PE can cause severe substernal pain mimicking MI from pulmonary-artery distention and RV strain (p.2153, p.2159). Pulmonary infarction usually signals a small (peripheral) PE and is exquisitely painful (p.2159). May-Thurner syndrome (left iliac vein compressed by the right iliac artery) should be considered in young women with recurrent left thigh swelling and associated DVT (p.2159). A diffusely edematous leg makes ordinary DVT unlikely, with phlegmasia cerulea dolens being the exception (p.2159). Many patients with PE have no demonstrable DVT because the leg thrombus has already embolized to the lungs (p.2158). McConnell's sign on echocardiography (RV free-wall hypokinesis with preserved/hyperkinetic RV apex) is the best-known indirect echo sign of PE (p.2161). Systemic arterial hypotension / cardiogenic shock indicating massive (high-risk) PE (p.2158) Syncope or cyanosis (p.2158, p.2153) RV dysfunction on echocardiography or RV enlargement on CT despite normal blood pressure (submassive/intermediate-risk PE) (p.2158, p.2162) Elevated troponin (from RV microinfarction) signaling high risk of clinical deterioration (p.2158, p.2162) Phlegmasia cerulea dolens (diffusely swollen, threatened limb) (p.2159) D-dimer is sensitive (>95%) but not specific; it rises with MI, pneumonia, sepsis, cancer, postoperative state, and the 2nd/3rd trimester of pregnancy, so it rarely helps in hospitalized patients (p.2159-2160). Wells criteria are validated in ambulatory patients, not in hospitalized patients (p.2159). A normal or near-normal chest x-ray and a normal ECG (or only sinus tachycardia) do not exclude PE (p.2160). Echocardiography is not a reliable rule-out test because most PE patients have normal echocardiograms (p.2161). Not all leg pain is DVT and not all dyspnea is PE; consider ruptured Baker's cyst, cellulitis, and muscle injury (p.2159). Virchow's triad of venous stasis, hypercoagulability, and endothelial injury, typically with an inflammatory trigger, recruits activated platelets that release microparticles and drive neutrophil extracellular trap formation, promoting thrombin generation; venous thrombi flourish in stasis, low oxygen tension, and proinflammatory gene upregulation. Detached lower-limb thrombi embolize through the vena cava and right heart to lodge in the pulmonary arteries (rarely paradoxically to the arterial circulation via a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect). The dominant gas-exchange defects are arterial hypoxemia and a widened alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient with increased dead space; additional mechanisms include raised pulmonary vascular resistance from obstruction and vasoconstrictors (e.g., serotonin), ventilation-perfusion mismatch remote from the embolus, reflex hyperventilation, increased airway resistance, and reduced compliance. Pulmonary-artery obstruction plus neurohumoral mediators raise pulmonary pressure and resistance; rising RV wall tension produces RV dilation, stretch and dysfunction (releasing BNP), septal bowing that impairs LV filling, and compression of the right coronary artery causing RV ischemia/microinfarction (releasing troponin), ultimately reducing LV output and systemic pressure, leading to circulatory collapse and death. Prothrombotic states include factor V Leiden, the prothrombin gene mutation, and deficiencies of antithrombin/protein C/protein S (rare); antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired thrombophilia predisposing to both venous and arterial thrombosis. (p.2156-2158) Low-risk PE (about 65-75% of cases) with normal blood pressure and normal RV carries an excellent prognosis; submassive (intermediate-risk) PE (~20-25%) has RV dysfunction despite normal pressure with raised cardiac biomarkers and a high risk of deterioration; massive (high-risk) PE (5-10%) presents with hypotension/shock and can lead to multisystem organ failure and death. A high-probability V/Q scan confers ~90% diagnostic certainty for PE. Roughly half of survivors report persistent dyspnea, fatigue, and reduced exercise capacity, and about one-quarter have persistent RV dysfunction on echo ('post-PE syndrome'); CTEPH is a less frequent late complication. Risk of recurrent VTE after stopping anticoagulation ranges from low (<3%/yr, e.g., major surgery/trauma) to intermediate (3-8%/yr) to high (>8%/yr, e.g., active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome) (ESC 2019). (p.2154-2155, 2158, 2161, 2163-2164) PE is stratified by hemodynamics and RV status: massive (high-risk, 5-10%) with systemic hypotension and extensive thrombosis (>=half of the pulmonary vasculature), hallmarks dyspnea/syncope/hypotension/cyanosis and possible cardiogenic shock; submassive (intermediate-risk, ~20-25%) with RV dysfunction and raised troponin despite normal blood pressure; and low-risk (~65-75%) with normal pressure and normal RV. RV strain markers (troponin, BNP/NT-proBNP, echo RV dysfunction, CT RV enlargement with RV/LV diameter ratio >1) drive risk stratification. (p.2158, 2160-2162)

mitochondrial aetiology in an infant with refractory anaemia Failing to anticipate metabolic decompensation during intercurrent illness Not recognising possible later evolution into Kearns-Sayre syndrome Pearson syndrome is caused by a single large-scale deletion of mitochondrial DNA, typically arising sporadically. Loss of genes encoding oxidative phosphorylation subunits and mitochondrial transfer RNAs impairs cellular energy production and disrupts mitochondrial iron handling, producing sideroblastic anaemia with ring sideroblasts. High-turnover tissues such as the bone marrow and exocrine pancreas are severely affected. The heteroplasmic burden of deleted genomes can shift with time, so surviving children may transition toward a Kearns-Sayre phenotype. Prognosis is poor, with high mortality in infancy from metabolic crises, infection and marrow failure. The anaemia may improve spontaneously in children who survive, but these survivors are at risk of progressing to Kearns-Sayre syndrome; management is supportive and multidisciplinary.

cartilages producing a sunken appearance It is often noticed in early childhood and typically becomes more pronounced during the adolescent growth spurt Many patients are asymptomatic, and the main deformities Progressive exertional dyspnoea or exercise intolerance suggesting significant cardiopulmonary compromise Echocardiographic evidence of marked cardiac compression or displacement Features of an underlying connective tissue disorder such as Marfan syndrome Arrhythmia or syncope on exertion warranting cardiac evaluation Dismissing the condition as purely cosmetic and overlooking genuine cardiopulmonary symptoms Failing to screen for associated connective tissue disorders and scoliosis Offering surgery based on appearance alone without objective severity and functional assessment anterior chest wall. The precise cause is unknown but is thought to involve disordered cartilage growth, and there is a familial tendency and links with connective tissue disease. In marked deformity the depressed sternum can compress and rotate the heart and reduce the space available for cardiac filling, which may impair cardiopulmonary performance, particularly during exertion. The deformity itself is rarely dangerous, and many patients do well without surgery. Operative correction in appropriately selected patients generally produces good cosmetic and functional results with high satisfaction, though the retrosternal bar requires later removal and there is a small risk of recurrence.

Pediatric Status Asthmaticus — status asthmaticus, acute severe asthma, severe asthma exacerbation Bronchiolitis or viral-induced wheeze in younger children Foreign body aspiration Anaphylaxis with bronchospasm Pneumonia with wheeze Vocal cord dysfunction Cardiac failure or a wheeze-mimicking cardiac lesion Continuous pulse oximetry and clinical severity scoring Blood gas in severe or deteriorating cases to assess for rising carbon dioxide Peak expiratory flow where age and cooperation allow Chest radiograph if complications such as pneumothorax, consolidation, or foreign body are suspected Electrolytes when high-dose beta-agonist therapy is used (risk of hypokalaemia) A severe, sustained asthma exacerbation that does not respond adequately to initial bronchodilator therapy and constitutes a medical emergency. Assessment combines clinical signs (work of breathing, accessory muscle use, air entry, mental state) with objective measures such as oxygen saturation and, where feasible, peak flow. A quiet chest with poor air entry is ominous, indicating severe airflow limitation rather than improvement. Rising carbon dioxide on blood gas in a tiring child signals impending respiratory failure; early in an attack hypocapnia is expected, so a normalising or high CO2 is a warning sign. First-line treatment uses inhaled short-acting beta-agonists, often with inhaled anticholinergic agents, and early systemic corticosteroids, alongside oxygen to maintain saturations. Escalation options for refractory cases include intravenous magnesium sulfate, continuous nebulised bronchodilator, and intravenous beta-agonist, with careful monitoring. Agitation, drowsiness, exhaustion, cyanosis, or a silent chest indicate life-threatening disease requiring intensive care and possible ventilatory support. Mechanical ventilation carries particular risks in asthma (air trapping and barotrauma) and is reserved for refractory respiratory failure using lung-protective, permissive strategies. Identifying and addressing triggers, ensuring correct inhaler technique, and providing a written action plan help prevent recurrence. Silent chest with poor air entry Exhaustion, drowsiness, confusion, or agitation indicating hypoxia and impending failure Rising or normalising carbon dioxide in a tiring child (impending respiratory failure) Cyanosis or falling oxygen saturation despite maximal therapy Poor response to initial bronchodilators or rapid clinical deterioration Misreading a quiet chest or a normalising carbon dioxide as improvement rather than deterioration Delaying systemic corticosteroids or under-treating a severe exacerbation Over-relying on oxygen saturation alone without assessing work of breathing and mental state Instituting mechanical ventilation without anticipating air trapping and barotrauma Discharging without addressing triggers, inhaler technique, and an action plan Acute severe asthma results from intense airway inflammation, bronchial smooth muscle constriction, mucosal oedema, and mucus plugging, producing widespread airflow obstruction that is worse on expiration. Air trapping and dynamic hyperinflation increase the work of breathing and impair gas exchange, causing ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxaemia. Early tachypnoea drives off carbon dioxide, but as the child fatigues and obstruction worsens, alveolar ventilation falls, carbon dioxide rises, and respiratory acidosis develops, heralding respiratory failure. Hyperinflation also impairs venous return and can compromise cardiac output. Most children with severe exacerbations recover fully with prompt, escalating treatment. A minority progress to respiratory failure requiring intensive care and ventilation, which carries higher risk. Poor prognostic factors include delayed treatment, prior life-threatening attacks, and inadequate preventive management; good discharge planning reduces relapse.

Peeling skin syndrome — PSS, acral peeling skin syndrome, CDSN, corneodesmosin deficiency, TGM5, deciduous skin Netherton syndrome Epidermolysis bullosa simplex (superficial forms) Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome Bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma Acral peeling from friction or exogenous causes Exfoliative ichthyosis Skin biopsy demonstrating superficial (subcorneal/intragranular) separation Molecular genetic testing of TGM5 and CDSN Assessment for erythroderma, atopy and raised IgE in the generalised form Examination of hair to help exclude Netherton syndrome Microbiological swabs to exclude staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome Family history and pedigree analysis Characterised by spontaneous, painless, continuous superficial peeling of the outer skin, often leaving no scarring An acral form (limited to hands and feet) is caused by TGM5 mutations, while a generalised inflammatory form is caused by CDSN (corneodesmosin) mutations The generalised inflammatory type is associated with erythroderma, pruritus and atopic features and can resemble Netherton syndrome Peeling is superficial (within the stratum corneum/granular layer), distinguishing it from the deeper blistering of epidermolysis bullosa The Nikolsky-like separation is at a more superficial plane than in immunobullous or staphylococcal scalded-skin disease Autosomal recessive inheritance; onset is usually at or soon after birth or in early childhood Management is supportive with emollients, gentle skin care and avoidance of friction; no curative therapy exists Extensive erythroderma with barrier failure, fluid loss or infection in infancy Failure to thrive in the generalised inflammatory form Recurrent skin infection from a compromised barrier Features suggesting Netherton syndrome requiring reappraisal Confusing the generalised form with Netherton syndrome or atopic erythroderma Interpreting superficial peeling as epidermolysis bullosa and over-investigating for deep blistering Mistaking it for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and giving unnecessary treatment Failing to distinguish the acral (TGM5) from the generalised (CDSN) form for counselling Peeling skin syndrome comprises autosomal recessive disorders of the cornified layer characterised by loss of cohesion between corneocytes at a superficial epidermal plane. The localised acral form is caused by mutations in TGM5, which encodes transglutaminase 5, an enzyme that cross-links structural proteins of the cornified cell envelope; its deficiency weakens the envelope so that the stratum corneum detaches from the underlying epidermis. The generalised inflammatory form results from mutations in CDSN encoding corneodesmosin, an adhesive component of corneodesmosomes that holds corneocytes together; loss of corneodesmosin causes separation high in the epidermis with associated barrier failure, inflammation and allergic sensitisation. In both, the split occurs superficially, giving painless peeling without deep blistering. Peeling skin syndrome is a chronic condition, but the localised acral form is generally mild and compatible with normal health, while the generalised inflammatory form can cause more troublesome erythroderma, itch and barrier problems. It is not life-limiting in most cases, though symptoms persist and require ongoing supportive care.

peliosis hepatis — hepatic peliosis, peliosis of the liver Hepatic metastases Pyogenic liver abscess Cavernous haemangioma Hepatic adenoma or adenomatosis Hepatocellular carcinoma Multifocal simple cysts or biliary hamartomas Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome or Budd-Chiari syndrome Multiphase contrast-enhanced CT of the liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic vasculature Careful, often transjugular, liver biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain Full liver function panel and coagulation profile Detailed drug and medication history including performance-enhancing agents Screen for underlying malignancy or chronic infection Peliosis hepatis is a rare vascular disorder in which the liver contains multiple blood-filled cystic spaces due to dilatation of the hepatic sinusoids. It is classically drug- or toxin-associated, with anabolic androgenic steroids, oestrogens and oral contraceptives, corticosteroids, tamoxifen and thiopurines such as azathioprine among the recognised culprits. It also complicates chronic wasting states such as advanced malignancy, tuberculosis and malnutrition, as well as solid-organ transplantation. Bacillary peliosis caused by Bartonella species in immunocompromised hosts is an important infective mimic to consider but is a separate entity. Most cases are asymptomatic and found incidentally; when symptomatic there may be hepatomegaly, cholestatic or mixed enzyme derangement and portal hypertension. The feared complication is spontaneous rupture of a peliotic cavity causing life-threatening intraperitoneal haemorrhage and haemodynamic collapse. Imaging is non-specific and easily confused with metastases, abscess or haemangioma, and percutaneous biopsy carries a significant bleeding risk. Withdrawal of the offending agent often leads to regression, and management is otherwise supportive, with embolisation or resection reserved for bleeding. Sudden severe abdominal pain with hypotension suggesting cavity rupture and haemoperitoneum Falling haemoglobin with haemodynamic instability Progressive hepatic dysfunction or synthetic failure New portal hypertension with variceal bleeding Performing a routine percutaneous biopsy of a vascular lesion and provoking major haemorrhage. Misdiagnosing the lesions as metastatic malignancy and subjecting the patient to unnecessary treatment. Failing to take a thorough medication and anabolic-steroid history. Overlooking the diagnosis as a cause of unexplained intra-abdominal haemorrhage. Peliosis hepatis results from injury to the hepatic sinusoidal endothelium and the reticulin framework that supports the hepatocyte plates. Loss of this support allows the sinusoids to dilate into blood-filled lacunar spaces distributed randomly throughout the parenchyma. Two histological patterns are described: a parenchymal type in which the cavities lack an endothelial lining and communicate with disrupted hepatocytes, and a phlebectatic type in which endothelium-lined spaces are centred on dilated central veins. Hormonal, cytotoxic and immunosuppressive agents are thought to weaken the sinusoidal wall and impair outflow, while chronic infection or wasting may act through endothelial injury and altered hepatic blood flow. Because the cavities are thin-walled and engorged they are prone to rupture, and extensive involvement can compress adjacent parenchyma and impair hepatic function. Drug-associated disease frequently regresses once the causative agent is stopped, but spontaneous rupture or extensive parenchymal involvement carries a high mortality and may precipitate hepatic failure.

mobility and causing contractures Seizures or airway compromise Failure to establish any developmental milestones Misdiagnosing early disease as cerebral palsy and not pursuing genetic testing Relying GJC2-related disorder Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease results from abnormalities of PLP1, which encodes proteolipid protein, a major myelin protein of the central nervous system produced by oligodendrocytes. Duplication, point mutation, or deletion of PLP1 disrupts oligodendrocyte function and myelin assembly, leading to failure of normal myelination (hypomyelination) rather than breakdown of previously formed myelin. Overexpression from duplication is toxic to oligodendrocytes, accounting for the common severe phenotype, while different mutation types produce distinct clinical severities. Outcome varies widely with phenotype; the connatal form carries a poor prognosis, the classic form progresses more slowly with survival into adulthood in some, and the allelic spastic paraplegia type 2 is milder. Care is supportive and directed at spasticity, feeding, and complications.

management of spasticity, physiotherapy, communication support and nutrition Failure to establish head control or feeding difficulty in a severely affected infant Progressive respiratory compromise from bulbar and truncal weakness Escalating spasticity or dystonia causing pain and contractures Unexpected rapid regression prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Testing only PLP1 and stopping when it is negative, thereby missing GJC2-related disease Discounting the diagnosis in an affected girl because Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease is X-linked Mistaking hypomyelination for delayed myelination without appropriate follow-up imaging Attributing the picture to hypoxic-ischaemic injury or cerebral palsy Not offering autosomal recessive genetic counselling to the family Pelizaeus-Merzbacher-like disease is caused by biallelic variants in GJC2, encoding connexin 47, a gap junction protein expressed by oligodendrocytes. Connexin 47 forms channels between oligodendrocytes and between oligodendrocytes and astrocytes that are essential for ionic and metabolic coupling in the white matter. Loss of functional connexin 47 disrupts this glial network, impairing the ability of oligodendrocytes to establish and maintain normal myelin. The result is a hypomyelinating leukodystrophy that phenotypically overlaps with the more common PLP1-related disease, in which a different oligodendrocyte protein is affected. The prognosis of Pelizaeus-Merzbacher-like disease spans a spectrum: severely affected children may never walk and have significant lifelong disability, whereas milder cases achieve more motor skills and a slower course. As with PLP1-related disease, many patients survive into adulthood with supportive care, and outcome depends largely on the severity of motor and bulbar involvement.

phototoxic dermatitis Dementia and confusional states from other causes Carcinoid syndrome as an underlying cause Dietary and drug history focusing on maize-based diets, alcohol, and isoniazid Urinary niacin metabolites where available Assessment for malabsorption and coexisting B-vitamin deficiencies Investigation for carcinoid syndrome when suggested clinically Skin examination and, if uncertain, biopsy to characterise the dermatitis Remembered by the triad of dermatitis, diarrhoea, and dementia, with death in untreated advanced disease The rash is a symmetrical, photosensitive, pigmented dermatitis on sun-exposed skin, classically a collar-like band over the neck (Casal's necklace) It occurs where maize or sorghum is the dietary staple because their niacin is poorly bioavailable and they are low in tryptophan Chronic alcohol use, malabsorption, carcinoid syndrome, and isoniazid therapy are recognised precipitants Neuropsychiatric features range from irritability and depression to confusion and frank dementia A glossitis, stomatitis, and diarrhoea reflect involvement of the whole gastrointestinal mucosa Clinical improvement after niacin repletion is rapid and helps confirm the diagnosis Progressive confusion or dementia indicating advanced central nervous system involvement Severe diarrhoea with dehydration and electrolyte disturbance Extensive dermatitis with secondary infection Rapid deterioration in a severely malnourished patient Misdiagnosing the rash as a primary photodermatosis and missing the nutritional cause Overlooking pellagra in patients on isoniazid or with carcinoid syndrome Failing to treat coexisting deficiencies in the malnourished or alcohol-dependent Attributing the neuropsychiatric picture solely to dementia or delirium of other cause Niacin, obtained from the diet or synthesised from tryptophan, is the precursor of the coenzymes NAD and NADP that are central to cellular energy metabolism and redox reactions. Deficiency impairs energy-dependent repair and turnover in tissues with high metabolic demand, explaining the prominence of skin, gut mucosa, and nervous system involvement. Diets based on untreated maize provide niacin in a bound, poorly absorbable form and little tryptophan; conditions that divert tryptophan, such as carcinoid tumours, or that impair absorption or metabolism, such as alcoholism and certain drugs, produce secondary deficiency. Prompt niacin repletion reverses skin, gastrointestinal, and early neuropsychiatric features quickly; advanced neurological disease may recover incompletely and untreated pellagra can be fatal.

keratometry to quantify against-the-rule astigmatism Serial imaging to monitor progression and guide cross-linking decisions A bilateral, non-inflammatory ectatic disorder featuring a band of inferior peripheral corneal thinning, typically between the 4 and 8 o'clock positions The cornea protrudes above the band of thinning, so the thinnest zone lies inferior to the point of maximal protrusion Produces characteristic high against-the-rule astigmatism, often with a claw- or crab-claw-shaped pattern on corneal topography (kissing doves / butterfly) The epithelium is intact and the eye is white and painless, distinguishing it from ulcerative peripheral thinning Vision loss is due to irregular astigmatism rather than central scarring, and often presents in the third to fifth decade It shares features with keratoconus but the thinning is inferior and peripheral rather than central Management begins with spectacles and specialty contact lenses, with corneal cross-linking, intrastromal ring segments, or large/eccentric grafts for advanced disease Acute hydrops from rupture of Descemet membrane can occur, causing sudden oedema and visual loss Sudden pain, redness, and marked visual loss suggesting acute hydrops Rapid progression of astigmatism indicating active ectasia Extreme thinning raising the risk of perforation Atypical inflammation or epithelial defect suggesting an alternative diagnosis Mislabelling it as keratoconus and missing the inferior peripheral pattern of thinning Attempting standard central grafting without accounting for peripheral thinning Overlooking acute hydrops as the cause of sudden visual loss Fitting standard contact lenses that fail to correct the irregular astigmatism Pellucid marginal degeneration is a non-inflammatory ectatic disorder characterised by a crescentic band of stromal thinning in the inferior peripheral cornea. Progressive weakening and thinning of the stroma allow the cornea just above the thinned band to protrude forward. This altered geometry flattens the vertical meridian centrally and produces high against-the-rule and irregular astigmatism, giving the typical crab-claw topographic appearance. The epithelium remains intact and the process is free of inflammation, but severe thinning and biomechanical weakness can lead to acute hydrops when Descemet membrane ruptures, causing sudden stromal oedema. Progression is usually slow, with vision limited by irregular astigmatism that can often be managed optically for years. Advanced disease may need surgical intervention, and grafting is technically challenging because the thinning is peripheral; acute hydrops usually resolves but can leave scarring.

Pelvic congestion syndrome — pelvic venous congestion, pelvic venous insufficiency, ovarian vein reflux, PCS Endometriosis Chronic pelvic inflammatory disease and adhesions Irritable bowel syndrome Interstitial cystitis or bladder pain syndrome Musculoskeletal or myofascial pelvic pain Ovarian or other pelvic mass Transvaginal ultrasound with Doppler to identify dilated pelvic veins and demonstrate reflux Transabdominal and transvaginal duplex assessment of ovarian vein diameter and flow direction Magnetic resonance venography or CT venography to map the pelvic venous anatomy Catheter venography, regarded as the reference standard, which also allows treatment at the same sitting Investigations to exclude other pelvic pathology, including laparoscopy where indicated Typically affects multiparous premenopausal women who describe a dull, aching chronic pelvic pain lasting more than six months The pain characteristically worsens towards the end of the day, on prolonged standing, and after intercourse, and eases on lying down Deep dyspareunia and a post-coital ache are common, and varicosities may be visible over the vulva, buttocks, or upper thighs Dilated, tortuous, incompetent ovarian and pelvic veins underlie the syndrome and can be demonstrated on Doppler imaging It is a diagnosis of exclusion; other causes of chronic pelvic pain must be considered before symptoms are attributed to venous congestion Ovarian and pelvic vein embolisation is the mainstay of definitive treatment, offering symptom relief in a majority of appropriately selected women Secondary causes of pelvic venous obstruction, such as left renal vein or iliac vein compression, should be sought before treatment Features suggesting an underlying secondary obstruction such as nutcracker or May-Thurner physiology A pelvic or renal mass causing venous compression Haematuria or flank pain pointing to left renal vein compression New or atypical symptoms that raise concern for malignancy Overdiagnosis, since pelvic varices are common and frequently asymptomatic incidental findings Failing to exclude a secondary obstructive cause such as renal or iliac vein compression Attributing all chronic pelvic pain to congestion without excluding coexisting pathology Offering intervention without correlating imaging findings with the clinical picture The syndrome results from incompetence and dilatation of the ovarian and internal iliac venous tributaries. Failure of the venous valves permits retrograde flow and pooling of blood within the pelvic veins, producing chronic venous congestion. Oestrogen has a venodilatory effect and, together with the increased pelvic venous capacity acquired during pregnancy, contributes to the tendency of the condition to occur in premenopausal parous women. The engorged veins and associated stasis are thought to generate the characteristic positional pelvic pain. Many women obtain durable relief of pain following ovarian vein embolisation, although symptoms may persist or recur, particularly if an underlying obstructive cause has not been addressed.

Pelvic inflammatory disease — PID, salpingitis, pelvic infection, endometritis-salpingitis-oophoritis Ectopic pregnancy Acute appendicitis Ovarian cyst accident (rupture, haemorrhage, or torsion) Endometriosis Urinary tract infection Functional or irritable bowel-related pelvic pain Pregnancy test to exclude ectopic pregnancy Endocervical or vaginal nucleic acid amplification testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea Microscopy and culture of genital tract samples Inflammatory markers and full blood count Pelvic ultrasound to detect tubo-ovarian abscess or pelvic collection Laparoscopy when the diagnosis is uncertain or the patient fails to respond PID is infection and inflammation of the upper female genital tract, encompassing endometritis, salpingitis, oophoritis, tubo-ovarian abscess, and pelvic peritonitis It is usually an ascending infection, most commonly caused by Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, often with anaerobes and other vaginal flora The clinical picture is variable and often subtle; classic findings are lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, abnormal discharge, and cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness Because sequelae are serious and diagnosis is imprecise, a low threshold for empirical treatment in at-risk women is recommended Antibiotic regimens are broad-spectrum to cover gonococcus, chlamydia, and anaerobes; sexual partners should be evaluated and treated to prevent reinfection Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis) causes right upper quadrant pain and can mimic hepatobiliary disease Intrauterine device users, recent instrumentation, and multiple sexual partners increase risk Long-term consequences include tubal-factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain, and risk rises with each recurrent episode Signs of a tubo-ovarian abscess such as a tender adnexal mass with high fever Peritonitis or suspicion of a ruptured abscess causing sepsis Haemodynamic instability or systemic sepsis Inability to tolerate oral therapy, pregnancy, or failure of outpatient treatment requiring admission Severe right upper quadrant pain raising concern for perihepatitis or an alternative surgical diagnosis Withholding treatment while awaiting definitive confirmation, allowing tubal damage to progress Missing an ectopic pregnancy by not performing a pregnancy test Neglecting to test for and treat sexual partners, leading to reinfection Failing to recognise or drain a tubo-ovarian abscess Assuming an absence of fever or normal inflammatory markers excludes PID PID arises when micro-organisms ascend from the vagina and cervix through the endometrial cavity to the fallopian tubes and adjacent structures. Sexually transmitted pathogens, chiefly Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, disrupt the cervical barrier and facilitate co-infection with endogenous aerobic and anaerobic vaginal flora. The resulting inflammation damages the tubal epithelium and cilia, leading to scarring, adhesions, and tubal occlusion. Progression can produce pyosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess, and pelvic peritonitis; spread to the hepatic capsule causes perihepatitis. Prompt, adequate antibiotic treatment usually resolves acute infection, but even treated PID carries appreciable risk of long-term tubal damage. Each recurrent episode further increases the likelihood of infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain, so prevention and partner treatment are central to a good outcome.

gestationis' Neglecting fetal monitoring for growth restriction and prematurity Failing to counsel about recurrence in future pregnancies and with oestrogen-containing contraception Pemphigoid gestationis is driven by IgG autoantibodies against BP180 (collagen XVII), a transmembrane component of the hemidesmosome at the dermo-epidermal junction. Aberrant expression of placental/amniotic basement-membrane antigens is thought to break self-tolerance, generating antibodies that cross-react with maternal skin. Antibody binding activates complement, recruiting eosinophils and other inflammatory cells that cleave the epidermis from the dermis to form tense subepidermal blisters. Because IgG crosses the placenta, the neonate may develop transient blistering that resolves as maternal antibody clears. Hormonal influences help explain peripartum flares and recurrence with oestrogen exposure. Pemphigoid gestationis usually resolves spontaneously in the weeks to months after delivery, though flares at parturition are common; there is a modest increase in prematurity and low birthweight, and recurrence in later pregnancies is frequent.

Pemphigus foliaceus — superficial pemphigus, anti-desmoglein-1 pemphigus, fogo selvagem (endemic pemphigus foliaceus), pemphigus erythematosus (Senear-Usher syndrome) Pemphigus vulgaris Seborrhoeic dermatitis Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus Impetigo and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome Subcorneal pustular dermatosis Widespread eczema or psoriasis with crusting Lesional skin biopsy for histology showing subcorneal/superficial acantholysis Perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence demonstrating intercellular IgG and C3 Indirect immunofluorescence on serum for circulating intercellular antibodies Serum ELISA for anti-desmoglein-1 (and anti-desmoglein-3 to help distinguish subtype) Drug history review to identify a possible drug-induced trigger Baseline investigations before immunosuppression (infection screen, glucose, bone health) A superficial autoimmune blistering disease driven by autoantibodies to desmoglein-1, producing a subcorneal (high epidermal) cleavage plane Intact bullae are rarely seen; instead there are crusted, scaly erosions on a seborrhoeic distribution (scalp, face, upper trunk) Mucous membranes are characteristically spared, distinguishing it from pemphigus vulgaris where desmoglein-3 involvement causes mucosal disease Nikolsky sign is positive, reflecting acantholysis and loss of keratinocyte cohesion in the upper epidermis Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular ('chicken-wire') IgG and C3 deposition, often most intense in the superficial epidermis An endemic form (fogo selvagem) occurs in parts of Brazil and is linked to environmental and insect-bite triggers Drug-induced cases, classically with thiol-containing agents, should be considered and the culprit withdrawn Extensive erosions with fluid loss, secondary infection, or sepsis in erythrodermic disease Rapid progression or failure to respond to first-line therapy Complications of prolonged systemic corticosteroid or immunosuppressive treatment New drug exposure temporally linked to disease onset requiring urgent withdrawal Mistaking crusted superficial lesions for seborrhoeic dermatitis or impetigo and delaying diagnosis Relying on histology alone without direct immunofluorescence to confirm the diagnosis Overlooking a drug trigger that could resolve with withdrawal Assuming mucosal involvement excludes pemphigus foliaceus rather than reconsidering pemphigus vulgaris Pemphigus foliaceus results from IgG autoantibodies directed against desmoglein-1, a desmosomal cadherin concentrated in the superficial (granular) layer of the epidermis. Antibody binding disrupts desmosomal adhesion between keratinocytes, causing acantholysis and a subcorneal split high in the epidermis. Because desmoglein-1 predominates in the skin rather than mucosa and mucosal desmoglein-3 compensates there, blistering is cutaneous and superficial with mucosal sparing. The fragile superficial roof breaks readily, so patients present with scale-crust and erosions rather than tense blisters. Genetic susceptibility, and in the endemic form environmental exposures, contribute to loss of tolerance. Pemphigus foliaceus is generally less severe than pemphigus vulgaris because it is superficial and spares mucosae, and many patients achieve durable remission with corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression or rituximab; relapses and treatment-related morbidity remain important concerns.

pemphigus vegetans — pemphigus vegetans of Neumann, pemphigus vegetans of Hallopeau pemphigus vulgaris (classical) Hailey-Hailey disease (benign familial pemphigus) condylomata lata of secondary syphilis granular parakeratosis and intertrigo with candidiasis halogenoderma (bromoderma / iododerma) pyoderma vegetans / blastomycosis-like pyoderma inverse psoriasis lesional biopsy for histopathology (suprabasal acantholysis, eosinophilic microabscesses, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia) perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence (intercellular IgG and C3) indirect immunofluorescence for circulating intercellular antibodies ELISA for desmoglein 1 and desmoglein 3 antibodies swabs and culture to exclude secondary bacterial or candidal infection syphilis serology when perianal or genital vegetations raise suspicion of condylomata lata baseline screening prior to immunosuppression (glucose, blood pressure, infection screen) A rare vegetating variant of pemphigus vulgaris characterised by hypertrophic, verrucous, exudative plaques favouring intertriginous and periorificial sites. Two forms are described: the Neumann type, which begins with flaccid bullae and erosions that evolve into vegetations, and the milder Hallopeau type, which starts with pustules. Flexural predilection includes the axillae, groin, inframammary folds, perianal region and the angles of the mouth; the scalp and face may also be affected. Oral mucosal involvement is common and may include cerebriform changes of the tongue, mirroring the mucosal disease of pemphigus vulgaris. Histology shows suprabasal acantholysis with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and characteristic intraepidermal eosinophilic microabscesses. Direct immunofluorescence demonstrates intercellular IgG and C3 in a net-like (chicken-wire) pattern, and serum antibodies target desmoglein 3 (and often desmoglein 1). The Hallopeau type generally follows a more indolent course and may respond to lower doses of systemic therapy than classical pemphigus vulgaris. Systemic corticosteroids with steroid-sparing immunosuppressants remain the mainstay, with rituximab increasingly used for refractory or steroid-dependent disease. extensive erosions with fluid loss, secondary infection or sepsis severe oropharyngeal involvement limiting oral intake and nutrition rapid progression or transformation to widespread classical pemphigus vulgaris signs of systemic infection arising from immunosuppressive therapy Mistaking flexural vegetations for intertrigo, candidiasis or condylomata lata and delaying biopsy. Biopsying only the vegetating surface and missing diagnostic acantholysis at the edge. Overlooking oral disease that may be the earliest and most persistent manifestation. Attributing treatment failure to disease when secondary bacterial or candidal colonisation is driving the plaques. Assuming the milder Hallopeau course applies to all patients and under-treating Neumann-type disease. Pemphigus vegetans is a clinical and histological variant of pemphigus vulgaris driven by IgG autoantibodies against the desmosomal cadherins desmoglein 3 and, in many cases, desmoglein 1. Antibody binding disrupts desmosomal adhesion between keratinocytes, producing suprabasal acantholysis and flaccid blistering. At intertriginous and periorificial sites, the warm moist environment and chronic irritation are thought to provoke an exuberant reparative epidermal response, giving rise to pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and the characteristic vegetating plaques studded with eosinophilic microabscesses. The reason certain patients develop vegetating rather than classical lesions is incompletely understood but may reflect host reactive patterns and local factors. With appropriate immunosuppression the disease is controllable, and the Hallopeau type in particular may follow a relatively benign, indolent course; however relapses are frequent and the Neumann type can be chronic and difficult to clear.

with fluid and protein loss and risk of sepsis Inability to eat or drink due to painful oropharyngeal involvement Signs of secondary bacterial infection or systemic instability Features suggesting misjudging severity and treatment intensity Under-appreciating infection risk from extensive barrier loss and immunosuppression Tapering immunosuppression too rapidly and precipitating relapse Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune disease in which IgG autoantibodies target desmoglein 3 (and desmoglein 1 in mucocutaneous disease), transmembrane desmosomal cadherins that mediate keratinocyte adhesion. Antibody binding disrupts desmosomal function and triggers intracellular signalling that causes loss of cell-to-cell adhesion (acantholysis). This produces a suprabasal split within the epidermis, giving rise to fragile flaccid blisters and erosions. Because desmoglein 3 is expressed strongly in mucosa, mucosal disease often predominates; involvement of both desmogleins produces combined mucosal and cutaneous lesions. Extensive erosions lead to fluid loss, protein depletion, and susceptibility to secondary infection and sepsis. Once frequently fatal, pemphigus vulgaris now has a much better outlook with immunosuppressive and B-cell-depleting therapy; however, it remains a serious chronic disease and much of the residual mortality relates to treatment complications and infection.

Pena-Shokeir syndrome — foetal akinesia deformation sequence, fetal akinesia deformation sequence, FADS, Pena-Shokeir phenotype type 1, arthrogryposis-pulmonary hypoplasia sequence Lethal multiple pterygium syndrome Congenital myotonic dystrophy Spinal muscular atrophy with arthrogryposis Congenital myasthenic syndromes Trisomy 18 and other chromosomal disorders Amyoplasia (survivable form) and other arthrogryposis syndromes Detailed prenatal ultrasound documenting reduced foetal movement, contractures and polyhydramnios Postnatal or postmortem examination and clinical photographs to define microarray or karyotype to exclude aneuploidy Maternal testing for myasthenia or myotonic dystrophy where relevant A phenotype (a sequence rather than a single disease) resulting from reduced foetal movement in utero, presenting with multiple congenital contractures The hallmark tetrad is foetal akinesia, multiple joint contractures, pulmonary hypoplasia and craniofacial anomalies Polyhydramnios reflects impaired foetal swallowing, and intrauterine growth restriction and a short umbilical cord are common Pulmonary hypoplasia, caused by absent foetal breathing movements, is the usual cause of death and is frequently lethal in the neonatal period Facial features include hypertelorism, a small mouth, micrognathia, low-set ears and depressed nasal tip It is aetiologically heterogeneous, arising from any process that limits foetal movement (neurogenic, myopathic, neuromuscular junction, connective tissue or restrictive uterine causes) Recurrence risk depends on the underlying cause, so establishing the aetiology is essential for counselling Neonatal respiratory failure from pulmonary hypoplasia, often not survivable Antenatal signs of severe akinesia and polyhydramnios indicating poor prognosis Feeding failure and inability to protect the airway Findings suggesting a treatable maternal cause such as myasthenia gravis Treating Pena-Shokeir as a single diagnosis rather than searching for its underlying cause Failing to counsel on recurrence, which varies widely by aetiology Overlooking a treatable maternal condition such as myasthenia gravis Not offering postmortem examination and genetic testing to guide future pregnancies Pena-Shokeir syndrome is the end result of the foetal akinesia deformation sequence: any insult that reduces or abolishes foetal movement during development produces a stereotyped set of secondary deformations. Immobility permits periarticular fibrosis and multiple joint contractures, absent breathing movements prevent normal lung expansion and cause pulmonary hypoplasia, and reduced swallowing leads to polyhydramnios and a small mouth. Causes are heterogeneous and may lie anywhere along the neuromuscular axis (central nervous system, anterior horn cell, peripheral nerve, neuromuscular junction or muscle) or in restrictive intrauterine conditions such as oligohydramnios or uterine anomaly. The prognosis is generally poor, with many affected infants stillborn or dying in the neonatal period from pulmonary hypoplasia; management is largely supportive and palliative, with counselling directed by the identified underlying cause.

Pendred syndrome — SLC26A4, pendrin deficiency, deafness with enlarged vestibular aqueduct and goitre, PDS Non-syndromic hearing loss with enlarged vestibular aqueduct (DFNB4) Branchio-oto-renal syndrome with inner-ear malformation Congenital hypothyroidism with dyshormonogenesis and goitre Other syndromic sensorineural hearing loss such as Waardenburg or Usher Acquired fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss from other causes Isolated multinodular goitre unrelated to hearing loss Audiometry with serial testing to document fluctuating or progressive loss High-resolution CT or MRI of the temporal bones for enlarged vestibular aqueduct and cochlear anomalies Thyroid function tests and thyroid ultrasound to assess goitre Perchlorate discharge test where genetic testing is unavailable SLC26A4 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Classic triad is sensorineural hearing loss, an enlarged vestibular aqueduct on imaging, and euthyroid goitre from an iodine organification defect Caused by biallelic mutations in SLC26A4, which encodes the anion transporter pendrin; inheritance is autosomal recessive Hearing loss is usually congenital or prelingual and may fluctuate or progress in a stepwise fashion, sometimes after minor head trauma Enlarged vestibular aqueduct (with or without cochlear incomplete partition) is the most consistent temporal-bone finding on CT or MRI Goitre often develops later, in later childhood or adolescence, and thyroid function is typically normal, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis A perchlorate discharge test can demonstrate the underlying iodine organification defect but is now largely superseded by genetic testing Advise patients to avoid activities with head-injury risk that may precipitate sudden drops in hearing Sudden or stepwise deterioration in hearing, especially after head trauma Progressive goitre or evolving thyroid dysfunction requiring endocrine review Vertigo or imbalance suggesting associated vestibular involvement Bilateral profound loss threatening speech and language development in a child Excluding Pendred because goitre is absent in a young child before it typically develops Overlooking an enlarged vestibular aqueduct on imaging as the key structural clue Not warning patients about head-injury and pressure-related hearing drops Assuming a euthyroid goitre is unrelated to the hearing loss Pendred syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in SLC26A4, encoding pendrin, a transmembrane anion (chloride/iodide/bicarbonate) exchanger expressed in the inner ear, thyroid and kidney. In the inner ear, impaired pendrin function disturbs endolymph ion and pH homeostasis, contributing to abnormal cochlear and vestibular development, an enlarged vestibular aqueduct, and sensorineural hearing loss. In the thyroid, defective iodide transport into the follicular lumen impairs organification of iodine, producing goitre while thyroid hormone levels are often maintained. The same gene can also cause non-syndromic hearing loss with enlarged vestibular aqueduct when thyroid involvement is absent. Hearing loss tends to be progressive and may fluctuate, with many patients eventually developing severe-to-profound loss suited to hearing aids or cochlear implantation; the goitre is usually benign and euthyroid, though thyroid function should be monitored over time.

Penetrating abdominal trauma — penetrating abdominal injury, stab wound abdomen, gunshot wound abdomen Superficial wound that has not breached the peritoneum Associated thoracic injury from a thoraco-abdominal track Retroperitoneal vascular or renal injury Diaphragmatic injury with thoraco-abdominal communication Concurrent blunt trauma Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) to detect free intraperitoneal fluid CT abdomen and pelvis in the stable patient to define trajectory and organ injury Local wound exploration in selected stab wounds to assess peritoneal breach Group and crossmatch with coagulation studies Erect chest radiograph to detect free air or associated thoracic injury Manage as a trauma patient using the primary survey, with haemorrhage control as the priority once the airway is secure A haemodynamically unstable patient or one with peritonitis or evisceration needs immediate surgery rather than further imaging Gunshot wounds usually breach the peritoneum and injure viscera and generally warrant laparotomy, whereas selected stab wounds may be managed non-operatively with close observation Do not remove an impaling object in the emergency setting; stabilise it and remove it in a controlled operative environment The trajectory can be deceptive, so consider injury to the chest, retroperitoneum, and pelvis and inspect the back and flanks for other wounds Serial abdominal examination detects evolving peritonitis in patients selected for conservative management Give tetanus prophylaxis and early antibiotics when hollow-viscus injury is likely, and resuscitate with blood products in shock Haemodynamic instability indicating major haemorrhage and the need for immediate laparotomy Peritonitis, evisceration, or a retained impaling object mandating surgical exploration Gunshot trajectory crossing the peritoneal cavity Rising lactate or persistent shock despite resuscitation Evolving peritoneal signs during observation of a non-operatively managed wound Removing an impaling object in the emergency department, which can trigger uncontrolled bleeding Being reassured by a benign initial abdomen when injury can evolve Underestimating trajectory and missing thoracic, retroperitoneal, or back wounds Delaying surgery in an unstable patient to obtain imaging Neglecting antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis when hollow viscus injury is likely A penetrating object breaches the abdominal wall and can lacerate solid organs (liver, spleen), causing haemorrhage, or hollow viscera (bowel, stomach), causing spillage of contents and peritoneal contamination. Vascular injury may produce rapid exsanguination into the peritoneal cavity or retroperitoneum. Low-energy stab wounds injure tissue along a relatively predictable track, whereas high-energy gunshot wounds transfer energy widely, causing cavitation and injury beyond the visible path. The result is a combination of haemorrhagic shock from bleeding and, later, peritonitis and sepsis from contamination. Prognosis depends on the organs injured, blood loss, and time to control of haemorrhage and contamination. Early surgery for unstable or peritonitic patients improves survival, whereas delay allows exsanguination or sepsis with high mortality.

appears protective It typically presents as a persistent penile ulcer, nodule, or warty growth that fails to heal, sometimes with foul discharge, and is frequently delayed by embarrassment or
