approaches such as topical therapy, laser, local excision, or glansectomy, preserving function where oncologically safe Advanced primary tumours may require partial or total penectomy, and management of inguinal nodes ranges from surveillance to lymphadenectomy depending on risk Platinum-based chemotherapy is used for bulky nodal or metastatic disease, sometimes combined with surgery or radiotherapy in a multimodal approach A non-healing penile ulcer or nodule persisting despite treatment for presumed infection Palpable or enlarging inguinal lymph nodes Bleeding, foul discharge, or destruction of penile tissue Fixed or ulcerated groin nodes suggesting advanced regional disease Treating a persistent penile lesion repeatedly as infection without biopsy Underestimating the importance of early inguinal node evaluation and management Delaying referral due to patient embarrassment, allowing progression Choosing organ-preserving therapy for lesions that are too advanced for safe conservation Penile squamous cell carcinoma develops from the epithelium of the glans and prepuce, arising either through human papillomavirus-driven pathways or through chronic inflammatory conditions such as lichen sclerosus and long-standing phimosis. Precursor penile intraepithelial neoplasia progresses to invasive carcinoma that infiltrates the corpora and surrounding tissues. The tumour spreads in a predictable stepwise fashion first to superficial and deep inguinal nodes and then to pelvic nodes, with distant metastasis occurring late. Prognosis correlates strongly with inguinal nodal status; localised node-negative disease has high cure rates with appropriate treatment, whereas extensive nodal involvement or distant metastasis markedly reduces survival.

Penile fracture — fracture of the penis, tunica albuginea rupture, traumatic rupture of the corpus cavernosum Rupture of a superficial or dorsal penile vein or artery ('false fracture') Dislocation of the penis Isolated urethral injury Penile haematoma without a tunical tear Painful Peyronie's plaque or acute Peyronie's disease Dorsal nerve or vessel injury Clinical assessment for the eggplant deformity and a palpable tunical defect Penile ultrasound to localise the tear MRI of the penis when the diagnosis is uncertain Retrograde urethrography to assess the urethra Flexible cystoscopy where urethral injury is suspected Urinalysis for haematuria Rupture of the tunica albuginea of an erect corpus cavernosum, usually during vigorous intercourse or forced bending of the erect penis The patient classically reports a sudden audible crack or pop, immediate pain, rapid detumescence, and swelling The typical aubergine (eggplant) deformity results from a haematoma confined by Buck's fascia, giving a swollen, bruised, and often deviated penis It is a surgical emergency, as prompt exploration and repair of the tunical defect give the best functional outcomes and reduce long-term erectile and deformity complications Always assess for an associated urethral injury - blood at the meatus, frank haematuria, or difficulty voiding raises this concern Diagnosis is largely clinical; ultrasound or MRI can localise the tear when the picture is equivocal, and retrograde urethrography or flexible cystoscopy evaluates the urethra Delayed or conservative treatment carries higher rates of penile curvature, painful nodules, and erectile dysfunction than early surgical repair Blood at the urethral meatus or gross haematuria, indicating urethral injury Inability to pass urine or acute urinary retention An expanding haematoma or bruising extending beyond Buck's fascia Features suggesting complete urethral disruption Managing conservatively when early surgical exploration would give better functional results Failing to evaluate the urethra and missing an associated urethral injury Mistaking a ruptured superficial vessel ('false fracture') for a true tunical tear, or vice versa Delaying theatre and increasing the risk of long-term penile deformity During erection the tunica albuginea covering the corpora cavernosa is stretched thin and taut. An abrupt bending force against the rigid erect penis, most often when it slips out and strikes the perineum or pubis during intercourse, sharply raises intracavernosal pressure and tears the tunica. Blood escapes from the corpus cavernosum and, while contained by Buck's fascia, collects as a localised haematoma that produces the characteristic eggplant deformity; if Buck's fascia is also breached, bruising spreads more widely. Because the urethra and corpus spongiosum lie ventrally, a forceful injury can extend to cause a concurrent urethral rupture, which must be actively sought. Early surgical repair generally restores good erectile function with low rates of curvature and nodules; delay or non-operative management is associated with higher rates of penile deformity and erectile dysfunction.

Penile Mondor disease — superficial dorsal penile vein thrombophlebitis Peyronie disease Penile lymphangitis (non-venereal sclerosing lymphangitis) Penile cellulitis or other infection Dorsal nerve or other penile pathology Thrombosed penile vascular malformation Clinical diagnosis from the palpable thrombosed dorsal cord Doppler ultrasound of the dorsal penile vein History of precipitating activity or trauma Assessment for a hypercoagulable state if recurrent Exclusion of Peyronie disease and infection Thrombophlebitis of the superficial dorsal vein of the penis, a benign self-limiting condition Presents as a palpable, cord-like, sometimes tender indurated structure along the dorsum of the penis It often follows vigorous or prolonged sexual activity, and other precipitants include trauma and pelvic procedures It is the penile analogue of Mondor disease of the chest/breast wall Diagnosis is usually clinical, supported by Doppler ultrasound showing a thrombosed non-compressible dorsal vein It resolves spontaneously over weeks with conservative measures such as anti-inflammatory treatment and abstinence Features suggesting infection (fever, purulence) Recurrent episodes suggesting a thrombophilia Progressive induration suggesting Peyronie disease Persistent symptoms beyond the expected course Confusing it with Peyronie disease or sclerosing lymphangitis Investigating or treating it as an infection Overlooking a hypercoagulable tendency in recurrent cases Causing undue alarm about a benign self-limiting condition Penile Mondor disease is a localised thrombophlebitis of the superficial dorsal vein of the penis. Endothelial injury and venous stasis, often from prolonged sexual activity, trauma or compression, promote thrombosis of the superficial vein, producing a palpable thrombosed cord with surrounding inflammation. It is a benign, self-limiting vascular condition confined to the superficial penile venous system, and recanalisation occurs over time. The condition is benign and resolves spontaneously over a few weeks with conservative management, with a good prognosis and low recurrence.

Pentasomy X (49,XXXXX) — 49,XXXXX, penta X syndrome, XXXXX syndrome Down syndrome, given the overlapping facial features Tetrasomy X (48,XXXX) and trisomy X (47,XXX) Other polysomy X or Y syndromes Syndromic intellectual disability of other cause Skeletal dysplasia featuring radioulnar synostosis Karyotype, which is diagnostic Chromosomal microarray Echocardiography Skeletal survey, including the forearm for radioulnar synostosis Developmental and cognitive assessment Endocrine and pubertal assessment with pelvic imaging for uterine and ovarian development Infection surveillance The most severe of the female X-polysomies, carrying three extra X chromosomes Moderate-to-severe intellectual disability is typical and more marked than in triple X Short stature is characteristic, in contrast to the tall stature of triple X, reflecting the escalating dosage effect at higher polysomies Characteristic facial features include upslanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, epicanthic folds, a flat nasal bridge, and coarse features that may superficially resemble Down syndrome Congenital heart defects, notably patent ductus arteriosus and septal defects, are common Skeletal anomalies include radioulnar synostosis, joint laxity or contractures, and clinodactyly Microcephaly, recurrent infections, and ovarian and uterine hypoplasia with delayed or absent puberty are frequent Significant congenital heart disease Recurrent or severe infections Failure to progress through puberty requiring endocrine input Mistaking the facial features for Down syndrome and not performing a karyotype Expecting tall stature, as in triple X, when short stature is typical Missing congenital heart disease or radioulnar synostosis Underestimating the degree of intellectual disability compared with lower-grade X-polysomies Pentasomy X arises from sequential non-disjunction during maternal meiosis, producing an egg with four X chromosomes and thus a 49,XXXXX conceptus. Although all but one X is inactivated, the burden of genes that escape X-inactivation rises with each additional X, so gene-dosage effects are amplified relative to trisomy X. This escalating imbalance explains why pentasomy X is far more severe, with pronounced intellectual disability, short stature, congenital malformations, and dysmorphism, illustrating the general rule that each additional sex chromosome worsens the phenotype. Guarded; most individuals have significant intellectual disability and need lifelong support, with outcome influenced by cardiac and other malformations, although survival into adulthood occurs.

Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase deficiency — PEPCK deficiency, PCK1 deficiency, PCK2 deficiency, cytosolic PEPCK deficiency, mitochondrial PEPCK deficiency Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency Glycogen storage disease type I Mitochondrial respiratory chain disorders with lactic acidosis Fatty-acid oxidation disorders with hypoglycaemia Secondary gluconeogenic dysfunction from liver failure or toxins Sepsis with lactic acidosis Blood glucose, blood gas and lactate during symptomatic fasting episodes Urine organic acids looking for elevated tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates Plasma amino acids and ammonia to assess for related metabolic defects Liver function tests to evaluate hepatic involvement PCK1 and PCK2 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Assessment for secondary causes of PEPCK dysfunction before attributing a primary defect Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase catalyses an early committed step of gluconeogenesis, and deficiency (cytosolic PCK1 or mitochondrial PCK2 forms) impairs glucose synthesis from lactate and amino acids Presents with fasting hypoglycaemia accompanied by lactic acidosis, often with hepatomegaly and evidence of liver dysfunction Historically a difficult and controversial diagnosis, as many reported cases reflected secondary or mitochondrial dysfunction rather than a primary enzyme defect Genetically confirmed PCK1 deficiency has been described with hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis and a characteristic urinary organic acid pattern including tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates Metabolic crises are typically triggered by fasting or intercurrent illness, with well periods in between Acute treatment corrects hypoglycaemia and lactic acidosis with intravenous glucose; long-term care focuses on avoidance of fasting and provision of frequent carbohydrate Confirmation now relies on PCK1 or PCK2 molecular testing, since enzyme measurement can be confounded by secondary causes Fasting hypoglycaemia with severe lactic acidosis in an infant or young child Hepatomegaly with liver dysfunction during crises Reduced consciousness or seizures from hypoglycaemia Recurrent metabolic decompensation triggered by fasting or illness Diagnosing primary PEPCK deficiency without excluding secondary mitochondrial or hepatic causes Relying on enzyme assays that can be confounded rather than confirming with molecular testing Failing to capture lactate and organic acids during the acute hypoglycaemic episode Permitting prolonged fasting for illness or procedures without protective glucose Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate, a rate-controlling step channelling gluconeogenic precursors toward glucose. It exists in cytosolic (PCK1) and mitochondrial (PCK2) isoforms. Deficiency impairs gluconeogenesis so that, once glycogen reserves are depleted during fasting, hypoglycaemia develops and gluconeogenic precursors such as lactate accumulate, producing lactic acidosis. Disruption of anaplerosis and the connection between the tricarboxylic acid cycle and glucose output leads to a distinctive organic acid pattern with elevated cycle intermediates. Hepatic involvement reflects the liver's central role in gluconeogenesis. Outcomes are variable and depend on the severity of crises and any coexisting mitochondrial dysfunction; with avoidance of fasting and prompt treatment of hypoglycaemia many children do reasonably well, but severe neonatal presentations carry a poorer prognosis.

Infiltrative/inflammatory mimics - Crohn's disease, sarcoidosis, eosinophilic infiltration, amyloidosis, lymphoma (pp.2523, 2532). Ischaemia and radiation-induced mucosal injury (p.2523). Idiopathic acid-hypersecretory states distinct from Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (p.2523). Around two-thirds of patients with peptic ulcer disease have no abdominal pain, and up to ~87% of those with NSAID-related mucosal injury first present with a complication (bleeding, perforation, or obstruction) without any preceding symptoms (p.2522). Classic duodenal ulcer pain comes on roughly 90 minutes to 3 hours after eating and is typically eased by food or antacids; pain that wakes the patient between midnight and 3 a.m. is the most discriminating symptom and is reported by about two-thirds of duodenal ulcer patients (p.2522). Gastric ulcer pain can instead be provoked by eating, and nausea and weight loss are commoner with gastric than duodenal ulcers (p.2522). Elderly and immunosuppressed patients are less likely to have typical pain and may present directly with bleeding or perforation (pp.2522-2523). H. pylori and NSAIDs are the dominant risk factors (US odds ratios ~3.7 and ~3.3); NSAIDs are now described as the most common cause of PUD, with only ~one-quarter of duodenal and ~one-sixth of gastric ulcers now attributable to H. pylori (pp.2518, 2520). More than half of patients with ulcer-related haemorrhage bleed without any preceding warning signs or symptoms (p.2522). Endoscopy detects an ulcer in fewer than 30% of patients investigated for dyspepsia, reflecting how poorly symptoms predict an actual ulcer (p.2522). Alarm features warranting prompt endoscopy rather than empirical test-and-treat - nausea, vomiting, weight loss, evidence of GI bleeding, or age >=60 years with new dyspepsia (pp.2523, 2531). Constant pain no longer relieved by food/antacids and radiating to the back suggests a penetrating ulcer (e.g. into the pancreas) (p.2522). Sudden severe generalised abdominal pain with a board-like, rigid abdomen (the triad of acute pain, tachycardia, and rigidity) suggests perforation (pp.2522-2523). Pain worsening with meals plus vomiting of undigested food, early satiety, weight loss, or a succussion splash suggests gastric outlet obstruction (pp.2522-2523). Tarry stools or coffee-ground emesis indicate bleeding; tachycardia and orthostasis suggest hypovolaemia from blood loss or vomiting (p.2522). Every gastric ulcer must be biopsied (multiple samples) at discovery because a GU may be malignant, and healing on therapy does not exclude cancer - about 70% of GUs ultimately found malignant show significant (usually incomplete) healing; repeat endoscopy with biopsy at 8-12 weeks is needed if the ulcer persists (pp.2519, 2531-2532). Abdominal pain has poor predictive value for an ulcer, and a normal exam or absent pain does not exclude PUD - many patients, especially the elderly or those on NSAIDs, present first with a complication (pp.2522-2523). Right-sided epigastric tenderness in about 20% of patients can mislead the examiner; epigastric tenderness overall has low predictive value (p.2522). Widespread PPI use can mask and delay the diagnosis of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and increase false-positive gastrin results (p.2534). Consider gastrinoma/ZES when ulcers occur in unusual locations (second part of duodenum or beyond), are multiple, are refractory, recur after acid-reducing surgery, present with frank complications, or arise without H. pylori or NSAID use (p.2535). Peptic ulcers are mucosal breaks >5 mm extending into the submucosa, occurring in the stomach (gastric ulcer, GU) or duodenum (duodenal ulcer, DU); >95% of DUs lie in the first part of the duodenum, within about 3 cm of the pylorus. The disease reflects an imbalance between aggressive factors (acid, pepsin) and mucosal defence. H. pylori and NSAIDs cause the majority of ulcers but act differently: H. pylori-associated benign GUs show antral gastritis, whereas NSAID-related GUs typically lack chronic active gastritis and instead show a chemical gastropathy (foveolar hyperplasia, lamina propria oedema). Duodenal ulcer patients tend to have increased basal and nocturnal acid secretion (with substantial overlap with controls) and reduced duodenal bicarbonate, both potentially influenced by H. pylori; gastric acid output in GU patients is usually normal or reduced, implying impaired mucosal defence. H. pylori is a gram-negative microaerophilic urease-producing rod living in the gastric mucous layer; virulence factors such as the cag pathogenicity island (delivering CagA), VacA, and urease determine the clinical outcome among colonisation, PUD, MALT lymphoma, and gastric adenocarcinoma (pp.2518-2520). More than 90% of both gastric and duodenal ulcers heal with conventional therapy; a GU not healed by 12 weeks or a DU not healed by 8 weeks is considered refractory. Eradicating H. pylori has cut duodenal ulcer recurrence by >80%. GI bleeding complicates roughly 15% of PUD with a 30-day mortality of about 2.5-10% (most deaths from non-bleeding causes such as multiorgan failure, pulmonary complications, and malignancy). Perforation occurs in ~6-7% of patients with 30-day mortality >20%, and penetration carries comparable mortality; gastric outlet obstruction is least common (~1-2%). Complications and mortality rise in patients over 60, partly reflecting greater NSAID use (pp.2522-2523, 2532).

Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders — PUD, Duodenal ulcer, Gastric ulcer, Acid peptic disease Functional (non-ulcer/essential) dyspepsia, including postprandial distress syndrome and epigastric pain syndrome (commonest cause of upper abdominal discomfort) Gastroesophageal reflux disease Proximal gastrointestinal tumors / gastric malignancy Pancreaticobiliary disease (biliary colic, chronic pancreatitis) Gastroduodenal Crohn's disease Mesenteric vascular disease Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma) Cytomegalovirus gastritis/ulceration (immunocompromised hosts) Herpes simplex virus gastritis/ulceration Helicobacter heilmannii infection Phlegmonous (bacterial) gastritis Infectious causes of large gastric folds mimicking Menetrier's disease (CMV, histoplasmosis, syphilis, tuberculosis) Upper endoscopy with biopsy (most sensitive/specific; biopsy gastric ulcers to exclude malignancy) H. pylori testing: rapid urease biopsy test, histology, culture (allows susceptibility testing) Noninvasive H. pylori tests: 13C-urea breath test and stool monoclonal antigen test (both >95% sensitivity/specificity); serology cannot distinguish active from prior infection Fasting serum gastrin (two occasions) when ZES is suspected Secretin stimulation test (rise >=120 pg/mL at 15 min) and gastric pH/acid analysis for gastrinoma Serum calcium, parathyroid hormone, prolactin, and pancreatic polypeptide to screen for MEN 1 in gastrinoma patients Tumor localization imaging and somatostatin-receptor-based studies for gastrinoma Screening blood/urine for surreptitious aspirin/NSAID use in refractory H. pylori-negative ulcers Functional dyspepsia Drug/toxin-induced ulceration (bisphosphonates, clopidogrel, glucocorticoids combined with NSAIDs, potassium chloride, mycophenolate, chemotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors, crack cocaine) Crohn's disease and eosinophilic gastroenteritis Sarcoidosis and other infiltrative disease Ischemia and radiation injury Menetrier's disease and gastric polyposis presenting as large gastric folds Idiopathic hypersecretory state A peptic ulcer is a break in the mucosa larger than 5 mm that extends into the submucosa; more than 90% of patients with the classic dyspepsia symptom complex have no ulcer, and many patients with true ulcers are asymptomatic (Harrison 22e p.2514, p.2522). Burning/gnawing epigastric pain typically occurs 90 minutes to 3 hours after eating in duodenal ulcer and is relieved by food or antacids; pain that wakes the patient between midnight and 3 A.M. is the most discriminating symptom (about two-thirds of DU patients), though it also occurs in roughly one-third with non-ulcer dyspepsia (Harrison 22e p.2522). In gastric ulcer the pain may instead be precipitated by food, and nausea and weight loss are more common than in duodenal ulcer (Harrison 22e p.2522-2523). H. pylori and NSAIDs are the two dominant risk factors (US odds ratios about 3.7 and 3.3); idiopathic and non-Hp/non-NSAID ulcers are rising as H. pylori prevalence falls (Harrison 22e p.2518, p.2522). Gastric ulcers can be malignant and must be biopsied at discovery; duodenal ulcers are almost never malignant (Harrison 22e p.2518). NSAID toxicity correlates poorly with symptoms: over 80% of patients with serious NSAID-related complications had no preceding dyspepsia, and even 75 mg/day of aspirin can cause serious ulceration, so no NSAID dose is completely safe (Harrison 22e p.2520-2521). About two-thirds of PUD patients have no abdominal pain, and up to 87% of those with NSAID-induced disease present with a complication without prior symptoms; more than 50% of ulcer hemorrhages occur without warning (Harrison 22e p.2522). Antral-predominant H. pylori gastritis predisposes to duodenal ulcer, whereas corpus-predominant gastritis predisposes to gastric ulcer, atrophy, and ultimately gastric carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.2519-2520). Endoscopy is the most sensitive and specific test; it detects an ulcer in fewer than 30% of patients presenting with dyspepsia, allows biopsy to exclude malignancy and detect H. pylori, and barium studies are now rarely used (Harrison 22e p.2523). A fasting serum gastrin above ten times normal strongly suggests Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, but two-thirds of ZES patients have gastrin levels that overlap with commoner causes; a secretin-stimulated rise of 120 pg/mL or more within 15 minutes is over 90% sensitive and specific (Harrison 22e p.2535-2536). Suspect gastrinoma with ulcers in unusual locations (second part of duodenum or beyond), refractory or recurrent ulcers, ulcers with complications, or ulcers without H. pylori or NSAID use; about 25% of gastrinomas arise in MEN 1 (Harrison 22e p.2534-2535). Stress-related mucosal injury (Cushing's ulcer after head injury, Curling's ulcer after burns) histologically lacks inflammation and H. pylori, so 'gastritis' is a misnomer; bleeding typically appears 48-72 h after the insult with mechanical ventilation and coagulopathy as key risk factors (Harrison 22e p.2536). Sudden severe generalized abdominal pain with a board-like, rigid abdomen suggesting perforation Tarry stools or coffee-ground emesis indicating gastrointestinal bleeding; tachycardia/orthostasis indicating hypovolemia Persistent pain no longer relieved by food/antacids and radiating to the back suggesting posterior penetration (pancreas) Early satiety, vomiting of undigested food, and a succussion splash suggesting gastric outlet obstruction Weight loss, anorexia, or new dyspepsia at age 60 or older warranting endoscopy before empiric therapy Ulcers in unusual locations, refractory/recurrent ulcers, or multiple ulcers prompting evaluation for gastrinoma Treating dyspepsia as PUD: abdominal pain has poor predictive value and most dyspeptic patients have no ulcer, so empiric assumptions can miss alternative diagnoses. Relying on symptoms to gauge NSAID risk: serious complications usually occur without preceding dyspepsia. Failing to biopsy a gastric ulcer to exclude malignancy. Misinterpreting an elevated fasting gastrin: PPIs, hypochlorhydria/achlorhydria, pernicious anemia, H. pylori, renal insufficiency, retained antrum, and G-cell hyperplasia all raise gastrin, and PPIs must be stopped (about 7 days, bridged with an H2 antagonist) before ZES testing to avoid false positives. Assuming serology proves active H. pylori infection, when it cannot distinguish current from prior infection and is unreliable for follow-up. Abruptly stopping PPIs in gastrinoma patients, which can precipitate severe acid-related complications. Calling stress-related mucosal injury 'gastritis' despite the absence of inflammation, or labeling endoscopic erythema as gastritis without histology. Ulcers result from an imbalance between mucosal aggressive factors (gastric acid secreted by parietal-cell H+,K+-ATPase, pepsin from chief cells) and mucosal defense/repair (a preepithelial mucus-bicarbonate-phospholipid layer, epithelial restitution and tight junctions, and a subepithelial microvascular bed), with prostaglandins, nitric oxide, and mucosal blood flow central to protection. H. pylori, a gram-negative microaerophilic urease-producing rod, colonizes gastric mucus, causes chronic active gastritis in nearly all infected individuals, and produces frank ulceration in only 10-15%; virulence factors include urease (generating ammonia), CagA delivered by a type IV secretion system from cag-PAI-positive strains, VacA, and adhesins. Antral-predominant gastritis raises acid and promotes duodenal ulcer, whereas corpus-predominant pangastritis lowers acid and favors gastric ulcer and carcinoma. NSAIDs injure mucosa both systemically (COX-1 inhibition depletes protective prostaglandins) and topically (weak acids that become trapped and ionized intracellularly), with neutrophil adherence to the gastric microcirculation initiating injury; H. pylori and NSAIDs act as independent and synergistic risk factors. In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, autonomous gastrin secretion from a neuroendocrine tumor drives acid hypersecretion, parietal-cell hyperplasia, ulceration, esophagitis, and diarrhea (Harrison 22e p.2514-2521, p.2534). Eradication of H. pylori reduces duodenal ulcer recurrence by more than 80%, and improving sanitation has steadily lowered ulcer incidence, surgery rates, and physician visits over the past decades. Complications still carry meaningful mortality: GI bleeding (the commonest, ~15% of patients) has a 30-day mortality of about 2.5-10% and is more frequent in those over 60; perforation occurs in about 6-7% of patients with 30-day mortality over 20%; gastric outlet obstruction is the least common (1-2%). Approximately 15,000 deaths per year in the US are attributed to complicated PUD. For gastrinoma, overall 5- and 10-year survival is about 62-75% and 47-53%; complete resection or negative laparotomy yields survival over 90%, while hepatic metastasis drops 5-year survival below 20% (Harrison 22e p.2514, p.2516, p.2522-2523, p.2536). PUD severity is framed clinically by the presence and type of complication: uncomplicated ulcer versus bleeding (commonest, ~15%, 30-day mortality ~2.5-10%), perforation/penetration (~6-7%, 30-day mortality >20%; DU penetrates posteriorly into pancreas, GU into left hepatic lobe), and gastric outlet obstruction (1-2%, may be inflammatory/reversible or fixed scar). For gastrinoma, prognosis is stratified by resectability and metastatic burden rather than a formal stage in this chapter (Harrison 22e p.2522-2523, p.2536).

Perforated peptic ulcer — peptic ulcer perforation, perforated duodenal ulcer, perforated gastric ulcer Acute pancreatitis Acute cholecystitis or biliary perforation Perforation elsewhere in the GI tract (colonic, appendiceal) Ruptured or leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm Myocardial infarction (inferior) Mesenteric ischaemia Ruptured ectopic pregnancy or ovarian pathology Erect chest radiograph to look for free subdiaphragmatic gas CT abdomen and pelvis as the most sensitive test for free air and to localise the perforation Bloods including full blood count, urea and electrolytes, amylase or lipase, CRP, and lactate Arterial blood gas and group and save or crossmatch for resuscitation and theatre Helicobacter pylori testing and, later, endoscopy to confirm ulcer healing and exclude malignancy in gastric ulcers Classically presents with sudden, severe, generalised abdominal pain in a patient who may have a history of dyspepsia or NSAID use Examination shows a rigid, board-like abdomen with generalised tenderness, guarding, and absent bowel sounds from peritonitis Perforation evolves through phases: initial chemical peritonitis from gastric acid, a deceptive period of apparent improvement, and then bacterial peritonitis with sepsis An erect chest radiograph often shows free air under the diaphragm, but its absence does not exclude perforation; CT is more sensitive Key risk factors are Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAID and aspirin use, smoking, and physiological stress Initial management is aggressive resuscitation, analgesia, nasogastric decompression, intravenous proton pump inhibition, and broad-spectrum antibiotics while preparing for surgery The standard operation is closure of the perforation, commonly with an omental (Graham) patch, and thorough peritoneal lavage; large or malignant gastric perforations may require resection Selected patients with a sealed perforation and no generalised peritonitis may be managed non-operatively with close monitoring Sudden severe pain with a rigid abdomen and generalised peritonitis (surgical emergency) Free intraperitoneal gas on imaging Sepsis, haemodynamic instability, or rising lactate indicating septic shock Deterioration after a deceptive symptom-free interval signalling established bacterial peritonitis Excluding perforation on the basis of a normal erect chest radiograph alone Being reassured by the transient improvement of the deceptive second phase Delaying resuscitation and surgery in a septic patient Failing to biopsy or follow up a perforated gastric ulcer to exclude malignancy Perforation occurs when a peptic ulcer erodes through the full thickness of the gastric or duodenal wall, allowing gastric and duodenal contents to spill into the peritoneal cavity. Mucosal breakdown is driven by an imbalance between aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, Helicobacter pylori, NSAIDs) and mucosal defence. Escaped acidic contents first cause a sterile chemical peritonitis, followed within hours by bacterial contamination and generalised bacterial peritonitis. The resulting inflammatory cascade produces fluid sequestration, sepsis, and, if untreated, septic shock and multi-organ failure. Duodenal and pyloric ulcers most often perforate anteriorly. Outcome depends on age, comorbidity, size of perforation, and, critically, the delay before surgery; early intervention gives good recovery, whereas delayed presentation with established peritonitis and sepsis carries high morbidity and mortality.

perforating folliculitis — perforating folliculitis of Mehregan and Coskey keratosis pilaris infective (bacterial or fungal) folliculitis Kyrle disease reactive perforating collagenosis prurigo nodularis follicular lichen planus perforating granuloma annulare skin biopsy demonstrating the plugged follicle with perforation of the follicular wall and eliminated debris renal function tests and estimated glomerular filtration rate fasting glucose and glycated haemoglobin swab of pustular lesions to exclude infective folliculitis where clinically suspected liver and thyroid function tests full blood count urinalysis for proteinuria A perforating dermatosis in which the perforation is centred on a hair follicle, presenting as discrete follicular keratotic papules, each often containing a curled or fragmented hair within a central plug. Favours the hair-bearing extensor surfaces of the limbs, buttocks and trunk, and is frequently pruritic. Regarded as part of the acquired perforating dermatosis spectrum and, like the others, associated with chronic kidney disease, haemodialysis and diabetes mellitus. Histology shows a dilated follicular infundibulum plugged with keratin, degenerate collagen and inflammatory debris, with a perforation through the follicular wall through which material is eliminated. A curled hair shaft is often trapped within the follicular plug and may act as the initiating foreign body driving the perforation. Differentiation from Kyrle disease and reactive perforating collagenosis rests on the follicular localisation of the perforating channel. Management follows the acquired perforating dermatosis approach: emollients, topical retinoids or corticosteroids, keratolytics, phototherapy and control of the underlying systemic disorder. Koebnerisation from scratching contributes to lesion development, so breaking the itch-scratch cycle is an important therapeutic goal. presentation without known renal or metabolic disease, warranting systemic screening pustular or tender lesions suggesting superimposed infective folliculitis requiring microbiological assessment widespread refractory disease indicating poorly controlled uraemia or diabetes signs of secondary bacterial infection from excoriation misdiagnosing pruritic follicular papules as ordinary keratosis pilaris or infective folliculitis and missing the perforating pathology not sectioning the biopsy through the follicle, so the follicular perforation is not visualised overlooking associated chronic kidney disease or diabetes relying on antibacterial therapy alone when the process is a non-infective perforating dermatosis Perforating folliculitis arises from injury to the follicular infundibulum, where retained keratin, a coiled or fractured hair shaft, and degenerate dermal connective tissue accumulate and are eliminated through a defect in the follicular wall. Follicular rupture provokes a foreign-body inflammatory response that facilitates transepithelial elimination of collagen and keratinous debris. In acquired cases the metabolic milieu of uraemia and diabetes, dermal microangiopathy, and repetitive scratch-induced trauma with Koebnerisation are considered key triggers, injuring the follicular epithelium and perpetuating the perforating process. The condition tends to be chronic and relapsing, with individual follicular papules resolving over weeks while new lesions continue to appear; improvement generally follows better control of the underlying systemic disease and reduction of scratching.

Perianal abscess — anorectal abscess, perirectal abscess, ischiorectal abscess Thrombosed external haemorrhoid Pilonidal abscess Hidradenitis suppurativa Bartholin's abscess in women Fournier's gangrene or other necrotising perineal infection Anal canal or rectal malignancy presenting with sepsis Examination under anaesthesia to locate and drain deep collections MRI of the pelvis for supralevator, complex, or recurrent collections Endoanal ultrasound to assess deep or intersphincteric collections Blood glucose and HbA1c, with screening for immunosuppression in recurrent disease Blood cultures and inflammatory markers if systemic sepsis is suspected Culture of drained pus and, in atypical cases, biopsy of the abscess wall Represents the acute suppurative phase of cryptoglandular anal gland infection, of which anal fistula is the chronic sequel Presents with severe, constant, throbbing perianal pain, a tender fluctuant swelling, erythema, and often fever Classified by the anatomical space involved: perianal (most common), ischiorectal (ischioanal), intersphincteric, and supralevator Deep abscesses (intersphincteric or supralevator) may cause severe pain and sepsis with little visible external swelling, requiring examination under anaesthesia and imaging The mainstay of treatment is prompt incision and drainage; antibiotics alone are inadequate and delay is dangerous A significant proportion of drained abscesses subsequently develop a fistula-in-ano Recurrent or atypical abscesses should prompt consideration of Crohn's disease, diabetes, immunosuppression, or malignancy A spreading, boggy, or crepitant perineum with systemic toxicity suggests necrotising infection (Fournier's gangrene), a surgical emergency Spreading erythema, crepitus, or perineal necrosis suggesting Fournier's gangrene Systemic sepsis, or diabetes or immunosuppression with pain out of proportion to findings Severe deep pain with minimal external signs suggesting an intersphincteric or supralevator abscess Recurrent abscesses suggesting Crohn's disease or underlying malignancy Relying on antibiotics instead of timely surgical drainage Missing a deep intersphincteric or supralevator collection because external signs are minimal Inadequate drainage leaving a loculated cavity and early recurrence Failing to recognise early Fournier's gangrene in a diabetic or immunosuppressed patient A perianal abscess usually begins with obstruction and infection of an anal gland in the intersphincteric plane (the cryptoglandular mechanism). Pus collects and tracks along planes of least resistance, caudally to the perianal skin, laterally through the external sphincter into the ischioanal fossa, or cephalad above the levators, forming abscesses in the corresponding spaces. It represents the acute phase of the same disease that, once drained or spontaneously discharging, may leave a chronic fistula. Diabetes, immunosuppression, and Crohn's disease predispose to more extensive or recurrent infection. Prompt incision and drainage resolves most simple abscesses, though a notable minority progress to a chronic fistula; delayed treatment or necrotising infection carries substantial morbidity and mortality.

Perianal fistula — fistula-in-ano, anal fistula, anorectal fistula, perianal fistula-in-ano Perianal or ischiorectal abscess Pilonidal sinus disease Hidradenitis suppurativa Crohn perianal disease Anal fistula secondary to tuberculosis Anorectal malignancy or fistulating carcinoma Examination under anaesthesia to define the tracks and internal opening MRI of the pelvis for complex or recurrent fistulae Endoanal ultrasound to map tracks and sphincter involvement Colonoscopy or ileocolonoscopy when Crohn disease is suspected Biopsy of atypical or non-healing tracks to exclude malignancy or tuberculosis Anorectal physiology and continence assessment when division of sphincter is contemplated A fistula-in-ano is an abnormal track lined by granulation tissue connecting the anal canal or rectum to the perianal skin, usually the sequel of a drained or spontaneously discharging anorectal abscess Typical symptoms are recurrent perianal discharge, intermittent pain and swelling that flares when the external opening blocks, and pruritus, often with a history of a previous abscess The Parks classification describes tracks in relation to the sphincters as intersphincteric, transsphincteric, suprasphincteric, and extrasphincteric Goodsall rule helps predict the internal opening: anterior openings tend to track radially, while posterior openings tend to curve to a posterior midline internal opening MRI of the pelvis and endoanal ultrasound accurately map complex tracks, secondary extensions, and the relationship to the sphincter complex before surgery The therapeutic balance is eradicating the fistula while preserving continence; low simple tracks may be laid open, whereas tracks involving significant sphincter muscle need sphincter-preserving techniques or a seton Recurrent, multiple, or complex fistulae should raise suspicion of Crohn disease, tuberculosis, or malignancy and prompt appropriate investigation Spreading perianal sepsis, cellulitis, or features of necrotising infection (Fournier gangrene) requiring emergency surgery Systemic sepsis from an undrained abscess Suspicion of underlying malignancy in a chronic, indurated, or non-healing fistula Extensive or multiple complex tracks suggesting Crohn disease with risk to continence Dividing significant sphincter muscle and causing incontinence, particularly in anterior fistulae in women or high tracks Missing a secondary track or the true internal opening, leading to early recurrence Laying open a fistula in a patient with undiagnosed Crohn disease with poor healing Treating an abscess without recognising or planning for an underlying fistula Failing to biopsy a chronic, atypical, or non-healing track and missing malignancy Most fistulae-in-ano arise from the cryptoglandular theory: infection of an anal gland in the intersphincteric plane at the level of the dentate line forms an abscess, which discharges and leaves a persistent epithelialising or granulating track between the internal opening in the anal canal and an external opening on the perianal skin. The course of the track relative to the internal and external anal sphincters determines its classification and surgical difficulty. Secondary tracks and horseshoe extensions can develop. A minority result from specific conditions such as Crohn disease, tuberculosis, pelvic sepsis, radiation, or malignancy, which alter management and prognosis. Simple low fistulae have a high cure rate after laying open with preservation of continence, whereas complex, high, or recurrent tracks carry greater risk of recurrence and incontinence and often require staged, sphincter-preserving strategies. Fistulae associated with Crohn disease are more difficult to heal and tend to recur, and outcomes depend on control of the underlying disease.

Perianal haematoma — thrombosed external haemorrhoid, external anal thrombosis, perianal thrombosis Prolapsed and thrombosed internal or mixed haemorrhoids Perianal or ischiorectal abscess Anal skin tag (non-acute, non-tender) Anal carcinoma or a pigmented perianal lesion such as melanoma Condylomata or other perianal skin lesion Anal fissure with sentinel tag Pilonidal or perianal cyst Inspection and gentle digital examination to confirm a tense subcutaneous clot at the verge Proctoscopy once acute pain allows, to assess for internal haemorrhoids Histology of excised tissue if the lesion is atypical or pigmented Assessment for constipation and straining as contributory factors Coagulation review if there are recurrent or spontaneous thromboses Exclusion of abscess by examination and, if needed, imaging when infection is suspected A perianal haematoma is an acute, painful, subcutaneous clot at the anal verge, often used interchangeably with a thrombosed external haemorrhoid; it is sometimes called a 'five-day painful pile' because pain peaks early and settles over several days It presents as a sudden, tense, tender, blue-purple lump at the anal margin, typically after straining, heavy lifting, constipation, or childbirth The lesion lies below the dentate line in somatically innervated tissue, which accounts for its marked pain, in contrast to painless internal haemorrhoidal bleeding Diagnosis is clinical on inspection; a smooth, tense, dark subcutaneous swelling at the verge is characteristic and does not require imaging Presenting early (within the first couple of days) while pain is severe favours evacuation or excision of the clot for rapid relief; later presentation with easing pain favours conservative management Conservative care comprises analgesia, warm baths, stool softening, topical measures, and reassurance, with most resolving spontaneously and sometimes leaving a residual skin tag Simple incision that only decompresses the clot has a higher recurrence and residual tag rate than complete excision of the thrombosed segment under local anaesthesia Recurrent or atypical lesions should prompt consideration of underlying causes and exclusion of other perianal pathology Signs of abscess such as spreading erythema, fluctuance, fever, or systemic upset A pigmented, indurated, or ulcerated lesion suggesting malignancy or melanoma Recurrent or multiple spontaneous thromboses suggesting a bleeding or clotting disorder Severe or worsening pain with systemic features Non-healing ulceration after clot discharge Confusing it with a perianal abscess and incising into infection or vice versa Performing simple incision rather than complete excision, leading to recurrence and residual tag Attempting evacuation late when the clot has organised and pain is already settling Missing a pigmented malignant lesion masquerading as a thrombosis Neglecting to address constipation and straining, allowing recurrence A perianal haematoma arises from rupture of a subcutaneous vein or venule of the external haemorrhoidal plexus, or from thrombosis within it, producing a clot within the perianal subcutaneous tissue below the dentate line. A sudden rise in venous pressure, typically from straining at stool, heavy lifting, coughing, or the second stage of labour, precipitates the event. The confined subcutaneous space and the tense clot stretch the richly innervated anoderm, generating acute severe pain that peaks within the first days and then eases as the clot organises and is gradually resorbed. Overlying skin may ulcerate and discharge the clot spontaneously. As the haematoma resolves, fibrosis of the redundant stretched skin may leave a residual anal skin tag. A perianal haematoma is benign and self-limiting; pain typically resolves within days to a week whether managed conservatively or by excision, and early excision gives the fastest relief with a low recurrence rate, though a residual skin tag may remain.

Periapical abscess — dentoalveolar abscess, apical abscess, acute periapical abscess, dental abscess Periodontal abscess arising from the gingival sulcus Irreversible pulpitis without abscess formation Periapical granuloma or radicular cyst Osteomyelitis of the jaw Odontogenic infection of adjacent teeth or sinus Pulp sensibility testing (expected non-vital response) Percussion, palpation, and mobility assessment Periapical radiography and, when needed, cone-beam CT for extent Assessment for fascial-space spread and airway compromise in swelling Culture and systemic markers if severe or spreading infection A periapical abscess is a localised collection of pus at the root apex arising from a necrotic, infected pulp Classic features are severe, well-localised pain, tenderness to percussion, and a feeling that the tooth is extruded or high on biting The affected tooth is typically non-vital, so pulp sensibility testing is negative while percussion and palpation are markedly positive Pus may drain spontaneously through a sinus tract (gum boil), which can relieve pain and produce a chronic, less symptomatic picture Early radiographs may look normal because bone changes lag behind, whereas chronic lesions show a periapical radiolucency Primary management is drainage and elimination of the source through root canal treatment or extraction; antibiotics are adjuncts reserved for spreading infection or systemic involvement Infection can track along fascial planes, so the pattern of swelling depends on tooth position relative to muscle attachments Recurrent or persistent sinus tracts indicate ongoing infection needing definitive endodontic or surgical treatment Rapidly spreading swelling of the floor of mouth or submandibular region raising concern for Ludwig angina and airway obstruction Trismus, difficulty swallowing, drooling, or voice change indicating deep-space infection Systemic sepsis, high fever, or periorbital/cavernous sinus spread from upper anterior teeth Immunocompromised or diabetic patients in whom infection can progress dangerously fast Prescribing antibiotics without draining the abscess or removing the source Being reassured by a normal early radiograph despite clear clinical signs Missing progression to a deep-space or airway-threatening infection Confusing a periodontal abscess with a periapical abscess and mistreating the cause A periapical abscess develops when pulp necrosis, usually secondary to caries or trauma, allows bacteria and their toxins to egress through the apical foramen into the periapical tissues. The host inflammatory response produces a purulent collection localised to the periradicular bone. Rising pressure causes intense pain and may resorb surrounding bone, seen later as a radiolucency. Pus follows the path of least resistance, perforating cortical bone and tracking into soft tissue, where the relationship of the perforation to muscle attachments determines whether a localised vestibular swelling, a draining sinus, or a spreading fascial-space infection results. With timely drainage and source control the prognosis is excellent, but delayed treatment risks spread to fascial spaces, osteomyelitis, airway compromise, or life-threatening sepsis.

Periarticular Disorders of the Extremities — Bursitis, Rotator cuff tendinitis, Impingement syndrome, Frozen shoulder, Adhesive capsulitis, Tennis elbow, Golfer's elbow, De Quervain's tenosynovitis, Plantar fasciitis, Iliotibial band syndrome, Calcific tendinitis Glenohumeral osteoarthritis Rheumatoid arthritis Gout and crystal arthropathy Spondyloarthritis Cervical radiculopathy referring to the shoulder Acromioclavicular joint pathology Intraarticular knee pathology (osteoarthritis, meniscal injury) versus periarticular knee pain Septic bursitis (e.g., olecranon or prepatellar) Infectious tenosynovitis Septic arthritis presenting as periarticular pain and swelling History and directed physical examination (often sufficient for diagnosis) Provocative maneuvers (painful abduction arc, drop-arm test, Finkelstein test, Yergason's test) Bursal aspiration with Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis when infection or gout is suspected Ultrasound (for bursitis, tendinitis, rotator cuff tears, calcific deposits, plantar fascia thickening, and guided injection) Plain radiographs (may show tendon calcification or incidental heel spurs) MRI (sensitive for rotator cuff tears, tendon integrity, and plantar fasciitis when diagnosis is unclear) Gouty bursitis/tendinitis (urate deposition) Calcium pyrophosphate or apatite crystal deposition Rheumatoid or inflammatory arthritis involving periarticular structures Referred pain from intraarticular degenerative joint disease Periarticular disorders are common soft-tissue musculoskeletal problems affecting people of any age, arising from structures around (rather than within) the joint such as bursae, tendons, fascia, and connective-tissue bands. Bursitis is inflammation of a synovial-lined sac; adults have over 150 bursae that ease gliding of tendons and muscles over bony prominences, and overuse, trauma, systemic disease (rheumatoid arthritis, gout), or infection can trigger inflammation. Subacromial (subdeltoid) bursitis is the most common bursitis and frequently coexists with rotator cuff tendinitis, presenting with anterolateral shoulder pain. Acutely inflamed olecranon or prepatellar bursitis with warmth/redness warrants aspiration with Gram stain, culture, and crystal examination to exclude infection or gout before assuming a mechanical cause. Rotator cuff tendinitis (impingement syndrome) is the leading cause of a painful shoulder; the supraspinatus tendon is most often affected due to impingement between the humeral head and the anterior acromion/coracoacromial ligament, classically producing a painful abduction arc of 60-120 degrees. Calcific tendinitis reflects hydroxyapatite (calcium salt) deposition within a tendon, most often the supraspinatus (involved in about 63% of cases), typically after age 40, and may be asymptomatic or cause sudden severe shoulder pain. De Quervain's tenosynovitis involves the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis at the radial styloid; a positive Finkelstein test (thumb tucked in fist with ulnar wrist deviation) reproduces radial styloid pain. Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) causes painful, globally restricted active and passive shoulder motion, usually without intrinsic joint disease, and is associated with diabetes, thyroid disease, chronic pulmonary disease, and prior myocardial infarction. Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) arises from repetitive resisted wrist extension/supination; most patients are injured by activities other than tennis such as pulling weeds, carrying briefcases, or using a screwdriver. Plantar fasciitis classically causes severe heel pain with the first steps in the morning or after rest, easing with initial activity then worsening with prolonged weight-bearing; tenderness localizes to the medial calcaneal attachment of the fascia. Drug-induced tendinopathy is increasingly recognized, with quinolones, glucocorticoids, aromatase inhibitors, and statins implicated; the Achilles tendon is most often affected and rupture can be the presenting event. Yergason's test (pain on resisted forearm supination with the elbow at 90 degrees) supports bicipital tendinitis; biceps tendon rupture in older patients may be painless and recognized by a retracted bulge of the long head. Acutely warm, red, tender bursa suggesting septic bursitis or gout requiring aspiration Weakness of abduction/external rotation or a positive drop-arm test suggesting a rotator cuff tear Acute tendon rupture (e.g., Achilles in drug-induced tendinopathy, biceps in active patients) Globally restricted active and passive shoulder motion suggesting adhesive capsulitis rather than a focal tendinitis Periarticular pain in the setting of systemic disease (rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, thyroid disease) prompting evaluation of the underlying condition Anserine bursitis is a frequently overlooked periarticular cause of knee pain. Assuming inflamed olecranon or prepatellar bursitis is mechanical without excluding infection or gout by aspiration. Mislabeling globally restricted shoulder motion as simple tendinitis when it is adhesive capsulitis. Attributing heel pain to a radiographic heel spur, which is of little diagnostic significance in plantar fasciitis. Overlooking medication as a cause of tendon pain or rupture (drug-induced tendinopathy), and reintroducing the offending agent. Confusing iliopsoas bursitis pain with pain originating within the hip joint itself. These are disorders of the soft tissues surrounding joints rather than the synovial joint itself. Bursitis is synovial inflammation of a bursa from frictional overuse, trauma, systemic inflammatory/crystal disease, or infection. Tendinopathies (rotator cuff, bicipital, patellar, epicondylar, De Quervain's) result from mechanical impingement and repetitive resisted loading producing microtears, inflammation, and degeneration at tendon insertions; the supraspinatus is uniquely vulnerable to impingement beneath the acromion. Calcific tendinitis is caused by hydroxyapatite deposition within tendon substance through poorly understood phases of calcification that can incite acute inflammation. Adhesive capsulitis features a thickened shoulder capsule with mild chronic inflammatory infiltrate and fibrosis, often after a period of immobility. Plantar fasciitis arises at the fascial origin on the medial calcaneal tuberosity from cumulative loading. Drug-induced tendinopathies have an unknown mechanism but are linked to specific drug classes. Most periarticular disorders are self-limited and respond to conservative measures. Adhesive capsulitis usually improves spontaneously over 1-3 years, though many patients retain some residual loss of shoulder motion. More than 80% of plantar fasciitis cases resolve within 12 months. Calcific tendinitis is largely self-limited. Rotator cuff tears vary in outcome depending on tear size, chronicity, pain, functional loss, and coexisting osteoarthritis. No formal grading system; rotator cuff tears are clinically characterized as acute, subacute, or chronic and as partial- or full-thickness, with management guided by tear severity, symptom duration, pain, functional loss, and coexisting osteoarthritis.

pericardial cyst — pleuropericardial cyst, spring-water cyst, mesothelial pericardial cyst bronchogenic cyst thymic cyst loculated pericardial effusion prominent epicardial or mediastinal fat pad cardiophrenic lymphadenopathy morgagni diaphragmatic hernia cystic mediastinal teratoma or other mediastinal mass contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax (water attenuation, non-enhancing, well-circumscribed) cardiac or thoracic MRI (low T1, high T2 signal, no enhancement) transthoracic echocardiography (echo-free space adjacent to the heart) chest radiography (smooth, rounded cardiophrenic-angle opacity) fluid analysis if aspirated (clear serous, benign mesothelial cells) PET imaging in selected cases to exclude a metabolically active/malignant mass interval imaging surveillance to document stability A pericardial cyst is a benign, thin-walled, mesothelium-lined fluid-filled sac that usually does not communicate with the pericardial cavity, most often congenital in origin. The classic location is the right cardiophrenic angle (roughly two-thirds of cases), with the left cardiophrenic angle next most common; atypical superior mediastinal locations occur but are rare. Most are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on chest radiography or cross-sectional imaging performed for another reason. When symptomatic, patients may report atypical chest discomfort, dyspnoea or cough from local compression; serious complications such as compression of a cardiac chamber, rupture or infection are uncommon. The typical 'spring-water' cyst contains clear serous fluid; the term reflects the classic clear appearance of aspirated contents. CT shows a well-defined, non-enhancing, homogeneous water-attenuation lesion abutting the pericardium; MRI demonstrates low T1 and high T2 signal without contrast enhancement of the contents. Asymptomatic, radiologically characteristic cysts can generally be managed conservatively with periodic imaging surveillance rather than intervention. Intervention (percutaneous aspiration or, more definitively, surgical/thoracoscopic excision) is reserved for symptomatic, enlarging, complicated or diagnostically uncertain lesions. rapid enlargement or interval change on serial imaging haemodynamic compromise or arrhythmia from cardiac chamber compression features suggesting infection of the cyst (fever, wall enhancement, surrounding inflammation) imaging characteristics atypical for a simple cyst (thick or enhancing wall, solid components, septations) acute chest pain with sudden change in cyst size suggesting rupture Mistaking a loculated pericardial effusion or a solid/malignant mediastinal mass for a simple benign cyst without cross-sectional confirmation. Proceeding to surgery for an incidental, asymptomatic, radiologically classic cyst that could be safely observed. Overlooking rare but important complications such as compression, infection or spontaneous rupture in a symptomatic patient. Relying on percutaneous aspiration alone, after which recurrence is common because the secretory lining remains. Failing to consider a Morgagni hernia, which can mimic a right cardiophrenic-angle cyst. Pericardial cysts are thought to arise from aberrant embryological development of the pericardial coelom, in which one of the mesenchymal lacunae that normally coalesce to form the pericardial sac fails to fuse and instead persists as an isolated, mesothelium-lined cavity. The resulting cyst has a thin fibrous wall lined by a single layer of mesothelial cells and typically contains clear serous fluid. Because it usually does not communicate with the pericardial space, it enlarges slowly by fluid secretion and is generally of little haemodynamic consequence. Rarely, acquired cysts follow inflammation, cardiac surgery or trauma. Mass effect, when it occurs, results from mechanical compression of adjacent structures rather than any intrinsic secretory or malignant behaviour. The prognosis is excellent; most pericardial cysts are benign, remain stable and never cause symptoms, and complete surgical excision when required is generally curative with a low recurrence rate.

Pericardial Disease — constrictive pericarditis, pericardial effusion Acute myocardial infarction (common confusion with acute pericarditis; in pericarditis ST elevations are upwardly concave, biomarker elevations are modest, and pain may precede or coincide with fever) (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2083) Restrictive cardiomyopathy (shares restriction of ventricular filling; must be distinguished from constrictive pericarditis because the latter is surgically correctable) (Harrison 22e p.2084) Right ventricular infarction (may mimic tamponade with hypotension, elevated JVP, slow y descent, occasional paradoxical pulse) (Harrison 22e p.2082) Cor pulmonale (systemic venous hypertension and paradoxical pulse, but Kussmaul's sign is negative and advanced parenchymal lung disease is apparent) (Harrison 22e p.2084) Tricuspid stenosis (congestive hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, ascites, venous distention, but characteristic murmur present) (Harrison 22e p.2084) Hepatic cirrhosis (constrictive pericarditis with hepatomegaly, jaundice, and intractable ascites may be mistaken for cirrhosis; inspection of distended neck veins avoids the error) (Harrison 22e p.2084) Viral pericarditis (coxsackievirus A and B, echovirus, influenza, mumps, herpes simplex, varicella-zoster, adenovirus, cytomegalovirus, HIV, post-acute COVID, mpox) (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2082) Tuberculous pericarditis (effusion, constriction, or effusive-constrictive disease; suggested by high adenosine deaminase or M. tuberculosis DNA by PCR, often requiring pericardial tissue) (Harrison 22e p.2082, p.2084) Pyogenic/purulent bacterial pericarditis (pneumococcus, Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Neisseria, Legionella, Chlamydia; from cardiothoracic surgery, lung/pleural extension, esophageal rupture, or valve-ring abscess; fever, chills, septicemia, poor prognosis) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083) Fungal pericarditis (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, aspergillosis, candidiasis) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083) Parasitic/protozoal and syphilitic pericarditis (amebiasis, toxoplasmosis, echinococcosis, trichinosis) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083) Transthoracic echocardiography: most widely used, sensitive, specific, bedside-capable; localizes and estimates pericardial fluid and shows late-diastolic collapse of the RV free wall and right atrium in tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2082) Doppler echocardiography: in tamponade and constriction, inspiratory increase in tricuspid/pulmonic flow velocities with decrease in pulmonary venous/mitral/aortic velocities and a leftward septal shift (respirophasic variation) (Harrison 22e p.2082, p.2084) CT and MRI: superior for loculated effusions, pericardial thickening, pericardial masses, calcification, and detecting pericardial inflammation; more accurate than echocardiography for confirming or excluding constriction (MRI assesses myocardial involvement) (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2084) ECG: stage 1-4 evolution in acute pericarditis; low QRS voltage and electrical alternans with large effusion/tamponade; low voltage and diffuse T-wave changes with atrial fibrillation in constriction (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2081, p.2083) Chest radiograph: enlarged cardiac silhouette with a 'water bottle' configuration in large effusion; pericardial calcification (most common in tuberculous constriction) (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2084) Pericardiocentesis with fluid analysis: cell counts, cytology for neoplastic cells, cultures, M. tuberculosis PCR and adenosine deaminase (Harrison 22e p.2082) Pericardial biopsy (e.g., via limited thoracotomy) when fluid analysis is non-diagnostic, especially for suspected tuberculous or neoplastic disease (Harrison 22e p.2082, p.2084) Laboratory: elevated C-reactive protein and white blood cell count in viral/idiopathic pericarditis (Harrison 22e p.2082) Uremic and dialysis-associated pericarditis (renal failure; fibrinous, serosanguinous effusions, friction rub common but pain usually mild) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083) Neoplastic pericarditis (lung and breast carcinoma, melanoma, lymphoma, leukemia; metastatic invasion, primary tumors, mesothelioma) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083) Postcardiac injury syndrome (postpericardiotomy, posttraumatic, post-MI Dressler's syndrome; hypersensitivity/autoimmune reaction to myocardial antigens 1-4 weeks after injury) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2082) Collagen vascular / autoimmune disease (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, ankylosing spondylitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, IgG4 disease, rheumatic fever, polyarteritis nodosa) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083) Drug-induced pericarditis (procainamide, hydralazine, phenytoin, isoniazid, minoxidil, anticoagulants, methysergide) (Harrison 22e p.2078) Postirradiation (mediastinal radiation) pericarditis, acute or chronic constrictive (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083) Aortic dissection with leakage into the pericardial sac (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2081) Acute myocardial infarction and metabolic causes (myxedema, cholesterol pericarditis) (Harrison 22e p.2078) Familial Mediterranean fever and other autoinflammatory syndromes (Harrison 22e p.2078) Acute pericarditis has four principal diagnostic features: chest pain, a pericardial friction rub, characteristic ECG changes, and pericardial effusion (Harrison 22e p.2078). Pericarditic chest pain is typically retrosternal/left precordial, often pleuritic, may radiate to the trapezius ridge, and is characteristically intensified by lying supine and relieved by sitting up and leaning forward (Harrison 22e p.2079). A pericardial friction rub is audible at some point in approximately 85% of patients with acute pericarditis; it may have up to three components per cycle and is best heard at end expiration with the patient upright and leaning forward (Harrison 22e p.2079). The ECG of acute pericarditis classically evolves through four stages: stage 1 widespread upwardly-concave ST elevation with PR-segment depression, stage 2 normalization of ST, stage 3 T-wave inversion, and stage 4 return to normal (Harrison 22e p.2079). Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade is hypotension, soft or absent heart sounds, and jugular venous distention with a prominent x descent but an absent y descent (Harrison 22e p.2081). Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory fall in systolic pressure >10 mmHg) is an important clue to tamponade, but also occurs in about one-third of constrictive pericarditis cases and in hypovolemic shock, obstructive airway disease, and pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.2081-2082). In constrictive pericarditis the rigid thickened pericardium limits ventricular filling only after early diastole (unimpeded in early diastole, then abruptly reduced), whereas in tamponade filling is impeded throughout diastole (Harrison 22e p.2083). Kussmaul's sign (failure of venous pressure to decline, or a rise, during inspiration) is common in chronic constrictive pericarditis but is also seen in tricuspid stenosis, right ventricular infarction, and restrictive cardiomyopathy; it is negative in cor pulmonale (Harrison 22e p.2083-2084). A pericardial knock, an early third heart sound at the apex from abrupt cessation of ventricular filling, is often conspicuous in constrictive pericarditis (Harrison 22e p.2083). Constrictive pericarditis produces an M-shaped atrial pressure contour with prominent x and y descents; the y descent (diminished/absent in tamponade) is the most prominent deflection, and the ventricular pressure pulse shows a 'square root' sign in diastole (Harrison 22e p.2083). In developing nations a high percentage of chronic constrictive pericarditis is tuberculous, but TB is now an uncommon cause in North America and Western Europe; other causes include prior viral/idiopathic pericarditis, cardiac surgery, mediastinal irradiation, and neoplasm (Harrison 22e p.2083). Cardiac tamponade: hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and unexplained sudden enlargement of the cardiac silhouette; may be rapidly fatal if not recognized and treated promptly (Harrison 22e p.2081) Reduced QRS amplitude with electrical alternans of P, QRS, or T waves raises suspicion of tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2081) Predictors of poor prognosis warranting hospitalization in acute pericarditis: fever >38C, subacute onset, large pericardial effusion, immunosuppression, or evidence of tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2080) Purulent (pyogenic) pericarditis carries a poor prognosis and requires immediate drainage and antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.2083) Without treatment, tuberculous pericardial disease can progress to constriction; constriction should be treated surgically (Harrison 22e p.2084) Distinguishing constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy is critical because constriction is surgically correctable; their hemodynamics overlap (square-root sign and equalized diastolic pressures occur in both) and echocardiography alone cannot definitively establish or exclude constriction, so MRI/CT is needed (Harrison 22e p.2083, p.2084). Acute pericarditis is commonly mistaken for AMI and vice versa; in pericarditis the ST elevations are upwardly concave, reciprocal depression is limited to aVR/V1, and biomarker rises (from epi-myocarditis) are modest relative to AMI (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2083). Pericardial calcification may occur without constriction, and constriction may occur without calcification, so calcification neither confirms nor excludes the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2084). Acute idiopathic pericarditis is a diagnosis of exclusion with no specific test; all other causes of fibrinous pericarditis must be considered (Harrison 22e p.2082-2083). Constrictive pericarditis with hepatomegaly, jaundice, and intractable ascites can be misdiagnosed as hepatic cirrhosis unless the distended neck veins with characteristic waveform are recognized (Harrison 22e p.2084). Pain is often absent in slowly developing tuberculous, postirradiation, neoplastic, and uremic pericarditis, so its absence does not exclude pericardial disease (Harrison 22e p.2079). Anticoagulants should be avoided in acute pericarditis because they could cause bleeding into the pericardial cavity and tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2080). The pericardium is a double-layered sac (visceral and parietal layers) separated by 15-50 mL of plasma ultrafiltrate; it restrains sudden cardiac chamber dilation and fixes cardiac position. In acute pericarditis, inflammation produces fibrinous or effusive disease. Cardiac tamponade occurs when fluid accumulates in the pericardial space in quantity sufficient to obstruct ventricular inflow, raising intrapericardial pressure and limiting diastolic filling throughout diastole, reducing stroke volume, cardiac output, and arterial pressure. As little as 200 mL can cause tamponade when fluid develops rapidly, versus >2000 mL when it accumulates slowly and the pericardium stretches. In chronic constrictive pericarditis, healing of fibrinous/serofibrinous pericarditis or resorption of effusion produces granulation tissue that contracts into a rigid, sometimes calcified scar encasing the heart; ventricular filling is unimpeded early in diastole then abruptly halts at the pericardium's elastic limit. End-diastolic pressures in both ventricles and mean atrial, pulmonary venous, and systemic venous pressures equalize within ~5 mmHg, while resting systolic function is typically normal or only mildly impaired (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2081, p.2083). Viral or idiopathic acute pericarditis usually runs its course in a few days to 4 weeks; recurrent (relapsing) pericarditis occurs in approximately one-fourth of patients, and both tamponade and constriction are possible but infrequent complications. Most patients with acute pericarditis can be managed as outpatients with careful follow-up. Untreated cardiac tamponade may be rapidly fatal. Purulent pericarditis generally has a poor prognosis. Without treatment, tuberculous pericardial disease may progress to constriction. Pericardial resection is the only definitive treatment of constrictive pericarditis, with benefits accruing progressively over months; operative mortality is in the range of 5-10% even at experienced centers, highest in the most severe disease, especially radiation-induced (Harrison 22e p.2080, p.2082, p.2083, p.2084). Clinical classification: I. Acute pericarditis (<6 weeks) - A. Fibrinous, B. Effusive (serous or sanguineous); II. Subacute pericarditis (6 weeks to 6 months) - A. Effusive-constrictive, B. Constrictive; III. Chronic pericarditis (>6 months) - A. Constrictive, B. Adhesive (nonconstrictive). Etiologic classification: infectious, noninfectious, and presumed autoimmune. Table 281-2 distinguishes tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, right ventricular myocardial infarction, and effusive-constrictive pericarditis by clinical, ECG, echocardiographic, and CT/MRI features (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2080).

Acute pericarditis — ECG (diffuse ST elevation, PR depression) Echocardiogram Inflammatory markers Tamponade if effusion enlarges Acute myocardial ischaemia / STEMI Acute aortic syndrome (dissection) Pulmonary embolism Pleuritis / pneumonia Musculoskeletal chest wall pain (e.g. costochondritis) Gastro-oesophageal reflux / oesophageal disease Herpes zoster Acute myocarditis (often viral; chest discomfort and ST/T-wave changes can overlap) Pneumonia / pleuritis 12-lead ECG looking for diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression (p.149) Chest radiograph (pericardial calcification suggests chronic pericarditis; usually unremarkable in acute disease) (p.150) Echocardiography to detect effusion (may be normal in 34-50% of acute cases) (p.90) Measurement of pulsus paradoxus when tamponade is suspected (p.312) Acute coronary syndrome / STEMI (diffuse ST elevation of pericarditis can be mistaken for infarction) Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy (ST elevation and biomarker rise mimicking MI) Aortic dissection extending into the pericardium Pulmonary embolism Diagnosis rests on the combination of characteristic chest pain, a pericardial friction rub, and characteristic ECG changes; echocardiography can be normal in roughly a third to half of cases, so a normal echo does not exclude pericarditis (p.90). The pericardial pain is typically pleuritic and positional: worse supine and on inspiration/coughing, relieved by sitting up and leaning forward (p.146, p.149). Pain referred to the trapezius ridge is characteristic of pericardial inflammation and is not typical of angina (p.149). Most of the pericardium is insensitive to pain; the discomfort of pericarditis is thought to arise largely from accompanying pleural inflammation, explaining its pleuritic, positional quality and referral to shoulder/neck (p.147). A pericardial friction rub on auscultation reflects pericardial inflammation and is a key physical sign (p.149). Pericarditis is an uncommon final diagnosis among undifferentiated acute chest pain presentations (about 4% in one ED series), so other causes are statistically more likely (p.145). Hypotension with significant tachycardia, suggesting tamponade and haemodynamic compromise (pericarditis with tamponade is a high-risk, potentially life-threatening cause of chest pain) (p.147, p.150) Abnormal jugular venous pulse pattern consistent with pericardial tamponade (p.149) Pulsus paradoxus (points to tamponade physiology) (p.312) Tamponade is a recognised cause of obstructive shock (p.102) Diffuse (multi-lead) ST-segment elevation not confined to a single coronary territory, together with PR-segment depression, helps distinguish pericarditis from acute MI; ascribing these ECG changes to ischaemia is a key pitfall (p.149). A normal echocardiogram does not exclude pericarditis (effusion absent in 34-50%) (p.90). Chest-wall tenderness does not exclude myocardial ischaemia, and an unremarkable physical exam is not reassuring (p.149). Low-grade fever is nonspecific and can accompany MI and thromboembolism as well as pericardial inflammation (p.149). Inflammation of the pericardium from infectious or noninfectious causes. Because the visceral and most of the parietal pericardium are insensitive to pain, the discomfort is attributed mainly to associated pleural inflammation, producing pleuritic, position-dependent pain that, via overlapping phrenic and C3-C5 somatic innervation, may be referred to the shoulder, neck, and trapezius ridge (p.147, p.149).

Periductal mastitis — Recurrent subareolar abscess, Periductal inflammation Mammary duct ectasia Lactational breast abscess Inflammatory breast carcinoma Tuberculous or granulomatous mastitis Idiopathic granulomatous mastitis Sebaceous or epidermoid cyst with infection Hidradenitis suppurativa involving the areola Clinical assessment including detailed smoking history Ultrasound of the subareolar region to detect an abscess or fistula Aspiration of any collection with microbiological culture including anaerobes Mammography in older patients or when malignancy is a concern Core biopsy of any persistent mass or if inflammatory carcinoma is suspected Fistulography or examination under anaesthesia for a suspected duct fistula Skin swab and pus culture to guide antibiotic choice Inflammation centred on the subareolar ducts, typically affecting younger women in contrast to the older women affected by duct ectasia. Very strongly associated with cigarette smoking, which is central to both causation and recurrence. Presents with periareolar pain, inflammation, a tender subareolar mass or a recurrent non-lactational abscess. Recurrent infection may discharge through the areolar margin and establish a mammary duct fistula between a subareolar duct and the skin. Nipple retraction at the site of the affected duct can develop and may mimic malignant retraction. Although classed as an inflammatory rather than infective process, secondary infection is often mixed, including anaerobes. Acute episodes are managed with antibiotics active against anaerobes and drainage of any abscess, ideally by aspiration. Definitive treatment of recurrent disease or fistula is total (major) duct excision, and smoking cessation is essential to reduce recurrence. Failure of an inflammatory episode to resolve, raising concern for inflammatory carcinoma A persistent hard mass after resolution of inflammation Diffuse skin oedema and peau d'orange Recurrent abscess with an established mammary duct fistula Associated axillary lymphadenopathy Confusing periductal mastitis in a young smoker with involutional duct ectasia Overlooking anaerobic cover when treating a non-lactational abscess Repeated incision and drainage that promotes fistula formation instead of definitive duct excision Mistaking non-resolving inflammation for infection and missing inflammatory carcinoma Neglecting to address smoking, the key driver of recurrence Periductal mastitis is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the large subareolar ducts distinct from involutional duct ectasia. Damage to the duct epithelium, strongly linked to the toxic and ischaemic effects of cigarette smoke, allows leakage of ductal secretions into surrounding tissue and provokes a periductal inflammatory response. Secondary bacterial colonisation, frequently mixed aerobic and anaerobic, leads to recurrent subareolar abscess formation.
