adults, or one year in children and adolescents, with fewer symptom-free intervals Associated symptoms may include poor appetite or overeating, sleep disturbance, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration, and feelings of hopelessness Because symptoms are long-standing, patients often regard the low mood as part of their personality and may not recognise it as a treatable illness A major depressive episode can be superimposed on the chronic baseline, a pattern often described as double depression, which increases severity and risk Suicide risk is present and should be assessed actively despite the seemingly milder day-to-day picture Management combines evidence-based psychotherapy with antidepressant pharmacotherapy, and chronic forms may need longer treatment to achieve and maintain response Screen for a history of hypomania or mania and for medical contributors such as hypothyroidism before attributing chronic low mood solely to a primary mood disorder Functional impairment accumulates over years, so early recognition and sustained treatment can substantially improve quality of life Active suicidal ideation with plan, intent, or access to means Emergence of a superimposed major depressive episode with worsening severity Emerging manic or hypomanic symptoms after starting an antidepressant Profound self-neglect or loss of function Assuming chronic low mood is fixed personality rather than a treatable disorder Underestimating suicide risk because symptoms appear mild day to day Missing a superimposed major depressive episode (double depression) Failing to screen for bipolarity before antidepressant treatment Ending treatment too early given the chronic, relapsing nature of the condition Persistent depressive disorder shares much of the neurobiology of major depression, with contributions from genetic vulnerability, monoamine dysregulation, and altered stress-axis and neuroplastic signalling, but is characterised by chronicity. Early adversity, ongoing psychosocial stressors, temperament, and reinforced negative cognitive styles are thought to sustain the persistent low-grade mood disturbance over years. Persistent depressive disorder is by definition chronic and can be more treatment-resistant than episodic depression, with high rates of relapse and comorbidity. Prognosis improves with sustained combined treatment and psychosocial support, but is worse with early onset, superimposed major depression, and untreated comorbid conditions.

Persistent fetal vasculature (PHPV) — persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous, PHPV, PFV, persistent foetal vasculature Retinoblastoma Congenital cataract Coats disease Retinopathy of prematurity Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy Toxocara or other infective endophthalmitis Norrie disease (in bilateral cases) B-scan ocular ultrasound to define the fibrovascular stalk and detect calcification MRI of the orbits and brain when retinoblastoma cannot be excluded clinically Examination under anaesthesia with fundus assessment of both eyes Intraocular pressure measurement and biometry for microphthalmia Wide-field retinal imaging where feasible Consideration of genetic evaluation in bilateral or syndromic presentations Results from failure of the embryonic hyaloid vascular system and primary vitreous to regress, usually unilateral and in an otherwise healthy full-term infant Typically presents with leukocoria, microphthalmia and, in the anterior form, a retrolental fibrovascular membrane with elongated ciliary processes drawn centrally Anterior disease can produce a shallow anterior chamber, cataract and secondary angle-closure glaucoma; posterior disease features a vitreous stalk and retinal folds or dysplasia A persistent Bergmeister papilla or Mittendorf dot may be seen as mild residua of the hyaloid system The critical differential is retinoblastoma, and any child with leukocoria requires urgent specialist assessment Ultrasound and MRI help distinguish the fibrovascular stalk and absence of calcification from a calcified retinoblastoma Early vitreoretinal surgery may preserve the eye and, in selected anterior cases, some vision, but the visual prognosis is generally guarded Leukocoria that could represent retinoblastoma requiring urgent exclusion Bilateral disease suggesting Norrie disease or a systemic disorder Secondary angle-closure glaucoma threatening a painful blind eye Rapid progression of cataract or vitreous haemorrhage Signs of raised intraocular pressure or buphthalmos Attributing leukocoria to PHPV without excluding retinoblastoma Failing to examine the fellow eye and consider a bilateral systemic cause Missing evolving secondary glaucoma in a microphthalmic eye Delaying referral and losing the window for sight-preserving surgery During normal development the hyaloid artery and primary vitreous nourish the developing lens and regress before birth. In persistent fetal vasculature this regression fails, leaving hyperplastic fibrovascular tissue in the vitreous cavity and behind the lens. The retained tissue exerts traction, causing microphthalmia, a retrolental membrane with dragged ciliary processes, cataract and, posteriorly, a vitreous stalk with retinal folds or dysplasia. Contraction and neovascular activity can precipitate cataract, shallowing of the anterior chamber, secondary glaucoma and vitreous haemorrhage. Most cases are sporadic and unilateral, though bilateral disease raises suspicion of a systemic or genetic disorder. Visual outcome is usually poor, particularly in posterior or combined disease, though early surgery for selected anterior cases can salvage the eye and occasionally yield useful vision; the priority is often preserving a comfortable, cosmetically acceptable globe.

Persistent mullerian duct syndrome (AMH/AMHR2) — PMDS, persistent Mullerian duct syndrome, hernia uteri inguinalis, anti-mullerian hormone deficiency Bilateral cryptorchidism without mullerian remnants Mixed gonadal dysgenesis Partial gonadal dysgenesis Ovotesticular disorder of sex development Testicular regression (vanishing testis) syndrome Karyotype confirming 46,XY Serum anti-mullerian testicular position Intraoperative identification and, where needed, histology of mullerian remnants Assessment of testicular function and fertility potential Occurs in otherwise normally virilised 46,XY males who retain a uterus and fallopian tubes because the anti-mullerian hormone pathway has failed External genitalia are typically male, since testosterone production and androgen action are intact Often discovered incidentally at surgery for cryptorchidism or inguinal hernia, where mullerian structures are found in the hernia sac (hernia uteri inguinalis) Caused by loss-of-function variants in the AMH gene (hormone deficiency) or in its receptor AMHR2 (hormone resistance), inherited in an autosomal recessive manner Bilateral cryptorchidism and transverse testicular ectopia are common associations Fertility is frequently impaired owing to undescended testes and disrupted duct anatomy Undescended testes carry a raised risk of germ cell malignancy, and persistent mullerian remnants require careful surgical judgement to preserve the vas deferens and testicular blood supply Long-standing intra-abdominal or undescended testes with malignancy risk An enlarging pelvic or inguinal mass Surgical injury to the vas deferens or testicular vessels when excising mullerian remnants Signs of malignant transformation within retained mullerian tissue Attempting complete excision of mullerian remnants and injuring the vas deferens or testicular vessels Failing to recognise mullerian structures found unexpectedly at hernia or orchidopexy surgery Overlooking the malignancy risk of retained intra-abdominal testes Confusing the condition with a disorder of androgen action given the normal male phenotype During normal male development the fetal Sertoli cells secrete anti-mullerian hormone, which acts through the AMHR2 receptor to trigger regression of the mullerian ducts. In persistent mullerian duct syndrome either the hormone is absent (AMH mutations) or its receptor is non-functional (AMHR2 mutations), so the mullerian ducts fail to regress and a uterus and fallopian tubes persist. Because Leydig cell testosterone secretion and androgen signalling are unaffected, wolffian derivatives and the external genitalia develop normally as male. The retained mullerian structures and the frequently maldescended testes distort normal anatomy and impair fertility. With orchidopexy and judicious management of mullerian remnants the outlook is generally good, though fertility is often reduced. The principal concerns are testicular malignancy in maldescended gonads and inadvertent damage to reproductive ducts during surgery.

persistent postural perceptual dizziness — PPPD, chronic subjective dizziness, phobic postural vertigo uncompensated peripheral vestibular hypofunction vestibular migraine recurrent benign paroxysmal positional vertigo bilateral vestibulopathy orthostatic hypotension or postural tachycardia syndrome cerebellar or other central balance disorders generalised anxiety or panic disorder and medication side effects pure-tone audiometry to detect a Menière's or retrocochlear contribution video head impulse testing, caloric testing, and vestibular evoked myogenic potentials to characterise any precipitating vestibular deficit MRI of the brain when central or progressive features are present orthostatic blood pressure and, where indicated, tilt-table testing posturography, which may demonstrate visual dependence and an abnormal reliance on surface cues validated anxiety and depression screening questionnaires and a medication review PPPD is among the commonest causes of chronic dizziness in working-age adults and is a functional disorder — neither a structural vestibular lesion nor a primary psychiatric illness. The defining symptom is persistent non-spinning dizziness, unsteadiness, or a rocking/swaying sensation present on most days for three months or longer, often worsening as the day progresses. Three core provocateurs characterise it: upright posture, active or passive self-motion, and exposure to moving or complex visual environments such as supermarket aisles, crowds, or scrolling screens. It is usually precipitated by an acute event that disturbs balance — vestibular neuritis, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, vestibular migraine, a panic attack, or another medical illness — after which symptoms persist despite recovery of the trigger. The mechanism is a maladaptive shift to visual and somatosensory dependence together with a stiff, high-risk postural control strategy that fails to relax once the initial threat has passed. Anxiety and neurotic traits are common comorbidities and predisposing factors but are not required for the diagnosis, which is positive and criteria-based rather than one of exclusion. Examination and vestibular tests are often normal or reflect only the resolved precipitant; repeated negative investigation tends to reinforce symptoms. Effective management combines patient education, vestibular rehabilitation with habituation and gaze stabilisation, serotonergic antidepressants (SSRIs or SNRIs), and cognitive behavioural therapy. progressive focal neurological signs or new spontaneous vertigo with nystagmus fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss suggesting Menière's disease gait ataxia, dysarthria, or limb incoordination suggesting cerebellar disease syncope or pre-syncope pointing to a cardiovascular cause acute severe headache or other features suggesting an evolving central lesion ordering repeated negative investigations, which reinforces illness behaviour and delays effective treatment dismissing the condition as purely psychological rather than explaining the functional balance model overlooking a treatable precipitant such as recurrent benign paroxysmal positional vertigo or vestibular migraine prescribing long-term vestibular suppressants, which impede compensation and often worsen chronic symptoms failing to give the patient a clear, positive explanation of the diagnosis, which undermines rehabilitation PPPD arises from a failure to re-establish normal postural control and spatial orientation after an acute vestibular, medical, or psychological insult. Rather than returning to the automatic, efficient balance strategy used before the event, the patient persists with a heightened, threat-adapted mode: a stiffened posture, conscious control of gait, and an over-reliance on visual and somatosensory cues (visual dependence). Functional neuroimaging suggests reduced activity and connectivity within central vestibular cortical networks alongside increased influence of visual and anxiety-related limbic circuits, so that ordinary motion and visually busy environments are processed as destabilising. Predisposing anxious and introspective personality traits amplify this reweighting. Importantly, the disorder is not explained by ongoing structural damage to the peripheral or central vestibular apparatus. Untreated PPPD tends to run a chronic, disabling course, but it responds well to a combined programme of vestibular rehabilitation, serotonergic medication, and cognitive behavioural therapy; early positive diagnosis and avoidance of repeated investigation improve outcome.

persistent pulmonary hypertension — PPHN, persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, persistent foetal circulation Cyanotic congenital heart disease (transposition of the great arteries, total anomalous pulmonary venous return, hypoplastic left heart) Meconium aspiration syndrome Neonatal sepsis or pneumonia (group B streptococcus) Respiratory distress syndrome from surfactant deficiency Congenital diaphragmatic hernia Pulmonary hypoplasia Polycythaemia and hyperviscosity Pre- and post-ductal pulse oximetry to detect differential saturations Echocardiography with Doppler (shunt direction, tricuspid regurgitation jet, exclusion of structural disease) Arterial blood gas with calculation of the oxygenation index Chest radiograph Sepsis screen including blood cultures, full blood count and inflammatory markers Hyperoxia test to help distinguish from cyanotic congenital heart disease Blood glucose and calcium Results from failure of the normal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance at birth, sustaining foetal-pattern right-to-left shunting across the patent foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus. Occurs mainly in term and near-term neonates and presents with cyanosis and hypoxaemia that is disproportionate to any parenchymal lung disease and often strikingly labile. A pre- to post-ductal oxygen saturation gradient (right hand higher than lower limb, typically by more than 5 to 10 percent) suggests right-to-left ductal shunting. Common precipitants include meconium aspiration syndrome, sepsis or pneumonia, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, respiratory distress syndrome, perinatal asphyxia, and idiopathic (maldeveloped vasculature) disease. Echocardiography is essential to confirm raised pulmonary pressures, define shunt direction and, critically, exclude structural congenital heart disease. Supportive care is foundational: optimise lung recruitment and oxygenation, correct acidosis, avoid hypothermia and agitation, and maintain systemic blood pressure to limit right-to-left shunting. Inhaled nitric oxide is the first-line selective pulmonary vasodilator, with agents such as sildenafil used as adjuncts. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is the rescue therapy when maximal medical management fails, with the oxygenation index guiding escalation. Severe labile hypoxaemia refractory to high inspired oxygen Rising oxygenation index despite maximal support, prompting ECMO consideration Systemic hypotension with poor perfusion Suspicion of duct-dependent congenital heart disease Failing to exclude cyanotic congenital heart disease before attributing hypoxaemia to PPHN. Giving inhaled nitric oxide in duct-dependent lesions or before echocardiography. Excessive handling, agitation and hypothermia, all of which worsen pulmonary vasoconstriction. Over-aggressive hyperventilation and induced alkalosis, which are associated with adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes. Overlooking the pre- to post-ductal saturation gradient. At birth, lung aeration and rising oxygen tension normally trigger pulmonary vasodilatation and a rapid fall in pulmonary vascular resistance. In PPHN this transition fails or reverses through one of three mechanisms: maladaptation (structurally normal vasculature with abnormal vasoconstriction driven by asphyxia, sepsis or acidosis), maldevelopment (remodelled, abnormally muscularised arteries following chronic intrauterine stress), or hypoplasia (a reduced cross-sectional vascular bed, as in congenital diaphragmatic hernia). Persistently high pulmonary vascular resistance maintains right-to-left shunting across the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, bypassing the lungs and causing severe hypoxaemia. Hypoxaemia and acidosis further raise pulmonary vascular resistance, creating a self-perpetuating cycle. With inhaled nitric oxide and ECMO the majority of infants survive, but PPHN still carries appreciable mortality and a risk of long-term neurodevelopmental and sensorineural hearing impairment, so structured follow-up is warranted.

pulmonary vasodilator The oxygenation index is used to gauge severity and to guide escalation, with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation reserved for refractory cases Severe refractory hypoxaemia with a rising oxygenation index despite maximal support Systemic hypotension and poor perfusion indicating cardiovascular decompensation Suspected duct-dependent congenital heart disease requiring urgent cardiology input Deterioration suggesting pneumothorax or other air leak Mistaking PPHN for cyanotic congenital heart disease, or vice versa, without echocardiography Provoking pulmonary vasoconstriction through excessive handling, pain, hypothermia, or acidosis Aggressive hyperventilation and over-ventilation causing lung injury without sustained benefit Failing to recognise and treat coexisting sepsis or an air leak Delaying referral for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in deteriorating refractory disease Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn arises from a failure of the normal postnatal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance. In foetal life high pulmonary resistance directs blood away from the lungs through the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale; at birth lung expansion and rising oxygen normally cause pulmonary vessels to dilate. In PPHN this transition fails because of maladaptation (reactive vasoconstriction from hypoxia, acidosis, or parenchymal disease), maldevelopment (abnormally muscularised pulmonary arteries), or underdevelopment (pulmonary hypoplasia). Sustained high pulmonary resistance maintains right-to-left shunting across the ductus and foramen ovale, producing profound hypoxaemia, and hypoxia and acidosis further raise pulmonary pressure in a self-perpetuating cycle. With modern management including inhaled nitric oxide and extracorporeal support most infants survive, but outcome depends heavily on the underlying cause and severity. Prolonged severe hypoxaemia carries a risk of neurodevelopmental impairment and sensorineural hearing loss, so structured follow-up is recommended.

Perthes' disease — Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children, coxa plana Transient synovitis (irritable hip) Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis of the hip Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (in older children) Developmental dysplasia of the hip Juvenile idiopathic arthritis Skeletal dysplasia or epiphyseal dysplasia (especially if bilateral) Hypothyroidism and avascular necrosis from other causes (e.g. sickle cell disease, steroids) Anteroposterior and frog-lateral radiographs of both hips to assess and stage the changes MRI for early detection before radiographic changes appear and to assess the extent of necrosis Clinical assessment of hip range of movement, particularly abduction and internal rotation Investigations to exclude infection or inflammatory arthritis when the presentation is acute Consideration of bilateral or systemic workup (e.g. thyroid function, skeletal survey) if presentation is atypical or bilateral An idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children, typically presenting between about 4 and 8 years and more common in boys Presents with a limp and hip, groin, or referred knee pain, often intermittent, with restricted abduction and internal rotation of the hip Knee pain in a child can be referred from the hip, so the hip must always be examined in a limping child Early radiographs may be normal; later changes include increased femoral head density, fragmentation, flattening, and eventual remodelling The key aims are to relieve symptoms, maintain hip movement, and keep the femoral head 'contained' within the acetabulum so it remodels into a congruent, spherical shape Younger children with more remaining growth and greater remodelling potential generally have a better prognosis than older children Treatment ranges from observation, activity restriction, and physiotherapy to containment by bracing or surgery (femoral or pelvic osteotomy) in more severe or older cases Bilateral or atypical presentations should prompt consideration of alternative diagnoses such as skeletal dysplasia or hypothyroidism Fever, systemic upset, and an acutely irritable hip suggesting septic arthritis requiring urgent exclusion Bilateral or atypical disease suggesting skeletal dysplasia or an underlying systemic cause Marked loss of hip movement and femoral head extrusion indicating a head at risk of permanent deformity An older child at presentation, associated with a poorer remodelling capacity Attributing a child's knee pain to the knee and failing to examine the hip Assuming a normal early radiograph excludes the disease and missing early presentation on MRI Not distinguishing Perthes' disease from septic arthritis in the acutely painful hip Overlooking bilateral involvement that should prompt evaluation for an underlying systemic disorder Perthes' disease results from a temporary interruption of the blood supply to the immature femoral head epiphysis, causing avascular necrosis. The precise trigger is unknown but the epiphysis undergoes a sequence of ischaemic necrosis, followed by fragmentation and resorption of dead bone, then reossification and remodelling as revascularisation occurs. During the biologically 'plastic' necrotic and fragmentation phases the softened femoral head is vulnerable to deformation under load, and can flatten and enlarge (coxa magna) or become incongruent if not well contained within the acetabulum. The ultimate shape of the healed head, and hence long-term function, depends on how well sphericity and containment are preserved through this self-limiting but prolonged process. The disease is self-limiting and many younger children with limited head involvement remodel to a near-normal, congruent hip; however, older children, extensive necrosis, and a poorly contained or deformed femoral head are associated with residual incongruity and an increased risk of premature hip osteoarthritis in adulthood.

Pertussis (Whooping Cough) — whooping cough, Bordetella pertussis Bordetella parapertussis (causes a similar but typically milder illness; does not express pertussis toxin gene) (p.1276). Bordetella holmesii (found in up to 20% of patients with a pertussis-like syndrome using improved PCR) (p.1276). Mycoplasma pneumoniae (p.1280). Chlamydia pneumoniae (p.1280). Adenovirus (p.1280). Influenza virus and other respiratory viruses (p.1280). Respiratory syncytial virus and rhinovirus -- isolated from patients with clinical pertussis but probably represent co-infection, particularly in children under 1 year (p.1280). Bordetella parapertussis infection (p.1280) Bordetella holmesii infection (p.1276) Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection (p.1280) Chlamydia pneumoniae infection (p.1280) Adenovirus, influenza, and other respiratory viral infections (p.1280) Nasopharyngeal culture (Bordet-Gengou or Regan-Lowe medium) -- gold standard owing to 100% specificity; cultures become positive by day 5 of incubation (p.1279). PCR / multitarget real-time PCR -- has replaced culture in most laboratories due to greater sensitivity and faster (hours) results; differentiates B. pertussis, B. parapertussis, and B. holmesii (p.1279). Nasopharyngeal aspiration is the best specimen; B. pertussis is highly sensitive to drying so specimens must be inoculated without delay or placed in transport medium (p.1279). Complete blood count for lymphocytosis (informative in young children, not in adolescents/adults) (p.1279). Serology -- enzyme immunoassays for IgA/IgG to pertussis toxin, filamentous hemagglutinin, pertactin, and fimbriae; increasingly used in adolescents, adults, and those symptomatic >4 weeks; single-specimen anti-pertussis-toxin serology is becoming standardized, especially for outbreaks and surveillance (p.1279). ACE inhibitor-induced cough (p.1280) Reactive airway disease (p.1280) Gastroesophageal reflux disease (p.1280) Acute respiratory tract infection caused by Bordetella pertussis; 'pertussis' means 'violent cough' and the inspiratory whoop at the end of a paroxysm gives the disease its common name (p.1276). Classic course runs through three stages: catarrhal phase (1-2 weeks of coryza, lacrimation, mild cough, low-grade fever, malaise, indistinguishable from a common cold), then paroxysmal phase (frequent spasmodic bursts of 5-10 coughs within a single expiration), then convalescent phase (p.1278-1279). Paroxysms may end in an audible whoop produced by rapid inspiration against a closed glottis; post-tussive vomiting is frequent and a mucous plug may be expelled (p.1279). During a coughing spasm there may be neck-vein distension, bulging eyes, tongue protrusion, and cyanosis; paroxysms can be precipitated by noise, eating, or physical contact and are often worse at night (p.1279). Between attacks the patient looks normal but shows increasing fatigue; fever is uncommon and, when present, suggests bacterial superinfection (p.1279). The convalescent phase lasts 1-3 months with gradual resolution; for 6-12 months afterward, intercurrent viral infections may trigger a recrudescence of paroxysmal cough (p.1279). Incubation period averages 7-10 days (p.1279). The whoop is variable: uncommon in infants 6 months of age or younger and frequently absent in older children and adults (p.1276). Lymphocytosis (absolute lymphocyte count >108-109/L) is common in young children and unusual with other infections, but is not a feature in adolescents and adults (p.1279). Highly communicable: attack rates of 80-100% among unimmunized household contacts; cyclical outbreaks occur every 3-5 years despite widespread immunization (p.1277). Severe morbidity and high mortality are restricted almost entirely to infants; in the US (2000-2017) infants under 2 months accounted for 84% of pertussis deaths (p.1278). Apnea in infants (occurred in 27.1% of children under 2 years hospitalized with pertussis) (p.1279). Cyanosis during coughing spasms (p.1279). Seizures and encephalopathy, thought to result from hypoxia of paroxysms/apnea (p.1278-1279). Very high leukocytosis and pulmonary hypertension in young infants -- frequently associated with death (p.1278). Pneumonia (occurs in up to 22% of infants with pertussis) (p.1278-1279). Infants, especially those under 2-3 months, carry the highest risk of complications and death and should generally be hospitalized (p.1278, 1279). In adolescents and adults the presentation is often atypical -- frequently no paroxysmal cough or whoop -- so pertussis is a commonly missed cause of prolonged cough; B. pertussis may be the agent in 12-30% of adults whose cough does not improve within 2 weeks (p.1278). Antibiotic therapy aims to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage; it does NOT substantially alter the clinical course unless given early in the catarrhal phase (p.1279). Cough suppressants are NOT effective and have no role in management; beta-adrenergic agonists and glucocorticoids have been advocated but are NOT proven effective (p.1280). Lymphocytosis is helpful in young children but is NOT a reliable feature in adolescents and adults (p.1279). There is only a small window for culture/PCR diagnosis because much of the period of organism recovery is during the catarrhal phase when pertussis is not yet suspected (p.1279). Cross-reactivity of antigens such as filamentous hemagglutinin and pertactin among Bordetella species makes diagnosis based on seroconversion of a single antibody type unreliable (p.1279). Suspect pertussis in any patient with a cough not improving within 14 days, a paroxysmal cough of any duration, cough followed by vomiting (adolescents/adults), or respiratory symptoms after contact with a laboratory-confirmed case (p.1280). Waning vaccine-derived immunity (faster with acellular vaccines) underlies resurgent outbreaks even in fully immunized older children, adolescents, and adults (p.1278). Infection begins with attachment of B. pertussis to ciliated epithelial cells of the nasopharynx, mediated by surface adhesins (pertactin, filamentous hemagglutinin) binding integrin-family proteins, probably with pertussis toxin. The organism multiplies locally and produces toxins causing mucosal damage (tracheal cytotoxin, dermonecrotic toxin); host defense is impaired by pertussis toxin and adenylate cyclase-hemolysin toxin. There is local cellular invasion with intracellular persistence, but systemic dissemination does NOT occur; systemic manifestations such as lymphocytosis result from the toxins. The cause of the hallmark paroxysmal cough is not known; a pivotal role for pertussis toxin has been proposed but not confirmed. Neurologic events (seizures, encephalopathy) are thought to result from hypoxia due to coughing paroxysms or apnea rather than from specific bacterial products. Deaths in young infants are frequently associated with very high leukocytosis and pulmonary hypertension (p.1278). With universal childhood immunization, reported cases fell by >90% and mortality declined even more dramatically. Severe morbidity and high mortality remain almost entirely restricted to infants; WHO estimates ~40 million cases and ~400,000 deaths globally each year, mostly among infants under 3 months. Immunity after natural infection is NOT lifelong; immunity after whole-cell vaccination is short-lived (little protection after 10-12 years) and wanes even faster (within 2-4 years of the fifth or sixth dose) in those immunized with acellular vaccines (p.1277-1278).

Pes anserine bursitis — pes anserinus bursitis, anserine bursopathy, medial knee bursitis, pes anserine pain syndrome Medial compartment knee osteoarthritis Medial meniscal pathology Medial collateral ligament injury Medial tibial stress fracture Saphenous nerve (infrapatellar branch) irritation Semimembranosus tendinopathy Clinical localisation of tenderness inferomedial to the joint line Ultrasound to assess for bursal fluid and adjacent structures MRI where meniscal, ligamentous or bony pathology is suspected Weight-bearing radiographs to assess medial compartment osteoarthritis Assessment of lower-limb biomechanics and alignment Medial knee pain and tenderness below the joint line at the insertion of the pes anserinus (sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus) Common in middle-aged and older people, those with knee osteoarthritis or obesity, and in some athletes, especially with valgus loading Pain is typically inferomedial to the joint line, helping distinguish it from medial joint-line pathology Frequently overlaps with or is secondary to medial compartment osteoarthritis Ultrasound may show bursal fluid, though the diagnosis is largely clinical and imaging often serves to exclude other causes Management is conservative with load and activity modification and addressing biomechanics and the hamstrings and adductors with physiotherapy; corticosteroid injection may help resistant cases Consider referred pain and intra-articular pathology when the picture is atypical Features suggesting a fracture such as focal bone tenderness in an at-risk athlete Locking or true mechanical symptoms suggesting meniscal pathology Systemic features suggesting infection or inflammatory arthritis A marked joint effusion suggesting intra-articular pathology Attributing all medial knee pain to the bursa while missing osteoarthritis or meniscal disease Over-reliance on imaging when the diagnosis is clinical Neglecting biomechanical contributors and weight management Repeated injection without addressing the underlying cause The pes anserine bursa lies deep to the conjoined insertion of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus on the anteromedial proximal tibia. Friction and overload from repetitive knee flexion and extension, valgus stress, tight hamstrings and altered biomechanics irritate the bursa. It is commonly associated with medial compartment osteoarthritis and with obesity and can be difficult to separate from these, forming part of a medial knee overload picture rather than always an isolated inflammatory bursitis. Generally responds to conservative management and correction of contributing factors, although it may persist or recur when associated osteoarthritis or biomechanical factors remain.

varus hindfoot Pes cavus is an elevation of the medial longitudinal arch that usually reflects a muscle imbalance across the foot rather than a primary bony abnormality. In the common cavovarus pattern, relative weakness of the tibialis anterior and peroneus brevis with preserved or overactive peroneus longus and tibialis posterior plantarflexes the first ray and drives the hindfoot into varus, while intrinsic weakness produces clawing of the toes. This imbalance is characteristically caused by hereditary motor and sensory neuropathies, most notably Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, but also by other neuromuscular disorders, spinal pathology, and sequelae of trauma or compartment syndrome. The rigid high arch concentrates load on the heel and metatarsal heads, producing metatarsalgia and callosities, and the varus hindfoot destabilises the ankle, leading to recurrent lateral ankle sprains, peroneal tendon overload, and lateral column stress injuries. Initially flexible, the deformity tends to stiffen and become fixed as it progresses. Prognosis is closely tied to the underlying cause. Idiopathic or mild cavus may remain stable and manageable with orthoses, but neuropathic cavovarus deformity, as in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, tends to be progressive and to recur even after surgery because the causative imbalance persists. Combined bony realignment and tendon transfers can restore a plantigrade, stable foot, but long-term orthotic support and monitoring are usually required.

asymptomatic flexible paediatric flatfoot that would resolve with growth Failing to distinguish flexible from rigid deformity and missing a tarsal coalition Overlooking tibialis posterior dysfunction foot presenting as a collapsing arch Pes planus reflects failure of the structures that maintain the medial longitudinal arch, which depends on the bony architecture, the spring and plantar ligaments and plantar fascia, and dynamic support from the tibialis posterior. In flexible flatfoot the arch collapses on standing but reconstitutes when load is removed or the great toe is dorsiflexed, tightening the windlass mechanism of the plantar fascia. Adult acquired flatfoot most often develops when the tibialis posterior tendon degenerates and elongates, so that it can no longer invert and lock the hindfoot for an efficient heel raise; the hindfoot drifts into valgus, the forefoot abducts, and the medial arch progressively flattens, giving the too-many-toes appearance and a failed single-limb heel raise. If uncorrected the deformity becomes fixed and secondary arthritis develops. A rigid flatfoot instead reflects an underlying structural cause such as tarsal coalition, arthritis, or neuromuscular imbalance. A tight gastrocnemius commonly coexists and increases deforming forces on the midfoot. Physiological flexible flatfoot in children usually improves with growth and rarely causes long-term problems. Adult acquired flatfoot from tibialis posterior dysfunction is progressive if untreated, moving from a flexible, correctable deformity to a fixed one with arthritis; early orthotic and physiotherapy treatment can control symptoms, and staged reconstructive surgery can restore alignment, whereas established rigid deformity may ultimately require arthrodesis.

grafting, or penile prosthesis when erectile dysfunction is also present Intervention decisions should await disease stability, since operating during the active phase risks recurrence and further change Rapidly enlarging or atypical penile mass raising concern for malignancy Acute severe pain with deformity suggesting penile fracture rather than Peyronie disease Deformity severe enough to prevent intercourse or urinary function Significant psychological distress or relationship impact Progressive deformity that has not stabilised, indicating ongoing active disease Operating during the active, unstable phase and risking recurrence Overlooking coexisting erectile dysfunction that alters the treatment approach Mistaking congenital curvature, which lacks a plaque, for Peyronie disease Failing to address the psychological impact on the patient and partner Assuming a penile mass is a benign plaque without excluding malignancy when features are atypical Peyronie disease is thought to begin with repetitive microtrauma to the tunica albuginea, most often during sexual activity, in a susceptible individual. The injury triggers an aberrant, exaggerated wound-healing response with local inflammation, fibroblast activation, and deposition of disorganised collagen and elastin. This forms a fibrous, sometimes calcified, plaque that is less elastic than the surrounding tunica. During erection the inelastic segment fails to expand normally, bending the penis toward the plaque and producing the characteristic curvature and deformity. Over time inflammation subsides and the plaque matures and stabilises, marking the transition to the chronic phase. The natural history is variable: a minority of men improve spontaneously, many stabilise with residual deformity, and a proportion progress. Pain from the active phase usually resolves over time. With appropriate treatment tailored to disease phase and severity, most men can achieve functional improvement, and surgery in stable disease offers reliable correction of significant curvature, though some penile shortening or altered sensation may persist.

hydrocephalus during follow-up Pfeiffer syndrome is driven by activating mutations in fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 or 2 that amplify FGF signalling in cranial sutures and limb buds. diagnosis is confirmed by PGM1 testing Hypoglycaemia, especially with fasting or intercurrent illness Rhabdomyolysis or acute muscle injury with exertion Signs of heart failure from dilated cardiomyopathy Cardiac arrhythmia Missing the diagnosis by overlooking the cleft palate or bifid uvula clue Not recognising PGM1-CDG as galactose-responsive and withholding treatment Attributing exercise intolerance solely to a primary glycogenosis Failing to screen for and monitor dilated cardiomyopathy Phosphoglucomutase 1 interconverts glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate, a step central both to glycogen turnover and to producing the UDP-glucose and UDP-galactose needed for glycosylation. Phacodonesis is a tremulous, wobbling movement of the crystalline lens seen on ocular saccades, signifying loss of zonular integrity and impending or partial lens subluxation It is a clinical sign rather than a diagnosis, and its presence should trigger a search for the underlying cause of zonular weakness In adults the commonest cause is pseudoexfoliation syndrome, in which fibrillar deposits progressively degrade the zonular attachments Blunt or penetrating ocular trauma is a frequent cause and may produce localised zonular dialysis with sectoral phacodonesis Heritable connective-tissue disorders are key associations, notably Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1), homocystinuria and Weill-Marchesani syndrome, and their systemic features must be sought It is best elicited at the slit lamp by asking the patient to make quick eye movements and observing oscillation of the lens, often accompanied by iridodonesis (tremulous iris) Phacodonesis markedly increases the risk of intra-operative complications such as zonular dialysis, capsular instability and dropped lens fragments, so it must be documented before cataract surgery Progression to frank lens subluxation or complete dislocation into the anterior chamber or vitreous can precipitate pupillary-block or lens-induced glaucoma Acute lens-induced or pupillary-block angle closure with pain and pressure rise Complete lens dislocation into the anterior chamber threatening corneal decompensation Features of Marfan syndrome warranting cardiovascular assessment for aortic root dilatation Homocystinuria with its risk of thromboembolism Sudden change from lens tremulousness to frank dislocation Overlooking subtle phacodonesis and encountering unexpected zonular dialysis during cataract surgery Failing to identify pseudoexfoliation as the underlying cause in an older patient Missing a systemic diagnosis such as Marfan syndrome or homocystinuria with life-threatening implications Not measuring intraocular pressure and assessing the angle in a mobile lens Assuming a stable lens when only iridodonesis is noted without testing lens movement The crystalline lens is suspended by the ciliary zonule, a system of fibrillin-rich microfibrils running from the ciliary body to the lens capsule that holds the lens centred and taut. Phacodonesis results when these fibres are reduced in number, stretched or disrupted, so the lens is inadequately anchored and oscillates with inertial movement of the eye. In pseudoexfoliation, abnormal fibrillar material and enzymatic degradation weaken the zonular insertions. In Marfan syndrome, mutations in the fibrillin-1 gene yield structurally deficient microfibrils; in homocystinuria, accumulated homocysteine disrupts zonular cross-linking; and trauma mechanically avulses zonular fibres. The common endpoint is a loss of stable zonular support that permits abnormal lens mobility and predisposes to subluxation. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause and on early recognition; with careful surgical planning using capsular support devices, good visual outcomes are achievable, though the presence of phacodonesis raises the risk of intra-operative and postoperative complications. Untreated progression to dislocation and secondary glaucoma can threaten sight and, in syndromic causes, systemic morbidity may dominate.

phacolytic glaucoma — lens protein glaucoma, phacolytic open-angle glaucoma acute primary angle-closure glaucoma phacomorphic glaucoma phacoanaphylactic (phacoantigenic) uveitis and glaucoma neovascular glaucoma acute anterior uveitis with secondary glaucoma endophthalmitis lens particle glaucoma following capsular rupture slit-lamp examination for hypermature cataract, pseudohypopyon and iridescent particles gonioscopy confirming an open angle intraocular pressure measurement B-scan ultrasonography to assess the posterior segment when the fundus is obscured aqueous aspirate cytology showing protein-laden macrophages when the diagnosis is uncertain corneal assessment for oedema and endothelial status before surgery biometry of the fellow eye to aid surgical planning Occurs with a hypermature or mature cataract, typically in an elderly patient with long-standing poor vision in the affected eye. Presents acutely with a very high intraocular pressure, pain, redness and corneal oedema, mimicking acute angle closure despite an open angle. The anterior chamber shows a characteristic pseudohypopyon or iridescent, floating particles representing macrophages laden with lens protein and calcium oxalate crystals. Gonioscopy reveals an open angle, distinguishing it from angle-closure glaucoma. Unlike phacoanaphylactic (lens-induced uveitic) glaucoma, the inflammation is a macrophage response to soluble high-molecular-weight lens proteins rather than a granulomatous reaction. Aqueous aspirate cytology shows swollen macrophages engorged with eosinophilic lens material. Definitive treatment is prompt cataract extraction after medical control of pressure and inflammation. Delay risks permanent optic nerve damage from sustained high pressure, so surgery should not be unduly postponed. acute painful eye with very high intraocular pressure and corneal oedema rapidly progressive optic nerve compromise from sustained pressure signs suggesting endophthalmitis rather than sterile lens-induced inflammation an only eye or bilateral hypermature cataracts requiring urgent intervention Mistaking the presentation for acute angle closure and performing iridotomy instead of addressing the lens. Confusing the pseudohypopyon with infective endophthalmitis and delaying appropriate surgery. Attempting prolonged medical control rather than proceeding to timely lens removal. Underestimating capsular fragility, which increases the risk of intraoperative capsular rupture and vitreous loss. Neglecting to counsel about guarded visual prognosis when the cataract is long-standing and the optic nerve status is unknown. In a hypermature or morgagnian cataract the lens capsule becomes permeable, and soluble high-molecular-weight lens proteins leak through microscopic capsular defects into the aqueous humour. These proteins, together with macrophages that engulf them, physically obstruct the trabecular meshwork. The engorged macrophages and the liberated protein and calcium oxalate material clog outflow channels, and the sheer volume of high-molecular-weight protein directly impedes aqueous drainage. Because the angle remains anatomically open, the obstruction is at the level of the meshwork rather than from iridocorneal apposition. The rapid rise in intraocular pressure produces an acute painful glaucoma. The process is a phacotoxic macrophage reaction rather than an immune granulomatous response to lens antigen. Prompt cataract extraction usually normalises intraocular pressure and the glaucoma resolves without long-term medication, though final vision depends on the health of the optic nerve and macula after any period of sustained high pressure.

pigmentokeratotica is understood as a form of twin spotting, in which a single post-zygotic somatic recombination event produces two genetically distinct daughter clones side by side, one giving rise to a pigmentary papular naevus spilus and the other to an organoid naevus sebaceus or epidermal naevus. Activating HRAS variants in the RAS-MAPK pathway have been implicated, which is why the condition overlaps mechanistically with naevus sebaceus and Schimmelpenning syndrome. When the mosaic clones also involve neuroectodermal, ocular and mesodermal tissue, the associated neurological, ocular and skeletal anomalies, hemihypertrophy and FGF23-mediated hypophosphataemic rickets develop. Prognosis depends on the extent of extracutaneous involvement; limited cutaneous disease has a good outlook, whereas neurological, skeletal or metabolic complications increase morbidity and require ongoing multidisciplinary management.

extraction is important Acute painful red eye with very high pressure and corneal oedema needing emergency pressure reduction A mature or intumescent unilateral cataract with unilateral angle closure Prolonged pressure elevation threatening irreversible optic-nerve damage Marked asymmetry of chamber depth signalling a lens-driven mechanism Treating it as primary angle closure and delaying the definitive lens extraction Overlooking the diagnosis by not comparing the two eyes for asymmetry Confusing it with phacolytic glaucoma, which involves lens protein leakage rather than pure angle crowding Assuming iridotomy alone will resolve pressure when the swollen lens must be removed Operating on a highly inflamed, high-pressure eye without first medically stabilising it Phacomorphic glaucoma occurs when a cataractous lens becomes enlarged and intumescent, swelling with fluid so that it thickens and shifts the iris-lens diaphragm forward. This exaggerates relative pupillary block by increasing lens-iris contact and simultaneously crowds the peripheral angle as the bulky lens pushes the peripheral iris against the trabecular meshwork. Aqueous outflow is obstructed and intraocular pressure rises acutely, producing corneal oedema, pain, and, if sustained, peripheral anterior synechiae and optic-nerve damage. The disparity in lens size and chamber depth compared with the fellow eye reflects the lens as the primary driver, distinguishing it from primary angle closure where both eyes share a predisposing anatomy. Prompt pressure control followed by cataract extraction usually resolves the angle closure and restores vision, but delayed treatment can leave permanent optic-nerve damage, synechial angle closure, and corneal decompensation, and the acutely inflamed eye carries higher surgical risk.

Phaeohyphomycosis — dematiaceous mould infection, dark mould infection, melanised fungal infection, cerebral phaeohyphomycosis Chromoblastomycosis (also caused by dematiaceous fungi but with distinct other benign subcutaneous cysts Tissue biopsy for histopathology, including Fontana-Masson stain to demonstrate melanised hyphae Fungal culture with molecular species identification Antifungal Clinical spectrum ranges from subcutaneous nodules and cysts after traumatic inoculation to allergic fungal sinusitis, keratitis, and life-threatening cerebral abscesses Cerebral phaeohyphomycosis, notably due to Cladophialophora bantiana, is striking because it can cause brain abscesses in apparently immunocompetent hosts and carries high mortality Immunosuppressed patients, including transplant recipients, are at risk of disseminated and invasive disease Management combines surgical excision or drainage with azole-based antifungal therapy, often prolonged, and outcomes for cerebral disease remain poor even with treatment Diagnosis rests on biopsy with histology showing pigmented hyphae, fungal culture, and molecular identification, since species determines prognosis and drug selection New focal neurological signs or a brain abscess on imaging Disseminated disease in an immunocompromised host Rapidly enlarging or invasive sinus disease Isolation of a known neurotropic species such as Cladophialophora bantiana Progressive lesions despite antifungal therapy, indicating the need for surgical intervention Failing to request a melanin stain, so pigmented hyphae are overlooked on histology Assuming cerebral abscess requires immunosuppression and dismissing it in an immunocompetent patient Relying on antifungals alone when surgical excision or drainage is often essential Not obtaining species identification, which strongly influences prognosis and drug choice Confusing it with chromoblastomycosis or other subcutaneous mycoses that require different management Phaeohyphomycosis is caused by melanised moulds acquired mainly through traumatic inoculation of contaminated soil or plant material into skin and subcutaneous tissue, or by inhalation leading to sinus and, rarely, cerebral disease. Melanin in the fungal cell wall is a virulence factor that scavenges free radicals and blunts host defences, contributing to the neurotropism of certain species. Localised disease produces subcutaneous cysts and nodules, whereas neurotropic species such as Cladophialophora bantiana can reach the brain and form abscesses even without evident immunosuppression; in immunocompromised hosts the fungi may invade tissue and disseminate more widely. Localised subcutaneous disease often responds well to excision and antifungal therapy, but cerebral phaeohyphomycosis carries a high mortality even with combined surgical and medical treatment, and disseminated disease in immunocompromised hosts also has a poor outlook.

have been implicated, linking it mechanistically to Sturge-Weber and phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica The current classification groups cases by vascular-plus-pigmentary combination and by the presence or absence of systemic involvement Extensive facial capillary malformation raises the risk of associated Sturge-Weber syndrome and Klippel-Trenaunay overgrowth Ocular melanocytosis (naevus of Ota) predisposes to glaucoma and warrants ophthalmological surveillance Management is generic: pulsed-dye laser for the vascular component, Q-switched laser for pigment, and screening for ocular and neurological complications Seizures or focal neurological signs suggesting leptomeningeal angiomatosis Raised intraocular pressure or visual symptoms from ocular melanocytosis Progressive limb overgrowth or venous complications Any change within a melanocytic lesion raising concern for melanoma Treating the birthmarks cosmetically without screening for Sturge-Weber, glaucoma or limb overgrowth Missing ocular melanocytosis and its lifelong glaucoma risk Attributing all vascular lesions to a simple port-wine stain and overlooking the pigmentary component Failing to arrange neuroimaging in extensive facial capillary malformation Phakomatosis pigmentovascularis is best understood as an example of twin spotting, in which post-zygotic somatic recombination or independent mosaic variants generate two genetically distinct cell populations that produce adjacent vascular and pigmentary birthmarks. Activating variants in the GNAQ and GNA11 genes, which encode G-protein alpha subunits, have been identified and account for the overlap with other GNAQ-driven conditions such as Sturge-Weber syndrome. The capillary malformation reflects dysregulated vascular development, while the coexisting dermal melanocytosis or naevus spilus reflects abnormal migration and persistence of dermal melanocytes. Where the mosaic clones involve leptomeningeal or ocular tissue, neurological and ocular complications ensue. Prognosis depends on associated systemic disease; purely cutaneous phakomatosis pigmentovascularis is benign and mainly a cosmetic concern, whereas coexisting Sturge-Weber, glaucoma or Klippel-Trenaunay overgrowth carries the associated morbidity of those conditions.

Phantom limb pain — PLP, phantom pain, post-amputation pain Residual limb (stump) pain from neuroma Prosthetic-related mechanical pain or pressure injury Residual limb infection or wound breakdown Ischaemia of the residual limb Referred pain from the spine or proximal joints Heterotopic ossification in the residual limb Clinical history and examination distinguishing phantom pain from stump pain and non-painful phantom sensation Inspection and palpation of the residual limb for neuroma, tenderness, and prosthetic fit Imaging of the residual limb where neuroma, heterotopic ossification, or bony spur is suspected Vascular assessment if ischaemia of the residual limb is a concern Assessment for infection when there are local inflammatory signs or wound problems Phantom limb pain is painful sensation perceived in a limb or body part that has been amputated, and must be distinguished from non-painful phantom sensation and from residual limb (stump) pain Most amputees experience some phantom phenomena; pain often begins within the first days to weeks after amputation and may follow a telescoping pattern where the phantom seems to shorten over time Pre-amputation limb pain and its intensity are recognised risk factors, and the phantom pain may echo the character of the pain felt before surgery Careful examination of the residual limb is essential to separate phantom pain from stump pain caused by neuroma, poor prosthetic fit, infection, or ischaemia Non-pharmacological approaches including mirror therapy, graded motor imagery, desensitisation, and early prosthetic use address the cortical reorganisation thought to drive the pain Pharmacological principles favour neuropathic agents such as gabapentinoids and certain antidepressants, with opioids reserved and used cautiously A multidisciplinary rehabilitation approach that combines prosthetic training, psychological support, and pain management gives the best functional outcomes Perioperative and preventive analgesic strategies may reduce the likelihood or severity of later phantom pain Residual limb signs of infection or wound dehiscence requiring urgent treatment Features of critical ischaemia in the residual limb Rapidly worsening or new pain pattern suggesting an alternative surgical or vascular cause Severe intractable pain with mood deterioration and suicidal ideation Confusing phantom pain with stump pain and missing a treatable neuroma or prosthetic-fit problem Neglecting early prosthetic fitting and rehabilitation, which can worsen cortical reorganisation Dismissing patient reports of pain in an absent limb as psychological Over-reliance on opioids for a fundamentally neuropathic pain problem Overlooking pre-amputation pain control that could reduce later phantom pain Phantom limb pain arises from maladaptive changes at multiple levels of the nervous system after amputation. Peripherally, injured axons form neuromas that generate ectopic and spontaneous discharge. In the spinal cord, deafferentation leads to central sensitisation and disinhibition of dorsal horn neurons. Within the brain, the somatosensory and motor cortices undergo reorganisation, with cortical territory representing the missing limb being invaded by adjacent regions; the degree of this remapping correlates with pain intensity. Psychological factors and pre-existing pain memory further modulate the experience. Phantom pain often diminishes in frequency and intensity over the months to years following amputation, and many patients cope well with a combination of therapy and prosthetic use. A subset develop persistent, treatment-resistant pain that requires ongoing multidisciplinary management.

associated structural anomalies Neurological review and, where regression occurs, psychiatric assessment A neurodevelopmental disorder with global developmental delay, intellectual disability, and include a long face, full brow, dolichocephaly, large fleshy hands, and dysplastic toenails, but these can be subtle Caused by deletion of the distal long arm of chromosome 22 (22q13.3) or by relies on chromosomal microarray to size the deletion, with sequencing to detect intragenic SHANK3 variants when the array is normal Developmental or behavioural regression, or new catatonia or psychiatric illness in adolescence or adulthood New seizures requiring evaluation Absent pain perception masking serious injury or intra-abdominal pathology Significant renal or cardiac anomaly identified on screening Labelling the presentation as idiopathic autism without performing microarray and SHANK3 testing Missing a parental balanced translocation and giving incorrect recurrence-risk advice Overlooking reduced pain perception, which can delay recognition of injury or illness Not anticipating and monitoring for regression and psychiatric change in later life Phelan-McDermid syndrome results from loss of functional SHANK3 at chromosome 22q13.3, either through a terminal deletion of varying size or a pathogenic sequence variant. SHANK3 encodes a scaffolding protein at the postsynaptic density of excitatory synapses that organises glutamatergic signalling, so its haploinsufficiency impairs synapse formation and function, producing hypotonia, developmental delay, absent speech, and autistic features. Larger deletions remove additional genes, contributing to more extensive systemic and dysmorphic features and greater phenotypic severity. Developmental disability and speech impairment are lifelong and most individuals need substantial support, while the risk of adolescent or adult regression and psychiatric illness adds long-term uncertainty. Larger deletions tend to correlate with greater severity, and multidisciplinary care improves quality of life.

Phenylketonuria — PKU, phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, hyperphenylalaninaemia Tetrahydrobiopterin (cofactor) deficiency disorders Transient hyperphenylalaninaemia of the newborn Other inborn errors of metabolism presenting with developmental delay Non-metabolic causes of intellectual disability and seizures Tyrosinaemia Newborn bloodspot screening for elevated phenylalanine Quantitative plasma amino acids (phenylalanine and tyrosine) Tetrahydrobiopterin loading test and pterin studies to exclude cofactor defects Dihydropteridine reductase activity measurement Genetic analysis of the PAH gene Serial blood phenylalanine monitoring to guide dietary treatment An autosomal recessive inborn error of amino acid metabolism caused most often by deficiency of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase. Untreated, accumulation of phenylalanine causes progressive and irreversible intellectual disability, seizures, and behavioural problems. Affected infants are typically normal at birth, so detection relies on newborn screening rather than clinical signs. Classic untreated features can include a musty or mousy body odour, eczema, and reduced pigmentation with fair hair and skin. Early diagnosis through screening and prompt dietary treatment prevent the neurological damage almost entirely. Treatment centres on a lifelong low-phenylalanine diet with a special protein substitute, guided by regular monitoring of blood phenylalanine levels. A subset of patients respond to the cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (sapropterin), and disorders of biopterin metabolism must be excluded as a separate cause of high phenylalanine. Maternal PKU with poorly controlled phenylalanine during pregnancy can damage the fetus, causing microcephaly, congenital heart disease, and developmental delay, so strict control is essential before and during pregnancy. Lifelong follow-up in a metabolic service supports adherence and long-term neurocognitive outcomes. Markedly elevated phenylalanine levels requiring urgent dietary intervention Seizures or neurological deterioration in an untreated infant Poor metabolic control during pregnancy (maternal PKU) risking fetal harm Failure of phenylalanine to fall despite dietary treatment, suggesting a cofactor defect Signs of nutritional deficiency from an overly restricted diet Assuming a normal newborn appearance excludes the diagnosis Failing to exclude tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency as a treatable alternative cause Relaxing dietary control in older children and adults, risking cognitive and neuropsychiatric effects Overlooking the need for strict preconception and pregnancy control in affected mothers Deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (or, less commonly, of its tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor) blocks the conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine. Phenylalanine therefore accumulates in blood and tissues and is diverted to alternative metabolites such as phenylketones. High phenylalanine levels are neurotoxic to the developing brain, interfering with amino acid transport across the blood-brain barrier, neurotransmitter synthesis, and myelination, producing the intellectual disability and neurological features of untreated disease. Reduced tyrosine availability also limits synthesis of melanin, contributing to hypopigmentation. With early diagnosis and consistent dietary control, cognitive development is normal or near-normal; delayed treatment or poor lifelong control leads to irreversible neurocognitive impairment, and maternal control critically affects offspring.

phenylketonuria maternal — maternal PKU syndrome, maternal hyperphenylalaninaemia embryopathy foetal alcohol spectrum disorder (overlapping facies, microcephaly, growth restriction and cardiac defects) congenital infections of the TORCH group causing microcephaly and growth restriction other teratogen embryopathies (anticonvulsants such as valproate, warfarin, retinoids) chromosomal and single-gene microcephaly-cardiac syndromes primary (non-maternal) inherited metabolic disease in the infant constitutional or placental-insufficiency intrauterine growth restriction tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor disorders in the mother mimicking classical PKU control problems serial maternal blood phenylalanine and tyrosine monitoring before and throughout pregnancy confirmation of maternal PKU genotype/phenotype and tetrahydrobiopterin (sapropterin) responsiveness testing detailed fetal anomaly ultrasound and fetal echocardiography serial fetal growth scans and monitoring of head circumference maternal nutritional assessment including protein, vitamin B12, iron and micronutrient status on restricted diet paediatric developmental and cardiac assessment of the neonate exclusion of foetal alcohol exposure and congenital infection where the phenotype overlaps Maternal PKU syndrome is a teratogenic embryopathy: the fetus is harmed by transplacental phenylalanine from a mother with poorly controlled phenylketonuria, not by an inherited enzyme defect in the child, who is usually a heterozygous carrier and biochemically normal. The classic tetrad in the offspring is microcephaly, congenital heart disease, intrauterine and postnatal growth restriction, and intellectual disability, often with a characteristic facial appearance resembling foetal alcohol syndrome. Phenylalanine is actively concentrated across the placenta, so fetal levels exceed maternal levels; the threshold for damage is lower than that for classical PKU brain injury, meaning even mildly elevated maternal levels can be teratogenic. Congenital heart defects, particularly coarctation of the aorta, tetralogy of Fallot and other conotruncal and left-sided lesions, arise from first-trimester exposure, so metabolic control must be achieved BEFORE conception, not merely once pregnancy is recognised. Preconception counselling and reinstitution of a strict phenylalanine-restricted diet with medical protein (phenylalanine-free amino acid mixture) is the cornerstone; many adult women previously told they could relax diet must resume it well before attempting to conceive. Adherence is a major problem because many women diagnosed by newborn screening discontinued diet in childhood ('diet for life' was not historically advised) and find the restricted diet difficult; structured multidisciplinary metabolic and obstetric care improves outcomes. Tyrosine becomes conditionally essential and must be supplemented, and tetrahydrobiopterin (sapropterin) responsiveness should be assessed as it can aid control in selected women; overtreatment causing maternal phenylalanine deficiency also harms the fetus. Because affected offspring do not have PKU themselves, a normal newborn screen in the baby does not exclude maternal PKU embryopathy; the diagnosis rests on maternal history and biochemistry. unplanned pregnancy or conception occurring while maternal phenylalanine is poorly controlled persistently elevated maternal blood phenylalanine during the first trimester fetal microcephaly, growth restriction or a structural cardiac anomaly detected on antenatal imaging maternal phenylalanine driven too low, risking amino-acid deficiency and fetal catabolic harm loss to follow-up of a woman of childbearing age with known PKU no longer on diet Assuming a normal newborn screen in the baby excludes harm; the offspring is usually an unaffected carrier yet may be severely damaged by intrauterine phenylalanine exposure. Achieving metabolic control only after pregnancy is confirmed, by which time cardiac organogenesis and early neurodevelopment have already occurred. Allowing women diagnosed in infancy to remain off diet without preconception planning, on the outdated view that diet can be stopped after childhood. Overzealous restriction causing maternal phenylalanine deficiency, which itself impairs fetal growth and development. Neglecting tyrosine and micronutrient supplementation and dietetic support, leading to maternal malnutrition on the restricted diet. Phenylketonuria results from deficiency of hepatic phenylalanine hydroxylase (or, less commonly, of its tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor), causing accumulation of phenylalanine. In pregnancy, phenylalanine is actively transported across the placenta and concentrated in the fetal compartment, so an inadequately treated affected mother exposes the developing embryo and fetus to sustained hyperphenylalaninaemia. Excess phenylalanine is directly neurotoxic and disrupts organogenesis: it impairs neuronal proliferation and migration and interferes with the metabolism of other large neutral amino acids and neurotransmitter precursors. First-trimester exposure disturbs cardiac neural crest and outflow-tract development, producing congenital heart disease, while ongoing exposure impairs brain growth and myelination, yielding microcephaly and intellectual disability, and restricts somatic growth. The severity of fetal damage correlates closely with the level and duration of maternal blood phenylalanine, especially periconceptional and first-trimester control; the fetus is affected regardless of its own genotype, being typically an unaffected carrier. When strict maternal metabolic control is achieved before conception and maintained throughout pregnancy, the risk of the embryopathy falls markedly and offspring outcomes approach those of the general population. Poor periconceptional and first-trimester control carries high rates of microcephaly, congenital heart disease, growth restriction and irreversible intellectual disability in the child.

function tests and renal function to detect organ involvement Inflammatory markers and temperature charting Skin biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain Screening for viral reactivation (e.g. HHV-6) in appropriate settings HLA typing (e.g. HLA-B*15:02, HLA-A*31:01) in at-risk populations before prescribing Thyroid function follow-up given the risk of late autoimmune sequelae A severe multiorgan drug reaction, part of the DRESS spectrum, classically caused by aromatic anticonvulsants such as phenytoin, carbamazepine and phenobarbital Onset is typically delayed, often two to eight weeks after starting the drug, distinguishing it from immediate reactions The triad of fever, widespread rash and internal organ involvement (especially hepatitis) is characteristic, frequently with lymphadenopathy Blood tests commonly show eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytes Facial oedema is a useful clinical clue to DRESS There is cross-reactivity among the aromatic anticonvulsants, so all should generally be avoided once one has caused the syndrome HLA associations exist (for example HLA-B*15:02 with carbamazepine-related Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis and HLA-A*31:01 with carbamazepine hypersensitivity), supporting pharmacogenomic screening in at-risk groups Management is prompt drug withdrawal, supportive care and systemic corticosteroids for significant organ involvement Marked transaminitis or evidence of acute liver failure Extensive rash with mucosal involvement or skin detachment suggesting overlap with SJS/TEN Renal impairment, myocarditis or pneumonitis Haemodynamic instability or high persistent fever Rapidly rising eosinophil count with organ dysfunction Attributing the delayed rash and fever to infection and continuing the anticonvulsant Switching to another aromatic anticonvulsant with which there is cross-reactivity Underestimating internal organ involvement because the rash appears mild Stopping corticosteroids too quickly and precipitating relapse Not screening at-risk populations for relevant HLA alleles before prescribing The syndrome is a delayed, T-cell-mediated drug hypersensitivity reaction. Aromatic anticonvulsants are metabolised by cytochrome P450 to reactive arene oxide intermediates, which are normally detoxified by epoxide hydrolase. Deficient or defective detoxification allows reactive metabolites to accumulate, act as haptens and trigger an immune response, with genetic variation in detoxifying enzymes contributing to susceptibility. Specific HLA alleles predispose to particular reactions by shaping which drug-modified peptides are presented to T cells. Reactivation of human herpesviruses, particularly HHV-6, is often associated with DRESS and may contribute to the prolonged, relapsing course. The immune activation produces fever, an extensive cutaneous eruption, eosinophilia and inflammation of internal organs, most often the liver but also kidneys, lungs and heart. With early drug withdrawal and supportive care most patients recover, but the syndrome can be fatal, largely from hepatic or other organ failure. The course may be prolonged and relapsing, and late autoimmune sequelae such as thyroid disease can occur, warranting follow-up.
