Genetic evaluation when a hereditary predisposition is suspected (MEN2/RET, von Hippel-Lindau, neurofibromatosis type 1, hereditary paraganglioma syndromes) (p.2140). Systemic mastocytosis — flushing and palpitation attacks; urinary metanephrines help exclude pheochromocytoma when evaluating mast-cell symptoms (mastocytosis chapter). Carcinoid tumour — overlapping flushing/paroxysmal symptoms; assessed together with metanephrines in differential testing (mastocytosis chapter). Stimulant (cocaine/amphetamine) toxicity producing a catecholaminergic crisis with hypertension and arrhythmia (cardiomyopathy chapter). Takotsubo (stress / apical ballooning) cardiomyopathy — catecholamine-mediated, can follow a surge resembling pheochromocytoma (cardiac trauma / cardiomyopathy chapters). The classic triad is episodic headache, palpitations and sweating (diaphoresis) occurring with paroxysmal hypertension (p.2140). Most patients present with hypertension at a relatively young age, often between 30 and 50 years (p.2140). Many patients have only non-specific symptoms; the florid paroxysmal presentation is not universal, so the diagnosis is easily missed (p.2140). Catecholamine-secreting tumours arise from chromaffin cells: roughly 80-85% are in the adrenal medulla, the remainder being extra-adrenal paraganglioma in paraganglion tissue (p.2140). Patients with pheochromocytoma frequently have postural (orthostatic) hypotension despite the hypertension, reflecting volume contraction and impaired sympathetic reflexes (cardiomyopathy chapter). Catecholamine excess can produce a hyperdynamic state and palpitations, and is one of the recognised endocrine causes alongside thyrotoxicosis and mastocytosis (palpitations chapter). Pheochromocytoma in crisis is named alongside aortic dissection and eclampsia as a hypertensive emergency demanding particularly rapid management; control blood pressure with a titratable IV agent (p.2141). Very labile blood pressure and heart rate with episodic palpitations occurring together with new heart failure should raise suspicion of pheochromocytoma (cardiomyopathy chapter). Coexisting postural hypotension with paroxysmal hypertension is a clue to catecholamine excess rather than essential hypertension (cardiomyopathy chapter). Representativeness-heuristic trap: clinicians overestimate the probability of pheochromocytoma when the classic headache-palpitations-sweating triad is present, because they neglect its low prevalence relative to common causes of hypertension; the triad also occurs in patients who do not have the tumour (clinical-reasoning chapter, p.~? — diagnostic reasoning). Conversely, non-specific or atypical presentations can lead to the diagnosis being missed entirely (clinical-reasoning chapter). Postural hypotension may be wrongly attributed to over-treatment of hypertension rather than recognised as a catecholamine-excess clue (cardiomyopathy chapter). Excess production of catecholamines, usually by a benign neuroendocrine tumour of chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla (80-85%) or in extra-adrenal paraganglion tissue (paraganglioma). The catecholamine surge drives paroxysmal hypertension, headache, sweating and cardiac arrhythmias, and produces a hyperdynamic catecholaminergic state. Chronic/episodic catecholamine exposure can cause microvascular myocardial ischaemia (microinfarcts similar to those seen with stimulant toxicity) and a catecholamine-mediated cardiomyopathy; the same mechanism of sudden catecholamine release underlies stress (takotsubo / apical ballooning) cardiomyopathy (hypertension, cardiomyopathy and cardiac-tumour chapters). A benign tumour is usual; definitive treatment is surgical extirpation (complete or partial adrenalectomy, typically minimally invasive), which is generally curative. Surgery requires prior alpha-adrenergic receptor blockade. Untreated catecholamine excess can precipitate hypertensive emergency, arrhythmia, catecholamine cardiomyopathy and heart failure (hypertension and cardiomyopathy chapters).

Pheochromocytoma — Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma, PPGL, Paraganglioma, Chromaffin cell tumor Essential hypertension Anxiety/panic attacks (may be mistaken for psychiatric illness) Cocaine or amphetamine use Mastocytosis or carcinoid syndrome (usually without hypertension) Intracranial lesions Clonidine withdrawal Autonomic epilepsy Factitious crises (sympathomimetic amine use) For an asymptomatic adrenal mass: nonfunctioning adrenal adenoma, aldosteronoma, cortisol-producing adenoma (Cushing's syndrome) 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines (high sensitivity for initial screening) Plasma free metanephrines (most sensitive, least stress-confounded) Contrast CT or T2-weighted MRI with gadolinium for localization (MRI somewhat better for extra-adrenal disease) Functional imaging: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT and 18F-DOPA PET/CT (very high sensitivity and specificity, >95%) 123I/131I-MIBG scintigraphy and 18F-FDG PET, useful in hereditary and metastatic disease Immunohistochemistry (chromogranin, synaptophysin, S-100, SDHB) on resected tissue Universal germline genetic panel testing Postoperative documentation of catecholamine normalization and ACTH stimulation test after bilateral cortex-sparing surgery Essential hypertension with adrenergic features Panic disorder / anxiety attacks Sympathomimetic drug effect (cocaine, amphetamines) Carcinoid syndrome and systemic mastocytosis Clonidine or other antihypertensive withdrawal Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas (PPGLs) are catecholamine-producing tumors arising from sympathetic (adrenal medulla, sympathetic trunk) or parasympathetic (carotid body, glomus tympanicum/jugulare/vagale) paraganglia; by WHO usage pheochromocytoma denotes the adrenal tumor and paraganglioma denotes tumors at all other sites. The classic triad is episodic palpitations, headache, and profuse sweating, present in roughly one-third of patients; the combination of this triad with hypertension makes pheochromocytoma a likely diagnosis, though tumors can remain asymptomatic for years. Hypertension is the dominant sign and may be paroxysmal (classic) or sustained (also common); paroxysms generally last under one hour. The classic 'rule of tens' states that about 10% are bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal, and 10% metastatic. Diagnosis rests on two equally important pillars: biochemical documentation of catecholamine excess and imaging localization of the tumor. Plasma free metanephrines are the most sensitive biochemical test and are less prone to false-positive elevation from stress including venipuncture; most tumors continuously leak O-methylated metabolites even when catecholamine secretion fluctuates. Values three times the upper limit of normal make the diagnosis highly likely regardless of assay; because the tumor is rare, borderline elevations are more likely to be false positives, so drug/dietary confounders should be excluded and testing repeated. On unenhanced CT, an adrenal mass with attenuation below 10 Hounsfield units makes pheochromocytoma unlikely; about 5% of adrenal incidentalomas prove to be pheochromocytomas on endocrine evaluation. Histology classically shows a 'Zellballen' pattern of neuroendocrine chief cell nests with peripheral sustentacular cells; chief cells stain for chromogranin and synaptophysin, sustentacular cells for S-100, and loss of SDHB staining suggests an underlying germline SDH mutation. About 25-33% of patients have an inherited syndrome (MEN 2, VHL, NF1, paraganglioma syndromes, TMEM127, MAX); these patients present on average about 15 years younger than those with sporadic tumors. Universal germline panel testing is the gold standard and identifies a genetic cause in up to about 30% of cases, with higher yield in early onset, extra-adrenal, multiple, or metastatic tumors or a family history. Pheochromocytoma in pregnancy may produce adrenergic crises, possibly via hCG/LHCG-receptor-mediated stimulation of epinephrine production, and is challenging to manage. Catecholamine crisis causing heart failure, pulmonary edema, arrhythmias, or intracranial hemorrhage Paroxysms precipitated by surgery, anesthesia/intubation, positional change, exercise, micturition (bladder paraganglioma), pregnancy, or drugs (tricyclics, opiates, metoclopramide) Paradoxical hypertensive response to antihypertensive drugs Beta blockade given before adequate alpha blockade (risk of worsened hypertension) Hypertensive crisis or adrenergic crisis during pregnancy Features suggesting a hereditary syndrome (early onset, bilateral/multifocal, extra-adrenal, family history, MTC, retinal/CNS/renal tumors) Borderline biochemical elevations are frequently false positives given tumor rarity; failing to exclude dietary/drug confounders (sympathomimetics, diuretics, tricyclics, alpha/beta blockers, levodopa withdrawal) and repeat testing leads to overdiagnosis. Serial catecholamine levels vary widely due to fluctuating secretion, so reliance on a single catecholamine measurement can miss the diagnosis; metanephrines are continuously leaked. Starting a beta blocker before adequate alpha blockade can precipitate severe hypertension. FNA of a presumed adrenal mass that is actually a pheochromocytoma can provoke a crisis. Standard histologic atypia, mitoses, and local invasion do not reliably establish malignancy. Symptoms can be misattributed to a primary psychiatric/panic disorder. NF1 germline mutations are essentially never found in sporadic pheochromocytoma, so NF1 testing is unnecessary without other neurofibromatosis features. Sequencing protocols may miss large single- or multi-exon deletions. PPGLs are well-vascularized neuroendocrine tumors derived from chromaffin cells of the sympathetic and parasympathetic paraganglial system. They synthesize and store catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine), and tumoral release drives the clinical syndrome; the name pheochromocytoma reflects the dark staining produced by chromaffin oxidation of catecholamines. The etiology of sporadic tumors is unknown, but 25-33% carry germline mutations. Susceptibility genes fall into three pathogenetic clusters: cluster 1 (pseudohypoxia: SDHx, FH, VHL, HIF2A), cluster 2 (kinase signaling: RET, NF1, TMEM127, MAX, HRAS, KIF1B-beta, PDH), and cluster 3 (Wnt signaling: CSDE1, MAML3). Most genes act as tumor suppressors with biallelic inactivation, while RET is a protooncogene whose mutations activate receptor tyrosine kinase activity; SDH is a Krebs-cycle/mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme, and the VHL protein is part of a ubiquitin E3 ligase whose loss upregulates cell-cycle, glucose metabolism, and oxygen-sensing pathways. Complete tumor removal is potentially curative and can prevent lethal hypertensive crises. About 5-10% of PPGLs are metastatic; histologic criteria alone are insufficient to define malignancy, and the WHO now uses 'metastatic' (lymph node or distant spread, commonly to lung, bone, or liver) rather than 'malignant.' The prognosis of metastatic disease is variable with 5-year survival of roughly 30-60%. Hereditary syndromes influence risk: about one-third of PGL4 (SDHB) patients develop metastases, the highest rate among the associated syndromes, and metastatic disease also occurs notably with VHL, NF1, and PGL1. Malignancy/recurrence risk is assessed by markers including tumor size >5 cm, the Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal gland Scaled Score (PASS), the Grading system for Adrenal Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma (GAPP), and SDHB status, although these remain controversial. Disease is now categorized by the WHO as localized versus metastatic (regional lymph node or distant metastasis) rather than benign versus malignant.

balanitis and secondary phimosis In the young child the foreskin is normally adherent to the glans and has a physiologically narrow opening; separation and retractility develop progressively over the Chronic inflammation, most importantly lichen sclerosus (balanitis xerotica obliterans) but also recurrent balanoposthitis and the trauma of repeated forcible retraction, drives dermal scarring that contracts the preputial ring into a rigid, non-distensible band. Physiological phimosis resolves spontaneously with growth, and many narrow non-scarred foreskins respond to topical steroid, whereas true scarring phimosis is effectively cured by circumcision, though associated lichen sclerosus of the glans or urethra may need continued attention.

phlegmasia alba dolens — painful white leg, milk leg, phlegmasia alba Acute arterial occlusion (embolic or thrombotic limb ischaemia) Uncomplicated deep vein thrombosis Compartment syndrome from another cause Necrotising soft tissue infection Acute cellulitis of the limb Lymphoedema complicated by cellulitis Ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst Duplex ultrasound to confirm and localise the venous thrombosis CT or MR venography to define the iliocaval extent and identify compressive lesions such as May-Thurner Assessment of arterial perfusion (ankle pressures and Doppler) to exclude arterial occlusion Full blood count with serial platelet monitoring for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and a coagulation profile Renal function and metabolic screen given fluid sequestration and possible tissue injury Evaluation for underlying malignancy and, where appropriate, thrombophilia Compartment pressure assessment and markers of tissue injury if gangrene or compartment syndrome is suspected Phlegmasia alba dolens ('painful white leg', 'milk leg') is a severe form of acute iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis in which massive venous outflow obstruction produces a swollen, painful, pale limb; it is classically described postpartum but occurs with any cause of extensive proximal thrombosis The pallor reflects tense subcutaneous oedema together with reflex arterial spasm, while patent collateral veins still permit some venous drainage, distinguishing it from the later cyanotic stage The condition lies on a continuum: untreated progression to phlegmasia cerulea dolens (a cyanotic, near-total venous occlusion involving the collaterals) and then to venous gangrene threatens both the limb and life Peripheral pulses are typically preserved in phlegmasia alba dolens, which helps differentiate it from acute arterial occlusion where the limb is likewise pale and painful Massive fluid sequestration into the affected limb can precipitate hypovolaemia and circulatory compromise, and severe swelling may cause a compartment syndrome Management centres on prompt therapeutic anticoagulation, limb elevation and consideration of catheter-directed thrombolysis or venous thrombectomy, alongside a search for underlying causes such as May-Thurner iliac vein compression or occult malignancy It is a limb- and life-threatening emergency requiring urgent vascular assessment; venous gangrene carries a high risk of amputation and significant mortality and is strongly associated with malignancy and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia Progression to cyanosis (phlegmasia cerulea dolens) or to skin blistering and gangrene Absent distal pulses or other signs of arterial compromise Tense swelling suggesting an evolving compartment syndrome Haemodynamic instability from fluid sequestration A falling platelet count suggesting heparin-induced thrombocytopenia Mistaking the pale, painful limb for acute arterial ischaemia and delaying anticoagulation Underestimating fluid sequestration and failing to resuscitate the circulation Missing an underlying iliac vein compression or occult malignancy Overlooking an evolving compartment syndrome Continuing heparin despite thrombocytopenia when heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is driving the thrombosis Extensive thrombosis of the iliofemoral venous segment obstructs venous outflow from the limb. In the alba stage the collateral veins remain patent, so the limb is pale, tensely swollen and painful, and reflex arterial vasospasm contributes to the pallor and to diminished distal perfusion. As thrombus propagates to involve the collateral and microvascular beds (phlegmasia cerulea dolens), venous drainage fails almost completely; capillary and venular pressures rise steeply, the limb becomes cyanotic and severely swollen, and large volumes of fluid sequester into the tissues, causing hypovolaemia. The resulting rise in tissue pressure, together with progressive microvascular thrombosis, impairs arterial inflow and can culminate in venous gangrene. With prompt anticoagulation and thrombus removal the white-leg stage can resolve, but progression to venous gangrene carries high rates of amputation and mortality. Long-term post-thrombotic syndrome is common in survivors, particularly after extensive iliofemoral thrombosis.

fasciotomy may be needed for compartment syndrome Carries a high risk of pulmonary embolism and of significant limb loss and mortality Progression to venous gangrene or absent arterial signals, indicating a threatened limb Compartment syndrome requiring fasciotomy Haemodynamic compromise from fluid sequestration or massive pulmonary embolism Rapidly advancing cyanosis and pain despite anticoagulation Mistaking it for acute arterial ischaemia and delaying anticoagulation Underestimating fluid sequestration and failing to resuscitate Delaying thrombolysis or thrombectomy until gangrene has developed Missing an occult underlying malignancy Phlegmasia cerulea dolens is the extreme of iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis, in which thrombus occludes not only the major deep veins but also the collateral channels, producing near-complete venous outflow obstruction. The resulting massive rise in interstitial and venous pressure causes gross oedema and cyanosis, and can exceed capillary and eventually arterial perfusion pressure, leading to ischaemia, venous gangrene, and compartment syndrome. Large volumes of fluid sequester in the limb, causing hypovolaemia and shock. An underlying hypercoagulable state, often malignancy, is common. A serious emergency with significant risk of limb loss, pulmonary embolism, and death; prompt anticoagulation and thrombus removal can salvage the limb, but venous gangrene carries a poor outcome and any underlying malignancy influences survival.

phlycten before prescribing steroids Overlooking central corneal scarring as a cause of reduced vision Failing to screen for tuberculosis and malnutrition in at-risk children Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis is a delayed-type hypersensitivity response to microbial antigens, most often staphylococcal proteins associated with chronic blepharitis, and historically tuberculoprotein. Sensitised T lymphocytes react to the antigen at the limbus, cornea, or conjunctiva, producing a localised nodular infiltrate (the phlycten) with surrounding vascular congestion. The overlying epithelium may ulcerate. Corneal phlyctens can advance centrally, drawing a wedge of new vessels and leaving a scar. Repeated episodes cause progressive corneal vascularisation, thinning, and scarring. As the disorder reflects an immune reaction to a remote antigen rather than active local infection, treatment targets both the antigenic source and the hypersensitivity response. Conjunctival phlyctens are usually self-limiting and resolve without sequelae, whereas recurrent corneal disease can cause scarring, vascularisation, and lasting visual impairment. Controlling the underlying trigger reduces recurrence and preserves vision.

triggers, transfusion or folate support for haemolysis, and seizure control as needed Acute rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria threatening acute kidney injury Severe anaemia requiring transfusion or causing cardiovascular compromise Stroke-like episodes or new focal neurological deficit Status epilepticus or rapid neurological deterioration Attributing exertional muscle symptoms to a glycogenosis without considering a glycolytic enzymopathy Missing the diagnosis in a boy with unexplained non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia Failing to counsel on avoidance of rhabdomyolysis triggers and prompt management of myoglobinuria Overlooking the X-linked inheritance in genetic counselling of the family Phosphoglycerate kinase catalyses an ATP-generating step of glycolysis, converting 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 3-phosphoglycerate. PGK1 is X-linked and expressed in almost all tissues, so deficiency impairs glycolytic ATP production broadly. In erythrocytes, which depend on glycolysis for energy, reduced ATP shortens red-cell survival and causes chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. In skeletal muscle, impaired glycolysis limits energy during anaerobic exertion, producing exercise intolerance, cramps, and rhabdomyolysis. In the brain, deficient energy metabolism underlies the intellectual impairment, seizures, and stroke-like episodes seen in some patients. The particular combination of features varies with the specific variant. The prognosis varies widely with phenotype; isolated haemolysis or myopathy may be manageable with supportive care, whereas significant CNS involvement carries a worse outlook, and recurrent rhabdomyolysis poses ongoing renal risk.

Deficiency impedes glycolytic energy production; in skeletal muscle this manifests as exercise intolerance, cramps and exertional muscle breakdown, while in the red cell, which relies wholly on glycolysis for ATP, reduced activity can shorten cell survival and cause a chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. The relative contribution of muscle and erythrocyte disease depends on which isoform and mutation are involved. The muscle disease is usually compatible with a normal lifespan provided provocative exertion is avoided; haemolysis, when present, is generally mild to moderate and well tolerated.

Photoallergic contact dermatitis is an acquired, immunologically mediated (type IV, cell-mediated) response. A chemical applied to or reaching the skin absorbs ultraviolet radiation, most often in the UVA range, and is thereby altered to form a photoproduct or a stable hapten-protein complex that becomes antigenic. After an initial sensitisation phase, subsequent exposure to both the chemical and light provokes a T-cell-driven eczematous reaction. Because an immunological memory response is required, only previously sensitised individuals react, the amount of allergen needed is small, and the eruption may extend to covered skin, distinguishing it from the direct, non-immunological tissue damage of a phototoxic reaction. The outlook is good once the responsible agent is identified and avoided, with resolution of the eczema and no long-term sequelae in most patients; a minority develop persistent light reactivity that may evolve towards chronic actinic dermatitis.

to a topical product while missing a systemic photosensitising drug Advising only ultraviolet-B sunscreens when the reaction is driven by ultraviolet A Failing to recognise pseudoporphyria and confusing it with true porphyria Overlooking the sparing of shaded sites that defines the photodistributed pattern Photodistributed drug eruptions arise when a systemic drug or its metabolite absorbs ultraviolet radiation in the skin. In phototoxic reactions the absorbed energy generates reactive oxygen species and other cytotoxic photoproducts that directly damage keratinocytes and other cutaneous cells, producing an exaggerated sunburn-like response that depends on the dose of both drug and light and can occur on first exposure. In photoallergic reactions the drug is converted by light into a photoproduct that acts as a hapten, provoking a delayed type IV, T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity that requires prior sensitisation and produces an eczematous eruption. The predominance of ultraviolet A in the action spectrum explains why reactions occur despite ordinary sunscreens and through glass. Most reactions resolve after the culprit drug is stopped and light exposure minimised, though phototoxic pigmentation and drug-induced photosensitivity can persist for a time after withdrawal, and rarely a lasting photosensitivity develops.

Photokeratitis — ultraviolet keratitis, snow blindness, welder's flash, arc eye Infective keratitis or corneal ulcer Corneal abrasion or foreign body Chemical eye injury Acute anterior uveitis Dry eye disease with keratopathy Clinical diagnosis from the exposure history and delayed bilateral symptoms Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein showing punctate epithelial staining Visual acuity assessment Exclusion of a retained foreign body or infective keratitis Assessment for occupational ultraviolet exposure An acute painful inflammation of the corneal epithelium caused by ultraviolet radiation exposure Typical sources are welding arcs, reflection of sunlight off snow or water, and sunlamps Symptoms are characteristically delayed by several hours after exposure and are bilateral Patients have intense pain, foreign-body sensation, watering, redness, blepharospasm and photophobia Examination shows diffuse punctate epithelial staining, and the condition is self-limiting Management is supportive with lubrication and analgesia, and prevention through appropriate eye protection Features suggesting infective keratitis such as a focal infiltrate A retained foreign body or penetrating injury Significant visual loss Failure to improve within the expected short timeframe Missing an infective keratitis or foreign body mistaken for simple photokeratitis Prescribing topical anaesthetics for ongoing use, which impairs healing Overlooking the occupational source and failing to advise eye protection Attributing delayed symptoms to another acute ocular condition Photokeratitis results from ultraviolet radiation damaging the corneal and conjunctival epithelium, causing death and shedding of surface epithelial cells. The injury behaves like a superficial burn, and because the epithelial damage and consequent nerve-ending exposure take hours to manifest, symptoms are characteristically delayed after the exposure. The corneal epithelium regenerates quickly, so the condition is painful but usually short-lived and heals without scarring. The condition is self-limiting and typically resolves within a day or two as the corneal epithelium heals, without long-term visual consequence.

Phyllodes tumour of the breast — phyllodes tumour, cystosarcoma phyllodes, phylloides tumour, fibroepithelial tumour of the breast, benign, borderline and malignant phyllodes tumour Fibroadenoma, especially the cellular and juvenile variants Primary breast sarcoma Metaplastic (spindle cell) carcinoma of the breast Hamartoma of the breast Periductal stromal tumour Fibromatosis of the breast Malignant heterologous elements mimicking a separate sarcoma Triple assessment with clinical examination, breast imaging and biopsy Core-needle biopsy, recognising its limitations in separating phyllodes tumour from cellular fibroadenoma Histological grading assessing stromal cellularity, atypia, mitoses, margins and stromal overgrowth Breast ultrasound and mammography, with MRI when extent is unclear Staging imaging for distant (haematogenous) metastasis in malignant tumours Molecular studies (for example MED12 and TERT promoter status) in selected diagnostically difficult cases A fibroepithelial neoplasm of the breast in which the stromal (mesenchymal) component drives the tumour, forming characteristic leaf-like (phyllodes) fronds projecting into cystic spaces Classified into a spectrum of benign, borderline and malignant grades based on stromal cellularity, atypia, mitotic activity, margin appearance and stromal overgrowth Typically presents in middle-aged women as a firm, rapidly enlarging, painless breast mass, often larger than a fibroadenoma Distinguishing benign phyllodes tumour from a cellular fibroadenoma can be difficult, and core biopsy may not reliably separate them Stromal overgrowth, defined as stroma without accompanying epithelium in a low-power field, is an important adverse feature MED12 mutations are shared with fibroadenoma, while progression to higher grade is associated with additional alterations such as TERT promoter mutations and other tumour-suppressor changes Wide local excision with an adequate rim of normal tissue is the goal; axillary dissection is not required because malignant tumours spread haematogenously, not typically to nodes Rapid increase in size of a breast mass Malignant-grade histology with marked stromal overgrowth, atypia and high mitotic activity Positive or close excision margins predicting local recurrence Signs of haematogenous metastasis, particularly to the lungs Heterologous sarcomatous differentiation within the tumour Diagnosing a cellular fibroadenoma on core biopsy and missing a phyllodes tumour Performing axillary lymph node dissection, which is unnecessary given haematogenous spread Excising with inadequate margins, leading to local recurrence Overlooking stromal overgrowth or heterologous sarcomatous elements when grading Underestimating recurrence risk in borderline tumours treated as clearly benign Phyllodes tumours are biphasic fibroepithelial lesions in which the neoplastic stroma is the driving component, producing exaggerated leaf-like architecture and, in higher grades, sarcomatous features. Early tumours often share MED12 mutations with fibroadenomas, indicating a common starting point, whereas progression towards borderline and malignant grades accumulates further genetic alterations, including TERT promoter mutations and loss of tumour-suppressor function, that increase stromal cellularity, atypia and proliferation. Malignant tumours can undergo heterologous sarcomatous differentiation and metastasise through the bloodstream rather than via lymphatics. Benign phyllodes tumours have an excellent prognosis when completely excised, with recurrence linked mainly to inadequate margins; borderline tumours recur more often, and malignant phyllodes tumours can metastasise haematogenously, most commonly to the lungs, carrying a significantly worse outlook, so wide excision with clear margins is the key determinant of local control across all grades.

Graded as benign, borderline or malignant using stromal cellularity, atypia, mitotic rate, stromal overgrowth and the nature of the tumour margin. Typically presents as a firm, mobile, painless mass that enlarges more rapidly than a fibroadenoma, often in women in their fourth to fifth decade. Core biopsy cannot reliably distinguish a phyllodes tumour from a cellular fibroadenoma; a report of 'cellular fibroepithelial lesion' warrants excision for definitive classification. Wide local excision aiming for a clear margin (conventionally around 1 cm) is the mainstay; enucleation predisposes to local recurrence. Axillary node dissection is not indicated as spread of malignant phyllodes is haematogenous, chiefly to lung and bone, rather than lymphatic. Malignant transformation is characterised by pure stromal sarcomatous overgrowth; heterologous elements such as liposarcoma may occur. Recurrence can show progression to a higher grade, so long-term clinical and imaging surveillance is advised after excision. Rapid interval enlargement of a previously stable breast mass Very large tumour with overlying skin stretching, ulceration or venous prominence Histological stromal overgrowth with high mitotic count and infiltrative margin New respiratory or skeletal symptoms suggesting haematogenous metastasis Repeated local recurrence with rising histological grade Mislabelling a phyllodes tumour as a fibroadenoma on core biopsy and undertreating with simple enucleation Performing unnecessary axillary surgery, since spread is haematogenous rather than nodal Failing to obtain an adequate margin, the principal driver of local recurrence Assuming benign histology excludes recurrence and omitting follow-up surveillance Overlooking sarcomatous heterologous elements that upgrade a lesion to malignant Phyllodes tumours are biphasic fibroepithelial neoplasms arising from the intralobular (periductal) hormone-responsive stroma. Unlike fibroadenomas, the stromal component is the neoplastic driver and shows variable hypercellularity, atypia and mitotic activity, producing the characteristic elongated leaf-like fronds lined by benign ductal and myoepithelial epithelium. Progressive accumulation of stromal genetic alterations, including MED12 mutations shared with fibroadenoma and additional changes such as TERT promoter mutations and later cytogenetic aberrations, underlies the spectrum from benign through borderline to frankly malignant lesions in which the stroma overgrows and behaves as a sarcoma. Benign phyllodes tumours have an excellent outlook after complete excision, though local recurrence may occur if margins are inadequate. Borderline and malignant lesions carry progressively higher recurrence and, for malignant tumours, a meaningful risk of distant metastasis that markedly worsens survival.

of dilated cardiomyopathy with conduction disease Hereditary lipid disorders (tendon, eruptive, or palmar xanthomas; lipemia retinalis) signaling atherosclerotic risk Noncardiac causes of dyspnea such as obstructive lung disease (barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing) The jugular venous pressure is the single most important bedside measurement for estimating volume status; the internal jugular vein is preferred over the external because the latter is valved and not directly in line with the superior vena cava and right atrium. Using the sternal angle (angle of Louis) as the reference point systematically underestimates central venous pressure, so it is better used to separate normal from elevated CVP than to quantify it; venous pulsations above the clavicle in the sitting position are clearly abnormal since the clavicle-to-right-atrium distance is at least 10 cm. The venous waveform is biphasic in sinus rhythm whereas the carotid pulse is monophasic; the venous pulse is not easily obliterated by palpation and changes with posture and inspiration, helping distinguish it from the arterial pulse. A cannon a wave occurs with atrioventricular dissociation when the right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve; in a wide-complex tachycardia, cannon a waves identify the rhythm as ventricular in origin. The a wave is absent in atrial fibrillation. Kussmaul's sign (a rise or lack of fall of the JVP with inspiration) is classically associated with constrictive pericarditis but also occurs with restrictive cardiomyopathy, massive pulmonary embolism, right ventricular infarction, and advanced left ventricular systolic heart failure, and is common after cardiac surgery. Pulsus parvus et tardus (weak and delayed carotid pulse) suggests severe aortic stenosis, whereas a sharp rapidly collapsing carotid upstroke (Corrigan's or water-hammer pulse) points to chronic severe aortic regurgitation. Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory fall in systolic pressure >10 mmHg) is seen in pericardial tamponade but also occurs with massive pulmonary embolism, hemorrhagic shock, severe obstructive lung disease, and tension pneumothorax; it reflects exaggerated interventricular dependence. Fixed splitting of S2 (a wide A2-P2 interval that does not vary with respiration) is characteristic of a secundum atrial septal defect, while reversed (paradoxical) splitting occurs with left bundle branch block, right ventricular pacing, severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, and acute myocardial ischemia. The mitral valve prolapse click-murmur complex moves away from S1 with maneuvers that increase preload (squatting) and closer to S1 on standing, a dynamic behavior that helps distinguish it from other systolic events. Lower extremity edema with an elevated JVP indicates volume overload (heart failure or constrictive pericarditis), whereas edema without jugular venous hypertension suggests hypoalbuminemia (nephrotic syndrome, liver failure), venous insufficiency, or dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker use. Janeway lesions (nontender hemorrhagic macules on palms and soles) and Osler's nodes (tender nodules on finger/toe pads), along with splinter hemorrhages in the mid-nail bed, are peripheral signs of infective endocarditis. An ankle-brachial index (ankle systolic pressure divided by the higher brachial systolic pressure) is a powerful predictor of long-term cardiovascular mortality; a >2% finger-to-toe oxygen saturation difference on pulse oximetry performs comparably for detecting lower extremity peripheral arterial disease. Markedly elevated JVP that does not pulsate with a dusky cyanotic head and neck, suggesting superior vena cava syndrome Pulsus paradoxus with elevated JVP and blunted y descent, suggesting pericardial tamponade An interarm systolic blood pressure difference >10 mmHg or femoral pulse delay, raising concern for aortic dissection or coarctation Differential cyanosis of the lower extremities with a large patent ductus and pulmonary hypertension (right-to-left shunting) New peripheral embolic stigmata with fever pointing toward infective endocarditis Orthostatic hypotension without compensatory tachycardia, suggesting autonomic insufficiency Using an inappropriately small blood pressure cuff overestimates pressure, while an oversized cuff underestimates it; the bladder should be about 80% of arm length and 40% of arm circumference. Examining the carotid upstrokes simultaneously, or before auscultating for a bruit, and applying heavy pressure can precipitate carotid hypersensitivity and syncope in susceptible elderly patients. A cervical bruit correlates poorly with the degree of carotid stenosis, and its absence does not exclude significant obstruction. Palpation alone is insufficiently accurate to diagnose an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and sensitivity falls with increasing body size. Homans' sign is neither sensitive nor specific for deep venous thrombosis. Arcus senilis lacks specificity as a marker of coronary heart disease risk. Physician-measured blood pressures tend to be higher than nurse- or self-recorded values, contributing to white coat hypertension; conversely masked hypertension can be missed when clinic pressures are normal despite target organ damage. Heart and pulse findings can be misleading in low cardiac output states and in stiffened arteries from aging, hypertension, or peripheral arterial disease. The cardiovascular examination derives diagnostic and prognostic information from the mechanical and hemodynamic consequences of cardiac and vascular disease. The jugular venous waveform reflects right atrial pressure dynamics: the a wave is presystolic right atrial contraction, the x descent is atrial relaxation, the c wave is the systolic bulging of the closed tricuspid valve, the v wave is atrial filling during ventricular systole, and the y descent is right atrial emptying after tricuspid opening. Reduced right ventricular compliance accentuates the a wave; tricuspid regurgitation accentuates the v wave with a rapid y descent and progressively 'ventricularizes' the waveform; obstruction to right ventricular inflow (tricuspid stenosis, tamponade) blunts or prolongs the y descent. Arterial pulse contour depends on stroke volume, ejection velocity, vascular compliance, and systemic vascular resistance, so fixed outflow obstruction blunts and delays the upstroke while wide pulse pressure states produce a bounding collapsing pulse. Heart sound intensity reflects valve leaflet excursion and mobility, ventricular contractility, and the PR interval, while the distance between the stethoscope and the cardiac event (obesity, lung disease, effusion) attenuates all sounds. Splitting of S2 depends on the relative timing of aortic and pulmonic valve closure, which is altered by conduction delays, shunts, and outflow obstruction. Bedside findings carry independent prognostic weight. In heart failure, an elevated JVP and a third heart sound predict the pulmonary artery wedge pressure and are associated with higher risk of heart failure hospitalization and death; an estimated right atrial pressure >10 mmHg predicted a wedge pressure >22 mmHg with high positive value in advanced heart failure. The ankle-brachial index is a powerful predictor of long-term cardiovascular mortality, and higher ambulatory systolic pressures independently predict cardiovascular events and all-cause death. Pulsus alternans indicates severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction, and when accompanied by electrocardiographic T-wave alternans the arrhythmic risk appears increased. No formal grading scale; specific findings convey severity within individual conditions (e.g., pulsus parvus et tardus and a soft A2 indicate severe aortic stenosis; the A2-opening snap interval in mitral stenosis is inversely proportional to the left atrial-left ventricular gradient; a JVP distance >4.5 cm above the sternal angle at 30 degrees, or any venous pulsation above the clavicle in the sitting position, is abnormal; orthostatic hypotension is a fall in systolic pressure >20 mmHg or diastolic >10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing).

Physiologic and Nonphysiologic Sinus Rhythm — Sinus tachycardia, Sinus arrhythmia, Sinus bradycardia, Inappropriate sinus tachycardia, IST, Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, POTS Focal atrial tachycardia arising near the sinus node (abrupt onset/offset favors AT) Premature atrial contractions causing rhythm irregularity (varying P-wave morphology) Inappropriate sinus tachycardia versus appropriate physiologic sinus tachycardia Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome Anxiety or panic disorder presenting with sinus tachycardia Fever or systemic infection driving appropriate (physiologic) sinus tachycardia Postviral autonomic dysfunction producing a POTS-like picture, including post-COVID-19 (long COVID) 12-lead ECG to confirm sinus P-wave morphology and axis Ambulatory / outpatient telemetry monitoring to distinguish gradual sinus tachycardia from paroxysmal atrial tachycardia Thyroid function testing to exclude hyperthyroidism as a reversible cause Hemoglobin / evaluation for anemia Orthostatic (supine-to-standing) heart rate and blood pressure assessment when POTS is suspected Invasive electrophysiology study in selected cases where the ECG distinction remains unclear Anemia Hyperthyroidism and other thyroid dysfunction Dehydration / volume depletion Pulmonary embolism Pheochromocytoma Decompensated heart failure or valvular disease Anxiety / panic attack Stimulant or drug effect (caffeine, sympathomimetics, cocaine, amphetamines, beta-blocker withdrawal) The sinus node sits at the lateral-superior junction of the right atrium and superior vena cava, within the upper portion of the crista terminalis where the smooth posterior wall (from the sinus venosus) meets the trabeculated anterior right atrium. Normal sinus rhythm runs between roughly 60 and 100 beats/min, with a sinus P wave that is upright in leads II, III, and aVF, negative in aVR, and initially positive/biphasic in V1, reflecting an inferiorly and leftward-directed frontal-plane axis. Sinus arrhythmia is a common, usually asymptomatic finding defined as a sinus-origin rhythm with P-P interval variation greater than 120 ms; when P-wave morphology also varies, premature atrial contractions rather than true sinus arrhythmia are the likely cause. Three patterns of sinus arrhythmia are described: respirophasic (vagal tone reflexively falls in inspiration and is restored in expiration), ventriculophasic (seen with heart block or after a PVC, where an interposed ventricular beat shortens the P-P interval), and nonphasic (P-P variation unrelated to cardiac or respiratory cycle). Sinus tachycardia (>100 beats/min) arises from sympathetic stimulation and/or vagal withdrawal; the earliest activation focus shifts more leftward toward the superior septal crista terminalis, producing taller inferior-lead P waves than in resting sinus rhythm. Sinus bradycardia is defined as a rate <60 beats/min but can be entirely normal during sleep and in physically fit individuals. A gradual rate rise with an identifiable trigger (such as exertion) favors sinus tachycardia, whereas abrupt onset and offset favor focal atrial tachycardia originating near the sinus node. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia (IST) is an uncommon disorder of autonomic dysregulation in which the sinus rate climbs at rest or out of proportion to physiologic demand; it most often affects women in their third or fourth decade. POTS is defined by symptomatic sinus tachycardia on standing, with a rate increase of at least 30 beats/min or to >120 beats/min within 10 minutes of standing in the absence of hypotension. POTS can follow a viral illness and may resolve spontaneously over 3-12 months; a POTS-like autonomic picture has been described in prolonged post-COVID-19 (long COVID) syndromes. Distinguishing IST from POTS is clinically critical because they require fundamentally different management approaches; conflating them risks worsening symptoms. Asymptomatic sinus arrhythmia is physiologic, is not considered pathogenic, and does not warrant further cardiac evaluation. Sinus tachycardia accompanied by hypotension, impaired consciousness, angina, or heart failure, suggesting a serious underlying cause requiring urgent attention Unexplained or persistent sinus tachycardia mandating exclusion of pulmonary embolism, myocardial ischemia, and structural/functional cardiac disease before labeling it nonphysiologic Syncope or disabling palpitations accompanying tachycardia Sinus tachycardia as a possible marker of underlying systemic illness (e.g., infection, malignancy, endocrine disorder) or drug toxicity Mislabeling rhythm irregularity with varying P-wave morphology as sinus arrhythmia when it is actually premature atrial contractions. Diagnosing nonphysiologic sinus tachycardia before excluding reversible drivers such as anemia, thyroid disease, and pulmonary embolism. Failing to separate inappropriate sinus tachycardia from POTS, since blood-pressure-raising strategies appropriate for POTS are inappropriate for IST, and sinus node modification is ineffective for POTS and may worsen its nontachycardia features. Pursuing catheter-based sinus node modification for IST, which often yields poor long-term symptom control and can lead to symptomatic sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, or chronotropic incompetence requiring a permanent pacemaker. Overtreating an asymptomatic, constitutionally elevated resting or exercise sinus rate with no identifiable underlying cause. Sinus rhythm originates from spontaneous depolarization of pacemaker cells in the sinus node at the right atrium-SVC junction within the crista terminalis. Heart rate is modulated by the autonomic balance between sympathetic input (which accelerates and shifts the activation focus) and parasympathetic (vagal) input (which slows the node). Sinus arrhythmia reflects normal beat-to-beat shifts in autonomic tone, classically respiratory-linked vagal modulation. Sinus tachycardia results from increased sympathetic drive and/or vagal withdrawal raising the rate of spontaneous nodal depolarization; when this is an appropriate response to exercise, stress, or illness it is physiologic. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is thought to stem from an imbalance between sympathetic and parasympathetic input to the node, altered membrane automaticity of sinus node cells, or both, though the precise mechanism remains poorly defined. POTS reflects orthostatic autonomic dysfunction, sometimes postviral. Sinus arrhythmia is benign and physiologic, requiring no treatment. Physiologic sinus tachycardia resolves with correction of the underlying condition and often needs no specific therapy. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia tends to be a chronic, often disabling condition that responds poorly to therapy and may be difficult to control long term. POTS frequently improves over time, and postviral POTS may resolve spontaneously within 3-12 months. Sinus tachycardia is rate-defined as >100 beats/min and sinus bradycardia as <60 beats/min, with normal sinus rhythm spanning 60-100 beats/min. POTS is defined diagnostically by an orthostatic heart-rate rise of >=30 beats/min (or to >120 beats/min) within 10 minutes of standing without hypotension. Sinus arrhythmia is defined by P-P interval variability >120 ms of sinus origin.

hands, can be mistaken for non-accidental injury or bruising Management is largely supportive with skin cleansing, treatment of the acute reaction, sun avoidance of affected areas and reassurance that the pigmentation fades slowly Extensive blistering or involvement of a large body surface requiring burns-type care Handprint or bruise-like marks in a child prompting a safeguarding assessment Systemic photosensitivity suggesting a drug cause or an underlying porphyria Ocular or mucosal involvement from plant sap contact Misdiagnosing the streaky pigmentation as bruising and raising unwarranted safeguarding concerns, or conversely dismissing genuine concerns Labelling it an allergic reaction and mismanaging it, when it is a phototoxic process affecting anyone Failing to elicit the plant or fruit exposure history that explains the bizarre pattern Not warning patients that the hyperpigmentation will persist long after the initial reaction resolves Phytophotodermatitis is a phototoxic reaction in which furocoumarins (psoralens) transferred to the skin from plants absorb ultraviolet A radiation and, in the excited state, form covalent adducts with DNA and damage cell membranes, causing direct keratinocyte injury, inflammation and blistering. This is the same class of psoralen-plus-ultraviolet-A photochemical reaction exploited therapeutically in PUVA. Subsequent stimulation of melanocytes produces the characteristic and often prolonged post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in the exact distribution of plant contact. The acute phototoxic reaction settles over days to a couple of weeks, but the resulting post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is often marked and can take many weeks to months to fade; the condition is entirely preventable by avoiding the combination of furocoumarin contact and sun exposure, and it does not recur without renewed exposure.

piebaldism — partial albinism, piebald trait Waardenburg syndrome (types I-IV) Segmental or focal vitiligo Naevus depigmentosus Tuberous sclerosis ash-leaf macules Hypomelanosis of Ito Naevus anaemicus Wood's lamp examination confirming true depigmentation with sharply demarcated borders and retained pigmented islands Molecular genetic testing for KIT and SNAI2 mutations Audiological assessment to exclude Waardenburg syndrome when clinical overlap exists Ophthalmological review for iris pigmentary changes and dystopia canthorum Skin biopsy showing absent or reduced melanocytes in depigmented areas (rarely required) Detailed three-generation family pedigree Autosomal dominant congenital leukoderma caused chiefly by loss-of-function mutations in the KIT proto-oncogene, with a minority due to SLUG/SNAI2 defects impairing melanoblast migration from the neural crest. The hallmark is a stable white forelock (poliosis) present at birth in most affected individuals, overlying a triangular or diamond-shaped depigmented patch of the central forehead. Depigmented patches favour the central forehead, ventral trunk, and mid-extremities, while the hands, feet, back, and a median dorsal strip are characteristically spared. Islands of normally pigmented or hyperpigmented macules lie within and at the borders of the amelanotic patches, a feature that helps distinguish piebaldism from vitiligo. Lesions are congenital and remain remarkably stable in relative size and distribution throughout life, expanding only in proportion to body growth. Histology of affected skin shows an absence or marked reduction of melanocytes, mirroring the failed migration and survival of melanoblasts. Overlap with Waardenburg syndrome should be considered; the presence of sensorineural deafness, dystopia canthorum, or heterochromia iridis points away from isolated piebaldism. Genotype-phenotype correlation exists: mutations affecting the KIT tyrosine kinase domain tend to produce more extensive depigmentation than those in the extracellular ligand-binding region. Associated sensorineural hearing loss suggesting Waardenburg syndrome rather than isolated piebaldism Progressive or acquired depigmentation, which argues against a congenital stable leukoderma Broad nasal root, dystopia canthorum, or heterochromia indicating a syndromic diagnosis Features of Hirschsprung disease or constipation raising suspicion of Waardenburg type IV Mislabelling stable congenital piebaldism as vitiligo, leading to inappropriate immunomodulatory therapy Overlooking the pigmented islands within depigmented patches, a clue that distinguishes piebaldism from vitiligo Failing to screen for deafness and other Waardenburg features when a white forelock is present Attributing depigmentation to trauma or inflammation despite its clearly congenital onset Assuming amelanotic skin is protected from sunburn and neglecting rigorous photoprotection advice Piebaldism arises from defective embryonic development, migration, proliferation, and survival of melanoblasts derived from the neural crest. The commonest cause is a heterozygous loss-of-function mutation in the KIT gene, which encodes the transmembrane tyrosine kinase receptor for stem cell factor (KIT ligand); reduced KIT signalling impairs the dorsolateral migration and survival of melanoblasts destined for the epidermis, so the affected skin regions never acquire melanocytes. Haploinsufficiency accounts for the dominant inheritance and the correlation between mutation severity and the extent of depigmentation. A smaller subset results from mutations in SNAI2 (SLUG), a transcription factor downstream of KIT signalling. Because the ventral and central regions are the last to be reached by migrating melanoblasts, they are preferentially left amelanotic, explaining the characteristic pattern of sparing of the extremities' extremes and a mid-dorsal strip. Piebaldism is a benign, non-progressive condition with a normal life expectancy, and the depigmented areas remain cosmetically stable throughout life. The principal long-term concern is photoprotection of amelanotic skin, since these areas lack the melanin defence against ultraviolet-induced damage.

positional obstruction to critical airway compromise requiring surgical intervention Severe or worsening obstructive apnoea with desaturation or cor pulmonale Failure to thrive from inability to feed safely Cyanotic episodes or respiratory distress unrelieved by positioning Recurrent aspiration Signs of a wider syndrome requiring urgent multisystem evaluation Treating it as a fixed syndrome rather than recognising an initiating sequence Failing to look for an underlying syndrome, especially Stickler Underestimating airway obstruction because the infant appears settled when prone Overlooking feeding failure as a marker of significant obstruction Delaying escalation when non-surgical measures are insufficient The sequence is initiated by early hypoplasia of the mandible. The small jaw leaves insufficient room in the oral cavity, so the tongue is displaced posteriorly and superiorly (glossoptosis), which in turn obstructs the airway and, during palatal shelf fusion, mechanically prevents the shelves meeting, producing the characteristic wide U-shaped cleft palate. The initiating mandibular deficiency may result from intrinsic developmental disturbance of the first branchial arch or from extrinsic constraint such as oligohydramnios limiting jaw movement in utero. Because a single early anomaly drives the downstream features, the condition is classified as a malformation sequence, and it may occur in isolation or as a component of a recognisable syndrome. Isolated Robin sequence generally has a favourable outlook as mandibular growth improves the airway over time, whereas syndromic cases and those with severe obstruction carry greater morbidity and depend on the associated condition.

Pigmentary glaucoma — pigment dispersion glaucoma, pigmentary dispersion syndrome, pigment dispersion syndrome, PDS Pseudoexfoliation glaucoma Primary open-angle glaucoma Pigment released by uveitis or intraocular tumour Post-traumatic angle recession glaucoma Pigment dispersion associated with a malpositioned intraocular lens Pigment liberation after intraocular surgery or laser Gonioscopy to document dense homogeneous trabecular pigmentation and iris configuration Slit-lamp examination for a Krukenberg spindle and iris transillumination defects Applanation tonometry, ideally with post-exercise or post-dilation testing to detect pigment-release pressure spikes OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer to assess for glaucomatous damage Automated perimetry to detect and monitor field loss Anterior segment imaging to demonstrate the concave peripheral iris where needed Results from liberation of pigment granules from the posterior iris that deposit throughout the anterior segment and clog the trabecular meshwork, raising intraocular pressure Typically affects young, myopic adults, more often men, and may be asymptomatic or cause blurring and haloes after exercise or pupillary dilation A vertical spindle-shaped deposit of pigment on the corneal endothelium (Krukenberg spindle) is a classic sign Mid-peripheral radial iris transillumination defects reflect loss of pigment where the iris chafes against the lens zonules Gonioscopy shows a heavily and homogeneously pigmented trabecular meshwork, often with a concave (posteriorly bowed) peripheral iris Reverse pupillary block, in which the iris is pushed back against the zonules, is thought to drive the pigment-releasing chafing Treatment lowers pressure with topical agents; laser peripheral iridotomy may flatten the concave iris and reduce chafing, and laser trabeculoplasty can be effective though it may cause pressure spikes in heavily pigmented angles Not all patients with pigment dispersion develop glaucoma; the term pigmentary glaucoma applies once pressure-related optic-nerve damage occurs Marked pressure spikes after exercise or pupil dilation that can cause acute symptomatic rises Established optic-nerve cupping and field loss in a young myopic patient Very high trabecular pigmentation predisposing to exaggerated pressure spikes after laser trabeculoplasty Progressive damage despite apparently modest baseline pressure Assuming pigment dispersion syndrome always progresses to glaucoma or, conversely, discharging patients who need long-term surveillance Missing exercise- or dilation-induced pressure spikes on isolated clinic readings Applying high-energy laser trabeculoplasty to a heavily pigmented meshwork and provoking a pressure spike Confusing dense trabecular pigment with pseudoexfoliation material Overlooking the diagnosis in a young myope with unexplained ocular hypertension In pigment dispersion the peripheral iris bows posteriorly and rubs against the anterior lens zonular bundles during physiological pupil movement, mechanically stripping melanin granules from the posterior iris pigment epithelium. A postulated reverse pupillary block, where aqueous is trapped in the anterior chamber and presses the iris backward, exaggerates this iridozonular contact. Liberated pigment circulates in the aqueous and is deposited on the corneal endothelium as a Krukenberg spindle, on the lens and iris, and within the trabecular meshwork. Accumulated pigment and associated trabecular cell dysfunction reduce aqueous outflow, and in susceptible eyes the resulting rise in intraocular pressure produces glaucomatous optic-nerve damage. Many patients with pigment dispersion syndrome never develop glaucoma, and pigment release often lessens with age as the iris becomes less concave, but those who progress to pigmentary glaucoma can have aggressive pressure elevation in young eyes requiring lifelong monitoring and treatment.

pigmentary glaucoma — pigment dispersion glaucoma, pigmentary dispersion syndrome with glaucoma primary open-angle glaucoma pseudoexfoliation glaucoma uveitic glaucoma with pigment dispersion post-traumatic pigment dispersion pigment dispersion from a malpositioned posterior chamber intraocular lens melanomalytic glaucoma from a pigmented iris or ciliary body tumour iris melanoma with secondary dispersion gonioscopy demonstrating dense homogeneous trabecular pigment and a concave peripheral iris slit-lamp examination for Krukenberg spindle and iris transillumination defects anterior segment optical coherence tomography or ultrasound biomicroscopy showing posterior iris bowing diurnal intraocular pressure phasing to capture exercise or dilatation-related spikes standard automated perimetry for glaucomatous field loss optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer and ganglion cell complex optic disc stereo-photography for baseline documentation Typically affects young, myopic Caucasian men in the third to fourth decade, in contrast to the older demographic of primary open-angle glaucoma. The classic triad is Krukenberg spindle (vertical pigment deposition on corneal endothelium), mid-peripheral iris transillumination defects in a radial spoke-like pattern, and heavy homogeneous trabecular meshwork pigmentation. Reverse pupillary block, in which the peripheral iris bows posteriorly against the zonules and lens, is the leading mechanism for iridozonular chafing and pigment liberation. Exercise or pupillary dilatation can precipitate a shower of pigment with an acute intraocular pressure spike, sometimes with corneal oedema and blurring. Not all patients with pigment dispersion syndrome develop glaucoma; conversion to glaucoma occurs in a minority over time and warrants ongoing surveillance. Laser peripheral iridotomy aims to flatten the iris and abolish reverse pupillary block, though evidence for preventing progression is inconsistent. Pilocarpine addresses both pressure and iris configuration by pulling the iris away from the zonules, but is poorly tolerated in young myopes because of induced myopia and retinal detachment risk. Laser trabeculoplasty is often effective given the heavily pigmented meshwork, but lower energy is prudent to avoid a marked post-laser pressure spike. acute intraocular pressure spike after exercise or pupil dilatation with corneal oedema and haloes progressive optic disc cupping or nerve fibre layer thinning despite treatment markedly asymmetric pressures or pigmentation suggesting an alternative intraocular tumour very high presenting pressures in a young myope at risk of rapid field loss Attributing a young myope's raised pressure to primary open-angle glaucoma and missing the diagnostic anterior segment signs. Prescribing standard-energy laser trabeculoplasty without anticipating an exaggerated post-laser pressure spike in a heavily pigmented meshwork. Overlooking exercise-induced pressure spikes because a single clinic reading is normal. Using pilocarpine in a young high myope without counselling about induced myopia and the risk of retinal detachment. Assuming all pigment dispersion syndrome will convert to glaucoma and over-treating patients who only require monitoring. Mechanical rubbing of the posterior iris pigment epithelium against the anterior packets of lens zonules liberates melanin granules into the aqueous. A posteriorly bowed, concave peripheral iris configuration, driven by reverse pupillary block where aqueous is trapped in the anterior chamber and raises its pressure relative to the posterior chamber, brings the iris into contact with the zonules during physiological pupil movement. Dispersed pigment is carried by aqueous convection currents and deposited throughout the anterior segment, most importantly within the trabecular meshwork. Phagocytosis of pigment by trabecular endothelial cells, subsequent cell death, meshwork collapse and sclerosis progressively reduce aqueous outflow facility, elevating intraocular pressure and producing a glaucomatous optic neuropathy identical in appearance to primary open-angle glaucoma. With early detection and pressure control the long-term visual prognosis is generally good, and pigment dispersion tends to diminish with age as the lens enlarges and the iris configuration flattens. Untreated or poorly controlled disease can progress to significant glaucomatous field loss and irreversible visual impairment.

Pigmented purpuric dermatosis — capillaritis, Schamberg disease, progressive pigmentary purpura, purpura pigmentosa chronica Leukocytoclastic (small-vessel) vasculitis Stasis dermatitis with haemosiderin deposition Thrombocytopenic or coagulopathic purpura Early mycosis fungoides (pigmented purpura-like) Drug-induced purpura Angioma serpiginosum Clinical assessment with dermoscopy showing coppery-red background and pigment dots Full blood count and platelet count to exclude thrombocytopenia Coagulation screen where a bleeding disorder is suspected Skin biopsy in atypical, persistent, or lichenoid cases to confirm capillaritis and exclude vasculitis or lymphoma Assessment of venous insufficiency in the lower limbs Medication review for a possible drug trigger A group of chronic benign eruptions caused by capillaritis, producing petechiae and golden-brown ('cayenne pepper') pigmentation, most often on the lower legs Schamberg disease is the commonest variant; other forms include Majocchi (annular telangiectodes), lichen aureus, Gougerot-Blum (lichenoid), and eczematoid-like (Doucas-Kapetanakis) types Lesions are typically asymptomatic or mildly itchy and are not associated with thrombocytopenia or a coagulation defect The characteristic colour reflects extravasated red cells and haemosiderin deposition in the dermis Contributing factors include venous hypertension, gravitational dependency, exercise, and sometimes drugs Persistent, unusually widespread, or lichenoid variants occasionally overlap with, or should prompt exclusion of, early mycosis fungoides It is a cosmetic and chronic nuisance rather than a systemic threat, and pigmentation resolves slowly if at all Palpable purpura or systemic symptoms suggesting true vasculitis rather than capillaritis Thrombocytopenia or abnormal clotting indicating a haematological cause of purpura Persistent, widespread, or lichenoid patches raising concern for early cutaneous T-cell lymphoma Progressive change in a long-standing lesion warranting biopsy Mistaking benign capillaritis for a bleeding disorder and ordering unnecessary extensive haematological workup, or conversely missing genuine thrombocytopenia Overlooking an evolving mycosis fungoides in persistent or lichenoid variants Confusing it with palpable-purpura vasculitis Ignoring contributory venous hypertension and aggravating drugs Pigmented purpuric dermatoses arise from a lymphocytic capillaritis: inflammation of dermal capillaries increases vascular permeability and fragility, allowing red cells to leak into the papillary dermis. Breakdown of extravasated erythrocytes leaves haemosiderin deposits in dermal macrophages, producing the characteristic golden-brown discolouration overlying fresh pinpoint (cayenne-pepper) petechiae. Platelet counts and coagulation are normal, so the purpura reflects vessel-wall inflammation rather than a bleeding diathesis. Venous hypertension, gravitational stasis, physical activity, and occasionally drug hypersensitivity contribute to the capillary damage. Pigmented purpuric dermatosis is benign and chronic, often persisting or recurring over months to years; pigmentation fades slowly and treatment is largely cosmetic, but atypical persistent disease occasionally warrants monitoring for mycosis fungoides.

Pigmented villonodular synovitis (tenosynovial giant cell tumour) — PVNS, tenosynovial giant cell tumour, TGCT, diffuse-type giant cell tumour, giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath Synovial deposition MRI showing haemosiderin-laden synovium with low signal and blooming on gradient-echo sequences Plain radiographs to assess soft-tissue swelling and juxta-articular bony erosions Joint aspiration revealing serosanguineous or brown haemosiderin-stained fluid Histological confirmation from synovial biopsy or resected tissue Assessment of CSF1 overexpression where targeted therapy is shows haemosiderin-laden proliferative synovium with characteristic low signal and 'blooming' artefact on gradient-echo sequences Driven in most cases by overexpression of colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF1), providing the rationale for CSF1R-directed therapy in advanced or unresectable disease Primary treatment is surgical synovectomy, with radiotherapy or CSF1R inhibition considered for diffuse, recurrent or inoperable disease Rapid growth or atypical features raising concern for malignant transformation or sarcoma Aggressive bony erosion and joint destruction in diffuse disease Repeated recurrence after synovectomy indicating incomplete disease control Neurovascular compromise from an expanding mass Mistaking recurrent haemarthrosis for injury or a bleeding disorder and delaying diagnosis Incomplete synovectomy in diffuse disease leading to recurrence Overlooking the diagnosis when gradient-echo MRI sequences are not obtained Confusing it with synovial chondromatosis or a malignant soft-tissue tumour Pigmented villonodular synovitis is a neoplastic proliferation of the synovial lining producing villous and nodular thickening with abundant haemosiderin-laden macrophages, multinucleated giant cells and foam cells. The majority of cases are driven by a translocation involving the colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF1) gene, leading to overexpression of CSF1; a small population of neoplastic cells recruits large numbers of non-neoplastic CSF1-receptor-bearing inflammatory cells that make up the bulk of the lesion (a 'landscape' effect). Recurrent microhaemorrhage within the hypervascular synovium deposits haemosiderin, giving the tissue its pigmented appearance and the characteristic MRI blooming. The proliferative synovium erodes cartilage and subchondral bone, causing progressive joint destruction, particularly in the diffuse form. The localised form has a good outcome after complete excision, whereas the diffuse form recurs frequently and can cause progressive joint destruction; malignant transformation is rare, and CSF1R-directed therapy has improved options for advanced disease.

pilar cyst — trichilemmal cyst, isthmus-catagen cyst, wen epidermoid cyst lipoma proliferating trichilemmal tumour dermoid cyst cylindroma scalp metastasis or adnexal tumour osteoma cutis clinical examination noting absence of a punctum ultrasonography showing a well-defined cystic scalp lesion, sometimes with calcification histopathology confirming trichilemmal keratinisation without a granular layer imaging and wide histological sampling if a proliferating trichilemmal tumour is suspected family history assessment given autosomal dominant inheritance Presents as a smooth, firm, mobile subcutaneous nodule, with the great majority occurring on the scalp. Unlike epidermoid cysts, pilar cysts lack a central punctum and characteristically shell out cleanly and intact at surgery. They are frequently multiple and show an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern in many affected families. The lining shows trichilemmal keratinisation without a granular layer, abruptly producing dense homogeneous keratin, often with calcification. Overlying hair may be thinned or lost due to pressure, but the lesions themselves are asymptomatic unless inflamed or ruptured. A proliferating trichilemmal tumour can arise within a long-standing cyst, presenting as a rapidly enlarging exophytic scalp mass. Complete excision with the intact capsule is curative and technically easier than for epidermoid cysts. Rarely, malignant proliferating trichilemmal tumours occur and may recur locally or metastasise, warranting histological review of atypical lesions. rapid enlargement or exophytic ulcerated growth suggesting a proliferating or malignant trichilemmal tumour fixation to deeper tissues or irregular infiltrative margins recurrence after apparently complete excision a solitary firm scalp nodule with atypical features that could represent metastasis Assuming a rapidly growing scalp cyst is simply inflamed and missing a proliferating or malignant trichilemmal tumour. Confusing a pilar cyst with an epidermoid cyst and expecting a punctum that is absent. Rupturing the fragile capsule during excision, complicating complete removal. Failing to submit an atypical or recurrent lesion for histopathology. Pilar cysts derive from the outer root sheath of the hair follicle at the level of the isthmus, and the lining epithelium undergoes trichilemmal keratinisation in which cells enlarge and keratinise abruptly without forming a granular layer. The cavity fills with compact, homogeneous keratin that frequently calcifies. A hereditary autosomal dominant tendency underlies the common multiplicity and scalp predilection, and clonal proliferation of the cyst lining can give rise to a proliferating trichilemmal tumour. Malignant change is rare but recognised, characterised by cytological atypia, infiltrative growth and occasionally metastatic potential. Pilar cysts are benign and excision of the intact capsule is curative with a low recurrence rate. Proliferating trichilemmal tumours are usually benign but may recur locally, and the rare malignant variant can metastasise.
