is supportive with gentle hair care and avoidance of trauma, and identifying any underlying syndrome is essential, since some acquired forms improve once the trigger resolves An infant with pili torti and neurodevelopmental regression suggesting Menkes disease Associated sensorineural hearing loss pointing to Bjornstad syndrome Features of an underlying ectodermal or systemic syndrome requiring urgent evaluation Missing Menkes disease in an infant and so delaying diagnosis of a serious metabolic disorder Overlooking associated deafness or ectodermal features Confusing pili torti with other hair-shaft defects without confirmatory microscopy Attributing brittle hair to hair care alone without examining the shaft Pili torti is a structural abnormality in which the hair shaft is flattened and rotated on its own axis, producing recurrent twists that create points of weakness and increased fragility. It may be a primary genetic defect of hair-shaft formation or occur as part of syndromes affecting ectodermal structures or metabolism; in Menkes disease deficient copper-dependent enzyme activity impairs disulphide bonding and keratin cross-linking. Acquired forms can follow inflammation, scarring or drug exposure. The twisting weakens the shaft so that hair breaks readily. Isolated classic pili torti often improves after puberty, but the outlook depends heavily on any associated syndrome; Menkes disease carries a poor neurological prognosis, whereas isolated or acquired forms may resolve when the cause is removed.

pilocytic astrocytoma — juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma, JPA medulloblastoma ependymoma haemangioblastoma ganglioglioma diffuse midline or paediatric-type diffuse low-grade glioma pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumour contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain showing cyst with enhancing mural nodule MRI of the whole neuraxis when dissemination is suspected surgical resection or biopsy for histological confirmation BRAF fusion and BRAF V600E molecular testing assessment for neurofibromatosis type 1, especially with optic pathway lesions formal ophthalmological and visual field assessment for optic pathway tumours endocrine evaluation for hypothalamic or chiasmatic involvement The commonest glioma of childhood and a CNS WHO grade 1 tumour, most often arising in the cerebellum, optic pathway, hypothalamus and brainstem. The characteristic cerebellar appearance is a cyst with an avidly enhancing mural nodule, producing signs of raised intracranial pressure and ataxia. Optic pathway pilocytic astrocytoma is strongly associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 and may present with visual loss or proptosis. Histology is biphasic with compact piloid areas containing Rosenthal fibres alternating with loose microcystic zones and eosinophilic granular bodies. The vast majority are driven by activation of the MAPK pathway, most commonly a KIAA1549-BRAF fusion, with BRAF V600E mutations in a minority. Gross total resection is often curative and may be the only treatment required for accessible cerebellar tumours. For unresectable, progressive or NF1-associated disease, MAPK-pathway-targeted agents such as MEK inhibitors are increasingly used. Contrast enhancement and even leptomeningeal dissemination do not imply aggressive behaviour, and malignant transformation is rare. obstructive hydrocephalus with headache, vomiting and papilloedema rapidly progressive visual loss in an optic pathway tumour brainstem involvement causing cranial nerve or long-tract signs new or worsening deficit suggesting unusual progression interpreting strong contrast enhancement as evidence of malignancy regarding leptomeningeal spread as inevitably aggressive overtreating an indolent grade 1 tumour with aggressive radiotherapy in a child missing an underlying diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 1 confusing piloid gliosis adjacent to other lesions with true neoplasm on small biopsies Pilocytic astrocytoma is a circumscribed, slow-growing glioma whose biology is dominated by constitutive activation of the RAS-MAPK signalling pathway. The characteristic event is a tandem duplication generating a KIAA1549-BRAF fusion gene that produces a constitutively active BRAF kinase; alternative drivers include BRAF V600E point mutations, other BRAF or RAF fusions, and, in the context of neurofibromatosis type 1, biallelic NF1 loss. Sustained MAPK signalling promotes a bland, biphasic astrocytic proliferation with piloid bipolar cells, Rosenthal fibres and eosinophilic granular bodies, together with glomeruloid vascular proliferation that accounts for the strong contrast enhancement. Despite a single dominant oncogenic pathway, the low proliferative index and tendency towards senescence explain the indolent, often self-limiting course. The outlook is excellent, with long-term survival and frequent cure after complete resection of accessible tumours; deep-seated or unresectable lesions may follow a more protracted course but malignant transformation is uncommon.

Pilomatricoma — pilomatrixoma, calcifying epithelioma of Malherbe, benign calcifying epithelioma Epidermoid or dermoid cyst Calcified lymph node Osteoma cutis Foreign-body granuloma Basal cell carcinoma (when ulcerated or facial) Pilomatrix carcinoma (malignant counterpart) Clinical examination for the tent sign and stony consistency Skin ultrasound showing a well-defined nodule with internal calcification and acoustic shadowing Excisional biopsy with histopathology demonstrating shadow cells and calcification Immunohistochemistry for nuclear beta-catenin in equivocal cases Evaluation for associated syndromes when lesions are multiple (e.g. myotonic dystrophy) A benign tumour of hair-follicle matrix differentiation, most common in children and young adults on the head, neck, and upper limbs Presents as a firm, sometimes stony-hard, mobile subcutaneous nodule, occasionally with a bluish or reddish hue through the overlying skin Stretching the overlying skin can reveal multiple facets and angulated edges, the so-called tent sign, reflecting internal calcification Driven by activating mutations of CTNNB1 leading to beta-catenin stabilisation and aberrant Wnt signalling in the follicular matrix Histology shows basaloid matrix cells maturing into anucleate eosinophilic shadow (ghost) cells, with dystrophic calcification and often foreign-body giant-cell reaction and ossification Usually solitary; multiple lesions may prompt consideration of associations such as myotonic dystrophy and other syndromes Treatment is simple surgical excision, which is curative; malignant transformation (pilomatrix carcinoma) is rare Rapid enlargement, ulceration, or infiltrative growth suggesting pilomatrix carcinoma Multiple pilomatricomas prompting evaluation for an underlying syndrome Recurrence after excision raising concern for incomplete removal or malignancy Mistaking the firm nodule for an epidermoid cyst or calcified lymph node and mismanaging it Failing to recognise the tent sign and characteristic clinical features Overlooking multiple lesions that may signal an associated systemic disorder Dismissing atypical rapidly growing lesions that could represent malignant transformation Pilomatricoma is a benign neoplasm derived from the matrix cells of the hair follicle. Activating mutations in CTNNB1, the gene encoding beta-catenin, prevent its normal degradation, so stabilised beta-catenin accumulates and constitutively activates Wnt signalling, driving proliferation of follicular matrix cells. These basaloid cells progressively lose their nuclei as they differentiate, producing sheets of eosinophilic anucleate shadow (ghost) cells. Over time the lesion undergoes dystrophic calcification and sometimes true ossification, with a surrounding foreign-body giant-cell and granulomatous reaction, accounting for the characteristic firm to stony consistency. Pilomatricoma is benign with an excellent prognosis; complete excision is curative and recurrence is uncommon. The rare malignant counterpart, pilomatrix carcinoma, can recur locally and occasionally metastasise.

Pilonidal disease — pilonidal sinus, pilonidal cyst, sacrococcygeal pilonidal disease, jeep disease Perianal or anal fistula tracking towards the natal cleft Hidradenitis suppurativa Furuncle, carbuncle, or infected sebaceous cyst Sacrococcygeal dermoid or teratoma Crohn's perianal disease Presacral sinus or osteomyelitis with cutaneous discharge Clinical inspection of the natal cleft for midline pits and secondary tracks Examination under anaesthesia with probing for complex or recurrent disease MRI in atypical, recurrent, or extensive disease to map tracks Assessment for Crohn's disease when perianal features are atypical Swab and culture of discharge if secondary infection is suspected Biopsy of chronic, non-healing lesions to exclude malignant change An acquired condition of the natal cleft in which loose hairs are driven into the skin, provoking a foreign-body reaction and forming midline pits and a chronic sinus Typically affects young, hirsute men, and is associated with a deep natal cleft, sedentary occupations, obesity, and poor local hygiene May present acutely as a painful fluctuant abscess or chronically with intermittent discharge and one or more midline pits, often with lateral secondary openings Characteristic midline pits in the intergluteal cleft, sometimes containing protruding hair tufts, are the diagnostic hallmark Acute abscesses are treated by incision and drainage placed off the midline; definitive treatment of the sinus follows once inflammation settles Definitive options range from minimally invasive (pit picking, phenol or laser ablation) to excision with off-midline or flap closure (Karydakis, Bascom cleft-lift, Limberg flap), which flatten the cleft and reduce recurrence Hair removal, hygiene, and keeping the cleft clean and dry reduce recurrence after treatment A chronic non-healing sinus with induration or a mass suggesting malignant (squamous) change Extensive or atypical tracks suggesting Crohn's disease or hidradenitis suppurativa Rapidly spreading sepsis in an immunocompromised or diabetic patient A fistulous communication with the anal canal Closing wounds in the midline, which heal poorly and recur Neglecting hair removal and hygiene advice after surgery Mistaking a pilonidal track for an anal fistula, or the reverse Overlooking rare malignant transformation in long-standing disease Pilonidal disease is now regarded as acquired rather than congenital. Friction and movement in the natal cleft, together with a hair-friendly microenvironment, allow shed hairs to penetrate the skin through enlarged follicles or midline pits. The embedded hair acts as a foreign body, provoking chronic inflammation, granulation, and a sinus lined by granulation tissue that discharges and can abscess. A deep cleft, hirsutism, obesity, and prolonged sitting perpetuate the cycle, and midline wounds that heal poorly predispose to recurrence. Pilonidal disease is prone to recurrence, particularly with midline wounds and persistent risk factors; off-midline closure techniques and diligent hair control substantially improve long-term healing.

pilonidal disease Neglecting hair control and hygiene advice, allowing recurrence Failing to biopsy a chronic non-healing sinus Pilonidal disease is now regarded as an acquired condition in which loose hairs are driven into the skin of the natal cleft, provoking a foreign-body inflammatory reaction and forming midline pits. The pits become epithelialised sinuses that trap further hair and debris, leading to chronic infection, abscess formation, and secondary tracks extending laterally. Friction, sweating, deep natal clefts, hirsutism, and prolonged sitting promote hair insertion and infection. Recurrent cycles of infection and incomplete healing perpetuate the disease. Acute abscesses settle with drainage, but pilonidal disease is prone to recurrence. Definitive excisional and flap-based procedures improve healing and lower recurrence, and long-term outcome is strongly influenced by ongoing hair control and hygiene.

transverse over-curvature of the plate that increases from proximal to distal, pinching the underlying soft tissue The tightening curve traps and compresses the nail bed and distal tissue, which is underlying phalanx, ill-fitting footwear, osteoarthritis, and some medications A dorsal bony spur or widening of the distal phalanx often underlies acquired cases and is best shown on radiograph As the curve deepens the lateral edges may roll inward, sometimes producing subungual hyperkeratosis and secondary changes Management ranges from conservative measures such as bracing and orthonyxia to surgical correction of the matrix or underlying bone in refractory cases Severe unremitting pain interfering with walking and function Secondary infection or ulceration of the pinched soft tissue Radiographic bony resorption or an aggressive-looking underlying lesion Rapidly progressive deformity or an atypical single-nail change suggesting a tumour Treating the nail as a simple ingrowing toenail and missing the underlying over-curvature Omitting a radiograph and overlooking a correctable bony spur Expecting conservative bracing alone to cure severe long-standing deformity Failing to address footwear and biomechanical contributors, leading to recurrence Pincer nail results from progressive transverse over-curvature of the nail plate, so that the two lateral edges curl toward each other and increasingly compress the nail bed and pulp as the nail grows distally. In many acquired cases an underlying bony change of the distal phalanx, such as a dorsal osteophyte or lateral widening, alters the shape of the tissue on which the matrix sits and forces the plate to curl. Hereditary forms reflect an intrinsic tendency of the matrix to produce an over-curved plate. The pinching action distorts and can even resorb the underlying soft tissue and bone, and the trapped nail bed generates pain and predisposes to secondary ingrowing and hyperkeratosis. Conservative bracing can relieve symptoms and partially flatten the curve but tends to relapse when discontinued, whereas surgery addressing the matrix or underlying bony spur offers the most durable correction in refractory, painful cases.

obstructive hydrocephalus with rapidly rising intracranial pressure Progressive dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) signs and deteriorating consciousness Evidence of CSF dissemination along the neuraxis test germline RB1 in a child with a pineal embryonal tumour Attributing early upgaze failure to a benign cause and missing tectal compression Understaging by omitting craniospinal imaging and CSF cytology Pineoblastoma is a poorly differentiated embryonal tumour arising from the parenchymal cells of the pineal gland. It shows primitive small round cells with high proliferative activity and a propensity to seed the cerebrospinal fluid pathways. A proportion of cases arise on a background of germline predisposition, most notably biallelic RB1 loss (the basis of trilateral retinoblastoma, in which a pineal or suprasellar tumour accompanies bilateral hereditary retinoblastoma) and germline DICER1 mutations, which impair microRNA processing. Its midline position adjacent to the tectum and cerebral aqueduct means that even modest growth readily obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow and compresses the dorsal midbrain. Prognosis is guarded and worse than for lower-grade pineal parenchymal tumours, being poorest in infants, those with metastatic disease, and germline RB1-associated trilateral retinoblastoma. Combined surgery, craniospinal radiotherapy and chemotherapy can achieve durable control in older children with localised disease, but survivors are at risk of significant treatment-related late effects.

Pinguecula — pingueculum, conjunctival pinguecula Pterygium (fibrovascular growth crossing the limbus onto cornea) Conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia / ocular surface squamous neoplasia Conjunctival dermoid or dermolipoma Amyloid deposition of the conjunctiva Bitot spot of vitamin A deficiency Conjunctival concretions Limbal nodule of phlyctenular or nodular scleritis Slit-lamp biomicroscopy to characterise the lesion and confirm the cornea is spared Documentation with anterior-segment photography for serial comparison Assessment of tear film and ocular surface (tear break-up time, staining) for associated dryness Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography where depth or atypia needs clarification Excisional or incisional biopsy with histopathology if neoplasia is suspected Corneal topography if a coexisting pterygium is inducing astigmatism A pinguecula is a yellowish-white, slightly raised amorphous deposit on the bulbar conjunctiva, characteristically at the nasal (and later temporal) limbus within the interpalpebral fissure but, unlike a pterygium, it does NOT encroach onto the cornea. It represents actinic (ultraviolet) elastotic degeneration of the subepithelial conjunctival stroma; chronic sun, wind and dust exposure are the principal drivers, so it is commoner in outdoor workers and low-latitude populations. The great majority are asymptomatic and require only reassurance; lubricants suffice for mild irritation or foreign-body sensation. Pingueculitis denotes episodic inflammation with localised hyperaemia and swelling, often after intense ultraviolet exposure or ocular-surface dryness, and is managed with lubricants and a short course of a mild topical anti-inflammatory. Photoprotection with wrap-around sunglasses and a broad-brimmed hat is the key preventive and progression-limiting measure. Excision is reserved for cosmetic concern, recurrent pingueculitis, interference with contact-lens wear, or diagnostic uncertainty; surgery carries a risk of scarring and recurrence. A lesion that grows atypically, becomes nodular, develops feeder vessels, pigmentation or leukoplakia, or does not respect the limbus should raise suspicion of ocular surface squamous neoplasia rather than a benign pinguecula. Pinguecula and pterygium share the same actinic aetiology and frequently coexist; a pinguecula may be a precursor stage but the two are distinguished by corneal involvement. Progressive growth, nodularity, feeder vessels, pigmentation or leukoplakia suggesting ocular surface squamous neoplasia or melanoma Encroachment onto the cornea indicating pterygium rather than pinguecula Persistent or recurrent inflammation unresponsive to lubricants and photoprotection Rapid change in size, colour or vascularity of a previously stable lesion Mistaking an atypical conjunctival neoplasm for a benign pinguecula and delaying biopsy Confusing a pinguecula with an early pterygium; the defining feature is whether the lesion crosses the limbus onto the cornea Over-treating an asymptomatic lesion with prolonged topical steroids, risking raised intraocular pressure and cataract Attributing all interpalpebral irritation to the pinguecula while overlooking coexisting dry eye disease Assuming excision is curative without warning the patient about recurrence and conjunctival scarring Chronic ultraviolet and environmental (wind, dust, dryness) exposure induces actinic damage to the bulbar conjunctival stroma within the interpalpebral zone, where light is focused nasally by the anterior segment. The result is elastotic degeneration: fragmentation and abnormal accumulation of elastin-like fibrillar material in the substantia propria, with hyalinisation of collagen, secondary calcification in some lesions, and a thinned or occasionally thickened overlying epithelium. Because the process is confined to the subepithelial conjunctiva and does not cross the limbal barrier, the cornea is spared, distinguishing it from pterygium. An entirely benign degenerative lesion with an excellent prognosis; most remain stable and asymptomatic for life. Even after excision for cosmesis or recurrent pingueculitis the outlook is good, though scarring and recurrence are recognised.

Pinta — Treponema carateum, carate, azul, mal del pinto Vitiligo (for late achromic lesions) Pityriasis versicolor and other superficial mycoses Other endemic treponematoses (yaws, bejel) Leprosy (hypopigmented patches) Post-inflammatory dyspigmentation Psoriasis or chronic eczema (for scaly plaques) Dark-field microscopy of scrapings from active lesions for spirochaetes Non-treponemal serology (e.g. RPR/VDRL) for activity and follow-up Treponemal serology (e.g. TPPA/TPHA) for confirmation Skin biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain PCR of lesion material where available Assessment of close contacts in endemic communities Pinta is a chronic non-venereal treponematosis caused by Treponema carateum and is confined to the skin, occurring in remote rural areas of Central and South America Transmission is by prolonged direct skin-to-skin contact with lesion material, favoured by crowding and poor hygiene; it is not sexually transmitted Unlike the other endemic treponematoses, pinta affects only the skin and does not involve bone, viscera or the nervous system The primary lesion is an erythematous scaly papule or plaque that slowly enlarges, usually on exposed limbs Secondary lesions (pintids) are disseminated scaly patches that undergo striking colour changes, becoming blue, violet, brown then depigmented Late pinta is characterised by symmetrical achromic (depigmented) and atrophic patches that resemble vitiligo and are cosmetically disfiguring Diagnosis uses dark-field microscopy and treponemal/non-treponemal serology (indistinguishable from syphilis); treatment for the endemic treponematoses is benzathine penicillin Extensive disfiguring depigmentation causing psychosocial harm Diagnostic uncertainty with vitiligo or leprosy delaying treatment Positive syphilis serology raising confusion about venereal infection Persistence or spread of active lesions despite treatment Mistaking late depigmented lesions for vitiligo and missing a treatable infection Interpreting positive treponemal serology as venereal syphilis Expecting depigmented skin to re-pigment fully after treatment Failing to treat contacts and interrupt transmission Confusing pinta with other endemic treponematoses without regional context Treponema carateum enters through breaks in the skin during prolonged close contact. It multiplies locally to form the primary lesion and then, over months, produces disseminated secondary skin lesions (pintids) through local and lymphatic spread. The immune response and disturbance of melanocytes produce the characteristic sequence of dyschromic changes, progressing from hyperpigmentation to permanent depigmentation and skin atrophy in late disease. Because the organism does not disseminate to deep tissues, pinta remains a purely cutaneous disease throughout its course. Early and secondary pinta respond fully to penicillin, but late achromic and atrophic skin changes are often permanent and cosmetically disfiguring even after cure; the disease carries no systemic morbidity.

piriformis syndrome — deep gluteal syndrome, extraspinal sciatic entrapment lumbosacral radiculopathy from disc herniation or stenosis sacroiliac joint dysfunction hip osteoarthritis or labral pathology greater trochanteric pain syndrome ischiofemoral impingement proximal hamstring tendinopathy gluteal or pelvic neoplasm compressing the sciatic nerve lumbosacral spine magnetic resonance imaging to exclude radiculopathy magnetic resonance neurography of the lumbosacral plexus and sciatic nerve electromyography and nerve conduction studies including H-reflex, with FAIR-position testing pelvic and hip imaging to exclude articular or mass lesions diagnostic ultrasound-guided perisciatic or intramuscular injection dynamic ultrasound of the deep gluteal space inflammatory and metabolic screen when a systemic cause is considered Extraspinal compression or irritation of the sciatic nerve within the deep gluteal space, classically as it relates to the piriformis muscle, producing buttock pain with radiation down the posterior leg. Deep, aching buttock pain aggravated by prolonged sitting, and tenderness over the sciatic notch, are more characteristic than the dermatomal back pain of lumbar radiculopathy. The Freiberg sign (pain on passive internal rotation of the extended hip) and the Pace sign (pain and weakness on resisted abduction and external rotation of the flexed hip) are supportive provocative tests. The FAIR position (flexion, adduction and internal rotation) reproduces symptoms and is sometimes combined with electrophysiological H-reflex testing. An anatomical variant in which the peroneal division pierces the piriformis is common and may predispose to entrapment. It is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion made only after lumbosacral radiculopathy and other causes of sciatica have been carefully ruled out. Magnetic resonance neurography and open or ultrasound-guided injections can support the diagnosis but none is fully specific. Symptoms typically lack the true neurological deficit of a compressive disc lesion, with preserved reflexes and only subjective sensory change in many cases. progressive foot drop or objective motor weakness suggesting significant nerve compromise bowel or bladder disturbance or saddle anaesthesia indicating cauda equina pathology night pain, weight loss or a palpable mass suggesting pelvic or gluteal malignancy bilateral symptoms or systemic features pointing to an alternative diagnosis diagnosing piriformis syndrome before adequately excluding lumbosacral radiculopathy over-reliance on provocative signs that are neither sensitive nor specific attributing all deep gluteal sciatic symptoms to the piriformis when other structures may be responsible missing a pelvic or gluteal tumour presenting as apparent entrapment The sciatic nerve exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen in intimate relation to the piriformis muscle within the deep gluteal (subgluteal) space. Hypertrophy, spasm, fibrosis, anatomical variation of the nerve or muscle, trauma, or a space-occupying lesion can compress or tether the nerve, producing mechanical irritation and secondary ischaemia. Fibrous bands and other deep gluteal structures may contribute, and the broader concept of deep gluteal syndrome recognises multiple potential sites of extraspinal sciatic entrapment. The result is buttock pain with variable referred symptoms along the sciatic distribution, usually without the discrete root-level deficit of intraspinal pathology. Most patients improve with physiotherapy, activity modification and targeted injections, and prognosis is generally favourable. A minority with refractory symptoms may require surgical decompression, with variable outcomes.

facial gestalt includes a broad, beaked nose, deep-set eyes, wide mouth with a cupid's-bow upper lip and full lips, and a square jaw, coarsening with age Caused by haploinsufficiency of TCF4 due to point variants, deletions or larger rearrangements, following autosomal dominant inheritance and almost always de novo Severe intellectual disability with absent or minimal speech and a happy, sociable demeanour is characteristic Constipation and Hirschsprung disease are recognised gastrointestinal associations Stereotypic hand movements, hypotonia and unsteady, broad-based gait are common Myopia and strabismus are frequent ophthalmological findings Apnoeic episodes causing cyanosis or requiring intervention Prolonged or refractory seizures Severe constipation or features suggesting Hirschsprung disease Feeding difficulty with aspiration risk Mistaking the breathing episodes for primary epilepsy or a psychiatric disorder Confusing the phenotype with Angelman syndrome and stopping at negative methylation testing Overlooking severe constipation or Hirschsprung disease Attributing the sociable demeanour and hand stereotypies solely to autism without genetic testing Pitt-Hopkins syndrome is caused by haploinsufficiency of TCF4 (transcription factor 4), a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor essential for neuronal development and differentiation in the central nervous system. Loss-of-function point variants, intragenic deletions and larger chromosomal rearrangements reduce functional TCF4, disrupting the transcriptional programmes that govern brain development and autonomic control. This underlies the severe neurodevelopmental impairment, the distinctive breathing abnormality reflecting brainstem autonomic dysregulation, and the associated craniofacial and gastrointestinal features. Individuals have severe, lifelong intellectual disability and require continuous support, but the condition is generally compatible with survival into adulthood and is associated with a characteristically cheerful temperament. Breathing episodes, while alarming, are not usually life-limiting on their own.

Pituitary apoplexy — pituitary tumour apoplexy, haemorrhagic pituitary infarction Subarachnoid haemorrhage Bacterial meningitis Migraine or other primary headache Cavernous sinus thrombosis Ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke Ruptured intracranial aneurysm Urgent MRI of the pituitary and sella to confirm haemorrhage or infarction and assess chiasmal compression CT head when MRI is unavailable or to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage Baseline anterior pituitary hormone panel and serum cortisol before or alongside starting steroids Serum electrolytes to detect hyponatraemia and monitor for diabetes insipidus Formal visual acuity and visual field assessment Pituitary apoplexy is a neuroendocrine emergency caused by sudden haemorrhage or infarction, usually within a pre-existing pituitary adenoma It presents abruptly with severe headache, visual disturbance, ophthalmoplegia, and often nausea, vomiting, and reduced consciousness Visual field loss (classically bitemporal from optic chiasm compression) and cranial nerve palsies affecting eye movements arise from expansion into the suprasellar region and cavernous sinus The most dangerous complication is acute secondary adrenal insufficiency from ACTH deficiency, which can cause life-threatening hypotension and hyponatraemia Empirical stress-dose corticosteroid cover is a cornerstone of initial management once apoplexy is suspected, before biochemical confirmation delays treatment MRI is the preferred imaging to demonstrate the pituitary lesion and haemorrhage, as CT may miss subtle changes Urgent surgical decompression is considered for severe or deteriorating visual loss or reduced consciousness, while selected stable cases may be managed conservatively with close monitoring Long-term follow-up is needed because many patients develop persistent hormone deficiencies requiring replacement Sudden severe headache with visual loss or ophthalmoplegia indicating an endocrine and neurosurgical emergency Haemodynamic instability and hyponatraemia from acute adrenal insufficiency requiring immediate corticosteroids Rapidly progressive or severe visual field loss needing urgent surgical decompression Declining conscious level or signs of raised intracranial pressure Withholding stress-dose steroids while awaiting hormone results in a suspected case Relying on CT alone and missing the diagnosis when MRI would reveal the lesion Mistaking the presentation for subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis and delaying endocrine treatment Failing to arrange long-term endocrine follow-up for evolving hormone deficiencies Pituitary apoplexy results from acute haemorrhage, infarction, or both within the pituitary gland, most commonly in an existing (often previously undiagnosed) adenoma. Rapid expansion of the gland within the confined sella and suprasellar space compresses adjacent structures: upward pressure on the optic chiasm impairs vision, and lateral extension into the cavernous sinus affects the oculomotor, trochlear, abducens, and trigeminal branches. Sudden loss of functioning pituitary tissue precipitates hypopituitarism, with acute corticotroph failure being the immediate threat to life. Leakage of blood and necrotic material can also cause meningism. With prompt corticosteroid cover and, when indicated, timely decompression, visual and neurological recovery is often good; however, permanent hypopituitarism is common and delayed recognition of adrenal crisis can be fatal.

another primary such as breast or lung, the reverse situation Other malignant sellar or parasellar tumours such as germ cell tumour, chordoma or sarcoma Craniopharyngioma Lymphoma or leukaemic infiltration of the sella Meningeal carcinomatosis of other origin Whole-neuraxis MRI of brain and spine to detect craniospinal metastases Systemic staging imaging with CT and functional imaging such as somatostatin-receptor PET for distant spread Histopathology showing high proliferation indices such as elevated Ki-67, mitoses and p53 to support aggressiveness Biopsy confirmation of a metastatic deposit to establish the diagnosis Serial hormone measurement for functioning tumours, for example ACTH and cortisol or prolactin Assessment of anterior and posterior pituitary function Very rare, and defined not by histological atypia alone but by the presence of craniospinal or systemic metastasis of a pituitary tumour Most evolve from an initially invasive adenoma, often ACTH- or prolactin-secreting, that progresses over years despite treatment It cannot be diagnosed on the primary tumour histology alone, since demonstration of discontinuous metastatic deposits is required Metastases may be craniospinal through the cerebrospinal fluid, involving leptomeninges, brain or spinal cord, or systemic to liver, bone or lymph nodes Presentation is with an aggressive, treatment-resistant pituitary tumour, sometimes with new neurological symptoms from metastases Functioning carcinomas continue to secrete hormone, for example persistent hypercortisolism or hyperprolactinaemia Management is multimodal with surgery, radiotherapy and increasingly temozolomide chemotherapy The prognosis is generally poor Rapid tumour progression or new neurological deficits despite prior treatment Discovery of discontinuous central nervous system or systemic lesions Escalating hormone levels refractory to therapy Leptomeningeal symptoms such as cranial neuropathies or radiculopathy Expecting histology alone to distinguish carcinoma from adenoma, when metastasis is the defining criterion Failing to image the whole neuraxis when an aggressive pituitary tumour progresses Overlooking a pituitary metastasis from an extracranial primary, which is more common than true pituitary carcinoma Delaying consideration of temozolomide in progressive disease Pituitary carcinoma is a malignant tumour of adenohypophyseal cells distinguished from an aggressive adenoma solely by the presence of metastasis outside the sellar region, either craniospinal spread through the cerebrospinal fluid or systemic dissemination. It typically develops through stepwise progression of an invasive, hormonally active adenoma, most commonly corticotroph or lactotroph, that accumulates further molecular alterations, increasing proliferative and invasive capacity over a prolonged latency. Continued hormone secretion by functioning tumours perpetuates the associated endocrine syndrome, while metastatic deposits cause site-specific neurological or systemic effects. Poor overall, with limited survival once metastasis is documented, although temozolomide and multimodal therapy can achieve responses and prolong survival in some patients.

Pituitary gigantism — pituitary gigantism, gigantism, childhood growth hormone excess, paediatric somatotroph adenoma Familial or constitutional tall stature Marfan syndrome and other connective tissue disorders Homocystinuria Klinefelter syndrome Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism) and other overgrowth syndromes Precocious puberty with early growth acceleration then early fusion Ectopic growth-hormone-releasing hormone secretion, which is rare Serum IGF-1 interpreted against age- and sex-specific reference ranges Oral glucose tolerance test with growth hormone measurement, showing failure of growth hormone to suppress Pituitary MRI to define the somatotroph adenoma and any invasion Assessment of the other pituitary axes and prolactin, as co-secretion is common Formal visual field testing if there is suprasellar extension Genetic testing for GPR101, AIP, GNAS, MEN1 and PRKAR1A with screening for associated syndromic features Growth hormone excess arising before fusion of the epiphyseal growth plates, producing excessive linear growth and very tall stature, in contrast to acromegaly which occurs after fusion Usually caused by a growth-hormone-secreting pituitary somatotroph adenoma, often a macroadenoma at diagnosis in children Frequently associated with genetic or syndromic conditions including X-linked acrogigantism (GPR101 duplication), AIP mutations in familial isolated pituitary adenoma, McCune-Albright syndrome (GNAS mosaicism), Carney complex and MEN1 Acromegalic features such as coarse facies, large hands and feet and prognathism coexist with on an elevated IGF-1 for age and failure of growth hormone to suppress during an oral glucose tolerance test, together with pituitary MRI Management combines transsphenoidal surgery with medical therapy using somatostatin analogues and the growth-hormone-receptor antagonist pegvisomant, and radiotherapy for residual disease Screening for associated syndromes and genetic testing is important, especially in young patients Rapidly accelerating growth crossing height centiles in a child Visual field loss or headache from a large invasive adenoma Features of McCune-Albright syndrome such as cafe-au-lait patches and fibrous dysplasia, or of Carney complex, prompting syndrome workup Cardiovascular or metabolic complications of growth hormone excess Attributing extreme tall stature to familial tall stature without measuring IGF-1 Failing to test for an underlying genetic syndrome in a young patient with gigantism Overlooking prolactin co-secretion or other pituitary hormone deficits Underestimating the aggressiveness and treatment resistance of syndromic somatotroph tumours Pituitary gigantism results from sustained growth hormone hypersecretion, almost always from a somatotroph pituitary adenoma, occurring while the epiphyseal growth plates are still open. Growth hormone stimulates hepatic and local production of insulin-like growth factor 1, which drives chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plates and accelerated linear growth, giving excessive height, while simultaneous periosteal and soft-tissue growth produces acromegalic features. A substantial proportion of paediatric cases are genetically determined, through germline or mosaic activation of growth-promoting pathways as in X-linked acrogigantism, AIP-related familial pituitary adenomas, McCune-Albright syndrome with activating GNAS mutations, Carney complex and MEN1, and these often produce larger, earlier and more aggressive tumours than sporadic disease. Control can be difficult because these tumours are often large and aggressive, especially in the genetic forms, and frequently require multimodal therapy; with biochemical control final height and complications are limited, but incomplete control risks continued growth and cardiovascular and metabolic morbidity.

Pituitary stalk interruption syndrome — pituitary stalk interruption syndrome, PSIS, ectopic posterior pituitary, pituitary stalk transection syndrome Other causes of congenital combined pituitary hormone deficiency without the imaging triad Septo-optic dysplasia and other midline developmental defects Craniopharyngioma or another sellar mass causing acquired hypopituitarism Hypophysitis Idiopathic isolated growth hormone deficiency Constitutional delay of growth and puberty Dedicated pituitary MRI to demonstrate a thin or absent stalk, anterior hypoplasia and an ectopic posterior bright spot Baseline anterior pituitary hormone panel including IGF-1, free thyroxine and TSH, morning cortisol and ACTH, gonadotropins and prolactin Dynamic pituitary stimulation testing such as growth hormone provocation and assessment of the cortisol response Blood glucose monitoring in the neonate for hypoglycaemia Assessment of posterior pituitary function, usually intact, if polyuria is present Genetic testing for developmental transcription-factor mutations where indicated A congenital condition defined by the imaging triad of a thin or absent (interrupted) pituitary stalk, an absent or hypoplastic anterior pituitary and an ectopic posterior pituitary bright spot It is a leading cause of congenital hypopituitarism, ranging from isolated growth hormone deficiency to combined or panhypopituitarism Neonatal presentation may include hypoglycaemia, prolonged jaundice and, in boys, micropenis and undescended testes; later features include short stature and delayed puberty Posterior pituitary function is often preserved despite the ectopic location, so diabetes insipidus is uncommon Diagnosis relies on dedicated pituitary MRI demonstrating the classic triad Some cases follow breech delivery or perinatal injury while others are associated with mutations affecting pituitary development such as HESX1, LHX4, PROP1, SOX3 and OTX2 Anterior hormone deficits may evolve over time, so longitudinal endocrine monitoring is essential Management is lifelong replacement of the deficient anterior pituitary hormones, including growth hormone, thyroxine, glucocorticoid and sex steroids as needed Neonatal hypoglycaemia and adrenal insufficiency, which are life-threatening if unrecognised Evolving cortisol deficiency during intercurrent illness Severe growth failure Emergence of new hormone deficits over time, indicating progressive hypopituitarism Attributing neonatal hypoglycaemia or prolonged jaundice to other causes and missing hypopituitarism Assuming a single hormone deficiency is fixed, when deficits can evolve and require repeated assessment Overlooking cortisol deficiency before starting growth hormone therapy, which can unmask adrenal insufficiency Expecting diabetes insipidus and being falsely reassured by its absence Pituitary stalk interruption syndrome is a developmental disorder of the pituitary in which the infundibulum is thin or absent, the anterior pituitary is hypoplastic and the posterior pituitary is ectopically located at the median eminence, seen as a displaced neurohypophyseal bright spot on MRI. Interruption of the stalk disrupts delivery of hypothalamic releasing hormones to the anterior pituitary and the normal migration of neurohypophyseal tissue, producing variable anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies. The aetiology is heterogeneous, with contributions from mutations in transcription factors governing pituitary organogenesis and from perinatal or traumatic mechanisms; because axonal antidiuretic hormone transport can terminate at the ectopic posterior lobe, vasopressin secretion is frequently spared. With early diagnosis and appropriate hormone replacement the prognosis is good, allowing normal growth and pubertal development; however deficiencies may progress, so lifelong endocrine surveillance is required, and unrecognised cortisol deficiency carries a risk of crisis.

TRH stimulation may provoke atypical gonadotropin/subunit rise TSH-secreting adenoma: free T4, free T3, TSH, alpha-subunit (inappropriately normal/high TSH with high free T4/T3) Immunohistochemistry for hormones and cell-specific transcription factors on resected tissue for histologic confirmation Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia (antipsychotics esp. risperidone, metoclopramide, methyldopa, verapamil, estrogens, opiates, H2 blockers) Primary hypothyroidism causing reflex hyperprolactinemia Chronic renal failure and cirrhosis (reduced PRL clearance) Pregnancy, lactation, chest-wall stimulation, stress and sleep as physiologic PRL elevation Polycystic ovarian syndrome (overlap with FSH/LH-secreting tumor causing ovarian hyperstimulation) Iatrogenic/exogenous glucocorticoid excess mimicking Cushing's disease Ectopic ACTH or ectopic CRH secretion mimicking Cushing's disease Adrenal adenoma/carcinoma or adrenal hyperplasia as ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome Ectopic GHRH (bronchial/abdominal carcinoid) or rare ectopic GH causing acromegaly Pituitary adenomas are benign monoclonal neoplasms arising from one of the five anterior pituitary cell types; the secreted hormone (PRL, GH, ACTH, TSH, or LH/FSH) determines the clinical syndrome. About one-third are clinically nonfunctioning, most of these originating from gonadotrope or null cells (p.3003-3004). Hormone output does not reliably track tumor size: small secretory microadenomas can be highly symptomatic, whereas large adenomas producing little hormone may stay clinically silent until mass effects appear (p.3003). Suprasellar extension classically compresses the optic chiasm to produce bitemporal hemianopia, often worse superiorly, because crossing nasal ganglion-cell fibers in the ventral chiasm are most vulnerable; loss of red color perception can be an early sign (p.2998-2999). The 'stalk section' phenomenon: any sellar mass that compresses the pituitary stalk and portal vessels causes early hyperprolactinemia (typically 30-100 ug/L) with later loss of other anterior pituitary hormones, even when the mass itself is not a prolactinoma (p.2998-2999). Hyperprolactinemia is the most common pituitary hypersecretion syndrome; PRL levels above 200 ug/L almost always indicate a prolactin-secreting adenoma, while milder elevations are more often drug-induced, stalk-related, or due to hypothyroidism or renal failure (p.3004-3005). Microprolactinomas show a marked female predominance (~20:1) and present early with amenorrhea/galactorrhea/infertility, whereas macroprolactinomas have a near 1:1 sex ratio and men tend to present later with larger, invasive tumors and mass effects (p.3005-3006). Acromegaly is typically indolent and may go undiagnosed for a decade or more; acral and soft-tissue overgrowth (frontal bossing, prognathism, enlarged hands/feet, coarse features) plus visceromegaly are characteristic, and GH excess before epiphyseal closure causes gigantism (p.3008-3009). Random single GH measurement is not diagnostic for acromegaly because of GH pulsatility; an age- and sex-matched IGF-1 is the screening test, and diagnosis is confirmed by failure of GH to suppress below threshold after an oral glucose load (p.3009). Cushing's disease (corticotrope adenoma) accounts for ~70% of endogenous Cushing's syndrome, is 5-10 times more common in women, and the tumors are usually small microadenomas, about half undetectable on MRI (p.3010-3011). Iatrogenic glucocorticoid use remains the most common overall cause of cushingoid features and must be excluded by history before pursuing an endogenous workup (p.3010). ACTH-secreting adenomas retain partial suppressibility by high-dose glucocorticoids, distinguishing them from ectopic ACTH sources; inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH (central:peripheral ratio >2 basal, >3 post-CRH) has >95% sensitivity for localizing a pituitary source (p.3011-3012). Nonfunctioning/gonadotrope adenomas are the most common adenoma type at presentation and are usually macroadenomas discovered through mass effect or as incidentalomas; mildly elevated PRL from stalk compression must not be mistaken for a true prolactinoma since these tumors do not shrink with dopamine agonists (p.3012-3013). Most pituitary glands harbor an unsuspected microadenoma at autopsy (up to one-quarter), and imaging detects clinically inapparent lesions (incidentalomas) in at least 10% of people; small nonsecretory intrasellar lesions can be safely followed with serial MRI (p.2999, p.3003). Progressive visual field loss or new bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal compression) Cranial nerve III/IV/VI palsy, diplopia, ptosis, or facial numbness indicating cavernous sinus invasion Severe sudden headache with visual loss or ophthalmoplegia suggesting pituitary apoplexy (intratumoral hemorrhage/infarction) Signs of raised intracranial pressure: headache, vomiting, papilledema, hydrocephalus Arginine vasopressin deficiency (polyuria) as a presenting feature, which suggests posterior pituitary involvement or a non-adenomatous lesion such as metastasis or germ cell tumor Rapid-onset hypercortisolism with hyperpigmentation, severe myopathy, and hypokalemic alkalosis suggesting an ectopic ACTH source Features of acute adrenal insufficiency from coexisting hypopituitarism Assuming PRL suppression by a dopamine agonist proves a prolactinoma: stalk-compression hyperprolactinemia from a nonfunctioning mass also falls with dopamine agonists even though the mass does not shrink. Very high prolactin levels (>1000 ug/L) may be reported falsely low due to assay 'hook' artifact unless the sample is diluted, leading to underestimation of macroprolactinoma. Falsely elevated PRL from biologically inactive macroprolactin can prompt unnecessary evaluation. Diagnosing acromegaly on a single random GH level is unreliable because of GH pulsatility; IGF-1 and a glucose-suppression test are required. Attributing every small pituitary lesion to a secretory tumor: incidental microadenomas are very common, and ~50% of ACTH adenomas are MRI-occult, so imaging cannot reliably localize the ACTH source. Overlap in basal ACTH levels between pituitary and ectopic ACTH sources means ACTH measurement alone cannot distinguish them; dynamic testing or petrosal sampling is needed. Mistaking iatrogenic glucocorticoid excess for endogenous Cushing's syndrome. Headache severity correlates poorly with adenoma size; a small intrasellar tumor can cause significant headache while a large tumor may not. Pituitary adenomas are benign, almost always monoclonal neoplasms derived from a single anterior pituitary cell lineage, implying acquisition of somatic mutation(s) conferring a growth advantage. Hormonally active tumors secrete autonomously with reduced responsiveness to physiologic feedback. Several molecular events are implicated: about 35% of GH-secreting tumors carry activating Gs-alpha mutations that lower GTPase activity, raise cyclic AMP, and drive somatotrope proliferation; growth factors (bFGF, EGFR signaling, the latter linked to USP8 mutation in some ACTH tumors), activated oncogenes (RAS, PTTG), loss of suppressors (e.g., MEG3), and loss of negative feedback (as in primary hypothyroidism/hypogonadism) also contribute. Hypothalamic hormones GHRH and CRH can additionally stimulate mitotic activity, so ectopic GHRH/CRH-producing chest or abdominal tumors can cause somatotrope or corticotrope hyperplasia. Familial settings include MEN 1 (MENIN, 11q13), MEN 4 (CDKN1B), Carney complex (PRKAR1A), McCune-Albright (mosaic Gs-alpha), and familial acromegaly (AIP). Clinical effects arise both from hormone hyper-/hyposecretion and from local mass effect: dorsal expansion lifts the optic chiasm, stalk compression disrupts dopaminergic inhibition of lactotropes (hyperprolactinemia) and portal hormone delivery, and lateral extension into the cavernous sinus impairs cranial nerves III, IV, VI and trigeminal branches. Pituitary tumors are overwhelmingly benign and slow growing; true carcinomas with extracranial metastases are exceedingly rare. Outcomes depend on tumor type and size and require lifelong follow-up. Prolactinomas respond well to dopamine agonists with normoprolactinemia and gonadal recovery in roughly 80% of microadenomas and tumor shrinkage in most macroadenomas; about 20% (especially men) are dopamine-resistant, and hyperprolactinemia may resolve spontaneously in up to 30% of hyperprolactinemic patients without a visible adenoma. Surgical PRL normalization reaches ~70% for microprolactinomas but only ~40% for macroadenomas, with substantial long-term recurrence (>50% for macroadenomas). In acromegaly, untreated GH excess roughly triples mortality and shortens survival by about 10 years, driven by cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and respiratory disease and increased colon cancer risk; transsphenoidal remission is ~70% for microadenomas and under 50% for macroadenomas. Cushing's disease has a microadenoma surgical remission of ~80% (<50% for macroadenomas), with ~5% biochemical recurrence and a postoperative period of ACTH deficiency. Untreated hypercortisolism carries excess mortality, chiefly cardiovascular, plus increased infection and suicide risk. Pituitary adenomas are conventionally classified by size into microadenomas (<10 mm) and macroadenomas (>=10 mm, often locally invasive with parasellar extension), and by secretory phenotype into functioning (lactotrope/PRL, somatotrope/GH, corticotrope/ACTH, thyrotrope/TSH, gonadotrope/FSH-LH, or plurihormonal) versus clinically nonfunctioning (frequently gonadotrope or null-cell). Sellar mass severity is further graded by anatomic impact in Table 392-1 (compression of pituitary, optic chiasm, hypothalamus, cavernous sinus, frontal lobe, or brain), as larger/invasive tumors carry higher surgical risk and lower cure rates.

pityriasis alba — pityriasis simplex faciei, erythema streptogenes Vitiligo Pityriasis versicolor Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation from other dermatoses Naevus depigmentosus Tinea corporis (faciei) Early morphoea Mycosis fungoides (hypopigmented variant) Skin scraping with potassium hydroxide microscopy to exclude pityriasis versicolor and dermatophytosis Wood's lamp examination showing mild, incomplete accentuation Dermoscopy revealing fine white scale and preserved pigment network Skin biopsy reserved for atypical, persistent, or treatment-resistant lesions to exclude hypopigmented mycosis fungoides Assessment for other features of atopic dermatitis Serial review to confirm gradual spontaneous resolution A common, benign, self-limiting hypomelanosis of children and adolescents, widely regarded as a minor or forme fruste manifestation of atopic dermatitis. Lesions are ill-defined, round to oval, hypopigmented patches with fine powdery scale, most often on the cheeks, lateral upper arms, and shoulders. It becomes most conspicuous in summer or in darker skin, when the surrounding skin tans and accentuates the pale patches. The typical evolution is from a faintly erythematous scaly stage to a residual hypopigmented, minimally scaly patch that gradually resolves. Wood's lamp shows only mild accentuation with partial preservation of pigment, in contrast to the sharp bright-white of vitiligo. It is a clinical diagnosis; scrapings for fungal microscopy help exclude pityriasis versicolor when there is diagnostic doubt. Hypopigmentation reflects post-inflammatory reduction in melanin and disturbed melanosome transfer, not melanocyte destruction. Management centres on emollients, gentle skin care, sun protection, and reassurance, with low-potency topical anti-inflammatories for troublesome cases. Persistence into adulthood or lesions that fail to resolve, prompting reconsideration of hypopigmented mycosis fungoides Progressive, atrophic, or indurated plaques suggesting morphoea or lymphoma Sharply demarcated, truly depigmented macules indicating vitiligo Widespread scaly lesions with positive mycology pointing to a fungal infection Mistaking it for vitiligo and causing undue alarm or inappropriate treatment Overlooking pityriasis versicolor by not performing mycological examination in scaly cases Attributing persistent adult lesions to pityriasis alba and missing hypopigmented mycosis fungoides Neglecting the underlying atopic dryness, so that emollient therapy is omitted Promising rapid resolution and undermining confidence when repigmentation is inevitably slow Pityriasis alba represents a low-grade, subclinical dermatitis, most commonly within the atopic spectrum, that culminates in post-inflammatory hypopigmentation. Mild eczematous inflammation and associated dryness disturb the orderly transfer of melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes and reduce the number and size of active melanosomes, while the overlying hyperkeratosis and scale scatter incident light and further diminish apparent pigmentation. Melanocytes are preserved but functionally quiescent, which is why repigmentation eventually occurs spontaneously. Ultraviolet exposure deepens the contrast by tanning the unaffected surrounding skin. Xerosis, frequent washing, sun exposure, and an atopic diathesis are recognised contributory factors, and the condition is regarded as one of the minor diagnostic criteria of atopic dermatitis. Pityriasis alba is entirely benign and self-limiting, with pigmentation returning spontaneously over months to a few years, though relapses are common during childhood. It carries no long-term sequelae and requires only supportive care and reassurance.

Pityriasis lichenoides (chronica/PLC spectrum) — pityriasis lichenoides chronica, PLC, guttate parapsoriasis, chronic pityriasis lichenoides Lymphomatoid papulosis Guttate psoriasis Pityriasis rosea Secondary syphilis Papular urticaria / arthropod bite reactions Small-plaque parapsoriasis (digitate dermatosis) Skin biopsy with histopathology to confirm the interface dermatitis and characterise the infiltrate Immunohistochemistry and T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies to exclude lymphomatoid papulosis or cutaneous lymphoma Serology for possible triggers such as Toxoplasma, Epstein-Barr virus, or HIV when clinically indicated Full blood count and inflammatory markers in patients who are febrile or systemically unwell Syphilis serology where secondary syphilis is a diagnostic consideration Photographic documentation to track the evolution of successive crops Belongs to a spectrum of benign, self-limiting T-cell-driven papulosquamous eruptions that runs from the chronic pole (PLC) to the acute pole (PLEVA) PLC produces recurrent crops of small red-brown papules capped by a characteristic adherent mica-like scale that can be lifted off in one piece Lesions appear in successive crops so that different stages coexist, usually healing with transient post-inflammatory hyper- or hypopigmentation rather than scarring Most common in children and young adults and typically follows a relapsing-remitting course over months to years The trunk and the proximal aspects of the limbs are the sites most often involved Usually asymptomatic or only mildly itchy, which helps separate it from more inflammatory dermatoses Diagnosis is clinical but supported by biopsy showing a lymphocytic interface reaction; clonality studies may be needed to distinguish it from lymphomatoid papulosis Management is generally conservative with emollients, topical corticosteroids, and phototherapy for extensive or persistent disease Evolution of the acute pole into febrile ulceronecrotic Mucha-Habermann disease with systemic upset Development of persistent, infiltrated, or ulcerating plaques raising concern for cutaneous lymphoma Atypical or clonal lymphoid infiltrate on histology requiring formal clonality assessment Failure to settle or progressive extension despite standard therapy Mistaking it for guttate psoriasis or pityriasis rosea and delaying diagnostic biopsy Overlooking the overlap with lymphomatoid papulosis, which can be histologically very similar Assuming a single self-limited episode when the relapsing, crop-by-crop pattern is characteristic Failing to recognise the rare but potentially serious ulceronecrotic variant Pityriasis lichenoides is best regarded as a reactive, sometimes clonal, T-lymphocyte-driven process rather than a true malignancy. It is thought to represent an exaggerated hypersensitivity reaction, possibly to infectious antigens (viruses and Toxoplasma have been implicated) or to circulating immune complexes, producing a lymphocytic vasculitis with interface change at the dermo-epidermal junction. The chronic end of the spectrum shows a milder, more superficial infiltrate with parakeratotic scale, giving the persistent scaly papules of PLC, whereas the acute pole shows a denser cytotoxic response with keratinocyte necrosis. Post-inflammatory pigmentary change reflects melanin disturbance at the dermo-epidermal interface. Generally benign and self-limiting, although the chronic form may relapse over months or years; the great majority resolve without scarring, but rare progression to a lymphoproliferative disorder justifies long-term follow-up of atypical cases.

The eruption reflects a T-cell-mediated inflammatory response in the skin producing spongiotic dermatitis with focal parakeratosis, which accounts for the fine collarette of scale. The alignment of lesions along Langer's cleavage lines gives the distinctive distribution. A clinically indistinguishable pityriasis rosea-like eruption can be triggered by certain drugs and vaccines through a similar hypersensitivity mechanism. The condition is benign and self-limiting, typically clearing over several weeks to a few months without scarring; post-inflammatory pigment change may persist for a while, especially in darker skin, and recurrence is uncommon.

unexplained erythroderma Pityriasis rubra pilaris is a chronic papulosquamous disorder of keratinisation whose precise cause is uncertain. The disordered maturation of keratinocytes leaves discrete areas of preserved skin, producing the diagnostic islands of sparing. The classic adult form often resolves spontaneously within one to several years, whereas other subtypes, particularly juvenile-onset familial and HIV-associated disease, tend to be more chronic and refractory.

care is symptomatic Rapid developmental regression with loss of vision and motor skills in an infant Progressive bulbar dysfunction with aspiration risk New seizures or status epilepticus Acute respiratory compromise from progressive neuromuscular weakness Excluding the diagnosis on the basis of a normal early MRI when brain iron has not yet accumulated Missing the early cerebellar atrophy that is often the first imaging clue Attributing adult-onset dystonia-parkinsonism to idiopathic Parkinson disease without considering a genetic cause Overlooking the peripheral nervous system involvement when interpreting neurophysiology PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration arises from biallelic variants in PLA2G6, which encodes a calcium-independent phospholipase A2 that remodels membrane phospholipids and maintains membrane integrity. surgical control Haemodynamic instability, tachycardia, and hypotension indicating major blood loss Placenta percreta with bladder or bowel involvement risking visceral injury and uncontrolled bleeding Coagulopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation complicating massive transfusion Unplanned delivery outside a specialist centre without blood products or surgical backup Failing to screen for accreta in a woman with placenta praevia and a previous caesarean scar Attempting to deliver the placenta manually and precipitating uncontrolled haemorrhage Delivering in a non-specialist setting without blood products, cell salvage, or surgical support Underestimating bladder involvement in percreta and omitting urological planning Assuming a conservative uterus-preserving approach is low risk when delayed haemorrhage and sepsis can follow The disorder arises from a defect in the decidua basalis, usually within a uterine scar, so that the normal Nitabuch fibrinoid layer that limits trophoblast invasion is deficient or absent. Chorionic villi therefore anchor directly onto or into the myometrium instead of the decidua. The depth of invasion determines the grade. Scar tissue is poorly vascularised and lacks a decidual cleavage plane, so at delivery the placenta cannot separate physiologically; disruption of the abnormal placental-myometrial interface tears richly vascular tissue and causes massive obstetric haemorrhage. Neovascularisation around the invasion front contributes to the bleeding risk. With antenatal diagnosis and planned management in an experienced multidisciplinary unit, maternal survival is high and morbidity is reduced, though many women require hysterectomy and lose future fertility. Undiagnosed cases presenting acutely carry a substantially higher risk of massive haemorrhage, intensive care admission, visceral injury, and maternal death. Recurrence risk relates to the underlying scarring and future uterine surgery.

Placenta accreta spectrum results from defective decidualisation, usually over a uterine scar, so that chorionic villi anchor directly to or invade the myometrium rather than the normal decidua The absent decidual plane prevents physiological placental separation after delivery, and attempts at removal tear deeply vascular tissue, producing torrential haemorrhage. Deeper invasion (increta and percreta) can breach the uterine serosa and involve adjacent structures such as the bladder, with abnormal neovascularisation increasing operative bleeding. Outcomes are substantially better with antenatal diagnosis and planned delivery at an experienced centre; unrecognised cases carry a high risk of massive haemorrhage, transfusion, bladder injury, and maternal death. Many women require hysterectomy, with consequent loss of fertility.

early-term window depending on symptoms, with senior obstetric and anaesthetic involvement and preparation for major haemorrhage A low-lying placenta detected in the mid-trimester often appears to heart rate abnormalities or absent fetal movements Bleeding with features suggestive of placenta accreta spectrum, such as a known anterior praevia over a prior scar Onset of painful contractions or caesarean scar Assuming a mid-trimester low-lying placenta will persist, or has resolved, without third-trimester re-imaging Under-preparing for delivery by not securing blood products, senior staff, and appropriate anaesthesia The placenta implants in the lower uterine segment rather than the well-vascularised fundus, so that placental tissue lies over or close to the internal cervical os. As the lower segment forms and stretches in the third trimester and the cervix begins to efface and dilate, the relatively inelastic placenta cannot accommodate the shearing forces, and the anchoring villi are torn from the decidua, opening maternal venous sinuses and causing painless bleeding. Because the lower segment contracts poorly after delivery, the placental bed is prone to continued haemorrhage. Abnormal implantation over scarred myometrium, as after caesarean section, is associated with deficient decidualisation and predisposes to a morbidly adherent placenta (accreta spectrum). Repeated or heavy bleeding can compromise both maternal circulating volume and uteroplacental perfusion, threatening the fetus. With antenatal diagnosis, planned caesarean delivery, and ready access to transfusion, maternal and perinatal outcomes are generally good. Praevia complicated by placenta accreta spectrum or major antepartum haemorrhage, however, carries a substantial risk of massive obstetric haemorrhage, hysterectomy, and perinatal morbidity.
