As the lower segment stretches and the cervix effaces in later pregnancy and labour, the inelastic placental attachment is disrupted from the underlying decidua, tearing maternal vessels and causing painless bleeding. Because the lower segment contracts poorly after delivery, the placental bed is prone to continued haemorrhage. Prior uterine scarring predisposes to abnormally adherent or invasive placentation (accreta spectrum). With antenatal diagnosis, planned caesarean delivery, and ready access to blood products, maternal and perinatal outcomes are generally good. Uncontrolled haemorrhage, particularly with coexisting accreta spectrum, remains a major cause of maternal morbidity, massive transfusion, and peripartum hysterectomy.

Placental abruption — abruptio placentae, placental abruptio, premature separation of the placenta Placenta praevia Uterine rupture Preterm labour Vasa praevia Local genital tract causes of bleeding Acute abdomen from a non-obstetric cause Continuous cardiotocography to detect fetal compromise and uterine hypertonicity Full blood count and serial haemoglobin Coagulation screen including fibrinogen to identify disseminated intravascular coagulation Group and cross-match for transfusion Ultrasound mainly to exclude praevia rather than to confirm abruption Kleihauer test in rhesus-negative women to quantify fetomaternal haemorrhage Abruption is premature separation of a normally sited placenta before delivery, classically presenting with painful vaginal bleeding and a tender, firm, or hypertonic uterus Bleeding may be concealed behind the placenta, so the degree of vaginal blood loss can badly underestimate the true haemorrhage Risk factors include hypertension and pre-eclampsia, trauma, cocaine or tobacco use, prior abruption, polyhydramnios with rapid decompression, and thrombophilia Fetal compromise or death can occur rapidly because the separated placenta cannot support gas exchange It is largely a clinical diagnosis; ultrasound is insensitive and a normal scan does not exclude abruption Disseminated intravascular coagulation is an important complication, particularly with large abruptions or fetal demise Management depends on maternal and fetal status: resuscitation, and prompt delivery (often by caesarean) when there is fetal distress or maternal instability Anti-D should be given to rhesus-negative women and blood products used to correct coagulopathy Maternal haemodynamic instability or shock, which may be disproportionate to visible blood loss due to concealed haemorrhage Non-reassuring or absent fetal heart activity Developing coagulopathy with falling fibrinogen and abnormal clotting A rigid, exquisitely tender uterus with frequent contractions Rapid clinical deterioration requiring emergency delivery Being falsely reassured by minimal external bleeding when concealed haemorrhage is severe Relying on ultrasound to rule out abruption Underestimating and undertreating evolving coagulopathy Delaying delivery in the face of fetal distress or maternal instability Failing to consider abruption after seemingly minor abdominal trauma in pregnancy Abruption begins with rupture of maternal decidual vessels, causing bleeding into the decidua basalis that splits the placenta from the uterine wall. The expanding retroplacental clot further separates the placenta, reducing the functional area for maternal-fetal exchange and provoking uterine irritability and contraction. Thromboplastins released from the disrupted placenta and decidua enter the maternal circulation and can trigger consumptive coagulopathy (disseminated intravascular coagulation), while extravasation of blood into the myometrium (Couvelaire uterus) impairs contractility and postpartum haemostasis. Small abruptions with a stable mother and reassuring fetus may allow expectant management with good outcomes. Large abruptions carry high risks of fetal death, maternal haemorrhage, coagulopathy, and organ injury, and abruption is a leading cause of perinatal mortality and antepartum stillbirth. Recurrence risk in future pregnancies is increased.

Placental insufficiency — uteroplacental insufficiency, placental dysfunction A constitutionally small-for-gestational-age but healthy fetus Incorrect gestational dating Fetal aneuploidy or a genetic syndrome causing growth restriction Congenital infection such as cytomegalovirus or toxoplasmosis A structural fetal anomaly Multiple pregnancy with twin-to-twin transfusion or selective growth restriction Oligohydramnios from ruptured membranes or a fetal renal anomaly Serial ultrasound biometry to assess fetal size and growth velocity Amniotic fluid volume assessment by deepest vertical pocket or amniotic fluid index Umbilical artery Doppler for placental resistance and end-diastolic flow Middle cerebral artery Doppler and cerebroplacental ratio for redistribution Ductus venosus Doppler in early-onset severe restriction to help time delivery Cardiotocography, including computerised analysis of short-term variation Investigations for an underlying cause, including maternal blood pressure and urinalysis, uterine artery Doppler, screening for infection, thrombophilia or autoimmune disease, and karyotype or anomaly assessment where indicated Placental insufficiency describes inadequate placental transfer of oxygen and nutrients, most often manifesting as fetal growth restriction, oligohydramnios, and, if progressive, fetal hypoxia It commonly underlies placenta-mediated disease, linking fetal growth restriction with pre-eclampsia through the shared mechanism of deficient spiral artery remodelling Risk factors include hypertensive disorders, maternal vascular and autoimmune disease such as antiphospholipid syndrome, pre-existing diabetes or renal disease, smoking, thrombophilia, and a previous growth-restricted or stillborn pregnancy Distinguishing a constitutionally small but healthy fetus from a growth-restricted fetus with placental dysfunction is central and rests on growth trajectory and Doppler studies rather than size alone Umbilical artery Doppler is the key surveillance tool: rising resistance, then absent, and finally reversed end-diastolic flow indicate worsening placental function and impending fetal compromise In late-onset disease the cerebroplacental ratio and middle cerebral artery Doppler ('brain-sparing') may reveal redistribution even when the umbilical artery Doppler appears near-normal Ductus venosus Doppler and computerised cardiotocography help time delivery in early-onset severe cases, where prematurity must be balanced against the risk of stillbirth Management centres on surveillance and optimally timed delivery, with antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity and magnesium sulphate for neuroprotection when very preterm birth is planned Absent or reversed umbilical artery end-diastolic flow Abnormal ductus venosus Doppler with an absent or reversed a-wave Reduced or absent fetal movements Static or declining fetal growth on serial scans Abnormal cardiotocography or reduced short-term variation Equating small fetal size with growth restriction, or vice versa, without Doppler and growth-trajectory assessment Over-relying on a single normal umbilical artery Doppler in late-onset disease and missing redistribution Inaccurate dating leading to misclassification Failing to investigate for underlying maternal or fetal causes Delivering too early or too late by not integrating the full surveillance picture In normal pregnancy, extravillous trophoblast invades and remodels the maternal spiral arteries into wide, low-resistance vessels that deliver a high, steady blood flow to the intervillous space. In placental insufficiency this transformation is incomplete, leaving high-resistance vessels prone to spasm and thrombosis; the resulting malperfusion causes placental ischaemia, infarction, and villous maldevelopment. Reduced surface area and impaired diffusion limit oxygen and nutrient transfer, restricting fetal growth. The fetus adapts by redistributing cardiac output to preserve the brain, heart, and adrenals at the expense of the kidneys and periphery, which reduces renal perfusion and amniotic fluid, producing oligohydramnios. Progressive hypoxaemia and acidaemia are reflected in deteriorating arterial and then venous Doppler indices and, ultimately, in abnormal cardiotocography and stillbirth if delivery is not achieved. Outcome depends on the severity and gestation at onset; late-onset, well-surveilled disease often does well with timely delivery, whereas early-onset severe insufficiency carries high risks of stillbirth, iatrogenic prematurity, and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment.

Plague — Yersinia pestis Acute focal lymphadenopathy of other etiologies (for bubonic plague): streptococcal or staphylococcal infection, tularemia, cat-scratch disease, tick typhus, infectious mononucleosis, lymphatic filariasis (p.1343). Tuberculosis (in differential of fever and hemoptysis in plague-endemic areas, as a small-airborne-particle-transmitted infection) (p.1347). Tonsillitis with peritonsillar abscess (resembles plague pharyngitis) (p.1344). Tularemia (Francisella tularensis) (p.1343) Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) (p.1343) Tick typhus (rickettsial) (p.1343) Infectious mononucleosis (p.1343) Lymphatic filariasis (p.1343) Streptococcal or staphylococcal lymphadenitis (p.1343) Tuberculosis (fever and hemoptysis differential) (p.1347) Bubo aspirate (bubonic), bronchoalveolar lavage fluid or sputum (pneumonic), and blood (septicemic) are the appropriate specimens; culture of postmortem organ biopsy can also be diagnostic. Transport medium such as Cary-Blair preserves viability (p.1345). Direct microscopy: Gram-negative coccobacilli with characteristic bipolar 'closed safety pin' appearance on Wayson or Wright-Giemsa stain; bipolar bacilli may be visible on direct blood smear in septicemic plague, indicating very high circulating bacterial numbers and a poor prognosis (p.1345). Culture on nutrient-rich media (sheep blood agar, brain-heart infusion broth) and selective agar (MacConkey, EMB, or Yersinia-specific CIN agar); optimal growth at <37 degC (25-29 degC). Y. pestis is oxidase-negative, catalase-positive, urease-negative, indole-negative, lactose-negative, and nonmotile (distinguishing it from other Yersinia species) (p.1345). F1 antigen detection: direct immunofluorescence and rapid immunochromatographic test strip (F1RDT), effective on bubo aspirates and sputum and widely used in endemic countries; a Pla antigen strip can detect F1-negative strains (p.1345). PCR/RT-PCR requiring positivity for at least two Y. pestis-specific targets (e.g., caf1, pla, and chromosomal genes); FDA-authorized BioFire FilmArray panels include Y. pestis (p.1346). Serology: rising hemagglutinating antibody titer to F1 antigen, or seroconversion/fourfold rise in paired sera; ELISA for IgG and IgM to F1 antigen (p.1345-1346). WHO case definitions (suspected/probable/confirmed) guide presumptive diagnosis followed by reference laboratory confirmation (p.1345). Plague is a systemic zoonosis caused by Yersinia pestis, predominantly affecting small rodents in rural areas of Africa, Asia, and the Americas and usually transmitted to humans by an arthropod (flea) vector; less often via contact with animal tissues or respiratory droplets (p.1341). Three principal clinical forms: bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic. Worldwide, bubonic plague is the predominant reported form; a minority (10-20%) present as primary septicemic or pneumonic disease (p.1343). Bubonic plague: after a 2-6 day incubation, sudden onset of fever (>38 degC), malaise, myalgia, dizziness, and increasing pain from progressive regional lymphadenitis. The bubo is a tense, tender swelling with a boggy consistency and underlying hard core, usually solitary and erythematous with periganglionic edema, most commonly inguinal but may be crural, axillary, cervical, or submaxillary depending on bite site (p.1343). Children most commonly present with cervical or axillary buboes; abdominal pain from intraabdominal node involvement can occur without other visible signs (p.1343). Primary pneumonic plague follows inhalation of infectious droplets from another person or animal with plague pneumonia; short incubation (a few hours to 2-3 days, range 1-7 days) with abrupt fever, headache, myalgia, weakness, nausea, vomiting, dizziness; respiratory signs (cough, dyspnea, chest pain, sputum with hemoptysis) typically appear after 24 h (p.1344). Primary pneumonic plague is generally the least common but most fatal of the main presentations; treated pneumonic plague has an estimated death rate of about 17% versus 98% for untreated pneumonic plague (p.1343). Primary septicemic plague (10-25% of infections) presents as gram-negative septicemia (hypotension, shock) WITHOUT preceding lymphadenopathy; occurs in all age groups but risk is elevated in persons over 40 (p.1344). WBC count is generally raised (10,000-20,000/uL) with neutrophilic leukocytosis and left shift; counts can be very high in children (>100,000/uL), but in some cases the WBC is normal or leukopenia develops. DIC occurs in a significant minority (p.1346). Appropriate treatment of bubonic plague resolves fever within 2-5 days, but buboes may remain enlarged for more than a week after initial treatment and can become fluctuant (p.1344). Pneumonic plague is transmissible person-to-person via respiratory droplets (productive cough), making it a public-health emergency requiring immediate isolation and notification (p.1344, 1347). Aerosolized Y. pestis is a recognized potential bioterrorism agent (Tier 1 select agent); an outbreak of primary pneumonic plague in a nonendemic region or urban setting should raise concern for intentional release (p.1342, 1344, 1345). Rapid progression of primary pneumonic plague from segmental pneumonitis to lobar and bilateral involvement with hemoptysis and ARDS within hours to days (p.1344). Bipolar bacilli visible on direct blood smear indicate very high circulating bacterial numbers and a poor prognosis (p.1345). Disseminated intravascular coagulation with shock in septicemic disease (p.1346). The term 'septicemic plague' can be confusing because most patients with buboes have detectable bacteremia at some stage, with or without systemic sepsis signs (p.1344). Automated biochemical or mass-spectrometry identification systems can misidentify Y. pestis as Y. pseudotuberculosis or other species (p.1345). Meningeal plague may be associated with suboptimal antimicrobial therapy (delayed treatment, penicillin use, or low-dose tetracycline) (p.1344). A single negative rapid antigen test is insufficient to exclude plague; WHO exclusion requires two negative F1RDT tests on specimens collected 24 h apart when confirmatory tests are unavailable (p.1345-1346). F1RDT specificity for culture-confirmed pneumonic plague was only 71%, so a positive sputum test in an endemic area identifies a probable case requiring treatment but needs additional confirmatory testing (p.1345-1346). Culture yield can be low after prehospital antimicrobial use (as observed in the 2017 Madagascar outbreak) (p.1345). Y. pestis is a gram-negative bacterium of the order Enterobacterales that recently evolved from the enteric pathogen Y. pseudotuberculosis. It has a two-stage life cycle alternating between arthropod (flea) and a wide range of mammalian hosts. In the flea, the organism multiplies and forms biofilm-embedded aggregates in the midgut; some fleas become 'blocked' at the proventriculus and regurgitate bacteria into the bite site, while early-phase unblocked transmission also occurs. In the mammalian host, dissemination from the inoculation site is initially dependent on plasminogen activator (Pla), which activates plasminogen, degrades complement, and binds laminin, and is essential for high-level virulence and bubo formation. Bacteria are rapidly transported to regional lymph nodes where Y. pestis replicates extracellularly with full expression of antiphagocytic systems (type III secretion machinery and effectors encoded by pYV plus the F1 capsule), producing a bubo (hemorrhagic/necrotic node with thrombosed vessels, replaced architecture, and abundant bacteria). LcrV targets phagocytes and exerts an anti-inflammatory effect, and modified lipopolysaccharide minimizes Toll-like receptor 4 stimulation, prolonging high-grade bacteremia. Spread via efferent lymphatics to the thoracic duct produces high-grade bacteremia and hematogenous seeding of spleen, liver, secondary buboes, lungs (secondary plague pneumonia), and meninges, with uncontrolled septicemia leading to death; the septicemic phase can occur without an obvious prior bubo (p.1342-1343). Untreated plague carries high mortality, but it is treatable with antimicrobials. Treated pneumonic plague has an estimated death rate of about 17% compared with 98% for untreated pneumonic plague. In the United States, case-fatality fell from 66% in 1900-1941 to 16% in the post-antibiotic era (1942 onward); in 2000-2018, mortality was 8% in patients receiving any antimicrobial and 4% in those receiving currently recommended high-efficacy agents. The global case-fatality rate notified to WHO for 2013-2018 was 17%. Visible bipolar bacilli on direct blood smear signal very high bacteremia and poor prognosis (p.1343, 1345). WHO case classification of plague: Suspected case (clinical presentation suggestive of plague plus an epidemiologic context of possible exposure within 10 days of onset); Probable case (suspected case plus one of: F1 antigen detected by rapid test or immunofluorescence, a single anti-F1 serology without prior infection/immunization, or direct microscopy showing bipolar-staining gram-negative coccobacilli); Confirmed case (suspected case plus one of: isolation of Y. pestis, seroconversion or fourfold anti-F1 titer change in paired sera, or species-specific PCR positivity); Not a case (suspected case with negative confirmatory testing) (p.1345).

PLAID (PLCG2-associated antibody deficiency and immune dysregulation) — PLCG2-associated antibody deficiency and immune dysregulation, familial cold urticaria with immunodeficiency, PLCG2, phospholipase C gamma 2 defect Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS) with cold-triggered features Acquired cold urticaria Common variable immunodeficiency APLAID (PLCG2 autoinflammation and immune dysregulation) variant Systemic autoimmune disease with cutaneous features Chronic spontaneous urticaria Genetic testing for PLCG2 mutations Evaporative cooling challenge reproducing cold urticaria Immunoglobulin levels and specific antibody responses Lymphocyte subset analysis including B-cell subsets Autoantibody panel to assess autoimmunity Assessment for granulomatous disease where clinically suggested Caused by mutations in PLCG2, which encodes phospholipase C gamma 2, a signalling enzyme important in immune cells Characterised by cold-induced urticaria triggered by evaporative cooling rather than by contact with a cold object Combines an autoinflammatory cold urticaria with features of humoral immunodeficiency and autoimmunity Antibody deficiency predisposes to recurrent sinopulmonary infection and may require immunoglobulin support Autoimmune and granulomatous manifestations, including autoantibodies, can coexist with the immunodeficiency The cold urticaria differs from classic acquired cold urticaria and from cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes Management is largely supportive, targeting infection risk, cold avoidance, and specific autoimmune complications Recurrent or severe sinopulmonary infections indicating significant antibody deficiency Anaphylaxis or airway involvement during cold exposure Emergence of serious autoimmune or granulomatous complications Bronchiectasis from repeated respiratory infection Confusing cold-evaporation urticaria with cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes and mistargeting therapy Overlooking the underlying antibody deficiency and infection risk Attributing autoimmunity to an unrelated primary autoimmune disease Testing only for classic contact cold urticaria and missing the evaporative trigger PLAID results from mutations in PLCG2 that alter phospholipase C gamma 2 signalling in immune cells such as B lymphocytes, natural killer cells, and mast cells. The abnormal enzyme shows enhanced activity at reduced temperatures, so mild cooling of the skin triggers mast cell activation and urticaria. The same signalling defect disturbs B-cell development and function, producing antibody deficiency alongside a paradoxical tendency to autoimmunity and, in some, granulomatous disease. This dual disturbance explains the coexistence of cold urticaria, immunodeficiency, and immune dysregulation. PLAID is a chronic condition; with cold avoidance, infection management, and treatment of autoimmune complications, many patients do well, though antibody deficiency and autoimmunity require ongoing care.

Plantar fasciitis — plantar fasciopathy, plantar heel pain, plantar fasciosis, heel spur syndrome Calcaneal stress fracture Fat-pad atrophy or contusion Tarsal tunnel syndrome or entrapment of the nerve to abductor digiti minimi (Baxter's nerve) S1 radiculopathy referring to the heel Inflammatory enthesitis from seronegative spondyloarthropathy Insertional Achilles or retrocalcaneal pathology (posterior heel) Usually diagnosed clinically without imaging Ultrasound to demonstrate a thickened, hypoechoic proximal plantar fascia MRI in atypical or refractory cases and to exclude calcaneal stress fracture or nerve entrapment Plain radiographs to identify a calcaneal stress fracture or other bony pathology Inflammatory screen and referral if a spondyloarthropathy is suspected The hallmark is sharp inferior heel pain that is worst with the first few steps in the morning or after periods of rest, then eases with activity Tenderness is maximal at the medial calcaneal tubercle where the plantar fascia originates It is a degenerative fasciopathy from repetitive overload rather than a primarily inflammatory condition, despite the -itis suffix Risk factors include obesity, prolonged standing, reduced ankle dorsiflexion, tight calf muscles, and a sudden increase in running load Diagnosis is clinical; a windlass test reproducing pain on passive great-toe dorsiflexion supports it Heel spurs seen on radiographs are common incidental findings and do not cause the pain Management principles are calf and plantar fascia stretching, load management, supportive footwear, and orthoses or heel cushioning Most cases resolve within a year with conservative care; corticosteroid injection gives short-term relief but risks fat-pad atrophy and fascial rupture Persistent bilateral heel pain, especially in a young person with inflammatory features, should prompt consideration of a seronegative spondyloarthropathy Features suggesting inflammatory arthropathy such as young age, bilateral disease, and other enthesitis or back symptoms Focal bony tenderness or night pain raising concern for stress fracture or tumour Numbness, tingling, or a positive Tinel sign suggesting nerve entrapment Systemic symptoms or signs of infection Attributing symptoms to an incidental heel spur Overusing corticosteroid injection with risk of fat-pad atrophy or fascial rupture Missing a calcaneal stress fracture or nerve entrapment presenting as heel pain Overlooking an underlying inflammatory spondyloarthropathy in bilateral or young patients Plantar fasciitis results from repetitive traction overload at the origin of the plantar aponeurosis on the medial calcaneal tuberosity. The tissue undergoes microtearing and a degenerative response with collagen disorganisation, mucoid change, and thickening of the fascia rather than sustained acute inflammation. Impaired ankle dorsiflexion and tight gastrocsoleus increase tensile strain, and the failed healing perpetuates pain. The large majority of patients improve within six to twelve months with conservative treatment, though symptoms can be protracted; recalcitrant cases may benefit from extracorporeal shockwave therapy before considering surgery.

Plantar fibromatosis — Ledderhose disease, plantar fascial fibromatosis, Morbus Ledderhose Plantar fibroma versus a soft-tissue sarcoma such as synovial sarcoma or fibrosarcoma Plantar fascial rupture or chronic plantar fasciitis with a fibrotic nodule Ganglion or epidermal inclusion cyst of the sole Foreign-body granuloma or infective granuloma Rheumatoid or other inflammatory nodule Giant cell tumour of tendon sheath or fibrolipoma MRI of the foot to characterise fascial origin, collagen-rich signal and extent before intervention Ultrasound demonstrating a hypoechoic fusiform nodule contiguous with the plantar fascia Examination of the hands and, where relevant, the penis for associated superficial fibromatoses Core or excisional biopsy with histology when malignancy cannot be excluded on imaging Screening for associated conditions such as diabetes and chronic liver disease Baseline photographic and clinical mapping of nodule number and size for monitoring A benign fibroblastic and myofibroblastic proliferation of the plantar aponeurosis, presenting as one or more firm, slowly enlarging nodules in the medial or central band of the arch Nodules are typically fixed to the fascia but mobile relative to overlying skin, and are often bilateral; unlike Dupuytren disease they seldom produce fixed toe contractures because the digital extensions of the fascia are less involved It forms part of the superficial fibromatosis or fibromatosis diathesis, so associations with Dupuytren contracture of the hand, Peyronie disease and Garrod knuckle pads should be sought Reported associations include diabetes, chronic alcohol use, chronic liver disease, epilepsy and long-term anticonvulsant therapy MRI is characteristic, showing an infiltrative fascial lesion that is typically low to intermediate in signal on both T1 and T2 owing to its dense collagen content, which helps distinguish it from a sarcoma Histology shows bland spindled myofibroblasts within dense collagen without atypia, distinguishing it from fibrosarcoma and other malignant soft-tissue tumours First-line treatment is non-operative with soft accommodative orthoses and padding to offload the nodule; surgery is reserved for disabling disease and carries a high recurrence rate Recurrence is substantially lower after wide or complete plantar fasciectomy than after simple local nodule excision, at the cost of greater morbidity Rapid growth, size beyond a few centimetres, or a deep and poorly defined mass suggesting sarcoma High T2 signal, marked enhancement or bony involvement on imaging atypical for benign fibromatosis Skin ulceration, fixation or neurovascular compromise Systemic symptoms or regional lymphadenopathy Mistaking an aggressive soft-tissue sarcoma for a benign fibroma and performing an unplanned marginal excision Undertaking simple nodule excision and underestimating the high recurrence risk compared with wider fasciectomy Damaging plantar nerves or creating a painful plantar scar and contracture during surgery Attributing arch pain solely to plantar fasciitis and missing an underlying fibromatosis nodule Plantar fibromatosis is a locally infiltrative but biologically benign proliferation of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts within the plantar aponeurosis, most often the medial band. Disordered wound-healing-type signalling with excess transforming growth factor beta and platelet-derived growth factor drives myofibroblast proliferation and deposition of dense type III and type I collagen, producing the palpable nodules. Repetitive microtrauma, a genetic predisposition shared with other superficial fibromatoses, and metabolic factors such as diabetes and alcohol are thought to contribute. Progression through cellular proliferative, involutional and residual collagenous phases parallels the pattern seen in Dupuytren disease, though contracture of the toes is far less common because the vertical and digital fascial extensions are relatively spared. Plantar fibromatosis is benign and does not metastasise, but it is prone to local recurrence, and postoperative recurrence is common after limited excision; symptoms are often controlled long term with orthoses, with surgery reserved for refractory disabling disease.

Plantar plate tear — plantar plate insufficiency, plantar plate rupture, lesser MTP joint instability, predislocation syndrome Interdigital (Morton's) neuroma Freiberg's infraction of the metatarsal head Metatarsophalangeal joint synovitis from inflammatory arthritis Metatarsal stress fracture Mechanical metatarsalgia from other causes Hammer or claw toe deformity from other mechanisms Capsulitis of the metatarsophalangeal joint Clinical examination including the modified drawer test and inspection for crossover deformity and the V-sign Weight-bearing foot radiographs to assess metatarsal length, alignment, and toe position Ultrasound to visualise the plantar plate and dynamic instability MRI to confirm and grade the tear and assess collateral ligament involvement Assessment for associated hallux valgus and metatarsal length abnormality Pedobarography to characterise forefoot overload where relevant Inflammatory markers and serology if a synovitic or inflammatory cause is suspected The plantar plate is the fibrocartilaginous plantar stabiliser of the lesser metatarsophalangeal joint, and its attrition or tear causes pain and progressive instability The second toe is most commonly affected, and patients describe plantar pain at the base of the toe, often with a feeling of walking on a lump and swelling of the joint The modified drawer (Lachman-type) test, in which long metatarsal that drives recurrence if uncorrected Assuming conservative treatment will heal a complete tear rather than merely control symptoms Missing an inflammatory arthropathy underlying multiple-joint synovitis The plantar plate is a thick fibrocartilaginous structure on the plantar surface of the lesser metatarsophalangeal joint that resists dorsiflexion and hyperextension and, together with the collateral ligaments, provides the main static stability of the joint. Chronic dorsiflexion overload, as occurs with a long metatarsal, hallux valgus that crowds the second toe, high-heeled footwear, or inflammatory disease, produces cumulative attritional injury that weakens and eventually tears the plate, usually near its insertion into the base of the proximal phalanx. As the plantar restraint fails, the proximal phalanx drifts dorsally and the toe becomes unstable, and asymmetrical involvement of the collateral ligaments allows medial deviation, giving the characteristic crossover second toe that overrides the hallux. Loss of the plantar cushioning contributes to metatarsalgia beneath the involved head. The process is typically gradual and degenerative rather than the result of a single acute event. Early and partial tears often stabilise or improve with offloading, taping, and footwear modification, though these measures control symptoms rather than heal the plate. Once fixed deformity or dislocation develops, conservative treatment is less effective and surgical plantar plate repair or reconstruction with deformity correction is required; results are generally good but some residual stiffness, recurrence, or floating toe may occur.

MRI of spine/pelvis for focal lesions Serum calcium, creatinine/creatinine clearance, and hemoglobin (to assess CRAB end-organ damage) VEGF level and evaluation for Castleman's disease when POEMS is suspected Tissue biopsy with Congo red staining and mass spectrometry-based typing when amyloidosis is suspected (SPEP/UPEP alone are inadequate screens for AL) M components in other lymphoid neoplasms (CLL, B- or T-cell lymphomas) M components in nonlymphoid neoplasms (chronic myeloid leukemia, breast cancer, colon cancer) Nonneoplastic conditions: cirrhosis, sarcoidosis, parasitic diseases, Gaucher's disease, pyoderma gangrenosum Autoimmune conditions: rheumatoid arthritis, myasthenia gravis, cold agglutinin disease Post organ-transplant immunosuppression (and rarely allogeneic transplant) Skin diseases with monoclonal gammopathy: lichen myxedematosus (papular mucinosis), necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (~10% progress to myeloma) Mixed cryoglobulinemia (IgM/IgA complexed with IgG) seen in rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune disease, usually not associated with malignancy Plasma cell disorders are monoclonal neoplasms of late B-lymphocyte lineage; the group includes multiple myeloma (MM), Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, primary (AL) amyloidosis, and the heavy chain diseases, also termed monoclonal gammopathies, paraproteinemias, plasma cell dyscrasias, or dysproteinemias (Harrison 22e p.883). MGUS is vastly more common than myeloma, occurring in ~1% of the population aged >50 and up to ~10% of those aged >75; no specific intervention is indicated and annual (or less frequent) follow-up is adequate, with closer monitoring only for higher-risk MGUS (Harrison 22e p.887-890). About ~1% of MGUS patients per year progress to myeloma, but essentially all cases of myeloma are preceded by MGUS (Harrison 22e p.887). Higher-risk MGUS features are non-IgG subtype, abnormal kappa/lambda free light chain ratio, and serum M-protein >15 g/L (1.5 g/dL); absence of all three predicts ~5% progression while presence of all three predicts ~60% progression over 20 years (Harrison 22e p.887). Diagnostic workup for a monoclonal protein uses serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) for quantitation and immunoelectrophoresis/immunofixation for confirmation of a single heavy and/or light chain; serum free light chain assay and urine studies (UPEP) detect light-chain-only and Bence Jones disease (Harrison 22e p.883-884). An M component must be present at ~5 g/L (0.5 g/dL) to be accurately quantitated by electrophoresis; the serum M-protein level is a reliable measure of tumor burden but is not specific enough to screen asymptomatic patients (Harrison 22e p.883-884). MGUS diagnostic criteria: serum monoclonal protein (non-IgM) <30 g/L, clonal bone marrow plasma cells <10%, and absence of myeloma-defining events or amyloidosis attributable to the plasma cell disorder (Harrison 22e p.888, Table 116-1). Waldenström's macroglobulinemia (WM) is a malignancy of IgM-secreting lymphoplasmacytoid cells; unlike myeloma it presents with lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly and its major manifestation is hyperviscosity syndrome (Harrison 22e p.893). A distinct MYD88 L265P somatic mutation is present in >90% of WM patients and the majority of IgM MGUS, and is used as a diagnostic test to discriminate WM from marginal zone lymphoma, IgM-secreting myeloma, and CLL with plasmacytic differentiation (Harrison 22e p.893). In WM the IgM may have specificity for myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG); a peripheral neuropathy may precede the neoplasm and about half of these patients are anti-MAG positive (Harrison 22e p.893). POEMS syndrome = Polyneuropathy, Organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, M-protein, and Skin changes; patients typically have a severe progressive sensorimotor polyneuropathy with sclerotic bone lesions, and polyneuropathy occurs in only ~1.4% of myelomas with POEMS being a rare subset (Harrison 22e p.893). AL (primary) amyloidosis is a plasma cell disorder most often caused by clonal bone marrow plasma cells secreting a misfolding monoclonal light chain; it can coexist with multiple myeloma, Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, or non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.896-897). Macroglossia and periorbital ('raccoon-eye') ecchymoses are pathognomonic but uncommon signs of AL amyloidosis, each seen in only ~10% of patients (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.897). Hyperviscosity syndrome in Waldenström's macroglobulinemia / IgM gammopathy: headache, visual disturbance, retinal vein segmentation and dilation, epistaxis, altered consciousness, paresis (most IgM is intravascular and responds to plasmapheresis) Myeloma-defining end-organ damage (CRAB): hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lytic lesions Spinal cord compression: new lower-extremity neurologic deficit, severe localized back pain, or loss of bowel/bladder control requiring emergency MRI and radiation/decompression Acute renal failure from light chain cast nephropathy, especially with dehydration Cardiac involvement in AL amyloidosis (70-80%) is the leading cause of death; low-voltage ECG with pseudo-infarct pattern and thickened ventricles on echo MGUS with severe polyneuropathy (consider causal IgM/anti-MAG neuropathy) Do not equate a monoclonal protein with malignancy: distinguish MGUS (clonal marrow plasma cells <10%, M-protein <30 g/L, no myeloma-defining events/amyloidosis) from multiple myeloma, which requires marrow plasmacytosis and myeloma-defining events / CRAB end-organ damage (Harrison 22e p.887-888). SPEP/UPEP are useful in myeloma but are NOT adequate screening tests for AL amyloidosis, because the clonal light chain is often insufficient to produce an M-spike; use serum/urine immunofixation and free light chain assay (>90% positive) (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.897). A monoclonal protein alone is not diagnostic of amyloidosis since MGUS is common in older patients; when MGUS coexists with biopsy-proven amyloidosis, AL type must be ruled out and 'smoldering myeloma' patients should be screened for AL (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.897). WM does not cause bone lesions or hypercalcemia (unlike myeloma); large IgM paraprotein causes little renal excretion so renal disease is uncommon (~20% excrete light chains)—reserve the diagnosis of IgM myeloma for lytic bone lesions with CD138+ plasma cells and t(11;14) (Harrison 22e p.893). Suspected cryoglobulin: draw blood into a warm syringe and transport in warm water to avoid errors in quantitation (Harrison 22e p.893). Rituximab can produce an IgM flare in WM—use plasmapheresis first or initially withhold rituximab in patients with high IgM levels (Harrison 22e p.894). Pseudohyponatremia and a decreased anion gap can occur in myeloma because the cationic M component retains chloride and displaces serum water (Harrison 22e p.887). In normal B-cell maturation, antigen exposure drives differentiation of mature B lymphocytes into antibody-secreting plasma cells; in plasma cell disorders this control is lost, producing a monoclonal expansion that secretes a single (monoclonal) immunoglobulin or fragment (M component). Clinical manifestations arise from neoplastic cell expansion, from the secreted products (intact immunoglobulin, free light/heavy chains, lymphokines), and from the host response. In multiple myeloma, recurrent chromosomal lesions include hyperdiploidy and 14q32 translocations (e.g., t(11;14), t(4;14), t(14;16)), with errors in immunoglobulin switch recombination implicated in early transformation. Waldenström's macroglobulinemia arises from a post-germinal-center IgM-bearing memory B cell, driven by MYD88 L265P (TLR/IL-1R IRAK and NF-kB signaling, plus BTK/HCK signaling) and frequently CXCR4 mutations. In AL amyloidosis, clonal plasma cells produce a monoclonal light chain (lambda predominates) that misfolds into insoluble amyloid fibrils deposited extracellularly in tissues (Harrison 22e p.883-884, 893; ch.117 p.896-897). MGUS carries a low malignant potential, with ~1% per year progression to myeloma (risk stratified by IgG vs non-IgG subtype, free light chain ratio, and M-protein level: ~5% at 20 years with no risk features vs ~60% with all three). Smoldering myeloma progresses to symptomatic MM in ~25% at 5 years with one risk feature and ~76% with all three high-risk features. Waldenström's macroglobulinemia is often indolent and may not require therapy; median survival is reported as ~50 months, with older age, male sex, general symptoms, and cytopenias defining a high-risk group. AL amyloidosis is often rapidly progressive and fatal if untreated (occurs after age 40); very low dFLC (<50 mg/L) predicts significantly better outcome (Harrison 22e p.887-888, 893-894; ch.117 p.896-898). MGUS vs smoldering (asymptomatic) myeloma vs symptomatic multiple myeloma per IMWG criteria (Harrison Table 116-1). MGUS: non-IgM serum M-protein <30 g/L, clonal marrow plasma cells <10%, no myeloma-defining events/amyloidosis. Smoldering MM: serum M-protein (IgG/IgA) >=30 g/L or urine M-protein >=500 mg/24h and/or clonal marrow plasma cells 10-60%, without myeloma-defining events. Symptomatic MM: clonal plasma cells (or plasmacytoma) plus a myeloma-defining event—CRAB end-organ damage (hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lesions) or a biomarker of malignancy (clonal marrow plasma cells >=60%, involved:uninvolved serum free light chain ratio >=100, or >1 focal MRI lesion). POEMS requires polyneuropathy + monoclonal plasma cell disorder + (sclerotic bone lesions / Castleman's / elevated VEGF) + an additional system feature.

Monoclonal immunoglobulin production and marrow infiltration drive end-organ damage, including renal impairment from light chains, hypercalcaemia and osteolytic bone disease with cytopenias. The aggressive biology reflects the accumulation of adverse genetic lesions and explains the rapid clinical course. Plasma cell leukaemia carries a significantly worse prognosis than multiple myeloma, though outcomes have improved with modern combination therapy and, in suitable patients, stem cell transplantation; secondary disease evolving from myeloma has a particularly poor outlook.

marrow-retention signals of ordinary myeloma and circulates freely in the blood, reflecting altered adhesion-molecule expression such as reduced CD56. Primary disease arises without an antecedent plasma-cell disorder, while secondary disease evolves from progressive multiple myeloma. The clone frequently harbours high-risk genomic changes, including TP53 loss through deletion 17p and MYC rearrangements, driving proliferation, genomic instability and extramedullary dissemination. Widespread infiltration of blood, marrow and extramedullary sites produces the profound cytopenias, end-organ damage and monoclonal protein burden that define the aggressive clinical picture. Plasma cell leukaemia carries a markedly worse prognosis than multiple myeloma, with shorter survival despite modern therapy; secondary disease is particularly aggressive, and outcomes are best when intensive combination treatment and autologous HSCT can be delivered to eligible patients.

have differentiated to the plasmablast stage, losing mature B-cell antigens while acquiring a plasma-cell secretory phenotype. It arises predominantly in immunodeficient hosts, in whom impaired immune surveillance permits Epstein-Barr virus-driven proliferation of terminally differentiating B-cells. Frequent rearrangement of the MYC oncogene amplifies proliferative drive, producing the characteristic high growth fraction and rapidly enlarging masses. Because the neoplastic cells resemble plasma cells, the tumour lies at the interface between lymphoma and plasma-cell neoplasia. The disease is aggressive with generally short survival, though control of HIV with antiretroviral therapy and intensive combination chemotherapy can improve outcomes; MYC rearrangement and advanced stage predict worse results.

and overlooking the inherited cause Plasminogen is the zymogen of plasmin, the principal enzyme of fibrinolysis. In severe deficiency, insufficient plasmin activity means fibrin deposited at sites of minor mucosal injury or inflammation cannot be cleared, so it accumulates as firm, woody pseudomembranes rich in fibrin. The defect is one of extravascular fibrin clearance on wet epithelial surfaces, which explains why the eyes, gums, airway and other mucous membranes are affected while systemic thrombosis is uncommon. Plasminogen replacement can markedly improve mucosal lesions, so prognosis has improved where such therapy is available.

plastic bronchitis — cast bronchitis, fibrinous bronchitis mucoid impaction in allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis aspirated foreign body causing lobar collapse thick tenacious secretions in cystic fibrosis or severe asthma endobronchial tumour or broncholith with obstruction pulmonary haemorrhage with organised clot cast diphtheritic or other pseudomembranous airway disease acute chest syndrome of sickle cell disease flexible or rigid bronchoscopy for cast extraction and airway inspection histopathological analysis of the cast to classify lymphatic versus inflammatory type chest CT to assess atelectasis, bronchiectasis and mediastinal or lymphatic abnormality dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance lymphangiography or intranodal lymphangiography echocardiography and assessment of Fontan haemodynamics in relevant patients evaluation for asthma and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis where inflammatory casts are found haemoglobinopathy screening where sickle cell disease is suspected Plastic bronchitis is characterised by the formation of large, cohesive, branching airway casts that take the shape of the bronchial tree and are expectorated or removed bronchoscopically. Expectoration of a rubbery, branching cast is virtually diagnostic; patients may describe coughing up a 'tree-shaped' or 'model' of their airways. In children it is classically associated with congenital heart disease following Fontan-type palliation, where abnormal lymphatic flow drives cast formation. Other associations include asthma and allergic bronchopulmonary disease, sickle cell acute chest syndrome, and lymphatic disorders or thoracic duct abnormalities. Casts are broadly divided into lymphatic/acellular fibrin-rich types (often in cardiac and lymphatic disease) and inflammatory eosinophil- or mucin-rich types (often in asthma and allergic disease). Acute large-cast impaction can cause lobar or whole-lung collapse and life-threatening airway obstruction, sometimes with sudden severe respiratory distress. Bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic, allowing extraction of casts and sampling to characterise their composition. In lymphatic disease, cross-sectional lymphatic imaging can identify abnormal pulmonary lymphatic flow amenable to lymphatic embolisation or surgical correction. acute severe respiratory distress from central cast impaction lobar or whole-lung collapse on imaging hypoxaemia or asphyxiation risk requiring urgent airway clearance recurrent casts in a Fontan patient indicating protein-losing lymphatic complications haemoptysis suggesting vascular involvement Failing to retrieve and analyse the cast, thereby missing the distinction between lymphatic and inflammatory types that dictates treatment. Treating recurrent Fontan-associated casts purely as mucus without investigating pulmonary lymphatic flow. Underestimating the risk of acute asphyxiation from a mobile central cast. Overlooking allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis or poorly controlled asthma as a driver of inflammatory casts. Relying on mucolytics or physiotherapy alone in refractory disease without escalating to bronchoscopy or lymphatic intervention. Plastic bronchitis involves the accumulation and consolidation of material within the airways into firm, cohesive casts that replicate the branching bronchial anatomy. In lymphatic-type disease, often after Fontan palliation of single-ventricle physiology, chronically elevated systemic venous and lymphatic pressures cause abnormal pulmonary lymphatic networks to leak protein-rich, fibrin-laden lymph into the airways, which coagulates into acellular fibrinous casts. In inflammatory-type disease, airway inflammation — as in asthma, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis or the acute chest syndrome of sickle cell disease — generates mucin, fibrin and cellular exudate (frequently eosinophil-rich) that inspissates into casts. Once formed, a cast behaves as an obstructing intraluminal plug: it impairs ventilation of the subtended lung, promotes atelectasis and post-obstructive infection, and, if it dislodges into a central airway, can cause acute critical obstruction. The composition of the cast reflects the underlying mechanism and guides directed therapy. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause: inflammatory casts related to asthma or allergic disease often respond to control of airway inflammation, whereas Fontan-associated lymphatic plastic bronchitis is more refractory, though lymphatic imaging and targeted embolisation have substantially improved outcomes in selected patients.

peripheral crowding Not distinguishing plateau iris syndrome from malignant glaucoma, which needs very different treatment In plateau iris the ciliary body and its processes sit abnormally far forward, mechanically supporting and displacing the peripheral iris towards the trabecular meshwork so that the angle is crowded. The central anterior chamber remains reasonably deep because the mechanism is peripheral rather than a generalised forward shift of the iris-lens diaphragm. A relative pupillary-block element may coexist, which a laser peripheral iridotomy relieves; when appositional angle closure persists despite a patent iridotomy, the residual peripheral crowding from the anteriorly placed ciliary processes defines plateau iris syndrome. Pupil dilation worsens the situation by folding the peripheral iris into the already narrow angle, and chronic apposition can lead to peripheral anterior synechiae and pressure elevation. With recognition and treatment, including iridotomy and iridoplasty where needed, angle closure is often controlled and the prognosis is good, but unrecognised plateau iris can cause progressive synechial closure and glaucomatous damage requiring ongoing surveillance and sometimes further intervention.

elevated in DIC) Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test if anemia present (rule out Evans syndrome) Secondary ITP workup: HIV, hepatitis C, SLE serology, serum protein electrophoresis, immunoglobulin levels, IgA deficiency / monoclonal gammopathy testing, H. pylori Complement regulatory gene DNA variant testing for atypical HUS Pseudothrombocytopenia from EDTA-induced platelet clumping (in vitro artifact) Myelodysplasia presenting as isolated thrombocytopenia Iron deficiency, inflammation, or malignancy causing reactive thrombocytosis (when evaluating platelet count abnormalities) Other microangiopathies: bone marrow transplant-associated, drug-induced, pregnancy-related, and vasculitis-associated Thrombocytopenia arises from one or more of three mechanisms: decreased bone marrow production, sequestration (usually in an enlarged spleen), and/or increased platelet destruction (Harrison 22e p.921). First step in evaluating thrombocytopenia is reviewing the peripheral blood smear and ruling out pseudothrombocytopenia, especially when there is no apparent cause (Harrison 22e p.921). Petechiae are pinpoint, nonblanching hemorrhages that usually signify a decreased platelet number rather than platelet dysfunction; they first appear in areas of increased venous pressure (ankles/feet in ambulatory patients) (Harrison 22e p.921-922). Wet purpura (blood blisters on the oral mucosa) and retinal hemorrhages are thought to denote an increased risk of life-threatening hemorrhage in the thrombocytopenic patient (Harrison 22e p.922, 924). Drugs are the most common cause of thrombocytopenia; in a patient with no apparent cause, all drugs (including herbal and OTC preparations) should be suspect and stopped or substituted if possible (Harrison 22e p.922). Infection is the most common noniatrogenic cause of thrombocytopenia; viral and bacterial infections can affect both platelet production and survival, and immune mechanisms may also contribute (Harrison 22e p.921-922). In HIT, thrombocytopenia is usually not severe (nadir rarely <20,000/uL) and is not associated with bleeding; instead it markedly increases the risk of thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.923). Most patients develop HIT 5-14 days after heparin exposure; onset before 5 days suggests prior heparin exposure within ~100 days with circulating anti-heparin/PF4 antibodies (Harrison 22e p.923). ITP is characterized by mucocutaneous bleeding and a low, often very low, platelet count with an otherwise normal peripheral blood smear and cell counts (Harrison 22e p.924). In thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP/HUS) the PT and aPTT are characteristically normal, which helps distinguish them from DIC, where a coagulopathy predominates with elevated PT and often aPTT (Harrison 22e p.924-925). An ADAMTS13 activity level of <10% is diagnostic of TTP (Harrison 22e p.925). Markedly elevated platelet counts (>1.5 million), usually in a myeloproliferative disorder, carry an increased risk of bleeding rather than thrombosis, due in part to acquired von Willebrand disease (Harrison 22e p.926). HIT: thrombosis (venous and/or arterial) despite a falling platelet count -- stop all heparin immediately (including LMWH, which cross-reacts) and start a non-heparin anticoagulant Wet purpura (oral mucosal blood blisters) and retinal hemorrhages herald life-threatening, including CNS, bleeding VITT: high D-dimer with thrombosis in unusual sites such as cerebral venous sinuses (fatal in ~20%) New thrombocytopenia with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes) suggesting TTP -- a devastating disease if not promptly diagnosed and treated Severe thrombocytopenia (<5000/uL) or signs of impending bleeding in ITP requiring urgent inpatient combined-modality therapy Introducing warfarin alone in HIT/HITT may precipitate thrombosis (e.g., venous gangrene) due to reduced protein C and S Pseudothrombocytopenia: EDTA-induced platelet agglutination is an in vitro artifact and not true thrombocytopenia; confirm with a smear and a count in citrate/heparin or fresh fingerstick blood. Anti-heparin/PF4 antibodies are common without clinical disease (e.g., ~50% after cardiopulmonary bypass), so the HIT immunoassay has low specificity; HIT remains a clinical diagnosis. The 4T score is very useful for excluding HIT but overdiagnoses it in settings (e.g., ICU) where thrombocytopenia and thrombosis from other causes are common. LMWH cross-reacts with HIT antibodies and must not be used to treat HIT. Starting warfarin alone in HIT/HITT may precipitate thrombosis and venous gangrene; overlap with a DTI, fondaparinux, or DOAC and start only after thrombocytopenia resolves. Serologic (antibody) testing in ITP is generally unhelpful due to low sensitivity and specificity. Plasma infusion/exchange has not been shown to alter the overall course of HUS or atypical HUS (except aHUS with antibodies to factor H). Petechiae indicate decreased platelet number, not platelet dysfunction -- excessive bruising can occur with disorders of either number or function. Hemostasis depends on platelets and the vessel wall. Platelets are activated on adhesion to von Willebrand factor (VWF) and collagen in exposed subendothelium after injury; adhesion (primarily via VWF) generates signals activating the GpIIb/IIIa (alphaIIb-beta3) receptor and aggregation, with release of granule contents and stabilization by a fibrin mesh. Normal platelet count is 150,000-450,000/uL; thrombopoietin (TPO), made in the liver, is the major regulator, and roughly one-third of platelets reside in the spleen. Thrombocytopenia results from decreased production, splenic sequestration, and/or increased destruction. In HIT, antibodies form to a complex of platelet factor 4 (PF4) and heparin/glycosaminoglycans; the anti-heparin/PF4 antibody activates platelets via the FcgammaRIIa receptor and also activates monocytes, endothelium, and coagulation, producing a prothrombotic state. ITP is immune-mediated platelet destruction with possible inhibition of platelet release from megakaryocytes. In TTP, deficiency of or antibodies to the metalloprotease ADAMTS13 leave ultra-large VWF multimers uncleaved, driving pathogenic platelet adhesion/aggregation and microvascular thrombosis. HUS features acute renal failure with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia; atypical HUS arises from genetic complement-regulatory defects or anti-complement-regulator antibodies causing chronic complement activation. ITP: in children usually acute, post-infectious, and self-limited; in adults more chronic, though some remit spontaneously within months. Patients with platelet counts >30,000/uL appear not to have increased mortality from the thrombocytopenia. TTP: introduction of plasma exchange reduced mortality from 85-100% to 10-30%; however 25-45% relapse within 30 days of remission and 12-40% have late relapses, with relapses more frequent in those with severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. HUS: diarrhea-associated HUS has overall mortality <5% (about 40% of children need dialysis), whereas non-diarrhea-associated HUS mortality is higher (~26%). VITT is fatal in about 20%. No single formal grading scale is given; clinically meaningful thresholds noted: ~5000-10,000/uL platelets needed to maintain microvascular integrity; severe ITP thrombocytopenia <5000/uL (or impending bleeding) warrants inpatient combined-modality therapy; ITP counts >30,000/uL not associated with increased mortality; HIT nadir rarely <20,000/uL; ADAMTS13 activity <10% diagnostic of TTP; platelet counts >1.5 million (myeloproliferative) carry bleeding risk. The 4Ts score is used for HIT pretest probability.

disease Genetic testing for syndromic forms such as Hermansky-Pudlak or gray platelet syndrome A group of inherited platelet secretion defects caused by deficiency of dense (delta) granules, alpha granules, or both, producing mild to moderate mucocutaneous bleeding Typical features are easy bruising, epistaxis, menorrhagia, and prolonged bleeding after surgery or dental procedures despite a normal platelet count Dense-granule deficiency can be part of syndromic disorders such as Hermansky-Pudlak (with oculocutaneous albinism) and Chediak-Higashi syndrome Alpha-granule deficiency defines gray platelet syndrome, in which platelets appear large and agranular (gray) on the blood film with a tendency to progressive myelofibrosis Light transmission aggregometry classically shows an absent secondary wave and impaired response to weak agonists, with a blunted ATP release The platelet count is usually normal or only mildly reduced, so the defect is qualitative rather than quantitative Management centres on avoiding antiplatelet drugs, using antifibrinolytics and local measures, and reserving platelet transfusion for significant bleeding or surgery Severe or unexpected perioperative or postpartum haemorrhage Bleeding compounded by inadvertent antiplatelet drug use Features of a syndromic disorder such as albinism or recurrent infections suggesting a broader diagnosis Progressive cytopenias or splenomegaly suggesting marrow fibrosis in gray platelet syndrome Overlooking the diagnosis because the platelet count is normal Missing an underlying syndrome such as Hermansky-Pudlak by not examining for albinism Attributing aggregation abnormalities to recent antiplatelet drug use without a proper drug-free interval Failing to give perioperative haemostatic cover for an apparently mild disorder Platelet storage pool disease reflects a failure to form, fill, or release the contents of platelet secretory granules. Dense (delta) granules store ADP, ATP, calcium, and serotonin, which amplify platelet activation and recruitment; their deficiency blunts the secondary aggregation response. Alpha granules store adhesive and procoagulant proteins including von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, and platelet factor 4, and their absence in gray platelet syndrome impairs platelet function and is associated with marrow fibrosis. The resulting defective granule release weakens the platelet activation amplification loop and produces a mucocutaneous bleeding tendency. Most patients have a mild, manageable bleeding tendency compatible with a normal life when antiplatelet agents are avoided and procedures are covered. Prognosis is modified by any associated syndrome, and gray platelet syndrome may progress to clinically significant myelofibrosis.

surgical closure of an intracardiac defect can be curative, whereas intrapulmonary causes are managed according to their underlying disease Severe positional hypoxaemia limiting the patient to a recumbent posture Hypoxaemia poorly responsive to supplemental oxygen, indicating true shunt Paradoxical embolic events such as stroke through an intracardiac shunt Rapidly progressive desaturation suggesting worsening shunt fraction Measuring oxygenation only supine and thereby missing orthodeoxia Assuming an incidental patent foramen ovale is sufficient without seeking the anatomical factor that makes it shunt Failing to distinguish intracardiac from intrapulmonary shunting before intervention Attributing positional breathlessness to deconditioning or anxiety Overlooking hepatopulmonary syndrome as an intrapulmonary cause Platypnoea-orthodeoxia syndrome arises from a right-to-left shunt whose magnitude increases in the upright posture. In the intracardiac form there is an interatrial communication such as a patent foramen ovale, but the shunt only becomes haemodynamically significant when an additional anatomical or functional factor, for example an elongated or dilated aortic root, right pneumonectomy, or pericardial change, alters the geometry of the atria so that inferior vena caval flow is preferentially directed across the septum on standing. In the intrapulmonary form, dilated or abnormal vessels at the lung bases, as seen in hepatopulmonary syndrome or arteriovenous malformations, receive more perfusion when upright, increasing the fraction of venous blood bypassing gas exchange. In both mechanisms, standing augments the shunt and produces the characteristic positional hypoxaemia and breathlessness. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; closure of a responsible intracardiac defect is frequently curative with immediate resolution of the positional hypoxaemia. Intrapulmonary causes carry the prognosis of the underlying pulmonary or hepatic disease.

Pleomorphic adenoma — Benign mixed tumour, Mixed tumour of salivary gland Warthin tumour Basal cell adenoma Myoepithelioma Adenoid cystic carcinoma Mucoepidermoid carcinoma Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma Schwannoma of the facial nerve Fine-needle aspiration cytology (with core biopsy where cytology is equivocal) Ultrasound of the gland and neck as first-line imaging MRI showing a well-defined, lobulated, markedly T2-hyperintense lesion CT where bony involvement or deep-lobe extension is suspected Assessment of facial nerve function before intervention Histological examination of the excised specimen with margin assessment The commonest salivary gland neoplasm overall, most often arising in the superficial lobe and tail of the parotid as a painless, slow-growing, mobile mass. Histologically biphasic and truly 'mixed': epithelial and myoepithelial cells set within a chondromyxoid or hyaline stroma, giving the classic myxoid appearance. Driven in most cases by PLAG1 rearrangement (8q12) or, less often, HMGA2 (12q), frequently through gene fusions such as CTNNB1-PLAG1. The capsule is characteristically incomplete with finger-like pseudopodia and satellite nodules, so simple enucleation predisposes to recurrence. Recommended treatment is complete excision with a cuff of normal tissue (superficial or partial parotidectomy for parotid lesions) with facial nerve preservation. Fine-needle aspiration cytology typically shows metachromatic fibrillary matrix with epithelial and myoepithelial cells; a hypercellular aspirate should not be over-called as malignant. Long-standing tumours carry a rising risk of malignant transformation to carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma, so a sudden change in a chronic lump is significant. Deep-lobe or parapharyngeal lesions may present as a dumbbell-shaped mass with medial displacement of the tonsil and soft palate. Sudden rapid growth or pain in a previously stable mass, suggesting malignant transformation Facial nerve weakness or palsy Fixation to skin or deep tissues or overlying skin ulceration New cervical lymphadenopathy Rapidly enlarging long-standing tumour present for many years Enucleation or capsular breach with tumour spillage leading to multinodular recurrence that is difficult to eradicate Over-interpreting a cellular aspirate as malignant on fine-needle aspiration cytology Overlooking a deep-lobe or parapharyngeal component on clinical examination Failing to recognise malignant transformation in a chronic, recently changed swelling Inadequate facial nerve identification during parotid surgery Pleomorphic adenoma arises from the terminal duct and myoepithelial cell compartment of salivary tissue and is characterised by both epithelial and mesenchymal-appearing differentiation from a common neoplastic clone. Recurrent chromosomal translocations activate the transcription factors PLAG1 or HMGA2, which reprogramme cellular growth and drive proliferation of ductal epithelial and modified myoepithelial cells. The neoplastic myoepithelial cells elaborate an abundant extracellular matrix that undergoes chondromyxoid, myxoid and occasionally osseous change, producing the tumour's distinctive heterogeneous stroma. Growth is expansile with a fibrous but frequently incomplete pseudocapsule, through which small tumour buds and satellite nodules extend, accounting for recurrence after incomplete removal and for the field of tumour left behind if the capsule is breached. Prognosis is excellent after adequate complete excision, with low recurrence when the capsule is respected. The principal long-term concern is malignant transformation, the risk of which rises with the duration the tumour has been present.

refractory seizures Leptomeningeal dissemination in higher-grade tumours Overcalling the marked pleomorphism as glioblastoma and overtreating a lower-grade tumour Failing to recognise anaplastic PXA and underestimating recurrence risk Not testing for BRAF V600E, missing a targetable alteration Incomplete resection of a superficial, potentially curable lesion Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma is an astrocytic tumour arising superficially in the cerebral hemispheres, characteristically in the temporal lobe and often reaching the leptomeninges. It is thought to derive from astrocytes or subpial progenitor cells. Despite alarming histological pleomorphism, including large bizarre and lipid-laden cells, the typical tumour is relatively circumscribed and lower grade. Activation of the MAP kinase pathway, most often via the BRAF V600E mutation, frequently combined with homozygous deletion of CDKN2A/B, drives tumorigenesis. Higher mitotic activity defines the anaplastic (grade 3) variant, which is more prone to recurrence and progression. Its cortical position accounts for the prominence of seizures. Prognosis for the grade 2 tumour is generally good after gross total resection, with prolonged survival, whereas the anaplastic (grade 3) variant recurs more readily and carries a poorer outlook. BRAF status, extent of resection and grade are the main determinants, and BRAF/MEK-directed therapy offers an option for recurrent or anaplastic BRAF V600E-mutant disease.

Pleural effusion — CXR / thoracic ultrasound Diagnostic pleural tap (Light's criteria) Empyema if infected — needs drainage Congestive heart failure (typically bilateral transudative effusions) (Harrison 22e p.314) Cirrhosis / hepatic hydrothorax (often right-sided) (Harrison 22e p.366, p.373) Nephrotic syndrome and other hypoalbuminemic states (Harrison 22e p.422) Parapneumonic effusion / empyema complicating pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1235) Malignant effusion (e.g., lung cancer, metastatic disease) (Harrison 22e p.662) Tuberculous pleurisy (Harrison 22e p.1430) Pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.314) Tuberculous pleural effusion — straw-colored (sometimes hemorrhagic) lymphocyte-predominant exudate that can mimic a parapneumonic or malignant effusion (Harrison 22e p.1430). Tuberculous empyema, usually from rupture of a cavity into the pleural space, sometimes with a bronchopleural fistula and air in the pleural space (Harrison 22e p.1431). Spontaneous bacterial empyema complicating hepatic hydrothorax in cirrhosis (Harrison 22e p.373). Diagnostic thoracentesis to determine whether the fluid is a transudate or an exudate and to identify the underlying cause (Harrison 22e p.1430). Pleural fluid pH — a value of ≤7.1 in a parapneumonic setting indicates empyema requiring drainage (Harrison 22e p.1235). Pleural fluid protein, glucose, and cell count/differential; in TB the fluid is an exudate with protein >50% of serum (often ~4-6 g/dL), normal-to-low glucose, pH ~7.3 (occasionally <7.2), and 500-6000 WBC/uL, with neutrophils early and lymphocyte predominance later (Harrison 22e p.1430). Pleural fluid adenosine deaminase (ADA) — an elevated level is consistent with TB and a very low level helps exclude it (Harrison 22e p.1430). Pleural fluid IFN-gamma and lysozyme as adjuncts for suspected tuberculous effusion (Harrison 22e p.1430). Pleural fluid cytology for malignancy, with repeat thoracentesis if the first sample is negative (Harrison 22e p.663). Needle (closed) pleural biopsy for suspected TB, which reveals granulomas and/or yields positive culture in up to ~80% of cases and is favored over fluid analysis (Harrison 22e p.1430). Xpert MTB/RIF on pleural biopsy tissue (positive in ~75%); testing pleural fluid itself with this assay is not recommended owing to low sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.1430). Serum-to-pleural-fluid albumin gradient — a value >=1.1 g/dL suggests hepatic hydrothorax (Harrison 22e p.373). Heart-failure transudate, which can be unilateral and be mistaken for a localized pathologic effusion (Harrison 22e p.314). Hepatic hydrothorax from cirrhosis, mimicking other right-sided effusions (Harrison 22e p.366, p.373). Malignant effusion, which may be exudative or bloody and can coexist with or be confused for a parapneumonic effusion (Harrison 22e p.663). On examination an effusion gives dullness to percussion, reduced or absent breath sounds, and decreased tactile fremitus over the fluid; this contrasts with consolidation, where fremitus is increased (Harrison 22e p.2243). Percussion helps separate the two causes of a quiet hemithorax: an effusion is dull, whereas a pneumothorax is hyper-resonant (Harrison 22e p.2243). Skodaic resonance, a band of hyper-resonance just above the dull effusion, is a classic percussion sign (Harrison 22e p.89). Bilateral effusions are characteristic of congestive heart failure (and some collagen-vascular disorders), whereas a unilateral effusion should raise suspicion of malignancy or pulmonary embolism, though heart failure and parapneumonic effusion can also be unilateral (Harrison 22e p.314). A right-sided pleural effusion can occur in advanced cirrhosis even when no ascites is clinically detectable (Harrison 22e p.366). In a malignant effusion an initially negative thoracentesis does not exclude cancer; repeating the tap is essential because cytologic yield improves with repeat sampling (Harrison 22e p.663). Frank pus, organisms on microscopy, or pleural fluid pH <=7.1 in a parapneumonic effusion — diagnostic of empyema and mandates aggressive complete drainage, usually via chest tube (Harrison 22e p.1235). New or persistent fever and leukocytosis after 4-5 days of appropriate antibiotics for pneumonia — suspect empyema (Harrison 22e p.1235). Exudative or bloody effusion — raises concern for malignancy (Harrison 22e p.663). Unilateral effusion without an obvious cause — investigate for malignancy or pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.314). Avoid attributing every quiet, dull hemithorax to effusion — confirm with percussion and fremitus, since pneumothorax and consolidation differ (Harrison 22e p.2243). A negative initial pleural cytology does not rule out malignancy; failing to repeat the tap is a diagnostic pitfall (Harrison 22e p.663). Do not assume a unilateral effusion is benign heart failure — it may be malignant or embolic (Harrison 22e p.314). Testing pleural fluid (rather than biopsy tissue) with Xpert MTB/RIF is unreliable for TB because of low sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.1430). AFB smears are rarely positive and cultures are often falsely negative in tuberculous effusions, so a negative smear/culture does not exclude pleural TB (Harrison 22e p.1430). In hepatic hydrothorax, chest-tube placement should be avoided (Harrison 22e p.373). Fluid abnormally accumulates in the pleural space when the balance of hydrostatic and oncotic forces, lymphatic drainage, or capillary permeability is disturbed. Transudates arise from systemic forces (raised hydrostatic pressure or low plasma oncotic pressure) as in the sodium-avid edematous states of heart failure, cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome (Harrison 22e p.422). Exudates result from local pleural or capillary processes such as infection, malignancy, or inflammation. In hepatic hydrothorax, ascitic fluid migrates through diaphragmatic fenestrae into the pleural space (Harrison 22e p.373). Tuberculous effusion typically reflects a hypersensitivity reaction to mycobacterial antigens after recent primary infection, or contiguous spread from parenchymal disease (Harrison 22e p.1430). Malignant effusions arise from pleural involvement or from lymphatic obstruction by tumor (Harrison 22e p.662). Tuberculous pleural effusion responds rapidly to antituberculous chemotherapy and may even resolve spontaneously; concurrent glucocorticoids may shorten fever and chest pain but are of unproven benefit (Harrison 22e p.1430). Parapneumonic effusions are usually a self-limited inflammatory response, whereas a true empyema requires drainage and carries a worse course if undrained (Harrison 22e p.1235). Parapneumonic effusions are distinguished from empyema by their character: an uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion is a self-limited reaction to adjacent pneumonia, whereas frank pus, visible organisms, or a pleural fluid pH <=7.1 defines empyema (a complicated/infected collection) that requires complete drainage (Harrison 22e p.1235).

Pleural empyema — empyema, empyema thoracis, pyothorax, complicated parapneumonic effusion Uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion Malignant pleural effusion Tuberculous pleural effusion Haemothorax Lung abscess Transudative effusion from heart failure Diagnostic pleural aspiration with fluid pH, glucose, LDH, protein, Gram stain, and culture Chest ultrasound to detect loculations and guide sampling and drainage Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest to define pleural collections and underlying pathology Blood cultures and inflammatory markers to assess systemic infection Cytology and mycobacterial studies where malignancy or tuberculosis is possible Empyema is the presence of pus within the pleural space, most commonly a complication of bacterial pneumonia (parapneumonic effusion) Presents with persistent or worsening fever, pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, and failure to improve despite pneumonia treatment Suspect empyema when a parapneumonic effusion is large, loculated, or associated with ongoing sepsis Pleural fluid sampling is key; frankly purulent fluid, positive Gram stain or culture, low pH, low glucose, and high LDH indicate a complicated effusion or empyema needing drainage Contrast CT and ultrasound help characterise loculations, pleural thickening, and the underlying lung and guide drainage Effective management combines prompt drainage of the infected space with appropriate antimicrobial therapy covering likely organisms Loculated or organising collections may require intrapleural fibrinolytics or surgical intervention such as decortication Anaerobes and mixed flora are common, particularly with aspiration, and treatment should reflect the likely microbiology Signs of severe sepsis or septic shock Large or rapidly accumulating collection causing respiratory compromise Failure to improve despite antibiotics and initial drainage, suggesting loculation or trapped lung Development of a bronchopleural fistula or spreading infection Managing an infected pleural collection with antibiotics alone without adequate drainage Delaying pleural fluid sampling in a non-resolving pneumonia Underestimating loculated collections on plain radiography without ultrasound or CT Overlooking anaerobic or aspiration-related organisms when choosing antimicrobial cover Empyema typically evolves through stages from an initial free-flowing exudative parapneumonic effusion, as infection and inflammation increase pleural capillary permeability. Bacterial invasion of the pleural fluid promotes neutrophil influx, fibrin deposition, and metabolic activity that lower fluid pH and glucose and raise LDH. Fibrin strands then organise the collection into loculations (fibrinopurulent stage). If untreated, fibroblast proliferation produces a thick, inelastic pleural peel that traps the lung and restricts expansion (organising stage), impairing recovery. With early recognition, adequate drainage, and appropriate antibiotics, most patients recover well; delayed or inadequate treatment allows loculation and pleural thickening, leading to prolonged illness, the need for surgery, chronic respiratory impairment, and higher mortality, particularly in frail or comorbid patients.
