Inhaled asbestos fibres, particularly long amphibole fibres, are transported to the parietal pleura where they provoke a low-grade chronic inflammatory response. Over many years this drives deposition of dense, acellular collagen that forms well-demarcated islands of hyaline fibrosis, which frequently mineralise and calcify. The plaques sit on the parietal surface and, unlike diffuse pleural thickening or malignant disease, remain localised and do not invade underlying lung. They are a durable biological marker of cumulative asbestos exposure rather than a lesion that itself transforms into cancer. Isolated pleural plaques are benign with an excellent outlook and do not shorten life, but they mark asbestos exposure that confers a lasting risk of mesothelioma and lung cancer, so any new pleural symptoms should prompt reassessment.

pleural plaques — hyaline pleural plaques, asbestos-related pleural plaques Diffuse pleural thickening (asbestos-related or post-inflammatory) Malignant pleural mesothelioma Pleural metastases Extrapleural fat pads Fibrothorax from healed empyema or haemothorax Rounded atelectasis Rib companion shadows and other plain-film mimics Chest radiograph High-resolution CT of the thorax for characterisation and to exclude other disease Detailed occupational and exposure history Pulmonary function tests (usually normal; to detect coexistent asbestosis) Comparison with previous imaging to confirm stability Further characterisation with PET or biopsy only if features suggest malignancy Pleural plaques are discrete, well-circumscribed areas of hyaline (collagenous) fibrosis of the parietal pleura and are the commonest manifestation of asbestos exposure. They characteristically involve the posterolateral chest wall, the domes of the diaphragm and the mediastinal pleura, while sparing the costophrenic angles and lung apices. There is a long latency, typically 20 to 40 years from first exposure. Plaques are usually asymptomatic incidental radiological findings and rarely cause meaningful functional impairment. Calcification is common with time and aids radiological recognition. They are a marker of asbestos exposure and hence of increased risk of other asbestos-related disease, but are not themselves premalignant and do not transform into mesothelioma. CT is more sensitive and specific than chest radiography and helps separate plaques from mimics such as extrapleural fat. Their main importance is as a marker of exposure prompting counselling on mesothelioma and lung cancer risk and on smoking cessation. Pleural thickening that is nodular, circumferential or associated with a mass, raising concern for mesothelioma A new pleural effusion Chest pain or unexplained weight loss Progressive or asymmetric thickening on serial imaging Misinterpreting plaques as metastases or mesothelioma, or vice versa. Wrongly telling a patient that plaques turn into cancer, causing unnecessary alarm; they are markers, not precursors. Confusing extrapleural fat or normal muscle shadows with plaques on plain films. Failing to counsel on smoking cessation, which multiplies asbestos-related lung cancer risk. Overlooking coexisting asbestosis or an early mesothelioma. Inhaled asbestos fibres, particularly the longer amphibole fibres, are carried to the parietal pleura via lymphatic channels. There they incite a low-grade, chronic inflammatory and fibrogenic response with deposition of dense, relatively acellular basket-weave hyaline collagen, forming discrete plaques on the parietal pleura and diaphragm. Over years these plaques may calcify. Unlike diffuse pleural thickening and mesothelioma, plaques remain localised, typically spare the visceral pleura and reflect cumulative exposure rather than a progressive malignant process. Pleural plaques themselves are benign with an excellent prognosis and rarely cause symptoms or meaningful functional impairment; their significance lies in signalling asbestos exposure and the associated lifetime risk of mesothelioma and lung cancer.

Pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis — PPFE, Idiopathic pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with a UIP pattern Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis Fibrotic sarcoidosis with upper-zone fibrosis Apical fibrosis following prior tuberculosis or radiation Ankylosing spondylitis-related apical fibrosis Chronic fibrosing pleuritis Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease HRCT thorax demonstrating upper-zone pleuroparenchymal fibrosis Pulmonary function tests, which show restriction with a characteristically preserved or raised residual volume relative to total lung capacity due to platythorax Surgical lung biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain Autoimmune serology and detailed exposure history Review of prior transplant, chemotherapy or recurrent infection history Assessment for coexistent lower-lobe interstitial lung disease Six-minute walk test with oximetry A rare fibrosing interstitial lung disease defined by fibrosis of the visceral pleura and subpleural parenchyma with striking upper-lobe predominance. May be idiopathic or associated with haematopoietic stem cell or lung transplantation, recurrent infection, chemotherapy, autoimmune disease and familial pulmonary fibrosis. A characteristic phenotype comprises a thin body habitus, a flattened thorax with reduced anteroposterior diameter (platythorax) and deepening of the suprasternal notch. Presents with breathlessness, dry cough, recurrent pneumothoraces and weight loss. HRCT shows dense upper-zone pleural and subpleural fibrosis with volume loss, traction bronchiectasis and architectural distortion, sparing the lower zones early in disease. Histology demonstrates intra-alveolar fibrosis with prominent elastosis and visceral pleural thickening (elastofibrosis). It frequently coexists with another interstitial lung disease pattern, such as UIP, in the lower lobes. No drug therapy is of proven benefit; antifibrotic agents are being explored and transplantation is considered in suitable patients. Recurrent or bilateral pneumothorax Rapidly progressive restrictive decline Significant weight loss or cachexia Coexisting lower-lobe fibrosis indicating combined disease with a worse outcome Dismissing apical changes as old infection or scarring Missing the characteristic body habitus and preserved lung volumes as diagnostic clues Overlooking coexisting lower-lobe interstitial lung disease Attributing recurrent pneumothorax to primary spontaneous pneumothorax Pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis is defined by dense fibroelastotic thickening of the visceral pleura and the immediately subpleural parenchyma, with elastin-rich fibrosis obliterating alveolar spaces predominantly in the upper lobes. Proposed mechanisms include recurrent injury and infection, immune dysregulation such as after transplantation, and genetic predisposition; the upper-zone distribution and marked elastosis are distinctive. The disease is often progressive with a poor outcome, particularly when combined with lower-lobe fibrosis; pneumothorax and progressive respiratory failure are common complications.

pleuropulmonary blastoma — PPB, pleuropulmonary blastoma of childhood Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) Congenital lobar emphysema Bronchogenic or other foregut duplication cyst Pulmonary sequestration Bronchopulmonary infection with cavitation or empyema Metastatic sarcoma or Wilms tumour to the lung Mediastinal germ cell tumour Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest to characterise cystic versus solid components Histopathology of the resected lesion with attention to the malignant cambium layer Germline and tumour DICER1 mutation testing Brain MRI to screen for cerebral metastases in solid types Bone imaging for skeletal metastases Echocardiography if there is mediastinal or cardiac displacement Thyroid ultrasound and abdominal/pelvic imaging for DICER1-associated tumours The commonest primary lung malignancy of early childhood, a dysembryonic mesenchymal tumour of lung and pleura, distinct from the epithelial pulmonary blastoma of adults. Classified into three progressive types: Type I is purely cystic, Type II is mixed cystic and solid, and Type III is purely solid, with prognosis worsening across the sequence. Type I may regress or, if untreated, progress to the aggressive Type II and III forms, so complete resection of Type I lesions is advocated. Around two-thirds of cases arise in DICER1 syndrome; identifying a germline DICER1 pathogenic variant unlocks family surveillance. It is frequently and dangerously mistaken for a benign congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) on imaging. Presentations include respiratory distress, persistent cough, chest pain, and spontaneous pneumothorax. The solid types metastasise with a particular predilection for the brain and bone. DICER1 syndrome also predisposes to cystic nephroma, Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour, multinodular goitre, ciliary body medulloepithelioma, and nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma. Spontaneous pneumothorax in a young child, which may herald an underlying cystic pleuropulmonary blastoma A presumed CPAM with solid components, septal thickening, or rapid enlargement Neurological signs suggesting cerebral metastasis A family history of DICER1-associated tumours Diagnosing a cystic lung lesion as benign CPAM without histological review, missing an early Type I pleuropulmonary blastoma. Adopting watchful waiting for complex cystic lung lesions in a child with a DICER1 background rather than resecting. Not sending DICER1 testing, missing the syndrome and surveillance opportunities for the child and relatives. Omitting brain imaging in solid-type disease and thereby missing metastases. Pleuropulmonary blastoma is a dysontogenetic tumour arising from the primitive mesenchyme of the developing lung and pleura. Most cases are associated with germline loss-of-function mutation in DICER1, an endoribonuclease essential for microRNA maturation; a characteristic somatic hotspot missense mutation in the RNase IIIb domain of the remaining allele deregulates microRNA processing and drives tumour formation. Disease begins as an epithelium-lined cystic lesion (Type I) harbouring a subtle malignant mesenchymal (cambium) layer beneath a benign-appearing epithelium; over time the mesenchyme overgrows to produce mixed (Type II) and then wholly solid, high-grade sarcomatous (Type III) tumours, which may display blastematous, rhabdomyosarcomatous, chondroid, and anaplastic elements. Type I disease that is completely resected has a favourable outcome, whereas Type II and especially Type III tumours carry a substantially worse prognosis with significant risk of recurrence and metastatic spread; cerebral metastases are a particularly poor prognostic feature.

chickenpox and missing the relapsing crop pattern Failing to recognise and treat the febrile ulceronecrotic variant promptly Overlooking the clinical and histological overlap with lymphomatoid papulosis Attributing residual varioliform scars to another cause PLEVA is regarded as a reactive, predominantly CD8-positive cytotoxic T-cell response that produces a lymphocytic vasculitis and epidermal injury. As with the chronic form, triggers are thought to include infectious antigens and, in some cases, drugs, which provoke an inflammatory cascade damaging both keratinocytes and dermal vessels. The intense cytotoxic reaction accounts for the vesiculation, haemorrhage, and necrosis of individual lesions and for the varioliform scarring that can follow. In the severe febrile ulceronecrotic variant an exaggerated response, sometimes with a large clonal T-cell population and cytokine release, drives widespread ulceration and systemic illness. Most cases resolve over weeks to months, though relapses are common and varioliform scarring may persist; the febrile ulceronecrotic variant carries appreciable morbidity and, rarely, mortality and warrants urgent aggressive treatment.

targeting the quadriceps and stretching, corticosteroid injection and arthroscopic resection for refractory cases True locking or an effusion suggesting a meniscal tear or loose body Significant chondral damage Features suggesting an inflammatory or septic arthritis Progressive mechanical symptoms Overdiagnosis, since asymptomatic plicae are common incidental findings Missing a meniscal or chondral lesion, as the diagnosis is one of exclusion Resecting an incidental plica that is not the source of symptoms Ignoring underlying patellofemoral dysfunction A synovial plica is a remnant of the embryonic septa that once divided the knee into compartments, and the medial patellar plica is the fold that most commonly becomes symptomatic. Repetitive overuse or direct trauma causes the plica to thicken, lose its elasticity and become fibrotic and inflamed, so that it impinges against the medial femoral condyle during flexion and extension. This produces pain, snapping and sometimes chondral damage. Asymptomatic plicae are common incidental findings and do not require treatment. Many patients settle with conservative treatment, and arthroscopic excision of a genuinely symptomatic plica gives good results.

Plummer-Vinson syndrome — Paterson-Brown-Kelly syndrome, Paterson-Kelly syndrome, sideropenic dysphagia Oesophageal web without iron deficiency Post-cricoid or hypopharyngeal carcinoma Peptic or other oesophageal stricture Eosinophilic oesophagitis Oropharyngeal or neuromuscular dysphagia Schatzki ring Full blood count with iron studies confirming iron-deficiency anaemia Barium swallow demonstrating a post-cricoid web Upper endoscopy with biopsy to confirm the web and exclude malignancy Investigation for the source of iron loss, including gastrointestinal blood loss Ear-nose-throat evaluation of the hypopharynx where indicated Classic triad of iron-deficiency anaemia, dysphagia, and upper (post-cricoid) oesophageal webs Most often affects middle-aged women and is now uncommon where iron deficiency is well managed Dysphagia is typically to solids and results from the cervical web narrowing the lumen Associated features include glossitis, angular cheilitis, koilonychia, and other signs of chronic iron deficiency Recognised as a premalignant condition with an increased risk of post-cricoid and upper oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma Cornerstone of management is iron repletion, which often improves the dysphagia, with endoscopic dilatation for persistent webs Long-term surveillance is warranted given the malignant potential Progressive dysphagia, weight loss, or hoarseness suggesting malignancy A post-cricoid mass or ulcer on imaging or endoscopy Occult gastrointestinal blood loss requiring source identification Persistent symptoms despite iron correction Treating the web without correcting the underlying iron deficiency Failing to investigate the cause of iron loss Missing an early post-cricoid carcinoma in a patient with sideropenic dysphagia Neglecting long-term surveillance given the premalignant nature of the condition Plummer-Vinson syndrome links chronic iron deficiency to the formation of upper oesophageal webs and dysphagia. Iron deficiency is thought to impair the turnover of the rapidly dividing oesophageal mucosa and reduce iron-dependent oxidative enzymes, leading to mucosal atrophy and web formation in the post-cricoid region. The web mechanically narrows the lumen, causing solid-food dysphagia, while the chronic atrophic and inflammatory changes are believed to underlie the increased long-term risk of squamous carcinoma of the hypopharynx and upper oesophagus. Dysphagia frequently improves with iron repletion, and webs respond to dilatation; the principal long-term concern is the elevated risk of upper aerodigestive squamous carcinoma, which justifies ongoing surveillance.

connection to the sublingual space on imaging Injuring the lingual nerve or submandibular duct during sublingual gland excision A plunging ranula is a variant of the sublingual gland mucus extravasation lesion in which mucus escapes into the neck rather than remaining confined to the floor of the mouth. Saliva leaking from a disrupted sublingual gland tracks posteriorly and inferiorly around the free posterior edge of mylohyoid, or through a congenital or acquired dehiscence within the muscle, descending into the submandibular and upper cervical spaces. The collection is a pseudocyst without a true epithelial lining, and because the sublingual gland continues to secrete, definitive resolution depends on removing that gland to stop the flow of mucus. Excision of the offending sublingual gland gives a high cure rate and resolves the cervical component. Procedures that drain or remove only the neck pseudocyst while leaving the gland in place commonly recur.

PMM2-CDG (CDG type Ia) — phosphomannomutase 2 deficiency, CDG-Ia, carbohydrate-deficient glycoprotein syndrome type Ia, PMM2 Other congenital disorders of glycosylation (e.g. ALG6-CDG, MPI-CDG) Congenital muscular dystrophies with cerebellar involvement Mitochondrial cytopathies (e.g. Leigh-like disease) Peroxisomal disorders such as Zellweger spectrum Pontocerebellar hypoplasia of other genetic cause Inherited coagulopathies presenting with unexplained bleeding/thrombosis Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry (type 1 pattern) Phosphomannomutase enzyme activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts PMM2 gene sequencing for confirmation and family counselling Coagulation studies including antithrombin, protein C, protein S and factor XI Thyroid function tests and liver function/transaminases Brain MRI to demonstrate cerebellar/pontocerebellar hypoplasia Echocardiography for pericardial effusion and cardiomyopathy Most common congenital disorder of glycosylation; a multisystem N-glycosylation defect caused by biallelic PMM2 variants Classic infantile presentation combines failure to thrive, developmental delay, hypotonia and a cerebellar/pontocerebellar hypoplasia picture Distinctive dysmorphic clues include inverted nipples and abnormal (fat pad) subcutaneous fat distribution over the buttocks and suprapubic area Non-neurological features include pericardial effusion, hepatopathy, coagulopathy, hypothyroidism and stroke-like episodes Older children develop retinitis pigmentosa, peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, skeletal changes and hypogonadism Screening test is serum transferrin isoform analysis showing a type 1 pattern (raised asialo- and disialotransferrin) reflecting whole-glycan loss Enzyme assay of phosphomannomutase in leukocytes/fibroblasts and PMM2 gene sequencing confirm the diagnosis Management is supportive and multidisciplinary; there is no disease-modifying therapy, though dietary mannose supplementation has been tried without proven benefit Stroke-like episodes or thrombotic events reflecting coagulation factor imbalance Life-threatening pericardial effusion or cardiac failure in infancy Severe hepatopathy with hypoalbuminaemia and protein-losing enteropathy Acute deterioration during intercurrent illness with multi-organ failure Progressive feeding failure and profound failure to thrive Attributing the picture to a non-specific 'cerebral palsy' and never testing transferrin glycoforms False-negative or false-positive transferrin patterns in neonates, intercurrent infection, galactosaemia or heavy alcohol exposure Overlooking treatable comorbidities such as hypothyroidism and coagulopathy before procedures Assuming mannose supplementation is effective, unlike its role in MPI-CDG Not screening for thrombosis/bleeding risk prior to surgery or anticoagulation decisions PMM2-CDG results from deficiency of phosphomannomutase 2, the cytosolic enzyme that converts mannose-6-phosphate to mannose-1-phosphate, an essential step in generating GDP-mannose and the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide precursor used for N-linked glycosylation of proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum. Reduced substrate limits assembly and transfer of the glycan, so many secretory and membrane glycoproteins are hypoglycosylated, with whole glycan chains missing from some sialylation sites. Because glycosylation is required across virtually every organ system, the resulting glycoprotein dysfunction produces the characteristic multisystem phenotype affecting the brain and cerebellum, liver, heart, endocrine glands, coagulation factors and connective tissue. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Infantile mortality can reach up to one in five, often from infection, cardiac or hepatic complications; survivors have static intellectual disability with slowly progressive neurological and multisystem involvement, and prognosis varies widely with genotype and severity.

Polymyalgia rheumatica — ESR/CRP (markedly raised) Assess for giant cell arteritis Watch for GCA — visual symptoms need urgent steroids Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis in the elderly, which can be difficult to distinguish from PMR; RA predominantly affects wrists/hands and ankles/feet at onset whereas PMR is girdle-predominant (p.2920). Remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema (RS3PE) — prominent distal limb pitting edema, prompt response to low-dose prednisone (p.2920). Other inflammatory arthropathies / seronegative RA in patients who develop a worsening pattern of peripheral arthritis (p.2945). Fibromyalgia — listed among conditions confused with PMR; PMR appears in the fibromyalgia differential (p.2965). Osteoarthritis and other noninflammatory nonarticular conditions (bursitis, tendinitis) (p.2938-2939). Rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) should be negative; positive results point toward seronegative-RA spectrum or other inflammatory arthropathy (p.2946). Serum creatine kinase is NOT elevated in PMR; elevation should prompt consideration of a myopathic process (p.2946). Normochromic or slightly hypochromic anemia and elevated alkaline phosphatase (liver function abnormalities) may accompany the inflammatory state in the GCA/PMR spectrum (p.2945). If GCA is suspected, evaluate temporal arteries (biopsy, or ultrasonography showing a noncompressible 'halo' sign) and consider vascular imaging (MR/CT, PET investigational) for large-vessel disease; therapy should not be delayed pending these studies (p.2945-2946). Inflammatory myopathy/myositis (polymyositis): PMR is included among nonarticular conditions to consider, but unlike myopathy it is not associated with true muscle weakness, and serum CK, EMG, and muscle biopsy are normal in PMR (p.2939, Ch.385). Fibromyalgia: a painful, noninflammatory myofascial syndrome with normal CK, ESR, EMG, and muscle biopsy — distinguished from PMR by normal inflammatory markers. Paraneoplastic syndromes (noted as mimics in the elderly inflammatory-arthritis context) (p.2920). Chronic tophaceous gout and hepatitis C-related arthropathy (mimics of inflammatory arthritis in the elderly) (p.2920). PMR causes stiffness, aching, and pain in the muscles of the neck, shoulders, lower back, hips, and thighs in a patient typically aged >50 years (p.2945). PMR and giant cell arteritis are regarded as different clinical expressions of a single underlying disease process, supported by clinical association and pathophysiologic data (p.2945). Although PMR most often occurs in isolation, it is found in roughly 40-50% of patients with giant cell arteritis (p.2945). About 10-20% of patients presenting initially with apparently isolated PMR later go on to develop giant cell arteritis, so reassessment for GCA features should occur at follow-up visits (p.2945). Inflammatory stiffness in PMR tends to be prolonged (lasting hours) and improves with activity, in contrast to the brief gel-phenomenon stiffness (<=45 min, worse with activity) of noninflammatory disorders such as osteoarthritis (p.2938). Fatigue can be profound in PMR, mirroring other inflammatory conditions (p.2938). Annual incidence of PMR in those aged >=50 years was 58.7 per 100,000 in Olmsted County, Minnesota (p.2945). New or worsening peripheral arthritis pattern — reconsider seronegative RA or another inflammatory arthropathy rather than PMR (p.2946). Elevated serum CK or true muscle weakness — argues against PMR and suggests inflammatory myopathy (p.2946). Jaw or tongue claudication, scalp tenderness, new headache, or a tender/thickened/nodular temporal artery — signal evolution to GCA with risk of ischemic optic neuropathy and sudden blindness (p.2945). Arm claudication, diminished pulses, or bruits — may indicate large-vessel (e.g., subclavian) GCA involvement or aortic aneurysm risk (p.2945-2946). Treating an IL-6-inhibitor-exposed patient: blockade of IL-6 signaling normalizes CRP and ESR, so these markers can no longer be used to monitor disease activity or detect infection (p.2945). Minor rises in ESR/CRP during tapering do not necessarily indicate disease exacerbation, particularly in an asymptomatic patient; ESR/CRP can also rise from infection (p.2946). Assuming PMR explains distal/peripheral arthritis — PMR can mimic RA, and persistent or worsening peripheral arthritis warrants reconsideration (p.2946). PMR sits on the same disease spectrum as giant cell arteritis, an antigen-driven panarteritis of medium- and large-sized vessels with mononuclear infiltrates and frequent giant cell formation. Activated CD4+ T lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells are central; restricted clonal T-cell receptor expansion suggests an antigen residing in the arterial wall. Two CD4 T-cell lineages (IFN-gamma-producing TH1 and IL-17-producing TH17) participate in vascular inflammation, with IL-6 signaling driving hepatic acute-phase protein (CRP, and effects on ESR) production. Familial aggregation and HLA-DR4 / HLA-DRB1*04 associations have been reported for the GCA end of the spectrum (p.2945). Isolated PMR generally responds promptly to low-dose treatment, and most patients can be managed without IL-6-directed agents. Recurrent polymyalgia symptoms develop in the majority of patients during steroid tapering. The principal long-term concern is progression toward giant cell arteritis (10-20% of initially isolated PMR), which carries risks of visual loss and, late, thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection (p.2945-2946).

pain out of proportion to physical findings suggesting mesenteric ischaemia Peritonitis, haemodynamic instability, or sepsis Rising lactate or metabolic acidosis Portal or mesenteric venous gas on imaging in an unwell patient Reflexively operating on benign incidental pneumatosis or, conversely, observing ischaemic pneumatosis that needs urgent surgery Relying on the radiological sign alone without integrating the clinical picture and lactate Underestimating the significance of portomesenteric venous gas in an unwell patient Overlooking a drug or lung-disease association that explains a benign form Pneumatosis intestinalis denotes the presence of gas within the wall of the bowel, and several mechanisms are proposed. In the benign cystic form, gas is thought to track into the submucosa and subserosa either mechanically (for example through mucosal breaks, raised intraluminal pressure, or from the lungs via the mediastinum in chronic lung disease) or through the action of gas-forming luminal bacteria. In the sinister form, ischaemia disrupts the mucosal barrier and, combined with bacterial gas production and gas dissection into damaged wall and mesenteric veins, signals transmural injury and impending or established necrosis; the same radiological sign therefore reflects widely differing underlying processes. Prognosis depends entirely on the underlying cause: benign, idiopathic pneumatosis is often self-limiting or stable with an excellent outlook, whereas pneumatosis due to bowel ischaemia or necrosis, particularly with portomesenteric venous gas, carries a high mortality without prompt surgical intervention.

lung tissue pathology is the gold standard for pneumonia Myocardial infarction Heart failure with atypical pulmonary oedema Pulmonary atelectasis Lung cancer (can produce round/spherical consolidation mimicking pneumococcal round pneumonia) S. pneumoniae can infect nearly any tissue; the four most common syndromes are otitis media, pneumonia, bacteraemia, and meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1191). There is no pathognomonic presentation of pneumococcal disease, and a microbiologically confirmed diagnosis is made in only a minority of cases, so empirical therapy covering S. pneumoniae is often indicated (Harrison 22e p.1191). In the elderly, pneumococcal pneumonia may present non-specifically with confusion or malaise without fever or cough; a high index of suspicion is required because delayed treatment leads to rapid, severe deterioration (Harrison 22e p.1192). Pneumococcal pneumonia can mimic an acute abdomen (upper abdominal pain from diaphragmatic pleural involvement); clinicians should remember to keep this non-abdominal process in the differential (Harrison 22e p.1192). Now that H. influenzae type b vaccine is in routine childhood use, S. pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis are the most common bacterial causes of meningitis in both adults and children (Harrison 22e p.1193). Pneumococcal meningitis can be a primary presentation or a complication of skull fracture, otitis media, mastoiditis, or bacteraemia; most cases arise from haematogenous spread rather than direct extension (Harrison 22e p.1191, 1193). A positive urinary pneumococcal antigen test is useful for etiologic attribution in adults (low nasopharyngeal colonization) but is generally uninformative in children and in high-colonization low-income settings (Harrison 22e p.1192-1193). Most pneumococcal pneumonia is non-bacteraemic; only ~5-20% of cases are accompanied by bacteraemia, and blood cultures are positive in fewer than 30% of cases (Harrison 22e p.1190, 1192). Empyema is the most common focal complication of pneumococcal pneumonia (<5% of cases); pleural fluid with frank pus, visible bacteria, or pH <=7.1 indicates empyema and demands complete drainage (Harrison 22e p.1192). Asplenia or splenic dysfunction (e.g., sickle cell disease) confers risk of overwhelming, fulminant pneumococcal sepsis Leukopenia in pneumococcal pneumonia (<10% of cases) is a poor prognostic sign associated with fatal outcome Hypotension and signs of severe pneumonia/sepsis at presentation predict higher case-fatality Meningitis features: altered consciousness, seizures, stiff neck, signs of raised intracranial pressure (bradycardia, hypertension), cranial nerve palsies In children: inability to drink, convulsions, lethargy, or severe malnutrition signify very severe disease warranting immediate antibiotics and referral Pleural effusion with persistent fever/leukocytosis after 4-5 days of appropriate therapy suggests empyema Treating an apparent acute abdomen while overlooking pneumococcal lower-lobe pneumonia causing referred abdominal pain (Harrison 22e p.1192). Relying on a normal early chest radiograph to exclude pneumonia; an infiltrate may be absent early or with dehydration and appear after rehydration (Harrison 22e p.1192). Over-interpreting a positive urinary pneumococcal antigen in children or in high-colonization settings, where it does not reliably attribute etiology (Harrison 22e p.1192-1193). Diagnosing otitis media from tympanic-membrane redness alone, which is insufficient (Harrison 22e p.1193). Attributing round/spherical consolidation solely to pneumococcus without considering other causes, especially cancer (Harrison 22e p.1192). Assuming PPSV23 reliably prevents non-bacteraemic pneumococcal pneumonia, particularly in the elderly and immunodeficient, where effectiveness is reduced and protection wanes after ~5 years (Harrison 22e p.1194). Pneumococci are encapsulated gram-positive diplococci that colonise the human nasopharynx from an early age; colonisation is common while disease is rare. All pneumococcal infection ultimately stems from nasopharyngeal acquisition. The anti-phagocytic polysaccharide capsule is the key virulence determinant, resisting complement deposition in the absence of type-specific antibody. The organism dynamically modulates capsule expression: it downregulates capsule in the nasopharynx (rough colonies) to evade immune recognition and upregulates it on tissue invasion (smooth colonies). From the nasopharynx, organisms spread haematogenously to distant sites (brain, joints, bone, peritoneum) or locally to mucosal surfaces (otitis media, pneumonia). Intercurrent viral respiratory infection increases susceptibility by upregulating epithelial adhesion factors, permitting adhesion via surface adhesins (PsaA, PspA, CbpA/PspC, pneumolysin, neuraminidases). Disease pathology is driven by host inflammation: cell-wall teichoic acids and peptidoglycan induce IL-1, IL-6, and TNF and activate the alternative complement pathway, and pneumolysin drives proinflammatory cytokine release. Host defence depends on intact respiratory epithelium, the cough reflex and mucociliary escalator, splenic function, complement, neutrophils/macrophages, CRP binding of cell-wall phosphorylcholine, and TLR2/TLR4 recognition, together with acquired anticapsular IgG (Harrison 22e p.1190-1191). Case-fatality varies with age, comorbidity, disease severity at presentation, and access to care. For pneumococcal pneumonia, CFR ranges from <5% in hospitalised patients aged 18-44 to >12% in those over 65, even with timely management; severity at presentation (rather than the presence of bacteraemia) drives mortality, and early deaths reflect a rapidly progressive cascade that often unfolds irrespective of antibiotic administration. Pneumococcal meningitis carries a mortality of ~20%, and up to 50% of survivors have acute or chronic sequelae (deafness, hydrocephalus, and cognitive impairment in children; diffuse brain swelling, subarachnoid bleeding, hydrocephalus, cerebrovascular complications, and hearing loss in adults) (Harrison 22e p.1190, 1193). Pneumococcal syndromes are classified as invasive (a normally sterile site is infected or bacteraemia is present, e.g., bacteraemic pneumonia, meningitis, bacteraemia) versus noninvasive (contiguous spread, e.g., otitis media, sinusitis, bronchitis); whether non-bacteraemic pneumonia counts as invasive is debated. In children, WHO IMCI algorithms stratify illness by danger signs (very severe disease: inability to drink, convulsions, lethargy, severe malnutrition) and by cough with tachypnoea plus lower chest-wall indrawing to guide antibiotics and referral; no equivalent validated algorithm exists for adults (Harrison 22e p.1191).

Pneumoconiosis — occupational lung disease, coal workers' pneumoconiosis, CWP, dust lung disease Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and other interstitial lung diseases Sarcoidosis Pulmonary tuberculosis (which may also complicate pneumoconiosis) Metastatic or miliary pulmonary nodular disease Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Pulmonary manifestations of connective tissue disease Chest radiography, ideally read against standardised classification of pneumoconiosis opacities High-resolution CT to characterise nodularity, fibrosis, and pleural disease Pulmonary function testing to quantify restrictive, obstructive, or mixed impairment and gas transfer Detailed occupational and environmental exposure documentation Screening for complicating tuberculosis or, with asbestos, for malignancy where clinically indicated A group of parenchymal lung diseases caused by chronic inhalation of inorganic mineral dusts, most often occupational (coal, silica, asbestos, beryllium) A detailed occupational and exposure history, including duration and intensity of dust contact and latency, is essential to diagnosis Many patients are asymptomatic early, with disease detected on surveillance chest imaging before dyspnoea and cough develop Chest radiography and CT typically show small rounded or irregular opacities, with characteristic patterns and distributions depending on the causative dust Coal workers' pneumoconiosis ranges from simple disease with small nodules to progressive massive fibrosis with large conglomerate masses There is no specific treatment to reverse the fibrosis; management centres on removal from exposure, supportive care, and prevention of complications Asbestos exposure additionally raises the risk of pleural plaques, mesothelioma, and bronchogenic carcinoma, warranting long-term vigilance Prevention through dust control, respiratory protection, and workplace exposure limits is the most effective strategy Rapidly enlarging masses or new nodules suggesting progressive massive fibrosis or malignancy Constitutional symptoms or haemoptysis raising concern for tuberculosis or cancer Rapid decline in lung function or new hypoxaemia Pleural effusion or thickening in an asbestos-exposed patient suggesting mesothelioma Failing to take an adequate occupational history and therefore missing the diagnosis Attributing all radiographic change to dust without excluding superimposed tuberculosis or malignancy Assuming a short exposure excludes disease, given the often long latency Overlooking the need to remove the worker from ongoing exposure Inhaled mineral dust particles that reach the distal airways and alveoli are engulfed by alveolar macrophages. Depending on particle size, surface reactivity, and burden, the macrophages are activated or killed, releasing inflammatory mediators, cytokines, and reactive oxygen species. Sustained exposure drives chronic inflammation and fibroblast activation, leading to collagen deposition, nodule formation, and, in advanced disease, coalescence into large fibrotic masses that distort lung architecture and impair gas exchange. The specific pattern reflects the fibrogenic potential of the particular dust. Simple pneumoconiosis may remain stable and cause little functional impairment, whereas progressive massive fibrosis and asbestos-related disease can lead to progressive respiratory failure; asbestos exposure carries a long-term risk of mesothelioma and lung cancer, and outcomes improve when further exposure is halted early.

Pneumocystis Pneumonia (PCP) — PCP, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, PJP Bacterial pneumonia (including community-acquired pneumonia) Pulmonary tuberculosis (especially with upper-lobe cavitary pattern seen after aerosolized pentamidine prophylaxis) Cytomegalovirus and other viral pneumonias in the immunocompromised host Other invasive fungal pneumonias (e.g., Aspergillus) Congestive heart failure Pulmonary embolism Pulmonary hypertension Drug toxicity Neoplastic process involving the lung Lymphoid interstitial pneumonitis (LIP) and nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis (NIP) in HIV Bacterial pneumonia Pulmonary tuberculosis Cytomegalovirus pneumonia Invasive aspergillosis / other fungal pneumonia Pulse oximetry / oxygen saturation at rest and with exertion, and arterial blood gases (hypoxaemia with widened alveolar-arterial gradient; used for staging severity and directing treatment) Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) - often elevated but neither sensitive nor specific High-resolution chest CT (diffuse ground-glass opacities; a normal chest CT essentially rules out PCP) Bronchoalveolar lavage with methenamine silver, toluidine blue O, Giemsa, or immunofluorescent staining Induced sputum examination (experienced-provider dependent) PCR of respiratory specimens (more useful for ruling out PCP when negative than for confirming it when positive; cannot distinguish colonization from disease and is not standardized) Serum (1->3)-beta-D-glucan (frequently elevated but neither perfectly sensitive nor highly specific) Transbronchial or open-lung biopsy when less invasive sampling is non-diagnostic Congestive heart failure Pulmonary embolism Pulmonary hypertension Drug-induced pulmonary toxicity Pulmonary neoplasm Lymphoid interstitial pneumonitis (LIP) / nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis (NIP) Caused by the fungus Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly P. carinii); the organism cannot be cultured and is host-specific to humans, infecting only via other humans (Harrison 22e p.1730-1731). An opportunistic pathogen of immunocompromised hosts: HIV infection, organ transplantation, haematologic malignancy, and those on high-dose glucocorticoids or certain immunosuppressive monoclonal antibodies (Harrison 22e p.1730). Among people with HIV, PCP incidence is inversely related to CD4+ T-cell count: at least 80% of cases occur at counts <200/uL and most actually develop at counts <100/uL (Harrison 22e p.1731-1732). Classic presentation is acute or subacute pneumonia, often beginning with a vague sense of dyspnoea alone, then progressing to fever, nonproductive cough, and progressive shortness of breath (Harrison 22e p.1731). Decreased oxygen saturation at rest or with exertion is characteristic; untreated it progresses to severe hypoxaemia (Harrison 22e p.1731). Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is often elevated from pulmonary damage (Harrison 22e p.1731). Classic chest radiograph shows diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates that are perihilar and symmetric, which can progress to alveolar filling (Harrison 22e p.1731). High-resolution chest CT shows diffuse ground-glass opacities in virtually all PCP patients, often before the plain chest radiograph becomes abnormal (Harrison 22e p.1731). Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) is the most common sampling method; demonstration of organisms in BAL fluid is almost 100% sensitive and specific for PCP (Harrison 22e p.1733). Since the organism cannot be cultured, diagnosis relies on staining of cyst or trophozoite forms in lung tissue/secretions with methenamine silver, toluidine blue O, Giemsa, or specific immunofluorescent antibody (Harrison 22e p.1733). An induced sputum sample, when obtained and interpreted by an experienced provider, can be highly sensitive and specific, but sensitivity is widely variable (55-90%); expectorated sputum and throat swabs have very low sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.1733). Adjunctive glucocorticoids improve survival in moderate-to-severe disease (initial room-air PaO2 <70 mmHg or alveolar-arterial gradient >=35 mmHg) by reducing the inflammation that follows organism die-off once specific therapy begins; they should be started when PCP therapy is initiated, even if the diagnosis is only suspected (Harrison 22e p.1734). Prophylaxis is the cornerstone of prevention; for HIV, CD4+ counts <200/uL (or CD4 percentage <15) are an indication to start or continue chemoprophylaxis, alongside prior PCP, unexplained prolonged fever, or recent oropharyngeal candidiasis (Harrison 22e p.1734). PCP now occurs more often from non-HIV-related immunosuppression than from HIV infection in many health care systems (Harrison 22e p.1731). PaO2 <70 mmHg on room air (or alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient >=35 mmHg) marking moderate-to-severe disease that warrants adjunctive glucocorticoids Profound or progressive hypoxaemia / progression to respiratory failure Development of pneumothorax (pneumatoceles and pneumothoraces are characteristic, especially in HIV) - associated with higher mortality Need for mechanical ventilation Distributive shock due to PCP (rare) Clinical deterioration after 3-4 days of therapy, or failure to improve by 7-10 days, prompting reevaluation for other or coexisting processes A normal LDH does not rule out PCP, and an elevated LDH is not specific for PCP (Harrison 22e p.1731). PCP can occur at CD4+ counts >200/uL in HIV (uncommon, especially at counts well above 200), and in non-HIV immunosuppression a CD4+ count >200/uL does not imply protection (Harrison 22e p.1731). PCR is so sensitive that it cannot reliably distinguish colonization from true pneumonia; there is no validated PCR threshold, so a positive result does not definitively attribute disease to Pneumocystis (Harrison 22e p.1733). Serum/BAL (1->3)-beta-D-glucan and serum PCR are not sufficiently sensitive or specific to establish or exclude PCP (Harrison 22e p.1733). If treated with specific therapy but without corticosteroids, patients of any severity often deteriorate during the first few days from inflammation induced by dying organisms (Harrison 22e p.1733). Initial chest radiograph may be normal in mild disease, and the classic dense perihilar infiltrate is unusual in AIDS; relying on plain film can delay diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1730-1731). Extrapulmonary pneumocystosis is rare and nonspecific; when present, the priority is to look for another concurrent infectious or neoplastic process (Harrison 22e p.1733). Pneumocystis jirovecii is a fungus with unique tropism for the lung. Organisms are inhaled into the alveolar space, presumably after being exhaled by another human; most people are exposed and infected early in life. Disease may arise from primary infection, reinfection, or reactivation of latent infection. Clinically apparent pneumonia occurs only in immunocompromised hosts, where defects in cellular and/or humoral immunity (congenital, HIV-related, or drug-induced) permit proliferation. CD4+ T cells are critical for host defence. The organism proliferates in the lung provoking a mononuclear cell response; alveoli fill with proteinaceous material and alveolar-capillary injury with surfactant abnormalities develops. Stained sections show foamy, vacuolated alveolar exudates of viable and nonviable organisms, with interstitial oedema and fibrosis. Much of the clinical deterioration after starting specific therapy is attributed to enhanced inflammation from dying organisms, the rationale for adjunctive glucocorticoids (Harrison 22e p.1731-1734). Untreated, PCP is invariably fatal. HIV-associated disease is often indolent, presenting early as mild exercise intolerance or chest tightness without fever or cough and a normal or near-normal chest radiograph, then progressing over days to months to fever, cough, diffuse alveolar infiltrates, and profound hypoxaemia; non-HIV immunosuppressed patients more often have acute disease progressing over days to respiratory failure. Mortality is influenced by age, degree of immunosuppression, preexisting lung disease, need for mechanical ventilation, and development of pneumothorax. With advances in critical care, prognosis for those requiring intubation has improved and depends largely on comorbidities and the underlying disease (Harrison 22e p.1733). Severity is staged largely by oxygenation. Moderate-to-severe disease is defined by an initial room-air PaO2 <70 mmHg or an alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient >=35 mmHg; this threshold identifies patients (with HIV, and probably other immunodeficiencies) who benefit from adjunctive glucocorticoids in addition to specific antimicrobial therapy. Arterial blood-gas measurement both aids diagnosis and directs treatment by staging severity (Harrison 22e p.1731, 1734).

Pneumopericardium — air in the pericardium, pneumo-pericardium, hydropneumopericardium (with fluid) Pneumomediastinum Pneumothorax, particularly on the medial aspect Pericardial effusion or haemopericardium Cardiac tamponade from fluid Diaphragmatic hernia with bowel adjacent to the heart Purulent pericarditis with gas-forming organisms Chest radiography showing air surrounding the heart within the pericardium Cardiac CT to confirm and quantify the pericardial air and identify a source or fistula Echocardiography to assess haemodynamic effect, though air can limit windows Evaluation for a communicating fistula, such as contrast studies or endoscopy when suspected Assessment of ventilation and airway pressures in ventilated or neonatal patients The presence of air or gas within the pericardial sac, ranging from an incidental finding to a life-threatening tension collection Causes include chest trauma, mechanical ventilation and barotrauma (especially in neonates), thoracic or cardiac surgery and other procedures, and fistulous communication with an air-containing viscus or infection with gas-forming organisms A characteristic auscultatory sign is a metallic or churning sound synchronous with the heartbeat (the bruit de moulin or mill-wheel murmur) The chest radiograph shows air outlining the heart bordered by the pericardium, and cardiac CT confirms the diagnosis and its extent Tension pneumopericardium is an emergency in which trapped air under pressure compresses the heart and causes tamponade physiology Small collections from a self-limiting cause may be managed conservatively with observation and treatment of the underlying process Tension physiology requires urgent decompression by pericardiocentesis or a pericardial window, together with correction of the source, such as adjusting ventilation or repairing a fistula Haemodynamic instability from tension pneumopericardium requiring emergency decompression Rapidly enlarging pericardial air on serial imaging A demonstrable fistula between the pericardium and airway or gastrointestinal tract Gas-forming infection producing purulent pneumopericardium Failing to recognise tension physiology and delaying decompression Mistaking pneumopericardium for pneumomediastinum or a medial pneumothorax on the radiograph Decompressing the air without identifying and correcting the source, such as a fistula Overlooking barotrauma from ventilator settings as the driver in neonates and ventilated patients Pneumopericardium develops when air gains access to the pericardial space, either directly through a breach of the pericardium from trauma or surgery, by tracking along tissue planes from alveolar rupture during barotrauma, through a fistula linking the pericardium to an air-containing structure such as the oesophagus or a bronchus, or from gas produced by infection with gas-forming organisms. If the air can escape freely the haemodynamic effect is limited, but when a valve-like mechanism allows air to enter but not leave, intrapericardial pressure rises to compress the cardiac chambers, impairing filling and reproducing the physiology of tamponade with falling output. Small, non-tension collections from a self-limiting cause often resolve with treatment of the underlying process, whereas tension pneumopericardium is rapidly fatal without prompt decompression, and the overall outlook reflects the precipitating condition.

Pneumothorax — CXR (or POCUS) Decompress if tension Tension pneumothorax → immediate needle decompression Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial infarction (Harrison 22e p.105) Acute aortic syndrome / aortic dissection (Harrison 22e p.104, p.105) Pericarditis with tamponade (Harrison 22e p.105) Pleurisy / pleuritis (Harrison 22e p.104) Pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.104) Esophageal disorders such as reflux or motility disorder mimicking angina (Harrison 22e p.105) Musculoskeletal chest-wall pain including costochondritis (Tietze syndrome) (Harrison 22e p.105) Panic disorder / anxiety state (Harrison 22e p.105) Pneumonia or pleuritis presenting with sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea (Harrison 22e p.104) Chest radiograph to confirm or exclude pneumothorax; it is the routine first-line image in acute chest discomfort and is useful for pneumothorax, though for tension it must not delay decompression (Harrison 22e p.105, p.2272). Point-of-care lung ultrasound (POCUS), which can rapidly diagnose pneumothorax (as well as pleural effusion and consolidation) at the bedside (Harrison 22e p.2272, shock evaluation chapter). Bedside physical examination as a diagnostic tool for tension pneumothorax: enlarged hemithorax with absent breath sounds, hyperresonance to percussion, mediastinal shift to the contralateral side, and hypotension (Harrison 22e p.2314). Percussion to distinguish causes of diminished breath sounds: pneumothorax is hyper-resonant whereas pleural effusion is dull (Harrison 22e respiratory-examination chapter). Palpation for subcutaneous emphysema as a sign of associated barotrauma (Harrison 22e respiratory-examination chapter). Pulmonary embolism, which like pneumothorax can cause sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, and hemodynamic compromise (Harrison 22e p.104, p.105) Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial infarction (Harrison 22e p.105) Aortic dissection / acute aortic syndrome (Harrison 22e p.104, p.105) Pericarditis with cardiac tamponade (Harrison 22e p.105, p.2293) Esophageal reflux or spasm mimicking angina (Harrison 22e p.105) Pneumothorax is simply gas within the pleural space; classify it as spontaneous (no preceding trauma) versus traumatic, and spontaneous further as primary (no underlying lung disease) versus secondary (underlying lung disease present) (Harrison 22e p.2313). A tension pneumothorax is defined physiologically as one in which pleural pressure stays positive throughout the entire respiratory cycle (Harrison 22e p.2313). Tension pneumothorax should be treated as a clinical emergency on the basis of bedside findings; do not wait for a confirmatory chest radiograph before relieving the pressure, because untreated tension leads to death from inadequate cardiac output or severe hypoxemia (Harrison 22e p.2314). When a tension pneumothorax is suspected, decompression precedes imaging: a large-bore needle is placed into the pleural space and a rush of escaping gas confirms the diagnosis (knowledge principle; no dose/technique detail) (Harrison 22e p.2314). Primary spontaneous pneumothorax typically results from rupture of small apical subpleural blebs (cystic spaces within or just beneath the visceral pleura) (Harrison 22e p.2313). Classic primary spontaneous pneumothorax patient is a young, tall, thin man; smoking, male sex, family history, and Marfan syndrome are recognized risk factors (Harrison 22e p.104, p.105). Symptom onset in primary spontaneous pneumothorax is usually sudden but dyspnea can be mild, so presentation to care is sometimes delayed (Harrison 22e p.104). Tension pneumothorax most often arises during mechanical ventilation or resuscitation; difficulty ventilating during resuscitation or high peak inspiratory pressures on the ventilator should strongly raise suspicion (Harrison 22e p.2314). Persistent air leak is a recognized entity, defined as a non-resolving pneumothorax with an air leak lasting longer than about 5-7 days (Harrison 22e p.2273). Tracheal/mediastinal shift to the contralateral side, absent breath sounds over an enlarged hemithorax, hyperresonant percussion, and hypotension — the bedside signs of tension pneumothorax (Harrison 22e p.2314). Hemodynamic collapse from trapped intrathoracic air defines tension pneumothorax as a medical emergency (Harrison 22e p.104). Tension pneumothorax is a cause of obstructive shock and of pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest, and is a reversible cause to consider during resuscitation (Harrison 22e shock and cardiac-arrest chapters). Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory systolic fall greater than 10 mmHg) can accompany tension pneumothorax and signals significant hemodynamic compromise (Harrison 22e p.1813). Tachycardia and hypotension in a patient with chest discomfort should trigger rapid evaluation for the most lethal causes, including tension pneumothorax (Harrison 22e p.105). Difficulty ventilating during resuscitation or rising peak inspiratory pressures on mechanical ventilation should prompt urgent suspicion of tension pneumothorax (Harrison 22e p.2314). Waiting for a chest radiograph to confirm a suspected tension pneumothorax instead of decompressing immediately — tension is a clinical diagnosis and delay can be fatal (Harrison 22e p.2314). Underestimating a secondary pneumothorax in a patient with COPD, asthma, or cystic fibrosis; because of poor reserve it can be far more dangerous than a primary event (Harrison 22e p.104, p.2313). Mild dyspnea in primary spontaneous pneumothorax can lead to delayed presentation, so a benign-seeming history does not exclude it (Harrison 22e p.104). Forgetting iatrogenic pneumothorax after thoracentesis, transthoracic needle aspiration, or central line placement (Harrison 22e p.2314). Attributing absent or diminished breath sounds to effusion when percussion (hyper-resonant in pneumothorax, dull in effusion) would distinguish them (Harrison 22e respiratory-examination chapter). Overlooking tension pneumothorax as a reversible cause of PEA arrest and obstructive shock (Harrison 22e shock and cardiac-arrest chapters). Pneumothorax is the accumulation of gas in the pleural space. In primary spontaneous pneumothorax, apical subpleural blebs rupture, allowing air to enter the pleural space without preceding trauma and in the absence of underlying lung disease. Secondary pneumothorax occurs when the same process complicates established lung disease, where loss of pulmonary reserve makes the event more dangerous. Traumatic pneumothorax results from penetrating or non-penetrating chest injury, and iatrogenic pneumothorax (a traumatic subtype) follows procedures such as transthoracic needle aspiration, thoracentesis, or central venous catheter insertion. In a tension pneumothorax, a one-way valve effect produces pleural pressure that remains positive across the whole respiratory cycle; this both severely compromises ventilation and transmits positive pressure to the mediastinum, reducing venous return to the heart and thereby cardiac output (Harrison 22e p.2313, p.2314). Roughly half of patients with an initial primary spontaneous pneumothorax experience a recurrence. Secondary pneumothorax carries a worse outlook than pneumothorax in otherwise normal lungs because the underlying lung disease leaves little pulmonary reserve, making the event potentially more life-threatening. Untreated tension pneumothorax is rapidly fatal from inadequate cardiac output or severe hypoxemia (Harrison 22e p.2313, p.2314). Harrison classifies pneumothorax by mechanism and risk rather than a numeric score: (1) primary spontaneous (no underlying lung disease, often young tall thin smokers, frequently manageable conservatively if asymptomatic/minimally symptomatic); (2) secondary spontaneous (underlying lung disease present, e.g., COPD, asthma, cystic fibrosis — more life-threatening because of limited reserve); (3) traumatic, including the increasingly common iatrogenic subtype; and (4) tension pneumothorax, defined by positive pleural pressure throughout the respiratory cycle and treated as a medical emergency. Persistent air leak is a recognized complication defined as a non-resolving pneumothorax with air leak beyond about 5-7 days (Harrison 22e p.2313, p.2314, p.2273).

Poisoning and Drug Overdose — xenobiotic poisoning, drug overdose, intoxication, toxic ingestion, acute poisoning Structural CNS lesion (focal neurologic findings are uncommon in poisoning and should prompt imaging) Sepsis or other infection causing altered mental status Primary psychiatric illness or psychogenic illness (fear of poisoning, mass hysteria) Metabolic encephalopathy (hepatic, renal, or respiratory failure) Hypoglycemia from non-toxic causes Trauma and occult head injury Sepsis with shock and multiorgan dysfunction (hypoxemia/shock from severe poisoning can mimic, and secondary aspiration pneumonia and sepsis can complicate poisoning) Anion-gap calculation (elevated AGMA in advanced methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate poisoning, and any poisoning causing organ failure, seizures, or shock; abnormally low anion gap suggests bromide, calcium, iodine, lithium, or magnesium) Serum lactate (typically low relative to anion gap in toxic-alcohol/salicylate poisoning, high and near-equal to the gap in hypoperfusion) Osmolal gap (>10 mmol/L difference suggests a low-molecular-weight solute such as a toxic alcohol or glycol) Serum glucose and ketones Electrolytes including potassium and calcium ECG (bradycardia/AV block, QRS and QT prolongation from membrane-active agents and hyperkalemia, ventricular tachyarrhythmias) Quantitative serum levels for acetaminophen, alcohols (including ethylene glycol and methanol), anticonvulsants, barbiturates, digoxin, heavy metals, iron, lithium, salicylate, theophylline, carboxyhemoglobin, and methemoglobin Qualitative urine drug screen (most useful when toxicity is severe or unexplained, e.g., coma, seizures, cardiovascular instability, acidosis, nonsinus rhythms) Radiography/abdominal CT (radiopaque densities suggest chloral hydrate, chlorinated hydrocarbons, heavy metals, drug packets, iodinated compounds, potassium salts, enteric-coated tablets, or salicylates; chest x-ray for pulmonary edema, metal fume fever, elemental mercury) Review of the state Prescription Monitoring Program for controlled-substance history PT/INR (useful for risk stratification in warfarin/rodenticide poisoning, but unreliable for direct oral anticoagulant overdose) Psychogenic illness and anxiety reactions, which can produce mild physiologic stimulation indistinguishable from a toxic cause without observation or ancillary testing Primary cardiac arrhythmia or conduction disease Endocrine emergencies (e.g., thyroid storm mimicking a sympathomimetic toxidrome) Neuroleptic malignant syndrome and serotonin syndrome (CNS syndromes that may overlap with stimulant toxidromes) Poisoning severity is dose-related, but individual responses to a given dose vary with genetic polymorphisms, enzyme induction or inhibition from co-ingested xenobiotics, and acquired tolerance; the functional reserve of the target organ (influenced by age and preexisting disease) also shapes severity and reversibility. Diagnosis of an unknown poisoning rests on pattern recognition: first characterize the overall physiologic state as stimulated, depressed, discordant, or normal, then look for a toxidrome and finally for agent-specific clues. Core temperature must be measured and reassessed frequently even in combative patients, because temperature elevation is the single most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant poisoning (e.g., cocaine) and in withdrawal states (e.g., alcohol, GHB). Mydriasis is characteristic of all stimulant states but is most marked in anticholinergic poisoning because pupillary reactivity is muscarinic; sympathomimetic poisoning also dilates pupils but some light reactivity persists, whereas the anticholinergic toxidrome adds hot, dry, flushed skin, decreased bowel sounds, and urinary retention. Rotatory nystagmus points specifically to phencyclidine or ketamine, the only physiologic stimulants that produce this sign. Miosis is most pronounced in opioid and cholinergic poisoning; cholinergic poisoning is distinguished by accompanying muscarinic and nicotinic features. A normal exam can be deceptive: 'toxic time-bombs' (slowly absorbed, slowly distributed, requiring metabolic activation, or disrupting metabolism) and the proliferation of once-daily extended-release formulations mean delayed, severe toxicity is increasingly common. A rapid response to a diagnostic antidote can confirm the cause: improvement within minutes of IV dextrose, naloxone, or flumazenil is essentially diagnostic of hypoglycemia, opioid poisoning, and benzodiazepine intoxication respectively. Qualitative urine drug-of-abuse screens are screening tests only: false positives and negatives are common (e.g., fluoroquinolones cause false-positive opiate screens), and newer agents such as synthetic cannabinoids (spice), cathinones (bath salts), and kratom are not detected at all. Symptomatic patients (e.g., apnea from opioids) should be managed on the basis of history, examination, and the observed toxidrome without waiting for laboratory confirmation. Effects after overdose typically begin sooner, peak later, and last longer than after a therapeutic dose, and the toxicokinetic profile differs from the published therapeutic pharmacokinetics in standard references. Most patients who are asymptomatic 6 h after ingestion are unlikely to develop later toxicity and can be discharged safely, but longer observation is mandatory after suspected toxic time-bomb ingestions. Coma or progressively decreasing level of consciousness Respiratory depression, apnea, or hypoxemia Hypotension or cardiovascular collapse Cardiac conduction abnormalities or arrhythmias (QRS/QT prolongation, ventricular tachyarrhythmias) Seizures Hyperthermia or hypothermia (temperature elevation is the most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant/withdrawal states) Suspected ingestion of a toxic time-bomb or an agent with toxic metabolites (acetaminophen, ethylene glycol, methanol) Body packing or body stuffing (concealment of illicit drug packets) Intentional (suicidal) overdose requiring continuous observation and self-injury precautions Relying on the gag reflex as an indicator of the need for intubation; it is not reliable, and a patient may protect the airway while stimulated but not when left alone. Treating a negative qualitative drug screen as exclusion of poisoning; the agent may be undetectable by the assay or present below the limit of detection, and repeat testing later may turn positive. Treating a positive qualitative screen as diagnostic or forensic; cross-reacting drugs cause false positives and confirmatory GC/MS may take weeks. Assuming blood levels correlate with toxicity during absorption/distribution (levels can exceed tissue concentrations) or during resolution (levels fall below tissue concentrations); rebound increases (e.g., lithium) can occur after extracorporeal removal stops. Discharging too early after ingestion of a toxic time-bomb (slow-absorption, slow-distribution, metabolic-activation, or metabolism-disrupting agents) on the basis of an initially benign presentation. Failing to consider all medications available in the home (including pet medications) when the history is unclear in a suspected poisoning. Overlooking intentional self-harm: failing to maintain continuous observation and self-injury precautions in patients who have attempted suicide. Using class IA, IC, or III antiarrhythmics, or beta blockers driven by sympathetic hyperactivity, for toxin-induced ventricular arrhythmias; sodium bicarbonate is the preferred first agent for membrane-active toxicity. Poisoning is the development of dose-related adverse effects from exposure to chemicals, drugs, or other xenobiotics. Effects may be local (skin, eyes, lungs) or systemic depending on the route of exposure and the chemical's physical properties and mechanism of action. Toxidromes reflect the net effect on autonomic and neuromuscular function: stimulated states arise from sympathetic, anticholinergic, or hallucinogen activity or from drug withdrawal; depressed states from functional sympatholytics, cholinergic agents, opioids, and sedative-hypnotic GABAergic agents; discordant states from asphyxiants, CNS syndromes, membrane-active agents, and anion-gap metabolic acidosis inducers. In opioid and sedative-hypnotic poisoning, vital-sign derangement is secondary to depression of central cardiovascular and respiratory centers (or resulting hypoxemia) and is seen only with marked depression of consciousness, whereas direct/peripheral sympatholytics can cause prominent cardiovascular depression without comparable CNS depression. Some agents (acetaminophen, ethylene glycol, methanol) owe their toxicity to metabolites more toxic than the parent compound. Overall mortality is low at less than 1% of all poisoning exposures, with most being minor or non-toxic and involving children under 6 years. Mortality is substantially higher (1-2%) among hospitalized patients with intentional (suicidal) overdose or complications from drugs of abuse, who account for most serious poisonings. Acetaminophen is the pharmaceutical most often implicated in fatal poisoning. Carbon monoxide is the overall leading cause of poisoning death, although it is underrepresented in hospital and poison-center statistics because such patients are typically dead when found and referred directly to medical examiners. Drug overdose deaths have risen steadily since 1999 (over 106,600 U.S. deaths in 2021; age-adjusted rate 32.4 per 100,000), driven largely by synthetic opioids such as fentanyl and emerging agents such as xylazine. Once the offending agent is eliminated, maintaining tissue perfusion is critical to complete recovery. Harrison grades physiologic stimulation and depression on a 1-4 scale. Stimulation: Grade 1 - anxious, irritable, tremulous with normal vital signs; Grade 2 - agitated, possible confusion/hallucinations but still able to converse and follow commands, mildly-to-moderately elevated vital signs; Grade 3 - delirious, unintelligible speech, uncontrollable motor hyperactivity, markedly raised vital signs, possible tachyarrhythmias; Grade 4 - coma, seizures, cardiovascular collapse. Depression: Grade 1 - lethargic/sleeping but arousable, able to converse; Grade 2 - responds to pain not voice, brainstem reflexes intact; Grade 3 - unresponsive to pain, depressed brainstem reflexes, decreased tone/respiration/temperature; Grade 4 - flaccid paralysis, absent brainstem reflexes and respirations, decreased cardiovascular vital signs.

POLR3-related leukodystrophy results from biallelic variants in genes encoding subunits of RNA polymerase III, the enzyme that transcribes small non-coding RNAs such as transfer RNAs and 5S ribosomal RNA. Impaired polymerase III activity is thought to reduce the supply of these RNAs needed for efficient protein synthesis, disproportionately affecting cells with high biosynthetic demands, including oligodendrocytes during myelination. The consequent failure of adequate myelin deposition produces hypomyelination, while involvement of other tissues explains the dental, endocrine and ocular manifestations that accompany the neurological picture. POLR3-related leukodystrophy is usually slowly progressive; many children develop skills before plateauing and then declining, with gait, coordination and speech becoming increasingly affected over years. Severity varies widely with genotype, from relatively mild adolescent-onset forms to more severe early-onset disease, and prognosis is influenced by the degree of motor and bulbar involvement.

chest wall protection Significant rib deficiency leaving thoracic viscera inadequately protected Paradoxical chest wall movement or respiratory compromise from extensive rib defects Coexisting cardiac or great vessel anomaly Features suggesting associated Moebius syndrome with feeding or airway risk Marked functional hand impairment requiring early rehabilitation Regarding it as a purely cosmetic chest deformity and missing functional hand impairment Overlooking rib deficiency that compromises thoracic protection or respiration Failing to assess for coexisting Moebius syndrome Not screening for cardiac anomalies, particularly with left-sided involvement Neglecting the psychosocial impact, especially breast asymmetry in adolescence Poland syndrome is thought to arise from a vascular disruption sequence, most commonly attributed to reduced blood flow through the subclavian artery and its branches during the sixth week of gestation. Interruption or hypoplasia of this vessel is proposed to compromise the developing chest wall and limb bud on the affected side, producing the absent pectoral muscle, chest wall and breast deficiency, and hand malformation. The degree and precise territory of the vascular compromise determine the pattern and severity of the anomalies, explaining the frequent unilaterality and the overlap with Moebius syndrome when the vertebral or brainstem circulation is also involved. Cases are overwhelmingly sporadic. The prognosis is generally good with normal life expectancy and cognition; management focuses on hand function, chest wall reconstruction where protection or appearance is a concern, and breast reconstruction in affected women.

Transmural inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis weakens the vessel wall, producing the microaneurysms characteristic of visceral angiography, while intimal proliferation and thrombosis cause luminal narrowing and downstream tissue infarction. Lesions are segmental and favour branch points. Unlike small-vessel vasculitides it does not typically involve capillaries, glomeruli, or the pulmonary circulation and is ANCA-negative. Immune complex mechanisms are implicated, particularly in hepatitis B-associated disease. Untreated disease has a poor outlook, but immunosuppression markedly improves survival. Prognosis is worse with significant gastrointestinal, renal, cardiac, or central nervous system involvement; hepatitis B-associated disease can respond well when the virus is also treated.
