Polycystic Kidney Disease — ADPKD, PKD Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD, PKHD1) - distal/collecting-duct cysts, oligohydramnios if severe, hypertension, congenital hepatic fibrosis and Caroli disease; absence of renal cysts in either parent >40y on ultrasound helps distinguish ARPKD from ADPKD (p.2430, p.2434) ADPKD-like disease (GANAB, DNAJB11) - normal-to-smaller kidneys with fewer cysts, variable liver cysts (p.2430-2432) Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (ADTKD; UMOD, MUC1, REN, HNF1B, SEC61A1) - small fibrotic kidneys, medullary cysts, gout in adults (p.2430) Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2) - renal cysts (20-30%), angiomyolipomas, increased risk of renal cell carcinoma, facial angiofibromas, CNS hamartomas; TSC2 is adjacent to PKD1 so a contiguous gene deletion can cause both ADPKD and TS (p.2430, p.2434) Von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL) - renal cysts, renal cell carcinoma, retinal angiomas, CNS hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytomas (p.2430) Nephronophthisis and other ciliopathies (e.g., Bardet-Biedl, Meckel-Gruber, Senior-Loken) - cystic kidney phenotypes with syndromic features (p.2430) Renal cysts and diabetes syndrome (HNF1B) - kidney cysts with aberrant nephrogenesis and diabetes (p.2430) Acquired simple renal cysts (increase in frequency with age and can confound diagnostic cyst counts) (p.2432-2433) Renal ultrasonography - first-line for presymptomatic screening and donor evaluation; age-stratified cyst-count criteria for diagnosis (p.2432-2433) CT and T2-weighted MRI (with/without contrast) - more sensitive than ultrasound, detect smaller cysts (MRI with gadolinium can detect 2-3 mm cysts); useful to distinguish malignancy from a complex cyst (p.2432-2433) Magnetic resonance angiography for presymptomatic intracranial aneurysm screening in patients with a positive family history of aneurysm (p.2432) CT scan as first diagnostic test for suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage, with lumbar puncture to confirm (p.2432) Genetic testing by linkage and mutational analysis for ambiguous cases; PKD1 analysis is difficult and costly owing to gene size and homologous pseudogenes (paired-end next-generation sequencing may improve this) (p.2433) Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common life-threatening monogenic disease, affecting ~12 million people worldwide (estimated prevalence 1:1000 to 1:400), and is a leading cause of kidney failure; it is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with complete penetrance but variable expressivity (p.2430-2431). ADPKD is caused by mutations in PKD1 (chromosome 16p13, ~85% of cases, encodes polycystin-1) and PKD2 (chromosome 4q21-q23, ~15% of cases, encodes polycystin-2); PKD2 patients tend to have milder disease and may be underdiagnosed. Polycystins are localized on the primary cilium, and defective ciliary function places ADPKD among the ciliopathies (p.2430-2431). It is characterized by progressive bilateral formation of epithelial-lined renal cysts; cysts arise in only ~5% of tubules but their enormous growth destroys surrounding tissue. Enlarged kidneys can reach a fourfold increase in length and up to 20 times the normal weight (p.2430-2431). Back or flank pain is a frequent symptom in ~60% of patients and may result from cyst infection, hemorrhage, or nephrolithiasis; gross hematuria from cyst rupture occurs in ~40% during the disease course, often recurrently (p.2432). Hypertension is common and typically occurs before any reduction in GFR; it is a risk factor for both cardiovascular and kidney disease progression. Cardiovascular complications are the major cause of mortality in ADPKD (p.2432). Intracranial (berry) aneurysm occurs four to five times more frequently than in the general population and causes high mortality; about 20-50% of patients may have 'warning headaches' preceding subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm (p.2432). Liver (biliary epithelial) cysts are the most common extrarenal complication; massive polycystic liver disease occurs almost exclusively in women, particularly those with multiple pregnancies. Mitral valve prolapse occurs in up to 30% of patients, and colonic diverticulae and abdominal wall hernias are also increased (p.2432). Diagnosis is typically made from a positive autosomal dominant family history plus bilateral kidney cysts on ultrasonography; in at-risk subjects aged 15-29 years, two renal cysts (unilateral or bilateral) suffice (sensitivity 96%, specificity 100%), with higher cyst counts required at older ages because simple cysts increase with age (p.2432-2433). Tolvaptan, a vasopressin V2-receptor (V2R) antagonist, inhibits the cAMP pathway in collecting ducts and reduces cell proliferation by lowering renal cAMP, slowing the decline of renal function; the FDA has indicated it only for patients at risk of rapidly progressing disease (p.2433). Infection is the second most common cause of death; up to half of patients have one or more renal infections, most commonly an infected cyst or acute pyelonephritis due to gram-negative bacteria, with fever and flank pain (p.2432). Sudden severe headache or 'warning headache' suggesting subarachnoid hemorrhage from ruptured intracranial (berry) aneurysm (p.2432) Positive family history of intracranial aneurysm - a risk factor for aneurysm rupture warranting presymptomatic MRA screening (p.2432) Fever and flank pain indicating infected cyst or acute pyelonephritis (with or without bacteremia); infection is the second most common cause of death (p.2432) Gross hematuria from cyst rupture (p.2432) Diffuse arterial dolichoectasia of the cerebral circulation predisposing to arterial dissection and stroke (p.2432) Proteinuria is usually only a MINOR feature of ADPKD, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis (p.2432). Renal cell carcinoma is NOT increased in frequency compared with the general population, but when it does occur in ADPKD it is more often bilateral, multicentric, and sarcomatoid; radiologic imaging is often unable to distinguish cyst infection from cyst hemorrhage due to their complexity (p.2432). Diagnostic cyst-count thresholds rise with age because simple renal cysts increase with age; criteria have lower sensitivity for PKD2 patients owing to late onset (p.2432-2433). No specific FDA-approved treatment prevents cyst growth or the decline of renal function; more rigorous blood pressure control does not equal greater benefit, and targeting systolic pressure to 110 mmHg in moderate/advanced disease may worsen progression by reducing renal blood flow (p.2433). Most renal cysts are not connected to glomerular filtration, so cyst infection requires lipid-soluble antibiotics that penetrate cyst walls (e.g., trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, quinolones, chloramphenicol), often for 4-6 weeks (p.2433). Polycystic liver disease in ADPKD is distinct from isolated autosomal dominant polycystic liver disease (ADPLD; PRKCSH/SEC63), which does NOT progress to renal failure (p.2432). ADPKD results from mutations in PKD1 and PKD2, encoding polycystin-1 (PC1, a large 11-transmembrane G-protein-coupled-receptor-like protein) and polycystin-2 (PC2, a calcium-permeable six-transmembrane TRP-family cation channel). PC1 and PC2 bind via their C-terminal tails to form a receptor-channel complex (proposed 1:3 PC1:PC2 stoichiometry) located on the primary cilium and at cell membranes and cell-cell junctions of tubular epithelium, functioning as a mechano-/chemosensor regulating calcium and G-protein signaling. Every cell carries a germline mutant allele, but cysts develop in only a small fraction of nephrons, thought to arise from clonal growth of cells sustaining a somatic 'second hit' in the normal allele; a 'third hit' such as renal injury or an additional genetic/epigenetic event may accelerate cyst formation. Loss of ciliary PC1/PC2 function is hypothesized to cause aberrant calcium signaling, increased adenylyl cyclase and decreased phosphodiesterase activity, raising cellular cAMP; increased cAMP promotes protein kinase A activity, driving cyst growth through proliferation and chloride/aquaporin-mediated fluid secretion. Cellular defects include increased proliferation and fluid secretion, decreased differentiation, and abnormal extracellular matrix; affected signaling pathways include Wnt, mTOR, STAT3, cMET, PI3K/Akt, GPCR, EGFR, and CFTR. Rarer ADPKD-associated genes GANAB and DNAJB11 affect PC1 trafficking and cause milder cystic disease. ADPKD progression shows striking inter- and intrafamilial variability; disease can present as early as in utero, but end-stage renal disease typically occurs in late middle age. Risk factors for progression include early diagnosis, hypertension, gross hematuria, multiple pregnancies, and large kidney size; PKD2 disease is generally milder with later onset. More than half of patients eventually require peritoneal dialysis, hemodialysis, or kidney transplantation. Cardiovascular complications are the major cause of mortality, and renal infection is the second most common cause of death (p.2431-2433). Harrison does not provide a formal stage-based severity classification for ADPKD. Genotype broadly stratifies severity (PKD1 disease ~85% of cases is more severe with earlier onset than PKD2 disease ~15%; GANAB/DNAJB11 mutations cause milder cystic disease). Risk of rapid progression - used to select patients for tolvaptan - is estimated by combining genotypic and imaging (kidney growth rate) information; recognized clinical risk factors for progression include early diagnosis, hypertension, gross hematuria, multiple pregnancies, and large kidney size (p.2431-2433).

somatostatin analogues can reduce liver volume Fever and localised pain suggesting cyst infection Sudden severe pain from cyst haemorrhage or rupture Jaundice or portal hypertension from biliary or vascular compression Lower-limb oedema or Budd-Chiari-like features from inferior vena cava/hepatic vein compression Failing to look for coexisting renal cysts and distinguish ADPKD from isolated PLD Mistaking a cystic neoplasm or hydatid cyst for a simple polycystic cyst Aspirating a cyst without sclerotherapy, leading to rapid recurrence Attributing abnormal liver tests to the cysts rather than seeking another cause Polycystic liver disease arises from abnormal proliferation of the biliary epithelium and defective ductal plate remodelling, producing fluid-filled cysts derived from biliary microhamartomas that lose continuity with the biliary tree. In isolated autosomal dominant disease, mutations in genes including PRKCSH (encoding hepatocystin) and SEC63 disrupt glycoprotein processing and protein translocation in cholangiocytes, promoting cyst formation. Cysts also accompany ADPKD (PKD1/PKD2). Progressive cyst growth, modulated by oestrogen and cyclic AMP-driven fluid secretion, leads to hepatomegaly and mass-effect complications while sparing hepatocellular function. Overall prognosis is good because hepatocellular function is generally preserved; symptoms relate to liver volume and complications, and even severely affected patients can be managed with volume-reducing procedures or, rarely, transplantation.

ovarian morphology and antral follicle count Oral glucose tolerance test and lipid profile to assess metabolic risk PCOS is diagnosed using the Rotterdam criteria, requiring at least two of oligo- or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound, after excluding mimics Common presentations include irregular or absent periods, hirsutism and acne, subfertility, and difficulty with weight Insulin resistance is central to the syndrome and is often present regardless of body weight, though obesity worsens it It is the leading cause of anovulatory infertility Unopposed oestrogen from chronic anovulation increases the long-term risk of endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma, so regular endometrial protection is important Lifestyle modification with weight management is the first-line intervention and can restore ovulation and improve metabolic profile Management is symptom-directed: cycle regulation and endometrial protection, treatment of hyperandrogenic features, and ovulation induction when fertility is desired Screening for and managing metabolic complications, including impaired glucose tolerance, type 2 diabetes, and dyslipidaemia, is an essential part of long-term care Rapid onset or severe virilisation suggesting an androgen-secreting tumour rather than PCOS Prolonged amenorrhoea with abnormal bleeding raising concern for endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma Markedly elevated androgens beyond the range typical of PCOS Features of Cushing syndrome Severe metabolic derangement such as newly diagnosed diabetes Diagnosing PCOS without excluding thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, and other mimics Relying on ultrasound alone, since polycystic ovarian morphology can occur in healthy women Overlooking endometrial protection in women with prolonged amenorrhoea Focusing only on fertility and neglecting long-term metabolic and cardiovascular risk Attributing severe or rapidly progressive virilisation to PCOS PCOS reflects a complex interplay of hormonal and metabolic disturbances. Insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinaemia stimulates ovarian theca cells to overproduce androgens and reduces hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin, raising free androgen levels. Altered gonadotrophin secretion, with a relatively high luteinising hormone drive, further promotes androgen production and disrupts follicular maturation, so multiple small antral follicles accumulate without a dominant follicle emerging, causing anovulation. Chronic unopposed oestrogen exposure from anovulation places the endometrium at risk of hyperplasia. PCOS is a lifelong condition whose reproductive symptoms often improve with weight management and targeted therapy, and many women conceive with or without ovulation induction. The main long-term concerns are metabolic, with increased risks of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and, through chronic anovulation, endometrial cancer; proactive metabolic surveillance improves outcomes.

Polycythaemia vera — polycythemia vera, primary polycythaemia, PV Secondary polycythaemia (hypoxia, erythropoietin-secreting tumour) Relative (apparent) polycythaemia from plasma volume contraction Essential thrombocythaemia or primary myelofibrosis Congenital polycythaemia Chronic myeloid leukaemia Full blood count and haematocrit JAK2 V617F and, if negative, exon 12 mutation analysis Serum erythropoietin (characteristically low) Bone marrow examination where needed Assessment of thrombotic risk factors A myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by autonomous overproduction of red cells, often with raised white cells and platelets Almost all cases carry a JAK2 mutation (V617F or exon 12) Symptoms include aquagenic pruritus, erythromelalgia, headache, plethora and thrombosis A low serum erythropoietin supports the diagnosis and helps distinguish it from secondary polycythaemia The dominant risks are arterial and venous thrombosis, with later potential to transform to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia Management combines venesection to a target haematocrit, aspirin and, in higher-risk patients, cytoreduction Arterial or venous thrombosis, including unusual-site thrombosis Very high haematocrit with hyperviscosity symptoms Progressive splenomegaly or cytopenias suggesting transformation to myelofibrosis Blasts suggesting leukaemic transformation Confusing it with secondary or relative polycythaemia Failing to control the haematocrit to target Overlooking JAK2-negative cases needing exon 12 testing Missing transformation signalled by new cytopenias or splenomegaly Polycythaemia vera is a clonal stem cell disorder driven in nearly all cases by activating JAK2 mutations, which render erythroid (and often myeloid and megakaryocytic) progenitors hypersensitive to, or independent of, erythropoietin. The resulting unregulated proliferation expands the red cell mass and frequently the granulocyte and platelet lines. The elevated haematocrit raises blood viscosity and, together with qualitative platelet and endothelial changes, produces the high thrombotic risk, while progressive marrow fibrosis or clonal evolution underlies transformation. With haematocrit control and thrombosis prevention many patients live for decades, but the disease carries thrombotic risk and a smaller long-term risk of transformation to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia.

Post-polycythaemia vera myelofibrosis — post-PV myelofibrosis, post-polycythaemic myelofibrosis Primary myelofibrosis Post-essential-thrombocythaemia myelofibrosis Reactive marrow fibrosis (for example infection, malignancy) Myelodysplastic syndrome with fibrosis Chronic myeloid leukaemia Full blood count and film for leucoerythroblastic changes and teardrop cells Bone marrow trephine demonstrating fibrosis JAK2 and driver-mutation status (usually known from prior PV) Assessment of spleen size and constitutional symptoms Prognostic scoring for myelofibrosis A recognised progression of polycythaemia vera to a myelofibrotic phase with marrow fibrosis It is marked by a falling need for venesection, anaemia, progressive splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms The blood film shows a leucoerythroblastic picture with teardrop cells Diagnostic criteria require established polycythaemia vera plus marrow fibrosis and additional features such as anaemia and splenomegaly It resembles primary myelofibrosis clinically and shares the risk of leukaemic transformation Management mirrors that of myelofibrosis, including JAK inhibition for symptoms and splenomegaly and transplantation in selected patients Rising blasts indicating transformation to acute leukaemia Severe anaemia or thrombocytopenia Massive or painful splenomegaly Profound constitutional symptoms and weight loss Attributing the falling haematocrit and anaemia to over-venesection rather than fibrotic transformation Confusing it with primary myelofibrosis without the prior PV history Missing leukaemic transformation Overlooking the need to reassess prognosis and management Post-polycythaemia vera myelofibrosis represents clonal evolution of the underlying JAK2-driven myeloproliferative neoplasm. Chronic cytokine release and megakaryocyte proliferation stimulate reactive deposition of reticulin and collagen fibrosis in the marrow, progressively impairing haematopoiesis. As the marrow fails, red cell production falls (so venesection is no longer needed and anaemia develops) and haematopoiesis shifts to the spleen and liver (extramedullary haematopoiesis), causing organomegaly and the leucoerythroblastic blood picture. The disease carries an increased risk of transformation to acute leukaemia. Transformation to a fibrotic phase generally worsens prognosis compared with polycythaemia vera, with outcomes similar to primary myelofibrosis and a risk of leukaemic transformation; allogeneic transplantation is the only cure.

Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms — Myeloproliferative neoplasms, MPN, PV, Primary myelofibrosis, PMF, Agnogenic myeloid metaplasia, Myelofibrosis with myeloid metaplasia, Essential thrombocytosis, Essential thrombocythemia, ET Relative (spurious/stress) erythrocytosis from plasma volume contraction (Gaisbock's syndrome) due to dehydration, diuretics, ethanol, androgens, or tobacco Hypoxic erythrocytosis (pulmonary disease, right-to-left shunt, sleep apnea, high altitude, carbon monoxide, high-oxygen-affinity hemoglobin) Tumor- or renal-disease-associated erythrocytosis (hypernephroma, hepatoma, cerebellar hemangioblastoma, uterine myoma, pheochromocytoma, renal artery stenosis, renal cysts, post-transplant) Congenital/familial erythrocytosis (erythropoietin receptor, VHL/Chuvash, 2,3-BPG, PHD2/EGLN1, HIF2alpha/EPAS1, LNK mutations) and recombinant erythropoietin or SGLT2-inhibitor effect Reactive thrombocytosis (iron deficiency, infection, inflammation, malignancy, hemorrhage, surgery, postsplenectomy, B12/folate-deficiency rebound) Chronic myeloid leukemia (BCR-ABL positive), myelodysplasia including 5q- syndrome and sideroblastic anemia (SF3B1) Secondary myelofibrosis (myelophthisis) from metastatic carcinoma, lymphoma, multiple myeloma, hairy cell leukemia, systemic mastocytosis, and nonmalignant causes such as HIV, tuberculosis, SLE, hyperparathyroidism, renal osteodystrophy, vitamin D deficiency HIV infection (can cause secondary myelofibrosis) Tuberculosis (can cause secondary myelofibrosis and constitutional symptoms) Quantitative next-generation-sequencing assay for JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutations (now supersedes surrogate tests for PV diagnosis) Red cell mass and plasma volume determination to confirm absolute versus relative erythrocytosis when hemoglobin is below ~20 g/dL Serum erythropoietin level (elevated level favors a secondary cause; a normal level does not exclude PV) Red cell count, mean corpuscular volume, and red cell distribution width (microcytic erythrocytosis narrows differential) Mutation testing for MPL and CALR (exon 9, type 1 deletions and type 2 insertions) in JAK2-negative ET/PMF FISH for BCR-ABL to exclude CML in JAK2-negative thrombocytosis Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy (megakaryocyte clustering/hyperplasia, reticulin/collagen fibrosis in PMF; absent stainable iron with hypercellularity favors PV) Cytogenetic analysis (del 20q, del 13q, trisomy 8/9, partial trisomy 1q; complex karyotype portends poor prognosis in PMF) Mutational analysis of ASXL1, EZH2, SRSF2, and IDH1/2 for refined PMF prognosis Ristocetin cofactor activity to detect acquired von Willebrand disease at very high platelet counts Serum lactate dehydrogenase and alkaline phosphatase (may be elevated in PMF), uric acid Reactive thrombocytosis from iron deficiency, inflammation, or malignancy mimicking ET Stress/spurious erythrocytosis (Gaisbock's syndrome) mimicking PV Chronic myeloid leukemia mimicking ET or PMF Myelodysplastic syndromes (5q- syndrome, sideroblastic anemia) presenting with thrombocytosis Metastatic carcinoma, lymphoma, or systemic mastocytosis causing myelophthisic marrow fibrosis Systemic lupus erythematosus, hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, and renal osteodystrophy causing nonmalignant myelofibrosis The classic chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms covered here (PV, PMF, ET) all arise from a hematopoietic stem cell and share constitutive activation of JAK2 through driver mutations in JAK2, MPL, or CALR; their natural histories are usually measured in decades, and leukemic transformation is uncommon in the absence of chemotherapy or radiation (Harrison 22e p.818). JAK2 V617F is expressed in more than 95% of PV patients and in roughly 50% of PMF and ET patients; most JAK2-negative PV patients carry a JAK2 exon 12 mutation, while a few have LNK or calreticulin mutations (Harrison 22e p.818-819). In PV the plasma volume is expanded, unlike other causes of true erythrocytosis, so an elevated red cell mass can be masked, especially in women; below a hemoglobin of about 20 g/dL (hematocrit 60%) one cannot reliably separate true erythrocytosis from plasma-volume contraction without red cell mass and plasma volume measurement (Harrison 22e p.819-820). PV should be suspected in any woman presenting with hepatic vein (Budd-Chiari) thrombosis, since this is the type of thrombosis particularly associated with JAK2 V617F; portal vein thrombosis is more common in male PV patients (Harrison 22e p.819). Aquagenic pruritus and erythromelalgia are the symptoms that can suggest PV over other causes of erythrocytosis; pruritus may reflect JAK2 V617F-driven mast cell activation, and Helicobacter pylori incidence is increased in PV (Harrison 22e p.819-820). Only three conditions cause microcytic erythrocytosis: beta-thalassemia trait, hypoxic erythrocytosis, and PV; the red cell distribution width is typically normal in thalassemia trait but may be elevated in hypoxic erythrocytosis or PV when iron deficiency coexists (Harrison 22e p.820). In a PV patient with massive splenomegaly, a 'normal' hematocrit or hemoglobin should be regarded as indicating an elevated red cell mass until proven otherwise, because the associated plasma volume increase masks the true red cell mass (Harrison 22e p.820). In PMF the peripheral smear shows a leukoerythroblastic picture with teardrop-shaped red cells, nucleated red cells, myelocytes, and promyelocytes; marrow is usually inaspirable ('dry tap') owing to fibrosis, and bone x-rays may show osteosclerosis (Harrison 22e p.821-822). PMF marrow fibroblasts are polyclonal and not part of the neoplastic clone; fibrosis is driven by overproduction of transforming growth factor beta, tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases, and thrombopoietin, while osteosclerosis relates to osteoprotegerin and angiogenesis to vascular endothelial growth factor (Harrison 22e p.821). In ET the large platelet mass can cause spurious (test-tube) hyperkalemia from platelet potassium release on clotting, with no electrocardiographic correlate, and can make arterial oxygen measurements inaccurate unless blood is collected on ice (Harrison 22e p.823). Very high platelet counts (above about 1 million/microL) are associated primarily with bleeding from acquired von Willebrand disease due to proteolysis of high-molecular-weight von Willebrand multimers, not with thrombosis; tobacco use is the most important thrombotic risk factor in ET (Harrison 22e p.823-824). PMF and ET diagnoses are largely diagnoses of exclusion: significant splenomegaly in apparent ET suggests another MPN, and FISH for BCR-ABL is preferred to exclude CML in JAK2-negative thrombocytosis because reverse-transcriptase PCR for BCR-ABL is prone to false positives (Harrison 22e p.823-824). Hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd-Chiari) in a young woman, or portal/mesenteric vein thrombosis, as a presenting feature of PV Neurologic hyperviscosity symptoms: vertigo, tinnitus, headache, visual disturbance, transient ischemic attack Arterial or venous thrombosis in cerebral, cardiac, or mesenteric vessels Platelet count above 1 million/microL with bleeding from acquired von Willebrand disease Sudden splenic enlargement with painful splenic infarction (fever, pleuritic chest pain) Development of transfusion-dependent anemia, increasing organomegaly, or peripheral blood blasts signaling marrow failure or accelerated/blastic transformation in PMF Constitutional symptoms (night sweats, fatigue, weight loss) suggesting a myeloproliferative rather than reactive process Spinal cord compression, pericardial tamponade, or ureteral/intestinal obstruction from exuberant extramedullary hematopoiesis in PMF Treating the platelet count rather than the patient in ET: a high platelet count alone does not establish thrombotic risk, and the cause of any symptom must be confirmed to be platelet-related before therapy Assuming a high platelet count causes thrombosis when very high counts more often cause hemorrhage via acquired von Willebrand disease; aspirin can promote bleeding in this setting Interpreting a normal hematocrit/hemoglobin as excluding elevated red cell mass in a PV patient with massive splenomegaly (plasma volume expansion masks it) Relying on a low-level JAK2 V617F allele burden (VAF 5% or less) to diagnose a blood disease, since not everyone with low burden has one Assuming a normal serum erythropoietin excludes PV (it does not), or overlooking that an elevated level points to a secondary cause Diagnosing ET in a JAK2 V617F-positive patient without red cell mass/plasma volume studies, since many such patients actually have PV Misreading spurious hyperkalemia or inaccurate arterial oxygen values caused by the large platelet mass in ET Mistaking secondary myelofibrosis/myelophthisis for PMF and missing a treatable underlying disorder Using leukemogenic agents (alkylating agents, radioactive phosphorus-32) and prolonged hydroxyurea, which is itself mutagenic and antagonizes TP53, in disorders with otherwise long survival These chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms originate in a single hematopoietic stem cell and produce overabundant mature blood elements without significant dysplasia, together with a tendency toward extramedullary hematopoiesis, myelofibrosis, and eventual leukemic transformation. PV, PMF, and ET share constitutive activation of the nonreceptor tyrosine kinase JAK2, the cognate kinase and chaperone for the erythropoietin and thrombopoietin receptors. The JAK2 V617F mutation in the autoinhibitory pseudokinase domain causes ligand-independent kinase activation, explaining erythropoietin hypersensitivity, erythropoietin-independent erythroid colony growth, increased Bcl-XL expression, and apoptosis resistance in PV progenitors. Loss of heterozygosity on chromosome 9p (uniparental disomy) leads to JAK2 V617F homozygosity, common in PV, less so in PMF, and rare in ET. JAK2 V617F alone does not account for the entire phenotype and is probably not the initiating lesion: the same mutation yields different phenotypes in ET versus PMF, familial PV can occur without it, and leukemia may arise in a JAK2-negative progenitor, implying an ancestral precursor. PMF and ET may instead carry MPL (thrombopoietin receptor) or CALR (calreticulin) mutations; mutant CALR binds and activates MPL at the cell surface. In PMF, marrow fibrosis is a reactive, polyclonal fibroblast response driven by cytokines from the clone (TGF-beta, thrombopoietin), with extramedullary hematopoiesis in liver and spleen. Megakaryocyte genome reduplication is endomitotic and thrombopoietin-driven; paradoxically, MPL expression is reduced and plasma thrombopoietin is increased across these MPNs despite the expanded megakaryocyte/platelet mass. PV is generally indolent, with a clinical course measured in decades; most patients live long lives without functional impairment when red cell mass is controlled, and the incidence of acute leukemia is very low in those not exposed to chemotherapy or radiation. Myelofibrosis is part of the natural history of PV but is usually reactive and reversible without prognostic significance, although about 15% develop hematopoietic stem cell failure with extramedullary hematopoiesis and transfusion-dependent anemia. PMF has the shortest survival of the three: it follows a course of progressive marrow failure and organomegaly, can evolve to an accelerated phase, and about 10% transform spontaneously to a treatment-refractory acute leukemia. PMF survival is stratified by IPSS, DIPSS, and DIPSS-Plus risk factors (anemia, leukocytosis, peripheral blasts, constitutional symptoms, age over 65, unfavorable karyotype, thrombocytopenia, transfusion dependence); ASXL1, EZH2, SRSF2, and IDH1/2 mutations and complex cytogenetics independently predict early death or leukemic transformation, and triple-negative PMF carries the worst prognosis. ET is more benign than previously thought; survival is comparable to the general population regardless of driver mutation, and leukemic evolution is more often a consequence of therapy than of the disease. For primary myelofibrosis, prognostic risk is estimated by the IPSS (2009), DIPSS (2010), and DIPSS-Plus (2011) scoring systems. Risk factors include anemia (hemoglobin <10 g/dL), leukocytosis (>25,000/microL), peripheral blood blasts (>=1%), constitutional symptoms, and age over 65; DIPSS-Plus adds unfavorable karyotype, platelet count <100,000/microL, and transfusion dependence. In DIPSS, anemia is weighted as 2 points. Categories run Low, Intermediate-1, Intermediate-2, and High by number/weight of factors. These systems are not accurate for risk assessment of PV or ET patients who have developed secondary myelofibrosis.

Polydactyly — supernumerary digit, preaxial polydactyly, postaxial polydactyly, central polydactyly, duplicated digit Syndactyly or polysyndactyly, which may coexist Macrodactyly (an enlarged rather than duplicated digit) Ulnar dimelia (mirror hand) Triphalangeal thumb Constriction ring sequence with accessory tissue Symphalangism Radiographs of the hand to define the level of skeletal duplication (for example Wassel-Flatt grading of the thumb) Family history and examination of relatives, as postaxial forms are often autosomal dominant Clinical screening for syndromic features affecting the heart, kidneys, retina, and growth Echocardiography where a heart-hand or VACTERL association is suspected Genetic evaluation when the pattern is syndromic, central, or bilateral Polydactyly is duplication of a digit and is classified by location: preaxial (thumb or radial side), central (index to ring), and postaxial (little finger or ulnar side) Postaxial polydactyly is common, frequently familial (autosomal dominant), and more prevalent in children of African ancestry; it may be isolated or syndromic Preaxial (thumb) duplication is graded by the Wassel-Flatt classification according to the most proximal level of skeletal duplication, from a bifid distal phalanx to a duplicated metacarpal Central polydactyly is less common, is often hidden within a syndactyly (polysyndactyly), and involves complex bony and tendinous connections that are difficult to reconstruct Syndromic associations must be considered: preaxial forms with conditions such as Holt-Oram syndrome and Fanconi anaemia, and postaxial forms with Ellis-van Creveld, Bardet-Biedl, Meckel-Gruber, and trisomy 13 A well-formed extra digit is not simply excised; reconstruction preserves the most functional bone, joint, ligaments, tendons, and nail, and reconstructs collateral ligament stability Surgery is timed to optimise function and appearance, generally in early childhood Features suggesting a serious syndrome, such as a cardiac anomaly, renal disease, retinal dystrophy, or marrow-failure risk Central polydactyly or polysyndactyly with complex functional impairment A duplicated thumb that is unstable or deviating, threatening pinch function Simply tying off or amputating a duplicated digit without reconstructing the collateral ligaments, leaving instability or deviation Discarding the more functional of two duplicated thumbs Failing to look for syndromic associations Underestimating the complexity of central polysyndactyly Polydactyly arises from disordered patterning of the developing limb bud along the anteroposterior (radioulnar) axis. Abnormal signalling, notably of the sonic hedgehog pathway acting through the zone of polarising activity, produces one or more supernumerary digits. The duplicated ray may be a rudimentary soft-tissue tag or a fully formed digit with its own bones, joints, and tendons. Depending on which part of the axis is affected, the extra digit lies on the radial (preaxial), central, or ulnar (postaxial) side of the hand, and disturbances of these same signalling pathways underlie the many syndromic forms. Isolated postaxial and most preaxial duplications have an excellent outcome after well-planned reconstruction; residual problems can include joint instability, angular deviation, stiffness, and a reconstructed thumb that is smaller than normal, while central forms are more prone to stiffness and imperfect appearance.

Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (APECED, AIRE) — APS-1, APECED, autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy, autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2 Isolated Addison disease Isolated idiopathic hypoparathyroidism DiGeorge syndrome (hypoparathyroidism with immunodeficiency) IPEX syndrome Isolated chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis from other immune defects AIRE gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis Calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone for hypoparathyroidism Morning cortisol with ACTH stimulation and adrenal autoantibodies for Addison disease Autoantibody panel including anti-interferon antibodies and organ-specific antibodies Screening for additional components: thyroid, gonadal and glucose testing, liver enzymes and full blood count Assessment of ectodermal features including dental and ophthalmic review A monogenic autoimmune disorder caused by mutations in the AIRE gene, which normally drives thymic negative selection of self-reactive T cells Defined by the classic triad of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), with two of the three needed for diagnosis Candidiasis usually appears first in childhood, followed by hypoparathyroidism and then adrenal failure A wide range of additional autoimmune features may develop, including hypogonadism, type 1 diabetes, autoimmune hepatitis, pernicious anaemia, alopecia and vitiligo Ectodermal features such as enamel hypoplasia, nail dystrophy and keratopathy support the diagnosis High-titre neutralising autoantibodies against type-1 interferons and interleukin-17/22 are characteristic and underlie susceptibility to candidiasis Because new component disorders emerge over years, lifelong surveillance for evolving endocrine and non-endocrine autoimmunity is essential Adrenal crisis from unrecognised or intercurrent-stress-precipitated adrenal insufficiency Symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany, laryngospasm or seizures Fulminant autoimmune hepatitis Invasive or oesophageal candidiasis, or squamous carcinoma arising in chronic candidiasis Managing each component in isolation and failing to anticipate emerging new autoimmune disorders Overlooking coexisting adrenal insufficiency when treating hypoparathyroidism, risking crisis Attributing recurrent candidiasis to simple infection rather than the underlying immune defect Missing autoimmune hepatitis or other non-endocrine components during follow-up Not offering genetic counselling and family screening APS-1 results from loss-of-function mutations in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene, which controls expression of tissue-specific self-antigens in thymic medullary epithelial cells. Defective AIRE impairs negative selection of autoreactive T cells, allowing escape of lymphocytes that attack multiple endocrine and non-endocrine tissues. The resulting organ-specific autoimmunity destroys the parathyroid glands and adrenal cortex among others, while neutralising autoantibodies against type-1 interferons and Th17 cytokines compromise mucosal antifungal immunity, explaining the characteristic chronic candidiasis. With hormone replacement and antifungal treatment most patients survive into adulthood, but the disease is lifelong and mortality is driven by adrenal crises, severe hypocalcaemia, fulminant hepatitis and complications of chronic candidiasis.

syndrome type 1 Isolated autoimmune Addison disease Isolated autoimmune thyroid disease Type 1 diabetes mellitus without additional endocrinopathy Secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary so cortisol status must be assessed first Periodic screening of at-risk relatives and of affected patients for evolving deficiencies is central to management Treatment is lifelong hormone replacement tailored to each affected gland Adrenal crisis with hypotension, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia Precipitation of crisis by thyroid hormone given before glucocorticoid replacement Diabetic ketoacidosis at diabetes onset Severe hypothyroidism Rapid clinical deterioration during intercurrent illness Starting levothyroxine before excluding or treating adrenal insufficiency and triggering a crisis Diagnosing a single endocrinopathy without considering the wider syndrome Failing to screen for evolving deficiencies over time Overlooking associated non-endocrine autoimmune disease such as coeliac disease Confusing the polygenic type 2 syndrome with the monogenic type 1 form Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 is an organ-specific autoimmune disorder in which loss of immune self-tolerance leads to lymphocytic destruction of multiple endocrine glands. Susceptibility is polygenic, driven strongly by human leucocyte antigen associations together with other immune-regulatory gene variants, rather than by a single-gene defect. Circulating autoantibodies against adrenal, thyroid and pancreatic islet antigens mark the underlying cell-mediated destruction, which progresses at different rates in different glands, producing the characteristic sequential emergence of adrenal insufficiency, thyroid dysfunction and type 1 diabetes over time. With prompt recognition and lifelong, appropriately balanced hormone replacement, patients can expect a near-normal life, though the ongoing risk of adrenal crisis and the potential for new autoimmune components to develop necessitate continued surveillance.

Polyhydramnios — hydramnios, amniotic fluid excess Multiple pregnancy Fetal macrosomia Large uterine fibroids or an adnexal mass Inaccurate gestational dating Maternal obesity giving a false impression of a large uterus An ovarian or other pelvic-abdominal cyst Ultrasound quantification of amniotic fluid by deepest vertical pool or amniotic fluid index Detailed fetal anomaly ultrasound, with attention to the stomach bubble, swallowing, and structural survey Maternal testing for diabetes by glucose tolerance testing or glycaemic assessment Assessment for fetal anaemia, such as middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity Doppler, and for hydrops Screening for congenital infection where indicated Consideration of fetal karyotype or microarray when structural anomalies are present Assessment of chorionicity and inter-twin fluid discordance in multiple pregnancy Polyhydramnios is an excessive volume of amniotic fluid, defined sonographically by a deepest vertical pool at or above a defined threshold or an amniotic fluid index above the ninety-fifth centile for gestation Causes fall into fetal, maternal, and placental groups; roughly half to two-thirds are idiopathic, but a cause should always be sought Fetal causes include anything that impairs swallowing or increases urine output, such as gastrointestinal obstruction (oesophageal or duodenal atresia), neurological and neuromuscular disorders, orofacial clefts, chest masses, cardiac anomalies, and hydrops Maternal diabetes, pre-existing or gestational, is a leading maternal cause through fetal hyperglycaemia and osmotic diuresis, so glycaemic control should be assessed In monochorionic twins, polyhydramnios in one sac with oligohydramnios in the other suggests twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome Symptoms and signs reflect uterine overdistension: abdominal discomfort and breathlessness, a large-for-dates uterus, a tense abdomen with difficulty palpating fetal parts, and a fluid thrill Complications arise chiefly from overdistension and sudden decompression, including preterm labour, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, malpresentation, cord prolapse, placental abruption after membrane rupture, and postpartum haemorrhage from atony Management targets the cause and the complications: optimise maternal glycaemia, monitor for preterm labour and malpresentation, consider amnioreduction in symptomatic cases, and assess the neonate for anomalies such as oesophageal atresia after birth Rapidly increasing fluid or acute maternal respiratory distress from massive polyhydramnios Preterm contractions or prelabour rupture of membranes Malpresentation or a high, unstable lie near term, carrying a cord prolapse risk Sonographic evidence of a major fetal anomaly, hydrops, or twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome Signs of placental abruption after membrane rupture Labelling polyhydramnios idiopathic without a thorough search for fetal anomaly, diabetes, and anaemia Overlooking oesophageal atresia antenatally and failing to assess the neonate, for example by passing a nasogastric tube, after birth Performing artificial rupture of membranes without controlling for the risk of cord prolapse and abruption from sudden decompression Neglecting the raised risk of postpartum haemorrhage from an overdistended, atonic uterus Missing twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome by not assessing chorionicity and inter-twin discordance Amniotic fluid volume in the second half of pregnancy is maintained by a balance between fetal urine production and lung fluid, which add fluid, and fetal swallowing and intramembranous absorption, which remove it. Polyhydramnios develops when production exceeds removal. Reduced swallowing or absorption occurs with upper gastrointestinal obstruction, in which the fetus cannot swallow fluid past an atresia, with neuromuscular disease impairing swallowing, and with external compression of the gut. Increased production occurs with fetal polyuria, as in maternal hyperglycaemia causing fetal osmotic diuresis, in high-output states such as fetal anaemia, and in the recipient twin of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome. The accumulating fluid overdistends the uterus, stretching the myometrium and predisposing to preterm contractions and, after membrane rupture, to rapid decompression that can shear the placenta or allow the cord to prolapse. Idiopathic mild polyhydramnios generally has a good outcome, but moderate-to-severe polyhydramnios and cases with an identifiable fetal anomaly or twin-to-twin transfusion carry higher perinatal morbidity and mortality; prognosis is largely determined by the underlying cause.

Polymicrogyria — PMG, bilateral perisylvian polymicrogyria, cortical dysplasia (polymicrogyria type), GPR56 (ADGRG1), TUBB2B Pachygyria and other lissencephaly-spectrum malformations Cobblestone malformation of the dystroglycanopathies Schizencephaly, which is frequently lined by polymicrogyria Focal cortical dysplasia Congenital cytomegalovirus-related cortical malformation Tubulinopathy-related cortical dysgenesis High-resolution brain MRI to define the distribution and extent of the malformation Testing for congenital cytomegalovirus infection, including stored newborn blood spot analysis where available Chromosomal microarray, including assessment for 22q11.2 deletion Gene panel or exome sequencing for cortical malformation genes Electroencephalography to characterise seizures Swallowing and speech assessment for perisylvian involvement A malformation of late cortical organisation in which the cortex forms excessive small, fused gyri with abnormal lamination, producing an irregular or bumpy cortical surface It is often bilateral and symmetric in recognised patterns, the perisylvian region being the most common site, giving the bilateral perisylvian syndrome MRI shows an irregular grey-white junction with numerous small gyri; the cortex may look deceptively thickened because the tiny folds are packed together Causes are heterogeneous and include genetic variants such as GPR56 and tubulin genes, chromosomal disorders including 22q11.2 deletion, and acquired insults, notably congenital cytomegalovirus infection and in-utero ischaemia The bilateral perisylvian form typically causes pseudobulbar palsy with oromotor dysfunction, dysarthria, feeding difficulty, epilepsy, and variable cognitive impairment Clinical severity depends on extent and location, ranging from focal, minimally symptomatic lesions to widespread malformation with severe disability Diagnosis rests on the MRI pattern combined with genetic testing and evaluation for congenital infection Severe oromotor dysfunction with aspiration and feeding failure Drug-resistant epilepsy Evidence of congenital cytomegalovirus infection with hearing loss requiring intervention Rapidly progressive neurological decline suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis Misreading the packed small gyri as a thick, smooth cortex and mistaking it for pachygyria Failing to test for congenital cytomegalovirus, an important and potentially preventable acquired cause Overlooking associated 22q11.2 deletion and its systemic implications Assuming all polymicrogyria is genetic and neglecting acquired prenatal causes in counselling Polymicrogyria is a disorder of the late stages of cortical development, arising after neurons have largely completed migration, during cortical organisation and lamination. Both genetic factors, including variants in genes governing the neuronal cytoskeleton and cortical patterning, and acquired prenatal insults such as congenital cytomegalovirus infection or focal ischaemia can disrupt normal gyral formation. The cortex develops an excess of small, abnormally laminated and fused convolutions. The distribution of the malformation, often bilateral and region-specific, determines the neurological consequences such as perisylvian oromotor dysfunction and epilepsy. Outcome ranges widely with the extent and location of involvement. Small focal lesions may be asymptomatic or cause only focal epilepsy, whereas extensive bilateral malformation causes significant motor, oromotor, cognitive, and seizure disability.

polymorphic eruption of pregnancy — pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy, PUPPP, toxaemic rash of pregnancy pemphigoid gestationis intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy atopic eruption of pregnancy drug eruption allergic or irritant contact dermatitis urticaria viral exanthem or scabies skin biopsy for histology (non-specific: dermal oedema with perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate and eosinophils) direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin (negative, to exclude pemphigoid gestationis) serum bile acids and liver function tests to exclude obstetric cholestasis full blood count (eosinophilia may occur but is non-specific) indirect immunofluorescence or BP180 ELISA if pemphigoid gestationis is suspected obstetric ultrasound to confirm multiple gestation and fetal wellbeing Typically arises in the third trimester (or immediately postpartum) in a primigravida, and characteristically begins within abdominal striae distensae. The periumbilical region is spared, an important clinical clue distinguishing it from pemphigoid gestationis which frequently involves the umbilicus. Lesions are polymorphic: urticarial papules and plaques predominate but vesicles, targetoid lesions, eczematous change and widespread erythema may all occur. Strongly associated with excessive maternal weight gain, multiple gestation (twins, triplets) and male fetal sex. It is a clinical diagnosis; direct immunofluorescence is negative and is used mainly to exclude pemphigoid gestationis when in doubt. Intensely pruritic but self-limiting, usually resolving within a few weeks of delivery without scarring. There is no associated maternal or fetal risk, distinguishing it prognostically from intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy and pemphigoid gestationis. First-line management is emollients and topical corticosteroids with oral antihistamines; a short course of systemic corticosteroid is reserved for severe cases. periumbilical involvement or tense blisters suggesting pemphigoid gestationis rather than polymorphic eruption pruritus without primary skin lesions plus dark urine or pale stools, raising intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy jaundice or right upper quadrant pain suggesting hepatic pathology reduced fetal movements or other signs of fetal compromise systemic upset, fever or mucosal involvement suggesting an alternative severe dermatosis or drug reaction Mislabelling any tense blistering as polymorphic eruption; umbilical involvement and positive direct immunofluorescence point to pemphigoid gestationis. Failing to check bile acids in a pruritic pregnant woman and missing intrahepatic cholestasis, which carries fetal risk. Assuming recurrence in later pregnancies and causing unnecessary anxiety when recurrence is in fact unusual. Overusing systemic corticosteroids for a benign self-limiting condition when topical therapy usually suffices. Attributing the eruption solely to striae and overlooking the strong link with multiple gestation, delaying recognition of a twin pregnancy. The aetiology is incompletely understood but is thought to relate to rapid abdominal wall distension in the third trimester causing damage to connective tissue within striae, exposing altered collagen that provokes an inflammatory response. This is supported by the strong associations with excessive weight gain, large fetal size and multiple gestation. A contribution from circulating fetal DNA and a mild immunological reaction to fetal antigens has been proposed, and the male-fetus association raises the possibility of a response to fetal cells in maternal skin, but no consistent hormonal or autoimmune mechanism has been confirmed. Unlike pemphigoid gestationis there is no autoantibody to the basement membrane zone. Excellent, with spontaneous resolution typically within one to six weeks of delivery and no scarring. There is no increased maternal or fetal morbidity and recurrence in subsequent pregnancies is uncommon.

in childhood, pointing to erythropoietic protoporphyria Skin fragility, blistering and scarring raising concern for a cutaneous porphyria A new photosensitivity temporally linked to a recently started desensitisation phototherapy in spring for patients with recurrent disabling episodes Polymorphic light eruption is thought to represent a delayed-type (T-cell mediated) hypersensitivity response to one or more endogenous cutaneous antigens that are generated or altered in the skin by ultraviolet radiation. Affected individuals appear relatively resistant to the ultraviolet-induced immunosuppression that would normally suppress such reactions in unaffected skin, permitting an inflammatory lymphocytic infiltrate to develop in sun-exposed areas. Repeated ultraviolet exposure gradually induces tolerance, or hardening, which accounts for the characteristic seasonal improvement, and a genetic predisposition with reduced regulatory immune activity is likely to contribute. The condition is benign and tends to improve each summer as hardening develops, and it may lessen or resolve over years, although many patients continue to experience recurrent spring and holiday flares that are usually well controlled by photoprotection and, where needed, prophylactic phototherapy.

Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation — Polymorphic VT, Torsades des pointes, Ventricular fibrillation, VF Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (implies a fixed structural substrate or automatic focus, unlike polymorphic VT) Acquired (drug- or electrolyte-induced) long QT with torsades des pointes Congenital long QT syndrome (LQTS-1, -2, -3) Short QT syndrome Brugada syndrome Early repolarization syndrome Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT (bidirectional VT) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Genetic dilated cardiomyopathies (e.g., Lamin A/C, SCN5A) 12-lead ECG with measurement of corrected QT (QTc); congenital LQTS typically prolongs QTc to >440 ms in men and >460 ms in women (p.1969) Short QT syndrome: QTc <360 ms, usually <300 ms (p.1970) Telemetry/rhythm strip to capture pause-dependent initiation of torsades and characteristic morphologies (p.1969) Genetic testing/genotyping for family screening and diagnostic reassurance in LQTS (p.1970) Provocative sodium channel blocker testing (e.g., flecainide, ajmaline, procainamide) to unmask Brugada ST elevation (p.1970) Assessment of residual LV function/ejection fraction to guide ICD decisions (p.1969) Reference resource crediblemeds.org to check whether a medication has been reported to prolong the QT interval (p.1969) Brugada pattern ST elevation must be distinguished from LV hypertrophy, pericarditis, myocardial ischemia/MI, hyperkalemia, hypothermia, right bundle branch block, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (p.1970) Asymptomatic Brugada ECG pattern versus the clinical Brugada syndrome (analogous to Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern versus syndrome) J-point elevation as a benign normal variant versus early repolarization syndrome associated with arrhythmia risk Sustained polymorphic VT shows a QRS configuration that changes continuously beat to beat, reflecting an ever-changing ventricular activation sequence; unlike monomorphic VT it does not necessarily imply a fixed structural abnormality or single automatic focus (p.1968). Sustained polymorphic VT commonly degenerates into ventricular fibrillation (p.1969). Acute myocardial infarction or ischemia is a frequent cause and should be the first consideration; roughly 10% of acute MI patients develop VT that degenerates to VF, with greatest risk in the first hour (p.1969). Polymorphic VT/VF occurring within the first 48 hours of acute MI carries higher in-hospital mortality, but survivors to discharge are not at increased risk of later arrhythmic sudden death (p.1969). Torsades des pointes is the polymorphic VT linked to QT prolongation and classically begins in a pause-dependent fashion: a PVC induces a pause, the following sinus beat has a longer QT, and a PVC interrupting that T wave starts the run (p.1969). Congenital long QT syndrome stems from ion-channel gene mutations; LQTS-1, -2, and -3 account for roughly 80-90% of cases, with LQTS-1/-2 involving potassium channels and LQTS-3 involving the sodium channel (p.1969-1970). Genotype influences triggers: LQTS-1 events tend to occur during exertion (notably swimming), LQTS-2 with sudden auditory stimuli or emotional upset, and LQTS-3 sudden death tends to occur during sleep (p.1970). Brugada syndrome causes syncope or cardiac arrest from polymorphic VT in the absence of structural heart disease; arrest may occur during sleep or be provoked by febrile illness, and males are more commonly affected (p.1970). Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT is a rare familial disorder of abnormal sarcoplasmic calcium handling producing arrhythmias resembling digitalis toxicity, often with bidirectional (alternating QRS morphology) VT, presenting in childhood with exertion- or emotion-induced events (p.1971). Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the most common genetic cardiovascular disorder (about 1 in 500), is a prominent cause of sudden death before age 35, typically via polymorphic VT/VF (p.1971). Ventricular fibrillation shows disordered electrical ventricular activation with no identifiable QRS complexes; spiral wave reentry and multiple circulating reentry wavefronts are proposed mechanisms (p.1971). After surviving acute MI and revascularization, poorly coupled but surviving Purkinje fibers (which tolerate ischemia owing to glycogen stores and oxygenation from the LV cavity) can trigger PVCs and ventricular fibrillation (p.1971). Near-syncope, syncope, or cardiac arrest as the presenting event (p.1969) Repeated episodes of polymorphic VT suggesting ongoing myocardial infarction/inadequate reperfusion (p.1969) QTc exceeding 500 ms, female gender, and prior syncope or cardiac arrest as markers of increased risk in LQTS (p.1970) Family history of sudden death (relevant in Brugada syndrome, early repolarization syndrome, and genetic cardiomyopathies) (p.1970-1971) Febrile illness provoking cardiac arrest in Brugada syndrome (p.1970) HCM features: young age, nonsustained VT, failure of blood pressure to rise with exercise, recent syncope (within 6 months), ventricular wall thickness >3 cm (p.1971) Assuming polymorphic VT implies a fixed structural focus as monomorphic VT does (p.1968) Overlooking ongoing ischemia/inadequate reperfusion when polymorphic VT/VF recurs after MI (p.1969) Failing to recognize numerous noncardiac QT-prolonging drugs and drug interactions that raise levels of an offending agent as precipitants of torsades (p.1969) Re-exposing a patient who had QT-prolongation-induced polymorphic VT to QT-prolonging medications; such patients should be considered susceptible and avoid all future exposure (p.1969) Misinterpreting benign J-point elevation (a common normal variant) as pathologic early repolarization syndrome (p.1971) Confusing the asymptomatic Brugada ECG pattern with true Brugada syndrome (p.1970) Polymorphic VT arises from a continually changing ventricular activation sequence. Proposed mechanisms include reentry with variable paths, spiral wave reentry, and multiple automatic foci, often near fibrotic myocardium and potentiated by damaged Purkinje cells or ventricular hypertrophy. Abnormal transmural dispersion of repolarization can drive it in the setting of channelopathies or antiarrhythmic drugs even without structural disease. In acute MI/ischemia, reentry through the infarct border zone is implicated, and surviving automatic Purkinje cells can initiate it. Torsades des pointes is associated with abnormal QT prolongation and pause-dependent initiation. Congenital LQTS reflects mutations in ion-channel genes governing repolarization (potassium channels in LQTS-1/-2, sodium channel in LQTS-3, and calcium channels in others). Short QT syndrome reflects a gain of function of the IKr potassium channel or reduced inward depolarizing currents. Brugada syndrome reflects dispersion of repolarization across the ventricular wall, with epicardial and M cells more affected than endocardial cells, localized to the right ventricular outflow tract; sodium channel mutations (SCN5A, SCN1B, SCN10A) are found in about 25% of cases. Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT results from cardiac ryanodine receptor (and less often calsequestrin 2) mutations causing abnormal sarcoplasmic calcium handling. Ventricular fibrillation represents disordered activation without organized QRS, frequently as degeneration of sustained polymorphic or monomorphic VT (p.1968-1971). Polymorphic VT/VF within the first 48 hours of acute MI is associated with greater in-hospital mortality, yet patients who survive to discharge are not at increased risk for later arrhythmic sudden death. Long-term risk after infarction is governed largely by residual LV function. In LQTS, higher risk is conferred by QTc >500 ms, female gender, and prior syncope or cardiac arrest. HCM is a prominent cause of sudden death before age 35; surgical myectomy carries a sudden death rate <1% per year, and transcoronary ethanol septal ablation has a reported annual rate of sustained VT or sudden death of roughly 1-5% (p.1969-1971). No single formal severity grade; risk is stratified by substrate. In post-MI patients, an ICD is indicated for persistent severe LV dysfunction (LV ejection fraction <35%). In LQTS, high-risk features include QTc >500 ms, female gender, and prior syncope/cardiac arrest. In HCM, high-risk markers include young age, nonsustained VT, failure of blood pressure to rise with exercise, recent syncope, and ventricular wall thickness >3 cm (p.1969-1971).

Polymorphous adenocarcinoma — Polymorphous low-grade adenocarcinoma, Terminal duct carcinoma Adenoid cystic carcinoma Pleomorphic adenoma Canalicular adenoma Basal cell adenoma Secretory carcinoma Adenocarcinoma not otherwise specified Incisional biopsy of the mucosal or submucosal lesion Immunohistochemistry including S100 and Ki-67 proliferation index MRI to assess soft-tissue extent and perineural spread Molecular testing for PRKD1 alterations where available CT to evaluate bony involvement of the palate or maxilla Ultrasound or cross-sectional imaging of the neck for nodal assessment A malignancy that arises almost exclusively in the minor salivary glands, with the palate being the classic site of origin. It is one of the commonest intraoral minor salivary gland malignancies and typically presents as a painless, slow-growing submucosal swelling. The defining paradox is cytological uniformity combined with architectural diversity: tubular, cribriform, solid, single-file streaming and concentric targetoid patterns coexist. Perineural invasion, often with a targetoid whorling pattern, is common yet usually consistent with indolent behaviour. The classic type harbours a recurrent PRKD1 hotspot mutation, whereas the cribriform-predominant variant more often shows PRKD1, PRKD2 or PRKD3 rearrangements. Tumour cells are typically S100 positive with a low proliferation index, and the main task is to separate it from adenoid cystic carcinoma. The cribriform variant, favouring the tongue base, more frequently involves regional lymph nodes yet still generally behaves indolently. Wide local excision is the mainstay, and distinguishing it from adenoid cystic carcinoma has major implications for treatment intensity. Rapid growth or mucosal ulceration Bone invasion of the palate or maxilla Extensive or symptomatic perineural spread Regional nodal metastasis, particularly with the cribriform variant Solid, high-grade-appearing areas within the tumour Misdiagnosing it as adenoid cystic carcinoma, leading to inappropriate treatment intensity Achieving inadequate margins because of the infiltrative growth pattern Failing to recognise the characteristic perineural invasion Mistaking it for a benign pleomorphic adenoma on a small biopsy Polymorphous adenocarcinoma is a malignant neoplasm derived from the terminal duct or intercalated duct cells of minor salivary glands, in which a single, cytologically bland cell population expresses a remarkably wide range of growth patterns. In most conventional tumours an activating hotspot mutation in the PRKD1 gene deregulates protein kinase D signalling, driving proliferation, while the cribriform-predominant variant is instead characterised by rearrangements of PRKD1, PRKD2 or PRKD3. The neoplastic cells infiltrate the surrounding tissue in tubules, cribriform islands, solid nests and single-file cords, and characteristically ensheath nerves in concentric layers, so that perineural invasion is a defining rather than an alarming feature. Despite this infiltrative and neurotropic growth, proliferative activity remains low, which underlies the tumour's generally indolent clinical course. Prognosis is generally favourable and the tumour is low-grade, with complete excision usually curative. The cribriform variant carries a higher rate of nodal metastasis but still tends to behave indolently, whereas misdiagnosis as adenoid cystic carcinoma risks unnecessary overtreatment.

inclusion body myositis in older patients and other myopathies must be considered before labelling weakness as polymyositis Muscle biopsy classically shows endomysial CD8 T-cell infiltration surrounding and invading non-necrotic fibres Corticosteroids are the mainstay of initial treatment, with steroid-sparing immunosuppressants added to control disease and limit steroid toxicity Rapidly progressive dyspnoea or hypoxia from interstitial lung disease, especially with antisynthetase antibodies Bulbar or respiratory muscle weakness causing dysphagia, aspiration, or ventilatory compromise Cardiac involvement with arrhythmia or heart failure Features suggesting an underlying occult malignancy Severe dysphagia risking aspiration pneumonia Diagnosing polymyositis without excluding inclusion body myositis and necrotising myopathy, which respond differently to therapy Overlooking interstitial lung disease, a major cause of morbidity and mortality Attributing weakness solely to steroid myopathy during treatment without reassessing disease activity Failing to screen for dysphagia and aspiration risk Missing an associated malignancy or overlap connective tissue disease Polymyositis is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy driven by cell-mediated autoimmunity. Cytotoxic CD8 T lymphocytes recognise antigens expressed on muscle fibres and invade non-necrotic myofibres, causing fibre necrosis and regeneration and consequent weakness. Upregulation of MHC class I on muscle fibres is characteristic. Associations with specific autoantibodies define distinct phenotypes, and there is overlap with other connective tissue diseases and, less strongly than in dermatomyositis, with malignancy. With treatment many patients regain strength, but relapses are common and prognosis is worse in the presence of interstitial lung disease, cardiac involvement, severe dysphagia, or associated malignancy. Long-term functional outcome depends on early treatment and control of extramuscular disease.

or anticholinergic drugs used together Unexplained functional or cognitive decline that may be iatrogenic Adding a drug to treat the side effect of another instead of reassessing the original agent Continuing medications indefinitely without reassessing ongoing indication or benefit Failing to adjust doses for declining renal function Stopping several drugs abruptly and precipitating withdrawal effects rather than tapering Overlooking over-the-counter drugs and supplements as sources of interactions With ageing, reduced lean body mass and total body water, increased fat, declining hepatic metabolism, and especially reduced renal excretion alter drug distribution and clearance, prolonging exposure to many agents and their metabolites. Pharmacodynamic sensitivity also changes, notably increased susceptibility to central nervous system depressants, anticholinergics, and drugs affecting blood pressure. As the number of medications rises, the probability of interactions grows combinatorially, and overlapping adverse effects (sedation, hypotension, anticholinergic load) summate to produce falls, delirium, and functional decline. Inappropriate polypharmacy is associated with increased adverse drug events, hospitalisation, falls, cognitive impairment, and mortality. Thoughtful deprescribing and ongoing medication optimisation can reduce these harms and improve quality of life without compromising the treatment of important conditions.

polysplenia — left atrial isomerism, left isomerism, bilateral left-sidedness asplenia syndrome (right isomerism) situs inversus with normal spleen accessory spleens or splenosis in situs solitus isolated interrupted inferior vena cava with azygos continuation isolated congenital heart block biliary atresia of non-syndromic type heterotaxy without clear isomerism pattern abdominal ultrasound demonstrating multiple splenic nodules and hepatic symmetry echocardiography with attention to systemic and pulmonary venous drainage cross-sectional imaging showing interrupted inferior vena cava with azygos continuation twelve-lead ECG and ambulatory monitoring for sinus node dysfunction or heart block peripheral blood film to assess functional splenic activity hepatobiliary imaging where biliary atresia is suspected in infancy genetic testing for laterality and ciliopathy genes in selected patients Polysplenia is the visceral hallmark of left atrial isomerism (bilateral left-sidedness), with multiple small spleens usually clustered along the greater curvature of the stomach. Bilateral bilobed lungs with hyparterial bronchi and paired morphologically left atrial appendages are the defining thoracic features. Interruption of the intrahepatic inferior vena cava with azygos or hemiazygos continuation is a characteristic and surgically important finding. Cardiac lesions are typically less severe than in asplenia but commonly include atrioventricular septal defect, partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection and left-sided obstructive lesions. Sinus node dysfunction and congenital complete heart block are frequent because the sinus node is hypoplastic, malpositioned or absent. Extracardiac associations include intestinal malrotation, a midline symmetrical liver, and biliary atresia, the last carrying significant hepatic morbidity. Despite multiple spleens, splenic function may be reduced, so immunisation status and splenic reserve should be assessed rather than assumed. Some individuals with mild cardiac anatomy present in adulthood incidentally on imaging performed for unrelated reasons. bradyarrhythmia, syncope or antenatally detected complete heart block bilious vomiting or abdominal signs suggesting volvulus from malrotation conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and pale stools indicating biliary atresia signs of overwhelming infection where splenic function is impaired progressive cyanosis or heart failure from evolving cardiac lesions Assuming normal splenic immune function simply because multiple spleens are present. Missing interruption of the inferior vena cava before catheterisation or cardiac surgery. Overlooking evolving heart block that may be silent until syncope or fetal compromise. Failing to investigate neonatal cholestasis for associated biliary atresia. Not screening for intestinal malrotation, risking acute volvulus. Polysplenia reflects a laterality defect in which the embryo fails to establish rightward differences and instead duplicates left-sided morphology on both sides of the body. Disruption of nodal cilia-driven leftward flow and the downstream Nodal-Lefty-Pitx2 pathway leads to bilateral 'left' patterning, so the lungs are both bilobed with hyparterial bronchi and the atrial appendages are both of morphologically left type. The spleen, normally a single left-sided organ, forms as multiple splenic nodules. Because the sinus node is a right-sided structure that fails to develop normally in bilateral left-sidedness, conduction is frequently abnormal with atrial rhythms or heart block. Interruption of the hepatic segment of the inferior vena cava occurs because the right-sided venous confluence does not form, and systemic venous return is rerouted through the azygos system. Associated abnormalities of gut rotation and of the biliary tree arise from the same failure of asymmetric organogenesis. Prognosis is generally more favourable than right isomerism and depends on the complexity of the cardiac defect, the presence of heart block, and whether biliary atresia supervenes. Many patients achieve good long-term survival with staged cardiac repair, pacing where indicated, and vigilant management of hepatic and infective complications.

Completing the secondary survey before life threats in the primary survey are addressed Over-resuscitation with crystalloid worsening dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia Anchoring on an obvious dramatic injury while missing a silent source of shock Failing to reassess after each intervention as physiology evolves Neglecting active warming and haemostatic resuscitation in the bleeding patient Polytrauma involves injury to two or more body regions or systems, at least one of which is life-threatening. Simultaneous tissue damage triggers haemorrhage, hypovolaemic shock, and a systemic inflammatory response. Hypoperfusion causes tissue hypoxia and lactic acidosis, while ongoing bleeding and crystalloid dilution impair clotting. Hypothermia further inhibits enzymatic coagulation, and the resulting lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy establishes a self-reinforcing cycle. Later, immune activation predisposes to systemic inflammatory response syndrome, acute respiratory distress, and multi-organ dysfunction. Outcome depends on injury burden, time to haemorrhage control, and physiological reserve. Early definitive control of bleeding and correction of the lethal triad improve survival, whereas prolonged shock and multi-organ dysfunction carry high mortality.

Pompe disease — acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, acid maltase deficiency, glycogen storage disease type II, GSD II Spinal muscular atrophy and other causes of infantile hypotonia Congenital muscular dystrophies and congenital myopathies Other causes of infantile hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Limb-girdle muscular dystrophies in later-onset presentations Other glycogen storage disorders affecting muscle Assay of acid alpha-glucosidase activity, including dried blood spot screening with confirmatory testing GAA molecular genetic testing Serum creatine kinase measurement Echocardiography and ECG to assess cardiomyopathy in infants Pulmonary function testing and muscle assessment in later-onset disease An autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme acid alpha-glucosidase (acid maltase), resulting in lysosomal glycogen accumulation; it is classified as glycogen storage disease type II It is unusual among the glycogenoses in being a lysosomal disorder rather than affecting cytoplasmic glycogen metabolism, so fasting hypoglycaemia is not a feature The classic infantile form presents in the first months with profound hypotonia, a rapidly enlarging heart (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), and feeding and respiratory difficulty A markedly enlarged tongue and prominent cardiomegaly on chest imaging are useful clues in infants Late-onset (juvenile and adult) forms present with progressive proximal and respiratory muscle weakness and often lack significant cardiac involvement Diaphragmatic weakness can cause respiratory failure that is disproportionate to limb weakness Serum creatine kinase is commonly elevated, reflecting the underlying myopathy Enzyme replacement therapy has transformed the outlook, particularly in infantile disease, and newborn screening enables earlier treatment Rapidly progressive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in an infant Respiratory compromise from diaphragmatic weakness Severe feeding difficulty with failure to thrive Progressive respiratory decline out of proportion to limb weakness in older patients Expecting hypoglycaemia and being misled when it is absent, since this is a lysosomal rather than cytoplasmic glycogenosis Attributing infantile hypotonia to a neuromuscular cause without checking for cardiomyopathy Underestimating respiratory muscle involvement in later-onset disease Delaying treatment when early initiation most influences outcome Pompe disease is caused by pathogenic variants in the GAA gene encoding acid alpha-glucosidase, the lysosomal enzyme that degrades glycogen to glucose within the lysosome. Deficient activity leads to progressive lysosomal glycogen accumulation, most damaging in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Lysosomal engorgement and subsequent autophagic dysfunction impair muscle architecture and function, producing cardiomegaly and hypotonia in infants and progressive skeletal and respiratory muscle weakness in later-onset disease. The degree of residual enzyme activity broadly correlates with age of onset and severity. Untreated classic infantile disease is usually fatal within the first year from cardiorespiratory failure. Enzyme replacement therapy substantially improves survival and cardiac outcomes, especially when started early, though respiratory and motor sequelae may persist. Late-onset disease progresses more slowly, with respiratory function being a key determinant of long-term outcome.
