CT typically reveals mosaic attenuation and air trapping on expiratory imaging rather than parenchymal opacities The chest radiograph is frequently normal or near-normal, which can lead to underdiagnosis Small-airway scarring narrows and obliterates terminal bronchioles, and established disease is largely irreversible Recognition of an occupational cluster among flavouring or food-production workers is a critical diagnostic pointer Rapidly progressive fixed airflow obstruction in a young non-smoker Continued workplace exposure after symptom onset Severe irreversible obstruction with respiratory failure A cluster of affected workers signalling ongoing hazardous exposure Mistaking the disease for ordinary asthma and relying on bronchodilators that do not reverse fixed obstruction Being reassured by a normal chest radiograph and omitting expiratory CT Missing the occupational history in a young non-smoker with obstruction Delaying removal from exposure until irreversible damage has occurred Volatile alpha-diketones such as diacetyl, released when heated flavourings are handled, are inhaled and cause direct toxic injury to the epithelium of the small conducting airways. The ensuing inflammation and repair lead to concentric peribronchiolar fibrosis that narrows and ultimately obliterates the lumen of terminal and respiratory bronchioles (constrictive bronchiolitis). Because the injury is confined largely to the small airways with sparing of the surrounding parenchyma, gas exchange may be relatively preserved while airflow obstruction becomes fixed and progressive. The scarring is not reversible, so the emphasis is on early detection and exposure cessation. Constrictive bronchiolitis from diacetyl is typically irreversible; some patients stabilise after removal from exposure, but others progress to severe disabling airflow obstruction and may require consideration of transplantation.

Popliteal artery aneurysm — Popliteal aneurysm, PAA Baker's (popliteal) cyst Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome Deep vein thrombosis presenting with a swollen, painful calf Cystic adventitial disease of the popliteal artery Soft-tissue tumour or sarcoma of the popliteal fossa Atherosclerotic occlusive disease causing claudication Popliteal abscess or enlarged lymph nodes Duplex ultrasound of both popliteal arteries for diagnosis, size and mural thrombus Abdominal aortic and iliac ultrasound to exclude coexistent aneurysm CT angiography of the lower limb MR angiography as an alternative for run-off assessment Catheter angiography, frequently with a view to thrombolysis or intervention Ankle-brachial pressure index and arterial waveform studies Dedicated imaging of the contralateral limb given the high bilaterality The commonest peripheral (non-aortic) arterial aneurysm, defined as focal dilatation of the popliteal artery, commonly more than 50% of the adjacent normal diameter or an absolute diameter typically exceeding around 2 cm. Strongly associated with male sex, smoking, hypertension and coexisting abdominal aortic aneurysm. Bilateral in roughly half of cases, and frequently associated with an abdominal aortic aneurysm, so both popliteal fossae and the aorta must be imaged. Complications are predominantly thromboembolic (acute limb ischaemia, distal embolisation, progressive obliteration of the tibial run-off) rather than rupture, which is uncommon. A prominent, easily palpable popliteal pulse should raise suspicion; a pulsatile popliteal mass is aneurysmal until proven otherwise. Presentation ranges from incidental and asymptomatic to intermittent claudication, limb-threatening acute ischaemia, or compressive symptoms such as venous obstruction and neuropathy. Duplex ultrasound is first-line for diagnosis, sizing and surveillance; CT or MR angiography defines run-off for intervention planning. Repair, by open bypass with aneurysm exclusion or endovascular stent-grafting, is indicated for symptomatic aneurysms and for asymptomatic aneurysms above a threshold size or with significant mural thrombus or poor run-off. Acute limb ischaemia with the six Ps (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishing cold), which is limb-threatening. Sudden loss of previously palpable distal pulses with a cold, painful foot. Progressive rest pain, tissue loss or trash foot from distal embolisation. A rapidly enlarging or tender popliteal mass. Compressive neurological deficit or acute venous outflow obstruction. Mistaking a pulsatile popliteal mass for a Baker's cyst and attempting aspiration. Failing to screen the contralateral popliteal artery and the abdominal aorta. Underestimating a thrombosed aneurysm because the mass is no longer pulsatile, delaying diagnosis in acute ischaemia. Delaying repair of an asymptomatic aneurysm harbouring large mural thrombus or compromised run-off. Attributing calf swelling solely to deep vein thrombosis and anticoagulating without imaging the artery. The popliteal artery undergoes segmental degeneration of the media with loss of elastin and smooth muscle, collagen remodelling and matrix metalloproteinase-driven wall weakening, mirroring aortic aneurysmal disease. Repetitive flexion at the knee, turbulent flow and mural stress promote progressive dilatation and deposition of laminated thrombus within the sac. The stagnant flow within the redundant lumen favours thrombus accumulation that embolises distally, progressively occluding the tibial run-off, or acutely thromboses the aneurysm to produce severe acute limb ischaemia with a poorly developed collateral bed. Rupture is uncommon because of the confining structures of the popliteal fossa. Asymptomatic aneurysms carry a substantial annual risk of thromboembolic complications, and once acute ischaemia occurs limb loss rates are high, particularly with poor distal run-off. Elective repair before complications develop yields good long-term patency and low amputation rates.

provocative dynamic studies Attributing exertional leg pain to a musculoskeletal or compartment cause in a young athlete Assessing only the symptomatic limb and missing bilateral disease Delaying treatment until irreversible arterial damage or thrombosis has occurred Confusing the syndrome with cystic adventitial disease, which requires different management Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome results from an abnormal anatomical or functional relationship between the popliteal artery and the muscles and tendons of the popliteal fossa, most often involving the medial head of gastrocnemius. In anatomical variants the artery follows an aberrant medial course or is crossed by an anomalous muscle slip, while in the functional form a normally positioned artery is compressed by hypertrophied musculature during contraction. Repeated dynamic compression, particularly during the plantarflexion of exercise, intermittently restricts arterial flow and produces exertional ischaemia. Over time the recurrent mechanical trauma damages the arterial wall, promoting intimal injury, post-stenotic dilatation or aneurysm formation, mural thrombus, and the risk of thrombotic occlusion or distal embolisation, so a functional problem can progress to fixed arterial disease. When recognised before fixed arterial damage develops, surgical release of the entrapment relieves symptoms and preserves the artery with good long-term outcomes. Delayed diagnosis allowing arterial degeneration, aneurysm, or thrombosis worsens the prognosis and may require arterial reconstruction.

Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome — PAES Chronic exertional compartment syndrome Medial tibial stress syndrome Atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease Cystic adventitial disease of the popliteal artery Nerve entrapment causing exertional leg pain Ankle-brachial index and pulse assessment at rest and with provocation Duplex ultrasound with active plantarflexion manoeuvres CT or MR angiography, including provocative positioning, to show compression and anatomy Assessment for arterial damage such as stenosis, thrombosis or aneurysm Exclusion of compartment syndrome An uncommon cause of exertional calf pain in young, often athletic, individuals due to compression of the popliteal artery It should be considered when a fit young person has claudication without atherosclerotic risk factors Symptoms are provoked by exercise, particularly activities using the calf muscles, and relieved by rest Compression usually results from an abnormal anatomical relationship between the artery and the gastrocnemius or popliteus, though a functional form exists Provocative manoeuvres with active plantarflexion can reproduce reduced pedal pulses and imaging changes Untreated repetitive compression can damage the artery, causing stenosis, thrombosis or aneurysm, so surgery is often required Signs of arterial thrombosis or acute limb ischaemia Distal embolisation or a popliteal aneurysm Rest pain or tissue loss Rapidly progressive symptoms Dismissing exertional leg pain in a young athlete as musculoskeletal Confusing it with chronic exertional compartment syndrome Relying on resting vascular studies, which may be normal without provocation Missing established arterial damage requiring reconstruction Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome arises when the popliteal artery is compressed within the popliteal fossa, most often by an anomalous course relative to the medial head of gastrocnemius or by an accessory muscle slip; a functional variant occurs with a hypertrophied but normally positioned muscle. Repetitive compression during exercise transiently reduces distal flow, causing claudication, and over time causes intimal injury that can progress to fixed stenosis, thrombosis or post-stenotic aneurysm with distal embolisation. The young age and absence of atherosclerotic risk factors distinguish it from typical peripheral arterial disease. With early diagnosis and surgical release, and vascular reconstruction if the artery is damaged, outcomes are generally good; delayed diagnosis risks permanent arterial injury and limb-threatening complications.

entrapment from the physiological compression that can occur in normal limbs during extreme plantarflexion, so as to avoid overdiagnosis Symptomatic anatomical entrapment is treated surgically by decompression, releasing the offending muscle slip or fibrous band, whereas functional entrapment without a structural anomaly is generally managed more conservatively Deep vein thrombosis in a young patient without conventional risk factors Coexisting arterial entrapment with claudication or limb ischaemia Recurrent thrombosis or post-thrombotic changes despite anticoagulation Progressive symptoms that increasingly limit activity Features suggesting pulmonary embolism Overdiagnosing entrapment from the physiological venous compression seen in normal limbs on extreme plantarflexion Missing the diagnosis in young patients with unexplained deep vein thrombosis or exertional leg swelling Failing to assess for a coexisting popliteal artery entrapment Relying on resting, non-provocative imaging, which may appear normal Treating recurrent deep vein thrombosis with anticoagulation alone without addressing the underlying compression The popliteal vein normally traverses the popliteal fossa alongside the artery, passing between the heads of gastrocnemius. In entrapment, an anomalous origin or accessory slip of the medial head of gastrocnemius, a fibrous band, or muscular hypertrophy compresses the vein, particularly during muscle contraction in plantarflexion or with certain knee positions. Repetitive compression produces intermittent venous outflow obstruction, venous hypertension and stasis, which give rise to exertional swelling and predispose to intimal injury and secondary thrombosis. In functional entrapment, hypertrophied but normally positioned muscles compress otherwise normal vessels, so imaging at rest may be unremarkable while provocative manoeuvres reveal the obstruction. With timely surgical decompression of an anatomical entrapment, symptomatic and functional outcomes are generally good. Delayed diagnosis may lead to established deep vein thrombosis, post-thrombotic syndrome and chronic venous insufficiency.

and CA 19-9 if carcinoma is suspected Cross-sectional staging imaging if a mass or malignancy is identified Assessment of surgical fitness for cholecystectomy Refers to calcification of the gallbladder wall, generally the end result of long-standing chronic cholecystitis and almost always associated with gallstones Frequently asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on plain radiography, CT, or ultrasound Historically linked to a high risk of gallbladder carcinoma, though contemporary series suggest the risk, while real, is lower than once believed The pattern of calcification may characterising the mural calcification Prophylactic cholecystectomy is commonly recommended given the malignancy association, particularly for surgically fit patients or when features are concerning Coexisting focal wall thickening or a mass should raise suspicion of established carcinoma Focal or asymmetric wall thickening or a soft-tissue mass suggesting carcinoma New pain, weight loss, or jaundice Regional lymphadenopathy or hepatic invasion on imaging Rising tumour markers in the appropriate context Overstating the cancer risk based on older literature, or conversely dismissing it entirely Confusing wall calcification with a gallbladder packed with calcified stones Overlooking a coexisting carcinoma masked by dense calcification Delaying cholecystectomy in a fit patient when malignancy risk warrants it Mistaking emphysematous cholecystitis for calcification on plain imaging Porcelain gallbladder develops from chronic inflammation of the gallbladder, almost invariably in the setting of gallstones and often after repeated or persistent cholecystitis. Prolonged mucosal injury and scarring lead to deposition of calcium salts within the fibrotic gallbladder wall, which may be laid down as a continuous intramural band (complete calcification) or as patchy calcification of the mucosa and inner layers (selective or incomplete calcification). The stiff, calcified wall is functionally useless and characteristically painless. The chronic inflammatory milieu that produces the calcification is also the substrate for malignant transformation, which accounts for the recognised association with gallbladder adenocarcinoma. An incidentally found, uncomplicated porcelain gallbladder has a good outlook, and cholecystectomy removes both symptoms and the associated cancer risk; prognosis is poor if invasive gallbladder carcinoma has already developed, which is why the malignancy association drives management.

Porphyria — acute intermittent porphyria, porphyria cutanea tarda Intestinal obstruction (acute abdomen) — pain of porphyria is usually difficult to distinguish because severe hyperperistalsis is prominent in both (p.3344-ch.40) Lead colic / lead intoxication (lead inhibits ALA-dehydratase, raising urinary ALA and coproporphyrin III) (p.3342, ch.40) Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 (succinylacetone inhibits ALA-dehydratase, mimicking acute porphyria) (p.3342) Guillain-Barre syndrome (acute attack with ascending weakness mimics GBS) (p.3603) Chronic liver disease (can cause nonspecific increases in urinary porphyrins leading to misdiagnosis) (p.3345) Spot (single-void) urine for porphobilinogen (PBG) — first-line; always raised in acute attacks of AIP/HCP/VP and specific; 24-h collection unnecessary (p.3345-3346) Quantitative urinary ALA, PBG, and creatinine on the same spot sample (also detects ADP) (p.3345) Total urinary porphyrins (interpret cautiously — often nonspecific) (p.3345) Urinary, fecal, and plasma porphyrins to distinguish AIP from HCP and VP (fecal porphyrins normal/minimal in AIP) (p.3346) Total plasma porphyrins with fluorometric scanning of diluted plasma at neutral pH (distinguishes VP from PCT; VP emission peak ~626 nm) for cutaneous porphyrias (p.3346, 3348) Erythrocyte protoporphyrin (more sensitive for EPP/XLP; confirm EPP by predominant free, not zinc, protoporphyrin) (p.3346) Isocoproporphyrins in feces — diagnostic of hepatic URO-decarboxylase deficiency (PCT) (p.3348) Erythrocyte URO-decarboxylase activity (~50% in type 2 PCT; markedly deficient, 3-10%, in HEP) (p.3348) Molecular genetic mutation analysis of the relevant heme-pathway gene (definitive; diagnostic even when precursor levels have normalized, and for latent heterozygotes/relatives) (p.3342, 3346) Acute surgical abdomen / intestinal obstruction (acute hepatic porphyria attack mimics this) (p.3344, ch.40) Lead poisoning (lead colic and neuropathy mimic acute porphyria) (p.3342) Guillain-Barre syndrome (ascending motor weakness in an acute attack) (p.3603) Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 (biochemical and clinical mimic of acute porphyria) (p.3342) The porphyrias are metabolic disorders, each from deficient (or, for XLP, increased) activity of a specific enzyme in the heme biosynthetic pathway; inherited as autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked, except porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) which is usually sporadic (p.3340). Classified as hepatic or erythropoietic (by primary site of porphyrin/precursor overproduction) and as acute or cutaneous (by clinical manifestation) (p.3340, 3344). Acute hepatic porphyrias (AIP, HCP, VP) usually present in adult life after puberty with acute attacks of neurovisceral symptoms and elevated urinary porphyrin precursors ALA and/or PBG (p.3344). Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is autosomal dominant from half-normal HMB-synthase (porphobilinogen deaminase) activity; the most common acute hepatic porphyria (~1 in 20,000 Caucasians), especially frequent in Scandinavia and Great Britain (p.3340, 3346). AIP abdominal pain is the most common symptom: poorly localized, often with cramping, ileus, distention, and decreased bowel sounds (though increased bowel sounds and diarrhea may occur) (p.3346). AIP attacks also feature nausea, vomiting, constipation, tachycardia, hypertension, mental symptoms, limb/head/neck/chest pain, muscle weakness, sensory loss, dysuria, and urinary retention; tachycardia, hypertension, restlessness, tremor, and sweating reflect sympathetic overactivity (p.3346). AIP peripheral neuropathy is due to axonal degeneration (not demyelination) and primarily affects motor neurons; proximal muscles (shoulders/arms) are involved first, and it may be focal or involve cranial nerves (p.3346). Mental symptoms in acute attacks include anxiety, insomnia, depression, disorientation, hallucinations, and paranoia; seizures may be neurologic or due to hyponatremia (p.3346). Diagnosis of an acute attack rests on substantial elevation of urinary PBG (and ALA); urinary PBG is always increased during acute attacks of AIP, HCP, and VP and is not substantially raised in any other condition, making a spot urine PBG both sensitive and specific (p.3345-3346). PCT is the most common porphyria overall; hepatic URO-decarboxylase is deficient in all types, and ~80% of patients have no UROD mutation (sporadic type 1) (p.3347). PCT presents with blistering, photosensitive skin lesions most commonly on the backs of the hands that rupture, crust, and scar, with skin friability, milia, hypertrichosis, and hyperpigmentation; neurologic features are absent (p.3347). An acute attack may begin with sharp abdominal pain, then agitation/hallucinations/seizures, with back and extremity pain followed by weakness several days later, mimicking Guillain-Barre syndrome; weakness may be asymmetric, proximal or distal, and involve facial/bulbar muscles (p.3602-3603). Urine may appear brownish during an attack due to high porphyrin metabolite concentration (p.3602-3603). Acute neurovisceral attack: severe poorly-localized abdominal pain with autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating), motor neuropathy/weakness, and psychiatric disturbance — the AIP acute hepatic porphyria red-flag constellation (p.3346) Hyponatremia (from inappropriate vasopressin secretion or electrolyte depletion) and seizures during an attack (p.3346) Markedly raised urinary PBG/ALA in a patient with abdominal pain after puberty (p.3345-3346) Exposure to a porphyria-precipitating drug, low-calorie diet, alcohol, infection, or surgery preceding the attack (p.3346) Progression to respiratory and bulbar paralysis; sudden death may result from sympathetic overactivity and cardiac arrhythmia, especially with delayed diagnosis/treatment (p.3346) A great mimic of the acute abdomen: porphyric (and lead colic) pain is hard to distinguish from intestinal obstruction because of prominent hyperperistalsis — risking unnecessary surgery (p.3344, ch.40). Because symptoms are nonspecific and rarely occur before puberty, diagnosis is often delayed; a high index of suspicion is required (p.3340, 3346). Measuring urinary porphyrins alone for screening should be avoided — minimal nonspecific increases (e.g., in chronic liver disease) cause misdiagnosis; use urinary PBG (p.3345). Erythrocyte HMB-synthase assay is not a useful first-line test: activity is not decreased in all AIP patients, borderline-low values are not diagnostic, and it is not deficient in other acute porphyrias; some HMBS mutations give normal erythrocyte enzyme so genetic testing is needed (p.3345-3346). ALA/PBG levels often remain high after symptoms resolve, so diagnosing an acute attack in a biochemically proven AIP patient relies primarily on clinical features (p.3346). Most antiseizure drugs can exacerbate AIP, making seizure treatment difficult (clonazepam may be safer than phenytoin or barbiturates) (p.3346). Abdominal tenderness, fever, and leukocytosis are usually absent or mild in AIP because the process is neurologic, not inflammatory — their prominence should prompt reconsideration (p.3346). In PCT, neurologic features are absent — abdominal/neurovisceral attacks should not be attributed to it (p.3347). Each porphyria results from deficient (or, in XLP, increased) activity of one of the eight enzymes of the heme biosynthetic pathway converting glycine and succinyl-CoA to heme. In acute hepatic porphyrias, half-normal enzyme activity becomes limiting when hepatic heme synthesis is increased: induction of the rate-limiting hepatic gene ALAS1 (regulated in part by PGC-1alpha, which is induced by fasting) leads to accumulation and urinary excretion of the porphyrin precursors ALA and PBG, which underlie the acute neurovisceral attacks. Common precipitating factors include endogenous and exogenous steroids (estrogens/progestins), porphyrinogenic drugs (often P450-metabolized), alcohol, low-calorie/low-carbohydrate diets, infections, and surgery. AIP is almost always latent before puberty, suggesting adult steroid hormone levels drive expression; symptoms are commoner in women, with premenstrual (luteal-phase progesterone) attacks. Hyponatremia results from hypothalamic involvement with inappropriate vasopressin secretion or from electrolyte depletion (vomiting, diarrhea, poor intake, renal sodium loss). In PCT, substantial deficiency of hepatic URO-decarboxylase (to ~20% of normal or less, via an iron- and oxidative-stress-dependent uroporphomethene inhibitor) causes accumulation of porphyrins that, on excitation by long-wave UV light in the skin, produce blistering photosensitivity (p.3340, 3345-3347). AIP can be disabling but is rarely fatal; the prognosis of individuals with HMBS mutations is generally favorable, and most heterozygotes remain latent. When an attack resolves, abdominal pain may disappear within hours and paresis begins to improve within days, sometimes continuing to improve over years; recovery from severe motor neuropathy may take months to years and depends on the degree of neuronal damage and early treatment. Long-term complications of AIP include increased risk of hypertension and chronic kidney disease (up to 59% develop CKD), chronic liver function abnormalities with increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (warranting hepatic imaging at least every 6 months), and persistent neuropathy, fatigue, chronic pain, nausea, depression, and anxiety. Homozygous dominant AIP usually presents in infancy and most affected children die at an early age. PCT can almost always be brought into complete remission with treatment, but patients characteristically have chronic liver disease, sometimes cirrhosis, and are at risk for hepatocellular carcinoma (p.3346-3348). Porphyrias are classified by primary overproduction site (hepatic vs erythropoietic) and by clinical manifestation (acute neurovisceral vs cutaneous). Acute hepatic porphyrias: AIP, HCP, VP (and the rare autosomal recessive ADP) present with acute neurovisceral attacks and raised ALA/PBG; AIP causes neurovisceral disease without photosensitivity, whereas HCP and VP can have both neurovisceral attacks and PCT-like cutaneous photosensitivity. Cutaneous: PCT (and HEP) present with chronic blistering photosensitivity. Erythropoietic porphyrias (CEP, EPP, XLP) present with cutaneous photosensitivity (EPP/XLP non-blistering, immediate and painful). Acute-attack severity ranges from mild (abdominal pain without paresis or hyponatremia, manageable with carbohydrate loading) to severe (paresis, hyponatremia, bulbar/respiratory paralysis) (p.3340, 3344, 3346-3347).

Porphyria cutanea tarda — PCT, uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency, UROD deficiency, symptomatic porphyria Pseudoporphyria from drugs (e.g. NSAIDs, diuretics) or renal dialysis Variegate porphyria and hereditary coproporphyria with skin involvement Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita Bullous pemphigoid and other subepidermal blistering disorders Hepatoerythropoietic porphyria (severe biallelic UROD deficiency) Polymorphic light eruption and other photodermatoses Quantitative urinary porphyrins showing uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl porphyrin excess Faecal porphyrin analysis for isocoproporphyrin, characteristic of the condition Plasma fluorescence scanning to support the porphyria diagnosis Iron studies and ferritin, with HFE genotyping where iron overload is present Hepatitis C and HIV serology, and assessment of alcohol intake and liver function UROD gene testing when a familial form is suspected The most common porphyria, resulting from deficient activity of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, the fifth enzyme of haem biosynthesis Predominantly acquired (type I) with a normal gene, occurring when hepatic enzyme activity is inhibited; a familial (type II) form has an inherited UROD mutation Presents as a chronic blistering photosensitivity with skin fragility, vesicles and bullae, milia, erosions and scarring on sun-exposed skin, especially the backs of the hands Additional features include hypertrichosis (notably on the temples and cheeks), hyperpigmentation and, in some, sclerodermoid change It is a purely cutaneous (non-acute) porphyria without neurovisceral attacks, as the accumulating porphyrins are photoreactive rather than neurotoxic precursors Key susceptibility factors include hepatic iron overload (often with HFE haemochromatosis variants), hepatitis C, HIV, alcohol excess and oestrogen exposure The biochemical hallmark is markedly raised urinary uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl porphyrin with raised isocoproporphyrin in faeces Management combines removal of contributory factors, iron reduction by venesection and low-dose antimalarial therapy, alongside sun protection Features of advanced chronic liver disease or hepatocellular carcinoma given the raised long-term risk Severe childhood-onset blistering suggesting hepatoerythropoietic porphyria Secondary infection or scarring of fragile skin lesions Unrecognised underlying hepatitis C or HIV Overlooking treatable drivers such as hepatitis C, HIV, alcohol, oestrogen use and iron overload Confusing it with pseudoporphyria, which has identical skin changes but normal porphyrins Failing to distinguish it from variegate porphyria, which can look identical on the skin Neglecting sun protection while awaiting the effect of definitive treatment Missing familial disease and the need for family assessment Porphyria cutanea tarda develops when hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity falls below a critical threshold, whether from acquired inhibition alone or on the background of an inherited mutation. The enzyme sequentially decarboxylates uroporphyrinogen, so its deficiency causes accumulation of highly carboxylated, water-soluble and photoreactive porphyrins, particularly uroporphyrin. Hepatic iron, oxidative stress and cofactors such as hepatitis C, alcohol and oestrogens generate an inhibitor of the enzyme. Circulating porphyrins deposit in the skin and, on ultraviolet and visible light exposure, generate reactive oxygen species that damage the dermo-epidermal junction, producing the characteristic fragility and blistering. Prognosis is good when contributory factors are addressed; skin lesions usually remit with iron reduction and antimalarial therapy, although there is a long-term risk of hepatic fibrosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, particularly with concurrent hepatitis C or alcohol excess.

port-wine stain results from a developmental malformation of the superficial dermal capillaries and postcapillary venules, which are abnormally dilated and increase in ectasia over time. Many cases are associated with somatic activating mutations in genes of the GNAQ/GNA11 pathway, arising during embryogenesis and affecting a clone of vascular and surrounding cells. Because the abnormality is structural rather than proliferative, the number of vessels is essentially fixed, but progressive vascular dilatation and, in some cases, associated soft-tissue overgrowth account for the darkening and thickening seen with age. The same mosaic mutations underlie the neurological and ocular features when the malformation extends beyond the skin. A port-wine stain is a lifelong lesion that persists and typically darkens and thickens over time; the skin lesion itself is benign, but associated syndromic features determine broader outcome, and laser treatment can substantially lighten many lesions though results vary and maintenance may be required.

portal biliopathy — portal cavernoma cholangiopathy, portal hypertensive biliopathy Primary sclerosing cholangitis Cholangiocarcinoma Primary choledocholithiasis IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis Iatrogenic or post-surgical bile duct stricture Recurrent pyogenic cholangitis Autoimmune pancreatitis with biliary involvement MRCP with MR portovenography Doppler ultrasound of the portal system Endoscopic ultrasound to distinguish collaterals from stones or tumour Liver function tests with fractionated bilirubin and cholestatic markers Thrombophilia and myeloproliferative neoplasm screen for the underlying cause ERCP reserved for therapeutic intervention Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to assess varices before any procedure Portal biliopathy describes abnormalities of the biliary tree, including strictures, dilatation, angulation and displacement, arising from long-standing portal hypertension, most often chronic extrahepatic portal vein obstruction with cavernoma. The term portal cavernoma cholangiopathy is preferred when a cavernoma is the demonstrable cause. Two mechanisms operate together: extrinsic compression by dilated paracholedochal veins of Petren and epicholedochal veins of Saint, and ischaemic fibrotic injury from the original thrombotic insult. Most patients remain asymptomatic despite striking cholangiographic changes; only a minority develop jaundice, biliary pain, cholangitis or secondary duct stones. MRCP combined with MR portovenography is the imaging modality of choice, showing both the biliary changes and the venous collaterals non-invasively. ERCP should be reserved for therapy such as stone extraction or stenting rather than diagnosis, because periductal collaterals bleed readily. Symptomatic disease is managed stepwise with endoscopic biliary drainage first, portosystemic shunt surgery to decompress the collaterals in refractory cases, and biliary bypass reserved for fixed strictures. Ascending cholangitis with fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain Progressive obstructive jaundice suggesting a fixed dominant stricture Secondary biliary cirrhosis from long-standing obstruction Variceal haemorrhage Features raising suspicion of superimposed cholangiocarcinoma Mistaking the cholangiographic appearances for primary sclerosing cholangitis or cholangiocarcinoma. Performing diagnostic ERCP and precipitating haemobilia or variceal bleeding from periductal collaterals. Attempting biliary surgery without first decompressing the portal system, risking catastrophic intraoperative haemorrhage. Overlooking and failing to treat the underlying prothrombotic disorder. Chronic obstruction of the extrahepatic portal vein leads to cavernous transformation, a leash of hepatopetal collateral veins around the obstructed segment. Two venous plexuses that normally drain the bile duct, the paracholedochal veins of Petren and the finer epicholedochal veins of Saint, become grossly dilated within and around the duct wall. These engorged collaterals compress and indent the common bile duct, and over time the sustained pressure together with ischaemia from the original thrombosis provokes fibrotic stricturing and wall thickening. The result is a spectrum ranging from smooth extrinsic indentations to fixed strictures, upstream ductal dilatation and intrahepatic involvement, which may be complicated by biliary stasis, stone formation and recurrent cholangitis. Most patients remain asymptomatic with a good long-term outlook, but those who develop symptomatic strictures may progress to recurrent cholangitis and secondary biliary cirrhosis if drainage is inadequate.

portal cavernoma — cavernous transformation of the portal vein, portal vein cavernoma Cirrhotic portal hypertension Non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis or idiopathic portal hypertension Budd-Chiari syndrome Portal vein tumour thrombus from hepatocellular carcinoma Congenital hepatic fibrosis Arterioportal fistula Hepatic schistosomiasis Doppler ultrasound of the portal system CT or MR portography Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy for varices Thrombophilia and myeloproliferative neoplasm screen including JAK2 mutation testing Full blood count to assess hypersplenism Liver function and synthetic tests to confirm preserved function MRCP if biliopathy is suspected A portal cavernoma is the network of hepatopetal collateral veins that develops around a chronically obstructed or thrombosed portal vein, a process termed cavernous transformation. It is the hallmark of chronic extrahepatic portal vein obstruction, and in the absence of cirrhosis liver synthetic function is typically well preserved. In children it commonly follows neonatal umbilical vein catheterisation, omphalitis or sepsis, whereas in adults prothrombotic states, myeloproliferative neoplasms, cirrhosis, abdominal sepsis and malignancy predominate. The dominant clinical problem is portal hypertension with gastro-oesophageal varices, splenomegaly and hypersplenism. Variceal bleeding is often surprisingly well tolerated because hepatic function is preserved. The collaterals can compress the biliary tree to produce portal cavernoma cholangiopathy, also called portal biliopathy. Doppler ultrasound shows the serpiginous collaterals replacing the normal portal vein, and CT or MR portography maps the anatomy for intervention. The Meso-Rex bypass, which restores physiological portal inflow, is the preferred operation in suitable children. Acute variceal haemorrhage with haematemesis or melaena Ascending cholangitis from associated biliopathy Extension of thrombosis into the mesenteric veins with bowel ischaemia Rapid splenic enlargement with severe cytopenias Assuming portal hypertension implies cirrhosis and overlooking a non-cirrhotic cavernoma with preserved liver function. Failing to screen for and treat an underlying prothrombotic or myeloproliferative disorder. Missing associated portal biliopathy as a cause of cholestasis. Delaying recognition of mesenteric extension causing intestinal ischaemia. When the main portal vein is obstructed by thrombosis, extrinsic compression or malformation, the portal circulation seeks alternative routes to reach the liver. Over weeks to months the pre-existing tiny peribiliary and paracholedochal veins in the porta hepatis dilate and proliferate into a leash of tortuous hepatopetal collaterals, the cavernoma, which partially bypasses the occluded segment. Because these collaterals cannot fully substitute for the calibre of the native vein, portal pressure rises and drives the formation of portosystemic collaterals including gastro-oesophageal varices, together with splenomegaly and hypersplenism. In extrahepatic obstruction the intrahepatic parenchyma and its arterial supply remain intact, so hepatic synthetic function is generally preserved and bleeding is better tolerated than in cirrhotic portal hypertension. The engorged periductal collaterals may in turn compress and distort the bile ducts, producing cholangiopathy. With preserved hepatic function the long-term outlook is generally good once varices are controlled, though recurrent bleeding, hypersplenism and biliopathy contribute to morbidity, and extension of thrombosis to the mesenteric veins is a serious threat.

syndrome, constrictive pericarditis) Endoscopy characterises and treats varices, while non-selective beta-blockade reduces portal pressure and the risk of first or recurrent bleeding Acute variceal bleeding is managed with resuscitation, vasoactive splanchnic vasoconstrictors, endoscopic band ligation, and antibiotic prophylaxis, with balloon tamponade or TIPS as rescue Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) and, less commonly, surgical shunts decompress the portal system but can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy Active variceal haemorrhage with haematemesis, melaena, and haemodynamic instability requiring emergency resuscitation and endoscopy Encephalopathy with reduced consciousness and risk of aspiration Rapidly accumulating tense ascites or spontaneous bacterial peritonitis Signs of decompensation (jaundice, coagulopathy, hepatorenal syndrome) indicating advanced liver failure Over-transfusing during variceal bleeding, which can raise portal pressure and worsen haemorrhage Omitting antibiotic prophylaxis in cirrhotic patients with gastrointestinal bleeding Aggressive correction of coagulopathy or platelet counts without regard to the rebalanced haemostasis of cirrhosis Creating a shunt without anticipating precipitation or worsening of hepatic encephalopathy Attributing all upper GI bleeding to varices and missing coexisting peptic ulceration or portal hypertensive gastropathy Portal hypertension results from increased resistance to portal blood flow combined with increased splanchnic inflow. In cirrhosis, fibrosis and regenerative nodules distort the hepatic architecture and raise sinusoidal resistance, compounded by intrahepatic vasoconstriction. Splanchnic arterial vasodilatation, mediated in part by nitric oxide, increases portal inflow and sustains the elevated pressure. As pressure rises, portosystemic collateral channels open at sites of communication between the portal and systemic circulations, producing varices at the gastro-oesophageal junction, rectum, and anterior abdominal wall. Splenic congestion causes splenomegaly and hypersplenism, and the combination of portal hypertension and hepatic dysfunction drives ascites and hepatic encephalopathy. Prognosis is dominated by the underlying liver disease and by whether decompensation has occurred; variceal bleeding carries substantial mortality, particularly in advanced cirrhosis. Effective prophylaxis, endoscopic therapy, and shunting reduce rebleeding, but long-term survival depends on hepatic reserve and, in suitable candidates, transplantation.

gastropathy results from the passive congestion of the gastric mucosal and submucosal microvasculature that accompanies raised portal venous pressure, usually from cirrhosis. Dilatation of mucosal capillaries and venules, with ectasia and oedema but relatively little inflammation, produces the characteristic mosaic or snake-skin appearance, and the fragile congested mucosa bleeds easily. The severity tends to track with the degree of portal hypertension, and it may become more apparent after endoscopic eradication of oesophageal varices diverts flow into the gastric mucosal bed. Portal hypertensive gastropathy is usually a chronic source of low-grade blood loss that is manageable, but its course mirrors the underlying liver disease and portal hypertension; severe or refractory bleeding carries a worse outlook and depends on control of portal pressure.

Portal vein thrombosis — PVT, Portal venous thrombosis Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic venous outflow obstruction) Tumour (hepatocellular carcinoma) invasion of the portal vein Cirrhotic portal hypertension without thrombosis Mesenteric arterial ischaemia Nodular regenerative hyperplasia or idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal hypertension Constrictive pericarditis or cardiac cirrhosis causing portal hypertension Congenital portosystemic shunt Doppler ultrasonography of the portal venous system Contrast-enhanced CT or MR portography to map thrombus extent Full blood count and JAK2 V617F mutation testing Thrombophilia screen (protein C and S, antithrombin, antiphospholipid antibodies, factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation) Liver function and synthetic markers with cause-specific liver workup Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy for varices Alpha-fetoprotein and cross-sectional imaging to exclude hepatocellular carcinoma Presents acutely with abdominal pain or is discovered chronically as cavernous transformation (portal cavernoma) with periportal collaterals. Cirrhosis is the commonest predisposing factor in adults; other causes include myeloproliferative neoplasms, abdominal sepsis, pancreatitis and malignancy. Distinguish bland thrombus from tumour thrombus (hepatocellular carcinoma): tumour thrombus expands the vein, enhances arterially and may show pulsatile flow on Doppler. Extension into the mesenteric veins is the feared complication, risking intestinal congestion, ischaemia and infarction. Doppler ultrasound is first line; contrast CT or MR portography defines the extent and mesenteric involvement. Anticoagulation promotes recanalisation and prevents extension in acute non-cirrhotic disease, balanced against variceal bleeding risk after endoscopic assessment. In non-cirrhotic patients, screen for an underlying myeloproliferative neoplasm including JAK2 V617F even when the standard thrombophilia screen is negative. Chronic portal cavernoma causes portal hypertension with varices and splenomegaly but relatively preserved hepatic synthetic function when non-cirrhotic. Severe worsening abdominal pain with lactic acidosis suggesting mesenteric ischaemia Peritonism or clinical signs of bowel infarction Variceal haemorrhage New ascites with fever suggesting concurrent sepsis Mistaking bland thrombus for tumour thrombus, or vice versa, which fundamentally alters management Withholding anticoagulation for fear of varices without first assessing and prophylaxing them Missing mesenteric extension and impending bowel infarction Overlooking an occult myeloproliferative neoplasm when the standard thrombophilia screen is negative Thrombosis within the extrahepatic portal vein or its intrahepatic branches arises from the elements of Virchow's triad: reduced portal flow (cirrhosis and portal hypertension), endothelial injury (inflammation, tumour invasion, sclerotherapy, surgery) and hypercoagulability (myeloproliferative neoplasms, inherited or acquired thrombophilias, pregnancy and oestrogen exposure). Obstruction raises portal pressure and, when persistent, drives the development of periportal venous collaterals termed cavernous transformation. If thrombus propagates into the superior mesenteric vein, venous congestion of the bowel can progress to ischaemia and transmural infarction. Acute non-cirrhotic portal vein thrombosis has a good outcome with prompt anticoagulation and high recanalisation rates, whereas chronic cavernoma carries a risk of portal hypertensive bleeding but usually preserved liver function. Thrombosis complicating cirrhosis or malignancy portends a worse prognosis.

later causes exertional breathlessness and fatigue Severity is important for liver transplant candidacy, as uncontrolled pulmonary hypertension markedly increases perioperative mortality Targeted pulmonary vasodilator therapy can lower pulmonary vascular resistance and may render some patients eligible for transplantation The severity of portal hypertension does not correlate with the severity of the pulmonary vascular disease Severe pulmonary hypertension in a transplant candidate, which greatly increases perioperative mortality Syncope or signs of right heart failure indicating advanced disease Rapid deterioration in exercise tolerance or breathlessness Pulmonary oedema after vasodilator initiation, prompting reassessment of the haemodynamic profile Diagnosing pulmonary hypertension from pressure alone without measuring pulmonary vascular resistance, thereby confusing a high-flow state with true PoPH Proceeding to liver transplantation without adequately treating significant pulmonary hypertension Confusing portopulmonary hypertension with hepatopulmonary syndrome, which has opposite vascular physiology Assuming pulmonary severity tracks liver severity when the two are independent Overlooking screening echocardiography in cirrhotic patients being assessed for transplant Portopulmonary hypertension is a pulmonary arteriopathy that develops in patients with portal hypertension. Portosystemic shunting allows vasoactive and proliferative mediators normally cleared or metabolised by the liver to reach the pulmonary circulation, where, together with the high cardiac output and shear stress of the hyperdynamic cirrhotic state, they promote endothelial dysfunction and vascular remodelling. The small pulmonary arteries undergo intimal proliferation, medial hypertrophy, and in situ thrombosis, raising pulmonary vascular resistance in a manner histologically similar to other forms of arterial pulmonary hypertension. The distinction from a simple high-flow state is critical, because volume overload alone raises pressure without raising resistance, whereas established portopulmonary hypertension reflects fixed remodelling that loads and eventually fails the right ventricle. Prognosis depends on both the severity of the pulmonary vascular disease and the underlying liver disease; untreated moderate to severe disease carries a poor outlook. Targeted therapy can improve haemodynamics and, in selected patients, restore eligibility for liver transplantation, after which the pulmonary hypertension may stabilise or improve.

pressure response Assuming the condition is always benign and omitting long-term glaucoma surveillance Missing an underlying cytomegalovirus or herpetic cause in recurrent cases Failing to examine the angle and confirm it is open Posner-Schlossman syndrome produces episodic acute rises in intraocular pressure with concurrent mild anterior chamber inflammation affecting the trabecular outflow. During an attack, low-grade trabeculitis and inflammatory obstruction of an open angle reduce aqueous outflow while aqueous production may also be altered, producing a pressure spike out of proportion to the modest cellular reaction. The angle remains open, distinguishing it from angle-closure mechanisms. Infective triggers, particularly cytomegalovirus and other herpesviruses detected in the aqueous of some patients, are thought to drive the recurrent inflammation in a subset. Between crises the eye typically returns to normal, but repeated or protracted episodes can cumulatively damage the trabecular meshwork and optic nerve. The visual prognosis is generally good because attacks are self-limiting and pressure normalises between episodes, but a minority develop chronic glaucomatous optic-nerve damage from recurrent crises, so periodic assessment of the disc and fields is advisable.

antiemetic in high-risk patients instead of combining agents Repeating the same drug class for breakthrough symptoms Overlooking modifiable contributors such as opioids, hypotension, and dehydration Assuming all postoperative vomiting is benign and missing a surgical or neurological cause Failing to risk-stratify and tailor prophylaxis preoperatively Nausea and vomiting are coordinated by brainstem centres receiving input from the chemoreceptor trigger zone, vestibular system, higher cortical centres, and vagal afferents from the gastrointestinal tract. Multiple neurotransmitters, including serotonin, dopamine, histamine, acetylcholine, and substance P, mediate these pathways. Anaesthetic agents, opioids, gastric distension, hypotension, and surgical stimulation activate one or more of these inputs. Because several receptor systems contribute, blocking a single pathway is often insufficient, which is why combining antiemetics acting at different receptors is more effective than escalating a single agent. PONV is usually self-limiting and responds to multimodal prophylaxis and treatment, but uncontrolled symptoms can delay recovery, cause dehydration, and rarely lead to aspiration or wound complications.

iliac vein stenting may help selected patients with proximal obstruction Features suggesting recurrent acute DVT rather than chronic sequelae A non-healing or atypical ulcer requiring biopsy Coexisting significant arterial disease making compression hazardous Rapidly progressive swelling suggesting new proximal obstruction or a mass Mistaking post-thrombotic changes for recurrent acute DVT, or the reverse Under-using compression therapy, the mainstay of control Overlooking a treatable proximal (iliac) obstruction Applying compression without excluding arterial disease Post-thrombotic syndrome develops when a deep vein thrombus fails to resolve fully, leaving residual venous obstruction and destroying venous valves through inflammation and recanalisation. common platelet antigen, most often human platelet antigen 1a, who has been sensitised by earlier transfusion or pregnancy.
