over-immunosuppression that drives the disorder Treating empirically without a tissue diagnosis and clonality and viral assessment Reducing immunosuppression without weighing the resulting risk of graft rejection Immunosuppression weakens cytotoxic T-cell control of Epstein-Barr-virus-infected B cells, allowing latently infected cells to proliferate unchecked. Proliferation is initially polyclonal and potentially reversible, but accumulating genetic changes can drive progression to clonal, autonomous lymphoma. A minority of cases are Epstein-Barr-virus-negative, tend to arise later, and are thought to develop through virus-independent mechanisms related to chronic immune dysregulation. Early lesions may regress with reduction of immunosuppression, whereas monomorphic and aggressive disease has a worse outlook, although rituximab-based therapy has improved survival; management requires balancing tumour control against the risk of graft rejection.

Postdural puncture headache — PDPH, post-lumbar puncture headache, low-pressure headache Migraine or tension-type headache Meningitis (infective) or chemical meningism Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis Subdural haematoma Pre-eclampsia or eclampsia in the obstetric patient Pneumocephalus or caffeine-withdrawal headache Clinical assessment focusing on the postural nature of the headache Neurological examination to exclude focal signs Brain imaging (CT or MRI) when features are atypical, worsening, or accompanied by neurological signs Investigations for pre-eclampsia in the postpartum patient when relevant Assessment for infection if fever or meningism is present A characteristically postural headache that worsens on sitting or standing and improves on lying flat, developing within a few days of dural puncture Typically frontal or occipital and may be accompanied by neck stiffness, photophobia, nausea, tinnitus, or hearing changes Risk is higher with larger-gauge and cutting (rather than pencil-point) needles, younger age, female sex, and after accidental dural puncture during epidural placement Diagnosis is largely clinical, but a headache lacking postural features or with neurological signs should prompt evaluation for other causes Initial management is conservative with rest as needed, hydration, simple analgesia, and reassurance, as many cases resolve spontaneously An epidural blood patch is the definitive treatment for severe or persistent headache and is generally highly effective Caffeine and other pharmacological measures have limited and temporary benefit compared with a blood patch Rare but serious complications of intracranial hypotension include subdural haematoma and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, so atypical or worsening features require imaging Loss of the postural component or a headache that becomes constant, suggesting an alternative or serious cause Focal neurological deficit, seizure, or reduced consciousness suggesting subdural haematoma or venous thrombosis Fever, neck stiffness, or photophobia raising concern for meningitis Sudden thunderclap onset or features suggesting subarachnoid haemorrhage Assuming every post-procedure headache is a postdural puncture headache and missing a dangerous cause Delaying an effective blood patch in severe, disabling headache Overlooking evolving neurological signs that indicate subdural haematoma or venous sinus thrombosis Failing to consider pre-eclampsia in a postpartum woman with headache Relying on caffeine or bed rest alone for persistent severe symptoms A persistent hole in the dura allows cerebrospinal fluid to leak into the epidural space faster than it is produced, lowering cerebrospinal fluid volume and pressure. In the upright position, reduced buoyant support causes traction on pain-sensitive intracranial structures such as the meninges and bridging veins, and compensatory cerebral vasodilation may contribute, producing the postural headache. Larger dural defects leak more and cause more severe symptoms. An epidural blood patch works by sealing the defect and raising epidural and cerebrospinal fluid pressure. Most postdural puncture headaches resolve within days to weeks with conservative care, and a blood patch relieves the majority of severe cases; rare progression to intracranial haemorrhage or venous thrombosis can cause serious morbidity.

Posterior cortical atrophy — PCA, Benson syndrome, visual variant of Alzheimer disease, posterior cortical atrophy syndrome Typical amnestic Alzheimer disease Dementia with Lewy bodies Corticobasal syndrome Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease Primary ophthalmological or optic pathway disease Occipital stroke or structural posterior lesion Delirium or a primary psychiatric disorder MRI of the brain to demonstrate parieto-occipital and posterior temporal atrophy FDG-PET to show posterior cortical hypometabolism Amyloid PET or cerebrospinal fluid amyloid and tau markers to confirm Alzheimer pathology Formal ophthalmological and visual acuity assessment to exclude primary eye disease Detailed neuropsychological testing of visuospatial and higher visual functions Assessment for parkinsonian or myoclonic features suggesting alternative pathology Presents with progressive impairment of higher visual and spatial processing, with early memory and insight relatively preserved Patients struggle with reading, judging distances, locating objects and dressing, despite normal basic acuity and eyes, reflecting cortical rather than ocular visual failure Features may include components of Balint syndrome (simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, oculomotor apraxia) and Gerstmann syndrome (acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation) Onset is often at a relatively young age, and patients are frequently referred first to ophthalmology because the problem seems visual Alzheimer disease is the most common underlying pathology, though corticobasal degeneration, Lewy body disease and prion disease can also produce the syndrome Imaging shows atrophy and hypometabolism concentrated in the parieto-occipital and posterior temporal cortex Amyloid imaging and cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers help confirm underlying Alzheimer pathology Rapid progression or myoclonus raising concern for prion disease Development of parkinsonism or asymmetrical limb apraxia suggesting corticobasal degeneration Visual disability causing falls, driving hazards and loss of independence Marked fluctuations or visual hallucinations pointing to Lewy body disease Repeatedly investigating the eyes when the problem is cortical visual processing Missing the diagnosis because early memory and insight are preserved Assuming all cases are Alzheimer disease without considering Lewy body, corticobasal or prion pathology Underestimating the safety impact of cortical visual failure on driving and daily living Posterior cortical atrophy is a clinical-radiological syndrome caused by neurodegeneration concentrated in the posterior cortical regions responsible for higher-order visual and spatial processing, including the occipital, parietal and posterior temporal lobes. The commonest underlying pathology is Alzheimer disease, in which amyloid plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles accumulate predominantly in these posterior networks rather than the medial temporal memory regions, producing a visual-predominant rather than amnestic phenotype. Progressive damage to the dorsal and ventral visual pathways disrupts the integration of visual information, spatial localisation and object recognition, while primary visual acuity and the eyes themselves remain intact. Posterior cortical atrophy is progressive, with worsening visual and spatial disability and eventual spread to involve broader cognitive domains resembling more generalised dementia; prognosis reflects the underlying pathology, and management is supportive with visual aids, environmental adaptation and caregiver support.

Posterior cruciate ligament injury — PCL tear, PCL rupture, posterior cruciate ligament sprain Anterior cruciate ligament injury (a false-positive anterior drawer from a posterior sag) Posterolateral corner injury Multiligament knee injury or reduced dislocation Meniscal tear Extensor mechanism disruption Posterior drawer and posterior sag tests, with dial test for posterolateral corner MRI of the knee to confirm and grade the tear Stress radiographs to quantify posterior translation Vascular assessment where a dislocation is suspected Examination under anaesthesia for multiligament injuries Classic mechanisms are a dashboard injury (posteriorly directed force on a flexed knee) or a fall onto a flexed knee with a plantarflexed foot The posterior drawer test is the most reliable examination sign, with a posterior sag observed in 90 degrees of flexion Isolated PCL injuries are often treated non-operatively with quadriceps rehabilitation, unlike many ACL tears High-grade or combined ligament injuries (especially with posterolateral corner injury) are more likely to require reconstruction A PCL injury raises suspicion of a multiligament injury or a reduced knee dislocation with vascular risk Quadriceps strengthening is central because the quadriceps dynamically substitutes for PCL function Chronic deficiency can lead to patellofemoral and medial compartment osteoarthritis Signs of knee dislocation with possible popliteal artery injury Combined posterolateral corner injury producing gross rotatory instability Common peroneal nerve palsy accompanying posterolateral injury Mistaking a posterior sag for a positive anterior drawer and diagnosing an ACL tear Missing an associated posterolateral corner injury, which compromises PCL reconstruction Overlooking a spontaneously reduced knee dislocation and its vascular risk Neglecting quadriceps rehabilitation in non-operative management The PCL is the primary restraint to posterior tibial translation. A posteriorly directed force on the proximal tibia of a flexed knee, or hyperflexion, exceeds its tensile strength and tears it, usually in the mid-substance. Posterior tibial subluxation alters joint contact and, if combined with posterolateral corner injury, produces rotatory instability; long-standing deficiency increases patellofemoral and medial compartment loading. Isolated low-grade PCL injuries usually do well with rehabilitation; combined injuries have poorer outcomes and often need reconstruction, and chronic deficiency predisposes to osteoarthritis.

Posterior embryotoxon — prominent Schwalbe line Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome or anomaly Normal anatomical variant Arcus lipoides (which is stromal, not at Schwalbe line) Peripheral corneal degenerations Iridocorneal endothelial syndrome Slit-lamp examination and gonioscopy Assessment of the iris for hypoplasia and corectopia Intraocular pressure measurement and glaucoma evaluation Systemic assessment for Axenfeld-Rieger features (dental, facial, umbilical) where relevant Family history and examination An anteriorly displaced and prominent Schwalbe line, seen as a fine white ring or arc just inside the limbus It is a common, usually incidental finding that can occur in normal eyes It is a hallmark feature of Axenfeld-Rieger spectrum when accompanied by iris strands and other anomalies In isolation it is benign, but as part of anterior segment dysgenesis it carries a significant glaucoma risk Gonioscopy demonstrates the prominent Schwalbe line and any attached iris processes Identification should prompt assessment for associated iris changes, glaucoma and systemic features of Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome Associated iris anomalies indicating Axenfeld-Rieger spectrum Raised intraocular pressure or glaucoma Systemic features of a syndrome Progressive angle changes Dismissing it without checking for associated iris changes and glaucoma Overlooking the systemic associations of Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome Confusing it with arcus or other peripheral corneal findings Failing to screen the family in syndromic cases Posterior embryotoxon represents an anteriorly positioned, thickened Schwalbe line, the peripheral termination of Descemet membrane at the angle. It arises from abnormal development of the neural crest-derived anterior segment tissues. When isolated it is a benign anatomical variant, but when it occurs with iridocorneal adhesions and iris hypoplasia it is part of the Axenfeld-Rieger spectrum of anterior segment dysgenesis, in which maldevelopment of the drainage angle predisposes to glaucoma. Isolated posterior embryotoxon is benign with no visual consequence; when part of anterior segment dysgenesis, prognosis depends on glaucoma control.

posterior interosseous syndrome — posterior interosseous nerve palsy, PIN syndrome, deep radial nerve entrapment Radial tunnel syndrome (pain without motor weakness) Extensor tendon rupture, for example in rheumatoid arthritis Main radial nerve palsy (which includes wrist drop and sensory loss) C7-C8 radiculopathy Neuralgic amyotrophy involving the posterior interosseous nerve Sagittal band rupture causing extensor tendon subluxation Nerve conduction studies and needle electromyography of posterior interosseous-innervated muscles with sparing of extensor carpi radialis longus and brachioradialis Tenodesis test to confirm extensor tendon integrity and exclude rupture High-resolution ultrasound of the radial tunnel to identify a mass or focal nerve change MRI of the elbow and proximal forearm to detect lipoma, ganglion or synovitis Plain radiographs if Monteggia fracture-dislocation or bony abnormality is suspected Inflammatory markers and rheumatoid serology when synovitis is considered A pure motor palsy of the posterior interosseous nerve, the deep motor branch of the radial nerve, most often entrapped at the arcade of Frohse (the proximal fibrous edge of supinator) within the radial tunnel The hallmark is finger drop with loss of metacarpophalangeal extension of the fingers and thumb, but with PRESERVED wrist extension and NO sensory loss because the superficial radial nerve is spared Wrist extension deviates radially because extensor carpi radialis longus (innervated proximal to the branch) is preserved while extensor carpi ulnaris is weak Common causes include a proximal mass such as a lipoma or ganglion, rheumatoid synovitis of the elbow, radial tunnel fibrous bands, and trauma including Monteggia fracture-dislocation It must be distinguished from radial tunnel syndrome, which causes pain over the mobile wad without motor deficit, and from extensor tendon rupture, differentiated by the tenodesis test showing intact tendons Onset may be gradual and painless in entrapment, or acute and painful, in which case inflammatory neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner) affecting the posterior interosseous nerve should be considered Management is initially conservative with splinting and observation for compressive or inflammatory cases, with surgical exploration and decompression indicated for a structural lesion or failure to recover Acute severe pain preceding weakness, suggesting neuralgic amyotrophy A palpable or imaging-detected mass in the proximal forearm Progressive weakness despite conservative treatment indicating a structural compressive lesion Antecedent Monteggia fracture-dislocation or elbow trauma Mistaking finger drop for extensor tendon rupture without performing the tenodesis test Diagnosing a full radial nerve palsy when wrist extension and sensation are in fact preserved Overlooking a proximal forearm mass such as a lipoma or ganglion as the cause Failing to consider neuralgic amyotrophy in acute painful presentations Confusing the painless motor syndrome with painful radial tunnel syndrome, which lacks true weakness After the radial nerve divides at the level of the elbow, the posterior interosseous nerve passes into the radial tunnel and dives between the two heads of supinator, most commonly compressed at the proximal fibrous margin known as the arcade of Frohse. Because this branch is purely motor, distal to the take-off of extensor carpi radialis longus and the superficial radial sensory nerve, entrapment produces selective weakness of the digital and thumb extensors, extensor carpi ulnaris and the radial abductors of the thumb, without sensory loss. Compression from fibrous bands, a space-occupying mass, proliferative synovitis or trauma causes focal demyelination and, if sustained, axonal loss; the preserved extensor carpi radialis longus explains the radial deviation on attempted wrist extension. Compressive lesions treated by removing or decompressing the offending structure, and inflammatory cases, commonly recover good extensor function, although recovery may take several months. Long-standing entrapment with axonal loss recovers less completely and may require tendon transfer to restore digital extension.

posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy — PION, retrobulbar ischaemic optic neuropathy Retrobulbar optic neuritis Compressive optic neuropathy Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy Chiasmal or retrochiasmal lesion Cortical visual loss Toxic or nutritional optic neuropathy Functional (non-organic) visual loss Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein to exclude giant cell arteritis Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits with contrast to exclude compression and inflammation Automated perimetry to characterise the field loss Optical coherence tomography, which later demonstrates nerve fibre layer thinning Review of perioperative records for hypotension, blood loss, positioning and fluid balance Temporal artery biopsy where an arteritic mechanism is suspected Infarction affects the retrobulbar optic nerve, so the optic disc appears normal at onset and only becomes pale after several weeks. Three recognised categories exist: arteritic (giant cell arteritis), non-arteritic, and perioperative. The perioperative form classically follows prolonged spinal or cardiac surgery with prone positioning, hypotension, anaemia, large fluid shifts and significant blood loss. Acute visual loss with a normal-looking disc should prompt consideration of a retrobulbar process, of which posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy is one cause. A relative afferent pupillary defect is present when involvement is unilateral, but perioperative cases are frequently bilateral. It is largely a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring neuroimaging to rule out compressive and inflammatory causes. In the perioperative setting visual loss may be profound and bilateral, making preventive haemodynamic management the priority. Optic atrophy developing four to eight weeks after acute loss with a previously normal disc supports the diagnosis retrospectively. Systemic or laboratory features of giant cell arteritis Bilateral visual loss on emergence from prolonged surgery Progressive visual loss suggesting a compressive lesion Pain on eye movement pointing to optic neuritis Expecting disc swelling and discounting the diagnosis when the early disc looks normal Overlooking giant cell arteritis as a cause in older patients Failing to image and thereby missing a compressive lesion Underestimating the risk in prolonged prone or cardiac surgery The intraorbital posterior optic nerve is supplied by a pial vascular plexus arising from small branches of the ophthalmic artery, and this segment represents a watershed zone particularly vulnerable to systemic hypoperfusion. Non-arteritic and perioperative disease result from a critical fall in perfusion pressure, often compounded by anaemia, oedema and raised orbital or intraocular venous pressure, producing infarction of the retrobulbar nerve. The arteritic form is caused by the granulomatous vasculitis of giant cell arteritis occluding the feeding vessels. Visual recovery is generally poor, particularly in the arteritic and perioperative forms where loss is often severe and permanent. In the perioperative setting prevention through meticulous haemodynamic and positioning management is the most important determinant of outcome.

posterior lenticonus — posterior lentiglobus, conical posterior lens Posterior polar cataract Persistent fetal vasculature (persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous) Anterior lenticonus Posterior lens coloboma Lamellar or total congenital cataract of other cause Retinoblastoma or other cause of leukocoria in a child Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with retro-illumination to demonstrate the posterior conical bulge and any opacity Retinoscopy and cycloplegic refraction to detect the oil-droplet reflex and anisometropia B-scan ultrasonography or anterior segment OCT to define posterior lens contour and integrity of the posterior capsule Assessment for amblyopia with age-appropriate visual acuity testing and fixation preference Systemic and metabolic evaluation for Lowe syndrome where clinically suspected Fundus examination to exclude persistent fetal vasculature and posterior segment pathology A localised posterior bulge of the posterior lens capsule and cortex into the vitreous, usually unilateral, sporadic and more common than anterior lenticonus It is an important cause of unilateral acquired or progressive cataract and amblyopia in infancy and childhood, and warrants early paediatric ophthalmology referral Retro-illumination shows a central 'oil-droplet' or fish-tail reflex, and the posterior curvature may progress with growth, later opacifying into a posterior polar or lamellar cataract The overlying posterior capsule is inherently thin and prone to spontaneous dehiscence, so a pre-existing or intra-operative posterior capsule defect should be anticipated Because it is frequently unilateral and progressive, dense amblyopia is a major threat and mandates refractive correction and occlusion alongside any surgery Most cases are isolated, but posterior lenticonus can occur in Lowe (oculocerebrorenal) syndrome and, less often, in the Alport spectrum, prompting a directed systemic review Surgical planning should account for the weak or absent posterior capsule, with a low threshold for anterior vitrectomy and careful intraocular lens placement Ultrasound or anterior segment imaging helps define the posterior lens contour and detect any capsular breach before intervention Dense unilateral cataract in an infant with high risk of irreversible deprivation amblyopia Evidence of spontaneous posterior capsule rupture with sudden lens swelling or fragments in the vitreous Leukocoria requiring urgent exclusion of retinoblastoma Rapid progression of lens opacity or myopic shift in the amblyogenic period Delaying referral and surgery so that dense amblyopia becomes irreversible Being unprepared for a pre-existing posterior capsule defect during cataract surgery Mistaking the oil-droplet reflex for a corneal or vitreous abnormality Neglecting occlusion therapy after successful lens surgery Failing to consider Lowe syndrome or other systemic associations Posterior lenticonus arises from a focal area of weakness and thinning in the posterior lens capsule, which normally lacks the epithelial support present anteriorly. The exact mechanism is debated but proposed causes include a primary developmental defect of the posterior capsule, abnormal persistence or traction of the hyaloid vascular system on the posterior pole, and relative overgrowth of lens fibres against a deficient capsule. The weakened region bulges backward under intralenticular forces, increasing local curvature and lens power; progressive stretching disrupts the adjacent cortical fibres and leads to focal opacification and eventual posterior polar cataract. Frank dehiscence of the attenuated capsule can occur spontaneously. With timely surgery, intraocular lens implantation and rigorous amblyopia therapy the visual prognosis for isolated posterior lenticonus can be favourable, though outcome depends heavily on the depth of amblyopia at presentation. Cases complicated by posterior capsule rupture or dense long-standing amblyopia have a more guarded visual outlook.

Posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy — PPCD, PPMD Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy Iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome Congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy Anterior segment dysgenesis Descemet membrane changes from other cause Slit-lamp examination and specular or confocal microscopy of the endothelium Assessment of the anterior chamber angle for adhesions Intraocular pressure measurement and glaucoma assessment Anterior segment imaging where needed Family history and genetic evaluation in selected cases A dystrophy of the corneal endothelium and Descemet membrane, usually inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern It is characterised by vesicular, band-like or diffuse lesions at the level of Descemet membrane Many patients are asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally, with a generally mild course The endothelial cells acquire epithelial-like characteristics and can migrate abnormally It may be associated with iridocorneal adhesions, corectopia and, in some, raised intraocular pressure or glaucoma Most cases need only monitoring, with corneal transplantation reserved for the minority developing significant oedema Raised intraocular pressure or glaucomatous damage Progressive corneal oedema and visual loss Extensive iridocorneal adhesions Features overlapping with ICE syndrome (usually unilateral, non-hereditary) Confusing it with the typically unilateral, acquired ICE syndrome Overlooking associated glaucoma Attributing corneal oedema to another cause Missing the autosomal dominant inheritance and need to examine relatives In posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy the corneal endothelial cells behave abnormally, taking on epithelial-like features with the capacity to proliferate and migrate across the posterior cornea and, at times, onto the anterior chamber angle and iris. This aberrant tissue produces the characteristic vesicular and band lesions of Descemet membrane and can form adhesions that distort the iris and impair aqueous outflow, causing glaucoma in a subset. Endothelial dysfunction can occasionally progress to corneal oedema. Most cases are mild and stable with a good prognosis; a minority develop glaucoma or corneal decompensation requiring specific treatment or transplantation.

posterior scleritis — posterior scleral inflammation Orbital inflammatory disease or orbital cellulitis Choroidal tumour such as melanoma or metastasis Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease Central serous chorioretinopathy Optic neuritis or papilloedema Uveal effusion syndrome B-scan ultrasonography seeking scleral thickening and the T-sign Optical coherence tomography to demonstrate subretinal fluid and choroidal folds Fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography Magnetic resonance imaging or computed tomography of the orbits when orbital or mass pathology is suspected Inflammatory and autoimmune serology including full blood count, ESR, CRP, ANA, ANCA, rheumatoid factor and angiotensin-converting enzyme Infective screen for syphilis and tuberculosis before starting immunosuppression A rare, potentially sight-threatening inflammation of the sclera posterior to the equator, often with minimal or absent anterior signs so it is easily missed. Pain is typically severe, deep and boring, worse on eye movement, and may radiate to the brow, jaw or temple with globe tenderness. It may produce proptosis, diplopia and restricted ocular motility, mimicking orbital disease. B-scan ultrasonography is the key investigation, showing scleral and choroidal thickening with fluid tracking into the sub-Tenon space producing the T-sign. Posterior segment signs include exudative retinal detachment, choroidal folds, disc oedema, uveal effusion, macular oedema and a subretinal mass mimicking a tumour. Around half of cases are associated with a systemic autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, lupus, relapsing polychondritis or IgG4-related disease. Management is graded by severity, using systemic non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression or biologics. Infective and masquerade causes should be excluded before committing to immunosuppression. Severe pain accompanied by significant visual loss Proptosis with restricted motility raising concern for orbital cellulitis Systemic features suggesting an underlying vasculitis A subretinal or choroidal mass raising suspicion of malignancy Misdiagnosis as orbital cellulitis or a choroidal tumour leading to inappropriate management Overlooking the diagnosis in a painful eye with a normal anterior segment Failing to investigate for an associated systemic autoimmune disorder Commencing corticosteroids without first excluding an infective cause Posterior scleritis is an immune-mediated inflammation of the collagen-rich posterior sclera, frequently occurring as an ocular manifestation of systemic autoimmune or vasculitic disease. Immune-complex deposition and cell-mediated hypersensitivity drive inflammatory infiltration and oedema that thicken the sclera and track into the sub-Tenon space and adjacent choroid. This produces the characteristic ultrasonographic findings and secondary changes such as choroidal effusion, exudative retinal detachment and disc swelling. The outlook is generally good when treatment is prompt and appropriately intensive, though recurrences occur and any associated systemic disease influences overall outcome. Delayed recognition and treatment risk permanent visual loss.

Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction — adult acquired flatfoot deformity, tibialis posterior tendinopathy, progressive collapsing foot deformity Tarsal coalition or accessory navicular causing a rigid or painful flatfoot Midfoot or hindfoot osteoarthritis and Charcot neuroarthropathy Inflammatory arthropathy such as rheumatoid or seronegative spondyloarthritis Deltoid or spring ligament injury without primary tendon disease Tarsal tunnel syndrome or medial ankle nerve entrapment Deep posterior compartment or medial ankle tenosynovitis of other tendons Weight-bearing foot and ankle radiographs assessing talonavicular coverage, talo-first metatarsal alignment and arch collapse MRI to grade tendon degeneration, tears and associated spring and deltoid ligament involvement Ultrasound for dynamic assessment of tendon integrity and tenosynovitis Standing hindfoot alignment view or weight-bearing CT for coronal deformity Single-limb heel-rise test and too-many-toes assessment documented over time Screening for inflammatory arthropathy and metabolic risk factors where clinically indicated The tibialis posterior is the principal dynamic stabiliser of the medial longitudinal arch; it inverts the hindfoot and locks the transverse tarsal joint to create a rigid lever for push-off, so its failure produces a progressive collapsing flatfoot It is the commonest cause of acquired adult flatfoot, classically in middle-aged women, and is associated with obesity, hypertension, diabetes, corticosteroid use and seronegative inflammatory arthropathy Early disease causes medial hindfoot pain and swelling behind the medial malleolus; as the arch collapses, lateral subfibular impingement pain can develop The too-many-toes sign and an inability to perform a single-limb heel raise with hindfoot inversion are key bedside tests of tendon competence The Johnson and Strom staging, with the Myerson modification, runs from tenosynovitis with a flexible foot, through a flexible then rigid flatfoot, to fixed deformity with ankle valgus and deltoid ligament failure A watershed zone of relative hypovascularity just distal and posterior to the medial malleolus predisposes the tendon to degeneration and rupture Flexible deformity is managed with orthoses, medial arch support or an ankle-foot orthosis and structured rehabilitation, whereas fixed deformity or ankle involvement requires reconstructive or fusion surgery A hot, deformed insensate foot suggesting Charcot neuroarthropathy, especially in diabetes Rapidly progressive deformity or fixed valgus with ankle involvement Features of an inflammatory or septic process rather than degenerative tendinopathy Neurovascular compromise or non-healing medial ankle ulceration Dismissing early medial ankle pain and swelling as a simple sprain and missing tenosynovitis Failing to distinguish a flexible from a rigid deformity, which fundamentally changes management Overlooking a hot deformed neuropathic foot and treating Charcot arthropathy as tendon dysfunction Attempting soft-tissue reconstruction alone without correcting hindfoot malalignment with osteotomy, so the reconstruction fails Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction begins as degenerative tendinosis and tenosynovitis within the watershed hypovascular segment behind the medial malleolus, where repetitive load, ageing and impaired healing lead to mucoid degeneration, elongation and eventual attritional rupture. As the tibialis posterior loses its inverting and arch-supporting action, the unopposed peroneus brevis and the body's weight drive progressive hindfoot valgus, forefoot abduction and collapse of the medial longitudinal arch. Secondary attenuation of the spring (plantar calcaneonavicular) ligament and later the deltoid ligament allows the talar head to plantarflex and the deformity to become fixed, with lateral subfibular and sinus tarsi impingement and, in advanced disease, valgus tilt of the ankle. Inflammatory arthropathy and metabolic factors accelerate this degenerative cascade. With early diagnosis, flexible deformity often responds well to orthoses and rehabilitation, and joint-preserving reconstruction can restore function; once deformity becomes rigid or the ankle is involved, arthrodesis is usually required and full correction of established deformity is less predictable.

Posterior urethral polyp — posterior urethral polyp, fibroepithelial polyp of posterior urethra, congenital urethral polyp Prostatic-type urethral polyp with prostatic epithelium Urethral or bladder visualise and localise the polyp Voiding or retrograde urethrography showing a mobile filling defect Urinalysis and urine cytology to assess haematuria Pelvic MRI or ultrasound if a mass or malignancy produces intermittent obstruction In adults it may cause haematuria, haematospermia, voiding symptoms, or be found incidentally It is a recognised benign cause of lower urinary tract symptoms and, when near the prostate, may be associated with PSA elevation as a benign mimic of malignancy Cystourethroscopy demonstrates a mobile pedunculated lesion, and urethrography may show a corresponding filling defect Histology shows a fibrovascular core covered by urothelium without malignant features Treatment is endoscopic transurethral resection, which is usually curative Persistent haematuria or atypical cytology suggesting urothelial malignancy Significant obstruction or urinary retention A rising or persistently elevated PSA warranting exclusion of prostate cancer Recurrent lesions after resection Attributing a raised PSA to the polyp and missing a coexisting prostate cancer Mistaking the polyp for posterior urethral valves in a child Incomplete resection of the stalk leading to recurrence Failing to send tissue for histology to exclude malignancy A posterior urethral polyp is a benign proliferation with a fibrovascular core lined by normal urothelium, generally considered congenital in boys and arising on a stalk near the verumontanum. Its mobility on a pedicle allows intermittent prolapse into the bladder neck, producing positional or intermittent obstruction, while surface trauma explains episodes of haematuria and haematospermia. Excellent; endoscopic resection is generally curative with a low recurrence rate, and the typical fibroepithelial polyp is benign with no malignant potential.

Posterior urethral valves — PUV, congenital obstructing posterior urethral membrane Ureteropelvic or ureterovesical junction obstruction Prune belly (Eagle-Barrett) syndrome Bilateral high-grade vesicoureteric reflux Neurogenic bladder Urethral atresia or stricture Voiding cystourethrogram to demonstrate the valves and assess reflux and bladder morphology Renal and bladder ultrasound to evaluate hydronephrosis and bladder wall thickness Serum electrolytes, urea, and creatinine to assess renal function (interpreted after the first days of life) Cystoscopy for direct visualisation and treatment of the valves Isotope renography to assess differential renal function and drainage The most common cause of congenital lower urinary tract obstruction in male infants, caused by obstructing membranous folds in the posterior urethra Many cases are suspected antenatally from bilateral hydronephrosis, a thick-walled distended bladder, a dilated posterior urethra (keyhole sign), and oligohydramnios Severe early obstruction and oligohydramnios can lead to pulmonary hypoplasia, which may be the immediate life-threatening problem at birth Postnatal presentation ranges from a palpable bladder, poor urinary stream, and straining to urosepsis or failure to thrive, and older boys may present with voiding difficulty or incontinence The voiding cystourethrogram is the key diagnostic study, showing a dilated posterior urethra, bladder trabeculation, and often vesicoureteric reflux Initial management is bladder decompression with a catheter, correction of fluid and electrolyte disturbance, and treatment of infection before definitive intervention Definitive treatment is endoscopic ablation of the valves, with temporary urinary diversion (vesicostomy) reserved for selected infants Long-term follow-up is essential because bladder dysfunction and progressive renal impairment can persist or evolve even after successful valve ablation Neonatal respiratory distress from pulmonary hypoplasia secondary to oligohydramnios, which is immediately life-threatening Urosepsis in an infant with obstruction requiring urgent decompression and antibiotics Acute kidney injury with electrolyte disturbance and rising creatinine Progressive deterioration in renal function or bladder function despite valve ablation Attributing an antenatal keyhole bladder or bilateral hydronephrosis to a benign cause and delaying evaluation Interpreting neonatal creatinine in the first day or two as the baby's true renal function rather than the mother's Assuming valve ablation cures the child and neglecting long-term renal and bladder surveillance Overlooking bladder dysfunction as an ongoing cause of upper tract deterioration Posterior urethral valves are congenital obstructing tissue folds in the posterior (prostatic) urethra of males that impede bladder emptying from early in fetal life. The resulting high-pressure obstruction causes bladder wall hypertrophy and trabeculation, vesicoureteric reflux, and back-pressure that dilates the ureters and damages the developing kidneys, producing dysplasia and impaired concentrating ability. Reduced fetal urine output causes oligohydramnios, which in turn impairs lung development and can result in pulmonary hypoplasia. The renal and bladder damage sustained in utero often determines lifelong outcome. Outcome depends largely on the degree of irreversible renal dysplasia established in utero. Many boys do well after valve ablation, but a significant proportion develop chronic kidney disease and bladder dysfunction, and some progress to end-stage renal failure requiring transplantation. Early nadir creatinine after treatment is a useful prognostic indicator.

Posterior uveitis — choroiditis, chorioretinitis, retinochoroiditis Intraocular lymphoma masquerading as chronic vitritis Central serous chorioretinopathy Retinal vein occlusion with macular oedema therapy Bilateral panuveitis after ocular injury or surgery raising concern for sympathetic ophthalmia Persistent vitritis in an older patient that may represent intraocular lymphoma Macular or optic nerve involvement with declining acuity requiring prompt treatment Starting immunosuppression before excluding an infective cause, which can allow infection to progress Overlooking cystoid macular oedema as the reason for reduced acuity in a quiet-looking eye Attributing chronic vitritis in an older patient to inflammation and missing masquerade lymphoma Failing to screen for a systemic disease that the eye findings are heralding Posterior uveitis is inflammation predominantly affecting the choroid and overlying retina, often with secondary vitreous involvement. It may arise from direct infection (for example Toxoplasma, tuberculosis, syphilis, viral retinitis) or from immune-mediated processes such as sarcoidosis, Behcet disease, or an autoimmune reaction to ocular antigens as in sympathetic ophthalmia. Inflammatory cells and mediators disrupt the outer blood-retinal barrier, causing exudation, oedema, and eventual chorioretinal scarring. Ischaemia and chronic inflammation can drive neovascularisation, and macular or optic nerve involvement determines the visual outcome. Outcome depends on the underlying cause and on whether the macula and optic nerve are spared; focal treatable infections such as toxoplasmosis often heal with scarring away from the fovea, but recurrent or immune-mediated disease can cause cumulative visual loss from macular oedema, scarring, or neovascular complications.

Posterior vitreous detachment — PVD, acute posterior vitreous detachment, vitreous separation Retinal tear or rhegmatogenous retinal detachment Vitreous haemorrhage from other causes such as proliferative retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion or a retinal macroaneurysm Retinal migraine or cortical or occipital photopsia Posterior uveitis or vitritis producing floaters Vitreomacular traction syndrome Ocular ischaemia or other retinal cause of photopsia Dilated slit-lamp biomicroscopy with peripheral retinal examination and scleral indentation Assessment for Shafer's sign (pigment in the anterior vitreous) B-scan ultrasonography when the fundus view is obscured, for example by vitreous haemorrhage, to detect PVD, tears or detachment OCT to demonstrate a Weiss ring, vitreomacular traction or coexisting macular pathology Documented visual acuity and confrontation or formal visual field assessment Repeat examination after an interval, or sooner if new symptoms develop, to detect delayed retinal breaks Age-related separation of the posterior vitreous cortex from the internal limiting membrane of the retina, driven by vitreous liquefaction (synchysis) and weakening of vitreoretinal adhesion Classic symptoms are the sudden onset of floaters together with flashing lights (photopsia) from vitreoretinal traction, often more noticeable in dim light or with eye movement A Weiss ring, the detached annulus of condensed vitreous from around the optic disc, is effectively pathognomonic when seen The principal danger is that traction may create a retinal tear, which can progress to rhegmatogenous retinal detachment; a meaningful proportion of symptomatic acute PVDs have a tear at presentation Pigmented cells in the anterior vitreous, described as tobacco dust or Shafer's sign, strongly suggest a retinal break and mandate careful peripheral examination Accompanying vitreous haemorrhage substantially raises the likelihood of a retinal tear and should prompt urgent, thorough retinal assessment All symptomatic patients need dilated fundus examination with scleral indentation; those with an initially normal examination warrant safety-netting and often repeat review because breaks can appear later Risk is increased in myopia, after cataract surgery, following trauma, and in the fellow eye of a patient who has had a PVD-related tear or detachment A curtain, shadow or progressive field defect suggesting retinal detachment A sudden shower of floaters or vitreous haemorrhage indicating a probable retinal tear Tobacco dust (Shafer's sign) in the anterior vitreous Progressive increase in floaters or flashes, or any loss of central vision Failing to perform, or to repeat, an adequate peripheral retinal examination with indentation and so missing a retinal break Discharging a patient with a vitreous haemorrhage without excluding a tear or arranging timely follow-up Ignoring new or changing symptoms after an initially normal examination Attributing all floaters to benign PVD without considering uveitis, haemorrhage or detachment With ageing the vitreous gel undergoes liquefaction (synchysis) while the adhesion between the posterior vitreous cortex and the internal limiting membrane weakens. When liquefied vitreous passes through a dehiscence in the posterior cortex into the retrohyaloid space, the cortex peels away from the retina, producing a posterior vitreous detachment. Where focal vitreoretinal adhesions persist, for example at the vitreous base, along retinal vessels or at areas of lattice degeneration, dynamic traction during separation can tear the retina or avulse a vessel, causing a retinal break and/or vitreous haemorrhage. Photopsiae arise from mechanical stimulation of the retina by this traction, while floaters reflect condensed vitreous and the Weiss ring casting shadows on the retina. An uncomplicated posterior vitreous detachment is benign, and symptoms usually diminish over weeks to months as floaters settle and the patient adapts. The overall prognosis depends on prompt detection and treatment of any associated retinal tear, which when treated early usually prevents progression to detachment.

exposure to deepen and prolong the pigmentation Cutaneous inflammation stimulates melanocytes to increase melanin synthesis through inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins, leukotrienes and cytokines, producing epidermal hypermelanosis. When the inflammation damages the basal layer and dermoepidermal junction, melanin is released and drops into the dermis (pigment incontinence), where it is engulfed by melanophages to give a deeper, longer-lasting dermal hyperpigmentation. The depth of pigment therefore reflects the intensity and level of the preceding inflammatory process. Epidermal post-inflammatory pigment usually fades gradually over months once the inflammation is controlled, whereas dermal pigment may persist for years or be effectively permanent; darker skin phototypes tend to have slower resolution.

Postpartum depression generally responds well to treatment, and most women recover, but there is an increased risk of recurrence in subsequent pregnancies and of future depressive episodes. Prognosis is better with early detection, treatment, and social support, and worse when the condition is unrecognised, when there is a bipolar diathesis, or when comorbidities and psychosocial adversity persist.

Postpartum haemorrhage — postpartum hemorrhage, PPH, obstetric haemorrhage after delivery Uterine atony Genital tract trauma including cervical or vaginal lacerations and haematomas Retained placenta slowly to mechanical and surgical measures when medical therapy fails Normal postpartum haemostasis depends on vigorous myometrial contraction that mechanically compresses the spiral arteries of the placental bed, supported by the clotting cascade. Postpartum haemorrhage results when one or more of these mechanisms fail: the uterus fails to contract (atony, often from overdistension, prolonged or augmented labour, infection, or retained tissue); vessels are torn by genital tract trauma; retained placental tissue or invasive placentation prevents effective contraction; or coagulation is impaired by dilution, consumption, or a pre-existing disorder. Ongoing loss can precipitate hypovolaemic shock and a self-perpetuating coagulopathy. With prompt recognition, resuscitation, and stepwise treatment most women recover fully. Delay in diagnosis or treatment can lead to shock, organ failure, need for hysterectomy with loss of fertility, and death; postpartum haemorrhage remains one of the leading causes of maternal mortality worldwide, particularly in low-resource settings.

Postpartum thyroiditis — postpartum thyroid dysfunction Graves disease presenting postpartum Silent (painless) thyroiditis unrelated to pregnancy Normal postpartum fatigue or postnatal depression Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis Sheehan syndrome (for postpartum hypothyroid symptoms) Thyroid function tests across the phases Thyroid peroxidase antibodies Radioactive iodine uptake if Graves disease must be excluded (avoiding breastfeeding considerations) Follow-up thyroid function to detect permanent hypothyroidism Screening in subsequent pregnancies given recurrence risk A painless autoimmune destructive thyroiditis occurring within about a year of delivery (or miscarriage) It classically follows a triphasic course of thyrotoxicosis, then hypothyroidism, then recovery, though many present with only one phase It is strongly associated with thyroid peroxidase antibodies detectable before or during pregnancy The thyrotoxic phase is destructive with low radioactive iodine uptake, distinguishing it from Graves disease Symptoms are easily mistaken for normal postpartum fatigue or postnatal depression A significant proportion develop permanent hypothyroidism and it tends to recur after future pregnancies Features suggesting Graves disease Symptoms mislabelled as postnatal depression Persistent hypothyroidism affecting the mother and breastfeeding Severe thyrotoxic symptoms Attributing symptoms to normal postpartum tiredness or depression Treating the thyrotoxic phase with antithyroid drugs Confusing it with Graves disease and giving radioactive iodine Not arranging follow-up for permanent hypothyroidism Postpartum thyroiditis is an autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis unmasked by the immune rebound that follows the relative immunosuppression of pregnancy. Immune-mediated destruction of thyroid follicles releases stored hormone, causing a transient thyrotoxic phase, after which hormone depletion produces hypothyroidism before the gland usually recovers. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies mark the underlying autoimmunity and predict risk. As a destructive process, radioactive iodine uptake is low and antithyroid drugs are unhelpful. Most women return to euthyroidism within a year, but many develop permanent hypothyroidism over subsequent years, and the condition frequently recurs after later pregnancies.

eating Recurrent syncope causing injury Postprandial angina or evidence of cardiac ischaemia Marked coexisting orthostatic hypotension suggesting autonomic failure Neurological features suggesting an underlying synucleinopathy Overlooking meals as the trigger for falls or syncope in older patients Timing antihypertensive medication so that its peak effect coincides with the postprandial fall Failing to look for coexisting orthostatic hypotension Attributing symptoms solely to hypoglycaemia without measuring blood pressure After a meal, blood pools in the splanchnic circulation as digestion increases mesenteric blood flow, and vasoactive gastrointestinal peptides promote splanchnic vasodilatation. In a healthy person the baroreflex compensates through increased sympathetic outflow, vasoconstriction elsewhere, and a modest rise in heart rate, keeping blood pressure stable. In postprandial hypotension this compensation is inadequate, typically because of impaired baroreflex or sympathetic function as in autonomic failure, ageing, diabetes, or Parkinson disease, so that splanchnic pooling causes a sustained fall in blood pressure. Rapid gastric emptying and carbohydrate-rich meals, which accelerate the insulin and gut-peptide response, exaggerate the effect. Postprandial hypotension is usually manageable with dietary and behavioural measures, but in frail older people and those with autonomic failure it is an important, sometimes recurrent cause of falls, syncope, and reduced quality of life.

poststeroid panniculitis — post-steroid panniculitis, corticosteroid-withdrawal panniculitis erythema nodosum subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn (in infants) infective panniculitis relapse of the underlying inflammatory or neoplastic disease with cutaneous involvement lupus panniculitis traumatic panniculitis cold panniculitis deep skin biopsy for histopathology (needle-shaped crystal clefts, lobular granulomatous panniculitis) review of the corticosteroid tapering schedule and timing relative to lesion onset serum calcium to exclude associated hypercalcaemia inflammatory markers and cultures to exclude infection assessment for relapse of the primary disease that prompted corticosteroid use full blood count and metabolic panel A rare lobular panniculitis that develops after rapid reduction or withdrawal of high-dose systemic corticosteroids, most often described in children. Firm, tender subcutaneous nodules and plaques appear typically within days to a few weeks of dose reduction. Lesions favour sites where corticosteroid-induced fat had accumulated, notably the cheeks, and may also affect the trunk and proximal limbs. The classic history is a child treated with high-dose corticosteroids (for example for rheumatic or neoplastic disease) whose therapy is tapered too quickly. Histology closely resembles subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn, with needle-shaped crystal clefts within adipocytes and a granulomatous, lipophagic infiltrate. The eruption is generally self-limiting and resolves over weeks to months without specific treatment. Reinstituting corticosteroids and then tapering more gradually may hasten resolution in symptomatic cases. Recognition avoids unnecessary investigation for infection or relapse of the underlying disease. features suggesting infection (fever, fluctuance, systemic upset) rather than sterile panniculitis hypercalcaemia analogous to that seen in neonatal fat necrosis signs of relapse of the underlying disease requiring corticosteroid reinstatement extensive or ulcerating lesions Mistaking the nodules for infection or for relapse of the treated disease and escalating therapy inappropriately. Failing to link lesion onset to a recent corticosteroid taper. Overlooking possible hypercalcaemia given the histological similarity to neonatal fat necrosis. Sampling too superficially to capture the diagnostic lobular fat changes. Reintroducing corticosteroids without then planning a slower taper. During high-dose corticosteroid therapy, lipid composition of subcutaneous fat shifts towards a higher proportion of saturated fatty acids with a raised melting point, and corticosteroids promote redistribution and accumulation of fat at characteristic sites. When corticosteroids are abruptly withdrawn, the altered, saturated-fat-rich adipose tissue is prone to crystallisation and necrosis. Liberated fatty acids provoke a lobular, lipophagic granulomatous inflammatory reaction, and histology reveals radial needle-shaped crystal clefts within adipocytes and giant cells, closely mirroring subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn. Gradual tapering allows the fat composition to normalise and prevents the crystallisation that underlies the panniculitis. The condition is benign and self-limiting, resolving spontaneously over weeks to months, particularly when corticosteroids are tapered more gradually.

Post-streptococcal Glomerulonephritis — PSGN, acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, APSGN, acute post-infectious glomerulonephritis IgA nephropathy Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Lupus nephritis Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) nephritis Haemolytic uraemic syndrome Alport syndrome or thin basement membrane disease Serum complement C3 (and C4) with follow-up to document normalisation Antistreptococcal serology (ASO, anti-DNase B) or streptozyme panel Throat or skin swab and culture if active infection present Urinalysis with microscopy for red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells Serum urea, creatinine, and electrolytes to assess renal function Renal biopsy only in atypical or progressive cases A classic cause of acute nephritic syndrome in children, most often between about 5 and 12 years of age. Follows infection with specific nephritogenic strains of group A streptococcus, typically 1-2 weeks after pharyngitis or 3-6 weeks after skin infection. Presents with the nephritic picture of haematuria (often cola- or tea-coloured urine), oedema, hypertension, and variable reduction in urine output. Complement C3 is characteristically low and typically returns to normal within about 6-8 weeks; persistently low C3 beyond this window suggests another diagnosis. Evidence of preceding streptococcal infection is supported by elevated or rising antistreptococcal antibodies such as ASO or anti-DNase B. Management is largely supportive, centred on salt and fluid restriction and control of hypertension and fluid overload. Antibiotics treat any active streptococcal infection but do not alter the course of the established nephritis. Renal biopsy is usually unnecessary and reserved for atypical features such as persistent low complement, progressive kidney failure, or nephrotic-range proteinuria. The prognosis in children is excellent, with the large majority recovering complete renal function. Severe or refractory hypertension, including hypertensive encephalopathy Rapidly rising creatinine suggesting rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis Pulmonary oedema or heart failure from fluid overload Marked oliguria or anuria Persistently low complement or nephrotic-range proteinuria indicating an alternative diagnosis Attributing every child with haematuria and low C3 to PSGN without follow-up complement testing Overlooking hypertensive complications by not monitoring blood pressure closely Failing to consider alternative glomerulonephritides when complement stays low beyond eight weeks Aggressive fluid administration worsening volume overload in an oliguric child Infection with nephritogenic strains of group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus triggers an immune-complex-mediated glomerular injury. Streptococcal antigens (such as nephritis-associated plasmin receptor and streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B) deposit in the glomeruli and, together with circulating and in situ immune complexes, activate the complement system, predominantly via the alternative pathway. The resulting inflammation causes endocapillary proliferation and neutrophil infiltration, reducing glomerular filtration and producing sodium and water retention, which manifests as haematuria, oedema, and hypertension. Most children recover fully; acute complications resolve over days to weeks, complement normalises within about two months, and microscopic haematuria may persist for up to a year with an excellent long-term outlook.

Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) — POTS, postural tachycardia syndrome, chronic orthostatic intolerance Orthostatic hypotension due to autonomic failure Inappropriate sinus tachycardia Anxiety or panic disorder Thyrotoxicosis Phaeochromocytoma Dehydration or anaemia Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia Active-stand (lying-to-standing) test with serial heart rate and blood pressure over ten minutes Head-up tilt-table testing where the active-stand test is equivocal Full blood count and thyroid function to exclude anaemia and thyrotoxicosis Supine and standing plasma catecholamines when a hyperadrenergic subtype is suspected Ambulatory ECG monitoring to exclude a primary arrhythmia Autonomic function testing including QSART where available Defined by a sustained rise in heart rate of at least 30 beats per minute (40 in adolescents) within ten minutes of standing or head-up tilt, without a significant fall in blood pressure Symptoms of orthostatic intolerance include palpitations, light-headedness, tremulousness, blurred vision, fatigue, and cognitive 'brain fog', all relieved by lying down Predominantly affects young women and frequently follows a viral illness, pregnancy, surgery, or trauma Commonly overlaps with chronic fatigue, fibromyalgia, migraine, joint hypermobility (Ehlers-Danlos type), and gastrointestinal dysmotility Recognised subtypes include hypovolaemic, neuropathic (partial dysautonomic), and hyperadrenergic forms that may coexist An active-stand (lying-to-standing) test and head-up tilt confirm the heart-rate criterion; a symptomatic orthostatic tachycardia sustained over the recording period is required Deconditioning perpetuates the syndrome, so prolonged bed rest should be avoided Management is primarily non-pharmacological: volume and salt expansion, compression garments, physical counter-manoeuvres, graded exercise reconditioning, and avoidance of triggers Syncope on exertion or causing injury, suggesting a cardiac cause A significant orthostatic fall in blood pressure indicating autonomic failure rather than POTS Features of phaeochromocytoma such as paroxysmal hypertension, headache, and sweating Progressive neurological signs suggesting a wider autonomic neuropathy Mislabelling the orthostatic tachycardia as anxiety and overlooking the reproducible heart-rate criterion Diagnosing POTS when an orthostatic fall in blood pressure actually indicates orthostatic hypotension Failing to exclude dehydration, anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, or medication effects before making the diagnosis Recommending prolonged rest, which worsens deconditioning and perpetuates symptoms Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome is a heterogeneous disorder of orthostatic intolerance in which assuming an upright posture provokes an exaggerated compensatory rise in heart rate without orthostatic hypotension. Several mechanisms may act, often in combination: reduced circulating blood volume, excessive venous pooling in the lower limbs and splanchnic bed, a partial peripheral autonomic (small-fibre) neuropathy that limits lower-body vasoconstriction, and a hyperadrenergic state with heightened central sympathetic outflow. Inadequate venous return lowers stroke volume, so heart rate rises steeply to preserve cerebral perfusion, generating the characteristic symptoms. Physical deconditioning and abnormal fluid regulation frequently perpetuate the cycle. Many patients, particularly those with a post-viral onset, improve substantially over months to years with reconditioning and non-pharmacological measures, although a proportion have persistent, disabling symptoms that require long-term multidisciplinary support.

spinal cord compression and requiring urgent evaluation for decompression Bladder or bowel dysfunction suggesting significant cord or cauda involvement Spinal instability or severe progressive kyphotic deformity Large cold abscess with systemic sepsis or rifampicin resistance Attributing chronic back pain to mechanical causes and delaying imaging, allowing deformity and deficit to progress malignant vertebral disease without confirmatory sampling Mycobacterium tuberculosis reaches the vertebral bodies by haematogenous spread, often via the paravertebral venous plexus, lodging in the well-vascularised anterior vertebral body near the endplate. Granulomatous infection with caseous necrosis destroys bone and later the intervertebral disc, and spreads beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament to contiguous vertebrae. Vertebral collapse causes angular kyphosis, while caseous material and pus form cold abscesses that dissect along tissue planes. Neurological compromise arises from mechanical compression of the cord by abscess, inflammatory tissue, bony sequestra or deformity, and occasionally from vascular compromise of the cord. With early diagnosis and prolonged multidrug therapy most patients recover well, and even established neurological deficits often improve substantially with treatment and timely surgery; delayed presentation with severe deformity or long-standing cord compression carries a higher risk of permanent disability.

Powassan virus encephalitis — Powassan virus infection, POWV infection, deer tick virus infection, Powassan encephalitis Herpes simplex virus encephalitis West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease Eastern equine encephalitis Lyme neuroborreliosis Bacterial meningoencephalitis Autoimmune encephalitis Serum and cerebrospinal fluid IgM serology for Powassan virus Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showing lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain for deep grey-matter, brainstem, and cerebellar involvement RT-PCR on cerebrospinal fluid or blood early in disease, recognising limited sensitivity Testing for co-transmitted Ixodes-borne infections such as Lyme disease, anaplasmosis, and babesiosis Testing to exclude herpes simplex encephalitis A North American and Russian Far East flavivirus in the tick-borne encephalitis serocomplex, transmitted by Ixodes ticks, with the deer-tick lineage sharing the vector of Lyme disease Transmission can occur very rapidly after tick attachment, often within minutes to hours, unlike the longer attachment needed to transmit Lyme borreliosis Many infections are asymptomatic, but neuroinvasive disease presents with encephalitis, meningitis, or meningoencephalitis, sometimes after a nonspecific febrile prodrome Magnetic resonance imaging may show involvement of the thalami, basal ganglia, brainstem, and cerebellum, similar to other tick-borne encephalitis serocomplex viruses Because it shares the Ixodes vector, co-infection with Lyme disease, anaplasmosis, or babesiosis should be considered There is no specific antiviral or licensed vaccine; management is intensive supportive care, and prevention relies on tick-bite avoidance Diagnosis is primarily serological (IgM in serum and cerebrospinal fluid), as viraemia is often brief by the time neurological disease appears Declining consciousness or coma Seizures or status epilepticus Brainstem or cerebellar signs Focal neurological deficits with characteristic deep grey-matter lesions on imaging Respiratory compromise from brainstem involvement Assuming prolonged tick attachment is required, since Powassan virus can transmit rapidly Delaying empirical aciclovir for possible herpes simplex encephalitis pending arboviral results Failing to test for co-infecting Ixodes-borne pathogens Relying on molecular testing when serology is usually the diagnostic modality Overlooking the tick-exposure history in endemic areas Powassan virus is inoculated during the bite of an infected Ixodes tick, and its presence in tick salivary glands allows unusually rapid transmission. After local replication and viraemia, which frequently produces only mild or unnoticed symptoms, the virus can cross into the central nervous system in susceptible hosts. There it infects neurons and triggers an inflammatory response, with a predilection for deep grey-matter structures, brainstem, and cerebellum, causing encephalitis with the potential for severe neuronal injury and lasting deficits. As with related flaviviruses, the antibody response is usually detectable by the neurological phase, underpinning serological diagnosis. Neuroinvasive Powassan virus disease carries appreciable mortality, and a large proportion of survivors are left with long-term neurological sequelae such as cognitive impairment, weakness, or recurrent headaches.

without typical pain Scoliosis and respiratory compromise requiring surveillance Attributing neonatal hypotonia to birth injury or a primary neuromuscular disorder and delaying methylation testing Underestimating the intensity of environmental food control required Missing hypogonadism and osteoporosis risk in adolescents and adults Overlooking central adrenal insufficiency and sleep apnoea Prader-Willi syndrome arises from loss of function of paternally expressed, imprinted genes in the 15q11-q13 region. Because maternal copies of these genes are normally silenced by imprinting, absence of the paternal contribution leaves the region functionally inactive. This most commonly results from a de novo paternal deletion, and less commonly from maternal uniparental disomy (two maternal copies and no paternal copy) or an imprinting defect. Hypothalamic dysfunction is central to the phenotype, driving the abnormal satiety regulation and hyperphagia, growth hormone deficiency, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and temperature and sleep disturbances. With rigorous dietary control, a structured food-secure environment, and growth hormone therapy, individuals can achieve improved health and function; without weight control, morbid obesity substantially shortens life expectancy.

Precocious Puberty — sexual precocity, central precocious puberty, peripheral precocious puberty, early puberty Premature thelarche (benign isolated breast development) Premature adrenarche (early pubic/axillary hair without other puberty) Congenital adrenal hyperplasia Gonadal or adrenal tumour McCune-Albright syndrome CNS lesion (hamartoma, tumour, prior irradiation, or injury) Exogenous sex steroid exposure Bone age radiograph Basal and GnRH-stimulated LH and FSH Sex steroid levels (oestradiol or testosterone) Adrenal androgens and 17-hydroxyprogesterone when a peripheral cause is suspected Pelvic ultrasound in girls to assess ovarian and uterine development MRI of the brain, particularly in boys or where a central lesion is suspected Precocious puberty is conventionally defined as the onset of secondary sexual characteristics before about 8 years in girls and 9 years in boys. It is broadly classified as central (gonadotropin-dependent, from early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis) or peripheral (gonadotropin-independent, from sex steroids produced outside the normal axis). Central precocious puberty is far more common in girls and is usually idiopathic, whereas in boys an underlying CNS lesion is more likely and must be excluded. Accelerated linear growth and advanced bone age are typical; paradoxically, premature epiphyseal fusion can compromise final adult height. A GnRH (or GnRH-agonist) stimulation test helps distinguish central from peripheral causes by assessing the gonadotropin response. Isolated premature thelarche or premature adrenarche are usually benign normal variants but should be monitored to ensure they are not the start of true precocity. Peripheral causes include congenital adrenal hyperplasia, gonadal or adrenal tumours, McCune-Albright syndrome, and exogenous sex steroid exposure. Beyond physical changes, early puberty can carry psychosocial consequences that warrant support for the child and family. Neurological signs, headaches, or visual disturbance suggesting an intracranial lesion Rapidly progressive virilisation or a palpable abdominal/gonadal mass suggesting a hormone-secreting tumour Precocious puberty in a boy, which more often has a serious underlying cause Very early or rapidly advancing puberty threatening severe height compromise Cafe-au-lait macules with bony abnormalities suggesting McCune-Albright syndrome Assuming precocious puberty is idiopathic in a boy without imaging to exclude a CNS lesion Confusing benign premature thelarche or adrenarche with true central precocity Overlooking the impact of advanced bone age on final adult height Neglecting the psychosocial needs of a child developing ahead of peers In central precocious puberty the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis reactivates prematurely, with pulsatile GnRH secretion stimulating pituitary gonadotropins and subsequent gonadal sex steroid production, reproducing normal but early puberty. In peripheral precocious puberty sex steroids arise independently of GnRH from the gonads, adrenals, tumours, or exogenous sources, producing secondary sexual characteristics without central axis activation. Sex steroids accelerate growth and skeletal maturation, so advanced bone age can ultimately limit final height. Idiopathic central precocious puberty generally has a good outcome, and appropriate treatment can preserve growth potential and address psychosocial concerns; prognosis in secondary forms depends on the underlying cause, such as a CNS lesion or hormone-secreting tumour.

Pre-eclampsia — preeclampsia, pre-eclampsia, PET, pregnancy-induced hypertension with proteinuria, gestational proteinuric hypertension Chronic (pre-existing) hypertension Gestational hypertension without organ involvement Chronic kidney disease with proteinuria Acute fatty liver of pregnancy Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or haemolytic uraemic syndrome Systemic lupus erythematosus flare Serial blood pressure measurement and urine protein quantification (protein:creatinine ratio or 24-hour collection) Full blood count for thrombocytopenia and evidence of haemolysis Liver transaminases and lactate dehydrogenase Renal function including serum creatinine and urate Angiogenic markers (sFlt-1/PlGF ratio) where available to aid risk stratification Fetal assessment with ultrasound growth, amniotic fluid volume, and umbilical artery Doppler Defined by new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks' gestation combined with proteinuria or evidence of maternal organ dysfunction (renal, hepatic, neurological, haematological) or uteroplacental compromise Proteinuria is no longer mandatory for diagnosis when hypertension is accompanied by features such as thrombocytopenia, raised transaminases, renal impairment, pulmonary oedema, or cerebral/visual symptoms Warning symptoms include persistent severe headache, visual disturbance (flashing lights, blurring), right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, and rapid oedema of the face and hands HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) is a severe variant that can occur with only modest blood pressure elevation Definitive treatment is delivery of the placenta; timing balances gestational age against maternal and fetal risk Magnesium sulfate is used for seizure prophylaxis in severe disease and to treat eclamptic seizures, not as an antihypertensive Antihypertensive therapy aims to lower dangerously high blood pressure to reduce maternal stroke risk while preserving placental perfusion Low-dose aspirin from early pregnancy reduces incidence in women at high risk (prior pre-eclampsia, chronic hypertension, renal disease, diabetes, multiple pregnancy, antiphospholipid syndrome) Severe hypertension unresponsive to treatment threatening maternal stroke Neurological signs (severe headache, visual loss, hyperreflexia with clonus) heralding impending eclampsia Right upper quadrant pain with abnormal liver enzymes suggesting HELLP or hepatic haematoma/rupture Pulmonary oedema or oliguria indicating organ failure Fetal growth restriction with abnormal Dopplers or non-reassuring fetal status Excluding the diagnosis because proteinuria is absent despite organ dysfunction Underestimating severity in HELLP syndrome where blood pressure may be only mildly raised Over-aggressive blood pressure lowering compromising placental perfusion Failing to continue monitoring postpartum, when eclampsia and severe hypertension can still occur Treating magnesium sulfate as an antihypertensive rather than as seizure prophylaxis Pre-eclampsia originates in abnormal placentation: inadequate remodelling of the maternal spiral arteries by trophoblast leads to a poorly perfused, ischaemic placenta. The ischaemic placenta releases anti-angiogenic factors (such as soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 and soluble endoglin) that antagonise vascular endothelial and placental growth factors, producing widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction. This causes vasospasm, increased vascular permeability, activation of coagulation, and multi-organ hypoperfusion, manifesting as hypertension, proteinuria, hepatic and cerebral involvement, and fetal growth restriction. With timely surveillance, blood pressure control, seizure prophylaxis, and appropriately timed delivery most women recover fully postpartum, though there is an increased lifetime risk of cardiovascular and renal disease. Severe or early-onset disease carries higher maternal and perinatal morbidity, and recurrence in future pregnancies is common.

Impaired perfusion causes bone death, and with continued loading the necrotic scaphoid can fragment and collapse, altering carpal mechanics and leading to degenerative wrist arthritis. Systemic risk factors for osteonecrosis contribute in some cases, while others remain idiopathic. Outcomes vary; early disease may stabilise with conservative treatment or revascularisation, but progressive collapse leads to arthritis that may require salvage surgery.
