reproductive (PCOS) risks Over-investigating mild, slowly progressive, isolated pubic hair development Adrenarche is the maturation of the adrenal zona reticularis and the associated increase in adrenal androgen secretion (especially DHEAS) that normally precedes gonadal puberty. In premature adrenarche this process begins early, producing androgen-dependent signs such as sexual hair and body odour while the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis remains quiescent, so gonadal maturation does not occur. The adrenal androgens are relatively weak and produced in modest amounts, which is why bone maturation and growth are usually little affected. The trigger for early adrenal maturation is incompletely understood but is linked in some children to insulin resistance and higher body weight, factors that also connect premature adrenarche with later polycystic ovary syndrome. Isolated premature adrenarche is usually benign with a normal adult height and pubertal course; the principal longer-term consideration is an increased risk of insulin resistance and polycystic ovary syndrome in a subset of girls, which merits metabolic awareness.

Premature ejaculation — PE, early ejaculation, rapid ejaculation Erectile dysfunction with compensatory rapid ejaculation Chronic prostatitis or pelvic pain contributing to ejaculatory symptoms Hyperthyroidism Performance anxiety and situational sexual dysfunction Relationship or psychosexual conflict Substance or medication effects Focused sexual and psychosocial history distinguishing lifelong from acquired patterns Assessment of erectile function to identify coexisting erectile dysfunction Thyroid function testing when an endocrine cause is suspected Evaluation for prostatitis or lower urinary tract symptoms where indicated Screening for depression, anxiety, and relationship stressors Premature ejaculation is the most common male sexual complaint and is defined by ejaculation occurring sooner than desired, with a perceived inability to delay it and associated distress It is classified as lifelong (present since first sexual experiences) or acquired (developing later after a period of normal control), which guides evaluation and management Diagnosis is clinical and rests on the history; the intravaginal ejaculatory latency time and degree of control, distress, and interpersonal difficulty frame the assessment Acquired cases warrant a search for contributing conditions such as erectile dysfunction, thyroid dysfunction, prostatitis, or psychological stressors Erectile dysfunction and premature ejaculation frequently coexist, and treating the erectile problem first may resolve the ejaculatory complaint Behavioural techniques such as the stop-start and squeeze methods can improve ejaculatory control, often combined with partner involvement and counselling Pharmacological options work by delaying the ejaculatory reflex, and topical desensitising agents or centrally acting serotonergic medication are used according to principle rather than fixed dosing A collaborative, non-judgemental approach that addresses relationship and psychological factors improves outcomes Sudden acquired premature ejaculation with erectile dysfunction, which may signal underlying vascular or endocrine disease Associated pelvic or perineal pain suggesting prostatitis Significant psychological distress, relationship breakdown, or depression Symptoms of thyrotoxicosis accompanying new-onset ejaculatory change Treating premature ejaculation in isolation while missing coexisting erectile dysfunction Neglecting the partner and relationship dimension, which strongly influences distress and outcome Overlooking treatable contributors such as thyroid disease or prostatitis in acquired cases Framing the problem as purely psychological when a neurobiological basis is likely in lifelong disease Ejaculation is a spinal reflex coordinated by sympathetic, parasympathetic, and somatic pathways and modulated by supraspinal serotonergic centres. Serotonin (5-HT) generally raises the ejaculatory threshold, and variation in central serotonergic tone and receptor sensitivity is thought to underlie lifelong premature ejaculation, giving it a substantial neurobiological and genetic basis. Acquired premature ejaculation is more often secondary, arising from erectile dysfunction (where a man rushes before losing his erection), prostatic or thyroid disease, or psychological factors such as anxiety and performance pressure that heighten sympathetic arousal and shorten latency. Premature ejaculation responds well to a combination of behavioural therapy, pharmacological delay of the reflex, and treatment of any coexisting condition, though lifelong forms may require ongoing management to maintain control.

development Neglecting to check for exogenous oestrogen exposure Relying on a single assessment rather than tracking the trajectory over time Premature thelarche is believed to result from transient or mildly increased oestrogen exposure of the breast tissue, without sustained activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Proposed mechanisms include small self-limited ovarian follicular cysts, intermittent low-level gonadotropin secretion characteristic of early childhood, or heightened breast tissue sensitivity to circulating oestrogen. Because the axis is not persistently activated, other oestrogen-dependent changes such as accelerated growth, bone-age advancement, and uterine maturation do not develop, and the breast tissue often regresses. The condition is therefore a benign variant rather than true puberty, distinguished from central precocious puberty by its lack of progression and normal skeletal maturation. Excellent, as the condition is self-limited and does not affect growth, bone maturation, or eventual pubertal timing and fertility; a minority of girls later develop true precocious puberty, which is why continued observation is worthwhile.

Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm — PVCs, Ventricular premature complexes, Ventricular ectopy, Nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, NSVT, Accelerated idioventricular rhythm, AIVR Idiopathic outflow-tract or fascicular ventricular arrhythmia (benign) Papillary muscle ectopy associated with mitral valve prolapse and mitral annular disjunction Sustained monomorphic VT (must be distinguished from NSVT by duration and hemodynamic impact) Supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction (wide-complex differential) Genetic arrhythmia syndromes: long QT, Brugada, short QT, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 12-lead ECG in sinus rhythm (benign idiopathic arrhythmia usually shows a completely normal ECG; any abnormality warrants further workup) Ambulatory/telemetry monitoring to quantify PVC burden and capture NSVT Transthoracic echocardiography to assess ventricular function, wall-motion abnormalities, and valvular disease Contrast-enhanced cardiac MRI to detect scar and late gadolinium enhancement suggesting underlying cardiomyopathy Exercise stress testing for effort-related symptoms or coronary risk Assessment of electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) during acute illness Family history evaluation and consideration of genetic syndromes when a family history of sudden death exists Electrolyte abnormality (especially hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia) provoking ectopy Stimulant or adrenergic effect (caffeine, alcohol, sympathomimetics) Myocardial ischemia presenting as new ventricular ectopy Drug or toxic effect on conduction (e.g., sodium-channel-blocking agents producing slowed, wide QRS rhythms) Ventricular ectopy spanning PVCs, nonsustained VT (NSVT), and accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR) is very common and is most often asymptomatic, detected incidentally on telemetry or prompted by palpitations. A PVC is a single ventricular beat occurring earlier than the next expected supraventricular beat; PVCs from one focus share an identical QRS morphology (unifocal), while differing morphologies indicate multifocal origin and raise suspicion for structural or myopathic disease. Two consecutive ventricular beats form a couplet; three or more consecutive beats above 100/min define VT, and VT terminating spontaneously within 30 seconds is termed nonsustained. QRS morphology localizes the focus: a dominant S wave in V1 (left bundle branch block-like) points to the right ventricle or septum, whereas a dominant R wave in V1 (right bundle branch block-like) points to the left ventricle; the frontal-plane axis distinguishes superior (inferior-wall) versus cranial origin. Most ventricular arrhythmias without structural disease have a left bundle branch block-like pattern, while a right bundle branch block configuration or multiple PVC morphologies more often signal structural heart disease. Idiopathic ectopy commonly arises from the right or left ventricular outflow tracts near the valve annuli, and also from papillary muscles and fascicular tissue; benign idiopathic NSVT is usually monomorphic with rates under 200/min. Bigeminy (every other beat a PVC) can cause pseudobradycardia because the premature beats may not generate a palpable pulse, so counted rate can read falsely low. In the peri-infarct period, PVCs and NSVT are common early manifestations of ischemia and can herald ventricular fibrillation. AIVR is defined as three or more ventricular beats at a rate slower than 100/min, usually due to enhanced automaticity; it is common during acute MI and may emerge during sinus bradycardia or sleep. Frequent ectopy can itself depress ventricular function (PVC-induced cardiomyopathy), but this rarely occurs unless PVCs account for at least 10-20% of total beats over 24 hours, and only a minority of such patients develop reversible cardiomyopathy. Smooth, sharp QRS deflections of a PVC suggest a focus in relatively normal myocardium, whereas broad notching and slurring suggest a diseased substrate. Recently inflammation has been recognized as contributing to PVC genesis in inflammatory and inherited cardiomyopathies. Syncope or near-syncope, especially without prodrome, during exertion, or with an abnormal ECG or structural heart disease Very rapid or polymorphic NSVT, or a 'short-coupled' first beat occurring before the peak of the T wave Family history of sudden death prompting evaluation for inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy Any abnormality on the 12-lead ECG (Q waves of prior infarction, ventricular hypertrophy, repolarization abnormalities of long QT/Brugada/ARVC) Right bundle branch block-like or multifocal PVC morphology suggesting structural disease Depressed ventricular function with frequent/repetitive ectopy Bigeminal PVCs can produce pseudobradycardia, leading to an erroneously low measured heart rate. Asymptomatic PVCs and NSVT discovered in a hospitalized or acutely ill patient generally do not require specific antiarrhythmic treatment beyond addressing the underlying illness and correcting aggravating factors. Assuming all ventricular ectopy is benign; very rapid, polymorphic, short-coupled, or multifocal patterns and any ECG/structural abnormality demand evaluation for sudden-death risk. Overlooking reversible PVC-induced cardiomyopathy in patients with very frequent ectopy and otherwise unexplained left ventricular dysfunction. Attributing a wide-complex rhythm to VT without distinguishing it from supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy. PVCs arise via enhanced (abnormal) automaticity, triggered activity, or localized reentry. They are frequently sympathetically sensitive and can reflect heightened sympathetic tone, myocardial ischemia, hypoxia, electrolyte disturbances (notably hypokalemia), or underlying structural heart disease. The site of earliest ventricular activation dictates the activation sequence and therefore the QRS morphology, allowing the surface ECG to suggest the anatomic origin and the likelihood of structural disease. In the setting of ischemia or structural disease, PVCs and NSVT can be harbingers of sustained VT or VF. AIVR is typically driven by automaticity, though rare reentrant circuits in diseased myocardium can produce it. PVC-induced ventricular dysfunction is thought to act through a mechanism akin to chronic tachycardia or through ventricular dyssynchrony. PVCs, NSVT, and AIVR are most often benign when they occur in structurally normal hearts with normal ECGs, and idiopathic ectopy generally has excellent long-term arrhythmia-free outcomes (catheter ablation suppresses idiopathic PVCs in roughly 90% of patients). In contrast, the same arrhythmias carry prognostic weight in the presence of structural disease: after MI and in heart failure, frequent (typically >10 PVCs/h), repetitive PVCs, couplets, and NSVT are markers of depressed ventricular function and increased mortality, and they are likewise associated with worse outcomes in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and congenital heart disease with ventricular dysfunction. AIVR is usually well tolerated, though loss of AV synchrony may cause hemodynamic compromise in susceptible patients. Risk is stratified less by ectopy count alone than by context: (1) structurally normal heart with normal ECG and monomorphic NSVT under 200/min - benign/low risk; (2) structural heart disease (post-MI, heart failure, HCM, congenital disease) where greater frequency and complexity (couplets, NSVT) mark more severe disease and higher mortality; (3) high-risk features warranting concern - syncope, very rapid/polymorphic/short-coupled NSVT, multifocal or RBBB-like morphology, abnormal ECG, or family history of sudden death. PVC burden of at least 10-20% of total beats over 24 hours is the threshold associated with potential PVC-induced ventricular dysfunction.

Premenstrual dysphoric disorder — PMDD, severe premenstrual syndrome, premenstrual dysphoria Premenstrual exacerbation of major depressive or anxiety disorder Bipolar affective disorder Thyroid dysfunction Perimenopausal mood symptoms Generalised anxiety disorder Premenstrual syndrome without severe dysphoria Prospective daily symptom diary over at least two menstrual cycles to confirm cyclical timing Mental health assessment to exclude an underlying mood or anxiety disorder Thyroid function testing where clinically indicated Screening for depression severity and suicide risk Review of contraceptive and other medication effects on mood Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is a severe form of premenstrual syndrome dominated by mood symptoms that markedly impair function and relationships The defining feature is the timing: symptoms appear in the luteal phase, remit shortly after menstruation begins, and are absent in the follicular phase Core symptoms include marked irritability, mood lability, depressed mood, anxiety, and a sense of being overwhelmed, alongside physical complaints such as bloating and breast tenderness Diagnosis should be confirmed by prospective daily symptom charting across at least two cycles rather than by retrospective recall alone It must be distinguished from premenstrual exacerbation of an underlying mood or anxiety disorder, which persists throughout the cycle Serotonergic antidepressants are a first-line treatment and can be given continuously or restricted to the luteal phase according to principle Suppressing ovulation, for example with combined hormonal contraception, can relieve symptoms by abolishing the cyclical hormonal trigger Lifestyle measures, cognitive behavioural therapy, and attention to suicide risk during the luteal phase are important adjuncts Suicidal ideation, which may intensify during the luteal phase Symptoms persisting throughout the cycle, suggesting a primary psychiatric disorder rather than PMDD Severe functional impairment or inability to maintain work and relationships Features suggesting bipolar disorder that would alter treatment choice Diagnosing on retrospective history without prospective symptom charting Missing an underlying mood disorder that is merely worsened premenstrually Underestimating luteal-phase suicide risk Attributing all cyclical physical symptoms to PMDD without considering other causes Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is thought to arise from an abnormal central nervous system sensitivity to the normal cyclical fluctuations of ovarian steroids rather than from any abnormal hormone level. Progesterone metabolites such as allopregnanolone, which modulate GABA-A receptor function, and interactions with serotonergic neurotransmission appear central, so susceptible women experience marked mood and behavioural symptoms during the luteal phase when these hormones fluctuate. Because the trigger is ovulatory cycling, symptoms resolve when the cycle ends and can be abolished by suppressing ovulation. The rapid response to serotonergic agents, often faster than in major depression, supports a serotonergic mechanism. With accurate diagnosis and treatment, most women achieve substantial symptom control; symptoms recur if treatment stops while ovulatory cycles continue and typically resolve after the menopause or with sustained ovulation suppression.

Prepatellar bursitis — housemaid's knee, carpet layer's knee, kneecap bursitis, prepatellar bursopathy Septic prepatellar bursitis Knee joint effusion or intra-articular pathology Gout or pseudogout Infrapatellar bursitis (clergyman's knee) Cellulitis of the anterior knee Patellar fracture or contusion Bursal aspiration for cell count, Gram stain and culture Polarised light microscopy for crystals Inflammatory markers, with blood cultures if systemically unwell Ultrasound to confirm a superficial bursal collection separate from the joint Plain radiographs if fracture or a foreign body is suspected Swelling over the front of the kneecap from inflammation of the superficial prepatellar bursa Classically related to prolonged or repetitive kneeling, hence 'housemaid's knee' As with the olecranon bursa, the superficial position makes it prone to septic bursitis Distinguishing septic from aseptic bursitis is the priority; warmth, erythema, fever and disproportionate pain suggest infection Aspiration for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystal microscopy guides management when infection is suspected The knee joint itself is usually uninvolved and joint range is typically preserved Aseptic cases are managed with avoidance of kneeling, protection and aspiration if symptomatic, with corticosteroid injection reserved for resistant aseptic cases and avoided when infection is possible Fever, spreading erythema and severe pain suggesting septic bursitis or cellulitis An overlying wound or immunosuppression Features of systemic sepsis A tense joint effusion or inability to bear weight suggesting intra-articular pathology Injecting a potentially infected bursa with corticosteroid Confusing a superficial bursal swelling with a true knee joint effusion Not analysing aspirate when infection is suspected Overlooking a foreign body or penetrating injury The prepatellar bursa lies superficially between the skin and the patella, allowing the skin to glide over the kneecap. Repetitive kneeling, friction or a direct blow provokes inflammation and effusion. Its superficial location makes it vulnerable to inoculation and infection, particularly through breaks in the overlying skin and typically with skin organisms such as staphylococci. Systemic causes such as gout and rheumatoid disease can also inflame the bursa. Because the bursa does not communicate with the knee joint, intra-articular structures are usually spared. Aseptic prepatellar bursitis usually resolves with protection and activity change, recurring if kneeling continues; septic bursitis typically responds to antibiotics and drainage.

Presbycusis — age-related hearing loss, presbyacusis, senile deafness Noise-induced hearing loss Ototoxic drug-induced hearing loss Cerumen impaction or middle ear disease causing conductive loss sensorineural pattern Speech audiometry to assess discrimination and predict hearing aid benefit Tympanometry to exclude a middle ear conductive component Otoscopy to exclude wax impaction and other hearing loss that accompanies ageing and is the commonest cause of hearing loss in older adults It characteristically begins with the high frequencies, so patients first struggle with consonant sounds and with speech in noisy or crowded settings A common complaint is that people can hear that someone is speaking but cannot make out the words, reflecting impaired speech discrimination Tinnitus and facial numbness raising concern for acoustic neuroma Associated neurological signs that point away from simple age-related loss Assuming all hearing loss in the elderly is presbycusis and missing wax, effusion or a tumour Overlooking asymmetry that warrants imaging Neglecting the impact of poor speech discrimination and recruitment on hearing aid success Failing to address modifiable contributors such as ongoing noise exposure and ototoxic medication Presbycusis results from cumulative degenerative changes in the auditory system with age. Several subtypes are described: sensory presbycusis from loss of hair cells in the basal (high-frequency) cochlea; neural presbycusis from loss of spiral ganglion neurons, which particularly impairs speech discrimination; strial or metabolic presbycusis from atrophy of the stria vascularis affecting the endocochlear potential across frequencies; and cochlear conductive (mechanical) presbycusis from stiffening of the basilar membrane. Central auditory pathway changes further degrade processing of speech, especially in noise. Genetic predisposition, lifelong noise exposure, vascular and metabolic disease and ototoxins accelerate these changes. Presbycusis is irreversible and slowly progressive, but most patients maintain good communication and quality of life with hearing aids and rehabilitation, and cochlear implantation can help those with severe loss and poor aided speech understanding.

The vestibular decline itself is not reversible, but rehabilitation, sensory optimisation, and falls-prevention strategies meaningfully reduce instability and injury risk in most older adults.

often combined with shear and friction Common sites include the sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities, greater trochanters, and occiput, reflecting where soft tissue is compressed against bone Staging nutrition Near the end of life, skin failure can occur despite excellent care, and goals may appropriately prioritise comfort over aggressive wound healing Spreading erythema, purulent discharge, or systemic features suggesting wound infection or sepsis Deep wounds exposing bone with suspected underlying osteomyelitis Rapidly deteriorating or new deep-tissue injury indicating ongoing unrelieved pressure Signs of necrotising soft-tissue infection requiring urgent surgical assessment Focusing on dressings while failing to relieve the underlying pressure Neglecting nutrition, which is essential to wound healing Missing deep-tissue injury because early damage lies beneath intact-looking skin Overlooking heels and medical-device-related sites during skin inspection Pursuing aggressive healing goals at the end of life when comfort should take priority Sustained pressure over a bony prominence exceeds capillary closing pressure, obstructing microcirculation and causing local ischaemia. If pressure is not relieved, ischaemia progresses to tissue hypoxia, inflammation, and cell death, with damage often beginning in deeper tissues adjacent to bone before it becomes visible at the surface. Shear forces distort and occlude vessels, and friction and moisture from incontinence weaken the epidermal barrier. Impaired perfusion, undernutrition, reduced sensation, and immobility all lower tissue tolerance and accelerate breakdown. Superficial pressure injuries can heal with consistent offloading and good wound and nutritional care, whereas deep, full-thickness injuries heal slowly and may recur. Pressure injuries are markers of illness severity and are associated with pain, infection, prolonged hospitalisation, and increased mortality, particularly in frail and end-of-life patients in whom prevention and comfort are paramount.

and an external surface. When interface pressure exceeds capillary closing pressure, local ischaemia and impaired lymphatic drainage lead to tissue hypoxia, accumulation of metabolic waste, and cell death. Superficial pressure injuries can heal with conservative care once pressure is relieved, but deep ulcers heal slowly and often require surgery. delivery at a very early gestation Mistaking true preterm labour for Braxton Hicks contractions and delaying steroids Overtreating with tocolytics when there is a contraindication such as chorioamnionitis or significant abruption Failing to give antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium neuroprotection within the appropriate window Not arranging timely transfer to a unit with adequate neonatal facilities Overlooking an underlying infection driving the labour Preterm labour is a syndrome with multiple pathways converging on premature activation of the mechanisms of labour: uterine contractility, cervical ripening, and decidual-membrane activation. Recognised triggers include intrauterine infection and inflammation, uteroplacental ischaemia or haemorrhage (decidual bleeding), excessive uterine distension (as in multiple pregnancy or polyhydramnios), cervical insufficiency, and maternal or fetal stress activating the corticotrophin-releasing hormone axis. Priapism — persistent erection, ischaemic priapism, low-flow priapism, non-ischaemic priapism Ischaemic (low-flow) versus non-ischaemic (high-flow) priapism distinction Stuttering (recurrent) priapism Penile trauma with fistula Drug-induced erection (intracavernosal agents, psychotropics, recreational drugs) Sickle cell disease or other haemoglobinopathy Pelvic or penile malignant infiltration Cavernosal blood gas analysis to differentiate ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism Penile colour Doppler ultrasound to assess cavernosal blood flow and identify a fistula Full blood count and film with haemoglobinopathy screen (sickle cell testing) Toxicology and medication review for causative agents Selective pudendal arteriography if embolisation of a high-flow fistula is planned Priapism is a prolonged penile erection (typically beyond four hours) unrelated to sexual stimulation, and the critical first step is to distinguish ischaemic (low-flow) from non-ischaemic (high-flow) types Ischaemic priapism is a painful, rigid erection representing a compartment syndrome of the corpora cavernosa and is a urological emergency because prolonged ischaemia causes fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction Non-ischaemic (high-flow) priapism is usually painless, semi-rigid, and follows perineal or penile trauma with an arteriolar-sinusoidal fistula; it is not an emergency and often resolves or is managed by embolisation Cavernosal blood gas analysis distinguishes the two: ischaemic blood is dark and hypoxic/acidotic, whereas high-flow blood is bright red with near-arterial values Common causes of ischaemic priapism include sickle cell disease, haematological malignancy, and drugs, notably intracavernosal vasoactive agents and certain psychotropic and recreational drugs Emergency management of ischaemic priapism proceeds stepwise from corporal aspiration and irrigation to intracavernosal sympathomimetic injection, and to surgical shunting if these fail Underlying conditions such as sickle cell disease require concurrent systemic treatment alongside local measures Stuttering (recurrent) priapism, common in sickle cell disease, warrants preventive strategies to reduce recurrent ischaemic episodes Ischaemic priapism is a urological emergency; delay leads to corporal fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction A rigid, painful erection persisting beyond four hours Underlying sickle cell crisis or haematological malignancy requiring urgent systemic treatment Failure of aspiration and intracavernosal therapy, mandating urgent surgical shunting Failing to distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism before treatment, leading to inappropriate management Delaying emergency intervention in ischaemic priapism and risking irreversible fibrosis Overlooking an underlying cause such as sickle cell disease or a causative medication Treating high-flow priapism as an emergency with aggressive corporal procedures Neglecting preventive management of recurrent stuttering priapism Priapism reflects a disturbance of the normal mechanisms that terminate erection. In ischaemic (low-flow) priapism, veno-occlusion persists so blood becomes trapped in the corpora cavernosa, producing stagnant, hypoxic, acidotic blood and a compartment-syndrome-like state; prolonged ischaemia leads to smooth muscle necrosis and corporal fibrosis. Causes include sickle cell disease and other haemoglobinopathies, leukaemic infiltration, and pharmacological agents. Non-ischaemic (high-flow) priapism results from unregulated arterial inflow, typically through a cavernosal artery fistula created by perineal or penile trauma, so oxygenation is maintained and tissue ischaemia does not occur. Prompt relief of ischaemic priapism improves the chance of preserved erectile function, but episodes lasting many hours frequently result in fibrosis and long-term erectile dysfunction; non-ischaemic priapism has a benign course and often resolves spontaneously or after embolisation.

Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System — Brain tumors, CNS tumors, Intracranial neoplasms, Glioma, Glioblastoma, Meningioma, Brain metastases, Leptomeningeal metastases, Epidural spinal cord compression High-grade glioma (glioblastoma, IDH wild-type) Low-grade IDH-mutant astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma Meningioma vs dural metastasis vs dural lymphoma Primary CNS lymphoma vs metastasis vs infection Vestibular schwannoma vs cerebellopontine-angle meningioma Brain metastasis vs primary brain tumor vs second malignancy in a cancer patient Brain abscess Toxoplasmosis (ring-enhancing lesions, especially in immunocompromised, mimicking PCNSL or metastases) Epidural abscess (mimicking epidural tumor) Subacute/chronic meningitis (leptomeningeal lymphoma can present this way) Gadolinium-enhanced cranial MRI (preferred for all suspected brain tumors); CT only if MRI not possible FLAIR sequences to detect non-enhancing low-grade glioma and infiltrative disease Functional MRI for presurgical mapping of eloquent cortex PET, MR perfusion, and MR spectroscopy to assess metabolic activity and help distinguish tumor progression from treatment-related necrosis Molecular/integrated histopathologic testing (IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT promoter methylation, H3 status, etc.) for classification and prognosis Stereotactic biopsy for histologic diagnosis of PCNSL (withhold glucocorticoids until biopsy where possible, as they are cytolytic to lymphoma) CSF cytology and flow cytometry for leptomeningeal and primary CNS lymphoma; HIV testing and EBV DNA in immunocompromised PCNSL Whole-spine MRI (or CT myelography if MRI impossible) for suspected epidural cord compression Demyelinating lesions Sarcoidosis Radiation necrosis in a previously treated patient Cerebral infarction or hemorrhage Migraine (when tumor headache has migrainous features) Depression (apathy/social withdrawal from a frontal tumor) Epidural hematoma, epidural lipomatosis, or extramedullary hematopoiesis (mimicking epidural tumor) Arthritic/degenerative back pain (vs epidural metastasis pain) Brain tumors of any histology tend to present with a mixture of generalized features (headache, nausea/vomiting, cognitive decline, personality change, gait disturbance from raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus) and focal features (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual-field defect) (Harrison 22e p.716). The classic morning-predominant brain tumor headache that eases through the day is actually seen in only a minority of patients; tumor headaches may be holocephalic, ipsilateral to the lesion, or even migraine-like with throbbing pain and scotoma (Harrison 22e p.716). Seizures occur in roughly 25% of patients with brain metastases or malignant gliomas but are the presenting symptom in up to 90% of low-grade gliomas; all tumor-related seizures have a focal onset whether or not that is clinically apparent (Harrison 22e p.716). Contrast (gadolinium) MRI is the preferred diagnostic study; CT is reserved for patients who cannot undergo MRI. Neuroimaging is generally the only test needed to diagnose a brain tumor, and laboratory tests are rarely useful (Harrison 22e p.716). Malignant tumors (primary or metastatic) typically enhance with gadolinium, show central necrosis, and are ringed by white-matter edema, whereas low-grade gliomas usually do NOT enhance and are best seen on FLAIR sequences (Harrison 22e p.716). Meningiomas are dural-based enhancing extra-axial masses with a characteristic dural tail that compress but do not invade brain; their principal differential is a dural metastasis or dural lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.716, p.722). Adult diffuse gliomas are now classified molecularly: IDH-mutant astrocytoma (1p/19q intact), IDH-mutant oligodendroglioma (1p/19q co-deleted), and IDH wild-type glioblastoma; these molecular markers carry major prognostic weight (Harrison 22e p.718-719). An unmethylated MGMT promoter predicts relative temozolomide resistance and a worse glioblastoma prognosis; MGMT promoter hypermethylation (gene silencing) predicts better response (Harrison 22e p.720). Meningiomas are the most common primary brain tumor (~35%), are more common in women and with prior cranial irradiation and NF2, and many are found incidentally; small asymptomatic ones can simply be monitored with serial MRI (Harrison 22e p.721-722). Most brain metastases lodge at the gray-white junction in watershed territories; ~85% are supratentorial and ~15% in the posterior fossa, and distribution roughly mirrors regional blood flow (Harrison 22e p.723). Melanoma has the greatest propensity to seed the brain (found in ~80% at autopsy), but lung and breast carcinomas are the most common sources overall; prostate and breast cancers also favor dural metastases that can mimic meningioma (Harrison 22e p.723). In epidural spinal metastasis, back pain is the presenting symptom in virtually all patients and may precede neurologic signs by weeks to months; the pain characteristically worsens on lying down, in contrast to arthritic pain which eases with recumbency (Harrison 22e p.725). Any cancer patient with severe back pain should undergo whole-spine MRI; plain films, bone scan, or CT may show bony disease but only MRI reliably delineates epidural tumor (Harrison 22e p.725). New focal neurologic deficit (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual-field loss) that is subacute and progressive New-onset focal seizures, especially in an adult without prior epilepsy Severe back pain in a cancer patient (suggests epidural metastasis) — warrants urgent whole-spine MRI Leg weakness, sensory level, or sphincter dysfunction suggesting evolving spinal cord compression (a neuro-oncologic emergency) New limb pain in a patient with breast, lung cancer, or melanoma (consider leptomeningeal spread) Signs of raised intracranial pressure / hydrocephalus (worsening headache, vomiting, declining consciousness) Multilevel neuraxis signs (combined cranial neuropathies plus radiculopathies) suggesting leptomeningeal carcinomatosis Assuming a tumor headache must be morning-predominant — most are not, and tumor headaches can mimic migraine. Misattributing frontal-lobe apathy and withdrawal to primary depression rather than tumor. Giving glucocorticoids before biopsy in suspected PCNSL — their cytolytic effect on lymphoma cells can yield non-diagnostic tissue. Relying on a single CSF cytology in suspected leptomeningeal disease — it is positive in only ~50% on first lumbar puncture and still misses ~10% after three samples; imaging is diagnostic in only ~75%. Forgetting that the smallest brain metastases can produce extensive edema while large ones cause little, and that imaging appearance is nonspecific. Overlooking that ~10% of systemic cancers can first present with a brain metastasis, sometimes requiring biopsy of the brain lesion when no accessible systemic site exists. Treating low-grade glioma as benign — most ultimately transform to higher grade. Delaying spine imaging in a cancer patient with back pain until neurologic deficits appear. Most primary brain tumors have no identified cause; established risk factors are limited to ionizing radiation exposure (meningiomas, gliomas, schwannomas) and immunosuppression (primary CNS lymphoma), while electromagnetic field/cell-phone exposure, head injury, dietary N-nitroso compounds, and occupational factors are not proven. Tumors arise through a multistep accumulation of genetic alterations: loss of tumor-suppressor genes (p53, CDKN2A/B, PTEN) and amplification/overexpression of proto-oncogenes (EGFR, PDGFR), producing uncontrolled growth; many gliomas show marked molecular heterogeneity. The 2016 and 2021 WHO classifications integrate molecular parameters (e.g., IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion, H3 K27/G34 alterations) with histology. Brain metastases spread hematogenously, lodging in terminal arterioles at the gray-white junction; leptomeningeal disease reaches the subarachnoid space via arterial circulation or retrograde venous flow and may also follow resection of a cerebellar metastasis. Epidural cord compression generally results from metastases to the axial skeleton (typically breast and prostate), though lymphoma can invade through an intervertebral foramen without bone destruction (Harrison 22e p.717, p.719, p.723, p.724-725). Outcome is highly histology- and molecular-subtype-dependent. Low-grade IDH-mutant astrocytomas have median survival around 10 years (most eventually transform to higher grade); oligodendrogliomas (1p/19q co-deleted) generally exceed 10 years. Glioblastoma carries a poor prognosis with median survival in the 15-18 month range with combined therapy and ~10% 5-year survival; adverse factors are older age, unmethylated MGMT promoter, poor Karnofsky status, and unresectable tumor. H3 K27-altered diffuse midline glioma has a median survival of roughly 1 year regardless of grade; H3 G34-mutant hemispheric glioma about 18-22 months. Medulloblastoma achieves long-term survival in ~70% but often with neurocognitive cost, varying by molecular subgroup (WNT best; group 3 worst). Completely resected meningiomas and schwannomas can be cured. Brain metastases treated with whole-brain radiotherapy alone yield median survival of only ~4-6 months, though stereotactic radiosurgery achieves local control in 80-90% and occasional cure. Leptomeningeal metastasis is treated palliatively with no curative therapy. In epidural metastasis, patients fare well if treated before a severe deficit develops, but overall survival is often short owing to widespread systemic disease (Harrison 22e p.718-725). Gliomas are graded by the WHO into grades 2-4 (low- vs high-grade) integrating histology with molecular markers (IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion; CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion upgrades an IDH-mutant astrocytoma to grade 4). Meningiomas are WHO grade I (benign), II (atypical), or III (malignant). Brain tumor symptoms are categorized as generalized (raised-ICP related) versus focal/lateralizing. Nervous-system metastatic disease is grouped clinically into intraparenchymal brain metastases, leptomeningeal (carcinomatous meningitis) metastases, and epidural spinal cord compression (Harrison 22e p.716, p.719, p.722).

spares large arteries on angiography Primary angiitis of the central nervous system is an idiopathic inflammatory vasculitis restricted to vessels of the brain, spinal cord, and meninges. Segmental infiltration of small and medium arterial walls by lymphocytes, granulomas, or necrotising inflammation leads to vessel wall thickening, luminal narrowing, and thrombosis, producing progressive multifocal ischaemia and occasionally haemorrhage. Because inflammation is patchy and confined to the CNS, systemic markers are typically unremarkable and diagnosis can be difficult, with progressive rather than reversible arterial narrowing distinguishing it from vasoconstrictive syndromes. Untreated PACNS is often severely disabling or fatal, but many patients stabilise or improve with immunosuppression; relapses occur and outcome depends on prompt diagnosis and treatment.

nausea, and vomiting to a gastrointestinal or neurological cause and missing the ocular emergency Dilating a susceptible shallow-chamber eye and precipitating an acute attack Failing to examine and treat the occludable fellow eye prophylactically Assuming laser iridotomy alone controls pressure when extensive synechial closure or coexisting open-angle damage requires further therapy Overlooking chronic painless angle closure presenting as apparent open-angle glaucoma In primary angle closure the peripheral iris comes into contact with the trabecular meshwork and obstructs aqueous drainage, causing intraocular pressure to rise. The commonest mechanism is relative pupillary block, where resistance to aqueous passing between the lens and iris margin lets pressure build in the posterior chamber, bowing the peripheral iris forward against the angle. Predisposing anatomy includes a shallow anterior chamber, short axial length (hypermetropia), a relatively anterior and thick lens, and a crowded angle; pupillary mid-dilation in dim light or with mydriatics can precipitate acute closure. Sustained apposition damages the trabecular meshwork and may form permanent peripheral anterior synechiae, while a sudden pressure spike causes corneal oedema, iris ischaemia, and optic-nerve injury. Prompt medical pressure reduction followed by laser iridotomy usually aborts an acute attack and prevents recurrence, but delayed treatment can cause permanent optic-nerve damage, peripheral anterior synechiae, cataract, and lasting visual loss. Chronic angle closure carries a substantial risk of progressive glaucomatous field loss if unrecognised.

A central mechanism is the aberrant (ectopic or over-expressed) presence of G-protein-coupled receptors on steroidogenic cells, so that ligands not normally driving cortisol, such as gastric inhibitory polypeptide released after meals, vasopressin, catecholamines or serotonin, inappropriately stimulate steroidogenesis. The condition is usually indolent with benign nodules, and metabolic and cortisol excess can be controlled by unilateral or bilateral adrenalectomy, though bilateral resection commits the patient to lifelong steroid replacement. Long-term outcome is generally good when hypercortisolism is corrected and associated cardiometabolic risk is managed.

sodium-dependent carnitine transporter expressed in heart, muscle, kidney and other tissues, responsible for cellular carnitine uptake and renal tubular reabsorption. Loss of function causes urinary carnitine loss and systemic carnitine depletion, so long-chain fatty acids cannot be shuttled into mitochondria for beta-oxidation because carnitine, the obligatory carrier, is lacking. The resulting energy deficit affects the heart and skeletal muscle, producing cardiomyopathy and myopathy, and impairs hepatic ketogenesis during fasting, causing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia; unlike downstream oxidation defects, the block is due to substrate (carnitine) deficiency rather than a defective enzyme. Prognosis is generally excellent with early diagnosis and consistent carnitine supplementation, which reverses cardiac and muscle disease; the main risks are arrhythmia and sudden death in untreated or non-adherent individuals.

Defective assembly or function of these structures impairs the coordinated beating of respiratory cilia, so mucociliary clearance fails and mucus and bacteria are retained throughout the airways and sinuses. The same defect in embryonic nodal cilia disrupts left-right patterning during development, explaining the frequent situs anomalies, while shared axonemal components account for impaired sperm and fallopian tube function. With early diagnosis and structured airway clearance many patients maintain reasonable lung function into adulthood, but chronic infection can cause progressive bronchiectasis, and outcomes vary with genotype, adherence to therapy, and access to specialist multidisciplinary care.

B-cell neoplasm, usually of diffuse large B-cell type, that arises within and remains confined to the central nervous system and eyes. The malignant cells are typically of activated B-cell origin and characteristically carry mutations activating B-cell receptor and toll-like receptor signalling, such as MYD88 and CD79B. Tumour cells cluster around blood vessels within the brain parenchyma, and how the clone becomes restricted to this immune-privileged site remains incompletely understood. In immunodeficient hosts, impaired surveillance allows Epstein-Barr virus to drive transformation, accounting for the EBV positivity seen in that setting. Untreated disease is rapidly fatal, but high-dose methotrexate-based regimens achieve remission in many patients; older age, poor performance status, and treatment-related neurotoxicity limit long-term outcomes, and relapse is common.

Primary central nervous system vasculitis — Primary angiitis of the central nervous system, PACNS, Primary CNS vasculitis Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome Intracranial atherosclerosis or embolic stroke Secondary CNS involvement by systemic vasculitis or connective tissue disease CNS infection (varicella zoster, tuberculosis, fungal, syphilitic arteritis) Intravascular lymphoma or other neoplastic vasculopathy Cerebral amyloid angiopathy with associated inflammation Moyamoya and other non-inflammatory vasculopathies MRI brain with diffusion and gradient-echo or susceptibility sequences High-resolution vessel-wall MRI to assess mural enhancement Catheter cerebral angiography where medium-vessel disease is suspected Cerebrospinal fluid analysis including cell count, protein, cytology and infection screen Systemic vasculitis and autoimmune serology (ANCA, ANA, complement) to exclude secondary causes Brain and leptomeningeal biopsy in selected cases Screening for infective and neoplastic mimics including varicella zoster PCR Primary CNS vasculitis is an inflammatory vasculopathy confined to the brain, spinal cord and leptomeninges, with no systemic vasculitis. Presentation is typically insidious with headache and cognitive decline, punctuated by multifocal strokes or transient ischaemic events in different vascular territories. Systemic inflammatory markers and ANCA are usually normal or negative, which helps distinguish it from systemic vasculitides. Cerebrospinal fluid commonly shows a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein; a completely normal CSF makes the diagnosis much less likely. Catheter angiography may show alternating stenosis and dilatation ('beading'), but is neither sensitive nor specific and can be normal in small-vessel disease. Brain and leptomeningeal biopsy is the reference standard but has significant sampling error because the disease is patchy. Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome is the key mimic and must be excluded before committing to prolonged immunosuppression. High-resolution vessel-wall MRI showing concentric enhancement can support the diagnosis and help differentiate it from non-inflammatory vasculopathy. Rapidly progressive encephalopathy or reduced consciousness Recurrent multifocal strokes despite treatment Intracranial haemorrhage Spinal cord involvement with evolving myelopathy New seizures with progressive cognitive decline Misdiagnosing reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome as vasculitis and giving unnecessary long-term immunosuppression. Relying on angiographic 'beading' as diagnostic when it is non-specific and often absent in small-vessel disease. Excluding the diagnosis on a single negative biopsy given the patchy distribution of disease. Overlooking infective arteritis, particularly varicella zoster, before starting immunosuppression. Attributing an isolated stroke in a young patient to atherosclerosis without considering CNS vasculitis. Primary CNS vasculitis is characterised by inflammatory infiltration and destruction of the walls of small and medium arteries and veins restricted to the central nervous system. Histology varies from granulomatous inflammation (often with vascular amyloid deposition) to lymphocytic or acute necrotising patterns. The inflammation narrows and occludes vessels, producing ischaemia and infarction, and may weaken walls to cause haemorrhage. The stimulus is unknown and, by definition, there is no systemic vasculitic process; the disease is heterogeneous, affecting different calibre vessels in different patients, which accounts for its variable clinical and radiological picture. Untreated disease can progress to disabling stroke, cognitive impairment or death, but many patients respond to immunosuppression; the granulomatous and small-vessel subtypes may relapse and require prolonged therapy. Early diagnosis and exclusion of mimics substantially improve outcomes.

dermis. In the common keratinic forms (lichen and macular amyloidosis), chronic friction and scratching are thought to cause apoptosis (filamentous degeneration) of basal keratinocytes; the resulting keratin fragments are converted into amyloid within the papillary dermis, which is why the deposits stain for cytokeratins and the disorder is perpetuated by the itch-scratch cycle. Genetic susceptibility, including variants in the oncostatin M receptor (OSMR) and interleukin-31 receptor (IL31RA) in familial disease, contributes in some patients. Nodular amyloidosis differs fundamentally, arising from local production of immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloid by a clonal infiltrate of cutaneous plasma cells. Primary cutaneous amyloidosis is benign and does not itself shorten life, but the keratinic forms tend to be chronic and troublesome because of persistent pruritus. Nodular amyloidosis is usually localised yet requires surveillance, as a minority progress to systemic amyloidosis.

Malignant transformation produces cells that retain a strong cytotoxic phenotype, expressing granule-associated proteins and often CD56, and that infiltrate the epidermis, dermis and subcutis in varying combinations. The disease is typically clinically aggressive with rapid progression and a tendency to disseminate to mucosal and other extranodal sites while often sparing lymph nodes. The prognosis is generally poor with short median survival, though outcomes improve with combination chemotherapy alongside effective antiretroviral therapy and control of the underlying immunodeficiency.

Sustained physical effort raising intrathoracic and intracranial pressure is the trigger, distinct from the brief Valsalva of cough headache. Because the same exertional stress can precipitate serious secondary events, vascular and cardiac causes must be excluded initially. The primary form is benign and frequently self-limiting over months to a few years, often manageable with pre-exercise prophylaxis; prognosis of secondary causes depends on the specific diagnosis.

Primary headache associated with sexual activity — orgasmic headache, pre-orgasmic headache, coital cephalalgia Subarachnoid haemorrhage Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome Cervical or intracranial arterial dissection Primary exercise headache Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis Phaeochromocytoma-related headache Urgent CT of the head and, if non-diagnostic, lumbar puncture for the first severe episode CT or MR angiography and venography for vascular causes MRI of the brain where indicated Repeat vascular imaging if reversible cerebral vasoconstriction is suspected Headache precipitated by sexual activity, occurring either as a dull bilateral ache that builds with arousal or as an explosive headache at orgasm The explosive orgasmic form can be indistinguishable from the thunderclap headache of subarachnoid haemorrhage on first presentation A first or severe episode therefore mandates exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage and other vascular causes Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome is an important cause of recurrent orgasmic thunderclap headache It is more common in men and in people who also have migraine The primary form is often self-limiting but may recur in bouts and can respond to preventive treatment First explosive orgasmic headache (treat as possible subarachnoid haemorrhage) Focal neurological deficit, seizures or reduced consciousness Recurrent thunderclap episodes suggesting vasoconstriction syndrome Neck pain suggesting dissection Assuming a benign cause for a first explosive orgasmic headache without imaging Failing to consider reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome in recurrent cases Overlooking arterial dissection when there is neck pain Not re-evaluating if the headache pattern changes Primary headache associated with sexual activity is linked to the abrupt rises in blood pressure, heart rate and muscular and intracranial pressure that accompany sexual excitement and orgasm, in the absence of a structural lesion. The explosive subtype coincides with the autonomic surge at orgasm. Because the same haemodynamic stress can precipitate aneurysmal rupture or reversible vasoconstriction, secondary causes must be excluded before the primary diagnosis is accepted. Once secondary causes are excluded the primary form is benign and frequently remits over weeks to months, though it may recur; preventive treatment can help during symptomatic bouts.

Primary focal hyperhidrosis — primary hyperhidrosis, focal hyperhidrosis, essential hyperhidrosis, idiopathic hyperhidrosis Secondary generalised hyperhidrosis from systemic disease (thyrotoxicosis, diabetes, phaeochromocytoma) Menopausal or hormonally driven sweating and flushing Drug-induced or withdrawal-related sweating Infection-related or malignancy-related night sweats Gustatory sweating (Frey syndrome) Anxiety and other psychiatric causes of sweating Clinical assessment against diagnostic criteria including symmetry, early onset and cessation during sleep Focused history and examination to exclude features of secondary hyperhidrosis Thyroid function tests and glucose when a systemic cause is suspected Gravimetric or starch-iodine testing to map and quantify affected areas when required Assessment for secondary skin infection such as pitted keratolysis or dermatophytosis Screening for phaeochromocytoma or other endocrine causes if the pattern is generalised or nocturnal Characterised by excessive eccrine sweating beyond physiological needs, focal and symmetrical, most often affecting the palms, soles, axillae and craniofacial skin Onset is usually in childhood or adolescence, and there is frequently a positive family history By definition the excess sweating stops during sleep, a key feature distinguishing it from secondary generalised hyperhidrosis It can cause considerable social, occupational and psychological impairment despite being a benign condition The eccrine glands are structurally normal, and the problem lies in their neural overstimulation rather than in gland pathology Diagnosis is clinical, supported by criteria such as focal symmetrical sweating for at least six months, early onset, family history and cessation during sleep Complications include maceration, secondary bacterial and fungal infection, pitted keratolysis and contact dermatitis Treatment follows a stepwise approach with topical antiperspirants (aluminium salts), iontophoresis for palms and soles, botulinum toxin injections for focal areas, and systemic anticholinergics or surgery in resistant cases Generalised, asymmetrical or night-time sweating suggesting a secondary systemic cause Associated weight loss, fever or lymphadenopathy pointing to infection or malignancy Unilateral sweating raising concern about underlying neurological or thoracic pathology Sudden onset in adulthood without a lifelong history Failing to distinguish primary focal from secondary generalised hyperhidrosis and missing an underlying systemic cause Underestimating the psychosocial burden of a benign condition Escalating to invasive treatment before trialling topical antiperspirants and iontophoresis Overlooking secondary skin infection such as pitted keratolysis Primary focal hyperhidrosis is thought to result from an exaggerated or dysregulated sympathetic response producing excessive cholinergic stimulation of structurally normal eccrine sweat glands. The eccrine glands are innervated by sympathetic fibres that release acetylcholine, and in affected individuals these glands are overstimulated out of proportion to thermoregulatory need, particularly at sites of high eccrine density such as the palms, soles and axillae. The frequent family history suggests a genetic predisposition, and emotional and thermal stimuli often exacerbate the sweating. The cessation of symptoms during sleep reflects the withdrawal of the emotional and cortical drive to sympathetic outflow. Primary focal hyperhidrosis is a benign, chronic condition that often persists for many years but frequently improves with age; quality of life can be substantially restored with appropriate stepwise treatment, and it carries no threat to general health.

Liver enzyme assay on biopsy in selected diagnostic uncertainty Assessment for systemic oxalosis when renal failure is present Primary hyperoxaluria is a group of inherited disorders of glyoxylate metabolism that cause marked overproduction of oxalate by the liver It typically presents with recurrent calcium oxalate kidney stones and nephrocalcinosis, often from childhood, and can progress to renal failure Type 1, from deficiency of the hepatic enzyme alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase, is the most common and generally the most severe form As renal function declines, oxalate can no longer be cleared and deposits throughout the body (systemic oxalosis), affecting bone, heart, retina, and vessels The diagnosis should be considered in any patient with recurrent oxalate stones, especially with early onset, a family history, or nephrocalcinosis Elevated urinary oxalate, genetic testing, and sometimes liver biopsy establish the diagnosis, and high fluid intake with crystallisation inhibitors is a supportive measure A subset of type 1 disease responds biochemically to pyridoxine, and definitive treatment historically involved combined or sequential liver and kidney transplantation, with newer RNA-targeted therapies now available Progressive decline in renal function toward end-stage disease Systemic oxalosis with cardiac, skeletal, retinal, or vascular involvement Recurrent obstructing stones with infection or acute kidney injury Early-onset stone disease with nephrocalcinosis suggesting a severe genotype Treating recurrent stones symptomatically without recognising an underlying inherited metabolic cause Confusing primary with enteric hyperoxaluria, which have different mechanisms and management Overlooking systemic oxalosis as renal function falls Performing isolated kidney transplantation in type 1 disease without addressing continued hepatic oxalate overproduction Primary hyperoxaluria results from autosomal recessive defects in enzymes of hepatic glyoxylate detoxification. In type 1, deficiency of the peroxisomal enzyme alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase allows glyoxylate to be oxidised to oxalate; types 2 and 3 involve other enzymes in the same pathway. The liver overproduces oxalate, which the kidneys excrete in high amounts, promoting calcium oxalate crystallisation, stone formation, and nephrocalcinosis. Because oxalate is poorly cleared once renal function fails, it accumulates systemically and is deposited in multiple tissues as oxalosis. The outlook varies with type and genotype; type 1 disease can progress to end-stage renal failure and life-threatening systemic oxalosis, whereas some pyridoxine-responsive and non-type-1 forms are milder, and early diagnosis with modern therapies has improved outcomes considerably.

Primary hyperparathyroidism — PHPT, primary HPT, parathyroid adenoma-related hypercalcaemia Malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia (PTH-related peptide or bony metastases) Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia Tertiary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease Vitamin D or vitamin A intoxication Granulomatous disease producing excess active vitamin D Thiazide diuretic or lithium effect on calcium Simultaneous serum calcium (corrected or ionised) and intact PTH Serum phosphate, magnesium, and renal function 25-hydroxyvitamin D level, as deficiency can worsen disease and confound interpretation 24-hour urinary calcium to help distinguish FHH and assess stone risk Bone mineral density including a cortical site such as the distal one-third radius Renal imaging for stones or nephrocalcinosis, and parathyroid localisation studies before surgery The leading cause of hypercalcaemia in ambulatory patients, most often detected incidentally on routine biochemistry The biochemical hallmark is hypercalcaemia with a PTH level that is elevated or inappropriately normal rather than suppressed Most cases are due to a single parathyroid adenoma; a minority reflect four-gland hyperplasia or, rarely, carcinoma Classic symptomatic disease is summarised as stones, bones, abdominal groans, and psychiatric moans, but most patients are now asymptomatic Skeletal effects include reduced bone density, particularly at cortical sites such as the distal radius, with fracture risk Renal complications include nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, and impaired renal function; urine calcium helps assess risk Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is a key mimic and is distinguished by a low urinary calcium excretion Parathyroidectomy is curative and is indicated for symptomatic disease and for asymptomatic patients meeting defined criteria on calcium, bone density, renal parameters, or age Severe hypercalcaemia with dehydration, confusion, or cardiac dysrhythmia Rapidly rising calcium with a palpable neck mass suggesting parathyroid carcinoma Acute kidney injury or symptomatic nephrolithiasis Very high PTH with markedly elevated calcium out of keeping with a simple adenoma Failing to distinguish familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, leading to unnecessary neck surgery Overlooking concurrent vitamin D deficiency that masks or modifies the biochemical picture Attributing hypercalcaemia to hyperparathyroidism when PTH is actually suppressed, indicating another cause Neglecting bone density and renal assessment that determine the need for surgery in asymptomatic patients Primary hyperparathyroidism results from autonomous overproduction of parathyroid hormone by one or more parathyroid glands, usually a benign adenoma. Excess PTH raises serum calcium by increasing bone resorption, enhancing renal tubular calcium reabsorption, and stimulating renal conversion of vitamin D to its active form, which augments intestinal calcium absorption. PTH also promotes renal phosphate excretion, tending to lower serum phosphate. The loss of normal calcium-mediated negative feedback on the parathyroid glands sustains the hypercalcaemia. Chronic PTH excess drives cortical bone loss and contributes to hypercalciuria and stone formation. Successful parathyroidectomy cures the disease, halts bone loss with partial recovery of density, and reduces stone recurrence; asymptomatic patients managed conservatively often remain stable but require monitoring, and parathyroid carcinoma has a worse outlook with a tendency to recur.

Primary Immunodeficiency — PID, common variable immunodeficiency, CVID Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) X-linked or autosomal-recessive agammaglobulinaemia Hyper-IgM (HIGM) syndromes (CD40L/CD40 or AID/UNG defects) IgA deficiency and selective IgG-subclass deficiency Selective antibody deficiency to polysaccharide antigens with normal total Ig Chronic granulomatous disease and other phagocyte killing defects Leukocyte adhesion deficiency and severe congenital neutropenia Complement component deficiencies (classic, alternative, lytic-phase) Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (IL-12-IFN-gamma axis defects) Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia, DiGeorge syndrome, hyper-IgE syndrome Regulatory-pathway disorders: HLH, ALPS, IPEX, APECED Recurrent pyogenic sinopulmonary infection from anatomical causes (e.g., cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis of other aetiology) mimicking antibody deficiency HIV/AIDS and other secondary (acquired) immunodeficiency producing an opportunistic-infection pattern resembling a T-cell PID Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia as a presenting opportunistic infection of T-cell or combined defects Recurrent or chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis Disseminated or recurrent nontuberculous mycobacterial infection (suggesting MSMD) Invasive aspergillosis or other filamentous-mould infection (suggesting CGD) Blood cell counts and morphology (neutrophil and lymphocyte counts adjusted for age; eosinophilia; Howell-Jolly bodies suggesting asplenia) Serum immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, IgM) and IgE Specific antibody responses to vaccination (tetanus toxoid; unconjugated pneumococcal polysaccharide antigens) Lymphocyte phenotyping: T-, B-, and NK-cell counts and subsets; switched (CD27+ IgM-IgD-) and non-switched (CD27+ IgM+IgD+) memory B cells Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) fluorescence or nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) assay for neutrophil reactive-oxygen-species production (chronic granulomatous disease) Complement functional assays CH50 and AP50 (classic and alternative pathways) Chest x-ray for thymic shadow (SCID, DiGeorge) and costochondral junctions (ADA deficiency); bone x-ray of metaphyses (cartilage-hair hypoplasia) Abdominal ultrasonography for spleen size (asplenia) Newborn TREC (T-cell receptor excision circle) screening on the Guthrie card for SCID Targeted gene-panel resequencing and/or whole-exome/genome sequencing for definitive molecular diagnosis Secondary hypogammaglobulinaemia from thymoma (profound hypogammaglobulinaemia observed in adults) Hypogammaglobulinaemia secondary to myelodysplastic syndrome (can present as agammaglobulinaemia) Protein-losing states (nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy) lowering immunoglobulin levels Drug-induced or malignancy-associated (e.g., CLL, lymphoma) immunosuppression Cytokine-neutralising autoantibodies (to IFN-gamma, IL-6, IL-7, type I interferon) that can mimic a PID VEXAS syndrome (somatic UBA1 mutation) presenting with late-onset inflammation, vasculitis, and cytopenias The most frequent symptom prompting the diagnosis of a PID is recurrent or unusually severe infection; recurrent allergic or autoimmune manifestations may also be the alerting feature (Harrison 22e p.2793). PIDs are classified by (1) the arm of the immune system that is defective and (2) the mechanism of the defect; the major categories are antibody/B-cell defects (agammaglobulinaemia, CVID, hyper-IgM, IgA deficiency), T-cell/cellular defects, combined defects (SCID), and innate-immune defects of phagocytes, complement, or innate receptors/signalling (Harrison 22e p.2794). The site of infection and the causal microorganism point to the affected compartment: respiratory-tract (sinus, bronchial) infection mostly suggests defective antibody responses; invasive bacterial infection can result from complement deficiency, innate-signalling defects, asplenia, or antibody defects; viral, recurrent Candida, and opportunistic infections suggest impaired T-cell immunity; skin infections and deep abscesses primarily reflect innate (phagocyte) defects such as chronic granulomatous disease (Harrison 22e p.2794). B-lymphocyte (antibody) deficiencies are the most frequent PIDs, accounting for 60-70% of all cases; T-cell deficiencies account for ~20% and innate-immune defects for ~10% (Harrison 22e p.2794, 2796, 2797). Encapsulated/pyogenic bacteria (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis) and recurrent sinopulmonary infection are the hallmark of defective antibody production; untreated recurrent bronchial infection leads to bronchiectasis, cor pulmonale, and death (Harrison 22e p.2801). Invasive Neisseria infection points to deficiencies of the complement lytic phase (C5-C9) or the alternative pathway (factors D, properdin); classic-pathway and lytic-phase complement deficiencies may also predispose to autoimmune disease, notably SLE (Harrison 22e p.2797). CVID is recognised predominantly in adults, although clinical manifestations can begin earlier in life; in most cases no molecular cause is identified and the diagnosis is made only after excluding hypomorphic agammaglobulinaemia mutations and more subtle T-cell defects, especially in children (Harrison 22e p.2802). First-line laboratory work-up is guided by the clinical picture and includes blood cell counts/morphology, serum immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE), specific antibody responses to vaccines (tetanus toxoid, unconjugated pneumococcal polysaccharide), and lymphocyte subset phenotyping; more specific (genetic) tests then confirm a definitive diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2794-2795). Even with profound B-cell deficiency, infections rarely occur before 6 months of age because of transplacental maternal IgG; conversely, in SCID clinical consequences typically appear within 3-6 months of birth (Harrison 22e p.2801, 2799). Immunoglobulin replacement should be guided by the occurrence of infection, not by laboratory IgG/antibody levels alone, to avoid unjustified infusions; it is lifelong therapy (Harrison 22e p.2802). A precise molecular/genetic diagnosis has become a milestone in the care of PID patients, guiding treatment selection, genetic counselling, and prenatal diagnosis; suspected cases should be referred to experienced centres (Harrison 22e p.2804). Recurrent, unusually severe, or persistent infections, or infection by unusual/opportunistic organisms A family history of early childhood deaths (suggesting X-linked or recessive inheritance, e.g., SCID) Lymphocytopenia in an infant (strongly suggestive of SCID in >90% of cases) or absent thymic shadow on chest x-ray Failure to thrive with protracted diarrhoea, recurrent oral candidiasis, or Pneumocystis pneumonia in early infancy Complications of live vaccines (e.g., BCG dissemination, rotavirus diarrhoea) signalling a severe T-cell defect Invasive Neisseria infection (complement lytic-phase or alternative-pathway deficiency) or recurrent encapsulated-organism sepsis with asplenia Recurrent infection accompanied by autoimmunity, lymphoproliferation, granulomatous disease, or lymphoma Absence of pus at sites of infection (hallmark of severe congenital neutropenia) CVID can present in adulthood and is easily missed; it is recognised predominantly in adults although manifestations may begin earlier (Harrison 22e p.2802). High variability of expression for a given PID (e.g., WAS, XLA, CTLA4 deficiency) can hamper diagnosis; modifier genes and environmental triggers such as EBV (in XLP) modulate the phenotype (Harrison 22e p.2804). Leaky BTK mutations causing mild hypogammaglobulinaemia with low but detectable B cells should not be confused with CVID (Harrison 22e p.2802). T-cell lymphopenia in SCID may be masked by maternally-engrafted T cells, so screening for maternal cells with genetic markers should be performed when needed (Harrison 22e p.2799). Somatic mutations in an affected gene can attenuate the phenotype of T-cell PIDs (described for ADA, X-linked SCID, RAG, NEMO, and most often WAS), while somatic mutations can also create PID-like disease (as in ALPS) (Harrison 22e p.2804). Cytokine-neutralising autoantibodies (to IFN-gamma, IL-6, IL-7, type I interferon) can mimic a PID (Harrison 22e p.2804). Caution with immunoglobulin replacement in patients with complete IgA deficiency and residual antibody production: anti-IgA antibodies can trigger anaphylactic shock, so IgA-free IgG preparations should be used (Harrison 22e p.2803). Ataxia-telangiectasia should be considered in young children with IgA deficiency and recurrent problematic infections, as ataxia and telangiectasia may not appear before age 3-4 years (Harrison 22e p.2799-2800). PIDs are predominantly Mendelian genetic diseases that arise whenever the expression or function of a nonredundant effector or mediator of the immune system is genetically impaired. More than 550 conditions have been described, with deleterious mutations identified in roughly 500 genes; estimated prevalence is 5-10 per 100,000 (probably an underestimate). They are increasingly grouped within the broader category of inborn errors of immunity that also includes autoinflammatory syndromes. Defects can involve any aspect of innate or adaptive immunity, cell differentiation, effector function, or immune regulation. The clinical consequence is multiple levels of vulnerability to infection, ranging from extremely broad (as in SCID, where T-cell development is blocked) to narrowly restricted to a single class of organism (as in Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, an IL-12-IFN-gamma axis defect). Antibody (B-cell) defects (agammaglobulinaemia from BTK and pre-B-cell-receptor gene defects, hyper-IgM from class-switch-recombination defects such as CD40L/CD40, IgA deficiency, and CVID) impair production or class switching of immunoglobulins, leaving patients unable to opsonise and neutralise pyogenic encapsulated bacteria. Cellular (T-cell) defects impair help for antibody production, macrophage activation, and cytotoxicity, causing susceptibility to viral, fungal (Candida), and opportunistic infections (e.g., Pneumocystis jirovecii, Cryptosporidium). Combined defects (SCID) abolish both arms. Innate defects affect phagocyte number (severe congenital neutropenia), adhesion (LAD), or microbial killing (chronic granulomatous disease, from defective NADPH-oxidase reactive-oxygen-species production), as well as complement components and innate receptor/signalling pathways (TLR adaptors IRAK4/MYD88). Beyond infection, PIDs can drive immunopathology including allergy, lymphoproliferation, autoimmunity, and an increased risk of malignancy (notably lymphoma) (Harrison 22e p.2793-2794, 2796-2802). Prognosis varies widely with the molecule and arm of immunity affected. T-cell and combined defects generally carry a poor prognosis and require early diagnosis and intervention; SCID is fatal in infancy without treatment, but allogeneic HSCT offers a high curative potential in patients in otherwise reasonable condition, and gene therapy has succeeded in X-linked (gamma-c) SCID, ADA-SCID, and Artemis deficiency. Functional T-cell defects carry a worse HSCT prognosis than SCID because many patients are already chronically infected at diagnosis. For antibody deficiencies, lifelong immunoglobulin replacement combined with management of chronic lung disease reduces respiratory infections and prevents progression to bronchiectasis and cor pulmonale; in CVID, lymphoproliferation, granulomatous disease, autoimmunity, and lymphoma define long-term prognosis. DNA-repair disorders such as ataxia-telangiectasia are progressive and carry a very high risk of lymphoma, leukaemia, and (in adulthood) carcinoma. Newborn TREC screening, by enabling treatment of uninfected SCID patients, maximises the chance of cure. Early diagnosis with referral to experienced centres is essential to optimal outcome (Harrison 22e p.2794, 2799-2800, 2802, 2804). PIDs are classified along two axes: (1) the arm of the immune system that is defective and (2) the mechanism of the defect (when known). The two main divisions are deficiencies of the innate immune system (phagocytic cells - impaired production [severe congenital neutropenia], asplenia, impaired adhesion [LAD], impaired killing [CGD]; innate-immunity receptors/signal transduction [TLR-signalling defects, MSMD]; complement deficiencies of the classical/alternative/lectin pathways and the lytic phase) and deficiencies of the adaptive immune system (T lymphocytes - SCID, DiGeorge, combined immunodeficiencies, hyper-IgE, DOCK8, CD40L, Wiskott-Aldrich, ataxia-telangiectasia and DNA-repair defects; B lymphocytes - X-linked/AR agammaglobulinaemia, hyper-IgM, CVID, IgA deficiency), together with regulatory defects (autoinflammatory syndromes, severe colitis, HLH, ALPS, autoimmunity such as IPEX and APECED). The classification is acknowledged to involve some arbitrary decisions because of overlap and incomplete data (Harrison 22e p.2794).

to exclude metabolic myelopathies HTLV-1 serology where exposure risk exists Genetic testing for hereditary spastic paraparesis genes when a familial pattern is suspected Cerebrospinal fluid analysis to help exclude inflammatory or infective myelopathy Presents with a slowly progressive, symmetrical spastic paraparesis that often begins in the legs and ascends, later involving the arms and bulbar decades rather than years Bladder urgency from a spastic bladder may develop, but sensory loss and prominent muscle atrophy should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis A proportion of apparently
