positive electromyogram, indicating conversion to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis A clear sensory level or sphincter disturbance suggesting a structural cord lesion Rapidly progressive weakness inconsistent with the expected indolent course Bulbar dysfunction causing unsafe swallowing and aspiration risk Diagnosing primary lateral sclerosis too early, before enough time has elapsed to exclude conversion to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis Overlooking a compressive cervical myelopathy that can mimic pure upper motor neurone disease Attributing emotional lability to a mood disorder rather than recognising pseudobulbar affect Missing a treatable metabolic or hereditary cause of progressive spastic paraparesis Primary lateral sclerosis is a rare degenerative disorder confined largely to the upper motor neurones, with selective loss of the large Betz cells of the primary motor cortex and degeneration of the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts. Unlike amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the anterior horn cells and lower motor neurones are relatively spared, at least for a prolonged period, which explains the predominance of spasticity over wasting. The condition is regarded as sitting at the upper motor neurone end of the motor neurone disease spectrum, and its precise molecular basis remains uncertain, although overlap with familial motor neurone disease genes is recognised in some cases. Primary lateral sclerosis progresses slowly over many years and is associated with a much longer survival than amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, although accumulating spasticity and eventual bulbar involvement cause substantial disability; a subset later develop lower motor neurone signs and are reclassified.

primary lymphoedema — hereditary lymphoedema, idiopathic lymphoedema chronic venous insufficiency with venous oedema lipoedema systemic oedema from cardiac, renal or hepatic failure hypothyroid myxoedema secondary lymphoedema from malignancy, surgery, radiotherapy or filariasis deep vein thrombosis and post-thrombotic syndrome chronic regional pain syndrome with limb swelling lymphoscintigraphy to assess lymphatic transport venous duplex ultrasonography to exclude venous disease MR or CT lymphangiography for anatomical mapping indocyanine green near-infrared lymphography targeted genetic testing and pedigree analysis in early-onset or syndromic cases thyroid function and renal, hepatic and cardiac assessment to exclude systemic oedema Arises from an intrinsic developmental or functional abnormality of the lymphatic conducting vessels or nodes, not from an identifiable external insult, distinguishing it from secondary lymphoedema. Classified by age of onset: congenital (present at or shortly after birth, includes Milroy disease), praecox (onset before 35 years, includes Meige disease) and tarda (onset after 35 years). A positive Stemmer sign, the inability to pinch and tent a skin fold at the base of the second toe, is a reliable bedside indicator and is rarely falsely positive. Swelling typically begins distally at the ankle or dorsum of the foot and ascends, is initially pitting and soft, then becomes non-pitting with dermal thickening, hyperkeratosis and peau d'orange. Recurrent cellulitis is both a consequence and an accelerant of disease, each episode causing further lymphatic destruction and worsening oedema. Several Mendelian forms exist, including FLT4 (VEGFR3) mutations in Milroy disease and FOXC2 mutations in lymphoedema-distichiasis, so a syndromic and family history is essential. Lymphoscintigraphy is the standard confirmatory investigation, demonstrating delayed or absent tracer transport, dermal backflow and abnormal or absent nodes. Chronic longstanding disease carries a small but important risk of cutaneous angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves phenomenon), warranting vigilance for new violaceous lesions. rapidly progressive or markedly asymmetrical swelling raising concern for underlying malignancy new violaceous or haemorrhagic cutaneous nodules suggesting angiosarcoma recurrent cellulitis with systemic sepsis skin breakdown, ulceration or lymphorrhoea unilateral limb swelling of recent onset in an older adult, mandating exclusion of pelvic or nodal tumour attributing chronic limb swelling to venous disease or simple obesity and missing lymphatic failure undertreating or delaying antibiotics in cellulitis, allowing further lymphatic damage overlooking associated syndromic features such as distichiasis, yellow nails or ptosis failing to elicit a family history and thereby missing a hereditary diagnosis dismissing new cutaneous lesions on a chronically swollen limb as bruising Primary lymphoedema results from a constitutional abnormality of lymphatic development or function, which may take the form of aplasia, hypoplasia, hyperplasia with valvular incompetence, or lymph node fibrosis. Impaired lymphatic transport allows protein-rich interstitial fluid to accumulate, and the persistent high-protein oedema drives chronic low-grade inflammation, fibroblast activation, adipose deposition and progressive dermal and subcutaneous fibrosis. This creates a self-perpetuating cycle in which tissue remodelling further compromises the remaining lymphatics and predisposes to recurrent bacterial infection, which in turn accelerates lymphatic obliteration. A growing number of causative germline mutations affecting lymphangiogenesis pathways (for example VEGFR3/FLT4, FOXC2, SOX18, GJC2 and CCBE1) have been identified, explaining the hereditary and syndromic patterns. Primary lymphoedema is a chronic, incurable condition that tends to progress without treatment, but structured decongestive therapy and infection prevention allow most patients to maintain limb function and quality of life. Prognosis worsens with recurrent cellulitis, advanced fibrosis and the rare development of angiosarcoma.

Primary myelofibrosis — PMF, myelofibrosis, chronic idiopathic myelofibrosis, agnogenic myeloid metaplasia Secondary (reactive) myelofibrosis from metastatic cancer or infection Post-polycythaemia vera or post-essential thrombocythaemia myelofibrosis Chronic myeloid leukaemia Myelodysplastic syndrome with fibrosis Hairy cell leukaemia and other marrow-infiltrating disorders Autoimmune myelofibrosis Full blood count and blood film for leucoerythroblastic changes and teardrop cells Bone marrow trephine biopsy with reticulin/collagen staining to grade fibrosis Molecular testing for JAK2, CALR, and MPL, plus high-molecular-risk mutation panels BCR-ABL1 testing to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia Cytogenetic analysis for prognostic stratification Abdominal imaging to document splenomegaly and extramedullary disease A myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by clonal proliferation with progressive marrow fibrosis and extramedullary haematopoiesis, classically producing marked splenomegaly Typical features include fatigue and anaemia, constitutional symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fever), and abdominal discomfort or early satiety from splenic enlargement The blood film shows a leucoerythroblastic picture with teardrop-shaped red cells (dacrocytes), nucleated red cells, and immature myeloid forms Attempts to aspirate marrow often yield a dry tap because of fibrosis, so a trephine biopsy demonstrating reticulin or collagen fibrosis is essential Driver mutations in JAK2, CALR, or MPL are present in most cases and support the diagnosis; additional high-risk mutations refine prognosis Prognostic scoring incorporates age, symptoms, cytopenias, blast count, and cytogenetic/molecular features to guide management decisions JAK inhibitors reduce spleen size and constitutional symptoms and can improve quality of life, though they are not curative Allogeneic stem cell transplant is the only curative therapy and is considered for suitable higher-risk patients; transformation to acute leukaemia is a feared complication Rapidly rising blast count or new cytogenetic changes indicating leukaemic transformation Severe anaemia or thrombocytopenia with bleeding requiring urgent support Massive symptomatic splenomegaly with risk of splenic infarction or rupture Portal hypertension or splanchnic vein thrombosis from extramedullary haematopoiesis and hypercoagulability Assuming a leucoerythroblastic film always indicates PMF without excluding marrow infiltration by malignancy or infection Relying on a marrow aspirate alone when fibrosis produces a dry tap and a biopsy is needed Failing to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia with BCR-ABL1 testing Overlooking prognostic mutations that would prompt earlier transplant referral Not recognising that a JAK inhibitor controls symptoms and spleen size but does not prevent progression Primary myelofibrosis originates from a clonal haematopoietic stem cell with dysregulated JAK-STAT signalling, most often driven by JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutations. The abnormal clone, particularly its megakaryocytes, secretes fibrogenic cytokines and growth factors (such as transforming growth factor-beta and platelet-derived growth factor) that stimulate marrow fibroblasts to deposit reticulin and collagen. As the marrow becomes progressively fibrotic, haematopoiesis relocates to the spleen and liver (extramedullary haematopoiesis), causing organomegaly and release of immature cells into the circulation. A chronic inflammatory cytokine state produces constitutional symptoms, and clonal evolution can culminate in acute leukaemia. Survival in primary myelofibrosis is highly variable, ranging from many years in low-risk disease to under two years in high-risk categories; adverse cytogenetics, high-risk mutations, transfusion dependence, and excess blasts predict poorer outcomes, and only allogeneic transplant offers cure.

Primary obstructive megaureter — primary obstructed megaureter, POM, congenital obstructive megaureter Refluxing megaureter (primary vesicoureteric reflux) Ureteropelvic junction obstruction Ureterocele causing ureteric dilatation Ectopic ureter Posterior urethral valves with secondary upper-tract dilatation Non-obstructive non-refluxing megaureter Renal and bladder ultrasound to characterise ureteric and pelvicalyceal dilatation MAG3 diuretic renogram to assess drainage and differential function Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) to exclude reflux and bladder outlet pathology Serial ultrasound for surveillance of antenatally detected dilatation Urinalysis and culture when infection is suspected MR urography in selected cases to define anatomy A congenitally dilated ureter caused by a narrowed, aperistaltic juxtavesical (distal) segment that impedes urine flow into the bladder, with the obstruction being functional rather than a fixed anatomical stenosis in most cases Classified within the megaureter spectrum as obstructed, refluxing, both, or neither; the primary obstructive type has obstruction without reflux Commonly detected on antenatal ultrasound as ureteric dilatation with variable pelvicalyceal dilatation, the ureter being widest just above the bladder May present later with urinary tract infection, loin pain, or haematuria The distal aperistaltic segment itself is typically of normal calibre; it is the segment above that is dilated Many cases, especially with preserved function and modest dilatation, improve spontaneously and are managed expectantly with surveillance and often prophylactic antibiotics Persistent or progressive obstruction with deteriorating function, breakthrough infection, or symptoms is treated by ureteric reimplantation with tapering or, in selected cases, temporising endoscopic or drainage procedures Declining differential renal function on serial renography Increasing ureteric or pelvicalyceal dilatation Febrile urinary tract infection or urosepsis in a dilated obstructed system Obstruction in a solitary functioning kidney Assuming all megaureters are obstructive when reflux or a non-obstructive non-refluxing pattern may be responsible Operating early on stable dilatation likely to resolve, rather than observing Misinterpreting a diuretic renogram in an immature kidney or with a full bladder Failing to exclude reflux and bladder outlet obstruction before attributing dilatation to the distal ureter In primary obstructive megaureter the terminal ureteric segment adjacent to the bladder is structurally abnormal, with disorganised smooth muscle and excess collagen that render it aperistaltic and non-compliant. Although this segment is usually of normal or near-normal calibre and not stenotic in the classic sense, it fails to transmit peristaltic waves and effectively obstructs the passage of urine into the bladder. Urine therefore accumulates proximally, producing progressive dilatation of the ureter above the junction and, in more severe cases, pelvicalyceal dilatation and impairment of renal function. There is no reflux, distinguishing it from refluxing megaureter. The majority of antenatally detected cases with reasonable function stabilise or resolve spontaneously over the first years of life, and reimplantation for persistent obstruction has good results; long-standing severe obstruction can leave permanent functional loss.

outflow through an anatomically open trabecular meshwork is impaired, raising resistance to drainage. The resulting intraocular pressure, sometimes within the normal range, contributes to mechanical and vascular stress at the optic nerve head, causing loss of retinal ganglion cell axons. This produces characteristic cupping of the optic disc and a corresponding pattern of arcuate and peripheral visual field loss that advances slowly over years. With early detection and sustained pressure control most patients retain useful vision for life, but untreated or poorly controlled disease progresses to irreversible visual field loss and blindness.

Loss of ovarian feedback removes inhibition of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, driving compensatory elevation of gonadotropins, especially FSH. Mechanisms include chromosomal abnormalities causing accelerated follicular atresia (as in Turner syndrome), the FMR1 premutation, other genetic and metabolic disorders (such as galactosaemia), autoimmune destruction of ovarian tissue, and iatrogenic gonadotoxic insults from chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery. The resulting oestrogen deficiency impairs pubertal development or causes menstrual cessation and predisposes to reduced bone mineral density. Fertility is substantially reduced and often permanently lost, though intermittent ovarian function means occasional spontaneous ovulation; with appropriate hormone replacement, secondary sexual characteristics, bone health, and cardiovascular risk can be well managed, and assisted reproduction with donor oocytes offers a route to pregnancy.

inheritable PRKAR1A-related condition PPNAD is a bilateral adrenocortical disorder in which numerous small cortisol-secreting micronodules, containing lipofuscin pigment, arise within an often Autonomous cortisol production suppresses pituitary ACTH. The condition is a component of Carney complex, a multiple neoplasia and lentiginosis syndrome. Cushing syndrome due to PPNAD is effectively cured by bilateral adrenalectomy, which necessitates lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement. Overall prognosis is dominated by other Carney complex manifestations, particularly cardiac myxomas, so lifelong surveillance is required.

decision-making capacity Mislabelling the language decline as a psychiatric or purely age-related change Failing to subtype the aphasia, which informs the likely underlying pathology Not testing for Alzheimer biomarkers in a logopenic presentation Overlooking evolving motor or behavioural features that reshape the diagnosis Primary progressive aphasia is an umbrella term for neurodegenerative syndromes in which the disease process selectively targets the language-dominant, usually left, perisylvian and temporal cortical networks. The underlying pathology varies by subtype: the non-fluent/agrammatic and semantic variants are most commonly associated with frontotemporal lobar degeneration due to abnormal tau or TDP-43 protein aggregation, while the logopenic variant is usually caused by Alzheimer disease pathology with amyloid plaques and tau tangles. Progressive neuronal loss within specific components of the language network determines whether speech production, grammar, single-word comprehension or word retrieval and repetition are predominantly affected. Primary progressive aphasia is progressive, with language impairment worsening and additional cognitive, behavioural or motor deficits typically emerging over years; the rate and later features depend on the underlying pathology, and management is supportive with speech and language therapy and caregiver support.

and inferior parietal cortex, regions important for phonological processing and verbal working memory. Primary stabbing headache — ice-pick headache, jabs and jolts syndrome, idiopathic stabbing headache Trigeminal neuralgia Short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks (SUNCT/SUNA) Nummular headache Occipital neuralgia Secondary stabbing pain from a structural lesion Clinical diagnosis based on the characteristic brief stabs Neurological examination to exclude focal signs Neuroimaging if pains are strictly fixed in location or examination is abnormal Review for coexisting migraine or other primary headache Transient ultra-brief stabs of head pain lasting seconds, occurring spontaneously without an identifiable trigger Pains are felt in the distribution of the first division of the trigeminal nerve in most cases but may move between areas There are no accompanying cranial autonomic features, which helps distinguish it from the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias Attacks may occur once or many times a day with an irregular pattern It is more common in people who also have migraine A subset responds to indometacin, though pains are often too brief to warrant treatment Stabs consistently confined to one fixed location Abnormal neurological examination New onset in an older patient with other concerning features Progressive change in pattern or associated deficits Assuming a fixed-site stab is primary without imaging Confusing it with trigeminal neuralgia, which has cutaneous triggers Overlooking coexisting migraine Overtreating pains that are too brief to target Primary stabbing headache is an idiopathic disorder thought to arise from transient spontaneous discharges within trigeminal nociceptive pathways, without structural cause in the primary form. Its association with migraine and other primary headaches suggests shared central pain-modulating mechanisms. When stabs are consistently localised to one fixed site, an underlying structural lesion in that region should be considered. The disorder is benign and often intermittent, with many patients needing no treatment and attacks tending to fluctuate over time.

Primary thunderclap headache — idiopathic thunderclap headache Subarachnoid haemorrhage Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis Cervical or intracranial arterial dissection Pituitary apoplexy Spontaneous intracranial hypotension Urgent non-contrast CT of the head Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia if CT is non-diagnostic CT or MR angiography and venography for vascular causes MRI of the brain for apoplexy, intracranial hypotension and other lesions Repeat vascular imaging if RCVS is suspected, as early studies can be normal A high-intensity headache of abrupt onset reaching maximum severity within one minute, mimicking a ruptured aneurysm It is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion made only after serious secondary causes have been ruled out Subarachnoid haemorrhage is the priority to exclude, followed by other vascular emergencies Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome is a common cause of recurrent thunderclap headache and must be actively sought Other secondary causes include cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, arterial dissection, pituitary apoplexy and spontaneous intracranial hypotension Because the primary label carries risk, a thorough vascular and cerebrospinal fluid evaluation is essential Any focal neurological deficit or reduced conscious level Neck stiffness or photophobia suggesting subarachnoid blood Recurrent thunderclap episodes suggesting vasoconstriction syndrome Papilloedema or seizures Labelling a headache primary before completing vascular and cerebrospinal fluid workup Stopping at a normal early angiogram and missing RCVS Overlooking venous sinus thrombosis or intracranial hypotension Failing to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage with lumbar puncture when CT is negative Thunderclap headache reflects sudden activation of pain-sensitive intracranial structures, most dangerously by acute vascular events such as aneurysmal subarachnoid bleeding or arterial vasoconstriction. In the primary form no cause is identified despite appropriate investigation, and its mechanism is poorly understood; it may overlap with disorders of cerebrovascular tone. The clinical imperative is that the presentation is treated as a vascular emergency until secondary causes are excluded. When secondary causes are excluded the primary form generally has a benign course, but the initial presentation always warrants urgent investigation because the dangerous mimics are time-critical.

Prion Diseases (CJD) — Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, CJD, spongiform encephalopathy Alzheimer's disease (can occasionally present as rapidly progressive dementia) Corticobasal degeneration (CBD) - rapid degenerative dementia with prominent movement abnormalities, more likely mistaken for CJD Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) - rapid degenerative dementia with prominent movement abnormalities, more likely mistaken for CJD Other rapidly progressive dementias Viral encephalitides Bacterial encephalitides Other CNS infections causing rapidly progressive dementia MRI diffusion-weighted imaging - restricted diffusion in cortical ribbon and/or basal ganglia (cortical ribboning); basal ganglia or thalamus hyperintensity on diffusion/FLAIR EEG - periodic complexes (repetitive bursts of diffuse high-amplitude sharp waves) Lumbar puncture/CSF - to exclude CNS infection or inflammation among rapidly progressive dementia mimics MRI/neuroimaging to exclude treatable structural causes (neoplasm, subdural hematoma, NPH) Hashimoto's encephalopathy CNS vasculitis CNS lymphoma Paraneoplastic/autoimmune syndromes (autoimmune encephalitis) Prolonged focal or generalized seizures (can rarely produce a similar imaging appearance) CJD is a rapidly progressive disorder associated with dementia, focal cortical signs, rigidity, and myoclonus, causing death less than 1 year after first symptoms appear (p.3525-3526). CJD is the classic cause of a rapidly progressive dementia (RPD: progression from symptom onset to dementia within a year or less), especially when associated with myoclonus, though more often RPD is due to AD, another neurodegenerative disorder, or autoimmune encephalitis (p.237). On examination, CJD is suggested by diffuse rigidity, an akinetic-mute state, and prominent, often startle-sensitive myoclonus (p.239). MRI diffusion-weighted imaging reveals restricted diffusion within the cortical ribbon and/or basal ganglia in most patients; basal ganglia or thalamus hyperintensity may also be seen on diffusion/FLAIR MRI (p.240, p.3526). EEG is not routinely used but can suggest CJD by showing repetitive bursts of diffuse high-amplitude sharp waves (periodic complexes) (p.241). Prion diseases such as CJD are rare (prevalence ~1 per million); the rapidity of progression distinguishes CJD from AD, though AD can occasionally present as a rapidly progressive dementia (p.3525-3526). Prion disease is one cause of subacute progressive ataxia, especially when an infectious etiology such as transmission from contaminated human growth hormone is responsible (p.3590). Rapidly progressive dementia (onset to dementia within a year or less) Dementia accompanied by myoclonus (often startle-sensitive) Diffuse rigidity and akinetic-mute state Subacute progressive ataxia Cortical ribboning / basal ganglia or thalamic hyperintensity on diffusion/FLAIR MRI Periodic complexes on EEG Must exclude treatable causes of rapidly progressive dementia (e.g., autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis, Hashimoto's encephalopathy, CNS vasculitis, CNS infection, lymphoma) before attributing a rapidly progressive dementia to CJD. More rapid degenerative dementias with prominent movement abnormalities (CBD, DLB) are more likely to be mistaken for CJD. Rarely, prolonged focal or generalized seizures can produce an MRI appearance similar to CJD. Prion diseases are caused by prions, host-encoded proteins (the prion protein) that adopt an alternative, abnormal conformation (misfolded PrPSc) which undergoes self-propagation. PrPSc imposes its conformation on the normal precursor protein, which in turn becomes self-templating, producing faithful copies; the misfolded protein is enriched for beta-sheet and assembles into amyloid fibrils. The amyloid plaques in kuru and CJD are filled with PrPSc prions assembled into fibrils. CJD is one of the major degenerative dementias characterized by abnormal aggregation of a specific protein (misfolded prion protein, PrPSc). Familial CJD is genetically linked to mutations in the PrP gene (p.237, p.3400-3401). Uniformly fatal. CJD causes death less than 1 year after the first symptoms appear (p.3525-3526). Etiologic classification of prion diseases (all caused by PrPSc): sporadic (e.g., classic CJD), familial/genetic (linked to PrP gene mutations - includes familial CJD, Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker disease [GSS], and fatal insomnia), iatrogenic (transmission e.g. from contaminated human growth hormone), and acquired/transmissible forms (kuru). PrPSc prions also cause animal spongiform encephalopathies including scrapie, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), and chronic wasting disease (p.3400-3401, p.3590).

Misdiagnosing it as sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and missing the glycogen storage basis Overlooking pre-excitation as a clue to the underlying metabolic disorder Underestimating the risk of rapidly conducted atrial fibrillation via an accessory pathway Neglecting family screening for an autosomal dominant condition PRKAG2 encodes a regulatory subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase, the cell's central energy sensor governing glucose and fatty acid metabolism. Activating or dysregulating variants disturb this energy-sensing function, causing excessive accumulation of glycogen within cardiomyocytes. Glycogen-laden myocytes produce ventricular hypertrophy that resembles hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and glycogen deposition also disrupts the annulus fibrosus, allowing anomalous atrioventricular connections that generate ventricular pre-excitation. Progressive infiltration and degeneration of the conduction system cause worsening atrioventricular block over time, while the accessory conduction and atrial disease predispose to tachyarrhythmias. The disorder is thus a metabolic (glycogen storage) cardiomyopathy with a distinctive electrophysiological signature. The disorder tends to progress over years, with many patients ultimately needing pacing for conduction disease and management of tachyarrhythmias; heart failure can develop in advanced disease, and prognosis is improved by early rhythm surveillance and device therapy.

Triggers include stress, sexual activity, and defecation, and a rare hereditary internal anal sphincter myopathy underlies some familial cases. Between episodes there is no demonstrable abnormality. and function Confusing preserved intelligence with other progeroid syndromes that feature cognitive impairment Underestimating cardiovascular risk in a young child and delaying cardiology involvement Attributing early features to a non-syndromic failure to thrive Overlooking the sclerodermatous skin as a diagnostic clue Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome is usually caused by a de novo point variant in LMNA that activates a cryptic splice site, producing progerin, a truncated lamin A that cannot be properly processed and remains farnesylated. Accumulation of progerin distorts the nuclear envelope, destabilises the nuclear lamina and disrupts chromatin organisation, DNA repair and mechanotransduction. This drives premature cellular senescence and, in vascular smooth muscle, accelerated atherosclerosis that dominates the clinical course. The condition is progressive and life-limiting, with death typically in the second decade, most often from myocardial infarction or stroke secondary to accelerated atherosclerosis. Multidisciplinary supportive care and cardiovascular risk management are central, and disease-modifying therapy targeting protein farnesylation has been developed.

In the SCN5A-related form, loss-of-function variants reduce cardiac sodium current, slowing conduction velocity through the His-Purkinje system and predisposing to bundle branch and atrioventricular block. Ageing-related fibrosis of the conduction system compounds the genetic defect, so block worsens over time, giving the characteristic progressive course. With timely recognition and pacing for symptomatic or high-grade block, prognosis is generally favourable, but untreated advanced conduction disease carries a risk of syncope and sudden death, and overlap phenotypes may add arrhythmic risk.

In inherited forms, mutations in genes encoding the cardiac sodium channel (SCN5A) and other conduction-related proteins reduce conduction reserve, so conduction slows and blocks over time, producing bundle branch block, then higher-grade atrioventricular block. In each case impaired bile acid secretion produces intracellular accumulation of bile acids, hepatocyte injury, and progressive cholestasis that evolves to fibrosis and cirrhosis. The characteristic difference in gamma-glutamyl transferase reflects whether the underlying lesion damages the bile duct epithelium (high, as in MDR3 disease) or not (low or normal, as in FIC1 and BSEP disease). Without intervention most subtypes progress to biliary cirrhosis and liver failure during childhood, though disease-modifying therapy such as ileal bile acid transport inhibitors, surgical biliary diversion, and liver transplantation can markedly improve outcomes. BSEP disease additionally carries a lifelong risk of hepatobiliary malignancy requiring surveillance.

the mainstay is restoration of immune function through immune reconstitution in HIV or withdrawal of the offending immunosuppressant Immune reconstitution can precipitate PML-IRIS, in which recovering immunity produces paradoxical clinical worsening with new gadolinium enhancement and oedema on imaging Rapidly progressive focal neurological deficit in an immunocompromised patient New enhancing lesions with oedema after immune reconstitution suggesting PML-IRIS Deteriorating conscious level or brainstem involvement Development of intractable seizures or profound cognitive collapse Attributing progressive deficits to the underlying condition or to multiple sclerosis relapse rather than considering PML in a treated patient Being falsely reassured by a single negative CSF JC virus PCR, since sensitivity is imperfect Failing to recognise PML-IRIS when clinical worsening follows immune recovery Overlooking natalizumab or other biological agents as a cause and delaying drug withdrawal The disease results from reactivation of latent JC polyomavirus, a common childhood infection that persists silently in the kidney and lymphoid tissue. The resulting confluent foci of demyelination enlarge and coalesce across the subcortical white matter, sparing axons relatively early but producing progressive neurological deficits. Astrocytes become bizarrely enlarged and oligodendrocyte nuclei acquire viral inclusions. Because inflammation is minimal while immunity is suppressed, lesions usually do not enhance until immune function recovers, when a brisk inflammatory response (immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome) may develop. Historically often fatal within months, outcomes have improved where immune function can be restored, particularly in HIV with effective antiretroviral therapy; nonetheless many survivors are left with substantial neurological disability, and PML-IRIS carries a risk of further deterioration or death.

Progressive nodular histiocytosis — PNH, progressive nodular histiocytoma Xanthoma disseminatum Multiple dermatofibromas Juvenile / adult xanthogranuloma Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis Erdheim-Chester disease Cutaneous involvement by Langerhans cell histiocytosis Eruptive xanthomas Skin biopsy sampling both superficial and deep lesions with immunohistochemistry (CD68, factor XIIIa, CD1a, langerin) Fasting serum lipid profile to confirm normolipaemia Serum and urine protein electrophoresis to exclude paraproteinaemia Assessment for diabetes insipidus to distinguish from xanthoma disseminatum Laryngoscopy if hoarseness or airway symptoms occur Imaging only if systemic involvement is clinically suspected Ophthalmological review where periorbital lesions threaten vision A rare, persistent and progressive non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis characterised by two coexisting lesion types: superficial yellowish xanthomatous papules and deeper firm red-brown to skin-coloured nodules. Lesions accumulate steadily over time without the spontaneous involution seen in other cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses. Extensive facial involvement can coalesce to produce a disfiguring leonine facies, and lesions around the eyes, mouth and larynx may impair function. In contrast to xanthoma disseminatum, lesions are not confined to flexures and there is characteristically no mucosal, pituitary or systemic organ involvement, though mucosal lesions are occasionally reported. Serum lipids are normal, and there is no consistent association with diabetes insipidus or paraproteinaemia. Histology reveals two populations of histiocytes: superficial foamy xanthomatous cells with Touton giant cells and deeper spindle-shaped histiocytes in a storiform arrangement resembling dermatofibroma. Immunohistochemistry shows CD68 positivity with CD1a and langerin negativity, consistent with a macrophage rather than Langerhans cell lineage. The condition is notoriously refractory to treatment, and surgical or physical removal of individual disfiguring or obstructing lesions is often the mainstay. Progressive facial infiltration producing leonine facies and functional impairment Periorbital or eyelid nodules threatening vision Laryngeal or perioral lesions causing airway or feeding compromise Rapid enlargement or ulceration of nodules Emergence of systemic features suggesting an alternative multisystem histiocytosis Mistaking the deep storiform lesions for multiple dermatofibromas and underestimating the disorder. Progressive nodular histiocytosis is a proliferative disorder of macrophage-derived histiocytes within the non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis group, distinguished by the coexistence of superficial lipidised xanthomatous histiocytes with Touton giant cells and deeper spindle-shaped histiocytes arranged in a storiform pattern. The lesional cells express macrophage markers such as CD68 and factor XIIIa but lack CD1a, langerin and Birbeck granules. Unlike the self-healing cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses, the infiltrate here proliferates progressively and does not regress, producing an ever-increasing burden of papules and nodules; the reason for this relentless behaviour in the absence of systemic involvement or a paraprotein is not fully understood, but it distinguishes progressive nodular histiocytosis as the most persistent and disfiguring of the purely cutaneous forms. The condition follows a chronic, relentlessly progressive course without spontaneous remission; it does not shorten life through systemic disease but causes substantial disfigurement and functional morbidity, and it is characteristically resistant to medical therapy.

Progressive non-fluent aphasia is the non-fluent/agrammatic variant of primary progressive aphasia, caused by neurodegeneration centred on the left inferior frontal, insular and premotor cortex that supports speech planning and grammatical processing. The most frequent underlying pathology is frontotemporal lobar degeneration associated with abnormal tau protein aggregation, and there is clinical and pathological overlap with corticobasal degeneration and progressive supranuclear palsy. Damage to these anterior language and motor-speech networks produces effortful, agrammatic output and apraxia of speech, with relative sparing of the temporal regions that store word meaning. The disorder progresses over years, with speech becoming increasingly sparse and eventual mutism in many patients, and frequent evolution of motor features; prognosis depends on the underlying pathology, and management is supportive with speech and language therapy and communication aids.

panencephalitis, as the two are clinically and mechanistically similar but follow different viruses Overlooking a distant history of congenital rubella when assessing adolescent cognitive decline Expecting the periodic EEG complexes of SSPE, which are absent in progressive rubella panencephalitis Attributing the decline to a primary neurodegenerative disorder and missing the raised CSF rubella antibody Progressive rubella panencephalitis reflects long-term persistence of the rubella virus within the central nervous system after congenital or, rarely, postnatal infection. The virus is not fully cleared and continues a smouldering, low-grade infection of brain tissue over many years. A chronic immune-mediated process, with intrathecal synthesis of rubella-specific antibody, accompanies slowly progressive destruction of both grey and white matter, hence panencephalitis. There is widespread neuronal loss, gliosis, perivascular inflammation, and a characteristic prominent involvement of the cerebellum, producing the ataxia that is a notable feature. The mechanism resembles that of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis after measles, in that a common childhood virus persists in the brain and drives a delayed, progressive, and ultimately fatal encephalitis. The condition is progressive and ultimately fatal, evolving over years to profound neurological disability and death, with no proven treatment able to halt its course.

tau aggregates as neurofibrillary tangles, tufted astrocytes, and coiled bodies in the basal ganglia, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra, midbrain tegmentum, and brainstem nuclei controlling eye Degeneration of the midbrain and its ocular motor circuitry produces the supranuclear gaze palsy, while nigral and striatal involvement causes the poorly levodopa-responsive parkinsonism. Damage to brainstem postural and gait pathways underlies the early instability and falls, and frontal-subcortical involvement drives the cognitive and behavioural features. PSP is relentlessly progressive with no disease-modifying therapy; mobility, communication, and swallowing decline over several years, and death is commonly related to aspiration and its complications.

very high levels are more specific for a true prolactinoma In large tumours with only mildly elevated prolactin, laboratory dilution may be needed to exclude the hook effect artefact Unlike most pituitary tumours, prolactinomas are usually managed medically with dopamine agonists rather than surgery as first line Dopamine agonist therapy typically lowers prolactin, restores gonadal function, and shrinks tumour volume Bitemporal visual field loss from chiasmal compression by a macroadenoma Sudden severe headache with visual or cranial nerve signs suggesting apoplexy Symptoms and signs of coexisting hypopituitarism, including adrenal insufficiency Very large invasive tumours threatening vision or requiring urgent decompression Diagnosing a prolactinoma without excluding drugs, hypothyroidism, renal failure, and pregnancy Missing the hook effect and underestimating prolactin in a large tumour, leading to inappropriate surgery Overlooking macroprolactin as a cause of asymptomatic elevation Failing to counsel on bone health and fertility implications of chronic hypogonadism A prolactinoma is a benign lactotroph adenoma of the anterior pituitary that autonomously secretes prolactin. Prolactin is normally under tonic inhibitory control by hypothalamic dopamine, which is why dopamine agonists are effective and dopamine-blocking drugs raise prolactin. Excess prolactin inhibits pulsatile gonadotrophin-releasing hormone secretion, reducing LH and FSH and causing hypogonadism, galactorrhoea, and infertility. Larger tumours (macroadenomas) may compress the optic chiasm and adjacent pituitary tissue, producing visual field defects and hypopituitarism. Non-tumoural hyperprolactinaemia from stalk disconnection, drugs, or systemic disease must be distinguished from a true adenoma. Most microprolactinomas respond well to dopamine agonists with normalisation of prolactin, restoration of fertility, and often no significant growth; macroadenomas also usually shrink with medical therapy, and in selected patients treatment can eventually be tapered, though relapse of hyperprolactinaemia is possible.

Prolidase deficiency — prolidase deficiency, PEPD deficiency, peptidase D deficiency, imidodipeptiduria, hyperimidodipeptiduria Chronic venous or arterial leg ulceration of other cause Pyoderma gangrenosum and other inflammatory ulcerative dermatoses Other genodermatoses with poor wound healing Immunodeficiency with recurrent skin and respiratory infection Systemic lupus erythematosus (some patients have lupus-like features) Vasculitic ulceration Urine amino acid and peptide analysis demonstrating marked imidodipeptiduria Prolidase enzyme activity assay in erythrocytes, leucocytes, or fibroblasts Molecular analysis of the PEPD gene Skin biopsy and wound swabs to characterise ulcers and infection Immunological workup given recurrent infections Imaging or examination for splenomegaly and associated features Caused by deficiency of prolidase (peptidase D, encoded by PEPD), the enzyme that cleaves dipeptides with proline or hydroxyproline at the C-terminus, a final step in collagen turnover The hallmark clinical feature is chronic, recalcitrant skin ulceration, especially of the lower legs, together with a characteristic facies and recurrent infections The diagnostic biochemical signature is massive urinary excretion of imidodipeptides (proline- and hydroxyproline-containing dipeptides) Splenomegaly, recurrent respiratory and skin infections, and variable intellectual disability may accompany the skin disease Impaired recycling of proline from collagen breakdown is thought to compromise wound healing and connective tissue integrity Management is largely supportive with meticulous wound care; topical approaches aiming to supply amino acids to ulcers have been explored Inheritance is autosomal recessive with wide phenotypic variability, from near-asymptomatic to severe British spelling applies (e.g. tumour, oedema) where relevant to descriptions Extensive or infected chronic ulceration with systemic sepsis risk Recurrent severe respiratory infections suggesting significant immune compromise Features of an associated autoimmune process such as lupus Managing leg ulcers as simple venous disease without considering a metabolic cause in atypical, treatment-resistant cases Overlooking associated immunodeficiency and infection risk Missing associated autoimmune or lupus-like features Assuming a uniform severe phenotype, when presentation ranges widely Prolidase hydrolyses dipeptides in which the C-terminal residue is proline or hydroxyproline, the last enzymatic step that releases these imino acids from collagen degradation for reuse in new collagen synthesis. When prolidase is deficient, imidodipeptides accumulate and are excreted in large amounts in the urine, while recycling of proline for collagen synthesis is impaired. The resulting defect in connective tissue turnover and wound healing underlies the chronic, poorly healing skin ulcers, and the dermatological and immune manifestations characteristic of the disorder. The course is highly variable; skin ulceration is often chronic and difficult to heal and may cause substantial morbidity, while some individuals remain mildly affected. Recurrent infection can be a significant contributor to morbidity.

In the T-cell form, rearrangements activating the TCL1 oncogene, together with ATM inactivation from chromosome 11 abnormalities, drive proliferation and impair DNA damage responses, producing an aggressive disease with high tumour burden. The B-cell form is a distinct clonal B-cell disorder. Extensive marrow, splenic and blood involvement accounts for the very high counts, cytopenias and organomegaly, while tissue tropism in T-cell disease explains skin and serosal involvement. T-cell prolymphocytic leukaemia is aggressive with historically poor survival, although targeted antibody therapy and, where feasible, allogeneic transplantation have improved outcomes; the B-cell form is also aggressive but somewhat variable.

pronator teres syndrome — proximal median nerve entrapment, pronator syndrome carpal tunnel syndrome anterior interosseous syndrome C6 or C7 cervical radiculopathy brachial plexopathy involving the lateral cord medial epicondylitis cervical rib or thoracic outlet syndrome flexor-pronator strain or tendinopathy nerve conduction studies and needle electromyography of median-innervated forearm and hand muscles elbow and humeral radiographs to identify a supracondylar spur high-resolution nerve ultrasound of the proximal forearm magnetic resonance imaging of the elbow and forearm for mass lesions or muscle oedema cervical spine imaging when radiculopathy is suspected comparison studies of the contralateral limb dynamic provocative examination during electrodiagnostic testing Proximal median nerve compression in the forearm presenting with volar forearm aching aggravated by repetitive pronation, distinguishing it from the nocturnal wrist-centred symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome. Sensory disturbance characteristically involves the thenar eminence via the palmar cutaneous branch, which arises proximal to the wrist and is therefore spared in carpal tunnel syndrome. Compression may occur at the ligament of Struthers, the lacertus fibrosus, between the two heads of pronator teres, or at the fibrous arch of flexor digitorum superficialis. A negative Tinel sign at the wrist with a positive provocative response over the proximal forearm supports the diagnosis. Provocative manoeuvres attempt to localise the site: resisted pronation with the elbow extended implicates pronator teres, resisted elbow flexion with supination implicates lacertus fibrosus, and resisted long-finger flexion implicates the superficialis arch. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography are frequently normal or non-localising, so the diagnosis remains largely clinical. Unlike anterior interosseous syndrome, weakness is usually mild and sensory symptoms predominate, though overlap occurs when the parent median nerve is affected. A supracondylar humeral spur with the ligament of Struthers is a rare bony cause and may be visible on radiographs. rapidly progressive motor weakness suggesting an alternative or compressive mass lesion constitutional symptoms or a palpable forearm mass indicating neoplasm bilateral or multifocal deficits suggesting a systemic or inflammatory neuropathy acute severe pain with swelling raising concern for compartment syndrome mislabelling proximal median symptoms as carpal tunnel syndrome and performing an unhelpful wrist release expecting confirmatory electrodiagnostic findings when studies are frequently normal overlooking a supracondylar spur by omitting elbow radiographs confusing the sensory-predominant picture with the pure motor deficit of anterior interosseous syndrome The median nerve traverses several potential compression points in the proximal forearm: a supracondylar spur bridged by the ligament of Struthers, the bicipital aponeurosis (lacertus fibrosus), the interval between the humeral and ulnar heads of pronator teres, and the proximal fibrous arch of flexor digitorum superficialis. Repetitive forceful pronation and gripping, muscular hypertrophy, anatomical anomalies, or a space-occupying lesion produce mechanical and ischaemic injury to the nerve. Because the palmar cutaneous and thenar motor branches arise at or distal to this level, both thenar sensation and, variably, thenar motor function may be affected, contrasting with the pattern seen in wrist-level entrapment. Many patients improve with activity modification, splinting and conservative measures, and surgical decompression is generally effective when a discrete compressive structure is identified. Recovery may be slow and incomplete when diagnosis is delayed or the compression is diffuse.

Properdin deficiency — Properdin deficiency, Factor P deficiency, Complement properdin deficiency Terminal complement component deficiencies (C5 to C9) Factor D or other alternative-pathway defects Asplenia or hyposplenism Antibody deficiency predisposing to infection Idiopathic invasive meningococcal disease Acquired complement consumption AH50 alternative-pathway assay (abnormal) CH50 classical-pathway assay (usually preserved) Specific properdin (factor P) level Genetic testing of the CFP gene Cultures and PCR during acute infection to identify serogroup Meningococcal and other vaccination status X-linked family screening and carrier assessment Properdin deficiency is the principal X-linked complement deficiency, so it predominantly affects males. It markedly increases susceptibility to fulminant meningococcal disease, which can be rapidly fatal even at first presentation. Meningococcal infection in properdin deficiency often presents acutely and with a high case-fatality rate rather than the recurrent pattern seen in terminal-pathway defects. Properdin is the only known positive regulator of complement, stabilising the alternative-pathway C3 convertase. The AH50 alternative-pathway assay is abnormal while the CH50 classical-pathway assay is typically preserved. A specific low or absent properdin level confirms the diagnosis after alternative-pathway dysfunction is shown. Meningococcal vaccination, including conjugate quadrivalent and serogroup B vaccines, and family screening are essential. Patient and family education about seeking urgent care for febrile illness can be life-saving. Fever with headache, neck stiffness or a non-blanching rash Rapidly progressive meningococcaemia or septic shock Any febrile illness in a known properdin-deficient individual Purpura fulminans Family history of fatal meningococcal disease Overlooking an X-linked complement defect in a male with severe meningococcal disease. Relying on a normal CH50 to exclude complement deficiency when the defect is in the alternative pathway. Failing to provide serogroup B and conjugate meningococcal vaccination. Not screening male relatives after an index case. Underestimating how rapidly meningococcaemia can progress in these patients. Properdin (factor P) is the sole positive regulator of the complement system: it binds and stabilises the alternative-pathway C3 convertase, prolonging its half-life and amplifying complement deposition on microbial surfaces. In its absence the alternative pathway cannot be sustained, so amplification of C3b deposition and downstream membrane attack complex formation on Neisseria is impaired. This leaves the host unable to mount rapid complement-mediated killing of meningococci, producing a striking vulnerability to fulminant meningococcal sepsis. Because the classical and lectin pathways remain functional, susceptibility is largely confined to neisserial organisms, and the disease is inherited in an X-linked pattern, so affected individuals are typically male. The main hazard is fulminant meningococcal disease with a high case-fatality if not treated immediately; with vaccination, education and prompt antibiotics the outlook is greatly improved. Because episodes can be overwhelming at first presentation, prevention and rapid response are paramount.

propiogenic amino acids, carnitine supplementation, and control of intercurrent catabolism, with metronidazole sometimes used to lower gut propionate Unlike some organic acidaemias this disorder is generally not cofactor-responsive, though biotin is often trialled Included in newborn screening via elevated C3 acylcarnitine, enabling early diagnosis Acute metabolic decompensation with severe acidosis and hyperammonaemia is a medical emergency Encephalopathy from hyperammonaemia during crises Cardiomyopathy or QT prolongation with risk of life-threatening arrhythmia Rapid clinical deterioration during infection, fasting or catabolic stress Confusing it with methylmalonic acidemia without checking that methylmalonic acid is not elevated Overlooking cardiac surveillance, since cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia can be fatal even with good metabolic control Attributing the acidotic neonate to sepsis and delaying specific therapy Under-recognising secondary hyperammonaemia as a driver of encephalopathy Propionic acidemia arises from deficient propionyl-CoA carboxylase, a mitochondrial biotin-dependent enzyme that converts propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA. This step is part of the catabolic pathway for the amino acids isoleucine, valine, methionine and threonine, as well as odd-chain fatty acids and cholesterol. Enzyme deficiency causes accumulation of propionyl-CoA and its derivatives (propionic acid, 3-hydroxypropionate, methylcitrate, propionylcarnitine). These organic acids produce severe metabolic acidosis, inhibit the urea cycle to cause hyperammonaemia, impair mitochondrial energy production, and are toxic to the myocardium, bone marrow, pancreas and basal ganglia. Propionic acidemia is among the more severe organic acidaemias, with high risk of recurrent metabolic crises and long-term neurological and cardiac complications despite treatment; early detection and rigorous metabolic management improve survival, and selected patients are considered for liver transplantation.

Propofol infusion syndrome — PRIS, propofol-related infusion syndrome, propofol infusion syndrome Sepsis with lactic acidosis and multiorgan dysfunction Cardiogenic shock from other causes Other causes of rhabdomyolysis Malignant hyperthermia Diabetic or other metabolic ketoacidosis Mitochondrial disease decompensation Ischaemia-related lactic acidosis Serial arterial blood gases and lactate Characterised by a severe high-anion-gap metabolic (lactic) acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury Cardiac features include bradyarrhythmias and progressive myocardial failure that can culminate in refractory cardiac arrest Risk rises with high infusion rates, prolonged duration, concurrent catecholamine or corticosteroid use, and low carbohydrate intake A rising lactate, unexplained metabolic acidosis or new arrhythmia in a patient on prolonged propofol should prompt immediate suspicion Management is immediate cessation of propofol, cardiorespiratory support and correction of acidosis and electrolytes Refractory cases may need pacing, extracorporeal support or renal replacement therapy to remove metabolites and manage acidosis and hyperkalaemia Prevention involves limiting the dose and duration of propofol and ensuring adequate carbohydrate provision Unexplained and worsening metabolic acidosis with rising lactate New bradyarrhythmia or conduction block during prolonged propofol infusion Rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalaemia Progressive myocardial dysfunction or refractory cardiac arrest Green or otherwise discoloured urine with deteriorating haemodynamics Continuing high-dose propofol despite an unexplained rising lactate or acidosis Attributing the metabolic derangement solely to sepsis Overlooking early bradyarrhythmia as a warning sign Failing to limit propofol dose and duration or to provide adequate carbohydrate in at-risk patients Propofol infusion syndrome is thought to arise from propofol-induced impairment of mitochondrial function. The drug interferes with the electron transport chain and with fatty acid oxidation, particularly the entry of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria, so cells cannot generate adequate energy from fat and become dependent on glucose. In critical illness, with high catecholamine and cortisol levels and often limited carbohydrate supply, this energy failure is unmasked. The result is accumulation of unused fatty acids, anaerobic metabolism with lactic acidosis, and injury to metabolically active tissues including cardiac and skeletal muscle, producing rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, renal impairment, myocardial depression and conduction abnormalities. Progressive cardiovascular collapse follows if the drug is not stopped. Once established with cardiovascular collapse, the syndrome carries a high mortality. Early recognition, immediate withdrawal of propofol and aggressive supportive care, including extracorporeal support in severe cases, offer the best chance of recovery.

Propriospinal myoclonus — PSM Functional (psychogenic) axial jerks Hypnic jerks (sleep starts) Spinal segmental myoclonus Cortical or subcortical myoclonus Startle syndromes Surface electromyography with polygraphy to show slow propagation and recruitment pattern Back-averaging to seek a premovement Bereitschaftspotential (suggesting functional origin) MRI of the spinal cord to exclude a structural lesion Assessment for functional signs such as variability and distractibility Sleep study if the relationship to sleep onset is prominent Sudden jerks producing flexion (or occasionally extension) of the trunk, neck and hips, arising from a generator in the spinal cord Jerks characteristically appear or worsen during relaxed wakefulness and the transition to sleep, often when lying down The movements spread slowly up and down the cord from a thoracic or abdominal origin, reflecting conduction along propriospinal pathways Neurophysiology can demonstrate the slow rostro-caudal propagation and a consistent muscle recruitment pattern A substantial proportion of clinically diagnosed cases are ultimately shown to be functional Back-averaging and the presence of a Bereitschaftspotential help distinguish organic from functional cases A structural spinal cord lesion on imaging Associated sensory level, weakness or sphincter disturbance Rapid progression Features suggesting a broader neurological disorder Assuming an organic spinal cause without seeking a Bereitschaftspotential Missing a structural spinal lesion in genuinely lesional cases Confusing it with benign hypnic jerks Not recognising the high proportion of functional cases Propriospinal myoclonus is generated within the spinal cord, with an initial focus in the mid-thoracic region from which activity propagates slowly up and down the cord along propriospinal interneuronal pathways, producing axial jerks. In some patients a structural spinal lesion is found, but many have no identifiable lesion and a significant number are demonstrated to be functional, in which a premovement Bereitschaftspotential and variable, distractible features indicate a voluntary-type mechanism experienced as involuntary. Prognosis varies with cause; lesional cases depend on the underlying pathology, while functional cases can improve with appropriate explanation and therapy, though the disorder is often persistent.

treat symptomatic bacterial prostatitis with antibiotics before biopsy, but routine antibiotics in an asymptomatic patient with elevated PSA are discouraged) Recurrent urinary tract infection as a complication of bladder-outlet obstruction Digital rectal exam (assesses size, symmetry, consistency, nodules; extended 12-core pattern; MRI-guided superior to ultrasound-guided) Gleason grading and the five-tier grade group system (grade group 1 = Gleason <=6 favorable, up to grade group 5 = Gleason 9-10) TNM staging (T1c PSA-detected, T2 palpable organ-confined, T3-T4 extraprostatic); risk stratification into low/intermediate(favorable vs unfavorable)/high/very-high risk PSMA PET scan (FDA approved for intermediate/high-risk disease; more sensitive/specific than conventional imaging but cannot detect low-volume microscopic disease) For BPH: AUA Symptom Index (AUASI) / International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), uroflowmetry, bladder ultrasound for postvoid residual, pressure-flow urodynamics, cystoscopy if hematuria, upper-tract imaging if hematuria/calculi/prior tract problems BPH-related induration on DRE mimicking carcinoma Prostatic calculi causing nodularity Degenerative spine disease, spinal stenosis, or osteoporotic vertebral collapse mimicking metastatic bone pain in advanced disease (require accurate diagnosis before attributing pain to metastases) Direct invasion of the prostate by colon cancer or bladder transitional cell carcinoma (true metastases TO the prostate are rare) Both benign and malignant prostate changes rise sharply with age: autopsies of men in the eighth decade show hyperplastic changes in >90% and malignant changes in >70%, so management is risk-adapted and weighed against competing causes of morbidity and mortality (p.695). BPH arises in the periurethral transition zone surrounding the urethra, whereas most cancers arise in the peripheral zone; peripheral-zone cancers may or may not be palpable on digital rectal exam (DRE) (p.696). BPH causes lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) split into obstructive symptoms (hesitancy, straining, weak stream, terminal dribbling, prolonged voiding, incomplete emptying) and irritative symptoms (frequency, urgency, urge incontinence, small voided volumes); LUTS reflect both prostatic enlargement and age-related detrusor dysfunction, not mass effect alone (p.703). PSA (kallikrein KLK3) is prostate specific, NOT prostate cancer specific: it can rise from prostatitis, BPH, or cancer; a lower free PSA fraction is more likely associated with cancer at biopsy (p.696-697). After radical prostatectomy PSA should become undetectable within about 6 weeks (no prostate = no detectable PSA); persistence of measurable PSA after gland removal is typical of recurrent cancer (p.696-697). Only 20-25% of patients with an abnormal DRE have prostate cancer; carcinoma is characteristically hard, nodular, irregular, asymmetric, but induration can also be BPH or calculi (p.696). >95% of prostate cancers are adenocarcinomas; the remainder are squamous, transitional cell, rarely carcinosarcoma or small-cell histologies (p.697). Most men diagnosed with prostate cancer will NOT die of it; the incidence/mortality ratio is extremely high relative to other malignancies, which drives the active-surveillance vs treatment balance (p.695). Multiparametric prostate MRI (mpMRI) graded by PI-RADS is now obtained in most cases BEFORE biopsy: PI-RADS 1-2 lesions can safely avoid biopsy; PI-RADS 3-5 lesions get targeted biopsy, reducing detection of indolent Gleason 6 (grade group 1) cancers without missing clinically relevant ones (p.697). Osteoblastic bone metastases (prostate cancer characteristically produces bone-forming metastases) presenting as back/skeletal pain; bone is the dominant site of metastatic and castration-resistant progression Spinal cord compression / cord compromise or base-of-skull symptoms from metastatic disease require EMERGENCY evaluation because loss of neurologic function may be permanent if not treated quickly GnRH agonists are relatively contraindicated in patients with significant urinary obstruction, cancer-related pain, or spinal cord compromise because the initial testosterone surge can cause a disease flare (AR antagonists are added to blunt flare; GnRH antagonists and abiraterone do not cause a surge) BPH danger signs mandating evaluation/treatment regardless of gland size: inability to urinate (acute urinary retention), gross hematuria, recurrent infection, or bladder stones Rising nadir PSA >4 ng/mL at 6-8 months after starting androgen deprivation predicts markedly inferior survival Marrow infiltration (myelophthisis), coagulopathy, or thromboembolism as manifestations of widespread metastatic disease PSA screening is controversial: it generates both false positives and false negatives and can lead to diagnosis and treatment of indolent cancers that pose little risk; the decision (USPSTF: individual shared decision for men 55-69, recommended AGAINST screening at age >=70; AUA: shared decision, earlier for Black ancestry/germline mutations/strong family history) must balance benefit against overtreatment harm. PSA is prostate specific, not cancer specific - do not equate an elevated PSA with cancer; BPH and prostatitis also raise it. There is NO PSA level below which prostate cancer risk is zero (Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial); a 'normal' PSA does not exclude cancer. DRE alone is inaccurate for staging (capsular invasion, seminal-vesicle and nodal involvement) and is not a validated screening test by itself. Patients misread Gleason 6 as 'mid-scale' and assume aggressive disease; the grade group system was created because Gleason 6 (grade group 1) is actually the lowest, favorable-risk category. PSMA PET, despite high sensitivity, cannot detect low-volume microscopic nodal disease - a negative scan does not exclude micrometastasis. A negative biopsy in a patient with elevated PSA does NOT rule out a future cancer diagnosis - continue follow-up. No agent is currently approved for prostate cancer prevention (5-alpha-reductase inhibitors reduced mainly low-risk indolent cancers; vitamins/supplements showed no benefit). No rationale to screen asymptomatic men with short life expectancy; antiandrogen monotherapy gives inferior cancer-specific outcomes versus castration. The prostate (pelvic, adjacent to rectum, bladder, neurovascular bundles and urinary sphincter) is composed of tubuloalveolar glands in fibromuscular stroma. PSA is produced by epithelial cells; both epithelial and stromal cells express androgen receptors (AR) and depend on androgens for growth. Testosterone is converted by prostatic 5alpha-reductase to the more potent dihydrotestosterone. BPH is non-malignant proliferation of the periurethral transition zone (begins at puberty, accelerates after age 55) producing bladder-outlet obstruction; symptoms also reflect age-related detrusor dysfunction. Malignancy usually arises in the peripheral zone; the cancer continuum runs from preneoplastic/localized lesion to metastatic, symptomatic, lethal disease over years to decades. Prostate cancer is AR-signaling dependent, so androgen deprivation is the mainstay of metastatic therapy; castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) progresses despite castrate testosterone (<=50 ng/mL) because most CRPCs continue to express and signal through the AR, and androgen-resistant cells are present from diagnosis (cure is not achieved by androgen depletion alone). (p.695-696, 702-703) Most men with prostate cancer do not die from it; >70-80% of newly diagnosed cancers are now organ-confined. Nonmetastatic disease is stratified low/intermediate/high (and very-high) risk; grade group system accurately predicts prognosis with grade group 1 (Gleason <=6) being favorable. A single PSA at age 60 correlates strongly (AUC 0.90) with lifetime risk of death from prostate cancer, and ~90% of prostate-cancer deaths occur in the top PSA quartile (>2 ng/mL), though only a minority of those men develop lethal disease. Androgen deprivation produces an initial response and dormant period but is not curative; PSA normalizes in 60-70% and measurable disease regresses in >50%, with survival inversely proportional to disease extent at treatment start and to the 6-8 month nadir PSA. Castration-resistant prostate cancer is lethal for most patients; multiple agents (abiraterone, enzalutamide, docetaxel, cabazitaxel, radium-223, Lu-177 PSMA-617, PARP inhibitors for BRCA/DNA-repair mutations, checkpoint inhibitors for MSI-high/dMMR) prolong survival. (p.695, 697, 701-703) Gleason grade group system: grade group 1 (Gleason <=6), 2 (3+4=7), 3 (4+3=7), 4 (4+4=8), 5 (Gleason 9-10). TNM staging: T1c clinically inapparent PSA-detected; T2 palpable, confined within prostate; T3 extends through capsule/seminal vesicles (T3b); T4 fixed or invading adjacent structures. Nonmetastatic risk groups: low (organ-confined, PSA <10, grade group 1); intermediate (organ-confined, PSA 10-20, or grade group 2 favorable / 3 unfavorable, with >50% positive cores = unfavorable); high (extraprostatic, PSA >20, or grade group 4-5); very-high (seminal vesicle T3b or adjacent-organ T4 invasion or multiple high-grade biopsy samples). Metastatic states: noncastrate metastatic (testosterone >50 ng/dL) vs castration-resistant (CRPC, testosterone <=50 ng/mL). (p.697-698, 701-703)

Protein-Losing Enteropathy — PLE, intestinal protein loss, gut protein loss Nephrotic syndrome Chronic liver disease with impaired synthesis Malnutrition or inadequate protein intake Malabsorption syndromes Congestive heart failure Sepsis or capillary leak states Serum albumin and total protein Stool alpha-1-antitrypsin (clearance) Serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte count Urinalysis to exclude renal protein loss Endoscopy with biopsy when mucosal disease is suspected Imaging or echocardiography to assess lymphatics and cardiac status This is a syndrome, not a single disease, in which excessive loss of plasma proteins into the gastrointestinal tract leads to hypoproteinaemia and oedema. It should be suspected in a child with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema once liver disease, kidney protein loss, and inadequate intake have been excluded. Underlying mechanisms fall into two broad groups: lymphatic obstruction or elevated lymphatic pressure, and mucosal disease with increased permeability or erosion. Lymphatic causes include intestinal lymphangiectasia and elevated central venous pressure after cardiac surgery (notably the Fontan circulation), while mucosal causes include inflammatory, allergic, infectious, and infiltrative enteropathies. Because losses are non-selective, other serum proteins such as immunoglobulins and clotting factors may also fall, sometimes causing lymphopenia and predisposing to infection. A stool alpha-1-antitrypsin measurement is a useful non-invasive marker of enteric protein loss because it is not degraded in the gut. Management is directed at the underlying cause together with nutritional support, and in lymphatic causes a low-fat diet enriched with medium-chain triglycerides can reduce lymphatic protein loss. Peripheral oedema, ascites, or effusions in a child with unexplained low albumin should prompt evaluation of the gut as a source. Severe hypoalbuminaemia with anasarca, ascites, or effusions Signs of immunodeficiency or recurrent infection from immunoglobulin loss Evidence of underlying serious cardiac or lymphatic disease Growth failure Features of an underlying inflammatory or malignant infiltrative process Attributing hypoalbuminaemia and oedema to renal or hepatic causes without considering the gut Overlooking accompanying immunoglobulin loss and infection risk Failing to identify and treat the specific underlying disorder Neglecting nutritional support and the role of a low-fat, medium-chain triglyceride diet in lymphatic loss Plasma proteins normally enter the gut lumen only in small amounts. In protein-losing enteropathy this loss is markedly increased by one of two general processes. In lymphatic disorders, obstructed or high-pressure intestinal lymphatics (from congenital lymphangiectasia or raised systemic venous pressure, as after Fontan surgery) leak protein-rich lymph into the lumen. In mucosal disorders, inflammation, ulceration, or increased epithelial permeability from infectious, allergic, inflammatory, or infiltrative disease allows serum proteins to escape across the damaged barrier. Because the loss is non-selective, albumin, immunoglobulins, and other proteins are depleted, producing hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and sometimes immune compromise. Outlook depends heavily on the underlying cause; some mucosal causes resolve when the primary disease is treated, whereas lymphangiectasia and Fontan-associated protein loss can be chronic and difficult to manage.

Prototheca species are ubiquitous unicellular algae that lack chlorophyll and reproduce asexually by internal division to form sporangia packed with endospores. Human disease follows inoculation of the organism through skin trauma or, less often, through mucosal or catheter-associated routes. In immunocompetent hosts, infection tends to remain localised as a granulomatous cutaneous or bursal lesion, whereas defects in cell-mediated immunity permit deeper and disseminated spread. The relatively indolent, granulomatous tissue response reflects the organism's slow replication and its resistance to clearance by impaired host defences. Localised cutaneous and bursal disease in immunocompetent hosts responds reasonably well to excision and antifungal therapy, but disseminated infection in the immunocompromised is difficult to treat and carries a poorer outcome, with relapse likely if immune suppression cannot be reduced.

electron microscopy often required in tissue Repeated stool sampling, duodenal fluid aspiration, and small-bowel biopsy when cyst/oocyst excretion is intermittent or low-level Wet-mount microscopy of vaginal or prostatic secretions for motile trichomonads (sensitivity only ~50-60%); NAATs on urine or vaginal/endocervical swabs are first-line Celiac disease / gluten-sensitive enteropathy Tropical sprue Inflammatory bowel disease (for invasive colonic balantidiasis) Functional/chronic diarrhea of uncertain cause Giardia (G. duodenalis, assemblages A and B in humans) is a non-invasive parasite confined to the proximal small bowel that does not spread hematogenously; an inoculum of as few as ~10 cysts can establish infection, and cysts resist routine chlorination but are killed by boiling or filtration. Giardiasis classically presents with upper-intestinal/small-bowel features (nausea, vomiting, bloating, belching, sulfurous flatus, abdominal pain) and non-bloody diarrhea; fever, blood, or mucus in stool point away from giardiasis toward colitis or a concomitant illness. Cryptosporidium (C. hominis, C. parvum) is self-limited (about 1-2 weeks) in immunocompetent hosts but causes chronic, profuse watery diarrhea with stool volumes ranging from 1 to 25 L/day in AIDS patients with CD4 counts below 100/uL. Cystoisospora belli is distinctive among enteric protozoa in that it can produce peripheral eosinophilia in immunocompetent hosts; in AIDS it mimics cryptosporidiosis with chronic profuse watery diarrhea. Cyclospora cayetanensis is linked to foodborne outbreaks from imported produce (basil, sweet peas, raspberries) and waterborne spread, and characteristically causes prolonged diarrhea that may persist beyond one month; absence of fecal blood and leukocytes indicates the small-bowel mucosa is not destroyed. Conventional ova-and-parasite (O+P) stool examination does NOT reliably detect Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, or microsporidia; specific tests (modified acid-fast stain, immunoassays, direct fluorescent antibody, or NAATs) must be requested explicitly. Microsporidia are obligate intracellular spore-forming organisms that are small and gram-positive; they are most often opportunistic in AIDS, where Enterocytozoon bieneusi and Encephalitozoon intestinalis cause chronic diarrhea and wasting and have been found in 10-40% of patients with chronic diarrhea. Encephalitozoon species can disseminate beyond the gut to cause keratoconjunctivitis, sinusitis, bronchiolitis/respiratory disease, cholangitis, nephritis, and cystitis, so microsporidiosis is not solely an intestinal disease. Balantidium coli is a large ciliated protozoan producing a large-bowel disease resembling amebiasis (mucosal invasion, focal necrosis, ulceration); it is zoonotic from pigs and, unlike amebiasis, only rarely disseminates hematogenously to other organs. Blastocystis hominis has uncertain pathogenicity; finding it in stool warrants a full search for other bacterial, viral, or protozoal causes of diarrhea before attributing symptoms to it. Dientamoeba fragilis is unique among intestinal protozoa in having only a trophozoite stage and no cyst stage; immediate fixation of stool improves detection of the labile trophozoites and NAATs outperform microscopy. Trichomonas vaginalis is one of the most prevalent protozoal parasites in the United States (an estimated 2-3 million infections per year); it is essentially always transmitted venereally, and most infected men are asymptomatic, serving as a reservoir for reinfection.
