boiling or submicron filtration is needed Diagnosing trichomonal vaginitis by wet mount alone, given its modest (~50-60%) sensitivity Treating trichomoniasis without concurrently treating sexual partners, leading to apparent treatment failure that is actually reinfection (true high-level metronidazole resistance also occurs) Most of these protozoa are acquired by fecal-oral ingestion of environmentally resistant cysts or oocysts (Trichomonas is the exception, being venereally transmitted). Giardia trophozoites excyst in the small intestine, adhere to but do not invade the proximal small-bowel epithelium, and may cause enterocyte apoptosis, epithelial barrier dysfunction, and malabsorption/secretion; the precise mechanism of diarrhea is unknown, and consequent loss of brush-border enzyme activity produces lactose intolerance and, in some chronic cases, malabsorption with villous flattening resembling tropical sprue or celiac disease. Cryptosporidium sporozoites infect intestinal epithelial cells within an intracellular vacuole, completing asexual and sexual cycles to generate immediately infectious oocysts; the means of secretory diarrhea are uncertain, infection can be patchy in the small bowel, and biliary tract involvement may cause papillary stenosis, sclerosing cholangitis, or cholecystitis, especially in AIDS. Cystoisospora and Cyclospora similarly invade small-bowel epithelial cells (Cyclospora oocysts must mature in the environment before becoming infectious). Microsporidia inject sporoplasm into host cells via an extruded polar tubule and replicate by merogony and sporogony, releasing spores in stool, urine, respiratory secretions, or other fluids. Hypogammaglobulinemia predisposes to prolonged, severe, treatment-refractory giardiasis, indicating humoral immunity is important for control. Outcomes depend heavily on immune status. Giardiasis ranges from asymptomatic carriage to fulminant diarrhea and malabsorption; most patients are cured, though some with chronic infection have delayed symptom resolution attributed to slow brush-border enzyme regeneration, and hypogammaglobulinemic or AIDS patients may have refractory disease. Cryptosporidiosis is self-limited (1-2 weeks) in immunocompetent hosts but can be chronic and severe in AIDS, where improved immune status from antiretroviral therapy can lead to resolution. Cystoisosporiasis and cyclosporiasis can be self-limited but tend to relapse and become chronic in HIV-infected patients. Microsporidiosis can be self-limited in the immunocompetent but contributes to chronic diarrhea and wasting in AIDS, and definitive therapy is not well established. Balantidiasis ranges from asymptomatic to fulminant dysentery; sarcocystosis and most Blastocystis or Dientamoeba infections are mild or self-limited. No formal staging; severity is gauged clinically by host immune status (notably CD4 count below 100/uL marking risk of severe cryptosporidiosis), stool volume and degree of fluid/electrolyte loss (up to 25 L/day in severe cryptosporidiosis), presence of malabsorption/weight loss/wasting, dehydration, growth retardation in children, and biliary or disseminated extraintestinal involvement.

18q deletion syndrome arises from an interstitial loss within the proximal long arm of chromosome 18, sparing the terminal segment. As a contiguous-gene disorder, its features result from haploinsufficiency of the particular dosage-sensitive genes contained in the deleted interval, which differ from those lost in the distal deletion; this accounts for the distinct phenotype, with a greater tendency to seizures and behavioural disturbance and relatively less effect on growth and hearing. The variability in the position and size of the interstitial deletion explains the heterogeneity between individuals. Most affected individuals have intellectual disability of variable degree with behavioural challenges, and seizure control is often an important determinant of function. With appropriate developmental, educational and neurological support, many reach adulthood, though the outlook varies with the extent of the deletion and the severity of epilepsy and behavioural problems.

proximal hamstring tendinopathy — high hamstring tendinopathy, hamstring origin tendinopathy Ischiogluteal bursitis Partial or complete proximal hamstring avulsion Deep gluteal syndrome with sciatic nerve entrapment Ischiofemoral impingement S1 lumbar radiculopathy Ischial apophysitis or apophyseal avulsion in adolescents Referred pain from the sacroiliac joint MRI of the pelvis and proximal thigh centred on the ischial origin Ultrasound to assess tendinosis, guide injection and perform dynamic evaluation Radiographs to identify apophyseal avulsion, enthesophytes or ischial changes Clinical and imaging assessment of the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joint Diagnostic peritendinous local anaesthetic injection Presents as deep, localised lower buttock pain at the ischial tuberosity that is characteristically aggravated by sitting on hard surfaces and by running, lunging and accelerating. Onset is usually insidious and overuse-related, and it is common in distance runners, sprinters and hurdlers. Pain is reproduced by resisted knee flexion and hip extension and by loaded lengthening of the hamstrings, and localises precisely to the ischial origin. Provocation tests such as the Puranen-Orava test, the bent-knee stretch test and the modified bent-knee stretch test help confirm the site. There is a compressive enthesopathic component, as the tendon is loaded against the ischial tuberosity in deep hip flexion, which explains aggravation by sitting and by hip-flexed activities. The sciatic nerve lies immediately deep and lateral to the origin, so peritendinous scarring can generate referred posterior thigh symptoms. Management centres on load management and progressive tendon loading, using isometric then heavy slow or eccentric resistance while correcting lumbopelvic mechanics and initially minimising compressive positions. Recalcitrant cases may be treated with extracorporeal shockwave therapy or peritendinous injections; surgical debridement or reattachment is rarely required. An acute painful pop with weakness and posterior thigh bruising, suggesting a proximal hamstring avulsion that may need timely surgery Progressive neurological deficit in the sciatic distribution Rest or night pain with systemic symptoms, raising concern for a neoplasm around the pelvis or ischium An adolescent with acute pain suggesting ischial apophyseal avulsion Missing a retracted complete avulsion that requires timely surgical repair by mistaking it for tendinopathy. Injecting corticosteroid close to the tendon and sciatic nerve, risking tendon rupture and nerve injury. Inadequate load progression or premature return to sprinting, leading to recurrence. Overlooking a lumbar spine or sacroiliac joint contribution to posterior pain. Repetitive tensile and compressive loading of the conjoint proximal hamstring origin on the ischial tuberosity provokes a failed healing response rather than true inflammation. Histologically there is collagen disorganisation, increased ground substance with mucoid degeneration, and neovascularisation with accompanying neural ingrowth. A compressive, insertional element arises because the tendon is loaded against the bony tuberosity when the hip is flexed, so activities and postures combining flexion with load are particularly provocative. Because the sciatic nerve runs immediately deep and lateral to the enthesis, peritendinous thickening and scarring may tether or irritate the nerve and contribute to posterior thigh symptoms. Symptoms are frequently protracted, but the majority improve with a structured, progressive loading programme over several months. Recalcitrant cases may respond to shockwave therapy or injection, and surgical debridement or reattachment is reserved for the small refractory minority.

Prune belly syndrome — Eagle-Barrett syndrome, triad syndrome, abdominal muscle deficiency syndrome Posterior urethral valves with secondary bladder and upper-tract dilatation Megacystis-microcolon-intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome Congenital bladder outlet obstruction of other cause Primary bilateral vesicoureteric reflux with dysplasia Urethral atresia or stenosis Non-syndromic bilateral cryptorchidism with unrelated hydronephrosis Renal and bladder ultrasound to characterise hydroureteronephrosis and bladder morphology Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) to assess reflux, bladder shape, and urethral anatomy MAG3 (or other radionuclide) renogram to assess differential function and drainage Serum creatinine and electrolytes with serial renal function monitoring Antenatal ultrasound findings and amniotic fluid assessment Echocardiography and skeletal/chest imaging for associated anomalies Defined by a classic triad: deficient or absent abdominal wall musculature, bilateral cryptorchidism, and dilatation of the urinary tract (large hypotonic bladder, dilated tortuous ureters, and hydronephrosis) Predominantly affects males; the wrinkled, lax abdominal wall gives the characteristic prune-like appearance in the neonate The urinary tract dilatation is typically non-obstructive, reflecting a dysmorphic smooth-muscle wall rather than mechanical blockage Renal outcome is dictated by the degree of associated renal dysplasia, which is present in a substantial proportion Associated anomalies are common, including pulmonary hypoplasia (potentially lethal, related to oligohydramnios), cardiac defects, and musculoskeletal deformities such as talipes Antenatal ultrasound may show a distended bladder, hydroureteronephrosis, and oligohydramnios Management is individualised and ranges from conservative surveillance to abdominoplasty, orchidopexy, and urinary tract reconstruction, with prophylactic antibiotics and monitoring of renal function Neonatal respiratory distress from pulmonary hypoplasia, which is a leading cause of early mortality Rising creatinine or oliguria signalling significant renal dysplasia or impairment Recurrent febrile urinary tract infections in a poorly draining, dilated system Signs of true obstruction (e.g. urethral atresia) superimposed on the baseline dilatation Assuming all upper-tract dilatation is obstructive and intervening surgically when the tract is non-obstructive Underestimating pulmonary hypoplasia as the immediate life-threatening problem in the neonate Overlooking associated cardiac, gastrointestinal, and orthopaedic anomalies Delaying orchidopexy for the intra-abdominal testes with implications for fertility and malignancy risk Prune belly syndrome is a rare congenital disorder whose precise cause is uncertain. Leading hypotheses include a primary mesodermal developmental defect affecting the abdominal wall and urinary tract smooth muscle, and transient early urinary tract obstruction producing massive bladder and ureteric distension that secondarily damages the abdominal wall musculature and prevents testicular descent. The result is a thin, poorly muscular abdominal wall, a large hypotonic bladder that often empties incompletely, dilated tortuous ureters with deficient peristalsis, and variable renal dysplasia. Bilateral intra-abdominal testes and, frequently, pulmonary hypoplasia from oligohydramnios complete the picture. Outcome varies widely and is largely determined by the severity of renal dysplasia and pulmonary hypoplasia; severely affected neonates may die from respiratory or renal failure, whereas mildly affected children can have near-normal life expectancy with careful urological and nephrological follow-up.

Prurigo nodularis — nodular prurigo, Hyde prurigo nodularis, chronic nodular prurigo, picker's nodules Hypertrophic lichen planus Lichen simplex chronicus Bullous pemphigoid (nodular/prurigo variant) hyperkeratotic nodules arising from a self-perpetuating itch-scratch cycle Nodules are typically symmetrical on the extensor limbs and trunk, sparing the mid-back where the hand cannot reach ('butterfly sign') Excoriation, crusting, and post-inflammatory hyper- or hypopigmentation commonly accompany the nodules It is a reaction pattern rather than a single disease, so an underlying cause of chronic pruritus should be sought Associated conditions include atopic dermatitis, chronic kidney disease, hepatobiliary disease, thyroid dysfunction, HIV, and, less commonly, lymphoma Neural hyperplasia and upregulation of itch-related mediators contribute to the persistence and severity of the pruritus Breaking the itch-scratch cycle is central to management, alongside treating any Rapidly growing or ulcerated nodules raising concern for malignancy Severe intractable itch with sleep disturbance and marked impairment of quality of life Treating the nodules symptomatically without investigating an underlying systemic cause of pruritus Missing an underlying bullous pemphigoid presenting in a prurigo-like form Underestimating the psychological impact and role of scratching behaviour Overlooking malignancy in solitary, rapidly changing, or ulcerated lesions Prurigo nodularis develops when chronic, intense pruritus drives repetitive scratching and rubbing, producing hyperkeratotic, fibrotic nodules. Persistent mechanical trauma and neuroimmune activation lead to dermal fibrosis, epidermal hyperplasia, and proliferation of cutaneous nerve fibres, with increased expression of pruritogenic cytokines and neuropeptides that sensitise itch pathways. This establishes a self-sustaining itch-scratch cycle. The underlying pruritus may be dermatological, systemic (renal, hepatic, haematological, endocrine), neuropathic, or psychogenic, so the nodules represent a common end-point rather than a distinct primary disorder. Prurigo nodularis is typically chronic and difficult to treat, with lesions persisting for months to years; outcome improves when an underlying cause is identified and treated and when the itch-scratch cycle can be interrupted.

prurigo of pregnancy — prurigo gestationis, Besnier prurigo gestationis, early-onset prurigo of pregnancy atopic eruption of pregnancy (eczematous and papular types) polymorphic eruption of pregnancy pemphigoid gestationis intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy scabies insect bite reactions folliculitis or pruritic folliculitis of pregnancy serum bile acids and liver function tests to exclude obstetric cholestasis total serum IgE (frequently elevated) skin biopsy if diagnosis uncertain (non-specific with parakeratosis, acanthosis and dermal inflammation) direct immunofluorescence to exclude pemphigoid gestationis in atypical cases skin scrapings for scabies mites where itch is severe and contacts affected full blood count for eosinophilia Presents with grouped excoriated papules and nodules, typically on the extensor surfaces of the limbs and sometimes the trunk. Often arises earlier than polymorphic eruption, commonly in the second trimester between around 25 and 30 weeks. Now widely regarded as part of the atopic eruption of pregnancy spectrum, occurring in women with an atopic diathesis. Lesions frequently show central excoriation or crusting reflecting the intense scratching that drives the picture. Diagnosis is clinical; there are no diagnostic laboratory findings and direct immunofluorescence is negative. Total serum IgE may be raised, reflecting the underlying atopic tendency. It is benign for mother and fetus, with no reported increase in adverse pregnancy outcomes. Management centres on emollients, topical corticosteroids and antihistamines, with attention to a possible atopic flare. widespread pruritus without primary lesions and abnormal bile acids indicating intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy tense blisters or umbilical involvement suggesting pemphigoid gestationis jaundice, pale stools or dark urine pointing to hepatobiliary disease burrows, involvement of web spaces or affected household contacts suggesting scabies signs of secondary bacterial infection of excoriated lesions Attributing generalised pruritus to prurigo and failing to measure bile acids, thereby missing intrahepatic cholestasis with its fetal risk. Overlooking scabies, which can closely mimic prurigo and requires treatment of contacts. Undertreating pruritus so the itch-scratch cycle perpetuates nodules and secondary infection. Regarding it as entirely distinct from atopic eruption of pregnancy and missing a broader atopic flare needing eczema care. Confusing persistent post-delivery lesions with treatment failure rather than expected slow resolution. Prurigo of pregnancy is considered a manifestation of an atopic tendency unmasked or exacerbated by the immunological shift of pregnancy. The normal gestational skew from T-helper-1 towards T-helper-2 cytokine dominance favours the atopic phenotype, promoting pruritus and the prurigo reaction pattern. Repeated scratching in response to itch produces the characteristic excoriated papules and nodules through a chronic itch-scratch cycle rather than a primary blistering or autoimmune process. There is no autoantibody and no consistent hormonal trigger, and the condition overlaps clinically and conceptually with the eczematous and papular forms grouped under atopic eruption of pregnancy. Benign and self-limiting, usually resolving in the weeks after delivery, although lesions and post-inflammatory pigmentation may persist for some weeks. There is no fetal risk, but recurrence in subsequent pregnancies can occur given the underlying atopic predisposition.

Prurigo pigmentosa — Nagashima disease, keto rash, prurigo pigmentosa Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis Dermatitis herpetiformis Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis Urticaria or urticarial dermatitis Ashy dermatosis / erythema dyschromicum perstans (for the pigmented phase) Transient acantholytic dermatosis (Grover disease) Pityriasis rosea Detailed dietary and weight history covering ketogenic dieting, fasting, and anorexia, together with diabetic control Urine or blood ketones and blood glucose or HbA1c where ketosis or diabetes is suspected Skin biopsy of an early papule showing a superficial neutrophilic infiltrate and of older lesions showing pigment incontinence A trial of a tetracycline as a supportive therapeutic test Direct immunofluorescence to exclude dermatitis herpetiformis if the diagnosis is unclear Presents with recurrent crops of intensely itchy erythematous papules and papulovesicles that resolve to leave a striking reticulate (net-like) hyperpigmentation Characteristically affects the trunk, particularly the back, chest, neck, and sacral area, in a symmetrical pattern First well described in and more frequently reported from Japan but recognised worldwide, typically in young adults and more often women Strongly linked to states of ketosis, including ketogenic and low-carbohydrate diets, fasting, poorly controlled diabetes with ketoacidosis, and anorexia, hence the lay term keto rash The active inflammatory papules are itchy, whereas the residual reticulate pigmentation is asymptomatic and can persist for months Ketone bodies are thought to accumulate around dermal vessels and provoke a neutrophilic and then lymphocytic inflammatory reaction Responds rapidly to tetracyclines (such as minocycline or doxycycline) or dapsone and to correction of the ketotic state with reintroduction of carbohydrate Topical corticosteroids are relatively ineffective, which itself is a useful diagnostic clue Underlying diabetic ketoacidosis presenting with the eruption and requiring urgent metabolic management Significant undernutrition or an eating disorder driving the ketosis Failure to respond to tetracyclines, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Failing to ask about ketogenic dieting, fasting, or diabetes Treating with topical corticosteroids, which typically do not work Mistaking the residual reticulate pigmentation for a primary pigmentary disorder Overlooking diabetic ketoacidosis as a precipitant The mechanism is incompletely understood, but the strong association with ketosis suggests that circulating ketone bodies accumulate around dermal blood vessels and act as a trigger for a sterile inflammatory response. Early lesions show a superficial neutrophilic infiltrate that evolves through a lichenoid or interface phase and finally leaves dermal melanophages, which accounts for the characteristic residual reticulate pigmentation. The dramatic response to tetracyclines and to correction of ketosis, together with the poor response to topical corticosteroids, supports a distinctive neutrophil-driven, metabolically triggered process rather than a simple eczematous or allergic reaction. Benign; the itchy papules clear rapidly with treatment and correction of ketosis, though the reticulate pigmentation fades slowly and recurrences accompany renewed ketotic states.

Pseudo-Hurler polydystrophy (mucolipidosis III) — mucolipidosis III, ML III, ML III alpha/beta (GNPTAB), ML III gamma (GNPTG), N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase deficiency (partial) epiphyseal dysplasia and other skeletal dysplasias Progressive pseudorheumatoid dysplasia Other lysosomal storage disorders with slowly progressive arthropathy Plasma or serum assay of multiple lysosomal enzymes showing raised activity Cultured fibroblast studies demonstrating reduced intracellular enzyme activity GNPTAB and GNPTG gene sequencing to define the subtype Skeletal survey and hip imaging for dysplasia Echocardiography for valvular involvement Slit-lamp examination for corneal changes Represents the milder, later-onset counterpart of I-cell disease within the same mannose-6-phosphate targeting pathway Results from partial deficiency of GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase, so lysosomal enzyme mistargeting is incomplete Presents in mid-childhood with progressive joint stiffness, particularly of the shoulders and hands, and slowly progressive skeletal changes Cognition is normal or only mildly affected, in contrast to the severe course of mucolipidosis II Like I-cell disease, plasma lysosomal enzyme activities are elevated while intracellular activities are reduced Two genetic forms exist: ML III alpha/beta from GNPTAB variants and ML III gamma from GNPTG variants Hip dysplasia, aortic valve involvement, and mild corneal changes can develop over time Progressive hip destruction impairing mobility Aortic or mitral valve dysfunction Cervical spine involvement with instability Marked functional decline from advancing joint contractures Mistaking early joint stiffness for inflammatory arthritis and delaying metabolic diagnosis Assuming normal intellect excludes a lysosomal disorder Overlooking the diagnostic pattern of high plasma lysosomal enzyme activity Failing to distinguish the milder ML III course from severe ML II Pseudo-Hurler polydystrophy is caused by partial deficiency of UDP-N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, the enzyme that generates the mannose-6-phosphate signal directing lysosomal hydrolases to the lysosome. Variants in GNPTAB (alpha/beta subunits, ML III alpha/beta) or GNPTG (gamma subunit, ML III gamma) leave greater residual phosphotransferase function than in mucolipidosis II, so enzyme mistargeting is incomplete and disease is milder and slower. Lysosomal hydrolases are partly secreted rather than delivered intracellularly, giving the same biochemical pattern of high plasma and low cellular enzyme activity, with gradual accumulation of undegraded substrate. The predominant clinical burden is on connective tissue and the skeleton. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The course is slowly progressive, and many patients survive into adulthood; the main long-term burden comes from joint contractures, hip disease, and cardiac valve involvement, which can cause significant disability.

are normal, distinguishing it clinically from achondroplasia, but there is marked ligamentous laxity and early progressive joint pain Radiographs show generalised epiphyseal and metaphyseal especially before anaesthesia Rapidly progressive lower-limb malalignment impairing walking Severe early-onset joint pain limiting function Neurological deficit suggesting spinal cord compression anaesthesia or sport Failing to anticipate and manage early degenerative joint disease Pseudoachondroplasia is caused by dominant variants in COMP, a glycoprotein of the cartilage extracellular matrix. Mutant protein is retained within the endoplasmic reticulum of chondrocytes rather than being secreted, forming characteristic inclusions and provoking cellular stress that impairs chondrocyte function and premature cell death. Disrupted cartilage matrix in the growth plates and articular surfaces causes disproportionate short stature, epiphyseal and metaphyseal abnormalities, joint laxity, and premature degenerative joint disease. Lifespan and intelligence are normal, but adult stature is significantly reduced and premature osteoarthritis, particularly of the hips and knees, frequently necessitates joint replacement in adulthood. Cervical instability requires vigilance to prevent neurological injury.

Pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia — PASH, Pseudoangiomatous hyperplasia of mammary stroma Low-grade angiosarcoma Fibroadenoma Benign phyllodes tumour Myofibroblastoma of the breast Hamartoma Fibromatosis Gynaecomastia (in male patients) Breast ultrasound to characterise a circumscribed solid mass Mammography as part of triple assessment Core needle biopsy for histological diagnosis Immunohistochemistry with CD34, factor VIII and hormone receptors MRI for large or rapidly enlarging lesions Excisional biopsy where imaging and pathology are discordant Interval imaging follow-up of conservatively managed lesions A benign myofibroblastic proliferation of breast stroma in which slit-like spaces mimic the vascular channels of a vascular lesion. Often an incidental microscopic finding, but can form a discrete palpable or mammographic mass (tumoural PASH). Typically affects premenopausal women or those exposed to hormones, reflecting the hormone responsiveness of the myofibroblasts. Also recognised as a common stromal component underlying gynaecomastia in men. Imaging shows a well-circumscribed, non-calcified oval mass that can resemble a fibroadenoma. The pseudovascular slits are lined by CD34-positive, factor VIII-negative myofibroblasts, distinguishing it from a true angiosarcoma. Small asymptomatic lesions confirmed on biopsy can be observed; symptomatic or enlarging masses are excised. Recurrence after excision can occur, but PASH has no metastatic potential. Rapid enlargement of a stromal breast mass Histological atypia, mitoses or true vascular channels suggesting angiosarcoma Discordance between benign biopsy and suspicious imaging Recurrent or multifocal rapidly growing lesions Skin involvement or diffuse breast enlargement Mistaking the pseudovascular slits for the channels of a low-grade angiosarcoma Confusing a tumoural mass with a fibroadenoma and not confirming histologically Over-treating small incidental microscopic PASH found on biopsy for another reason Failing to correlate benign histology with imaging, missing a discordant lesion Overlooking PASH as the stromal basis of male gynaecomastia Pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia results from proliferation of myofibroblasts within the interlobular breast stroma, producing a network of anastomosing, empty, slit-like spaces set in dense collagenous tissue. These spaces superficially resemble vascular channels but contain no red cells and are lined by spindled myofibroblasts rather than endothelium, hence the term pseudoangiomatous. The myofibroblasts express hormone receptors, and the lesion's association with the reproductive years, hormone therapy and gynaecomastia points to hormonal, particularly progestogenic, stimulation as a driver of the proliferation. The process is entirely benign and lacks the cytological atypia, mitoses and true vascular differentiation of angiosarcoma. PASH is benign with an excellent prognosis and no malignant or metastatic potential. Local recurrence may follow incomplete excision or reflect ongoing hormonal stimulation, but does not indicate malignant behaviour.

pseudochylothorax — chyliform pleural effusion, cholesterol pleurisy True chylothorax Empyema (may also appear turbid or milky) Parapneumonic effusion Malignant pleural effusion Rheumatoid or other connective tissue disease effusion Chronic tuberculous pleural effusion Pleural fluid cholesterol and triglyceride levels Pleural fluid microscopy for cholesterol crystals and lipoprotein analysis for chylomicrons Pleural fluid cell count, protein, LDH, glucose and pH (Light's criteria) Pleural fluid adenosine deaminase and mycobacterial culture for tuberculosis Rheumatoid factor and connective tissue serology CT thorax to assess pleural thickening, calcification and trapped lung Pleural biopsy where the underlying cause remains unclear Pseudochylothorax is a cholesterol-rich, lipid-laden pleural effusion that looks milky or turbid but arises from chronic pleural inflammation rather than thoracic duct disruption. It classically develops in long-standing effusions (often present for years) with markedly thickened, fibrotic or calcified pleura. The two commonest causes are chronic tuberculous pleuritis and rheumatoid pleuritis; historical artificial (therapeutic) pneumothorax is another. It is distinguished from true chylothorax biochemically: pseudochylothorax has high cholesterol (typically markedly elevated) and/or cholesterol crystals, with low triglycerides and no chylomicrons. True chylothorax, by contrast, has high triglycerides and chylomicrons and reflects a thoracic duct leak. Cholesterol crystals appear as rhomboid, notched plates on polarised light microscopy of the fluid. Many patients are relatively asymptomatic despite turbid fluid, with symptoms determined by the underlying disease and any trapped lung. Management targets the underlying cause, with therapeutic aspiration for symptoms and decortication reserved for trapped lung or persistent symptomatic effusion. Features suggesting active tuberculosis (fever, weight loss) requiring treatment A new or enlarging pleural mass raising concern for malignancy Signs of superimposed empyema or sepsis Progressive breathlessness from a trapped, non-expandable lung Confusing pseudochylothorax with true chylothorax and pursuing an unnecessary search for thoracic duct injury. Assuming turbid fluid always represents empyema. Overlooking underlying tuberculosis or rheumatoid disease that needs specific treatment. Repeatedly aspirating a trapped lung without addressing the underlying pleural thickening. Pseudochylothorax develops when a pleural effusion persists for a prolonged period within a thickened, poorly reabsorbing pleural space. Chronic inflammation and slow fluid turnover lead to accumulation of cholesterol and lecithin-globulin complexes, probably derived from degenerating red and white cells, within the trapped fluid. The fibrotic pleura impairs lipid clearance, so cholesterol concentrates and may crystallise, producing the characteristic opalescent, turbid appearance. Because the retained lipid is cholesterol rather than triglyceride-rich chyle, the thoracic duct is intact, which is the key distinction from chylothorax. The condition is generally benign and its outlook is dictated by the underlying disease; the effusion itself is chronic and often stable, though a trapped lung may cause persistent breathlessness that requires decortication.

Pseudoexfoliation glaucoma — PXF glaucoma, PEX glaucoma, exfoliation glaucoma, pseudoexfoliation syndrome Primary open-angle glaucoma Pigmentary glaucoma True exfoliation (capsular delamination) from heat or infrared exposure Uveitic glaucoma with anterior segment deposits Amyloid deposition in the anterior segment Phacolytic or lens-related glaucoma Dilated slit-lamp examination for the target-like lens deposits, pupillary ruff changes, and phacodonesis Gonioscopy to assess trabecular pigmentation and exclude angle closure Applanation tonometry with attention to pressure fluctuation OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer to quantify glaucomatous damage Automated perimetry to monitor field loss Assessment of zonular integrity before planning cataract surgery A common secondary open-angle glaucoma caused by deposition of greyish-white fibrillar pseudoexfoliation material throughout the anterior segment that obstructs the trabecular meshwork The classic lens sign is a central disc and a peripheral band of deposited material separated by a clear zone where the mobile iris wipes the surface Deposits and pigment loss at the pupillary ruff, along with dense trabecular pigmentation on gonioscopy, are supportive signs, and dilation may reveal material on the lens periphery and zonules It is a systemic elastic-tissue disorder linked to variants in the LOXL1 gene, with material also found in extraocular tissues Zonular weakness is a hallmark, increasing the risk of lens subluxation, capsule rupture, and vitreous loss during cataract surgery, and phacodonesis may be visible Intraocular pressure is often higher and more fluctuating than in primary open-angle glaucoma, so the disease can be more aggressive with poorer prognosis Treatment lowers pressure with topical agents and laser trabeculoplasty, which often works well initially, with drainage surgery reserved for uncontrolled cases Both eyes should be examined even when signs appear unilateral, as involvement is frequently asymmetric Very high or widely fluctuating intraocular pressure driving rapid optic-nerve damage Phacodonesis or lens subluxation warning of high surgical risk from zonular weakness Advanced field loss at presentation because the disease was under-recognised Sudden pressure decompensation or angle closure from lens instability Failing to dilate the pupil and missing the peripheral lens deposits that confirm the diagnosis Underestimating the aggressive pressure behaviour and monitoring too infrequently Not anticipating zonular weakness and capsule instability during cataract surgery Mistaking dense trabecular pigment for pigmentary glaucoma Assuming the fellow eye is unaffected without examining it Pseudoexfoliation is a generalised disorder of elastic microfibril metabolism, strongly associated with variants in the LOXL1 gene, in which abnormal greyish fibrillar material is produced and deposited in ocular and systemic tissues. In the eye this material accumulates on the anterior lens capsule, pupil margin, zonules, ciliary body, iris, and corneal endothelium. Material and liberated iris pigment progressively obstruct the trabecular meshwork and damage trabecular cells, reducing aqueous outflow and raising intraocular pressure, often with large fluctuations. Deposition also weakens the zonular apparatus, predisposing to lens instability. The optic nerve sustains glaucomatous damage that tends to progress more rapidly than in primary open-angle glaucoma. Pseudoexfoliation glaucoma generally follows a more aggressive course than primary open-angle glaucoma, with higher and more variable pressures and faster progression, so close monitoring is needed; cataract surgery carries elevated risk from zonular weakness but may itself modestly lower pressure.

Pseudogout (acute CPP crystal arthritis) — acute CPP crystal arthritis, calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis, pseudogout, acute CPPD arthritis Gout (urate crystal arthritis) Septic arthritis Acute flare of osteoarthritis Rheumatoid arthritis Reactive arthritis Haemarthrosis or trauma Joint aspiration with polarised microscopy for positively birefringent rhomboid CPP crystals and to exclude sepsis Synovial fluid Gram stain, culture, and cell count Radiographs to demonstrate chondrocalcinosis Metabolic screen in younger or atypical cases: ferritin and transferrin saturation, calcium and parathyroid hormone, magnesium, and alkaline phosphatase Ultrasound to detect crystal deposition within cartilage Serum urate to help distinguish the condition from gout An acute crystal-induced arthritis caused by calcium pyrophosphate (CPP) crystals, presenting as a hot, swollen, painful joint that clinically mimics gout or septic arthritis The knee is the most commonly affected joint, followed by the wrist; the first metatarsophalangeal joint, so classic for gout, is less typically involved Synovial fluid polarised microscopy shows rhomboid or rod-shaped, weakly positively birefringent CPP crystals, in contrast to the needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals of urate Radiographs frequently show chondrocalcinosis, the linear calcification of fibrocartilage (such as the knee menisci and the triangular fibrocartilage of the wrist) and hyaline cartilage Attacks may be provoked by intercurrent illness, surgery, or trauma, and increasing age is a strong risk factor Younger patients or florid, polyarticular disease should prompt a search for metabolic associations, particularly haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia, and hypophosphatasia Acute attacks are treated with anti-inflammatory measures (a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, colchicine, a corticosteroid, or joint aspiration and injection), as no therapy dissolves CPP crystals A hot swollen joint that could be septic arthritis until proven otherwise Chondrocalcinosis in a young patient signalling an underlying metabolic disease Systemic upset with fever closely mimicking infection Assuming a hot joint is gout without confirming the crystal type on microscopy Missing an underlying metabolic disorder in a young patient with chondrocalcinosis Failing to exclude septic arthritis Expecting urate-lowering therapy to help, when it has no effect on CPP crystals Calcium pyrophosphate crystals form within cartilage, producing chondrocalcinosis, as a result of altered inorganic pyrophosphate metabolism and calcium handling in ageing or metabolically abnormal cartilage. Shedding of these crystals into the joint space triggers their phagocytosis and an inflammasome-driven inflammatory response similar to that of gout, producing the acute attack. Underlying metabolic disorders such as haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, and hypomagnesaemia predispose to crystal formation, which is why they must be considered, particularly in younger patients. Individual acute attacks are self-limiting and respond to anti-inflammatory treatment, but recurrent attacks and chronic CPP-related joint damage are common; because no treatment removes the crystals, management is directed at symptoms and at any underlying metabolic cause.

Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 — PHA1, NR3C2, mineralocorticoid receptor deficiency, ENaC loss-of-function, SCNN1A, SCNN1B, SCNN1G, aldosterone resistance Primary adrenal insufficiency (aldosterone deficiency, e.g. salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia) Aldosterone synthase deficiency Transient pseudohypoaldosteronism secondary to urinary tract infection or obstructive uropathy in infants Cystic fibrosis (salt loss with respiratory disease, mimicking the systemic form) Renal tubular acidosis type 4 Congenital adrenal hypoplasia Serum sodium, potassium and bicarbonate to document salt-wasting hyperkalaemic acidosis Plasma renin and aldosterone (both markedly elevated) Urinary electrolytes to confirm renal sodium loss Sweat chloride testing to assess systemic involvement and exclude cystic fibrosis Renal tract imaging to exclude secondary/transient causes such as obstruction or infection Molecular genetic testing of NR3C2 and the ENaC subunit genes Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 is a state of target-organ resistance to aldosterone, so despite very high aldosterone the kidney cannot retain sodium normally The autosomal dominant (renal) form is due to loss-of-function variants in NR3C2, the mineralocorticoid receptor, and tends to be milder and to improve with age The autosomal recessive (systemic) form is due to loss-of-function variants in the epithelial sodium channel subunits (SCNN1A, SCNN1B, SCNN1G) and is more severe and persistent The biochemical signature is salt wasting with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis, alongside markedly elevated renin and aldosterone In the systemic form, sodium loss also affects sweat, salivary glands and colon, and recurrent respiratory symptoms can mimic cystic fibrosis It is effectively the mirror image of Liddle syndrome, with an underactive rather than overactive sodium channel pathway Management rests on generous sodium supplementation and control of hyperkalaemia; the recessive systemic form typically needs lifelong high-dose salt replacement Life-threatening neonatal salt-wasting crisis with severe hyperkalaemia Cardiac arrhythmia from hyperkalaemia Severe dehydration and circulatory collapse Failure to thrive despite feeding Recurrent respiratory infections in the systemic form Misdiagnosing it as adrenal insufficiency and giving mineralocorticoid replacement, which is ineffective because the defect is resistance, not deficiency Failing to distinguish the transient secondary form (infection/obstruction) from inherited disease Overlooking systemic salt loss and confusing the recessive form with cystic fibrosis Underestimating the very large sodium requirements of the systemic form Not appreciating the mode of inheritance when counselling families Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 is caused by failure of aldosterone signalling in the distal nephron. In the dominant renal form, loss-of-function variants in the mineralocorticoid receptor gene NR3C2 blunt the response to aldosterone; in the recessive systemic form, loss-of-function variants in the epithelial sodium channel subunits prevent sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct and in other epithelia. Because sodium cannot be reabsorbed and the electrochemical gradient for potassium and hydrogen secretion is lost, the kidney wastes salt while retaining potassium and hydrogen ion, producing hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis. The salt loss and hypovolaemia strongly stimulate renin and aldosterone, but the target tissues cannot respond, so the very high hormone levels coexist with continued salt wasting. The dominant renal form often attenuates with age and may need little treatment in adulthood, whereas the recessive systemic form is severe, persists lifelong, and requires continuous salt supplementation and careful management of hyperkalaemia.

Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2 — PHA2, Gordon syndrome, familial hyperkalaemic hypertension, WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3, CUL3 Chronic kidney disease with hyperkalaemia and hypertension Renal tubular acidosis type 4 (hypoaldosteronism) Addison disease / primary adrenal insufficiency Drug-induced hyperkalaemia (RAAS inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics) Primary hypertension with incidental hyperkalaemia Diabetic hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism Serum potassium, chloride and bicarbonate to define hyperkalaemic hyperchloraemic acidosis Plasma renin (suppressed) and aldosterone Renal function to demonstrate hyperkalaemia despite preserved glomerular filtration Review of medications that raise potassium Assessment of blood-pressure and biochemical response to thiazide therapy Molecular genetic testing of WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3 and CUL3 Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2, also called Gordon syndrome or familial hyperkalaemic hypertension, is caused by variants in WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3 or CUL3 that increase activity of the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule The characteristic combination is hypertension with hyperkalaemia and a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, essentially the mirror image of Gitelman syndrome Renin is suppressed while aldosterone is variable, and importantly hyperkalaemia occurs despite a normal glomerular filtration rate Excess distal sodium-chloride reabsorption expands volume and reduces the sodium delivery needed for distal potassium and hydrogen secretion, causing potassium and acid retention It responds strikingly to a thiazide diuretic, which inhibits the overactive cotransporter and corrects both the blood pressure and the electrolyte abnormalities The KLHL3 and CUL3 variants disrupt the ubiquitin-mediated degradation of WNK kinases, increasing their signalling to the cotransporter Consider it in patients with hyperkalaemia and hypertension that seem out of proportion to renal function Severe hyperkalaemia with electrocardiographic changes Resistant hypertension with end-organ damage Marked acidosis Family history of early hypertension with hyperkalaemia Attributing hyperkalaemia to renal failure when the glomerular filtration rate is actually preserved Prescribing renin-angiotensin blockade for the hypertension, which can worsen the hyperkalaemia Missing the diagnosis by not recognising the mirror-image relationship to Gitelman syndrome Overlooking the excellent and specific response to thiazide treatment Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2 results from dysregulation of the WNK kinase signalling network that controls the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Variants in WNK1 or WNK4, or in the KLHL3 and CUL3 components of the ubiquitin ligase complex that normally degrades WNK kinases, lead to excessive kinase activity and increased cotransporter abundance and function. Enhanced distal sodium-chloride reabsorption expands extracellular volume and raises blood pressure, and by consuming luminal sodium it reduces the electrochemical driving force for potassium and hydrogen secretion in the downstream nephron. The net effect is salt-dependent, low-renin hypertension with hyperkalaemia and a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, which is reversed by inhibiting the cotransporter with a thiazide. Prognosis is generally excellent because low-dose thiazide therapy typically normalises blood pressure and electrolytes; untreated disease carries the usual cardiovascular risks of hypertension and the hazards of hyperkalaemia.
