rounded face, and shortened metacarpals Resistance may extend to other Gs-coupled hormones, producing features such as hypothyroidism from TSH resistance Parental origin of the mutation influences the phenotype because GNAS is subject to tissue-specific imprinting Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism shares the physical phenotype but has normal calcium biochemistry Symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany, laryngospasm or seizures requiring urgent correction Prolonged QT interval on the electrocardiogram from severe hypocalcaemia Features of resistance to multiple hormones indicating broad Gs-alpha involvement Ectopic ossification or other complications requiring specialist assessment Mistaking the high-PTH, low-calcium pattern for secondary hyperparathyroidism of renal disease Confusing pseudohypoparathyroidism with pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism, which has normal calcium Overlooking coexisting hormone resistance such as subclinical hypothyroidism Aiming for high-normal calcium and risking hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis Parathyroid hormone acts through a receptor that signals via the stimulatory G-protein to generate cyclic AMP in target tissues such as kidney and bone. In pseudohypoparathyroidism, GNAS mutations impair this Gs-alpha signalling, so target organs fail to respond to PTH despite adequate or elevated hormone levels. The renal resistance reduces calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion, producing hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia, while the low calcium drives compensatory secondary rises in PTH. Because GNAS is imprinted, the parent from whom the mutation is inherited determines whether multi-hormone resistance and the osteodystrophy phenotype are expressed. With calcium and active vitamin D therapy guided by PTH and calcium targets, biochemical control and symptom prevention are generally achievable, although the skeletal phenotype and any additional hormone resistance persist and require ongoing management.

Pseudomyxoma peritonei — jelly belly, gelatinous ascites, mucinous ascites of the peritoneum Malignant ascites from ovarian, gastric, colorectal, or pancreatic carcinoma Mucinous ovarian tumour with peritoneal spread Peritoneal carcinomatosis of other origin Cirrhotic or transudative ascites Peritoneal tuberculosis Mucinous neoplasm of the colon or pancreas Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) showing loculated mucinous ascites with scalloping of visceral surfaces Assessment of the appendix as the likely primary site Tumour markers including CEA, CA19-9, and CA125 for baseline and monitoring Colonoscopy and gastrointestinal evaluation to identify or exclude a bowel primary Histological and cytological examination of mucin and peritoneal deposits with grading Immunohistochemistry to confirm gastrointestinal (often appendiceal) origin A clinical syndrome of progressive accumulation of gelatinous mucinous material within the peritoneal cavity, colloquially termed jelly belly Most cases originate from a low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm; ovarian involvement is usually secondary, so a coexisting ovarian mucinous tumour is often a metastasis rather than the source Presents insidiously with increasing abdominal distension, a rising waistband, vague discomfort, and sometimes a new hernia or reduced appetite Mucin preferentially redistributes to dependent and low-flow areas of the peritoneum while relatively sparing the small bowel surface, the so-called redistribution phenomenon Imaging shows loculated, non-mobile mucinous ascites with characteristic scalloping of the liver and splenic margins Graded from low-grade (disseminated peritoneal adenomucinosis) to high-grade mucinous carcinomatosis, which strongly influences outcome Optimal treatment is cytoreductive surgery combined with heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy at specialist centres Progressive abdominal distension with gelatinous ascites and a suspected appendiceal lesion Signs of bowel obstruction from accumulating mucin High-grade histology indicating mucinous carcinomatosis Nutritional decline or a new hernia signalling advanced intra-abdominal disease Attributing the disease to a primary ovarian mucinous tumour and overlooking the appendiceal source Simply draining mucinous ascites without addressing the underlying neoplasm Underestimating low-grade disease as benign despite its relentless progression Managing complex cases outside specialist cytoreduction and intraperitoneal chemotherapy centres Pseudomyxoma peritonei develops when mucin-producing neoplastic epithelial cells disseminate across the peritoneum and secrete copious mucin that gradually fills the abdominal cavity. In the great majority the primary lesion is a low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm that perforates and seeds the peritoneum; the appendiceal wall ruptures and epithelial cells and mucin escape, then follow peritoneal fluid currents to accumulate in dependent regions while largely sparing the peristaltic small bowel. Because the ovaries lie in a dependent position and readily take up peritoneal deposits, apparent ovarian mucinous tumours in this setting are frequently secondary. The tumour cells are typically indolent but the relentless mucin production causes mass effect, bowel obstruction, and nutritional decline, so the disease is defined more by its progressive local behaviour than by distant metastasis. Highly dependent on grade and completeness of surgery; low-grade disease treated with complete cytoreduction and intraperitoneal chemotherapy can achieve prolonged survival, whereas high-grade mucinous carcinomatosis carries a markedly worse outlook, and the disease tends to recur and progress locally over time.

Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism — PPHP Pseudohypoparathyroidism Primary hypoparathyroidism Other causes of brachydactyly or short stature Acrodysostosis Turner syndrome Serum calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone (normal) Assessment of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy features GNAS genetic testing and parent-of-origin assessment Radiographs for brachydactyly and ossifications Family evaluation and genetic counselling A condition with the physical features of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy but normal calcium and normal parathyroid hormone responsiveness Features of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy include short stature, a round face, brachydactyly (notably short fourth metacarpals) and subcutaneous ossifications Unlike pseudohypoparathyroidism, there is no hormone resistance and biochemistry is normal It is caused by GNAS mutations inherited from the father, whereas maternal inheritance of the same mutation causes pseudohypoparathyroidism (an example of imprinting) It sits within the same family as pseudohypoparathyroidism and is distinguished biochemically Management is mainly of the skeletal and cosmetic features, with genetic counselling Biochemical hormone resistance, which would indicate pseudohypoparathyroidism instead Significant functional impact of ossifications Features suggesting an alternative syndrome Associated endocrine abnormalities suggesting resistance Confusing it with pseudohypoparathyroidism despite normal biochemistry Overlooking the imprinting/parent-of-origin basis in counselling Attributing brachydactyly to another syndrome Missing the diagnosis in a relative of a pseudohypoparathyroidism patient Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism arises from a heterozygous inactivating GNAS mutation affecting the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G protein. Because GNAS is imprinted, the phenotype depends on the parent of origin: paternal transmission produces the Albright hereditary osteodystrophy physical phenotype without hormone resistance (pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism), whereas maternal transmission additionally causes resistance to parathyroid hormone and other hormones (pseudohypoparathyroidism) because the maternal allele is the active one in key tissues. Hence calcium and parathyroid hormone signalling are normal here despite the shared skeletal features. The condition is benign biochemically, and prognosis relates to the skeletal and cosmetic features rather than to calcium disturbance.

Pseudoxanthoma elasticum — PXE, Groenblad-Strandberg syndrome, ABCC6-related disorder Cutis laxa Elastosis perforans serpiginosa Solar (actinic) elastosis Beta-thalassaemia-associated PXE-like syndrome Other causes of angioid streaks such as Paget disease of bone Fibroelastolytic papulosis of the neck Skin biopsy with elastic-tissue staining to demonstrate calcified fragmented elastic fibres Dilated fundus examination and retinal imaging for angioid streaks and neovascularisation Molecular genetic testing of ABCC6 Ankle-brachial pressure index and vascular imaging for peripheral arterial disease Cardiovascular risk assessment including blood pressure and lipids Investigation for gastrointestinal bleeding when clinically indicated Autosomal recessive disorder caused by variants in ABCC6, leading to progressive mineralisation and fragmentation of elastic fibres Skin changes are the earliest sign: yellowish papules (a 'plucked chicken skin' appearance) coalescing into lax plaques in flexural areas such as the neck and axillae Angioid streaks of the retina are a hallmark ocular finding and predispose to choroidal neovascularisation and central visual loss Cardiovascular involvement includes premature peripheral arterial disease, intermittent claudication, and increased risk of ischaemic events Gastrointestinal haemorrhage can occur from mineralisation of arteries in the gastric mucosa Diagnosis rests on characteristic skin and eye findings, skin biopsy showing calcified fragmented elastic fibres, and ABCC6 molecular testing Management is supportive and preventive: retinal surveillance with prompt treatment of neovascularisation, cardiovascular risk reduction, and avoidance of antiplatelet or anticoagulant excess where bleeding risk is high Genetic counselling should reflect the autosomal recessive inheritance and carrier implications for the family Sudden central visual distortion or loss suggesting choroidal neovascularisation or retinal haemorrhage Gastrointestinal bleeding from mineralised mucosal arteries Symptoms of myocardial or cerebral ischaemia Rapidly worsening claudication or critical limb ischaemia Ocular trauma in a patient with fragile Bruch membrane Dismissing early flexural skin papules as a cosmetic issue rather than a diagnostic sign Failing to arrange retinal surveillance, allowing preventable neovascular visual loss Overlooking premature cardiovascular disease in a relatively young patient Prescribing antithrombotic therapy without weighing the heightened bleeding risk Not recognising angioid streaks as a pointer to systemic disease Pseudoxanthoma elasticum is caused by loss of function of ABCC6, a transporter expressed mainly in the liver and kidney. Reduced ABCC6 activity lowers circulating levels of inorganic pyrophosphate, a key inhibitor of ectopic mineralisation. The resulting imbalance allows calcium and phosphate to deposit on elastic fibres in the skin, the Bruch membrane of the eye, and the arterial wall. Progressive calcification and fragmentation of these elastic fibres produce the characteristic cutaneous papules, retinal angioid streaks with neovascular complications, and premature arterial disease with a tendency to haemorrhage. Life expectancy is usually near normal, but progressive visual loss from retinal complications and the burden of premature vascular disease are the main sources of morbidity. Early retinal surveillance and cardiovascular risk management improve outcomes.

Psoriasis — psoriasis vulgaris, plaque psoriasis, chronic plaque psoriasis Seborrhoeic dermatitis (especially on the scalp and face) Chronic eczema or lichen simplex chronicus Tinea corporis or tinea capitis Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides) Pityriasis rubra pilaris Secondary syphilis in atypical guttate-like eruptions Largely a clinical diagnosis; skin biopsy reserved for atypical presentations Throat swab or streptococcal serology when guttate psoriasis is suspected Joint assessment and imaging when psoriatic arthritis is suspected Baseline and monitoring bloods (including liver function and infection screening) before systemic or biologic therapy Metabolic screening for cardiovascular risk factors, lipids, and glucose Classic lesions are well-demarcated, salmon-pink plaques with adherent silvery scale, favouring extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp, and the lumbosacral region Gentle removal of scale may reveal pinpoint bleeding points (Auspitz sign), and new plaques can appear at sites of trauma (Koebner phenomenon) Nail changes such as pitting, onycholysis, and oil-drop discolouration are common and support the diagnosis Up to a third of patients develop psoriatic arthritis, so ask about joint pain, stiffness, and dactylitis at every review Recognise clinical variants: guttate (often post-streptococcal in younger patients), inverse/flexural, pustular, and erythrodermic forms Treatment is stepped: topical agents (corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues) for limited disease, phototherapy for widespread involvement, and systemic or biologic immunomodulators for severe or refractory disease Screen for and address associated cardiometabolic risk, obesity, and depression, as psoriasis is a systemic inflammatory condition Avoid abrupt withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids, which can precipitate a pustular or erythrodermic flare Erythroderma with widespread redness, scaling, and impaired thermoregulation requiring urgent care Generalised pustular psoriasis with fever and systemic upset Rapidly progressive joint destruction or dactylitis suggesting aggressive psoriatic arthritis Signs of secondary infection or sepsis in extensive skin breakdown Mislabelling scalp or flexural psoriasis as seborrhoeic dermatitis or fungal infection Overlooking psoriatic arthritis until irreversible joint damage has occurred Using potent topical steroids in flexures or on the face without appropriate caution Precipitating pustular or erythrodermic flares by withdrawing systemic corticosteroids Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated disorder driven by dysregulated activation of the innate and adaptive immune systems, particularly the interleukin-23/T-helper-17 axis and tumour necrosis factor signalling. Activated T cells and dendritic cells release cytokines that drive keratinocyte hyperproliferation and abnormal differentiation, dramatically shortening epidermal turnover time and producing thickened, scaly plaques. Dilated dermal vessels and a neutrophilic and lymphocytic infiltrate account for the erythema and, in pustular variants, sterile collections of neutrophils. A strong polygenic predisposition (including PSORS1/HLA-C associations) interacts with triggers such as infection, trauma, drugs, and stress. Psoriasis is a lifelong relapsing-remitting condition; most patients achieve good control with appropriate therapy, but disease severity fluctuates and associated arthritis and cardiometabolic disease influence long-term outcomes.

Psoriatic arthritis — PsA, arthritis psoriatica, psoriatic arthropathy Rheumatoid arthritis Ankylosing spondylitis and other spondyloarthritides Reactive arthritis Gout and other crystal arthropathies Osteoarthritis, particularly of distal interphalangeal joints Undifferentiated inflammatory arthritis Examination of skin and nails for psoriasis, pitting, and onycholysis Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies to help distinguish from rheumatoid arthritis Radiographs of hands, feet, and axial skeleton for erosions, new bone, and pencil-in-cup change Ultrasound or MRI to detect enthesitis, synovitis, and dactylitis Inflammatory markers and metabolic/cardiovascular risk screening An inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis; skin disease usually precedes joint involvement but arthritis can appear first or without evident skin lesions Presents in several patterns including asymmetric oligoarthritis, symmetric polyarthritis resembling rheumatoid arthritis, distal interphalangeal predominant disease, spondylitis, and the destructive arthritis mutilans Dactylitis ('sausage digit') and enthesitis are hallmark features that help distinguish it from rheumatoid arthritis Nail changes such as pitting and onycholysis correlate with distal interphalangeal joint involvement Usually seronegative for rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies Radiographs may show combined erosion and new bone formation, with the classic 'pencil-in-cup' deformity in advanced disease Associated comorbidities include uveitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and increased cardiovascular and metabolic risk Treatment is guided by domains involved (peripheral joints, axial disease, enthesitis, dactylitis, skin, nails), using NSAIDs, conventional DMARDs, and biologic or targeted synthetic agents (TNF, IL-17, IL-23, JAK inhibitors) Rapidly progressive, deforming or mutilating arthritis with joint destruction (arthritis mutilans) Acute painful red eye indicating uveitis requiring ophthalmology review Features suggesting axial disease with neurological compromise Symptoms of undiagnosed inflammatory bowel disease Extensive or erythrodermic/pustular skin disease indicating severe systemic involvement Missing the diagnosis when arthritis precedes or occurs without obvious skin psoriasis Mislabelling it as rheumatoid arthritis and overlooking dactylitis, enthesitis, and nail disease Failing to assess and treat all involved domains rather than joints alone Neglecting cardiovascular, metabolic, and uveitis comorbidities Assuming seronegativity excludes an inflammatory arthritis Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy resulting from immune-mediated inflammation in genetically predisposed individuals. Dysregulation of the TNF and IL-23/IL-17 axes drives inflammation at synovium, entheses, and skin. Unlike rheumatoid arthritis, both bone erosion and pathological new bone formation occur, producing the mixed destructive and proliferative changes seen radiographically. Enthesitis is considered a primary lesion, and there are associations with HLA-B27 (particularly axial disease) and other HLA alleles. Course ranges from mild intermittent arthritis to progressive erosive disease with joint destruction and disability. Early recognition and treat-to-target therapy improve outcomes; poor prognostic markers include polyarticular involvement, elevated inflammatory markers, early erosions, and dactylitis.

Psychiatric Disorders — Mental disorders, Anxiety disorders, Mood disorders, Depression, Bipolar disorder, Schizophrenia, Somatic symptom disorder, Eating disorders, Personality disorders Major depression vs bipolar depression vs depression secondary to general medical illness or substance use Major depressive episode vs normal bereavement/grief (grief features emptiness and wave-like pangs with preserved self-esteem) Generalized anxiety disorder vs panic disorder (they segregate independently in families) Schizophrenia vs schizophreniform disorder (shorter duration), schizoaffective disorder, delusional disorder, and brief psychotic disorder Somatic symptom disorder vs illness anxiety disorder vs conversion (functional neurologic symptom) disorder vs factitious disorder vs malingering Anorexia nervosa vs avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (the latter lacks fear of weight gain and body-image distortion) HIV-associated depression and CNS disease (lifetime depression prevalence in HIV-positive individuals ~22-45%) Chronic hepatitis C-associated depression, which may worsen with interferon-alpha therapy AIDS as a cause of secondary mania Targeted history, physical exam, and focused labs to exclude medical mimics of anxiety (e.g., thyroid studies, glucose, catecholamine workup as indicated) ECG and echocardiography when a cardiovascular cause of panic-like symptoms is suspected Thyroid function testing in mood disorders and in rapid-cycling bipolar disorder (lithium has antithyroid effects) TCA plasma levels to guide dosing and interpret apparent treatment resistance or toxicity Lithium blood levels (target ~0.8-1.2 meq/L acutely) given the narrow therapeutic-to-toxic window; valproate level 50-125 ug/mL; carbamazepine 4-12 ug/mL In anorexia nervosa: CBC (leukopenia/relative lymphocytosis), electrolytes (hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis with purging), BUN, and bone-density assessment for osteoporosis Pheochromocytoma, thyrotoxicosis, and hypoglycemia presenting as anxiety/panic Hyperthyroidism, Huntington's disease, Wilson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, and cerebrovascular accidents presenting as secondary mania Hypothyroidism (including subclinical) and hyperthyroidism presenting with depressed mood and cognitive/memory impairment Frontal-lobe tumor presenting as personality change with a normal neurologic exam Depressive pseudodementia in the elderly mimicking neurodegenerative dementia Cardiovascular conditions (paroxysmal atrial tachycardia, mitral valve prolapse) detected on ECG/echocardiography in patients labeled with panic Drug- or medication-induced psychosis (parkinsonian agents, clonidine, quinacrine, procaine derivatives) mimicking schizophrenia Mental or substance use disorders affect roughly 30% of the U.S. population, yet only about one-third of those affected are currently in treatment; four of the ten leading causes of global disability are psychiatric in origin, and depression is the single largest contributor to disability worldwide. Brief validated office instruments (PRIME-MD / Patient Health Questionnaire, SDDS-PC, the four-item PC-PTSD screen) take only minutes and map patient responses onto formal DSM criteria, helping primary care clinicians make the initial diagnosis. Panic attacks reach peak intensity within about 10 minutes and usually resolve within an hour; up to ~75% of panic disorder patients eventually meet criteria for major depression, and panic is a frequent occult cause of chest pain with normal coronary angiograms and of unexplained syncope. Agoraphobia and housebound behavior are often concealed out of embarrassment, so the syndrome is missed unless the clinician asks directly; about one-third of patients presenting with anxiety have an underlying medical etiology. Major depression requires depressed mood or anhedonia plus a total of at least 5 of 9 symptoms for a minimum of 2 weeks; key distinguishing features from grief are pervasive worthlessness/self-loathing and persistent (rather than wave-like) dysphoria. Suicide risk must be probed by direct, empathic questioning: about 4-5% of depressed patients die by suicide, and most have seen a physician within the month before death; coexisting anxiety, panic, or agitation raises near-term risk. Recognizing a bipolar diathesis in a patient presenting with depression is essential because antidepressant monotherapy can worsen symptoms and accelerate cycling; clues include childhood onset, antidepressant treatment failure, atypical features (hypersomnia, weight gain), and marked irritability/impulsivity. Anorexia nervosa carries the highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder (~5.1 per 1000 untreated); characteristic lab and exam findings include leukopenia with relative lymphocytosis, raised BUN, metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia with purging, amenorrhea, lanugo, hypotension, hypothermia, and sinus bradycardia. Bulimia nervosa usually occurs at normal or slightly above-normal weight, and physical exam is often unremarkable except for dental enamel erosion and parotid gland enlargement; medical danger stems from purging-related fluid/electrolyte disturbance and cardiac conduction abnormalities. Schizophrenia requires at least two characteristic symptoms (positive and/or negative) over a 1-month period with continuous signs for at least 6 months; about 10% of patients die by suicide, and negative symptoms predominate in roughly one-third and predict poor drug response. Personality change can be the first manifestation of serious neurologic, endocrine, or other medical disease (e.g., a frontal-lobe tumor presenting with altered motivation while the neurologic exam stays normal), so a personality disorder is a diagnosis that requires exclusion of such causes. In somatic symptom disorder the defining feature is the patient's disproportionate interpretation and preoccupation with symptoms, not the absence of a medical explanation; patients with genuine medical disease can still qualify, and repeated tests and exploratory surgery are counterproductive. Suicidal or homicidal ideation, a specific plan, or prior attempts - warrants immediate referral to a mental health specialist Psychotic symptoms, mania, or severe depression/anxiety failing first-line treatment - indications for psychiatric consultation or transfer of care Coexisting anxiety, panic, or agitation in a depressed patient, which raises near-term suicide risk Critical weight loss, hypotension, hypothermia, bradycardia, or electrolyte/cardiac conduction abnormalities in eating disorders Refeeding syndrome risk when restoring weight too rapidly in anorexia nervosa (target gain ~0.5-1 lb/week) Serotonin syndrome (myoclonus, agitation, abdominal cramping, hyperpyrexia, hypertension) - a contraindication to combining MAOIs with SSRIs Hypertensive crisis from tyramine-containing foods or sympathomimetics in patients taking MAOIs New-onset psychosis requiring exclusion of a drug/medication cause before diagnosing schizophrenia Basing psychiatric referral on the mere absence of a physical explanation rather than on positive signs/symptoms of a mental disorder Failing to ask directly about agoraphobia, OCD behaviors, or suicidal ideation, all of which patients commonly conceal Subjecting somatic symptom disorder patients to repeated tests and exploratory surgery, or confronting them in a way that causes humiliation and treatment abandonment Treating an unrecognized bipolar depression with antidepressant monotherapy, risking induction of mania or cycle acceleration Prescribing benzodiazepines beyond 4-6 weeks (tolerance, abuse, dependence) and not anticipating withdrawal, which can include seizures Giving benzodiazepines or SSRIs in the immediate aftermath of trauma, and using debriefing, which does not prevent PTSD and may worsen symptoms Using TCAs in patients with serious cardiovascular risk or bundle branch block, and providing large supplies to suicidal patients (TCA overdose can be lethal, desipramine highest risk) Overlooking lithium's narrow therapeutic index and its antithyroid/renal effects during maintenance monitoring Psychiatric disorders are conceptualized as CNS disorders arising from interacting genetic, developmental, and environmental factors, with substantial heritability and considerable overlap of genetic risk variants across diagnoses (pleiotropy). Anxiety and panic involve noradrenergic discharge from the locus coeruleus and serotonergic dorsal-raphe pathways, with lactate, yohimbine, CCK-4, and CO2 capable of provoking attacks; generalized anxiety implicates the GABA-A receptor/chloride-channel complex and serotonergic modulation. PTSD is associated with excessive locus coeruleus norepinephrine release facilitating fear-memory encoding, insular threat-detection overactivity, and blunted pituitary-adrenal responses. OCD involves orbitofrontal cortex-caudate-globus pallidus circuitry. Major depression shows elevated cortisol and CRH, dexamethasone non-suppression, blunted TSH response to TRH, shortened REM latency with increased REM density and reduced slow-wave sleep, altered proinflammatory cytokines and neurotrophins, oxidative stress, telomere shortening, and possible gut-microbiome changes; delayed therapeutic action of antidepressants implicates adaptive second-messenger and neurotrophic changes. Bipolar disorder shows very high monozygotic concordance (approaching 80%) with risk genes (CACNA1C, ANK3, NCAN, ODZ4, TRANK1) shared with schizophrenia and autism, plus circadian and calcium dysregulation. Schizophrenia involves dopamine D2/D3 signaling in the ventral striatum, many small-effect GWAS loci and rare copy-number variants, and pathways of immunity, inflammation, and cell signaling. Outcomes vary widely by disorder. Panic disorder responds to treatment in 75-85% of patients, though complete remission is somewhat lower. Most depressed patients (60-70%) respond to an adequately dosed antidepressant over 6-8 weeks, and about three-quarters improve by ~2 months; the best predictor of recurrence is the number of prior episodes (50-60% of first-episode patients have at least one or two recurrences). Bipolar disorder is recurrent and requires maintenance therapy; lithium responses are 70-80% in acute mania and a sustained level >=0.8 meq/L reduces suicide risk. About 4-5% of depressed and ~10% of schizophrenic patients die by suicide. Anorexia nervosa has the highest mortality of any psychiatric condition (~5.1/1000 untreated), though most patients achieve remission within 5 years; binge-eating disorder has the most favorable prognosis among eating disorders. Schizophrenia often has a poor outcome with insidious onset, but positive symptoms tend to attenuate with age and permanent remission occasionally occurs. Diagnoses are framed by DSM-5-TR (with ICD-10-CM used more widely worldwide); alternative research frameworks include NIMH RDoC and the dimensional HiTOP taxonomy, none yet adequately validated. Severity and subtyping markers within disorders include: bipolar I (full manic episode >=1 week) vs bipolar II (hypomania >=4 days plus recurrent depression) vs cyclothymia (>=2 years of subthreshold fluctuations); rapid cycling defined as >=4 mood episodes per year; persistent depressive (dysthymic) disorder as chronic symptoms >=2 years; PTSD specifiers (with dissociative symptoms, with delayed expression >=6 months); anorexia nervosa restricting type vs binge-eating/purging type; and Munchausen's syndrome as the most severe form of factitious disorder.

Pterygium — surfer's eye, pterygia Pinguecula Pseudopterygium (from prior injury or inflammation) Ocular surface squamous neoplasia (conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia) Conjunctival naevus or other pigmented lesion Limbal dermoid Slit-lamp examination to document size, vascularity, and encroachment onto the cornea Refraction and corneal topography to assess induced astigmatism Serial photography to monitor progression Excision biopsy with histology when ocular surface neoplasia is suspected A pterygium is a wing-shaped fibrovascular growth of conjunctival tissue that encroaches onto the cornea, most commonly on the nasal side Strongly associated with chronic exposure to ultraviolet light, wind, and dust, and therefore more common in people living in sunny, outdoor environments near the equator It is distinguished from a pinguecula, which is a similar degenerative conjunctival lesion that does not cross onto the cornea Symptoms range from a cosmetic concern and irritation or redness to visual disturbance when it induces astigmatism or approaches the visual axis A leading edge (Stocker's line of iron deposition) and a fibrovascular head advancing over the cornea are characteristic Management is conservative with lubricants and UV protection for mild lesions; surgical excision is indicated for visual axis threat, marked astigmatism, discomfort, or cosmesis Recurrence after excision is common, and adjuncts such as conjunctival autografting reduce this risk compared with bare-scleral excision Atypical or rapidly growing lesions should be evaluated to exclude ocular surface squamous neoplasia Rapid growth, marked thickening, or leukoplakic change suggesting ocular surface squamous neoplasia Encroachment onto or across the visual axis threatening vision Significant induced astigmatism degrading acuity Restricted ocular motility from a large or recurrent lesion with scarring Assuming all fleshy conjunctival lesions are benign pterygia and missing ocular surface neoplasia Operating too early on quiescent lesions given the risk of recurrence Using bare-scleral excision alone, which has a high recurrence rate compared with grafting Neglecting UV protection advice, allowing progression or recurrence A pterygium is a degenerative and proliferative condition of the bulbar conjunctiva in which chronic ultraviolet and environmental exposure causes elastotic degeneration of subepithelial collagen along with fibrovascular proliferation. The abnormal tissue invades the superficial cornea, disrupting Bowman's layer and the corneal architecture at its advancing head. Progressive growth can flatten the cornea and induce astigmatism, and encroachment onto the visual axis reduces vision. Most pterygia are benign and slowly progressive with a good prognosis; surgery is effective for symptomatic or vision-threatening lesions, though recurrence is a recognised problem, particularly with bare-scleral techniques and in younger patients.

Ptosis — blepharoptosis, drooping eyelid Aponeurotic (involutional) ptosis Third nerve palsy Horner syndrome Myasthenia gravis and other myogenic causes Mechanical ptosis from lid mass or oedema Pseudoptosis from dermatochalasis, brow ptosis, or contralateral lid retraction Measurement of margin-reflex distance, palpebral aperture, levator function, and skin crease position Pupil examination to identify Horner syndrome or third nerve palsy Assessment for fatigability and ice-pack or targeted testing when myasthenia is suspected Neuroimaging when a compressive or neurogenic cause is suspected Systemic and antibody testing for suspected myasthenia gravis Ptosis is abnormal drooping of the upper eyelid; severity is gauged by the margin-reflex distance and the effect on the visual axis Assessing levator function is central to classification and surgical planning Aponeurotic (involutional) ptosis is the commonest, showing good levator function, a high skin crease, and often thinning of the eyelid A ptosis with a small pupil and ipsilateral anhidrosis suggests Horner syndrome; a ptosis with a dilated pupil and an eye deviated down and out suggests a third nerve palsy Variable, fatigable ptosis worsening through the day points to myasthenia gravis and warrants systemic evaluation Congenital ptosis usually reflects levator dystrophy with poor function and risks amblyopia if the visual axis is occluded in a child The rare Marcus Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon links lid elevation to jaw movement Painful ptosis with a dilated pupil and ophthalmoplegia suggesting a compressive third nerve palsy (possible aneurysm) requiring urgent imaging Ptosis with anisocoria and anhidrosis (Horner syndrome), which may indicate serious underlying pathology such as an apical lung lesion or carotid dissection Fatigable or variable ptosis with diplopia or bulbar symptoms suggesting myasthenia gravis Ptosis occluding the visual axis in a child, threatening amblyopia Treating ptosis as purely cosmetic and missing a serious neurological cause such as third nerve palsy or Horner syndrome Failing to test for fatigability and overlooking myasthenia gravis Not recognising amblyopia risk in congenital ptosis Mistaking pseudoptosis from brow droop or dermatochalasis for true ptosis Ptosis results from impaired elevation of the upper lid, which is normally raised by the levator palpebrae superioris (oculomotor nerve) and Muller muscle (sympathetic). Aponeurotic ptosis is caused by dehiscence or stretching of the levator aponeurosis with age. Neurogenic ptosis follows interruption of the nerve supply, as in third nerve palsy or sympathetic denervation (Horner syndrome). Myogenic ptosis reflects muscle disease such as myasthenia gravis, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, or myotonic dystrophy. Mechanical ptosis arises from lid mass or scarring, and congenital ptosis from maldevelopment of the levator muscle. Aponeurotic and congenital ptosis generally respond well to surgery; the outlook for neurogenic and myogenic ptosis depends on the underlying cause, and childhood ptosis carries a risk of amblyopia if not managed promptly.

Post-traumatic stress disorder — PTSD, post traumatic stress disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder Acute stress disorder Adjustment disorder Major depressive disorder Panic disorder and other anxiety disorders Obsessive-compulsive disorder Substance use disorder Psychosis when flashbacks are mistaken for hallucinations Traumatic brain injury Structured trauma history and PTSD symptom rating scales Suicide risk assessment Screening for comorbid depression and substance use Assessment for traumatic brain injury where relevant Evaluation of sleep disturbance and nightmares Develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, whether directly experienced, witnessed, or learned about affecting a close other Core symptom clusters are intrusion (flashbacks, nightmares, distressing memories), avoidance of trauma reminders, negative alterations in mood and cognition, and heightened arousal and reactivity Symptoms persist beyond about one month and cause significant distress or impairment; an acute stress reaction is the label used within the first month Hyperarousal features include hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, irritability, sleep disturbance, and concentration problems Trauma-focused psychotherapies (such as trauma-focused CBT and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing) are first-line treatments Pharmacotherapy principles favour SSRIs or SNRIs; prazosin may help trauma-related nightmares, and benzodiazepines are generally avoided Screen for common comorbidities including depression, substance use, and suicidal ideation, and for traumatic brain injury in relevant populations Dissociative symptoms and delayed onset (months to years after the event) are recognised presentations Suicidal ideation or self-harm Severe dissociative episodes with risk to safety Escalating substance or alcohol use to cope with symptoms Aggression or risk to others during flashbacks or heightened arousal Using benzodiazepines, which do not treat core symptoms and may impair recovery Missing comorbid depression, substance use, and suicide risk Overlooking delayed-onset presentations by not taking a trauma history Mislabelling normal early stress reactions as PTSD before the required duration Failing to refer for evidence-based trauma-focused psychotherapy Post-traumatic stress disorder reflects dysregulated fear processing, with exaggerated amygdala responses, impaired prefrontal inhibition, and hippocampal changes affecting contextual memory, alongside altered hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and noradrenergic stress responses. These changes underpin persistent conditioned fear, impaired extinction of trauma memories, and chronic hyperarousal. Many people recover within the first year, especially with early trauma-focused treatment, but a substantial minority develop a chronic course. Prognosis is worse with severe or prolonged trauma, lack of social support, and comorbid depression or substance use.

with diffusing capacity to quantify restriction and gas-transfer impairment Serum calcium, phosphate, and renal function to exclude metastatic calcification Echocardiography to screen for pulmonary Failure to clear alveolar phosphate leads to deposition of countless calcium-phosphate concretions (microliths, calcospherites) filling the alveolar spaces Striking clinico-radiological dissociation is characteristic, with extensive calcified change on imaging in a patient who may be minimally symptomatic for years The chest radiograph classically shows a diffuse fine sand-like micronodular pattern (a 'sandstorm' lung) that is densest in the lower zones High-resolution CT demonstrates calcified micronodules, subpleural calcific interlobular septal thickening, and dense posterior/basal consolidation, sometimes with a subpleural 'black pleural line' Diagnosis is often made confidently on imaging in the right context and can be confirmed by identifying microliths in sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage, or biopsy, or by genetic testing Familial clustering is common and screening of siblings is worthwhile given the recessive inheritance There is no proven disease-modifying therapy; management is supportive and lung transplantation is considered for end-stage disease Progressive breathlessness and hypoxaemia signalling advancing restrictive disease Signs of pulmonary hypertension or right heart strain Pneumothorax, which can complicate the stiff calcified lung Rapid functional decline suggesting need for transplant assessment Mistaking the dramatic calcified imaging for widespread infection such as miliary tuberculosis and treating inappropriately Assuming severe disease because imaging looks alarming, when symptoms may be mild for years Overlooking the recessive inheritance and failing to screen affected siblings Attributing the calcification to renal metabolic disease without checking calcium, phosphate, and renal function Pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in SLC34A2, which encodes the sodium-dependent phosphate cotransporter normally expressed on alveolar type II pneumocytes. This transporter clears phosphate liberated by the turnover of surfactant phospholipid from the alveolar lining fluid. When it is deficient, phosphate accumulates and combines with calcium to precipitate as innumerable laminated calcium-phosphate microliths within the alveoli. Progressive filling of the air spaces and later interstitial fibrosis and ossification impair gas exchange and lung compliance over decades, eventually producing restrictive physiology and pulmonary hypertension. The disease usually progresses very slowly over decades, and many patients remain stable for long periods, but a subset develop relentless restrictive fibrosis, respiratory failure, and pulmonary hypertension for which lung transplantation is the only definitive option.

Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis — PAP, Alveolar proteinosis, Alveolar lipoproteinosis Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia Cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema Exogenous or endogenous lipoid pneumonia Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia and other ground-glass interstitial lung disease Invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma Acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis HRCT thorax showing crazy paving Serum anti-GM-CSF autoantibody titre Bronchoalveolar lavage with characteristic milky PAS-positive fluid Pulmonary function tests with transfer factor, showing restriction and markedly reduced gas transfer Serum lactate dehydrogenase, which is often raised Transbronchial or surgical biopsy if lavage is non-diagnostic Screening for secondary causes with blood film or marrow examination, occupational dust history and immune function tests Characterised by accumulation of surfactant-derived lipoproteinaceous material within the alveoli. Three forms exist: autoimmune (over ninety per cent, mediated by anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies), secondary (haematological malignancy, inhaled dusts such as silica, immunodeficiency or infection) and hereditary (GM-CSF receptor or surfactant gene mutations, chiefly in children). Insidious breathlessness and cough occur, and clinical signs are often disproportionately mild relative to imaging, a clinico-radiological dissociation. HRCT shows 'crazy paving': ground-glass opacity with superimposed interlobular septal thickening in a geographical distribution. Bronchoalveolar lavage is both diagnostic and therapeutic, yielding opaque, milky, periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) positive effluent. An elevated serum anti-GM-CSF autoantibody confirms the autoimmune form. Whole-lung lavage is the standard treatment for significant disease, with inhaled or subcutaneous GM-CSF an option in autoimmune disease. There is an increased risk of secondary infection, including with Nocardia and mycobacteria. Superimposed opportunistic infection with Nocardia, mycobacteria or fungi Progressive hypoxaemic respiratory failure Rapid deterioration suggesting secondary disease from a haematological malignancy Development of secondary pulmonary fibrosis Mistaking crazy paving for infection or pulmonary oedema Not measuring the anti-GM-CSF autoantibody to classify disease Missing an underlying haematological malignancy in secondary disease Failing to consider opportunistic infection when a patient deteriorates Surfactant homeostasis depends on granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) signalling for alveolar macrophage maturation and surfactant clearance. In autoimmune disease, neutralising anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies impair macrophage function; secondary and hereditary forms disrupt the same pathway through reduced macrophage numbers or function or through receptor defects. The result is progressive alveolar filling with surfactant material that impairs gas exchange. Autoimmune disease often responds well to whole-lung lavage with good long-term survival; the prognosis of secondary disease depends on the underlying disorder, and some cases resolve spontaneously.

pulmonary arterial hypertension — PAH, pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension (WHO Group 1) Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease (Group 2) Pulmonary hypertension due to lung disease or hypoxia (Group 3) Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (Group 4) Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease or pulmonary capillary haemangiomatosis Congenital systemic-to-pulmonary shunts Deconditioning or other causes of exertional dyspnoea High-output states (anaemia, thyrotoxicosis) Right heart catheterisation with acute vasoreactivity testing Transthoracic echocardiography Ventilation/perfusion scan to exclude chronic thromboembolic disease Pulmonary function tests with DLCO Connective tissue disease serology (ANA, anti-centromere, anti-Scl-70), HIV test and liver studies Cardiac MRI and CT pulmonary angiography Six-minute walk test and natriuretic peptides for risk assessment PAH is pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension (WHO Group 1): mean pulmonary arterial pressure above 20 mmHg with a pulmonary artery wedge pressure of 15 mmHg or less and pulmonary vascular resistance greater than 2 Wood units at right heart catheterisation. Subtypes include idiopathic, heritable (commonly BMPR2 mutations), drug or toxin induced (for example dexfenfluramine, methamphetamine), and forms associated with connective tissue disease, congenital heart disease, portal hypertension, HIV and schistosomiasis. Systemic sclerosis is the commonest connective tissue disease association and warrants annual screening. Right heart catheterisation is mandatory for diagnosis; echocardiography only estimates probability and cannot confirm PAH. Acute vasoreactivity testing identifies the minority (mainly idiopathic, heritable or drug induced) who respond to and benefit from calcium channel blockers. Risk stratification using functional class, exercise capacity, natriuretic peptides and haemodynamics guides escalation and the intensity of therapy. Targeted therapies act on three pathways: endothelin (endothelin receptor antagonists), nitric oxide (phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators) and prostacyclin (prostacyclin analogues and receptor agonists). Upfront combination therapy is now standard for most patients, with parenteral prostacyclins reserved for high-risk disease and transplantation for refractory cases. Exertional syncope or presyncope, a marker of severe disease Signs of right heart failure (raised JVP, ascites, peripheral oedema) Rapidly declining exercise capacity or functional class Haemodynamic instability or systemic hypotension Diagnosing PAH on echocardiography alone without confirmatory right heart catheterisation. Missing an elevated wedge pressure and mislabelling Group 2 (left heart) disease as PAH. Prescribing calcium channel blockers to non-vasoreactive patients, which can be harmful. Failing to screen at-risk groups such as those with systemic sclerosis, BMPR2 carriers and portal hypertension. Overlooking pulmonary veno-occlusive disease or capillary haemangiomatosis, in whom vasodilators can precipitate pulmonary oedema. PAH results from a progressive vasculopathy of the small pulmonary arteries driven by endothelial dysfunction, with an imbalance between vasoconstrictor and mitogenic mediators (endothelin-1, thromboxane) and vasodilator and antiproliferative mediators (nitric oxide, prostacyclin). This favours vasoconstriction, smooth muscle and endothelial proliferation, in-situ thrombosis and adventitial remodelling, producing intimal fibrosis, medial hypertrophy and plexiform lesions. Impaired bone morphogenetic protein signalling, classically through BMPR2 loss of function, promotes this angioproliferation. The resulting rise in pulmonary vascular resistance increases right ventricular afterload, leading initially to right ventricular hypertrophy and ultimately to dilatation and failure, which determines symptoms and survival. Once uniformly fatal within a few years, prognosis has improved substantially with modern risk-based combination therapy. Nonetheless PAH remains a progressive, incurable disease short of lung transplantation, and outcome depends heavily on right ventricular function and treatment response.

perfusion scan) Screening and genetic assessment for hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia Cerebral imaging when neurological symptoms or abscess are suspected Assessment for anaemia and iron deficiency from associated bleeding An abnormal direct connection between a pulmonary artery and vein that bypasses the capillary bed, creating a right-to-left shunt The majority are associated with hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease), so screening and family assessment are important The right-to-left shunt causes hypoxaemia, and the loss of capillary filtration allows paradoxical embolism, predisposing to stroke and brain abscess Classic features include dyspnoea, cyanosis, digital clubbing, and, when related to HHT, epistaxis and mucocutaneous telangiectasia Platypnoea and orthodeoxia (breathlessness and desaturation on sitting or standing) can occur with basal lesions Contrast (bubble) echocardiography is a sensitive screening test for right-to-left shunt, with CT pulmonary angiography defining the feeding vessels Transcatheter embolisation of feeding arteries is the mainstay of treatment and reduces the risk of neurological complications and haemorrhage Neurological symptoms suggesting paradoxical stroke or cerebral abscess Massive haemoptysis or haemothorax from lesion rupture Progressive hypoxaemia and cyanosis Enlarging lesions, especially during pregnancy, increasing complication risk Failing to consider a pulmonary AVM in unexplained hypoxaemia, clubbing, or paradoxical embolism Not screening for hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and missing familial disease Omitting antibiotic prophylaxis advice for procedures given the risk of brain abscess Overlooking small lesions that still permit paradoxical embolism despite minimal hypoxaemia A pulmonary arteriovenous malformation is a thin-walled abnormal vascular sac or channel connecting a feeding pulmonary artery directly to a draining pulmonary vein, bypassing the normal capillary network. This produces a right-to-left shunt that lowers arterial oxygenation and, critically, removes the capillary filter that normally traps small emboli and bacteria, so venous clots and septic material can pass directly into the systemic circulation and cause paradoxical stroke and cerebral abscess. Most lesions arise in the context of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, an autosomal dominant disorder of vascular development, and they tend to enlarge over time and during pregnancy. The fragile vessel walls can also rupture, causing haemoptysis or haemothorax. With embolisation of the feeding arteries, oxygenation improves and the risk of serious neurological and haemorrhagic complications falls substantially; untreated lesions carry a significant risk of stroke, brain abscess, and life-threatening haemorrhage, and lifelong surveillance is needed as lesions can recur or grow.

pulmonary artery sling — aberrant left pulmonary artery, PA sling Complete vascular rings such as double aortic arch or right arch with aberrant subclavian Innominate artery compression syndrome Primary tracheomalacia or bronchomalacia Congenital tracheal stenosis without a sling Bronchiolitis or recurrent viral wheeze Foreign body aspiration Mediastinal mass compressing the airway CT angiography of the thorax MR angiography Transthoracic echocardiography to delineate the anomalous origin and associated cardiac lesions Flexible and rigid bronchoscopy to assess complete rings and stenosis Contrast oesophagogram showing an anterior oesophageal indentation Chest radiograph noting asymmetric aeration, a low right hilum and air trapping Ventilation-perfusion or pulmonary function assessment in older children The left pulmonary artery arises anomalously from the right pulmonary artery and courses between the trachea and oesophagus to reach the left lung, forming a sling around the distal trachea and right main bronchus. It is the only vascular anomaly that passes between the trachea and oesophagus, giving a unique anterior indentation on the oesophagus at barium swallow. It frequently coexists with complete (O-shaped) tracheal cartilage rings and long-segment congenital tracheal stenosis, the so-called ring-sling complex. Infants typically present early with stridor, wheeze, recurrent respiratory infection and respiratory distress from airway compression. Because associated tracheal stenosis often dominates the clinical picture, airway assessment is as important as defining the vascular anatomy. CT or MR angiography demonstrates the aberrant vessel, and bronchoscopy is essential to evaluate the trachea for complete rings and the level and length of stenosis. Surgical treatment involves division and re-implantation of the left pulmonary artery onto the main pulmonary artery, typically on cardiopulmonary bypass. Coexisting significant tracheal stenosis is addressed concurrently, commonly by slide tracheoplasty. Severe stridor with respiratory distress or apnoeic episodes in infancy Cyanotic spells or acute deterioration Recurrent or lobar pneumonia with persistent air trapping Difficult intubation or inability to pass beyond a narrowed trachea Focusing on the vascular anomaly and failing to assess the trachea for complete rings and stenosis. Misinterpreting the anterior oesophageal indentation, which is unique to this lesion. Delayed diagnosis through mislabelling as asthma or recurrent bronchiolitis. Not planning simultaneous airway reconstruction when significant stenosis is present. Assuming that vessel re-implantation alone will relieve fixed intrinsic tracheal narrowing. The left pulmonary artery normally develops from the left sixth aortic arch; in a pulmonary artery sling it fails to form from this precursor and instead arises from the right pulmonary artery, so that to reach the left hilum it must pass over the right main bronchus and course posteriorly between the trachea and oesophagus. This aberrant vessel forms a partial sling that compresses the distal trachea and right main bronchus anteriorly and, lying behind the trachea, indents the oesophagus anteriorly. The developmental disturbance is frequently accompanied by intrinsic tracheal maldevelopment with complete cartilage rings and diffuse narrowing, compounding the extrinsic compression and producing severe fixed airway obstruction. With modern surgical re-implantation and, where needed, tracheal reconstruction, outcomes have improved substantially, though prognosis is worse with extensive long-segment tracheal stenosis or associated cardiac anomalies.

Pulmonary atresia — pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum, pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect Critical pulmonary stenosis Tetralogy of Fallot Tricuspid atresia Other duct-dependent pulmonary circulation lesions Ebstein anomaly with functional pulmonary atresia Echocardiography defining outflow obstruction and ventricular size Assessment for coronary sinusoids and right-ventricle-dependent coronary circulation Imaging of pulmonary arteries and any aortopulmonary collaterals Pre- and post-ductal saturations Cardiac catheterisation for detailed anatomy Complete obstruction of the right ventricular outflow to the pulmonary arteries, so there is no antegrade pulmonary blood flow It occurs with an intact ventricular septum or with a ventricular septal defect, which differ in physiology and management Pulmonary blood flow is duct-dependent, so neonates become profoundly cyanotic as the duct closes In the intact-septum form the right ventricle is often hypoplastic and may have coronary sinusoids or right-ventricle-dependent coronary circulation The form with a ventricular septal defect resembles severe tetralogy of Fallot and may have major aortopulmonary collaterals Prostaglandin to maintain the duct is the immediate priority, followed by staged surgical or catheter intervention Profound cyanosis as the duct closes Right-ventricle-dependent coronary circulation (contraindicates decompression) Inadequate or discontinuous pulmonary arteries Severe hypoxaemia despite prostaglandin Failing to start prostaglandin promptly Decompressing a right ventricle that supplies the coronary circulation, causing ischaemia Underestimating collateral-dependent pulmonary supply Confusing the two subtypes, which need different strategies In pulmonary atresia there is no patent pathway from the right ventricle to the pulmonary arteries, so pulmonary perfusion depends on the arterial duct or on aortopulmonary collateral arteries. With an intact ventricular septum, blood cannot leave the right ventricle, which becomes hypertensive and often hypoplastic, sometimes maintaining fistulous connections (sinusoids) to the coronary arteries; closure of the duct causes life-threatening hypoxaemia. With a ventricular septal defect, the right ventricle decompresses through the defect and pulmonary supply comes from the duct or collaterals, giving a spectrum that overlaps with severe tetralogy of Fallot. Outcome depends on the subtype and pulmonary artery and right ventricular anatomy; many children require staged intervention, achieving biventricular or single-ventricle circulations with variable long-term results.

Pulmonary barotrauma — pulmonary overinflation syndrome, burst lung Decompression sickness Spontaneous pneumothorax of another cause Acute coronary syndrome Immersion pulmonary oedema Asthma exacerbation Chest imaging for pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum and surgical emphysema Assessment for arterial gas embolism, which takes management priority Oxygenation and ventilation assessment Evaluation of underlying airway disease as a risk factor Monitoring for tension physiology Overexpansion and rupture of lung tissue caused by expanding gas that cannot escape, classically during ascent from a dive Breath-holding during ascent or air trapping from airway disease markedly increases the risk Consequences include pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, surgical emphysema and arterial gas embolism It can also occur with positive-pressure mechanical ventilation at high airway pressures Presentation ranges from chest pain and breathlessness to catastrophic arterial gas embolism Management targets the specific complication, with recompression for gas embolism and chest decompression for tension pneumothorax Neurological symptoms indicating arterial gas embolism Signs of tension pneumothorax Rapidly worsening respiratory distress Haemodynamic instability Overlooking arterial gas embolism while focusing on a pneumothorax Missing air trapping from undiagnosed airway disease as the cause Delaying chest decompression in tension pneumothorax Allowing a diver with lung bullae to continue diving Pulmonary barotrauma results from Boyle's law: as ambient pressure falls during ascent, gas in the lungs expands, and if it cannot be exhaled the alveoli overdistend and rupture. Escaping gas tracks into the pleural space (pneumothorax), the mediastinum and soft tissues (pneumomediastinum and surgical emphysema), or into the pulmonary veins to cause arterial gas embolism. Air trapping from breath-holding, bronchospasm or bullous disease localises the overpressure and predisposes to rupture. Isolated small air leaks often resolve with supportive care, but arterial gas embolism or tension pneumothorax can be life-threatening; prompt treatment of complications determines outcome.

pulmonary capillary haemangiomatosis — PCH, capillary haemangiomatosis of the lung Idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage syndromes Hypersensitivity pneumonitis or other diffuse interstitial lung disease Lymphangitis carcinomatosa or metastatic pulmonary calcinosis Right heart catheterisation (wedge pressure often normal despite venous congestion) High-resolution CT of the thorax Full pulmonary function testing with DLCO (markedly reduced) EIF2AK4 genetic testing Bronchoalveolar lavage for haemosiderin-laden macrophages Transthoracic echocardiography Surgical lung biopsy (rarely performed owing to bleeding risk; diagnosis is often clinico-radiological) Rare pulmonary vascular disease classified within WHO Group 1 prime alongside pulmonary veno-occlusive disease (PVOD), with which it shares clinical, genetic and histological overlap along a disease continuum. Biallelic (recessive) loss-of-function mutations in EIF2AK4 (encoding GCN2) underlie heritable forms and are shared with PVOD, supporting the view that the two are variants of one entity. Histology shows proliferation of thin-walled capillaries infiltrating alveolar septa, bronchovascular bundles, pleura and the walls of pulmonary veins and arteries. Presents like idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension (progressive exertional dyspnoea, right heart failure) but with a disproportionately low DLCO and marked hypoxaemia. Haemoptysis and occult alveolar haemorrhage (haemosiderin-laden macrophages on lavage) are clues that help separate it from idiopathic PAH. HRCT typically shows diffuse or centrilobular ground-glass nodules, smooth interlobular septal thickening and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Life-threatening pulmonary oedema may be precipitated by PAH-targeted vasodilators, especially prostacyclins, a hallmark shared with PVOD. Lung transplantation is the only definitive therapy, so early referral to a transplant centre is essential. Acute pulmonary oedema after starting PAH-targeted vasodilators Rapidly progressive hypoxaemic respiratory failure Massive haemoptysis Decompensated right heart failure with syncope or hypotension Misdiagnosis as idiopathic PAH leading to aggressive vasodilator therapy and fatal pulmonary oedema. Attributing the low DLCO and ground-glass changes to interstitial lung disease rather than a pulmonary vascular cause. Delaying transplant referral because pulmonary pressures initially appear to respond to therapy. Assuming a normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure excludes a post-capillary or venous component. PCH is characterised by abnormal proliferation of pulmonary capillaries that invade and infiltrate the alveolar interstitium and, importantly, the walls of pulmonary veins and arteries as well as the pleura and airways. Capillary infiltration and obstruction at and beyond the post-capillary level produce venous congestion and pulmonary hypertension with a venous-obstructive component, explaining the overlap with PVOD. Biallelic EIF2AK4 mutations impair the integrated stress response and are thought to predispose to dysregulated angioproliferation. The remodelled capillary bed raises pulmonary vascular resistance, and because the obstruction lies at or beyond the capillary level, potent arterial vasodilators can flood an unprotected downstream bed and precipitate acute pulmonary oedema. The course is progressive and generally poor, with median survival of only a few years from diagnosis without transplantation. Lung transplantation is potentially curative and offers the best long-term outcome.

pulmonary veno-occlusive disease and the EIF2AK4 genotype Pulmonary capillary haemangiomatosis is characterised by uncontrolled proliferation of thin-walled capillaries that infiltrate the alveolar septa, bronchovascular bundles, pleura, and the walls of pulmonary veins and arteries. This proliferating capillary network encroaches on and obstructs the microvascular bed, raising pulmonary vascular resistance and producing pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension. Because the proliferating vessels compress and involve the post-capillary venules, the disorder shares physiology and imaging features with pulmonary veno-occlusive disease, and many familial cases carry biallelic loss-of-function mutations in EIF2AK4. The key clinical hazard is that the obstruction lies downstream of the arterioles, so pulmonary vasodilators increase flow into a fixed distal obstruction and can flood the capillary bed, precipitating acute pulmonary oedema. The prognosis is poor, with progressive pulmonary hypertension and limited response to medical therapy, and death from right heart failure or vasodilator-precipitated pulmonary oedema. Lung transplantation is the only definitive treatment and offers the best chance of survival, so early referral is critical.

supportive measures include oxygen, pulmonary rehabilitation, and vaccination Acute exacerbations cause rapid deterioration and carry high mortality; lung transplantation should be considered in suitable candidates Rapid worsening of dyspnoea with new diffuse ground-glass change suggesting an acute exacerbation Resting hypoxaemia or significant desaturation on exertion Signs of pulmonary hypertension or right heart failure Features suggesting an underlying treatable systemic disease that alter management Labelling fibrosis as idiopathic without excluding occupational, drug, and connective tissue causes Using corticosteroids or immunosuppression indiscriminately in IPF, where they may be harmful Missing coexisting emphysema, which can mask spirometric restriction Delaying transplant referral until the patient is too deconditioned to be a candidate Repeated microinjury to the alveolar epithelium in a susceptible (often ageing, genetically predisposed) individual triggers aberrant wound-healing rather than normal repair. Activated fibroblasts and myofibroblasts accumulate in fibroblastic foci and deposit excess extracellular matrix, progressively distorting and stiffening the lung architecture. The result is loss of functional alveolar units, honeycomb cystic change, impaired gas exchange, and reduced compliance, producing a restrictive physiology with worsening hypoxaemia. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is generally progressive with a poor prognosis and median survival of only a few years from diagnosis, though the course is variable; antifibrotic drugs slow decline and transplantation can prolong survival in eligible patients, while acute exacerbations markedly worsen outcome.

liver function and hepatitis serology; methamphetamine screening where relevant Vasoreactivity testing (idiopathic/hereditary PAH only) Asthma (overlapping nonspecific dyspnoea) Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction Physical deconditioning Obstructive sleep apnoea / obesity-hypoventilation syndrome Sarcoidosis with pulmonary vascular involvement PH is diagnosed when mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) is >20 mmHg by right heart catheterisation; this threshold was lowered from the older >=25 mmHg cut-off to emphasise earlier disease detection (p.2185, 2191). The most common causes of PH are left heart disease or primary lung disease; pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is an uncommon but distinct subtype with an obliterative arteriopathy (p.2185). Most patients present with dyspnoea and/or fatigue; oedema, chest pain, presyncope and syncope are less common and signal more advanced disease (p.2188). The current WSPH classification (last revised 2018, Sixth World Symposium) defines five groups: 1 = PAH; 2 = PH due to left heart disease; 3 = PH due to chronic lung disease/hypoxia or sleep-disordered breathing; 4 = chronic thromboembolic PH (CTEPH); 5 = miscellaneous/multifactorial (p.2191). Echocardiography with agitated-saline (bubble) study is the most important initial screening test; estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure >35 mmHg, a notched continuous-wave Doppler waveform, or a hypertrophied/dilated right ventricle supports the diagnosis (p.2188). Hemodynamic subtypes by RHC: precapillary PH = PAWP/LVEDP <=15 mmHg with PVR >2.0 Wood units; isolated postcapillary PH = PAWP >15 mmHg with PVR <=2.0 WU; combined pre-/postcapillary PH = mPAP >20 mmHg with PAWP >15 mmHg and PVR >2.0 WU (p.2191). In PAH, an isolated reduction in diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) on pulmonary function testing is a classic finding (p.2189). BNP and NT-proBNP correlate with right ventricular dysfunction, hemodynamic severity and functional status in PAH, and NT-proBNP can serve as a biomarker of treatment response once a baseline is established (p.2191). Vasoreactivity testing (with short-acting agents such as inhaled nitric oxide or inhaled epoprostenol) is reserved for idiopathic or hereditary PAH; a positive response is a fall in mPAP by >=10 mmHg to an absolute level <=40 mmHg without a fall in cardiac output, seen in <5% of patients but carrying a particularly favourable prognosis (p.2191). CTEPH is curable in many patients by surgical pulmonary endarterectomy but is widely underdiagnosed; ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scanning remains the primary screening test and should be considered in any PH of unclear cause (p.2190-2191). Syncope or presyncope (signals advanced disease) Signs of right ventricular failure: elevated jugular venous pressure, lower-extremity oedema, ascites Rapid progression of symptoms with severely reduced exercise capacity Decompensated right heart failure (the major cause of mortality if untreated) Significant decline in exercise tolerance from baseline even when CPET appears reassuring (e.g. in athletes - may indicate early PAH or subacute PE) Right heart catheterisation - not echocardiography - is the diagnostic gold standard; echocardiography only screens, and an echo in which tricuspid regurgitation is simply not detected does NOT exclude PH (PH is found in one-third of such patients). PH symptoms are nonspecific, insidious and overlap with asthma, HFpEF and deconditioning, so the diagnosis is frequently missed without a reasonable index of suspicion. Do not assume that PH in patients with comorbid cardiopulmonary disease (e.g. ILD, mitral valve disease) is merely an extension of the underlying condition rather than a specific entity. Patients with left heart disease aggressively diuresed before RHC may falsely appear to have an isolated precapillary (PAH-like) profile - diuresis can mask the true hemodynamic classification. A low peak VO2 occurs across the heart-lung disease spectrum and is NOT diagnostic of PH per se. Chronic thromboembolic disease (thrombotic remodelling with reduced exercise capacity but without PH) requires consideration in patients with prior PE and dyspnoea even when echocardiography is reassuring. PAH arises from apoptosis resistance, cell proliferation, dysregulated metabolism and increased oxidant stress in pulmonary vascular cells, pericytes and adventitial fibroblasts, producing hypertrophic, fibrotic and plexogenic remodelling of distal (small) pulmonary arterioles with extracellular-matrix expansion, reduced vascular compliance and in-situ thrombosis. This raises pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) and mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP). To preserve cardiac output against the elevated right-ventricular afterload, RV work increases; sustained overload depletes myocardial energy and causes right ventricular-pulmonary arterial uncoupling, and in end-stage disease cardiac output and mPAP both fall. The most common germline driver of hereditary PAH is a BMPR2 variant (a TGF-beta superfamily receptor) with variable penetrance (as low as ~20%); other drivers include TBX4 and SOX17, and EIF2AK4 for pulmonary veno-occlusive disease. In group 2 PH the hallmark is elevated left atrial pressure causing pulmonary venous hypertension, venule sclerosis and secondary arteriolar remodelling. (p.2185-2192) If left untreated, PH carries a high mortality rate, largely owing to decompensated right heart failure. Idiopathic PAH is progressive and leads to right heart failure and early mortality; in left-sided heart failure or HFpEF even mildly elevated mPAP carries adverse outcome. Among IPAH, prevalence favours women ~3:1 but hemodynamics are more severe and prognosis less favourable in men. Hereditary BMPR2 PAH presents younger with more severe hemodynamics and greater clinical risk (conversion ~2.3%/year in carriers). Vasoreactive responders (<5%) have a particularly favourable prognosis. Scleroderma-associated PAH and HIV-PAH carry especially poor prognoses; portopulmonary hypertension is a marker of adverse post-liver-transplant outcome (up to 100% mortality reported with mPAP >=50 mmHg in one study). Peak VO2 <15 mL/kg/min is prognostic. (p.2185, 2191-2192) World Symposium on Pulmonary Hypertension (WSPH) clinical classification (revised 2018) into 5 groups: Group 1 - pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH: idiopathic, heritable, drug/toxin-associated, or associated with connective tissue disease, HIV, portal hypertension, congenital heart disease, schistosomiasis; plus PVOD/PCH and persistent PH of the newborn); Group 2 - PH associated with left heart disease (HFpEF, HFrEF, valvular, congenital/acquired postcapillary); Group 3 - PH associated with lung disease and/or hypoxia (obstructive, restrictive, mixed, hypoventilation, high-altitude hypoxia, developmental); Group 4 - PH associated with pulmonary artery obstruction (CTEPH and other obstructions); Group 5 - PH with unclear/multifactorial mechanisms (haematological, systemic, metabolic, chronic renal failure +/- haemodialysis, pulmonary tumour thrombotic microangiopathy, fibrosing mediastinitis). hypertension due to left heart disease is a post-capillary disorder driven by elevated left-sided filling pressures. Systolic or diastolic left ventricular dysfunction, or left-sided valvular disease, raises left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure, which is transmitted backward into the pulmonary capillaries and arteries, producing a passive rise in pulmonary artery pressure while the wedge pressure remains elevated. Over time, chronic pulmonary venous congestion can trigger vasoconstriction and structural remodelling of the pulmonary arteries, adding a pre-capillary component and producing combined post- and pre-capillary disease in which pulmonary vascular resistance also rises. This superimposed arteriopathy further loads the right ventricle and worsens outcome. Because the primary problem is upstream in the left heart, therapy that dilates the pulmonary arteries can increase transpulmonary flow into a congested left heart and precipitate pulmonary oedema. The prognosis is largely determined by the underlying left heart disease, and the development of pulmonary hypertension, particularly a combined post- and pre-capillary pattern, marks more advanced disease and a worse outlook. Optimising treatment of the left heart condition can lower pulmonary pressures, whereas an established pulmonary vascular component is less reversible.
