pulmonale Not referring a severe pulmonary vascular phenotype to a specialist pulmonary hypertension centre Pulmonary hypertension due to lung disease and hypoxia is driven principally by alveolar hypoxia, which provokes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction as an adaptive mechanism to divert blood away from poorly ventilated lung. When hypoxia is chronic and widespread, this vasoconstriction becomes sustained and is accompanied by structural remodelling of the pulmonary arteries with medial hypertrophy and intimal thickening. In parenchymal diseases such as emphysema and fibrosis, destruction and distortion of the alveolar-capillary bed reduces the cross-sectional area of the pulmonary vasculature, further raising resistance. Acidosis and hypercapnia potentiate the vasoconstriction, and the chronically elevated afterload leads to right ventricular hypertrophy and eventual failure. The pulmonary hypertension is typically proportionate to the underlying disease, and a disproportionately severe pattern suggests an additional or alternative process. The presence of pulmonary hypertension marks more advanced lung disease and predicts reduced exercise capacity and survival, with a severe pulmonary vascular phenotype carrying the worst outlook. Correcting chronic hypoxaemia with oxygen and optimising the underlying respiratory disease can slow progression, but the pulmonary hypertension is rarely fully reversible.

pulmonary hypoplasia — lung hypoplasia, pulmonary hypodysplasia Respiratory distress syndrome from surfactant deficiency Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (both cause and differential) Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn Congenital pneumonia or sepsis Meconium aspiration syndrome Alveolar capillary dysplasia with misalignment of pulmonary veins Congenital surfactant protein deficiencies Antenatal ultrasound with lung-to-head ratio and amniotic fluid assessment Foetal MRI for lung volume estimation Chest radiograph noting a small bell-shaped thorax and low lung volumes Echocardiography to assess pulmonary hypertension and associated cardiac anomalies Arterial blood gas and pre- and post-ductal saturation monitoring Renal ultrasound and genetic or karyotype testing to identify the underlying cause Post-mortem lung weight-to-body-weight ratio and radial alveolar count where applicable Defined as incomplete development of the lung with a reduced number of airway generations, alveoli and pulmonary vessels, giving an abnormally low lung weight and volume for body size. Primary (isolated) hypoplasia is rare; the majority of cases are secondary to an identifiable intrathoracic or extrathoracic cause. Major secondary mechanisms include thoracic space restriction (congenital diaphragmatic hernia, effusion or hydrops, masses), oligohydramnios (renal agenesis or Potter sequence, prolonged rupture of membranes), thoracic cage constraint (skeletal dysplasias, neuromuscular disease) and reduced foetal breathing movements. Normal lung growth requires adequate amniotic fluid volume, sufficient intrathoracic space and regular foetal breathing movements, particularly during the canalicular and saccular stages. Affected neonates typically present with respiratory distress from birth, are difficult to ventilate and are prone to air leaks such as pneumothorax. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn frequently coexists because the pulmonary vascular bed is both reduced in number and abnormally muscularised. Antenatal predictors of severity in congenital diaphragmatic hernia include the lung-to-head ratio and the degree of liver herniation on ultrasound and foetal MRI. Management is supportive with lung-protective ventilation, pulmonary vasodilators and treatment of the underlying cause, with extracorporeal support reserved for selected severe cases. Severe refractory hypoxaemia and hypercapnia unresponsive to escalating support Suprasystemic pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular failure Recurrent or tension pneumothorax Inability to achieve adequate ventilation despite optimal settings, suggesting severe hypoplasia Attributing neonatal respiratory failure solely to surfactant deficiency and missing underlying hypoplasia. Underestimating the contribution of pulmonary hypertension to hypoxaemia. Using aggressive ventilation that causes barotrauma in small, non-compliant lungs. Failing to search for the underlying renal, skeletal or diaphragmatic cause once hypoplasia is recognised. Providing over-optimistic counselling before severity has been fully assessed. Normal lung growth depends on sufficient intrathoracic space, an appropriate volume of amniotic and intrapulmonary fluid maintaining distending pressure, and regular foetal breathing movements; interference with any of these during the critical canalicular and saccular phases arrests branching morphogenesis and alveolarisation. Space-occupying lesions and effusions compress the developing lung, oligohydramnios removes the distending fluid pressure and allows lung liquid to drain, and thoracic or neuromuscular constraint prevents the mechanical stretch that drives growth. The result is a lung with fewer bronchial divisions, fewer and simplified alveoli, and a diminished, abnormally muscularised vascular bed that predisposes to hypoxaemia and pulmonary hypertension after birth. Outcome depends chiefly on the severity of hypoplasia and its underlying cause: severe bilateral disease, as in Potter sequence, is frequently fatal, whereas milder secondary hypoplasia may improve with postnatal lung growth.

Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis — PLCH, Pulmonary histiocytosis X, Pulmonary eosinophilic granuloma Lymphangioleiomyomatosis Centrilobular emphysema Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome Respiratory bronchiolitis-ILD and desquamative interstitial pneumonia Metastatic or infective cavitating nodules Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Sarcoidosis HRCT thorax demonstrating nodules and cysts with upper- and mid-zone predominance Detailed smoking history Pulmonary function tests with transfer factor, often showing a reduced gas transfer with obstructive, restrictive or mixed defects Bronchoalveolar lavage with increased CD1a-positive cells as supportive evidence Lung biopsy with CD1a and S100 immunostaining where the diagnosis is unclear BRAF mutation testing in progressive or multisystem disease Echocardiography and, where indicated, right heart catheterisation for pulmonary hypertension A smoking-related disease of young to middle-aged adults; almost all patients are current or former smokers. Presents with cough and breathlessness, and up to a quarter present with spontaneous pneumothorax; constitutional symptoms may also occur. The HRCT hallmark is a combination of nodules, which cavitate, and bizarrely shaped thick-walled cysts, with upper- and mid-zone predominance and sparing of the costophrenic angles. Early disease is nodular and evolves to a predominantly cystic pattern over time. Histology shows bronchiolocentric stellate nodules of Langerhans cells that are CD1a and S100 positive, with Birbeck granules on electron microscopy and admixed eosinophils. BRAF V600E and other activating MAPK-pathway mutations are found in a substantial proportion, supporting a clonal neoplastic basis. Smoking cessation is essential and can lead to regression; progressive disease may require systemic therapy. Pulmonary hypertension is a recognised and prognostically important complication. Spontaneous or recurrent pneumothorax Signs of pulmonary hypertension or right heart failure Multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis with diabetes insipidus, bone lesions or skin involvement Rapid progression despite smoking cessation Diagnosing the disease in a lifelong non-smoker without reconsideration Mistaking cysts for emphysema or lymphangioleiomyomatosis Not testing for BRAF mutations in progressive or multisystem disease Failing to screen for pulmonary hypertension and underestimating the risk of recurrent pneumothorax Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis involves accumulation and proliferation of Langerhans-type dendritic cells that form bronchiolocentric granulomatous nodules, driven by tobacco smoke exposure in clonally susceptible individuals who frequently harbour activating MAPK-pathway mutations such as BRAF V600E. Nodules undergo cavitation and cystic transformation to produce the characteristic nodulocystic upper-zone disease and, over time, fibrosis and pulmonary vascular remodelling. The course is variable; many patients stabilise or improve with smoking cessation, but a subset progresses to cystic destruction, fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension and respiratory failure, with pulmonary hypertension worsening the outlook.

Pulmonary regurgitation — pulmonary valve insufficiency Aortic regurgitation (early diastolic murmur) Pulmonary hypertension with functional regurgitation Residual lesions after congenital heart surgery Endocarditis of the pulmonary valve Absent pulmonary valve syndrome Echocardiography assessing the valve and right ventricle Cardiac MRI to quantify regurgitant fraction and right ventricular volumes Electrocardiogram and monitoring for arrhythmia Assessment of pulmonary artery pressure Serial follow-up in post-tetralogy patients Backflow across the pulmonary valve, very often iatrogenic after repair of tetralogy of Fallot or pulmonary valvotomy Other causes include pulmonary hypertension, endocarditis and congenital valve abnormalities Mild pulmonary regurgitation is common and usually of no consequence Chronic severe regurgitation causes progressive right ventricular dilatation and eventual dysfunction The murmur is an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge (a Graham Steell murmur when due to pulmonary hypertension) Timing of pulmonary valve replacement in post-tetralogy patients is guided by right ventricular size and function on cardiac MRI Progressive right ventricular dilatation or dysfunction Exercise intolerance or arrhythmia in post-tetralogy patients Signs of right heart failure Endocarditis Dismissing chronic severe regurgitation because symptoms appear late Relying on echocardiography alone without MRI for right ventricular assessment Delaying valve replacement until right ventricular dysfunction is irreversible Confusing the murmur with aortic regurgitation Pulmonary regurgitation occurs when the pulmonary valve fails to prevent diastolic backflow from the pulmonary artery into the right ventricle. The commonest setting is after surgical relief of right ventricular outflow obstruction (as in tetralogy of Fallot), where the valve is rendered incompetent. The regurgitant volume chronically overloads the right ventricle, causing progressive dilatation; over years this leads to right ventricular dysfunction, exercise intolerance and an increased risk of arrhythmia. Pulmonary hypertension can also cause functional regurgitation through pulmonary artery and annular dilatation. Mild pulmonary regurgitation is benign, but chronic severe regurgitation after congenital repair can cause right ventricular decline; timely pulmonary valve replacement can preserve or improve right ventricular function.

pulmonary sequestration — bronchopulmonary sequestration, accessory lung Congenital pulmonary airway malformation Congenital diaphragmatic hernia or eventration Bronchogenic cyst Posterior mediastinal mass such as neuroblastoma Congenital lobar emphysema Pulmonary abscess or necrotising pneumonia Bronchial atresia with mucocoele CT pulmonary and aortic angiography to define the feeding artery and venous drainage Contrast-enhanced MRI or MR angiography (avoids ionising radiation, useful in children) Antenatal and postnatal Doppler ultrasound Echocardiography to assess shunt burden and exclude associated cardiac anomalies Digital subtraction angiography if embolisation is planned Histopathological examination of the resected specimen Renal and spinal imaging where associated anomalies are suspected in extralobar disease Defined as non-functioning lung tissue that lacks normal communication with the tracheobronchial tree and receives an anomalous systemic arterial supply, most often from the descending thoracic or abdominal aorta. Two subtypes exist: intralobar (shares the visceral pleura of normal lung and typically presents later in childhood or adulthood with recurrent infection) and extralobar (has its own pleural investment, presents earlier and is frequently associated with other anomalies). Intralobar sequestration predominates and characteristically involves the posterobasal segment of the left lower lobe. Venous drainage differs by subtype: intralobar lesions usually drain to the pulmonary veins, whereas extralobar lesions typically drain to systemic veins such as the azygos or hemiazygos system. CT angiography is the investigation of choice because it demonstrates the anomalous systemic feeding vessel that clinches the diagnosis. Extralobar lesions are commonly detected antenatally and may coexist with congenital diaphragmatic hernia, congenital pulmonary airway malformation (hybrid lesions) and cardiac defects. Definitive management is surgical resection (lobectomy for intralobar disease, simple excision for extralobar), while catheter embolisation of the feeding artery is an option in selected cases. Meticulous identification and secure control of the systemic feeding artery is essential, as an unrecognised retracted vessel can cause catastrophic haemorrhage. Mislabelling a hybrid lesion as pure sequestration or pure congenital pulmonary airway malformation. Overlooking an infradiaphragmatic feeding vessel arising from the abdominal aorta. Attributing recurrent left basal pneumonia to ordinary infection rather than an underlying sequestration. Assuming all lesions drain to pulmonary veins and misjudging the venous anatomy at surgery. During foetal development an accessory lung bud arises from the primitive foregut caudal to the normal lung bud, and because it develops separately it fails to establish communication with the tracheobronchial tree and retains its embryonic systemic arterial supply from the aorta rather than acquiring a pulmonary arterial connection. Whether the ectopic tissue is incorporated within the developing lung before or after pleural formation determines the intralobar phenotype (no separate pleura) versus the extralobar phenotype (separate pleural investment). The sequestered tissue is non-aerated or ventilated only through collateral channels, predisposing to mucus stasis and recurrent infection, while its systemic arterial supply creates a shunt that can rarely produce high-output cardiac strain or life-threatening haemoptysis. Prognosis is excellent after complete resection, with low recurrence and preserved long-term pulmonary function. Outcome in antenatally detected disease depends on lesion size, associated anomalies and the presence of hydrops.

rapid deterioration solely to pneumonia or thromboembolism and missing an occult cancer Overlooking the diagnostic clue of concurrent microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia Expecting targeted pulmonary vasodilators to reverse a fundamentally malignant microvascular process Delaying a search for the primary tumour that determines any therapeutic option Pulmonary tumour thrombotic microangiopathy occurs when malignant cells embolise into the small pulmonary arteries and arterioles and, rather than simply occluding them mechanically, provoke a local activation of coagulation and the release of growth factors. This stimulates a fibrocellular intimal proliferation and in situ thrombosis that progressively narrows and obstructs the microvasculature. The widespread microvascular obstruction rapidly raises pulmonary vascular resistance and imposes an acute pressure load on the right ventricle, producing rapidly progressive pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale. The same microvascular thrombotic process shears red cells and consumes platelets, generating the microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia that often accompany the syndrome. The prognosis is extremely poor, with most patients deteriorating over days to weeks, and the diagnosis is frequently confirmed only post mortem. Occasionally, prompt recognition and treatment of the underlying malignancy can slow progression, but survival is generally measured in weeks.

valve is narrowed, most often by commissural fusion of a congenitally domed valve or by thickened, poorly mobile dysplastic leaflets. The obstruction imposes a pressure load on the right ventricle, which hypertrophies to maintain output across the narrowed orifice; the resulting high-velocity jet produces post-stenotic dilatation of the pulmonary trunk. With severe, chronic obstruction the hypertrophied right ventricle may fail, right atrial pressure rises, and any coexisting atrial communication can permit right-to-left shunting with cyanosis. Mild pulmonary stenosis carries an excellent outlook and rarely progresses, while moderate to severe obstruction responds well to balloon valvuloplasty or surgery with durable relief and regression of right ventricular hypertrophy.

Administering arterial vasodilators increases flow into a bed that cannot drain, precipitating acute pulmonary oedema. Pulmonic Valve Disease — Pulmonary valve disease, Pulmonic stenosis, Pulmonic regurgitation, PS, PR Aortic regurgitation (the Graham Steell murmur of PR can mimic the AR murmur) Other causes of a midsystolic murmur such as aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive physiology, or an atrial septal defect with enhanced pulmonic flow Pulmonary hypertension as the dominant clinical problem rather than the valve lesion itself Infective endocarditis of the pulmonic valve (an etiology of both PS from bulky vegetations and PR) ECG: right axis deviation, RV hypertrophy, and right atrial enlargement in severe PS; RVH/RA enlargement may appear in PR depending on etiology and severity Chest x-ray: poststenotic dilation of the main pulmonary artery on the frontal view, retrosternal airspace filling from RV enlargement on the lateral view, and apex lifted off the left hemidiaphragm in some patients Transthoracic echocardiography (Doppler): definitive diagnosis in most cases, with jet velocity, gradient, RV function, pulmonary artery pressures (which should be low in PS), and associated lesions; RV systolic pressure estimated from the tricuspid regurgitant jet Transesophageal echocardiography: better delineation of the RV outflow tract and infundibular hypertrophy when needed Cardiac MR: greater anatomic detail and precise RV volume/function assessment, especially in repaired congenital heart disease Cardiac catheterization: not routinely required; if performed in PS, pressures are taken just below and above the valve with attention to a possible dynamic gradient Carcinoid heart disease causing mixed pulmonic valve lesions Obstructing tumors producing RV outflow obstruction that mimics valvular PS Idiopathic dilation of the pulmonary artery / annulus causing functional PR Marfan syndrome-related annular enlargement Pulmonic stenosis is overwhelmingly a congenital lesion; the valve is typically domed in isolated cases, and the pulmonic valve is only very rarely affected by the rheumatic process. Dysplastic pulmonic valves occur as a feature of Noonan syndrome (mapped to chromosome 12), with PTPN1 gene mutations identified in roughly half of Noonan cases. The pulmonic ejection sound (click) is the single right-sided acoustic event that DECREASES in intensity with inspiration, because elevated RV end-diastolic pressure pre-opens the valve. As pulmonic stenosis worsens, the ejection sound migrates toward S1 and eventually becomes inaudible, the systolic murmur peaks later and may extend past A2, and P2 becomes reduced or absent. The systolic murmur of pulmonic stenosis is mid-systolic and crescendo-decrescendo, best heard in the left second interspace, and it increases in intensity during inspiration. The Graham Steell murmur of pulmonic regurgitation is a high-pitched, decrescendo diastolic murmur along the left sternal border that can be mistaken for aortic regurgitation; it tends to grow louder with inspiration. In survivors of childhood tetralogy of Fallot or PS/pulmonary atresia repair, an RV-PA conduit lacking a valve can be freely regurgitant, producing a misleadingly low-pitched, short diastolic murmur despite significant PR and RV volume overload. Right ventricular dysfunction from afterload mismatch appears earlier and at lower peak systolic pressures in pulmonic stenosis than left ventricular failure does in aortic stenosis, because the RV tolerates pressure overload poorly. Cardiac output is maintained until late in pulmonic stenosis, so many patients with mild or even moderate disease are asymptomatic and are detected only by an incidental murmur or click. A reduction in RV ejection fraction may be an early sign of hemodynamic compromise in pulmonic regurgitation, before overt symptoms develop. Trace or mild pulmonic regurgitation of no hemodynamic significance is frequently seen on transthoracic echocardiography even when the valve is structurally normal. Carcinoid characteristically produces mixed pulmonic valve disease, combining both regurgitation and stenosis. Exertional dyspnea or early-onset fatigue indicating severe pulmonic stenosis Anginal chest pain from RV oxygen supply-demand mismatch, or syncope, with very severe obstruction Destabilizing triggers (atrial fibrillation, fever, infection, anemia, pregnancy) precipitating decompensation in severe PS Signs of right heart failure (hepatomegaly, ascites, peripheral edema) from RV systolic dysfunction Abdominal fullness/bloating and lower-extremity swelling in progressive severe PR with RV dysfunction The Graham Steell murmur of PR is easily confused with aortic regurgitation along the left sternal border. A valveless RV-PA conduit after congenital repair can give a low-pitched, short diastolic murmur that understates the true severity of PR and RV volume overload. Doppler peak instantaneous gradient correlates only weakly with the catheterization peak-to-peak gradient; the catheter peak-to-peak value tends to track better with the Doppler MEAN gradient. Trace or mild PR seen on echocardiography is usually of no clinical or hemodynamic consequence and should not be over-interpreted. Relying on the systolic ejection sound can mislead in severe PS, where the click moves toward S1 and may become inaudible. Pulmonic stenosis is defined hemodynamically by a systolic pressure gradient between the right ventricle and the main pulmonary artery. Sustained obstruction to RV outflow drives RV hypertrophy and prolongs systolic ejection; because the RV adapts poorly to pressure overload, dysfunction from afterload mismatch develops earlier and at lower pressures than analogous left-sided changes in aortic stenosis. The right atrial a wave rises in proportion to the higher pressures needed to fill a stiff, hypertrophied RV, and a prominent RA v wave reflects functional tricuspid regurgitation from RV and annular dilation; cardiac output is preserved until late. Pulmonic stenosis rarely progresses when mild but can worsen with age in moderate disease owing to valve thickening and calcification. In pulmonic regurgitation, severe disease causes RV chamber enlargement and eccentric hypertrophy, creating a state of increased preload and afterload. The diastolic pressure gradient from pulmonary artery to RV that drives the regurgitant flow falls progressively through diastole, explaining the decrescendo murmur, and the murmur shortens as RV diastolic pressure rises. Forward output is preserved early but fails to augment normally with exercise and declines over time; advanced stages show marked RV and RA enlargement with elevated jugular venous pressure. PR arises from primary valve pathology, annular enlargement (e.g., long-standing severe pulmonary hypertension dilating the valve ring), or their combination, and may follow surgical relief of RV outflow obstruction or balloon valvotomy. Mild pulmonic stenosis rarely progresses, whereas moderate disease may worsen with age due to valve thickening and calcification. Because cardiac output is maintained until late, many patients remain asymptomatic for years; severe disease eventually brings RV dysfunction and, uncommonly and only very late, overt right heart failure. In pulmonic regurgitation, forward output is preserved early but does not rise normally with exertion and declines over time, with a falling RV ejection fraction serving as an early marker of compromise and advanced disease producing marked RV/RA enlargement and elevated jugular venous pressure. Pulmonic stenosis severity (normal systolic function and cardiac output): severe = peak systolic gradient >64 mmHg (mean gradient >35 mmHg, Doppler jet velocity >4 m/s); moderate = peak gradient 36-64 mmHg (jet velocity 3-4 m/s); mild = jet velocity <3 m/s (peak gradient <36 mmHg).

from advancing caries, reach the pulp through dentinal tubules or direct exposure, triggering an inflammatory response within the rigid, low-compliance confines of the pulp chamber. Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability raise intrapulpal pressure, and because the pulp cannot expand, this compresses vessels and nerves, amplifying pain. In reversible disease the inflammation is limited and the pulp can recover once the irritant is removed. With continued insult the inflammation becomes irreversible, progressing to ischaemia, localised then total pulp necrosis, and eventual extension of infection through the apical foramen into the periapical tissues. Reversible pulpitis usually resolves fully after the irritant is treated, while irreversible pulpitis will not recover and needs endodontic treatment or extraction; treated teeth generally have a good outcome when infection is eliminated.

is a neurodegenerative disorder confined largely to the peripheral autonomic nervous system. Misfolded alpha-synuclein accumulates within postganglionic sympathetic and parasympathetic neurons and causes their degeneration. Loss of postganglionic sympathetic fibres impairs noradrenaline release, so vasoconstriction fails on standing and blood pools in the lower body, producing orthostatic hypotension. Pure autonomic failure generally progresses slowly and carries a better outlook than multiple system atrophy, but a meaningful proportion of patients phenoconvert to a central synucleinopathy over years, and disabling orthostatic symptoms with supine hypertension require ongoing management.

pure motor hemiparesis — pure motor stroke, pure motor lacunar syndrome Cortical (large-vessel) infarct with predominant motor involvement Small deep intracerebral haemorrhage in the capsule or pons Sensorimotor lacunar stroke Subdural haematoma or mass lesion compressing the internal capsule Todd's paresis following a focal seizure Demyelinating lesion of the corticospinal tract Diffusion-weighted and T2/FLAIR MRI of the brain Non-contrast CT head to exclude haemorrhage acutely Vascular imaging of carotids and intracranial vessels to seek an alternative embolic source ECG and prolonged rhythm monitoring for atrial fibrillation Fasting glucose, HbA1c and lipid profile Blood pressure profiling including ambulatory measurement The commonest lacunar syndrome, classically caused by a small deep infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule or the basis pontis. Weakness affects the face, arm and leg roughly equally on one side, without sensory loss, visual field defect, aphasia or neglect. The complete absence of 'cortical' signs (aphasia, apraxia, agnosia, hemianopia, gaze deviation) is what distinguishes it from a cortical territory infarct. Dysarthria and mild transient sensory symptoms may occur, but objective sensory loss argues against the pure motor label. Small-vessel lipohyalinosis and microatheroma from chronic hypertension and diabetes are the dominant mechanisms rather than embolism. A capsular warning syndrome, with stuttering, fluctuating or crescendo hemiparesis, heralds impending completed capsular infarction and warrants urgent attention. CT is frequently normal acutely; diffusion-weighted MRI best demonstrates the small deep infarct and excludes mimics. Long-term management centres on aggressive control of blood pressure, glycaemia and lipids plus antiplatelet therapy. Stuttering or crescendo weakness suggesting capsular warning syndrome and impending completed infarct Depressed conscious level or headache raising suspicion of haemorrhage Rapid worsening with new cortical signs indicating larger-territory ischaemia Fever or systemic sepsis suggesting an alternative or infective cause Labelling a stroke 'pure motor' when subtle objective sensory loss or a visual field defect is present, which points instead to a larger lesion. Assuming a normal acute CT excludes stroke and thereby missing a small deep infarct visible only on diffusion MRI. Attributing all deficits to small-vessel disease and failing to screen for a treatable embolic source. Overlooking a small capsular or pontine haemorrhage that can mimic the syndrome exactly. Under-treating vascular risk factors because the initial deficit seems mild. Pure motor hemiparesis results from occlusion of a single small penetrating (perforating) artery supplying the corticospinal tract where its fibres are compactly arranged, most often the lenticulostriate branches to the posterior limb of the internal capsule or paramedian pontine perforators from the basilar artery. Chronic hypertension and diabetes drive lipohyalinosis and microatheromatous change within these end-arteries, producing a small (typically under 15 mm) ischaemic cavity or lacune. Because the lesion lies in white matter tracts distant from cortex, motor fibres to face, arm and leg are interrupted together while sensory, visual and higher cortical pathways are spared, giving the characteristic isolated motor deficit. Functional recovery is often good, with many patients regaining substantial motor function, but recurrent lacunar events and vascular cognitive impairment are common without rigorous risk-factor control. The capsular warning syndrome carries a high short-term risk of completed disabling infarction.

syndrome results from occlusion of a single small penetrating artery, typically due to lipohyalinosis or microatheroma from chronic hypertension and diabetes, producing a small deep infarct (lacune). The lesion interrupts the densely packed corticospinal fibres where they are concentrated in a small volume, most often the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the corona radiata, or the basis pontis. Because these sites carry motor fibres without accompanying sensory, visual, or higher cortical pathways, the deficit is a proportionate contralateral weakness of face, arm, and leg with no sensory loss, hemianopia, or cortical dysfunction, defining the pure motor pattern. Individual lacunar strokes often recover well with rehabilitation, but recurrent lacunes and progressive small-vessel disease can lead to cumulative disability, gait disorder, and vascular cognitive impairment.

Several mechanisms converge on this outcome: direct viral cytotoxicity to erythroid progenitors by parvovirus B19, which infects them via the P antigen; T-cell or antibody-mediated immune attack on erythroid precursors as in thymoma-associated and large granular lymphocytic leukaemia-associated disease; and neutralising antibodies against erythropoietin or its receptor. Prognosis depends on the cause; parvovirus-related and drug-related cases often recover once the trigger is removed or treated, thymoma-associated disease may improve after thymectomy, and idiopathic or immune forms frequently need ongoing immunosuppression.

pure sensory stroke — pure sensory lacunar syndrome, thalamic lacunar sensory stroke Sensory seizure or migraine aura with marching paraesthesiae Small thalamic haemorrhage Cortical parietal infarct causing sensory loss with discriminative features Peripheral or radicular sensory disturbance Functional (non-organic) sensory symptoms Multiple sclerosis plaque affecting sensory tracts Diffusion-weighted and T2/FLAIR MRI focusing on the thalamus and brainstem Non-contrast CT head to exclude thalamic haemorrhage Carotid and intracranial vascular imaging ECG and prolonged cardiac rhythm monitoring HbA1c, fasting glucose and lipid profile Blood pressure assessment including ambulatory monitoring Caused most often by a small lacune in the ventral posterolateral or ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus supplied by thalamogeniculate perforators. Presents with unilateral numbness, tingling or a subjective 'heavy' or 'swollen' sensation of the face, arm, trunk and leg without weakness or cortical signs. Involvement of all sensory modalities in a hemibody distribution that respects the midline is characteristic of a thalamic lesion. Objective sensory findings can be strikingly subtle even when symptoms are prominent, so patient-reported distribution is diagnostically valuable. Dejerine-Roussy thalamic pain syndrome may emerge weeks to months later as delayed, distressing central post-stroke pain in the affected region. Motor power, visual fields, language and coordination are, by definition, preserved. MRI with diffusion weighting is far more sensitive than CT for the small thalamic or lemniscal infarct. Hypertension and diabetes-related small-vessel disease underlie most cases; a cardioembolic or large-artery source should still be excluded. Reduced consciousness, headache or vomiting suggesting thalamic haemorrhage Progressive extension of symptoms into motor or cortical domains Severe delayed central pain heralding thalamic pain syndrome Bilateral or fluctuating sensory disturbance suggesting an alternative diagnosis Dismissing prominent subjective numbness as functional because objective signs are minimal. Missing a small thalamic haemorrhage that can present identically to the ischaemic syndrome. Failing to warn patients about, or later recognise, delayed thalamic pain. Relying on an early normal CT and not proceeding to diffusion MRI. Neglecting embolic-source screening on the assumption of pure small-vessel disease. Pure sensory stroke arises from occlusion of a small penetrating artery, classically a thalamogeniculate branch of the posterior cerebral artery supplying the ventral posterior thalamic nuclei, the principal relay for the spinothalamic and medial lemniscal pathways. A small lacune here interrupts crossed sensory fibres from the contralateral hemibody while sparing the internal capsule motor fibres, optic radiations and cortex. Less commonly the responsible lesion lies in the lemniscal pathway of the pons or in the parietal white matter. The underlying arteriopathy is typically hypertensive lipohyalinosis or microatheroma of end-arteries, producing the small deep cavity that defines a lacunar infarct. Sensory symptoms often improve over weeks and the immediate functional outcome is usually favourable, but a minority develop chronic, treatment-resistant central post-stroke (thalamic) pain, and recurrent small-vessel events remain a risk without risk-factor control.

the breakdown of inosine, guanosine and deoxyguanosine. Its deficiency causes accumulation of deoxyguanosine triphosphate, which is particularly toxic to developing and dividing T lymphocytes, producing a progressive T-cell lymphopenia and combined immunodeficiency while sparing B-cell numbers more than adenosine deaminase deficiency. The same toxic metabolites are thought to injure the central nervous system, accounting for the developmental and motor abnormalities. The metabolic block also diverts purines away from uric acid production, giving the characteristic hypouricaemia. The prognosis is poor without treatment, with death from infection in childhood; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can restore immune function, but the neurological impairment already present tends to persist and shapes the long-term outcome.

distinctive sign The retinopathy results from occlusion of retinal arterioles and precapillary vessels by microemboli, which may consist of fat, air, fibrin or aggregated leucocytes. pustular psoriasis of pregnancy — impetigo herpetiformis, generalised pustular psoriasis of pregnancy acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis subcorneal pustular dermatosis (Sneddon-Wilkinson disease) pemphigoid gestationis polymorphic eruption of pregnancy generalised pustular psoriasis unrelated to pregnancy widespread bacterial or candidal pustular infection drug reaction with pustulation skin biopsy (spongiform pustules of Kogoj, parakeratosis and neutrophilic infiltrate) serum calcium, albumin, phosphate and parathyroid hormone full blood count and inflammatory markers (leucocytosis, raised C-reactive protein and ESR) swabs and pustule culture to confirm sterility and exclude infection renal and liver function tests fetal surveillance with cardiotocography and growth ultrasound; consider IL36RN genetic testing Regarded as generalised pustular psoriasis presenting in pregnancy; the historical name impetigo herpetiformis is a misnomer as it is neither infective nor herpetic. Typically presents in the third trimester with erythematous patches fringed by sterile subcorneal pustules that extend centrifugally, often starting in the flexures. Systemic upset is characteristic, with fever, malaise, delirium, and features of hypocalcaemia such as tetany, and it can be life-threatening. Unlike the other pregnancy dermatoses it is often not markedly itchy; pain, burning and systemic illness dominate. Hypocalcaemia, hypoalbuminaemia and secondary hypoparathyroidism may occur and require correction. It carries a genuine risk of placental insufficiency, stillbirth and neonatal death, so fetal surveillance is essential. First-line treatment is systemic corticosteroid; ciclosporin is an option in resistant disease and delivery may be needed if the fetus is compromised at term. It tends to recur in subsequent pregnancies, often with earlier onset and greater severity. high fever, rigors, delirium or haemodynamic instability indicating systemic sepsis-like decompensation tetany, perioral or peripheral paraesthesiae or seizures from hypocalcaemia reduced fetal movements, growth restriction or abnormal cardiotocography signalling placental insufficiency rapidly extending confluent pustulation with skin failure and fluid or electrolyte loss signs of secondary bacterial infection or septicaemia Mistaking sterile pustules for infection and delaying corticosteroid while pursuing antibiotics. Failing to measure and correct calcium, risking tetany and seizures from unrecognised hypocalcaemia. Underestimating fetal risk and omitting fetal surveillance, missing placental insufficiency. Attributing the eruption to a benign pregnancy dermatosis and undertreating a potentially fatal condition. Abruptly stopping systemic corticosteroid after delivery, precipitating a rebound flare. Pustular psoriasis of pregnancy is a variant of generalised pustular psoriasis in which the pregnant state acts as a trigger, and a subset of patients carry mutations in IL36RN encoding the interleukin-36 receptor antagonist, leading to unopposed interleukin-36 signalling and intense neutrophilic inflammation. This produces the characteristic sterile spongiform pustules of Kogoj within the epidermis. Contributory factors include the relative hypocalcaemia and reduced parathyroid hormone activity of pregnancy and possible hormonal influences. The neutrophil-rich sterile pustulation and systemic inflammatory response account for the fever, leucocytosis and constitutional illness, while placental dysfunction underlies the associated fetal risk. With prompt systemic treatment, correction of electrolyte disturbance and fetal monitoring, maternal outcome is usually good, but there is a real risk of stillbirth, fetal growth restriction and neonatal death from placental insufficiency. It characteristically recurs in later pregnancies, frequently earlier and more severely.

cathepsin K biology has informed development of antiresorptive drug targets Recurrent or non-healing fractures, particularly of the long bones and mandible Severe obstructive sleep apnoea causing hypoxaemia Basilar skull deformity or neurological compromise Signs suggesting marrow failure that would point instead to osteopetrosis Assuming dense bone is strong and underestimating the high fracture risk Confusing it with osteopetrosis and expecting marrow failure or with osteogenesis imperfecta on the basis of fractures alone Overlooking acro-osteolysis and delayed fontanelle closure as diagnostic clues Neglecting airway and dental complications during anaesthesia and routine care Pycnodysostosis results from biallelic mutations in CTSK, the gene encoding cathepsin K, a cysteine protease secreted by osteoclasts that degrades the organic collagen matrix of bone during resorption. Because the enzyme is defective, osteoclasts can demineralise but cannot properly break down the collagenous matrix, leaving behind poorly remodelled, densely mineralised but structurally weak bone. This uncoupling of mineral removal from matrix degradation explains the paradox of a sclerotic, radiodense skeleton that fractures readily. Impaired remodelling at the acral skeleton produces the characteristic acro-osteolysis, and defective skull remodelling underlies the delayed fontanelle closure and craniofacial features. Lifespan is usually normal, but patients face recurrent fragility fractures, orthopaedic deformity, dental complications, and potential airway problems that require long-term multidisciplinary management.

prominent skull involvement and cranial-nerve compression Assuming the bulky metaphyses are strong when the thin cortices predispose to fracture Attributing an Erlenmeyer-flask deformity solely to Pyle disease without considering osteopetrosis or Gaucher disease Overlooking the autosomal recessive inheritance when counselling families Pyle disease results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in SFRP4, which encodes a secreted frizzled-related protein that normally antagonises WNT signalling and helps regulate the modelling of bone during growth. Loss of this antagonist disturbs the coordinated resorption and shaping that narrows the metaphysis into the diaphysis, so the metaphyses remain broad and undermodelled, giving the Erlenmeyer-flask appearance. The expanded metaphyseal bone has thinned cortices, accounting for a degree of fragility despite the bulky radiographic appearance. Because the skull is relatively spared compared with the craniotubular dysplasias, the disorder lacks the severe cranial-nerve and craniofacial complications seen in those conditions. The prognosis is generally good, with normal intelligence and life expectancy; morbidity relates mainly to limb deformity and occasional fractures rather than the neurological complications of the craniotubular dysplasias.

Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis — infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, IHPS, pyloric stenosis, congenital pyloric stenosis Gastro-oesophageal reflux Overfeeding Malrotation with volvulus (bilious vomiting) Gastroenteritis Cow's milk protein intolerance Metabolic disorders or raised intracranial pressure causing vomiting Adrenal insufficiency (salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia) Abdominal ultrasound to measure pyloric muscle thickness and channel length Serum electrolytes, chloride, and bicarbonate Blood gas to characterise the alkalosis Assessment of hydration status and weight Blood glucose Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle causing gastric outlet obstruction, typically presenting between 3 and 6 weeks of age and more common in firstborn males. The hallmark is progressive, forceful non-bilious (projectile) vomiting shortly after feeds, with the infant remaining hungry and eager to feed again. The classic metabolic picture is a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric acid and chloride. A palpable olive-shaped mass in the epigastrium/right upper quadrant and visible gastric peristalsis are classic but not always present. Ultrasound is the diagnostic investigation of choice, demonstrating a thickened and elongated pyloric muscle. The vomiting is characteristically non-bilious, because the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla of Vater; bilious vomiting should prompt consideration of other diagnoses. Initial management is medical resuscitation: correcting dehydration and the electrolyte and acid-base disturbance before any operation. Definitive treatment is surgical pyloromyotomy, which is not an emergency and should follow adequate fluid and electrolyte correction. Signs of significant dehydration or shock Severe electrolyte or acid-base derangement Bilious vomiting, which points away from pyloric stenosis toward a surgical emergency such as volvulus Lethargy or reduced responsiveness from dehydration and electrolyte imbalance Rushing to surgery before correcting fluid and electrolyte abnormalities Mistaking the illness for simple reflux or overfeeding and delaying diagnosis Overlooking that vomiting is characteristically non-bilious, and failing to reconsider the diagnosis if it is bilious Underestimating the degree of dehydration and metabolic alkalosis Progressive hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the circular smooth muscle of the pylorus narrows and elongates the pyloric channel, obstructing gastric emptying. The exact cause is unknown but involves genetic and environmental factors. Persistent vomiting of gastric contents leads to loss of hydrogen and chloride ions, producing a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; ongoing losses and renal compensation drive potassium loss and, later, paradoxical aciduria. Fluid losses cause dehydration. The obstruction is proximal to the biliary drainage, so vomitus is non-bilious. Prognosis is excellent after appropriate resuscitation and pyloromyotomy, with prompt recovery and no long-term gastrointestinal sequelae.

underlying immunocompromising condition Pyomyositis is a suppurative infection arising within skeletal muscle, thought to require transient bacteraemia together with muscle that has been rendered susceptible by trauma, strenuous exercise, or underlying compromise. Skeletal muscle is normally resistant to infection, but injury allows haematogenously seeded bacteria to establish a focus that progresses from diffuse inflammation to a walled-off intramuscular abscess. Without drainage the infection can extend, cause systemic sepsis, and, if untreated, seed distant sites. With timely antibiotics and adequate drainage the outlook is generally good; delayed diagnosis, extensive or multifocal disease, and progression to septic shock worsen outcomes, and immunocompromised patients are at higher risk of complications.

Pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase deficiency — P5N deficiency, P5'N-1 deficiency, pyrimidine 5-prime nucleotidase deficiency, NT5C3A gene Lead poisoning Thalassaemia and other causes of basophilic stippling Pyruvate kinase deficiency Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Sideroblastic anaemias Red-cell pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase enzyme assay Blood film examination for coarse basophilic stippling Blood lead concentration to exclude lead poisoning Red-cell nucleotide profile showing pyrimidine accumulation Haemolysis screen with bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin Molecular testing of the NT5C3A gene One of the commoner enzyme defects of red-cell nucleotide metabolism, causing chronic non-spherocytic, Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia The blood film hallmark is prominent coarse basophilic stippling, an unusual finding for an inherited haemolytic anaemia Because lead inhibits this same enzyme, the picture closely mimics lead poisoning and the two must be distinguished Inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, so consanguinity or affected siblings may be present Retained pyrimidine nucleotides accumulate in the red cell and can be detected as an abnormal nucleotide profile Diagnosis rests on reduced enzyme activity on assay together with the characteristic stippling and NT5C3A mutation testing Management is supportive with folate and transfusion when needed; the anaemia is usually mild to moderate and splenectomy gives limited benefit Failure to exclude lead poisoning, which is treatable and potentially serious Aplastic crisis after parvovirus B19 infection Symptomatic anaemia requiring transfusion Transfusional iron overload in more severe disease Failing to check a blood lead level and missing treatable lead intoxication that mimics the disorder Attributing basophilic stippling to thalassaemia without considering an enzyme defect Expecting splenectomy to substantially improve the anaemia Overlooking the abnormal red-cell nucleotide profile that supports the diagnosis Pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase dephosphorylates pyrimidine nucleotides during the degradation of RNA as reticulocytes mature, allowing the breakdown products to leave the cell. When the enzyme is deficient, pyrimidine nucleotides accumulate within the red cell, aggregate with ribosomal remnants to produce the coarse basophilic stippling seen on the film, and disturb nucleotide balance and glycolytic metabolism, shortening cell survival and causing a chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. Because lead directly inhibits the enzyme, lead intoxication reproduces the same biochemical and morphological picture. The anaemia is typically mild to moderate and lifelong but well tolerated, with a generally good prognosis once lead poisoning has been excluded.

disorders Multiple carboxylase deficiency (biotinidase or holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency) Urea cycle disorders Organic acidaemias with secondary lactic acidosis Fatty acid oxidation defects blood glucose during metabolic decompensation Enzyme activity assay in cultured fibroblasts Molecular genetic testing of the PC gene Neuroimaging assessing white matter and structural changes Autosomal recessive disorder caused by variants in the PC gene, encoding the biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme pyruvate carboxylase The enzyme converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate, an anaplerotic step essential for gluconeogenesis, the citric acid cycle and neurotransmitter synthesis Presents with lactic acidosis, often accompanied by hypoglycaemia, and a raised lactate-to-pyruvate ratio The severe neonatal (type B, often French) form causes overwhelming lactic acidosis, hyperammonaemia, citrullinaemia and early death The milder infantile (type A, North American) form causes developmental delay, seizures and recurrent metabolic acidosis with lactic acidaemia A characteristic biochemical pattern includes raised lactate, ketones, ammonia, citrulline and lysine with low aspartate Anaplerotic therapy and avoidance of fasting form the mainstay of supportive management, but outcomes are generally poor Because pyruvate carboxylase is biotin-dependent, it should be distinguished from biotinidase and holocarboxylase synthetase deficiencies Severe neonatal lactic acidosis with hyperammonaemia and encephalopathy Recurrent hypoglycaemia with metabolic acidosis Rapid neurological deterioration during intercurrent illness Failure of acidosis to respond to conventional resuscitation Confusing it with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, which typically shows a normal lactate-to-pyruvate ratio Missing the diagnosis when lactic acidosis is attributed to sepsis or tissue hypoperfusion Overlooking hyperammonaemia and the urea cycle contribution Failing to prevent catabolism and fasting, which precipitate crises Pyruvate carboxylase catalyses the ATP-dependent, biotin-requiring carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate within mitochondria. This reaction replenishes citric acid cycle intermediates (anaplerosis) and provides oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis and, in the brain, for aspartate and glutamate synthesis. Enzyme deficiency blocks gluconeogenesis, causing fasting hypoglycaemia, and diverts pyruvate towards lactate, producing lactic acidosis with an elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratio. Depletion of oxaloacetate impairs the malate-aspartate shuttle and urea cycle function, contributing to hyperammonaemia and abnormal amino acids, while cerebral aspartate deficiency disturbs myelination and neurotransmitter metabolism. The severe neonatal form carries a very poor prognosis with early death, and even the milder infantile form is usually associated with significant developmental delay and recurrent metabolic crises. Rare attenuated cases with more residual enzyme activity have better outcomes.

dichloroacetate has been used to lower lactate Not a standard target of newborn screening, so diagnosis rests on recognising congenital lactic acidosis and neurological features and confirming enzymatically or genetically Severe neonatal lactic acidosis with encephalopathy is a metabolic emergency Acute worsening of lactic acidosis and neurological function after carbohydrate loading Rapidly progressive encephalopathy or brainstem involvement in a Leigh-syndrome presentation Intractable seizures or apnoea in the neonatal period Loading a hypotonic, acidotic infant with intravenous glucose, which can worsen lactic acidosis Confusing it with respiratory chain disease by not checking the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio Overlooking treatable thiamine-responsive variants Missing affected females because the common defect is X-linked The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts pyruvate, the end product of glycolysis, into acetyl-CoA, linking carbohydrate metabolism to the citric acid cycle and oxidative energy production. When the complex is deficient, pyruvate cannot enter the cycle and is instead diverted to lactate and alanine, producing lactic acidosis with a normal lactate-to-pyruvate ratio. The brain, which depends heavily on glucose oxidation for energy, is particularly affected, resulting in structural malformations, neurodegeneration and a Leigh-like phenotype. Providing fat-derived ketones and acetyl-CoA through a ketogenic diet bypasses the enzymatic block and supplies the brain with usable fuel. Prognosis is generally guarded and correlates with the severity of residual enzyme activity; severe neonatal forms often have a poor outcome, whereas milder and thiamine-responsive variants and early ketogenic dietary treatment can improve neurological outcome, though the disorder is not curable.

It releases biflagellate motile zoospores that are attracted to and encyst on damaged skin, cornea, or the gut wall, then germinate to produce invasive hyphae. Because its cell wall is built of cellulose and beta-glucans and its membranes lack ergosterol, the organism is intrinsically resistant to antifungal agents that target ergosterol synthesis. In the vascular form the hyphae invade arterial walls, provoking a necrotising, thrombosing arteritis that progressively occludes vessels and produces limb ischaemia; the tendency for this angioinvasive disease is greatly increased in patients with thalassaemia and iron overload. Host immune responses are largely granulomatous and eosinophil-rich but insufficient to contain the aggressive tissue invasion. Vascular pythiosis carries a high risk of limb loss and death unless there is early radical surgery combined with medical and immunotherapy; ocular disease often leads to loss of the eye, whereas localised cutaneous disease treated promptly has a better outcome.

In chronic disease the organism persists at sites such as damaged or prosthetic heart valves and vascular tissue, driving endovascular infection. rather than immediate Quebec platelet disorder is caused by a tandem duplication of PLAU, the gene encoding urokinase-type plasminogen activator. Overexpression of urokinase within developing megakaryocytes leads to accumulation of the enzyme in platelet alpha granules, where it generates plasmin intracellularly. This premature, localised plasmin activity degrades stored alpha-granule proteins such as factor V, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, and others. Failure to recognise the disorder can lead to preventable, sometimes serious, delayed haemorrhage.

CT usually normal; EEG nonspecific Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (especially young females; behavioral changes, autonomic instability, hypoventilation, seizures) Other antibody-mediated autoimmune encephalitis Guillain-Barre syndrome Rabies hysteria (somatic symptom disorder) with shorter course and eventual recovery Psychiatric disorder Rabies is a rapidly progressive acute CNS infection by rabies virus (a lyssavirus, family Rhabdoviridae), normally transmitted via the bite of an infected animal; it has encephalitic and paralytic forms that progress to death (p.1650). Worldwide, ~99% of human rabies is transmitted from dogs in countries with endemic canine rabies; endemic canine rabies causes an estimated 59,000 human deaths annually, with most deaths in Asia and Africa and rural populations and children disproportionately affected (p.1650-1651). Incubation period is usually 20-90 days but in rare cases may be as short as a few days or longer than 1 year (p.1651). Earliest specific neurologic symptoms are paresthesias, pain, or pruritus near the exposure site, occurring in 50-80% of patients and strongly suggesting rabies; the wound has usually healed by this point (p.1652). Two acute neurologic forms occur: encephalitic (furious) in ~80% and paralytic (dumb) in ~20% (p.1652). Encephalitic rabies presents as atypical encephalitis with relative preservation of consciousness; episodes of hyperexcitability alternate with periods of complete lucidity that shorten as disease progresses (p.1652). Early brainstem involvement produces the classic hydrophobia (involuntary painful contraction of diaphragm and accessory respiratory, laryngeal, and pharyngeal muscles on swallowing liquids) and aerophobia (same response to a draft of air) (p.1652). Autonomic dysfunction is common and may cause hypersalivation, gooseflesh, cardiac arrhythmia, and priapism; hypersalivation plus pharyngeal dysfunction produces the classic 'foaming at the mouth' (p.1652). Paralytic rabies features early prominent flaccid weakness often beginning in the bitten extremity, progressing to quadriparesis and facial weakness, with sphincter involvement common and sensory involvement usually mild (p.1652). The Negri body (eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion in brain neurons, e.g. cerebellar Purkinje cells and hippocampal pyramidal neurons) is the most characteristic pathologic finding, but is NOT seen in all cases (p.1651-1652). Diagnosis should be considered in patients with acute atypical encephalitis or acute flaccid paralysis, including those in whom Guillain-Barre syndrome is suspected; absence of an animal-bite history is common in North America due to unrecognized bat exposures (p.1653). Postexposure prophylaxis must be initiated after a recognized exposure and before any symptoms or signs develop; the emphasis for prevention is on PEP (p.1652). Near-100% fatal once symptomatic, so post-exposure prophylaxis is everything - do NOT delay PEP after a recognized exposure. Paresthesias, pain, or pruritus at a healed animal-bite site preceding neurologic illness strongly suggest rabies. Hydrophobia or aerophobia with preserved consciousness (atypical encephalitis) is essentially diagnostic of encephalitic rabies. Absence of a recalled animal bite does NOT exclude rabies - bat exposures are frequently unrecognized; consider PEP when a small child or sleeping adult shared a space with a bat and an unrecognized bite cannot be reliably excluded. Negative antemortem rabies-specific laboratory tests never exclude the diagnosis; repeat testing may be needed. Acute flaccid paralysis resembling Guillain-Barre syndrome may be paralytic rabies - fever, bladder dysfunction, normal sensory exam, and CSF pleocytosis favor rabies. Rabies is often not considered until late in the clinical course in North America even with a typical presentation. Relying on a history of animal bite to make the diagnosis - many cases (especially bat-associated) have no recalled exposure. Assuming absence of hydrophobia excludes rabies - lack of hydrophobia is not unusual. Misdiagnosing paralytic rabies as Guillain-Barre syndrome. Treating negative antemortem rabies-specific tests as exclusionary. Severe CSF pleocytosis (>1000 white cells/uL) is unusual for rabies and should prompt a search for an alternative diagnosis. Delaying local wound care while awaiting the 10-day animal observation period - wound care should not be delayed. Administering passive immunization (RIG) more than 7 days after the first vaccine dose, when endogenous antibody production has begun and passive immunization may be counterproductive; rabies vaccine and RIG must never be given at the same site. Minor deviations from current PEP recommendations can lead to prophylaxis failure. Rabies virus, a single-strand negative-sense RNA lyssavirus (family Rhabdoviridae), is usually inoculated by an animal bite. During most of the incubation period the virus remains at or near the inoculation site; in muscle it binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junctions. It spreads centripetally along peripheral nerves toward the spinal cord or brainstem by retrograde fast axonal transport (up to ~250 mm/d, with ~12-h delays at each synapse). Once in the CNS it disseminates rapidly along neuroanatomic connections; neurons are prominently infected while astrocyte infection is unusual. After CNS infection is established there is centrifugal spread along sensory and autonomic nerves to salivary glands, heart, adrenal glands, and skin; viral replication in salivary gland acinar cells leads to secretion in saliva (the vehicle of animal transmission). There is no well-documented evidence for hematogenous spread. CNS inflammatory changes are mild (mononuclear infiltrate, perivascular cuffing, microglial Babes nodules) with little neuronal death; clinical disease is attributed to neuronal dysfunction rather than death, with oxidative stress from mitochondrial dysfunction implicated. (p.1650-1652) Rabies is an almost uniformly fatal disease but is nearly always preventable after recognized exposures with appropriate postexposure therapy during the early incubation period. Most patients die within several days of symptom onset despite aggressive critical-care support. There is no established treatment and no antiviral has demonstrated efficacy; aggressive supportive care has yielded at least 33 documented survivors (many recently reported from India), but recent treatment failures (>60) have far outnumbered successes. All but 2 of the 33 documented survivors had received one or more doses of rabies vaccine before disease onset, and the unvaccinated survivors had neutralizing antibodies in CSF at presentation. A palliative approach may be appropriate for patients who are not candidates for aggressive management. (p.1654) Clinical stages: incubation period (20-90 days, asymptomatic); prodrome (2-10 days: fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting; paresthesias/pain/pruritus at the wound site); acute neurologic disease - encephalitic form (~80%, 2-7 days: anxiety, agitation, hyperactivity, bizarre behavior, hallucinations, autonomic dysfunction, hydrophobia) or paralytic form (~20%, 2-10 days: flaccid limb paralysis progressing to quadriparesis with facial paralysis); then coma and death (0-14 days; recovery rare). (p.1653)

With markedly reduced insulin signalling, tissues cannot take up glucose or grow normally despite very high insulin levels, and hepatic glucose output is poorly suppressed. The result is severe insulin resistance manifest as fasting hypoglycaemia alternating with pronounced postprandial hyperglycaemia, together with acanthosis nigricans, growth impairment, and the characteristic dysmorphic, dental, and nail features. Because residual receptor function is greater than in Donohue syndrome, the course is less rapidly fatal but progresses to overt, ketosis-prone diabetes. Children with Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome generally survive longer than those with Donohue syndrome, often into the second decade or beyond, but face progressive, difficult-to-control diabetes with ketoacidosis and chronic complications; IGF-1-based therapy may improve control.

Radial longitudinal deficiency (radial club hand) — radial club hand, radial dysplasia, radial longitudinal deficiency, RLD, preaxial deficiency of the upper limb Ulnar longitudinal deficiency (postaxial deficiency) Isolated thumb hypoplasia without radial deficiency Cleft hand or central longitudinal deficiency Constriction ring (amniotic band) sequence affecting the forearm Arthrogryposis with fixed wrist contracture Acquired radial deficiency following trauma, infection, or tumour resection Radiographs of the whole upper limb to grade radial, carpal, and thumb deficiency Full blood count and blood film to screen for thrombocytopenia (TAR syndrome) Chromosomal breakage testing (diepoxybutane or mitomycin C) to exclude Fanconi anaemia before surgery Echocardiography and cardiology spectrum of preaxial (radial-side) failure of formation, ranging from a mildly hypoplastic thumb to complete absence of the radius with the hand deviated radially at the wrist The forearm is usually short and bowed, the unsupported carpus deviates radially (the 'club hand' appearance), and the thumb is frequently hypoplastic or absent Severity is graded (Bayne and later modifications) from a deficient distal radial epiphysis through partial to complete radial aplasia, incorporating thumb and carpal deficiency Strong systemic associations mandate a syndrome search: VACTERL association,
