and a full blood count) is essential before any surgery Early treatment centres on stretching and splinting to correct wrist alignment, with surgical centralisation or radialisation of the carpus over the ulna reserved for suitable cases Thumb reconstruction by pollicisation of the index finger restores pinch when the thumb is absent or non-functional Undiagnosed Fanconi anaemia, which can progress to marrow failure and malignancy if missed before surgery Severe thrombocytopenia in TAR syndrome risking perioperative haemorrhage Associated cardiac or renal anomalies (Holt-Oram or VACTERL) needing evaluation before anaesthesia Bilateral severe deformity with limited elbow extension compromising hand-to-mouth function Treating the hand deformity without screening for Fanconi anaemia or TAR, thereby missing a life-threatening haematological disorder Overlooking associated cardiac, renal, or vertebral anomalies Performing aggressive centralisation when elbow extension is limited, which can worsen function by preventing hand-to-mouth movement Neglecting thumb function, which is often more disabling than the wrist deformity itself The deformity arises from failure of formation along the preaxial (radial) margin of the developing upper limb bud in early gestation, affecting the radius, radial carpal bones, thumb ray, and the associated muscles, radial nerve, and vessels. The degree of radial deficiency determines the radial deviation of the hand and the instability of the wrist, as the carpus loses its bony support. Because the same limb-patterning and progenitor pathways influence blood formation and cardiac development, radial longitudinal deficiency is frequently part of systemic disorders affecting haematopoiesis (Fanconi anaemia, thrombocytopenia-absent-radius) or the heart (Holt-Oram syndrome), which must always be sought. With appropriate splinting, centralisation, and pollicisation, function and appearance improve substantially, but recurrence of radial deviation and continued forearm shortening are common as the child grows; the overall outlook is heavily influenced by any underlying syndrome, particularly the haematological disorders.

radial nerve palsy — radial neuropathy, Saturday night palsy, spiral groove syndrome Posterior interosseous nerve syndrome (finger drop without wrist drop or sensory loss) C7 radiculopathy Posterior cord brachial plexopathy Central lesion causing pseudo-radial upper-limb weakness (cortical hand knob stroke) Lead neuropathy causing bilateral wrist drop Extensor tendon rupture at the wrist Nerve conduction studies to localise the lesion and identify conduction block at the spiral groove Needle electromyography sampling triceps, brachioradialis, extensor and forearm muscles to define the level and axonal loss Plain radiographs of the humerus if fracture or callus entrapment is suspected High-resolution ultrasound or MRI neurography to demonstrate focal nerve enlargement, mass or entrapment Serum lead concentration when bilateral wrist drop is present Cervical spine imaging if radiculopathy is a competing diagnosis The commonest site of injury is the spiral (radial) groove of the humerus, producing wrist drop, finger drop and weak thumb extension with sensory loss over the dorsal first web space The classic compressive 'Saturday night palsy' follows prolonged external pressure on the arm, often with sleep after alcohol; humeral shaft fracture (notably the Holstein-Lewis distal-third fracture) is a key traumatic cause A spiral-groove lesion spares triceps and the elbow-extension reflex because branches to triceps arise proximally, whereas a very proximal axillary lesion (for example crutch palsy) also weakens triceps Brachioradialis and supinator weakness helps localise a lesion at or above the elbow, and the radially deviated posture on attempted wrist extension reflects preserved extensor carpi radialis longus with weak extensor carpi ulnaris Finger drop with preserved wrist extension and no sensory loss indicates a posterior interosseous (deep motor branch) lesion rather than a main radial trunk palsy Apparent hand-grip weakness is often spurious, resulting from loss of wrist extension that shortens the finger flexors; grip normalises when the wrist is passively supported Most neuropraxic and compressive lesions recover spontaneously; a cock-up wrist splint maintains function, and tendon transfers are considered when there is no recovery after adequate time and electrophysiological follow-up Wrist drop developing acutely after humeral fracture or fracture manipulation, suggesting nerve entrapment or laceration Bilateral wrist drop raising concern for lead toxicity or a systemic neuropathy Rapidly progressive or painful onset suggesting inflammatory neuralgic amyotrophy or vasculitis Associated triceps weakness and axillary sensory loss indicating a proximal plexus or cord lesion Interpreting grip weakness as median or ulnar dysfunction when it is secondary to loss of wrist extension Missing a posterior interosseous lesion by not testing for preserved wrist extension and intact sensation Failing to recognise triceps sparing as evidence for a spiral-groove rather than axillary lesion Overlooking a humeral fracture or delayed entrapment in callus as the cause Not considering neuralgic amyotrophy or lead toxicity in atypical, painful or bilateral presentations The radial nerve, the terminal continuation of the posterior cord (C5-T1), descends through the axilla, winds around the humerus in the spiral groove between the heads of triceps, then pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to reach the anterior compartment at the elbow, where it divides into the superficial (sensory) radial nerve and the posterior interosseous (deep motor) branch. Its close apposition to the humerus in the spiral groove and its tethering at the lateral intermuscular septum render it susceptible to external compression, fracture and traction. Compression typically produces focal demyelination with conduction block and good prognosis, whereas transection or severe traction causes axonal loss requiring regeneration over months; the motor deficit reflects paralysis of the wrist, finger and thumb extensors and, in proximal lesions, the elbow extensors. Compressive and neuropraxic palsies usually recover fully over weeks to a few months once conduction block resolves. Lesions with significant axonal loss recover more slowly and incompletely, and those associated with nerve transection require surgical repair with a more guarded outcome.

Radial scar — Complex sclerosing lesion, Radial sclerosing lesion Tubular carcinoma Invasive carcinoma of no special type presenting as a spiculated mass Sclerosing adenosis Fat necrosis with scarring Postsurgical scar Complex sclerosing lesion with atypia Low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma Diagnostic mammography with additional projections Tomosynthesis to characterise the stellate lesion Targeted ultrasound of the mammographic abnormality Image-guided core or vacuum-assisted biopsy Diagnostic surgical or vacuum-assisted excision for definitive assessment Histology with myoepithelial immunohistochemistry Radiological-pathological concordance review at multidisciplinary meeting A benign sclerosing lesion with a fibroelastic core from which ducts and lobules radiate, termed a complex sclerosing lesion when larger than about 1 cm. Usually impalpable and detected on screening mammography as a stellate or spiculated lesion that closely mimics invasive carcinoma. The mammographic appearance may show a radiolucent centre and long radiating spicules, sometimes varying between projections ('black star'). Frequently harbours or is associated with atypical hyperplasia, in situ carcinoma or, less often, invasive carcinoma at its periphery. Core biopsy sampling can under-represent associated atypia, so diagnostic excision or vacuum-assisted excision is usually recommended. The lesion itself is benign but is regarded as a marker of modestly increased future breast cancer risk. Preserved myoepithelial layer around entrapped tubules distinguishes it from tubular carcinoma histologically. Careful radiological-pathological correlation is essential given the strong radiological overlap with malignancy. Associated atypical hyperplasia or in situ carcinoma on biopsy Discordance between imaging and core biopsy findings Increasing size or a developing palpable mass Foci suspicious for tubular carcinoma at the lesion periphery Suspicious microcalcification within the lesion Confidently diagnosing malignancy on imaging alone, or conversely dismissing a spiculated lesion as benign Relying on limited core biopsy that misses associated atypia or carcinoma Misinterpreting entrapped tubules as invasive tubular carcinoma without myoepithelial stains Failing to ensure radiological-pathological concordance Neglecting ongoing surveillance given the increased future risk A radial scar forms around a central zone of fibroelastic (fibroelastotic) tissue into which ducts and lobules are drawn and distorted, creating a stellate architecture with entrapped, sometimes distorted, tubules at the centre. The radiating arms show a range of proliferative changes including adenosis, ductal hyperplasia, cyst formation and papillomatosis. Although the process is benign and probably reflects a localised reparative or sclerosing response, the entrapment of tubules within dense stroma can mimic stromal invasion, and the associated proliferative epithelium may progress to atypical hyperplasia or carcinoma, explaining both the diagnostic difficulty and the increased cancer risk. The radial scar itself is benign, and after appropriate excision the outlook is excellent. It signals a mild-to-moderate increase in long-term breast cancer risk, warranting continued participation in screening.

Radiation enteritis — radiation enteropathy Recurrent malignancy causing obstruction Inflammatory bowel disease Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth Adhesional small-bowel obstruction Coeliac or other malabsorptive disease History of abdominal/pelvic radiotherapy Cross-sectional imaging or contrast studies of the small bowel Assessment of nutritional status and malabsorption Endoscopy where accessible bowel is involved Evaluation for bacterial overgrowth and bile acid malabsorption Small-bowel injury from abdominal or pelvic radiotherapy, in acute and chronic forms Acute enteritis causes nausea, cramping, diarrhoea and malabsorption during and shortly after treatment and usually settles Chronic radiation enteropathy develops months to years later with obstruction, malabsorption, bleeding or fistulae Fixed loops of small bowel in the pelvis (for example after surgery) are especially vulnerable Chronic disease reflects progressive obliterative endarteritis, ischaemia and fibrosis Management is largely supportive and nutritional; surgery for strictures or fistulae is high-risk in irradiated tissue Small-bowel obstruction Enteric fistula formation Significant gastrointestinal bleeding Severe malnutrition or features suggesting recurrent tumour Attributing chronic symptoms to recurrent cancer without considering radiation enteropathy (and vice versa) Underestimating the surgical risk in irradiated bowel Overlooking bacterial overgrowth and bile acid malabsorption as treatable contributors Neglecting nutritional support Radiation enteritis arises from ionising radiation injury to the rapidly dividing small-bowel mucosa and to the bowel vasculature. Acute injury causes mucosal cell loss, villous blunting and inflammation with malabsorption and diarrhoea, and usually recovers. Chronic radiation enteropathy results from progressive submucosal fibrosis and obliterative endarteritis, producing ischaemia, strictures, dysmotility, bacterial overgrowth, bleeding from telangiectasia and fistula formation. Risk relates to dose, technique and factors that fix bowel loops within the radiation field. Acute enteritis usually resolves after treatment; chronic enteropathy is progressive and difficult to manage, with surgery carrying high complication rates in irradiated bowel.

Radiation pneumonitis — radiation-induced lung injury, radiation lung injury, post-radiation pneumonitis Infective pneumonia, including opportunistic infection Lymphangitic carcinomatosis or tumour progression in the lung Pulmonary embolism Drug-induced or immune checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema Exacerbation of underlying interstitial lung disease Chest radiograph and high-resolution CT correlating changes with the radiation field Oxygen saturation and, where indicated, arterial blood gas and lung function testing Inflammatory markers and cultures to help exclude infection Bronchoscopy with lavage in selected cases to exclude infection or alternative diagnoses Review of the radiotherapy plan and concurrent systemic therapy including immunotherapy It is a subacute inflammatory lung injury that typically develops weeks to a few months after thoracic radiotherapy, most often for lung, breast, oesophageal, or mediastinal tumours Presenting features include dry cough, exertional breathlessness, low-grade fever, and sometimes pleuritic chest pain, which can mimic infection or cancer progression Risk is influenced by the volume of lung irradiated, total dose and fractionation, pre-existing lung disease, and concurrent or prior chemotherapy or immunotherapy Imaging classically shows ground-glass or consolidative change corresponding to the radiation field, though the distribution may extend beyond classic field borders with modern conformal techniques It is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring careful exclusion of infection, pulmonary embolism, lymphangitic tumour spread, and drug-induced pneumonitis Mild cases may be managed with observation and supportive care, while symptomatic disease is treated principally with corticosteroids and gradual tapering Concurrent immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy can potentiate or complicate lung toxicity, making the distinction from immune-related pneumonitis important Untreated or severe pneumonitis can progress over months to irreversible radiation-induced pulmonary fibrosis Rapidly worsening breathlessness with hypoxaemia High fever or purulent sputum suggesting superimposed infection Extensive bilateral changes extending beyond the radiation field Progression toward respiratory failure despite corticosteroid therapy Assuming symptoms represent infection and delaying appropriate anti-inflammatory treatment Missing tumour progression or pulmonary embolism by anchoring on radiation pneumonitis Tapering corticosteroids too rapidly and provoking a symptom flare Failing to consider concurrent immune-related pneumonitis in patients on checkpoint inhibitors Ionising radiation damages alveolar epithelial and vascular endothelial cells within the treated lung volume, triggering release of inflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species. This produces an acute to subacute alveolitis with increased capillary permeability, protein-rich exudate, and impaired gas exchange, seen clinically as radiation pneumonitis. If inflammation and fibroblast activation persist, the process evolves into progressive collagen deposition and radiation fibrosis with permanent architectural distortion and volume loss. The severity relates to the dose delivered and the volume of normal lung exposed, modified by patient and treatment factors. Most mild to moderate cases respond well to corticosteroids and resolve, but severe pneumonitis, extensive lung involvement, or progression to fibrosis can cause lasting respiratory impairment and, uncommonly, death.

Radiation proctitis — radiation proctopathy Inflammatory bowel disease proctitis Infective proctitis Ischaemic proctitis Recurrent or new pelvic malignancy Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome History of pelvic radiotherapy Sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy documenting telangiectasia and mucosal change Cautious biopsy given fistula risk in irradiated tissue Full blood count and iron studies for chronic bleeding Imaging if stricture, fistula or recurrent tumour is suspected Rectal injury from pelvic radiotherapy, occurring in acute (during/soon after treatment) and chronic (months to years later) forms Acute proctitis causes diarrhoea, urgency, tenesmus and mucus; chronic disease causes rectal bleeding from telangiectasia It commonly follows radiotherapy for prostate, cervical, rectal or other pelvic cancers Chronic radiation proctopathy is characterised by mucosal telangiectasia, ischaemia and fibrosis Endoscopy shows friable mucosa with telangiectasia, and biopsy carries a fistula risk in irradiated tissue Treatment ranges from topical therapies to endoscopic ablation (for example argon plasma coagulation) for bleeding Severe or transfusion-dependent rectal bleeding Fistula formation (for example rectovaginal or rectovesical) Stricturing with obstruction Features suggesting recurrent malignancy Aggressive biopsy of irradiated rectum precipitating a fistula Attributing bleeding to radiation without excluding recurrent tumour Confusing it with inflammatory bowel disease Underestimating chronic progressive change Radiation proctitis results from ionising radiation damage to the rectal mucosa and vasculature. Acute injury reflects direct mucosal cell death and inflammation during treatment, which usually recovers. Chronic radiation proctopathy develops later from progressive obliterative endarteritis and fibrosis, producing mucosal ischaemia and fragile telangiectatic vessels that bleed, and in severe cases strictures, ulceration or fistulae. The chronic changes are progressive and relate to the radiation dose and technique. Acute proctitis usually settles after treatment ends; chronic proctopathy tends to be persistent or progressive but bleeding is often controllable with endoscopic and medical measures.

Acute radiation syndrome — ARS, radiation sickness, acute radiation syndrome Acute gastroenteritis or food poisoning Sepsis of other cause Chemotherapy or other cytotoxic drug toxicity Acute leukaemia or bone marrow failure of other cause Chemical or toxic exposure causing vomiting Serial full blood counts with attention to the rate of lymphocyte decline Estimation of absorbed dose using time to vomiting and available dosimetry Biological dosimetry such as chromosome aberration analysis where available Assessment and monitoring for radioactive contamination Baseline organ function tests and cultures to guide supportive care Acute radiation syndrome follows a high, acute whole-body or large partial-body dose of penetrating ionising radiation, as in criticality accidents or radiological incidents It classically evolves through a prodromal phase (nausea, vomiting, malaise), a latent phase, a manifest illness phase and then either recovery or death The speed of onset of vomiting is a useful early guide to dose severity, with earlier vomiting indicating higher exposure Recognised dose-dependent sub-syndromes affect the bone marrow (haematopoietic), the gastrointestinal tract, and at very high doses the cardiovascular and central nervous systems Serial lymphocyte counts over the first day or two are a practical biological indicator of the dose received and prognosis Management is supportive with infection prevention, blood product and fluid support, and treatment of the failing organ systems, ideally with specialist and haematology input Contamination with radioactive material must be distinguished from irradiation, and decontamination plus staff protection are early priorities Localised high-dose exposure can cause cutaneous radiation injury with erythema, blistering and later necrosis, sometimes appearing after a delay MEDICAL EMERGENCY: high-dose exposure with very early vomiting, rapidly falling lymphocytes, or neurological or cardiovascular signs indicates severe, potentially fatal illness Signs of gastrointestinal syndrome with intractable diarrhoea and bleeding Profound neutropenia with infection or sepsis Confusion, hypotension or seizures suggesting a very high dose Mistaking early prodromal vomiting for simple gastroenteritis Being reassured by the latent phase and underestimating impending marrow failure Confusing external irradiation with radioactive contamination and neglecting decontamination Failing to protect staff and control the scene during care Not obtaining serial lymphocyte counts for dose estimation Ionising radiation deposits energy that damages DNA and cellular structures, with the greatest harm to rapidly dividing tissues. Loss of proliferating stem cells in the bone marrow causes pancytopenia, while injury to the intestinal crypt cells breaks down the mucosal barrier, leading to fluid loss, bleeding and sepsis. Very high doses cause vascular and neurological injury. The clinical course reflects the differing turnover rates of these tissues, giving the characteristic phased illness. Outcome is strongly dose-dependent: lower doses causing mainly marrow suppression may recover with intensive support, whereas gastrointestinal and neurovascular syndromes from very high doses carry a poor to near-uniformly fatal outlook despite treatment.

Radiculopathy — nerve root compression, pinched nerve, cervical radiculopathy, lumbosacral radiculopathy Peripheral entrapment neuropathy or mononeuropathy Brachial or lumbosacral plexopathy Referred pain from shoulder, hip, or joint disease Spinal cord compression or myelopathy Peripheral polyneuropathy Infective or neoplastic root involvement (e.g. epidural abscess, metastasis, meningeal disease) MRI of the relevant spinal region to identify compressive pathology CT or CT myelography when MRI is contraindicated Electromyography and nerve conduction studies to localise the root and exclude mimics Inflammatory markers and imaging for infection or malignancy when red flags are present Plain radiographs for alignment, instability, or degenerative change in selected cases Results from dysfunction of one or more spinal nerve roots, producing pain, sensory change, and weakness in a dermatomal and myotomal distribution Pain characteristically radiates along the affected root and is often aggravated by manoeuvres that raise intraspinal pressure such as coughing or straining The commonest cause is a degenerative disc or spondylotic osteophyte compressing the root within or near the intervertebral foramen Localising signs follow the root: for example L5 causes foot-drop with weak dorsiflexion, while S1 reduces the ankle reflex and plantar flexion Provocative tests such as straight-leg raise (lumbar) or Spurling manoeuvre (cervical) support a root cause Most cases are self-limiting and improve with conservative management, so imaging is guided by red flags and by persistence or progression of deficits MRI is the preferred imaging test to correlate structural compression with the clinical level Electromyography helps confirm the affected root and distinguish radiculopathy from plexopathy or peripheral neuropathy New bladder or bowel dysfunction, saddle anaesthesia, or bilateral leg symptoms suggesting cauda equina syndrome (surgical emergency) Progressive or severe motor weakness rather than isolated pain Fever, systemic illness, or immunosuppression raising concern for spinal infection History of cancer, unexplained weight loss, or night pain suggesting malignant infiltration Missing cauda equina syndrome by not asking about sphincter and saddle symptoms Over-reliance on incidental imaging findings that do not match the clinical level Attributing radicular pain to a benign disc when infection or malignancy is the true cause Delaying surgical referral in progressive motor weakness Confusing peripheral entrapment or plexopathy with root disease without electrophysiology Radiculopathy reflects mechanical compression, inflammation, or ischaemia of a nerve root, most often where a herniated disc or degenerative spondylotic change narrows the intervertebral foramen or lateral recess. Compression and local inflammatory mediators disrupt axonal conduction and cause both ectopic pain signals and conduction failure, producing radicular pain, dermatomal sensory loss, and myotomal weakness. Chronic compression may lead to axonal loss with denervation. Non-degenerative causes include infection, malignant infiltration, and inflammatory or infiltrative processes affecting the roots. Most degenerative radiculopathies resolve or substantially improve with conservative treatment over weeks to a few months; persistent severe compression, marked motor deficit, or a serious underlying cause predicts a poorer outcome and may require surgery.

Ranula — sublingual mucocoele, oral ranula, simple ranula, sublingual gland retention cyst Plunging (cervical) ranula Dermoid or epidermoid cyst of the floor of mouth Sublingual or submandibular gland tumour Mucocoele of a minor salivary gland Lymphatic or venous malformation Thyroglossal or branchial anomaly when near the midline or neck Ultrasound of the floor of mouth and neck to characterise specimen Assessment of salivary gland duct anatomy when obstruction is suspected A mucus extravasation or retention lesion arising from the sublingual gland, presenting as a soft cystic swelling in the floor of the mouth The classic oral ranula appears as a bluish, dome-shaped, translucent swelling lateral to the midline that may fluctuate in size It is termed a pseudocyst when it results from extravasated mucus without a true epithelial lining, the commonest mechanism Large lesions can displace the tongue and interfere with speech, chewing and swallowing Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by imaging to define extent and distinguish a simple oral ranula from a plunging variant Definitive management usually involves excision of the sublingual gland along with the ranula, which addresses the source of mucus Marsupialisation alone is associated with a higher recurrence rate than removal of the offending gland Recurrence and the possibility of a plunging component should be considered when the lesion extends toward the neck Rapid enlargement causing tongue displacement and difficulty with speech or swallowing Airway compromise from a very large floor-of-mouth swelling Features atypical for a simple ranula suggesting neoplasm Extension into the neck indicating a plunging ranula Treating with incision and drainage alone, which commonly leads to recurrence Failing to recognise a plunging component presenting as a neck mass Mistaking a solid salivary neoplasm for a benign cystic ranula Injuring the lingual nerve or submandibular duct during sublingual gland excision A ranula develops when saliva from the sublingual gland escapes into the surrounding floor-of-mouth tissues, most often because a duct or acinus is disrupted by trauma or obstruction. The extravasated mucus incites a surrounding reaction and collects as a pseudocyst lacking a true epithelial lining, though less commonly a true retention cyst forms behind a ductal obstruction. Continued salivary secretion causes the swelling to enlarge and fluctuate. If mucus tracks around or through the mylohyoid muscle into the neck, a cervical (plunging) ranula results. The prognosis is excellent once the sublingual gland is removed, with low recurrence. Simple drainage or marsupialisation without gland removal is more likely to recur.

Rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism — RDP, DYT12, ATP1A3, Na+/K+-ATPase alpha-3 disorder, DYT-ATP1A3 Young-onset Parkinson disease and other genetic parkinsonism Dopa-responsive dystonia DYT1 and other early-onset dystonias Wilson disease Functional (psychogenic) movement disorder given the abrupt stress-related onset Other ATP1A3-related phenotypes (alternating hemiplegia of childhood, CAPOS syndrome) ATP1A3 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Brain MRI, expected to be unremarkable, to exclude structural causes Dopaminergic (presynaptic) imaging, typically normal, to distinguish degenerative parkinsonism A levodopa trial, which characteristically shows little benefit, helping separate it from dopa-responsive conditions Serum copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude Wilson disease Autosomal dominant disorder caused by variants in ATP1A3, which encodes the alpha-3 subunit of the neuronal sodium-potassium ATPase Hallmark is abrupt or subacute onset of dystonia and parkinsonism, often over hours to days, frequently triggered by physical or emotional stress, fever, childbirth, or alcohol Symptoms characteristically follow a rostrocaudal gradient, with prominent bulbar and upper-limb involvement (dysarthria, dysphagia, arm dystonia) more than lower limbs Parkinsonian features such as bradykinesia and postural instability accompany the dystonia, but there is typically little or no tremor and a poor response to levodopa After the dramatic initial onset the deficit tends to stabilise, sometimes with a second abrupt worsening, rather than steadily progressing ATP1A3 variants cause a spectrum that also includes alternating hemiplegia of childhood and the CAPOS syndrome, which can overlap Brain imaging and dopaminergic imaging are typically unremarkable, distinguishing it from degenerative parkinsonism Diagnosis rests on the distinctive stress-triggered abrupt onset and is confirmed by ATP1A3 molecular testing; treatment is largely supportive as levodopa is generally ineffective Abrupt bulbar dysfunction with dysphagia and aspiration or airway risk Severe generalised dystonia or status dystonicus following a trigger Rapid neurological deterioration during febrile illness or physiological stress Secondary decompensation with dehydration or immobility during an acute episode Misdiagnosing the stress-triggered abrupt onset as a functional movement disorder Expecting and relying on a levodopa response, which is characteristically poor Overlooking the diagnosis because imaging is normal Not recognising the broader ATP1A3 spectrum and its overlapping phenotypes when counselling families Rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism is caused by dominant variants in ATP1A3, encoding the alpha-3 subunit of the neuronal sodium-potassium ATPase that maintains transmembrane ion gradients essential for repolarisation and neuronal excitability. The variants reduce pump function, and this reserve deficit is thought to become clinically manifest when metabolic demand rises, which is why physiological stressors such as fever, exertion, emotional stress, or childbirth precipitate the abrupt onset. Impaired ion homeostasis within cerebellar and basal ganglia circuits produces combined dystonia and parkinsonism without frank neurodegeneration, accounting for the normal structural and dopaminergic imaging. After the characteristic abrupt onset the disorder tends to plateau rather than progress steadily, though a further stepwise deterioration can occur; disability is often significant, particularly from bulbar and upper-limb involvement, and response to medication is generally limited.

Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis — RPGN, crescentic glomerulonephritis, crescentic GN Acute tubular necrosis Acute interstitial nephritis Thrombotic microangiopathy Atheroembolic renal disease Severe acute post-infectious glomerulonephritis Accelerated hypertension with renal injury Urine microscopy for dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts Kidney biopsy for crescent quantification and immunofluorescence pattern ANCA testing (including antigen-specific assays) and anti-GBM antibody titres Complement levels and other autoimmune serologies including antinuclear and anti-dsDNA antibodies Chest imaging when pulmonary haemorrhage is suspected Quantification of proteinuria and serial renal function monitoring RPGN is a nephrological emergency defined by a rapid loss of renal function over days to weeks, accompanied by a nephritic urine sediment with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts The histological hallmark is crescent formation in a large proportion of glomeruli, reflecting severe glomerular injury and rupture of capillary walls It is classified into three immunopathological groups: anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, immune-complex-mediated disease, and pauci-immune (usually ANCA-associated) disease Coexisting pulmonary haemorrhage with glomerulonephritis (pulmonary-renal syndrome) suggests anti-GBM disease or ANCA-associated vasculitis and demands urgent evaluation Early kidney biopsy is central to diagnosis and to gauging the balance of active (treatable) crescents versus fibrous (irreversible) scarring Serological testing for ANCA, anti-GBM antibodies, complement levels, and other markers helps categorise the disease and guide treatment Outcome depends critically on how quickly immunosuppression is started, since delay allows crescents to organise into irreversible fibrosis Management principles centre on prompt aggressive immunosuppression, with plasma exchange added in anti-GBM disease and in selected severe or dialysis-dependent vasculitis cases Pulmonary haemorrhage with haemoptysis and hypoxaemia indicating a pulmonary-renal syndrome Rapidly rising creatinine or oliguria threatening imminent dialysis dependence Severe hypertension or fluid overload Systemic vasculitic features such as mononeuritis, purpura, or ENT involvement Delaying biopsy and treatment while awaiting serology, allowing crescents to become irreversible Missing coexisting pulmonary haemorrhage that changes urgency and management Assuming a negative ANCA excludes vasculitis, since a minority are seronegative Starting heavy immunosuppression in a kidney already dominated by fibrous scarring with little chance of recovery Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis describes a clinical syndrome of accelerating renal failure caused by severe inflammatory glomerular injury, characterised pathologically by extensive crescents. Crescents form when damage to the glomerular capillary wall allows plasma proteins, fibrin, and inflammatory cells to enter Bowman space, where proliferating parietal epithelial cells and macrophages compress the glomerular tuft. Three mechanisms underlie the syndrome: linear deposition of antibodies against the glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM disease), deposition of immune complexes as seen in lupus, post-infectious, and IgA-related disease, and a pauci-immune process typically associated with ANCA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis. In all forms, unchecked inflammation rapidly destroys glomeruli and, without timely treatment, progresses to fibrous scarring and end-stage kidney disease. Untreated RPGN progresses to end-stage kidney disease within weeks. With early immunosuppression many patients recover useful renal function, but prognosis worsens sharply with delayed treatment, a high proportion of fibrous crescents, dialysis dependence at presentation, and anti-GBM disease with advanced injury. Relapse is common in ANCA-associated disease and requires ongoing surveillance.

Significant gastrointestinal bleeding from mucosal ulceration Severe malnutrition or weight loss Removing the bezoar without treating the underlying trichotillomania, inviting recurrence Underestimating the extent of the small-bowel tail before intervention Missing complications such as ulceration, obstruction, or perforation Failing to consider the diagnosis in a young woman with an epigastric mass and weight loss Rapunzel syndrome arises when compulsively ingested hair (trichophagia), which is indigestible and slippery, becomes trapped in the gastric folds and enmeshes with mucus and food debris to form a trichobezoar. Over time the mass conforms to the shape of the stomach and a long tail extends through the pylorus into the small intestine. The accumulating mass impairs gastric emptying, causes mucosal pressure necrosis and ulceration, and can precipitate obstruction or perforation; the behavioural substrate is an impulse-control/psychiatric disorder driving repeated hair ingestion. With complete removal of the bezoar and effective treatment of the underlying psychiatric disorder the prognosis is good, but failure to address the hair-pulling behaviour commonly leads to recurrence.

focal seizures Epilepsia partialis continua, in which continuous focal motor seizure activity affects part of the body, is a characteristic feature The clinical course brings progressive hemiparesis, cognitive decline and, when the dominant hemisphere is involved, language impairment Serial MRI shows progressive unilateral hemispheric atrophy, often with insular and periventricular involvement The presumed mechanism is a cell-mediated immune process with T-lymphocyte-driven inflammation and neuronal loss confined to one hemisphere Immunotherapy may slow progression and help seizures, but definitive seizure control usually requires functional disconnection or hemispherectomy Hemispherectomy typically stops the intractable seizures at the cost of a predictable fixed hemiparesis and visual field deficit Epilepsia partialis continua that is refractory to antiseizure medication Rapidly progressive hemiparesis or cognitive and language decline Status epilepticus requiring intensive management Progressive hemispheric atrophy on serial imaging Attributing early focal seizures to ordinary focal epilepsy and missing the progressive inflammatory course Delaying surgical referral in a dominant-hemisphere case for fear of deficits, allowing further decline Failing to obtain serial imaging to demonstrate characteristic progressive atrophy Overlooking mimics such as mitochondrial disease or a structural lesion before committing to diagnosis Rasmussen encephalitis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory disorder characteristically restricted to a single cerebral hemisphere. Histopathology shows T-cell-dominant perivascular inflammation, microglial nodules, reactive gliosis and progressive neuronal loss, supporting a predominantly cell-mediated cytotoxic process, although humoral and antigen-driven mechanisms have also been proposed. Ongoing inflammation drives relentless cortical damage and hemispheric atrophy, producing the combination of drug-resistant focal seizures, epilepsia partialis continua and progressive contralateral neurological and cognitive deficits. Untreated, Rasmussen encephalitis progresses to a fixed severe hemiparesis, cognitive impairment and intractable seizures. Immunotherapy may modify the tempo, but seizure freedom generally requires hemispherectomy or hemispheric disconnection, which halts the epilepsy while leaving a predictable permanent motor and visual deficit; earlier surgery may better preserve overall function.

Rat-bite fever — Streptobacillus moniliformis infection, Spirillum minus infection, streptobacillary rat-bite fever, Haverhill fever, sodoku Meningococcaemia and other causes of fever with petechial rash Disseminated gonococcal infection (fever, rash, arthritis) Rocky Mountain spotted fever and other rickettsioses Leptospirosis Secondary syphilis (rash on palms and soles) Reactive or septic arthritis of other cause Infective endocarditis from other organisms Blood cultures (prolonged incubation for the fastidious organism) and culture of joint aspirate Dark-field microscopy of blood, lesion exudate or lymph node aspirate for Spirillum minus Molecular testing (PCR/16S sequencing) for Streptobacillus moniliformis Full blood count and inflammatory markers Echocardiography if endocarditis is suspected Joint imaging or aspiration in arthritis, and lumbar puncture if meningitis is suspected Rat-bite fever has two forms: streptobacillary disease (Streptobacillus moniliformis), predominant in the Americas and Europe, and spirillary disease (Spirillum minus, 'sodoku'), predominant in Asia Acquired from the bite or scratch of rats or other rodents, or by handling them; streptobacillary disease may also be foodborne (Haverhill fever) from contaminated milk or water Streptobacillary disease presents abruptly with fever, rigors, myalgia, a maculopapular or petechial rash favouring the extremities including palms and soles, and a migratory polyarthritis Spirillary disease has a longer incubation, relapsing fever, induration or ulceration at the healed bite site with regional lymphadenopathy, and a rash, but arthritis is uncommon Diagnosis of streptobacillary disease relies on culture of blood or joint fluid (fastidious organism) or molecular methods; Spirillum minus cannot be cultured and is identified by dark-field microscopy of lesion or blood material Untreated disease can lead to endocarditis, myocarditis, meningitis, abscesses and septic arthritis, with appreciable mortality Penicillin-class antibiotics are the treatment of choice, with alternatives for penicillin allergy and escalation for endocarditis Features of endocarditis, myocarditis or a new murmur Meningism or altered consciousness suggesting central nervous system involvement Septic arthritis or deep abscess formation Haemodynamic instability or sepsis Persistent or relapsing fever despite initial treatment Not eliciting a history of rodent exposure, which is key to considering the diagnosis Discarding blood cultures too early before the fastidious organism grows Attempting to culture Spirillum minus, which does not grow on artificial media Mistaking the rash and arthritis for meningococcaemia or disseminated gonococcal infection without pursuing exposure history Under-treating when endovascular or CNS involvement is present The causative bacteria are commensals of the rodent nasopharynx and are introduced into humans through bites, scratches, handling or ingestion of contaminated food and water. Streptobacillus moniliformis, a fastidious pleomorphic Gram-negative bacillus, disseminates haematogenously to produce systemic febrile illness, immune-mediated rash and a reactive or septic polyarthritis, and can seed heart valves and other sites. Spirillum minus, a spiral organism, causes relapsing fever with characteristic reactivation of the healed inoculation site and regional lymphadenitis. Both can progress to metastatic infection and endovascular involvement if untreated. With prompt antibiotic therapy the prognosis is excellent, but untreated rat-bite fever carries substantial mortality, largely from endocarditis and other metastatic complications.

Rathke cleft cyst — Rathke cleft cyst, Rathke pouch cyst, RCC, pars intermedia cyst Cystic pituitary adenoma Craniopharyngioma, especially the cystic adamantinomatous form Arachnoid cyst Empty sella Epidermoid or dermoid cyst Hypophysitis Suprasellar germ cell tumour Pituitary MRI with contrast, showing a non-enhancing cyst and any intracystic nodule Anterior pituitary hormone profile to detect hypopituitarism Serum prolactin, which may be mildly elevated from a stalk effect Assessment of posterior pituitary function with plasma and urine osmolality if diabetes insipidus is suspected Formal visual field testing when there is suprasellar extension Histology after drainage to confirm the epithelial lining and exclude craniopharyngioma A benign, non-neoplastic epithelial cyst arising from remnants of Rathke pouch, usually located between the anterior and posterior pituitary and intrasellar with or without suprasellar extension Often an incidental imaging finding and asymptomatic When symptomatic it can cause headache, visual disturbance from chiasmal compression and hypopituitarism, and diabetes insipidus may occur Hyperprolactinaemia from a stalk effect can cause menstrual disturbance or galactorrhoea MRI typically shows a non-enhancing cystic sellar lesion, and a non-enhancing intracystic nodule is a characteristic feature It should be distinguished from a cystic pituitary adenoma and from craniopharyngioma, both of which it can mimic Asymptomatic cysts are managed conservatively with surveillance, whereas symptomatic cysts may need transsphenoidal drainage or fenestration rather than complete excision Recurrence can occur after drainage, so follow-up imaging is advisable Progressive visual field loss from chiasmal compression New hypopituitarism or diabetes insipidus Features suggesting cyst apoplexy or rupture with acute headache Rapid enlargement or atypical imaging suggesting an alternative neoplasm Attempting aggressive complete excision, which raises the risk of hypopituitarism and cerebrospinal fluid leak, when drainage or fenestration suffices Misdiagnosing it as a cystic adenoma or craniopharyngioma Missing associated hypopituitarism or diabetes insipidus before surgery Failing to arrange surveillance imaging given the recurrence risk Rathke cleft cysts derive from the embryonic Rathke pouch, the ectodermal invagination that forms the anterior and intermediate pituitary. Persistence and expansion of the cleft between the pars anterior and pars nervosa produces a cyst lined by ciliated cuboidal or columnar epithelium, often with goblet cells, containing mucoid or serous fluid. Most remain small and clinically silent, but progressive fluid accumulation can enlarge the cyst to compress the normal pituitary, the stalk (raising prolactin by disinhibition) and the optic chiasm, and can disrupt antidiuretic hormone pathways. Rupture or inflammation of the cyst contents may provoke symptoms. Generally excellent; incidental cysts often remain stable and symptomatic cysts usually improve after drainage or fenestration, although endocrine deficits may persist and cysts can recur, warranting follow-up imaging.

Raynaud phenomenon — Raynaud's phenomenon, Raynaud syndrome, primary Raynaud, secondary Raynaud Systemic sclerosis and other connective tissue diseases (secondary Raynaud) Thoracic outlet syndrome and other causes of arterial compression Atherosclerotic or embolic peripheral arterial disease Vibration-induced (hand-arm) vascular injury and occupational causes Drug- or toxin-induced vasospasm antibodies Inflammatory markers and assessment for features of systemic autoimmune disease Vascular assessment for fixed arterial obstruction when ischaemia is asymmetric or severe Targeted investigations for occupational, drug, or haematological causes when suspected Episodic, reversible digital vasospasm provoked by cold or emotional stress, classically producing a triphasic colour change of pallor, then cyanosis, then reactive hyperaemia Primary Raynaud is common, typically begins in young women, is symmetric, and occurs without an underlying disease or tissue damage Secondary Raynaud arises from an underlying condition, most importantly connective tissue disease, and carries a greater risk of digital ischaemia and ulceration Features favouring a secondary cause include older age at onset, asymmetry, digital ulcers or pitting scars, and abnormal nailfold capillaries A positive antinuclear antibody and abnormal nailfold capillaroscopy suggest an evolving connective tissue disease, often systemic sclerosis General measures emphasise cold avoidance, keeping the whole body warm, and smoking cessation Pharmacological therapy, when needed, uses vasodilators (calcium channel blockers first-line, with other agents for refractory or ischaemic disease) Critical digital ischaemia is an emergency requiring urgent assessment and consideration of secondary causes Digital ulceration, gangrene, or critical ischaemia threatening tissue loss Asymmetric or unilateral symptoms suggesting fixed arterial obstruction or embolism New Raynaud phenomenon in an older adult indicating a likely secondary cause Accompanying features of connective tissue disease such as skin tightening, dysphagia, or breathlessness Abnormal nailfold capillaries with positive autoantibodies signalling evolving systemic sclerosis Labelling all Raynaud as benign primary disease without screening for secondary causes Missing evolving systemic sclerosis by not performing nailfold capillaroscopy and autoantibody testing Underestimating critical digital ischaemia as ordinary vasospasm Overlooking drug, occupational, or vascular contributors Neglecting non-pharmacological measures such as whole-body warming and smoking cessation Raynaud phenomenon results from exaggerated vasoconstriction of digital arteries, precapillary arterioles, and cutaneous arteriovenous shunts in response to cold or stress. In primary disease this reflects a functional imbalance of vascular tone with heightened sympathetic and local vascular reactivity and no structural vessel damage. In secondary disease, structural vasculopathy, endothelial dysfunction, and abnormal balance of vasoconstrictors (such as endothelin) and vasodilators (such as nitric oxide), often in the setting of systemic sclerosis or other connective tissue disease, produce fixed narrowing that predisposes to persistent ischaemia, ulceration, and tissue loss. Primary Raynaud phenomenon is benign, usually stable or improving over time, and rarely causes tissue damage. Secondary Raynaud has a more variable outlook determined by the underlying disease and carries a real risk of digital ulceration and loss, particularly in systemic sclerosis.

Reactive perforating collagenosis — RPC, acquired reactive perforating collagenosis, acquired perforating dermatosis Other perforating dermatoses (elastosis perforans serpiginosa, perforating folliculitis, Kyrle disease) Prurigo nodularis Folliculitis Hypertrophic lichen planus Perforating granuloma annulare Multiple keratoacanthomas Dermatofibroma (for a solitary lesion) Skin biopsy showing a cup-shaped epidermal invagination with transepidermal elimination of collagen Special stains (such as Masson trichrome and elastic stains) to characterise the eliminated material and distinguish it from elastic-fibre perforating disease Fasting glucose and HbA1c to screen for diabetes mellitus Renal function tests (urea, creatinine, eGFR) to detect chronic kidney disease Assessment of dialysis status and adequacy in renal patients Screening for other causes of pruritus (for example liver and thyroid function) where relevant One of the perforating dermatoses, characterised by umbilicated papules and nodules with a central keratotic plug through which altered collagen is extruded (transepidermal elimination) Lesions are often intensely itchy and show the Koebner phenomenon, appearing in linear arrays along scratch marks The acquired adult form is strongly associated with diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease, particularly in patients on dialysis A rare inherited childhood form exists, precipitated by superficial trauma or cold Commonly affects the extensor limbs, trunk, and backs of the hands, with lesions typically resolving over weeks to leave scars or hyperpigmentation as new crops appear Diagnosis is confirmed on biopsy showing a cup-shaped epidermal depression with elimination of degenerate, basophilic collagen bundles through the epidermis Pruritus and scratching are central to pathogenesis, so lesions cluster where the patient can reach Management addresses the underlying disease and the itch, using emollients, topical corticosteroids, keratolytics, antihistamines, phototherapy, and control of pruritus Newly diagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes or chronic kidney disease uncovered by the skin findings Intractable pruritus with a marked impact on quality of life and sleep Secondary infection of excoriated, ulcerated lesions Atypical or rapidly growing nodules requiring biopsy to exclude malignancy Overlooking undiagnosed diabetes or renal disease in an adult presenting with perforating papules Treating the skin without addressing the underlying itch and metabolic cause Confusing it with prurigo nodularis or the other perforating dermatoses without biopsy Underestimating the role of scratching in perpetuating lesions Reactive perforating collagenosis is a disorder of transepidermal elimination in which altered dermal collagen is extruded through the epidermis. Superficial trauma and, in acquired cases, the metabolic disturbances of diabetes and renal failure are thought to damage dermal collagen and provoke an epidermal response that channels the degenerate collagen to the surface. Persistent scratching in response to itch perpetuates the trauma and drives the characteristic Koebnerised, umbilicated papules, so that lesions cluster at accessible, frequently scratched sites and continue to recur while itch and the underlying systemic disturbance persist. The acquired form runs a chronic, relapsing course tied to control of the underlying systemic disease; individual lesions heal, often with scarring, but new crops recur while itch and metabolic disturbance persist.

Recluse (Loxosceles) spider envenomation — loxoscelism, brown recluse bite, Loxosceles bite, violin spider bite, necrotic arachnidism Bacterial skin and soft-tissue infection or abscess Necrotising fasciitis Cutaneous anthrax or other necrotic infection Vasculitis or pyoderma gangrenosum Other arthropod bite or chemical/thermal injury Diabetic or ischaemic ulcer Full blood count and blood film for haemolysis Haptoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase, reticulocytes and bilirubin for intravascular haemolysis Urinalysis for haemoglobinuria and renal function tests Coagulation studies if disseminated intravascular coagulation is suspected Wound assessment over serial reviews to track demarcation Consideration of infective causes when a necrotic lesion lacks clear envenomation history Loxoscelism ranges from a self-limiting local lesion to a necrotic ulcer, and less commonly a systemic (viscerocutaneous) illness with haemolysis The bite is often initially painless; over hours a central blister with surrounding pallor and erythema may evolve into a sinking, dusky lesion and eschar A dependent or gravity-influenced spread of discolouration and the classic red-white-blue appearance suggest developing dermonecrosis Systemic loxoscelism, more common in children, features fever, malaise and intravascular haemolysis, sometimes with haemoglobinuria and acute kidney injury Most necrotic wounds attributed to spiders are actually other conditions; confirmed recluse exposure requires the spider to be endemic and ideally identified Management is largely supportive with wound care, analgesia and monitoring for haemolysis; surgical debridement is deferred until the lesion has fully demarcated There is no local pain-predominant cramping syndrome as in widow bites, which aids differentiation Systemic features of fever, malaise and dark urine suggesting haemolysis Falling haemoglobin or evidence of acute kidney injury Rapidly spreading necrosis or signs of superadded necrotising infection Haemodynamic instability Coagulopathy Over-diagnosing recluse bites for necrotic wounds outside the spider's endemic range, missing infection or other pathology Performing early aggressive debridement before the lesion has demarcated, worsening the defect Failing to screen for and monitor systemic haemolysis, especially in children Treating a necrotising soft-tissue infection as a benign spider bite Recluse venom contains sphingomyelinase D (phospholipase D), which acts on cell membranes and endothelium to trigger complement activation, neutrophil recruitment and intravascular thrombosis. This produces localised vascular occlusion and ischaemic dermonecrosis, with a characteristic gravity-dependent spread of injury. In systemic loxoscelism the enzyme induces complement-mediated haemolysis of red cells, releasing free haemoglobin that can precipitate acute kidney injury; disseminated intravascular coagulation may accompany severe cases. The delayed, evolving nature of the lesion reflects progressive microvascular thrombosis rather than direct cytolysis alone. Most bites heal with conservative wound care, though large necrotic ulcers may take weeks to months and can scar. Systemic loxoscelism with haemolysis is uncommon but potentially life-threatening, particularly in children, and requires close monitoring.

Rectal intussusception — internal rectal prolapse, internal intussusception, recto-rectal/recto-anal intussusception External full-thickness rectal prolapse Rectocele or enterocele causing obstructed defecation Anismus (paradoxical puborectalis contraction) Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome as coexisting pathology Rectal neoplasm acting as a lead point Haemorrhoidal or mucosal prolapse Slow-transit constipation Defecating proctography to grade the intussusception (Oxford classification) Dynamic pelvic-floor MRI to assess associated compartment defects Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion for evacuatory function Endoanal ultrasound where incontinence or sphincter injury is suspected Flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy to exclude a neoplastic lead point and inspect for solitary rectal ulcer Colonic transit study where slow-transit constipation is considered Rectal intussusception is an internal telescoping of the rectal wall that does not protrude through the anus, distinct from external (full-thickness) rectal prolapse It is graded by the Oxford radiological classification according to whether the intussusception is recto-rectal, recto-anal, or descends into the anal canal Typical presentations are obstructed defecation with a sensation of incomplete evacuation and blockage, and, when the lead point reaches the anal canal, faecal incontinence and mucus leakage It is strongly associated with solitary rectal ulcer syndrome, where the intussuscepting mucosa is subjected to trauma and ischaemia Defecating proctography or dynamic MRI is the key investigation, demonstrating the intussusception and any associated rectocele, enterocele, or perineal descent Internal intussusception is a common finding in asymptomatic individuals, so symptoms must correlate with the radiological grade before intervention First-line management is conservative with fibre, stool regulation, avoidance of straining, and biofeedback pelvic-floor retraining Surgery, such as ventral mesh rectopexy or a stapled transanal resection in selected cases, is reserved for high-grade symptomatic intussusception refractory to conservative care Rectal bleeding or a mass suggesting neoplasia acting as a lead point A persistent rectal ulcer requiring biopsy to exclude malignancy New or worsening faecal incontinence Symptoms disproportionate to a low-grade intussusception, prompting a broader assessment Progression to external full-thickness prolapse Operating on an incidental low-grade intussusception that does not explain the symptoms Overlooking coexisting anismus or enterocele that will limit surgical benefit Failing to biopsy a solitary rectal ulcer and missing malignancy Attributing all evacuatory symptoms to the intussusception when a functional disorder predominates Proceeding to surgery before an adequate trial of biofeedback and bowel regulation Rectal intussusception occurs when a segment of the rectal wall invaginates into the lumen of the rectum or anal canal during straining, without protruding externally. Weakness and redundancy of the rectal wall and its supporting attachments, often with a deep pouch of Douglas and pelvic-floor dysfunction, allow the wall to fold in on itself as intrarectal pressure rises. The intussusceptum acts as a lead point that obstructs the outflow of stool, producing a sensation of blockage and incomplete evacuation and prompting further straining, which perpetuates the process. Repeated shearing and impaction of the prolapsing mucosa against the anal canal cause the mucosal ischaemia, ulceration, and fibrosis of solitary rectal ulcer syndrome. When the lead point repeatedly descends into the anal canal it disrupts the sphincter mechanism and produces incontinence. Many patients improve with conservative management and biofeedback; surgery for well-selected high-grade symptomatic intussusception can improve obstructed defecation and incontinence, but functional results are variable and recurrence and persistent symptoms are recognised, particularly when other pelvic-floor disorders coexist.

Rectal prolapse — procidentia, complete rectal prolapse, full-thickness rectal prolapse, rectal procidentia Prolapsing (third- or fourth-degree) haemorrhoids Mucosal-only rectal prolapse Internal rectal intussusception Prolapsing rectal polyp or tumour Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome Anal or perianal skin tags or condylomata Examination with the patient straining to reproduce the prolapse Colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy to exclude a lead-point lesion or synchronous colorectal pathology Defecating proctography or dynamic pelvic MRI for internal intussusception and pelvic floor assessment Anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound when incontinence is prominent Colonic transit studies where significant constipation coexists Full-thickness (complete) rectal prolapse is protrusion of the entire rectal wall through the anus, with concentric mucosal folds, whereas mucosal prolapse and internal intussusception are distinct, less severe entities It is most common in older women and in children, and is frequently associated with chronic straining, pelvic floor weakness, and a redundant sigmoid colon Typical symptoms are a protruding mass on defecation, mucous discharge, bleeding, and a sensation of incomplete evacuation, with faecal incontinence in a large proportion The diagnosis is often made by asking the patient to strain, ideally on a commode, to reproduce the prolapse; concentric rings distinguish it from the radial folds of prolapsing haemorrhoids Defecating proctography or dynamic MRI can demonstrate internal intussusception and associated pelvic floor abnormalities when clinical findings are equivocal Coexisting incontinence and constipation should be assessed, and colonic evaluation is prudent to exclude a lead point or synchronous pathology Definitive treatment is surgical and is broadly divided into abdominal approaches (rectopexy, with or without resection) and perineal procedures, chosen according to fitness, symptoms, and surgeon preference Irreducible, incarcerated prolapse with congestion, ulceration, or impending strangulation requiring urgent reduction or surgery Ischaemic or gangrenous prolapsed bowel Significant bleeding or a palpable mass suggesting an underlying tumour Acute large prolapse in a frail patient with obstruction Confusing full-thickness prolapse with prolapsing haemorrhoids and offering inappropriate treatment Failing to reproduce the prolapse on examination and therefore missing or underestimating it Not excluding a colorectal neoplasm acting as a lead point before elective repair Ignoring coexisting incontinence or constipation, leading to poor functional results despite anatomical success Delaying intervention in an incarcerated or ischaemic prolapse Full-thickness rectal prolapse is understood as a circumferential intussusception of the rectum that progresses until the bowel protrudes through the anal canal. Contributing factors include a deep rectovaginal or rectovesical pouch, loss of the normal posterior rectal fixation, a redundant mobile rectosigmoid, weak pelvic floor and anal sphincter musculature, and chronically raised intra-abdominal pressure from straining. Repeated prolapse stretches and damages the pudendal nerves and sphincter complex, which explains the frequent association with faecal incontinence, while chronic mucosal exposure produces discharge, bleeding, and ulceration. Surgical repair relieves the prolapse in most patients with acceptable recurrence rates that vary by procedure, and continence often improves over time though it may not fully recover if pelvic floor and nerve damage is longstanding. Constipation can persist or occasionally worsen, and outcomes are best when associated functional problems are addressed alongside the anatomical repair.

Rectal varices — anorectal varices Haemorrhoids Other causes of lower gastrointestinal bleeding (angiodysplasia, neoplasm, diverticular) Ischaemic or inflammatory proctitis Rectal neoplasm Colonic varices Endoscopic identification distinguishing varices from haemorrhoids Assessment for portal hypertension and its cause (liver disease, portal vein thrombosis) Cross-sectional or Doppler imaging of the portal system Full blood count and coagulation/liver function tests Assessment of overall variceal burden Dilated portosystemic collateral veins in the rectum arising in portal hypertension They are distinct from haemorrhoids, which are dilatations of the normal haemorrhoidal cushions They appear as serpentine submucosal veins extending upward from the anorectum on endoscopy They can cause significant, sometimes massive, lower gastrointestinal bleeding Recognising portal hypertension is essential, as management differs from haemorrhoid treatment Treatment targets portal pressure (for example with portosystemic shunting) alongside local haemostatic measures; conventional haemorrhoid procedures can provoke severe bleeding Massive or recurrent rectal bleeding Haemodynamic instability Decompensated liver disease Coagulopathy compounding bleeding Mistaking rectal varices for haemorrhoids and treating with banding or excision, risking severe bleeding Failing to recognise underlying portal hypertension Overlooking other bleeding sources in portal hypertension Not addressing coagulopathy Rectal varices form when portal hypertension drives blood through portosystemic collaterals between the superior rectal veins (portal system) and the middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic system). The resulting dilated submucosal veins can rupture and bleed. Unlike haemorrhoids, which are downward displacements of vascular cushions, rectal varices are true varices reflecting elevated portal pressure, so definitive control often requires reducing portal pressure rather than local excision. Bleeding can be controlled and prognosis is largely determined by the underlying portal hypertension and liver disease; recurrence is likely unless portal pressure is addressed.
