Anismus (paradoxical puborectalis contraction) causing obstructed defecation Cystocele or uterine/vault prolapse contributing to pelvic-floor symptoms Slow-transit constipation Anterior mucosal or full-thickness rectal prolapse Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome Defecating proctography to assess rectocele size and barium trapping Dynamic pelvic-floor MRI to evaluate all three compartments Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion testing for evacuatory function Endoanal ultrasound if sphincter injury or incontinence is suspected Colonic transit studies where slow-transit constipation is considered Examination in the lithotomy and standing positions with straining A rectocele is a herniation of the anterior rectal wall into the posterior vaginal wall through a weakened rectovaginal septum, most common in parous women Typical symptoms are obstructed defecation, a sensation of incomplete evacuation, vaginal bulging, and the need for vaginal or perineal digitation to empty the rectum Small rectoceles are a common incidental finding on imaging in asymptomatic women, so symptoms must correlate with anatomical findings before intervention Risk factors include vaginal childbirth, chronic straining, ageing with connective-tissue laxity, prior pelvic surgery, and oestrogen deficiency Defecating proctography or dynamic MRI demonstrates the size, barium trapping, and associated pelvic-floor abnormalities such as enterocele or intussusception Rectocele frequently coexists with other pelvic-floor disorders, so a global structural and functional assessment is essential rather than treating it in isolation First-line treatment is conservative: fibre, stool softening, avoidance of straining, and biofeedback/pelvic-floor physiotherapy Surgical repair (transvaginal, transperineal, transanal, or as part of a ventral rectopexy or stapled procedure) is reserved for significant symptomatic rectoceles with demonstrable contrast trapping Rectal bleeding, weight loss, or change in bowel habit suggesting neoplasia A non-reducing or ulcerated prolapsing mass New-onset faecal incontinence or a suspected sphincter defect Symptoms disproportionate to a small rectocele, prompting search for another cause Signs of coexisting enterocele obstructing the small bowel Operating on an incidental rectocele that does not correlate with the patient's symptoms Overlooking coexisting enterocele, intussusception, or anismus that will limit surgical benefit Failing to treat constipation and straining, leading to recurrence Attributing obstructed defecation solely to the rectocele when a functional disorder predominates Neglecting pelvic-floor physiotherapy before considering surgery The rectovaginal septum is a fibromuscular layer that separates the rectum from the vagina and supports the anterior rectal wall. Weakening or disruption of this septum and its fascial attachments, most often following vaginal delivery, chronic straining, ageing, or oestrogen deficiency, allows the anterior rectal wall to bulge forward into the posterior vaginal lumen during defecation. As intrarectal pressure rises with straining, stool preferentially fills the outpouching rather than passing through the anal canal, producing trapping of stool, a sensation of incomplete evacuation, and a vicious cycle of increased straining that enlarges the defect. Associated pelvic-floor weakness, perineal descent, and coexisting prolapse of other compartments compound the functional obstruction. Many symptomatic rectoceles improve substantially with conservative measures and biofeedback; surgical repair of well-selected patients with demonstrable contrast trapping gives good functional results, though recurrence and persistent evacuatory symptoms can occur, particularly when other pelvic-floor abnormalities are unaddressed.

Recurrent isolated sleep paralysis — RISP, isolated sleep paralysis, sleep paralysis Narcolepsy, in which sleep paralysis is one feature Nocturnal panic attacks Nocturnal seizures, for example of frontal lobe origin Cataplexy Hypokalaemic or other periodic paralysis Nightmare disorder with awakening Clinical history establishing the timing, preserved awareness and brief duration of episodes Screening for narcolepsy features such as excessive sleepiness and cataplexy Sleep diary and assessment of sleep deprivation and schedule regularity Polysomnography and multiple sleep latency testing if narcolepsy is suspected Review of stress, psychiatric symptoms and substance use Recurrent episodes of inability to move the trunk and limbs while falling asleep or on waking, with full awareness of the surroundings Episodes last seconds to a few minutes and resolve spontaneously or when the person is touched or spoken to Frightening hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations are common, such as a sensed intruder, chest pressure or a floating sensation The term isolated indicates that it occurs without narcolepsy, and recurrent troublesome episodes define the disorder It represents intrusion of the muscle atonia of REM sleep into wakefulness Sleep deprivation, irregular sleep schedules, the supine position and psychological stress are recognised precipitants Management centres on reassurance and improved sleep habits, while persistent daytime sleepiness or cataplexy should prompt evaluation for narcolepsy Excessive daytime sleepiness or cataplexy suggesting narcolepsy Features atypical for sleep paralysis that suggest nocturnal seizures Episodes occurring away from the sleep-wake transition Severe distress or avoidance of sleep because of the episodes Missing underlying narcolepsy when sleepiness or cataplexy is also present Mistaking episodes for nocturnal seizures or panic attacks Underestimating the fear and sleep avoidance the episodes can cause Neglecting sleep deprivation and irregular schedules as remediable triggers Sleep paralysis occurs when the muscle atonia that normally accompanies REM sleep persists into, or intrudes upon, wakefulness at the boundaries of sleep. The person is conscious but temporarily unable to move voluntary muscles, while dream-related imagery may carry over as vivid hallucinations. Factors that disrupt or fragment REM sleep, such as sleep deprivation and irregular schedules, increase the likelihood of these dissociated states. The condition is benign and often improves with better sleep habits and reassurance; episodes may recur intermittently, especially with sleep loss or stress, but do not indicate serious disease once narcolepsy has been excluded.

Recurrent pericarditis — relapsing pericarditis, recurrent acute pericarditis, incessant pericarditis Acute coronary syndrome Pulmonary embolism Pleuritis or pneumonia Pericarditis from systemic autoimmune disease such as lupus Post-cardiac injury syndrome Myopericarditis with myocardial involvement Electrocardiography for widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation and PR depression Inflammatory markers including C-reactive protein to confirm activity and guide tapering Echocardiography to detect and size a pericardial effusion and assess for tamponade Cardiac MRI to demonstrate pericardial inflammation and late gadolinium enhancement in uncertain cases Targeted screening for autoimmune or systemic causes when features suggest secondary disease A recurrence of pericarditis after a symptom-free interval following a first episode, typically presenting with the same pleuritic chest pain that eases on sitting forward Most cases are presumed immune-mediated following an initial viral or idiopathic episode, and an autoinflammatory mechanism is increasingly recognised Diagnosis rests on recurrent pericarditic pain with supportive features such as a friction rub, typical electrocardiographic changes, a new or worsening effusion, or a rise in inflammatory markers Colchicine added to anti-inflammatory therapy reduces the risk of further recurrences and is a cornerstone of treatment Corticosteroids relieve symptoms but promote steroid dependence and further relapses, so they are reserved for specific indications and used sparingly Refractory, corticosteroid-dependent disease may respond to interleukin-1 blockade, reflecting the autoinflammatory basis The long-term outlook is generally good, and progression to constriction is uncommon in idiopathic recurrent disease Signs of cardiac tamponade such as hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure, and pulsus paradoxus A large or rapidly accumulating pericardial effusion Features of evolving constriction with right heart failure Troponin rise or ventricular dysfunction indicating significant myocardial involvement Early or excessive use of corticosteroids, which fosters dependence and further recurrences Omitting colchicine, thereby losing its proven protection against relapse Stopping anti-inflammatory therapy abruptly rather than tapering guided by symptoms and C-reactive protein Advising undue restriction of activity or missing an underlying systemic autoimmune cause Recurrent pericarditis usually follows an initial acute episode of viral or idiopathic pericarditis and is thought to reflect a dysregulated immune or autoinflammatory response rather than persistent infection. Inflammation of the pericardial layers produces the characteristic pleuritic pain, a friction rub, and often a small effusion, with release of inflammatory mediators, particularly the interleukin-1 pathway, driving relapses. Incomplete treatment of the first attack and early or high reliance on corticosteroids favour recurrence. Repeated inflammation can occasionally lead to pericardial thickening, but in idiopathic disease progression to significant constriction is unusual. Most patients have a favourable long-term outcome with control of recurrences, and although relapses can be troublesome and prolonged, progression to constrictive pericarditis is rare in idiopathic recurrent disease.

Recurrent pregnancy loss — RPL, recurrent miscarriage, recurrent spontaneous abortion, habitual abortion Antiphospholipid syndrome Parental balanced chromosomal translocation Uterine anomalies, submucosal fibroids, or intrauterine adhesions Thyroid dysfunction or poorly controlled diabetes Inherited thrombophilia Unexplained recurrent loss Antiphospholipid antibody testing (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I) with confirmatory repeat testing Parental karyotyping and, where available, cytogenetic analysis of pregnancy tissue Pelvic imaging such as ultrasound or hysteroscopy to assess uterine anatomy Thyroid function tests and glycaemic assessment Selective thrombophilia screening where clinically indicated Recurrent pregnancy loss is generally defined as two or more consecutive clinical pregnancy losses and warrants systematic evaluation of both partners Despite thorough investigation, a large proportion of cases remain unexplained, and even then the prognosis for a future successful pregnancy is often favourable Antiphospholipid syndrome is the most important treatable cause and should be specifically excluded, since it is amenable to anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy Sporadic early losses are most often due to embryonic chromosomal abnormalities, whereas recurrent loss prompts a search for maternal and parental factors Parental balanced chromosomal rearrangements are an uncommon but important cause identified by karyotyping both partners Uterine anatomical abnormalities, endocrine disorders such as thyroid disease and poorly controlled diabetes, and inherited thrombophilias should be considered Maternal age and the number of previous losses are the strongest predictors of further loss Management combines treatment of any identified cause, notably antiphospholipid syndrome, with supportive early-pregnancy care and reassurance Positive or suspected antiphospholipid syndrome requiring confirmatory testing and antithrombotic management in future pregnancy Second-trimester loss suggesting cervical insufficiency or a uterine anomaly A parental chromosomal rearrangement necessitating genetic counselling Significant psychological distress and grief requiring support Failing to test for and treat antiphospholipid syndrome, the key reversible cause Not confirming antiphospholipid antibodies with appropriately spaced repeat testing Omitting parental karyotyping when a chromosomal rearrangement is possible Neglecting the substantial psychological impact and need for supportive counselling Recurrent pregnancy loss is a heterogeneous problem in which established pregnancies fail repeatedly. Genetic causes include embryonic aneuploidy (rising sharply with maternal age) and inherited parental balanced translocations that yield unbalanced gametes. Antiphospholipid syndrome, an acquired autoimmune thrombophilia, causes loss through placental thrombosis and impaired trophoblast function driven by antibodies such as lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I. Anatomical uterine factors (congenital malformations, adhesions, submucosal fibroids, and possibly cervical insufficiency in later loss) impair implantation or placentation. Endocrine disturbances, including thyroid dysfunction and poorly controlled diabetes, disrupt the hormonal environment needed to sustain pregnancy. In many couples no cause is found, and losses are attributed to unrecognised embryonic or implantation factors. The outlook for a subsequent successful pregnancy is often good, particularly when a treatable cause such as antiphospholipid syndrome is identified and managed, and even most couples with unexplained recurrent loss eventually achieve a live birth, though the chance declines with maternal age and the number of prior losses.

Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (HPV 6/11) — RRP, laryngeal papillomatosis, juvenile-onset recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, adult-onset recurrent respiratory papillomatosis Vocal cord nodules or polyps Laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma Vocal fold granuloma Croup or other infective laryngitis Subglottic stenosis or haemangioma in children Foreign body of the airway Flexible and rigid laryngoscopy to map lesion distribution Microlaryngoscopy under anaesthesia with biopsy for histology HPV typing of excised tissue Cross-sectional imaging or bronchoscopy when distal tracheobronchial or pulmonary spread is suspected Voice assessment and serial documentation of disease burden to guide treatment intervals Caused by human papillomavirus, predominantly types 6 and 11, producing recurrent benign papillomata of the aerodigestive tract, most commonly the larynx Juvenile-onset disease is thought to arise from vertical transmission around delivery from maternal genital HPV, while adult-onset disease is often sexually acquired Progressive hoarseness or an abnormal cry is the typical presenting feature; stridor and airway obstruction develop as lesions enlarge In a child with persistent hoarseness and stridor, RRP should be considered and can be mistaken for asthma or croup Diagnosis rests on laryngoscopy showing exophytic, frond-like lesions, confirmed histologically with HPV typing Disease behaviour is highly variable, ranging from a single lesion to aggressive recurrence needing frequent procedures, with HPV 11 associated with a more aggressive course Management centres on repeated surgical debulking to preserve airway and voice while sparing normal tissue, with adjuvant medical therapies in aggressive cases Distal spread into the trachea and lungs and rare malignant transformation are recognised complications Stridor, respiratory distress or rapidly worsening airway obstruction Rapid recurrence or bulky disease requiring increasingly frequent procedures New pulmonary lesions suggesting distal spread Suspicion of malignant transformation on histology or unusually rapid growth Mistaking childhood stridor and hoarseness for asthma or recurrent croup and delaying laryngoscopy Aggressive deep excision causing scarring and permanent voice damage Performing tracheostomy unnecessarily, which may promote distal seeding of disease Neglecting surveillance for malignant change in long-standing or aggressive disease Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis results from infection of respiratory epithelium by low-risk human papillomavirus, chiefly types 6 and 11. The virus infects basal epithelial cells and drives proliferation of squamous epithelium into exophytic papillomata with fibrovascular cores, showing a predilection for zones of ciliated-to-squamous epithelial transition such as the vocal folds. Latent virus in clinically normal-appearing adjacent mucosa accounts for the characteristic recurrence after removal. Host immune factors and viral type influence disease aggressiveness, and repeated growth can extend distally through the tracheobronchial tree with rare progression to squamous carcinoma. The course is unpredictable: some patients experience spontaneous remission while others require repeated procedures over many years to maintain the airway and voice. Distal pulmonary spread and malignant transformation are uncommon but serious, and HPV vaccination is expected to reduce future incidence.

Vancomycin infusion (red man) reaction — red man syndrome, red neck syndrome, vancomycin flushing reaction, vancomycin infusion reaction, vancomycin flushing syndrome True IgE-mediated anaphylaxis to vancomycin or a co-administered drug Other drug-induced anaphylactoid reactions Carcinoid or mastocytosis-related flushing Sepsis with vasodilatation Systemic hypersensitivity or DRESS from vancomycin (linear IgA disease with vancomycin is a separate entity) Panic or vasovagal reaction Clinical observation of the temporal relationship to infusion rate Vital sign monitoring for hypotension during infusion Serum tryptase where true anaphylaxis needs to be excluded Review of co-administered histamine-releasing drugs Assessment for urticaria, angio-oedema or bronchospasm suggesting true allergy Trial of slowed infusion with observation under supervision An infusion-rate-related reaction to vancomycin causing flushing, erythema and pruritus over the face, neck and upper trunk It is a non-immune (anaphylactoid) reaction driven by direct mast-cell degranulation, not a true IgE-mediated allergy Onset is typically during or shortly after a rapid infusion, and it often eases when the infusion is slowed or paused More severe episodes can include hypotension, chest and back pain, and muscle spasm Prevention centres on slowing the infusion rate; antihistamine pre-treatment can reduce or blunt the reaction Distinguishing it from true anaphylaxis is important, as the reaction does not necessarily contraindicate future vancomycin use with a slower infusion Other agents that provoke histamine release (for example certain opioids or muscle relaxants) can potentiate the reaction The presence of urticaria beyond the infusion, angio-oedema or bronchospasm should raise concern for true allergic anaphylaxis Significant hypotension or cardiovascular instability during infusion Angio-oedema, bronchospasm or stridor suggesting true anaphylaxis Widespread urticaria persisting after the infusion Chest pain or severe muscle spasm Mislabelling the reaction as a true penicillin-class-style allergy and permanently avoiding an effective antibiotic Failing to slow the infusion and instead abandoning treatment unnecessarily Missing genuine anaphylaxis by assuming all vancomycin flushing is benign Overlooking co-administered histamine-releasing drugs that potentiate the reaction The reaction results from direct, non-immunological degranulation of mast cells and basophils provoked by vancomycin, releasing histamine into the circulation. Because it does not require prior sensitisation or drug-specific IgE, it can occur on first exposure and is closely related to the rate and concentration of the infusion, with rapid administration causing a larger histamine surge. Histamine produces cutaneous vasodilatation and flushing, pruritus and, when release is marked, hypotension and muscle discomfort. This anaphylactoid mechanism contrasts with true type I hypersensitivity, in which drug-specific IgE cross-links mast-cell receptors; the distinction guides whether the drug can be cautiously continued at a slower rate. The reaction is usually mild and self-limiting once the infusion is slowed or stopped, and vancomycin can often be continued with a slower infusion and antihistamine cover. Severe hypotensive episodes are uncommon but require prompt supportive treatment.

Reducing body myopathy (FHL1) — FHL1-related reducing body myopathy, RBM, four-and-a-half LIM domain 1 myopathy, X-linked reducing body myopathy Other FHL1-related myopathies (X-linked myopathy with postural muscle atrophy, scapuloperoneal myopathy, Emery-Dreifuss-like phenotype) Myofibrillar myopathies Congenital myopathies with cores or aggregates Rigid spine syndrome from SELENON-related myopathy Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy Inflammatory myopathy Serum creatine kinase Nerve conduction studies and electromyography Muscle biopsy with the menadione-NBT reaction, FHL1 immunostaining, and electron microscopy to demonstrate reducing bodies Muscle MRI to define involvement, including paraspinal muscles Cardiac evaluation and respiratory function testing Targeted FHL1 sequencing Caused by variants in FHL1 on the X chromosome, encoding the four-and-a-half LIM domain protein 1; inheritance is X-linked so males are typically more severely affected than heterozygous females Presents with progressive proximal and axial weakness, and rigid spine or scoliosis can be prominent features The clinical spectrum ranges from severe early-childhood-onset disease to milder later-onset forms Cardiac involvement and respiratory muscle weakness can occur, given FHL1 expression in cardiac and skeletal muscle, so cardiorespiratory surveillance is important The defining biopsy feature is reducing bodies, cytoplasmic inclusions that stain intensely with menadione-linked nitro-blue tetrazithium (menadione-NBT) in the absence of substrate, reflecting their reducing activity Reducing bodies contain aggregated mutant FHL1 protein and can be confirmed with FHL1 immunostaining and electron microscopy Creatine kinase is normal to moderately elevated and electromyography shows myopathic, sometimes irritable, changes Diagnosis combines the reducing-body biopsy finding with FHL1 genetic testing Cardiomyopathy or conduction abnormality on cardiac assessment Respiratory muscle weakness or nocturnal hypoventilation Rapidly progressive weakness or severe early-onset disease Progressive rigid spine or scoliosis compromising respiration Missing reducing bodies unless the menadione-NBT reaction is specifically performed on the biopsy Neglecting cardiac and respiratory surveillance given the FHL1 gene's cardiac role Failing to recognise the X-linked inheritance pattern and its counselling implications Confusing the inclusions with other cytoplasmic bodies without confirmatory staining Reducing body myopathy is caused by variants in FHL1, an X-linked gene encoding a LIM-domain protein involved in sarcomere assembly, mechanotransduction, and cytoskeletal signalling in striated muscle. Disease-associated variants, frequently affecting the zinc-coordinating residues of the second LIM domain, cause the mutant protein to misfold and self-aggregate. These aggregates form the characteristic reducing bodies, which have intrinsic reducing activity demonstrable with the menadione-NBT reaction, and their accumulation is toxic to muscle fibres, producing progressive weakness. Because FHL1 is also expressed in cardiac muscle, some patients develop cardiomyopathy. Prognosis varies with age of onset and sex: severe early-onset disease in males can progress rapidly with loss of ambulation and significant cardiorespiratory involvement, whereas later-onset and female cases may follow a milder course; cardiac and respiratory complications are important determinants of outcome.

Reduplicative Paramnesia — Delusional place reduplication, Environmental reduplication Capgras and Fregoli delusions of person misidentification Delirium Dementia (Alzheimer's, vascular, or Lewy body type) Traumatic brain injury with confabulation Korsakoff syndrome and other confabulatory states Right-hemisphere stroke or tumour Primary psychotic disorder, less commonly Structural neuroimaging (MRI or CT) attentive to right frontal and parietal pathology Cognitive assessment including memory, executive function, and orientation Delirium screen for infection and metabolic disturbance Bloods including vitamin B12, thyroid function, glucose, and calcium EEG where seizures or encephalopathy are suspected Neuropsychological testing Collateral history on onset and progression A delusional misidentification syndrome for place: the conviction that a location, such as the hospital, has been duplicated, relocated, or exists in two places at once. The patient may insist that the current hospital is a replica situated near their home, despite clear evidence to the contrary. Strongly associated with organic brain disease, especially right-hemisphere and bifrontal lesions from trauma, stroke, tumour, or dementia. One of the classic content-specific, monothematic delusions, alongside the Capgras and Fregoli delusions. Often accompanied by confabulation, disorientation, and anosognosia. The term was originally introduced by Pick, with place reduplication as the prototypical form. Its presence should prompt neurological and neuroimaging evaluation rather than an assumption of primary psychiatric illness. A new focal neurological deficit Acute onset with fluctuating consciousness suggesting delirium or encephalitis Rapidly progressive cognitive decline Signs of raised intracranial pressure or a space-occupying lesion Mistaking an organic delusion for primary psychiatric illness and omitting neuroimaging Overlooking coexisting delirium Attempting to argue the patient out of the belief rather than investigating the cause Missing associated anosognosia and its safety implications Reduplicative paramnesia is a monothematic delusion arising from combined right-hemisphere and frontal dysfunction. Right-hemisphere damage impairs the perceptual, spatial, and familiarity mechanisms that anchor a place to a single location, while frontal executive dysfunction impairs the monitoring and belief-evaluation processes that would normally reject the incongruity, so the patient accepts and maintains the reduplication belief. It commonly co-occurs with confabulation and disorientation, reflecting shared frontal contributions, and is typically seen in traumatic brain injury, stroke, tumours, and neurodegenerative disease affecting these regions. Prognosis depends on the underlying neurological cause; reduplication may resolve as an acute brain insult recovers but tends to persist or progress in neurodegenerative disease.

Refeeding syndrome — refeeding hypophosphataemia, nutritional recovery syndrome Sepsis with metabolic derangement Primary cardiac failure or arrhythmia of other cause Other causes of hypophosphataemia such as renal loss Diabetic ketoacidosis and its treatment-related electrolyte shifts Adrenal insufficiency Baseline and frequent monitoring of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium Glucose, sodium, and fluid balance assessment during refeeding ECG monitoring for arrhythmia in high-risk patients Assessment of nutritional risk before starting feeding Renal function and, where indicated, markers of rhabdomyolysis It is a potentially fatal set of metabolic shifts triggered when nutrition, especially carbohydrate, is reintroduced to a malnourished or starved patient The hallmark biochemical abnormality is a sharp fall in serum phosphate, often with falls in potassium and magnesium and fluid retention Highest-risk groups include those with very low body mass index, prolonged fasting or minimal intake, chronic alcohol use, anorexia nervosa, and severe malnutrition Clinical consequences include cardiac arrhythmia and failure, respiratory muscle weakness, seizures, confusion, and rhabdomyolysis Prevention is key: identify at-risk patients, correct electrolytes, give thiamine before feeding, and start nutrition cautiously with slow escalation Electrolytes must be monitored frequently during early refeeding and replaced as they fall rather than waiting for symptoms It can complicate refeeding in any setting, including treatment of severe childhood malnutrition and hospital nutritional support Rapidly falling phosphate, potassium, or magnesium after feeding begins Cardiac arrhythmia or acute heart failure during refeeding Respiratory muscle weakness or respiratory failure Seizures, confusion, or reduced consciousness attributable to electrolyte shifts or thiamine deficiency Starting full-rate nutrition immediately in a severely malnourished patient Being falsely reassured by normal pre-feeding serum electrolytes despite depleted body stores Omitting thiamine before a carbohydrate load Monitoring electrolytes too infrequently to catch the early post-feeding fall During prolonged starvation the body shifts to fat and protein catabolism, depletes intracellular electrolytes and vitamins despite near-normal serum levels, and reduces insulin secretion. Reintroducing carbohydrate causes a surge of insulin that drives glucose, phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells and stimulates synthesis of phosphorylated intermediates, abruptly lowering their serum concentrations. Thiamine, needed for carbohydrate metabolism, is rapidly consumed and can become critically deficient. Insulin also promotes sodium and water retention. The combination of hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, thiamine deficiency, and fluid overload produces the cardiac, neurological, and neuromuscular manifestations. With early identification of at-risk patients, cautious feeding, thiamine, and proactive electrolyte replacement the syndrome is largely preventable and recoverable; unrecognised, it can cause fatal arrhythmia and multi-organ dysfunction.

Reflex (vasovagal) syncope — vasovagal syncope, neurocardiogenic syncope, neurally mediated syncope, common faint Cardiac (arrhythmic or structural) syncope Orthostatic hypotension Carotid sinus hypersensitivity Epileptic seizure Situational syncope (cough, micturition, defecation) Functional (dissociative) episodes Detailed history and eyewitness account of the event and its prodrome 12-lead ECG to screen for arrhythmia or conduction disease Lying and standing blood pressure to detect orthostatic hypotension Head-up tilt-table testing in recurrent or uncertain cases Ambulatory ECG or an implantable loop recorder for infrequent unexplained episodes Echocardiography where structural heart disease is suspected The commonest cause of transient loss of consciousness, resulting from a reflex fall in heart rate and/or blood pressure with transient global cerebral hypoperfusion Typical triggers include prolonged standing, heat, pain, venepuncture, emotion, or the sight of blood A prodrome of light-headedness, nausea, sweating, pallor, and visual greying usually precedes the faint, helping distinguish it from cardiac syncope and seizures Brief myoclonic jerks (convulsive syncope) can occur and be mistaken for epilepsy Recovery is rapid with little or no confusion, unlike the post-ictal state after a seizure Diagnosis is clinical from a good history and eyewitness account; head-up tilt testing can support it in uncertain cases Cardioinhibitory, vasodepressor, and mixed haemodynamic patterns are recognised Management: education, trigger avoidance, adequate fluid and salt intake, recognising the prodrome and lying down, and physical counter-pressure manoeuvres Syncope during exertion or when supine, suggesting a cardiac cause Absence of a prodrome, or syncope causing serious injury Family history of sudden cardiac death or an abnormal ECG Palpitations preceding collapse or known structural heart disease Misdiagnosing convulsive syncope as epilepsy and starting antiepileptic drugs Failing to exclude cardiac syncope, which carries a worse prognosis Over-relying on tilt testing, which has limited sensitivity and specificity Not teaching counter-pressure manoeuvres and prodrome recognition Reflex (vasovagal) syncope results from a transient, inappropriate autonomic reflex. Triggers such as prolonged standing or emotional stress lead, in susceptible people, to a paradoxical withdrawal of sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone together with a surge of vagal (parasympathetic) activity. This produces vasodilatation (the vasodepressor component) and/or bradycardia or asystole (the cardioinhibitory component), causing a sudden fall in blood pressure and transient global cerebral hypoperfusion with loss of consciousness. Because the mechanism is self-limiting and posture-dependent, lying flat restores cerebral perfusion and consciousness returns quickly. Reduced venous return from lower-body pooling and relative hypovolaemia predispose to the reflex. Reflex syncope is benign in terms of mortality, but recurrent episodes can cause injury and impair quality of life; most patients respond well to education, trigger avoidance, and physical counter-manoeuvres.

Reflux hypersensitivity — oesophageal reflux hypersensitivity Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease Functional heartburn Eosinophilic oesophagitis Oesophageal motility disorder Cardiac chest pain Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsies to exclude mucosal and eosinophilic disease Ambulatory pH-impedance monitoring showing normal acid exposure but positive symptom association Oesophageal manometry to exclude a motility disorder Assessment of response to prior acid suppression Evaluation of psychological contributors Heartburn or chest pain triggered by reflux events despite physiologically normal oesophageal acid exposure It is distinguished from functional heartburn by a positive association between symptoms and reflux episodes on monitoring It is distinguished from reflux disease by the absence of excessive acid exposure and of mucosal injury Both acidic and weakly acidic reflux events can trigger symptoms in sensitised patients Diagnosis rests on endoscopy plus ambulatory pH-impedance monitoring with symptom-association analysis Treatment may combine acid suppression or reflux-reducing measures with neuromodulators targeting hypersensitivity Alarm features such as dysphagia, weight loss or bleeding Chest pain with cardiac features Objective testing not supporting the diagnosis Progressive symptoms Confusing it with functional heartburn (which lacks symptom-reflux correlation) Assuming reflux disease and escalating acid suppression alone Omitting symptom-association analysis on reflux monitoring Missing eosinophilic oesophagitis or cardiac chest pain Reflux hypersensitivity is a disorder of gut-brain interaction in which the oesophagus perceives physiological reflux as painful. Although total acid exposure is within normal limits and the mucosa is intact, peripheral and central sensitisation lowers the threshold at which reflux events, whether acidic or weakly acidic, provoke symptoms. The positive temporal correlation between reflux episodes and symptoms defines the condition and separates it from functional heartburn, in which no such correlation exists. The condition is benign, and symptom control is often achievable by reducing reflux events and using neuromodulators to lower hypersensitivity.

Reflux nephropathy — chronic pyelonephritis with reflux, vesicoureteric reflux nephropathy Chronic pyelonephritis without reflux Other causes of chronic kidney disease with scarring Obstructive uropathy Renal dysplasia or hypoplasia Analgesic or other tubulointerstitial nephropathy Renal ultrasound and DMSA scintigraphy for scarring Assessment of blood pressure, proteinuria and renal function Micturating cystourethrography where active reflux is investigated Urinalysis and culture for infection Long-term monitoring of renal function Renal scarring resulting from vesicoureteric reflux, typically with childhood urinary tract infections It is an important cause of chronic kidney disease and of hypertension in children and young adults Characteristic imaging shows focal cortical scars overlying dilated calyces, often at the poles It may present with hypertension, proteinuria, recurrent infections or incidentally reduced renal function Established scarring is irreversible, so prevention and early detection are key Management focuses on blood pressure and proteinuria control and prevention of further infection and scarring Progressive chronic kidney disease Difficult-to-control hypertension Significant proteinuria Recurrent pyelonephritis causing new scarring Failing to control hypertension and proteinuria that drive progression Attributing the scarring purely to infection without recognising reflux Overlooking reflux nephropathy as a cause of young-adult hypertension Missing ongoing preventable urinary infections Reflux nephropathy develops when vesicoureteric reflux, particularly with intrarenal reflux and urinary infection during early childhood, damages the renal parenchyma and produces focal scarring. The scars disrupt nephrons and, once a critical amount of renal mass is affected, trigger hyperfiltration injury in the remaining nephrons, causing progressive proteinuria, glomerulosclerosis and declining function. Activation of the renin-angiotensin system contributes to the associated hypertension, which further accelerates renal injury. Prognosis depends on the extent of scarring; limited disease may remain stable, but extensive bilateral scarring can progress to end-stage kidney disease, especially with uncontrolled hypertension or proteinuria.

Bardet-Biedl syndromes Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy Charcot-Marie-Tooth and other hereditary neuropathies Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata (PEX7-related, with high phytanic acid) Generalised peroxisome biogenesis disorders (Zellweger spectrum) Abetalipoproteinaemia and vitamin E deficiency Plasma phytanic acid level, which is markedly elevated Plasma pristanic acid and very-long-chain fatty acids to distinguish from generalised peroxisomal disorders Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showing raised protein with normal cell count Ophthalmological assessment with electroretinography for pigmentary retinopathy Nerve conduction studies and audiometry PHYH and PEX7 molecular genetic testing Classic Refsum disease is an autosomal recessive peroxisomal disorder of phytanic acid alpha-oxidation, usually from PHYH mutations and less often from PEX7 defects The cardinal tetrad is retinitis pigmentosa, chronic peripheral polyneuropathy, cerebellar ataxia and raised cerebrospinal fluid protein without pleocytosis (albuminocytological dissociation) Night blindness and progressively constricted visual fields from pigmentary retinopathy are often the earliest and most consistent feature Additional clues include anosmia, sensorineural deafness, ichthyosis, skeletal abnormalities such as a shortened fourth toe, and cardiac conduction disturbance Diagnosis rests on a markedly elevated plasma phytanic acid with normal or only mildly elevated very-long-chain fatty acids, distinguishing it from generalised peroxisomal disorders Because phytanic acid is entirely of dietary (exogenous) origin, strict dietary restriction of phytanic acid, avoiding ruminant fats, dairy and certain fish, is the mainstay of treatment Rapid weight loss and fasting mobilise phytanic acid from fat stores and can precipitate acute deterioration, so these are avoided; plasma exchange is used generically for acute severe episodes Cardiac arrhythmia or conduction block, a recognised cause of sudden death Acute worsening of weakness or ataxia after fasting, illness or rapid weight loss Rapidly progressive visual or hearing loss Severe polyneuropathy compromising mobility or respiration Permitting rapid weight loss or fasting, which mobilises stored phytanic acid and can trigger acute deterioration Failing to measure phytanic acid, so a treatable disorder is mistaken for another hereditary neuropathy or retinopathy Overlooking cardiac conduction disease that requires monitoring Not distinguishing classic Refsum disease from generalised peroxisomal disorders by checking very-long-chain fatty acids Classic Refsum disease is a peroxisomal single-enzyme disorder in which deficiency of phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase (encoded by PHYH), or less commonly a defect of the peroxisomal targeting receptor PEX7, blocks the alpha-oxidation of phytanic acid. Phytanic acid is a branched-chain fatty acid derived exclusively from the diet, and because its beta-methyl group prevents beta-oxidation it must first undergo alpha-oxidation. When this pathway fails, phytanic acid accumulates in blood and lipid-rich tissues, where it is incorporated into membranes and disrupts myelin, retinal and neural function, producing the neuropathy, retinopathy and ataxia. Its wholly dietary origin is what makes dietary restriction effective. With early diagnosis and sustained dietary phytanic acid restriction the neuropathy and ataxia can stabilise or partially improve and progression slows, although retinopathy, deafness and anosmia tend to persist; untreated disease progresses and carries a risk of fatal cardiac complications.

with the mucosa billowing on inspiration Smoking cessation is the single most important intervention and can halt progression Bulky disease is treated by microlaryngeal surgery to evacuate the gelatinous material and redrape the mucosa, staged for each side to avoid webbing Sudden change or a firm focal area in a heavy smoker should prompt exclusion of coexisting dysplasia or carcinoma A firm or leukoplakic focal area suggesting dysplasia or carcinoma Impaired vocal fold mobility Stridor or exertional dyspnoea from bulky airway-narrowing folds Rapid unilateral change out of keeping with symmetrical polypoid degeneration Operating on both vocal folds simultaneously with aggressive mucosal removal, risking an anterior glottic web Failing to insist on smoking cessation, allowing recurrence Overlooking coexisting carcinoma masked by diffuse polypoid change Attributing the low voice solely to habit and missing treatable hypothyroidism Reinke oedema is a chronic accumulation of oedematous, myxoid material within the superficial lamina propria of the vocal fold, the potential space known as Reinke's space. Prolonged irritation, above all from tobacco smoke, together with phonotrauma and reflux, increases vascular permeability and impairs lymphatic drainage in this loosely bound layer, so fluid and mucoid matrix collect and the covering mucosa becomes lax and redundant. The increased mass lowers the fundamental frequency of vibration, producing the typical low, rough voice, and in advanced disease the pendulous folds can narrow the airway. Progression usually halts with smoking cessation, and surgery reliably reduces bulk and raises vocal pitch, though the deepened voice may not fully normalise; continued smoking leads to recurrence and carries ongoing malignant risk.

Reis-Bucklers corneal dystrophy — corneal dystrophy of Bowman layer type 1, granular corneal dystrophy type 3 Thiel-Behnke corneal dystrophy Granular corneal dystrophy Lattice corneal dystrophy Map-dot-fingerprint dystrophy Anterior corneal scarring from other cause Slit-lamp examination of the superficial opacities TGFBI genetic testing to confirm and subtype Corneal topography and imaging (for example anterior segment OCT) Family history and examination of relatives Assessment of visual impact and erosion frequency An autosomal dominant dystrophy affecting the Bowman layer, associated with mutations in the TGFBI gene Presents in childhood with recurrent painful corneal erosions Progressive superficial opacities develop at the level of Bowman layer, reducing vision over time It shares its TGFBI genetic basis with other classic stromal dystrophies (granular, lattice, Thiel-Behnke) Erosions tend to lessen with age as opacification and scarring increase It commonly recurs in grafts after keratoplasty, so superficial ablative procedures are often preferred Progressive visual loss from opacification Infective keratitis complicating an erosion Recurrence within a previous graft Severe recurrent erosion episodes Confusing it with Thiel-Behnke or other TGFBI dystrophies without genetic testing Performing penetrating keratoplasty when a superficial procedure would avoid rapid recurrence Missing infective keratitis during erosions Overlooking the autosomal dominant family history Reis-Bucklers corneal dystrophy is caused by mutations in the transforming growth factor beta-induced (TGFBI) gene, leading to deposition of abnormal protein at the level of the Bowman layer and superficial stroma. The abnormal material disrupts and replaces the Bowman layer, causing surface irregularity, poor epithelial adhesion with recurrent erosions in early life, and progressive superficial opacification that degrades vision. Because the underlying epithelial and anterior stromal cells continue to produce the abnormal protein, the dystrophy characteristically recurs in corneal grafts. Vision declines gradually with superficial opacification; superficial keratectomy or phototherapeutic ablation can improve vision, though the dystrophy tends to recur, including in grafts.

and erosions characteristically recur superficially after treatment, including within grafts Frequent severe erosions causing disabling pain in childhood Non-healing epithelial defect with risk of secondary infection Progressive superficial scarring and irregular astigmatism reducing vision Rapid recurrence of deposits after phototherapeutic keratectomy or grafting Confusing it with Thiel-Behnke dystrophy without histological or genetic confirmation Attributing childhood erosions to trauma and missing the hereditary dystrophy Assuming a single procedure is curative despite the tendency to recur Overlooking reduced corneal sensation and its impact on healing Reis-Bucklers corneal dystrophy is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the transforming growth factor beta-induced gene (TGFBI). Abnormal mutant protein accumulates as hyaline (granular) deposits that replace and disrupt the Bowman layer and superficial stroma. Destruction of the Bowman layer weakens epithelial adhesion, producing frequent painful erosions in early life, while progressive deposition and superficial scarring create an irregular, hazy surface that reduces vision over time. Because the deposits arise from an inherited protein abnormality, they tend to recur in the superficial cornea after surgical removal. Painful recurrent erosions dominate early life and later diminish as superficial scarring reduces vision. Superficial procedures can improve the surface, but deposits and erosions commonly recur, sometimes requiring repeated intervention.

Relapsing Fever — Louse-borne relapsing fever, LBRF, Soft tick relapsing fever, STRF, Hard tick relapsing fever, HTRF, Borrelia recurrentis infection, Borrelia miyamotoi disease Rocky Mountain spotted fever and other rickettsioses Ehrlichiosis Anaplasmosis Tick-borne viral infection (including a viral encephalitis transmitted by Ixodes) Babesiosis Lyme disease (especially when STRF presents with Bell's palsy in co-endemic areas) Malaria Typhoid fever Epidemic (louse-borne) typhus Dengue Leptospirosis Trench fever (Bartonella quintana, also louse-transmitted) Influenza (LBRF cough plus fever and myalgia can mimic it) Undifferentiated sepsis (notably with B. miyamotoi disease) Malaria (periodic fever, co-endemic, can coexist as co-infection) Typhoid fever Epidemic louse-borne typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii) and other rickettsioses Leptospirosis Dengue Lyme disease (cross-reactive serology and shared Bell's palsy) Anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis, and babesiosis Influenza Wright, Giemsa, or Giemsa-Wright-stained thin blood smear examined over several oil-immersion fields (sensitive when spirochete density is >= 10^5/mL), ideally drawn at or just before the fever peak Thick blood smear treated with 0.5% acetic acid before staining, or a wet mount of citrated blood examined by phase-contrast/dark-field microscopy for motile spirochetes PCR / nucleic acid amplification testing of blood or CSF (more sensitive than thin smear, especially between febrile episodes; preferred for B. miyamotoi and B. lonestari) Culture of blood or CSF in Barbour-Stoenner-Kelly broth medium (slow, rarely offered) GlpQ-based serologic assay (specific for relapsing-fever Borrelia and negative in Lyme disease species, but often negative when smear/PCR are positive) CSF analysis in any case with signs of meningitis/meningoencephalitis (mononuclear pleocytosis and mildly-to-moderately elevated protein support CNS involvement) Complete blood count (normocytic anemia; variable leukocyte count; thrombocytopenia, sometimes <50,000/uL) C-reactive protein and procalcitonin (elevated) Liver enzymes and coagulation studies (elevated aminotransferases; PT/PTT may be moderately prolonged) ECG and chest radiography where myocarditis is suspected (prolonged QTc, cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema) Relapsing fever is caused by several Borrelia spirochete species and occurs in three epidemiologic forms: louse-borne (LBRF, B. recurrentis), soft tick-borne (STRF, multiple Ornithodoros-transmitted species), and hard tick-borne (HTRF, mainly B. miyamotoi and B. lonestari) (p.1444). The hallmark is two or more febrile episodes separated by afebrile intervals of well-being; the relapsing course reflects antigenic variation of the spirochete's surface lipoproteins, with each variant cleared as specific antibody develops (p.1444-1446). In LBRF the first fever is typically unremitting for 3-6 days and is usually followed by a single milder relapse, whereas STRF produces multiple febrile periods of 1-3 days each; interfebrile intervals span roughly 4-14 days (p.1446). A 'crisis' may terminate the first fever episode (rigors, a further rise in temperature, increased pulse and blood pressure for about 15-30 min), followed by drenching sweats, falling temperature, and hypotension lasting several hours (p.1446). Soft ticks (Ornithodoros) feed briefly, often under 30 minutes and usually while the victim sleeps, then leave undetected, so the exposure may go unrecognized (p.1445). Transovarial transmission in soft ticks means infection risk can persist in a dwelling for years, and a case may be diagnosed long after the last reported local case (p.1445-1447). LBRF is acquired not from the louse bite itself but by rubbing crushed louse hemolymph into the bite site or auto-inoculating it into conjunctivae or a wound; humans are the sole reservoir of B. recurrentis (p.1445). Jaundice, epistaxis, and subconjunctival hemorrhages are common in LBRF but typically absent in STRF and HTRF; splenomegaly or splenic tenderness is common in both LBRF and STRF (p.1446). Localizing neurologic signs are more frequent in STRF than in LBRF/HTRF; B. turicatae is notably neurotropic, and unilateral or bilateral Bell's palsy (cranial neuritis) characteristically appears in the second or third febrile episode rather than the first (p.1446). B. miyamotoi disease (HTRF) is less distinctive, often presenting as acute fever with chills, headache, and myalgia 1-2 weeks after a tick bite, and has been mistaken for undifferentiated sepsis; meningoencephalitis occurs particularly in patients with impaired humoral immunity (e.g., after rituximab) (p.1446). Diagnosis of LBRF/STRF rests on direct microscopic detection of spirochetes in blood (Wright, Giemsa, or Giemsa-Wright stain), best collected at or just before the fever peak; spirochete density in B. miyamotoi/B. lonestari may be too low for smear alone (p.1447). Outbreaks of LBRF (often alongside typhus) cluster in settings of famine, war, refugee migration, homelessness, and incarceration, and can appear in migrant camps far from the country of origin (p.1445). Signs of meningitis or meningoencephalitis (warrants CSF analysis and consideration of CNS-directed therapy) Cranial neuritis, especially uni- or bilateral Bell's palsy, or visual impairment from iridocyclitis/panophthalmitis (which may be permanent) Myocarditis: gallop rhythm, prolonged QTc, cardiomegaly, and pulmonary edema Acute respiratory distress syndrome Diffuse bleeding, jaundice, and poor liver function Stupor or coma on admission Pregnancy (high risk of abortion, stillbirth, or perinatal death) Concurrent malaria, typhus, or typhoid Abrupt clinical worsening within 1-3 h of starting antibiotics (Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction with hypotension and falling platelets), which can be fatal without monitoring Whole-cell serologic assays (including ELISA and the C6 peptide ELISA for Lyme disease) can be falsely positive in relapsing fever due to antigenic cross-reactivity among spirochetes (p.1447). Serology cannot distinguish among Borrelia species as the cause, and a positive IgG on a single specimen may reflect past infection rather than the current illness (p.1447). Specific serologic assays (e.g., GlpQ-based) are commonly negative at the very time a blood smear or PCR would be positive (p.1447). Spirochete density in B. miyamotoi or B. lonestari infection may be too low for diagnosis by blood smear alone, so PCR is preferred (p.1447). Smears drawn during afebrile intervals may miss spirochetemia; sampling at/just before the fever peak (or using NAAT) improves yield (p.1447). For B. miyamotoi HTRF, prompt removal of an embedded tick may not prevent infection because transmission occurs soon after feeding begins (p.1447). STRF presenting with Bell's palsy can be misdiagnosed as Lyme disease in co-endemic regions (p.1447). Co-infections (malaria, typhus, typhoid with relapsing fever; B. miyamotoi with Lyme disease) may obscure the diagnosis (p.1447). A Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can be provoked even by antibiotics with suboptimal antiborrelial activity (e.g., ciprofloxacin) given for an unsuspected case (p.1448). Borrelia are slender, double-membrane spirochetes that are extracellular pathogens with a limited biosynthetic genome about one-quarter the size of E. coli; their flagella lie between the two membranes. Tick-borne spirochetes enter in tick saliva at the onset of feeding, and from a small inoculum STRF organisms proliferate in blood (doubling roughly every 6 h) to 10^6-10^7/mL or more, while HTRF organisms grow more slowly to lower densities. Although they lack potent exotoxins and lack lipopolysaccharide endotoxin, abundant Borrelia lipoproteins activate Toll-like receptors, driving an endotoxemia-like proinflammatory response with elevated TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IL-8. Spirochete binding to erythrocytes causes red cell aggregation, splenic/hepatic sequestration, hepatosplenomegaly, and anemia; bleeding reflects thrombocytopenia, impaired hepatic clotting-factor production, and small-vessel blockage by aggregates of spirochetes, erythrocytes, and platelets. Serotype-specific IgM appears after a few days and lyses circulating bacteria by bactericidal action or opsonization; release of bacterial products from dying organisms drives a spontaneous 'crisis,' the antibiotic-triggered counterpart of which is the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. Antigenic variation of surface lipoproteins produces successive bacteremic relapses, each ended by variant-specific antibody. Some species are neurotropic and enter the relatively immune-sheltered brain, and spirochetes can cross the maternal-fetal barrier to cause placental damage, intrauterine growth retardation, and congenital infection (p.1444-1447). Untreated mortality is approximately 10-70% for LBRF and 4-10% for STRF, depending heavily on coexisting conditions (e.g., malnutrition, other infection) and available medical support. With prompt antibiotic treatment, mortality falls to about 2-5% for LBRF and under 2% for STRF; no deaths from HTRF have been reported. Poor-prognosis features include concurrent malaria, typhus, or typhoid; pregnancy; stupor or coma at admission; diffuse bleeding; poor liver function; myocarditis; and bronchopneumonia. The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction in LBRF carries roughly a 5% mortality without adequate monitoring and resuscitation. LBRF or STRF in pregnancy frequently causes abortion, stillbirth, or perinatal death, though congenital malformations have not been reported. Documented posttreatment sequelae and prolonged disability have not been established for any form, and partial immunity to reinfection appears to develop in residents of perennially high-risk areas (p.1448). No formal numeric severity score is given. Clinically, severity is stratified by relapsing-fever type and complications: LBRF carries higher untreated mortality (about 10-70%) than STRF (about 4-10%), while HTRF/B. miyamotoi disease is mildest with no reported deaths. CNS involvement (confirmed or suspected meningitis/meningoencephalitis, supported by CSF mononuclear pleocytosis and elevated protein) marks severe disease warranting parenteral therapy. Features defining a severe/poor-prognosis course include concurrent malaria, typhus, or typhoid; pregnancy; stupor or coma at admission; diffuse bleeding; poor liver function; myocarditis; and bronchopneumonia (p.1446-1448).

Relapsing Polychondritis — RP Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) - distinguished by ANCA positivity and glomerulonephritis, which are not features of RP (p.2920) Autoinflammatory diseases (p.2920) VEXAS syndrome - especially in older males with cytopenia, macrocytosis, and lymphopenia (p.2920) Rheumatoid arthritis - the small-joint pattern can mimic RA but RP arthritis is nonerosive and nondeforming (p.2919) Behcet's syndrome - overlap via MAGIC syndrome (p.2920) Adult-onset asthma - airway chondritis is frequently misattributed to asthma (p.2919) Infectious diseases of the external ear mimicking ear chondritis (p.2920) Infectious diseases mimicking nasal chondritis (p.2920) Infectious airway disease mimicking airway chondritis (p.2920) Audiometry to assess for conductive and sensorineural hearing loss in all suspected patients (p.2920) Dynamic expiratory-phase chest CT to evaluate tracheobronchomalacia (p.2920) Direct laryngoscopy to visualize upper-airway cartilage damage; bronchoscopy of the lower airway can exacerbate disease and must be used with caution (p.2920-2921) Echocardiography to assess valvular heart disease (p.2921) FDG-PET to detect inflammation in large arteries and larger airways (p.2921) Vestibular testing (finger-to-nose, Romberg, nystagmus) when dizziness is present (p.2920) Genetic testing for UBA1 and bone marrow assessment for VEXAS in older males with cytopenias (p.2920) Cartilage biopsy reserved for excluding mimics (infection, malignancy) since findings are nonspecific (p.2918, 2921) Traumatic otohematoma and red ear syndrome (ear) (p.2920) Cutaneous diseases of the external ear (p.2920) Angiocentric centrofacial lymphoma (nasal chondritis) (p.2920) Traumatic airway stenosis and congenital airway disorders (p.2920) Rare systemic disease defined by recurrent inflammation of cartilaginous structures, with the ears, nose, respiratory tract, and joints as hallmark sites; the eyes, inner ear, nervous system, skin, and cardiovascular system may also be involved (p.2917). Ear involvement is the most common manifestation, affecting roughly 80-90% of patients, and typically spares the non-cartilaginous lobule; pain may occur with minimal visible swelling or erythema (p.2918). Triggers for ear pain often include minor trauma (lying on the affected side, wearing glasses) or temperature change; 'cauliflower ear' from cartilage damage occurs only in a small subset after recurrent episodes (p.2918). Nasal disease often presents as a pressure sensation at the bridge of the nose; a saddle-nose deformity may develop but is not universal, and unlike GPA the nasal perforations in RP are usually anterior rather than septal (p.2918-2919). Airway involvement such as subglottic stenosis may be misdiagnosed as adult-onset asthma; severe narrowing can cause stridor and is a medical emergency, and chronic damage can lead to tracheomalacia, bronchomalacia, or tracheal calcification (p.2919). Costochondral joint inflammation can produce severe bilateral chest pain that is reproducible on palpation and not movement-related, sometimes mimicking acute coronary syndrome and prompting emergency evaluation (p.2919-2920). Recurrent chondritis of the ears and nose in older male patients with severe systemic inflammation and progressive bone marrow failure should prompt evaluation for VEXAS syndrome (somatic UBA1 mutation) (p.2917, 2920). Episcleritis is the most frequent ocular manifestation; scleritis is rare but warrants urgent ophthalmologic evaluation given the risk of vision loss, scleromalacia, or globe rupture (p.2920). Because disease activity is intermittent and patients may appear non-inflamed during a clinic visit, a longitudinal history and review of patient-provided photographs are essential to diagnosis (p.2918). MAGIC syndrome (mouth and genital ulcers with inflamed cartilage) overlaps with Behcet's syndrome features such as pathergy and GI involvement and may include large-vessel vasculitis of the aorta (p.2920). Some patients carry concurrent rheumatologic diagnoses such as Sjogren's syndrome or systemic lupus erythematosus (p.2917). Neurologic attribution to RP is a diagnosis of exclusion; infection and malignancy must be ruled out first, though encephalitis and meningitis can occur in RP (p.2920). Stridor from severe airway/subglottic narrowing - a medical emergency requiring urgent attention to avoid mortality (p.2919) Features of scleritis - urgent ophthalmology referral due to risk of vision loss, scleromalacia, or globe rupture (p.2920) Cytopenia with macrocytosis and lymphopenia in older males - suggests VEXAS and possible progressive bone marrow failure (p.2917, 2920) Severe costochondral chest pain that can mimic acute coronary syndrome (p.2919-2920) Airway involvement is commonly misdiagnosed as adult-onset asthma, delaying treatment and risking chronic large-airway damage (p.2919) Normal ESR and CRP do not exclude active RP, as acute-phase reactants are not reliably elevated (p.2918) There is no diagnostic blood or tissue biomarker; relying on a single test is a pitfall - diagnosis rests on clinical pattern recognition over time (p.2918, 2920) Cartilage biopsy yields nonspecific findings and can cause morbidity; it should not be expected to confirm RP (p.2918, 2921) Patients may appear non-inflamed at a single visit because disease activity is intermittent (p.2918) Published diagnostic criteria were derived from small cohorts, are largely expert-opinion-based, and have not been formally validated (p.2920) Assuming a saddle nose implies GPA - in RP the deformity usually lacks septal perforation (perforations are anterior) (p.2918-2919) The exact mechanisms remain unclear despite study of genetic, environmental, and immunologic factors. Limited animal-model data suggest autoimmunity against cartilage components may contribute: immunizing certain animals against type II collagen, type IX collagen, or matrilin-1 can reproduce aspects of the human phenotype. However, autoantibodies (including anti-type II collagen) are neither sensitive nor specific enough for diagnosis, and observational data showing B-cell-depleting therapy is not particularly effective argue against a dominant antibody-mediated mechanism. Proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines linked to both innate and adaptive immunity have been associated with RP but are inconsistent. Histologically, acute cartilage shows a mixed myeloid and lymphoid inflammatory infiltrate at the cartilage interface; over time there is lacunar breakdown, loss of chondrocytes, and replacement by fibrosis (p.2918). Outcomes depend heavily on organ involvement. Airway disease can progress to tracheomalacia, bronchomalacia, or tracheal calcification, and severe subglottic narrowing carries mortality risk. Scleritis can lead to vision loss or globe rupture. VEXAS-associated disease involves progressive bone marrow failure and is potentially life-threatening, so prompt recognition is essential. Acute-phase reactants (ESR, CRP) are not reliably elevated, so they cannot be used to gauge severity (p.2917-2920). No formally validated severity grading exists. Several diagnostic schemes have been proposed: McAdam's criteria require 3 of 6 features (bilateral auricular chondritis, nonerosive seronegative inflammatory polyarthritis, nasal chondritis, ocular inflammation, respiratory-tract chondritis, vestibular/cochlear dysfunction); the Damiani-Levine modification accepts 3 clinical features, or 1 feature plus histologic chondritis, or 2 features plus clinical response to treatment; Michet's criteria use 3 major criteria (ear, nose, or respiratory-tract inflammation) and 4 minor criteria (ocular inflammation, hearing loss, vestibular dysfunction, seronegative inflammatory arthritis), requiring 2 major or 1 major plus 2 minor. All are limited by lack of precise organ-involvement definitions (p.2920).

Relentless placoid chorioretinitis — ampiginous choroiditis, relentless placoid chorioretinopathy Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy Serpiginous choroiditis Tuberculous serpiginous-like choroiditis Syphilitic placoid chorioretinitis Birdshot chorioretinopathy Fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography Fundus autofluorescence to map active and healed lesions Optical coherence tomography for outer-retinal and RPE changes Workup to exclude tuberculosis and syphilis before immunosuppression Serial wide-field imaging to monitor the relapsing course A rare placoid inflammatory chorioretinopathy considered to sit on a spectrum between APMPPE and serpiginous choroiditis (hence 'ampiginous') Characterised by numerous placoid lesions, often more than fifty over the disease course, involving both posterior pole and periphery Follows a prolonged, relapsing course over months rather than the self-limiting behaviour of classic APMPPE Lesions show the typical early hypofluorescence and late staining of placoid disease on fluorescein angiography Vision can be preserved but is threatened by foveal involvement and recurrent activity Long-term immunosuppression is often required to control the relentless course Foveal or peripapillary lesions threatening central vision Frequent relapses despite treatment Features suggesting an infective (tuberculous/syphilitic) mimic Progressive enlargement resembling serpiginous spread Assuming a self-limiting APMPPE course and undertreating Starting immunosuppression before excluding tuberculosis and syphilis Underestimating relapse risk on stopping therapy Overlooking peripheral lesions by examining only the posterior pole The condition is an idiopathic inflammatory disorder of the choriocapillaris and overlying retinal pigment epithelium, producing placoid lesions similar to those of acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy and serpiginous choroiditis. Unlike self-limiting APMPPE, the inflammatory process recurs relentlessly, generating a large number of lesions across the fundus over an extended period, with choriocapillaris hypoperfusion contributing to the angiographic and imaging findings. The course is protracted with repeated relapses, but with sustained immunosuppression many eyes retain useful vision unless the fovea is repeatedly involved.

can be provoked by antidepressants, other drugs, alcohol withdrawal or brainstem lesions Emerging parkinsonism, cognitive decline or autonomic failure suggesting evolving synucleinopathy Onset in a young person or focal neurological signs pointing to a structural or demyelinating lesion Serious injury to the patient or bed partner Atypical features suggesting nocturnal seizures rather than a parasomnia Attributing dream enactment to nightmares without confirmatory polysomnography Missing obstructive sleep apnoea causing pseudo-RBD Neglecting bedroom safety advice, leaving the patient or partner at risk of injury Failing to counsel appropriately and to monitor for later neurodegenerative disease Overlooking an antidepressant or other drug as a precipitant During normal REM sleep, brainstem circuits centred on the sublaterodorsal nucleus of the pons actively inhibit spinal motor neurones, producing the characteristic muscle atonia. In REM sleep behaviour disorder these circuits fail, so the motor accompaniments of dreaming are no longer suppressed and dreams are acted out. Because these pontine and medullary structures are affected early by alpha-synuclein pathology, the disorder often heralds a neurodegenerative synucleinopathy years before other features appear. Symptoms are usually controllable with clonazepam or melatonin together with a safe sleep environment; however, most people with idiopathic RBD will develop a neurodegenerative synucleinopathy over subsequent years, so long-term neurological follow-up is advised.

Without this atonia, the motor commands accompanying dreaming are expressed as movement. Degeneration of these brainstem nuclei by alpha-synuclein pathology explains the strong link between idiopathic RBD and later development of a synucleinopathy, often years after the sleep disorder appears. Symptoms are usually controllable with bedroom safety measures and medication, but isolated RBD carries a high long-term risk of conversion to a defined neurodegenerative synucleinopathy.

or failed interaction between the ureteric bud and the metanephric blastema; the unilateral form is relatively common and often silent, whereas the bilateral form is rare and incompatible with tract anomalies owing to shared mesonephric and Mullerian development: in girls a unicornuate uterus, Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome or the obstructed hemivagina with ipsilateral renal agenesis (OHVIRA / Herlyn-Werner-Wunderlich) syndrome, and in boys seminal vesicle cysts or absence of the vas deferens It may be isolated or part of a syndrome such as the VACTERL association, branchio-oto-renal syndrome, Kallmann syndrome or renal coloboma syndrome, so extrarenal features should prompt genetic evaluation and family screening Lifelong surveillance of the solitary kidney, with attention to blood pressure, proteinuria and renal function and avoidance of nephrotoxic insults, is advised Bilateral agenesis with severe oligohydramnios and anticipated pulmonary hypoplasia requiring perinatal counselling Hypertension, proteinuria or declining function in a solitary kidney An acute illness threatening the only functioning kidney An obstructive genital anomaly such as OHVIRA presenting with cyclical pain around menarche Diagnosing agenesis when the kidney is in fact ectopic or crossed and fused, without searching elsewhere Overlooking associated genital tract anomalies, particularly Mullerian anomalies in girls Failing to arrange lifelong surveillance of the solitary kidney Mistaking an involuted multicystic dysplastic kidney for primary agenesis Not offering genetic counselling and family screening despite recognised heritable forms Renal agenesis results from failure of the metanephros to develop, most often because the ureteric bud fails to form from the mesonephric (wolffian) duct, fails to reach the metanephric blastema, or fails to induce it. As the ureteric bud also gives rise to the ureter and the corresponding hemitrigone, its absence explains the missing ipsilateral ureter and hemitrigone. The shared embryological origin with the genital ducts underlies the frequent Mullerian anomalies in females and wolffian anomalies in males. In bilateral agenesis the fetus produces little or no urine; because fetal urine is the principal component of amniotic fluid in the later part of pregnancy, profound oligohydramnios develops, compressing the fetus and preventing normal lung expansion, and so producing the pulmonary hypoplasia and deformational features of the Potter sequence. Unilateral renal agenesis with a normal solitary kidney generally has a good prognosis, though it carries a modestly increased lifetime risk of hypertension, proteinuria and chronic kidney disease that warrants monitoring. Bilateral renal agenesis is almost uniformly fatal in the neonatal period from pulmonary hypoplasia, with only rare reported survival following intensive intervention.

Renal angiomyolipoma — AML, renal AML Fat-poor angiomyolipoma versus renal cell carcinoma Clear cell or papillary renal cell carcinoma Retroperitoneal liposarcoma involving the kidney Oncocytoma Renal lipoma or other fatty lesion Wilms tumour in children CT or MRI to demonstrate macroscopic fat and characterise the lesion Assessment of lesion size and intratumoural aneurysms to gauge bleeding risk Screening for tuberous sclerosis features when lesions are multiple or bilateral Renal mass biopsy when imaging is indeterminate and malignancy cannot be excluded Baseline renal function, particularly before intervention A benign renal tumour composed of blood vessels, smooth muscle and mature fat, part of the PEComa family Most are sporadic, solitary and found incidentally; multiple bilateral lesions suggest tuberous sclerosis complex The presence of macroscopic fat on CT or MRI is characteristic and usually allows a confident diagnosis Fat-poor variants can mimic renal cell carcinoma and may require biopsy or excision to clarify Larger lesions carry a risk of spontaneous, potentially life-threatening retroperitoneal haemorrhage (Wunderlich syndrome) Aneurysms within the feeding vessels increase the bleeding risk and can be targeted by embolisation Epithelioid angiomyolipoma is an uncommon variant with malignant potential Acute flank pain with hypotension suggesting spontaneous haemorrhage Rapidly enlarging lesion or a large lesion with prominent aneurysms Features suggesting the epithelioid variant or malignancy New multiple bilateral lesions raising concern for a syndrome with other organ involvement Assuming all angiomyolipomas are benign and overlooking the epithelioid variant Misdiagnosing a fat-poor lesion as, or overlooking, renal cell carcinoma Failing to evaluate for tuberous sclerosis when lesions are multiple Underestimating haemorrhage risk in large or aneurysmal lesions Angiomyolipomas are benign mesenchymal neoplasms arising from perivascular epithelioid cells and containing a variable mixture of dysmorphic thick-walled vessels, smooth muscle and adipose tissue. In tuberous sclerosis, biallelic inactivation of the TSC1 or TSC2 genes leads to constitutive activation of the mTOR pathway, driving multiple and often larger tumours. The abnormal, aneurysm-prone vasculature accounts for the tendency of larger lesions to bleed. The epithelioid variant shows atypical cells and can behave in a malignant fashion. Most angiomyolipomas are benign with an excellent prognosis; the main risks are haemorrhage from larger lesions and, rarely, malignant behaviour of the epithelioid variant, both of which can be mitigated by surveillance and timely intervention.

Choosing a repair approach that unnecessarily sacrifices renal parenchyma A renal artery aneurysm is a localised dilatation resulting from weakening of the arterial wall, commonly at branch points where haemodynamic stress is greatest. Medial degeneration from fibromuscular dysplasia, atherosclerotic wall damage, and inherited connective tissue disease reduce wall integrity, allowing progressive dilatation. Disturbed flow within the aneurysm can generate thrombus and distal embolisation causing renal ischaemia and activating the renin-angiotensin system, which contributes to secondary hypertension. Increasing wall tension with growth raises rupture risk, which is amplified by the physiological and hormonal changes of pregnancy. Most incidental aneurysms remain stable and can be monitored, with elective repair offering good outcomes and often preserving renal function; rupture is rare but carries high mortality, especially in pregnancy, and secondary hypertension may improve after successful treatment.
