renal artery occlusion Reflexively stenting atherosclerotic lesions when evidence favours medical therapy for most patients Stopping renin-angiotensin blockade for a modest, stable creatinine rise that is actually acceptable Missing fibromuscular dysplasia as a curable cause of hypertension in a young woman Failing to recognise bilateral disease as the cause of recurrent flash pulmonary oedema Renal artery stenosis reduces perfusion pressure to the affected kidney, which the kidney interprets as volume depletion and responds to by activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. The resulting angiotensin-mediated vasoconstriction and aldosterone-driven sodium retention raise systemic blood pressure. When only one kidney is affected, the contralateral kidney can excrete the retained sodium, so hypertension is predominantly renin-driven. With bilateral disease or a single functioning kidney, sodium and volume retention dominate and drive the hypertension. Chronic hypoperfusion also causes ischaemic injury with tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis, and glomerulosclerosis, producing ischaemic nephropathy. Renin-angiotensin blockade can precipitate a fall in glomerular filtration because efferent arteriolar tone, needed to maintain filtration pressure in the underperfused kidney, is removed. Fibromuscular dysplasia generally responds well to angioplasty with a good chance of improving or curing hypertension. Atherosclerotic disease reflects generalised vascular disease and carries substantial cardiovascular risk; for most such patients optimal medical therapy gives outcomes comparable to intervention, and prognosis is driven largely by comorbid cardiovascular disease and the degree of established ischaemic nephropathy.

Renal Cell Carcinoma — RCC, kidney cancer Simple/complex renal cysts (p.689) Benign neoplasms: adenoma, angiomyolipoma, oncocytoma (p.689) Inflammatory lesions: pyelonephritis or renal abscess (p.689) Transitional (urothelial) cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis (p.689) Renal sarcoma (p.689) Renal lymphoma (p.689) Wilms' tumor (p.689) Metastases from cancers originating in other organs (p.689) Pyelonephritis (inflammatory renal lesion in the differential of a renal mass) (p.689) Renal abscess (inflammatory renal lesion in the differential of a renal mass) (p.689) CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis - part of standard evaluation of a suspected renal tumor (p.689) Chest radiograph; CT of the chest if metastatic disease is suspected on chest x-ray (p.689) Urine analysis (p.689) MRI - useful for evaluating inferior vena cava when tumor thrombus/invasion is suspected, or when IV contrast for CT is precluded by impaired renal function (p.689) Needle biopsy to confirm histology in small tumors managed with radiographic surveillance before delayed surgery (p.689) Renal cysts (p.689) Angiomyolipoma (p.689) Oncocytoma (p.689) Renal adenoma (p.689) RCC accounts for 90-95% of malignant neoplasms arising from the kidney; the remaining 5-10% are transitional (urothelial) cell carcinomas of the renal pelvis (covered separately in Chap. 91) (p.687-688). The classic triad of hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable abdominal mass is now uncommon; most tumors are detected incidentally on cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI) performed for other reasons (p.688-689). Other presenting features include fever, weight loss, anemia, and a varicocele (p.688). Once called the "internist's tumor" because it was frequently first detected via a paraneoplastic syndrome before modern imaging was common (p.688-689). Clear cell is the predominant histology (~70% of cases) and is found in >80% of patients who develop metastases; it arises from epithelial cells of the proximal tubules (p.688). Any solid renal mass should be considered malignant until proven otherwise; a definitive diagnosis is required (p.689). Most common sites of distant metastasis are the lungs, lymph nodes, liver, bone, and brain; the clinical course can be unpredictable and protracted (p.689). RCC is associated with anecdotal reports of spontaneous regression (p.687). Increasing detection of incidental low-stage tumors has improved 5-year survival and increased use of nephron-sparing surgery (partial nephrectomy) (p.689). Gross hematuria (p.688) Flank or abdominal pain (p.688) Palpable abdominal/flank mass (p.688) Constitutional symptoms: fever, weight loss, anemia (p.688) New varicocele (p.688) Paraneoplastic features: erythrocytosis, hypercalcemia, nonmetastatic hepatic dysfunction (Stauffer's syndrome) (p.688) Relying on the classic triad (hematuria, flank pain, palpable mass) for diagnosis - it is now uncommon, and most tumors present incidentally (p.688-689). Assuming chemotherapy will help - metastatic RCC is refractory to cytotoxic chemotherapy; treatment relies on molecularly targeted agents and checkpoint immunotherapy (p.689). Treating a solid renal mass as benign without proof - any solid renal mass should be considered malignant until proven otherwise (p.689). Despite many candidate biomarkers investigated for predictive value in metastatic RCC, none have been validated for clinical use to date (p.690). Renal vein or inferior vena cava invasion does not preclude surgical resection if no metastases are present (p.689). RCC is a heterogeneous group of tumors. Most cases are sporadic, but familial forms exist. Clear cell RCC (the predominant subtype) is characterized by loss of chromosome 3p as the earliest event, causing loss of heterozygosity for 3p genes including VHL, PBRM1, BAP1, and SETD2. VHL encodes a tumor-suppressor protein that regulates transcription of VEGF and other effectors via ubiquitination of hypoxia-inducible factors (HIF); VHL inactivation upregulates VEGF signaling, promoting tumor angiogenesis and growth and rendering clear cell RCC susceptible to antiangiogenic therapy. Clear cell RCC also arises in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (autosomal dominant, VHL gene on chromosome 3p), which carries a ~70% lifetime risk of clear cell RCC. Papillary subtypes are linked to activating MET mutations or gain of chromosome 7; chromophobe tumors originate from the distal nephron and typically show aneuploidy. Early loss of chromosome 9p confers high risk of early metastatic dissemination and correlates with poor cancer-specific survival (p.687-688). Staging uses the AJCC TNM system. Stage I tumors are <=7 cm and confined to the kidney; stage II are >7 cm and confined to the kidney; stage III extend through the renal capsule but remain within Gerota's fascia, grossly infiltrate the renal vein, or involve regional nodes (N1); stage IV invades adjacent organs or involves nonregional nodes or distant metastases. About 65% present at stage I-II, 15-20% at stage III, and 15-20% at stage IV. Overall 5-year survival is currently ~77% but varies greatly by stage. For metastatic disease, the IMDC risk model uses six factors associated with worse survival (poor performance status, low hemoglobin, high serum calcium, high neutrophils, high platelets, and <1-year interval from diagnosis to systemic treatment). Zero risk factors confer significantly longer median survival (>=5 years) than one to two factors (~4 years) or three to six factors (~3 years) with first-line checkpoint-inhibitor-containing regimens. Projected overall survival for newly diagnosed metastatic disease has tripled over the past 15-20 years (p.688-690). AJCC TNM staging (stages I-IV; Fig. 90-1): Stage I <=7 cm confined to kidney; Stage II >7 cm confined to kidney; Stage III extends through renal capsule within Gerota's fascia, infiltrates renal vein, or N1 nodal involvement; Stage IV invades adjacent organs or has nonregional nodal or distant metastases. For metastatic disease, the IMDC (International Metastatic RCC Database Consortium) risk model stratifies prognosis using six clinical/laboratory factors (p.688-689).

Renal / ureteric colic — Non-contrast CT KUB Urinalysis (haematuria) Fever with obstruction → emergency (infected obstructed system) Ruptured/impending-rupture abdominal aortic aneurysm — abdominal pain radiating to the flank, sacral region, or genitalia should always raise suspicion of a leaking AAA; pain may precede rupture by days (p.154). Acute mesenteric ischemia (pain out of proportion to exam in a vascular patient) (p.154). Other causes of acute lower abdominal pain such as appendicitis, salpingitis, ectopic pregnancy, inguinal hernia, inflammatory bowel disease, and bowel obstruction (p.18 abdominal pain differential table). Ureteric obstruction due to extrinsic malignancy (pelvic/prostatic/gynecologic tumors, retroperitoneal nodes) or post-radiation ureteric fibrosis, which can mimic stone-related obstruction (p.631). Acute pyelonephritis (flank pain, fever, pyuria) (p.1118). Perinephric or renal abscess — flank/abdominal pain, fever in at least half; suspect when pyelonephritis remains febrile after 4-5 days, when urine culture is polymicrobial, when stones are known, or when fever and pyuria coexist with a sterile urine culture (p.1118). Renal ultrasonography — useful to identify hydronephrosis/ureteric and pelvic dilation, though it may be falsely negative early or when ureteric dilation is prevented (e.g., retroperitoneal fibrosis or tumor encasement) (p.383, p.631). Abdominal CT and renal ultrasound are the most useful modalities when perinephric/renal abscess is suspected (p.1118). Urinalysis showing alkaline urine plus a urease-producing organism (e.g., Proteus) may prompt evaluation for urolithiasis, though Harrison notes clinical support for routine action on this finding is lacking (p.1334). Serum calcium / PTH and metabolic workup when an underlying stone-promoting metabolic disorder (e.g., primary hyperparathyroidism) is suspected (p.406). Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm with flank/genital radiation, especially in older patients (p.154). Ureteric obstruction from malignancy or retroperitoneal fibrosis presenting with flank pain (p.631). Renal colic is classic visceral pain from distention of a hollow viscus (the obstructed collecting system/ureter): cramping and intermittent rather than constant (p.551). Stones obstructing urinary flow are the single most important risk factor for perinephric/renal abscess; 20-60% of patients with perinephric abscess have renal stones (p.1118). Urea-splitting organisms (notably Proteus, also other urease producers) alkalinize the urine, favoring precipitation of struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) and carbonate-apatite, which can form staghorn calculi in the renal pelvis (p.1118, p.1334). Struvite stones act as a persistent nidus for recurrent UTI and typically cannot be eradicated by antibiotics alone without removal of the stone (p.1118, p.1334). Stone-associated obstruction is a recognized cause of postrenal azotemia/AKI; because one functioning kidney clears adequately, obstructive renal failure from stones generally requires bilateral ureteric obstruction or unilateral obstruction in a solitary/single functioning kidney (p.383). Nephrolithiasis can be the presenting feature of an underlying metabolic disorder such as primary hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcemia (p.406). Imaging of the upper tracts is advised in any patient with hematuria, a history of calculi, or prior urinary tract problems (p.747). Pain radiating to flank, sacral region, or genitalia in an older patient — exclude a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm (p.154). Rising serum creatinine, oliguria, or anuria — suggests obstruction of a solitary kidney or bilateral obstruction and warrants immediate evaluation (p.383, p.631). Persistent fever after several days of treatment for presumed pyelonephritis, polymicrobial urine, or fever/pyuria with sterile culture — suspect perinephric/renal abscess complicating an obstructing stone (p.1118). Assuming flank pain radiating to the groin is always a stone — in older patients a ruptured/leaking AAA can present identically and is rapidly fatal if missed (p.154). Relying on a negative ultrasound to exclude obstruction; dilation may be absent early or when the ureter cannot distend (p.383). Failing to recognize an infected obstructed system / perinephric abscess in a patient with known stones who stays febrile or has polymicrobial or sterile-but-pyuric urine (p.1118). Overlooking an underlying metabolic cause (e.g., hyperparathyroidism) in a stone former (p.406). Colicky flank pain arises from acute distention of the renal collecting system and ureter when a stone obstructs urinary outflow, producing visceral cramping pain (p.551). Obstruction proximal to the bladder produces hydroureter and renal pelvic dilation (hydronephrosis); if unrelieved this impairs glomerular filtration and causes postrenal azotemia (p.383). In urease-producing infection (e.g., Proteus), hydrolysis of urea to ammonia raises urinary pH; the resulting alkaline environment precipitates struvite and carbonate-apatite, building staghorn calculi that perpetuate infection and obstruction (p.1118, p.1334). Stones also serve as a chronic nidus that promotes recurrent and recalcitrant urinary infection (p.1118). Stone-related obstruction is usually reversible if relieved promptly; urinary tract obstruction accounts for under 5% of acute renal failure and must be excluded early because it is correctable (p.383). When obstruction is complicated by infection (abscess), diagnosis is frequently delayed and mortality is appreciable, though lower than historically (p.1118). Struvite/staghorn stones tend to recur and perpetuate infection unless the stone is removed (p.1118, p.1334).

Renal hypouricaemia (URAT1/GLUT9) — renal hypouricaemia, hereditary renal hypouricaemia, URAT1, SLC22A12, GLUT9, SLC2A9 Fanconi syndrome with urate wasting Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (associated hypouricaemia) Drug-induced hypouricaemia (uricosuric agents) Acquired urate wasting in malignancy or liver disease Xanthine oxidase deficiency (xanthinuria) Dietary or laboratory causes of low measured urate Serum uric acid demonstrating persistent hypouricaemia Fractional excretion of urate showing inappropriately high renal loss Renal function testing during and after episodes of exercise-induced injury Renal ultrasound for urate stones or nephrocalcinosis Urinalysis for haematuria and crystals SLC22A12 and SLC2A9 gene sequencing Caused by loss-of-function variants in the urate transporters URAT1 (SLC22A12) or GLUT9 (SLC2A9), leading to renal urate wasting Defined biochemically by a low serum uric acid with an inappropriately high fractional excretion of urate Most individuals are asymptomatic and identified incidentally on a low serum urate The classic complication is exercise-induced acute kidney injury, typically after intense anaerobic exertion Urate stones and haematuria are the other recognised complications from heavy urinary urate excretion Management is preventive: avoiding strenuous anaerobic exercise, maintaining good hydration, and considering antioxidant strategies around exertion GLUT9 defects tend to cause more profound hypouricaemia and a higher complication risk than URAT1 defects Acute kidney injury following intense exercise, often with loin pain Obstructing urate calculi or gross haematuria Recurrent episodes of exertional renal impairment Dismissing an isolated low serum urate as unimportant and missing the diagnosis Failing to advise against strenuous anaerobic exercise in an at-risk patient Attributing post-exercise acute kidney injury to rhabdomyolysis alone Overlooking urate stones as the cause of haematuria URAT1 and GLUT9 are the principal transporters mediating reabsorption of filtered urate in the proximal tubule; URAT1 exchanges urate across the apical membrane while GLUT9 returns urate to the blood across the basolateral membrane. Loss of either transporter impairs urate reabsorption, so a large fraction of filtered urate is excreted, producing a low serum concentration with a high fractional excretion. The heavy urinary urate load predisposes to crystal formation, stones, and haematuria. Exercise-induced acute kidney injury is thought to arise because urate is an important circulating antioxidant, and its deficiency, combined with exertional generation of reactive oxygen species, promotes renal vasoconstriction and tubular injury. Long-term outlook is usually good with preventive measures, and baseline renal function is typically normal; however, recurrent exercise-induced acute kidney injury or obstructing stones can cause lasting renal damage if unrecognised.

sickle cell trait when a medullary renal mass is found Misclassifying it as clear cell carcinoma and offering ineffective targeted therapy Delaying tissue diagnosis in a rapidly progressive tumour Renal medullary carcinoma arises from the distal collecting duct or calyceal epithelium within the renal medulla. The chronic hypoxic, hypertonic medullary environment in individuals with sickling haemoglobinopathies is thought to promote genomic instability and malignant transformation. Loss of function of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling subunit SMARCB1 (INI1) is a defining molecular event, driving an aggressive, poorly differentiated tumour with early lymphovascular invasion and rapid metastatic spread. The prognosis is generally poor, with most patients presenting with advanced disease and short survival; localised disease treated with surgery combined with systemic chemotherapy offers the best, though still limited, outcomes.

Renal oncocytoma — oncocytoma of kidney Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma Clear cell renal cell carcinoma with eosinophilic features Papillary renal cell carcinoma, eosinophilic type Epithelioid angiomyolipoma Hybrid oncocytic tumour in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome Succinate dehydrogenase-deficient renal tumour CT or MRI to characterise the solid renal mass Renal mass biopsy where the result would change management Immunohistochemistry to help separate it from chromophobe carcinoma Assessment for Birt-Hogg-Dube features when tumours are multiple Surveillance imaging when a conservative approach is chosen A benign renal epithelial tumour arising from the intercalated cells of the collecting duct Usually discovered incidentally as a well-defined solid cortical mass May show a central stellate scar on imaging, though this is neither sensitive nor specific Cannot be reliably distinguished from chromophobe renal cell carcinoma by imaging alone Renal mass biopsy can suggest the diagnosis but sampling and hybrid oncocytic tumours limit certainty Multiple oncocytomas or oncocytosis may occur in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome Because malignancy cannot always be excluded preoperatively, many lesions are still resected Interval growth or new symptoms suggesting the lesion is not benign Imaging features overlapping with malignancy Multiple renal and cutaneous lesions suggesting a hereditary syndrome Any histological atypia raising doubt about the benign diagnosis Relying on a central scar on imaging to diagnose it confidently Assuming biopsy fully excludes chromophobe carcinoma Missing an underlying Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome Over-treating a benign lesion or, conversely, under-treating a misclassified carcinoma Renal oncocytoma is composed of oncocytes, cells packed with mitochondria that give an eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, and is thought to derive from the intercalated cells of the collecting duct. It is a benign neoplasm without metastatic potential, but it shares histological and immunophenotypic features with chromophobe renal cell carcinoma, which complicates diagnosis. Hybrid oncocytic-chromophobe tumours occur, particularly in the setting of Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, reflecting overlap in their cell of origin. Renal oncocytoma is benign with an excellent prognosis and does not metastasise; the main challenge is diagnostic certainty rather than tumour behaviour, and outcomes are excellent whether managed by surveillance or excision.

renal osteodystrophy — CKD-MBD bone disease, uraemic bone disease osteoporosis osteomalacia from other causes primary hyperparathyroidism Paget's disease of bone myeloma or metastatic bone disease aluminium-related bone disease dialysis-related beta-2 microglobulin amyloidosis serum calcium, phosphate, PTH and bone-specific alkaline phosphatase 25-hydroxyvitamin D intact FGF23 radiographs for subperiosteal resorption and rugger-jersey spine DXA for fracture risk bone biopsy with double tetracycline labelling in uncertainty imaging of vascular calcification Renal osteodystrophy is the bone component of chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD), spanning a spectrum from high-turnover to low-turnover bone disease. It is driven by phosphate retention, reduced 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, hypocalcaemia, FGF23 excess and secondary hyperparathyroidism. High-turnover disease (osteitis fibrosa cystica) results from secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism, whereas low-turnover forms are adynamic bone disease and, historically, osteomalacia from aluminium or vitamin D deficiency. Adynamic bone disease is increasingly common with over-suppression of PTH, diabetes and peritoneal dialysis, and carries fracture and vascular calcification risk. Bone histomorphometry using the turnover-mineralisation-volume (TMV) classification after tetracycline labelling is the gold standard; PTH and bone-specific alkaline phosphatase serve as surrogate markers. Management targets phosphate control (dietary restriction and phosphate binders), correction of vitamin D deficiency, active vitamin D analogues and calcimimetics for hyperparathyroidism. Vascular and soft-tissue calcification is a major consequence, so excessive calcium load and over-suppression of turnover should be avoided. Parathyroidectomy is indicated for severe refractory tertiary hyperparathyroidism, calciphylaxis or intractable symptoms. calciphylaxis with painful skin necrosis symptomatic hypercalcaemia from tertiary hyperparathyroidism fragility fractures spontaneous tendon rupture rapidly rising PTH suggesting autonomous gland activity relying on DXA alone, which cannot distinguish high- from low-turnover disease over-suppressing PTH and inducing adynamic bone disease using excessive calcium-containing binders and promoting vascular calcification overlooking aluminium toxicity treating biochemistry without regard to the underlying bone-turnover state As renal function declines, phosphate excretion falls and FGF23 rises to maintain phosphate balance, while reduced functioning renal mass lowers 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity and hence calcitriol. Falling calcitriol and calcium, together with hyperphosphataemia, stimulate parathyroid hyperplasia and PTH secretion (secondary hyperparathyroidism); persistent stimulation can lead to autonomous tertiary hyperparathyroidism. High PTH increases osteoclastic and osteoblastic activity, producing high-turnover osteitis fibrosa cystica with marrow fibrosis. Conversely, over-suppression of PTH, skeletal PTH resistance, aluminium or diabetes can produce low-turnover adynamic bone. The disordered mineral milieu also promotes ectopic vascular and soft-tissue calcification. The disorder is chronic and progresses with declining renal function; it is controllable with CKD-MBD management but is associated with increased fracture risk and cardiovascular mortality.

prevent progression Sepsis from infection with obstruction by necrotic tissue Acute kidney injury, especially with bilateral papillary involvement Massive haematuria Rapid deterioration in a solitary functioning kidney Mistaking a sloughed papilla for a calculus on imaging Failing to look for multiple coexisting causes, such as diabetes together with analgesics Overlooking analgesic overuse in the drug history Missing an infected obstructed system caused by necrotic tissue The renal papilla lies at the tip of the medulla and is perfused by the vasa recta in a region of relatively low oxygen tension, making it highly susceptible to ischaemia. Conditions that reduce medullary blood flow or heighten its metabolic vulnerability, such as diabetic microvascular disease, analgesic-induced vascular injury, sickling of red cells within the hypertonic medulla, infection with oedema and raised intrarenal pressure, and obstruction, cause coagulative necrosis of one or more papillae. The necrotic tissue may calcify in situ or detach and pass down the ureter, where it can obstruct and mimic a calculus. Outcome depends on the number of papillae affected and control of the underlying causes; an isolated event with a single reversible cause may have little lasting impact, whereas recurrent necrosis, as in combined diabetes and analgesic use, can cause progressive chronic kidney disease.

Renal tubular acidosis — RTA, distal RTA, type 1 RTA, proximal RTA, type 2 RTA, type 4 RTA, hyperkalaemic RTA Diarrhoea and other gastrointestinal bicarbonate losses Early or advanced chronic kidney disease with reduced ammoniagenesis Ureteral diversion into bowel Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor or other drug effect Dilutional acidosis from rapid saline infusion Addison disease or hypoaldosteronism from other causes Serum electrolytes with calculation of the plasma anion gap to confirm a normal-gap acidosis Simultaneous urine pH and urine electrolytes to calculate the urine anion gap and assess ammonium excretion Serum potassium to help classify the subtype (low in types 1 and 2, high in type 4) Urinalysis for glycosuria, proteinuria, and evidence of proximal tubular dysfunction Renal imaging for nephrocalcinosis or stones, especially in distal RTA Plasma renin and aldosterone when a hyperkalaemic (type 4) picture is suspected RTA produces a normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis despite relatively preserved glomerular filtration, distinguishing it from the high anion gap acidosis of advanced renal failure Type 1 (distal) RTA reflects failure of the distal nephron to secrete hydrogen ions, so urine pH stays inappropriately high (typically above 5.5) in the face of systemic acidosis, and is usually accompanied by hypokalaemia Type 2 (proximal) RTA arises from impaired proximal reabsorption of bicarbonate; once serum bicarbonate falls below the lowered threshold, distal acidification can still generate acidic urine Type 4 RTA is a hyperkalaemic form driven by aldosterone deficiency or resistance, most commonly seen in diabetic kidney disease, and impairs both acid and potassium excretion Nephrocalcinosis and calcium-containing stones are characteristic of distal RTA because of hypercalciuria, low urinary citrate, and alkaline urine The urine anion gap is a useful bedside tool: a positive (or inappropriately non-negative) value in the presence of acidosis points to impaired renal ammonium excretion rather than gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss Proximal RTA frequently coexists with generalised proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome), so glycosuria, phosphaturia, and aminoaciduria should be sought Management principles centre on alkali replacement; distal RTA usually needs modest alkali plus potassium, while proximal RTA requires larger alkali loads and often potassium supplementation because bicarbonate therapy worsens kaliuresis Severe hypokalaemia causing muscle weakness, paralysis, or arrhythmia in distal or proximal RTA Dangerous hyperkalaemia in type 4 RTA, particularly with concurrent potassium-retaining drugs Growth failure, rickets, or osteomalacia in children and adults from chronic acidosis and phosphate loss Recurrent stones or progressive nephrocalcinosis threatening renal function Attributing a normal anion gap acidosis to diarrhoea without checking the urine anion gap or urine ammonium Giving bicarbonate in proximal RTA without adequate potassium, precipitating worsening hypokalaemia Overlooking type 4 RTA as a cause of unexplained hyperkalaemia in a diabetic patient Failing to search for Fanconi syndrome features when proximal RTA is diagnosed Assuming a high urine pH always indicates distal RTA without excluding urinary infection with urea-splitting organisms The renal tubular acidoses are disorders in which the kidney fails to appropriately acidify the urine or reclaim filtered bicarbonate despite normal or near-normal glomerular filtration, producing a hyperchloraemic (normal anion gap) metabolic acidosis. In distal (type 1) RTA the collecting duct cannot secrete hydrogen ions effectively, so net acid excretion falls and the urine cannot be maximally acidified. In proximal (type 2) RTA the proximal tubule cannot reabsorb the filtered bicarbonate load, leading to bicarbonate wasting until serum levels reach a new lower steady state. Type 4 RTA results from deficient or ineffective aldosterone action, reducing distal sodium reabsorption and potassium and hydrogen secretion, which produces hyperkalaemia and a mild acidosis. Potassium behaves differently across subtypes: distal and proximal forms tend toward hypokalaemia, whereas the aldosterone-related form causes hyperkalaemia. With appropriate alkali and electrolyte correction most patients do well, and complications such as bone disease, stones, and growth impairment can be prevented or limited. Outcome depends heavily on the underlying cause; type 4 RTA linked to diabetic nephropathy tends to progress with the primary kidney disease, while inherited distal RTA requires lifelong therapy.

renal venous renin sampling is now rarely used due to false results Kidney biopsy: confirms atheroembolic disease (cholesterol-crystal cleft in microvessels) Renal parenchymal disease causing secondary hypertension Primary aldosteronism Hypertensive nephrosclerosis Cholesterol atheroembolism mimicking vasculitis (livedo reticularis, eosinophilia, elevated ESR, hypocomplementemia) Renovascular disease is a specifically treatable 'secondary' cause of hypertension because restoring renal perfusion pressure can reverse the pressor pathways it activates (Harrison 22e p.2150). Roughly 90% of renovascular hypertension is due to atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis (ARAS), which is typically unilateral with a discrete lesion near the renal artery origin in older patients with a broader atherosclerotic risk profile (Harrison 22e p.2139, 2150). Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) accounts for a minority of cases and characteristically affects younger patients aged ~15 to 50, predominantly women; lesions are more diffuse with an irregular 'sawtooth/string-of-beads' appearance located in the distal renal artery (Harrison 22e p.2139, 2150). FMD should be suspected with abrupt-onset hypertension (especially in young women) or resistant/recently worsening hypertension; ARAS should be suspected in older patients with other ASCVD evidence or otherwise unexplained decline in kidney function (Harrison 22e p.2139). Critical stenosis (usually >70 to 80% luminal obstruction) reduces perfusion pressure, activating the renin-angiotensin system, reducing sodium excretion, and engaging sympathetic pathways (Harrison 22e p.2150). Early renovascular hypertension is angiotensin-dependent and marked by widely varying pressures, loss of circadian BP rhythm, and accelerated target organ injury including left ventricular hypertrophy and renal fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2150). An abdominal renal artery bruit, or carotid/femoral bruits, may be audible and supports the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2139, 2150). When large-vessel disease primarily threatens kidney function the entity is termed ischemic nephropathy; gradually reduced flow can leave function reduced but stable for years, whereas advanced disease produces cortical hypoperfusion and overt tissue hypoxia (Harrison 22e p.2150). ARAS commonly coexists with preexisting small-vessel disease from hypertension, aging, and diabetes; nearly 85% of patients considered for revascularization already have stage 3 to 5 CKD (eGFR <60) (Harrison 22e p.2150). The presence of ARAS independently predicts cardiovascular morbidity and mortality regardless of whether revascularization is performed (Harrison 22e p.2150). Atheroembolic renal disease most often follows arterial procedures (e.g., coronary angiography), with cholesterol crystals lodging in downstream microvessels; manifestations typically appear 1 to 14 days after the inciting event (Harrison 22e p.2152). Thromboembolic renal disease can cause flank pain, fever, leukocytosis, nausea and vomiting, and a transient extreme rise in LDH if infarction occurs; bilateral involvement causes precipitous functional decline and reduced urine output (Harrison 22e p.2153). Rapidly progressive or resistant hypertension failing optimal medical therapy Progressive decline in GFR during BP treatment, or decline associated with ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy Recurrent flash pulmonary edema / congestive heart failure not explained by LV dysfunction Abrupt-onset hypertension in a young woman (suggests FMD) or worsening kidney function in an older patient with ASCVD (suggests ARAS) New worsening hypertension and deteriorating renal function days after an arterial/angiographic procedure (atheroembolism), possibly reaching a malignant phase Acute flank pain with fever and markedly elevated LDH suggesting renal infarction; anuria with bilateral acute occlusion Plasma renin activity is transient and influenced by drugs/sodium/timing, so it does not reliably predict response to revascularization; over-reliance on it is misleading (Harrison 22e p.2151). Multiple randomized trials show no compelling benefit of revascularization over optimal medical therapy for moderate ARAS regarding BP or renal function over 3 to 5 years; revascularization should not be assumed beneficial just because flow is restored (Harrison 22e p.2139, 2150). Revascularization rarely normalizes BP alone because most patients have preexisting hypertension and need continued drug therapy (Harrison 22e p.2150). Atheroembolic complications of revascularization can be catastrophic and accelerate the very hypertension and renal failure the procedure intended to prevent (Harrison 22e p.2151). Atheroembolic renal disease is frequently underdiagnosed and is often a diagnosis of exclusion; systemic features (fever, abdominal pain, weight loss) are present in fewer than half of patients (Harrison 22e p.2152). Hypertensive nephrosclerosis is often assigned without specific etiologic proof; nephrosclerosis changes also occur with aging, dyslipidemia, and glucose intolerance with only modest association with BP, and antihypertensive therapy does not alter its course (Harrison 22e p.2154). The renal cortex receives high arteriolar flow in excess of its metabolic needs for filtration, while the postglomerular medullary circulation has lower flow yet high oxygen consumption, leaving the deeper medulla near the margin of hypoxemia. Large-vessel occlusive disease (atherosclerosis, fibromuscular dysplasia, dissection, extrinsic compression, aortic stent graft) reduces perfusion pressure to the kidney. Once stenosis is hemodynamically significant (typically >70 to 80% lumen occlusion), the drop in perfusion pressure activates the renin-angiotensin system, reduces sodium excretion, and stimulates sympathetic adrenergic pathways, producing angiotensin-dependent systemic hypertension. Sustained pressure and ischemia drive endothelial injury (reflected by increased urinary albumin excretion), microvascular proliferation in early atherosclerosis and later microvascular rarefaction in chronic ischemia, with consequent tubulointerstitial fibrosis and loss of function. In atheroembolic disease, cholesterol crystals from fractured plaque occlude microvessels leaving a characteristic 'cleft' on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.2150-2152). FMD patients are usually younger with otherwise normal vessels and long life expectancy and often respond well to angioplasty; FMD seldom threatens kidney function. Untreated ARAS progresses in nearly 50% of cases over 5 years, sometimes to total occlusion, though intensive BP and statin therapy slow progression. After endovascular stenting renal function recovers in only ~25%, is unchanged in ~50%, and deteriorates in the remainder. ARAS independently predicts cardiovascular events and death. Atheroembolic renal disease carries an ominous prognosis with 1-year mortality exceeding 38%; untreated malignant hypertension historically had 1-year mortality over 90% (and >50% at 6 to 12 months with target organ injury), but current 5-year survival exceeds 50% with effective antihypertensive therapy (Harrison 22e p.2150-2154). No formal staging is given; severity is gauged by degree of luminal stenosis (hemodynamically critical at >70 to 80% occlusion), CKD stage (most revascularization candidates are stage 3 to 5 with eGFR <60), and clinical syndrome (stable medically managed disease versus rapidly progressive/resistant disease). Table 289-2 outlines clinical factors favoring revascularization plus medical therapy (progressive GFR decline, medical failure of BP control, GFR decline with ACEi/ARB, recurrent unexplained heart failure) versus medical therapy with surveillance (controlled BP with stable function, stable non-progressing stenosis, advanced age/limited life expectancy, high atheroembolic risk, concomitant parenchymal disease with proteinuria) (Harrison 22e p.2152).

Resistance to thyroid hormone — RTH, RTH-beta, THRB mutation, thyroid hormone resistance, Refetoff syndrome Thyroid-stimulating-hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma Assay interference or heterophile antibodies producing spurious results Familial dysalbuminaemic hyperthyroxinaemia Ordinary primary hyperthyroidism MCT8 transporter defect Non-thyroidal illness affecting thyroid function tests Repeat and confirmatory thyroid function tests including free thyroxine, free triiodothyronine, and thyroid-stimulating hormone THRB genetic testing and family screening Alpha-subunit measurement and dynamic testing to exclude a pituitary adenoma Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging when an adenoma is suspected Assay interference checks such as alternative platforms or dilution studies Markers of peripheral thyroid hormone action such as sex hormone binding globulin Characterised by reduced tissue responsiveness to thyroid hormone, most commonly from mutations in the beta thyroid hormone receptor (THRB) The paradoxical biochemistry is a raised free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine with a thyroid-stimulating hormone that is not suppressed (normal or elevated) Usually autosomal dominant, so a family history of similar abnormal thyroid function tests is common and very helpful Clinical features are variable and mixed, because tissues differ in their receptor dependence; goitre is common, and tachycardia can occur where beta-receptor-independent tissues remain responsive Often discovered incidentally when thyroid function tests do not fit the usual patterns of hyper- or hypothyroidism Most patients are clinically euthyroid overall and require no thyroid-directed treatment, as elevated hormone levels compensate for the resistance The key differential is a thyroid-stimulating-hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma, which produces a similar biochemical picture but is a distinct disorder Features suggesting a thyroid-stimulating-hormone-secreting adenoma such as a pituitary mass or visual field defect Significant symptomatic tachycardia or arrhythmia Inappropriate antithyroid or ablative treatment causing iatrogenic hypothyroidism Severe or homozygous disease presenting in childhood with growth and developmental problems Misreading the raised hormones with unsuppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone as ordinary hyperthyroidism and prescribing antithyroid drugs Failing to distinguish the condition from a thyroid-stimulating-hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma Ablating the thyroid and creating lifelong management difficulty Not checking family members with similar unexplained results Resistance to thyroid hormone usually results from dominant-negative mutations in the beta isoform of the thyroid hormone receptor. The mutant receptor binds hormone poorly yet still occupies target genes, interfering with normal receptor function. Because the pituitary and hypothalamus rely on the beta receptor for feedback, they sense hormone inadequately and continue to drive thyroid-stimulating hormone despite high circulating thyroid hormone. Peripheral tissues vary in their reliance on the affected receptor, so the same person can show features of both hormone excess and deficiency depending on the tissue. Most people with resistance to thyroid hormone lead normal lives without specific treatment because compensatory high hormone levels maintain a euthyroid state; the main harm comes from misdiagnosis leading to unnecessary antithyroid therapy or thyroid ablation.

Respiratory acidosis — respiratory acidosis, hypercapnic acidosis, CO2 retention, ventilatory failure Metabolic alkalosis with compensatory hypoventilation Mixed acid-base disorders Acute versus chronic respiratory acidosis differentiation Causes of acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (opioid overdose, acute severe asthma, COPD exacerbation) Neuromuscular disorders such as Guillain-Barre syndrome or myasthenic crisis Arterial blood gas analysis to confirm hypercapnia and assess pH and bicarbonate Assessment of the expected compensation to identify mixed disorders Chest imaging and pulmonary function or bedside respiratory assessment to find the cause Investigations for central, neuromuscular, or airway causes as clinically directed Serum electrolytes to evaluate accompanying metabolic derangements Respiratory acidosis results from alveolar hypoventilation, causing carbon dioxide retention and a fall in arterial pH Arterial blood gases show a raised PaCO2 with low pH; bicarbonate rises as compensation develops Acute and chronic forms are distinguished by the degree of renal (metabolic) compensation, with bicarbonate rising modestly in acute and substantially in chronic disease Clinical features range from headache, drowsiness, and confusion to asterixis and, in severe hypercapnia, coma (CO2 narcosis) Causes include central respiratory depression (drugs, CNS lesions), neuromuscular weakness, airway obstruction, and severe parenchymal or chest wall disease Management targets the underlying cause and restoration of adequate alveolar ventilation, sometimes with non-invasive or invasive ventilation In chronic CO2 retainers, excessive supplemental oxygen can blunt respiratory drive and worsen hypercapnia, so oxygen is titrated carefully Correcting hypercapnia too rapidly risks post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis if the compensatory bicarbonate is not accounted for Depressed conscious level or CO2 narcosis indicating severe hypercapnia Rapidly rising PaCO2 with falling pH suggesting impending ventilatory failure Signs of exhaustion in a patient with increased work of breathing Severe acidaemia causing haemodynamic instability Giving high-flow oxygen indiscriminately to a chronic CO2 retainer and precipitating worsening hypercapnia Failing to recognise acute-on-chronic decompensation by misreading compensation Missing a coexisting metabolic disorder in a mixed acid-base picture Delaying ventilatory support in a tiring patient with rising PaCO2 Carbon dioxide is generated by metabolism and normally excreted by alveolar ventilation, keeping PaCO2 constant. When ventilation is inadequate relative to CO2 production, PaCO2 rises; through the carbonic acid equilibrium this increases hydrogen ion concentration and lowers pH. The body compensates in two phases: acutely, tissue and blood buffers slightly raise bicarbonate, while over days the kidneys enhance hydrogen ion excretion and bicarbonate reabsorption, producing a larger rise in bicarbonate that returns pH toward normal in chronic respiratory acidosis. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause and its reversibility; acute respiratory acidosis from a rapidly correctable insult often resolves fully, whereas chronic hypercapnia reflects advanced or progressive disease, and acute-on-chronic decompensation can be life-threatening without prompt ventilatory support.

Respiratory bronchiolitis interstitial lung disease — RB-ILD, Smoking-related interstitial lung disease Desquamative interstitial pneumonia Subacute hypersensitivity pneumonitis Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with emphysema Early or subclinical idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis Detailed smoking history and HRCT thorax Pulmonary function tests, which may show a mixed obstructive-restrictive pattern with reduced transfer factor Bronchoalveolar lavage demonstrating pigmented macrophages Exclusion of hypersensitivity pneumonitis with precipitins and exposure history Surgical lung biopsy only if the diagnosis remains unclear after multidisciplinary review Six-minute walk test with oximetry A smoking-related interstitial lung disease occurring almost exclusively in current or heavy former smokers. Forms part of a spectrum with desquamative interstitial pneumonia; asymptomatic respiratory bronchiolitis is a common incidental finding in smokers, whereas RB-ILD is the symptomatic form. Presents with mild breathlessness and cough; crackles may be present but finger clubbing is uncommon. HRCT shows centrilobular nodules, patchy ground-glass opacity and bronchial wall thickening, often upper-zone predominant, together with centrilobular emphysema. Histology demonstrates pigmented 'smoker's' macrophages accumulating within respiratory bronchioles and surrounding alveoli with mild peribronchiolar fibrosis. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows characteristic golden-brown pigmented macrophages. Smoking cessation is the cornerstone of management and may lead to stabilisation or improvement. Corticosteroids are reserved for progressive disease, where the supporting evidence is limited. Progressive decline despite smoking cessation, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Development of honeycombing suggesting an alternative fibrotic interstitial lung disease Significant resting or exertional hypoxaemia Radiological features raising concern for Langerhans cell histiocytosis or malignancy Diagnosing RB-ILD in a lifelong non-smoker without reconsidering the diagnosis Not prioritising smoking cessation as the primary therapy Confusing incidental respiratory bronchiolitis with symptomatic RB-ILD Overtreating with immunosuppression when smoking cessation would suffice Chronic inhalation of cigarette smoke provokes accumulation of pigment-laden macrophages within respiratory bronchioles and adjacent alveolar spaces, accompanied by mild bronchiolocentric inflammation and fibrosis. This bronchiolocentric distribution and the strong causal link to tobacco distinguish RB-ILD from the more diffuse alveolar macrophage filling of desquamative interstitial pneumonia, with which it overlaps. The outlook is generally favourable, particularly with smoking cessation; most patients stabilise, although some have persistent symptoms and a minority progress.

and venous insufficiency Positional discomfort and habitual foot tapping Periodic limb movement disorder without the sensory urge Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation to assess iron status Renal which can be documented on polysomnography Iron deficiency is a key and treatable contributor, so serum ferritin and transferrin saturation should be checked even when the haemoglobin is normal Common suggesting a neuropathy or radiculopathy rather than primary RLS Augmentation on dopaminergic therapy with earlier, more intense, and spreading symptoms Symptoms secondary to unrecognised chronic kidney disease or severe iron deficiency Severe sleep deprivation with significant mood disturbance or impaired daytime function Failing to check and correct iron status, missing a readily treatable driver of symptoms Overlooking culprit medications that provoke or worsen the syndrome Relying on long-term dopamine agonists and precipitating augmentation Confusing the condition with akathisia, cramps, or neuropathy and treating the wrong problem Restless legs syndrome is a sensorimotor disorder linked to dysfunction of central dopaminergic transmission and to abnormal brain iron handling, since iron is a cofactor for dopamine synthesis. Reduced iron availability within the central nervous system, even with normal peripheral stores, is thought to impair dopaminergic signalling in circuits including the spinal cord and diencephalon. There is a strong genetic contribution, and it may be primary or secondary to iron deficiency, uraemia, pregnancy, or neuropathy. Primary restless legs syndrome is usually a chronic condition that can fluctuate over time, often worsening with age. Secondary forms may resolve when the underlying cause, such as iron deficiency or pregnancy, is corrected. Most patients achieve good symptom control with appropriate treatment, though augmentation can complicate long-term dopaminergic therapy.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy — RCM, restrictive heart disease, infiltrative cardiomyopathy Constrictive pericarditis Cardiac amyloidosis and other infiltrative diseases Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in a non-dilated phase Hypertensive heart disease with severe diastolic dysfunction Right heart failure from other causes Pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology Echocardiography demonstrating restrictive filling with biatrial enlargement and preserved cavity size Cardiac MRI for tissue characterisation and to help identify infiltration Specific evaluation for amyloidosis, including relevant imaging, laboratory testing, and sometimes biopsy Invasive haemodynamic study when distinguishing restriction from constriction is difficult 12-lead ECG, which may show low voltages or conduction disease in infiltrative disease Endomyocardial biopsy in selected cases to establish the underlying cause Restrictive cardiomyopathy is characterised by stiff, non-compliant ventricles causing impaired diastolic filling with preserved or near-preserved systolic function and normal or reduced ventricular cavity size early on The dominant physiology is diastolic dysfunction with raised filling pressures, so patients present with signs of both right- and left-sided heart failure, prominent among them systemic venous congestion Causes include infiltrative diseases such as amyloidosis, storage disorders, endomyocardial fibrosis, and post-radiation or idiopathic fibrosis; amyloidosis is a leading cause to actively exclude A key clinical challenge is distinguishing restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis, because the latter is potentially curable with surgery Atrial enlargement is characteristic because the atria bear the burden of filling stiff ventricles, predisposing to atrial fibrillation Multimodality imaging including echocardiography and cardiac MRI, sometimes with biopsy or specific tests for amyloid, is used to establish the cause Management is largely directed at the underlying cause and at cautious control of congestion, since these patients are sensitive to changes in filling Because the ventricles depend on adequate preload, excessive diuresis or loss of atrial contribution can precipitate a marked fall in output Progressive heart failure refractory to therapy indicating advanced disease Haemodynamic deterioration after aggressive diuresis due to preload dependence Conduction disease or arrhythmia, particularly with infiltrative causes such as amyloidosis, raising the risk of syncope or sudden death Features suggesting cardiac amyloidosis, which carries specific prognostic and treatment implications Failing to distinguish restrictive cardiomyopathy from potentially curable constrictive pericarditis Missing cardiac amyloidosis as an underlying cause Over-diuresing a preload-dependent ventricle and precipitating a fall in output Attributing raised filling pressures to systolic failure when systolic function is preserved In restrictive cardiomyopathy the ventricular myocardium or endocardium becomes abnormally stiff, either from infiltration by abnormal material (as in amyloidosis or storage disease), fibrosis (as in endomyocardial fibrosis or after radiation), or idiopathic processes. The stiff ventricle resists filling, so filling pressures rise sharply for only small increases in volume and most filling occurs rapidly in early diastole. This raises atrial and venous pressures, dilates the atria, and produces pulmonary and systemic congestion while systolic ejection is initially preserved. As disease advances, systolic function and conduction may also be affected, and the physiology can closely mimic constrictive pericarditis. Prognosis is largely determined by the underlying cause; idiopathic and infiltrative forms, especially advanced cardiac amyloidosis, often carry a poor outlook, whereas identifying a treatable cause or distinguishing curable constrictive pericarditis can markedly change the trajectory.

Restrictive dermopathy — ZMPSTE24, LMNA, lethal restrictive dermopathy, tight skin contracture syndrome Neu-Laxova syndrome Harlequin ichthyosis Congenital ichthyoses with taut skin Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita Stiff skin syndrome Other perinatally lethal contracture syndromes Molecular testing of ZMPSTE24 and LMNA Skin biopsy with histology showing a thin dermis and abnormal epidermis Chest imaging for pulmonary hypoplasia Detailed dysmorphology examination and clinical photography Placental and fetal assessment where a pregnancy history is available Genetic counselling and consideration of prenatal testing in future pregnancies A rare, typically lethal neonatal genodermatosis defined by rigid, taut, thin skin that severely restricts movement The tight skin causes a fixed facial expression, small pinched nose, open O-shaped mouth, micrognathia and multiple joint contractures Pulmonary hypoplasia and respiratory insufficiency from restricted chest movement are the usual cause of early death, often within days of birth Most cases result from loss-of-function variants in ZMPSTE24, the enzyme that processes prelamin A into mature lamin A; some arise from LMNA variants There is often a history of polyhydramnios, reduced fetal movements and premature birth Skin may show erosions and a characteristic thin, tightly adherent epidermis on histology Management is almost always palliative given the near-uniform lethality; genetic counselling is central for recurrence risk Progressive respiratory failure from pulmonary hypoplasia and restricted chest expansion Severe feeding difficulty from restricted facial and oral movement Skin erosions with risk of infection and fluid loss Any presentation is inherently critical given the near-uniform neonatal lethality Mistaking the taut skin for a severe congenital ichthyosis such as harlequin ichthyosis Pursuing aggressive intervention when the condition is near-uniformly lethal, rather than focusing on palliation Overlooking the laminopathy basis and its implications for recurrence-risk counselling Failing to arrange confirmatory genetics to guide future pregnancies Restrictive dermopathy is a laminopathy caused by failure of normal maturation of the nuclear lamina protein lamin A. Loss-of-function variants in ZMPSTE24, the zinc metalloprotease that cleaves the farnesylated prelamin A precursor, or certain LMNA variants, lead to accumulation of abnormal farnesylated prelamin A. This toxic precursor distorts nuclear architecture and impairs the function of skin and connective tissue cells, producing the rigid, hypoplastic dermis, taut skin, joint contractures and secondary pulmonary hypoplasia that characterise the lethal phenotype. The prognosis is extremely poor: restrictive dermopathy is almost always lethal in the neonatal period, usually from respiratory insufficiency, so care is generally palliative and directed at comfort and family support.

Retained placenta — retained placenta, adherent placenta Placenta adherens due to uterine atony Trapped or incarcerated placenta behind a constriction ring or closed cervix Placenta accreta, increta, or percreta A succenturiate lobe left in situ Uterine inversion presenting as failure to deliver the placenta A constriction ring or hourglass contraction from mismanaged third stage Clinical assessment of blood loss, uterine tone, and maternal haemodynamic status Full blood count and group-and-save or crossmatch, with coagulation studies if bleeding is heavy Examination of the delivered placenta and membranes for completeness Bedside ultrasound to assess for retained tissue and features suggesting abnormal placentation Review of antenatal imaging for placenta accreta spectrum when the placenta will not separate over a scar Observations and inflammatory markers if delayed retention presents with suspected endometritis Retained placenta is failure to deliver the placenta within a defined interval after birth, commonly thirty minutes with active management of the third stage or up to an hour with physiological management Three broad mechanisms are recognised: a separated placenta trapped behind a closed cervix (trapped placenta), a placenta that fails to separate because of inadequate uterine contraction (placenta adherens), and a morbidly adherent placenta of the accreta spectrum It is an important cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage, both because the uterus cannot contract effectively around retained tissue and because partial separation opens maternal sinuses Risk factors include a previous retained placenta, previous uterine surgery or curettage, preterm delivery, placenta praevia, and grand multiparity; abnormal placentation should be considered when the uterus is scarred Initial steps are to ensure the bladder is empty, encourage breastfeeding or nipple stimulation, give a uterotonic, and attempt controlled cord traction; injudicious traction risks cord avulsion or uterine inversion If these measures fail, manual removal of the placenta under regional or general anaesthesia is required, with antibiotic cover and careful assessment for completeness If the placenta cannot be separated and morbid adherence is evident, forced removal must be avoided; senior help and preparation for major haemorrhage and possible hysterectomy are needed After delivery of the placenta, examine it for completeness, since retained fragments can cause ongoing or secondary haemorrhage and endometritis Heavy or continuing postpartum bleeding with the placenta still undelivered Signs of hypovolaemic shock Inability to separate the placenta with suspicion of accreta spectrum Uterine inversion, with sudden pain, haemorrhage, and a mass at or beyond the introitus Fever and offensive lochia suggesting infected retained tissue Applying vigorous cord traction against a poorly contracted uterus, causing cord avulsion or uterine inversion Failing to empty the bladder, which impedes uterine contraction and placental delivery Persisting with attempts at manual removal when placenta accreta is evident Not inspecting the placenta for missing cotyledons or a succenturiate lobe Underestimating cumulative blood loss and delaying escalation Normal placental separation depends on brisk contraction and retraction of the myometrium after delivery of the fetus, which shears the placenta from the decidua basalis along the plane of the spongy layer and then closes off the underlying spiral arteries. Retention arises when this sequence fails. In placenta adherens, poor and often localised myometrial contraction prevents shearing, so the placenta remains attached. In a trapped placenta, the placenta separates but the cervix contracts down before expulsion, imprisoning it. In placenta accreta spectrum, deficient decidua, typically over a scar, allows chorionic villi to invade the myometrium so that no cleavage plane exists. Because retained tissue prevents the uterus from contracting fully, the exposed vascular placental bed continues to bleed, linking retained placenta closely with postpartum haemorrhage. With prompt uterotonics, bladder emptying, and timely manual removal, most cases resolve without lasting harm; delay increases the risk of major haemorrhage, and cases complicated by placenta accreta spectrum carry a significant risk of massive haemorrhage and hysterectomy.

neutropenia (e.g. ELANE, HAX1) Kostmann syndrome Cartilage-hair hypoplasia Congenital infection with marrow suppression Other mitochondrial disorders affecting haematopoiesis Full blood count and loss-of-function variants Represents the most severe form of severe combined immunodeficiency, presenting in the neonatal period with overwhelming infection and failure to thrive The defining combined loss of T and NK cells with impaired B-cell function alongside the agranulocytosis Sensorineural hearing loss is a distinctive extra-haematopoietic feature that separates it from other forms of SCID The bone marrow shows a maturation arrest of the granulocytic lineage with preserved erythroid and megakaryocytic lines Inheritance is autosomal recessive, from biallelic loss-of-function stem cell transplantation is the only curative treatment and correction of the immune defect does not reverse the deafness Neonatal sepsis or overwhelming infection in an infant with agranulocytosis and lymphopenia Failure of neutrophil count to respond to granulocyte colony-stimulating factor Signs of graft-versus-host disease after non-irradiated blood products Complications of live vaccine administration in an undiagnosed infant Progressive failure to thrive with intractable infection Mistaking the agranulocytosis for isolated severe congenital neutropenia and overlooking the lymphopenia Giving live vaccines or non-irradiated blood products before the diagnosis is recognised Failing to test hearing and missing the diagnostic association with deafness Delaying referral for transplantation while pursuing infection control alone Assuming successful transplantation will also correct the hearing loss AK2 (adenylate kinase 2) is a mitochondrial enzyme that maintains the balance of adenine nucleotides in the intermembrane space and supports the energy metabolism needed for cell differentiation. Its absence causes energy failure and increased apoptosis in the leucocyte precursors that are especially dependent on this pathway, producing a maturation arrest of both the granulocytic and lymphoid lineages while erythroid and megakaryocytic development is largely spared. The consequence is congenital agranulocytosis combined with severe lymphopenia and defective adaptive immunity. AK2 is also required within the developing inner ear, which accounts for the associated sensorineural deafness. Reticular dysgenesis is uniformly fatal in early infancy without treatment; allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, ideally performed early, can be curative for the immune and myeloid defect, although the sensorineural deafness persists.

Retinal detachment — RD, detached retina, rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, RRD, tractional retinal detachment, exudative retinal detachment Posterior vitreous detachment without tear Vitreous haemorrhage Retinoschisis Choroidal detachment or mass Central serous chorioretinopathy Migraine with visual aura Dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral indentation to locate breaks Slit-lamp examination and assessment for pigment cells in the anterior vitreous (tobacco dust) B-scan ultrasonography when the view is obscured by haemorrhage or cataract Optical coherence tomography to determine macular status Assessment of visual acuity and for a relative afferent pupillary defect Classic warning symptoms are sudden floaters and flashing lights (photopsia) followed by a curtain or shadow spreading across the field of vision Central vision is preserved until the macula detaches ('macula-on' versus 'macula-off'), which is the key prognostic and timing factor The commonest type is rhegmatogenous, caused by a retinal tear that lets fluid pass under the retina; tractional and exudative types have different mechanisms Risk factors include high myopia, previous cataract surgery, ocular trauma, lattice degeneration, and a detachment in the fellow eye Fundoscopy shows an elevated, mobile, often corrugated grey retina; a relative afferent pupillary defect may be present in large detachments Treatment is surgical (laser/cryo for tears, pneumatic retinopexy, scleral buckle, or vitrectomy) and is prioritised urgently when the macula is still attached A posterior vitreous detachment with a fresh tear can be treated with prophylactic retinopexy to prevent progression Sudden new floaters and flashes with a visual field defect — sight-threatening, refer urgently A 'macula-on' detachment is a surgical emergency because prompt repair preserves central vision Rapidly enlarging shadow or curtain indicating extension toward the macula New symptoms in the fellow eye of a patient with previous detachment Dismissing floaters and flashes without a dilated peripheral retinal examination Delaying referral in a macula-on detachment and allowing the macula to detach Missing a small peripheral break because the retina was not examined with indentation Attributing symptoms to migraine or vitreous floaters without excluding a tear In rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, a full-thickness retinal break (usually from vitreous traction as the vitreous separates with age) allows liquefied vitreous to track through the tear into the potential space between the neurosensory retina and the retinal pigment epithelium, lifting the photoreceptor layer off its blood supply. Tractional detachment occurs when contracting fibrovascular membranes (as in proliferative diabetic retinopathy) pull the retina forward, and exudative detachment when fluid accumulates beneath an intact retina from inflammatory, vascular, or neoplastic processes. Separated photoreceptors become ischaemic and, if not reattached, degenerate. Anatomical reattachment is achieved in most cases with modern surgery, but final visual outcome depends heavily on whether the macula was detached and for how long before repair.

Some macroaneurysms undergo spontaneous thrombosis and sclerosis, involuting without treatment. The outlook is often favourable, as many macroaneurysms involute spontaneously; the visual outcome depends chiefly on whether the fovea is involved by exudate or haemorrhage.

caused by mutations in numerous genes essential to photoreceptor and retinal pigment epithelium function. Progressive apoptosis of rod photoreceptors, followed later by cones, leads to loss of peripheral and night vision that spreads centrally over time. Degenerating photoreceptors and migration of retinal pigment epithelial cells into the retina produce the characteristic bone-spicule pigmentation, while secondary changes cause arteriolar narrowing and optic disc pallor. The underlying genetic defect determines the pattern of inheritance and the rate of progression. Retinitis pigmentosa is generally slowly progressive, and although many patients retain useful central vision into adulthood, most eventually experience severe peripheral field loss; prognosis varies with genotype and inheritance pattern.

Retinoblastoma — RB, retinal blastoma Coats disease Persistent fetal vasculature (persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous) Toxocariasis (ocular larva migrans) Retinopathy of prematurity Congenital cataract Endophthalmitis or other causes of leukocoria Detailed dilated fundus examination under anaesthesia by an ocular oncology team Ocular ultrasound and MRI of the orbits and brain RB1 genetic testing and genetic counselling Examination of the fellow eye and screening of at-risk relatives Evaluation for metastatic or trilateral (pineal) disease when clinically indicated The most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, usually diagnosed before 5 years of age. Leukocoria (a white pupillary reflex, sometimes first noticed in photographs) is the most common presenting sign and warrants urgent ophthalmology referral. Strabismus is the second most common presentation and should never be dismissed without excluding an intraocular cause. Disease may be unilateral or bilateral; bilateral and multifocal tumours are almost always heritable. Heritable retinoblastoma arises from germline mutation of the RB1 tumour suppressor gene and carries a lifelong risk of second malignancies, especially osteosarcoma. Diagnosis is made clinically by an experienced ophthalmologist under examination, supported by imaging; biopsy is avoided because of the risk of tumour seeding. Treatment aims to save life first, then preserve the eye and vision, using approaches such as chemotherapy, focal therapies, and enucleation for advanced disease. Children with heritable disease and affected families need genetic counselling and long-term surveillance for new tumours and secondary cancers. Leukocoria in any child requires urgent same-pathway ophthalmology referral to exclude retinoblastoma New-onset strabismus without an obvious benign cause Rapidly progressive proptosis or an inflamed, painful eye suggesting advanced or extraocular spread Bilateral disease or a family history indicating heritable retinoblastoma Signs of intracranial (trilateral) disease such as neurological deterioration Dismissing leukocoria or a subtle white reflex noticed in photographs as artefact Attributing strabismus solely to a benign squint without a dilated fundus examination Delaying urgent referral, which can be the difference between saving and losing an eye or life Overlooking the need for genetic testing and family screening in apparently unilateral disease Retinoblastoma results from biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumour suppressor gene in developing retinal cells. In heritable disease one mutated allele is inherited or arises in the germline, and a second somatic hit inactivates the remaining allele, producing early, often bilateral, multifocal tumours (consistent with the two-hit hypothesis). Loss of functional RB protein removes control of the cell cycle at the G1-S checkpoint, driving unregulated proliferation of retinal precursor cells and tumour formation. With early diagnosis and modern therapy, survival in high-resource settings exceeds 95 percent for intraocular disease; extraocular or metastatic spread markedly worsens outcome. Children with heritable disease remain at elevated lifelong risk of second malignancies.

leukocoria and allowing progression to advanced disease Performing intraocular biopsy and risking tumour dissemination Assuming a unilateral presentation excludes a germline mutation without genetic testing Neglecting lifelong surveillance for second malignancies in germline carriers Failing to screen and counsel at-risk relatives Retinoblastoma arises from developing retinal cells and is driven by biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumour-suppressor gene, whose protein normally restrains cell-cycle progression. In hereditary disease one defective RB1 allele is present in every cell as a germline mutation (the first hit), and loss or mutation of the remaining functional allele within a retinal cell (the second hit) allows unregulated proliferation and tumour formation, in keeping with Knudson's two-hit hypothesis. Because the first hit is already present throughout the body, tumours tend to be bilateral and multifocal and to arise early, and the germline defect predisposes other tissues to malignancy later in life. With early diagnosis and modern treatment, survival from intraocular retinoblastoma is high in well-resourced settings, and eye-preserving therapy is often possible; however, patients with a germline RB1 mutation carry a lifelong increased risk of second malignancies, and extraocular or metastatic disease and trilateral retinoblastoma carry a much poorer prognosis.
