detachment quickly Any signs of tractional retinal detachment (stage 4 or 5) Missed or delayed screening in eligible infants, risking preventable blindness Failing to screen eligible preterm infants or examining them too late to intervene Underestimating aggressive posterior disease that lacks the classic ridge appearance Poor regulation of supplemental oxygen increasing the risk and severity of disease Discharging treated infants without long-term follow-up for refractive and detachment risks Retinopathy of prematurity results from disordered development of the retinal vasculature in the incompletely vascularised preterm retina. In an initial phase, the relatively hyperoxic extrauterine environment (worsened by supplemental oxygen) suppresses vascular growth factors and halts normal vessel growth, leaving peripheral avascular retina. As the metabolically active retina matures, the resulting hypoxia drives excessive vascular endothelial growth factor production and pathological neovascularisation at the junction of vascular and avascular retina. These new vessels can bleed and form fibrovascular tissue, exerting traction that leads to retinal detachment. Mild ROP frequently regresses spontaneously with a good visual outcome, but severe disease can progress to retinal detachment and blindness if untreated. Timely screening and treatment markedly reduce the risk of severe visual loss, though treated eyes and preterm survivors remain prone to refractive error, strabismus, and amblyopia.

Retractile testis — retractile testicle Undescended (cryptorchid) testis Ascending (acquired undescended) testis Ectopic testis Absent (vanishing) testis Gliding testis Careful examination in a warm, relaxed setting to overcome the cremasteric reflex Confirmation that the testis stays in the scrotum after manipulation Serial follow-up to detect an ascending testis No routine imaging required Referral if the testis cannot be kept in the scrotum A testis that intermittently withdraws from the scrotum into the groin due to an overactive cremasteric reflex, but can be brought down and stays in the scrotum It is a normal variant in prepubertal boys and must be distinguished from a truly undescended (cryptorchid) testis The key clinical feature is that the testis, once manipulated into the scrotum, remains there without tension until the reflex is re-triggered The cremasteric reflex is most active in mid-childhood, when retractile testes are commonest A minority become ascending (acquired undescended) testes over time, so periodic review is advised No surgery is needed for a genuinely retractile testis, but an ascending testis requires orchidopexy A testis that will not stay in the scrotum (undescended/ascending) Testicular asymmetry or atrophy Associated hypospadias or ambiguous genitalia Loss of a previously scrotal testis on follow-up Labelling an undescended or ascending testis as merely retractile Examining in a cold or anxious setting and misjudging position Failing to arrange follow-up for possible ascent Reassuring without confirming the testis stays down A retractile testis results from a brisk cremasteric reflex that pulls a normally descended testis up toward the external ring, particularly with cold or handling. Because the spermatic cord is of adequate length, the testis can be drawn back into and remain in the scrotum, distinguishing it from cryptorchidism. In some boys relative shortening of the cord with growth converts a retractile testis into an ascending (acquired undescended) testis, which no longer stays down. A truly retractile testis is benign and typically resolves at puberty, but the small risk of progression to an ascending testis warrants monitoring.

Retrocalcaneal bursitis — retrocalcaneal bursopathy, posterior heel bursitis, Haglund-associated bursitis, subtendinous calcaneal bursitis Insertional Achilles tendinopathy Mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy Haglund deformity Calcaneal stress fracture Sever's disease (calcaneal apophysitis in children) Spondyloarthropathy-related enthesitis Ultrasound to show bursal fluid and assess the Achilles insertion MRI to characterise bursitis, insertional tendinopathy and bone oedema Lateral radiograph to assess a Haglund prominence and insertional calcification Inflammatory markers and HLA-B27 with rheumatological review if spondyloarthropathy is suspected Clinical localisation of tenderness anterior to the tendon Posterior heel pain from inflammation of the bursa between the calcaneus and the Achilles tendon insertion Often associated with insertional Achilles tendinopathy and with a prominent posterosuperior calcaneal process (Haglund deformity) Tenderness is anterior to the Achilles tendon on either side of its insertion, distinguishing it from mid-portion tendinopathy Aggravated by ankle dorsiflexion and by footwear pressure on the heel counter Can occur in inflammatory arthropathies such as the spondyloarthritides, so consider systemic causes in bilateral or atypical presentations Ultrasound or MRI shows bursal fluid and any associated insertional tendinopathy or bony prominence Management is load and footwear modification, heel lift or shoe changes to reduce pressure, and physiotherapy; corticosteroid injection is used cautiously given proximity to the Achilles and rupture risk Features of inflammatory arthropathy such as bilateral heel pain, inflammatory back pain or other enthesitis Sudden posterior pain and weakness suggesting Achilles rupture Focal bone pain suggesting a calcaneal stress fracture Systemic upset suggesting infection Corticosteroid injection near the Achilles with its attendant rupture risk Confusing bursitis with mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy and mistreating it Missing an underlying spondyloarthropathy Overlooking a calcaneal stress fracture The retrocalcaneal bursa sits between the posterosuperior calcaneus and the Achilles tendon. Repetitive compression and friction during ankle dorsiflexion, often aggravated by a prominent posterosuperior calcaneal tuberosity (Haglund deformity) and by rigid heel counters, inflame the bursa. It commonly coexists with insertional Achilles tendinopathy, the two forming part of a posterior heel overload picture. Inflammatory arthropathies such as the spondyloarthritides can also produce a genuine inflammatory bursitis and enthesitis at this site. Usually improves with footwear and load modification and rehabilitation; cases linked to a Haglund deformity or insertional tendinopathy can be persistent and occasionally require surgery.

Retrograde ejaculation — backward ejaculation, retrograde ejaculation into the bladder, dry orgasm from retrograde flow Failure of seminal emission (anejaculation) Ejaculatory duct obstruction producing low ejaculate volume Congenital absence of the vasa and seminal vesicles Hypogonadism reducing ejaculate volume Androgen-deficiency-related reduction in ejaculate Psychogenic ejaculatory dysfunction Post-orgasmic urine analysis for the presence of sperm, the confirmatory test Standard semen analysis assessing ejaculate volume and sperm content Blood glucose or HbA1c to identify diabetes Medication review focusing on alpha-blockers and other implicated drugs Surgical and neurological history including bladder-neck, prostate, and retroperitoneal procedures Scrotal or transrectal ultrasound where an anatomical or obstructive cause is also considered Men describe orgasm with little or no antegrade ejaculate, and the first urine passed afterwards is characteristically cloudy from admixed semen The diagnosis is confirmed by finding sperm in a post-orgasmic urine specimen, distinguishing it from failure of emission where no semen is produced at all The common causes are diabetic autonomic neuropathy, bladder-neck or prostate surgery, retroperitoneal surgery, and alpha-blocker medication It is a recognised and treatable cause of low-volume ejaculate and of male-factor infertility Alkalinisation and appropriate preparation of the post-orgasmic urine allow sperm to be harvested for assisted reproduction when medical treatment fails Medical treatment aims to restore bladder-neck closure using sympathomimetic or alpha-agonist agents, most useful when the cause is neuropathic rather than anatomical Anatomical causes following bladder-neck resection generally do not respond to drugs, so assisted conception is planned from the outset when fertility is the goal New retrograde ejaculation as an early clue to undiagnosed diabetes Recent retroperitoneal or pelvic surgery with additional neurological deficits Associated bladder or voiding symptoms suggesting broader outflow pathology Complete absence of orgasmic sensation pointing to a different neurological problem Confusing retrograde ejaculation with true anejaculation by not examining post-orgasmic urine Attempting drug treatment for an anatomical bladder-neck defect that will not respond Missing underlying diabetes as the driver of a neuropathic cause Overlooking a culprit alpha-blocker that could simply be adjusted Failing to alkalinise and prepare urine promptly, reducing the yield of viable sperm Normal ejaculation depends on coordinated closure of the bladder neck at the moment of emission so that semen is propelled forward through the urethra rather than back into the bladder. When the internal urethral sphincter fails to close, seminal fluid takes the path of least resistance and flows retrogradely into the bladder. This failure may be neurogenic, as in diabetic autonomic neuropathy or after retroperitoneal lymph-node dissection that interrupts sympathetic outflow; anatomical, following transurethral or open bladder-neck and prostate surgery that destroys the sphincter mechanism; or pharmacological, notably with alpha-adrenergic blocking drugs that relax the bladder neck. The result is a reduced or absent antegrade ejaculate with sperm recoverable from the post-orgasmic urine. The condition is benign and does not threaten general health; fertility is frequently achievable, either by restoring antegrade ejaculation with medication in neuropathic cases or by retrieving sperm from post-orgasmic urine for assisted reproduction when the cause is anatomical.

Retronychia — proximal nail ingrowing, retronychia Chronic paronychia Onychocryptosis (lateral ingrowing toenail) Pyogenic granuloma of the nail fold Acute bacterial paronychia or felon Subungual or periungual tumour Nail changes of psoriasis affecting the proximal fold Clinical assessment for proximal fold inflammation with arrested distal nail growth Onychoscopy to detect stacked nail plates and proximal embedding Ultrasound to demonstrate multiple overlapping plates when the diagnosis is unclear Swab of any discharge if secondary bacterial infection is suspected History of preceding proximal nail fold rather than into the lateral folds It typically affects the great toenail and presents with proximal pain, swelling, redness, and chronic inflammation of the proximal fold Recurrent granulation tissue and discharge from beneath the proximal fold are characteristic, and it is often misdiagnosed as simple chronic paronychia A key sign is the arrest of normal distal nail growth, inflammation and allows a new, correctly aligned nail to grow Persistent proximal fold inflammation unresponsive to treatment for presumed paronychia Signs of spreading soft-tissue infection requiring prompt intervention Atypical granulation or a mass suggesting an underlying tumour Recurrent disease after treatment indicating incomplete removal or ongoing trauma Repeatedly treating retronychia as chronic paronychia with antimicrobials or topical agents alone Overlooking the diagnostic clue of arrested distal nail growth Delaying avulsion, which prolongs the inflammation unnecessarily Failing to address ongoing trauma or footwear factors, leading to recurrence Retronychia arises when the longitudinal growth of the nail plate is interrupted, usually after trauma, so that the plate loses its normal forward advance and is instead pushed proximally into the tissue of the proximal nail fold. Continued matrix activity produces new plates behind the disconnected leading nail, and these become stacked one beneath another, embedding into the proximal fold. The buried plate acts as a foreign body, provoking persistent inflammation, granulation tissue, and discharge, which explains why the condition mimics and is frequently confused with chronic paronychia. Retronychia responds well to nail plate avulsion, after which inflammation settles and a normally growing nail usually returns, although recovery takes months and recurrence can occur if predisposing trauma continues.

obstruction Acute kidney injury or anuria from bilateral ureteric obstruction Features suggesting underlying malignancy such as marked weight loss or atypical imaging Anterior displacement of the aorta on imaging raising concern for lymphoma Vascular compromise from encasement of major arteries or veins Labelling the disease idiopathic without excluding malignancy, drugs, and infection Missing silent bilateral ureteric obstruction and progressive renal failure Overlooking a diagnosis of IgG4-related disease and its multi-organ implications Assuming a periaortic mass is inflammatory when imaging features suggest lymphoma Relieving obstruction without treating the underlying inflammatory process Retroperitoneal fibrosis is characterised by a chronic inflammatory and fibrotic plaque in the retroperitoneum, frequently centred on the abdominal aorta (chronic periaortitis). Many idiopathic cases represent a manifestation of IgG4-related disease, with an immune-mediated infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils driving progressive collagen deposition. An exaggerated inflammatory response to atherosclerotic aortic antigens has also been proposed. The expanding fibrous tissue encases and constricts adjacent structures, most importantly the ureters, producing obstructive uropathy and hydronephrosis. Idiopathic and IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis generally responds well to corticosteroids with regression of the mass and relief of obstruction, though relapse is common and long-term monitoring of renal function is needed; malignancy-associated disease carries the prognosis of the underlying tumour.

transoral route in the acute form The infection can spread inferiorly into the mediastinum along fascial planes, which is a dangerous complication Chronic (tuberculous) retropharyngeal abscess presents more insidiously and is drained by an external approach rather than transorally Stridor, drooling, or respiratory distress indicating airway compromise that demands urgent airway management Rapid spread with signs of descending mediastinitis such as chest pain and sepsis Torticollis with neurological signs suggesting cervical spine involvement Sepsis or vascular complications such as jugular vein thrombosis Failing to anticipate and secure a threatened airway before other interventions Attempting transoral drainage of a chronic tuberculous abscess instead of an external approach Missing downward spread into the mediastinum Overlooking underlying cervical spine tuberculosis in an insidious presentation The retropharyngeal space lies between the buccopharyngeal fascia covering the pharynx and the prevertebral fascia, and contains lymph nodes that drain the nasopharynx, adenoids, and posterior nasal structures. In young children an upper respiratory infection can seed these nodes, which suppurate to form an acute abscess; these nodes largely regress with age, making the acute form rare in adults, where trauma or foreign body is more often responsible. The chronic form arises from caries of the cervical vertebrae (Pott disease), where tuberculous pus tracks forward into the space. Because the space communicates inferiorly with the mediastinum, infection can descend to cause mediastinitis. With prompt airway protection, appropriate antibiotics, and timely surgical drainage the acute abscess resolves well in most children; delay can lead to airway obstruction, aspiration on rupture, or life-threatening mediastinitis, and the chronic tuberculous form requires prolonged antitubercular treatment alongside drainage.

Rett syndrome — MECP2, RTT, methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 disorder CDKL5 deficiency disorder FOXG1-related disorder (congenital Rett variant) Autism spectrum disorder with regression Angelman syndrome Other developmental and epileptic encephalopathies Neurodegenerative and metabolic disorders with regression MECP2 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, with wider gene testing if negative EEG, which commonly shows epileptiform abnormalities and background slowing Brain MRI to exclude alternative structural pathology Assessment of growth and head circumference over time Multidisciplinary evaluation of feeding, breathing, spine and development Classic Rett syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked MECP2 gene and occurs almost exclusively in girls There is a period of apparently normal early development followed by regression, typically between six and eighteen months of age Loss of purposeful hand use with characteristic midline hand stereotypies such as wringing and washing movements is a defining feature Regression brings loss of acquired language, gait abnormalities or loss of ambulation, and deceleration of head growth causing acquired microcephaly Epilepsy develops in a large proportion of patients, alongside breathing dysregulation, autonomic disturbance and scoliosis Diagnosis rests on established clinical criteria supported by MECP2 genetic testing Care is multidisciplinary and supportive, targeting seizures, feeding, orthopaedic and respiratory complications Developmental regression with loss of purposeful hand skills and language Deceleration of head growth producing acquired microcephaly New or worsening seizures superimposed on stereotyped movements Progressive scoliosis or feeding and respiratory compromise Mistaking early regression for idiopathic autism and delaying MECP2 testing Assuming a normal MECP2 result excludes a Rett-like disorder such as CDKL5 or FOXG1 Overtreating stereotypies as seizures without EEG correlation Neglecting scoliosis, feeding and breathing complications that drive morbidity Rett syndrome is caused by loss-of-function variants in MECP2, which encodes methyl-CpG-binding protein 2, a transcriptional regulator essential for mature neuronal function and synaptic maintenance. MeCP2 deficiency does not cause neurodegeneration but arrests and disrupts postnatal synaptic development and network refinement, so early milestones are attained and then lost. X-linkage and X-inactivation explain the female predominance and clinical variability, while the widespread neuronal dysfunction underlies the epilepsy, movement, breathing and autonomic manifestations. Rett syndrome causes lifelong severe disability with variable epilepsy, motor and communication impairment, but many individuals survive into adulthood with supportive care. Life expectancy is somewhat reduced, with cardiorespiratory complications and, less commonly, sudden death contributing to mortality.

Recurrent thunderclap headaches, which mandate exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage New focal neurological deficit or seizure suggesting stroke or oedema Cortical subarachnoid haemorrhage on imaging Persistent or worsening narrowing that raises concern for true vasculitis Misdiagnosing it as CNS vasculitis and giving prolonged immunosuppression Missing an underlying vasoactive drug or postpartum trigger Failing to repeat vascular imaging to confirm reversibility Using corticosteroids, which may worsen outcomes in this condition Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome is a transient disturbance of cerebral arterial tone in which dysregulation of vascular smooth muscle produces multifocal segmental vasoconstriction of medium and large cerebral arteries. The abnormal vasomotor control, often provoked by vasoactive substances, hormonal changes, or the postpartum state, causes waves of constriction and dilatation that account for the recurrent thunderclap headaches. Impaired perfusion can lead to ischaemic infarction, while vessel wall stress and reperfusion contribute to cortical subarachnoid haemorrhage and posterior reversible encephalopathy; the vasoconstriction characteristically resolves over weeks to a few months. Most patients recover fully within days to weeks as the vasoconstriction resolves, but a minority suffer permanent deficits from stroke or haemorrhage, and recurrence is uncommon but possible.

Reye Syndrome — Reye's syndrome, acute encephalopathy with fatty liver Inborn errors of metabolism (fatty acid oxidation defects, urea cycle disorders, organic acidaemias) Toxic ingestion or drug-induced hepatotoxicity Acute encephalitis or meningitis Fulminant viral hepatitis Diabetic ketoacidosis Haemorrhagic shock and encephalopathy syndrome Serum ammonia Liver transaminases, bilirubin, and coagulation profile Blood glucose monitoring Metabolic screen: plasma amino acids, urine organic acids, acylcarnitine profile Neuroimaging to assess cerebral oedema and exclude other causes Lumbar puncture only when safe and to exclude CNS infection Liver biopsy in atypical or diagnostically uncertain cases A rare but potentially fatal disorder marked by acute non-inflammatory encephalopathy occurring alongside fatty change in the liver and other organs. Classically follows a viral illness, especially influenza or varicella, during the recovery phase. Salicylate (aspirin) exposure during a preceding viral infection is a well-recognised association, and the sharp decline in incidence tracks with public advice to avoid aspirin in children. Typical evolution is protracted vomiting followed by progressive neurological deterioration: irritability or lethargy advancing to confusion, delirium, seizures, and coma. Liver dysfunction is present but jaundice is characteristically absent or minimal, which can be a useful discriminating clue. Laboratory findings include raised transaminases, hyperammonaemia, prolonged prothrombin time, and often hypoglycaemia in younger children. In any child presenting with this picture, an underlying inborn error of metabolism (particularly a fatty acid oxidation or urea cycle defect) must be excluded, as these mimic Reye syndrome. Management is supportive with a focus on controlling raised intracranial pressure, correcting metabolic derangements, and protecting cerebral perfusion. Prognosis correlates strongly with the depth of coma and the degree of hyperammonaemia at presentation. Rapidly progressive encephalopathy or declining conscious level (EMERGENCY) Signs of raised intracranial pressure: abnormal posturing, pupillary changes, bradycardia with hypertension Marked or rising hyperammonaemia Seizures or status epilepticus Coagulopathy with bleeding Progression to coma requiring airway protection and intensive care Attributing the illness to Reye syndrome without excluding an inborn error of metabolism, which is now a more common cause of this presentation Being reassured by absent jaundice despite significant hepatic derangement Delaying management of raised intracranial pressure while awaiting confirmatory tests Overlooking hypoglycaemia, especially in infants and young children Failing to elicit a history of aspirin or salicylate-containing product use The core lesion is acute, generalised mitochondrial injury. Diffuse mitochondrial dysfunction in the liver impairs the urea cycle and fatty acid oxidation, producing microvesicular fatty infiltration of hepatocytes, hyperammonaemia, and disturbed intermediary metabolism. In the brain this mitochondrial failure, combined with hyperammonaemia, drives cytotoxic cerebral oedema and raised intracranial pressure, which underlie the encephalopathy. Salicylate metabolites are thought to potentiate mitochondrial injury in susceptible children following a viral trigger. Outcome depends heavily on how advanced the encephalopathy is at presentation; children who remain in earlier stages often recover well, whereas deep coma and severe hyperammonaemia carry high risk of death or lasting neurological deficit. Early recognition and aggressive management of intracranial pressure improve survival.

anti-D dose is inadequate When Rh(D)-positive fetal red cells enter the circulation of a Rh(D)-negative mother, her immune system mounts an antibody response, initially IgM and then IgG anti-D. In a later pregnancy with a Rh(D)-positive fetus, maternal IgG crosses the placenta, binds fetal red cells, and leads to their destruction in the fetal reticuloendothelial system. The resulting fetal anaemia drives extramedullary haematopoiesis and, when severe, high-output cardiac failure with generalised oedema known as hydrops fetalis, alongside accumulation of bilirubin that threatens the neonate after birth. With routine antenatal screening, effective anti-D prophylaxis, non-invasive monitoring, and intrauterine transfusion, most affected pregnancies now achieve good outcomes. Prognosis worsens with early-onset severe anaemia and hydrops, and sensitised pregnancies tend to be affected earlier and more severely in successive gestations, making specialist surveillance essential.

Rhabdomyolysis — Creatine kinase (markedly raised) Renal function, K⁺ Urine myoglobin Aggressive fluids; watch hyperkalaemia and AKI Clostridial myositis/myonecrosis — predictably precipitates acute rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096). Streptococcal (group A) myositis — also predictably causes acute rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096). Viral myositis — influenza, echovirus, coxsackievirus and Epstein-Barr virus infections may be associated with rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096). Legionella infection — reported association with rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096). Urine dipstick for blood with microscopy — dipstick blood-positive but RBC-negative supports myoglobinuria rather than true haematuria (Harrison 22e p.343). Urine sediment / microscopy for muddy-brown (pigmented) granular casts and tubular epithelial cells, indicating accompanying acute tubular necrosis (Harrison 22e p.343). Serum phosphate and calcium — hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia accompany acute muscle injury (Harrison 22e p.359, p.363). Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) — may be <1% in early rhabdomyolysis-associated ATN, limiting its discriminatory value (Harrison 22e p.343). Myoglobinuria characteristically produces a positive urine dipstick for blood while urine microscopy shows no (or few) red cells — a key clue distinguishing pigment nephropathy from true haematuria (Harrison 22e p.343). In rhabdomyolysis-associated acute tubular necrosis the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) may be paradoxically low (<1%), unlike the classic >1% of established ATN, because the injury is often early/non-oliguric (Harrison 22e p.343). Rhabdomyolysis is listed among the 'don't-miss' metabolic emergencies whose urgency can be underappreciated, alongside malignant hyperthermia and tumour lysis syndrome (Harrison 22e p.102). Heat-related exertional rhabdomyolysis is a recognised, albeit rare, cause of sudden death in sickle cell trait carriers during strenuous exercise — a reason to counsel carriers before sports participation (Harrison 22e p.818). Hyperkalaemia from release of intracellular potassium during muscle necrosis — predictable and potentially life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.359). Rising creatinine with pigmented granular casts signalling evolving pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis (Harrison 22e p.343). Interpreting a dipstick-positive 'haematuria' as bleeding from the urinary tract when no RBCs are seen on microscopy — this pattern reflects myoglobinuria in rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.343). Relying on a low FENa to exclude ATN: rhabdomyolysis-related ATN can present with FENa <1% (Harrison 22e p.343). Acute rhabdomyolysis typically causes hypocalcaemia, but the recovery phase (with renal failure) can produce rebound hypercalcaemia — calcium should not be over-corrected early (Harrison 22e p.362, p.363). Massive skeletal muscle breakdown releases intracellular contents — including myoglobin, potassium, phosphate and creatine kinase — into the circulation. Filtered myoglobin (a heme protein) is nephrotoxic and contributes to pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis; the released heme pigment also causes a false-positive dipstick reaction for blood. Concurrent volume sequestration into injured muscle produces a prerenal/hypovolaemic insult that compounds the tubular injury (Harrison 22e p.343). Rhabdomyolysis-associated acute kidney injury is frequently of the milder, non-oliguric ATN type and is potentially reversible with adequate perfusion; the recovery phase may be complicated by rebound hypercalcaemia (Harrison 22e p.343, p.362).

rhabdoid tumour — malignant rhabdoid tumour, malignant rhabdoid tumour of the kidney, extracranial rhabdoid tumour Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma) Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney Congenital mesoblastic nephroma Neuroblastoma Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour when the central nervous system is involved Epithelioid sarcoma (also INI1-deficient) at soft-tissue sites Renal medullary carcinoma (also SMARCB1-deficient) in older children SMARCB1/INI1 (and SMARCA4) immunohistochemistry on tumour tissue Molecular and cytogenetic testing for SMARCB1 deletion or mutation Germline SMARCB1/SMARCA4 testing and genetic counselling Brain and whole-spine MRI to exclude synchronous central nervous system rhabdoid tumour Cross-sectional imaging of chest, abdomen, and pelvis for staging Serum calcium to detect paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia Bone imaging for skeletal metastases A highly aggressive malignancy of infancy and early childhood; the kidney is the prototypical site (malignant rhabdoid tumour of the kidney), but soft tissue, liver, and other viscera are also affected. Defined by biallelic inactivation of SMARCB1 (INI1/hSNF5) on chromosome 22q11.2, with a small subset driven by SMARCA4 (BRG1) loss. Loss of nuclear INI1 (SMARCB1) expression on immunohistochemistry is the diagnostic hallmark and distinguishes it from mimics such as Wilms tumour. A substantial minority arise within rhabdoid tumour predisposition syndrome from a germline SMARCB1 or SMARCA4 mutation, so germline testing and genetic counselling are essential. Synchronous or metachronous central nervous system atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour occurs, making brain imaging mandatory at staging. Hypercalcaemia is a recognised paraneoplastic feature of renal rhabdoid tumour. Presentation is often with a rapidly growing abdominal or flank mass, haematuria, and systemic upset in a very young infant. Metastatic disease at diagnosis is common and the prognosis is among the worst of paediatric solid tumours. Neurological signs or a brain lesion indicating synchronous atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour Symptomatic hypercalcaemia A rapidly enlarging mass with systemic deterioration in an infant Tumour rupture with intraperitoneal haemorrhage Misclassifying the tumour as Wilms tumour or another blastemal-rich neoplasm without performing INI1 immunohistochemistry. Omitting brain imaging and thereby missing a synchronous central nervous system rhabdoid tumour. Failing to arrange germline SMARCB1/SMARCA4 testing, missing predisposition syndrome and family risk. Attributing hypercalcaemia to another cause and overlooking a paraneoplastic mechanism. Rhabdoid tumours are driven by loss of function of the SWI/SNF (BAF) chromatin-remodelling complex, most often through biallelic inactivation of SMARCB1 (INI1) and less commonly SMARCA4 (BRG1). Loss of a core subunit deregulates chromatin accessibility and enhancer activity, impairing differentiation and driving proliferation despite an otherwise remarkably stable, near-diploid genome with few additional mutations. Tumours are composed of characteristic rhabdoid cells with eccentric nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and eosinophilic cytoplasmic hyaline inclusions corresponding to whorls of intermediate filaments. A germline SMARCB1 or SMARCA4 alteration (rhabdoid tumour predisposition syndrome) predisposes to multifocal, very early-onset disease, including concurrent central nervous system tumours. Extracranial rhabdoid tumour carries a poor prognosis, particularly in infants and in those with metastatic disease or a germline predisposition. Intensified multimodal therapy achieves long-term survival in only a minority.

Rhabdomyolysis — muscle breakdown syndrome Acute kidney injury of another cause Myocardial infarction (for raised enzymes) Inflammatory myopathy Haemolysis causing pigmenturia Compartment syndrome Primary hyperkalaemia Serum creatine kinase and serial trends Renal function, potassium, phosphate and calcium Urinalysis showing blood on dipstick without red cells (myoglobinuria) Electrocardiogram for hyperkalaemic changes Investigation of the underlying cause, including compartment pressures if indicated Breakdown of skeletal muscle releases intracellular contents, notably myoglobin, potassium, phosphate and creatine kinase, into the circulation The classic triad is muscle pain, weakness and dark (tea-coloured) urine, though many patients lack all three A markedly raised creatine kinase is the key laboratory finding Acute kidney injury from myoglobin, and life-threatening hyperkalaemia, are the main dangers Causes are diverse, including crush and trauma, prolonged immobility, extreme exertion, seizures, drugs, toxins, ischaemia and metabolic myopathies Early and generous intravenous fluid resuscitation to maintain urine output is the cornerstone of treatment Hyperkalaemia with electrocardiographic changes Oliguria or established acute kidney injury Signs of compartment syndrome Very high or rising creatine kinase with volume depletion Delaying fluid resuscitation Missing hyperkalaemia as an immediate threat Overlooking compartment syndrome Attributing dark urine to haematuria without checking for myoglobinuria Rhabdomyolysis occurs when injury to skeletal muscle disrupts the sarcolemma and releases myoglobin and other intracellular constituents. Myoglobin is filtered by the kidney where it causes tubular obstruction, direct tubular toxicity and renal vasoconstriction, producing acute kidney injury, particularly when the patient is volume-depleted and the urine is acidic. Release of potassium and phosphate and sequestration of calcium in damaged muscle cause dangerous electrolyte disturbances, while a compartment syndrome can both cause and result from the muscle injury. With prompt fluid resuscitation many patients avoid or recover from kidney injury; prognosis worsens with severe hyperkalaemia, established renal failure or the underlying precipitating condition.

pelvic mass Features of disseminated disease such as bone pain or cytopenias suggesting marrow involvement Assuming morphology alone predicts behaviour rather than confirming fusion status by molecular testing Underestimating central nervous system risk in parameningeal disease and omitting appropriate neuraxis staging Inadequate biopsy planning that jeopardises subsequent local control Overlooking regional lymph node assessment, which is particularly important at extremity and paratesticular sites Neglecting long-term surveillance for late effects of chemotherapy and radiotherapy in survivors Rhabdomyosarcoma is a malignancy of primitive mesenchymal cells committed to skeletal muscle differentiation but arrested before maturation. The alveolar subtype is characteristically driven by a PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1 fusion gene that generates a potent chimeric transcription factor promoting proliferation and blocking myogenic maturation. Embryonal tumours generally lack these fusions and instead show a range of alterations, frequently involving the RAS pathway and loss of imprinting at chromosome 11p15. Because fusion status correlates better with behaviour than morphology alone, molecular classification into fusion-positive and fusion-negative disease now guides risk assessment. Prognosis is determined by fusion status, stage and clinical group, primary site, patient age, and histological subtype; localised, fusion-negative embryonal tumours at favourable sites do well, whereas fusion-positive, metastatic, or unfavourable-site disease carries a substantially worse outlook.

rheumatic fever — acute rheumatic fever, ARF septic or reactive arthritis juvenile idiopathic arthritis systemic lupus erythematosus infective endocarditis viral myocarditis Lyme disease disseminated gonococcal infection throat swab culture and rapid antigen testing for group A streptococcus serial anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B titres inflammatory markers (ESR and C-reactive protein) electrocardiogram for PR-interval prolongation and conduction disturbance echocardiography with Doppler to detect subclinical valvulitis full blood count and blood cultures to exclude sepsis or endocarditis Acute rheumatic fever is a delayed immune-mediated sequela of group A streptococcal pharyngitis, typically emerging a few weeks after the sore throat, and is a diagnosis of the whole child rather than any single test. Diagnosis rests on the revised Jones criteria, which now stratify populations into low-risk and moderate-to-high-risk to improve sensitivity where the disease remains endemic. Migratory polyarthritis of the large joints is the commonest major manifestation and is characteristically exquisitely responsive to salicylates. Carditis is the only manifestation that causes long-term morbidity; a pancarditis, its hallmark is valvulitis with the mitral valve most often affected, followed by the aortic valve. Sydenham chorea may appear in isolation and late, after other manifestations have resolved, and can be the sole criterion sufficient for diagnosis. Subcutaneous nodules and erythema marginatum are uncommon but highly specific minor major manifestations, nodules correlating with severe carditis. Evidence of preceding streptococcal infection (rising anti-streptolysin O or anti-DNase B titres, or positive throat culture) is essential except in isolated chorea or indolent carditis. Secondary prophylaxis with long-acting penicillin is the cornerstone of preventing recurrent attacks and progressive rheumatic heart disease. new or changing cardiac murmur with signs of heart failure indicating severe carditis pericardial rub or effusion suggesting pancarditis high-grade atrioventricular block recurrent attack in a child with established rheumatic heart disease Attributing a febrile arthritis to rheumatic fever without documented antecedent streptococcal infection, especially in low-incidence settings. Starting salicylates or steroids before the joint picture has declared itself, masking the diagnostic migratory pattern. Overlooking subclinical carditis detectable only on echocardiography in a child with apparently isolated arthritis. Failing to institute and sustain secondary prophylaxis, the single most important determinant of long-term outcome. Misreading isolated late-onset chorea as a functional or psychiatric disorder. Acute rheumatic fever follows pharyngeal infection with rheumatogenic strains of group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus in a genetically susceptible host. Molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens, particularly M protein and the group A carbohydrate N-acetyl-glucosamine, and human tissue proteins such as cardiac myosin and laminin drives a cross-reactive humoral and T-cell response. Antibody binding to valvular endothelium up-regulates adhesion molecules, recruiting CD4+ T cells that release inflammatory cytokines and produce the granulomatous Aschoff bodies pathognomonic of rheumatic carditis. The same autoimmune mechanism targets the basal ganglia to produce chorea, the joints to produce arthritis, and the skin. Repeated episodes amplify valvular scarring, leading to chronic rheumatic heart disease. Arthritis and chorea resolve without sequelae, but the prognosis is dictated by the severity of carditis, which may progress to chronic rheumatic heart disease. Faithful secondary prophylaxis markedly reduces recurrence and can allow mild valve lesions to regress.

presenting with functional valve regurgitation Transthoracic and, when needed, transoesophageal echocardiography to define valve morphology and severity 12-lead ECG to detect atrial fibrillation and chamber enlargement Chest radiography for chamber size, pulmonary congestion, and valve calcification Evidence of prior streptococcal infection and inflammatory markers in suspected acute disease Assessment of pulmonary pressures and right heart consequences Blood cultures and endocarditis workup when infection is suspected Rheumatic heart disease is the chronic valvular sequel of acute rheumatic fever, an immune-mediated complication of group A streptococcal infection, and remains a major cause of valve disease in many parts of the world The mitral valve is most often affected, and mitral stenosis is the most characteristic lesion, though mixed mitral and aortic valve involvement is common Patients may be asymptomatic for years before developing exertional breathlessness, fatigue, palpitations from atrial fibrillation, or features of heart failure Although the valve damage itself is non-infective, these valves are prone to infective endocarditis, which must be considered when there is fever or clinical deterioration Mitral stenosis predisposes to atrial fibrillation and left atrial thrombus, and to systemic embolism including stroke Echocardiography is central to assessing valve morphology, severity, and haemodynamic consequences Prevention relies on prompt treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis and long-term secondary antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrent rheumatic fever Advanced disease may require balloon valvuloplasty for suitable mitral stenosis, or surgical repair or valve replacement Fever or systemic features suggesting superimposed infective endocarditis on a damaged valve New atrial fibrillation with embolic risk, or acute systemic embolism such as stroke Acute pulmonary oedema or rapidly progressive heart failure Haemoptysis or severe pulmonary hypertension in advanced mitral stenosis Overlooking superimposed infective endocarditis when a patient with known rheumatic valve disease develops fever Failing to maintain long-term secondary antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrent rheumatic fever Underestimating stroke risk from atrial fibrillation and left atrial thrombus in mitral stenosis Delaying valve intervention until irreversible pulmonary hypertension or ventricular dysfunction has developed Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis in susceptible individuals, in whom molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens and host tissue drives a cross-reactive immune response affecting the heart, joints, skin, and nervous system. Recurrent or severe carditis produces chronic inflammation and scarring of the valves, with leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, and chordal shortening. Over years this yields stenosis, regurgitation, or mixed dysfunction, most commonly of the mitral valve. The resulting pressure and volume loading leads to atrial enlargement, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension, and eventually heart failure. Prognosis depends on the valves involved, severity, and access to secondary prophylaxis and intervention; secondary prophylaxis and timely valve intervention allow many patients to do well, but advanced disease with pulmonary hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and heart failure carries significant morbidity and mortality.

Rheumatic mitral stenosis — mitral stenosis Degenerative (calcific) mitral stenosis Congenital mitral stenosis Left atrial myxoma obstructing the valve Cor triatriatum Other causes of pulmonary hypertension and breathlessness Echocardiography with valve area and gradient and morphology scoring Electrocardiogram (atrial fibrillation, left atrial enlargement) Chest radiograph for left atrial enlargement and pulmonary congestion Assessment for left atrial thrombus (often transoesophageal) Right heart assessment for pulmonary hypertension Narrowing of the mitral valve orifice, worldwide most often a late consequence of rheumatic fever Presents with exertional breathlessness, fatigue, haemoptysis and, frequently, atrial fibrillation The classic auscultatory findings are a loud first heart sound, an opening snap and a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex Left atrial enlargement predisposes to atrial fibrillation and to left atrial thrombus with systemic embolism Pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure develop as the disease advances Assessment of severity and valve morphology guides balloon valvuloplasty or surgery; anticoagulation is needed for atrial fibrillation or thrombus New atrial fibrillation with rapid deterioration Systemic embolism or left atrial thrombus Severe pulmonary hypertension or right heart failure Haemoptysis or pulmonary oedema Missing left atrial thrombus before valvuloplasty Failing to anticoagulate atrial fibrillation Attributing breathlessness to lung disease alone Underestimating pulmonary hypertension Rheumatic mitral stenosis results from chronic post-inflammatory scarring after rheumatic fever, with leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and chordal shortening progressively narrowing the mitral orifice. The obstruction raises left atrial pressure, which is transmitted back to the pulmonary circulation causing pulmonary congestion and, over time, pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain. Left atrial dilatation and stasis promote atrial fibrillation and thrombus formation with embolic risk. Although the valve injury is a sequela of infection, the established stenosis is a structural, non-infective disorder. The condition is progressive; symptoms and complications are well controlled and prognosis improved by timely balloon valvuloplasty or valve surgery, though atrial fibrillation and embolism carry ongoing risk.

Rheumatoid arthritis — RF, anti-CCP, ESR/CRP X-rays of hands/feet Septic arthritis can complicate a known RA joint Primary Sjogren's syndrome - polyarthralgia and mild synovitis can mimic RA, and ~50% are RF-positive; distinguished by predominant sicca symptoms, ANA positivity and anti-Ro/SSA in about two-thirds (Harrison 22e p.2847). Spondyloarthropathies (psoriatic arthritis, enteropathy-associated arthritis) - distinguished by sacroiliitis, enthesopathy, and presence of psoriasis or inflammatory bowel disease (Harrison 22e p.2847). Polymyalgia rheumatica in elderly patients - can resemble seronegative RA; PMR centres on neck/shoulder and hip girdle, whereas RA predominantly affects wrists/hands and ankles/feet, especially at onset (Harrison 22e p.2847). Remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema (RS3PE) - features prominent distal-limb pitting edema (unusual in RA) and responds promptly to low-dose prednisone (Harrison 22e p.2847). Paraneoplastic syndromes - may be confused with early RA (Harrison 22e p.2847). Virus-related polyarthritis syndromes - can mimic RA and cause transient RF production, but usually resolve within 2-3 weeks (Harrison 22e p.2847). Hepatitis C-related arthropathy - often involves small joints of the hands and is RF-positive in about half of cases, but generally anti-CCP negative (Harrison 22e p.2847). Subacute bacterial endocarditis and chronic hepatitis B/C - chronic infections that can produce a positive RF and confound interpretation (Harrison 22e p.2847). Anti-CCP (ACPA) antibodies - high specificity (~95%) for RA; useful diagnostically and prognostically (Harrison 22e p.2847). Synovial fluid aspiration with cell count and crystal/microbiology analysis - confirms inflammatory arthritis and excludes infection or crystal disease (Harrison 22e p.2847). MRI - greatest sensitivity for synovitis, effusions and early bone/bone-marrow changes; bone marrow edema predicts subsequent erosions (Harrison 22e p.2848). Musculoskeletal ultrasound with power Doppler - detects synovitis, increased joint vascularity and erosions, often more than plain films; portable and radiation-free (Harrison 22e p.2848). ANA and ANCA - may be positive in RA (~30% ANA, occasional p-ANCA), but anti-MPO/anti-PR3 should be negative (Harrison 22e p.2847). High-resolution chest CT - to detect and characterise interstitial lung disease (UIP vs NSIP patterns) when respiratory symptoms arise (Harrison 22e p.2840). Chronic tophaceous gout - can mimic severe RA, and tophi may be mistaken for rheumatoid nodules (Harrison 22e p.2847). Pseudogout (CPPD crystal arthritis) - inflammatory arthritis excluded via synovial fluid crystal analysis (Harrison 22e p.2847). Osteoarthritis - non-inflammatory; DIP involvement and synovial fluid under 2,000 WBC/uL favour OA over RA (Harrison 22e p.2839, p.2847). Early-morning joint stiffness lasting more than 1 hour that improves with activity is characteristic; the earliest joints involved are typically the small joints of the hands and feet (Harrison 22e p.2839). Wrists, MCP and PIP joints are most often affected; isolated DIP involvement usually reflects coexistent osteoarthritis rather than RA itself (Harrison 22e p.2839). Flexor tendon tenosynovitis is a frequent hallmark, producing reduced range of motion, weakened grip and trigger fingers, and can lead to tendon rupture (most commonly flexor pollicis longus) (Harrison 22e p.2839-2840). Anti-CCP (ACPA) and RF are useful both diagnostically and as prognostic biomarkers; anti-CCP carries the most value for predicting worse outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2839, p.2847). Anti-CCP has sensitivity similar to RF but much higher specificity (approaching 95%), so a positive anti-CCP in early inflammatory arthritis helps distinguish RA from other arthritides; testing both RF and anti-CCP adds incremental yield because some patients are positive for only one (Harrison 22e p.2847). About three-quarters of RA patients are seropositive (RF and/or ACPA) and one-quarter are seronegative; seronegative RA is a clinical diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2847). A fever above 38.3C (101F) at any point in the course should raise suspicion of systemic vasculitis or superimposed infection rather than being attributed to RA activity alone (Harrison 22e p.2840). Approximately 30% of RA patients are ANA-positive and some have p-ANCA, but anti-MPO and anti-PR3 are not expected and their presence points to an ANCA-associated vasculitis instead (Harrison 22e p.2847). Synovial fluid in RA is inflammatory (typically 5,000-50,000 WBC/uL, neutrophil-predominant) versus under 2,000 WBC/uL in osteoarthritis; aspiration is most useful to confirm inflammation and to exclude infection or crystal arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2847). Fever above 38.3C (101F) during the course should prompt evaluation for systemic vasculitis or infection rather than being ascribed to RA activity (Harrison 22e p.2840). RA patients have the highest incidence of septic (most often S. aureus) arthritis due to chronically inflamed joints, glucocorticoid therapy and breakdown of nodules/vasculitic ulcers; TNF inhibitors add risk of mycobacterial and other infections (Harrison 22e Chap. 124, p.~). Atlantoaxial (C1-C2) subluxation can cause compressive myelopathy; neurologic signs may evolve slowly with progressive instability (now seen in under 10% of patients) (Harrison 22e p.2840). New-onset numbness, tingling or focal weakness (mononeuritis multiplex) suggests systemic rheumatoid vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2841). Two- to fourfold increased risk of lymphoma (most often diffuse large B-cell), greatest with high disease activity or Felty's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2841). The 2010 ACR-EULAR criteria are classification (not diagnostic) criteria intended to identify early patients likely to progress; a positive RF or anti-CCP alone does not establish the diagnosis without supporting clinical features (Harrison 22e p.2847). A negative RF does not exclude RA - IgM RF is found in only ~75% of patients, and RF also occurs in other connective tissue diseases, chronic infections and 1-5% of healthy people (Harrison 22e p.2847). Accelerated growth of subcutaneous nodules can occur in up to 10% of patients on long-term methotrexate and should not automatically be read as worsening disease (Harrison 22e p.2840). Rheumatoid nodules and chronic tophaceous gout tophi can be confused with one another (Harrison 22e p.2840, p.2847). Periarticular osteopenia, the classic earliest x-ray finding, is difficult to appreciate on plain (especially digitised) films, so early radiographs may appear normal (Harrison 22e p.2848). RA is a chronic, systemic, symmetric erosive polyarthritis driven by an interaction of genetic predisposition (e.g., the HLA shared epitope) and environmental triggers such as cigarette smoking. Antigen-presenting cells activate synovial CD4+ T cells (via TCR-MHC class II and CD28-CD80/86 co-stimulation), which differentiate into TH1 and TH17 subsets. These activate B cells that mature into plasma cells producing autoantibodies (RF and anti-CCP/ACPA); immune complexes form within the joint and activate complement, amplifying inflammation. T effector cells stimulate synovial macrophages and fibroblasts to release pro-inflammatory cytokines, with TNF-alpha playing a central role by upregulating endothelial adhesion molecules and driving IL-1, IL-6 and GM-CSF production. TNF-alpha also disrupts the bone balance: it raises DKK-1 (inhibiting Wnt-driven osteoblastic bone formation) and promotes osteoclastogenesis through M-CSF and RANKL signalling, with osteoprotegerin acting as a decoy that limits bone loss. The net result is pannus formation, cartilage and bone erosion, and generalised inflammatory bone loss (Harrison 22e p.2845). Most patients show persistent, waxing-and-waning progressive disease; about 10% (particularly seronegative) remit spontaneously within 6 months, while a minority follow either a relapsing explosive course or an aggressively erosive course (now less common with modern therapy). Early disability is driven mainly by joint inflammation (potentially reversible) and later by cumulative irreversible joint damage. Overall mortality is roughly twice that of the general population, with excess deaths from respiratory illness, cardiovascular disease and infection; median life expectancy is shortened by about 7 years in men and 3 years in women. Worse survival is associated with systemic extraarticular involvement, low functional capacity, low socioeconomic status, low education and chronic prednisone use. Cardiovascular disease is the most common cause of death (Harrison 22e p.2848). Seropositivity for RF and especially anti-CCP predicts worse outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2847). Diagnosis is supported by the 2010 ACR-EULAR classification criteria (for patients with at least one joint of definite clinical synovitis not better explained by another disease), scored 0-10 across four domains - joint involvement (0-5), serology (RF/ACPA, 0-3), acute-phase reactants (CRP/ESR, 0-1), and symptom duration (0-1); a score of 6 or more fulfils requirements for definite RA. Disease activity (the main driver of treatment decisions) is tracked with composite indices: ACR 20/50/70 improvement criteria (mainly for trials) and continuous measures including DAS, SDAI, CDAI and RAPID3 used in practice. Functional disability is measured with the Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) (Harrison 22e p.2847-2848).

Rhinophyma — phymatous rosacea of the nose Other phymas of rosacea (for example of the chin or ears) Basal or squamous cell carcinoma of the nose Sarcoidosis or other granulomatous infiltration Nasal lymphoma or other tumour Sebaceous hyperplasia Clinical diagnosis from the characteristic appearance and rosacea history Biopsy of any suspicious nodule or ulcer to exclude carcinoma Assessment of the extent and functional impact including nasal airway Photography to monitor progression Dermatological review of associated rosacea Progressive enlargement, thickening and lobulation of the nose from sebaceous gland hyperplasia and fibrosis, representing the phymatous form of rosacea It predominantly affects the lower nose, producing a bulbous, irregular contour with dilated follicular openings It occurs far more often in men and usually develops in the context of long-standing rosacea Contrary to popular belief, it is not caused by alcohol excess A rare but important concern is squamous or basal cell carcinoma arising within or mimicking rhinophyma Advanced disease is managed surgically or with ablative techniques to recontour the nose A non-healing ulcer, bleeding nodule or rapidly growing lesion suggesting malignancy Nasal airway obstruction from bulk Atypical rapid progression Features suggesting granulomatous or lymphomatous infiltration Attributing the condition to alcohol and stigmatising the patient Missing a carcinoma arising within rhinophymatous tissue Overlooking nasal airway compromise Neglecting treatment of the underlying rosacea Rhinophyma is the end stage of phymatous rosacea, in which chronic inflammation drives marked hyperplasia of sebaceous glands, dermal fibrosis and connective-tissue overgrowth of the nasal skin. Progressive sebaceous and fibrous expansion distorts the nasal contour and enlarges follicular openings. The underlying rosacea-associated vascular and inflammatory changes, rather than any dietary or alcohol factor, account for the disfigurement, and occasionally cutaneous malignancy develops within the thickened tissue. The condition is benign but progressive if untreated and can be cosmetically and functionally disabling; surgical recontouring generally gives good results, though rosacea persists.

mucosa by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis, an encapsulated Gram-negative bacillus acquired by inhalation, typically in conditions of overcrowding and poor sanitation. The organism is engulfed by macrophages but resists intracellular killing, giving rise to the distinctive foamy Mikulicz cells that dominate the granulomatous stage. A sustained inflammatory response with plasma cells and Russell bodies leads progressively to fibrosis and scarring. This staged process explains the transition from non-specific catarrhal symptoms through proliferative masses to the sclerotic deformity and airway narrowing of late disease. With prolonged appropriate antibiotics the infection can be controlled, but late fibrotic disease may leave permanent structural deformity and airway narrowing, and relapse can occur if therapy is inadequate in duration.

disseminated cases Rhinosporidiosis is caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi, now regarded as an aquatic protistan parasite, which is thought to enter the mucosa through minor trauma after contact with contaminated stagnant water. The organism proliferates within the mucosa, maturing through trophic stages into large sporangia packed with endospores. Rupture of a sporangium releases endospores that seed adjacent tissue, driving formation of highly vascular polypoidal granulomatous masses. The rich vascularity accounts for the marked tendency to bleed, and local dissemination of endospores explains frequent recurrence after incomplete removal. Complete excision with cautery of the base usually gives a good outcome, but recurrence is common owing to local spread of endospores, and disease occasionally disseminates to other mucosal sites; the condition is chronic and can be troublesome to eradicate fully.

that establish the diagnosis Overlooking treatable contributors such as elevated phytanic acid in the PEX7 form Failing to arrange early cataract assessment and airway or feeding support Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata is a disorder of peroxisomal metabolism in which the import or activity of a small group of peroxisomal enzymes is disrupted. In the common PEX7 form, the receptor for the peroxisomal targeting signal 2 fails, so enzymes bearing that signal, including those for plasmalogen biosynthesis and phytanic acid alpha-oxidation, are not correctly delivered to the peroxisome. Types 2 and 3 involve direct deficiency of the plasmalogen synthetic enzymes encoded by GNPAT and AGPS. The shared consequence is severely deficient plasmalogen synthesis, which impairs formation of myelin and other specialised membranes; accumulation of phytanic acid contributes in the PEX7 form. These defects underlie the skeletal, ocular and neurological features. The classic form carries a poor prognosis with severe developmental impairment and reduced survival, many affected children not surviving early childhood, although milder variants with residual enzyme function can survive longer with a less severe course.

and bacteraemia The organism may be dismissed as a diphtheroid contaminant in the laboratory, so a compatible clinical picture should prompt careful identification, aided by its salmon-pink colonies Cavitating pneumonia with bacteraemia in an immunocompromised patient Neurological signs suggesting brain abscess from dissemination Rapid clinical deterioration or respiratory failure Relapse or persistent infection despite therapy indicating inadequate immune reconstitution Dismissing the isolate as a diphtheroid skin contaminant and missing a true pathogen Using single-agent or short-course therapy, which promotes relapse and resistance Overlooking the animal or soil exposure history in an immunocompromised patient with cavitary pneumonia Failing to address the underlying immunosuppression, without which cure is difficult Rhodococcus equi is an environmental actinomycete found in soil enriched by the manure of horses and other herbivores. Humans are usually infected by inhalation of contaminated dust, and less often through wound inoculation or ingestion. As a facultative intracellular organism it is taken up by alveolar macrophages, where a virulence plasmid encoding virulence-associated proteins allows it to survive and replicate within the phagosome, subverting normal killing. Effective containment depends on T-cell-mediated macrophage activation, which explains why serious disease is concentrated in patients with defective cellular immunity. Uncontrolled intracellular growth drives a granulomatous, necrotising, and often cavitating pneumonia; sometimes the histology shows malakoplakia with characteristic intracytoplasmic inclusions. Haematogenous dissemination can seed the brain, bone, and other sites. Outcome hinges on immune status and prompt, prolonged combination therapy; with restoration of cell-mediated immunity (for example effective antiretroviral therapy) many patients recover, but disseminated disease in profoundly immunosuppressed hosts carries appreciable mortality and a risk of relapse.

ribbing disease — multiple diaphyseal sclerosis, hereditary multiple diaphyseal sclerosis Camurati-Engelmann diaphyseal dysplasia osteoid osteoma chronic sclerosing osteomyelitis osteosarcoma or sclerotic metastasis stress fracture with periosteal reaction Paget disease of bone chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis plain radiography of the long bones for diaphyseal cortical thickening bone scintigraphy to localise active lesions MRI to assess marrow and exclude a nidus or tumour CT to characterise cortical sclerosis and exclude an osteoid osteoma nidus inflammatory markers and cultures to exclude infection family history assessment and, where indicated, TGFB1 gene testing Ribbing disease is a rare sclerosing dysplasia characterised by endosteal and periosteal new bone formation confined to the diaphyses of the long bones, most often the tibia and femur. It typically presents after puberty in adults, distinguishing it from the childhood-onset Camurati-Engelmann disease it otherwise resembles radiologically. Involvement is often asymmetrical and may be limited to one or a few bones, unlike the symmetrical pattern of Camurati-Engelmann disease. The dominant symptom is deep, activity-related bone pain in the affected limb, and many cases are discovered when investigating unexplained leg pain. There is no associated myopathy, cranial involvement or systemic features, which helps separate it from diaphyseal dysplasia with neuromuscular signs. Bone scintigraphy shows increased uptake at active sites and helps map disease and exclude alternative causes of sclerosis. It is frequently a diagnosis of exclusion after osteoid osteoma, chronic osteomyelitis, and sclerosing malignancy have been ruled out. Management is largely symptomatic; the pain can be difficult to control and the natural history is variable. night pain unresponsive to rest suggesting osteoid osteoma or malignancy systemic features such as fever or weight loss pointing to infection or tumour a soft-tissue mass or cortical destruction on imaging rapidly progressive symptoms warranting biopsy Mistaking focal diaphyseal sclerosis for osteosarcoma or metastasis and proceeding to aggressive intervention. Overlooking a small osteoid osteoma nidus within thickened cortex. Assuming symmetry and thereby confusing it with Camurati-Engelmann disease. Attributing the pain to soft-tissue causes and delaying dedicated bone imaging. Performing unnecessary biopsy when the radiological and clinical picture is characteristic. Ribbing disease is a disorder of bone modelling in which excessive endosteal and periosteal apposition thickens the diaphyseal cortex and narrows the medullary canal. The molecular basis is incompletely understood; some pedigrees suggest autosomal recessive inheritance, and it is regarded by many authorities as part of a spectrum with Camurati-Engelmann disease, which is linked to activating mutations in the TGF-beta 1 gene that increase osteoblastic bone formation. Unlike the generalised, symmetrical, childhood-onset TGF-beta 1 disorder, Ribbing disease is later in onset, focal and asymmetrical, and spares the skull and the neuromuscular system, implying a distinct or attenuated mechanism of dysregulated diaphyseal bone turnover. Ribbing disease is benign and does not undergo malignant transformation, but chronic bone pain may be persistent and refractory, and the clinical course fluctuates over years.

it encompasses the Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere and Fazio-Londe phenotypes The biochemical profile can mimic multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenation deficiency (MADD), with an abnormal acylcarnitine pattern and organic aciduria, because flavin cofactors are needed for fatty-acid oxidation flavoenzymes Features include sensorineural deafness, bulbar palsy, axial and limb weakness, sensory ataxia, optic atrophy and respiratory compromise Plasma flavin levels may be low but can be normal, so a normal result does not exclude the diagnosis High-dose riboflavin supplementation frequently stabilises or reverses neurological decline and normalises the MADD-like metabolites Treatment should be started on clinical suspicion rather than deferred until genetic confirmation The MADD-like biochemistry can be a helpful clue that points towards a riboflavin-responsive disorder Respiratory insufficiency from bulbar and diaphragmatic weakness Rapidly progressive dysphagia with aspiration risk Acute metabolic decompensation during catabolic illness Progressive visual loss from optic atrophy Diagnosing genetic MADD and missing the riboflavin-responsive transporter defect Withholding empirical riboflavin pending genetic results Interpreting normal plasma flavin levels as excluding the diagnosis Attributing the picture to an untreatable motor neurone disease Riboflavin transporter deficiency is caused by impaired cellular uptake of riboflavin (vitamin B2) owing to loss-of-function variants in SLC52A2 or SLC52A3. Reduced riboflavin uptake depletes the flavin cofactors FAD and FMN, which are essential for many flavoenzymes, including the acyl-CoA dehydrogenases and electron-transfer flavoprotein of mitochondrial fatty-acid beta-oxidation. Cofactor deficiency therefore produces a secondary, riboflavin-responsive phenocopy of multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenation deficiency, with a corresponding acylcarnitine and organic acid signature, and drives neurodegeneration of cranial motor nuclei, anterior horn cells and the auditory and optic pathways. Because the underlying problem is cofactor delivery, supraphysiological riboflavin can restore flavoenzyme function and improve both the metabolic and neurological abnormalities. Without treatment the disorder is progressive and potentially fatal, but early high-dose riboflavin supplementation often halts and partly reverses neurological deterioration, making prompt recognition decisive for outcome.

Because the accumulated polyols concentrate in the brain, cerebral magnetic resonance spectroscopy is especially informative. The disorder is progressive but often unusually slowly, with accumulating neurological disability over years; there is no curative therapy and long-term outcome depends on the extent of central and peripheral nervous system involvement.

the toxicity is due to tyrosine crystal deposition Dietary restriction of tyrosine and phenylalanine improves the ocular and cutaneous features and may protect neurodevelopment Corneal lesions are typically bilateral, which helps distinguish them from infective dendritic ulcers Severe or ulcerating keratitis threatening vision Marked, persistent hypertyrosinaemia despite treatment Progressive developmental or behavioural concerns Diagnostic confusion with recurrent herpetic keratitis leading to inappropriate antiviral or steroid use Misdiagnosing the bilateral pseudodendritic keratitis as herpes simplex and treating accordingly Overlooking hypertyrosinaemia as the unifying cause of eye and skin findings Assuming hepatorenal involvement as in tyrosinaemia type I Delaying dietary treatment and allowing corneal or neurological damage Richner-Hanhart syndrome is caused by deficiency of hepatic cytosolic tyrosine aminotransferase, the first enzyme of tyrosine catabolism, due to biallelic TAT variants. The block causes tyrosine to accumulate in blood and tissues. Supersaturated tyrosine crystallises within cells, and the resulting crystalline deposition triggers an inflammatory response in the cornea and skin, producing the characteristic pseudodendritic keratitis and painful palmoplantar keratoderma. Elevated tyrosine may also affect the developing brain, accounting for the variable intellectual disability. Because the disorder does not involve the downstream toxic metabolites of tyrosinaemia type I, the liver and kidneys are spared; lowering tyrosine through dietary restriction of tyrosine and phenylalanine reverses the crystal-driven ocular and skin disease. With early dietary restriction of tyrosine and phenylalanine the ocular and skin lesions resolve and neurodevelopmental outcome can be favourable; untreated disease risks corneal scarring and cognitive impairment.

progression of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or small lymphocytic lymphoma into an aggressive lymphoma. In the majority of large-cell cases the transformed clone is genetically derived from the original leukaemic clone, having acquired additional driver lesions such as TP53 disruption, MYC activation, CDKN2A loss and NOTCH1 mutation that confer a proliferative, chemoresistant phenotype. A minority of large-cell cases and many Hodgkin-type transformations are clonally unrelated and, in the latter, Epstein-Barr virus frequently contributes within the immunosuppressed microenvironment of the underlying disease. The clonal relationship and the accumulated genetic damage largely determine the aggressive behaviour and generally poor response to therapy. Clonally related diffuse large B-cell-type Richter transformation carries a poor prognosis with short survival despite intensive therapy, particularly when TP53 is disrupted; clonally unrelated cases and Hodgkin-type transformation generally fare better, and allogeneic HSCT offers the main prospect of durable remission in eligible responders.

CSF analysis when meningoencephalitis is suspected Immune thrombocytopenic purpura / thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura Kawasaki disease Drug hypersensitivity / drug rash Immune-complex (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis Acute abdomen prompting exploratory laparotomy when abdominal pain and tenderness dominate Rickettsiae are small, obligately intracellular, gram-negative coccobacilli/short bacilli, most spread by a tick, mite, flea, or louse; except for louse-borne typhus, humans are incidental hosts. The agents span seven genera (Rickettsia, Orientia, Ehrlichia, Anaplasma, Neorickettsia, Candidatus Neoehrlichia, and Coxiella). During the first roughly 5 days the acute presentations are largely indistinguishable: fever, headache, and myalgia, with or without nausea, vomiting, and cough; later differentiating features such as rash, eschar, pneumonitis, or meningoencephalitis emerge. Heightened clinical suspicion based on exposure history should prompt empiric antibiotics rather than waiting for confirmation (p.1454). A characteristic laboratory triad supports the diagnosis across many of these infections: thrombocytopenia, a normal or low white-cell count, mildly to moderately elevated hepatic aminotransferases, and hyponatremia (p.1454). Coxiella burnetii, R. prowazekii, and R. typhi can survive long periods outside the host and are highly infectious by inhalation (a single Coxiella organism can cause pneumonia), making several agents bioterrorism concerns (p.1454). In Rocky Mountain spotted fever the rash is progressive and unreliable: present in only about 14% on day 1 and roughly 49% by day 3, appearing on day 6 or later in ~20% and never appearing in about 10% of cases; classic palm/sole involvement tends to come late and may not occur at all (p.1456-1457). Only about 3% of RMSF patients show the classic triad of fever, rash, and tick exposure in the first 3 days, and only ~60% recall a tick bite; serology is typically negative at presentation, so treatment must not await a positive result (p.1457). An eschar (tache noire) at the bite site is a useful clue in several spotted fevers (notably African tick-bite fever ~90%, rickettsialpox, Mediterranean spotted fever ~50%) and in scrub typhus, but is absent in the typhus group (epidemic and murine typhus have no eschar) (p.1455). Ehrlichioses/anaplasmoses (Anaplasmataceae) target hematopoietic cells: E. chaffeensis (HME) and E. muris infect mononuclear phagocytes, while E. ewingii and A. phagocytophilum (HGA) infect neutrophils; intracytoplasmic morulae may be seen on blood smear but only in a minority (about 20% or less in HME, 20-75% in HGA) (p.1460-1462). Of the Rickettsiaceae, in descending case-fatality order the life-threatening species are R. rickettsii (RMSF), R. prowazekii (louse-borne typhus), Orientia tsutsugamushi (scrub typhus), R. conorii (MSF), and R. typhi (murine typhus); many spotted-fever species (e.g., R. parkeri, R. africae, R. akari, R. felis) have never been documented to cause a fatal illness (p.1456). Of the rickettsial agents, only C. burnetii is documented to cause chronic illness, and only R. prowazekii causes a recrudescent illness (Brill-Zinsser disease) when latent infection reactivates years after the acute episode (p.1454, p.1459). Q fever is an inhalational zoonosis from sheep, goats, and cattle (organism shed heavily in parturition material); the infectious dose is extremely low (probably 1-10 organisms) and ~60% of infections are asymptomatic seroconversions. Acute disease presents geographically as either pneumonia or hepatitis (p.1462). Scrub typhus shows remarkable antigenic diversity with rapid loss of cross-protective immunity, so reinfection can occur within weeks to months; the classic eschar/rash/lymphadenopathy triad is often absent, with under half of travelers developing an eschar and under 40% a rash (p.1460).
