delay worsens outcome and empiric doxycycline should not be withheld Excluding RMSF because there is no rash or no recalled tick bite (~10% never rash; only ~60% recall a bite) or because palms/soles are not involved Interpreting a single acute-phase positive titer as diagnostic in endemic areas - cross-reactive preexisting antibody (e.g., from the highly prevalent R. amblyommatis or in HGA-endemic regions) can mislead; the recent apparent RMSF surge largely reflects cross-reactive single-titer enzyme immunoassays rather than true R. rickettsii disease Relying on blood PCR for RMSF or typhus - insufficiently sensitive because organisms reside in endothelium, not blood; skin/eschar biopsy is preferable Assuming negative HME serology because E. chaffeensis tests can cross-react when the true agent is another Ehrlichia; separate specific tests are needed for HME vs HGA Overlooking chronic Q fever as a cause of culture-negative endocarditis or unexplained infected aneurysm/vascular prosthesis - median latency from primary infection is ~13 months and can exceed 9 years Mislabeling epidemic typhus as typhoid fever in tropical/resource-limited settings Attributing prolonged post-Q-fever fatigue to active infection and prescribing antibiotics - a randomized trial showed long-term doxycycline did not reduce fatigue versus placebo The spotted fever and typhus group organisms (Rickettsia and Orientia) infect vascular endothelial cells and disseminate lymphohematogenously, producing widespread small-vessel infection. The fundamental injury is increased vascular permeability rather than occlusive thrombosis or ischemic necrosis; resulting edema, hypovolemia, and tissue ischemia drive the clinical picture. Platelet consumption causes thrombocytopenia in roughly a third to half of RMSF cases, but overt DIC with hypofibrinogenemia is rare; thrombin generation and fibrinolysis appear to be homeostatic responses to nonocclusive hemostatic plugs at sites of endothelial injury. Hyponatremia reflects appropriate ADH secretion in response to hypovolemia. Pathogenic rickettsiae have small, reductively evolved genomes lacking biosynthetic genes for intracellularly available molecules. Ehrlichia and Anaplasma instead parasitize vacuoles of hematopoietic cells; vasculitis and granulomas are not features of HME or HGA. Coxiella burnetii is genetically distinct from the Rickettsiaceae, survives harsh environments, escapes macrophage killing by inhibiting the final step of phagosome maturation, and adapts to the acidic phagolysosome. Outcome depends heavily on early recognition and prompt empiric therapy. RMSF mortality was 20-25% before antibiotics and is roughly 3-5% now, principally driven by diagnostic/treatment delay; confirmed-case fatality is higher (~9-10% in regions where R. rickettsii is the sole spotted-fever species), is highest in children under 10 and adults over 70, and approaches 50% in parts of Mexico and Brazil for unknown reasons. Untreated fatal RMSF typically dies 8-15 days after onset. Survivors usually recover fully, but severe disease can leave permanent neurologic deficits or gangrene requiring amputation. Mediterranean spotted fever has a severe form (~50% mortality) in patients with diabetes, alcoholism, or heart failure. Epidemic (louse-borne) typhus is fatal in 7-40% of untreated cases. Untreated classic scrub typhus has ~6% case-fatality. Acute Q fever case-fatality is ~1-2%; chronic Q fever carries high mortality (~25% in proven Dutch-outbreak cases, highest at 33% when both endocarditis and vascular infection are present). Q fever fatigue syndrome follows up to 20% of acute cases. Many SFG species (e.g., R. parkeri, R. africae, R. akari, R. felis) have never caused documented fatal illness, and African tick-bite fever is typically mild. No single unified rickettsial severity score; severity is judged by organ-system involvement and progression. Across the group, escalating clinical lines after nonspecific fever are: (1) macular/maculopapular rash; (2) eschar at the bite site; (3) vesicular rash; (4) pneumonitis with radiographic opacities/rales; (5) meningoencephalitis; and (6) progressive hypotension and multiorgan failure (sepsis/toxic-shock-like). For Q fever, the Dutch consensus group classifies chronic disease as proven, probable, or possible based on PCR positivity in blood/tissue or phase I IgG IFA >=1:800/1:1024 combined with endocarditis (modified Duke criteria), proven large-vessel/prosthetic infection on imaging, or compatible clinical and histologic findings.

It infects vascular endothelium, producing a focal dermal vasculitis at the inoculation site that forms the initial papule and subsequent eschar. Haematogenous dissemination leads to a mild generalised endothelial infection manifesting as the disseminated papulovesicular rash, but the vasculitis is limited in severity, accounting for the benign, self-limiting course. Rickettsialpox is a benign self-limiting illness that resolves within a week or two even without treatment, and doxycycline shortens the fever; no deaths have been attributed to it.

Rift Valley fever — RVF, Rift Valley fever virus infection, enzootic hepatitis Malaria Leptospirosis Viral hepatitis Other viral haemorrhagic fevers such as Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever or Ebola virus disease Q fever and other zoonotic febrile illnesses Dengue and other arboviral fevers RT-PCR on blood for viral RNA in the acute viraemic phase Serology for Rift Valley fever IgM and IgG antibodies Liver function tests to detect hepatitis and hepatic necrosis Full blood count and coagulation studies to assess for haemorrhagic disease Ophthalmological examination for retinitis in patients with visual symptoms Lumbar puncture and neuroimaging when encephalitis is suspected A mosquito-borne phlebovirus zoonosis of sub-Saharan Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, with epizootics in livestock heralding human outbreaks, often after heavy rainfall and flooding Humans are most often infected through direct contact with the blood or tissues of infected animals (abattoir workers, herders, veterinarians) as well as by mosquito bites Most infections are a self-limiting influenza-like febrile illness, but a minority develop severe disease with haemorrhagic fever, hepatitis, encephalitis, or retinitis A characteristic delayed ocular complication is macular or paramacular retinitis that can cause permanent visual loss weeks after the acute illness The haemorrhagic form features jaundice, mucosal bleeding, and hepatic necrosis and carries a high mortality Management is supportive; there is no licensed specific antiviral, and ribavirin has been considered in some settings for other viral haemorrhagic fevers but is not established for Rift Valley fever Diagnosis uses RT-PCR and serology (IgM/IgG), and laboratory handling requires enhanced biosafety because of aerosol infectivity Jaundice with mucosal or gastrointestinal bleeding indicating the haemorrhagic form Rapidly rising transaminases signalling fulminant hepatitis Altered consciousness or focal neurological signs of encephalitis Sudden visual loss from retinitis Shock or disseminated intravascular coagulation Assuming a benign course when severe hepatic, haemorrhagic, or neurological disease can develop in a minority Failing to recognise delayed retinitis presenting weeks after apparent recovery Inadequate biosafety precautions given aerosol transmissibility in the laboratory and abattoir setting Overlooking the animal-contact or outbreak history in endemic regions Confusing early disease with malaria and delaying appropriate isolation and diagnostics Rift Valley fever virus is transmitted by infected mosquitoes and by direct contact with aerosols or fluids from viraemic animals during slaughter or handling. After entry the virus replicates widely and is markedly hepatotropic, producing hepatocellular necrosis. Severe disease reflects a combination of direct viral injury, cytokine-driven vascular dysfunction, and coagulopathy, leading to haemorrhage, hepatic failure, or central nervous system and retinal involvement. Immune-mediated inflammation contributes to the delayed retinitis and encephalitic complications. The great majority recover fully from the uncomplicated febrile illness, but the haemorrhagic and encephalitic forms carry substantial mortality, and retinitis may leave permanent visual impairment.

right aortic arch — right-sided aortic arch Double aortic arch Pulmonary artery sling Innominate artery compression syndrome Aberrant right subclavian artery with a left aortic arch Mediastinal mass causing tracheal deviation Tetralogy of Fallot or truncus arteriosus (as associated conditions) Primary tracheomalacia or laryngomalacia CT angiography of the aortic arch and great vessels MR angiography Transthoracic echocardiography to detect associated intracardiac defects Barium swallow demonstrating a posterior oesophageal indentation Bronchoscopy for airway compression 22q11.2 deletion testing by FISH or microarray Chest radiograph noting a right-sided arch and an absent left aortic knuckle The aortic arch passes to the right of the trachea and crosses the right main bronchus rather than the left. Two principal patterns exist: right arch with mirror-image branching and right arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery. Mirror-image branching carries a very high association with cyanotic congenital heart disease, particularly tetralogy of Fallot and truncus arteriosus. A right arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery arising from a Kommerell diverticulum, combined with a left-sided ligamentum arteriosum, completes a vascular ring. This ring-forming configuration is strongly linked to 22q11.2 deletion, so genetic testing and cardiac evaluation are warranted. Many isolated right arches are asymptomatic and found incidentally, but a ring may cause stridor, dysphagia and recurrent respiratory infection. CT or MR angiography delineates the branching pattern, the presence of a Kommerell diverticulum and any airway compression. Symptomatic vascular rings are treated surgically by dividing the ligamentum and, when the diverticulum is large, addressing it directly. Cyanosis or a murmur suggesting associated cyanotic heart disease Progressive stridor or respiratory distress from ring compression Dysphagia with feeding difficulty and failure to thrive Aneurysmal enlargement of a Kommerell diverticulum Overlooking the strong association between mirror-image branching and cyanotic congenital heart disease. Failing to test for 22q11.2 deletion when an aberrant subclavian and ring are present. Missing an enlarging Kommerell diverticulum that may require resection. Assuming any right arch forms a ring, or conversely that all are innocuous. Achieving incomplete symptom relief if the Kommerell diverticulum or ligamentum is not adequately addressed. A right aortic arch arises when the embryonic left arch regresses and the right fourth arch and right dorsal aorta persist, reversing the normal pattern. In mirror-image branching the regression occurs distal to the ductus, producing branching that mirrors normal anatomy and rarely forming a ring, but coexisting conotruncal cardiac malformations are common. When instead the left dorsal aorta regresses between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, the left subclavian arises aberrantly from the descending aorta via a Kommerell diverticulum and passes behind the oesophagus; together with a left-sided ligamentum arteriosum this encircles the trachea and oesophagus to form a loose vascular ring that may compress these structures. An isolated asymptomatic right aortic arch requires no treatment and has an excellent prognosis; when it forms a symptomatic ring or accompanies congenital heart disease, outcome depends on surgical relief of compression and repair of the underlying cardiac lesion.

self-limiting viral illness and discharging without follow-up Substituting a beta-lactam, which is ineffective against rickettsiae Rickettsia rickettsii is an obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium that, following inoculation by a feeding tick, invades and multiplies within vascular endothelial cells and to a lesser extent smooth muscle of small and medium vessels. Widespread infection of the endothelium produces a systemic small-vessel vasculitis with increased vascular permeability, microvascular leak, oedema, activation of coagulation and localised microthrombi. This vascular injury underlies the rash, the tissue oedema and hypovolaemia, and end-organ damage affecting the brain, lungs, kidneys and other organs, and in severe disease can progress to shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation and multi-organ failure. With prompt doxycycline most patients recover fully, but untreated or late-treated disease carries a high case-fatality rate; survivors of severe illness may be left with neurological deficits or, rarely, limb loss from vascular compromise.

disorder of uncertain cause with several contributing mechanisms. Dysregulation of the innate immune system with abnormal cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide processing promotes inflammation and vascular changes. Neurovascular dysregulation drives flushing and persistent erythema, while an increased density of Demodex mites and altered cutaneous microbiome may stimulate the inflammatory response. Ultraviolet radiation, chronic inflammation, and vascular and lymphatic changes contribute to telangiectasia and, over time, the fibrous and sebaceous overgrowth of phymatous disease. Genetic predisposition and environmental triggers modulate expression. Rosacea is a chronic relapsing condition that is controllable but not curable; symptoms often persist for years with fluctuating severity, and phymatous changes, once established, tend to be permanent without procedural treatment.

tissues. The hallmark is emperipolesis, the presence of intact inflammatory cells within histiocyte cytoplasm. Although historically considered reactive and possibly infection- or immune-triggered, a subset harbours clonal MAPK pathway mutations, placing it within the histiocytic neoplasm spectrum. The infiltrating S100-positive histiocytes expand lymph nodes and infiltrate extranodal sites, producing the clinical manifestations. Most patients, particularly those with isolated nodal disease, follow a benign self-limiting or relapsing-remitting course, but extensive extranodal disease, central nervous system involvement, or associated immune dysregulation confers a more guarded prognosis.

Roseola infantum — sixth disease, exanthem subitum, HHV-6 infection, three-day fever Measles Rubella Scarlet fever Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) Drug hypersensitivity eruption Enteroviral exanthem Measles Rubella Enteroviral rash illness Early meningococcal or other bacterial infection presenting with high fever Clinical diagnosis is usually sufficient in a well child with the typical fever-then-rash sequence HHV-6 PCR or serology reserved for atypical, severe, or immunocompromised presentations Basic bloods to exclude bacterial sepsis when the febrile child appears unwell Neuroimaging and CSF studies if encephalitis or complicated seizures are suspected Classically affects infants and toddlers between roughly 6 months and 2 years, caused mainly by human herpesvirus 6 (and less often HHV-7) The hallmark pattern is several days of high fever in a child who otherwise looks relatively well, followed by defervescence and then the eruption of a rash The rash typically appears as the fever breaks: small rose-pink macules or maculopapules starting on the trunk and spreading to the neck and limbs, usually non-pruritic and fading within days Febrile seizures are a recognised complication because of the height of the fever, and can be the presenting concern Diagnosis is generally clinical; The virus infects lymphocytes and other cells, producing a viraemia that drives the high fever. As host immunity controls the viraemia the temperature falls and the characteristic exanthem appears. Like other herpesviruses, HHV-6 then persists in a latent state and can reactivate later, particularly under immunosuppression, where it is linked to encephalitis, marrow suppression, and graft complications. In healthy infants the illness is self-limiting with full recovery and no long-term sequelae; complications such as encephalitis are rare and are seen chiefly in immunocompromised hosts.

hydrocephalus Rosette-forming glioneuronal tumour is a rare, low-grade neoplasm with both neuronal and glial differentiation, arising most often in the midline posterior fossa around the fourth ventricle and adjacent structures, and sometimes in the pineal region or aqueduct. It is characterised by a biphasic architecture: a neurocytic component forming neurocytic rosettes and perivascular pseudorosettes, and a glial component resembling pilocytic astrocytoma. The neurocytic elements express synaptophysin, confirming neuronal differentiation. Recurrent molecular alterations, particularly of the FGFR1 gene and sometimes PIK3CA and NF1, drive its development. Growth is slow, and clinical features arise mainly from its periventricular location and obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow rather than from aggressive behaviour. Prognosis is generally favourable given the indolent, grade 1 nature of the tumour, and gross total resection can be curative. However, its midline posterior fossa location adjacent to the brainstem and cerebellar structures often limits complete removal and carries a risk of surgical morbidity, so residual tumour may be monitored or, uncommonly, treated further.

paraneoplastic process Recurrent heat-related collapse Focusing on the hyperhidrosis and missing the underlying anhidrosis and autonomic diagnosis Failing to recognise the tonic pupil and areflexia that complete the triad Attempting to suppress compensatory sweating, which may worsen heat intolerance Not distinguishing it from Holmes-Adie syndrome and the wider dysautonomia spectrum Ross syndrome is a progressive partial dysautonomia characterised by degeneration of postganglionic cholinergic autonomic neurons. Ross syndrome tends to progress slowly, with the area of anhidrosis gradually enlarging over years; it is not life-threatening, but heat intolerance and troublesome compensatory hyperhidrosis can impair quality of life.

Tendon integrity is compromised by age-related degeneration, hypovascularity near the supraspinatus insertion, and mechanical impingement beneath the coracoacromial arch, making tears increasingly common with age. Repetitive overhead loading and acute trauma superimpose on this degeneration. Once a tear occurs, the tendon tends to retract and the corresponding muscle undergoes atrophy and fatty infiltration over time, reducing repairability and allowing superior migration of the humeral head, which can eventually produce cuff-tear arthropathy. Many small and degenerative tears remain functionally acceptable with rehabilitation, but larger or acute traumatic tears repaired promptly generally do better than chronic retracted tears with fatty muscle degeneration; untreated massive tears can progress to cuff-tear arthropathy with persistent weakness and pain.

Most cases improve with structured loading rehabilitation over weeks to months, although recovery can be slow and recurrence is common if load is not managed; large or full-thickness tears may need surgical consideration.

Rotavirus Gastroenteritis — rotavirus diarrhoea, rotavirus infection, viral gastroenteritis (rotavirus) Norovirus and other viral gastroenteritis Bacterial enteritis (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, enterotoxigenic E. coli) Parasitic infection (Giardia, Cryptosporidium) Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea Systemic infection presenting with diarrhoea (e.g. urinary tract infection, sepsis) Surgical abdomen (intussusception) when vomiting and lethargy predominate Stool rotavirus antigen enzyme immunoassay or PCR when confirmation is needed Serum electrolytes, urea, and creatinine in moderate to severe dehydration Capillary or venous blood gas to assess acid-base status in severe illness Blood glucose in a lethargic or severely dehydrated child Stool culture if bacterial infection is suspected (blood, mucus, high fever) A leading cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea in infants and young children, especially between about 3 and 24 months of age. Typically presents with abrupt onset of vomiting followed by profuse watery, non-bloody stools, often with fever. Spread is faecal-oral; the virus is highly contagious and stable in the environment, so outbreaks in daycare and hospital settings are common. Assessment of hydration status guides management far more than laboratory testing, which is rarely needed for diagnosis. Oral rehydration therapy is the cornerstone of treatment for mild to moderate dehydration; intravenous fluids are reserved for severe dehydration or failed oral therapy. Early refeeding with an age-appropriate diet is encouraged once rehydration is achieved; prolonged fasting and dilute feeds are discouraged. Antibiotics and antimotility agents have no role and may be harmful; routine antiemetics are generally avoided in young children. Live oral rotavirus vaccines given in infancy substantially reduce severe disease and hospitalisation. Antigen immunoassay or PCR on stool can confirm the pathogen when confirmation is required for epidemiologic or infection-control purposes. Signs of severe dehydration or hypovolaemic shock Persistent vomiting preventing oral rehydration Altered consciousness, lethargy, or seizures Bloody stools or high fever suggesting alternative or complicating diagnosis Abdominal distension or severe pain raising concern for intussusception Underestimating fluid deficit and failing to reassess hydration during treatment Using dilute or lactose-heavy feeds and prolonged fasting instead of prompt refeeding Prescribing antibiotics or antimotility drugs that offer no benefit Missing intussusception in a child with vomiting, lethargy, and abdominal signs Rotavirus infects the mature enterocytes at the tips of the small intestinal villi, causing villous blunting and loss of absorptive surface. This produces malabsorption of nutrients and water with an osmotic diarrhoea, while the viral nonstructural protein NSP4 acts as an enterotoxin that triggers secretory diarrhoea and disrupts calcium homeostasis. The combination of impaired absorption, secretion, and reduced disaccharidase (including lactase) activity leads to voluminous watery stool and rapid fluid and electrolyte losses. Most children recover fully within about a week with appropriate rehydration; mortality is low where fluid therapy is accessible but remains significant in resource-limited settings due to severe dehydration.

RECQL4-related and genetically heterogeneous forms Rothmund-Thomson syndrome type 2 is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in RECQL4, encoding a RecQ-family DNA helicase that participates in DNA replication and repair and in maintaining genomic and mitochondrial stability. For individuals without malignancy, life expectancy may be near normal, but the elevated risk of osteosarcoma, most pronounced in RECQL4-associated disease and typically in childhood or adolescence, is the main determinant of outcome. Later skin cancers and the cumulative effects of photosensitivity add to long-term morbidity.

A portion of conjugated bilirubin normally effluxes from hepatocytes back into the sinusoids and is then re-taken up by these transporters. neuropathy Rapidly worsening tremor or ataxia out of keeping with slowly progressive inherited disease New bulbar or breathing symptoms requiring review Treating the presentation as isolated essential tremor and overlooking the underlying neuropathy Attributing the ataxia to a cerebellar lesion rather than sensory deafferentation Regarding Roussy-Levy as a separate disorder rather than a CMT1 phenotype Missing a treatable acquired demyelinating neuropathy Roussy-Levy syndrome is now understood as a phenotypic variant of demyelinating CMT, most often associated with PMP22 or MPZ variants that impair peripheral myelin. The demyelinating neuropathy causes distal weakness and prominent loss of large-fibre sensory function; the resulting deafferentation of proprioceptive pathways produces sensory ataxia and contributes to the characteristic postural tremor. The tremor is thought to arise from disturbed sensorimotor feedback rather than a distinct central lesion. As in other CMT1 subtypes, repeated demyelination and remyelination generate onion-bulb formations and secondary axonal loss, and the diffuse myelin involvement explains the uniformly slow conduction velocities. Typically slowly progressive with long preservation of ambulation; the tremor and ataxia can be functionally limiting but the overall course mirrors that of other CMT1 subtypes with normal life expectancy.

Increased vascular permeability, linked to raised levels of vascular endothelial growth factor and pro-inflammatory cytokines, is thought to underlie the prominent subcutaneous oedema surrounding the inflamed tendon sheaths. The condition may be idiopathic or arise as a paraneoplastic phenomenon accompanying solid organ or haematological malignancy, and it shares immunopathogenic features with polymyalgia rheumatica and other seronegative arthropathies of the elderly. Idiopathic RS3PE usually remits within months and responds excellently to low-dose corticosteroids with a favourable long-term outlook; however, paraneoplastic cases carry the prognosis of the underlying malignancy, making cancer surveillance essential.

Rubella (German Measles) — German measles, three-day measles, Rubivirus infection, Congenital rubella syndrome, CRS Measles (rubeola) Scarlet fever Roseola (exanthem subitum) Toxoplasmosis Fifth disease (erythema infectiosum / parvovirus B19) Zika virus infection Other febrile illnesses with suboccipital and postauricular lymphadenopathy Measles (rubeola) Roseola Fifth disease (parvovirus B19) Toxoplasmosis Zika virus infection For CRS: other intrauterine (TORCH) infections such as cytomegalovirus and toxoplasmosis producing nonspecific neonatal findings Serology: rubella IgM in an acute-phase serum specimen, or a fourfold rise in IgG titer between acute- and convalescent-phase sera; IgM-capture ELISA is regarded as most accurate (Harrison 22e p.1644). Timing of paired sera: acute specimen within 7-10 days of illness onset, convalescent specimen about 14-21 days later; repeat IgM testing if an early specimen (before day 5 after rash) is negative (Harrison 22e p.1644). IgG avidity testing to distinguish primary infection (low-avidity antibodies, recent infection) from reinfection (mature high-avidity IgG indicating infection at least ~2 months earlier); especially useful in pregnant women to assess CRS risk (Harrison 22e p.1644). RT-PCR for viral RNA detection (preferred from nasopharyngeal swab; throat swab or urine acceptable), collected as soon as possible after onset, ideally 1-3 days and no later than 7 days; virus isolation by culture also possible (Harrison 22e p.1644). CRS confirmation: serum IgM (normally present up to ~6 months, sometimes up to 1 year; may be absent at birth and require retesting at 1 month), and persistence of rubella IgG beyond the expected decline of passively transferred maternal antibody (titer not declining at the expected twofold-per-month rate); RT-PCR/culture of nasopharyngeal, throat, or urine specimens, most likely positive within the first 6 months (Harrison 22e p.1644). Routine prenatal screening for rubella IgG; a positive IgG indicates immunity (Harrison 22e p.1644-1645). Scarlet fever (toxin-mediated streptococcal exanthem clinically similar to rubella) Other drug or hypersensitivity maculopapular eruptions Caused by rubella virus, an enveloped single-stranded positive-sense RNA virus of the Matonaviridae family (genus Rubivirus); only a single antigenic type exists and humans are the only known reservoir (Harrison 22e p.1643). Acquired rubella typically presents as a mild generalized maculopapular rash lasting up to about 3 days, but as many as roughly half of infections are subclinical or occur without a rash (Harrison 22e p.1643). Incubation period averages 14 days (range about 12-23 days); in older children and adults a 1- to 5-day prodrome of low-grade fever, malaise, and upper respiratory symptoms may precede the rash, whereas in young children rash is often the first sign (Harrison 22e p.1643). Occipital and postauricular lymphadenopathy is characteristic and may appear during the second week after exposure (Harrison 22e p.1643). Arthralgia and arthritis are common complications in infected adults, particularly women; thrombocytopenia and encephalitis are less common (Harrison 22e p.1643). Persons with acquired rubella may shed virus from about 7 days before rash onset to roughly 5-7 days afterward, and both clinical and subclinical infections are considered contagious (Harrison 22e p.1643). The most serious consequence is congenital rubella syndrome (CRS), which results from maternal infection during pregnancy, especially the first trimester; the classic triad is cataracts, hearing impairment, and heart defects (Harrison 22e p.1644). Hearing impairment is the single most common defect of CRS, and the classic complete triad is seen in only about 10% of CRS infants (Harrison 22e p.1644). Maternal infection within the first 10 weeks of gestation carries roughly a 90% risk of delivering an infant with CRS; risk declines later in pregnancy and fetal defects are rare after about 16 weeks, though sensorineural hearing deficit can still occur with infection up to about 20 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1644-1645). Infants with CRS can shed large quantities of virus (notably from throat secretions and urine) for up to 1 year, so only rubella-immune individuals should care for them (Harrison 22e p.1643). Reinfection with rubella virus, although uncommon, is possible and may produce detectable IgM antibodies (Harrison 22e p.1644). Rubella is no longer endemic in the United States (endemic transmission interrupted by 2001), but importations and sporadic cases continue, so vigilance is warranted in adults migrating from or returning from areas without rubella control (Harrison 22e p.1643). Maternal rubella infection during the first trimester (highest risk of CRS, up to ~90% within the first 10 weeks of gestation) (Harrison 22e p.1644). A susceptible pregnant woman with exposure to or symptoms of a rubella-like illness, requiring IgM testing and low-avidity IgG confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1645). A neonate with cataracts, hearing impairment, congenital heart defects, or 'blueberry muffin' purpura suggestive of CRS (Harrison 22e p.1644). Encephalitis or significant thrombocytopenia complicating acquired rubella (Harrison 22e p.1643). An index case of CRS in a nosocomial or congregate setting, given prolonged viral shedding and outbreak potential (Harrison 22e p.1643). Relying on clinical diagnosis is unreliable because rubella mimics many rash illnesses, has varied presentations, and is frequently subclinical or mild; laboratory confirmation is the only reliable way to confirm acute disease (Harrison 22e p.1644). A negative rubella IgM drawn before day 5 after rash onset does not exclude infection and should be repeated (Harrison 22e p.1644). Rubella IgM testing is not recommended in pregnant women without a history of illness or contact with a rubella-like illness because of the risk of false-positive results (Harrison 22e p.1645). An infant with suspected CRS who tests IgM-negative shortly after birth should be retested at 1 month, since IgM may not yet be detectable (Harrison 22e p.1644). Worldwide rubella case counts are likely underestimated because disease is often mild, care may not be sought, cases may go unrecognized or unreported, and some countries detect cases only through measles surveillance (Harrison 22e p.1643). Live attenuated rubella-containing vaccine should not be given to women known to be pregnant, and pregnancy should be avoided for 28 days after vaccination; however, inadvertent vaccination during pregnancy is not ordinarily a reason to consider termination, as no CRS occurred among ~3000 such pregnancies followed (Harrison 22e p.1645). Rubella virus spreads person to person via respiratory droplets. After primary implantation and replication in the nasopharynx it spreads to regional lymph nodes, followed by viremia. In pregnant women the viremia frequently infects the placenta; placental replication can then seed fetal organs. In the infected fetus nearly all organs may be involved, and the hallmark is a chronic infection that persists throughout intrauterine development and for up to 1 year after birth. Tissue effects of rubella virus range from no obvious impact to cell destruction. The pathology of postnatal (acquired) rubella is limited because the disease is mild, whereas the pathology of CRS is well defined even though its pathogenesis remains poorly delineated (Harrison 22e p.1643). Acquired rubella is generally a mild, self-limited illness; the rash usually resolves within about 3 days, and serious complications such as encephalitis and thrombocytopenia are uncommon. The major prognostic concern is congenital infection: maternal infection in early pregnancy may lead to miscarriage, fetal death, premature delivery, or live birth with severe and often permanent defects (eyes, ears, heart, and CNS). Permanent CRS manifestations include deafness, congenital heart defects, cataracts and other eye defects, microcephaly, and neurodevelopmental sequelae, whereas manifestations such as hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenic purpura, and adenopathy are transient. Immunity following infection or a single dose of rubella-containing vaccine (seroconversion in >=95%) is considered long-term and probably lifelong (Harrison 22e p.1644-1645). No formal severity grading system is described. Clinically, infection is categorized by host and timing: subclinical/mild acquired rubella; symptomatic acquired rubella (rash with possible arthralgia/arthritis, rarely thrombocytopenia or encephalitis); congenital rubella virus infection without apparent signs; and congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) with transient versus permanent manifestations, where fetal risk is greatest with maternal infection in the first 10 weeks of gestation (~90%) and declines markedly after ~16 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1644-1645).

Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome — RTS, RSTS, broad thumb-hallux syndrome, CREBBP, EP300 Cornelia de Lange syndrome Floating-Harbor syndrome Saethre-Chotzen syndrome Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome Cohen syndrome Kabuki syndrome Sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis of CREBBP and EP300 Chromosomal microarray to detect 16p13.3 microdeletions involving CREBBP Echocardiography for congenital heart disease Renal tract ultrasound for structural anomalies Ophthalmology review for refractive error, strabismus, glaucoma and lacrimal duct obstruction Hearing assessment and monitoring for recurrent otitis media Broad, often angulated thumbs and great toes are the signature finding and a key diagnostic clue The facial gestalt includes down-slanting palpebral fissures, a beaked or convex nose with the columella extending below the alae, highly arched eyebrows, and a grimacing smile Postnatal growth failure, microcephaly and intellectual disability with a friendly, sociable temperament are typical Most cases arise from de novo autosomal dominant variants in CREBBP; a minority involve EP300 and tend to be milder facially but may include maternal pre-eclampsia in pregnancy Both genes encode histone acetyltransferases, so the condition is a disorder of chromatin regulation Keloid formation, recurrent respiratory and ear infections, and feeding difficulties are common There is an increased lifetime risk of benign and malignant tumours, warranting attention to new lesions New or rapidly enlarging masses given the increased neoplasia risk Signs of raised intraocular pressure or glaucoma threatening vision Recurrent aspiration or severe apnoea related to airway and feeding problems Anaesthetic difficulty from a narrow airway and reported arrhythmia risk Missing the diagnosis when digital broadening is subtle and the facial features are mild, as in some EP300 cases Overlooking treatable glaucoma or lacrimal duct obstruction Failing to warn about keloid risk before elective surgery Inadequate preoperative airway and cardiac assessment before anaesthesia Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome results from haploinsufficiency of transcriptional coactivators with intrinsic histone acetyltransferase activity, encoded by CREBBP and its paralogue EP300. These proteins acetylate histones and remodel chromatin to permit transcription of numerous developmental genes. Reduced acetyltransferase dosage impairs the coordinated gene expression required for skeletal, craniofacial and neuronal development, producing the characteristic broad digits, dysmorphism, growth impairment and cognitive deficit. The same chromatin-regulatory role underlies the elevated tumour predisposition. Most individuals survive into adulthood with moderate intellectual disability and require lifelong support; overall outlook is shaped by cardiac anomalies, infection burden and tumour surveillance. Life expectancy can approach normal with good multidisciplinary care.

regurgitation as refractory reflux and escalating acid suppression Ordering repeated procedures instead of recognising the postprandial effortless pattern Confusing the condition with an eating The bleeding tendency is usually manageable, but the defining concern is the high lifetime risk of myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukaemia; outcomes depend on early detection through surveillance and on timely allogeneic transplantation using a mutation-negative donor when transformation supervenes.

Ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm — sinus of Valsalva aneurysm rupture Coronary arteriovenous fistula Patent ductus arteriosus Ventricular septal defect with aortic regurgitation Aortopulmonary window Aortic dissection involving a sinus Transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiography Cardiac CT or MRI to define the aneurysm and rupture site Assessment of shunt magnitude and cardiac function Evaluation for associated ventricular septal defect and aortic regurgitation Exclusion of endocarditis where relevant An aneurysm of an aortic sinus that ruptures, usually into a right-sided chamber, creating an aorto-cardiac shunt The right coronary sinus is most commonly involved, often rupturing into the right ventricle or atrium Rupture may be acute with chest pain, breathlessness and heart failure, or more insidious It produces a loud continuous murmur from the aorto-cardiac shunt It may be congenital or associated with connective tissue disease, infection or trauma Diagnosis is by echocardiography and surgical or transcatheter closure is usually required Acute heart failure or haemodynamic collapse at rupture Large shunt with rapid decompensation Associated endocarditis Compression of adjacent structures or coronary compromise by an unruptured aneurysm Attributing the continuous murmur to a patent ductus or coronary fistula Missing an associated ventricular septal defect or aortic regurgitation Delaying closure until heart failure is advanced Overlooking endocarditis as a precipitant A sinus of Valsalva aneurysm is a localised dilatation of an aortic sinus, typically from congenital weakness at the junction of the aortic media and the annulus, sometimes exacerbated by connective tissue disease or infection. When it ruptures, high-pressure aortic blood flows through the defect into a lower-pressure cardiac chamber, most often the right ventricle or atrium, creating a left-to-right (aorto-cardiac) shunt. The resulting volume load causes heart failure, and the continuous pressure gradient generates a characteristic continuous murmur. Untreated rupture leads to progressive heart failure, but surgical or transcatheter closure generally gives good results, particularly when performed before severe ventricular dysfunction develops.

neonatal hepatopathy for another cause of infantile liver failure Failing to distinguish it from MAT I/III and GNMT deficiency, which have very different implications S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase removes S-adenosylhomocysteine, the product formed whenever S-adenosylmethionine donates a methyl group. Because SAH is a potent feedback inhibitor of methyltransferases, its clearance is essential to keep transmethylation running. When the enzyme is deficient, SAH accumulates and inhibits methylation reactions throughout the body, while methionine and S-adenosylmethionine also rise as the cycle backs up. Impaired methylation, particularly of substrates important for muscle and liver, together with disturbed creatine and phosphatidylcholine synthesis, is thought to produce the myopathy, hepatopathy and neurodevelopmental features. Prognosis depends on early recognition and treatment; dietary and supplementary therapy can improve muscle, liver and developmental outcomes, whereas late diagnosis carries a risk of persistent neurological and hepatic impairment.

saber sheath trachea — sabre-sheath trachea, scabbard trachea post-intubation or post-tracheostomy tracheal stenosis tracheomalacia and excessive dynamic airway collapse extrinsic tracheal compression by goitre or mediastinal mass relapsing polychondritis tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica tracheobronchial amyloidosis tracheobronchomegaly chest CT with measurement of coronal and sagittal tracheal diameters pulmonary function testing to characterise the associated obstructive disease chest radiograph demonstrating the coronal narrowing on the frontal view bronchoscopy where an intrinsic stenosing or infiltrative process needs exclusion dynamic expiratory CT if coexisting tracheomalacia is suspected assessment of smoking history and alpha-1 antitrypsin status where indicated arterial blood gas or oximetry in advanced obstructive disease A fixed deformity of the intrathoracic trachea in which the coronal (side-to-side) diameter is markedly reduced while the sagittal (front-to-back) diameter is preserved or increased, giving a scabbard-like cross-section. It is strongly associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and is regarded as a radiological marker of long-standing airflow obstruction, typically in older men with a heavy smoking history. The narrowing is confined to the intrathoracic trachea; the extrathoracic cervical portion is characteristically spared, and the deformity abruptly resolves at the thoracic inlet. Tracheal cartilage may ossify and the lumen appears flattened laterally on axial CT, with a coronal-to-sagittal ratio well below normal. Most patients' symptoms reflect the underlying COPD (chronic cough, sputum, dyspnoea) rather than the tracheal shape itself, which is usually an incidental imaging finding. It should be distinguished from tracheomalacia; in the classic saber-sheath deformity the abnormal shape is relatively fixed, although coexisting expiratory collapse can occur. The condition is thought to arise from chronically raised intrathoracic pressure and altered mechanical stresses transmitted to the tracheal cartilage over years. Recognising the pattern prevents misinterpretation as an intrinsic stenosing or infiltrative tracheal disease. new stridor or focal fixed narrowing suggesting a superimposed stenosing lesion haemoptysis prompting evaluation for malignancy rapidly progressive dyspnoea out of keeping with baseline COPD features of systemic cartilage disease such as auricular or nasal inflammation Mistaking the coronal narrowing for an intrinsic stenosing or infiltrative tracheal disease and pursuing unnecessary intervention. Overlooking coexisting tracheomalacia by relying only on static inspiratory imaging. Assuming the deformity accounts for a patient's dyspnoea rather than attributing it to the underlying COPD. Failing to note that the cervical trachea is spared, a key discriminating feature. Saber-sheath trachea is a chronic remodelling deformity of the intrathoracic trachea associated with obstructive lung disease. Repeated coughing and the chronically elevated, widely fluctuating intrathoracic pressures generated in COPD are thought to impose abnormal mechanical loading on the tracheal cartilages, leading to lateral flattening with compensatory sagittal widening; the cartilages frequently calcify or ossify and become rigid, so the deformed shape is largely fixed. Because the deforming pressures act within the thorax, the cervical trachea above the thoracic inlet retains its normal rounded contour, producing the characteristic abrupt transition at that level. The altered geometry modestly increases airflow resistance, but the dominant functional impairment in affected patients is the underlying emphysema and small-airways disease rather than the tracheal deformity per se. The tracheal deformity itself is usually clinically inconsequential and stable, with outcome determined by the severity and management of the underlying chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

The outlook is excellent, as saccharopinuria is generally an asymptomatic biochemical trait with no established link to progressive disease. Recognition mainly serves to avoid misdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment.

persistently elevated or rising levels after resection raise concern for malignant (yolk sac) elements or recurrence Large vascular tumours detected antenatally can cause high-output cardiac failure and fetal hydrops due to arteriovenous shunting Definitive treatment is complete surgical excision including the coccyx, since leaving the coccyx behind markedly increases recurrence Long-term follow-up with clinical review and tumour markers is required to detect recurrence and to monitor bowel and bladder function Antenatal high-output cardiac failure or hydrops from a large vascular tumour, which is life-threatening Rapid tumour growth or haemorrhage requiring urgent surgical planning Rising alpha-fetoprotein after resection suggesting malignant recurrence Delayed presentation of an internal tumour, which carries higher malignancy risk Failing to remove the coccyx, which greatly increases recurrence risk Missing a predominantly internal (presacral) tumour on external examination alone Neglecting postoperative alpha-fetoprotein surveillance for recurrence Overlooking associated anorectal or spinal anomalies and later functional problems Sacrococcygeal teratoma is a germ cell tumour thought to arise from pluripotent cells near the primitive streak (Hensen's node) at the caudal end of the embryo. It therefore contains tissues derived from multiple germ layers and grows at the coccygeal region, extending externally, into the pelvis, or both. Large, highly vascular tumours can act as arteriovenous shunts, causing high-output heart failure and hydrops in the fetus. Malignant transformation, usually to yolk sac tumour, becomes more likely with delayed diagnosis and with predominantly internal, poorly detected lesions. Benign lesions completely excised in the neonatal period with removal of the coccyx have an excellent prognosis. Prognosis worsens with malignant histology, incomplete excision, delayed diagnosis, and antenatal complications such as hydrops. Even after benign resection, some children have long-term bowel or bladder dysfunction.

thrust, compression, distraction (gapping), and Gaenslen manoeuvres A commonly used rule is that three or more positive provocation tests raise the likelihood of a sacroiliac source Pain often worsens with transitional movements, prolonged sitting or standing, and climbing stairs An image-guided intra-articular anaesthetic block is the reference standard for diagnosis Management is largely conservative (physiotherapy, pelvic stabilisation, analgesia), with image-guided injection and, rarely, joint fusion for refractory cases Inflammatory features (young patient, morning stiffness, alternating buttock pain, good response to anti-inflammatories) suggesting axial spondyloarthritis Constitutional symptoms suggesting infection or malignancy Progressive neurological deficit Missing inflammatory sacroiliitis by not considering axial spondyloarthritis Relying on a single provocation test rather than a cluster Overlooking hip pathology presenting as buttock or groin pain Sacroiliac joint dysfunction encompasses pain generated by the sacroiliac joint, a large, partly synovial joint that transmits load between the spine and pelvis and is stabilised by strong ligaments. Pain may result from altered joint mechanics (hypermobility or hypomobility), ligamentous strain, degenerative change, pregnancy-related laxity, leg-length discrepancy, or previous lumbar fusion increasing adjacent load. The joint and its ligaments are innervated by branches from the dorsal rami, and both intra-articular and extra-articular (ligamentous) sources can contribute to the pain. Most cases improve with conservative treatment and correction of contributing factors; image-guided injections often give useful relief, and outcomes are generally favourable, although a minority have persistent pain.

Sacroiliitis — inflammation of the sacroiliac joint Axial spondyloarthritis / ankylosing spondylitis Septic (infective) sacroiliitis Mechanical low back pain Osteitis condensans ilii Sacral insufficiency fracture Referred pain from the hip or lumbar spine MRI of the sacroiliac joints for active inflammation Radiographs for structural change HLA-B27 and inflammatory markers Assessment for features of spondyloarthritis and its extra-articular manifestations Blood cultures and joint sampling where infection is suspected Inflammation of the sacroiliac joint, a hallmark of axial spondyloarthritis but with several causes Presents with inflammatory-type buttock or low back pain, often alternating, with morning stiffness Common causes are the spondyloarthritides (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic, reactive and enteropathic arthritis) Infective (septic) sacroiliitis is an important distinct cause, usually unilateral with acute severe pain and systemic features MRI detects active inflammation (bone marrow oedema) earlier than radiographic changes Management depends on the cause: immunomodulation for inflammatory disease, antimicrobials for infection Acute severe unilateral pain with fever suggesting septic sacroiliitis Immunosuppression or injecting drug use raising infection risk Progressive structural damage Neurological deficit suggesting an alternative diagnosis Missing septic sacroiliitis, which needs urgent antimicrobial therapy Relying on radiographs and missing early inflammation seen on MRI Attributing inflammatory back pain to mechanical causes Overlooking associated spondyloarthritis features Sacroiliitis is inflammation of the sacroiliac joint that may be immune-mediated or infective. In spondyloarthritis, enthesitis and synovial inflammation at the joint are driven by genetic susceptibility (HLA-B27) and dysregulated immunity, producing bone marrow oedema, erosion and, over time, ankylosis. Septic sacroiliitis results from haematogenous or contiguous infection of the joint. Mechanical and degenerative processes can also inflame the joint. The pattern (unilateral versus bilateral, acute versus chronic) and systemic features help distinguish the causes. Prognosis depends on the cause; inflammatory sacroiliitis is controllable with modern therapy though it may progress to ankylosis, and septic sacroiliitis does well with prompt antimicrobial treatment.

Saethre-Chotzen syndrome — acrocephalosyndactyly type III, TWIST1-related craniosynostosis, ACS3 Muenke syndrome (FGFR3 coronal synostosis, can look similar) Crouzon syndrome (FGFR2) Apert syndrome (severe syndactyly) Baller-Gerold syndrome (craniosynostosis with radial defects) Non-syndromic unilateral coronal synostosis Craniofrontonasal syndrome (EFNB1) Molecular testing of TWIST1, including to document asymmetry and ptosis MRI of the brain if raised intracranial pressure or structural anomaly is suspected Developmental assessment, particularly where a large deletion is identified
