dominant pattern with variable expressivity Typically presents with coronal synostosis (often unilateral, producing plagiocephaly) with a low frontal hairline and facial asymmetry Ptosis of the eyelids is a characteristic and helpful diagnostic clue The external ears are small with a prominent crus, and there may be mild cutaneous syndactyly, usually of the second and third fingers Intelligence is usually normal, distinguishing it from some other craniosynostosis syndromes, though large deletions involving neighbouring genes can be associated with learning difficulty Brachydactyly, broad great toes and other minor digital anomalies may be present Larger contiguous gene deletions at the TWIST1 locus should prompt consideration of developmental delay and require specific genetic evaluation Management is by a craniofacial team, with cranial vault surgery guided by suture involvement and monitoring for raised intracranial pressure Signs of raised intracranial pressure from multisuture involvement Ptosis severe enough to obscure the visual axis and risk amblyopia Developmental regression or delay suggesting a larger contiguous gene deletion Progressive facial asymmetry needing surgical planning Mislabelling the condition as Muenke syndrome without molecular testing, as the phenotypes overlap Overlooking amblyopia risk from ptosis Not performing deletion analysis, thereby missing large TWIST1 deletions associated with delay Assuming a purely cosmetic problem and failing to monitor intracranial pressure Saethre-Chotzen syndrome results from haploinsufficiency of TWIST1, a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that regulates the balance between proliferation and differentiation of osteoprogenitor cells in the cranial sutures. Reduced TWIST1 activity disturbs the normal restraint on osteogenic differentiation at the coronal suture, leading to premature fusion and the resulting craniofacial dysmorphology. Because the defect is loss of function, whole-gene deletions and larger contiguous deletions of adjacent genes can broaden the phenotype. Most individuals have normal cognition and a good outcome after craniofacial surgery, but those with large deletions may have additional developmental problems, and lifelong monitoring for intracranial pressure and visual complications is advisable.

Subarachnoid hemorrhage — Non-contrast CT head (urgent) LP for xanthochromia if CT negative CT angiography Thunderclap headache is SAH until proven otherwise — image immediately Primary thunderclap headache / reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) — many otherwise-undiagnosed thunderclap headaches are attributed to RCVS (p.3462) Cervicocephalic arterial dissection (p.3462) Cerebral venous (sinus) thrombosis (p.3462) Ruptured arteriovenous malformation — but blood is usually intraparenchymal, not deposited in the basal cisterns, and symptomatic vasospasm is rare (p.3457) Dural arteriovenous fistula (a recognised cause of SAH) (p.3457) Noncontrast CT detects >95% of cases when obtained within 72 h; sensitivity falls as time from ictus increases (p.3459) Four-vessel conventional x-ray (catheter) angiography — gold standard to localise/define aneurysm anatomy and detect additional aneurysms; ruptured aneurysm can be treated at the same sitting (p.3459) CT perfusion imaging — adjunct to identify potentially reversible ischaemic deficits in suspected delayed cerebral ischaemia (p.3459) Transcranial Doppler ultrasound — daily/alternate-day bedside monitoring detects rising flow velocities of vasospasm (p.3459) Serial (daily or twice-daily) serum electrolytes to detect early hyponatraemia (p.3459) ECG and echocardiography to detect neurogenic cardiac changes and stress (catecholamine) cardiomyopathy (p.3459-3460) Thunderclap migraine — a migraine variant that can simulate SAH; a definitive workup to exclude aneurysm/other intracranial pathology is required before attributing sudden severe headache to it (p.3458) The single most important feature of aneurysmal SAH headache is its sudden (abrupt) onset, even more than its severity; ruptures may occasionally present as only moderate headache or as a change in the patient's usual headache pattern (p.3458). Transient loss of consciousness occurs in nearly half of patients at the moment of rupture, reflecting an abrupt rise in intracranial pressure; many patients only report the headache after regaining consciousness (p.3458). A third nerve palsy with pupillary dilation and pain around/behind the eye suggests an expanding aneurysm at the posterior communicating artery-internal carotid junction; a sixth nerve palsy may indicate a cavernous-sinus aneurysm (p.3458). Quivering, jerking, or extensor posturing accompanying loss of consciousness at SAH onset is usually caused by the sharp ICP rise rather than true seizure activity (p.3461). ECG changes mimicking cardiac ischaemia (ST/T changes, long QT, peaked or deeply inverted T waves) and a reversible (catecholamine-mediated) cardiomyopathy with regional wall-motion abnormalities can occur after SAH; an asymptomatic troponin rise is common (p.3459-3460). Nimodipine improves outcomes in aneurysmal SAH, apparently by limiting ischaemic injury rather than by reducing vasospasm itself (knowledge, no dose) (p.3461). Perimesencephalic (idiopathic) SAH localised to the perimesencephalic cisterns is benign, probably venous/capillary in origin, and angiography is typically unrevealing (p.3458). Sudden unexplained headache of any location may represent a sentinel bleed (small aneurysmal leak) heralding imminent major haemorrhage and must be investigated (p.3459) Declining mental status with worsening headache 4-14 days after SAH suggests delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm (p.3459-3460) High ICP refractory to treatment is a poor prognostic sign (p.3461) A normal CT does not exclude SAH, especially as time elapses or with small or infratentorial bleeds; if CT is non-diagnostic and there is no mass lesion/obstructive hydrocephalus, lumbar puncture for xanthochromia is required (p.3458-3459). Xanthochromia (yellow CSF from haemoglobin-to-bilirubin conversion) takes 6-12 h to appear, peaks at ~48 h, and persists 1-4 weeks; an LP performed too early may miss it (p.3459). Free-water restriction should NOT be used to treat SAH-associated hyponatraemia (cerebral salt wasting): the resulting hypovolaemia/hypotension can precipitate cerebral ischaemia (p.3459, p.3461). Marked hyponatraemia of several days' duration must not be corrected too rapidly because of the risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome (p.3461). Lumbar puncture before imaging is appropriate only when CT is unavailable at the time of suspected SAH (p.3459). Excluding trauma, the commonest cause is rupture of a saccular ('berry') aneurysm, which forms at bifurcations of large- to medium-sized intracranial arteries (about 89% in the anterior circulation, mostly on the circle of Willis). Aneurysm walls show loss of the internal elastic lamina at the neck base with medial thinning and replacement of smooth muscle by connective tissue; rupture is usually at the thin-walled dome through a tear often <=0.5 mm. Rupture deposits blood in the subarachnoid space of the basal cisterns (and sometimes adjacent parenchyma), abruptly raising ICP. Other causes include vascular malformations (AVM, dural arteriovenous fistula) and subarachnoid extension of a primary intracerebral haemorrhage. Roughly 2% of adults harbour intracranial aneurysms and about 20% of affected patients have multiple aneurysms (frequently mirror-image bilateral). Delayed cerebral ischaemia is thought to arise from clot breakdown products acting on basal arteries to cause vasospasm and vessel-wall thickening, but also from vasospasm-independent mechanisms (microthrombosis, inflammation, microvascular dysregulation, cortical spreading depolarisation). Hyponatraemia results from natriuresis with volume depletion ('cerebral salt wasting'), mediated by atrial and brain natriuretic peptides (p.3457-3461). Overall mortality of aneurysmal SAH is about 35%, with roughly a third dying before reaching hospital; over half of survivors are left with significant neurologic deficits from the initial bleed, delayed cerebral ischaemia, or hydrocephalus. Outcome worsens with increasing presentation grade: grade 1 (Hunt-Hess) patients rarely die if treated, whereas mortality for grades 4-5 may reach about 60%. In an untreated aneurysm, rebleeding risk is about 20% in the first 2 weeks, 30% in the first month, then about 3% per year; rerupture (~30% in the first month, peaking in the first 7 days) carries about 50% mortality. Delayed cerebral ischaemia occurs in about 30% and is the leading cause of delayed morbidity and death among initial survivors. Unruptured aneurysms <7 mm had ~0% 5-year rupture risk in a large study (though many ruptured aneurysms are <6 mm); giant aneurysms (>25 mm) carry ~8-10% annual rupture risk (p.3458-3460). Two presentation-based clinical grading scales are used: the Hunt-Hess scale (1 = asymptomatic/minimal headache and slight nuchal rigidity through 5 = coma with reflex posturing or flaccidity) and the World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies (WFNS) scale based on Glasgow Coma Scale score and motor deficits (1 = GCS 15 no motor deficit through 5 = GCS 3-6). Higher grade predicts worse outcome. The modified Fisher CT grading system predicts symptomatic vasospasm by the amount and distribution of subarachnoid/intraventricular blood ('thin' <1 mm vs 'thick' >=1 mm), with risk rising from 0% (grade 0) to ~40% (grade 4, thick blood with intraventricular blood) (p.3459-3460).

Salicylate poisoning — aspirin poisoning, salicylate toxicity, acetylsalicylic acid overdose, salicylism, oil of wintergreen (methyl salicylate) poisoning Diabetic or other high anion-gap ketoacidosis Sepsis with lactic acidosis Toxic alcohol (methanol or ethylene glycol) poisoning Theophylline or iron toxicity Sympathomimetic toxicity or thyroid storm Primary central nervous system infection causing hyperpnoea and confusion Serial serum salicylate concentrations to track absorption and elimination Arterial blood gas with anion-gap and acid-base interpretation Serum electrolytes, particularly potassium, and glucose Renal function and lactate Coagulation profile and paracetamol level in intentional overdose Chest radiograph if pulmonary oedema is suspected and urine pH monitoring during alkalinisation The classic acid-base picture is a mixed primary respiratory alkalosis and primary high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, most evident in adults Early features include tinnitus, deafness, nausea, vomiting, hyperventilation and hyperpyrexia A normal or rising blood pH with low carbon dioxide reflects the respiratory alkalosis, but falling pH signals dangerous progression A single salicylate concentration can mislead, so serial levels are needed because of delayed and erratic absorption, especially with enteric-coated preparations or bezoars Concentrated liquid methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen) can cause rapid severe toxicity from a small volume Acidaemia increases the non-ionised fraction that crosses into the central nervous system, so intubation with inadequate ventilation can be catastrophic Urinary alkalinisation enhances salicylate elimination and limits central penetration, while haemodialysis is used for severe toxicity, high levels or end-organ effects Maintaining potassium is essential, as hypokalaemia prevents effective urinary alkalinisation Altered mental status, seizures or coma indicating central nervous system toxicity A falling or normalising pH after initial alkalosis, signalling decompensation Pulmonary or cerebral oedema Hyperthermia, haemodynamic instability or intractable acidosis Very high or rising salicylate concentrations, or need for airway control Relying on a single salicylate level and missing continued absorption Intubating and under-ventilating, causing acidaemia and rapid neurological deterioration Allowing hypokalaemia, which defeats urinary alkalinisation Misinterpreting the early respiratory alkalosis as reassuring Delaying haemodialysis in patients with high levels or end-organ toxicity Salicylate directly stimulates the medullary respiratory centre, producing hyperventilation and a primary respiratory alkalosis. Simultaneously it uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, impairs the citric acid cycle and promotes accumulation of organic acids and lactate, generating a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis and heat production with hyperthermia. As pH falls, a greater proportion of salicylate becomes non-ionised and crosses the blood-brain barrier, worsening neurotoxicity. Salicylate also interferes with glucose metabolism, coagulation and gastrointestinal integrity, and in severe cases causes pulmonary and cerebral oedema. Prompt recognition, urinary alkalinisation and timely haemodialysis when indicated usually yield good outcomes, but delayed treatment, marked acidaemia and central nervous system involvement are associated with high mortality.

Salicylate toxicity — Salicylate level (serial) ABG (mixed acid-base) Glucose, electrolytes Consider urinary alkalinisation / dialysis Serial quantitative serum salicylate level (guides management) (p.3706) Anion gap and serum lactate (lactate typically lower than the anion gap in salicylate vs near-equal in shock/organ failure) (p.3705) Serum glucose and calcium (risk of hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia) (p.3714) Potassium (hypokalemia) (p.3714) Abdominal x-ray/CT may show radiopaque enteric-coated salicylate tablets or concretions (p.3706) Other high-anion-gap metabolic acidoses: methanol, ethylene glycol, alcoholic/diabetic/starvation ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, kidney failure (p.412) Other causes of ketosis: acetone, isopropyl alcohol, alcoholic ketoacidosis (p.3705) Other causes of drug-induced respiratory alkalosis: theophylline/aminophylline; also sepsis, hepatic failure, pregnancy/progesterone (p.376) Classic course: early nausea/vomiting and hyperventilation with respiratory alkalosis and alkaline urine, evolving to a mixed respiratory alkalosis plus high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with paradoxical aciduria; late stages show acidemia with CNS and respiratory depression (p.3714). Salicylates are the most common cause of drug-induced respiratory alkalosis, acting by direct stimulation of the medullary respiratory chemoreceptor (p.376). Only part of the elevated anion gap is attributable to salicylate itself; concurrent lactic acid production and other endogenous unmeasured anions also contribute (p.370, p.3714). Cerebral and pulmonary edema can develop in severe poisoning; non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema (ARDS) is a recognized complication (p.3705, p.3714). Hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hypokalemia, and seizures can occur in salicylate toxicity (p.3714). Ketosis can accompany salicylate poisoning and may mimic other causes of ketoacidosis (p.3705). Salicylate is detected on quantitative serum assay; serum levels guide management and are usually available within an hour (p.3706). Enteric-coated and sustained-release salicylate preparations cause delayed/slow absorption and can form gastric concretions (bezoars), acting as a 'toxic time-bomb' with continued rising levels (p.3705, p.3752). Coma, seizures, cerebral edema (p.3714) Pulmonary edema / ARDS (p.3705, p.3714) Renal failure (impairs clearance) (p.376) Progressive acid-base disturbance / late acidemia with CNS and respiratory depression (p.3714) Salicylate level >7 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) after acute overdose (p.3714) Vigorous gastric lavage, if used, should be with isotonic saline, NOT NaHCO3 (p.370). Only a portion of the anion gap is due to salicylate itself; do not assume the whole gap reflects drug level (p.370). Acid (acidic) diuresis is never indicated and is potentially harmful (p.3752). Acetazolamide can cause systemic metabolic acidosis if excreted bicarbonate is not replaced, which markedly reduces salicylate clearance (p.370). Delayed/slow absorption from enteric-coated, sustained-release, or concretion-forming salicylate means a single early level can underestimate toxicity; repeat levels (p.3705, p.3752). Salicylate increases sensitivity of the CNS respiratory center and directly stimulates the medullary chemoreceptor, driving hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis. It also uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, inhibits Krebs cycle enzymes, and stimulates carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, generating unmeasured endogenous anions (and increased lactate) that produce a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (p.376, p.3714). Stages by clinical/acid-base course: (1) early respiratory alkalosis with alkalemia, alkaluria, nausea/vomiting and hyperventilation; (2) mixed respiratory alkalosis plus high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with paradoxical aciduria; (3) late acidemia with CNS and respiratory depression, cerebral and pulmonary edema in severe cases. Severe-toxicity markers include coma, cerebral edema, seizures, pulmonary edema, renal failure, progressive acid-base disturbance, and salicylate level >7 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) after acute overdose (p.3714).

Salivary gland tumor — salivary gland neoplasm, parotid tumour, salivary gland cancer Reactive or infective lymphadenopathy near the gland Sialadenitis or salivary duct stones with gland swelling Salivary gland cyst or sialocele Lymphoma involving the salivary gland Metastatic disease to intraparotid lymph nodes Benign lymphoepithelial lesions and autoimmune sialadenitis Ultrasound as first-line imaging, often with guided fine-needle aspiration cytology MRI or CT to define tumour extent, deep lobe involvement, and perineural or nodal spread Assessment of facial nerve function in parotid lesions Histopathological examination of the excised specimen for type, grade, and margins Staging imaging for high-grade or clinically malignant tumours Most salivary gland tumours occur in the parotid gland and the majority of these are benign, whereas tumours of the smaller submandibular, sublingual, and minor salivary glands carry a proportionally higher risk of malignancy The typical presentation is a slow-growing, painless lump, and pleomorphic adenoma is the most common benign tumour while mucoepidermoid and adenoid cystic carcinomas are common malignant types Features suggesting malignancy include rapid growth, pain, fixation to surrounding tissue, skin involvement, cervical lymphadenopathy, and especially facial nerve weakness in parotid lesions Facial nerve palsy in association with a parotid mass is a strong indicator of malignant invasion and demands urgent evaluation Fine-needle aspiration cytology and imaging help characterise the lesion, though definitive diagnosis often rests on excisional histology Adenoid cystic carcinoma is notable for perineural spread and a tendency to late recurrence and distant metastasis, requiring prolonged follow-up Surgery is the primary treatment, with parotidectomy performed to preserve the facial nerve whenever oncologically feasible, and appropriate gland excision for other sites Radiotherapy is used adjuvantly for high-grade tumours, positive margins, perineural invasion, or nodal disease, while enucleation of pleomorphic adenoma is avoided due to recurrence and malignant transformation risk Facial nerve weakness accompanying a parotid mass A rapidly enlarging, painful, or fixed salivary gland lump Skin ulceration or infiltration over the gland Associated cervical lymphadenopathy suggesting nodal metastasis Assuming all salivary lumps are benign and missing malignant features such as pain or nerve palsy Enucleating a pleomorphic adenoma, risking recurrence and later malignant transformation Underestimating perineural spread and late recurrence of adenoid cystic carcinoma Inadequate facial nerve assessment and counselling before parotid surgery Salivary gland tumours arise from the epithelial and myoepithelial cells of the major and minor salivary glands and comprise a diverse group with widely varying behaviour. Benign tumours such as pleomorphic adenoma grow slowly and are well circumscribed but can recur if incompletely excised and, rarely, undergo malignant transformation over time. Malignant tumours vary from low-grade to aggressive high-grade carcinomas that invade locally, track along nerves (notably adenoid cystic carcinoma), and metastasise to regional nodes and distant sites. The inverse relationship between gland size and malignancy risk reflects the differing tumour types that predominate in each gland. Benign tumours have an excellent prognosis after complete excision; malignant tumour outcomes depend on grade, stage, and histological type, with high-grade and adenoid cystic carcinomas prone to recurrence and late distant spread despite treatment.

Nontyphoidal Salmonellosis — nontyphoidal Salmonella, NTS, nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis, invasive NTS disease Other bacterial enteric pathogens (Campylobacter, Shigella, enteroinvasive/enterotoxigenic E. coli) Norovirus and other viral gastroenteritis Intestinal parasites Pseudoappendicitis (NTS can mimic acute appendicitis) Inflammatory bowel disease (NTS rarely produces an IBD-like illness) Enteric (typhoid) fever - especially with invasive NTS presenting as nonspecific febrile illness Enteric (typhoid/paratyphoid) fever from S. Typhi/S. Paratyphi presenting as undifferentiated febrile illness Other causes of community-acquired bloodstream infection in endemic regions (malaria co-infection common) Other bacterial gastroenteritides (Campylobacter, Shigella, E. coli) Stool culture (freshly passed) with primary isolation even after culture-independent molecular detection Blood cultures - obtain whenever fever is prolonged or recurrent; high-grade bacteremia defined as >50% of three or more blood-culture sets positive suggests endovascular infection Culture-independent molecular diagnostic panels for enteric pathogens Serotyping of all NTS isolates via public health laboratories Echocardiography to evaluate suspected endocarditis CT imaging to localize deep/focal infection Indium-labeled white-cell scanning to identify localized infection Culture of joint fluid aspirate, bone biopsy, abscess drainage, or CSF when localized infection is suspected Antimicrobial susceptibility testing with attention to ciprofloxacin MIC (Etest or alternative method) given the lowered susceptibility breakpoint and decreased-ciprofloxacin-susceptibility strains not reliably detected by nalidixic acid screening or standard disk diffusion Acute appendicitis (pseudoappendicitis) Inflammatory bowel disease Postinfectious irritable bowel syndrome / functional dyspepsia (recognized sequelae) NTS infection most often produces a gastroenteritis that is clinically indistinguishable from that caused by other enteric pathogens, with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea beginning 6-48 h after ingestion of contaminated food or water; stools are usually loose, nonbloody, and of moderate volume, though large-volume watery stools, bloody stools, or frank dysentery can occur (p.1320). NTS gastroenteritis is usually self-limited: diarrhea resolves within 3-7 days and fever within 72 h; stool cultures may remain positive for 4-5 weeks after infection (p.1320). Globally S. Typhimurium and S. Enteritidis are the most common serotypes causing human disease; in the United States NTS is the second most common cause of foodborne outbreaks after norovirus (p.1319). Unlike S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi (human-only reservoir), NTS is acquired from multiple animal and plant reservoirs - especially eggs, poultry, undercooked ground meat, and dairy, plus produce contaminated with animal waste and contact with animals (reptiles, amphibians, chicks, etc.) (p.1319). Up to 8% of patients with NTS gastroenteritis develop bacteremia, and of those 5-10% develop localized (metastatic) infections; bacteremia and metastatic infection are most common with S. Choleraesuis and S. Dublin and among infants, the elderly, and the immunocompromised, especially those with HIV (p.1320). Invasive NTS disease (predominantly S. Typhimurium ST313 and S. Enteritidis ST11) is a leading cause of bacteremia in children and HIV-infected adults in sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia; it typically presents as a nonspecific febrile illness resembling enteric fever and uncommonly causes diarrhea (p.1319-1320). Diagnosis rests on isolating the organism from freshly passed stool or from blood or another normally sterile fluid; culture-independent molecular tests are increasingly used but positive specimens should still undergo primary isolation, and all NTS isolates should be referred to public health for serotyping (p.1320-1321). Reactive arthritis can follow NTS gastroenteritis, occurring most frequently in persons carrying the HLA-B27 antigen (p.1321). Localized NTS infections include intraabdominal (hepatic/splenic abscess, cholecystitis), CNS (meningitis - chiefly in infants 1-4 months and HIV-infected adults), pulmonary (lobar pneumonia), urinary/genital, and bone/joint disease; Salmonella osteomyelitis classically affects the femur, tibia, humerus, or lumbar vertebrae and is strongly linked to sickle cell disease and hemoglobinopathies (p.1320-1321). Invasive disease / bacteremia and endovascular seeding in the elderly, immunocompromised (including HIV), infants/neonates, and patients with sickle cell disease or other hemoglobinopathies High-grade or persistent bacteremia, particularly with preexisting valvular heart disease, atherosclerotic vascular disease, prosthetic vascular graft, or aortic aneurysm - suspect NTS endovascular infection Prolonged fever with back, chest, or abdominal pain after an episode of gastroenteritis in an elderly patient - suspect arteritis/mycotic aneurysm NTS meningitis in infants 1-4 months of age or HIV-infected adults - severe sequelae and death in up to 60% of cases Persons >50 years with known or suspected atherosclerosis (increased risk of invasive infection and endovascular seeding) Antibiotics should NOT be used routinely to treat uncomplicated NTS gastroenteritis - the illness is usually self-limited and antibiotics do not significantly shorten fever or diarrhea, while they have been associated with increased relapse rates, prolonged fecal/gastrointestinal carriage, and adverse drug reactions. Only ~1% of clinical isolates ferment lactose, so a high index of suspicion is needed to detect rare lactose-fermenting strains. Decreased-ciprofloxacin-susceptibility NTS strains may not be reliably detected by nalidixic acid susceptibility testing or standard ciprofloxacin disk diffusion, risking missed resistance and treatment failure. Neonates, the elderly, and immunosuppressed patients with NTS gastroenteritis are especially prone to dehydration and invasive infection and may need hospitalization and antibiotic therapy - they are exceptions to the no-routine-antibiotics rule. All Salmonella infections begin with ingestion of organisms, usually in contaminated food or water; the infectious dose ranges from ~200 to 10^6 CFU, and the ingested dose helps determine incubation period and severity. Conditions reducing gastric acidity (age <1 year, acid-suppression therapy, achlorhydria) or compromising intestinal integrity (inflammatory bowel disease, cytotoxic chemotherapy, prior GI surgery, antibiotic-induced microbiome alteration) increase susceptibility. In contrast to enteric fever (mononuclear infiltration of small-bowel mucosa), NTS gastroenteritis is characterized by massive polymorphonuclear leukocyte infiltration into both large- and small-bowel mucosa. This response depends largely on induction of interleukin 8, a strong neutrophil chemoattractant secreted by intestinal cells in response to NTS colonization and translocation of bacterial proteins and LPS into host cytoplasm with subsequent inflammasome activation; neutrophil degranulation and release of toxic substances damages the mucosa, producing inflammatory diarrhea. NTS persistence is aided by its ability to use tetrathionate (generated from thiosulfate via inflammatory reactive oxygen species) for metabolism in a microaerophilic, inflamed gut, allowing it to outcompete endogenous flora. Unlike typhoidal serotypes, NTS effectively colonizes the intestinal tract rather than evolving as a primarily systemic pathogen. NTS gastroenteritis is usually self-limited, with diarrhea resolving in 3-7 days and fever within 72 h; chronic carriage develops in <1% of cases. Outcomes worsen markedly with invasive disease: endocarditis and arteritis are rare (<1%) but carry serious, potentially fatal complications (valve perforation, endomyocardial abscess, infected mural thrombus, pericarditis, mycotic aneurysm, aneurysm rupture, aortoenteric fistula, vertebral osteomyelitis), and NTS meningitis is fatal in up to 60% of cases. In 2017 there were ~535,000 invasive NTS cases and ~77,500 deaths worldwide, ~80% in sub-Saharan Africa. Acute NTS gastroenteritis was associated with a threefold increased risk of dyspepsia and irritable bowel syndrome at 1 year in a Spanish study. Harrison does not provide a formal graded severity score for NTS. Disease is described along a clinical spectrum: (1) uncomplicated self-limited gastroenteritis; (2) bacteremia (low-grade defined as <50% of blood cultures positive vs high-grade >50% of three or more sets positive, the latter raising concern for endovascular infection); and (3) localized/metastatic infection (intraabdominal, CNS, pulmonary, urinary/genital, bone/joint/soft tissue) and endovascular infection (endocarditis, arteritis). Host-risk stratification for invasive disease includes neonates (up to ~3 months), persons >50 years with atherosclerosis, and those with immunosuppression, cardiac valvular/endovascular abnormalities, or significant joint disease.

Episodes characteristically cluster around or shortly after feeds and abate during sleep, a temporal pattern that helps distinguish them from epileptic seizures. Consciousness is fully preserved throughout episodes and there is no post-ictal drowsiness, a key discriminator from seizure activity. The posturing is thought to be a reflexive or learned manoeuvre that relieves the discomfort of acid reflux or reduces oesophageal obstruction, rather than a primary neurological disorder. It typically presents in infancy and early childhood and is over-represented in children with neurodisability, in whom reflux is common and communication limited. Effective treatment of the underlying reflux — positional and feeding measures with acid suppression — usually abolishes the movements, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Associated features may include feeding refusal, irritability, faltering growth, iron-deficiency anaemia and, occasionally, apparent apnoeic or brief resolved unexplained events. Misdiagnosis as epilepsy, infantile spasms or a primary dystonia is common and frequently leads to unnecessary neurological investigation and antiepileptic exposure. Altered awareness, cyanosis or apnoea during episodes, suggesting seizure or airway compromise Faltering growth, persistent vomiting or haematemesis Focal neurological signs, developmental regression or an abnormal interictal examination Episodes unrelated to feeds or persisting despite adequate reflux treatment Bilious vomiting raising concern for malrotation with volvulus Labelling episodes as epilepsy and starting antiepileptic drugs unnecessarily Overlooking reflux because posturing rather than regurgitation dominates the presentation Attributing the torticollis solely to a musculoskeletal cause Failing to consider Sandifer syndrome in neurodisabled children in whom reflux is common Stopping anti-reflux therapy prematurely before symptoms have resolved Sandifer syndrome is a movement phenomenon secondary to gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and sometimes hiatus hernia, rather than a disorder of the central nervous system. Acid or volume reflux into the distal oesophagus is thought to provoke discomfort and vagally mediated afferent stimulation, and the stereotyped extension and lateral flexion of the neck and trunk are believed to be a protective postural response that lengthens and straightens the oesophagus, reduces reflux, relieves pain and may safeguard the airway. Because the movements are reflexive and non-epileptic, the electroencephalogram is normal and awareness is retained; resolution of the reflux, whether through maturation of the lower oesophageal sphincter or with therapy, characteristically resolves the posturing. The prognosis is excellent; the condition is self-limiting and typically resolves with maturation of the lower oesophageal sphincter and control of reflux during infancy. When correctly identified and treated there are no long-term neurological sequelae.

which differ in exposure, presentation and diagnosis Overlooking sarcocystosis in a traveller with fever, myalgia and eosinophilia Relying on stool testing to diagnose muscular disease, in which stool is typically negative Missing dietary history of raw or undercooked meat Sarcocystis has an obligatory predator-prey life cycle. When humans eat undercooked meat containing mature tissue cysts, the parasite completes sexual reproduction in the intestinal wall and sporocysts are shed in the stool, producing intestinal sarcocystosis. When humans instead ingest sporocysts shed by another carnivore, the parasite behaves as if in an intermediate host: released sporozoites disseminate haematogenously and encyst in skeletal and cardiac muscle, causing muscular sarcocystosis. The intramuscular cysts and the inflammatory, often eosinophilic, response to them account for the myalgia, muscle swelling and enzyme release seen in the muscular form, while intestinal invasion produces a milder self-limiting enteritis. Intestinal sarcocystosis is self-limiting; muscular sarcocystosis tends to run a relapsing but ultimately self-limiting course over weeks to months, though prolonged myalgia can cause considerable morbidity.

malignancy/chemoimmunotherapy Lymphoma presenting with hilar/mediastinal adenopathy Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease of unknown cause; the lung is involved in over 90% of cases, but roughly half of patients have extrapulmonary disease and almost any organ can be affected (p.2921, p.2924). Diagnosis rests on three criteria: a compatible clinical picture, nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation on tissue, AND exclusion of other causes of granulomas — it is never made with absolute certainty, so new signs during follow-up should be re-evaluated (p.2923-2924). Löfgren syndrome (fever, erythema nodosum, ankle arthralgias, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy) occurs in up to ~10% of cases and, like Heerfordt syndrome, carries an excellent prognosis with frequent spontaneous resolution (p.2923). Heerfordt syndrome = facial nerve palsy, fever, anterior uveitis, and bilateral parotid gland enlargement (p.2923, p.2928). In very compelling presentations (classic Löfgren, Heerfordt, lupus pernio, or asymptomatic symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy), biopsy may be deferred, but close clinical follow-up is still required (p.2924). A BAL CD4:CD8 lymphocyte ratio >3.5 supports the diagnosis when combined with consistent clinical/radiographic findings, but a normal ratio does NOT exclude sarcoidosis; BAL is also important to exclude infection (p.2924). Endobronchial ultrasound-guided lymph node sampling has high diagnostic yield with low procedural risk when hilar/mediastinal nodes are the prominent feature (p.2924). Sarcoidosis is upper-lobe predominant on imaging with a lymphangitic (perilymphatic/subpleural/peribronchovascular) nodular distribution; airflow obstruction can occur in up to one-third of patients despite the classically restrictive pattern (p.2924-2925). Every sarcoidosis patient should be screened for cardiac involvement (baseline ECG) because severity of lung disease does not predict cardiac sarcoidosis and sudden death can be the initial presentation (p.2925-2926). Baseline workup in every patient should include PFTs, chest imaging, an ophthalmologic exam (to detect clinically silent uveitis), an ECG, and serum creatinine/alkaline phosphatase/calcium/CBC (p.2924). Hypercalcemia from dysregulated macrophage/granuloma production of calcitriol (1,25-(OH)2 vitamin D) occurs despite suppressed PTH; patients should limit vitamin D intake, avoid excess sunlight, and stay hydrated (p.2927-2928). Optic neuropathy in ocular sarcoidosis is an emergency requiring immediate immunosuppression to prevent sudden permanent vision loss (p.2927). Smoking is a consistent NEGATIVE predictor of incident sarcoidosis (reduced odds), an unusual feature among lung diseases (p.2921-2922). Exclude infection (especially TB and fungi such as histoplasmosis) before starting immunosuppression — abundant necrosis on biopsy points away from sarcoidosis toward infection Acute symptomatic hypercalcemia can require hospital admission and urgent corticosteroids Optic neuropathy threatens sudden permanent vision loss and is an ophthalmologic emergency Cardiac involvement (new-onset AV block, ventricular arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy in younger patients) carries risk of sudden death and can be the first presentation Neurologic involvement (basal/cranial nerve disease, mass lesions, meningitis) can cause neurologic demise Untreated hypercalcemia leads to nephrocalcinosis and renal failure New reproductive-organ nodules/masses require exclusion of malignancy given the rarity of genital sarcoidosis A normal BAL CD4:CD8 ratio, normal PFTs, or a normal lung exam does NOT exclude sarcoidosis despite active granulomatous inflammation (p.2924). Serum ACE has low sensitivity and is not a reliable diagnostic or prognostic test; it only roughly tracks granuloma burden and is best used to monitor activity (p.2929). Scadding (CXR) stages reveal overall resolution rates but do NOT predict disease activity, lung-function progression, or extrapulmonary involvement in an individual (p.2929). Cardiac involvement is frequently subclinical and endomyocardial biopsy has poor sensitivity (patchy granulomas, basal predominance, sparing of the right ventricle), so a negative biopsy does not exclude cardiac sarcoidosis (p.2926). Failing to screen for cardiac, ocular, and neurologic disease at baseline misses life- or sight-threatening involvement because pulmonary severity does not predict it (p.2924-2926). Isolated extrapulmonary sarcoidosis (cardiac, hepatic, neurologic) can occur without lung disease and is easily overlooked (p.2926-2927). Loosely formed granulomas suggest hypersensitivity pneumonitis and abundant necrosis suggests infection — misreading these as sarcoidosis is a classic error (p.2924). Always re-evaluate alternative causes for isolated hepatic granulomas, which carry a broad differential (p.2927). Sarcoidosis is thought to arise from a heightened, antigen-driven host immune response to an undetermined (likely inhaled bioaerosol or inorganic) environmental antigen in a genetically susceptible person; the inciting antigen may differ between individuals/populations. A poorly degradable material is presented to lymphocytes by dendritic cells/macrophages via MHC, triggering an innate cytokine/chemokine cascade and recruitment of adaptive immune cells. The immunopathologic hallmark is highly polarized CD4+ TH1 lymphocytes (less so CD8+) producing IFN-gamma, with upregulation of TH1-promoting cytokines/chemokines (IL-1, IL-2, IL-15, IL-18, CXCR3) that activate macrophages and drive formation of tightly organized nonnecrotizing (noncaseating) granulomas. Altered regulatory T-cell and TH17 responses are implicated in failure to resolve and in progression to fibrosis. Granulomas comprise macrophages, epithelioid cells, and multinucleated giant cells rimmed by lymphocytes/fibroblasts (CD4+ central, CD8+ and B cells peripheral). Mycobacterial proteins (mKatG, ESAT-6, superoxide dismutase A, antigen 85A, heat-shock proteins) and Cutibacterium acnes have been disproportionately implicated; the transmissibility seen with the Kveim-Siltzbach reagent and via organ transplantation supports an antigenic trigger (p.2922-2923). Disease resolves spontaneously in just over half of patients, but 30-40% develop chronic disease threatening vital organs or causing debilitating symptoms. Most patients show radiographic or spirometric improvement by 2 years (treated or untreated). Death attributable to sarcoidosis occurs in roughly 1-5%, most often from progressive respiratory insufficiency/pulmonary fibrosis (leading cause in the US/Northern Europe) or cardiac involvement (predominant cause of death in Japan). A robust acute initial immune response predicts a better outcome: Löfgren and Heerfordt syndromes remit spontaneously in up to ~80%, and immunosuppression is rarely needed. Adverse prognostic factors include lupus pernio, chronic uveitis, older age, chronic hypercalcemia, nephrocalcinosis, African ancestry, pulmonary hypertension, fibrotic pulmonary disease, sinus involvement, cystic bone lesions, neurosarcoidosis, and cardiac involvement. Relapses are common and associated with shorter treatment duration (p.2928-2929). Scadding chest x-ray stages describe the pulmonary pattern and correlate with spontaneous resolution rates (NOT with activity or prognosis in the individual): Stage 1 = bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy without parenchymal involvement (resolution ~55-90%); Stage 2 = bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy WITH parenchymal involvement (resolution ~40-70%); Stage 3 = parenchymal involvement without lymphadenopathy (resolution ~10-20%); Stage 4 = pulmonary fibrosis with architectural distortion and volume loss (resolution ~0%) (p.2925).

corticosteroids are reserved for significant or progressive organ involvement, with immunosuppressants as steroid-sparing options Symptoms or findings suggesting cardiac sarcoidosis such as arrhythmia, heart block, or heart failure Neurosarcoidosis with cranial nerve or central nervous system involvement Significant hypercalcaemia with renal impairment Progressive pulmonary fibrosis or pulmonary hypertension Diagnosing sarcoidosis without excluding tuberculosis and other infective granulomatous disease Relying on serum ACE levels for diagnosis or disease monitoring Missing clinically silent but dangerous cardiac or neurological involvement Treating asymptomatic or mildly affected patients who may remit without therapy Sarcoidosis is thought to arise when an unknown antigen triggers an exaggerated cell-mediated immune response in a genetically susceptible host. Antigen-presenting cells activate CD4 T-helper lymphocytes that secrete Th1 cytokines, driving accumulation of macrophages and their organisation into compact non-caseating epithelioid granulomas. In the lung these granulomas cluster along lymphatics and around bronchovascular structures. Granulomas may resolve or, with persistent inflammation, be replaced by fibrosis, causing irreversible architectural distortion and functional impairment. Prognosis is generally favourable, with a substantial proportion of patients undergoing spontaneous remission, especially in acute presentations such as Loefgren syndrome; however, chronic progressive disease with pulmonary fibrosis, cardiac involvement, or neurosarcoidosis carries greater morbidity and mortality.

It is at least partly reversible: resistance training combined with adequate protein intake can improve strength and performance, and earlier intervention yields better results.

The fertilised female mite burrows into the stratum corneum, laying eggs and depositing faeces as she tunnels. The clinical eruption and intense pruritus are largely due to a delayed type IV hypersensitivity response to the mite, its eggs, and its excreta, which explains the delay in symptoms after primary infestation. In classic scabies the mite burden is low (typically a small number of adult mites), whereas in crusted scabies impaired immune control permits proliferation of thousands to millions of mites, producing thick hyperkeratotic crusts and extreme infectivity. Prognosis is excellent with correct treatment of the patient and all contacts; failures usually reflect incomplete application, missed contacts, or re-infestation rather than true drug resistance.

Short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase catalyses the initial dehydrogenation of short-chain (predominantly butyryl-CoA) substrates in the final rounds of mitochondrial beta-oxidation. Reduced activity leads to accumulation of butyryl-CoA and its derivatives, detectable as raised C4 acylcarnitine and as ethylmalonic and methylsuccinic acids in urine. Because short-chain oxidation contributes relatively little to overall energy generation and the block is late in the pathway, the biochemical abnormality often occurs without a clear clinical syndrome, and many carriers of the common variants remain well. The great majority of screen-detected individuals remain healthy with a normal outlook, and current evidence does not support classifying isolated SCAD deficiency as a reliably harmful disorder; reported symptoms often reflect coincidental or alternative conditions.

Scaphoid fracture — carpal scaphoid fracture, scaphoid waist fracture, carpal navicular fracture Distal radius fracture De Quervain tenosynovitis Scapholunate ligament injury Simple wrist sprain Fracture of the trapezium or other carpal bones First carpometacarpal osteoarthritis Dedicated scaphoid radiographic series including a posteroanterior view in ulnar deviation, oblique and lateral projections Repeat radiographs after an interval of immobilisation when initial films are normal but clinical suspicion persists MRI for early detection of an occult fracture and marrow oedema CT to characterise fracture displacement, humpback deformity and to assess union Radionuclide bone scan as an alternative when MRI is unavailable Most commonly fractured carpal bone, typically following a fall on the outstretched hand with the wrist dorsiflexed and radially deviated Hallmark signs are tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, tenderness over the scaphoid tubercle, and pain on axial compression of the thumb The scaphoid receives its blood supply retrogradely through vessels entering distally, so waist and proximal pole fractures place the proximal fragment at risk of avascular necrosis and non-union Initial radiographs are frequently normal (occult fracture); a clinically suspected scaphoid injury should be immobilised and re-imaged, or evaluated earlier with MRI or CT Dedicated scaphoid views, including a posteroanterior projection in ulnar deviation, improve fracture detection compared with standard wrist films Undisplaced waist fractures are usually managed with cast immobilisation, whereas displaced, unstable or proximal pole fractures often require percutaneous or open fixation Untreated non-union may progress to a predictable pattern of carpal collapse and arthritis (scaphoid non-union advanced collapse) Proximal pole fracture carrying a high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union Fracture displacement or humpback (flexion) deformity indicating instability Delayed presentation with established non-union or sclerosis A snuffbox-tender wrist discharged on the basis of normal initial radiographs Discharging a clinically suspicious, snuffbox-tender wrist because early radiographs appear normal Underestimating the vascular vulnerability of proximal pole fractures Inadequate duration or quality of immobilisation leading to non-union Overlooking associated carpal ligament injury or instability The scaphoid spans the proximal and distal carpal rows and derives most of its blood supply from vessels that enter the distal pole and dorsal ridge, perfusing the bone in a retrograde direction. A fracture, most often across the waist, can interrupt flow to the proximal fragment, which becomes prone to delayed union, non-union and avascular necrosis. Because the bone is largely covered by articular cartilage with little periosteum, healing depends heavily on this tenuous vascular supply and on adequate immobilisation or fixation to prevent motion at the fracture. Persistent non-union alters carpal kinematics and leads over time to progressive degenerative collapse of the wrist. Undisplaced waist fractures usually unite with adequate immobilisation, but proximal pole and displaced fractures carry substantially higher rates of non-union and avascular necrosis; unaddressed non-union can culminate in carpal collapse and post-traumatic arthritis.

scaphoid nonunion — scaphoid fracture nonunion, ununited scaphoid fracture Acute scaphoid fracture Congenital bipartite scaphoid Kienböck disease Scapholunate dissociation or SLAC wrist Preiser disease (idiopathic scaphoid osteonecrosis) Radial styloid or trapezial osteoarthritis De Quervain tenosynovitis PA, lateral, oblique and dedicated scaphoid-view radiographs CT reconstructed along the scaphoid long axis for union and deformity assessment MRI to evaluate proximal pole vascularity Contralateral comparison radiographs Intraoperative assessment of punctate bleeding to gauge bone vascularity Metabolic or inflammatory screen in atypical presentations Scaphoid nonunion typically follows a missed, inadequately immobilised or displaced waist fracture, and the retrograde blood supply predisposes the proximal pole to avascular necrosis. The blood supply enters distally via dorsal ridge branches of the radial artery, so more proximal fractures heal least reliably. Untreated nonunion produces a humpback (flexion) deformity with a DISI posture and a predictable arthritic cascade termed SNAC. SNAC progresses from radial styloid and distal scaphoid arthritis to periscaphoid and midcarpal degeneration, characteristically sparing the radiolunate joint. CT reconstructed along the long axis of the scaphoid best defines union, displacement and humpback deformity. MRI assesses proximal pole vascularity and helps decide between vascularised and non-vascularised bone grafting. Vascularised bone grafting is favoured for an avascular proximal pole, whereas structural wedge grafting is used to correct humpback deformity. Proximal pole sclerosis or fragmentation indicating avascular necrosis Established humpback deformity with DISI Radiographic SNAC changes signalling irreversible arthritis Persistent wrist pain and functional decline in a young manual worker Missing the original fracture on initial radiographs and mislabelling it a sprain. Assuming union on plain films without CT confirmation. Neglecting proximal pole vascularity assessment before selecting a graft. Failing to correct humpback deformity and leaving residual malalignment. Overlooking established SNAC arthritis when planning reconstruction. The scaphoid is largely covered by articular cartilage and receives most of its blood supply retrogradely from branches of the radial artery entering the distal dorsal ridge. A fracture, particularly of the waist or proximal pole, can devascularise the proximal fragment. Persistent motion combined with poor vascularity prevents bridging bone and produces a fibrous or sclerotic nonunion. Volar bone resorption causes the scaphoid to collapse into flexion, the humpback deformity, with compensatory lunate extension producing DISI. Altered load transmission then drives progressive periscaphoid and midcarpal arthritis, the SNAC pattern. With appropriate grafting and fixation before arthritis develops, union rates are good, but established SNAC arthritis is irreversible and ultimately requires salvage surgery.

scapholunate dissociation — scapholunate ligament injury, rotatory subluxation of the scaphoid, SL dissociation Distal radius fracture with associated ligament injury Scaphoid fracture Lunotriquetral ligament injury Kienböck disease Radiocarpal or midcarpal osteoarthritis Dorsal wrist ganglion or occult ganglion De Quervain tenosynovitis Standard PA, lateral and clenched-fist stress radiographs with contralateral comparison views Measurement of the scapholunate gap and scapholunate angle on plain films MRI focused on the scapholunate interosseous ligament MR arthrography or CT arthrography to assess ligament integrity Wrist arthroscopy for definitive staging using the Geissler classification Fluoroscopic or cineradiographic dynamic motion studies Grip-loaded views to provoke dynamic gapping The most common and most significant carpal instability pattern, resulting from disruption of the scapholunate interosseous ligament, particularly its stronger dorsal component. The Watson scaphoid shift test reproduces dorsal pain and a clunk as the scaphoid subluxates over the dorsal rim of the radius on radial deviation. Classic static radiographic signs are a widened scapholunate gap (Terry Thomas sign) on the PA view and a cortical ring sign from the abnormally flexed scaphoid seen end-on. A clenched-fist PA view stresses the interval and may unmask dynamic instability not evident on standard films. On the lateral radiograph an increased scapholunate angle indicates a dorsal intercalated segment instability (DISI) posture, with the lunate extended. Untreated complete injuries progress predictably to scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC) arthritis over years. Management differs sharply between an acute repairable ligament, a chronic reducible deformity without arthritis, and a chronic irreducible or arthritic wrist. Arthroscopy remains the reference standard for staging partial versus complete tears when imaging is equivocal. Progressive dorsal wrist pain and loss of grip after a fall, suggesting evolving instability Radiographic DISI or scapholunate gapping indicating complete ligament disruption Early radioscaphoid narrowing or osteophytes signalling onset of SLAC collapse High-energy mechanism with associated perilunate instability or dislocation Dismissing the injury as a simple sprain and missing the window for primary ligament repair. Relying only on static radiographs and overlooking dynamic instability. Failing to notice scapholunate widening on a distal radius fracture film. Attributing dorsal wrist pain solely to a ganglion. Not comparing with the contralateral wrist, since scapholunate distances vary between individuals. The scapholunate interosseous ligament, together with secondary stabilisers such as the dorsal intercarpal ligament, scaphotrapeziotrapezoid ligament and radioscaphocapitate ligament, maintains the tight kinematic linkage between scaphoid and lunate. When the dorsal scapholunate ligament and its secondary restraints fail, typically after a fall on the extended, ulnar-deviated and supinated wrist, the scaphoid loses restraint and rotates into flexion and pronation while the lunate, still tethered to the triquetrum, extends into a DISI posture. The resulting rotatory subluxation of the scaphoid concentrates load on the radioscaphoid articulation and initiates a predictable degenerative cascade. Acute, well-reduced injuries repaired before arthritis develops have the best functional outcome, whereas untreated complete tears progress over years to SLAC arthritis with pain and stiffness.

scapular dyskinesis — scapular dyskinesia, SICK scapula syndrome Long thoracic nerve palsy causing serratus anterior winging Spinal accessory nerve palsy causing trapezius winging Subacromial impingement syndrome Rotator cuff pathology Glenohumeral instability Fascioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy Cervical radiculopathy Structured clinical observation of scapular motion from behind during repeated elevation Scapular assistance and scapular retraction corrective manoeuvres Electromyography and nerve conduction studies if neurological winging is suspected Assessment of posterior capsular and pectoralis minor tightness MRI or ultrasound of the shoulder to identify associated cuff, labral or instability pathology Cervical spine and neurological assessment when a proximal cause is suspected Scapular dyskinesis is an alteration in the normal position and movement of the scapula, most often observed as prominence of the medial or inferomedial border during arm elevation and lowering. It is usually a response to or a contributor to other shoulder pathology rather than a discrete disease, so search for an underlying cause. The scapula must protract, upwardly rotate and posteriorly tilt to maintain a stable base for the glenohumeral joint and to preserve the subacromial space during elevation. Common contributors include periscapular muscle weakness or fatigue (notably serratus anterior and lower trapezius), pain inhibition, posterior capsular tightness and altered thoracic posture. A neurological cause such as long thoracic nerve palsy (serratus anterior) or spinal accessory nerve palsy (trapezius) must be excluded when winging is prominent. The scapular assistance and scapular retraction tests help demonstrate that correcting scapular mechanics relieves symptoms and predicts response to rehabilitation. The SICK scapula (scapular malposition, inferomedial border prominence, coracoid pain and dyskinesis) describes an overuse pattern in overhead athletes. Management is overwhelmingly rehabilitative, restoring scapular control and flexibility and addressing the primary shoulder disorder, with surgery reserved for specific structural or neurological causes. Prominent static winging suggesting a long thoracic or spinal accessory nerve palsy Progressive, symmetrical periscapular wasting suggesting an underlying myopathy or dystrophy A palpable mass beneath the scapula such as an osteochondroma or elastofibroma Associated neurological deficit or neck pain suggesting cervical or brachial plexus pathology Treating scapular dyskinesis as a standalone diagnosis without identifying the underlying shoulder or neurological cause. Missing a long thoracic or spinal accessory nerve palsy presenting as winging. Overlooking an underlying muscular dystrophy in bilateral or progressive cases. Focusing rehabilitation on the glenohumeral joint alone while neglecting periscapular and postural control. Normal shoulder function depends on coordinated scapulothoracic motion that positions the glenoid optimally beneath the humeral head throughout elevation, maintaining the length-tension relationship of the rotator cuff and preserving subacromial clearance. Scapular dyskinesis arises when this coordination is disrupted by muscular, capsular, postural or neurological factors. Weakness or fatigue of the serratus anterior and lower trapezius, imbalance with an overactive upper trapezius, pain-related inhibition, a tight posteroinferior capsule and pectoralis minor, or denervation of the periscapular muscles all alter scapular upward rotation, posterior tilt and external rotation. The malpositioned scapula reduces the subacromial space, alters glenohumeral contact and increases loads on the rotator cuff and static stabilisers, predisposing to or perpetuating impingement, instability and labral pathology. Thus dyskinesis is frequently both a consequence and a driver of other shoulder conditions. When it accompanies another shoulder disorder, correcting scapular control through targeted rehabilitation improves symptoms and complements treatment of the primary problem, with a generally good outcome. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause, being more guarded when there is an established nerve palsy or a progressive neuromuscular disorder.

pattern with facioscapulohumeral dystrophy Overlooking the wide TRPV4 phenotypic spectrum, including CMT2C and skeletal features Assuming a myopathic cause without electrophysiology to identify a neurogenic process Missing vocal cord involvement that carries airway risk Scapuloperoneal spinal muscular atrophy is a lower motor neurone disorder in which degeneration of anterior horn cells produces weakness in a distinctive scapuloperoneal pattern. The dominant TRPV4-associated form results from variants in a calcium-permeable transient receptor potential channel; the mutations are thought to alter channel gating and calcium handling in motor neurones, leading to selective vulnerability of the neurones supplying shoulder-girdle and peroneal muscles. Because the pathology is largely confined to motor neurones and their axons, sensory function is typically preserved, and the electrophysiology reflects denervation with normal sensory responses. TRPV4 variants can also affect the peripheral nerve and skeleton, explaining the associated phenotypes. Usually slowly progressive with long preservation of function, though severity is variable; congenital TRPV4-related forms and those with vocal cord or respiratory involvement can be more severe.

The primary focus is usually the pharynx. With prompt antibiotic therapy the outlook is excellent and most children recover fully; the main concern with untreated or inadequately treated disease is the risk of rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis, and suppurative spread.

identification, since histology cannot distinguish it from Aspergillus and management differs Overlooking a near-drowning history in a patient with brain abscesses Failing to pursue surgical debridement and source control alongside antifungals Underestimating the near pan-resistance of Lomentospora prolificans Scedosporium and Lomentospora species are inhaled as conidia, aspirated in contaminated water, or directly inoculated through trauma. In immunocompetent hosts localised disease such as mycetoma or airway colonisation predominates, whereas aspiration of polluted water during near-drowning can seed the brain and produce abscesses even in previously healthy people. In immunosuppressed hosts the moulds are angioinvasive, causing vascular thrombosis, tissue infarction, and haematogenous dissemination that is histologically indistinguishable from aspergillosis. Their intrinsic and often multidrug resistance, especially in Lomentospora prolificans, is central to the difficulty of treatment. Outcomes are poor for disseminated and central nervous system disease, particularly with the highly resistant Lomentospora prolificans; prognosis is better for localised infection in immunocompetent hosts amenable to surgery, and depends heavily on immune status and the feasibility of source control.

Truncating variants on the active paternal allele abolish or reduce functional protein, which normally participates in hypothalamic development, circadian and autonomic regulation, and protein trafficking within neurones. Loss of this function disturbs hypothalamic-driven control of feeding, sleep, and endocrine signalling and contributes to abnormal neurodevelopment, while the accompanying joint contractures reflect reduced foetal movement during development. Because expression is imprinted, a variant on the maternally inherited allele is generally silent, so parent of origin critically determines whether disease results. The course is variable but generally involves lifelong intellectual disability and autism-related needs; early mortality can occur in severely affected infants with respiratory or feeding compromise, whereas milder cases stabilise with supportive care, and long-term issues centre on neurodevelopment, sleep-disordered breathing, contracture management, and, in some, obesity-related complications.

junction, with squamous epithelium above and columnar epithelium below. Its exact cause is debated, but chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux and mechanical factors are implicated in its development and in progressive narrowing. The ring reduces the maximal luminal diameter, so large solid boluses intermittently lodge above it, producing episodic dysphagia and, when a bolus fully obstructs the lumen, acute food impaction. Dilatation of a symptomatic ring is usually effective and safe, though rings can recur; addressing coexisting reflux may reduce the recurrence rate.

syndrome arises from biallelic pathogenic variants in the IDUA gene, which encodes the lysosomal hydrolase alpha-L-iduronidase. Residual enzyme activity is greater than in Hurler syndrome, producing a milder phenotype within the same disease continuum. Impaired breakdown of the glycosaminoglycans dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate leads to their progressive accumulation within lysosomes of connective tissue, cornea, cartilage, heart valves, and other organs. The stored substrate is also excreted in excess in the urine. Because intellectual function is generally spared, the clinical burden is dominated by musculoskeletal, ocular, and cardiac involvement that worsens slowly over years. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Life expectancy can approach normal in many patients, though progressive cardiac valve disease, corneal clouding, and joint limitation cause substantial long-term morbidity. Enzyme replacement therapy may help systemic manifestations but does not correct established corneal or valvular changes.

search for another cause Mislabelling a rigid structural kyphosis as flexible postural round-back and under-treating it Failing to appreciate the diagnostic requirement for wedging of several consecutive vertebrae Overlooking neurological compromise in a severe or painful thoracic curve Attributing all back pain to Scheuermann disease without excluding infection, fracture or tumour Scheuermann disease is an osteochondrosis affecting the ring apophyses and cartilaginous endplates of the growing vertebral bodies. Disordered endochondral ossification and mechanical stress at the vertebral growth zones impair the normal anterior growth of the vertebral bodies, so that the anterior height falls behind the posterior height and the vertebrae become wedged. Herniation of disc material through weakened endplates produces Schmorl nodes, and endplate irregularity with disc space narrowing follows. The cumulative anterior wedging of several adjacent vertebrae results in an increased, rigid thoracic (or thoracolumbar) kyphosis that, unlike postural round-back, does not correct with extension. A genetic predisposition and repetitive loading during rapid growth are thought to contribute. Most adolescents have a stable curve and do well with observation, physiotherapy or bracing during growth; severe curves may progress and cause pain or cosmetic concern into adulthood, and neurological compromise is rare but important to recognise.

intracranial pressure Visual compromise from an ocular choristoma or coloboma Assuming an extensive naevus sebaceus is purely cosmetic and not screening for neurological, ocular or skeletal disease Overlooking hypophosphataemic rickets as a treatable cause of skeletal symptoms Attributing every secondary nodule to malignancy when benign trichoblastoma is more common Delaying neuroimaging in a child presenting with seizures and a segmental head-and-neck naevus Schimmelpenning syndrome is a mosaic RASopathy caused by a post-zygotic activating variant, most commonly in HRAS and less often KRAS, occurring early in embryogenesis. Because the variant arises after fertilisation, only the clonal population of cells descended from the mutated progenitor is affected, producing lesions distributed along the lines of Blaschko. In the skin this drives an organoid naevus sebaceus with sebaceous and epidermal overgrowth, while involvement of neuroectodermal, ocular and mesodermal progenitors accounts for the associated brain, eye and skeletal anomalies. Persistent RAS-MAPK signalling within the naevus also underlies the tendency to develop secondary appendageal tumours over time. Prognosis depends on the extent of extracutaneous involvement; isolated cutaneous disease has an excellent outlook, whereas extensive neurological involvement with refractory seizures and developmental delay carries a poorer prognosis, and lifelong dermatological surveillance is needed for secondary tumours.

Relying only on glycosaminoglycan screening and missing the oligosaccharide pattern Assuming a single uniform phenotype given the wide clinical spectrum Schindler disease is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in NAGA, encoding lysosomal alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase. This enzyme removes terminal alpha-N-acetylgalactosamine residues from glycoproteins, glycopeptides, and glycolipids during lysosomal degradation. Its deficiency leads to accumulation of these incompletely degraded compounds and their excretion in the urine. The mechanism linking substrate storage to the severe infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy of type I remains incompletely understood, but the phenotype features widespread axonal swellings (spheroids). Type II (Kanzaki disease) presents in adulthood with cutaneous angiokeratomas and only mild neurological involvement, and intermediate presentations occur. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The infantile type I form is severe with profound neurological deterioration and a poor outlook, whereas the adult type II form follows a much milder course compatible with long survival. No disease-modifying therapy is established.

cercariae penetrate intact human skin within a few minutes (p.1826). A travel/migration history of freshwater exposure (bathing, washing, fishing, rice-field work, swimming) in an endemic area is central to the diagnosis, especially in travelers (p.1827, p.1829). Most disease manifestations are due to immunologic granulomatous reactions to eggs retained in host tissues, not to the adult worms; about half of eggs are trapped in tissue (p.1827). Cercarial dermatitis ('swimmer's itch') is a maculopapular rash from cercarial skin penetration; a severe form follows exposure to avian schistosomes (e.g., lakes in Europe/US) that die in the skin (p.1828). Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever) occurs 2 weeks to 3 months after exposure, usually in first-time-infected travelers, with fever, myalgia, malaise, headache, nonproductive cough, and abdominal symptoms (p.1828). Eosinophilia is a common finding and is often associated with schistosomiasis; transient pulmonary infiltrates may accompany Katayama fever (p.1828, p.1829). Intestinal schistosomiasis (S. mansoni, S. japonicum): worms in mesenteric veins; eggs trapped in intestinal tissue cause granulomatous inflammation, microulceration, intermittent abdominal pain, and sometimes bloody diarrhea (p.1829). Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis (S. mansoni, S. japonicum): late disease produces periportal (Symmers clay-pipestem) fibrosis with portal vein occlusion, portal hypertension, splenomegaly, esophageal varices, and hematemesis; hepatic function usually remains normal (p.1827, p.1829). Urogenital schistosomiasis (S. haematobium): hallmark of the active stage is painless terminal hematuria, with dysuria and suprapubic discomfort; eggs in bladder mucosa cause inflammation, fibrosis, 'sandy patches', and possible ureteric obstruction with hydronephrosis (p.1829). S. haematobium is an IARC group 1 carcinogen; chronic infection is associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder (p.1829). Detection of schistosome eggs in stool or urine indicates active infection and is the standard diagnostic method; S. haematobium eggs (terminal spine) are excreted in urine, other species (S. mansoni lateral spine, S. japonicum small lateral knob) in feces (p.1826, p.1829). Neuroschistosomiasis is one of the most severe forms: S. mansoni/S. haematobium can cause transverse myelitis (an acute complication in returning travelers), while S. japonicum causes cerebral granulomas with seizures and focal neurologic deficits (p.1829). Hematemesis or melena from esophageal varices in hepatosplenic disease - the most severe complication; death may result from massive blood loss (p.1829) Acute transverse myelitis or other cerebral/spinal cord manifestations - neuroschistosomiasis, even from light infections (p.1829) Severe Katayama fever with weight loss, dyspnea, diarrhea, and hepatomegaly; rarely fatal (p.1829) Painless terminal hematuria in a traveler/migrant from an endemic area (urogenital S. haematobium) (p.1829) Obstructive uropathy progressing to uremia from ureteral fibrosis (p.1829) Patients with periportal fibrosis (late hepatosplenic disease) may excrete very few or no eggs in feces, so a negative stool exam does not exclude advanced disease (p.1829). In the chronic urogenital stage, urinary egg excretion may be sparse or absent despite ongoing urogenital tract pathology (p.1829). Egg excretion may be very low in people from nonendemic areas (travelers), requiring larger samples and concentration methods (p.1829). Katayama fever is rare in people chronically exposed in S. mansoni- or S. haematobium-endemic areas, so its absence does not exclude infection in residents (p.1829). CAA/CCA antigen detection is not currently suitable for diagnosing travelers, who have low worm burdens (p.1830). Serology is less useful in people from endemic areas with ongoing transmission (p.1829-1830). Free-swimming cercariae released from infected freshwater snails penetrate intact skin within minutes, transform into schistosomula, enter veins/lymphatics, traverse the lungs and heart, and mature in the portal vein into paired adult male and female worms that migrate to the mesenteric (S. mansoni, S. japonicum) or pelvic/vesical (S. haematobium) venous plexus. The prepatent period is 5-7 weeks (up to 12 for S. haematobium). About half of the eggs produced are excreted in feces or urine; the remainder become trapped in tissue. Most morbidity results from egg-induced, TH2-driven granulomatous immune responses (lymphocytes, eosinophils, alternatively activated macrophages; IL-4/5/13). Egg antigen excess early in infection forms soluble immune complexes causing a serum sickness-like illness (Katayama fever). Hepatic egg deposition leads to periportal (Symmers) fibrosis, portal-branch occlusion, and portal hypertension; S. haematobium egg deposition in the bladder/ureters causes inflammation, fibrosis, obstructive uropathy, and predisposes to squamous bladder carcinoma (p.1826-1829). Many patients recover spontaneously from acute schistosomiasis after 2-10 weeks, though some follow a more severe course, and the acute syndrome can rarely be fatal. In hepatosplenic disease, hepatic function usually remains normal even with marked periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension; however, severe periportal (Symmers) fibrosis is often irreversible, and hematemesis from variceal bleeding may be fatal. Early inflammatory hepatosplenomegaly in children generally decreases over time as immunity develops. Ureteral fibrosis can cause irreversible obstructive uropathy progressing to uremia. The adult worm lifespan averages 3-5 years but can reach 30 years (p.1826-1829). Disease is staged clinically by duration and intensity of infection into three phases - acute (cercarial dermatitis and Katayama fever), active/established, and chronic (e.g., late hepatosplenic periportal fibrosis with portal hypertension, or chronic urogenital fibrosis with sandy patches and obstructive uropathy). Severity of early hepatosplenomegaly is closely associated with infection intensity (p.1828-1829).

nerve hypoplasia Not screening for hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction when septo-optic features coexist Confusing a large open-lip cleft with hydrocephalus or hydranencephaly on imaging Schizencephaly is a disorder of cortical formation in which a cleft lined by dysplastic grey matter spans the full thickness of the hemisphere from the ventricle to the cortical surface. It is thought to arise most often from a disruptive prenatal insult, such as a vascular event, that damages the germinal zone and developing cortex, sometimes combined with genetic susceptibility affecting cortical patterning. Because the injury occurs while the cortex is still developing, the cleft becomes lined by abnormal, typically polymicrogyric grey matter, and associated failure of midline structures such as the septum pellucidum and optic apparatus is common. Prognosis depends on the size, type, and laterality of the cleft. Unilateral closed-lip schizencephaly may cause only mild hemiparesis and manageable epilepsy, whereas bilateral open-lip disease is typically associated with severe motor and cognitive disability and refractory seizures.

Missing substance-induced or medical causes of combined mood and psychotic symptoms Making a firm diagnosis prematurely without longitudinal observation Schizoaffective disorder is conceptualised as lying on a spectrum between schizophrenia and the mood disorders, sharing neurobiological features with both, including dopaminergic dysregulation implicated in psychosis and monoaminergic and stress-axis disturbances implicated in mood pathology. Genetic vulnerability overlapping with both schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, neurodevelopmental factors, and altered corticolimbic circuitry are thought to contribute. The prognosis of schizoaffective disorder is generally intermediate between that of schizophrenia and the mood disorders, tending to be better than schizophrenia but worse than a pure mood disorder. Outcome is more favourable with predominant mood symptoms, good treatment adherence, and strong psychosocial support, and less favourable with prominent persistent psychosis and poor functioning between episodes.

Structural and functional brain changes, synaptic pruning abnormalities, and gene-environment interactions such as obstetric complications and cannabis exposure contribute to the emergence of illness. Better outcomes are associated with acute onset, good premorbid functioning, prominent mood symptoms, and early treatment, whereas insidious onset, prominent negative symptoms, and long untreated psychosis predict poorer functional recovery.

chondrodysplasia is caused by dominant variants in COL10A1, encoding type X collagen, which is produced by hypertrophic chondrocytes in the growth plate. Mutant chains misfold and are retained within the endoplasmic reticulum, triggering an unfolded-protein/ER-stress response that disrupts the orderly progression of hypertrophic chondrocytes and mineralisation at the metaphysis. The result is metaphyseal disorganisation, flaring and coxa vara, while epiphyseal cartilage and vertebral growth, which rely less on type X collagen, remain largely spared. Generally favourable: short stature is mild, radiographic metaphyseal changes tend to remodel with growth, and life expectancy is normal, though residual bowing may occasionally warrant orthopaedic correction.

defining monoclonal gammopathy Not arranging long-term haematological surveillance for lymphoproliferative transformation Confusing it with a late-onset cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome without appropriate testing Schnitzler syndrome is an acquired autoinflammatory condition in which excessive activation of the innate immune system, particularly interleukin-1-driven inflammation, produces a neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis and systemic inflammation. It occurs in the context of a monoclonal gammopathy, most often IgM kappa, and although the precise link between the paraprotein and the inflammatory drive is not fully defined, the disease behaves as an interleukin-1-mediated process, as evidenced by its striking response to interleukin-1 blockade. Chronic overproduction of interleukin-1 beta and downstream cytokines accounts for the fever, bone changes and acute phase response, while the underlying clonal B-cell process explains the association with, and risk of evolution to, lymphoproliferative malignancy. Inflammatory symptoms are usually well controlled with interleukin-1 inhibition and quality of life can be restored, but the disorder is chronic and carries a persistent long-term risk of evolving into a lymphoproliferative malignancy, so lifelong monitoring is required.
