Although the corneal defect is local, affected individuals frequently have systemic dyslipidaemia, so the cornea can be a marker of a broader lipid abnormality. Vision declines slowly over decades; systemic lipid management is important, and superficial ablation or keratoplasty can help visually significant disease, though deposits may recur.

malignant change is very rare Rapid growth, pain, or new neurological deficit suggesting malignant transformation Bilateral vestibular tumours or multiple schwannomas indicating an underlying syndrome Progressive hearing loss, tinnitus, or brainstem compression from a vestibular lesion Spinal lesions causing cord or root compression A large deep tumour with atypical imaging features Resecting the nerve unnecessarily when the tumour can be dissected free with preservation of function Overinterpreting the degenerative atypia of ancient schwannoma as malignancy Failing to investigate for neurofibromatosis type 2 or schwannomatosis when tumours are multiple or bilateral Confusing schwannoma with neurofibroma and thereby misjudging the risk of malignant transformation Schwannoma is a benign neoplasm arising from the Schwann cells that form the myelin sheath of peripheral nerves. It grows as a well-encapsulated mass eccentric to the nerve, displacing rather than engulfing the fascicles, which is why it can often be enucleated with preservation of nerve function. Most sporadic tumours show biallelic inactivation of the NF2 gene on chromosome 22, whose product merlin normally restrains cell proliferation; loss of merlin function drives Schwann cell overgrowth. Germline NF2 alterations produce neurofibromatosis type 2 with its hallmark bilateral vestibular schwannomas, whereas germline SMARCB1 or LZTR1 variants underlie schwannomatosis. Histologically the tumour alternates between organised, cellular Antoni A tissue with palisaded Verocay bodies and hypocellular, myxoid Antoni B tissue, and it characteristically has thick-walled hyalinised vessels. Malignant transformation is exceptional, in contrast to the neurofibroma of neurofibromatosis type 1. Schwannoma is benign with an excellent prognosis; careful enucleation is usually curative and preserves nerve function, and recurrence is uncommon. Malignant transformation is very rare, and the main determinants of outcome are tumour site and any associated tumour syndrome.

rather than schwannomatosis Rapid tumour growth, new neurological deficit, or features suggesting malignant transformation Spinal cord or cauda equina compression from an enlarging intraspinal schwannoma Intractable pain with functional decline requiring specialist intervention Diagnosing schwannomatosis without excluding bilateral vestibular schwannomas and thereby missing NF2 Assuming pain is proportional to tumour bulk and under-treating disabling neuropathic pain Pursuing aggressive resection of all tumours rather than targeting symptomatic or growing lesions Relying on blood testing alone, since tumour tissue analysis often clarifies the genetic diagnosis Schwannomatosis is a tumour predisposition syndrome caused by germline variants in the tumour suppressor genes SMARCB1 or LZTR1, both situated on chromosome 22q close to NF2. Tumour development typically follows a multi-hit mechanism in which the germline variant is compounded by somatic loss of the region encompassing both the predisposing gene and NF2, so that the resulting schwannomas show combined inactivation. This shared chromosomal neighbourhood explains the clinical overlap with NF2 while the preservation of at least one functional NF2 allele in constitutional tissue accounts for the absence of the bilateral vestibular schwannomas that define NF2. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance, and many cases appear sporadic. Life expectancy is generally normal because the tumours are benign and malignant change is uncommon. The principal burden is chronic pain and the cumulative morbidity of multiple tumours and their surgical treatment; quality of life depends heavily on effective pain control and judicious, function-preserving surgery.

channelopathy and missing the skeletal chondrodysplasia that defines the syndrome Overlooking the anaesthetic and airway risks in a child with facial and jaw stiffness Confusing the continuous discharges with the discharges of Isaacs syndrome or true myotonia Failing to arrange orthopaedic and ophthalmological surveillance for the skeletal and eye complications Schwartz-Jampel syndrome is caused by mutations in HSPG2, which encodes perlecan, a large heparan sulphate proteoglycan that is a major structural and signalling component of basement membranes and of cartilage extracellular matrix. Deficient or dysfunctional perlecan disrupts cartilage development, producing the chondrodysplasia, short stature and skeletal deformities. At the neuromuscular junction, perlecan anchors acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic basal lamina, and its deficiency reduces cholinesterase activity so that acetylcholine action is prolonged, contributing, together with abnormal muscle-membrane excitability, to the sustained muscle activity and stiffness that clinically resembles myotonia. Prognosis varies with severity, but many children with the classic form survive into adulthood with persistent stiffness and skeletal deformity, whereas a rarer severe neonatal presentation carries higher early morbidity; the disorder is generally non-progressive once established but causes lasting orthopaedic and functional handicap.

mechanically compresses and inflames the root. Other causes include degenerative foraminal or central canal stenosis, spondylolisthesis, and less often tumour or infection. Nerve root inflammation and ischaemia generate the characteristic radiating pain and neurological signs in the corresponding dermatome and myotome. The majority of disc-related cases resolve within six to twelve weeks with conservative treatment, but a proportion have persistent or recurrent symptoms; surgery gives faster relief of leg pain in selected patients, and outcomes worsen if significant neurological deficit is not treated promptly.

anomalous systemic arterial supply, which can cause pulmonary overcirculation if left untreated Assuming an isolated atrial septal defect and overlooking the anomalous venous drainage Underappreciating pulmonary hypertension confined to the affected lung Failing to recognise postoperative scimitar vein stenosis as a cause of persistent symptoms Scimitar syndrome is part of the pulmonary venolobar spectrum arising from abnormal development of the right lung bud and its venous drainage. All or part of the right lung drains anomalously through a scimitar-shaped vein into the inferior vena cava, right atrium, portal or hepatic veins rather than the left atrium, creating a left-to-right shunt. The affected lung is typically hypoplastic, pulling the heart rightward, and often receives an anomalous systemic arterial supply directly from the descending aorta, which adds a further left-to-right contribution and can cause pulmonary hypertension in the affected segment. The overall haemodynamic burden depends on the volume of anomalous flow, the aberrant arterial supply and any associated shunt lesions. The adult form is often well tolerated with a good outlook, while the infantile form with pulmonary hypertension and associated defects has a more guarded prognosis; surgical repair can be complicated by scimitar vein stenosis.

Scleredema (of Buschke) — scleredema of Buschke, scleredema adultorum, scleredema diabeticorum, Buschke disease Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) Scleromyxoedema Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis Eosinophilic fasciitis Myxoedema of hypothyroidism Chronic graft-versus-host disease with sclerosis Skin biopsy showing dermal thickening, separated collagen bundles, and mucin deposition Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation for monoclonal gammopathy Fasting glucose and HbA1c to assess for diabetes Streptococcal and viral serology when a post-infectious form is suspected Thyroid function to exclude myxoedema Autoantibody screen to help exclude systemic sclerosis A deposition dermatosis with diffuse, non-pitting induration and thickening of the skin, typically over the upper back, posterior neck, and shoulders The affected skin feels woody and firm, and movement of the neck and trunk can become restricted Three recognised clinical settings: a post-infectious form after streptococcal or viral illness, an association with monoclonal gammopathy, and a form linked to long-standing diabetes (scleredema diabeticorum) Unlike systemic sclerosis it spares the fingers and lacks Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and nailfold capillary changes Histology shows thickened dermis with widely separated collagen bundles and accumulation of mucin (glycosaminoglycans) The diabetes-associated form tends to be chronic and persistent, whereas the post-infectious form may resolve over months There is no uniformly effective treatment; options explored include physiotherapy, phototherapy, and immunomodulatory approaches, alongside management of the underlying association Detection of a monoclonal protein warranting haematological evaluation for myeloma or related dyscrasia Restriction of chest wall movement or dysphagia from extensive induration Rapidly progressive or widespread skin involvement Features suggesting an alternative systemic sclerosing disease Mistaking it for systemic sclerosis and missing that the fingers are spared without Raynaud phenomenon Failing to screen for a monoclonal gammopathy that may herald a plasma-cell disorder Overlooking poorly controlled diabetes as the underlying association Interpreting the non-pitting swelling as simple oedema Scleredema is characterised by excessive deposition of collagen and mucopolysaccharide (mucin) in the reticular dermis, which thickens the skin and produces its firm, non-pitting induration. Fibroblasts in affected skin appear to be stimulated to overproduce collagen and glycosaminoglycans. The mechanisms differ by clinical context: a post-infectious immune response is implicated after streptococcal or viral illness, non-enzymatic glycosylation and altered collagen metabolism are thought relevant in diabetes, and a paraproteinaemic form is associated with monoclonal gammopathy, sometimes progressing to a plasma-cell dyscrasia. The dermal expansion, not oedema fluid, explains why the swelling does not pit. The post-infectious form often improves spontaneously over months to a couple of years, whereas the diabetes-associated and paraproteinaemic forms tend to be chronic and refractory; overall prognosis depends on any underlying disorder.

sclerema neonatorum — sclerema neonatorum, sclerema adiposum subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn neonatal scleroderma / stiff skin syndromes neonatal sepsis with oedema and induration cold injury / neonatal cold syndrome diffuse neonatal oedema (hydrops, hypoproteinaemia) congenital ichthyosis with taut skin full septic screen including blood cultures, lumbar puncture and cultures as indicated full blood count, C-reactive protein and coagulation studies serum electrolytes, glucose, urea and creatinine blood gas analysis for hypoxia and acidosis skin biopsy for histopathology when diagnosis is uncertain (wide septa, crystal clefts, scant inflammation) core temperature monitoring chest radiograph and other imaging directed at the underlying illness A rare, diffuse hardening of the skin and subcutaneous fat affecting critically ill, usually premature or low-birth-weight neonates in the first week of life. The skin becomes cold, board-like, waxy and immobile, spreading rapidly from the buttocks and lower limbs to involve most of the body, sparing the palms, soles and genitalia. It is almost always a marker of severe underlying illness such as sepsis, dehydration, hypothermia, hypoxia or congenital malformation, rather than a primary skin disease. Unlike subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn, affected infants are gravely unwell and the induration is diffuse rather than nodular. The rigid skin restricts respiration and feeding, compounding the underlying condition. Histology shows widened fibrous septa and needle-shaped clefts within enlarged adipocytes, with little or no inflammatory infiltrate and minimal fat necrosis. Management is directed at the underlying illness, aggressive supportive care, warming, correction of fluid and electrolyte disturbances and treatment of sepsis. Mortality is high and correlates with the severity of the precipitating illness rather than the skin changes themselves. rapidly spreading induration in a hypothermic, hypotensive or septic neonate respiratory compromise from restricted chest-wall movement haemodynamic instability and multi-organ dysfunction severe metabolic acidosis or coagulopathy inability to feed or maintain temperature despite supportive measures Regarding the skin hardening as the primary problem instead of a sign of critical systemic illness. Confusing it with the far more benign subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn. Delaying sepsis evaluation and empirical treatment while investigating the skin. Underestimating the respiratory impact of diffuse cutaneous rigidity. Attributing induration to primary scleroderma in a neonate. Sclerema neonatorum reflects the physicochemical vulnerability of neonatal subcutaneous fat, which has a high ratio of saturated to unsaturated fatty acids and thus a high melting point. In a critically ill, hypothermic and hypoperfused infant, this fat solidifies and crystallises, producing diffuse induration. Enzymatic defects in fatty-acid mobilisation and impaired thermoregulation are thought to contribute. Histologically there is little inflammation or true necrosis; instead adipocytes enlarge and contain needle-shaped crystal clefts, and the fibrous septa thicken. The process is best understood as a physical solidification of fat in a decompensating infant, so the condition is essentially an epiphenomenon of severe systemic illness. The prognosis is poor, with high mortality driven by the severity of the underlying illness; survival depends on prompt and effective treatment of the precipitating condition rather than of the skin changes.

Scleritis — anterior scleritis, posterior scleritis, necrotising scleritis, scleromalacia perforans Episcleritis Anterior uveitis Conjunctivitis Orbital cellulitis or orbital inflammatory disease (posterior scleritis) Infective (e.g. herpetic or pseudomonal) scleritis Choroidal tumour or exudative retinal detachment (posterior scleritis) Slit-lamp examination with assessment of deep vessel involvement and response to topical phenylephrine B-scan ultrasonography for posterior scleritis (scleral thickening and T-sign) Inflammatory and autoimmune workup: full blood count, ESR/CRP, ANA, ANCA, rheumatoid factor Investigations for infective causes (including syphilis and tuberculosis) when indicated Imaging or systemic referral when an underlying vasculitis is suspected Presents with severe, deep, boring ocular pain that is often worse at night, may radiate to the face or jaw, and characteristically disturbs sleep The redness has a bluish or violaceous hue from involvement of the deep scleral vessels, unlike the bright red of episcleritis Scleral vessels do not blanch with topical phenylephrine, which helps distinguish scleritis from episcleritis Classified into anterior (diffuse, nodular, or necrotising) and posterior forms; necrotising scleritis is the most destructive and sight-threatening Scleromalacia perforans is a painless necrotising form seen in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis Roughly half of cases are associated with systemic disease, especially rheumatoid arthritis and ANCA-associated vasculitis such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis Posterior scleritis can mimic other conditions with proptosis, pain on eye movement, and disc swelling, and is confirmed on ultrasound (T-sign) Management is with systemic anti-inflammatory therapy: oral NSAIDs for milder disease and systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppression for necrotising or refractory cases Necrotising scleritis with scleral thinning or threatened perforation Severe pain with reduced vision indicating posterior segment or optic nerve involvement Features of systemic vasculitis (e.g. granulomatosis with polyangiitis) requiring urgent systemic treatment Rapid progression despite therapy suggesting infective scleritis or aggressive vasculitis Mistaking scleritis for the benign, self-limiting episcleritis and undertreating it Failing to search for and treat an underlying systemic vasculitis or connective-tissue disease Missing posterior scleritis, which lacks obvious external redness and mimics orbital disease Using topical steroids alone when systemic immunosuppression is required for necrotising disease Scleritis is inflammation of the sclera, frequently immune-mediated and often a manifestation of systemic autoimmune or vasculitic disease. Immune-complex deposition and T-cell-mediated inflammation cause oedema and cellular infiltration of the sclera and episclera; in necrotising disease, occlusive vasculitis of the deep episcleral vessels leads to scleral ischaemia, necrosis, and thinning, with risk of perforation. Chronic or severe inflammation can extend to adjacent structures causing keratitis, uveitis, glaucoma, and, in posterior disease, exudative retinal detachment and optic nerve involvement. Diffuse and nodular anterior scleritis usually respond to anti-inflammatory treatment with good visual outcomes, but necrotising scleritis is associated with significant ocular morbidity and, when linked to systemic vasculitis, increased mortality if the underlying disease is untreated.

It reflects abnormal neural crest-derived anterior segment development and often coexists with other dysgenetic features. The corneal opacification obstructs the visual axis in severe cases, causing form-deprivation amblyopia, while the abnormal anterior segment can predispose to glaucoma. Mild peripheral sclerocornea has little visual impact, whereas total sclerocornea carries a poor visual prognosis even with corneal transplantation because of associated dysgenesis and amblyopia.

failure Falling platelets with schistocytes signalling thrombotic microangiopathy Withholding or stopping angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition because creatinine rises initially Missing a normotensive presentation and attributing renal failure to another cause Confusing the microangiopathy with primary thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and giving inappropriate plasma exchange alone Using unnecessary glucocorticoids in high-risk early diffuse disease Scleroderma renal crisis arises from obliterative vasculopathy of the renal arcuate and interlobular arteries, with intimal proliferation and luminal narrowing reducing renal blood flow. Consequent activation of the renin-angiotensin system produces severe hypertension, which further injures the vessel walls in a self-amplifying cycle. Endothelial damage in the small vessels drives a thrombotic microangiopathy with mechanical fragmentation of red cells and platelet consumption. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition interrupts the renin-angiotensin drive and is therefore central to management. Before the era of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition renal crisis was almost uniformly fatal; timely blood pressure control now allows many patients to recover renal function, though some remain dialysis-dependent and overall mortality stays significant.

scleroedema — scleroedema of Buschke, scleroedema adultorum, scleroedema diabeticorum Systemic sclerosis and morphoea Scleromyxoedema Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis Eosinophilic fasciitis Myxoedema of hypothyroidism Chronic sclerodermatous graft-versus-host disease Skin biopsy from involved back or neck showing dermal thickening with mucin between collagen bundles Fasting glucose and glycated haemoglobin to assess for diabetes Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to detect a paraprotein Antistreptolysin O titre and infection history in the post-infectious form Thyroid function tests to exclude myxoedema Assessment of chest wall and joint mobility where induration is extensive A mucinosis characterised by diffuse, symmetrical, non-pitting woody induration of the skin, typically beginning on the posterior neck, upper back and shoulders Three clinical types are recognised: a post-infectious form (often after streptococcal or viral upper respiratory infection) that tends to resolve, a form associated with monoclonal gammopathy, and scleroedema diabeticorum linked to long-standing insulin-dependent diabetes The skin over the upper trunk becomes thickened and bound down, sometimes with an orange-peel appearance and reduced ability to pinch or wrinkle the skin The hands and feet are characteristically spared, helping to distinguish it from systemic sclerosis, and Raynaud phenomenon and sclerodactyly are absent Extensive disease can restrict movement of the neck, back and chest wall, and rarely involves the tongue, pharynx or heart Histology shows a thickened reticular dermis with collagen bundles separated by mucin, producing characteristic fenestration, best demonstrated with colloidal iron or Alcian blue Treatment is often unsatisfactory; phototherapy (particularly UVA1 or PUVA), optimisation of glycaemic control and physiotherapy are used, and the post-infectious form may resolve spontaneously Restriction of chest wall movement causing respiratory compromise Cardiac involvement in extensive disease Dysphagia or airway symptoms from pharyngeal or tongue involvement Rapidly progressive induration or associated systemic symptoms prompting reassessment Confusing scleroedema with systemic sclerosis, despite the sparing of the hands and absence of Raynaud phenomenon Overlooking an underlying monoclonal gammopathy requiring monitoring Failing to distinguish the self-limiting post-infectious form from the persistent diabetic form when advising on prognosis Taking a superficial biopsy that misses the deep dermal mucin and collagen changes Neglecting glycaemic optimisation and physiotherapy in the diabetic form Scleroedema is a primary cutaneous mucinosis in which fibroblasts deposit excess collagen and glycosaminoglycans, chiefly hyaluronic acid, throughout a markedly thickened reticular dermis. In the post-infectious form, an immune response to preceding infection is thought to stimulate fibroblast activity transiently. In the diabetes-associated form, chronic hyperglycaemia is believed to promote non-enzymatic glycation of collagen, increase resistance to degradation and stimulate mucin production, accounting for its persistence. The paraproteinaemic form is associated with a monoclonal gammopathy that, as in scleromyxoedema, may drive fibroblast stimulation, although the mechanism is incompletely defined. The post-infectious form usually resolves over months to a couple of years, whereas the diabetes-associated and paraprotein-related forms tend to be chronic and persistent. Serious systemic complications are uncommon, and prognosis is largely determined by the underlying association and the extent of functional restriction.

Scleromalacia perforans — necrotising scleritis without inflammation, anterior necrotising scleritis without inflammation Necrotising scleritis with inflammation (painful, injected) Diffuse or nodular anterior scleritis Infective (e.g. pseudomonal or fungal) scleritis and surgically induced necrotising scleritis Scleral thinning from prior surgery or trauma Senile scleral hyaline plaques Choroidal or ciliary body melanoma showing through thin sclera Blue sclera of osteogenesis imperfecta or other collagen disorders Slit-lamp examination with red-free light to map scleral thinning and avascular necrotic areas Rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP antibodies and inflammatory markers ANCA, antinuclear antibody and complement to screen for systemic vasculitis Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography or high-frequency ultrasound to quantify residual scleral thickness Screening for infection when a necrotising process could be microbial, including scrape and culture Systemic vasculitis and infection screen (chest imaging, urinalysis, renal function) in liaison with rheumatology Scleromalacia perforans is a form of anterior necrotising scleritis occurring characteristically WITHOUT inflammation and WITHOUT pain, which is why it is so easily overlooked despite being sight- and globe-threatening. It is strongly associated with long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, typically in older women with severe deforming disease, and is regarded as a marker of systemic vasculitic activity. The hallmark is progressive scleral thinning with the appearance of yellow-grey necrotic plaques and increasingly visible bluish underlying uvea; despite the name, actual perforation is uncommon unless trauma or raised intraocular pressure supervenes. Because it is painless and quiet, patients may present late with an incidental blue-grey patch or with astigmatic visual change rather than with a red painful eye. Management is fundamentally systemic: aggressive immunosuppression, frequently with corticosteroids plus a steroid-sparing agent or a biologic, in close liaison with rheumatology, because the eye disease reflects underlying systemic vasculitis with excess mortality. Topical therapy is largely supportive; ocular lubrication and protection are used but do not alter the necrotising process. Surgery is avoided where possible because the necrotic sclera heals poorly; scleral or tectonic patch grafting is reserved for impending or actual perforation. New-onset necrotising scleritis mandates a work-up for systemic vasculitis and exclusion of infection, as an underlying connective-tissue or ANCA-associated disorder frequently coexists and dictates prognosis. Rapidly progressive scleral thinning with staphyloma formation or impending perforation Exposure of uvea through frankly necrotic sclera Systemic features of active vasculitis (renal, pulmonary or neurological involvement) Signs suggesting infective scleritis, which mimics and requires urgent culture-directed antimicrobials Any globe rupture following minor trauma to markedly thinned sclera Dismissing a white, painless eye as benign and missing sight-threatening necrotising scleritis Treating the eye in isolation without instituting or escalating systemic immunosuppression Failing to exclude infective scleritis before committing to immunosuppression Undertaking scleral surgery on actively necrotic tissue, precipitating further melt (surgically induced necrotising scleritis) Overlooking the associated excess systemic mortality and not co-managing with rheumatology The lesion is driven by immune-complex-mediated occlusive microvasculitis of the deep episcleral and scleral vessels, most often in the setting of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. Vascular occlusion produces ischaemia of the avascular scleral collagen, and infiltrating macrophages and matrix metalloproteinases degrade the scleral matrix, causing progressive necrosis and thinning. Uniquely, the classic cellular inflammatory response is muted or absent, so the eye remains white and painless while the sclera melts away, exposing the underlying dark uvea. Continued matrix breakdown risks staphylomatous ectasia and, rarely, perforation. Ocular prognosis is guarded and depends on early control of the underlying systemic disease; untreated it can progress to staphyloma or perforation. Its appearance signals severe systemic vasculitis and is associated with increased mortality, so outcome is tied to systemic rather than purely ocular management.

paraprotein Failing to perform serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation in a patient with unexplained waxy skin induration Overlooking systemic and neurological involvement Assuming absence of myeloma excludes significant disease Tracking treatment response by paraprotein level rather than clinical activity Scleromyxoedema is a generalised form of lichen myxoedematosus characterised by deposition of mucin (glycosaminoglycans) in the dermis together with proliferation of fibroblasts and increased collagen. It is almost invariably associated with a monoclonal gammopathy, usually IgG lambda, though the paraprotein's precise pathogenic role is unclear and disease activity does not track paraprotein levels. Circulating factors are thought to stimulate dermal fibroblasts to overproduce mucin and collagen, and the process may extend to internal organs, producing systemic and, in the dermato-neuro syndrome, central neurological complications. Scleromyxoedema is a chronic, often progressive disorder; skin disease may respond to intravenous immunoglobulin and immunomodulation, but systemic and central nervous system involvement, particularly the dermato-neuro syndrome, can be life-threatening.

condition for systemic sclerosis and missing the distinctive papular and doughnut-sign features Not recognising dermato-neuro syndrome, a treatable but rapidly fatal emergency, as part of the disease which fibroblasts, apparently stimulated by circulating factors, proliferate and deposit excess glycosaminoglycans (chiefly hyaluronic acid) together with increased collagen in the upper and mid A monoclonal gammopathy is almost always present, and the paraprotein or associated cytokines are thought to drive fibroblast activation and mucin production, though the precise mechanism linking the two is not fully understood. Scleromyxoedema is a chronic, unpredictable and potentially progressive disorder that can be complicated by fatal systemic and neurological involvement. Response to intravenous immunoglobulin and other therapies has improved outcomes, but relapses are common and the dermato-neuro syndrome carries a high mortality.

with a small increase in future breast cancer risk, greater when accompanied by atypical hyperplasia Suspicious microcalcification or architectural distortion on imaging Histological features overlapping with tubular carcinoma or associated atypia A discrete or enlarging palpable mass Discordant triple assessment findings Coexisting atypical hyperplasia, which raises future cancer risk Overcalling the lesion as invasive carcinoma on imaging or biopsy owing to its infiltrative appearance Failing to use myoepithelial markers to distinguish it from cancer Missing coexisting atypia or malignancy in an adjacent radial scar or papilloma Ignoring discordance between suspicious imaging and a benign biopsy Underestimating the associated future cancer risk when atypia is present Sclerosing adenosis is characterised by an increase in the number of acini within the lobule (adenosis) accompanied by proliferation of fibrous stroma that compresses and distorts the proliferating glands. This combination of glandular proliferation and stromal sclerosis produces a swirling, infiltrative-looking architecture that can closely resemble invasive carcinoma, and dystrophic calcification within the lesion often generates suspicious microcalcification on mammography. The key feature confirming benignity is preservation of the outer myoepithelial cell layer around the distorted glands, which is retained in adenosis but lost in invasive cancer, and which can be highlighted with immunohistochemical markers. Sclerosing adenosis is benign with a good prognosis once malignancy is excluded, requiring no treatment in most cases, though it confers a modest increase in future breast cancer risk that is greater if atypical hyperplasia is also present.

the endometrium Performing radical rather than fertility-sparing surgery in a young woman Sclerosing stromal tumour is a benign ovarian sex cord-stromal neoplasm characterised by a pseudolobular growth pattern in which cellular areas alternate with hypocellular, oedematous, or collagenised sclerotic zones. The cellular regions contain a mixture of spindled fibroblast-like cells and rounded cells with vacuolated, lipid-laden cytoplasm, and a conspicuous thin-walled branching vasculature reminiscent of a haemangiopericytoma. Some of the vacuolated cells can produce steroids, which accounts for the oestrogenic manifestations seen in a proportion of patients, particularly during pregnancy when hormonal activity may be accentuated. Despite a sometimes alarming cellularity and rich vascular pattern, the tumour behaves in a uniformly benign fashion. Excellent, as the tumour is benign and cured by simple excision, with hormonal effects resolving after removal and no established tendency to recur or metastasise.

bisphosphonates are not effective at reducing bone mass Signs of raised intracranial pressure such as headache, papilloedema, and vomiting Progressive facial-nerve palsy or rapidly worsening hearing or vision Brainstem or cerebellar signs suggesting posterior fossa crowding Sudden neurological deterioration requiring urgent decompression Confusing sclerosteosis with Van Buchem disease, distinguished by the presence of syndactyly and generally greater severity in sclerosteosis Attributing progressive facial palsy to idiopathic Bell palsy rather than bony entrapment Failing to monitor and treat rising intracranial pressure Expecting antiresorptive drugs to reduce the excess bone mass Sclerosteosis is caused by biallelic inactivating mutations in SOST, the gene encoding sclerostin, a protein secreted by osteocytes that normally inhibits the Wnt/beta-catenin signalling pathway in bone. Without functional sclerostin, Wnt signalling is unrestrained, driving markedly increased osteoblastic bone formation throughout the skeleton. The result is progressive, dense, sclerotic bone with cortical and skull thickening. Overgrowth of the calvaria and skull base narrows cranial foramina, entrapping cranial nerves and, in severe cases, elevating intracranial pressure. The same pathway biology has informed development of anti-sclerostin therapy for osteoporosis. The disorder is progressive; without intervention, cranial nerve entrapment and raised intracranial pressure can cause serious neurological disability, and severe cases may be life-limiting, though timely surgical decompression can relieve complications.

SCN8A encodes Nav1.6, a voltage-gated sodium channel concentrated at the axon initial segment and nodes of Ranvier where it drives action potential initiation and repetitive firing. Gain-of-function variants shift channel gating so that neurons become hyperexcitable, for example through impaired inactivation or a persistent inward sodium current, producing early severe epilepsy and encephalopathy. Loss-of-function variants reduce channel availability and are generally associated with milder phenotypes without early catastrophic seizures. Because the therapeutic response depends on the functional consequence of the variant, distinguishing gain from loss of function guides rational selection of antiseizure medication. Outcome varies widely by variant: gain-of-function developmental and epileptic encephalopathy often carries drug-resistant seizures, significant intellectual disability, and a raised risk of sudden unexpected death, whereas milder self-limited or predominantly movement-disorder phenotypes may have better cognitive outcomes.

Scoliosis — spinal curvature, adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, lateral curvature of the spine Postural (non-structural) scoliosis that corrects on forward bending Leg-length discrepancy causing compensatory curvature Congenital vertebral anomalies Neuromuscular scoliosis (cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, spinal muscular atrophy) Syndromic scoliosis (e.g. neurofibromatosis, Marfan syndrome) Intraspinal pathology (syrinx, tethered cord, tumour) causing an atypical or painful curve Standing posteroanterior and lateral spinal radiographs to measure the Cobb angle and assess balance Assessment of skeletal maturity (e.g. Risser sign, hand/wrist bone age) Forward-bending (Adam's) test with a scoliometer to gauge rotation MRI of the whole spine for atypical, painful, rapidly progressive, or early-onset curves, or when there are neurological signs Pulmonary function testing for large thoracic or neuromuscular curves A three-dimensional deformity combining lateral curvature and vertebral rotation, most commonly adolescent idiopathic scoliosis in otherwise healthy children, predominantly girls It is often painless and detected as asymmetry of the shoulders, waist, or scapulae; a rib hump on the forward-bending (Adam's) test reflects the rotational component Curve magnitude is quantified by the Cobb angle on a standing radiograph, and skeletal maturity (e.g. Risser sign) helps predict the risk of progression Significant back pain, a rapidly progressive curve, an atypical (e.g. left thoracic) curve, or neurological signs should prompt a search for an underlying cause and MRI Scoliosis may be idiopathic, congenital (vertebral anomalies), or neuromuscular (e.g. cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy), and management differs accordingly Small curves are observed, moderate curves in a growing child may be braced to limit progression, and large or progressive curves are considered for surgical correction and fusion The likelihood of progression is greatest during the adolescent growth spurt, so monitoring is intensified during rapid growth Severe thoracic curves can restrict pulmonary function, an important consideration in early-onset and neuromuscular disease Neurological signs or symptoms suggesting an intraspinal cause requiring MRI Significant or persistent back pain, unusual for idiopathic scoliosis Rapid curve progression or an atypical curve pattern (e.g. left thoracic) Respiratory compromise from a severe thoracic curve Assuming all scoliosis is benign idiopathic disease and missing an underlying intraspinal or neuromuscular cause Overlooking a painful or atypical curve that warrants MRI Failing to monitor closely during the adolescent growth spurt when progression is most likely Confusing a compensatory postural curve from leg-length discrepancy with structural scoliosis Scoliosis is a structural lateral deviation of the spine accompanied by rotation of the vertebrae, which produces the characteristic rib or paravertebral prominence. In adolescent idiopathic scoliosis the cause is unknown but multifactorial, with genetic, growth-related, and neuromuscular balance factors implicated, and the deformity tends to worsen during periods of rapid skeletal growth. Congenital scoliosis results from failures of vertebral formation or segmentation present from birth, while neuromuscular scoliosis arises from asymmetrical muscle forces acting on the growing spine in conditions such as cerebral palsy. Progressive rotation and wedging of vertebrae make the curve increasingly rigid, and large thoracic curves can distort the chest and compromise lung capacity. Most mild adolescent idiopathic curves remain stable and require only monitoring, and bracing can prevent progression of moderate curves during growth; large or progressive curves may need surgical correction, and untreated severe curves can cause deformity, back pain, and in extreme thoracic cases cardiopulmonary compromise, while neuromuscular and congenital curves tend to be more progressive.

Scombroid (histamine) fish poisoning — scombroid, histamine fish poisoning, scombrotoxism, mahi-mahi/tuna histamine poisoning True IgE-mediated seafood allergy or anaphylaxis Ciguatera fish poisoning Anaphylaxis to another allergen Carcinoid or other flushing syndrome Panic attack or vasomotor flushing Medication or alcohol-related flushing reaction Clinical diagnosis based on rapid onset after fish and characteristic flushing Corroborating history of others affected by the same meal Observation of response to antihistamines to support the diagnosis Electrocardiography and monitoring if palpitations or hypotension occur Measurement of histamine in the implicated fish where laboratory capability exists Results from eating fish (typically dark-fleshed species such as tuna, mackerel, mahi-mahi, sardines) that have been inadequately refrigerated, allowing bacterial conversion of histidine to histamine Onset is rapid, usually within minutes to an hour, mimicking an allergic reaction despite being a toxin-mediated illness Features include flushing of the face and upper body, headache, palpitations, urticaria, sweating, and gastrointestinal upset; a peppery or metallic taste to the fish may be reported Because it mimics IgE-mediated allergy, it is often misdiagnosed as a seafood allergy, which has implications for future advice Management is largely supportive with antihistamines; severe reactions with bronchospasm or hypotension are treated as for anaphylaxis, including adrenaline Multiple diners becoming ill after the same fish, or normal tolerance of the same species previously, points to scombroid rather than true allergy The fish often looks and smells normal, and the histamine is heat-stable, so cooking does not prevent poisoning Airway compromise, stridor or severe bronchospasm Hypotension or shock Rapidly progressive symptoms requiring treatment as anaphylaxis Reaction in a patient with significant cardiac or respiratory comorbidity Severe or persistent symptoms despite antihistamines Mislabelling the patient as fish-allergic, leading to unnecessary lifelong avoidance Assuming cooking or the fish smelling normal excludes the diagnosis, as histamine is heat-stable Under-treating a severe reaction that warrants adrenaline as for anaphylaxis Failing to consider a common-source outbreak and report a food-safety issue When scombroid and related fish are stored at inadequate temperatures, bacteria decarboxylate the naturally abundant amino acid histidine in the flesh into histamine and other biogenic amines. Ingesting this preformed histamine produces a pharmacological reaction that mimics an allergic response, with vasodilatation, flushing, increased vascular permeability and, in severe cases, bronchospasm and hypotension. The reaction is not immunologically mediated and does not require prior sensitisation, and because histamine is heat-stable it is not removed by cooking; other amines may potentiate the effect by inhibiting histamine breakdown. Scombroid poisoning is usually mild and self-limiting, resolving within hours, and responds well to antihistamines; severe reactions are uncommon but can resemble anaphylaxis and require the same emergency treatment.

Scorpion envenomation — scorpion sting, scorpionism, Centruroides envenomation, Leiurus (deathstalker) sting, Androctonus sting Sympathomimetic toxidrome from drug ingestion Anaphylaxis to the sting or another allergen Primary myocarditis or acute coronary syndrome Seizure disorder or CNS infection in an agitated child Hymenoptera or spider envenomation Thyroid storm or phaeochromocytoma crisis Electrocardiography for ischaemic changes and arrhythmia Cardiac troponin and echocardiography if myocardial involvement is suspected Chest imaging for pulmonary oedema Blood glucose, electrolytes and lactate given catecholamine-driven derangements Creatine kinase and renal function if muscle activity is marked Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring in graded systemic envenomation Most stings cause only intense local pain with minimal swelling; systemic envenomation is species-dependent and most severe in young children Medically important genera (Centruroides, Leiurus, Androctonus, Tityus, Hottentotta) produce an autonomic storm from massive neurotransmitter release Sympathetic overdrive causes tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, agitation and hyperthermia, sometimes alternating with cholinergic features such as hypersalivation and vomiting Neuromuscular excitation may produce roving eye movements, fasciculations, restlessness and involuntary limb movements, especially in children Catecholamine surge can precipitate myocarditis, pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock, which are the main causes of death Grading of severity (local only, systemic autonomic, cardiorespiratory failure) guides the need for antivenom and intensive support Management principles include analgesia, species-appropriate antivenom for systemic envenomation, and cautious afterload reduction for the hyperadrenergic state and cardiac dysfunction Signs of pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock Persistent hypertension with end-organ compromise Marked neuromuscular excitation or airway-threatening secretions in a young child Altered consciousness or seizures Rapid clinical deterioration after an initially mild sting Underestimating a sting in a young child, in whom systemic envenomation and cardiac failure develop rapidly Attributing pulmonary oedema to fluid overload rather than venom-induced myocardial dysfunction and giving excess fluid Delaying antivenom while treating only the autonomic symptoms Failing to monitor for evolving cardiac injury after the initial autonomic phase Scorpion venom contains neurotoxins that bind voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels on excitable membranes, prolonging depolarisation and causing repetitive firing of autonomic and somatic nerves. This triggers a massive release of catecholamines and acetylcholine, producing a mixed sympathetic and parasympathetic autonomic storm. The catecholamine surge increases myocardial oxygen demand and can cause a stress cardiomyopathy or myocarditis with left ventricular dysfunction, capillary leak and pulmonary oedema. Local venom effects on nociceptors account for the severe pain that is often disproportionate to visible tissue changes. Isolated local stings resolve within hours to a day. Systemic envenomation, particularly in children, carries a risk of life-threatening cardiopulmonary failure, but with timely antivenom and intensive supportive care outcomes are generally good.

Scorpion sting — scorpion envenomation, scorpion bite, scorpionism Other venomous envenomation (snakebite, spider bite) Acute myocarditis from other causes Sympathomimetic drug toxicity Acute anaphylaxis Acute coronary syndrome with pulmonary oedema Continuous ECG monitoring for arrhythmia and ischaemic changes Echocardiography to assess left ventricular function in systemic envenomation Cardiac biomarkers (troponin) where myocardial injury is suspected Chest imaging for pulmonary oedema Blood glucose, electrolytes, and arterial blood gas in severe cases Venom is a mixture of neurotoxins that activate sodium channels and drive a massive autonomic (catecholamine) surge, producing a mixed sympathetic and parasympathetic toxidrome Local effects are often minor (intense pain, tingling, minimal swelling), so systemic severity can be underestimated from the sting site alone Early cholinergic features (vomiting, profuse sweating, salivation, priapism) are typically followed by an adrenergic phase with hypertension, tachycardia, and agitation The feared complication is myocardial dysfunction with acute pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock, particularly in children Prazosin, an alpha-blocker, is a key pharmacological measure to counter the catecholamine storm and offload the heart in significant envenomation Species-specific scorpion antivenom may be indicated for systemic envenomation where available, ideally given early Supportive care includes analgesia, close cardiorespiratory monitoring, and management of pulmonary oedema; dobutamine may help the failing heart Children and those presenting late with signs of myocarditis or shock carry the greatest risk and need intensive monitoring Acute pulmonary oedema, respiratory distress, or frothy sputum indicating myocardial involvement Signs of cardiogenic shock or cool clammy peripheries Priapism, profuse sweating, and repeated vomiting signalling significant systemic envenomation Young children with any systemic feature, who deteriorate rapidly New arrhythmia or ECG changes suggesting myocarditis Judging severity by the local reaction and missing evolving systemic toxicity Delaying prazosin or antivenom while awaiting overt pulmonary oedema Aggressive fluid loading in a patient with myocardial dysfunction, worsening pulmonary oedema Under-monitoring children, who can deteriorate abruptly Scorpion venom contains peptide neurotoxins that delay inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels and block potassium channels at nerve terminals, causing repetitive depolarisation and unregulated release of neurotransmitters. This produces an initial cholinergic outpouring followed by an overwhelming sympathetic (catecholamine) surge. The resulting effects include hypertension, tachyarrhythmias, increased systemic vascular resistance, and direct catecholamine-mediated myocardial injury. Myocarditis, transient left ventricular dysfunction, and increased capillary permeability lead to acute pulmonary oedema, which is the principal cause of death, especially in children. Most stings cause only local pain and resolve without sequelae, but systemic envenomation with myocardial dysfunction and pulmonary oedema can be fatal, particularly in children; early alpha-blockade, antivenom where indicated, and intensive supportive care markedly improve outcomes.

Scott syndrome — Scott syndrome, Platelet procoagulant deficiency, Phospholipid scramblase deficiency Mild haemophilia A or B von Willebrand disease Platelet storage pool or secretion defects Factor XI deficiency Acquired coagulopathy or anticoagulant effect Vascular/connective tissue bleeding disorder Combined factor V and factor VIII deficiency Platelet-dependent thrombin generation assay (reduced) Flow-cytometric annexin V binding to activated platelets (decreased phosphatidylserine exposure) Assessment of platelet-derived microparticle formation Prothrombin consumption / serum prothrombin time Standard coagulation screen and platelet aggregometry (typically normal) ANO6 (TMEM16F) gene sequencing von Willebrand factor and coagulation factor assays to exclude alternatives An exceptionally rare inherited bleeding disorder caused by defective exposure of procoagulant phosphatidylserine on the activated platelet surface. Most cases result from autosomal recessive mutations in ANO6 (TMEM16F), which encodes a calcium-activated phospholipid scramblase. Platelet count, morphology and standard aggregation studies are normal, so routine coagulation and platelet testing are typically unremarkable. Bleeding is characteristically deep and delayed after trauma or surgery, resembling a coagulation defect more than a typical platelet disorder. The defect impairs assembly of tenase and prothrombinase complexes on the platelet membrane because the phosphatidylserine platform is not externalised. Diagnosis relies on specialised assays showing reduced platelet-dependent thrombin generation and diminished annexin V binding by flow cytometry. Failure of microparticle release and impaired factor Va/factor Xa binding are hallmark laboratory findings. Management centres on antifibrinolytics and platelet transfusion for significant bleeding, since no specific replacement therapy exists. Severe delayed haemorrhage following surgery, dental extraction or trauma Post-partum haemorrhage Bleeding disproportionate to normal routine coagulation and platelet tests Large deep haematoma or intramuscular bleeding Recurrent bleeding requiring repeated transfusion with alloimmunisation risk Excluding a bleeding disorder because routine coagulation and platelet function tests are normal. Overlooking the need for specialised phosphatidylserine-exposure and thrombin-generation assays. Assuming platelet transfusion alone always suffices without antifibrinolytic support. Failing to plan haemostatic cover before elective surgery in a known patient. Confusing the delayed deep bleeding pattern with a coagulation factor deficiency and misdirecting factor replacement. Scott syndrome is caused by failure of the transmembrane phospholipid scrambling that normally follows platelet activation. In health, a rise in cytosolic calcium activates the scramblase encoded by ANO6 (TMEM16F), which collapses membrane phospholipid asymmetry and externalises phosphatidylserine on the outer leaflet of activated platelets, red cells and microparticles. This anionic surface is the essential catalytic platform for assembly of the tenase (factor VIIIa/IXa) and prothrombinase (factor Va/Xa) complexes that accelerate thrombin generation. In Scott syndrome, loss-of-function mutations abolish scramblase activity, so phosphatidylserine remains sequestered internally, microparticle formation is deficient and localised thrombin generation at the platelet surface is markedly impaired despite normal clotting factors and platelet aggregation. The result is a haemostatic defect that manifests chiefly after surgical or traumatic challenge. With awareness of the diagnosis and appropriate peri-procedural haemostatic support the prognosis is good and spontaneous bleeding is uncommon. The main hazard is unanticipated severe bleeding during surgery or trauma when the disorder has not been recognised.

recurrence is possible after excision Overlooking secondary infection of a discharging nodule Scrotal calcinosis is characterised by deposits of calcium within the dermis of the scrotal skin. Excellent with restoration of vitamin C intake; bleeding and gum changes resolve within days to weeks and full recovery is expected.

loss of SDHA staining specifically indicates an SDHA mutation Frequently harbours germline SDH mutations, so identification should prompt genetic counselling and evaluation for hereditary paraganglioma-phaeochromocytoma syndromes Associated with the Carney triad (gastric GIST, paraganglioma and pulmonary chondroma) and the Carney-Stratakis dyad (GIST and paraganglioma with germline SDH mutation) Behaves differently from conventional GIST, with frequent lymph node metastasis yet often an indolent, protracted course even with metastatic disease Characteristically resistant to standard imatinib therapy because it does not depend on KIT or PDGFRA signalling Young patient with a gastric mass and multifocal or nodal disease Coexisting paraganglioma or phaeochromocytoma suggesting a hereditary syndrome Family history of paraganglioma, phaeochromocytoma or GIST Progressive metastatic disease despite the typically indolent course Symptomatic gastrointestinal bleeding from an ulcerating gastric tumour Assuming all GISTs will respond to imatinib and overlooking the wild-type, SDH-deficient subset Not performing SDHB immunohistochemistry in a young patient with a gastric GIST Failing to recognise the hereditary implications and omitting germline testing and family screening Applying conventional GIST risk-stratification schemes, which do not reliably predict behaviour in this subset Interpreting nodal metastasis as necessarily indicating a poor outcome SDH-deficient GIST results from loss of function of the mitochondrial succinate dehydrogenase complex, through germline or somatic mutation of one of its subunit genes or, in some cases, epigenetic silencing of SDHC. Failure of this enzyme causes accumulation of succinate, which inhibits prolyl hydroxylases and stabilises hypoxia-inducible factors, producing a pseudohypoxic state that drives angiogenesis and tumour growth. Because the disease is independent of KIT and PDGFRA activation, it forms a biologically separate group with distinct morphology, natural history and treatment response. SDH-deficient GIST tends to follow an indolent, protracted course, and patients may live for many years even with lymph node or liver metastases; conventional tyrosine kinase inhibitors are largely ineffective, so complete surgical resection is the mainstay, and lifelong surveillance is needed because of multifocality and the risk of associated syndromic tumours.

post-synaptic and pre-synaptic neurotoxins that block neuromuscular transmission, producing a descending flaccid paralysis of cranial, bulbar and respiratory muscles similar to terrestrial elapids. Potent myotoxins additionally damage skeletal muscle, causing pain, stiffness and rhabdomyolysis with release of myoglobin and potassium. Myoglobinuria can precipitate acute kidney injury, and hyperkalaemia poses a direct cardiac threat. Local tissue effects are typically minimal, which can mask the seriousness of the systemic envenomation. With early pressure immobilisation, timely antivenom, ventilatory support and management of rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemia, recovery is usually complete. Delay increases the risk of fatal respiratory failure, hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest or renal failure.

Sebaceous carcinoma — sebaceous gland carcinoma, sebaceous adenocarcinoma, meibomian gland carcinoma Chalazion or recurrent chalazion Chronic blepharitis or blepharoconjunctivitis Basal cell carcinoma of the eyelid Squamous cell carcinoma and its in-situ forms Sebaceous adenoma and sebaceoma Ocular surface squamous neoplasia (for conjunctival pagetoid spread) Amelanotic melanoma Full-thickness or incisional biopsy of any suspicious or recurrent eyelid lesion Lipid staining on fresh (frozen) tissue and immunohistochemistry including adipophilin and EMA Map (multiple conjunctival) biopsies to delineate pagetoid intraepithelial spread Mismatch-repair protein immunohistochemistry and consideration of Muir-Torre / hereditary cancer evaluation Regional nodal assessment and imaging for staging in higher-risk tumours Ophthalmic examination to assess conjunctival and orbital involvement A malignant tumour of sebaceous differentiation that most often arises in the periocular region from meibomian and Zeis glands, but also occurs at extraocular sites Periocular lesions notoriously masquerade as a recurrent chalazion or chronic blepharoconjunctivitis, so a firm or recurrent eyelid lesion warrants biopsy Pagetoid intraepithelial spread through the overlying epidermis or conjunctiva is characteristic and contributes to multifocal disease and margin difficulty Histology shows lobules of atypical cells with foamy, vacuolated lipid-laden cytoplasm; lipid stains on fresh tissue and markers such as adipophilin and EMA support the diagnosis Association with Muir-Torre syndrome links sebaceous neoplasms to mismatch-repair deficiency and internal (often colorectal and genitourinary) malignancy Immunohistochemistry for mismatch-repair proteins can flag Muir-Torre syndrome and should prompt consideration of hereditary cancer screening Treatment is complete surgical excision, often with Mohs micrographic surgery or wide excision with map (conjunctival) biopsies, and radiotherapy in selected cases Recurrent or atypical chalazion that fails to resolve or recurs after drainage Unilateral chronic blepharoconjunctivitis unresponsive to conventional treatment Loss of eyelash follicles (madarosis) or eyelid architecture over a firm lesion Diffuse conjunctival injection with an underlying eyelid mass suggesting pagetoid spread Personal or family history suggesting Muir-Torre syndrome and internal malignancy Treating a recurrent eyelid lesion repeatedly as a chalazion without biopsy Underestimating margins because of occult pagetoid intraepithelial spread Failing to test for mismatch-repair deficiency and missing an underlying Muir-Torre syndrome Overlooking multifocal or extraocular disease in the staging assessment Sebaceous carcinoma is a malignant neoplasm showing sebaceous differentiation, thought to arise from the adnexal sebaceous glands, prominently the meibomian and Zeis glands of the eyelid. Tumour cells proliferate as lobules and sheets with atypical nuclei and characteristic finely vacuolated cytoplasm reflecting intracytoplasmic lipid. A distinctive feature is pagetoid spread, in which malignant cells migrate individually through the overlying epithelium of the skin or conjunctiva, producing clinically deceptive diffuse involvement and complicating margin assessment. A subset arises in the context of Muir-Torre syndrome, a phenotypic variant of hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer, where germline mismatch-repair deficiency underlies both the sebaceous neoplasia and associated visceral cancers. Prognosis depends on tumour size, extent of pagetoid spread, and stage; periocular tumours can recur locally and metastasise to regional nodes, and delayed diagnosis from chalazion masquerade worsens outcome. Complete excision of localised disease carries a reasonable prognosis, but advanced or metastatic disease is associated with significant mortality.

lipid stains on fresh tissue and markers such as adipophilin and EMA support the diagnosis Management is complete excision, often Mohs micrographic surgery or wide excision, with map (conjunctival) biopsies to map pagetoid spread and radiotherapy in selected cases An association with Muir-Torre syndrome links the tumour to mismatch-repair deficiency and internal malignancy, warranting consideration of hereditary cancer screening A recurrent chalazion that fails to resolve or recurs after drainage Chronic unilateral blepharoconjunctivitis unresponsive to conventional treatment Madarosis or destruction of eyelid margin architecture over a firm lesion Diffuse conjunctival injection suggesting pagetoid spread or orbital signs suggesting invasion Personal or family history pointing to Muir-Torre syndrome Treating a recurrent eyelid lesion repeatedly as a chalazion without biopsy and delaying diagnosis Underestimating margins because of occult pagetoid intraepithelial spread Failing to test for mismatch-repair deficiency and missing an underlying Muir-Torre syndrome Overlooking orbital or nodal involvement during staging Eyelid sebaceous gland carcinoma is a malignant tumour of sebaceous differentiation arising predominantly from the meibomian glands within the tarsal plate and the glands of Zeis at the lid margin, with the upper eyelid most often affected. Malignant cells proliferate as lobules and sheets with atypical nuclei and characteristic finely vacuolated cytoplasm reflecting intracytoplasmic lipid. A defining behaviour is pagetoid intraepithelial spread, in which individual malignant cells migrate through the overlying conjunctival and epidermal epithelium, producing diffuse periocular involvement that mimics inflammatory disease and obscures the true tumour extent. A subset occurs within Muir-Torre syndrome, where germline mismatch-repair deficiency predisposes to both the sebaceous neoplasia and associated visceral cancers. The tumour spreads to regional preauricular and cervical nodes and can invade the orbit. Eyelid sebaceous carcinoma is aggressive, and prognosis worsens with delayed diagnosis, larger tumours, extensive pagetoid spread, and orbital or nodal involvement; complete excision of localised disease gives a reasonable outlook, but regional or distant spread carries significant mortality.

sebaceous hyperplasia — senile sebaceous hyperplasia, premature sebaceous gland hyperplasia basal cell carcinoma sebaceous adenoma molluscum contagiosum intradermal melanocytic naevus fibrous papule of the face trichoepithelioma sebaceous carcinoma dermoscopy to demonstrate crown vessels and central umbilication punch or shave biopsy where basal cell carcinoma cannot be excluded histopathology confirming enlarged mature sebaceous lobules assessment for Muir-Torre syndrome in extensive or early-onset disease mismatch-repair immunohistochemistry on sebaceous neoplasms when syndrome suspected Presents as soft, yellowish, umbilicated papules on the forehead, cheeks and nose of middle-aged and older adults. The central umbilication corresponds to a dilated sebaceous duct surrounded by enlarged sebaceous lobules, giving a doughnut-like configuration. Lesions are often multiple in individuals with seborrhoeic, sun-damaged skin and in those on long-term ciclosporin after organ transplantation. Dermoscopy shows a central crater with surrounding cream-yellow lobules and a 'crown' of unbranched or minimally branched peripheral vessels. The crown vessels do not cross the midline of the lesion, helping to distinguish it from the arborising telangiectasia of basal cell carcinoma. The main clinical challenge is differentiation from basal cell carcinoma, which may require dermoscopy or biopsy. Treatment is for cosmetic reasons only and includes light electrodesiccation, laser, photodynamic therapy or topical/oral retinoids. Widespread early-onset lesions can be a feature of the Muir-Torre syndrome, particularly when sebaceous adenomas or carcinomas coexist. arborising telangiectasia, pearly rolled border or ulceration suggesting basal cell carcinoma numerous sebaceous lesions at a young age suggesting Muir-Torre syndrome a firm, rapidly growing or bleeding lesion raising concern for sebaceous carcinoma coexisting visceral malignancy or strong family history of colorectal cancer Misdiagnosing basal cell carcinoma as sebaceous hyperplasia and delaying appropriate treatment. Failing to recognise the Muir-Torre association in patients with multiple or early lesions. Aggressive destructive treatment causing scarring for a purely cosmetic lesion. Confusing lesions with molluscum contagiosum in immunosuppressed patients. Sebaceous hyperplasia represents a benign enlargement of otherwise normal sebaceous glands, in which numerous mature sebaceous lobules cluster around a centrally dilated excretory duct. The process reflects reduced epidermal cell turnover and diminished androgen-driven basal sebocyte replacement with ageing, causing retention and accumulation of crowded mature sebocytes. Chronic ultraviolet exposure and immunosuppression, especially ciclosporin, accelerate the process. Although a benign hamartomatous proliferation, extensive and early lesions may reflect the sebaceous gland dysregulation seen in the Muir-Torre variant of Lynch syndrome, mediated by mismatch-repair deficiency. Sebaceous hyperplasia is entirely benign and of cosmetic significance only, although individual lesions persist and new ones accumulate with age. Recurrence after superficial destruction is common because the deeper gland is often incompletely removed.

(including cradle cap) and again in adults The condition is linked to the commensal yeast Malassezia, so antifungal agents are a mainstay of treatment Management combines antifungal shampoos or creams with short courses of low-potency topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors for inflammation, and recognises that it is a relapsing condition needing maintenance Unusually severe, extensive, atopic or contact dermatitis based on distribution and morphology Severe, extensive, or abrupt-onset disease prompting evaluation for immunosuppression such as HIV Erythroderma with widespread involvement Failure to respond to appropriate first-line therapy suggesting an alternative diagnosis Secondary bacterial infection of excoriated or fissured plaques Confusing it with psoriasis or dermatophyte infection and choosing the wrong therapy Relying on topical corticosteroids alone and neglecting antifungal treatment of the yeast component Overusing potent steroids on the face, risking atrophy and rosacea-like changes Failing to investigate unusually severe or refractory disease for underlying HIV or neurological disease Seborrhoeic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory disorder occurring in sebaceous-rich skin, driven by an abnormal host inflammatory response to Malassezia yeasts that are part of the normal skin flora. The yeasts metabolise sebum lipids, releasing free fatty acids and other products that irritate the skin and provoke inflammation in susceptible individuals. Sebaceous gland activity, an altered skin barrier, individual immune reactivity, and neurological or immunosuppressive comorbidities all influence expression. This explains its predilection for sebum-rich sites, its association with hormonal activity in infancy and adulthood, and its increased severity in HIV infection and Parkinson's disease. Seborrhoeic dermatitis is a benign but chronic relapsing condition; infantile disease usually resolves within months, whereas adult disease tends to persist with periodic flares and is controlled rather than cured.

seborrhoeic keratosis — seborrhoeic wart, basal cell papilloma, senile wart melanocytic naevus malignant melanoma (particularly heavily pigmented or irritated lesions) pigmented basal cell carcinoma viral wart actinic keratosis solar lentigo epidermal naevus dermoscopy to identify milia-like cysts and comedo-like openings clinical photography for lesion monitoring shave or punch biopsy of atypical lesions excisional biopsy with histopathology where melanoma cannot be excluded screening for occult malignancy if the sign of Leser-Trelat is suspected Presents as a well-demarcated, 'stuck-on' waxy or verrucous papule or plaque, most often on the trunk, face and scalp of middle-aged and older adults. Colour ranges from pale tan through brown to almost black; heavily pigmented lesions on the face are a common source of melanoma referral. Surface horn cysts (keratin-filled pseudocysts) and comedo-like plugged follicular openings are characteristic and best appreciated on dermoscopy. Dermoscopic hallmarks include milia-like cysts, comedo-like openings, a cerebriform 'brain-like' pattern, fat fingers and sharply demarcated moth-eaten borders. The dermatosis papulosa nigra and stucco keratosis variants represent phenotypic subtypes seen respectively in darker skin and on the distal lower limbs. The sudden eruption of numerous lesions with pruritus (the sign of Leser-Trelat) may rarely signal an internal adenocarcinoma and warrants malignancy screening. Irritated lesions can become inflamed, crusted and clinically alarming, mimicking melanoma or squamous cell carcinoma. No treatment is needed for asymptomatic lesions; cryotherapy, curettage or shave excision are used for symptomatic or diagnostically uncertain lesions, with histology if malignancy is suspected. rapid eruption of multiple lesions with pruritus (sign of Leser-Trelat) prompting a search for internal malignancy asymmetry, irregular pigment network or ulceration suggesting melanoma recent change in size, colour or bleeding within a pre-existing lesion a solitary rapidly enlarging keratotic nodule raising concern for squamous cell carcinoma Misdiagnosing a heavily pigmented or irritated lesion as benign when it is actually melanoma, or vice versa, leading to inappropriate management. Destroying a lesion by cryotherapy or curettage without histology when the clinical diagnosis is uncertain, thereby losing the specimen. Overlooking the sign of Leser-Trelat and failing to investigate for an underlying adenocarcinoma. Confusing a solitary lesion with a viral wart and applying inappropriate keratolytic treatment. Seborrhoeic keratoses are benign epidermal proliferations composed of monomorphous basaloid keratinocytes with variable squamous differentiation, forming acanthotic plaques containing horn cysts and pseudo-horn cysts. Activating somatic mutations in FGFR3 and in the PIK3CA gene are frequently identified, indicating clonal keratinocyte expansion, yet the lesions have negligible malignant potential. Accumulation of melanin within the proliferating keratinocytes accounts for the variable pigmentation. Their prevalence rises steeply with age and there is a clear familial predisposition, with ultraviolet exposure implicated in facial and truncal lesions. Seborrhoeic keratoses are entirely benign with no intrinsic malignant potential, although individual lesions persist indefinitely and new ones accumulate with age. Recurrence after superficial removal is common if the lesion is incompletely destroyed.

to intrauterine environmental factors and missing the recessive genetic cause Failing to counsel consanguineous families about substantial recurrence risk Seckel syndrome is a genetically heterogeneous microcephalic primordial dwarfism arising from biallelic variants in genes controlling the DNA damage response, DNA replication, and centrosome function, of which ATR is the prototype. Impaired handling of replication stress and defective cell-cycle control reduce the number of cell divisions during development, most conspicuously in the brain, producing severe proportionate growth restriction and profound microcephaly. The same genome-maintenance defects underlie the associated haematological and other systemic complications. Growth restriction and microcephaly are lifelong and stature remains far below normal, while cognitive impairment is usually significant. Prognosis is influenced by the specific gene involved and by haematological and other systemic complications, and survival into adulthood is possible with supportive care.

Secondary peritonitis — acute secondary peritonitis, surgical peritonitis, generalised peritonitis Primary (spontaneous bacterial) peritonitis Acute pancreatitis Mesenteric ischaemia Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm Intra-abdominal abscess without generalised peritonitis Medical causes of acute abdomen (diabetic ketoacidosis, inferior myocardial infarction) Bloods including full blood count, urea and electrolytes, CRP, amylase or lipase, blood cultures, and lactate Arterial blood gas to assess acid-base status and organ perfusion Erect chest radiograph for free subdiaphragmatic gas CT abdomen and pelvis to identify the source and any collections Peritoneal fluid sampling and culture when the diagnosis or source is unclear Results from bacterial contamination of the peritoneal cavity following perforation, ischaemia, or inflammation of an abdominal viscus, unlike primary (spontaneous) peritonitis Presents with severe, constant abdominal pain worsened by movement, with tenderness, guarding, rigidity, and rebound, and the patient characteristically lies still Common sources include perforated peptic ulcer, perforated appendix, perforated diverticular disease, and bowel ischaemia or anastomotic leak Systemic features of sepsis develop rapidly: fever, tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria, and, if untreated, septic shock and multi-organ failure The management triad is aggressive resuscitation, appropriate broad-spectrum antibiotics, and prompt source control of the underlying cause Source control, achieved surgically or by radiological drainage, is the definitive step; antibiotics and resuscitation support but do not replace it Faeculent peritonitis from colonic perforation carries a particularly heavy bacterial and endotoxin load and a high mortality Peritoneal contamination is often graded (localised, diffuse, purulent, faeculent) and guides the extent of surgery and lavage Generalised peritonitis with sepsis, hypotension, or rising lactate indicating septic shock (surgical emergency) Faeculent contamination from colonic perforation with heavy sepsis burden Progressive organ dysfunction (oliguria, confusion, respiratory compromise) Failure to improve after resuscitation, indicating inadequate source control Delaying source control while awaiting response to antibiotics and fluids Under-resuscitating a patient with large third-space and septic losses Attributing peritonism to a medical cause and missing a surgical source Inadequate peritoneal lavage or failing to address ongoing contamination at surgery Secondary peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum caused by spillage of gastrointestinal contents and micro-organisms into the peritoneal cavity following a breach of a hollow viscus or transmural necrosis. Gut flora, typically a mix of coliforms and anaerobes, provoke an intense inflammatory response with fibrinopurulent exudate, large third-space fluid losses, and paralytic ileus. Absorption of bacteria and endotoxin across the vast peritoneal surface drives systemic inflammatory response, sepsis, and septic shock. The peritoneum may localise infection into abscesses, but diffuse contamination overwhelms these defences and threatens life. Outcome hinges on early recognition, prompt resuscitation, and timely source control; delay, faeculent contamination, advanced age, and comorbidity markedly increase mortality, which remains high in established diffuse peritonitis with septic shock.

Secretory carcinoma of salivary gland — Mammary analogue secretory carcinoma, MASC Acinic cell carcinoma Low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma Cystadenocarcinoma Polymorphous adenocarcinoma Adenocarcinoma not otherwise specified Salivary duct carcinoma (high-grade lesions) Fine-needle aspiration cytology Core or excisional biopsy for histology Immunohistochemistry including S100, mammaglobin, SOX10 and DOG1 Molecular testing for ETV6-NTRK3 and variant fusions MRI of the primary with ultrasound or CT of the neck for staging NTRK fusion testing to determine eligibility for targeted therapy in advanced disease A salivary malignancy defined by an ETV6-NTRK3 gene fusion, morphologically analogous to secretory carcinoma of the breast. It most often arises in the parotid but also occurs in the intraoral minor glands, typically as a slow-growing painless mass. Many cases were historically misclassified as acinic cell carcinoma before the fusion was recognised. Histology shows microcystic and tubular structures with abundant eosinophilic intraluminal secretions and vacuolated cytoplasm, but no true zymogen granules. The immunophenotype is characteristic: S100, mammaglobin and SOX10 positive, with DOG1 negative, which helps separate it from acinic cell carcinoma. The defining ETV6-NTRK3 fusion, or variant fusions such as ETV6-RET, can be demonstrated by fusion-directed molecular testing. The NTRK fusion is therapeutically important, as it renders advanced disease potentially responsive to tropomyosin receptor kinase inhibitors. Most tumours are indolent, but high-grade transformation is described and carries a worse outlook. Rapid growth or new pain Histological features of high-grade transformation Facial nerve weakness or palsy Cervical nodal or distant metastasis Recurrence after apparently complete excision Misdiagnosing it as acinic cell carcinoma and thereby overlooking a targetable NTRK fusion Failing to perform NTRK or fusion testing in advanced or recurrent cases Misinterpreting DOG1 or S100 staining and reaching the wrong diagnosis Underrecognising high-grade transformation on limited sampling Secretory carcinoma is driven by a balanced translocation that fuses the ETV6 gene with NTRK3, generating a chimeric protein with constitutively active tropomyosin receptor kinase signalling that promotes proliferation and survival through downstream RAS-MAPK and PI3K pathways. The neoplastic cells display apocrine-type secretory differentiation, producing abundant intraluminal and intracytoplasmic eosinophilic secretory material within microcystic, tubular and solid architecture, closely mirroring secretory carcinoma of the breast. Unlike acinic cell carcinoma, the cells do not form true serous zymogen granules, which is reflected in a DOG1-negative, S100- and mammaglobin-positive immunophenotype. The presence of an actionable kinase fusion links the tumour's biology directly to targeted therapy, and progression is usually slow unless high-grade transformation supervenes. Prognosis is generally favourable for conventional low-grade tumours treated with complete excision. Identification of the NTRK fusion offers a targeted therapy option for recurrent or metastatic disease, whereas high-grade transformation worsens the outlook.
