to general anaesthesia, and patients can drift into a deeper level than intended, so providers must be able to rescue from the next deeper level The most common serious complications are respiratory: airway obstruction, hypoventilation, apnoea, and hypoxaemia, which can progress rapidly if unrecognised Cardiovascular effects include hypotension and bradycardia, and combining sedatives with opioids for opioids and a benzodiazepine antagonist for benzodiazepines) can be used, but their duration may be shorter than the sedative, risking re-sedation Elderly, frail, obese, and sleep-apnoea patients, saturation Unintended progression to deep sedation or general anaesthesia without rescue capability Significant hypotension or bradycardia Aspiration during sedation in an at-risk patient Providing sedation without the skills or equipment to rescue a deeper-than-intended level Relying on oximetry alone and missing early hypoventilation that capnography would detect Underestimating the additive respiratory depression of sedative-opioid combinations Assuming a reversal agent fully solves the problem despite its shorter duration and risk of re-sedation Inadequate pre-procedure assessment of airway, comorbidity, and aspiration risk Sedative and analgesic agents depress the central nervous system in a dose-dependent way, reducing conscious level, blunting protective airway reflexes, and depressing respiratory drive and upper airway muscle tone. Loss of pharyngeal tone causes obstruction, while reduced central drive causes hypoventilation and apnoea, together producing hypoxaemia and hypercapnia. Many agents also cause vasodilation and myocardial depression, leading to hypotension, and some blunt compensatory reflexes. Because effects are additive, combinations of sedatives and opioids produce disproportionate respiratory and cardiovascular depression. Depressed reflexes also raise the risk of aspiration in patients with a full stomach. With appropriate patient selection, monitoring, and prompt rescue, procedural sedation is generally safe; unrecognised respiratory depression can cause hypoxic injury or death, and most serious events are linked to inadequate monitoring or rescue.

See-saw nystagmus — seesaw nystagmus Pituitary or other parasellar mass Craniopharyngioma Mesodiencephalic stroke or lesion Congenital or retinal-dystrophy-associated nystagmus Other acquired pendular nystagmus (for example demyelinating) Oculopalatal tremor MRI of the brain focused on the sellar, suprasellar and mesodiencephalic regions Formal visual field testing for a bitemporal hemianopia Neuro-ophthalmological and orthoptic assessment Endocrine evaluation if a sellar mass is found Electroretinography when a retinal cause is suspected A distinctive nystagmus in which one eye rises and intorts while the other falls and extorts, then the cycle reverses, resembling a see-saw The pendular form is classically associated with parasellar or suprasellar masses compressing the chiasm and optic pathways A bitemporal hemianopia frequently accompanies the pendular form because of chiasmal involvement The jerk (hemi-see-saw) form points to a mesodiencephalic lesion, often in the region of the interstitial nucleus of Cajal It may also occur with severe congenital visual loss and some retinal dystrophies MRI directed at the sellar, suprasellar and mesodiencephalic regions is central to the workup Bitemporal hemianopia or other chiasmal field loss Signs of a sellar or suprasellar mass, including endocrine disturbance Additional brainstem or diencephalic signs Progressive visual loss Failing to image the sella and chiasm when see-saw nystagmus is identified Overlooking an accompanying bitemporal hemianopia Not distinguishing the pendular from the jerk (hemi-see-saw) form and their different localisations Missing a congenital or retinal cause in a child See-saw nystagmus arises from disruption of the vestibulo-ocular and visual pathways that coordinate torsional and vertical eye movements, particularly around the diencephalon and rostral midbrain. The pendular form is linked to large parasellar or suprasellar lesions that damage the chiasm and adjacent structures, plausibly removing visual and vestibular stabilising signals, whereas the jerk hemi-see-saw form reflects a focal lesion of the interstitial nucleus of Cajal and its connections. The result is the conjugate torsional and disjunctive vertical oscillation that defines the sign. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; the nystagmus may improve if a compressive lesion is treated, but it can persist, and associated visual field loss may not fully recover.

segmental neurofibromatosis — mosaic neurofibromatosis type 1, localised neurofibromatosis Generalised neurofibromatosis type 1 Isolated multiple café-au-lait macules without neurofibromatosis Schwannomatosis or segmental schwannomas Becker naevus or other segmental pigmentary mosaicism Congenital melanocytic naevus Piebaldism or naevus spilus with associated lesions Dermatological mapping of the segmental distribution and midline demarcation Skin biopsy of a representative nodule for histological confirmation Molecular testing for NF1 mutation on lesional tissue rather than peripheral blood Ophthalmological review for Lisch nodules or optic pathway involvement MRI of the affected region if deep plexiform or nerve involvement is suspected Family assessment and genetic counselling for reproductive risk A mosaic form of neurofibromatosis type 1 in which café-au-lait macules, freckling and/or neurofibromas are confined to one or a few body segments, often respecting the midline. It results from a post-zygotic somatic NF1 mutation, so features are limited to the clonal cutaneous territory rather than being generalised. Lesions frequently follow a broad dermatomal or Blaschkoid distribution and stop abruptly at the midline. Most patients have no family history, but gonadal (germline) mosaicism means offspring can rarely inherit generalised NF1. Systemic complications such as optic glioma and skeletal dysplasia are uncommon, though they can occur if deeper tissues carry the mutation. Diagnosis is largely clinical; skin biopsy of a neurofibroma confirms the lesion type and mosaic NF1 can be demonstrated on lesional (not blood) tissue. New or rapidly enlarging, painful nodules within the affected segment warrant assessment for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour. Genetic counselling should address the small but real reproductive risk from possible germline involvement. Rapid growth, new pain or neurological deficit in a lesion suggesting malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour Extension beyond the original segment or emergence of generalised features Unexplained skeletal deformity within the affected region Visual disturbance suggesting optic pathway involvement Testing peripheral blood for NF1 and reporting a false-negative result because the mutation is confined to lesional tissue. Reassuring patients that offspring cannot be affected, overlooking possible gonadal mosaicism. Mistaking segmental disease for benign isolated café-au-lait macules and omitting surveillance. Failing to investigate a rapidly changing nodule for malignant transformation. Assuming no systemic features can ever occur when deeper tissues may share the mutation. Segmental neurofibromatosis is caused by a somatic loss-of-function mutation in the NF1 tumour-suppressor gene occurring after fertilisation, during embryonic development. Because the mutation arises in a single progenitor cell and is propagated only to its clonal descendants, neurofibromin deficiency is restricted to a delimited region of skin and sometimes underlying tissue, producing the characteristic segmental, midline-respecting distribution of café-au-lait macules, freckling and neurofibromas. Loss of neurofibromin removes negative regulation of Ras signalling within the affected clone, promoting the same Schwann-cell and melanocytic proliferations seen in generalised NF1 but confined to the mosaic territory. If the mutation also involves germ cells, offspring may inherit a constitutional NF1 mutation and develop generalised disease. The prognosis is generally favourable with disease confined to the affected segment and a low rate of systemic complications, though there is a small lifelong risk of malignant transformation within neurofibromas and a rare reproductive risk of transmitting generalised NF1.

Segmental testicular infarction — segmental testicular infarct Testicular tumour Testicular torsion Epididymo-orchitis with abscess Focal orchitis Intratesticular haematoma Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler and, where available, contrast-enhanced ultrasound MRI in equivocal cases to characterise the lesion Tumour markers (alpha-fetoprotein, beta-hCG, LDH) Assessment for a hypercoagulable or vasculitic cause Interval imaging to demonstrate a decreasing lesion supporting a benign diagnosis Infarction of a portion of the testis rather than the whole gland, presenting with acute testicular pain It is an uncommon cause of the acute scrotum and an important mimic of testicular tumour on imaging Many cases are idiopathic, though causes include epididymo-orchitis, trauma, sickle cell disease, vasculitis and hypercoagulable states Ultrasound shows a wedge-shaped or rounded avascular area, and contrast-enhanced imaging confirms absent perfusion of the segment The main concern is distinguishing it from a testicular neoplasm to avoid unnecessary orchidectomy Where imaging is confident and tumour markers are normal, it can be managed conservatively with follow-up Imaging or markers suggesting a testicular tumour Progressive enlargement of the lesion Features suggesting torsion or abscess An underlying thrombophilia or vasculitis needing treatment Mistaking it for a tumour and performing unnecessary orchidectomy Failing to use contrast imaging or follow-up to clarify the diagnosis Overlooking an underlying prothrombotic or vasculitic cause Confusing it with torsion or abscess Segmental testicular infarction results from occlusion or compromise of a branch of the testicular vasculature supplying part of the testis, producing ischaemic necrosis of that segment while the rest of the gland remains perfused. Precipitants include local inflammation (epididymo-orchitis) causing vascular compression, trauma, sickling in sickle cell disease, vasculitis and thrombophilia, although many cases are idiopathic. The resulting focal avascular lesion can radiologically resemble a tumour, which is the key diagnostic challenge. Idiopathic segmental infarction generally has a benign course with the lesion shrinking over time, and the testis can often be preserved when malignancy is confidently excluded.

Segond fracture — lateral capsular avulsion fracture, lateral tibial rim avulsion, anterolateral ligament avulsion Arcuate (fibular head avulsion) fracture indicating posterolateral corner injury Reverse Segond (medial avulsion) with PCL injury Tibial plateau fracture Iliotibial band or biceps femoris avulsion Isolated ACL rupture without avulsion Radiographs of the knee (the fragment is best seen on the AP view) MRI to confirm ACL rupture and detect meniscal injury Lachman and pivot-shift examination for anterior instability Assessment for associated posterolateral corner injury A small avulsion fracture off the lateral margin of the proximal tibia, just distal to the joint line It results from internal rotation and varus stress and represents avulsion of the anterolateral capsuloligamentous complex Its great importance is as a radiographic marker: it is strongly associated with (nearly pathognomonic of) anterior cruciate ligament rupture It is frequently accompanied by meniscal injury as well as the ACL tear A reverse Segond (medial tibial rim avulsion) is instead associated with PCL and medial meniscal injury The fleck of bone can be subtle on radiographs, so its recognition should trigger MRI of the knee Treatment is directed at the associated intra-articular injuries rather than the small bony fragment itself Multiligament injury or a reduced knee dislocation with vascular risk Locked knee suggesting a displaced meniscal fragment Gross rotatory instability implying posterolateral corner involvement Overlooking the subtle bony fleck and thereby missing the associated ACL rupture Treating the fragment in isolation while ignoring intra-articular injury Confusing it with an arcuate fracture that signals posterolateral corner injury Failing to obtain MRI after identifying the sign Excessive internal rotation and varus loading of the knee places tension on the anterolateral structures of the proximal tibia, avulsing a small cortical fragment at their insertion. The same mechanism ruptures the anterior cruciate ligament, which is why the Segond fragment is a reliable secondary sign of ACL injury; the bony fragment itself is usually clinically insignificant compared with the associated ligamentous and meniscal damage. The fracture itself heals without specific treatment; the outcome is determined by the associated ACL and meniscal injuries and their management.

mandatory in all HIV-infected patients even without signs of infection (p.3417) Serum and CSF autoantibody testing when epilepsy onset is fulminant or accompanied by psychiatric/cognitive disturbance (autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis) (p.3417) MRI preferred over CT for detecting structural lesions; CT performed emergently when MRI is not immediately available or when a mass/infection is suspected (p.3417-3418) Interictal and ictal EEG, with activating procedures (hyperventilation, photic stimulation, sleep, sleep deprivation); a normal routine interictal EEG does NOT exclude epilepsy - it is normal in 50-80% of known epileptics initially (p.3416-3417) Continuous video-EEG telemetry for poorly characterized events or seizures that are difficult to control, and to distinguish epileptic from psychogenic events (p.3417, p.3419) Genetic testing in infants/children with suspected genetic epilepsy syndromes, and selected older patients with an undiagnosed early-life epilepsy syndrome (p.3418) Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES) - nonepileptic behaviors, often a conversion reaction; clues include side-to-side head turning, ictal eye closure, asynchronous large-amplitude limb shaking, four-limb twitching without loss of consciousness, pelvic thrusting, and prolonged waxing/waning episodes; surface EEG may be normal especially for frontal-lobe-like events, and PNES can coexist with true epilepsy (p.3419) Convulsive syncope - a brief (1-10 s) burst of convulsive movements at the onset of a faint, especially if the patient stays upright; postictal confusion is much less prominent than after a true seizure (p.3419) Alcoholic blackouts and delirium tremens (p.3419) Hypoglycemia and hypoxia as metabolic mimics of seizure (p.3419) Hyperventilation and panic attack (p.3419) Effects of psychoactive drugs / hallucinogens (p.3419) A seizure is a transient event from abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity; epilepsy is the distinct condition of recurrent unprovoked seizures from a chronic underlying process. A single seizure, or seizures due to a correctable/avoidable cause, is not by itself epilepsy (p.3408). Operationally, epilepsy is defined as two or more unprovoked seizures, though a single seizure with clinical or EEG features portending high recurrence risk can establish the diagnosis (p.3408-3409). Seizures are fundamentally classified as focal (network limited to one hemisphere; often structural) versus generalized (rapidly engaging both hemispheres) versus unknown onset; the older terms 'partial', 'simple/complex partial' are no longer used (p.3409). Focal seizures are subclassified by awareness (intact vs impaired) and onset (motor vs nonmotor); a focal seizure can evolve to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure (formerly 'secondary generalization') (p.3409). Distinguishing a focal seizure that evolves to generalized from a primary generalized tonic-clonic seizure is critical but difficult, because bystanders emphasize the dramatic convulsive phase and overlook the subtle focal onset; a careful history for a preceding aura or focal features, and EEG, are needed because evaluation and treatment differ substantially (p.3410). Status epilepticus is continuous seizures, or repetitive discrete seizures with impaired consciousness between them; for generalized convulsive status epilepticus the practical operational threshold is seizures lasting beyond 5 minutes (older definitions used 15-30 min) (p.3425). Generalized convulsive status epilepticus (GCSE) is a medical emergency: prolonged seizures cause cardiorespiratory dysfunction, hyperthermia, and metabolic derangements that can produce irreversible CNS injury (p.3425-3426). Treatment principle for status epilepticus is an escalating sequence beginning with a benzodiazepine, followed by an IV antiseizure drug, with anesthetic agents for refractory cases - alongside attention to airway, oxygenation, glucose, and reversible metabolic causes (no doses given here) (p.3426). After 30-45 min of uninterrupted GCSE the motor signs can become very subtle (only fine finger twitching or rapid eye movements); if a patient stops overt convulsions yet remains comatose, an EEG is required to exclude ongoing (nonconvulsive) status epilepticus (p.3426). If the sole cause of a seizure is a correctable metabolic disturbance (e.g., electrolyte or glucose abnormality), or a precipitant drug/illicit substance, treatment targets the underlying problem and chronic antiseizure drugs are usually unnecessary (p.3419). An apparently unprovoked first seizure carries a recurrence risk estimated at roughly 31-71% in the first 12 months; accepted risk factors favoring treatment are prior brain insult (stroke/trauma), epileptiform EEG, a significant imaging abnormality, or a nocturnal seizure (p.3420). A serum prolactin rise in the 30 min after most generalized and some focal seizures can support an epileptic cause, but it is unreliable because baseline levels are rarely available and some drugs elevate prolactin (p.3419). The clinical range of focal seizure behaviors is extremely broad, so caution is advised before dismissing paroxysmal stereotypic bizarre episodes as non-epileptic (p.3409). The age of the patient strongly informs the likely etiology of new seizures - e.g., febrile seizures and genetic/developmental causes in young children versus cerebrovascular disease, tumor, metabolic disturbance and degenerative disease in older adults (p.3411-3414). Generalized convulsive status epilepticus - immediate emergency due to risk of cardiorespiratory failure, hyperthermia, metabolic derangement, and irreversible CNS injury (p.3425-3426) Persistent coma after overt convulsions stop - suspect ongoing nonconvulsive status epilepticus and obtain EEG (p.3426) Focal features, focal neurologic deficit, or abnormal/changing neurologic exam - points to a structural cause (mass, stroke, infection, trauma, degenerative disease) requiring imaging (p.3416) Fulminant new-onset seizures with psychiatric symptoms and cognitive change - suspect autoimmune/antibody-mediated encephalitis (p.3413-3414, p.3417) First seizure in a patient with HIV - lumbar puncture is mandatory even without signs of infection (p.3417) Atonic ('drop attack') seizures - substantial risk of direct head injury from the fall (p.3410) Failing to exclude a treatable provoking cause (metabolic, toxic, structural, or infective) before labeling a patient as having epilepsy - many such seizures need only correction of the underlying problem, not chronic antiseizure drugs (p.3408, p.3419, p.3416-3417). Assuming a normal interictal EEG rules out epilepsy - the initial routine EEG is normal in 50-80% of patients with known epilepsy, and EEG has limited sensitivity (p.3417). Missing nonconvulsive status epilepticus: in altered consciousness or persistent coma without overt convulsions, NCSE can be present and is only revealed by EEG; intermittent seizures with prolonged postictal states are easily overlooked as causes of unexplained encephalopathy (p.3426). Overlooking a focal onset by focusing on the dramatic generalized convulsive phase, thereby misclassifying the seizure and choosing the wrong evaluation/treatment pathway (p.3410). Mistaking psychogenic nonepileptic seizures for epilepsy (or vice versa) on clinical grounds alone - even experienced epileptologists err; PNES and epilepsy can coexist, and video-EEG is the arbiter (p.3419). Misinterpreting convulsive syncope (brief convulsive jerks at the start of a faint) as a primary seizure (p.3419). Relying on headache or incontinence to distinguish seizure from syncope - these features are unreliable (p.3419). Forgetting that the postictal Todd's paralysis (focal weakness for minutes to hours after a focal seizure) can mimic an acute structural deficit such as stroke (p.3409). Misdiagnosing childhood absence epilepsy as attention deficit disorder or simple 'daydreaming' (p.3410). A seizure reflects a shift in the normal balance between excitation and inhibition in the CNS. At the cellular level the hallmark of focal seizure activity is the electrographic spike, generated by near-simultaneous bursting (the 'paroxysmal depolarization shift') of local excitatory neurons - a prolonged membrane depolarization driven by calcium influx that opens voltage-gated sodium channels, followed by a GABA- or potassium-mediated hyperpolarizing afterpotential. Surrounding inhibition normally limits spread; when recruitment overwhelms it (via rising extracellular potassium, presynaptic calcium accumulation with enhanced transmitter release, NMDA-receptor activation, and ephaptic effects), activity propagates through local cortical and long commissural pathways (e.g., corpus callosum). Generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges of absence seizures arise from thalamocortical oscillatory circuits involving GABA-B receptors, T-type calcium channels, and potassium channels. Many causes converge on three interacting factor classes: endogenous (genetic/developmental seizure-threshold) factors, epileptogenic factors (CNS injury such as severe penetrating head trauma, stroke, infection, or neurodegeneration that, over months to years, transforms a normal network into a chronically hyperexcitable one - 'epileptogenesis'), and precipitating factors (sleep deprivation, stress, hormonal change, toxins, certain drugs, photic stimulation). Many inherited epilepsies are channelopathies due to ion-channel mutations (p.3411-3415). About half of people respond to the first antiseizure drug; roughly 30% have ongoing seizures despite drug combinations (refractory epilepsy). People with epilepsy have a 2-3 times higher mortality than matched controls, mostly driven by the underlying etiology (e.g., tumor, stroke); excess deaths also arise from accidents, status epilepticus, and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP), which typically affects young patients with convulsive seizures and tends to occur at night, possibly via brainstem-mediated cardiorespiratory/arousal effects. Simple febrile seizures do not raise the risk of later epilepsy, whereas complex febrile seizures carry a 2-5% risk. Severe penetrating head trauma carries up to a ~45% (penetrating/depressed fracture/hemorrhage/prolonged coma: 30-50%) risk of subsequent epilepsy, closed head injury with contusion 5-25%, and mild concussion only slightly increased risk. Favorable factors for staying seizure-free after planned drug withdrawal include 1-5 years of control, a single seizure type, normal exam/intelligence, normal EEG, and no family history (p.3411, p.3414, p.3420, p.3424, p.3426-3427). Seizures are classified (ILAE 2017) by onset: (1) Focal onset (with intact or impaired awareness; motor or nonmotor onset; may evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic); (2) Generalized onset - motor (tonic-clonic, or other such as atonic/myoclonic) or nonmotor (absence); (3) Unknown onset. Status epilepticus is staged by duration/refractoriness in management terms: impending/early (5-30 min), established and early-refractory (30 min to 48 h), and late refractory (>48 h), with subtypes generalized convulsive (GCSE) versus nonconvulsive (NCSE) (p.3409, p.3425-3426).

emergent CT when MRI unavailable or mass/infection suspected Routine bloods - electrolytes, glucose, calcium, magnesium, hepatic and renal function; toxicology screen of blood and urine Lumbar puncture when meningitis/encephalitis suspected, and mandatory in HIV-infected patients Serum and CSF autoantibody testing in fulminant epilepsy with psychiatric or cognitive features Genetic testing in suspected genetic epilepsy syndromes (diagnostic and may guide therapy choice and predict drug toxicity, e.g., HLA-B*1502 and severe cutaneous reactions) Functional imaging (PET, SPECT) and advanced localization (high-density EEG/ESI, magnetoencephalography/MSI) in medically refractory focal epilepsy Convulsive syncope (brief tonic-clonic-like movements during a faint, especially when kept upright) Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (side-to-side head movement, ictal eye closure, asynchronous limb shaking, pelvic thrusting, waxing-waning prolonged events) Transient ischemic attack Migraine aura Movement disorders and parasomnias A seizure is a transient event caused by abnormal excessive or hypersynchronous neuronal activity; epilepsy is the distinct condition of a chronic underlying tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures, so a single or provoked seizure does not by itself constitute epilepsy (though a single seizure with high-risk clinical/EEG features may suffice). Roughly 5-10% of people experience at least one seizure in life, with peaks in early childhood and late adulthood; epilepsy prevalence is approximately 5-30 per 1000. The 2017 ILAE scheme classifies seizures by onset as focal, generalized, or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness (intact vs impaired) and motor vs nonmotor onset, replacing the older 'simple/complex partial' and 'secondary generalization' terms. Focal motor seizures may show a Jacksonian march (spread along the motor strip), and a postictal focal weakness (Todd's paralysis) lasting minutes to hours can mimic a stroke. Auras are themselves focal seizures with intact awareness; temporal-lobe auras include rising epigastric sensations, foul smells/tastes, fear, deja vu, and micropsia/macropsia. Typical absence seizures produce brief lapses of consciousness without postural loss or postictal confusion, with a 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave EEG provoked by hyperventilation; they are frequently misdiagnosed as attention-deficit disorder or daydreaming. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures begin with a tonic phase (ictal cry, apnea/cyanosis, tongue biting, sympathetic surge) evolving to a clonic phase, followed by postictal flaccidity, confusion, headache, and myalgia. Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis is the most common cause of focal seizures with impaired awareness and is characteristically medically refractory but responds well to surgery. Etiology is strongly age-dependent: neonates - perinatal hypoxia-ischemia, infection, and metabolic derangements; young children - febrile seizures; adolescents/young adults - trauma, genetic syndromes, drugs, autoantibodies; older adults - cerebrovascular disease (up to ~50% of new epilepsy over 65), tumor, and degenerative disease. Distinguishing seizure from syncope: aura, cyanosis, prolonged motor activity (30-60 s), and many minutes to hours of postictal confusion favor seizure, whereas brief loss of consciousness with rapid recovery, pallor, and provocation by pain/standing favor syncope; headache and incontinence are unreliable discriminators. A transient serum prolactin rise in the first 30 minutes after most generalized and some focal seizures can support a true seizure over a psychogenic event, but is unreliable without a baseline and because some drugs elevate prolactin. Penetrating head injury carries up to a 45% risk of subsequent epilepsy via epileptogenesis, illustrating how an acquired structural lesion can permanently lower seizure threshold. Generalized convulsive status epilepticus - continuous or repetitive seizures (practically, GCSE lasting beyond ~5 min); a medical emergency that can cause cardiorespiratory failure, hyperthermia, metabolic derangement, and irreversible CNS injury After 30-45 minutes of uninterrupted seizures the clinical signs may become subtle while damaging electrographic seizures continue, including in patients paralyzed by neuromuscular blockade Fulminant new-onset seizures with psychiatric symptoms and cognitive change suggesting autoimmune (e.g., anti-potassium-channel or anti-glutamate-receptor) epilepsy New seizure in an older adult suggesting cerebrovascular disease, tumor, or degenerative disease First seizure with focal features, persistent neurologic deficit, fever, or suspected CNS infection prompting urgent imaging and possible lumbar puncture Atonic 'drop attacks' with high risk of head injury Failing to distinguish a focal seizure that secondarily generalizes from a primary generalized tonic-clonic seizure because bystanders emphasize the convulsive phase and overlook subtle focal onset/aura - a distinction that materially changes evaluation and treatment. Misdiagnosing absence epilepsy as attention-deficit disorder or simple daydreaming. Concluding bizarre paroxysmal stereotyped behavior is non-epileptic; focal (especially frontal-lobe) seizures can produce highly unusual behaviors. Assuming a normal interictal EEG excludes epilepsy, or that epileptiform discharges by themselves prove epilepsy. Over-relying on incontinence or headache to separate seizure from syncope, as these are unreliable. Assuming psychogenic nonepileptic seizures exclude true epilepsy - the two frequently coexist. Misreading subtle late-stage status epilepticus as resolution when damaging electrographic seizures persist. Seizures arise from a shift in the normal balance between neuronal excitation and inhibition in the CNS. Focal seizure activity begins in a discrete cortical region and can invade surrounding cortex; the hallmark is the electrographic spike produced by near-simultaneous bursting of many excitatory neurons (hypersynchronization). At the cellular level, a prolonged paroxysmal depolarization shift driven by calcium influx opens voltage-dependent sodium channels and generates repetitive action potentials, followed by a GABA- or potassium-channel-mediated hyperpolarizing afterpotential. Spread is normally limited by intact hyperpolarization and feedforward surround inhibition; recruitment of neighboring neurons occurs through rising extracellular potassium, presynaptic calcium accumulation enhancing transmitter release, NMDA-receptor activation, and ephaptic effects, allowing propagation via local and commissural (corpus callosum) pathways. Epilepsy results from a dynamic interplay of endogenous (often genetic, maturational) factors, epileptogenic factors (e.g., severe head trauma, stroke, infection, neurodegeneration, developmental malformations), and precipitating factors (sleep deprivation, stress, hormonal change, toxins, photic stimulation). Many gene mutations affecting ion channels (e.g., SCN1A, KCNQ2), neurotransmitter receptors, and metabolic transporters (e.g., SLC2A1/GLUT-1) underlie specific syndromes. Outcome varies widely by syndrome and etiology. Typical absence epilepsy and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy generally respond well to medication (though JME remission is uncommon), whereas mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and epilepsies tied to structural lesions or developmental delay are often refractory. About half of patients do not respond to the first medication, and roughly 30% have ongoing seizures despite optimal drug therapy. Favorable predictors for successfully discontinuing therapy include 1-5 years of complete control, a single seizure type (generalized carrying a better prognosis than focal), normal neurologic examination and intelligence, no family history of epilepsy, and a normal EEG; a normal EEG generally implies a better prognosis. People with epilepsy have a death rate roughly 2-3 times that of matched controls, mostly attributable to the underlying cause but also to accidents, status epilepticus, and SUDEP. Seizures are classified by ILAE 2017 onset: focal (with intact or impaired awareness, motor or nonmotor), generalized (motor such as tonic-clonic, atonic, myoclonic; or nonmotor/absence), or unknown onset. Severity at the syndromic extreme is status epilepticus: continuous or repetitive seizures with impaired interictal consciousness, subdivided into generalized convulsive status epilepticus (GCSE) and nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE). Although traditionally defined as 15-30 minutes of activity, GCSE is practically treated as an emergency when convulsions last beyond about 5 minutes. Febrile seizures are graded as simple (single, brief, symmetric) versus complex (repeated, lasting over 15 minutes, or with focal features).

Selective IgA deficiency — IgA deficiency, selective immunoglobulin A deficiency, sIgAD Common variable immunodeficiency (may share features and can evolve from IgA deficiency) Transient low IgA in early childhood before immune maturation Drug-induced IgA suppression (e.g. certain anticonvulsants) IgG subclass or specific antibody deficiency presenting with recurrent infection Coeliac disease and other associated autoimmune disorders Secondary immunodeficiency from protein loss Serum IgA, IgG, and IgM to confirm isolated IgA deficiency IgG subclass levels and vaccine-specific antibody responses to assess for broader deficiency Coeliac evaluation using IgG-based serology or duodenal biopsy given unreliable IgA-based tests Screening for associated autoimmune disease when clinically indicated Testing for anti-IgA antibodies before transfusion in patients with prior reactions Periodic reassessment of immunoglobulins to detect evolution toward CVID Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency and is defined by a very low or absent serum IgA with normal IgG and IgM and otherwise intact immunity The majority of affected individuals are asymptomatic and are detected incidentally, so a low IgA alone does not equate to clinical disease When symptomatic, patients tend to have recurrent sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infections, reflecting the loss of secretory IgA at mucosal surfaces There is a recognised association with atopy and with autoimmune conditions such as coeliac disease, so unexplained IgA deficiency warrants screening for these Coeliac serology based on IgA antibodies can be falsely negative in IgA deficiency, so IgG-based testing or histology should be used instead A minority have severe anaphylactic reactions to blood products because of anti-IgA antibodies, so washed or IgA-deficient blood components may be required There is no specific replacement therapy because IgA cannot be effectively replaced; management centres on prompt treatment of infections and, where needed, prophylactic antibiotics A small proportion, particularly those with associated IgG subclass deficiency or poor vaccine responses, can progress over time toward common variable immunodeficiency and need monitoring Anaphylactic transfusion reaction from anti-IgA antibodies, requiring IgA-deficient or washed blood products Progressive fall in IgG or poor vaccine responses signalling evolution to CVID Recurrent severe or invasive infection prompting reassessment of the full antibody profile Unexplained malabsorption or systemic autoimmune features suggesting an associated disorder Interpreting an incidental low IgA as clinically significant disease in an asymptomatic person Missing coeliac disease because of falsely negative IgA-based serology Transfusing standard blood products in a patient with anti-IgA antibodies Failing to reassess immunoglobulins over time and thus missing progression to CVID Selective IgA deficiency results from a failure of terminal differentiation of IgA-committed B cells into IgA-secreting plasma cells, so that little or no IgA reaches serum and mucosal secretions. The loss of secretory IgA impairs mucosal immune exclusion of pathogens at the respiratory and gastrointestinal surfaces, though compensatory secretory IgM often limits the clinical impact. The precise molecular basis is usually unknown; it shares genetic susceptibility loci (including MHC haplotypes and TACI variants) with CVID, and the two conditions can occur within the same families and occasionally evolve into one another. Immune dysregulation underlies the associated atopic and autoimmune disease. Most individuals with selective IgA deficiency remain well and have a normal life expectancy. Symptomatic patients generally do well with treatment of infections, but a subset with additional immune defects have more infections and may progress to CVID, and rare transfusion anaphylaxis is a serious hazard.

caused by neurodegeneration focused on the anterior temporal lobes, which serve as a hub for conceptual and semantic knowledge. The commonest underlying pathology is frontotemporal lobar degeneration associated with abnormal TDP-43 protein aggregation. Progressive loss of neurones in the anterior temporal cortex erodes the store of meaning for words, objects and, in right-predominant cases, faces, while the more posterior and perisylvian regions supporting fluent speech output, grammar and repetition remain relatively intact until later. This produces fluent, well-articulated but semantically empty speech with severe naming and comprehension deficits. Semantic dementia progresses over years, with widening loss of conceptual knowledge and eventual emergence of behavioural change and broader cognitive decline; prognosis reflects the underlying frontotemporal lobar degeneration, and management is supportive with speech and language and behavioural strategies.

Pure seminoma has an excellent prognosis, with cure rates approaching those of other stages of testicular cancer; localised disease is almost universally curable and even metastatic seminoma has high cure rates with cisplatin-based chemotherapy.

intellect is typically preserved Decompensated hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or heart failure Life-threatening arrhythmia Severe neonatal lactic acidosis with cardiorespiratory compromise Rapid clinical deterioration during intercurrent illness or metabolic stress Treating congenital cataracts in isolation without evaluating the heart, thereby missing the cardiomyopathy Attributing the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to a sarcomeric cause and overlooking a metabolic origin Assuming cognitive impairment, when intellect is characteristically preserved Exposing patients to mitochondrial toxins that can worsen the energy deficit Sengers syndrome is caused by recessive loss-of-function mutations in AGK, which encodes acylglycerol kinase. This mitochondrial enzyme phosphorylates monoacylglycerol and diacylglycerol and also functions as a component of the TIM22 carrier import machinery that inserts certain proteins, including the adenine nucleotide translocator, into the inner mitochondrial membrane. Loss of AGK disturbs mitochondrial membrane lipid composition and impairs import of key carriers, secondarily compromising oxidative phosphorylation and ATP export. Tissues with high and sustained energy demand, notably cardiac and skeletal muscle, and the metabolically specialised lens are preferentially affected, giving the cardiomyopathy, myopathy and cataracts. Prognosis is bimodal: the severe neonatal form usually causes death in infancy from cardiomyopathy and lactic acidosis, whereas the milder form permits survival into adulthood with cataract, myopathy and manageable cardiac disease, cardiac status being the main prognostic factor.

senile chorea — senile chorea of the elderly, late-onset sporadic chorea Late-onset Huntington disease Huntington disease-like syndromes and C9orf72 expansion Neuroacanthocytosis and related syndromes Vascular (post-stroke) chorea Drug-induced chorea and tardive dyskinesia Metabolic chorea (non-ketotic hyperglycaemia, thyrotoxicosis, polycythaemia) Autoimmune and paraneoplastic chorea HTT CAG repeat genetic testing for Huntington disease Genetic testing for Huntington disease phenocopies (C9orf72, JPH3, others) where indicated MRI brain to assess caudate atrophy and vascular or structural lesions Peripheral blood film for acanthocytes and creatine kinase Metabolic screen including glucose, thyroid function and full blood count Autoimmune and paraneoplastic antibody panel where clinically suspected Serum caeruloplasmin and copper studies in younger-appearing presentations Senile chorea is a controversial descriptive label for late-onset chorea in the elderly without dementia, psychiatric decline or a family history of Huntington disease. It is a diagnosis of exclusion; many historical cases would now be reclassified as late-onset Huntington disease, Huntington disease-like syndromes or secondary chorea. Chorea is typically generalised, symmetrical and predominantly affects the limbs and orobuccolingual region. Cognition is characteristically preserved, distinguishing it from the cognitive and behavioural decline of Huntington disease. Genetic testing for the HTT CAG repeat expansion and for C9orf72 and other phenocopies is essential before accepting the label. Structural basal ganglia lesions, metabolic derangement, drugs and autoimmune causes must be systematically excluded. Progression, if any, is generally slow and confined to the movement disorder without the relentless multisystem decline of Huntington disease. Treatment is symptomatic and reserved for functionally disabling chorea, using dopamine-depleting or dopamine-blocking agents cautiously in view of age and comorbidity. Emerging cognitive decline or psychiatric change suggesting Huntington disease rather than isolated senile chorea Abrupt onset or focal signs indicating a vascular or structural lesion Systemic features suggesting paraneoplastic or autoimmune aetiology Rapid progression prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Metabolic derangement such as marked hyperglycaemia requiring urgent correction Accepting the label without genetic testing and thereby missing late-onset Huntington disease. Assuming a negative family history excludes Huntington disease, which may reflect non-paternity, early parental death or reduced penetrance. Overlooking reversible metabolic causes such as non-ketotic hyperglycaemia. Attributing chorea to ageing and not screening for drug-induced or tardive movement disorders. Using dopamine antagonists without regard to fall risk, sedation and anticholinergic burden in older patients. Senile chorea is best understood as a clinical syndrome rather than a unified pathological entity, reflecting age-related or acquired dysfunction of the striatal indirect pathway. In many patients neuropathological or genetic re-evaluation reveals late-onset Huntington disease with reduced-penetrance CAG expansions, or Huntington disease phenocopies. In genuinely sporadic cases, degeneration or vascular and gliotic change within the caudate and putamen is thought to reduce inhibitory striatal output to the globus pallidus, disinhibiting thalamocortical drive and producing chorea. The relative sparing of cognition suggests that pathology is more restricted to motor striatal circuits than in classical Huntington disease, though the boundaries of the concept remain debated. When a serious underlying cause is excluded, senile chorea tends to follow a relatively benign, slowly progressive or static course with preserved cognition and reasonable functional outlook. Prognosis worsens substantially if the presentation ultimately proves to be late-onset Huntington disease or another neurodegenerative disorder.

Senior-Loken syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in nephronophthisis-associated genes that encode proteins localising to the primary cilium, basal body, and centrosome. Defective ciliary function in renal tubular epithelium leads to progressive tubulointerstitial nephropathy with tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis, and cyst formation at the corticomedullary junction, the hallmark of nephronophthisis. The same proteins are essential for the connecting cilium of photoreceptors, so their loss produces photoreceptor degeneration and inherited retinal dystrophy, explaining the combined renal and retinal phenotype. The renal disease is progressive and most affected individuals reach end-stage kidney disease during childhood or adolescence, requiring renal replacement therapy. Visual prognosis depends on the retinal genotype, ranging from profound early blindness to slowly progressive visual loss.

sensorimotor lacunar stroke — sensorimotor lacunar syndrome, thalamocapsular lacunar stroke Large-vessel cortical infarct with combined sensorimotor deficit Thalamocapsular or capsular intracerebral haemorrhage Pure motor hemiparesis or pure sensory stroke early in evolution Space-occupying lesion compressing thalamus and capsule Demyelinating lesion involving sensory and motor tracts Postictal (Todd's) deficit after a focal seizure Diffusion-weighted and T2/FLAIR MRI of the brain Non-contrast CT head to exclude deep haemorrhage Carotid duplex and intracranial vascular imaging ECG and extended cardiac rhythm monitoring Fasting glucose, HbA1c and lipid profile Ambulatory blood pressure measurement Combines unilateral weakness and sensory loss of the face, arm and leg without cortical signs, classically from a lacune at the junction of the thalamus and adjacent posterior internal capsule. The lesion typically involves thalamocapsular territory supplied by penetrating arteries, interrupting both ascending sensory relay and descending corticospinal fibres. Absence of aphasia, neglect, hemianopia and gaze palsy distinguishes it from a large middle cerebral artery cortical infarct. It is one of the classical Fisher lacunar syndromes and shares hypertensive small-vessel pathology with the pure motor and pure sensory variants. A comparable clinical picture can arise from a small primary intracerebral haemorrhage in the same region, so imaging is essential. Diffusion-weighted MRI reliably localises the small deep infarct when CT is unrevealing. Because the deficit is 'complete' across motor and sensory domains, functional impact can exceed that of the single-modality lacunar syndromes. Secondary prevention rests on blood pressure, glycaemic and lipid control together with antiplatelet therapy. Deteriorating conscious level or severe headache suggesting haemorrhage Emergence of cortical signs indicating larger-territory infarction Stuttering or crescendo progression of the deficit New brainstem signs implying more extensive posterior-circulation ischaemia Mistaking a thalamocapsular haemorrhage for ischaemic lacunar stroke without imaging. Classifying the event as cortical and pursuing unnecessary investigation when cortical signs are genuinely absent. Assuming a normal early CT excludes infarction rather than proceeding to diffusion MRI. Underestimating rehabilitation needs given the combined sensory and motor loss. Failing to screen for a co-existent embolic source in a patient with small-vessel disease. Sensorimotor lacunar stroke is produced by occlusion of a small penetrating artery supplying the region where the ventral posterior thalamic nuclei lie immediately adjacent to the posterior limb of the internal capsule. A single lacune here simultaneously interrupts the crossed sensory pathways relaying through the thalamus and the descending corticospinal motor fibres in the capsule, yielding combined contralateral sensory loss and weakness affecting face, arm and leg. As with other lacunar strokes, the responsible arteriopathy is usually hypertensive lipohyalinosis or microatheroma of a deep perforating end-artery, producing a small cavitated infarct without involvement of the overlying cortex. Recovery is variable and often slower than in single-modality lacunar syndromes because both motor and sensory function are affected, though many patients still regain useful independence; recurrent small-vessel events and vascular cognitive decline remain important risks.

early recognition can transform the motor and developmental outcome Progressive dystonia and parkinsonism in a child mislabelled as cerebral palsy Marked diurnal fluctuation with severe evening deterioration limiting function Recurrent oculogyric crises and developmental regression Behavioural or mood disturbance suggesting serotonergic deficiency needing treatment adjustment Assuming a normal newborn phenylalanine screen excludes a BH4-related disorder Treating only the dopaminergic deficit and omitting serotonin-precursor therapy Not performing CSF pterin and neurotransmitter analysis, which is central to the diagnosis Overlooking the diagnosis in older children presenting with fluctuating dystonia and learning difficulty Sepiapterin reductase catalyses the final step of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthesis. BH4 is the essential cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase and tryptophan hydroxylase, so its deficiency impairs synthesis of both dopamine and serotonin. Because alternative pathways can regenerate enough BH4 for hepatic phenylalanine hydroxylase, systemic phenylalanine metabolism is preserved and newborn screening is normal, yet central monoamine neurotransmission is deficient. The result is a mixed dopaminergic and serotonergic deficiency causing levodopa-responsive dystonia and parkinsonism with diurnal variation, and accumulation of upstream pterins such as sepiapterin and dihydrobiopterin. With early combined neurotransmitter-precursor therapy many patients show substantial and sustained improvement in motor and developmental function, whereas delayed treatment may leave residual cognitive and motor deficits. The disorder is treatable rather than curable, and long-term follow-up guides dose adjustment.

rapidly Assuming an inflamed bursa is gouty or traumatic and missing infection Confusing septic bursitis with septic arthritis, which requires more aggressive intervention Injecting corticosteroid into a bursa without excluding infection Stopping treatment prematurely and precipitating relapse A bursa is a synovial-lined sac that reduces friction over bony prominences. Superficial bursae such as the olecranon and prepatellar sit just beneath the skin and are readily seeded by direct trauma or overlying cellulitis. Introduced bacteria, usually skin flora, provoke an inflammatory exudate within the bursal cavity, producing pain, swelling, warmth, and sometimes abscess formation. Because the bursa is anatomically separate from the joint, infection tends to remain localised unless it extends into surrounding tissue. Superficial septic bursitis generally resolves well with aspiration and appropriate antibiotics; recurrence or chronicity is more likely with repeated trauma or delayed treatment, and a minority require surgical bursectomy.

Disruption of the developmental programme, occasionally attributable to mutations in transcription factors such as HESX1 but usually of unknown cause, leads to a spectrum of malformations. Hypoplasia of the optic nerves reduces the ganglion cell axon population, midline defects reflect failed commissural and septal development, and hypothalamic-pituitary maldevelopment produces variable anterior and posterior pituitary hormone deficiencies. The heterogeneous phenotype mirrors which structures are most affected. Outcome depends on the balance of the three components; visual impairment is usually stable, but timely diagnosis and lifelong hormone replacement are critical to prevent morbidity and mortality from endocrine failure.

nucleotides, glycine, and D-serine, so deficiency severely affects the developing nervous system The classic infantile phenotype is congenital microcephaly, intractable seizures, and profound psychomotor retardation The severe end of the spectrum is Neu-Laxova syndrome, a lethal condition with severe microcephaly, ichthyosis, and multiple congenital anomalies The biochemical clue is low prenatal or presymptomatic treatment is being explored for at-risk pregnancies British spelling applies (paediatric) Intractable neonatal or infantile seizures with microcephaly requiring urgent evaluation Progressive neurological deterioration in an untreated infant Features of Neu-Laxova syndrome indicating a severe, often lethal phenotype Missed opportunity for early treatable intervention Overlooking a treatable cause of microcephaly and seizures by not measuring serine Relying on plasma alone when CSF serine is more revealing Delaying serine supplementation, which reduces the chance of benefit Not recognising Neu-Laxova syndrome as part of the same biosynthetic defect L-serine is synthesised de novo from the glycolytic intermediate 3-phosphoglycerate in three steps catalysed by 3-phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase, phosphoserine aminotransferase, and phosphoserine phosphatase. Because the blood-brain barrier limits serine entry, the brain depends heavily on local synthesis, so a block in this pathway causes a functional serine deficiency in the central nervous system. Serine is required for synthesis of glycine, D-serine (an NMDA-receptor co-agonist), phospholipids, and nucleotides essential for neuronal growth and myelination. Deficiency therefore impairs brain development, producing microcephaly, seizures, and severe neurological impairment, with the most profound defects causing the multisystem malformations of Neu-Laxova syndrome. Untreated infantile disease causes severe neurological impairment, but early L-serine (with glycine) supplementation can markedly reduce seizures and improve development, making early recognition critical. The Neu-Laxova end of the spectrum is typically lethal.

Serotonin syndrome / NMS — Medication review (serotonergics/antipsychotics) CK, renal function Temperature Hyperthermia + rigidity — stop agent, cooling, supportive ICU care Neuroleptic malignant syndrome vs serotonin syndrome (mutual differential; distinguish by onset speed, neuromuscular pattern and offending drug class) Lithium toxicity (tremor, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, encephalopathy, may include hyperthermia and seizures in severe cases) Anticholinergic toxidrome Sympathomimetic toxicity (amphetamines, cocaine) Strychnine poisoning Withdrawal syndromes (ethanol, sedative-hypnotics) Meningitis Encephalitis (including brainstem encephalitis) Cerebral abscess Sepsis / systemic inflammatory response syndrome Malaria Typhoid Tetanus Core temperature measurement (most reliable prognosticator of poor outcome in stimulant/withdrawal-type toxidromes) Creatine kinase (markedly elevated in NMS; rhabdomyolysis complicates both) Lactate / arterial blood gas (lactic acidosis is a recognised complication) Coagulation studies (monitor for disseminated intravascular coagulation when hyperthermia is sustained) Toxicology screen and detailed medication review (serotonergic agents, dopamine antagonists, recent dose changes or dopaminergic withdrawal) Cranial CT and CSF analysis if mental status fails to improve, to exclude structural or infectious CNS causes Malignant hyperthermia (e.g. after general anesthesia) Heatstroke / exertional and classic heat illness Thyroid storm Pheochromocytoma Diabetic ketoacidosis Status epilepticus Anticholinergic toxidrome Stimulant/sympathomimetic toxicity Serotonin syndrome and NMS overlap closely (both cause fever, altered mental status, rigidity and autonomic instability), but prominent myoclonus is characteristically a feature of serotonin syndrome and helps separate it from NMS (p.3517). NMS typically evolves over days to weeks after a neuroleptic/dopamine-antagonist is started or up-titrated, i.e. a comparatively slow, subacute onset (p.3517). NMS is not only triggered by antipsychotics: it can also be precipitated by abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic medication in Parkinson's disease patients (p.3517). Serotonin syndrome arises from agents with serotonin-like activity or that block serotonin reuptake (e.g. tryptophan, MDMA/'ecstasy', meperidine, SSRIs), and is rare but potentially fatal (p.3517). The serotonin-syndrome picture is attributed to hyperstimulation of brainstem 5-HT1A (and 5-HT2) receptors (p.3667). The antibiotic linezolid (and to a lesser degree tedizolid) is a monoamine-oxidase inhibitor: combined with serotonergic agents such as SSRIs it can precipitate serotonin syndrome (p.1172). Combining an MAOI with an SSRI is an absolute contraindication because of serotonin-syndrome risk; serotonergic agonists (tryptophan, fenfluramine, triptans) carry a similar hazard (p.3667). Both syndromes are toxidromes in the CNS-syndrome / 'stimulated' physiologic category, alongside lithium toxicity, extrapyramidal reactions and strychnine (p.3715). Hyperthermia — sustained core temperature elevation predicts poor outcome and can progress to irreversible cellular injury Rhabdomyolysis with markedly elevated creatine kinase Autonomic instability — labile blood pressure, tachycardia, diaphoresis Acute renal failure Lactic acidosis Disseminated intravascular coagulation / coagulopathy Coma, seizures or multisystem organ failure Mistaking one syndrome for the other: rapid-onset hyperreflexia/myoclonus/clonus after a serotonergic drug points to serotonin syndrome, whereas slow (days-to-weeks) lead-pipe rigidity with bradyreflexia after a dopamine-antagonist points to NMS — the offending drug class and onset tempo are the key discriminators (p.3517). Overlooking non-psychiatric culprits: the antibiotic linezolid is an MAOI and can trigger serotonin syndrome with concurrent SSRIs (p.1172). Forgetting that NMS can be precipitated by stopping dopaminergic drugs (not only by starting antipsychotics) in Parkinson's disease (p.3517). Anchoring on infection: the fever-plus-rigidity-plus-altered-mental-status picture closely mimics meningitis/encephalitis and sepsis, and structural/infectious causes should be excluded if mental status does not improve (p.3715, p.3773). Dantrolene is ineffective for hyperthermia not caused by malignant hyperthermia, so a hyperthermia mechanism must be identified rather than assumed (p.3776). Some atypical antipsychotics (e.g. chlorpromazine used for agitation) can themselves cause or worsen NMS — adding a neuroleptic to an undifferentiated hyperthermic patient can be harmful (p.3776). Serotonin syndrome results from excess CNS and peripheral serotonergic activity — promotion of serotonin release, inhibition of its reuptake, or direct stimulation of serotonin receptors (chiefly 5-HT1A and 5-HT2), occurring alone or when serotonergic drugs are combined. NMS, in contrast, is linked to dopamine-antagonist (neuroleptic) exposure or abrupt loss of dopaminergic tone, producing central hyperthermia, rigidity and autonomic dysfunction; central dopamine depletion impairs hypothalamic (preoptic/anterior) thermoregulation. Both are classified among the hypothalamic disorders of autonomic/temperature regulation (Harrison 22e p.3541, p.3517, p.3715). Both syndromes are potentially fatal; serotonin syndrome is described as rare but able to progress to death, and NMS can be lethal (e.g. typical neuroleptics in Lewy body disease can cause NMS and death). The duration of hyperthermia drives morbidity and mortality, and progression to rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, DIC and multisystem organ failure marks severe disease (Harrison 22e p.3517, p.3715, p.3773). Harrison frames severity by the physiologic toxidrome state (stimulated vs depressed vs discordant) and by the degree of physiologic derangement on serial vital signs; escalating findings — hyperthermia, lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis and multisystem organ failure — mark severe serotonin syndrome, while marked CK elevation with renal failure and labile autonomic signs marks severe NMS. No formal numeric grading scale is given in the source (Harrison 22e p.3715, p.3517).

Serotonin syndrome — serotonin toxicity, serotonergic syndrome, SSRI toxicity, serotonin toxidrome Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Anticholinergic toxidrome Sympathomimetic toxicity Malignant hyperthermia Meningitis or encephalitis Thyroid storm Sedative or alcohol withdrawal Careful medication and drug history to identify serotonergic agents and interactions Core temperature monitoring Creatine kinase for rhabdomyolysis Renal function, electrolytes and coagulation profile Arterial blood gas and lactate in severe cases Exclusion of infection (including lumbar puncture) where meningitis is possible A potentially life-threatening toxidrome caused by excess serotonergic activity, often from combining serotonergic drugs or from overdose The clinical triad is neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, rigidity), autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia, sweating, diarrhoea) and altered mental state (agitation, confusion) Inducible and spontaneous clonus, often more prominent in the lower limbs, is a particularly useful diagnostic sign Onset is typically rapid, within hours of a dose change or added serotonergic agent, distinguishing it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome Culprits include SSRIs, SNRIs, MAO inhibitors, tramadol, triptans, linezolid, certain opioids and recreational drugs; MAOI combinations are especially dangerous Neuromuscular findings help distinguish it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which causes lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia and a slower onset Management is withdrawal of serotonergic agents, aggressive cooling and supportive care, benzodiazepines for agitation, and cyproheptadine as a serotonin antagonist in significant cases Severe hyperthermia may require sedation, paralysis and intubation to control muscle activity Severe hyperthermia Marked rigidity limiting ventilation Rhabdomyolysis with renal impairment Seizures or rapidly declining consciousness Disseminated intravascular coagulation or cardiovascular instability Confusing it with neuroleptic malignant syndrome and missing the distinguishing clonus and hyperreflexia Overlooking non-psychiatric serotonergic drugs such as tramadol, linezolid or triptans Underestimating the danger of MAO inhibitor combinations Failing to control hyperthermia aggressively in severe cases Attributing agitation and fever to the underlying illness rather than drug toxicity Serotonin syndrome results from excessive stimulation of central and peripheral serotonin receptors, particularly the 5-HT2A subtype. Excess serotonergic activity can arise from increased synthesis or release, reduced reuptake, reduced metabolism (as with monoamine oxidase inhibitors), or direct receptor agonism, and is greatly amplified when drugs acting by different mechanisms are combined. The over-stimulation drives neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia, rigidity), autonomic dysregulation (hyperthermia, tachycardia, blood pressure lability, diaphoresis, gastrointestinal hurry) and altered mental status. Severe hyperthermia is generated largely by sustained muscular activity and can lead to rhabdomyolysis, metabolic acidosis, disseminated intravascular coagulation and multiorgan failure if untreated. Most cases resolve within a day or two of stopping the offending drugs and providing supportive care. Severe hyperthermic cases can be fatal or leave lasting organ injury, so early aggressive treatment is important.

cystadenomas arise from centroacinar or ductal epithelial cells and are lined by a single layer of glycogen-rich, cuboidal serous epithelium that secretes thin, watery fluid. neovascularisation Lesion activity threatening or approaching the fovea New subretinal fluid, haemorrhage or exudate suggesting choroidal neovascularisation Evidence of underlying tuberculosis requiring antimicrobial rather than purely immunosuppressive therapy Rapid centrifugal progression despite treatment Treating with immunosuppression without excluding tuberculosis-associated disease inflammatory disorder targeting the choriocapillaris and overlying retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptors. Recurrent bouts of inflammation cause ischaemia and destruction of the choriocapillaris, producing geographic areas of chorioretinal atrophy that spread centrifugally from the peripapillary region. Each recurrence extends from the edge of previously healed lesions, giving the characteristic serpentine advancing border. Serpiginous choroiditis is a chronic relapsing disease; vision is preserved when the fovea is spared, but foveal involvement or secondary choroidal neovascularisation can cause permanent central visual loss, and recurrences may continue over many years.

The Leydig component frequently secretes testosterone and other androgens, which suppress normal ovarian function and produce the clinical progression from defeminisation to virilisation. Histological differentiation ranges from well-formed tubules in well-differentiated tumours to poorly organised, mitotically active sheets in poorly differentiated lesions, and retiform or heterologous (for example mucinous or mesenchymal) elements may occur. Intermediate and poorly differentiated tumours carry a real risk of recurrence and malignant behaviour, so outlook depends heavily on grade and stage.

sertoli leydig cell tumour — arrhenoblastoma, androblastoma, Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour of ovary granulosa cell tumour steroid (lipid) cell tumour of the ovary adrenocortical tumour producing androgens polycystic ovary syndrome congenital adrenal hyperplasia (non-classic) ovarian stromal hyperthecosis gynandroblastoma serum total testosterone and free androgen index serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate to help localise the androgen source serum inhibin and anti-Mullerian hormone transvaginal pelvic ultrasound and MRI of the pelvis CT of abdomen and pelvis for staging in higher-grade disease DICER1 mutation testing on tumour and consideration of germline testing inhibin, calretinin and SF-1 immunohistochemistry A rare sex-cord stromal tumour of young women that classically produces androgens, causing progressive virilisation: oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, hirsutism, acne, clitoromegaly, deepening of the voice and loss of female body contour. Preceding defeminisation (breast atrophy, cessation of menses) often heralds the androgenic phase, and symptoms may regress after resection of a localised tumour. Tumours are graded as well, moderately or poorly differentiated, and a subset contains heterologous elements (most often mucinous epithelium or, less commonly, cartilage or skeletal muscle) or a retiform pattern. A significant proportion, especially those with a retiform pattern or heterologous elements in young patients, harbour DICER1 mutations, prompting consideration of the hereditary DICER1 syndrome and its associated tumours. Serum testosterone is characteristically raised while dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate is usually only mildly elevated or normal, helping to distinguish an ovarian source from an adrenal one. Immunohistochemistry typically shows positivity for inhibin, calretinin, SF-1 and often FOXL2, with Leydig cells sometimes highlighting crystalloids of Reinke. Most are unilateral and confined to the ovary at diagnosis, so fertility-sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is appropriate for well-differentiated, stage-confined disease in young women. Prognosis correlates strongly with differentiation and stage: well-differentiated tumours are effectively benign, whereas poorly differentiated or ruptured tumours carry a real risk of recurrence and metastasis. rapidly progressive virilisation suggesting an androgen-secreting neoplasm rather than functional hyperandrogenism markedly elevated serum testosterone with a palpable or imaged adnexal mass tumour rupture with haemoperitoneum or an acute abdomen poorly differentiated histology or extra-ovarian spread indicating aggressive potential personal or family history suggesting DICER1 syndrome, such as pleuropulmonary blastoma or thyroid nodular disease Attributing hirsutism and menstrual disturbance to polycystic ovary syndrome and missing a virilising tumour when testosterone is disproportionately high. Failing to consider and test for DICER1 syndrome in young patients or those with retiform or heterologous tumours. Assuming an adrenal source without checking that dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate is not markedly elevated. Underestimating a poorly differentiated tumour by sampling only well-differentiated areas. Rupturing the tumour intra-operatively, which upstages the disease and worsens prognosis. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumours are sex-cord stromal neoplasms composed of Sertoli cells, Leydig cells and, in less differentiated forms, primitive gonadal stroma recapitulating testicular development in the ovary. The Leydig cell component secretes androgens, chiefly testosterone, producing the virilising syndrome; some tumours instead secrete oestrogen or are hormonally silent. Many arise on a background of germline or somatic DICER1 mutation, which impairs microRNA processing and predisposes to this and other DICER1-associated tumours, particularly in the young and in tumours showing retiform or heterologous differentiation. Degree of differentiation reflects how closely the tubular Sertoli architecture is preserved; poorly differentiated tumours show sarcomatoid stroma, mitotic activity and loss of organised tubules, and correlate with a more aggressive, potentially metastatic course. Well-differentiated tumours are essentially benign and cured by conservative surgery, whereas moderately and poorly differentiated tumours, those with heterologous mesenchymal elements, and ruptured or advanced-stage tumours carry a substantial risk of recurrence and metastasis with correspondingly poorer survival.

Serum sickness — serum sickness reaction, type III hypersensitivity reaction, serum-sickness-like reaction Serum-sickness-like reaction to antibiotics (e.g. cefaclor) Acute viral infection (e.g. hepatitis B, parvovirus) with rash and arthralgia Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective-tissue disease Urticarial vasculitis and other small-vessel vasculitides Acute drug reaction such as DRESS or an urticarial drug eruption Reactive or infectious arthritis Serum C3 and C4, which fall during the active immune-complex phase Full blood count and inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) Urinalysis to detect renal involvement Assessment for circulating immune complexes or cryoglobulins where available Serologies to exclude viral and autoimmune mimics Skin biopsy in atypical cases to evaluate for vasculitis Serum sickness is the classic immune-complex (type III) hypersensitivity reaction, presenting with fever, rash, arthralgia or arthritis, and lymphadenopathy Symptoms characteristically begin about one to three weeks after first exposure to the offending agent, with a faster onset on re-exposure because the patient is already sensitised Historically it followed heterologous (animal) antiserum, and today it is most often triggered by antitoxins, antivenoms, therapeutic antibodies, and certain drugs The rash is often urticarial or a serpiginous purplish eruption at the border of the palms and soles, a helpful clinical clue During the active phase complement is consumed, so serum C3 and C4 fall and can be used to support the diagnosis and track resolution A serum-sickness-like reaction, most often attributed to antibiotics such as cefaclor, resembles serum sickness clinically but lacks the true immune-complex and hypocomplementaemic features and is generally benign The condition is usually self-limiting once the causative agent is withdrawn, with recovery over days to a couple of weeks Management principles are stopping and avoiding the trigger, symptomatic relief with antihistamines and anti-inflammatory agents, and corticosteroids for severe or systemic disease Significant renal involvement with proteinuria, haematuria, or rising creatinine Concurrent anaphylaxis or angioedema at the time of re-exposure to the antigen Neurologic involvement or severe systemic illness suggesting extensive immune-complex disease Features pointing to a severe drug reaction such as DRESS rather than simple serum sickness Failing to take a careful exposure history for antisera, antivenoms, or therapeutic antibodies given weeks earlier Confusing serum sickness with an acute IgE-mediated allergic reaction and mismanaging the tempo of illness Overlooking renal involvement by not checking urinalysis and renal function Re-administering the same heterologous protein or drug without recognising the sensitisation risk Serum sickness is mediated by circulating antigen-antibody (immune) complexes. After exposure to a foreign protein or drug-protein conjugate, the host mounts an antibody response; as antibody rises while antigen is still present, soluble immune complexes form in antigen-relative excess. These complexes deposit in small vessels of the skin, joints, kidneys, and elsewhere, where they activate complement and recruit neutrophils, producing local inflammation and tissue injury (a type III hypersensitivity reaction). Complement activation consumes C3 and C4, accounting for the transient hypocomplementaemia. Once the antigen is cleared and complexes are removed, the process resolves. Serum-sickness-like reactions produce a similar clinical picture through incompletely understood mechanisms without demonstrable immune-complex disease. Serum sickness is generally self-limiting and resolves without sequelae once the causative agent is removed, with symptoms settling over days to a couple of weeks. Recovery may be hastened by corticosteroids in severe cases; significant organ involvement is uncommon but warrants closer follow-up.

suggesting gout or infection Progressive pain with imaging changes suggesting osteonecrosis or established stress fracture Rest or night pain or a destructive lesion suggesting infection or tumour Mistaking a bipartite sesamoid for a fracture, or vice versa, on plain radiographs Attributing plantar first metatarsophalangeal pain to sesamoiditis while missing a stress fracture or osteonecrosis
