the cause of an acutely inflamed joint The hallucal sesamoids are two small bones enclosed within the tendons of flexor hallucis brevis on the plantar surface of the first metatarsal head, where they increase the mechanical advantage of the flexor, absorb load, and protect the flexor hallucis longus tendon. During push-off the great toe dorsiflexes and the sesamoids are drawn distally and loaded heavily, so repetitive high forces, as in running, dancing, and jumping, or sustained pressure from hard or high-heeled footwear, produce an overload inflammation of the sesamoid and its surrounding soft tissues. A cavus foot or a plantarflexed first ray increases the load borne by the sesamoids and predisposes to symptoms. Persistent overload may progress to a stress reaction or stress fracture, and impaired blood supply can lead to osteonecrosis, while a congenitally bipartite sesamoid can be a source of confusion on imaging and a site of symptomatic stress. Most cases of overload sesamoiditis settle with offloading, footwear modification, and activity reduction, though recovery can be slow because the sesamoids are heavily loaded with every step. Stress fractures and osteonecrosis take longer and occasionally fail to heal, and sesamoidectomy usually relieves pain but can alter first-ray mechanics and, if both sesamoids are removed, cause deformity, so it is reserved for resistant cases.

Sever disease — calcaneal apophysitis, Sever's disease, os calcis apophysitis, posterior heel apophysitis Achilles tendinopathy or insertional Achilles tendinitis Retrocalcaneal or superficial calcaneal bursitis Calcaneal stress fracture Plantar fasciitis Osteomyelitis or bone tumour of the calcaneus Tarsal coalition presenting with hindfoot pain Clinical squeeze (compression) test of the heel reproducing pain Assessment of gastrocnemius-soleus tightness and ankle dorsiflexion Plain radiographs primarily to exclude fracture, infection or tumour Magnetic resonance imaging reserved for atypical, persistent or unilateral cases Inflammatory markers if infection or inflammatory arthropathy is suspected Gait and footwear assessment in the active child A traction apophysitis of the calcaneal (heel) apophysis rather than a true osteonecrosis Affected site is the posterior calcaneal apophysis at the insertion of the Achilles tendon Typically affects active children roughly eight to fourteen years of age around a growth spurt, often bilaterally Presents with activity-related posterior heel pain relieved by rest, with tenderness on medial-lateral squeeze of the heel It is a clinical diagnosis; radiographs are usually obtained to exclude other causes rather than to confirm the condition Sclerosis and fragmentation of the calcaneal apophysis is a normal developmental appearance and does not by itself establish the diagnosis A positive squeeze test and tight gastrocnemius-soleus complex on examination support the diagnosis Management is conservative with activity modification, heel cups or orthoses, calf and hamstring stretching and physiotherapy as needed Rest pain, night pain or systemic features suggesting infection or malignancy A discrete focal bony lesion or fracture line on imaging Persistent unilateral pain not settling with conservative measures Swelling, warmth or erythema over the heel pointing to an alternative diagnosis Interpreting the normal fragmented, sclerotic apophysis on radiographs as diagnostic or as osteonecrosis Missing a calcaneal stress fracture, infection or tumour presenting as atypical heel pain Failing to address tight calf musculature that perpetuates apophyseal traction Complete immobilisation and deconditioning when relative activity modification would suffice Sever disease is a traction apophysitis of the posterior calcaneal apophysis, arising where the powerful Achilles tendon inserts onto the still-cartilaginous growth centre of the heel. During periods of rapid growth the bones lengthen faster than the surrounding muscle-tendon units, increasing tension across the apophysis, while repetitive impact from running and jumping adds cyclical traction and compression. This repetitive microtrauma at the vulnerable cartilaginous apophysis produces inflammation and pain. The radiographic sclerosis and fragmentation often seen at the apophysis represent normal variation in ossification rather than avascular necrosis, and the condition resolves once the apophysis fuses at skeletal maturity. The prognosis is excellent; symptoms are self-limiting and resolve with skeletal maturity as the apophysis fuses, with activity modification and stretching controlling pain in the interim and no long-term sequelae expected.

Severe acute malnutrition — SAM, severe malnutrition, marasmus, kwashiorkor, protein-energy malnutrition Oedema from nephrotic syndrome or cardiac/hepatic failure Chronic infection (including tuberculosis and HIV) Malabsorption syndromes (e.g. coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis) Chronic diarrhoeal disease Underlying malignancy or chronic illness causing wasting Weight, height/length, and mid-upper arm circumference with oedema assessment Blood glucose (to detect hypoglycaemia) Electrolytes including potassium, magnesium, and phosphate Haemoglobin and assessment for anaemia Screening for infection (including tuberculosis, HIV where relevant) and malaria in endemic areas Assessment of hydration status, which is difficult to judge clinically in SAM Defined in young children by severe wasting (weight-for-height well below the reference median, or a very low mid-upper arm circumference) and/or bilateral pitting oedema of nutritional origin. Marasmus is severe wasting from overall energy deficit; kwashiorkor is characterised by oedema, and mixed pictures occur. Kwashiorkor features include oedema, sparse depigmented hair, skin changes (flaky-paint dermatosis), an enlarged fatty liver, and apathy. Children with SAM are highly vulnerable to hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and overwhelming infection, which is often present without classic signs. Refeeding must be cautious and staged to avoid refeeding syndrome; overly rapid feeding and excess fluid or sodium can precipitate cardiac failure and death. Initial stabilisation prioritises treating and preventing hypoglycaemia and hypothermia, correcting dehydration carefully, and giving broad micronutrient support. Rehydration is preferably oral or nasogastric with a low-sodium, higher-potassium solution, because intravenous fluids readily cause fluid overload. Management follows a stabilisation phase with cautious feeding, followed by a rehabilitation phase with catch-up growth once appetite and stability return. Hypoglycaemia and hypothermia Signs of shock or severe dehydration (difficult to assess and easy to overtreat) Developing signs of heart failure during rehydration or refeeding (refeeding syndrome) Severe anaemia requiring careful transfusion Lethargy, hypothermia, or hypoglycaemia as subtle markers of serious infection Feeding too much too quickly and precipitating refeeding syndrome and heart failure Using standard intravenous rehydration and causing fluid overload Relying on usual signs of infection, which are often absent Missing hypoglycaemia and hypothermia because signs are subtle Treating oedema as fluid overload rather than recognising nutritional kwashiorkor Prolonged inadequate intake of energy, protein, and micronutrients forces the body into a state of reductive adaptation: metabolic rate falls, organ function is downregulated, and body composition shifts with loss of fat and muscle. Sodium-potassium pump activity is impaired, causing intracellular sodium retention and total-body potassium and magnesium depletion despite oedema. Hepatic and cardiac function, immune competence, and thermoregulation are all compromised. In kwashiorkor, hypoalbuminaemia and increased capillary permeability contribute to oedema. These adaptations make the child dangerously intolerant of the metabolic demands of aggressive feeding and fluid loads. With careful phased management and treatment of complications, most children recover, but case fatality is high when complications such as hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, sepsis, or refeeding syndrome are missed or when rehydration is too aggressive.

with severe thymic hypoplasia Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome Secondary immunodeficiency and severe malnutrition Newborn screening for low T-cell receptor excision circles where available Full blood count with lymphocyte subset quantification Immunoglobulin levels and functional lymphocyte proliferation studies Molecular genetic testing to define the specific subtype Adenosine deaminase enzyme assay and chest imaging for thymic assessment Group of inherited disorders defined by profound impairment of T-cell development, with variable B-cell and natural killer cell involvement, causing severe combined immune failure Affected infants typically present in the first months of life with recurrent, severe, or opportunistic infections, chronic diarrhoea, and failure to thrive Persistent or excision circles enables presymptomatic detection and early treatment Definitive treatment is immune reconstitution, principally haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, with gene therapy and enzyme replacement for specific subtypes Early diagnosis before infections develop markedly improves transplant outcomes This is a paediatric emergency: suspected SCID requires immediate specialist referral and protective isolation Live vaccines, including BCG and rotavirus, are contraindicated and can cause fatal disseminated infection Blood products must be irradiated, cytomegalovirus-safe, and leucodepleted to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease Any infection can rapidly become life-threatening and needs urgent aggressive management Administering live vaccines before immunodeficiency is excluded Transfusing non-irradiated blood products Delaying referral by attributing recurrent infections to ordinary childhood illness Overlooking lymphopenia on a routine full blood count Severe combined immunodeficiency comprises a genetically diverse group of disorders that share a failure of adaptive immunity due to absent or non-functional T lymphocytes, with associated defects in B-cell and sometimes natural killer cell function. Underlying defects disrupt lymphocyte development or function through varied mechanisms, such as impaired cytokine receptor signalling in common gamma-chain deficiency, toxic metabolite accumulation in adenosine deaminase deficiency, or failure of antigen-receptor gene rearrangement. Without functional T cells, the coordinated immune response to pathogens collapses, leaving infants unable to clear common and opportunistic organisms. Most forms are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, with the common gamma-chain form being X-linked. Without immune reconstitution the condition is usually fatal within the first year or two of life, but early haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, particularly before infections occur, offers a high chance of long-term survival and immune recovery.

omphalitis, skin abscesses, and pneumonia Autosomal dominant ELANE mutations are the commonest cause, whereas classic autosomal recessive Kostmann syndrome results from HAX1 mutations The marrow characteristically shows maturation arrest of the myeloid series at the promyelocyte or myelocyte stage Most patients respond to granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), which raises neutrophil counts and reduces infection There is a lifelong risk of clonal evolution to myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukaemia, often heralded by acquired CSF3R and RUNX1 mutations Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the definitive option for G-CSF-refractory disease or when leukaemic transformation supervenes Diagnosis combines persistent severe neutropenia, marrow maturation arrest, and targeted genetic testing while excluding autoimmune and secondary causes Recurrent life-threatening bacterial or fungal infection with an absolute neutrophil count persistently very low New cytogenetic abnormality, rising blasts, or acquired CSF3R/RUNX1 mutation signalling leukaemic transformation Escalating G-CSF requirement with declining response Sepsis or deep-seated infection in a febrile neutropenic infant requiring urgent broad-spectrum cover Mistaking severe congenital neutropenia for autoimmune neutropenia and delaying G-CSF Failing to perform serial marrow surveillance and missing early clonal evolution Attributing a poor G-CSF response solely to under-dosing rather than considering transformation Overlooking syndromic features that point to a specific genetic diagnosis Severe congenital neutropenia is a group of inherited disorders of granulopoiesis in which neutrophil precursors fail to mature. ELANE mutations produce a misfolded neutrophil elastase that triggers the unfolded protein response and endoplasmic reticulum stress, driving apoptosis of promyelocytes; HAX1 mutations remove a protein that maintains mitochondrial membrane potential, again promoting precursor apoptosis. Other genes converge on similar pathways of accelerated myeloid progenitor death or defective intracellular trafficking. The net effect is arrest of myeloid maturation with near-absent circulating neutrophils. Chronic G-CSF stimulation of a genetically unstable myeloid compartment, together with acquisition of CSF3R and other somatic mutations, underlies the elevated risk of transformation to myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukaemia. G-CSF has transformed survival by controlling infection, but patients carry a substantial lifelong risk of transformation to myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukaemia, so surveillance is essential and transplantation is curative for high-risk or refractory disease.

Sever's disease — calcaneal apophysitis Achilles tendinopathy or retrocalcaneal bursitis Calcaneal stress fracture Plantar fasciitis Bone cyst or tumour of the calcaneus Osteomyelitis (if systemic features) Clinical diagnosis from the age, activity and positive squeeze test Radiographs only to exclude other pathology if the picture is atypical Assessment of calf flexibility and footwear Review of training load Further imaging if there are red flags for another diagnosis A common cause of heel pain in physically active children and early adolescents, related to traction at the calcaneal growth plate Pain is felt at the back and sides of the heel, worse with running and jumping and eased by rest It typically occurs during the growth spurt and often around a period of increased sporting activity The squeeze test, compressing the sides of the calcaneus, reproduces the pain It is a self-limiting condition that resolves once the calcaneal apophysis fuses Management is with activity modification, calf stretching, heel cushioning and reassurance Night pain, rest pain or systemic features suggesting infection or tumour Focal bony swelling Failure to settle with appropriate measures Significant unilateral symptoms without a clear activity link Over-investigating a classic clinical presentation Missing a calcaneal stress fracture, infection or tumour when features are atypical Failing to address calf tightness and training load Advising complete rest rather than activity modification Sever's disease is a traction apophysitis of the calcaneus, in which repetitive tensile load from the Achilles tendon on the still-open calcaneal growth plate, combined with the impact of running and jumping, produces stress and inflammation at the apophysis. The vulnerability of the growth plate during the adolescent growth spurt, when bone growth may outpace muscle-tendon flexibility, increases traction across the apophysis. It is a benign, self-limiting overuse condition rather than a structural or destructive process. The condition is benign and resolves spontaneously with skeletal maturity, and symptoms are well controlled in the meantime with conservative measures.

Sertoli-Leydig tumours with DICER1 mutations) Management is primarily surgical, with fertility-sparing resection where feasible, and the histological subtype and stage guide the need for any further therapy A palpable or radiologically evident gonadal mass with signs of sex-steroid excess Rapidly progressive virilisation or feminisation suggesting an active tumour Features of a tumour-predisposition syndrome pointing to hereditary risk Abdominal pain, distension, or ascites suggesting a large or advanced tumour Recurrence of hormonal signs after resection, indicating residual or recurrent disease Attributing precocious puberty to central causes without recognising a hormone-secreting gonadal tumour Failing to perform a GnRH stimulation test to establish gonadotropin independence Overlooking an associated genetic syndrome and its implications for the patient and family Assuming all such tumours are benign and omitting appropriate staging and follow-up Missing a small contralateral or recurrent lesion after initial surgery Sex cord-stromal tumours develop from the steroidogenic and supporting cells of the gonad rather than from germ cells, and they often retain the capacity to synthesise sex steroids. Depending on the cell of origin, they may secrete oestrogens, causing feminising effects and isolated pseudopuberty, or androgens, causing virilisation; some are hormonally silent. Because the hormone production is autonomous and independent of pituitary drive, gonadotropins are suppressed and the changes represent precocious pseudopuberty rather than true, centrally driven puberty. The clinical picture therefore combines the local effects of a gonadal mass with the systemic consequences of the particular hormone being produced, and a subset arises in the context of tumour-predisposition syndromes. Many sex cord-stromal tumours in children are of low stage and behave in a benign or indolent fashion with an excellent outcome after complete resection, and hormone-driven signs typically regress once the tumour is removed; higher-stage or aggressive histological subtypes carry a less favourable outlook and require additional treatment and surveillance.

Female sexual dysfunction — FSD, female sexual dysfunction, hypoactive sexual desire disorder, female sexual arousal disorder, female orgasmic disorder Hypoactive sexual desire disorder Female sexual arousal disorder Female orgasmic disorder Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder (vaginismus, dyspareunia) Depression, anxiety, or relationship dysfunction Medication-induced or endocrine (menopausal) sexual dysfunction Comprehensive biopsychosocial and sexual history including relationship context Review of medications, particularly antidepressants, and chronic medical conditions Pelvic examination to identify atrophy, pain, or structural causes Targeted endocrine assessment where indicated, including menopausal status Screening for depression, anxiety, and history of sexual trauma Female sexual dysfunction spans disorders of desire, arousal, orgasm, and sexual pain, and is only a clinical diagnosis when the problem is persistent and causes personal distress The female sexual response is better understood as a circular, intimacy-driven model rather than a rigid linear sequence, so context and relationship factors are central Causes are typically multifactorial, combining biological, psychological, and interpersonal contributors that should all be explored Hormonal changes, especially the oestrogen decline of menopause, commonly reduce arousal and lubrication and contribute to genitourinary and pain symptoms Many common medications, particularly serotonergic antidepressants, and chronic illnesses such as diabetes, depression, and vascular disease impair sexual function A sensitive, open history that legitimises the concern is essential, as patients often will not raise the topic themselves Management addresses reversible contributors, optimises relationship and psychological factors, and considers psychosexual therapy alongside targeted treatments such as local oestrogen for genitourinary symptoms Persistent pain with intercourse points towards specific disorders such as vaginismus or dyspareunia that require directed assessment Sexual pain or bleeding suggesting an underlying gynaecological pathology History of sexual abuse or trauma requiring sensitive, specialised support Coexisting depression with suicidal ideation New sexual dysfunction accompanying signs of significant systemic or neurological disease Not asking about sexual health, so distressing problems go unrecognised Attributing dysfunction to a single cause when it is usually multifactorial Overlooking medication, especially antidepressants, as a reversible contributor Neglecting relationship and psychological dimensions in favour of a purely biomedical approach Female sexual function integrates neurological, vascular, hormonal, and psychological systems. Sexual arousal depends on genital vasocongestion and lubrication mediated by autonomic and nitric-oxide pathways, while desire and orgasm involve central dopaminergic, serotonergic, and hormonal modulation. Dysfunction arises when any of these are disrupted: oestrogen deficiency thins and dries the vaginal epithelium and reduces blood flow, vascular and neurological disease (as in diabetes) impairs the genital response, and medications such as SSRIs blunt desire and orgasm. Psychological factors including depression, anxiety, past trauma, body image, and relationship conflict powerfully influence desire and arousal, and pain disorders can create a self-reinforcing cycle of anticipatory anxiety and avoidance. The circular, context-dependent nature of female sexual response means these factors interact rather than act in isolation. Outcomes are generally good when contributing factors are identified and addressed; genitourinary symptoms of menopause respond well to local oestrogen, medication-related effects may improve with adjustment, and psychosexual and relationship interventions can substantially help desire and arousal disorders.

Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach — STI overview, STD overview, Sexually transmitted diseases, Venereal disease Acute epididymitis must be distinguished from testicular torsion (a surgical emergency with sudden pain, testicular elevation, and absent Doppler flow), testicular tumor, and trauma (Harrison 22e p.1101) Dysuric women: STI-associated urethral syndrome (sterile pyuria, <10^2 conventional uropathogens/mL) versus bacterial cystitis (single uropathogen >=10^2/mL) versus acute pyelonephritis (costovertebral tenderness/fever) (Harrison 22e p.1100-1101) Persistent genital ulcer not resolving with syndrome-based therapy: consider donovanosis, carcinoma, and other nonvenereal dermatoses on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.1108) Pelvic inflammatory disease that is not due to specific STIs (secondary to appendicitis, regional ileitis, diverticulitis, hematogenous tuberculosis or staphylococcal bacteremia, or tropical disease such as schistosomiasis) (Harrison 22e p.1104) Chronic granulomatous epididymal disease such as tuberculosis mimicking sexually acquired epididymitis when symptoms persist after therapy (Harrison 22e p.1101) Risk assessment using a structured sexual-history questionnaire (e.g., the eleven-question STD/HIV risk assessment) to guide screening and presumptive treatment decisions (Harrison 22e p.1098) Urethral Gram's stain to confirm urethritis and detect gram-negative diplococci, recognizing that up to ~30% of gonococcal urethral infections can yield a negative Gram's stain (Harrison 22e p.1099) Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, M. genitalium, and T. vaginalis on appropriate genital/urine specimens (Harrison 22e p.1099-1100) Genital ulcer workup: dark-field examination, direct fluorescent antibody, or PCR for T. pallidum; RPR/VDRL/EIA serology for syphilis; culture, FA, ELISA, or PCR for HSV; HSV-2 type-specific serology; PCR or culture for H. ducreyi in chancroid-endemic settings (Harrison 22e p.1108-1109) Biopsy of a genital ulcer persisting beyond the expected natural history (herpes 2-3 weeks; chancroid or syphilis up to 6 weeks) to exclude donovanosis and malignancy (Harrison 22e p.1108) Aspiration of fluctuant inguinal nodes for culture/PCR (H. ducreyi) plus Gram's stain to exclude other pyogenic bacteria (Harrison 22e p.1108) Cervical ectopy (columnar epithelium on the ectocervix), often mislabeled 'cervical erosion,' confused with infectious endocervicitis but showing clear/cloudy mucus and intact epithelium on colposcopy (Harrison 22e p.1104) Testicular tumor or trauma presenting as scrotal pain/swelling mimicking epididymitis (Harrison 22e p.1101) Genital carcinoma or nonvenereal dermatoses presenting as a persistent genital ulcer (Harrison 22e p.1108) STIs are syndrome-driven in practice: most patients are managed initially by presenting symptoms, signs, and risk factors rather than by a confirmed microbial diagnosis, with common syndromes including male urethritis, epididymitis, mucopurulent cervicitis, vulvovaginitis, genital/perianal ulcers, PID, and proctitis (Harrison 22e p.1100). More than 40 microorganisms are now recognized as predominantly sexually transmitted or frequently sexually transmissible, spanning bacteria, viruses, protozoa, fungi, and ectoparasites (Harrison 22e p.1096). The initial rate of spread of any STI in a population is the product of three factors: the rate of sexual exposure of susceptible to infectious persons, the per-exposure transmission efficiency, and the duration of infectivity (Harrison 22e p.1096). Genital HPV is described as the most common sexually transmitted pathogen in the United States, and HPV and hepatitis B virus remain major causes of cervical and hepatocellular carcinoma respectively in the developing world (Harrison 22e p.1096-1097). Reported syphilis in the United States in 2022 (207,255 cases, all stages and congenital) was the highest since 1950, with congenital syphilis rate of 102.5 per 100,000 live births and 282 congenital syphilis-related stillbirths/infant deaths (Harrison 22e p.1097). All four major curable STIs (gonorrhea, chlamydial infection, syphilis, trichomoniasis) plus bacterial vaginosis have been associated with increased risk of HIV transmission or acquisition (Harrison 22e p.1097). Acute epididymitis in sexually active men under 35 is most often due to C. trachomatis (less often N. gonorrhoeae) and usually accompanies overt or subclinical urethritis, whereas in older men or after urinary instrumentation it is usually caused by urinary pathogens (Harrison 22e p.1101). Unsolicited reporting of abnormal vaginal discharge (increased amount or abnormal odor) most often denotes bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis, not cervical gonorrhea or chlamydia, which usually do not increase discharge volume or odor (Harrison 22e p.1101). Sexually transmitted HSV causes most genital ulcer disease worldwide; HSV-2 produces more frequent genital recurrences and is more infectious to partners than HSV-1, so typing has prognostic value (Harrison 22e p.1097, 1108). STI control combines reducing exposure (education, behavior change, post-exposure prophylaxis), shortening infectivity (early diagnosis and curative or suppressive treatment), and reducing per-exposure transmission (condoms, vaccines, male medical circumcision) (Harrison 22e p.1096). Despite the strong epidemiologic HSV-HIV link, randomized trials of antiviral HSV suppression showed no protective effect against HIV acquisition or transmission (Harrison 22e p.1097). Sudden severe testicular pain with testicular elevation and absent Doppler flow indicating testicular torsion, a surgical emergency (Harrison 22e p.1101) Costovertebral angle pain/tenderness or fever in a dysuric woman suggesting acute pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.1100) Genital ulcer in a patient with HIV risk (e.g., MSM, known HIV infection): treat presumptively for syphilis rather than awaiting seroconversion given high syphilis rates (Harrison 22e p.1108) Suspected PID with peritoneal extension (pelvic or generalized peritonitis, perihepatitis, perisplenitis, or pelvic abscess) (Harrison 22e p.1104) Congenital syphilis exposure in pregnancy, given the sharp recent rise including syphilis-related stillbirths and infant deaths (Harrison 22e p.1097) Treating genital symptoms without performing the microbiologic tests needed to establish a cause; self-diagnosis of vulvovaginal candidiasis is often incorrect (Harrison 22e p.1101) Relying on urethral Gram's stain alone to exclude gonorrhea, since up to ~30% of gonococcal urethral infections are smear-negative (Harrison 22e p.1099) Misreading cervical ectopy as infectious endocervicitis and unnecessarily cauterizing it (Harrison 22e p.1104) Assuming a positive HSV-2 serology proves current lesions are herpetic, when nearly one-fifth of the U.S. population becomes HSV-2 seropositive in early adulthood and type-specific assays are not 100% specific (Harrison 22e p.1108) Failing to evaluate and treat sexual partners with contact in the relevant window (e.g., within the prior 60 days for urethritis), allowing reinfection (Harrison 22e p.1099) Withholding presumptive syphilis treatment in a high-risk patient with a genital ulcer while awaiting seroconversion (Harrison 22e p.1108) Attributing male urethritis recurrence to treatment failure without considering reexposure to an untreated partner or M. genitalium (often resistant to doxycycline and azithromycin) (Harrison 22e p.1100, 1099) STIs are acquired through sexual exposure to a susceptible person from an infectious one, with spread amplified within highly interconnected sexual networks marked by high partner-change rates or concurrent partners (e.g., transactional sex, some MSM, drug-using populations), while infections such as chlamydia, genital HPV, and genital herpes propagate efficiently even in relatively low-risk populations. Many of these organisms colonize or invade genital, anal, oral, or systemic epithelium; ascending spread from cervix or vagina to endometrium and fallopian tubes underlies PID, with potential extension to pelvic peritonitis, perihepatitis, perisplenitis, or abscess. Immunopathology contributes to tissue damage in chlamydial salpingitis, where repeated exposure produces the greatest inflammation. Hormonal and anatomic factors modulate susceptibility (e.g., cervical ectopy may increase susceptibility to gonococcus, chlamydia, and HIV; oral contraceptives favor ectopy persistence; menstruation appears to facilitate ascending gonococcal/chlamydial infection). Many STIs are curable when diagnosed and treated early, and prompt treatment shortens infectivity and reduces onward transmission. Outcomes worsen with delayed care: untreated chlamydial and gonococcal infection can ascend to cause PID with risk of tubal damage and infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain, and immunopathology contributes to chlamydial tubal injury. HPV and HBV carry long-term oncogenic risk (cervical and other anogenital cancers; hepatocellular carcinoma). HSV-2 causes lifelong recurrent infection with asymptomatic shedding and ongoing transmission risk. In men, urethritis with neither chlamydiae nor gonococci detected carries a higher risk of recurrent nongonococcal urethritis, and most persistent urethritis is attributable to M. genitalium. Congenital syphilis can result in stillbirth or infant death. No single staging system applies to STIs as a group; severity is assessed by syndrome and complications. Localized lower-tract syndromes (uncomplicated urethritis, cervicitis, vulvovaginitis, genital ulcer) are distinguished from complicated or upper-tract/disseminated disease (PID with peritonitis, perihepatitis, perisplenitis, or pelvic abscess; disseminated gonococcal infection; epididymo-orchitis), and from long-term oncologic or reproductive sequelae (cervical/anogenital neoplasia, infertility). Genital ulcer evaluation also uses lesion natural-history timelines (herpes 2-3 weeks; chancroid and syphilis up to ~6 weeks) to flag atypical persistence (Harrison 22e p.1104, 1108).

replacement and precipitating adrenal crisis Failing to consider the diagnosis years after the causative delivery Overlooking hyponatraemia as a manifestation of cortisol or thyroid deficiency Assuming posterior pituitary involvement and over-investigating for diabetes insipidus Sheehan syndrome arises when major obstetric haemorrhage and circulatory collapse cause ischaemic infarction of the anterior pituitary. During pregnancy the gland hypertrophies, largely due to lactotroph expansion, increasing its metabolic demand while its low-pressure portal blood supply leaves it prone to infarction if perfusion falls. The resulting loss of anterior pituitary tissue produces variable, often panhypopituitary, hormone deficiencies affecting prolactin, gonadotrophins, growth hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone and corticotrophin. The posterior lobe is usually preserved, so diabetes insipidus is comparatively rare, and the infarcted gland gradually atrophies, sometimes leaving an empty sella. With appropriate and lifelong hormone replacement, patients generally do well, but unrecognised disease carries a real risk of life-threatening adrenal crisis; deficits are permanent because infarcted pituitary tissue does not recover.

Shigellosis — bacillary dysentery Salmonella infection Campylobacter jejuni infection Clostridium difficile colitis Yersinia enterocolitica infection Entamoeba histolytica (amebic dysentery) Inflammatory bowel disease (first flare of Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis), particularly in industrialized countries Enteroinvasive E. coli (can cause a shigellosis-like dysentery) Salmonellosis Campylobacter jejuni enteritis Clostridium difficile colitis Yersinia enterocolitica enterocolitis Amebic dysentery (Entamoeba histolytica) Enteroinvasive E. coli dysentery Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) infection (predominant cause of HUS in industrialized countries) Stool culture is the gold standard; sample the bloody/mucopurulent portion directly, or use rectal swabs (highest yield in the acute phase). Because Shigella is fragile and dies during transport, use a holding medium (buffered glycerol saline or Cary-Blair) with prompt inoculation onto isolation media. Use multiple media to raise yield: nonselective (bromocresol-purple lactose), low-selectivity (MacConkey, eosin-methylene blue), and high-selectivity (Hektoen, Salmonella-Shigella, or xylose-lysine-deoxycholate agar). Microscopy of stool smears: bacterial enteroinvasive infection (including shigellosis) shows high PMN counts per field, whereas E. histolytica shows erythrophagocytic trophozoites with very few PMNs. Identify shigellae as non-lactose-fermenting colonies that are glucose-positive (usually no gas), lactose-negative, H2S-negative, and nonmotile; confirm serogroup by slide agglutination. Blood cultures are positive in fewer than 5% of cases but should be obtained when there is a clinical picture of severe sepsis. Abdominal x-ray when toxic megacolon is suspected (transverse colon dilation, thumbprinting, loss of haustra, pseudopolyps; pneumoperitoneum if perforated). In HUS: full blood count and smear (schizocytes), platelets, LDH, free hemoglobin, reticulocytes, creatinine; Coombs test (HUS is Coombs-negative). PCR for Shigella virulence genes or mass spectrometry are available but not yet standardized for global use. Inflammatory bowel disease - Crohn's disease Inflammatory bowel disease - ulcerative colitis Classic dysentery is a syndrome of fever, intestinal cramps, and frequent passage of small, bloody, mucopurulent stools; tenesmus is characteristic (p.1322). Shigella has a very low infectious dose; experimental infection of volunteers occurs with as few as ~100 CFU, accounting for high attack rates in day-care centers (33-73%) and high secondary attack rates among family members (26-33%) (p.1322). Spread is primarily fecal-oral via hand carriage; the organism survives gastric passage owing to acid resistance, and can also be transmitted sexually (p.1322-1323). Shigellosis typically evolves through four phases: incubation (usually 1-4 days, up to 8), watery diarrhea, dysentery, and a postinfectious phase (p.1323). Dysentery reflects invasion of the colonic mucosa, producing acute colitis mainly involving the distal colon and rectum, with uninterrupted small-volume bloody mucopurulent stools, tenesmus, and cramps (p.1323). Of the four species, S. flexneri predominates in least-developed areas while S. sonnei is more common in industrialized/emerging economies; S. dysenteriae type 1 (Shiga-toxin producer) drives the most severe epidemic disease (p.1322). With effective antibiotics, clinical improvement occurs within ~48 h, with fewer complications, shorter symptoms, and clearance of Shigella from stool; in the US every culture-confirmed case is recommended for treatment because of transmissibility (p.1324). Reactive arthritis (arthritis, ocular inflammation, urethritis) can develop weeks to months after infection, almost exclusively after S. flexneri and in HLA-B27-positive patients (about 3% of S. flexneri infections) (p.1323-1324). Nonbloody diarrhea, moderate-to-severe dehydration, bacteremia, absence of fever, abdominal tenderness, and rectal prolapse are risk factors for death in clinically severe cases. Altered consciousness (seizures, delirium, coma), especially in children under 5, carries a poor prognosis. Abdominal distention and tenderness suggesting toxic megacolon, with or without peritonitis. Pallor, asthenia, irritability, oliguria, increasing edema, or mucosal bleeding heralding hemolytic-uremic syndrome (most often after several days of diarrhea). Fever persisting beyond 48-72 h in toxic megacolon raises the possibility of local perforation or abscess. Severe, unusual manifestations such as meningitis in the absence of serious malnutrition may indicate an inborn innate-immune defect (e.g., IRAK-4 deficiency) and warrant genetic investigation. Avoid antimotility agents in bloody diarrhea: they have been implicated in prolonged fever in shigellosis, are suspected of increasing the risk of toxic megacolon, and were implicated in HUS in children with EHEC infection. Because shigellosis often manifests only as watery diarrhea, systematic attempts to isolate Shigella are necessary - a watery presentation does not exclude the diagnosis. Shigella is fragile and commonly disappears during transport with changes in temperature and pH; failure to use a holding medium and prompt inoculation leads to false-negative cultures. Negative initial blood cultures do not exclude shigellosis (positive in fewer than 5% of cases). Predisposing factors for toxic megacolon - hypokalemia and use of opioids, anticholinergics, loperamide, psyllium seeds, and antidepressants - should be sought and addressed. In HUS, oral rehydration solutions and potassium-rich nutrition must be discontinued (water restriction is required), in contrast to routine rehydration management. Bacteriologic proof in mild adult cases often arrives only after symptoms have resolved, so empiric decisions cannot await culture in fragile patients. Pathogenicity is governed by a ~214-kb virulence plasmid encoding a type III secretion system that injects effectors into host cells. After acid-resistant passage through the stomach, bacteria invade colonic epithelium either directly at crypt openings or after crossing M cells over mucosal lymphoid follicles; they induce apoptosis of resident macrophages, drive cytoskeletal uptake, lyse the containing vacuole to reach the cytosol, then spread cell-to-cell using actin-based motility. A massive cytokine-driven influx of polymorphonuclear leukocytes destabilizes the epithelial barrier and produces the acute colitis of shigellosis. Early watery diarrhea is attributed to combined enterotoxin (ShET-1) action and mucosal inflammation. In S. dysenteriae type 1, Shiga toxin (an A1-B5 toxin binding globotriaosylceramide and inhibiting protein synthesis via 28S rRNA N-glycosidase activity) is translocated into the circulation and, by acting on renal target cells, can cause hemolytic-uremic syndrome (p.1322-1323). Most episodes are self-limited and resolve without treatment within about 1 week; with appropriate therapy recovery occurs within a few days to a week, usually without sequelae. Acute life-threatening complications occur most often in children under 5 (especially the malnourished) and the elderly. In HUS, acute renal failure occurs in 55-70% of cases but renal function recovers in most (up to ~70%). S. dysenteriae type 1 epidemics historically caused high mortality. Shigellosis is a major contributor to stunted growth among children in endemic regions because of the exudative enteropathy and anorexia it causes. Harrison does not provide a formal grading scale. Severity is described as depending on infecting serotype and, more importantly, on host age, immunologic and nutritional status. The clinical course is staged in four phases (incubation, watery diarrhea, dysentery, postinfectious). Severe/complicated disease is recognized by markers of poor outcome (nonbloody diarrhea, moderate-to-severe dehydration, bacteremia, absence of fever, abdominal tenderness, rectal prolapse, altered consciousness) and by major complications: intestinal (toxic megacolon, perforation, rectal prolapse), metabolic (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, dehydration), and HUS (in S. dysenteriae type 1).

parachute mitral valve, subaortic stenosis and coarctation of the aorta Incomplete forms with two or three components are common, and lesions may be at valvar, subvalvar or supravalvar level coarctation component Severe pulmonary venous hypertension or pulmonary oedema Rising left atrial pressure with a restrictive mitral apparatus Progressive left ventricular dysfunction from combined obstructions Relieving one obvious obstruction while overlooking additional serial lesions that limit benefit Underestimating the mitral component, which frequently dictates long-term outcome Assuming an isolated coarctation and missing the wider complex Failing to reassess for progression of previously mild lesions after intervention Shone complex is a spectrum of developmental left-heart obstructions occurring in series, so that blood entering and leaving the left ventricle meets resistance at multiple levels. A supravalvar mitral ring and a parachute mitral valve (chordae inserting into a single papillary muscle) impede left atrial emptying and mimic mitral stenosis, raising pulmonary venous pressure. Subaortic and aortic obstruction, together with coarctation, impede left ventricular ejection and impose pressure loading. Because the obstructions are additive, even individually mild lesions can combine to produce significant pulmonary venous hypertension, left atrial and pulmonary vascular changes, and impaired systemic output. The neonatal coarctation component may render the systemic circulation duct-dependent. Outcome depends on the number and severity of lesions and especially on the mitral valve, which is difficult to repair and prone to residual stenosis; multilevel and mitral-dominant disease carries a guarded prognosis and often needs repeated intervention.

dependent on parenteral support Severe dehydration with acute kidney injury or dangerous electrolyte disturbances Catheter-related bloodstream infection or sepsis in patients on parenteral nutrition Progressive intestinal-failure-associated liver disease or cholestasis Central venous thrombosis threatening long-term access for parenteral nutrition Underestimating fluid and electrolyte losses, particularly magnesium, in high-output patients Withholding enteral nutrition entirely and thereby delaying adaptation Overlooking vitamin B12 and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency after ileal resection Missing small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth or catheter sepsis as causes of deterioration Short bowel syndrome arises when the absorptive surface of the small intestine is reduced below the level needed to maintain nutrition and hydration, most often after massive resection. The functional consequences depend on which segment is lost: jejunal loss reduces overall absorptive surface, while ileal loss additionally impairs vitamin B12 and bile-salt reabsorption, disrupting the enterohepatic circulation and causing bile-salt diarrhoea and fat malabsorption. Loss of the ileocaecal valve accelerates transit and predisposes to small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth. Rapid transit and reduced surface lead to fluid, electrolyte, and nutrient losses. Over time the remnant intestine adapts through mucosal hyperplasia and slowed transit, partially restoring absorptive capacity. Outlook depends on residual bowel length and anatomy and on adaptation. Many patients eventually achieve enteral autonomy, while those with very short remnants or absent colon may need lifelong parenteral nutrition, whose complications (liver disease, line sepsis, thrombosis) drive much of the long-term morbidity and mortality.

Short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase (ECHS1) deficiency — ECHS1 deficiency, SCEH deficiency, crotonase deficiency, mitochondrial short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase 1 deficiency Leigh syndrome from mitochondrial DNA or nuclear respiratory chain defects Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency Biotinidase and biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease Other organic acidaemias causing basal ganglia injury 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA hydrolase (HIBCH) deficiency in the same valine pathway Acquired or hypoxic-ischaemic basal ganglia injury Brain MRI to identify symmetrical basal ganglia and brainstem lesions Blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate measurement Urine organic acids for valine-pathway metabolites (e.g. 2-methyl-2,3-dihydroxybutyrate) Plasma acylcarnitine and amino acid profiles ECHS1 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Enzyme activity or functional studies in fibroblasts where genetics are inconclusive Autosomal recessive deficiency of mitochondrial short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase (ECHS1 gene), an enzyme acting in valine catabolism and fatty-acid oxidation Characteristically causes a Leigh or Leigh-like syndrome with developmental regression, dystonia, and symmetrical basal ganglia lesions on MRI Presentation is often in infancy or early childhood, frequently with regression triggered or worsened by intercurrent illness The mechanism is thought to involve accumulation of toxic valine-pathway intermediates rather than simple energy failure, which has prompted interest in valine (protein) restriction Biochemical markers can be subtle, but urine organic acids may show metabolites such as 2-methyl-2,3-dihydroxybutyrate and S-(2-carboxypropyl)cysteine derivatives; lactate may be raised ECHS1 deficiency is an important, potentially treatable cause of Leigh-like disease that can be missed if only the respiratory chain is investigated Management is largely supportive, with dietary valine/protein restriction and avoidance of catabolic stress explored as disease-modifying approaches Developmental regression with new dystonia or movement disorder Acute neurological deterioration during intercurrent illness Progressive Leigh-like lesions on serial imaging Feeding difficulties, respiratory compromise or brainstem dysfunction Attributing Leigh-like disease solely to a respiratory chain defect and not testing ECHS1 Being reassured by subtle or near-normal routine metabolic screening Overlooking the related valine-pathway disorder HIBCH with a similar presentation Failing to consider dietary valine restriction as a potentially modifying intervention Short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase (ECHS1, crotonase) catalyses hydration of short-chain enoyl-CoA esters and participates in the catabolism of the branched-chain amino acid valine as well as in fatty-acid beta-oxidation. Deficiency is believed to cause disease predominantly through accumulation of reactive valine-pathway intermediates (such as methacrylyl-CoA and acryloyl-CoA derivatives) that damage mitochondrial proteins, producing a Leigh-like encephalopathy with characteristic basal ganglia injury. Secondary impairment of energy metabolism, with lactate elevation, may accompany this. Because the toxic intermediates arise chiefly from valine, restricting valine intake is a rational, if still investigational, strategy. The disorder is frequently severe and progressive, with a Leigh-like course and significant neurological disability or early death in classic cases; milder phenotypes exist, and valine/protein restriction is being studied as a potential disease-modifying measure.

Short QT syndrome — SQTS, short QT interval syndrome, KCNH2-related short QT, familial short QT Normal QT variant or measurement error Hypercalcaemia causing QT shortening Hyperkalaemia with peaked T waves Effects of digoxin on the ST segment and QT Early repolarisation syndrome Brugada syndrome (with overlapping calcium channel variants) 12-lead ECG with careful measurement of the corrected QT interval and T-wave morphology Serial or repeat ECGs to confirm a persistently short QT Ambulatory monitoring for atrial and ventricular arrhythmia Correction and reassessment after excluding electrolyte and drug causes of QT shortening Echocardiography to confirm a structurally normal heart Genetic testing for potassium and calcium channel variants with family cascade screening A rare inherited channelopathy defined by an abnormally short QT interval and a high risk of atrial and ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death May present with palpitations, syncope, atrial fibrillation at a young age, or aborted cardiac arrest, sometimes as the first event The ECG shows a persistently short QT interval with tall, peaked, symmetrical T waves and often a short or absent ST segment Most identified variants are gain-of-function changes in potassium channel genes (such as KCNH2, KCNQ1 and KCNJ2) that shorten repolarisation; some loss-of-function calcium channel variants overlap with a Brugada phenotype Diagnosis rests on the corrected QT interval together with symptoms, family history and genetic findings, as the QT alone can overlap with normal variants An implantable cardioverter defibrillator is the mainstay for those who survive cardiac arrest or are at high risk Quinidine can prolong the QT interval and is used to reduce arrhythmic events, particularly when a defibrillator is unsuitable Family screening is important because the first manifestation may be sudden death Aborted cardiac arrest or documented ventricular fibrillation Unexplained syncope in a young person with a short QT Atrial fibrillation presenting at an unusually young age Family history of sudden cardiac death Overlooking a short QT interval because attention focuses on QT prolongation Attributing a short QT to hypercalcaemia or digoxin without reassessing after correction Relying on the QT value alone without integrating symptoms, family history and genetics Failing to screen relatives given that sudden death can be the first event Assuming a structurally normal heart excludes life-threatening arrhythmia Short QT syndrome is caused by ion channel dysfunction that accelerates cardiac repolarisation. Gain-of-function variants in potassium channel genes increase outward repolarising currents, shortening the action potential duration and thereby the QT interval; loss-of-function variants in calcium channel subunits can produce a similar phenotype. The abbreviated and heterogeneous repolarisation shortens refractory periods across the atria and ventricles, creating a substrate for re-entry that predisposes to atrial fibrillation and to polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation, and hence sudden death, in a structurally normal heart. The natural history is dominated by the risk of sudden arrhythmic death, which can occur across all ages including infancy; appropriate defibrillator therapy and, where used, QT-prolonging drug therapy substantially improve outcome for high-risk individuals.

may later develop progressive renal and hepatic disease requiring surveillance Severe thoracic insufficiency and respiratory failure in the newborn Recurrent respiratory infection with failure to thrive Progressive renal impairment Hepatic fibrosis with portal hypertension Excluding the diagnosis simply because polydactyly is absent Underestimating the risk of progressive renal or hepatic disease in survivors Failing to anticipate and plan for a difficult respiratory course Assuming a uniformly lethal outcome across the whole spectrum The short-rib thoracic dysplasias result from biallelic variants in genes encoding components of the intraflagellar transport system and the cytoplasmic dynein-2 retrograde motor, most often DYNC2H1. These proteins are essential for building and maintaining the primary cilium, through which hedgehog and other signals that pattern the developing skeleton are transduced. Disrupted ciliary signalling in growth-plate chondrocytes impairs endochondral ossification, producing the characteristically short ribs, narrow thorax and shortened limbs, while abnormal hedgehog signalling in the limb bud underlies the polydactyly seen in some subtypes. Because the same cilia are required in kidney, liver, retina and pancreas, affected individuals may also develop cystic kidney disease, hepatic fibrosis, retinal degeneration and other visceral abnormalities. Outcome is highly variable across the spectrum: the lethal short-rib polydactyly forms are fatal in the perinatal period, whereas Jeune syndrome has a variable respiratory course, and survivors of the early years remain at risk of progressive renal and hepatic disease.

Short Stature — growth failure, poor linear growth, faltering height, paediatric short stature Familial (genetic) short stature Constitutional delay of growth and puberty Growth hormone deficiency Hypothyroidism Chronic systemic disease (e.g. coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, renal or cardiac disease) Turner syndrome and other genetic/syndromic causes Skeletal dysplasia Undernutrition or psychosocial deprivation Accurate serial height and weight with growth velocity calculation Bone age radiograph Screening bloods (full blood count, renal and liver function, inflammatory markers, coeliac serology) Thyroid function and, where indicated, IGF-1 and growth hormone provocation testing Karyotype or genetic testing in girls (to exclude Turner syndrome) and where a syndrome is suspected Skeletal survey if disproportion suggests a dysplasia Short stature is generally defined as height more than about 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and sex, but the growth velocity and trajectory matter more than a single measurement. The two most common causes are normal variants: familial (genetic) short stature and constitutional delay of growth and puberty. Serial, accurately measured heights plotted on a growth chart are the single most valuable assessment, since a falling growth velocity is a key warning sign. Bone age radiography helps distinguish constitutional delay (delayed bone age, preserved height potential) from familial short stature (bone age near chronological age). A low or crossing-down growth velocity with poor weight gain suggests systemic disease or malnutrition, whereas short but proportionate growth with normal velocity favours a normal variant. Endocrine causes such as growth hormone deficiency and hypothyroidism typically produce a child who is relatively overweight for height, in contrast to malnutrition or chronic illness. Disproportionate short stature points towards a skeletal dysplasia and warrants assessment of body segment ratios. Estimating mid-parental target height helps interpret whether a child's growth is appropriate for their genetic background. A crossing-down growth velocity or fall across major height centiles Short stature with neurological signs, headaches, or visual disturbance suggesting an intracranial lesion Disproportionate short stature suggesting a skeletal dysplasia Poor growth with weight loss or gastrointestinal symptoms suggesting chronic disease Dysmorphic features or other findings suggesting a genetic syndrome Relying on a single height measurement rather than growth velocity over time Labelling a child as a normal variant without excluding treatable disease when velocity is poor Missing an intracranial cause of growth hormone deficiency Failing to consider Turner syndrome in a short girl Linear growth depends on an intact growth plate responding to growth hormone, insulin-like growth factor 1, thyroid hormone, and sex steroids, supported by adequate nutrition and freedom from chronic illness. Short stature arises when any of these are disturbed: genetic determination of a lower height potential, temporary delay in the tempo of maturation, endocrine deficiency, chronic systemic disease, undernutrition, or intrinsic bone/cartilage disorders. The pattern of growth velocity, body proportions, and bone age reflects which mechanism predominates. Normal variants such as familial short stature and constitutional delay have an excellent prognosis with normal health, and constitutional delay usually reaches a normal adult height; outcomes for pathological causes depend on early identification and treatment of the underlying condition.

abdomen (e.g. large abdominal mass, hydrops) Locked twins Uterine or contraction abnormality causing prolonged second stage Cephalopelvic disproportion with obstructed labour Immediate clinical recognition rather than investigation is the priority in the acute event Neonatal assessment of the arms, clavicles, and neurology for brachial plexus injury or fracture after delivery Cord blood gas analysis to document the degree of any acidosis Maternal assessment for postpartum haemorrhage and perineal or anal sphincter trauma Antenatal estimation of fetal weight and screening for diabetes in at-risk pregnancies Shoulder dystocia is failure of the shoulders to deliver after the head, caused by impaction of the anterior shoulder behind the maternal pubic symphysis, and is a time-critical obstetric emergency The warning sign is the turtle sign, where the delivered head retracts tightly against the perineum, and failure of restitution and of routine gentle traction to deliver the body Risk factors include fetal macrosomia, maternal diabetes, previous shoulder dystocia, obesity, prolonged labour, and instrumental delivery, but many cases occur without identifiable risk factors so all birth attendants must be prepared Management follows a structured sequence: call for help, avoid the harmful HELPER pitfalls, and apply the McRoberts manoeuvre with suprapubic pressure as first-line steps If initial measures fail, internal rotational manoeuvres (such as delivery of the posterior arm or rotational techniques) are used, and the mother should not be pushed while shoulders are impacted Fundal pressure must be avoided because it worsens impaction and increases the risk of uterine rupture Excessive or downward traction on the fetal head is the main modifiable cause of brachial plexus injury and should be avoided Complications include brachial plexus palsy (Erb palsy), clavicular or humeral fracture, hypoxic injury from delay, and maternal postpartum haemorrhage and perineal trauma Accurate contemporaneous documentation of the sequence, manoeuvres, timings, and personnel is essential given the medicolegal significance OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY: head delivered with turtle sign and shoulders not delivering despite routine traction, requiring immediate structured manoeuvres Prolonged head-to-body delivery interval with rising risk of hypoxic-ischaemic injury Signs of neonatal brachial plexus injury or limb fracture after delivery Maternal postpartum haemorrhage or severe perineal and anal sphincter trauma Use of fundal pressure or excessive head traction indicating unsafe technique Applying fundal pressure, which worsens impaction and can cause uterine rupture Using excessive downward traction on the head, the leading cause of brachial plexus injury Encouraging maternal pushing while the shoulder remains impacted Failing to summon senior and neonatal help early Poor documentation of manoeuvres and timings in a medicolegally significant event After the fetal head delivers, the shoulders normally rotate into the wider oblique diameter of the pelvis. In shoulder dystocia the anterior shoulder fails to rotate and becomes wedged above the pubic symphysis (or, less commonly, the posterior shoulder impacts on the sacral promontory). Because the fetus can no longer descend, the umbilical cord is compressed within the pelvis and placental gas exchange is impaired, so fetal hypoxia and acidosis progress with time. Rotational manoeuvres and delivery of the posterior arm work by reducing the shoulder-to-shoulder (bisacromial) diameter or moving it into a larger pelvic diameter, freeing the impaction. Most shoulder dystocias are relieved with recognised manoeuvres and the majority of infants have no lasting harm. Brachial plexus injuries are the commonest fetal complication and most resolve within the first year, though a minority are permanent. Prolonged impaction risks hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy or death. Women who have had shoulder dystocia have an increased recurrence risk in subsequent pregnancies.

from craniosynostosis Severe scoliosis compromising respiratory function Airway or feeding difficulties from craniofacial anomalies Labelling the patient as having Marfan syndrome and missing the craniosynostosis and intellectual disability Assuming aortic involvement is absent and omitting cardiovascular surveillance Overlooking raised intracranial pressure from suture fusion Attributing developmental delay to an unrelated cause Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome is a heritable connective-tissue disorder caused by pathogenic variants in SKI, which encodes a repressor of transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) signalling. Loss of normal SKI-mediated repression is thought to enhance TGF-beta signalling, a mechanism shared with Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes, disturbing the development and integrity of connective tissue, bone and the cardiovascular system. This produces the marfanoid skeletal habitus, the craniofacial features including premature fusion of cranial sutures (craniosynostosis), and connective-tissue laxity, alongside the neurodevelopmental impairment that distinguishes the condition. Aortic root involvement reflects the same connective-tissue vulnerability but tends to be less severe than in related aortopathies. Prognosis depends on the severity of skeletal, neurological and cardiovascular involvement; intellectual disability is common, and although aortic disease is usually milder than in Marfan syndrome, cardiovascular surveillance remains important.

Shuddering attacks of infancy — shuddering spells, shivering attacks Epileptic seizures (especially myoclonic or spasms) Benign myoclonus of early infancy Tics Chills from fever or infection Gratification behaviour or other benign paroxysmal events Clinical diagnosis from the characteristic brief shivering with preserved awareness Home video of episodes to support the diagnosis Electroencephalogram only if seizures cannot be excluded clinically Developmental and neurological assessment confirming normal findings Family history of tremor Brief episodes of rapid shivering or shuddering of the head, shoulders and trunk, as if experiencing a cold chill Consciousness is fully preserved and there is no postictal drowsiness, distinguishing episodes from seizures Attacks are very short, may occur many times a day and often happen during excitement, feeding or frustration Onset is usually in infancy or early childhood and the episodes are benign and self-limiting The electroencephalogram is normal, both during and between episodes A possible association with later essential tremor has been suggested, and a family history of tremor may be present Loss of awareness or postictal features suggesting seizures Developmental delay or regression Abnormal neurological examination Change in the pattern or emergence of new event types Misdiagnosing shuddering as epileptic seizures and starting unnecessary treatment Ordering extensive investigation for a clearly benign event Overlooking a family history of tremor Failing to reassess if awareness is lost or the pattern changes Shuddering attacks are a benign non-epileptic paroxysmal event of early childhood, characterised by brief tremulous shivering movements with retained awareness. The mechanism is not fully understood but the movements resemble an exaggerated shiver, and the reported association with a family history of essential tremor has led to the hypothesis that they may be an early manifestation of a tremor tendency. There is no underlying structural or epileptic disorder. The attacks are entirely benign and typically resolve during early childhood without treatment; development and later neurological health are normal.

Genomic instability of the marrow underlies the predisposition to clonal evolution and leukaemic transformation. With enzyme replacement and infection management many patients do well in childhood, but the lifelong risk of marrow failure, myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukaemia dominates long-term prognosis and mandates surveillance; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is used for marrow failure or malignant transformation.

infection Ultrasound of the gland to assess for stones, abscess or a mass Culture of pus expressed from the duct or obtained at drainage Plain radiography or CT to detect calculi Sialography or MR sialography for ductal anatomy in recurrent disease Blood tests including inflammatory markers and, where relevant, mumps serology and autoimmune screening Fine needle aspiration or biopsy if a neoplasm is suspected Sialadenitis is inflammation of a salivary gland, most commonly affecting the parotid or submandibular gland Acute bacterial infection typically develops in dehydrated, debilitated or postoperative patients with reduced salivary flow, classically ascending parotitis It presents with a painful, tender, swollen gland, and gentle massage may express pus from the duct opening in the mouth Staphylococcus aureus is the usual organism in acute suppurative parotitis, whereas viral parotitis (mumps) is a key non-bacterial cause Submandibular sialadenitis is often related to a stone (sialolith) obstructing the duct, causing pain and swelling that worsen at mealtimes General measures such as good hydration, oral hygiene, warm compresses, gland massage and sialogogues promote salivary flow and recovery, alongside appropriate antibiotics for bacterial disease An enlarging, fluctuant, non-resolving gland may indicate abscess formation needing drainage Recurrent or chronic sialadenitis warrants imaging to look for stones, strictures or an underlying mass or systemic disease Rapidly spreading swelling, systemic sepsis or airway compromise from a deep neck or floor of mouth extension (an emergency) A persistent hard gland mass, facial nerve weakness or skin fixation suggesting malignancy Fluctuant swelling indicating an abscess requiring drainage Failure to resolve with appropriate treatment, prompting imaging and reassessment Bilateral gland involvement with systemic features suggesting a systemic or autoimmune cause Overlooking dehydration and reduced salivary flow as the precipitant, especially postoperatively Missing an obstructing calculus in recurrent mealtime swelling Assuming all salivary swellings are infective and overlooking a tumour Delaying drainage of an established abscess Neglecting facial nerve assessment when a hard parotid mass is present Salivary glands are normally protected from ascending infection by continuous salivary flow, which flushes the ducts, and by antibacterial constituents of saliva. When flow is reduced, by dehydration, poor oral intake, debility, medications that dry the mouth, or mechanical obstruction from a duct stone or stricture, oral bacteria ascend the duct and infect the gland, producing acute suppurative sialadenitis with parenchymal inflammation and pus. Stasis of saliva also predisposes to stone formation, and calculi in turn obstruct outflow, causing painful mealtime swelling and recurrent infection. Repeated episodes lead to chronic inflammation, ductal changes and glandular fibrosis. Viral sialadenitis such as mumps causes a non-suppurative inflammatory swelling. Acute bacterial sialadenitis usually resolves with rehydration, salivary stimulation and antibiotics, and outcomes are good when the cause is treated; recurrent obstruction from stones or strictures and chronic sialadenitis may require repeated treatment or gland surgery.

autoimmune disease Mistaking diffuse bilateral swelling for recurrent sialadenitis and giving repeated antibiotics Overlooking an underlying eating disorder in a patient with painless parotid enlargement Failing to exclude Sjogren syndrome, lymphoma, or a neoplasm Attributing gland enlargement solely to the salivary glands without seeking a systemic cause Proceeding to unnecessary surgery for a benign, systemically driven condition Sialadenosis is a non-inflammatory, non-neoplastic enlargement of the salivary glands caused by an underlying metabolic or systemic disturbance. It is thought to reflect a peripheral autonomic (sympathetic) neuropathy affecting the secretory acinar cells, leading to dysregulated protein synthesis and secretion. The acinar cells become hypertrophied and engorged with secretory granules, producing diffuse, symmetrical gland enlargement without inflammation or duct obstruction. Recognised associations include diabetes and other endocrine disorders, chronic alcoholism with liver disease, malnutrition, and the repeated vomiting of bulimia nervosa. Sialadenosis itself is benign; the swelling often persists but may regress if the underlying metabolic or systemic condition is treated. The prognosis is largely determined by the associated disorder, and recognising the swelling can prompt diagnosis of a hidden condition such as an eating disorder.

care is supportive with developmental, neurological and, where relevant, renal support Non-immune hydrops fetalis or severe multisystem disease in the neonate Nephrotic-range proteinuria with renal involvement Progressive neurological regression with spasticity Feeding difficulty and respiratory compromise in the infantile form Not measuring urinary free sialic acid in unexplained hypotonia with hypomyelination Confusing free sialic acid storage disease with sialidosis, where bound sialic acid metabolism differs Overlooking renal involvement in the infantile form Attributing a milder phenotype to cerebral palsy without metabolic evaluation Sialin is a proton-driven transporter in the lysosomal membrane that carries free sialic acid (N-acetylneuraminic acid) generated by glycoconjugate degradation out of the lysosome into the cytoplasm. When sialin is defective, free sialic acid accumulates within lysosomes across many tissues, which are consequently distended by storage. The nervous system is particularly affected, with disturbed myelination underlying the hypotonia, developmental impairment and progressive motor signs, while severe transporter loss produces the multisystem infantile phenotype with visceromegaly, bone changes and, in the most severe cases, hydrops. Infantile free sialic acid storage disease is severe and usually fatal in early childhood, whereas Salla disease follows a slower course with prolonged survival and predominantly neurological disability; prognosis depends on residual sialin function.

gene testing Progressive myoclonus and seizures unresponsive to standard therapy Rapid visual deterioration Hydrops fetalis or severe neonatal presentation in the congenital form Cardiorespiratory decline in type 2 disease Attributing progressive myoclonic epilepsy to an idiopathic cause and missing the cherry-red spot Failing to distinguish sialidosis from galactosialidosis by not assaying beta-galactosidase Screening only for glycosaminoglycans and missing the sialylated oligosaccharide pattern Overlooking sialidosis in the differential of non-immune hydrops fetalis Sialidosis is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in NEU1, encoding lysosomal alpha-N-acetylneuraminidase (sialidase). This enzyme removes terminal sialic acid residues from sialylated glycoconjugates during their lysosomal degradation. Its deficiency causes accumulation of sialyloligosaccharides and sialylated glycopeptides within lysosomes and their excretion in the urine. The severity spectrum reflects residual enzyme activity: type 1 causes a progressive myoclonic epilepsy with visual decline and preserved somatic appearance, while type 2 causes earlier, more generalised storage disease with dysmorphism, skeletal changes, and visceromegaly, including a congenital hydropic form. Neuraminidase normally functions in a complex with beta-galactosidase and the protective protein cathepsin A, and defects in that protective protein instead cause galactosialidosis. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Type 1 follows a slowly progressive course with disabling myoclonus and visual loss but relatively preserved somatic health, whereas type 2, especially the congenital form, is severe with high early mortality. No disease-modifying therapy is established, so care is supportive.

Sialoblastoma — Congenital basal cell adenoma, Embryoma of salivary gland Congenital haemangioma Teratoma Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma Basal cell adenoma or adenocarcinoma Adenoid cystic carcinoma Neuroblastoma or other small round blue cell tumour MRI of the head and neck to define extent and relation to the facial nerve Ultrasound of the mass Biopsy with histology and immunohistochemistry for ductal and myoepithelial markers Serum alpha-fetoprotein interpreted in the neonatal context, and to help exclude teratoma Staging imaging where malignant behaviour is suspected Screening for associated hepatoblastoma A rare congenital or perinatal salivary neoplasm, arising most often in the parotid and less commonly the submandibular gland. It presents at birth or in the neonatal period as a firm mass, and may be detected on antenatal imaging. Histology recapitulates primitive salivary anlage, with basaloid epithelial cells in organoid nests showing peripheral palisading and both ductal and myoepithelial differentiation. Behaviour is variable and best regarded as of low to intermediate malignant potential, with a real risk of local recurrence and occasional metastasis. Recognised associations include hepatoblastoma, nevus sebaceus and other congenital anomalies, and molecular studies have identified HRAS, PIK3CA and beta-catenin alterations. Complete surgical excision with facial nerve preservation where feasible is the mainstay of management. Chemotherapy has a role for unresectable, incompletely excised or aggressive tumours. It must be distinguished from other congenital head and neck masses such as teratoma, haemangioma and embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma. Rapid growth of the mass Facial nerve weakness Skin ulceration or fixation Infiltrative margins or incomplete excision Evidence of regional or distant metastasis Mistaking it for a benign basal cell adenoma and undertreating Underestimating the risk of local recurrence after excision Achieving incomplete excision, particularly around the facial nerve in a neonate Overlooking an associated hepatoblastoma Sialoblastoma is thought to arise from retained primitive (blastematous) salivary gland epithelium that fails to complete normal differentiation, producing a tumour that mirrors the embryonic developing gland. Neoplastic basaloid cells are organised into solid and organoid nests with peripheral palisading and focal ductal lumina, reflecting arrested dual epithelial and myoepithelial differentiation. Molecular studies have implicated activation of growth-signalling pathways, with reported HRAS and PIK3CA mutations and beta-catenin (WNT pathway) alterations driving proliferation of the primitive epithelium. The recognised association with hepatoblastoma and certain cutaneous and congenital anomalies suggests that, in some cases, sialoblastoma forms part of a broader developmental or embryonal tumour predisposition. Prognosis is variable; complete excision offers a good outcome, but local recurrence is not uncommon and close surveillance is required. Metastasis is infrequent but reported, and outcome is worse with incompletely excised or aggressive tumours.
