sepsis or spreading floor-of-mouth infection A firm, fixed or rapidly enlarging gland mass suggesting neoplasm rather than a stone Facial nerve weakness, which is not expected with benign stone disease and suggests malignancy Airway compromise from significant floor-of-mouth swelling or abscess Assuming all obstructive gland swelling is due to a stone and missing an underlying tumour Overlooking secondary infection that requires antimicrobial treatment and drainage Proceeding to gland excision before trying gland-preserving techniques Failing to recognise multiple or proximal stones that alter the treatment approach Sialolithiasis develops when calcium phosphate and other salts deposit around an organic nidus within a salivary duct or gland, gradually forming a calculus. Stasis of saliva, changes in its composition, ductal inflammation and dehydration favour stone formation. The submandibular gland is most often affected because its saliva is more viscous and alkaline and its duct runs upward against gravity with a relatively narrow orifice. An obstructing stone impedes salivary outflow, producing the characteristic painful mealtime swelling, and the resulting stasis predisposes to ascending bacterial infection and, over time, chronic gland damage and fibrosis. Most cases resolve with conservative measures or minimally invasive gland-preserving stone removal, and outcomes are generally good. Recurrent obstruction and chronic infection can cause irreversible gland damage, occasionally requiring gland excision.

Sialuria — French type sialuria, sialuria, infantile type (historical distinction), free sialic acid overproduction, GNE Sialic acid storage disorders (Salla disease, infantile free sialic acid storage disease) Other lysosomal storage disorders with coarse facies and hepatomegaly Mucopolysaccharidoses Congenital disorders of glycosylation GNE myopathy (allelic but distinct phenotype) Other causes of hepatomegaly with developmental delay Quantitative urinary free sialic acid (markedly elevated) Measurement of bound versus free sialic acid to distinguish storage disorders GNE molecular genetic testing Liver function tests and abdominal imaging for hepatomegaly Developmental assessment Metabolic screening to exclude alternative storage disorders A dominantly inherited disorder of sialic acid overproduction caused by activating (dominant-negative) variants in the allosteric site of GNE Characterised by massive urinary excretion of free (unconjugated) N-acetylneuraminic acid, the sialic acid intermediate It differs fundamentally from the sialic acid storage disorders, where the problem is lysosomal accumulation rather than cytoplasmic overproduction Clinical features are variable and often relatively mild: coarse facies, hepatomegaly, recurrent infections, and variable developmental delay Diagnosis rests on demonstrating grossly elevated free sialic acid in urine, distinguishing it from bound sialic acid disorders The same GNE gene, when affected by different loss-of-function variants, causes GNE myopathy, illustrating gene-specific allelic diversity There is no specific therapy; management is supportive with monitoring of growth and development Prognosis is generally more favourable than for the severe sialic acid storage diseases Significant developmental regression prompting reassessment for an alternative diagnosis Recurrent serious infections Progressive hepatomegaly with functional impairment Failure to thrive Confusing sialuria (overproduction, free sialic acid excreted) with sialic acid storage disease (lysosomal accumulation) Failing to distinguish free from bound sialic acid on testing Assuming a severe storage-disease prognosis and counselling incorrectly Overlooking the shared GNE gene basis with the distinct GNE myopathy Sialuria is caused by variants that disrupt the allosteric feedback site of GNE, the bifunctional enzyme UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 2-epimerase/N-acetylmannosamine kinase that catalyses the rate-limiting steps of sialic acid biosynthesis. Normally the end-product, CMP-sialic acid, feeds back to inhibit this enzyme. When the regulatory site is disrupted, feedback inhibition is lost and the cytoplasm overproduces free N-acetylneuraminic acid, which is then excreted in large amounts in the urine and accumulates in tissues. This is distinct from the sialic acid storage disorders, in which a lysosomal transporter defect traps sialic acid within lysosomes. The overproduction phenotype tends to be milder, with variable somatic and developmental features. Generally more benign than the sialic acid storage disorders, with variable outcome; many affected individuals have relatively mild disease, though developmental delay may occur.

sinoatrial node or failure of conduction from the node to the surrounding atrium. The most common cause is idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the node and perinodal tissue with ageing. Ischaemia, infiltrative and inflammatory diseases, prior cardiac surgery, and autonomic influences also contribute, and many drugs suppress node function. In the tachy-brady syndrome, atrial remodelling supports tachyarrhythmias, while the diseased node produces prolonged pauses when the tachyarrhythmia stops because of overdrive suppression of an already impaired pacemaker. Sick sinus syndrome is rarely immediately life-threatening but causes considerable morbidity from recurrent symptoms; pacing effectively relieves bradycardic symptoms, and overall outcome is largely determined by associated atrial fibrillation and thromboembolic risk and by underlying cardiac disease.

narrow mesenteric pedicle, producing a closed-loop large bowel obstruction. Chronic constipation and a lengthy, mobile sigmoid on a narrow mesenteric base predispose to torsion. The twist obstructs the lumen at both ends, and progressive distension raises intraluminal and intramural pressure. If the mesenteric vessels are compromised by the torsion, the loop becomes ischaemic, progressing to gangrene and perforation with faeculent peritonitis and sepsis. Massive gaseous distension of the closed loop is characteristic. Uncomplicated cases usually respond to endoscopic decompression but recur frequently unless definitive surgery is performed. Emergency surgery for gangrenous or perforated bowel in typically frail, elderly patients carries substantial morbidity and mortality.

Pathogenic variants disturb this signalling, altering the transcriptional response to neuronal activity and impairing normal circuit maturation. The resulting dysfunction produces both the severe early epilepsy and the profound developmental impairment, with the mechanism residing in disrupted intracellular signalling rather than direct membrane excitability changes. Most affected children have severe developmental impairment with drug-resistant epilepsy, although seizure frequency and the electroencephalographic picture may evolve over time.

atelectasis, begins with obstruction of the maxillary sinus outflow at the osteomeatal complex. Trapped secretions are gradually resorbed and, with ventilation cut off, a persistent negative pressure develops within the sealed sinus. Over time this sub-atmospheric pressure draws the thin sinus walls inwards, so the antrum contracts and the orbital floor bows downward. Because the orbital floor descends and the maxillary volume falls, the orbital contents sink, producing the painless enophthalmos and hypoglobus that dominate the clinical picture, all typically without the pain or discharge of overt sinusitis. Silent thyroiditis — painless thyroiditis, subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis Graves disease Subacute (de Quervain) granulomatous thyroiditis Postpartum thyroiditis Amiodarone-induced thyroiditis Factitious thyrotoxicosis Thyroid function tests through the phases Thyroid radioactive iodine uptake (low in the thyrotoxic phase) Thyroid autoantibodies Inflammatory markers (usually normal, unlike subacute thyroiditis) Follow-up thyroid function to detect permanent hypothyroidism A painless autoimmune destructive thyroiditis causing transient thyrotoxicosis followed by hypothyroidism and usually recovery Unlike subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis it is painless, and unlike Graves disease there is no ophthalmopathy Radioactive iodine uptake is low during the thyrotoxic phase, distinguishing it from Graves disease It is considered part of the autoimmune thyroid disease spectrum and is related to postpartum thyroiditis The thyrotoxic phase is managed symptomatically with beta-blockade rather than antithyroid drugs A minority develop permanent hypothyroidism, so follow-up thyroid function testing is needed Features suggesting Graves disease (ophthalmopathy) needing different management Severe thyrotoxic symptoms Persistent hypothyroidism Diagnostic uncertainty with amiodarone exposure Treating the thyrotoxic phase with antithyroid drugs, which do not work in destructive thyroiditis Misdiagnosing it as Graves disease and giving radioactive iodine Failing to monitor for permanent hypothyroidism Overlooking the link with the postpartum period Silent thyroiditis is an autoimmune lymphocytic inflammation of the thyroid that transiently destroys follicular cells, releasing preformed thyroid hormone and causing a self-limited thyrotoxic phase. As stored hormone is depleted and the gland recovers, a hypothyroid phase often follows before euthyroidism is usually restored. Because the process is destructive rather than hyperfunctioning, radioactive iodine uptake is low, and antithyroid drugs are ineffective. It shares its autoimmune basis and biphasic course with postpartum thyroiditis. Most patients recover normal thyroid function within months, though some develop permanent hypothyroidism and recurrence can occur.

Silicosis — silicosis, silica pneumoconiosis, quartz dust lung disease Other pneumoconioses such as coal workers' pneumoconiosis Pulmonary tuberculosis (which may coexist) Sarcoidosis Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and other interstitial lung diseases Metastatic or miliary nodular lung disease Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Chest radiography with attention to upper-zone nodularity and eggshell nodal calcification High-resolution CT to characterise nodules and detect progressive massive fibrosis Pulmonary function testing to quantify restrictive, obstructive, or mixed impairment Screening for tuberculosis given the heightened risk Detailed occupational exposure history including engineered-stone and sandblasting work Silicosis is a fibrotic lung disease caused by inhaling crystalline silica dust, seen in mining, quarrying, sandblasting, stone-cutting, and engineered-stone work Chronic silicosis develops after prolonged exposure and may be asymptomatic initially, later causing exertional dyspnoea and cough Accelerated and acute (silicoproteinosis) forms follow intense exposure and progress far more rapidly Chest imaging classically shows small upper-zone nodular opacities, sometimes with eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes Simple nodular disease can coalesce into progressive massive fibrosis, producing large conglomerate masses and significant impairment Silica exposure substantially increases susceptibility to tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis), which should be actively sought and treated There is no treatment that reverses fibrosis; management focuses on stopping exposure, supportive care, and screening for and treating complications Silica is also associated with increased risks of lung cancer, chronic airflow obstruction, and certain autoimmune diseases New constitutional symptoms, haemoptysis, or cavitation suggesting tuberculosis or malignancy Rapidly progressive breathlessness indicating accelerated or acute silicosis Enlarging conglomerate masses consistent with progressive massive fibrosis Development of respiratory failure or cor pulmonale Failing to elicit an occupational silica exposure history, especially newer engineered-stone work Overlooking coexisting tuberculosis in a patient with silicosis Attributing all nodular change to silicosis without considering malignancy Not removing the worker from ongoing dust exposure Inhaled crystalline silica particles reaching the alveoli are taken up by macrophages. The reactive silica surface is toxic to these macrophages, triggering activation of inflammasome pathways, cell death, and release of inflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species. This provokes recruitment of further inflammatory cells and stimulation of fibroblasts, which lay down collagen to form the characteristic silicotic nodules. Continued or intense exposure sustains the cycle, with nodules enlarging and coalescing into progressive massive fibrosis, while impaired macrophage function increases vulnerability to mycobacterial infection. Chronic simple silicosis may remain stable with limited impairment, but progressive massive fibrosis, accelerated, and acute forms carry a poor prognosis with progressive respiratory failure; the lifelong increased risk of tuberculosis and lung cancer means continued surveillance is important, and outcomes improve when exposure ceases early.

Silver-Russell syndrome is an imprinting disorder most often caused by hypomethylation of the paternally derived IC1 domain at chromosome 11p15, which reduces expression of the growth-promoting gene IGF2, or by maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7. Reduced IGF2-driven growth signalling produces profound intrauterine and postnatal growth restriction with relative sparing of head growth. Because the affected loci are imprinted, the parental origin of the epigenetic or chromosomal change determines the phenotype, and body asymmetry reflects mosaic distribution of the molecular defect. With early nutritional optimisation, hypoglycaemia prevention, and endocrine management, growth and general health improve, though final stature is often below average. Cognition is usually normal or near normal, and adult outcomes are generally favourable with appropriate support.

Early detection of embryonal tumours through structured screening improves outcomes.

Repetitive, forceful contraction of the quadriceps during jumping and running transmits tension through the patellar tendon to this immature bone-tendon junction. The prognosis is favourable; symptoms are self-limiting and typically resolve as the patella matures and traction loads decrease, with activity modification and rehabilitation controlling pain and no significant long-term sequelae.

Single-organ vasculitis — Single-organ vasculitis, Isolated vasculitis, Localised vasculitis Systemic vasculitis with early or limited organ involvement ANCA-associated vasculitis Vasculitis secondary to connective tissue disease Infection-related vasculitis Malignancy-associated or paraneoplastic vasculitis Drug-induced vasculitis Non-inflammatory vasculopathy mimicking vasculitis Tissue biopsy of the affected organ to characterise vessel size and inflammation ANCA, ANA and complement to screen for systemic and autoimmune disease Inflammatory markers and full systemic review of symptoms Cross-sectional or vascular imaging appropriate to the organ involved Screening for infective triggers including relevant serology Age-appropriate malignancy screening where clinically indicated Longitudinal follow-up to detect later systemic conversion Single-organ vasculitis denotes vasculitis confined to one organ or organ system without features of a systemic vasculitis, a category formalised in the current consensus nomenclature. Recognised examples include isolated cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis, isolated aortitis, single-organ vasculitis of the gastrointestinal tract, testis, breast or urinary bladder, and isolated peripheral nerve vasculitis. It is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring a thorough search for systemic disease before the 'single-organ' label is applied. The distribution may be unifocal or multifocal within the affected organ, but by definition does not cross into other systems. A subset of apparently localised disease later declares itself as systemic vasculitis, so ongoing surveillance is essential. Histology (leukocytoclastic, granulomatous or necrotising) reflects the vessel size involved and helps frame differentials. Management is often more conservative than systemic vasculitis; some cutaneous forms are self-limiting, while an isolated organ lesion such as focal aortitis may be treated surgically. Isolated aortitis is frequently discovered incidentally in surgical aortic specimens and warrants assessment for large-vessel disease. Emergence of constitutional symptoms or new organ involvement suggesting systemic conversion Progressive organ dysfunction despite treatment Aortic dilatation or dissection in isolated aortitis Rapidly evolving mononeuropathy in isolated nerve vasculitis Positive ANCA or other systemic serology on follow-up Prematurely labelling disease as single-organ without excluding systemic vasculitis. Failing to arrange follow-up, so later systemic conversion is missed. Over-treating benign self-limiting cutaneous vasculitis with aggressive immunosuppression. Overlooking incidental aortitis in surgical specimens and its implications for large-vessel disease. Assuming a single negative serology permanently excludes systemic disease. Single-organ vasculitis is inflammation of blood vessel walls restricted to a single organ or anatomical region, without the systemic distribution or serological markers of a defined systemic vasculitis. The vessel calibre involved varies by site and determines the histological pattern, ranging from leukocytoclastic small-vessel injury in isolated cutaneous disease to granulomatous or necrotising inflammation in isolated aortitis or nerve vasculitis. The initiating stimulus is usually unknown and may be immune-complex-mediated, cell-mediated or triggered by local factors. Because the same histology can be the first manifestation of a systemic process, single-organ vasculitis is defined partly by the absence of evidence for wider involvement over time. Many single-organ forms have a favourable outlook, particularly self-limiting cutaneous disease, but prognosis depends on the organ affected and on whether the process later becomes systemic. Isolated aortitis and isolated nerve vasculitis carry organ-specific risks that require targeted follow-up.

viral nucleic acids. The mutant sensors are inappropriately activated, driving constitutive production of type I interferons even without genuine infection. Chronic interferon signalling promotes ectopic calcification of the aorta and cardiac structures, disturbs tooth and bone development, and causes systemic inflammatory features. The interferon-dominant mechanism links the dental, cardiovascular, and skeletal manifestations and provides the rationale for JAK inhibition to reduce interferon signalling. The prognosis is largely determined by cardiovascular calcification, which can cause serious morbidity; interferon-directed therapy may modify disease, but established calcification and dental loss are difficult to reverse.

The hallmark is proliferation of the epithelium in an endophytic pattern, inverting into the stroma while maintaining an intact basement membrane. Although benign, it erodes and remodels adjacent bone and can extend widely through the sinuses, and it has a well-recognised association with squamous cell carcinoma arising synchronously or over time. With complete excision including the site of attachment, most benign inverted papillomas are controlled, though recurrence is not uncommon and mandates long-term surveillance. When associated squamous cell carcinoma is present, prognosis depends on the stage and grade of that malignancy.

sinonasal undifferentiated carcinoma — SNUC, sinonasal anaplastic carcinoma High-grade esthesioneuroblastoma (olfactory neuroblastoma) Sinonasal neuroendocrine or small cell carcinoma NUT carcinoma SMARCB1 (INI-1)-deficient sinonasal carcinoma Poorly differentiated or non-keratinising squamous cell carcinoma Sinonasal lymphoma (extranodal NK/T-cell type) Mucosal melanoma or rhabdomyosarcoma Endoscopic biopsy with a broad immunohistochemistry panel (pancytokeratin, p40/p63, synaptophysin, chromogranin, NUT, INI-1/SMARCB1, S100, CD45, HMB-45) Contrast-enhanced MRI of the sinuses and brain to map dural, orbital and intracranial extension CT of the sinuses to define bony destruction and skull-base involvement Whole-body PET-CT for distant staging Molecular testing (IDH2 mutation, NUT rearrangement) to subtype the tumour Ophthalmology and neurosurgical assessment where orbital or intracranial invasion is present Serum LDH and lymphoma work-up when lymphoma remains in the differential Highly aggressive, poorly differentiated epithelial malignancy of the sinonasal tract that is distinct from squamous cell and neuroendocrine carcinomas. Typically presents with a short history and rapidly progressive nasal obstruction, epistaxis, facial pain, proptosis, diplopia and cranial neuropathies. Usually bulky at diagnosis with extensive invasion of the orbit, skull base and anterior cranial fossa. It is largely a diagnosis of exclusion requiring immunohistochemistry to rule out NUT carcinoma, SMARCB1-deficient carcinoma, neuroendocrine carcinoma, lymphoma, melanoma and olfactory neuroblastoma. Tumour cells are pancytokeratin positive, typically negative or only focally positive for neuroendocrine markers, and show no squamous or glandular differentiation. Retained INI-1 (SMARCB1) helps separate it from SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, and NUT immunostaining excludes NUT carcinoma; an IDH2-mutant subset is increasingly recognised. Management is multimodal, often induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiotherapy or surgery guided by treatment response and resectability. Local recurrence and distant metastasis are common, so response-adapted therapy and close surveillance are central to care. Rapid tumour growth over weeks with new cranial nerve palsies Orbital apex or cavernous sinus involvement with visual loss Intracranial extension with headache and altered mental state Midface or cheek numbness indicating perineural or skull-base spread Sudden severe epistaxis from a friable bulky mass Labelling a tumour as SNUC without first excluding NUT carcinoma and SMARCB1-deficient carcinoma, which carry different management and prognosis Under-staging the true intracranial and orbital extent of disease Managing the tumour as ordinary squamous cell carcinoma Attributing early nonspecific symptoms to chronic sinusitis and delaying biopsy Omitting distant staging before committing to an aggressive local treatment plan Sinonasal undifferentiated carcinoma is a carcinoma of uncertain histogenesis thought to arise from the Schneiderian mucosa or olfactory epithelium of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses. It is composed of sheets, nests and trabeculae of medium-to-large cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, prominent nucleoli, brisk mitotic activity, frequent tumour necrosis and lymphovascular invasion, and by definition lacks squamous or glandular differentiation. The entity is molecularly heterogeneous, and recognition of related but distinct tumours such as IDH2-mutant carcinoma, NUT carcinoma and SMARCB1-deficient carcinoma has refined its definition as a diagnosis of exclusion. Prognosis is generally poor, with a strong tendency to local recurrence and distant metastasis. Multimodality treatment and a good response to induction chemotherapy are associated with better outcomes, but overall long-term survival remains low.

Sinus barotrauma — barosinusitis, aerosinusitis, sinus squeeze Ear barotrauma Acute or chronic sinusitis Dental barotrauma (barodontalgia) Migraine or tension headache Trigeminal neuralgia Facial pain from temporomandibular joint dysfunction Clinical assessment correlating facial pain and epistaxis with the dive or flight profile Anterior rhinoscopy or nasendoscopy to identify ostial obstruction, polyps, or inflammation Otoscopy to assess for coexisting ear barotrauma Sinus imaging (CT) in recurrent, severe, or diagnostically unclear cases Assessment for underlying rhinitis or structural nasal abnormality Occurs when a paranasal sinus cannot equalise pressure with the environment because its ostium is obstructed, classically during descent The frontal and maxillary sinuses are most often affected, producing pain over the forehead, cheek, or around the eye On descent the trapped sinus air is compressed relative to the surroundings, creating a squeeze that causes mucosal swelling, infection, allergic rhinitis, nasal polyps, and other causes of ostial obstruction Management is decongestion, avoiding diving or flying until the sinuses can equalise, and treating any underlying nasal pathology Prevention centres on not diving or flying with nasal or sinus congestion and controlling rhinitis Severe or persistent headache with neurological or visual symptoms Features suggesting orbital or intracranial extension of infection Recurrent barotrauma indicating significant untreated nasal or sinus disease Signs of secondary bacterial sinusitis Continuing to dive or fly with nasal congestion and provoking recurrence Overlooking coexisting ear barotrauma Failing to identify and treat underlying rhinitis, polyps, or structural obstruction Missing secondary bacterial sinusitis after the injury The paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities that equalise pressure through their ostia into the nasal cavity. When an ostium is blocked by mucosal swelling, polyps, or secretions, the air within the sinus cannot equalise with rising ambient pressure on descent. The resulting relative negative pressure within the sinus draws fluid and blood from the mucosa into the cavity and causes mucosal engorgement and haemorrhage, producing pain and bleeding. On ascent, expanding trapped air or dislodged material can cause further discomfort and epistaxis. Sinus barotrauma usually settles within days to a couple of weeks with decongestion and avoidance of pressure changes; recurrence is likely if underlying nasal or sinus disease is not addressed, but serious complications are uncommon.

arteriosus rather than a ruptured aneurysm Missing an incidental unruptured aneurysm that warrants surveillance Overlooking associated lesions such as ventricular septal defect or bicuspid aortic valve Delaying repair once rupture or significant enlargement is evident A sinus of Valsalva aneurysm results from a deficiency in the elastic and muscular tissue where the aortic media meets the annulus fibrosus, allowing the affected aortic sinus to bulge. The weakness may be congenital or acquired through infection such as endocarditis, connective tissue disease, atherosclerosis, or trauma. Over time the thin-walled aneurysm enlarges under aortic pressure and may compress neighbouring structures or interfere with the aortic valve and coronary ostia. If the wall gives way, blood jets from the high-pressure aorta into an adjacent lower-pressure chamber, most often on the right side of the heart, establishing a left-to-right shunt with volume overload and, if large, acute heart failure. Unruptured aneurysms may remain stable for years, but rupture carries significant risk and, if untreated, can lead to progressive heart failure; surgical or transcatheter repair generally has good outcomes when performed promptly.

Blood flows bidirectionally through this connection so that the extracranial venous pouch fills when intracranial venous pressure rises and empties with compression or upright posture. The anomaly may be developmental or arise after trauma, and its clinical significance hinges on whether it merely drains scalp veins or also carries important intracranial venous outflow. Many lesions are stable and can be observed with a good prognosis; when treatment is indicated for cosmetic, symptomatic or safety reasons, outcomes are generally favourable provided the venous drainage pattern is defined beforehand to avoid compromising intracranial outflow.

The resulting post-sinusoidal outflow obstruction produces portal hypertension, hepatocellular necrosis and cholestasis, clinically manifest as tender hepatomegaly, weight gain, ascites and jaundice, and in severe disease progressing to hepatorenal and multi-organ failure. Mild and moderate SOS often resolves with supportive care, but severe or very severe disease with multi-organ failure carries a high mortality; early recognition and timely use of defibrotide improve outcomes.

tumour type and stage A new firm or ulcerated umbilical nodule in an adult, which mandates urgent evaluation for malignancy Associated ascites, weight loss, or a palpable abdominal mass indicating disseminated disease Bleeding or discharge from the nodule Rapid growth of the lesion Mistaking the nodule for a benign umbilical lesion such as a hernia or granuloma and delaying diagnosis Biopsying Malignant cells are thought to reach the umbilicus by several routes, including direct extension through the anterior abdominal wall, lymphatic spread along embryological remnants, haematogenous dissemination, and contiguous spread along the obliterated umbilical vessels and the urachal or falciform ligament remnants. The nodule signifies advanced malignancy with peritoneal or systemic dissemination and is associated with a poor prognosis and short median survival, although outcome varies with the primary tumour type and response to systemic therapy.

statins are relatively ineffective and this must be distinguished from familial hypercholesterolaemia Premature coronary artery disease or sudden cardiac event in a young patient Extensive xanthomata in childhood, particularly with normal or near-normal cholesterol Significant haemolytic anaemia or bleeding from macrothrombocytopenia Family history of early cardiovascular death Misdiagnosing it as familial hypercholesterolaemia and relying on statins, which are relatively ineffective Missing the diagnosis because routine cholesterol assays do not measure plant sterols Overlooking haematological clues such as haemolysis and large platelets Underestimating cardiovascular risk when cholesterol appears near normal Failing to advise dietary restriction of plant and shellfish sterols Sitosterolaemia results from loss of function of the ABCG5/ABCG8 heterodimeric transporter expressed on enterocytes and hepatocytes. Normally this pump exports non-cholesterol sterols back into the gut lumen and into bile, keeping absorption of dietary plant sterols very low. When it is defective, plant sterols such as sitosterol and campesterol, along with cholesterol, are absorbed in excess and poorly excreted, so they accumulate in plasma and tissues. Deposition in tendons and skin causes xanthomata and in arterial walls accelerates atherosclerosis, while incorporation of abnormal sterols into red cell and platelet membranes underlies the haemolysis and macrothrombocytopenia. With early diagnosis, sterol-restricted diet and sterol-absorption-blocking therapy, plant sterol levels fall, xanthomata regress and cardiovascular risk improves; undiagnosed disease carries a substantial risk of premature atherosclerotic events.

situs inversus — situs inversus totalis, situs transversus, situs oppositus heterotaxy syndrome (situs ambiguus) situs solitus with isolated dextrocardia dextroposition from pulmonary hypoplasia or diaphragmatic hernia congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries primary ciliary dyskinesia without laterality defect asplenia or polysplenia syndromes acquired mediastinal shift mimicking cardiac malposition transthoracic echocardiography with formal segmental analysis abdominal ultrasound documenting hepatic, splenic and gastric position chest radiograph noting cardiac apex, gastric bubble and aortic arch side ECG with both standard and mirror-image lead placement nasal nitric oxide measurement and ciliary studies where primary ciliary dyskinesia is suspected cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) for detailed situs and vascular mapping before intervention genetic testing for ciliopathy and laterality genes in selected cases Situs inversus totalis denotes complete mirror-image reversal of both thoracic and abdominal viscera, with cardiac apex, aortic arch, stomach and spleen on the right and liver on the left. In contrast to heterotaxy, situs inversus totalis carries a relatively low incidence of major congenital heart disease, most affected individuals having structurally normal hearts in mirror-image configuration. Roughly a quarter of individuals with situs inversus totalis have primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome), so persistent sinopulmonary disease, chronic otitis and subfertility should prompt ciliary evaluation. Congenitally corrected transposition and other conotruncal lesions occur more often in situs inversus than in the general population and warrant careful segmental echocardiographic assessment. Atypical presentation of common disease is the rule: left-sided appendicitis, left-sided biliary colic and a right-sided cardiac apex on examination are classic traps. Standard ECG electrode placement produces a spurious picture (inverted P in lead I, reversed praecordial progression); mirror-image lead placement restores a normal-appearing trace. A segmental (sequential) approach naming atrial situs, ventricular loop and great-artery relationship is essential before any surgical or catheter intervention. Interventional and surgical teams must anticipate reversed anatomy for central venous access, coronary angiography, and abdominal surgery to avoid wrong-side procedures. chronic productive cough, recurrent sinusitis or bronchiectasis suggesting primary ciliary dyskinesia cyanosis, murmur or failure to thrive indicating associated structural heart disease atypical or contralateral pain suggesting missed left-sided appendicitis or biliary disease unexplained subfertility in the context of a laterality defect planned surgery or intervention where reversed anatomy risks a wrong-side procedure Assuming a normal heart and omitting a full segmental echocardiographic assessment. Misinterpreting the ECG as ischaemic or abnormal when electrodes are placed conventionally. Overlooking primary ciliary dyskinesia in a patient presenting only with situs inversus. Diagnosing situs inversus when the true picture is heterotaxy, thereby underestimating cardiac and splenic risk. Failing to communicate reversed anatomy to surgical, anaesthetic and interventional teams. Situs inversus arises from disruption of the normal left-right axis patterning established during early embryogenesis at the primitive node, where motile monocilia generate a leftward extra-embryonic fluid flow (nodal flow) that biases asymmetric expression of the Nodal-Lefty-Pitx2 signalling cascade. When this laterality signal is randomised or reversed, the viscera and cardiac tube loop in mirror-image fashion, producing complete reversal (situs inversus totalis) when the process is coordinated across all organ fields. In primary ciliary dyskinesia the nodal cilia are immotile or dyskinetic, so laterality is determined at random, explaining why about half of affected individuals have situs inversus and half situs solitus. Because the reversal is usually symmetric and complete, atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial concordance is preserved in mirror image and the heart is typically structurally normal, distinguishing this condition from the abnormal midline symmetry of heterotaxy. Isolated situs inversus totalis with a structurally normal heart is compatible with a normal lifespan and requires mainly awareness for atypical disease presentation. Prognosis is chiefly determined by any coexisting congenital heart disease or by the respiratory and fertility consequences of associated primary ciliary dyskinesia.

Strongly female-predominant (female-to-male ratio roughly 10–20:1) and chiefly affects middle-aged women, but can present at any age including childhood; prevalence is approximately 0.5–1%. Earlier age at onset tends to mark a more aggressive phenotype with more systemic manifestations and more serum autoantibodies. Can occur alone or in association with other systemic rheumatic diseases, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis, limited scleroderma, and systemic lupus erythematosus; 5–20% of patients with other autoimmune diseases can have sicca features. Principal oral symptom is dryness (xerostomia) with difficulty swallowing dry food, burning mouth, increased dental caries; examination may show dry erythematous sticky mucosa, atrophic tongue papillae, and a deeply fissured tongue. Intermittent or persistent enlargement of the parotid or other major salivary glands occurs in about two-thirds of patients. Ocular involvement classically produces a sandy or gritty sensation under the lids, with burning, stranded secretions at the inner canthi, reduced tearing, redness, and photosensitivity from corneal and conjunctival epithelial destruction (keratoconjunctivitis sicca). Extraglandular (systemic) manifestations occur in about one-third of patients and are categorized as nonspecific, periepithelial, immune complex–mediated, and lymphoma. Carries the highest risk of lymphoma among all autoimmune diseases; most are extranodal, low-grade, marginal zone (MALT) B-cell lymphomas, often found incidentally on labial minor salivary gland biopsy. Most patients (about two-thirds) have an elevated ESR, hypergammaglobulinemia, antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, and anti-Ro52/Ro60 and anti-La autoantibodies. The disease course is usually slow and benign in the majority of patients; antecedent major stressful life events have been reported prior to onset. Recently described as triggerable by PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor therapy. Parotid or major salivary gland enlargement, especially persistent or with a lymph node mass >7 cm — concern for lymphoma Palpable purpura, urticarial lesions, skin ulcerations, or mononeuritis multiplex (immune complex–mediated vasculitis) Low C4 complement, monoclonal gammopathy (paraproteinemia), and cryoglobulins — lymphoma risk markers Heavy focal lymphocytic infiltrates with germinal center formation on salivary biopsy — lymphoma risk B symptoms (constitutional) with lymphadenopathy Severe tongue atrophy and leukopenia in the appropriate context Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis with mixed type II/III cryoglobulinemia Myelitis with anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies (rare CNS involvement) Failing to take a careful medication history — diuretics, antihypertensives, anticholinergics, and antidepressants can themselves cause dryness and mimic or worsen sicca. Overlooking HIV- or HCV-associated sicca syndrome, which can closely resemble Sjögren’s but lacks anti-Ro/La and has distinct demographics and glandular infiltrate phenotype. Missing renal tubular dysfunction: interstitial nephritis may be asymptomatic, presenting only as hyposthenuria or renal tubular acidosis, and untreated acidosis can progress to nephrocalcinosis. Attributing all salivary gland enlargement to benign disease and missing an incidental MALT lymphoma on labial biopsy. Not excluding sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, IgG4-related disease, graft-versus-host disease, and prior head/neck radiation before diagnosing Sjögren’s disease. Assuming arthritis is erosive — arthritis in primary Sjögren’s disease is characteristically nonerosive (may lead to Jaccoud’s arthropathy). Activated T lymphocytes are the major infiltrating cells in affected exocrine (chiefly salivary and lacrimal) glands, with B-cell populations prevailing in heavily infiltrated labial minor salivary gland tissue; follicular, myeloid, and plasmacytoid dendritic cells and macrophages are also present, the latter (with inflammasome activation) being linked to lymphoma risk. Ductal and acinar epithelial cells play an active pathogenic role: they aberrantly express costimulatory molecules and surface Ro/La autoantigens, secrete proinflammatory cytokines and lymphocyte-attracting chemokines that support ectopic germinal center formation, express innate-immunity Toll-like receptors (TLR3, 7, 9), and display immunoregulatory molecules (ICAM, CD40). Epithelial cells produce B cell–activating factor (BAFF), induced by type I and II interferons, and circulating BAFF is elevated (especially with hypergammaglobulinemia and autoantibodies), exerting an antiapoptotic effect on B lymphocytes; epithelial cells themselves show increased apoptosis. Disease initiation and perpetuation reflect interplay of endogenous triggers (intracellular stress, inappropriate expression of endogenous nucleic acids) and exogenous triggers (viruses, hormonal factors, stressful life events) on a genetically hyperactive immune background. Established genetic loci include HLA-DQA1*0501, interferon/BAFF axis variants (IRF5, STAT4, BAFF), B-cell function genes (EBF1, BLK), and combined deficiencies of the classical complement pathway. The disease usually evolves slowly and follows a benign course in most patients. The dominant adverse outcome is malignant transformation: Sjögren’s disease carries the highest lymphoma risk of any autoimmune disease, with clinical (parotid enlargement, severe tongue atrophy, palpable purpura), hematologic/serologic (leukopenia, autoantibodies, low C4, monoclonal gammopathy, cryoglobulins), and histopathologic (germinal center formation, heavy focal lymphocytic infiltrates) risk factors. Survival is reduced in patients with B symptoms, lymph node mass >7 cm, and high or intermediate histologic grade. Patients also have an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, paralleling rheumatoid arthritis and SLE. Diagnosis/classification per the 2016 ACR-EULAR criteria: suspect in patients with dry eyes and/or dry mouth (or systemic features such as major salivary gland enlargement, fatigue, Raynaud’s, small-joint arthralgia/arthritis, palpable purpura/urticaria, renal tubular acidosis/membranoproliferative GN, ILD/small airway disease, autoimmune cholangitis, peripheral neuropathy, or MS-like lesions), supported by objective findings: unstimulated whole saliva flow ≤0.1 mL/min, Schirmer’s test ≤5 mm/5 min, ocular staining score ≥5 (or van Bijsterveld ≥4), serum anti-Ro antibodies, and minor salivary gland biopsy focus score ≥1. Exclusions include prior head/neck radiation, active HCV, AIDS, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, graft-versus-host disease, and IgG4-related disease. Extraglandular disease severity is gauged by the categories of involvement (nonspecific, periepithelial, immune complex–mediated, and lymphoma).

Sjogren-Larsson syndrome — ALDH3A2, fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase deficiency, FALDH deficiency, SLS Other congenital ichthyoses (lamellar ichthyosis, congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma) Refsum disease and other peroxisomal disorders Chanarin-Dorfman syndrome (neutral lipid storage disease with ichthyosis) Cerebral palsy of other cause with coincidental xerosis Trichothiodystrophy with ichthyosis Netherton syndrome Assay of fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase activity in cultured fibroblasts or leucocytes Molecular genetic testing of ALDH3A2 Ophthalmological examination for glistening macular dots and photophobia Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain (white-matter change) and MR spectroscopy showing an abnormal lipid peak Skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis with a variably reduced or thickened granular layer Developmental and neurological assessment Classic triad of congenital ichthyosis, spastic diplegia or tetraplegia, and intellectual disability The ichthyosis is generalised with fine to plate-like scaling, often prominent in flexures, and pruritus is characteristic A pathognomonic ophthalmological sign is glistening white/yellow dots (crystalline maculopathy) at the macula Autosomal recessive; caused by mutations in ALDH3A2 encoding fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase (FALDH) Neurological features typically emerge in infancy with delayed motor milestones and spasticity, and seizures may occur Photophobia and reduced visual acuity accompany the macular changes Management is supportive with emollients/keratolytics for the skin, physiotherapy and spasticity care, and specialist neurological and ophthalmological follow-up Progressive loss of motor function or new-onset seizures Marked visual deterioration Feeding difficulty or failure to thrive in the affected infant Barrier compromise with recurrent skin infection Diagnosing isolated cerebral palsy and missing the associated ichthyosis and macular dots Attributing pruritus to eczema rather than recognising it as a characteristic feature Failing to arrange fundoscopy, which can reveal the near-specific glistening dots Overlooking the recessive inheritance and the value of genetic counselling for the family Sjogren-Larsson syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in ALDH3A2, which encodes fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase, a component of the fatty alcohol:NAD oxidoreductase complex. Deficient enzyme activity blocks the oxidation of long-chain fatty aldehydes and alcohols, which accumulate and are incorporated abnormally into lipids. In the epidermis this disrupts the lamellar lipid membranes essential for the permeability barrier, producing ichthyosis; in the developing central nervous system abnormal lipid metabolism and myelin disturbance underlie the spasticity and cognitive impairment; and lipid deposition in the retina produces the characteristic glistening macular dots. Neurological impairment is usually static or slowly progressive and largely irreversible; most patients have lasting spasticity and intellectual disability. The ichthyosis and pruritus can be controlled but not cured, and lifespan varies with the severity of neurological and swallowing involvement.

Sjögren syndrome — SS, sicca syndrome, Sjogren's syndrome, autoimmune epithelitis Age-related or medication-induced sicca (anticholinergics) Sarcoidosis and IgG4-related disease affecting salivary glands Chronic viral infection (hepatitis C, HIV) Radiation-induced glandular damage Other connective tissue diseases with secondary sicca Amyloidosis Anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies, ANA, and rheumatoid factor Schirmer test and ocular surface staining for aqueous tear deficiency Unstimulated whole salivary flow and salivary gland ultrasound or imaging Labial minor salivary gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis Serum immunoglobulins and protein electrophoresis; monitoring for lymphoma if persistent gland enlargement or new lymphadenopathy Characterised by dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia) from immune-mediated destruction of lacrimal and salivary glands Predominantly affects middle-aged women and may be primary or secondary to another connective tissue disease such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus Systemic features include fatigue, arthralgia, Raynaud phenomenon, parotid gland swelling, and cutaneous vasculitis Anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies are characteristic, along with positive antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor Objective sicca can be confirmed with Schirmer test, ocular surface staining, and unstimulated salivary flow; labial minor salivary gland biopsy shows focal lymphocytic sialadenitis There is a markedly increased lifetime risk of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, particularly MALT lymphoma Anti-Ro antibodies in pregnancy carry a risk of neonatal lupus and congenital heart block Management centres on symptomatic relief of dryness (tear and saliva substitutes, secretagogues) with immunosuppression reserved for significant systemic involvement Persistent unilateral parotid enlargement, lymphadenopathy, or new cytopenias suggesting lymphoma transformation Signs of systemic vasculitis, mononeuritis multiplex, or interstitial lung disease Renal involvement such as renal tubular acidosis or interstitial nephritis Pregnancy with anti-Ro antibodies given the risk of fetal congenital heart block Severe corneal complications from untreated dry eye Dismissing sicca symptoms as trivial and missing systemic or lymphomatous complications Failing to consider mimics such as IgG4-related disease, sarcoidosis, or viral infection Not counselling and monitoring anti-Ro-positive women in pregnancy for fetal heart block Overlooking increased dental caries and ocular surface damage from chronic dryness Attributing new persistent gland swelling to disease flare rather than investigating for lymphoma Sjögren syndrome is a chronic autoimmune exocrinopathy in which lymphocytic (mainly CD4 T-cell and B-cell) infiltration of the exocrine glands destroys secretory epithelium, sometimes termed autoimmune epithelitis. B-cell hyperactivity produces autoantibodies (anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB) and hypergammaglobulinaemia, and sustained clonal B-cell proliferation underlies the elevated lymphoma risk. Type I interferon signalling and genetic HLA associations contribute to disease susceptibility. Extraglandular disease reflects immune complex deposition and lymphocytic infiltration of organs including skin, joints, lungs, kidneys, and nervous system. Most patients have a good prognosis with a slowly progressive course dominated by sicca symptoms, but systemic involvement and, importantly, lymphoma development can worsen outcomes. Lifelong monitoring for lymphoproliferative disease is warranted.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome / TEN — Stop the culprit drug Dermatology review SCORTEN severity Skin detachment — manage like a burn; high mortality Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) - may resemble early SJS but erosions are superficial and prominent mucosal involvement is lacking Drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome / DRESS (DIHS) - can have TEN-like overlap features Overlap hypersensitivity syndromes (DIHS-TEN-like, AGEP-TEN-like) - up to ~20% of severe drug eruptions show overlap, supporting a clinical spectrum Reactive infectious mucocutaneous eruption (RIME) - Mycoplasma and other respiratory infections in children cause prominent mucositis with limited cutaneous involvement Erythema multiforme associated with herpes simplex virus - painful mucosal erosions and target lesions, typically acral, with limited skin detachment Frozen-section skin biopsy for rapid diagnosis; histology shows full-thickness epidermal necrosis (distinguishes from AGEP's superficial/subcorneal neutrophilic pustules) Calculate BSA of epidermal detachment to classify SJS vs overlap vs TEN Assess for renal insufficiency and consider underlying malignancy (both poor-prognosis markers) Patch testing with the responsible drug (after recovery) and use of the ALDEN algorithm to rank likelihood of drug causality Staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome (SSSS) - diffuse tender erythema with bullae/desquamation and positive Nikolsky's sign; cleavage is superficial (subcorneal), spares mucosa DRESS / drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome - maculopapular eruption, facial edema, eosinophilia, multiorgan (especially hepatic) involvement Erythema multiforme major - target lesions with mucous-membrane involvement Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) - sterile pustules on erythema, flexural predominance Exfoliative erythroderma syndrome - diffuse erythema/scaling, may be drug-induced Autoimmune blistering disease (e.g., bullous pemphigoid, which can also be drug-induced/exacerbated) SJS/TEN is a single disease spectrum of full-thickness epidermal necrosis with blistering and mucosal/epidermal detachment, separated only by the extent of body surface area (BSA) detachment. Drugs cause roughly 80% of cases; the most frequently implicated agents are sulfonamide antibiotics, allopurinol, antiepileptics (lamotrigine, phenytoin, carbamazepine), oxicam NSAIDs, beta-lactam and other antibiotics, and nevirapine. Onset is typically delayed, around 5-28 days after starting the culprit drug. Prodrome: fever >39 C (102.2 F), sore throat, and conjunctivitis precede or accompany the rash; lesions are painful, dusky, atypical and target-like. It is uncommon in children and over-represented among people with HIV, SLE, certain HLA types, and slow acetylators. Mucosal surfaces are characteristically involved, and Nikolsky's sign is positive. SJS/TEN is mediated by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells recognizing a drug-HLA class I complex; granulysin released by these cells is thought to be the principal mediator of keratinocyte death. Strong, drug- and phenotype-specific HLA associations exist: HLA-B*15:02 with carbamazepine SJS/TEN (Han Chinese), HLA-B*58:01 with allopurinol, HLA-B*13:01 with dapsone/sulfonamide. Frozen-section skin biopsy can aid rapid diagnosis and distinguish SJS/TEN (full-thickness epidermal necrosis) from mimics. Loss of skin barrier integrity leads to dehydration and secondary sepsis, which are major causes of death. Extensive/rapidly progressing epidermal detachment (BSA toward TEN range) - maximal-severity form Older age, malignancy, or renal insufficiency - independently associated with poor prognosis Signs of sepsis or dehydration from loss of skin barrier integrity Mucosal (ocular, oral, urogenital, respiratory) involvement - risk of acute and long-term sequelae Early SJS may be hard to distinguish from AGEP; in AGEP erosions are superficial and prominent mucosal involvement is NOT present. Drugs may be implicated even when the eruption appears shortly AFTER the drug has been discontinued (delayed-type reactions). A risk HLA allele does NOT by itself cause SJS/TEN - most carriers remain drug-tolerant; other factors (e.g., drug metabolism) are required. Designation of a single diagnosis is NOT always possible in overlap hypersensitivity syndromes; manage according to the dominant evolving clinical features. Skin biopsy helps characterize the reaction but does NOT by itself establish drug causality. A delayed, T-cell-mediated (type IVa, cytotoxic) severe cutaneous adverse reaction. A drug or metabolite-altered antigen is presented in association with a risk HLA class I allele by keratinocytes or other antigen-presenting cells; a restricted T-cell receptor on skin-enriched CD8+ T cells recognizes this drug-HLA complex, triggering activation and release of cytolytic mediators (notably granulysin) that cause full-thickness epidermal keratinocyte death and detachment. Proposed antigen-presentation models include hapten/prohapten covalent binding, the pharmacologic-interaction (p-i) noncovalent model, and the altered-peptide-repertoire model (as proven for abacavir-HLA-B*57:01). Carbamazepine SJS/TEN shows a highly restricted V-alpha/V-beta TCR repertoire shared among HLA-B*15:02 patients. A risk HLA allele alone is insufficient; non-MHC factors such as drug metabolism (e.g., CYP2C9*3 slow metabolism with phenytoin) contribute. (Harrison 22e p.417-420) Mortality is substantial and rises with the extent of epidermal detachment: at least ~10% of SJS and ~30% of TEN patients die from the disease (overall reported mortality up to ~30%). Older age, greater BSA detachment, malignancy, and renal insufficiency are independent poor-prognostic factors. Best outcomes follow early diagnosis and immediate withdrawal of the culprit drug. (Harrison 22e p.142, p.424-425) Classified by percent body surface area (BSA) of epidermal detachment: SJS = <10% BSA; SJS/TEN overlap = 10-30% BSA; TEN = >30% BSA (maximal form). (Harrison 22e p.142, p.424). SCORTEN (severity-of-illness score for TEN) is the standard prognostic tool; note the source text does not enumerate its parameters.

Skew deviation — skew deviation with ocular tilt reaction Fourth nerve (superior oblique) palsy Partial third nerve palsy Myasthenia gravis Thyroid eye disease Orbital restrictive disease Dissociated vertical deviation HINTS examination in acute vestibular syndrome Upright-supine test to demonstrate reduction of the deviation when supine MRI of the brain with attention to the brainstem and cerebellum Orthoptic assessment including measurement of ocular torsion Vascular risk-factor evaluation when stroke is suspected An acquired vertical misalignment of the eyes caused by disturbance of the otolithic (utricular) vestibular pathways, not by a single ocular muscle palsy It may occur alone or as part of the ocular tilt reaction with head tilt, ocular torsion and skew toward the lower eye It is an important mimic of fourth nerve palsy and of other causes of vertical diplopia The upright-supine test helps distinguish it: a skew deviation typically decreases when the patient lies supine It usually signals brainstem or cerebellar disease, so acute skew with other signs may indicate stroke Within the HINTS assessment of acute vestibular syndrome, skew deviation is a central (worrying) sign Acute onset with vertigo, ataxia or other brainstem signs Direction-changing or gaze-evoked nystagmus Any feature suggesting posterior circulation stroke Reduced conscious level or rapidly evolving deficits Misdiagnosing skew as a benign fourth nerve palsy and missing a stroke Failing to perform HINTS in acute vestibular syndrome Overlooking the associated ocular tilt reaction Attributing vertical diplopia to orbital disease without considering a central cause Skew deviation results from an imbalance in the graviceptive otolithic pathways that project from the utricle through the brainstem to the ocular motor nuclei, producing a vertical divergence of the visual axes. Lesions of these pathways in the pons, medulla, midbrain or cerebellum disturb the normal tonic balance that keeps the eyes level, and when the full ocular tilt reaction occurs the head tilt, ocular torsion and hypotropia all deviate toward the side of a lower pontomedullary lesion (or opposite a higher one). Because these pathways lie in the posterior circulation, skew deviation frequently accompanies brainstem or cerebellar ischaemia. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; skew from a self-limiting or treatable lesion may resolve, but as a sign of brainstem or cerebellar stroke it carries the prognosis of that event.

Skin Cancer — melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma Benign nevomelanocytic nevus (vs melanoma) Dysplastic/atypical nevus Seborrheic keratosis Lentigo Nummular eczema and psoriasis (may mimic superficial BCC) Wart or callus (may mimic SCC when inflammation is minimal) Keratoacanthoma (rapidly growing low-grade SCC variant) Merkel cell carcinoma Cutaneous B- or T-cell lymphoma Extramammary Paget's disease Excisional biopsy with 1-3 mm narrow margins (preferred) for any changing/suspicious pigmented lesion; incisional (shave, saucerization, or punch) biopsy of the most nodular/darkest area when excision is impractical - incisional biopsy does not facilitate melanoma spread Histopathology report should include Breslow thickness, mitotic rate, ulceration, lymphatic/vascular/neural invasion, regression, microsatellitosis, and margin status Dermoscopy (low-level magnification with polarized light or water interface) and total-body photography for surveillance in high-risk patients Genetic expression profiles (GEP, e.g. 31-gene), FISH with multiple probes, or comparative genomic hybridization to distinguish difficult melanomas from benign nevi and estimate prognosis Complete blood count, complete metabolic panel, and serum LDH (LDH is part of AJCC stage IV criteria) Sentinel lymph node biopsy for pathologic staging CT, PET, or combined CT/PET (and MRI) when symptoms, exam, or abnormal labs suggest metastatic disease Genetic testing for individuals with >=3 primary melanomas or with families having >=1 invasive melanoma plus >=2 cases of melanoma and/or pancreatic cancer, ocular melanoma, mesothelioma, or renal cell carcinoma on one side Superficial BCC mimicking nummular eczema or psoriasis SCC mistaken for a wart or callus when inflammatory response is minimal Pigmented (nodular) BCC mimicking melanoma Desmoplastic melanoma mimicking nodular basal cell carcinoma Benign nevus mimicking melanoma Apply the ABCDE rule to pigmented lesions to detect melanoma early: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variegation, Diameter >6 mm (pencil-eraser size), and Evolving (any change in size, shape, color, elevation, or new symptoms such as bleeding, itching, or crusting) (p.601). The 'ugly duckling' sign: any nevus that looks atypical and different from the rest of an individual's nevi should be considered suspicious (p.601). Melanoma is an aggressive malignancy of melanocytes and accounts for over half of all deaths from skin cancer, even though it is far less common than nonmelanoma skin cancer (p.598). Basal cell carcinoma is among the most common cancers; its natural history is a slowly enlarging, locally invasive neoplasm with low metastatic potential (~0.1% in immunocompetent patients), though the risk of recurrence or a new primary NMSC is about 40% over 5 years (p.607). Nodular BCC classically presents as a pearly nodule with tortuous telangiectatic vessels, rolled borders, and a central crust; pigmented BCC may contain melanin and be confused with melanoma (p.606-607). Squamous cell carcinoma arises from keratinizing epidermal cells on sun-exposed skin and can metastasize (0.3-5.2%), most often to regional lymph nodes; lower-lip and ear tumors metastasize in 13% and 11% respectively (p.606-607). Actinic keratoses and actinic cheilitis are premalignant forms of SCC; SCC in situ (Bowen's disease) presents as a scaling erythematous plaque, and treating premalignant/in-situ lesions reduces subsequent invasive disease (p.607). NMSCs (SCC ~80%, BCC ~18% of cases) are the most common cancers in the US, with an estimated >5.3 million cases annually (p.606). Breslow thickness (greatest tumor thickness measured from the top of the granular layer or ulcer base to the bottom of the tumor) is the best predictor of melanoma recurrence and, with ulceration, defines the T stage (p.601-602). Any pigmented lesion that has changed (size, shape, color, elevation) or that meets ABCDE criteria is a candidate for biopsy An 'ugly duckling' nevus that differs from a patient's other nevi New bleeding, itching, or crusting in a pigmented lesion Thick and/or ulcerated melanoma (key adverse T-stage features) Microsatellite lesions, in-transit metastases, nodal involvement, elevated LDH, or distant metastases to brain/liver/bone SCC on the lower lip or ear, recurrent SCC (~30% metastatic risk), or SCC in scars/chronic ulcers, genital/mucosal surfaces, or in immunosuppressed patients (aggressive behavior) Rapidly expanding lesion in an older, immunosuppressed, UV-exposed patient (MCC: AEIOU - Asymptomatic, Expanding rapidly, Immunosuppression, Older than 50, UV-exposed site) Morpheaform, infiltrative, and micronodular BCCs have indistinct borders and subtle presentation, so treatment is often delayed and tumors are more extensive than they appear clinically SCC can be mistaken for a benign wart or callus when the inflammatory response is minimal Pigmented BCC may be confused with melanoma; desmoplastic melanoma can mimic nodular BCC Melanoma frequently develops on non-sun-exposed skin (acral, mucosal); in dark-skinned, Hispanic, and East Asian populations melanoma is often non-UV-related, diagnosed at higher stage, and has worse outcomes The 31-gene GEP can estimate distant-relapse probability but has not supplanted prognostic estimates from surgical staging, and genomic pathway data are not yet incorporated into AJCC staging Standard labs and imaging rarely detect occult metastatic disease in early melanoma and should be directed by symptoms/exam findings Melanoma is a malignancy of melanocytes, neural-crest-derived pigment-producing cells; most melanomas arise in skin but can occur in mucosa, eye, meninges, and upper esophagus. UV radiation is the dominant environmental driver, and cutaneous melanomas carry one of the highest somatic mutation rates of any cancer (>10 mutations/Mb), the majority bearing a UV signature. Key driver mutations affect the MAP-kinase and PI3K/AKT proliferative pathways: BRAF (commonly V600E) in 40-50% of cutaneous melanomas, NRAS in ~20%, and loss-of-function NF1 in 10-15%; germline CDKN2A (p16/ARF, RB and p53 pathways), CDK4, MITF, BAP1, POT1, TERT, and moderate-risk MC1R variants underlie inherited susceptibility. Nonmelanoma skin cancers are also UV-driven: SCC is associated with p53 and N-RAS damage, whereas BCC is driven by hedgehog (Hh) pathway activation, usually loss of function of the tumor-suppressor PTCH1 (which normally inhibits SMO). Merkel cell carcinoma is linked to the oncogenic Merkel cell polyomavirus, present in ~80% of tumors (p.598-607). Melanoma prognosis is dominated by Breslow thickness and ulceration (T stage); favorable primary sites are the forearm and leg, unfavorable sites the scalp, hands, feet, and mucous membranes. 10-year melanoma-specific survival ranges from >99% for stage 0 (in situ) and ~98% for stage IA down to ~24-30% for stage IIID. Women with stage I/II disease and younger patients do better; older men have worse outcomes (delayed diagnosis, thicker tumors, more head/neck, acral and BRAF wild-type tumors). High mitotic rate and lymphatic/vascular invasion are additional adverse factors. Overall melanoma mortality has been falling, attributed to immunotherapy and targeted therapy. BCC rarely metastasizes (~0.1% in immunocompetent patients) but recurs frequently. Cutaneous SCC metastasizes in 0.3-5.2% of cases overall, higher for lip/ear/recurrent/immunosuppressed disease. Merkel cell carcinoma is aggressive: ~90% cure with local disease but ~52% survival with nodal and ~10% with distant disease (p.602-609). Melanoma is staged by the AJCC TNM system (T stage built primarily on Breslow thickness and ulceration; pathologic stage incorporates sentinel lymph node biopsy results), from stage 0 (in situ, Tis) through stage IV (distant metastasis); 10-year melanoma-specific survival is depicted by stage in Table 81-3. Merkel cell carcinoma has its own TNM staging incorporating tumor size (<2 cm vs >2 cm), nodal status, and distant metastases (p.602-609).

slac wrist — scapholunate advanced collapse, SLAC arthritis SNAC wrist (scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse) Rheumatoid or other inflammatory arthritis Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (pseudogout) arthropathy Kienböck disease with secondary arthritis Post-traumatic radiocarpal arthritis from an intra-articular distal radius fracture Primary radiocarpal osteoarthritis Gout PA and lateral radiographs to stage the degenerative pattern Clenched-fist and contralateral comparison views CT for detailed articular assessment and surgical planning MRI to evaluate cartilage and the capitate head before proximal row carpectomy Diagnostic wrist arthroscopy to grade chondral surfaces Inflammatory and crystal screen if an inflammatory arthropathy is suspected SLAC is the most common pattern of degenerative wrist arthritis and usually arises from untreated scapholunate dissociation. Degeneration follows a predictable sequence: the radial styloid-scaphoid articulation first, then the whole radioscaphoid joint, then the capitolunate and midcarpal joint. The radiolunate joint is characteristically spared, which underpins motion-preserving salvage procedures. Scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse (SNAC) follows an analogous but distinct degenerative pattern originating from scaphoid nonunion. Stage guides surgery: radial styloidectomy with scapholunate treatment early, proximal row carpectomy or scaphoid excision with four-corner fusion later, and total wrist fusion for pancarpal disease. Proximal row carpectomy depends on preserved cartilage on the capitate head and in the lunate fossa. Wrist denervation via anterior and posterior interosseous neurectomy can relieve pain while preserving motion in selected patients. Rapidly progressive pain and deformity suggesting advanced collapse Features of inflammatory or crystal arthropathy requiring systemic work-up Capitate head chondral loss that would contraindicate proximal row carpectomy Choosing proximal row carpectomy when the capitate head cartilage is already compromised. Failing to distinguish SLAC from SNAC, which changes the pattern of joint involvement. Mistaking crystal or inflammatory arthropathy for degenerative SLAC. Underestimating radial styloid involvement in early disease. Chronic scapholunate dissociation allows the scaphoid to assume a fixed flexed and rotated position, shifting radiocarpal contact to a small area at the radial styloid. Abnormal, concentrated loading erodes articular cartilage first at the radioscaphoid articulation and then across the midcarpal joint as the capitate migrates proximally into the gap between scaphoid and lunate. Because the lunate remains congruent within the lunate fossa, the radiolunate joint is preserved, which allows salvage operations that offload the diseased articulations while retaining some wrist motion. SLAC is progressive and non-reversible, but stage-appropriate salvage surgery reliably relieves pain, albeit at the cost of some grip strength and wrist motion.

Assessment for glenohumeral internal rotation deficit in throwers A tear of the superior glenoid labrum centred on the biceps anchor, extending anterior and posterior to the attachment of the long head of biceps tendon Typical mechanisms are a fall onto an outstretched hand, a traction injury, or repetitive overhead throwing (the peel-back mechanism in athletes) Patients describe deep shoulder pain, painful clicking or catching, and loss of throwing velocity rather than frank instability Provocative tests such as O'Brien active compression, the crank test and the biceps load tests support the diagnosis but none is highly specific Commonly classified into types I-IV (Snyder), with type II (detachment of the labrum and biceps anchor) the most frequently treated surgically MR arthrography is more sensitive than plain MRI, but asymptomatic labral change is common with age so imaging must be correlated clinically Coexisting rotator cuff pathology, internal impingement and instability are frequent and influence management Recurrent frank dislocation suggesting significant instability rather than an isolated labral tear Rapidly progressive weakness or a mass suggesting biceps rupture or tumour Night pain and constitutional symptoms prompting exclusion of neoplasia or infection Over-diagnosing symptomatic SLAP tears from MRI when age-related labral change is incidental Attempting labral repair in older patients in whom biceps tenodesis or non-operative care gives better results Missing associated rotator cuff or instability lesions that drive symptoms Relying on any single provocative test given their limited specificity The superior labrum anchors the long head of biceps tendon to the supraglenoid tubercle. Acute traction or compression loads, or the repetitive torsional and peel-back forces of overhead throwing, avulse or fray the superior labrum and destabilise the biceps-labral complex. This disrupts the labral contribution to glenohumeral concavity-compression and biceps load transfer, producing pain and mechanical symptoms; in throwers it often coexists with posterosuperior internal impingement and a glenohumeral internal rotation deficit. Many SLAP lesions, particularly in older patients or as incidental findings, respond to rehabilitation; surgically treated type II tears in young athletes have variable return-to-sport rates, and outcomes of repair versus biceps tenodesis depend on age, activity and associated pathology.

slap tear — superior labrum anterior to posterior lesion, superior labral tear Rotator cuff tear or tendinopathy Subacromial impingement syndrome Internal (posterosuperior) impingement in the overhead athlete Glenohumeral instability Biceps tendinopathy or instability of the long head Normal labral variants (sublabral foramen, Buford complex) Paralabral cyst causing suprascapular nerve compression MR arthrography, the most accurate imaging for superior labral pathology Standard MRI to assess the cuff, biceps and any paralabral cyst Plain radiographs to exclude bony and degenerative causes Diagnostic arthroscopy for direct assessment and dynamic peel-back testing Assessment for glenohumeral internal rotation deficit and posterior capsular tightness Electrophysiological studies if suprascapular neuropathy from a paralabral cyst is suspected A SLAP lesion is an injury to the superior labrum extending anterior to posterior around the biceps anchor at the supraglenoid tubercle. Two dominant mechanisms are recognised: a fall onto an outstretched or abducted arm (compression), and repetitive overhead throwing generating a peel-back force on the biceps-labral complex. The Snyder classification describes four principal types, ranging from fraying to bucket-handle detachment with biceps anchor involvement and extension into adjacent labrum. Symptoms are often vague deep-seated pain, clicking or catching, and loss of throwing velocity, making clinical diagnosis difficult. Provocative tests such as O'Brien active compression, the biceps load and dynamic labral shear tests aid diagnosis but individually lack accuracy, so combine several. A key mimic and normal variant is the sublabral foramen and Buford complex; misinterpreting these leads to overdiagnosis. In older patients an incidental degenerate superior labral change is common and repairing it may worsen stiffness, so treat the symptomatic lesion, not the image. Biceps tenodesis or tenotomy is often preferred over labral repair in older patients and those with biceps pathology, whereas anatomical repair suits younger overhead athletes with true unstable lesions. Associated large rotator cuff tear with significant weakness Features of a paralabral cyst compressing the suprascapular nerve with infraspinatus wasting Mechanical locking suggesting a displaced bucket-handle labral fragment Coexisting instability with recurrent subluxation or dislocation Overdiagnosing a SLAP tear by mistaking normal labral variants for pathology. Repairing a degenerate superior labrum in an older patient and precipitating stiffness. Relying on a single provocative test given their limited individual accuracy. Failing to address associated internal impingement, cuff pathology or a paralabral cyst. The superior labrum anchors the long head of biceps tendon at the supraglenoid tubercle and contributes to glenohumeral stability by deepening the socket. SLAP lesions arise when this biceps-labral complex is disrupted, either by an acute traction or compression load or by repetitive microtrauma. In overhead throwers, the late cocking position generates a posterosuperior peel-back force that progressively strips the superior labrum from the glenoid; associated posterior capsular tightness and glenohumeral internal rotation deficit shift the contact point and amplify this stress. Acute injuries typically follow a fall on an outstretched arm or a sudden traction event. An unstable superior labrum destabilises the biceps anchor, alters humeral head kinematics and can produce pseudolaxity, pain and mechanical symptoms; with time degenerative fraying accumulates independently of a discrete injury. Younger overhead athletes with a true unstable lesion can achieve good pain relief with repair, though return to the previous level of throwing is less predictable. In older patients and those with degenerative changes, biceps tenodesis or tenotomy generally provides more reliable relief than labral repair.

genetic diagnosis is confirmed Failing to consider the ketogenic diet given the metabolic basis of the disorder Missing the associated enamel defects and dental care needs SLC13A5 encodes NaCT, a plasma-membrane sodium-coupled citrate transporter that moves extracellular citrate into neurons, where citrate feeds the tricarboxylic acid cycle, fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis, and neurotransmitter production. Loss of transporter function limits neuronal citrate availability, disturbing cellular energy metabolism and biosynthetic pathways and leaving citrate to accumulate in the cerebrospinal fluid. The resulting metabolic derangement impairs neuronal function and lowers the seizure threshold, and the same energy-substrate deficiency provides the rationale for ketogenic dietary therapy that supplies ketone bodies as an alternative fuel. Seizures often improve beyond the neonatal and early infantile period, and some children achieve reasonable control, but most have persistent developmental impairment; outcomes are variable and a subset respond well to dietary therapy.

galactosyltransferases. Impaired transport starves the Golgi of UDP-galactose, so galactose is not added to maturing complex N-glycans, leaving truncated antennae and defining a type II processing defect on transferrin analysis. deterioration affecting safety Diagnosing generic Doose syndrome and not testing for SLC6A1 Overlooking pre-seizure developmental concerns because early milestones seemed adequate Assuming a normal MRI excludes a genetic epilepsy Using vigabatrin-type strategies without recognising the underlying GABAergic transport defect SLC6A1 encodes GAT1, the principal transporter that clears the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA from the synaptic cleft into neurons and astrocytes, terminating inhibitory signalling and recycling GABA. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants reduce transporter function through haploinsufficiency or dominant-negative effects, disturbing the normal spatial and temporal control of GABAergic inhibition. Dysregulated inhibitory neurotransmission destabilises cortical and thalamocortical networks, producing the generalised epilepsy, and impairs the balance of excitation and inhibition needed for normal cognitive development. The resulting picture combines myoclonic-atonic epilepsy with intellectual disability and autistic features. Most individuals have mild to moderate intellectual disability with epilepsy that is variably responsive to treatment; seizures may improve over time in some. Long-term outcome depends on seizure control and cognitive impact, and management is supportive and multidisciplinary.
