linked to neonatal lupus, congenital heart block, sicca, photosensitivity, SCLE (p.2831-2832) Antihistone antibodies — suggest drug-induced lupus (positive in ~75% of DIL) (p.2832, 2835) Antiphospholipid panel: anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-1 (IgG/IgM/IgA) plus lupus anticoagulant by dilute Russell viper venom time (~50% prevalence) (p.2831-2832) Random urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCr) or 24-h urine protein with eGFR and serum creatinine; renal biopsy when UPCr >0.5 and/or declining function (p.2830, 2832) Renal biopsy with ISN/RPS lupus nephritis classification (the only single finding that alone meets EULAR/ACR criteria — class III or IV) (p.2827, 2830) CK and aldolase with muscle biopsy if inflammatory myopathy suspected (p.2829) Emerging urinary biomarkers of renal inflammation/fibrosis: urinary IL-16, CD163, type 1 IFN, TGF-beta (p.2832) Quarterly screening of CBC and renal indices in asymptomatic patients, since hematologic and renal flares can be silent (p.2832) Atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome / TTP-like microvascular thrombotic crisis (hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, microvascular thrombosis, schistocytes, low ADAMTS13, high LDH) (p.2831) Antiphospholipid syndrome thrombotic events presenting as stroke, DVT/PE, Budd-Chiari, or Libman-Sacks embolism (p.2829-2831) Glucocorticoid-induced complications mimicking active disease (steroid myopathy, hyperglycemia, psychosis, avascular necrosis) (p.2829, 2833) Macrophage activation syndrome / hemophagocytic syndrome (acute hemophagocytic syndrome listed among severe SLE manifestations) (p.2833, and HLH associated with SLE p. table 67824 region) Roughly 90% of SLE patients are women, most of childbearing age; prevalence is highest among Black women, then Hispanic, White, and Asian/Pacific Islander women; disease tends to be more severe in non-White patients (p.2827). Autoantibodies can be detectable years before clinical diagnosis, so a positive serology in a symptomatic patient supports attributing nonspecific complaints to SLE (p.2827, 2829). Most patients have active disease despite therapy or recurrent flares; treatment goals are low disease activity (SLEDAI 0-4) or remission on ≤5 mg/day prednisone equivalent (p.2829, 2832). A proposed clinical split distinguishes type 1 lupus (classic inflammatory/organ manifestations such as nephritis, arthritis, vasculitis that respond to immunosuppression) from type 2 lupus (fatigue, diffuse pain, brain fog, depression, sleep disturbance that respond poorly to immunosuppression) (p.2827). Anti-dsDNA titers and C3/C4 levels track disease activity: anti-dsDNA is produced by short-lived plasmablasts that turn over quickly, and complement falls during high activity as it is consumed by immune complexes (p.2832). Rising anti-dsDNA and falling C3/C4 can serve as warning signs of impending active nephritis even in an asymptomatic patient (p.2830). Lupus arthritis is typically non-erosive (Jaccoud-like reversible deformity from ligamentous laxity); overlap with rheumatoid arthritis is termed 'rhupus' (p.2829). Pain out of proportion in a single hip, shoulder, or knee — especially with prior corticosteroid use — should raise concern for avascular necrosis of bone (p.2829). Accelerated atherosclerosis is a major cause of premature death, notably myocardial infarction and stroke in young patients without traditional risk factors, and is the leading cause of death after ~5 years of disease (p.2829, 2836). Antiphospholipid antibodies/APS coexist in about a third of SLE patients and markedly raise risk of arterial/venous thrombosis, stroke (reported in up to 19%), Libman-Sacks endocarditis, and pregnancy loss (p.2829, 2830, 2831). Rapidly declining eGFR, rising proteinuria, or active urinary sediment — class III/IV proliferative lupus nephritis; ~20% of class IV patients die or reach ESRD within 10 years (p.2830) Crescentic / rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (cellular crescents or fibrinoid necrosis) — poor prognostic features (p.2834) Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage with capillaritis (p.2829) Mesenteric vasculitis — risk of intestinal perforation, bleeding, and ischemia (p.2830) Neuropsychiatric flare: seizures, acute psychosis/confusion, transverse myelitis (p.2829) Atypical HUS/TTP-like crisis: hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, schistocytes, low ADAMTS13, microvascular thrombosis (p.2831) Severe thrombocytopenia (<20-50 x10^9/L) with bleeding risk; severe hemolytic anemia (p.2830, 2833) Stroke or arterial/venous thrombosis suggesting APS (p.2829-2830) Pulmonary arterial hypertension, prior arterial thrombosis, or severe end-organ damage — highest maternal mortality; pregnancy should strongly be reconsidered (p.2836) Distinguishing flare from infection is a central challenge: cytopenias and constitutional symptoms can stem from disease activity, medication, OR infection, and acute lupus pneumonitis can look identical to pneumonia on imaging — infection must be excluded before escalating immunosuppression (p.2829-2830). Classification criteria (2019 EULAR/ACR; 2012 SLICC) were built for trial enrollment, not diagnosis — diagnosis remains an individualized clinical judgment; relying on criteria alone can mislead, and ANA-negative or incomplete-lupus patients are excluded by EULAR/ACR (p.2827). A positive ANA or even antihistone antibody alone does not confirm SLE — many drugs induce a positive ANA in patients who never develop symptoms, and antihistone antibodies occur in most SLE cases too (p.2835). Drug-induced lupus can be hard to separate from SLE because skin biopsy and many labs overlap; presence of additional SLE-specific autoantibodies (rarely seen in DIL) and symptom resolution after stopping the drug help distinguish (p.2835). Acute psychosis/confusion may be glucocorticoid-induced rather than neuropsychiatric lupus — and infectious encephalitis must also be ruled out (p.2829). Single-joint pain out of proportion may be avascular necrosis (steroid-related), not arthritis flare (p.2829). Estrogen-containing contraceptives/HRT should be avoided in patients with antiphospholipid antibodies or moderate-severe/active lupus due to thromboembolism risk (p.2836). SLE arises from overactive innate and adaptive immunity with autoantibodies directed at nuclear components (nucleic acids, nucleosomes, RNA-binding proteins). Impaired clearance of cellular debris — driven by high neutrophil turnover/NETosis and defective complement-mediated phagocytosis — overwhelms macrophages and dendritic cells. Accumulated nucleic acids engage toll-like receptors and nucleic-acid sensors in plasmacytoid dendritic cells, driving type 1 interferon production that primes the immune response. Autoreactive B cells (including expanded age-associated B cells) lose tolerance and, with help from T follicular/T peripheral helper cells, mature into autoantibody-secreting plasma cells, while regulatory T-cell function is defective. Resulting immune complexes deposit in tissues and cause inflammation, repair, and eventual fibrosis after recurrent flares. Strong genetic component (monozygotic twin concordance 24% vs 2% dizygotic; >150 GWAS loci, with the MHC the strongest and nearly half of loci linked to type 1 interferon; monogenic complement-pathway deficiencies — C1q, C1r/s, C2, C4 — cause severe SLE). Environmental triggers include UV light, smoking, crystalline silica, mercury/toxins, sex hormones, EBV, and gut microbiome/permeability changes (p.2827-2829). Prognosis and survival vary widely by geography, race/ethnicity, and access to care/medications. Renal disease, especially class IV nephritis, carries substantial risk of ESRD and death (~20% within 10 years), and is more severe in non-White patients. Accelerated atherosclerosis is a major cause of premature death and the leading cause after ~5 years of disease, driven by both traditional risk factors and lupus-specific factors (antiphospholipid antibodies, high disease activity, low C3, high glucocorticoid dose, high homocysteine/leptin). Glucocorticoid exposure independently accrues irreversible organ damage (cataracts, osteoporotic fractures, avascular necrosis, diabetes) even at doses as low as 5 mg prednisone equivalent. Class V (membranous) nephritis has a better prognosis than class III/IV. Sustained low disease activity (LLDAS) for 2+ years is associated with significantly less damage. Recent meta-analyses suggest an increased overall cancer risk and cancer-related mortality (p.2830, 2835-2836). Disease activity is graded for treatment using SLEDAI/SLEDAI-2K (low disease activity = SLEDAI 0-4; remission/DORIS = SLEDAI 0). EULAR severity tiers: mild (constitutional symptoms, mild arthritis, rash <=9% BSA, platelets 50-100, SLEDAI <=6); moderate (RA-like arthritis, rash 9-18% BSA, platelets 20-50, serositis, SLEDAI 7-12); severe (major organ-threatening disease e.g. cerebritis, myelitis, pneumonitis, mesenteric vasculitis; platelets <20; TTP-like or acute hemophagocytic syndrome; rash >18% BSA; SLEDAI >12). Lupus nephritis is graded by ISN/RPS renal biopsy classes I-V (class I mesangial deposits; II mesangial proliferative; III focal proliferative; IV diffuse proliferative; V membranous; III/IV +/- V combinations), with class III/IV (and III/IV+V) being proliferative forms warranting aggressive therapy (p.2827, 2830-2831, 2833-2834).

Sleep Apnea — obstructive sleep apnea, OSA, central sleep apnea Narcolepsy (multiple sleep latency / maintenance of wakefulness testing helps distinguish from OSA) Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea Nocturnal asthma Acid reflux with laryngospasm Insomnia (common in the general population, may coexist with OSA) Obesity-hypoventilation / hypoventilation syndromes Periodic limb movement disorder Overnight in-laboratory polysomnography (PSG) - gold standard Home sleep test (respiratory and cardiac channels) for cost-effective diagnosis Apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) and respiratory disturbance index (RDI) quantification Overnight oximetry profile (mean, nadir, time at low saturation) Multiple sleep latency test / maintenance of wakefulness test (quantify sleepiness, distinguish narcolepsy) Upper-airway imaging (cephalometry, MRI, CT) and fibreoptic endoscopy to identify anatomic risk factors (not routine; useful for surgical planning) Cardiac evaluation for systolic/diastolic dysfunction or structural abnormality Overnight blood-pressure monitoring (may show nondipping pattern) Arterial blood gas (usually normal awake; waking hypoxaemia/hypercarbia suggests cardiopulmonary disease or hypoventilation) Drug-induced sleep endoscopy (for hypoglossal-nerve stimulation candidacy) Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea Nocturnal asthma Acid reflux with laryngospasm Narcolepsy Cheyne-Stokes / central sleep apnoea of heart failure OSA diagnosis requires either symptoms of nocturnal breathing disturbance (snoring, snorting, gasping, breathing pauses) impairing quality of life or unexplained daytime sleepiness/fatigue, PLUS at least 5 obstructive apnoeas/hypopnoeas per hour of sleep (apnoea-hypopnoea index, AHI) on a sleep study; OSA may also be diagnosed without symptoms if AHI is at least 15 episodes/h (p.2277-2278). Each apnoea/hypopnoea is a reduction in breathing for at least 10 s, commonly causing a fall in oxygen saturation of at least 3% or a cortical arousal (p.2278). The major risk factors for OSA are obesity, male sex, and older age; roughly 40-60% of cases are attributable to excess weight, but the absence of obesity does NOT exclude the diagnosis (p.2278). Snoring is the most common symptom, but its absence does NOT exclude OSA because pharyngeal collapse can occur without tissue vibration; the most common daytime symptom is excessive sleepiness, though women preferentially report fatigue rather than sleepiness (p.2279). Dyspnoea is unusual in OSA, and its absence generally distinguishes OSA from paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, nocturnal asthma, and acid reflux with laryngospasm (p.2279). Overnight in-laboratory polysomnography (PSG) is the gold standard for diagnosis; a negative in-lab PSG usually rules out OSA, but false-negatives can occur with night-to-night variation, insufficient REM sleep, or less supine sleep than typical (p.2279). Home sleep tests recording only respiratory and cardiac channels are a cost-effective option; when prior probability of OSA is high, a negative home study should be followed by PSG (p.2279). CPAP is the standard medical therapy with the highest level of evidence; it acts as a mechanical splint to hold the airway open during sleep, and auto-titrating (APAP) home devices have eliminated the need for titration studies in many patients (p.2281). Although CPAP reduces 24-h ambulatory blood pressure, the overall effect is modest (averaging 2-4 mmHg), with larger improvements in patients with high AHI, daytime sleepiness, or resistant hypertension (p.2280-2281). Large randomized trials have FAILED to show that CPAP reduces cardiovascular/stroke events or prolongs survival, possibly because sleepy patients (who may have the greatest risk) were excluded and because of limited treatment adherence (p.2281). Central sleep apnoea (CSA) is less common than OSA and may occur alone or, more often, combined with obstructive events as mixed apnoeas; it is often driven by increased sensitivity to PCO2 causing unstable breathing, and a prolonged circulation delay (as in congestive heart failure) produces the crescendo-decrescendo Cheyne-Stokes pattern (p.2282). Treatment of CSA has NOT been shown to improve long-term health outcomes, so specific treatment is generally indicated only for symptomatic CSA; unlike OSA, treatment is difficult and depends on the underlying cause (p.2282). Waking hypoxaemia or hypercarbia, suggesting coexisting cardiopulmonary disease or a hypoventilation syndrome Evidence of cor pulmonale, suggesting a comorbid cardiopulmonary condition (OSA alone is NOT thought to cause right-heart failure) Resistant or uncontrolled hypertension Excessive daytime sleepiness with occupational accident or motor-vehicle-crash risk (drowsy driving) Coexisting heart failure (raises risk of both OSA and CSA) Severe nocturnal hypoxaemia with elevated haemoglobin Assuming absence of snoring excludes OSA - pharyngeal collapse can occur without tissue vibration. Assuming a normal weight excludes OSA - absence of obesity does NOT exclude the diagnosis. Underrecognising OSA in women, who have a lower arousal threshold, shorter and more REM-predominant apnoeas, and tend to report fatigue/insomnia rather than classic sleepiness. Relying on symptoms/signs to gauge severity - they do not accurately predict the severity of sleep-related breathing disturbance; objective measurement is required. Treating a single negative home sleep study as definitive when prior probability is high - follow with PSG. Attributing right-heart failure/cor pulmonale to OSA alone, which is not thought to cause it - look for a comorbid cardiopulmonary condition. Using adaptive servoventilation in patients with CSA and LVEF below 45% (FDA warning following increased mortality). Sedative-hypnotics have inconsistent effects and should be avoided in most patients with moderate-to-severe OSA; opioids worsen CSA in a dose-dependent way. In OSA the pharyngeal airway lacks fixed bony/cartilaginous support, so patency depends on pharyngeal dilator muscles. Inspiration generates increasingly negative intraluminal pressure (a suctioning force); at sleep onset neuromuscular output to these muscles declines, and in a collapsible airway this causes transient pharyngeal collapse (apnoea) or near-collapse (hypopnoea), typically terminated by an arousal that restores muscle activity. Collapse sites include the soft palate (most common), tongue base, lateral pharyngeal walls, and epiglottis. OSA is often worst in REM sleep (lowest skeletal-muscle output) and supine (gravity). A small pharyngeal lumen (soft-tissue enlargement from fat, lymphoid tissue, or genetic variation; craniofacial factors such as mandibular retroposition/micrognathia), low lung volume (reduced caudal pharyngeal traction, pronounced in obesity), and high nasal resistance all predispose to collapse. Pharyngeal muscle activation is linked to ventilatory drive: an over-sensitive ventilatory control system, a low arousal threshold (preempting CO2-mediated muscle compensation), or a high arousal threshold (prolonging apnoeas) all contribute. In OSA-related disease, sleep fragmentation, cortical arousals, and intermittent hypoxaemia/hypercapnia drive sympathetic overactivity, blood-pressure surges, a prothrombotic/proinflammatory state, insulin resistance, and large negative intrathoracic pressure swings that alter cardiac preload/afterload and promote cardiac/electrical remodelling. CSA is usually caused by increased PCO2 sensitivity producing hyperventilation alternating with apnoea, plus prolonged circulatory delay (heart failure) giving Cheyne-Stokes breathing. OSA is the most common medical cause of daytime sleepiness and reduces quality of life. It is strongly associated with cardiac, cerebrovascular and metabolic disease (coronary artery disease, heart failure with and without reduced EF, atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, atherosclerosis, stroke, diabetes), premature death, and increased risk of certain cancers. Untreated OSA carries a roughly twofold risk of occupational accidents and a two- to threefold increase in motor-vehicle crashes. CPAP improves alertness, mood, quality of life, blood pressure and insulin sensitivity, but randomized trials have NOT shown that CPAP reduces cardiovascular/stroke events or prolongs survival. CSA carries increased risk for heart failure and atrial fibrillation, and its treatment has not been shown to improve long-term outcomes; adaptive servoventilation showed no cardiovascular or mortality benefit and increased mortality in patients with LVEF below 45%. OSA severity by apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI = apnoeas plus hypopnoeas per hour of sleep): mild OSAHS = AHI 5-14 events/h; moderate OSAHS = AHI 15-29 events/h; severe OSAHS = AHI at least 30 events/h. The respiratory disturbance index (RDI) additionally counts respiratory effort-related arousals (RERAs). Each AHI level can be further qualified by the degree of sleepiness and associated hypoxaemia (Table 308-2, p.2280).

another hypnotic as the trigger Missing coexisting restless legs syndrome that is driving the arousals Neglecting kitchen and home safety, leaving a risk of injury or fire Sleep-related eating disorder is regarded as a disorder of arousal, a non-REM parasomnia in which incomplete transition from deep sleep to wakefulness allows automatic feeding behaviour to occur while consciousness and memory systems remain largely offline. Conditions that fragment sleep, such as restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movements, and drugs that promote complex sleep-related behaviours, especially certain hypnotics, lower the threshold for these partial arousals and the associated eating. The disorder tends to be chronic if untreated, but many patients improve substantially once precipitating drugs are stopped and any underlying restless legs or arousal disorder is treated; safety measures reduce the risk of injury in the meantime.

Sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy — SHE, nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy, autosomal dominant nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy NREM parasomnias (sleepwalking, sleep terrors, confusional arousals) REM sleep behaviour disorder Obstructive sleep apnoea with arousals Nocturnal panic attacks Paroxysmal nocturnal movement disorders Video-EEG and video polysomnography to capture and characterise events MRI of the brain to seek a structural focus Detailed semiological description and event stereotypy assessment Genetic evaluation where an autosomal dominant pattern is present Family history of nocturnal events Stereotyped hyperkinetic or dystonic seizures arising predominantly from sleep, often in clusters through the night Attacks are brief, sudden and highly stereotyped for a given patient, distinguishing them from parasomnias Seizures frequently originate in the frontal lobe, though other cortical origins occur An autosomal dominant form is linked to mutations in neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit genes and others Events emerge mainly from non-REM sleep and the patient may be aware during or immediately after them Video-EEG and video polysomnography help separate it from NREM parasomnias and REM sleep behaviour disorder Frequent nocturnal clusters causing injury or major sleep disruption Daytime seizures or new focal neurological signs A structural lesion on imaging Diagnostic uncertainty between seizures and parasomnia Misdiagnosing stereotyped nocturnal seizures as parasomnias or psychiatric events Relying on routine daytime EEG, which is often normal Overlooking a family history pointing to the inherited form Failing to capture events with video for accurate classification Sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy is a focal epilepsy in which seizures are strongly modulated by sleep, arising most often from mesial or other frontal regions and producing dramatic hyperkinetic, dystonic or ambulatory motor behaviour. In the inherited form, mutations affecting neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and related genes alter cholinergic modulation of the sleep-wake and arousal networks, lowering the threshold for seizures during non-REM sleep. The stereotypy and brevity of events reflect their epileptic rather than parasomnic origin. Seizures often respond to antiseizure medication, though a proportion are drug-resistant; the disorder is typically lifelong but many patients achieve good control.

Sleep-related leg cramps — nocturnal leg cramps Restless legs syndrome Periodic limb movement disorder Peripheral neuropathy or radiculopathy Peripheral arterial disease with claudication Dystonia or myopathy with cramps Electrolyte disturbance (for example low potassium, calcium or magnesium) Clinical diagnosis from the description and relief by stretching Review for dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and culprit medications Assessment for peripheral vascular and neurological disease when frequent Targeted blood tests where a secondary cause is suspected Further neurological evaluation if cramps are severe, generalised or progressive Sudden painful involuntary contractions, usually of the calf or small foot muscles, occurring during the sleep period The cramp produces a palpably hard, tight muscle and is relieved by forceful stretching or massage of the affected muscle Unlike restless legs syndrome, the problem is frank painful muscle contraction rather than an urge to move with relief on movement Prevalence rises with age and cramps are common in pregnancy Secondary contributors include dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, peripheral vascular or neurological disease and certain drugs Management emphasises stretching, addressing reversible contributors and reviewing culprit medications Cramps with progressive weakness, wasting or sensory loss Features of significant peripheral arterial disease Widespread or daytime cramps suggesting a systemic or neuromuscular disorder Marked electrolyte abnormalities Confusing leg cramps with restless legs syndrome and mismanaging them Overlooking peripheral vascular or neurological disease when cramps are frequent Not reviewing medications that can provoke cramps Missing correctable dehydration or electrolyte disturbance Sleep-related leg cramps arise from sustained involuntary hyperexcitable motor-unit discharge in a muscle, producing a sudden painful contraction; the tendency is increased by muscle shortening during sleep and by factors that alter neuromuscular excitability. Ageing, pregnancy, fluid and electrolyte shifts, and peripheral nerve or vascular disease can lower the threshold for these discharges. In many people the cramps are idiopathic, reflecting benign motor-neuron hyperexcitability rather than a defined underlying disease. The cramps are benign though disruptive to sleep; many respond to stretching and correction of reversible contributors, and idiopathic cases often fluctuate over time.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis — SCFE, SUFE, slipped upper femoral epiphysis, femoral head epiphysis slip Perthes' disease Transient synovitis of the hip Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis Juvenile idiopathic arthritis Femoral neck stress fracture or trauma Muscle strain or apophyseal avulsion Referred pain from other hip or spinal pathology Anteroposterior and frog-lateral pelvic radiographs of both hips (the lateral view is key for subtle slips) Assessment of Klein's line and the physeal appearance MRI or ultrasound in equivocal cases or to assess a pre-slip Endocrine and metabolic workup (e.g. thyroid function, renal function) in young, atypical, or bilateral presentations Careful hip examination for loss of internal rotation and obligatory external rotation on flexion A displacement of the proximal femoral epiphysis through the growth plate, typically in overweight adolescents around the time of the pubertal growth spurt Presents with hip, groin, thigh, or referred knee pain and a limp; knee or thigh pain in an adolescent must always prompt examination of the hip A characteristic sign is obligatory external rotation of the hip when it is passively flexed, with limited internal rotation Radiographs should include a frog-lateral view, as subtle slips are best seen laterally; a line along the superior femoral neck (Klein's line) normally intersects the epiphysis Slips are classified by symptom duration (acute, chronic, acute-on-chronic) and by whether the child can weight-bear (stable versus unstable), which strongly influences the risk of avascular necrosis It is an orthopaedic urgency: once suspected the child should stop weight-bearing and be referred promptly, as further slipping worsens the outlook Treatment is surgical stabilisation, usually in-situ pinning to prevent progression, and the contralateral hip may be pinned if at high risk Consider an underlying endocrine or metabolic disorder (e.g. hypothyroidism, renal disease) in atypical, young, or bilateral cases SURGICAL URGENCY: suspected SCFE requires immediate non-weight-bearing and prompt referral to prevent further slip Unstable slip (inability to weight-bear) carrying a high risk of avascular necrosis Adolescent knee or thigh pain that could be referred from an undiagnosed hip slip Bilateral or very young presentation suggesting an underlying endocrine or metabolic disorder Attributing knee or thigh pain to the knee and failing to image the hip, leading to missed or late diagnosis Allowing continued weight-bearing on a suspected slip, risking further displacement and avascular necrosis Missing a subtle slip by not obtaining a frog-lateral radiograph Overlooking an underlying endocrine cause in atypical or bilateral cases Slipped capital femoral epiphysis occurs when shear forces exceed the strength of the proximal femoral physis, allowing the epiphysis to displace, typically posteriorly and inferiorly, relative to the femoral neck (so the neck effectively rotates anteriorly and externally on the head). The physis is mechanically weakest during the adolescent growth spurt, and obesity increases the mechanical load, while hormonal factors influence physeal strength, explaining associations with endocrine disorders. In unstable slips the epiphyseal blood supply, which runs along the femoral neck, is at high risk of disruption, predisposing to avascular necrosis. Residual deformity from a healed slip alters femoral head-neck morphology and can cause femoroacetabular impingement and early osteoarthritis. Stable slips treated promptly with in-situ fixation generally do well, whereas unstable slips carry a substantial risk of avascular necrosis and chondrolysis; even after successful fixation, residual femoral head-neck deformity can cause impingement and predispose to premature osteoarthritis, so long-term follow-up is important.

testing Overlooking cervical spine and cardiac surveillance Sly syndrome is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in GUSB, encoding the lysosomal enzyme beta-glucuronidase. This enzyme participates in the degradation of dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate, and chondroitin-4/6-sulfate, so its deficiency causes accumulation of all these glycosaminoglycans within lysosomes across many tissues. The resulting storage produces multisystem disease affecting the skeleton, connective tissue, viscera, cardiovascular system, and, in more severe forms, the central nervous system. Severe cases can present antenatally with non-immune hydrops fetalis. Excess glycosaminoglycans are excreted in the urine. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and the degree of residual enzyme activity broadly correlates with the wide clinical spectrum. Prognosis depends heavily on the phenotype; severe neonatal disease with hydrops carries high early mortality, while attenuated forms may allow survival into adulthood with variable disability. Enzyme replacement therapy can improve some somatic manifestations.

Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcaemic type — SCCOHT, hypercalcaemic small cell carcinoma of the ovary, SMARCA4-deficient ovarian carcinoma, ovarian small cell carcinoma of hypercalcaemic type Adult granulosa cell tumour and other sex cord-stromal tumours Dysgerminoma and other malignant germ cell tumours Small cell carcinoma of pulmonary type involving the ovary Metastatic small round blue cell tumours (e.g. lymphoma, neuroblastoma) Poorly differentiated (high-grade) ovarian carcinoma Primary neuroendocrine carcinoma Histopathology with immunohistochemistry showing loss of SMARCA4 (BRG1) expression Serum corrected calcium and parathyroid hormone-related protein assessment Cross-sectional imaging of the abdomen, pelvis, and chest for staging Serum tumour markers to help exclude germ cell and epithelial tumours Germline SMARCA4 genetic testing and genetic counselling Baseline renal function and electrocardiography in the context of hypercalcaemia This is a rare, highly aggressive ovarian malignancy that characteristically affects adolescents and young women rather than older adults About two-thirds of patients have paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia, which may cause fatigue, nausea, constipation, polyuria, and confusion and can be the presenting clue Despite the historical name, it is not of neuroendocrine origin; it is now defined by loss of the chromatin-remodelling protein SMARCA4 (BRG1) It shares molecular features with malignant rhabdoid tumours, and some cases are associated with germline SMARCA4 variants, so family history and genetic assessment matter Tumours are usually large and unilateral at diagnosis and frequently present at an advanced stage with extra-ovarian spread Diagnosis rests on histology with immunohistochemistry demonstrating loss of SMARCA4 (BRG1) expression, distinguishing it from other small round cell tumours Management is delivered by a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team and combines tumour-directed surgery with aggressive chemotherapy, and the hypercalcaemia typically resolves as the tumour is controlled Severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia with dehydration, arrhythmia, or altered consciousness requiring urgent correction A rapidly enlarging pelvic or abdominal mass with constitutional symptoms Evidence of advanced-stage disease with extra-ovarian spread A young patient with an ovarian mass and unexplained hypercalcaemia Assuming ovarian cancer is a disease of older women and discounting it in a young patient Attributing hypercalcaemia to bony metastases rather than recognising a paraneoplastic mechanism Misclassifying the tumour as a germ cell or sex cord-stromal neoplasm without SMARCA4 immunohistochemistry Overlooking the possibility of a germline SMARCA4 variant and omitting genetic referral Small cell carcinoma of the ovary of hypercalcaemic type is a chromatin-remodelling-driven malignancy defined by inactivation of SMARCA4, the gene encoding BRG1, a core ATPase subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling complex. Loss of this subunit disrupts the complex's control of gene expression and differentiation, driving an undifferentiated, highly proliferative tumour that resembles malignant rhabdoid tumours molecularly. The paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia is attributed to tumour production of parathyroid hormone-related protein, which promotes bone resorption and renal calcium retention independent of bony metastasis. A subset of patients carry germline SMARCA4 variants, linking the tumour to an inherited rhabdoid tumour predisposition. The tumour is aggressive and carries a poor prognosis overall, particularly when it presents at an advanced stage, though outcomes are better for early-stage disease treated with multimodal therapy. Younger age and higher stage generally portend a worse outcome, and relapse is common.

others include Sjogren and other autoimmune disease, amyloidosis, sodium-channel gene variants, alcohol, and drugs, while a large proportion remain idiopathic The pain is neuropathic in character and is often worse at night Management: treat any underlying cause, use neuropathic-pain measures, address autonomic symptoms, and avoid neurotoxic exposures Rapidly progressive or profoundly disabling symptoms suggesting vasculitis or amyloidosis Prominent autonomic failure suggesting a systemic or amyloid process Systemic features such as weight loss or organ involvement pointing to a serious underlying cause Motor weakness or large-fibre signs indicating a broader neuropathy Excluding the diagnosis because nerve conduction studies are normal Failing to search for treatable causes such as impaired glucose tolerance or Sjogren syndrome Overlooking autonomic involvement Attributing genuine neuropathic pain to a purely functional or psychological cause Small fibre neuropathy is a disorder of the small-diameter peripheral nerve fibres, the thinly myelinated A-delta and unmyelinated C fibres, that carry pain and temperature sensation and mediate autonomic function. Damage to these fibres, which may be length-dependent (beginning in the feet) or non-length-dependent, produces spontaneous neuropathic pain and impaired thermal and pain sensation, together with autonomic disturbances of sweating, cardiovascular regulation, and visceral function. The underlying mechanisms are diverse, including metabolic injury from diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance, immune-mediated damage, amyloid deposition, toxic and drug exposures, and gain-of-function sodium-channel gene variants that render nociceptors hyperexcitable; in many patients no cause is found. Because large fibres are spared, routine nerve conduction studies are typically normal. Prognosis depends on the cause: where a treatable driver such as impaired glucose tolerance or an autoimmune disorder is identified and managed, symptoms may stabilise or improve, whereas idiopathic and amyloid-related forms tend to progress; pain and autonomic symptoms are often the main long-term burden.

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth — SIBO Irritable bowel syndrome Coeliac disease Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency Carbohydrate malabsorption (for example lactose) Inflammatory bowel disease Bile acid diarrhoea Carbohydrate breath testing (for example glucose or lactulose) Assessment for underlying motility disorders or anatomical abnormalities Nutritional studies including vitamin B12 and fat-soluble vitamins in suspected malabsorption Coeliac serology and pancreatic assessment to exclude mimics Small-bowel imaging where structural causes are suspected Excessive numbers of bacteria in the small intestine causing bloating, flatulence, diarrhoea and, when severe, malabsorption It is a consequence of impaired clearance of small-bowel bacteria rather than a communicable infection Predisposing factors include disordered motility, anatomical changes such as blind loops and strictures, and loss of protective gastric acid Severe or long-standing cases can cause fat and vitamin B12 malabsorption with weight loss and deficiency Breath testing after a carbohydrate load is commonly used, though it has recognised limitations Treatment combines antibiotics with correction of the underlying predisposing factor where possible Weight loss and features of malabsorption Vitamin deficiency states An underlying structural lesion such as a stricture or fistula Failure to respond to appropriate treatment Diagnosing it on symptoms alone given overlap with irritable bowel syndrome Treating recurrent episodes without addressing the underlying motility or anatomical cause Over-reliance on breath tests despite their limitations Missing malabsorption and nutritional deficiencies Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth develops when the mechanisms that normally keep the small-bowel bacterial population low, principally propulsive motility, gastric acid and an intact ileocaecal valve, are impaired. Overgrowth of predominantly colonic-type bacteria in the small bowel leads to fermentation of carbohydrates, producing gas and bloating, deconjugation of bile salts causing fat malabsorption, and competition for and altered handling of nutrients such as vitamin B12. It is therefore a disorder of dysbiosis and impaired clearance secondary to motility or structural abnormalities, not a primary infective disease. Symptoms usually improve with antibiotic treatment, but recurrence is common when the underlying predisposing factor persists, so addressing the cause is important for durable control.

keratin negativity excludes an epithelial or carcinoma-related process Failing to test for BRG1 loss in an undifferentiated thoracic mass Misinterpreting co-loss of BRM as an unrelated finding rather than part of the characteristic profile Overreliance on a single marker rather than the integrated morphological and immunohistochemical picture This tumour is defined by biallelic loss of function of SMARCA4, which encodes the BRG1 ATPase at the heart of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling complex. Loss of BRG1 disrupts nucleosome positioning and the regulation of differentiation-associated genes, producing a highly undifferentiated, often rhabdoid phenotype. The strong link with tobacco exposure suggests a background of heavy mutational damage, and the resulting dependence on residual chromatin-remodelling and epigenetic pathways is being explored as a therapeutic vulnerability. The tumour behaves very aggressively, with rapid progression, frequent metastasis and short median survival despite chemotherapy and radiotherapy; complete resection is often not feasible because of extent at presentation, and immune checkpoint inhibition has shown responses in some patients, keeping treatment approaches under active investigation.

nerve compromise Inadequate follow-up allowing undetected re-displacement A force directed onto the dorsum of a flexed wrist, or a fall onto the back of the hand, fractures the distal radial The pull of the forearm muscles and the inherent instability of the pattern tend to recreate volar angulation after reduction, so maintenance of reduction in plaster is difficult. Volar displacement can also crowd the carpal tunnel, threatening the median nerve, and articular extension of the fracture line predisposes to incongruity and later arthritis. Because volar-displaced fractures are unstable and prone to re-displacement, many require operative fixation; anatomical volar plate fixation generally restores good function, whereas malunion causes deformity, weakness and median nerve symptoms.

sequencing Escalating or refractory seizures requiring urgent neurological review Rapidly increasing head circumference or signs of raised intracranial pressure Developmental regression Feeding difficulties with faltering growth in infancy Overlooking somatic mosaicism, so that standard blood testing yields a falsely negative result Confusing the picture with tuberous sclerosis and missing the specific MTOR diagnosis Attributing macrocephaly to a benign familial cause and delaying evaluation of developmental delay and seizures Initiating mTOR inhibition outside a specialist framework without appropriate monitoring MTOR encodes the catalytic kinase of two complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, which integrate growth-factor and nutrient signals to drive protein synthesis, cell growth and proliferation while restraining autophagy. Gain-of-function variants lock the kinase in an overactive state, so downstream signalling proceeds even without normal upstream cues. In the developing brain this excessive signalling enlarges neurons and disturbs cortical organisation, producing megalencephaly, epilepsy and intellectual disability, while its effects in other tissues account for the overgrowth and pigmentary skin changes. Because the abnormality lies in a well-characterised and pharmacologically accessible pathway, rational suppression of mTOR activity is an area of active therapeutic interest. The condition is lifelong, with intellectual disability that ranges from mild to severe and epilepsy that may be difficult to control in some children; overall outlook depends heavily on seizure burden and developmental trajectory, and emerging mTOR-pathway therapies may in future modify aspects of the phenotype though evidence remains preliminary.

Ambiguous genitalia requiring urgent endocrine evaluation Feeding difficulties, failure to thrive and recurrent illness Signs of adrenal insufficiency during stress Measuring only total cholesterol, which can be normal, rather than specific sterol profiling Missing adrenal insufficiency during intercurrent illness or surgery Attributing the phenotype to a chromosomal syndrome without sterol testing Assuming cholesterol supplementation reliably improves neurodevelopment 7-Dehydrocholesterol reductase catalyses the last step of cholesterol synthesis, reducing 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholesterol. In Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome this enzyme is deficient, so cholesterol production falls and the immediate precursor 7-dehydrocholesterol and its isomer accumulate. Cholesterol is essential for cell membranes, myelin, bile acids, steroid hormones and Sonic hedgehog signalling during embryogenesis. Deficiency during development therefore disrupts morphogenesis (explaining the malformation pattern, including holoprosencephaly-spectrum features from impaired hedgehog signalling), while accumulated precursor sterols may exert additional toxic effects. Impaired steroidogenesis contributes to the genital and adrenal manifestations. Prognosis correlates with disease severity: the most severely affected infants have major malformations and high early mortality, whereas milder cases survive with variable intellectual disability and behavioural difficulties. Cholesterol supplementation may improve some physical parameters, but its benefit for cognition and behaviour is not clearly established.

circadian sleep-wake rhythm with an inverted melatonin cycle (melatonin secreted during the day rather than at night), causing daytime sleepiness and marked night-time waking Characteristic established by chromosomal microarray to detect the 17p11.2 deletion, or by RAI1 sequencing when a deletion is not found Severe self-injurious behaviour causing significant tissue damage Profound sleep deprivation affecting safety and daytime functioning New or worsening scoliosis with respiratory or neurological compromise Acute behavioural crisis posing risk to the patient or others Attributing the sleep disturbance to primary behavioural insomnia and missing the underlying inverted melatonin rhythm Overlooking the diagnosis in a child labelled with non-syndromic autism or intellectual disability Failing to recognise the characteristic self-injurious and self-hugging behaviours as diagnostic clues Not arranging chromosomal microarray, or stopping at a normal microarray without considering RAI1 sequencing Smith-Magenis syndrome results from haploinsufficiency of RAI1 (retinoic acid-induced 1), whether through the common 17p11.2 microdeletion or a point variant within the gene. RAI1 is a transcriptional regulator with widespread roles in neurodevelopment and, importantly, in the control of circadian gene expression. Reduced RAI1 dosage disrupts the molecular circadian clock, producing the hallmark inversion of the melatonin secretion rhythm and the resulting sleep-wake disturbance, while its broader transcriptional effects account for the cognitive, behavioural, craniofacial, and multisystem features of the syndrome. Smith-Magenis syndrome is a lifelong condition; intellectual disability and behavioural and sleep difficulties persist, but life expectancy is generally not markedly reduced and structured behavioural, sleep, and developmental interventions can meaningfully improve quality of life.

Snakebite envenomation — venomous snakebite, elapid envenomation, viper envenomation, crotalid envenomation, ophidism Non-venomous or dry bite with anxiety and local trauma Other envenomation (scorpion, spider) or arthropod bite Anaphylaxis to an unrelated allergen Cellulitis or necrotising soft-tissue infection Primary neuromuscular disorder (myasthenic crisis, Guillain-Barre syndrome) Sepsis or another cause of consumptive coagulopathy 20-minute whole-blood clotting test at the bedside as a screen for coagulopathy Full coagulation studies including prothrombin time, fibrinogen and D-dimer Full blood count for thrombocytopenia and evolving anaemia Creatine kinase, renal function and urinalysis for rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria Serial spirometry or forced vital capacity to track neurotoxic respiratory decline Electrocardiography and continuous monitoring in systemic envenomation Broad syndromes vary by family: elapids (cobras, kraits, mambas, taipans) tend to produce neurotoxic descending paralysis, while vipers cause local cytotoxicity, coagulopathy and haemorrhage A dry bite (no envenomation) is common; observe for a meaningful period before excluding envenomation, as neurotoxic and coagulation effects may be delayed Ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, bulbar weakness and progressive respiratory muscle failure are the hallmarks of neurotoxic envenomation and mandate close airway monitoring Venom-induced consumption coagulopathy (VICC) can render blood incoagulable; a bedside 20-minute whole-blood clotting test is a useful field indicator of systemic viper envenomation Progressive local swelling, blistering, bruising and tissue necrosis characterise cytotoxic bites and can cause compartment syndrome Species-appropriate antivenom is the definitive treatment for systemic envenomation; timing, dose to effect and monitoring for anaphylactoid reactions are key principles Pressure immobilisation is appropriate for neurotoxic elapid and sea-snake bites to delay systemic spread, but is NOT recommended for cytotoxic viper bites where it may worsen local tissue injury Reassess repeatedly, as neurotoxicity and coagulopathy can evolve or recur and may require repeat antivenom dosing Progressive bulbar or respiratory muscle weakness threatening the airway Spontaneous systemic bleeding or an incoagulable 20-minute clotting test Rapidly advancing limb swelling with features suggesting compartment syndrome Shock, oliguria or acute kidney injury Anaphylactoid reaction to antivenom during infusion Applying arterial tourniquets or incising/sucking the wound, which increase local tissue damage without benefit Delaying antivenom in evolving systemic envenomation while awaiting definitive species identification Discharging early after an apparent dry bite before delayed neurotoxicity or coagulopathy has been excluded Using pressure immobilisation for cytotoxic viper bites where it aggravates local necrosis Failing to monitor for and treat recurrent coagulopathy or neurotoxicity after initial improvement Snake venoms are complex mixtures of enzymes and peptides that produce syndrome-specific injury. Pre-synaptic and post-synaptic neurotoxins block neuromuscular transmission to cause a descending flaccid paralysis affecting cranial, bulbar and respiratory muscles. Procoagulant and fibrinolytic components activate the clotting cascade and consume fibrinogen, producing venom-induced consumption coagulopathy with a risk of spontaneous haemorrhage, while haemorrhagins damage vascular endothelium. Cytotoxins, phospholipases and metalloproteinases cause local tissue oedema, blistering and necrosis, and some venoms produce myotoxicity with rhabdomyolysis or systemic capillary leak and shock. With timely species-appropriate antivenom and supportive care including ventilation for neurotoxic paralysis, most patients recover fully. Delayed treatment increases the risk of death from respiratory failure or haemorrhage, and severe cytotoxic bites may leave permanent tissue loss or amputation.

Snakebite envenomation — venomous snakebite, snake envenoming Dry bite or non-venomous snakebite Other arthropod or animal envenomation Cellulitis or wound infection Anaphylaxis to the bite Primary bleeding or neuromuscular disorder Whole-blood clotting test and coagulation studies Full blood count for thrombocytopenia and haemolysis Renal function and creatine kinase for kidney injury and myotoxicity Serial neurological assessment for progressive paralysis Species identification where safely possible to guide antivenom choice Effects depend on the species and venom, broadly divided into local tissue injury, systemic coagulopathy, neurotoxicity and, with some species, myotoxicity Not every bite by a venomous snake injects venom, so a proportion are dry bites without envenoming Progressive local swelling, spontaneous bleeding and a positive whole-blood clotting test point to significant envenoming Neurotoxic envenoming may cause ptosis, ophthalmoplegia and progressive descending paralysis with respiratory failure Antivenom is the specific treatment for systemic envenoming, given according to clinical and laboratory features Pressure immobilisation may be appropriate for some neurotoxic elapid bites, whereas tourniquets and incision are harmful Spontaneous systemic bleeding or incoagulable blood Progressive weakness, ptosis or respiratory compromise Rapidly advancing local swelling or compartment syndrome Oliguria or evidence of acute kidney injury Applying harmful first aid such as tourniquets, incision or suction Assuming a dry bite too early and discharging before observation Delaying antivenom in evolving systemic envenoming Overlooking airway and ventilatory support in neurotoxic envenoming Snake venoms are complex mixtures of enzymes and toxins that damage tissue and disrupt physiological systems. Depending on species, components cause local cytotoxic and necrotic injury, consumptive coagulopathy through activation or destruction of clotting factors, presynaptic or postsynaptic neuromuscular blockade producing paralysis, and rhabdomyolysis. The resulting syndromes include painful progressive local swelling, systemic bleeding, flaccid paralysis and acute kidney injury from myoglobinuria or the coagulopathy. With timely antivenom and supportive care many patients recover fully, but delayed treatment, severe neurotoxicity, coagulopathy or local necrosis can lead to disability, limb loss or death.

Snapping hip syndrome (coxa saltans) — coxa saltans, dancer's hip, iliopsoas tendon snapping Greater trochanteric pain syndrome or trochanteric bursitis Iliopsoas bursitis or tendinopathy Labral tear or femoroacetabular impingement Intra-articular loose body or chondral lesion Hip osteoarthritis Femoral neck stress fracture Athletic pubalgia Dynamic ultrasound as a first-line study to demonstrate the snapping tendon Clinical reproduction manoeuvres for the external and internal types Plain radiographs to assess bony morphology, impingement and osteoarthritis MRI or MR arthrography to evaluate the labrum and intra-articular structures A diagnostic injection into the iliopsoas sheath or bursa to confirm the pain source The hallmark is an audible or palpable snap or clunk felt during hip movement The external type is caused by the iliotibial band or gluteus maximus tendon flicking over the greater trochanter, giving lateral symptoms The internal type is caused by the iliopsoas tendon shifting over the iliopectineal eminence or femoral head, giving anterior or groin symptoms The intra-articular type is caused by a labral tear, loose body or chondral lesion It most often affects young active people such as dancers and athletes and is frequently painless, though it can become symptomatic The external snap can often be reproduced and even seen by the patient, whereas the internal snap is elicited by extending the hip from a flexed, abducted, externally rotated position Dynamic ultrasound is particularly useful to demonstrate the offending tendon snapping in real time Generic management includes activity modification, stretching and physiotherapy, corticosteroid injection into the bursa or iliopsoas sheath, and surgical lengthening, release or arthroscopy for refractory or intra-articular causes Intra-articular mechanical symptoms such as locking suggesting a loose body or labral tear Night pain or systemic features raising concern for tumour or infection Progressive activity-related pain suggesting a femoral neck stress fracture Progressive loss of function Missing intra-articular pathology by labelling all snapping as a benign tendon cause Overtreating asymptomatic snapping that needs only reassurance Causing iatrogenic weakness through excessive tendon lengthening Failing to use dynamic imaging to confirm the mechanism Snapping hip syndrome describes a snapping sensation produced when a tendon or band catches on a bony prominence, or when an intra-articular lesion mechanically catches. In the external type the iliotibial band or gluteus maximus tendon flicks across the greater trochanter, while in the internal type the iliopsoas tendon abruptly shifts over the iliopectineal eminence or femoral head as the hip extends from a flexed position. The intra-articular type stems from labral tears or loose bodies. Repetitive movement of the offending structure commonly leads to a secondary tendinopathy or bursitis that generates pain. Most patients respond to conservative measures, and surgery reserved for refractory cases generally gives good results, though intra-articular causes require specific treatment.

Snapping scapula syndrome — scapulothoracic bursitis, snapping scapula, scapulothoracic crepitus, washboard syndrome Isolated scapulothoracic bursitis Osteochondroma or other bony lesion of the scapula or ribs Scapular dyskinesis or muscle imbalance Long thoracic or spinal accessory nerve palsy causing scapular winging Cervicothoracic referred pain Rotator cuff or glenohumeral pathology Plain radiographs including tangential scapular views CT to define bony lesions such as an osteochondroma or a prominent angle MRI or ultrasound to assess the bursae and soft tissues Clinical assessment of scapular motion, winging and dyskinesis Diagnostic bursal injection where scapulothoracic bursitis is suspected Painful audible or palpable snapping or grating (crepitus) of the scapula on the chest wall during shoulder movement Arises at the scapulothoracic articulation, with scapulothoracic bursitis and/or bony or soft-tissue abnormalities at the medial and superomedial scapula Often related to overuse in overhead and throwing activities and to scapular dyskinesis and posture Causes include inflamed scapulothoracic bursae, muscle atrophy or fibrosis, and bony lesions such as osteochondroma or a prominent superomedial angle Examination looks for crepitus, tenderness, scapular winging and dyskinesis Imaging (radiographs, CT for bony lesions, MRI or ultrasound for soft tissue and bursae) is used when a structural cause is suspected Most cases respond to conservative management with postural and scapular stabilisation rehabilitation, load modification and sometimes bursal injection; surgery is reserved for structural lesions or refractory bursitis Fixed scapular winging suggesting a nerve palsy (long thoracic or spinal accessory) A firm mass or rapidly growing lesion suggesting tumour Night pain or systemic features suggesting neoplasm or infection Progressive neurological deficit Attributing symptomatic crepitus to a benign cause without excluding an osteochondroma or other bony lesion Missing a nerve palsy as a cause of associated winging Neglecting scapular dyskinesis and posture in rehabilitation Rushing to surgery before a trial of conservative care in non-structural cases The scapula glides over the posterior chest wall at the scapulothoracic articulation, cushioned by bursae. Snapping scapula syndrome arises when this smooth gliding is disturbed, whether by inflamed or fibrotic scapulothoracic bursae, by altered muscle bulk or scarring, or by bony incongruity such as an osteochondroma, a prominent superomedial angle or a malunited rib or scapular fracture. Repetitive overhead loading, scapular dyskinesis and poor posture contribute. The result is symptomatic crepitus and pain as the scapula tracks over the chest wall. The majority improve with scapular rehabilitation and load management; outcomes are good after excision when a discrete bony lesion is the cause.

Sneddon syndrome — Sneddon's syndrome, livedo racemosa with cerebrovascular disease, idiopathic livedo reticularis with cerebrovascular accidents Antiphospholipid syndrome without the full livedo picture Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue disease Systemic vasculitis such as polyarteritis nodosa Cholesterol embolisation syndrome Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and other thrombotic microangiopathies Cryoglobulinaemia Antiphospholipid antibody panel including lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I Brain MRI and MR angiography to document infarcts and small-vessel disease Skin biopsy taken from the white centre of the livedo net to capture occluded arterioles Connective tissue and vasculitis serology to exclude alternative causes Echocardiography and thrombophilia screening to assess embolic and prothrombotic sources Defined by the combination of widespread livedo racemosa and recurrent ischaemic cerebrovascular events Livedo is a persistent, broken, irregular net-like violaceous pattern that often precedes strokes by years Affects predominantly young to middle-aged women and presents with strokes, transient ischaemic attacks, and progressive cognitive decline A substantial subset have antiphospholipid antibodies, linking it to the antiphospholipid syndrome spectrum Hypertension, headache, and vascular dementia are frequent accompaniments Skin biopsy from the border of livedo may show a non-inflammatory occlusive vasculopathy of small dermal arteries Management centres on antithrombotic therapy and control of vascular risk factors rather than a specific cure Recurrent strokes in a young patient with persistent livedo Rapidly progressive cognitive decline Catastrophic thrombotic events suggesting antiphospholipid syndrome New focal neurological deficits despite antithrombotic therapy Dismissing livedo racemosa as benign livedo reticularis and missing the underlying vasculopathy Failing to test for antiphospholipid antibodies, which alters anticoagulation decisions Taking skin biopsy from the wrong site so the occlusive lesion is missed Attributing young-onset stroke to a single episode rather than a systemic vasculopathy Sneddon syndrome is a non-inflammatory occlusive arteriopathy affecting small and medium arteries of the skin and brain. Progressive endothelial injury and subintimal proliferation lead to partial then complete occlusion of dermal and cerebral vessels, producing the characteristic livedo racemosa and recurrent cerebral ischaemia. In antiphospholipid-antibody-positive cases a prothrombotic autoimmune mechanism contributes, whereas seronegative cases appear to reflect a primary vasculopathy; both converge on chronic small-vessel occlusion and cumulative brain injury. The condition tends to be progressive, with recurrent strokes and stepwise cognitive decline leading to vascular dementia in many patients; antithrombotic therapy and risk-factor control may slow but rarely halt the course.

Social anxiety disorder — social phobia, SAD Normal shyness or introversion Panic disorder with or without agoraphobia Generalised anxiety disorder Avoidant personality disorder Autism spectrum disorder with social difficulties Major depressive disorder with social withdrawal Body dysmorphic disorder driving social avoidance Structured clinical interview focusing on feared and avoided situations Standardised social anxiety rating scales to gauge severity and track response Screening for comorbid depression and alcohol or substance use Developmental history to distinguish from autism spectrum and personality disorders The defining feature is marked, persistent fear of one or more social or performance situations in which the person feels exposed to possible scrutiny, with fear of acting in a way that will be humiliating or negatively judged Feared situations are avoided or endured with intense distress, and the anxiety is out of proportion to any real threat and typically lasts many months A performance-only subtype exists, confined to situations such as public speaking, and often responds well to targeted strategies Onset is usually in childhood or adolescence, and the disorder is frequently underrecognised because sufferers are quiet and avoidant rather than disruptive Comorbidity with depression, other anxiety disorders, and alcohol misuse is common, and alcohol is often used as maladaptive self-medication First-line treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy with graded exposure and cognitive restructuring, with SSRIs or SNRIs as effective pharmacological options For circumscribed performance anxiety, beta-adrenergic blockade can dampen peripheral symptoms such as tremor and palpitations, used situationally rather than daily Distinguish from normal shyness by the degree of distress, avoidance, and functional impairment it causes Emerging suicidal ideation, particularly with comorbid depression Escalating alcohol or sedative use to cope with social situations Progressive social isolation with collapse of education, employment, or relationships Dismissing the presentation as mere shyness and missing significant impairment Overlooking comorbid alcohol misuse used as self-medication Failing to include exposure-based work, which is central to durable improvement Prescribing daily benzodiazepines and risking dependence Stopping SSRIs prematurely before an adequate response has developed Social anxiety disorder reflects an interaction between heritable temperamental traits, notably behavioural inhibition in early childhood, and altered function of fear and threat-appraisal circuits involving the amygdala and prefrontal cortex. Dysregulation of serotonergic and dopaminergic systems, heightened sensitivity to social evaluation, and learned avoidance that prevents disconfirmation of feared outcomes together maintain the condition. Social anxiety disorder is often chronic and, if untreated, can persist for many years with substantial functional impairment. Prognosis improves with cognitive behavioural therapy and pharmacotherapy, and is better with earlier onset of treatment and fewer comorbidities; the performance-only subtype generally carries a more favourable outlook.

Soft Tissue & Bone Sarcoma — sarcoma, osteosarcoma, GIST, Ewing sarcoma Benign soft tissue tumor / well-differentiated liposarcoma (atypical lipomatous tumor) - lacks metastatic potential Benign bone lesions with malignant potential: enchondroma and osteochondroma (to chondrosarcoma); fibrous dysplasia, bone infarcts, Paget's disease (to UPS or osteosarcoma) Lymphoma, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, and small-cell carcinoma (can be confused with the small round blue cells of Ewing's sarcoma) Osteoporosis vs metastatic spine disease in older patients (cortical bone preserved in osteoporosis; cortical destruction with metastases) Plasma cell tumors (the most common malignant tumor of bone) Core-needle (cutting needle) or small-incision biopsy of all new, persistent, or growing masses, placed so it can be encompassed in the definitive resection Plain radiographs and MRI for primary tumors of extremities or head/neck (MRI best for intramedullary and soft-tissue extension) CT for tumors of the chest, abdomen, or retroperitoneum (CT best for bone destruction and calcification pattern in osteosarcoma) Chest radiograph and chest CT to detect lung metastases Bone scan or FDG-PET to detect skeletal metastases (almost all osteosarcomas are hypervascular and PET-avid) Radionuclide bone scanning (sensitive to new bone formation) for osteoblastic lesions; plain radiography for osteolytic lesions (may not be apparent until >1 cm) Serum alkaline phosphatase (elevated with prominent osteoblastic activity) and monitoring for hypercalcemia (osteolytic) or hypocalcemia (extensive osteoblastic) Osteoporotic vertebral disease mimicking spinal bone metastasis in older patients Benign enchondroma / osteochondroma mimicking low-grade chondrosarcoma (difficult to distinguish by x-ray or histology; new pain, inflammation, or progressive size increase suggests malignancy) Well-encapsulated benign-appearing lesion produced by the compressed pseudocapsule of a soft tissue sarcoma Sarcomas are rare (<1% of all malignancies) mesenchymal neoplasms arising in bone and soft tissues, usually of mesodermal origin and biologically distinct from the more common epithelial cancers (p.727). The most common presentation of a soft tissue sarcoma is an asymptomatic mass; mechanical symptoms from pressure, traction, or entrapment of nerves or muscles may also occur (p.728). Approximately 60% of soft tissue sarcomas arise in the extremities (lower limbs involved three times as often as upper), 30% in the trunk (retroperitoneum = 40% of trunk lesions), and 10% in the head and neck (p.727). The pulmonary parenchyma is the most common site of metastasis for soft tissue sarcomas; lung radiograph plus chest CT is important for detecting lung metastases (p.728). Histologic grade and primary tumor size are the most important prognostic factors; prognosis is related to AJCC stage and cure is common in the absence of metastatic disease (p.728). About one-third of soft tissue sarcomas carry a characteristic translocation with diagnostic/prognostic relevance (e.g., t(X;18)(p11;q11) involving SYT in ~90% of synovial sarcomas) (p.728). Most malignant GISTs carry activating c-kit mutations causing ligand-independent KIT receptor tyrosine kinase activation; ~5-10% have PDGFRA mutations, and KIT/PDGFRA wild-type GISTs may show SDH B/C/D mutations (p.728). Osteosarcoma accounts for almost 45% of bone sarcomas, is a spindle-cell neoplasm producing osteoid/bone, with predilection for metaphyses of long bones (distal femur, proximal tibia, proximal humerus); ~60% occur in the second decade (p.729-730). Classic osteosarcoma radiographic findings: a destructive moth-eaten lesion, spiculated periosteal reaction (sunburst appearance), and a cuff of periosteal new bone at the soft-tissue mass margin (Codman's triangle) (p.730). The most important predictive factor for long-term survival in osteosarcoma is response to chemotherapy; long-term survival in extremity osteosarcoma ranges from 60-80% (p.730). Ewing's sarcoma (~10-15% of bone sarcomas) peaks in the second decade, shows an 'onion peel' periosteal reaction with a soft-tissue mass, expresses p30/32 (MIC-2 product), and carries the t(11;22) translocation fusing fli-1 (chr 11) and ews (chr 22) (p.730). Chondrosarcoma (~20-25% of bone sarcomas) is a tumor of adulthood/old age (peak 4th-6th decades) with predilection for flat bones (shoulder, pelvic girdles); it has an indolent natural history and is mostly chemoresistant, with surgical resection the mainstay (p.730). Prostate, breast, and lung primaries account for 80% of all bone metastases; metastatic bone tumors are more common than primary bone tumors (p.730). Bone is a common metastatic site for prostate, breast, lung, kidney, bladder, and thyroid carcinomas and for lymphomas and sarcomas; in descending frequency the sites are vertebrae, proximal femur, pelvis, ribs, sternum, proximal humerus, and skull (p.730). When a patient with back pain develops neurologic signs or symptoms, emergency evaluation for spinal cord compression is indicated (p.730). An enlarging, deep, or large soft tissue mass requires biopsy - all new, persistent, or growing masses should be biopsied rather than ignored Back pain with new neurologic signs or symptoms mandates emergency evaluation for spinal cord compression New onset of pain, signs of inflammation, and progressive size increase in a cartilaginous lesion suggest malignant (chondrosarcoma) transformation Bone pain that develops gradually over weeks, is localized, and is more severe at night suggests bone metastasis Pathologic fracture, nerve root or cord compression, or myelophthisis from a destructive bony lesion Hypercalcemia symptoms in the setting of bony destruction Soft tissue sarcomas grow along fascial planes and compress surrounding tissue into a pseudocapsule, giving a deceptive well-encapsulated appearance; 'shelling out' (marginal excision / enucleation) results in a 50-90% probability of local recurrence - wide excision with a negative margin incorporating the biopsy site is standard. A biopsy of an enlarging/deep/large mass must be planned so the tract can be encompassed in the definitive resection and does not compromise a limb-sparing operation; an inappropriately placed incision compromises future limb salvage. Low-grade chondrosarcoma is difficult to distinguish from benign lesions on x-ray or histology, so diagnosis is influenced by clinical history and examination. Osteosarcoma is radioresistant - radiation therapy has no role in routine management. Forgetting non-pulmonary metastatic patterns: GISTs metastasize to liver, myxoid liposarcomas seek fatty tissue (retroperitoneum, mediastinum, subcutaneous), clear cell sarcomas may go to bone, and alveolar soft part sarcoma to CNS. In older patients (especially women), metastatic spine disease must be distinguished from osteoporosis - cortical bone is preserved in osteoporosis but destroyed by metastatic cancer. Sarcomas are mesenchymal neoplasms (mostly mesodermal, occasionally neuroectodermal) classified into ~20 groups by their pattern of differentiation toward normal tissue (e.g., rhabdomyosarcoma shows skeletal-muscle cross-striations, leiomyosarcoma shows smooth-muscle spindle fascicles, liposarcoma contains adipocytes). Malignant transformation of benign soft tissue tumors is extremely rare, except that malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (neurofibrosarcoma, malignant schwannoma) can arise from neurofibromas in neurofibromatosis. Etiologic contributors include radiation (tumor arises in the irradiated field, risk rising with time), scar tissue (prior surgery, burn, fracture, foreign body), chemical carcinogens (polycyclic hydrocarbons, asbestos, dioxin), HHV-8 (Kaposi's sarcoma - the only sarcoma virus-associated), and immunodeficiency/immunosuppression. Genetic syndromes include Li-Fraumeni (germline p53), neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1 on chr 17, encoding neurofibromin which inhibits ras), and germline RB1 mutation (chr 13q14, predisposing to osteosarcoma and radiation-unrelated soft tissue sarcomas). About one-third of soft tissue sarcomas carry characteristic translocations; most malignant GISTs have activating c-kit (KIT receptor tyrosine kinase) mutations, fewer have PDGFRA mutations. Bone metastases occur via hematogenous spread (or local invasion); tumors produce osteolytic lesions (via PTH-related peptide, vitamin D-like steroids, prostaglandins, IL-1, TNF inducing osteoclasts) and/or osteoblastic lesions (cytokines activating osteoblasts), with most lesions showing a mix. For soft tissue sarcoma, histologic grade and size are the most important prognostic factors and prognosis tracks AJCC stage; cure is common without metastatic disease, and a small number with metastases can still be cured. Metastatic soft tissue sarcomas are largely incurable, but up to 20% achieving complete response become long-term survivors. Historically most stage IV patients died within 12 months, but with multiple treatment lines, median survival in second-line and beyond is now 13-18 months and some live with stable/slowly progressive disease for years. Extremity osteosarcoma long-term survival is 60-80%, with response to chemotherapy the key predictor. Ewing's sarcoma overall cure rates approach 60-70% for localized tumors. For bone metastases, overall survival is related to the prognosis of the underlying tumor; some (lymphoma, Hodgkin's lymphoma) are curable while most are treated palliatively. Soft tissue sarcomas use the AJCC (8th edition) TNM/grade system: T1 (<=5 cm), T2 (>5-10 cm), T3 (>10-15 cm), T4 (>15 cm); N0/N1; M0/M1; with grade G1-G3 driving stage grouping (e.g., Stage IA = T1 N0 M0 G1; Stage IV = any T N1 M0, or any T any N M1). Bone sarcomas use the Musculoskeletal Tumor Society system (stage I low grade, II high grade, III nodal/distant metastases; A = intracompartmental, B = extracompartmental) and a TNM system: T1 (<=8 cm), T2 (>8 cm), T3 (discontinuous tumors in the primary bone); M1a (lung) vs M1b (other sites); grade G1-G4 (Ewing's always G4).

solar retinopathy — foveomacular retinitis, solar maculopathy, eclipse retinopathy Laser pointer or welding-arc phototoxic maculopathy Macular hole or impending macular hole Acute idiopathic maculopathy Central serous chorioretinopathy Poppers (amyl nitrite) maculopathy Torpedo maculopathy or other focal outer retinal defect Occult macular dystrophy Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography of the fovea for outer retinal and ellipsoid zone defects Fundus autofluorescence to detect focal pigment epithelial change Amsler grid testing to map the central scotoma and metamorphopsia Fluorescein angiography to exclude exudative or inflammatory maculopathy Microperimetry to quantify central sensitivity loss Colour vision testing for acquired dyschromatopsia Multifocal electroretinography in atypical or medicolegal cases Caused by direct or prolonged viewing of the sun, classically after solar eclipse gazing, sun worship, or telescope viewing without adequate filters, and increasingly reported after use of hallucinogens or psychiatric illness where sun-staring occurs. Patients present hours to a day or two after exposure with bilateral (occasionally asymmetrical) central or paracentral scotoma, blurred vision, metamorphopsia, dyschromatopsia and sometimes chromatopsia or micropsia. Visual acuity is often only mildly to moderately reduced despite marked symptomatic disturbance, and a positive history of sun exposure is the key to diagnosis. Early fundus signs are subtle, a small yellow-white foveal spot, later evolving into a sharply defined reddish foveal lesion, and may be missed without careful stereoscopic macular examination. Optical coherence tomography is the most sensitive investigation, characteristically showing a focal defect in the outer retinal layers at the fovea with disruption of the ellipsoid zone and interdigitation zone. The injury is predominantly photochemical (and to a lesser extent thermal) damage to the photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelium rather than a burn from focused heat alone. Fluorescein angiography is often normal or shows only a subtle window defect, helping to distinguish it from exudative maculopathies. No proven specific treatment exists; management centres on preventing further exposure, patient education and observation, with corticosteroids of unproven benefit. History of prolonged or repeated unprotected sun-gazing suggesting cumulative bilateral injury Persistent dense central scotoma beyond the expected recovery window indicating permanent foveal damage Bilateral involvement threatening reading and driving vision Underlying psychiatric illness or substance use driving compulsive sun-staring and re-injury Progressive enlargement of the foveal defect suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis Missing the diagnosis because visual acuity is relatively preserved and early fundus findings are subtle, without eliciting the exposure history. Mistaking the small foveal lesion for an early macular hole and pursuing surgical rather than conservative management. Relying on ophthalmoscopy alone rather than obtaining optical coherence tomography, which is far more sensitive for the outer retinal defect. Prescribing corticosteroids as if for an inflammatory maculopathy despite absence of proven benefit. Neglecting to counsel on eye protection and address any underlying behavioural or psychiatric driver, risking recurrent phototoxic injury. Solar retinopathy results chiefly from photochemical injury to the outer retina when short-wavelength (blue) and near-ultraviolet light from direct solar viewing is focused by the optics of the eye onto the fovea. Absorbed radiant energy generates reactive oxygen species that damage photoreceptor outer segments and the underlying retinal pigment epithelium, with a smaller contribution from thermal energy that raises local tissue temperature. The fovea is preferentially affected because it lies at the point of optical focus and lacks the protective screening of inner retinal vasculature and, being cone-rich, is metabolically vulnerable. The acute insult produces oedema and disruption of the photoreceptor layer; over subsequent weeks the pigment epithelium and photoreceptors may partially recover or leave a permanent focal outer retinal defect, sometimes a small lamellar cavity, accounting for the residual scotoma. Predisposing factors include a clear atmosphere, dilated pupils, youth with clear ocular media, and pharmacological or behavioural states that prolong sun-gazing. Most patients experience partial or substantial recovery of visual acuity over weeks to months, though a small residual central or paracentral scotoma and subtle metamorphopsia frequently persist owing to the focal outer retinal defect. Prognosis is worse with more prolonged exposure, bilateral involvement or repeated injury.

Solar urticaria — SU, light-induced urticaria, sun-induced urticaria Polymorphic light eruption Erythropoietic protoporphyria Drug-induced or chemical photosensitivity Cholinergic urticaria triggered by heat from sun exposure Systemic lupus erythematosus Heat or contact urticaria from other stimuli Phototesting to reproduce weals and define the action spectrum History clarifying the immediate onset and rapid resolution that distinguish it from delayed photodermatoses Plasma, urine and faecal porphyrins to exclude erythropoietic protoporphyria Antinuclear antibody testing to exclude lupus erythematosus Photopatch testing where a photoallergic contact cause is suspected Baseline assessment for systemic reactions in those with extensive exposure symptoms An immediate photodermatosis in which itching, erythema and weals appear within minutes of sun exposure and typically settle within an hour or two of moving into shade Any waveband may be responsible, and defining the individual action spectrum (ultraviolet B, ultraviolet A or visible light) by phototesting guides both diagnosis and protection strategy Habitually exposed skin such as the face and hands may be relatively
