tolerant, so weals are often most striking on normally covered areas that are suddenly exposed Extensive exposure can provoke systemic symptoms including headache, wheeze, syncope and, rarely, anaphylaxis, particularly with sunbathing over a large body surface It must be distinguished from other immediate reactions such as erythropoietic protoporphyria, which causes burning and pain rather than true weals Management centres on trigger avoidance, appropriate photoprotection, and non-sedating antihistamines, with omalizumab a useful option for antihistamine-resistant disease Phototherapy hardening can raise the threshold for symptoms and induce tolerance in selected patients Systemic symptoms such as wheeze, dizziness or collapse indicating anaphylaxis risk with widespread exposure Burning pain rather than weals, especially from childhood, suggesting erythropoietic protoporphyria Photosensitivity with systemic features or autoantibodies suggesting lupus New symptoms coinciding with a recently introduced drug or topical agent Mistaking the immediate weals for delayed polymorphic light eruption and thereby misdirecting treatment Failing to warn patients about the risk of systemic reactions during whole-body exposure such as sunbathing or swimming Overlooking that visible light can be the trigger, which many sunscreens do not adequately block Not defining the action spectrum, leading to inappropriate or inadequate photoprotection advice Solar urticaria is considered an immediate (type I) hypersensitivity reaction in which ultraviolet or visible radiation converts a precursor in the skin or circulation into a photoallergen; this in turn triggers IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation with histamine release, producing the characteristic weal and flare within minutes. The specific wavelengths capable of generating the photoallergen constitute the patient's action spectrum, which varies between individuals. Because the reaction depends on newly formed antigen, brief exposure can rapidly precipitate widespread urticaria and, when extensive, systemic mediator release. Solar urticaria is often a persistent condition, but many patients achieve good control with photoprotection, antihistamines and, where required, omalizumab or phototherapy hardening; spontaneous remission occurs in a proportion of cases over several years, while the main risk lies in systemic reactions during extensive exposure.

Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas — SPN, solid pseudopapillary tumour, Frantz tumour, papillary cystic neoplasm Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour Mucinous cystic neoplasm of the pancreas Serous cystadenoma Pancreatoblastoma (in younger patients) Cystic degeneration of an adenocarcinoma Acinar cell carcinoma Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to define the encapsulated solid-cystic mass and haemorrhagic components Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle biopsy for tissue diagnosis Immunohistochemistry including beta-catenin, CD10, and progesterone receptor Cyst or lesion fluid analysis when cystic degeneration predominates Staging imaging to assess for hepatic or peritoneal spread Serum tumour markers (usually normal) to help exclude other diagnoses A rare epithelial neoplasm of low malignant potential that arises predominantly in young women Often presents as a large, well-circumscribed mass with mixed solid and cystic components, sometimes with haemorrhage or a fibrous capsule Frequently asymptomatic or causes vague abdominal discomfort, and may be found after minor trauma to a bulky lesion Immunohistochemistry typically shows nuclear beta-catenin staining reflecting an underlying CTNNB1 mutation, along with markers such as CD10 and progesterone receptor Imaging shows an encapsulated lesion with heterogeneous internal architecture and areas of degeneration; calcification may be present The mainstay of treatment is complete surgical resection, which is curative in the great majority of cases Even lesions with local invasion or limited metastases can have a favourable outcome after resection, reflecting the indolent biology Local invasion of adjacent organs or vessels on imaging Hepatic or peritoneal metastases Rapid growth or rupture with haemorrhage Older or male patients or atypical histology, which may portend more aggressive behaviour Mistaking the mass for a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour or adenocarcinoma and misdirecting treatment Assuming benignity and forgoing resection, given the recognised though low malignant potential Overlooking the diagnosis in the rare male or older patient because of the female predominance Incomplete excision leaving a positive margin in a curable tumour Solid pseudopapillary neoplasms are uncommon tumours of uncertain cell lineage that are strongly linked to activating mutations of the CTNNB1 gene and consequent abnormal Wnt/beta-catenin signalling, demonstrable as aberrant nuclear beta-catenin accumulation. The neoplastic cells are poorly cohesive and tend to fall away from delicate fibrovascular cores, creating the characteristic pseudopapillary pattern, while areas of the tumour undergo cystic degeneration and haemorrhage, producing the typical mixed solid and cystic mass. The marked female predominance and hormone-receptor expression suggest a hormonal influence on growth. Malignant potential is low, but a minority show local invasion or metastasis, most often to the liver or peritoneum. Overall prognosis is very good, with high cure rates after complete resection even for large tumours; a small proportion recur or metastasise, but survival remains favourable, and resection of limited metastatic disease is often worthwhile.

Solitary fibrous tumour — SFT, haemangiopericytoma, NAB2-STAT6 fusion tumour Synovial sarcoma Desmoid-type fibromatosis Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour Spindle cell lipoma Gastrointestinal stromal tumour in abdominal sites MRI or CT to define the well-circumscribed mass and its vascularity Core biopsy with histological assessment of the patternless pattern and staghorn vessels STAT6 immunohistochemistry as a highly specific diagnostic marker Molecular confirmation of the NAB2-STAT6 fusion in uncertain cases Blood glucose evaluation if symptoms suggest tumour-related hypoglycaemia A fibroblastic tumour of intermediate behaviour that can arise almost anywhere, historically described in the pleura but common in extrapleural soft tissue Usually a slow-growing, well-circumscribed mass; deep-seated lesions may reach a large size before detection Defined molecularly by a recurrent NAB2-STAT6 gene fusion, which produces diffuse nuclear STAT6 expression on immunohistochemistry Histology shows a patternless architecture of bland spindle cells, ropey collagen and branching staghorn-shaped thin-walled vessels The term haemangiopericytoma is now regarded as part of the solitary fibrous tumour spectrum A minority secrete insulin-like growth factor and cause hypoglycaemia, known as Doege-Potter syndrome Complete surgical excision is the mainstay of treatment, with long-term follow-up because late recurrence and metastasis can occur Large size, high mitotic count or necrosis indicating a malignant solitary fibrous tumour Rapid growth or evidence of distant spread on staging Symptomatic hypoglycaemia suggesting a functioning tumour Late local recurrence or metastasis during follow-up Assuming all solitary fibrous tumours are benign and omitting long-term follow-up Confusing it with synovial sarcoma or other spindle-cell tumours without STAT6 testing Overlooking tumour-associated hypoglycaemia as a paraneoplastic clue Relying on morphology alone when the molecular signature clarifies the diagnosis Solitary fibrous tumour is a fibroblastic neoplasm defined by an intrachromosomal NAB2-STAT6 gene fusion arising from an inversion on chromosome 12. This fusion converts the normally repressive NAB2 into a transcriptional activator of EGR1 target genes, driving cell proliferation, and results in nuclear relocation of STAT6 that can be detected immunohistochemically. The tumour is composed of a haphazard arrangement of bland ovoid to spindled cells set in variably collagenous stroma with characteristic dilated, branching thin-walled vessels. Although most behave in an indolent fashion, a subset shows malignant features and can metastasise, so behaviour is stratified using mitotic activity, size, necrosis and age. Most solitary fibrous tumours are cured by complete excision, but the entity has intermediate malignant potential, and a subset recurs or metastasises, sometimes many years later. Risk stratification using size, mitoses, necrosis and age guides surveillance intensity.

Solitary mastocytoma — mastocytoma of skin Juvenile xanthogranuloma Spitz naevus Congenital melanocytic naevus Other cutaneous mastocytosis Insect bite reaction Clinical diagnosis with a positive Darier sign Skin biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain Baseline tryptase if multiple lesions or systemic features Reassurance and monitoring for spontaneous regression Trigger history A solitary (or few) cutaneous accumulation of mast cells, usually appearing in infancy Presents as a single red-brown or yellowish plaque or nodule, sometimes with a peau d'orange surface Stroking produces urtication and can cause blistering in infants (a strong Darier sign) Vigorous rubbing may provoke flushing from localised mediator release It is benign and typically regresses spontaneously during childhood Management is conservative with reassurance and trigger avoidance; systemic disease is rare with a solitary lesion Multiple lesions or systemic symptoms suggesting broader mastocytosis Marked flushing or hypotension on stimulation Atypical features suggesting an alternative diagnosis Persistence or growth into later childhood Provoking blistering or flushing by vigorously rubbing the lesion Confusing it with a melanocytic or xanthogranulomatous lesion Assuming systemic disease from a single lesion Unnecessary excision of a self-limiting lesion A solitary mastocytoma is a localised benign collection of mast cells within the skin, part of the cutaneous mastocytosis spectrum. Mechanical stimulation degranulates the concentrated mast cells, releasing histamine and other mediators to produce a brisk weal-and-flare and, in infants, blistering. Because the mast cell burden is limited to a small area, systemic mediator effects are uncommon, and the lesion generally involutes as the child grows. The prognosis is excellent, with most solitary mastocytomas regressing spontaneously during childhood and rarely causing systemic problems.

Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome — SRUS, solitary rectal ulcer, mucosal prolapse syndrome Rectal adenocarcinoma Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn's) Ischaemic or infective proctitis Rectal polyp or villous adenoma Endometriosis involving the rectum Traumatic or radiation proctitis Flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy with biopsy for diagnosis and to exclude malignancy Histology demonstrating fibromuscular obliteration of the lamina propria Defecography (fluoroscopic or MR) to demonstrate internal or external prolapse and evacuatory dysfunction Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion to assess dyssynergia Endoanal ultrasound where sphincter or prolapse assessment is required Colonoscopy to exclude synchronous colonic pathology A benign but often misdiagnosed disorder linked to internal rectal (mucosal) prolapse and chronic straining, frequently with paradoxical pelvic floor contraction Presents with rectal bleeding, mucus discharge, straining, a sense of incomplete evacuation, and sometimes the need to digitate to evacuate Despite the name, lesions may be single or multiple and ulcerated, polypoid, or merely erythematous, typically on the anterior rectal wall a few centimetres above the anal verge Biopsy shows the characteristic fibromuscular obliteration of the lamina propria, with smooth muscle extending upward between the crypts, and features of mucosal prolapse Endoscopy with biopsy is essential to distinguish it from malignancy and inflammatory bowel disease, both of which it can mimic First-line management targets the underlying evacuatory disorder: bulking agents, bowel retraining, and biofeedback to correct straining and dyssynergia Surgery, such as rectopexy for overt or internal prolapse, is reserved for refractory cases or associated full-thickness prolapse An endoscopic appearance mimicking malignancy, making biopsy mandatory before treatment Progressive bleeding, weight loss, or anaemia Failure to heal despite treatment of the evacuatory disorder Development of a stricture or mass Mistaking the lesion for carcinoma or Crohn's disease, or the reverse, without biopsy Treating the ulcer topically while ignoring the underlying evacuatory disorder Overlooking dyssynergic defecation amenable to biofeedback Proceeding to surgery without confirming prolapse on defecography Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome arises from chronic mechanical trauma to the rectal mucosa, driven by internal intussusception or mucosal prolapse and repeated straining, often with paradoxical (dyssynergic) contraction of the puborectalis. The prolapsing mucosa is subjected to shear, ischaemia, and direct trauma, including self-digitation, producing ulceration, hyperaemia, or polypoid change. Histology reflects this, with fibromuscular obliteration of the lamina propria and derangement of the muscularis mucosae characteristic of mucosal prolapse. The name is a misnomer, as lesions vary in number and appearance. A benign condition, but frequently chronic and difficult to treat; symptoms improve with correction of straining and biofeedback in many patients, while refractory cases with prolapse may require surgery with variable success.

Somatic symptom disorder — SSD, somatization, somatisation disorder, somatoform disorder Illness anxiety disorder Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder) Factitious disorder and malingering Major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders with somatic features Panic disorder Undiagnosed genuine medical illness Body dysmorphic disorder Focused, proportionate medical evaluation guided by objective findings rather than repeated broad testing Review of prior investigations to avoid duplication Screening for comorbid depression and anxiety Assessment of functional impairment and healthcare utilisation patterns Defined by one or more distressing physical symptoms accompanied by excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviours related to those symptoms The diagnosis rests on the disproportionate and persistent nature of the response, not on whether the symptoms are medically explained Features include disproportionate and persistent worry about the seriousness of symptoms, high health-related anxiety, and excessive time and energy devoted to symptoms or health concerns Symptoms are typically persistent (often more than six months) even if individual complaints vary over time Distinguish from illness anxiety disorder (preoccupation with having illness with few or no somatic symptoms) and from conversion disorder (neurological symptoms incompatible with recognised disease) Management principles emphasise a consistent single coordinating clinician, regular scheduled visits, limiting unnecessary tests and referrals, and validating distress while gently shifting focus toward functioning Cognitive behavioural therapy is the best-supported psychotherapy; treat comorbid depression and anxiety, where SSRIs or SNRIs may help A genuine coexisting medical illness does not exclude the diagnosis, so maintain appropriate but restrained medical vigilance New objective clinical signs suggesting an emergent genuine medical condition Suicidal ideation associated with comorbid depression Escalating analgesic or sedative use and dependence Iatrogenic harm from repeated invasive investigations or procedures Ordering repeated investigations and referrals that reinforce illness behaviour and risk iatrogenic harm Dismissing symptoms as not real, which damages the therapeutic alliance Assuming the diagnosis excludes genuine disease and missing a new medical problem Failing to identify and treat comorbid depression and anxiety Lack of a single coordinating clinician leading to fragmented, duplicated care Somatic symptom disorder is understood through a biopsychosocial model in which heightened attention to and amplification of bodily sensations, cognitive misinterpretation of benign symptoms as dangerous, and autonomic and stress responses interact. Predisposing factors include early adverse experiences, trauma, comorbid anxiety and depression, and learned illness behaviour, with reinforcement from repeated medical attention perpetuating the pattern. Somatic symptom disorder is often chronic and fluctuating, but consistent, coordinated care can reduce distress, unnecessary investigations, and healthcare costs while improving function. Prognosis is worse with prolonged illness, multiple comorbidities, and ongoing reinforcement through repeated medical intervention.

Somatostatinoma — somatostatin-secreting tumour, somatostatin-secreting neuroendocrine tumour, D-cell tumour Other functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours such as glucagonoma or VIPoma Non-functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma Chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency Cholelithiasis from unrelated causes Coeliac disease or other malabsorptive states Fasting plasma somatostatin concentration Somatostatin-receptor imaging such as gallium DOTATATE positron emission tomography Cross-sectional imaging and endoscopic ultrasound to localise and stage the tumour Assessment of glycaemic status and pancreatic exocrine function Abdominal imaging to document gallstones Screening for neurofibromatosis type 1 and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 where relevant The classic triad reflects somatostatin's inhibitory actions: diabetes mellitus, gallstones, and steatorrhoea with weight loss The full syndrome is uncommon; many tumours are found incidentally or present with mass effect rather than florid hormonal features Pancreatic tumours more often produce the complete inhibitory syndrome, whereas duodenal or periampullary lesions may present with obstructive jaundice or bleeding Diabetes tends to be mild because somatostatin suppresses both insulin and glucagon Gallstones arise from reduced gallbladder contractility and diminished cholecystokinin-driven emptying Steatorrhoea results from inhibition of pancreatic exocrine secretion and bile flow A markedly elevated plasma somatostatin supports the diagnosis, and somatostatin-receptor imaging aids localisation and staging Duodenal tumours may be associated with neurofibromatosis type 1, and pancreatic lesions with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 Obstructive jaundice from a periampullary tumour Hepatic metastases at presentation Progressive weight loss and malnutrition from severe steatorrhoea Gastrointestinal haemorrhage from a duodenal lesion Features suggesting an inherited tumour syndrome Missing the diagnosis because the full inhibitory triad is often incomplete or subtle Attributing the mild diabetes and gallstones to common coincidental disease Overlooking a periampullary tumour presenting purely with obstructive symptoms Failing to screen for associated neurofibromatosis type 1 or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 Assuming resectability without adequate somatostatin-receptor and cross-sectional staging Somatostatinoma is a rare neuroendocrine tumour of pancreatic delta cells or duodenal somatostatin-producing cells. Excess somatostatin exerts broad inhibitory effects across the gastroenteropancreatic axis, suppressing insulin and glucagon (producing mild diabetes), reducing gallbladder motility and cholecystokinin action (favouring gallstone formation), and dampening pancreatic exocrine and biliary secretion (causing fat malabsorption and steatorrhoea). Many tumours are large and metastatic at diagnosis, and periampullary lesions may declare themselves through local obstruction rather than hormonal excess. Outlook depends heavily on stage; small, completely resected tumours can be cured, but a large proportion are advanced with hepatic or nodal metastases at diagnosis, when surgical resection and somatostatin analogues aim to control disease and symptoms rather than cure.

Sorsby fundus dystrophy — SFD, TIMP3, Sorsby pseudoinflammatory macular dystrophy, hereditary haemorrhagic macular dystrophy Neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration Pattern dystrophies and Best disease Malattia leventinese / Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy Late-onset autosomal dominant macular dystrophies Central areolar choroidal dystrophy Myopic choroidal neovascularisation Optical coherence tomography for subretinal fluid, deposits and neovascular membranes Fluorescein and/or indocyanine green angiography or OCT-angiography to detect choroidal neovascularisation Dark adaptometry demonstrating the characteristic prolonged rod recovery Fundus autofluorescence to map retinal pigment epithelium atrophy Full-field electroretinography as disease advances Molecular genetic testing for TIMP3 mutations Autosomal dominant macular dystrophy caused by TIMP3 mutations, with onset of symptoms typically in the fourth to fifth decade Patients often report early nyctalopia and difficulty with dark adaptation, followed by sudden central visual loss from choroidal neovascularisation Fundus shows confluent yellow-white drusen-like deposits at the level of Bruch's membrane, later with atrophy, pigmentary change and subretinal neovascular membranes and haemorrhage It resembles neovascular age-related macular degeneration but occurs earlier and with a clear dominant family history A characteristic finding is thickening of Bruch's membrane with abnormal deposits, reflecting impaired extracellular matrix turnover Choroidal neovascularisation is common and responds to anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy, so prompt recognition of new distortion is important Management combines anti-angiogenic treatment of neovascular membranes, low-vision support and genetic counselling; some patients report benefit from vitamin A supplementation for the dark-adaptation defect Acute central distortion, scotoma or metamorphopsia indicating choroidal neovascularisation needing urgent treatment Subretinal haemorrhage at the macula Early unexplained night-vision difficulty in a patient with a relevant family history Affected relatives requiring surveillance given dominant inheritance Diagnosing early-onset neovascular disease as ordinary age-related macular degeneration and missing the hereditary cause Overlooking the early dark-adaptation defect that can precede visual loss Delaying treatment of choroidal neovascularisation, which is often treatable Failing to counsel and screen relatives for a dominantly inherited condition Sorsby fundus dystrophy is caused by dominant mutations in TIMP3, the tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-3, which regulates extracellular matrix turnover and angiogenesis in the retinal pigment epithelium and Bruch's membrane. Mutant TIMP3 accumulates and thickens Bruch's membrane with abnormal deposits, impairing transport between the choroid and retina and disturbing the visual cycle, which produces the early dark-adaptation defect. The abnormal, thickened Bruch's membrane and dysregulated angiogenesis predispose to choroidal neovascularisation, haemorrhage and subsequent chorioretinal atrophy. Without treatment, choroidal neovascularisation frequently causes severe central visual loss, but timely anti-angiogenic therapy can preserve vision; peripheral vision is generally retained while progressive chorioretinal atrophy limits central acuity long term.

Sotos syndrome — cerebral gigantism, NSD1-related overgrowth, Sotos sequence Weaver syndrome (EZH2-related overgrowth) Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome Fragile X syndrome and other macrocephaly-associated intellectual disability syndromes Malan syndrome (NFIX-related overgrowth) Marfan syndrome and other tall-stature connective tissue disorders Molecular testing for NSD1 sequence variants and 5q35 deletion by targeted analysis, microarray, or overgrowth gene panel Chromosomal microarray to detect contiguous 5q35 microdeletion and other copy-number causes Bone age radiograph, which is characteristically advanced Developmental and neuropsychological assessment for learning and behavioural needs Echocardiography and renal ultrasound to evaluate associated structural anomalies Cranial imaging where indicated to characterise ventricular or midline brain findings Classic triad of prenatal and postnatal overgrowth (tall stature and macrocephaly), a characteristic facial gestalt, and variable learning difficulty The facial pattern includes a broad prominent forehead, sparse frontotemporal hair, downslanting palpebral fissures, malar flushing, and a long narrow chin Advanced bone age and rapid early growth are typical, although final adult height is often within or near the normal range Caused by haploinsufficiency of NSD1 on chromosome 5q35, usually from a de novo point mutation or a 5q35 microdeletion Inheritance is autosomal dominant with most cases arising de novo; microdeletions are more common in some populations and tend to give more marked learning difficulty Neonatal hypotonia, feeding difficulty, jaundice, and delayed early motor and speech milestones are common, with behaviour and autistic features seen in a proportion Tumour risk is modestly increased but low overall, so intensive tumour surveillance is generally not recommended for isolated NSD1 disease Rapidly enlarging head circumference or neurological signs prompting exclusion of hydrocephalus or an intracranial lesion Seizures requiring assessment and management New mass or unexplained systemic symptoms raising concern for an embryonal tumour Feeding failure or profound neonatal hypotonia needing supportive care Attributing tall stature or macrocephaly to familial variation and missing the diagnosis Confusing Sotos with Weaver syndrome, which shares overgrowth but has distinct facial features and gene Applying intensive tumour surveillance protocols that are not warranted by the low risk Overlooking behavioural and autistic features that need targeted intervention Sotos syndrome results from loss of function of NSD1, a gene encoding a histone methyltransferase that regulates chromatin and transcription of growth and developmental pathways. Haploinsufficiency, whether from an intragenic mutation or a contiguous 5q35 microdeletion, disturbs regulation of growth-promoting genes, producing generalised pre- and postnatal overgrowth with disproportionate head growth. The same disturbance of neuronal chromatin regulation underlies the cognitive and behavioural phenotype, while the recognisable facial gestalt reflects altered craniofacial patterning. Most individuals have a good general prognosis with growth normalising through childhood and adult height often near the normal range, though learning difficulty and behavioural challenges frequently persist and require support. Overall tumour risk is low and life expectancy is generally normal.

Sparganosis (Spirometra) — Spirometra infection, sparganum infection, larval diphyllobothriid disease, plerocercoid larva migrans Cutaneous larva migrans and other migratory helminth infection Neurocysticercosis and other cerebral cystic or granulomatous disease Coenurosis and hydatid disease of the central nervous system or soft tissue Soft-tissue lipoma, cyst or abscess Orbital cellulitis or other periorbital inflammatory lesion Primary or secondary intracranial tumour MRI or CT to localise migrating tracks, granulomas or intracranial lesions Full blood count for eosinophilia Serology for sparganum antigens where available Histological examination of the excised larva to confirm the diagnosis Ophthalmological assessment in suspected ocular disease Exclusion of other cystic cestode infection by appropriate serology Caused by migrating plerocercoid (sparganum) larvae of Spirometra tapeworms, with humans as accidental intermediate hosts Acquired by drinking water containing infected copepods, eating raw or undercooked frog, snake or other paratenic hosts, or applying raw amphibian flesh as a traditional poultice The larva does not mature but migrates through tissues, producing a slowly moving, sometimes painful subcutaneous nodule that may appear and disappear Ocular sparganosis causes periorbital swelling, pain and lid oedema, while cerebral sparganosis can cause seizures, headache and focal neurological deficits Peripheral eosinophilia is common and imaging may show a migrating or serpiginous track or an enhancing granuloma Definitive treatment is surgical removal of the whole larva; anthelmintic drugs are generally ineffective against the tissue-dwelling sparganum Prevention includes drinking safe water, cooking meat thoroughly and avoiding the practice of applying raw amphibian tissue to wounds or eyes Seizures or focal neurological signs indicating cerebral involvement Progressive ocular swelling threatening vision An enlarging or migrating intracranial lesion with mass effect Recurrent or incompletely excised larva with persistent symptoms Relying on anthelmintic drugs, which rarely eradicate the tissue-dwelling sparganum Incomplete surgical removal leaving viable larva and causing relapse Mistaking a migrating subcutaneous nodule for a benign lipoma or cyst Overlooking the history of raw-flesh poultice application or untreated water consumption Spirometra species are diphyllobothriid tapeworms whose adults live in cats, dogs and other carnivores. Their life cycle uses copepods as first intermediate hosts and amphibians, reptiles and other vertebrates as second intermediate or paratenic hosts harbouring the plerocercoid larva, the sparganum. Humans become accidental hosts by swallowing infected copepods in water, by eating raw or undercooked intermediate hosts, or by direct inoculation when raw frog or snake flesh is applied to skin, eyes or wounds as a poultice. The larva cannot mature in humans; instead it migrates through subcutaneous tissue, muscle, the eye or the central nervous system, provoking a local inflammatory and eosinophilic reaction with granuloma formation and, in the brain, surrounding oedema and mass effect. The living, motile larva accounts for the characteristic migratory and space-occupying features of the disease. Prognosis is good when a subcutaneous or ocular larva is completely removed, but cerebral sparganosis can cause lasting neurological deficits and may recur if the larva is not fully excised.

Spasmodic dysphonia (laryngeal dystonia) — laryngeal dystonia, spastic dysphonia, adductor spasmodic dysphonia, abductor spasmodic dysphonia Muscle tension dysphonia Vocal tremor (essential tremor of the voice) Psychogenic (functional) dysphonia Vocal fold paresis or paralysis Structural vocal fold lesions (nodules, polyps) Neurodegenerative dysarthria Reflux-related laryngeal irritation Flexible fibreoptic laryngoscopy and stroboscopy during connected speech and other vocal tasks Perceptual and acoustic voice analysis by a speech and language therapist Laryngeal electromyography in selected or atypical cases Neurological examination for other focal dystonias or tremor MRI of the brain if an atypical or secondary dystonia is suspected Trial of botulinum toxin as both a therapeutic and confirmatory measure A focal, task-specific laryngeal dystonia in which involuntary spasms of the intrinsic laryngeal muscles disrupt voice during speech but spare other laryngeal functions The adductor type is most common, producing a strained, strangled, effortful voice with abrupt voice breaks on vowels The abductor type produces breathy breaks and aphonic whispered segments, especially on voiceless consonants Symptoms are task-specific: the voice may be normal during whispering, singing, laughing, or crying but abnormal during connected speech It is frequently accompanied by voice tremor and may coexist with other focal dystonias Diagnosis is clinical, supported by perceptual voice assessment and flexible laryngoscopy showing task-specific spasms with a structurally normal larynx Botulinum toxin injection into the affected laryngeal muscles is the mainstay of treatment, giving temporary relief that requires periodic repetition Associated stridor or airway compromise suggesting a different or additional laryngeal disorder Progressive generalised neurological signs suggesting a wider neurodegenerative process A structural vocal fold lesion on endoscopy Rapid onset after a clear psychological precipitant suggesting a functional disorder Misdiagnosing it as muscle tension or psychogenic dysphonia and delaying appropriate treatment Failing to assess the voice across multiple tasks to reveal its task-specific nature Overlooking coexisting vocal tremor, which affects treatment response Confusing abductor spasmodic dysphonia with vocal fold paresis Attributing all voice breaks to reflux or structural lesions Spasmodic dysphonia is a focal task-specific dystonia of the larynx, considered a disorder of central motor control within the basal ganglia and their cortical and brainstem connections rather than a structural or purely psychogenic problem. Abnormal, involuntary co-contraction of the laryngeal muscles occurs selectively during the fine motor task of speech. In the adductor form the vocal folds press together excessively, interrupting phonation with strained breaks; in the abductor form inappropriate opening produces breathy, aphonic breaks. The larynx is structurally normal and the dystonia typically does not affect breathing or swallowing. Spasmodic dysphonia is a chronic condition without spontaneous cure, but botulinum toxin injections reliably improve the voice for several months at a time, and combined botulinum toxin and voice therapy allow most patients to maintain functional communication.

Spasmus nutans — spasmus nutans syndrome Optic pathway or suprasellar glioma Congenital (infantile) nystagmus syndrome Retinal dystrophy causing sensory nystagmus Bobble-head doll syndrome Acquired nystagmus from posterior fossa disease MRI of the brain and anterior visual pathways Detailed ophthalmological and fundus examination Electroretinography where a retinal dystrophy is suspected Ocular motility and orthoptic assessment Developmental and neurological review A benign disorder of infancy defined by a triad of fine rapid asymmetric nystagmus, head nodding and an anomalous head posture The nystagmus is typically small-amplitude, high-frequency and often dissociated or intermittent between the two eyes Onset is usually in the first year of life and the condition tends to resolve spontaneously within a few years It is a diagnosis of exclusion because chiasmal and suprasellar tumours (such as optic pathway gliomas) can mimic it Neuroimaging is mandatory to exclude an intracranial lesion before accepting a benign diagnosis Retinal dystrophies can produce similar nystagmus and may need electrophysiological testing to exclude Optic disc pallor or afferent pupillary defect Failure to resolve or progression of signs Associated neurological deficit or failure to thrive Monocular or grossly asymmetric visual loss Accepting the diagnosis without neuroimaging and missing an optic pathway glioma Overlooking a retinal dystrophy as the cause of the nystagmus Confusing it with congenital nystagmus syndrome Attributing the head nodding to a primary movement disorder Spasmus nutans is an idiopathic, usually self-limiting disorder of ocular motor control in infancy of unknown mechanism, in which the head nodding is thought to be a partially compensatory response to the shimmering nystagmus. Because an identical clinical picture can be produced by anterior visual pathway tumours compressing the chiasm and by certain retinal dystrophies, the benign form can only be diagnosed once these structural and retinal causes have been excluded. The idiopathic form is benign and usually resolves spontaneously over months to a few years; prognosis otherwise depends entirely on excluding and, if present, treating a structural or retinal cause.

Spasticity management — spasticity, hypertonia, upper motor neuron syndrome spasticity Rigidity of parkinsonian or extrapyramidal origin Dystonia Fixed contracture without active hypertonia Paratonia (gegenhalten) Rigidity from neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin syndrome Local joint pathology limiting movement Structured tone assessment using the Modified Ashworth or Tardieu scale Evaluation for noxious triggers including urinalysis, review of bowel and bladder function, and skin inspection Goal-setting assessment and gait or functional analysis to guide treatment targets Dynamic assessment with diagnostic nerve or motor point blocks to distinguish dynamic spasticity from fixed contracture Imaging or electrophysiology where an evolving or new central lesion is suspected Spasticity is a velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone with exaggerated tendon reflexes, arising as part of the upper motor neuron syndrome after brain or spinal cord injury It should be assessed for its functional impact using scales such as the Modified Ashworth Scale, since not all spasticity is harmful and some may aid standing or transfers A key first step is to identify and remove noxious triggers such as infection, pressure injury, constipation, urinary retention, ingrown nails, or poor positioning that can suddenly worsen tone Management follows a stepped approach beginning with therapy and physical measures: stretching, positioning, splinting, serial casting, and an appropriate seating and standing programme Focal spasticity affecting a few muscles is well suited to intramuscular botulinum toxin injection to reduce tone in targeted muscles and enable therapy Generalised spasticity may require oral agents such as baclofen, tizanidine, dantrolene, or benzodiazepines, weighing benefit against sedation and weakness Severe, diffuse spasticity refractory to oral treatment may be managed with intrathecal baclofen delivered by an implanted pump Treatment goals should be explicit and functional, whether to improve mobility, ease care and hygiene, relieve pain, or prevent contracture, and outcomes reassessed regularly Untreated spasticity can lead to fixed contractures, pain, pressure injury, and impaired hygiene, so proactive management is important A sudden, unexplained increase in tone that may signal infection, pressure injury, fracture, or another noxious stimulus New or rapidly progressive spasticity suggesting an evolving spinal cord or intracranial lesion such as syringomyelia Signs of intrathecal baclofen withdrawal, which can be life-threatening with high fever, rebound spasticity, and rhabdomyolysis Developing pressure injury or contracture threatening skin integrity and function Treating spasticity aggressively when it is actually providing useful functional support for standing or transfers Failing to look for and remove a noxious trigger before escalating drug therapy Over-sedating patients with oral agents, causing weakness and functional decline Missing intrathecal baclofen pump malfunction or abrupt withdrawal Neglecting stretching, positioning, and therapy while relying solely on medication Spasticity results from loss of descending inhibitory control over spinal reflex circuits following upper motor neuron lesions. Reduced supraspinal inhibition leads to hyperexcitability of the stretch reflex arc, with increased alpha motor neuron excitability, altered interneuronal modulation, and diminished presynaptic and reciprocal inhibition. Over time, secondary changes within muscle and connective tissue, including altered viscoelastic properties and contracture, add a non-neural component to the increased resistance felt on passive movement. With individualised, goal-directed treatment most patients achieve meaningful reductions in tone, pain, and care burden, though spasticity in progressive neurological disease may continue to evolve. Early and consistent management reduces the risk of irreversible contracture and secondary complications.

specific granule deficiency — neutrophil-specific granule deficiency, SGD, CEBPE deficiency Chronic granulomatous disease Leukocyte adhesion deficiency Chediak-Higashi syndrome Myeloperoxidase deficiency Congenital or cyclic neutropenia Myelodysplasia with acquired Pelger-Huet anomaly Glycogen storage disease type Ib with neutrophil dysfunction Peripheral blood film for bilobed, hypogranular neutrophils (pseudo-Pelger-Huet appearance) Assays of neutrophil granule proteins such as lactoferrin and defensins demonstrating deficiency CEBPE and SMARCD2 gene sequencing Neutrophil functional studies including chemotaxis and bactericidal assays Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to assess granulopoiesis Flow cytometry or immunofluorescence for specific-granule proteins Targeted infection work-up with imaging of suspected deep abscesses A rare congenital neutrophil disorder in which neutrophils (and often eosinophils) fail to produce secondary (specific) and tertiary granules together with their antimicrobial contents Classically caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in CEBPE, encoding the myeloid transcription factor CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein epsilon; variants in SMARCD2 produce a closely related phenotype The blood film characteristically shows neutrophils with bilobed or hypolobated nuclei resembling the Pelger-Huet anomaly and strikingly agranular cytoplasm Patients suffer recurrent, often severe pyogenic infections of skin, ears, lungs and lymph nodes, commonly with Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas and enteric organisms, and may develop deep abscesses Functional defects include impaired chemotaxis, disordered receptor up-regulation and reduced bactericidal activity, compounded by absence of defensins, lactoferrin and other granule proteins Demonstrating markedly reduced or absent specific-granule proteins such as lactoferrin, alongside the typical morphology, supports the diagnosis pending genetic confirmation Management centres on aggressive treatment and prophylaxis of infection, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation considered in severe cases Recurrent deep-seated abscesses or invasive bacterial infection Sepsis in a child with the characteristic agranular blood film Faltering growth with chronic suppurative infection Progressive pulmonary infection or evolving bronchiectasis Mistaking the bilobed hypogranular neutrophils for acquired myelodysplasia rather than a congenital defect Attributing recurrent infection to a commoner immunodeficiency without inspecting granule morphology Overlooking the diagnosis because neutrophil counts are typically normal Failing to separate it from myeloperoxidase deficiency or chronic granulomatous disease by functional testing Delaying genetic confirmation and appropriate family counselling CEBPE encodes a transcription factor essential for terminal neutrophil maturation and for driving expression of secondary and tertiary granule proteins. Biallelic loss-of-function abolishes production of specific granules (containing lactoferrin, transcobalamin and collagenase) and gelatinase granules together with their antimicrobial peptides, notably defensins, while also disturbing nuclear segmentation to give the bilobed morphology. The resulting neutrophils show defective chemotaxis, impaired mobilisation of surface receptors and reduced bactericidal capacity, predisposing to recurrent bacterial infection. SMARCD2, a subunit of the BAF chromatin-remodelling complex, acts in concert with CEBPE during granulopoiesis, so its deficiency yields an overlapping disorder. With vigilant antimicrobial treatment and prophylaxis many patients survive into adulthood, although recurrent severe infections cause considerable morbidity; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be curative in selected severe cases.

Specific phobia — simple phobia, isolated phobia Panic disorder with situational attacks Agoraphobia Social anxiety disorder when avoidance centres on scrutiny Post-traumatic stress disorder with stimulus and avoidance Assessment of functional impairment attributable to the phobia Screening for comorbid anxiety, mood, and substance use disorders In blood-injection-injury type, evaluation of any history of syncope The hallmark is marked, disproportionate fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation that almost always provokes an immediate response and is actively avoided or endured with intense distress Common types include animals, the natural environment such as heights or storms, blood-injection-injury, situational triggers such as flying or enclosed spaces, and other stimuli The blood-injection-injury type is distinctive because it can provoke a vasovagal response with fainting, unlike most phobias where arousal is heightened Diagnosis generally requires that the fear is persistent, typically lasting six months or more, and causes clinically significant distress or impairment Exposure-based cognitive behavioural therapy, especially graded in vivo exposure, is the treatment of choice and is often highly effective, sometimes in a single prolonged session Pharmacotherapy plays only a limited, adjunctive role, and long-term medication is usually unnecessary for isolated phobias For blood-injection-injury phobia, applied tension techniques help counter the drop in blood pressure and prevent fainting during exposure Assess how much the phobia genuinely restricts the person's life, since avoidance of rare triggers may need no treatment while others cause major impairment Phobic avoidance that prevents essential medical care, such as avoidance of injections or blood tests in a patient needing treatment Syncope with injury risk in blood-injection-injury phobia Comorbid depression with emerging suicidal ideation Avoiding exposure work in favour of reassurance, which maintains the fear Overlooking a phobia that blocks necessary medical procedures Relying on as-needed sedatives that undermine exposure learning Mislabelling situational panic or agoraphobia as an isolated phobia Failing to teach applied tension in blood-injection-injury phobia Specific phobia is understood through models of classical fear conditioning and its persistence, in which a stimulus becomes associated with danger and avoidance prevents extinction of the learned fear. Heritable predisposition, heightened amygdala-driven threat responses, evolutionary preparedness for certain stimuli, and vicarious or informational learning all contribute, while the blood-injection-injury type involves a biphasic autonomic response predisposing to vasovagal syncope. Specific phobias arising in childhood may remit spontaneously, whereas those persisting into adulthood tend to be chronic if untreated. The prognosis with exposure-based therapy is generally excellent, with many patients achieving lasting improvement, though untreated phobias affecting essential activities can cause enduring impairment.

variant in the RAS pathway, with HRAS and KRAS implicated, affecting a clone of neural-crest-derived melanocytes during development. This produces the background tan café-au-lait patch with superimposed darker melanocytic macules and papules characteristic of a naevus spilus, distributed segmentally. When the same or a partner clone involves peripheral nerve, muscle or skeletal tissue, the syndrome's segmental sensory disturbance, hyperhidrosis, weakness and skeletal anomalies develop. The melanocytic component carries a small potential for malignant transformation, accounting for the recognised, though low, melanoma risk within these lesions. Prognosis is generally good for limited disease; the main long-term concern is the small melanoma risk within the melanocytic component, while extensive neurological or skeletal involvement in the syndromic form determines additional morbidity.

A true spermatic cord lipoma is benign and cured by excision with an excellent prognosis; the principal caveat is ensuring that a well-differentiated liposarcoma has not been overlooked, as the latter can recur locally and requires wider management.

Growth is usually slow, and the lesion is entirely benign with no malignant potential. Excellent, as spermatoceles are benign and frequently stable; even after excision the outlook is good, though surgery carries a small risk to epididymal patency and thus fertility.

Prognosis depends on the subtype: patients with objective obstructive findings may benefit from sphincterotomy, whereas those with pain alone often gain little and remain at risk of procedural complications, so expectations must be set carefully.

bifida results from failure of the neural tube to close completely during early embryonic development, leaving a midline defect in the vertebral arches and, in open forms, in the overlying tissues. In myelomeningocele the meninges and dysplastic spinal cord protrude through the defect, so neural function below the lesion is impaired. Disordered cerebrospinal fluid dynamics and the commonly associated Chiari II malformation predispose to hydrocephalus. In occult forms the cord may be abnormally low and tethered by a thickened filum or lipoma, and growth-related traction can produce progressive neurological, urological, or orthopaedic deterioration. Outcome varies widely with the level and severity of the lesion; occulta is usually benign, whereas myelomeningocele typically causes lasting motor, sensory, and sphincter deficits, though multidisciplinary care and timely surgery improve function and reduce complications.

motor weakness, sensory loss, or bladder/bowel dysfunction suggesting cord or cauda equina compression Severe or worsening back pain with neurological signs after neuraxial block Failing to anticipate and promptly treat sympathetic-blockade hypotension and bradycardia Not recognising an ascending high spinal early enough to support ventilation Overlooking neuraxial haematoma risk in anticoagulated space blocks nerve roots and the spinal cord, producing sensory, motor, and autonomic blockade. Sympathetic blockade causes vasodilation and, with higher blocks, loss of cardiac accelerator fibre activity, leading to hypotension and bradycardia. Excessive cephalad spread can impair respiratory muscles and brainstem perfusion. Dural puncture allows cerebrospinal fluid leakage, lowering intracranial pressure and producing a postural headache. Mechanical trauma, mass lesions such as haematoma or abscess, or neurotoxicity can compress or injure neural tissue, causing ischaemia and potentially permanent deficit if not decompressed promptly. Common physiological effects such as hypotension resolve with treatment and most postdural puncture headaches settle, but a missed compressive haematoma or abscess can cause permanent paralysis, so outcome depends on rapid recognition and decompression.

Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (Kennedy disease) — SBMA, Kennedy disease, Kennedy's disease, X-linked bulbospinal neuronopathy, AR CAG repeat disorder Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis / motor neuron disease Adult-onset (type 4) spinal muscular atrophy (SMN1 related) Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy Myasthenia gravis with bulbar features Inclusion body myositis Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy Genetic testing for the androgen receptor CAG repeat expansion, which is diagnostic Electromyography and nerve conduction studies showing chronic neurogenic changes with reduced sensory action potentials Serum creatine kinase, often moderately elevated Endocrine assessment including testosterone, gonadotrophins and lipids/glucose given metabolic associations Swallowing assessment to quantify aspiration risk Family history and genetic counselling regarding X-linked inheritance An X-linked recessive lower motor neuron disorder affecting adult men, caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the androgen receptor gene (AR) Presents in mid-adult life with slowly progressive proximal limb weakness, cramps, and prominent bulbar involvement including dysarthria, dysphagia and tongue atrophy Perioral and chin fasciculations and a characteristic postural or action tremor are useful clinical clues Partial androgen insensitivity produces gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy and reduced fertility The disorder is a polyglutamine disease; longer CAG expansions tend to correlate with earlier onset Sensory involvement is frequently detectable on nerve conduction studies even when clinically silent, reflecting a sensory neuronopathy component It must be distinguished from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which it can mimic but from which it differs by its slower course, absence of upper motor neuron signs, and androgen features Significant dysphagia with aspiration and weight loss Recurrent aspiration pneumonia Choking episodes or nocturnal respiratory symptoms Rapid deterioration suggesting an alternative motor neuron disease Misdiagnosing the condition as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and giving an inappropriately grave prognosis Overlooking the androgen features (gynaecomastia, subfertility) that point to the diagnosis Failing to recognise the subclinical sensory neuronopathy on nerve conduction studies Not counselling about X-linked inheritance and carrier status in female relatives Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy is caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat encoding a polyglutamine tract in the androgen receptor. The expanded, ligand-activated receptor misfolds and accumulates, exerting a toxic gain of function that preferentially damages lower motor neurons in the brainstem and spinal cord, together with dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons. Because the toxicity is androgen-dependent, disease is largely confined to men, while the same receptor dysfunction produces partial androgen insensitivity with gynaecomastia and reduced fertility. Progressive motor neuron degeneration leads to bulbar and proximal limb weakness and muscle atrophy. The condition progresses slowly over decades and life expectancy may be near normal or only modestly reduced, with morbidity and mortality driven mainly by bulbar dysfunction, aspiration and falls. Most affected men remain ambulant for many years before requiring aids.

cervical injury Signs of sepsis from urinary infection or pressure injury Symptoms of pulmonary embolism in an immobilised patient Failing to recognise and treat autonomic dysreflexia promptly in at-risk patients Relying on indwelling catheters and neglecting upper urinary tract protection Inadequate pressure relief leading to preventable pressure injuries in insensate skin Overlooking respiratory decline in high cervical injuries until failure occurs Underestimating the psychological impact and the need for coordinated long-term support Spinal cord injury involves a primary mechanical insult to the cord followed by a secondary injury cascade of ischaemia, oedema, excitotoxicity, inflammation, and free-radical damage that extends the initial neurological loss. Interruption of ascending and descending tracts produces motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction below the lesion. After the initial period of spinal shock with flaccid areflexia resolves, reflex activity returns below the level of injury, giving rise to spasticity, neurogenic bladder and bowel, and, in higher lesions, disordered autonomic control including autonomic dysreflexia and orthostatic hypotension. Prognosis depends chiefly on the neurological level and completeness of injury; incomplete injuries and preserved sacral function carry a better outlook for recovery. Most neurological recovery occurs within the first months, and long-term outcomes are strongly influenced by prevention of complications such as pressure injury, urinary tract deterioration, and respiratory disease.

decline with exertional or postural worsening in an older man Ascending sensory level with developing sphincter involvement Abrupt deterioration suggesting venous thrombosis or the Foix-Alajouanine syndrome Neurological worsening after corticosteroid administration Misdiagnosing the condition as transverse myelitis and giving corticosteroids, which may precipitate marked deterioration Overlooking the dorsal serpentine flow voids on MRI that signal the diagnosis Failing to proceed to spinal angiography when imaging suggests a vascular myelopathy Attributing progressive myelopathy to degenerative spinal disease and missing a treatable fistula Not recognising exertional and postural symptom fluctuation as a clue to venous congestion A spinal dural arteriovenous fistula is an acquired direct shunt situated in the dura near a spinal nerve root, where a dural branch of a radiculomeningeal artery connects to a radicular (medullary) vein without an intervening capillary bed. Arterial pressure is transmitted into the normally low-pressure, valveless coronal venous plexus that drains the cord, raising spinal venous pressure and reducing the arteriovenous pressure gradient. The consequent failure of venous drainage causes chronic venous congestion, interstitial oedema and cord hypoxia, producing a progressive myelopathy; unlike intramedullary arteriovenous malformations, the low-flow dural shunt rarely bleeds, and superimposed venous thrombosis can precipitate abrupt, often irreversible deterioration. Gait and motor function commonly improve after treatment by endovascular embolisation or surgical ligation, provided intervention occurs before fixed deficits develop, whereas sphincter recovery is less reliable. Delayed diagnosis allows irreversible cord injury and can result in permanent paraplegia.

The abscess damages the cord through two mechanisms: direct mechanical compression and, importantly, vascular compromise causing ischaemic or venous infarction of the cord, which can produce deficits out of proportion to the degree of compression. Outcome hinges on the speed of diagnosis and decompression; patients treated before significant weakness often recover well, whereas established paralysis or delayed intervention frequently leaves permanent deficits, and severe sepsis carries appreciable mortality.

Attributing canal compromise solely to degenerative stenosis and missing the excess epidural fat Spinal epidural lipomatosis is the abnormal accumulation of histologically normal adipose tissue within the epidural space. It is most commonly driven by states of corticosteroid excess, whether from prolonged exogenous steroid use or endogenous Cushing syndrome, and by obesity, although idiopathic cases are also described. The excess fat encroaches on the limited epidural space and compresses the thecal sac and its neural contents. In the lumbar region the compressed sac takes on a characteristic stellate or Y-shaped configuration, whereas thoracic disease can compress the cord and cause myelopathy. Symptoms often stabilise or improve when the underlying cause is addressed, notably with weight loss and reduction of corticosteroids; severe or myelopathic cases may need surgery, after which outcomes depend on the degree and duration of pre-operative compression.

Spinal Muscular Atrophy — SMA, SMN-related spinal muscular atrophy Congenital myopathies Congenital muscular dystrophies Neonatal or congenital myasthenic syndromes Hypoxic-ischaemic or metabolic encephalopathy causing hypotonia Prader-Willi syndrome and other central causes of hypotonia Pompe disease and other metabolic myopathies Genetic testing for SMN1 deletion/mutation with SMN2 copy number Newborn screening result where available Assessment of respiratory function and swallowing safety Creatine kinase (usually normal or only mildly elevated, helping distinguish from dystrophies) Electromyography and nerve conduction studies if genetic testing is inconclusive Nutritional and growth assessment An autosomal recessive disorder of anterior horn (lower motor neuron) degeneration, most commonly caused by homozygous loss of function of the SMN1 gene. It produces progressive, symmetrical muscle weakness and wasting that is typically more marked proximally and in the legs more than the arms. Disease severity is graded into types (from severe infantile-onset to milder later-onset forms) and correlates broadly with the number of copies of the modifying SMN2 gene. Severe infantile SMA (type 1) presents with profound hypotonia, poor head control, a weak cry, feeding and swallowing difficulty, and paradoxical (belly) breathing with a bell-shaped chest. Tongue fasciculations and absent deep tendon reflexes are characteristic, while cognition and sensation are preserved. Respiratory muscle and bulbar weakness drive the major morbidity and mortality, particularly recurrent aspiration and respiratory failure in the most severe forms. Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing showing biallelic SMN1 loss, with SMN2 copy number providing prognostic information. Disease-modifying therapies that increase SMN protein have substantially changed the outlook, and newborn screening enables early, presymptomatic treatment. Multidisciplinary supportive care addresses respiratory support, nutrition, orthopaedic complications such as scoliosis and contractures, and physiotherapy. Respiratory failure or hypoventilation from progressive respiratory muscle weakness Bulbar weakness with unsafe swallowing and recurrent aspiration Rapidly progressive weakness and loss of motor milestones in an infant Weak cough and impaired airway clearance during intercurrent respiratory infection Signs of impending ventilatory decompensation such as paradoxical breathing and rising work of breathing Attributing infantile hypotonia to a central cause and missing the lower motor neuron pattern Overlooking tongue fasciculations and preserved cognition as clues to anterior horn disease Underestimating respiratory and bulbar risk, especially during intercurrent illness Delaying genetic confirmation and thereby missing the window for early therapy Failing to organise multidisciplinary respiratory, nutritional, and orthopaedic support Loss of functional SMN protein, resulting from homozygous deletion or mutation of SMN1, leads to degeneration and loss of the motor neurons of the anterior horn of the spinal cord and brainstem motor nuclei. The nearly identical SMN2 gene produces only a small amount of full-length functional protein, so a higher SMN2 copy number partially compensates and mitigates severity. Denervation of skeletal muscle causes progressive weakness and atrophy, with the respiratory and bulbar musculature critically affected in severe forms, resulting in hypoventilation, impaired airway clearance, aspiration, and respiratory failure. Historically severe infantile-onset disease carried a very poor prognosis with early respiratory failure, while later-onset forms had longer survival with variable disability. Early diagnosis through newborn screening and initiation of SMN-directed disease-modifying therapy have markedly improved motor outcomes and survival, especially when started presymptomatically.

atrophy is a dominant motor neurone disorder caused by variants in components of the cytoplasmic dynein transport machinery: DYNC1H1 encodes the dynein heavy chain and BICD2 encodes an adaptor that decompressive surgery is considered for disabling or progressive symptoms Progressive myelopathy in cervical stenosis or any sphincter disturbance warrants prompt specialist assessment Imaging findings of stenosis are common with age and must be correlated with symptoms rather than treated in isolation New or progressive cauda equina symptoms such as saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention, or bowel dysfunction requiring urgent evaluation Rapidly progressive cervical myelopathy with worsening gait or hand function Bilateral neurological deficit or significant motor weakness Features suggesting infection or malignancy, such as fever, night pain, or weight loss Treating incidental imaging stenosis that does not match the clinical picture Confusing neurogenic with vascular claudication and missing peripheral arterial disease Overlooking early cervical myelopathy, mistaking gait and hand changes for ageing Failing to recognise cauda equina features as an emergency Spinal stenosis is narrowing of the spinal canal, lateral recesses, or neural foramina that compresses the cord, cauda equina, or nerve roots. It is most often degenerative, resulting from intervertebral disc bulging, osteophyte formation, facet joint hypertrophy, and buckling or thickening of the ligamentum flavum, sometimes compounded by spondylolisthesis or congenitally narrow canals. In the lumbar spine, compression of the cauda equina and roots produces neurogenic claudication, aggravated by extension which further narrows the canal and relieved by flexion. In the cervical spine, cord compression can cause myelopathy through direct pressure and ischaemia. Symptoms often follow a fluctuating or slowly progressive course; many patients are managed conservatively for years, and decompression can relieve claudication and stabilise myelopathy, though established cord damage in cervical disease may not fully reverse.

Spindle cell haemangioma — Spindle cell haemangioendothelioma Kaposi sarcoma Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma Venous malformation with organising thrombi Epithelioid haemangioendothelioma Angiosarcoma Pyogenic granuloma Excisional biopsy with histology showing cavernous vessels, phleboliths, spindle cells and vacuolated endothelium IDH1/IDH2 mutation analysis Radiographs or MRI of the affected limb to detect enchondromas Skeletal survey when Maffucci syndrome is suspected Surveillance imaging for malignant transformation of enchondromas Benign vascular neoplasm, formerly termed spindle cell haemangioendothelioma, typically arising in the distal extremities of adolescents and young adults. Presents as one or several firm, sometimes painful, blue-red dermal or subcutaneous nodules that may recur locally or appear in crops. Strongly associated with Maffucci syndrome (multiple enchondromas plus spindle cell haemangiomas). Somatic IDH1 (and less often IDH2) mutations are characteristic and are shared with the enchondromas of Maffucci syndrome. Histology shows cavernous vessels with organising thrombi and phleboliths alongside a spindled component with vacuolated epithelioid endothelial cells. Does not metastasise, but new lesions commonly develop in the same anatomical region. In Maffucci syndrome there is a substantial lifetime risk of chondrosarcoma and other malignancies, warranting surveillance. Excision is used for symptomatic lesions, though recurrence and new lesions are frequent. Rapid growth or increasing pain in a pre-existing enchondroma, suggesting chondrosarcoma New deep bony lesions in Maffucci syndrome Atypical histological features raising concern for angiosarcoma Neurovascular compromise from an enlarging lesion Mistaking the lesion histologically for Kaposi sarcoma or angiosarcoma. Failing to evaluate for Maffucci syndrome and its malignancy risk. Regarding local recurrence as evidence of malignancy. Neglecting long-term skeletal surveillance. Spindle cell haemangioma is a benign vascular tumour combining thin-walled cavernous blood vessels, often containing organising thrombi and phleboliths, with solid areas of bland spindle cells and epithelioid, vacuolated endothelial cells. Somatic mosaic mutations in IDH1 (rarely IDH2) produce the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate, which alters cellular metabolism and epigenetic regulation; the same mutations drive the enchondromas of Maffucci syndrome, explaining the association. The lesion is thought to reflect a reactive, malformation-like process on a background of abnormal, stasis-prone vessels rather than a truly malignant proliferation. The tumour itself is benign and does not metastasise, though local recurrence and new lesions are common. In Maffucci syndrome the overall prognosis is dominated by the high risk of malignant transformation of enchondromas.

Spindle cell lipoma is a benign adipocytic neoplasm in which mature fat is replaced in varying proportion by bland spindle cells set within a matrix of characteristic thick, eosinophilic ropey collagen fibres, frequently accompanied by myxoid change and scattered mast cells. The tumour, together with its pleomorphic lipoma variant and mammary-type myofibroblastoma, is defined molecularly by deletions of the long arm of chromosome 13 that involve the RB1 tumour suppressor locus; loss of RB1 function drives the proliferation while permitting continued differentiation, so the cells remain cytologically banal. The spindle cells consistently express CD34. This molecular profile is fundamentally different from that of atypical lipomatous tumour and well-differentiated liposarcoma, which are characterised by amplification of MDM2 and CDK4, and the distinction is central to avoiding overtreatment of what is a wholly benign lesion. Spindle cell lipoma is benign with an excellent prognosis, and marginal excision is curative with recurrence being rare. The principal clinical value lies in confidently separating it from atypical lipomatous tumour to avoid unnecessarily aggressive management.

In the common polyglutamine subtypes, expanded CAG repeats produce abnormal proteins that misfold, aggregate, and cause neuronal dysfunction and loss, with a threshold repeat length determining disease and longer expansions producing earlier, more severe disease. Most subtypes are slowly progressive over years to decades with gradual loss of independent mobility and speech; life expectancy is often reduced in more severe subtypes, largely through complications such as aspiration, while relatively pure subtypes may follow a more benign course.

management is supportive and multidisciplinary Progressive dysphagia and aspiration risk from bulbar involvement Rapid functional decline or falls compromising safety Respiratory compromise in advanced disease Assuming a specific subtype from clinical features alone rather than confirming with gene-specific testing Overlooking prominent pyramidal signs that are a useful clue to SCA1 Failing to counsel about anticipation and reproductive implications Neglecting proactive management of dysphagia and aspiration risk SCA1 is a polyglutamine (polyQ) neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expanded CAG repeat in the ATXN1 gene. The elongated polyglutamine tract confers a toxic gain of function on the ataxin-1 protein, promoting its abnormal accumulation and formation of nuclear inclusions, disrupting transcriptional regulation and protein homeostasis. This leads to progressive degeneration predominantly of cerebellar Purkinje cells, brainstem (pontine and olivary) nuclei, and spinocerebellar tracts, producing the olivopontocerebellar pattern of atrophy. Neuronal dysfunction and loss accumulate over years, and the repeat length inversely correlates with age of onset, explaining the phenomenon of genetic anticipation. SCA1 is progressive over one to a few decades, with SCA1 tending to progress somewhat faster than several other dominant ataxias; disability accumulates steadily and premature death commonly results from bulbar and respiratory complications.

recurrence SCA10 is caused by a markedly expanded ATTCT pentanucleotide repeat located within an intron of ATXN10. Because it is non-coding, the disorder is attributed to an RNA-mediated toxic gain-of-function in which the expanded repeat transcript sequesters RNA-binding proteins and disrupts normal RNA processing, rather than to a polyglutamine protein. This leads to Purkinje cell and cerebellar cortical degeneration and, through mechanisms that remain incompletely understood, a lowered seizure threshold in many patients. The large, unstable expansion accounts for variable repeat size, anticipation and the strong founder effect observed in Amerindian-derived populations. SCA10 generally progresses slowly over years to decades; seizure control is achievable in most patients and, when adequate, ataxia remains the main determinant of long-term disability. Prognosis is more guarded in those with frequent seizures or additional systemic features.

In developmental (early-onset) variants this disturbance additionally affects cerebellar development, so the phenotype can combine neurodevelopmental impairment with cerebellar dysfunction, whereas adult-onset variants tend to cause progressive Purkinje cell degeneration and ataxia. In the early-onset form disability is often relatively static but combined with lasting developmental and cognitive impact, whereas the adult-onset form is slowly progressive; overall course and severity vary with the specific variant, and many patients retain useful mobility for extended periods.

ATXN8OS/ATXN8 locus. The region is bidirectionally transcribed: the ATXN8OS strand yields a CUG-containing non-coding RNA thought to exert an RNA toxic gain-of-function similar to the myotonic dystrophies, while the opposite ATXN8 strand encodes a nearly pure polyglutamine protein via a CAG expansion. Both mechanisms are implicated in Purkinje cell and cerebellar degeneration. The considerable variability in expansion length, incomplete penetrance and presence of expanded alleles in the general population make genotype-phenotype correlation less clear-cut than in other repeat ataxias. SCA8 usually follows a slowly progressive course over years to decades with generally preserved life expectancy, though disability from gait ataxia and dysarthria accumulates over time. Reduced penetrance means some expansion carriers remain mildly affected or asymptomatic.

Splenic abscess — abscess of the spleen, splenic suppuration, pyogenic splenic abscess Splenic infarct Splenic cyst (including hydatid cyst) or pseudocyst Subphrenic abscess Left-sided pyelonephritis or perinephric abscess Pancreatic tail abscess or pseudocyst Splenic tumour or lymphoma Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen to characterise the abscess Blood cultures and inflammatory markers to identify the organism and monitor response Echocardiography to seek infective endocarditis as a source Ultrasound for bedside assessment and to guide percutaneous drainage Aspirate microscopy, culture, and sensitivity from drained material Screening for immunocompromise (including HIV and diabetes) where relevant Splenic abscess is uncommon but important, and classically presents with fever, left upper quadrant pain, and left-sided tenderness, sometimes with referred left shoulder-tip pain It most often arises from haematogenous seeding, with infective endocarditis a notable source, and is increasingly seen in immunocompromised and diabetic patients A left pleural effusion, basal atelectasis, or raised hemidiaphragm may be present and can distract from the underlying splenic pathology Contrast CT is the imaging modality of choice and defines the size, number, and character of collections, while ultrasound is a useful bedside adjunct Blood cultures and identification of the causative organism guide targeted antimicrobial therapy; polymicrobial, fungal (especially Candida in the immunosuppressed), and mycobacterial causes occur Management combines appropriate antibiotics with drainage; image-guided percutaneous drainage may suffice for a unilocular collection, while splenectomy is often required for multiloculated or refractory disease An untreated or ruptured splenic abscess can lead to overwhelming sepsis, so prompt diagnosis and source control are essential Signs of rupture with peritonitis and haemodynamic instability requiring emergency surgery Septic shock or multi-organ dysfunction from uncontrolled infection Rapid clinical deterioration despite antibiotics indicating inadequate source control Underlying infective endocarditis with ongoing embolic risk Attributing left upper quadrant pain and fever to pneumonia or a pleural effusion and missing the splenic source Relying on antibiotics alone for a large or multiloculated abscess that requires drainage Failing to seek and treat an underlying source such as endocarditis Neglecting post-splenectomy sepsis prophylaxis and vaccination Overlooking fungal or atypical organisms in immunocompromised patients Splenic abscesses develop when organisms reach and proliferate within splenic tissue, most commonly by haematogenous spread from a distant focus such as infective endocarditis, or from contiguous infection, penetrating trauma, or infarction of the spleen (as in sickle cell disease) that subsequently becomes infected. Immunosuppression, diabetes, and intravenous drug use increase susceptibility and broaden the range of pathogens to include fungi and unusual bacteria. Localised suppuration forms a walled-off collection of pus; as it enlarges it can rupture into the peritoneal cavity, causing peritonitis, or into adjacent structures, and can seed the bloodstream to produce systemic sepsis. With early diagnosis, effective antimicrobial therapy, and adequate drainage or splenectomy the outlook is generally favourable. Mortality rises sharply with delayed treatment, rupture, multiloculated or fungal infection, and significant immunocompromise. After splenectomy patients require lifelong precautions and vaccination against encapsulated organisms.
