near the splenic hilum There is a marked female predominance, and multiparity and pregnancy are important associations Portal hypertension and cirrhosis substantially increase both prevalence and size of these aneurysms Most are asymptomatic, but larger or symptomatic lesions may cause left upper quadrant or epigastric pain Rupture is the feared complication and can present as a two-stage bleed, initially contained within the lesser sac before free intraperitoneal haemorrhage Rupture risk is especially high in pregnancy, where it carries grave maternal and fetal mortality, and this drives aggressive treatment in women of childbearing potential Repair, by endovascular embolisation or open or laparoscopic surgery, is generally advised for large, symptomatic, or pregnancy-associated aneurysms Sudden severe abdominal pain with hypotension suggesting rupture A two-stage presentation with transient stabilisation before collapse Rapidly enlarging or large aneurysm on serial imaging Any splenic artery aneurysm identified in a pregnant patient given the high rupture-related mortality Dismissing an incidental calcified splenic lesion without appreciating rupture risk in higher-risk groups Underestimating the danger of even modest-sized aneurysms during pregnancy Confusing a true aneurysm with a post-inflammatory pseudoaneurysm, which has different management urgency Failing to identify and address underlying portal hypertension A splenic artery aneurysm is a focal dilatation of the splenic artery caused by weakening of the arterial wall, with degeneration of elastic and muscular layers and medial fibrodysplasia. Hormonal and haemodynamic changes of pregnancy, portal hypertension with increased splenic blood flow, atherosclerosis and fibromuscular dysplasia all contribute to wall stress and progressive enlargement. As the aneurysm grows, wall tension rises and the risk of rupture increases; rupture may initially be tamponaded within the lesser sac, producing transient stability before catastrophic free intraperitoneal haemorrhage and haemodynamic collapse. Unruptured aneurysms treated electively have an excellent outcome, whereas rupture carries high mortality, particularly in pregnancy; elective repair of high-risk lesions therefore markedly improves prognosis, and small low-risk aneurysms can be safely surveyed.

splenic artery steal — splenic artery steal syndrome, splenic steal syndrome, SASS Hepatic artery thrombosis Hepatic artery stenosis or kinking Coeliac axis stenosis from median arcuate ligament compression or atherosclerosis Acute cellular rejection Primary graft non-function or preservation injury Biliary anastomotic stricture Portal vein stenosis or thrombosis Doppler ultrasound of the Coeliac axis blood is preferentially diverted through a high-flow, often dilated splenic artery, diminishing flow to the hepatic artery Pre-transplant splenomegaly, portal hypertension, hypersplenism and a large splenic-to-hepatic artery calibre ratio are the principal risk factors Typically presents with otherwise unexplained graft dysfunction, cholestatic derangement of liver enzymes and angiography confirms poor hepatic arterial filling with a prominent splenic artery and is both diagnostic and a platform for treatment Proximal splenic artery embolisation is the preferred treatment, redirecting flow into the hepatic artery, with splenectomy or splenic artery ligation as alternatives The concept remains debated, and some regard the picture as reflecting inadequate hepatic arterial inflow rather than true competitive steal Rising cholestatic liver enzymes with evolving ischaemic cholangiopathy Progressive graft dysfunction despite a patent arterial anastomosis Doppler features that cannot exclude hepatic artery thrombosis, a surgical emergency Deterioration unresponsive to treatment of presumed rejection Attributing graft dysfunction to rejection and overlooking the arterial steal Failing to exclude hepatic artery stenosis or thrombosis before diagnosing steal Overlooking marked splenomegaly as a predisposing risk factor before or after transplantation Embolising too distally within the splenic artery, risking splenic infarction and abscess In the coeliac circulation the hepatic and splenic arteries share a common origin. After liver transplantation, a combination of a relatively small or low-flow hepatic artery and a high-flow splenic artery, the latter enlarged by pre-existing splenomegaly, portal hypertension and hypersplenism, can result in preferential diversion of coeliac flow towards the spleen. The transplanted liver, having lost its portal autoregulatory buffer response and being dependent on arterial inflow for biliary perfusion, is left relatively ischaemic despite a technically patent arterial anastomosis. The resulting hypoperfusion impairs graft function and, because the biliary tree is supplied almost entirely by the hepatic artery, predisposes to ischaemic cholangiopathy and biliary strictures. Whether this represents genuine haemodynamic steal or simply inadequate hepatic inflow is contested, but redirecting flow towards the liver reverses the abnormality. When recognised early and treated with splenic artery embolisation, hepatic arterial flow and graft function usually improve rapidly with a good outcome. Left untreated, persistent hypoperfusion risks ischaemic biliary strictures and graft loss.

Splenic cyst — splenic epidermoid cyst, true (epithelial) splenic cyst, congenital splenic cyst Post-traumatic splenic pseudocyst Parasitic (hydatid) cyst Splenic abscess Cystic neoplasm such as lymphangioma, haemangioma or cystic metastasis Pancreatic pseudocyst or cyst indenting the spleen Organising intrasplenic haematoma Cystic lymphangioma, particularly in children Ultrasound with Doppler to demonstrate an anechoic, well-defined lesion and assess the wall Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to characterise the wall, septa and any enhancement Serum CA 19-9 and CEA, which may be raised with epithelial cysts Hydatid serology and indirect haemagglutination where parasitic disease is possible Full blood count and inflammatory markers if secondary infection or abscess is suspected Histological examination of the excised specimen to confirm the lining type Splenic cysts are classified as true (primary) cysts, which possess an epithelial or mesothelial lining, or false (secondary) pseudocysts, which lack a lining and most often follow trauma; congenital epidermoid cysts are the commonest true non-parasitic type Congenital epidermoid cysts are lined by squamous epithelium and are thought to arise from embryonic inclusion of surface mesothelium within the developing spleen, typically presenting in children and young adults Most are asymptomatic incidental findings; larger cysts cause left upper quadrant pain or fullness, early satiety, referred left shoulder-tip pain or a palpable mass The lining epithelium can secrete CA 19-9 and CEA, so serum levels may be raised and then normalise after excision; this is a diagnostic clue and not a marker of malignancy On imaging a true cyst is a well-defined, thin-walled, non-enhancing fluid lesion, whereas wall calcification and trabeculation favour a pseudocyst, though imaging cannot always separate the two A parasitic (hydatid) cyst must always be excluded before intervention through exposure history, serology and the search for daughter cysts, because inadvertent spillage can cause anaphylaxis and dissemination Spleen-preserving surgery such as partial splenectomy, deroofing or decapsulation is preferred over total splenectomy where feasible, to retain immune function and avoid overwhelming post-splenectomy infection Acute abdomen or hypovolaemia from cyst rupture or intracystic haemorrhage Fever and sepsis suggesting secondary infection or abscess formation Rapid enlargement or solid, septated components raising concern for a neoplasm A large thin-walled cyst at risk of traumatic rupture Interpreting a raised CA 19-9 as evidence of malignancy rather than a benign epithelial cyst Relying on simple percutaneous aspiration, which frequently leads to recurrence Missing a parasitic (hydatid) cyst and risking spillage and anaphylaxis at operation Performing total splenectomy when spleen-preserving surgery would suffice Neglecting vaccination and infection-prevention advice when splenectomy is unavoidable True congenital splenic (epidermoid) cysts are believed to develop from embryonic entrapment of surface mesothelium within the splenic parenchyma, or from metaplasia of these inclusions, producing a cyst lined by squamous or cuboidal epithelium. This epithelium can elaborate CA 19-9 and CEA, accounting for the raised serum markers seen in some patients. Pseudocysts, in contrast, have no epithelial lining and usually represent the organised, liquefied remnant of a previous haematoma, most often post-traumatic. Progressive accumulation of fluid enlarges the cyst, thins the overlying parenchyma and capsule and predisposes to rupture, intracystic haemorrhage or secondary infection. Benign congenital splenic cysts carry an excellent prognosis, and spleen-preserving surgery gives durable results with a low recurrence rate, whereas simple aspiration alone commonly recurs. Malignant transformation is very rare.

splenic infarction — splenic infarct, ischaemic necrosis of the spleen Left-sided pyelonephritis or renal infarction Left lower lobe pneumonia with pleuritic pain Acute pancreatitis Splenic abscess Splenic rupture or subcapsular haematoma Perforated peptic ulcer Diverticulitis of the splenic flexure Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen to demonstrate the wedge-shaped perfusion defect and complications Transthoracic and, if needed, transoesophageal echocardiography to seek a cardioembolic source ECG and ambulatory monitoring for atrial fibrillation Full blood count and peripheral blood film, with JAK2 and myeloproliferative screening where indicated Thrombophilia and antiphospholipid antibody screen, particularly in younger patients Blood cultures where infective endocarditis is suspected Haemoglobin electrophoresis when a sickling disorder is possible Results from occlusion of the splenic artery or its branches, producing the classic wedge-shaped peripheral hypodense lesion on contrast-enhanced CT with its base against the capsule Two dominant mechanisms are cardioembolic disease (atrial fibrillation, infective endocarditis, mural thrombus) and haematological disease (myeloproliferative neoplasms, sickle cell disease and massive splenomegaly of any cause) In a young patient without a cardiac source, actively seek an underlying hypercoagulable state such as antiphospholipid syndrome or an inherited thrombophilia Left upper quadrant pain radiating to the left shoulder tip (Kehr sign) reflects diaphragmatic irritation, but a large proportion of infarcts are clinically silent and found incidentally In sickle cell disease repeated infarction causes autosplenectomy and functional hyposplenism; splenic infarction may also occur in sickle cell trait or HbSC disease at high altitude Global rather than segmental infarction points to splenic artery or vein thrombosis, or to torsion of a wandering spleen Most uncomplicated cases are managed conservatively with analgesia and treatment of the underlying cause, reserving intervention for complications Complications to anticipate include splenic abscess, haemorrhage, subcapsular haematoma, pseudocyst formation and rupture Haemodynamic instability or peritonism suggesting splenic rupture and haemorrhage Persistent swinging fever and rising inflammatory markers indicating abscess formation An enlarging tender mass or falling haemoglobin from a subcapsular haematoma New embolic phenomena elsewhere pointing to an untreated cardiac source Attributing left upper quadrant pain to pneumonia or pancreatitis and overlooking the infarct on imaging Failing to pursue an embolic source or a myeloproliferative or thrombophilic cause Missing an evolving abscess or rupture during conservative management Overlooking resulting functional hyposplenism and the need for immunisation and infection prophylaxis Splenic infarction occurs when arterial inflow through the splenic artery or its segmental branches is interrupted, causing ischaemic necrosis of the dependent parenchyma. Because the spleen has a largely end-arterial segmental supply, occlusion typically produces a wedge-shaped lesion with its base at the capsule. Emboli arising from the heart or aorta, in-situ thrombosis in hypercoagulable and myeloproliferative states, sickling and sludging of red cells within the microcirculation, mechanical compromise of the pedicle in a wandering spleen, or infiltration and expansion in massive splenomegaly can each precipitate ischaemia. Necrotic tissue may resolve with scarring and contraction, liquefy to form a pseudocyst, become secondarily infected to form an abscess, or bleed and rupture through the capsule. Uncomplicated splenic infarction usually settles with conservative management and its outlook is largely determined by the underlying disorder. Development of abscess, significant haemorrhage or rupture worsens the prognosis and may necessitate splenectomy.

symptomatic disease is treated with anti-CD20 targeted therapy, and splenectomy or chemoimmunotherapy in selected cases Rapid splenic enlargement, new B symptoms or rising lactate dehydrogenase suggesting transformation to aggressive lymphoma Severe cytopenias causing bleeding or infection risk Symptomatic autoimmune haemolysis or immune thrombocytopenia Splenic rupture or infarction from massive splenomegaly Failing to test for hepatitis C virus and missing a case treatable with antiviral therapy Confusing the disease with hairy cell leukaemia or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia without full immunophenotyping Overlooking the intrasinusoidal bone marrow pattern that supports the diagnosis Attributing cytopenias solely to marrow infiltration when hypersplenism or autoimmunity is responsible Missing transformation in a patient with sudden clinical change Splenic marginal zone lymphoma arises from a post-germinal-centre memory B cell of the splenic marginal zone. Chronic antigenic stimulation, including that associated with hepatitis C virus infection in a subset of cases, is thought to drive clonal B-cell expansion, and this dependence explains why antiviral therapy can produce regression when HCV is present. The tumour replaces splenic white pulp and infiltrates the red pulp, and typically shows involvement of splenic hilar nodes and an intrasinusoidal pattern in the bone marrow. Recurrent mutations affecting NOTCH2 and the NF-kappaB and marginal-zone differentiation pathways contribute to the neoplastic phenotype. Most patients follow an indolent course with prolonged survival, and HCV-associated cases may regress with antiviral therapy; adverse outcomes are associated with transformation to aggressive large B-cell lymphoma and with certain molecular features such as TP53 abnormalities.

splenic tissue and permit testis-sparing surgery A scrotal mass misinterpreted as malignancy prompting orchidectomy A hard or rapidly enlarging testicular mass requiring urgent tumour work-up Associated limb reduction defects or micrognathia indicating the syndromic form An undescended testis with its attendant malignancy and torsion risk Removing the testis for a presumed tumour without frozen section or splenic scintigraphy Not considering the diagnosis in a boy with a left scrotal mass and a limb anomaly Attributing a waxing and waning scrotal swelling to a hernia Failing to preserve the gonad in a child when benign splenic tissue is confirmed Overlooking associated cryptorchidism and its long-term surveillance needs During the second month of embryogenesis the splenic primordium develops within the dorsal mesogastrium in close proximity to the left urogenital ridge, mesonephros and gonad. If splenic tissue adheres abnormally to the gonadal anlage before the gonad begins its descent, the splenic tissue is either tethered to or carried along with the gonad. In the continuous type a cord, sometimes beaded with splenic nodules, connects the orthotopic spleen to the gonad; in the discontinuous type an isolated mass of splenic tissue is fused to the gonad. The preponderance of left-sided and male cases reflects these embryological relationships, and the association with limb reduction defects in the continuous type reflects the timing of the developmental insult. Splenogonadal fusion is benign and the prognosis is excellent when it is recognised and treated with testis-sparing excision of the ectopic splenic tissue. The principal avoidable morbidity is unnecessary orchidectomy resulting from misdiagnosis as a testicular tumour.

found throughout the abdomen and pelvis, and rarely in the thorax, liver or subcutaneous tissue at old wound sites Imaging features that cannot confidently be distinguished from malignancy and require exclusion Gastrointestinal bleeding or bowel obstruction attributable to an implant Haemoptysis or pleuritic symptoms in thoracic splenosis Misinterpreting implants as malignancy and proceeding to needless biopsy or resection Assuming splenosis fully restores immune function and omitting vaccination and prophylaxis Not considering the diagnosis in a patient with prior splenic trauma and new peritoneal or pleural nodules Confusing splenosis with a congenital accessory spleen Splenosis develops when splenic pulp is disseminated during traumatic rupture or at splenectomy, seeding the peritoneal cavity, omentum, serosal surfaces of the bowel, mesentery and diaphragm, or the pleural space when the diaphragm is breached. The viable red pulp fragments implant on vascularised surfaces and induce neovascularisation, deriving a blood supply from the surrounding host tissue rather than from the splenic artery. The resulting nodules are histologically splenic and retain some filtering and immune capacity, but their total mass and disordered architecture usually provide only incomplete restoration of splenic function. Because they enlarge slowly and appear as multiple soft-tissue nodules, they frequently masquerade radiologically as metastatic or peritoneal malignancy. Splenosis is benign and the great majority of patients remain asymptomatic for life, needing no treatment. The principal hazard is misdiagnosis as malignancy leading to unnecessary intervention.

Spondyloarthritis — ankylosing spondylitis, axial spondyloarthritis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis Mechanical (nonspecific) back pain - the etiology in 95-96% of chronic back pain; axSpA accounts for only 4-5% (Harrison 22e p.2885) Fibromyalgia / central sensitization (especially mistaken for SpA in women, delaying diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.2885) Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) - noninflammatory, flowing osteophytes over >=4 contiguous vertebrae, normal sacroiliac joints, in obese diabetic males >50; can be mistaken for bamboo spine (Harrison 22e p.2886) Osteitis condensans ilii (OCI) - asymptomatic triangular iliac-side sclerosis in multiparous women; lack of erosions distinguishes from axSpA (Harrison 22e p.2886) Osteoarthritis of the spine - horizontal osteophytes vs vertical syndesmophytes (Harrison 22e p.2884) Rheumatoid arthritis - symmetric polyarticular MCP/PIP disease, RF/nodules present (Harrison 22e p.2879) Hypothyroidism and hypovitaminosis D in young patients with generalized body pain (Harrison 22e p.2886) Septic sacroiliitis from tuberculosis, brucellosis, fungi, or other infectious agents - can cause inflammatory back pain with sclerotic sacroiliac changes (Harrison 22e p.2886) Osteomyelitis (consider with red-flag features) (Harrison 22e p.2886) Infectious enterocolitis-like acute gut inflammation seen histologically in SpA terminal ileum (Harrison 22e p.2891) HLA-B27 typing - supportive but neither necessary nor sufficient for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2884) ESR and CRP - elevated in only 30-40% of active axSpA; neither sensitive nor specific, but useful for monitoring (Harrison 22e p.2884, 2888) Plain AP or Ferguson pelvic radiograph for sacroiliitis (multiple oblique views add little and increase gonadal radiation) (Harrison 22e p.2884) MRI of sacroiliac joints/spine - detects active osteitis/bone marrow edema (STIR) and structural lesions (sclerosis, fat metaplasia, erosions, backfill, ankylosis) early; not indicated for routine monitoring (Harrison 22e p.2885, 2888) Low-dose CT of sacroiliac joints/spine - emerging alternative to radiography for diagnosis and progression (Harrison 22e p.2885) Synovial fluid analysis in monoarthritis - WBC >2000/mL with negative crystals/Gram stain/culture suggests inflammatory arthritis; rules out septic and crystal arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2888) Fecal calprotectin (elevated with microscopic gut inflammation in SpA) (Harrison 22e p.2891) Disease activity indices: BASDAI, ASDAS; function: BASFI; metrology: BASMI (Harrison 22e p.2886) Postpartum sacral insufficiency fracture (Harrison 22e p.2886) Osteoporotic vertebral fracture (Harrison 22e p.2886) Metastatic disease / malignancy, including acute lymphoblastic leukemia presenting with inflammatory back pain and sacroiliac sclerosis (Harrison 22e p.2886) MRI osteitis-like changes from mechanical stress in athletes, postpartum women, and normal individuals >40 (risk of overdiagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.2885) Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD) and gout (may coexist with/mimic PsA) (Harrison 22e p.2889) SAPHO and hidradenitis suppurativa (may mimic palmoplantar psoriasis/PsA) (Harrison 22e p.2889) Spondyloarthritis (SpA) is a family of immune-mediated inflammatory arthritides sharing clinical, genetic, and pathologic features; classified by ASAS (2009) into axial (axSpA) and peripheral (pSpA). Axial skeletal involvement is hinted at in the name but is NOT mandatory (Harrison 22e p.2879). axSpA is subdivided into radiographic (r-axSpA, = ankylosing spondylitis [AS]) and nonradiographic (nr-axSpA), the difference based on presence/absence of definitive sacroiliitis on plain radiographs; the two share the same clinical features and disease burden (Harrison 22e p.2880, 2883). pSpA encompasses psoriatic arthritis (PsA), reactive arthritis (ReA), IBD-associated arthritis, and undifferentiated pSpA; SAPHO, acne-associated, and hidradenitis suppurativa-associated arthritis are sometimes included (Harrison 22e p.2880). HLA-B27 is the strongest genetic risk factor: present in 85-90% of r-axSpA and 50-90% of nr-axSpA, versus ~5% of the healthy Caucasian population (Harrison 22e p.2881). Inflammatory back pain (IBP): insidious onset, age <45, chronic (>3 months), improves with exercise/activity but NOT with rest, worse in second half of night with improvement after getting up, and prolonged (>30 min) morning stiffness; this distinguishes it from mechanical back pain (Harrison 22e p.2883). Characteristic SpA pattern is asymmetric mono-/oligoarticular (<=4 joints) inflammatory arthritis of large lower-limb joints (usually knee) with enthesitis, tendonitis, and dactylitis (sausage digits), contrasting with the symmetric polyarticular MCP/PIP involvement of rheumatoid arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2879). Hips are the most common nonspinal ('root') joints affected in axSpA; peripheral arthritis occurs in ~30-40% of axSpA patients (Harrison 22e p.2883). Uveitis is the most common extramusculoskeletal manifestation (~40% of axSpA), typically acute, anterior, unilateral, and episodic; other extra-articular features include psoriasis (~10%) and IBD (frank IBD ~10%, subclinical gut inflammation up to 50%) (Harrison 22e p.2883-2884). Enthesitis (inflammation at tendon/ligament insertions) is common in axSpA, presenting as heel pain (plantar fasciitis, Achilles insertion), chest wall pain, epicondylitis, or pelvic rim pain; dactylitis is relatively rare in axSpA but common in PsA (Harrison 22e p.2883). Persistent axial inflammation leads to bony fusion of sacroiliac and apophyseal joints and syndesmophyte formation; complete ankylosis of the spine is termed 'bamboo spine,' seen in only a very small percentage of late-stage AS patients (Harrison 22e p.2880, 2884). Typical SpA syndesmophytes are vertically oriented, distinguishing them from the horizontal osteophytes of spinal osteoarthritis; PsA syndesmophytes are often chunky and nonmarginal (Harrison 22e p.2884, 2889). Reactive arthritis follows infectious gastroenteritis (Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter) or genitourinary Chlamydia; classic features include urethritis, conjunctivitis, mucosal ulcers, and keratoderma blennorrhagica (Harrison 22e p.2880). IBD-associated arthritis: r-axSpA develops in up to 10% of IBD patients and pSpA in 10-30%; conversely axSpA patients have a 5-10% risk of developing IBD. HLA-B27 is NOT a risk factor for IBD itself (Harrison 22e p.2891-2892). Fever, weight loss, advanced age, or past malignancy in a back-pain patient - prompt evaluation for osteomyelitis, osteoporotic fracture, or metastatic disease (Harrison 22e p.2886) Cauda equina syndrome (urinary hesitancy and/or saddle anesthesia) - late axSpA complication (Harrison 22e p.2884) Cardiac conduction abnormalities (heart block) at any stage; aortic valve insufficiency as a late complication (Harrison 22e p.2884) AA (renal) amyloidosis causing nephrotic syndrome after prolonged uncontrolled inflammation; IgA nephropathy with microscopic hematuria (Harrison 22e p.2884) Spinal fractures in ankylosed (bamboo) spine - consider if back pain persists/relapses despite therapy (Harrison 22e p.2888) Atlantoaxial subluxation (rare, in PsA) with potentially serious neurologic consequences (Harrison 22e p.2889) Acute anterior uveitis (eye pain, redness, photophobia, miosis) requiring urgent ophthalmologic care (Harrison 22e p.2884) PITFALL: confusing inflammatory back pain with common mechanical back pain - mechanical causes must be considered first since axSpA is the etiology in only 4-5% of chronic back pain; conversely IBP improves with exercise and worsens with rest, the reverse of mechanical pain (Harrison 22e p.2883, 2885). The term 'inflammatory back pain' is itself a partial misnomer - only ~15% of patients with IBP have demonstrable axial inflammation (Harrison 22e p.2883). Diagnostic delay of 5-14 years is common, worse in women (back pain/enthesitis mistaken for fibromyalgia) and in nonwhite populations with lower HLA-B27 prevalence (Harrison 22e p.2884). Interreader reliability for distinguishing r-axSpA from nr-axSpA on radiographs is poor (kappa 0.35-0.45), even between trained musculoskeletal radiologists (Harrison 22e p.2883). MRI overdiagnosis: osteitis-type and fat-metaplasia changes occur from mechanical stress in athletes, postpartum women, degenerative arthritis, and normal individuals >40 (Harrison 22e p.2885). Normal/negative inflammatory markers do NOT exclude axSpA - ESR/CRP elevated in only 30-40% of active disease (Harrison 22e p.2884). Plain spine radiographs should generally be avoided in chronic back pain; multiple oblique sacroiliac views add little but increase gonadal radiation (Harrison 22e p.2884). Avoid glucocorticoid injection around lower-extremity weight-bearing entheses due to risk of tendon rupture; in IBD-associated arthritis anti-IL17 therapy is contraindicated and NSAIDs may trigger IBD flares (Harrison 22e p.2890-2892). SpA is a prototypic chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease that couples inflammation to structural damage, with the unique feature that inflammation-induced bone loss coexists with pathologic new bone formation at specific skeletal sites (sacroiliac joints, anterior spinal ligaments, peripheral entheses). HLA-B27, an MHC class I allele, is the strongest genetic risk factor; proposed mechanisms include the arthritogenic peptide theory (HLA-B27 presenting microbial peptides to CD8+ T cells with molecular mimicry), HLA-B27 homodimerization engaging innate receptors (KIR3DL2) to drive IL-17, and unfolded protein response/autophagy promoting IL-23-driven type 17 immunity. Disease requires additional factors beyond HLA-B27 (only ~5% of HLA-B27-positive people, and 20% of HLA-B27-positive first-degree relatives, develop axSpA); key instigators are loss of intestinal barrier integrity with microbial dysbiosis (germ-free HLA-B27 transgenic rats fail to develop disease) and aberrant response to mechanical stress. The IL-23/IL-17 axis and TNF-alpha are central, with overlapping yet domain-distinct cytokine signatures across gut, joint, entheses, and skin (Harrison 22e p.2880-2882). Course is variable: ~50% of patients progress from nonradiographic to radiographic stage over 20 years, but <10% progress to significant spinal involvement with bamboo spine. Risk factors for osteoproliferation (worse structural outcome) include male sex, persistent inflammation (MRI sacroiliac/spine activity, high CRP), existing syndesmophytes, HLA-B27 positivity, and smoking. With increased awareness and earlier treatment, structural damage has steadily decreased over recent decades, with a shift toward higher prevalence of nr-axSpA over r-axSpA. axSpA significantly impairs well-being, function, productivity, and quality of life. Reactive arthritis is often self-limiting but may become chronic, with HLA-B27 linked to chronicity (Harrison 22e p.2880, 2884, 2891). axSpA is classified as radiographic (r-axSpA / ankylosing spondylitis) vs nonradiographic (nr-axSpA) using definitive sacroiliitis on plain radiographs per the modified New York criteria: definitive = grade 2 bilateral OR grade 3-4 unilateral or bilateral (r-axSpA); lower-grade sacroiliitis = nr-axSpA. ASAS criteria further split SpA into axial (axSpA) and peripheral (pSpA). Diagnosis of axSpA in chronic back pain follows the schema of Figure 374-2 (definite sacroiliitis on x-ray -> AS; otherwise count SpA features >=4 or compelling clinical picture plus MRI sacroiliitis/HLA-B27 -> nr-axSpA). Disease activity graded with BASDAI/ASDAS; PsA classified with CASPAR criteria, activity by DAPSA/MDA (Harrison 22e p.2883-2884, 2889).

normal lung growth and ventilation In DLL3-related disease the spine may show a characteristic 'pebble beach' or generalised vertebral disorganisation on radiographs Distinguish from spondylothoracic dysostosis, in which symmetric posterior rib fusion gives a 'crab-like' or fan-shaped thorax Respiratory distress or failure from thoracic insufficiency, especially in infancy Rapidly progressive scoliosis compromising lung development Signs of spinal cord involvement or neurological deficit Recurrent respiratory infections indicating restrictive lung disease Focusing on the scoliosis while underestimating the life-limiting thoracic insufficiency Confusing spondylocostal with spondylothoracic dysostosis, which differ in rib pattern and prognosis Missing associated visceral anomalies by not screening beyond the skeleton Assuming dominant inheritance when most forms are autosomal recessive, giving incorrect counselling Spondylocostal dysostosis results from disruption of the Notch signalling pathway that drives the segmentation clock during somitogenesis, most commonly through recessive variants in DLL3, MESP2, LFNG or HES7, or from TBX6-related mechanisms. Faulty oscillatory gene expression disturbs the orderly formation and boundary specification of somites, the embryonic precursors of vertebrae and their associated ribs. The result is multiple, often widespread vertebral segmentation and rib anomalies. Because the axial skeleton and thorax form abnormally, chest volume and compliance are reduced, producing thoracic insufficiency and restrictive respiratory disease. Outcome depends chiefly on the severity of thoracic insufficiency: milder cases have good survival with orthopaedic management of the spine, whereas severe early respiratory compromise carries significant mortality. Multidisciplinary respiratory and orthopaedic care is central.

cartilage and the vitreous, caused by dominant variants in COL2A1. Defective type II collagen impairs the cartilage template for endochondral ossification, particularly affecting the vertebral bodies and epiphyses, producing platyspondyly, short trunk, and epiphyseal dysplasia. Because type II collagen is also a major component of the vitreous and inner ear, affected individuals are prone to myopia, retinal detachment, and hearing loss, placing the condition within the broader spectrum of type II collagenopathies. Intelligence and lifespan are typically normal, but adult stature is markedly reduced and morbidity arises from spinal deformity, premature osteoarthritis, cervical instability, and ocular complications that require lifelong surveillance.

Spondylolisthesis — isthmic spondylolisthesis, degenerative spondylolisthesis, vertebral slip Mechanical low back pain Lumbar disc herniation Lumbar spinal stenosis without slip Vertebral fracture or pathological lesion Sacroiliac joint dysfunction Standing lateral radiographs to demonstrate and grade the slip Flexion-extension views to assess dynamic instability MRI to evaluate neural compression, disc, and root involvement CT or oblique views to characterise a pars defect when suspected Bone imaging (e.g. SPECT or MRI) in young athletes for a suspected active pars stress injury Spondylolisthesis is forward (or occasionally backward) slippage of one vertebra on the one below, most often at the lumbosacral junction Isthmic slips relate to a defect in the pars interarticularis (spondylolysis), often from repetitive extension stress in young athletes, while degenerative slips occur in older adults from facet and disc degeneration Many slips are asymptomatic; when symptomatic, patients report low back pain, hamstring tightness, and sometimes radicular leg pain or neurogenic claudication Severity is commonly graded by the degree of slip relative to the vertebral body width, which helps guide monitoring and management Standing lateral and flexion-extension radiographs are useful to demonstrate the slip and any dynamic instability Most cases are managed conservatively with activity modification, physiotherapy focusing on core stabilisation, and analgesia Surgery, typically decompression with or without fusion, is considered for persistent disabling symptoms, neurological deficit, or progressive high-grade slips High-grade slips in the skeletally immature warrant closer surveillance because of the potential for progression New or progressive neurological deficit or radiculopathy Cauda equina symptoms such as saddle anaesthesia or sphincter disturbance High-grade or progressive slip, particularly in a young or skeletally immature patient Severe unremitting pain or features suggesting infection or malignancy Relying on supine imaging, which can underestimate a slip that is only apparent when standing Missing dynamic instability by omitting flexion-extension views Overlooking a pars stress injury in a young athlete with extension-related back pain Attributing all symptoms to the slip without excluding coexisting stenosis or disc pathology Spondylolisthesis is displacement of one vertebra relative to the adjacent vertebra, usually anterior translation of the upper on the lower body. In isthmic disease a stress-related defect or fracture of the pars interarticularis (spondylolysis) allows the anterior elements to slip forward. In degenerative disease, age-related disc narrowing and facet joint arthropathy reduce the segment's stability and permit gradual slippage, typically without a pars defect. The malalignment can narrow the central canal and neural foramina, tethering or compressing nerve roots and, in higher grades, causing back pain and radicular or claudicant symptoms. Most low-grade, degenerative, and isthmic slips remain stable and respond well to conservative care; higher-grade slips and those with neurological compromise are more likely to need surgery, which generally improves symptoms though progression can occur in growing patients.

surgical repair or fusion is reserved for refractory pain or a progressive slip Neurological deficit or radicular symptoms suggesting nerve-root compression from a high-grade slip Rapidly progressive slip on serial imaging Constitutional symptoms or night pain suggesting infection or tumour Relying on plain radiographs alone, which miss early stress reactions Failing to monitor for slip progression during adolescent growth Attributing all adolescent back pain to spondylolysis without excluding other causes Spondylolysis is a defect of the pars interarticularis, the bony bridge linking the superior and inferior articular processes of a vertebra. It usually represents a fatigue (stress) fracture from repetitive hyperextension and rotational loading rather than an acute injury, and there is a recognised genetic and dysplastic predisposition. The lowest lumbar level (L5) bears the greatest shear stress and is most often affected. When the defect is bilateral the vertebral body can slip forward on the one below, producing isthmic spondylolisthesis, which may in turn narrow the foramen and place the exiting nerve root under tension. Many young patients achieve pain-free return to activity with conservative management, and early stress reactions may heal with rest; high-grade or progressive slips and persistent pain may require surgical stabilisation, but outcomes are generally good.

syndrome Overlooking subtle angiographic appearances without using intracoronary imaging Failing to screen for fibromuscular dysplasia and other arteriopathies after diagnosis Neglecting the elevated recurrence risk when counselling and following up patients Spontaneous coronary artery dissection occurs when blood accumulates within the coronary arterial wall, either through a tear in the intima or through spontaneous haemorrhage from the vasa vasorum, creating a false lumen or intramural haematoma. The expanding haematoma compresses the true lumen and restricts coronary flow, producing myocardial ischaemia or infarction without the atherosclerotic plaque rupture that underlies most acute coronary syndromes. The arterial wall is thought to be predisposed by an underlying arteriopathy, most commonly fibromuscular dysplasia, rendering it vulnerable to hormonal influences and to shear stress from emotional or physical triggers, which explains the strong female and peripartum predominance. Because the primary problem is a wall haematoma rather than a fixed plaque, the vessel often heals over weeks, and mechanical instrumentation risks extending the dissection. Most stable patients managed conservatively do well, with spontaneous angiographic healing over subsequent weeks, though there is a recognised risk of recurrence, particularly in the context of underlying arteriopathy. High-risk anatomy or haemodynamic instability worsens the short-term outlook and may necessitate intervention despite its hazards.

Sporotrichosis — rose gardener's disease, Sporothrix schenckii infection, lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis Cutaneous nocardiosis (sporotrichoid pattern) Atypical mycobacterial infection (e.g. Mycobacterium marinum) Cutaneous leishmaniasis Tularaemia Bacterial lymphangitis or cutaneous tuberculosis Mycobacterium marinum fish-tank granuloma Nocardia brasiliensis lymphocutaneous infection Cutaneous leishmaniasis Cutaneous tuberculosis (scrofuloderma or lupus vulgaris) Fungal culture of aspirate, exudate or tissue as the diagnostic gold standard Histopathology of biopsy for granulomatous inflammation and yeast forms with asteroid bodies Imaging of bone and joints when osteoarticular disease is suspected Chest imaging in suspected pulmonary involvement Assessment of immune status including HIV testing in disseminated disease A subacute-to-chronic infection caused by the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix, acquired through traumatic inoculation of soil, thorns, sphagnum moss or plant material into the skin The classic lymphocutaneous form begins as a papule or nodule at the inoculation site that ulcerates, followed by a chain of nodules tracking along lymphatic channels (sporotrichoid spread) A fixed cutaneous form remains localised at the inoculation site without lymphatic progression Occupational and recreational exposure among gardeners, farmers and forestry workers is a key historical clue Extracutaneous disease, including osteoarticular, pulmonary and disseminated forms, occurs mainly in immunocompromised or alcoholic patients Diagnosis is confirmed by fungal culture of pus, tissue or aspirate, with histopathology sometimes showing yeast forms and asteroid bodies Itraconazole is the preferred agent for cutaneous and lymphocutaneous disease, with amphotericin-based therapy reserved for severe, disseminated or meningeal infection; saturated potassium iodide remains a low-cost option in some settings Disseminated or multifocal disease suggesting significant immunosuppression Pulmonary involvement with cavitation or systemic symptoms Osteoarticular disease with joint destruction Meningeal involvement, which is rare but serious and difficult to treat Stopping antifungal therapy too early before lesions have fully resolved, risking relapse Overlooking the inoculation history and misdiagnosing bacterial infection Failing to investigate for immunosuppression in disseminated cases Not distinguishing sporotrichoid spread from other causes of nodular lymphangitis Sporothrix species exist as mould in the environment and convert to a yeast form at body temperature after traumatic inoculation into skin or subcutaneous tissue. A localised suppurative and granulomatous (mixed pyogranulomatous) inflammatory response develops. The organism spreads proximally along lymphatic vessels, producing successive nodules. In immunocompromised hosts or after inhalation, haematogenous or pulmonary dissemination can occur, involving bones, joints, lungs and rarely the meninges. Cell-mediated immunity is central to containment, explaining severe disease in those with impaired T-cell function. Lymphocutaneous and fixed cutaneous disease respond well to prolonged azole therapy with an excellent outcome, whereas disseminated, pulmonary and meningeal forms carry a much poorer prognosis and require aggressive treatment, particularly in immunocompromised hosts.

Overlooking an omovertebral bone that limits movement and complicates surgery Attributing the asymmetry to posture or torticollis Neglecting associated scoliosis and rib anomalies Underestimating the psychosocial effect of visible shoulder asymmetry Sprengel deformity results from failure of the normal caudal descent of the scapula during embryonic development. The scapula forms in the cervical region and normally migrates to its thoracic position by around the third month of gestation; arrested or incomplete descent leaves it elevated, hypoplastic, and often medially rotated. An abnormal osseous, cartilaginous, or fibrous connection (the omovertebral bar) may tether the superomedial scapula to the lower cervical vertebrae, tethering it in position and restricting movement. Because the disturbance occurs during the same period as cervical vertebral segmentation and rib formation, associated anomalies such as Klippel-Feil fusion, scoliosis, and rib defects frequently coexist. Most cases are sporadic. The deformity itself is not life-limiting; mild cases need only observation, while surgical repositioning in selected children can improve appearance and shoulder function, with outcome influenced by associated spinal and girdle anomalies.

multidisciplinary setting Emphasise sun protection, treatment of field damage, and regular surveillance, and consider reducing immunosuppression in transplant patients where feasible A rapidly enlarging, ulcerating, or bleeding lesion, especially at high-risk sites such as the lip or ear Palpable regional lymphadenopathy or new neurological symptoms suggesting perineural or nodal spread A tumour arising in a chronic wound, scar, or previously irradiated skin (potential for aggressive behaviour) Multiple or aggressive tumours in an immunosuppressed or transplant patient Underestimating the metastatic potential and treating cutaneous SCC as casually as basal cell carcinoma Failing to biopsy and assess an indurated or growing lesion within a field of actinic damage Omitting lymph node examination and staging in high-risk tumours Not recognising the heightened risk and aggressive course in immunosuppressed and transplant patients Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is a malignant proliferation of epidermal keratinocytes that have acquired full-thickness atypia and then breached the basement membrane to invade the dermis. Cumulative ultraviolet radiation is the dominant driver, producing signature mutations including in TP53 and other tumour-suppressor and oncogene pathways, with additional contributions from immunosuppression, human papillomavirus in some tumours, chronic inflammation or scarring, and carcinogen exposure. Progression typically follows a continuum from dysplastic keratinocytes (actinic keratosis) through in-situ disease (Bowen's) to invasive carcinoma. Invasive nests of atypical keratinocytes with variable keratinisation can track along nerves and invade lymphatics, giving the potential for metastasis that distinguishes it from basal cell carcinoma. Most low-risk cutaneous SCCs are cured by complete excision, but prognosis worsens with high-risk features such as large size, deep invasion, poor differentiation, perineural involvement, high-risk sites, and immunosuppression, which raise the likelihood of recurrence and metastasis; early detection and adequate treatment are key to good outcomes.

no specific corrective therapy exists Diagnosis is confirmed by SRD5A3 molecular genetic testing Progressive visual loss or severe congenital ocular malformation Developmental regression or worsening cerebellar signs Refractory seizures Failure to thrive with multisystem involvement Managing the eye findings in isolation without recognising an underlying glycosylation disorder Misattributing the transferrin abnormality to secondary causes Overlooking the coagulopathy before surgery Delaying molecular testing when a type I pattern accompanies ocular anomalies SRD5A3 encodes polyprenol reductase, which converts polyprenol to dolichol, the lipid carrier required to build the oligosaccharide precursor for N-glycosylation and other glycan pathways. Reduced dolichol availability limits assembly of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide, so N-linked sites are under-occupied and transferrin shows a type I pattern. The strikingly ocular-predominant phenotype reflects the sensitivity of eye development to glycosylation, while widespread hypoglycosylation accounts for the neurological, cutaneous and dysmorphic features. Visual impairment is often significant and may progress, while neurodevelopmental outcome varies with disease severity; overall prognosis depends on the burden of neurological and systemic complications. There is no treatment that corrects the underlying defect.

ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction — STEMI, Acute ST-elevation MI, Q-wave myocardial infarction, Transmural myocardial infarction Acute pericarditis (radiation of discomfort to the trapezius favors pericarditis and is not seen in STEMI) Pulmonary embolism Acute aortic dissection Costochondritis Gastrointestinal disorders (the xiphoid/epigastric location can mimic indigestion) Serial 12-lead ECG to detect ST-segment elevation and evolution of Q waves Cardiac troponin T or I (high-sensitivity assays preferred); a rise and/or fall with at least one value above the 99th percentile upper reference limit defines myocardial injury/infarction CK and CK-MB historically used; a CK-MB mass to CK activity relative index of 2.5 or greater suggests but is not diagnostic of myocardial origin, and CK-MB's rapid decline can help detect early reinfarction Two-dimensional echocardiography for regional wall-motion abnormalities, LV function, RV infarction, ventricular aneurysm, pericardial effusion, LV thrombus, and Doppler detection of VSD and mitral regurgitation Radionuclide myocardial perfusion imaging (e.g., 99mTc-sestamibi) shows a 'cold spot' but cannot distinguish acute infarct from chronic scar Acute pericarditis Pulmonary embolism Acute aortic dissection Costochondritis Esophageal and other gastrointestinal causes of chest pain Type 2 MI from oxygen supply-demand imbalance unrelated to acute atherothrombosis STEMI typically arises when coronary flow drops abruptly after a thrombus forms over an atherosclerotic plaque that has eroded or ruptured; slowly progressive high-grade stenoses less often cause STEMI because collaterals develop over time (Harrison 22e p.2113). Plaques prone to disruption tend to have a large lipid core and a thin fibrous cap, yet fewer than 5% of such thin-capped fibroatheromas actually become the nidus for an acute MI during long-term follow-up (Harrison 22e p.2113). Deep, visceral chest pain described as heavy, squeezing, or crushing, usually central and/or epigastric and lasting longer than angina, is the most common presentation; it may radiate to the arms, back, lower jaw, or neck but not below the umbilicus (Harrison 22e p.2114). Pain is not universal: painless STEMI is more frequent in patients with diabetes mellitus and increases with age, and the event may instead present as sudden breathlessness, syncope, confusion, profound weakness, arrhythmia, peripheral embolism, or an unexplained fall in blood pressure (Harrison 22e p.2114). Anterior infarction may produce sympathetic overactivity (tachycardia/hypertension), whereas inferior infarction may produce parasympathetic overactivity (bradycardia/hypotension) (Harrison 22e p.2114). Substernal chest pain lasting more than 30 minutes combined with diaphoresis strongly suggests STEMI (Harrison 22e p.2114). The 12-lead ECG is the pivotal triage tool: total epicardial coronary occlusion produces ST-segment elevation, and most patients presenting with ST elevation ultimately evolve Q waves (Harrison 22e p.2115). Cardiac troponin T and I are the preferred biomarkers when measured with high-sensitivity assays and may rise to roughly 20-50 times the upper reference limit in classic MI, remaining elevated for at least 7-10 days after STEMI (Harrison 22e pp.2115-2116). Because urgent reperfusion decisions rest on clinical and ECG findings, high-sensitivity troponin is of less immediate value in confirmed STEMI than in the broader chest-pain workup (Harrison 22e p.2116). Wall-motion abnormalities on two-dimensional echocardiography are almost universal in STEMI and aid triage, but acute infarction cannot be distinguished from old scar or severe acute ischemia by echo alone (Harrison 22e p.2116). The two major classes of complications determining prognosis in the primary-PCI era are electrical (arrhythmias) and mechanical (pump failure); most out-of-hospital STEMI deaths result from sudden ventricular fibrillation (Harrison 22e p.2117). Temperature can rise up to 38 degrees C during the first week, and a nonspecific leukocytosis (often 12,000-15,000/microL) appears within hours and persists 3-7 days, with the ESR rising more slowly and peaking in the first week (Harrison 22e pp.2114, 2116). Sudden development of ventricular fibrillation, the leading cause of out-of-hospital STEMI death, with most such deaths occurring within the first 24 hours and over half within the first hour Hypotension or unexplained drop in arterial pressure Sudden loss of consciousness, confusional state, or profound weakness as an atypical STEMI presentation New apical systolic murmur suggesting mitral valve apparatus dysfunction, a serious mechanical complication Inferior infarction with elevated jugular venous pressure, clear lungs, and hypotension suggesting right ventricular infarction Pericardial friction rub in transmural STEMI Signs of pump failure / cardiogenic shock and mechanical complications such as ventricular septal defect Equating absence of pain with absence of STEMI: painless infarction is common in diabetics and older patients and may present only as dyspnea, syncope, or hypotension (Harrison 22e p.2114). Misattributing xiphoid/epigastric pain to indigestion, compounded by the patient's own denial of a heart attack (Harrison 22e p.2114). Older terms Q-wave/non-Q-wave and transmural/nontransmural MI correlate poorly with pathology and have been replaced by STEMI and NSTEMI; Q-wave development depends more on infarct volume than on transmurality (Harrison 22e p.2115). Peak biomarker concentration correlates only weakly with infarct size, and early reperfusion causes earlier biomarker peaking from rapid washout, so peak levels should not be used to gauge infarct size (Harrison 22e p.2116). Echocardiographic wall-motion abnormalities cannot distinguish acute STEMI from old scar or severe acute ischemia (Harrison 22e p.2116). Radionuclide perfusion 'cold spots' cannot distinguish acute infarct from chronic scar, so they are not specific for acute MI (Harrison 22e p.2117). STEMI usually results from abrupt thrombotic occlusion of a coronary artery already affected by atherosclerosis. Vascular injury promoted by smoking, hypertension, lipid accumulation, and inflammation leads to disruption of an atherosclerotic plaque by erosion or rupture, exposing its contents to blood under conditions favoring thrombogenesis. A platelet monolayer forms first; agonists such as collagen, ADP, epinephrine, and serotonin activate platelets, releasing thromboxane A2 (a local vasoconstrictor) and converting the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor to a high-affinity state that binds fibrinogen and cross-links platelets. Exposure of tissue factor activates the coagulation cascade (factors VII and X), generating thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin; an autoamplifying thrombin reaction culminates in an occlusive thrombus of platelet aggregates and fibrin. The extent of necrosis depends on the territory supplied, completeness and duration of occlusion, collateral supply, myocardial oxygen demand, endogenous thrombolysis, and adequacy of reperfusion. Microvascular dysfunction can produce no-reflow. Healing proceeds through acute (first hours-7 days), healing (7-28 days), and healed (29+ days) stages, with polymorphonuclear leukocytes then proinflammatory and reparative monocytes driving clearance, angiogenesis, extracellular matrix production, scar formation, and ventricular remodeling (Harrison 22e pp.2113-2116). About half of AMI-related deaths occur before the patient reaches the hospital. In-hospital mortality after admission for AMI has fallen from roughly 10% to about 5%, and the 1-year mortality after AMI is approximately 15%. Mortality is roughly fourfold higher in patients older than 75 years than in younger patients. Up to one-third of STEMI patients achieve spontaneous reperfusion of the infarct-related artery within 24 hours with improved healing. Outcome hinges largely on electrical (arrhythmic) and mechanical (pump failure) complications (Harrison 22e pp.2113, 2117). Patients with prolonged ischemic discomfort are first classified as an acute coronary syndrome and triaged by the 12-lead ECG into ST-segment elevation versus no ST-segment elevation; biomarkers then separate unstable angina from NSTEMI. The Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction classifies MI into five types: type 1 (atherothrombotic), type 2 (oxygen supply-demand imbalance unrelated to acute atherothrombosis), type 3 (cardiac death with presumed new ischemic ECG changes before troponin became available), type 4 (PCI-related, including 4a, 4b stent thrombosis, 4c restenosis), and type 5 (CABG-related). Procedure-related MI within 48 h is defined by troponin elevation greater than 5-fold (type 4a) or greater than 10-fold (type 5) the 99th percentile URL with additional ischemic criteria (Harrison 22e pp.2114, 2117-2118).

Stable angina pectoris — chronic stable angina, exertional angina, stable ischaemic heart disease, SIHD Acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI) Gastro-oesophageal reflux and oesophageal spasm Musculoskeletal or costochondral chest pain Pericarditis Aortic dissection Pulmonary embolism Anxiety or panic disorder Resting 12-lead ECG and comparison with prior tracings Exercise or pharmacological stress testing with ECG or imaging to demonstrate inducible ischaemia Coronary CT angiography to define anatomy in low to intermediate risk patients Invasive coronary angiography when high-risk features or refractory symptoms are present Assessment for anaemia, thyroid dysfunction, and metabolic risk factors including lipids and glucose Resting echocardiography to assess left ventricular function and exclude structural disease Classic presentation is retrosternal chest discomfort or pressure precipitated by exertion or emotion and relieved within minutes by rest or short-acting nitrates Discomfort commonly radiates to the left arm, neck, or jaw, and anginal equivalents such as exertional breathlessness or fatigue are frequent in older adults, women, and people with diabetes Symptoms are reproducible and stable over weeks to months; a change in the threshold, frequency, or duration signals progression toward an acute coronary syndrome The resting ECG is often normal between episodes, so a normal tracing does not exclude significant coronary disease Functional imaging or stress testing establishes inducible ischaemia, while coronary CT angiography is increasingly used to assess anatomy in patients at low to intermediate risk Management combines aggressive risk-factor and lifestyle modification, antianginal therapy to control symptoms, and antiplatelet and statin therapy to reduce cardiovascular events Revascularisation is considered for symptoms refractory to medical therapy or for high-risk anatomy such as significant left main or proximal multivessel disease Grading anginal severity (for example by the Canadian Cardiovascular Society classes) helps track response to treatment and guide escalation Angina occurring at rest, at low workload, or with escalating frequency or duration, suggesting an evolving acute coronary syndrome Chest pain with haemodynamic instability, syncope, or new heart failure Tearing or interscapular pain suggesting aortic dissection Prolonged pain unrelieved by rest or nitrates that may indicate infarction Assuming a normal resting ECG excludes significant coronary disease Overlooking atypical or equivalent presentations in women, older adults, and people with diabetes Attributing new rest or crescendo symptoms to stable angina rather than recognising an acute coronary syndrome Focusing on symptom relief while neglecting event-reducing secondary prevention Stable angina results from a mismatch between myocardial oxygen demand and supply, most often caused by fixed atherosclerotic narrowing of one or more epicardial coronary arteries. When demand rises with exertion, a flow-limiting stenosis cannot augment supply sufficiently, producing transient subendocardial ischaemia and the sensation of angina. Endothelial dysfunction, coronary microvascular disease, and vasospasm can contribute or cause ischaemia even without high-grade obstruction. Ischaemia is reversible and resolves once demand falls, distinguishing it from the sustained supply-demand failure of infarction. Prognosis depends on the extent and location of coronary disease, left ventricular function, and control of risk factors; many patients do well for years on guideline-directed medical therapy, but left main or extensive multivessel disease and impaired ventricular function carry higher event rates.

weigh salvage against nephrectomy Serum renal function and inflammatory markers Metabolic screen for a non-infective stone nidus A large branching stone that fills the renal pelvis and extends into two or more calyces, taking the shape of a stag's horn Most are struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate and carbonate apatite) related to chronic infection with urease-producing organisms, though a minority are cystine or uric acid They may be surprisingly asymptomatic or present with vague loin ache, recurrent urinary infection or haematuria rather than classic colic Complications include recurrent pyelonephritis, sepsis, progressive loss of renal function and, rarely, squamous cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis Non-contrast CT defines the stone burden and pelvicalyceal anatomy for treatment planning Left untreated, a staghorn calculus carries a substantial risk of kidney loss and life-threatening sepsis Treatment aims for complete stone clearance, most often by percutaneous nephrolithotomy, because residual fragments perpetuate infection and regrowth Culture-directed antibiotics against the urease organism are an essential adjunct to surgical clearance Sepsis from an infected obstructed staghorn kidney Rapidly deteriorating renal function A poorly functioning kidney harbouring chronic infection Suspicion of squamous cell carcinoma within a chronic staghorn Managing with antibiotics alone without addressing the stone Accepting incomplete clearance, which virtually guarantees recurrence Failing to assess residual renal function before deciding on treatment Overlooking malignancy in a chronically infected, calcified kidney A staghorn calculus is defined by its shape and extent rather than its composition, but the great majority arise from chronic infection with urease-producing bacteria that alkalinise the urine and drive rapid precipitation of struvite and carbonate apatite within the pelvicalyceal system. Because bacteria are incorporated into the stone, infection persists and the calculus enlarges to occupy the collecting system. Continuing infection and obstruction cause inflammation, scarring and progressive parenchymal destruction; non-infective staghorns can also form from cystine or uric acid when a heavy solute load fills the collecting system. Complete clearance with eradication of infection offers the best chance of preserving function and preventing recurrence; incompletely treated staghorns frequently recur, and long-standing disease can lead to a non-functioning kidney requiring nephrectomy.

stannosis — tin oxide pneumoconiosis, tin pneumoconiosis silicosis mixed-dust fibrosis baritosis and other benign inert-dust pneumoconioses siderosis (iron oxide pneumoconiosis) coal workers' pneumoconiosis pulmonary sarcoidosis miliary tuberculosis or other miliary nodular disease detailed occupational history of tin smelting, refining or fume exposure chest radiography demonstrating dense, discrete nodular opacities high-resolution CT to characterise nodules and assess for fibrosis pulmonary function tests to confirm preserved lung function assessment of co-existing silica or other fibrogenic dust exposure workplace air sampling and dust characterisation biopsy or mineralogical analysis only if the diagnosis is uncertain Stannosis is a benign inert-dust pneumoconiosis caused by inhalation of tin oxide (stannic oxide) fume and dust, without fibrosis or functional impairment. It is a classic example of a radiologically dramatic but clinically silent pneumoconiosis, because tin is radiodense and highly opaque on imaging. Chest radiographs show numerous small, very dense, sharply defined nodular opacities distributed widely through the lungs, sometimes with dense hilar and even pleural or perihilar deposits. The striking radiographic density reflects the high atomic number of tin rather than any tissue reaction, so appearances greatly overstate the biological effect. Exposure occurs in tin smelting and refining, tin-oxide production, and processes generating tin fume; the ore cassiterite may co-contain silica, which must be considered separately. Patients are typically asymptomatic with normal lung function and no increased risk of progressive fibrosis, tuberculosis or malignancy from the tin itself. The key clinical task is to distinguish benign stannosis from silicosis, mixed-dust fibrosis or other serious pneumoconioses that share nodular patterns but carry a worse prognosis. Occupational history and knowledge of the specific exposure are essential; regression is not expected but progression is also not seen once exposure ceases. development of true fibrosis or functional impairment suggesting co-exposure to silica progressive breathlessness or cough not explained by benign dust retention radiographic features atypical for inert-dust deposition such as masses or cavitation constitutional symptoms or weight loss prompting exclusion of infection or malignancy coalescing or conglomerate opacities indicating a fibrotic pneumoconiosis Misinterpreting the dramatic dense nodular radiograph as silicosis or malignancy. Attributing coexisting fibrosis to tin rather than to concomitant silica exposure. Subjecting an asymptomatic worker to unnecessary invasive investigation. Failing to take an accurate occupational history and therefore missing the diagnosis. Assuming all radiodense pneumoconioses are harmful and causing undue alarm. Inhaled tin oxide particles are deposited in the alveoli and small airways and taken up by alveolar macrophages. Tin oxide is biologically inert and does not stimulate the fibrogenic macrophage response seen with silica, so the particles accumulate as dust-laden macrophage aggregates in a perivascular and peribronchiolar distribution without collagen deposition, granuloma formation or architectural distortion. The result is a non-fibrotic accumulation of dust (a benign 'inert-dust' pneumoconiosis) that leaves alveolar structure and gas exchange intact. The high radiographic density arises purely from the high atomic number and radio-opacity of tin, causing prominent nodular shadowing that is disproportionate to the negligible tissue reaction. Any fibrosis or functional loss in a tin worker should prompt a search for co-exposure to silica or other fibrogenic dusts. Stannosis is benign: it does not cause symptoms, functional impairment or progressive disease, and there is no increased risk of fibrosis or malignancy from tin oxide alone. The radiographic changes persist but do not progress once exposure ceases.

Staphylococcal Infections — Staph aureus infection, MRSA Group A streptococcal infection (overlaps with staphylococci in impetigo, cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis, and toxic shock syndrome) (p.389, p.993) Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (more often with overt soft-tissue infection/necrotizing fasciitis and bacteremia, less prominent exanthem) (p.993) Toxic epidermal necrolysis and severe drug eruptions (in the differential of widespread skin blistering versus SSSS) (p.389, p.402) Kawasaki disease and scarlet fever (other causes of scarlatiniform rash with palm/sole desquamation) (p.402) Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome Scarlet fever (group A streptococcal erythrogenic toxin) Clostridium sordellii toxic shock (childbirth-associated or black-tar heroin injection; fever typically absent) Blood cultures, repeated from both central and peripheral sites, to confirm bacteremia and distinguish true infection from skin-flora contamination/catheter colonization (differential time-to-positivity can localize a catheter source) (p.581) Frozen section of the blister roof or exfoliative cytology of blister contents to distinguish SSSS from toxic epidermal necrolysis rapidly (p.402) Culture of lesional material from skin/soft-tissue infection to guide therapy and detect MRSA (p.389) mecA gene detection as the genotypic basis of methicillin resistance, enabling rapid genotypic MRSA identification (p.1195) Double-disk diffusion (D-zone) test to detect inducible clindamycin resistance when an isolate is erythromycin-resistant but clindamycin-susceptible (p.383) Echocardiography and a search for metastatic foci in S. aureus bacteremia to evaluate for endocarditis (p.994) Toxic epidermal necrolysis / severe drug eruption (mimics SSSS) Kawasaki disease (polymorphous rash, conjunctival injection, desquamation; clues are cervical lymphadenopathy, cheilitis, thrombocytosis) SARS-CoV-2-associated multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children Staphylococcus aureus causes a wide spectrum of disease, ranging from localized skin and soft-tissue infection to invasive bloodstream, endocardial, and bone infection and to toxin-mediated syndromes; methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) is now common in both community and health-care settings (p.1195, p.389). Furunculosis (boils) is caused by S. aureus and has risen in prominence with community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA); patients frequently mistake furuncles for spider or insect bites, and family members or close contacts may also be affected (p.389). Whenever possible, send lesional material from staphylococcal skin infection for culture; incision and drainage may be adequate therapy for a small solitary furuncle without surrounding cellulitis or systemic symptoms (p.389). Impetigo is caused most often by S. aureus (and sometimes group A streptococci) and forms a characteristic honey-colored crust; bullous impetigo, with tense clear bullae, is produced by S. aureus exfoliative toxin (phage type II) (p.389). In staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome (SSSS) the site of staphylococcal infection is usually extracutaneous (e.g., conjunctivitis, rhinorrhea, otitis media, pharyngitis) and the skin lesions themselves are sterile, whereas in bullous impetigo the skin lesions are the actual site of infection (p.402). Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is defined by clinical criteria — fever, diffuse macular (sunburn-type) erythroderma, hypotension, and multiorgan involvement — with three criteria involving mucocutaneous sites (diffuse skin erythema, desquamation of palms and soles 1-2 weeks after onset, and mucous-membrane hyperemia of the vagina, oropharynx, or conjunctivae) (p.402, p.993). In staphylococcal TSS, the vagina or a postoperative wound is typically colonized rather than overtly infected, and mucosal areas appear hyperemic but not infected; this contrasts with streptococcal TSS, which is more often linked to overt skin/soft-tissue infection and bacteremia (p.993). Acute bacterial endocarditis from S. aureus follows a far more aggressive course than subacute endocarditis, can attack previously normal native valves, and native-valve S. aureus (including MRSA) endocarditis is increasing in frequency (p.994). Coagulase-negative staphylococci are skin commensals; a single positive blood-culture bottle for skin flora (especially one taking >24 h to turn positive) should raise suspicion of contamination or catheter colonization rather than true bloodstream infection, and cultures should be repeated from both central and peripheral sites (p.581). S. aureus bacteremia warrants an active search for infective endocarditis and metastatic/seeded foci, because any primary focus can give rise to bloodstream infection with secondary seeding (p.994). In TSS, rapid hypotension developing within hours of symptom onset, and early renal failure preceding hypotension, are warning features (early renal failure helps distinguish TSS from other septic shock syndromes) (p.993). Acute S. aureus endocarditis: a changing murmur, congestive heart failure, rapid valvular destruction (especially aortic) with pulmonary edema and hypotension, myocardial abscess with conduction block/arrhythmia, and large friable vegetations causing arterial emboli, metastatic infection, or stroke (p.994). Widespread skin blistering or radial perioral crusting with diffuse tenderness suggests SSSS and demands prompt evaluation (p.402). S. aureus among organisms that can present as intractable hypotension/septic shock with a primary soft-tissue focus (p.993). Attributing a single positive blood culture for coagulase-negative staphylococci to true bacteremia when it may represent skin-flora contamination or catheter colonization — repeat paired cultures and assess time-to-positivity (p.581). Assuming a primary skin focus is present in staphylococcal TSS; colonization (vaginal or wound) without overt infection is typical, so the portal may be subtle (p.993). Missing the diagnosis of S. aureus endocarditis in older patients, whose nonspecific presentation delays recognition (p.994). Confusing SSSS with toxic epidermal necrolysis or severe drug eruption; SSSS occurs mainly in infants/toddlers, is more superficial, spares the oral mucosa, and is toxin- rather than drug-mediated (p.402). Inducible clindamycin resistance can cause treatment failure in apparently clindamycin-susceptible isolates unless the double-disk (D-zone) test is performed (p.383). S. aureus expresses cell wall-anchored adhesins called MSCRAMMs (microbial surface components recognizing adhesive matrix molecules, e.g., SdrC) that mediate binding to host extracellular-matrix proteins and underpin adherence and colonization (p.967). Like other extracellular pathogens it can form biofilms, which contribute to device- and prosthesis-associated infection (p.967). Disease is driven partly by potent secreted toxins. Superantigens — including toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1) and the staphylococcal enterotoxins — bind invariant regions of MHC class II molecules and the T-cell receptor, nonspecifically activating vast numbers of T cells and triggering a cytokine storm responsible for fever, rash, and the shock of TSS (p.974, p.402). S. aureus also produces an erythrotoxin causing scarlatiniform rash and exfoliative toxin ("exfoliatin") that cleaves the superficial epidermis to produce bullous impetigo and SSSS (p.402, p.389). It elaborates several pore-forming toxins — leukocidins, alpha- and gamma-hemolysins, and phenol-soluble modulins — that lyse host cells, protect the organism from phagocytosis, and impair development of protective adaptive immunity (p.975). Methicillin resistance results from acquisition of the mobile mecA gene carried on the SCCmec cassette, which has spread widely through the S. aureus population (p.1195). Outcome varies sharply by syndrome. For TSS, reported mortality is about 5% for menstruation-associated and 10-15% for nonmenstrual disease (compared with 30-70% for streptococcal TSS) (p.993). Acute bacterial endocarditis, including native-valve S. aureus/MRSA disease, carries mortality of roughly 10-40%, and older patients with S. aureus endocarditis often present with nonspecific symptoms that delay diagnosis and worsen prognosis (p.994). Rapid recognition and intervention are crucial across invasive staphylococcal syndromes. No single graded severity scale is presented; staphylococcal disease is categorized by clinical syndrome and invasiveness — superficial skin/soft-tissue infection (impetigo, furunculosis), toxin-mediated syndromes (TSS, SSSS, scarlatiniform eruption), and invasive disease (bacteremia, infective endocarditis, osteomyelitis, septic intracranial/epidural infection). TSS is defined by formal clinical criteria (fever, diffuse erythroderma, hypotension, multiorgan involvement with mucocutaneous features) (p.402, p.993).

is useful for monitoring progression Patients should avoid high-dose vitamin A supplementation, which may accelerate lipofuscin accumulation Rapid or asymmetric visual decline prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Widespread (rather than macular) retinal dysfunction on ERG indicating a poorer-prognosis phenotype Inadvertent high-dose vitamin A intake potentially accelerating disease Labelling early cases as functional or refractive when acuity loss precedes visible fundus change Recommending or overlooking high-dose vitamin A supplements that may worsen the disease Confusing it with age-related macular degeneration in older patients and mismanaging accordingly Failing to arrange genetic testing and counselling for recessive inheritance Stargardt disease is caused by defects in ABCA4, a transporter in photoreceptor outer-segment discs that clears retinoid by-products of the visual cycle. Loss of transporter function allows toxic bisretinoid compounds to accumulate and form excessive lipofuscin (including A2E) within the retinal pigment epithelium. This lipofuscin overload is cytotoxic to the retinal pigment epithelium, leading to its dysfunction and death and secondary loss of the overlying photoreceptors, concentrated at the macula. The result is progressive central photoreceptor and pigment-epithelial atrophy with the characteristic flecks representing lipofuscin-laden cells. Central vision is progressively lost, often to the level of legal blindness, while peripheral vision is usually preserved; the rate of progression varies with genotype and age of onset, and gene- and pharmacologically-targeted therapies are under active investigation.
