infection without considering targeted therapy STAT1 is a signal transducer activated downstream of type I, type II and type III interferons and of interleukin-27. Gain-of-function variants impair the normal dephosphorylation of STAT1, leaving it persistently phosphorylated and producing exaggerated interferon-driven gene expression. This heightened STAT1 activity suppresses the differentiation of interleukin-17-producing T-helper-17 cells, which are essential for mucosal defence against Candida, explaining the chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. The same interferon over-activity fosters loss of immune tolerance with autoimmunity, contributes to vascular pathology and, together with chronic mucosal inflammation, raises the risk of squamous malignancy. The course ranges from relatively mild mucocutaneous disease to severe multisystem involvement; life-limiting complications include invasive infection, squamous malignancy and vascular events, though targeted JAK inhibition has improved outcomes in refractory cases.

STAT3 loss-of-function (autosomal dominant hyper-IgE / Job syndrome) — STAT3 loss-of-function deficiency, autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome, AD-HIES, Job syndrome, signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 deficiency DOCK8 deficiency autosomal recessive hyper-IgE syndrome PGM3 deficiency Severe atopic dermatitis with reactive IgE elevation Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome Chronic granulomatous disease with recurrent abscesses Cystic fibrosis or other causes of recurrent pneumonia with cavitation Comel-Netherton syndrome Serum IgE with full blood count and eosinophil quantification Enumeration of interleukin-17-producing T-helper cells Quantitative immunoglobulins and specific antibody responses Genetic sequencing of STAT3 Chest imaging to detect pneumatocoeles and monitor for secondary fungal infection Bone density assessment and skeletal or dental review Vascular imaging where aneurysm or tortuosity is suspected An autosomal dominant multisystem disorder caused by dominant-negative mutations in STAT3, classically presenting as the hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome The immunological hallmark is a triad of recurrent staphylococcal skin abscesses (often cold, lacking the usual warmth and inflammation), recurrent pneumonias with pneumatocoele formation, and a markedly elevated serum IgE Chronic eczematoid dermatitis and mucocutaneous candidiasis are common and often begin in infancy Connective-tissue and skeletal features are characteristic: a distinctive coarse facial appearance, hyperextensible joints, recurrent fractures with reduced bone density, and scoliosis Retained primary teeth from failure of normal deciduous tooth shedding is a classic dental clue Vascular abnormalities including aneurysm formation and tortuosity may develop, and pneumatocoeles can become secondarily infected with fungi such as aspergillus Diagnosis integrates a clinical scoring approach with a high IgE, reduced interleukin-17-producing T cells, and confirmatory STAT3 sequencing; management centres on antistaphylococcal and antifungal prophylaxis, skin care, and vigilant treatment of lung complications Recurrent cold staphylococcal abscesses with a very high IgE Pneumatocoeles or cavitary lung disease with secondary aspergillus or other fungal infection Pathological fractures or progressive scoliosis Aneurysm formation or coronary/cerebral vascular abnormality Extensive mucocutaneous candidiasis in infancy Mistaking cold abscesses for simple recurrent boils and missing the underlying syndrome Draining or operating on pneumatocoeles without recognising the risk of secondary fungal colonisation and poor healing Attributing a high IgE solely to atopy Overlooking the non-immune skeletal, dental, and vascular features that aid diagnosis Underusing antifungal and antistaphylococcal prophylaxis in established disease STAT3 is a transcription factor that relays signals from numerous cytokines, including interleukin-6, interleukin-10, interleukin-21, and interleukin-23. Dominant-negative mutations produce a protein that interferes with the normal STAT3 encoded by the intact allele, so STAT3-dependent signalling is broadly reduced. A key consequence is failure to generate interleukin-17-producing T-helper cells, which are needed to defend skin and mucosa against Staphylococcus aureus and candida, explaining the abscesses and candidiasis. Impaired STAT3 signalling also disturbs the regulation of inflammation (contributing to the paradoxically cold abscesses and elevated IgE), and because the same pathway participates in bone remodelling, connective-tissue maintenance, vascular integrity, and dental development, the disorder extends well beyond immunity into the skeletal, dental, and vascular abnormalities that define the syndrome. Many patients survive into adulthood with attentive antimicrobial prophylaxis and skin care, but chronic lung damage with secondary fungal infection is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality, and vascular and skeletal complications add to the long-term burden.

malformation of the pilosebaceous unit centred on the sebaceous duct. In familial disease, dominant variants in KRT17 disturb the keratin cytoskeleton of the sebaceous duct and associated epithelium, producing multiple cysts lined by stratified squamous epithelium with a characteristic crenulated eosinophilic cuticle and containing sebaceous lobules. The cysts accumulate sebaceous secretions, and when they rupture the released contents provoke inflammation, which in the suppurativa variant leads to abscess-like lesions and scarring. The condition is benign with no malignant potential; cysts persist and slowly accumulate over time, and the main impact is cosmetic, though the suppurativa variant can cause scarring.

Stercoral colitis — stercoral ulceration Ischaemic colitis Diverticulitis Infective or inflammatory colitis Colonic obstruction or pseudo-obstruction Colorectal malignancy CT of the abdomen and pelvis Assessment of the degree of faecal impaction Inflammatory markers and lactate Evaluation of constipation cause and comorbidities Surgical review where perforation or necrosis is suspected Inflammation and ulceration of the colonic wall caused by pressure from impacted, hardened faeces (a faecaloma) It occurs in patients with severe chronic constipation, typically elderly, immobile or institutionalised The rectosigmoid and the antimesenteric border are most often affected It can progress to ischaemic pressure necrosis, ulceration and stercoral perforation, which is life-threatening CT shows a distended faeces-filled colon with wall thickening, pericolonic changes or, if perforated, free air Management includes disimpaction and bowel decompression, with surgery for perforation or necrosis Peritonitis or free air indicating stercoral perforation Signs of colonic necrosis or systemic toxicity Marked colonic distension with impending perforation Rapid clinical deterioration Underestimating the perforation risk of severe faecal impaction Confusing it with diverticulitis or ischaemic colitis Failing to address the underlying chronic constipation Overlooking the diagnosis in a frail, constipated patient with abdominal pain Stercoral colitis develops when a hard, impacted faecal mass exerts sustained pressure on the colonic wall, exceeding capillary perfusion pressure and causing localised ischaemia. The resulting mucosal and mural injury produces inflammation and stercoral ulcers, which can deepen to full-thickness necrosis and perforation. The rectosigmoid is predisposed because of its narrower lumen and firmer stool, and chronic constipation with reduced colonic motility and sensation underlies the impaction. Uncomplicated cases improve with disimpaction and bowel care, but stercoral perforation carries a high mortality, so early recognition is important.

Sternocostoclavicular hyperostosis — SCCH, sternoclavicular hyperostosis, acquired hyperostosis syndrome, anterior chest wall hyperostosis SAPHO syndrome (broader multifocal disease) Sternoclavicular septic arthritis or osteomyelitis Metastatic disease of the sternum or clavicle Paget disease of bone Condensing osteitis of the clavicle Ankylosing spondylitis with anterior chest wall involvement Bone scintigraphy to demonstrate the anterior chest wall 'bull's head' uptake pattern CT of the anterior chest wall to define hyperostosis, sclerosis and ossification MRI to assess active osteitis and adjacent soft-tissue involvement Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), often mildly to moderately raised Venography or vascular imaging if subclavian vein compression is suspected A chronic hyperostotic and osteitic process centred on the sternum, medial clavicles and first ribs, causing anterior chest wall pain and bony swelling Considered by many to be the anterior chest wall expression of SAPHO syndrome, and frequently accompanied by palmoplantar pustulosis Presents with recurrent episodes of anterior chest pain and firm swelling over the sternoclavicular region, sometimes with restricted shoulder girdle movement Bone scintigraphy classically demonstrates increased tracer uptake in the 'bull's head' distribution across the sternoclavicular joints The process is sterile; cultures are negative and it is not a pyogenic infection despite the osteitis Ossification and hyperostosis can compress adjacent structures, occasionally causing subclavian vein compression and venous congestion of the arm Managed like SAPHO with NSAIDs first-line, and bisphosphonates or DMARDs including TNF inhibition for refractory disease Features of true infection (fever, rigors, positive cultures) requiring exclusion of septic arthritis or osteomyelitis Destructive lesion or mass raising concern for malignancy Arm swelling and venous distension suggesting subclavian vein compression or thrombosis Rapidly progressive deformity or neurological symptoms at the thoracic inlet Misdiagnosing sterile osteitis as pyogenic infection and giving prolonged antibiotics or surgery Failing to recognise the link with SAPHO syndrome and palmoplantar pustulosis Overlooking subclavian vein compression as a cause of arm swelling Attributing anterior chest pain to a cardiac cause and missing the bone pathology Sternocostoclavicular hyperostosis is a chronic sterile osteitis with reactive new bone formation affecting the sternum, medial clavicles and first ribs, and their connecting joints and ligaments. It is regarded as part of the SAPHO/autoinflammatory spectrum, in which dysregulated innate immunity drives neutrophilic bone inflammation and progressive hyperostosis and ossification of the anterior chest wall soft tissues and joints. The association with palmoplantar pustulosis and severe acne, and the proposed role of skin commensals such as Cutibacterium acnes as immune triggers, mirror the mechanisms of SAPHO syndrome. Progressive ossification produces bony expansion that can bridge joints and encroach on neurovascular structures at the thoracic inlet. The condition follows a chronic relapsing course; pain and swelling often persist over years, and although it is benign, progressive hyperostosis can cause lasting anterior chest wall discomfort and occasionally vascular compression.

Steroid cell tumour of the ovary — lipid cell tumour, lipoid cell tumour, steroid cell tumour not otherwise specified Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour Polycystic ovary syndrome Congenital adrenal hyperplasia Androgen- or cortisol-secreting adrenal tumour Luteoma of pregnancy Metastatic tumour with luteinised stroma Serum testosterone and full androgen profile to confirm hyperandrogenism Cortisol and adrenal axis testing when a Cushingoid picture is present Transvaginal ultrasound to identify a solid ovarian mass Adrenal and pelvic cross-sectional imaging to localise the hormone source Histology with assessment of size, mitoses, necrosis, and atypia to gauge malignant potential Immunohistochemistry (e.g. inhibin, calretinin, Melan-A) to confirm the diagnosis A rare sex cord-stromal tumour composed of cells resembling steroid-secreting cells, frequently producing androgens and causing virilisation Most commonly secretes testosterone, so hirsutism, oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, and virilisation are typical presenting features Some tumours instead secrete oestrogen or cortisol, occasionally producing a Cushingoid picture Subclassified into stromal luteoma, Leydig cell tumour, and steroid cell tumour not otherwise specified, the last being the most common and having the greatest malignant potential Leydig cell tumours may contain characteristic cytoplasmic Reinke crystals Usually unilateral; larger size, mitotic activity, necrosis, and atypia point towards malignant behaviour Managed surgically, with fertility-sparing options for benign-appearing tumours in young women and resolution of androgenic features after removal Rapidly progressive virilisation with markedly raised testosterone and an ovarian mass A Cushingoid presentation from cortisol secretion Histological features (large size, mitoses, necrosis, atypia) suggesting malignancy Evidence of metastatic spread at presentation Attributing hyperandrogenism to polycystic ovary syndrome and missing a small functioning tumour Failing to separate an ovarian from an adrenal source of steroid excess Assuming all steroid cell tumours are benign and overlooking malignant features Neglecting to reassess hormone levels after surgery to confirm cure Steroid cell tumours are sex cord-stromal neoplasms made up of cells with abundant eosinophilic or lipid-rich cytoplasm that resemble luteinised stromal cells, Leydig cells, or adrenocortical cells, and characteristically synthesise steroid hormones. Androgen production, most often testosterone, is the usual functional consequence and drives virilisation, although some tumours elaborate oestrogen or, less commonly, cortisol with resulting Cushingoid features. The category is divided into stromal luteoma and Leydig cell tumour, which are almost always benign, and steroid cell tumour not otherwise specified, which accounts for most cases and carries a definite risk of malignant behaviour. Malignancy is suggested by larger size, increased mitotic activity, necrosis, haemorrhage, and nuclear atypia rather than by hormonal output. Stromal luteomas and Leydig cell tumours are almost always benign and cured by excision, with hormonal effects regressing afterwards; steroid cell tumours not otherwise specified are benign in most cases but a substantial minority behave malignantly, so outlook depends on histological features and stage.

steroid induced glaucoma — corticosteroid-induced glaucoma, steroid responder glaucoma primary open-angle glaucoma uveitic glaucoma where the underlying inflammation also raises pressure pigmentary glaucoma pseudoexfoliation glaucoma normal-tension glaucoma with incidental steroid use traumatic or angle-recession glaucoma ocular hypertension unrelated to steroids detailed corticosteroid exposure history across all routes gonioscopy confirming an open angle intraocular pressure measurement and comparison with pre-treatment baseline optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer and ganglion cell complex standard automated perimetry optic disc examination and photography review for a periocular or intravitreal steroid depot on examination or imaging Any route of corticosteroid delivery can raise intraocular pressure, including topical eye drops, periocular and intravitreal injections, inhaled, nasal, dermatological and systemic preparations. The angle is open and the clinical picture otherwise resembles primary open-angle glaucoma, so a medication history is essential. Response usually develops within weeks of starting topical steroid, but potent intravitreal depots can cause a delayed and prolonged rise. Around a third of the general population are moderate responders and a smaller proportion are high responders; primary open-angle glaucoma patients and their relatives respond more frequently and more strongly. Children, particularly young ones, can respond rapidly and severely, sometimes within days. Drop potency matters: more potent molecules cause larger rises, whereas weaker or ester-based steroids and some newer agents carry a lower risk. The mainstay of management is stopping or reducing the steroid, or switching to a lower-potency agent, alongside pressure-lowering therapy. Pressure usually normalises after topical steroid withdrawal, but an intravitreal depot may require surgical removal or filtration surgery if the effect persists. markedly raised pressure in a child on corticosteroids persistent high pressure after an intravitreal steroid depot glaucomatous optic nerve damage discovered at first presentation very high pressures threatening rapid field loss in a known high responder Failing to ask about non-ophthalmic steroids such as inhalers, nasal sprays and skin creams. Continuing potent topical steroid for chronic conditions without monitoring pressure. Assuming pressure will fall quickly after an intravitreal depot when the effect can persist for months. Overlooking the heightened and rapid susceptibility of children. Attributing the raised pressure solely to steroids in a uveitic eye where inflammation also contributes. Corticosteroids reduce aqueous outflow facility at the trabecular meshwork through several interacting mechanisms. They promote accumulation of extracellular matrix material, including glycosaminoglycans, fibronectin and cross-linked actin networks, within the juxtacanalicular meshwork, and they suppress the normal turnover of this matrix by reducing phagocytic activity and matrix metalloproteinase expression in trabecular cells. Changes in trabecular cell cytoskeleton and gene expression, including induction of myocilin, further stiffen the outflow pathway. The net effect is increased resistance to aqueous drainage through an anatomically open angle, raising intraocular pressure. Susceptibility is partly genetically determined, which parallels the shared predisposition seen in primary open-angle glaucoma. When recognised early and the steroid is withdrawn, intraocular pressure usually returns to normal without lasting damage; prolonged unrecognised elevation, or an inescapable long-acting depot, can produce permanent glaucomatous optic neuropathy.

stewart treves syndrome — lymphangiosarcoma in chronic lymphoedema, post-mastectomy angiosarcoma Kaposi sarcoma traumatic bruising or haematoma on an oedematous limb cellulitis or erysipelas recurrent or metastatic cutaneous breast carcinoma radiation-associated atypical vascular lesion benign vascular tumours such as haemangioma or pyogenic granuloma amelanotic or pigmented melanoma incisional skin biopsy with endothelial immunohistochemistry (CD31, CD34, ERG) magnetic resonance imaging of the affected limb to delineate extent staging computed tomography of chest, abdomen and pelvis positron emission tomography for occult multifocal or metastatic disease sentinel or regional nodal assessment where indicated review of prior oncological history and radiotherapy fields A cutaneous angiosarcoma that arises within a chronically lymphoedematous limb, classically described after post-mastectomy arm lymphoedema but reported in any longstanding lymphoedema including congenital and filarial forms. The latency is long, typically around a decade from the onset of chronic lymphoedema to tumour appearance. Early lesions are subtle violaceous or red-blue macules, papules or bruise-like patches that are easily mistaken for simple ecchymosis on an oedematous limb. Lesions are frequently multifocal, with satellite nodules that enlarge, coalesce, ulcerate and bleed. Diagnosis rests on full-thickness incisional biopsy with immunohistochemistry demonstrating endothelial markers such as CD31, CD34, ERG and factor VIII-related antigen. The tumour is aggressive with a strong tendency to early haematogenous metastasis, particularly to the lungs. Wide surgical excision, often amputation, is the mainstay of treatment, with radiotherapy and chemotherapy as adjuncts, yet outcomes remain poor. Any new or changing pigmented or violaceous lesion on a chronically swollen limb should prompt urgent biopsy rather than reassurance. new violaceous, red-blue or bruise-like cutaneous lesions on a chronically lymphoedematous limb rapid growth, ulceration or spontaneous bleeding of a skin lesion multifocal or coalescing nodules over the affected territory systemic symptoms or respiratory features suggesting pulmonary metastasis a non-healing lesion previously dismissed as bruising or infection mistaking early lesions for bruising, cellulitis or benign vascular change and delaying biopsy taking an inadequate or superficial biopsy that misses the malignant endothelium underestimating multifocality and performing insufficiently wide excision failing to stage for pulmonary metastasis at presentation attributing the swelling and skin change solely to the pre-existing lymphoedema Stewart-Treves syndrome represents malignant transformation of vascular endothelium within a field of chronic lymphoedema. Persistent stasis of protein-rich lymph is thought to create a locally immunocompromised, immunologically privileged microenvironment in which impaired immune surveillance, sustained tissue remodelling, aberrant lymphangiogenic and angiogenic signalling, and chronic inflammation promote accumulation of oncogenic changes in endothelial cells. The result is a high-grade angiosarcoma composed of atypical, anastomosing vascular channels lined by malignant endothelium that infiltrates dermis and subcutis. The same predisposing stasis explains why the tumour tends to be multifocal across the affected territory. The prognosis is poor: Stewart-Treves angiosarcoma is aggressive, frequently multifocal and metastasises early, so five-year survival is low even after radical surgery. Early recognition and wide excision offer the only realistic chance of prolonged survival.

Stickler syndrome - hearing/otological features — hereditary arthro-ophthalmopathy, COL2A1, COL11A1, COL11A2, Stickler syndrome Marshall syndrome with overlapping facial and sensory features Other syndromic hearing loss such as branchio-oto-renal or Waardenburg syndrome Isolated cleft palate or Pierre Robin sequence with secondary otitis media with effusion Other inherited collagenopathies affecting connective tissue Isolated high myopia with vitreoretinal degeneration Non-syndromic mixed hearing loss from chronic middle-ear disease Audiometry with tympanometry to distinguish conductive, sensorineural and mixed loss Ophthalmic assessment for high myopia, vitreous abnormality and retinal detachment risk Examination of the palate and airway for clefting and Robin sequence Skeletal and joint assessment for features of the associated arthropathy Molecular genetic testing of collagen genes to confirm the subtype A hereditary connective-tissue (collagenopathy) disorder in which hearing loss is one component alongside ocular, orofacial and skeletal features Hearing loss may be sensorineural, conductive from middle-ear disease, or mixed, and is often high-frequency Caused by mutations in collagen genes including COL2A1, COL11A1 and COL11A2; most subtypes are autosomal dominant The COL11A2 subtype (type 3) shows the syndrome's systemic features with hearing loss but without the ocular involvement Cleft palate or a Pierre Robin sequence contributes to conductive hearing loss through Eustachian tube dysfunction and recurrent middle-ear effusion The associated high myopia carries a significant risk of retinal detachment, so ophthalmology assessment is essential A child with cleft palate, midface hypoplasia and hearing loss should be assessed for Stickler syndrome Sudden visual symptoms suggesting retinal detachment in a highly myopic patient Airway compromise in an infant with Pierre Robin sequence Progressive hearing loss impairing speech and language development Recurrent middle-ear effusions causing persistent conductive loss Managing recurrent middle-ear effusion without recognising an underlying syndrome Failing to arrange retinal-detachment prophylaxis and surveillance in high myopia Assuming hearing loss is purely conductive and missing a sensorineural component Overlooking the diagnosis in the ocular-sparing COL11A2 subtype Stickler syndrome is caused by mutations in genes encoding types II and XI collagen, which are important structural components of cartilage, the vitreous of the eye and the connective tissue of the inner and middle ear. Defective collagen impairs the integrity of these tissues, producing the characteristic vitreoretinal degeneration and myopia, orofacial abnormalities such as cleft palate and midface underdevelopment, joint and skeletal problems, and hearing loss. Middle-ear collagen abnormality and Eustachian tube dysfunction related to palatal clefting contribute a conductive element, while cochlear collagen involvement contributes a sensorineural element, giving frequently mixed hearing loss. Hearing loss is usually mild to moderate and manageable with amplification or middle-ear treatment, but the main threats to long-term outcome are sight-threatening retinal detachment and, in infancy, airway compromise from Robin sequence; overall prognosis is good with coordinated multidisciplinary care.

failing to arrange ophthalmology surveillance Overlooking hearing loss because ocular features dominate the picture Assuming high myopia is simple refractive error rather than syndromic Not offering genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal dominant inheritance Stickler syndrome results from defects in the fibrillar collagens types II and XI, which are major structural components of the vitreous, cartilage, and inner ear. Variants in COL2A1 or the type XI collagen genes disrupt normal collagen fibril assembly, producing an abnormal vitreous gel that predisposes to retinal tears and detachment, cartilage that is prone to early degeneration and mild skeletal dysplasia, and inner-ear structures vulnerable to sensorineural hearing loss. The same collagen deficiency during craniofacial development underlies the midface and palatal anomalies, including the Pierre Robin sequence. Most patients have a normal lifespan, but vision is threatened by retinal detachment, which is the principal preventable cause of morbidity, and joint and hearing problems accumulate over time. Outcomes improve markedly with proactive ophthalmic surveillance and detachment prophylaxis.

in a young patient Recurrent venous thromboembolism without an obvious cause Recurrent pregnancy loss after exclusion of other causes Thrombosis recurring despite an otherwise negative thrombophilia workup Diagnosing it without first excluding established inherited and acquired thrombophilias Relying on non-standardised aggregometry protocols with variable cut-offs Overinterpreting transient platelet hyperreactivity from recent stress or sampling artefact Attributing all thrombotic events to it while missing a coexisting definitive cause Sticky platelet syndrome is described as a heritable tendency of platelets to aggregate excessively when exposed to low concentrations of ADP and adrenaline, suggesting heightened responsiveness of platelet activation pathways. This hyperreactivity is proposed to promote platelet-driven thrombus formation in both the arterial and venous circulations, particularly under conditions of physiological stress with catecholamine surges. The precise molecular basis is unresolved, no single causative gene has been established, and the entity remains debated, so it is best regarded as a clinico-laboratory phenotype pending further validation. Because the entity is not firmly established, prognosis is uncertain; reported cases suggest that reducing platelet reactivity can lessen thrombotic events, but the evidence base is limited. Outcomes are strongly influenced by coexisting, better-defined thrombotic risk factors.

Stiff-person syndrome — SPS, stiff-man syndrome, Moersch-Woltman syndrome Tetanus Neuromyotonia and other peripheral hyperexcitability syndromes Dystonia and other movement disorders Parkinsonism and progressive supranuclear palsy with axial rigidity Functional (psychogenic) movement disorder Myelopathy with spasticity Anti-GAD65 antibodies, with glycine receptor and amphiphysin antibodies when indicated Electromyography demonstrating continuous motor unit activity Screening for associated autoimmune disease including diabetes and thyroid disorders Investigation for an underlying malignancy in suspected paraneoplastic cases MRI to exclude structural spinal or cerebral causes of rigidity An immune-mediated disorder of central nervous system inhibition characterised by progressive axial and proximal muscle rigidity with superimposed painful spasms Rigidity typically involves the trunk and abdominal wall, producing an exaggerated lumbar lordosis and a stiff, board-like posture Spasms are often triggered by startle, emotional stress, or sudden movement and can be severe enough to cause falls or fractures Most cases are associated with high-titre antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD65); a smaller subset relate to antibodies against amphiphysin or glycine receptors It commonly coexists with other autoimmune conditions, particularly type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease, and pernicious anaemia A paraneoplastic form, often linked to amphiphysin antibodies and breast or other tumours, should be considered especially with atypical or rapidly progressive disease Electromyography characteristically shows continuous motor unit activity in agonist and antagonist muscles that persists at rest Treatment principles combine GABA-enhancing symptomatic therapy for rigidity and spasm with immunotherapy directed at the underlying autoimmune process Spasms severe enough to impair breathing or cause fractures and falls Rapid progression or atypical features suggesting a paraneoplastic cause Autonomic instability during severe spasm episodes New systemic symptoms prompting malignancy search Mistaking the disorder for a functional or psychiatric condition given the stress-sensitive spasms Failing to check for associated autoimmune diseases and an occult malignancy Overlooking the diagnostic value of anti-GAD antibodies and characteristic EMG findings Relying on symptomatic drugs alone without considering immunotherapy Stiff-person syndrome is thought to arise from impaired GABAergic inhibition in the central nervous system, largely on an autoimmune basis. Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase, the enzyme that synthesises the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA, or to other synaptic proteins such as glycine receptors and amphiphysin, are associated with reduced inhibitory tone in spinal and brainstem circuits. The loss of descending and segmental inhibition leads to continuous co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles, producing sustained rigidity and stimulus-sensitive spasms. The course is usually chronic and progressive but often responsive, at least partially, to symptomatic and immunomodulatory treatment; some patients stabilise or improve, while paraneoplastic cases depend on treatment of the underlying tumour and can be more refractory.

Stingray injury — stingray envenomation, stingray sting Other marine envenomation (stonefish, weeverfish) Simple laceration or puncture wound Retained foreign body without envenomation Secondary wound infection or cellulitis Allergic reaction to the sting Wound exploration and imaging to identify retained spine fragments Assessment of the depth and structures involved, especially for truncal wounds Consideration of tetanus status and infection risk Observation for systemic symptoms in severe envenoming Surgical review for deep or penetrating body-cavity wounds Injury combines a penetrating or laceration wound from the barbed spine with envenomation by a heat-labile venom Pain is typically immediate, intense and out of proportion to the visible wound Immersion of the affected part in hot (not scalding) water helps relieve pain by denaturing the venom Retained spine or sheath fragments in the wound are common and can be missed Wounds are prone to secondary infection, including marine organisms, so wound care and consideration of antibiotics are important Truncal or penetrating chest and abdominal wounds can be life-threatening and need urgent surgical assessment Penetrating chest, abdominal or neck wounds Signs of systemic envenoming or haemodynamic compromise Evidence of deep infection or necrosis Neurovascular compromise of a limb Failing to search for and remove retained spine fragments Prematurely closing a contaminated marine wound Underestimating pain and delaying hot-water immersion Missing deep penetrating injury to vital structures Stingray injury results from the tail spine penetrating tissue while releasing venom from glandular tissue along the spine. The venom is a heat-labile mixture that causes intense local pain, vasoconstriction and tissue injury, while the barbed spine produces mechanical laceration and can retain fragments. Local necrosis and a high infection risk follow from the combination of envenomation, tissue trauma and contamination, and deep penetrating wounds may damage vital structures. Most limb injuries do well with hot-water analgesia, wound care and removal of foreign material, but truncal penetrating wounds and severe infections can be serious or fatal.

Stonefish envenomation — Synanceia sting, stonefish sting, stinging fish envenomation, reef stonefish injury, venomous fish spine injury Other venomous fish spine injury (lionfish, scorpionfish, weeverfish, stingray) Sea urchin spine injury Simple puncture wound with secondary infection Cellulitis or necrotising soft-tissue infection Retained foreign body without envenomation Marine bacterial infection (e.g. Vibrio, Mycobacterium marinum) Wound imaging (ultrasound or radiography) to detect retained spine fragments Assessment of neurovascular status of the affected limb Electrocardiography and monitoring in systemic envenomation Inflammatory markers and wound cultures if infection is suspected Renal function and creatine kinase in severe systemic cases Stonefish (Synanceia) have dorsal spines that inject venom when trodden on, causing immediate and often excruciating pain out of proportion to the wound Local effects include intense pain, rapid swelling, discolouration and sometimes tissue necrosis, with retained spine fragments a common complication Hot-water immersion of the affected part at a tolerable temperature is a key first-aid measure, as the venom is heat-labile and this can relieve pain Systemic features may include nausea, sweating, weakness and, uncommonly, cardiovascular and respiratory effects with severe envenomation Stonefish antivenom is available and used for severe pain or systemic envenomation; wound exploration for retained spine and foreign material is important Secondary wound infection is common, so wound care, tetanus prophylaxis and monitoring for infection including marine organisms are essential Distinguish envenomation pain and swelling from evolving secondary soft-tissue infection during follow-up Systemic features such as hypotension, arrhythmia or respiratory compromise Signs of compartment syndrome or extensive necrosis Spreading soft-tissue infection or systemic sepsis Retained deep foreign material near neurovascular structures Uncontrolled severe pain despite first aid Using very hot water that scalds the anaesthetised, painful limb Missing retained spine fragments leading to persistent pain and infection Neglecting tetanus prophylaxis and marine wound care Attributing later worsening solely to venom rather than recognising secondary infection Stonefish venom, delivered through grooved dorsal spines, contains a pore-forming protein (verrucotoxin/stonustoxin family) that disrupts cell membranes and causes intense local pain, oedema and potential tissue necrosis. Systemic absorption can produce cardiovascular effects including hypotension and arrhythmia, and the venom has actions on skeletal and cardiac muscle. Many venom components are heat-labile, which underlies the analgesic benefit of hot-water immersion. Puncture wounds frequently retain spine fragments and are prone to secondary infection by marine and skin flora. Most stings cause severe transient pain that improves with hot-water immersion and analgesia, with full recovery. Complications arise chiefly from retained spines, secondary infection and, rarely, systemic envenomation; delayed or inadequate wound care prolongs morbidity.

Platelet storage pool disease — Storage pool deficiency, Platelet granule deficiency, SPD von Willebrand disease Glanzmann thrombasthenia Bernard-Soulier syndrome Aspirin or other antiplatelet drug effect Mild coagulation factor deficiency Acquired platelet dysfunction from uraemia or myeloproliferative disease Vascular or connective tissue bleeding disorders Full blood count and blood film for platelet number and morphology Light transmission platelet aggregometry with multiple agonists Whole-mount transmission electron microscopy for dense granule count Flow-cytometric mepacrine uptake and release studies Platelet nucleotide (ADP/ATP) content and secretion assays von Willebrand factor antigen and activity to exclude von Willebrand disease Targeted genetic testing (for example NBEAL2, HPS genes, LYST) A heterogeneous group of inherited platelet disorders defined by deficient granule content, comprising dense granule (delta), alpha granule (grey platelet syndrome) and combined (alpha-delta) forms. Patients present with lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding: easy bruising, epistaxis, menorrhagia and prolonged bleeding after surgery or dental extraction. Platelet count is usually normal, though grey platelet syndrome is characteristically associated with mild thrombocytopenia and large agranular platelets. Light transmission aggregometry typically shows absent second-wave aggregation and a blunted response to ADP, adrenaline and collagen. Dense granule deficiency can be confirmed by whole-mount electron microscopy showing reduced granule number or by flow-cytometric mepacrine uptake studies. Storage pool defects may be isolated or part of syndromes such as Hermansky-Pudlak (with oculocutaneous albinism) and Chediak-Higashi. Grey platelet syndrome arises from NBEAL2 mutations and may progress to marrow fibrosis and splenomegaly. Management centres on antifibrinolytics, desmopressin for minor procedures and platelet transfusion for major bleeding, with judicious use given alloimmunisation risk. Life-threatening haemorrhage after trauma, surgery or childbirth Progressive splenomegaly and marrow fibrosis in grey platelet syndrome Pulmonary fibrosis or colitis suggesting underlying Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome Recurrent severe infections or lymphohistiocytosis suggesting Chediak-Higashi syndrome Severe menorrhagia causing symptomatic anaemia Attributing mucocutaneous bleeding to a normal platelet count and overlooking a qualitative defect. Missing an underlying syndrome such as Hermansky-Pudlak by not examining for oculocutaneous albinism. Interpreting aggregometry without accounting for recent antiplatelet or non-steroidal drug exposure. Repeated platelet transfusion leading to alloimmunisation and refractoriness. Failing to give peri-operative antifibrinolytic cover for mucosal surgery. Platelet storage pool disease results from defective formation, cargo loading or retention of platelet secretory granules. Dense (delta) granules normally store ADP, ATP, calcium and serotonin that amplify platelet activation and recruitment; their deficiency impairs the secondary wave of aggregation. Alpha granules store adhesive and haemostatic proteins including von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, factor V and platelet factor 4; their absence, as in grey platelet syndrome from NBEAL2 mutation, produces agranular platelets and can drive marrow fibrosis through unregulated growth-factor release. In syndromic forms such as Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi, mutations in genes governing lysosome-related organelle biogenesis and vesicle trafficking affect melanosomes and granules alike, explaining the associated albinism. The common consequence is impaired granule secretion and a functional platelet defect causing mucocutaneous bleeding despite an often normal platelet count. Bleeding is usually mild to moderate and lifelong, and most patients have a normal life expectancy with appropriate peri-procedural precautions. Prognosis is chiefly determined by any associated syndrome, such as pulmonary fibrosis in Hermansky-Pudlak or the immunodeficiency of Chediak-Higashi.

Strabismus — squint, ocular misalignment, esotropia, exotropia, heterotropia Pseudostrabismus from prominent epicanthic folds or facial asymmetry Cranial nerve palsy (third, fourth, or sixth nerve) Restrictive myopathy (e.g. thyroid eye disease, orbital fracture) Myasthenia gravis Internuclear ophthalmoplegia and other supranuclear disorders Retinoblastoma or other cause of sensory deprivation in a child Cover-uncover and alternate cover tests to detect and measure the deviation Assessment of visual acuity in each eye to detect amblyopia Cycloplegic refraction to identify a correctable refractive cause Ocular motility examination and assessment of binocular function/stereopsis Neuroimaging when an incomitant or paralytic squint suggests a neurological lesion Strabismus is a misalignment of the visual axes and is described by direction: esotropia (inward), exotropia (outward), hypertropia (upward), and hypotropia (downward) It is classified as concomitant (the deviation is similar in all directions of gaze, typical of childhood squints) or incomitant (varying with gaze, suggesting a nerve palsy or restriction) In children the main concern is amblyopia in the deviating eye, whereas new-onset strabismus in adults usually causes diplopia The cover test (cover-uncover and alternate cover) is the key clinical method for detecting and characterising a manifest or latent deviation Accommodative esotropia is linked to uncorrected hypermetropia and often improves substantially with the appropriate glasses A new incomitant squint, especially with a cranial nerve palsy pattern, warrants investigation for a neurological cause Management principles include correcting refractive error, treating any amblyopia (e.g. occlusion), and surgical realignment of the extraocular muscles when indicated Leukocoria or a sudden squint in a child requires urgent examination to exclude retinoblastoma or other serious pathology New-onset incomitant squint with features of a cranial nerve palsy suggesting intracranial pathology Leukocoria or a squint accompanying poor vision in a child, raising concern for retinoblastoma Sudden diplopia with headache or other neurological signs Painful or restricted eye movements suggesting orbital or inflammatory disease Dismissing a genuine squint as pseudostrabismus and delaying amblyopia treatment Failing to perform cycloplegic refraction and missing correctable accommodative esotropia Not investigating a new incomitant or paralytic squint for a neurological cause Overlooking a serious underlying cause such as retinoblastoma in a child presenting with a squint Strabismus arises from a failure of the normal binocular alignment maintained by coordinated extraocular muscle action and central fusional control. Causes include refractive error (notably hypermetropia driving accommodative esotropia), sensory deprivation from poor vision in one eye, abnormalities of the neuromuscular pathways (cranial nerve palsies), mechanical restriction of muscles, and disorders of central fusion. In children, misalignment during the critical period of visual development leads to suppression of the deviating eye's image and can result in amblyopia and loss of binocular single vision. Outcomes are generally favourable when strabismus and any associated amblyopia are detected and treated early in childhood, with good prospects for alignment and, in some cases, binocular vision; late detection reduces the chance of restoring binocularity, and adult acquired strabismus depends on the underlying cause.

Streptococcal Infections — group A strep, GAS, Streptococcus pyogenes, group B strep, GBS, Streptococcus agalactiae Scarlet fever differential: measles and other viral exanthems, Kawasaki disease, toxic shock syndrome, and systemic allergic/drug eruptions (p.1209) Pharyngitis differential includes group C/G streptococci, mixed anaerobes (Vincent's angina), Arcanobacterium haemolyticum, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, EBV/CMV/HIV, and other viruses (Table 153-2, p.1208) Impetigo differential: bullous impetigo due to S. aureus, and herpetic lesions (orolabial HSV, chickenpox, or zoster), distinguished by grouped discrete vesicles and positive Tzanck/PCR (p.1210) Staphylococcus aureus cellulitis/soft tissue infection mimicking streptococcal cellulitis (suspect S. aureus when cellulitis develops around a wound or ulcer) (p.1210-1211) Bullous impetigo (S. aureus) mimicking streptococcal impetigo (p.1210) Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome (shares features with streptococcal TSS, but staph TSS patients are usually not bacteremic) (p.1211-1212) Herpes simplex virus or varicella-zoster lesions mimicking impetigo (p.1210) Throat culture (gold standard; vigorous rubbing of both tonsillar pillars) and rapid antigen test (latex agglutination/EIA, specificity >95%, relative sensitivity 70-90%); confirm negative rapid test with culture in higher-risk individuals (p.1208) Antibody tests to streptolysin O (ASO) and DNase B for serodiagnosis of preceding streptococcal infection in suspected ARF or PSGN (p.1207) emm-typing by PCR/sequencing of the variable region of the emm gene (CDC database) for strain typing (p.1207) In streptococcal TSS, laboratory findings: marked left shift with immature granulocytes, hypocalcemia, hypoalbuminemia, and thrombocytopenia (worsening on day 2-3) (p.1211) Blood cultures (most streptococcal TSS patients are bacteremic) (p.1211-1212) Early surgical exploration of suspected necrotizing fasciitis for diagnosis (reveals fascial-plane necrosis and inflammatory fluid without muscle involvement) (p.1211) Cultures of vesicular fluid in difficult impetigo cases; culture to rule out MRSA if empirical treatment fails (p.1210) Kawasaki disease (mimics scarlet fever) (p.1209) Systemic allergic reactions / drug eruptions (mimic scarlet fever) (p.1209) Group A Streptococcus (GAS; S. pyogenes) is the only common cause of sore throat that should be treated with antibiotics; GAS accounts for 20-40% of exudative pharyngitis in children and is rare under age 3 (p.1208). Streptococcal pharyngitis cannot be reliably diagnosed on clinical grounds alone given overlap with many viral and bacterial causes; throat culture remains the diagnostic gold standard, with rapid antigen tests (specificity >95%) a useful adjunct (p.1208). Antibiotic treatment of GAS pharyngitis is given primarily to prevent suppurative complications and acute rheumatic fever; symptoms resolve in 3-5 days and are shortened little by treatment (p.1208). Prevention of ARF depends on eradicating the organism from the pharynx (not just symptom resolution) and requires a 10-day penicillin course; a single dose or short course is inadequate (p.1208). Penicillin treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis reduces the likelihood of ARF but NOT of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (p.1209). Worldwide, GAS infections and their post-infectious sequelae (chiefly ARF and rheumatic heart disease) cause an estimated 500,000 deaths/year; incidence of GAS disease and RHD is roughly tenfold higher in resource-limited countries (p.1206-1207). Scarlet fever is streptococcal infection (usually pharyngitis) plus a rash from pyrogenic exotoxins: blanching sandpaper-textured papular rash on trunk and extremities sparing palms and soles, with circumoral pallor, strawberry tongue, and Pastia's lines in skin folds, followed by desquamation of palms and soles (p.1209). Impetigo is most often a superficial GAS infection (occasionally other streptococci or S. aureus) of young children; honey/amber crusted lesions on face and legs; lesions are generally NOT painful and fever is NOT a feature — if fever is present, suspect deeper infection or another diagnosis (p.1209-1210). Erysipelas is a streptococcal cellulitis of the superficial dermis: bright red, warm, shiny, edematous plaque with a sharply demarcated raised border and peau d'orange texture, typically on the face (malar) or lower extremities, with abrupt onset, fever and chills; classic cases are almost always due to beta-hemolytic streptococci (usually GAS) (p.1210). Streptococcal cellulitis favors sites of disrupted lymphatic drainage (prior cellulitis, post-mastectomy/axillary dissection arm, prior DVT or lymphedema leg, saphenous vein harvest site); treating tinea pedis can stop recurrent leg cellulitis after vein harvest (p.1210-1211). GAS is among the few pathogens producing wound infection and surrounding cellulitis within the first 24 h after surgery, with thin exudate and rapid spread (p.1211). Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency: GAS is implicated in ~60% of cases; early surgical exploration and extensive debridement are diagnostic, therapeutic, and life-saving, with antibiotics as a critical adjunct (p.1211). Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (TSS) features fever, hypotension, renal impairment, and respiratory distress; in contrast to staphylococcal TSS, most patients with streptococcal TSS are bacteremic, rash usually does NOT develop, and the most common associated infection is a soft tissue infection (necrotizing fasciitis, myositis, or cellulitis) (p.1211-1212). Streptococcal TSS carries a mortality rate of >=30%, mostly from shock and respiratory failure; because of its rapidly progressive lethal course, early recognition is essential (p.1212). Group B Streptococcus (GBS; S. agalactiae) is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis and of peripartum fever; early-onset disease (first week, median 20 h) is acquired from the colonized maternal genital tract, while late-onset disease (1 week-3 months) most often presents as meningitis, frequently capsular type III (p.1212-1213). GBS infection in adults increasingly affects the elderly and those with chronic illness (e.g., diabetes, malignancy), presenting as cellulitis/soft-tissue infection including diabetic ulcers, UTI, pneumonia, endocarditis, and septic arthritis (p.1213-1214). Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency: severe pain out of proportion to physical findings, with only minimal early skin erythema; progression over hours to dusky/mottled erythema and edema; tenderness evolving into anesthesia from infarction of cutaneous nerves — demands early surgical exploration and debridement (p.1211) Streptococcal TSS: rapidly progressive, lethal (mortality >=30%) with hypotension and multiorgan failure; early recognition essential (p.1211-1212) Fever in a patient with impetigo suggests extension to deeper tissues or an alternative diagnosis (p.1210) GAS bacteremia without an identified source raises the possibility of endocarditis, occult abscess, or osteomyelitis (p.1212) Unusually severe or prolonged pharyngitis, or localized pain with high fever and toxic appearance, suggests a peritonsillar or parapharyngeal abscess (p.1209) Diagnosing streptococcal pharyngitis on clinical grounds alone is unreliable; clinicians over-prescribe antibiotics for sore throat (p.1208) Rapid antigen tests are less sensitive than culture (relative sensitivity 70-90%), so a negative rapid test should be confirmed by throat culture in higher-risk patients (p.1208) Improper swab technique lowers rapid-test sensitivity; both tonsillar pillars (and any exudate/ulceration) must be vigorously sampled (p.1208) In necrotizing fasciitis, early physical findings may be unimpressive despite severe pain; relying on skin appearance delays diagnosis (p.1211) Macrolide resistance is common in many countries and rising in invasive US GAS isolates (>30% since 2021); avoid macrolides where resistance exceeds 5-10% unless susceptibility is known (p.1208-1209) Clindamycin resistance occurs in >=30% of invasive GAS isolates; susceptibility should not be assumed without in vitro testing before relying on clindamycin (p.1212) Aggressive eradication of asymptomatic GAS pharyngeal carriage is usually not justified (carriers have lower risk of ARF and of transmission than symptomatic patients); exceptions arise when a carrier is a source of transmission to others (p.1209) Endocarditis due to nonenterococcal group D streptococci (S. gallolyticus/S. bovis group) is associated with occult GI neoplasm (often colon carcinoma/polyp; abnormalities in >60%) and should prompt GI evaluation (p.1214) GAS (S. pyogenes) is the single species of Lancefield group A, a beta-hemolytic, chain-forming, gram-positive facultative anaerobe. M protein (encoded by the emm gene, >200 emm types) is the major surface protein and chief virulence factor: it resists phagocytic killing partly by binding plasma fibrinogen and interfering with complement deposition, and type-specific anti-M antibody confers protection only against the same M type. A hyaluronic acid capsule (a weak immunogen owing to structural identity with mammalian connective tissue) protects against phagocytosis and aids pharyngeal colonization via CD44 binding; capsule is not essential for virulence. GAS elaborates streptolysins S and O, streptokinase, DNases, SpyCEP (cleaves IL-8 to impair neutrophil recruitment), and pyrogenic exotoxins (formerly erythrogenic toxins) that cause the scarlet fever rash and act as superantigens triggering T-cell cytokine release, implicated in severe invasive disease including necrotizing fasciitis and streptococcal TSS. The post-infectious sequelae ARF (uniquely associated with S. pyogenes) and PSGN are thought to result from immune responses to streptococcal infection. GBS is encapsulated by 1 of 10 polysaccharides; the capsule is a key virulence factor and type-specific anticapsular antibody is protective. Uncomplicated GAS pharyngitis is self-limited, with symptoms resolving in 3-5 days. Suppurative complications (peritonsillar/retropharyngeal abscess, cervical lymphadenitis, sinusitis, otitis, meningitis, bacteremia, endocarditis, pneumonia) are now uncommon with antibiotics; nonsuppurative sequelae are ARF and PSGN. Necrotizing fasciitis and streptococcal TSS are rapidly progressive and life-threatening; streptococcal TSS has a mortality rate of >=30%. Globally GAS sequelae account for ~500,000 deaths/year. Neonatal GBS incidence has fallen from ~2-3 to ~0.6 per 1000 live births with prenatal screening. Recurrent invasive GBS in adults occurs in ~4% of cases. Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome case definition (CDC, 1993; updated 2010; Table 153-4): I. Isolation of GAS from (A) a normally sterile site or (B) a nonsterile site; II. Clinical signs of severity = (A) hypotension AND (B) >=2 of: renal impairment, coagulopathy, liver function impairment, ARDS, generalized erythematous macular rash that may desquamate, or soft tissue necrosis (including necrotizing fasciitis or myositis) or gangrene. A DEFINITE case meets IA + IIA + IIB; a PROBABLE case meets IB + IIA + IIB if no other etiology is identified. Pharyngitis pretest risk is stratified clinically by the Centor criteria (fever history, absence of cough, tender anterior cervical adenopathy, tonsillar exudate/swelling).

Stress fracture — fatigue fracture, insufficiency fracture, march fracture, bone stress injury Medial tibial stress syndrome (shin splints) Chronic exertional compartment syndrome Tendinopathy or muscle strain Nerve entrapment Osteomyelitis or bone infection Osteoid osteoma or other bone tumour Pathological fracture from metastasis or metabolic bone disease Plain radiographs, recognising they are frequently normal early and may show periosteal reaction or a fracture line later MRI as the preferred sensitive test to grade bone marrow oedema and confirm the fracture Radionuclide bone scan as an alternative sensitive investigation CT for suspected navicular or other fractures needing detailed cortical assessment Metabolic and endocrine workup, vitamin D, and bone density assessment in recurrent, atypical, or insufficiency fractures Presents as gradually worsening, activity-related localised bone pain that eases with rest, typically after a change or increase in training load Fatigue fractures occur when normal bone is subjected to repetitive abnormal load, whereas insufficiency fractures occur when normal load acts on weakened bone such as osteoporotic or pathological bone Common sites include the metatarsals (march fracture), tibia, navicular, and femoral neck, with the tibia most frequent in runners Focal bony tenderness, pain on hopping or percussion, and pain reproduced by loading the bone support the diagnosis Early plain radiographs are often normal, and MRI or bone scan is more sensitive for detecting bone stress injury Certain high-risk sites, including the tension side of the femoral neck, anterior tibial cortex, navicular, and base of the fifth metatarsal, are prone to non-union or completion and need protected weight-bearing or surgical referral Management of low-risk fractures is relative rest, activity modification, and graduated return to loading once pain-free In female athletes consider the female athlete triad / relative energy deficiency in sport, with attention to energy availability, menstrual function, and bone health Recurrent or multiple stress fractures warrant assessment for metabolic bone disease, vitamin D deficiency, and endocrine causes High-risk sites such as the femoral neck (especially tension side), anterior tibia, tarsal navicular, and fifth metatarsal base that risk non-union or displacement Groin or hip pain with weight-bearing suggesting femoral neck stress fracture requiring urgent assessment Features of pathological or insufficiency fracture such as minimal trauma, older age, or known malignancy Systemic symptoms or signs suggesting infection or tumour Excluding a stress fracture on the basis of a normal early radiograph Failing to recognise high-risk sites and continuing loading with risk of completion or non-union Overlooking relative energy deficiency in sport or metabolic bone disease in recurrent cases Returning to full training too early before the bone has healed A stress fracture develops when repetitive submaximal loading causes microdamage to accumulate faster than bone can remodel and repair it. Osteoclastic resorption temporarily outpaces osteoblastic formation, weakening the cortex and, if loading continues, progressing from a stress reaction to a frank fracture line. Fatigue fractures reflect excessive load on normal bone, while insufficiency fractures reflect normal load on abnormally weak bone. Low-risk stress fractures generally heal fully within six to twelve weeks with load modification and graded return, whereas high-risk fractures may progress to non-union or complete fracture and can require prolonged protection or surgery.

Stress Urinary Incontinence — stress urinary incontinence, stress incontinence, SUI, effort urinary incontinence, exertional incontinence Urgency urinary incontinence / overactive bladder Mixed urinary incontinence Overflow incontinence from chronic retention Urinary tract infection causing transient symptoms Vesicovaginal or urethrovaginal fistula (continuous leakage) Urethral diverticulum Functional incontinence from mobility or cognitive impairment Bladder (frequency-volume) diary to characterise the pattern of leakage Cough stress test to demonstrate leakage with raised abdominal pressure Urinalysis and culture to exclude infection Post-void residual measurement to exclude incomplete emptying Pad testing to quantify leakage where useful Urodynamic studies in complex, mixed, recurrent, or pre-surgical cases Stress urinary incontinence is involuntary leakage of urine on effort or exertion, such as coughing, sneezing, laughing, or physical activity, when abdominal pressure rises It results from a weakened sphincter mechanism or poor support of the bladder neck and urethra, so that a rise in intra-abdominal pressure overcomes urethral closure Key risk factors include vaginal childbirth, ageing and menopause, obesity, chronic cough or straining, and previous pelvic surgery It must be distinguished from urgency incontinence (leakage with a sudden compelling desire to void); many women have a mixed picture with features of both Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by a bladder diary, cough stress test, and exclusion of infection and significant post-void residual urine First-line management is conservative: supervised pelvic floor muscle training, weight loss, treatment of chronic cough or constipation, and lifestyle measures Adjuncts include continence pessaries or devices, and duloxetine may be considered in selected cases where surgery is unsuitable or declined Surgical options for persistent bothersome stress incontinence include mid-urethral slings, colposuspension, and urethral bulking agents, chosen according to patient factors and shared decision-making Urodynamic testing is reserved for complex, mixed, or recurrent cases or before surgery where the diagnosis is uncertain, rather than being routine Visible haematuria requiring exclusion of urinary tract malignancy Continuous leakage suggesting a fistula Significant post-void residual or voiding difficulty indicating retention with overflow New neurological symptoms suggesting a neurological cause Recurrent urinary infections or pain warranting further evaluation Labelling all incontinence as stress type without identifying a mixed or urgency component Proceeding to surgery without a trial of conservative therapy or without clarifying the diagnosis Missing overflow incontinence by not checking post-void residual Overlooking a fistula in a patient with continuous leakage, especially after surgery or childbirth Attributing symptoms to stress incontinence when haematuria or infection needs investigation Continence during exertion depends on adequate urethral closure pressure and on the bladder neck and urethra being well supported so that rises in abdominal pressure are transmitted equally to the bladder and proximal urethra. Two overlapping mechanisms cause stress incontinence: urethral hypermobility, in which weakened pelvic floor and endopelvic fascial support (often after childbirth or with ageing) allows the bladder neck to descend and the pressure transmission to become unequal; and intrinsic sphincter deficiency, in which the urethral closure mechanism itself is weakened, for example after surgery, radiation, or oestrogen deficiency. In either case a cough or exertion transiently raises bladder pressure above urethral resistance and urine escapes. Stress incontinence is not life-threatening but can substantially impair quality of life. Many women improve significantly with conservative measures, particularly sustained pelvic floor muscle training and weight loss. Surgical procedures offer high rates of symptom improvement in appropriately selected patients, though some experience recurrence or complications, so treatment is individualised through shared decision-making.

Stress urinary incontinence — SUI, Stress incontinence, Effort incontinence Urgency urinary incontinence / overactive bladder Mixed urinary incontinence Overflow incontinence from chronic retention Urethral diverticulum or fistula (vesicovaginal, urethrovaginal) Ectopic ureter presenting with continuous leakage Functional incontinence from mobility or cognitive impairment Extraurethral leakage or vaginal discharge mistaken for urine Cough stress test with a comfortably full bladder Frequency-volume bladder diary Pad test to quantify leakage severity Post-void residual measurement Urinalysis and culture to exclude infection Multichannel urodynamics in complex, mixed or recurrent cases Cystourethroscopy or imaging when fistula, diverticulum or prior mesh complication is suspected Stress urinary incontinence is the involuntary leakage of urine on effort, exertion, coughing or sneezing, reflecting failure of the sphincteric closure mechanism to withstand rises in abdominal pressure. In women it is usually related to urethral hypermobility from pelvic floor and support weakness after childbirth and with ageing, or to intrinsic sphincter deficiency; the two frequently coexist. In men it is most commonly iatrogenic, particularly following radical prostatectomy or other prostatic surgery that damages the sphincteric mechanism. Mixed urinary incontinence, combining stress and urgency components, is common, and the more bothersome component should guide initial treatment. A cough stress test demonstrating synchronous leakage, together with a bladder diary and pad testing, supports the diagnosis and quantifies severity. Supervised pelvic floor muscle training is the first-line treatment and benefits both women and men, including after prostatectomy. Surgical options in women include the midurethral sling and colposuspension, while intrinsic sphincter deficiency and post-prostatectomy incontinence may require slings or an artificial urinary sphincter. Urodynamic assessment is reserved for complex, mixed, recurrent or pre-surgical cases and to confirm the diagnosis when it is unclear. Continuous leakage suggesting a fistula or ectopic ureter rather than true stress incontinence Associated haematuria, pain or a pelvic mass Significant post-void residual indicating retention with overflow New neurological symptoms suggesting a neurogenic cause Recurrent incontinence or pain after previous continence surgery or mesh insertion Missing a coexisting overactive bladder component and operating on a patient whose main problem is urgency Failing to exclude a fistula or ectopic ureter when leakage is actually continuous rather than effort related Offering surgery before an adequate trial of supervised pelvic floor training Overlooking chronic retention with overflow, which mimics stress leakage but requires very different management Neglecting reversible contributors such as obesity, constipation, chronic cough and atrophic changes Continence during effort depends on the urethra remaining a competent, well-supported closure mechanism so that intraurethral pressure exceeds intravesical pressure when abdominal pressure suddenly rises. In stress urinary incontinence this mechanism fails by two overlapping routes. Loss of anatomical support, from weakening of the pelvic floor musculature, endopelvic fascia and vaginal wall attachments, allows the bladder neck and proximal urethra to descend and rotate (urethral hypermobility), so abdominal pressure is no longer transmitted equally to the urethra. Alternatively, or additionally, intrinsic sphincter deficiency, from denervation, scarring, atrophy or surgical damage, leaves the urethra unable to generate adequate closure pressure regardless of support. Contributing factors include vaginal childbirth, ageing and oestrogen deficiency, obesity, chronically raised intra-abdominal pressure, pelvic surgery and, in men, prostatic surgery. The result is leakage synchronous with transient increases in abdominal pressure and no accompanying detrusor contraction. Conservative pelvic floor muscle training improves or cures symptoms in a substantial proportion of patients, and appropriately selected surgery achieves high continence rates. Outcomes are less favourable with severe intrinsic sphincter deficiency, obesity, previous failed surgery and a large mixed urgency component.

Striate palmoplantar keratoderma — SPPK, Brünauer-Fuhs-Siemens keratoderma, DSG1, DSP Diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma (Unna-Thost / Vörner) Focal palmoplantar keratoderma of pachyonychia congenita Punctate palmoplantar keratoderma Naxos disease and Carvajal syndrome (cardiocutaneous keratodermas) Acquired keratoderma from friction or eczema Keratosis palmoplantaris of Wachters Molecular genetic testing of DSG1, DSP and related desmosomal genes Skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis with acantholytic-like widening of intercellular spaces Family history and pedigree analysis Cardiac assessment (history, ECG and echocardiography) where a DSP variant or cardiocutaneous syndrome is suspected Nail and hair examination to exclude syndromic keratoderma Clinical photography to document the striate pattern An autosomal dominant focal palmoplantar keratoderma with linear (striate) hyperkeratosis running along the palms and fingers and focal thickening on the soles Caused by heterozygous variants in desmosomal genes, most often DSG1 (desmoglein 1) or DSP (desmoplakin), and occasionally KRT1 The linear pattern follows lines of mechanical stress, so the fingers and weight-bearing soles are typically involved Because desmoplakin also functions in cardiac desmosomes, some DSP variants are associated with cardiocutaneous syndromes, so a cardiac history should be considered Nails and hair are usually normal, helping to distinguish it from syndromic keratodermas Diagnosis is clinical with family history; biopsy shows hyperkeratosis with widened intercellular spaces and can be supported by molecular testing Management is supportive with keratolytics, emollients, mechanical paring and protective measures, with oral retinoids reserved for severe disease Personal or family history of arrhythmia, syncope or cardiomyopathy suggesting a cardiocutaneous desmoplakin syndrome Woolly hair with keratoderma raising concern for Carvajal or Naxos syndrome Painful fissuring causing functional impairment Secondary infection of fissured keratoderma Failing to consider cardiac evaluation in desmoplakin-related disease Confusing the linear pattern with a friction or occupational keratoderma Overlooking woolly hair as a clue to a cardiocutaneous syndrome Relying on systemic retinoids before optimising topical and mechanical care Striate palmoplantar keratoderma results from haploinsufficiency or dominant-negative effects of variants in desmosomal proteins, chiefly desmoglein 1 and desmoplakin, which anchor keratin filaments to cell-cell junctions in the epidermis. Weakened desmosomal adhesion is most consequential in acral skin subjected to shearing and pressure, where impaired keratinocyte cohesion triggers compensatory hyperkeratosis along lines of mechanical stress, producing the characteristic striate pattern. Certain desmoplakin variants additionally impair cardiac desmosomes, linking the skin phenotype to arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy in some families. The cutaneous prognosis is good, with lifelong but manageable focal keratoderma; overall prognosis depends on excluding the cardiac involvement associated with some desmoplakin variants.

Stroke rehabilitation — post-stroke rehabilitation, CVA rehabilitation, cerebrovascular accident rehabilitation Recurrent or extending stroke Post-stroke seizure with transient worsening Metabolic or reintegration and vocational return are integral to the rehabilitation programme New or worsening neurological deficit suggesting recurrent or extending stroke or haemorrhagic transformation Signs of aspiration or pneumonia in a patient with dysphagia Symptoms of pulmonary embolism or deep vein thrombosis in an immobile patient Sudden severe headache, reduced consciousness, or new seizures Rapidly developing pressure injury or sepsis Allowing oral intake before dysphagia screening and risking aspiration Delaying rehabilitation until the patient is deemed fully stable, losing the early window for gains Neglecting shoulder positioning and support, leading to painful subluxation Overlooking post-stroke depression and cognitive impairment that limit engagement Failing to address secondary prevention and carer support alongside physical recovery Stroke causes focal brain injury through either ischaemia or haemorrhage, producing loss of function referable to the affected vascular territory. The initial deficit reflects both the infarct or haematoma core and the surrounding penumbra and oedema. Functional recovery over subsequent weeks and months depends on resolution of oedema and diaschisis together with neuroplastic reorganisation, including recruitment of perilesional and contralateral networks, synaptic remodelling, and cortical remapping. Rehabilitation harnesses these adaptive processes through repetitive, goal-directed activity, while maladaptive changes such as spasticity and learned non-use can impede recovery. Recovery is most rapid in the first weeks to months and can continue for a year or more, though the extent varies with stroke size, location, initial severity, age, and comorbidity. Early, intensive, multidisciplinary rehabilitation improves functional outcome, while persisting severe deficits, cognitive impairment, and depression predict greater long-term disability.

Strongyloidiasis — Strongyloides stercoralis infection, threadworm infection, strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome Other soil-transmitted helminth infections (hookworm, ascariasis) Peptic ulcer disease or functional dyspepsia Inflammatory bowel disease Chronic urticaria of other cause Hypereosinophilic syndromes Drug-induced eosinophilia Allergic/atopic disease with urticaria Other causes of Gram-negative sepsis in the immunosuppressed Eosinophilic gastroenteritis Serology for Strongyloides antibodies, which is more sensitive than single stool testing Repeated stool microscopy with concentration or agar-plate culture to detect larvae Full blood count looking for eosinophilia (which may be absent in dissemination) Examination of sputum, duodenal aspirate or other fluids for larvae in suspected hyperinfection Screening for HTLV-1 and assessment of immune status in severe disease A soil-transmitted intestinal nematode acquired when larvae in contaminated soil penetrate skin, endemic in warm, humid parts of India Uniquely among common helminths it can complete its life cycle within the host (autoinfection), so infection may persist silently for decades Chronic infection is often mild, with intermittent abdominal symptoms, urticaria, and a characteristic migratory serpiginous rash (larva currens); eosinophilia is a common clue The feared complication is hyperinfection/disseminated disease, precipitated by immunosuppression, especially corticosteroids and HTLV-1 co-infection Screening and treating latent infection before starting immunosuppression is a key preventive principle Disseminated strongyloidiasis often carries Gram-negative bacteraemia or meningitis as larvae transport gut bacteria A single stool examination is insensitive; serology and repeated or concentrated stool studies improve detection Antiparasitic therapy with ivermectin is the treatment principle, with prolonged/repeated courses needed in disseminated disease Hyperinfection or dissemination in an immunosuppressed patient, a life-threatening emergency Gram-negative bacteraemia or meningitis complicating heavy larval migration Planned corticosteroid or other immunosuppression in someone from an endemic area without prior screening Rapid respiratory or gastrointestinal deterioration with detectable larvae Starting corticosteroids or immunosuppression without screening at-risk patients, precipitating fatal hyperinfection Relying on a single negative stool sample to exclude infection Assuming eosinophilia will always be present, as it is often absent in dissemination Failing to give a sufficiently prolonged antiparasitic course in disseminated disease Filariform larvae penetrate the skin, migrate through the circulation to the lungs, ascend the airways and are swallowed, maturing into adult worms in the small intestine. Females produce eggs that hatch into rhabditiform larvae; some transform into infective filariform larvae within the gut or perianal skin and reinvade the host, sustaining autoinfection. When host cellular immunity is impaired, this autoinfective cycle accelerates uncontrollably, causing massive larval migration through multiple organs (hyperinfection and dissemination) and carrying enteric bacteria that seed the bloodstream, meninges and other sites. Chronic uncomplicated infection responds well to antiparasitic therapy and has an excellent outlook, though eradication should be confirmed given the autoinfection risk. Hyperinfection and disseminated disease, by contrast, carry very high mortality despite treatment, particularly when diagnosis is delayed.
