thyroid histology Neglecting thyroid-directed surveillance after removal of malignant struma Struma ovarii is a germ-cell tumour of the ovary in which mature thyroid tissue forms the dominant or exclusive component. The ectopic thyroid follicular cells can retain the capacity to synthesise thyroid hormone, and when active in sufficient quantity they cause thyrotoxicosis independent of pituitary control, thereby suppressing thyroid-stimulating hormone and the normal cervical thyroid. Most tumours are benign, but the same follicular epithelium can rarely undergo malignant change resembling papillary or follicular thyroid carcinoma, with potential for spread. The mass itself may produce local pelvic symptoms or, uncommonly, ascites and pleural effusion. The great majority are benign and cured by surgical removal, with resolution of any associated thyrotoxicosis; malignant struma ovarii is uncommon and generally indolent, though it warrants thyroid-cancer-style follow-up.

Struvite (infection) nephrolithiasis — struvite stones, infection stones, triple phosphate stones, magnesium ammonium phosphate stones, urease stones Calcium stones forming a staghorn configuration Cystine staghorn calculus Uric acid stone with secondary infection Renal tuberculosis with calcification Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis Medullary sponge kidney with stones Non-contrast CT to define the stone burden and staghorn configuration Urine culture to identify the urease-producing organism and guide antibiotics Urine pH, which is characteristically alkaline, and microscopy for crystals Stone analysis confirming struvite and carbonate apatite composition Serum renal function and, in bilateral disease, assessment of split renal function Metabolic evaluation to exclude a coexisting metabolic stone nidus Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones form only in urine infected by urease-producing organisms, classically Proteus mirabilis and also Klebsiella, Pseudomonas and Ureaplasma The enzyme urease splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, alkalinising the urine and supplying the ammonium and carbonate needed for crystallisation These are the archetypal stones that grow rapidly and fill the collecting system as staghorn calculi They occur more often in women and in patients with recurrent urinary infection, neurogenic bladder, indwelling catheters or urinary diversion A persistently alkaline urine with recurrent urea-splitting organisms is an important diagnostic clue Coffin-lid shaped crystals may be seen on urine microscopy Cure requires complete surgical clearance of every fragment, because residual material harbours bacteria and seeds regrowth Culture-directed antibiotics against the urease organism, sometimes with a urease inhibitor and urinary acidification, support treatment but cannot substitute for complete stone clearance Sepsis arising from an infected obstructed system Rapid staghorn growth threatening renal function Progressive loss of function in the affected kidney Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis that may require nephrectomy Treating with antibiotics alone and expecting cure without complete stone removal Leaving residual fragments that reseed both infection and stone Missing a coexisting metabolic abnormality that acted as the initial nidus Underestimating the sepsis risk when instrumenting an infected stone Struvite stones are a direct consequence of chronic urinary infection with bacteria that produce urease. Urease hydrolyses urea to ammonia and carbon dioxide; the ammonia raises the urine pH and generates ammonium while carbon dioxide yields carbonate. In this persistently alkaline environment magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) and carbonate apatite become supersaturated and precipitate rapidly, frequently incorporating bacteria within the stone matrix. Because organisms are sequestered inside the stone, infection cannot be eradicated by antibiotics alone, and any retained fragment allows the process to recur and the stone to enlarge. If every fragment is cleared and infection eradicated, cure is achievable; incomplete clearance leads to a high recurrence rate, and long-standing staghorn calculi can destroy renal function and, rarely, are associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the collecting system.

Strychnine poisoning — strychnine toxicity, strychnine intoxication, nux vomica poisoning, rodenticide strychnine poisoning Tetanus Generalised seizure or status epilepticus Dystonic reaction to antidopaminergic drugs Neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin syndrome Stiff-person syndrome Hypocalcaemic tetany Creatine kinase and myoglobin to assess rhabdomyolysis Arterial blood gas and lactate for acidosis and ventilation Renal function and electrolytes including potassium and calcium Core temperature monitoring for hyperthermia Analytical confirmation of strychnine in blood, urine or gastric contents Electrocardiogram and continuous cardiac monitoring Strychnine causes generalised muscle rigidity and violent, exaggerated startle-provoked spasms with a fully preserved level of consciousness between episodes Classic signs include opisthotonos, risus sardonicus and trismus, closely mimicking tetanus but with much more rapid onset after ingestion Spasms are triggered by minimal sensory stimulation, so a dark, quiet environment with minimal handling is an important supportive measure Unlike a true seizure there is no post-ictal confusion, because the mechanism is spinal disinhibition rather than cortical discharge Severe sustained contractions can cause hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, lactic acidosis and myoglobinuric renal injury Death results from respiratory failure due to spasm of the muscles of respiration and diaphragm rather than direct central depression Management is supportive: aggressive control of spasms with sedation and neuromuscular blockade with ventilation when needed, plus treatment of hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis Sources include some rodenticides and adulterated illicit drugs, and diagnosis is largely clinical with confirmatory analytical testing Frequent or prolonged spasms involving respiratory muscles Hyperthermia with rigidity Marked rhabdomyolysis or myoglobinuric renal injury Metabolic acidosis or haemodynamic instability Inability to maintain the airway or adequate ventilation Mistaking spasms for epileptic seizures and overlooking preserved consciousness Excessive stimulation, examination or lighting that provokes further spasms Failing to secure the airway and provide ventilation once neuromuscular blockade is used Underestimating hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis Delaying sedation while awaiting analytical confirmation Strychnine competitively antagonises glycine, the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter at postsynaptic receptors of spinal cord and brainstem motor neurons. Loss of this inhibitory tone removes the normal reciprocal control of motor neurons, so both agonist and antagonist muscle groups contract simultaneously in response to any stimulus. The result is generalised rigidity with intermittent violent extensor spasms while consciousness is spared, because the toxin acts on the spinal cord rather than the cortex. Sustained muscular hyperactivity generates heat, acid and muscle breakdown, and respiratory muscle involvement causes fatal hypoventilation. If ventilation and spasms are controlled early and complications such as hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis are managed, recovery within a few days is usual as the toxin is metabolised; untreated severe poisoning is rapidly fatal from respiratory failure.

Sturge-Weber syndrome — SWS, encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis Isolated port-wine birthmark without systemic involvement Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome PHACE syndrome Other causes of infantile seizures with focal deficits Megalencephaly-capillary malformation syndrome Brain magnetic resonance imaging with contrast to demonstrate leptomeningeal angiomatosis Electroencephalography for seizure assessment Regular ophthalmological review including intraocular pressure measurement for glaucoma Neurodevelopmental assessment and monitoring Imaging for cortical calcification when clinically indicated Neurocutaneous disorder characterised by a facial capillary malformation (port-wine birthmark), leptomeningeal angiomatosis, and eye involvement The facial birthmark typically follows the distribution of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, and upper facial involvement raises the risk of brain and eye disease Leptomeningeal angiomatosis predisposes to seizures, which often begin in infancy and can be difficult to control Stroke-like episodes, hemiparesis, and progressive cognitive impairment may occur from impaired cortical perfusion Glaucoma is a common ocular complication and requires ongoing monitoring of intraocular pressure Caused by a somatic mosaic activating mutation in the GNAQ gene arising during early development, so it is not typically inherited Characteristic tram-track cortical calcification may be seen on imaging in affected brain regions A port-wine birthmark alone, without brain or eye involvement, does not constitute the full syndrome Poorly controlled or prolonged seizures requiring urgent treatment to limit neurological injury Stroke-like episodes with acute focal deficits Rising intraocular pressure or visual deterioration from glaucoma Progressive developmental regression signalling worsening cortical involvement Assuming any facial port-wine birthmark implies the full syndrome without assessing brain and eye involvement Failing to monitor for glaucoma, which can present at any age Undertreating early seizures with consequences for development Not recognising the mosaic somatic cause and incorrectly counselling about heritability Sturge-Weber syndrome is caused by a somatic activating mutation in the GNAQ gene occurring in a subset of cells during early embryogenesis, producing a mosaic distribution that explains the segmental capillary malformations. The mutation dysregulates signalling in vascular and other tissues, leading to abnormal capillary-venous malformations in the skin, leptomeninges, and eye. The leptomeningeal vascular malformation impairs normal venous drainage and cortical perfusion, causing chronic ischaemia, cortical atrophy, calcification, and a lowered seizure threshold. Because the mutation is somatic and mosaic rather than germline, the condition arises sporadically and is not inherited. Outcome varies with the extent of brain and eye involvement; some individuals have well-controlled seizures and near-normal development, while extensive leptomeningeal disease can lead to refractory epilepsy, hemiparesis, and cognitive impairment.

STXBP1 developmental and epileptic encephalopathy — STXBP1, Munc18-1 encephalopathy, early infantile epileptic encephalopathy 4 (EIEE4), STXBP1-related disorder KCNQ2 or SCN2A neonatal epileptic encephalopathy CDKL5 deficiency disorder Ohtahara and West syndromes of other causes Pyridoxine-dependent and other treatable metabolic epilepsies Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy Other developmental and epileptic encephalopathies EEG to identify burst-suppression, hypsarrhythmia or other epileptiform patterns Brain MRI to exclude structural or acquired causes Metabolic screen including a trial addressing treatable causes such as pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy Chromosomal microarray and STXBP1-inclusive gene panel or exome sequencing Developmental and movement-disorder assessment A common cause of early-infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, with seizures often beginning in the neonatal period or early infancy Seizure types are varied and may include epileptic spasms with a burst-suppression or hypsarrhythmia EEG (Ohtahara or West syndrome patterns) Some individuals have significant developmental impairment with little or no epilepsy, so the disorder spans an encephalopathy-with-or-without-seizures spectrum Prominent features include hypotonia, movement disorders such as tremor, dystonia and ataxia, and later autistic behaviours Caused by heterozygous loss-of-function or dominant-negative variants in STXBP1 (Munc18-1), usually de novo and autosomal dominant Seizures may respond well to certain antiseizure medications even when development remains severely affected Brain MRI is frequently normal or shows only non-specific findings Neonatal-onset seizures or epileptic spasms Burst-suppression or hypsarrhythmia on EEG Status epilepticus or clustering seizures Feeding difficulty and failure to thrive Assuming controlling the seizures will normalise development Not considering STXBP1 in developmental impairment without epilepsy Omitting a trial for treatable metabolic epilepsies before concluding the diagnosis Interpreting a normal MRI as excluding a genetic encephalopathy STXBP1 encodes Munc18-1, a syntaxin-binding protein essential for assembly of the SNARE complex that mediates synaptic vesicle docking and calcium-triggered neurotransmitter release. Heterozygous loss-of-function or dominant-negative variants reduce functional protein through haploinsufficiency and, in some cases, aggregation of misfolded protein, impairing synaptic transmission across excitatory and inhibitory networks. The resulting disturbance of neurotransmission produces cortical hyperexcitability and abnormal circuit function, manifesting as early epileptic encephalopathy, movement disorder and intellectual disability. The developmental impairment can be substantial even when seizures are controlled, reflecting the protein's ongoing role in synaptic function. Most individuals have moderate to severe intellectual disability regardless of seizure control, though epilepsy can improve or remit over time in some. Outcome is variable across the spectrum, and management is supportive with attention to seizures, movement disorder and development.

considered when systemic features are present Fever, erythema and marked tenderness suggesting septic bursitis Acute loss of active movement after trauma suggesting a cuff tear Systemic upset or immunosuppression raising infection risk Progressive night pain unresponsive to treatment Treating bursitis in isolation while ignoring the underlying cuff tendinopathy Repeated corticosteroid injections without addressing load Missing septic bursitis in an atypically hot, swollen presentation Over-reliance on imaging findings that may be incidental The subacromial-subdeltoid bursa reduces Usually settles with treatment of the underlying cuff disorder and activity modification; recurrence relates to ongoing overload or unaddressed cuff pathology.

subacromial impingement syndrome — subacromial pain syndrome, rotator cuff impingement Rotator cuff tear (partial or full thickness) Calcific tendinitis of the shoulder Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) Acromioclavicular joint osteoarthritis Glenohumeral instability with secondary impingement Cervical radiculopathy referring to the shoulder Glenohumeral osteoarthritis Plain radiographs including an outlet (scapular Y) view to assess acromial morphology and spurs Ultrasound of the rotator cuff and subacromial bursa, including dynamic assessment during elevation MRI to characterise cuff tendinopathy, partial or full-thickness tears and bursal changes Diagnostic subacromial local anaesthetic injection test Assessment of scapular kinematics and posture Cervical spine imaging if radicular features are present Presents as a painful arc during mid-range abduction, typically with anterolateral shoulder pain that is worse on overhead reach and at night when lying on the affected side. The term subacromial pain syndrome is increasingly preferred, reflecting a shift away from a purely mechanical model towards a spectrum including bursitis, tendinopathy and partial cuff pathology. Neer and Hawkins-Kennedy provocation tests are sensitive but not specific; a positive subacromial injection test supports the diagnosis by transiently abolishing pain and improving cuff strength. Acromial morphology matters: a hooked (Bigliami type III) acromion and a laterally downsloping acromion are associated with increased mechanical narrowing of the subacromial space. Distinguish primary (extrinsic mechanical) impingement from secondary impingement arising from glenohumeral instability or scapular dyskinesis, as the latter requires rehabilitation rather than decompression. Structured physiotherapy targeting rotator cuff and scapular stabiliser strengthening is first-line and resolves symptoms in the majority without surgery. Consider an alternative or coexisting diagnosis when weakness is profound or there is loss of active elevation, suggesting a full-thickness cuff tear rather than isolated impingement. Subacromial corticosteroid injection can provide short-term relief and aid engagement with rehabilitation, but repeated injections risk tendon deterioration. Profound weakness or inability to actively elevate the arm suggesting a large or massive cuff tear Rest and night pain unresponsive to conservative measures raising concern for tumour or infection History of significant trauma with acute loss of function suggesting acute cuff rupture or fracture Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss or a palpable mass Attributing all anterolateral shoulder pain to impingement while missing an underlying full-thickness cuff tear or glenohumeral pathology. Proceeding to acromioplasty without first correcting scapular dyskinesis or instability, leading to persistent secondary impingement. Over-reliance on radiographic acromial shape, which correlates poorly with symptoms in individual patients. Repeated corticosteroid injections that mask progression and may compromise tendon integrity. Impingement describes mechanical compression and irritation of the rotator cuff tendons (chiefly supraspinatus) and the subacromial bursa within the coracoacromial arch during elevation of the arm. Extrinsic factors include acromial shape, subacromial spurs and coracoacromial ligament thickening, which narrow the outlet, while intrinsic tendon degeneration, hypovascularity of the critical zone and age-related collagen changes weaken the tendon. Dynamic contributors such as scapular dyskinesis, glenohumeral instability and rotator cuff or periscapular muscle imbalance reduce effective humeral head depression, allowing superior migration and repetitive abrasion. The resulting inflammatory and degenerative cascade produces bursitis, tendinopathy and progressive partial tearing, forming part of a continuum that may culminate in cuff failure. Most patients improve substantially with a sustained programme of physiotherapy and activity modification, and outcomes of subacromial decompression are comparable to structured exercise in appropriately selected cases. Prognosis is less favourable when impingement is secondary to unaddressed instability, dyskinesis or an established cuff tear.

Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord — SCD, SACD, subacute combined degeneration, B12 myelopathy Copper deficiency myelopathy (clinically near-identical picture) Multiple sclerosis and other demyelinating myelopathy Compressive cervical myelopathy or spondylotic myelopathy Tabes dorsalis and other causes of sensory ataxia Hereditary spastic paraplegia HTLV-1 associated myelopathy Serum vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid and homocysteine when B12 is borderline Full blood count and blood film for macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils Intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies to identify pernicious anaemia MRI of the spine showing high T2 signal in the dorsal columns (inverted V or dot sign) Serum copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude copper deficiency mimicking the syndrome Nerve conduction studies if a coexisting peripheral neuropathy is suspected Caused by vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency, which preferentially damages the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts of the spinal cord Typically presents with symmetrical distal paraesthesiae, loss of vibration and joint-position sense, and a progressive spastic-ataxic gait Combines upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, extensor plantars) with impaired proprioception and sometimes absent ankle reflexes, giving a mixed picture Neuropsychiatric features such as cognitive slowing, irritability, or depression may accompany or precede the myelopathy Serum B12 can be borderline or normal, so raised methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are more sensitive markers of tissue deficiency Common causes include pernicious anaemia, malabsorption, strict vegan diet, gastric surgery, and prolonged nitrous oxide exposure Early replacement of B12 can halt and partially reverse deficits; delayed treatment risks permanent disability Macrocytic anaemia may be absent, so neurological disease can occur without haematological changes Rapidly progressive myelopathy causing gait failure or sphincter disturbance Recent or repeated nitrous oxide use with acute neurological decline Severe anaemia or pancytopenia requiring urgent evaluation Coexisting cognitive decline suggesting advanced or long-standing deficiency Relying on a normal serum B12 and missing functional deficiency demonstrable by methylmalonic acid Assuming anaemia must be present, thereby overlooking purely neurological presentations Failing to ask about recreational or repeated medical nitrous oxide exposure Overlooking copper deficiency, which produces an indistinguishable myelopathy Attributing spastic-ataxic gait solely to spondylosis and delaying B12 assessment Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Deficiency impairs myelin synthesis and maintenance, leading to vacuolar demyelination and axonal degeneration that begins in the dorsal columns and later involves the lateral (corticospinal) columns, hence the term 'combined'. Nitrous oxide irreversibly oxidises the cobalt core of cobalamin and can precipitate the disorder in those with marginal stores. The pathology accounts for the combination of sensory ataxia from posterior column loss and spasticity from corticospinal tract involvement. Recovery depends on how early replacement begins; symptoms present for less than a few months often improve substantially, whereas long-standing deficits may only stabilise, leaving residual sensory ataxia or spasticity.

Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (measles) — SSPE, Dawson encephalitis, measles inclusion encephalitis (chronic), subacute sclerosing leukoencephalitis Progressive rubella panencephalitis Other viral or autoimmune encephalitides Neurodegenerative disorders and leukodystrophies of childhood and adolescence Inborn errors of metabolism presenting with regression Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and other prion disorders Epileptic encephalopathies with myoclonus Electroencephalography demonstrating periodic complexes synchronous with myoclonus Cerebrospinal fluid measles antibody titre with paired serum for antibody index and oligoclonal bands MRI of the brain showing white-matter change and later cerebral atrophy Detailed history of prior measles infection, especially in infancy, and immunisation status Molecular detection of measles virus RNA in brain tissue in atypical cases Exclusion of metabolic, prion, and autoimmune causes of progressive encephalopathy A rare, progressive, and fatal encephalitis caused by persistence of a defective measles virus in the brain, typically developing years after the initial measles infection The risk is greatest when natural measles is acquired in infancy, and the latent interval before SSPE is often 6 to 10 years or more It evolves through recognisable stages, beginning with subtle cognitive and behavioural change and declining school performance The hallmark second stage is periodic myoclonic jerks, followed by progressive dementia, spasticity, rigidity, and eventually a vegetative state The electroencephalogram characteristically shows periodic complexes that coincide with the myoclonic jerks Cerebrospinal fluid reveals markedly raised measles-specific antibody with oligoclonal bands and evidence of intrathecal antibody synthesis, with normal or mildly raised protein There is no curative therapy; agents such as interferon and isoprinosine have been tried with limited benefit, and prevention through measles immunisation is paramount Progressive cognitive decline with new periodic myoclonic jerks in a child or adolescent Rapid neurological deterioration into rigidity or a vegetative state Loss of safe swallowing and airway protection Intractable seizures or autonomic instability in advanced disease Dismissing early behavioural and academic decline as a psychological or educational problem Not recognising the diagnostic value of periodic EEG complexes coinciding with myoclonus Relying on serum measles antibody alone rather than demonstrating intrathecal antibody synthesis Underestimating the importance of measles vaccination in prevention, especially where infants are infected Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis results from persistence of the measles virus in neurones and glia after apparently complete recovery from acute measles. Over the ensuing years the virus accumulates mutations, particularly affecting the matrix and other envelope genes, so that it can no longer produce complete infectious particles but continues to spread cell to cell within the brain. This defective, persistent infection provokes a chronic inflammatory and immune response, with intense intrathecal production of anti-measles antibody, alongside slowly progressive destruction of both grey and white matter, hence the term panencephalitis. Neurones and oligodendrocytes contain viral inclusions, and there is perivascular inflammation, gliosis, and demyelination. The relentless accumulation of neuronal loss underlies the stepwise clinical deterioration from cognitive decline through myoclonus to a vegetative state and death. SSPE is usually relentlessly progressive and fatal, most patients dying within a few years of onset; occasional cases follow a more prolonged or fluctuating course, but spontaneous long-term remission is rare and no treatment reliably arrests it.

antimicrobials Marked thyrotoxic symptoms with cardiac compromise Persistent hypothyroid symptoms indicating the need for hormone replacement Compressive symptoms or an atypical mass raising concern for malignancy Mistaking destructive thyrotoxicosis for Graves' disease and prescribing ineffective antithyroid drugs Failing to check radioiodine uptake or ultrasound vascularity to separate the two Overlooking the later hypothyroid phase and not monitoring thyroid function through recovery Attributing a painful gland to malignancy without recognising the inflammatory picture Subacute thyroiditis is thought to result from a viral infection or post-viral inflammatory response affecting the thyroid, producing granulomatous inflammation with giant cells and destruction of thyroid follicles. Disruption of follicles releases stored thyroid hormone into the circulation, causing an initial destructive thyrotoxicosis with suppressed TSH and low radioiodine uptake. As follicular stores are depleted and the gland heals, patients pass through a hypothyroid phase before glandular recovery restores normal hormone production in most cases. The illness is usually self-limiting over weeks to months with full recovery of thyroid function in most patients, though pain can be prolonged, recurrences occur occasionally, and a small proportion develop permanent hypothyroidism.

Subaortic stenosis — subvalvular aortic stenosis, discrete subaortic stenosis Valvular aortic stenosis Supravalvular aortic stenosis Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (dynamic) Coarctation (as another left-heart obstruction) Tunnel-type left ventricular outflow obstruction Echocardiography localising the obstruction and measuring the gradient Assessment of aortic valve for secondary regurgitation Evaluation of left ventricular hypertrophy and function Exclusion of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and valvular stenosis Serial follow-up given progression and recurrence Fixed obstruction below the aortic valve, most often from a discrete fibrous or fibromuscular ridge in the left ventricular outflow tract It is usually acquired and progressive during childhood, and may recur after resection The turbulent subvalvular jet can damage the aortic valve, causing progressive aortic regurgitation It must be distinguished from valvular aortic stenosis and from hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (a dynamic obstruction) An ejection systolic murmur is heard, and unlike valvular stenosis there is no ejection click Surgical resection is considered for significant gradients or progressive aortic regurgitation, but recurrence is common Rapidly progressive gradient Developing or worsening aortic regurgitation Symptoms of outflow obstruction (syncope, angina, breathlessness) Recurrence after surgical resection Confusing fixed subaortic stenosis with dynamic hypertrophic obstruction Overlooking progressive aortic regurgitation from the subvalvular jet Assuming cure after resection without follow-up for recurrence Mislocalising the level of obstruction Discrete subaortic stenosis is characterised by a fibrous or fibromuscular membrane or ridge in the left ventricular outflow tract beneath the aortic valve, producing a fixed obstruction to ejection. Abnormal outflow tract geometry and shear stress are thought to stimulate proliferation of the obstructing tissue, which explains its progressive nature and tendency to recur after removal. The high-velocity subvalvular jet strikes the aortic valve leaflets, causing thickening and regurgitation over time, while the pressure-loaded left ventricle hypertrophies. Resection relieves the obstruction and can protect the aortic valve, but the lesion may recur and aortic regurgitation can persist, so long-term surveillance is required.

Subclavian steal syndrome — subclavian steal syndrome, subclavian steal phenomenon, vertebral-subclavian steal Vertebrobasilar insufficiency from intrinsic posterior circulation atherosclerosis Vestibular or inner-ear causes of vertigo Cardiac arrhythmia or other causes of syncope Thoracic outlet syndrome causing arm symptoms Carotid territory transient ischaemic attack Large-vessel vasculitis (e.g. Takayasu arteritis) Bilateral arm blood pressure measurement to document an inter-arm gradient Duplex ultrasound of the vertebral and subclavian arteries demonstrating reversed vertebral flow CT or MR angiography of the aortic arch and great vessels to localise the proximal lesion Catheter angiography when intervention is planned Provocative arm-exercise testing to reproduce symptoms and flow reversal Assessment for large-vessel arteritis when atherosclerosis is not the obvious cause Caused by proximal subclavian (or innominate) artery stenosis or occlusion, so blood is drawn in reverse down the ipsilateral vertebral artery to supply the arm, at the expense of the posterior cerebral circulation Classically presents with arm claudication and posterior-circulation (vertebrobasilar) symptoms such as dizziness, vertigo, visual disturbance or syncope, provoked by exercising the affected arm A hallmark examination finding is a significant inter-arm systolic blood pressure difference, with the lower pressure on the affected side The affected arm may also have a weaker or delayed radial pulse and a supraclavicular bruit It is far more common on the left, reflecting the higher frequency of proximal left subclavian atherosclerosis The reversed vertebral flow (steal) is often an asymptomatic imaging finding; During arm exercise, demand in the limb increases and the pressure gradient reverses flow in the ipsilateral vertebral artery, so blood is siphoned retrogradely from the basilar and contralateral vertebral system into the arm. This diversion can transiently reduce perfusion of the posterior cerebral circulation, producing vertebrobasilar symptoms, while the arm experiences exertional ischaemia. The underlying lesion is usually atherosclerotic, though large-vessel arteritis, prior surgery or congenital anomalies can be responsible. Asymptomatic subclavian steal is generally benign and often needs no intervention, while symptomatic disease usually responds well to revascularisation with relief of arm and neurological symptoms; long-term outlook is largely determined by the burden of underlying atherosclerotic disease.

Subclinical (mild autonomous cortisol secretion) Cushing syndrome — subclinical Cushing syndrome, mild autonomous cortisol secretion, MACS, autonomous cortisol secretion Overt clinical Cushing syndrome Non-functioning adrenal adenoma Pseudo-Cushing states related to alcohol, depression or obesity Exogenous glucocorticoid effect Metabolic syndrome of another cause Phaeochromocytoma as part of the incidentaloma workup Overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test as the key screening test Plasma ACTH, expected to be low or suppressed, and DHEAS Late-night salivary cortisol and 24-hour urinary free cortisol to gauge overall cortisol burden Assessment of comorbidities including blood pressure, glucose or HbA1c, lipids and bone density Adrenal CT to characterise the adenoma Metanephrines and aldosterone-to-renin ratio as part of the incidentaloma screen Refers to autonomous cortisol secretion from an adrenal adenoma without the overt clinical features of Cushing syndrome; The circulating cortisol, although insufficient to produce classic Cushingoid features, suppresses pituitary ACTH and the contralateral adrenal cortex. Subconjunctival haemorrhage — subconjunctival hemorrhage, hyposphagma, SCH Conjunctivitis (bacterial, viral, haemorrhagic) Ruptured globe with subconjunctival bleeding after trauma Conjunctival or Kaposi lesion mimicking haemorrhage Anterior uveitis or scleritis (painful red eye) Bleeding from orbital or retrobulbar haemorrhage Blood pressure measurement, especially in recurrent cases Review of anticoagulant and antiplatelet medication Coagulation studies and platelet count when bleeding is recurrent or spontaneous Slit-lamp examination to exclude other causes of red eye Assessment for globe rupture or orbital injury when trauma is involved Presents as a painless, flat, bright red patch of blood beneath the conjunctiva with a sharply defined border and normal vision Usually benign and self-limiting, resolving over one to two weeks as the blood is reabsorbed and changes colour Common precipitants include Valsalva-type events such as coughing, sneezing, straining, or vomiting, minor trauma, and rubbing Recurrent or bilateral haemorrhages should prompt review of hypertension, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, and bleeding disorders The absence of pain, discharge, and visual disturbance distinguishes it from more serious causes of a red eye A haemorrhage without a visible posterior margin after trauma may indicate a source from behind the orbit, raising concern for orbital fracture or ruptured globe Reassurance is the mainstay; Because blood is confined to this superficial layer, it appears as a well-demarcated red sheet without affecting the cornea or intraocular structures. Rises in venous pressure (Valsalva), fragile vessels, trauma, or impaired haemostasis predispose to rupture. The blood is gradually cleared by resorption, passing through the usual colour changes of a resolving bruise. Isolated spontaneous subconjunctival haemorrhage resolves completely without treatment and carries no visual risk; prognosis depends on any underlying systemic or traumatic cause.

dermatosis is a neutrophilic dermatosis in which sterile neutrophils accumulate immediately beneath the stratum corneum to form subcorneal pustules, without acantholysis or infection. The precise trigger is unknown, but dysregulated neutrophil chemotaxis is central, and cytokine or immunoglobulin abnormalities, notably IgA monoclonal gammopathy, are implicated in a proportion of cases. Unlike IgA pemphigus it lacks demonstrable intercellular immunoglobulin deposition, indicating that the pustulation is driven by neutrophil recruitment rather than by autoantibodies to desmosomal adhesion molecules. or ulcerating lesions with possible secondary infection Thrombocytopenia or metabolic derangement Discharging without arranging prolonged calcium monitoring, so delayed hypercalcaemia is missed hypercalcaemia has passed Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn is an injury to neonatal fat that follows perinatal stresses such as hypoxia, hypothermia and trauma, often in the setting of therapeutic hypothermia. Neonatal fat is rich in saturated fatty acids with a higher solidification point, making it prone to crystallisation and necrosis when subjected to cold or ischaemia. The damaged adipocytes provoke a granulomatous inflammatory response with characteristic needle-shaped crystal clefts. Granulomatous tissue can produce excess 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, driving intestinal calcium absorption and the delayed hypercalcaemia that is the key systemic risk. The skin lesions almost always resolve spontaneously over weeks to months, sometimes with transient atrophy; the outlook is good provided hypercalcaemia is detected and managed, as untreated hypercalcaemia can cause significant morbidity.

subcutaneous fat necrosis of newborn — subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn, SCFN sclerema neonatorum neonatal cellulitis or abscess cold panniculitis (popsicle panniculitis) bacillus Calmette-Guerin or other iatrogenic injection-site reactions congenital infantile haemangioma or other vascular tumours poststeroid panniculitis (in infants weaned off corticosteroids) serial serum calcium (including ionised calcium) for several weeks to months serum phosphate, magnesium, parathyroid hormone and vitamin D metabolites full blood count for thrombocytopenia serum triglycerides and glucose skin biopsy for histopathology when diagnosis is uncertain (needle-shaped clefts, granulomatous panniculitis) renal ultrasound and urinary calcium if nephrocalcinosis is suspected electrocardiogram if significant hypercalcaemia is detected A self-limiting lobular panniculitis of term and post-term neonates, typically appearing in the first days to weeks of life as firm, indurated, red-violaceous nodules and plaques. Characteristic sites are areas rich in fat and subject to pressure: the back, buttocks, shoulders, cheeks and proximal limbs. Risk factors include perinatal asphyxia, hypothermia (including therapeutic cooling), meconium aspiration, pre-eclampsia and maternal factors such as gestational diabetes. The infant is usually otherwise well, in contrast to sclerema neonatorum which affects sick, premature neonates diffusely. The principal and potentially life-threatening complication is hypercalcaemia, which may be delayed for weeks after the skin lesions appear. Histology shows fat necrosis with a granulomatous infiltrate and pathognomonic needle-shaped clefts (radial crystals of triglyceride) within adipocytes and giant cells. Other metabolic derangements include thrombocytopenia, hypertriglyceridaemia and hypoglycaemia, warranting monitoring. Skin lesions resolve spontaneously over weeks to months, but serum calcium must be monitored well beyond cutaneous resolution. hypercalcaemia causing irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy or seizures nephrocalcinosis or renal impairment from sustained hypercalcaemia extensive or ulcerating lesions predisposing to secondary infection cardiac arrhythmia associated with severe hypercalcaemia systemically unwell infant suggesting sclerema neonatorum or sepsis rather than isolated fat necrosis Discharging the infant once skin lesions improve without arranging prolonged calcium monitoring. Confusing it with sclerema neonatorum, which carries a far graver prognosis and different clinical context. Attributing hypercalcaemic symptoms to feeding difficulties or sepsis. Failing to recognise therapeutic hypothermia as a precipitating factor. Overlooking thrombocytopenia or hypertriglyceridaemia in the metabolic work-up. Neonatal subcutaneous fat has a high ratio of saturated (stearic and palmitic) to unsaturated fatty acids and a higher melting point than adult fat, predisposing it to crystallise and solidify under stress. Perinatal hypoxia, hypothermia and local pressure cause ischaemic injury to this metabolically vulnerable fat, triggering crystallisation and necrosis of adipocytes with liberation of fatty acids. A granulomatous inflammatory response ensues, with foreign-body giant cells containing characteristic radially arranged needle-shaped crystal clefts. The associated hypercalcaemia is attributed largely to extrarenal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity within the granulomatous infiltrate producing 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, augmented by prostaglandin E and release of calcium from necrotic fat. The cutaneous prognosis is excellent, with spontaneous resolution over weeks to months, but the outcome hinges on detecting and managing hypercalcaemia, which can be delayed and, if unrecognised, cause metastatic calcification or renal damage.

associated haemophagocytic syndrome that dominates the clinical picture By definition the neoplastic infiltrate is confined to subcutaneous fat, rimming individual adipocytes, without dermal or epidermal involvement Tumour cells are cytotoxic T-lymphocytes of the alpha-beta lineage, typically CD8-positive and betaF1-positive, with expression of cytotoxic granule proteins It must be separated from primary cutaneous gamma-delta T-cell lymphoma, which involves dermis and epidermis, is more aggressive, and carries a worse prognosis An overlap exists with lupus erythematosus panniculitis, and the two can be difficult to distinguish or may coexist In the absence of haemophagocytic syndrome the course is often relatively indolent Development of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis with cytopenias, high ferritin, and organ dysfunction Rapid dissemination or transformation to a more aggressive phenotype Extensive ulcerating disease suggesting a gamma-delta lymphoma rather than SPTCL Systemic deterioration with high fever and multi-organ involvement Misdiagnosing the lesions as benign panniculitis and delaying biopsy Failing to distinguish SPTCL from the more aggressive gamma-delta cutaneous lymphoma Overlooking a developing haemophagocytic syndrome Confusing the condition with lupus panniculitis, which it can closely resemble or coexist with Subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma is a cytotoxic T-cell neoplasm derived from alpha-beta T-lymphocytes that selectively infiltrates subcutaneous adipose tissue. The malignant cells characteristically surround individual fat cells, producing a lobular panniculitis-like pattern with fat necrosis and karyorrhexis while sparing the overlying dermis and epidermis. Cytotoxic activity and cytokine release can drive macrophage activation, precipitating a haemophagocytic syndrome that accounts for much of the disease's morbidity. Some cases arise on a background of, or overlap with, autoimmune disease, blurring the boundary with lupus panniculitis. Without haemophagocytic syndrome the prognosis is generally favourable and disease may be controlled with immunosuppression or systemic therapy, but an associated haemophagocytic syndrome markedly worsens outcome.

Subdural haematoma — Non-contrast CT head Coagulation; reverse anticoagulation Neurosurgical review Expanding bleed — may need evacuation Epidural haematoma (lenticular/lens-shaped on CT, usually arterial from a torn middle meningeal artery, classic lucid interval, more rapid evolution) Cerebral contusion / convexity contusion (can produce focal deficits such as aphasia or mild hemiparesis) Carotid or vertebral artery dissection (can mimic focal deficits seen with subdural) Posttraumatic headache syndrome (chronic subdural may mimic this) (p.160) MRI reliably identifies both subacute and chronic subdural haematomas and is useful when CT is equivocal (p.3573) Contrast-enhanced imaging demonstrates enhancement of the vascular fibrous capsule surrounding a chronic collection (p.3573) Serial imaging for clinical observation of small chronic collections without mass effect (p.3573) Transient ischemic attack (rarely chronic subdural causes brief episodes of hemiparesis or aphasia indistinguishable from TIA) (p.3573) Dementia / Alzheimer or other neurodegenerative disease (chronic subdural is a treatable cause of dementia, often on a background of cortical atrophy) (pp.238, 3527) Stroke (subdural is considered when excluding stroke in older fallers) (p.3929) Normal-pressure hydrocephalus and other reversible dementia causes (listed alongside subdural among treatable dementias) (p.238) Direct cranial trauma may be minor and is not always required for an acute subdural bleed, particularly in the elderly and those on anticoagulants; acceleration forces alone (e.g. whiplash) can suffice (p.3572). Up to one-third of patients with acute subdural haematoma have a lucid interval of minutes to hours before coma supervenes, but most are drowsy or comatose from the moment of injury (p.3572). A unilateral headache with a slightly enlarged pupil on the side of the haematoma is frequently, though not invariably, present (p.3572). Small subdural haematomas may be asymptomatic and usually do not require evacuation unless they enlarge (p.3572). In chronic subdural haematoma, drowsiness, inattentiveness and incoherent thinking are generally more prominent than focal signs such as hemiparesis (p.3573). Chronic subdural haematoma headache typically fluctuates in severity, sometimes with changes in head position (p.3573). A history of trauma may be absent in chronic subdural haematoma; the injury may have been trivial and forgotten, especially in the elderly and those with clotting disorders (p.3572). Recurrent falls in older adults place them at risk for subdural haematoma; brain imaging is warranted when neurologic signs are present (pp.222-223, 3927, 3929). Trauma should be considered in any patient with an unexplained acute neurologic deficit (hemiparesis, stupor, confusion), particularly after a fall (p.3498). Stupor or coma, hemiparesis, and unilateral pupillary enlargement indicate a larger acute haematoma (p.3572) Acutely deteriorating patient requiring emergency craniotomy (p.3572) Repetitive vomiting, nystagmus, drowsiness and unsteadiness may signal a posterior fossa subdural haematoma (p.3619) Large bleed after only minor trauma should raise concern for coagulopathy or anticoagulant therapy (p.3573) Subacute pitfall: between roughly 2 and 6 weeks after the initial bleed the clot becomes isodense relative to adjacent brain on non-contrast CT and may be inapparent/missed (p.3573). Acute subdural produces more horizontal displacement (mass effect) than expected from its thickness because of its large rostral-caudal extent, so mass effect can be underestimated from clot thickness alone (p.3572). Absence of a trauma history does not exclude chronic subdural haematoma in the elderly or anticoagulated (p.3572). Skull fractures are markers of injury site/severity, not the haematoma itself, and may be absent (p.3572). Bleeding occurs beneath the dura (subdural space). The bleeding producing larger subdural haematomas is primarily venous in origin, classically from torn bridging veins, although arterial bleeding sites are occasionally found at operation and a few large haematomas are purely arterial. Chronic subdural haematomas develop days to weeks after (often trivial) injury, favoured by age-related cerebral atrophy that stretches bridging veins; they organise into a vascular fibrous capsule, and weeks-old collections often contain a mixture of blood and serous fluid. Anticoagulant-related intracranial haemorrhages are often subdural and may continue to evolve over 24-48 h if coagulopathy is insufficiently reversed (pp.3572-3573, 3498). In contrast to epidural haematomas, acute subdural haematomas requiring surgery carry significant morbidity and mortality, partly reflecting frequently associated underlying cortical brain damage. Chronic subdural collections evacuated through burr holes are usually treated successfully when a postoperative cranial drain is used; encapsulating fibrous membranes may require craniotomy to prevent recurrent fluid accumulation (pp.3572-3573). Harrison frames subdural haematoma by acuity and imaging appearance rather than a numeric grade: ACUTE — non-contrast CT shows a hyperdense crescentic clot with an irregular brain interface; SUBACUTE (~2-6 weeks) — clot becomes isodense and easily overlooked, often with mixed blood and serous fluid; CHRONIC — hypodense crescentic collection over one or both convexities, most often frontotemporal (pp.3572-3573).

mass Over-treating an incidental, asymptomatic benign lesion Misinterpreting a mixed subependymoma-ependymoma as pure subependymoma and underestimating recurrence risk Attributing symptoms to the tumour when they are due to unrelated pathology Failing to recognise and relieve obstructive hydrocephalus in a symptomatic case Subependymoma is a slow-growing, benign glial tumour thought to arise from the subependymal glial cells lining the ventricles, possibly from a mix of ependymal and astrocytic progenitor cells. It grows as a well-demarcated nodular mass projecting into the ventricular lumen and is composed of small clusters of uniform, cytologically bland cells embedded in an abundant fibrillary glial matrix, commonly with microcysts and calcification. Proliferative activity is very low, accounting for its indolent behaviour, and it lacks the aggressive molecular features seen in higher-grade ependymal tumours. Clinical problems arise mechanically when the tumour is large enough to impede cerebrospinal fluid circulation. Prognosis is excellent, as subependymoma is benign and slow-growing; complete surgical resection of a symptomatic tumour is generally curative, and incidental asymptomatic lesions can often simply be monitored. Recurrence after gross total resection is uncommon.

Neonatal subgaleal haemorrhage — subgaleal haematoma, subaponeurotic haemorrhage Caput succedaneum Cephalohaematoma Coagulopathy causing bleeding Intracranial haemorrhage Other causes of neonatal shock Serial head circumference measurement and clinical assessment of the swelling Full blood count and serial haematocrit Coagulation studies Continuous vital sign monitoring for hypovolaemia Bilirubin monitoring during resorption Bleeding into the loose potential space between the scalp aponeurosis and the periosteum, which can hold a large volume of blood It is the most dangerous of the extracranial birth haemorrhages because it can cause life-threatening blood loss It is strongly associated with vacuum-assisted (and sometimes forceps) delivery The swelling is diffuse, boggy and fluctuant, crosses sutures and may shift with position, sometimes with a fluid thrill Signs of hypovolaemia (tachycardia, pallor, falling haematocrit) and expanding head circumference indicate ongoing bleeding Management requires close monitoring, volume and blood-product resuscitation and correction of coagulopathy Expanding swelling with rising head circumference Tachycardia, pallor or falling haematocrit indicating significant blood loss Signs of shock or coagulopathy Reduced conscious level Mistaking it for benign caput succedaneum and underestimating blood loss Failing to monitor head circumference and haematocrit serially Delaying resuscitation and blood products Overlooking an associated coagulopathy Subgaleal haemorrhage occurs when shearing forces, characteristically from vacuum extraction, rupture the emissary veins traversing the subgaleal space. Because this space is large and unconfined by suture attachments, it can accommodate a substantial proportion of the neonate's blood volume, leading to significant, sometimes catastrophic, haemorrhage. The resulting hypovolaemia and any accompanying coagulopathy can cause shock, and breakdown of the extravasated blood contributes to jaundice. With early recognition and aggressive resuscitation most infants recover, but delayed diagnosis of a large or ongoing bleed can be fatal; the condition demands vigilance after assisted delivery.

a decompensating infant Overlooking an underlying coagulopathy that perpetuates bleeding Not anticipating later hyperbilirubinaemia during resorption of the collection Subgaleal haemorrhage results from rupture of the emissary veins that connect the scalp veins to the intracranial dural sinuses, or from shearing of these vessels during delivery. Blood collects in the subgaleal space, a large loosely bound plane beneath the epicranial aponeurosis that is not limited by cranial sutures, so bleeding can dissect widely across the scalp. Traction and shearing forces, especially from vacuum extraction, and impaired haemostasis from coagulopathy predispose to this injury. Because the space can accommodate a large volume, continued bleeding leads to progressive expansion of the swelling, significant blood loss, hypovolaemia, and anaemia, and later hyperbilirubinaemia as the extravasated blood is broken down. With early recognition and prompt supportive care most infants recover fully. However, unrecognised or large subgaleal haemorrhage can cause severe hypovolaemic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and death, so mortality is significant when diagnosis is delayed. Survivors of severe blood loss are at risk of associated hypoxic-ischaemic injury.

Like cutaneous infantile haemangiomas it is typically absent or minimal at birth, proliferates over the first months of life, and then slowly involutes over subsequent years. During proliferation the lesion enlarges and encroaches on the already narrow infant subglottis, and because this is the least distensible part of the paediatric airway even modest swelling produces significant obstruction and biphasic stridor. Mucosal engorgement with crying or infection transiently worsens the narrowing, and spontaneous regression during the involutional phase underlies the tendency for symptoms to abate with time. The natural history is favourable because the lesion ultimately involutes, and with propranolol many infants avoid surgery and do well; the risk lies in airway obstruction during the proliferative phase, so timely diagnosis and treatment are important.

The congenital form reflects abnormal development of the cricoid cartilage producing an inherently narrow lumen. The acquired form typically follows mucosal injury, most often from a tightly fitting or prolonged endotracheal tube, which causes pressure ischaemia, ulceration, perichondritis, and healing by fibrosis with scar contracture; trauma, infection, inflammatory disease, and prior airway surgery are other causes. Because the cricoid is a complete non-expansile ring, even modest circumferential scarring or oedema markedly reduces the lumen and airflow. Mild congenital stenosis often improves as the airway grows, and mild acquired disease may respond to endoscopic measures; more severe or long-segment stenosis usually needs open reconstruction, which has good success in restoring an adequate airway, though multiple procedures and temporary tracheostomy are sometimes required.

from repeated activation of the mesolimbic dopaminergic reward pathway, producing neuroadaptations in reward, motivation, memory, and executive control circuits that drive compulsive use and craving. Genetic vulnerability, early exposure, psychiatric comorbidity, and environmental and social stressors interact with these neuroadaptations, while allostatic changes in stress and reward systems underlie tolerance, withdrawal, and relapse liability. Substance use disorders are chronic, relapsing conditions, but many people achieve sustained remission, particularly with sustained treatment engagement and social support. Prognosis is worse with early onset, severe dependence, polysubstance use, untreated psychiatric comorbidity, and limited social stability, and better with strong recovery support and continuity of care.

surface of the distal phalanx, usually of the hallux, into the space beneath or beside the nail. It is generally regarded as a reactive proliferation, often linked to previous trauma or chronic irritation, rather than an inherited skeletal disorder, and it differs from a true osteochondroma in its cartilage cap and clinical setting. As the bony mass enlarges it pushes upward against the nail bed and plate, causing elevation, distortion, or partial destruction of the nail and producing pain when compressed by shoes. Subungual exostosis is benign and is cured by complete surgical excision, after which the nail usually regrows, although incomplete removal can lead to recurrence and some residual nail deformity may persist.

Subungual haematoma — Subungual haemorrhage, Bleeding under the nail Subungual melanoma Melanocytic naevus of the nail matrix Squamous cell carcinoma of the nail unit Glomus tumour (painful lesions) Subungual exostosis Pseudomonas or fungal pigmentation Splinter haemorrhages from other causes Dermoscopy of the nail plate to characterise the pigment pattern and margins Radiograph of the digit to exclude underlying phalangeal fracture Serial review to confirm distal migration of the pigment with nail growth Nail plate paring or clipping to assess whether pigment is blood or melanin Nail matrix biopsy if melanoma cannot be excluded Assessment of footwear and activity in recurrent toenail lesions A collection of blood beneath the nail plate, usually following acute crush or stubbing trauma, or repetitive microtrauma from ill-fitting footwear in runners and hikers. Acute lesions are intensely painful because of pressure within the closed subungual space; chronic or repetitive ones may be painless. Colour evolves over time from red-purple to blue-black and finally brown, and the pigment characteristically migrates distally with nail growth, moving away from the proximal fold. Dermoscopy typically shows a homogeneous red-black globular or streaked pattern with peripheral fading and sometimes tiny blood spots, without the parallel pigment network of melanocytic lesions. Acute painful haematomas involving a large fraction of the nail benefit from trephination (nail plate perforation) to release pressure and relieve pain. A key clinical rule is that a pigmented subungual lesion that does not move distally over weeks, or that is associated with nail dystrophy or periungual pigment, warrants biopsy to exclude melanoma. Associated finger or toe fractures, particularly distal phalangeal tuft fractures, should be considered and imaged when the mechanism is significant. Complete resolution follows the pace of nail growth, which is slower in toenails than fingernails. A pigmented band or lesion that fails to migrate distally over several weeks Hutchinson sign with pigment extending onto the proximal or lateral nail fold Subungual pigmentation without a convincing history of trauma, especially in a single digit Associated nail plate dystrophy, ulceration or bleeding suggesting malignancy Significant crush injury with suspected open fracture or nail bed laceration Reflexively attributing all subungual pigment to trauma and missing a melanoma Failing to image a significant crush injury and overlooking a distal phalangeal fracture or nail bed laceration Delaying trephination in a painful acute lesion when prompt drainage would relieve symptoms Not arranging follow-up to confirm distal migration of the pigment Trauma to the nail apparatus ruptures the rich vascular network of the nail bed and matrix, and extravasated blood becomes trapped between the firmly adherent nail plate and the underlying bed. Because this compartment is relatively non-distensible, even a small volume of blood raises pressure sharply and stimulates nociceptors, producing the throbbing pain of an acute lesion. Haemoglobin breakdown accounts for the evolving colour changes. As the nail plate grows outward from the matrix, the adherent pigmented blood is carried distally, which is the basis of the diagnostically useful distal migration. Repetitive low-grade trauma, as in athletes, produces recurrent painless haemorrhage often affecting several toenails symmetrically. Uncomplicated subungual haematoma resolves completely as the nail grows out, though large matrix injuries can leave permanent nail dystrophy. The main clinical hazard is misattributing a subungual melanoma to trauma and delaying diagnosis.

Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency (GABA metabolism) — succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency, SSADH deficiency, ALDH5A1 deficiency, 4-hydroxybutyric aciduria, gamma-hydroxybutyric aciduria, GHB aciduria Other causes of global developmental delay with prominent language impairment Autism spectrum disorder with regression Other neurotransmitter metabolism disorders Mitochondrial disorders with bilateral pallidal signal change Other genetic epileptic encephalopathies GHB ingestion or intoxication (acquired) as a mimic of the biochemistry Urine organic acids with specific detection of 4-hydroxybutyric acid (may be missed on standard screens) Quantification of gamma-hydroxybutyrate in plasma and CSF Brain MRI for symmetric globus pallidus, subthalamic, and dentate signal change EEG in those with seizures Enzyme activity assay in leucocytes or lymphocytes Molecular analysis of the ALDH5A1 gene Caused by deficiency of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH5A1), the second enzyme of GABA degradation, so succinic semialdehyde is diverted to gamma-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB) The diagnostic biochemical hallmark is accumulation of 4-hydroxybutyric acid (gamma-hydroxybutyrate) in urine, plasma, and CSF, which is not detected on routine organic acid screening unless specifically sought Typical features are global developmental delay, prominent expressive language delay, hypotonia, ataxia, and behavioural/psychiatric problems, with epilepsy in many Both GABA and GHB accumulate, and the balance of GABA-B and GHB receptor effects is thought to explain the mixed excitatory and sedative neurological picture Brain MRI often shows a characteristic symmetric high T2 signal in the globus pallidus, subthalamic nuclei, and dentate nuclei It is generally a slowly progressive or static encephalopathy rather than an acute metabolic crisis illness; management is supportive and antiepileptic, with vigabatrin used cautiously given theoretical benefit and risk Inheritance is autosomal recessive British spelling and paediatric context apply Worsening seizures or status epilepticus requiring urgent management Significant neuropsychiatric deterioration or behavioural crisis Regression or unexpected rapid decline prompting reassessment Suspected GHB intoxication needing differentiation from the inherited disorder Missing the diagnosis because 4-hydroxybutyrate is not reliably seen on routine organic acid analysis Overlooking the characteristic MRI pattern Confusing the biochemical finding with exogenous GHB exposure Using antiepileptic agents without regard to the disturbed GABA metabolism The inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA is catabolised via GABA transaminase to succinic semialdehyde, which succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase then oxidises to succinate for entry into the citric acid cycle. When this enzyme is deficient, succinic semialdehyde is instead reduced to gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), which accumulates along with GABA in the brain and body fluids. GHB and elevated GABA act on GHB and GABA-B receptors, disturbing neurotransmission in ways that produce the developmental, motor, epileptic, and behavioural manifestations. The build-up of these neuroactive compounds, rather than an energy-failure crisis, characterises the disorder, giving a comparatively static or slowly evolving encephalopathy. The course is usually that of a static or slowly progressive encephalopathy with intellectual disability, language impairment, and variable epilepsy; many survive into adulthood. Outcome varies, and behavioural and psychiatric symptoms can be prominent later.

long-term management relies on strict avoidance of fasting with an emergency illness regimen Confirmation is by OXCT1 molecular testing or enzyme assay in fibroblasts, as biochemical markers can be subtle Neonatal or infant presentation with severe high-anion-gap ketoacidosis Persistent ketosis that does not resolve with feeding Rapid deterioration with obtundation or cardiorespiratory compromise during a crisis Recurrent unexplained severe ketoacidotic episodes Overlooking the diagnosis because newborn screening and acylcarnitine profiles are typically normal Interpreting persistent ketosis as dietary or presuming diabetes rather than a ketolysis defect Allowing prolonged fasting for procedures without a protective glucose regimen Assuming normal interictal biochemistry excludes the disorder when persistent low-grade ketosis is actually a clue SCOT (succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase) catalyses the rate-limiting first step of ketone-body utilisation in extrahepatic tissues, transferring coenzyme A from succinyl-CoA to acetoacetate to form acetoacetyl-CoA. When the enzyme is deficient, peripheral tissues cannot use ketone bodies for energy, so ketones accumulate and are not cleared even when glucose is available. This produces persistent ketosis and a tendency to severe, life-threatening ketoacidosis during any period of increased ketogenesis, such as fasting or intercurrent illness. Because only ketone bodies accumulate, the organic acid and acylcarnitine profiles lack the specific markers seen in the isoleucine-pathway ketolysis defect. With prompt recognition and rigorous avoidance of fasting, many individuals do well and crises become less frequent with age, but early or severe ketoacidotic episodes can be fatal or cause neurological injury before diagnosis.

Variants in SI reduce or abolish the activity of the sucrase-isomaltase complex, which normally hydrolyses sucrose and the alpha-1,6 and some alpha-1,4 bonds of starch-derived oligosaccharides. Sudden Infant Death Syndrome — SIDS, cot death, crib death Accidental asphyxia or unsafe sleep-related suffocation Undiagnosed infection or sepsis Inborn errors of metabolism (e.g. fatty acid oxidation defects) Cardiac channelopathy or arrhythmia (e.g. long QT syndrome) Non-accidental injury or inflicted harm Occult congenital or structural abnormality Full postmortem examination (autopsy) Detailed death scene investigation and review of circumstances Comprehensive clinical and family history review Metabolic screening including postmortem samples where indicated Genetic testing for cardiac channelopathies in selected cases Microbiology and toxicology as part of the exclusion process Defined as the sudden and unexpected death of an infant under one year that remains unexplained after a thorough death scene investigation, review of history, and complete postmortem examination. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and forms part of the broader category of sudden unexpected infant death (SUID). Incidence peaks between about 2 and 4 months of age, and most deaths occur during sleep. Prone and side sleeping positions are major modifiable risk factors; supine sleep is strongly protective. Additional risks include soft bedding, bed-sharing, overheating, maternal smoking during and after pregnancy, prematurity, and low birth weight. Protective measures include breastfeeding, immunisation, pacifier use at sleep, and room-sharing without bed-sharing. The prevailing model proposes a vulnerable infant meeting an exogenous stressor during a critical developmental period (the triple-risk hypothesis). Safe-sleep counselling for every family is a core preventive intervention, and any death requires a compassionate, thorough investigation to exclude other causes. Modifiable risk factors that mandate active safe-sleep counselling for prevention Non-supine sleep position, soft bedding, or bed-sharing Exposure to tobacco smoke before or after birth History or scene findings suggesting suffocation or non-accidental injury Recurrent unexplained infant deaths in a family, warranting careful evaluation Prematurity or low birth weight increasing baseline risk Assigning the label SIDS without a complete investigation that excludes other causes Failing to deliver safe-sleep advice at every relevant contact Overlooking an unsafe sleep environment as a contributing factor Not considering metabolic or cardiac causes in apparently unexplained deaths Neglecting sensitive support and follow-up for the bereaved family SIDS is thought to arise when an underlying vulnerability, an environmental stressor, and a critical developmental window coincide (the triple-risk model). The vulnerability is believed to involve abnormalities in brainstem regions that regulate arousal, cardiorespiratory control, and responses to hypoxia and hypercarbia, including serotonergic network dysfunction. When such an infant encounters a stressor, for example a prone position, rebreathing of expired air, or overheating during sleep, an impaired protective arousal and autonomic response may fail to correct hypoxia, leading to death. SIDS is by definition fatal; the clinical focus is prevention through consistent safe-sleep practices, which have substantially reduced incidence, and supportive bereavement care for affected families.

loss reflects acute dysfunction of the cochlea or auditory nerve. Although often idiopathic, proposed mechanisms include viral infection or inflammation of the labyrinth, microvascular compromise of the cochlear blood supply, rupture of intracochlear membranes, and autoimmune injury. These processes damage the delicate hair cells and neural elements or disturb the cochlear ionic and metabolic environment, producing abrupt hearing loss. A minority result from identifiable structural causes such as a vestibular schwannoma compressing the cochlear nerve, which is why imaging is required. Outcome is variable; a substantial proportion recover partially or fully, particularly with early treatment, but severe loss, delayed presentation, vertigo and poor initial audiometry are associated with worse recovery.

When SUOX is defective, sulphite accumulates and reacts with cystine to form S-sulphocysteine, a structural analogue of glutamate that is thought to act as an excitotoxin at NMDA receptors. Sulphite is also directly toxic and can disrupt cerebral connective tissue and lens zonules, explaining the lens dislocation. The result is severe neuronal injury, cystic white matter change and progressive cerebral atrophy in the classic neonatal form. The classic neonatal form carries a poor prognosis, with severe neurodevelopmental impairment and often early death. Later-onset, attenuated forms follow a more variable course but still cause significant neurological disability; effective disease-modifying therapy is currently lacking.

pancreatitis ERCP for direct visualisation, sump clearance, and therapeutic sphincterotomy Sump syndrome is a late complication of side-to-side choledochoduodenostomy in which the segment of common bile duct distal to the anastomosis becomes a poorly drained blind pouch, or sump, that accumulates food debris, biliary sludge, and stones The stagnant distal duct collects material that cannot clear through the papilla, leading to recurrent cholangitis, biliary obstruction, pain, and occasionally pancreatitis or hepatic abscess It is chiefly of historical and residual relevance because conversion to a Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy with closure of the distal duct Acute cholangitis with fever, rigors, jaundice, and haemodynamic compromise Development of hepatic abscess or persistent sepsis despite antibiotics Acute pancreatitis complicating the obstruction Progressive jaundice suggesting anastomotic stricture or fixed obstruction Recurrent severe episodes indicating need for surgical revision Failing to elicit the history of a previous side-to-side choledochoduodenostomy and so missing the diagnosis Misinterpreting expected post-anastomotic pneumobilia as evidence of infection or gas-forming disease Attributing recurrent cholangitis to simple retained stones without recognising the underlying sump anatomy Overlooking a hepatic abscess or pancreatitis as a complication of chronic biliary stasis Persisting with repeated endoscopic clearance when definitive surgical revision is warranted A side-to-side choledochoduodenostomy joins the common bile duct to the duodenum above the papilla, leaving the segment of duct between the anastomosis and the sphincter of Oddi as a dependent cul-de-sac. Because bile preferentially drains through the more proximal, wider anastomosis, this distal segment is no longer flushed by normal bile flow and loses its physiological clearance. Reflux of enteric contents introduces food particles, vegetable matter, and bacteria into the poorly emptying pouch, where stasis promotes accumulation of debris and biliary sludge, precipitation of stones, and bacterial overgrowth. The trapped material intermittently obstructs the papilla or the anastomosis and provokes recurrent ascending cholangitis; persistent stasis and infection can extend to cause pancreatitis when the pancreatic orifice is involved, or seed hepatic abscesses. The clinical picture therefore reflects chronic stagnation and infection within an anatomically dependent, non-draining distal duct rather than a primary stone or stricture elsewhere. Endoscopic sphincterotomy with clearance of the sump is effective in most patients and relieves recurrent cholangitis, giving a good outlook; recurrent or refractory disease that requires surgical conversion to a Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy also generally does well once the dependent distal segment is eliminated.

Posterior hypothalamic activation is seen on functional imaging, and neurovascular compression of the trigeminal nerve is identified in a proportion of cases, giving clinical overlap with trigeminal neuralgia. The course is variable, ranging from single bouts to a chronic unremitting pattern; many patients improve with preventive drugs such as lamotrigine, and identifying a symptomatic cause can allow targeted treatment.
