or fixed mass suggesting deep fibromatosis or malignancy Severe progressive contracture threatening hand function Atypical location or appearance not fitting classic palmar or plantar disease Recurrent or aggressive disease after multiple interventions Mistaking a palmar or plantar nodule for a ganglion or a soft tissue sarcoma Intervening too early before a functionally significant contracture has developed Underestimating the high recurrence rate when counselling patients before surgery Failing to recognise a strong diathesis and its implications for prognosis and recurrence Superficial fibromatosis is a benign but locally persistent proliferation of myofibroblasts within the palmar or plantar aponeurosis. The process evolves through a proliferative phase of cellular nodules, an involutional phase in which myofibroblasts align and contract, and a residual phase of dense, relatively acellular collagen forming cords. Myofibroblast contraction, mediated by their smooth muscle-like contractile apparatus and by remodelling of the surrounding collagen, produces the progressive flexion deformity that characterises palmar disease. Dysregulated Wnt and beta-catenin signalling, together with profibrotic growth factors, is implicated in driving the proliferation, and many lesions show nuclear beta-catenin. A genetic predisposition interacts with metabolic and lifestyle factors such as diabetes, alcohol, and smoking, explaining the familial clustering and the recognised disease associations. Superficial fibromatosis is benign and does not metastasise, but it is often progressive and recurrent, and palmar disease in particular can cause substantial functional disability from fixed contracture. Outcome after treatment depends on disease severity and the strength of the underlying diathesis, with recurrence being frequent.

Superficial Fungal Infections — Dermatophytosis, Ringworm, Tinea, Pityriasis versicolor, Tinea versicolor, Onychomycosis, Mucocutaneous candidiasis Contact dermatitis Eczema Psoriasis (can mimic both tinea corporis and onychomycosis) Erythrasma Intertriginous candidiasis Vitiligo (for tinea versicolor; differentiated by absence of scale) Bacterial folliculitis Seborrheic dermatitis / dandruff Leukoplakia (for oral thrush) Intertriginous candidiasis (vs tinea cruris) Bacterial folliculitis (vs Malassezia folliculitis) Oral leukoplakia from other infections vs Candida thrush KOH (potassium hydroxide) microscopy of scrapings from the lesion edge to detect hyphae Fungal culture, indicated when an outbreak is suspected or when there is no response to therapy KOH preparation showing budding bottle-shaped yeasts with short septate hyphae for Malassezia Culture of Malassezia requires sterile olive oil added to the medium for suspected disseminated infection Skin biopsy or nail clippings with culture and microscopy for skin and nail candidiasis Biopsy of oral/esophageal tissue to distinguish invasive thrush (yeasts, pseudohyphae, and hyphae invading epithelium) from mere colonization (superficial yeast forms only) and from mimics such as leukoplakia Culture and microscopy of vaginal secretions (swab) for vulvovaginal candidiasis Psoriasis Eczema Contact dermatitis Vitiligo Seborrheic dermatitis Mucosal leukoplakia Superficial fungal infections are caused by molds and yeasts that colonize the outer skin layers, hair follicles, and nails without invading deeper tissue; they are the most common human fungal infections but rarely cause serious disease. Dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) are not part of normal skin flora and confine themselves to keratinized structures; symptoms arise from inflammatory reaction to fungal antigens rather than tissue invasion, and an estimated billion people are affected worldwide. The annular, ring-shaped cutaneous lesion ('ringworm') results from centrifugal outward growth of the organism in the stratum corneum; the term tinea (Latin for worm) is preferred and is paired with the affected body site. Tinea capitis predominantly affects children aged 3 to 7 years, producing well-demarcated scaly patches with hair shafts broken off near the skin surface and possible alopecia. Tinea pedis typically begins in the toe web spaces with peeling, maceration, and pruritus, and is a recognized portal of entry for streptococci and staphylococci, predisposing to lower-extremity cellulitis through interdigital fissures. Onychomycosis affects toenails more often than fingernails, is most common in those with tinea pedis, and shows thickened, discolored, crumbling nails with onycholysis; older age, vascular disease, diabetes, and nail trauma are risk factors. Malassezia yeasts (notably M. furfur, M. pachydermatis) are lipophilic commensals of sebum-rich areas (back, chest, scalp, face) and cause tinea/pityriasis versicolor, folliculitis, and seborrheic dermatitis; cutaneous IL-17 signaling normally controls them. Tinea versicolor appears as flat round scaly hypo- or hyperpigmented patches on the neck, chest, or upper arms, usually asymptomatic, and can be confused with vitiligo (which is non-scaly). KOH (potassium hydroxide) preparation of lesion-edge scrapings demonstrating hyphae is the key bedside diagnostic test; Malassezia shows a characteristic mix of budding bottle-shaped yeasts and short septate hyphae. Mucocutaneous candidiasis is most often caused by Candida albicans; oral thrush yields white mucosal plaques that scrape off, and antibiotic use, diabetes, and pregnancy are major risk factors for vulvovaginal candidiasis. Candida auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant species that persistently colonizes human skin, hair follicles, healthcare environments, and devices, grows avidly in human sweat, and drives nosocomial outbreaks. Seborrheic dermatitis (a Malassezia-associated condition) can be especially severe in patients with AIDS, and Malassezia fungemia, though rare, occurs almost exclusively in premature neonates receiving parenteral lipid nutrition. Tinea pedis with interdigital fissuring predisposing to lower-extremity cellulitis from streptococcal/staphylococcal entry Severe seborrheic dermatitis as a clue to AIDS / advanced immunosuppression Malassezia fungemia/disseminated infection in premature neonates on parenteral lipid nutrition Candida auris colonization as a nosocomial multidrug-resistant outbreak risk Recurrent or extensive mucocutaneous candidiasis suggesting inborn errors of immunity (e.g., STAT1 gain-of-function, IL-17 signaling defects) or AIDS Moderate-to-severe oral thrush or esophageal involvement requiring systemic evaluation Diagnosing onychomycosis clinically without confirmation, since psoriasis can mimic nail fungal disease (usually with associated skin lesions) Mistaking tinea versicolor for vitiligo; the absence of scale distinguishes vitiligo Interpreting superficial yeast forms on oral/esophageal biopsy as invasive candidiasis when they actually represent colonization only Overlooking tinea pedis as a portal for bacterial cellulitis Not pursuing culture when a patient fails to respond to empiric therapy or when an outbreak is suspected Superficial fungi inhabit only the keratinized superficial layers (stratum corneum, hair follicles, nail plate) and do not invade beneath the stratum corneum. Dermatophytes live within keratin and produce disease through host inflammatory responses to fungal antigens rather than by direct tissue invasion; nail involvement begins via the lateral or superficial nail plate then spreads, and hair-shaft invasion may be intra- or peri-shaft. Host defense is mediated by IL-17 responses, which restrict dermatophyte growth and control cutaneous Malassezia; infections are more frequent in males, and progesterone can inhibit dermatophyte growth. Malassezia organisms are lipophilic commensals of sebaceous areas that elicit little inflammation but, when IL-17 responses are excessive, can exacerbate atopic inflammation. Candida species are mucosal/cutaneous commensals; control depends on IL-17-producing lymphoid cells (TH17, gamma-delta T cells, innate lymphoid cells) at barrier sites, and defects in IL-17 signaling predispose to oral and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. Superficial fungal infections rarely cause serious disease. Malassezia skin infections are benign and self-limited, though recurrences are common. Dermatophyte infections generally respond well to therapy, but onychomycosis is slow to clear and prone to relapse. The outcome of rare systemic Malassezia infection depends on the host's underlying condition, though most affected neonates do well. Clinically stratified by extent and site: localized cutaneous tinea versus extensive tinea and onychomycosis; for mucocutaneous candidiasis, mild oral thrush is distinguished from moderate/severe or esophageal disease that requires systemic management.

spinal dural defect Confusing infratentorial superficial siderosis with cortical siderosis of cerebral amyloid angiopathy Attributing hearing loss and ataxia to ageing or unrelated causes and missing the imaging signature Assuming the condition is untreatable and not pursuing a correctable dural or vascular lesion Superficial siderosis of the central nervous system arises from persistent or recurrent haemorrhage into the subarachnoid space, releasing blood that breaks down to deposit haemosiderin along the pial and subpial surfaces of the neuraxis. Iron-laden macrophages and free iron promote oxidative injury and the accumulation of ferritin and haemosiderin in tissues rich in Bergmann glia and microglia, which accounts for the particular vulnerability of the cerebellum and the eighth cranial nerve. Progressive neuronal and glial damage produces the characteristic sensorineural deafness, cerebellar ataxia and myelopathy. Identifying and treating the chronic source of bleeding, such as a dural tear, is central to halting progression. Superficial siderosis is usually slowly progressive, and neurological deficits such as hearing loss and ataxia are often irreversible; identifying and repairing the bleeding source may arrest further deterioration, so prognosis depends heavily on early recognition and treatment of the cause.

recurrent cases Not arranging duplex assessment when clot proximity to the deep system would change management Superficial thrombophlebitis is thrombosis with accompanying inflammation of a superficial vein. The elements of Virchow's triad apply: venous stasis (notably in varicose veins), endothelial injury (for example from cannulation), and hypercoagulability. Thrombus formation within the superficial vein triggers a local inflammatory response producing the characteristic tender palpable cord. Because superficial and deep systems communicate through perforators and saphenous junctions, thrombus can propagate into the deep veins, linking the condition to venous thromboembolism. Localised superficial thrombophlebitis in varicose veins is usually self-limiting with a good outcome, whereas extensive disease or thrombus near a deep junction carries a meaningful risk of progression to deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism. Recurrence is common when underlying venous disease or a prothrombotic state persists.

underlying malignancy in migratory thrombophlebitis Not recognising suppurative (septic) thrombophlebitis, which needs antibiotics and possible vein excision Providing an inadequate duration or intensity of anticoagulation for extensive or junction-related disease Superficial vein thrombosis develops through the components of the Virchow triad acting on a superficial vein: venous stasis (typically within tortuous varicosities), endothelial injury (from cannulation, trauma or chemical irritation) and hypercoagulability. Thrombus forms within the lumen and provokes an inflammatory response in the vein wall and surrounding tissue, producing the characteristic tender, indurated, erythematous cord. When the process involves the great or small saphenous trunk it can propagate proximally and extend through the saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal junction into the deep venous system, or shed thrombus to the pulmonary circulation, which underlies the recognised association with deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Most localised superficial vein thrombosis settles over a few weeks with conservative measures and, where indicated, a course of anticoagulation. However, proximal extension and venous thromboembolism can occur, and recurrence is common in those with varicose veins or an underlying thrombophilia.

Superior laryngeal neuralgia — SLN neuralgia, laryngeal neuralgia, superior laryngeal nerve neuralgia Glossopharyngeal neuralgia Carotidynia Eagle syndrome Thyroid pathology (thyroiditis or nodular disease) Laryngeal or hypopharyngeal malignancy Cervical spine referred pain Post-surgical neuroma of the neck Palpation for a trigger point over the thyrohyoid membrane reproducing the pain Diagnostic superior laryngeal nerve block with local anaesthetic Flexible laryngoscopy to exclude a mucosal or supraglottic lesion Ultrasound of the neck and thyroid to exclude local pathology MRI or CT of the neck if a structural or neoplastic cause is suspected Review of any prior neck or thyroid surgery Causes paroxysms of sharp, shooting pain in the lateral neck, over the thyrohyoid membrane, radiating to the angle of the jaw, ear, and supraclavicular region Attacks are triggered by swallowing, phonation, coughing, yawning, or turning the head A tender trigger point is often found over the thyrohyoid membrane where the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve pierces it It may follow upper respiratory infection, neck surgery (including thyroid surgery and endarterectomy), or trauma Diagnostic and therapeutic superior laryngeal nerve block at the trigger point relieving the pain strongly supports the diagnosis First-line medical therapy uses anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine; repeated nerve blocks or nerve sectioning help refractory cases The distribution and swallow-triggered pattern distinguish it from glossopharyngeal neuralgia and carotidynia A neck or laryngeal mass suggesting malignancy Progressive hoarseness, stridor, or dysphagia Constant rather than paroxysmal pain with systemic features New cranial nerve deficits Confusing it with glossopharyngeal neuralgia given overlapping triggers Overlooking laryngeal or thyroid malignancy as a cause of lateral neck pain Failing to seek and test the thyrohyoid trigger point Attributing the referred otalgia to primary ear disease Superior laryngeal neuralgia is a paroxysmal neuralgia of the superior laryngeal nerve, usually its internal branch, which supplies sensation to the supraglottic larynx and pierces the thyrohyoid membrane. Irritation, entrapment, or injury of the nerve, sometimes after infection, surgery, or trauma to the neck, is thought to generate ectopic afferent discharges triggered by laryngeal movement during swallowing and phonation. The resulting lancinating pain is referred throughout the sensory field of the nerve, and a focal trigger point overlying its entry through the thyrohyoid membrane is characteristic. The condition is benign and frequently responds to anticonvulsant medication or superior laryngeal nerve blocks, with many cases settling over time; refractory pain can be controlled by repeated blocks or nerve sectioning.

from persistent vomiting Profound weight loss and malnutrition Gastric or duodenal dilatation risking perforation or aspiration Features of an underlying eating disorder requiring integrated care Dismissing symptoms as functional or as an eating disorder without imaging the duodenum Overlooking the syndrome as a complication of rapid weight loss or spinal treatment Proceeding to surgery before an adequate trial of nutritional restoration Failing to correct dehydration and electrolytes before intervention Superior mesenteric artery syndrome results from compression of the third part of the duodenum in the narrow angle between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta. Normally a pad of mesenteric and retroperitoneal fat holds the artery away from the aorta, keeping the aorto-mesenteric angle wide enough for the duodenum to pass. Marked weight loss, catabolic states or altered spinal anatomy reduce this fat cushion, narrowing the angle and trapping the duodenum. The resulting partial obstruction causes proximal dilatation, vomiting and further weight loss, which in turn worsens the compression in a self-perpetuating cycle. Many patients improve with nutritional restoration and conservative measures; those with anatomical fixation or failure of conservative treatment may need surgery, which is generally effective.

Superior oblique myokymia — superior oblique microtremor, SOM Ocular neuromyotonia Nystagmus (acquired pendular or see-saw) Trochlear nerve palsy with aberrant regeneration Orbital myopathy or restrictive strabismus Functional eye-movement disorder Slit-lamp or fundus observation of the fine torsional movements MRI of the brain and orbits to exclude posterior fossa or trochlear-nerve lesions Orthoptic assessment of ocular alignment and motility Video-oculography where available to characterise the movements A benign paroxysmal disorder of the superior oblique muscle causing brief episodes of monocular oscillopsia and torsional-vertical diplopia Attacks are typically short, frequent and precipitated by looking in the direction of the affected superior oblique The high-frequency low-amplitude movements may be hard to see and are best appreciated on slit-lamp or fundus examination It is usually idiopathic but has been attributed to neurovascular compression of the trochlear nerve Most cases are benign, though MRI is warranted to exclude a posterior fossa lesion Membrane-stabilising drugs or, in refractory cases, surgery or microvascular decompression may be considered Associated other cranial neuropathies suggesting a structural lesion Progressive or persistent (non-paroxysmal) diplopia New neurological signs Onset after head trauma with additional deficits Overlooking the subtle movements and labelling symptoms functional Omitting MRI and missing a compressive posterior fossa lesion Confusing it with ocular neuromyotonia, which causes sustained rather than shimmering deviation Assuming persistent diplopia rather than the characteristic paroxysms Superior oblique myokymia is thought to arise from ephaptic transmission or aberrant regeneration within the trochlear nerve, in some cases related to vascular compression at the nerve root exit, producing spontaneous high-frequency contraction of the superior oblique muscle. The resulting small torsional and vertical eye movements are perceived as shimmering monocular oscillopsia and transient diplopia. The disorder is benign and may remit spontaneously or respond to medical therapy; symptoms can be intrusive but do not threaten sight.

imaging the fissure The superior orbital fissure is the cleft between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid that transmits the oculomotor, trochlear, and abducens nerves, the ophthalmic Causes include trauma, tumour, granulomatous inflammation, infection, and vascular lesions in the region. Prognosis depends on the cause; traumatic and inflammatory cases may recover partially or fully with appropriate management, whereas neoplastic causes are more guarded, and some ophthalmoplegia and sensory loss can persist.

surgical canal plugging or resurfacing via a middle-fossa or transmastoid approach Disabling vertigo or oscillopsia interfering with daily function or driving Symptoms suggesting a coexisting intracranial process such as raised intracranial pressure or an encephalocoele through the defect Progressive sensorineural hearing loss beyond the expected pseudo-conductive pattern New cerebrospinal fluid leak or meningitic features Misdiagnosing the low-frequency air-bone gap as otosclerosis and performing unnecessary stapes surgery Relying on CT alone, since thin or dehiscent bone is common and may be asymptomatic or overcalled by volume averaging Overlooking autophony and pulsatile or self-sound symptoms that point to a third-window disorder Failing to counsel about the small operative risk to hearing before canal surgery The superior semicircular canal normally lies enclosed within dense bone beneath the floor of the middle cranial fossa. When this bony covering is congenitally thin or eroded, a dehiscence creates an abnormal 'third mobile window' in addition to the oval and round windows. Acoustic and pressure energy that would normally drive the cochlea is instead partly shunted through the dehiscence, abnormally stimulating the vestibular apparatus and dissipating sound energy. This explains sound- and pressure-evoked vertigo, the low-frequency pseudo-conductive hearing pattern with preserved bone conduction, autophony, and the hypersensitive VEMP responses. Many patients have mild symptoms that can be managed conservatively by avoiding provoking stimuli. When symptoms are disabling, surgical plugging or resurfacing of the canal relieves sound- and pressure-induced vestibular symptoms in most cases, though there is a small risk of hearing loss and symptoms may occasionally recur or arise on the contralateral side.

superior vena cava obstruction — SVCO, superior vena cava syndrome, SVC syndrome Cardiac tamponade or constrictive pericarditis Congestive cardiac failure Angioedema Retrosternal thyroid goitre or other benign mediastinal mass Fibrosing mediastinitis Nephrotic syndrome with generalised oedema Catheter-associated central venous thrombosis without malignancy Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax Chest radiograph for mediastinal widening or a right hilar mass Tissue sampling by sputum cytology, bronchoscopy, EBUS, mediastinoscopy or core biopsy Serum LDH, beta-hCG and alpha-fetoprotein when lymphoma or germ-cell tumour is possible Venography or CT venography to delineate the obstruction and thrombus Full blood count and coagulation screen Cross-sectional staging to assess disease extent Malignancy causes the majority of cases—lung cancer (particularly small-cell and squamous), lymphoma, thymoma and germ-cell tumours—while an increasing minority are due to thrombosis around indwelling central catheters or pacemaker leads. Typical features are facial and neck swelling, plethora, distended non-pulsatile neck and chest-wall veins, headache worsened by bending forward, and a positive Pemberton's sign on raising the arms. Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax defines the level, cause and collateral circulation and guides the safest route to a tissue diagnosis. Wherever the airway and haemodynamics permit, obtain a histological diagnosis before treatment, because chemosensitive tumours (lymphoma, small-cell lung cancer, germ-cell) are highly treatable and empirical radiotherapy can render subsequent biopsy uninterpretable. Endovascular stenting provides the most rapid symptomatic relief and is increasingly first-line for severe or refractory obstruction irrespective of histology. Definitive treatment is directed at the cause—systemic chemotherapy for small-cell lung cancer, lymphoma and germ-cell tumours, radiotherapy for radioresponsive disease, and anticoagulation with catheter management for thrombotic causes. The routine benefit of corticosteroids is unproven except where the tumour is steroid-responsive (lymphoma) or to reduce radiotherapy-associated oedema. Laryngeal or cerebral oedema and haemodynamic compromise convert a subacute presentation into a true emergency requiring immediate airway assessment and vascular intervention. Stridor or other signs of airway compromise Laryngeal oedema Reduced consciousness or other features of cerebral oedema Haemodynamic instability Rapidly progressive facial and upper-body swelling Giving empirical radiotherapy or corticosteroids before histology in a potentially curable chemosensitive tumour Assuming every case is malignant and missing catheter-associated thrombosis Delaying airway and vascular assessment in a patient with stridor or cerebral symptoms Attempting biopsy without imaging-guided planning of the safest approach Overlooking concurrent venous thromboembolism requiring anticoagulation Obstruction of the thin-walled, low-pressure superior vena cava—by external compression from a mediastinal mass, direct tumour invasion, or intraluminal thrombosis—impedes venous return from the head, neck and upper limbs. Pressure rises in the tributary veins, producing oedema, plethora and the recruitment of collateral pathways through the azygos, internal mammary and superficial chest-wall veins; the gradual development of these collaterals explains why chronic obstruction may be surprisingly well tolerated. When obstruction is rapid or complete, or extends to compromise the airway or raise intracranial venous pressure, life-threatening laryngeal and cerebral oedema can develop. Symptomatic prognosis is generally good because stenting and tumour-directed therapy relieve obstruction effectively, but overall survival is dictated by the underlying malignancy. Chemosensitive tumours may be curable, whereas SVCO from advanced non-small-cell lung cancer signals a poor outlook.

Superior vena cava syndrome — SVC syndrome, SVC obstruction, superior vena cava obstruction Congestive cardiac failure Cardiac tamponade or constrictive pericarditis Mediastinal fibrosis (for example fibrosing mediastinitis or post-radiation) Nephrotic syndrome or other causes of facial oedema Angioedema Bilateral internal jugular vein thrombosis Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest to define the level, extent, and cause Tissue diagnosis (sputum cytology, bronchoscopy, or biopsy of a nodal or mediastinal mass) to guide oncological treatment CT or MR venography to map the obstruction and collaterals Chest radiograph as an initial screen for mediastinal widening or mass Venography at the time of stenting Assessment for catheter- or lead-related thrombosis where relevant Caused by obstruction of the superior vena cava, either extrinsic compression or invasion by tumour or intraluminal thrombosis Malignancy is the leading cause, particularly bronchogenic carcinoma (small-cell and squamous) and non-Hodgkin lymphoma Thrombotic causes are increasingly common with indwelling central venous catheters and pacemaker leads Presents with facial and neck swelling and plethora, distended neck and chest wall veins, arm swelling, headache, and dyspnoea, typically worse on bending forward or lying flat Pemberton's sign (facial congestion on raising the arms) supports the diagnosis Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest defines the level and cause of obstruction and guides biopsy; a tissue diagnosis is important because management depends on tumour type Management is directed at the cause, treating the underlying malignancy (chemotherapy or radiotherapy) or thrombus (anticoagulation), with endovascular stenting for prompt symptom relief in severe or refractory cases Stridor, laryngeal oedema, or respiratory compromise (an airway emergency) Cerebral oedema with confusion, severe headache, or altered consciousness Haemodynamic instability Rapid onset of severe symptoms without collateral formation Starting empirical radiotherapy before obtaining a tissue diagnosis in a stable patient, potentially obscuring histology Overlooking a catheter- or lead-related thrombus as the cause Failing to recognise airway or cerebral compromise requiring urgent intervention Assuming all SVC obstruction is malignant Superior vena cava syndrome results from obstruction to venous return through the SVC to the right atrium. Most cases are due to malignant mediastinal disease, commonly lung cancer or lymphoma, that compresses or invades the thin-walled, low-pressure SVC; thrombosis, frequently related to intravascular devices, is a growing non-malignant cause. Obstruction raises venous pressure in the head, neck, and upper limbs, producing oedema, venous distension, and the recruitment of collateral chest wall veins. The severity of symptoms depends on how rapidly the obstruction develops and whether collaterals have had time to form, with airway and cerebral oedema being the most dangerous consequences. Outcome depends chiefly on the underlying cause; malignant SVC syndrome reflects the prognosis of the tumour, although stenting and oncological therapy give rapid symptom relief, whereas benign thrombotic causes generally respond well to anticoagulation and stenting.

Superwarfarin (long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide) poisoning — long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide poisoning, brodifacoum poisoning, superwarfarin toxicity, bromadiolone poisoning, long-acting concentration in plasma where available to confirm and monitor Investigations for the site of bleeding, including imaging when haemorrhage is suspected Superwarfarins such as brodifacoum are far more potent and vastly longer acting than warfarin, so coagulopathy can persist for weeks to months Coagulopathy is delayed, typically appearing a day or two after ingestion, because existing clotting factors must first be depleted A single acute exploratory ingestion by a child rarely causes clinically significant coagulopathy, whereas large or repeated ingestion can Consider covert or intentional exposure in an adult with unexplained prolonged coagulation and no prescribed anticoagulant Bleeding can be occult, so haematuria, bruising, gum bleeding, gastrointestinal or intracranial haemorrhage should prompt assessment of coagulation Vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) is the specific antidote and must often be continued in high oral doses for a prolonged period given the long half-life Acute major bleeding is treated with factor replacement such as prothrombin complex concentrate or fresh frozen plasma in addition to vitamin K Prophylactic vitamin K should not be started routinely after a trivial ingestion, as it can mask evolving coagulopathy; the INR is followed instead Active bleeding, especially intracranial or gastrointestinal haemorrhage Markedly prolonged INR with clinical bleeding Large deliberate ingestion or repeated exposure Falling haemoglobin or haemodynamic instability Rebound coagulopathy when vitamin K is reduced or stopped too early Checking coagulation only at presentation and missing delayed coagulopathy Stopping vitamin K prematurely and allowing rebound anticoagulation Giving prophylactic vitamin K after a trivial ingestion, masking evolving coagulopathy Relying on vitamin K alone in major bleeding rather than replacing clotting factors Failing to consider covert or intentional poisoning in unexplained coagulopathy Superwarfarins inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase, the enzyme that regenerates reduced vitamin K, which is the essential cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and of proteins C and S. Without functional vitamin K these factors cannot be activated, producing an anticoagulant state. Because factor VII has the shortest half-life, the prothrombin time and INR prolong first, but full coagulopathy is delayed until preformed factors are consumed. Unlike warfarin, superwarfarins are highly lipophilic, extensively tissue-bound and slowly eliminated, so their anticoagulant effect is markedly prolonged. With adequate and sustained vitamin K therapy and treatment of any acute bleeding, prognosis is generally good, although therapy and monitoring may be required for weeks to months; life-threatening haemorrhage before treatment carries significant risk.

suprascapular neuropathy — suprascapular nerve entrapment, suprascapular nerve palsy, spinoglenoid notch syndrome Rotator cuff tear (supraspinatus or infraspinatus) C5-C6 cervical radiculopathy Neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner syndrome) Upper-trunk brachial plexopathy Glenohumeral or acromioclavicular joint pathology Quadrilateral space syndrome (axillary neuropathy) as an alternative cause of shoulder wasting Needle electromyography of supraspinatus and infraspinatus to localise the lesion to the suprascapular or spinoglenoid notch Nerve conduction studies measuring suprascapular motor latencies to the two muscles MRI of the shoulder to detect a ganglion cyst, labral tear and the pattern of muscle oedema or fatty atrophy Magnetic resonance or ultrasound arthrography if a posterosuperior labral tear is suspected Cervical spine imaging when C5-C6 radiculopathy is a competing diagnosis Diagnostic suprascapular nerve block in selected cases Entrapment or injury of the suprascapular nerve, most often at the suprascapular notch beneath the transverse scapular ligament or more distally at the spinoglenoid notch The level of the lesion determines the deficit: a suprascapular notch lesion weakens both supraspinatus and infraspinatus, whereas a spinoglenoid notch lesion selectively weakens infraspinatus, sparing supraspinatus Clinically there is weakness of shoulder external rotation and of the initial phase of abduction, with a deep, poorly localised posterolateral shoulder ache; the nerve carries no cutaneous sensory territory, so there is no skin numbness A spinoglenoid notch ganglion cyst, frequently associated with a posterosuperior glenoid labral tear, is a classic and treatable cause of isolated infraspinatus wasting Repetitive overhead activity, particularly in volleyball players and other overhead athletes, and traction injuries or scapular fractures are recognised mechanisms Visible infraspinatus wasting in the infraspinatus fossa is often the presenting sign, and can be mistaken for a rotator cuff tear or C5-C6 radiculopathy Management is conservative with physiotherapy and activity modification for traction or overuse cases, decompression or aspiration for a compressive ganglion, and repair of an associated labral tear where present Acute severe shoulder-girdle pain followed by weakness and wasting, suggesting neuralgic amyotrophy A spinoglenoid or suprascapular notch mass on imaging indicating a compressive ganglion or tumour Rapidly progressive or profound wasting despite conservative treatment Associated mechanical symptoms of a labral tear such as clicking, catching or instability Attributing external rotation weakness and infraspinatus wasting to a rotator cuff tear without imaging or electrophysiology Missing a spinoglenoid notch ganglion and its associated labral tear as a treatable cause Confusing the deep aching pain with primary glenohumeral joint disease Overlooking neuralgic amyotrophy in acute painful presentations Failing to localise the lesion by not distinguishing isolated infraspinatus from combined supraspinatus and infraspinatus involvement The suprascapular nerve arises from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5-C6, occasionally C4) and runs laterally to pass through the suprascapular notch beneath the transverse scapular ligament, where it gives motor branches to supraspinatus, before curving around the base of the scapular spine through the spinoglenoid notch to supply infraspinatus. Both notches are relatively fixed fibro-osseous tunnels that tether the nerve, making it vulnerable to compression and to repetitive traction during overhead and cross-body movement. A ganglion cyst arising from a labral tear characteristically compresses the nerve at the spinoglenoid notch, selectively denervating infraspinatus, while ligamentous or bony narrowing at the suprascapular notch affects both muscles. Because the nerve is essentially purely motor, injury produces weakness and muscle wasting with pain but without cutaneous sensory loss. Traction and overuse cases and those with a decompressed or aspirated ganglion generally recover strength over months, particularly when an associated labral tear is addressed. Long-standing entrapment with established fatty atrophy of the muscle recovers less completely, leaving persistent weakness of external rotation.

Supraventricular tachycardia — SVT, paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, PSVT, AVNRT, AVRT Atrial fibrillation Atrial flutter Ventricular tachycardia (especially with aberrant conduction) Sinus commonly AV nodal reentrant tachycardia and AV reentrant tachycardia using an accessory pathway Typical presentation is abrupt-onset, regular palpitations with sudden termination, often with lightheadedness, chest discomfort, or breathlessness The QRS is usually narrow unless there is aberrant conduction or a pre-existing bundle branch block, when it can mimic ventricular tachycardia usual next step Synchronised cardioversion is indicated when the patient is haemodynamically unstable Catheter ablation offers a high cure rate for recurrent AVNRT and AVRT and is a definitive long-term option A regular narrow-complex tachycardia should be distinguished from atrial flutter and atrial fibrillation, which have different management Haemodynamic instability with hypotension, ischaemic chest pain, pulmonary oedema, or reduced consciousness, requiring urgent synchronised cardioversion Wide-complex tachycardia that cannot be confidently distinguished from ventricular tachycardia, which should be treated as VT until proven otherwise Pre-excited tachycardia where AV nodal blocking drugs may be hazardous Recurrent syncope during episodes Giving AV nodal blocking drugs in a pre-excited tachycardia, which can accelerate ventricular response Misdiagnosing a wide-complex tachycardia as SVT with aberrancy when it is actually ventricular tachycardia Delaying cardioversion in an unstable patient while attempting pharmacological control Overlooking reversible precipitants such as stimulants, thyroid disease, or electrolyte disturbance Most paroxysmal SVT is caused by reentry. In AV nodal reentrant tachycardia a functional circuit forms within or near the AV node using fast and slow pathways. In AV reentrant tachycardia the circuit incorporates an accessory pathway connecting atrium and ventricle, as in Wolff-Parkinson-White. Atrial tachycardias instead arise from an ectopic atrial focus with enhanced automaticity or microreentry. In reentrant mechanisms a premature beat finds one limb refractory and conducts down the other, then returns retrogradely, establishing a self-sustaining loop that the AV node often participates in, which is why AV nodal blockade frequently terminates the arrhythmia. Most forms of SVT are not life-threatening and carry an excellent prognosis, with catheter ablation curing the majority of reentrant cases; prognosis worsens when SVT complicates structural heart disease or occurs as pre-excited tachycardia with a risk of rapid ventricular rates.

SURF1-related Leigh syndrome — SURF1 deficiency, cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) deficiency, COX-deficient Leigh syndrome, subacute necrotising encephalomyelopathy (SURF1) Leigh syndrome from other nuclear or mitochondrial DNA mutations Other complex IV assembly-factor defects (e.g. SCO2, COX10, COX15) MELAS and other mitochondrial encephalopathies Biotinidase deficiency and biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease (treatable mimics) Wilson disease and other basal ganglia disorders in older children Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis or infective encephalitis Blood and CSF lactate and pyruvate concentrations Brain MRI to demonstrate symmetrical basal ganglia and brainstem lesions Muscle biopsy with histochemistry showing cytochrome c oxidase deficiency and respiratory-chain enzymology SURF1 gene sequencing and broader mitochondrial gene panels Plasma amino acids and urine organic acids to exclude treatable metabolic mimics Cardiac and ophthalmological assessment given multisystem mitochondrial involvement Autosomal recessive Leigh syndrome caused by SURF1 mutations, in which a complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) assembly factor is deficient, giving isolated COX deficiency Typically presents in infancy or early childhood with psychomotor regression, hypotonia, feeding and swallowing difficulty, and brainstem signs, often triggered or worsened by intercurrent illness Brain MRI classically shows symmetrical T2-hyperintense lesions of the basal ganglia and brainstem, the imaging hallmark of Leigh syndrome Elevated lactate in blood and cerebrospinal fluid supports a mitochondrial energy-generation defect, and CSF lactate can be raised even when blood is near-normal SURF1 disease tends to produce a relatively consistent phenotype with hypertrichosis reported in some patients and a notably poor tolerance of anaesthesia and metabolic stress Diagnosis rests on the MRI pattern, isolated COX deficiency on muscle histochemistry/biochemistry, and SURF1 sequencing; management is supportive with avoidance of catabolic stress Acute neurological deterioration during intercurrent illness signalling a metabolic crisis Brainstem dysfunction with respiratory irregularity or apnoea Progressive bulbar involvement compromising airway and feeding safety Anaesthetic exposure without mitochondrial precautions, risking decompensation Overlooking treatable mimics of Leigh syndrome (such as biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease) before concluding an untreatable defect Missing raised CSF lactate when blood lactate is normal Failing to take mitochondrial anaesthetic and fasting precautions, precipitating crises Attributing acute deterioration solely to infection without recognising metabolic decompensation SURF1 encodes an assembly factor required for correct biogenesis of complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), the terminal enzyme of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations reduce assembled, functional complex IV, impairing oxidative phosphorylation and cellular ATP production. Highly energy-dependent neurons, particularly in the basal ganglia and brainstem, undergo the characteristic subacute symmetrical necrosis of Leigh syndrome, with reactive lactate accumulation. Metabolic crises are commonly precipitated by infection, fasting, or other catabolic stress that further strains oxidative metabolism. SURF1-related Leigh syndrome is typically progressive with a poor prognosis, and many affected children die in early childhood, often during metabolic crises, although the rate of decline varies. Care is supportive, aiming to prevent and manage crises and optimise nutrition and neurological function.

progressive hearing loss New focal neurological deficits indicating ongoing microinfarction Misdiagnosing it as multiple sclerosis and missing the distinguishing central callosal lesions Not permitting irreversible organ damage Attributing cognitive symptoms to a psychiatric cause Susac syndrome is an immune-mediated microangiopathy (endotheliopathy) affecting the small vessels (precapillary arterioles) of the brain, retina, and inner ear. Sustained Ventricular Tachycardia — Sustained monomorphic VT, Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, Idiopathic VT, Belhassen's VT, Verapamil-sensitive VT, Bundle branch reentry VT, Outflow tract VT Supraventricular tachycardia with left or right bundle branch block aberrancy Supraventricular tachycardia conducted to the ventricles over an accessory pathway (pre-excited tachycardia) Rapid ventricular pacing (appropriate or inappropriate) in a patient with a pacemaker or defibrillator Telemetry noise and movement artifact simulating VT 12-lead ECG during tachycardia analyzing AV dissociation, aVR morphology, and V1-V6 concordance to differentiate VT from SVT with aberrancy Comparison of tachycardia QRS morphology with the baseline sinus-rhythm QRS (identical morphology in a known bundle branch block favors SVT but is not definitive) Echocardiography to assess ventricular function and detect segmental wall-motion abnormalities indicating scar Cardiac MRI for delayed gadolinium enhancement to identify and localize fibrosis (intramural/subepicardial in nonischemic cardiomyopathy) Nuclear imaging for wall-motion abnormalities Cardiac biomarkers (troponin, CK-MB) to evaluate myocardial injury, recognizing that acute MI rarely causes sustained monomorphic VT and modest elevations usually reflect demand ischemia during the arrhythmia rather than an acute coronary event Electrophysiologic study when noninvasive criteria leave the diagnosis uncertain SVT with aberrant conduction (bundle branch block) Antidromic AV reentrant tachycardia / pre-excited SVT over an accessory pathway Pacemaker-mediated rapid ventricular pacing Sustained monomorphic VT is a wide-QRS ventricular arrhythmia lasting at least 30 seconds, or one requiring intervention (antitachycardia pacing or cardioversion) for termination; each QRS resembles the others, pointing to a single focal origin or repetitive exit from a fixed reentry circuit. In structural heart disease the usual substrate is patchy replacement fibrosis from prior infarction, fibrosis, inflammation, or previous cardiac surgery, which sets up anatomic or functional reentry; less often VT arises from reentry or automaticity in diseased Purkinje conduction tissue. Clinical tolerance depends on rate, baseline ventricular function, and autonomic response: rapid VT may cause hypotension and syncope (especially with poor LV function), while patients with normal function may have only palpitations despite fast rates. Hemodynamic stability during a wide-complex tachycardia does NOT distinguish VT from supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy; tolerance of the rhythm should never be used to exclude VT. Ventriculoatrial (AV) dissociation is a reliable marker of VT, provided the atrial rate is slower than the ventricular rate; however a P wave following every QRS does not exclude VT because 1:1 ventriculo-atrial conduction can occur. A monophasic R or Rs complex in lead aVR, or concordance (all monophasic R or all S waves) across V1 to V6, is relatively specific for VT. In a patient with known structural heart disease, a wide-QRS tachycardia is most likely VT regardless of QRS morphology; depressed LV function or evidence of structural disease makes scar-related reentry the most likely mechanism of sustained monomorphic VT. Scar is suggested by pathologic Q waves on ECG, segmental wall-motion abnormalities on echo or nuclear imaging, and areas of delayed gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI. Idiopathic VT occurs in structurally normal hearts (normal sinus ECG, normal function and no scar on imaging), is provoked by sympathetic stimulation or acute sympathetic withdrawal (e.g. immediately post-exercise), and is generally benign with low risk of sudden death. Outflow tract VT most often arises in the right ventricular outflow tract, producing a left bundle branch block pattern in V1 with an inferiorly directed axis (tall R waves in II, III, aVF); a prominent R wave in V1 or V2 suggests a left ventricular outflow tract or aortic-root origin. LV fascicular VT (Belhassen's / verapamil-sensitive VT) is the second most common idiopathic form: it shows a right bundle branch block-like configuration negative in the inferior leads and is due to a small reentry circuit near the septal ramifications of the left Purkinje system; despite being reentrant its course is typically benign. Repeated incessant bursts of nonsustained monomorphic VT (repetitive monomorphic VT) can produce a tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy with depressed ventricular function that recovers once the arrhythmia is suppressed. Hypotension, impaired consciousness, or pulmonary edema accompanying the tachycardia (hemodynamic instability) Rapid VT in a patient with significant ventricular dysfunction (high risk of syncope and degeneration to VF) VT presenting as resuscitated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest where VF was the initial recorded rhythm Sustained monomorphic VT in the setting of structural heart disease (high recurrence and sudden-death risk) Frequent recurrent or incessant VT episodes Syncope or cardiac arrest as the presenting event in inherited cardiomyopathies (ARVC, repaired tetralogy of Fallot) Using hemodynamic stability to rule out VT - tolerance of the rhythm does not exclude VT. Assuming a P wave after every QRS excludes VT, when 1:1 ventriculo-atrial conduction can mimic this. Relying on a single QRS-morphology criterion; all such criteria have limitations and are unreliable in severe heart disease, and bundle branch reentry VT can closely resemble the native sinus QRS. Interpreting troponin/CK-MB elevations during VT as proof of an acute coronary event - these usually reflect demand ischemia from hypotension and fixed coronary disease; acute MI is rarely the cause of sustained monomorphic VT. Mistaking telemetry noise or movement artifact for VT, leading to unnecessary tests and interventions. Attributing a typical outflow-tract QRS morphology automatically to benign idiopathic VT, since cardiomyopathies (notably ARVC) can produce PVCs/VT from the same region and must be excluded. Failing to recognize repetitive monomorphic (incessant nonsustained) VT as a reversible cause of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. Sustained monomorphic VT most commonly results from reentry around a fixed substrate. In structural heart disease this substrate is an area of patchy replacement fibrosis (from infarction, inflammation, fibrosis, or surgical scar) creating anatomic or functional reentrant circuits; the uniform QRS reflects a single focal origin or repetitive exit from a stable circuit. In coronary artery disease the typical setting is a remote large myocardial infarction with a remodeled ventricle and depressed LV function, where the infarct scar provides a durable reentry substrate that is not generally dependent on ongoing acute ischemia. In nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, scar-related reentry from progressive replacement fibrosis underlies VT, with scars often intramural or subepicardial and frequently adjacent to a valve annulus; sarcoidosis, Chagas' disease, and Lamin A/C mutation cardiomyopathy are particularly associated. Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy involves fibrofatty replacement chiefly of right ventricular myocardium producing a left bundle branch block-like VT. Bundle branch reentry VT (about 5% of monomorphic VT with structural disease) uses a macroreentrant circuit through the Purkinje system, usually retrograde up the left bundle and anterograde down the right bundle, generating a left bundle branch block configuration. Idiopathic VT in structurally normal hearts arises either from focal triggered automaticity (outflow tract foci near the pulmonic or aortic annuli) or from small reentry circuits in the Purkinje system (fascicular VT). Rapid or scar-associated monomorphic VT may degenerate into ventricular fibrillation. Prognosis hinges on the presence and type of underlying heart disease. Scar-related monomorphic VT in structural heart disease carries a high recurrence risk; with ischemic cardiomyopathy and a prior large MI, up to 70% of patients have arrhythmia recurrence within 2 years, and even after device-based secondary prevention the depressed-ejection-fraction population remains at risk for heart failure, recurrent ischemic events, and recurrent VT, with a 5-year mortality exceeding 30%. Device shocks and antitachycardia pacing are themselves adverse events linked to higher rates of heart failure, mortality, and psychological stress. By contrast, idiopathic VT in a structurally normal heart is generally benign, sudden death is rare, and a defibrillator is not recommended; LV fascicular (Belhassen's) VT likewise follows a benign course despite being reentrant. In ARVC, clinical heart failure is rare until late stages and survival to advanced age can be expected provided the VT is controlled. In repaired tetralogy of Fallot the risk of sudden cardiac death may reach roughly 1% per year in adulthood by the fourth or fifth decade. Harrison classifies sustained ventricular arrhythmias by substrate/etiology rather than a graded severity scale: (1) idiopathic VT without structural heart disease - outflow tract (RV outflow: LBBB pattern in V1 with inferior axis and late precordial transition; LV outflow: inferior axis with early precordial transition and prominent R in V2-V3), LV fascicular VT (RBBB pattern in V1 with left axis deviation), and papillary muscle VT; (2) ischemic cardiomyopathy (monomorphic VT common after large prior MI); (3) nonischemic cardiomyopathy (fibrotic scar VT, e.g. sarcoidosis, Chagas', Lamin A/C); (4) arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy (RV-origin LBBB-pattern VT); (5) repaired tetralogy of Fallot (RV-origin VT); (6) hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; and (7) genetic arrhythmia syndromes (long QT, Brugada, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, short QT/early repolarization). Practically, the most important severity distinction is between benign idiopathic VT in a structurally normal heart and scar-related VT in structural heart disease, the latter conferring substantial sudden-death risk.

Malignancy (lung cancer, lymphoma, metastatic tumours) accounts for most cases, but benign causes now make up at least 40% owing to widespread use of intravascular devices (central venous catheters, pacemaker/defibrillator leads). Lung cancer—particularly small-cell and squamous-cell histology—causes around 85% of malignant SVCS. In a young adult/young man with a mediastinal mass and SVCS, think lymphoma versus primary mediastinal germ cell tumour. Symptoms are characteristically worse on bending forward or lying supine; facial swelling and plethora are exacerbated when supine. The clinical picture is milder when the obstruction is above the azygos vein. Symptoms may actually improve over time as collateral venous circulation develops, and most patients improve partly for this reason. Small-cell lung cancer patients with SVCS have a higher incidence of brain metastases than those without SVCS; new seizures more likely reflect brain mets than venous cerebral oedema. Tissue diagnosis (bronchoscopy, percutaneous needle biopsy, mediastinoscopy, endobronchial/oesophageal ultrasound-guided aspiration, or even thoracotomy) can generally be obtained safely without major bleeding risk despite the venous congestion. For a patient with no prior cancer history, a full evaluation is essential to exclude benign causes and define a specific diagnosis before directing therapy; in known cancer, treatment may begin after a thoracic CT. Signs/symptoms of cerebral and/or laryngeal oedema — rare but carry a poorer prognosis and demand urgent evaluation Upper airway/tracheal obstruction from a superior mediastinal mass — the one potentially life-threatening complication, demands emergent therapy Cardiorespiratory symptoms at rest, especially with positional change — indicate significant airway/vascular obstruction and limited physiologic reserve Risk of cardiac arrest or respiratory failure, particularly with sedation or general anaesthesia Proptosis, glossal and laryngeal oedema, and obtundation indicate severe disease Postural hypotension with severe symptoms Variceal (downhill oesophageal varices) bleeding as a late complication of chronic SVCS Do not assume SVCS is always malignant — benign device/catheter-related causes now account for at least 40% of cases. A normal chest radiograph does not exclude SVCS when other characteristic findings are present. Attributing seizures to venous cerebral oedema when brain metastases are the more likely cause (especially in small-cell lung cancer). Sedatives or general anaesthesia in a patient with airway/vascular obstruction may precipitate cardiac arrest or respiratory failure. In a patient without known cancer, omitting a full diagnostic workup risks missing benign causes and a treatable specific diagnosis. SVC syndrome results from obstruction of the superior vena cava causing a severe reduction in venous return from the head, neck, and upper extremities. Obstruction may be due to external compression, direct tumour invasion, intraluminal thrombosis (often device-related), or fibrosis. Venous congestion produces facial/upper-body swelling, distended neck veins, and development of collateral venous channels over the chest wall. The 'hot quadrate' focal hepatic hotspot on CT reflects portosystemic shunting between the SVC and portal vein. Chronic SVCS can produce 'downhill' oesophageal varices (cephalad-to-caudad flow, opposite to portal-hypertension 'uphill' varices), which may bleed late. Clinical improvement occurs in most patients, partly attributable to the development of adequate collateral circulation. Mortality is determined by the underlying cause rather than by the caval obstruction itself. SVCS recurs in roughly 10-30% of patients. Cerebral or laryngeal oedema portends a worse prognosis. Harrison does not provide a formal severity grading scale. Severity is described clinically by features such as presence of cerebral/laryngeal oedema, proptosis, glossal/laryngeal oedema, obtundation, postural hypotension, and cardiorespiratory symptoms at rest with positional change, which together denote severe, potentially life-threatening disease; obstruction above the azygos vein produces a milder picture.

tightness as a contributor Ignoring the metacarpophalangeal joint in rheumatoid arthritis Attempting to splint a rigid joint that will not correct Swan-neck deformity reflects an imbalance of the extensor mechanism producing proximal interphalangeal hyperextension and distal interphalangeal flexion. It may begin distally, where a chronic mallet finger allows extensor force to concentrate on the proximal interphalangeal joint and hyperextend it, or at the proximal interphalangeal joint itself through volar plate attenuation, flexor digitorum superficialis insufficiency or intrinsic muscle tightness, with the lateral bands displacing dorsally. It is common in rheumatoid arthritis, where synovitis, metacarpophalangeal joint subluxation and intrinsic contracture combine to create and perpetuate the deformity. The outlook varies with the cause and the flexibility of the joints; flexible deformities respond well to splinting and soft-tissue procedures, whereas established or arthritic deformities usually require joint surgery and give less predictable results.

It is thought to reflect a hypersensitivity-type response driven by cytokines and colony-stimulating factors that recruit and activate neutrophils, rather than by infection or primary vasculitis. Dysregulated innate immune activation and possible clonal myeloid contributions underlie the neutrophil-rich inflammation. Classic and drug-induced disease usually responds rapidly to glucocorticoids and often resolves, though recurrences occur; malignancy-associated disease tends to follow the course of the underlying cancer and may relapse with disease activity.

Swimming-induced pulmonary oedema — SIPE, immersion pulmonary oedema Aspiration or near-drowning Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from primary cardiac disease Pulmonary barotrauma or decompression illness in divers Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction Pneumonia Clinical assessment and oxygen saturation during and after the event Chest imaging showing pulmonary oedema without aspiration Cardiac evaluation including echocardiography for underlying disease Blood pressure assessment for hypertension Exclusion of diving-specific causes such as barotrauma in divers Acute pulmonary oedema arising during surface swimming or diving in the absence of water aspiration or a primary cardiac event Presents with breathlessness, cough, frothy or blood-tinged sputum and hypoxaemia during or soon after immersion It typically affects otherwise healthy swimmers, divers and triathletes, sometimes recurrently Cold water, exertion, overhydration and tight wetsuits are recognised contributing factors Symptoms usually improve rapidly on leaving the water and with oxygen and rest Recurrence is common, and evaluation for hypertension or underlying cardiac disease is advised Severe hypoxaemia or respiratory distress Features suggesting a primary cardiac event Haemoptysis with haemodynamic compromise Recurrent episodes indicating an underlying cardiovascular disorder Confusing it with near-drowning from aspiration Overlooking an underlying cardiac or hypertensive cause In divers, missing barotrauma or decompression illness Underestimating the risk of recurrence with continued open-water activity Swimming-induced pulmonary oedema is attributed to the combination of immersion and exertion raising pulmonary capillary pressure. Water immersion and cold shift blood centrally and cause peripheral vasoconstriction, while exertion increases cardiac output and pulmonary blood flow; the resulting rise in pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure exceeds the threshold for fluid to leak into the alveoli. Factors that further raise preload or afterload, such as overhydration, cold and constrictive suits, and any underlying cardiac or hypertensive tendency, augment the pressure and precipitate oedema. The acute episode usually resolves quickly with removal from water, oxygen and rest, but recurrence is frequent and an identified cardiac or hypertensive predisposition needs management.

swyer james syndrome — Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome, unilateral hyperlucent lung endobronchial obstruction by tumour or foreign body causing air trapping congenital lobar emphysema congenital absence or hypoplasia of a pulmonary artery compensatory overinflation after contralateral lobar collapse or resection bullous or panlobular emphysema (including alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency) pulmonary embolism with regional oligaemia technical or rotational causes of asymmetric radiographic lucency inspiratory and expiratory CT to demonstrate air trapping and mosaic attenuation ventilation-perfusion scintigraphy showing matched reduction on the affected side chest radiograph in inspiration and expiration pulmonary function testing including assessment of airflow obstruction and gas trapping bronchoscopy where endobronchial obstruction needs exclusion CT pulmonary angiography if absent or hypoplastic pulmonary artery is considered assessment for bronchiectasis-related infection with sputum culture Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome is a form of post-infectious constrictive (obliterative) bronchiolitis producing a hyperlucent, hypoperfused lung or lobe that is usually smaller than normal. It follows a severe lower respiratory infection in early childhood — often viral (adenovirus, measles) or Mycoplasma — that injures the developing distal airways and alveoli. The classic chest radiograph shows unilateral hyperlucency with a small or normal-sized lung and reduced vascular markings, distinguishing it from compensatory overinflation. Air trapping is the functional hallmark: expiratory imaging shows the affected side remaining lucent and failing to empty, sometimes with mediastinal shift on expiration. CT typically reveals mosaic attenuation, bronchiectasis, reduced vessel calibre and areas of low attenuation reflecting the obliterated small airways. Many patients are asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally; others have recurrent infection, chronic cough, exertional dyspnoea or bronchiectasis. Perfusion imaging demonstrates markedly reduced perfusion to the affected lung, matching the ventilation abnormality. It must be distinguished from other causes of a unilateral hyperlucent lung, including endobronchial obstruction, congenital lobar emphysema, absent pulmonary artery and prior pneumonectomy or lobar disease. recurrent or severe lower respiratory infections with declining lung function haemoptysis prompting exclusion of another cause of hyperlucency progressive dyspnoea suggesting extension of disease or a superimposed process new focal obstruction raising concern for an endobronchial lesion Misinterpreting the hyperlucency as emphysema, compensatory overinflation or a technical artefact. Omitting expiratory imaging, without which the diagnostic air trapping may be missed. Overlooking an endobronchial obstruction that can mimic the appearance. Failing to recognise and treat associated bronchiectasis and recurrent infection. Assuming the small hyperlucent lung is congenitally absent tissue rather than post-infectious small-airway obliteration. Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome arises when a severe lower respiratory infection during the period of ongoing lung growth in early childhood injures the terminal and respiratory bronchioles. Healing produces constrictive (obliterative) bronchiolitis, with fibrous narrowing and obliteration of small airways that impairs both ventilation and normal alveolar multiplication in the affected region. The damaged lung is chronically underventilated, and reflex and structural reduction of the pulmonary vascular bed leads to diminished perfusion and attenuated vessels, accounting for the radiographic hyperlucency. Collateral air drift allows air to enter distal units but the obliterated broncholes impede its egress, so air trapping develops and the affected lung fails to deflate normally on expiration. Because the insult occurs during development, the affected lung or lobe often remains smaller than normal, and coexisting bronchiectasis reflects proximal airway damage from the original infection and subsequent recurrent infection. Many patients remain stable and minimally symptomatic for life, but those with extensive bronchiectasis or recurrent infection may have progressive symptoms; management is largely supportive, with treatment of infection and, rarely, resection for a destroyed lobe causing intractable problems.

mass suggesting gonadoblastoma or dysgerminoma Signs of virilisation, which would suggest an alternative diagnosis or a hormonally active tumour Severe osteoporosis or fragility fracture from untreated oestrogen deficiency Delayed diagnosis leaving Y-bearing gonads in situ into adulthood Mislabelling the condition as simple delayed puberty and missing the karyotype Leaving dysgenetic gonads with Y material in place and overlooking tumour risk Confusing it with androgen insensitivity, in which no uterus is present Neglecting bone protection and psychological support during hormone induction In Swyer syndrome the karyotype is 46,XY but the bipotential gonad fails to differentiate into a testis, resulting in fibrous streak gonads. This failure of testis determination most often reflects disruption of the SRY gene or of downstream sex-determining transcription factors. Without functioning Sertoli cells there is no anti-mullerian hormone, so the mullerian ducts develop into a uterus, cervix and upper vagina; without Leydig cell testosterone the wolffian ducts regress and the external genitalia default to a female pattern. The streak gonads retain Y-derived germ cell material, which predisposes to malignant germ cell tumours, chiefly gonadoblastoma and dysgerminoma. With timely gonadectomy of the dysgenetic gonads and appropriate hormone replacement, individuals have a good long-term outlook and can achieve pregnancy via oocyte donation. The main threat is malignant transformation of retained Y-bearing streak gonads, which is largely preventable with early gonadectomy.

sydenham chorea — chorea minor, rheumatic chorea, St Vitus dance Systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid antibody syndrome chorea Chorea gravidarum and oral contraceptive-related chorea Drug-induced chorea (neuroleptics, stimulants, anticonvulsants) Benign hereditary chorea and other genetic choreas Wilson disease Tics and Tourette syndrome Functional (psychogenic) movement disorder Throat swab culture and anti-streptolysin O / anti-DNase B titres Echocardiography to detect subclinical rheumatic valvulitis Inflammatory markers (ESR, C-reactive protein) and full blood count Autoantibody screen (antinuclear, antiphospholipid antibodies) to exclude lupus Serum caeruloplasmin and copper studies to exclude Wilson disease MRI brain (often normal or showing reversible striatal signal change) Electrocardiogram for evidence of rheumatic carditis Post-streptococcal autoimmune chorea and the commonest cause of acquired chorea in childhood, typically arising 1-6 months after group A streptococcal pharyngitis. One of the major Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever, and may occur in isolation (pure chorea) when other manifestations have resolved. Peaks between ages 5 and 15 with a female preponderance; onset is often subacute over days to weeks. Clinical triad of chorea, hypotonia and emotional lability; obsessive-compulsive symptoms and attention difficulties frequently accompany the movement disorder. Classic bedside signs include the 'milkmaid grip' (rhythmic squeezing on sustained grasp), 'darting' or serpentine tongue on protrusion, and pronator (spooning) sign with wrist flexion on arm elevation. Chorea may be markedly asymmetrical or strictly unilateral (hemichorea) in up to a fifth of cases. Antineuronal antibodies cross-reacting with basal ganglia epitopes are implicated; anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B titres may already be falling by the time chorea appears. Secondary penicillin prophylaxis against recurrent streptococcal infection and rheumatic carditis is essential regardless of whether cardiac involvement is evident. Signs of active carditis (new murmur, cardiac failure, pericardial rub) requiring urgent cardiology assessment Severe generalised chorea causing dehydration, exhaustion or injury (chorea paralytica) Fever, encephalopathy or focal deficits suggesting an alternative encephalitic process Marked psychiatric disturbance or self-harm risk from emotional lability Recurrence of chorea suggesting inadequate streptococcal prophylaxis Attributing fidgetiness or emotional change to behavioural problems and missing an evolving chorea. Excluding rheumatic fever because pharyngitis was not recalled or streptococcal titres have already normalised. Omitting echocardiography because a murmur is not audible, thereby missing subclinical valvulitis. Failing to institute or continue secondary penicillin prophylaxis, risking carditis with recurrent infection. Over-sedating with dopamine antagonists when symptoms are mild and would settle spontaneously. Sydenham chorea is an autoimmune disorder triggered by group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal infection in a genetically susceptible host. Molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens (notably M protein and N-acetyl-beta-D-glucosamine) and neuronal epitopes generates cross-reactive antibodies that bind surface antigens on basal ganglia neurons, particularly within the caudate and putamen. Antibody binding activates calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II signalling and disturbs dopaminergic neurotransmission, producing dysfunction of the striatal indirect pathway and the disinhibited, involuntary movements characteristic of chorea. Neuroimaging and functional studies show reversible striatal inflammation and hypermetabolism, correlating with the usually self-limiting course as the immune response wanes. Most cases are self-limiting and resolve over weeks to months, though symptoms may persist up to two years and recur in a third of patients, particularly during pregnancy or with oestrogen exposure. Long-term outcome is dominated by the risk of rheumatic heart disease, making secondary antibiotic prophylaxis the key determinant of prognosis.

or fever suggesting an alternative severe drug reaction Mucosal involvement or skin detachment inconsistent with the diagnosis Failure to settle after drug withdrawal Signs of secondary infection in the affected folds Mistaking it for an infective or inverse-psoriasis intertrigo and missing the drug cause Failing to recognise that no external contact allergen is required for the flexural eruption Overlooking that recurrence follows re-exposure to the culprit drug Confusing it with acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis when pustules develop Symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema is regarded as a systemically induced delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction to a drug, without the need for prior sensitisation through skin contact. A systemically administered drug or its metabolite is thought to reach the flexural skin and provoke a T-cell-mediated inflammatory response, with the characteristic predilection for the buttocks and major body folds possibly reflecting local factors such as occlusion, sweat, and a higher density of eccrine structures or drug delivery to these sites. The reaction is confined to the skin, and the lack of systemic features and organ involvement distinguishes it mechanistically from severe cutaneous adverse reactions. The prognosis is excellent, with resolution over one to two weeks once the responsible drug is stopped and no long-term sequelae, although the reaction will recur on re-exposure.

Symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema — SDRIFE, baboon syndrome Intertrigo Inverse psoriasis Allergic contact dermatitis Fixed drug eruption Other drug exanthems Drug history correlating onset with a systemic drug Clinical recognition of the symmetrical flexural distribution Skin biopsy in atypical cases Patch or drug testing where confirmation is needed Exclusion of intertrigo and inverse psoriasis A distinctive drug eruption with symmetrical erythema of the gluteal/perianal area and the major flexures The gluteal V-shaped erythema gives the historical name baboon syndrome It occurs after systemic exposure to a drug, without prior sensitisation at those sites There are typically no systemic symptoms and no mucosal involvement Common culprits include beta-lactam antibiotics and other systemic drugs It resolves on stopping the culprit drug and has a benign course Systemic symptoms or mucosal involvement suggesting a more serious reaction Extensive or atypical distribution Features suggesting a severe cutaneous adverse reaction Failure to resolve after stopping the drug Confusing it with intertrigo or inverse psoriasis Failing to identify the systemic drug trigger Overtreating a benign self-limiting eruption Not documenting the culprit for future avoidance Symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema is a T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity reaction to a systemically administered drug (or occasionally systemically absorbed contact allergen). For reasons that are not fully understood, the reaction localises symmetrically to the gluteal region and flexures. The immune response produces the characteristic well-demarcated erythema without the systemic features or mucosal involvement of more severe cutaneous adverse reactions, and it settles when the drug is withdrawn. The condition is benign and self-limiting, clearing within days to a couple of weeks after the culprit drug is discontinued.
