ophthalmia until proven otherwise Rapidly progressive bilateral visual loss requiring urgent immunosuppression Exudative retinal detachment threatening the macula Development of the disease in a patient's only functioning eye Attributing fellow-eye inflammation to something benign and missing early sympathetic ophthalmia Under-dosing or prematurely tapering immunosuppression and precipitating a relapse Assuming enucleation of the exciting eye after onset will halt established disease Failing to exclude infective and neoplastic mimics before committing to long-term immunosuppression Overlooking the risk following seemingly minor intraocular surgery, not just major trauma Sympathetic ophthalmia is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune granulomatous inflammation directed against previously sequestered uveal and retinal antigens. Penetrating trauma or surgery exposes these ocular antigens to the systemic immune system, breaking immune privilege and sensitising the host. The resulting autoreactive response attacks the uvea of both eyes, producing a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis characterised by diffuse choroidal infiltration by lymphocytes and epithelioid cells and by Dalen-Fuchs nodules. Because the response targets shared antigens, the uninjured sympathising eye is affected in parallel with the exciting eye. With prompt and sustained immunosuppression, many patients retain useful vision, but the disease is chronic and relapsing; delayed treatment or recurrent flares can lead to severe bilateral visual loss and secondary complications such as cataract, glaucoma and macular scarring.

Sympathomimetic toxidrome — adrenergic toxidrome, stimulant toxidrome Anticholinergic toxidrome Serotonin syndrome Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Thyroid storm Alcohol or sedative withdrawal Sepsis or CNS infection Clinical recognition and a substance-use history Electrocardiogram and cardiac assessment for ischaemia and arrhythmia Temperature, creatine kinase and renal function for hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis Neuroimaging if focal signs or severe headache suggest intracranial haemorrhage Glucose and electrolytes to exclude mimics Characterised by agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, dilated pupils and prominent sweating Typical causes include cocaine, amphetamines and related stimulants and some decongestants The presence of sweating and usually preserved bowel sounds distinguishes it from the dry anticholinergic toxidrome Benzodiazepines are the cornerstone of treatment, controlling agitation, tachycardia and hypertension Complications include seizures, myocardial ischaemia, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and intracranial haemorrhage Traditional teaching cautions against beta-blocker monotherapy in cocaine toxicity because of concern about unopposed alpha stimulation Chest pain or electrocardiographic evidence of ischaemia Severe hyperthermia Seizures or focal neurological signs Uncontrolled hypertension with end-organ compromise Confusing it with the anticholinergic toxidrome (sweaty versus dry skin) Under-sedating agitated patients and allowing hyperthermia to progress Overlooking myocardial ischaemia or intracranial haemorrhage Giving beta-blocker monotherapy in cocaine toxicity against traditional caution The sympathomimetic toxidrome results from excessive stimulation of adrenergic receptors through increased release or reduced reuptake of catecholamines, or direct receptor agonism. The resulting adrenergic overdrive raises heart rate, blood pressure and temperature, dilates pupils and stimulates sweating, while central stimulation causes agitation and can provoke seizures. End-organ complications arise from vasoconstriction and increased metabolic demand, including myocardial ischaemia, cerebral haemorrhage and hyperthermia with rhabdomyolysis. Most patients recover with sedation and supportive care, but severe hyperthermia, myocardial infarction, intracranial haemorrhage or status epilepticus can be fatal.

Synchysis scintillans — cholesterolosis bulbi, cholesterol crystals of the vitreous Asteroid hyalosis (calcium soaps suspended in a formed gel that do not sediment) Vitreous or anterior chamber haemorrhage Vitreous amyloidosis Inflammatory vitreous cells or uveitis Retained intraocular foreign body or changes of long-standing retinal detachment Crystalline retinopathies with intraretinal deposits Slit-lamp and dilated fundus examination noting settling of crystals inferiorly at rest B-scan ultrasonography demonstrating mobile echoes that settle with gravity, particularly where the fundus view is poor Detailed history and examination for previous trauma, haemorrhage or chronic intraocular disease Examination of the fellow eye to assess laterality and any systemic pattern Investigation of the underlying cause of recurrent or chronic vitreous haemorrhage where relevant Fundus imaging where the media are clear enough to document the crystals and underlying retina Consists of cholesterol crystals that form within a liquefied (synchytic) vitreous, characteristically in an eye already damaged by previous trauma, chronic vitreous haemorrhage or long-standing severe intraocular disease Crystals are flat, angular and golden-brown or multicoloured with a highly refractile glitter, in contrast to the round white spheres of asteroid hyalosis Because the vitreous is liquefied the crystals move freely and settle inferiorly under gravity when the eye is still, then swirl through the cavity on movement like a snow-globe Often unilateral when secondary to prior injury or haemorrhage in one eye, but may be bilateral where systemic or metabolic factors contribute Typically arises in an eye with vision already reduced by the underlying disease; the crystals themselves seldom cause additional visual loss Cholesterol crystals may also accumulate in the anterior chamber (cholesterolosis) in a blind or severely damaged eye Diagnosis is essentially clinical, and management is directed at the underlying condition rather than at the inert crystals themselves Recurrent or new vitreous haemorrhage indicating active underlying disease such as proliferative retinopathy or a retinal tear Signs of a retained intraocular foreign body or occult penetrating trauma A painful blind eye raising concern about other end-stage complications New visual symptoms in the fellow eye Confusing it with asteroid hyalosis and missing the clue that a liquefied vitreous with sedimenting crystals signifies a previously diseased eye Overlooking a treatable underlying cause of recurrent vitreous haemorrhage Attempting to treat the crystals rather than the primary pathology Failing to examine the fellow eye and assess for systemic contributors Synchysis scintillans, or cholesterolosis bulbi, develops when cholesterol released from the breakdown of blood or degenerating tissue after haemorrhage, trauma or chronic intraocular disease crystallises within a vitreous that has already undergone liquefaction. Loss of the normal gel structure allows the dense crystals to move freely and to sediment inferiorly under gravity between eye movements. It therefore signifies a previously diseased eye, distinguishing it from asteroid hyalosis, in which calcium-phospholipid bodies remain suspended in a still-formed gel and do not settle. The cholesterol crystals themselves are inert and generally do not threaten vision; the visual outcome is determined almost entirely by the underlying ocular disease that gave rise to them. Many affected eyes already have poor vision from the causative pathology.

it is classified as simple (soft tissue only) or complex (with bony fusion), and as complete (to the fingertips) or incomplete Complicated syndactyly involves additional or abnormal bones, tendons, or neurovascular structures beyond a simple bony bridge The third web space (long-ring) is most often affected; the condition is frequently bilateral and may be familial (autosomal dominant with variable penetrance) Border-digit and unequal-length pairings (such as ring-little or thumb-index) should be separated earlier, because tethering causes progressive angular and rotational deformity as the digits grow at different rates Syndromic links include Apert syndrome (complex symmetrical syndactyly producing a 'mitten hand'), Poland syndrome (with chest-wall and pectoral deficiency), and constriction ring (amniotic band) sequence Surgical separation uses interdigitating (zig-zag) incisions to resurface the sides of the digits and reconstructs the web (commissure) with local flaps, frequently supplemented by skin grafts The two sides of a single digit are generally not released at the same operation, so as to protect that digit's blood supply Complex or complicated syndactyly with a shared neurovascular bundle risking devascularisation at separation Progressive deformity of border digits from tethered unequal growth Features of Apert or another syndrome requiring multidisciplinary care Releasing both sides of the same digit at one operation and compromising its blood supply Delaying separation of unequal-length border digits, allowing fixed deformity to develop Reconstructing the web too shallow or narrow, leading to web creep Underestimating shared bony or neurovascular anatomy in complex syndactyly Syndactyly results from failure of the normal programmed cell death (apoptosis) that separates the digital rays during limb development, so adjacent digits remain joined by skin and, in complex forms, by bone. It represents a failure of differentiation and may occur in isolation, be inherited, or form part of a syndrome in which broader signalling defects affect both the hand and other structures, as in the acrocephalosyndactyly of Apert syndrome or the vascular disruption of constriction ring sequence. Simple isolated syndactyly has excellent results after zig-zag separation and web reconstruction; complex and syndromic forms, especially Apert syndrome, are more likely to need multiple procedures and to leave residual stiffness, distal migration of the web ('web creep'), and imperfect appearance.

involving SYNGAP1 Gene panel or exome sequencing for SYNGAP1 and other epileptic-encephalopathy genes Developmental, speech and autism assessment Combines moderate to severe intellectual disability, dominant, encoding a synaptic Ras/Rap GTPase-activating protein Language is often more impaired than expected for the overall cognitive level Frequent drop attacks risking injury Status epilepticus or clusters of atypical absences Feeding difficulty with aspiration or faltering growth Escalating aggression or self-injury affecting safety Attributing the epilepsy to a generic idiopathic syndrome and not testing for SYNGAP1 Missing eating-triggered reflex seizures because EEG is not recorded around meals Assuming a normal MRI excludes a monogenic cause Underestimating the disproportionate language and communication impairment SYNGAP1 encodes a synaptic Ras/Rap GTPase-activating protein highly enriched at excitatory glutamatergic postsynaptic densities, where it regulates AMPA-receptor trafficking and the maturation of dendritic spines. Haploinsufficiency from loss-of-function variants disturbs the balance of synaptic excitation, accelerating spine maturation and impairing synaptic plasticity underlying learning. The resulting cortical hyperexcitability and abnormal circuit development produce the intellectual disability, autistic features and generalised, frequently reflex-triggered epilepsy. The gene is dosage-sensitive, so a single functional copy is insufficient for normal synaptic function. Most individuals have lifelong intellectual disability and ongoing, often drug-resistant epilepsy, with variable but usually limited functional independence. Seizure burden and behaviour tend to be the main determinants of quality of life, and care is supportive and multidisciplinary.

Synovial chondromatosis — synovial osteochondromatosis, primary synovial chondromatosis, Reichel syndrome Secondary osteochondromatosis from osteoarthritis or trauma Pigmented villonodular synovitis Loose bodies from osteochondritis dissecans Synovial chondrosarcoma Rheumatoid or other inflammatory synovitis Intra-articular tumour or synovial sarcoma Plain radiographs showing multiple calcified intra-articular bodies of similar size MRI to detect non-calcified cartilaginous bodies and characterise the synovial disease CT to define ossified loose bodies and bony involvement Ultrasound to demonstrate effusion and intra-articular bodies Histological examination of resected tissue to confirm the diagnosis and exclude chondrosarcoma A benign proliferative disorder in which the synovium undergoes cartilaginous metaplasia, forming multiple cartilage nodules that detach as loose bodies Typically monoarticular, most often affecting the knee, followed by the hip, elbow and shoulder Presents with joint pain, swelling, stiffness, crepitus and mechanical symptoms such as locking or catching from the loose bodies When the loose bodies calcify or ossify they become visible on plain radiographs as multiple similarly sized calcified bodies within the joint Non-mineralised cartilaginous bodies may be radiographically occult, so MRI is valuable to demonstrate them and the synovial disease Diagnosis is confirmed histologically, and malignant transformation to synovial chondrosarcoma is rare but recognised Treatment is surgical removal of loose bodies with synovectomy, and recurrence can occur if active synovial disease remains Rapid growth, aggressive bone destruction or a soft-tissue mass suggesting chondrosarcoma Recurrent disease after surgery raising concern for persistent active or malignant synovium Progressive joint destruction with severe mechanical impairment Atypical extra-articular extension of the process Missing non-calcified cartilaginous loose bodies on plain radiographs and relying on them alone Confusing it with pigmented villonodular synovitis on imaging Failing to consider malignant transformation in aggressive or recurrent disease Removing loose bodies without addressing the active synovium, leading to recurrence Synovial chondromatosis is a benign neoplastic or metaplastic process in which the synovial membrane produces multiple foci of hyaline cartilage. These nodules enlarge, may calcify or ossify, and can detach from the synovium to become free-floating intra-articular loose bodies that continue to grow by drawing nutrition from the synovial fluid. Primary synovial chondromatosis arises de novo from the synovium and is now recognised to be a true clonal neoplastic process in many cases, whereas secondary chondromatosis develops from cartilage and bone fragments in a joint already damaged by osteoarthritis or trauma. The loose bodies mechanically damage articular cartilage and produce the locking, effusion and secondary degenerative change seen clinically. Primary synovial chondromatosis is benign and treatable with surgery, but recurrence is not uncommon when active synovium persists and untreated disease can cause secondary osteoarthritis; malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma is rare but carries a worse outlook.

Synovial sarcoma (SS18-SSX) — SS18-SSX fusion sarcoma, SYT-SSX sarcoma, monophasic synovial sarcoma, biphasic synovial sarcoma, poorly differentiated synovial sarcoma Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour Fibrosarcoma and other spindle-cell sarcomas Solitary fibrous tumour Leiomyosarcoma Mesothelioma (for biphasic pleural lesions) Benign nerve sheath tumours and other slow-growing soft-tissue masses MRI of the primary site to assess deep extent and relation to joint and neurovascular structures Plain radiographs to detect characteristic soft-tissue calcification Chest CT for pulmonary metastatic surveillance Whole-body functional imaging in higher-risk or large tumours Core or open biopsy with careful tract planning and molecular testing for SS18 rearrangement Immunohistochemistry including cytokeratins, EMA, TLE1, and SS18-SSX-specific antibodies Typically affects adolescents and young adults, though it can occur at any age, without a strong sex predilection Characteristically arises in para-articular deep soft tissue of the extremities, especially around the knee and thigh, but despite the name does not originate from synovium Often presents as a slowly enlarging, sometimes long-standing and painful deep mass, which can lead to misdiagnosis as a benign lesion Calcification within the tumour on imaging is a helpful, relatively characteristic feature Defined by the t(X;18) translocation producing an SS18-SSX fusion gene (SSX1, SSX2, or less often SSX4), demonstrable by molecular testing and increasingly by SSX and SS18-SSX antibody immunohistochemistry Morphology ranges from monophasic spindle cell to biphasic (spindle plus epithelial) and poorly differentiated patterns, with variable cytokeratin and EMA positivity Local control relies on wide surgical excision, frequently combined with radiotherapy, and multi-agent chemotherapy is considered in selected higher-risk cases A tendency to late local recurrence and metastasis, chiefly to lung, mandates prolonged follow-up A deep-seated, enlarging soft-tissue mass, especially near a joint in a young patient, wrongly labelled benign A long-standing mass that begins to grow more rapidly or becomes painful New respiratory symptoms suggesting pulmonary metastases Recurrence at the primary site after apparently adequate excision Dismissing a deep soft-tissue mass as benign because of slow growth or long duration Failing to obtain molecular confirmation of the SS18 fusion when morphology is ambiguous Poorly planned biopsy that contaminates compartments and complicates limb-sparing surgery Curtailing follow-up too early, missing late local or pulmonary recurrence Interpreting focal keratin positivity in isolation without the full immunohistochemical and molecular context Synovial sarcoma is a translocation-associated malignancy of uncertain differentiation defined by fusion of SS18 on chromosome 18 with an SSX gene on the X chromosome. The resulting SS18-SSX fusion protein disrupts normal chromatin-remodelling complexes of the SWI/SNF (BAF) family, hijacking transcriptional programmes and derepressing target genes that drive proliferation and block normal differentiation. This epigenetic dysregulation, rather than any true synovial origin, underlies the tumour and its capacity for both spindle-cell and epithelial (biphasic) phenotypes; detection of the fusion is the diagnostic gold standard. Outcome is influenced by tumour size, depth, grade, patient age, and adequacy of resection; smaller, completely excised tumours in younger patients fare better, but late recurrence and pulmonary metastasis are well recognised, so long-term survival can be worse than early results suggest.

Syphilis — lues, Treponema pallidum infection Primary chancre vs herpes simplex virus genital ulceration (Harrison 22e p.1430) Primary chancre vs chancroid (Harrison 22e p.1430) Primary chancre vs donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) (Harrison 22e p.1430) Primary chancre vs traumatic genital injury (Harrison 22e p.1430) Neonatal congenital syphilis vs rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex, toxoplasmosis, and erythroblastosis fetalis (Harrison 22e p.1432) Genital herpes simplex virus infection (Harrison 22e p.1430) Chancroid (Harrison 22e p.1430) Donovanosis (Harrison 22e p.1430) Other treponemal infections (yaws, pinta, bejel) that also give reactive treponemal serology (Harrison 22e p.1433) RPR or VDRL lipoidal (nontreponemal) serology for screening and quantitation, confirmed by a treponemal test (FTA-ABS or TPPA) (Harrison 22e p.1433) Treponemal EIA/CIA automated assays as screening tests in large laboratories, with reflex TPPA confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1433-1434) Dark-field microscopy or direct fluorescent antibody of moist lesions to demonstrate T. pallidum (rarely available outside research settings) (Harrison 22e p.1433) PCR of lesion swabs, tissue, blood, CSF, ocular fluid, urine, or oropharyngeal/rectal swabs (not commercially available; in-house validated assays) (Harrison 22e p.1433) CSF examination (mononuclear pleocytosis >5/uL, protein >45 mg/dL, CSF VDRL) for suspected neurosyphilis; CSF VDRL is highly specific but insensitive (Harrison 22e p.1432, p.1434) HIV testing in all patients with newly diagnosed syphilis (Harrison 22e p.1434) Traumatic genital injury mimicking a primary chancre (Harrison 22e p.1430) Rectosigmoid mass of secondary syphilis mistaken for malignancy (Harrison 22e p.1431) Ocular syphilis (uveitis/iritis) mistaken for non-infectious uveitis when it fails to respond to topical steroids (Harrison 22e p.1431) Chronic systemic infection by Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum, usually sexually transmitted, characterized by episodes of active disease separated by asymptomatic latent periods (Harrison 22e p.1428). Staging is the organizing framework: a primary chancre at the site of inoculation, then generalized secondary mucocutaneous disease, followed by latency, and in a minority of untreated patients tertiary disease (gumma, cardiovascular, late neurosyphilis) (Harrison 22e p.1428, p.1430). Primary chancre is typically a single painless papule that erodes into an indurated ulcer with a firm cartilaginous edge; it is accompanied by regional (usually inguinal) lymphadenopathy that is firm, nonsuppurative, and painless, and heals spontaneously in about 4-6 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1430). Secondary syphilis classically produces a widespread macular-to-papular, nonpruritic rash that frequently involves the palms and soles, plus generalized nontender lymphadenopathy (noted in ~85% of patients) (Harrison 22e p.1430-1431). Condylomata lata (broad, moist, highly infectious lesions in intertriginous areas, ~10% of secondary cases) and mucous patches (painless silver-gray erosions of oral/genital mucosa) are characteristic secondary lesions (Harrison 22e p.1431). Latent syphilis is defined by reactive serology with a normal CSF and no clinical manifestations; early latent is within the first year, late latent is >=1 year or of unknown duration (Harrison 22e p.1431). Two classes of serologic tests: lipoidal (nontreponemal) RPR/VDRL, which are quantitative and reflect disease activity, and treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, TPPA, EIA/CIA); a reactive lipoidal screen must be confirmed by a treponemal test (Harrison 22e p.1433). RPR is preferred for rapid serologic diagnosis; the VDRL remains the standard for CSF examination and is superior to RPR for that purpose (Harrison 22e p.1433-1434). After treatment of early syphilis a fourfold (two-dilution) fall in VDRL/RPR titer (e.g., 1:32 to 1:8) signals adequate response; treponemal tests typically remain reactive and are not useful for monitoring therapy (Harrison 22e p.1433, p.1435). Penicillin is the drug of choice for all stages as a principle; its efficacy against T. pallidum remains undiminished after decades of use (Harrison 22e p.1434). Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (fever, chills, myalgia, headache, tachycardia) may follow the start of therapy, thought to be a response to lipoproteins released by dying treponemes; it occurs in ~50% of primary and ~90% of secondary cases, defervesces within 12-24 h, is self-limited, and does not require steroids (Harrison 22e p.1435). Earliest manifestations of early congenital syphilis include rhinitis ('snuffles'), mucocutaneous lesions, periostitis/bone changes, and hepatosplenomegaly; classic late stigmata include Hutchinson's teeth, mulberry molars, saddle nose, and saber shins (Harrison 22e p.1432-1433). Neurosyphilis at any stage: meningeal syphilis (headache, neck stiffness, cranial nerve involvement, seizures, mental status change), meningovascular syphilis (stroke syndrome in a relatively young adult), or late parenchymatous disease (general paresis, tabes dorsalis) (Harrison 22e p.1432) Ocular syphilis (uveitis, iritis, optic neuritis, pupillary abnormalities)—permanent blindness may result without prompt diagnosis and treatment (Harrison 22e p.1431) Otic syphilis (sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo, tinnitus)—deafness may result if untreated (Harrison 22e p.1431) Cardiovascular syphilis: aortitis with aortic regurgitation, saccular aneurysm of the ascending aorta, or coronary ostial stenosis (Harrison 22e p.1432) Maternal syphilis in pregnancy: high risk of fetal loss, stillbirth, prematurity, neonatal death, and congenital syphilis (Harrison 22e p.1432) Serum RPR titer >=1:32 marks higher risk of neurosyphilis (Harrison 22e p.1432, p.1434) Prozone phenomenon: a high-titer specimen may give a nonreactive or only weakly reactive lipoidal test with undiluted serum that becomes reactive only on dilution—a falsely negative screen if dilution is not performed (Harrison 22e p.1433). Primary syphilis is often missed in women and in MSM because chancres on the cervix, vaginal wall, anal canal, rectum, or mouth go unseen; atypical or trivial dark-field-negative genital lesions should still prompt consideration of syphilis (Harrison 22e p.1430). Both lipoidal and treponemal tests may be nonreactive in early primary syphilis; an early primary ulcer can present with nonreactive serology, so negative serology does not exclude it (Harrison 22e p.1431-1433). Biological false-positive lipoidal tests occur (usually titer <=1:8, e.g., in autoimmune disease or injection drug use); a nonreactive treponemal test excludes syphilis in this setting (Harrison 22e p.1433-1434). Treponemal tests usually remain reactive for life after treatment and cannot distinguish active from past infection or gauge response to therapy (Harrison 22e p.1433, p.1435). CSF VDRL is highly specific but insensitive—it may be nonreactive even in symptomatic neurosyphilis—and RPR must not be substituted for VDRL on CSF (Harrison 22e p.1434). Benzathine penicillin does not achieve treponemicidal levels in CSF even at high doses, so it is inadequate for neurosyphilis and viable T. pallidum has been recovered from CSF after such treatment (Harrison 22e p.1434). Syphilis is a 'great imitator': its protean mucocutaneous and systemic features overlap with many other diseases, so it must be considered broadly (Harrison 22e p.1430-1431). Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum is a thin spiral organism with a lipid-rich outer membrane and periplasmic endoflagella that drive motility; it has severely limited metabolic capacity and depends on host amino acids, carbohydrates, and lipids. Humans are the only known natural host. After penetrating intact mucous membranes or skin abrasions, treponemes reach the lymphatics and blood within hours, producing systemic dissemination and metastatic foci well before the primary lesion appears (median incubation ~21 days, rarely >6 weeks). Tissue damage reflects the host immune response rather than a direct treponemal toxin: lesions show perivascular infiltration by CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, plasma cells, and macrophages with endarteritis obliterans (obliteration of small vessels). Antigenic variation of the TprK outer-membrane protein allows immune evasion and persistence, explaining the paradoxical appearance of secondary lesions after primary lesions clear. Tertiary lesions (gumma, aortitis of the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta, parenchymal neurosyphilis) arise from a slowly progressive inflammatory process that begins early in infection (Harrison 22e p.1428-1430, p.1432). Untreated primary and secondary lesions resolve spontaneously, but infection persists. In the preantibiotic era about one-third of untreated patients with latent infection progressed to tertiary disease; the Tuskegee Study showed untreated syphilis raised the death rate ~17%, largely from cardiovascular disease. With early treatment, prognosis is excellent and tertiary syphilis is now nearly eliminated in Western countries; the clinical response to therapy for benign tertiary (gumma) disease is usually impressive. Congenital syphilis prognosis is poor when fulminant disease is clinically apparent at birth, but adequate maternal treatment before the 16th week of pregnancy should prevent fetal damage. Response to therapy is monitored by a fourfold decline in VDRL/RPR titer (Harrison 22e p.1430, p.1432, p.1435). Disease is described by clinical stage rather than a graded severity score: primary syphilis (chancre with regional lymphadenopathy); secondary syphilis (generalized mucocutaneous rash including palms and soles, condylomata lata, mucous patches, constitutional symptoms); latent syphilis (reactive serology, normal CSF, no clinical signs; early latent <1 year vs late latent >=1 year or unknown duration); tertiary/late syphilis (gumma, cardiovascular syphilis, late neurosyphilis). Neurosyphilis spans a continuum: early (asymptomatic meningitis, meningeal and meningovascular syphilis) and late parenchymatous disease (general paresis, tabes dorsalis). Congenital syphilis is divided into early (within first 2 years) and late (after 2 years) (Harrison 22e p.1428, p.1431-1433).

missing a continuous cervical syrinx Underestimating occult central sleep-disordered breathing and aspiration risk Syringobulbia is a slit-like, gliosis-lined cavity within the brainstem, most commonly dissecting through the medullary tegmentum, and in the majority of cases it is continuous with a cervical cord syrinx. It is thought to arise from disordered cerebrospinal fluid dynamics at the craniovertebral junction, classically in association with a Chiari I malformation, which alters pressure gradients and drives fluid into and along the neuraxis. As the cavity enlarges it disrupts adjacent structures, including the nuclei and intramedullary fibres of the glossopharyngeal, vagus and hypoglossal nerves, the spinal tract and nucleus of the trigeminal nerve, descending sympathetic pathways, the medial longitudinal fasciculus and vestibular connections, producing the characteristic constellation of bulbar, sensory, oculomotor and autonomic signs. The course is usually slowly progressive over years, and treatment directed at the underlying cause, such as posterior fossa decompression for Chiari I malformation, may arrest or partially reverse deficits. Established bulbar and cranial nerve deficits often persist, and advanced disease carries a risk of life-threatening aspiration and respiratory compromise.

options include ablative or destructive methods, with recurrence common because lesions are numerous An indurated infiltrative plaque rather than discrete papules, raising concern for microcystic adnexal carcinoma Rapid change or ulceration atypical for benign syringoma Widespread eruptive lesions prompting evaluation for an associated systemic condition Confusing periorbital syringomas with xanthelasma and pursuing lipid-lowering rather than dermatological assessment Misinterpreting the sclerotic ductal histology as microcystic adnexal carcinoma or morphoeic basal cell carcinoma Promising complete cosmetic clearance despite a high recurrence rate Overlooking the association with systemic conditions in eruptive presentations Syringoma is a benign adnexal neoplasm derived from the intraepidermal portion of the eccrine sweat duct. Histologically it consists of numerous small ducts and solid epithelial strands set within a fibrous, often sclerotic, dermal stroma; the ducts are lined by two layers of cuboidal cells and many acquire a characteristic comma-like or tadpole configuration. The lesions represent a proliferation of well-differentiated ductal structures rather than an aggressive process, so they remain confined to the dermis without invasion or metastatic potential. Hormonal and genetic influences are thought to contribute, reflected in the female predominance, the tendency to periorbital clustering, and the eruptive forms associated with certain systemic conditions. Syringomas are entirely benign with no malignant potential; they are cosmetically bothersome and tend to persist, and treatment can be complicated by recurrence and scarring given the number and depth of lesions.

Syringoma (eyelid) — eyelid syringoma, eccrine syringoma Xanthelasma palpebrarum Milia Sebaceous hyperplasia Trichoepithelioma and other benign adnexal tumours Microcystic adnexal carcinoma Morphoeic (sclerosing) basal cell carcinoma Flat warts or lichen planus papules Slit-lamp and external examination of the periorbital distribution Dermoscopy to assess surface and vascular pattern Skin biopsy with histopathology when diagnosis is uncertain or a lesion is atypical External photography to document distribution and monitor after treatment Evaluation for associated conditions (e.g. Down syndrome) where clinically indicated Deeper or excisional biopsy if microcystic adnexal carcinoma is suspected Syringomas are benign adnexal tumours of the eccrine sweat ducts presenting as multiple small, soft, skin-coloured to yellowish papules clustered on the lower eyelids and upper cheeks. They are typically bilateral and symmetrical, appear around puberty or in early adulthood, and are commoner in women. Individual papules are small and firm; they are usually asymptomatic and the concern is almost entirely cosmetic. The periorbital region, especially the lower lids, is the classic site, and the clustered, symmetrical distribution is a helpful diagnostic clue. There is a recognised association with Down syndrome, and an eruptive variant can appear on the trunk; diabetes has been linked to a clear-cell histological variant. Diagnosis is usually clinical, but biopsy with histology confirms the characteristic ductal structures when there is doubt. Treatment is for cosmesis only and is difficult, as lesions are dermal and multiple; options include ablative laser, electrocautery, excision and chemical peels, all with a tendency to recur and a risk of eyelid scarring. Syringomas must be distinguished from xanthelasma, milia, sebaceous hyperplasia and, importantly, from the more aggressive microcystic adnexal carcinoma and morphoeic basal cell carcinoma when a lesion is solitary, indurated or growing. A solitary, indurated, enlarging or ill-defined lesion suggesting microcystic adnexal carcinoma or morphoeic basal cell carcinoma Ulceration, bleeding or loss of eyelashes Rapid change in a previously stable lesion Deep infiltration or recurrence after excision suggesting a more aggressive adnexal tumour Confusing syringomas with xanthelasma and thereby missing an opportunity to counsel on lipids, or vice versa Mistaking an infiltrative microcystic adnexal carcinoma for benign syringomas and delaying appropriate excision Aggressive ablative treatment of lower-lid lesions causing scarring, dyspigmentation or ectropion Promising complete cosmetic clearance despite the high recurrence rate of dermal lesions Failing to biopsy an atypical or solitary lesion before cosmetic destruction Syringomas are benign proliferations (hamartomatous or adenomatous) of the intraepidermal eccrine sweat duct. Histology shows small ducts and solid epithelial cords embedded in a fibrous dermal stroma, with characteristic comma-shaped or tadpole-like ductal profiles lined by two layers of cuboidal cells. The proliferation is confined to the superficial to mid dermis without invasion, and hormonal influence is implicated by the tendency to appear or worsen around puberty and in women. Because the lesions are dermal and multifocal, they neither regress spontaneously nor respond to superficial treatment, and their depth explains the difficulty of complete cosmetic clearance. Benign with an excellent prognosis and no threat to vision; lesions persist indefinitely. Cosmetic treatment is often only partially effective and recurrence is common, with a risk of scarring on the delicate eyelid skin.

wasting solely to motor neuron disease without imaging the cord Not counselling patients about protecting insensate areas from burns and injury Syringomyelia is characterised by a longitudinal cavity within the spinal cord that disrupts neural tissue from the centre outward. Altered cerebrospinal fluid dynamics, often related to obstruction at the craniocervical junction as in Chiari I malformation, are thought to drive fluid accumulation and cavity expansion. The central location preferentially damages the decussating spinothalamic fibres, producing dissociated sensory loss, and progressive enlargement affects anterior horn cells, long tracts, and autonomic pathways. Syringomyelia often progresses slowly over years, with a stepwise or gradual accumulation of deficits. Treating the underlying cause, particularly decompressing a Chiari malformation, can stabilise or improve symptoms, but established neurological deficits may not fully reverse and some patients continue to deteriorate despite surgery.

lymphoma of childhood develops when Epstein-Barr virus infects T cells and, against a background of genetically impaired antiviral immunity, drives a clonal and rapidly proliferating population of virus-infected cytotoxic T lymphocytes. The infected clone and the surrounding immune response release large quantities of inflammatory cytokines, activating macrophages and precipitating haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis with its attendant cytopenias, coagulopathy and multi-organ dysfunction. long-term monitoring for growth impairment and joint damage Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis is best understood as an autoinflammatory disorder driven by dysregulated innate immunity rather than adaptive autoimmunity. Excess production of the proinflammatory cytokines interleukin-1, interleukin-6 and interleukin-18, together with activated neutrophils and macrophages, produces the systemic features of fever, rash, serositis and reticuloendothelial activation. Uncontrolled macrophage and T-cell activation can tip into a cytokine storm known as macrophage activation syndrome, a form of secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Persistent joint inflammation in the chronic phase may reflect a shift towards adaptive immune mechanisms and can lead to erosive, destructive arthritis if inadequately controlled. Outcomes have improved substantially with early cytokine-targeted therapy; some children achieve durable remission, whereas others develop persistent destructive polyarthritis or recurrent systemic flares. Macrophage activation syndrome carries appreciable mortality and requires prompt recognition and intensive immunosuppression.

cutaneous, musculoskeletal, and renal systems are most often affected, followed by pulmonary, hematologic, cardiovascular, serosal, and CNS involvement (p.2827). Roughly 90% of patients are women, most of childbearing age; in the US the highest prevalence is in Black women, then Hispanic, White, and Asian/Pacific Islander women, and non-White patients tend to have more severe disease (p.2827). Autoantibodies can be detectable years before clinical diagnosis, so seropositivity helps attribute nonspecific constitutional symptoms to SLE (p.2827, p.2830). ANA at a titer of at least 1:80 is the best screening test and is present in nearly all patients; repeatedly negative immunofluorescence ANA makes the diagnosis unlikely, though about 5% of patients are ANA-negative (p.2832). Anti-dsDNA (present in ~40-60%, specificity ~75-99%) and anti-Sm (present in ~30%, highly specific) are the only ANA subtypes in the EULAR/ACR criteria; rising anti-dsDNA with falling C3/C4 signals active disease, especially impending nephritis (p.2832, p.2830). Lupus arthritis is a nonerosive polyarthritis of wrists, MCP/PIP joints, and knees; periarticular ligament damage can cause reversible Jaccoud-like deformities, and overlap with rheumatoid arthritis is termed 'rhupus' (p.2829). The classic malar 'butterfly' rash spares the nasolabial folds (distinguishing it from rosacea); subacute cutaneous lupus is photosensitive and linked to anti-Ro/SSA, while discoid lesions are the most common chronic cutaneous form (p.2829). Nephritis occurs in about 35% of patients, may be asymptomatic, and warrants screening every 3 months with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio; biopsy is generally prompted by UPCr >0.5 or declining renal function (p.2830, p.2833). Antiphospholipid antibodies are present in ~50% of patients and markedly raise risk of arterial/venous thrombosis, thrombocytopenia, recurrent fetal loss, Libman-Sacks endocarditis, and stroke (p.2830, p.2832). Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies can cross the placenta and cause neonatal lupus (transient rash/lab abnormalities or, less commonly, congenital heart block); high-titer Ro warrants fetal echocardiography screening (p.2836). Avascular (osteo)necrosis should be suspected when pain is out of proportion in a single hip, shoulder, or knee, particularly with prior corticosteroid use (p.2829). Some patients are categorized as 'type 1 lupus' (classic immune-driven features such as nephritis, arthritis, vasculitis, generally steroid-responsive) versus 'type 2 lupus' (fatigue, diffuse pain, cognitive dysfunction/'brain fog', less responsive to immunosuppression) (p.2827-2828). Excluding SLE because ANA is negative: about 5% of patients are ANA-negative, where anti-Ro/SSA can support the diagnosis. Missing asymptomatic lupus nephritis or cytopenias by not screening quarterly, since renal and hematologic disease can be present without symptoms. Attributing acute pulmonary infiltrates to lupus pneumonitis when infection looks identical on imaging. Ascribing psychosis or confusion to neuropsychiatric lupus without ruling out glucocorticoid-induced psychosis and infectious encephalitis. Overlooking avascular necrosis as a cause of disproportionate single-joint pain in patients on corticosteroids. Confusing drug-induced lupus (antihistone-positive, usually sparing kidney/brain, resolving after withdrawal) with idiopathic SLE. Using estrogen-containing contraceptives or HRT in patients with antiphospholipid antibodies or active disease, increasing thromboembolism risk. Using direct oral anticoagulants instead of warfarin for concomitant APS, or continuing teratogenic agents (mycophenolate, methotrexate, warfarin) in pregnancy. SLE arises from multiple immunoregulatory defects in genetically predisposed individuals interacting with environmental triggers. There is a strong genetic component (24% vs 2% concordance in monozygotic vs dizygotic twins; >150 GWAS susceptibility loci), with the MHC the most common association and nearly half of loci tied to type 1 interferon production or signaling (e.g., TLR7, IRF5/7/8, STAT4); complement-cascade defects (C1q, C1r, C1s, C2, C4) impair clearance of apoptotic debris and immune complexes and underlie severe monogenic disease. Environmental contributors include UV light, crystalline silica, smoking, sex hormones, Epstein-Barr virus, and gut-microbiome-related increased intestinal permeability. Innate defects cause excess cellular debris (high neutrophil turnover and NETosis) that overwhelms macrophage/dendritic clearance, triggering nucleic-acid sensors and TLRs in plasmacytoid dendritic cells to produce type 1 interferon, which sensitizes the adaptive immune system. Loss of B- and T-cell tolerance (including expansion of age-associated B cells, T follicular/peripheral helper cell help, and defective regulatory T cells) drives production of pathogenic autoantibodies; autoantibody-nucleic acid immune complexes deposit in tissue, activate monocytes, and produce inflammation, repair, and eventually fibrosis after recurrent flares. Prognosis and survival vary widely by geographic region, race/ethnicity, and access to care and medications. Most patients have active disease despite therapy or recurrent flares; about 15% have relatively mild disease. Renal disease is a major determinant of outcome: roughly 20% of US patients with class IV lupus nephritis die or develop ESRD within 10 years, and non-White patients more often progress to ESRD. Accelerated atherosclerosis becomes a leading cause of death after about 5 years of disease, with elevated myocardial infarction and stroke rates driven by both traditional risk factors and lupus-specific factors (antiphospholipid antibodies, high disease activity, low C3, high glucocorticoid dose, elevated homocysteine/leptin). Glucocorticoids contribute to irreversible, dose-dependent organ damage (cataracts, osteoporotic fractures, avascular necrosis, diabetes) even at low doses; class V nephritis carries a better renal prognosis than class III/IV. Sustained low disease activity (LLDAS) for 2 or more years is associated with significantly less damage, and meta-analyses suggest an increased overall risk of cancer and cancer-related death. Lupus nephritis is graded by the International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society (ISN/RPS) classes: I (mesangial deposits without hypercellularity), II (mesangial proliferative), III (focal proliferative glomerulonephritis), IV (diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis), and V (membranous), with III/IV +/- V combinations carrying the highest risk; class V (~20% of nephritis) more often presents with nephrotic syndrome but has a better prognosis than III/IV. Disease activity is quantified with the SLEDAI (and SLEDAI-2K), where low disease activity is a score of 0-4 and remission a score of 0 (with stable hydroxychloroquine/immunosuppressive use and prednisone equivalent 5 mg/day or less). Overall disease severity is also stratified clinically as mild (constitutional symptoms, mild arthritis, rash <=9% BSA, platelets 50-100, SLEDAI <=6), moderate (rheumatoid-like arthritis, rash 9-18% BSA, platelets 20-50, serositis, SLEDAI 7-12), and severe (major organ-threatening disease such as cerebritis, myelitis, pneumonitis, mesenteric vasculitis; platelets <20; TTP-like or hemophagocytic syndrome; rash >18% BSA; SLEDAI >12). Treat-to-target endpoints include LLDAS and DORIS remission, and trials use SRI, BICLA, and CLASI instruments.

These mast cells infiltrate the bone marrow and frequently the gastrointestinal tract, liver, spleen and bone, and release mediators such as histamine and tryptase either spontaneously or in response to triggers. In lcSSc, Raynaud's phenomenon typically precedes sclerodactyly and other manifestations, sometimes by years; the CREST constellation (calcinosis cutis, Raynaud's, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia) is a distinct lcSSc subset (p.2859). SSc-specific autoantibodies are mutually exclusive and aid risk stratification: anti-centromere is associated with lcSSc and isolated PAH (renal crisis rare); anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) with dcSSc, extensive skin, early ILD and cardiac involvement; anti-RNA polymerase III with rapidly progressive skin, renal crisis and contemporaneous cancer (p.2864, 2871). Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are detectable in virtually all SSc patients, even in early/preclinical stages (p.2864, 2871). Nailfold capillaroscopy distinguishes primary Raynaud's disease (regular, evenly spaced parallel hairpin loops) from secondary Raynaud's/SSc (giant capillaries, dilated and distorted loops, microhemorrhages, capillary dropout) and helps establish early SSc diagnosis (p.2867, 2871). ILD and pulmonary vascular disease together account for the majority of SSc-related deaths; survival is particularly poor when both coexist (p.2868). Scleroderma renal crisis presents with accelerated hypertension plus acute kidney injury, occurs in <15% of patients almost always within 4 years of onset, and is associated with diffuse/progressive skin involvement and anti-RNA polymerase III (up to 50%); anti-centromere appears protective (p.2870-2871). Palpable tendon friction rubs are associated with increased risk of renal and cardiac complications and reduced survival, and may be a harbinger of impending renal crisis (p.2871). SSc patients should be screened for PAH at initial evaluation and annually thereafter, and screened for ILD with regular pulmonary monitoring for several years after diagnosis (p.2868, 2872). SSc sine scleroderma: characteristic Raynaud's plus typical clinical/serologic features of SSc in the absence of detectable skin thickening (~10% of patients) (p.2859, 2866, 2872). Scleroderma renal crisis: accelerated/new hypertension (generally >150/90 mmHg) with progressive oliguric renal failure - a medical emergency (note ~10% present normotensive, with poorer outcome) (p.2870-2871) Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with fragmented red cells and thrombocytopenia (hallmark of renal crisis) (p.2871) New unexplained anemia, thrombocytopenia, pericardial effusion or new tendon friction rubs as harbingers of impending renal crisis (p.2871) Pulmonary arterial hypertension: exertional dyspnea, near-syncope, loud P2, right heart failure - 3-year survival of untreated PAH <50% (p.2868) Rapidly progressive ILD with declining FVC (can fall ~30%/year), most rapid in the first 3-5 years (p.2868) Critical digital ischemia with fingertip ulceration/necrosis and acro-osteolysis (p.2867) Early dcSSc may present with only upper-extremity edema and puffy fingers and Raynaud's may be absent, leading to misdiagnosis as arthritis, SLE, myositis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease (p.2872) Scleroderma renal crisis can be misdiagnosed as TTP or other thrombotic microangiopathy; renal biopsy and von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease activity may help (p.2871) Glucocorticoids (especially prednisone >=10 mg/d) are associated with precipitating scleroderma renal crisis and should be used only when essential and at low dose in high-risk patients (p.2870) PFTs and conventional echocardiography are relatively insensitive for early ILD and early cardiac involvement, respectively (p.2868, 2871) Echocardiography can over- or underestimate pulmonary artery pressures, so PAH must be confirmed by cardiac catheterization (p.2868) SSc sine scleroderma can be missed because diagnostic skin induration is absent despite organ involvement (p.2872) SSc is a chronic, often progressive disease of unknown etiology defined pathologically by widespread microangiopathy (fibroproliferative vasculopathy with capillary loss and obliteration) combined with multiorgan fibrosis, on a background of autoimmunity. An initial vascular insult in a genetically predisposed individual (modest HLA class II and immune-regulatory gene associations) triggers inflammation, generation of SSc-specific autoantibodies, and sustained activation of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts driven by mediators such as TGF-beta, IL-6, CTGF, PDGF and endothelin. Maladaptive repair leads to replacement of normal tissue with rigid, avascular, acellular connective tissue affecting skin, lungs, heart, GI tract, kidneys and other organs (p.2859-2866). Highly variable; dcSSc carries a more rapidly progressive course and worse prognosis than lcSSc. SSc confers a fivefold to eightfold higher age/sex-adjusted mortality, with median survival ~11 years; 5- and 10-year survival are ~70%/55% in dcSSc and ~90%/75% in lcSSc. Major causes of death are PAH, pulmonary fibrosis, GI involvement and cardiac disease. Scleroderma renal crisis carries ~30% 3-year mortality (markedly improved by ACE inhibitors). Poor-prognosis markers include male sex, African ancestry, older age at onset, extensive truncal skin involvement, palpable tendon friction rubs, significant/progressive visceral involvement, and laboratory findings of elevated ESR, anemia, proteinuria and anti-topoisomerase I antibodies (p.2873). ACR/EULAR classification criteria are >90% specific and sensitive but are intended for research rather than clinical practice; weighted items include skin thickening proximal to MCP joints (score 9), sclerodactyly/puffy fingers, fingertip lesions, telangiectasia, abnormal nailfold capillaries, ILD/PAH, Raynaud's phenomenon, and SSc-specific autoantibodies (anti-centromere, Scl-70, RNA polymerase III). Clinically, patients are stratified into limited cutaneous and diffuse cutaneous subsets by extent of skin involvement (p.2860).

Humans are the definitive host for both Taenia saginata and Taenia solium. Ingesting viable cysticerci in undercooked beef or pork releases a larva whose scolex attaches to the small-intestinal wall and matures into an adult tapeworm producing a chain of egg-laden proglottids shed in the faeces. For Taenia saginata the human is only the definitive host, so disease is confined to the gut. Taenia solium is more dangerous because, in addition to the intestinal adult, humans can act as an intermediate host: ingested eggs hatch, and the oncospheres disseminate to encyst in tissues including muscle, subcutaneous tissue, eye and brain, producing cysticercosis. Neurocysticercosis results when cysts lodge in the central nervous system, and the inflammatory response as they degenerate provokes seizures and other neurological effects. Intestinal taeniasis is readily cured and generally benign; the outlook is dominated by Taenia solium cysticercosis, where neurological involvement can cause significant long-term morbidity despite treatment.

catecholamine source as an underlying cause Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is thought to arise from a surge in circulating catecholamines, often provoked by acute emotional or physical stress, that produces transient myocardial stunning. The apex of the left ventricle, with its relatively high density of adrenergic receptors, is particularly susceptible, leading to the characteristic apical ballooning with preserved or hypercontractile basal segments. Proposed mechanisms include catecholamine-mediated microvascular dysfunction, direct myocyte injury, and transient coronary vasospasm, without a fixed obstructive coronary lesion to explain the regional dysfunction. Because the injury is functional rather than infarction, systolic function typically recovers once the catecholamine stress subsides. Most patients recover left ventricular function within days to weeks with a generally favourable outlook, but the acute phase can be complicated by heart failure, arrhythmia, and shock, and recurrence occurs in a minority.

molluscum contagiosum Talaromyces marneffei is inhaled as conidia that convert to a pathogenic yeast-like form dividing by fission at body temperature. In hosts with intact cell-mediated immunity infection is usually contained, but in advanced HIV or other T-cell deficiency the organism proliferates within macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system. Haematogenous dissemination follows, seeding skin, bone marrow, liver, spleen and lymph nodes, producing a granulomatous, suppurative or necrotising reaction depending on immune status. Uncontrolled fungaemia leads to sepsis and multiorgan involvement. Untreated disseminated talaromycosis is almost uniformly fatal, but early antifungal induction and consolidation with antiretroviral therapy and secondary prophylaxis achieve good outcomes; mortality remains high when diagnosis is delayed or the patient presents with sepsis.

In inhalational disease the particles deposit in airways and interstitium, and any accompanying silica or asbestos amplifies fibrosis. In intravenous talcosis, filler particles lodge in pulmonary arterioles and capillaries, seeding perivascular granulomas that can coalesce into fibrotic conglomerate masses, obliterate the vasculature to cause pulmonary hypertension, and, through mechanisms not fully understood, promote basal panacinar emphysema. Cardiac tamponade — Urgent echocardiogram ECG (electrical alternans) Obstructive shock — urgent pericardiocentesis Constrictive pericarditis (also impairs cardiac filling via a thick, noncompliant pericardium; on the differential for dyspnea) (p.1938) Acute right ventricular dysfunction (can mimic the elevated JVP / characteristic jugular waveform pattern) (p.147) Sepsis (can produce a paradoxical-type arterial waveform) (p.1906) Pericardiocentesis under echocardiographic guidance, with pericardial fluid sent for biochemical, cytologic, and microbiologic analysis (p.630, p.1432) Pericardial fluid cytology when malignancy is suspected (diagnostic in most malignant cases; fluid may be serous, serosanguineous, or hemorrhagic) (p.630) Pericardial/epicardial biopsy and pericardioscopy to distinguish neoplastic from benign disease (p.630) Chest CT, CMR, or echocardiography to assess effusion size and pericardial thickness (p.1432, p.1938) In suspected tuberculous etiology, pericardial fluid adenosine deaminase, lysozyme, and IFN-gamma, plus culture/biopsy (fluid is exudative, lymphocyte/monocyte-rich, often hemorrhagic) (p.1432) Massive pulmonary embolism (shares hypotension/tachycardia and pulsus paradoxus) (p.147, p.1906) Tension pneumothorax (life-threatening cause of obstructive shock and pulsus paradoxus) (p.147, p.1906) Hemorrhagic shock (cause of pulsus paradoxus) (p.1906) Severe obstructive lung disease / asthma (cause of pulsus paradoxus) (p.1906) Acute MI with cardiogenic shock (hypotension + tachycardia in chest-pain patient) (p.147) Acute aortic dissection (may extend into the pericardium and itself cause tamponade) (p.147, p.1938) Tamponade is fundamentally a clinical diagnosis in an unstable patient; the textbook triad is hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure with neck-vein distention, and quiet/muffled heart sounds (p.630). It is the balance between intrapericardial pressure and ventricular (especially right ventricular) filling pressure that drives compression, not the absolute volume of fluid (p.1938). Rate of accumulation matters more than total volume: slowly forming effusions (e.g. malignant) can become large without classic tamponade physiology, whereas rapid accumulation (e.g. cardiac rupture, perforation, aortic dissection into the pericardium) can cause tamponade with only a small effusion (p.1938). Pulsus paradoxus is an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mmHg and represents an exaggerated form of normal interventricular dependence (p.1906). Measure pulsus paradoxus by deflating the cuff slowly and noting the gap between the pressure where Korotkoff sounds are first heard (only in expiration) and the pressure where they are heard with every beat regardless of respiration; a difference >15 mmHg may even be palpable at the brachial or femoral pulse (p.1906). A pulsus paradoxus exceeding 12 mmHg in a patient with a large pericardial effusion is highly predictive of tamponade (reported sensitivity ~98%, specificity ~83%) (p.1910). The ECG triad of sinus tachycardia, low QRS voltage, and total electrical alternans (beat-to-beat P-QRS-T alternation) strongly suggests pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology, though it is insensitive (p.1917). Total electrical alternans (whole-complex) is relatively specific for effusion/tamponade; in contrast, pure repolarization (ST-T/U-wave) alternans signals electrical instability and risk of ventricular arrhythmia, not tamponade (p.1917). Echocardiography is the initial test of choice for suspected effusion/tamponade and can usually be done rapidly at the bedside (p.1938). Hypotension with tachycardia in a chest-pain patient mandates rapid evaluation for tamponade as one of the immediately life-threatening causes (p.147) Life-threatening hemodynamic instability with acute tamponade requires immediate fluid drainage (p.630) Hemorrhagic tamponade from cardiac rupture, procedural perforation, or aortic dissection into the pericardium can be catastrophic at small effusion volumes (p.1938) Do not delay decompression in a hemodynamically unstable patient waiting for confirmatory tests; tamponade is a clinical/emergency diagnosis and instability requires immediate drainage (p.147, p.630). Failing to appreciate the urgency of the situation is a recognized diagnostic error for tamponade (listed among can't-miss time-critical diagnoses) (p.102). Pulsus paradoxus can be hard to measure or unreliable in tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, or tachypnea (p.1906). A large slowly-accumulating effusion may lack classic tamponade signs, while a small rapidly-accumulating effusion may already be causing tamponade; judging severity by volume alone is misleading (p.1938). In malignant tamponade, relatively specific signs (paradoxical pulse, diminished heart sounds, pulsus alternans, friction rub) are LESS common than in nonmalignant disease, so their absence does not exclude tamponade (p.630). ECG and chest radiograph are abnormal in ~90% of malignant pericardial cases but about half of those abnormalities are nonspecific (p.630). Pericardial fluid accumulates between the visceral (epicardial) and parietal pericardial layers. Tamponade develops when intrapericardial pressure rises enough to exceed the filling pressures of the cardiac chambers, generally the right ventricle, impairing diastolic filling. Because the relatively non-distensible pericardial sac determines tolerance, the rate of fluid accumulation is more important than absolute volume: slow accumulation allows large effusions without compromise, while rapid accumulation (trauma, cardiac rupture, procedural perforation, aortic dissection into the pericardium) causes tamponade at small volumes. Inspiratory augmentation of right-heart filling at the expense of the left, mediated by exaggerated interventricular dependence within the fixed pericardial space, produces pulsus paradoxus (p.1906, p.1938). Outcome depends heavily on cause and timeliness of drainage. Untreated tuberculous pericarditis is usually fatal and even treated TB pericarditis carries case-fatality rates up to ~40% in some series, with risk of progression to constrictive pericarditis. Cancer patients whose pericardial fluid contains malignant cells on cytology have very poor survival. After percutaneous catheter drainage of malignant effusions the recurrence rate is ~20%, and a subset develop paradoxical hemodynamic worsening after drainage (post-drainage low cardiac output syndrome) (p.630, p.1432).

temperature loss Overlooking a very low HDL as a clue and attributing neuropathy to a more common cause Mistaking the pseudosyringomyelic sensory loss for a primary spinal cord lesion Assuming low total cholesterol is protective and neglecting cardiovascular risk Failing to examine the tonsils, which show the characteristic orange discolouration Tangier disease is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in ABCA1, a transporter that mediates the efflux of cellular cholesterol and phospholipid onto lipid-poor apolipoprotein A-I to form nascent high-density lipoprotein. Without functional ABCA1, apolipoprotein A-I is not lipidated and is rapidly catabolised, so plasma HDL and apolipoprotein A-I fall to very low levels and total cholesterol is reduced. Unesterified cholesterol and cholesteryl esters accumulate within macrophages throughout the reticuloendothelial system, producing the enlarged orange tonsils, hepatosplenomegaly and foam-cell infiltration. Lipid accumulation within Schwann cells and nerves is thought to underlie the demyelinating and axonal neuropathy, which can be multifocal and relapsing or produce a syringomyelia-like dissociated sensory loss. The neuropathy may relapse and remit or slowly progress and can cause substantial disability; long-term outlook is also influenced by an increased risk of premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

tardive akathisia — tardive akathisic syndrome, chronic neuroleptic-induced akathisia acute drug-induced akathisia psychomotor agitation of the underlying psychiatric disorder restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movements tardive dyskinesia with stereotypic leg movements anxiety or agitated depression hyperthyroidism or stimulant/substance-related restlessness drug-withdrawal states structured temporal history of all dopamine-blocking agents including antiemetics and any recent dose changes standardised assessment with the Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale for severity and monitoring mood, impulsivity and suicide-risk evaluation given the recognised association screening for restless legs syndrome including iron studies where the history overlaps thyroid function tests to exclude a metabolic driver of restlessness review for coexisting tardive dyskinesia, dystonia or parkinsonism on examination A persistent, late-onset movement disorder of inner restlessness and a compelling urge to move, developing after prolonged exposure to dopamine-receptor-blocking agents and continuing well after acute akathisia would be expected to settle. Distinguished from acute akathisia by its delayed emergence, chronicity, and tendency to persist or worsen when the offending drug is reduced or withdrawn, rather than on initiation or dose increase. The subjective distress (tension, dysphoria, inability to keep still) is often more prominent than in tardive dyskinesia and can be mistaken for anxiety, agitation or worsening of the underlying psychiatric illness. Characteristic motor features include marching on the spot, shifting weight, crossing and uncrossing legs, truncal rocking and inability to remain seated. It frequently coexists with tardive dyskinesia and tardive dystonia, and complex stereotypic leg movements may blur the boundary between restlessness and dyskinesia. Increasing the causative antipsychotic may transiently suppress symptoms (masking), reinforcing a cycle of escalating exposure; the diagnosis requires a careful temporal drug history. Recognised because of its strong association with dysphoria, impulsivity and heightened suicide risk, warranting proactive mood and safety assessment. Management centres on reviewing the need for and dose of the dopamine blocker, considering a switch to an agent with lower liability, and specific pharmacological strategies including VMAT2 inhibitors and, in selected cases, beta-adrenergic blockade. emergent suicidal ideation, severe dysphoria or impulsive behaviour escalating distress prompting inappropriate increases in the causative drug features suggesting an evolving neuroleptic malignant syndrome such as rigidity, fever and autonomic instability profound functional impairment or inability to rest and sleep misattributing the restlessness to worsening psychosis, anxiety or agitation and escalating the antipsychotic dose overlooking the heightened suicide and impulsivity risk associated with the disorder failing to distinguish tardive from acute akathisia by ignoring the temporal relationship to drug changes missing coexisting restless legs syndrome that may respond to iron repletion or dopaminergic strategies not recognising covert dopamine antagonists such as metoclopramide as the responsible agent Tardive akathisia is attributed to chronic postsynaptic dopamine D2-receptor blockade producing receptor supersensitivity and dysregulation of mesocortical, mesolimbic and nigrostriatal dopaminergic pathways that subserve motor drive and reward. Imbalance between dopaminergic and noradrenergic tone, and altered signalling in ventral striatal and limbic circuits, is thought to generate both the subjective restlessness and the semi-voluntary movements. As with other tardive syndromes, cumulative and high-potency drug exposure, and individual genetic and neurochemical vulnerability, shape the risk and persistence. Tardive akathisia is often chronic and may persist for years, and can worsen transiently on withdrawal of the causative agent; some patients improve gradually once the offending drug is stopped or switched. The associated dysphoria and suicide risk make early recognition clinically important.

dose to mask movements, which perpetuates the underlying problem Misdiagnosing spontaneous orofacial dyskinesia or Huntington's disease as tardive dyskinesia Failing to review the ongoing need for, and dose of, dopamine-blocking medication Tardive dyskinesia is thought to develop from chronic blockade of dopamine D2 receptors, leading to postsynaptic dopamine-receptor supersensitivity and up-regulation, altered signalling within striatal output pathways, and possible oxidative injury to vulnerable neurones. This maladaptive plasticity disturbs basal ganglia control of movement and produces the characteristic involuntary, often orofacial, hyperkinesias. Because the underlying changes can become fixed, the movements may persist long after the offending drug has been withdrawn. The course is variable; some patients improve or remit after the offending agent is reduced or stopped, but a substantial proportion have persistent or irreversible movements. Early recognition and review of the causative drug improve outcome, and VMAT2-inhibiting therapy can meaningfully reduce symptoms. Prevention through judicious prescribing and regular monitoring remains the most effective strategy.

tardive dystonia — tardive dystonic syndrome, neuroleptic-induced tardive dystonia idiopathic (primary) focal or segmental dystonia acute dystonic reaction to dopamine-blocking drugs Wilson disease and other inherited metabolic dystonias tardive dyskinesia and other tardive syndromes dystonia of Huntington disease or neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation functional (psychogenic) dystonia structural basal ganglia lesion or paraneoplastic movement disorder detailed longitudinal drug-exposure history including antiemetics and hidden dopamine blockers serum caeruloplasmin, copper studies and slit-lamp examination to exclude Wilson disease in younger patients MRI brain to exclude structural, iron-deposition or degenerative pathology genetic testing for inherited dystonia syndromes where phenotype or family history suggests standardised rating with the Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale and dystonia severity scales for monitoring review for coexisting parkinsonism or tardive dyskinesia on structured examination A form of tardive syndrome characterised by sustained or repetitive muscle contractions producing twisting, patterned postures, arising after prolonged exposure to dopamine-receptor-blocking agents (typical and atypical antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine). Unlike classic tardive dyskinesia, it favours younger adults and men, and frequently involves axial and cranial musculature, producing retrocollis, opisthotonic trunk posturing, and characteristic arm extension with internal rotation and wrist flexion. Onset may follow months of exposure rather than years, and by definition persists beyond a defined interval after the offending drug is stopped; it may be irreversible. Blepharospasm, oromandibular dystonia and a fixed 'tardive' grimace overlap with tardive dyskinesia, but the sustained, directional, action- or posture-related nature distinguishes dystonia. Sensory tricks (geste antagoniste) may transiently relieve the posturing, mirroring idiopathic focal dystonias. Paradoxically, cautious increase of the causative dopamine blocker can mask symptoms while worsening the underlying disorder ('masking'); withdrawal often unmasks or intensifies the dystonia. Anticholinergics may help tardive dystonia (in contrast to tardive dyskinesia, which they often worsen), and this differential drug response is a useful bedside clue. VMAT2 inhibitors, tetrabenazine-class agents, botulinum toxin for focal distributions, and deep brain stimulation of the globus pallidus internus are recognised options for refractory disease. laryngeal or pharyngeal dystonia threatening the airway or causing stridor and dysphagia opisthotonic or severe axial posturing risking respiratory compromise or spinal injury rapidly progressive dystonia with autonomic instability or rigidity suggesting an emerging neuroleptic malignant syndrome new focal neurological deficit or atypical features prompting urgent structural imaging mislabelling sustained posturing as tardive dyskinesia and prescribing anticholinergics inappropriately, or withholding them when they might help dystonia increasing the causative antipsychotic to 'treat' worsening movements, thereby masking and perpetuating the disorder overlooking covert dopamine antagonists such as metoclopramide and prochlorperazine in the exposure history attributing early or reversible posturing to a functional disorder and delaying drug withdrawal failing to screen younger patients for Wilson disease before ascribing dystonia solely to drug exposure Prolonged blockade of striatal postsynaptic dopamine D2 receptors by antipsychotics or antiemetic dopamine antagonists is thought to induce receptor supersensitivity and maladaptive plasticity within striato-pallido-thalamocortical motor circuits, alongside altered signalling in the indirect and direct basal ganglia pathways. Compared with tardive dyskinesia, tardive dystonia is postulated to reflect a distinct imbalance favouring sustained co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles, with contributions from dysregulated GABAergic and cholinergic tone and possible oxidative injury to striatal neurones. Individual susceptibility is modulated by genetic factors, cumulative and potency-weighted drug exposure, and coexisting mood or psychotic illness. Tardive dystonia is frequently persistent and may be permanent even after the offending agent is withdrawn, though a minority remit over months to years. Early recognition and cessation of the causative drug improve the chance of partial or complete recovery.

imbrication, although recurrence is a recognised problem New or progressive bladder, bowel, or sexual dysfunction Progressive neurological deficit Features suggesting a solid sacral tumour rather than a simple cyst Attributing symptoms to an incidental cyst without careful correlation Overlooking an alternative, treatable cause of sacral radicular symptoms Underestimating the risk of cerebrospinal fluid leak and recurrence after intervention Tarlov (perineural) cysts are dilatations of the meningeal sheath around the posterior nerve root and dorsal root ganglion, most often in the sacral region. They contain cerebrospinal fluid and, characteristically, nerve-root fibres within their wall or lumen. A ball-valve mechanism is proposed, whereby cerebrospinal fluid enters the cyst but leaves less readily, allowing gradual enlargement, and raised cerebrospinal fluid pressure such as during the Valsalva manoeuvre may drive expansion. Progressive growth can compress adjacent nerve roots and erode the surrounding bone, producing radicular or sphincter symptoms in the minority who become symptomatic. Most perineural cysts are asymptomatic and require only reassurance; symptomatic cysts have a more variable course, and although intervention can relieve symptoms in selected patients, recurrence and cerebrospinal-fluid-related complications temper outcomes.

restricted subtalar motion Proceeding to resection when extensive coalition or established arthritis would be better served by arthrodesis Tarsal coalition results from a failure of normal segmentation of the primitive mesenchyme during foetal development, so that two or more tarsal bones remain abnormally joined by bone (synostosis), cartilage (synchondrosis) or fibrous tissue (syndesmosis). Early in life a fibrous or cartilaginous coalition may permit some movement and remain asymptomatic, but as the child grows the bar tends to ossify and progressively restrict motion at the affected joint, most often the subtalar or calcaneonavicular articulation. The loss of hindfoot mobility transfers abnormal stress to adjacent joints and provokes protective spasm of the peroneal muscles, producing the characteristic rigid, everted flatfoot. Over time the restricted, abnormally loaded joints are prone to secondary degenerative change. Many patients improve with conservative measures, particularly when a limited coalition is treated before secondary arthritis develops; larger coalitions, established degenerative change or persistent pain may require surgery, with resection favoured for smaller bars and arthrodesis for extensive coalitions or arthritic joints.

tarsal tunnel posterior — posterior tarsal tunnel syndrome, tibial nerve entrapment at the ankle plantar fasciitis peripheral polyneuropathy, including diabetic S1 lumbosacral radiculopathy Morton neuroma medial plantar nerve entrapment (jogger's foot) calcaneal stress fracture posterior tibial tendinopathy nerve conduction studies of medial and lateral plantar nerves with tibial motor studies needle electromyography of intrinsic foot muscles magnetic resonance imaging of the ankle to identify a space-occupying lesion high-resolution ultrasound of the tarsal tunnel weight-bearing foot radiographs to assess alignment and bony anomalies screening for diabetes and other causes of polyneuropathy contralateral comparison electrodiagnostic studies Entrapment of the posterior tibial nerve or its terminal branches beneath the flexor retinaculum behind the medial malleolus, producing burning plantar pain and paraesthesiae. Symptoms are typically worse with standing and walking and may radiate proximally along the medial calf (the Valleix phenomenon). A Tinel sign behind the medial malleolus, and reproduction of symptoms with sustained eversion and dorsiflexion, support the diagnosis. Selective involvement of the medial or lateral plantar branch, or the calcaneal branch, produces a restricted sensory pattern that aids localisation. A space-occupying lesion such as a ganglion, varicosity, lipoma, accessory muscle or tenosynovitis is identified in a substantial proportion of cases and should be actively sought. The condition is markedly less common than carpal tunnel syndrome, and overdiagnosis is a recognised problem when plantar symptoms have another cause. Electrodiagnostic studies with distal tibial motor and mixed or sensory plantar conductions help confirm the diagnosis but can be technically difficult. Hindfoot malalignment, particularly a valgus or planovalgus foot, increases traction on the nerve and predisposes to entrapment. a rapidly enlarging or firm mass within the tarsal tunnel suggesting neoplasm progressive motor weakness or intrinsic foot muscle wasting constitutional symptoms or features of systemic inflammatory or infiltrative disease bilateral or diffuse sensory loss pointing to a generalised neuropathy rather than local entrapment diagnosing tarsal tunnel syndrome when a distal polyneuropathy is the true cause of plantar symptoms failing to image the tunnel and thereby missing a treatable space-occupying lesion over-interpreting technically difficult plantar nerve conduction studies neglecting hindfoot malalignment that will cause recurrence after surgery The posterior tibial nerve passes through the fibro-osseous tarsal tunnel behind the medial malleolus, bounded by the flexor retinaculum, where it divides into the medial and lateral plantar and calcaneal branches. Increased pressure within this confined space from a ganglion, tenosynovitis, varicosities, an accessory or hypertrophied muscle, post-traumatic fibrosis, or biomechanical traction in hindfoot valgus produces focal demyelination and axonal injury. Branch-specific compression within separate compartments accounts for the variable sensory patterns, and systemic conditions causing nerve vulnerability may lower the threshold for symptomatic entrapment. Outcomes are best when a discrete compressive lesion is found and released, whereas idiopathic cases respond less predictably to decompression. Conservative measures including orthoses and corticosteroid injection help many patients with milder or biomechanical presentations.
